report: Abstract: The reviewed object is the 55-page author manuscript arXiv:0910.0078v4, dated 1 July 2020, by Ciprian Manolescu, Peter S. Ozsváth and Dylan P. Thurston. Two defects affect steps used by the printed core construction or its finiteness argument. A third false general hyperbox statement has no demonstrated downstream core impact. Each finding has an explicit algebraic check or counterexample. These are findings about this manuscript version. The 2025 journal Version of Record was not acquired or compared; no claim about its current defects follows.

Title: Scientific initial review: M25-0001
Grid diagrams and Heegaard Floer invariants
# Object, scope, and version control

The frozen journal identity is Annals of Mathematics 201 (2025), 1–78, DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.201.1.1 [S2]. The reviewed PDF and its bound author TeX are the earlier arXiv v4 [S1]. The publisher records a revision on 16 February 2021, after this v4. The arXiv history exposed in the version check lists v4 as its latest revision. A bounded search by the exact title and arXiv identifier with correction/erratum/error terms did not identify a separate correction. This does not establish the absence of corrections or intervening changes.

All 55 PDF pages, including references, were read as extracted text. The author TeX was inspected statically at the relevant definitions, formulas and proof passages. Sixteen source pages were also rendered and visually checked: 1, 3–8, 11, 23–25, 38, 42, and 44–46. Source-manifest bindings were checked by byte size and SHA-256. No author code was executed. No separately verified computational repository or supplement was available in the acquired input.

The claims are over \(\mathbb F_2\). Theorem 1.2 concerns completed minus and infinity groups and the plus group, with a sparse grid as input. Theorem 1.3 assumes a closed four-manifold with \(b_2^+>1\), a cut-link presentation, and a sparse grid. This review does not extend these claims to integer coefficients or arbitrary four-manifolds.
# F01: the filtered projection is not defined on its printed domain
## Location and claim

Equation reference: eq:printed. Section 2.2, pp. 7–8, the filtration defining \(\mathfrak A^-(G,s)\) and equation (4); bound file `hf+.tex`, lines 666, 669 and 674–679. The ordinary complex \(\mathbf A^-(G,s)\) is the part of \(C^-(G)\) with Alexander filtration \(A_i\leq s_i\). Its coefficient ring is \(\mathcal R=\mathbb F_2[[U_1,\ldots,U_n]]\), which has no negative \(U\) exponents. The intermediate complex has \[\mathfrak F_i(x)=-A_i(x),\quad
 \mathfrak F_i(U_{i,1})=-1,\quad \mathfrak F_i(V_{i,j})=1\ (j\geq2),\] and the other variables have filtration zero. The printed domain is \(\mathfrak F_i\leq s_i\). Put \(J=\{(i,j):1\leq i\leq\ell,\ 2\leq j\leq p_i\}\). On a monomial without \(Y\) factors, the asserted \(\mathcal R\)-linear projection is \[
 \widetilde P\left(\prod_{(i,j)\in J}V_{i,j}^{n_{i,j}}x\right)
 =
 \prod_{i=1}^{\ell} U_{i,1}^{A_i(x)-s_i-\sum_{j=2}^{p_i}n_{i,j}}
 \prod_{(i,j)\in J}U_{i,j}^{n_{i,j}}x .\]
## An allowed sparse counterexample

Use a \(4\) by \(4\) toroidal grid, with rows and columns \(0,1,2,3\). The following coordinates denote cells, with markings at their centres: \[\begin{array}{c|l}
\text{linked }O &(0,0),(2,2)\\
\text{free }O &(1,1),(3,3)\\
X &(0,2),(2,0).
\end{array}\] There is one \(O\) in every row and column, at most one \(X\) in each, and the rows and columns of the two free \(O\) markings contain no \(X\). The linked arcs form one rectangular component, an unknot. The \(X\) rows and columns are separated, including cyclically, by free rows and columns, so the grid is sparse.

Choose the state \(x\) formed by the four diagonal intersections \((0,0),(1,1),(2,2),(3,3)\) of the grid circles. These are vertices, distinct from marking centres. Put \(a=A_1(x)\in\mathbb Z\); the affine Alexander lattice for a knot is \(\mathbb Z\). Choose the permitted integer parameter \(s=|a|+1\). This argument does not need a particular absolute Alexander normalization. The single monomial \(x\) satisfies the boundedness condition (3), and \[\mathfrak F_1(x)=-a\leq s,\qquad
 \widetilde P(x)=U_{1,1}^{a-|a|-1}x,\qquad a-|a|-1\leq-1.\] It therefore lies in the printed domain but its purported image does not lie in \(C^-(G)\) over \(\mathcal R\), or in \(\mathbf A^-(G,s)\).
## Counterevidence, local repair, and core impact

Power-series completion does not admit negative exponents. The different Laurent coefficient ring used later for the infinity theory does not rescue this minus map. Sparsity does not exclude the example. No stated reindexing of \(x\) or \(s\) changes these explicit definitions.

Changing the cutoff to \(\mathfrak F_i\leq -s_i\) is a plausible local repair. For \(U_{1,1}^r\prod_{j\geq2}V_{1,j}^{n_j}x\), set \(N=\sum_jn_j\). The changed inequality would give \[-a-r+N\leq-s\ \Longrightarrow\ r+a-s-N\geq0.\] The image then has Alexander filtration \(a-(r+a-s-N)-N=s-r\leq s\). Additional nonnegative \(U\) powers only decrease that target filtration. This proves this local well-definedness calculation; it does not establish the quasi-isomorphism or globally repair the subsequent conventions.

Equation (9), p. 11, repeats the exponent in the projection-inclusion map \(I_s^{\vec M}\). Taking the whole knot as sublink with its given orientation reproduces the obstruction. Equation (29), p. 23, composes this map into \(\Phi_s^{\vec M}\). These maps enter the surgery differential on p. 24, Theorem 2.10 on p. 25, and the construction used for Theorem 1.2 on pp. 45–46. Thus a printed core construction is undefined on an allowed input. Classification: Major in v4. The computability theorem itself is not disproved; a consistently propagated sign correction may repair the construction.
# F02: local hyperbox relations do not imply the asserted total differential
## Location and claim

Section 2.1, p. 5, equation (1) and the subsequent total-complex paragraph; p. 6, the induced map of those total complexes. Bound TeX: lines 514–528 and 553. Relations (1) are imposed for displacements \(\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^n\). The text then claims that the sum of local maps is a differential on \[C_*=\bigoplus_{\varepsilon\in E(\mathbf d)}
 C^\varepsilon_{*+\|\varepsilon\|}\] for a general hyperbox, before compression.
## Complete finite counterexample

Let \(n=1\), \(d_1=2\), and \(C^0=C^1=C^2=\mathbb F_2\), each concentrated in internal degree zero. All vertex differentials vanish, and both consecutive edge maps are identities. Their internal degree is zero, as required. Relations (1) for displacement zero are \(d^2=0\) and those for displacement one are \(df+fd=0\); all hold. No condition is imposed for displacement two.

On the total space let \(e_j\) be the vector at vertex \(j\), of total degree \(-j\). Then \[De_0=e_1,\quad De_1=e_2,\quad De_2=0,\quad D^2e_0=e_2\ne0.\] With columns representing inputs, the independent matrix calculation over \(\mathbb F_2\) is \[D=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 D^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&0\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] There is no convergence or sign ambiguity.
## Counterevidence and limited impact

In a unit hypercube all endpoint displacements belong to \(\{0,1\}^n\), so (1) supplies every component of \(D^2=0\). Compression of this example gives the two-vertex cube \(C^0\xrightarrow{\operatorname{id}}C^2\), whose total differential squares to zero. Restricting the claim to hypercubes, or compressing first, removes the obstruction.

The descent construction and pp. 42, 45 explicitly use compression. The surgery complex has the unit-cube indexing by sublinks. No core dependence on the false totalization of an uncompressed general hyperbox was established. Classification: Minor. The p. 5 statement and related p. 6 assertion need qualification; this example does not invalidate the later surgery formula.
# F03: a global finite-dimensional truncation cannot preserve the minus tower
## Location and claim

Page 46, first paragraph in the proof of Theorem 1.2; bound TeX lines 2476–2477. After acknowledging the completed minus complex is infinite dimensional, the proof claims it can be replaced by a quasi-isomorphic complex finite dimensional over \(\mathbb F_2\), using vertical and horizontal truncation in manuscript reference [14, Section 10]. This supplies the final finiteness step.
## Counterexample and complete dimension obstruction

Take the allowed sparse unknot grid in F01 and framing \(+1\). Surgery gives \(S^3\), with its unique \(\operatorname{Spin}^c\) structure. The genus-zero, one-generator minus Floer complex of \(S^3\) has zero differential: the symmetric product of degree zero is a point and there is no index-one disk contributing a differential. With the completion explicitly used by Theorem 1.2, \[\mathbf{HF}^{-}(S^3)\cong\mathbb F_2[[U]].\] For every \(N\geq0\), the elements \(1,U,\ldots,U^N\) are linearly independent by uniqueness of formal power-series coefficients. The homology thus has infinite \(\mathbb F_2\)-dimension.

A complex of finite total dimension \(m\) has homology \(\ker d/\operatorname{im}d\) of dimension at most \(m\). A quasi-isomorphism preserves homology. Consequently no such finite complex can be quasi-isomorphic to this completed minus complex. This analytic argument, not a finite experiment, establishes the obstruction.
## Alternative interpretations and consequence

A finite presentation or finite rank over \(\mathbb F_2[[U]]\) is compatible with the example. A finite grading window or a specified-degree calculation can also be meaningful. These are different from the unqualified global assertion of finite dimension over \(\mathbb F_2\) on p. 46. Surrounding discussion of ranks motivates checking a narrower intended reading, but that restriction is not stated in this step.

Infinite groups can have finite algorithmic descriptions, so computability itself is not refuted. A repair must specify the output representation, retained tower information, and any degree restriction, and show that the chosen truncation recovers that object. This review does not certify that replacement argument or re-prove the external truncation theorem. Classification: Major in v4: the printed core finiteness justification fails.
# Positive checks and coverage limitations

For the last numerical inference in Proposition 3.10, the inequality \(I\geq(\epsilon_1-1)/2\), with \(\epsilon_1\in\{0,1\}\) and \(I\in\mathbb Z\), does imply \(I\geq0\). This checks the final inference, not every preceding geometric step.

The use of Theorem 4.4 in Lemma 4.8 has the required degree range: for every \(k\geq2\), \(1-k<0\) and \(1-k<2-k\), hence \(1-k<\min(0,2-k)\). In the cocycle calculation on pp. 44–45, substituting the induction relations produces associative triple products occurring in pairs, which cancel in characteristic two.

The text was read for definitions, quantifiers, coefficients, hypotheses, boundary values and dependency directions. This did not amount to independent reconstruction of all holomorphic-disk counts, transversality arguments, sparse-domain case analyses, or external surgery results. No further supported issue is asserted. This is not a certificate of correctness for every proof.
# Conclusion
ID | Assessment | Established consequence
F01 | Major, v4 | A printed core projection leaves its coefficient ring on an allowed sparse input.
F02 | Minor, v4 | Local hyperbox relations do not ensure the uncompressed total differential; later compression limits impact.
F03 | Major, v4 | A finite-total-dimensional \(\mathbb F_2\) complex cannot retain the completed minus homology of \(S^3\).

The mathematical clarifications needed are a consistent filtration sign convention; an appropriately restricted totalization statement; and a precise finite representation or degreewise algorithm in the last step of Theorem 1.2. Compare the exact journal text and later corrections before assigning any finding to the 2025 publication. No editorial decision or author contact is part of this initial review.
# Supporting checks

The reviewer-authored `independent_checks.py` uses Python standard-library arithmetic and JSON. Its actual output records the matrix square, grid incidence/sparsity checks, and 25 F01 instances with \(a=-12,\ldots,12\). It also checks 9,465 admitted monomials for the proposed local cutoff repair, with \(a,s=-5,\ldots,5\), \(N=0,\ldots,6\), and \(r=0,\ldots,14\). No negative output exponent or target-filtration violation occurs. The universal proof is in F01; the scan is corroboration only. The degree inequality was also evaluated for \(k=2,\ldots,14\).
The evidence directory includes the extraction, rendered source pages and logs, independent script and actual output, and coverage, findings and provenance records.
Exact report-source, compiler, dependency and output-PDF hashes are in the external build and provenance records; a self-referential PDF hash is deliberately not embedded here.
# Execution record and remaining limits

Scientific analysis, independent calculations, static source checks, report creation and visual checks were performed by the assistant. No backend equivalence was inferred, no independent routing evidence established a mismatch, and no model switch was requested or performed.

The existing native `/usr/bin/pdflatex` was independently verified. The user-authorized portable Tectonic 0.17.0 binary was hash verified. Author TeX was inspected, not executed. No software installation, author-code execution, shell escape, or author communication was used.

A direct PDF extraction tool failed; installed Poppler `pdftotext` succeeded. A console read encountered a Windows character-encoding error and was rerun read-only with UTF-8 output. An arXiv HTML fetch for the external surgery paper timed out, so that attempt did not provide its complete proof. These failures are not evidence of a scientific defect. Human adjudication and full-text comparison with the journal publication remain outside this completed, version-limited initial review.

report: Abstract: The reviewed object is the 59-page author manuscript arXiv:2204.13674v1, dated 28 April 2022, by L. Alexander Betts and Jakob Stix. One demonstrated defect concerns the period-map comparison used in the core finiteness argument; one concerns the unnecessary generality of the abstract principal trichotomy. Both admit explicit counterexamples to the particular printed assertions. Neither counterexample disproves the main finiteness theorem. The 2025 journal Version of Record was not acquired or compared, and these findings are not attributed to it.

Title: Scientific initial review: M25-0002
Galois sections and \(p\)-adic period mappings
# Reviewed object and scope

The frozen journal identity is Annals of Mathematics 201 (2025), 79–166, DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.201.1.2 [S2]. The publisher records revision on 24 May 2024 and acceptance on 28 May 2024, substantially after the reviewed v1 [S1]. The arXiv record exposed in the version check lists only v1. The author’s publication list links the same arXiv identifier and journal article [S3]. Bounded searches of the exact title and identifier with correction, erratum, and revision terms did not identify a specific separate correction. This is not a proof that none exists.

All 59 PDF pages, including references and Appendix A, were read. The active author TeX was inspected statically at the definitions and proof passages relevant to the findings. The input sequence in `main.tex`, lines 133–143, excludes the older file `prelims.tex`; material in that inactive file is not evidence of a defect in the PDF. Source-manifest file bindings were verified by size and SHA-256. Source pages 16, 33, 40–42, 44, 46–47, 49, and 51 were also visually inspected. No author code was executed.

The main assertion concerns smooth projective curves of genus at least two over number fields without a CM subfield, with finiteness of the local image of Selmer sections. The intermediate local theorem uses a self-conjugate place. Smoothness, projectivity, the genus restriction, the place condition, and the Hodge–Tate weight restrictions are not discarded in this review. Reading the whole manuscript does not amount to independently reproving every cited theorem of \(p\)-adic Hodge theory.
# F01: the formal period map uses transport in the wrong direction
Classification: Major; demonstrated invalid core derivation.
## Location and assertion

Definition 3.1, continued on p. 16, defines the period filtration by pulling back along horizontal transport \[T^\nabla:\mathcal O_U\otimes_{K_v}\mathcal E_{y_0}\longrightarrow \mathcal E|_U.\] In Section 5.2, pp. 40–42, the connection is written \(\nabla=d+\omega\), the filtration is made constant in a chosen frame, and equation (5.1) specifies \(dT=-\omega T\), \(T(0)=I\). The manuscript then constructs \(\widehat\Phi\) from the first columns of \(T\), identifies these with the analytic period coordinates, and uses this identification in Lemmas 5.5 and 5.6. The exact source locations are `big_monodromy.tex`, lines 76–112 and 116–137. Definition 3.1 is `reps_in_families.tex`, lines 10–29.

With the displayed direction of \(T^\nabla\), the pullback of a subspace \(F\) is \(T^{-1}F\). Its coordinates in the reference fibre are therefore columns of \(T^{-1}\), not columns of \(T\). This distinction can change the Zariski closure, so it cannot be dismissed merely as a different parametrization of the same image.
## A counterexample satisfying the stated setup

Take \(K_v=\mathbb Q_3\), \(Y=\mathbb A^1_{\mathbb Q_3}\), \(y_0=0\), \(\mathcal E=\mathcal O_Y^3\), and the constant filtration \[F^i\mathcal E=
\begin{cases}
\mathcal E,&i\leq0,\\
\mathcal O_Y e_1,&i=1,\\
0,&i\geq2.
\end{cases}\] It is exhaustive and separated, and all graded pieces are vector bundles. Set \[T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\t&1&0\\t^2&t&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
T^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\-t&1&0\\0&-t&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\omega=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\-1&0&0\\-t&-1&0\end{pmatrix}dt .\] Direct multiplication gives \(TT^{-1}=T^{-1}T=I\), \(T(0)=I\), and \[\omega=-T'T^{-1}\,dt,\qquad dT+\omega T=0.\] The algebraic connection is flat: on this smooth one-dimensional base, both \(d\omega\) and \(\omega\wedge\omega\) vanish. Its horizontal frame is the polynomial matrix \(T\), invertible on the entire affine line. In particular, on the closed unit disc \(U=\operatorname{Sp}(\mathbb Q_3\langle t\rangle)\) it has a full horizontal basis and \(H^0_{\mathrm{dR}}(U/\mathbb Q_3)=\mathbb Q_3\). Even Griffiths transversality, which Definition 3.1 does not require, holds, since \(\nabla(F^1)\subset F^0\otimes\Omega^1\).

The actual period map prescribed by Definition 3.1 is \[t\longmapsto T(t)^{-1}\langle e_1\rangle=[1:-t:0].\] Its Zariski closure in \(\mathbb P^2\) is the line \(X_2=0\): a polynomial in the remaining affine coordinate vanishing on all \(t\in\mathbb Q_3\) with \(|t|_3\leq1\) is zero. The printed formal construction instead gives \[\widehat\Phi(t)=[1:t:t^2],\] whose scheme-theoretic image is the conic \(X_0X_2-X_1^2=0\). Indeed, on \(X_0\ne0\), the kernel of \(\mathbb Q_3[u,v]\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_3[[t]]\), \((u,v)\mapsto(t,t^2)\), is exactly \((v-u^2)\): divide by the monic polynomial \(v-u^2\) and use injectivity of \(\mathbb Q_3[u]\to\mathbb Q_3[[t]]\). For the actual map the kernel is \((v)\). These are different ideals. Shrinking the disc does not remove the difference. The same matrices over \(\mathbb C\) give the same discrepancy for Lemma 5.6.

The independently written checking script performs exact polynomial matrix arithmetic; both inverse products and the differential-equation residual were checked coefficient by coefficient. The ideal arguments above are algebraic proofs, not conclusions drawn from sampling.
## Counterevidence, dependency, and repair

Remark 5.7 on p. 42 explicitly returns to the correct intrinsic description by pullback along \(\widehat T\). This supports the intended construction, but contradicts the preceding column formulas rather than validating them. Changing the direction of transport only in the interpretation would conflict with Definition 3.1 and equation (5.1).

The dependency is direct: Lemmas 5.5 and 5.6 are used immediately to prove Proposition 5.3. That comparison enters Lemma 5.9 and Corollary 5.10, and hence the finiteness applications in Corollaries 6.10 and 6.16, Theorem 6.5, and Theorem A together with Theorem 7.1. Under the prescribed review standard, a demonstrated invalid derivation on this core path is Major even when a local repair is available.

The example is a filtered flat bundle allowed by the general comparison setup; it is not asserted to arise from an abelian-by-finite family. It does not refute Theorem A or the true comparison of analytic period images. A uniform repair of the displayed construction is to use columns of \(T^{-1}\) on both analytic sides and in \(\widehat\Phi\). Since \(T(0)=I\), the inverse exists formally and on a sufficiently small analytic neighbourhood. Inversion commutes with the field embedding \(\iota:K_v\hookrightarrow\mathbb C\), so the corrected complex coordinates are the images of the corrected \(v\)-adic coordinates. The kernel base-change argument then applies to these coordinates. Thus the defect and its algebraic repair are both established here; the report does not claim that the principal finiteness conclusion is false.
# F02: the principal trichotomy allows algebras for which its count fails
Classification: Minor relative to the paper’s core result; demonstrated false extra generality.
## Location and complete example

Proposition 6.7 on p. 46, also summarized as Proposition 1.8, permits the symplectic pairs of Definitions 4.3–4.4 (pp. 33–34). Those definitions allow a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Q_p\)-algebra \(A\) without requiring it to be split or reduced. The proposition sets \(\Sigma=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Q_p\text{-alg}}(A,\mathbb Q_p)\). Its alternatives (a) and (b) require an orbit of local size at least four, whereas (c) requires at least \(\dim_{\mathbb Q_p}(A)/(d+1)\) elements in local orbits of size less than four. See `locus.tex`, lines 142–163.

Let \(K=\mathbb Q\), \(p=3\), \(v=3\), and \[A=\mathbb Q_3[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^3)\] with trivial \(G_\mathbb Q\)-action. Let \(E/\mathbb Q\) be the elliptic curve \(y^2=x^3-x\), let \(B=H^1_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(E_{\overline{\mathbb Q}},\mathbb Q_3)\), and put \[V=A\otimes_{\mathbb Q_3}B,\qquad
L=A\otimes_{\mathbb Q_3}\mathbb Q_3(-1).\] The cup-product pairing on \(B\) extends to a perfect alternating \(A\)-bilinear, \(G_\mathbb Q\)-equivariant pairing \(V\times V\to L\). Here \(V\) is free of rank \(2\) over \(A\), so \(d=1\), and \(L\) is free of rank one. The actions are continuous and compatible with all structures.

The place is self-conjugate because \(\mathbb Q\) has no CM subfield. The elliptic curve has discriminant \(64\), hence good reduction outside \(2\). Taking \(S=\{2,3,\infty\}\), \(B\) is unramified, pure and integral of weight one away from \(S\), is de Rham at \(3\), and has Hodge–Tate weights \(\{0,1\}\), as for the smooth proper cohomology used throughout the manuscript. As a \(\mathbb Q_3\)-representation \(V\) is three copies of \(B\), so it satisfies the same hypotheses; \(A\) is unramified everywhere. These standard cohomological facts, not a finite numerical test, supply the arithmetic hypotheses of the example.

Every \(\mathbb Q_3\)-algebra homomorphism \(A\to\mathbb Q_3\) sends \(\epsilon\) to zero, since a field has no nonzero nilpotents. Thus \(\Sigma\) has exactly one element, fixed by \(G_\mathbb Q\) and \(G_v\). Alternatives (a) and (b) are impossible because its local orbit has size \(1<4\). Alternative (c) would require \[1\ \geq\ \frac{\dim_{\mathbb Q_3}A}{d+1}=\frac32,\] which is false. All three alternatives therefore fail.
## Failed inference and restricted valid argument

In the preliminary reduction on p. 46, the proof argues from an orbit proportion bounded below by \(1/(d+1)\) and \(\#\Sigma\leq\dim_{\mathbb Q_p}A\) to (c). The inequality has the wrong direction for this inference. In the example it compares \(1\) with \(3\). The natural map \(A\to\prod_{\psi\in\Sigma}\mathbb Q_p\) forgets its nilpotent directions, which contribute to the denominator but not the count.

There is decisive counterevidence against treating this as a failure of the main theorem: Remark 6.3 on p. 44 states that an interpolating \(A\) in the Lawrence–Venkatesh locus is isomorphic as an algebra to \(\mathbb Q_p^\delta\). Remark 6.6 on p. 46 displays this fact for geometric degree-zero cohomology. Thus the actual application already has \(\#\Sigma=\dim_{\mathbb Q_p}A\).

Restricting Proposition 6.7 to split reduced algebras \(A=\mathbb Q_p^\delta\) removes this counterexample and validates the orbit reduction. Merely requiring a finite étale algebra does not ensure this equality, because the homomorphisms in the statement have target \(\mathbb Q_p\), not \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_p\). For a transitive split component, write \(m=\dim W\), \(s=\#\Sigma_{<4}\) and \(\delta=\#\Sigma\). Failure of (b), the integral Hodge–Tate dimensions, and the averaged weight identity give \[\frac{m\delta}{2}
 \leq\frac{m-1}{2}(\delta-s)+ms,
\qquad
\delta\leq(m+1)s\leq(d+1)s.\] The last step uses isotropy, \(m\leq d\). Summing the transitive split components yields the stated count. This reconstruction confirms why the restriction is sufficient for the intended application. The false abstract generality deserves correction, but no core failure from this second issue has been demonstrated.
# Independent positive checks and boundaries
## Four Lagrangians and the degree-four threshold

The argument in Sublemma 6.18 on p. 51 was reconstructed. Over an algebraic closure choose complementary Lagrangians \(E_0=\langle e_i\rangle\) and \(F_0=\langle f_i\rangle\), and graphs of maps \(\psi_3(e_i)=f_i\) and \(\psi_4(e_i)=\lambda_i f_i\), where the nonzero \(\lambda_i\) are distinct. All pairs are complementary except possibly the two graphs. If a nonzero isotropic \(W\) met each Lagrangian in dimension at least \(\dim(W)/2\), complementary pairs force \(\dim W\) to be even and \[W=(W\cap E_0)\oplus(W\cap F_0),\qquad
\psi_3(W\cap E_0)=\psi_4(W\cap E_0)=W\cap F_0.\] Hence \(W\cap E_0\) is invariant under the diagonal map \(\psi_3^{-1}\psi_4\). A nonzero invariant subspace for a diagonal map with distinct eigenvalues contains an eigenvector, by polynomial spectral projection. Thus \(e_i\) and \(f_i\) both belong to \(W\) for some \(i\), contradicting \(\omega(e_i,f_i)=1\). The proper incidence projection then gives the required proper closed bad locus; \(r>4\) follows from the first four factors.

As a separate finite check, the reviewer enumerated all subspaces of \(\mathbb F_5^4\) of dimensions one and two using reduced row-echelon matrices: 156 lines and 806 planes, of which 156 planes are isotropic. None of the 312 nonzero isotropic subspaces meets all four chosen Lagrangians in at least half its dimension. This finite instance is supporting evidence; the preceding argument supplies the universal proof. The strict dimension estimate at the degree-four threshold also checks exactly: \[4\,\frac{d(d+1)}2-d(2d+1)=d>0\quad(d>0).\]
## Arithmetic bounds, local conditions, and dependencies

The final inequality used in Proposition 6.20 was checked algebraically. Writing \(q-1=2k\), with \(g\geq2\) and \(k\geq2\), \[4k^{g-1}\geq 2^g k\geq2gk>(2g-1)k+1.\] Together with \(\zeta(2g)<9/8\) and \(2k\geq9n_v\), this gives the required upper bound for the proportion of short orbits. Exact rational tests for 741 pairs \((g,k)\) supplement this argument. For the stated genus three illustrations, \(q=11\) gives \(d_q=25\) and \(9/500<1/26\); \(q=23\) gives \(d_q=55\) and \(9/2662<1/56\). The Chinese-remainder congruences used with Dirichlet’s theorem are compatible and prime to their modulus. These checks concern the inequalities, not practical runtime of a point-finding algorithm.

The determinant and induction argument for averaged Hodge–Tate weights was checked with the local degree factors retained. For Proposition 2.16 the required endomorphism dimension bound can be justified by Frobenius descent: a shortest normalized linear relation among Frobenius-fixed endomorphisms, after applying Frobenius and subtracting, forces all coefficients to be Frobenius-fixed, hence in \(\mathbb Q_p\). Averaging only under \(G_v\) requires care when its unramified fixed field exceeds \(\mathbb Q_p\); this does not provide a counterexample to the dimension bound itself.

The closed-polydisc condition in the analytic finiteness step, the properness used for the global finite cover, the self-conjugate-place restriction, and the basepoint/conjugacy compatibility of the section construction were checked along their displayed applications. The degree-two and degree-three unramified extensions used when the residue field has two elements give the necessary coprime subgroup indices. The manuscript explicitly includes the Scholze erratum in its filtered-derived discussion; it was not silently treated as the uncorrected source.
# Assessment and remaining limits

The supported result is one Major finding and one Minor finding for the specified v1. The first invalidates a printed core proof step, with a concrete correction and no counterexample to the final finiteness conclusion. The second concerns generality excluded by the actual application. They are not combined into an unsupported claim that Theorem A is false.

The review covers the entire manuscript at reading level and the displayed proof chains at the level described above. The full external proofs of the Scholze–Shimizu comparison results, the Faltings finiteness input, and the Lawrence–Venkatesh monodromy construction were not all independently rederived. No journal-final comparison was performed. The report therefore neither certifies global correctness nor establishes which issues, if any, survived the 2024 journal revision.
# Compact conclusion table
Item | Judgment | Repair and remaining decision

F01, period transport | Major; core displayed step invalid | Use the inverse transport matrix consistently. The explicit connection refutes the printed step; it does not disprove Theorem A. The corrected full proof remains to be adopted and checked.

F02, Proposition 6.7 | Minor; nonreduced generality | Exclude the nilpotent-algebra counterexample by the reduced/split hypothesis available in the application. No core dependency failure shown there.

Scope and decision | v1 initial review complete | Full journal-final comparison and all external comparison/monodromy proofs remain outside the established coverage. Author adoption was not requested; editorial disposition remains pending.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the 45-page author manuscript arXiv:2208.03108v2, dated 19 August 2022, by Simon Eberle, Alessio Figalli and Georg S. Weiss. A false power-integral estimate enters the core paraboloid-envelope argument. A complete replacement estimate is supplied here; the classification theorem is not disproved. Title: Scientific initial review: M25-0003
Complete classification of global solutions
to the obstacle problem
# Object, versions, and review coverage

The frozen journal identity is Annals of Mathematics 201 (2025), 167–224, DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.201.1.3 [S2]. The publisher lists revision on 8 November 2023 and acceptance on 7 October 2024. The arXiv history inspected lists v1 and v2, with v2 dated 19 August 2022 [S1]. Bounded exact-title and identifier searches, including an authoritative-domain check for correction and erratum, identified no separate correction notice. This does not establish that no correction exists.

An author-hosted 45-page PDF [S3] differs from v2: it includes Appendix A and strengthens Definition 2.8(ii). Its HTTP Last-Modified field is 10 October 2024, which is transport metadata, not proof of its scientific revision date or journal-final status. The inspected passages retain the power-estimate chain and the unnormalized uniqueness wording; the choice of \(\delta\) on p. 14 is changed from equality to \(\delta\leq1/3\). These observations do not establish a correction of F01 or F02. The reviewed object remains v2.

All 45 v2 PDF pages, including references, were read. Active author TeX was inspected statically at the stated definitions, estimates and proof dependencies. The bound source filename is `Classification-of-global-solutions-in-the-obstacle-problem—V3.03.tex`; line references below refer to that file. Source pages 3, 6, 11–12, 14, 22, and 27–28 were also visually checked. No author code was executed. The input PDF, source file and manifest bindings were hash-verified.

The principal problem is \(\Delta u=\chi_{\{u>0\}}\), \(u\geq0\), on \(\mathbb R^N\). The monotone theorem requires all four conditions of Definition 2.8: nonempty contact interior, placement in a half-space with the origin on its boundary, \(\partial_Nu\leq0\), and a transverse positive-definite quadratic blow-down of trace one. These hypotheses are retained throughout the analysis. The distinction between \(N\geq4\) and \(N=3\) is essential.
# F01: bounded and logarithmic power-integral regimes are lost
Classification: Major; demonstrated invalid derivation on a core proof path.
## Exact location

Equations (3.5)–(3.6), pp. 11–12, estimate integrals over \[T_\delta=\{(y',t):t\geq0,\ |y'|^2<t^{1+\delta}\},\qquad 0<\delta<1.\] In (3.6) the integral of \(t^{(N-1)(1+\delta)/2+1-N}\) is bounded by a constant times \((1+|x|)^{(N-1)(1+\delta)/2+2-N}\), without a bounded-term or logarithmic case. See source lines 908–923. The proof of Proposition 4.1, p. 14, explicitly invokes (3.5) and (3.6) for its middle integral and then chooses \(\delta=1/3\) to infer \(V_{\mathcal C}(x)\geq-C(1+|x|)\); see lines 1058–1067. The lower-cutoff symbol \(B_R\) in that display is not defined there. The preceding decomposition uses the fixed ball \(B_{2\widehat r}\). The failure below already occurs in the unambiguous estimate (3.6), independently of this notation problem.
## An explicit failure at the selected exponent

Take \(N=4\) and \(\delta=1/3\). The exponent of the one-dimensional integrand in (3.6) is \(-1\), whereas the exponent of its proposed bound is zero. For fixed \(a>0\), \[\int_a^R\frac{dt}{t}=\log(R/a)\longrightarrow\infty.\] The same obstruction holds for the actual geometric integral, not only for an overly rough upper bound. Choose \(a>\max\{2\widehat r,1\}\) and \(R>a\), and restrict to \[a<t<R,\qquad |y'|<t^{2/3}.\] This region lies in \(T_{1/3}\cap(B_{2R}\setminus B_{2\widehat r})\), because \(t\leq|y|\leq\sqrt2\,t\) for \(t\geq1\). Its cross-sectional volume is \(|B_1^3|t^2\). Consequently, \[\int_{T_{1/3}\cap(B_{2R}\setminus B_{2\widehat r})}|y|^{-3}\,dy
 \geq \frac{|B_1^3|}{2^{3/2}}\log(R/a).\] No constant independent of \(R\) can satisfy (3.6) in this case. In the Proposition 4.1 majorant the moment is multiplied by \(|x|=R\), producing an \(R\log R\) term. It cannot be replaced by \(CR\) by the printed estimate.

There is also a bounded-integral error when the proposed power is negative. For example, \(N=4,\delta=1/4\) gives the integrand \(t^{-9/8}\). Its integral from a fixed positive lower limit tends to a strictly positive constant, whereas the printed power is \((1+R)^{-1/8}\to0\). Equation (3.5) has the corresponding issue in higher dimensions. These failures concern the explicit auxiliary integrals, rather than numerical rounding or a disputed coincidence set. No claim is made that \(T_{1/3}\) itself is a coincidence set.
## A complete replacement estimate

The defect is repairable without assuming Proposition 4.1 in advance. For its \(N\geq4\) proof choose \(\delta=1/4\) in Lemma 2.10 and set \(a_N=5(N-1)/8\). With a fixed lower cutoff at least one, the first-moment integral is bounded because \[a_N+1-N=-\frac{3(N-1)}8\leq-\frac98,\qquad
\int_a^{2R}t^{a_N+1-N}\,dt\leq C.\] The potential integral and tail obey \[\begin{aligned}
\int_a^{2R}t^{a_N+2-N}\,dt
 &\leq C(1+R^{7/8}),\\
R^2\int_R^\infty t^{a_N-N}\,dt
 &= C_N R^{a_N+3-N}\leq C_N R^{7/8}.\end{aligned}\] The first inequality follows by comparing the integrand to \(t^{-1/8}\) for \(t\geq1\), and remains valid when the actual integral is bounded. Retaining the bounded near contribution and multiplying the first moment by \(R\) gives \[V_{\mathcal C}(x)\geq-C(1+R)-CR^{7/8}\geq-C'(1+R),
\qquad R=|x|\geq1.\] The expansion \(u=p+V_{\mathcal C}\) and transverse coercivity \(p(x')\geq c_p|x'|^2\) then yield, for \(x\in\mathcal C\), \[c_p|x'|^2\leq C(1+|x'|+x_N).\] Young’s inequality absorbs the linear \(|x'|\) term and gives \(|x'|^2\leq C'(1+x_N)\), which is the needed envelope.

The earlier subquadratic estimate in Lemma 3.3 can also be justified without the false intermediate powers. For \(N\geq3\) and \(t\geq1\), compare the three relevant integrands directly to the \(N=3\) powers \(t^\delta,t^{\delta-1},t^{\delta-2}\) before integrating. The first two contributions are \(O(1+R^{1+\delta})\), and the tail is \(O(R^{1+\delta})\). The translated singular kernel integrated over transverse balls contributes \(O(R^{(3+\delta)/2})\). Setting \(\delta=1/2\) gives \(O(1+R^{7/4})\). This validates the regularized-potential construction and its subsequent Liouville expansion at this step.
## Impact and counterevidence

Proposition 4.1 supplies the envelope needed by Lemma 5.1, the linear matching in Corollary 6.3, the ACF ordering in Proposition 7.1, and the \(N\geq4\) part of Theorem 1.2. The false estimate is therefore on a core derivation, warranting Major under the prescribed standard. The replacement above is strong counterevidence to any claim that the geometric theorem is false. It establishes a repair of this particular proof step; it does not certify all remaining dependencies. The separate \(N=3\) envelope proof is not refuted by this calculation.
# F02: quadratic blow-down does not determine the scale of the ellipsoid
Classification: Minor; a false uniqueness assertion not needed by the core construction.

Lemma 6.1, pp. 27–28, asserts uniqueness of an ellipsoid \(E'\) for the specified quadratic blow-down \(p\), without a volume, semiaxis, or other scale normalization. The same claim appears in Step 1 of its proof, source lines 1673–1709.

If \(P=P_{E'}\) is one such paraboloid and \(u_P\) its solution, the rescaling explicitly given in the lemma, \[u_{\gamma P}(x)=\gamma^2u_P(x/\gamma),\] satisfies the same obstacle equation and has the same quadratic blow-down \(p\), since \(p\) is homogeneous of degree two. But \(\gamma P_{E'}=P_{\sqrt\gamma E'}\); taking \(\gamma\ne1\) changes the ellipsoid. Thus the existence and scaling parts of the lemma are incompatible with its unnormalized uniqueness claim.

There is also a direct potential check. In dimension \(d=N-1\) let \(E'_a\) be the ball of radius \(a>0\). Its radial Newtonian potential \(V_a\) satisfies \(-\Delta V_a=1\) inside this ball. Regularity at the centre and the radial equation give \[V_a(r)-V_a(0)=-\frac{r^2}{2d},\qquad 0\leq r\leq a.\] This holds for every \(a\), including the logarithmic kernel for \(d=2\). Hence the identity cited in Step 1 cannot determine \(a\).

For an independent realization by actual three-dimensional obstacle solutions, fix \(s>0\), write \(\rho^2=x_1^2+x_2^2\), and define \[Z=x_3-s/2,\quad
q=\sqrt{\rho^2+Z^2},\quad
\xi=q-Z,\quad \eta=q+Z.\] For \(\xi>s\) put \[\begin{aligned}
g(\xi)&=\frac{s}{4}\{\xi\log(\xi/s)-\xi+s\},\\
h(\xi)&=\frac14\{\xi-s-s\log(\xi/s)\},&
u_s&=g(\xi)+\eta h(\xi),\end{aligned}\] and set \(u_s=0\) for \(\xi\leq s\). Both \(g\) and \(h\) are nonnegative for \(\xi\geq s\), and \(g(s)=h(s)=g'(s)=h'(s)=0\). The axisymmetric Laplacian gives \[\Delta u_s=
\frac4{\xi+\eta}
 \left\{(\xi g')'+h+\eta(\xi h')'\right\}=1
 \quad\text{where }\xi>s,\] because the expression in braces is \((\xi+\eta)/4\). The zero extension has no first-derivative jump and is locally \(C^{1,1}\). Its contact set is \(\rho^2\leq2s x_3\), while its quadratic blow-down is \(\rho^2/4\), independent of \(s\): \(\xi\eta=\rho^2\), and the remaining terms grow at most \(O(R\log R)\) on \(B_R\); inside the contact set \(\rho^2=O(R)\). Compactness upgrades this blow-down to the regularity used in the lemma. Thus \(s=1\) and \(s=2\) give different cross-sectional disks with the same \(p\).

Exact coefficient checks of the PDE identity were executed; Cartesian finite-difference checks were used only as a sanity check. The identity and boundary conditions supply the proof. The subsequent construction requires a choice of one \(E'\) and then deliberately varies \(\gamma\). It does not require absolute uniqueness. Delete that claim or specify a scale normalization and its appropriate uniqueness theorem. No breakdown of the classification argument from this extra claim is demonstrated.
# F03: the zero solution is omitted from the general blow-down lemma
Classification: Minor; an excluded degenerate case needs an explicit convention.

Lemma 2.3, p. 5, source lines 499 onward, is stated for a global nonnegative solution of (1.1), and lists only a half-space blow-down or a quadratic form with trace-one Hessian. The smooth global function \(u\equiv0\) satisfies \(\Delta u=0=\chi_{\{u>0\}}\) and \(u\geq0\), but all its quadratic rescalings are zero. Zero is neither listed alternative. The lemma needs \(u\not\equiv0\) or an additional zero alternative.

This case cannot enter the main monotone proof: Definition 2.8(ii) excludes its contact set \(\mathbb R^N\), and condition (iv) also excludes a zero blow-down. Theorem 1.1 should likewise make its nontrivial-solution convention explicit, or explicitly include the full space as a degenerate contact set. Whether a zero-dimensional base is permitted in the term cylinder is a convention; the counterexample to Lemma 2.3 is independent of it. This is a scope correction, not evidence of a new nontrivial geometric class missing from the result.
# Checks of the remaining argument

The regularized kernel was checked for sign, normalization, homogeneity and cancellation. Its value and first derivative vanish at \(x=0\), its far-field remainder is \(O(|x|^2|y|^{-N})\), and its distributional Laplacian is the negative source density. The harmonic difference \(u-p-V_{\mathcal C}\) is subquadratic, hence affine; the value and gradient at the origin eliminate that affine part. The first moment for a true paraboloid is integrable starting at \(N=4\), whereas the unregularized potential needs \(N\geq6\). The cross-sectional power count confirms these thresholds.

For the three-dimensional envelope, the chain from convexity of sections to concavity of \(\sqrt{H}\), the one-dimensionalized potential, the running maximum \(\Psi\), and differential comparison was checked. With \[h(z)=-Cz-z\log z,\qquad
G(t)=A\log t-A(C+\log A),\] one has \(h(G')=G/t\) exactly. For \(A=t_0^{2\delta}\) the coefficient of \(\log t_0\) in \(G(t_0)/t_0^{2\delta}\) is \(1-2\delta\), not the \(2-2\delta\) printed on p. 22. The required domination still holds for \(0<\delta<1/2\) and sufficiently large \(t_0\). Asymptotic thresholds can be enlarged after fixing \(A\). This local arithmetic slip does not refute the section-growth conclusion.

For differences of two obstacle solutions, \(w\Delta w\geq0\) yields subharmonic positive and negative parts and the Caccioppoli estimate. The ACF scaling was checked explicitly: \[\Phi\bigl(v(r\,\cdot)/r,\rho\bigr)=\Phi(v,r\rho).\] The weighted energy on \(B_\delta\) contributes the factor \(\delta^2\), as in (8.9), preventing concentration at the origin in the ACF limit. The strong-convergence proof needs only \(w_k\Delta w_k\geq0\) and a harmonic weak limit, so it applies to the linear rescalings even though their summands are no longer normalized obstacle solutions.

The zero-scale limit in Section 8 must be interpreted as the solution \(p\) specified by the text, rather than as the literal set product \(0P\). Its zero set is the vertical axis. That axis, as well as a half-axis, has locally zero Sobolev \(2\)-capacity in \(\mathbb R^3\): a transverse logarithmic cutoff has energy \(O(1/|\log\epsilon|)\). Using the axis in the removable-set argument therefore does not obstruct the harmonic-limit step. The two ACF alternatives, horizontal translation by \(Q^{-1}b'\), the \(R/\log R\) adjustment, and the ordering/continuity argument were traced to the final classification. In the zero-scale case the sign of \(b_3\) can be tested at \(-e_3/2\), inside the ball of convergence in (8.11).

For Section 9 the directional ACF argument forces a single sign in each null direction. A two-dimensional kernel would contain a direction orthogonal to the gradient at a fixed positive point, contradicting strict monotonicity. After choosing the orientation to agree with Definition 2.8, the remaining null direction gives the monotone case. These checks distinguish the intended proof from local sign or radius slips; no further nontrivial counterexample has been established.
# Assessment and limits

The findings are one Major derivation defect and two Minor statement defects for v2. A concrete repair is proved for the Major estimate. The other defects concern information not needed in the nontrivial monotone construction. Their combination does not demonstrate failure of the classification theorem.

All manuscript pages were read, and the algebraic, scaling, boundary, and dependency checks above were performed independently. The full external proofs of free-boundary regularity, the ACF equality case, the compact-coincidence classification, and the cited stability of quadratic blow-down under translated limits were not all rederived. The author-hosted comparison was selective, not a second full review. No journal-final comparison or whole-paper correctness certification is claimed. Coverage, findings, provenance, independent code and results, actual compiler/dependency hashes, logs, and every-page report inspection are supplied separately.

Item | Judgment | Repair and remaining decision

F01, potential estimate | Major; power-integral bound invalid | The report supplies a corrected fixed-\(\delta\) bound and lower-potential argument for the required paraboloid containment. No counterexample to the classification theorem.
F02, Lemma 6.1 | Minor; uniqueness fails under scaling | Retain the existence statement actually used. The explicit scaled family refutes uniqueness, not the subsequent existence construction.
F03, Lemma 2.3 | Minor; zero-solution omission | Include the zero solution among the general alternatives. Definition 2.8 excludes it from the later nontrivial monotone case.

Scope and decision | v2 initial review complete | Later author-copy comparison was selective; full journal-version equivalence remains unestablished. Repairs are proposed, not author-adopted. Editorial decision remains pending.

Title: Scientific initial review: M25-0004
Fundamental groups and the Milnor conjecture
# Version, scope, and assessment

This review concerns only the manifest-bound manuscript of E. Bruè, A. Naber and D. Semola, arXiv:2303.15347v3 (20 November 2023), 56 PDF pages, with its bound 2497-line `source.tex`. The input PDF SHA256 is
Page numbers below refer to this manuscript.

The checked arXiv record still lists v3 as its latest version. All 56 pages were read. The principal dependency is the equivariant positive-Ricci path (Section 6), its constant-volume refinement and neck (Section 7), and the action-extension gluing (Section 8), feeding the direct limit in Section 3. This review identifies three Major derivation defects and three Minor scope/description defects in v3. Major here means a demonstrated invalid step on a core dependency; it does not mean that the main existence theorem has been disproved. The independent calculations, static-source locations, coverage, version records, build evidence and page checks are supplied separately.
# F01: the fixed connection is not Yang–Mills throughout the proposed deformation

Major. The locations are Lemma 6.3(ii), p. 29; (67)–(75), pp. 29–31; and the harmonic-extension assertion in Section 6.6, p. 34. The corresponding source ranges are 1072–1178 and 1257–1265. The assertion that the displayed family has zero mixed Ricci curvature is false. It is not a consequence of the two diagonal Christoffel identities in (70).
## Direct computation from the actual ansatz

Suppress the parameter \(t\), and use the orthonormal frame in (67): \[\begin{gathered} T=f^{-1}(U_1+kV_1),\quad X_2=U_2,\quad X_3=U_3,\\
 W_1=a^{-1}(-kU_1+V_1),\quad
 W_2=(ab)^{-1}V_2,\quad W_3=(ab)^{-1}V_3.\end{gathered}\] Here \(a,b,f>0\). Using the paper’s simultaneous bracket-sign convention, the bracket \([T,W_2]\) is \(2kW_3/f\), not \(2kX_3/f\) as printed in (68). A simultaneous sign reversal for right-invariant frames does not change any Ricci calculation below.

Take \(k=1,\ a=1,\ b=1/2,\ f=1/10\). This is a smooth positive invariant metric of exactly the displayed form, with constant-length circle fibers and the fixed connection \(\eta_0\). It gives \[\operatorname{Ric}(T,W_1)=\frac34,\qquad
 \operatorname{Ric}(T,T)=\frac{17}{200},\qquad
 \operatorname{Ric}(W_1,W_1)=\frac{17}{2}.\] Since the circle fibers have constant length, the mixed Ricci formula in Proposition 4.4 makes nonzero mixed curvature equivalent, up to the stated nonzero scalar and sign convention, to nonzero divergence of the curvature form. Thus (74), and the zero assertion in (75), fail.
## Why the endpoint requirements do not remove the problem

For \(k\ne0\), (R1) vanishes precisely when \(ab=1\). Rounding the quotient \(S^3\) fibers requires \(b=1/(1+k^2)\), by the three lengths displayed on p. 30. Consequently zero mixed curvature at that round endpoint would force \(a=1+k^2\). Direct computation of the base Ricci component gives \[\operatorname{Ric}_{N}(X_2,X_2)=4-\frac{2k^2a^2}{(1+k^2)^2}.
 \tag{R2}\] At this endpoint it equals \(4-2k^2\), which is negative for \(|k|\ge2\). For example \(k=2,a=5,b=1/5\) gives \(-4\). Therefore the proposed fixed-connection ansatz cannot simultaneously provide the stated Yang–Mills property, round fibers and positive base Ricci curvature for these values of \(k\). This conclusion concerns the constructed ansatz; it is not a classification of all possible metrics in the lemma.

There is also an immediate incompatible condition at source lines 1102–1104: \(b\) is required to be nondecreasing from \(1/\sqrt{1+k^2}\) to the smaller number \(1/(1+k^2)\). Reversing this inequality repairs that particular sign, but does not repair (R1) or the endpoint obstruction. Nor does correcting the isolated bracket index repair the Yang–Mills assertion.
## Dependency, counterevidence, and required repair

Section 6.6 chooses the unique harmonic curvature representative and asserts that it agrees with the already constructed curvature for all \(t\in[0,1/2]\). This agreement uses precisely the false divergence claim. One therefore needs a different connection/path construction, or a proved transition to harmonic representatives with full mixed-curvature control. The dependency is Lemma 6.3 \(\to\) Section 6.6 \(\to\) Theorem 6.1 \(\to\) Lemma 7.2 and Proposition 7.1 \(\to\) the induction for Theorem 1.1. The issue is consequently Major.

The calculation also supplies substantial counterevidence against an overstated conclusion: the \(T,W_1\) block has determinant \[\operatorname{Ric}(T,T)\operatorname{Ric}(W_1,W_1)-\operatorname{Ric}(T,W_1)^2
   =\frac{4f^2}{(1+k^2)^2a^2b^4}>0.\] In the explicit \(k=1\) example the other four diagonal entries are \(699/200,699/200,198/25,198/25\), and all other cross entries vanish. The total metric in that example has positive Ricci curvature despite not being Yang–Mills. This finding invalidates the printed proof step, not the possibility of a corrected positive-Ricci deformation.
# F02: the neck Ricci formula omits the second variation of its cross section

Major. The location is (128), p. 45, source lines 1694–1699, and its use in (135), p. 46. For \(G=dr^2+h(r)^2g(r)\) with constant cross-section volume form, the printed tangential formula has no \(g''\) term. Such a term cannot be eliminated by constant volume.

An explicit test uses \(S^3\times S^3\) with \[h(r)=1,\qquad
 g(r)=e^{2c(r-1)^2}g_{S^3}\oplus e^{-2c(r-1)^2}g_{S^3},\qquad c>0.
 \tag{R3}\] This is smooth on an open interval about \(1\), has constant volume form, and is invariant under every Hopf action under discussion. At \(r=1\), \(g'=0\), while \(g''\) has blocks \(4c\,g_{S^3}\) and \(-4c\,g_{S^3}\). Formula (128) predicts Ricci curvature \(2\) in a unit direction of the first sphere. The ordinary doubly warped formula, or a direct shape-operator calculation, gives instead \[\operatorname{Ric}_G(X_1,X_1)=2-2c.
 \tag{R4}\] For \(c=2\) these values are \(2\) and \(-2\), respectively. All prerequisites for the general formula are satisfied; the test does not purport to be the authors’ particular final neck.

The estimate (135) does not bound this missing term. A repair must bound the second derivative of the compact smooth metric family and use \[g''=\ddot{\widetilde g}\,(t')^2+\dot{\widetilde g}\,t''.\] Slow reparametrization offers a plausible way to make these errors small; compact smoothness supplies finite higher derivative bounds. These are counterevidence to claiming the neck cannot be constructed. They do not make the printed estimate valid, and this review has not certified a replacement set of simultaneous constants. The defect is on the Proposition 7.1 neck construction used by Theorem 1.1, so it is Major.
# F03: the volume normalization does not justify the Moser equation

Major. Equations (118)–(120), p. 43, source lines 1618–1650, assert constant volume after defining \[\widetilde g_r=a_r\varphi_r^*\widehat g_r,\qquad
 a_r=\widetilde a\,\operatorname{Vol}(\widehat g_r)^{-1/6}.\] With the displayed tensor multiplication in dimension six, \[\operatorname{Vol}(a_r\widehat g_r)
  =a_r^3\operatorname{Vol}(\widehat g_r)
  =\widetilde a^{\,3}\operatorname{Vol}(\widehat g_r)^{1/2},\] which is not generally constant. A diffeomorphism cannot alter the total volume. Moreover the subsequent definition is \(\nu_r=dv_{\widehat g_r}\), so even replacing the exponent alone would leave the stated density equation unnormalized.

A complete countertest to this normalization step is \(\widehat g_r=c(r)g_0\), with \(c>0\) smooth, equal to \(1\) near both endpoints and nonconstant in the interior. For \(k=0\) this is already an admissible positive-Ricci equivariant path with the specified standard endpoints; one may also insert a scalar bump in any admissible path. Its volume is \(V_0c(r)^3\). The proposed scaled tensor has volume \(\widetilde a^3V_0^{1/2}c(r)^{3/2}\), which varies.

The obstruction to (120) is exact, not a numerical concern: the weighted integral of its left side is zero by integration by parts, whereas the required integral of its right side is \(-\frac{d}{dr}\int\nu_r\). This is nonzero where the above volume changes. Thus the stated solvability condition need not hold.

A concrete algebraic repair is to use the tensor factor \(a_r=\widetilde a\,\operatorname{Vol}(\widehat g_r)^{-1/3}\) and then define \(\nu_r=dv_{a_r\widehat g_r}\). Equivalently one can consistently use a length scale and its square in every metric formula. With this repair the integral obstruction vanishes, and the usual invariant weighted elliptic equation yields an equivariant Moser isotopy. This does not address F01 or F02. The incorrect normalization is itself used to obtain Lemma 7.2(3), an explicit prerequisite for the neck calculation, and is Major under the required core-derivation standard despite its elementary repair.
# Three Minor defects with explicit limiting counterevidence
## F04: coprime weights do not ensure freeness at the zero section

The location is p. 11, Section 2.2.1, and Propositions 3.1(4) and 5.1(4), pp. 16 and 24; source lines 423, 569 and 840. In the constructed product model, take \((a,b)=(2,1)\). These weights are coprime and \(a\ne0\). At any \((u,0)\in S^3\times\mathbb R^4\), the nonidentity element \(\theta=\pi\) acts by \((e^{2i\pi}u,e^{i\pi}0)=(u,0)\). More generally the zero-section stabilizer has order \(|a|\). Away from the zero section, coprimality does eliminate the simultaneous stabilizer. Global freeness for this model requires \(|a|=1\).

The actual inductive construction uses weights \((1,k)\), which pass this test, and its cyclic subactions are free. Restricting the overgeneral assertion to \(|a|=1\) leaves that mechanism available. This is therefore Minor, not a counterexample to the free action needed by the theorem.
## F05: the universal metric-cone description contradicts the stated cylinder limit

The final paragraph of Section 2.2, p. 14 (source line 494), says that every tangent at infinity is a metric cone. Section 2.2.7, p. 13, equation (22), and the introduction explicitly include a limit \(\mathbb R^3\times S^1\) when \(k_j\to\infty\). A full metric cone contracts to its vertex by radial contraction and is contractible. The cylinder has fundamental group \(\mathbb Z\), so it is not isometric or homeomorphic to any such cone, regardless of basepoint. Both assertions cannot be retained simultaneously.

A bounded sequence of indices can avoid this particular limit; the statement in question was not restricted to that case, and Example 2.3 allows unbounded indices. Delete or restrict the universal description, and distinguish a general pointed blow-down limit from a metric cone. This is a descriptive contradiction in the outline, not an obstruction to the inductive manifold construction, hence Minor.
## F06: the mapping-class argument silently omits orientation reversal

Equation (173) and the four-generator conclusion on p. 54 are written for all of \(\operatorname{Diff}(S^3\times S^3)\) with image in \(\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\). The diffeomorphism \(\sigma(x,y)=(y,x)\) acts on \(H_3\) by \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), whose determinant is \(-1\). It therefore disproves that stated image restriction and the claim that the four determinant-one maps generate every component.

The needed distinction is the orientation-preserving subgroup. This particular omitted case can be repaired without a new curvature construction: \(\sigma\) is an isometry of the standard equal-sphere product. If \(\phi\) reverses orientation, then \(\psi=\sigma\circ\phi\) preserves orientation and \(\psi^*g_0=\phi^*g_0\). A path for \(\psi\) is already a path with the required endpoint for \(\phi\). Subject to the earlier positive-Ricci construction, this completes the omitted reduction. The defect is Minor; it does not disprove Lemma 1.2.
# Coverage, positive checks, and limits

The group decomposition was checked as a compatible nested sequence of finite cyclic groups. Any finite set of elements of \(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\) has a common denominator and generates a cyclic finite subgroup. Compatible generators can be chosen inductively by lifting units in a cyclic quotient. The carry in (17) is needed because the splitting is only a splitting of sets. In (32), exactly one wrap occurs after \(k\) applications of the new generator, giving the old generator on each piece. This identity was independently enumerated for 56 pairs of subgroup order and index, and the general one-wrap proof was checked.

Topologically, each punctured \(S^3\times D^4\) piece and every gluing \(S^3\times S^3\) boundary is simply connected. The incidence graph has no cycles, and every finite collection of vertices has a common ancestor because the cyclic subgroups exhaust \(\Gamma\). Van Kampen on finite subtrees, followed by compactness of any loop, supplies simple connectivity of the increasing union. Stabilized metric balls with radii tending to infinity provide completeness of the direct limit; properness of the action additionally uses the separation of the newly inserted orbits, not just freeness. These mechanisms were traced through the inductive conditions and the gluing construction. No purely topological contradiction was established.

The base-model Ricci formula (53), the ordinary doubly warped formulas, the circle-bundle correspondence, the \(S^3\)-bundle triviality over \(S^2\), the gauge correction at the endpoint and the order of parameter choices were checked. The explicit map \(\phi_1(u,z)=(u,u^{-1}z)\) does intertwine the two specified actions, and its inverse is \((u,w)\mapsto(u,uw)\). The singular zero section has no bearing on freeness of the weight-one action. The induction for finite or trivial \(\Gamma\) also has direct product/lens-space models and does not require an infinite strictly increasing chain.

Several displayed local normalizations need reconciliation in a revision. For example the convex interpolation of \(f\) on p. 40 requires the maximum, rather than the printed minimum, of its two affine functions. The affine tail on p. 25 has cone coordinate \(r+\epsilon10^{-4}/(1-\epsilon)\), so the stated cutoff is not exact. These have explicit local corrections and are not counted again as independent demonstrated obstructions. Small-radius statements must be read with explicit smallness choices; for the constructed product a whole \(S^3_\delta\) cannot lie in a fixed-radius ball when \(\delta\) is arbitrarily large. The differing weight labels in the restatement of Proposition 8.1 likewise need to be reconciled with the actual action in (171). These observations do not substitute for a complete repaired construction.

The exact independent execution comprised 24 rational Koszul-curvature cases, four warped-metric specializations, and 56 finite carry-action cases, with all assertions passing. The analytical identities above, rather than a finite parameter grid, establish the findings. Eight source pages were visually checked to disambiguate the key formulas; all source pages were read as text.

The full external classification of the mapping class group, all cited compactness results and every smoothing constant in a corrected construction were not independently reproved. In particular this review does not certify a replacement proof after F01–F03. The verdict is version-limited: demonstrated defects in the acquired v3 derivations, with no claim that the 2024 revision or 2025 journal-final article retains them, and no claim that the main theorem is false.
# Compact conclusion table
Item | Judgment | Repair and remaining decision

F01, connection/Ricci | Major; asserted mixed term vanishing fails | Reconcile the connection, Yang–Mills condition and metric ansatz. The tested alternative also has a curvature obstruction; no complete repaired construction is certified.

F02, radial Ricci | Major; missing second metric derivative | Include the \(g''\) term and redo the neck estimate. The exact warped counterexample refutes the formula, not the final existence theorem.

F03, volume normalization | Major; tensor power inconsistent | Use the dimension-six tensor normalization exponent \(-1/3\) and recheck the volume/neck estimates. No full repaired induction is supplied.
F04, weight action | Minor; asserted general freeness fails | Restrict to the weight-one action used in the construction; the broader weighted claim has nontrivial isotropy.

F05, blow-down description | Minor; incompatible cone statement | Reconcile the universal cone assertion with the displayed \(\mathbb R^3\times S^1\) example. No independent refutation of the construction.
F06, mapping-class image | Minor; missing orientation case | Include the determinant-\(-1\) product factor interchange. It supplies the required local correction.
Scope and decision | v3 initial review complete | No attribution to the unverified 2024 revision or journal final. Author adoption was not requested; scientific/editorial disposition remains pending.

problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 13 Pdf pages: 14 Labels: (22) Labels: last paragraph Section 2.2 Source lines: 494
claim: Recorded check: Universal metric-cone claim conflicts with stated cylindrical blow-down
analysis: The final paragraph of Section 2.2, p. 14 (source line 494), says that every tangent at infinity is a metric cone. Section 2.2.7, p. 13, equation (22), and the introduction explicitly include a limit \(\mathbb R^3\times S^1\) when \(k_j\to\infty\). A full metric cone contracts to its vertex by radial contraction and is contractible. The cylinder has fundamental group \(\mathbb Z\), so it is not isometric or homeomorphic to any such cone, regardless of basepoint. Both assertions cannot be retained simultaneously.

A bounded sequence of indices can avoid this particular limit; the statement in question was not restricted to that case, and Example 2.3 allows unbounded indices. Delete or restrict the universal description, and distinguish a general pointed blow-down limit from a metric cone. This is a descriptive contradiction in the outline, not an obstruction to the inductive manifold construction, hence Minor.
result: Recorded evidence: Proof: R3 x S1 has fundamental group Z, whereas a full metric cone is contractible by radial contraction. The k_j->infinity limit in (22) cannot also be a metric cone.

claim: Recorded check: Orientation-reversing mapping classes are omitted
analysis: Equation (173) and the four-generator conclusion on p. 54 are written for all of \(\operatorname{Diff}(S^3\times S^3)\) with image in \(\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\). The diffeomorphism \(\sigma(x,y)=(y,x)\) acts on \(H_3\) by \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), whose determinant is \(-1\). It therefore disproves that stated image restriction and the claim that the four determinant-one maps generate every component.

The needed distinction is the orientation-preserving subgroup. This particular omitted case can be repaired without a new curvature construction: \(\sigma\) is an isometry of the standard equal-sphere product. If \(\phi\) reverses orientation, then \(\psi=\sigma\circ\phi\) preserves orientation and \(\psi^*g_0=\phi^*g_0\). A path for \(\psi\) is already a path with the required endpoint for \(\phi\). Subject to the earlier positive-Ricci construction, this completes the omitted reduction. The defect is Minor; it does not disprove Lemma 1.2.
