Title: Scientific initial review: M25-0005
The optimal paper Moebius band
# Assessment and exact version
No Issue Found in the scientific arguments within the review scope specified below. This is an initial-review result, not a certificate that every statement or external dependency is correct.
The reviewed input is Richard Evan Schwartz’s arXiv:2308.12641v12, 14 October 2024, with 16 PDF pages. Its PDF SHA256 is

`2170d49196cf30b557fc5c78a051499d98fa398c2c6cc6b15a23610fd4cc50dd`. The associated source and all 28 manifest file bindings were verified. All pages, including the discussion and references, were read; source pages 6–11 and their figures were also inspected visually.

The checked repository lists v12 as latest. Its author comment calls it the final intended publication version; that statement is recorded as author metadata, not independently proved equivalence to the journal PDF. The publisher lists revision and acceptance on 11 October 2024, and publication in Annals of Mathematics 201 (2025), 291–305, DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.201.1.5. The journal Version of Record was not acquired.

The historical erratum found in the author’s search-indexed material, dated 27 August 2023, concerns An improved bound on the optimal paper Moebius band, a different paper. The present v12 itself explains on p. 4 that the earlier parallelogram claim was wrong and that the present proof supersedes that earlier argument. The current proof uses a symmetric trapezoid. The historical error is therefore not counted against this input. A search-indexed distinct author copy is dated 12 November 2024; direct bounded retrieval of that copy and of the historical erratum timed out. Their full contents were not compared, and no identity with the journal final is asserted.
# Definitions, hypotheses, and the bend foliation

The object on p. 2 is a smooth arc-length-preserving embedding of the flat quotient \[M_\lambda=([0,\lambda]\times[0,1])/
       \bigl((0,y)\sim(\lambda,1-y)\bigr)\] into \(\mathbb R^3\). Arc-length preservation gives a positive-definite induced metric and hence an immersion; injectivity is separately required. The distinction matters: the proof needs disjoint bends, and the strict bound is not asserted for arbitrary immersed or sharply folded objects. The triangular folded model is a limit outside the smooth embedded class. It is consequently consistent to have the strict inequality \(\lambda>\sqrt3\) and infimum \(\sqrt3\).

The central dependency is \[\text{bend foliation}\ \longrightarrow\
 \text{embedded T-pattern}\ \longrightarrow\
 \text{trapezoid bound and equality analysis}.\] The nonzero-curvature part of the foliation in Lemma 2.1, p. 6, has the following local differential-geometric check. Choose an orthonormal principal frame \(e_1,e_2\) with shape operator \(Ae_1=0,\ Ae_2=\kappa e_2,\ \kappa\ne0\). Write \(\nabla_{e_1}e_1=a e_2\) and \(\nabla_{e_2}e_1=b e_2\). Codazzi gives \(a=0\) and \(e_1\kappa=-b\kappa\). Flatness gives \(e_1b=-b^2\). Along a unit-speed \(e_1\) curve, \[b(s)=\frac{b(0)}{1+s b(0)},\qquad
 \kappa(s)=\frac{\kappa(0)}{1+s b(0)}.
 \tag{R1}\] Its ambient acceleration is zero because both its intrinsic acceleration and its normal curvature vanish. It is a straight ruling. Formula (R1) prevents its nonzero curvature from becoming zero at a finite regular interior endpoint, while a pole would contradict smoothness. This supports continuation to the boundary, the key fact used by the cited developability results.

Distinct such rulings cannot cross at a nonflat point: two independent null directions would force the shape operator to vanish. After their closure is taken, the flat complementary strips can be filled by straight segments in the developed flat domain. If their side equations are \(x=u(y)\) and \(x=v(y)\), where \(u,v\) are affine and \(u(y)<v(y)\) for \(0\le y\le1\), the interpolation \[x_t(y)=(1-t)u(y)+t v(y),\qquad 0\le t\le1,\] is affine in \(y\), stays in the strip and has disjoint leaves. This supplies the elementary interpolation needed in Proposition 2.2. The treatment of limiting flat components still uses the global developability/foliation framework cited in that proposition; no claim is made to have re-proved every version of the external regularity theorems.

There is a local editorial clarification at p. 6, `2proof.tex` lines 81–84: for nonparallel sides the interpolated supporting lines are concurrent, meeting at the common intersection of the extended sides. The word coincident would mean identical lines and should be replaced. The explicit interpolation above verifies the intended construction; no scientific obstruction follows from this wording.
# Independent check of the T-pattern argument

The bend parameter is a circle. The centerline-intersection check on p. 7 is sufficient for this parametrization: a pre-bend long enough to wind past a fundamental strip would have length at least \(\sqrt{1+\lambda^2}>\lambda\), whereas its two endpoints split the boundary loop of total length \(2\lambda\) into two arcs, each at least as long as their straight spatial chord. This is impossible. A transverse pre-bend in a single developed strip crosses the centerline once.

For ordered distinct bends, the configuration space is a cylinder. Collapsing its two ends gives a sphere. The explicit coordinates on p. 12, \[(\theta,\phi)\longmapsto
       (x_0,x_1)=(\theta-\phi,\theta+\phi),
 \quad 0<\phi<\pi,\quad \theta\in\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z),\] are bijective, continuous with continuous inverse, and extend across the collapsed ends. Swapping the ordered entries is precisely \((\theta,\phi)\mapsto(\theta+\pi,\pi-\phi)\), the antipodal map. This identity was also checked independently at twenty sample pairs, including pairs near both ends.

Transporting a ruling orientation once around a Moebius band reverses it. Thus the two functions in (2), p. 8, \[g=u_0\cdot u_1,\qquad
 h=(m_0-m_1)\cdot(u_0\times u_1),\] are well-defined under simultaneous reversal of both chosen directions. Reversing the order of the bends gives the transported pair \((u_1,-u_0)\), so both \(g\) and \(h\) change sign. Continuity at the two added points gives respectively \((1,0)\) and \((-1,0)\); compactness bounds the midpoint difference, while the cross product tends to zero.

The odd-map form of Borsuk–Ulam therefore supplies a common zero away from the two added points. The author’s alternative winding argument was also checked: every path between the poles would have the same half-integer winding, but the antipodal transformation followed by reversal changes its sign, an impossibility. At a zero, the directions are perpendicular and the scalar triple product vanishes. The supporting lines are coplanar and intersect. The segments remain disjoint because they belong to the fixed foliation. The argument proves exactly the embedded T-pattern required by Lemma G; it does not require that the intersection of the extended lines lie on both segments.
# The trapezoid bound, strictness, and global optimization

Figure 2 and (3), p. 9, were checked together. Cutting along one pre-bend gives the symmetric trapezoid. The two remaining boundary paths satisfy \[H+D=2\lambda,\qquad D-H=2t,\] where \(t\) is a signed horizontal displacement. Neither step requires \(t\ge0\). One of the two disjoint perpendicular bends can be chosen entirely on one open ray of its supporting line away from the line intersection. This makes the comparison triangle’s height strictly greater than the length of that bend, and hence strictly greater than or equal to \(1\).

For a triangle of base length \(B=\sqrt{1+t^2}\) and height \(h\ge1\), reflection of one base endpoint across the line through the apex gives \[\text{sum of the other two sides}\ \ge\
       \sqrt{B^2+4h^2}\ \ge\sqrt{5+t^2}.
 \tag{R2}\] The first equality requires the apex to lie above the midpoint; the second requires \(h=1\). The unrestricted horizontal coordinate of the apex is allowed in this proof. In the embedded T-pattern situation the height inequality is strict, so the strict inequality needed in (3) is justified.

Independently define \[\delta(t)=\sqrt{1+t^2}+\sqrt{5+t^2},\qquad
 \nu(t)=2\sqrt{5+t^2}-2t.\] The two path estimates yield \(2\lambda>\max(\delta(t),\nu(t))\). At \(t_0=1/\sqrt3\), both functions equal \(2\sqrt3\). Moreover \[\delta'(t)=\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+t^2}}+\frac{t}{\sqrt{5+t^2}}>0
       \quad(t>0),\qquad
 \nu'(t)=\frac{2t}{\sqrt{5+t^2}}-2<0
       \quad(t\in\mathbb R).\] For \(t>t_0\) the first branch exceeds \(2\sqrt3\); for \(t<t_0\) the second branch does. Thus the minimax has its unique minimum \(2\sqrt3\) at \(t_0\), and the strict geometric inequality proves \(\lambda>\sqrt3\). In particular negative displacements are covered. The independently executed 4001-point grid and ninety triangle checks are numerical corroboration; the derivative and reflection arguments, not the grid, prove the universal statement.
# The triangular limit and uniform convergence of maps

For \(\lambda_n\to\sqrt3\), the minimax is squeezed between \(2\sqrt3\) and \(2\lambda_n\). Its coercivity and unique minimizer therefore give \(t_n\to1/\sqrt3\), rather than just convergence along one unspecified subsequence. The base lengths tend to \(2/\sqrt3\). The perimeter bound and the equality case in (R2) force the comparison height to tend to \(1\) and its apex to the midpoint position, giving the equilateral limiting triangle after rigid motions.

The other bend has length \(\sqrt{1+b_n^2}\le h_n\), hence \(b_n\to0\). Its gap from the horizontal supporting line also tends to zero. This supplies the midpoint assertion used at the beginning of p. 11. The boundary length excess vanishes, so the four boundary arcs converge to the appropriate straight segments, with lengths \(1/\sqrt3,1/\sqrt3,2/\sqrt3,2/\sqrt3\). For a curve of length \(L\) with endpoint distance \(d\), every point lies within distance at most \(\sqrt{L^2-d^2}/2\) of the endpoint segment: it lies inside the prolate ellipsoid defined by the two endpoint distances. This supplies a quantitative check on the disappearance of bending when \(L-d\to0\). Arc-length parametrization also rules out uncontrolled backtracking in the limit.

The final passage from triangle boundaries to interiors can be proved without assuming that an arbitrary bent surface is planar. Let \(p=\sum_i\alpha_i v_i\) with \(\alpha_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i\alpha_i=1\), in one of the three limiting triangles, and let \(A\) be the affine isometry fixed by its three vertices. If \(J\) is a 1-Lipschitz limiting map fixing these vertex images, then \[\begin{aligned}
 \sum_i\alpha_i|J(p)-A(v_i)|^2
 &=|J(p)-A(p)|^2+
       \sum_i\alpha_i|A(p)-A(v_i)|^2\notag\\
 &\le \sum_i\alpha_i|p-v_i|^2.
 \tag{R3}\end{aligned}\] The variance sums on the two sides coincide, so \(J(p)=A(p)\). The approximate version gives uniform control as the vertex errors vanish. This identity was verified with exact rational arithmetic for 66 choices of barycentric weights. Alternatively, common Lipschitz bounds give compactness and every subsequential limit is forced by (R3), establishing convergence of the full normalized sequence.

The changing domains are handled by the converging cut trapezoids and their three corresponding triangles; uniform convergence is understood using these natural piecewise affine domain identifications. Rigid motions normalize the images. The proof does not assert convergence of derivatives or curvature, and it permits the folded limiting map to cease being an embedding. The additional foliation discussion on p. 11 was checked separately and is not used to prove either main theorem.
# Supporting checks

The active source driver `0paper.tex`, lines 78–81, inputs `1intro`, `2proof`, `3remarks` and `refs`. The bound file `4bends.tex` is not included in this v12 driver. It was not silently treated as a current appendix or as a proof printed in the reviewed PDF. Static source inspection confirms that the current optimization uses a trapezoid and the displayed functions checked above. No author source was executed.

The discussion of other twists, cylinders and ribbon knots was read as context. The external smoothing results needed to transfer statements to folded ribbon knots were not independently re-proved in full. Reference labels `[HN]` and `[Ma]` on p. 6 should be reconciled with the printed `[HL]` and `[Mas]` entries; this is a traceability clarification, not a demonstrated false theorem. No present scientific finding is inferred from typographical slips or from the acknowledged error in the superseded earlier paper.

All independent script assertions passed: 4001 minimax samples, 90 triangle samples, 20 configuration-space coordinate checks and 66 exact variance identities. The analytic arguments in this report explain the mathematical conclusions and the limitations of those checks. The complete external developability literature, all historical results, and the inaccessible later author copy and journal final were not certified. Within these explicit limits, no demonstrated Major or Minor scientific defect was established in the manifest-bound v12 main proof or its triangular-limit argument.
# Compact conclusion table
Item | Judgment | Evidence and remaining decision

Main bound and limit | No Issue Found within coverage | Ruling/configuration-space argument, strict trapezoid bound, minimax calculation and triangular-limit rigidity checked as described. No whole-paper correctness certificate.

Historical error | Not a current v12 finding | The earlier parallelogram error belongs to a different, superseded paper and is acknowledged in this manuscript. The active proof uses the trapezoid argument.

Scope and decision | v12 initial review complete | External developability/smoothing inputs and the inaccessible later copy/journal final were not fully verified. No scientific repair proposed; author adoption is not applicable. Editorial disposition remains pending.

Title: Scientific initial review of M25-0006
On approximation to a real number by algebraic numbers of bounded degree
=3em
# Identity, scope, and disposition

The reviewed object is Anthony Poëls’s arXiv:2405.08341v1, dated 14 May 2024, comprising 21 PDF pages. The frozen journal identity is Annals of Mathematics 201 (2025), 307–330, DOI `10.4007/annals.2025.201.1.6`. These identities correspond, but equivalence to the journal Version of Record has not been established. All seven manifest file bindings passed the actual byte-count and SHA-256 checks. The reviewed PDF SHA-256 is
00001TOKEN.

All 21 pages were read. Definitions, the quantifiers in the approximation exponents, the polynomial construction, generalized resultants, the finite-dimensional minimization and final constant were checked. Pages 1, 13, 14, 16, 19 and 20 were also inspected as rendered source images. The 1,367-line bound author TeX was parsed statically; it was not executed. There are no active external input commands in that source.

Disposition: one Minor finding, restricted to the v1 abstract; no demonstrated Major defect in the reviewed core argument. Several compressed steps and local formula slips are resolved explicitly below. This is a scientific initial review with the stated coverage, not a whole-paper correctness certificate or verification of every cited theorem. In particular, the positive conclusion is conditional on the classical geometry-of-numbers and transference results identified below.
# F01: the abstract defines the exponent using the wrong extremum
Severity and location. Minor. PDF page 1, abstract, third sentence; `source.tex`, line 326. The abstract uses infimum where the body uses supremum, in the definition of \(\omega_n^*(\xi)\).

Equation reference: eq:down. Complete check. Let \(E\) be the set of exponents \(w\) for which infinitely many algebraic numbers of degree at most \(n\) satisfy \[
 0<|\xi-\alpha|\le H(\alpha)^{-w-1}.\] For \(H(\alpha)\ge1\), if \(w\in E\) and \(v<w\), the same solutions satisfy the inequality for \(v\). Thus \(E\) is downward closed. It is nonempty: for irrational \(\xi\), rational convergents have \(|\xi-p/q|\le q^{-2}\) and \(H(p/q)=\max(|p|,q)\ll_\xi q\), which gives every fixed \(0<w<1\) after discarding finitely many convergents. Consequently its infimum is \(-\infty\) if all real exponents are allowed, or \(0\) if the domain is restricted to positive exponents. Neither is the positive exponent claimed in the abstract. The supremum has the required meaning.

Counterevidence and impact. Equation (1.2) on the same page and Section 2 on page 4 correctly specify the supremum. The construction and Theorem 6.1 use arbitrarily large heights and then let \(\varepsilon\) decrease to zero in this correct sense. The defect is local to the abstract and does not invalidate Theorem 1.1. Replacing the single extremum word repairs it.

Version attribution. The current publisher abstract already uses the correct extremum. The publisher page records a revision dated 19 July 2024, after v1. This verifies correction in the publisher’s abstract only; it does not verify the entire journal PDF or show exactly when the correction was made. F01 is not alleged to remain in the journal article.
# Polynomial construction and dependency checks
## Quantifiers, minima, and irreducible factors

The distinction between a solution for every sufficiently large height and one for arbitrarily large heights is maintained. The reduction \(\omega_n(\xi)=\infty\Rightarrow\omega_n^*(\xi)=\infty\) uses the stated classical transference inequality; the finite case permits the uniform lower bound (4.3) after finitely many small polynomials are excluded. Transcendence ensures that a nonzero integer polynomial never vanishes at \(\xi\) and that a bounded-height collection is finite.

For the convex body on page 4, its volume is comparable to \(e^{-q}\) with constants depending on \(n,\xi\): the coefficient of the constant term in evaluation is 1, and fixed smaller boxes give the lower bound. Minkowski’s second theorem therefore gives \(\sum L_i(q)=q+O(1)\). The unboundedness of \(L_1\) follows by finiteness of integer polynomials of bounded height. In Lemma 3.1 the strict height inequality can be obtained by first choosing an exponent strictly between the working exponent and the uniform exponent, then using a fixed factor smaller than the target height. The exponent margin absorbs this factor.

For Lemma 3.3, changing signs of the initial \(Q_i\) so that their values have the sign of \(Q_1(\xi)\) makes the floor subtraction immediately satisfy the displayed factor-2 norm estimate. Such sign changes preserve successive-minimum realization and independence. Subtracting multiples of \(Q_1\) preserves independence; sorting the resulting heights preserves the upper bounds by the ordered successive minima. The integer determinant expanded in its evaluation row supplies the lower product bound, while Minkowski supplies the upper bound. Without the harmless sign convention, the printed elementary estimate needs a larger absolute constant; this does not change any later exponent.

The infinitude of the irreducible family in Section 4 uses a standard factor argument. Factor sufficiently good integer polynomials into their content and at most \(n\) irreducible factors. Product-height comparability and an exponent margin imply that at least one factor has the required small value. A finite collection of possible factors, with multiplicities bounded by \(n\), cannot account for values tending to zero with unbounded heights. Constants are absorbed by the fixed positive exponent margin. The invoked transference and product-height theorems are retained as external inputs, rather than presented as newly proved here.
## The two branches of Lemma 4.1

The maximal \(q\) with \(L_1(q)=\log(e^{-n}\lVert P\rVert)\) exists for the large heights in use. Its terminal trajectory has slope 1. Gelfond’s inequality and irreducibility give coprimality of \(P\) and \(Q\), including the possibility that their degrees are smaller than \(n\). Adding \(3P\) only to the low-height basis vectors makes their heights exceed \(\lVert P\rVert\) while preserving spanning together with \(P\). A basis-exchange argument then retains \(Q,P\) and removes one of the other vectors.

In the \(P_0\) branch, \(q<q_P\) implies \(e^{-n}|P(\xi)|\le|Q(\xi)|\); in the other branch, \(q\ge q_P\) implies \(|Q(\xi)|<|P(\xi)|\). Together with the determinant lower bound these yield respectively the exponent ranges around \(\widehat\omega_n\) and \(\omega_n\). Their union supplies the weaker uniform estimate needed in Theorem 6.1. The constants depending on \(n,\xi\) are fixed before the height tends to infinity; thresholds may depend on \(\varepsilon\).
# Generalized resultants, including the endpoint height branch
## Dimension and root estimates

The cited dependency [13], On uniform polynomial approximation, arXiv:2405.07219v1, Section 6, was consulted directly. Its Lemma 6.3 and Proposition 6.2 have the required hypotheses. The essential argument can also be reconstructed: writing \(V_i=V_i(\mathcal A)\), one has \(V_{i+1}=V_i+XV_i\). The quotient map from \(V_i\) to \(V_{i+1}/XV_i\) is onto and its kernel contains \(XV_{i-1}\). Hence the dimension increments decrease. Strict increase follows from a shifted nonzero polynomial of degree \(i+1\). If \(\gcd(\mathcal A)=1\), a Bezout identity puts 1 in some \(V_\ell\), and sufficiently high spaces are full. Concavity then gives the dimension bound used in Lemma 5.2. For the actual sets containing a coprime pair, full dimension at \(2n-1\) also follows directly by the Sylvester-map injection.

The degree-padding factors \((X-\lambda_i)^{n-\deg P_i}\) can be chosen with \(\lambda_i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\) avoiding the other polynomial’s roots and each other when necessary. Thus they preserve coprimality and have controlled heights and values. The basis extension has the asserted dimension. Taylor translation has determinant 1, so the generalized resultant remains a nonzero integer after translation.
## Why the index \(m=1\) may be removed in Corollary 5.4

The passage from Proposition 5.1 to (5.6), page 14, is compressed: the proposition permits \(m=1\), whereas the corollary writes \(m\ge2\). It requires justification, especially at \(k=n+1\). Here is a direct completion, with constants independent of \(C,y\).

Set \(r=n-k+2\). If \(k\le n\) and the root in Proposition 5.1 comes from the first-height group, its distance is bounded by \[\delta^2 H_1^{r-2}H_2^r H_3\cdots H_k
 \le \delta^2 H_2^{2r-2}H_3\cdots H_k.\] Its height is at most a fixed multiple of \(H_1\le H_2\), so this is precisely the required estimate with height index 2. Other indices work directly.

Equation reference: eq:refine. For \(k=n+1\), use the first two rows of the determinant expansion before discarding height information. Give its \(k\) columns height budgets \(B_1=H_1,B_2=H_2,\ldots,B_k=H_k\), allowing fixed factors from degree padding. Even if an actual column has smaller height, these budgets remain valid. If the derivative is in column 1, the value row must use another column with budget at least \(H_2\). If it is in another column, the remaining smallest budget is at least \(H_1\). Consequently, with \(M_i=\max(B_i,H_2)\), \[
 1\ll \delta\,\frac{\prod_i B_i}{H_1}
          \sum_i\frac{|S_i'(\xi)|}{M_i}.\] Choose a largest summand, and apply the nearest-root estimate. It gives \[|\xi-\alpha|\ll
 \delta^2\,\frac{H_2\cdots H_k}{M_i},
 \qquad H(\alpha)\ll M_i.\] Here \(M_i\) is one of \(H_2,\ldots,H_k\), exactly as (5.6) requires. This resolves the endpoint, rather than assuming \(H_1\) and \(H_2\) are comparable.

The sentence after (5.4), page 13, writes \(|S_\ell'(\xi)|/\lVert S_\ell\rVert^{-1}\) (source line 876). The largest summand actually needed is \(|S_\ell'(\xi)|/\lVert S_\ell\rVert\), as displayed in (5.4). This local selection typo and the omitted branch explanation have a complete direct resolution above; they are not evidence that the approximation bound or main theorem is false.

With \(A_k\ge0\), conversion from a height budget to \(H(\alpha)\) has the correct inequality direction. In Theorem 6.1, \(A_k(x,a)\ge1\) and \(\varepsilon<1/2\) ensure this sign condition. There are finitely many \(k\), so maximizing over \(k\) does not lose uniformity. The independent bound \(|\xi-\alpha|\ll H_2^{-1}\) forces \(H(\alpha)\to\infty\), excluding recycling finitely many roots. The exponent margin also absorbs the fixed constant in the definition of \(\omega_n^*\).
# Minimization and boundary analysis

For \(x=n\), the feasible vector is \((1,\ldots,1)\) and \(F=n\). For \(x\ge(3n-1)/2\), the \(k=2\) term is at least \(n\). The trial vector \((1,\ldots,1,1+\varepsilon)\), \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), has every ratio below \(n\). The page-16 display (source line 1028) should label its left side \(A_{n+1}/a_{n+1}\): the numerator itself is \(n+\varepsilon\), and the required ratio is \((n+\varepsilon)/(1+\varepsilon)\). This local label slip does not prevent the stated strict bound for \(F\). Compactness yields a minimizer with strict interior \(x\) bounds.

Reducing one coordinate immediately after a strict jump lowers all other ratios. At a minimizer this forces the jump ratio to be active. The same fact rules out coordinates at least 2 and equal consecutive coordinates above the initial plateau. This proves the active-set structure in Lemma 7.2 without assuming differentiability of a maximum.

The recurrence for the remaining coordinates is \[a_{k+1}=\frac{F}{F+1}a_k+\frac2{F+1}.\] Its explicit solution gives the sum constraint (7.6). At \(\theta=1/2\), that constraint makes \(F=(2n-\ell+1)/2\) rational. Writing \(F/(F+1)=a/b\) in lowest terms, \(2a^m=b^m\) with \(m=n+1-\ell\) forces \(m=1,a=1,b=2\). Thus \(F=1,\ell=n\) and \(n=1\), contrary to \(n\ge2\). Division by \(1-2\theta\) in the perturbation argument is therefore legitimate. The strict bounds persist for a small decrease of \(F\), contradicting minimality unless \(F=2(x-n)+\ell-1\).

Finally, the two minimizing identities give \[(3-2\theta)F_n=2n+1-\ell,\qquad
 F_n\log\theta\ge-(n+1-\ell).\] The second inequality follows from \(\log(1+u)\le u\), \(u>0\), with the sign checked after multiplication by \(-(n+1-\ell)\). Adding them yields \((3-2\theta+\log\theta)F_n\ge n\). The scalar function has derivative \(-2+1/\theta\) and negative second derivative, hence global maximum \(2-\log2\) at \(\theta=1/2\). This proves the final lower bound. The exceptional value excluded for an exact minimizer is used only as a global upper bound on this scalar function, which is logically consistent.

claim: Abstract incorrectly defines omega-star by infimum.
analysis: Severity and location. Minor. PDF page 1, abstract, third sentence; `source.tex`, line 326. The abstract uses infimum where the body uses supremum, in the definition of \(\omega_n^*(\xi)\).

Equation reference: eq:down. Complete check. Let \(E\) be the set of exponents \(w\) for which infinitely many algebraic numbers of degree at most \(n\) satisfy \[
 0<|\xi-\alpha|\le H(\alpha)^{-w-1}.\] For \(H(\alpha)\ge1\), if \(w\in E\) and \(v<w\), the same solutions satisfy the inequality for \(v\). Thus \(E\) is downward closed. It is nonempty: for irrational \(\xi\), rational convergents have \(|\xi-p/q|\le q^{-2}\) and \(H(p/q)=\max(|p|,q)\ll_\xi q\), which gives every fixed \(0<w<1\) after discarding finitely many convergents. Consequently its infimum is \(-\infty\) if all real exponents are allowed, or \(0\) if the domain is restricted to positive exponents. Neither is the positive exponent claimed in the abstract. The supremum has the required meaning.

Counterevidence and impact. Equation (1.2) on the same page and Section 2 on page 4 correctly specify the supremum. The construction and Theorem 6.1 use arbitrarily large heights and then let \(\varepsilon\) decrease to zero in this correct sense. The defect is local to the abstract and does not invalidate Theorem 1.1. Replacing the single extremum word repairs it.

This verifies correction in the publisher’s abstract only; it does not verify the entire journal PDF or show exactly when the correction was made. F01 is not alleged to remain in the journal article.

report: Abstract: This report reviews Manjul Bhargava’s Galois groups of random integer polynomials and van der Waerden’s Conjecture, arXiv:2111.06507v3, the exact 34-page supplied manuscript. Six Major findings concern three false statements at their stated scope and three defective derivations of principal results. No counterexample to the named van der Waerden theorem is asserted. Several proof completions and an explicit parameter repair are supplied. The unavailable journal-final text is not adjudicated.
Author: ChatGPT
Date: 25 October 2026

Title: Version-limited scientific initial review
M25-0007
=3em
# Identity, scope, and principal assessment

The frozen journal identity is Annals of Mathematics 201 (2025), 339–377, DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.201.2.1. The reviewed version is arXiv v3, submitted 28 September 2024; its PDF front matter displays 1 October 2024. Neither date establishes equivalence to the journal version. The input PDF SHA-256 is
00000TOKEN.

All 34 pages were read, including references; selected source pages 2–5, 11, 15, 23–24 and 26–30 were rendered and visually inspected. The bound source is one 1464-line `source.tex`; active input and executable-construct checks found none. Page references below are the manuscript’s printed page numbers; source lines are one-based.

The central mechanism combines permutation-index bounds, ramification conditions, finite-field Fourier estimates, number-field counting and a three-region argument in conductor/discriminant space. The review checked the definitions, quantifiers, tame/wild distinction, characteristic restrictions, prime-factor splitting, elimination steps, exponents and intransitive convolution. The disposition Major follows the specified standard for a demonstrated invalid derivation of a principal contribution, even where a repair is short.
# Problem F01: Theorem 2 includes intransitive groups but counts fields

Source and location. The definition of \(F_n(G,X)\) on p. 2, Theorem 2 on p. 3 (source lines 165–185), and Section 6, pp. 26–27, especially (23), use a field-counting exponent \(a(G)\) for any permutation group, while \(K_f=\mathbb Q[x]/(f)\) is then an étale algebra.

Complete check. Let \(n=3\) and let \(G=\langle(12)\rangle\) fix the third letter. Then \(\operatorname{ind}(G)=1\) and \(u=0\). No degree-three number field has this intransitive permutation Galois group, so the defined \(F_3(G,X)\) is zero. Thus \(a(G)=1/8\) satisfies exactly the stated hypothesis. The second alternative in Theorem 2 would give \[N_3(G,H)=O(H^{(2\cdot3-2)/8+1}\log^2H)
          =O(H^{3/2}\log^2H).\] For \(H\) a positive multiple of four, take \[f_{b,c}(x)=x(x^2+bx+c),\qquad |b|\le H,\quad 2\mid b,
 \quad 0<c\le H,\quad c\equiv2\pmod4.\] The quadratic is Eisenstein at 2, has nonzero discriminant, and has no zero root. The three roots are therefore distinct, and the exact permutation group of \(f_{b,c}\) is the specified \(C_2\) with one fixed point. Its coefficient height is at most \(H\). There are exactly \(H(H+1)/4\) such polynomials. This is \(\Omega(H^2)\), contradicting the asserted bound.

Counterevidence and interpretation. Defining \(F_n\) to count étale algebras would remove the vacuous field-counting hypothesis, but it is a different definition and would require corresponding counting inputs. Both p. 2 and Section 6 explicitly say number fields. Theorem 7’s separate treatment of intransitive groups is consistent with the likely intended restriction, but does not restrict Theorem 2 as written.

Impact and repair. Major: the advertised general scope of Theorem 2 is false. Restrict it to transitive groups, or formulate and prove an algebra-counting variant. The counterexample does not contradict Theorem 1: its order \(H^2\) is exactly the permitted exceptional order in degree three. Evidence: `independent_checks.py/json`, exact Eisenstein-family counts.
# Problem F02: Corollary 6 omits a necessary degree restriction

Source and location. Corollary 6 on pp. 4–5, source lines 258–266, asserts \(N_n(G,H)=O(H^{3n/11+1.164})\) for every regular permutation group of order \(n\), citing the exponent \(a(G)=3/8+\epsilon\).

Complete check. For \(n=2\), \(G=C_2=S_2\) is genuinely regular. The quadratics \(x^2+bx+c\) just constructed give \(\Omega(H^2)\) distinct polynomials of this group, whereas the claimed exponent is \[\frac6{11}+1.164=\frac{4701}{2750}<2.\] This is a direct counterexample within all the displayed hypotheses.

Dependency verification and counterevidence. The published Ellenberg–Venkatesh paper, Proposition 1.3, printed p. 725, explicitly assumes \(n>4\) for this Galois-extension estimate. The older author-hosted 2003 draft encountered in verification has a different lower-degree condition and is not substituted for the published theorem. The input’s reference does not authorize the missing low degrees. High-degree cases are not refuted by the quadratic family.

Impact and repair. Major: a stated quantitative corollary is false. Restore the degree restriction required by the actual cited input, and state low-degree bounds separately; degree two needs an exponent at least two. Evidence: the exact counts and the primary published Proposition 1.3 [EV].
# Problem F03: Corollary 8 fails for \(S_9\times M_{11}\)

Source and location. Corollary 8 and its proof, p. 5, source lines 280–284: all \(G\subset S_k\), \(k\le9\), are assigned the bound \(O(H^{8.686})\). The manuscript’s use of \(\subset\) includes equality, explicitly so for \(G=S_n\) after Theorem 2.

Construction. Fix a monic integral degree-eleven polynomial \(h\) with Galois group \(M_{11}\) in its natural action. Existence follows from the regular \(M_{11}\) realizations over \(\mathbb Q(t)\) recalled in König’s Section 2 [Koenig] and Hilbert irreducibility. In a resulting \(M_{11}\)-Galois extension of \(\mathbb Q\), the fixed field of a point stabilizer in its natural eleven-point action has degree eleven and Galois closure group \(M_{11}\), since the action is faithful. An integral primitive element of that fixed field gives a monic integral polynomial. This existence theorem is an identified external dependency, not an unverified assertion that one arbitrary specialization works.

There is a positive-density coefficient class of monic degree-nine polynomials \(q\) having group \(S_9\). An explicit independently computed class, in ascending coefficient order, is \[(a_0,\ldots,a_9)\equiv
 (323,1594,1589,3841,2809,1924,3976,3358,1162,1)
 \pmod {4199},\] where \(4199=13\cdot17\cdot19\). The three squarefree factorization patterns are respectively \((9)\), \((8,1)\), and \((2,1,1,1,1,1,1,1)\). The exact finite-field tests are saved. Frobenius gives a 9-cycle, hence transitivity, and an 8-cycle fixing a point, hence 2-transitivity. The transposition then forces \(S_9\): the normal subgroup generated by its conjugates is generated by edges of a connected invariant graph, and is the full symmetric group. Thus the coefficient class contains \(\Omega(B^9)\) such \(q\) of height at most \(B\).

Let \(L_h,L_q\) be splitting fields. Their intersection is Galois over \(\mathbb Q\). Since \(M_{11}\) is simple, a nontrivial common quotient would be \(M_{11}\) itself; this is impossible for \(S_9\), since \(11\) divides \(|M_{11}|\) and does not divide \(9!\). Thus the fields are linearly disjoint, and \[\operatorname{Gal}(hq)=S_9\times M_{11}.\] The irreducible degrees differ, so the product is squarefree. With the fixed constant \(M_h=\sum|\text{coefficients of }h|\) and \(H(q)\ge1\), coefficient convolution gives \(H(hq)\le M_hH(q)\). Multiplication by \(h\) is injective. Choosing \(B=H/M_h\) proves \[N_{20}(S_9\times M_{11},H)\gg H^9,\] contradicting \(O(H^{8.686})\).

Counterevidence, impact, repair. The isolated bound for \(N_{11}(M_{11},H)\) is not contradicted. Theorem 7 itself predicts a maximum of the factor exponents, and the \(S_9\) factor has exponent nine. Major: Corollary 8’s stated range is false. The specific obstruction is removed by taking \(k\le8\), by excluding \(S_9\) when \(k=9\) and supplying the exceptional-group bound, or by allowing exponent nine in this case. No claim is made that merely editing the statement completes every other proof obligation. Evidence: the saved CRT construction and [Koenig].
# Problem F04: the stated small parameter does not close the main bound

Source and location. Section 5, p. 23, chooses \(\delta\) small, suggesting \(1/(2n)\) (source line 895); Case II, p. 24 (line 912 and following display), needs \[E=1+(2+2\delta)(a-u)<n-1\] to absorb its positive logarithmic factor. Here \(a=(n+2)/4\) for \(n\ge6\) and \(u=1/[n(n-1)]\).

Check. At \(n=6\), the proposed \(\delta=1/12\) gives \[E=1+\frac{13}{6}\left(2-\frac1{30}\right)
   =\frac{947}{180}>5.\] At \(n=4\), using the stated \(a=1\), it gives \(E=49/16>3\). An \(O(H^E\log^{n-1}H)\) estimate with these exponents does not imply the required \(O(H^{n-1})\).

Repair, fully checked. One may instead use \(\delta=1/(4n^2)\) uniformly. For \(n\ge7\), \[E\le\frac{n+4}{2}+\frac{n+2}{8n^2}<n-1,\] and direct rational substitution proves the same strict inequality for \(n=4,5,6\), with \(a=1\) for 4 and 5. For \(n=6\) the sharp requirement here is \(\delta<1/59\). The proposed repair also satisfies the monic Fourier condition \(\delta<1/(2n-1)\), and the squarefull tails retain room for \(\epsilon<\delta/2\). This restores the numerical step in the three-region proof.

There is a related dependency mismatch in Section 6, p. 26: \(\delta<1/(n-1)\) is announced and the binary-form Proposition 26 is invoked for monic polynomials. The monic Corollary 33 supplies only \(\delta<1/(2n-1)\). The same smaller common choice fixes this application; the larger stated monic range is not established by that citation.

Counterevidence and impact. The freedom to choose \(\delta\) small makes repair straightforward; it does not make the specified numerical value valid. Major under the review standard because this invalid estimate lies directly on the proof of Theorem 1. It is a defective derivation, not a counterexample to Theorem 1. The Case II replacement of \(D^{-u}\) by \(Y^{-u}\) additionally needs partial summation: if \(A(X)\ll X^a\) and \(a>u\), then \(\sum_{D\le Y}D^{-u}\ll Y^{a-u}\), including the integral term. This supplies the estimate; a pointwise inequality would have the wrong direction. The actual exponents used here satisfy \(a>u\).
# Problem F05: Theorem 7 differentiates a cumulative upper bound

Source and location. Section 8, p. 30, source lines 1146–1155, especially line 1153, replaces the number of polynomials of exact height \(H_1\) by \(O(H_1^{\alpha_1-1}\log^{\beta_1}H_1)\) using only the cumulative hypothesis \(N_1(T)=O(T^{\alpha_1}\log^{\beta_1}T)\).

Complete logical test. Put \(m(2^j)=2^{2j}\) and \(m(t)=0\) at other positive integers. Then \[\sum_{t\le T}m(t)\le\frac43T^2,
 \qquad \frac{m(2^j)}{2^j}=2^j\longrightarrow\infty.\] Thus a cumulative \(O(T^2)\) bound does not imply the exact-height \(O(T)\) bound used in the proof. This sequence is a counterexample to the inference from the stated hypothesis; it is not claimed to be an actual polynomial counting sequence.

Repair in the applications. For the positive power exponents and nonnegative logarithmic exponents used here, a dyadic argument proves the desired convolution estimate without an exact-height estimate. Use \(H_*=\max(1,|\text{coefficients}|)\); fixed-degree comparison with the multiplicative Mahler measure implies \(\prod_i H_*(f_i)\ll H_*(\prod_i f_i)\). Put \(H_*(f_i)\) in dyadic intervals \([2^{j_i},2^{j_i+1})\). Then \(\sum j_i\le L=\log_2(CH)\), up to a harmless fixed adjustment, and the cumulative hypotheses bound the sum by \[\sum_{\substack{j_i\ge0\\\sum j_i\le L}}
 2^{\sum_i\alpha_i j_i}\prod_i(1+j_i)^{\beta_i}.\] If \(\alpha=\max_i\alpha_i>0\), divide by \(2^{\alpha L}\). Every index with \(\alpha_i<\alpha\) has a geometrically decaying weight. The indices with \(\alpha_i=\alpha\) contribute a composition sum of order \(L^{\sum_{\alpha_i=\alpha}(\beta_i+1)-1}\); summing the remaining slack is geometric. This proves the claimed form for these parameter ranges, with upper bounds throughout. Constants in product heights and zero coefficient-height factors must be treated as above. The manuscript does not explicitly restrict arbitrary \(\beta_i\); this repair is not claimed for every negative-logarithm regime.

Counterevidence and impact. Theorem 7’s conclusion can survive the invalid proof step in its applications. Major: the step is indispensable to the printed proof of a separately advertised general theorem and to its quantitative applications. The dyadic repair does not rescue F03, since there the maximum exponent is nine. Evidence: exact sparse-shell calculations and the analytic argument just given.
# Problem F06: quantitative exponent comparisons fail at stated endpoints

Scope and repair. These are counterexamples to the printed exponent deductions, not number fields refuting the endpoint conclusions. Stronger index information or a separately proved bound could restore the announced thresholds. As sufficient scalar conditions, \(k\ge6,n\ge36\) give \(s> (10/3)(n-1)/(n+2)>3\), and \(k\ge13,n\ge56\) give \(s>(48/13)(n-1)/(n+2)>7/2\). Any use of these repairs must also establish the required group-index assumptions. In the non-elemental branch with \(a=4,k=7\), the denominator furnished by Theorem 2 is \(34/7-u\), not the \(4-u\) printed in (28); its saving is still greater than six at \(n\ge53\), so that branch’s intended conclusion is not refuted by this correction.

Related logarithmic comparison. Section 6, p. 28 (source line 1060), asserts \[b=(c-1)-(c-n)\frac{1-1/k}{a+1-1/k-u}<c.\] For the primitive group \(\operatorname{AGL}_2(\mathbb F_3)\) in degree nine, independent enumeration of all 432 affine maps gives index three, so \(c=q(3,6)=3\). Taking the permissible loose field-count exponent \(a=3\) and \(u=1/72\) gives \(b=814/263>3\). The inequality as stated is false. A sharper choice of \(a\) may still imply the advertised theorem bound; this calculation alone does not disprove that bound. Retaining the actual \(b\), or a valid larger logarithmic exponent, avoids this algebraic step.

Impact and counterevidence. Major: these invalid comparisons directly support the paper’s advertised quantitative improvements. Other checked thresholds, \(n=10,k=3\) and \(n=16,k=4\), have strictly sufficient savings. No endpoint group counterexample has been inferred from scalar arithmetic. Evidence: exact fractions, the affine-group enumeration, and preserved failed check attempts.
# Positive checks, resolved concerns, and dependency limits
## Group theory and ramification

The transposition argument closes after adding reflexivity to the equivalence relation; conjugation supplies transitivity. For a nontrivial inertia element, the orbit count gives the wild discriminant lower bound; tame primes \(p>n\) give equality for the inertia generator. Small primes form a fixed finite set with bounded degree-dependent discriminant exponents.

Lemma 24, p. 15, prints \(v_p(D)=ef\) and assigns index \(e\) to \(x^e\). The correct quantities are \((e-1)f\) and \(e-1\). Over an unramified splitting extension, the \(f\) conjugate factors have reduction \((x-c_i)^e\), so their total index is at least \(f(e-1)\). Translation signs can likewise be corrected. These paired local errors do not refute the lemma’s needed statement and are not separately inflated into an additional Major finding.

The induction for the movement inequality (6), p. 11, omits the fully paired odd-\(k\) case and boundary cases where its induction hypothesis changes range. An independent completion avoids those cases. Write \(Y=\lfloor m/2\rfloor\) and start with \(Y\) disjoint transpositions. Choose \(y\) of them uniformly. Every \(k\)-set moved by the full family is hit by at least one asymmetric pair; the probability that a chosen pair hits is at least \(y/Y\). Thus \(f(m,k,y)\ge(y/Y)f(m,k,Y)\). For even \(m\), odd \(k\) has no fixed \(k\)-sets; for even \(k\ge2\), the fixed proportion \(\binom{Y}{k/2}/\binom{2Y}{k}\) is at most \(1/(2Y-1)\le1/5\) in the relevant range, by the ratio between successive even \(k\). For odd \(m\), the fixed proportion is at most \(1/m\), by the analogous parity-wise ratios starting at \(k=1,2\). These bounds imply the required \[f(m,k,y)\ge \frac{8y}{5k}\binom{m-1}{k-1}.\] The small allowed cases are immediate. Exact enumeration checked 17,545 parameter triples with \(3\le m\le60\); the universal argument, rather than this finite test, supplies the completion.
## Geometry, Fourier estimates, and the three regions

The Vandermonde argument in Proposition 22 uses the no-zero-subset-sum assumption to exclude solutions at infinity and gives the stated finite intersection bound. In Proposition 21, \(p>n\) ensures that positive multiplicities and their subset sums remain nonzero and that Newton identities can be inverted. The monic-to-binary normalization in Remark 23 needs the scalar factor \(t^{-n}\); with it the translation/dilation orbit argument works. The zero binary form must be removed before asserting a bounded factorization multiplicity; nonzero points retain the requisite density.

For the monic Fourier bound, the highest nonzero dual coordinate supplies a nonconstant translation-phase polynomial of degree at most \(n\); its leading binomial coefficient is nonzero for \(p>n\). The square-root bound and the CRT strata then have the necessary hypotheses. The distinction between binary and monic exponents is retained in F04.

In Case III the double discriminant is a nonzero polynomial: the family \(x^n+bx+c\) supplies a direct nonvanishing specialization. Its zero locus gives \(O(H^{n-2})\) choices before the last coefficient. Large prime factors have bounded number because the double discriminant has polynomial height and each such prime exceeds a fixed positive power of \(H\). In the other subcase, a greedy product of primes at most \(H^{\delta/2}\) crosses \(H^{1+\delta/2}\) without exceeding \(H^{1+\delta}\). The powerful-integer tails have strict power savings after the repaired choice of \(\delta\).

Section 6’s triangular elimination needs more than dimension alone. The earlier weighted moment equations give a finite projection to the first \(n-k\) coordinates; integrality supplies monic annihilating relations for the remaining coordinates. This justifies the bounded intermediate fibers required by the counting argument. Theorem 20’s trace-zero lattice count and the primitive-extension condition were checked together: every nonrational element generates in that setting, and the discriminant divisibility constraints fit the successive coefficient ranges.
## What this review does not establish

The manuscript uses classification-based group-index estimates, classical number-field counting, geometry-of-numbers results, Weil bounds and Hilbert irreducibility as external theorems. Their stated interfaces and relevant restrictions were checked; this report is not a fresh proof of the whole cited literature. No author executable or computational output was run or adopted as independent verification. The special hyperelliptic application was read with its genus/degree conventions; no unqualified low-genus objection is asserted. Finite computations test the explicit algebra above and do not certify all degrees or all proofs.

report: Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Scientific initial review M25-0008
The Alperin–McKay conjecture for the prime 2

=3em Object and disposition. This review concerns Lucas Ruhstorfer’s arXiv:2204.06373v1, submitted 13 April 2022, with 54 PDF pages and the earlier title printed above. It identifies two Major issues in the written proof chain and five Minor groups of local errors. No counterexample to the Alperin–McKay conjecture or Brauer’s height-zero conjecture is asserted. Proposed repairs are distinguished from adopted conclusions.

The frozen journal identity is The Alperin–McKay and Brauer’s height zero conjecture for the prime 2, Annals of Mathematics 201 (2025), 379–457, DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.201.2.2. The supplied identity recovery links this DOI and arXiv identifier in the same zbMATH record 8014492 and supplies corroborating references. This establishes correspondence, not equality of texts. The 2025 Version of Record was not obtained; no finding below is attributed to that uninspected version. The earlier manuscript already states a height-zero corollary on page 1.
# Scope, version, and method

All 54 source PDF pages were read. The review followed definitions, quantifiers, block and character parametrizations, Sylow and root calculations, extension maps, local-to-global criteria, and the exceptional-case assembly. Twelve source pages were additionally inspected as rendered images: 7, 9, 17, 19, 31, 34, 36, 44, 46, 47, 51, and 52. The 13 manifest file bindings were checked by size and SHA256. No author TeX source is supplied for this item; static inspection is limited to the actual PDF and the reviewer’s own sources. No author code was run.

The arXiv history checked for this review lists v1 only. The publisher page records receipt on 14 April 2022, revision on 7 August 2024, acceptance on 13 March 2024, and online publication on 12 March 2025; the unusual displayed ordering of revision and acceptance is retained as metadata, not silently corrected. Bounded searches did not identify an article-specific erratum; this is not proof that none exists. Remark 4.6, page 17, corrects an assertion in Cabanes’s 2018 work, and Lemma 7.4, page 26, supplies an omitted centralizer in Malle’s 2018 work. Those are historical issues acknowledged in the reviewed manuscript, not new defects assigned to it.

Primary dependency checks included Ruhstorfer’s local criterion [Ruh], Brough–Späth’s extension construction [BS], and the original character tables of Simpson–Frame [SF]. Classification, general Deligne–Lusztig theory, all tables in Kessar–Malle, and every cited equivalence theorem have not been independently re-proved. These are explicit limits on coverage, not assertions that such inputs are false.
# Major issue F01: the local subgroup hypothesis cannot hold
Location. Theorem 9.3, page 31, first sentence; its application in Theorem 11.3, pages 41–42; compare Lemma 6.6(a), page 24, and Definition 9.1, page 31.

Claim and complete check. Theorem 9.3 demands a proper \(\operatorname{Aut}(G)_b\)-stable subgroup \(M\) containing \(N_G(P)\). Every inner automorphism fixes a block \(b\): a block idempotent is central in the group algebra. Thus \[\operatorname{Inn}(G)\leq\operatorname{Aut}(G)_b,\qquad
 M\text{ is }\operatorname{Aut}(G)_b\text{-stable}\ \Longrightarrow\ M\lhd G.\] In the quasisimple groups at issue every proper normal subgroup is central. Since \(P\leq N_G(P)\leq M\) and the relevant defect group is noncentral, the demanded proper subgroup does not exist. This is an incompatibility of the stated hypotheses, not a counterexample to an implication with impossible hypotheses.

Lemma 6.6(a) proves the different assertion that \(N_G(L)\) is stable under \(\operatorname{Aut}(G)_{P,b}\). Theorem 11.3 explicitly selects \(M=N_G(L)\) and says that Lemma 6.6 verifies the assumptions of Theorem 9.3. It does not verify the printed \(\operatorname{Aut}(G)_b\)-stability condition. The same overly large stabilizer reappears in the argument of Corollary 14.3 on page 51.

Counterevidence and repair. Definition 9.1 uses the appropriate group \(N_{\operatorname{Aut}(H)}(D,b)\), which preserves the chosen defect group. Moreover, Theorem 2.1 of the primary source [Ruh], page 8 of arXiv:2010.04499v2, is formulated with \(M=N_G(Q)\), for \(Q\) characteristic in a defect group, rather than with the impossible invariance under all inner automorphisms. These strongly support a missing stabilizer subscript. The repair must state the correct local criterion, verify its normalizer/characteristic-subgroup formulation or the required generalization to \(N_G(L)\), and then check its remaining character and block conditions. Merely retaining the printed vacuous criterion does not do this.

Core impact and judgment. The affected application is the final iAM verification in Theorem 11.3, used in the noncyclic-stabilizer branch of Theorem 14.6; Lemma 9.6 and other subsequent uses also require the corrected criterion. This is a demonstrated invalid derivation on the main proof path, hence Major under the supplied standard, even though a local notational repair is plausible. The main conjectures are not refuted.
# Major issue F02: a factor-swap cannot be in the extension kernel
Location. Lemma 12.6, last paragraph of page 44 and first paragraph of page 45; Remark 12.4, page 44; application in Theorem 12.8, page 45.

Here \(L_0=\operatorname{SL}_3(q)\times\operatorname{SL}_3(q)\), \(W_{(d)}\simeq S_3\), its subgroup of order three centralizes \(L_0\), and its involutions interchange the two simple factors. The proof claims an extension of \(\psi_0\) to \(L_0\rtimes W_{(d)}\) with all of \(W_{(d)}\) in its kernel, and uses it to construct the character denoted \(\psi_0\Gamma(\nu)\).

Let \(K=\operatorname{SL}_3(q)\) and let \(\tau\) swap the factors. Any representation \(D\) with \(D(\tau)=I\) must satisfy \[D(a,1)=D\bigl(\tau(a,1)\tau^{-1}\bigr)=D(1,a)\quad(a\in K).\] The two commuting copies of \(K\) therefore have the same image, and that image is abelian. Since \(K\) is perfect for the cases here, \(D|_{K\times K}\) is trivial. Thus no nontrivial \(\psi_0\) of the required kind can have such an extension.

Equivalently, for \(\psi_0=\chi\otimes\chi\), the swap must act by a tensor permutation: \[F(v\otimes w)=w\otimes v,\qquad
 F(\rho(a)\otimes I)F^{-1}=I\otimes\rho(a).\] Replacing \(F\) by \(I\) forces \(\rho(a)\) to be scalar for every \(a\). The obstruction is not restricted to a toy representation. The relevant \(A_2\) series is nontrivial on the simple factors; for example at the allowed split parameter \(q=13\), its exceptional constituent has degree \((q-1)^2(q+1)/3=672\), as also described in Section 12.4. Its tensor square cannot satisfy the claimed kernel condition. An explicit \(4\)-by-\(4\) matrix calculation in the independent script checks the swap relation and the failure of the identity operator, while the argument above proves the general obstruction.

Counterevidence and repair. The canonical tensor-permutation extension does exist. Its kernel contains \(C_{W_{(d)}}(L_0)\), the subgroup of order three, not the whole permutation group. Proposition 4.2 of [BS], page 16, requires an actual extension representation \(D'\); its formula (4.1) retains the factor \(D'(\rho(v))\). It does not permit dropping a nontrivial swap operator. Replace the false kernel assertion, carry the tensor-permutation action through the construction on \(L_0V_{(d)}\), and check the \(E'\)-stabilizer and induction steps on page 45 with that action retained.

Core impact and judgment. The displayed construction supplies the equivariant extension map used in Theorem 12.8 for the \(A_2(\varepsilon q^3).3\) cases, part of the final exceptional-group coverage. Its printed justification cannot be executed. This is Major; the existence of a plausible corrected extension is counterevidence against claiming that Lemma 12.6 itself, or the main result, is false.
# Minor issues with explicit checks
## F03: unequal orbit lengths in Theorem 1.4(a)
Location. Page 7, Theorem 1.4(a) and the last paragraph of its proof.

Take \(\mathbf G=\operatorname{SL}_2\) over \(\mathbb F_5\), with dual \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\), and let \(s\) be the image of \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\). Here \(Z_F=C_2\), \(C^\circ_{\mathbf G^*}(s)\) is a split torus, and \(A(s)=C_2\). The torus has only the trivial unipotent character, so its \(A(s)\)-orbit has size one.

For the regular embedding in \(\operatorname{GL}_2(5)\), let \(\eta\) be the nontrivial quadratic character of \(\mathbb F_5^\times\). The principal series induced from \((1,\eta)\) is irreducible of degree six: the two Bruhat double cosets give endomorphism dimension one when the two inducing characters differ. Twisting by \(\eta\circ\det\) interchanges the two inducing characters and fixes this representation. These are exactly the two determinant twists fixing it. Cyclic Clifford theory therefore gives two distinct degree-three constituents on \(\operatorname{SL}_2(5)\), interchanged by diagonal conjugation. Their \(Z_F\)-orbit has size two. Thus the corresponding orbit lengths are \(2\) and \(1\), not equal.

For \(a=|A(s)|\) and \(r\) the unipotent orbit length, the relevant cyclic Clifford relations are \[\#(\text{diagonal orbit})=a/r,\qquad
 \chi(1)=\widetilde\chi(1)\,r/a,\qquad
 \psi(1)=r\,\widetilde\psi(1).\] The printed formulas divide \(\widetilde\chi(1)\) by \(r\) and multiply \(\widetilde\psi(1)\) by \(a/r\) instead. In this example they would give \(6\) and \(2\), whereas the actual degrees are \(3\) and \(1\). The script enumerates \(\operatorname{GL}_2(5)\) (480 elements), \(\operatorname{SL}_2(5)\) (120), and the centralizers (orders 16 upstairs and 8 projectively), corroborating the degree indices.

Counterevidence/impact. The quotient of the two corrected degree formulas still yields the degree formula in part (c). Lemma 2.3 constructs its later correspondence through additional Clifford arguments. No use of the false equality of orbit lengths that defeats the final AM count was established. Correct the orbit statement and its proof; classify this verified auxiliary error as Minor, without promoting it to a counterexample to part (c).
## F04: the Cabanes tests have overstrong quantifiers
Location. Proposition 4.2 and Lemma 4.4, page 17; compare the quotient-involution argument in Theorem 4.10, pages 18–20.

Proposition 4.2 claims necessity as well as sufficiency of the absence of nontrivial quadratic cosets. For necessity take \(H=S_4\) and \(A=V_4\). This \(A\) is the unique maximal abelian normal subgroup. Indeed, for any abelian normal \(B\), minimal normality of \(A\) gives \(B\cap A=1\) or \(A\). In the second case \(B\leq C_H(A)=A\); in the first, \([B,A]\leq B\cap A=1\) gives the same conclusion. Yet a transposition induces a nontrivial involution on \(A\simeq\mathbb F_2^2\), and in characteristic two \((h-I)^2=h^2-2h+I=0\). This is the forbidden quadratic coset in a group satisfying the printed conclusion. The independent enumeration checks the abelian normal closures and the action.
The sufficient direction survives: if an abelian normal \(B\) is not contained in \(A\), choose \(h\in B\setminus A\). Then \([h,A]\subseteq B\cap A\) centralizes \(h\), making the coset quadratic.

Lemma 4.4 incorrectly asks for an actual involution in \(H\setminus A\). Take \(H=Q_8\) and \(A=\langle i\rangle\). The quotient is \(C_2\), there is no involution outside \(A\), and \(H\) has three maximal abelian normal subgroups of order four. Its nontrivial coset is involutory and acts quadratically on \(A\), but its representatives have order four. The correct obstruction is an involutory coset acting on \(A\). For such a coset the action squares to one, and the quadratic condition becomes \([h,t]^2=1\) for all \(t\in A\). The further implication from equality of squares to \({}^ht\in\{t,t^{-1}\}\) is also invalid for general abelian \(A\) and is unnecessary.

Counterevidence/impact. The proof of Theorem 4.10 tests involutions in the Weyl quotient, which is the corrected type of test; it does not depend on finding order-two lifts in the Sylow group. Thus these two finite counterexamples do not refute its Sylow conclusion. Retain sufficiency, use cosets, and remove the unnecessary equality-of-squares step. This is a Minor group of false auxiliary assertions, with no demonstrated failure of the core Sylow conclusion.
## F05: the three \(A_2\) subgroups do not share pairwise a \(C_3\)
Location. Section 10.3, page 34, last paragraph; simply connected torus convention on page 33.

The root subgroups \(G_1,G_2,G_3\) have bases \(\{\alpha_1,\alpha_3\}\), \(\{\alpha_5,\alpha_6\}\), and \(\{\alpha_0,\alpha_2\}\). The text asserts \(G_i\cap G_j=Z\) of order three for every \(i\ne j\). But \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) commute and have independent coordinate subtori in the simply connected torus, whose simple coroots form a basis. Their intersection is central in both, hence lies in those subtori, and is trivial. The same calculation applies to the other pairs.

There is a genuine order-three kernel in the product map. With the order of simple coroots used in the paper, its lattice matrix has columns \[e_1,\ e_3,\ e_5,\ e_6,\ -(1,2,2,3,2,1)^t,\ e_2\] and determinant of absolute value three. The kernel involves all three factors diagonally; it is not a common pairwise intersection. Exact determinant arithmetic and enumeration on the three-torsion subtori give pairwise intersection sizes \(1,1,1\) and product-kernel size \(3\).

Counterevidence/impact. The correct central-product description and rank are close to the intended statement. The discrepancy concerns odd central torsion; the subsequent explicit two-local calculations do not thereby become false. No necessary later use of a nontrivial pairwise intersection was identified. Replace the assertion by the product-kernel formulation. Minor.
## F06: central characters must be normalized by degree
Location. Lemma 12.9(a),(b), pages 46–47.

Part (a) prints \(\operatorname{Res}_{Z(U)}^U(\phi)\phi(1)=\operatorname{Res}_{Z(U)}^H(\chi)\chi(1)\). At the identity this would require \(\phi(1)^2=\chi(1)^2\), even when restriction has nontrivial multiplicity. All hypotheses are met by \[H=S_3\times C_3,\quad H_0=U=C_3,\quad Z=1,\quad
 \chi=\chi_{\rm std}\otimes1,\quad\phi=1_U.\] Here \(\chi(1)=2\), \(\phi(1)=1\), and the multiplicity is two. The printed identity is \(1=4\).

Schur’s lemma gives the correct statement \[\frac{\operatorname{Res}_{Z(U)}^U\phi}{\phi(1)}
   =\frac{\operatorname{Res}_{Z(U)}^H\chi}{\chi(1)}.\] Part (b) must use the corresponding normalized central character on \(Z(U)Z\). If \(\lambda_\chi\) denotes the scalar central character of \(\chi\), the extension is explicitly \(\widehat\rho(uz)=\rho_\phi(u)\lambda_\chi(z)\); agreement on \(U\cap Z\) proves it well defined, and determines it uniquely.

Counterevidence/impact. The proof in words already establishes equality of scalar central characters, and Proposition 12.10 needs that normalized assertion. The correction is fully supplied here; its odd-multiplicity argument is checked separately below. Thus Minor, not evidence that the claimed odd multiplicity is false.
## F07: the defining union for \(\mathcal E_\ell(G,s)\) omits \(s\)
Location. Section 1.6, page 9, first display.

The union is printed with \(\mathcal E(G,t)\) instead of \(\mathcal E(G,st)\). Take \(\mathbf G=\mathbb G_m\) over \(\mathbb F_7\), so \(G=C_6\), \(\ell=2\), and \(s\) has exponent \(2\) and order \(3\) in its dual. The displayed union selects characters of exponents \(\{0,3\}\), whereas the series associated with \(s\) is \(\{2,5\}\). These are different \(2\)-blocks. In a torus the printed expression loses its dependence on \(s\) altogether.

Counterevidence/impact. Lemma 2.3, page 11, explicitly uses the products \(st\). Thus this is a local missing factor, not an independently demonstrated failure of the later parametrization. Insert \(s\) in the defining union. Minor.
# Positive checks and resolved concerns
## An independent verification of the character-table calculation

Proposition 12.10, page 47, invokes CHEVIE for an odd-multiplicity claim. The following derivation checks its split \(\operatorname{SL}_3(q)\) calculation directly from the original tables [SF], Tables 1a–1b, with \(q\equiv1\pmod3\). It uses no author code and no CHEVIE execution.

Write \(r=q-1\), \(s=q+1\), \(t=q^2+q+1\), \(r'=r/3\), and \(D=r^2s/3\). The six exceptional characters of degree \(D\) have indices \(\chi_{u,v}\), \(u=0,1,2\), \(v=1,2\). With \(\omega^3=1\), their relevant nonzero values are: \(D\omega^{vk}\) on the three central classes, \(-r'\omega^{vk}\) on the three transvection classes, \((q\delta_{\ell u}-r')\omega^{vk}\) on the nine regular-unipotent classes, and \(\omega^{vk}\) on irreducible-torus classes. The corresponding centralizer orders are \(q^3r^2st\), \(q^3r\), \(3q^2\), and \(t\); the last class family has \((t-3)/3\) members.

For the subfield case on the same page, a regular element of order \(q^2+q+1\) remains in the irreducible-torus class family over \(\mathbb F_{q^2}\). The embedding exponent \(q^2-q+1\) is \(1\) modulo three. The table therefore gives a third root of unity for the relevant exceptional character value. Among constituents nonzero at that element and with its nontrivial central character, the exceptional and generic cuspidal degrees have the required common two-part; the other relevant characters vanish. If all their multiplicities were even, a third root of unity divided by two would be an algebraic integer, which is impossible (its norm in \(\mathbb Q(\omega)\) is \(1/4\)). This verifies the parity mechanism used there. No blanket verification of every unitary table entry or every Ennola substitution is claimed.
## Root, group-action, and case-assembly checks

The independent program constructs all 72 \(E_6\) roots, identifies the 36 positive roots, and verifies the coefficient assertion of Lemma 4.8 for that root system. Orthogonality to the tori in Section 12.2 gives 12 and 14 roots, agreeing with the claimed \(A_2^2\) and \(A_2^2A_1\) Levi types. These checks also support the lattice calculation in F05.

The statement about an odd group acting on a power-of-two set in the argument of Lemma 2.3 needs its actual context: here the relevant odd component group is at most \(C_3\). Since \(3\) does not divide a power of two, a fixed point exists; the commuting transitive diagonal action then propagates fixedness. An arbitrary odd group acting on an arbitrary power-of-two set would not justify the same shortcut. No separate defect is assigned after restoring the context.

Similarly, the coprime-orbit argument in Proposition 8.3 uses the commuting action supplied by the cyclic outer automorphism setup. A permutation commuting with a transitive abelian action acts as a translation on the orbit; coprimality then forces the required trivial action. Coprimality alone, without this structure, would not suffice.

The final cyclic-stabilizer sentence in Theorem 14.6 cites Proposition 14.4, whose statement excludes two centralizer types. The already proved Theorem 12.8 and Lemma 14.5 address those excluded cases. The final assembly should cite them explicitly. This is not recorded as a new missing-case obstruction.
