report: Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Scientific initial review M25-0009
De Rham algebras of closed quasiregularly elliptic manifolds are Euclidean

=3em Object and disposition. This report reviews Susanna Heikkilä and Pekka Pankka’s arXiv:2302.11440v2, dated 7 December 2023, 25 PDF pages. It records two Major issues in the written argument or its advertised scope and one Minor issue in an example. One Major issue has a complete local repair supplied below. The other concerns a missing implication for an arbitrary given smooth structure, not a constructed counterexample to the classification. Neither finding disproves the principal algebra-embedding theorem.

The corresponding journal identity is Annals of Mathematics 201 (2025), 459–488, DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.201.2.3. The journal Version of Record was not obtained or verified as textually identical. All findings in this report are confined to the supplied v2.
# Scope, versions, and method

All 25 PDF pages were read, including definitions, all proof sections, examples, appendices, and references. Source PDF pages 2, 4, 14, 17, 19, 22, 23, and 24 were additionally inspected as images. The supplied 1,437-line author TeX file was inspected statically; it was not executed or compiled. The manifest’s seven file bindings were actually hashed and matched. Independent calculations below use only the reviewing assistant’s own Python standard-library script.

The review followed the chain from the rescaling/hunting argument to bounded normalized pullbacks, compact homotopy primitives, weak wedge convergence, the top-degree limit measure, multiplicativity, Poincaré-duality injectivity, and pointwise evaluation. It also checked the bounded-energy alternative, the singular sphere example, intersection-form bounds, and the PL-to-quasiregular interface.

The arXiv history inspected during this review lists v1 on 22 February 2023 and v2 on 7 December 2023. The publisher metadata reports a later revision on 20 November 2024 and publication online on 12 March 2025; its displayed acceptance date, 16 May 2024, precedes that revision and is retained as displayed rather than silently reordered. The official Helsinki research portal lists an accepted manuscript named Heikkila-Pankka_QR-cohomology-revised-Nov-2024. A bounded retrieval received HTTP 403. A publicly indexed Helda reprint was also found, but opening it encountered an access-denied challenge. That barrier was not bypassed. An indexed excerpt cannot establish the content of the entire later manuscript. No claim is made that any issue below persists in, or was repaired by, either later text. Bounded publisher/arXiv searches did not identify an erratum; absence of a search hit is not proof of absence.
# F01 — Major: division by a possibly zero top-degree pairing

Equation reference: eq:bad. Exact location. Proposition 5.1, PDF page 14, the displayed assertion immediately after the case \(k_1+k_2=n\) begins; author TeX lines 860–870, especially line 862. For arbitrary classes \(c_1,c_2\) in complementary positive degrees, the proof selects \(\tau\) such that \[
 \operatorname{vol}(N)h(c_1)\wedge h(c_2)
 = I\bigl(\operatorname{vol}_N+d\tau\bigr),\qquad
 I=\int_N c_1\wedge c_2 .\] Here \(h(c)\) is the harmonic representative. No nonzero-pairing hypothesis is imposed in this proposition. If \(I=0\), this would require the harmonic representatives to have identically zero wedge, which need not hold.
## A counterexample satisfying the actual surrounding setup

Let \(N=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3\) with coordinates \(x,y,z\) modulo one, oriented by \(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz\). Put \(a(z)=\frac12\sin(2\pi z)\) and choose the smooth metric whose inverse matrix is \[(g^{ij})=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&a&0\\ a&1&0\\0&0&(1-a^2)^{-1}
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 (g_{ij})=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 (1-a^2)^{-1}&-a(1-a^2)^{-1}&0\\
 -a(1-a^2)^{-1}&(1-a^2)^{-1}&0\\
 0&0&1-a^2
 \end{pmatrix}.\] Both matrices are positive definite, \(\det g=1\), and the largest eigenvalue of \(g\) is at most two because \(|a|\le1/2\). Hence \(\operatorname{vol}(N)=1\) and \(\operatorname{vol}_N=dx\wedge dy\wedge dz\). Directly from the defining identity for the Hodge star, \[*dx=dy\wedge dz+a\,dz\wedge dx,\qquad
 *dy=a\,dy\wedge dz+dz\wedge dx .\] These two forms are closed: each differentiated coefficient already multiplies a factor \(dz\). Thus \(dx\) and \(dy\) are closed and coclosed. Set \[\alpha=dx,\qquad \beta=*dy.\] The form \(\beta\) is closed, and \(*\beta=dy\) is closed, so \(\beta\) is also harmonic. With \(c_1=[\alpha]\) and \(c_2=[\beta]\), uniqueness of harmonic representatives gives \(h(c_1)=\alpha\), \(h(c_2)=\beta\). However, \[\alpha\wedge\beta=a(z)\operatorname{vol}_N,\qquad
 \int_N\alpha\wedge\beta=0,\qquad
 a(1/4)=1/2.\] The left side of [eq:bad] (#eq:bad) is nonzero and its right side is zero for every \(\tau\). For clarity, the nonzero wedge is exact: \[\alpha\wedge\beta=d\eta_0,\qquad
 \eta_0=-\frac{\cos(2\pi z)}{4\pi}\,dx\wedge dy .\] Exactness is weaker than pointwise vanishing.

This example is not placed on a target excluded by the unbounded-area hypothesis. For every positive integer \(j\) take \[f_j:B_2^3\longrightarrow N,\qquad u\longmapsto ju\pmod{\mathbb Z^3}.\] Its Jacobian is \(j^3\), and \(\|Df_j\|^3\le2\sqrt2\,j^3\). Writing \(\omega_3=\operatorname{vol}_{\mathbb R^3}(B^3)\), one obtains \[A(f_j)=\omega_3j^3\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad
 \int_{B_2^3}f_j^*\operatorname{vol}_N=8A(f_j).\] Thus \(f_j\in\mathcal F_{2\sqrt2,8}(N)\) with fixed constants. The target is closed, connected, oriented, and not a rational homology sphere. The normalized pullbacks of a finite harmonic basis are bounded in the required \(L^{3/k}\) spaces. Weak compactness and compactness of the Poincaré operator give a Sobolev–Poincaré subsequence, exactly as in Lemma 4.1, independently of the invalid assertion [eq:bad] (#eq:bad). In the two specified degrees the normalized forms are explicitly \[f_j^\#(c_1)=\omega_3^{-1/3}dx,\qquad
 f_j^\#(c_2)=\omega_3^{-2/3}
       \bigl(a(jz)\,dy\wedge dz+dz\wedge dx\bigr).\] Periodic averaging makes the oscillatory coefficient converge weakly to zero. The limiting product is zero, as the proposition’s desired conclusion requires.
## Repair, counterevidence, and core impact

Equation reference: eq:repair. The correct top-cohomology decomposition, valid also when \(I=0\), is \[
 h(c_1)\wedge h(c_2)=\frac{I}{\operatorname{vol}(N)}\operatorname{vol}_N+d\eta .\] Its difference has integral zero and hence is exact on the closed connected oriented \(N\). Applying normalized pullback, testing against a compactly supported smooth function, using Proposition 4.2 for weak wedge convergence, Lemma 3.2 for the vanishing exact term, and Theorem 4.4 for the volume-form limit gives \[d\widehat L(c_1)\wedge d\widehat L(c_2)
  =\frac{I}{\operatorname{vol}(N)}\,\nu_{d\widehat L}
  =\Phi_{d\widehat L}(c_1\wedge c_2).\] This supplies the missing zero-pairing case without division by \(I\). The earlier use of a similar formula in Theorem 4.4, page 12, explicitly chooses \(I\ne0\) by Poincaré duality and is not defective for this reason.

The invalid step lies on Proposition 5.1 \(\to\) Theorem 1.7 \(\to\) Theorem 1.3 \(\to\) Theorem 1.1. Under standard 0.7.1 it is Major because a core written derivation fails under its own hypotheses, although the local repair is complete and no main-theorem counterexample results. The repaired statement is adopted locally in this report; that adoption does not retroactively change the reviewed source.
# F02 — Major: the sufficiency argument changes the smooth/PL scope

Exact location. Corollary 1.2 and the two preceding paragraphs on PDF page 2, author TeX lines 398–415; compare Proposition B.1 on page 23, lines 1206–1213. The definition on page 1 is for a given Riemannian manifold. The corollary asserts an if-and-only-if condition on that manifold using only its homeomorphism type. Its sufficiency argument, however, constructs torus branched covers for the displayed connected sums with their standard PL structures compatible with the usual smooth structures.

Dependency verification. The inspected primary version of Piergallini–Zuddas [PZ], Theorem 1.3, constructs branched covers onto the standard connected-sum models. Remark 1.4 explains the torus consequence and expressly leaves the exotic counterparts outside that conclusion. Corollary 1.5 constructs covers from an exotic counterpart to a standard model, not covers in the reverse direction. This describes the scope of that primary source; it is not a claim about the current status of every exotic case.

The missing implication. Let \(X\) be a manifold with its given smooth structure and let \(N_0\) be a standard model on the list. The supplied premises give \[X\cong_{\mathrm{TOP}}N_0,\qquad
 \mathbb R^4\longrightarrow\mathbb T^4\longrightarrow N_0
 \quad\hbox{quasiregular}.\] To conclude that \(X\) itself is quasiregularly elliptic by this construction requires a suitable quasiregular transfer to \(X\), or a separate branched-cover construction for its compatible PL structure. An arbitrary homeomorphism \(N_0\to X\) has no stated Sobolev or bounded-distortion control. Proposition B.1 does not supply it: that proposition requires a PL map and PL structures compatible with both given smooth structures. A topological classification alone does not verify those hypotheses. Nor can a branched covering \(X\to N_0\) simply be inverted and composed.

Consequently, the proof establishes a precise weaker classification: every closed simply connected quasiregularly elliptic smooth four-manifold has one of the listed homeomorphism types, and every listed type has a quasiregularly elliptic standard smooth representative. It does not establish, by the cited steps, the stronger sufficiency for every given smooth structure on such a type. No existence assertion about a particular exotic structure in this small range, and no nonelliptic exotic example, is needed or claimed here.

Counterevidence and resolution. The standard models really do have the required torus covers. The necessary intersection-form bounds \(\beta_2^\pm\le3\) are independently checked below. Changing the smooth Riemannian metric on a fixed closed smooth manifold is harmless: uniform equivalence of the metrics controls distortion. These facts do not address a change of compatible PL/smooth structure. The repair is either to state the weaker homeomorphism-type classification explicitly or to provide the missing theorem for the stronger quantifier. The abstract’s advertised classification and Corollary 1.2 are a main application, so this demonstrated scope gap is Major. The truth of the stronger formulation remains unresolved by this review; it is not labeled false.
# F03 — Minor: the zoom in Example 7.3 includes a transition annulus

Exact location. Example 7.3, PDF page 17, author TeX lines 992–996. First, the prescribed balls \(B(2^j e_1,j)\) are not mutually disjoint for all \(j\ge1\): the pairs \((1,2)\) and \((2,3)\) overlap. Starting at \(j=3\) repairs this finite-prefix defect.

Even after that repair, the positive zoom \(f_{a_j,r_j/2}\) is defined on \(B_2^n\). It sees the whole ball of radius \(r_j\), not only the inner ball on which \(h_Q\) is the fixed rotation \(Q\). In normalized coordinates its map is \[H(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 Qx,& |x|\le1,\\
 Q_{2-|x|}x,&1\le |x|<2.
 \end{cases}\] This is independent of \(j\). Taking \(Q_t=\exp(tA)\) with \(A\) skew-symmetric, the derivative of a radial twist \(x\mapsto Q_{t(|x|)}x\) has determinant \[\det Q_t\left(1+\frac{t'(|x|)}{|x|}x\cdot Ax\right)=1.\] Consequently normalization does not remove the annular derivative: its degree-one pullback is \(\operatorname{vol}(B^n)^{-1/n}dH\), not the constant form specified by \(Q^*L_\pi\) on all of \(B_2^n\).

For an explicit check, take \(n=2\), \(Q\) a rotation by \(\theta=\pi/2\), and \(x=(3/2,0)\). Then \[DH(x)=R_{\pi/4}
 \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-3\pi/4&1\end{pmatrix},\] which is different from \(Q=R_{\pi/2}\). Continuity on the open annulus gives a positive-measure discrepancy, not just a single exceptional point. The independent numerical check gives a maximum entrywise difference approximately \(2.37319\).

Use the positive zoom \(f_{a_j,r_j/4}\) instead. Its full domain \(B_2^n\) then lies in the inner rotation ball. For a particularly transparent identity zoom, use \(f_{-j^2e_1,j}\) with \(j\ge3\); its full image ball lies in the negative half-space and misses all supports. The two normalized embeddings are exactly \(Q^*L_\pi\) and \(L_\pi\). Uniform derivative and inverse-derivative bounds follow from \(|t'(r)|r\le2\) in every rescaled annulus, so the patched map remains quasiconformal. This repairs the intended nonuniqueness example. The main proof does not depend on the stated numerical choices, hence Minor.
# Positive checks, boundary cases, and rejected concerns

Sobolev algebra and exact forms. For degrees \(k,\ell\) with \(k+\ell\le n\), Hölder exponents obey \(k/n+\ell/n=(k+\ell)/n\). The product derivative has the same integrability because each exterior derivative is controlled in the corresponding degree’s \(L^{n/k}\) space. For \(1\le k<n\), \(n/k>1\), so weak compactness is available; the top degree is handled separately as a measure. The independent script checks 680 such exponent cases for \(2\le n\le16\), supplementing this general calculation.

For an exact \(k\)-form \(d\eta\), integration by parts against a compact test form and the bound on \(f^*\eta\) leave the factor \(A(f)^{-k/n} A(f)^{(k-1)/n}=A(f)^{-1/n}\). This tends to zero. Degree zero uses a constant harmonic representative, not an unavailable reflexive \(L^\infty\) argument. Compactness of the regularized Poincaré operator produces strongly convergent primitives on a finite harmonic basis. Combining one strong primitive with one weak closed pullback and integrating by parts proves the distributional wedge limit, including total degree \(n\). The general operator theorem remains an external analytic input, not an independently reproved monograph.

Top measure and injectivity. For a non-rational-homology-sphere target, a single nonzero dual pair yields an \(L^1\) density for the vague Jacobian limit. Nonnegativity follows from positive approximating measures. Absolute continuity makes the unit sphere a null set, so restriction to \(\overline B^n\) preserves the normalized mass one. Poincaré duality then makes a nonzero class pair to a nonzero multiple of that top class, proving injectivity. In the rational-homology-sphere case the intermediate cohomology vanishes and a normalized top form can be chosen directly; the argument does not assert the same Jacobian-limit regularity there.

For pointwise evaluation in Section 7, choose representatives of a finite homogeneous basis and extend linearly. Intersect the finitely many full-measure sets on which the basis multiplication identities hold, and choose a point where the top density is nonzero. There is no need to intersect uncountably many full-measure sets. Evaluation is then a graded homomorphism, injective by the same duality argument.

Growth and compactness dependencies. Bonk–Heinonen [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 1.11]{BH}] supplies a positive growth exponent depending on dimension and distortion for the required nonzero intermediate cohomology. Its exact primary statement was checked; the apparent concern about an unmentioned target-dependent exponent was rejected. The hunting step extracts a fixed doubling constant and unbounded normalized area.

The bounded-area argument in Section 9 uses a local bounded-energy bubbling statement, whereas the prominently cited Pankka–Souto theorem is phrased for closed sources and fixed degree. The local proof ingredients in [Retained latex: \cite[Propositions 3.1--3.2]{PS}] were checked: uniform energy bounds the number of bad balls; an exhaustion and diagonal subsequence give finitely many interior concentration points; finite-energy removable singularities yield spherical bubbles. A nonconstant sphere-to-\(N\) map would have positive degree, forcing an injection of intermediate cohomology into that of the sphere. Thus a target which is not a rational homology sphere has no such bubbles. This supplies the local adaptation used here, subject to those external compactness/removability inputs.

Crucially, Corollary 1.4 and Theorem 9.1 really contain the closure \(\overline{\mathcal F_{K,D}(N)}\). The overbar is visible in the source PDF and author TeX, although lost by plain-text extraction. Shrinking maps converging to a constant therefore do not refute the printed statements. This candidate concern was explicitly rejected.

Examples and four-dimensional algebra. For the sphere construction in Section 8, the tripling map fixes the equator as required for gluing. Each small inserted bubble has mass \(\operatorname{vol}(S^n)+O(j^{-n})\), the normalized weights are \(1/j+O(j^{-n-1})\), and the mass outside the small balls tends to zero. Uniform continuity and the midpoint Riemann sum give the claimed half-length measure on the segment. This is consistent with the exclusion of rational homology spheres in the absolute-continuity theorem.

On \(\bigwedge^{2m}\mathbb R^{4m}\), interpret the top-degree pairing as the coefficient of the fixed oriented volume element. Each complementary pair of basis monomials gives a \(2\)-by-\(2\) block with eigenvalues \(+1,-1\). There are \(\frac12\binom{4m}{2m}\) such blocks, proving the claimed signature bound. Exact checks give \((3,3)\), \((35,35)\), \((462,462)\), and \((6435,6435)\) for dimensions \(4,8,12,16\). The integral over all of \(\mathbb R^{4m}\) printed in Appendix A should be read as this algebraic evaluation (or integration over a unit-volume cube); a literal improper integral of a nonzero constant top form would not be finite. This notational repair leaves the signature argument intact and is not counted as a separate obstruction.

The PL argument in Appendix B has a locally evident composition-order typo, \(p\circ\iota\) in place of \(\iota\circ p\). With the corrected order, finite-simplex derivative bounds, cancellation of opposite boundary faces in Stokes’ formula, and a positive minimum Jacobian on each compact simplex give the asserted Sobolev regularity and finite distortion. This verification preserves the compatibility hypotheses emphasized in F02.

problems.title: Zero-pairing harmonic wedge cannot be written as pairing times volume plus exact form
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Zero-pairing harmonic wedge cannot be written as pairing times volume plus exact form
claim: Recorded check: Zero-pairing harmonic wedge cannot be written as pairing times volume plus exact form
analysis:
Equation reference: eq:bad. Exact location. Proposition 5.1, PDF page 14, the displayed assertion immediately after the case \(k_1+k_2=n\) begins; author TeX lines 860–870, especially line 862. For arbitrary classes \(c_1,c_2\) in complementary positive degrees, the proof selects \(\tau\) such that \[
 \operatorname{vol}(N)h(c_1)\wedge h(c_2)
 = I\bigl(\operatorname{vol}_N+d\tau\bigr),\qquad
 I=\int_N c_1\wedge c_2 .\] Here \(h(c)\) is the harmonic representative. No nonzero-pairing hypothesis is imposed in this proposition. If \(I=0\), this would require the harmonic representatives to have identically zero wedge, which need not hold.

Let \(N=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3\) with coordinates \(x,y,z\) modulo one, oriented by \(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz\). Put \(a(z)=\frac12\sin(2\pi z)\) and choose the smooth metric whose inverse matrix is \[(g^{ij})=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&a&0\\ a&1&0\\0&0&(1-a^2)^{-1}
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 (g_{ij})=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 (1-a^2)^{-1}&-a(1-a^2)^{-1}&0\\
 -a(1-a^2)^{-1}&(1-a^2)^{-1}&0\\
 0&0&1-a^2
 \end{pmatrix}.\] Both matrices are positive definite, \(\det g=1\), and the largest eigenvalue of \(g\) is at most two because \(|a|\le1/2\). Hence \(\operatorname{vol}(N)=1\) and \(\operatorname{vol}_N=dx\wedge dy\wedge dz\). Directly from the defining identity for the Hodge star, \[*dx=dy\wedge dz+a\,dz\wedge dx,\qquad
 *dy=a\,dy\wedge dz+dz\wedge dx .\] These two forms are closed: each differentiated coefficient already multiplies a factor \(dz\). Thus \(dx\) and \(dy\) are closed and coclosed. Set \[\alpha=dx,\qquad \beta=*dy.\] The form \(\beta\) is closed, and \(*\beta=dy\) is closed, so \(\beta\) is also harmonic. With \(c_1=[\alpha]\) and \(c_2=[\beta]\), uniqueness of harmonic representatives gives \(h(c_1)=\alpha\), \(h(c_2)=\beta\). However, \[\alpha\wedge\beta=a(z)\operatorname{vol}_N,\qquad
 \int_N\alpha\wedge\beta=0,\qquad
 a(1/4)=1/2.\] The left side of [eq:bad] (#eq:bad) is nonzero and its right side is zero for every \(\tau\). For clarity, the nonzero wedge is exact: \[\alpha\wedge\beta=d\eta_0,\qquad
 \eta_0=-\frac{\cos(2\pi z)}{4\pi}\,dx\wedge dy .\] Exactness is weaker than pointwise vanishing.

This example is not placed on a target excluded by the unbounded-area hypothesis. For every positive integer \(j\) take \[f_j:B_2^3\longrightarrow N,\qquad u\longmapsto ju\pmod{\mathbb Z^3}.\] Its Jacobian is \(j^3\), and \(\|Df_j\|^3\le2\sqrt2\,j^3\). Writing \(\omega_3=\operatorname{vol}_{\mathbb R^3}(B^3)\), one obtains \[A(f_j)=\omega_3j^3\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad
 \int_{B_2^3}f_j^*\operatorname{vol}_N=8A(f_j).\] Thus \(f_j\in\mathcal F_{2\sqrt2,8}(N)\) with fixed constants. The target is closed, connected, oriented, and not a rational homology sphere. The normalized pullbacks of a finite harmonic basis are bounded in the required \(L^{3/k}\) spaces. Weak compactness and compactness of the Poincaré operator give a Sobolev–Poincaré subsequence, exactly as in Lemma 4.1, independently of the invalid assertion [eq:bad] (#eq:bad). In the two specified degrees the normalized forms are explicitly \[f_j^\#(c_1)=\omega_3^{-1/3}dx,\qquad
 f_j^\#(c_2)=\omega_3^{-2/3}
       \bigl(a(jz)\,dy\wedge dz+dz\wedge dx\bigr).\] Periodic averaging makes the oscillatory coefficient converge weakly to zero. The limiting product is zero, as the proposition’s desired conclusion requires.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Theorem4.4 explicitly uses a nonzero pairing and is unaffected. Correct decomposition h(c1) wedge h(c2)=I/vol(N) vol_N+d eta proves the proposition using the existing weak-wedge/exact-form lemmas.

problems.title: Standard PL representatives do not prove sufficiency for every given smooth structure of a homeomorphism type
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Standard PL representatives do not prove sufficiency for every given smooth structure of a homeomorphism type
claim: Recorded check: Standard PL representatives do not prove sufficiency for every given smooth structure of a homeomorphism type
analysis: Exact location. Corollary 1.2 and the two preceding paragraphs on PDF page 2, author TeX lines 398–415; compare Proposition B.1 on page 23, lines 1206–1213. The definition on page 1 is for a given Riemannian manifold. The corollary asserts an if-and-only-if condition on that manifold using only its homeomorphism type. Its sufficiency argument, however, constructs torus branched covers for the displayed connected sums with their standard PL structures compatible with the usual smooth structures.

Dependency verification. The inspected primary version of Piergallini–Zuddas [PZ], Theorem 1.3, constructs branched covers onto the standard connected-sum models. Remark 1.4 explains the torus consequence and expressly leaves the exotic counterparts outside that conclusion. Corollary 1.5 constructs covers from an exotic counterpart to a standard model, not covers in the reverse direction. This describes the scope of that primary source; it is not a claim about the current status of every exotic case.

The missing implication. Let \(X\) be a manifold with its given smooth structure and let \(N_0\) be a standard model on the list. The supplied premises give \[X\cong_{\mathrm{TOP}}N_0,\qquad
 \mathbb R^4\longrightarrow\mathbb T^4\longrightarrow N_0
 \quad\hbox{quasiregular}.\] To conclude that \(X\) itself is quasiregularly elliptic by this construction requires a suitable quasiregular transfer to \(X\), or a separate branched-cover construction for its compatible PL structure. An arbitrary homeomorphism \(N_0\to X\) has no stated Sobolev or bounded-distortion control. Proposition B.1 does not supply it: that proposition requires a PL map and PL structures compatible with both given smooth structures. A topological classification alone does not verify those hypotheses. Nor can a branched covering \(X\to N_0\) simply be inverted and composed.

Consequently, the proof establishes a precise weaker classification: every closed simply connected quasiregularly elliptic smooth four-manifold has one of the listed homeomorphism types, and every listed type has a quasiregularly elliptic standard smooth representative. It does not establish, by the cited steps, the stronger sufficiency for every given smooth structure on such a type. No existence assertion about a particular exotic structure in this small range, and no nonelliptic exotic example, is needed or claimed here.

Counterevidence and resolution. The standard models really do have the required torus covers. The necessary intersection-form bounds \(\beta_2^\pm\le3\) are independently checked below. Changing the smooth Riemannian metric on a fixed closed smooth manifold is harmless: uniform equivalence of the metrics controls distortion. These facts do not address a change of compatible PL/smooth structure. The repair is either to state the weaker homeomorphism-type classification explicitly or to provide the missing theorem for the stronger quantifier. The abstract’s advertised classification and Corollary 1.2 are a main application, so this demonstrated scope gap is Major. The truth of the stronger formulation remains unresolved by this review; it is not labeled false.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Necessary beta2+/-<=3 bound and existence of standard QR representatives are valid. Weaker homeomorphism-type classification follows. No nonelliptic exotic example and no assertion of existence of any particular exotic structure in small range.

problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Nonuniqueness example uses overlapping initial balls and a zoom that includes a transition annulus
claim: Recorded check: Nonuniqueness example uses overlapping initial balls and a zoom that includes a transition annulus
analysis: Exact location. Example 7.3, PDF page 17, author TeX lines 992–996. First, the prescribed balls \(B(2^j e_1,j)\) are not mutually disjoint for all \(j\ge1\): the pairs \((1,2)\) and \((2,3)\) overlap. Starting at \(j=3\) repairs this finite-prefix defect.

Even after that repair, the positive zoom \(f_{a_j,r_j/2}\) is defined on \(B_2^n\). It sees the whole ball of radius \(r_j\), not only the inner ball on which \(h_Q\) is the fixed rotation \(Q\). In normalized coordinates its map is \[H(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 Qx,& |x|\le1,\\
 Q_{2-|x|}x,&1\le |x|<2.
 \end{cases}\] This is independent of \(j\). Taking \(Q_t=\exp(tA)\) with \(A\) skew-symmetric, the derivative of a radial twist \(x\mapsto Q_{t(|x|)}x\) has determinant \[\det Q_t\left(1+\frac{t'(|x|)}{|x|}x\cdot Ax\right)=1.\] Consequently normalization does not remove the annular derivative: its degree-one pullback is \(\operatorname{vol}(B^n)^{-1/n}dH\), not the constant form specified by \(Q^*L_\pi\) on all of \(B_2^n\).

For an explicit check, take \(n=2\), \(Q\) a rotation by \(\theta=\pi/2\), and \(x=(3/2,0)\). Then \[DH(x)=R_{\pi/4}
 \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-3\pi/4&1\end{pmatrix},\] which is different from \(Q=R_{\pi/2}\). Continuity on the open annulus gives a positive-measure discrepancy, not just a single exceptional point. The independent numerical check gives a maximum entrywise difference approximately \(2.37319\).

Use the positive zoom \(f_{a_j,r_j/4}\) instead. Its full domain \(B_2^n\) then lies in the inner rotation ball. For a particularly transparent identity zoom, use \(f_{-j^2e_1,j}\) with \(j\ge3\); its full image ball lies in the negative half-space and misses all supports. The two normalized embeddings are exactly \(Q^*L_\pi\) and \(L_\pi\). Uniform derivative and inverse-derivative bounds follow from \(|t'(r)|r\le2\) in every rescaled annulus, so the patched map remains quasiconformal. This repairs the intended nonuniqueness example. The main proof does not depend on the stated numerical choices, hence Minor.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Use r_j/4 for pureQ zoom and negative center -j^2 e1,scalej for pureidentity. Uniform radial-twist derivative/inverse bounds prove globalquasiconformality. Nonuniqueness survives.

# Identity, scope, and judgment

This review concerns Ravi Shankar and Yu Yuan, Hessian estimates for the sigma-2 equation in dimension four, arXiv:2305.12587v2, submitted 3 December 2024, 25 PDF pages. The frozen journal identity is Annals of Mathematics 201 (2025), 489–513, DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.201.2.4. All seven manifest file bindings were independently checked. The reviewed input PDF SHA-256 is
00000TOKEN. The bound author TeX has 1,170 lines and SHA-256
00001TOKEN.

Judgment: zero Major findings and one Minor finding. The general, zero-order-dependent stability proof in Lemma 6.1 evaluates its operator at a function that does not touch the approximating solution. A complete counterexample to that displayed inequality is given below, together with its repair. The actual application is to a pure Hessian operator, so the omitted constant does not invalidate that application. No demonstrated failure of the main Hessian estimates was found. This is a version-limited initial review, not a certificate of whole-paper correctness.

All 25 pages were read; source pages 2, 5, 9, 11, 14, 16, 17, 19, 21, and 22 were visually inspected to resolve notation and location. The TeX was inspected statically; the inactive comment blocks at lines 275–281, 307–330, and 369–393 were excluded from the active proof. No author code was executed. An author-hosted journal-formatted PDF was subsequently acquired for selected comparisons, including the exact Lemma 6.1 passage; this does not replace the manifest input or constitute a full review of the later text.

The dispatcher reported the account Minhao Liu’s Group—Academic Researchers, Chat mode, webpage model 6Pro. Those are dispatcher observations. The visible assistant performed the scientific reading, proofs, computations, static inspection, compilation, and page inspection.
# F01: the contact value in the general stability argument

Equation reference: eq:wrong. Location and claim. Lemma 6.1, PDF page 22, author-source lines 1012–1032, especially line 1030. The lemma concerns continuous elliptic equations \(F(D^2u,Du,u,x)=0\) and uniformly convergent viscosity solutions \(u_k\). In its proof, after setting \[Q_\varepsilon=Q+\varepsilon|x-x_0|^2-\varepsilon^4,\] the maximum of \(u_k-Q_\varepsilon\) is positive and occurs at \(x_\varepsilon\). The proof then asserts \[
 0\le F(D^2Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),DQ_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),
                 Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),x_\varepsilon).\] The test function touching \(u_k\) is instead \(Q_\varepsilon+m_\varepsilon\), where \(m_\varepsilon=(u_k-Q_\varepsilon)(x_\varepsilon)>0\). Its value is \(u_k(x_\varepsilon)\), not \(Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon)\).

Complete check under the stated assumptions. In dimension \(n=4\), on \(B_1(0)\), take \[F(M,p,z,x)=(\operatorname{tr}M)^5+z,\qquad u_k=u=0,\qquad Q=0,\quad x_0=0.\] This \(F\) is smooth and elliptic in the monotonicity sense: for \(N\ge0\), \(F(M+N,p,z,x)\ge F(M,p,z,x)\), strictly if \(N\ne0\). It is not uniformly elliptic, which the lemma does not require. No monotonicity in \(z\) is stated there. The zero functions solve the equation classically and in the viscosity sense: an upper test has nonnegative Hessian at contact, and a lower test has nonpositive Hessian. Convergence is uniform and \(Q\ge u\) with equality.

Here \(x_\varepsilon=0\) and \(m_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^4\). For \(\varepsilon<1/4\) the annulus estimate in the proof holds. Taking \(\varepsilon=1/65536=1/[2(2n)^5]\) gives \[F(2\varepsilon I,0,-\varepsilon^4,0)
       =(8\varepsilon)^5-\varepsilon^4
       =-\frac{\varepsilon^4}{2}<0,\] contradicting [eq:wrong] (#eq:wrong). In fact it is negative for every \(0<\varepsilon<(2n)^{-5}\), so choosing a still smaller perturbation does not fix the step. The genuine touching test is \(\varepsilon|x|^2\); its value gives \((8\varepsilon)^5>0\), as the viscosity condition requires. Nine exact rational checks for \(2\le n\le10\) reproduce this distinction; the dimension-four wrong value is \(-1/36893488147419103232\).

Repair and counterevidence. Use \(\phi_\varepsilon=Q_\varepsilon+m_\varepsilon\) and write \[0\le F(D^2Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),DQ_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),
                    u_k(x_\varepsilon),x_\varepsilon).\] Since \(Q\ge u\), \(0<m_\varepsilon\le\left\lVert u_k-u\right\rVert_{L^\infty}+\varepsilon^4\to0\) after the indicated choice of \(k(\varepsilon)\). Also \(x_\varepsilon\to x_0\), and continuity now gives the required inequality for \(u\). The lower-test argument is analogous. Thus this is not a counterexample to the stability lemma.

The operator actually needed in the compactness argument has no \(z\) or gradient dependence. Adding \(m_\varepsilon\) therefore leaves that operator unchanged. Consequently no broken dependency from this error to Theorem 1.1, the higher-dimensional conditional estimate, or the four-dimensional viscosity regularity result has been demonstrated. The finding is Minor, concerning the overgeneral form of the written proof. If an additional properness condition in the zero-order variable were intended, it should be stated; the repair above needs no such extra assumption. The same unshifted zero-order value was directly checked in the author-hosted journal-formatted copy, printed page 510 (PDF page 22).
# Jacobi inequality: definitions, algebra, and limiting cases

Write \(H=D^2u\), \(s=\operatorname{tr}H>0\), and \(f_i=s-\lambda_i\). From \(\sigma_2(H)=1\), \[s^2=2+|H|^2,\qquad f_i>0,\qquad
 \sum_i f_i^2=(n-1)s^2-2=:\mathcal F.\] Thus the linearization is elliptic throughout the positive branch. The negative branch is handled by \(u\mapsto-u\), rather than silently included in the positive-branch argument. For \(n\ge5\) the stated dynamic hypothesis is \(\lambda_{\min}/s\ge-c_n\), where \[c_n=\frac{\sqrt{3n^2+1}-n+1}{2n}.\] For \(n=4\), the admissible-cone inequality \(\lambda_{\min}/s>-1/2\) supplies the corresponding condition automatically.

I redifferentiated \(\sigma_2=1\) and regrouped all symmetric third derivatives. Put \(b=\log s\), \(\delta=1+\varepsilon\), and \(t_i=(u_{11i},\ldots,u_{nni})\). Then \(Df\cdot t_i=0\) and \[s\bigl(\Delta_F b-\varepsilon|\nabla_F b|^2\bigr)
 =6\sum_{i<j<k}u_{ijk}^2+\sum_i
 \left[3|t_i|^2-2t_{i,i}^2-
       \left(1+\delta\frac{f_i}{s}\right)
                \left(\sum_j t_{i,j}\right)^2\right].\] This accounts for repeated and three-distinct-index terms; ignoring their multiplicities would change the result.

Let \(E\) and \(L\) be the orthogonal projections of \(e_i\) and \((1,\ldots,1)\) onto \(Df^\perp\). Direct projection gives \[|E|^2=1-\frac{f_i^2}{\mathcal F},\quad
 |L|^2=1-\frac{2(n-1)}{\mathcal F},\quad
 E\cdot L=1-\frac{(n-1)sf_i}{\mathcal F}.\] The nontrivial restriction is \(3I-2E\otimes E-\eta L\otimes L\) with \(\eta=1+\delta f_i/s\). Its trace is \(6-2|E|^2-\eta|L|^2\), and its determinant is \[d_i=9-6|E|^2-3\eta|L|^2
           +2\eta\bigl(|E|^2|L|^2-(E\cdot L)^2\bigr).\] An exact simplification, retaining favorable terms, is \[\begin{aligned}
 \frac{\mathcal F}{sf_i}d_i
 &=q_\delta(y)+\frac{6\delta}{s^2}
                   +\frac{2(n-1)\eta}{sf_i},\qquad y=\frac{f_i}{s},\\
 q_\delta(y)
 &=(n-1)(4-3\delta)
    +(6-2n+4(n-1)\delta)y-2n\delta y^2.\end{aligned}\] For \(\delta=1\), its roots are \(y_\pm=(n+1\pm\sqrt{3n^2+1})/(2n)\), and \(q_1(y)=2n(y_+-y)(y-y_-)\). The coefficient of \(\varepsilon\) is \(-3(n-1)+4(n-1)y-2ny^2>-3(n-1)\) for \(0<y<2(n-1)/n\). Therefore the paper’s choice \[\varepsilon=
 \frac{-2ny_-}{3(n-1)}
       \left(y_+-\frac{f_n}{s}\right)\ge0\] makes \(q_\delta\ge0\) for every \(i\). The trace bound and \(\delta\le3n/[2(n-1)]\) give positivity of the other invariant. Dependent \(E,L\) are covered by continuity; at a round spectrum the remaining eigenvalues can also be read directly. The case \(\varepsilon=0\) at the higher-dimensional dynamic boundary is allowed, not discarded by an implicit strict inequality.

The four-dimensional degenerating family \[(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\lambda_4)
       =(a,a,a,-a+1/(3a))\] has \(\sigma_2=1\) and \(\varepsilon=1/(18a^2+3)\to0\). Nevertheless \(f_4\lambda_4^2/s^3\to3/8\). This directly checks why the gradient term in the next argument rescues the regime where a fixed positive Jacobi constant would fail. For dimension three the separate \(\varepsilon=1/3\) calculation uses the sharp negative eigenvalue bound. The strict positive-edge inequality printed in Lemma 2.1 has equality at the round spectrum; its needed weak form suffices. This numerical notation issue is not counted as a scientific finding.
# Doubling, scaling, and the dependence of constants

The maximum-principle test on pages 10–13 combines \(2\log\rho\), \(\alpha(x\cdot Du-u)\), \(\beta|Du|^2/2\), and the logarithm of the truncated excess of \(b=\log\Delta u\) over its \(B_1\) maximum. The boundary term tends to \(-\infty\). If the excess is below the truncation threshold, the desired bound is immediate; otherwise differentiation is legitimate at the interior maximum.

For \(\lambda_{\min}/s\le-c_n/2\), the term \(f_n\lambda_n^2\ge(c_n/2)^2s^3\) controls the bad gradient terms after the first-derivative equation is substituted. For \(\lambda_{\min}/s\ge-c_n/2\), the Jacobi coefficient has a fixed positive lower bound. Splitting according to whether the coordinate in the largest-eigenvalue direction has square greater than \(1/n\) yields the two alternatives used in the paper: either the \(\alpha\) term is effective, or a transverse direction has \(f_k\ge(1-1/\sqrt2)s\) and a definite cutoff derivative. The possible equality in the dynamic hypothesis lies in the first regime and is therefore covered.

With \(\Gamma\) the stated gradient-size parameter, the choices \[\gamma=\frac1{2C},\qquad
 \alpha=\frac{\gamma^4}{\Gamma},\qquad
 \beta=\frac{\gamma^6}{\Gamma^2}\] are compatible for a sufficiently large dimensional \(C\). Indeed \(\alpha^2/\beta=\Gamma\beta/\alpha=\gamma^2\), and the final positive coefficient is proportional to \(\gamma^6(1-C\gamma-C\gamma^5)>0\). I checked these inequalities directly, including 162 exact parameter cases. They give the required exponential control of the ratio of Laplacians.

The translated-ball step is supported by the inclusions \(B_1(0)\subset B_{4/3}(y)\subset B_{5/3}(y)\subset B_2(0)\) for \(|y|<1/3\). The subsequent iteration uses \[u_k(x)=t^{2k}u\bigl(y+t^{-k}(x-y)\bigr),\qquad t=5/4.\] Its argument stays in \(B_3\) for \(x\in B_3\), and \(\left\lVert u_k\right\rVert_{C^1(B_3)}\le t^{2k}\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{C^1(B_3)}\). Hence a bound involving the square of that norm scales as \(t^{4k}\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{C^1}^2\). The page-14 line for \(C_k\) (source line 764) should be read with this power, rather than its printed \(t^{2k}\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{C^1}\). For example, \(u=M+|x|^2/(2\sqrt6)\) shows why a squared norm cannot be bounded uniformly by the printed linear norm. Since only finitely many steps depending on the target radius are used, the corrected estimate still has exactly the asserted dependence \(C(n,r,\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{C^1})\). This is a local quantitative correction, not a failed qualitative doubling theorem.

The page-11 numerical comment concerning the three-dimensional split has its comparison direction reversed. For instance \((3,3,-4/3)\) is an admissible spectrum in the first regime. The proof already handles both regimes, and no step needs that regime to be empty. This is recorded as counterevidence against escalating a numerical slip into a theorem failure.
# Alexandrov differentiability and the compactness argument
## Dependency hypotheses and a complete density argument

The proof uses two different inputs that must not be conflated. Chaudhuri–Trudinger, Theorem 2.4 [CT], gives signed Radon measures for the distributional Hessian for every \(2\le k\le n\); the stronger assumption \(k>n/2\) belongs to other conclusions of that reference. Thus its use for \(k=2,n=4\) is legitimate. The local measure argument follows by testing the dual cone with \(\mu I\) and \(\mu I-e\otimes e\), then polarizing.

The weighted gradient estimate in Trudinger–Wang, Corollary 3.4 [TW], applies to the constant-Hessian-measure equation as used here; it does not impose an extra negative-sign condition on \(u\). Its norm in (2.11), Theorem 3.2’s smooth Dirichlet problem, and the comparison/approximation interface were inspected. A ball is uniformly \((k-1)\)-convex; smooth boundary approximations and comparison give the stated uniform limit and interior gradient bound. This checks the hypotheses actually needed, without asserting a new proof of the entire Dirichlet theory.

At a point of differentiability and finite density of the Hessian measure, the mollified Taylor calculation in Lemma 4.1 is dominated by \(\left\lVert D^2u\right\rVert(B_{rt+\epsilon})/(rt+\epsilon)^n\le C\) for small radii. Its singular density tends to zero and its absolutely continuous part has a Lebesgue value. The resulting integral in \(t\) is bounded and yields the averaged second-order remainder \(o(r^2)\).

Two local presentations benefit from an explicit completion. At page 17, source line 842, the Taylor remainder centered at \(x\) should use \(Du(x)\) and \(D^2u(x)\), not the displayed values at 0 unless \(x\) has first been translated to 0. For the admissible quadratic \(u(y)=|y|^2/(2\sqrt6)\) and \(x=e_1/4\), the uncorrected remainder is \((y_1-1/4)/(4\sqrt6)\), whose mean absolute value on \(B_r(x)\) is \(4r/(15\pi\sqrt6)\); the correctly centered remainder is zero. The subsequent proof uses the centered version.

In Lemma 4.2, pages 21–22, a bad-set bound \(\varepsilon|B_r|\) by itself does not guarantee a good point within distance \(\varepsilon r\) in dimension \(n>1\). The established little-oh estimate supplies the stronger choice needed. Write \(\operatorname{Av}_B\) for the integral mean over \(B\). Fix \(0<\tau<1/2\) and take \(r\) sufficiently small that \[\operatorname{Av}_{B_r}|h|\le\frac12\tau^{n+1}r^2.\] Then \(\{|h|\ge\tau r^2\}\) has volume at most \(\tfrac12\tau^n|B_r|<|B_{\tau r}|\). Every \(y\in B_{r/2}\) therefore has a good point \(z\in B_{\tau r}(y)\). The gradient estimate (4.7), together with \(\operatorname{Av}_{B_{2r}}|h|=o(r^2)\), gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(h)\le Cr\). Consequently \(|h(y)|\le\tau r^2+C\tau r^2\). First choosing \(\tau\) small and then \(r\) small proves the desired \(\sup_{B_{r/2}}|h|=o(r^2)\), with the same hypotheses. These explicit basepoint and parameter corrections complete the argument; they are not separate formal findings or counterexamples to Alexandrov differentiability.
## Savin’s local ellipticity requirements and order of choices

At an Alexandrov point with Taylor Hessian \(H\), the upper and lower tests \(Q\pm\epsilon|x-y|^2\) imply \(\sigma_2(H)=1\) and the positive branch relation. The shifted operator used for the perturbation is \[G_H(M)=\operatorname{tr}(M+H)-\sqrt{2+|M+H|^2}.\] It is globally elliptic, since \[DG_H(M)=I-\frac{M+H}{\sqrt{2+|M+H|^2}}>0,\] and on \(|M|\le1\) it has the uniform lower bound \(1-(|H|+1)/\sqrt{2+(|H|+1)^2}>0\); its second derivatives are bounded there and \(G_H(0)=0\). Savin’s hypotheses H1, H2, H4 and Theorem 1.3 [Savin] require precisely global monotonicity and local uniform ellipticity near zero, not a global uniform ellipticity constant. This resolves a potential objection to the invocation.

Choose the spatial radius using the limit function’s Taylor error first, then choose the sequence index using uniform convergence. The perturbation theorem gives a neighborhood independent of that later index. The local Hessian bound combined with the moving-center doubling estimate contradicts the assumed blow-up. For \(n\ge5\), the original smooth sequence retains the dynamic condition; the approximation used solely to establish Alexandrov differentiability of the limit need not retain it. The authors do not assert unrestricted viscosity regularity in those higher dimensions.

For \(n=4\), the Hessian bound yields uniform ellipticity on compact subsets, allowing the indicated concavity and regularity theory to apply. The entire-solution quadratic-growth consequence uses \(u_R(x)=R^{-2}u(Rx)\); uniform local \(C^{2,\alpha}\) bounds then force oscillation of the Hessian on fixed balls to vanish as \(R\to\infty\). The general \(k\)-Hessian discussion establishes the stated differentiability/partial-regularity route, not global regularity of every admissible solution.

problems.title: Missing contact-value shift in the zero-order-dependent stability proof
problems.source_location: Pdf page: 22 Lemma: 6.1 Source lines: 1012 Source lines: 1032 Exact step line: 1030
claim: At the positive maximum of u_k-Q_epsilon, the printed proof evaluates F at zero-order value Q_epsilon instead of u_k.
analysis:
Equation reference: eq:wrong. Location and claim. Lemma 6.1, PDF page 22, author-source lines 1012–1032, especially line 1030. The lemma concerns continuous elliptic equations \(F(D^2u,Du,u,x)=0\) and uniformly convergent viscosity solutions \(u_k\). In its proof, after setting \[Q_\varepsilon=Q+\varepsilon|x-x_0|^2-\varepsilon^4,\] the maximum of \(u_k-Q_\varepsilon\) is positive and occurs at \(x_\varepsilon\). The proof then asserts \[
 0\le F(D^2Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),DQ_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),
                 Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),x_\varepsilon).\] The test function touching \(u_k\) is instead \(Q_\varepsilon+m_\varepsilon\), where \(m_\varepsilon=(u_k-Q_\varepsilon)(x_\varepsilon)>0\). Its value is \(u_k(x_\varepsilon)\), not \(Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon)\).

Complete check under the stated assumptions. In dimension \(n=4\), on \(B_1(0)\), take \[F(M,p,z,x)=(\operatorname{tr}M)^5+z,\qquad u_k=u=0,\qquad Q=0,\quad x_0=0.\] This \(F\) is smooth and elliptic in the monotonicity sense: for \(N\ge0\), \(F(M+N,p,z,x)\ge F(M,p,z,x)\), strictly if \(N\ne0\). It is not uniformly elliptic, which the lemma does not require. No monotonicity in \(z\) is stated there. The zero functions solve the equation classically and in the viscosity sense: an upper test has nonnegative Hessian at contact, and a lower test has nonpositive Hessian. Convergence is uniform and \(Q\ge u\) with equality.

Here \(x_\varepsilon=0\) and \(m_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^4\). For \(\varepsilon<1/4\) the annulus estimate in the proof holds. Taking \(\varepsilon=1/65536=1/[2(2n)^5]\) gives \[F(2\varepsilon I,0,-\varepsilon^4,0)
       =(8\varepsilon)^5-\varepsilon^4
       =-\frac{\varepsilon^4}{2}<0,\] contradicting [eq:wrong] (#eq:wrong). In fact it is negative for every \(0<\varepsilon<(2n)^{-5}\), so choosing a still smaller perturbation does not fix the step. The genuine touching test is \(\varepsilon|x|^2\); its value gives \((8\varepsilon)^5>0\), as the viscosity condition requires. Nine exact rational checks for \(2\le n\le10\) reproduce this distinction; the dimension-four wrong value is \(-1/36893488147419103232\).

Repair and counterevidence. Use \(\phi_\varepsilon=Q_\varepsilon+m_\varepsilon\) and write \[0\le F(D^2Q_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),DQ_\varepsilon(x_\varepsilon),
                    u_k(x_\varepsilon),x_\varepsilon).\] Since \(Q\ge u\), \(0<m_\varepsilon\le\left\lVert u_k-u\right\rVert_{L^\infty}+\varepsilon^4\to0\) after the indicated choice of \(k(\varepsilon)\). Also \(x_\varepsilon\to x_0\), and continuity now gives the required inequality for \(u\). The lower-test argument is analogous. Thus this is not a counterexample to the stability lemma.

The operator actually needed in the compactness argument has no \(z\) or gradient dependence. Adding \(m_\varepsilon\) therefore leaves that operator unchanged. Consequently no broken dependency from this error to Theorem 1.1, the higher-dimensional conditional estimate, or the four-dimensional viscosity regularity result has been demonstrated. The finding is Minor, concerning the overgeneral form of the written proof. If an additional properness condition in the zero-order variable were intended, it should be stated; the repair above needs no such extra assumption. The same unshifted zero-order value was directly checked in the author-hosted journal-formatted copy, printed page 510 (PDF page 22).
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: reports/0010.tex Section2

report: Abstract: This review checks the finite-entropy argument for the entropic polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa theorem and its conversion to the covering theorem in arXiv:2311.05762v2. No substantive issue was found within this inspected scope. The compactness step, conditional distributions, fibring identity, two estimates, endgame constants, and covering argument were checked. Two local sign misprints admit immediate, fully checked readings already used by the subsequent argument; they are recorded as excluded typographical observations. This is an initial review of the bound author manuscript, not a certification of the journal-final text.
Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Initial scientific review of On a conjecture of Marton
# Identity, materials, and scope

Paper M25-0011 is W. T. Gowers, B. Green, F. Manners, and T. Tao, On a conjecture of Marton, associated with DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.201.2.5 (https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2025.201.2.5). The reviewed scientific text is the 33-page author manuscript arXiv:2311.05762v2, dated 12 December 2023 on its first page [paper]. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages; these agree with printed pages 1–33. All 33 pages were read as extracted text and inspected as rendered images. Selected source-TeX passages were cross-checked; the source was not compiled.

The detailed proof review covers Theorem 1.8, Proposition 2.1, Sections 2 and 4–7, Appendices A and B, and the resulting Theorem 1.2. Definitions and motivating discussion in Sections 1 and 3 were also read. The reductions to Theorem 1.3, Corollaries 1.4–1.7, and the sketch in Remark 2.4 rely on external works that were not independently re-proved here. Historical comparisons and their numerical constants were not fully audited against those external texts. This limitation is not an adverse finding about those claims.

A pinned, later Lean repository snapshot was inspected statically [repo]; it is not identified with the manuscript’s original formalization state. No author code, Lean build, dependency download, or empirical reproduction was run. The author’s earlier corrected sign discrepancy, acknowledged in footnote 4 on page 18, is kept distinct from current observations. No new search for errata or journal-final correspondence was performed.
# Definitions and quantifiers

The main proof fixes the finite elementary abelian group \(G=\mathbb F_2^n\). Entropies use natural logarithms and the continuous convention \(0\log 0=0\). The distance is \[\mathrm d[X;Y]=\mathrm H[X'-Y']-\tfrac12\mathrm H[X']-\tfrac12\mathrm H[Y'],\] where the primed variables are independent with the prescribed marginals (page 4, (1.1)). Thus neither a given coupling of \(X,Y\) nor equality of their underlying sample spaces is an assumption. The conditional distance in (A.14), page 27, averages over product marginal weights. The single common-fibre average in Lemma A.2 is a different expression; the manuscript explicitly distinguishes it. Fibres of zero probability are omitted, so no conditional distribution at an impossible event is needed.

All minima below are over pairs of probability distributions on a fixed finite group. The product of the two closed simplices is compact, and entropy, convolution, and the functional \(\tau\) are continuous up to the boundary. The combinatorial conversion uses a nonempty set \(A\), as required to form \(U_A\); then the doubling assumption implies \(K\ge1\). This is the natural nonempty-set domain of that formulation, also explicit in the inspected Lean theorem. The empty set is not used as a purported counterexample. Point masses, \(n=0\), \(K=1\), and \(k=0\) cause no division by zero in the proof.
# Checked proof chain
## Compactness and the constants 11 and 6

For \(\eta=1/9\), write \[\tau[X_1;X_2]=\mathrm d[X_1;X_2]
       +\eta\mathrm d[X_1^0;X_1]+\eta\mathrm d[X_2^0;X_2].\] Proposition 2.1 forces a minimizer to have \(k=\mathrm d[X_1;X_2]=0\). The zero-distance conclusion of Lemma 2.2 is consistent with the equality case of entropy concavity: \(H(X-X')=H(X)\) forces the law of \(X\) to be invariant under all differences of its support. Its support is a coset of the subgroup generated by those differences, and its law is uniform there. Applying the distance-zero equalities to the two marginals gives the same subgroup. Translation invariance then gives \(U_H\).

The comparison in the proof on page 7 is with the swapped reference pair \((X_2^0,X_1^0)\). With \(d_0=\mathrm d[X_1^0;X_2^0]\), this gives \[\eta\{\mathrm d[X_1^0;U_H]+\mathrm d[X_2^0;U_H]\}
 \le(1+2\eta)d_0,\] hence the sum bound \(11d_0\). The Ruzsa triangle inequality bounds the difference of the two terms by \(d_0\), giving each term at most \(6d_0\). For completeness, that triangle inequality follows by taking independent \(X,Y,Z\), observing \(\mathrm H[X-Y\mid X-Z]\ge\mathrm H[Y]\), and then using \(\mathrm H[X-Y,Y-Z]\le\mathrm H[X-Y]+\mathrm H[Y-Z]\). This checks the needed inequality without executing a proof assistant.
## Fibring and the two estimates

For independent \(Z_1,Z_2\) and a homomorphism \(\pi\), the chain rule gives exactly the nonnegative defect in Proposition 4.1 (page 15): \[\begin{aligned}
 &\mathrm d[Z_1;Z_2]-\mathrm d[\pi Z_1;\pi Z_2]
      -\mathrm d[Z_1\mid\pi Z_1;Z_2\mid\pi Z_2]\notag\\
 &=\mathrm I[Z_1-Z_2:(\pi Z_1,\pi Z_2)\mid\pi(Z_1-Z_2)].\end{aligned}\] The independence assumptions and the coordinate change used for Corollary 4.2 were checked. Product-fibre averaging of the universal minimality inequality gives (3.15); it does not presume that two original conditioning variables are independent.
## Endgame and exact numerical margin

Let \(R=2\eta k-I_1\ge0\), and use the variables \(U,V,W,S\) of Section 7. The relation \(U+V+W=0\) uses characteristic two essentially. The checked bounds on pages 21–25 are \[\widetilde\delta\le6\eta k-\frac{1-5\eta}{1-\eta}R,\qquad
 \sum_{i=1}^2\sum_{T\in\{U,V,W\}}
  \bigl(\mathrm d[X_i^0;T\mid S]-\mathrm d[X_i^0;X_i]\bigr)
 \le(6-3\eta)k+3R.\] For the last two costs, \(W'=W+S\); at fixed \(S=s\) this is a fixed translation, so the conditional distance is unchanged. Lemma 7.2 uses the common-fibre BSG bound, then averages the six permutations of the triple. A positive-probability fibre and a permutation no larger than their averages exist. This justifies the existence step without an unwarranted simultaneous choice of unrelated fibres.

Equation reference: margin. Substitution gives \[k\le(8\eta+\eta^2)k-
 \left(\frac{1-5\eta}{1-\eta}(1+\eta/3)-\eta\right)R.\] At \(\eta=1/9\), independent exact rational calculation gives \[
 \frac8{81}k+\frac{11}{27}R\le0.\] Nonnegativity forces \(k=R=0\). This verifies the contradiction required for Proposition 2.1, including its boundary case.
## From entropy to covering

Appendix B uses \(\mathrm d[U_A;U_A]\le\log K\) and the equal-reference case of Theorem 1.8 to get \(\mathrm d[U_A;U_H]\le(11/2)\log K\). The entropy difference bound gives \(K^{-11}|A|\le|H|\le K^{11}|A|\). The largest-atom entropy bound yields a translate with \[|B|:=|A\cap(H+x_0)|\ge K^{-11/2}|A|^{1/2}|H|^{1/2}.\] A maximal disjoint collection of translates \(a+B\), \(a\in A\), has at most \(|A+B|/|B|\) members and covers \(A\) after enlargement by \(B-B\). Since \(B-B\subset H\), this gives at most \(K^{13/2}\sqrt{|A|/|H|}\) cosets. If \(|H|\le|A|\), the bound is \(K^{12}\). Otherwise a subspace \(H'\le H\) with \(|A|/2<|H'|\le|A|\) exists by the powers-of-two subgroup sizes. Refining the cover multiplies its size by less than \(2|H|/|A|\), giving at most \(2K^{12}\). No integrality or endpoint obstruction was found.
# Excluded observations and counterevidence
These observations are not substantive findings under the requested exclusion of typography alone.

On page 16, the first mutual-information expression in the proof of Corollary 4.2 conditions on \(\pi(Z_1)+\pi(Z_2)\); the preceding proposition and the next line require \(\pi(Z_1)-\pi(Z_2)\). Source TeX line 616 contains the plus sign. Replacing that sign gives exactly the stated identity by substitution; in the main characteristic-two application the two forms already coincide. No changed hypothesis or result is needed.

On page 29, (A.22) prints \(\mathrm H[A_2,B_1]\le\mathrm H[A]-\mathrm H[B]\). The correct subadditivity bound is \[\mathrm H[A_2,B_1]\le\mathrm H[A_2]+\mathrm H[B_1]=\mathrm H[A]+\mathrm H[B].\] Both the source TeX label `bsg-25` and the image confirm the minus. To test the literal printed line, take independent uniform bits \(A,B\) in \(\mathbb F_2\), \(Z=A+B\), and construct conditionally independent trials by choosing \(Z,A_1,A_2\) independent uniform bits and setting \(B_i=Z-A_i\). Each \((A_i,B_i)\) has the required original law, and the two pairs are independent conditional on \(Z\). Then \((A_2,B_1)\) is uniform on four points, so its entropy is \(2\log2\), whereas the printed right side is zero. The corrected right side is \(2\log2\).

The correction suffices in full: (A.20) gives \(2\mathrm H[A,B]-\mathrm H[Z]\) for the middle joint entropy in (A.19); the corrected (A.22) and (A.21) each give \(\mathrm H[A]+\mathrm H[B]\). Consequently \(\mathrm H[A_1-B_2]\le2\mathrm I[A:B]+\mathrm H[Z]\). Conditioning and \(\mathrm H[A_1\mid Z]=\mathrm H[B_2\mid Z]=\mathrm H[A,B]-\mathrm H[Z]\) give precisely (A.16), with its original constants. For the uniform-bit example, both sides of (A.16) are zero. The manuscript’s very next displayed bound uses this plus-sign calculation. This is decisive counterevidence against interpreting the misprint as a failed BSG lemma or a new substantive gap in the core result.
# Outcome and remaining limits

No supported Major or Minor concern is retained in the inspected core proof. The finite computations below corroborate selected inequalities; the analytic checks above carry the general reasoning. The external application reductions, historical optimization claims, journal-final correspondence, and the full Lean dependency graph remain outside this completed initial-review scope. Later repository refinements are not substituted for the bound manuscript. No author adoption or human scientific approval is claimed.
Dimension | Result
Issue judgment | No Issue Found within the inspected scope; typography excluded.
Repair verification | Two local sign readings checked analytically; no theorem repair proposed.
Adoption | Not requested; no source manuscript modified.

# Supporting checks

The reviewer-authored `independent_checks.py` was executed with Python and installed SymPy 1.13.3. Exact simplification produced the coefficients \(73/81\), \(11/27\), and \(8/81\) in the endgame. Enumeration of all 165 binary joint laws with masses in multiples of \(1/8\) found no violation of (A.16). The 729 triples of Bernoulli laws with parameters in \(\{0,1/8,\ldots,1\}\) gave maximal residuals \(0\) and \(1.11\,10^{-16}\) for (5.5) and (5.6), with a \(10^{-12}\) tolerance. # Identity, scope, and principal assessment

The reviewed work is The endoscopic fundamental lemma for unitary Friedberg–Jacquet periods, by Spencer Leslie, associated by the supplied metadata with DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.201.3.1. All page references are to physical PDF pages 1–89, agreeing with printed pages, of arXiv 1911.07907v3. They are not asserted to describe the final journal article.

All 89 pages of extracted text were read and all 89 rendered source pages were visually inspected. The principal proof chain checked is Theorem 11.1, Theorem 5.3, Proposition 5.2, Proposition 4.8, Theorem 3.5, Proposition 3.12, and Theorem 2.12. The review checks definitions, regular semisimple restrictions, quantifiers, contraction maps, normalizations, central quotients, local spherical computations, and globalization. External results remain distinguished from independently checked arguments.

Lemma 11.5, p. 83, is false under the stated assumptions. Integral invertible points and \(Z\)-regularity do not imply that central orbital support consists only of units. The lemma is used to obtain nonzero central orbital factors in Proposition 11.4, then cancelled in proving Theorem 11.1. This is a Major defect in the core derivation under the requested criterion. A finite enlargement of the bad-place set provides a natural repair; its corrected local lemma is proved below.

The rational orbit quantified over in Lemma 10.6 is too large for its spherical normalization. The fixed-lattice equivalence after (3.8) is also false. Both have limited demonstrated impact, as their respective applications use a smaller orbit and a variable intermediate lattice.
# Checks of the mathematical architecture

In Sections 1.5–2, ordinary, stable, and relative orbits are distinguished. For the split model \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&X\\Y&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the characteristic polynomial is \(\det(t^2I-XY)\). A zero eigenvalue of \(XY\) would give a repeated zero root. Thus Lemma 2.4 correctly puts the regular semisimple locus inside the invertible locus, where Lemma 2.3’s torsor argument is used. The fibre integration and centralizer identification in Lemma 2.5 respect that domain. External cohomological and convergence inputs were not independently re-proved.

The minus sign in contraction (2.1) and the later positive Gram-matrix notation in density formula (3.8) were kept distinct. The \(q\) powers of Lemma 3.2 agree with \(q_E=q^2\) and the substitutions \(Z_i\mapsto q^{-b}X_i\) and \(Z_{a+j}\mapsto q^{-a}Y_j\). For \(n=a+b\) and \(d=d_a+d_b\), \[d(n-1)-d_ab-d_ba=d_a(a-1)+d_b(b-1).\] This checks the factorization in Proposition 3.12. Its unipotent volume \(q^{2\sum(i-1)\lambda_i}\) combines with \(\langle\lambda,2\rho\rangle\) to give \(q^{d(n-1)}\), also correctly at \(d=0\).

The two Jacquet–Rallis transfers (4.3) and (4.7) were followed separately. The parabolic descent Jacobian in Proposition 4.8 is \(|\det m_1|_F^b\); combining it with the modular character gives the stated twist. Base change squares Satake variables, so the twist \(|\cdot|_F^{s/2}\) reproduces the twist over \(E\). This checks commutation directly, without relying on the explanatory support assertion on p. 39.

For Proposition 5.2, support gives vanishing for \(|q(a)|_F>1\), and the unit-norm reduction handles \(|q(a)|_F=1\). Fourier invariance of the self-dual lattice and upper-unipotent invariance for parameters in \(\mathfrak p_F^{-1}\) then give the conclusion using the standard Weil representation. The generation assertion on p. 43 is consistent: upper and lower elementary matrices with such parameters produce a diagonal uniformizer matrix, whose conjugations give elementary matrices at arbitrarily negative valuations. They generate \(\mathrm{SL}_2(F)\). Local constancy and density handle \(q(a)=0\). The cited Fourier-transfer theorem remains an external input.

The four central twists in Section 9 agree with the index-four norm subgroup in the two-dimensional centre. The factors \(4\) and \(4L(1,\eta)^2\) were traced through (9.4)–(9.5), including the idele-class volume ratio on p. 72. The restrictions to nice functions and two distinct split places are material. Lemma 11.2 uses the norm subgroup, whose even valuations explain the character period \(\pi/\log q\). Its Fourier uniqueness argument agrees with that quotient. The rank shift of Section 11.2, using \(\mathbf 1_{K_{n-1,E}}\otimes\varphi\), has the correct contraction and proves the stated dependence of Theorem 2.12 on Theorem 11.1.

The spectral expansions, smooth transfer, nonvanishing, FLO functional construction, and external global representation theory were not independently re-proved. Another scope point remains: Lemma 8.6 assumes odd residue characteristic, whereas the subsequent unramified argument states no such restriction. No counterexample in residue characteristic two was established. Independent verification of the needed normalization extension is pending; this is not counted as an additional proved defect.
# Problem 1: central support lemma
## Location and claim

Severity: Major. Lemma 11.5, p. 83, after the choice of \(S\) in Proposition 11.4 on p. 82, asserts \[\operatorname{Orb}(\mathbf 1_{K'_v},bz)\ne0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z\in Z_{G'}(\mathcal O_v). \tag{P1}\] Outside \(S\), the stated assumptions are \(a\in K_v\) and \(b\in K'_v\). The points are \(Z\)-regular semisimple: the two specified invariants are nonzero, not necessarily units. The supplied TeX has the choice and proof at lines 3304–3332, with the claim at 3315–3320.
## A counterexample in the original domain

Let \[F=\mathbb Q_3,\quad E=F(s),\quad s^2=2,\quad \bar s=-s,\quad
 a=1+s,\quad c=2as=4+2s.\] Since \(t^2-2\) is irreducible modulo 3 with unit discriminant, \(E/F\) is unramified quadratic. We have \(\operatorname{Nm}(a)=-1\) and \(\operatorname{Nm}(c)=8\); thus \(a,c,s,2\) are units. Write \(M^*=\bar M^t\) and set \[B=\begin{pmatrix}1&c\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 B'=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&c\end{pmatrix},\quad D=\operatorname{diag}(1/3,3).\] Both \(B,B'\in\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathcal O_E)\), and \[BB^*=\begin{pmatrix}9&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}=:T,\qquad
 B'B'^*=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&9\end{pmatrix}=DTD. \tag{1}\] Their determinants are \(-c,c\); \(\det T=8\). First use the Hermitian model \((x,y)=(1,I_2)\). Then \(b=(1,B)\in K'\) matches \(\gamma=(1,T)\in K\). Both off-diagonal coordinates of \(T\) are 1, so their nonzero product gives a closed orbit of maximal dimension under the rank-one Jacquet–Rallis action. Thus it is regular semisimple. Also \(\operatorname{Tr}(A)=9\ne0\) and \(d=1\ne0\), giving \(Z\)-regularity. All stated local integrality conditions hold.

Take \[z=(9,3I_2),\qquad h_1=9\in H'(F),\qquad u=(DB)^{-1}B'.\] Equation (1) implies \(uu^*=I_2\). With \(h_2=(1,u)\in U(1)\times U(I_2)\) the embedding of Section 6 gives \[h_1^{-1}bzh_2=(1,B')\in K'. \tag{2}\] The nonnegative integrand of \(\operatorname{Orb}(\mathbf 1_{K'},bz)\) is 1 on a nonempty open neighborhood of \((h_1,h_2)\), of positive Haar measure. Regular semisimplicity gives convergence, hence \[\operatorname{Orb}(\mathbf 1_{K'},bz)>0,\qquad z\notin Z_{G'}(\mathcal O_F), \tag{3}\] contradicting (P1).

To use exactly the Part 2 form, put \(w_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(\xi=s\), and \(y_0=sw_2\). Set \[P=\begin{pmatrix}a&1\\-a/2&1/2\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q=\operatorname{diag}(s,1)P.\] Then \(PP^*=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(QQ^*=y_0\), \(\det P=a\), and \(\det Q=sa\). In particular \(Q\in\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathcal O_E)\). Let \(B_0=BQ^{-1}\), \(B'_0=B'Q^{-1}\), and \(u_0=QuQ^{-1}\). We have \[B_0y_0B_0^*=T,\quad u_0y_0u_0^*=y_0,\quad
 \operatorname{diag}(1/9,1)B_0(3I_2)u_0=B'_0.\] Moreover \(\det B_0=-2\) and \(\det B'_0=2\). Thus no nonintegral change of compact subgroup is hidden in the example. These matrices are algebraic over \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\).

For the trivial unramified central character the nonunit central coset of \(z\) contributes positively. The next displayed formula in Lemma 11.5, which restricts the central integral to units, omits this contribution. No numerical integration is needed.
## Diagnosis, counterevidence, and impact

The proof uses a nonzero integral invariant as if it were a unit. Also (7.8) gives the true scalings: \(\operatorname{Tr}(A)\) scales by \(\operatorname{Nm}(z_2/z_1)\) and \(d\) by \(\operatorname{Nm}(z_2)\). The linear scalings on p. 83 do not describe that action.

Counterevidence limiting the conclusion is the freedom to enlarge a finite set of bad places. The example has the nonunit \(\operatorname{Tr}(A)=9\) at precisely a place that such an enlargement can exclude. It does not refute Proposition 11.4 or the main theorem. Nevertheless the stated lemma is false and supplies the central nonvanishing/equality used in Proposition 11.4. The final paragraph on p. 85 cancels the other local factors to obtain (11.2), leading through Theorems 11.1, 5.3, and 3.5 to 2.12. This is a core derivation defect even though repair is possible.
## A verified local repair

Enlarge \(S\) to contain every place where \(\operatorname{Tr}(A(b))\) or \(d(b)\) is not a unit, and any bad places for forms and unimodular lattices. This is finite because the invariants are fixed nonzero global algebraic numbers.

Assume locally that \(b\in K'\), both these invariants are units, and the forms are integral unimodular. Put \(r=v_E(z_1)\), \(t=v_E(z_2)\). If the orbit of \(bz\) meets \(K'\), invariant integrality gives \(t-r\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\). The contracted determinant must be a unit; its central scaling is \(\operatorname{Nm}(z_2)^{n+1}\operatorname{Nm}(z_1)^{-n}\). Therefore \[(n+1)t-nr=0.\] For \(n\ge1\), \(0=(n+1)t-nr\ge t\ge0\), so \(r=t=0\). Conversely unit central elements preserve \(K'\), and \(b\in K'\) gives a positive orbital integral. This proves the corrected equivalence. An unramified character is trivial on unit central elements, so the stipulated unit-volume normalization also gives the corrected central integral equality.
This proves the local repair and shows why the finite global adjustment is available. It does not certify every remaining analytic step of a revised proof or assert author adoption.
# Problem 2: the orbit in the spherical normalization
## Location and claim

Severity: Minor. Lemma 10.6, p. 76, quantifies over \((x,y)\in G'(F)*(w_n,w_{n+1})\), with a fixed spherical test function, and asserts \[J^{x,y,\natural}_{\operatorname{BC}(\pi)}(f')=I^\natural_\pi(\operatorname{BC}(f')). \tag{P2}\] Its proof invokes Lemma 8.6, p. 61, whose normalization concerns the integral orbit \(K'*(w_n,w_{n+1})\) and odd residue characteristic. Relevant source TeX is at lines 3056–3067, with diagonal equivariance in Section 8.3 and the relative character in Definition 8.10.
## Counterexample and calculation

Use the same unramified extension of \(\mathbb Q_3\), an unramified additive character, and \(n=1\). Let \(\chi\) be the unramified unitary character with \(\chi(3)=i\). Its base change \(\Pi_1=\chi\circ\operatorname{Nm}\) satisfies \(\Pi_1(3)=\chi(9)=-1\). Choose an irreducible tempered unramified generic \(\pi_2\) of \(\operatorname{GL}_2(F)\), for example normalized induction of \(1\) and the unramified quadratic character. Their ratio is not \(|\cdot|^{\pm1}\), so this principal series is irreducible; its base change is also generic. Set \(\pi=\chi\boxtimes\pi_2\) and \(f'=\mathbf 1_{K'}\). For these tempered parameters the normalizing local factors are finite and nonzero.

## Impact, counterevidence, and repair

Restrict Lemma 10.6 to \(K'*(w_n,w_{n+1})\). Diagonal equivariance and \(K'\)-invariance of the spherical vector preserve the FLO value at the integral base point. This proves the orbit portion of the corrected assertion using the manuscript’s normalization theorem in odd residue characteristic.

The application on p. 85 uses the fixed base pair \((w_n,w_{n+1})\), not the false extension to every rationally equivalent form. This directly limits the demonstrated impact. Corollary 10.8 on p. 78 also invokes the overbroad computation and unit test functions, so its proof requires a scope check. The counterexample does not by itself disprove its comparison constant after test functions have been correctly transported. No such stronger conclusion is asserted. The residue-characteristic-two normalization remains a separate unchecked input.
# Problem 3: fixed and variable intermediate lattices
## Location and claim

Severity: Minor. The paragraph after (3.8), p. 28, asserts that integrality of \(T=xx^\tau\) is equivalent to \[L=x^\tau\Lambda\ \subset\ \Lambda\ \subset\
 L^\vee=x^{-1}\Lambda. \tag{P3}\] This substitutes a fixed lattice for the arbitrary intermediate self-dual lattice in the following argument. The claim occurs in the supplied Section 3.3 TeX paragraph describing the normalized local representation density.
## A regular counterexample

Because \(y,y^*\) preserve \(\Lambda\), \[L=x^*\Lambda=h^{-1}\Lambda=L^\vee.\] But \(h^{-1}e_1=(5/3,-4/(3a))^t\) is not integral, so \(L\not\subset\Lambda\). Likewise \(he_1\) is not integral, giving \(\Lambda\not\subset L\). Both containments in (P3) fail. Nevertheless \(xh^{-1}=y\in\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathcal O_E)\), so the density integral in (3.8) is positive. The matrix identities were checked exactly.
## Correct statement and limited effect

Applying \(x^{-1}\) to \(xx^*\Lambda\subset\Lambda\) proves \[T\text{ integral}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\subset L^\vee.\] For a specified \(u\in U(I_2)\) the stronger condition is \[xu\in\operatorname{End}(\Lambda)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\subset u\Lambda\subset L^\vee.\] The right-hand inclusion is \(xu\Lambda\subset\Lambda\), and duality gives the other. In the example the intermediate lattice may be \(L\) itself.

The next paragraph on p. 28 already uses \(L'=u\Lambda\) and gives the correct bijection. Remark 3.9, p. 29, says that the density interpretation is not used in the paper. The subsequent integral/Hecke calculation does not require the false fixed-lattice equivalence. These are direct counterevidence to a main-theorem failure. The corrected equivalences repair the explanation without refuting the density identity.
