report: Abstract: This report concerns Bogdan Zavyalov’s author manuscript arXiv:2111.01830v3, not an independently matched journal version. All 101 source PDF pages were read and visually inspected. The principal finding is an incompatible normalization in the two local definitions used to glue Faltings’ trace: the generic-fiber diagram introduces an extra factor \((1-\zeta_p)^{-d}\). A smooth one-dimensional formal torus verifies the contradiction under all the stated hypotheses. This is a Major defect in the printed core construction, with a verified local correction; it does not refute mod-\(p\) Poincaré duality. A second, Minor finding concerns a false multiplication isomorphism for semistable character spaces. Scope and shift clarifications are recorded separately. External foundational results were not independently reproved in full.

Title: Scientific initial review of
Mod-\(p\) Poincaré duality in \(p\)-adic analytic geometry
# Identity, version, and outcome

The paper is Mod-\(p\) Poincaré Duality in \(p\)-adic analytic geometry by Bogdan Zavyalov, assigned identifier M25-0013 and journal DOI https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2025.201.3.2. The reviewed object is the 101-page author manuscript https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.01830v3, dated 21 February 2024, with its matching supplied `main.tex` and `main.bbl`. Page numbers below are the PDF’s one-based pages, which agree with its printed page numbers. TeX line numbers are one-based in the supplied 4,666-line `main.tex`.
The source PDF has SHA-256
The TeX source has SHA-256

These values were independently recomputed locally and matched the acquired manifest. No equality with the journal Version of Record has been established. Every finding in this report is therefore version-bound to the supplied v3.

Assessment 1.  One Major and one Minor mathematical concern are supported. Problem 1 invalidates the simultaneous compatibility conditions in Theorem 3.5.2 as literally defined earlier. The corrected generic-fiber normalization resolves this particular obstruction. Problem 2 refutes a local algebraic assertion; the manuscript’s later nonunit argument does not rely on that assertion in its false generality. Neither problem supplies a counterexample to the principal cohomological duality theorem. Independent acceptance and all author adoption decisions remain pending.
# Definitions, hypotheses, and coverage

The main theorem concerns a smooth proper rigid-analytic \(K\)-space of pure dimension \(d\), for a complete rank-one valued mixed-characteristic \((0,p)\) field \(K\). Write \(C\) for its completed algebraic closure. The geometric pairing has the form \[H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_C,\mathbf F_p)\otimes_{\mathbf F_p}
H^{2d-i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_C,\mathbf F_p(d))
 \longrightarrow H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_C,\mathbf F_p(d))
 \xrightarrow{t_X}\mathbf F_p.\] It is asserted to be perfect and Galois-equivariant. Connectedness is used in constructing the top-degree identification, then removed by taking the finite disjoint union of connected components. The pure-dimension hypothesis is retained throughout.

For local trace constructions, a nice formal scheme means a separated admissible formal \(\mathcal O_C\)-scheme with smooth pure-dimensional generic fiber and reduced special fiber (Definition 3.5.1). The manuscript’s admissible formal schemes are qcqs. The almost category is relative to the maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m_C\); a module killed by one nonzero element of \(\mathfrak m_C\) need not be almost zero. The distinction matters in both counterexamples below.

The following reading and verification were actually performed. The complete extracted text, 13,068 lines, was read to its end, with truncated tool output re-read where needed. The 101 original PDF page images were individually viewed. The whole TeX file was scanned statically for relevant labels, expressions, and execution directives; selected critical passages were additionally read verbatim. This is not a claim that every TeX line was separately human-style read in addition to the complete PDF.

- Sections 1–2, pp. 2–29: theorem hypotheses; twists and almost conventions; compactification and dualizing-complex dependencies; bottom cohomology and flatness; reflexivity; the Hartogs intersection construction; formal and generic-fiber traces; reduced formal models.

- Section 3, pp. 30–47: removal of \(p^\infty\)-torsion, exterior/cup products including \(p=2\); the BMS map; Fontaine’s twist comparison; smooth and generic definitions of \(\Psi\); torus/Kummer normalization; gluing and functoriality of Faltings’ trace.

- Section 4, pp. 48–74: standard polystable models and their perfectoid towers; character decompositions; Koszul cohomology and annihilators; the algebraic semistable trace; derived duality of character-class modules; almost passage from sums to products; rig-isomorphism and finite-group descent.

- Section 5, pp. 74–83: model independence; global almost duality; primitive comparison and ordinary mod-\(p\) detection; Berkovich trace compatibility; local systems; derived mod-\(p^n\), integral and rational coefficient extensions, with the shift clarification below.

- Appendices A–D, pp. 84–99: the adic/Berkovich passage and trace adjunctions; algebraization and reduced fibers; exact generic-fiber functors; proper base change in the stated coherent range; finite étale pro-étale traces and the explicit Cartan–Leray comparison. The bibliography on pp. 99–101 was also read and visually checked.

No independent complete proof of the external almost-coherent formalism, altered local uniformization, BMS comparison, primitive comparison, or Huber/Berkovich foundations is claimed. These are substantial dependencies, not automatically verified merely because the manuscript cites them. No separate computational implementation or supplement was identified in the supplied bounded acquisition record; this does not prove that none exists.
# Problem 1: incompatible normalization of the trace (Major)
## Exact source claim and dependency

Theorem–Definition 3.4.13, p. 43, diagram (3.7), defines the generic-fiber map \((\Psi'^n_{\mathfrak X})_C\). Both left corners of the diagram are \[E_C:=\left(\widetilde{R^n\nu_*\widehat{\mathcal O}_X^+}\right)_C .\] The upward left arrow is explicitly multiplication by \((1-\zeta_p)^n\), while the bottom horizontal arrow is \((\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C^{-1}\). This is also explicit in `main.tex`, line 2027, within lines 2023–2035. Remark 3.4.15, p. 44, nevertheless identifies the resulting map with the inverse of Scholze’s comparison. Theorem 3.5.2, p. 44 (TeX lines 2060–2085), then requires a trace whose restriction to the smooth formal locus is the map of Definition 3.3.5, and whose generic fiber is the map of Definition 3.4.14.
The suspect step is the last sentence of the proof of Theorem 3.5.2: the two prescribed maps are said to coincide on the overlap. They do not coincide with diagram (3.7) as printed.
## Exact scalar calculation

Equation reference: eq:bad-normalization. Put \(q=1-\zeta_p\) and \[j=\operatorname{id}\otimes(\operatorname{dlog}^{\vee})^{\otimes n}.\] Theorem 3.4.12, pp. 42–43, gives, under its stated canonical identifications, \[(\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C=\operatorname{Sch}_X^n\circ j.\] Thus diagram (3.7) says \[(\Psi'^n_{\mathfrak X})_C\circ(q^n\operatorname{id})
       =j\circ(\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C^{-1}
       =(\operatorname{Sch}_X^n)^{-1}.\] Consequently its actual definition is \[
(\Psi'^n_{\mathfrak X})_C=q^{-n}(\operatorname{Sch}_X^n)^{-1}.\] All these are equalities of maps over \(C\); there is no integrality ambiguity in cancelling \(q^n\).

Equation reference: eq:good-normalization. By contrast, Theorem–Definition 3.3.4, pp. 36–37, uses the submodule \((\zeta_p-1)^nE\) at the lower left and its inclusion into \(E\). Its proof gives the explicit formula \[\Psi'^n_{\mathrm{sm}}(x)
 =\frac{j\big((\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})^{-1}((\zeta_p-1)^nx)\big)}
              {(\zeta_p-1)^n}.\] After inverting \(p\), linearity cancels the two factors, so \[
(\Psi'^n_{\mathrm{sm}})_C
   =j(\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C^{-1}=(\operatorname{Sch}_X^n)^{-1}.\] The sign difference between \(\zeta_p-1\) and \(1-\zeta_p\) cannot cure the discrepancy: the generic diagram adds a nonunit factor, not merely a sign.
## Counterexample with every original hypothesis

Take \(p=2\), \(C=\widehat{\overline{\mathbf Q}_2}\), and \[\mathfrak X=\operatorname{Spf}\mathcal O_C\langle T,T^{-1}\rangle,\qquad d=n=1.\] This is affine, hence separated and qcqs. It is an admissible smooth formal \(\mathcal O_C\)-scheme, flat and topologically of finite type. Its generic fiber is the smooth one-dimensional analytic torus and its special fiber is the reduced scheme \(\operatorname{Spec}k[T,T^{-1}]\). It is therefore nice. The formal smooth locus is all of \(\mathfrak X\). The prime \(2\) is allowed by the manuscript; no odd-prime hypothesis occurs in the cited constructions. Here \(\zeta_2=-1\), so \(q=2\).

There is an additional integrality obstruction: \(\omega/2\) does not belong to the free \(\mathcal O_C\langle T,T^{-1}\rangle\)-lattice generated by \(\omega\). Even an almost interpretation cannot identify this lattice with its \(1/2\)-rescaling. For example, an element \(a\in C\) with \(a^2=2\) lies in \(\mathfrak m_C\), but \(a/2\notin\mathcal O_C\). Thus \((\tfrac12\mathcal O_C)/\mathcal O_C\) is not annihilated by all of \(\mathfrak m_C\). No appeal to almostification repairs the printed equality.
## Counterevidence and verified correction

The surrounding text strongly indicates the intended normalization: Remark 3.4.15 explicitly says \((\operatorname{Sch}_X^n)^{-1}\), the smooth formula already gives that map, and Lemma 3.5.4 uses that same inverse. These are evidence for a local correction rather than for failure of the underlying duality theorem.

Replace the upward left arrow in diagram (3.7) by the identity, leaving the two copies of \(E_C\) and the bottom map unchanged. Then the defining relation is precisely \[(\Psi'^n_{\mathfrak X})_C=j(\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C^{-1}
              =(\operatorname{Sch}_X^n)^{-1}.\] On the overlap with the smooth locus this equals [eq:good-normalization] (#eq:good-normalization). The Hartogs intersection property of Theorem 2.5.5 therefore applies exactly as the proof of Theorem 3.5.2 requires: the maps to the smooth-locus sheaf and the generic-fiber sheaf agree in their common target, and hence factor through their intersection. The uniqueness argument is unaffected. Alternatively, retain the upward multiplication by \(q^n\) and replace the bottom map by \((\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C^{-1}\circ(q^n\operatorname{id})\); this gives the same corrected map.

This verification restores the specific gluing step, its smooth normalization, and the claimed generic-fiber identity. It is not a substitute for independently verifying every later external theorem. Merely relabelling the upper map, or asserting that both vertical arrows are isomorphisms over \(C\), does not restore their compatibility with the already fixed integral smooth map.
## Impact

The dependency is direct: Theorem 3.5.2 constructs the trace used in Definitions 3.5.3 and 3.5.5; the local duality theorems in Section 4 use that trace; Section 5 globalizes the resulting pairing. As printed, there is no trace with the two simultaneous restrictions, already on the smooth torus above. This is an invalid derivation tied to the main construction, hence Major under standard 0.7.1 even though the scalar repair is local. No failure of the principal mod-\(p\) pairing, after the correction, has been demonstrated. No journal-version or author-adoption claim is made.
# Problem 2: multiplication of character spaces (Minor)
## Source assertion and exact example

Equation reference: eq:false-product. On p. 53 after (4.6), and in Lemma 4.2.15 on p. 54, the manuscript says that multiplication induces isomorphisms \[
V_\chi\otimes_{\mathcal O_C}V_{\chi'}\xrightarrow{\sim}V_{\chi+\chi'}\] for all characters, including rational characters at each finite tower level \(m\). These assertions occur in TeX lines 2470–2472 and 2492–2500.

Use the same \(C\) and \(p=2\) as above, and choose the permitted standard polystable model \[R^+=\mathcal O_C\langle t_0,t_1\rangle/(t_0t_1-2).\] In the notation of the paper, \(l=1\), \(n_1=1\), \(d=1\), \(\varpi_1=2\), and take \(m=0\). The parameter \(\varpi_1\) is nonzero, as required; it is not required to be a unit. The normal form with basis \(1,t_0^r,t_1^s\), \(r,s\geq1\), shows \(\mathcal O_C\)-torsion-freeness and hence flatness. The generic fiber is smooth since \(t_0t_1=2\) makes the two partial derivatives \(t_1,t_0\) never simultaneously zero. The special fiber \(k[t_0,t_1]/(t_0t_1)\) is reduced. Thus this lies in the very semistable class under discussion.

The torus is \(T=\{(u,u^{-1})\}\). For the character \(\chi(u,u^{-1})=u\), the paper’s own normalized-monomial definition gives \[V_\chi=\mathcal O_Ct_0,\quad V_{-\chi}=\mathcal O_Ct_1,\quad V_0=\mathcal O_C.\] Multiplication sends \(t_0\otimes t_1\) to \(2\). Its image is \(2\mathcal O_C\), and its cokernel is \(\mathcal O_C/2\), which is nonzero. It is not even almost zero: an element of valuation strictly between \(0\) and \(v(2)\) does not kill the class of \(1\). This verifies failure of [eq:false-product] (#eq:false-product) under all original hypotheses, already at \(m=0\).
## Correct general formula

Equation reference: eq:correct-product. Write the normalized exponent vectors of the two characters as \(a=(a_{ij})\) and \(b=(b_{ij})\), with nonnegative entries and \(\min_j a_{ij}=\min_j b_{ij}=0\) in every block \(i\). Put \(c_i=\min_j(a_{ij}+b_{ij})\). The defining relations give \[
t^a t^b=\left(\prod_i\varpi_i^{c_i}\right)t^{\,a+b-c},\] where \(c_i\) is subtracted from every exponent in block \(i\). For rational exponents, use the compatible roots fixed in the tower. The rightmost monomial is the normalized generator for \(\chi+\chi'\).

Thus multiplication between these free rank-one \(\mathcal O_C\)-modules is injective and has image the principal ideal \(\prod_i\varpi_i^{c_i}\) times the target generator. It is an isomorphism precisely when that scalar is a unit. In particular, it is an isomorphism if all relevant parameters are units, or after inverting \(p\). Formula [eq:correct-product] (#eq:correct-product), rather than [eq:false-product] (#eq:false-product) in full generality, is a verified replacement. The reviewer-owned symbolic script additionally checked 49 normalized integer-exponent pairs in the two-variable model. That finite check illustrates, but is not the proof of, the general monomial identity.
## Counterevidence, downstream use, and severity

Warning 4.2.22, p. 55, correctly says that the character-class modules \(R^+_{\bar\chi}\) need not be free or even flat over \(R^+\). These are different objects from the individual \(\mathcal O_C\)-lines \(V_\chi\). For example, at \(m=0\) the class module is \(R^+\) itself; its ordinary self-duality is not contradicted by \(V_\chi V_{-\chi}=2\mathcal O_C\).

Proposition 4.3.6, pp. 61–62, is also important counterevidence. Its Case 1 uses \(V_\chi V_{-\chi}\simeq\mathcal O_C\) only when \(\varpi\) is a unit, where [eq:correct-product] (#eq:correct-product) verifies that assertion. Its Case 2 uses reduction modulo a suitably small pseudouniformizer and Theorem 4.3.2, rather than the false multiplication isomorphism for individual nonunit weight lines. The additive decompositions remain valid. The inspected proof therefore does not establish a core dependency on the false general statement. Replace the multiplication assertion by [eq:correct-product] (#eq:correct-product), retaining the unit case. The supported severity is Minor. No failure of derived duality for \(R^+_{\bar\chi}\) has been proved.
# Scope clarifications and rejected concerns
The following checks are retained for a faithful audit but are not counted as additional severity-bearing findings.
## Reduced special fiber in Theorem 4.4.24

Theorem 4.4.24, p. 74, omits reduced special fiber from its displayed hypotheses. Read literally, this is broader than the definition of Faltings’ pairing in Definition 4.1.1 and the nice-model restriction in Definitions 3.5.1–3.5.5. The opening of Section 4.4, p. 66, explicitly retains reduced special fiber, and Remark 3.5.6, p. 45, explains that the earlier more general construction was removed.

The omission is not a consequence of smooth generic fiber. For example, \[A=\mathcal O_C\langle T,S\rangle/(S^2-2T)\] is finite free of rank two over \(\mathcal O_C\langle T\rangle\), hence \(\mathcal O_C\)-flat, topologically of finite type and admissible. Its generic fiber is smooth of pure dimension one since the derivative with respect to \(T\) is the invertible scalar \(-2\) over \(C\). Its special fiber is \(k[T,S]/(S^2)\), which is not reduced. For this model the cited nice-model trace has not been defined in v3.

The precise supported reading is to retain the reduced-special-fiber hypothesis in Theorem 4.4.24 and its application of the local uniformization statement. This matches Theorem 4.1.2 and the nice formal models actually used in Section 5. No counterexample to a separately extended trace on nonnice models is asserted. Because the section explicitly supplies the missing scope and the global application stays within it, this is recorded as a scope clarification, not as another demonstrated core failure.
## Cohomological shifts in Section 5.5

The derived pairings in Theorems 5.5.2, 5.5.4, and 5.5.6, pp. 81–83, print target \(\Lambda\) without the required shift \([-2d]\), for \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/p^n\mathbf Z,\mathbf Z_p,\mathbf Q_p\). The duality maps in the proof of Theorem 5.5.2 have the same omission (TeX lines 3771–3801, 3814–3819, and 3832–3839). The trace is actually defined on \(H^{2d}(-,\Lambda(d))\). The correctly typed derived statement is

The literal unshifted formula is incompatible even with the paper’s Theorem 5.4.2: for nonempty geometrically connected \(X\), \(d>0\), that theorem gives \(H^{2d}(X_C,\mathbf F_p(d))\ne0\). The unshifted dual has nonzero cohomology in degree \(-2d\), whereas \(\mathbf R\Gamma(X_C,\mathbf F_p)\) has none in negative degrees. For a projective line, the degree pattern is \(0,2\) on the left and \(-2,0\) for the unshifted dual. The corrected shift restores \(0,2\). This is a degree check, not a numerical experiment.

The correct shift is explicit in the preceding almost-duality formula (5.1), and the ordinary \(\mathbf Q_p\)-pairing on p. 83 correctly pairs degrees \(i\) and \(2d-i\). Inserting the shift throughout makes the finite-level base-change square and the derived Nakayama argument compatible with Theorem 5.4.4; the integral limit and rational scalar-extension arguments preserve the shift. This is treated as a systematic notation clarification under the task’s exclusion of typographical errors alone, not as a separate claim that the intended \(p\)-adic duality theorem fails. For integral coefficients the valid assertion remains derived; one must not infer perfect pairings of torsion-containing individual \(\mathbf Z_p\)-cohomology groups without further qualifications.
## Checks that did not yield additional findings

The nonunit case of Proposition 4.3.6 can choose the auxiliary pseudouniformizer small enough in valuation to divide both \(p\) and the relevant root \(\varpi^{1/p^m}\). The available value group over \(C\) allows this. The appearance of \(n\) instead of \(m\) in that bound does not create a demonstrated existence obstruction.

In Lemma 2.5.3 and the proof of Lemma 2.5.4, the needed injectivity of restriction to a dense formal open can be justified directly using the normalization of a nonzero function supplied by Lemma B.6. If a nonzero function vanished on that open, scale it into \(A\) with nonzero reduction; its reduction would vanish on a dense open of the reduced special fiber, a contradiction. This avoids overreading connectedness as irreducibility. Similarly, the Hartogs argument only needs the canonical restriction to sections on the reduced open; it does not need an unrestricted commutation of nonaffine global sections with reduction.

For \(p=2\), the alternating exterior-power construction in Section 3 uses the torsion-free quotient. Graded commutativity gives \(2(x\cup x)=0\), and removal of \(2^\infty\)-torsion gives \(x\cup x=0\). Thus characteristic two does not invalidate the smooth comparison used in Problem 1.

For a character Koszul complex, an annihilator can be tracked at the chain level. If \(d=a\,e_1\wedge+b\,e_2\wedge\), contraction \(h\) with \(e_1\) satisfies \(dh+hd=a\operatorname{id}\). This identity survives reduction modulo \(p\). It supports the needed annihilation without the invalid general inference that an annihilator of cohomology always survives arbitrary derived base change.

The passage from completed direct sums to products in Section 4 uses the fact that for each fixed annihilator tolerance only finitely many character denominators remain exceptional. For each \(a\in\mathfrak m_C\), choose a sufficiently small valuation bound; the tail is killed by \(a\), and the finite exceptional part is already in the sum. The role of the almost category is essential.

Finite-group descent in Section 4.4 uses homotopy invariants and coinvariants, not division by \(|G|\). On a split torsor the regular module has vanishing higher group cohomology, the augmentation identifies coinvariants with the base module, and the norm vector identifies the base module with invariants. These statements remain valid when \(p\mid |G|\). They do not assert that the composite of restriction and trace on the base is invertible in that case.

For local systems in Theorem 5.4.5, the cover associated to a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup has degree prime to \(p\), and the restricted finite \(p\)-group representation over \(\mathbf F_p\) has a filtration with trivial quotients. The split trace and exact-sequence argument therefore have the required different roles. Finiteness of the coefficient groups in Lemma 5.5.1 gives the Mittag–Leffler condition; no surjectivity of every transition map is required.
# Overall impact and disposition

The central issue is the normalization needed to compare the integral smooth trace with the generic-fiber trace. Retaining the printed scalar breaks an actual existence assertion, not merely an explanation of it. Removing it is supported by the manuscript’s comparison theorem and its explicit smooth formula. The resulting overlap equality restores the specified use of the Hartogs theorem. This is the exact extent of the repair verification here.

The local multiplication correction preserves the weight decomposition and the unit-parameter calculation. The nonunit derived-duality proof takes a separate route, so the counterexample does not disprove that result. The two additional clarifications state the hypotheses and cohomological degrees needed for the later arguments.
Item | Judgment | Verified repair or disposition | Remaining work
Problem 1 | Major; trace gluing fails literally | Identity left arrow in (3.7) restores overlap equality | Independent acceptance; check any journal counterpart

Problem 2 | Minor; weight multiplication not always an isomorphism | Formula [eq:correct-product] (#eq:correct-product) with the parameter factor; unit case retained | Check any revised text; no adoption claimed
Scope | Clarification only | Retain reduced special fiber in local duality | No general nonnice extension verified
Shifts | Clarification only | Use \(\Lambda[-2d]\) in derived pairings | Apply consistently if preparing a revision
Delivery | Recoverable TeX only | Evidence and structured ledgers saved | Genuine compile and all report-page QA

No later version or erratum was independently compared to these exact passages during this review. The acquisition’s identification of the author manuscript is not evidence that either concern survives in the journal text. No experiments, author execution, or author contact are needed to verify the two analytic counterexamples; none was performed.
# Evidence and actual computation

The source PDF was extracted with the already installed Poppler `pdftotext.exe`, and all 101 pages were rendered with `pdftoppm.exe` to PNGs of maximum dimension 1600. The actual commands, source hashes, page counts, return codes and output paths are recorded in `verification/0013/evidence/extraction_log.json` and `verification/0013/evidence/render_1_101.json`. problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 36 Pdf pages: 37 Pdf pages: 42 Pdf pages: 43 Pdf pages: 44 Pdf pages: 45 Source: Theorem-Definition 3.4.13 (3.7), Remark 3.4.15, Theorem 3.5.2; compare Theorem-Definition 3.3.4 Tex lines: 2027
claim:
The main theorem concerns a smooth proper rigid-analytic \(K\)-space of pure dimension \(d\), for a complete rank-one valued mixed-characteristic \((0,p)\) field \(K\). Write \(C\) for its completed algebraic closure. The geometric pairing has the form \[H^i_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_C,\mathbf F_p)\otimes_{\mathbf F_p}
H^{2d-i}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_C,\mathbf F_p(d))
 \longrightarrow H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_C,\mathbf F_p(d))
 \xrightarrow{t_X}\mathbf F_p.\] It is asserted to be perfect and Galois-equivariant. Connectedness is used in constructing the top-degree identification, then removed by taking the finite disjoint union of connected components. The pure-dimension hypothesis is retained throughout.

For local trace constructions, a nice formal scheme means a separated admissible formal \(\mathcal O_C\)-scheme with smooth pure-dimensional generic fiber and reduced special fiber (Definition 3.5.1). The manuscript’s admissible formal schemes are qcqs. The almost category is relative to the maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m_C\); a module killed by one nonzero element of \(\mathfrak m_C\) need not be almost zero. The distinction matters in both counterexamples below.

- Section 3, pp. 30–47: removal of \(p^\infty\)-torsion, exterior/cup products including \(p=2\); the BMS map; Fontaine’s twist comparison; smooth and generic definitions of \(\Psi\); torus/Kummer normalization; gluing and functoriality of Faltings’ trace.

- Section 5, pp. 74–83: model independence; global almost duality; primitive comparison and ordinary mod-\(p\) detection; Berkovich trace compatibility; local systems; derived mod-\(p^n\), integral and rational coefficient extensions, with the shift clarification below.
Generic and smooth trace definitions coincide on the overlap.
analysis: Theorem–Definition 3.4.13, p. 43, diagram (3.7), defines the generic-fiber map \((\Psi'^n_{\mathfrak X})_C\). Both left corners of the diagram are \[E_C:=\left(\widetilde{R^n\nu_*\widehat{\mathcal O}_X^+}\right)_C .\] The upward left arrow is explicitly multiplication by \((1-\zeta_p)^n\), while the bottom horizontal arrow is \((\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C^{-1}\). This is also explicit in `main.tex`, line 2027, within lines 2023–2035. Remark 3.4.15, p. 44, nevertheless identifies the resulting map with the inverse of Scholze’s comparison. Theorem 3.5.2, p. 44 (TeX lines 2060–2085), then requires a trace whose restriction to the smooth formal locus is the map of Definition 3.3.5, and whose generic fiber is the map of Definition 3.4.14.
The suspect step is the last sentence of the proof of Theorem 3.5.2: the two prescribed maps are said to coincide on the overlap. They do not coincide with diagram (3.7) as printed.

Equation reference: eq:bad-normalization. Put \(q=1-\zeta_p\) and \[j=\operatorname{id}\otimes(\operatorname{dlog}^{\vee})^{\otimes n}.\] Theorem 3.4.12, pp. 42–43, gives, under its stated canonical identifications, \[(\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C=\operatorname{Sch}_X^n\circ j.\] Thus diagram (3.7) says \[(\Psi'^n_{\mathfrak X})_C\circ(q^n\operatorname{id})
       =j\circ(\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C^{-1}
       =(\operatorname{Sch}_X^n)^{-1}.\] Consequently its actual definition is \[
(\Psi'^n_{\mathfrak X})_C=q^{-n}(\operatorname{Sch}_X^n)^{-1}.\] All these are equalities of maps over \(C\); there is no integrality ambiguity in cancelling \(q^n\).

Equation reference: eq:good-normalization. By contrast, Theorem–Definition 3.3.4, pp. 36–37, uses the submodule \((\zeta_p-1)^nE\) at the lower left and its inclusion into \(E\). Its proof gives the explicit formula \[\Psi'^n_{\mathrm{sm}}(x)
 =\frac{j\big((\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})^{-1}((\zeta_p-1)^nx)\big)}
              {(\zeta_p-1)^n}.\] After inverting \(p\), linearity cancels the two factors, so \[
(\Psi'^n_{\mathrm{sm}})_C
   =j(\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C^{-1}=(\operatorname{Sch}_X^n)^{-1}.\] The sign difference between \(\zeta_p-1\) and \(1-\zeta_p\) cannot cure the discrepancy: the generic diagram adds a nonunit factor, not merely a sign.

Take \(p=2\), \(C=\widehat{\overline{\mathbf Q}_2}\), and \[\mathfrak X=\operatorname{Spf}\mathcal O_C\langle T,T^{-1}\rangle,\qquad d=n=1.\] This is affine, hence separated and qcqs. It is an admissible smooth formal \(\mathcal O_C\)-scheme, flat and topologically of finite type. Its generic fiber is the smooth one-dimensional analytic torus and its special fiber is the reduced scheme \(\operatorname{Spec}k[T,T^{-1}]\). It is therefore nice. The formal smooth locus is all of \(\mathfrak X\). The prime \(2\) is allowed by the manuscript; no odd-prime hypothesis occurs in the cited constructions. Here \(\zeta_2=-1\), so \(q=2\).

There is an additional integrality obstruction: \(\omega/2\) does not belong to the free \(\mathcal O_C\langle T,T^{-1}\rangle\)-lattice generated by \(\omega\). Even an almost interpretation cannot identify this lattice with its \(1/2\)-rescaling. For example, an element \(a\in C\) with \(a^2=2\) lies in \(\mathfrak m_C\), but \(a/2\notin\mathcal O_C\). Thus \((\tfrac12\mathcal O_C)/\mathcal O_C\) is not annihilated by all of \(\mathfrak m_C\). No appeal to almostification repairs the printed equality.

The dependency is direct: Theorem 3.5.2 constructs the trace used in Definitions 3.5.3 and 3.5.5; the local duality theorems in Section 4 use that trace; Section 5 globalizes the resulting pairing. As printed, there is no trace with the two simultaneous restrictions, already on the smooth torus above. This is an invalid derivation tied to the main construction, hence Major under standard 0.7.1 even though the scalar repair is local. No failure of the principal mod-\(p\) pairing, after the correction, has been demonstrated. No journal-version or author-adoption claim is made.
result: The surrounding text strongly indicates the intended normalization: Remark 3.4.15 explicitly says \((\operatorname{Sch}_X^n)^{-1}\), the smooth formula already gives that map, and Lemma 3.5.4 uses that same inverse. These are evidence for a local correction rather than for failure of the underlying duality theorem.

Replace the upward left arrow in diagram (3.7) by the identity, leaving the two copies of \(E_C\) and the bottom map unchanged. Then the defining relation is precisely \[(\Psi'^n_{\mathfrak X})_C=j(\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C^{-1}
              =(\operatorname{Sch}_X^n)^{-1}.\] On the overlap with the smooth locus this equals [eq:good-normalization] (#eq:good-normalization). The Hartogs intersection property of Theorem 2.5.5 therefore applies exactly as the proof of Theorem 3.5.2 requires: the maps to the smooth-locus sheaf and the generic-fiber sheaf agree in their common target, and hence factor through their intersection. The uniqueness argument is unaffected. Alternatively, retain the upward multiplication by \(q^n\) and replace the bottom map by \((\Phi^n_{\mathfrak X})_C^{-1}\circ(q^n\operatorname{id})\); this gives the same corrected map.

This verification restores the specific gluing step, its smooth normalization, and the claimed generic-fiber identity. It is not a substitute for independently verifying every later external theorem. Merely relabelling the upper map, or asserting that both vertical arrows are isomorphisms over \(C\), does not restore their compatibility with the already fixed integral smooth map.
Impact: Theorem 3.5.2 -> integral/mod-p Faltings trace -> Section 4 local duality -> Section 5 global duality. No counterexample to corrected principal theorem.

Multiplication V_chi tensor V_chi' -> V_chi+chi' is always an OC-isomorphism.
analysis:
Equation reference: eq:false-product. On p. 53 after (4.6), and in Lemma 4.2.15 on p. 54, the manuscript says that multiplication induces isomorphisms \[
V_\chi\otimes_{\mathcal O_C}V_{\chi'}\xrightarrow{\sim}V_{\chi+\chi'}\] for all characters, including rational characters at each finite tower level \(m\). These assertions occur in TeX lines 2470–2472 and 2492–2500.

Use the same \(C\) and \(p=2\) as above, and choose the permitted standard polystable model \[R^+=\mathcal O_C\langle t_0,t_1\rangle/(t_0t_1-2).\] In the notation of the paper, \(l=1\), \(n_1=1\), \(d=1\), \(\varpi_1=2\), and take \(m=0\). The parameter \(\varpi_1\) is nonzero, as required; it is not required to be a unit. The normal form with basis \(1,t_0^r,t_1^s\), \(r,s\geq1\), shows \(\mathcal O_C\)-torsion-freeness and hence flatness. The generic fiber is smooth since \(t_0t_1=2\) makes the two partial derivatives \(t_1,t_0\) never simultaneously zero. The special fiber \(k[t_0,t_1]/(t_0t_1)\) is reduced. Thus this lies in the very semistable class under discussion.

The torus is \(T=\{(u,u^{-1})\}\). For the character \(\chi(u,u^{-1})=u\), the paper’s own normalized-monomial definition gives \[V_\chi=\mathcal O_Ct_0,\quad V_{-\chi}=\mathcal O_Ct_1,\quad V_0=\mathcal O_C.\] Multiplication sends \(t_0\otimes t_1\) to \(2\). Its image is \(2\mathcal O_C\), and its cokernel is \(\mathcal O_C/2\), which is nonzero. It is not even almost zero: an element of valuation strictly between \(0\) and \(v(2)\) does not kill the class of \(1\). This verifies failure of [eq:false-product] (#eq:false-product) under all original hypotheses, already at \(m=0\).

Equation reference: eq:correct-product. Write the normalized exponent vectors of the two characters as \(a=(a_{ij})\) and \(b=(b_{ij})\), with nonnegative entries and \(\min_j a_{ij}=\min_j b_{ij}=0\) in every block \(i\). Put \(c_i=\min_j(a_{ij}+b_{ij})\). The defining relations give \[
t^a t^b=\left(\prod_i\varpi_i^{c_i}\right)t^{\,a+b-c},\] where \(c_i\) is subtracted from every exponent in block \(i\). For rational exponents, use the compatible roots fixed in the tower. The rightmost monomial is the normalized generator for \(\chi+\chi'\).

Thus multiplication between these free rank-one \(\mathcal O_C\)-modules is injective and has image the principal ideal \(\prod_i\varpi_i^{c_i}\) times the target generator. It is an isomorphism precisely when that scalar is a unit. In particular, it is an isomorphism if all relevant parameters are units, or after inverting \(p\). Formula [eq:correct-product] (#eq:correct-product), rather than [eq:false-product] (#eq:false-product) in full generality, is a verified replacement. The reviewer-owned symbolic script additionally checked 49 normalized integer-exponent pairs in the two-variable model. That finite check illustrates, but is not the proof of, the general monomial identity.
result: Warning 4.2.22, p. 55, correctly says that the character-class modules \(R^+_{\bar\chi}\) need not be free or even flat over \(R^+\). These are different objects from the individual \(\mathcal O_C\)-lines \(V_\chi\). For example, at \(m=0\) the class module is \(R^+\) itself; its ordinary self-duality is not contradicted by \(V_\chi V_{-\chi}=2\mathcal O_C\).

Proposition 4.3.6, pp. 61–62, is also important counterevidence. Its Case 1 uses \(V_\chi V_{-\chi}\simeq\mathcal O_C\) only when \(\varpi\) is a unit, where [eq:correct-product] (#eq:correct-product) verifies that assertion. Its Case 2 uses reduction modulo a suitably small pseudouniformizer and Theorem 4.3.2, rather than the false multiplication isomorphism for individual nonunit weight lines. The additive decompositions remain valid. The inspected proof therefore does not establish a core dependency on the false general statement. Replace the multiplication assertion by [eq:correct-product] (#eq:correct-product), retaining the unit case. The supported severity is Minor. No failure of derived duality for \(R^+_{\bar\chi}\) has been proved.
Impact: No demonstrated core dependency on false nonunit generality; additive decomposition and derived R_chibar duality not disproved.

report: Abstract: This review concerns Xinliang An’s 90-page author manuscript arXiv:2401.02003v1. All source pages were read and visually inspected. Two Major concerns are supported: an impossible signed parameterization of a nonnegative shear norm in the instability theorems, and an incorrect induced-metric calculation in the spacelikeness proof. Explicit corrections and their precise limits are given. Two local Minor concerns concern a missing background term in an expansion estimate and a false extreme Weyl-component equation. Neither the corrected horizon mechanism nor the general physical censorship conclusion is refuted by these checks. Uniformity and low-regularity existence remain evidence questions.

Title: Scientific initial review of
Naked singularity censoring with anisotropic apparent horizon
# Identity, version, and assessment

The assigned paper is Naked singularity censoring with anisotropic apparent horizon, by Xinliang An, M25-0014, associated with https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2025.201.3.3. The actually reviewed version is https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02003v1, dated January 2024. The manifest-bound PDF has 90 pages. Page references below use one-based PDF pages, agreeing with printed page numbers. Source-line references are one-based in the supplied 5,364-line `source.tex`. The DOI transcription amendment is metadata evidence, not a scientific finding.
The PDF SHA-256 is
The TeX SHA-256 is
All seven manifest-bound inputs were rehashed and matched. No comparison establishing equality with the journal Version of Record was performed. The findings concern this author version exclusively.

Assessment 1.  The overall initial judgment is Major, with two Major and two Minor supported concerns. Problem 1 contradicts the literal all-real-parameter initial-data statement, including arbitrarily small negative parameters. Problem 2 invalidates a core geometric derivation; the estimates already available suggest a verifiable repair for fixed positive barrier constants. Problems 3–4 are localized errors without demonstrated failure of the corrected core argument. Pending uniformity and regularity questions are not counted as proved defects. Independent scientific acceptance and author adoption remain pending.
# Definitions, hypotheses, and checked scope

Equation reference: metric. For clarity this report writes \(v=\underline u\), \(r=|u|\), \(\mu=\mu^*\in(0,1)\), and \(k=\mu/(1-\mu)\). This \(v\) is not the separately rescaled coordinate \(v=4\underline u\) introduced on source p. 20. The field equations are \[\operatorname{Ric}_{\alpha\beta}=\partial_\alpha\phi\,\partial_\beta\phi,
 \qquad \Box_g\phi=0.\] The introductory gauge on p. 2 is \[
 g=-2\Omega^2(\mathrm du\otimes\mathrm dv+\mathrm dv\otimes\mathrm du)
 +h_{AB}(\mathrm d\theta^A-d^A\mathrm dv)(\mathrm d\theta^B-d^B\mathrm dv),\] with \(e_3=\Omega^{-1}\partial_u\), \(e_4=\Omega^{-1}(\partial_v+d^A\partial_A)\), and \(g(e_3,e_4)=-2\). The shift vanishes on the initial \(H_{-1}\). Equation (2.1), p. 14, prints \(d^A\mathrm du\) instead of \(d^A\mathrm dv\). This conflicts with the introduction and its displayed frame. The analysis of Problem 2 uses [metric] (#metric); its shift-free diagnostic is independent of this isolated coordinate discrepancy.

On \(v=0\), the prescribed spherical background has \[h=r^2\gamma_{\mathbb S^2},\quad
 \Omega_0^2=r^k,\quad
 \Omega^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\chi=\frac{2(1-\mu)}r,\quad
 \Omega\operatorname{tr}\underline\chi=-\frac2r,\quad
 \Omega\underline\omega=\frac{\mu}{4(1-\mu)r}.\] Theorem 1.1 combines weighted initial bounds through five angular and three outgoing derivatives, a small region \(v\le r\Omega_0^{2-\widetilde\delta}\), and an energy profile \[\int_0^v\left(|\widehat\chi|^2+
     |\Omega e_4\phi-(\Omega e_4\phi)_{\mathrm{corner}}|^2\right)\mathrm dv'
 =vf(\omega,v),\quad 0\le f\le1,\quad f\ge m>0
 \ \hbox{on a fixed ball }B_p(\epsilon).\] The parameter \(a\ge1\) is retained in later sections and may be set to one. Constants depending on fixed \(\mu,m,\epsilon\) are not uniform as \(\mu\to0,1\) or \(m,\epsilon\to0\). The elliptic unknowns are related by \[R=(va)^{1-\mu}e^{-(1-\mu)\widetilde\varphi}
   =(va)^{1-\mu}\psi^\lambda,\qquad
 \psi=e^{-\mu\widetilde\varphi}>0,\quad
 \lambda=\frac{1-\mu}{\mu}.\] The constructed MOTS is \(u=-R(\omega,v)\). Uniqueness proved in the elliptic argument uses the positive barrier and a priori bounded class. This review does not extend it to arbitrary uncontrolled graphs or to all notions of apparent horizon.

The entire extracted text, 14,583 lines, was read to zero remaining lines, and every source PDF page 1–90 was actually viewed. The complete TeX was machine-scanned statically; critical passages were also read verbatim. The latter does not mean every TeX line was separately read in addition to the full PDF. The coverage ledger records:
- pp. 1–13: all main theorem quantifiers; characteristic data; energy positivity; the degenerating \(C^0\) profile; hyperbolic/elliptic region matching and parameter dependence.
- pp. 14–24: metric/frame conventions; null structure and Bianchi systems; renormalized variables; derivative counts; initial norms; bootstrap smallness \(v a^{1/2}/(r\Omega^{3/2})\).
- pp. 25–35: transport weights, metric comparability and Sobolev use; background-subtracted expansions; Ricci-coefficient bounds; the scalar transport estimate and the nonzero background source.
- pp. 36–49: commutation and top angular scalar-energy pairing; cancellation of paired highest derivatives; Hodge estimates and auxiliary mass-aspect/torsion quantities.

- pp. 50–65: top Ricci and curvature estimates, renormalized curvature-energy pairs and closure strategy. Reciprocal references between estimates were not treated as circularity without a failed absorption argument. External existence/extension theorems were not independently reproved.
- pp. 66–74: MOTS equation, barrier direction, coordinate changes, natural quadratic gradient term, Moser and Schauder dependencies. The nested exponential in \(C(\kappa)\), (9.15), was retained.
- pp. 75–81: linearization, principal eigenfunction, maximum principle, continuation and uniqueness in the controlled class; smooth parameter dependence and the induced horizon metric.
- pp. 82–90: background cancellation in the instability proof; all-real amplitude quantifiers; \(C^0\) profile and intrinsic \(\dot H^{1/2}\) estimate; conformal free data and the full bibliography.
# Problem 1: a nonnegative norm cannot carry all signed amplitudes
## Claim and location

Theorem 1.3, pp. 4–5 (TeX lines 478–487), and Theorem 13.2, p. 84 (lines 5005–5032), prescribe the first component of the data as \[|\widehat\chi|(-1,v,\omega)=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f_i(v,\omega)\] for arbitrary real \(\lambda_i,\lambda'_i\), not all zero, and assert injectivity of the pair of displayed initial-data components. The proof on pp. 84–85 chooses \(f_i\ge0\), supported on disjoint discs, with \(f_i\ge m_i a^{1/2}>0\) on a smaller ball. The \(C^0\) version on p. 87 replaces this lower bound by \(m_i g(v)^{1/2}a^{1/2}>0\) for every \(v>0\).
## Complete check

Take \(k=1\), \(\lambda_1=-\varepsilon\) with any \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(\lambda'_1=0\). Then the required nonzero-parameter condition is satisfied. Choose \(v>0\) and \(\omega\) in the smaller ball supplied by the proof. All stated support, positivity and smoothness properties of \(f_1\) are retained, but \[\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(v,\omega)<0,\qquad
 |\widehat\chi|_h(v,\omega)\ge0\] for every real tensor and positive definite induced sphere metric \(h\). No such data exist. The same contradiction applies to the continuous profiles because \(g(v)>0\) for \(v>0\). Taking \(\varepsilon\) arbitrarily small rules out interpreting the obstruction as merely excessive amplitude in an upper energy bound.

This is an impossibility of the quantified data prescription. It is not a purported Einstein solution violating the horizon theorem; there is no admissible data tensor realizing the prescribed negative norm. Even without the proof’s nonnegative choice, an arbitrary nonzero real \(f_1\) cannot make both \(f_1\) and \(-f_1\) nonnegative everywhere. Injectivity prevents taking every \(f_i=0\).
## Counterevidence and a precise repair

Appendix A, p. 89 (lines 5230–5269), actually supplies signed free conformal data, which is the natural place for the amplitudes. In a local angular chart let \[m=\exp\!\left(\sqrt{2a}\,x
       \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\right),\qquad \det m=1.\] Direct differentiation, using the manuscript’s shear formula, gives \[|\widehat\chi|^2
 =\frac14\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl(m^{-1}m'm^{-1}m'\bigr)=a(x')^2,\qquad
 |\widehat\chi|=\sqrt a\,|x'|.\] The reviewer computed this exact identity independently in SymPy; no author code was executed. Thus one may set \[x'=a^{-1/2}\sum_i\lambda_i f_i\] and state the theorem for the resulting conformal metric or actual trace-free shear tensor, with the displayed norm replaced by \(\left|\sum_i\lambda_i f_i\right|\). Disjoint support still makes the squared energy a sum of \(\lambda_i^2 f_i^2\). For any nonzero shear amplitude, a corresponding smaller ball gives the required positive energy density. The scalar-field amplitudes remain signed scalar data.

The norm alone then loses the sign information: replacing all \(\lambda_i\) by \(-\lambda_i\) gives the same norm. Injectivity must be stated for the full free data. With \(x(0,\omega)=0\), the unique symmetric logarithm of the positive matrix \(m\) recovers \(x\), differentiation recovers \(x'\), and disjoint supports recover the coefficients. This verifies injectivity of this corrected free-data map. The characteristic constraints and the hypotheses of the evolution theorem still have to be imposed; the algebraic correction alone is not an independent existence theorem. Restricting to nonnegative coefficients would instead give a cone, not the printed all-real linear family.
## Impact and judgment

This is Major because the advertised arbitrary-dimensional instability family in Theorems 1.3 and 13.2 is a central explicit contribution, and its literal data prescription is impossible. The positive-energy mechanism and the qualitative availability of many signed conformal perturbations are substantial counterevidence against reading this as a refutation of the physical instability conclusion. Theorem 1.1 for valid initial data is not contradicted. Evidence: source pp. 84, 87, 89 and `verification/0014/evidence/independent_checks.json`.
# Problem 2: the spacelikeness proof uses the wrong induced metric
## Claim and location

Proposition 12.4 and (12.5), p. 81, TeX lines 4851–4897, assert spacelikeness under the extra smallness condition on \(v\partial_v f\). After deriving \(R_v\ge (1-\mu)R/(2v)>0\), the proof prints \[g'_{AB}=h_{AB},\qquad g'_{Av}=2R_A,\qquad g'_{vv}=4R_v.\] These are not the pullback of the metric and frame specified on p. 2. The same paragraph also reverses the direction of a barrier bound.
## Exact pullback and positivity criterion

Equation reference: schur. Pull back [metric] (#metric) under \((\omega,v)\mapsto(-R(\omega,v),v,\omega)\). Since \(\mathrm du=-R_A\mathrm d\theta^A-R_v\mathrm dv\), one obtains \[\begin{aligned}
 g'_{AB}&=h_{AB},\\
 g'_{Av}&=2\Omega^2 R_A-h_{AB}d^B,\\
 g'_{vv}&=4\Omega^2R_v+h_{AB}d^Ad^B.\end{aligned}\] All coefficients are evaluated on the horizon. The angular block is positive definite, so its Schur complement is \[
 4\Omega^2\left(
 R_v+d^AR_A-\Omega^2 h^{AB}R_AR_B\right).\] An independent symbolic multiplication of the full \(4\times4\) metric and the \(4\times3\) tangent matrix verified every entry and [schur] (#schur).

Already at \(d=0\) and \(R_A=0\), the actual coefficient is \(4\Omega^2R_v\), whereas the printed coefficient is \(4R_v\). The paper’s interior lapse is small and is not normalized to one there. This diagnostic does not depend on the shift typo in (2.1). It refutes the displayed tensor identity, not positivity of its corrected version. No unproved realization of an arbitrary graph as a MOTS is needed for the pullback calculation.

For the barrier, (9.13), p. 68, gives \(\widetilde\varphi\ge\log(3/2)\), and hence \[\psi=e^{-\mu\widetilde\varphi}\le(2/3)^\mu.\] The last paragraph on p. 81 uses the reverse inequality \(\psi\ge(2/3)^\mu\). Theorem 11.6 actually places the solution strictly between the barriers. A valid positive lower bound instead comes from the upper bound \(\widetilde\varphi\le\bar\kappa(m,\epsilon)\): \(\psi\ge e^{-\mu\bar\kappa}\).
## A checked repair with the required restrictions

The corrected criterion is positivity of the bracket in [schur] (#schur). Fix \(0<\mu<1\), \(a\), and the positive barrier constants. The preceding barrier and derivative estimates then give \[R\asymp v^{1-\mu},\quad R_v\ge cR/v,\quad
 |\nabla_\omega\log R|\le C,\quad
 h\asymp R^2\gamma_{\mathbb S^2},\quad \Omega^2\asymp R^k.\] Consequently \[\frac{\Omega^2|\nabla_hR|^2}{R_v}
 \le C\frac{\Omega^2v}{R}=O(v^{2\mu})\longrightarrow0.\] The omitted shift must also be controlled. In the paper’s frame, \(\zeta=(\eta-\underline\eta)/2\); the angular part of the frame commutator gives \[\partial_u d^A=4\Omega^2\zeta^A,\qquad d(-1,v,\omega)=0.\] The torsion estimate of Proposition 4.5 with the sphere Sobolev estimate gives \(|\zeta|_h\le Cv/r^2\), for fixed \(a\) and bounded bootstrap norms. Raising to angular coordinates supplies one further factor \(r^{-1}\). Integration from \(r=1\) to \(r=R\) yields \[|d|_{\mathrm{coord}}\le Cv\int_R^1 s^{k-3}\mathrm ds
 \le C v
 \begin{cases}

The positive \(R_v\) bound is real evidence in favor of the intended conclusion. The lapse factor makes the angular-gradient subtraction smaller in the actual criterion. The shift has a controllable rate. Accordingly, this finding does not exhibit a timelike apparent horizon.

Nevertheless the printed proof establishes positivity of a different quadratic form and invokes an incorrect barrier inequality. Spacelikeness of the constructed horizon is a central geometric claim, so this invalid derivation is Major under standard 0.7.1 even though the specific local correction is feasible. The manuscript’s more general achronality statement on p. 80 also uses its external forthcoming reference [7]; that theorem was not independently read here. The repair above is for Proposition 12.4 under its additional derivative assumption, not a replacement proof of that general theorem. Evidence: source pp. 2, 68, 80–81 and `verification/0014/evidence/geometry_checks.json`.
# Problem 3: a background expansion term is lost at derivative zero
## Claim, assumptions, and contradiction
## Correction and downstream check

The proposition’s first, background-subtracted estimate is consistent: \[\sum_{i\le4}\|r^{i+1}\nabla^i
 [\Omega\operatorname{tr}\chi-\Omega^2(\Omega^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\chi)_0]\|_2
 \lesssim va\mathcal O^2.\] Together with the already stated lapse and angular-torsion bounds it gives the corrected form \[\sum_{i\le4}\|r^i\nabla^i(\Omega\operatorname{tr}\chi)\|_2
 \lesssim \Omega_0^2+\frac{va\mathcal O^2}{r}.\] The background-free estimate can also be restricted to positive angular orders, with the lapse derivatives estimated as in the proof.

In Proposition 5.1, p. 35, treating \(-\tfrac12(\Omega\operatorname{tr}\chi)(\Omega e_3\phi)\) as entirely \(O(v)\) loses this zeroth-order background contribution. Its weighted transport integral is nevertheless finite: the background size reduces to \(\int_r^1s^{k-1}\mathrm ds=(1-r^k)/k\), for fixed \(\mu>0\). Restoring an \(O(1)\) contribution is compatible with the required \(O(a^{1/2})\) estimate because \(a\ge1\). It does not justify the incorrectly stronger \(O(v)\) intermediate bound.
## Counterevidence and impact

Equation (4.4), p. 32, retains a \(1/r\) background term. The Raychaudhuri application on p. 83 explicitly writes \(2(1-\mu)\Omega^2/r\) back into the estimate. The decisive trapped-surface calculation uses the valid background-subtracted expansion, and the highest angular estimates remove the constant background. The supported finding is therefore a localized false estimate and its overstated intermediate source bound, not a demonstrated failure of the core bootstrap after the background is restored. Judgment: Minor. The check and corrected transport integral are analytic; the exact background norm is also recorded in the independent-check result.
# Problem 4: the extreme Weyl equation has nonzero pure-trace matter
## Claim and exact location

Equation reference: badmatter. The first line of (2.13), p. 18, TeX lines 1132–1133, presents the \(\nabla_3\alpha\) equation with matter contribution \[
 \left[\frac14(D_3\operatorname{Ric}_{44}-D_4\operatorname{Ric}_{43})
          +\frac16e_4\operatorname{Scal}\right]h_{AB}.\] Here \(\alpha_{AB}=W(e_A,e_4,e_B,e_4)\) is trace-free. All its displayed vacuum terms are trace-free as well. The scalar coefficient in [badmatter] (#badmatter) does not vanish on all Einstein–massless-scalar solutions.
## An exact solution satisfying the identity’s assumptions

For \(t>0\), use the spatially flat scalar-field FLRW solution \[g=-\mathrm dt^2+t^{2/3}(\mathrm dx^2+\mathrm dy^2+\mathrm dz^2),\qquad
 \phi=c\log t,\quad c=\sqrt{2/3}.\] Direct calculation gives \[\operatorname{Ric}_{tt}=\frac{2}{3t^2},\quad \operatorname{Ric}_{ij}=0,\quad
 \operatorname{Scal}=-\frac{2}{3t^2},\quad \Box_g\phi=0,\quad W=0.\] Thus the exact field equations used in Section 2.2 hold. For sphere sections one can equivalently use radial spatial coordinates away from their center and take \(e_4=\partial_t+t^{-1/3}\partial_\rho\), \(e_3=\partial_t-t^{-1/3}\partial_\rho\); then \(g(e_3,e_4)=-2\). The following contractions are the same as for a unit Cartesian spatial direction at a point. Let \(H=D^2\phi\). They are \[H_{44}=-\frac{4c}{3t^2},\qquad
 H_{34}=-\frac{2c}{3t^2},\qquad
 e_3\phi=e_4\phi=\frac ct.\] Since \(D\operatorname{Ric}=D(\mathrm d\phi\otimes\mathrm d\phi)\), \[D_3\operatorname{Ric}_{44}=-\frac8{9t^3},\qquad
 D_4\operatorname{Ric}_{43}=-\frac4{3t^3},\qquad
 e_4\operatorname{Scal}=\frac4{3t^3}.\] Consequently [badmatter] (#badmatter) equals \[\left(\frac1{9t^3}+\frac2{9t^3}\right)h_{AB}
 =\frac1{3t^3}h_{AB}\ne0.\] Every Weyl quantity in the first equation vanishes because \(W=0\), so the printed equation says \(0=h_{AB}/(3t^3)\). The trace is \(2/(3t^3)\), already nonzero at \(t=1\).

The reviewer independently computed the Christoffel symbols, full Ricci tensor, all 256 Weyl components, the scalar wave operator, and these covariant-derivative contractions using exact SymPy expressions. All seven grouped checks in the saved result passed. This spacetime verifies the assumptions of the universal local Einstein–scalar identity. It does not satisfy, and is not claimed to satisfy, the special naked-singularity characteristic data of Theorem 1.1. The finding is precisely the false identity in Section 2.2.
## Counterevidence, correction limits, and impact

Section 8 develops energy estimates for the renormalized \(\beta,K,\check\sigma,\underline\beta\) system rather than evolving the extreme \(\alpha,\underline\alpha\) components by this line. The static source scan and the inspected energy argument did not establish a core use of the false extreme-component equation. Judgment: Minor.

A valid correction requires rederiving its complete symmetric trace-free matter contribution from the divergence identity (2.12). Simply declaring the displayed pure-trace term to be projected away does not establish the missing anisotropic terms in a general scalar field. No unverified full replacement equation is proposed. The unused incorrect identity can instead be removed without changing the inspected renormalized energy argument. Evidence: source p. 18, Section 8, the independent script and its result.
# Unresolved evidence questions and excluded concerns
## Uniform smallness in the angular concentration

The main statements write \(\delta=\delta(B)\). The barrier construction and region match in (1.15) and (9.16), pp. 12 and 68, visibly involve \(m,\epsilon\). For example put \(s=m\epsilon^{\tau+2}\), \(a=1\), and \(c_0=\mu\widetilde\delta/2\in(0,1)\). A required smallness inequality of the form \(s\ge(vs)^{c_0}\) is equivalent to \[v\le s^{(1-c_0)/c_0}.\] There is no fixed positive \(v\) satisfying this as \(s\downarrow0\). The a priori \(C^2\) barrier constants also deteriorate with \(m,\epsilon\). The manuscript should specify whether the horizon interval is shrunk after these data are fixed and whether that shrinkage is included in the notation \(\delta(B)\).

This proves a limitation of the displayed proof’s uniformity. It does not prove nonexistence of MOTSs for concentrated data beyond that sufficient range. Classification: Needs Evidence, not an additional proved Major issue.
## Weighted norms, the auxiliary initial norm, and continuous data

Page 23 defines \(\mathcal I^{(0)}\) using unweighted outgoing derivatives through order five and angular derivatives through order six. Page 24 permits implicit constants to depend on initial-data quantities, while the theorem’s displayed controlled norm has only three weighted outgoing derivatives and five angular derivatives. The continuous example on pp. 85–88 uses \[h(v)=[\log\log(1/v)]^{-1/4},\qquad
 h'(v)=\frac{1}{4v\log(1/v)[\log\log(1/v)]^{5/4}}.\] Thus \(h'(v)\to\infty\), but \(v^j h^{(j)}(v)\to0\) for \(j=1,2,3\). The latter three limits were symbolically checked. This satisfies the intended pointwise weighted-derivative behavior, not the unweighted \(\mathcal I^{(0)}\) bound.

There is also a notational ambiguity: some displayed theorem expressions place \(v^j\) outside an \(L^\infty_v\) norm. If that is taken literally as a multiplier after an infinite unweighted supremum, the continuous example fails it. The function space should explicitly put the weight inside the supremum.

Even in a smooth one-sided family, low derivative control does not by itself control five outgoing derivatives: a profile \(C+b(1+N^{-3}\sin Nv)\), with fixed small \(b>0\), has uniformly bounded derivatives through order three on a fixed interval, whereas its fifth derivative has size \(bN^2\). It can retain a uniformly positive, bounded energy density after normalization. This elementary family shows that a bound for \(\mathcal I^{(0)}\) cannot simply be inferred from the displayed low-order norm. It is not a construction of a failed Einstein evolution.

To complete the continuous-data assertion, one needs an existence and limiting argument whose lifespan and necessary estimates are uniform in smooth approximations of these profiles, or a direct theorem in the specified weighted function space. The manuscript’s many estimates use angular rather than high outgoing derivatives, which is genuine evidence that such a repair may be possible. The reference to standard local existence and extension on p. 65 alone does not record that uniform argument. This remains Needs Evidence; no failure of the claimed low-regularity solution has been proved here.
## Checks that do not support additional findings

Proposition 13.4 estimates the intrinsic Slobodeckij seminorm on \([0,\delta]\). Its near/far diagonal decomposition gives the stated smallness; the logarithmic substitutions and integration bounds were checked. The zero extension to \(v<0\) would instead have cross energy comparable to \(\int_0^\delta h(v)^2\,\mathrm dv/v=\infty\). Because the proposition explicitly uses the one-sided interval, this does not refute it. The intrinsic result must not be advertised as a global critical norm bound across the junction without further work.

The linearized principal term is \[\Delta_\gamma-\mu-\frac{1-\mu}{2}f\psi^{-1/\mu}.\] For fixed \(\mu>0\), its negative zeroth-order contribution remains coercive even where \(f=0\). Thus the p. 86 informal global notation \(f\psi^{-1/\mu}\asymp1\) is too strong outside the support, but a positive lower bound everywhere is not needed in this argument. The positive barrier context must be retained when lemmas say nonnegative \(\psi\), because negative powers are used.

The nested bound (9.15) is \(C(\kappa)=(Ce^\kappa)^{C e^{4\Lambda\kappa e^\kappa}}\). For the log-log profile, fixed angular-data constants add to \(\kappa\); they cannot be discarded in exact equalities. Nevertheless \(4\Lambda\kappa e^\kappa=o(\log\log(1/v))\) as \(v\downarrow0\) for that profile, so the qualitative domination by arbitrarily small powers of \(v^{-1}\) survives after shrinking the interval. No extra false-conclusion finding is supported.

Isolated coordinate, sign and numerical-normalization inconsistencies were not counted without a demonstrated substantive dependency. The manuscript’s external reference [7] is listed as in preparation. Its absence from this review is a dependency limitation, not a missing-citation finding. Neither global future null infinity nor a global formulation of cosmic censorship was independently established by this local review.

Take \(k=1\), \(\lambda_1=-\varepsilon\) with any \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(\lambda'_1=0\). Then the required nonzero-parameter condition is satisfied. Choose \(v>0\) and \(\omega\) in the smaller ball supplied by the proof. All stated support, positivity and smoothness properties of \(f_1\) are retained, but \[\sum_i\lambda_i f_i(v,\omega)<0,\qquad
 |\widehat\chi|_h(v,\omega)\ge0\] for every real tensor and positive definite induced sphere metric \(h\). No such data exist. It is not a purported Einstein solution violating the horizon theorem; there is no admissible data tensor realizing the prescribed negative norm. Even without the proof’s nonnegative choice, an arbitrary nonzero real \(f_1\) cannot make both \(f_1\) and \(-f_1\) nonnegative everywhere. Injectivity prevents taking every \(f_i=0\).

This is Major because the advertised arbitrary-dimensional instability family in Theorems 1.3 and 13.2 is a central explicit contribution, and its literal data prescription is impossible. result:
Appendix A, p. 89 (lines 5230–5269), actually supplies signed free conformal data, which is the natural place for the amplitudes. In a local angular chart let \[m=\exp\!\left(\sqrt{2a}\,x
       \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\right),\qquad \det m=1.\] Direct differentiation, using the manuscript’s shear formula, gives \[|\widehat\chi|^2
 =\frac14\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl(m^{-1}m'm^{-1}m'\bigr)=a(x')^2,\qquad
 |\widehat\chi|=\sqrt a\,|x'|.\] The reviewer computed this exact identity independently in SymPy; no author code was executed. Thus one may set \[x'=a^{-1/2}\sum_i\lambda_i f_i\] and state the theorem for the resulting conformal metric or actual trace-free shear tensor, with the displayed norm replaced by \(\left|\sum_i\lambda_i f_i\right|\). Disjoint support still makes the squared energy a sum of \(\lambda_i^2 f_i^2\). For any nonzero shear amplitude, a corresponding smaller ball gives the required positive energy density. The scalar-field amplitudes remain signed scalar data.

The norm alone then loses the sign information: replacing all \(\lambda_i\) by \(-\lambda_i\) gives the same norm. Injectivity must be stated for the full free data. With \(x(0,\omega)=0\), the unique symmetric logarithm of the positive matrix \(m\) recovers \(x\), differentiation recovers \(x'\), and disjoint supports recover the coefficients. This verifies injectivity of this corrected free-data map. The characteristic constraints and the hypotheses of the evolution theorem still have to be imposed; the algebraic correction alone is not an independent existence theorem. Restricting to nonnegative coefficients would instead give a cone, not the printed all-real linear family.
Impact: Literal arbitrary-dimensional family in Theorems 1.3/13.2 false; valid-data horizon mechanism not refuted.

 h\asymp R^2\gamma_{\mathbb S^2},\quad \Omega^2\asymp R^k.\] Consequently \[\frac{\Omega^2|\nabla_hR|^2}{R_v}
 \le C\frac{\Omega^2v}{R}=O(v^{2\mu})\longrightarrow0.\] The omitted shift must also be controlled. Date: 25 October 2026

Title: Scientific Initial Review
M25-0015
# Identity, version, and location convention

The reviewed work is Andrei Jaikin-Zapirain and Marco Linton, On the coherence of one-relator groups and their group algebras. The associated journal DOI is 10.4007/annals.2025.201.3.4 (https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2025.201.3.4). The actual scientific source is the manifest-bound author manuscript arXiv:2303.05976v4: its arXiv stamp is 4 February 2025 and its title-page manuscript date is 5 February 2025. These two dates are retained separately. The PDF has 40 pages; page references below mean one-based PDF pages, which agree with the printed manuscript numbers. The journal Version of Record was not compared with this manuscript.
The PDF SHA-256 is
The manuscript source is `Coherence_accepted_version.tex`; its SHA-256 is
> afd0f1e8645548d9252c5db4af17a32a4ca9adcc9323a0ae9acc097b97dfb776.
A filename containing accepted does not establish journal-version identity.
# Checked claims, outcome, and scope

Outcome: No Issue Found within the inspected core scope. No substantive counterexample or false indispensable inference was established. This is a bounded initial-review result, not a certification of the paper or of its external foundations. All 40 PDF pages were read as extracted text and individually inspected as rendered images. The complete 1,544-line TeX file was machine-scanned; selected critical ranges were read verbatim. Reviewer-owned exact calculations were run; no author program was executed.

The principal chains checked were the homological-coherence criterion (Theorems 1.2 and 3.6), the tree-action upgrade from \(\mathrm{FP}_2(k)\) to finite presentability (Theorems 4.4–4.6), one-relator coherence (Theorem 1.1), weak dimension and group-algebra coherence (Theorems 1.6–1.7 and Section 5), and the intersection-rank argument (Theorem 6.9). The finite bireducible-complex argument and its Magnus-subgroup intersection step were also inspected. Characteristic restrictions, trivial-group cases, proper powers, cyclic intersections, and module sidedness were explicitly considered.

A proof-scope question remains for the passage from an arbitrary total staggering order in Section 2.5 to the integer-indexed infinite presentation used on page 33. It is recorded below as Needs Evidence, without claiming a counterexample or a Major/Minor defect. Several recoverable notation inconsistencies are likewise separated from substantive findings.
# Definitions, assumptions, quantifiers, and dependencies

Rings are associative and unital. In the tree-action statements the coefficient ring \(k\) is commutative and nonzero: the conclusion from vanishing \(N_{\rm ab}\otimes k\) for a free group \(N\) uses \(k\ne0\). The augmentation ideal \(I_G\) has left- and right-module versions; induction, the inverse-involution operation, and tensor products with diagonal action must retain their stated sides. The involution is not a vector-space dual.

The embedding of a group algebra into a Hughes-free division ring is an explicit hypothesis in statements over an arbitrary field. Its existence for the locally indicable groups used in characteristic zero is supplied by external results cited by the authors. The Linnell linear-independence property is stronger-looking input obtained there from Hughes freeness. This review checked the uses of these properties but did not independently reprove the cited division-ring existence theorem.

Non-positive immersions concern compact connected immersed complexes and allow the trivial-fundamental-group exception. The stronger NTPI inequality has an exception for free products of finite cyclic groups. That exception cannot be discarded when using Proposition 2.10. The asphericity conclusion in Corollary 2.8 also has a trivial-group alternative.

Reducibility involves a reducing edge which remains strictly involved; the absence of proper powers is a statement in the appropriate fundamental group after removing the cell. It is not merely a claim that a displayed word has no visible repetition. Bireducibility supplies two distinct reductions when at least two cells are present. Lemma 2.12 supplies the embeddings needed when passing between reductions and one-cell subcomplexes.

For the torsion variant in Theorem 5.6, the characteristic is coprime to the relevant finite orders. For Theorem 6.9, the ideal used in the quotient to the division ring is the two-sided kernel associated with the normal closure of \(W\). Confusing it with a one-sided augmentation ideal would invalidate the final zero-versus-one dimension calculation.

External foundations used but not independently reproved in full include the cited Freiheitssatz and one-relator torsion results, the domination theorem for tree actions of finitely presented groups, the Magnus–Moldavanskii hierarchy, the cited virtual free-by-cyclic theorem, the division-ring existence theorem, and the relevant immersion and \(L^2\)-Betti-number results. The report does not describe these references as independently retrieved or verified.
# Detailed mathematical verification and residual questions
## Projective modules and the homological criterion

Pages 16–18, Lemma 3.1 through Corollary 3.5, were checked without assuming that the ambient division ring is flat over the group algebra. For Lemma 3.1, let \(P\) be projective and let finitely many elements of \(P\) span \(D\otimes_RP\). Embed \(P\) as a summand of a free module \(L\) and choose a finite free summand \(L_1\) containing these elements. If \(N\) is the module they generate, right exactness gives \(D\otimes_R(P/N)=0\). The image of \(P\) in \(L/L_1\) therefore has zero tensor product with \(D\). Any submodule of the free module \(L/L_1\) maps injectively to its scalar extension as far as its own elements are concerned: its composite map to \(D\otimes_R(L/L_1)\) is injective because \(R\hookrightarrow D\). Consequently that image is zero. Thus \(P\subset L_1\), and projection from \(L_1\) onto the summand \(P\) proves finite generation. This resolves the apparent risk of illicitly using flatness.

For a finitely generated module of projective dimension at most one, its presentation kernel is projective. The long exact Tor sequence, together with the preceding finite-dimensional criterion, gives Proposition 3.2. If the ring has global dimension at most two and the division ring has weak dimension at most one, a finitely generated ideal \(J\) has \(\operatorname{Tor}_1(D,J)=\operatorname{Tor}_2(D,R/J)=0\); the criterion gives finite presentation and hence coherence, as in Corollary 3.3.

The scalar-extension step in Proposition 2.2 does not require arbitrary coefficient modules to be flat over \(\mathbb Z\). A projective resolution of \(\mathbb Z\) over \(\mathbb ZG\) splits as a complex of underlying abelian groups in the required short exact pieces, since the kernels are free abelian. Tensoring those pieces remains exact. The diagonal action on a free induced module is untwisted by \(g\otimes m\mapsto g\otimes g^{-1}m\). This justifies the cohomological-dimension bound used later.

The ascending-HNN argument in Theorem 3.4 was checked through the locally free kernel, the skew Laurent ring, Ore localization, and the passage from finitely presented modules to arbitrary modules by filtered colimits. In Theorem 3.6 rationalization is compatible with the Tor calculation because \(\mathbb Q\) is flat over \(\mathbb Z\). The proof is not an assertion that all group algebras are division-ring subrings in positive characteristic.
## The tree-action step

On pages 20–22 the decisive point is the passage from an \(\mathrm{FP}_2(k)\) group to a finitely presented cover with a \(k\)-acyclic relation-module kernel, followed by the cited domination theorem for trees. Let \(1\to N\to H\to G\to1\) be the cover, let \(H_i\) be the relevant vertex stabilizers, and put \(K=\langle\!\langle N\cap H_i\rangle\!\rangle\). The quotient tree is a tree because \(K\) is generated by elliptic stabilizers. In \(H/K\), the group \(N/K\) intersects each image of \(H_i\) trivially: an element represented in \(H_i\) and trivial in \(G\) lies in \(N\cap H_i\), which was killed. Hence \(N/K\) acts freely on the quotient tree and is free.

The quotient map on abelianizations gives \((N/K)_{\rm ab}\otimes k=0\) from \(N_{\rm ab}\otimes k=0\). A nontrivial free group has a nonzero free abelianization, whose tensor product with a nonzero ring is nonzero. Therefore \(N/K=1\). This establishes the step which could otherwise have concealed an unjustified passage from homological to ordinary coherence. The finite-presentability conclusion then uses finitely presented vertex groups and finitely generated edge groups. It does not require edge groups to be finitely presented.

The one-relator application still relies on the external hierarchy and virtual-subgroup inputs named above. Their invocation was traced; they were not reconstructed from first principles in this review.
## Flatness, Fox coefficients, and finite torsion

Lemma 5.1, pages 22–23, is a leading-degree argument for a diagonal module \(V\otimes_KD\). Its support condition is essential: the group elements in the chosen support have distinct images in the locally indicable quotient. After choosing an epimorphism of the finitely generated image to \(\mathbb Z\), the extreme-degree coefficient has fewer support terms. Clearing Ore denominators on the right commutes with the left action, and a leading-degree cancellation contradicts the inductive injectivity statement. No finite-dimensionality of \(V\) is used.

In the augmentation-ideal induction, the two factor modules are flat after induction and scalar extension. The relation-module map is injective by the Fox-coefficient support argument and Lemma 5.1. The Tor exact sequence then gives flatness; the inverse-involution and the augmentation sequence supply the dimension shift to weak dimension at most one.

For the torsion relation \(w=u^\ell\), let \(N_\ell=1+u+\cdots+u^{\ell-1}\). In the regular group algebra, multiplication by \(N_\ell\) gives an injection from coinvariants by \(u-1\): this is seen coset by coset in the cyclic subgroup of order \(\ell\). For an arbitrary module \(M\), if \(\ell\) is invertible and \(N_\ell m=0\), then \[m=\ell^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}(1-u^i)m\in (u-1)M.\] Together with \(N_\ell(u-1)=0\), this proves \(\ker N_\ell=(u-1)M\). The coprimality hypothesis in Theorem 5.6 therefore has exactly the role required by the proof.

The earlier Fox-coefficient injection on the regular group algebra can be justified without an illicit flatness assumption. The equivariant map \[KG\longrightarrow KG\otimes_KD_{\overline G},\qquad
 g\longmapsto g\otimes\overline g\] is injective, and the distinct-support lemma applies on the target. The image is not the non-equivariant map \(v\mapsto v\otimes1\). This supplies the implicit justification of the injection used with the norm factor.

## Intersection ranks and boundary cases

The Mackey decomposition in Section 6.4 is a decomposition of the permutation module by double cosets. Applying Tor gives the sum of the ordinary ranks of the intersections, so cyclic intersections must not be silently discarded by replacing ordinary rank with reduced rank.

For the quotient to \(D\), the image of a left ideal \(L\) has dimension zero if \(L\) lies in the two-sided kernel \(I\), and dimension one otherwise: a nonzero element of its image is invertible in \(D\). The augmentation presentation then gives \[\dim_D\operatorname{Tor}_1(D,\mathbb QF/L)=\operatorname{rank}L-1+\delta,\qquad
 \delta=\begin{cases}1&L\subset I,\\0&L\not\subset I.\end{cases}\] The lifted flat module from Theorem 5.11 kills the other Tor term. This is the algebraic source of the two branches of Theorem 6.9. For \(L=0\) the expression is \(0-1+1=0\); for \(L=\mathbb QF\) it is \(1-1+0=0\). The trivial subgroup belongs to the normal closure, so the negative bound in the other branch is never asserted for it.

Five explicit folded core graphs in the free group on \(x,y\) were checked with \(W=\langle x\rangle\). For \(U=\langle x,yxy^{-1}\rangle,\langle x,y^2\rangle,
