# Substantive findings
## Problem 1 (Major): integral fundamental-cycle normalization fails for torsion
Location. Proposition 2.27, pages 22–23, the homology surjection and diagram (2.4.2); Corollary 2.29, page 24. See `Coherent-Eisenstein-classes.tex`, lines 792–852, especially 811–831.

The proof asserts that, for a free finite-index \(\Gamma'\), homological transfer \(H_{d-1}(\Gamma,\mathbb Z)\to H_{d-1}(\Gamma',\mathbb Z)\) is onto. It chooses an integral preimage of a generator and requires evaluation after cohomological restriction to be \([\Gamma:\Gamma']\) times evaluation before restriction.

Take \(L=\mathbb Q(\zeta_3)\), \(d=1\), \(\Gamma=\{1,-1\}\), and \(\Gamma'=1\). Both \(H_0\)’s are \(\mathbb Z\). Inclusion-induced corestriction is the identity, whereas transfer sends \([1]\mapsto[1]+[-1]=2[1]\). It has image of index two and no generator has an integral preimage. This directly contradicts the step used to choose \(\xi\).

The obstruction is integral, not an orientation choice. Let \(R=\mathbb Z[\zeta_3,1/3]\), so \(2\notin R^\times\), and take the critical weight \(\overline\sigma-\sigma\), i.e. \(\alpha=0,\beta=1\). The coefficient line is a trivial \(\Gamma\)-module, and restriction on \(H^0(\Gamma,R)=R\) is the identity. Free-group evaluation is the identity. Diagram (2.4.2) would require an \(R\)-linear evaluation \(a\mapsto ca\) with \(2c=1\), impossible in this \(R\). This base is compatible with CM geometry: \(y^2+y=x^3\) has discriminant \(-27\), admits the \(\zeta_3\)-action, and is smooth at two. The universal group-homology failure is independent of a chosen nonzero class.

Counterevidence. For torsion-free groups of rank \(d-1\), top transfer between finite-index lattices is an isomorphism. Over \(\mathbb Q\), or after inverting the torsion order, a rational fundamental cycle provides the intended normalization. Sections explicitly restricted to torsion-free groups avoid this obstruction.

Repair and impact. Restrict the integral proposition to torsion-free groups, or invert \(|\Gamma_{\rm tors}|\), and then prove the required integral descent for congruence units. Definition 2.28, Corollary 2.29 and Lemma 5.15 use this normalization. No counterexample to the final regularized \(L\)-value is established. The full norm-one subgroup of \((L\otimes\mathbb R)^\times\) on page 23 is also not the contractible positive-real model later supplied on page 33; correcting that notation does not remove the transfer obstruction.
## Problem 2 (Major): the refined comparison omits an isogeny-degree factor
Location. Theorem 2.30, pages 24–25; Proposition 2.31, pages 25–26; `Coherent-Eisenstein-classes.tex`, lines 873–993.

Work over \(\mathbb C\), with \(d=1,\Gamma=1\), and a square CM elliptic curve \(E\). Let \(\mathfrak f=(3)\), \(\mathfrak c=(2)\). Identify \(E(\mathfrak f^{-1})\) with \(E\) by multiplication by three on the fractional ideal. The isogeny \([\mathfrak f]\) and its dual are then \([3]\). Transport the chosen bases consistently and take \(\alpha=\beta=0\), of critical type \(-\sigma\).

At the zeroth moment the bundle map \([3]_\#\) is the identity. The construction on page 24 additionally applies \([3]^{\vee *}\) to the top differential, multiplying it by three. The left side of Proposition 2.31 then applies \([3]^*\), multiplying by three again. For a zeroth specialization \(s(x)\omega\), this gives \[[3]^*({}_{[3]}\operatorname{EK}^{0,0}(f,x))=9s(x)\omega,\qquad
 \operatorname{TSym}^0([3]_\#)\operatorname{EK}^{0,0}(f,x)=s(x)\omega.\]

A nonzero admissible specialization exists without numerical approximation. Use \(f=\delta_0-\delta_t\) on \(E[2]\), with \(t\neq0\) two-torsion. It is trace zero and \(\Gamma\)-invariant. The zeroth component is a meromorphic differential with residues \(1,-1\) at two distinct points. It has two simple poles and at most two zeros on an elliptic curve. Of the eight nonzero three-torsion points, none is a pole and some \(x\) is not a zero. This \(x\) meets the original hypotheses. The displayed comparison therefore requires \(9s(x)=s(x)\neq0\).

Counterevidence. The proof’s connection and moment diagrams do express functoriality over the localized base. They account for derivative and moment factors, but not the extra top differential inserted before differentiating. Transporting all structures under the curve isomorphism does not turn two multiplication-by-three maps into the identity.

Repair and impact. This comparison needs the factor \(\deg[3]=9\). The analogous determinant composition accounts for an isogeny degree in higher dimension. Dividing the refined construction by that degree can repair the rational comparison, but is not an integral repair when the degree is not a unit. Theorem 4.9 explicitly invokes Proposition 2.31 for denominator control, so that proof needs reconstruction. No counterexample to Theorem 4.10 is asserted. The non-etale pulled-back connection is a further question recorded below.

Location. Theorem 5.27, Step 1, pages 74–75: exact sequence, \(G\), \(q\), and (5.7.1). See `p-adic-interpolation.tex`, lines 1217–1250.

For nontrivial tame modulus \(\mathfrak f\), the kernel of \[\operatorname{Gal}(L(p^\infty\mathfrak f)/L)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(L(\mathfrak f)/L)\] is \((\mathcal O_L\otimes\mathbb Z_p)^\times/\overline{\mathcal O_{\mathfrak f}^\times}\), where \(\mathcal O_{\mathfrak f}^\times=\{u:u\equiv1\bmod\mathfrak f\}\). Location. Proposition 3.13, page 35; Mellin proof, page 36. Take \(d=1,\Lambda=\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z,H(z,z)=|z|^2,\mu=0,z=w=0\). ## Problem 8 (Minor): subgroup change must track the torsion-coset stabilizer

Location. Definition 3.24 and Lemma 3.25, page 43; proof, page 44. The definition permits arbitrary torsion \(t'\), not only a \(\Gamma\)-fixed coset. It sums over \(\Gamma\backslash(\Lambda+\Gamma t')\). The lemma claims a factor \([\Gamma:\Gamma']\) under group change.

Absolute convergence holds since \(2>(0-2)/2+1=0\). The sets \(\Lambda+t'\) and \(\Lambda-t'\) are disjoint. Every \(\Gamma\)-orbit in their union has exactly one representative in \(\Lambda+t'\), and \(g(\lambda)=1/(\lambda^2|\lambda|^4)\) is even. Consequently \(E_{\Gamma'}(t',2)=E_\Gamma(t',2)\), not twice it.

This value is nonzero: the \(\lambda=t'\) term is \(10^6\). For all other \(\lambda=t'+m+in\), use shells \(\max(|m|,|n|)=k\). There are \(8k\) points and \(|\lambda|\geq k-1/10\geq9k/10\), so their absolute sum is bounded by \[8(10/9)^6\zeta(5)<16.\] Thus the two unequal multipliers cannot accidentally give the same value.

Equivalently, account for the splitting of the entire \(\Gamma\)-orbit of \(t'\) into \(\Gamma'\)-orbits. When \(t'\) is \(\Gamma\)-fixed, the printed factor is correct. These are counterevidence to a claim that every later transfer formula is false, but they do not prove Lemma 3.25 with its stated quantifiers.
## Problem 9 (Minor): a critical \(L\)-value need not be nonzero

Location. Corollary 4.15 and Remark 4.16, page 54; the repeated conclusion on page 55; corresponding introduction statement. The corollary puts \(L_{\mathfrak f}(\chi,0)/c^+_\tau\) in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}^\times\), with no nonvanishing hypothesis.

Let \(E_5:y^2=x^3-25x\), which has CM by \(\mathbb Z[i]\). Let \(\psi_5\) be its CM Hecke character over \(\mathbb Q(i)\), with infinity type \(\sigma\) under the paper’s convention. One explicit description away from \(2,5\) is \(\psi_5(\mathfrak a)=\psi_1(\mathfrak a)(5/N\mathfrak a)\), where \(\psi_1\) chooses the primary Gaussian generator congruent to \(1\bmod(2+2i)\). The CM Euler-factor identity gives \(L(\psi_5,s)=L(E_5,s)\). Set \(\chi=\psi_5N^{-1}\). Its infinity type is \(\sigma-(\sigma+\overline\sigma)=-\overline\sigma\). Thus \(s=0\) is critical by Definition 1.2: choose the attached CM type \(\{\overline\sigma\}\), \(\alpha=1,\beta=0\). Taking the exact conductor, \[L_{\mathfrak f}(\chi,0)=L(E_5,1).\]

The functional equation of \(E_5\) has sign \(-1\) (the congruent-number root-number formula for \(5\bmod8\)). Hence its completed central value equals its negative, so \(L(E_5,1)=0\). This uses no BSD conjecture or numerical rank inference. For a separate arithmetic check, \(E_1:y^2=x^3-x\) has conductor \(32\) and sign \(+1\); the coprime quadratic twist by discriminant \(5\) changes the sign by \((5/-32)=-1\). The root-number statement was checked against Elkies’ author research page [Elkies]; Tian’s treatment [Tian], selected passages on printed page 1994, also gives central vanishing for square-free \(n\equiv5,6,7\bmod8\). Its CM discussion on printed page 2005 identifies the elliptic and Hecke \(L\)-functions. These external inputs are identified as such, not claimed as newly reproved here.

Deligne’s period is nonzero, so the ratio in the corollary is zero, which is not in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}^\times\). Counterevidence and repair. The period comparison itself is a comparison of nonzero periods and can remain in \(\mathbb C^\times/\overline{\mathbb Q}^\times\). The \(L\)-value conclusion should be in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\), or explicitly assume nonvanishing. Theorem 4.10 permits zero, and its integrality assertion is not refuted by this example. This is a mathematical boundary-case correction, not a complaint about a missing reference.
## Problem 10 (Minor): the Borel comparison proof falsely asserts flabbiness

Location. Appendix A.2, page 81, proof of (A.2.1); `Relation-to-de-Rham-polylog.tex`, lines 517–558. The proof claims that an injective equivariant sheaf \(\mathcal I\) pulls/descent-transforms to a flabby sheaf \(\widetilde{\mathcal I}\) on \(E\Gamma\times_\Gamma X\). It identifies sections on an arbitrary open set with invariant sections over its projection to \(X\).

Take the smooth zero-dimensional manifold \(X=\{\ast\}\), \(\Gamma=\mathbb Z\), \(E\Gamma=\mathbb R\), and \(I=\operatorname{Map}(\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q)\) with the shift action. It is an injective \(\mathbb Z[\mathbb Z]\)-module: it is coinduced from the injective abelian group \(\mathbb Q\), and coinduction is right adjoint to the exact forgetful functor. The descended sheaf on \(S^1\) is the local system with fiber \(I\) and shift monodromy. Its global sections are \(I^\mathbb Z\), the constant sequences, isomorphic to \(\mathbb Q\). On a proper contractible arc \(U\), sections are all of \(I\). Restriction is the inclusion of constant sequences in all sequences, and is not onto; the sequence with a single \(1\) at index zero is not in its image. Thus the local system is not flabby.

Moreover \(p(q^{-1}U)=X\), so the specific second section isomorphism in the proof would identify \(I\) with \(I^\mathbb Z\) through restriction, which is false. Openness of \(p\) does not provide that isomorphism.

Counterevidence, repair, impact. The Borel/group-cohomology comparison itself is standard and is not contradicted by this example. For the circle, coinduction is group-cohomologically acyclic: the map shift minus identity on all rational sequences is onto (solve the difference equation recursively in both directions). Use acyclicity and a descent or Cartan–Leray argument, rather than flabbiness, to prove the comparison. This is an auxiliary proof error with a standard replacement, not a new obstruction to equivariant cohomology or to the corrected current model.
# Impact, unresolved checks, and counterevidence

Problems 1–5 concern core normalization, comparison, explicit-current, translation, or measure-construction steps, and meet the major threshold even if the intended repair is local. They block acceptance of the displayed proof chain as it stands. They do not collectively prove that the final Hecke \(L\)-value or interpolation theorem is false. Problems 6–10 concern broader auxiliary statements, normalization, or side consequences; their counterexamples do not automatically propagate to the locally free, invariant, or completed cases actually needed later.
Three questions remain Needs Evidence, not additional established theorem counterexamples:

1. In Theorem 2.30, page 24, the expression \([\mathfrak f]^*(\nabla^a)\) is written with target \([\mathfrak f]^*\operatorname{TSym}^a\Omega_B^1\) although \([\mathfrak f]\) need not be etale. A connection pulled back in the usual sense lands in \(\Omega_A^1\); an inverse differential or divisibility argument is needed for this target. The review has not established all higher-order integral divisibilities. Problem 2 is already a closed zeroth-order counterexample independent of this concern.

2. Lemma 5.11, page 61, needs a precise formal-connection calculation. The displayed equation \(p^2\eta_\Sigma=p\eta_\Sigma\) is attributed to multiplication by \(p\), while \([p]\) acts by \(p\) on both parts of characteristic-zero \(H^1\), and pullback also changes the coefficient functions. A Frobenius/unit-root argument would require its own definitions. The types in (5.2.6) should be reconciled with the Hodge splitting. No counterexample to the final commutative diagram has been established here.

3. Theorem 5.27, Step 4, page 79, infers that a pseudomeasure is a measure from integral values on individual Hecke characters and density of their linear span. This needs a uniform norm bound, Kummer congruences, or an Iwasawa-algebra divisibility argument. Density alone does not supply continuity. For a diagnostic, on polynomials over \(\mathbb Q_2\) let \(D(P)=P'(0)\). It is integral on all monomials, but \[D\binom{x}{m}=\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}m,\qquad m=2^r,\] has unbounded \(2\)-adic norm, although \(\binom{x}{m}\) is integer-valued on \(\mathbb Z_2\). This disproves that generic inference, not the specific pseudomeasure’s boundedness. The cited de Shalit argument in Step 2 was not retrieved and fully checked in this review.

The phrase \(i\neq d\) in the proof of Corollary 2.34, page 27, overstates the preceding vanishing \(i<d\). The low-degree spectral sequence conclusion used there only needs the latter. That local overstatement is not counted as a separate substantive problem. Likewise, the finite-character discussion on page 73 should specify the tame-congruence condition on principal generators; no additional independent counterexample is counted beyond the ray-group issue.

Recorded check: Integral fundamental-cycle normalization
analysis: Location. Proposition 2.27, pages 22–23, the homology surjection and diagram (2.4.2); Corollary 2.29, page 24. See `Coherent-Eisenstein-classes.tex`, lines 792–852, especially 811–831.

The proof asserts that, for a free finite-index \(\Gamma'\), homological transfer \(H_{d-1}(\Gamma,\mathbb Z)\to H_{d-1}(\Gamma',\mathbb Z)\) is onto. It chooses an integral preimage of a generator and requires evaluation after cohomological restriction to be \([\Gamma:\Gamma']\) times evaluation before restriction.

Take \(L=\mathbb Q(\zeta_3)\), \(d=1\), \(\Gamma=\{1,-1\}\), and \(\Gamma'=1\). Both \(H_0\)’s are \(\mathbb Z\). Inclusion-induced corestriction is the identity, whereas transfer sends \([1]\mapsto[1]+[-1]=2[1]\). It has image of index two and no generator has an integral preimage. This directly contradicts the step used to choose \(\xi\).

The obstruction is integral, not an orientation choice. Let \(R=\mathbb Z[\zeta_3,1/3]\), so \(2\notin R^\times\), and take the critical weight \(\overline\sigma-\sigma\), i.e. \(\alpha=0,\beta=1\). The coefficient line is a trivial \(\Gamma\)-module, and restriction on \(H^0(\Gamma,R)=R\) is the identity. Free-group evaluation is the identity. Diagram (2.4.2) would require an \(R\)-linear evaluation \(a\mapsto ca\) with \(2c=1\), impossible in this \(R\). This base is compatible with CM geometry: \(y^2+y=x^3\) has discriminant \(-27\), admits the \(\zeta_3\)-action, and is smooth at two. The universal group-homology failure is independent of a chosen nonzero class.

Counterevidence. For torsion-free groups of rank \(d-1\), top transfer between finite-index lattices is an isomorphism. Over \(\mathbb Q\), or after inverting the torsion order, a rational fundamental cycle provides the intended normalization. Sections explicitly restricted to torsion-free groups avoid this obstruction.

Repair and impact. Restrict the integral proposition to torsion-free groups, or invert \(|\Gamma_{\rm tors}|\), and then prove the required integral descent for congruence units. Definition 2.28, Corollary 2.29 and Lemma 5.15 use this normalization. No counterexample to the final regularized \(L\)-value is established. The full norm-one subgroup of \((L\otimes\mathbb R)^\times\) on page 23 is also not the contractible positive-real model later supplied on page 33; correcting that notation does not remove the transfer obstruction.

analysis: Location. Theorem 2.30, pages 24–25; Proposition 2.31, pages 25–26; `Coherent-Eisenstein-classes.tex`, lines 873–993.

Work over \(\mathbb C\), with \(d=1,\Gamma=1\), and a square CM elliptic curve \(E\). Let \(\mathfrak f=(3)\), \(\mathfrak c=(2)\). Identify \(E(\mathfrak f^{-1})\) with \(E\) by multiplication by three on the fractional ideal. The isogeny \([\mathfrak f]\) and its dual are then \([3]\). Transport the chosen bases consistently and take \(\alpha=\beta=0\), of critical type \(-\sigma\).

At the zeroth moment the bundle map \([3]_\#\) is the identity. The construction on page 24 additionally applies \([3]^{\vee *}\) to the top differential, multiplying it by three. The left side of Proposition 2.31 then applies \([3]^*\), multiplying by three again. For a zeroth specialization \(s(x)\omega\), this gives \[[3]^*({}_{[3]}\operatorname{EK}^{0,0}(f,x))=9s(x)\omega,\qquad
 \operatorname{TSym}^0([3]_\#)\operatorname{EK}^{0,0}(f,x)=s(x)\omega.\]

A nonzero admissible specialization exists without numerical approximation. Use \(f=\delta_0-\delta_t\) on \(E[2]\), with \(t\neq0\) two-torsion. It is trace zero and \(\Gamma\)-invariant. The zeroth component is a meromorphic differential with residues \(1,-1\) at two distinct points. It has two simple poles and at most two zeros on an elliptic curve. Of the eight nonzero three-torsion points, none is a pole and some \(x\) is not a zero. This \(x\) meets the original hypotheses. The displayed comparison therefore requires \(9s(x)=s(x)\neq0\).

Counterevidence. The proof’s connection and moment diagrams do express functoriality over the localized base. They account for derivative and moment factors, but not the extra top differential inserted before differentiating. Transporting all structures under the curve isomorphism does not turn two multiplication-by-three maps into the identity.

Repair and impact. This comparison needs the factor \(\deg[3]=9\). The analogous determinant composition accounts for an isogeny degree in higher dimension. Dividing the refined construction by that degree can repair the rational comparison, but is not an integral repair when the degree is not a unit. Theorem 4.9 explicitly invokes Proposition 2.31 for denominator control, so that proof needs reconstruction. No counterexample to Theorem 4.10 is asserted. The non-etale pulled-back connection is a further question recorded below.

Write \(\varphi:A'=A_{(n)}\to A\) for the etale isogeny. Equation (5.5.1) defines \(f'=\varphi^*f\) on the entire \(D'=\varphi^{-1}D\). At \(\mathfrak s=\mathfrak t=0\), the theorem states \[\vartheta_A(f,x)=\sum_{a\in\ker\varphi}

analysis: Location. Theorem 5.27, Step 1, pages 74–75: exact sequence, \(G\), \(q\), and (5.7.1). See `p-adic-interpolation.tex`, lines 1217–1250.

For nontrivial tame modulus \(\mathfrak f\), the kernel of \[\operatorname{Gal}(L(p^\infty\mathfrak f)/L)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(L(\mathfrak f)/L)\] is \((\mathcal O_L\otimes\mathbb Z_p)^\times/\overline{\mathcal O_{\mathfrak f}^\times}\), where \(\mathcal O_{\mathfrak f}^\times=\{u:u\equiv1\bmod\mathfrak f\}\). The proof quotients by the closure of all \(\mathcal O_L^\times\).

Take \(L=\mathbb Q(i)\), \(\mathfrak f=(3)\), \(p=5\). The class number is one; the four units have distinct residues modulo three, so \(\mathcal O_{\mathfrak f}^\times=1\). Principal ideals modulo generators congruent to one give \[|\operatorname{Cl}(3)|=(9-1)/4=2.\] Since \(\mathcal O_L/(5^n)\simeq(\mathbb Z/5^n)^2\), \[|(\mathcal O_L/5^n)^\times|=16\,5^{2n-2},\quad
 |\operatorname{Cl}(3\cdot5^n)|=32\,5^{2n-2}.\] The onto map to \(\operatorname{Cl}(3)\) therefore has kernel of order \(16\,5^{2n-2}\). Quotienting the local units by all four global units instead gives \(4\,5^{2n-2}\). At \(n=1\) these are \(16\) and \(4\). analysis: Location. Proposition 3.13, page 35; Mellin proof, page 36. Take \(d=1,\Lambda=\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z,H(z,z)=|z|^2,\mu=0,z=w=0\). The uncompleted series is \[K(s)=\sum_{(m,n)\neq(0,0)}(m^2+n^2)^{-s}=4\zeta(s)\beta(s).\] The equality follows by grouping representations as sums of two squares; \(r_2(N)=4\sum_{a\mid N}\chi_{-4}(a)\). Using \(\zeta(0)=-1/2\), \(\beta(0)=1/2\), and \(\beta(1)=\pi/4\), one gets \[K(0)=-1,\quad \operatorname{Res}_{s=0}K(s)=0,\quad \operatorname{Res}_{s=1}K(s)=\pi.\] For example \(\beta(s)=4^{-s}(\zeta(s,1/4)-\zeta(s,3/4))\) and \(\zeta(0,a)=1/2-a\) give \(\beta(0)=1/2\); the alternating odd reciprocal series gives \(\beta(1)=\pi/4\). The standard zeta residue at one is one.

The printed residues are instead \(-1\) at zero and \(1\) at one for this unit-volume example. They are exactly the residues of \(\pi^{-s}\Gamma(s)K(s)\). Counterevidence and repair. The Mellin integral in the proof already represents the completed expression, and later current formulas contain \(\Gamma(s)K(s)\). State the residue assertion for that completed function and adjust wording on possible poles. This local analytic normalization error is separate from the missing current sign in Problem 3. No claim about the functional-equation phase in full generality is certified here.

analysis: Location. Definition 3.24 and Lemma 3.25, page 43; proof, page 44. The definition permits arbitrary torsion \(t'\), not only a \(\Gamma\)-fixed coset. It sums over \(\Gamma\backslash(\Lambda+\Gamma t')\). The lemma claims a factor \([\Gamma:\Gamma']\) under group change.

Take \(L=\mathbb Q(i),\Lambda=\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z,\Gamma=\{\pm1\},\Gamma'=1\), \(t'=1/10,\alpha=2,\beta=0,s=2\). Type \(-2\sigma\) is critical and trivial on \(\Gamma\). Absolute convergence holds since \(2>(0-2)/2+1=0\). The sets \(\Lambda+t'\) and \(\Lambda-t'\) are disjoint. Every \(\Gamma\)-orbit in their union has exactly one representative in \(\Lambda+t'\), and \(g(\lambda)=1/(\lambda^2|\lambda|^4)\) is even. Consequently \(E_{\Gamma'}(t',2)=E_\Gamma(t',2)\), not twice it.

This value is nonzero: the \(\lambda=t'\) term is \(10^6\). For all other \(\lambda=t'+m+in\), use shells \(\max(|m|,|n|)=k\). There are \(8k\) points and \(|\lambda|\geq k-1/10\geq9k/10\), so their absolute sum is bounded by \[8(10/9)^6\zeta(5)<16.\] Thus the two unequal multipliers cannot accidentally give the same value.

Repair. For abelian \(\Gamma\), the orbitwise factor is \([\Gamma_{t'}:\Gamma_{t'}\cap\Gamma']\), with stabilizer taken modulo \(\Lambda\). Equivalently, account for the splitting of the entire \(\Gamma\)-orbit of \(t'\) into \(\Gamma'\)-orbits. When \(t'\) is \(\Gamma\)-fixed, the printed factor is correct. Weighted sums over all torsion orbits can also recover the aggregate factor needed later. These are counterevidence to a claim that every later transfer formula is false, but they do not prove Lemma 3.25 with its stated quantifiers.
result: Impact: Auxiliary lemma quantifiers false; not all later aggregate formulas refuted.

analysis: Location. Appendix A.2, page 81, proof of (A.2.1); `Relation-to-de-Rham-polylog.tex`, lines 517–558. The proof claims that an injective equivariant sheaf \(\mathcal I\) pulls/descent-transforms to a flabby sheaf \(\widetilde{\mathcal I}\) on \(E\Gamma\times_\Gamma X\). It identifies sections on an arbitrary open set with invariant sections over its projection to \(X\).

Take the smooth zero-dimensional manifold \(X=\{\ast\}\), \(\Gamma=\mathbb Z\), \(E\Gamma=\mathbb R\), and \(I=\operatorname{Map}(\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q)\) with the shift action. It is an injective \(\mathbb Z[\mathbb Z]\)-module: it is coinduced from the injective abelian group \(\mathbb Q\), and coinduction is right adjoint to the exact forgetful functor. The descended sheaf on \(S^1\) is the local system with fiber \(I\) and shift monodromy. Its global sections are \(I^\mathbb Z\), the constant sequences, isomorphic to \(\mathbb Q\). On a proper contractible arc \(U\), sections are all of \(I\). Restriction is the inclusion of constant sequences in all sequences, and is not onto; the sequence with a single \(1\) at index zero is not in its image. Thus the local system is not flabby.

Moreover \(p(q^{-1}U)=X\), so the specific second section isomorphism in the proof would identify \(I\) with \(I^\mathbb Z\) through restriction, which is false. Openness of \(p\) does not provide that isomorphism.

Counterevidence, repair, impact. The Borel/group-cohomology comparison itself is standard and is not contradicted by this example. For the circle, coinduction is group-cohomologically acyclic: the map shift minus identity on all rational sequences is onto (solve the difference equation recursively in both directions). Use acyclicity and a descent or Cartan–Leray argument, rather than flabbiness, to prove the comparison. This is an auxiliary proof error with a standard replacement, not a new obstruction to equivariant cohomology or to the corrected current model.
result: Impact: Auxiliary proof incorrect, standard comparison not refuted.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use acyclicity and descent/Cartan-Leray argument.

report: Abstract: The reviewed author-hosted proof develops Euclidean and hyperbolic characterizations of Weil–Petersson curves. All 78 source pages were read and visually inspected. Three core proof estimates fail in explicit admissible examples: the upper Fubini estimate for Möbius energy, the Euclidean distortion estimate for normal reflection, and the boundary-curvature estimate in the renormalized-area argument. Two peripheral claims require restricted parameter ranges. The first core estimate has an analytic repair supplied here; general repairs for the latter two remain unverified. A single-basepoint dyadic-cylinder interpretation and a smooth-welding interpretation are separately clarified, with the manuscript’s own counterevidence retained. No counterexample to the main Weil–Petersson equivalences is established.
Title: Scientific initial review of M25-0017
# Identity, version, and page convention

Christopher J. Bishop, Weil-Petersson curves, \(\beta\)-numbers, and minimal surfaces, associated journal DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.202.1.2 (https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2025.202.1.2). The actual input is the author-hosted black-and-white Annals proof at https://www.math.stonybrook.edu/~bishop/papers/wp_annals_bw.pdf. Its PDF metadata records creation on 17 June 2025. It has provisional pages 1–78, whereas the publisher metadata gives journal pages 111–188. The DOI is an identity link, not evidence of byte-for-byte or mathematical equivalence to the journal final.

# Definitions, assumptions, and dependency limits

A chord-arc Jordan curve \(\Gamma\) has a constant \(C\) such that the length \(\ell(x,y)\) of its shorter connecting subarc satisfies \(|x-y|\leq\ell(x,y)\leq C|x-y|\). Its unit tangent \(\tau\) exists almost everywhere. The central Euclidean comparison concerns \[\operatorname{M\ddot ob}(\Gamma)
 =\int_\Gamma\!\int_\Gamma\left(\frac1{|z-w|^2}-\frac1{\ell(z,w)^2}\right)|dz|\,|dw|
\quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \int_\Gamma\!\int_\Gamma\frac{|\tau(x)-\tau(y)|^2}{|x-y|^2}|dx|\,|dy|.\] These are nonnegative integrals; Tonelli is available even before finiteness is known. The admissible integration domain after interchanging variables still matters.

The geometric conditions include a scale-normalized \(\beta\) number for \(3Q\cap\Gamma\), a reflection-distortion number \(\rho(Q)\) measuring Euclidean departure from isometry, and a fat-ball quantity \(\varepsilon_\Gamma(Q)\). In hyperbolic upper-half-space the operative metric for the curvature/area calculations is \(ds_\rho^2=(|dx|^2+dt^2)/t^2\), of curvature \(-1\). The thickness \(\delta\) of the hyperbolic convex hull vanishes for a round circle. A totally geodesic hemisphere then has both principal curvatures zero. These elementary special cases obey, rather than evade, the hypotheses used in Problems 2 and 3.

For a minimal surface \(S\subset\mathbb H^3\), its principal curvatures are \(\pm\kappa\), and \(K=-1-\kappa^2\). For a regular height truncation \(S_t\), \[A_\rho(S_t)-L_\rho(\partial S_t)
 =-2\pi\chi(S_t)-\int_{S_t}\kappa^2\,dA_\rho
   +\int_{\partial S_t}(\kappa_g-1)\,dL_\rho.\] The final boundary integral must tend to zero to obtain the stated formula for renormalized area. Finiteness of an area integral by itself is not a pointwise or trace estimate.

The paper’s existence assertions about a minimal disk, its assertions about every minimal surface with a given boundary, and its statements for a surface with finite Euler characteristic are different quantifiers. They are kept separate throughout this report. None of the elementary counterexamples below refutes the existence of a suitable minimal spanning surface for a WP curve.
# Supported substantive problems

Problem 1 (Major: the upper Fubini estimate uses a divergent enlargement).  Location and source claim. Lemma 9.1, especially the last chain of comparisons on page 36, is used to identify Definitions 7 and 8 and hence to prove Theorem 1.2. With \(s=\ell(\Gamma)/2\), the printed upper comparison replaces the domain \(\sigma(x,y)=\{(z,w):x,y\in\gamma(z,w)\}\) by the product of two length-\(s\) arcs and writes \[J(x,y)=
 \int_{z\in\sigma(x,y,s)}\int_{w\in\sigma(y,x,s)}
       |x-w|^{-4}|dz|\,|dw|
 \simeq
 \int_{w\in\sigma(y,x,s)}|x-w|^{-3}|dw|
 \simeq |x-y|^{-2}.\] Here \(\gamma(z,w)\) is the shorter arc. The first displayed comparison is false.

Complete admissible check. Take the unit circle, a smooth closed chord-arc Jordan curve, with angular coordinates \(x=0\) and \(y=d\), \(0<d<\pi/8\). Its total length is \(2\pi\), so \(s=\pi\). The two arcs in the printed product are \([-\pi,0]\) and \([d,d+\pi]\), understood modulo \(2\pi\). Since the integrand is independent of \(z\), \[J(d)=\pi\int_d^{d+\pi}\frac{dw}{(2\sin(w/2))^4}
      \sim \frac{\pi}{3d^3}\qquad(d\downarrow0).\] The last claimed quantity is \((2\sin(d/2))^{-2}\sim d^{-2}\), so no uniform comparison holds. On this circle \(|\tau(x)-\tau(y)|^2=|x-y|^2\); the final tangent integral is finite, whereas the printed intermediate integral has a local logarithmic divergence after multiplication by this tangent difference and integration in \(d\).

Merely changing the denominator to \(|z-w|^4\) does not repair the argument. The two semicircles overlap on an arc of length \(d\) (represent the first as \([\pi,2\pi]\)). Their product contains an open segment of the diagonal, and \(\int\int|z-w|^{-4}|dz|\,|dw|=\infty\). Thus a domain correction is necessary in addition to any typographical correction.

Analytic repair. Retain the shorter-arc condition. For \(d=\ell(x,y)\leq\ell(\Gamma)/8\), parametrize \(z\) at backward arclength \(a\geq0\) from \(x\) and \(w\) at forward arclength \(b\geq0\) from \(y\). The correct domain satisfies \[a+b+d\leq \ell(\Gamma)/2.\] The chord-arc hypothesis gives \(|z-w|\geq C^{-1}(a+b+d)\) on this domain. Including the opposite orientation changes only a factor of two. Consequently the inner kernel is bounded above by \[2C^4\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty(a+b+d)^{-4}\,da\,db
 =\frac{C^4}{3d^2}.\] For a lower bound, restrict to \(0\leq a,b\leq d\). This is admissible because \(3d\leq3\ell(\Gamma)/8<\ell(\Gamma)/2\), and the chord length is at most \(a+b+d\leq3d\). The kernel is at least \(d^2/(3d)^4=1/(81d^2)\) for one orientation. Pairs \((x,y)\) outside this small-separation region contribute a finite bounded amount: every containing shorter arc has length at least \(\ell(\Gamma)/8\), hence its chord is bounded below by the chord-arc hypothesis. This proves the intended comparability using the actual domain.

Counterevidence, impact, and repair status. The circle satisfies both claimed finiteness conclusions. The preceding proof repairs the central comparison and supports the theorem rather than refuting it. Nevertheless the printed upper derivation is invalid in an admissible, maximally regular case and lies directly on the proof of Theorem 1.2, which supports Major under standard 0.7.1. The exact quadrant integral and illustrative values of \(d^3J(d)\) are recorded in `independent_checks.json`; the analytic proof above, not those finite numerical samples, establishes the repair.

Problem 2 (Major: hyperbolic flatness does not eliminate Euclidean reflection distortion).  Location and source claim. In the proof of Lemma 18.2 on page 53, the center of the boundary sphere of the normal hyperplane at \(z=(x,t)\) is asserted to lie within \(O(t\sup_w\max_j|\kappa_j(w)|)\) of \(x\). The normal antipodal construction is then used to assert \(\rho(Q)=O(K_r(z))\), where \(K_r\) bounds the principal curvatures on a fixed hyperbolic ball. This is the quantitative step in the higher-dimensional implication (16)\(\Rightarrow\)(13).

Parameters and assumptions. Set \(n=2\), let \(\Gamma=\{|z|=1\}\subset\mathbb R^2\), and let \[S=\{(x,y,t):x^2+y^2+t^2=1,\ t>0\}\subset\mathbb H^3.\] This is a smooth, properly embedded, complete, totally geodesic disk with asymptotic boundary \(\Gamma\). Both principal curvatures are zero everywhere. In particular, they tend to zero at the boundary and their square integral is zero, so the surface obeys the curvature requirements of Definition 16. Any fixed-ball supremum \(K_r\) is zero.

At \(p=(x,0,t)\in S\), \(0<x<1\), the Euclidean center of the normal geodesic is at horizontal coordinate \(a=1/x\). Its endpoints are \[r_-=\frac{1-t}{x},\qquad r_+=\frac{1+t}{x},
 \qquad r_-r_+=1.\] These formulas follow by taking a Euclidean circle orthogonal to the plane \(t=0\) and tangent at \(p\) to the Euclidean normal \((x,0,t)\); the upper-half-space metric is conformal, so the normal direction is unchanged. Thus \[a-x=\frac{t^2}{x}>0,\] whereas the asserted \(O(t\sup|\kappa|)\) is identically zero. This remains a boundary counterexample: take \(x=(1-u^2)/(1+u^2)\), \(t=2u/(1+u^2)\) and let \(u\downarrow0\).

The antipodal pairing of the two endpoints is precisely \[R(z)=\frac1{\overline z}.\] Its Euclidean differential has norm \(|z|^{-2}\). In a nondegenerate Whitney cube off the unit circle this differs from one at some point, so the local distance distortion \(\rho(Q)\) is positive. The proposed bound by \(K_r=0\) is false.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. Hyperbolic isometric normalization at a point cannot remove the Euclidean scale distortion in the definition of \(\rho(Q)\); a Möbius transformation is not a Euclidean isometry. For this same circle, inversion does satisfy \(\rho(Q)=O(\operatorname{diam}Q)\) near the circle, and the resulting square sum is finite: there are \(O(h^{-1})\) relevant cubes at side length \(h\), each contributing \(O(h^2)\). Hence the existence of a reflection in Definition 13 survives.

The paper itself recognizes on page 49 that \(\delta=0\) for a circle while \(\varepsilon_\Gamma\) is nonzero, so a size term is needed when passing from hyperbolic to Euclidean geometry. That observation is relevant counterevidence against reading the omitted scale term as harmless.

Impact and remaining repair. The displayed estimate cannot prove the central implication as written. A possible form of a replacement must include a scale or background-circle term, for example a properly normalized \(O(\operatorname{diam}Q)\) contribution, in addition to curvature information. This report does not assert a general bound of that form without proof. One must also justify replacing an \(L^2\) curvature integral by an \(L^2\) integral of fixed-ball suprema. For a general smooth function such a replacement fails: disjoint bumps of amplitude \(k^{-1/2}\) supported in disks of radius \(2^{-k}\) have finite square integral, whereas their fixed-radius local suprema have divergent square integral on disjoint fixed-radius neighborhoods. This diagnostic is not a constructed surface counterexample, but identifies an additional estimate the repair must supply. No counterexample to the existential equivalence is claimed.

Problem 3 (Major: the boundary error estimate fails on a totally geodesic disk).  Location and source claim. Lemma 20.1, page 55, asserts \(\kappa_g=1+O(\delta^2)\) and equation (20.1), \[\int_{\partial S_t}(\kappa_g-1)\,dL_\rho
       =O\!\left(\int_{\partial S_t}\delta^2\,dL_\rho\right),\] then uses a trace-to-area estimate to make the left side vanish. This is central to (15)\(\Rightarrow\)(19), Corollary 1.7 and formula (1.6).

Full check. Use the same unit hemisphere as in Problem Problem 2 (#prob:reflection). Its round boundary is WP, its convex hull is the totally geodesic plane itself, \(\delta\equiv0\), \(\kappa\equiv0\), and \(\chi(S)=1\). Every \(0<t<1\) is a regular truncation height, so all conditions of the displayed calculation hold.

Write \(r=\sqrt{1-t^2}\). Direct integration of the induced hyperbolic metric gives \[L_\rho(\partial S_t)=\frac{2\pi r}{t},\qquad
 A_\rho(S_t)=2\pi\left(\frac1t-1\right).\] Intrinsically \(S\) is the hyperbolic plane and this section is a geodesic circle with \(\cosh R=1/t\). Therefore \[\kappa_g=\coth R=\frac1{\sqrt{1-t^2}}>1,\qquad
 \int_{\partial S_t}(\kappa_g-1)\,dL_\rho
   =\frac{2\pi(1-\sqrt{1-t^2})}{t}
   =\pi t+O(t^3)>0.\] The right side of (20.1) is zero. The assertion that the horizontal curvature contribution is bounded by the surface’s principal curvatures also fails in this example: the surface is totally geodesic, while its horizontal sections are Euclidean circles.

Counterevidence and exact consequence. The error nevertheless tends to zero. Indeed \[\lim_{t\downarrow0}\{A_\rho(S_t)-L_\rho(\partial S_t)\}=-2\pi,\] which agrees with the claimed renormalized-area formula. Thus this is a counterexample to the proof estimate, not to Corollary 1.7. The example exhibits the missing background term explicitly: \(\kappa_g-1=\tfrac12t^2+O(t^4)\) even when \(\delta=0\).

Repair requirements. A valid argument must retain such a scale term and control its integrated boundary contribution for the surfaces under consideration, as well as establish a genuine trace estimate. On the round disk an \(O(t^2)\) term integrates to \(O(t)\), but this special case is not a proof of the general estimate. The printed annulus \(A_t=S_t\setminus S_{t+1}\) does not escape compact subsets as \(t\downarrow0\), so finite total integral does not imply its integral tends to zero. A geometric-height annulus such as \(S_t\setminus S_{2t}\) would have the correct escaping property; its required comparison with the boundary trace still needs proof. The formula involving distance from an interior point at the end of page 55 concerns geodesic spheres and retains a \(\coth r\) term; it does not justify dropping the corresponding error for height sections. General repair and the all-minimal-surface scope remain unverified.

Problem 4 (Minor: the half-space distance comparison needs a small-gap hypothesis).  Location and claim. Lemma 16.1, page 49, states that disjoint Euclidean balls of equal radius \(r\) separated by \(\varepsilon\) have corresponding hyperbolic half-spaces at distance \(\rho\simeq\sqrt{\varepsilon/r}\), without restricting \(\varepsilon/r\).

Complete calculation. Let \(\eta=\varepsilon/r>0\). In the two-dimensional section through the centers the boundary geodesics are semicircles of radius \(r\) with centers \(2r+\varepsilon\) apart. Their inversive distance gives \[\cosh\rho=\frac{(2r+\varepsilon)^2-2r^2}{2r^2}
          =1+2\eta+\frac{\eta^2}{2},
 \qquad
 \rho=2\operatorname{arcosh}(1+\eta/2).\] These balls are disjoint for every \(\eta>0\), so they meet all printed assumptions. At small \(\eta\), \(\rho/\sqrt\eta\to2\). At large \(\eta\), \(\rho=2\log\eta+O(\eta^{-1})\) and \(\rho/\sqrt\eta\to0\). The stated two-sided uniform comparison therefore fails.

Counterevidence, impact and verified correction. The proof uses a local expansion whose optimizing height would exceed the radius when the gap is large. The next lemma’s application explicitly requires \(\varepsilon_\Gamma(Q)<1/100\), so the relevant small-gap use is not refuted. Restricting \(0<\eta\leq\eta_0\) for a fixed finite \(\eta_0\) gives a valid square-root comparison, by continuity and the limit at zero. The exact formula above works for all positive gaps. This is a Minor range error, not a failure of the subsequent small-thickness implication.

Problem 5 (Minor: smooth curves need not have finite knot energy at the claimed endpoint).  Location and claim. Section 23, page 61, defines \[E^{j,p}(\Gamma)
 =\int_\Gamma\!\int_\Gamma
   \left(|x-y|^{-j}-\ell(x,y)^{-j}\right)^p\,|dx|\,|dy|\] and asserts finiteness for smooth curves if \(jp\leq2p+1\).

Counterexample with all conditions. Take the smooth embedded unit circle, \(j=3\) and \(p=1\). These parameters satisfy \(jp=2p+1=3\). For shorter arclength \(h\downarrow0\) the chord is \(2\sin(h/2)\), and \[(2\sin(h/2))^{-3}-h^{-3}
 =\frac1{8h}+\frac{17h}{1920}+O(h^3).\] The positive integrand consequently has a logarithmically divergent integral near the diagonal. Thus \(E^{3,1}(\Gamma)=\infty\) despite the asserted smoothness and endpoint condition.

Repair and limits. For a unit-speed smooth curve with nonzero curvature at a point, \[|x(s+h)-x(s)|=|h|\left(1-\frac{\kappa(s)^2h^2}{24}+O(h^3)\right).\] For \(j,p>0\) the energy integrand has leading order \((j\kappa(s)^2/24)^p|h|^{p(2-j)}\). Local integrability at nonzero curvature requires the strict inequality \(jp<2p+1\). The unit circle calculation rigorously excludes the printed equality case without relying on any numerical integration. The main Möbius energy corresponds to \(j=2,p=1\) and is strictly inside this range. The issue is therefore peripheral and Minor; no failure of Theorem 1.2 is inferred from it.
# Scope clarifications and counterevidence
These items are not added to the supported Major/Minor totals. Their purpose is to state exactly which reading is justified and to prevent an overbroad adverse conclusion.
## A single dyadic cylinder is insufficient, but the main theorem already quantifies correctly

Definition 20 on page 28 refers to the dyadic cylinder \(X\) corresponding to \(\Gamma\). Read in isolation as a condition on one basepoint, it is too weak. Let \(\Gamma\) be the boundary of the unit square, of length four, and choose a vertex as the arclength origin. Its \(2^n\)-vertex equalarclength polygon equals the square for \(n\geq2\), with only collinear subdivision. For \(n=1\) its closed two-edge length is \(2\sqrt2\), so \[\sum_{n\geq1}2^n\{\ell(\Gamma)-\ell(\Gamma_n)\}=8-4\sqrt2<\infty.\] Using exactly the page-28 layers \(\Gamma_n\times(2^{-n},2^{-n+1}]\), for \(0<t<1/2\) the lateral area and bottom-section length satisfy \[A_\rho(X_t)=2\sqrt2+4(1/t-2),\qquad
 L_\rho(\partial X_t)=4/t.\] The renormalized area is the finite constant \(2\sqrt2-8\). Adding or changing finitely many upper layers or caps only changes a finite constant. The harmless indexing inconsistency in Section 12 does not affect this example.
The square is not WP. Across a corner, the two unit tangents differ by a fixed nonzero vector and \[\int_0^\varepsilon\int_0^\varepsilon\frac{da\,db}{(a+b)^2}=\infty.\]

Equivalently, for dyadic \(Q=(-h,0]^2\) adjacent to a corner at the origin, \(3Q\cap\Gamma\) contains \((0,0),(h,0),(0,h)\). The smallest strip half-width containing this triangle is \(h/(2\sqrt2)\). With the paper’s normalized \(\beta\) this gives \(\beta_\Gamma(Q)\geq1/(3\sqrt2)\) at every sufficiently fine scale, and the square sum diverges.

The omitted uniformity is real: shifting the arclength origin by \(1/3\) yields corner fractions \(1/3\) and \(2/3\) at every dyadic scale \(n\geq2\), so \[2^n\{\ell(\Gamma)-\ell(\Gamma_n)\}
 =16\left(1-\frac{\sqrt5}{3}\right)>0.\] This series diverges.

Counterevidence controlling the judgment. Theorem 1.3 on page 4 and Lemma 12.1 on page 40 explicitly require every basepoint with a uniform bound. Those statements exclude this square and are not refuted. Definition 20’s reference to Theorem 1.3 can reasonably be read as importing that qualification. Accordingly this report records a scope clarification: carry the universal basepoint and uniform-bound requirement explicitly into Definition 20 and its use in Lemma 22.1 on page 60. It does not count the abbreviated wording as a separate demonstrated core defect.
## Smooth weldings require a nondegeneracy qualification

The transition across pages 15–16 says that an \(H^s\) welding and an \(H^s\) arclength parametrization are equivalent for \(s>3/2\), using Hölder continuity of the welding derivative to infer nonvanishing conformal derivatives and biLipschitz behavior. Hölder continuity alone does not imply a positive lower bound.

For the unqualified interpretation there is an explicit test. Let \(M(z)=z/(1+z)\), \[f(z)=M(z^{1/2})\quad(z\in\mathbb H^+),\qquad
 g(w)=M(w^{3/2})\quad(w\in\mathbb H^-),\] with arguments in \((0,\pi)\) and \((-\pi,0)\), respectively. The image of \(f\) is the upper half-disk bounded by the segment \([0,1]\) and the upper semicircle of radius \(1/2\); the image of \(g\) is its complementary domain on the sphere. Both are conformal bijections. Their welding on the extended real line is \(f^{-1}g(t)=t^3\): for \(t<0\), the lower-branch power is \(i|t|^{3/2}\) and the upper-branch square root of \(-|t|^3\) is the same. After Cayley changes of source coordinates the welding is a smooth circle homeomorphism. At infinity its local expression is again \(u^3\), and it is quasisymmetric. It belongs to every \(H^s\), but its derivative vanishes at two points. The curve has two right-angle corners, so its arclength tangent is not in \(H^{1/2}\) by the preceding corner integral.

The next paragraph explicitly discusses \(H^s\) diffeomorphisms, and an implicit restriction to the WP class could also exclude this example. Consequently the precise correction is to distinguish an \(H^s\) circle homeomorphism from a nondegenerate \(H^s\) diffeomorphism and state the intended domain of the equivalence. This report does not count the example as refuting a theorem restricted to WP weldings or diffeomorphisms. It also does not claim to have reproved the full higher-\(s\) equivalence under the corrected hypotheses.
## Restore the scale and incidence conditions in the fat-ball definition

The planar wording around Definition 14 on page 23 must be read with the incidence and normalization visible in Figure 6 and the later construction: the near-contact point lies in the relevant cube and the gap is measured relative to its diameter, while the ball radii are controlled from below at the appropriate inverse scale. If one omits incidence and uses only a line through \(Q\), two arbitrarily large balls can be placed arbitrarily far along that line, separated by an arbitrarily small gap and missing any fixed bounded curve. The resulting infimum would vanish even for a square. The later proof on pages 46–48 uses the intended local geometry. This is recorded as restoration of the definition, not inflated into a separate scientific error after ignoring its figure and usage.

Other observed notation or extraction discrepancies are excluded from the issue count. In particular, the page-18 image includes the square root in the triangle-curvature expression, and the page-7 curvature identity has the intended absolute-value bars. Fractional tangent phases require their circle factor and orientation convention; these do not produce a new counterexample to Theorem 1.1. Obvious indexing, naming, and survey-formula slips are not used as substitutes for substantive findings.
# Needs Evidence and dependence of the overall claims
## NE1: the quantifier over all minimal surfaces

Theorem 1.6(4), page 7, and page 55 involve every minimal surface, whereas Lemma 19.1 on page 53 is stated for an embedded minimal disk. The step from small convex-hull thickness to uniform local curvature, a single boundary sheet, finite Euler characteristic, and the integrated estimate requires hypotheses that control this distinction.

Selected portions of Seppi’s arXiv:1411.3412v4 were inspected: Lemma 4.11, the local compactness discussion, Proposition 4.14, Lemma 4.15 and formula (32). Proposition 4.14 allows a fixed quasicircle bound \(K_0\) and a fixed radius, with constants depending on them; it must not be misrepresented as requiring \(K_0\) arbitrarily close to one merely to state that local estimate.

Huang–Lowe–Seppi, arXiv:2309.00599v2, Section 1.4, explicitly discusses a stability requirement in the earlier compactness argument, and removes it in a globally small-quasicircle regime using a new uniqueness result. This is a relevant later dependency, not evidence that every arbitrary WP boundary satisfies that global smallness hypothesis. Only the indicated selected portions were consulted, not either entire external proof.

The pending task is to give a complete localization and stability/topology argument for every surface in the original quantifier, or explicitly restrict the affected intermediate result. No surface violating the final theorem with a WP asymptotic boundary has been constructed here. NE1 therefore remains Needs Evidence rather than a supported theorem counterexample.
## NE2: the reverse exhaustion argument and boundary regularity

Definition 18 on page 28 assumes finite Euler characteristic and a nested compact exhaustion with controlled length minus area. In Section 21, pages 56–59, the proof uses a height end that is an annulus, a small-curvature regime, and then a sharper Euler-characteristic constant. Finite Euler characteristic alone does not identify a particular height function’s regular sublevel sets with the desired annular exhaustion. The implication to the stated height-based limit, especially in the non-WP case where the desired value is \(-\infty\), needs those transitions supplied.

Similarly, the extension of the boundary graphical and normal-foliation arguments from the regularity assumptions of the cited Lin result to the WP setting is asserted in Sections 18 and 22. The full Lin paper was not acquired and checked here. The report records this dependency rather than inventing a regularity theorem. The Fiala-type differential inequality and its intended geometric use were inspected; a complete proof of all the exhaustion and foliation prerequisites was not obtained. This is a remaining proof obligation, not a fabricated counterexample.
## What survives, what needs repair, and later versions

Problems 1–3 affect different edges of the equivalence diagram. The correct Fubini argument restores the tangent/Möbius edge. The normal-reflection and height-trace bounds need additional geometric work; their round examples show exactly why an estimate depending only on extrinsic hyperbolic curvature or thickness is insufficient. These facts do not negate the other Euclidean characterizations, nor do they show that the stated renormalized-area limit is false. Problems 4 and 5 have restricted, analytically verified repairs and do not undermine their cited main applications.

A narrow public search for an author correction or an erratum specific to this paper did not identify one. This is a bounded negative search, not proof that no correction exists. The author-hosted proof and the journal final were not compared, so adoption or correction status in the final publication is unknown. The selected later minimal-surface paper is used only to clarify a dependency. No new empirical experiment or author-code execution is needed to verify the explicit failures in this report; general geometric repair requires proof.

A chord-arc Jordan curve \(\Gamma\) has a constant \(C\) such that the length \(\ell(x,y)\) of its shorter connecting subarc satisfies \(|x-y|\leq\ell(x,y)\leq C|x-y|\). Its unit tangent \(\tau\) exists almost everywhere. The central Euclidean comparison concerns \[\operatorname{M\ddot ob}(\Gamma)
 =\int_\Gamma\!\int_\Gamma\left(\frac1{|z-w|^2}-\frac1{\ell(z,w)^2}\right)|dz|\,|dw|
\quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \int_\Gamma\!\int_\Gamma\frac{|\tau(x)-\tau(y)|^2}{|x-y|^2}|dx|\,|dy|.\] These are nonnegative integrals; Tonelli is available even before finiteness is known. The admissible integration domain after interchanging variables still matters.

Upper Fubini product-domain kernel is comparable to |x-y|^-2.
analysis:
Location and source claim. Lemma 9.1, especially the last chain of comparisons on page 36, is used to identify Definitions 7 and 8 and hence to prove Theorem 1.2. With \(s=\ell(\Gamma)/2\), the printed upper comparison replaces the domain \(\sigma(x,y)=\{(z,w):x,y\in\gamma(z,w)\}\) by the product of two length-\(s\) arcs and writes \[J(x,y)=
 \int_{z\in\sigma(x,y,s)}\int_{w\in\sigma(y,x,s)}
       |x-w|^{-4}|dz|\,|dw|
 \simeq
 \int_{w\in\sigma(y,x,s)}|x-w|^{-3}|dw|
 \simeq |x-y|^{-2}.\] Here \(\gamma(z,w)\) is the shorter arc. The first displayed comparison is false.

Complete admissible check. Take the unit circle, a smooth closed chord-arc Jordan curve, with angular coordinates \(x=0\) and \(y=d\), \(0<d<\pi/8\). Its total length is \(2\pi\), so \(s=\pi\). The two arcs in the printed product are \([-\pi,0]\) and \([d,d+\pi]\), understood modulo \(2\pi\). Since the integrand is independent of \(z\), \[J(d)=\pi\int_d^{d+\pi}\frac{dw}{(2\sin(w/2))^4}
      \sim \frac{\pi}{3d^3}\qquad(d\downarrow0).\] The last claimed quantity is \((2\sin(d/2))^{-2}\sim d^{-2}\), so no uniform comparison holds. On this circle \(|\tau(x)-\tau(y)|^2=|x-y|^2\); the final tangent integral is finite, whereas the printed intermediate integral has a local logarithmic divergence after multiplication by this tangent difference and integration in \(d\).

Merely changing the denominator to \(|z-w|^4\) does not repair the argument. The two semicircles overlap on an arc of length \(d\) (represent the first as \([\pi,2\pi]\)). Their product contains an open segment of the diagonal, and \(\int\int|z-w|^{-4}|dz|\,|dw|=\infty\). Thus a domain correction is necessary in addition to any typographical correction.

Analytic repair. Retain the shorter-arc condition. For \(d=\ell(x,y)\leq\ell(\Gamma)/8\), parametrize \(z\) at backward arclength \(a\geq0\) from \(x\) and \(w\) at forward arclength \(b\geq0\) from \(y\). The correct domain satisfies \[a+b+d\leq \ell(\Gamma)/2.\] The chord-arc hypothesis gives \(|z-w|\geq C^{-1}(a+b+d)\) on this domain. Including the opposite orientation changes only a factor of two. Consequently the inner kernel is bounded above by \[2C^4\int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty(a+b+d)^{-4}\,da\,db
 =\frac{C^4}{3d^2}.\] For a lower bound, restrict to \(0\leq a,b\leq d\). This is admissible because \(3d\leq3\ell(\Gamma)/8<\ell(\Gamma)/2\), and the chord length is at most \(a+b+d\leq3d\). Pairs \((x,y)\) outside this small-separation region contribute a finite bounded amount: every containing shorter arc has length at least \(\ell(\Gamma)/8\), hence its chord is bounded below by the chord-arc hypothesis. This proves the intended comparability using the actual domain.

The preceding proof repairs the central comparison and supports the theorem rather than refuting it. Nevertheless the printed upper derivation is invalid in an admissible, maximally regular case and lies directly on the proof of Theorem 1.2, which supports Major under standard 0.7.1. The exact quadrant integral and illustrative values of \(d^3J(d)\) are recorded in `independent_checks.json`; the analytic proof above, not those finite numerical samples, establishes the repair.
result: Impact: Invalid core derivation of Definitions 7 iff 8 / Theorem 1.2.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Retain a+b+d<=length/2; chord-arc gives kernel upper <=2C^4/(6d^2), lower from a,b in [0,d]; large separated pairs bounded.

problems.source_location: Lemma 18.2 proof, p.53

Normal-boundary-sphere center displacement O(t sup|kappa|), and rho(Q)=O(K_r).
analysis: Location and source claim. In the proof of Lemma 18.2 on page 53, the center of the boundary sphere of the normal hyperplane at \(z=(x,t)\) is asserted to lie within \(O(t\sup_w\max_j|\kappa_j(w)|)\) of \(x\). The normal antipodal construction is then used to assert \(\rho(Q)=O(K_r(z))\), where \(K_r\) bounds the principal curvatures on a fixed hyperbolic ball. This is the quantitative step in the higher-dimensional implication (16)\(\Rightarrow\)(13).

Parameters and assumptions. Set \(n=2\), let \(\Gamma=\{|z|=1\}\subset\mathbb R^2\), and let \[S=\{(x,y,t):x^2+y^2+t^2=1,\ t>0\}\subset\mathbb H^3.\] This is a smooth, properly embedded, complete, totally geodesic disk with asymptotic boundary \(\Gamma\). Both principal curvatures are zero everywhere. In particular, they tend to zero at the boundary and their square integral is zero, so the surface obeys the curvature requirements of Definition 16. Any fixed-ball supremum \(K_r\) is zero.

At \(p=(x,0,t)\in S\), \(0<x<1\), the Euclidean center of the normal geodesic is at horizontal coordinate \(a=1/x\). Its endpoints are \[r_-=\frac{1-t}{x},\qquad r_+=\frac{1+t}{x},
 \qquad r_-r_+=1.\] These formulas follow by taking a Euclidean circle orthogonal to the plane \(t=0\) and tangent at \(p\) to the Euclidean normal \((x,0,t)\); the upper-half-space metric is conformal, so the normal direction is unchanged. Thus \[a-x=\frac{t^2}{x}>0,\] whereas the asserted \(O(t\sup|\kappa|)\) is identically zero. This remains a boundary counterexample: take \(x=(1-u^2)/(1+u^2)\), \(t=2u/(1+u^2)\) and let \(u\downarrow0\).

The antipodal pairing of the two endpoints is precisely \[R(z)=\frac1{\overline z}.\] Its Euclidean differential has norm \(|z|^{-2}\). In a nondegenerate Whitney cube off the unit circle this differs from one at some point, so the local distance distortion \(\rho(Q)\) is positive. The proposed bound by \(K_r=0\) is false.

Alternative readings and counterevidence. Hyperbolic isometric normalization at a point cannot remove the Euclidean scale distortion in the definition of \(\rho(Q)\); a Möbius transformation is not a Euclidean isometry. For this same circle, inversion does satisfy \(\rho(Q)=O(\operatorname{diam}Q)\) near the circle, and the resulting square sum is finite: there are \(O(h^{-1})\) relevant cubes at side length \(h\), each contributing \(O(h^2)\). Hence the existence of a reflection in Definition 13 survives.

The paper itself recognizes on page 49 that \(\delta=0\) for a circle while \(\varepsilon_\Gamma\) is nonzero, so a size term is needed when passing from hyperbolic to Euclidean geometry. That observation is relevant counterevidence against reading the omitted scale term as harmless.

Impact and remaining repair. The displayed estimate cannot prove the central implication as written. A possible form of a replacement must include a scale or background-circle term, for example a properly normalized \(O(\operatorname{diam}Q)\) contribution, in addition to curvature information. This report does not assert a general bound of that form without proof. One must also justify replacing an \(L^2\) curvature integral by an \(L^2\) integral of fixed-ball suprema. For a general smooth function such a replacement fails: disjoint bumps of amplitude \(k^{-1/2}\) supported in disks of radius \(2^{-k}\) have finite square integral, whereas their fixed-radius local suprema have divergent square integral on disjoint fixed-radius neighborhoods. This diagnostic is not a constructed surface counterexample, but identifies an additional estimate the repair must supply. No counterexample to the existential equivalence is claimed.
result: Impact: Quantitative core implication (16)->(13) not established by printed estimate.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Requires Euclidean scale term, foliation justification and an L2 local-supremum estimate; no general replacement proved.

kappa_g=1+O(delta^2) and corresponding boundary-integral estimate.
analysis:
Location and source claim. Lemma 20.1, page 55, asserts \(\kappa_g=1+O(\delta^2)\) and equation (20.1), \[\int_{\partial S_t}(\kappa_g-1)\,dL_\rho
       =O\!\left(\int_{\partial S_t}\delta^2\,dL_\rho\right),\] then uses a trace-to-area estimate to make the left side vanish. This is central to (15)\(\Rightarrow\)(19), Corollary 1.7 and formula (1.6).

Full check. Use the same unit hemisphere as in Problem Problem 2 (#prob:reflection). Its round boundary is WP, its convex hull is the totally geodesic plane itself, \(\delta\equiv0\), \(\kappa\equiv0\), and \(\chi(S)=1\). Every \(0<t<1\) is a regular truncation height, so all conditions of the displayed calculation hold.

Write \(r=\sqrt{1-t^2}\). Direct integration of the induced hyperbolic metric gives \[L_\rho(\partial S_t)=\frac{2\pi r}{t},\qquad
 A_\rho(S_t)=2\pi\left(\frac1t-1\right).\] Intrinsically \(S\) is the hyperbolic plane and this section is a geodesic circle with \(\cosh R=1/t\). Therefore \[\kappa_g=\coth R=\frac1{\sqrt{1-t^2}}>1,\qquad
 \int_{\partial S_t}(\kappa_g-1)\,dL_\rho
   =\frac{2\pi(1-\sqrt{1-t^2})}{t}
   =\pi t+O(t^3)>0.\] The right side of (20.1) is zero. The assertion that the horizontal curvature contribution is bounded by the surface’s principal curvatures also fails in this example: the surface is totally geodesic, while its horizontal sections are Euclidean circles.

Counterevidence and exact consequence. The error nevertheless tends to zero. Indeed \[\lim_{t\downarrow0}\{A_\rho(S_t)-L_\rho(\partial S_t)\}=-2\pi,\] which agrees with the claimed renormalized-area formula. Thus this is a counterexample to the proof estimate, not to Corollary 1.7. The example exhibits the missing background term explicitly: \(\kappa_g-1=\tfrac12t^2+O(t^4)\) even when \(\delta=0\).

Repair requirements. A valid argument must retain such a scale term and control its integrated boundary contribution for the surfaces under consideration, as well as establish a genuine trace estimate. On the round disk an \(O(t^2)\) term integrates to \(O(t)\), but this special case is not a proof of the general estimate. The printed annulus \(A_t=S_t\setminus S_{t+1}\) does not escape compact subsets as \(t\downarrow0\), so finite total integral does not imply its integral tends to zero. A geometric-height annulus such as \(S_t\setminus S_{2t}\) would have the correct escaping property; its required comparison with the boundary trace still needs proof. The formula involving distance from an interior point at the end of page 55 concerns geodesic spheres and retains a \(\coth r\) term; it does not justify dropping the corresponding error for height sections. General repair and the all-minimal-surface scope remain unverified.
result: Impact: Invalid boundary estimate in core (15)->(19) and renormalized-area derivation.

paragraphs: Must retain scale/background error, prove integrated trace control, and replace the nonescaping S_t minus S_(t+1) annulus; general proof pending.

rho comparable to sqrt(epsilon/r) for all disjoint equal-radius balls.
analysis: Location and claim. Lemma 16.1, page 49, states that disjoint Euclidean balls of equal radius \(r\) separated by \(\varepsilon\) have corresponding hyperbolic half-spaces at distance \(\rho\simeq\sqrt{\varepsilon/r}\), without restricting \(\varepsilon/r\).

Complete calculation. Let \(\eta=\varepsilon/r>0\). In the two-dimensional section through the centers the boundary geodesics are semicircles of radius \(r\) with centers \(2r+\varepsilon\) apart. Their inversive distance gives \[\cosh\rho=\frac{(2r+\varepsilon)^2-2r^2}{2r^2}
          =1+2\eta+\frac{\eta^2}{2},
 \qquad
 \rho=2\operatorname{arcosh}(1+\eta/2).\] These balls are disjoint for every \(\eta>0\), so they meet all printed assumptions. At small \(\eta\), \(\rho/\sqrt\eta\to2\). At large \(\eta\), \(\rho=2\log\eta+O(\eta^{-1})\) and \(\rho/\sqrt\eta\to0\). The stated two-sided uniform comparison therefore fails.

Counterevidence, impact and verified correction. The proof uses a local expansion whose optimizing height would exceed the radius when the gap is large. The next lemma’s application explicitly requires \(\varepsilon_\Gamma(Q)<1/100\), so the relevant small-gap use is not refuted. Restricting \(0<\eta\leq\eta_0\) for a fixed finite \(\eta_0\) gives a valid square-root comparison, by continuity and the limit at zero. The exact formula above works for all positive gaps. This is a Minor range error, not a failure of the subsequent small-thickness implication.

paragraphs: Assume bounded small eta or state exact formula.

Smooth curves have finite E^(j,p) when jp<=2p+1.
analysis:
Location and claim. Section 23, page 61, defines \[E^{j,p}(\Gamma)
 =\int_\Gamma\!\int_\Gamma
   \left(|x-y|^{-j}-\ell(x,y)^{-j}\right)^p\,|dx|\,|dy|\] and asserts finiteness for smooth curves if \(jp\leq2p+1\).

Counterexample with all conditions. Take the smooth embedded unit circle, \(j=3\) and \(p=1\). These parameters satisfy \(jp=2p+1=3\). For shorter arclength \(h\downarrow0\) the chord is \(2\sin(h/2)\), and \[(2\sin(h/2))^{-3}-h^{-3}
 =\frac1{8h}+\frac{17h}{1920}+O(h^3).\] The positive integrand consequently has a logarithmically divergent integral near the diagonal. Thus \(E^{3,1}(\Gamma)=\infty\) despite the asserted smoothness and endpoint condition.

Repair and limits. For a unit-speed smooth curve with nonzero curvature at a point, \[|x(s+h)-x(s)|=|h|\left(1-\frac{\kappa(s)^2h^2}{24}+O(h^3)\right).\] For \(j,p>0\) the energy integrand has leading order \((j\kappa(s)^2/24)^p|h|^{p(2-j)}\). Local integrability at nonzero curvature requires the strict inequality \(jp<2p+1\). The unit circle calculation rigorously excludes the printed equality case without relying on any numerical integration. The main Möbius energy corresponds to \(j=2,p=1\) and is strictly inside this range. The issue is therefore peripheral and Minor; no failure of Theorem 1.2 is inferred from it.
result: Impact: False peripheral endpoint statement.

paragraphs: For j,p>0 use jp<2p+1; at nonzero curvature equality diverges.

report: Abstract: The acquired September 2024 manuscript asserts an effective equidistribution alternative for a unipotent flow on the space of unimodular three-dimensional lattices. An explicit rational lattice satisfies the stated two-sided compactness test with a strict factor-two margin, while every point of the tested orbit contains the same fixed vector. A compactly supported test function therefore contradicts the main theorem. The same example makes the initial deletion step remove the whole orbit. A separate small-window calculation disproves the parameter-recovery estimate in Lemma 11.4. A short-time separation claim also needs a restricted range. All 63 source pages and the complete matching TeX and bibliography were inspected. These conclusions concern arXiv version 6 only; no mathematical equivalence to the journal final has been established.
Title: Scientific initial review of M25-0018
# Identity, version, and scope

Lei Yang, Effective version of Ratner’s equidistribution theorem for \(\operatorname{SL}(3,\mathbb R)\), associated journal DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.202.1.3 (https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2025.202.1.3). The actual scientific input is arXiv:2208.02525v6 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.02525v6), dated 19 September 2024, 63 pages. All page references below are printed manuscript pages, equal to one-based PDF pages. Publisher metadata gives journal pages 189–264; that identity information does not establish equivalence of the acquired 63-page manuscript and the final publication.
The PDF `papers/0018/0018.pdf`, 554,813 bytes, has SHA256
> 6ad6199b4aaf27439d4ee3baa0f3b3bb86d8809aa969a6604469ecab4178ba0a.
The source manifest has SHA256

All eight manifest-bound files were rehashed successfully. The matching source tree contains `main.tex` (3,360 lines) and `main.bbl` (201 lines). Both were read to the end. No separate computational code release or standalone supplement was acquired. Author code and author TeX were not executed.
# Checked claims and outcome

The initial review read Sections 1–12 and the complete bibliography. It traced the dependence of Theorems 1.2–1.3 on the initial nondivergence/deletion step, transverse dimension improvement, and the high-dimension equidistribution input. It inspected Corollaries 1.4 and 1.6, the Lie-algebra and coordinate calculations, all stated scale ranges, the heavy/unstructured/structured decompositions, and the final measure approximation.

The supported outcome is Major: the acquired main theorem is false as stated. Problem 1 is a complete counterexample, with both primal and exterior-square conditions checked for all relevant times. Problem 2 independently invalidates a core counting estimate; it does not by itself show that every subsequent counting conclusion is false. Problem 3 is a local short-time defect whose later application uses large times. Three other transitions remain Needs Evidence and are not counted as supported defects.

1–5 | Definitions of \(X_\varpi\), \(a,a_0,U\), Theorems 1.2–1.3, line and curve applications | Complete counterexample to the main alternative; graph-coordinate and Taylor issues distinguished.

6–12 | Lie-algebra decomposition, BCH estimates, high-dimension input, nondivergence and separation | Basic brackets and weights checked; Problem 3. External mixing/nondivergence proofs not independently reproduced.

18–30 | Flow boxes, projections, tube coordinates, intersections and hyperbolas | Coordinate formulas and their domains inspected; cross-section boundary control remains pending.

31–43 | Heavy, strange, unstructured and coarse-scale dimension estimates | Exponents and normalization dependencies traced; later normalization factors provide counterevidence to one earlier omission.
44–59 | Structured part, parameter recovery and curve counting | Problem 2; full downstream repair not verified.
59–63 | Final decomposition, iteration, theorem proof and references | Scale budget checked; exact versus weak measure equality remains pending.
# Definitions and quantifiers

Let \(G=\operatorname{SL}(3,\mathbb R)\), \(\Gamma=\operatorname{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\), and \(X=G/\Gamma\). A point \(g\Gamma\) represents the lattice \(\Lambda=g\mathbb Z^3\). The manuscript defines \[u(r)=I+rE_{23},\qquad
 a(t)=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{t/2},e^{-t/2}),\qquad
 a_0(\ell)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{\ell/3},e^{-\ell/6},e^{-\ell/6}).\] Its compact set is \[X_\varpi=\{g\Gamma:\|gv\|\geq\varpi
 \text{ for all }0\ne v\in\mathbb Z^3\text{ and all }0\ne v\in\wedge^2\mathbb Z^3\}.\] The exterior-square condition is essential: checking only lattice vectors would not test the theorem. For an oriented unimodular Euclidean three-dimensional lattice, the Hodge map identifies \(\wedge^2\Lambda\) isometrically with the dual lattice \(\Lambda^*=g^{-T}\mathbb Z^3\).

The notation \([L]\) means \([-L/2,L/2]\). Section 5 fixes \[\delta_1=\delta_2=10^{-5},\ d_0=10^{-6},\ C_1=10^7,\quad
 0<\theta<10^{-10},\quad \varepsilon_2=10^{-26}\theta,\quad N_1=10^5/\varepsilon_2,\] \[\varepsilon=e^{-10^5N_1},\quad\beta=e^{-\varepsilon^3t},\quad

# Supported substantive problems

Problem 1 (Major: an explicit lattice contradicts the main alternative).  Location and suspect implication. Theorems 1.2–1.3, page 3; Definition 6.1 and equation (6.7), page 13; final proof, pages 61–62. The two-sided \(a_0\) test in [eq:main2] (#eq:main2) does not exclude an \(AU\) orbit lying in a proper fixed-vector locus. Consequently the claimed small deletion and the subsequent dimension argument cannot establish [eq:main1] (#eq:main1).

Parameters and every compactness condition. Set \[g=\begin{pmatrix}2&1/2&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1/2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad x_0=g\Gamma.\] Then \(\det g=1\), and \[\begin{aligned}
 \Lambda&=\{(2p+q/2,q,r/2):p,q,r\in\mathbb Z\},\\
 \Lambda^*&=\{(p/2,q-p/4,2r):p,q,r\in\mathbb Z\}.\end{aligned}\] The inverse transpose is \[g^{-T}=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0&0\\-1/4&1&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}.\] These formulas are exact, including the denominator four in the dual.

For \(L\geq12\log2\), put \(z=e^{L/6}\geq4\). The compactness threshold is \(e^{-L/3}=z^{-2}\). After dividing all coordinates by that threshold, the vectors in the four lattices to be checked are: \[\begin{array}{c|c}
 a_0(L)\Lambda &(z^4(2p+q/2),\,zq,\,zr/2)\\
 (a_0(L)\Lambda)^* &(p/2,\,z^3(q-p/4),\,2z^3r)\\
 a_0(-L)\Lambda &(2p+q/2,\,z^3q,\,z^3r/2)\\
 (a_0(-L)\Lambda)^* &(z^4p/2,\,z(q-p/4),\,2zr).
\end{array}\] For every nonzero integer triple, the maximum absolute coordinate is at least two:

1. In the first row, if \(2p+q/2\ne0\), its magnitude is at least \(1/2\), so the first coordinate is at least \(z^4/2\geq128\). If it is zero, at least one of \(q,r\) is nonzero, and the last two coordinates have maximum at least \(z/2\geq2\).

2. In the second row, if \((q-p/4,2r)\ne(0,0)\), the maximum of its coordinates is at least \(1/4\), so the corresponding maximum is at least \(z^3/4\geq16\). Otherwise \(r=0,p=4q\), and nonzeroness gives \(|p/2|=2|q|\geq2\).
3. In the third row, if \((q,r)\ne(0,0)\), the maximum of the last two coordinates is at least \(z^3/2\geq32\). Otherwise \(|2p|\geq2\).
4. In the fourth row, \(p\ne0\) gives a first coordinate at least \(z^4/2\). If \(p=0\), then \((q,r)\ne(0,0)\) and the maximum of the last coordinates is at least \(z\geq4\).

Equation reference: eq:strict. Thus, in both the usual Euclidean and maximum-coordinate norms, \[a_0(L)x_0,\ a_0(-L)x_0\in X_{2e^{-L/3}}\subset X_{e^{-L/3}}
 \qquad(L\geq12\log2).\] The exterior-square checks are the second and fourth rows, not omitted assumptions. Therefore [eq:main2] (#eq:main2) is false for every allowed \(\ell\) once \(t\geq12\log2/0.99\). This is a strict factor-two example, not an issue about equality at the boundary of \(X_\varpi\).

Failure of the equidistribution alternative. The vector \(v=2e_1\) lies in \(\Lambda\), and \(a(t)u(r)v=v\) for all real \(r,t\). Hence every lattice \(a(t)u(r)x_0\) lies in \[S_v=\{\Lambda'\in X:v\in\Lambda'\}.\] This set is closed. Indeed, in a local chart choose representatives \(g_n\to g\) for a convergent sequence of lattices in \(S_v\). If \(g_nk_n=v\) with \(k_n\in\mathbb Z^3\), then \(k_n=g_n^{-1}v\) stays bounded. A subsequence is constant, so \(v\in g\mathbb Z^3\).

The set is proper: the unimodular diagonal lattice represented by \(\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt2,1,1/\sqrt2)\) does not contain \(2e_1\), since \(2/\sqrt2\) is not an integer. Choose a nonzero nonnegative smooth compactly supported function \(f\) in a relatively compact open subset of \(X\setminus S_v\). Such a function exists in a manifold chart. Haar measure has positive mass on every nonempty open subset, so \[I:=\int_X f\,d\mu_G>0,\qquad
 \int_{-1/2}^{1/2}f(a(t)u(r)x_0)\,dr=0
 \quad\hbox{for all }t.\] The left side of [eq:main1] (#eq:main1) is the fixed positive number \(I\), whereas its proposed upper bound tends to zero. Taking \(t\geq\max(t_0,12\log2/0.99)\) and then \(t\) sufficiently large contradicts both alternatives. Theorem 1.2 is contradicted by the same calculation with its starting point \(a(t)x_0\), exactly as in the equivalence given on page 3.

The first failed proof step is also explicit. Write \(s=(1-\delta_1)t\) and \(\mathcal E=a(s)u([1])x_0\). Every \(y\in\mathcal E\) contains \(2e_1\). Definition 6.1 permits \(\ell=0\) and \(\ell'=-2\delta_1t\). Then \(a_0(\ell')a(-\ell)y\) contains \[2e^{-2\delta_1t/3}e_1.\] For \[t>\frac{\log2}{2\delta_1/3-\varepsilon^3/4},\] whose denominator is positive by the listed constants, its length is less than \(\beta^{1/4}=e^{-\varepsilon^3t/4}\). Every point is therefore removed: \(\mathcal F=\varnothing\). The removed proportion is one, while the bound claimed before (6.7) is \(O(s^2\beta^{\alpha_2})\to0\). The normalized measure on \(\mathcal F\) is not defined. This identifies an actual failure in the proof, beyond the abstract theorem counterexample.

Counterevidence, alternative readings, and repair limits. The familiar lattice \(\mathbb Z^3\) would already expose a boundary-equality concern, but it is unnecessary: [eq:strict] (#eq:strict) has a margin. Including the dual lattice does not rescue the statement. Replacing a norm by another fixed norm does not rescue a uniform theorem either. For a positive integer \(N\), use \[g_N=\begin{pmatrix}N&1/N&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1/N\end{pmatrix},

A slower decay threshold \(e^{-(1/3-\kappa)|\ell|}\) with fixed \(\kappa>0\) would eventually detect the fixed-axis examples, but this observation is not a proof of a corrected theorem. A valid replacement must establish the quantitative implication needed for Definition 6.1, with all primal and dual obstruction heights controlled. No such global repair is claimed here.

Impact and evidence. This is material damage to the central theoretical guarantee, hence Major under 0.7.1. It does not refute Ratner’s qualitative theorem: the obstruction is precisely that the orbit remains in a proper locus. The proof is analytic and covers infinitely many integer vectors and all sufficiently large times. The reviewer-owned script separately verifies determinant, dual, Hodge matrix, fixed vector, and 58,944 illustrative finite-box inequalities; finite enumeration is not substituted for the coordinate proof.
