# Needs Evidence: unresolved transitions
These items are not additional supported problems. The checks below identify what is missing without claiming counterexamples to conclusions whose full hypotheses have not been tested.
## NE1: the curve linearization needs a smaller scale or a different argument

Corollary 1.6, page 5, divides a smooth nondegenerate graph into pieces of length \(e^{-t/2}\) and claims exponentially small error after applying \(a_1(t)\), where \(a_1(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{t/3},e^{t/3},e^{-2t/3})\). For the admissible graph \(\psi(r)=(r,r^2)\), the first and second derivatives span \(\mathbb R^2\) at every point. At an increment \(\Delta=q e^{-t/2}\) the quadratic Taylor remainder is \(\Delta^2E_{13}\) before conjugation. Since \(\operatorname{Ad}(a_1(t))E_{13}=e^tE_{13}\), the left group-coordinate remainder is exactly \[e^t\Delta^2E_{13}=q^2E_{13}.\] For fixed nonzero \(q\in[-1/2,1/2]\) it does not tend to zero.

This disproves the direct exponentially small group-Taylor estimate, but it has not been turned into a uniform lower bound for quotient distance or for the tested orbit integrals: cusp identifications and the relevant norms must be controlled. It is therefore recorded as Needs Evidence concerning the corollary’s derivation, not as a counterexample to the corollary. Using pieces of length \(e^{-(1/2+c)t}\) gives the precise group-coordinate bound \(O(e^{-2ct})\) for bounded second derivative, but then the expansion time, diagonal factors and nondivergence argument all change. No completed repair of the corollary is claimed.

Two additional proof obligations belong to this same application: a general nondegenerate curve need not globally be the displayed graph without charts and Jacobian weights; and controlling each exceptional set for a fixed real \(\ell\) does not itself control their uncountable union. An explicit time mesh and a compactness-threshold margin can potentially address the latter. The manuscript’s stronger \(e^{-t/10}\) threshold supplies useful slack, which is counterevidence against treating the union step as an immediate false theorem.
## NE2: exact positive decomposition versus weak approximation

Proposition 12.1 and (12.1), pages 59–61, state an exact positive measure decomposition after discarding a small positive part. The construction then projects orbit pieces and proves only a \(C^1\)-dual estimate (12.5), of size \(O(\beta)\). A small weak error need not be a positive discarded measure. Also, normalizing restrictions to an overlapping cover does not by itself yield a probability decomposition with the displayed weights; disjoint cells or a partition of unity and the induced weights must be specified.

The final theorem proof on page 61 actually uses an \(O(\beta)\) remainder. That is significant counterevidence: a weak approximation may suffice for the intended application. The remaining obligation is a precise decomposition in the correct topology, with masses summing appropriately, overlap controlled, and the projected transverse measures satisfying the needed dimension bound. No counterexample satisfying all of Proposition 12.1’s dimension assumptions was constructed here, so this remains Needs Evidence.
## NE3: cross-section boundary control

Lemma 8.5, pages 20 and 23, claims uniformly long intersections with every cross-section for every point of the full playground. Its proof controls the longitudinal coordinate \(f_y(r)\), but membership in the cross-section also imposes transverse-coordinate bounds. The displayed formulas (8.8)–(8.10) show that these transverse coordinates move. For example, in the subcase \(w_2=0\), the positive coordinate moves as \(v_1(r)=v_1+rv_2\); a point close to a box face can leave that face while the longitudinal coordinate is brought to zero.

The relevant global injectivity, boundary trimming and full-playground hypotheses were not all established for a single proposed counterexample, so no failed lemma is asserted on that basis. The needed evidence is a nested/fattened-box formulation or a quantified boundary deletion which proves the uniform intersection lengths actually used in Lemmas 8.6 and 8.13. Merely solving the longitudinal equation does not supply that evidence.
# Scope clarifications and counterevidence retained
## The sign in Proposition 4.1 is not counted as a separate substantive finding

On page 11 the hypothesis literally says both \(a_0(\pm s)x\) are outside \(X_{e^{-s/3}}\), whereas the contradiction proof needs them inside. The literal statement is false: for \(s=1\) and \(g_\delta=\operatorname{diag}(\delta,1,\delta^{-1})\), both tests are outside for sufficiently small \(\delta\), and every \(a(1)u(r)g_\delta\Gamma\) contains \(\delta e_1\). Taking \(\beta=\sqrt\delta\) makes the exceptional proportion one and the claimed \(O(\beta^\alpha)\) bound tend to zero. The proof and later intended use identify the sign correction. As an apparent negation transcription error it is recorded here, not used to inflate the substantive count. Correcting that sign does not repair Problem 1 or (6.7).
## Normalization in Lemma 8.6

Page 21 defines \(\widetilde\mu=\mu|_{\Pi}/\mu(\Pi)\) but bounds a normalized mass by the corresponding unnormalized mass. For a measurable subset \(A\subset\Pi\) of positive mass and \(p=\mu(\Pi)<1\), the exact relation is \(\widetilde\mu(A)=\mu(A)/p>\mu(A)\). The available full-playground condition gives \(p\geq\beta^{15}\) and therefore a factor \(\beta^{-15}\), not factor one. The manuscript itself includes this factor in Lemma 9.4 on page 32 and again in the application on page 39. These later formulas are the relevant counterevidence and indicate the intended correction. No additional core failure is inferred solely from the earlier missing factor, and the exact unchanged statement of Lemma 8.6 is not declared proved.
## A finite cover must cover a compact relevant region

The first line of the proof of Proposition 7.2, page 17, covers the whole noncompact space \(X\) by finitely many translates of a bounded local box. A finite union of their compact closures cannot cover \(X\). The trajectory being studied starts from a compact parameter interval, and the argument also retains thick points; a relevant compact region can replace \(X\). The required cardinality and overlap bounds still need an actual covering argument on that region. This is a scope clarification, not a claim that compact truncation is impossible.
## Greedy counting can use first ownership

On page 57 the greedy construction is described as giving each selected curve many cells not covered by any other selected curve. The construction directly ensures only that its newly added cells were not covered by earlier selections. For a lower bound on the union, assign each cell to the first selected curve that covers it. These assigned new-cell sets are disjoint, so their cardinalities add. This repairs that local interpretation of the greedy union count and does not address the parameter estimate in Problem 2.
## Correct scale and algebra checks

The reviewer checked \([\mathbf u,\mathbf v_2]=\mathbf v_1\), \([\mathbf u,\mathbf w_2]=-\mathbf w_1\), and \([\mathbf v_1,\mathbf w_1]=\mathbf u\) directly. The elapsed-time identity \[(1-\delta_1)t+\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}s_j=t-2s_i\] is correct. There is also adequate formal room in the stated structured-dimension range: \[10^{11}C_1\varepsilon_1=2\cdot10^{-8}\theta<\theta.\] Thus the restriction in Proposition 11.1 is compatible with stopping at dimension \(4-\theta\). These checks do not validate the missing initial dimension input. They prevent an incorrect additional allegation about the iteration budget.

 \delta_3=10^{-5}\theta\varepsilon,\quad \varepsilon_1=2\varepsilon_2.\] The iteration uses \(s_i=2^{-i}\delta_1t/2\) and \(d_i=d_0+i\varepsilon_2\). These constants, however extreme, are positive and fixed before \(t\) tends to infinity. No floating-point underflow is used to replace them by zero.
Two-sided a0 compactness alternative guarantees effective Haar equidistribution.
analysis: Location and suspect implication. Theorems 1.2–1.3, page 3; Definition 6.1 and equation (6.7), page 13; final proof, pages 61–62. The two-sided \(a_0\) test in [eq:main2] (#eq:main2) does not exclude an \(AU\) orbit lying in a proper fixed-vector locus. Consequently the claimed small deletion and the subsequent dimension argument cannot establish [eq:main1] (#eq:main1).

Parameters and every compactness condition. Set \[g=\begin{pmatrix}2&1/2&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1/2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad x_0=g\Gamma.\] Then \(\det g=1\), and \[\begin{aligned}
 \Lambda&=\{(2p+q/2,q,r/2):p,q,r\in\mathbb Z\},\\
 \Lambda^*&=\{(p/2,q-p/4,2r):p,q,r\in\mathbb Z\}.\end{aligned}\] The inverse transpose is \[g^{-T}=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0&0\\-1/4&1&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}.\] These formulas are exact, including the denominator four in the dual.

For \(L\geq12\log2\), put \(z=e^{L/6}\geq4\). The compactness threshold is \(e^{-L/3}=z^{-2}\). After dividing all coordinates by that threshold, the vectors in the four lattices to be checked are: \[\begin{array}{c|c}
 a_0(L)\Lambda &(z^4(2p+q/2),\,zq,\,zr/2)\\
 (a_0(L)\Lambda)^* &(p/2,\,z^3(q-p/4),\,2z^3r)\\
 a_0(-L)\Lambda &(2p+q/2,\,z^3q,\,z^3r/2)\\
 (a_0(-L)\Lambda)^* &(z^4p/2,\,z(q-p/4),\,2zr).
\end{array}\] For every nonzero integer triple, the maximum absolute coordinate is at least two:

1. In the first row, if \(2p+q/2\ne0\), its magnitude is at least \(1/2\), so the first coordinate is at least \(z^4/2\geq128\). If it is zero, at least one of \(q,r\) is nonzero, and the last two coordinates have maximum at least \(z/2\geq2\).

2. In the second row, if \((q-p/4,2r)\ne(0,0)\), the maximum of its coordinates is at least \(1/4\), so the corresponding maximum is at least \(z^3/4\geq16\). Otherwise \(r=0,p=4q\), and nonzeroness gives \(|p/2|=2|q|\geq2\).
3. In the third row, if \((q,r)\ne(0,0)\), the maximum of the last two coordinates is at least \(z^3/2\geq32\). Otherwise \(|2p|\geq2\).
4. In the fourth row, \(p\ne0\) gives a first coordinate at least \(z^4/2\). If \(p=0\), then \((q,r)\ne(0,0)\) and the maximum of the last coordinates is at least \(z\geq4\).

Equation reference: eq:strict. Thus, in both the usual Euclidean and maximum-coordinate norms, \[a_0(L)x_0,\ a_0(-L)x_0\in X_{2e^{-L/3}}\subset X_{e^{-L/3}}
 \qquad(L\geq12\log2).\] The exterior-square checks are the second and fourth rows, not omitted assumptions. Therefore [eq:main2] (#eq:main2) is false for every allowed \(\ell\) once \(t\geq12\log2/0.99\). This is a strict factor-two example, not an issue about equality at the boundary of \(X_\varpi\).

Failure of the equidistribution alternative. The vector \(v=2e_1\) lies in \(\Lambda\), and \(a(t)u(r)v=v\) for all real \(r,t\). Hence every lattice \(a(t)u(r)x_0\) lies in \[S_v=\{\Lambda'\in X:v\in\Lambda'\}.\] This set is closed. Indeed, in a local chart choose representatives \(g_n\to g\) for a convergent sequence of lattices in \(S_v\). If \(g_nk_n=v\) with \(k_n\in\mathbb Z^3\), then \(k_n=g_n^{-1}v\) stays bounded. A subsequence is constant, so \(v\in g\mathbb Z^3\).

The set is proper: the unimodular diagonal lattice represented by \(\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt2,1,1/\sqrt2)\) does not contain \(2e_1\), since \(2/\sqrt2\) is not an integer. Choose a nonzero nonnegative smooth compactly supported function \(f\) in a relatively compact open subset of \(X\setminus S_v\). Such a function exists in a manifold chart. Haar measure has positive mass on every nonempty open subset, so \[I:=\int_X f\,d\mu_G>0,\qquad
 \int_{-1/2}^{1/2}f(a(t)u(r)x_0)\,dr=0
 \quad\hbox{for all }t.\] The left side of [eq:main1] (#eq:main1) is the fixed positive number \(I\), whereas its proposed upper bound tends to zero. Taking \(t\geq\max(t_0,12\log2/0.99)\) and then \(t\) sufficiently large contradicts both alternatives. Theorem 1.2 is contradicted by the same calculation with its starting point \(a(t)x_0\), exactly as in the equivalence given on page 3.

The first failed proof step is also explicit. Write \(s=(1-\delta_1)t\) and \(\mathcal E=a(s)u([1])x_0\). Every \(y\in\mathcal E\) contains \(2e_1\). Definition 6.1 permits \(\ell=0\) and \(\ell'=-2\delta_1t\). Then \(a_0(\ell')a(-\ell)y\) contains \[2e^{-2\delta_1t/3}e_1.\] For \[t>\frac{\log2}{2\delta_1/3-\varepsilon^3/4},\] whose denominator is positive by the listed constants, its length is less than \(\beta^{1/4}=e^{-\varepsilon^3t/4}\). Every point is therefore removed: \(\mathcal F=\varnothing\). The removed proportion is one, while the bound claimed before (6.7) is \(O(s^2\beta^{\alpha_2})\to0\). The normalized measure on \(\mathcal F\) is not defined. This identifies an actual failure in the proof, beyond the abstract theorem counterexample.

Counterevidence, alternative readings, and repair limits. The familiar lattice \(\mathbb Z^3\) would already expose a boundary-equality concern, but it is unnecessary: [eq:strict] (#eq:strict) has a margin. Including the dual lattice does not rescue the statement. Replacing a norm by another fixed norm does not rescue a uniform theorem either. For a positive integer \(N\), use \[g_N=\begin{pmatrix}N&1/N&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1/N\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 g_N^{-T}=\begin{pmatrix}1/N&0&0\\-1/N^2&1&0\\0&0&N\end{pmatrix}.\] Both the primal and dual intersections with the first coordinate axis have primitive generator \(Ne_1\). All nonaxis normalized vectors eventually grow under the same coordinate cases. Choosing \(N\) large handles any fixed equivalent-norm constant. This also shows that merely inserting a fixed multiplicative constant in the threshold cannot uniformly repair the theorem over all starting lattices.

A slower decay threshold \(e^{-(1/3-\kappa)|\ell|}\) with fixed \(\kappa>0\) would eventually detect the fixed-axis examples, but this observation is not a proof of a corrected theorem. A valid replacement must establish the quantitative implication needed for Definition 6.1, with all primal and dual obstruction heights controlled. No such global repair is claimed here.

Impact and evidence. This is material damage to the central theoretical guarantee, hence Major under 0.7.1. It does not refute Ratner’s qualitative theorem: the obstruction is precisely that the orbit remains in a proper locus. The proof is analytic and covers infinitely many integer vectors and all sufficiently large times. The reviewer-owned script separately verifies determinant, dual, Hodge matrix, fixed vector, and 58,944 illustrative finite-box inequalities; finite enumeration is not substituted for the coordinate proof.

claim:
Let \(G=\operatorname{SL}(3,\mathbb R)\), \(\Gamma=\operatorname{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\), and \(X=G/\Gamma\). A point \(g\Gamma\) represents the lattice \(\Lambda=g\mathbb Z^3\). The manuscript defines \[u(r)=I+rE_{23},\qquad
 a(t)=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{t/2},e^{-t/2}),\qquad
 a_0(\ell)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{\ell/3},e^{-\ell/6},e^{-\ell/6}).\] Its compact set is \[X_\varpi=\{g\Gamma:\|gv\|\geq\varpi
 \text{ for all }0\ne v\in\mathbb Z^3\text{ and all }0\ne v\in\wedge^2\mathbb Z^3\}.\] The exterior-square condition is essential: checking only lattice vectors would not test the theorem. For an oriented unimodular Euclidean three-dimensional lattice, the Hodge map identifies \(\wedge^2\Lambda\) isometrically with the dual lattice \(\Lambda^*=g^{-T}\mathbb Z^3\).

The notation \([L]\) means \([-L/2,L/2]\). Section 5 fixes \[\delta_1=\delta_2=10^{-5},\ d_0=10^{-6},\ C_1=10^7,\quad
 0<\theta<10^{-10},\quad \varepsilon_2=10^{-26}\theta,\quad N_1=10^5/\varepsilon_2,\] \[\varepsilon=e^{-10^5N_1},\quad\beta=e^{-\varepsilon^3t},\quad
 \delta_3=10^{-5}\theta\varepsilon,\quad \varepsilon_1=2\varepsilon_2.\] The iteration uses \(s_i=2^{-i}\delta_1t/2\) and \(d_i=d_0+i\varepsilon_2\). These constants, however extreme, are positive and fixed before \(t\) tends to infinity. No floating-point underflow is used to replace them by zero.
C' in A exp(-3s') neighborhood implies |w-w'|<=A exp(-s'+2ell).
analysis: Location and dependency. Lemma 11.4(1), equation (11.2), pages 44–46, asserts parameter recovery from proximity of two hyperbolas in \(\mathfrak C=[1.2\beta e^{-s'}]^2\). It is explicitly applied on pages 49 and 51 in Lemmas 11.5 and 11.7, which enter Proposition 11.1 and hence the central dimension-improvement Proposition 9.1. The proof replaces the available \(\beta e^{-s'}\) window by an \(e^{-s'}\) scale when extracting coefficients.

Full admissible construction. Write \(S=s'>0\), \(E=e^S\), and \(h=C_1\varepsilon_1\). Choose the manuscript parameters at sufficiently large \(t\) so that \[0<\beta\leq10^{-2},\quad E^2\geq4\beta^{-2},\quad
 e^{-10hS}\leq\beta/4.\] Take \[\ell=0,\quad k=k'=1,\quad A=1,\quad
 w=\beta E/4,\quad w'=w+\beta^{-1}E^{-1}.\] Then \(|k|\in[e^\ell,e^{\ell+1}]\), \(0\leq\ell\leq S\), and \[e^{S-10hS}\leq w<w'\leq\tfrac12\beta E<\beta E.\] Also \(0<A<e^{(2-h)S}\) because \(0<h<2\). Thus every parameter restriction in part (1) is met.

These are compatible with the actual hierarchy, not merely freely chosen surrogate parameters. Indeed \(S=ct\) at an iteration scale, with \(c\geq10^{-5}2^{-N_1-1}\) for \(i\leq N_1\). Since \(\varepsilon^3=e^{-3\cdot10^5N_1}\), \[c>\varepsilon^3,\qquad 10C_1\varepsilon_1c>\varepsilon^3.\] For the second inequality, its left side at the displayed lower bound for \(c\) is \((10^8/N_1)2^{-N_1}\), much larger than \(e^{-300000N_1}\). These inequalities can be checked by logarithms, using \(N_1>10^{41}\) and \(\log N_1<N_1\). They ensure all three conditions above once \(t\) is large. In particular no forbidden interchange of constants and time is used.

The conclusion (11.2), however, requires \(|w-w'|\leq AE^{-1+0}=E^{-1}\), whereas \[|w-w'|=\beta^{-1}E^{-1}.\] The ratio \(\beta^{-1}=e^{\varepsilon^3t}\) is unbounded. An absolute implicit constant cannot cover the discrepancy. This is not a boundary, sign, zero-denominator, or \(k'=0\) example.

Counterevidence and a precisely limited correction. The subsequent arguments allow large exponential slack, and the hierarchy has \(\log\beta^{-1}\ll\varepsilon_1s'\) throughout the required finite iteration. It is therefore plausible that explicitly retaining a fixed power of \(\beta^{-1}\) could be absorbed later. That possibility does not validate the displayed implication or establish the repaired counting argument.

In a restricted graph regime where \(k,k'\) are comparable to \(e^\ell\), denominators stay comparable to them, and the horizontal (same-\(Y\)) discrepancy is at most \(\rho\) on two points \(Y=\pm b\) with \(b\asymp\beta e^{-S}\), the exact identity gives \[|\Delta k\pm b\Delta w|\leq C\rho e^{2\ell}/b.\] Adding and subtracting yields the defensible local bounds \[|\Delta k|\leq C\rho e^{2\ell}/b,\qquad
 |\Delta w|\leq C\rho e^{2\ell}/b^2.\] With \(\rho=Ae^{-3S}\) these contain respectively \(\beta^{-1}\) and \(\beta^{-2}\). This is a conditional elementary correction, not a replacement of all parts of Lemma 11.4. A full repair must also justify denominator comparability, conversion from Euclidean neighborhood to a same-\(Y\) horizontal discrepancy bound, truncated-curve endpoints, and propagation through Lemmas 11.5–11.7.

Impact and evidence. The invalid coefficient estimate is a demonstrated derivation error in the core dimension argument and is Major even if a corrected exponent budget ultimately works. No separate counterexample to every downstream counting bound is claimed. The exact rational separation identity and the uniform small-window upper bound are verified in the reviewer-owned script; the all-time admissibility argument is analytic.

analysis: Location and claim. Lemma 4.2 on page 12 is stated for every \(\ell\geq1\). Under its injectivity and coordinate hypotheses it concludes that the negative-weight coefficient pair has norm at least \(\beta e^{-\ell/2}\). The proof first uses \(\ell\) sufficiently large to exclude the identity lattice element; that step is false at the stated lower endpoint.

Complete check in the standard coordinate norm. Choose \(0<\beta<10^{-10}\), \(\ell=1\), \(x=a(1)\Gamma\), \[r_1=r_3=0,\qquad r_2=\beta/4,\qquad
 \mathbf v=e^{1/2}\beta E_{21}/4.\] Here \(\mathbf v_1=E_{21}\) as defined on page 6. The parameters lie in \([\beta]\) and their Euclidean triple norm is \(\beta/4\). The coefficient norm of \(\mathbf v\) is \(e^{1/2}\beta/4<\beta\); this also holds for the Frobenius norm and twice that norm. Moreover \(a(-1)x=\Gamma\in X_{\beta^{1/4}}\). The equality of the two exponential actions in the hypothesis is an identity of group elements: \[\exp(r_1e^\ell\mathbf u+r_2e^{\ell/2}\mathbf v_1+
                   r_3e^{\ell/2}\mathbf w_1)=\exp(\mathbf v).\] The \(\mathbf u^*\), \(\mathbf v_2\), and \(\mathbf w_2\) coefficients of \(\mathbf v\) are all zero. Thus \(|u^*|<\beta e^{-1}\), while the claimed conclusion would read \(0\geq\beta e^{-1/2}>0\). In the proof the lattice element is exactly the identity.

Any fixed-norm formulation should state the required lower time depending on that convention. The later application in Section 6 uses time proportional to a large parameter, so this example does not establish failure of that application. report: Abstract: This review concerns Alex Cohen’s arXiv:2305.05022v2 author manuscript, dated 5 October 2024, with 42 PDF pages. One supported Minor issue concerns the pointwise interpretation of a boundary-derivative lemma under a merely \(C^1\) hypothesis. An explicit compactly supported \(C^1\) example has infinite normal derivative at one boundary point. The subsequent core applications assume \(C^2\) or \(C^3\) regularity, so this example does not refute the fractal uncertainty theorem or the higher-dimensional multiplier construction. No Major issue was established in the inspected core. Several scale and normalization details are made explicit below, with local supporting arguments. All original pages and all supplied mathematical TeX/bibliography files were read; nine groups of reviewer-owned checks were executed. This is an initial review, not independent acceptance or certification of all external dependencies.
Author: AI-assisted scientific review; human decision pending

Title: Scientific initial review of
Fractal uncertainty in higher dimensions
# Identity, version, and scope

The assigned paper is M25-0019, Alex Cohen, Fractal uncertainty in higher dimensions, DOI https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2025.202.1.4. The actual scientific input is the manifest-bound arXiv:2305.05022v2 author manuscript. Its first page says 5 October 2024; the TeX filename contains 10-4-24 and the PDF creation metadata is later. Those are different metadata fields, not evidence of different mathematical versions.

All page references below mean the one-based pages of the 42-page acquired PDF; its printed page numbers agree. The journal Version of Record was not compared. Findings must not be attributed to that final version without a corresponding comparison.

The review covered the main statements, definitions and quantifiers, Sections 1–6, Appendix A, all 42 original page images, and the full 1782-line mathematical TeX file, 312-line bibliography output, and 446-line bibliography source. The three supplied illustrative figure assets were inspected as rendered in the main PDF on pages 2 and 33. No separate experimental data or numerical author program is present in this source bundle. No author code was executed. The review is analytic, with small symbolic and numerical cross-checks; it does not reproduce an empirical experiment.
# Claims, assumptions, and checked dependence

The Fourier convention is \[\widehat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,dx.\] Theorem 1.1, page 1, assumes \(X\subset[-1,1]^d\) is \(
u\)-porous on balls from scales \(h\) to 1, and \(Y\subset[-h^{-1},h^{-1}]^d\) is \(
u\)-porous on lines from scales 1 to \(h^{-1}\). Here \(0<h<1/100\), and the standing convention is \(0<
u\leq1/3\). Porosity means that every tested ball or line segment has a point admitting a ball of radius \(
u\) times its diameter or length that misses the set. The quantifier over all line segments is essential; ordinary ball porosity of both sets is insufficient.

The asserted conclusion is \[\operatorname{supp}\widehat f\subset Y
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \|f1_X\|_2\leq C h^\beta\|f\|_2,
 \qquad C,\beta>0\ \hbox{depending only on }\nu,d.\] The intermediate multiplier theorem, Theorem 1.4 on page 5, assumes a nonpositive weight \(\omega\), vanishing on \(B_2\), with \[|D^a\omega(x)|\leq C_{\rm reg}\langle x\rangle^{1-a}\quad(0\leq a\leq3),
 \qquad
 \int_0^\infty\frac{G^*(r)}{1+r^2}\,dr\leq C_{\rm gr},\] where \(G(x)=\int_{1/2}^2|\omega(sx)|\,ds\) and \(G^*(r)=\sup_{|x|=r}G(x)\). The positive constants in upper bounds may always be enlarged, including in the zero-weight case. The theorem supplies a nonzero \(L^2\) multiplier with Fourier support in \(B_\sigma\), a uniform lower bound near zero, and exponential decay controlled by \(\sigma\omega\).

The logical dependence inspected was: Proposition 3.1 and Lemmas 4.1–4.5 give the plurisubharmonic extension in Proposition 2.2; the weighted \(\bar\partial\) argument in Section 5 gives Proposition 2.3; their combination gives Theorem 1.4; line porosity gives the damping functions in Proposition 1.7; the stated Han–Schlag conditional theorem, with the conversions in Appendix A.1, yields Theorem 1.1. The imported weighted \(\bar\partial\) and Paley–Wiener theorems were treated as established external results with their stated hypotheses. Their full original proofs were not independently reconstructed.
## Extension and real-boundary positivity

For the operator \[E\omega(x+iy)=\frac1\pi\int_\mathbb R\frac{\omega(x+ty)}{1+t^2}\,dt,\] the compact-support calculation on pages 17–19 is consistent: \[\partial\bar\partial E\omega(x+iy)
 =\frac1{4\pi}\int_\mathbb RD^2\omega(x+ty)\,dt.\] The mixed imaginary coefficients cancel by equality of mixed derivatives. Changing variables gives the factor \(1/|y|\). The X-ray transform is constant along its integration line, so its Hessian annihilates the longitudinal direction. For \(v=v_\perp+r\widehat y\) this gives the transverse formula (3.15). Meanwhile, \[\partial\bar\partial|y|=\frac{I-\widehat y\widehat y^{\,T}}{4|y|}.\] Consequently the line-integral lower bound in Proposition 3.1 offsets exactly the possible negative transverse Hessian. No missing \(4\), \(\pi\), or \(|y|\) factor was found here.

At a real point, pages 20–21 use \(C>C_1\) first. The positive term \(\varepsilon\,\operatorname{avg}_\theta|\operatorname{Im}(e^{i\theta}v)|\) is at least \(\varepsilon|v|/2\) and dominates the negative quadratic Taylor remainder for small \(|v|\). Passing \(C\) down to its limiting value is legitimate by local uniform convergence. This step uses \(C^2\) regularity, not merely the hypothesis challenged in Problem 1.

For noncompact weights, the uniform tail estimate on page 16 includes both a term of size \(R^{-1/2}C_{\rm gr}\) and the integrable tail \(M\int_{\sqrt R}^{\infty}G^*(t)/(1+t^2)\,dt\). It therefore gives convergence uniformly on compact subsets, including as \(y\) tends to zero. The same domination supports Lemma 3.5 for the specific nonpositive partial sums constructed later.
## Dyadic modification and cancellation

The integration-by-parts sign in Lemma 4.1, page 22, was checked: \[\int_0^\infty D^2_{vv}f(t\widehat y)\,dt
 =\pi_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}f(\widehat y)
  +\left.\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}
    \pi_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}f(\widehat y\cos\theta+v\sin\theta)
   \right|_{\theta=0}.\] Compact support away from the origin removes the boundary term. Making each large dyadic piece have constant spherical projection \(q_k\) leaves the line integral equal to \(2q_k\) on the full line. The correction \(p_k^{-1}\psi_k(q_k-\pi\omega_k)\) is nonpositive, so the new weight stays below the old one. The summability of \(|q_k|\), together with the third derivative bound, controls the large-scale translation errors in Lemmas 4.4–4.5. The low, middle, and high scales have respectively summable geometric bounds, a bounded number of terms, and the summable \(|q_k|\) terms.

The audit retains the nonpositivity of the constructed pieces in (4.13). Reading Lemma 4.3 as a theorem about arbitrary signed pieces solely from the abbreviated list (ii)–(v) would discard information used in the absolute-integral bounds. The actual constructed pieces have that information; no defect in their use was established. Likewise the displayed projection normalization \(p_k\asymp2^{-k}\) is used for \(k\geq1\), not for the partition piece meeting the origin.
## The weighted \(\bar\partial\) step

Pages 28–31 use \[\varphi=2u+20d\log|z|_\infty+\rho u_0
              +\frac{\rho}{2}(\langle y\rangle-1).\] The singular logarithm is plurisubharmonic; the source expressly permits distributional Hessians in the invoked theorem. The positive correction has \[\partial\bar\partial\langle y\rangle
 =\frac{(1+|y|^2)I-yy^T}{4(1+|y|^2)^{3/2}},
 \qquad \lambda_{\min}=\frac1{4\langle y\rangle^3}.\] Thus the stated lower bound \(\kappa=\rho/(8\langle y\rangle^3)\) is correct. The cutoff derivative is supported away from zero, where the weight is bounded below. The solution \(g\) is holomorphic near zero, and the weighted submean estimate gives \[|g(x)|\leq C_d\rho^{-1/2}|x|^{9d}e^{3\rho|x|}.\] For \(|x|\leq c_d\min(\rho,\rho^{-1})\), the right side is uniformly small after choosing \(c_d\) sufficiently small. For \(\rho\leq1\) the power is \(\rho^{9d-1/2}\); for \(\rho\geq1\) it is \(\rho^{-9d-1/2}\), while the exponential is bounded in both regimes.

The additional negative weight at infinity absorbs logarithmic growth and makes the real restriction square integrable. The complex bound \(Ae^{2\rho|y|}\) gives Fourier support in \(B_{\rho/\pi}\) under this Fourier convention. The rescaling on page 14 then gives the announced support in \(B_\sigma\). Appendix A.3 is explicitly a sketch; its contour-shift sketch is not a substitute here for a full Paley–Wiener proof.
## Line porosity and the exponent

In Section 6, \(W_k=2^k/k^s\) and the weight height is \(2^k/k^\alpha\). Its derivatives through order 3 obey the required symbol bounds when \(3s<\alpha\). Restricting thickened porous sets to a line and using Appendix A.2 yields a gain \(k^{-s\gamma}\). Accordingly, \[G^*(r)\lesssim \frac{r}{(\log(2+r))^{\alpha+s\gamma}},\] and integrability requires \(\alpha+s\gamma>1\). After reducing \(\gamma\) if needed to \(0<\gamma\leq1\), the choice \(s=1/5\), \(\alpha=1-\gamma/10\) gives \[\alpha-3s=2/5-\gamma/10\geq3/10,\qquad
 \alpha+s\gamma-1=\gamma/10>0.\] These are compatible strict margins. The porosity counting identity \((L^d-1)^nL^{-nd}=(1-L^{-d})^n\) and the exponent \(-\log(1-L^{-d})/\log L\) also agree with the volume argument.
# Problem 1: pointwise normal derivative under a \(C^1\) hypothesis
## Source claim and exact location

Judgment: Minor, for the classical pointwise reading. Lemma 3.3, PDF page 17, equation (3.9), asserts for \(\omega\in C^1_0(\mathbb R)\) and its bounded harmonic extension to the upper half-plane that \[\partial_yu(x+i0)=H[-\omega'].\] The TeX label is `lem:normal_derivative_harmonic_extension`. The proof ends by passing through the Hilbert transform from \(C^1\) convergence of the boundary approximations. Such convergence does not imply finite pointwise convergence of the Hilbert transforms of their continuous derivatives.
## Explicit admissible example and complete check

Put \(r_0=1/8\) and \(r_1=1/4\). Define an even cutoff \(\chi\) by \[\chi(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,& |x|\leq r_0,\\
 1-3s^2+2s^3,\quad s=(|x|-r_0)/(r_1-r_0),
       &r_0<|x|<r_1,\\
 0,&|x|\geq r_1.
 \end{cases}\] The polynomial has zero derivative at both endpoints and takes values in \([0,1]\). Thus \(\chi\) is compactly supported and \(C^1\). Set \[\omega(0)=0,\qquad
 \omega(x)=\frac{\chi(x)|x|}{\log(e/|x|)}
   \quad(0<|x|<r_1),\qquad
 \omega(x)=0\quad(|x|\geq r_1).\] Near zero, with \(L(t)=\log(e/t)\), \[\frac{\omega(x)}x\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 \omega'(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(x)
       \bigl(L(|x|)^{-1}+L(|x|)^{-2}\bigr)\longrightarrow0.\] The cutoff endpoints have matching values and derivatives. Hence \(\omega\in C^1_0(\mathbb R)\) exactly as required, is real-valued, bounded and nonnegative, and \(\omega'(0)=0\). Lemma 3.3 does not require a sign; replacing \(\omega\) by \(-\omega\) also gives a nonpositive example if a weight convention is imposed.
## Counterevidence, impact, and verified correction

The distributional identity is valid; so is an appropriate \(L^2\) boundary-trace formulation. Since \(\omega'\) is compactly supported and in \(L^2\), Hilbert-transform continuity in \(L^2\) supplies that weaker interpretation. The lemma need not be read as claiming a new failure of that standard operator identity. Its pointwise notation and the displayed limiting argument should specify the intended topology.

A sufficient classical correction is to assume \(\omega\in C_c^{1,\alpha}(\mathbb R)\) for some \(0<\alpha\leq1\), or more generally a Dini modulus for \(\omega'\). In the symmetric principal value, the local numerator is bounded by a constant times \(t^\alpha\), so the integrand is integrable as \(t^{\alpha-1}\). The tails are finite. The resulting continuous boundary function is recovered by Poisson approximation, giving the finite classical normal derivative and the identity. In particular, \(C_c^2\) is sufficient.

This defect is peripheral to the inspected core. Lemma 3.4 on the same page assumes \(C^2_0(\mathbb R^d)\); its one-dimensional application on pages 17–18 uses \(C^2_0(\mathbb R)\) explicitly. Proposition 3.1 also assumes \(C^2\), the modified weights have three controlled derivatives, and Lemma A.9 assumes \(C^2_0\). Those uses meet the sufficient corrected hypothesis. The example verifies an overstated pointwise regularity range, not a counterexample to Theorems 1.1 or 1.4. A wording clarification in a distributional formulation, or the stated strengthening for a classical formulation, resolves the identified issue. Author adoption and final-version status remain unknown.

The following are recorded to make the checked argument reproducible. They are not additional supported Major findings and are not counted as separate typographical complaints.
## The final Schwartz factor, pages 34–35

The text introduces a scaled factor and then suppresses its scale in the product notation. Its normalization should ensure a nonzero value at zero, not merely an integral normalization for the untransformed factor. A fully specified choice is to take \(\eta\in C_c^\infty(B_1)\), \(\eta\geq0\), \(\int\eta=1\), put \(\Phi=\check\eta\), and use \(\Phi_\delta(x)=\Phi(\delta x)\) with \(\delta=c_d\sigma\leq\sigma/2\). ## The upper end of the line scales, pages 33–34

The segment length \(2^k/\sqrt d\) may exceed \(N=h^{-1}\) for the outermost nonempty annuli. A direct way to stay within the stated porosity range is to use \[R_k=\min(2^k/\sqrt d,N/2).\] Since a nonempty annulus has \(2^k\leq3\sqrt d\,N\), this length is comparable to \(2^k\) with constants depending only on \(d\). u\) is below \(R_k\), Corollary A.8 gives exactly the same power \(k^{-s\gamma}\). If \(a_k\geq R_k\), then \(k^s\leq24d/
u\); the trivial length bound is therefore at most a constant depending on \(

Title: Scientific initial review of M25-0020
# Identity, version and outcome

Paper. M. Dafermos and J. Luk, The interior of dynamical vacuum black holes I: The \(C^0\)-stability of the Kerr Cauchy horizon. Assigned identifier M25-0020; DOI https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2025.202.2.1. The bibliographic journal placement is Annals of Mathematics 202 (2025), 309–630. This review is bound to arXiv:1710.01722v1, submitted 4 October 2017, with 5 October 2017 printed on its title page. Both dates are retained; neither is substituted for the other. The 2025 journal text was not compared.

Page convention. All source page references below are one-based PDF pages of the acquired 217-page manuscript. Its printed pagination agrees with those page numbers. TeX line references, where supplied, are one-based lines of `KerrInterior.postedversion.tex`.

Decision within this review. Problem 1 is Major because a demonstrated invalid coordinate-limit argument is used directly in Theorem 16.14, the final continuity step of the principal extension theorem. Problem 2 is Minor because its degenerate data satisfy the local proposition as stated but are excluded by the main theorem’s actual data. There is no claim of a counterexample to the main nonlinear Einstein theorem, no claim about an unexamined journal version, and no independently accepted scientific decision.

Decisive evidence. For exact Kerr with \(M=1\), \(a=3/5\), the manuscript’s angular change is \[\phi_{*,\mathcal{CH}^{+}}=\phi_*-3v,\qquad
 F_{\mathrm K}(v,x)=R(-3v)x\] in either specified stereographic chart. Consequently \(D_xF_{\mathrm K}\) alternates between \(\mathrm I\) and \(-\mathrm I\) along two sequences approaching the same old-coordinate boundary point. The estimate (16.55) would force their difference to tend to zero. This is an exact calculation at admissible rotating subextremal parameters. Problem 2 uses smooth Minkowski annular data \(u=-\tau^3\), \(v=\tau\); the eikonal equation forces \(\mathrm du=0\) at \(\tau=0\), which a coordinate function cannot have.
# Claims, hypotheses and coverage
## What the main theorem does and does not assert

The principal result studied here is the construction, from a spacelike interior hypersurface asymptotic to rotating subextremal Kerr and satisfying the specified weighted smallness assumptions, of a nontrivial Cauchy-horizon portion with a continuous nondegenerate Lorentzian extension. The comparison parameters obey \(0<|a|<M\). This review does not add the Schwarzschild endpoint \(a=0\), the extremal endpoint \(|a|=M\), or uniform constants in either endpoint limit.

The introduction also describes event-horizon and bifurcate-horizon formulations and consequences for strong cosmic censorship conditional on further exterior/interior results. Theorems 2 and 3 and the cited subsequent projects are not silently identified with the theorem proved in this manuscript. Likewise, the cosmological-constant discussion on pp. 34–36 is separated from the vacuum \(\Lambda=0\) proof. Section 17 supplies upper regularity estimates; it is not a proof of generic blow-up or failure of unweighted \(H^1\) regularity.

The initial parameter is \(\tau\geq1\), with the actual optical data \(v=\tau\) and \(u=C_R-\tau\). The initial weighted norms include metric derivatives through order five and second-fundamental-form derivatives through order four, with polynomial weight \(\tau^{1/2+\delta}\) and \(\delta>0\). The proof uses the detailed initial, null-flux, and sphere norms of Section 4; these are not replaced by a bare informal small-perturbation assumption. Large \(N\) is chosen first, then sufficiently small \(\epsilon\) and sufficiently negative \(u_f\) in the order prescribed in the argument.
## Basic conventions checked

Equation reference: review:metric. For the double-null metric \[
 g=-2\Omega^2(\mathrm du\otimes\mathrm dv+\mathrm dv\otimes\mathrm du)
 +\gamma_{AB}(\mathrm d\theta^A-b^A\mathrm dv)
                \otimes(\mathrm d\theta^B-b^B\mathrm dv),\] the manuscript uses \[e_3=\partial_u,\qquad
 e_4=\Omega^{-2}(\partial_v+b^A\partial_{\theta^A}),\qquad
 g(e_3,e_4)=-2.\] A pointwise diagonal angular-metric check gives \(\det g=-4\Omega^4\gamma_{11}\gamma_{22}\) and \(g^{uu}=g^{vv}=0\). The normalization of the unit timelike and spacelike hypersurface normals was checked algebraically, including their squared norms \(-1\), \(1\), and zero inner product. This checks signs and factors, not every component of the Einstein equations.

The gauge identities \(\omega=0\), \(\underline\omega=-\partial_u\log\Omega\), \(\zeta=\eta\), \(\nabla\log\Omega=(\eta+\underline\eta)/2\), and \(\partial_u b=2\Omega^2(\eta-\underline\eta)^\sharp\) were followed into their uses. The renormalizations \[K=-\rho+\tfrac12\widehat\chi\mathbin{\cdot}\widehat{\underline\chi}
                  -\tfrac14\operatorname{tr}\chi\operatorname{tr}\underline\chi,
 \qquad
 \check\sigma=\sigma+\tfrac12\widehat{\underline\chi}\wedge\widehat\chi\] are essential to the curvature-pair cancellations; replacing them by unrenormalized components would change the proof.

# Problem 1: rotating Kerr contradicts the asserted coordinate limit
## Location and source claim

Severity: Major. The linked assertions occur in Section 16.1.2, p. 166, especially (16.2); Lemma 16.8, p. 176; (16.44), p. 177; Proposition 16.11, pp. 178–181, including (16.45) and (16.50)–(16.55); Corollary 16.13, p. 182; and Theorem 16.14, pp. 182–183, especially (16.59)–(16.60). The defining Kerr comparison is in Appendix A.5.2, p. 206, with the smooth-extension discussion in A.5.6, p. 207. Related Kerr shift formulas are (A.43), p. 202, and (A.47), p. 203.

Equation reference: review:false-tail. The manuscript compares the old compactified coordinates \((u,v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}},\theta^1,\theta^2)\) with new coordinates \((u,v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}},\theta^1_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}},\theta^2_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}})\). It asserts the same continuous structure, while allowing a different differentiable structure. Proposition 16.11 asserts both an \(O(\epsilon)\) difference between the actual and Kerr angular Jacobians and continuous extension of the actual angular Jacobian in the old coordinates. Its final estimate (16.55) bounds the same-old-angle difference at two values of \(v\) by a constant times \[
 |v_m^{-2\delta}-v_n^{-2\delta}|^{1/2}
 \left(1+\left\lVert v^{1/2+\delta}\nabla\widetilde b\right\rVert
                _{L^\infty_uL^2_vL^\infty(S)}\right).\] Corollary 16.13 then transfers continuous extendibility of an arbitrary \(S\)-tangent tensor from the old to the new coordinates. Theorem 16.14 explicitly invokes this transfer and the angular-Jacobian limit in proving continuity of the metric.
## Admissible parameters and all relevant assumptions

Equation reference: review:kerr-values. Set \[
 M=1,\quad a=\frac35,\quad
 r_-=\frac15,\quad r_+=\frac95,\quad
 \omega_-=\frac{4Mar_-}{(r_-^2+a^2)^2}=3,\quad
 c=\frac{r_+-r_-}{r_-^2+a^2}=4.\] These satisfy \(0<a<M\) strictly. Use exact Kerr initial data on the comparison hypersurface. They solve the vacuum constraints and agree identically with the comparison Kerr data, including all derivatives: the difference size is zero. Therefore every stated smallness requirement on those differences is satisfied for any allowed positive \(\epsilon\), and every positive \(\delta\) is admissible for that comparison. Fix an allowed \(N\), take \(u_f\) as negative as required, and restrict to \(u\leq u_f\). All sequences used below can be started sufficiently late that \(u+v\geq C_R\), the selected initial sphere has been passed, and the exponential formula for \(v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}}\) applies. Thus neither an early-time boundary nor an excluded parameter endpoint is used.

Equation reference: review:kerr-map. In the large-\(v\) region, \(v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}}=-e^{-4v}/4\), which tends to zero. The manuscript’s Kerr angular map, defined by Appendix A.5.2, is \[
 (\theta_*,\phi_*)\longmapsto
 (\theta_*,\phi_{*,\mathcal{CH}^{+}})=(\theta_*,\phi_*-3v)
 \quad \text{modulo }2\pi.\] An additive initial phase, if retained, merely translates the sequences below and changes none of the conclusions.
## Exact Jacobian and topological contradiction

Equation reference: review:rotation, review:sequences. Let \[J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 R(t)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t\\ \sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}.\] In either of the manuscript’s stereographic charts, the angular coordinate is \[x=\rho(\theta_*)(\cos\phi_*,\sin\phi_*),
 \qquad \rho=\tan(\theta_*/2)\ \text{or}\ \cot(\theta_*/2).\] Consequently the map [review:kerr-map] (#review:kerr-map) and its derivative are exactly \[
 F_{\mathrm K}(v,x)=R(-3v)x,\qquad D_xF_{\mathrm K}(v,x)=R(-3v).\] Choose \(x_0=(1,0)\) on the equator and the two sequences \[
 v_n=\frac{2\pi n}{3},\qquad
 w_n=\frac{2\pi n+\pi}{3}.\] Then \[F_{\mathrm K}(v_n,x_0)=x_0,\quad F_{\mathrm K}(w_n,x_0)=-x_0,\qquad
 D_xF_{\mathrm K}(v_n,x_0)=\mathrm I,\quad D_xF_{\mathrm K}(w_n,x_0)=-\mathrm I.\] Both images stay in the prescribed sets \(\mathcal V_i'\) with squared radius less than \(2\), and hence in \(\mathcal V_i''\) with squared radius less than \(3\). There is no chart-edge or polar singularity. The Jacobian norm difference is \(2\), and its \((1,1)\) entry has difference \(2\).

The old-coordinate sequences \((u,v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}}(v_n),x_0)\) and \((u,v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}}(w_n),x_0)\) converge to the same boundary point \((u,0,x_0)\). Their new angular coordinates have distinct limits. Thus the identity transition on the common interior has no continuous extension between these two proposed completions. In particular, they cannot give the same \(C^0\) structure in the sense asserted for that transition. Each completion may be abstractly homeomorphic to a product; that weaker observation does not give the identity-compatible boundary map the proof requires.

The right side of [review:false-tail] (#review:false-tail), for the exact Kerr comparison and any fixed \(\delta>0\), tends to zero, since \[0<v_n^{-2\delta}-w_n^{-2\delta}<v_n^{-2\delta}\longrightarrow0.\] The left side for the Kerr angular Jacobian equals \(2\). This is a direct failure of the supposedly trivial Kerr-background estimate in (16.55).

There is a separate ambiguity in the manuscript’s forced coordinate equation, discussed below. The contradiction does not require pretending that its inconsistent stereographic equation has already been solved by [review:kerr-map] (#review:kerr-map). If its actual solution is used instead, Proposition 16.11 still asserts a uniform componentwise bound \(|D_xF-D_xF_{\mathrm K}|\leq C\epsilon\) and continuity of \(D_xF\). Choose an admissible small \(\epsilon\) with \(C\epsilon<1/2\), using the stated uniform estimate. Along [review:sequences] (#review:sequences), the \((1,1)\) entries of \(D_xF\) differ by at least \(2-2C\epsilon>1\). They cannot converge to a common boundary value. Exact Kerr satisfies the data hypotheses for this choice; even though \(u_f\) may depend on the smallness choice, the argument applies at that fixed allowed \(u_f\) and arbitrarily large \(v\). The asserted closeness and continuity therefore cannot both hold.
## Failure of the unrestricted tensor-continuity transfer

For the intended exact Kerr map, take the globally smooth scalar on the sphere \[f(\theta_*,\phi_*)=\sin\theta_*\cos\phi_*
                 =\frac{2x_1}{1+x_1^2+x_2^2}.\] It is independent of \(u\) and \(v\), so it extends smoothly in the old compactified coordinates. In the new coordinates it is \[f=\sin\theta_*\cos(\phi_{*,\mathcal{CH}^{+}}+3v).\] At \(\theta_*=\pi/2\), \(\phi_{*,\mathcal{CH}^{+}}=0\) its values along [review:sequences] (#review:sequences) are \(1\) and \(-1\). It has no continuous new-coordinate extension. If the phrase \(S\)-tangent tensor is intended to exclude scalars, use \(f\) times the unit round metric; that metric is rotation-invariant, and the same failure is present in its tensor components. This checks the actual universal continuity-transfer assertion rather than a condition imposed only on axisymmetric metric coefficients.
## Why the Kerr derivative estimate used in the proof fails

Equation reference: review:shift-derivative. Write the exact Kerr shift as \(b_{\mathrm K}=B\,\partial_{\phi_*}\), where \[B=\frac{4Mar}{(r^2+a^2)^2-a^2\sin^2\theta\,\Delta},
 \qquad \Delta=r^2-2Mr+a^2.\] At the inner horizon \(B\to\omega_-=3\). In stereographic coordinates this vector field is \(B J_0x\). On compact chart subsets its limiting component derivative is \[
 D_x b_{\mathrm K}\longrightarrow 3J_0\ne0.\] The derivatives of the scalar coefficient \(B\) tend to zero; derivatives of the rotating basis field do not. Formula (A.47) controls special scalar-coordinate derivatives. It cannot be used to conclude that all stereographic component derivatives of \(b_{\mathrm K}\) are \(O(\Omega_{\mathrm K}^2)\).

The estimate used before (16.51), p. 181, consequently does not give \(\int^\infty |D_xb_{\mathrm K}|\,\mathrm dv<\infty\): already an off-diagonal component tends to \(3\) in absolute value. This also explains why treating the background rotation as a negligible transport coefficient is invalid. A rotation can preserve geometric distances without having a small componentwise Jacobian generator; the two statements are different.
## Chart consistency requires the derivative at the image point

There is a related coordinate issue in Lemma 16.8 and equations (16.39)–(16.44). If an angular map \(F\) satisfies \[(\partial_v+b\mathbin{\cdot}\partial_x)F=q(x),\] then a nonlinear target-chart change \(\Psi\) gives \[(\partial_v+b\mathbin{\cdot}\partial_x)(\Psi\circ F)
       =D\Psi(F(x))q(x).\] The components of the old-point vector field in the changed chart instead use \(D\Psi(x)q(x)\). The proof equates these derivative evaluations without justification. The elementary local diagnostic \(F(v,x)=x+v\), \(\Psi(x)=x^2\) on \(x>0\) gives \(2(x+v)\) on the left and \(2x\) for the asserted transformed forcing. This diagnostic is only a chain-rule check; the Kerr calculation supplies the counterevidence in the relevant spacetime.

Equation reference: review:covariance-residual. Even granting the natural correction of the subtracted constant in (16.40) to \(\omega_-\), the polar Kerr equation reads \[(\partial_v+B\partial_{\phi_*})\phi_{*,\mathcal{CH}^{+}}=B-\omega_-.\] For the stereographic Kerr map [review:rotation] (#review:rotation), its correct left side is \((B-\omega_-)J_0R(-\omega_-v)x\). The stated old-point forcing in (16.44) is \((B-\omega_-)J_0x\). Their difference is \[
 (B-\omega_-)(R(-\omega_-v)-\mathrm I)J_0x,\] which is generally nonzero before the horizon. At the equator with the parameters [review:kerr-values] (#review:kerr-values), simplification gives \[B(r)=\frac{12/5}{r^3+(9/25)r+18/25},\qquad r_-<r<r_+.\] Its denominator is strictly increasing for \(r>0\) and gives \(B(r_-) =3\); hence \(B(r)<3\) for every interior \(r>r_-\). For any fixed allowed \(u_f\), late finite \(v\) has \(r>r_-\), and infinitely many such \(v\) have a nonidentity rotation. The residual is therefore nonzero at legitimate late points. For illustration, \(r=1/2\) gives \(B=96/41\), and algebraic substitution of \(R=-\mathrm I\), \(x=(1,0)\) gives residual \((0,54/41)\). This last numerical pair is a finite algebra illustration, not an additional assertion that a prescribed fixed-\(u_f\) orbit simultaneously takes those illustrative values.
## Counterevidence and precise impact

Several facts limit the conclusion. First, the exact Kerr spacetime is smoothly extendible in the regular rotating coordinates described in the appendix; the calculation above does not refute that. Second, \(R(-3v)\) is invertible with determinant \(1\) for every finite \(v\). Failure of its boundary limit is not a failure of interior diffeomorphism. Third, the Kerr metric has axisymmetry, which can cancel rotations in transformed metric components even when a generic tensor does not extend. Fourth, local polar angular derivatives can hide the rotating phase, but they do not remove it or supply a globally regular stereographic boundary map. Reversing the rotation sign or using the inverse map leaves the nonconvergence unchanged.

Proposition 16.6’s conversion of transport control into fixed-old-angle continuity also deserves care because the relevant vector contains an angular shift. This report does not count that observation as a further demonstrated counterexample to its metric conclusion: exact Kerr’s symmetry gives genuine cancellations. Likewise, the ordinary matrix exponential written in the proof of Proposition 16.11 would require commutation or a correctly ordered fundamental solution; it is not counted as an additional independent issue here.
## Supported repair ingredient and remaining nonlinear work
A precise limited replacement ingredient is available, but it is not a completed repair of Section 16.

Lemma 1.  Let \(V\) generate a fixed round-sphere rotation, let \(\omega\) be constant, and let \(b(v)=\omega V+q(v)\) be a smooth time-dependent vector field on \(\mathbb S^2\). Suppose \(\int_{v_0}^\infty \left\lVert q(v)\right\rVert_{C^1(\mathbb S^2)}\,\mathrm dv<\infty\). If \(\Phi_v\) is its forward flow from \(v_0\) and \(Q_t\) is the rotation flow of \(V\), then \(Q_{-\omega(v-v_0)}\circ\Phi_v\) converges in \(C^1\) to a \(C^1\) diffeomorphism.

Proof. Conjugating by the round rotation produces a flow \(\Psi_v\) with vector field \[\widetilde q_v=(Q_{-\omega(v-v_0)})_*q_v.\] Rotations preserve the relevant norms up to a fixed equivalent choice of \(C^1\) norm. Thus \[\int\left\lVert\widetilde q_v\right\rVert_{C^1}\,\mathrm dv<\infty.\] Its displacement between times \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) is bounded by \(\int_{v_1}^{v_2}\left\lVert\widetilde q_v\right\rVert_{C^0}\,\mathrm dv\). The derivative equation is \(\partial_vD\Psi_v=D\widetilde q_v(\Psi_v)D\Psi_v\). Gronwall gives a uniform derivative bound; integration of that equation gives a uniform Cauchy estimate for \(D\Psi_v\) with the \(C^1\) tail integral. The inverse derivatives are uniformly bounded by the same integrable-coefficient argument. Hence the limit is locally invertible and globally bi-Lipschitz. Surjectivity follows by compactness: for each target, take a convergent subsequence of its preimages under \(\Psi_v\). The limit and inverse are \(C^1\) by local inversion, giving the assertion. ◻

This lemma removes the persistent rigid rotation before asking for convergence. To use it in the full problem one must construct an intrinsic compatible sphere map, establish the needed bounds in the precise mixed norms and on the relevant hypersurfaces, and prove continuity of the transformed metric directly or through a valid relative-coordinate transfer. Lemma 16.8, the applicable part of Proposition 16.6, Proposition 16.11, Corollary 16.13, and Theorem 16.14 would need corresponding revisions. Those nonlinear revisions have not been proved in this review. Simply deleting the nondecaying rotation from one displayed estimate does not verify the original conclusion.
# Problem 2: strict monotonicity does not prevent a degenerate optical coordinate
## Location, claim and severity

Severity: Minor. Proposition 2.1, pp. 38–39, constructs local double-null coordinates near the embedded spacelike hypersurface \(\Sigma=\ell\times\mathbb S^2\). The simple curve \(\ell:(a,b)\to\mathbb R^2\) supplies smooth functions \(u|_\Sigma\) and \(v|_\Sigma\) that are assumed strictly decreasing and strictly increasing, respectively, in its parameter \(\tau\). The proposed coordinates satisfy the eikonal equations and metric form (2.1). The stated strict monotonicity, in its ordinary mathematical meaning, does not imply nonzero derivatives.
## Complete counterexample to the stated local proposition

Equation reference: review:degenerate-curve. Consider the annular region of Minkowski spacetime \[g=-\mathrm dt^2+\mathrm d\tau^2+(2+\tau)^2g_{\mathbb S^2},
 \qquad -1<\tau<1,\] where \(g_{\mathbb S^2}\) is the unit round metric and the ordinary spatial radius is \(2+\tau>0\). Take \(\Sigma=\{t=0\}\) with all of \(\mathbb S^2\), and \[
 \ell(\tau)=(-\tau^3,\tau),\qquad
 u|_\Sigma=-\tau^3,\qquad v|_\Sigma=\tau.\] The ambient metric is smooth and Lorentzian. The induced metric on \(\Sigma\) is positive definite, so the embedding is spacelike and isometric with the specified induced metric. The curve is smooth and injective; its derivative \((-3\tau^2,1)\) never vanishes, so it is a regular simple curve with smooth inverse parameter \(v\). The function \(-\tau^3\) is strictly decreasing and \(\tau\) strictly increasing on the whole interval. Thus this is not a nonsmooth parameterization or a curve cusp. Additive constants may be added to \(u\) and \(v\) if a coordinate-range translation is desired.

At any point of the sphere \(\tau=0\), all tangential derivatives of \(u|_\Sigma\) vanish. With \(N=\partial_t\) the unit normal, any smooth extension of \(u\) has \[g^{-1}(\mathrm du,\mathrm du)
       =-(Nu)^2+|\mathrm d_\Sigma u|^2
       =-(Nu)^2\] at that point. The required eikonal equation therefore gives \(Nu=0\). Hence \(\mathrm du=0\) as a full spacetime covector at that point. A function whose differential vanishes cannot be one member of a coordinate system there. In particular, it cannot give the asserted nonsingular double-null metric with positive finite lapse.

The proposition asserts the existence of such coordinates near every point (and the associated sphere neighborhood); the point \(\tau=0\) contradicts that assertion. The counterexample satisfies every stated geometric and monotonicity hypothesis, while the asserted conclusion is impossible.
## Alternative reading, supported correction and limited impact

If strictly decreasing/increasing was intended to mean that the derivatives are strictly negative/positive everywhere, that is the missing explicit assumption and excludes [review:degenerate-curve] (#review:degenerate-curve). These meanings are not equivalent for smooth real functions.

The precise local correction is to require \[\partial_\tau u|_\Sigma<0,\qquad
 \partial_\tau v|_\Sigma>0\] pointwise, in addition to the existing smooth spacelike hypotheses. The functions are constant on each initial sphere. If \(n\) is the unit normal to those spheres within \(\Sigma\), oriented by \(n\tau>0\), then \(nu<0\) and \(nv>0\). Choosing the appropriate eikonal branches gives nonzero \(Nu\) and \(Nv\). The normal derivative of the eikonal equation, viewed as an equation for the normal first derivative, is \(-2Nu\) or \(-2Nv\) and is nonzero. Thus the ordinary smooth noncharacteristic local construction applies, with the prescribed branch; compactness of the sphere permits a common sufficiently small neighborhood. This verifies the missing nondegeneracy ingredient of the proposition, not a new global existence statement.

The actual main data (4.5), p. 52, are \(u=C_R-\tau\) and \(v=\tau\). Their derivatives are \(-1\) and \(1\). Equations (4.8)–(4.10), p. 55, have the positive factor \(n\tau=(\Phi-|w|^2)^{-1/2}\) under the spacelike condition. Accordingly the degenerate example does not invalidate the invocation for these main data. This supported defect remains local and Minor. The reciprocal normalization appearing in the nearby proof is not counted as another issue: the geometric normal calculation and later formulas make the intended normalization recoverable, and isolated typographical defects are outside this review’s issue count.

Strict 0<a<M; any fixed allowed delta>0, large N, small epsilon and corresponding sufficiently negative u_f. Start sequences late enough for u+v>=C_R and compactifying-coordinate formula. Equator in both specified chart interiors; no endpoint or chart-boundary exception.
analysis: Severity: Major. The linked assertions occur in Section 16.1.2, p. 166, especially (16.2); Lemma 16.8, p. 176; (16.44), p. 177; Proposition 16.11, pp. 178–181, including (16.45) and (16.50)–(16.55); Corollary 16.13, p. 182; and Theorem 16.14, pp. 182–183, especially (16.59)–(16.60). The defining Kerr comparison is in Appendix A.5.2, p. 206, with the smooth-extension discussion in A.5.6, p. 207. Related Kerr shift formulas are (A.43), p. 202, and (A.47), p. 203.

Equation reference: review:false-tail. The manuscript compares the old compactified coordinates \((u,v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}},\theta^1,\theta^2)\) with new coordinates \((u,v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}},\theta^1_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}},\theta^2_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}})\). It asserts the same continuous structure, while allowing a different differentiable structure. Proposition 16.11 asserts both an \(O(\epsilon)\) difference between the actual and Kerr angular Jacobians and continuous extension of the actual angular Jacobian in the old coordinates. Its final estimate (16.55) bounds the same-old-angle difference at two values of \(v\) by a constant times \[
 |v_m^{-2\delta}-v_n^{-2\delta}|^{1/2}
 \left(1+\left\lVert v^{1/2+\delta}\nabla\widetilde b\right\rVert
                _{L^\infty_uL^2_vL^\infty(S)}\right).\] Corollary 16.13 then transfers continuous extendibility of an arbitrary \(S\)-tangent tensor from the old to the new coordinates. Theorem 16.14 explicitly invokes this transfer and the angular-Jacobian limit in proving continuity of the metric.

Equation reference: review:kerr-values. Set \[
 M=1,\quad a=\frac35,\quad
 r_-=\frac15,\quad r_+=\frac95,\quad
 \omega_-=\frac{4Mar_-}{(r_-^2+a^2)^2}=3,\quad
 c=\frac{r_+-r_-}{r_-^2+a^2}=4.\] These satisfy \(0<a<M\) strictly. Use exact Kerr initial data on the comparison hypersurface. They solve the vacuum constraints and agree identically with the comparison Kerr data, including all derivatives: the difference size is zero. Therefore every stated smallness requirement on those differences is satisfied for any allowed positive \(\epsilon\), and every positive \(\delta\) is admissible for that comparison. Fix an allowed \(N\), take \(u_f\) as negative as required, and restrict to \(u\leq u_f\). All sequences used below can be started sufficiently late that \(u+v\geq C_R\), the selected initial sphere has been passed, and the exponential formula for \(v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}}\) applies. Thus neither an early-time boundary nor an excluded parameter endpoint is used.

Equation reference: review:kerr-map. In the large-\(v\) region, \(v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}}=-e^{-4v}/4\), which tends to zero. The manuscript’s Kerr angular map, defined by Appendix A.5.2, is \[
 (\theta_*,\phi_*)\longmapsto
 (\theta_*,\phi_{*,\mathcal{CH}^{+}})=(\theta_*,\phi_*-3v)
 \quad \text{modulo }2\pi.\] An additive initial phase, if retained, merely translates the sequences below and changes none of the conclusions.

Equation reference: review:rotation, review:sequences. Let \[J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 R(t)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t\\ \sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix}.\] In either of the manuscript’s stereographic charts, the angular coordinate is \[x=\rho(\theta_*)(\cos\phi_*,\sin\phi_*),
 \qquad \rho=\tan(\theta_*/2)\ \text{or}\ \cot(\theta_*/2).\] Consequently the map [review:kerr-map] (#review:kerr-map) and its derivative are exactly \[
 F_{\mathrm K}(v,x)=R(-3v)x,\qquad D_xF_{\mathrm K}(v,x)=R(-3v).\] Choose \(x_0=(1,0)\) on the equator and the two sequences \[
 v_n=\frac{2\pi n}{3},\qquad
 w_n=\frac{2\pi n+\pi}{3}.\] Then \[F_{\mathrm K}(v_n,x_0)=x_0,\quad F_{\mathrm K}(w_n,x_0)=-x_0,\qquad
 D_xF_{\mathrm K}(v_n,x_0)=\mathrm I,\quad D_xF_{\mathrm K}(w_n,x_0)=-\mathrm I.\] Both images stay in the prescribed sets \(\mathcal V_i'\) with squared radius less than \(2\), and hence in \(\mathcal V_i''\) with squared radius less than \(3\). There is no chart-edge or polar singularity. The Jacobian norm difference is \(2\), and its \((1,1)\) entry has difference \(2\).

The old-coordinate sequences \((u,v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}}(v_n),x_0)\) and \((u,v_{\mathcal{CH}^{+}}(w_n),x_0)\) converge to the same boundary point \((u,0,x_0)\). Their new angular coordinates have distinct limits. Thus the identity transition on the common interior has no continuous extension between these two proposed completions. In particular, they cannot give the same \(C^0\) structure in the sense asserted for that transition. Each completion may be abstractly homeomorphic to a product; that weaker observation does not give the identity-compatible boundary map the proof requires.

The right side of [review:false-tail] (#review:false-tail), for the exact Kerr comparison and any fixed \(\delta>0\), tends to zero, since \[0<v_n^{-2\delta}-w_n^{-2\delta}<v_n^{-2\delta}\longrightarrow0.\] The left side for the Kerr angular Jacobian equals \(2\). This is a direct failure of the supposedly trivial Kerr-background estimate in (16.55).

There is a separate ambiguity in the manuscript’s forced coordinate equation, discussed below. The contradiction does not require pretending that its inconsistent stereographic equation has already been solved by [review:kerr-map] (#review:kerr-map). If its actual solution is used instead, Proposition 16.11 still asserts a uniform componentwise bound \(|D_xF-D_xF_{\mathrm K}|\leq C\epsilon\) and continuity of \(D_xF\). Choose an admissible small \(\epsilon\) with \(C\epsilon<1/2\), using the stated uniform estimate. Along [review:sequences] (#review:sequences), the \((1,1)\) entries of \(D_xF\) differ by at least \(2-2C\epsilon>1\). They cannot converge to a common boundary value. Exact Kerr satisfies the data hypotheses for this choice; even though \(u_f\) may depend on the smallness choice, the argument applies at that fixed allowed \(u_f\) and arbitrarily large \(v\). The asserted closeness and continuity therefore cannot both hold.

For the intended exact Kerr map, take the globally smooth scalar on the sphere \[f(\theta_*,\phi_*)=\sin\theta_*\cos\phi_*
                 =\frac{2x_1}{1+x_1^2+x_2^2}.\] It is independent of \(u\) and \(v\), so it extends smoothly in the old compactified coordinates. In the new coordinates it is \[f=\sin\theta_*\cos(\phi_{*,\mathcal{CH}^{+}}+3v).\] At \(\theta_*=\pi/2\), \(\phi_{*,\mathcal{CH}^{+}}=0\) its values along [review:sequences] (#review:sequences) are \(1\) and \(-1\). It has no continuous new-coordinate extension. If the phrase \(S\)-tangent tensor is intended to exclude scalars, use \(f\) times the unit round metric; that metric is rotation-invariant, and the same failure is present in its tensor components. This checks the actual universal continuity-transfer assertion rather than a condition imposed only on axisymmetric metric coefficients.

Equation reference: review:shift-derivative. Write the exact Kerr shift as \(b_{\mathrm K}=B\,\partial_{\phi_*}\), where \[B=\frac{4Mar}{(r^2+a^2)^2-a^2\sin^2\theta\,\Delta},
 \qquad \Delta=r^2-2Mr+a^2.\] At the inner horizon \(B\to\omega_-=3\). In stereographic coordinates this vector field is \(B J_0x\). On compact chart subsets its limiting component derivative is \[
 D_x b_{\mathrm K}\longrightarrow 3J_0\ne0.\] The derivatives of the scalar coefficient \(B\) tend to zero; derivatives of the rotating basis field do not. Formula (A.47) controls special scalar-coordinate derivatives. It cannot be used to conclude that all stereographic component derivatives of \(b_{\mathrm K}\) are \(O(\Omega_{\mathrm K}^2)\).

The estimate used before (16.51), p. 181, consequently does not give \(\int^\infty |D_xb_{\mathrm K}|\,\mathrm dv<\infty\): already an off-diagonal component tends to \(3\) in absolute value. This also explains why treating the background rotation as a negligible transport coefficient is invalid. A rotation can preserve geometric distances without having a small componentwise Jacobian generator; the two statements are different.

There is a related coordinate issue in Lemma 16.8 and equations (16.39)–(16.44). If an angular map \(F\) satisfies \[(\partial_v+b\mathbin{\cdot}\partial_x)F=q(x),\] then a nonlinear target-chart change \(\Psi\) gives \[(\partial_v+b\mathbin{\cdot}\partial_x)(\Psi\circ F)
       =D\Psi(F(x))q(x).\] The components of the old-point vector field in the changed chart instead use \(D\Psi(x)q(x)\). The proof equates these derivative evaluations without justification. The elementary local diagnostic \(F(v,x)=x+v\), \(\Psi(x)=x^2\) on \(x>0\) gives \(2(x+v)\) on the left and \(2x\) for the asserted transformed forcing. This diagnostic is only a chain-rule check; the Kerr calculation supplies the counterevidence in the relevant spacetime.

Equation reference: review:covariance-residual. Even granting the natural correction of the subtracted constant in (16.40) to \(\omega_-\), the polar Kerr equation reads \[(\partial_v+B\partial_{\phi_*})\phi_{*,\mathcal{CH}^{+}}=B-\omega_-.\] For the stereographic Kerr map [review:rotation] (#review:rotation), its correct left side is \((B-\omega_-)J_0R(-\omega_-v)x\). The stated old-point forcing in (16.44) is \((B-\omega_-)J_0x\). Their difference is \[
 (B-\omega_-)(R(-\omega_-v)-\mathrm I)J_0x,\] which is generally nonzero before the horizon. At the equator with the parameters [review:kerr-values] (#review:kerr-values), simplification gives \[B(r)=\frac{12/5}{r^3+(9/25)r+18/25},\qquad r_-<r<r_+.\] Its denominator is strictly increasing for \(r>0\) and gives \(B(r_-) =3\); hence \(B(r)<3\) for every interior \(r>r_-\). For any fixed allowed \(u_f\), late finite \(v\) has \(r>r_-\), and infinitely many such \(v\) have a nonidentity rotation. The residual is therefore nonzero at legitimate late points. For illustration, \(r=1/2\) gives \(B=96/41\), and algebraic substitution of \(R=-\mathrm I\), \(x=(1,0)\) gives residual \((0,54/41)\). This last numerical pair is a finite algebra illustration, not an additional assertion that a prescribed fixed-\(u_f\) orbit simultaneously takes those illustrative values.
A precise limited replacement ingredient is available, but it is not a completed repair of Section 16.

Lemma 1.  Let \(V\) generate a fixed round-sphere rotation, let \(\omega\) be constant, and let \(b(v)=\omega V+q(v)\) be a smooth time-dependent vector field on \(\mathbb S^2\). Suppose \(\int_{v_0}^\infty \left\lVert q(v)\right\rVert_{C^1(\mathbb S^2)}\,\mathrm dv<\infty\). If \(\Phi_v\) is its forward flow from \(v_0\) and \(Q_t\) is the rotation flow of \(V\), then \(Q_{-\omega(v-v_0)}\circ\Phi_v\) converges in \(C^1\) to a \(C^1\) diffeomorphism.

Proof. Conjugating by the round rotation produces a flow \(\Psi_v\) with vector field \[\widetilde q_v=(Q_{-\omega(v-v_0)})_*q_v.\] Rotations preserve the relevant norms up to a fixed equivalent choice of \(C^1\) norm. Thus \[\int\left\lVert\widetilde q_v\right\rVert_{C^1}\,\mathrm dv<\infty.\] Its displacement between times \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) is bounded by \(\int_{v_1}^{v_2}\left\lVert\widetilde q_v\right\rVert_{C^0}\,\mathrm dv\). The derivative equation is \(\partial_vD\Psi_v=D\widetilde q_v(\Psi_v)D\Psi_v\). Gronwall gives a uniform derivative bound; integration of that equation gives a uniform Cauchy estimate for \(D\Psi_v\) with the \(C^1\) tail integral. The inverse derivatives are uniformly bounded by the same integrable-coefficient argument. Hence the limit is locally invertible and globally bi-Lipschitz. Surjectivity follows by compactness: for each target, take a convergent subsequence of its preimages under \(\Psi_v\). The limit and inverse are \(C^1\) by local inversion, giving the assertion. ◻

This lemma removes the persistent rigid rotation before asking for convergence. To use it in the full problem one must construct an intrinsic compatible sphere map, establish the needed bounds in the precise mixed norms and on the relevant hypersurfaces, and prove continuity of the transformed metric directly or through a valid relative-coordinate transfer. Lemma 16.8, the applicable part of Proposition 16.6, Proposition 16.11, Corollary 16.13, and Theorem 16.14 would need corresponding revisions. Those nonlinear revisions have not been proved in this review. Simply deleting the nondecaying rotation from one displayed estimate does not verify the original conclusion.
result: Several facts limit the conclusion. First, the exact Kerr spacetime is smoothly extendible in the regular rotating coordinates described in the appendix; the calculation above does not refute that. Second, \(R(-3v)\) is invertible with determinant \(1\) for every finite \(v\). Failure of its boundary limit is not a failure of interior diffeomorphism. Third, the Kerr metric has axisymmetry, which can cancel rotations in transformed metric components even when a generic tensor does not extend. Fourth, local polar angular derivatives can hide the rotating phase, but they do not remove it or supply a globally regular stereographic boundary map. Reversing the rotation sign or using the inverse map leaves the nonconvergence unchanged.

Proposition 16.6’s conversion of transport control into fixed-old-angle continuity also deserves care because the relevant vector contains an angular shift. This report does not count that observation as a further demonstrated counterexample to its metric conclusion: exact Kerr’s symmetry gives genuine cancellations. Likewise, the ordinary matrix exponential written in the proof of Proposition 16.11 would require commutation or a correctly ordered fundamental solution; it is not counted as an additional independent issue here.

Impact: Invalid core derivation in the reviewed 2017 v1: Proposition 16.11 and Corollary 16.13 are explicitly used by Theorem 16.14 and the main C0 extension argument. A replacement nonlinear proof is needed. Does not establish failure of the main geometric conclusion or of the unexamined 2025 journal text.

claim: Smooth strictly decreasing u and strictly increasing v on the spacelike initial curve suffice for local nonsingular double-null coordinates solving the eikonal equations.

Smooth injective regular curve, derivative (-3tau^2,1) never zero; smooth inverse parameter v; -tau^3 strictly decreasing, tau strictly increasing; radius positive; smooth isometric spacelike embedding.
analysis: Severity: Minor. Proposition 2.1, pp. 38–39, constructs local double-null coordinates near the embedded spacelike hypersurface \(\Sigma=\ell\times\mathbb S^2\). The simple curve \(\ell:(a,b)\to\mathbb R^2\) supplies smooth functions \(u|_\Sigma\) and \(v|_\Sigma\) that are assumed strictly decreasing and strictly increasing, respectively, in its parameter \(\tau\). The proposed coordinates satisfy the eikonal equations and metric form (2.1). The stated strict monotonicity, in its ordinary mathematical meaning, does not imply nonzero derivatives.

Equation reference: review:degenerate-curve. Consider the annular region of Minkowski spacetime \[g=-\mathrm dt^2+\mathrm d\tau^2+(2+\tau)^2g_{\mathbb S^2},
 \qquad -1<\tau<1,\] where \(g_{\mathbb S^2}\) is the unit round metric and the ordinary spatial radius is \(2+\tau>0\). Take \(\Sigma=\{t=0\}\) with all of \(\mathbb S^2\), and \[
 \ell(\tau)=(-\tau^3,\tau),\qquad
 u|_\Sigma=-\tau^3,\qquad v|_\Sigma=\tau.\] The ambient metric is smooth and Lorentzian. The induced metric on \(\Sigma\) is positive definite, so the embedding is spacelike and isometric with the specified induced metric. The curve is smooth and injective; its derivative \((-3\tau^2,1)\) never vanishes, so it is a regular simple curve with smooth inverse parameter \(v\). The function \(-\tau^3\) is strictly decreasing and \(\tau\) strictly increasing on the whole interval. Thus this is not a nonsmooth parameterization or a curve cusp. Additive constants may be added to \(u\) and \(v\) if a coordinate-range translation is desired.

At any point of the sphere \(\tau=0\), all tangential derivatives of \(u|_\Sigma\) vanish. With \(N=\partial_t\) the unit normal, any smooth extension of \(u\) has \[g^{-1}(\mathrm du,\mathrm du)
       =-(Nu)^2+|\mathrm d_\Sigma u|^2
       =-(Nu)^2\] at that point. The required eikonal equation therefore gives \(Nu=0\). Hence \(\mathrm du=0\) as a full spacetime covector at that point. A function whose differential vanishes cannot be one member of a coordinate system there. In particular, it cannot give the asserted nonsingular double-null metric with positive finite lapse.

The proposition asserts the existence of such coordinates near every point (and the associated sphere neighborhood); the point \(\tau=0\) contradicts that assertion. The counterexample satisfies every stated geometric and monotonicity hypothesis, while the asserted conclusion is impossible.
result: If strictly decreasing/increasing was intended to mean that the derivatives are strictly negative/positive everywhere, that is the missing explicit assumption and excludes [review:degenerate-curve] (#review:degenerate-curve). These meanings are not equivalent for smooth real functions.

The precise local correction is to require \[\partial_\tau u|_\Sigma<0,\qquad
 \partial_\tau v|_\Sigma>0\] pointwise, in addition to the existing smooth spacelike hypotheses. The functions are constant on each initial sphere. If \(n\) is the unit normal to those spheres within \(\Sigma\), oriented by \(n\tau>0\), then \(nu<0\) and \(nv>0\). Choosing the appropriate eikonal branches gives nonzero \(Nu\) and \(Nv\). The normal derivative of the eikonal equation, viewed as an equation for the normal first derivative, is \(-2Nu\) or \(-2Nv\) and is nonzero. Thus the ordinary smooth noncharacteristic local construction applies, with the prescribed branch; compactness of the sphere permits a common sufficiently small neighborhood. This verifies the missing nondegeneracy ingredient of the proposition, not a new global existence statement.

The actual main data (4.5), p. 52, are \(u=C_R-\tau\) and \(v=\tau\). Their derivatives are \(-1\) and \(1\). Equations (4.8)–(4.10), p. 55, have the positive factor \(n\tau=(\Phi-|w|^2)^{-1/2}\) under the spacelike condition. Accordingly the degenerate example does not invalidate the invocation for these main data. This supported defect remains local and Minor. The reciprocal normalization appearing in the nearby proof is not counted as another issue: the geometric normal calculation and later formulas make the intended normalization recoverable, and isolated typographical defects are outside this review’s issue count.
Impact: Peripheral/local overstatement; no demonstrated damage to the main-data invocation.
