report: Abstract: This claim-focused initial review checks the local Euler linearization, its use in the energy proof, and the refined Gronwall lemma in the manifest-pinned author manuscript. A factor-of-two error in the linearized wave equation is established both analytically and by an exact smooth Euler solution. It propagates to the displayed Riemann-invariant wave system used in the core energy argument. The supported judgment is Major for this invalid core derivation, not a counterexample to the main a priori theorem. A local correction is derived; the complete corrected bootstrap proof has not been verified. No issue was found in the inspected Gronwall argument.
Date: 25 October 2026

Title: Scientific review of M25-0021:
a linearization coefficient in rarefaction-wave energy estimates
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is Tian-Wen Luo and Pin Yu, On the stability of multi-dimensional rarefaction waves I: the energy estimates, arXiv:2302.09714v2, revised 19 September 2024. The supplied PDF has 100 pages; page references below are physical, one-based PDF pages (matching the printed numbers at the cited locations). The journal identifier is DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.202.2.2. This review binds to the supplied author manuscript, not to an independently compared journal final version. Their equivalence has not been established.
All 30 manifest-listed input files matched their recorded SHA-256 hashes. The PDF hash is
The principal TeX source is `I-Rarefaction_waves_final-version.tex`, with 4970 lines and SHA-256

The actual text-reading scope was PDF pp. 1–8, 23–38, 50–55, 65–67, and 89–91. Source line ranges 790–820, 1058–1075, and 1385–1420 were read. Actual page images inspected were pp. 1, 23, 28, 33, 34, 37, 53–55, 65–66, and 89–90. Extraction of the remaining pages does not constitute reading or visual inspection. This is not a certification of the full 100-page proof.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and the main theorem

The paper studies two spatial dimensions, with the second coordinate periodic, isentropic pressure \(p=k_0\rho^\gamma\), \(k_0>0\), and \(1<\gamma<3\). In the irrotational potential formulation, \[v=-\nabla\phi,\qquad
h=\phi_t-\tfrac12|\nabla\phi|^2=\frac{c^2}{\gamma-1},
\qquad c^2=p'(\rho).\] Here \(\psi_\mu=\partial_\mu\phi\), in particular \(\psi_i=-v^i\) for \(i=1,2\). The acoustic metric and scalar contraction are \[g=-c^2dt^2+(dx^1-v^1dt)^2+(dx^2-v^2dt)^2,\qquad
Q_g(f,k)=g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu f\,\partial_\nu k.\] Equation (2.16), p. 28, defines \[w=\frac{c}{\gamma-1}+\frac{\psi_1}{2},\qquad
\underline{w}=\frac{c}{\gamma-1}-\frac{\psi_1}{2}.\] The main theorem on p. 37 is an a priori estimate under the specific rarefaction data conditions \((I_0),(I_2),(I_\infty)\) and the preceding irrotational setting. It requires \(N_{\rm top}\geq9\) and gives an \(\varepsilon_0\) and energy constants independent of \(0<\delta<1/2\). Its conclusion includes \(t^2\varepsilon^2\) energy control. These special data assumptions are much stronger than the local smooth Euler assumptions under which the identities in Section 2 are derived. The example below tests those local identities; it is not asserted to meet the global rarefaction-data ansatz.

The manifold has two spatial dimensions, as explicitly stated and as visible in its metric. The three-dimensional-space conformal convention cannot be substituted silently. A material mitigating fact is that the corrected system consists of the same family of quadratic null forms. The structural assertion of Remark 3.1, p. 34, survives: no new derivative order is introduced. The inspected beginnings of Sections 6 and 8 estimate general linear combinations of these forms, with constants absorbed in inequalities. This supports the possibility of a repair of the proof strategy; it does not itself check every commutator, sign, bootstrap constant, or boundary argument.
## Dependence and supported impact

Section 6 explicitly starts from (3.7) on p. 55 to prove the lowest-order energy estimates. Section 8 starts from the same equation on p. 65 and constructs differentiated source terms. Section 8.5, pp. 89–90, combines these bounds to close the energy bootstrap used for the main theorem on p. 37. This is a demonstrated core dependency, not a peripheral typographical use of an isolated formula.

The issue is therefore classified Major: invalid core derivation in the reviewed author manuscript. It does not establish that the final theorem is false, that all energy bounds fail, or that the journal final version contains the same formulas. Completing the repair requires substituting the corrected sources throughout the affected estimates and checking the full bootstrap closure, including Section 9. No empirical experiment is needed to establish the local algebraic discrepancy; the independent symbolic computation corroborates, rather than replaces, the analytic proof.
# A separate check with no issue found

Lemma 5.2, pp. 53–55, assumes nonnegative smooth \(E,F\) with the stated monotonicities and \[E(t,u)+F(t,u)\leq At^2+B\int_0^uF(t,v)\,dv
+C\int_\delta^t E(\tau,u)\,\frac{d\tau}{\tau}.\] Its conclusion under \(e^{Bu^*}C\leq1\) is \(E+F\leq3Ae^{Bu}t^2\). The Volterra resolvent in \(u\), followed by monotonicity of \(E\) in \(u\), gives \[E+F\leq Ae^{Bu}t^2+D Y(t),\qquad
D=e^{Bu}C,\quad Y(t)=\int_\delta^t E(\tau,u)\,\frac{d\tau}{\tau}.\] Consequently \((Y/t^D)'\leq Ae^{Bu}t^{1-D}\), \(Y(\delta)=0\). Since \(0<D\leq1\), \[Y(t)\leq\frac{Ae^{Bu}}{2-D}
  (t^2-\delta^{2-D}t^D)
\leq\frac{Ae^{Bu}}{2-D}t^2 .\] This even implies \(E+F\leq2Ae^{Bu}t^2\); the paper’s looser intermediate factor two yields its claimed factor three. The auxiliary function \(H\) need not be nonnegative for the integrated Volterra comparison used here. The displayed choice \(a_0=1/(2C_0)\) and \(u_0^*=(\log2)/(2C_0^2)\) on p. 90 satisfies the lemma’s smallness condition. This check does not independently establish all inequalities fed into that application.

Title: Scientific review of M25-0022:
wave identities and compactness in rarefaction-wave existence
# Identity and exact coverage

Tian-Wen Luo and Pin Yu, On the stability of multi-dimensional rarefaction waves II: existence of solutions and applications to Riemann problem, arXiv:2305.06308v2, 19 September 2024, is the reviewed author manuscript. The corresponding journal identifier is DOI 10.4007/annals.2025.202.2.3. Equivalence to the journal final version has not been established, so no finding is attributed to that unexamined version.
The supplied PDF has 88 pages. Page numbers here are one-based physical PDF pages, matching the printed page numbers at cited locations. Its SHA-256 is
All 40 manifest-listed source files passed hash verification. The principal TeX file is
> `II-Rarefaction_waves_final-version.tex`.
It has 4491 lines and SHA-256

Actual PDF text-reading ranges were pp. 1–12, 17–24, 57–63, and 77–86. Actual rendered page images inspected were pp. 1, 10, 19–20, 23–24, 60–62, and 82–86. Source lines 638–677 and 1333–1340 were read. The initial-data construction in most of Section 3, the full Goursat construction, and all geometry estimates were not exhaustively verified.
# Assumptions and dependencies

The equation of state is \(p=k_0\rho^\gamma\), \(k_0>0\), \(1<\gamma<3\). Space is \(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)\); the background is a nondegenerate two-rarefaction Riemann solution away from vacuum. Definition 1.1, pp. 7–8, requires smooth data on both closed half-tubes, sufficiently small high-order Sobolev perturbations of fixed constant states, and distributional irrotationality across the initial interface. The fixed positive separation between the two wave families is part of the smallness comparison. Theorem 1 constructs compatible rarefaction data at \(t=\delta\). Corollary 1, p. 19, expressly uses the companion paper’s a priori energy estimates. Section 4 then passes to \(\delta\downarrow0\) on compact sets bounded away from \(t=0\).

The local potential identities on p. 10 have a different scope from these global perturbation hypotheses: they are asserted for smooth irrotational solutions of the stated Euler system. We use that local scope in Problem 1 and do not claim a counterexample to the small-data existence theorem.
# Problem 1: an incorrect local wave equation in a core dependency
## Claim, location, and analytic verification

u}=-ho g^{\mu
u}\). Its variation therefore satisfies \[\partial_\mu(ho g^{\mu

## Exact test and all applicable conditions

On \(0<t<1\), \(x\in\mathbb R\), \(y\in\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)\), write \(s=1+t\) and take \[\gamma=2,\quad k_0=\tfrac12,\quad
\rho=s^{-1},\quad c=s^{-1/2},\quad p=\tfrac12s^{-2},\quad
v=(x/s,0),\quad
\phi=-x^2/(2s)+\log s .\] These are smooth positive-density fields, periodic in \(y\), with \(v=-\nabla\phi\) and zero curl. The pressure and sound-speed laws hold. For \(B=\partial_t+v\cdot\nabla\), \[B\rho+\rho\operatorname{div}v=-s^{-2}+s^{-2}=0,\qquad
Bv+\rho^{-1}\nabla p=(0,0).\] Moreover \(\phi_t-\frac12|\nabla\phi|^2=1/s=c^2/(\gamma-1)\), and the nondivergence potential equation (1.9) vanishes. Time translation supplies an exact one-parameter family with variation \(\psi_0=\phi_t\).

Direct evaluation of the divergence-form wave operator gives \[\Box_g\psi_0=\frac1{2s^2},\qquad
Q_g(\log(\rho/c),\psi_0)=-\frac1{2s^2}.\] The predicted right side of [bad] (#bad) is \(1/(4s^2)\), leaving a nonzero residual \(1/(4s^2)\). The corrected residual is zero. Furthermore \[w=s^{-1/2}-x/(2s),\quad \underline{w}=s^{-1/2}+x/(2s),\quad \psi_2=0,\] \[Q_g(w,w)=Q_g(\underline{w},\underline{w})=0,\qquad
Q_g(w,\underline{w})=-1/(2s^2),\qquad
\Box_gw=0.\] Equation [badw] (#badw) predicts \(-1/(8s^{3/2})\); [goodw] (#goodw) predicts zero.

The affine velocity is not claimed to meet Definition 1.1’s global Sobolev smallness or the rarefaction data ansatz. The example refutes the asserted local identities only. It does not refute Theorems 1–3 or Proposition 2.12.
## Counterevidence, dependence, and severity

Constant \(\rho/c\) makes the differing term vanish, and \(\gamma=3\) would also do so, but the paper’s allowed case \(\gamma=2\) does not. Reinterpreting \(\Omega\) as its square contradicts its explicit definition on p. 10. The direct metric and source checks rule out a text-extraction ambiguity.

The same identities occur in the manifest-pinned companion paper, arXiv:2302.09714v2, equations (2.2) and (3.7), whose Sections 6 and 8 use them in the core energy proof. In this paper, Corollary 1 on p. 19 and the uniform estimates on p. 60 expressly invoke that companion result; those estimates feed the compactness construction in pp. 61–62. This establishes the core dependency.

The supported judgment is Major for the repeated invalid core derivation and affected proof dependency. It is one shared mathematical error across the two manuscripts, not two independently discovered mechanisms. The corrected sources remain quadratic null forms, which is significant counterevidence against claiming that the strategy or theorem must fail. A complete correction requires rechecking the energy argument and all transferred estimates. No such full repair is claimed here. The independent computation is exact symbolic verification, not an empirical experiment.
# Problem 2: the Sobolev embedding used in the limit passage
## Source and complete check

Section 4.3, p. 62, takes strong convergence in \(H^{N_{\rm top}}(K_k)\) and cites an embedding into \(C^{N_\infty}\) with \(N_\infty=N_{\rm top}-1\). But \(K_k\) is a three-dimensional space-time domain, not a two-dimensional spatial slice. In three dimensions, this claimed Sobolev embedding is false.
## Local repair and impact

The existence of a classical solution needs much less than \(C^{m-1}\) when \(m\) is large. The erroneous embedding is therefore Minor, with a supported local repair using the paper’s own displayed bound. This repair is conditional on that bound and does not resolve Problem 1 or certify all higher-order boundary statements. It is not a separate Major claim based merely on an inaccurate regularity sentence.
# Additional checks and rejected readings

A possible objection based on restricting a centered fan to a smaller \(u\)-interval was rejected after inspecting the actual p. 24 image and source line 1337. Although a region subscript contains an extra prime, the displayed union uses the same interval \(u'\in[0,u^*]\), and the conclusion compares regions at that common extent. A counterexample using unequal interval lengths would not test that reading of the proposition. No additional scientific finding is assigned to this notation.
# Conclusion and version limits

The consulted arXiv history lists v2 of 19 September 2024 as the last revision. The Annals landing page identifies volume 202(2), pp. 753–855, with online publication on 26 September 2025. No correction notice was observed on those pages; a targeted search did not identify a correction. This does not establish global absence of errata. The journal final PDF has not been compared.

Not established | Falsity of existence/uniqueness theorems; full repaired proof; journal-final defect.

report: Abstract: This claim-focused review concerns the manifest-pinned author manuscript of Lawrence and Sawin, arXiv:2004.09046v5. Two local defects are identified in the supplied numerical verification program: a factor of \(n\) is inverted in a logarithmic comparison, and a computed summand is omitted from another comparison. Independent exact arithmetic and analytic bounds verify the corresponding mathematical inequalities. The supported judgment is therefore Minor for the ancillary verification implementation, not a refutation of the finiteness theorems. The geometric and \(p\)-adic arguments are not certified in their entirety.
Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Scientific initial review of M25-0023
# Identity, version, and scope

The paper is The Shafarevich conjecture for hypersurfaces in abelian varieties, by Brian Lawrence and Will Sawin, DOI https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2025.202.3.1. The inspected PDF is arXiv:2004.09046v5, dated 16 October 2025, with 121 physical PDF pages. All page references below count physical PDF pages starting at one. The source archive and its ancillary program are the exact manifest-listed files. All 20 listed input hashes matched. Equivalence with the journal’s final PDF or separately hosted code has not been established.

PDF text was read on pages 1–7, 85–92, 105–112, and 116–118. Actual rendered PDF pages inspected were 1, 2, 85, 87, 88, 89, 90, 91, 92, 105, 111, 116, 117, and 118. The full 482-line ancillary `eulerian.py` and the full 40-line `eulerian_output.txt` were read statically. No author program was executed or imported. The selected checks concern theorem quantifiers and the isogeny reduction, Appendix A’s numerical bound, and selected Eulerian inequalities used in Appendices B and C. They do not constitute a complete audit of the Tannakian, monodromy, or \(p\)-adic period arguments.
# Claims, definitions, and dependencies

Equation reference: rec. Write \(\mathsf A(n,k)\) for the Eulerian number counting permutations of \(n\) letters with \(k\) descents, and put it equal to zero outside \(0\leq k<n\). Its recurrence is \[
 \mathsf A(n,k)=(k+1)\mathsf A(n-1,k)+(n-k)\mathsf A(n-1,k-1).\] The main finiteness statement fixes a number field \(K\), a finite set of excluded primes, an abelian variety \(A/K\), and an ample Neron–Severi class \(\phi\). For \(\dim A\geq4\), smooth hypersurfaces in that class with the prescribed good reduction are finite up to translation. In dimension three the theorem excludes multiples of certain specified intersection numbers.

The primitive case in Theorem 9.2 and the quotient-isogeny reduction in Corollary 9.3 distinguish an equality exclusion from a divisibility exclusion. If \(\pi:A\to A'\) is the relevant isogeny and \(\phi=\pi^*\phi'\), then \[\frac{\phi^n}{n!}=(\deg\pi)\frac{(\phi')^n}{n!}.\] Thus an exceptional primitive degree becomes a possible exceptional multiple before passage to the quotient. This explains the stronger exclusion in the final dimension-three formulation; confusing these two scopes would create a spurious objection. The sequence \(a_1=1,a_2=5,a_{i+2}=4a_{i+1}+1-a_i\) gives \(d_i=\binom{a_i+a_{i+1}}{a_i}\), with the first three values \(6,53130,216182590635135019896\), independently calculated.

The main proof on pages 85–87 invokes the preceding large-monodromy and arithmetic results and the numerical condition of Lemma A.1. Appendix B uses numerical inequalities for representation-theoretic multiplicity bounds. The issues below are in the supplied checks of particular inequalities, not demonstrated failures of these inequalities.
# Problem 1: inverted factor in an ancillary logarithmic bound
## Source and suspect step

Equation reference: strong. In `anc/eulerian.py`, function `verify_bound_m1b_mult1a`, lines 304–318, the advertised large-\(n\) comparison is \[
 \mathsf A(n,4)<\frac{\mathsf A(n,1)^3}{200n},\qquad 20\leq n\leq199.\] Line 316 instead constructs the logarithmic right-hand side as

Code:
np.log(1/200)+np.log(n)+3*np.log(normeuler[n][1])
    +3*logfact[n]-.1

Here `normeuler[n][1]` represents \(\mathsf A(n,1)/n!\). In ideal exact arithmetic this is \[\log\!\left(\frac{n\mathsf A(n,1)^3}{200}\right)-0.1,\] whereas the intended expression has \(-\log n\). Consequently the tested right-hand side differs by a factor \(n^2\) from the correspondingly buffered intended bound. At \(n=20\) the factor is 400. The buffer does not repair the sign error.
## Complete check and counterevidence

Equation reference: b23. This finding follows by elementary logarithm identities and static inspection, without executing the program. A true comparison with the larger right-hand side alone does not imply [strong] (#strong). Page 111, Lemma B.23, uses the related inequality \[
 78n\mathsf A(n,4)<(\mathsf A(n,1)-1)^3,\qquad n\geq5.\] The small-\(n\) branch directly tests the latter expression.

Neither [strong] (#strong) nor [b23] (#b23) is false. A separate reviewer program using arbitrary-precision integers verified [b23] (#b23) for every \(5\leq n\leq199\), and [strong] (#strong) for every \(20\leq n\leq199\). There is also a short all-range argument. For \(n\geq5\), \[\mathsf A(n,1)=2^n-n-1,\quad
 \mathsf A(n,1)-1\geq \tfrac34\,2^n,\quad
 \mathsf A(n,4)\leq5^n.\] The exact integer inequalities \[64\cdot78\cdot20\cdot5^{20}<27\cdot8^{20},
 \qquad
 64\cdot200\cdot20\cdot5^{20}<27\cdot8^{20}\] were checked independently. Since \(n(5/8)^n\) decreases for \(n\geq20\), these prove both requested inequalities for all \(n\geq20\). The remaining cases of [b23] (#b23) were checked exactly.
## Impact and judgment

The implemented logarithmic test does not match its stated target. Replacing \(+\log n\) by \(-\log n\) corrects that algebraic expression; a claim that a floating-point implementation is a certified verifier would still require an explicit rounding-error analysis. The independent integer and analytic arguments above supply the mathematical verification without that additional claim. This is a supported Minor defect in the ancillary verification artifact. No invalidity of Lemma B.23 or of the core finiteness conclusion is demonstrated.
# Problem 2: omitted summand in a second ancillary comparison
## Source and exact discrepancy

Equation reference: b15. The numerical bound on page 105, Lemma B.15, is, for \(n\geq11\), \[
 \begin{split}
 S_n={}&2\mathsf A(n,1)
 +\sqrt{\frac{48\mathsf A(n,3)\mathsf A(n,1)}{11}}+1
 +\frac{48\mathsf A(n,3)}{11\mathsf A(n,1)}\\
 &+\sqrt{\frac{96\mathsf A(n,5)}{11\mathsf A(n,1)}}+1
 <\mathsf A(n,2).
 \end{split}\] The intervening zero term in the five-bound presentation is immaterial. In `verify_bound_m1a_final`, lines 147–170, the \(20\leq n\leq199\) branch calculates `bde` but its comparison at line 165 sums only the exponentials corresponding to `bda`, `bdb`, `bdc`, and `bdd`. The final `bde` contribution is omitted. Moreover, the retained value `bdb=0` contributes \(1\) after exponentiation, rather than a zero summand.
## Alternative reading and independent verification

Some other logarithmic terms include positive buffers. Such buffers could compensate for an omitted term at the particular values tested. Thus the source discrepancy is not evidence that the comparison actually accepted a false inequality, nor is an observed failure of [b15] (#b15) alleged. It does mean that the literal sum does not implement the displayed five-bound test, and no justification for exchanging the missing term against the other buffers is given in this code segment.

The reviewer independently formed every term in \(S_n\) for \(11\leq n\leq199\), bounding each square root above by a rational number on a grid of size \(10^{-20}\). Each bound was verified by exact integer squaring. All 189 resulting rational strict inequalities passed.
## Impact and judgment

The omission is a Minor implementation discrepancy. The full mathematical bound has been independently verified. An appropriate repair is to evaluate all specified terms with certified bounds, or to replace the numerical check by a documented exact finite calculation and tail estimate. The original program was neither modified nor run, and no inference is made about which code generated an author’s historical result.
# Other checks and limits
## Appendix A

The coefficients \[a_i=\frac{\sum_k\mathsf A(n,k)\mathsf A(n,k-i)}{(n!)^2}\] form a symmetric log-concave probability sequence as used in the appendix, with second moment \((n+1)/6\). Conditional on the appendix’s stated log-concavity and moment identities, the tail argument for \(a_0\leq1/2\) is consistent. Indeed, if \(a_0>1/2\), the positive tail has total mass below \(1/4\). Log-concavity, applied after multiplication by \(2\,3^i\), forces each tail sum to be strictly below the corresponding tail of \(1/(2\,3^i)\): otherwise an earlier index below that geometric comparison, together with the value above one at zero, forces every later index below it, a contradiction. The resulting total second moment is below \(3/2\), contradicting \((n+1)/6\) for odd \(n\geq9\). For even \(n\), symmetry of the unpaired-middle-free Eulerian row gives maximal normalized entry at most \(1/2\), hence \(a_0\leq1/2\). The remaining odd cases give \(a_0(3)=1/2\), \(a_0(5)=571/1440\), and \(a_0(7)=6907/20160\). No issue was found in this inspected numerical mechanism. The original references underlying all general identities were not independently reproved.
## Additional finite and asymptotic checks

Lemma C.5’s \(27\mathsf A(n,2)<\mathsf A(n,1)^2\) was checked exactly for \(11\leq n\leq199\). It also follows for \(n\geq14\) from \(\mathsf A(n,2)\leq3^n\), \(\mathsf A(n,1)\geq(3/4)2^n\), and \(48(3/4)^{14}<1\); cases 11–13 complete that proof. Selected base cases of Lemma C.4, \[\mathsf A(n,r-1)(\mathsf A(n,r-1)-1)>2\mathsf A(n,3r-2),
 \quad 5\leq n\leq20,\quad3\leq r\leq n-2,\] were checked exactly. The entire induction and all other Appendix B inequalities were not audited.

The source’s arrays created with `np.zeros` use floating-point storage. They therefore do not in general contain exact Eulerian integers: \(\mathsf A(19,8)=27862280567093358\) is not representable in binary64. This is a representability observation, not a reconstructed runtime result. The supplied output file records only a subset of checks. It does not establish the execution history of every function. These limitations are retained as provenance qualifications, not additional claims that the mathematical statements fail.
# Dependence, version history, and conclusion

The consulted arXiv page lists v5 as its latest revision. The journal metadata page links both arXiv ancillary files and a separate code DOI; the latter was not downloaded or compared. No correction notice was observed on the consulted primary pages. This limited observation does not establish that no erratum exists anywhere, nor that the same code discrepancies occur in the journal-associated files.
Item | Judgment | Repair or remaining work
Logarithmic factor | Minor | Intended inequalities independently verified.
Omitted summand | Minor | Complete bound independently verified.
Selected numerical lemmas | No Issue Found | Scope and assumptions stated above.
Full finiteness proof | Not certified | Tannakian, monodromy, and period arguments remain.
Human acceptance / adoption | Pending / not requested | No decision attributed to a human or author.
# Supporting checks

The reviewer-authored `independent_eulerian.py` computes [rec] (#rec) with Python arbitrary-precision integers and verifies row sums \(n!\) and symmetry through \(n=199\). It uses `Fraction` and integer square roots for certified upper bounds. The saved result records 198 checks of \(a_0\), 189 of C.5, 195 of [b23] (#b23), 180 of [strong] (#strong), 189 of [b15] (#b15), and 136 selected C.4 base cases, with no failed predicate. The actual command was Python with `-B` on that reviewer script, under this task’s staging tree. Process 25268 completed with exit code zero after the tail-base checks were added. The author program was not executed or imported.

Title: Scientific initial review of M25-0024
# Identity and actual coverage

The paper is Loop structure on equivariant \(K\)-theory of semi-infinite flag manifolds, by Syu Kato, DOI https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2025.202.3.2. The manifest binds arXiv:1805.01718v9, posted 25 December 2024. Its internal title-page date is 30 December 2024; these are distinct recorded dates, not a basis for a mathematical finding. The PDF has 64 pages. All page references count physical PDF pages from one. All eight manifest-listed input files passed hash validation. The journal-final text has not been compared.

Text was read on pages 1–11, 18–32, 41–46, 56–61, and 63. Actual source-PDF images inspected were pages 1, 3, 11, 19, 20, 21, 29, 30, 31, 44, 56, 60, and 61. The rank-one source was also read at lines 1246–1310 of `mu241220.tex`. Reading these ranges does not imply that every intermediate result or every cited theorem was independently proved. No separate computational repository was supplied or needed for the checks below; no author code was run.
# Scope of the principal statements

The setting is a connected, simply connected, simple complex algebraic group \(G\), with a fixed maximal torus \(H\), finite Weyl group \(W\), weight lattice \(P\), and coroot lattice \(Q^\vee\). The coefficients are complexified. The localized affine-Grassmannian group carries the Pontryagin product, not the ordinary product on the affine flag \(K\)-group. Theorem 2.12 gives a dense embedding into the semi-infinite group whose image consists of finite Schubert combinations. Theorem 3.11 and Corollary 3.13 instead compare that semi-infinite group with the completed, localized quantum group.

This distinction is explicit on pages 2–4, 20–24, 29, and 60. Remark 1.28 further distinguishes the transported ring identity \([\mathcal O_{\mathbf Q_G}]\) from a hypothetical class of the entire ind-scheme’s structure sheaf. Consequently, the infinite positive-twist formulas below do not contradict the finite product statement for Schubert classes in Corollary 4.22. An isomorphism of the uncompleted source with the entire completed target is not what the precise statement asserts.
# Checked reasoning
## Localization and independence of choices

Write \(x_w=[\mathcal O_{\operatorname{Gr}_w}]\). Theorem 1.8, page 11, states \[x_w\odot x_{t_\beta}=x_{wt_\beta},
 \qquad w\in W_{\rm af}^{-},\quad
 \langle\beta,\alpha_i\rangle<0\ \text{for every }i.\] The proof uses the length-additivity and left \(W\)-invariance of the relevant Demazure element, then projects from the smash product to its translation subalgebra. The distinction between multiplication before projection and the commutative Pontryagin product is maintained in equation (1.8).

Conditional on this translation identity, the localization does not kill a nonzero finite Schubert combination: right translation of the distinct basis indices is injective. The independence of \[h_i=x_{s_it_\beta}\odot x_{t_\beta}^{-1}\] can be checked by comparing two choices \(\beta,\beta'\) with their common sum \(\beta+\beta'\), which remains strictly antidominant. Similarly, if \(\gamma=\beta_1-\beta_2=\beta'_1-\beta'_2\), then \(\beta_1+\beta'_2=\beta'_1+\beta_2\); multiplication of numerator and denominator by the corresponding translation classes proves choice-independence of \(t_\gamma\). Every coroot can be expressed as such a difference by choosing the subtracted coroot sufficiently antidominant. No additional boundary case with a merely weakly antidominant denominator was inserted into the theorem.
## Cyclic-module endomorphism comparison

Pages 26–30 give the transported Demazure action and its product compatibility. For \(i\in I\), \(D_i^\#\xi=\xi\) is equivalent to finite-reflection invariance of \(\xi\); this makes multiplication by \(\xi\) commute with \(D_i^\#\). Invariance under all finite simple reflections likewise gives commutation with \(D_0^\#\) through the highest-root reflection, as calculated in Lemma 2.4.

The comparison in Theorem 2.12 is consequently more than equality on one arbitrary vector. Both \[\Theta_i=e^{-\varpi_i}(1-h_i\odot)
 \quad\text{and}\quad \Xi(-\varpi_i)\] commute with the indicated Hecke and translation actions, and the module is cyclic by Lemma 2.8. Thus equality on its cyclic vector implies equality everywhere. The \(j=i\) calculation on page 30 uses \[D_i e^{-\varpi_i}
 =e^{-\varpi_i+\alpha_i}D_i+
   \frac{e^{-\varpi_i}-e^{-\varpi_i+\alpha_i}}{1-e^{\alpha_i}},\] whose second coefficient is \(e^{-\varpi_i}\). The first term vanishes when applied to the indicated difference of Schubert classes. This verifies the displayed local algebra, conditional on the stated geometric action and cyclicity inputs. No invalid cancellation was found in this comparison.
## Independent rank-one calculation

For \(G=SL(2)\), set \(z=e^\varpi\), \(t=t_{\alpha^\vee}\), and order the Schubert basis as \(e,s\). At \(q=1\), the positive and negative twists on pages 31–32 have matrices \[M=\frac1{1-t}
 \begin{pmatrix}z&zt\\z^{-1}&z^{-1}\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 N=\begin{pmatrix}z^{-1}&-zt\\-z^{-1}&z\end{pmatrix}.\] Direct multiplication gives \(MN=NM=I\). Hence \[H=I-zN=
 \begin{pmatrix}0&z^2t\\1&1-z^2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad H^2-(1-z^2)H-z^2tI=0.\] These are rational identities over \(\mathbb C(z,t)\), and also identities in the formal completion because \(1-t\) is invertible there. The reviewer-authored SymPy calculation independently returned zero for all three matrix residuals.

In particular, at \(z=1\) the relation becomes \(H^2=tI\). This gives a useful nonequivariant boundary check on the signs. Applying negative translations recovers the two finite products on page 32. The same computation explains why \(N\) is finite but \(M\) contains \(\sum_{m\geq0}t^m\); the latter belongs to the completed target. No numerical sampling or analytic convergence assumption is involved.

The duplicated argument in one intermediate display on page 31 is resolved by the immediately preceding two distinct twist formulas, the following two product formulas, and source lines 1277–1288. It is not treated as a separate substantive problem.
## Completion and the final finite-rank step

The definition \(qK_H(\mathcal B)=K_H(\mathcal B)[[Q^\vee_+]]\) on page 23 and the formal coefficient description on page 20 give the coefficientwise completed ring \(R=\mathbb C[P][[Q_1,\ldots,Q_r]]\), followed by localization in the Novikov monomials. Ordinary algebraic tensor products should not be silently interchanged with this completion.

The algebraic mechanism needed at the end of Theorem 3.11 can be made explicit. For a continuous \(R\)-linear map between finite free modules, if its reduction modulo \((Q_1,\ldots,Q_r)\) is invertible, write its matrix \(F=F_0+\Delta\). Then \[F^{-1}=\sum_{m\geq0}(-F_0^{-1}\Delta)^mF_0^{-1}.\] Each coefficient has finitely many contributing terms. This proves invertibility before localization, and localization preserves it. The classical quotient comparison in Proposition 1.29 is the relevant input; density alone, without the completed-module structure, would not suffice. This check explains the finite-rank step under that coefficientwise interpretation. It is not a complete verification of the \(q\)-dependent convergence and specialization arguments used to construct the map in the first place.
# Geometric dependencies and historical issues

Pages 45–46 identify the geometric inputs. Theorem 4.13, pages 56–57, supplies rational singularities; Corollary 4.15 and Proposition 4.16 then support the Schubert-class comparison in Theorem 4.17. Corollaries 4.20–4.22 combine that comparison with Theorem 2.12 to obtain the Peterson-type map and finite quantum products. This dependency was traced, but the full transversal-slice construction in Sections 3.2 and 4.2–4.3 was not independently audited.

The footnote on page 3 explicitly attributes gaps to earlier versions and explains the separate normality treatment in the author’s Frobenius splitting of Schubert varieties of semi-infinite flag manifolds, Forum of Mathematics, Pi 9 (2021), e5, cited as [34]. The current manuscript imports that result in Theorem 4.4. This is retained as a historical issue acknowledged by the author; this review neither relabels it a demonstrated current defect nor claims to have independently certified the entire repair.

The consulted arXiv metadata lists v9 as the latest revision and describes its changes from v8 as typographical. The journal metadata was consulted without obtaining or comparing the final PDF. No additional correction notice was observed on those primary pages or in the targeted search. This is not proof of worldwide absence of an erratum.

Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Scientific initial review of M25-0025
# Paper identity and coverage

The paper is Independence of \(\ell\) for Frobenius conjugacy classes attached to abelian varieties, by Mark Kisin and Rong Zhou, DOI https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2025.202.3.3. The inspected source is the manifest-pinned author manuscript arXiv:2103.09945v2, 7 October 2024, 63 PDF pages. Page numbers below are physical PDF page numbers starting at one. All eight input hashes matched the manifest. Journal-final equivalence has not been established.

Text was read on pages 1–6, 33–34, and 42–61. Images actually viewed were pages 1, 2, 34, 43, 46, 49, 52, 54, 55, 58, 59, and 60. Source lines 1950–1995 in `l-independence__arXiv.tex` were also read. This is a systematic review of selected claims and their dependencies, not a complete line-by-line verification of Sections 2–4. No author code was executed.
# Assumptions and exact theorem scope

Let \(A/E\) be an abelian variety over a number field with a fixed complex embedding, and let \(G/\mathbb Q\) be its Mumford–Tate group. The base field is first enlarged so that the Galois representations factor through \(G(\mathbb Q_\ell)\) for every \(\ell\). For a place \(v\mid p\) of good reduction with \(p>2\), Theorems 1.1 and 6.2.7 produce \[\gamma\in\operatorname{Conj}_G(\mathbb Q),\qquad
 \gamma_{\mathbb Q_\ell}
   =\chi_G\bigl(\rho_\ell^G(\operatorname{Frob}_v)\bigr)
       \quad(\ell\ne p).\] Here \(\operatorname{Conj}_G=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Q[G]^G\) records geometric semisimple conjugacy classes. A rational point of this quotient need not have a representative in \(G(\mathbb Q)\), nor does it by itself identify rational conjugacy classes in \(G(\mathbb Q_\ell)\).

The stronger rational-representative statement on page 60 assumes that \(G^{\rm der}\) is simply connected and \(G_{\mathbb Q_p}\) is quasi-split, and permits one exceptional prime away from \(p\). The main theorem makes neither the \(p=2\) assertion nor the \(\ell=p\) crystalline assertion. Good reduction is essential to the stated theorem. These are boundaries of the result, not defects.

The intermediate Shimura statement assumes a strongly acceptable triple (Definition 4.2.2): Hodge type, the indicated Weil restrictions of split derived groups, an induced-torus condition on the specified central subgroup, and a very special parahoric. The \(\mu\)-ordinary lifting result is used under these hypotheses, not asserted here for every Shimura variety or every level.
# Checked descent and compatibility arguments
## Why curve points must preserve residue fields

Proposition 5.2.3 and Corollary 5.2.7 construct a smooth curve over \(\mathbb F_q\) with an \(\mathbb F_q\)-rational point above the chosen \(\mathbb F_q\)-point of the stratum. If the point above it had residue field \(\mathbb F_{q^d}\), its Frobenius would give the \(d\)-th power of the original element. Equality of powers would not in general recover the original semisimple class. The actual statements retain \(d=1\); the introduction explicitly identifies this issue on page 4. Thus the proof’s use of curves is not interchangeable with an arbitrary curve after a field extension.

The later finite extension of the number field in the proof of Theorem 6.2.7, page 59, also preserves the residue field at the selected place. This can be justified directly. The inverse image \(U\) of the chosen compact open subgroup under the continuous Galois representation is an open subgroup containing the chosen lift \(\widetilde\sigma_q\) of geometric Frobenius. Take the finite fixed field of \(U\). The local decomposition subgroup intersected with \(U\) still contains that lift, so its image in the procyclic residue Galois group is all of that group. The chosen place therefore has residue degree one. An arbitrary finite extension would not have this property; the specific subgroup construction does.
## Companions and semisimplification

Proposition 5.3.5, page 54, uses Chin’s Theorem 4.6. The primary text of that theorem was consulted: it applies to semisimple lisse sheaves on smooth curves whose algebraic Frobenius eigenvalues are units at every finite place away from \(p\). It allows an enlargement of the coefficient number field. Thus being a unit only at the initial \(\ell\)-adic place, in isolation, would not state the complete hypothesis.

In the present geometric setting the stronger property follows. For the faithful abelian-variety representation the eigenvalues, or their inverses according to the homology convention, are units away from \(p\): the Weil eigenvalues and \(q/\alpha\) are algebraic integers. At every prime not dividing \(q\), both valuations are nonnegative and sum to zero. Tensor products, duals, and subquotients preserve this property. Every algebraic representation of \(G\) occurs in the tensor category generated by a faithful representation. Consequently the representations used in Proposition 5.3.5 have the required property.

One may apply the companion theorem to semisimplifications, since characteristic polynomials of every group element are unchanged. Equality on the dense open part of the curve then identifies the semisimplifications by Chebotarev, giving equality at the selected point. This is sufficient for the semisimple conjugacy quotient; no assertion about unipotent parts is required. No missing finite-order determinant hypothesis is imposed by the cited version of the companion theorem.
## Descent of the common algebraic class to \(\mathbb Q\)

The final step on page 55 uses more than rationality in a single completion. Let \(F\) be the residue field of the common algebraic point, \(F'/\mathbb Q\) its Galois closure, and put \(\Gamma=\operatorname{Gal}(F'/\mathbb Q)\), \(H=\operatorname{Gal}(F'/F)\). An embedding \(F\hookrightarrow\mathbb Q_\ell\), for every unramified \(\ell\ne p\), implies that its Frobenius conjugacy class in \(\Gamma\) meets \(H\). Chebotarev therefore forces every conjugacy class to meet \(H\). Omitting the one prime \(p\) and finitely many ramified primes does not affect this inference.

For clarity, the finite-group conclusion has a short complete proof. The transitive action of \(\Gamma\) on \(\Gamma/H\) has average number of fixed points equal to one, by orbit counting. If \(H\) meets every conjugacy class, every element fixes at least one coset. If \([\Gamma:H]>1\), the identity fixes more than one, contradicting that average. Hence \(H=\Gamma\), \(F=\mathbb Q\), and the class is rational. No issue was found in this descent.
## Returning from the auxiliary group

Lemma 6.2.6, pages 58–59, uses \[G\hookrightarrow H\subset\operatorname{Res}_{F/\mathbb Q}G_F.\] Over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\), the first embedding is diagonal. If two diagonal elements become conjugate in the product group, any one component of the conjugating element already conjugates them in \(G\). The subsequent central modification \(H_1=H\times^{Z_H}T\) also preserves geometric conjugacy classes of \(H\): conjugation of \((h,1)\) by a pair \((h',t)\) changes only the first component by \(h'\). Equality modulo the central anti-diagonal does not introduce an extra ambiguity, since equality of the second components forces that central element to be the identity. Thus the asserted injection of geometric conjugacy classes is valid. Since it is Galois-equivariant, a rational auxiliary class with a preimage has a unique Galois-fixed preimage. This verifies the final descent mechanism, conditional on construction of the auxiliary Shimura datum.
# Exact check of the ramified \(SU_3\) calculation

Page 52, Case (3) of Proposition 5.2.3, uses \(p>2\), a uniformizer \(u\) with \(\tau(u)=-u\), and a nonzero constant \(x\). The defining unipotent condition for \(u_-(x,-x^2/2)\) holds because \(x^2-x^2/2-x^2/2=0\). The three matrices in the displayed factorization multiply to \[R=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 0&0&-2/(ux^2)\\
 0&1&-2/x\\
 ux^2/2&ux&-u
 \end{pmatrix}.\] An independent symbolic calculation verified this equality, \(\det R=1\), and \(R^{\tau\,t}JR=J\), where \(J\) is the anti-diagonal identity matrix. For \(s=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,u)\), one obtains \[s^{-1}Rs=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 0&0&-2/x^2\\
 0&1&-2u/x\\
 x^2/2&x&-u
 \end{pmatrix}.\] All entries are integral in the \(u\)-valuation, since \(x\) and \(2\) are units. Its determinant is one, so its inverse is also integral. This establishes membership in the indicated non-standard parahoric for the displayed matrix. The formula for the curve itself extends at \(x=0\), where it is the identity. The denominators in the factorization are used only for \(x\ne0\).

This check verifies a genuine local ingredient. It does not verify all root-orbit and Schubert-order reductions in Proposition 5.2.3, the entire classification of parahorics, or every stack-theoretic passage in Corollary 5.2.7.
# Dependence, outcome, and limits

The proof proceeds from canonical liftings on the \(\mu\)-ordinary locus to compatible systems along curves, then to all strata and finally to the abelian-variety statement through auxiliary groups. The role of the \(\mu\)-ordinary lifting in Corollary 4.4.13 was traced; the full \(p\)-divisible-group deformation construction was not independently audited.

Title: Initial scientific review of M25-0026
# Identity and scope

The paper is David Martí-Pete, Lasse Rempe and James Waterman, Eremenko’s conjecture, wandering Lakes of Wada, and maverick points, arXiv:2108.10256v5, posted 30 October 2024, 43 PDF pages. The title page is dated 31 October 2024. The associated journal identifier is DOI 10.1090/jams/1049. All page references below are one-based pages of the acquired PDF; these agree with its printed page numbers. The original PDF SHA-256 is

All 25 manifest-listed files matched their recorded hashes. The journal final PDF was not acquired, and equivalence to that version has not been established. This review is confined to the author manuscript.

The extracted text of all 43 pages was read. Actual rendered PDF images were inspected for pages 1, 3, 6, 12–14, 20, 23–24, 27, 30–39. Reading all text does not mean that every assertion was independently proved. The principal completed checks are described below.
# Definitions, quantifiers and dependencies

For an entire function \(f\), the escaping set is \(I(f)=\{z:f^n(z)\to\infty\}\). The bungee set \(\operatorname{BU}(f)\) consists of points with unbounded orbits that do not tend to infinity. A compact set is full when its complement is connected. A wandering domain is a Fatou component whose forward component itinerary never repeats. Theorem 1.2 requires a nonempty, full, connected compact set. Theorem 1.7 allows a full compact set with countable prescribed sets \(Z_I,Z_{\operatorname{BU}}\), but no interior component may meet both. This restriction is necessary for the normal-family argument on a Fatou component; the paper does not prescribe incompatible behaviours within one component.

A maverick boundary point is distinguished by subsequence accumulation behaviour, not just by its unparameterised omega-limit set. Lemma 8.1 expresses this as \(\limsup_n\operatorname{dist}^\#(f^n(z),f^n(\zeta))>0\), where \(\zeta\) is an interior point. Boundedness of the domain itself is not boundedness of its orbits.

The core dependencies are the stated Arakelyan approximation theorem, uniform perturbation estimates in Section 2, and the strip system of Section 4. Section 7 does not depend on the boundary interpolation result of Section 9. Sections 5–6 use that result. The harmonic-measure argument uses Osborne–Sixsmith’s Lemma 4.1 and the previously established behaviour of multiply connected wandering domains.
# Completed analytic checks
## Perturbations and limits

In Lemma 2.3, pp. 12–13, fix \(\delta<\operatorname{dist}(A,\partial U)/2\) and \(\rho=\delta\inf_A|\phi'|/4\). Koebe’s theorem gives a uniform image disc of radius \(\rho\). For \(\varepsilon<\rho/2\), points outside the source \(\delta\)-disc cannot have the same perturbed image as its centre. Within that disc the two boundary curves differ by less than \(2\varepsilon<\rho\); the argument principle gives exactly one zero, counted with multiplicity. Cauchy’s estimate gives \(|f'-\phi'|\leq\varepsilon/\delta<\inf_A|\phi'|/2\). These arguments handle an unbounded closed \(A\) because the constants are uniform.

Lemma 2.5 explicitly requires a single modulus of continuity on the finite orbit union. With that interpretation, the recursive choice \[\delta_{n+1}(\epsilon)=
 \min\{\delta_n(\epsilon),\delta_n(\delta'(\epsilon)),\epsilon/2\}\] keeps the perturbed orbit in the domain and bounds the next error by \(\epsilon\). For Corollary 2.7 one may first thicken \(K\) inside \(G\); the estimates on this neighbourhood supply the uniform closeness needed for the injectivity argument. This is the relevant reading of its use in the unbounded construction.

The approximation sets in the inductive constructions exhaust the plane and preserve previous sets. If \(\epsilon_{j+1}\leq\epsilon_j/2\), then the tail error relative to \(g_j\) is at most \(2\epsilon_j\). The stability thresholds are chosen for this total error before approximation. Consequently the locally uniform entire limit retains the finitely many requirements imposed at each stage. Mere convergence on compact sets, without this uniform tail control on the unbounded sets, would not suffice.
## Strip itinerary and prescribed escaping behaviour

The arithmetic in (4.1)–(4.2), p. 20, gives \[N_j=\frac{j(j+3)}2,\qquad N_{j+1}-N_j=j+2.\] For \(\Phi(z)=5z\), the image of \(S_j\) contains both \(S_{j+1}\) and \(T_{j+1}\) with positive vertical margins. If \(|f-\Phi|<1/2\), then \[|\operatorname{Re}f(z)|\geq5|\operatorname{Re}z|-1/2
   >4|\operatorname{Re}z|\quad (|\operatorname{Re}z|\geq1).\] Thus the expansion applies on either side of the imaginary axis.

The conditions of Proposition 5.2 imply unbounded orbits for all points of \(K\) by visits to \(T_j\). A prescribed bungee point has infinitely many visits to the bounded part of \(S_0\) because it occurs infinitely often in the scheduling sequence. A prescribed escaping point eventually belongs to every finite set \(Z_j\), and condition (e) gives a lower bound \(j\) throughout each interval \([N_j+1,N_{j+1}]\). These intervals cover all sufficiently large times, not merely a subsequence.

There is also a direct check of pairwise disjointness of the compacta. If \(f^n(K)\) and \(f^m(K)\) intersect with \(n<m\), choose \(j\) sufficiently large that \(N_j>m\) and \(j+1>m-n\). Iterating an intersection point for \(N_j-m\) steps would give an intersection of \(T_j\) with an image in one of the preceding \(S\) strips. This contradicts their disjointness. Interior normality follows because all images omit a fixed open disc; the approximating boundary sets entering that disc show \(\partial K\subseteq J(f)\). Hence the interior components are whole Fatou components, with wandering itineraries.

Lemma 5.4, p. 24, uses simple connectedness and the lower bound for the hyperbolic metric to obtain \[\operatorname{dist}_{U_m^\zeta}(\zeta,\omega)
 \geq\frac12\log\left(1+\frac{|\zeta-\omega|}{2\delta_m}\right)
 \longrightarrow\infty.\] The crossing of \(\partial K\) is justified both when an endpoint is on that boundary and when the endpoints are in different interior components. Countability of the prescribed points allows the subsequent diagonal subsequence selection.
## Connected components, rather than only paths

For Theorem 7.1, pp. 31–35, the half-strip boundaries enter a bounded forward-invariant disc. They are disjoint from \(J(f)\cup I(f)\cup\operatorname{BU}(f)\). For every point outside \(K=\bigcap_jK_j\), some such boundary separates it from \(K\). This excludes a connected subset of that union from meeting both \(K\) and its complement; the argument does not merely exclude paths.

For each fixed \(t>0\), the inclusion \(1/(j+2)\leq t\leq j+2\) holds for all sufficiently large \(j\). Thus condition (e) gives bounded returns for every non-endpoint of the ray, while the visits to \(T_j\) give unbounded suborbits. Condition (f), on the full intervening time intervals, makes the endpoint escape. These facts imply that the endpoint is a singleton component of \(I(f)\). The bungee orbit also rules out a polynomial of degree at least two; the prescribed strip expansion and bounded invariant disc rule out the affine cases.

Lemma 7.2’s derivative estimate is consistent with the change of variables \(\zeta=e^{-z}\) and \(\psi(\zeta)=\lambda\zeta+O(\zeta^2)\): \[\phi'(z)=\frac{\zeta\psi'(\zeta)}{\psi(\zeta)}
          =1+O(e^{-\operatorname{Re}z}).\] This supplies control at the unbounded end; compactness and univalence supply bounds on the remaining, strictly interior portion. In the general-continuum construction, equation (7.3) has an absolute value, verified in both the actual PDF image and source line 2023. The plain-text extraction dropped this symbol. A purported sign objection based on that extraction would be invalid.
## Lakes of Wada and harmonic measure

Given a Lakes of Wada continuum \(X\), take the complement of its unbounded complementary domain to obtain the full compactum used in Theorem 1.7. Its bounded complementary domains are interior components with boundary \(X\). Prescribing escaping behaviour in one and oscillating behaviour in another is permitted. Harmonic measures seen from these different domains need not agree. Thus having full harmonic measure for escaping points from one domain and for nonescaping points from another is not a contradiction.

For Theorem 1.11, pp. 37–38, select precisely those times when the interior orbit lies within spherical distance \(\delta\) of \(\xi\). The maps between those successive wandering domains are iterates of \(f\), and their compositions are the selected iterates. This ensures the eventual interior proximity assumption of the original Osborne–Sixsmith Lemma 4.1, whose statement was checked in its primary published PDF, p. 567. The change from all sufficiently large times in that lemma to selected times in the present paper is justified by this reindexing.

For a maverick point, compactness of the sphere gives a subsequence of interior images tending to \(\xi'\) with boundary images a definite distance away. Choose rational \(0<\delta<1\) sufficiently small, and \(\xi\in\mathbb Q(i)\) within \(\delta/2\) of \(\xi'\). Triangle inequalities give interior distance less than \(\delta\) and boundary distance greater than \(2\delta\) infinitely often. The countable union over such \(\xi,\delta\) therefore covers every maverick point and has harmonic measure zero. Rational finite points are dense in the sphere, so the case \(\xi'=\infty\) is included.

Finally, for the finite-set formula (9.1), p. 39, \(\operatorname{Im}\psi'(z)>0\) throughout the upper half-plane. For two distinct points, integrate \(\psi'\) on their straight segment: the quotient \((\psi(z_2)-\psi(z_1))/(z_2-z_1)\) still has positive imaginary part. This proves global injectivity, rather than only nonvanishing derivative. The integral version has the same positivity, conditional on the stated Evans measure theorem.
# Limits, alternative readings and impact

No substantive Problem is asserted. Several apparent transcription issues do not establish a failure: (7.3) retains absolute values, and in the disc example on p. 30 the needed convergence is \(\pi_m(Z_{\rm mav})=(r/r_m)\Xi\to\Xi\), regardless of the displayed equality there. Typographical errors alone are outside the assigned scope.

The following work remains: a full independent proof of the uniform kernel-convergence assertion for arbitrary full continua in Theorem 1.2; the positive-area Jordan-arc construction and its conformal collapse in Theorem 1.14; reconstruction of the omitted construction in the second part of Proposition 7.6; verification of every auxiliary remark, including the fast-escape variant; and full proofs of the external approximation, potential-theoretic and topological results. No computational experiment is needed to replace these analytic tasks.

Abstract: The manifest-pinned 2022 manuscript has an incorrect numerical criterion for an affine moduli scheme. A genus-two, rank-one example satisfies the stated criterion but has additive stabilizers. A stronger criterion restores the auxiliary construction and is compatible with the later choice of a sufficiently large divisor. Separately, an explicit elliptic-curve calculation reproduces a core component-indexing gap that was corrected in a later author manuscript. The highest supported impact in the pinned version is Major, from that historical core proof gap; the unresolved threshold finding is Minor. These are findings about the identified versions, not findings about an unexamined journal-final PDF.

Title: Scientific initial review of M25-0027
# Identity, outcome, and scope

The paper is Joakim Færgeman and Sam Raskin, Non-vanishing of geometric Whittaker coefficients for reductive groups. The assigned journal identifier is DOI 10.1090/jams/1051. The reviewed source is arXiv 2207.02955v1, submitted 6 July 2022; the PDF itself displays 8 July 2022. It has 64 pages. All page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages, agreeing with the printed numbering. The source manifest classifies acquisition as version-limited; equivalence to the journal version is unestablished.

The highest supported impact in the pinned v1 manuscript is Major, owing to the independently reproduced historical component-indexing gap in Problem 2. The component classification is false for disconnected center and feeds directly into the main conservativity argument. This is a known historical issue reproduced; subsequent correction is credited, and it is not counted as a new unresolved defect. The unresolved numerical-threshold finding in Problem 1 is Minor: Definition 5.1.7.1 does not imply Lemma 5.1.7.2. A complete counterexample and a supported stronger hypothesis are given below. The later author’s complete replacement proof has not been independently verified; no journal-final equivalence is asserted.

All 64 pages were read as extracted text. Actual rendered pages 1, 5, 14, 17, 18, 27, 28, 35, 37, 39, 42–44, 46–48, 50, 52, and 53 were inspected visually. Selected exact TeX ranges were compared with the decisive displays. Reading all pages does not mean re-proving all results: the full microlocal index theorem, the entire critical-level localization construction, and the cited foundational results were not independently established.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and dependency checks

The manuscript works in characteristic zero, with a smooth geometrically connected projective curve \(X\) and a split reductive group \(G\). There is no global connected-center assumption (pp. 5, 14). The sheaf category in the main argument is the specified regular-holonomic/ind-constructible \(D\)-module context; its statements are not unrestricted assertions about arbitrary \(\ell\)-adic sheaves.

Theorems A and B concern the enhanced coefficient functor and conservativity; neither asserts full faithfulness. The first coefficient alone is not asserted to detect every tempered object before Hecke operations. The shifted coefficient functor \(\operatorname{coeff}[\dim\operatorname{Bun}_G]\) is the one whose exactness is used.

Several formal steps were checked conditionally on the cited inputs. In Section 7, exact baby-Whittaker averaging makes its kernel stable under truncations and subobjects, permitting the quotient \(t\)-structure. Right exactness of Hecke action is transferred through the conservative quotient functor; left exactness follows by adjunction using the dual representation. The fully faithful adjoint to this quotient is the left adjoint, as the manuscript states.

In Section 8.2 the identity \(\operatorname{coeff}\simeq\operatorname{coeff}_![-2d]\), \(d=\dim\operatorname{Bun}_G\), gives the stated Verdier-duality compatibility after shift by \(d\). In Lemma 10.1.1.1 the authors first reduce to a constructible object in the heart. Exactness then places its coefficient in a single degree, so the Euler-characteristic argument is legitimate in that reduction; it is not the invalid implication that an arbitrary complex with zero Euler characteristic vanishes. These checks do not remove Problems 1 and 2.
# Problem 1: the large-divisor bound does not remove stabilizers
## Claim and location

Equation reference: oldbound. Definition 5.1.7.1, equation (5.1.1), p. 28, declares \(D\) sufficiently large if \[
 \langle\alpha,\deg D\rangle>g-1
 \qquad(\alpha>0).\] Lemma 5.1.7.2 on the same page then asserts that \(\operatorname{Bun}_N^{\Omega(-D)}\) is an affine scheme. The exact source is `coeffs.tex`, lines 3126–3148. The reduction to additive groups does not prove the claim: a torsor stack can retain \(H^0\) as its automorphism group.
## Counterexample with all parameters specified

Work over \(k=\mathbb C\). Let \(X\) be the smooth projective completion of \[y^2=x^5-x,\] and let \(P\) be the point at infinity. The polynomial is square-free: at \(x=0\) its derivative is \(-1\), and at any nonzero root \(x^4=1\) its derivative is \(5x^4-1=4\). The degree-five hyperelliptic cover has six branch points, including infinity, so Riemann–Hurwitz gives genus \(g=2\). It is geometrically connected and smooth after its stated completion.

At \(P\), \(x\) and \(y\) have orders \(-2\) and \(-5\). Hence \(\eta=dx/y\) has order \(-3-(-5)=2\). It is nonzero and regular at the finite branch points, as is seen using \(y\) as a local parameter, and has no other zeroes. Thus \[\operatorname{div}(\eta)=2P,\qquad
 \Omega_X\simeq\mathcal O_X(2P).\] Choose the square root \(\mathcal O_X(P)\).

Equation reference: actualstack. Take the split reductive group \(G=PGL_2\) with its upper Borel. Its center is trivial, so this example is independent of Problem 2. There is a single positive root \(\alpha\), and \(\check\rho\) is an integral dominant coweight with \(\langle\alpha,\check\rho\rangle=1\). Set \[D=2\check\rho\cdot P.\] It is a dominant coweight-valued divisor and satisfies every inequality in [oldbound] (#oldbound), since \(2>2-1\). However [rootline] (#rootline) gives \[L_\alpha=\Omega_X(-2P)\simeq\mathcal O_X.\] Therefore the twisted unipotent group is the constant \(\mathbb G_a\), and its torsor stack has isomorphism classes \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\) and automorphism group \(H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)\) at every object. Over \(\mathbb C\), after a linear splitting, it is \[
 \operatorname{Bun}_{\mathbb G_a}\simeq \mathbb A^2\times B\mathbb G_a.\] In particular the trivial torsor has automorphism group \(\mathbb G_a\ne1\). A scheme has trivial automorphism groups at its geometric points. Thus the actual stack is not a scheme, contradicting the lemma, and a fortiori is not an affine scheme.
## Alternative readings and supported repair

The object is defined as a fiber over a fixed \(T\)-bundle, not a coarse moduli space of isomorphism classes. Passing silently to \(H^1\) would change that definition and its sheaf operations. The choice of theta characteristic does not halve the root bundle: the displayed definition uses \(2\check\rho\) on \(\Omega_X^{1/2}\), and [rootline] (#rootline) follows. Both points were checked in the actual p. 27 image.

Equation reference: newbound. A sufficient replacement, for the reductive groups under discussion, is \[
 \langle\alpha_i,\deg D\rangle>2g-2
 \quad\hbox{for every simple root }\alpha_i.\] Here is the proof of the auxiliary assertion under this new hypothesis. If \(\alpha=\sum_i n_i\alpha_i>0\), then \(\langle\alpha,\check\rho\rangle=\sum_i n_i\). Thus \[\deg L_\alpha
 =(2g-2)\sum_i n_i-\sum_i n_i
       \langle\alpha_i,\deg D\rangle<0.\] It follows that \(H^0(X,L_\alpha)=0\); also \(H^2(X,L_\alpha)=0\) because \(X\) is a curve. Use the \(T\)-stable central filtration of \(N\) by positive-root height. Its successive central quotients, after twisting, are sums of these additive line bundles. For a central extension by such a vector group, the obstruction to lifting a torsor lies in \(H^2\), the lifts form a torsor under \(H^1\), and relative automorphisms lie in \(H^0\). The first and last vanish. Inductively, therefore, the moduli of lifts is a torsor under a finite-dimensional vector group over the previous affine scheme. Such a torsor over an affine scheme is affine (indeed trivial after using vanishing of first quasi-coherent cohomology). Starting with the trivial group proves that \(\operatorname{Bun}_N^{\Omega(-D)}\) is an affine scheme under [newbound] (#newbound). This is a strengthened hypothesis, not a proof of the original numerical claim.
## Impact and calibration

Step 1 of Theorem 8.3.0.1 (p. 43) uses this affineness to bound cohomological amplitude, so its invocation for every \(D\) satisfying [oldbound] (#oldbound) is unsupported. Nevertheless Step 2 explicitly permits \(\check\lambda=2n\check\rho\) with \(n\gg0\) at a chosen point. Such a divisor satisfies [newbound] (#newbound) as well. The same Steps 2 and 3 then transfer exactness to \(D=0\) and to general \(D\), conditional on the other stated inputs. The incorrect numerical threshold is therefore locally repairable without altering that main exactness statement or the allowed class of groups. This is the reason for the Minor calibration; mere ease of repair is not being used to dismiss a damaged core conclusion. No counterexample to the coefficient exactness theorem is claimed.
# Problem 2: a corrected historical component-indexing gap
## Old claim and its precise failure

Proposition 2.5.4.1(3), p. 17, asserts connectedness of \(\mathring{\operatorname{Nilp}}^{\check\lambda}\) whenever all \(\langle\alpha_i,\check\lambda\rangle+2g-2\) are nonnegative. The next paragraph declares the component-indexing map \(c\) injective. Section 2.5.6, p. 18, identifies the components of the everywhere regular locus with \(\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb G_m,Z_G)\) and identifies the entire degree \((2-2g)\check\rho\) stratum with the Kostant component. The TeX confirms these statements at lines 1955–2002 and 2123–2148.

Let \(k=\mathbb C\), \(G=SL_2\), and let \(X\) be the elliptic curve \(y^2=x^3-x\) with origin \(O\) at infinity. Fix a nowhere-zero differential \(\eta\) and the trivial square root of \(\Omega_X\). Take \(\check\lambda=0\). All numerical hypotheses are satisfied since \(g=1\). This is a split reductive group and an allowed curve.

There are four distinct two-torsion line bundles \[L_P=\mathcal O_X(P-O),\qquad
 P\in\{O,(0,0),(1,0),(-1,0)\}.\] For the three finite points, the divisor of \(x-x(P)\) is \(2P-2O\), giving \(L_P^2\simeq\mathcal O_X\); the usual identification of \(X\) with \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)\) distinguishes them. Choose these square trivializations and define determinant-trivial rank-two bundles and Higgs fields \[E_P=L_P\oplus L_P,\qquad
 \phi_P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\eta.\] Each field is trace-zero, squares to zero, and has rank one everywhere. Its unique kernel line is \(L_P\), of degree zero. Hence every point belongs to the asserted connected stratum.

Conversely, in this stratum a generically nonzero map \(L^{-1}\to L\otimes\Omega_X\) has degree zero; therefore it is an isomorphism. The kernel line consequently satisfies \(L^2\simeq
\mathcal O_X\). Its isomorphism class defines a map to the finite etale four-point space \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)[2]\). All four fibers are nonempty by the construction above and are open and closed. Thus the stratum cannot be connected.

One can count its components exactly. If \(M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) and \(f=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), then \[Mf-fM=\begin{pmatrix}-c&a-d\\0&c\end{pmatrix}.\] With \(\det M=1\), centralizing \(f\) means \(c=0\), \(d=a\), \(a^2=1\). The centralizer is \(\mu_2\times\mathbb G_a\), using \(b/a\) as the additive coordinate. The everywhere regular stratum is its torsor stack. \(\operatorname{Bun}_{\mu_2}\) has four components, while \(\operatorname{Bun}_{\mathbb G_a}\simeq\mathbb A^1\times B\mathbb G_a\) is connected. There are exactly four components, whereas \(\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb G_m,\mu_2)=0\) predicts one. This calculation verifies the discrepancy directly; no sheaf with an arbitrary prescribed singular support has been assumed to exist.
## Old core dependency and counterevidence

The old proof of Theorem 9.1.0.1 chooses an entire degree stratum inside \(\operatorname{SS}(\mathcal F)\) from the existence of one irreducible component meeting it (Section 9.3.2, p. 46, source lines 5077–5086). On p. 47 it then puts a particular canonical Higgs point into \(\operatorname{SS}(\mathcal F)\) solely from membership in that stratum. The example shows why the degree label alone cannot justify these steps. Its four components have the same degree, discrepancy zero, and first Chern class zero.

The chain continues through Corollary 10.1.1.2, the enhanced-coefficient conservativity statement, and Theorem 10.3.3.1 to Theorems A and B. The invalid classification is therefore a Major historical proof defect. This does not establish that the main conservativity theorem is false, nor that the four Higgs points themselves supply a counterexample to a statement about all sheaves.
## Later-version attribution

The author-hosted manuscript [FRnew], dated 9 May 2025, changes Proposition 2.5.4.1 to account for disconnected center and central torsors, restricts the Kostant-stratum equality, and incorporates central translations into Section 9 and the subsequent conservativity argument. It also includes an \(SL_2\) example. These changes corroborate the historical issue. The replacement global proof has not been fully audited here. Its Lemma 5.1.7.2 retains the numerical bound considered in Problem 1. This comparison does not establish equivalence of either author manuscript to the journal-final PDF.
# Remaining dependencies and rejected overclaims

Section 8 cites a result of Kevin Lin as forthcoming at the time of writing. A primary manuscript is now available as arXiv 2211.05282v1 [Lin]; its introduction and stated relationship between Poincare series and duality were consulted. This is not currently an absent source, but its full proof and all normalization identifications have not been independently checked. The cited alternative topological argument was not audited.

Section 11 distinguishes irreducible from very irreducible local systems; the latter has automorphism group exactly \(Z_{\check G}\). The finite-group example on p. 52 is compatible with this distinction. For semisimple \(G\), the proof bounds the length of the normalized eigensheaf by \(|\pi_1^{\mathrm{alg}}(G)|\) and obtains the reverse bound from nonzero restrictions to every component. Conditional on exact conservative coefficients, equality forces length one on each component. For general reductive \(G\), the central coweight quotient addresses the infinite-component issue. These are conditional formal checks, not a reconstruction of the full existence theorem.

The paper itself acknowledges a general-parabolic extension of the Eisenstein-series input as folklore, with incomplete literature proofs (Remark 11.1.4.2). Appendix A invokes substantial oper and localization machinery. These remain external-proof limitations; they are not converted into additional established defects. The semisimplicity statement for arbitrary irreducible local systems is presented as expected in Remark 11.1.4.3 and is not accepted here as an unconditional theorem. No claims about unperformed experiments or author-code execution are made.
