Title: Scientific initial review of M25-0028
# Identity, outcome, and coverage

This report concerns Chenyang Xu and Ziquan Zhuang, Stable degenerations of singularities, assigned DOI 10.1090/jams/1055. The exact reviewed input is the 42-page author manuscript arXiv 2205.10915v2, submitted 17 January 2025. Page numbers refer to one-based physical PDF pages and agree with the printed numbering. The manifest does not establish equivalence to the journal version of record; no journal-final defect is asserted.

The supported outcome is Minor, Problem 1 below. All 42 PDF pages were read as extracted text. Actual rendered pages 1, 5, 8, 9, 13, 15–17, 22, 27, and 30–40 were inspected visually (21 pages). The decisive lemma was also checked against exact TeX lines 409–438 of `HRFG-local.tex`. All seven manifest-listed input files passed hash validation. This is a claim-focused initial review, not a certification of every proof or of the imported birational geometry.

The principal checks concern the valuation conventions, the complement/minimizer argument in Lemmas 3.2–3.4, the role of Kollár models and their integral degenerations, and the deduction of finite generation in Corollary 4.10 and Theorem 1.1. A reviewer-written exact calculation checked a concrete instance of the asymptotic count in Lemma 3.3. No author code was run.
# Definitions and dependency structure

The general setting is a normal affine variety over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, with an effective \(\mathbb Q\)-boundary and a klt singularity at a closed point \(x\). A real valuation takes finite real values on every nonzero element of the function field. The centered valuations in \(\operatorname{Val}_{X,x}\) are nonnegative on the local ring and positive on its maximal ideal. The ideal at threshold \(\lambda\) is \[\mathfrak a_\lambda(v)=\{f:v(f)\geq\lambda\}.\] The normalized volume is \(A_{X,\Delta}(v)^n\operatorname{vol}(v)\). Its scale invariance follows from \(A(cv)=cA(v)\) and \(\operatorname{vol}(cv)=c^{-n}\operatorname{vol}(v)\); uniqueness of a minimizer is therefore understood up to scaling.

The main proof has two substantial branches. First, Lemma 3.3 establishes the threshold identity needed in Lemma 3.2, and Lemma 3.4 makes the minimizing valuation a monomial lc place of a special complement. The ample strict-transform condition avoiding the strata is essential here; the paper does not assert that any lc complement has this consequence. Second, Theorem 3.14 and Corollary 3.18 produce Kollár models, and Propositions 4.5–4.6 construct their compatible degenerations. Lemmas 4.8–4.9 then identify the filtered ideals; Corollary 4.10 supplies finite generation. Theorem 4.1 combines these implications, and Theorem 1.1 applies it to the minimizing valuation.

This dependency map matters for calibration. Lemma 2.7 is invoked inside the final branch, but its missing assumption can be proved from the definitions at that invocation. The defect does not require replacement of the main geometric construction.
# Problem 1: the filtered-ring criterion needs separatedness
## Source claim and suspect step

Equation reference: eq:sup. Lemma 2.7, PDF p. 8, and source lines 425–429 assert that a decreasing multiplicative sequence of ideals of a domain whose associated graded ring is integral is the sequence of ideals of a discrete valuation. The proof defines \[
 v(f)=\sup\{i:f\in\mathfrak a_i\}\qquad(0\ne f\in R)\] and uses products of nonzero initial forms to establish multiplicativity. The product argument is valid when the initial forms exist. What has not been shown is that the supremum in [eq:sup] (#eq:sup) is finite for every nonzero \(f\).

Equation reference: eq:separated. The definition of a graded sequence in the preliminary conventions requires multiplicativity, and the lemma adds decreasingness. Neither requirement supplies \[
 \bigcap_{i\geq0}\mathfrak a_i=0.\]
## Complete counterexample

Work over \(\mathbb C\) and take \[R=\mathbb C[x,y],\qquad \mathfrak a_0=R,\qquad
 \mathfrak a_i=(x,y^i)\quad(i\geq1).\] The ring is an integral domain, indeed a regular finitely generated ring, and its affine spectrum with zero boundary is smooth and klt. Each positive-index ideal is nonzero, proper, and \((x,y)\)-primary. The sequence decreases because \((x,y^{i+1})\subseteq(x,y^i)\). For \(i,j\geq1\), \[(x,y^i)(x,y^j)
  =(x^2,xy^i,xy^j,y^{i+j})\subseteq(x,y^{i+j}).\] The cases with an index zero are immediate. Thus every stated filtration assumption holds, even with the extra primary-ideal property later used in the paper.

Reduction modulo \(x\) identifies the successive quotients with those of the \(y\)-adic filtration of \(\mathbb C[y]\). Consequently \[R/\mathfrak a_1\simeq\mathbb C,\qquad
 \mathfrak a_i/\mathfrak a_{i+1}=\mathbb C\,[y^i]\ (i\geq1),\qquad
 \operatorname{gr}(R,\mathfrak a_\bullet)\simeq\mathbb C[t],\quad \deg t=1.\] Multiplication sends \([y^i][y^j]\) to \([y^{i+j}]\), so this is an isomorphism of graded rings, not just of vector spaces. In particular the graded ring is an integral domain with nonzero positive-degree pieces.

However \(0\ne x\in\mathfrak a_i\) for every \(i\). Any valuation satisfying \(\mathfrak a_i=\mathfrak a_i(v)\) would have \(v(x)\geq i\) for every positive integer \(i\), which contradicts the required finite real value of \(v(x)\). The proposed formula instead assigns \(v(x)=+\infty\). It gives a semivaluation supported on the nonzero prime ideal \((x)\), rather than a valuation of \(\mathbb C(x,y)\). Indeed \(\bigcap_i\mathfrak a_i=(x)\), exactly the missing separation.
## Alternative readings and counterevidence

Allowing a nontrivial support for a semivaluation would make the formula meaningful, but changes the definition of valuation used on p. 7 and the function-field conclusion of the lemma. Requiring positive-degree graded pieces, proper ideals, primary ideals, a Noetherian ring, or a smooth ambient variety does not remove this example. The usual separated filtration convention would remove it, but no such condition is stated in the relevant definition or in Lemma 2.7. The proof itself needs this convention explicitly.
## Supported corrected statement and proof

Let \(R\) be a domain and \((\mathfrak a_i)_{i\geq0}\) a decreasing, multiplicative sequence with \[\mathfrak a_0=R,\quad 0\ne\mathfrak a_1\subsetneq R,\quad
 \bigcap_i\mathfrak a_i=0,\] and suppose \(\operatorname{gr}(R,\mathfrak a_\bullet)\) is a domain. Then [eq:sup] (#eq:sup) defines a nontrivial discrete valuation on \(\operatorname{Frac}(R)\) whose threshold ideals at integral indices are exactly the \(\mathfrak a_i\).

For \(f\ne0\), separatedness and decreasingness give a unique finite largest index \(i\) with \(f\in\mathfrak a_i\). The properness of \(\mathfrak a_1\) gives \(v(1)=0\). If \(v(f)=i\) and \(v(g)=j\), their nonzero initial forms have nonzero product in the graded domain. Thus \(fg\in\mathfrak a_{i+j}\setminus\mathfrak a_{i+j+1}\), proving \(v(fg)=v(f)+v(g)\). Ideal membership proves \(v(f+g)\geq\min(v(f),v(g))\) whenever \(f+g\ne0\). The formula \(v(f/g)=v(f)-v(g)\) is well-defined by the product identity. The value group is a nonzero subgroup of \(\mathbb Z\), hence discrete. Finally, decreasingness gives \(f\in\mathfrak a_i\) if and only if \(v(f)\geq i\). This proves exactly the corrected assertion, with no completeness assumption on \(R\).
## Verification that the actual application is separated

Equation reference: eq:containment. Corollary 4.10 on p. 38 invokes the lemma for the filtration \[I_{s,\lambda}
 =\operatorname{Span}\{f\in R:\textstyle\sum_j s_jv_j(f)\geq\lambda\},
 \tag{4.3 of the manuscript}\] where \(v_j=\operatorname{ord}_{E_j}\) lie in one quasi-monomial cone, and initially \(0\ne s\in\mathbb N^r\) after rescaling rational weights. Write \(\alpha^j\) for the weight vector of \(v_j\). The quasi-monomial valuation \(v_s\) with weight \(\sum_j s_j\alpha^j\) satisfies, for a local monomial expansion, \[v_s(f)
 =\min_\beta\sum_j s_j\langle\alpha^j,\beta\rangle
 \ \geq\ \sum_j s_j\min_\beta\langle\alpha^j,\beta\rangle
 =\sum_j s_jv_j(f).\] The valuation inequality for sums therefore gives \[
 I_{s,\lambda}\subseteq\mathfrak a_\lambda(v_s).\] This is also the first observation in the proof of Lemma 4.8, p. 35, and does not presuppose the equality being proved.

Because \(v_s(f)\) is finite for \(f
e0\), [eq:containment] (#eq:containment) proves \( igcap_{i\geq0}I_{s,i}=0\). Centeredness gives \(I_{s,0}=R\) and properness of \(I_{s,1}\). For any \(0
e h\) in the maximal ideal of \(x\), a sufficiently large power \(h^N\) has \(\sum_j s_jv_j(h^N)\geq1\), proving \(I_{s,1}
e0\). Thus all extra hypotheses of the corrected lemma hold at the integer-weight invocation. Its integral graded ring is supplied by Propositions 4.5–4.6 as in the manuscript. Lemma 4.8 then identifies the resulting valuation with \(v_s\); Lemma 4.9 treats the remaining real weights.

The counterexample falsifies the unrestricted auxiliary lemma, but this direct separation argument repairs its actual use. The supported severity is therefore Minor. It is not a counterexample to Theorems 1.1–1.3.
# Other checked reasoning and boundaries
## The strict threshold in Lemma 3.3

Set \(A(v_0)=1\), \(q=v_0(f)>0\), \(rD=\operatorname{div}(f)\), and \(V=\operatorname{vol}(v_0)\). The counts on pp. 13–15 give \[N_m\sim\frac{Vm^n}{n!},\qquad
 w_m=mN_m-\sum_{j=1}^mN_j
       \sim\frac{nVm^{n+1}}{(n+1)!},\] and \[\mu_m=\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor m/q\rfloor}
            \ell(R/\mathfrak a_{m-jq}(v_0))
       \sim\frac{Vm^{n+1}}{q(n+1)!}.\] Hence \(r\mu_m/w_m\longrightarrow1/(n v_0(D))\). The strict assumption \(v_0(D)<1/n\) makes this limit larger than one and yields domination of \(D\) for sufficiently large \(m\). The argument does not prove the same statement at equality. The simultaneous-basis and K-semistability inputs remain cited dependencies rather than new results verified here.

As an exact check, take the smooth plane with \(v_0=\operatorname{ord}_0/2\), \(D=\frac14\{x=0\}\), \(r=4\), and \(f=x\). Then \(A(v_0)=1\), \(v_0(D)=1/8\), and \(\mathfrak a_m=\mathfrak m^{2m}\). Counting monomials gives \[N_m=m(2m+1),\quad
 w_m=\frac{m(m-1)(8m+5)}6,\quad
 \mu_m=\frac{(2m-1)(2m)(2m+1)}6.\] Thus \(4\mu_m/w_m\to4=1/(2v_0(D))\). The independent program checked all three integer formulas for \(m=2,\ldots,50\) (147 equalities) and the exact symbolic limit. It is a check of these counts, not an empirical reproduction or a substitute for the general argument.
## Local approximation and geometric induction

In Lemma 3.2, the needed Lipschitz bound is local near \(v_0\), which lies in the interior of the relevant cone. Finite convexity supplies local Lipschitz continuity there. A general global Lipschitz assertion on an entire closed cone does not follow from convexity alone; no counterexample to the specific function in this manuscript was established, and the local form suffices for the stated nearby approximants.

The inspection of Propositions 4.5–4.6 included the compatibility of the simultaneous induction, the restriction-surjectivity input from Lemma 3.13, and the use of qdlt normal strata together with connectedness. The integrality claim is not justified by flatness alone, nor is that the paper’s only argument. A complete reconstruction of every relative MMP and adjunction input was not performed.
## Rational weights, real weights, and downstream scope

Lemma 4.9 uses a finite set of weights below a fixed threshold, rather than one perturbation preserving the ordering of infinitely many monomials. The coefficients in the chosen \(\mathbb Q\)-independent weight decomposition distinguish the relevant finite tuples. Positive coordinates and restriction to the active face handle the local finiteness of the weight set. In Corollary 4.10 the input divisorial valuations are the integral orders \(\operatorname{ord}_{E_i}\), so the integral rescaling step has its required meaning. These observations support the specific rational-to-real passage used there. Full globalization of every quasi-monomial model appearing in the general formulation was not independently reconstructed.

The same-open-face conclusion for \(\operatorname{gr}_{v_s}R\) concerns the underlying algebras. The numerical real gradings can change with the Reeb weights. It does not assert a grading-preserving identification across different numerical weights, nor an identification across all boundary faces.

For Theorem 1.3, the \(\mathbb Q\)-boundary and the rational Reeb-volume function are relevant to algebraicity after normalization \(A=1\). The cited results on the minimizer are still external inputs. The theorem is not interpreted here as a result for arbitrary real boundary coefficients. For Theorem 1.6, deleting faces may produce a locally closed polyhedral subset; it need not be a closed cone.

A basic compatible boundary check is the positive monomial valuation on smooth \(\mathbb A^n\): \[A(v)=\sum_iw_i,\qquad \operatorname{vol}(v)=(\prod_iw_i)^{-1},\qquad
 \widehat{\operatorname{vol}}(v)=\frac{(\sum_iw_i)^n}{\prod_iw_i}\geq n^n.\] Equality is attained at equal weights. Irrational weights do not prevent the associated algebra from being a polynomial algebra. This calculation gives no contradiction to the finite-generation assertion or its scaling conventions.

The arXiv record identifies v2 as the accepted manuscript. The consulted author research page and targeted correction searches did not reveal a correction of the separatedness claim. This is a limited search observation, not a claim of exhaustive novelty. Neither an acceptance comment nor a DOI establishes bytewise or mathematical equivalence to the journal-final version.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the manifest-pinned arXiv author manuscript 2304.05881v3, not an independently verified journal-final version. Three defects are supported: a missing value-group condition in the axiomatization used for decidability transfer, an incorrect discriminant identity, and a characteristic-two boundary failure in an illustrative example. A countermodel, an exact cubic calculation, and a cyclotomic identity establish the respective defects. Explicit local repairs are justified. No failure of the main elementary-embedding or Fontaine–Wintenberger conclusions is demonstrated. The outcome is Major for the invalid proof of the advertised decidability transfer; the other two defects are Minor. These judgments are limited to the recorded inspection scope.

Title: Scientific initial review of
Beyond the Fontaine–Wintenberger theorem
# Identity, scope, and outcome

The reviewed paper is by Franziska Jahnke and Konstantinos Kartas, Beyond the Fontaine–Wintenberger theorem, arXiv:2304.05881v3, dated 19 December 2024, 60 PDF pages. The assigned bibliographic DOI is https://doi.org/10.1090/jams/1056. All locations below refer to the one-based pages of the supplied PDF, which agree with its printed numbering. All seven manifest-listed inputs passed SHA-256 verification. The reviewed PDF hash is
> 3bada3b6aa929fa70f17f95e1a39ab4a193a02cb1a5add9b60b0cf5d93948cc8.
Equivalence with the published journal PDF has not been established. Consequently, the findings are attributed only to this author manuscript.

Problem 1 invalidates the proof-enumeration procedure for the decidability transfer advertised as Corollary 1.7.6 (page 9) and proved as Corollary 5.3.5 (page 37). This explicitly promoted model-theoretic transfer result supports a Major judgment, limited to its original derivation. The main embedding proof does not use the incomplete theory. Problems 2 and 3 remain Minor: the former has a norm argument proving exactly the unit criterion used later, and the latter affects the prime boundary of an illustrative witness.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and main checks

A perfectoid field here is a non-discretely valued, complete, real-valued field of residue characteristic \(p>0\), with surjective Frobenius on \(\mathcal O_K/(p)\). Its tilt is denoted \(K^\flat\). The enlarged class \(\mathcal C\) permits higher-rank henselian valuations, with a distinguished nonzero nonunit \(\varpi\), semiperfect \(\mathcal O_v/(p)\), and algebraically maximal \(\mathcal O_v[\varpi^{-1}]\). Rank one must not silently be imposed on arbitrary models of this elementary class.

The valuation \(w\) in Theorem 6.2.3 is the coarsest coarsening of the ultrapower valuation \(v_U\) with \(w\varpi>0\). The assertion that finite extensions are unramified concerns \((K_U,w)\). It does not assert that every finite extension is unramified for \(v_U\) or for the original valuation of \(K\). The infinitesimal convex subgroup relative to \(v\varpi\) is collapsed in passing to \(w\).
The following checks support the scope of the review.

1. In Theorems 5.1.2 and 5.1.4, the quotient-ring and value-group conditions are substantive. Taking reduced quotients and then fraction fields retains the induced residue valuation. The resplendent embedding step must retain that extra structure. Regular density explains where value-group conditions can be omitted; it is not automatic for an arbitrary higher-rank model of \(\mathcal C\).

2. In Lemma 6.1.2, for a compatible system \(x=(x_n)\), \(v(x_n)=p^{-n}v(x_0)\). For nonzero \(x\) these values become infinitesimal relative to a fixed positive standard value. Thus \(x^\natural\) is a \(w\)-unit. Addition modulo \(p\) on integral elements gives addition in the residue field. General elements reduce to this case after multiplication by a common integral denominator, whose image remains a \(w\)-unit.

3. In Theorem 6.1.3, the nonstandard iterated Frobenius on \(\mathcal O_{v_U}/(\varpi)\) is surjective with kernel generated by \(\pi=\operatorname{ulim}\varpi^{1/p^i}\). Its induced isomorphism, together with the elementary diagonal map, proves the claimed elementarity of the truncated-ring map. The containment \(\mathfrak m_w\subseteq\pi\mathcal O_{v_U}\) justifies the next quotient. The final application of Theorem 5.1.4 uses the stated regular-density and class-\(\mathcal C\) hypotheses, independently of Problem 1.

4. In Lemma 6.2.1, the discriminant congruence and the strict inequality \(v(\operatorname{disc}f)<v\varpi\) imply \(v(\operatorname{disc}g)=p^{-1}v(\operatorname{disc}f)\). The Hensel–Rychlik step produces a root of \(f\) in \(K(\beta)\). Then \([K(\beta):K]\leq\deg g=\deg f\), while containment of a root of irreducible \(f\) gives the reverse bound. This supplies the degree argument implicit in the conclusion. Integral-generator normalization is needed when passing to general monic polynomials in the subsequent discussion.

5. In Theorem 7.2.5, countable cofinality of positive values for the original rank-one field matters in identifying the kernel of the ultrapower-localization functor with almost-zero modules. Tensor maps are initially natural comparison maps; their being isomorphisms is established under the appropriate uniform finiteness hypotheses. Faithfulness reflects isomorphisms of morphisms, and does not assert that arbitrary isomorphic image objects lift to isomorphic objects.

6. In Lemma 7.2.19, the choice \(p\,w\varepsilon<w\varpi<2p\,w\varepsilon\) gives both required ideal containments. Two successive lifts yield \(x=y_1^p+\varepsilon^p y_2^p+\varepsilon^{2p}x_2\). Reduction modulo \(\varpi\) removes the final term and the mixed binomial terms, since \(p\in\varpi\mathcal O_v\).
Full independent reconstructions of the external tame-field embedding theorems, all resplendence arguments, and the general Gabber–Ramero almost-module results were not performed.
# Problem 1: the theory used for decidability transfer is incomplete
## Source claim and suspect inference

Corollary 5.3.5, PDF page 37, claims that \(\operatorname{Th}(K^\flat,v^\flat)\) is decidable relative to \(\operatorname{Th}(K,v)\). Its proof constructs a theory \(T\) of perfect henselian characteristic-\(p\) valued fields \((F,u,t)\) for which \(\mathcal O_F[t^{-1}]\) is algebraically maximal, and adds \[\mathcal O_F/(t)\equiv\mathcal O_{K^\flat}/(t)\cong\mathcal O_K/(p).
 \tag{3.1}\] It then asserts, using Theorem 5.1.7, that \(T\) decides every \(L_{\rm val}\)-sentence exactly as \(K^\flat\) does.

Theorem 5.1.7 on page 34 additionally requires elementary equivalence of the pointed value groups \((\Gamma,u(t))\). That information is not among the listed axioms of \(T\). Source lines 1567–1572 confirm the omission; it is not an extraction artifact.
## A countermodel satisfying every listed condition

Fix a prime \(p\), let \(K=\mathbb C_p\), and let \(E=K^\flat\). The rank-one value group is \(\Gamma_E=\mathbb Q\), normalized so that \(v_E(t)=1\), where \(t=(p,p^{1/p},p^{1/p^2},\ldots)\). This choice exists in \(\mathbb C_p\), and \[\mathcal O_E/(t)\cong\mathcal O_K/(p).\] Set \(G=\mathbb Z[1/p]\) with its usual order and form the full Hahn field \[F=E((z^G)).\] Give it the Hahn valuation \(w_z\), with residue field \(E\), and then the composite valuation \(u=w_z\circ v_E\). Explicitly, if \(f=\sum c_gz^g\neq0\) has least exponent \(g_0\), then \[u(f)=(g_0,v_E(c_{g_0}))\in G\mathbin{\mathrm{lex}}\mathbb Q.
 \tag{3.2}\] Regard \(t\) as a constant series. The assumptions are checked as follows.

1. \(F\) has characteristic \(p\) and is perfect: \(E\) is perfect, \(G\) is \(p\)-divisible, and taking coefficientwise \(p\)-th roots and dividing every exponent by \(p\) preserves well-ordered support.

2. The full Hahn field is spherically complete for \(w_z\). Indeed, a nested family of balls prescribes compatible initial coefficient segments. Their union has well-ordered support: a hypothetical decreasing sequence in that support would lie below one prescribed radius and hence in a single center’s well-ordered support. Choosing all unspecified coefficients to be zero gives a point in every ball. Thus \(w_z\) is maximal, in particular henselian and algebraically maximal. The coefficient valuation \(v_E\) is henselian because \(E\) is a complete rank-one valued field. Their composite \(u\) is henselian.

3. \(u(t)=(0,1)>0\), so \(t\) is a nonzero nonunit. Inverting \(t\) clears any negative leading-coefficient value when the leading exponent is zero, while it cannot change a negative leading exponent. Therefore \[\mathcal O_u[t^{-1}]=\mathcal O_{w_z}.
 \tag{3.3}\] The localization is algebraically maximal, as required.

4. The residue map \(\mathcal O_u\longrightarrow\mathcal O_E\) for \(w_z\) is onto, and its kernel \(\mathfrak m_{w_z}\) is contained in \(t\mathcal O_u\): division by the constant \(t\) preserves positive \(z\)-order. Consequently \[\mathcal O_u/(t)\cong\mathcal O_E/(t)
 \tag{3.4}\] as rings, which is stronger than (3.1).
Thus both \(E\) and \(F\), with these choices of \(t\), satisfy the listed theory \(T\).

Choose a prime \(\ell\neq p\). The interpretable value-group sentence \[\sigma_\ell:\quad
 \forall\gamma\ \exists\delta\;(\ell\delta=\gamma)
 \tag{3.5}\] holds in \(E\), since \(\mathbb Q\) is divisible. It fails in \(F\): the element \((1,0)\) of \(\mathbb Z[1/p]\mathbin{\mathrm{lex}}\mathbb Q\) has no \(\ell\)-th part. Hence neither \(\sigma_\ell\) nor its negation follows from \(T\). Enumerating proofs of those alternatives from the stated \(T\) need not terminate.
## Counterevidence, precise repair, and impact

The higher-rank field \(F\) is not claimed to be perfectoid. That is not an escape from the example: the proof explicitly axiomatizes a larger elementary class, whose members need not have rank one. The countermodel concerns completeness of this \(T\), not the truth of the corollary.

There is a direct repair using the same oracle. In mixed characteristic choose \(t\in\mathcal O_{K^\flat}\) with \(\mathcal O_{K^\flat}/(t)\cong\mathcal O_K/(p)\) and \(v^\flat(t)=v(p)\); the first coordinate of the distinguished Witt-vector generator supplies such a choice. Add to \(T\) the complete theory \[\operatorname{Th}(\Gamma_K,v(p))
 \quad\text{on the pointed group }(\Gamma_F,u(t)).
 \tag{3.6}\] The ring \(\mathcal O_K/(p)\) and the pointed value group \((\Gamma_K,v(p))\) are uniformly interpretable in \((K,v)\), with the fixed integer \(p\) supplying the parameter. Their theories can therefore be enumerated using the same \(L_{\rm val}(K)\) oracle. The resulting theory \(T^*\) is consistent because \(K^\flat\) is a model. Every model now meets all the hypotheses of Theorem 5.1.7 relative to \(K^\flat\), so its \(L_{\rm val}\)-reduct is elementarily equivalent to \(K^\flat\). Proof enumeration from this oracle-recursive theory terminates for every sentence or its negation. In characteristic \(p\), tilting identifies \(K^\flat\) with \(K\), so the decidability assertion is immediate.

The incomplete theory \(T\) invalidates the proof-enumeration procedure used to establish the decidability transfer advertised as Corollary 1.7.6 (page 9) and proved as Corollary 5.3.5 (page 37). This is a demonstrated invalid derivation of an explicitly promoted model-theoretic transfer result and is assessed as Major. The countermodel does not refute the corollary itself: the augmented theory \(T^*\) supplies a corrected proof conditional on the stated AKE theorem, whose proof is not independently reconstructed here. The main embedding Theorem 6.1.3 applies Theorem 5.1.4 directly and does not depend on the incomplete theory \(T\); no failure of the main embedding or Fontaine–Wintenberger conclusions is established.
# Problem 2: a derivative square is substituted for a norm
## Source claim

In the proof of Fact 2.4.7, page 18, implication \((iii)\Leftrightarrow(iv)\), the manuscript writes \[\operatorname{disc}(m_a)=m_a'(a)^2=\delta_{K'/K}(a)^2.
 \tag{4.1}\] The same formula appears at source line 715. Page 17 defines a signed discriminant: \[D(f)=(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}\prod_{i<j}(r_i-r_j)^2.\] This convention is respected here; the issue is not its sign.
## Complete exact check

Take the henselian field \(K=\mathbb Q_7\), \(f(X)=X^3-2\), and \(a\) a root, with \(K'=K(a)\). The cubes modulo \(7\) are \(0,1,6\), so \(f\) has no residue root and is irreducible modulo \(7\). It is therefore irreducible over \(\mathbb Q_7\). Characteristic zero gives separability, and \(a\) is integral and a unit. Thus all assumptions needed for the displayed identity hold, with extension degree three.

The derivative is \(f'(a)=3a^2\), and \[f'(a)^2=9a^4=18a.
 \tag{4.2}\] Multiplication by \(3a^2\), in the basis \(1,a,a^2\), has matrix \[\begin{pmatrix}0&6&0\\0&0&6\\3&0&0\end{pmatrix},\] whose determinant is \(108\). Accordingly \[D(f)=\operatorname{N}_{K'/K}(f'(a))=108\neq18a=f'(a)^2.
 \tag{4.3}\] The inequality follows also because \(a\notin\mathbb Q_7\). The ordinary unsigned-convention discriminant is \(-108\). An independent exact symbolic check reproduced the determinant, resultant, and polynomial remainders; no author code was run.
## Correct criterion and impact

The valid identity under the manuscript’s convention is \[D(m_a)=\operatorname{N}_{K'/K}(m_a'(a)).
 \tag{4.4}\] Because the valuation is henselian, all conjugates of \(m_a'(a)\) have the same extended valuation. For \(n=[K':K]\), \[v(D(m_a))=n\,v'(m_a'(a)).
 \tag{4.5}\] The derivative is integral, so this gives exactly \[D(m_a)\in\mathcal O_K^\times
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 m_a'(a)\in\mathcal O_{K'}^\times.\] In the explicit example, both quantities are units; the example disproves the algebraic equality, not the unramifiedness criterion. The subsequent uses inspected require that criterion or valuation bounds for discriminants, not the false square identity. Replacing (4.1) by (4.4)–(4.5) restores the local equivalence: Minor, with no demonstrated main-theorem failure.
# Problem 3: the distinguishing element in Example 5.3.2 fails for \(p=2\)
## Location and exact calculation

Example 5.3.2, page 36, source lines 1533–1534, compares \[K=\widehat{\mathbb Q_p(p^{1/p^\infty})},
 \qquad
 K'=\widehat{\mathbb Q_p(\zeta_{p^\infty})},\] and distinguishes them by the asserted absence of \(p^{1/p}\) from \(K'\). No odd-prime restriction is imposed there.

For \(p=2\), let \(\zeta=\zeta_8\). This element belongs already to the indicated cyclotomic union, before completion. Since \(\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2}=0\), \[(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})^2=2.
 \tag{5.1}\] Thus \(K'\) contains a square root of \(2\). Both fields satisfy \(\exists x\;(x^2=2)\), so this proposed distinguishing sentence does not distinguish them. The exact remainder of \((z-z^3)^2-2\) modulo \(z^4+1\) is zero.
## Alternative readings and a supported restriction

The earlier assumption \(p\neq2\) in the separate example of Section 1.6.1 does not govern Example 5.3.2; it is also explicitly restated for the other relevant example in Section 7. No claim is made here that these two fields are elementarily equivalent when \(p=2\), or that no different distinguishing sentence exists.

The displayed argument is valid after restricting this example to odd primes. Indeed \(X^p-p\) is Eisenstein. If \(\mathbb Q_p(p^{1/p})/\mathbb Q_p\), of degree \(p\), were Galois, it would contain \(\zeta_p\), forcing \(p-1\) to divide \(p\), impossible for odd \(p\). Each finite subextension of the cyclotomic \(p\)-power union is abelian and hence Galois. Further, completion does not add algebraic elements over \(\mathbb Q_p\) to that union: if an algebraic \(\alpha\) lay in its completion, approximation by an element of one finite cyclotomic field and Krasner’s lemma would place \(\alpha\) in such a finite field. Consequently \(p^{1/p}\) is absent for odd \(p\), as required.

This is a boundary defect in an illustrative argument: Minor. Restricting that argument to odd \(p\) preserves the claimed existence of non-elementarily-equivalent untilts with isomorphic tilts. A replacement witness for \(p=2\) was not constructed and is not asserted.

Thus \(x^\natural\) is a \(w\)-unit. Addition modulo \(p\) on integral elements gives addition in the residue field. General elements reduce to this case after multiplication by a common integral denominator, whose image remains a \(w\)-unit.

3. In Theorem 6.1.3, the nonstandard iterated Frobenius on \(\mathcal O_{v_U}/(\varpi)\) is surjective with kernel generated by \(\pi=\operatorname{ulim}\varpi^{1/p^i}\). Its induced isomorphism, together with the elementary diagonal map, proves the claimed elementarity of the truncated-ring map. The containment \(\mathfrak m_w\subseteq\pi\mathcal O_{v_U}\) justifies the next quotient. The final application of Theorem 5.1.4 uses the stated regular-density and class-\(\mathcal C\) hypotheses, independently of Problem 1.

4. In Lemma 6.2.1, the discriminant congruence and the strict inequality \(v(\operatorname{disc}f)<v\varpi\) imply \(v(\operatorname{disc}g)=p^{-1}v(\operatorname{disc}f)\). The Hensel–Rychlik step produces a root of \(f\) in \(K(\beta)\). Then \([K(\beta):K]\leq\deg g=\deg f\), while containment of a root of irreducible \(f\) gives the reverse bound. This supplies the degree argument implicit in the conclusion. Integral-generator normalization is needed when passing to general monic polynomials in the subsequent discussion.

6. In Lemma 7.2.19, the choice \(p\,w\varepsilon<w\varpi<2p\,w\varepsilon\) gives both required ideal containments. Two successive lifts yield \(x=y_1^p+\varepsilon^p y_2^p+\varepsilon^{2p}x_2\). Reduction modulo \(\varpi\) removes the final term and the mixed binomial terms, since \(p\in\varpi\mathcal O_v\).
p^(1/p) is absent from completed Qp(zeta_p-infinity), with no odd-prime restriction.
analysis:
Example 5.3.2, page 36, source lines 1533–1534, compares \[K=\widehat{\mathbb Q_p(p^{1/p^\infty})},
 \qquad
 K'=\widehat{\mathbb Q_p(\zeta_{p^\infty})},\] and distinguishes them by the asserted absence of \(p^{1/p}\) from \(K'\). No odd-prime restriction is imposed there.

For \(p=2\), let \(\zeta=\zeta_8\). This element belongs already to the indicated cyclotomic union, before completion. Since \(\zeta^2+\zeta^{-2}=0\), \[(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})^2=2.
 \tag{5.1}\] Thus \(K'\) contains a square root of \(2\). Both fields satisfy \(\exists x\;(x^2=2)\), so this proposed distinguishing sentence does not distinguish them. The exact remainder of \((z-z^3)^2-2\) modulo \(z^4+1\) is zero.
result: The earlier assumption \(p\neq2\) in the separate example of Section 1.6.1 does not govern Example 5.3.2; it is also explicitly restated for the other relevant example in Section 7. No claim is made here that these two fields are elementarily equivalent when \(p=2\), or that no different distinguishing sentence exists.

The displayed argument is valid after restricting this example to odd primes. Indeed \(X^p-p\) is Eisenstein. If \(\mathbb Q_p(p^{1/p})/\mathbb Q_p\), of degree \(p\), were Galois, it would contain \(\zeta_p\), forcing \(p-1\) to divide \(p\), impossible for odd \(p\). Each finite subextension of the cyclotomic \(p\)-power union is abelian and hence Galois. Further, completion does not add algebraic elements over \(\mathbb Q_p\) to that union: if an algebraic \(\alpha\) lay in its completion, approximation by an element of one finite cyclotomic field and Krasner’s lemma would place \(\alpha\) in such a finite field. Consequently \(p^{1/p}\) is absent for odd \(p\), as required.

This is a boundary defect in an illustrative argument: Minor. Restricting that argument to odd \(p\) preserves the claimed existence of non-elementarily-equivalent untilts with isomorphic tilts. A replacement witness for \(p=2\) was not constructed and is not asserted.
Impact: One witness and prime boundary of an illustration fail; existence of different untilts remains supported for odd primes.

Title: Initial scientific review of
Dens, nests and the Loehr–Warrington conjecture
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is by J. Blasiak, M. Haiman, J. Morse, A. Pun, and G. H. Seelinger, assigned ID M25-0030 and DOI 10.1090/jams/1057 (https://doi.org/10.1090/jams/1057). The actual input is arXiv:2112.07070v2, whose header is dated 15 December 2021; its internal first-page date is 16 December 2021. All page references below are the manuscript’s printed pages 1–57, equal to the one-based PDF page indices. The 2025 journal record establishes identity, not textual equivalence.

All 57 pages were read as extracted text. Thirty-one selected pages were also inspected as actual rendered images; the exact list is in Appendix A. The relevant source ranges and all eight manifest input hashes were checked. The review gives particular attention to Definitions 3.1.1 and 3.4.4, Lemma 3.2.1, Theorems 3.5.1, 5.5.4, 6.1.3 and 7.1.1, and the proof in Section 7.2. Reading all text does not mean every assertion and every cited external proof has been independently established.
# Definitions, assumptions, and checked correspondence

A den has a positive integer \(h\), an irrational real slope \(p\), and integer sequences \(d,e\) indexed by \(0,\ldots,h\). The endpoint inequalities, balance \(\sum d_i=\sum e_i\), and the two strict slope inequalities (21)–(23) are essential. The general den theorem does not assume \(p>0\). The positive coprime parameters \(m,n\) belong to the Loehr–Warrington specialization, not to every den. The path counts are \[g_k=\sum_{i<k}(d_i-e_i),\qquad 1\leq k\leq h.\] Sources are ordered from left to right and then bottom to top, and sinks from right to left and then bottom to top. Paths use south and east steps, end with an east step, and obey head bounds at non-sink vertices. Nested paths may share south steps; replacing nesting by vertex-disjointness would change the theorem.

Combining (21) and (22) gives \(d_j-e_j\leq d_i-e_i+1\) for \(0<i<j<h\). Thus a negative interior difference cannot precede a positive one. Together with the endpoint conditions this places sources before sinks and gives the required positive, unimodal \(g\). In Lemma 3.2.1 (pp. 12–13), if \(y_{k,i}\) are increasing east-step heights, \[(\lambda_{(k)})_i=e_k-g_k+i-y_{k,i}.\] The head bounds, strict nesting, and starting/ending intervals make these partitions of length at most \(\min(g_k,g_{k+1})\). The converse recovers the paths: inequality (30) is precisely the compatibility of the two successive east-step lists. The area is \(|\lambda|\). Empty intervals and paths that end at the current column must be retained when checking this correspondence.

The vertical-run construction in Section 3.4 gives skew rows and adjusted contents, including the strict inequality in the positive-label condition between adjacent paths. Its attack condition is \(0<\widetilde c(b)-\widetilde c(a)<1\). The choice of the reference line changes the presentation but not the resulting LLT expression. Empty rows matter later: the triples in Section 5.5 depend on the row presentation and its boundaries, not just the set of occupied boxes.
# Checks of the proof chain
## Polynomial part and LLT series

For Theorem 5.5.4 (pp. 39–41), the dominant regular weights and coordinatewise condition \(\alpha\leq\beta\) cannot be omitted. In Lemma 5.5.5 a nonidentity permutation of a strictly dominant \(\alpha\) has an ascent. Subtracting it from strictly dominant \(\beta\) then forces an adjacent difference at least two, incompatible with a vector of zeros and ones. The vertical-strip chain that remains gives the negative tableaux used in the proof. The inversion increments are between blocks and correspond to the specified triples, with the endpoint conventions for empty rows. This supports the polynomial-part formula used in Section 7.2; it is not a test of arbitrary weights outside its hypotheses.
## Cauchy identity and specialization

Theorem 6.1.3 requires the same block maxima, the prescribed almost-monotone block minima, and compatible artificial extrema for zero-length blocks. These conditions were tracked through Lemmas 6.1.5–6.1.16 (pp. 42–48). In the specialization proof, if the omitted coordinate is strictly above its minimal bound, the partition has full block length and vanishes on setting the variable to zero. At the bound, deleting the coordinate preserves the relevant permutation sign. This verifies the two cases in (166), including the reason that zero-length blocks are allowed.

For equal compositions, the dual-basis coefficient in (168) reduces to the reproducing identity (169). Taking the block constant term in the first alphabet uses ordinary Cauchy reproduction; after substitution, the remaining factors with that block cancel. Iterating gives the stated result. For unequal compositions, the common enlargement \(r'_i=M_i-N+1\), with \(N\) below all minima, has no empty block. Specialization then uses the preceding lemma. These operations are coefficientwise in \(t\), where only finitely many partitions contribute at each degree.
## Winding permutations and the final matching

The operative signs in (179)–(181) agree with the Hecke normalization (77), and with the two possibilities for the difference of winding descent indicators. Intermediate comparison-word typos do not alter the correctly displayed operator identities or their applicable signs. They are not recorded as independent scientific findings.

In Theorem 7.1.1, the choices \(r=(0,\gamma_h,\ldots,\gamma_1)\) and \(s=(\gamma_h,\ldots,\gamma_1,0)\) meet the Cauchy hypotheses: the symbol \(\infty\) in (193) means a sufficiently large finite artificial minimum. The balance \(\gamma_{i+1}-\gamma_i=u_i-v_{i+1}\) matches the block maxima. The winding identity then supplies (199).

For the final application (pp. 55–56), write \[f_i=\lfloor s-pi\rfloor,\quad
 u_i=f_i-e_i,\quad v_i=f_{i-1}-d_{i-1},\quad
 b_i=f_{i-1}-f_i.\] The almost-monotonicity inequalities (187) reduce exactly to the two den slope inequalities. Taking \(\gamma=g\) gives \(u_i-v_i+b_i=d_{i-1}-e_i\), the required Catalanimal weight. The condition \(\alpha\leq\beta\) in (203)–(204) becomes (30); the surviving terms therefore are exactly the nests. The row identifications in (205) match the previously defined \(\nu(\pi)\), while \(|\lambda|=a(\pi)\). Finally, the line-crossing condition \[0<c(b)-c(a)+c_i-c_j<1\] has precisely the two integer-content cases distinguished by \(c_i<c_j\) and \(c_i>c_j\). These are the triples counted in the LLT formula, so their number is \(\operatorname{dinv}_p(\pi)\). This checks the stated final statistic matching, including non-sink points on zero-length vertical runs.

The appearance of \(q^{-1}\) in the LLT argument alone would not prove nonnegative exponents. Here the formula first gives nonnegative \(t\) exponents; the \(q,t\) symmetry of this Catalanimal and the nonnegative combinatorial coefficients rule out negative \(q\) exponents. No contradictory boundary case was established in these checks.
# Independent exact finite checks

A reviewer-written Python program, saved with this report, enumerates south/east words directly. It does not use the partition parametrization to generate nests and does not import or execute author code. It imposes the source/sink order, last-east-step rule, head bounds, nesting inequalities, and positive-label conditions. Separate semistandard-tableau enumeration evaluates the Schur side.

There are also 75 exact checks of the Hecke quadratic/inverse identities on Laurent monomials of exponents \(-2,\ldots,2\), and 18 checks of \(T y T=q x\) and \(T^{-1}xT^{-1}=q^{-1}y\) on exponents \(-1,0,1\). All passed, with process exit code zero. These finite checks support the normalization and inspected examples; they are not a proof for arbitrary rank.
# Dependencies, historical correction, and limits

The import from the companion paper [companion], Theorem 8.3.1 and Remarks 8.3.2–8.3.3, was checked at statement level. For a single shape there is no cross-component attack factor. The stretching rules for the magic number and diagonal statistic give the sign and \((qt)\) normalization used here in Theorem 2.4.2. The companion theorem’s full proof and its shuffle-algebra foundations were not independently rederived.

=2em Section 4.3 of the reviewed manuscript explicitly credits a correction to the older Loehr–Warrington definition. The middle indicator in equation (11) of the inspected original preprint [LW] is \(\chi(a\leq b)\); the reviewed paper specifies the ordered tie condition \(\chi(a<b\text{ or }(a=b\text{ and }u<v))\). This is a historical correction already identified by the authors, not a new defect of this manuscript. The present review checked its location and attribution, not every case of the original paper independently.

The arXiv version record still lists v2, and a later author-hosted manuscript was located; no line-by-line comparison with that file or with the journal version was performed. The limited correction search did not identify an explicit new erratum. It cannot establish the absence of an erratum or novelty of an observation. No essential separate supplement or computational repository was identified as missing for the inspected claims. Higher-rank exhaustive calculations and complete independent reconstruction of the imported symmetric-function results remain outside this review.
# Conclusion

Scientific outcome | No Issue Found in the recorded claim-focused scope; no whole-paper correctness certification.
Repair | No new substantive correction proposed. Historical correction retains its original attribution.
Finite checks | All listed exact checks passed; generality is limited to the stated cases and the accompanying analytic reasoning.
Acceptance/adoption | Independent scientific acceptance pending; author adoption has not been requested.
Delivery | TeX, compiled PDF and structured evidence saved. Exact-input build and every report page inspection recorded.

Title: Selected rigidity arguments: initial verification
# Identity, version, and scope

The assigned paper is M25-0031, Local rigidity of weak or no hyperbolicity algebraic actions, DOI 10.1090/jams/1058. The inspected original is the 98-page author manuscript arXiv:1908.10496v3, posted 19 March 2025. All page references below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with printed pages on the inspected pages. The PDF SHA-256 is
`a0aa39b077cac09ead24f9ccc58176d820fef346820361865b42cb3e2ad58ebf`.
No correspondence with the journal final text has been established.

The review traces Corollary 1.7 through Section 11.4, Theorem 9.2, and Section 3.1(11); checks the algebraic hypothesis used in Section 11.1; and recomputes the commuting-perturbation identity in Lemma 5.1 and the affine regularity recurrence in Appendix A. Definitions and statements on pp. 3, 6–7, 21–22, 27–29, 63–64, and 86–87 were read, with surrounding introductory text. This is a claim-focused, partial initial review. It does not certify Sections 6–10, Appendix C, or the paper as a whole.

The ambient assumptions include a compact quotient by a torsion-free cocompact irreducible lattice, the stated semisimple group hypotheses, and smooth continuous actions. Strong local rigidity permits a group automorphism of the acting group (p. 3). Geometric stability is the quantitative condition (5.4), not merely an informal stability assertion (pp. 28–29).
# Problem 1: the scope of Corollary 1.7
## Source claim and dependency

Corollary 1.7 (p. 7) is phrased for an \(\mathbb R^m\) action of upper triangular unipotents in \[G=SL(2,\mathbb R)\times SL(2,k_1)\times\cdots\times SL(2,k_n),
\qquad m\leq 1+n .\] Section 11.4 (p. 86; released `main.tex`, lines 4997–4998) obtains a splitting directly from Theorem 9.2. However, the latter uses the generating set \(E\) fixed in Section 3.1(11), p. 22: in the product case it contains \(u=E_{12}\) in the first factor and a nonzero nilpotent \(v\) from another factor. Section 9.2 (p. 64) expressly retains this choice. The definition of a friendly pair also excludes zero vectors (p. 22).
## Complete boundary check

Take \(n=1\), \(k_1=\mathbb R\), \(m=1\), and fix any quotient satisfying the ambient lattice assumptions. Define \[A=\{(I+tE_{12},I):t\in\mathbb R\}.\] Because \(E_{12}^2=0\), multiplication adds parameters, inversion negates them, and the parameter is recovered from the \((1,2)\) entry. Thus \(A\) is a closed abelian subgroup isomorphic to \(\mathbb R\), consisting of upper triangular unipotents. It obeys \(m=1\leq2\). Its Lie algebra is \[\mathop{\mathrm{Lie}}(A)=\mathbb R(E_{12},0),\qquad
\mathop{\mathrm{Lie}}(A)\cap(0\oplus\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb R))=\{0\}.\] Consequently no generating set for this action contains the required nonzero second-factor vector. A change of the one-dimensional acting-group coordinate does not change that intersection. The direct application of Theorem 9.2 therefore does not cover this boundary case.

This calculation is a counterexample to the implication from the displayed corollary hypotheses to the hypotheses of the cited splitting theorem. It is not a counterexample to transversal local rigidity itself. In particular, no nonconjugate deformation or failure of every possible transversal family has been proved here.
## Counterevidence, impact, and disposition

The sentence immediately before Corollary 1.7 describes removing the geometric-stability assumption from Theorem 1.1. This strongly suggests that the nonzero cross-factor condition was intended to remain in force. Such an interpretation excludes the example and is material counterevidence against declaring the intended result false. Conversely, the displayed corollary does not explicitly retain that condition, and the one-sentence reduction does not supply an alternative splitting for all its written cases.

The judgment is Needs Evidence: resolve the intended action class and demonstrate the splitting hypotheses for that class. The affected dependency is the stated range of Corollary 1.7. No defect in Theorems 1.1 or 1.2 has been established. No complete repair, author adoption, or human acceptance is claimed.
# Checks with no issue found within their scope
## Commuting perturbations

For commuting generators \(E_i\) and perturbations \(E_i+p_i\) that still commute, \[[E_i,p_j]-[E_j,p_i]=-[p_i,p_j].\] This follows by expanding \([E_i+p_i,E_j+p_j]=0\). For each nonnegative integer \(t\), the usual product estimate obtained by Leibniz expansion and interpolation gives \[\|[p_i,p_j]\|_{C^t}\leq C_t\|p\|_{C^0}\|p\|_{C^{t+1}}.\] The interpolation step matters: the coarser displayed bound (5.2) alone is not the sharp tame estimate. In the invariant frame, integration of derivative terms against Haar measure vanishes. Averaging the linearized expression thus gives the second bound in Lemma 5.1 at \(t=0\). This verifies the local commuting-error calculation on p. 28; it does not verify the later nonlinear iteration.
## The Jordan-block regularity recurrence

Condition on the scalar estimate in Theorem A.2 (p. 87). Put \(F(t)=s_2t+s_1\). Solving the triangular system from the last coordinate upward composes \(F\) once per coordinate, so after \(j\) coordinates, \[F^{\circ j}(t)=s_2^jt+s_1\sum_{r=0}^{j-1}s_2^r .\] The base case is immediate; composing this expression with \(F\) proves the next case. This matches the recurrence (A.2) and the displayed component estimate. The independent SymPy calculation checked \(j=1,\ldots,8\) with exact zero residuals; the induction, rather than that finite calculation, establishes the formula for arbitrary finite \(j\). Theorem A.2 and its external analytic dependencies were not independently reproved. The additional last-line assertion bounding \(\lambda\) by \(\dim\mathfrak g\) was not established by this check.
## The explicit rectangular subgroup

In \(SL(6,\mathbb R)\), the nine matrices \(E_{ij}\) with \(i\in\{1,3,5\}\) and \(j\in\{2,4,6\}\) commute: both Kronecker symbols in \[[E_{ij},E_{kl}]=\delta_{jk}E_{il}-\delta_{li}E_{kj}\] vanish. They contain \(E_{12},E_{34},E_{56}\), whose three disjoint root pairs give commuting \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) triples. Their pairwise root differences are not roots. This checks the root-space part of the reduction in Section 11.1, conditional on the geometric-stability result.

A scope clarification is retained separately: maximal abelian in Remark 1.5 and Corollaries 1.3–1.4 must be read consistently with the specific large-dimensional rectangular subgroup used in (3.1). Maximality by inclusion alone does not identify that subgroup. The proof’s explicit normal form is counterevidence against treating this terminology alone as a new substantive defect.
# Conclusion and remaining work
Item | Judgment | Repair/adoption
Corollary 1.7 range | Needs Evidence | No verified repair; adoption not requested
Lemma 5.1 local identity | No Issue Found | No repair proposed
Appendix A recurrence | No Issue Found, conditional | Scalar estimate not reverified
Rectangular-root reduction | Scope clarification | Geometric stability not reverified

The principal outstanding scientific work is the full verification of directional smoothing, global splitting, KAM convergence, the geometric-stability proof, and external cited results. The arXiv record inspected on 25 October 2026 lists v3 as its latest revision. A bounded title/identifier search and the author’s publication page did not identify a separate erratum; this is not a proof that none exists. No later-version or journal-final comparison was performed. No experiments are needed for the displayed algebraic checks.

The symbolic package was SymPy 1.13.3. No author code was run.

Title: Negligible classes and non-liftable representations: initial verification
# Identity and scope

M25-0032 is Alexander Merkurjev and Federico Scavia, Galois representations modulo \(p\) that do not lift modulo \(p^2\), DOI 10.1090/jams/1059. The reviewed item is the author manuscript arXiv:2410.12560v1, 16 October 2024, 21 pages. Its PDF SHA-256 is

Every page was read as extracted text and actually viewed as a rendered original page. Page references are one-based PDF pages, equal to the printed numbering. Relevant released `main.tex` passages were inspected statically. This author version was not compared with the journal final version.

The internal review covers definitions and quantifiers in Section 2, the construction and sign of \(\gamma\) in Section 3, the divisor argument in Section 4, and the reduction and matrix/weight arguments in Section 5. This is an initial mathematical audit, not a machine-checked formalization. The generic-extension theorem quoted as Proposition 2.1, the cited cohomological machinery, and the Chu–Kang rationality theorem remain external dependencies. Bibliography inspection does not certify every cited result.
# Problem 1: the unrestricted statement of Lemma 4.1
## Claim and exact failure

On pp. 12–13, Lemma 4.1 asserts for an arbitrary field \(F\) and finite \(H\)-module \(B\) that \((B\otimes F(V)^\times)^H\) is generated by the constant invariants and all \[N_{H/H_x}(b\otimes f_x),\qquad b\in B^{H_x},\quad \operatorname{div}(f_x)=x .\] The statement is in released `main.tex`, line 561; its proof is lines 565–573. A listed element need not be invariant.

Take \(F=\mathbb R\), \(H=C_2=\{1,s\}\), \(V=\mathbb A^1_\mathbb R\) with coordinate \(t\) and faithful sign action \(s(t)=-t\), and \(B=\mathbb Z/2\) with trivial action. All groups and modules have the finiteness required in the lemma. Let \(x\) be the codimension-one origin. Then \(H_x=H\), \(f_x=t\), and \(\operatorname{div}(t)=x\) on this affine line. With \(b=1\), the prescribed norm is just the identity, so the proposed generator is the class \([t]\) in \[B\otimes \mathbb R(t)^\times=\mathbb R(t)^\times/\mathbb R(t)^{\times2}.\] But \(s[t]-[t]=[-1]\ne0\). Indeed, if a real rational function squared were \(-1\), evaluation at any real point avoiding its finitely many poles would give a negative real square. Thus the purported generator is not in the group it is claimed to generate. Multiplying \(f_x\) by a real nonzero constant does not change this obstruction.

The proof correctly describes the invariants of the permutation divisor module. It does not, in this generality, show that those invariant divisor generators lift to invariant elements of \(B\otimes F(V)^\times\). Taking invariants is only left exact.
## Counterevidence and verified restricted correction

This does not invalidate the actual use with \(B=A(-1)\) in Theorem 1.3. Write \(n=e(A)\) and \(e=e(H)\). Its hypotheses include \(\mu_{ne}\subset F\). For \(h\in H_x\), the character calculation on pp. 13–14 gives \[h(f_x)/f_x=\chi_x(h)\in\mu_e\subset F^{\times n}.\] If \(nB=0\), then \(b\otimes\chi_x(h)=0\), so \(b\otimes f_x\) is \(H_x\)-invariant. Its coset norm is consequently a well-defined \(H\)-invariant lift of the stated divisor norm. Decomposing an invariant divisor into its finite set of orbits, subtracting these invariant lifts, and using exactness of the tensorized divisor sequence leaves precisely a constant invariant. This proves the generation assertion under these additional hypotheses, including its needed application.

The disposition is Minor, local overstatement. The counterexample refutes the independent general lemma; the main theorem already supplies the condition needed by the verified restricted argument. The classification is based on this dependency check, not on how easy correction might be. No author adoption or journal-version defect is asserted.
# Problem 2: restriction in Lemma 5.3

On p. 15, `main.tex` line 697, the alternative proof says that every element of the preimage \(E\) preserves \(\widetilde V\) and therefore defines a restriction map to \(\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}(\widetilde V)\). For \(p=3\) and rank-one summands, \[g=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}\in\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}_2(\mathbb Z/9)\] reduces to the identity, so belongs to \(E\). But \(g(1,0)=(1,3)\) does not belong to the first summand. Literal restriction is therefore not the asserted endomorphism.

The required map nevertheless exists as the upper-left block, with projection back onto \(\widetilde V\) understood. In general write \[g=\begin{pmatrix}A&pB\\pC&I+pD\end{pmatrix}\in E.\] Since \(\bar A\) is invertible, \(A\) is invertible over \(\mathbb Z/p^2\). For two such matrices, the upper-left block of their product is \(AA'+p^2BC'=AA'\). Therefore \(\pi(g)=A\) is a group homomorphism, reduces to the required identity on \(\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}(V)\), and restricts on the kernel to the linear projection \(\mathfrak{gl}(V\oplus W)\to\mathfrak{gl}(V)\). The extension diagram commutes. Pullback followed by this pushforward proves Lemma 5.3, and the same map applies to a particular lifted representation, proving the pointwise use on p. 20.

The judgment is Minor, incorrect map description; the needed block-map argument has been checked for arbitrary finite ranks, not only for the displayed example. The paper also cites an external proof, which was not relied upon here. An author-hosted October 2017 version of that reference has different numbering, so the cited Lemma 3.4 was not certified by that lookup.
# Problem 3: locally incorrect formulas
## Inflation target

Equation (2.3), p. 6, released `main.tex` lines 305–306, has target \(H^2(L,A)\) and is called a short exact sequence. The inflation target in the displayed Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre sequence must instead be \(H^2(K,A)\), and the displayed three terms are an exact segment, without asserted injectivity or surjectivity at the ends.

For a direct check, take \(L=\mathbb C\), \(K=\mathbb R\), \(H=C_2\) and trivial \(A=\mathbb Z/2\). Then \(H^1(L,A)=H^2(L,A)=0\) but \(H^2(C_2,A)=\mathbb Z/2\). The printed sequence is \(0\to\mathbb Z/2\to0\) and is not exact at its middle term. With target \(H^2(\mathbb R,A)\), inflation is the identity under \(\Gamma_\mathbb R=C_2\), restoring exactness. The preceding spectral sequence already has abutment \(H^{i+j}(K,A)\), and Proposition 2.1 has the fixed-field target. These are strong internal counterevidence against a deeper error in Corollary 2.4. The consequence is a Minor formula/terminology correction.
## Character and cross-reference

The first lines of p. 19 identify \(H^2(Z,\mathbb Z)\) with the character \(\tau_{13}\); the action convention on p. 18 instead gives \(\tau_{31}\). For \(t=\operatorname{diag}(t_1,t_2,t_3)\), \[(t\chi_{13})(I+cE_{13})=\chi_{13}(t^{-1}(I+cE_{13})t)
=(t_3/t_1)c .\] This is \(\tau_{31}\), which differs from \(\tau_{13}\), for example at \(p=5\) and \(t=\operatorname{diag}(2,1,1)\). With the inverse character, the ensuing invariant subspace and vanishing calculation on p. 19 are correct. At \(p=3\) the two characters coincide; the paper separately excludes the extra \(E_{31}\) vector because it is not in \(A^Z\). This is a local label error, not failure of the invariant-subspace conclusion. Similarly, the application of Lemma 3.4 on p. 11 should refer to (3.3), whose terms are trivial \(H\)-modules, rather than (3.2). Both observations are retained within this Minor formula item rather than counted as independent core failures.
# Positive checks, boundaries, and dependency chain

Negligibility quantifies over every extension \(K/F\) and every continuous map \(\Gamma_K\to H\). Kummer lifting in Example 2.2 works over every such \(K\), since the roots of unity remain present and \(K^\times/K^{\times mn}\to K^\times/K^{\times m}\) is surjective. Its alternating use of \(F\) and \(K\) in the prose does not defeat that argument.

The construction of \(\beta_f\) uses \(\mu_e\subset L^{\times n}\), so changing \(f\) by \(\mu_e\) changes its tensor by zero. The transgression sign in Proposition 3.1 agrees with minus the extension factor-set convention. Lemma 3.4 uses trivial coefficient actions; applying it to (3.3) supplies the required input. Constants are killed by \(\gamma\) after base change to an algebraic closure, because a finite module tensored with its divisible multiplicative group is zero and the right-hand \(H^2(H,A)\) map remains the identity. These checks support the two inclusions in Theorem 1.3 subject to Proposition 2.1 and the standard functoriality of cohomology.

For Lemma 5.2, conjugation by \((I+N)^i=I+iN\), with \(N^2=0\), is quadratic in \(i\). For \(p>3\), all sums of powers of degrees \(0,1,2\) vanish in \(\mathbb F_p\), so the norm is zero and the order-\(p\) lift is impossible. The hypothesis \(p>3\) is essential for this argument. For \(p=3\), the independent symbolic calculation reproduces \[N_{\sigma_{12}}(a)=a_{21}E_{12},\qquad
\bigl(-(\sigma_{13}-1)a+(\sigma_{12}-1)b\bigr)_{23}=a_{21}.\] The order condition forces \(a_{21}=-1\) and commutation forces \(a_{21}=0\). The calculation uses arbitrary symbolic entries, not a sample of lifts.

The centralizers \(A^U=\langle I,E_{13}\rangle\) and \(A^N=\langle I,E_{12},E_{13}\rangle\) follow by commuting with the indicated elementary matrices. Exactness of \(T\)-invariants uses \(p\nmid(p-1)^3\). The character products for the \(U\) term have no trivial constituent for odd \(p\). The \(N\) term has the two stated invariant generators. For the first, the norm of \(E_{12}\) is \(\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}(E_{12}-jE_{13})=0\); projection gives zero. For the second, the norm of \(\chi_{13}\) vanishes since \(p\) and \(p(p-1)/2\) are zero modulo \(p\). Finally, \(A^Z\) is upper triangular, so with the corrected dual character its only relevant invariant is \(E_{13}\otimes\partial\chi_{13}\); restriction followed by corestriction multiplies it by \(p\) and kills it. The script’s character checks for \(p=3,5,7\) supplement these general calculations.

Theorem 5.1 may enlarge \(F\) to adjoin \(\mu_{p^2}\): non-negligibility over that larger base implies non-negligibility over the smaller one. This is the correct direction of Lemma 2.3(5). Theorem 1.4 only assumes \(\mu_p\subset F\); the stronger root assumption is used after this enlargement for the obstruction, not imposed on the final rational function field. For odd \(p\), \(U_3(\mathbb F_p)\) has exponent \(p\). Its faithful \(p\)-dimensional representation is obtained from the cyclic shift and diagonal matrices on a basis indexed by \(\mathbb F_p\), with primitive \(\zeta_p\) diagonal entries; their commutator is a nontrivial scalar. Identification of the invariant field as purely transcendental still depends on Chu–Kang. The publisher result was identified, but direct page retrieval returned HTTP 403, so its exact Theorem 1.6 and proof remain unverified here.

report: Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Initial scientific review: M25-0033
# Identity, version, and decision

Paper: Tongmu He, Perfectoidness via Sen theory and applications to Shimura varieties, DOI 10.1090/jams/1060. The reviewed object is the 59-page author manuscript arXiv:2407.14488v2 (arXiv submission 23 July 2025; internal manuscript date 24 July), with supplied source00000TOKEN. Its PDF SHA-256 is
Despite the source filename, no comparison with the published journal version has been performed. Every assessment below concerns this exact author manuscript.

Judgment: No Issue Found within the inspected scope. No demonstrated invalid derivation or counterexample was established in the checks below. This is a bounded initial review, not certification of all 59 pages or of the external foundations. In particular, the construction of the Faltings extensions, several ramification estimates, and the full comparison with geometric Sen operators remain outside the independent verification completed here.
# Actual coverage and dependency map

The text of PDF pages 1–6, 16–18, 39–44, 46–51, and 56–57 was read. Images of pages 1, 3–6, 16–18, 40–41, 43–44, 46–51, and 56–57 were inspected for the statements and formulas used below. Critical occurrences in the supplied TeX were checked, including lines 284, 362, 1159–1161, 2250–2252, 2640, 2976, and 3037. Extraction of the full PDF and hashing the supplied sources do not constitute a complete semantic review.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and boundaries

The relevant hypothesis in Theorem 8.9 is injectivity of the geometric Sen action at the specified geometric valuative point, not merely that the map is nonzero. For geometric dimension greater than one, a nonzero linear map can have a kernel. Corollary 9.13 requires its valuative-point hypothesis for every point in the stated range, and separately for each generic component with the stipulated Galois extension. One favorable point cannot establish the global conclusion.

The distinction between a pre-perfectoid field and its completed perfectoid field is retained throughout this report. The inspected statements establish the stated valuation-theoretic conclusions; they are not, by themselves, a proof that a chosen global infinite-level space is a perfectoid space.

An apparent ground-field concern was rejected after checking the original image of page 4 and TeX line 362: Theorem 1.19 is formulated over \(\overline K\). The overline is lost in some plain-text extraction. A proposed arithmetic example over \(K\) instead of \(\overline K\) therefore does not satisfy the statement’s hypotheses and is not a counterexample. This is recorded as counterevidence, not as a paper defect.

The dimension-zero case is consistent with the inspected linear algebra: the geometric part has dimension zero while the arithmetic contribution still has to be nonzero. When the normal-crossings divisor is empty, the requirement to divide its local equations is vacuous. No vanishing at the boundary degree \(q=\dim Y\) is asserted.
# Supporting checks
## The Lie bracket in Section 8.2 (page 41)

Let \(E\) be the relevant vector space and let \(\lambda=\iota^*\) be the linear functional used in the construction. The proposed bracket is \[[x,y]=\lambda(x)y-\lambda(y)x .\] It is alternating and bilinear, and \(\lambda([x,y])=0\). Its iterated bracket is \[[[x,y],z]=-\lambda(z)\lambda(x)y+\lambda(z)\lambda(y)x .\] The cyclic sum cancels term by term, proving Jacobi. Thus \(\ker\lambda\) is an abelian ideal. If \(\lambda(e)=1\), then \([e,v]=v\) for \(v\in\ker\lambda\), giving the advertised semidirect-product description. This verifies the algebraic step conditional on the previously constructed extension and functional; it does not reconstruct that extension.
## Invariant dimension and the connecting homomorphism

In Lemma 4.22 (page 17) and Lemma 7.18 (page 40), the invariant sequence has the relevant shape \[0\longrightarrow \widehat F(1)\longrightarrow E^G
 \xrightarrow{j} V\xrightarrow{\delta} H^1(G,\widehat{\overline F}(1)),
 \qquad \dim_{\widehat F}V=d .\] The hypotheses fixing the necessary roots of unity and the identification of invariant scalars are essential. Under those hypotheses the left term has dimension one. Exactness gives \[\dim E^G=1+\dim\ker\delta\leq 1+d.\] Consequently maximal dimension is equivalent to surjectivity of \(j\), and to \(\delta=0\). This argument uses the connecting homomorphism and left exactness; it does not assume that taking invariants is right exact. The same computation remains valid for \(d=0\).
## The trace contradiction in Theorem 4.23 (pages 17–18)

The proof uses torsion-freeness of \(M=\Omega^1_{\mathcal O_F/\mathcal O_{\overline K}}\) and the previous normalized-trace results. Conditional on torsion-freeness, \(M\) embeds in its fraction-field differential space. If a transcendence-basis differential \(dt_i\) is infinitely \(p\)-divisible in \(M\), then for any \(a\in F\) the height-one valuation permits an integer \(n\) with \(p^n a\in\mathcal O_F\), and \[a\,dt_i=(p^na)\,(dt_i/p^n)\in M.\] If all basis differentials have this property, \(M\) equals the indicated \(F\)-linear differential space.

In the contrary case the Kummer cocycle \(\xi_t\) represents the connecting class. Vanishing of that class gives a coboundary \(x\). The kernel of the Kummer character and the invariant-field identification place \(x\) in the completed Kummer extension. The normalized trace \(T\) is an equivariant retraction to \(\widehat F\). Hence the nonzero value \((\tau-1)x=\xi_t(\tau)\) would lie both in \(\widehat F\) and in \(\ker T\), impossible since their intersection is zero. This checks the final contradiction using the precise retraction property. It is conditional on the established trace estimates and on the cited differential/pre-perfectoidness results. Remark 4.24 explicitly says that stronger estimates used for the homeomorphism in 4.19(3) are not required here; they were not treated as dependencies of this particular deduction.
## Theorem 8.9: geometric to full injectivity (pages 43–44)

The diagram in 8.8 has geometric and arithmetic exact rows. The cyclotomic hypothesis ensures that the arithmetic map is injective on its one-dimensional source. If \(x\) is in the kernel of the full action, its arithmetic image vanishes; injectivity of the arithmetic map forces \(x\) into the geometric subspace, where geometric injectivity forces \(x=0\). This is a direct diagram chase.

Dualizing an injective map of finite-dimensional vector spaces gives a surjection to the Faltings extension. Under the stated Galois and cyclotomic hypotheses the appropriate source basis is invariant. Its images are invariant and span the target. This proves the required invariant-dimension conclusion without incorrectly asserting that an arbitrary surjection remains surjective after applying invariants. The dimension count also requires the full target Lie algebra to have dimension at least \(d+1\) in this situation. The implication from the resulting zero connecting map to pre-perfectoidness and to boundary \(p\)-power roots uses 7.19 and 7.20. The last Kummer contradiction in 7.20 was followed; the entire earlier construction was not independently reproved.
## Corollary 9.9: from almost vanishing to actual vanishing

Here the ground field in 9.6 is explicitly an algebraically closed valuation field of height one (page 46). The cohomological comparison 9.7 and the pre-perfectoid calculation 9.8 are used conditionally. The subsequent dimension and coefficient arguments were checked.

For a proper, flat, finitely presented model, fiber dimension is locally constant; the valuation base is connected. The invoked Stacks Project lemmas 0D4J and 0E7D have the appropriate flatness, finite-presentation, properness, and quasi-coherent hypotheses. For \(q\) exceeding the fiber dimension the higher direct image vanishes, and the affine base has no further quasi-coherent cohomology. The passage along the directed system uses the cited continuity results.

There is no general principle that an almost zero module must be zero. The particular module here is \(V\otimes_{\mathbf F_p}\mathcal O_L/p\), where \(V\) is an \(\mathbf F_p\)-vector space. If \(V\ne0\), choose a basis vector; its span gives a direct summand isomorphic to \(\mathcal O_L/p\). This module is not almost zero: since \(L\) is algebraically closed, choose \(\pi\) with \(0<v(\pi)<v(p)\). Then \(\pi\in\mathfrak m_L\) but \(\pi\cdot1\ne0\) modulo \(p\). Thus the asserted almost vanishing forces \(V=0\).

The coefficient induction also preserves the degree bound. The short exact sequence with successive quotients \(\mathbf Z/p\) gives a long exact sequence; if both adjacent \(H^q\) groups vanish for \(\mathbf Z/p^{n-1}\) and \(\mathbf Z/p\), then \(H^q\) with \(\mathbf Z/p^n\) vanishes. The completed-cohomology definition in the introduction is an ordinary inverse limit of these already zero direct limits. No interchange of derived inverse limit and cohomology, or unproved \(\varprojlim^1\) vanishing, is needed for this final step.
## The Shimura application (pages 56–57)

Theorem 11.2 is an external input asserting locally split injectivity. Its proof was not independently verified. Conditional on it and the comparison in 10.4–10.5, the application gives the stated vanishing over \(\overline{\mathbf Q}_p\).

The transfer to \(\mathbf C\) uses invariance of torsion etale cohomology under extensions of separably closed fields (Stacks 0F0B). At finite level the varieties are quasi-projective and hence quasi-compact and quasi-separated; the torsion order is invertible in characteristic zero. One can compare both fields through an algebraic closure of the reflex field with compatible embeddings, and then pass to the specified filtered colimit. The fields need not be canonically embedded into one another. These are the hypotheses behind the short sentence in the proof; no violation of the cited base-change theorem was found.
# Findings and counterevidence

> d24a021751b5d26f1b80883ea62bacff1faa8

The manuscript explicitly offers alternative methods; that counterevidence is retained below.

All 35 pages were read as extracted text. Original images of pages 1, 3, 6–11, 14, 16–29, and 30–32 were inspected.
