# Claims, assumptions, and dependencies

The main finite-field analysis uses \(x^2+y^2+z^2=xyz\), while the introduction and arithmetic application use \(x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz\). For \(p\ne3\), multiplication of all coordinates by \(3\) gives the correspondence and conjugates the Vieta moves. Small-prime exclusions must be retained.

The main chain is: a connected cage and large-order endgame; a power-saving middle-game estimate used to increase rotation order; a cyclotomic argument preventing very small nonzero components; and the exceptional-prime and integer-sieving arguments. Proposition 14 and Corollary 15 are explicitly part of this chain (pages 18–25). The final sieve further depends on precise transitivity results of Meiri–Puder and an equidistribution input of Mirzakhani.

For \(\mathcal M^s\), multiplicities are part of the statement. The proof does not resolve the uniqueness conjecture or automatically establish an unweighted density statement. Theorem 19’s displayed meaning is that, for each fixed \(\nu\), the proportion with at most \(\nu\) distinct prime factors tends to zero. It does not assert the conventional extremal-divisor meaning of a highly composite number.
# Problem 1 (Major): invalid subgroup verification in Proposition 14
## Claim and location

Pages 20–21, equations (71)–(76), seek to verify the nonconcentration hypothesis of Theorem 13 for \[\Phi(t)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 t&-\sigma t^2-4(1-\sigma)\\1&-t
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma\ne1.\] The argument asserts that every proper subgroup of \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbf F_p)\) has trivial second derived group and reduces the verification to a double commutator. It also specifies a scalar normalization and a family \(g_t\). Three exact checks show that this verification cannot be accepted as written.
## Check A: the normalization does not give determinant one
## Check B: equation (72) has an incorrect entry
## Check C: proper subgroups need not be metabelian

In \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbf F_{97})\), take \[i=\begin{pmatrix}22&0\\0&75\end{pmatrix},\quad
 j=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\96&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 u=\begin{pmatrix}59&60\\59&37\end{pmatrix},\quad
 q=\begin{pmatrix}57&7\\90&40\end{pmatrix}.\] Every determinant is one. Exhaustive multiplication closure gives a subgroup \(H\) of order \(48\), whereas \(|\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbf F_{97})|=912576\), so \(H\) is proper. Closing all commutators gives \(|H'|=24\) and \(|H''|=8\). In particular, \(H''\) contains the nonscalar matrix \(i\). Its projective second derived group has order four, so the exception is not removed by discarding the center.

These examples belong to an algebraic family. For \(p\equiv1\pmod8\), choose \(a^2=-1\), \(b^2=2\), and set \[i=\operatorname{diag}(a,-a),\quad
 j=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 k=ij,\quad u=(-I+i+j+k)/2,\quad q=(i+j)/b.\] The quaternion relations, cyclic conjugation by \(u\), and the transposition up to signs induced by \(q\) give the binary octahedral group, with normal quaternion subgroup and quotient \(S_3\). Its successive derived groups are the binary tetrahedral and quaternion groups. The construction works for arbitrarily large such primes, so a large-prime qualification does not remove the issue. The accompanying program verifies the specified finite example and a binary tetrahedral example independently; no author code is executed.
## Counterevidence, dependency, and repair

The cited Bourgain preprint describes a bicommutator characterization of large proper subgroups (arXiv:1208.4008v1, Section 4). Separating bounded exceptional subgroups and showing that the actual polynomial image cannot lie in them is a plausible part of a repair. It is not a completed replacement for (71)–(76), especially after the corrected matrix computation.

Page 18 supplies two alternative routes: an auxiliary-polynomial argument and a Corvaja–Zannier estimate. Conditional on the quoted bound \[20\max\{(l_1l_2)^{1/3},\,l_1l_2/p\},\] summing over \(l_2\le l_1\) dividing \(p^2-1\), for \(p^\epsilon\le l_1\le p^{1/2+\delta_0}\) and fixed \(\delta_0<1/2\), gives \[p^{o(1)}O(l_1^{2/3}+l_1^2/p)=o(l_1).\] Thus this quoted estimate can provide the increasing-order mechanism if all its application hypotheses hold. Its original proof was not independently verified here. The principal theorem is not disproved by the present finding.

The Major classification concerns a demonstrated invalid derivation in a method explicitly developed for the central middle-game step, used in Corollary 15 and the main proof. It does not require all alternative arguments to fail or repair to be difficult. A complete repair is not verified.
# Problem 2 (Minor): Lemma 12 allows a reducible constant-map case
Location: pages 16–17, Lemma 12 and its fiber-product proof.

The assumptions require \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3\) not all zero and \(\alpha_3\pm2\sqrt{\alpha_1\alpha_2}\ne\pm2\), but allow \(\alpha_1=\alpha_2=0\). Choose \[p=13,\quad d=e=1,\quad \alpha_1=\alpha_2=0,\quad\alpha_3=1.\] The prime is odd, both positive exponents are less than \(p\), the coefficients are not all zero, and \(1\ne\pm2\). Every printed assumption holds. In the two-dimensional torus the equation becomes \[1=x+x^{-1},\qquad x^2-x+1=(x-4)(x-10).\] It is the union of two distinct nonempty vertical tori, reducible even over \(\mathbf F_{13}\). The proposed map \(g(y)\) is constant and is not the degree-\(2e\) cover invoked in the proof. The same degeneration occurs over the algebraic closure for any \(p>3\).

Counterevidence and impact. In the nondegenerate application (59), \(\alpha_1=1/4\) and \(\alpha_2=(B_2-B_1)^2/4\) are both nonzero. This counterexample does not refute that application. The supported issue is local overstatement. Requiring \(\alpha_1\alpha_2\ne0\) excludes this example and matches the branch-cycle proof’s setup, but the full corrected monodromy argument and the coincident-coordinate cases remain to be verified. No complete repaired theorem is certified here.
# Problem 3 (Minor): Corollary 21 includes inversion
Location: page 29, Corollary 21; its application to Corollary 22 is on page 30.

The printed assertion is \[|\sigma(U_t)\cap U_t|\ll t^{3/4},\qquad
t\mid p-1,\quad t\le p^{3/4},\quad
\sigma\in\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbf F_p),\quad \sigma\ne1.\] Take \(\sigma(x)=x^{-1}\), represented by \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). For odd \(p\) this is a nonidentity projective transformation with nonzero determinant and no pole on \(U_t\subset\mathbf F_p^\times\). Inversion permutes all \(t\) roots, so the left side equals \(t\). For arbitrarily large \(t\), Dirichlet’s theorem supplies primes \(p\equiv1\pmod t\) with \(p>t^{4/3}\). Both restrictions on \(t\) hold, while \(t/t^{3/4}=t^{1/4}\) is unbounded. Hence the uniform estimate is false.

Counterevidence. Proposition 20 assumes disjoint divisors for \(S\) and \(T\). The pair \(S(x)=x\), \(T(x)=x^{-1}\) violates that assumption, both supports being \(\{0,\infty\}\). Explicitly carrying that restriction into the corollary would exclude this example; its self-contained printed statement only excludes the identity. On page 30 the relevant map is \((b\eta-1)/(\eta-1)\), whose zero and pole avoid \(0,\infty\) for \(b\ne0,1\). Thus the inversion example does not refute the needed nondegenerate case. The \(b=0\) boundary and exact exponent derivation need separate verification. Merely deleting inversion is not asserted to repair every case. This is a local false auxiliary statement without a demonstrated failure of the core application.
# Positive checks and additional limits
## Conic and genus calculations

For \(x=w+w^{-1}\) and \(\kappa=x^2/(x^2-4)\), substitution of \(y=t+\kappa/t\), \(z=tw+\kappa/(tw)\) gives \[x^2+y^2+z^2-xyz=x^2+\kappa(4-x^2)=0.\] The nondegenerate hypotheses \(x\ne0,\pm2\) are essential. The norm calculation similarly explains the elliptic parametrization.

In Lemma 9 the quartic \(P(\xi)=\xi^4+2(B_1+B_2)\xi^2+(B_2-B_1)^2\) has four distinct roots if \(B_1B_2(B_1-B_2)\ne0\) and the characteristic is odd: its two roots in \(\xi^2\) are distinct by discriminant \(16B_1B_2\), and neither is zero. This verifies the genus-one double-cover step, not every later irreducibility application.

A local enumeration check is also retained: on page 9, omitting \(\eta=0\) from the quadratic-character sum in the stated \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) case changes the result to \(1-\chi(\xi^2-4)\). At \(p=11,\xi=1\), the sum is \(2\) and the elliptic conic meets six other-coordinate fibers; page 10 prints five. An exhaustive finite check is saved. No failure of the subsequent diameter argument is inferred. A local sign in the parabolic rotation formula is likewise recorded in the evidence, not used to justify the Major judgment.
## Cyclotomic opening

If \(a,b,c\in[-2,2]\) satisfy \(a^2+b^2+c^2=abc\), then \[a^2+b^2+c^2=|abc|
\le (|a|^3+|b|^3+|c|^3)/3
\le 2(a^2+b^2+c^2)/3,\] forcing all three to vanish. Thus the cyclotomic integer in (82) is nonzero unless the trace triple is zero. Every conjugate has absolute value at most \(12+8=20\), and \(|N(\eta)|\le20^{\varphi(n)}\le20^n\). A prime ideal containing it has norm no larger; combining with \(n=\operatorname{lcm}(l_1,l_2,l_3)\le\max(l_j)^3\) gives the logarithmic bound in the semisimple cases. Parabolic rotations have order at least \(p\) and require a direct case, rather than being lifted as roots of unity of order \(p\) in that unramified argument.
## Sieve and limits

For \(p\equiv1\pmod4\), the zero-coordinate fiber has \(2p-2\) nonzero points. Summing the conic sizes gives \(p^2+3p\) total points, so its proportion is \(2/p+O(p^{-2})\). Products over fixed finite \(Q\) give \(\exp(-2L_Q+O(1))\); summing subsets of at most \(\nu\) primes gives the polynomial factor in (102). The proof correctly fixes \(Q,\nu\) before taking the height limit, and only afterwards makes \(L_Q\) large. An exceptional-prime count with exponent less than one gives a convergent exceptional reciprocal sum by dyadic summation, preserving the divergent good-prime sum in the progression \(1\bmod4\).

This verifies the elementary sieve conditional on transitivity and equidistribution. The Meiri–Puder block/sign conventions, passage between Vieta-only and permutation-extended actions, elliptic endgame, full auxiliary-polynomial proof, and exact CKSZ dependency remain explicit tasks. They are neither certified nor promoted to unsupported defects.

Title: Initial scientific review: M25-0035
# Identity, version, and outcome

Alexander Smith, The distribution of \(\ell^\infty\)-Selmer groups in degree \(\ell\) twist families I,DOI 10.1090/jams/1062. The reviewed object is the supplied 73-page author manuscript arXiv:2207.05674v2, submitted 8 February 2023, with internal date 9 February 2023, and its supplied TeX sources. PDF SHA-256:
All page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with printed pages. No comparison with the journal-final article was available.

Overall judgment: Minor. The unrestricted rank comparison in Example 4.4 fails for a concrete rational four-torsion example. The ramification assumptions of the main grid theorem exclude this example; no failure of the main distribution theorem is established. Positive checks and substantial remaining dependencies are distinguished below.

This is a systematic claim-focused initial review, not a full independent reconstruction of the 73-page proof. Text pages 1–10, 22–34, 41–58, and 68–71 were read (45 pages). Original page images were inspected for pages 1–8, 22–27, 29–34, 41–47, 49–56, and 68–71 (39 pages). Selected author TeX, including `selmer.tex` lines 27–63, was checked against the PDF.
# Claim structure and assumptions

The main theorem proved here is Theorem 4.18, a distribution statement within a grid class that is ready for higher work. Definition 4.19 imposes quantitative size, rank, prefix, and independent-pairing conditions. This is not an unconditional theorem for every twist of every abelian variety. The introduction explicitly assigns the overarching theorem and its applications to Part II, including the passage from natural families to these grids.

The alternating case requires \(\#\mathbb F=2\) and vanishing of the Poonen–Stoll class, not merely symmetry in characteristic two (pages 30 and 34). In the other case the transition matrix has shape \((n-u)\times n\), with \(u\) the difference of the fixed-point ranks of the module and its dual. Its absorbing state is \(\max(0,u)\). In the class-group application \(u=-r_2-r'_1\), and the hypothesis \(\mu_{2\ell}\not\subset F\) must be retained (pages 6–7).

The dependency chain is: ramification sections and symbols; fixed-point grid classes; bilinear character estimates; Fourier reduction and regridding; grid-module algebra; governing expansions; and the main distribution estimate. The applications in the introduction additionally require Part II. External Cassels–Tate duality results are inputs rather than results independently proved in this review.
# Finding 1 (Minor): the unrestricted rank comparison misses rational higher torsion
## Location and exact assertion

Definition 4.3 on page 23 defines the torsion portion using the connecting map \[\delta:H^0(G_F,N^\chi[\omega])\longrightarrow H^1(G_F,N^\chi[\omega])\] for \[0\longrightarrow N^\chi[\omega]\longrightarrow N^\chi[\omega^2]
 \xrightarrow{\omega}N^\chi[\omega]\longrightarrow0.\] It divides \(\omega^{k-1}\operatorname{Sel}^{\omega^k}N^\chi\) by this image. The last sentence of Example 4.4, on the same page, identifies the resulting ranks with those of Section 1.1. Section 1.1, page 2, instead removes the Kummer image of all rational torsion. The source repeats the finite-level connecting sequence in `selmer.tex` lines 42–45 and the comparison in line 58. Example 4.4 does not assume new ramification or exclude the trivial character.
## Counterexample with hypotheses checked

Take \(F=\mathbb Q\), \(\ell=2\), \(k_0=1\), \(\xi=-1\), \(\omega=-2\), the trivial character \(\chi\), and \[E:\ y^2=x^3+4x,\qquad N=E[2^\infty].\] This is an abelian variety of positive dimension with nonzero discriminant \(-4096\); its \(2\)-primary torsion is a twistable module of the required form. Choose \(\mathcal V_0\) to contain \(2,\infty\) and any additional places needed for unpacking. The usual Kummer local conditions are precisely those of Example 4.4. The choice of auxiliary unpacking places does not change the following rational-torsion comparison.

The point \(P=(2,4)\) has doubling slope \(2\), hence \(2P=(0,0)=T\) and \(P\) has order four. The only nonzero rational two-torsion point is \(T\), since the other roots of \(x(x^2+4)\) are not rational. Direct enumeration gives \[\#E(\mathbb F_3)=4,\qquad \#E(\mathbb F_5)=8.\] Both primes are of good reduction. Injectivity of reduction on prime-to-residue-characteristic rational torsion implies that the \(2\)-primary torsion has order at most four; the two primes also exclude all odd torsion. Thus \(E(\mathbb Q)_{\rm tors}=\langle P\rangle\simeq\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z\). The independent enumeration and exact doubling calculation are saved.

Multiplication by \(2\) from \(E(\mathbb Q)[4]\) onto \(E(\mathbb Q)[2]\) is surjective, so \(\delta(E(\mathbb Q)[2])=0\). On the other hand, the Kummer image of \(E(\mathbb Q)_{\rm tors}\) in \(\operatorname{Sel}^2 E\) has dimension one. Indeed, \(P\) is not twice a rational point: such a point would be torsion of order eight, contradicting the torsion computation. Writing \(d=\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\operatorname{Sel}^2 E\), the displayed definitions give \[r_2(N)=d,\qquad r_2(E/\mathbb Q)=d-1.\] No computation of \(d\), no rank conjecture, and no assumption about the Tate–Shafarevich group is needed. The claimed equality already fails at \(k=1\).
## Counterevidence and impact

Definition 4.7 requires a nonempty set of new primes outside \(\mathcal V_0\) and generating ramification characters. At such a prime \(N\) is unramified, whereas inertia on the twist contains multiplication by \(\xi\). Every rational invariant \(m\) of \(N^\chi\) therefore satisfies \((\xi-1)m=0\). Consequently \[H^0(G_F,N^\chi)=H^0(G_F,N^\chi[\omega]).\] The analogous local equality is used explicitly in Proposition 4.8, page 26. In this grid setting the full torsion Kummer image agrees with the finite-level image used in Definition 4.3. Thus the example above is not a counterexample to Theorem 4.18, and it is not evidence that the asserted asymptotic distributions fail.

The supported impact is a false unrestricted compatibility statement and a misleading general interpretation of the defined torsion portion. A sufficient repair is to restrict the rank comparison to twists whose rational \(\omega\)-primary torsion is killed by \(\omega\), explaining why the grids satisfy that condition. A global redefinition using the full Kummer image would require checking all subsequent conventions; that larger repair has not been certified. Focused AI acceptance confirms this local counterexample and the stated restriction; human scientific adjudication remains pending.
# Independent positive checks: algebra and probability
## Transition probabilities and boundary states

Exhaustive reviewer-owned matrix enumeration reproduced the Figure 1.1 transitions: \[\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{matrix family}&\text{nullity counts}\\ \hline
\operatorname{Alt}_3(\mathbb F_2)&1:7,\ 3:1\\
\operatorname{Alt}_4(\mathbb F_2)&0:28,\ 2:35,\ 4:1\\
\operatorname{Mat}_3(\mathbb F_2)&0:168,\ 1:294,\ 2:49,\ 3:1 .
\end{array}\] The denominators are respectively \(8,64,512\). Alternating ranks have the required parity. General rectangular matrices have kernel dimension at least \(\max(0,u)\). Every nonterminal state has self-transition probability less than one, so a nonincreasing path almost surely reaches a terminal state. These calculations check the finite matrix model, not its arithmetic equidistribution.

For the class-group quotient on pages 6 and 24, the norm operator sends the group to its invariant subgroup, so the quotient is annihilated by the cyclotomic polynomial. The pairing induced by \((1-\sigma)\) descends because its annihilator in the dual is precisely the invariant subgroup. This supports the dual-quotient identification. The assertion that the injection (4.1) is an isomorphism outside a negligible family remains a Part II input.
## Zero sums on lines and grid bases

In Proposition 7.4, division by a coefficient of minimal valuation stays in the DVR and produces a unit coefficient, justifying removal of a dependent basis point. The boundary set in Proposition 7.7 spans by the alternating cube relation. A purported nonzero line-sum relation on it has a nonzero coefficient minimizing the number of base coordinates; the line condition produces a point with one fewer such coordinate, a contradiction. Therefore \[|B|=|X|-\prod_s(|X_s|-1)\le |X|\sum_s|X_s|^{-1}.\] Singleton factors are allowed and give the full boundary. The nonempty-index assumption matters. The closure notion cannot simply be replaced by a rational-rank notion: Remark 7.3 explicitly records dependence on \(\ell\).

For Proposition 7.9, put \(N=|X|\) and \(\delta^2=M\log(\ell N)\sum_s|X_s|^{-1}\). The Hoeffding bound for a fixed \(Y\), followed by the count of compatible functions and closed-set choices, gives \[2\exp(-2\delta^2N^2/|Y|)(\ell N)^{M|B|}\ell^N<\ell^N\] when \(N>1\), using \(|Y|\le N\) and the basis bound. The singleton case is separate. Constant shifts preserve the zero-sum constraints because the index set is nonempty; hence one choice of the forcing function works for all target values, without an extra union bound over those values.
## Four-twist subquotient and commutator sign

For the quadratic specialization of Example 7.16, take triples \((a,b,c)\in N[4]^3\) with \(2a=2b=2c\) and put \(d=b+c-a\). The alternating square relation holds, the first three projections determine the fourth, and diagonal triples give surjectivity onto \(N[4]\). For twist signs \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2\in\{\pm1\}\), the discrepancy from equivariance is \[(\lambda_1-\lambda_1\lambda_2)b+
 (\lambda_2-\lambda_1\lambda_2)c+
 (\lambda_1\lambda_2-1)a=0.\] This follows from the common doubles and \(4a=0\). The saved finite check verifies all 64 scalar cases modulo four. Together with the analytic identity this validates the advertised quadratic subquotient, without asserting that a finite computation proves the full general module construction.

With the commutator convention on page 56 and a cocycle vanishing at \(\tau\), while \(\sigma\) acts trivially, the cocycle identity gives \(\phi([\tau^{-1},\sigma^{-1}])=(\tau-1)\phi(\sigma)\). The sign used in Construction 7.18 is consistent. The iterated governing-field application still requires its stated module and ramification hypotheses.
# Reduction to the main theorem and remaining dependencies

The accumulated error is at most \(|W|(\log\log H)^{-1/4}\) times the base-class size. Put \(h=\log^{(3)}H\). The rank bound gives \(\log|W|=O(h^{1/2})\), making this smaller than \(e^{-3h/16}\) for large \(H\). The passage to an infinite rank sequence does not rely solely on convergence of finite cylinders: pages 44–45 separately bound slow paths. The number of valid fragments is at most \(\exp(O(h^{5/16}))\), while their probabilities decay like \(\exp(-c h^{1/2})\). This preserves a vanishing total error. These checks are conditional on Theorem 6.2 and the intermediate arithmetic statements.

In the final governing-class estimates, \(2/3<11/16\) allows the class-count exponent in Proposition 8.16 to be absorbed by the density threshold. This checks a needed scale separation. It does not independently prove the governing expansion, Theorems 8.5 and 8.12, or Corollary 8.13. The complete bilinear character-sum proof, ramification-symbol machinery, exact external Cassels–Tate inputs, and substantial portions of Section 8 remain unverified. These are coverage limits, not asserted errors.

report: Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Initial scientific review: M25-0036
# Identity, version, and outcome

Alexander Smith, The distribution of \(\ell^\infty\)-Selmer groups in degree \(\ell\) twist families II, DOI 10.1090/jams/1063. The reviewed object is arXiv:2207.05143v2, submitted 8 February 2023, internal date 9 February 2023, 65 pages, together with the supplied author TeX. PDF SHA-256:

> d8f2b5f5d033d7163d292da86d794f4a3e2
> b780755c5eebb6f3ce093a68abcee.
Page numbers are one-based PDF pages and agree with printed numbers. There was no journal-final comparison.

Overall judgment: Major for the false interpolation estimate used in the proof of the main theorem, with three local Minor findings. The main Selmer distribution theorem is not disproved. A weaker interpolation bound is proved below and is compatible with the relevant asymptotic scales. Severity refers to the demonstrated invalid core derivation in the supplied version, irrespective of repair difficulty.

Text pages 1–23 and 56–62 were read (30 pages). Original images of pages 1–3, 6–22, and 56–62 were inspected (27 pages). Selected author source was inspected directly: `introB.tex` lines 16–40, `results.tex` lines 121–178, and `distribution.tex` lines 93–129, with additional targeted search context. This is a claim-focused review, not certification of the full analytic machinery.
# Main claims and dependency map

Theorem 2.14 compares the empirical distribution of entire nonincreasing Selmer-rank sequences with a Markov law in total variation. It requires admissible twists, fixed globally realizable local data, favored twists, and either Case 2.12 or Case 2.13. Conditions on cofavored submodules, connecting-map automorphisms, universal Selmer elements, and parity cannot be omitted. For higher prime-power twisting groups, admissibility requires full inertia at every new ramified prime.

The core route is cofavored-module classification (Section 4), local character expressions and negligible terms (Sections 5–7), gridding and rough moments (Sections 8–9), refined moments (Proposition 10.3), moment identification (10.4), coefficient recovery (10.5), and Part I’s higher-grid distribution theorem. Theorem 2.14’s proof explicitly invokes Proposition 10.5 on page 61. This is the dependency supporting the Major finding.
The average-rank application in Theorem 1.1 instead uses Theorem 2.6 and the isogeny construction of Example 3.9. Its small-parameter defect below does not establish failure of bounded average rank.
# Problem 1 (Major): Proposition 10.5 has false uniform coefficient bounds
## Claim, location, and failed step

On pages 59–60, Proposition 10.5 asserts a universal \(C>0\). For real coefficients \(a_i\), an integer \(m\ge1\), a rational prime \(\ell\), and finite \[B=\sum_{i\ge0}|a_i|\ell^{mi},\] small values of \(f(z)=\sum_i a_i z^i\) on \(1,\ell,\ldots,\ell^{m-1}\) are claimed to imply \[|a_i|\le \ell^{(-i+C)m}(B\ell^{-m^2/2}+\epsilon)\quad(i\ge0).
 \tag{R1}\] With both signs of those nodes, the gain is claimed to be \(\ell^{-m^2}\) instead. The exact statements appear in `distribution.tex` lines 105 and 107.

The proof correctly obtains a Cauchy estimate for coefficients of \(q=(f-g)/p\), where \(p\) is the node polynomial and \(g\) is the interpolation polynomial. It then transfers the factor \(\ell^{-im}\) to coefficients of \(f=g+pq\) merely because \(p\) has bounded coefficients (source line 125). This transfer is invalid: the coefficient convolution includes \(b_{i-r}\), whose bound has the additional factor \(\ell^{rm}\).
## Counterexample to the first bound, for every proposed constant

Fix \(\ell=2\) and take \[f_m(z)=\prod_{r=0}^{m-1}(1-z/2^r).\] This polynomial has real coefficients, finite \(B\), and is zero at every required node. Its leading coefficient and weighted coefficient sum are \[|a_m|=2^{-m(m-1)/2},\qquad
 B=\prod_{s=1}^{m}(1+2^s)
 =2^{m(m+1)/2}\prod_{s=1}^{m}(1+2^{-s})
 <e\,2^{m(m+1)/2}.\] For \(i=m\), the ratio of the \(B\) term on the right of (R1) to \(|a_m|\) is less than \[e\,2^{-m^2/2+Cm}.\] For any fixed proposed \(C\), choose an integer \(m\) sufficiently large that this is less than \(1/2\). Choose \[0<\epsilon\le
 \min\{1,\ |a_m|/[4\,2^{(-m+C)m}]\}.\] All node conditions still hold, while the full claimed right side is less than \(3|a_m|/4\). Thus no universal \(C\) can make (R1) true. This verifies all hypotheses rather than relying on one guessed value of the unspecified constant.
## Counterexample to the signed-node bound

Use \[f_m(z)=\prod_{r=0}^{m-1}(1-z^2/2^{2r}).\] It vanishes at all \(2m\) signed nodes, has \[|a_{2m}|=2^{-m(m-1)},\qquad
 B=\prod_{s=1}^{m}(1+2^{2s})
 <e^{1/3}2^{m(m+1)}.\] For \(i=2m\), the ratio of the claimed \(B\) term to the actual coefficient is at most \(e^{1/3}2^{-m^2+Cm}\), again tending to zero. The same positive-\(\epsilon\) choice finishes the contradiction. Exact rational computations for \(m=8\), \(\ell=2\), illustrative \(C=1\), and \(\epsilon=1\) are saved for both parts; the analytic families, not those finite examples alone, disprove universality.
## Counterevidence: a weaker sufficient-range estimate

A valid replacement, for \(0\le i\le m\), is \[|a_i|\le \ell^{C'm}(B\ell^{-m^2/2}+\epsilon)
 \tag{R2}\] in the first case, and the same expression with \(\ell^{-m^2}\) in the signed case, for an absolute \(C'\).

Here is a proof of the stated replacement. The manuscript’s interpolation construction gives, on the disk of radius \(\ell^m\), \[|q|\le B\ell^{-m(m-1)/2}
       +4m\epsilon\ell^{2m+1}.\] On \(|z|=1/2\), the node polynomial has magnitude at most \(\prod_{r\ge0}(1+(2\ell^r)^{-1})\le e\). The Lagrange denominators have magnitude at least \(1/4\), so \(|g|\le4em\epsilon\) there. Hence \(|f|\le e|q|+4em\epsilon\) on this smaller circle. Cauchy’s estimate contributes \(2^i\le\ell^m\) for \(i\le m\), and all remaining factors are absorbed in \(\ell^{C'm}\), proving (R2).

For signed nodes write \(f(z)=F(z^2)+zG(z^2)\). Both \(F\) and \(G\) are bounded by \(\epsilon\) at \(\ell^{2r}\), because \(F(\ell^{2r})=(f(\ell^r)+f(-\ell^r))/2\) and \(G(\ell^{2r})=(f(\ell^r)-f(-\ell^r))/(2\ell^r)\). Their weighted coefficient sums for base \(\ell^2\) are at most \(B\) and \(B/\ell^m\). Applying the preceding proof, which works for every real base at least two, gives the signed version of (R2).

On page 61 the relevant \(B\) grows like \(\ell^{m^2/2+O(m)}\) in the alternating case and \(\ell^{m^2/4+O(m)}\) otherwise. The signed or unsigned replacement still gives exponential decay in \(m^2\). The target coefficient index is at most \((\log^{(3)}H)^{1/4}\), far smaller than an admissible interpolation order of size \((\log\log H)^{1/8-\eta}\). Thus this local repair is compatible with the required range and scale, after choosing margins in \(\eta\). This does not certify the entire remaining arithmetic proof or all constants.
The supported conclusion is that an explicitly used core lemma and its final coefficient step are false as written. It is not a counterexample to Theorem 2.14 or to the arithmetic rank distributions.
# Problems 2–4: separate local defects
## Problem 2 (Minor): finite alternating transition formula

Case 2.13, page 9, and `results.tex` line 161 display a numerator \(\prod_{k=1}^{j}(1-2^{-n-j+k})\). For \(n=j=2\), the two alternating matrices are the zero matrix and \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Therefore \(P(2\mid2)=P(0\mid2)=1/2\). The printed formula instead gives \(P(2\mid2)=7/8\), so its row sums to \(11/8\).

Counterevidence is substantial: the preceding verbal definition uses genuine uniform random matrices, Part I’s Figure 1.1 gives the correct finite probabilities, and the fixed-\(j\) limiting numerator tends to one in either expression. Proposition 10.4 counts kernels directly. This is a local erroneous formula, with a verified replacement, rather than evidence of an incorrect intended Markov model. Any use of the displayed finite formula requires correction.
## Problem 3 (Minor): the small-positive-parameter range of Theorem 1.1

Page 2 and `introB.tex` lines 20–21 quantify over every \(m>0\) without an integer restriction and bound the mean of \(e^{m\operatorname{rank}(A/K)}\) by \(e^{Cm^2}\). This cannot hold for all positive real \(m\).

Take \(F=\mathbb Q\), \(\ell=2\), and \(E:y^2=x^3-2\). The point \((3,5)\) is nontorsion: good-reduction counts at \(5\) and \(7\) are \(6\) and \(7\), which, by prime-to-residue-characteristic injectivity, force rational torsion to be trivial. The curve is nonsingular, with discriminant \(-1728\). Thus \(\operatorname{rank}(E/K)\ge1\) for every quadratic extension \(K\). For any proposed \(c,C>0\), choose \(H>\max(C,8,e^e)\), so the extension set is nonempty, and choose \(0<m<\min(1/C,c\log\log\log H)\). Then its mean is at least \(e^m>e^{Cm^2}\).

Theorem 2.6 explicitly uses a positive integer moment order, and Example 3.9 applies it to obtain boundedness. That is the natural intended reading. Restricting to \(m\ge1\), or explicitly to positive integer \(m\), removes this counterexample. If a real-parameter bound for all \(m>0\) is desired, a linear term in the exponent is needed: a bound at \(m=1\) gives \(e^{Dm}\) for \(0<m\le1\) by concavity, and together with a large-\(m\) estimate gives \(e^{D(m+m^2)}\). No failure of the bounded-average-rank conclusion is inferred. The literal endpoint quantifier, not the existence of a useful moment bound, is the defect.
## Problem 4 (Minor): favored density needs the subsequent hypotheses

Immediately after Example 1.2, page 3, the density of favored squarefree \(d\) is stated to be \(1/2\) under only \(b(a^2-4b)\ne0\). Take \(a=0,b=-1\). Then \(E:y^2=x^3-x\) is nonsingular, \(K=\mathbb Q\), and \(K_0=\mathbb Q(i)\). At every eligible prime, splitting in \(K_0\) contributes at most the splitting count in the trivial extension \(K\). Every squarefree \(d\) is favored, giving density one.

The following Proposition 1.3 and Theorem 1.4 explicitly require \(K,K_0\) to be distinct nontrivial quadratic extensions. The example violates those later hypotheses and does not refute either result. The earlier density sentence should carry those restrictions; the repair of the full density theorem is not reproved here.
# Positive checks and qualifications
## Favored twists and cofavored modules

The exact-sequence cardinality calculation in Proposition 2.5, page 18, gives the displayed local Tamagawa factor after new ramification forces invariants into \(\omega\)-torsion. The global lower bound remains conditional on the cited Euler-characteristic theorem.

For Proposition 4.3, positivity of the common weight makes equality of the summed invariant-dimension inequalities force equality at each group element. Adding a positive constant to a superlative is legitimate using the unweighted inequality. For Proposition 4.5, a submodule with zero intersection with the second summand and full first projection is a graph. Its connecting map is the difference \(\beta\delta_1-\delta_2\beta\), giving precisely the commuting condition. The resulting finite division-ring argument and the subspace description explain the Gaussian-binomial contribution to the moments. The induction in Proposition 4.7 must be read on \(\omega\)-torsion; local omitted torsion notation and the reversed sign in the final dimension display are not treated as separate substantive findings. With the correct sign, varying the quotient dimension gives the stated contradiction.
## Moments, parity, and tails

For \(m\) vectors spanning dimension \(d\), an alternating random matrix kills them with probability \(2^{-nd+d(d+1)/2}\). Counting the span relations gives \[\operatorname{gr}_2(d,m)\prod_{r=0}^{d-1}(2^n-2^r)\;\text{tuples}.\] This validates the finite counting step of Proposition 10.4 and gives limiting first moments \(3\) and \(15\) for orders one and two. In the rectangular case the first moment is \(1+\ell^u\).

Parity information is essential: equal unsigned moments alone do not select between the even and odd limiting laws. The signed-node step on page 61 uses fixed parity. For an odd-degree hyperelliptic polynomial with full symmetric Galois action, the fixed-space dimension on \(\mathbb F_2^{2g+1}/\langle(1,\ldots,1)\rangle\) is the number of permutation cycles minus one. Its parity is the sign character, consistent with the parity-invariant designation in Example 3.7. This does not independently verify the cited rational-point bounds in Theorem 3.8.

The rough moment bound yields a rank tail of size \(\exp(-cR^2)\) by choosing an integer moment proportional to \(R\). At \(R=(\log^{(3)}H)^{1/4}\) this moment lies within Theorem 2.6’s permitted logarithmic range and gives the required \(\exp(-c\sqrt{\log^{(3)}H})\) scale, conditional on the positive density of the fixed-local favored family.

Part I’s rational higher-torsion issue is recorded separately in M25-0035. Part II explicitly imposes new ramification in Remark 2.11; its admissible nontrivially ramified twists force rational invariants to be killed by \(\omega\). The finite exceptional family does not itself damage an asymptotic theorem. The class-group roots-of-unity exclusion and \(u=-r_2-r'_1\) agree with Part I. The precise global duality, parity, Chebotarev, and gridding estimates have not all been independently verified.
# Impact, repairs, and remaining work
Overall | Major for Proposition 10.5’s directly used invalid estimate; three separate local Minor findings.
Core conclusion | Theorem 2.14 not disproved; a weaker coefficient estimate compatible with its scales is proved here.
Repair status | (R2) and (R3) locally verified; full revised arithmetic proof and final constants not certified.
Remaining | Sections 5–9 in full; external arithmetic and rational-point dependencies; complete Part I interface; journal-final comparison.
Adoption | No author contact or author adoption; focused AI acceptance complete, human adjudication pending.

Here is a proof of the stated replacement. The manuscript’s interpolation construction gives, on the disk of radius \(\ell^m\), \[|q|\le B\ell^{-m(m-1)/2}
       +4m\epsilon\ell^{2m+1}.\] On \(|z|=1/2\), the node polynomial has magnitude at most \(\prod_{r\ge0}(1+(2\ell^r)^{-1})\le e\). The Lagrange denominators have magnitude at least \(1/4\), so \(|g|\le4em\epsilon\) there. Hence \(|f|\le e|q|+4em\epsilon\) on this smaller circle. Cauchy’s estimate contributes \(2^i\le\ell^m\) for \(i\le m\), and all remaining factors are absorbed in \(\ell^{C'm}\), proving (R2).

For signed nodes write \(f(z)=F(z^2)+zG(z^2)\). Both \(F\) and \(G\) are bounded by \(\epsilon\) at \(\ell^{2r}\), because \(F(\ell^{2r})=(f(\ell^r)+f(-\ell^r))/2\) and \(G(\ell^{2r})=(f(\ell^r)-f(-\ell^r))/(2\ell^r)\). Their weighted coefficient sums for base \(\ell^2\) are at most \(B\) and \(B/\ell^m\). Applying the preceding proof, which works for every real base at least two, gives the signed version of (R2).

On page 61 the relevant \(B\) grows like \(\ell^{m^2/2+O(m)}\) in the alternating case and \(\ell^{m^2/4+O(m)}\) otherwise. The signed or unsigned replacement still gives exponential decay in \(m^2\). The target coefficient index is at most \((\log^{(3)}H)^{1/4}\), far smaller than an admissible interpolation order of size \((\log\log H)^{1/8-\eta}\). Thus this local repair is compatible with the required range and scale, after choosing margins in \(\eta\). This does not certify the entire remaining arithmetic proof or all constants.
The supported conclusion is that an explicitly used core lemma and its final coefficient step are false as written. It is not a counterexample to Theorem 2.14 or to the arithmetic rank distributions.
Impact: Invalid directly used core lemma; main Selmer distribution not disproved.

report: Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Initial scientific review: M25-0037
# Identity, scope, and outcome

Shubhodip Mondal and Emanuel Reinecke, Unipotent homotopy theory of schemes, DOI 10.1090/jams/1064. The reviewed object is the supplied 95-page author manuscript arXiv:2302.10703v3, 18 August 2025, and its matching `main_revision.tex`. PDF SHA-256:
Page references are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with printed numbers. The journal version was not compared.

Overall judgment: Major for an invalid boundary derivation in the principal suspension theorem. The theorem itself is not disproved: a complete replacement argument for that boundary is supplied below. The later Calabi–Yau computations use higher connectivity and are not refuted by this example. The rating follows the prescribed criterion for an invalid derivation directly supporting a core theoretical guarantee, independently of repair difficulty.

Text pages 1–8, 10–12, 24–38, 49–54, 71–75, and 81–92 were read (49 pages). Images of pages 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 11, 12, 24, 26–28, 30–38, 49–54, 71–75, and 81–92 were inspected (43 pages). Static author-source inspection covered lines 1681–1720, including complete long lines relevant to the finding, plus targeted search context. This is a systematic claim-focused initial review, not full independent certification.
# Claims and dependencies

The construction is affinization \(\mathrm U(X)=\operatorname{Spec}R\Gamma(X,\mathcal O)\) among higher fpqc stacks. Pointed cohomological connectedness makes the homotopy sheaves unipotent affine group schemes. Proposition 3.1.7 compares the first group with Nori’s unipotent fundamental group through pointed torsor universal properties.

Principal guarantees include profiniteness for proper pointed cohomologically connected schemes in positive characteristic, maximal pro-etale quotient comparison, Freudenthal suspension, recovery of formal Lie groups, and derived invariance for Calabi–Yau varieties. The suspension theorem is stated as Theorem 1.0.16 on page 7 for all integers \(n\ge0\), through Proposition 3.4.10 and Corollary 3.4.11 on pages 37–38. The defect is in the explicitly used \(n=0\) derivation.

For \(n\ge1\), the proof uses finite-dimensional cohomology, Postnikov-stage finiteness, preservation of certain pullbacks by affinization, and right exactness of commutative unipotent completion. Proposition 7.2.15 later uses the simply connected formal two-sphere, hence the \(n=1\) suspension case, followed by higher connectivity. It does not require the erroneous \(n=0\) group sequence.
# Problem 1: the EHP group sequence fails at zero connectivity
## Claim and exact location

Proposition 3.4.10, page 37, equation (3.4.4), asserts \[\pi_{2n+2}(X\wedge X)\longrightarrow
 \pi_{2n+1}(X)\longrightarrow
 \pi_{2n+2}(\Sigma X)\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{R1}\] The following paragraph identifies the first arrow with a bilinear Whitehead product and, at \(n=0\), the commutator map. It explicitly uses this sequence to obtain the zero-connectivity surjection. The same text is in `main_revision.tex`, lines 1702–1709.

At \(n=0\), the first term is an abelian homotopy sheaf, whereas the kernel of the second arrow can be a nonabelian derived subgroup. Thus (R1) cannot be an exact sequence of group sheaves with the asserted arrows. The commutator also does not factor bilinearly through the abelianizations in Lemma 3.4.3.
## All hypotheses verified

Let \(k=\mathbf F_2\), let \(G\) be the constant group scheme of \(U_5(\mathbf F_2)\), the upper triangular \(5\) by \(5\) matrices with diagonal entries one, and set \(X=BG\). The group has order \(2^{10}\).

Every nonzero representation of a finite \(2\)-group in characteristic two has a nonzero invariant vector. Indeed, a central element \(z\) of order two has \((z-1)^2=0\), so its nonzero kernel is group-stable, and induction on the quotient group proves the assertion. Infinite-dimensional representations reduce to a nonzero finite-dimensional cyclic subrepresentation. Hence \(G\) is unipotent in the paper’s definition.

The stack \(BG\) is pointed, connected, and affine by Theorem 2.1.17. Every \(H^i(BG,\mathcal O)\) is finite-dimensional: the finite-group bar cochain complex has degree-\(i\) dimension \(|G|^i\). Both assumptions of Proposition 3.4.10 therefore hold for \(n=0\).

For a connected classifying space, the suspension map \[G=\pi_1(BG)\longrightarrow\pi_2(\Sigma BG)=G_{\mathrm{ab}}\] is abelianization, by degree-two Hurewicz and suspension homology. This persists for constant sheaves because the constant-object functor preserves finite limits and colimits. The kernel is the constant sheaf \(G'\).

Writing \(e_{ij}\) for elementary matrices and \([a,b]=aba^{-1}b^{-1}\), set \[A=I+e_{12},\quad B=I+e_{23},\quad
 C=I+e_{34},\quad D=I+e_{45}.\] Direct multiplication gives \[h=[A,B]=I+e_{13},\qquad v=[C,D]=I+e_{35},
 \qquad [h,v]=I+e_{15}\ne I. \tag{R2}\] Thus \(h,v\in G'\) do not commute. These identities were independently checked by original reviewer-written exact arithmetic modulo two.

But \(\pi_2(X\wedge X)\) is abelian. The image of a group-sheaf homomorphism from it must be abelian and cannot equal \(G'\). This disproves (R1) at \(n=0\). Also, \(h\) has zero class in \(G_{\mathrm{ab}}\) but \([h,v]\ne1\), independently ruling out the claimed bilinear commutator factorization.
## Impact and counterinterpretation

This is not only a label error: the ordinary EHP group sequence must be restricted to positive connectivity. Even interpreting the word sheaves as pointed sets would not validate the stated bilinear description. The manuscript expressly invokes the invalid sequence for the boundary part of a principal theorem, supporting the prescribed Major rating. No main theorem is claimed false, and no failure of the later Calabi–Yau applications follows from this example.
# Counterevidence and complete repair of the affected boundary

Let \(X\) be a pointed connected affine stack and \(G=\pi_1(X)\). For every commutative unipotent affine group scheme \(H\), adjunction gives \[\begin{split}
 [\mathrm U(\Sigma X),K(H,2)]_*
 &\simeq[\Sigma X,K(H,2)]_*\\
 &\simeq[X,BH]_*
 \simeq\operatorname{Hom}(G,H).
\end{split}\tag{R3}\] Brackets mean pointed homotopy classes. The last step uses one-truncation because \(BH\) is one-truncated.

The suspension is simply connected, and its first coherent cohomology vanishes. The paper’s Hurewicz criterion therefore gives \(\pi_1(\mathrm U(\Sigma X))=0\). The left side of (R3) is \(\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_2(\mathrm U(\Sigma X)),H)\), so the universal property yields \[\pi_2(\mathrm U(\Sigma X))\simeq G^{\mathrm{ab}}_{\mathrm{aff}}.\] Here the right side means abelianization in unipotent affine group schemes, not an assumption that an arbitrary sheaf quotient is representable. The suspension unit induces the quotient map, which is surjective by Remark 3.3.9. This proves the \(n=0\) conclusion without (R1), even without finite-dimensional cohomology.

The repair is complete within the established affine-stack framework. It explains why the conclusion survives the false auxiliary sequence. It does not certify the uninspected foundations or all positive-connectivity EHP inputs.
# Additional mathematical checks
## Definitions and universal properties

The Nori comparison on pages 24–26 uses the same pointed torsor functor on both sides, and the one-truncation step is appropriate. The Hurewicz statement on page 28 explicitly defines trivial degree-zero cohomology to mean \(H^0=k\); an objection based on \(H^0=0\) would be spurious. Its induction uses unipotence and vanishing of \(\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_i,\mathbf G_a)\), conditional on the stated Postnikov comparison.

The product formula retains quasicompactness and quasiseparatedness for its Kunneth input. No extension to arbitrary schemes was inferred. The introductory suspension theorem’s more general wording is compatible with the affine version because the left adjoint satisfies \(\mathrm U(\Sigma\mathrm U(X))\simeq\mathrm U(\Sigma X)\).
## Spectral-sequence degree logic

In Lemma 3.4.7 and Proposition 4.3.7, fibre cohomology vanishes for \(0<j\le n\). The term \(E_2^{0,n+1}\) has no incoming differentials; outgoing differentials before \(d_{n+2}\) land in zero rows, and the sole possible later differential lands at \((n+2,0)\). Thus \(E_{n+3}^{0,n+1}=E_\infty^{0,n+1}\).

A map from an infinite-dimensional vector space to a finite-dimensional one has infinite-dimensional kernel. Similarly, torsion Frobenius modules are closed under extensions, so a non-torsion term cannot be killed by a torsion target. These yield the stated contradictions against the abutment. This checks the degree logic conditional on the base-change, Frobenius-representation, and profiniteness criteria; those entire foundational sections were not re-proved.
## Formal groups and sphere reconstruction

In Proposition 6.2.3, the symmetric algebra on degree two has \(H^1=H^3=0\). The first nonzero homotopy group lies in degree two, and its \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(-,\mathbf G_a)\) vanishes by injection into \(H^3\). The finite-dimensional formal-Lie criterion then applies. The final map is an isomorphism on algebras generated in degree two, not merely an equality of graded dimensions.

Lemma 6.1.18 proves vanishing only for \(i>2\). Its inverse-limit argument correctly uses vanishing of degree-three cohomology of successive Verschiebung kernels to obtain surjectivity on the degree-two tower and remove \(\lim^1\).

For Proposition 7.2.14 the obstruction is \(H^{r+3}(BE^\vee,\pi_{n+r+1})\), which vanishes for all \(r\ge0\). Later ambiguities involve \(H^{r+2}\) and vanish for \(r\ge1\), leaving the first-stage \(H^2\) torsor. The Milnor argument explicitly handles inverse-limit ambiguity. The nontwisted Postnikov construction uses \(n\ge2\).

For the algebraically closed Calabi–Yau applications, symmetrization \(x\otimes y\mapsto x\otimes y+y\otimes x\) explains the weak wedge. In the split height-one characteristic-two case the cokernel of multiplication by two on \(\mathbf Z_2\) is \(\mathbf Z/2\). In odd characteristic the symmetric bilinear functional is killed by the weak-wedge relation. The final uniqueness argument retains both \(n>2\) and \(p>2\).
# Remaining work and scope boundaries

The full quasi-coherent/base-change foundations, Frobenius-representation theory, curve and abelian-variety sections, formal duality, and Artin–Mazur comparison were not independently verified. External results of Toen, Nori, Barcus/Whitehead, replete-topos theory, and Antieau–Bragg remain dependencies; their complete original statements were not checked.

The dimension-zero and dimension-one cases of general derived invariance were not certified by the inspected \(n\ge2\) formal-sphere argument. Nonsplit height-one formal groups over non-algebraically-closed perfect fields remain a scope question; no counterexample to the algebraically closed applications is asserted.

Uninspected pages/source and journal-final comparison remain outstanding. Focused AI acceptance of the stated finding and local repair is complete; human adjudication remains pending. A bounded public version/correction search found the official v3 record and no relevant correction in the retrieved results; absence of a correction is not established.
# Scope and limitations

The evidence folder contains extracted text, actually inspected source images, targeted static-source search, original exact matrix checks, and public lookup results. The main assistant performed all scientific reasoning, source inspection, calculation, and image inspection. No author code was run.

The original compiler-absence probe preceded the authorized portable Tectonic follow-up. Its build and page inspections remain preserved as historical evidence. The current report is compiled from this exact TeX with Tectonic 0.17.0 in untrusted, cached-only mode. Exact input, dependency, log, PDF and page-image hashes, together with actual inspection of changed or reflowed pages, are recorded in the accompanying provenance. Original-review actions retain their original attribution; focused AI acceptance is recorded separately. Scientific adjudication remains pending, with no human review or author adoption claimed.
# References

9 S. Mondal and E. Reinecke, Unipotent homotopy theory of schemes, arXiv:2302.10703v3 (18 August 2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.10703. The staged PDF and matching TeX are the primary reviewed evidence. Source manifest M25-0037, `papers/0037/source_manifest.json`. This binds the author manuscript and hashes, not equality with the journal version.

report: Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Initial scientific review: M25-0038
# Identity, exact version, and outcome

Ben Heuer and Daxin Xu, p-Adic non-abelian Hodge theory for curves via moduli stacks, DOI 10.1090/jams/1065. This review concerns the supplied 49-page author manuscript arXiv:2402.01365v1, submitted 2 February 2024, and its matching 3212-line `main.tex`. Page references below are physical PDF pages, numbered from the first page, and agree with the printed article numbering. PDF SHA-256:

> a20c65048e39da7e8b8ceee24570e1f0b1f
> b8b2feafa1814da45f8c22f3bff9c
No journal-final comparison was performed. None of the findings is represented as a verified defect of the journal version.

Outcome: Major, with two individually Minor findings. The proof of perfectoid GAGA invokes a false density statement (Problem 1). This is a demonstrated invalid premise in a chain supporting one of the paper’s main results. An exact local replacement argument is supplied and checked below; the GAGA theorem is not refuted. An introductory comparison isomorphism is false on a nonreduced spectral fibre, but the body explicitly uses the weaker correct comparison (Problem 2). A spectral-locus assertion lacks a genus restriction already present in later statements (Problem 3).

All 49 pages were read as extracted text and all 49 rendered source-page images were actually inspected. This is a systematic claim-focused review, not an independent proof of every theorem or cited dependency. The original TeX was searched throughout and selected evidence ranges were read; the complete TeX was not independently semantically audited.
# Definitions, assumptions, and checked reasoning

Throughout the paper, \(K\) is an algebraically closed complete extension of \(\mathbb Q_p\), \(X/K\) is a smooth projective connected curve, and \(G\) is a connected reductive group unless a narrower scope is specified. Write \(\Omega=\widetilde\Omega_X=\omega_X(-1)\). For \(G=\operatorname{GL}_n\), the Hitchin base is \[\mathcal A=\prod_{i=1}^n H^0(X,\Omega^{\otimes i})\otimes\mathbf G_a,\] and the spectral cover \(\pi:Z_b\to X\) is defined by the monic characteristic polynomial. The regular centralizer has Lie algebra \(\pi_*\mathcal O_{Z_b}\). In the discussion of relative cohomology, distinguish the projection \(q:X\times\mathcal A\to\mathcal A\) from \(\pi':Z\to\mathcal A\).
The following checks were made.

1. Sections 2–3, pp. 6–12: right torsor conventions, anti-diagonal contracted products and the inverse difference torsor; the logarithm’s kernel and the need for a \(p\)-surjective open subgroup for surjectivity; the distinction between left exactness in general and the stronger assertions subsequently proved for the algebraic centralizer.

2. Section 4, pp. 13–16: the use of commuting local representations in the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff calculation, invariance of the canonical Higgs field under its exponential action, change-of-chart reduction to a faithful linear representation, and zero-Higgs descent conditional on the cited local Simpson correspondence.

3. Sections 5–6, pp. 16–29: regular-centralizer equivariance, the identity \(d a(\tau)=\varphi\), the sign in the local exponential twist, and cancellation by the inverse torsor. The constructed Higgs field on the resulting etale bundle is distinguished from the canonical Higgs field of that underlying etale bundle. The relative Hodge–Tate sequence, its vector-bundle base changes and the construction of the torsor of splittings were traced, conditional on the quoted cohomological input. Functoriality is restricted by the stated compatibility with Kostant sections.

4. Section 7, pp. 30–36: the comparison diagram and its kernel isomorphism, rather than an isomorphism of all Lie-algebra cohomology; the use of one-dimensional fibres; torsion freeness of \(\Lambda\) and the inverse-limit hypotheses; the restriction \(p\nmid |W|\) where Weyl invariants are used. The \(\operatorname{GL}_n\) result and the more restricted general reductive result were kept separate. The pointwise continuous exponential yields the claimed condensed comparison and homeomorphism, not an asserted analytic isomorphism.

5. Section 8, pp. 36–44: the double-coset argument, generation and finite presentation for vector bundles, the Fitting-ideal step, reduction from a curve to \(\mathbb P^1\) by a finite flat map, and the dependence of the Higgs-stack comparison on GAGA. The regular spectral-fibre/Picard argument was traced conditional on the cited representability and BNR input.

6. Section 9, pp. 44–48: representation stacks include a \(G\)-torsor on the test space; naive conjugacy classes alone do not give the required stack. The adjunction and faithful-representation reductions were checked. For the degree-zero argument, determinant and tensor reduction, Riemann–Hurwitz, and the growth of sections of a positive-degree subbundle on finite etale covers were checked: \(g'-1=n(g-1)\) and Riemann–Roch gives \(h^0\geq n(d-g+1)\), contradicting the bounded invariant-section space when the tensor power makes \(d>g-1\).
# Problem 1: a false density premise in the GAGA proof
## Claim and exact location

Lemma 8.2.7, p. 39, with proof in `main.tex`, lines 2398–2414, asserts that a double coset has a representative \[A'\in \operatorname{GL}_r(R\langle T^{\pm1}\rangle)
       \cap T^{-m}M_r(R\langle T\rangle).\] The proof claims that \(\operatorname{GL}_r(R[T^{\pm1}])\) is dense in \(\operatorname{GL}_r(R\langle T^{\pm1}\rangle)\), and uses this to obtain \[\operatorname{GL}_r(R\langle T^{\pm1}\rangle)
 =\operatorname{GL}_r(R[T^{\pm1}])U(R\langle T^{\pm1}\rangle),
 \qquad U(S)=1+\mathfrak m_KM_r(S^+).\] The claimed density, at source line 2404, is false.
## Complete countercheck, including hypotheses

Indeed, the highest and lowest exponents of a nonzero Laurent polynomial add under multiplication over a field, so a product equal to \(1\) forces both factors to have exponent width zero. This uses openness of invertibility and continuity of inversion, together with the open subgroup \(U\) already used in the paper. It does not claim \(P\in\operatorname{GL}_r(R[T^{\pm1}])\).

By the same vanishing/Čech argument as in the original proof, \(A_1=A_+A_-\) with \(A_+\in U(R\langle T\rangle)\) and \(A_-\in U(R\langle T^{-1}\rangle)\). # Problem 2: an introductory isomorphism contradicted by a spectral fibre
## Claim, location, and strongest charitable reading

Theorem 1.4.1, p. 4, source lines 488–490, calls \[\psi:R^1 f_{v*}\operatorname{Lie}J\longrightarrow\Lambda\otimes_{\mathbb Z_p}\mathbf G_a\] a canonical isomorphism, where \(\Lambda\) is the first etale cohomology of the spectral curve. The introduction reuses \(f\) inconsistently. Interpret the source using \(q:X\times\mathcal A\to\mathcal A\) and the target using \(\pi':Z\to\mathcal A\), exactly as the body does. The asserted isomorphism is false even under that well-typed reading.
## Parameters, assumptions, and dimensions

Take \(K=\mathbb C_3\), \(G=\operatorname{GL}_2\), and let \(X\) be the smooth projective completion of \(y^2=x^5-x\). The polynomial has five simple roots, since its greatest common divisor with its derivative is \(1\). Including the branch point at infinity, the hyperelliptic cover has six branch points and genus \(2\). Thus \(X\) is a smooth projective connected curve in characteristic zero and \(G\) is a permitted connected reductive group.

Choose \(b=(0,0)\) in the full Hitchin base. There is no regular-spectral-fibre restriction in Theorem 1.4.1. Use the monic characteristic polynomial explicitly displayed at the start of Section 5.5: the spectral equation is \(t^2=0\). The finite flat degree-two cover is the nilpotent thickening with \[\pi_*\mathcal O_{Z_b}=\mathcal O_X\oplus\Omega^{-1},
 \qquad \operatorname{Lie}J_b=\mathcal O_X\oplus\Omega^{-1}.\] The Hodge–Tate sequence used in (6.1.13) gives, at this fibre, \[\dim_K H_v^1(X,\mathcal O_X)=h^1(\mathcal O_X)+h^0(\Omega)=2+2=4.\] It also gives \[\dim_K H_v^1(X,\nu^*\Omega^{-1})
 =h^1(\Omega^{-1})+h^0(\mathcal O_X)=3+1=4,\] because Serre duality and Riemann–Roch give \(h^1(\Omega^{-1})=h^0(\omega_X^2)=3\). Tate twists do not change these dimensions. The source fibre therefore has dimension \(8\).

The etale site is unchanged by this nilpotent thickening, so \(H^1_{\mathrm{et}}(Z_b,\mathbb Z_p)=H^1_{\mathrm{et}}(X,\mathbb Z_p)\) has rank \(4\). Hence the target fibre has dimension \(4\), and \(\psi\) cannot be an isomorphism. More generally the same calculation gives dimensions \(5g-2\) and \(2g\) for \(g\geq2\). The nilpotent summand is invisible on reduced perfectoid test spaces.
## Existing counterevidence and local correction

Theorem 7.0.1 and Corollary 7.0.2, p. 30, use a comparison morphism and the Cartesian diagram. Remark 7.0.5 on that page explicitly warns that this map need not be an isomorphism, including for nonreduced spectral curves; source lines 1944–1945 corroborate this. Proposition 7.2.3, p. 33, establishes the needed kernel isomorphism. The Cartesian property is enough for the exponential splitting and the later homeomorphism argument.

The precise correction is to replace the introductory isomorphism claim by the comparison morphism and Cartesian assertion of Theorem 7.0.1/Corollary 7.0.2. The body already contains the necessary distinction. Consequently this is an individually Minor local overstatement: no invalid downstream derivation of the main correspondence has been demonstrated from it.

The displayed ideal formula near Definition 5.5.1 omits the monic term in its typography. The counterexample above deliberately uses the correct monic polynomial already given in the same subsection; it does not exploit that omission.
# Problem 3: the dense smooth connected spectral locus needs a genus condition
## Claim and counterexamples

Section 5.5, p. 22, source line 1411, states without a genus restriction that there is an open dense \(\mathcal A^\circ\subseteq\mathcal A\) over which the spectral family is smooth proper with geometrically connected fibres.

Take again \(K=\mathbb C_3\) and \(G=\operatorname{GL}_2\), but let \(X=\mathbb P^1\). These satisfy the subsection’s general curve and group assumptions. Since \(\Omega\simeq\mathcal O(-2)\) as a line bundle, \[H^0(X,\Omega)=H^0(X,\Omega^2)=0.\] Thus \(\mathcal A\) is the single zero point and its spectral cover has equation \(t^2=0\). It is a nonreduced finite flat double cover of \(X\), so it is not smooth. A dense open of this one-point base must contain that point; none has the asserted property.

For an elliptic curve, \(\Omega\) is trivial and the coefficients of the degree-two spectral polynomial are constants in \(K\). If it has distinct roots, the cover is the disjoint union of two copies of \(X\), hence is smooth but disconnected. A repeated root gives a nonreduced cover. Thus there is no smooth geometrically connected spectral fibre in this case either.
## Impact and counterevidence

Theorem 1.1.3, p. 2, Section 8.5, p. 41, and Theorem 8.6.2, p. 42, already impose genus at least \(2\) where the regular-locus geometry is developed. The main twisted correspondence of Section 6 uses all spectral covers and does not require this dense locus. No additional main-theorem failure has been established.

Restrict the assertion in Section 5.5 to \(g(X)\geq2\), as in the later treatment. Rank one can be handled separately: its spectral cover is \(X\) itself for every genus. This is Minor, a supported local scope defect with a matching later restriction.

The constant-coordinate description of \(\tau_\Omega\) in the same subsection should also be read with \(n\geq2\); in rank one the characteristic relation gives \(T=b\). Section 6.5 uses the appropriate rank-one dependence. This is retained as an unrated scope clarification, not an additional substantive finding.

The repairs in Problems 1–3 are distinct: an analytic replacement proof, restoration of the body’s weaker comparison statement, and restoration of a later genus condition. None constitutes verification of an author revision.

Section 7, pp. 30–36: the comparison diagram and its kernel isomorphism, rather than an isomorphism of all Lie-algebra cohomology; the use of one-dimensional fibres; torsion freeness of \(\Lambda\) and the inverse-limit hypotheses; the restriction \(p\nmid |W|\) where Weyl invariants are used. The \(\operatorname{GL}_n\) result and the more restricted general reductive result were kept separate. The pointwise continuous exponential yields the claimed condensed comparison and homeomorphism, not an asserted analytic isomorphism.

5. Section 8, pp. 36–44: the double-coset argument, generation and finite presentation for vector bundles, the Fitting-ideal step, reduction from a curve to \(\mathbb P^1\) by a finite flat map, and the dependence of the Higgs-stack comparison on GAGA. The regular spectral-fibre/Picard argument was traced conditional on the cited representability and BNR input.

6. Section 9, pp. 44–48: representation stacks include a \(G\)-torsor on the test space; naive conjugacy classes alone do not give the required stack. The adjunction and faithful-representation reductions were checked. For the degree-zero argument, determinant and tensor reduction, Riemann–Hurwitz, and the growth of sections of a positive-degree subbundle on finite etale covers were checked: \(g'-1=n(g-1)\) and Riemann–Roch gives \(h^0\geq n(d-g+1)\), contradicting the bounded invariant-section space when the tensor power makes \(d>g-1\).

Section 5.5, p. 22, source line 1411, states without a genus restriction that there is an open dense \(\mathcal A^\circ\subseteq\mathcal A\) over which the spectral family is smooth proper with geometrically connected fibres.

Take again \(K=\mathbb C_3\) and \(G=\operatorname{GL}_2\), but let \(X=\mathbb P^1\). These satisfy the subsection’s general curve and group assumptions. Since \(\Omega\simeq\mathcal O(-2)\) as a line bundle, \[H^0(X,\Omega)=H^0(X,\Omega^2)=0.\] Thus \(\mathcal A\) is the single zero point and its spectral cover has equation \(t^2=0\). It is a nonreduced finite flat double cover of \(X\), so it is not smooth. A dense open of this one-point base must contain that point; none has the asserted property.

For an elliptic curve, \(\Omega\) is trivial and the coefficients of the degree-two spectral polynomial are constants in \(K\). If it has distinct roots, the cover is the disjoint union of two copies of \(X\), hence is smooth but disconnected. A repeated root gives a nonreduced cover. Thus there is no smooth geometrically connected spectral fibre in this case either.
