report: Abstract: This claim-focused review concerns the acquired author manuscript arXiv:1909.07649v3, not an independently compared journal version. A false assertion about geometric injectivity of saturation occurs in the proof of Lemma 8.4, on the dependency path to associativity. An explicit family of monoids disproves that assertion. The offending points are outside the actual closed monomial fibre: a direct argument restores the particular uniqueness statement needed there. The supported judgment is Major for the demonstrated core proof-step defect, with no demonstrated counterexample to the lemma or the main theorems. The checked scope comprises 90 of 175 text pages and 68 visually inspected original pages. This is not a whole-paper correctness certification.
Title: Initial scientific review of Intrinsic mirror symmetry
# Identity, version, and scope

Paper M25-0039 is Mark Gross and Bernd Siebert, Intrinsic mirror symmetry, DOI https://doi.org/10.1090/jams/1066. The reviewed PDF is https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.07649v3, submitted 30 September 2025, with internal date 1 October 2025, 175 PDF pages. Page references below use the PDF’s one-based page numbers, which agree with its printed numbering. The locally acquired released source is the corresponding v3 source tree. In particular, PDF Section 8 is in the file `section7.tex`.

The source manifest identifies this as an author manuscript. The journal version was not acquired or compared; the source-preparation record reports an AMS rate limit. The official arXiv abstract record was also consulted for version identity. Its version description is not proof of equality with journal pagination or text. This report makes no claim that the identified issue persists in the journal version, and does not claim an exhaustive later-version or erratum search.

Text actually read: pp. 1–24, 35–38, 51–61, 69–83, 93–100, 105–106, and 132–157 (90 pages). Original images actually inspected: pp. 1, 7, 10–16, 19–23, 35–37, 51–54, 57–60, 69, 73–75, 81–83, 93–100, 105–106, and 132–157 (68 pages). The exact machine-readable lists are in `coverage.json` and `evidence/visual_inspection.json`. Extraction of all pages and rendering 90 pages are recorded separately and are not counted as reading or visual inspection.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and checked structure

The setup is over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Basic Setup 1.1 requires a projective logarithmically smooth map to a point or to the specified non-complete logarithmic curve, with the stated Zariski and global-generation hypotheses. Basic Setup 1.6 includes the curve-class monoid, finite-type stable-map conditions, and the co-Artinian monomial ideal. These assumptions are substantive inputs to finiteness and properness.

Theorem 1.9 allows the logarithmic first Chern class to be nef or anti-nef. Theorem 1.15 instead uses the log Calabi–Yau setup, the nonnegative boundary coefficients for the negative logarithmic first Chern class, and the subcomplex \(B\) of good rays. It does not replace \(B(\mathbb Z)\) with all of \(\Sigma(X)(\mathbb Z)\). The structure constants use a logarithmic point constraint and a negative output contact order; they are defined to vanish unless \(A\cdot c_1(\Theta_{X/k})=0\).
# Problem 1: saturation is not globally injective on geometric points
## Location and exact logical issue

Equation reference: eq:normalization. Lemma 8.4, proof Step 3, p. 142, introduces \(P=Q_\lambda^{\mathrm{fine}}=Q\oplus_R^{\mathrm{fine}}R_\lambda\subset Q^\mathrm{gp}\). It then reasons from torsion-freeness of \(Q^\mathrm{gp}\), and hence of the saturation \(P^\mathrm{sat}\), to geometric injectivity of \[\operatorname{Spec}k[P^\mathrm{sat}]\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}k[P].
\tag{1}\] This implication is false. The same statement is present in released `section7.tex`, lines 451–454, so it is not a PDF extraction error. Step 4 uses Step 3 to establish pure-dimensionality in Lemma 8.4(1).
## Complete countercheck of the asserted affine-chart implication

Equation reference: eq:explicit. Take \(k=\mathbb C\), fix integers \(\mu\geq1\) and \(N\geq1\), and set \[Q=\mathbb Ne_1+\mathbb Ne_2,\quad
 \delta=e_2,\quad \ell_q=2e_1+\mu e_2,\quad \ell=\ell_q,\quad
 \lambda=\mu+2N.\] Thus \(Q\) is a sharp rank-two fine saturated monoid, \(Q^\mathrm{gp}=\mathbb Z^2\) is torsion-free, and \(Q\) is rationally generated by \(\delta\) and \(\ell_q-\mu\delta=2e_1\), as in the nearby local model of Lemma 8.3. Let \[R=\mathbb N\delta+\mathbb N\ell,\qquad
 R_\lambda=\mathbb N\delta+\mathbb N(\ell-\lambda\delta)\subset R^\mathrm{gp}.\] These are fine saturated free monoids in their own common group: \(R^\mathrm{gp}=R_\lambda^\mathrm{gp}\). Use the homomorphism \(\theta:R\to Q\) with the displayed images. It has the form (8.2) with \(a=1,b=0\). The integral image of the pushout, hence the fine pushout, is \[P=\mathbb Ne_1+\mathbb Ne_2+\mathbb N(2e_1-2Ne_2)\subset\mathbb Z^2.\] Its group is \(\mathbb Z^2\). It is finitely generated, integral and sharp: the functional \((a,b)\mapsto(N+1)a+b\) is positive on each nonzero displayed generator. Its saturation is \[P^\mathrm{sat}=\mathbb Ne_2+\mathbb N(e_1-Ne_2).\] Indeed these two vectors are a lattice basis, of determinant \(-1\), and generate the rational cone of \(P\). Writing \(x=\chi^{e_1}\), \(y=\chi^{e_2}\), \(z=\chi^{2e_1-2Ne_2}\), and \(t=\chi^{e_1-Ne_2}\), one obtains \[k[P]=k[x,y,z]/(x^2-y^{2N}z),\qquad
 k[P^\mathrm{sat}]=k[y,t],\qquad
 x\mapsto y^Nt,\quad y\mapsto y,\quad z\mapsto t^2.
\tag{2}\] For completeness, the relation is the primitive lattice relation on the three generators; the rank-two semigroup algebra has this prime height-one relation ideal. The element \(t\) is integral (\(t^2=z\)) and lies in the fraction field (\(t=x/y^N\)); the polynomial ring \(k[y,t]\) is normal. This also verifies the normalization description directly.

The distinct geometric points \((y,t)=(0,1)\) and \((0,-1)\) both map to \((x,y,z)=(0,0,1)\). Thus (1) is not one-to-one, even though all the stated local algebraic conditions above hold. Taking \(N\) arbitrarily large makes \(\lambda-\mu\) arbitrarily large. A requirement that \(\lambda\) be sufficiently large does not establish the false affine-chart assertion.
## Counterevidence and the exact scope of the counterexample

This is a counterexample to the unrestricted affine-chart assertion in Step 3. It is not an example of two punctured stable maps in the actual fibre of \(i\), and does not refute Lemma 8.4. The counterexample point has \(z=1\), whereas the new positive generator of \(R_\lambda\) vanishes on the closed monomial stratum used in \(B\mathbb G_m^\ddagger\). The paper’s geometric application therefore has a further restriction which excludes precisely these points.

The surrounding argument fixes a geometric ghost stalk, so the disputed sentence admits the intended reading that uniqueness is asserted only over its closed characteristic point. That restricted statement is valid by the argument below. The finding concerns the explicitly written global affine-chart premise; it does not establish a failure of the actual geometric-fibre conclusion.

This restriction is enough to supply a direct replacement argument. It must be stated explicitly instead of asserting injectivity of (1) everywhere. The distinction between the ambient chart and its closed monomial fibre is essential to both the diagnosis and the repair.
## Verified replacement for the needed geometric-fibre statement

Claim 1.  Let \(P\) be a sharp fine monoid embedded in a torsion-free group, and let \(P^\mathrm{sat}\) denote its saturation in \(P^\mathrm{gp}\). The closed monomial point of \(\operatorname{Spec}k[P]\) has exactly one geometric point above it in \(\operatorname{Spec}k[P^\mathrm{sat}]\).

Proof. The saturation is sharp. If \(q\in P^\mathrm{sat}\setminus\{0\}\), then \(mq\in P\setminus\{0\}\) for some positive integer \(m\). At any geometric lift, \((\chi^q)^m=\chi^{mq}=0\), so \(\chi^q=0\) in its residue field. Thus every nonzero monomial has a uniquely determined value. The map sending all such monomials to zero and the zero monomial to one exists because the monoid is sharp, so this determines precisely one geometric point. ◻

Apply this after choosing the local charts already used in Step 3 and trivializing the relevant torus torsors over the algebraically closed residue field. Nonzero elements of the ghost \(Q\) vanish at the chosen geometric point. Nonzero elements of \(R_\lambda\) likewise vanish on the closed monomial classifying stack. Hence every nonzero generator of the fine pushout has value zero. At a nonempty such point a positive generator cannot become a unit: it would have to map both to zero and to a unit. The characteristic monoid is therefore sharp as required. The identity of group completions used in Step 3 supplies the common lattice; no additional character choices arise from a changed group. The claim gives the unique geometric lift required for that fibre.

Together with the finite-surjective saturation and reduced-surjectivity argument already established in Step 3, this gives its intended bijection and supplies the input to Step 4. It proves only the needed geometric-fibre statement. It does not say the underlying nonreduced morphism is an isomorphism, nor that every multiplicity is preserved.

For example, the displayed family has \(K=(y,x^2)\subset k[Q]\), giving \(k[x]/(x^2)\), of length two. The corresponding saturated quotient is \(k[t]/(t^2)\), also of length two, but the induced map sends \(x=y^Nt\) to zero. Thus equality of these lengths is compatible with a nonisomorphic nonreduced morphism, exactly as the caution in footnote 8 on p. 140 allows. General multiplicity matching still uses Lemmas 8.3 and 8.10.
## Impact and judgment

The demonstrated defect is an invalid inference in a stated proof on the associativity dependency path. Under the specified core-contribution calibration its judgment is Major, proof-step defect. This judgment does not rely on an assertion that the entire mirror construction is false, that the repair is difficult, or that an offending ambient toric point is an actual punctured-map point. The closed-fibre repair above is analytically verified. Human acceptance of the finding and repair remains pending, and author adoption has not been requested. The repair is a review contribution, not an attributed author correction.
# Other checks and exclusions
## Product finiteness, degree zero, and the unit

Lemma 4.1 (p. 57) uses the balancing constraint of Remark 2.13 (pp. 35–37): the contact order has a fixed image in the space of global linear functionals. Global generation gives injectivity on each cone, and the finite cone complex gives only finitely many possibilities. The monomial quotient supplies the finite set of relevant classes. Finite units in the curve monoid do not by themselves make the coefficient quotient a field; the review does not use such an assumption.

For degree-zero three-point maps (Lemma 1.18, pp. 51–54), the checked argument uses the stable genus-zero three-point domain, cone balancing, quotienting logarithmic enhancements by the ghost-character action, and \(H^1(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(-1)^d)=0\). The asserted moduli properties still depend on the punctured-map foundations cited by the authors. Input symmetry gives commutativity.

In the unit argument (pp. 93–98), the evaluation correction includes the output contact term and the change in the conormal line. Forgetting a marking and pushing the zero-dimensional class to the dimension-minus-one Artin-stack target gives the required vanishing under the stated obstruction-theory compatibility. The \(A=0\) case and the convention for nonzero Chern degree are separate. The construction and properness of all preceding forgetful stacks were not independently reproved.
## Tropical and virtual-dimension checks

Proposition 4.21 (pp. 73–75) uses a two-dimensional miniversal tropical family, no terminal tail, and an unbounded length at fixed \(\delta\). The checked recurrence for consecutive vertex positions yields a nonnegative splitting direction by rescaling in a closed cone. The case \(r=0\) retains the independent parameter \(\delta\). This does not by itself exclude an internal tail.

For Lemma 7.17 (pp. 133–136), the review checked why the output belongs to the open stratum \(Z_r^\circ\), why \(r\) must lie in \(B(\mathbb Z)\) in the log Calabi–Yau case, and why the tail degree is nonpositive. If a positive boundary coefficient had negative intersection, the negative contact order would force the output component into that boundary divisor, contrary to the point constraint. The relative virtual dimension is \(A_1c_1(\Theta_{X/k})-\dim X\leq-\dim X\). The two-point genus-zero prestable base has dimension \(-1\); integrality and idealized logarithmic etaleness give the strict negative total virtual dimension needed for the cited vanishing theorem. The general virtual-pullback theorem in Appendix A was not independently proved in this review.

For Lemma 8.8 (pp. 144–151), the checked split separates non-dominating components and contact orders outside the skeleton from the remaining no-tail reduction. The finite-type restriction is essential to choose one sufficiently large \(\mu\) for finitely many cone conditions. The \(s=0\) case is explicitly accommodated by footnote 9. For Lemma 8.10 (p. 151), absence of internal tails gives coefficient one in \(\ell=\ell_q+b\delta\), the exact hypothesis needed for multiplicity matching in Lemma 8.3. Theorems 8.11–8.12 compare weighted components after tail vanishing; they do not assume all nonreduced spaces are isomorphic.

In Theorem 8.12 (pp. 152–157), the constraints \(\lambda\geq a+b\) and \(\lambda\geq b+\mu a\) make the chosen node vanish and the splitting factor through the modified base. The argument chooses \(\mu\) before \(\lambda\) after restricting to the finitely many relevant types (pp. 137–138 and 156). The two-sided inverse is asserted on the tail-free locus, where the splitting node is unique. The last monomorphism is a monomorphism of log stacks, justified by the group completion, not an assertion about all underlying stacks.
## Examples and scope clarification

The blow-up and line–conic examples (pp. 20–22) were checked at the level of curve intersections and possible contact orders. For the line–conic pair the equations are \(d=1-a_1,\ 2d=1-a_2\) for the first product, and \(d=2-a_1,\ 2d=2-a_2\) for the second. With nonnegative degree and coefficients these give the listed possibilities. The enumerativity of each punctured invariant is not an independent outcome of those elementary equations.

The relation calculation in Example 4.5 (pp. 59–60) reproduces its coefficient two algebraically. This is a check within the displayed algebraic presentation, not an independent count of maps or a proof of associativity from scratch. For \(\mathbb P^1\) with three boundary points in Example 1.27 (p. 23), the logarithmic tangent bundle has degree \(2-3=-1\), hence is anti-nef. The sign wording there is recorded as an unrated scope/typographical clarification: Theorem 1.9 already allows anti-nefness and Theorem 1.15 uses the negative Chern class. It is not a separate substantive finding.
# Remaining work and conclusion

Eighty-five text pages were not read. In particular, the full evaluation and virtual-smoothness foundations, all forgetful-map constructions, the intermediate adjacent-cone argument, the complete gluing proof, the remainder of Section 9, and Appendix A have not received an independent complete audit here. External punctured-map and virtual-pullback references were not fully reverified. The additional 22 rendered pages that were not displayed are not claimed as visually inspected.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the acquired 69-page author manuscript arXiv:2210.09581v2. All 69 text pages were read and all 69 original page images were inspected. One Major issue and two Minor issues are substantiated: an invalid volume comparison for cubically rounded shadings in Lemma 3.3; a false uniform projection proposition without control of the additive constant of the slope function; and an incorrect mass-retention estimate in the construction of Lemma 8.3. Admissible tests, counterevidence, impacts, and repair limits are provided. None is claimed to disprove the main dimension theorem. Reading every page is not independent verification of every proof: several core transitions and external inputs remain unresolved. The journal version was not compared. The third-party Lean repository was inspected statically only, without a build or kernel validation. Focused acceptance supplies an exact local multiplicity repair for the first issue; current report-build evidence is recorded below.
Title: Initial scientific review of Sticky Kakeya sets and the sticky Kakeya conjecture
# Identity and evidence boundary

Paper M25-0040 is Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl, Sticky Kakeya sets and the sticky Kakeya conjecture, DOI https://doi.org/10.1090/jams/1067. The reviewed PDF is the author manuscript https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.09581v2, submitted 7 October 2025, with internal date 9 October 2025, 69 pages. All page references are one-based PDF pages, equal to printed numbering. The source filename `251007_sticky_kakeya_final.tex` does not establish equality with a journal proof or published text.
The PDF SHA-256 is
The main TeX SHA-256 is

Acquired files, extraction/render logs, original page images, own arithmetic checks, and source excerpts are retained under `verification/0040/evidence/`. The source-preparation record reports an AMS rate limit. Findings apply to the acquired author version; no persistence in the journal text is asserted. The limited primary-source lookup did not establish an exhaustive later-version or erratum history.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and checked dependency structure

Stickiness controls packing dimension of the family of lines, not merely its Hausdorff dimension. The near-sticky formulation has the order for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\eta>0\). Section 2 uses the bounded line chart \(\mathcal L_n\), a fixed dimensional tube thickness, and shadings that are unions of \(\delta\)-grid cubes. Covering is defined through the line metric.

Definition 2.1 requires essential distinctness, a directional multiplicity bound for covers at every intermediate scale, and a lower bound for total shading mass. A leaf-scale condition alone is insufficient. \(M(s,t,\delta)\) is an infimum of union volume subject to these conditions. \(N(s,t)\) uses a limsup of logarithmic ratios; \(\sigma_n\) is obtained in the small-parameter regime. Extremal families are obtained along a sequence, not necessarily at every small scale. In the checked argument of Proposition 2.1, packing dimension supplies a countable upper-box decomposition, followed by a positive-direction piece and scale pigeonholing. The sign reversal on dividing by \(\log\delta<0\) and the limsup choice are essential.
# F1 — Minor: an unnecessary rounded-volume equivalence fails
## Location and precise claim

Definition 3.2, p. 11, defines rescaled shading as the union of \((\delta/\rho)\)-cubes meeting the affine image of the shading. In Lemma 3.3, pp. 12–13, equation (3.5) asserts, for \(n=3\), \[\left|\bigcup_{T\in\mathbb T}Y(T)\right|
 \sim \rho^2
 \left|\bigcup_{\widehat T\in\widehat{\mathbb T}}
              \widehat Y(\widehat T)\right|.
 \tag{F1.1}\] Its justification (3.4) is a Jacobian identity for raw images, not for their cubical enlargement. Relevant TeX lines are 420–425, 456–494, and 516–526. The final average-multiplicity identity on p. 13 also needs a separate justification after enlargement.
## An admissible family

Fix \(\varepsilon=1/4\). For any \(\eta>0\) selected by the lemma, put \[a=\min(\eta/2,1/8),\quad \rho=\delta^{1/2},\quad
 L=\lceil\delta^{-a}\rceil,\quad h=\delta/\rho.\] As \(\delta\to0\), we have \(\rho\in[\delta^{1-\varepsilon},1]\), \(L\rho\to0\), and \(a<\eta\). Let \(c=c(3)>0\) be the fixed constant in Definition 3.2. Choose a fixed \(K\ge100/c\), enlarged by a dimensional constant if needed. For \[u\in(K\delta\mathbb Z)^2\cap[-\rho/1000,\rho/1000]^2\] take the tube \(T_u\) with axis \(\ell_u=\{(uz,z):z\in\mathbb R\}\). There are \(J\asymp_K(\rho/\delta)^2\) such tubes. Their lines pass through the origin, are in \(\mathcal L_3\), and have third unit-direction coordinate at least \(1/2\). Direction separation is at least a fixed multiple of \(K\delta\), so the tubes are essentially distinct. The vertical \(\rho\)-tube covers them all.

For every \(\tau\in[\delta,1]\), choose a maximal angular net in this cap at a sufficiently small fixed multiple of \(\tau\), with the same base point. The corresponding \(\tau\)-tubes cover the family. Sphere packing gives only \(O(1)\) members essentially parallel to any common \(\tau\)-tube, hence at most \(\delta^{-\eta}\) for sufficiently small \(\delta\). This verifies the full every-scale hypothesis.

For integers \(m\) with \(mL\delta\in[1/2,3/4-\delta]\), choose the grid cube \(Q_{u,m}\) containing \[(u(mL\delta+\delta/2),\,mL\delta+\delta/2).\] Use a fixed half-open grid convention; boundaries have no volume. Every cube lies within \(\sqrt3\delta\) of the axis and inside the ambient cube, so it is a legitimate shading cube. Let \(Y(T_u)=\bigcup_m Q_{u,m}\). At these heights, distinct slopes are separated by a fixed multiple of \(K\delta\), and different layers are disjoint. All chosen cubes are disjoint, so the shading multiplicity equals one. With \(M\asymp(L\delta)^{-1}\) layers, \[|E|=\sum_u|Y(T_u)|=JM\delta^3\asymp_K\rho^2/L
 \ge\delta^\eta\rho^2\] for sufficiently small \(\delta\), since \(a<\eta\). Thus all hypotheses of Lemma 3.3 hold. That lemma does not assume extremality of its input.
## Failure after every permitted refinement

The rescaling here is \[\phi(x,y,z)=(cx/\rho,cy/\rho,cz),\qquad
 |\det\phi|=c^3\rho^{-2}.\] The rescaled axes remain essentially distinct by the choice of \(K\). Any permitted refinement retains a polylogarithmic fraction of shading mass. Its shadings remain unions of the original disjoint fine cubes; denote their union by \(E'\).

An \(h\)-grid cube can meet images of at most \(C/(L\rho)\) retained cubes from one tube: its vertical preimage has length at most \(h/c+O(\delta)\), whereas layers have period \(L\delta\). It cannot meet images from two distinct tubes. At the chosen heights their rescaled horizontal separation is at least a fixed multiple of \(cKh\). Variation within a coarse vertical cell and the widths of images are only \(O(h)\), and the fixed choice of \(K\) separates them.

Assign each retained fine cube to any coarse cube meeting its image. If \(N'\) fine cubes are retained, at least \(c_0N'L\rho\) distinct coarse cubes are assigned. The rounded union satisfies \[|\widehat E'|\ge c_0N'L\rho h^3
             =c_0L\rho^{-2}|E'|.\] A permitted refinement has \(|E'|\ge(\log(1/\delta))^{-C_1}|E|\) for a fixed \(C_1\). It follows that \[\frac{\rho^2|\widehat E'|}{|E|}
 \ge c_0L(\log(1/\delta))^{-C_1}\longrightarrow\infty.
 \tag{F1.2}\] The power growth beats every fixed polylogarithmic loss. Thus (3.5) fails even after the allowed refinement and even if its comparability notation tolerates polylogarithms.
## Counterevidence and the exact error boundary

The Jacobian identity for \(\phi(E')\) is correct. Definition 3.2 and Figure 1 explicitly include rounding, so \(\widehat Y\) cannot simply be read as a raw image. A constant-multiplicity refinement does not fix the issue: this example already has multiplicity one, and (F1.2) holds for every allowed mass-retaining refinement.

This does not disprove the conclusion of Lemma 3.3. Its original multiplicity is one and satisfies that conclusion. The example is not claimed to be extremal for Proposition 3.2. It disproves the precise intermediate volume comparison under the hypotheses of its proof. The final multiplicity identity needs a separate justification, but this multiplicity-one example alone does not disprove that separate identity.
## A sufficient multiplicity inequality and verified local repair

Set \(h=\delta/\rho\), and retain the constant-multiplicity refinement \((\mathbb T',Y')_\delta\) constructed in the proof. Write its multiplicity as \(\mu\), and let \((\widehat{\mathbb T},\widehat Y)_h\) be its unit rescaling. Every \(h\)-cube \(Q\) in \(\widehat E=\bigcup_{\widehat T}\widehat Y(\widehat T)\) meets \(\phi(E_{\mathbb T'})\). Choose \(q=\phi(p)\) in that intersection. Since \(p\) belongs to exactly \(\mu\) retained original shadings, \(Q\) belongs to at least \(\mu\) rounded shadings. These correspond to distinct tubes: \(\phi\) is invertible, and the preceding refinement makes the rescaled coaxial lines essentially distinct. Thus, integrating over the half-open grid cubes, \[\mu|\widehat E|
 \le \sum_{\widehat T\in\widehat{\mathbb T}}|\widehat Y(\widehat T)|.
 \tag{F1.3}\] Repeated intersections of a cube with one tube do not enter this count. No rounded-volume equivalence is used.

This proves the precise multiplicity conclusion of Lemma 3.3 used in Proposition 3.2, Step 2, within the existing parameter hierarchy. Delete (3.5), and replace the final multiplicity equality by (F1.3). The demonstrated error concerns an unnecessary stronger volume equivalence; the inspected downstream argument needs only the valid one-sided inequality. Its classification is therefore Minor on the basis of actual dependence, rather than the length or ease of repair. The false volume equivalence is not restored, and this local repair does not certify the remaining steps of Proposition 3.2 or the main theorem.
# F2 — Major: Proposition 7.1 omits intercept control
## Location and uniform quantifiers

Proposition 7.1 and (7.1), p. 47, assert \[\left\|\sum_{T\in\mathbb T}\chi_{\pi_f(T)}\right\|_{L^{3/2}(\mathbb R^2)}
 \le\delta^{-1-\varepsilon},\qquad
 \pi_f(x,y,z)=(x+f(z)y,z),
 \tag{F2.1}\] for direction-separated tubes and \(1\le|f'|\le2\), \(|f''|\le1/100\). The threshold \(\delta_0\) is chosen from \(\varepsilon\) before \(f\). There is no condition on \(f(0)\) or \(\|f\|_\infty\). Lemma 7.3 on p. 47 does assume \(f(0)=0\). Its proof and the proof of Proposition 7.1 on p. 48 use the resulting bound on \(|f|\). Relevant TeX lines are 2027–2034, 2068–2077, and 2109–2125.
## Complete counterexample
## A normalized local replacement

Adding \(f(0)=0\) gives \(|f|\le2\) on \([-1,1]\). Conditional on the cited Pramanik–Yang–Zahl theorem, the following verifies the intended local projection argument. For \(g=a+bf+dtf\) the coefficient-to-jet matrix is \[A(t)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&f&tf\\0&f'&f+tf'\\0&f''&2f'+tf''
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \det A(t)=2(f')^2-ff''\ge1.98.\] Entries and inverse are uniformly bounded. The coefficient norm, the pointwise jet norm, and the induced \(C^2\) norm have the required uniform comparisons. This gives cinematic separation and diameter bounds. Three-dimensional coefficient space gives a uniform doubling constant. The two halves of \([-1,1]\) are treated using \(f(t)\) and \(f(-t)\).

Partition directions into fixed charts and \(O(\delta^{-1})\) bins for the first slope. In each bin the second slopes are separated up to bounded multiplicity. Norm equivalence bounds the number of curves in any \(C^2\) ball of radius \(r\ge\delta\) by \(O(r/\delta)\). Bounded \(f\) puts every projected tube inside a fixed \(C\delta\)-neighborhood of its graph. The literal \(2\delta\) constant is unnecessary and must accommodate the manuscript’s dimensional tube thickness. Apply the cinematic estimate with a smaller auxiliary loss and sum the bins; after reducing \(\delta_0\), the bound is \(\delta^{-1-\varepsilon}\).

The external text actually consulted was Definition 1.6, Theorem 1.7, and its whole-plane consequence in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.02259v1. Its Frostman scale range is \(r\ge\delta\) and its loss parameter can be chosen below the target loss. Its proof was not independently reconstructed. The statement was first read as retrieved text. After an unsuccessful browser screenshot request, the exact v1 PDF was acquired, and its original p. 3 was rendered and actually inspected. The saved external PDF, page image, acquisition hash, and inspection record are in the evidence directory. This does not constitute verification of the external theorem’s proof.
## Counterevidence and the unresolved preceding interface

The introductory outline on p. 5 has a bounded \(C^2\) norm, and Lemma 7.3 explicitly has the normalization. These favor a missing-hypothesis interpretation, but do not insert the condition into Proposition 7.1. Proposition 6.1, p. 46, uses \(\widetilde f(z)=100m^{-2}f(mz/100)\), which can enlarge an unchecked intercept. After translating a height \(z_0\) to zero, the bounded shear \(x'=x+f(z_0)y\) subtracts the intercept before derivative rescaling. The preceding bounded \(C^2\) class makes this shear controlled. Its effects on the tube chart, lengths, separation, shadings, and all exponent losses still need full verification. That interface is not completed here. The final uniform estimate is false as stated on the main dependency chain, so the classification is Major. The normalized replacement is compatible with the intended main conclusion; no main-theorem counterexample is established.
# F3 — Minor: the specified threshold does not retain \(1-c\) mass
## Location and admissible test

Lemma 8.3, p. 53, starts with a Borel set \(E\) of product probability at least \(1-c\). It forms \(E'\) from the whole product grid cells whose relative \(E\)-density is at least \(c\), then asserts that the discarded mass is less than \(c\). Relevant source lines are 2347–2361; the thin-tube estimate continues on p. 54.

Let \(c=1/10\), let \(G_1\) be one \(\delta\)-square, and let \(G_2\) consist of 200 disjoint \(\delta\)-squares. For sufficiently small \(\delta\) they fit inside the unit square. Each product cell has probability \(1/200\). Let \(E\) fill 179 cells and occupy a measurable coordinate slice of relative volume \(1/20\) in each of the other 21. Then \[(
u_1	imes
u_2)(E)
 = rac{179+21/20}{200}
 = rac{3601}{4000}> rac9{10}.\] Set \( eta=0\) and \(K=1\). For every base point, every line through it, and every \(r>0\), the thin-tube slice has \(
u_2\)-measure at most \(1=Kr^0\). All continuous thin-tube hypotheses therefore hold.

The prescribed threshold discards the 21 partly filled cells. It gives \[|E'|/(|G_1||G_2|)=179/200<9/10.\] This disproves the mass assertion for that construction, not existence of some other discretized thin-tube set. For this \(\beta=0\) example, the whole product already works.
## A verified weaker replacement and its limits

If the discarded cells have total probability \(q\), their missing \(E\)-density is greater than \(1-c\). Thus \[(1-c)q\le1-(\nu_1\times\nu_2)(E)\le c,\qquad
 q\le c/(1-c)\le2c\quad(0<c<1/2).\] The construction retains at least \(1-2c\). It also gives thin-tube constant \(5^\beta K/c\). Indeed, any \(\delta\)-square meeting \(N_r(\ell)\) is inside \(N_{(1+\sqrt2)r}(\ell)\) when \(r\ge\delta\). Moving the line parallel to a different point in the base square adds at most \(\sqrt2r\), so radius \(5r\) suffices. Integrate the original bound over the base square and use the density threshold \(c\) to obtain the factor \(K/c\). This proves a replacement with retained mass \(1-2c\). The endpoint \(c=0\) is excluded, consistently with division by \(c\) in the asserted constant.

A continuous loss \(3c\) followed by this discretization is bounded by \(6c\). After \(N\) fixed bootstrap steps, a fixed multiple of \(6^Nc\) replaces one of \(3^Nc\). In the application \(c\) is a positive power of \(\delta\), whereas \(N\) depends only on fixed parameters. For example, \(2\cdot6^N\delta^{\alpha'}\le\delta^{\alpha'/2}\) holds after reducing the scale threshold. This changes constants and thresholds, not the powers in that particular bookkeeping step. Thin-tube constants must also be updated through the recurrence. The other steps of Lemma 8.8 and the external bootstrap are not certified by this calculation.

This is Minor: the specified construction is invalid but a weaker bound has the required finite-iteration type of loss. Exact retention \(1-c\) in the original lemma has not been recovered, nor has the whole Section 8 proof been repaired.
# Other checked steps and explicit unresolved transitions
These are substantive checks with the stated limitations, not a whole-proof certification.

The Section 4 broad/narrow mechanism was checked at the level of determinant transversality, weak planiness, and transverse pairs, conditional on multilinear Kakeya. The planar hairbrush sum has the harmonic inverse-angle loss. The plane-field comparison uses a slab error of order \(\tau^2\) and needs \(\tau^2\le\rho\) where applied.

Theorem 5.2 has different quantifiers in its two alternatives. The large-projection alternative concerns every admissible large hypergraph and can be vacuous if the sets are too small. In its application, the target loss must be smaller than \(\sigma\) to contradict the AD upper bound of dimension \(1-\sigma\). This is on the contradiction branch \(\sigma>0\). In the nested-rectangle construction, matching cutoff jets, disjoint support at each level, and telescoping on the finest chain explain the intended \(C^2\) bound. Summability requires a small auxiliary exponent; literal cutoff constants and unrestricted parameter wording have not been certified.

The inequality in Lemma 6.2 gives \[\delta^\varepsilon\tau\rho^{-1/2}
 \le\delta^{-\varepsilon}(\tau\rho^{-1/2})^\alpha
 \ \Longrightarrow\
 \tau\le\delta^{-2\varepsilon/(1-\alpha)}\rho^{1/2}.\] Here \(\alpha<1\) is essential. The small-derivative branch of Lemma 6.3 crowds directions and needs the right order of \(\sigma\), losses, and \(\eta\). The mass/Hölder calculation of Corollary 6.5 gives exponent \(-1-\sigma/3+O(\varepsilon)\) conditional on the preceding refinements and bounded projection width in F2.

The charging argument of Lemma 8.1 allocates losses over the finitely many coordinate subsets and gives the stated retained-density estimate. The checked energy computation in Theorem 8.2 uses \(\gamma<\alpha\le\beta\le1\) and the indicated dependence on Frostman constant and retained mass. In Proposition 8.5, the fact that \(\lambda\) depends on the target loss but not the later non-concentration exponent is necessary for the subsequent choice order.
The following remain unrated, because full hypothesis checks or complete propagation have not been established:
1. The skew coordinates on pp. 35–36 require a unified check of the translated slope argument, a sign in the dot-product expression, and the coordinate ordering.

2. The close-pair cutoff and angular estimates in Lemma 8.8, pp. 57–58, need a complete reconstruction. The apparent exponent and distance-factor concerns have not been turned into an admissible counterexample or full repair.

3. On pp. 63–65 the dual affine map is described as a transpose. For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/w)\), the needed identity uses \(D=w^{-1}A^{-T}=\operatorname{diag}(1/w,1)\): \[a\cdot(b_1-b_2)=w\,Da\cdot A(b_1-b_2).\] The complete transfer of grids, Frostman constants, and hypergraph density under the intended maps remains unchecked.
4. The unrestricted plane-field formulation and the piecewise-constant fields used in applications, including all associated losses, need reconciliation.

Reciprocal/sign slips in some displayed small-power estimates were not counted as additional findings. The false volume comparison in F1 persists after those slips are corrected, but (F1.3) supplies the multiplicity argument actually needed. The above unresolved points are remaining work, not substantiated errors.

With \(M\asymp(L\delta)^{-1}\) layers, \[|E|=\sum_u|Y(T_u)|=JM\delta^3\asymp_K\rho^2/L
 \ge\delta^\eta\rho^2\] for sufficiently small \(\delta\), since \(a<\eta\). Thus all hypotheses of Lemma 3.3 hold. That lemma does not assume extremality of its input.

The rescaling here is \[\phi(x,y,z)=(cx/\rho,cy/\rho,cz),\qquad
 |\det\phi|=c^3\rho^{-2}.\] The rescaled axes remain essentially distinct by the choice of \(K\). Any permitted refinement retains a polylogarithmic fraction of shading mass. Its shadings remain unions of the original disjoint fine cubes; denote their union by \(E'\).

An \(h\)-grid cube can meet images of at most \(C/(L\rho)\) retained cubes from one tube: its vertical preimage has length at most \(h/c+O(\delta)\), whereas layers have period \(L\delta\). It cannot meet images from two distinct tubes. At the chosen heights their rescaled horizontal separation is at least a fixed multiple of \(cKh\). Variation within a coarse vertical cell and the widths of images are only \(O(h)\), and the fixed choice of \(K\) separates them.

Assign each retained fine cube to any coarse cube meeting its image. If \(N'\) fine cubes are retained, at least \(c_0N'L\rho\) distinct coarse cubes are assigned. The rounded union satisfies \[|\widehat E'|\ge c_0N'L\rho h^3
             =c_0L\rho^{-2}|E'|.\] A permitted refinement has \(|E'|\ge(\log(1/\delta))^{-C_1}|E|\) for a fixed \(C_1\). It follows that \[\frac{\rho^2|\widehat E'|}{|E|}
 \ge c_0L(\log(1/\delta))^{-C_1}\longrightarrow\infty.
 \tag{F1.2}\] The power growth beats every fixed polylogarithmic loss. Thus (3.5) fails even after the allowed refinement and even if its comparability notation tolerates polylogarithms.

Set \(h=\delta/\rho\), and retain the constant-multiplicity refinement \((\mathbb T',Y')_\delta\) constructed in the proof. Write its multiplicity as \(\mu\), and let \((\widehat{\mathbb T},\widehat Y)_h\) be its unit rescaling. Every \(h\)-cube \(Q\) in \(\widehat E=\bigcup_{\widehat T}\widehat Y(\widehat T)\) meets \(\phi(E_{\mathbb T'})\). Choose \(q=\phi(p)\) in that intersection. Since \(p\) belongs to exactly \(\mu\) retained original shadings, \(Q\) belongs to at least \(\mu\) rounded shadings. These correspond to distinct tubes: \(\phi\) is invertible, and the preceding refinement makes the rescaled coaxial lines essentially distinct. Thus, integrating over the half-open grid cubes, \[\mu|\widehat E|
 \le \sum_{\widehat T\in\widehat{\mathbb T}}|\widehat Y(\widehat T)|.
 \tag{F1.3}\] Repeated intersections of a cube with one tube do not enter this count. No rounded-volume equivalence is used.

This proves the precise multiplicity conclusion of Lemma 3.3 used in Proposition 3.2, Step 2, within the existing parameter hierarchy. Delete (3.5), and replace the final multiplicity equality by (F1.3). The demonstrated error concerns an unnecessary stronger volume equivalence; the inspected downstream argument needs only the valid one-sided inequality. Its classification is therefore Minor on the basis of actual dependence, rather than the length or ease of repair. The false volume equivalence is not restored, and this local repair does not certify the remaining steps of Proposition 3.2 or the main theorem.
result: The Jacobian identity for \(\phi(E')\) is correct. Definition 3.2 and Figure 1 explicitly include rounding, so \(\widehat Y\) cannot simply be read as a raw image. A constant-multiplicity refinement does not fix the issue: this example already has multiplicity one, and (F1.2) holds for every allowed mass-retaining refinement.

This does not disprove the conclusion of Lemma 3.3. Its original multiplicity is one and satisfies that conclusion. The example is not claimed to be extremal for Proposition 3.2. It disproves the precise intermediate volume comparison under the hypotheses of its proof. The final multiplicity identity needs a separate justification, but this multiplicity-one example alone does not disprove that separate identity.

The valid inequality mu*|Ehat|<=sum|Yhat| and the original parameter hierarchy restore the exact Lemma 3.3 conclusion used in Proposition 3.2 Step 2. Recorded check: Uniform projection proposition lacks intercept control
analysis:
Proposition 7.1 and (7.1), p. 47, assert \[\left\|\sum_{T\in\mathbb T}\chi_{\pi_f(T)}\right\|_{L^{3/2}(\mathbb R^2)}
 \le\delta^{-1-\varepsilon},\qquad
 \pi_f(x,y,z)=(x+f(z)y,z),
 \tag{F2.1}\] for direction-separated tubes and \(1\le|f'|\le2\), \(|f''|\le1/100\). The threshold \(\delta_0\) is chosen from \(\varepsilon\) before \(f\). There is no condition on \(f(0)\) or \(\|f\|_\infty\). Lemma 7.3 on p. 47 does assume \(f(0)=0\). Its proof and the proof of Proposition 7.1 on p. 48 use the resulting bound on \(|f|\). Relevant TeX lines are 2027–2034, 2068–2077, and 2109–2125.

Adding \(f(0)=0\) gives \(|f|\le2\) on \([-1,1]\). Conditional on the cited Pramanik–Yang–Zahl theorem, the following verifies the intended local projection argument. For \(g=a+bf+dtf\) the coefficient-to-jet matrix is \[A(t)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&f&tf\\0&f'&f+tf'\\0&f''&2f'+tf''
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \det A(t)=2(f')^2-ff''\ge1.98.\] Entries and inverse are uniformly bounded. The coefficient norm, the pointwise jet norm, and the induced \(C^2\) norm have the required uniform comparisons. This gives cinematic separation and diameter bounds. Three-dimensional coefficient space gives a uniform doubling constant. The two halves of \([-1,1]\) are treated using \(f(t)\) and \(f(-t)\).

Partition directions into fixed charts and \(O(\delta^{-1})\) bins for the first slope. In each bin the second slopes are separated up to bounded multiplicity. Norm equivalence bounds the number of curves in any \(C^2\) ball of radius \(r\ge\delta\) by \(O(r/\delta)\). Bounded \(f\) puts every projected tube inside a fixed \(C\delta\)-neighborhood of its graph. The literal \(2\delta\) constant is unnecessary and must accommodate the manuscript’s dimensional tube thickness. Apply the cinematic estimate with a smaller auxiliary loss and sum the bins; after reducing \(\delta_0\), the bound is \(\delta^{-1-\varepsilon}\).

The external text actually consulted was Definition 1.6, Theorem 1.7, and its whole-plane consequence in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2207.02259v1. Its Frostman scale range is \(r\ge\delta\) and its loss parameter can be chosen below the target loss. Its proof was not independently reconstructed. The statement was first read as retrieved text. After an unsuccessful browser screenshot request, the exact v1 PDF was acquired, and its original p. 3 was rendered and actually inspected. result: The introductory outline on p. 5 has a bounded \(C^2\) norm, and Lemma 7.3 explicitly has the normalization. After translating a height \(z_0\) to zero, the bounded shear \(x'=x+f(z_0)y\) subtracts the intercept before derivative rescaling. The preceding bounded \(C^2\) class makes this shear controlled. Its effects on the tube chart, lengths, separation, shadings, and all exponent losses still need full verification. That interface is not completed here. The final uniform estimate is false as stated on the main dependency chain, so the classification is Major. The normalized replacement is compatible with the intended main conclusion; no main-theorem counterexample is established.
Impact: False uniform statement is the final projection bound compared with Corollary 6.5 to force sigma=0.

u_1	imes
u_2)(E)

u_2\)-measure at most \(1=Kr^0\). All continuous thin-tube hypotheses therefore hold.

report: Abstract: This review checks selected definitions, the annulus calculation used for the Tate twist, and specified steps of the cancellation argument in arXiv:2412.03382v3. One Major finding concerns a false root-location criterion used to identify the coefficient fibers in Proposition 5.19, whose annulus model and compactness enter the cancellation proof. An exact counterexample and a complete local correction are given. The corrected coefficient domain remains contractible, so the finding does not refute Proposition 5.19 or the cancellation theorem. No additional substantive issue was established in the inspected scope. The journal version was not compared with this author manuscript.
Date: 25 October 2026

Title: Focused initial verification of
Berkovich motives
# Identity, version, and review scope

The assigned paper is M25-0041, Peter Scholze, Berkovich motives, journal DOI 10.1090/jams/1068. The actual reviewed object is the 65-page author manuscript arXiv:2412.03382v3, submitted 22 January 2026; its first page internally dates the document 23 January 2026. All page references below are one-based PDF pages, equal to the printed manuscript page numbers. The source SHA-256 and the separately acquired TeX binding are recorded in Appendix 6 (#app:provenance).

The current arXiv record describes v3 as the final author version, but this is not a bytewise or textual comparison against the publisher’s version. The journal record has an electronic publication date in 2025 and a 2026 volume designation. Findings here apply only to the pinned author manuscript. Neither the annual assignment nor the journal title converts the acquired manuscript into a verified journal-final source.

Text was read on pp. 1–6, 18–20, 24–28, 33–36, 40–43, and 53–54. The substantive checks below concern the definitions on pp. 3 and 26, Proposition 5.6, Proposition 5.19, selected steps in Theorem 7.1 and Lemma 7.3, and the hypotheses of Theorem 1.12 and Proposition 10.3. All source pages specifically used as decisive evidence were also visually inspected: 1, 3, 6, 24, 26–28, 34–35, 40–43, 53–54. Merely extracting all 65 pages was not counted as reading or verification.

This is a claim-focused initial review. It does not independently reconstruct every descent argument, all of Theorem 6.3, the construction of the six-functor formalism, the general existence and descent of the spaces in the cancellation correspondence, or the generation argument of Proposition 10.1. These are explicit remaining dependencies, not findings of invalidity.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and checked implications

An effective motive is a finitary, ball-invariant arc-hypersheaf of complexes. The finitary requirement in Definition 1.2 is tested on filtered colimits of strictly totally disconnected Banach rings; it is not asserted for arbitrary filtered colimits of every Banach ring. Definition 5.1 requires \[M(A)\longrightarrow M(A\langle T\rangle_1)\] to be an equivalence for every Banach ring over the base. Corollary 5.4 reduces this test to nondiscrete algebraically closed Banach fields using arc-descent and the preservation of finitary sheaves in Theorem 4.20. That theorem explicitly assumes a proper, zero-truncated map of finite cohomological dimension. Omitting its finiteness assumption would change the argument.

For Proposition 5.6 (pp. 27–28), the checked local implication is the passage from equality of endpoint pullbacks to ball-invariance. Let \(p:\mathbb B_A\to A\) and let \(i:A\to\mathbb B_A\) be the zero section. Then \(p i=\mathrm{id}\), while multiplication \(H(s,t)=st\) joins \(i p\) to \(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb B_A}\). Consequently, once the stated endpoint homotopy for the localized presheaf is available, \[i^*p^*=\mathrm{id},\qquad p^*i^*\simeq\mathrm{id}.\] Thus \(p^*\) is an equivalence. This verifies that specific implication; it is not a replacement proof of all coherence and descent statements needed to construct the localization.

The relative rigidity statement retains its hypotheses: Theorem 1.12 (p. 6) and Proposition 10.3 (p. 54) require an analytic Banach base of finite cohomological dimension in the affine case. The more general version on p. 54 adds qcqs and the specified quasi-pro-étale geometric-point condition. No unconditional rigidity assertion for an arbitrary small arc-stack is inferred.
# Problem 1: the annulus coefficient criterion is false
## Exact claim and location

Equation reference: eq:printed. In the proof of Proposition 5.19, pp. 34–35, fix \(\mathbb T(r_1,r_2)=\{z:r_1<|z|<r_2\}\), with \(0<r_1<1<r_2\), and a monic polynomial \[f(X)=X^n+a_{n-1}X^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1X+a_0,
\qquad r_1^n<|a_0|<r_2^n.\] The first display on p. 35 characterizes all roots lying in \(\mathbb T\) by \[
|a_i|<\max\{r_2^{\,n-i},|a_0|r_1^{-i}\},
\qquad 1\leq i<n.\] The same \(\max\) is present in the acquired TeX at line 1267. This is not a PDF-extraction ambiguity.
## Exact counterexample and all assumptions

Take \(C=\mathbb C_3\), the completed algebraic closure of \(\mathbb Q_3\), with \(|3|=1/3\). It is a nondiscrete algebraically closed nonarchimedean Banach field, so its geometric-point base meets the reduction used in the proof. Choose \[n=2,\quad r_1=1/27,\quad r_2=3,\quad
f(X)=(X-9)(X-1/9)=X^2-\frac{82}{9}X+1.\] Both radii belong to the value group, \(0<r_1<1<r_2\), and \[r_1^2=\frac1{729}<|a_0|=1<9=r_2^2.\] Since \(82\) is not divisible by \(3\), \[|a_1|=\left|-\frac{82}{9}\right|_3=9
 <\max\{3,27\}=27.\] Thus every inequality in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) holds. Nevertheless the exact roots have norms \[|9|_3=\frac19,\qquad |1/9|_3=9.\] The second root lies outside the upper boundary \(3\). The printed criterion is therefore false even in degree two and within the stated nonarchimedean setting. Exact rational arithmetic independently verified both roots and every displayed comparison; no floating-point root solver was used.
## Correct criterion and proof

Equation reference: eq:correct. The correct criterion is \[
|a_i|<\min\{r_2^{\,n-i},|a_0|r_1^{-i}\},
\qquad 1\leq i<n.\] Here and below the assumed bounds on \(a_0\) remain in force.

Necessity. If the roots are \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\), all with \(r_1<|\alpha_j|<r_2\), the ultrametric inequality applied to the elementary symmetric functions gives \[|a_i|<r_2^{\,n-i}.\] Apply the same argument to the monic polynomial \(a_0^{-1}X^n f(1/X)\), whose roots are \(\alpha_j^{-1}\). Its coefficient corresponding to \(a_i\) yields \[|a_i/a_0|<r_1^{-i}.\] Both bounds must hold simultaneously, which gives the minimum.

Sufficiency. Suppose [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) holds. If a root \(\alpha\) satisfied \(|\alpha|\geq r_2\), then for each \(i<n\), \[|a_i\alpha^i|<|\alpha|^n,\] including \(i=0\) by the bound on \(a_0\). The leading term would strictly dominate every other term, impossible in a vanishing nonarchimedean sum. If instead \(|\alpha|\leq r_1\), the bounds give \[|a_i\alpha^i|<|a_0|\quad(1\leq i<n),
\qquad |\alpha|^n\leq r_1^n<|a_0|.\] The constant term would strictly dominate, again impossible. Every root is therefore in the required annulus.

For fixed \(a_0\), the corrected coefficient domain is the product of the open balls \[|a_i|<R_i(a_0),\qquad
R_i(a_0)=\min\{r_2^{\,n-i},|a_0|r_1^{-i}\}>0.\] It contains the origin. The homotopy \[(s,(a_1,\ldots,a_{n-1}))
 \longmapsto (s a_1,\ldots,s a_{n-1}),\qquad |s|\leq1,\] preserves every strict inequality and contracts the fiber onto the polynomial \(X^n+a_0\). Its roots have norm \(|a_0|^{1/n}\), which lies strictly between \(r_1\) and \(r_2\). This proves the specific fiber-contractibility assertion needed at that step. For \(n=1\), there are no coefficient inequalities and the fiber is a point, consistently with the corrected statement.
## Counterevidence, dependency, and classification

The defect is in the coefficient description, not in the conclusion that the fibers are contractible. Proposition 5.19 supplies the annulus model and compactness of the Tate twist used on p. 41 in Theorem 7.1, so the dependency has been checked explicitly. The proof above establishes the same needed local conclusion with the corrected domain. It does not refute either Proposition 5.19 or the cancellation theorem.

The finding is Major: the false equivalence is the calculation used to identify the fibers as open balls in Proposition 5.19, and that proposition supplies the annulus model and compactness explicitly used in the core cancellation proof. It is therefore an invalid core proof step, even though replacing maximum by minimum restores the needed local conclusion. The ease of this repair and survival of the stated theorems do not remove that dependency. The proved repair is restricted to the coefficient criterion and fiber contraction; it does not independently reconstruct every descent argument in Proposition 5.19 or Theorem 7.1. The author’s intent has not been established, and no author contact or adoption request has occurred.
# Cancellation: additional checks and boundaries

Theorem 7.1 states full faithfulness for every small arc-stack. The inspected argument reduces the adjunction unit to strictly totally disconnected bases and then geometric points, using proper pushforward and the annulus model. The rational free-sheaf expression on p. 41 invokes Theorem 6.1, whose coefficient inversion and rationalization qualifications are explicit on p. 35; those qualifications were retained.
Three algebraic aspects of the remaining argument were checked.

First, the splitting on p. 42 compares multiplicity \(N\) with multiplicity \(N-1\), so its composite is multiplication by \(1\). In residue characteristic \(p\), counting distinct roots would be incorrect. The manuscript explicitly includes multiplicities for the \(N-1\) term. Indeed, writing \(m=p^a u\), \(p\nmid u\), gives \[T^m-1=(T^u-1)^{p^a}\] over a characteristic-\(p\) field; the total multiplicity remains \(m\). This checks the arithmetic of the asserted splitting, not the entire geometric construction of \(Y_2\).

Second, for the basepoint contribution the equality is \(p_2=1\). Both loci are then defined by \(p_1^N=1\); their difference is zero. Thus the checked construction annihilates the indicated basepoint summand and is compatible with the pointed quotient at this level. The overline on \(\overline{\mathbb G_m}=\mathbb G_m/(1+\mathcal O_{<1})\) was confirmed in both the page images and the TeX, rather than erased by plain-text extraction.

Third, Lemma 7.3 on p. 43 uses the degree-zero condition \(\sum_i n_i=0\) to show that translation by \(-1\) changes \(\prod_i\overline{x}_i^{\,n_i}\) by \((-1)^{\sum_i n_i}=1\). The later swap on \(\overline{\mathbb G_m}\otimes\overline{\mathbb G_m}\) has the sign coming from the shift in \(\mathbb Z(1)=\overline{\mathbb G_m}[-1]\). The proof uses that swap twice, producing sign \(+1\). The text distinguishes elementwise triviality from homotopy-coherent triviality and does not use the latter as an unproved premise to finish cancellation.

No additional substantive defect was established in these checked steps. Uniform construction over the base, the eventual-sequence formalism, and all transfer/descent inputs remain outside an independently completed proof reconstruction.
# Version history, outcome, and remaining work

The opened arXiv history lists v1 (4 December 2024), v2 (19 November 2025), and v3 (22 January 2026). The author’s publications page was also inspected; no separate erratum was linked beside this paper there. This is a scoped search result, not a claim that no correction exists anywhere. No old version or journal-final text was substituted for the pinned manuscript.
Item | Current determination
Local coefficient formula | False as printed; exact counterexample supplied.
Local repair | Minimum criterion and fiber contraction proved here.
Substantive severity | One Major finding in the core annulus calculation; no additional counted finding.
Core theorem | Not refuted; full proof not independently certified.
Version scope | Author manuscript v3 only; journal correspondence unverified.
Adoption / acceptance | Neither author adoption nor human scientific acceptance established.
Remaining work | Full dependency reconstruction, uninspected sections, and journal-version comparison.

All roots are in the open annulus iff |a_i| < max(r2^(n-i), |a0| r1^(-i))
analysis:
Equation reference: eq:printed. In the proof of Proposition 5.19, pp. 34–35, fix \(\mathbb T(r_1,r_2)=\{z:r_1<|z|<r_2\}\), with \(0<r_1<1<r_2\), and a monic polynomial \[f(X)=X^n+a_{n-1}X^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1X+a_0,
\qquad r_1^n<|a_0|<r_2^n.\] The first display on p. 35 characterizes all roots lying in \(\mathbb T\) by \[
|a_i|<\max\{r_2^{\,n-i},|a_0|r_1^{-i}\},
\qquad 1\leq i<n.\] The same \(\max\) is present in the acquired TeX at line 1267. This is not a PDF-extraction ambiguity.

Take \(C=\mathbb C_3\), the completed algebraic closure of \(\mathbb Q_3\), with \(|3|=1/3\). It is a nondiscrete algebraically closed nonarchimedean Banach field, so its geometric-point base meets the reduction used in the proof. Choose \[n=2,\quad r_1=1/27,\quad r_2=3,\quad
f(X)=(X-9)(X-1/9)=X^2-\frac{82}{9}X+1.\] Both radii belong to the value group, \(0<r_1<1<r_2\), and \[r_1^2=\frac1{729}<|a_0|=1<9=r_2^2.\] Since \(82\) is not divisible by \(3\), \[|a_1|=\left|-\frac{82}{9}\right|_3=9
 <\max\{3,27\}=27.\] Thus every inequality in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) holds. Nevertheless the exact roots have norms \[|9|_3=\frac19,\qquad |1/9|_3=9.\] The second root lies outside the upper boundary \(3\). The printed criterion is therefore false even in degree two and within the stated nonarchimedean setting. Exact rational arithmetic independently verified both roots and every displayed comparison; no floating-point root solver was used.

Equation reference: eq:correct. The correct criterion is \[
|a_i|<\min\{r_2^{\,n-i},|a_0|r_1^{-i}\},
\qquad 1\leq i<n.\] Here and below the assumed bounds on \(a_0\) remain in force.

Necessity. If the roots are \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n\), all with \(r_1<|\alpha_j|<r_2\), the ultrametric inequality applied to the elementary symmetric functions gives \[|a_i|<r_2^{\,n-i}.\] Apply the same argument to the monic polynomial \(a_0^{-1}X^n f(1/X)\), whose roots are \(\alpha_j^{-1}\). Its coefficient corresponding to \(a_i\) yields \[|a_i/a_0|<r_1^{-i}.\] Both bounds must hold simultaneously, which gives the minimum.

Sufficiency. Suppose [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) holds. If a root \(\alpha\) satisfied \(|\alpha|\geq r_2\), then for each \(i<n\), \[|a_i\alpha^i|<|\alpha|^n,\] including \(i=0\) by the bound on \(a_0\). The leading term would strictly dominate every other term, impossible in a vanishing nonarchimedean sum. If instead \(|\alpha|\leq r_1\), the bounds give \[|a_i\alpha^i|<|a_0|\quad(1\leq i<n),
\qquad |\alpha|^n\leq r_1^n<|a_0|.\] The constant term would strictly dominate, again impossible. Every root is therefore in the required annulus.

For fixed \(a_0\), the corrected coefficient domain is the product of the open balls \[|a_i|<R_i(a_0),\qquad
R_i(a_0)=\min\{r_2^{\,n-i},|a_0|r_1^{-i}\}>0.\] It contains the origin. The homotopy \[(s,(a_1,\ldots,a_{n-1}))
 \longmapsto (s a_1,\ldots,s a_{n-1}),\qquad |s|\leq1,\] preserves every strict inequality and contracts the fiber onto the polynomial \(X^n+a_0\). Its roots have norm \(|a_0|^{1/n}\), which lies strictly between \(r_1\) and \(r_2\). This proves the specific fiber-contractibility assertion needed at that step. For \(n=1\), there are no coefficient inequalities and the fiber is a point, consistently with the corrected statement.
result: The defect is in the coefficient description, not in the conclusion that the fibers are contractible. Proposition 5.19 supplies the annulus model and compactness of the Tate twist used on p. 41 in Theorem 7.1, so the dependency has been checked explicitly. The proof above establishes the same needed local conclusion with the corrected domain. It does not refute either Proposition 5.19 or the cancellation theorem.

The finding is Major: the false equivalence is the calculation used to identify the fibers as open balls in Proposition 5.19, and that proposition supplies the annulus model and compactness explicitly used in the core cancellation proof. It is therefore an invalid core proof step, even though replacing maximum by minimum restores the needed local conclusion. The ease of this repair and survival of the stated theorems do not remove that dependency. The proved repair is restricted to the coefficient criterion and fiber contraction; it does not independently reconstruct every descent argument in Proposition 5.19 or Theorem 7.1. The author’s intent has not been established, and no author contact or adoption request has occurred.

Impact: Invalidates the printed root-location equivalence used in the annulus proof. The minimum criterion and fiber contraction are proved in the report; no refutation of Proposition5.19 or cancellation and no complete reconstruction of all descent dependencies is claimed.

# Identity, version and disposition

The title page prints DOI `10.4310/ACTA.2025.v235.n2.a1`. The frozen assignment instead records `10.4310/acta.2025.n235.n2.a1`. The volume-prefix discrepancy is preserved as metadata, not silently rewritten or counted as a scientific defect. The source is `papers/0042/0042.pdf`; its SHA-256 is

Disposition: No Issue Found within the substantive coverage below. There are zero confirmed Major and zero confirmed Minor findings. Observation X01 is excluded from those counts as an isolated display inconsistency: the relevant preceding corollary supplies the correctly shifted conclusion. This classification does not assert author intent or independent human acceptance.
# Claims, hypotheses and independent checks
## Additivity is a condition on squares

Definition 1.6.3, p. 203 (PDF 55), requires a reduced functor, a target admitting finite limits, and preservation of the appropriate class of squares. Proposition 1.6.4, p. 204 (PDF 56), permits replacement by sequences when the target is stable. The text explicitly retains the stronger square condition for a space-valued functor.

This distinction is necessary in the proof of Theorem 2.5.3 on p. 259 (PDF 111): one square recognises cocartesian arrows and another supplies their lifts. Merely assuming that a space-valued functor preserves sequences would not justify applying it to these squares. The actual definition supplies the stronger assumption, so this potential objection is rejected. The split condition on the projection is also explicit in Theorem 2.5.3, p. 249 (PDF 101), and the failure of an unrestricted nonsplit extension is acknowledged in Remark 2.5.4(ii), p. 250 (PDF 102).

The terminal/zero case is consistent: reducedness forces the invariant of the zero Poincaré category to be terminal; for a stable target this is the zero object. Thus no extra summand occurs when one term of a split sequence is zero.
## Why realisation preserves the square at issue

The proof of Theorem 2.5.1 on pp. 250–251 (PDF 102–103) does not use an unrestricted assertion that geometric realisation preserves pullbacks. It uses a bicartesian fibration and the straightening functor into categories with adjoints.

Here is the relevant independent implication. If \(L\dashv R\), its unit and counit induce homotopies \[|\mathrm{id}|\simeq |R||L|,\qquad |L||R|\simeq|\mathrm{id}|.\] Hence \(|L|\) is an equivalence. The straightening transition functors therefore become equivalences after groupoid completion and factor through the groupoid completion of the base. Unstraightening this space-valued local system commutes with base change; this is exactly the restricted pullback needed on p. 250.

The last step of Theorem 2.5.3, p. 259, also uses the self-opposite symmetry of the hermitian \(Q\)-construction to obtain the cartesian half from the cocartesian half. The recognition step is compatible with the stronger square-based definition of additivity. The full horn and Poincaré-structure calculations in Lemmas 2.6.3–2.6.7 were not all reconstructed; the preceding implication is checked conditional on those lemmas, rather than presented as a new proof of the whole additivity theorem.
## Bott–Genauer rotation and the \(U,V\) conventions

Corollary 4.3.1, p. 317 (PDF 169), identifies \(\mathrm{GW}(\mathrm{Met}(\mathcal C,\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}))\) with \(\mathrm{GW}(\mathrm{Hyp}(\mathcal C))\) and then with \(K(\mathcal C)\). The resulting sequence on p. 318 (PDF 170) is \[\mathrm{GW}(\mathcal C,\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^{[-1]})\longrightarrow K(\mathcal C)
 \longrightarrow\mathrm{GW}(\mathcal C,\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}).\] Write \(G_j=\mathrm{GW}(\mathcal C,\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^{[j]})\). With the paper’s definitions, \[U(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^{[2]})=\operatorname{fib}(K\to G_2)=G_1.\] Applying the sequence to \(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^{[1]}\) gives \(G_0\to K\to G_1\); rotation in spectra gives \[V(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}})=\operatorname{fib}(G_0\to K)=\Omega G_1.\] Consequently \(U(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^{[2]})\simeq\Sigma V(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}})\), exactly Corollary 4.3.3. Neither a shift by \(-2\) nor an unshifted \(U\simeq V\) follows. This checks the stated rotation; the equivalence between metabolic and hyperbolic theories remains dependent on the cited constructions.
## Bordification and the fundamental fibre sequence

Theorem 4.4.11, p. 329 (PDF 181), compares \(\mathrm{GW}^{\mathrm{bord}}\) with \(\mathrm{L}\). Its reduction from negative to all degrees is valid provided the natural negative-degree comparison holds for every shifted Poincaré structure, as asserted through Corollaries 3.6.17 and 4.4.9. For any integer \(i\), choose \(k>i\). For a bordism-invariant functor \(F\), \[F(\mathcal C,\mathord{\mathrm{Q}})\simeq \Sigma^k F(\mathcal C,\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^{[-k]}),\qquad
 \pi_iF(\mathcal C,\mathord{\mathrm{Q}})=\pi_{i-k}F(\mathcal C,\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^{[-k]}).\] The right-hand degree is negative. Applying this to both functors and to their natural comparison proves the claimed extension of the isomorphism. Negative-degree agreement for just one unshifted category would be insufficient; the quantification over shifted inputs is essential.

Corollary 4.4.13, p. 330 (PDF 182), identifies a cartesian square with bottom row \(K^{hC_2}\to K^{tC_2}\). Taking horizontal fibres yields \(K_{hC_2}\to\mathrm{GW}\to\mathrm{L}\), because the fibre of the norm cofibre map is the homotopy-orbit spectrum. The orbit and fixed-point terms must not be interchanged.

For Corollary 4.4.14, the displayed composite from \(K[1/2]_{hC_2}\) through \(\mathrm{GW}[1/2]\) to \((K[1/2])^{hC_2}\) is the norm. Its equivalence after inverting 2 gives a retraction and hence the splitting. The proof uses a map to the fixed points of the localised spectrum; it does not require an unjustified blanket commutation of localisation with arbitrary limits.
## Localisation, idempotent completion, and a rejected extraction alarm

Corollary 4.5.1 on p. 330 is Verdier localisation. Examples 1.6.9(iii)–(iv), p. 206 (PDF 58), distinguish connective \(K\), nonconnective \(K\), and connective \(K\) after idempotent completion. The introduction’s claim therefore does not assert that connective \(K\) sends every idempotent-completed quotient sequence to a fibre sequence.

Remark 4.5.2, p. 331 (PDF 183), retains involution-closed subgroups \(c\subseteq d\subseteq K_0(R)\) and explicitly cites paper IV for the cofinality squares. Direct page inspection establishes that its Grothendieck–Witt remainder is \[H(d/c)^{hC_2},\] with a superscript. The text extraction obscured this distinction. For an abelian group \(A\) with \(C_2\)-action, \(H(A)^{hC_2}\) has \(\pi_{-j}=H^j(C_2;A)\) for \(j\geq0\) and no positive homotopy groups. The long exact sequence consequently gives isomorphisms in positive degrees and injectivity in degree zero, as stated. An objection based on positive group homology would instead concern \(H(A)_{hC_2}\) and is not an objection to the printed paper. The cited cofinality theorem in paper IV was not independently proved here.
## Genuine periodicity and its range

Theorem 3.7.5, p. 311 (PDF 163), identifies the rotated metabolic sequence with the tensor of a genuine spectrum by \[\mathbb S[C_2]\longrightarrow\mathbb S\longrightarrow S^\sigma.\] Thus \(F^{\mathrm{ghyp}}(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^{[-1]})\simeq
S^{\sigma-1}F^{\mathrm{ghyp}}(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}})\), and replacing \(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}\) by \(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^{[1]}\) gives the \(1-\sigma\) shift in Corollary 4.6.3, p. 336 (PDF 188). The representation \(1-\sigma\) has underlying dimension zero and fixed dimension one. These two tests give unchanged nonequivariant suspension degree for \(K\), and suspension degree one for geometric fixed points \(\mathrm{L}\). They do not imply ordinary one-periodicity of connective \(K\).

Corollary 4.6.4, p. 337 (PDF 189), retains the \(n\sigma\)-orientation, the involution-closed subgroup, and an additional connectivity hypothesis for the truncated structures \(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^{\geq m}\). For \(n=2\) it gives \[\mathrm{KR}(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}_{-M}^{\geq m+1})\simeq
 S^{2-2\sigma}\mathrm{KR}(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}_M^{\geq m}).\] Taking \(m=0,1\) gives the genuine symmetric/even/quadratic chain with the correct sign change of \(M\). The homotopical structures \(\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^s,\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^q\) have the stated period; these should not be confused with an assertion that every genuine truncated structure is four-periodic without changing its form parameter.
# Excluded observation X01: final display on page 338

Location. The last display of §4.6, p. 338 (PDF 190), after Corollary 4.6.7, prints \[\Sigma^4 L_{\mathrm{gq}}\simeq
 \Sigma^2 L_{\mathrm{ge},-M}\simeq L_{\mathrm{gs}},
 \tag{X01-printed}\] where the suppressed category is \(\mathcal D^c(R)\) and the other two coefficients are \(M\).

Exact algebraic check. Corollary 4.6.5 on p. 337 instead gives \[S^{2\sigma-2}\mathrm{KR}_{\mathrm{gq}}\simeq
 \mathrm{KR}_{\mathrm{ge},-M}\simeq S^{2-2\sigma}\mathrm{KR}_{\mathrm{gs}}.\] Geometric fixed points send \(a+b\sigma\) to degree \(a\). Therefore \[\Sigma^{-2}L_{\mathrm{gq}}\simeq
 L_{\mathrm{ge},-M}\simeq\Sigma^2L_{\mathrm{gs}},\] and suspension by two gives \[L_{\mathrm{gq}}\simeq
 \Sigma^2L_{\mathrm{ge},-M}\simeq\Sigma^4L_{\mathrm{gs}}.
 \tag{X01-derived}\] This agrees with the stabilisation expression on p. 156 (PDF 8). In particular, the printed final chain is not the chain obtained by the stated derivation. Reversing the direction of an equivalence does not keep a suspension on the same side: from \(A\simeq\Sigma^2B\) one gets \(B\simeq\Sigma^{-2}A\).

Counterevidence and impact. The immediately preceding genuine-spectrum corollary, the general shift theorem, and the introduction all supply the consistent direction. The final display is not used in the inspected proof of those results. Remark 4.6.8(i), printed p. 339 (PDF 191), explicitly states that genuine \(L\)-spectra are not periodic in general and refers to a computation of \(L(\mathcal D^p(\mathbb Z),\mathord{\mathrm{Q}}^{\mathrm{gs}})\) in paper III. The printed middle equivalence \(\Sigma^2L_{\mathrm{ge},-M}\simeq L_{\mathrm{gs}}\), combined with \(L_{\mathrm{ge},-M}\simeq\Sigma^2L_{\mathrm{gs}}\) from Corollary 4.6.5, would force \(\Sigma^4L_{\mathrm{gs}}\simeq L_{\mathrm{gs}}\). The adjacent nonperiodicity statement supplies concrete counterevidence to interpreting the reversed chain as an additional periodicity theorem. The cited computation over \(\mathbb Z\) was not independently reconstructed here; no new ring-level calculation or refutation of the main theorem is claimed. The evidence supports correcting the placement of suspensions in this summary display. Because only this local display inconsistency has been established, it is recorded outside the substantive Major/Minor counts under the task’s exclusion of typographical errors alone. No claim about the author’s intended keystroke is needed.

Title: Initial scientific review: M25-0043
Perverse filtrations and Fourier transforms
# Identity, version and disposition

The reviewed source is Davesh Maulik, Junliang Shen and Qizheng Yin, Perverse filtrations and Fourier transforms, Acta Mathematica 234 (2025), 1–69, DOI `10.4310/acta.2025.v234.n1.a1`. Printed and one-based PDF page numbers agree. The assigned file is `papers/0043/0043.pdf`, SHA-256
