> 5667a4726deedff6ebfe8e1b230df.

The complete manifest and file bindings were verified at intake. Their parsing does not count as mathematical review. The later author manuscript is comparison evidence and has not replaced the publisher PDF.

Disposition. One known-issue reproduction, K01, concerns the proof of Corollary 5.3. Its dependency on a main application makes the gap Major-level for the frozen proof, but it is not reported as a new unresolved defect in the authors’ current manuscript. There are zero additional confirmed Major and zero additional confirmed Minor findings. No counterexample to the corollary or to Theorem 0.6 is asserted.
# Scope, definitions and positive checks

Text inspected: pp. 1–8, 12–16, 21–31, 40–42, 55–60 and 66–67 (35 of 69 pages). Actual source images inspected: pp. 1, 3, 7, 14, 15, 23, 24, 26, 27, 30, 31, 41, 42, 57, 58 and 60. The following are substantive checks, not a claim that every dependency on those pages was reconstructed.
## Hypotheses and ranges

The paper works over \(\mathbb C\) with rational coefficients. Its abelian fibrations have smooth irreducible total space and base, are proper and equidimensional, and admit the specified group action. Definition 1.2, pp. 15–16, includes inverse Fourier kernels, a convolution kernel with the requisite codimension bound, and full support of the perverse summands for the indicated fibration. These are hypotheses, not consequences of being any singular family of abelian varieties.

Theorem 0.1, p. 3, uses Fourier vanishing (FV). The compactified-Jacobian application in Theorem 0.2, p. 4, concerns integral projective planar curves, a section through the smooth locus, and a nonsingular total compactified Jacobian. Theorem 0.6, p. 7, asserts \(P\supset C\) for coprime \((r,\chi)\), \(r\geq3\), only in cohomological degrees at most \(2(r-2)\), not unrestricted \(P=C\).

With the paper’s unshifted direct-image convention, p. 14, \[P_kH^d(M)=\operatorname{im}\bigl[
 H^d(B,{}^p\tau_{\leq k+\dim B}R\pi_*\mathbb Q_M)\longrightarrow H^d(M,\mathbb Q)\bigr].\] The base-dimension shift is consequential in K01.
## Riemann–Roch normalization and projectors

The two Fourier classes on pp. 22–24 have deliberately asymmetric Todd factors. With \[T_{M^\vee\times_B M}
 =\operatorname{pr}_1^*T_{M^\vee}+\operatorname{pr}_2^*T_M-\pi^*T_B,\] the factors in the convolution cancel as required by Lemma 2.3. The proof uses the base-changed diagonal and flatness. Replacing its localized Chern character by an ordinary Chern character on an arbitrary singular product would be unjustified; the inspected proof does not do so.

Definition 2.5, p. 24, requires \(F_i^{-1}F_j=0\) for \(i+j<2g\) as relative Chow correspondences. No vanishing for \(i+j>2g\) is assumed. Set \(a_i=F_iF^{-1}_{2g-i}\). The proof on p. 26 has \(\sum_i a_i=1\) and \(a_i a_j=0\) for \(i>j\), since \(2g-i+j<2g\). For \(p_k=\sum_{j\leq k}a_j\), \[p_k=1p_k=\sum_i\sum_{j\leq k}a_i a_j
       =\sum_{i\leq k}\sum_{j\leq k}a_i a_j=p_k^2 .\] Thus \(q_{k+1}=1-p_k\) is its orthogonal complement. Only the stated one-sided vanishing is used. For \(g=0\) this reduces to \(p_0=1\).

The realization step on p. 27 uses full support and semisimplicity to exclude additional boundary-supported perverse summands. Generic agreement alone would not identify arbitrary derived morphisms; the split image and complementary summands permit the truncation identification here.
## Multiplicativity and degree bookkeeping

In the proof on pp. 28–30, a possibly nonzero component of the projected cup product must satisfy \[j_1\geq2g-k,\qquad j_2\geq2g-\ell,\qquad j_3\geq k+\ell+1.\] The convolution correspondence has degree at least \(-g\). Hence the total degree is at least \[(g-k)+(g-\ell)+(k+\ell+1-g)-g=1.\] The projected cup product is homogeneous of correspondence degree zero, so vanishes. This is a grading argument, without the missing opposite half of (FV). The Chern inclusion on p. 31 similarly uses \(2g-i+k<2g\) for \(i\geq k+1\).

For the subsequent motive splitting the preliminary projectors obey \(p_\ell p_k=p_k\) when \(\ell>k\). The replacement \(t_k=p_kp_{k+1}\cdots p_{2g}\) is nested on both sides: in \(t_\ell t_k\), successive \(p_i p_k\) collapse; in \(t_k t_\ell\), collapse the factors to the right down to \(p_\ell\). Thus \(t_\ell t_k=t_k t_\ell=t_k\) for \(k\leq\ell\), and \(t_k-t_{k-1}\) are orthogonal projectors. Commutativity of the original \(p_k\) is not assumed.
## Supporting checks

On pp. 40–42 the localized character of \(\psi^N\mathcal P\) scales in degree \(j\) by \(N^j\). Conditional on the support theorem used there, for fixed total degree below \(2g\) one obtains a finite relation \[\sum_{i+j=k}N^{j+\dim B}A_{ij}=0
 \qquad\text{for every positive integer }N.\] Taking as many distinct \(N\) as coefficients gives an invertible rational Vandermonde matrix after dividing the common nonzero power. Every \(A_{ij}\) therefore vanishes, even for an infinite-dimensional ambient Chow group. The Todd expansion has nonnegative index \(j'\) and replaces \(j\) by \(j-j'\leq j\), preserving the strict inequality. The preceding support theorem has not itself been reconstructed.
# Problem 1: known missing strictness step (K01)
## Exact source and suspect inference

Corollary 5.3, pp. 57–58, claims that restriction to the integral-curve locus \(W\) induces an isomorphism of perverse-filtered cohomology in degrees \(d\leq2r-4\), for every index \(k\). After triangle (5.5), p. 58 asserts low-degree ordinary and perverse bounds and claims an isomorphism of perverse cohomology sheaves for \(i\leq2r-4\).

The missing implication is strictness with respect to the whole perverse filtration in those ordinary cohomological degrees. Ordinary cohomological degree, absolute perverse-sheaf degree, and filtration index are different variables. The printed final inference does not supply that implication.
## Complete check of the inference

Let \(c=r-1\). Grant the geometric bound \(\operatorname{codim}_M Z\geq c\) used in the proof. The ordinary support bound and long exact sequence give an isomorphism \(H^d(M)\to H^d(M_W)\) for \(d\leq2c-2\): both adjacent support groups vanish. This proves the unfiltered assertion.

A filtered linear isomorphism need not be a filtered isomorphism: take \(V=W=\mathbb Q\), \(\phi=1\), with \(P_0V=0\), \(P_0W=\mathbb Q\) and \(P_1V=P_1W=\mathbb Q\), extended constantly above and by zero below. Then \(\phi(P_kV)\subseteq P_kW\) for every \(k\) and \(\phi\) is bijective, but \(\phi(P_0V)\ne P_0W\). This is a counterexample to the abstract inference, not a geometric counterexample to Corollary 5.3.

The perverse-sheaf range as printed also does not address every required truncation. Here \(N=\dim|rH|=r(r+3)/2\), and \(P_k\) uses cutoff \(k+N\). For \(r=3\), the printed bound is \(i\leq2\), whereas the \(P_0\) cutoff is \(9\). Even granting that low-degree perverse isomorphism does not yield the asserted filtered isomorphism.

An arbitrary proper direct image does not preserve all lower perverse bounds. For example, for \(f:\mathbb P^1\to\mathrm{pt}\), \(\mathbb Q_{\mathbb P^1}[1]\) is perverse but \[Rf_*(\mathbb Q_{\mathbb P^1}[1])=\mathbb Q[1]\oplus\mathbb Q[-1].\] This rules out one possible general justification; it does not show that the particular perverse bound in the paper is false. K01 rests on the missing strictness bridge.

The base-boundary count agrees with Lemma 5.2: if \(N_d=d(d+3)/2\), then \(N_r-N_a-N_{r-a}=a(r-a)\geq r-1\) for \(1\leq a<r\). Geometry transferring a base bound to the inverse image remains a dependency; that transfer is not proved by this polynomial identity.
## Counterevidence, known revision and repair

The arXiv record for `2308.13160v3`, dated 8 October 2025, records an update of the proof of Corollary 5.3. The revised proof combines the ordinary cohomology isomorphism with functoriality of a Deligne splitting, citing [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 3.3]{dms}]. That lemma and its proof were read on printed p. 937 of the primary source. The HTML rendering date is not treated as the manuscript version date.

Here is the strictness bridge independently completed. Choose an \(h\)-relative ample class \(\eta\); its restriction is relative ample for \(h_W\). Restriction is a graded ring map, preserves the perverse filtration by open-base-change naturality, and carries \(\eta\) to its restriction. The comparison lemma makes it preserve the first Deligne summands: \(\phi(G_kH^d(M))\subseteq G_kH^d(M_W)\). Fix \(d\leq2r-4\), where \(\phi\) is an ordinary isomorphism. For \(w\in G_kH^d(M_W)\), decompose its unique preimage as \(v=\sum_jv_j\) with \(v_j\in G_jH^d(M)\). The target direct sum implies \(\phi(v_j)=0\) for \(j\ne k\), so injectivity gives \(v_j=0\). Thus \(\phi\) is an isomorphism on every \(G_k\), and hence every \(P_k=\bigoplus_{j\leq k}G_j\).

This proves the missing bridge under the stated geometric and splitting inputs. It agrees with the later author proof and requires no all-degree ordinary isomorphism. It does not reprove all background geometry or the decomposition theorem.

Theorem 0.6, p. 60, explicitly uses Corollary 5.3 to reduce to \(M_W\). Descending its perverse-degree bound requires the inverse restriction to preserve the filtration, exactly the missing point. The gap is core-linked even though repair is available. Frozen-proof severity is Major-level; reporting status is known-issue reproduction, later repaired, not a new current Major. Neither the abstract Fourier theorem nor the multiplicativity argument checked above is refuted.

# Identity, version and outcome

Emanuel Milman and Joe Neeman, The structure of isoperimetric bubbles on \(\mathbb R^n\) and \(\mathbb S^n\), Acta Mathematica 234 (2025), 71–188, DOI `10.4310/ACTA.2025.v234.n1.a2`. The supplied publisher PDF, `papers/0044/0044.pdf`, is the reviewed version. Printed page equals one-based PDF page plus 70. Its SHA-256 is

The hash above is line-broken for readability; the machine-readable source binding is authoritative. The entire supplied manifest was parsed and bound files verified before review. This is not counted as scientific inspection.

Outcome: one supported Minor finding, M01; zero confirmed Major findings. M01 concerns a peripheral example asserting necessity of an assumption. No damage to a proved main conclusion has been demonstrated. No whole-paper correctness certificate is issued.
# Definitions, coverage and main dependencies

A \(q\)-cluster includes the exterior cell; a single bubble therefore has \(q=2\). Individual cells need not be connected. In \(\mathbb R^n\) only the exterior cell has infinite volume. Total perimeter counts each interface once. Reflection symmetry means invariance of each labelled cell, not just invariance of the union of interfaces.

Definitions 2.26 and 2.28, printed p. 100 (PDF 30), require stationarity and \[\delta_X^1 V=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 Q(X)=\delta_X^2 A-\langle\lambda,\delta_X^2V\rangle\geq0
 \qquad (X\in C_c^\infty).\] Perturbations are not restricted to reflection-symmetric fields or to preserving each connected component’s volume.

Theorem 1.3 concerns bounded stable regular clusters with reflection symmetry. The stable-cluster extension in Theorem 1.9 additionally assumes connected total boundary and finitely many cell components. The global minimizing conclusion in Theorem 1.13 is \(2\leq q\leq\min(5,n+1)\). Statements 1.14 and 1.16 are explicitly announced without proof in this paper; they are not treated as completed proofs here.

Text inspected: PDF pp. 1–18, 29–31, 39–41, 62–69, 83–91 and 97–110 (55 of 118 pages, including contents and figures). Actual source images inspected: PDF pp. 1, 8, 11, 12, 30, 64, 66, 67, 68, 83, 84, 87, 89, 91, 97, 98, 105, 106 and 108. Reading a page does not mean independently reconstructing every theorem it cites.
# Problem 1: reflected copies need not be stable (M01)
## Source claim and exact scope

Remark 9.14, printed p. 161 (PDF 91), proposes taking a stable \(q\)-cluster whose \(q-1\) finite cells lie in one open hemisphere and reflecting it about the equator. It states that the resulting \(q\)-cluster is stable and has disconnected cells, as an example showing why connectedness of the total boundary is needed in Theorem 1.9.
The suspect step is preservation of stability when a cell and its reflected copy receive the same label. The volume constraint then permits transferring volume between those two components.
## An explicit input satisfying the construction

Take \(M=\mathbb R^2\), \(n=2\), \(q=2\), equator \(\{y=0\}\), and \[D_+=B((0,2),1),\qquad D_-=B((0,-2),1).\] Start with the standard single bubble \((D_+,\mathbb R^2\setminus\overline{D_+})\), understood up to its null boundary. Its finite cell lies entirely in \(\{y>0\}\). It is bounded in the paper’s sense (compact total boundary), regular and stationary. It is stable: for a unit circle and a normal variation \(f\) of mean zero, \[Q(f)=\int_0^{2\pi}\bigl((f')^2-f^2\bigr)\,d\theta\geq0\] by the Fourier expansion, since every nonzero frequency has \(m^2-1\geq0\). Tangential fields do not change the constrained index.

Reflect and retain the same cell labels, exactly as required to obtain a \(q=2\) cluster with disconnected finite cell: \[\Omega_1=D_+\cup D_-,\qquad
 \Omega_2=\mathbb R^2\setminus(\overline{D_+}\cup\overline{D_-}).\] This is a regular stationary cluster; both circles have outward curvature 1 and the same pressure difference. It is bounded, each labelled cell is reflection invariant, and it has finitely many components. Also \(q=2\leq n+1=3\). It is not asserted to satisfy stability: that is the conclusion of the construction which the next calculation disproves.
## Two exact checks of instability

Equation reference: eq:disk. For \(|t|<1/2\) keep the centers fixed and set \[r_+(t)=\sqrt{1+t},\qquad r_-(t)=\sqrt{1-t}.\] The two disks stay disjoint and in their respective half-planes. Their total area is exactly \[V_1(t)=\pi r_+(t)^2+\pi r_-(t)^2=2\pi.\] The cluster perimeter is \[A(t)=2\pi\bigl(\sqrt{1+t}+\sqrt{1-t}\bigr),\qquad
 A'(0)=0,\qquad A''(0)=-\pi<0.                 \] This is an admissible smooth volume-preserving deformation near the compact interfaces, extendible by cutoffs in disjoint neighborhoods.

The same conclusion follows directly from the paper’s definition. Choose a smooth compactly supported ambient field with normal component \(f=1/2\) on the upper circle and \(f=-1/2\) on the lower one. Disjoint annular neighborhoods allow such a field, for example using local radial fields and cutoffs equal to 1 near each circle. Its first variation is \[\delta_XV_1=(1/2)(2\pi)-(1/2)(2\pi)=0,\qquad
 \delta_XV_2=-\delta_XV_1=0.\] There are no triple junctions, \(\operatorname{Ric}=0\), and \(|\mathrm{II}|^2=1\). Formula (2.15) gives \[Q(X)=\sum_{\pm}\int_{\partial D_\pm}(0-f^2)\,ds
      =-2(2\pi)(1/4)=-\pi.\] Thus the claimed stable output is unstable under the paper’s actual definition. Both computations are analytic; an independent exact-rational script also verifies the coefficient and index arithmetic.
## Alternative readings and precise consequence

Constraining the two disks’ volumes separately removes this variation, but changes the cluster’s labelled-volume constraints. Giving the reflected copy a different label also changes \(q\) and makes reflection exchange cells, contrary to the per-cell symmetry definition. Requiring only symmetric perturbations would define a weaker notion of stability than Definition 2.28. None of these readings validates the printed example under the existing definitions.

The example refutes the asserted stability-preservation construction, not Theorem 1.9 and not the existence of every possible different counterexample to dropping its connected-boundary assumption. Remark 9.14 follows the completed proof and is not used to establish the theorem or the minimizer classification. The demonstrated impact is therefore local and supports Minor. The precise safe correction is to remove the unsupported construction and leave necessity of that hypothesis unclaimed pending an example satisfying the actual stability condition. This review does not propose removing the hypothesis from the theorem.

The inspected arXiv v4 (20 April 2025) retains the same Remark 9.14. No correction of this point was identified in the inspected author publication listing; this limited search is not proof of novelty or absence of all errata.
# Checks of the central arguments
## The sign producing perpendicular sphericity

u-kp\). Lemma 7.8 gives \[L_{m Jac}x=|\mathrm{II}_0|^2x-(n-1)kz.\] Trace stability yields \(0\leq-\int x^2|\mathrm{II}_0|^2+(n-1)\int kxz\). The cutoff conformal-field estimate on the sphere yields \(0\leq-(n-1)\int\langle N,

In Euclidean space the required zero integral comes from Lemma 7.9, whose proof explicitly uses global \(L^2\) curvature control, rather than merely control away from the singular set. Full proofs of the earlier approximation and integrability results remain dependencies.

There is an independent check of the Euclidean isotropy formula in Remark 7.10. For a trace-free symmetric matrix \(B\), the flow \(\exp(tB)\) preserves every cell volume. With a cutoff agreeing near the compact boundary, stationarity and the surface Jacobian give \[0=\int_{\Sigma^1} igl(\operatorname{tr}B-

## Connectedness and the dimension restriction

The strict maximum statement of Lemma 9.12, p. 157 (PDF 87), uses positive edge weights and connectedness after deleting the source vertex. On the set \(W\) of maximum values of the solution of \(L_Aa=e_1-e_V\), the sink cannot occur. Positivity of the boundary flux forces \(1\in W\), and every vertex of \(\partial W\) must be 1. If \(W\) contained any other vertex, deleting 1 would disconnect the graph. Hence \(W=\{1\}\), establishing the strict inequality actually used.

The cusp argument on pp. 158–159 uses \(h_{ij}=a_{ij}|\langle N,p\rangle|\) with zero first volume variation and \(Q(h)=0\). Proposition 9.2 compares quadratic integrands almost everywhere; it does not apply a smooth integration-by-parts formula directly to the cusp. Elliptic regularity then contradicts its nonzero normal derivative jump. This reasoning is conditional on the scalar-field approximation and regularity lemmas, not on a claim that the cusp is initially smooth.

For Proposition 9.13, \(s\leq q-1\leq n\) equatorial cells leave a nonzero direction orthogonal to the first \(s-1\) constraint normals; its sign can be chosen to satisfy the last inequality. A ray in that direction stays in the open polyhedron and reaches the unit sphere, contradicting density of the equatorial cells. The argument explains the bound \(q\leq n+1\) and does not extend automatically to \(q=n+2\).
## Complete interfaces and small adjacency graphs

For Proposition 10.10, pp. 167–168 (PDF 97–98), all interfaces imply \(G(e_i-e_j,e_i-e_j)=1\). To verify that these data determine \(G\), set \(u_i=e_i-e_q\). A symmetric form \(B\) vanishing on all \(e_i-e_j\) satisfies \(B(u_i,u_i)=0\) and \(B(u_i-u_j,u_i-u_j)=-2B(u_i,u_j)=0\), hence \(B=0\). Consequently \(G=\tfrac12 I\) on the sum-zero subspace, with the paper’s factor \(\tfrac12\) correct.

Corollary 11.3 uses Taylor’s classification only when the effective cone dimension is at most 3. In the remaining \(d=4\), \(q=5\) case, affine independence of five generators gives a simplex normal fan, so every pair shares an interface; it does not presume classification of all four-dimensional minimizing cones.

The graph list in Figure 11.5 is complete: a five-vertex graph of minimum degree 3 has complement of maximum degree 1, hence a matching of size 0, 1 or 2. Independent enumeration gives respectively 1, 10 and 15 labelled graphs, exactly three isomorphism types. The subsequent geometric exclusions use minimization and contact regularity; the graph count alone is not their proof. The angle inequality in Lemma 11.6 gives \(120(q-1)<180(q-3)\), hence \(q>7\), consistent with the stated nondegenerate range.
# Later clarification, limitations and conclusion

The authors’ subsequent paper [boundary], Remark 1.6, explicitly identifies the simple-connectedness input implicitly used in the volume-preserving boundary-motion argument of Lemma 9.3, printed pp. 153–154. The original model spaces in dimensions \(n\geq2\) have that property. This is recorded as a known clarification, separately from M01; no counterexample to Lemma 9.3 in its stated model spaces is established. Only the later introduction and stated topological input were inspected, not its full proof.

Unperformed work includes the full regularity and scalar-to-vector approximation machinery, the complete simplicial-homology/Voronoi construction in Section 8, all singular maximum-principle details, the omitted properness and differential arguments in the volume-parameterization sketch, and all external foundations. No author code was supplied in the manifest or executed. No empirical experiment is relevant to the explicit counterexample.

# Identity, version and review scope

Fabrice Bethuel, Asymptotics for 2-dimensional vectorial Allen–Cahn systems, Acta Mathematica 234 (2025), 189–314, DOI `10.4310/ACTA.2025.v234.n2.a1`. The exact supplied publisher PDF `papers/0045/0045.pdf` is reviewed. Printed page equals one-based PDF page plus 188. Its SHA-256 is
The line break does not belong to the hash. All manifest identities and file bindings were checked before scientific review. Index parsing is not counted as proof inspection.

Outcome: one Major finding, M01, concerning a false domain-general clearing-out statement; no separate supported Minor finding. This is a systematic claim-focused initial review, not certification of the entire 126-page paper. Text was actually read on PDF pages 1–30, 48–54, 64–66, 69–89, 109–117 and 121–124 (74 distinct pages). Twenty-five source pages were rendered and visually checked, including every decisive page for M01. The full extraction is merely a navigation artifact.

Equation reference: eq:pde. The standing assumptions are a smooth bounded \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2\), smooth nonnegative \(V:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R\), finitely many zeroes with positive definite Hessians, coercivity and the radial growth condition (H3), together with solutions \[
 \Delta u_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-2}\nabla V(u_\varepsilon),\qquad
 E_\varepsilon(u_\varepsilon)=\int_\Omega
 \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|\nabla u_\varepsilon|^2+
 \frac{V(u_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\right)\le M_0 .\] The limits \(\nu_\star\) and \(\zeta_\star\) refer respectively to full energy and potential energy. The main results concern interior concentration, rectifiability, local straight segments away from an \(\mathcal H^1\)-null exceptional set, and stationarity of the potential-energy varifold. No boundary condition is imposed in these hypotheses. Remark 1.4 explicitly treats Neumann boundary orthogonality as an additional question.
# Problem 1: the clearing-out statement needs an interior restriction
## Source claim and failing step

Equation reference: eq:claimed. Theorem 1.16, printed p. 211/PDF 23, asserts, for an open \(U\subset\Omega\) and \(\delta>0\), \[
 \nu_\star(V_\delta)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \nu_\star(\overline U)=0 ,
 \qquad
 U_\delta=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,U)\le\delta\},\
 V_\delta=U_\delta\setminus U .\] The overline on \(U\) in the conclusion was confirmed in the page image; text extraction suppresses it. The preceding prose allows general regular subdomains and does not require \(\overline U\subset\Omega\) or a positive distance to the exterior boundary.

Section 7.3, printed p. 273/PDF 85, invokes Proposition 4.15. The latter, printed p. 252/PDF 64, writes \(U_\delta\subset\Omega\), but this is already automatic for the clipped definition (1.67). Its proof uses Proposition 3.11, printed p. 242/PDF 54, where a smooth cutoff equals one on \(U_{\delta/2}\) and vanishes outside \(U_\delta\), and the test field \(X(z)=z\chi_\delta(z)\) is inserted in the compact-support identity (3.19). Such a cutoff is unavailable when \(U_{\delta/2}\) reaches \(\partial\Omega\). This is a boundary-support obstruction, not a numerical approximation error.
## Complete counterexample

Take \[\Omega=\{x_1^2+x_2^2<1\},\quad k=2,\quad
 V(a,b)=\frac{(1-a^2)^2}{4}+\frac{b^2}{2},\qquad
 u_\varepsilon(x)=\left(\tanh\frac{x_1}{\sqrt2\,\varepsilon},0\right).\] This is genuinely a map to the allowed two-component target, even though one component is constant.

Potential assumptions. The zero set is \(\{(-1,0),(1,0)\}\), so (H1) holds with \(q=2\). The Hessian at either zero is \(\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), establishing (H2). The polynomial is smooth, nonnegative and tends to infinity as \(|(a,b)|\to\infty\). Moreover, \[\begin{aligned}
 (a,b)\cdot\nabla V&=a^4-a^2+b^2\\
 &=(a^2-\tfrac34)^2+\tfrac12(a^2+b^2)+\tfrac12b^2-\tfrac9{16}\\
 &\ge \tfrac14(a^2+b^2)\quad\text{if }|(a,b)|>2.
\end{aligned}\] Thus (H3) holds with \(R_\infty=2\) and \(\alpha_\infty=1/4\).

Equation and uniform energy. Writing \(w=\tanh(x_1/(\sqrt2\varepsilon))\) gives \[w_{x_1x_1}=\varepsilon^{-2}(w^3-w),\qquad
 \nabla V(w,0)=(w^3-w,0).\] Consequently [eq:pde] (#eq:pde) holds for every \(0<\varepsilon\le1\). Its energy density is \[e_\varepsilon(u_\varepsilon)
 =\frac1{2\varepsilon}\operatorname{sech}^4
       \left(\frac{x_1}{\sqrt2\varepsilon}\right).\] The integral in the \(x_1\) direction is \[c=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\int_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{sech}^4 s\,ds
   =\frac{2\sqrt2}{3},\] because \(t=\tanh s\) changes the integral to \(\int_{-1}^1(1-t^2)\,dt=4/3\). Every vertical slice of the unit disk has length at most two. Therefore \(E_\varepsilon\le2c=4\sqrt2/3<2\) for every allowed \(\varepsilon\); choose \(M_0=2\).

Actual limiting measure. Changing variables \(x_1=\sqrt2\varepsilon s\) in the integral against any compactly supported continuous test function, then using the integrable dominating function \(\operatorname{sech}^4s\), proves \[\nu_\star=c\,\mathcal H^1\mathbin{\rule[0.3ex]{0.07ex}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.07ex}}L,\qquad
 L=\{(0,x_2):-1<x_2<1\}.\] The same calculation gives \(\zeta_\star=(c/2)\mathcal H^1\mathbin{\rule[0.3ex]{0.07ex}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.07ex}}L\). These limits hold along every sequence \(\varepsilon\to0\); no subsequence choice can remove the counterexample.

Subdomain and contradictory conclusion. Set \[U=\{4x_1^2+x_2^2<1\},\qquad \delta=	frac14.\] This is a bounded, connected, smooth, proper open subset of \(\Omega\). Its closure touches \(\partial\Omega\) only at \((0,\pm1)\), and \(L\subset U\). By the printed definition, \(V_\delta\subset\Omega\setminus U\), hence \[ oxed{
u_\star(V_\delta)=0,\qquad
        
u_\star(\overline U\cap\Omega)=2c= rac{4\sqrt2}{3}>0.}\] If \(
u_\star\) is extended by zero outside \(\Omega\), the second value is exactly \(
u_\star(\overline U)\). If all sets are interpreted relatively in \(\Omega\), the value is unchanged. Thus both conventional interpretations contradict [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed). This example does not use equality \(U=\Omega\), an irregular subdomain, a degenerate well, unbounded energy, or a boundary condition absent from the theorem.

For completeness, the corresponding finite-\(\varepsilon\) exterior energy tends to zero as well. For almost every \(x_2\in(-1,1)\), the ellipse contains a positive-width interval around \(x_1=0\). The one-dimensional energy mass outside that interval tends to zero and is bounded by \(c\). Dominated convergence in \(x_2\) proves \(\int_{\Omega\setminus U}e_\varepsilon\to0\). Meanwhile the potential energy on \(U\) tends to \(c>0\). Thus Proposition 3.11’s estimate also fails in this boundary-touching range for any fixed finite constant independent of \(\varepsilon\).
## Alternative readings, impact and severity

The most favorable reading is that every subdomain in this argument was intended to be relatively compact, or that \(U_\delta\) was intended to be an ambient neighborhood contained in \(\Omega\). Either reading excludes the example. Neither is stated in Theorem 1.16, and the explicit \(x\in\Omega\) in (1.67) makes the displayed inclusion in Proposition 4.15 insufficient by itself. The correction must state an interior separation, not just repeat that inclusion.

The dependency is explicit: Theorem 1.16 is used in Proposition 7.4 to eliminate separated interior components; Proposition 1.17 and the rectifiability part of Theorem 1.2 then use this connectedness. A false theorem and unavailable test field on this core proof route warrant Major under the assigned calibration. Repair difficulty is not the severity criterion.

There is decisive counterevidence against a broader adverse conclusion. In Section 7.4, printed pp. 274–276/PDF 86–88, the application is constructed inside \(D^2(x_0,r)\) with \(D^2(x_0,2r)\subset\Omega\). The separated component and its small thickening are compactly contained in that interior disk. They satisfy the additional restriction below. The present finding therefore does not refute Theorems 1.2, 1.3, 1.5, 1.8 or 1.9; the example itself has a straight stationary interior interface.
# A precise restricted repair

A defensible corrected statement is: assume \(U\) is bounded and open and \[K_\delta=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\operatorname{dist}(x,\overline U)\le\delta\}
 \Subset\Omega .\] Define \(V_\delta=K_\delta\setminus U\). Under the paper’s PDE and energy hypotheses, \(\nu_\star(V_\delta)=0\) implies \(\nu_\star(\overline U)=0\).

Choose \(0<\delta_0<\min\{\delta,1\}\). Then \(K_{\delta_0}\Subset\Omega\) and \(V_{\delta_0}=K_{\delta_0}\setminus U\subset V_\delta\), so \(\nu_\star(V_{\delta_0})=0\). The cutoff in Proposition 3.11 can now be chosen with compact support in \(\Omega\): take it equal to one on \(K_{\delta_0/2}\) and supported in the interior of \(K_{\delta_0}\). The stress identity gives the potential bound because derivatives of the cutoff occur only in the exterior band, where the energy controls the tensor. This permits the use of Proposition 4.15 in its interior setting and with its explicit width condition \(\delta_0<1\).

The passage to the measure limit can also be stated rigorously. \(V_{\delta_0}\) is compact and closed in \(\Omega\), so weak convergence and its zero limiting mass give \(\limsup
u_{\varepsilon_n}(V_{\delta_0})\le0\). For sufficiently large \(n\) the smallness threshold of Proposition 4.15 holds, and \[
u_{\varepsilon_n}(U_{\delta_0/4})
 \le C\{
u_{\varepsilon_n}(V_{\delta_0})+\varepsilon_nM_0\}\longrightarrow0.\] An open neighborhood of \(\overline U\) contained in \(U_{\delta_0/4}\) then has zero limiting mass, proving the corrected conclusion. If only \(\overline U\Subset\Omega\) is assumed, choose the smaller width below \(\delta\), one, and the distance to \(\partial\Omega\); its exterior band is still a subset of the original band.

This verifies the support and limiting steps of the restricted repair, conditional on the earlier interior energy estimates used in Proposition 4.15. It is not an independent reconstruction of all level-set estimates in Section 4. The original boundary-general claim is not restored, and no replacement boundary theorem is proposed.
# Other mathematical checks and their limits
## Scaling and the fast-decay recurrence

Equations (1.52)–(1.61), printed pp. 208–209, have the correct two-dimensional scaling: \(\widetilde\varepsilon=\varepsilon/r\), \(\widetilde u(x)=u(rx+x_0)\) and \(E_{\widetilde\varepsilon}(\widetilde u,D)=E_\varepsilon(u,D_r)/r\). The scaled decay has terms \(r^{-1/2}E^{3/2}\) and \((\varepsilon/r)E\).

For the recurrence in Section 6.2, printed pp. 261–265, putting \(A_n=-\log E_n\) gives \(A_{n+1}\ge(3/2)A_n-f_n\), with \(f_n=(n/2)\log2+\log K_{\rm dec}\ge0\). Direct induction gives the exact lower bound \[A_n\ge(3/2)^n\left(A_0-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(2/3)^{j+1}f_j\right).\] The infinite sum is \(2\log2+2\log K_{\rm dec}\). Choosing \(A_0\) larger by one yields the double-exponential energy estimate and the logarithmic stopping-radius bound. The printed summation to \(n\) is weaker in this application precisely because \(f_n\ge0\); that endpoint cannot be used without qualification for arbitrary signed forcing. This is an index-level correction, not an additional substantive finding. The \(r\ge\varepsilon\) stopping condition is essential. The complete level-set derivation of Proposition 1.12 and every explicit constant/radius in Sections 5–6 were not certified.
## Stress tensor, potential monotonicity and singular mass

The singular-part argument in Lemmas 9.4–9.6 was checked as an argument about measures, not pointwise derivatives. With radial projection \(\Pi(x)=|x-x_0|\), the relevant exceptional set of radii is \(\Pi(E_\star)\), which is Lebesgue-null since \(\Pi\) is Lipschitz. On its complement the pushforward of \(N\) is positive. On that set, the identity \[\Pi_\#N=4\left(\Pi_\#\zeta_\star-\frac{Z(r)}r\,dr\right)\] is positive because the absolutely continuous \(Z(r)dr/r\) term vanishes there. This establishes positivity of the distributional derivative of \(Z(r)/r\). It does not assume away the possible singular mass at the start. The displayed inverse-image symbol and dropped positive factors in the surrounding text are not needed for this verified argument and are not counted as separate scientific issues.

Corollary 9.8’s abbreviated appeal to a finite density at \(\lambda\)-almost every point would not, in isolation, exclude a singular measure. The available stronger input is Lemma 9.7 for every interior center together with the locally uniform bound \(\zeta_\star(D_r(x))\le C r\) from monotonicity. It gives \(\nu_\star(D_s(x))\le C' s\) uniformly on compact subsets. Covering an \(\mathcal H^1\)-null set by small balls proves zero \(\nu_\star\) mass. Thus this step is supportable without the invalid general inference from almost-everywhere finiteness alone. No optimal numerical constant in (9.21) is asserted by this review.
The derivation of Proposition 1.20 from the projected-moment analysis in Section 8 is a substantive unverified input here. The conditional checks above do not certify it.
## Stationarity and the distinction between the two energies

In a tangent-normal frame, write the gradient-density matrix as \(\operatorname{diag}(a,a+2\Theta)\) using Theorem 1.9. Then \(
u=a+2\Theta\), and the limiting stress is \[
u I-\mu=2\Theta\,t\otimes t .\] Consequently its divergence-free identity is exactly \(\int \operatorname{div}_{T_xS_\star}X\,d\zeta_\star=0\). This independently checks the sign and factor in Section 11, printed pp. 311–312. Tangential energy \(a\) need not vanish. Therefore stationarity of \(\zeta_\star\) does not, by itself, assert \(
u_\star=2\zeta_\star\). No unsupported energy-equipartition substitution is needed.
# Overall disposition and remaining work

The proof route supports an interior interpretation of the clearing-out tool, and the inspected connectedness use satisfies that interpretation. The unrestricted printed formulation needs correction. Neither arbitrary boundary behavior nor higher-dimensional or parabolic extensions follow from this review.
Item | Disposition
M01 | Major: boundary-touching case falsifies Theorem 1.16 as stated and the unrestricted supporting estimate.
Repair | Interior restriction and limiting step verified, conditional on the earlier interior energy estimates.
Main results | No counterexample established; inspected local use survives the restriction.
Other checks | Scaling, recurrence structure, tensor algebra and final measure arguments checked within stated dependencies.
Adoption/acceptance | Author adoption not requested; independent human scientific acceptance pending.
Remaining work | Full level-set estimates, Section 8 projected moments, all Section 10 steps, quantitative constants, and cited geometric-measure-theory foundations.

No separate supplement or computational repository is included in the acquired manifest. No author code was run; its absence is not evidence of correctness or a defect. The pseudo-profile construction cited as work in preparation was not reconstructed. The complete paper and all external dependencies have not been verified.
# Supporting checks

The source-page images actually inspected are PDF pages 1, 4, 6, 8, 9, 18, 21, 23, 49, 53, 54, 64, 73, 74, 75, 85, 86, 87, 88, 111, 114, 115, 116, 123 and 124. The full extracted text, source PDF information and actual I/O events are retained alongside them. The reviewer-authored `independent_checks.py`, in the evidence directory, was actually executed with existing Windows Python. It checks the rational mass integral, all four polynomial coefficients in the corrected (H3) identity, the positive radial-growth margin at radius two, and twenty exact recurrence steps using only the standard library. The initial report omitted \(b^2/2\) from the identity and its original script checked only two coefficients; focused acceptance corrected both and executed the updated check. The JSON result records the analytic counterexample parameters and exact values. Finite recurrence checks corroborate arithmetic; induction, PDE satisfaction and weak convergence are proved above, not inferred from those checks. This is not empirical reproduction.

Version checks consulted arXiv `2003.10189`, whose inspected submission history lists v1, 23 March 2020. It was not substituted for the supplied 2025 publisher PDF. Targeted correction searches did not identify a correction for this theorem; this limited negative result does not prove no correction exists or establish novelty. The publisher landing-page open returned HTTP 403; the supplied PDF remained available, and its identity was visually verified. No claim of reading the blocked landing page is made.

report: Date: 25 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review of
The Landau equation does not blow up

Assigned source. Nestor Guillen and Luis Silvestre, Acta Mathematica 234 (2025), 315–375, DOI 10.4310/acta.2025.v234.n2.a2. The reviewed object is the supplied 61-page publisher PDF. Printed page equals PDF page plus 314. Its SHA-256 is

`b0389fb345eb1aca3199ddce58db99e83c3`
`bf80a431e4dcde631531cc30e29f1`.

Outcome. One Major proof-justification issue, M01, is established in the explicit approximation and convergence argument on pp. 364 and 371–372. The counterexample concerns that approximation, not blow-up of a Landau solution. The central lifted dissipation calculation and its spherical constant survive the checks below. No additional substantive issue was established in the declared scope. Independent human scientific acceptance remains pending.
# Scope and actual coverage

This is a systematic claim-focused initial review under scientific prompt 0.7.1. All 61 PDF pages were exposed as extracted text, including the reference pages; that does not mean that every referenced theorem or every analytic estimate has been independently proved. Source page images actually inspected were PDF pages 1–3, 18–20, 32, 34–35, 37, 44, 46–47, 49–51 and 54–58 (21 pages). A truncated combined read of pages 9–17 was recovered by smaller complete reads.

The mathematical work concentrated on the hypotheses of Theorems 1.1–1.2; mass normalization and projection in Section 3; rotational vector fields and commutators in Sections 4–8; the entire constant-producing chain in Section 9; the coordinate transfer in Section 10; weighted interpolation and continuation in Section 11; and the admissibility and convergence of the explicit approximations in Appendix B. Appendix A was read and its circle spectral-gap argument checked at the level described below.

The manifest supplies the publisher PDF and metadata HTML, without a separate computational repository or supplement. No author program was run. The reviewer wrote and executed a small exact-rational arithmetic check for the mass and energy divergence, the constants \(19/4,19/2\), and the interpolation choice \(p=2\). This corroborates analytic calculations; it does not simulate the PDE.

Not independently reconstructed: the complete local existence, uniqueness, moment propagation and conditional regularity theorems cited in Section 2; all coefficient and Schauder estimates in Appendix B; a complete solution-stability proof after replacing the defective approximation; optimal constants or the full later extensions; or every historical/reference claim. The absence of a supplied code repository is not a defect. This report does not certify the entire paper.
# M01: the proposed approximants have divergent mass
## Location and assertion

Equation reference: badapprox. The last displayed initial-data formula on printed p. 371 (PDF 57), with the stated cutoff directly below it, is \[
 f^\varepsilon(0,v)
 =(f_0(v)+\varepsilon)\eta(\varepsilon v)
 +(1-\eta(\varepsilon v))e^{-|v|^2},
 \qquad
 0\leq\eta\leq1,\quad
 \eta|_{B_1}=1,\quad
 \operatorname{supp}\eta\subset B_2.\] The first paragraph of p. 372 (PDF 58) then asserts convergence of the solutions, including weighted \(L^{\infty,k}\) convergence for \(f\), for any \(k\), and \(L^\infty([0,T],H^1(\mathbb R^3))\) convergence for their square roots. It uses this to transfer monotonicity of Fisher information to the original solution. The approximation is explicitly connected to the proof of Theorem 1.1 on p. 364 and to the justification of the integral manipulations on p. 368.
## Complete obstruction, including a unit-mass example

Choose the admissible, nonzero, smooth unit-mass Maxwellian \[f_0(v)=\pi^{-3/2}e^{-|v|^2}.\] It has every polynomial moment, finite Fisher information, and the upper bound required by Theorem 1.2. It is a stationary solution for every applicable power-law kernel: the difference of logarithmic gradients is \(-2(v-w)\), which is annihilated by \(a(v-w)\).

Equation reference: mass, energy. On \(B_{1/\varepsilon}\), equation [badapprox] (#badapprox) gives \(f^\varepsilon(0,v)=f_0(v)+\varepsilon\). Therefore \[\begin{aligned}
 m_\varepsilon:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f^\varepsilon(0,v)\,\mathrm dv
 &\geq\varepsilon |B_{1/\varepsilon}|
   =\frac{4\pi}{3}\varepsilon^{-2}\longrightarrow\infty,\\
 \int_{\mathbb R^3}|v|^2f^\varepsilon(0,v)\,\mathrm dv
 &\geq\varepsilon\int_{B_{1/\varepsilon}}|v|^2\,\mathrm dv
   =\frac{4\pi}{5}\varepsilon^{-4}\longrightarrow\infty.\end{aligned}\] These bounds hold for every cutoff permitted in the paper, independently of its transition behavior.

For each \(\varepsilon>0\), the approximant is integrable and has a Gaussian tail, so the objection is not that an individual three-dimensional datum is inadmissible. It is the absence of convergence and of uniform hydrodynamic bounds. At time zero, \[\|\sqrt{f^\varepsilon(0)}-\sqrt{f_0}\|_{L^2}
 \geq \sqrt{m_\varepsilon}-1\longrightarrow\infty.\] Mass conservation, recalled on p. 324, gives the same lower bound at every common time of existence of \(f^\varepsilon\) and the stationary \(f_0\). Thus this also rules out the asserted essential-supremum-in-time \(H^1\) convergence; the problem cannot be avoided by discarding the time-zero endpoint.
## The related six-dimensional formula

Printed p. 364 (PDF 50) proposes \[F_\varepsilon(v,w)=(F(v,w)+\varepsilon)\eta(\varepsilon v,\varepsilon w)
 +(1-\eta(\varepsilon v,\varepsilon w))e^{-|v|^2}.\] As printed, the tail has no \(w\)-decay. For fixed \(v\) and all sufficiently large \(w\), it equals \(e^{-|v|^2}\), and hence is not integrable on \(\mathbb R^6\); it need not be symmetric under \(v\leftrightarrow w\), either. These facts prevent its direct use in Proposition 10.2. Inserting the missing Gaussian factor in \(w\) alone still leaves the constant floor on an expanding six-dimensional ball, of mass at least \(\omega_6\varepsilon^{-5}\). The substantive issue is the unproved passage to a limit with these actual approximants, not the isolated missing factor. Both formulas belong to the same issue M01.
## Counterevidence and precise impact

The argument through Lemma 10.1 and Proposition 10.2 is a valid formal dissipation argument for sufficiently controlled, positive, symmetric inputs, subject to the analytic integrations being justified. Sections 3–10 do not require the divergent plateau to produce the constants. The later continuation argument in Section 11 is coherent once the monotonicity estimate is available for its solution class. A Gaussian stationary solution itself is not a counterexample to either global existence or Fisher monotonicity.

Moreover, Lemma 3.3 on p. 333 already uses an integrable symmetric Gaussian perturbation for a different limiting argument. That is useful evidence that an appropriate repair is plausible. However, it does not prove the solution convergence asserted on p. 372 for [badapprox] (#badapprox). Renormalizing [badapprox] (#badapprox) alone is not a remedy: its mass tends to infinity while it tends pointwise to \(f_0\), so division by its mass sends the initial data locally to zero.

The issue is rated Major because the defective passage is presented as the justification for extending the main Fisher-information theorem beyond the specially controlled class and for applying that estimate in the global theorem. The demonstrated result is a failure of the supplied proof step. It is not a claim that Theorems 1.1 or 1.2 are false, nor that no alternative proof exists. Its repair must supply convergence of the relevant solutions and Fisher information, rather than merely alter a displayed symbol.
## A checked initial-data repair and its remaining obligation

For the Gaussian-upper-bound class of Theorem 1.2, choose a positive Gaussian \(M\) with \(f_0\leq C M\), and set \[g^\varepsilon_0=f_0+\varepsilon M.\] Then \(\varepsilon M\leq g^\varepsilon_0\leq(C+\varepsilon)M\), and every finite polynomial moment of \(g^\varepsilon_0-f_0\) tends to zero. When \(\sqrt{f_0}\in H^1\), this also repairs initial square-root \(H^1\) convergence. Indeed, \[\|\sqrt{g^\varepsilon_0}-\sqrt{f_0}\|_2^2
 \leq\varepsilon\|M\|_1,\qquad
 i(f_0+\varepsilon M)\leq i(f_0)+\varepsilon i(M).\] The latter inequality is pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz applied to \(|\nabla(f_0+\varepsilon M)|^2/(f_0+\varepsilon M)\). Weak compactness and lower semicontinuity, combined with the upper bound, give convergence of the gradient norms and then strong \(H^1\) convergence.

This proves an initial-data replacement in the stated finite-Fisher class. It does not by itself prove convergence of the corresponding Landau solutions in \(L^\infty_tH^1\), or justify passage of the dissipation inequality at arbitrary positive times. Those stability and time-shift arguments must be supplied with uniform hypotheses. The more general polynomial-tail statement at the end of Appendix B requires further construction and appropriately restricted weights; it is not repaired here. No claim of a fully repaired main theorem is made.
# Independent checks supporting the unaffected calculations
## Equation scope and the lifting argument

Theorems 1.1–1.2 concern the three-dimensional space-homogeneous equation. Theorem 1.1 is an a priori estimate for classical solutions with adequate decay, under \(\sup_{r>0}r|\alpha'(r)|/\alpha(r)\leq\sqrt{19}\). For \(\alpha(r)=r^\gamma\), this ratio is \(|\gamma|\); the physical interval \([-3,1]\) is included. Theorem 1.2 assumes a Gaussian upper bound on the initial datum. Rough data are interpreted through positive-time smoothness and weak attainment at zero, as explained in Theorem 2.1. The unit-mass convention on p. 324 is respected by the counterexample above; zero initial mass is not used to manufacture a separate issue.

For unit-mass \(f\), direct differentiation of the tensor product gives \(I(f\otimes f)=2i(f)\). For symmetric \(F(v,w)\), Cauchy–Schwarz in \(w\) yields \[\frac{|\nabla\pi F(v)|^2}{\pi F(v)}
 \leq \int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{|\nabla_vF(v,w)|^2}{F(v,w)}\,\mathrm dw.\] Integration in \(v\) and symmetry give \(i(\pi F)\leq I(F)/2\). At \(F(0)=f\otimes f\), equality holds. The right derivative at zero of the nonpositive difference \(i(\pi F)-I(F)/2\) is nonpositive, proving the direction of Lemma 3.4. This suffices; the optional two-sided-curve discussion in Remark 3.5 is not needed.
## Rotations, radial error and signs

Writing \(B_k=\widetilde b_k\cdot\nabla\), the identities \(\sum_k b_k\otimes b_k=|v-w|^2 I-(v-w)\otimes(v-w)\), \(B_k\alpha=0\), and \(\operatorname{div}\widetilde b_k=0\) give \(Q=\sum_k\alpha B_k^2\). The fields are rotations on the fixed center-of-mass and relative-radius layers. The parallel Fisher information and the spherical Fisher information are separately invariant under the weighted rotations; the two nonzero commutator contributions cancel in the sum.

For \(n\) as in (4.7), \(n\cdot\nabla\alpha=\sqrt2\,\alpha'\) and \([n,\widetilde b_k]=0\). Setting \(u=\log F\), \(h=B_k u\), the integrand before the final square completion in Lemma 7.1 is \[-2\alpha F(nh)^2-2(n\alpha)Fh(nh).\] It equals \[-2F\bigl(n(\sqrt\alpha\,h)\bigr)^2+
 \frac{(n\alpha)^2}{2\alpha}Fh^2
 =
 -2F\bigl(n(\sqrt\alpha\,h)\bigr)^2+
 \frac{(\alpha')^2}{\alpha}Fh^2.\] Thus the sign and coefficient of the radial error are correct.

The intermediate displays (8.2) on p. 348 and the first display on p. 349 omit a minus sign before the respective Fisher Hessian term. The negative signs follow directly from Lemma 7.1 and (8.1), and the lemma statement and final expanded expression have the correct sign. These are recorded as excluded local transcription errors, not additional substantive findings: the required identity has been reconstructed without changing the argument.
## The \(19/4\) sphere constant

Put \(B_i=b_i\cdot\nabla_\sigma\), \(u=\sqrt f\), \(A_g=(B_iB_jg)_{ij}\), and let \(M_g,N_g\) be its symmetric and antisymmetric parts. The commutators give \[\|N_g\|^2=\frac12\sum_i(B_i g)^2.\] For a divergence-free rotational field \(B\), integration by parts gives the one-direction identity \[\int f(B^2\log f)^2
 =4\int\left((B^2u)^2+\frac{(Bu)^4}{3u^2}\right)
 \geq4\int(B^2u)^2.\] Averaging over \(B=b_e\cdot\nabla\), with fourth spherical moments \(\int e_1^2e_2^2=4\pi/15\) and \(\int e_1^4=4\pi/5\), gives Lemma 9.8.

The pointwise relation \(\sum_i\sigma_i B_i=0\) implies \(\sigma^T A_g=0\), so \(A_g\) has rank at most two. In a basis with a unit kernel vector first, its first diagonal entry is zero. The squared Frobenius norm of its symmetric part dominates the sum of squares of the other two diagonal entries, giving \(2\|M_g\|^2\geq|\operatorname{tr}M_g|^2\). This verifies the rank step of Lemmas 9.9–9.10.

The Casimir \(\Delta_\sigma=\sum_i B_i^2\) commutes with each rotation, and integration by parts yields \[\sum_{i,j}\int(B_iB_j u)^2=\int(\Delta_\sigma u)^2,\qquad
 \int\|M_u\|^2=\int(\Delta_\sigma u)^2- rac12\int|
abla_\sigma u|^2.\] Consequently Lemma 9.10 implies \[\int f\|M_{\log f}\|^2
 \geq 3\int(\Delta_\sigma u)^2-\int|
abla_\sigma u|^2.\] If \(f\) is even, then \(u\) and each \(B_j u\) are even. Each \(B_j u\) has integral zero because \(B_j\) is divergence free. The first allowed nonconstant spherical harmonic degree is two, of eigenvalue six. Hence \(\sum_{i,j}\int(B_iB_j u)^2\geq6\sum_j\int(B_j u)^2\). The last lower bound is therefore \(17\int|
abla_\sigma u|^2
=(17/4)\int f|
abla_\sigma\log f|^2\). Adding the antisymmetric contribution \(1/2\) gives \(19/4\). Dropping evenness would invalidate this improved spectral-gap step.
## Transfer and continuation

With \(v=z+r\sigma,\ w=z-r\sigma\), the six-dimensional Jacobian is \(8r^2\), and \(\widetilde b_k\cdot\nabla=2B_k\). The factors in (8.3)–(8.4) give \(16\) and \(8\) times the corresponding sphere integrals. Thus \(D_{\rm spherical}\geq(19/2)R_{\rm spherical}\), exactly compensating the error coefficient \(\sup r^2(\alpha')^2/(2\alpha^2)\). Remark 10.3’s \(Q=4\alpha(2r)\Delta_\sigma\) also follows. The earlier informal geometric normalization is not needed for these explicit computations.

For Section 11, finite Fisher information at \(t_0>0\) controls \(L^3\) by the Sobolev estimate for \(\sqrt f\). The weighted interpolation can be made explicit: \[\|f\|_{L^2_k}
 \leq\|f\|_{L^1_{4k}}^{1/4}\|f\|_{L^3}^{3/4}.\] For \(\gamma\in[-3,-2)\), \(2>3/(5+\gamma)\), so this meets the displayed conditional criterion of Theorem 2.2. Moment bounds may depend on the fixed finite proposed blow-up time; they need not be uniform as time tends to infinity. The Gaussian upper estimate then controls every finite \(L^\infty_k\) weight and closes the stated continuation criterion, conditional on the Fisher estimate and the cited analytic inputs. Constants must depend on the actual positive-time Fisher bound and the moments used; finiteness of \(i(f_0)\) is not silently assumed for every rough datum in Theorem 1.2.

For Appendix A, even functions on \(S^1\) exclude odd Fourier modes, giving the first positive allowed eigenvalue four. The same one-direction identity gives the displayed constant four and hence the lifted factor eight. This does not independently establish every higher-dimensional suggestion in that appendix.
# Supporting checks

The assigned publisher PDF remains the reviewed version. The arXiv record https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09420 lists v2 dated 27 January 2025. The v2 HTML at https://arxiv.org/html/2311.09420v2, specifically its Appendix B formula and following paragraph, was actually opened and still contains the same constant-floor approximation and convergence assertion. Limited correction searches and the authors’ publication pages https://math.uchicago.edu/~luis/preprints.html and https://www.ndguillen.com/research.html did not identify an explicit correction to M01. This does not prove novelty or absence of an unpublished repair. The improvement to \(\sqrt{22}\) attributed to Ji is already acknowledged on publisher p. 316; it is an improvement, not evidence against the paper’s weaker constant, and its proof was not audited here.

The evidence directory contains original-page renders, extracted source text, read/render events, reviewer-written exact arithmetic and its actual output, and version/correction-search records. Actual compiler, support-input, log, TeX/PDF and report-page inspection hashes are bound in the current `build_record.json` and shared support manifest. No author code was executed or compiler executable installed. The controller’s reported Chat/6Pro UI observation and the worker’s self-description remain separately attributed; no backend equivalence is asserted. Human scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Initial scientific review of
Deformation theory and partition Lie algebras
# Identity, version and scope

This report concerns M25-0047, D. Lukas B. Brantner and Akhil Mathew, Deformation theory and partition Lie algebras, Acta Mathematica 235 (2025), 1–148, DOI 10.4310/acta.2025.v235.n1.a1 [BM]. The assigned 148-page publisher PDF was reviewed; printed and PDF page numbers coincide. Its SHA-256 is
The later arXiv v5, dated 27 November 2025, was consulted for a limited comparison; it does not replace the publisher file.

The review exposed 82 of 148 pages as text: 1–18, 24–29, 44–50, 59–68, 77–91, 96–101, 103–114, 121–123 and 130–134. Twenty-four source pages were also inspected as rendered images. Full extraction and theorem indexing served navigation; neither constitutes review of unread pages. Targets were the classification hypotheses, comonadicity and completion, the relative-base reduction, explicit partition-complex formulas, and selected basis-calculation steps. This is a systematic claim-focused initial review, not a line-by-line verification of all 148 pages.
# Problem M01: the many-generator derivation loses equivariant information
Severity: Major, confined to a demonstrated core proof calculation.
## Exact locations and dependency

On p. 132, the proof of Proposition 7.40 first gives a binomial expansion for finite pointed \(X\), finite \(V\), and arbitrary integers \(\ell_i\), then extends it to (7.7). It pulls suspension factors outside subgroup coinvariants while leaving the permutation action on \(V^{\otimes n}\) untwisted. The last display on p. 132, repeated after dualisation on p. 133, makes a further assertion for arbitrary \(V\). The proof of Theorems 7.3 and 7.4 ends on p. 134 by using Proposition 7.40 for every number of generators greater than one. These are the advertised basis theorems, restated as Theorems 1.18 and 1.22. The invalid calculation thus has an explicit dependency on a core contribution.
## Complete counterexample to the binomial expansion

Equation reference: signed. Take \[p=3,\quad n=2,\quad m=1,\quad
 \ell_1=1,\quad V=\mathbb F_3,\quad X=S^0\] with trivial \(\Sigma_2\)-action on the single non-basepoint. All the displayed finiteness and integrality assumptions hold. Put \(W=\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb F_3\). The transposition on \(W^{\otimes2}\) acts by \(-1\), since both factors have odd degree. Hence \[
 \mathbb F_3[X]\otimes_{\Sigma_2} W^{\otimes2}=0.\] The coinvariant relation identifies a generator \(z\) with \(-z\), so \(2z=0\), and 2 is invertible. There are no hidden derived higher coinvariants: averaging makes invariants and coinvariants exact when the group order is invertible. Homotopy orbits give the same answer.

Equation reference: untwisted. The printed right-hand side has only \(n_1=2\), and gives \[
 \Sigma^{-2}\bigl(\mathbb F_3[X]\otimes_{\Sigma_2}V^{\otimes2}\bigr)
 =\Sigma^{-2}\mathbb F_3\ne0.\] Thus the preliminary expansion is false. Formula (7.7) has the same problem: in this semisimple arity, \(F_{S^0}\) is the second symmetric-power summand on complexes, so \[F_{S^0}(\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb F_3)=0,\qquad
 \Sigma^{-2}F_{S^0}(\mathbb F_3)=\Sigma^{-2}\mathbb F_3.\] This is not a distinction between strict and homotopy coinvariants.

A valid binomial expansion retains \[\bigotimes_i(\Sigma^{-\ell_i}V)^{\otimes n_i}\] inside the coinvariants for \(H=\prod_i\Sigma_{n_i}\). For discrete \(V\), pulling the total suspension outside must retain the character \(\bigotimes_i\operatorname{sgn}_{n_i}^{\ell_i}\) on \(V^{\otimes n}\). Derived extensions must carry the corresponding equivariant suspension data; an untwisted scalar shift cannot replace it.
## A second check excludes a correction of only one sign

Write \(C_r=\Sigma|\Pi_r|^\diamond\), with the intended convention \(C_1=S^0\). The last display on p. 132 uses the exponent \(1+\sum_i(1-\ell_i)n_i/d\), whereas the desired dual input requires \(-1+\sum_i(1-\ell_i)n_i/d\). Changing that sign alone does not make the assertion true for arbitrary \(V\).

Work over \(\mathbb F_5\), take \(n=2\), \(m=2\), \(\ell_1=\ell_2=0\), and \(V=\mathbb F_5^2\). Inspect mixed multidegree \((n_1,n_2)=(1,1)\). Since \(C_2=S^1\) with trivial \(\Sigma_2\)-action, the left-hand mixed summand is \[\Sigma(V\otimes V),\qquad \dim_{\mathbb F_5}=4.\] This is also the mixed term of \(\Sigma\operatorname{Sym}^2(V\oplus V)\). The right has only \(d=1\) and the Lyndon word \(x_1x_2\). Even after correcting the suspension sign, its term is \[F_{C_1}(\Sigma V)=\Sigma V,\qquad \dim_{\mathbb F_5}=2.\] A tensor power has disappeared. This example is in nonnegative degrees and semisimple characteristic, independently of the odd-shift example. The general-input formula must retain the appropriate \(V^{\otimes n/d}\), or specialise to \(V=\mathbb F_p\) before the simplification.
## Counterevidence, repair and restricted impact

There is strong counterevidence to interpreting this as a false main theorem. Proposition 7.40 is stated for sums of shifts of the one-dimensional \(\mathbb F_p\); it does not assert the false arbitrary-\(V\) identity. Its exponent \(1+\sum_i(\ell_i-1)|w|_i\) has the expected bracket degree. Theorem 7.39 retains permutation spheres and provides the correct starting point.

After specialising \(V=\mathbb F_p\), retain all shifted factors in the \(H\)-equivariant binomial expansion. For \(d\mid\gcd(n_i)\), restriction to the diagonal \(\Sigma_d\) groups these as the \(d\)-fold tensor power of \[\bigotimes_i(\Sigma^{-\ell_i}\mathbb F_p)^{\otimes n_i/d}.\] The sphere \((S^{n/d-1})^{\wedge d}\) in Theorem 7.39 combines with them to give the \(d\)-fold tensor power of a line in degree \[a=n/d-1-\sum_i\ell_i n_i/d
   =-1+\sum_i(1-\ell_i)n_i/d.\] Duality gives \(-a=1+\sum_i(\ell_i-1)n_i/d\), exactly the exponent in the statement of Proposition 7.40. Keeping the grouped tensor factors retains their Koszul action. In the spectral case this is compatible with the bounded-above formula of Proposition 5.35. The strict case requires the corresponding genuine-equivariant and right-left-extension argument, rather than (7.7). A full reconstruction of that extension argument for every shift is not claimed here.

The established impact is an invalid step in the multigenerator basis proof, with a clear correction route. Neither a counterexample to Theorems 7.3–7.4 nor damage to the separate classification Theorems 1.12, 1.21 and 6.27 has been established. Major follows the specified standard for a demonstrated invalid derivation used by a core theorem; repairability does not remove that dependency. The later v5 HTML still contains the untwisted expansion and general-\(V\) formula. Limited primary-source checks found no explicit erratum for this issue; novelty is not certified.
# Other reasoning and boundary checks
## Formal-moduli hypotheses and completion

Definitions 1.3 and 1.5 distinguish finite total homotopy for Artinian inputs from degreewise finite type for complete Noetherian objects. The designated maps in the pullback condition must be surjective on \(\pi_0\). Claims about arbitrary nonconnective algebras or arbitrary pullbacks were not substituted.

In Proposition 2.11, pp. 17–18, a sufficiently high finite skeleton of a simplicial connective object computes a fixed homotopy degree uniformly across the filtration. Finite colimits preserve complete filtered objects; the Milnor \(\lim\) and \(\lim^1\) terms can then be controlled degree by degree. This does not say arbitrary colimits preserve completeness.

In Theorem 4.20, pp. 61–65, a cotangent equivalence gives an associated-graded equivalence, and completeness gives conservativity. Totalisation uses a cotangent-split cosimplicial object and its adic lift, not an unrestricted interchange of cotangent fibres and limits. For square-zero inputs, duality exchanges the relevant pullback with a pushout and the free functor preserves the pushout. The general step uses cobar resolutions, \(\pi_0\)-surjectivity and coherence. The underlying filtered-totalisation lemmas were traced but not all independently reproved.

Lemma 5.21 and Proposition 5.22, pp. 77–78, use bounded-below almost-perfect modules and Nakayama’s lemma; the least nonzero homotopy degree is legitimate. The cotangent-space map makes the map on complete local rings surjective, after which the relative cotangent module is almost perfect. The formal-etale and connectivity criteria remain external dependencies. Proposition 5.28, p. 80, uses finite positive filtration degrees and completion of a finitely generated graded module, not an arbitrary direct-sum/product interchange.
## Relative bases and duality

Propositions 6.5–6.6 and Theorem 6.7, pp. 97–99, retain derived completeness and connectivity. Perfect approximations to an almost-perfect \(N\) have increasingly connective cofibres, giving degreewise control of tensor product versus totalisation. The Cech nerve splits after tensoring with \(k\), and conservativity on complete connective modules gives descent. This would not justify descent for all unbounded modules.

Theorems 6.15 and 6.24, pp. 103–107, reduce to the case over \(k\). Their duality is on degreewise finite coconnective objects. Double duality was not extended to arbitrary infinite-dimensional modules. The formal-moduli identification in Theorem 6.27 also invokes Lurie’s axiomatic deformation theorem; that external theorem was not independently reconstructed.
## Partition complexes and low weights

Proposition 5.35 uses a right-left extension for arbitrary \(V\); the simpler homotopy-fixed-point formula requires \(V\) bounded above. Proposition 5.49 instead uses strict fixed points in a cosimplicial model for simplicial commutative rings. These are not interchangeable in positive characteristic.

At arity one, the bar model on p. 84 has one non-basepoint simplex with all partitions equal, giving \(T(1)=S^0\). Literal use of the empty proper-partition nerve would be misleading. The primary source [AB, p. 84] explicitly specifies \(C_1=S^0\); the apparent unit discrepancy is therefore resolved by an actual convention and is not a finding.

Reviewer-written finite-field chain calculations enumerated the proper-partition posets and all chains for \(2\le n\le5\). Over each of \(\mathbb F_2,\mathbb F_3,\mathbb F_5\), reduced homology is concentrated in degree \(n-3\), with dimensions \(1,2,6,24\). Double suspension gives degrees \(n-1\), as expected. This finite check is not a proof for all arities.

At \(p=2\), spectral weight two on a class of degree \(\ell\) is \(\Sigma^{2\ell-1}\mathbb F_2^{hC_2}\), with one class in every degree at most \(2\ell-1\). The basis condition \(i_1\le\ell\), with degree \(\ell+i_1-1\), agrees. For odd primes, the extra self-bracket of an even-degree class has weight two and degree \(2\ell-1\), as required by the shifted Lie convention.

Corollary 7.9, p. 114, prints even where Proposition 7.8 and the surrounding odd-generator proof require odd degree at odd primes. The context and separate even-generator argument identify the intended correction. This isolated parity-word error and the isolated suspension-sign transcription on pp. 132–133 are not separate substantive findings. M01 rests on the independent action and dimension counterexamples.
# Evidence and limitations

The coverage ledger records the inspected pages and claims. Evidence includes source-page images, a reviewer-written exact-arithmetic script and actual output, source bindings, and compilation records. No author program was supplied in the acquired manifest or executed; the package contains a publisher PDF and metadata rather than a computational repository.

Unverified material includes the complete extension calculus in Section 3; all filtered convergence lemmas; the full operadic generalisation in Section 5.3; Appendix A’s hypercoverings and Kan extensions; the full Bredon matching and degeneration argument; the topological-algebra construction of the even-generator cofibration; and the external foundations and every cited theorem. The correction route for M01 is not promoted to a fully verified new proof of the article.

The outcome is one supported Major proof-calculation issue with restricted impact, and no additional substantive issue established in the inspected classification arguments. Scientific acceptance remains pending. This report does not certify whole-paper correctness or record author adoption.
