Title: Initial scientific review of
Generalizing Lusztig’s total positivity
# Version and assessment

The reviewed object is the 93-page publisher PDF of [GW], DOI 10.1007/s00222-024-01303-y, published online on 10 January 2025. Printed page numbers equal PDF page numbers plus 706. The independently read Benoist manuscript is identified separately below.

The review followed the positivity definitions, representation criterion, classification, explicit invariant cones, open and closed unipotent semigroups, parameter maps, tangent cone, and selected flag-variety arguments. Independent calculations include exact weight and stabilizer computations, a symbolic nilpotent matrix logarithm, an exceptional Weyl-group calculation, and orthogonal rank-two transition equations. No author program was executed.

Assessment: one Major finding M01, comprising two related defects in the same representation-theoretic foundation, and two Minor findings M02–M03. The Major label refers to verified invalid inputs in a central proof chain. It does not assert a counterexample to the final classification. The coverage limits in Section 6 (#sec:limits) are part of this assessment.
# M01—The representation criterion and its cone consequence are overstated
## Location and dependency

Section 3.2, printed p. 725 (PDF p. 19), defines evenness by \(\lambda(H_\alpha)\in2\mathbb Z\) for every weight \(\lambda\) and root \(\alpha\), or \(R(V)\subset2P\), and then asserts that for an irreducible representation it suffices to test the highest weight. The order defining that highest weight is also specified there. Proposition 3.6(1) uses these notions to characterize invariant acute cones; Proposition 3.6(2) identifies the whole interior, up to sign, with vectors fixed by some maximal compact subgroup.

These statements are explicit inputs to Proposition 3.7 and the proof of Theorem 3.4 on pp. 726–727 (PDF pp. 20–21). Proposition 3.6(2) is also cited for uniqueness of cones in Remark 3.2, p. 724, and Section 5.1, p. 731. The problem is therefore mathematical, rather than bibliographical.
## The all-weights criterion fails in an actual classified example

Equation reference: eq:weights. Let \(S=\operatorname{SL}_3(\mathbb R)\) act on \[V=\operatorname{Sym}^2(\mathbb R^3)=\{M=M^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R)\},\qquad g\cdot M=gMg^{\mathsf T}.\] The positive semidefinite cone is nonzero, closed, convex, pointed, and invariant. Its interior is the positive definite cone. For \(H_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0)\) and \(H_2=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,-1)\), the weights give \[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrr}
\lambda&2e_1&2e_2&2e_3&e_1+e_2&e_1+e_3&e_2+e_3\\ \hline
\lambda(H_1)&2&-2&0&0&1&-1\\
\lambda(H_2)&0&2&-2&1&-1&0 .
\end{array}\] The usual highest weight \(2e_1=2\omega_1\) is even on both simple coroots, but three other weights have odd evaluations. Thus the asserted equivalence and Proposition 3.6(1), with the printed all-weights definition, are false.

The hypotheses are checkable directly. The six distinct Cartan weights have one-dimensional spaces. Root operators replace one monomial factor \(e_j\) by \(e_i\), connecting all six weight spaces. Cartan spectral projections followed by these operators show that every nonzero invariant subspace is all of \(V\). This proves real irreducibility. The element \(\operatorname{diag}(t,1,t^{-1})\), \(t>1\), has unique largest eigenvalue \(t^2\) on \(V\), with one-dimensional eigenspace, so the representation is proximal in the usual sense.

The printed order \(\lambda\leq\mu\) iff \(\lambda(H_\alpha)\leq\mu(H_\alpha)\) for every positive root is another problem: [eq:weights] (#eq:weights) has no greatest element for this order. Such an element would need both simple-coroot coordinates at least \(2\), and none does. Consequently the claim that every irreducible representation admits a highest weight for that order is false. The usual root-dominance order must be used.

This is not an unrelated representation. For \(G=\operatorname{Sp}(6,\mathbb R)\), \(\Theta=\{\alpha_3\}\), the semisimple Levi action on \(\mathfrak u_{\alpha_3}\) is precisely this symmetric-square action. The paper describes that matrix model on pp. 723 and 732 (PDF pp. 17 and 26). The printed all-weights definition would reject a positive structure explicitly included in Theorem 3.4.
## The interior need not consist of maximal-compact-fixed vectors

Take \(S=\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\) acting on binary quartics \(V=\operatorname{Sym}^4(\mathbb R^2)\), and set \[C_{\max}=\{f:f(x,y)\geq0\text{ for all }(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\}.\] This is a nonzero closed pointed invariant convex cone with nonempty interior. The five distinct weight lines are connected by the raising and lowering operators, which proves irreducibility. The representation has weights \(4,2,0,-2,-4\), and is proximal. It satisfies even the printed all-weights parity condition.

Equation reference: eq:stab. The quartic \(q=x^4+y^4\) lies in \(\operatorname{int}C_{\max}\), because \(q\geq(x^2+y^2)^2/2\); sufficiently small coefficient perturbations stay positive on the unit circle. Its infinitesimal stabilizer satisfies, up to the harmless choice of contragredient convention, \[
(a x\partial_x+b y\partial_x+c x\partial_y-a y\partial_y)q
=4a(x^4-y^4)+4b x^3y+4c xy^3 .\] The three polynomials on the right are independent. Thus the stabilizer Lie algebra is zero and cannot contain a conjugate of \(\mathfrak{so}_2\), the one-dimensional maximal compact Lie algebra. This disproves Proposition 3.6(2)’s asserted equality.

General uniqueness up to sign also fails. Let \(C_{\min}\) be the cone generated by \((a x+b y)^4\). Normalize \(a^2+b^2=1\). The generators are compact and their integrals over the unit circle are a fixed positive constant; their convex hull is compact in that affine hyperplane, proving closedness of the generated cone. Five distinct slopes give independent quartics by the Vandermonde determinant, so the cone has nonempty interior. It is pointed, invariant, and contained in \(C_{\max}\). However, \[(x^2-y^2)^2\in C_{\max}\setminus C_{\min},\] since its \(x^2y^2\) coefficient is \(-2\), whereas any positive sum of fourth powers has that coefficient nonnegative. The two cones are distinct and are not negatives of one another.
## Primary source, counterevidence, and repair

Benoist’s Proposition 4.7 and proof in [B] were actually read on manuscript pp. 27–28 (PDF pp. 29–30). They use the highest restricted weight in \(2P\), together with proximality. They neither impose \(R(V)\subset2P\) nor say that all interior vectors have maximal compact stabilizers. The cited primary source therefore does not support the stronger printed claims.

There is substantial counterevidence against a broader negative conclusion. The classification calculation on p. 727 actually tests the extremal weight \(\beta(H_\alpha)\), consistent with the correct criterion. The Section 5 modules are special symmetric-cone models: positive matrices, Lorentz cones, and the exceptional Jordan cone. The binary quartic example is not one of these modules and does not refute their homogeneity or uniqueness.

The required repair is to use the usual highest-weight order and the highest-restricted-weight parity condition, retain only the valid direction that a nonzero maximal-compact-fixed vector lies up to sign in the interior, and justify uniqueness and stabilizers for the specific Section 5 models. For the one-way assertion, average an interior point over a maximal compact subgroup and use the one-dimensional fixed-vector space; this does not imply uniqueness of arbitrary invariant cones. The false general criterion and false general cone consequence share the same central dependency and are counted together as M01. The actual classified models and the repaired extremal-weight calculation must be kept in the assessment; no counterexample to the four-family list is established.
# M02—Long restricted roots need not have multiplicity one (Minor)
Location: the last root-multiplicity paragraph of Section 2.2, printed p. 716 (PDF p. 10). Under the general real semisimple setup it asserts that a long restricted-root space is one-dimensional.

Let \(G=\operatorname{Sp}(4,\mathbb C)\), viewed as a real Lie group. It is connected and real semisimple with finite center. With \[\mathfrak a=\{\operatorname{diag}(h_1,h_2,-h_1,-h_2):h_i\in\mathbb R\},\] the restricted roots form \(C_2\), with long simple root \(2e_2\), and \[\mathfrak g_{2e_2}=\mathbb CE_{24}=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{E_{24},iE_{24}\}.\] For \(J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(E_{24}^{\mathsf T}J+JE_{24}=0\) and \([H,E_{24}]=2h_2E_{24}\). The same identities hold for \(iE_{24}\); these are real-linearly independent. The real multiplicity is \(2\).

This refutes the unrestricted background assertion. It does not refute the classification, whose p. 727 proof separately requires multiplicity one by proximality and consults the restricted-root classification. This group fails that test. Delete the general sentence or restrict it to the families for which multiplicity one is established. The demonstrated effect is local.
# M03—The BCH bound is local, not globally quadratic (Minor)

Equation reference: eq:bad. Location: Lemma 10.21(2), printed pp. 768–769 (PDF pp. 62–63). It quantifies over every \(v=(v_i)\) in the indicated root spaces and asserts \[
 \left\|\log(\exp v_1\cdots\exp v_N)-\sum_i v_i\right\|
 \leq C\max_i\|v_i\|^2 .\] No smallness restriction is imposed.

Equation reference: eq:bch. For split \(\operatorname{SL}_4(\mathbb R)\), use the longest reduced word \((1,2,3,1,2,1)\), put \(v_1=tE_{12},v_2=tE_{23},v_3=tE_{34}\), and set the other three parameters to zero, with \(t>0\). These lie even in the closed positive cones. Multiplication and the terminating formula \(\log(I+N)=N-N^2/2+N^3/3\) give \[
 \log(\exp v_1\exp v_2\exp v_3)
 =t(E_{12}+E_{23}+E_{34})
  +\frac{t^2}{2}(E_{13}+E_{24})+\frac{t^3}{3}E_{14}.\] The squared Frobenius norm of the remainder is \(t^4/2+t^6/9\), so its ratio to \(t^2\) is unbounded. This contradicts [eq:bad] (#eq:bad).

There is a complete repair sufficient for the downstream use. The finite BCH polynomial gives, for \(r=\max_i\|v_i\|\leq1\), \[\|R(v)\|\leq\sum_{k=2}^{d}C_kr^k\leq
 \left(\sum_{k=2}^{d}C_k\right)r^2 .\] Proposition 10.10 bounds \(r\leq D\|X\|\) for \(X=\log F_\gamma(v)\) in the closed cone parameterization. This proves Proposition 10.22(1) near zero. Away from zero, say \(\|X\|\geq\delta\), use \[\|X-p_1X\|\leq\|I-p_1\|\|X\|
 \leq\frac{\|I-p_1\|}{\delta}\|X\|^2.\] Thus the conclusion of Proposition 10.22(1) still has a global proof. Its tangent-cone limit and Trotter product argument need only the local BCH estimate. The unbounded-parameter counterexample does not invalidate those conclusions or Theorem 10.24. This bounded impact is the reason for Minor severity.
# Additional mathematical checks

The reviewed semigroup proof uses injectivity through Bruhat lengths, openness through invariance of domain, properness through the abelianization, exclusion of boundary parameters from the open Bruhat cell, and a common split-subgroup component to compare reduced words (Sections 10.2–10.7). The properness inequality has a direct proof: choose a linear functional positive on the compact unit section of a pointed closed cone; applying it to a sum bounds each summand by the norm of that sum. This justifies the substantive estimate in Proposition 10.10. The argument first gives a homeomorphism; a complete differential-rank proof for every claimed diffeomorphism was not reconstructed.

The open/closed distinction is essential. Remark 10.20 and Section 11.2 explicitly allow noninjectivity on the entire closed parameter cone. Vanishing scalar parameters merge vector parameters. This is acknowledged behavior, not a new finding.

For Lemma 11.2, write \(A=q(v_1)\), \(B=b(v_1,v_2)\), \(C=q(v_2)\), and \(S=q(v_1+v_2)=A+2B+C\). Then \[q\big(Sv_1-A(v_1+v_2)\big)
 =S^2A-2SA(A+B)+A^2S=SAC.\] For future timelike vectors this is positive; connectedness and \(v_1=v_2\) fix the future component. All seven transition equations (11.2)–(11.8) also passed an exact rational example with strictly interior inputs and outputs.

The Appendix C reflection matrices were reconstructed from its four \(F_4\) roots. The product \(\sigma_1\sigma_2\) has order six and \((\sigma_1\sigma_2)^3s_3s_4s_3=-I_4\). The root system has 24 positive roots, matching the expanded word length. This verifies the displayed longest-element calculation, not all earlier exceptional Lie-algebra constructions.

For the \(\operatorname{SL}_3\) examples of Section 12.4, multiplication yields \[r(a+a')(b+b')-(c+c'+ab')
 =(rab-c)+(ra'b'-c')+ra'b+(r-1)ab'\geq0\] when \(r\geq1\). Larger sharp invariant semigroups therefore really occur; Theorem 12.1 concludes inclusion rather than equality. The stronger Bruhat-component assumption in Theorem 12.2 must be preserved.

For flags, uniqueness of the opposite diamond follows from inversion of the same semigroup in a fixed unipotent chart. Transversality between opposite diamonds reduces to multiplication of positive elements. The distinction between \(\operatorname{Aut}_1(\mathfrak g)\) and \(G\), and the finite-index qualification in the properness proof for positive triples, were preserved.
# Coverage and limitations

Text was actually read on PDF pp. 1–10, 16–29, 55–85, and 90–93: 59 distinct pages. Twenty-four source pages were visually inspected, including all formal finding locations. Full extraction and indexing are not counted as scientific verification.

This claim-focused initial review is not a correctness proof of all 93 pages. The entire \(\Theta\)-system and split-subalgebra construction in Sections 5.5–7, all Bruhat-length inputs in Sections 8–9, the case-by-case boundary parameterization of Proposition 11.5, the bracket-generation argument in Lemma 12.9, the continuity step in Proposition 13.4, and the remaining cyclic-order discussion were not fully reconstructed. Some downstream checks are conditional on these inputs. Exceptional Jordan theory and the complete external bibliography were not reproved.

Local sign, index, and base-case slips with an immediate intended correction were separated from substantive findings. For example, Proposition 13.26’s quadruple criterion needs \(n\geq4\); for \(n=3\) the positive-triple condition must remain because the displayed quadruple test is empty. The contraction parameter in Proposition 13.4 must likewise have the sign consistent with contraction of positive root spaces. Neither observation is used to allege a false main positivity theorem.

The acquired manifest has the publisher PDF and metadata, with no separately bound author program or supplement. A limited version/correction search and earlier author-preprint metadata do not establish absence of all corrections. No current erratum repairing these specific statements was established. Independent specialist examination of the repairs and human acceptance remain pending.

Title: Initial scientific review of
Iterations of symplectomorphisms and
\(p\)-adic analytic actions on the Fukaya category
# Identity, scope, and assumptions

The reviewed source is the 64-page publisher PDF of [K], DOI 10.1007/s00222-024-01308-7, published online on 13 January 2025. Printed page equals PDF page plus 800. The frozen source hash is recorded in Appendix 6 (#app:record). The author preprint [Kv3], dated 17 December 2024, was consulted for targeted comparison; it does not replace this source.

All 64 pages were exposed and read as text, including both appendices. Twenty-nine source pages were actually inspected as images. This is a systematic claim-focused initial review, not independent verification of every transversality, compactness, orientation, or generation theorem in the external Fukaya-category literature. The supplied manifest contains the publisher PDF and metadata, without a separate supplement or author code repository. No author code was run.

Theorem 1.1 retains Assumption 1.2: a smooth Fukaya category with finitely many split generators of minimal Maslov number at least three, with the stated torsion-image or simultaneous Bohr–Sommerfeld monotonicity conditions. The paper’s ambient monotonicity is the global relation \(c_1(M)=\lambda[\omega_M]\) with \(\lambda\ne0\) (p. 809), not merely a vacuous condition on \(\pi_2\). The branes \(L,L'\) remain tautologically unobstructed with minimal Maslov number at least three. Removing their additional Bohr–Sommerfeld condition at pp. 842–843 does not remove these remaining hypotheses.

Theorem 1.9 instead uses Assumption 1.10, including \(\pi_2(M)=0\), a smooth proper uncurved category, split generation, and the specified unobstructed branes. Definition 5.4 imposes that the flux-period group meet the energy group only in zero. It is a condition on the chosen data. The torus translation of Example 1.8 is an acknowledged periodic example outside the relevant hypotheses, not a counterexample discovered here. Replacing a symplectomorphism by an autonomous flux flow is used up to the Hamiltonian invariance of the quantities at issue.
# Problem 1: the periodic resolution lift need not exist
## Claim and precise location

Lemma A.2, pp. 856–857 (PDF pp. 56–57), first reduces to a two-periodic complex \(B\) with \(H^0(B)=0\). It fixes a finite free resolution of \(H^1(B)\) in (A.9), lifts its first terms into the unrolled complex \(B\), and asserts that the lift extends inductively in (A.11). Periodizing then supposedly gives the quasi-isomorphism (A.12). The existence of a finite free resolution of the module is supported by Kedlaya’s Proposition 6.5 [Ked]. It does not imply this particular lift into a periodic complex. Odd-degree cohomology can obstruct the later lifting steps.
## A counterexample to the asserted construction

Equation reference: eq:koszul. Take the exact coefficient ring and residue field \[A=\mathbb Q_3\langle x_1,x_2,x_3\rangle,\qquad
 \mathfrak m=(x_1,x_2,x_3),\qquad k=A/\mathfrak m=\mathbb Q_3.\] All radii are one and satisfy the lemma’s norm hypothesis. Let \(K^{-j}=\bigwedge^j A^3\) be the Koszul resolution of \(k\), with \[d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_j})
 =\sum_{a=1}^j(-1)^{a-1}x_{i_a}
 e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat e_{i_a}\cdots\wedge e_{i_j}.
 \] The variables form a regular sequence, so \(H^0(K)=k\) and all other cohomology vanishes. Let \(P\) be its two-periodization: each parity has rank four, with \(H^0(P)=k\) and \(H^1(P)=0\).

Equation reference: eq:cone, eq:coho. Define an odd map \(f:P\to P\) by \(f(e_1e_2e_3)=1\) and zero on the other exterior degrees. Since \(df+fd=0\), it is a chain map \(P\to P[1]\). Set \[B=\operatorname{Cone}(P\xrightarrow{f}P[1])
   =P[1]\oplus P[1],\qquad
 D=\begin{pmatrix}-d&f\\0&-d\end{pmatrix}.
 \] Thus \(D^2=0\). The cone long exact sequence gives \(H^0(B)=0\) and \(0\to k\to H^1(B)\to k\to0\). This extension splits as an \(A\)-module: the two empty-wedge elements \((1,0),(0,1)\) are odd cycles lifting the two generators. Every \(x_i\) multiple of either is a boundary, since \(D(-e_i,0)=(x_i,0)\) and \(D(0,-e_i)=(0,x_i)\). Consequently \[H^0(B)=0,\qquad H^1(B)=k^2.
 \] All module-finiteness and parity assumptions of the reduced argument hold.

An allowed choice for (A.9) is two copies of the ordinary Koszul resolution of \(k\). Its periodization, placed in odd cohomology, is \(F=P[1]\oplus P[1]\) with the block diagonal differential. If (A.11)–(A.12) existed for this resolution, it would give a quasi-isomorphism \(F\to B\).

Equation reference: eq:fiber. Evaluate at \(\mathfrak m\). For \(F\), the differential is zero and the fiber cohomology has dimensions \((8,8)\) in the two parities. For \(B\), the single entry \(f(e_1e_2e_3)=1\) survives. Its differential has rank one from the even to the odd part, and rank zero in the reverse direction. The fiber dimensions are therefore \[(\dim H^0,\dim H^1)(F\otimes_A k)=(8,8),\qquad
 (\dim H^0,\dim H^1)(B\otimes_A k)=(7,7).
 \]

Here this fiber comparison is legitimate, rather than an unjustified ordinary-tensor argument. An acyclic two-periodic complex of finite projective \(A\)-modules is contractible. Indeed, its cycles are finite modules, have finite projective dimension by [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition~6.5]{Ked}], and the two exact sequences with projective middle terms yield two-step dimension shifting. All their positive Ext groups vanish after sufficient shifting, so the cycles are projective and both sequences split. Thus a quasi-isomorphism between finite projective periodic complexes has contractible cone and remains a quasi-isomorphism on every fiber. Equation [eq:fiber] (#eq:fiber) rules out the claimed map. This refutes the lifting procedure, not merely an arbitrary choice of the first lift.
## A complete replacement argument
The statement of Lemma A.2 can be recovered without asserting formality. The following construction also supplies the projective version in Corollary A.5.

Equation reference: eq:syzygy. Let \(B_0=B\). Choose a finite graded free module \(G_j\), with zero differential, and a cycle map \(G_j\to B_j\) surjective on cohomology in both parities. Put \(B_{j+1}=\operatorname{Cone}(G_j\to B_j)\). The long exact sequence gives, for \(i\) modulo two, \[H^i(B_{j+1})=
 \ker\bigl(G_j^{i+1}\longrightarrow H^{i+1}(B_j)\bigr).
 \] These are the successive syzygies, with alternating parity, of the two original finite cohomology modules. Choose the surjections along finite projective resolutions. After finitely many steps both cohomology modules are projective. At that stage they lift to cycles and give a quasi-isomorphism from a finite graded projective module with zero differential to \(B_N\).

Reconstruct \(B_{N-1},\ldots,B_0\) through the triangles \(G_j\to B_j\to B_{j+1}\to G_j[1]\), retaining the connecting maps. A finite complex obtained by finitely many cones from graded projective modules is homotopically projective: applying its Hom complex to an acyclic periodic complex is acyclic. This starts with projectivity of a graded module and is preserved by cones. Therefore each required connecting morphism can be represented by an actual closed chain map from the model already constructed for \(B_{j+1}\). Its cone, shifted once, models \(B_j\). The result has finite projective modules in both parities. Over the Tate algebra those projectives are free by [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition~6.6]{Ked}]. Over the annular algebras, the projective conclusion is precisely what Corollary A.5 needs.

This construction keeps extension information, including the map \(f\) in [eq:cone] (#eq:cone); simply periodizing a resolution of \(H^1\) loses it. It proves the existence statements used later, under their stated finite resolution assumptions.
## Dependency, counterevidence, and assessment

Lemma 3.20 explicitly invokes A.2 at p. 831. Corollaries 3.22–3.23 use it to control convolutions and cones. Corollary A.5 repeats the same argument for the multivariable Novikov annulus, and the proof of Lemma 3.5 at p. 862 invokes A.5 to obtain the finite model needed for semicontinuity. Lemma 4.6 and Proposition 4.1 then use this comparison in the main rank theorem. The annular parameter rank is not uniformly bounded by one or two.

The one-variable Tate computations alone do not exhibit the three-variable obstruction. Moreover, \(B\) above is itself finite free, so it cannot refute the existence conclusion of A.2. The replacement proof supplies that conclusion. The supported judgment is Major: an invalid derivation on the central proof chain, with an algebraically verified repair. It is not a counterexample to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 1.9, or the group-like family construction.
# Problem 2: the strict positive lattice monoid is not finitely generated
## Source and exact check

In Lemma 5.1, p. 844 (PDF p. 44), equation (5.2) imposes \(\omega_i(\beta)>0\) for every \(i\), together with \(\omega_i(\beta)\in N^{-1}\mathbb Z\), and adjoins zero. Using the indicated rational basis, the text asserts that this monoid is finitely generated. The next paragraph on p. 845 applies Lemma 5.2 to its energy image on that basis.

Already for the permitted algebraic parameters \(n'=2\), \(N=1\), the assertion is false: \[S=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^2:a\ge1,\ b\ge1\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] For every \(m\ge1\), \((1,m)\) is indecomposable into two nonzero members of \(S\), because their first coordinates would sum to at least two. Any generating set must therefore contain all \((1,m)\). This is an infinite proof, not an inference from a bounded enumeration. Nor does passage to a positive energy functional automatically remove the problem: \((a,b)\mapsto a+b\sqrt2\) is positive on \(S\setminus\{0\}\) and injective, so its image has the same infinite family of indecomposables. The resulting energy set is locally finite and lies in a finitely generated additive group.

This tests exactly the auxiliary lattice-monoid implication used in the proof. It does not purport to construct holomorphic curves realizing every one of these classes, or a symplectic counterexample to Lemma 5.1.
## Verified repair and bounded impact

Replace the auxiliary set by the containing nonnegative orthant \[\overline S=(N^{-1}\mathbb Z_{\ge0})^{n'}.\] It contains all classes that the paper placed in \(S\) and is generated by the \(n'\) coordinate vectors \(e_i/N\). If \(\omega_M=\sum_i c_i\omega_i\) with \(c_i>0\), its image is the monoid generated by the positive numbers \(c_i/N\), all in the required rational energy span. Apply Lemma 5.2 to this larger finitely generated monoid. Its positive rationally independent generators contain all the required energies. Thus the algebraic part of the desired conclusion is restored without asserting finite generation of (5.2) itself.

An intended nonnegative reading is strong counterevidence to serious damage to the theorem. However, the strict inequalities and the finite-generation inference are explicit in the frozen PDF and in [Kv3]. This is a false algebraic premise, not an unverified missing-citation complaint. Lemma 5.1 supplies the generators sent into \(p\mathbb Z_p\) in (5.5); these ensure convergence of the nonmonotone families used for Theorem 1.9. Under the assigned core-derivation criterion this is Major with restricted impact and a verified local repair. The geometric perturbation argument preceding (5.2) is a separate dependency, not certified by the orthant repair. The monotone Theorem 1.1 does not require Lemma 5.1.
# Other checked reasoning
## Arithmetic and field comparisons

For \(p>2\) and \(v=1+pu\), the polynomial coefficients of \(\binom{t}{j}(pu)^j\) have valuation at least \[j-v_p(j!)\ \ge\ j\frac{p-2}{p-1}\ \longrightarrow\ \infty.\] This verifies the Tate convergence used for \(v^t\). The prime-to-\(p\) roots used to extend \(\mathbb Q(T^G)\to\mathbb Q_p\) to \(\mathbb Q(T^{G_{(p)}})\) are compatible under common denominators. The argument does not embed the entire Novikov field in \(\mathbb Q_p\).

The later finite extension \(\widetilde K/K\) is finitely generated over \(K\); \(K\) itself need not be finitely generated over \(\mathbb Q\). Countability permits a transcendence basis to be sent into \(\mathbb Q_p\), then the remaining finite algebraic extension embeds in some finite extension \(\mathbb Q_p'\). Finite perfect presentations justify the relevant field base changes; no unrestricted infinite Hom-base-change assertion is required.
## From local families to integer iterates

The group-like property is first obtained over \(p^n\mathbb Z_p\), an additive subgroup. The geometric Fukaya comparison is initially local in the real parameter. Lemma 4.9 uses a finite subdivision of a compact real interval with subdivision points in the dense subgroup \(p^n\mathbb Z_{(p)}\). Combining these local comparisons with the group-like identity yields the stated rational-time comparison. The paper explicitly does not require a fully coherent group action for this dimension argument.

For a finite periodic free complex over the one-variable Tate algebra, the exact sequence for multiplication by \(t-a\) includes the torsion kernel as well as the cokernel. The PID decomposition and finiteness of zeros of a nonzero Tate function then give finitely many exceptional parameters in each residue class. It would be incorrect to ignore the kernel term at exceptional fibers; the paper retains it.

Here is the last arithmetic step in full. Suppose a sequence agrees outside finite sets with residue values \(c_a\) modulo \(m=p^n\) and \(d_b\) modulo \(n=(p')^{n'}\), where \(\gcd(m,n)=1\). For every pair \((a,b)\), the Chinese remainder theorem gives an infinite progression satisfying both congruences. Choose a term outside the two finite exceptional sets. Then \(c_a=d_b\). Since this holds for every pair, all residue values agree. Hence the sequence is constant off a finite set. This does not imply the same assertion for all real times, a limitation already acknowledged in Remark 4.13.
## Genericity, semicontinuity, and applications

For the nonmonotone construction, disjoint energy and period groups give independent exponent directions. The energy degree tends to infinity, which is the convergence condition needed for the analytic functions in Lemma 5.5. With a common prime-to-\(p\) denominator, the finitely many period monomials at any fixed energy degree are distinct Laurent monomials in analytic roots of \(1+pY_j\); they cannot vanish identically. A nonzero analytic coefficient and the one-variable zero theorem, followed by induction and Fubini, establish a null zero set. Countability of the chosen coefficient ring allows simultaneous avoidance. This does not prove injectivity for the entire uncountable ring \(R_{\rm big}\), which the paper expressly avoids claiming.

The contraction argument of A.1 has a radius uniform in the cycle being solved. The finite-tail valuation argument of B.4 and the two adjacent differential minors of B.6 justify the semicontinuity statements once the finite projective replacement has been supplied correctly.

For Corollary 1.12, the abelian \(\pi_1(L)\) hypothesis is used to split off a \(\mathbb Z\) factor on which the flux is nonzero. The local-system differential \(T^{f\alpha(C)}-1\) is invertible for \(f\ne0\), killing the group cohomology. Semicontinuity can be applied degree by degree, while \(H^1(L;\Lambda)\ne0\) drops. Arbitrarily small nonzero real elements of \(p^n\mathbb Z_{(p)}\) contradict cofinite constancy at the self-Floer rank if a nontrivial iterate is isomorphic to \(L\). This checks the stated empty/singleton/all alternative conditional on the geometric local-system identification. Corollary 1.11 concerns the unweighted categorical entropy computed by (6.1); bounded finitely many generator-pair ranks give zero exponential growth.
# Dependence, limitations, and disposition

The two problems concern distinct algebraic steps and are not duplicate counts. Their repairs establish the needed algebraic assertions, but do not certify every analytic construction of the Fukaya category. The moduli-space compactifications, coherent perturbation choices, all orientation signs, external generation theorems, and reverse isoperimetric estimates were not rebuilt in full. In particular, this review does not independently establish the uniform geometric energy positivity preceding (5.2) for all allowed perturbation data.

Targeted comparison with [Kv3] retains both relevant passages. The limited publisher/arXiv and correction searches did not establish a published correction. This is not proof that none exists and not a claim of priority. Immediate isolated notation slips, such as the inverse parameter in (A.14), are not additional substantive findings; the subsequent general formula (A.15) has the needed product \(T^{c-b}\).

problems.title: the periodic resolution lift need not exist
problems.source_location: LemmaA.2 printed856-857/PDF56-57 equationsA.9-A.12; CorollaryA.5 printed858; dependencies831,836,862
claim: Lemma A.2, pp. 856–857 (PDF pp. 56–57), first reduces to a two-periodic complex \(B\) with \(H^0(B)=0\). It fixes a finite free resolution of \(H^1(B)\) in (A.9), lifts its first terms into the unrolled complex \(B\), and asserts that the lift extends inductively in (A.11). Periodizing then supposedly gives the quasi-isomorphism (A.12). The existence of a finite free resolution of the module is supported by Kedlaya’s Proposition 6.5 [Ked]. It does not imply this particular lift into a periodic complex. Odd-degree cohomology can obstruct the later lifting steps.
analysis:
Equation reference: eq:koszul. Take the exact coefficient ring and residue field \[A=\mathbb Q_3\langle x_1,x_2,x_3\rangle,\qquad
 \mathfrak m=(x_1,x_2,x_3),\qquad k=A/\mathfrak m=\mathbb Q_3.\] All radii are one and satisfy the lemma’s norm hypothesis. Let \(K^{-j}=\bigwedge^j A^3\) be the Koszul resolution of \(k\), with \[d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_j})
 =\sum_{a=1}^j(-1)^{a-1}x_{i_a}
 e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat e_{i_a}\cdots\wedge e_{i_j}.
 \] The variables form a regular sequence, so \(H^0(K)=k\) and all other cohomology vanishes. Let \(P\) be its two-periodization: each parity has rank four, with \(H^0(P)=k\) and \(H^1(P)=0\).

Equation reference: eq:cone, eq:coho. Define an odd map \(f:P\to P\) by \(f(e_1e_2e_3)=1\) and zero on the other exterior degrees. Since \(df+fd=0\), it is a chain map \(P\to P[1]\). Set \[B=\operatorname{Cone}(P\xrightarrow{f}P[1])
   =P[1]\oplus P[1],\qquad
 D=\begin{pmatrix}-d&f\\0&-d\end{pmatrix}.
 \] Thus \(D^2=0\). The cone long exact sequence gives \(H^0(B)=0\) and \(0\to k\to H^1(B)\to k\to0\). This extension splits as an \(A\)-module: the two empty-wedge elements \((1,0),(0,1)\) are odd cycles lifting the two generators. Every \(x_i\) multiple of either is a boundary, since \(D(-e_i,0)=(x_i,0)\) and \(D(0,-e_i)=(0,x_i)\). Consequently \[H^0(B)=0,\qquad H^1(B)=k^2.
 \] All module-finiteness and parity assumptions of the reduced argument hold.

An allowed choice for (A.9) is two copies of the ordinary Koszul resolution of \(k\). Its periodization, placed in odd cohomology, is \(F=P[1]\oplus P[1]\) with the block diagonal differential. If (A.11)–(A.12) existed for this resolution, it would give a quasi-isomorphism \(F\to B\).

Equation reference: eq:fiber. Evaluate at \(\mathfrak m\). For \(F\), the differential is zero and the fiber cohomology has dimensions \((8,8)\) in the two parities. For \(B\), the single entry \(f(e_1e_2e_3)=1\) survives. Its differential has rank one from the even to the odd part, and rank zero in the reverse direction. The fiber dimensions are therefore \[(\dim H^0,\dim H^1)(F\otimes_A k)=(8,8),\qquad
 (\dim H^0,\dim H^1)(B\otimes_A k)=(7,7).
 \]

Here this fiber comparison is legitimate, rather than an unjustified ordinary-tensor argument. An acyclic two-periodic complex of finite projective \(A\)-modules is contractible. Indeed, its cycles are finite modules, have finite projective dimension by [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition~6.5]{Ked}], and the two exact sequences with projective middle terms yield two-step dimension shifting. All their positive Ext groups vanish after sufficient shifting, so the cycles are projective and both sequences split. Thus a quasi-isomorphism between finite projective periodic complexes has contractible cone and remains a quasi-isomorphism on every fiber. Equation [eq:fiber] (#eq:fiber) rules out the claimed map. This refutes the lifting procedure, not merely an arbitrary choice of the first lift.
The statement of Lemma A.2 can be recovered without asserting formality. The following construction also supplies the projective version in Corollary A.5.

Equation reference: eq:syzygy. Let \(B_0=B\). Choose a finite graded free module \(G_j\), with zero differential, and a cycle map \(G_j\to B_j\) surjective on cohomology in both parities. Put \(B_{j+1}=\operatorname{Cone}(G_j\to B_j)\). The long exact sequence gives, for \(i\) modulo two, \[H^i(B_{j+1})=
 \ker\bigl(G_j^{i+1}\longrightarrow H^{i+1}(B_j)\bigr).
 \] These are the successive syzygies, with alternating parity, of the two original finite cohomology modules. Choose the surjections along finite projective resolutions. After finitely many steps both cohomology modules are projective. At that stage they lift to cycles and give a quasi-isomorphism from a finite graded projective module with zero differential to \(B_N\).

Reconstruct \(B_{N-1},\ldots,B_0\) through the triangles \(G_j\to B_j\to B_{j+1}\to G_j[1]\), retaining the connecting maps. A finite complex obtained by finitely many cones from graded projective modules is homotopically projective: applying its Hom complex to an acyclic periodic complex is acyclic. This starts with projectivity of a graded module and is preserved by cones. Therefore each required connecting morphism can be represented by an actual closed chain map from the model already constructed for \(B_{j+1}\). Its cone, shifted once, models \(B_j\). The result has finite projective modules in both parities. Over the Tate algebra those projectives are free by [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition~6.6]{Ked}]. Over the annular algebras, the projective conclusion is precisely what Corollary A.5 needs.

This construction keeps extension information, including the map \(f\) in [eq:cone] (#eq:cone); simply periodizing a resolution of \(H^1\) loses it. It proves the existence statements used later, under their stated finite resolution assumptions.

Lemma 3.20 explicitly invokes A.2 at p. 831. Corollaries 3.22–3.23 use it to control convolutions and cones. Corollary A.5 repeats the same argument for the multivariable Novikov annulus, and the proof of Lemma 3.5 at p. 862 invokes A.5 to obtain the finite model needed for semicontinuity. Lemma 4.6 and Proposition 4.1 then use this comparison in the main rank theorem. The annular parameter rank is not uniformly bounded by one or two.

The one-variable Tate computations alone do not exhibit the three-variable obstruction. Moreover, \(B\) above is itself finite free, so it cannot refute the existence conclusion of A.2. The replacement proof supplies that conclusion. The supported judgment is Major: an invalid derivation on the central proof chain, with an algebraically verified repair. It is not a counterexample to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 1.9, or the group-like family construction.
result: Impact: Invalid foundational derivation explicitly reused for multivariable Novikov finite models and local group-law/Fukaya comparison. No main theorem counterexample.

problems.title: the strict positive lattice monoid is not finitely generated
problems.source_location: Lemma5.1 printed844-845/PDF44-45 equation5.2 and following finite-generation inference
claim: Strict positive rational lattice orthant plus zero is finitely generated
analysis: In Lemma 5.1, p. 844 (PDF p. 44), equation (5.2) imposes \(\omega_i(\beta)>0\) for every \(i\), together with \(\omega_i(\beta)\in N^{-1}\mathbb Z\), and adjoins zero. Using the indicated rational basis, the text asserts that this monoid is finitely generated. The next paragraph on p. 845 applies Lemma 5.2 to its energy image on that basis.

Already for the permitted algebraic parameters \(n'=2\), \(N=1\), the assertion is false: \[S=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z^2:a\ge1,\ b\ge1\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] For every \(m\ge1\), \((1,m)\) is indecomposable into two nonzero members of \(S\), because their first coordinates would sum to at least two. Any generating set must therefore contain all \((1,m)\). This is an infinite proof, not an inference from a bounded enumeration. Nor does passage to a positive energy functional automatically remove the problem: \((a,b)\mapsto a+b\sqrt2\) is positive on \(S\setminus\{0\}\) and injective, so its image has the same infinite family of indecomposables. The resulting energy set is locally finite and lies in a finitely generated additive group.

This tests exactly the auxiliary lattice-monoid implication used in the proof. It does not purport to construct holomorphic curves realizing every one of these classes, or a symplectic counterexample to Lemma 5.1.
result: Impact: Lemma5.1 supplies energy generators needed for p-adic convergence in Theorem1.9; monotone Theorem1.1 unaffected. Major follows assigned core-derivation criterion despite short repair.

report: Abstract: The assigned publisher version of Crowley, Goette and Nordström, Inventiones mathematicae 239 (2025), 865–907, is reviewed. One Major concern identifies an invalid variational inference in the small-eigenvalue argument on the main gluing proof chain. A completely specified operator countermodel proves the failure of that inference. A coercivity argument repairs the relevant cutoff contradiction on the diagonal \(r=\ell\); the full two-parameter estimates are not certified. Independent exact calculations reproduce the five lattice examples and the characteristic-class and Maslov-angle arithmetic. No counterexample to the asserted \(G_2\) gluing formula or disconnected-moduli examples is established.
Author: Paper identifier: M25-0050

Title: Initial scientific review of
An analytic invariant of \(G_2\) manifolds
# Identity and declared coverage

The reviewed object is the 43-page publisher PDF of [CGN], DOI 10.1007/s00222-024-01310-z, published online on 23 January 2025. Printed page is PDF page plus 864. The assigned manifest binds this PDF and a publisher metadata file; no separate computational supplement or author repository was identified in that manifest. Its actual source hash appears in Appendix 5 (#app:record).

All 43 pages were read as text; 29 selected pages were also inspected as rendered images. This is a claim-focused initial review, not a claim that every geometric construction or cited theorem has been independently proved. The definitions and mod-48 relation in Section 1, gluing and configuration conventions in Section 2, all five numerical lattice examples in Section 3, the finite-dimensional signature calculation in Section 4, and the selected operator constructions and small-spectrum arguments in Section 5 were checked. The author’s preprint [CGNv5], dated 3 October 2024, was consulted at the passages relevant to the finding; it does not replace the frozen publisher version.

The construction requires closed spin seven-manifolds and compatible spin structures, ACyl Calabi–Yau pieces, the specified cyclic actions, and a hyper-Kähler rotation compatible with the torus gluing. The angle satisfies \(0<\vartheta<\pi\), and \(\rho=\pi-2\vartheta\in(-\pi,\pi)\). Spectral symmetry of the pieces is used only when \(k_\pm\leq2\). The general gluing formula retains the piece contributions. The rectangular case in Corollary 3 is read with the ordinary twisted-connected-sum convention clarified on p. 877; the review does not extend it to arbitrary cyclic quotients merely because \(\vartheta=\pi/2\).
# Problem 1: an eigenvalue exclusion is used as a coercive estimate
## Location, claim, and dependency

Equation reference: eq:sourcequotient. Proposition 5.4, pp. 898–899 (PDF 34–35), excludes small eigenspinors on each half under strict APS boundary conditions. For the negative half, the allowed trace is \(F^+(A)\), with no component in \(\ker A\). Proposition 5.5, pp. 899–902 (PDF 35–38), constructs spinors \(\psi_\pm\) that vanish at the outer boundary. Equations (54)–(55) imply, for one half, \[
 \|\psi_-\|\geq\tfrac12,\qquad
 \frac{\|D_{M_-,\ell,r}\psi_-\|}{\|\psi_-\|}
 \leq \frac{C c}{r}+O(e^{-r/C}).\] The first paragraph of p. 902 then infers a small Dirichlet eigenvalue of the first-order Dirac operator, contradicting Proposition 5.4. This inference is invalid for the boundary realization being used.

The dependence is explicit: Proposition 5.5 provides the spectral gap used in Proposition 5.7 (p. 905) to exclude spectral flow in the deformation from the modified operator to the geometric one. The final proof of Theorem 1 (p. 906) invokes Proposition 5.7 and the Dirac gluing theorem. Thus the defect concerns a core analytic justification, rather than an unrelated estimate. It is Major under the assigned core-derivation standard. This classification does not assert that Theorem 1 is false.
## The domain obstruction

Write the boundary Green form as \(\omega(u,v)=\langle u,\gamma v\rangle\), where \(\gamma A=-A\gamma\). The article itself states on p. 897 that the symplectic annihilator of \(F^+(A)\) is \[F^+(A)\oplus\ker A.\] Here \(\dim_\mathbb R\ker A=4\) (Remark 5.2). Consequently the strict APS realization is symmetric but is not self-adjoint: the adjoint admits additional zero-mode boundary traces. Imposing full Dirichlet trace zero also does not give a self-adjoint first-order Dirac realization. Adding a Lagrangian half of \(\ker A\) gives a different, self-adjoint modified APS problem, as distinguished earlier in Sections 4.1 and 5.2.

A small quotient \(\|T u\|/\|u\|\) bounds a singular value of \(T\), or an eigenvalue of \(T^*T\) with its own domain. It need not produce an eigenvalue of \(T\) with the original boundary condition. The paper requires precisely this unjustified change of spectral problem.
## Complete countermodel to the inference

Fix \(L>0\) and set \[\mathcal H=L^2((0,L);\mathbb C),\qquad
 T=-i\frac{d}{dx},\qquad \operatorname{dom}T=H^1_0((0,L);\mathbb C).\] This is a densely defined closed symmetric first-order Dirac operator with full Dirichlet trace zero. Integration by parts gives \(\operatorname{dom}T^*=H^1((0,L);\mathbb C)\), strictly larger than \(\operatorname{dom}T\). For any complex \(\lambda\), \(Tf=\lambda f\) implies \(f(x)=a e^{i\lambda x}\); the condition \(f(0)=0\) forces \(a=0\). Thus \(T\) has no nonzero eigenspinor for any \(\lambda\).

Nevertheless the admissible function \(f(x)=\sin(\pi x/L)\) satisfies \[\|f\|^2=\frac L2,\qquad
 \|Tf\|^2=\frac{\pi^2}{2L},\qquad
 \frac{\|Tf\|}{\|f\|}=\frac{\pi}{L}.\] Taking \(L>\pi/\varepsilon\) gives a quotient below any prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\), while the alleged first-order eigenvalue still does not exist. The second-order operator \(T^*T\) has the familiar Dirichlet eigenvalue \(\pi^2/L^2\); it is a different conclusion. This countermodel verifies every assumption of the abstract variational inference. It is not presented as an extra-twisted connected sum or as a counterexample to Proposition 5.5’s geometric statement.
## A second limitation of the printed estimate

This checks the logic of the estimate, not the existence of a zero eigenspinor on the actual manifold. Along \(r=\ell\), the exponential errors are absorbable. The proof of Proposition 5.7 explicitly chooses that diagonal. A missing square in the preceding gradient display and a choice of constants in the scalar inequality do not resolve the domain obstruction or the stated two-parameter quantifier.
## Verified repair for the cutoff contradiction on \(r=\ell\)

The needed replacement is a lower bound for all Dirichlet spinors on a half, not merely exclusion of eigenvectors. Here is a proof in the geometry already constructed in Sections 2 and 4.2. It supplies the diagonal statement used below.

A half consists of a fixed connected compact core and an end whose length \(L\) is comparable to \(\ell+r\), with metrics uniformly equivalent to a fixed product metric. The finite quotient does not alter these estimates. For a scalar function \(f\) vanishing at the outer end, the fundamental theorem of calculus on the cylinder gives \[\int_{[0,L]\times X}|f|^2
 \leq C L^2\int_{[0,L]\times X}|df|^2,\qquad
 \|f|_{\{0\}\times X}\|^2
 \leq C L\int_{[0,L]\times X}|df|^2.\] On the fixed core \(K\), the trace Poincaré inequality \[\|f\|_{L^2(K)}^2\leq C_K
 \bigl(\|df\|_{L^2(K)}^2+\|f|_{\partial K}\|^2\bigr)\] follows, for example, by compactness: a violating normalized sequence would converge to a nonzero constant with zero boundary trace. Combining the estimates, with \(L\geq1\), gives \(\|f\|\leq C L\|df\|\), with \(C\) independent of the neck length. Kato’s inequality therefore implies \[\|\psi\|\leq C L\|\nabla\psi\|
 \quad\text{for every spinor with zero outer boundary trace.}\]

Equation reference: eq:coercive, eq:diagonal. Let \(D_{\rm geom}\) denote the geometric Dirac operator for the gluing metric. Equations (38)–(39) give \(D=D_{\rm geom}+E_\ell\) with \(\|E_\ell\|_\infty\leq C e^{-a\ell}\). The scalar curvature is zero off the transition regions and bounded below by \(-C e^{-a\ell}\) there. For a zero-trace spinor there is no boundary term in the integrated Lichnerowicz identity. Hence \[\begin{aligned}
 \|D\psi\|^2
 &\geq \tfrac12\|D_{\rm geom}\psi\|^2-\|E_\ell\psi\|^2 \notag\\
 &\geq \left(\frac{c_0}{L^2}-C e^{-a\ell}\right)\|\psi\|^2.
 \end{aligned}\] For \(r=\ell\) and \(\ell\) sufficiently large, this proves \[
 \|D_{M_\pm,\ell,\ell}\psi\|
 \geq\frac{c_1}{\ell}\|\psi\|.\] There is no appeal to a nonexistent Dirichlet eigenvalue of \(D\).

The cutoff construction (50)–(55) can now be used directly. The coefficients \(b,e,f\) are controlled by Green’s identity and \(\sin\vartheta\ne0\), and \(|a|\leq C/\sqrt r\). For \(r=\ell\), its nonzero boundary modes decay exponentially and its zero-mode cutoff error is \(O(c/\ell)\). Equation [eq:sourcequotient] (#eq:sourcequotient) then contradicts [eq:diagonal] (#eq:diagonal) after choosing \(c\) small enough and \(\ell\) large. The kernel spinor supplied by (40) remains. This proves the diagonal version of the gap assertion in Proposition 5.5.

The proof above establishes exactly that repair. It does not establish the uniform claim for arbitrary \(r/\ell\), nor replace every nonresonance and limit argument in the full Dirac gluing theorem. Those stronger statements remain to be supplied or explicitly restricted by the authors.
## Metric deformation and the actual size of the perturbation

Proposition 5.7, p. 905, also calls \(D_{\ell,r,w}-D_{\ell,r,1}\) an operator of degree zero for all \(w\in[0,1]\). The construction on pp. 893–895 changes the metric for \(0\leq w<1/2\). Such a difference is generally first order: the square of its geometric Dirac principal symbol records \(-|\xi|_{g_w}^2\). Equality of symbols would force equality of the metrics. Identifying the spinor bundles does not remove this fact. For \(w\geq1/2\) the metric is fixed, so the degree-zero description does apply there.

This does not obstruct the diagonal repair. The actual estimate is \[\|(D_w-D_1)u\|
 \leq C e^{-a\ell}\bigl(\|\nabla u\|+\|u\|\bigr).\] Uniform metric bounds and the integrated Lichnerowicz formula give \(\|\nabla u\|\leq C\|u\|\) for \(u\in\ker D_w\): \(D_{{\rm geom},w}u=-E_wu\), the zeroth-order term is bounded, and the scalar curvature has a uniform lower bound. Thus \(\|D_1u\|\leq C e^{-a\ell}\|u\|\) on that kernel. If \(\dim\ker D_w>1\), choose \(u\) in it perpendicular to the known one-dimensional kernel of the self-adjoint closed-manifold operator \(D_1\). The repaired diagonal gap contradicts this estimate. The known spinor \(s_{\ell,w}\) supplies the opposite inequality \(\dim\ker D_w\geq1\). Possible changes of volume density under the bundle identification are uniformly equivalent, or can be removed unitarily, with the same first-order bound.

This proves the kernel-control mechanism on the diagonal with the appropriate relative estimate. Exponentially small local eta-variation densities integrated over volume \(O(\ell)\) still have exponential decay after decreasing the exponent. A complete independent reconstruction of every eta-gluing and arbitrary-length limit is not claimed.
## Counterevidence, versions, and precise impact

The intended conclusion is plausible and has a substantial verified repair in the range actually chosen in Proposition 5.7. The invariant construction in Section 1 and the finite-dimensional Maslov arithmetic do not depend on the invalid variational inference. The review finds no incorrect numerical lattice value and no \(G_2\) manifold contradicting Theorems 1, 4 or 5.

The same strict-APS statement, Dirichlet-eigenvalue inference and degree-zero description occur in the targeted passages of [CGNv5]. Limited title/DOI/correction searches did not identify an applicable erratum; this is not proof that none exists. Bunke’s original theorem [Bunke] distinguishes self-adjoint Lagrangian boundary realizations and imposes regularity assumptions on its simplified formula. Its invertible-kernel simplification cannot simply be substituted here, since the two boundary Lagrangians share \(s\). The article’s additional treatment of that common zero mode is essential.
# Independent checks and positive evidence
## Normalization of the analytic invariant

Using formal tangent Chern roots \(x_1,\ldots,x_4\), the four positive-spin weights can be chosen as \[\tfrac12(x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4),\
 \tfrac12(x_1+x_2-x_3-x_4),\
 \tfrac12(x_1-x_2+x_3-x_4),\
 \tfrac12(x_1-x_2-x_3+x_4).\] Their product, with the paper’s orientation convention, is \((p_1^2-4p_2+8e)/16\). Substitution of \(\widehat A_8=(7p_1^2-4p_2)/5760\) and \(L_8=(7p_2-p_1^2)/45\) verifies equation (3) exactly: \(2e(S^+)=48\widehat A_8+e-3L_8\). Combining the APS index, signature and zero-count formulas yields the coefficients \(-24(\eta+h)(D)+3\eta(B)\) in Theorem 1.2.

For a parallel spinor the Berezin-degree parity argument in Lemma 1.3 gives a vanishing Mathai–Quillen term. The Lichnerowicz identity, \(SM\cong\mathbb R\oplus TM\), and the Bochner identity give \(h(D)=1+b_1(M)\) on the closed Ricci-flat manifold. Thus \(\nu=\bar\nu+24(1+b_1)\) modulo 48; the full-holonomy case has \(b_1=0\). These deductions verify integrality and local constancy within the stated holonomy locus, not on the space of arbitrary metrics.

The corrected homogeneous coefficients already acknowledged in Example 1.8 were not relabeled as a new issue. The rational contribution is exactly \[24\,\frac{12923}{2\cdot3^2\cdot5^6}
 -3\,\frac{4817}{3^2\cdot5^6}=1,\] and the displayed Chern–Simons terms cancel.
## Maslov angles, endpoints, and lattice examples

The image of boundary cohomology is Lagrangian by the pair exact sequence and Poincaré–Lefschetz duality. Paired non-middle degrees have conjugate spectra, so their Maslov contributions cancel. On \(H^3(X)\), the product decomposition and Hodge signs give the angles \(\alpha_j^+-\rho\) and \(\alpha_j^-+\rho\) in (35). Reducing these to \((-\pi,\pi]\) and excluding the endpoint \(\pi\) gives the endpoint weight one and the interior weight two in Proposition 4.7. The case \(\rho=0\) must be treated separately. The positive-space angles then contribute \(-\operatorname{sign}\rho\) and give \[m_{H^3(X)}=-16\rho/\pi+m_\rho,\qquad
 m_{\ker A}=\rho/\pi.\] Consequently \(3(-16\rho/\pi+m_\rho)-24\rho/\pi
=-72\rho/\pi+3m_\rho\), with the signs and factor 72 as printed.

For each example, the review formed exact rational orthogonal projections from the printed Gram matrix: \[P_E=E(E^tGE)^{-1}E^tG,\qquad A_E=2P_E-I,\] and computed the characteristic polynomial and signature of the span of the two polarising lattices. The product is the identity on its orthogonal complement.
Example | signature of span | characteristic polynomial | \(m_\rho\) | \(\bar\nu\)

In Example 3.8 the \(-1\) eigenvector \((0,-3,1)\) has Gram norm \(-16\), so the \(\pi\) angle is in the negative space. The values for the first three examples use \(\rho/\pi=1/2\); the last two use \(2/3\). Orientation reversal changes their signs. The endpoint conventions were additionally checked in 13,338 exact rational-angle cases. These finite checks supplement the branch calculation; they do not prove geometric realization of arbitrary lists of angles.

For the examples used in Theorems 4 and 5, the topology inputs were cross-checked against [N], Examples 8.1 and 8.17: the ranks are 97 and 109 and the divisor of \(p_1/2\) is two. The two entries in [CHNP], Table 3, row \(b=74\), and the three entries at \(b=86\), have divisor of \(p_1\) equal to four. The table uses \(b_3=b+23\), explaining the row labels. These checks corroborate the cited classification data; the underlying building-block and classification proofs were not reconstructed. The target article gives \(
u=12\) for the \(-36\) example and \(
u=24\) for the \(-48\) example, by its own normalization. An inconsistent \(
u=36\) sentence in the earlier external Example 8.1 is not imported as evidence against the reviewed article.
## Operator calculations and excluded local notation

The self-adjoint finite-rank corrections (38)–(39) annihilate the specified spinors, and the cylinder modes (45) satisfy the eigenvalue equation. For instance, \(\mu=13\), \(\lambda=5\) and \(\sqrt{\mu^2-\lambda^2}=12\) give an exact check obeying \(2|\lambda|<\mu\). The boundary equations following (62) have determinant \[\cos^2(z\pi/2)+\sin^2\vartheta\,\sin^2(z\pi/2)>0\] in the \((w,y)\) block. They give \(w=y=0\), with the remaining two zero modes only at \(z=1\). The two endpoint branches approach zero from opposite signs, giving the stated spectral-flow count once the analytic exclusion of other modes is justified. That last justification is not replaced by the finite-dimensional determinant calculation.

There is a separate local notation issue in the proof of Proposition 4.6, p. 889. With the conventional pullback \(R=\kappa^*\) on differential forms, \(RB=-BR\) already follows from \(R d=dR\) and \(R\bar *=-\bar *R\). The extra \(c_v\) in the printed \(c_v\kappa^*\) does not give the stated anticommutator. In an oriented orthonormal frame \((dx_1,\ldots,dx_6,dv)\), formula (26) gives \[(c_vR c_{x_1}+c_{x_1}c_vR)(1)=2\,dx_1\wedge dv\ne0.\] This was checked on the exterior algebra, including all 3,136 Clifford basis identities. The natural pullback \(R\) is the direct repair: it anticommutes with the odd signature operator and the boundary complex structure, commutes with \(A\), and preserves the cohomological image \(L_B\) by naturality. It therefore preserves the modified APS domain and proves spectral symmetry. A coefficientwise reflection in a separately specified product trivialization would be a different meaning of \(\kappa^*\). problems.title: an eigenvalue exclusion is used as a coercive estimate
problems.source_location: Proposition5.4 pp898-899/PDF34-35; Proposition5.5 ending pp901-902/PDF37-38; Proposition5.7 p905/PDF41; Theorem1 dependency p906/PDF42
claim: A small Dirichlet norm quotient for the first-order Dirac operator produces a small eigenvalue excluded by the strict-APS eigenvector statement
analysis:
Equation reference: eq:sourcequotient. Proposition 5.4, pp. 898–899 (PDF 34–35), excludes small eigenspinors on each half under strict APS boundary conditions. For the negative half, the allowed trace is \(F^+(A)\), with no component in \(\ker A\). Proposition 5.5, pp. 899–902 (PDF 35–38), constructs spinors \(\psi_\pm\) that vanish at the outer boundary. Equations (54)–(55) imply, for one half, \[
 \|\psi_-\|\geq\tfrac12,\qquad
 \frac{\|D_{M_-,\ell,r}\psi_-\|}{\|\psi_-\|}
 \leq \frac{C c}{r}+O(e^{-r/C}).\] The first paragraph of p. 902 then infers a small Dirichlet eigenvalue of the first-order Dirac operator, contradicting Proposition 5.4. This inference is invalid for the boundary realization being used.

The dependence is explicit: Proposition 5.5 provides the spectral gap used in Proposition 5.7 (p. 905) to exclude spectral flow in the deformation from the modified operator to the geometric one. The final proof of Theorem 1 (p. 906) invokes Proposition 5.7 and the Dirac gluing theorem. Thus the defect concerns a core analytic justification, rather than an unrelated estimate. It is Major under the assigned core-derivation standard. This classification does not assert that Theorem 1 is false.

Write the boundary Green form as \(\omega(u,v)=\langle u,\gamma v\rangle\), where \(\gamma A=-A\gamma\). The article itself states on p. 897 that the symplectic annihilator of \(F^+(A)\) is \[F^+(A)\oplus\ker A.\] Here \(\dim_\mathbb R\ker A=4\) (Remark 5.2). Consequently the strict APS realization is symmetric but is not self-adjoint: the adjoint admits additional zero-mode boundary traces. Imposing full Dirichlet trace zero also does not give a self-adjoint first-order Dirac realization. Adding a Lagrangian half of \(\ker A\) gives a different, self-adjoint modified APS problem, as distinguished earlier in Sections 4.1 and 5.2.

A small quotient \(\|T u\|/\|u\|\) bounds a singular value of \(T\), or an eigenvalue of \(T^*T\) with its own domain. It need not produce an eigenvalue of \(T\) with the original boundary condition. The paper requires precisely this unjustified change of spectral problem.

Fix \(L>0\) and set \[\mathcal H=L^2((0,L);\mathbb C),\qquad
 T=-i\frac{d}{dx},\qquad \operatorname{dom}T=H^1_0((0,L);\mathbb C).\] This is a densely defined closed symmetric first-order Dirac operator with full Dirichlet trace zero. Integration by parts gives \(\operatorname{dom}T^*=H^1((0,L);\mathbb C)\), strictly larger than \(\operatorname{dom}T\). For any complex \(\lambda\), \(Tf=\lambda f\) implies \(f(x)=a e^{i\lambda x}\); the condition \(f(0)=0\) forces \(a=0\). Thus \(T\) has no nonzero eigenspinor for any \(\lambda\).

Nevertheless the admissible function \(f(x)=\sin(\pi x/L)\) satisfies \[\|f\|^2=\frac L2,\qquad
 \|Tf\|^2=\frac{\pi^2}{2L},\qquad
 \frac{\|Tf\|}{\|f\|}=\frac{\pi}{L}.\] Taking \(L>\pi/\varepsilon\) gives a quotient below any prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\), while the alleged first-order eigenvalue still does not exist. The second-order operator \(T^*T\) has the familiar Dirichlet eigenvalue \(\pi^2/L^2\); it is a different conclusion. This countermodel verifies every assumption of the abstract variational inference. It is not presented as an extra-twisted connected sum or as a counterexample to Proposition 5.5’s geometric statement.

This checks the logic of the estimate, not the existence of a zero eigenspinor on the actual manifold. Along \(r=\ell\), the exponential errors are absorbable. The proof of Proposition 5.7 explicitly chooses that diagonal. A missing square in the preceding gradient display and a choice of constants in the scalar inequality do not resolve the domain obstruction or the stated two-parameter quantifier.

Proposition 5.7, p. 905, also calls \(D_{\ell,r,w}-D_{\ell,r,1}\) an operator of degree zero for all \(w\in[0,1]\). The construction on pp. 893–895 changes the metric for \(0\leq w<1/2\). Such a difference is generally first order: the square of its geometric Dirac principal symbol records \(-|\xi|_{g_w}^2\). Equality of symbols would force equality of the metrics. Identifying the spinor bundles does not remove this fact. For \(w\geq1/2\) the metric is fixed, so the degree-zero description does apply there.

This does not obstruct the diagonal repair. The actual estimate is \[\|(D_w-D_1)u\|
 \leq C e^{-a\ell}\bigl(\|\nabla u\|+\|u\|\bigr).\] Uniform metric bounds and the integrated Lichnerowicz formula give \(\|\nabla u\|\leq C\|u\|\) for \(u\in\ker D_w\): \(D_{{\rm geom},w}u=-E_wu\), the zeroth-order term is bounded, and the scalar curvature has a uniform lower bound. Thus \(\|D_1u\|\leq C e^{-a\ell}\|u\|\) on that kernel. If \(\dim\ker D_w>1\), choose \(u\) in it perpendicular to the known one-dimensional kernel of the self-adjoint closed-manifold operator \(D_1\). The repaired diagonal gap contradicts this estimate. The known spinor \(s_{\ell,w}\) supplies the opposite inequality \(\dim\ker D_w\geq1\). Possible changes of volume density under the bundle identification are uniformly equivalent, or can be removed unitarily, with the same first-order bound.

This proves the kernel-control mechanism on the diagonal with the appropriate relative estimate. Exponentially small local eta-variation densities integrated over volume \(O(\ell)\) still have exponential decay after decreasing the exponent. A complete independent reconstruction of every eta-gluing and arbitrary-length limit is not claimed.
result: The intended conclusion is plausible and has a substantial verified repair in the range actually chosen in Proposition 5.7. The invariant construction in Section 1 and the finite-dimensional Maslov arithmetic do not depend on the invalid variational inference. The review finds no incorrect numerical lattice value and no \(G_2\) manifold contradicting Theorems 1, 4 or 5.

The same strict-APS statement, Dirichlet-eigenvalue inference and degree-zero description occur in the targeted passages of [CGNv5]. Limited title/DOI/correction searches did not identify an applicable erratum; this is not proof that none exists. Bunke’s original theorem [Bunke] distinguishes self-adjoint Lagrangian boundary realizations and imposes regularity assumptions on its simplified formula. Its invertible-kernel simplification cannot simply be substituted here, since the two boundary Lagrangians share \(s\). The article’s additional treatment of that common zero mode is essential.

Impact: Proposition5.5 gap is used to remove spectral flow in5.7, which is cited in the final Theorem1 proof. Major follows assigned core-derivation rule, without claiming the main invariant/formula or disconnected-moduli examples are false.
