report: Abstract: This initial review examines the publisher version of Vytnova and Wormell’s Hausdorff dimension of the Apollonian gasket. A complete rational counterexample disproves the parameter enclosure in Theorem 4.2 under the specified Hardy-space interpretation of its operator assumptions. The same unsafe choice of denominator occurs in the pinned public rigorous implementation. A second problem is the asserted density of analytic functions in the usual Hölder norm in Proposition 2.3; a replacement argument restores that spectral identification. Both concerns affect the proof of the central certificate. The review does not establish that the published numerical value is false. The parameter-enclosure repair is proved here; applying it to the authors’ actual high-precision residual remains outstanding. Focused independent acceptance retains both findings; human adjudication remains pending.
Date: 25 October 2026
Title: Verification of the Apollonian dimension certificate
# Identity, evidence and inspected scope

Paper. Polina L. Vytnova and Caroline L. Wormell, Hausdorff dimension of the Apollonian gasket, Inventiones mathematicae 239 (2025), 909–946, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-024-01311-y. The reviewed document is the 38-page publisher version of record, published online on 22 January 2025 [VW]. Paper ID: M25-0051. The page convention is one-based PDF page = printed page minus 908.

The entire extracted main text, including references, was read. Detailed checks concentrated on the dimension-to-spectrum bridge (Proposition 2.3), the two-dimensional Chebyshev estimate and its role in error control (Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 3.3), the residual-to-parameter enclosure (Theorems 4.1–4.2), and the dependency of the final certificate on these steps (Propositions 6.4–6.5 and Section 7). The repository was pinned to commit `4f73a6a1807ea7cb28313c379ffeeaf1410ff1d6` of 13 February 2025 [code]; its identity as the exact revision used for the published run is unverified.

The acquired arXiv TeX archive, version 2406.04922v1 of 7 June 2024, is a separate source version; it was not substituted for the journal text. The optional `APriori.ipynb` was not acquired. Its absence is a coverage limitation and is not a mathematical finding. No author code, notebook, JLD input or 448-bit computation was executed. The review does not certify every numerical constant, interval-library operation, or every general-dimensional endpoint in Section 3. The accompanying coverage ledger distinguishes reading from independently verified reasoning.
# Problem 1: the parameter enclosure fails for negative residuals

Judgment: Major; demonstrated invalid theorem and certification step. The issue is in Theorem 4.2, printed pp. 928–929 (PDF pp. 20–21). Its significance is explicit in the introduction, p. 911, and the proof of Theorem 1.1, p. 943.
## Claim and suspect step

Equation reference: derivative, printed. For a positive parameterized transfer operator, the theorem assumes \[
-D^-\sup\psi\ \le\ \frac{d}{ds}(\mathcal L_s\psi)(x)\
 \le\ -D^+\inf\psi <0,
\qquad D^\pm>0.\] The source states (29) for every bounded \(\psi>0\). Here \(\mathcal L_s\) is the operator (13) on the Hardy space (11), whose restrictions to the compact real cube are continuous; every strictly positive function in that domain has positive infimum. The counterexample below satisfies (29) for every such function, and more generally for every bounded function bounded away from zero. If bounded \(\psi>0\) were instead read as all pointwise-positive bounded functions, its terminal strict inequality would be impossible for functions with zero infimum. The enclosure failure is established under the coherent Hardy-space (or uniformly positive bounded-function) interpretation, without relying on that wording ambiguity. For a trial function \(0<\phi^-\le\phi\le\phi^+\), it assumes \[\varepsilon^-<(\mathcal P_K\mathcal L_{s_0}\phi-\lambda\phi)(x)<\varepsilon^+,
 \qquad
 \mathrm{err}=\|\mathcal L_{s_0}\phi-\mathcal P_K\mathcal L_{s_0}\phi\|_\infty.\] The printed conclusion is \[
 s_0+\frac{\varepsilon^--\mathrm{err}}{D^-\phi^+}
 <s_*<
 s_0+\frac{\varepsilon^++\mathrm{err}}{D^+\phi^-},
 \qquad \rho(\mathcal L_{s_*})=\lambda.\] The proof treats a forward parameter displacement and then describes the lower bound as analogous. A negative displacement reverses the relevant integral inequality. Dividing a negative residual by the larger bound \(D^-\phi^+\) can move the proposed lower endpoint to the wrong side of the root.
## Counterexample satisfying the assumptions

Fix \(d=1\), any Bernstein ellipse radii \(0<r<R\), and \(p=2\). Use a single analytic branch and weight \[v(z)=0,\qquad w_s(z)=2-s,\qquad
 s\in[1/2,3/2],\qquad
 (\mathcal L_sf)(z)=(2-s)f(0).\] The branch maps the larger ellipse into the smaller one. The weight is holomorphic and bounded, and the family is differentiable in \(s\). The operator is positive and rank one, with spectrum \(\{2-s,0\}\), a simple positive leading eigenvalue and a spectral gap for every parameter in the specified interval. Thus the analytic, summability, positivity and spectral assumptions all hold.

For every strictly positive continuous test function \(\psi\), \[\frac{d}{ds}\mathcal L_s\psi=-\psi(0),\qquad
 -2\sup\psi\le-\psi(0)\le-\inf\psi<0.\] Consequently [derivative] (#derivative) holds with \(D^-=2\), \(D^+=1\). These are valid bounds; the theorem imposes no optimality condition on them.

Now choose \[\phi\equiv1,\quad \phi^-=\phi^+=1,\quad K=1,\quad
 \lambda=1,\quad s_0=\frac54,\quad
 \varepsilon^-=-\frac13,\quad \varepsilon^+=\frac18.\] Chebyshev interpolation preserves constants, so \(\mathrm{err}=0\). The actual residual is \[\mathcal P_1\mathcal L_{5/4}\phi-\phi=-\frac14,
 \qquad -\frac13<-\frac14<\frac18.\] The unique exact root is \(s_*=1\), because \(\rho(\mathcal L_s)=2-s\). In contrast, [printed] (#printed) asserts \[\frac{13}{12}
 =\frac54+\frac{-1/3}{2}
 <s_*<
 \frac54+\frac18=\frac{11}{8}.\] Both proposed endpoints are within the original parameter interval, but the asserted lower endpoint exceeds the true root. This is a counterexample to the theorem, not a floating-point discrepancy. A separately authored 17-line Python check using exact `fractions.Fraction` arithmetic reproduces these fractions; the operator and domain assumptions are verified analytically above.
## Static implementation evidence and counterevidence
The rigorous Julia source sets \(D^-=33/10\) and \(D^+=59/100\) at lines 27–28, as in Proposition 6.5. Its function `dimensionbound`, lines 340–350, returns at line 349:

> s + hull(minmaxest.lo/(Dminus*phi_plus),
> minmaxest.hi/(Dplus*phi_minus))

where the displayed ASCII names stand for the corresponding Greek-named variables in the source. The lower residual is divided by \(D^-\phi^+\) regardless of its sign. Taking the hull of the two selected quotients cannot restore a missing, smaller quotient. For a valid residual enclosure \([-1/3,1/8]\) and denominator interval \([1,2]\), this rule again produces \([13/12,11/8]\) after adding \(5/4\).

This static match is evidence that the error is not confined to an isolated printed sign. It does not establish the sign, width or value of the actual residual in the publication-time run. The README’s stated output interval is a repository assertion, not an execution receipt from this review. The printed Algorithm 3, p. 944 (PDF p. 36), also contains subtraction signs that differ from the theorem and source return expression; it was not used to infer the execution history.
## A precise repair

Equation reference: repair. Let \[\ell=\varepsilon^--\mathrm{err},\quad u=\varepsilon^++\mathrm{err},\qquad
 m=D^+\phi^->0,\quad M=D^-\phi^+\ge m.\] Assume that the root exists in the stated parameter interval, as in the original theorem, and retain its positive-operator min–max implications. A valid enclosure is \[
 s_0+\min\{\ell/m,\ell/M\}
 <s_*<
 s_0+\max\{u/m,u/M\}.\] Equivalently, use the full interval quotient \([\ell,u]/[m,M]\). Endpoints outside the known parameter interval can be intersected with that interval. The theorem’s original hypotheses alone should not be read as an additional existence proof for a root at an arbitrary \(\lambda\).

Verification of the repair. Put \(F_s(x)=\mathcal L_s\phi(x)-\lambda\phi(x)\). Then \(-M\le\partial_sF_s\le-m\) and \(\ell<F_{s_0}(x)<u\). For a nonnegative displacement \(\delta\), \[F_{s_0}(x)-M\delta\le F_{s_0+\delta}(x)
 \le F_{s_0}(x)-m\delta.\] For a negative displacement, \[F_{s_0}(x)-m\delta\le F_{s_0+\delta}(x)
 \le F_{s_0}(x)-M\delta.\] Thus at \(\delta_-=\ell/M\) when \(\ell\ge0\), or \(\delta_-=\ell/m\) when \(\ell<0\), one has \(F_{s_0+\delta_-}>0\). At \(\delta_+=u/m\) when \(u\ge0\), or \(\delta_+=u/M\) when \(u<0\), one has \(F_{s_0+\delta_+}<0\). The min–max comparison and monotonicity place the root between these parameters whenever the comparison endpoints lie in the parameter interval; an endpoint beyond its outer edge gives a trivial bound from the known location of the root. These are exactly the endpoints in [repair] (#repair). ◻

For the counterexample the repaired interval is \([11/12,11/8]\), which contains \(1\). In the common case \(\ell<0<u\), both safe endpoints use the smaller denominator \(D^+\phi^-\). This is a repair of the enclosure theorem. It does not by itself revalidate the published numerical interval: that requires the actual residual, eigenfunction bounds and error quantities, followed by outward-rounded evaluation of the corrected endpoints.
## Core impact

Theorem 4.2 is expressly presented as a general contribution in the introduction. Section 7 then invokes it to transform validated transfer operator errors into the interval asserted in Theorem 1.1. The counterexample invalidates that stated general guarantee, and the same rule appears in the acquired rigorous source. This warrants Major under the specified calibration even if a corrected run preserves all reported digits. No such run was performed here. The mathematical value of the Apollonian dimension and the numerical truth of the particular printed interval have not been disproved.
# Problem 2: analytic functions are not dense in the stated Hölder norm

Judgment: Major core proof gap; analytic repair verified. The final paragraph of the proof of Proposition 2.3, printed p. 917 (PDF p. 9), takes \[B_0=B_1=\mathcal H^{2,2}_{R_A},\qquad B_2=C^\alpha([-1,1]^2)\] and asserts density in \(B_2\) before applying Baladi–Tsujii, Lemma A.1 [BT]. That lemma requires density in both Banach norms (author-manuscript PDF pp. 36–37). Density in the uniform norm is insufficient.
## Complete obstruction under the usual convention

An explicit little-Hölder convention would change the space, but the paper calls \(C^\alpha\) the space of Hölder continuous functions and does not state that convention. It cannot be silently supplied to validate this invocation. The following repair avoids that ambiguity.
## Replacement proof with the original inputs

Retain the original proof’s Hölder Ruelle–Perron–Frobenius conclusion: \(T=\mathcal A_s\) has a positive leading eigenvalue \(\rho>0\), a nonnegative nonzero eigenfunction \(h\), and a spectral gap. Normalize \(\|h\|_\infty=1\). Also retain compactness of the operator \(L=\mathcal A_s\) on the Hardy space, which the original argument establishes. The constant function \(1\) lies in that space with norm one. Positivity gives \[T^n1\ge T^nh=\rho^nh,\qquad
 \|L^n\|\ge\|L^n1\|_{\mathcal H}\ge\|T^n1\|_\infty\ge\rho^n.\] The spectral-radius formula yields \(r_{\mathcal H}(L)\ge\rho\).

If \(r_{\mathcal H}(L)>\rho\), compactness, after complexification if necessary, supplies a nonzero analytic eigenfunction with eigenvalue \(\mu\) satisfying \(|\mu|=r_{\mathcal H}(L)>\rho\). Restriction to the real square is nonzero by analytic uniqueness and belongs to \(C^\alpha(X)\); it is therefore a Hölder eigenfunction with eigenvalue \(\mu\), contradicting the Hölder spectral-radius bound. Hence \(r_{\mathcal H}(L)=\rho\). Compactness and the Hölder spectral gap identify the Hardy leading eigenvalue as the same positive eigenvalue. Restriction also injects its generalized eigenspace into the Hölder generalized eigenspace, preserving simplicity.

This restores the required spectral identification and therefore the original monotonicity and dimension correspondence, conditional on the same RPF and compactness inputs already used by the authors. It does not reprove the underlying graph-directed-system theory or the computer-assisted mapping bounds. The supported error is the printed density argument; Proposition 2.3 itself has not been refuted. Because that proposition connects the computed Hardy spectrum to the dimension, the gap is in a core dependency rather than a peripheral citation. Its repair is already analytically verified here.
# Checked reasoning, alternative readings and remaining work

The finite-rank strategy is coherent: summable analytic weights give the operator norm bound, interpolation controls the difference on the real cube, and a positive trial eigenfunction allows pointwise residual bounds to constrain the spectral radius. The two-dimensional \(p=2\) coefficient-decay argument yields \(e^{-R\|\mathbf k\|_2}\), and the shell-counting integral gives the stated \(E_{2,K}\) expression. This review did not certify all endpoint cases of the separate general-\(d,p\) formulation.

An apparent Euler–Maclaurin sign problem was checked against counterevidence and was not retained as an additional substantive finding. The code uses the standard negative Bernoulli derivative correction (`apollonian-rigorous.jl`, line 273; `apollonian-nonrigorous.jl`, line 181). The opposite-sign Bernoulli–zeta identity printed on p. 934 provides further context against reading one isolated sign as proof of an incorrect executed tail calculation. Likewise, unavailable optional material and non-rigorous preliminary eigenvectors are not defects: the intended second stage is a validated calculation, and the present finding addresses its final enclosure rule.

The public arXiv record checked on 25 October 2026 lists only v1. The inspected publisher record and targeted correction search did not identify a linked erratum resolving these concerns; this is the scope of that check, not proof that no correction exists anywhere. The acquired public repository revision is later than online publication and is kept separate from the publication-time execution provenance.
# Conclusion and disposition
Item | Judgment | Repair and remaining work
Theorem 4.2 and source return rule | Major; theorem falsified | Signed interval-division repair proved; actual high-precision certificate not recomputed.
Proposition 2.3 density step | Major proof gap under usual Hölder convention | Replacement proof verified from original RPF and compactness inputs.
Published 128-place interval | Numerical validity unresolved here | No counterexample to the actual dimension; original residual data and corrected outward-rounded certification are needed.
Adoption and acceptance | Human decision pending | No author contact or adoption; focused independent checks completed; human review record empty.

The initial-review outcome is Major, supported by explicit mathematics and fixed-version source evidence. The demonstrated consequence is a defect in the claimed certificate and a repairable spectral proof gap. A corrected numerical certificate may retain the reported precision; the present work supplies no result about that recomputation.

 s_0+\frac{\varepsilon^--\mathrm{err}}{D^-\phi^+}
 <s_*<
 s_0+\frac{\varepsilon^++\mathrm{err}}{D^+\phi^-},
 \qquad \rho(\mathcal L_{s_*})=\lambda.\] The proof treats a forward parameter displacement and then describes the lower bound as analogous. A negative displacement reverses the relevant integral inequality. Dividing a negative residual by the larger bound \(D^-\phi^+\) can move the proposed lower endpoint to the wrong side of the root.
analysis: Judgment: Major; demonstrated invalid theorem and certification step. The issue is in Theorem 4.2, printed pp. 928–929 (PDF pp. 20–21). Its significance is explicit in the introduction, p. 911, and the proof of Theorem 1.1, p. 943.

Fix \(d=1\), any Bernstein ellipse radii \(0<r<R\), and \(p=2\). Use a single analytic branch and weight \[v(z)=0,\qquad w_s(z)=2-s,\qquad
 s\in[1/2,3/2],\qquad
 (\mathcal L_sf)(z)=(2-s)f(0).\] The branch maps the larger ellipse into the smaller one. The weight is holomorphic and bounded, and the family is differentiable in \(s\). The operator is positive and rank one, with spectrum \(\{2-s,0\}\), a simple positive leading eigenvalue and a spectral gap for every parameter in the specified interval. Thus the analytic, summability, positivity and spectral assumptions all hold.

For every strictly positive continuous test function \(\psi\), \[\frac{d}{ds}\mathcal L_s\psi=-\psi(0),\qquad
 -2\sup\psi\le-\psi(0)\le-\inf\psi<0.\] Consequently [derivative] (#derivative) holds with \(D^-=2\), \(D^+=1\). These are valid bounds; the theorem imposes no optimality condition on them.

Now choose \[\phi\equiv1,\quad \phi^-=\phi^+=1,\quad K=1,\quad
 \lambda=1,\quad s_0=\frac54,\quad
 \varepsilon^-=-\frac13,\quad \varepsilon^+=\frac18.\] Chebyshev interpolation preserves constants, so \(\mathrm{err}=0\). The actual residual is \[\mathcal P_1\mathcal L_{5/4}\phi-\phi=-\frac14,
 \qquad -\frac13<-\frac14<\frac18.\] The unique exact root is \(s_*=1\), because \(\rho(\mathcal L_s)=2-s\). In contrast, [printed] (#printed) asserts \[\frac{13}{12}
 =\frac54+\frac{-1/3}{2}
 <s_*<
 \frac54+\frac18=\frac{11}{8}.\] Both proposed endpoints are within the original parameter interval, but the asserted lower endpoint exceeds the true root. This is a counterexample to the theorem, not a floating-point discrepancy. A separately authored 17-line Python check using exact `fractions.Fraction` arithmetic reproduces these fractions; the operator and domain assumptions are verified analytically above.
The rigorous Julia source sets \(D^-=33/10\) and \(D^+=59/100\) at lines 27–28, as in Proposition 6.5. Its function `dimensionbound`, lines 340–350, returns at line 349:

> s + hull(minmaxest.lo/(Dminus*phi_plus),
> minmaxest.hi/(Dplus*phi_minus))

where the displayed ASCII names stand for the corresponding Greek-named variables in the source. The lower residual is divided by \(D^-\phi^+\) regardless of its sign. Taking the hull of the two selected quotients cannot restore a missing, smaller quotient. For a valid residual enclosure \([-1/3,1/8]\) and denominator interval \([1,2]\), this rule again produces \([13/12,11/8]\) after adding \(5/4\).

This static match is evidence that the error is not confined to an isolated printed sign. It does not establish the sign, width or value of the actual residual in the publication-time run. The README’s stated output interval is a repository assertion, not an execution receipt from this review. The printed Algorithm 3, p. 944 (PDF p. 36), also contains subtraction signs that differ from the theorem and source return expression; it was not used to infer the execution history.

Equation reference: repair. Let \[\ell=\varepsilon^--\mathrm{err},\quad u=\varepsilon^++\mathrm{err},\qquad
 m=D^+\phi^->0,\quad M=D^-\phi^+\ge m.\] Assume that the root exists in the stated parameter interval, as in the original theorem, and retain its positive-operator min–max implications. A valid enclosure is \[
 s_0+\min\{\ell/m,\ell/M\}
 <s_*<
 s_0+\max\{u/m,u/M\}.\] Equivalently, use the full interval quotient \([\ell,u]/[m,M]\). Endpoints outside the known parameter interval can be intersected with that interval. The theorem’s original hypotheses alone should not be read as an additional existence proof for a root at an arbitrary \(\lambda\).

Verification of the repair. Put \(F_s(x)=\mathcal L_s\phi(x)-\lambda\phi(x)\). Then \(-M\le\partial_sF_s\le-m\) and \(\ell<F_{s_0}(x)<u\). For a nonnegative displacement \(\delta\), \[F_{s_0}(x)-M\delta\le F_{s_0+\delta}(x)
 \le F_{s_0}(x)-m\delta.\] For a negative displacement, \[F_{s_0}(x)-m\delta\le F_{s_0+\delta}(x)
 \le F_{s_0}(x)-M\delta.\] Thus at \(\delta_-=\ell/M\) when \(\ell\ge0\), or \(\delta_-=\ell/m\) when \(\ell<0\), one has \(F_{s_0+\delta_-}>0\). At \(\delta_+=u/m\) when \(u\ge0\), or \(\delta_+=u/M\) when \(u<0\), one has \(F_{s_0+\delta_+}<0\). The min–max comparison and monotonicity place the root between these parameters whenever the comparison endpoints lie in the parameter interval; an endpoint beyond its outer edge gives a trivial bound from the known location of the root. These are exactly the endpoints in [repair] (#repair). ◻

For the counterexample the repaired interval is \([11/12,11/8]\), which contains \(1\). In the common case \(\ell<0<u\), both safe endpoints use the smaller denominator \(D^+\phi^-\). This is a repair of the enclosure theorem. It does not by itself revalidate the published numerical interval: that requires the actual residual, eigenfunction bounds and error quantities, followed by outward-rounded evaluation of the corrected endpoints.

Theorem 4.2 is expressly presented as a general contribution in the introduction. Section 7 then invokes it to transform validated transfer operator errors into the interval asserted in Theorem 1.1. The counterexample invalidates that stated general guarantee, and the same rule appears in the acquired rigorous source. This warrants Major under the specified calibration even if a corrected run preserves all reported digits. No such run was performed here. The mathematical value of the Apollonian dimension and the numerical truth of the particular printed interval have not been disproved.

problems.title: analytic functions are not dense in the stated Hölder norm
problems.source_location: Publisher PDF9 / printed917, final paragraph of Proposition2.3 proof Baladi-Tsujii math/0606434v2 PDF36-37, LemmaA.1
claim: Recorded check: analytic functions are not dense in the stated Hölder norm
analysis: Judgment: Major core proof gap; analytic repair verified. The final paragraph of the proof of Proposition 2.3, printed p. 917 (PDF p. 9), takes \[B_0=B_1=\mathcal H^{2,2}_{R_A},\qquad B_2=C^\alpha([-1,1]^2)\] and asserts density in \(B_2\) before applying Baladi–Tsujii, Lemma A.1 [BT]. That lemma requires density in both Banach norms (author-manuscript PDF pp. 36–37). Density in the uniform norm is insufficient.

An explicit little-Hölder convention would change the space, but the paper calls \(C^\alpha\) the space of Hölder continuous functions and does not state that convention. It cannot be silently supplied to validate this invocation. The following repair avoids that ambiguity.

Retain the original proof’s Hölder Ruelle–Perron–Frobenius conclusion: \(T=\mathcal A_s\) has a positive leading eigenvalue \(\rho>0\), a nonnegative nonzero eigenfunction \(h\), and a spectral gap. Normalize \(\|h\|_\infty=1\). Also retain compactness of the operator \(L=\mathcal A_s\) on the Hardy space, which the original argument establishes. The constant function \(1\) lies in that space with norm one. Positivity gives \[T^n1\ge T^nh=\rho^nh,\qquad
 \|L^n\|\ge\|L^n1\|_{\mathcal H}\ge\|T^n1\|_\infty\ge\rho^n.\] The spectral-radius formula yields \(r_{\mathcal H}(L)\ge\rho\).

If \(r_{\mathcal H}(L)>\rho\), compactness, after complexification if necessary, supplies a nonzero analytic eigenfunction with eigenvalue \(\mu\) satisfying \(|\mu|=r_{\mathcal H}(L)>\rho\). Restriction to the real square is nonzero by analytic uniqueness and belongs to \(C^\alpha(X)\); it is therefore a Hölder eigenfunction with eigenvalue \(\mu\), contradicting the Hölder spectral-radius bound. Hence \(r_{\mathcal H}(L)=\rho\). Compactness and the Hölder spectral gap identify the Hardy leading eigenvalue as the same positive eigenvalue. Restriction also injects its generalized eigenspace into the Hölder generalized eigenspace, preserving simplicity.

This restores the required spectral identification and therefore the original monotonicity and dimension correspondence, conditional on the same RPF and compactness inputs already used by the authors. It does not reprove the underlying graph-directed-system theory or the computer-assisted mapping bounds. The supported error is the printed density argument; Proposition 2.3 itself has not been refuted. Because that proposition connects the computed Hardy spectrum to the dimension, the gap is in a core dependency rather than a peripheral citation. Its repair is already analytically verified here.

report: Abstract: This review concerns Gerber and Kunde’s 82-page arXiv manuscript 2109.06086v2, dated 9 December 2024. A complete construction shows that the fixed-strip analytic diffeomorphism space defined in Section 10.1 is nonseparable in the stated metric. An ergodic modification also makes the relation itself nonseparable, disproving the analytic classification in Theorem 27 under the manuscript’s definition. This does not refute the non-Borel reduction, the measurable theorem, or the smooth theorem. Two local corrections concern a matching inequality and the convention for continuous analytic completeness. The publisher version has not been textually compared. Independent scientific acceptance and human review remain pending.
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Initial mathematical review:
Non-classifiability of ergodic flows up to time change
# Identity, scope and evidence

M25-0052. Marlies Gerber and Philipp Kunde, Non-classifiability of ergodic flows up to time change, arXiv:2109.06086v2 [paper]. The associated journal article is Inventiones mathematicae 239 (2025), 527–619, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-024-01312-x. Every page reference below is to the reviewed arXiv PDF, whose printed page and one-based PDF page agree. No finding is attributed to the 2025 version of record without a textual comparison.

All 82 pages, including references, were read across the primary reviewer and three native session assistants. The primary reviewer checked the main reduction, the local matching calculation, the topology construction below, selected substitution estimates, and the tower argument at the end. The auxiliary audits identify their actual page ranges and dependencies. Reading is not a claim to have independently reproved all 97 numbered statements or the cited realization and coding theorems.

The structural chain examined is: strongly uniform uniquely readable words give an ergodic symbolic system; compatible odd group elements encode an infinite branch; finite coding and Feldman-pattern separation force such compatible elements from equivalence to the inverse; circular realization then supplies the smooth and analytic extensions. The conditional reduction in Theorems 22–23 (p. 18) is correct: continuity of \(T\mapsto(T,T^{-1})\) transfers the reduction of ill-founded trees. Analyticity is an additional input, explicitly cited in the introduction. The sigma-finite construction was checked for finite height almost everywhere, infinite mean height, and the two endpoint cases of the tower-reversal conjugacy.

A targeted version/correction search and the primary arXiv record identified v2 as the latest listed revision. No separate correction was identified in those retrieved results; this limited search does not establish that none exists. Publisher access returned a subscription preview. Optional code was not needed for the mathematical checks and its absence is not a finding. No author code was executed.
# Major: the declared analytic ambient space is not Polish
## Precise location and scope

Section 10.1, p. 68, defines \(C^\omega_\rho(\mathbb T^2)\) using bounded holomorphic extension to the open strip \(\Omega_\rho=\{|\operatorname{Im}z_1|,|\operatorname{Im}z_2|<\rho\}\), with its supremum norm. Both a diffeomorphism and its inverse must have such displacement functions. The metric \(d_\rho\) takes the maximum of their displacement distances, allowing integer changes of lift. The paragraph then infers that this space is Polish from completeness. The following family satisfies all these stated conditions and disproves separability.
## Complete separated-family construction

Consider the torus shear \[F_\theta(x,y)=(x+h_\theta(y),y)\pmod{\mathbb Z^2}.\] It is a real-analytic diffeomorphism, preserves area since its Jacobian determinant is \(1\), and is homotopic to the identity through the shears with displacement \(t h_\theta\). Its inverse is \((x,y)\mapsto(x-h_\theta(y),y)\). Both displacement functions have exactly the required bounded holomorphic extensions on \(\Omega_\rho\).

For \(\theta\ne\phi\), approach the lower strip boundary radially, choosing \(z_r=\theta/(2\pi)-i(2\pi)^{-1}\log(Rr)\) as \(r\uparrow1\). Then \(u(z_r)=r e^{i\theta}\). Thus \[H_\theta(z_r)\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 |H_\phi(z_r)|\longrightarrow1 .\] Indeed, the exponent for \(\theta\) is \(-(1+r)/(1-r)\), whereas for \(\phi\ne\theta\) the boundary quotient has real part zero. On the reflected approach, \(|u(\bar z_r)|\to R^{-2}\), so the difference of the two reflected terms has limiting superior at most \(2R^{-2N}\). The reverse triangle inequality gives \[\|h_\theta-h_\phi\|_\rho
 \ge \frac{1-2R^{-2N}}{16}\ge\frac1{32}.\] Also \(\|h_\theta-h_\phi\|_\rho\le1/4\). Every nonzero integer change of lift therefore has norm at least \(3/4\). Taking the infimum over lifts does not remove the lower bound: \[d_\rho(F_\theta,F_\phi)\ge1/32 .\] A separable metric space has no uncountable uniformly separated subset: balls of radius \(1/100\) about these points are pairwise disjoint, and each would contain a different point of a countable dense set. The stated ambient space is therefore nonseparable, hence not Polish.
## The relation itself is nonseparable

The defect also affects the ergodic relation, not only its ambient space. Put \(\beta=\sqrt2\bmod1\) and \(\alpha=\sqrt3\bmod1\), and replace the shears by \[E_\theta(x,y)=(x+\alpha+h_\theta(y),\,y+\beta).\] Their inverse displacements are \(-\alpha-h_\theta(y-\beta)\) and \(-\beta\); hence they have all the required extensions and the same separation bound \(d_\rho(E_\theta,E_\phi)\ge1/32\).

Since \(H_\theta\) has a Taylor series in \(u\) with zero constant term, \(h_\theta\) has zero mean. Write its Fourier coefficients as \(a_{\theta,k}\). The disk bound gives \(|a_{\theta,k}|\le R^{-|k|}/16\) for \(k\ne0\). For a nearest integer \(m\) to \(k\sqrt2\), \(k\ge1\), the nonzero integer \(2k^2-m^2\) yields \[\operatorname{dist}(k\sqrt2,\mathbb Z)\ge(4k)^{-1},
 \qquad |e^{2\pi ik\beta}-1|\ge k^{-1}.\] The same estimates hold with \(|k|\) for negative \(k\). Thus the Fourier coefficients \[b_{\theta,k}=\frac{a_{\theta,k}}{e^{2\pi ik\beta}-1}\quad(k\ne0),
 \qquad b_{\theta,0}=0\] define a real-valued real-analytic periodic function \(g_\theta\) on every narrower strip. It satisfies \(g_\theta(y+\beta)-g_\theta(y)=h_\theta(y)\). The area-preserving shear \(G_\theta(x,y)=(x+g_\theta(y),y)\) therefore obeys \(G_\theta R_{(\alpha,\beta)}G_\theta^{-1}=E_\theta\). Rational independence of \(1,\sqrt2,\sqrt3\) makes this translation ergodic; it follows, for example, by testing invariant functions on Fourier characters. Hence every \(E_\theta\) is ergodic.

The relation in Theorem 27 (p. 19) contains every diagonal pair \((E_\theta,E_\theta)\), an uncountable uniformly separated family. It is a metric subspace and is therefore nonseparable. Every Borel subset of a Polish space is separable and second countable, and its continuous image is separable. The relation cannot be analytic under Definition 16, which defines analyticity by such a continuous image. It consequently cannot be complete analytic as stated.
## Impact and limited repair

This is a Major defect in the real-analytic conclusion of Theorem 27 for the specified topology. The construction checks ergodicity as well as every membership requirement, so it does not rely on a nonergodic counterexample to a statement restricted to ergodic maps.

The continuous-reduction argument for non-Borelness can still work in a non-Polish target: the inverse image of a Borel set under a continuous map is Borel. Accordingly this finding does not refute that conclusion, the measurable result, or the smooth result. The complete-analytic formulation itself is false for this metric relation; recovering it requires a changed category or topology.

A limited correction is to state the non-Borel conclusion in the stated topology, subject to its existing reduction proof. To retain a Polish complete-analytic formulation, one must specify a separable complete analytic category, prove its relevant descriptive properties, and verify that the realization and its continuity land there. A closed-strip continuous-extension category, or an appropriate separable closure of the realization class, is a possible route; these are repair obligations, not a fully verified replacement theorem in this review.
# Minor: matching size versus matching deficit

In Lemma 14, p. 12, cases (I) and (II), and p. 13, Case 1, the printed implication replaces the factor \(1-\alpha\) by \(\alpha\). For a best match of size \(L(C,D)\), \[\overline f(C,D)=1-\frac{2L(C,D)}{|C|+|D|}.\] Thus \(\overline f(C,D)\ge\alpha\) implies, for every match \(K\), \[2|K|\le(1-\alpha)(|C|+|D|),
 \qquad |C|+|D|-2|K|\ge\alpha(|C|+|D|).\] If the premise is strict, the appropriate upper bound is strict. For example, \(C=0000\), \(D=0001\), and \(\alpha=1/10\) give \(\overline f(C,D)=1/4>\alpha\) and a best match of size \(3\); the printed bound \(6<\alpha\cdot8\) fails. This example tests that local implication, not all hypotheses of Lemma 14.

The final deficit estimate on p. 16 uses precisely the corrected form. There are at most \(2n\) short pairs, each of total length less than \(7L/(3R)\); hence their contribution to the discarded length is at most \(14Ln/(3R)\). Since \(n\le m\), this is at most \(3L(n+m)/R\). The resulting normalized estimate has loss \(3\alpha/R<1/R\) because \(\alpha<1/7\). Replacing the three matching-size inequalities and respecting non-strict premises restores this local step. No counterexample to Lemma 14 or its intended separation bound was found.
# Minor: convention for complete analyticity

Definition 17, p. 16, says that every analytic set can be continuously reduced to the target, without restricting the source space. Fact 20, p. 18, then calls ill-founded trees complete analytic under this wording. Take the analytic subset \(\{0\}\) of the connected Polish space \([0,1]\). Every continuous map from \([0,1]\) into the zero-dimensional tree space has connected, hence singleton, image. It cannot reduce \(\{0\}\) to ill-foundedness. This proves that the unrestricted wording is too strong.

The standard usable correction is to restrict the source spaces of the continuous-reduction definition to zero-dimensional Polish spaces, or to use Borel reductions for arbitrary standard Borel spaces. The reduction and the non-Borel argument on p. 18 survive either conventional correction. This is a definition/scope correction, not a counterexample to the measurable anti-classification result.
# Coverage, counterevidence and outstanding checks

The middle audit checked the coding/substitution parameter losses, including the displayed estimates of Lemma 43 and Proposition 45. For example, the augmentation loss in (7.10), the short-pair removal in (7.13), and the final \(1-4/2^e\) estimate in (7.14) were compared with actual page images. The positive lower bound in the proof of Proposition 58 requires \(\int f\,d\mu>1\), which is its nontrivial integer-valued roof case. The inverse-limit compatibility argument in Lemmas 76 and 96 was traced to the tree criterion; it was not replaced by an unsupported inference that an arbitrary circular functor preserves non-Kakutani equivalence.

No exhaustive independent reconstruction of all parameter choices, every finite-code case, the external smooth/analytic realization theorems, or the full reference literature was performed. The tower identification’s asserted continuity in Section 11 remains an external/detail-level dependency, not an established defect. All retained findings above have complete checks in this report. Additional candidate concerns in auxiliary notes are not findings unless included in the findings ledger.
# Supporting checks
The staged source PDF has SHA-256

The exact report source is compiled using the authorized Tectonic 0.17.0 executable, with shell escape disabled, task-local bounded cache and temporary directories, and recorded compiler/dependency/PDF hashes. The native assistants perform bounded auxiliary audits and are not an independent acceptance panel.
Human reviews are empty; independent scientific acceptance is pending.

Title: Initial mathematical review:
Joint ergodicity for commuting transformations
# Identity and scope

M25-0053. Nikos Frantzikinakis and Borys Kuca, Joint ergodicity for commuting transformations and applications to polynomial sequences, arXiv:2207.12288v2 [paper]. Associated journal DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-024-01313-w. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, equal to the printed numbers.

All 66 pages were actually read across the primary reviewer and three native session assistants, assigned pp. 1–22, 23–44 and 45–66. The primary reviewer independently checked the retained counterexamples, the exact statements and proof errors, the principal dependency on Appendix A, and selected source-page images. Full reading is distinguished from exhaustive independent reproof. The coverage ledger names the remaining external and technical dependencies.

The hypotheses distinguish commuting invertible transformations, pairwise independent zero-constant integer polynomials in Theorem 2.8, and linearly independent polynomials in Theorem 2.10 (p. 9). Characteristic-factor approximation in (8) is different from existence of the average limit in (9); Corollary 2.3 explicitly includes rational convergence. These distinctions are essential to the findings below.
# Major: the uniformity assertions in Appendix A are false
## A complete counterexample to Proposition A.2

The statement is on p. 57. Set \(\ell=2\), \(m=2\), and \[X_1=X_2=X'_1=X'_2=\ell^2(\mathbb N;\mathbb R),\qquad
 A(x,y)=\langle x,y\rangle,\qquad
 q(y)=\left(\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{y_j^2}{j^2}\right)^{1/2}.\] Use the ordinary Hilbert norm for all four norms appearing in the hypotheses. These spaces are separable, reflexive Banach spaces. The auxiliary subspaces are dense, their norms dominate the ambient norms with constant one, and their unit balls are closed. The bilinear functional is continuous, since \(|A(x,y)|\le\|x\|_2\|y\|_2\). Moreover \(q(y-z)\le\|y-z\|_2\), so norm convergence controls the seminorm on the required ball.

The qualitative hypothesis holds: \(q(y)=0\) implies \(y=0\). But for the standard unit vectors \(e_n\), \[q(e_n)=1/n\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 \sup_{\|x\|_2\le1}|A(x,e_n)|=1.\] For \(\varepsilon=1/2\), no \(\delta>0\) can satisfy the quantitative conclusion. This checks every stated hypothesis and refutes the claimed equivalence, rather than merely identifying an incomplete argument.

The precise invalid step is the last scaling on p. 60. After obtaining a bound only for \(x_\ell\in B_{X'_\ell}\), the proof applies it to \((2/r_0)^{\ell-1}x_\ell\). A small value of the controlled seminorm does not put that scaled vector in \(B_{X'_\ell}\). The parameter \(r_0\) depends on the earlier Baire argument, and replacing \(\varepsilon\) by an unspecified smaller number does not cure this failure.
## A direct counterexample to Proposition A.1

The assertion on p. 56 is false even with the stated ergodic seminorm. Use the fixed compact group \(X=\mathbb Z_3\) of 3-adic integers with Haar probability measure, and the odometer \(T(x)=x+1\). Put \[T_1=T_2=T,\quad a_1(n)=a_2(n)=n,\quad
 \mathcal Y_1=\mathcal Y_2=\mathcal X,\quad s=2,\quad m=2.\] These transformations commute and are invertible. Characters of finite quotients \(\mathbb Z/3^k\mathbb Z\) span a dense subspace of \(L^2(X)\): cylinder functions are dense and each finite quotient has a Fourier basis. The only \(T\)-invariant character is the constant one, so \(T\) is ergodic and has pure point spectrum.

For every bounded \(f_1,f_2\), \[\mathbb E_{n\le N} T^n f_1\,T^n f_2
 =\mathbb E_{n\le N}T^n(f_1f_2)\longrightarrow\int f_1f_2\,d\mu
 \quad\hbox{in }L^2.\] Thus the mean-convergence hypothesis holds. The Kronecker factor is the whole space, so \(\lVert f\rVert_{2,\mathrm{HK}}=0\) implies \(f=0\). This follows also from \(\lVert f\rVert_{2,\mathrm{HK}}^4=\sum_\chi|\widehat f(\chi)|^4\). Therefore the qualitative seminorm-control hypothesis holds for all bounded inputs.

Choose \(f_1=\overline{f_M}\) and \(f_2=f_M\). Every term of every average is exactly \(1\), whereas \(\lVert f_2\rVert_{2,\mathrm{HK}}=M^{-1/4}\to0\). Thus for the same fixed system and subspaces, no uniform \(\delta\) exists for \(\varepsilon=1/2\). This is precisely the dependence claimed in the remark following A.1, so allowing \(\delta\) to depend on the system does not repair it.

An independently written finite calculation corroborated the cube identity for \(M=3,9,27,81\) by reducing the integer root-of-unity polynomial modulo the cyclotomic polynomial. The exact results were \(1/3,1/9,1/27,1/81\); the averaged product was \(1\) in every case. Script, exact inputs and results are saved. This calculation is supplementary to the proof above; no author code was run.
## Core impact, counterevidence and restricted repair

Corollary 8.5, p. 49, explicitly invokes A.1 to obtain a \(\delta\) uniform over the functions and dual sequences. This is a necessary step in the stated seminorm-smoothing induction of Section 8. The failure therefore creates a Major proof dependency gap in the characteristic-factor argument and results that invoke it.

The odometer example has \(p_1=p_2=n\), so it does not satisfy pairwise independence. It is not a counterexample to Theorem 2.8, Theorem 2.10 or Corollary 8.5 itself. The specific polynomial application could admit a different uniform estimate; this review does not supply one. The pointwise-in-the-other-inputs conclusion proved in the first step of A.2 is also not refuted.

Here is a valid limited repair of A.2. Add the hypothesis that the induced linear map \[L:X_m\longrightarrow
 \mathcal B(X_1,\ldots,\widehat X_m,\ldots,X_\ell;\mathbb R),
 \qquad L(y)=A(\,\cdot\,,y,\,\cdot\,),\] is compact in the norm of bounded multilinear forms. If the quantitative conclusion failed, choose \(y_n\in B_{X'_m}\) with \(q(y_n)\to0\) and \(\|Ly_n\|\ge\varepsilon\). Reflexivity gives a weakly convergent subsequence \(y_n\rightharpoonup y\). The norm-closed convex ball is weakly closed. Mazur convex combinations of tails converge in norm to \(y\) inside that ball, and the seminorm continuity plus \(q(y_n)\to0\) gives \(q(y)=0\). The qualitative hypothesis and density imply \(Ly=0\). Compactness then gives \(Ly_n\to Ly\) in norm, a contradiction. Thus the added hypothesis suffices. No such compactness is established for the paper’s ergodic application, and the odometer example shows that it cannot be silently assumed.
# Minor: Corollary 2.7 claims too much convergence
On p. 8 the irrational-equidistribution branch refers to (9), the existence of a limit on p. 7. It lacks rational convergence. A full counterexample is already available for one nilrotation.

Let \(N_0=0\), \(N_k=2^{2^k}\) for \(k\ge1\), and set \(b(n)=k\bmod2\) for \(N_{k-1}<n\le N_k\), \(a(n)=2n+b(n)\). For irrational \(t\), the exponential sum on each block has modulus at most \(2/|1-e^{4\pi it}|\), by the geometric-series formula. There are \(O(\log\log N)\) blocks up to \(N\), including the final partial block, so \(\mathbb E_{n\le N}e^{2\pi i a(n)t}\to0\). This is exactly irrational equidistribution as defined in the paper.

However, \[\left|\frac1{N_k}\sum_{n\le N_k}(-1)^{a(n)}-(-1)^k\right|
 \le \frac{2N_{k-1}}{N_k}\longrightarrow0.\] On the allowed circle nilmanifold take \(T(x)=x+1/2\) and \(f(x)=e^{2\pi ix}\). Then \(T^{a(n)}f=(-1)^{a(n)}f\), whose averages do not converge in \(L^2\). The footnote defining a nilrotation does not exclude rational rotations.

A limited correction is to replace the reference to (9) by the characteristic-factor approximation (8). Alternatively, add rational convergence when asserting existence of the limit. In this example the rational Kronecker factor is the whole space, so (8) holds identically. The surrounding Theorem 2.2 and Corollary 2.3 already make this distinction; the example does not refute them.
# Local proof and notation corrections
## Dual-function index in Lemma 3.3 (Minor)

The proof on p. 22 uses \(\mathcal D_s\) to generate \(\mathcal Z_s\), whereas the definition and identity (32) on p. 21 place these dual functions in \(\mathcal Z_{s-1}\). For \(s=1\) and an ergodic irrational circle rotation, \(\mathcal D_1f=\int\bar f\,d\mu\) is constant, while \(\mathcal Z_1\) contains every Fourier character. Thus the claimed dense set in that proof does not have the stated density. Use \(\mathcal D_{s+1}\) throughout this construction, with the matching component identity and density theorem. Choose the approximating family countable and dense in each bounded continuous ball, and rational complex coefficients when working over \(\mathbb C\). On uniformly bounded sets the dual operation is continuous in \(L^2\) by a telescoping estimate, which justifies passage from the dense family. This repairs the local construction; the lemma’s conclusion is not refuted.
## Ties in Proposition 4.3 (Minor)

On p. 25, the sets \(E_k\) are defined by equality with the maximum of finitely many coordinate moduli. They can overlap. On a two-point ergodic cycle take \(\chi_1=1\), \(\chi_2=(-1)^x\), and \(f=(\chi_1+\chi_2)/2\). Both coordinates have modulus \(1/2\), so the printed definition gives \(E_1=E_2=X\). The constructed sum \(\chi_1+\chi_2\) has values \(2,0\), violating the required modulus \(0\) or \(1\) of a non-ergodic eigenfunction (p. 22). Replace \(E_k\) by the invariant measurable set where \(k\) is the least maximizing index. The sets then partition the space; the maximum estimate and phase correction survive, and the pasted function is an admissible eigenfunction. This is a local construction repair, not a refutation of the inverse theorem.
## Difference-box estimate in Lemma 5.2 (Minor)
## Relative density in Corollary 2.14 (scope clarification)

The final sentence on p. 11 uses positive lower density in the relative sense supplied by the preceding paragraph: density within \(\mathbb P-1\). Every subset of \(\mathbb P-1\) has ordinary natural density zero, since the primes do. The preceding paragraph explicitly uses relative density inside \(\mathbb P\), which supplies the intended interpretation. This is a scope clarification, not a separately established substantive defect; the existence assertion and the intended relative-density conclusion are unaffected.
# Supporting checks

The audits traced the non-ergodic eigenfunction and ergodic-decomposition quantifiers, the subsequence choices in Sections 6–7, the induction types and zero-constant convention in Section 8, and the Appendix B PET hypotheses. In particular, the ability to pass to subsequences while preserving the averaged strong-convergence property is explicitly provided by Proposition 5.6. No additional failure was established in that degree-lowering chain. An attempted Appendix B example with a nonzero polynomial constant term was rejected because it violated the standing assumption; it is not a finding.

The review does not independently reconstruct all Host–Kra structure theory, external PET/convergence results, all smoothing parameter cases, the prime-number inputs or every application. No identity with the journal text or subsequent correction is asserted. The primary arXiv record still lists v2; the targeted search produced no verified separate correction. Failed follow-up page retrievals are recorded as failures, not as evidence that corrections are absent.

report: Abstract: This report consolidates the preserved claim-focused review of Yang Li’s 2025 publisher version. No substantive mathematical defect is established within that review’s scope. A printed subgradient sign is corrected and checked on an admissible example. The regularization needed for the stability argument is made explicit, and a local integral estimate replaces an unsupported stronger intermediate expression. The report retains the precise dependencies of these conclusions. Scientific adjudication and independent acceptance remain pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical verification of
Intermediate complex structure limit
for Calabi–Yau metrics
# Paper identity and review scope

The reviewed work is Yang Li, Intermediate complex structure limit for Calabi–Yau metrics, Inventiones mathematicae 240 (2025), 459–496, DOI 10.1007/s00222-024-01314-9 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-024-01314-9) [Li2025]. The source is the 38-page publisher version of record, published online on 26 February 2025. Throughout this report, PDF page means the one-based page in that file; the corresponding printed page is PDF page plus 458. Source identity and the exact SHA-256 are recorded in Appendix 7 (#app:record).

This delivery continues an interrupted review. It incorporates the preserved early, middle and late audits, covering the extracted text of PDF pages 1–13, 14–26 and 27–38, respectively, and the two subsequently saved bounded checks. Those records contain the actual checks and their limits. Their work is attributed to the earlier sessions; this recovery has not repeated a full scientific review.

The inherited review follows the chain from the family assumptions and section decomposition, through the convex transport construction and complex ansatz, to the stability and global potential estimates. It checks normalization, signs, quantifiers and the use of cited inputs. In particular, it preserves the distinction between convergence of normalized potentials and convergence of metric tensors or microscopic geometries. The latter is not a conclusion of the main theorem.
# Hypotheses, notation and dependencies

In the setting of [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~460--461]{Li2025}], let \(M\) be a smooth Fano manifold of complex dimension \(n+1\), let \(L\) be ample, and let positive integers \(d_i\) satisfy \[-K_M=\left(\sum_{i=0}^{m}d_i\right)L,\qquad 1\leq m\leq n-1.\] The sections \(F_i\) of \(d_iL\) and \(F\) of \(-K_M\) are sufficiently generic that the stated divisors are smooth and their intersections are transverse. The smooth fibers under consideration are \[X_t=\{F_0\cdots F_m+tF=0\}\subset M .\] The bound on \(m\) makes the deepest complete intersection \(E_0\cap\cdots\cap E_m\) positive-dimensional; the connectedness and section-lifting arguments use this restriction.

Write \[\Delta=\{x_i\geq0:\ \textstyle\sum_i x_i=1\},\qquad
 \Delta^\vee=\bigcup_{k=0}^{m}
 \{p_i\leq0,\ p_k=0,\ \textstyle\sum_i d_ip_i\geq-1\}.\] The target is understood in the quotient by \(\mathbb R(1,\ldots,1)\). The convex representation and duality in [Retained latex: \cite[Eqs.~(12)--(15), p.~472]{Li2025}] use \[u(x)=\sup_{p\in\Delta^\vee}\{\langle x,p\rangle-\widetilde u(p)\}.\] On the target facets, the weighted measure has density \[W(p)=\left(1+\sum_i d_ip_i\right)^{n-m},\qquad
 C_1=\int_{\Delta^\vee}W(p)\,dp
 =\frac{(\sum_i d_i)(n-m)!}{n!\prod_i d_i}.\] Here \(\mu_0\) is normalized Lebesgue measure on \(\Delta\), and the intended weighted Monge–Ampère equation is \(M_u=C_1\mu_0\).

For the complex estimates, set \[\lambda=|\log|t||,\qquad V=(L^n),\qquad
 \omega_{\mathrm{CY},t}=\omega_t+\lambda dd^c\psi_t,\qquad
 \min_{X_t}\psi_t=0.\] The normalized Calabi–Yau measure is denoted by \(\mu_t\). The inherited normalization checks connect the weighted transport equation to the ansatz volume comparison and its total mass \(V\).

The review tracks the applications of the non-archimedean existence, uniqueness and domination results, Brenier transport and regularity, the uniform Skoda and stability estimates, and the Ohsawa–Takegoshi extension estimate. It does not independently reprove those external theorems. The following clarifications state exactly what the saved bounded arguments establish.
# The subgradient sign and its checked correction
## Printed claim and coordinate convention

Equation reference: eq:printed. On PDF page 16 / printed page 474, the displayed definition in Section 4.1 reads, literally, \[
 \nabla_{\rm print}u(x)=
 \{p\in\Delta^\vee:\ u(x')\geq u(x)+\langle x-x',p\rangle
       \ \hbox{for every }x'\in\Delta\}.\] This sign is inconsistent with the supporting-plane convention in (12)–(13), the Brenier map \(T=\nabla u\) on printed page 475, and the explicit formula (18) on page 476.

For \(m=1\), put \(x=(s,1-s)\) and \(q=p_0-p_1\). The effective coordinate \(q\) is invariant under addition of a diagonal vector. The pairing in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) is \((s-s')q\). At an interior differentiability point, taking \(s'=s+h\) with both signs of \(h\) forces \(q=-U'(s)\), where \(U(s)=u(s,1-s)\). The conventional subgradient has \(q=U'(s)\). A quotient-coordinate convention therefore does not remove the sign discrepancy.
## Admissible example and exact discrepancy

The saved bounded check uses \(n=2\), \(m=1\), \(d_0=1\), \(d_1=2\). These parameters are realized by a smooth quadric threefold \(M=Q^3\subset\mathbb P^4\), with \(L=\mathcal O_Q(1)\). Adjunction gives \(K_Q=(-5+2)L=-3L\). Generic sections of \(L,2L,3L\) give the required smooth transverse divisors. The resulting anticanonical pencil has smooth general fibers; shrinking the punctured parameter disk avoids its exceptional parameters. Its deepest stratum is a smooth connected curve. The example meets the stated family and dimension assumptions.

Equation reference: eq:example. The target interval is \(q\in[-1,1/2]\). Equation (18) of the paper gives \[
 U'(s)=
 \begin{cases}
 -1+\sqrt{3s/2},&0\leq s\leq2/3,\\[2pt]
 (1-\sqrt{3(1-s)})/2,&2/3\leq s\leq1.
 \end{cases}\] The branches are increasing, agree at zero, and have total range \([-1,1/2]\); integration yields a convex \(U\). This function also has the required representation (12): for \(q=p_0-p_1\), take \[\widetilde U(p)=p_1+\sup_{0\leq s\leq1}\{qs-U(s)\}.\] This is bounded on the compact target, and convex duality recovers \(U(s)\) as the supremum of \(\langle(s,1-s),p\rangle-\widetilde U(p)\).

Equation reference: eq:mass. Let \(E=(0,1/6)\). On this interval, \(-1<U'(s)<-1/2\). The literal definition [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) requires \(q=-U'(s)\in(1/2,1)\), outside the target. Its subgradient set is empty, so its weighted image mass is zero. In contrast, \[
 C_1=\frac{1}{2d_0}+\frac{1}{2d_1}=\frac34,\qquad
 C_1\mu_0(E)=\frac34\cdot\frac16=\frac18.\] This is an exact contradiction between the literal definition and its stated application to the paper’s example.
## Repair, counterevidence and impact

Replace \(\langle x-x',p\rangle\) by \(\langle x'-x,p\rangle\). Then the image of \(E\) is \((-1,-1/2)\), on which \(W(q)=1+q\), and \[\int_{-1}^{-1/2}(1+q)\,dq=\frac18.\] On each open branch of [eq:example] (#eq:example), \(W(U')U''=3/4\): the factors are \(\sqrt{3s/2}\) and \(3/(4\sqrt{3s/2})\) on the first branch, and \(\sqrt{3(1-s)}\) and \(3/(4\sqrt{3(1-s)})\) on the second. Continuity of \(U'\) at \(2/3\) introduces no atom there.

The surrounding convex-duality and transport derivation explicitly use this corrected convention. The saved result is retained as a verified printed definition/sign correction, excluded from the substantive severity tally under the task’s rule for typographical errors alone. The exact local discrepancy is preserved; it is not presented as a counterexample to the intended Calabi–Yau theorem. The reason is the absence of a demonstrated failure in the intended derivation, rather than the ease of repairing the symbol.
# Regularization in the stability application
## The sufficient total-variation estimate

The relevant passages are Proposition 5.6, Corollary 5.7 and Remark 5.8, PDF pages 23–24 / printed pages 481–482, followed by Theorems 6.1–6.3 and Corollary 6.4, pages 25–26 / 483–484. The saved check uses the local smooth approximation asserted in Remark 5.8, in addition to small potential error.

Fix \(t
e0\), and write \(\mu=V\mu_t\), \(
u=\omega_t^n\). Both measures have total mass \(V\). For a prescribed small \(\eta>0\), the good-region comparison allows \(t\) sufficiently small and a compact set \(K\) in the smooth good region such that \[\mu(K^c)\leq\eta V,\qquad
 \int_K|d
u-d\mu|\leq\eta V .\] Passing to a compact set uses inner regularity and can be absorbed in the choice of tolerance.

Equation reference: eq:tv. Let \(\omega_{t,j}\) be a smooth Kähler regularization in the same class, with locally smooth convergence near \(K\) and arbitrarily small potential difference, as asserted in Remark 5.8. For the already fixed \(t,K\), choose \(j\) so that, with \(
u_j=\omega_{t,j}^n\), \(\int_K|d
u_j-d
u|\leq\eta V\). Then \(a=\int_K|d
u_j-d\mu|\leq2\eta V\), while positivity and equal total mass give \(
u_j(K^c)\leq\mu(K^c)+a\). With the integral absolute-difference convention for total variation, \[
 \|
u_j-\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \leq a+
u_j(K^c)+\mu(K^c)
 \leq2a+2\mu(K^c)\leq6\eta V .\] Thus the normalized tolerance \(\gamma^{2n+3}\) is obtained by first choosing \(\eta<\gamma^{2n+3}/6\), then \(t\), then the smoothing accuracy. No uniform smoothing scale is required.
## The perturbation in Corollary 6.4

Let \(\phi_{t,j}\) regularize the ansatz potential \(\phi_t\). For \(\omega=\omega_{\mathrm{CY},t}/\lambda\), the smooth test function is \[q_j=-\psi_t+\frac{\phi_{t,j}-\phi_t}{\lambda},
 \qquad
 \omega+dd^cq_j=\frac{\omega_{t,j}}{\lambda}.\] Choose \(\|q_j+\psi_t\|_{C^0}<\delta/8\). Then \(\sup q_j\geq-\delta/8\). If the contrary hypothesis of Corollary 6.4 holds, the set \(\{\psi_t>\delta\}\) has \(\mu_t\)-measure greater than \(\delta\), and \(q_j<-7\delta/8\) on it. The mass hypothesis of Theorem 6.3 holds with \(a=-\delta/2\), \(b=\delta\). The uniform bound on the test function is retained with a fixed margin.

Choose \(\gamma\) below the theorem’s threshold and so that \(C\gamma<\delta/8\). Then choose \(t\) and the regularization as above. The stability estimate implies \(\sup q_j\leq-3\delta/8\), contradicting \(\sup q_j\geq-\delta/8\). The uniform Skoda estimate, its permitted change of reference potential, and the existence of the stated regularization remain explicit analytic inputs.

Equation [eq:tv] (#eq:tv) establishes the asymptotic application relative to \(V\mu_t\). It does not prove the stronger fixed-\(t\) assertion of arbitrarily small total variation relative to \(\omega_t^n\). Nor does arbitrary \(C^0\) approximation alone imply total-variation convergence. The stronger statement was not independently settled in the saved checks; no counterexample to it was established. This open verification limit does not increase supported severity.
# The integration domain in Proposition 6.12

On PDF page 32 / printed page 490, the displayed lower-bound chain inserts an unweighted integral over all \(X_t\) after a weight estimate known only on \(U_{y,t}\). That stronger intermediate expression is not justified by the stated local estimate. The terminal local bound needed by the proof follows directly.

The finite decomposition and the point normalization \(|s(z)|=1\) select an exponent tuple using \(z\) and \(s\), independently of \(y\). This preserves the quantifier needed for the subsequent Legendre optimization. The error is \(C/l+C\varepsilon+C(l)/\lambda\), and \(t\) is chosen small after \(l\) and \(\varepsilon\) are fixed. The final optimization uses \(u(x)\geq\langle p,x\rangle-u^*(p)\), including when the actual logarithmic coordinates \(x\) do not lie on \(\Delta\).

The correction is to pass directly through [eq:local] (#eq:local) and delete the unnecessary global unweighted intermediate line. It supports the already used terminal inequality under its local hypotheses. The preserved record does not establish that the stronger printed inequality is false in every instance, or that the intended core conclusion fails. This is retained as a local presentation/domain clarification, with the supported replacement shown explicitly.
# Overall outcome and remaining scope

The inherited checks establish no substantive Major or Minor issue within their inspected scope. The sign discrepancy and the integration-domain expression remain documented with their exact local corrections. Title: A scoped verification of curvature and log-quasimode growth
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

The reviewed work is Xiaoqi Huang and Christopher D. Sogge, Curvature and sharp growth rates of log-quasimodes on compact manifolds, Inventiones mathematicae 239 (2025), 947–1008, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01315-2 [HS]. The acquired 62-page PDF is the publisher version of record. In this report, PDF page 1 is printed page 947, so a printed page is its PDF page plus 946.

Sections 1–4 were read from the acquired PDF’s extracted text. The independent calculations focus on Theorems 1.1–1.2; Proposition 2.4 and equations (2.50)–(2.71); the orthogonal spectral-window argument on printed page 973; and the use of Lemmas A.1–A.2 on printed pages 986–988. Selected original page images were checked to resolve mathematical notation. The detailed global parametrix estimates in Lemma 2.5, the full variable-coefficient bilinear argument in the Appendix, and the complete Bieberbach-group periodization are not independently established here. No separate supplement or released computation was required for these analytic checks.
# The two logarithmic gains

Let \(n\ge2\), \(q_c=2(n+1)/(n-1)\), and \[\mu(q)=\frac{n-1}{2}\left(\frac12-\frac1q\right),
 \qquad 2<q\le q_c,\qquad T=c_0\log\lambda.\] Theorem 1.1 assumes a connected compact Riemannian manifold with all sectional curvatures nonpositive, or strictly negative for its stronger conclusion. The exponent \(q\) is fixed; the negative-curvature constant may depend on \(q\).

The equality case \(\alpha=q/(q-2)\) would instead leave a dyadic factor \(\log T\) before the square root. Proposition 2.4 correctly excludes it. Likewise, \(q=2\) is not included, and letting \(q\downarrow2\) does not supply a uniform constant. The proof does not obtain the negative-curvature subcritical improvement merely by interpolating the critical estimate with the trivial \(L^2\) bound: it uses (2.45), then (2.52), as required.

For the Appendix’s high-ceiling calculation, put \(\bar q=2(n+2)/n\). Direct simplification gives \[(q_c-\bar q)\left(\frac{3(n-1)}{16}-\frac18\right)
 =\frac{3n-5}{4n(n-1)}>0,\quad n\ge2.\] For \(n=2\) it equals \(1/8\), consistent with the separate treatment on printed page 988. At \(q=\bar q\), (A.12) gives a power saving of \(3/(4n)-\varepsilon\) relative to \(\lambda^{\mu(\bar q)\bar q}\); hence it supplies the endpoint that is not stated in (A.13). These checks verify the displayed exponent arithmetic and absorption margins, conditional on the bilinear input estimates themselves.
# Sharpness, quantifiers, and an independent flat model

The definition immediately before Theorem 1.2 (printed p. 951) explicitly uses \[f=\Theta(g)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 0<\limsup_{\lambda\to\infty} f(\lambda)/g(\lambda)<\infty .\] It is not a lower bound at every sufficiently large frequency. Empty spectral windows, assigned value zero in the theorem, therefore do not contradict it.

The square-root window factor on printed page 973 follows from orthogonality. Partition a unit frequency interval into \(J\lesssim\delta^{-1}\) disjoint spectral pieces \(I_j\) of length at most \(\delta\). For \(K=\max_j\left\lVert\chi_{I_j}\right\rVert_{2\to q}\), \[\left\lVert\chi_{[\lambda,\lambda+1]}f\right\rVert_q
 \le K\sum_j\left\lVert\chi_{I_j}f\right\rVert_2
 \le K\sqrt J\,\left\lVert f\right\rVert_2 .\] Consequently sharp unit-band lower bounds imply a subsequential \(\delta^{1/2}\lambda^{\mu(q)}\) lower bound for some narrow windows. This is the precise implication used by the paper, taking the cited unit-band sharpness theorem as an external input. It does not prove a pointwise lower bound at every window.
# A local notation clarification and its limits

Equation (2.26), printed page 961, labels the time at which a geodesic meets \(\Pi=\{x_n=0\}\) by \(s=d_g(x,\Pi)\). In ordinary distance notation this cannot literally specify the hitting time for generic directions. In the Euclidean two-dimensional model, \(x=(0,h)\), \(h>0\), and a unit covector \(\xi=(\epsilon,\sqrt{1-\epsilon^2})\) with \(0<\epsilon<1\) give \((\Phi_h(x,\xi))_2=h+h\sqrt{1-\epsilon^2}>0\). The signed intersection time is instead \(s=-h/\xi_n\).

The preceding transverse-section construction and the explicit invariance requirement (2.27) identify the intended definition: extend the initial cutoff constantly along each geodesic, using its unique local intersection with \(\Pi\). Transversality \(\xi_n\ne0\) makes that hitting time smooth and yields (2.27). This replacement changes no theorem statement or decay exponent. This report records the local notation clarification and does not treat it as evidence that the main microlocal construction or the estimates fail. It also does not certify every subsequent symbol calculation merely from this correction.
# Conclusion

The checked interpolation, summation, spectral-window, and model sharpness calculations support the stated conclusions within their hypotheses. No substantive defect is established within this scope. In particular, the limsup convention, the strict inequalities in Proposition 2.4, and the fixed-\(q\) constants remove several apparent endpoint objections.

Abstract: This scoped review identifies a missing finite-family restriction in Proposition 8.5 of Even-Zohar, Lakrec, and Tessler’s paper. Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: A finite-family restriction in the topological assembly of the BCFW triangulation
# Identity and scope

The reviewed source is Chaim Even-Zohar, Tsviqa Lakrec, and Ran J. Tessler, The amplituhedron BCFW triangulation, Inventiones mathematicae 239 (2025), 1009–1138, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01316-1 [paper]. The acquired 130-page PDF is the publisher version of record. PDF page \(p\) is printed page \(1008+p\).

The inspected scope comprises the main statements and domino/chord definitions; the linear-algebra mechanism in Lemma 4.35 and Proposition 5.1; the six-case structure of the separation induction; the topological assembly in Proposition 8.5 and its application; and a complete small example. The released `bcfw.sage`, README, and \(n=6\) separator output were read statically at commit `c0974f741ef51f7e05abf97c4b701b7bb5399fb6` (1 June 2022). No author code was executed. The entire 130-page argument, all boundary-pairing cases, and Section 9 were not independently reproved.

Definition 1.1 (printed p. 1011) requires injectivity on each open cell, disjoint open-cell images, and an open dense union of those images. It does not require the union of open images to contain its walls. The principal statements assume integers \(k\ge1\), \(n\ge k+4\), and an \(n\times(k+4)\) real matrix with strictly positive ordered maximal minors.
# A missing restriction in Proposition 8.5

Problem 1 (The local boundary conditions do not control an infinite family).  Proposition 8.5 (printed pp. 1120–1121; PDF pp. 112–113) is stated for a collection \(\{S_a\}_{a\in A}\) without explicitly assuming that \(A\) is finite. Its conclusion \[f\left(\bigcup_{a\in A}\overline{S_a}\right)=K\] is false for a general infinite family under the stratified-frontier convention used in the cell application.
## Original hypotheses and exact counterexample

The proposition assumes a smooth submersion \(f:B\to N\) between manifolds without boundary, \(\dim N=n\), a connected open \(L\subset B\) with compact closure, and \(K=f(\overline L)\). The \(n\)-dimensional submanifolds \(S_a\subset\overline L\) have disjoint images, compact closures with finite boundary stratifications, shared codimension-one boundaries unless their images lie in \(\partial K\), and an injective restriction with continuous inverse on each cell together with its shared boundaries.

Equation reference: eq:example. Set \[
 \begin{aligned}
 &B=N=\mathbb R,\quad f=\mathrm{id},\quad n=1,\quad
 L=(0,1),\quad K=[0,1],\\
 &a_j=\frac12+\frac1{2j},\qquad S_j=(a_{j+1},a_j),\qquad j\ge1.
 \end{aligned}\] Every hypothesis can be checked directly.

First, \(f\) is a smooth submersion, \(L\) is connected and open, and \(\overline L\) is compact. Each \(S_j\) is a smooth embedded one-dimensional manifold without boundary contained in \(L\), and distinct \(S_j\) have disjoint images.

Second, \(\overline{S_j}=[a_{j+1},a_j]\) is compact. Its two boundary strata are the singleton sets \(\{a_{j+1}\}\) and \(\{a_j\}\), both smooth zero-dimensional manifolds. Each has empty frontier \(\overline{\{a\}}\setminus\{a\}\), so the lower-stratum requirement holds. Here the boundary of a stratum is understood as its frontier, as required in the proposition’s stratified-cell application; it is not the ambient boundary of a lower-dimensional closed subset.

Third, \(a_1=1\) belongs to \(\partial K\). Every \(a_j\), \(j\ge2\), lies in the interior of \(K\) and is the common boundary point of \(S_{j-1}\) and \(S_j\). Therefore every codimension-one boundary stratum not mapped to \(\partial K\) is shared, exactly as required.

Finally, the identity map is injective and has continuous inverse on each interval together with its shared endpoints. This checks the fourth condition without an unstated differentiability assumption on the inverse.

Equation reference: eq:failure. Nevertheless, \[
 f\left(\bigcup_{j\ge1}\overline{S_j}\right)
 =\left(\frac12,1\right]\ne[0,1]=K .\] In particular, the interior point \(1/4\) is missing. Even taking the closure of the entire union would not repair coverage of that point. The only nonshared boundary stratum is \(\{1\}\), so the proposition’s additional description of \(\partial K\) also misses \(0\). This is an exact analytic counterexample, not a finite numerical surrogate.
## Where finiteness enters the proof

Lemma 8.6, quoted immediately after the proposition, explicitly assumes a finite collection of lower-dimensional submanifolds. Applying it to the combined boundary strata requires a corresponding finiteness condition that is absent from the proposition’s statement. The next page (printed p. 1122) also treats the union of the compact images \(f(\overline{S_a})\) as closed. That inference is valid for finite unions, but fails in [eq:example] (#eq:example): the union accumulates at \(1/2\), which it omits.
These are specific failures in the stated level of generality, rather than objections to stratification terminology or to an untested computational implementation.
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair

The actual BCFW family is finite. Its explicit cardinality on printed page 1011 is \[\frac1{k+1}\binom{n-3}{k}\binom{n-4}{k}.\] The counterexample therefore does not belong to the main triangulation application. It establishes neither failure of Theorems 1.3–1.5 nor failure of a finite-family version of the assembly argument.

A narrow repair is to require \(A\) to be finite and nonempty, or to state the proposition only for the finite stratified family used in its application. This excludes [eq:example] (#eq:example), makes the union of the compact images closed, and makes the combined finite boundary stratifications eligible for Lemma 8.6. These two repairs are verified. The present check does not certify every other aspect of a revised abstract proposition.

The supported impact is Minor: a local overgeneralization with no demonstrated damage to the central triangulation theorem. If finiteness is explicitly adopted as a standing contextual restriction, the issue is instead resolved by scope clarification. The finding is not a claim of first discovery or of absence of a later erratum.
# Independent checks supporting the bounded conclusion
## Linear algebra and the child case

In Lemma 4.35 (printed pp. 1067–1068), let \(U=\operatorname{span}(Y_1,\ldots,Y_k)\) and \(V=\operatorname{span}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{m+1})\) in \(\mathbb R^{k+m}\). The stated rank and nonzero mixed-minor assumptions give \(\dim(U+V)=k+m\) and therefore \(\dim(U\cap V)=1\). The alternating mixed-cofactor vector \[\sum_{j=1}^{m+1}(-1)^{j-1}
 \det(Y,Z_1,\ldots,\widehat Z_j,\ldots,Z_{m+1})\,Z_j\] belongs to that intersection and is nonzero by the independence of the \(Z_j\). This verifies the local reconstruction mechanism.

Positive ordered maximal minors imply that every subset of at most \(k+4\) rows of \(Z\) is independent. The six-row independence used for a nonsticky child in Proposition 5.1 is compatible with this bound because a child requires \(k\ge2\); it is not silently applied when \(k=1\). This check does not replace the full combinatorial nonvanishing proof.
## A complete \(k=1,n=6\) example

Take \(Z_i=(1,i,i^2,i^3,i^4)\) for \(1\le i\le6\). The six ordered maximal minors, in lexicographic row-subset order, are \[288,\ 1440,\ 2880,\ 2880,\ 1440,\ 288,\] so this matrix satisfies the required strict positivity. The three BCFW supports in this case are \[\{1,2,3,4,6\},\qquad\{1,2,4,5,6\},\qquad\{2,3,4,5,6\}.\] Normalize each nonnegative row \(c\) by \(\sum_i c_i=1\). The left kernel of \(Z\) is generated by \[r=(-1,5,-10,10,-5,1),\qquad rZ=0,\qquad\sum_i r_i=0.\] The independence of the five supported rows proves injectivity on each cell. If positive rows on two distinct supports, missing odd indices \(i\) and \(j\), had the same image, then \(c-d=t r\). The \(i\)th coordinate forces \(t>0\), whereas the \(j\)th forces \(t<0\), since both corresponding entries of \(r\) are negative. Thus the open images are disjoint.

For any nonnegative normalized \(c\), let \[t=\min\{c_1,c_3/10,c_5/5\},\qquad d=c+t r.\] Then \(d\ge0\), \(\sum_i d_i=1\), \(dZ=cZ\), and at least one odd coordinate vanishes. Hence the three closed simplices cover the polytope. Their open interiors have an open dense union because their omitted faces form a finite union of lower-dimensional sets. This proves the three triangulation properties for this fixed \(Z\).

The independent exact calculation also reproduces the relevant separator signs in the stored \(n=6\) output. For positive support coefficients \(a,b,c,d,e\), the paired expressions include \(1440c\) versus \(-2880d\), \(1440a\) versus \(-288d\), and \(-4147200a(c+2d)\) versus \(414720b(c+2d)\). No sampled positivity assumption or author-code execution is used. This verifies the bounded example, not all values of \(k,n\) or the complete Sage implementation.
# Conclusion

The finite-family omission in Proposition 8.5 has a complete counterexample and a precisely limited consequence. The actual BCFW family meets the missing finite restriction. The independent small example and local linear algebra provide positive checks, without being presented as a general proof of the paper.

Title: Two quantitative corrections to the stated sheeting estimates
# Source identity, conventions, and scope

The reviewed work is Costante Bellettini, Extensions of Schoen–Simon–Yau and Schoen–Simon theorems via iteration à la De Giorgi, Inventiones mathematicae 240 (2025), 1–34, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01317-0 [B]. The complete extracted text was read by the native scientific helper. Independent proof checks concentrate on the scale and amplitude dependence of Theorems 6–7, the curvature iteration at dimension six, the tilt truncation algebra, and the recurrence in Lemma B.1. Eighteen original pages were visually inspected by the helper; the primary executor rechecked the decisive statement and proof images.
