paragraphs: For rational beta>1/(p-1), exp-1 and log(1+T) are inverse analytic coordinates on the closed radius p^{-beta} disc; log(1+T)/T is a unit and coordinatewise Koszul rescaling is invertible.

report: Abstract: A clopen two-move example disproves the assertion in Lemma 72 that the explicitly defined tree \(Q\) is a quasi-strategy for Player I. The tree restricts Player II and can change a game won by II into one won by I, preventing the selection of the required auxiliary strategy. This is a Major defect in the written proof of the second separation reduction theorem. A replacement using actual winning positions and an additional escape phase repairs this local strategy argument. No counterexample to the determinacy theorem itself is established. Independent scientific acceptance remains pending.
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review of
The metamathematics of separated determinacy
# Identity and review boundaries

This report concerns J. P. Aguilera, The metamathematics of separated determinacy, Inventiones mathematicae 240 (2025), 313–457, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01322-3 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01322-3) [paper]. The reviewed file is the acquired 145-page publisher version of record. Its SHA-256 is
Printed page \(q\) is one-based PDF page \(q-312\).

This is a systematic, claim-focused initial review, not a line-by-line certification of all 145 pages. The text actually read covers the introduction and definitions, the first separation reduction proof, the second reduction proof through Lemma 81, the third reduction statement and Part I proof, the classification statements, the generalized Borel theorem and its proof, and selected concluding limitations. The exact ranges and distinct levels of checking are in `coverage.json`. The suitable-model construction and reversal in §6.3–6.5, all classification subcases and the two appendices were not independently reconstructed. No whole-paper correctness claim follows from this report.

No separate essential supplement was identified in the acquired manifest. Public author TeX and paper-specific software were unavailable in the recorded search; neither absence is treated as a defect. Only an independent small game-checking script was run.
# Definitions, quantifiers and checked dependencies

Here \(\mathbb R\) is Baire space \(\mathbb N^\mathbb N\). Write \([s]=\{x:s\preccurlyeq x\}\) for a basic cylinder. According to p. 328 (PDF 16), a game tree has no terminal nodes, a player moving outside it loses immediately, and a quasi-strategy for I must leave all II moves unrestricted. This last requirement is the decisive one below.

The full Wadge reduction definition on p. 329 (PDF 17) requires both sides of the membership equivalence, not just preservation of positive membership. Definable classes in Definition 3 require effective uniform coding of continuous preimages. These coding conditions are essential over \(\mathsf{RCA}_0\); external descriptions of ordinal classes must not be substituted for internally available codes without justification.

Equation reference: eq:layer. Definition 9, p. 335 (PDF 23), requires the compatibility \[
 W=\bigcup_i(A_i\cap C_i)\cup\bigl(B\setminus\bigcup_i C_i\bigr),
 \qquad W\cap C_i=A_i\cap C_i.\] The layers need not initially be disjoint. Lemma 10 disjointifies the \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^0_\xi\) layers; for \(\xi=2\), enumerating their closed pieces and assigning each point to its first piece verifies the required reduction. The compatibility in [eq:layer] (#eq:layer) is precisely what preserves the payoff on overlaps.

Theorem 40, p. 347 (PDF 35), assumes effective treeability and strategic replacement: a coded countable family of games has a coded countable family of winning strategies. Its proof, pp. 348–350 (PDF 36–38), uses this family both to form the winner-index set and to assemble a strategy after the first open layer is entered. For II, compatibility in [eq:layer] (#eq:layer) is indispensable. In the converse role-selection game, a strategy purported to beat both roles yields opposing strategies for the same game and hence a contradiction. These mechanisms were checked; ordinary determinacy alone cannot silently replace strategic replacement.

Theorem 69, p. 362 (PDF 50), takes a union \(\Gamma=\bigcup_l\Gamma_l\) of definable, effectively treeable classes, with \(\Gamma_{2l+1}=\check\Gamma_{2l}\). It relates \(\operatorname{LU}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^0_2,\Gamma)\) determinacy and strategic replacement to \(\Gamma\)-SR plus the union-operator monotone-induction principle of Definition 65. The latter is not merely the scheme \(\forall l\,(\Game\Gamma_l\text{-MI})\). The proof explicitly uses the paired dual classes in the reversal. Lemma 72 is needed in the forward direction and in identifying the winning-position set used for comprehension in (5.2).

Theorem 91, p. 380 (PDF 68), has additional projective-complexity and \(\beta\)-model hypotheses. Theorem 94, p. 381 (PDF 69), is a restricted reversal requiring \(\boldsymbol{\Pi}^1_3\) transfinite induction; Conjecture 93 is not a proved general reversal. Likewise, the one-way classification list in Theorem 164, p. 423 (PDF 111), does not claim that every listed case is non-transferable. Its stated open cases must be retained. Theorem 175, p. 429 (PDF 117), is a boldface ZFC transfer theorem, uses ordinary Borel determinacy, and does not claim its lightface analogue. The limitations on replacing \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^0_2\) by \(\boldsymbol{\Pi}^0_2\) were checked at the level of the displayed reductions in Propositions 180–182; their external consistency-strength inputs were not reproved.
# Problem 1: the tree in Lemma 72 can restrict the wrong player
## Exact source claim

Equation reference: eq:badQ. Lemma 72 starts on p. 364 (PDF 52) with \(p\notin P\). For a fixed pair \((i,n)\) it considers \[H_{i,n}=\{x:\exists k\ (x\upharpoonright k\in P)\}\cup C_{i,n}.\] In Case II on p. 365 (PDF 53), I wins \(H_{i,n}\). The paper explicitly defines \(Q\) by \[
 q\in Q\ \Longleftrightarrow\
   \bigl(\exists r\preccurlyeq q\ (r\in P)\bigr)\ \lor\ q\in T(C_{i,n}),\] where \(T(C_{i,n})\) is the tree of finite prefixes of the closed set, using the paper’s convention. It then asserts that \(Q\) is a quasi-strategy for I, so an I-winning strategy in \(G(W_{i,n}(P),Q)\) would also win the unrestricted game. Since I does not win the unrestricted game, the proof selects a II-winning strategy in the restricted game. The original PDF image confirms this exact formula and inference.
## Parameters and verification of all local hypotheses

Choose the paired pointclasses \[\Gamma_{2l}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^0_2,\qquad \Gamma_{2l+1}=\boldsymbol{\Pi}^0_2
 \quad(l\in\mathbb N).\] They are definable, effectively treeable Wadge classes: their codes are uniformly closed under union with an open set and intersection with a closed set, and the two classes are dual. Work with the ordinary full interpretation of Baire-space games. In the usual monotone-induction interpretation, strategic replacement and the required fixed points are available in ZFC. The particular fixed point needed below is, more strongly, exhibited directly.

Equation reference: eq:example. Set \[
\begin{aligned}
 A_0&=[1],& C_0&=[0]\cup[1,0],& C_{0,n}&=C_0\quad(n\in\mathbb N),\\
 A_i&=\varnothing,&C_i&=\varnothing,&C_{i,n}&=\varnothing\quad(i>0).
\end{aligned}\] All sets are recursive clopen sets, hence lie in the required classes. The layer family is pairwise disjoint, its closed decomposition is increasing (constant in \(n\)), and \[W=A_0\cap C_0=[1,0].\] Thus layered compatibility also holds. Take the initial position \(p=\varnothing\) and the pair \((i,n)=(0,0)\).

Equation reference: eq:P, eq:fixed. Let \[
 P=\{q\in\mathbb N^{<\mathbb N}:(1,0)\preccurlyeq q\}.\] We verify the fixed point rather than assuming it. From a position extending \((1,0)\), the payoff \(W\) is already guaranteed. From the empty position, II can answer a first move \(1\) with \(1\); from position \((1)\), II can again choose \(1\); and every other position outside \(P\) either still allows this response or has already made \(W\) impossible. Hence \(\Phi(\varnothing)=P\). Reaching \(P\) is equivalent to the final play lying in \([1,0]\), so [eq:Wi] (#eq:Wi) with \(X=P\) again has precisely \(P\) as its I-winning positions (also for the empty layers). Therefore \[
 \Phi(\varnothing)=P=\Phi(P)=\Phi^\infty,\qquad
 \varnothing\notin P.\] This particular induction has one nonempty stage. Even the printed stage-comparison convention can be satisfied for this example by the single-equivalence-class relation \(P\times P\); no transfinite-order ambiguity is needed for the counterexample.
## The claimed and actual outcomes
Because reaching \(P\) is just \([1,0]\), we have \[H_{0,0}=[1,0]\cup C_0=C_0.\] I wins \(H_{0,0}\) by choosing \(0\) initially. Thus the example is in Case II, exactly as required.

Every extension of a position in \(P\) is already a prefix of a real in \(C_0\). Formula [eq:badQ] (#eq:badQ) therefore gives \[Q=T(C_0).\] The node \((1)\) lies in \(Q\), while \((1,1)\) does not. At \((1)\) it is II’s turn. Consequently \(Q\) restricts II’s move \(1\) and is not a quasi-strategy for I. This tree is pruned and has no terminal nodes; dead-end coding is not the explanation.

The unrestricted game \(G(W_{0,0}(P))=G([1,0])\) is won by II: answer the initial move \(1\) with \(1\), and otherwise the payoff is already lost by I. But in the restricted game \(G([1,0],Q)\), I wins by choosing \(1\). If II chooses \(0\), the play lies in \([1,0]\); if II chooses any other number, II immediately loses by moving outside \(Q\). Thus \[\text{unrestricted winner}=\mathrm{II},\qquad
 \text{restricted winner}=\mathrm{I}.\] The II-winning strategy required by the displayed proof does not exist for this example.

The independent script `clopen_game_check.py` checked the nine pairs of move types \(0,1,\geq2\). This is an exact finite quotient of the above cylinder games: all integers at least \(2\) have identical membership and legality effects, and subsequent moves are irrelevant. It confirms, rather than replaces, the analytic verification.
## Counterevidence and alternative readings

There certainly exists a genuine I quasi-strategy for \(H_{0,0}\): I may choose \(0\) and leave every II move free. This does not make the explicitly defined \(Q\) a quasi-strategy. Replacing the displayed set by actual winning positions changes the construction and also requires checking the transition when I leaves the new tree.

The terminology canonical non-losing cannot override the explicit membership formula. Nor does restricting to the component reachable under some other fixed I strategy justify deleting the offending node \((1)\) from the displayed \(Q\). The source’s own game-tree convention makes illegal moves immediate losses, and the example uses that convention exactly.

The final statement of Lemma 72 survives this example: II really does win \(W\). The example refutes the construction and strategy-transfer inference used to prove that statement, not determinacy or the second separation reduction theorem as a statement.
## Core impact

The finding is Major. Lemma 72 completes the implication (3)\(\Rightarrow\)(1) of Theorem 69 and is explicitly used with Lemma 71 on p. 366 (PDF 54) to obtain the comprehension assertion (5.2). These are core parts of the second separation reduction theorem. Conclusions that rely on that proof need a corrected local argument. The evidence does not invalidate every theorem, the independent first reduction argument, or the entire classification program. Repairability does not remove the demonstrated core dependency.
# A precise repair of the local strategy construction

The following replacement addresses both the wrong-player restriction and the exit transition. It is given at the level of the game’s mathematical construction; the entire paper has not been mechanically formalized over \(\mathsf{RCA}_0\).

Fix \(i,n\), put \(C=C_{i,n}\) and \(H=H_{i,n}\), and let \[D=\{q:\text{I has a winning strategy for }H\text{ from }q\}.\] The family of these auxiliary games, for all pairs and starting positions, is countable and uniformly coded from \(P\) and the original codes. The strategic-replacement and effective-treeability hypotheses used in the source provide the winner-index sets and strategies. This use should be explicit; \(D\) is not claimed to be recursive in \(P\) alone.

Equation reference: eq:D. Two elementary observations will be used. First, if I can force a visit to \(P\) from \(q\), then I wins \(W_{i,n}(P)\) from \(q\), so \(q\in\Phi(P)=P\). In particular, \(P\) is closed under extension. Second, \[
 P\subseteq D,\qquad D\setminus P\subseteq T(C).\] For the second inclusion, if \(q\notin T(C)\), membership in the closed part \(C\) is already impossible. Winning \(H\) from \(q\) then means forcing a visit to \(P\), which puts \(q\) in \(P\).

If I wins \(H\) from the current position \(p\notin P\), form \(Q'\) from the histories extending \(p\) all of whose intermediate positions remain in \(D\). At an I position in \(D\), a winning strategy has a next move in \(D\). At a II position in \(D\), every legal next move lies in \(D\), by restricting an I-winning strategy after that move. Thus \(Q'\) is a pruned I quasi-strategy. It does not restrict II.

There is no I-winning strategy for \(G(W_{i,n}(P),Q')\), since such a strategy would win the unrestricted game, contradicting \(p\notin P\). By determinacy and treeability, choose a II-winning strategy for this restricted game. As long as I stays in \(Q'\), follow it. Any infinite play that stays in \(Q'\) avoids \(P\) and lies outside \(A_i\cap C\) by the II-winning property. Equation [eq:D] (#eq:D) puts all its prefixes in \(T(C)\), so it actually lies in \(C\setminus A_i\), hence outside \(W\) by disjointness or layered compatibility.

If I leaves \(Q'\) at a position \(q\), then \(q\notin D\), and therefore \(q\notin P\). Now use a II-winning strategy for \(H\) from \(q\). This additional escape phase avoids \(P\) and must reach a finite position outside \(T(C)\), since otherwise it would lose \(H\). At that position, and only then, continue with the paper’s next pair \((i',n')\).

The countable auxiliary strategies can be collected by the same strategic-replacement hypotheses. If infinitely many pairs are processed, the resulting play avoids every \(C_{i,n}\) and hence \(W\). If the process eventually remains in one \(Q'\), the preceding argument gives a play outside \(W\). An escape phase cannot itself last forever along a II-winning strategy for \(H\). This proves the corrected local II strategy.

This repair verifies the mathematical strategy argument underlying Lemma 72. It adds a winning-position construction and an escape phase; merely relabeling the old \(Q\) is insufficient. Full weak-theory formalization, the reversal proof and all subsequent applications still require separate acceptance checks. Author adoption is neither requested nor observed.
# Scope clarifications and disposition

The printed stage relation (5.1) and Definition 63 on p. 360 (PDF 48) reverse the usual arguments; the later construction on p. 367 (PDF 55) uses \(W_a=\Phi(W_{<a})\) with the usual initial-segment direction. The standard consistent formulation is \[a\leq_\Phi b\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 a,b\in\Phi^\infty\ \wedge\
 \forall\eta\,(b\in\Phi^\eta\Rightarrow a\in\Phi^\eta),
 \qquad a\leq_\Phi b\ \Longleftrightarrow\ a\in\Phi(W_{<b}).\] This is recorded as a notation clarification, not a separate severity-counted finding. Problem 1 uses a one-stage fixed point and remains valid independently of this transposition. Similarly, the introductory one-sided wording of Wadge reducibility is not treated as a scientific finding because the full operational definition appears in §2.

The publisher record and exact-title correction searches did not identify a specific erratum for Lemma 72. This was a limited search, not an exhaustive assertion that no correction exists. No later version was substituted for the acquired PDF.

Choose the paired pointclasses \[\Gamma_{2l}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^0_2,\qquad \Gamma_{2l+1}=\boldsymbol{\Pi}^0_2
 \quad(l\in\mathbb N).\] They are definable, effectively treeable Wadge classes: their codes are uniformly closed under union with an open set and intersection with a closed set, and the two classes are dual. Work with the ordinary full interpretation of Baire-space games. In the usual monotone-induction interpretation, strategic replacement and the required fixed points are available in ZFC. The particular fixed point needed below is, more strongly, exhibited directly.

Equation reference: eq:example. Set \[
\begin{aligned}
 A_0&=[1],& C_0&=[0]\cup[1,0],& C_{0,n}&=C_0\quad(n\in\mathbb N),\\
 A_i&=\varnothing,&C_i&=\varnothing,&C_{i,n}&=\varnothing\quad(i>0).
\end{aligned}\] All sets are recursive clopen sets, hence lie in the required classes. The layer family is pairwise disjoint, its closed decomposition is increasing (constant in \(n\)), and \[W=A_0\cap C_0=[1,0].\] Thus layered compatibility also holds. Take the initial position \(p=\varnothing\) and the pair \((i,n)=(0,0)\).

Equation reference: eq:P, eq:fixed. Let \[
 P=\{q\in\mathbb N^{<\mathbb N}:(1,0)\preccurlyeq q\}.\] We verify the fixed point rather than assuming it. From a position extending \((1,0)\), the payoff \(W\) is already guaranteed. From the empty position, II can answer a first move \(1\) with \(1\); from position \((1)\), II can again choose \(1\); and every other position outside \(P\) either still allows this response or has already made \(W\) impossible. Hence \(\Phi(\varnothing)=P\). Reaching \(P\) is equivalent to the final play lying in \([1,0]\), so [eq:Wi] (#eq:Wi) with \(X=P\) again has precisely \(P\) as its I-winning positions (also for the empty layers). Therefore \[
 \Phi(\varnothing)=P=\Phi(P)=\Phi^\infty,\qquad
 \varnothing\notin P.\] This particular induction has one nonempty stage. Even the printed stage-comparison convention can be satisfied for this example by the single-equivalence-class relation \(P\times P\); no transfinite-order ambiguity is needed for the counterexample.
Because reaching \(P\) is just \([1,0]\), we have \[H_{0,0}=[1,0]\cup C_0=C_0.\] I wins \(H_{0,0}\) by choosing \(0\) initially. Thus the example is in Case II, exactly as required.

Every extension of a position in \(P\) is already a prefix of a real in \(C_0\). Formula [eq:badQ] (#eq:badQ) therefore gives \[Q=T(C_0).\] The node \((1)\) lies in \(Q\), while \((1,1)\) does not. At \((1)\) it is II’s turn. Consequently \(Q\) restricts II’s move \(1\) and is not a quasi-strategy for I. This tree is pruned and has no terminal nodes; dead-end coding is not the explanation.

The unrestricted game \(G(W_{0,0}(P))=G([1,0])\) is won by II: answer the initial move \(1\) with \(1\), and otherwise the payoff is already lost by I. But in the restricted game \(G([1,0],Q)\), I wins by choosing \(1\). If II chooses \(0\), the play lies in \([1,0]\); if II chooses any other number, II immediately loses by moving outside \(Q\). Thus \[\text{unrestricted winner}=\mathrm{II},\qquad
 \text{restricted winner}=\mathrm{I}.\] The II-winning strategy required by the displayed proof does not exist for this example.

The independent script `clopen_game_check.py` checked the nine pairs of move types \(0,1,\geq2\). This is an exact finite quotient of the above cylinder games: all integers at least \(2\) have identical membership and legality effects, and subsequent moves are irrelevant. It confirms, rather than replaces, the analytic verification.

The finding is Major. Lemma 72 completes the implication (3)\(\Rightarrow\)(1) of Theorem 69 and is explicitly used with Lemma 71 on p. 366 (PDF 54) to obtain the comprehension assertion (5.2). These are core parts of the second separation reduction theorem. Conclusions that rely on that proof need a corrected local argument. The evidence does not invalidate every theorem, the independent first reduction argument, or the entire classification program. Repairability does not remove the demonstrated core dependency.
result: There certainly exists a genuine I quasi-strategy for \(H_{0,0}\): I may choose \(0\) and leave every II move free. This does not make the explicitly defined \(Q\) a quasi-strategy. Replacing the displayed set by actual winning positions changes the construction and also requires checking the transition when I leaves the new tree.

The terminology canonical non-losing cannot override the explicit membership formula. Nor does restricting to the component reachable under some other fixed I strategy justify deleting the offending node \((1)\) from the displayed \(Q\). The source’s own game-tree convention makes illegal moves immediate losses, and the example uses that convention exactly.

The final statement of Lemma 72 survives this example: II really does win \(W\). The example refutes the construction and strategy-transfer inference used to prove that statement, not determinacy or the second separation reduction theorem as a statement.
Impact: Demonstrated invalid core derivation; no counterexample to the determinacy theorem statement, first reduction theorem or whole classification program.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use D of actual I-winning H positions, retain histories whose intermediate positions stay in D, and after I exits use a II-winning H escape phase until leaving T(C). Countably select auxiliary strategies using stated strategic replacement/treeability.

report: Abstract: A concrete normal-crossing Stein surface shows that the fiber product prescribed in the normalization reduction of Proposition 4.2 need not kill the cohomology class. An extra component, arising from two different normalization branches, retains a nonzero class in degree one with coefficients in \(\mathbb Z/2\). Taking the product over the normalization repairs this local construction. This is a Major defect in a proof step used by the main comparison theorem, not a counterexample to that theorem. A separate Minor scope defect concerns the ambient-dimension equality stated in Theorem 0.4; the body already states the appropriate pure-dimension hypothesis. The review concerns only the acquired arXiv v3 manuscript. Independent scientific acceptance remains pending.
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review of
Étale cohomology of algebraic varieties over Stein compacta
# Identity, version and inspected scope

The assigned paper is Olivier Benoist, Étale cohomology of algebraic varieties over Stein compacta, M25-0063. The exact reviewed file is arXiv:2305.06054v3, dated 3 February 2025, with 36 PDF pages. Printed page numbers and one-based PDF page numbers agree. The acquired PDF SHA-256 is

The associated journal record is Inventiones mathematicae 240 (2025), 497–536, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01323-2 [paper, publisher]. The publisher version of record was not acquired. The arXiv record’s description of its version as final does not establish file or content identity with the journal article. None is asserted here.

All 1,939 lines of the native text extraction were read, including references; truncated display segments were retrieved again. Nineteen original PDF pages were also inspected visually. The scientific review concentrated on the hypotheses and dependency chain of Propositions 2.4, 4.1–4.3, Theorems 3.9, 5.1, 5.5–5.10, Corollary 5.11, Remark 5.12 and the sums-of-squares applications. Reading the text is not an independent reproof of every cited theorem. The released TeX was inspected statically at the disputed formulas and the corresponding body statements; it was not compiled or executed. No separate essential supplement was identified. Optional software absence is not a defect.
# Definitions, quantifiers and proof dependencies

A Stein compact subset has a basis of Stein open neighborhoods. \(\mathcal O(K)\) and \(\mathcal M(K)\) are rings of germs on neighborhoods of \(K\); they are not rings of functions merely on the underlying point set. In §1.1 the paper permits general second-countable complex spaces, without an implicit connectedness or pure-dimension assumption. Normality is local and does not force distinct connected components to have the same dimension.

Theorem 5.1, pp. 26–28, compares cohomology only after taking the directed limit over Stein neighborhoods of \(K\). The algebraic scheme is interiorly of finite type and the sheaf is torsion; either interior properness or interior constructibility is required. Corollary 5.2 removes the neighborhood-limit presentation under properness. These alternatives cannot both be dropped: the source’s Remark 3.10 explicitly gives a counterexample.

The checked dependency chain is as follows. Proposition 2.4 kills a positive-degree class after a finite, possibly ramified, cover, using a degree-one cyclic cover and a Mayer–Vietoris induction through bumps. Proposition 4.1 uses the relative comparison Theorem 3.9 and a finite-cover annihilation theorem to obtain local vanishing on a normal space. Proposition 4.2 extends this to general Stein spaces and all points over a chosen base point. Proposition 4.3 globalizes that result so a ramified class extends. Theorem 5.1, Step 5, combines Propositions 4.3 and 2.4 to kill higher direct images in the qfh comparison. Problem 1 concerns the first reduction in Proposition 4.2, before its separate Galois-closure argument.

For the equivariant application, \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb C/\mathbb R)\) acts antilinearly. Theorem 5.5 uses a comparison of Hochschild–Serre spectral sequences. The absence of fixed points in Theorem 5.6 is essential: it permits the equivariant Artin vanishing input. The statement of that external input was checked in [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem~2.6]{vanishing}]; taking its compact subset empty and using an empty fixed locus yields the vanishing used here. Its entire proof was not independently reproduced.
# Problem 1: the product in the normalization reduction has extra components
## Source claim and location

Proposition 4.2 is on pp. 23–24. Its proof starts with the normalization \(
u:\widetilde S	o S\), the points \(\widetilde s_i\) above \(s\), and finite surjections \(p_i:T_i	o\widetilde S\) which kill \(
u^*\alpha\) over disjoint neighborhoods \(\Omega_i\) of \(\widetilde s_i\). The first sentence on p. 24 asserts that the fiber product over \(S\) of the maps \(
u\circ p_i\) solves the original problem. The same construction is explicit in the released `compactStein.tex`, line 1299 (one-based). The essential inference is \[p_i^*
u^*\alpha=0\ \hbox{over }p_i^{-1}(\Omega_i\setminus
u^{-1}Z)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 p^*\alpha=0\ \hbox{near }p^{-1}(s)\setminus p^{-1}Z\] for \(p:\prod_S T_i	o S\). It need not hold.
## Explicit parameters and verification of every local assumption

Let \[\begin{aligned}
 S&=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb C^3:xy=0\},&
 A&=\{y=0\},\quad B=\{x=0\},\\
 s&=(0,0,0),&
 U&=S,\quad Z=\{z=0\}\cap S .
\end{aligned}\] This is a reduced Stein space, being a closed analytic subspace of \(\mathbb C^3\); \(U\) is open in \(S\), \(s\in U\), and \(Z\) is a closed analytic subset. The two planes \(A\) and \(B\) meet in the \(z\)-axis. The normalization is the finite surjection \[\nu:\widetilde S=A\amalg B\longrightarrow S.\] It has precisely two points over \(s\). Take \(k=1\) and \(m=2\). Let \(\eta\in H^1(\mathbb C^*,\mathbb Z/2)\) be the nonzero class, and define \[\alpha=z^*\eta\in H^1(S\setminus Z,\mathbb Z/2).\] The inclusion of the punctured \(z\)-axis is a section of \(z:S\setminus Z\to\mathbb C^*\), so \(\alpha\) is nonzero.

Define two covers of \(\widetilde S\): \[\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &\text{over }A&\text{over }B\\ \hline
p_A:T_A\to\widetilde S &(u,t)\mapsto(u,0,t^2)&(v,z)\mapsto(0,v,z)\\
p_B:T_B\to\widetilde S &(u,z)\mapsto(u,0,z)&(v,t)\mapsto(0,v,t^2).
\end{array}\] Each source is a disjoint union of two copies of \(\mathbb C^2\). Each map is holomorphic, finite and surjective, since its component maps are a degree-two polynomial map and an identity. Thus these maps are allowed inputs to the reduction.

Choose \(\Omega_A=A\) and \(\Omega_B=B\), viewed as disjoint open subsets of the normalization. They are neighborhoods of the respective preimages of \(s\); their union is all of \(\widetilde S\). On \(p_A^{-1}(\Omega_A\setminus
u^{-1}Z)\), the map on the punctured coordinate is \(t\mapsto t^2\), so \[p_A^*
u^*\alpha=2\eta=0\quad	ext{in }H^1(-,\mathbb Z/2).\] The same calculation gives \(p_B^*
u^*\alpha=0\) over \(\Omega_B\). Hence every input vanishing condition asserted in the reduction holds. For every neighborhood \(\Omega\) of \(s\) one also has \(
u^{-1}(\Omega)\subset\Omega_A\cup\Omega_B\).
## The prescribed output and its actual cohomology

Form the prescribed product \[T=T_A\times_S T_B,\qquad p:T\to S .\] It is again finite and surjective. However, take the open-and-closed part in which the first factor is the identity copy over \(B\) and the second is the identity copy over \(A\). This part is \[D=B\times_S A=\{x=y=0\}\simeq\mathbb C_z.\] The map \(p|_D\) is the identity onto the intersection axis. Consequently \[(p^*\alpha)|_{D\setminus p^{-1}Z}=\eta\ne0.\] This obstruction persists after every shrinking of \(\Omega\) around \(s\): a sufficiently small circle on the punctured \(z\)-axis lies in \(\Omega\) and has evaluation \(1\) against the restricted mod-two class. Thus the claimed vanishing is false for this permitted product. It is not a failure to choose a sufficiently small neighborhood.

An independent finite calculation of cyclic covering degrees confirms the four branch-pair cases. For branch pair \(AA,AB,BA,BB\), respectively, the degrees of the two coordinate covers are \((2,1),(2,2),(1,1),(1,2)\). Over a punctured base, their fiber product has \(\gcd(d,e)\) components, each with winding \(\operatorname{lcm}(d,e)\). The respective winding parities are \[(0,0,1,0).\] Only the \(BA\) component already proves the contradiction. The analytic construction above, rather than this finite calculation, verifies the Stein and neighborhood hypotheses.
## Counterevidence, interpretation and core impact

The proposition’s existence statement is not disproved: there are covers which kill the class, including the corrected product below. Nor is the normal-space Galois-closure argument in the second paragraph of the proof contradicted. The issue is the explicit reduction from a general Stein space to its normalization.

Taking products over \(\widetilde S\) would force the factors to have the same normalization lift. That is a different mathematical object from the stated product of \(\nu\circ p_i\) over \(S\). The example verifies a nonzero cohomology class on an actual additional component, rather than merely detecting an ambiguous symbol or an OCR error. The original PDF and the matching released TeX both specify the latter construction.

The supported severity is Major. Proposition 4.2 is the local input explicitly invoked in Proposition 4.3, p. 24, and Proposition 4.3 is explicitly invoked in Theorem 5.1, Step 5, p. 28. The written general-space proof of the main comparison theorem therefore needs this reduction corrected. This conclusion does not refute the comparison isomorphism, the dimension bounds, or the sums-of-squares theorem. An easy local repair does not remove the demonstrated dependency.
## Precise local repair and its boundary

Replace the prescribed product by \[T'=\prod_{\widetilde S}T_i,\qquad
 \widetilde p:T'	o\widetilde S,\qquad p'=
u\circ\widetilde p.\] This is finite and surjective. Because \(
u\) is finite and the disjoint neighborhoods \(\Omega_i\) contain the whole fiber over \(s\), choose \(\Omega\) around \(s\) with \(
u^{-1}(\Omega)\subset igcup_i\Omega_i\). The subsets \(\widetilde p^{-1}(\Omega_i\cap
u^{-1}\Omega)\) are disjoint and cover \((p')^{-1}\Omega\). On the \(i\)th such subset, the projection \(T'	o T_i\) pulls back the already vanishing class. Cohomology of a finite disjoint union is the product of the component cohomology groups. Therefore \((p')^*\alpha\) vanishes on \((p')^{-1}(\Omega\setminus Z)\), for every degree \(k\) in the proposition.

This proves the corrected normalization reduction in its stated generality. In the example it retains only the \(AA\) and \(BB\) parts, whose winding parities are both zero. It does not independently certify all subsequent Cech refinement arguments, hypercover descent, or external analytic inputs. Author adoption has not been requested or observed.
# Problem 2: ambient dimension in the introductory equality
## Exact statement and counterexample

Theorem 0.4 on p. 3 asserts \(\operatorname{cd}\mathcal M(K)=n\) for a connected Stein compact subset \(K\) of a normal Stein space \(S\) of dimension \(n\). The abstract on p. 1 has the same dimensional scope. In contrast, Remark 5.12(ii), p. 31, explicitly assumes that \(S\) has pure dimension \(n\) and \(K\) is nonempty.

Under the conventions of §1.1, take \[S=\{\ast\}\amalg\mathbb C,\qquad K=\{\ast\},\qquad n=1.\] This is a normal, second-countable Stein space of dimension one. The compact set \(K\) is nonempty and connected, and is Stein because it is itself an open Stein component and hence has a basis of Stein neighborhoods. These verify every stated assumption of Theorem 0.4. But restriction to that open component gives \[\mathcal O(K)=\mathcal M(K)=\mathbb C,\qquad \operatorname{cd}\mathcal M(K)=0,\] since \(\mathbb C\) is algebraically closed and has trivial absolute Galois group. The displayed conclusion would instead give \(1\). Adding an unrelated component changes \(\dim S\) without changing the germ along \(K\).
## Counterevidence, impact and correction

Normality does not exclude this example, and the theorem states connectedness of \(K\), not of \(S\). The important counterevidence is supplied by the paper itself: Corollary 5.11 only asserts an upper bound, and Remark 5.12(ii) already states the pure-dimension assumption needed for its lower bound. The above example satisfies the upper bound \(0\le1\) and does not meet the remark’s pure-dimension hypothesis.

This is a Minor scope defect in the introductory restatement. There is no demonstrated defect in the body result under its explicit hypotheses. The sums-of-squares bound in Theorem 6.4 uses the upper bound, so this example does not damage that quantitative application. The correction is to include nonemptiness of \(K\) and pure dimension \(n\) in Theorem 0.4, following Remark 5.12(ii), or to state the dimension of the normal connected component containing \(K\). The first formulation is already supported by the author’s body argument; it is not a new result claimed by this report.
# Other checked reasoning and limits

The Mayer–Vietoris step in Proposition 2.4 was checked at the level of the exact sequence: the two restrictions of the degree-\(k\) class vanish, so it lifts to a degree-\((k-1)\) class on the overlap; the induction hypothesis kills that lift on a finite cover, and naturality kills the original class after shrinking. Holomorphic convexity of the pulled-back compact set is supplied by Proposition 1.6(i). The bump construction and the cited approximation theorems were read but not independently reproved.

The relative comparison Theorem 3.9 preserves the properness/constructibility alternatives and uses dimension induction after reduction to regular closed strata. The terminal local calculation is the cohomology of a punctured complex normal slice, with nonzero degrees \(0\) and \(2c-1\), matched to purity. No contrary calculation was established in that inspected reduction.

For Theorem 5.1, Step 5, p. 28, the factorization is printed with finite target map to \(Y_U\), while the following inverse image of \(K\subset U\) and Steinness argument require a finite map to \(X_U=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O(U)\). A precise consistent reading is to factor the composite \(W\to X_U\) by Zariski’s Main Theorem, which is legitimate because it is separated and quasi-finite of finite presentation. Then \(\overline W^{\mathrm{an}}\) is finite over the Stein space \(U\), the inverse image of \(K\) is compact and holomorphically convex, and the finite cover restricted to \(W\) still refines the original cover of \(Y_U\). This restores the stated uses of Propositions 4.3 and 2.4 at this point. This forced base-label clarification is recorded without a separate severity count; the report does not claim the literal label already provides the required compactification. Unlike Problem 1, no additional counterexample to a separately specified gluing output is being counted here.

Theorem 5.6 requires an affine scheme and empty real fixed locus. Passing to the function field in Theorem 5.7 uses distinguished affine opens and a filtered colimit, not an assertion that arbitrary nonaffine schemes have the same bound. In Proposition 6.3 the descending argument is also consistent at the endpoint: to descend to the symbol of degree \(n+1\), injectivity uses vanishing in degree \(n+1\) over \(F(\sqrt{-1})\), which follows from the bound \(\le n\). The split quadratic algebra and characteristic-two cases do not furnish a counterexample. Theorems 6.4–6.5 retain compactness and their local-ring hypotheses; no extension to every noncompact real-analytic space is inferred.

The limited exact-title, publisher and arXiv checks did not identify a specific erratum addressing the two findings. This is not an exhaustive absence claim. No newer or journal text was substituted for the pinned manuscript.

 \widetilde p:T'	o\widetilde S,\qquad p'=
u\circ\widetilde p.\] This is finite and surjective. Because \(
u\) is finite and the disjoint neighborhoods \(\Omega_i\) contain the whole fiber over \(s\), choose \(\Omega\) around \(s\) with \(
u^{-1}(\Omega)\subset igcup_i\Omega_i\). The subsets \(\widetilde p^{-1}(\Omega_i\cap
u^{-1}\Omega)\) are disjoint and cover \((p')^{-1}\Omega\). On the \(i\)th such subset, the projection \(T'	o T_i\) pulls back the already vanishing class. Theorem 5.1, pp. 26–28, compares cohomology only after taking the directed limit over Stein neighborhoods of \(K\). analysis: Theorem 0.4 on p. 3 asserts \(\operatorname{cd}\mathcal M(K)=n\) for a connected Stein compact subset \(K\) of a normal Stein space \(S\) of dimension \(n\). Under the conventions of §1.1, take \[S=\{\ast\}\amalg\mathbb C,\qquad K=\{\ast\},\qquad n=1.\] This is a normal, second-countable Stein space of dimension one. The compact set \(K\) is nonempty and connected, and is Stein because it is itself an open Stein component and hence has a basis of Stein neighborhoods. But restriction to that open component gives \[\mathcal O(K)=\mathcal M(K)=\mathbb C,\qquad \operatorname{cd}\mathcal M(K)=0,\] since \(\mathbb C\) is algebraically closed and has trivial absolute Galois group. Title: Initial scientific review of
Poisson spacing statistics for lattice points on circles
# Identity, version and coverage

The assigned paper is Pär Kurlberg and Stephen Lester, Poisson spacing statistics for lattice points on circles, M25-0064, Inventiones mathematicae 240 (2025), 537–585, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01324-1 [paper]. The reviewed original is the acquired publisher version of record, 49 PDF pages. Throughout this report, printed page \(p\) corresponds to one-based PDF page \(p-536\). Its SHA-256 is

All 3,029 lines of its native text extraction, including references, were read continuously. Nineteen original PDF pages were inspected visually, including every page containing a figure (PDF pages 3 and 24), the theorem statements, both findings, and the concluding proof. This is claim-focused reading and checking, not an independent reconstruction of every external analytic theorem.

The acquired arXiv:2112.08522v1 source, dated 15 December 2021, is an older author version [arxiv]. Targeted static inspection of its `merge-arxiv.tex`, lines 1071–1096 and 2167–2200, corroborated the complex-exponent wording and the reindexing expression. It was not treated as the source of the journal PDF, compiled, or executed. All 12 manifest-listed files had actual byte counts and SHA-256 values checked. No separate essential supplement is missing. The absence of an identified paper-specific program is not a defect.
# Claims, hypotheses and dependencies

Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 assert exponential nearest-neighbor and joint consecutive-gap laws along a density-one subsequence of the sums of two squares. Density is relative to \(\mathcal S\), and the number \(\ell\) of consecutive gaps is fixed. The angle variable is modulo \(\pi/2\), \(N=r(n)=r_2(n)/4\), and the gap scale is \(N/(\pi/2)\). The result does not assert Poisson behavior along every sequence of radii or uniformly for growing \(\ell\).

The proof freezes a square factor and a fixed integer \(n_0\), writing \(n=n_0n_1\) with \(n_1\) square free, odd, composed of split primes, and coprime to \(n_0\). If \(M\) is its number of prime factors, then \(N=2^M r(n_0)\). Theorem 3.1 matches the first two arithmetic moments to those of a random subset-sum model, with error \[O_{f,r,n_0,A}\bigl((\log\log x)^{-1}+M^{-10}\bigr),
 \qquad 1\le M\le A\log\log x.\] The constants do not assert uniformity for arbitrary growing \(n_0\). The final slowly growing cutoff and diagonalization are needed for that reason.

Proposition 4.1 supplies the arithmetic average. Propositions 5.1 and 5.8 remove its arithmetic factor after averaging frequencies. Section 6 identifies the resulting expressions with the random model. The rank estimates in Section 7 give Poisson correlations; Section 8 combines variance, density estimates, sieving, and diagonalization to obtain spacings. Problem 1 lies on the second-moment branch of this chain. Problem 2 concerns the final density-one selection itself.
# Problem 1: adding a relation does not restrict a stratum
## Source and suspect step

In Section 5.1, printed p. 559 (PDF 23), the paper defines \[V_S^\star=\ker M_S\setminus
       \bigcup_{S_1\supsetneq S}\ker M_{S_1}.\] For a nonempty stratum, \(S\) is the exact set of complementary subset classes whose associated forms vanish. Thus forms outside \(S\) are required to be nonzero; this is stronger than merely belonging to \(\ker M_S\).

In the proof of Proposition 5.8, equation (5.36), p. 569 (PDF 33), the sum over each \(V_S^\star\) still has the constraint \(k_r=0\). On p. 570 (PDF 34), first paragraph and first unnumbered display, the paper sets \[\mu=[\{0,\ldots,r-1\}],\qquad
 \widetilde S=S\cup\{\mu\},\qquad
 \widetilde V^\star=V_{\widetilde S}^\star\] and replaces the constrained sum by a sum over \(\widetilde V^\star\), while retaining the outer sum over all original \(V^\star\in\mathcal V_{2r}\). This replacement is false. If \(\mu\notin S\), the original stratum requires \(k_\mu\ne0\), so its intersection with \(k_r=k_\mu=0\) is empty. Adding \(\mu\) to the label instead creates a different stratum, which can be nonempty and already appears elsewhere in the outer sum.
## Complete countercheck with all parameters

Take correlation order \(r=2\) and \(n_0=1\). These are allowed by Proposition 5.8; \(M\) can be any positive integer in its stated range, and \(N=2^M\). The frequency space for the second moment is \(\mathbb R^3\), with \(k_0=k_4=0\), and \(\mu=[\{0,1\}]\) gives \(k_\mu=k_2\).

Represent each class of subsets of \(\{0,1,2,3\}\) by the member not containing 3. Write \(S_0=\{[\varnothing]\}\) and \(S_1=\{[\varnothing],\mu\}\). The generic stratum \(V_{S_0}^\star\) is nonempty but contains no point with \(k_2=0\). In contrast, \[U:=V_{S_1}^\star
   =\{(a,0,b): a b
e0,\ a
e b,\ a
e-b\}.\] Indeed, the four increments are \((a,-a,b,-b)\); under these exclusions the only zero-sum subset classes are \([\varnothing]\) and \(\mu\). The point \((1,0,3)\) supplies an explicit witness. Thus both \(S_0\) and \(S_1\) label nonempty original strata, but the printed mapping sends both to \(S_1\): \[S_0\cup\{\mu\}=S_1,\qquad S_1\cup\{\mu\}=S_1.\] The original constrained sum counts each point of \(U\) once; the replacement counts it twice. This argument uses precisely the primed/stratified definition, not a different convention for ordinary kernels.

The independent exact-arithmetic check in `verification/0064/evidence/reviewer_checks.json` enumerated all 18 nonempty strata for this arrangement. It confirmed the two preimages, the zero classes of \((1,0,3)\), and all cube-intersection bounds \(\alpha_V\le 2^{3-\dim V}\) in this finite case. In the box \(|a|,|b|\le4\), \(U\) has 48 integer points; each has the stated duplicate. These finite calculations corroborate the general set-theoretic argument.
## The duplicate is of main-term size
## Counterevidence, repair and impact

The exact Fourier expansion before this reindexing is not contradicted, and the statement of Proposition 5.8 is not disproved. A possible informal reading is that the sum is intended to range only over distinct nonempty resulting strata, with duplicates removed. That convention is absent from the displayed outer index and would be a substantive correction to the equality as written.

The affected second moment feeds Theorem 3.1(3.4), then the variance estimate (8.1), and hence the density-one Poisson conclusion. The demonstrated invalid core derivation therefore supports Major under the specified calibration, even though the local repair is short. No counterexample to Theorems 1.1 or 1.2 is claimed.
# Problem 2: the final multiplicative-function invocation fails its hypothesis
## Location and exact failed condition

On p. 543 (PDF 7), Section 2 explicitly defines the multiplicity-counting function \[\Omega_1(n)=\sum_{\substack{p^a\Vert n\\p\equiv1\pmod4}} a.\] On p. 583 (PDF 47), after (8.2), the proof quotes the bound \[\sum_{n\le x}h(n)\ll\frac{x}{\log x}
       \prod_{p\le x}\left(1+\frac{h(p)}p\right)
 \quad\text{for multiplicative }0\le h(n)\le d(n),
                                                               \tag{R2}\] where \(d(n)\) is the divisor count. It then applies that bound with \(h(n)=b(n)2^{\Omega_1(n)}\), where \(b\) is the indicator of sums of two squares.

This chosen \(h\) is nonnegative and multiplicative, but it does not satisfy the displayed upper hypothesis. For \(n=25=5^2\), one has \[b(25)=1,\quad \Omega_1(25)=2,\quad h(25)=4,\quad d(25)=3.\] All conventions agree with the source: \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), multiplicity is two, and 25 is a sum of two squares. More generally, \(h(5^a)=2^a>a+1=d(5^a)\) for every \(a\ge2\), with unbounded ratio. Thus even inserting a fixed implied constant in the pointwise domination would not fix it. The saved exact check records exponents \(1\le a\le8\); the general inequality is elementary.

This is a counterexample to the invocation’s required hypothesis, not to the desired summatory estimate or density conclusion. If a stronger external multiplicative-function theorem is intended, its broader hypotheses and verification must replace the restricted form actually stated. Reinterpreting \(\Omega_1\) as a distinct-prime count silently changes the explicit definition in Section 2.
## Verified repair preserving the density estimate

Define instead \[\omega_1(n)=\#\{p\mid n:p\equiv1\pmod4\},\qquad
 h_*(n)=b(n)2^{\omega_1(n)}.\] This is nonnegative and multiplicative. At split prime powers its value is 2, at powers of 2 it is 1, and at inert prime powers it is 0 or 1. Consequently \(h_*(p^a)\le a+1\) at every prime power, and \(h_*(n)\le d(n)\) for all \(n\). Its values at primes are the same as those of the function used in the source. Applying (R2), with the same split-prime reciprocal-sum estimate as in the paper, gives \[\sum_{n\le x}h_*(n)\ll x.\]

The error occurs in the final proof that the restricted set of radii has full density, an essential part of both main statements. It is a demonstrated invalid application on that core chain, so it is rated Major under the requested standard. The ease of the verified repair and survival of the claimed bound are explicit counterevidence against any stronger conclusion about the paper’s validity.
# Additional checked reasoning and unresolved scope

The first-moment calculation, the cube-intersection bound, the rank-counting strategy, and the distinctions between all tuples and distinct tuples were read and checked at their main logical transitions. For fixed \(r\), generic binary tuples contain the required coordinate patterns with probability tending to one. For a nontrivial low-rank relation, the positive-pair argument in Proposition 7.5 gives \(o(N^{d+1})\) configurations, rather than only \(o(N^r)\). This stronger scale is what is needed against a contribution of size \(N^{-d}\). No new counterexample to that estimate was established.

For Lemma 7.8, distinct points may have the same subset \(J\) but different deterministic shifts. This does not alone invalidate the argument: for fixed \(n_0\) the finitely many distinct shifts have positive minimum separation on the torus, while a compactly supported test requires all points in a contributing tuple to be within \(O_{r,f}(N^{-1})\) of one another. Hence such omitted tuples contribute zero for sufficiently large \(N\). The fixed-\(n_0\) qualification is essential.

For the extension from a countable test family to all compactly supported smooth functions, positivity and cutoff functions can supply the needed local mass bound. A bound on an expected functional alone should not be interpreted as an automatic uniform bound on every deterministic radius. These details were considered in interpreting the standard diagonalization, without asserting a separate disproved theorem.
## Complex powers in Proposition 4.4: scope clarification

Equation (4.17), p. 550 (PDF 14), prints a restriction on \(|\operatorname{Re}z|\), whereas the coefficient bound just above it, (4.14), assumes \(|z|\le A\). The proof of (4.17) is omitted as similar to that of (4.16); the later application in Lemma 5.6 uses fixed real integer powers \(u\).

An interpretation uniform over arbitrary imaginary \(z\) would be false. Fix \(k=1\), let \(y=2^J\) be sufficiently large, and put \(z=iT\). The truncated Dirichlet sum is a polynomial in \(z\) of degree \(J\) with nonzero leading coefficient \[\frac{(-1)^J}{2^J J!}.\] The unique degree-\(J\) contribution at norms at most \(2^J\) is the ideal \((1+i)^J\); any replacement of a norm-2 prime ideal by another prime ideal increases the norm. On the other hand, the paper’s \(L(1,4)>0\) implies \(|L(1,4)^{iT}|=1\). Thus the polynomial grows unboundedly with \(|T|\), although \(\operatorname{Re}z=0\) satisfies the printed range. A uniform error depending only on \(y,k,A,n_0\) cannot hold in this interpretation.

The prior bounded-\(z\) context and unspecified parameter dependence for this second formula leave an alternative reading. Accordingly this is retained as an unrated scope clarification, not added to the supported issue count. Explicitly retaining bounded \(|z|\) (in particular the fixed real powers actually used) avoids this countercheck. This review does not claim to have verified a larger growing-complex-\(z\) range.

The cited estimates for Hecke \(L\)-functions, coefficient extraction, and the external theorem transferring correlations to gaps were not independently reproved from their primary proofs. All extracted source text was read, but this limitation precludes a whole-paper correctness certificate. The plots were visually checked as illustrations; their underlying data were not independently regenerated. They are not needed for the two analytic findings.
# Disposition, versions and remaining work

The acquired journal PDF and the targeted older TeX passages both contain the reindexing under discussion. This is not evidence of an unpublished correction or author adoption. A limited exact-title/DOI correction search and inspection of the publisher and arXiv records did not identify a specific erratum. The arXiv record exposes v1; no later author file was substituted for the frozen input. The search does not exclude all later commentary or corrections.
Item | Judgment | Repair verification | Adoption / remaining work
F01 | Major | Correct restriction (R1), no duplicates, and summed error verified | Not requested; independent acceptance and full downstream audit pending
F02 | Major | \(h_*\) satisfies the stated bound’s hypotheses and restores density estimate | Not requested; independent acceptance pending
(4.17) | Unrated scope | Unbounded-imaginary uniform reading ruled out; fixed-real use distinguished | Clarify intended constant dependence and range

The supported conclusion concerns two invalid derivations in the printed proof. The proposed local corrections preserve the intended statements on the dependencies checked here. No new empirical experiment is required to validate either calculation. External analytic dependencies, a complete independent proof of the final spacing transfer, and independent scientific acceptance remain outside the completed initial review.

report: Abstract: No substantive issue was established in the inspected scope. The review followed the reduction to free directions or canonical scaling, checked the local parity arguments, and examined the dependence on prior classification results. A short argument below makes explicit why a translated pair cannot leave the specified parity hyperplane in the no-free-direction branch. Exact finite checks corroborate this argument and several case tables. They do not reproduce the external classification of 110244 types or certify every cited geometric result. The reviewed object is arXiv:1906.05193v6, not an independently acquired journal version. Scientific acceptance remains pending.
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review of
Voronoi conjecture for five-dimensional parallelohedra
# Identity and actual coverage

The assigned paper is Alexey Garber, Voronoi conjecture for five-dimensional parallelohedra, M25-0065. The acquired original is arXiv:1906.05193v6, dated 31 January 2025, 41 pages [paper]. Page numbers in this report are the manuscript’s printed pages, equal to one-based PDF pages. The associated journal record is Inventiones mathematicae 240 (2025), 587–631, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01325-0 [journal]. That record does not establish byte or mathematical equivalence with the reviewed manuscript.

All 1978 lines returned by the native PDF text extraction were read, including references and Appendix A. Twenty-two original PDF pages were inspected as images: \[1,4,7,11,12,14,15,16,17,19,20,23,24,26,28,29,30,31,32,33,34,35.\] This includes all five figure pages, 4, 7, 26, 30 and 33. Static inspection of the supplied v6 TeX covered selected passages concerning translated pairs, Lemma 7.2, coherence and external dependencies; the whole TeX file was not independently read or compiled. All ten manifest-listed files were hash checked.

The reading was systematic and claim focused. It was not a formal verification or a complete independent reconstruction of every geometric subcase and cited theorem. The absence of executable author code in this source package is not a defect.
# Definitions, hypotheses and dependence

The central claim, Theorem 4.1 on p. 12, concerns every convex five-dimensional polytope that tiles \(\mathbb R^5\) by translations: it is an affine image of a lattice Dirichlet–Voronoi polytope. The argument uses the associated face-to-face lattice tiling. A dual cell \(\mathcal D(F)\) is the set of centers of tiles incident to a face \(F\); its dimension label initially records the codimension of \(F\). One must not assume the general dimension conjecture for dual cells, which the manuscript explicitly leaves open beyond the known cases.

The parity group \(\Lambda/2\Lambda\) and the midpoint-class group \((\tfrac12\Lambda)/\Lambda\) are distinct quotients, each isomorphic to \(\mathbb F_2^5\). In the computations below, doubling identifies a midpoint class with the sum of its endpoint parity classes. Equality of such classes alone does not imply equality of real segment vectors. Lemmas 3.3–3.5, pp. 11–12, provide the geometric translation and facet-vector restrictions needed to make that passage. Lemma 3.6 excludes the parity sum of a facet triangle; Lemma 3.7 turns a covered four-dimensional midpoint hyperplane into a free direction. Its proof uses the nontrivial intersection of a two-dimensional triangle-midpoint subspace with that hyperplane and the fact that a midpoint representing a facet cannot instead represent a non-facet contact face.

The checked dependence chain has the following structure. Lemma 5.3 obtains the Voronoi conclusion from a free direction, using Theorem 5.2, the four-dimensional theorem, the cited combinatorially Voronoi result, and Lemma 2.15. Definition 5.1 requires equivalence of tilings together with a compatible lattice isomorphism; equality of the face lattices of the individual polytopes alone is insufficient. Theorem 5.2 constructs this stronger equivalence by separating the tiling into lattice layers and taking the segment long enough that only neighboring layers meet. The proof was checked at the level of the stated layer properties and the induced face-incidence correspondence; the external projection and saturation results were not reproved.

A cubical dual 3-cell produces a free direction by Lemma 6.1. In the remaining prismatic case, Lemmas 7.1–7.2 reduce the primal face to a triangle and its three edge-dual cells to prisms over tetrahedra or pyramids over triangular prisms. Their number of prismatic cells is \(3,2,1,\) or \(0\), giving the exhaustive four branches of Sections 8–11. Section 8 uses a disconnected red Venkov graph; Sections 9–10 reconstruct an impossible centrally symmetric tetrahedral contact face unless a free direction already exists. Section 11 extends gain across parallelograms and proves coherence or a free direction. The local cycle relations and their use in constructing canonical scaling were followed; the full external local Ordine argument remains a cited input.
# A checked expansion of the translation argument

The assertions on p. 17, Case 7.1.2 and Subcase 7.1.2.00, and the introductory paragraph of Case 7.1.3 on p. 18 restrict translated endpoints to the parity plane \(x_4=0\). A lattice translation does not preserve that plane merely because the original segment is parallel to it. The following verification supplies the relevant alternative: an escaped translated pair itself forces a free direction, so it is excluded in the branch where no free direction exists. This is a proof clarification, not a counterexample to the lemma.

Let \(e_1,\ldots,e_5\) be a basis of \(\mathbb F_2^5\), and put \[F=\langle e_1,e_2,e_5\rangle,\qquad
 P_0=\{0,e_1,e_2,e_5,e_1+e_5,e_2+e_5\},\qquad A=e_3.\] These are the six prism classes and one additional class in the normalization on p. 16. Write \[M(S)=\{s+t:s,t\in S\}.\] Then \(M(P_0)=F\). Suppose a translated pair, lying in the same edge-dual cell, has midpoint class encoded by \(A+v\), where \(v\in P_0\), but has endpoints outside \(x_4=0\). Their classes have the form \[R=e_4+u,\qquad S=e_3+e_4+u+v,\qquad u\in F.\] Choose \(i\in\{1,2\}\) with \(v_i=0\); this is possible for every \(v\in P_0\). Define the nonzero linear functional \[L(w)=w_i+u_iw_4,\qquad K=\ker(L|_F).\] The four-element subspace \(K\) is contained in \(P_0\): the only elements of \(F\) omitted from \(P_0\) have both first two coordinates equal to one. Moreover, \[L(A)=L(R)=L(S)=0.\] The four distinct cosets \[K,\quad A+K,\quad R+K,\quad S+K\] therefore fill \(\ker L\), a four-dimensional subspace. Each lies in \(M(P_0\cup\{A,R,S\})\): the first lies in \(M(P_0)\) and the others arise by pairing \(A,R,S\) with points of \(K\). Thus the midpoint classes of this edge-dual cell contain \(\ker L\). Lemma 3.7 gives a free direction. Consequently the endpoint restriction is justified when the proof continues under the complementary no-free-direction assumption.

This argument also explains why merely checking the printed parity table would be inadequate. The reviewer-written computation exhausts all \(6\cdot8=48\) choices of \((v,u)\) and finds a hyperplane witness in every case. The analytic argument establishes the reason for those witnesses; the finite run corroborates the encoding.
# Finite checks and their mathematical limits

The exact \(\mathbb F_2^5\) checks in `parity_checks.py` use integer XOR, with \(e_i\) represented by bit \(i-1\). No floating-point tolerance or author program is involved. All assertions passed. In addition to the 48 cases above, the checks established:
- the six midpoint completions in Case 7.1.1, and the sixteen midpoint classes of a cube plus an outside parity class;
- the partition in Lemma 9.1, p. 24: ten occupied classes, fourteen distinct triangle-forbidden classes, and exactly eight remaining classes in \(x_3=x_4=1\);
- the corresponding counts in Lemma 10.1, pp. 27–28: nine occupied classes, twelve distinct forbidden classes, and eleven remaining classes;

- all fifteen nonzero first-four-coordinate classes required for Lemma 8.3, p. 23, using actual diagonal midpoint classes of the indicated parallelograms; the argument only requires one non-facet class in each pair differing in the fifth coordinate;
- the fourteen midpoint classes and the two missing classes in Case 10.1.00110;

- the completion used in Lemma 11.3, p. 33. Of 32 parity/orientation possibilities for the second prism, 28 would make a known facet midpoint class represent a non-facet contact face. In each of the four remaining possibilities, its two non-facet classes are precisely the two missing midpoint classes.

The final check explicitly uses the known facet status of the six apex edges. Counting the union of arbitrary sets of parity classes without that geometric restriction would not justify the conclusion. Conversely, these finite tests neither construct arbitrary configurations as real tilings nor prove the external classification. The geometric incidence arguments and their hypotheses were read separately from the computations.
# Outcome, external inputs and remaining work

No supported substantive defect was found in the inspected arguments. No claim of whole-paper correctness, independent scientific acceptance, or author adoption follows. The version record consulted on 26 October 2026 still listed v6 as the latest arXiv revision. A limited title/erratum search did not identify a specific correction; it was not an exhaustive search.

Section 12, pp. 34–35, explicitly identifies the 110244-type classification and the verification of a combinatorial condition on those types as inputs to Lemma 5.3. The primary classification record reports multiple implementations and a mass-formula check [classification]; that is the authors’ evidence, not a reproduction performed here. The statement of the combinatorially Voronoi dependency was cross-checked against its author record [combinatorial]. The present review did not run that classification, PORTA, or any author code. The discussion on p. 34 removes a particular Ordine computation in dimension five; it does not remove the separate classification dependency.

Appendix A was read as an explanation of the author’s assessment of Engel’s approach. The cited historical works were not independently audited, and no adverse finding about those works is adopted here. A further acceptance review could independently inspect the external classification certificates and the local-to-global canonical-scaling inputs. Such work concerns proof assurance, not a currently demonstrated error or a required new empirical experiment.

Abstract: Proposition 2.3 is false with the stated arbitrary dependence of the second input on the scale variable. A family of real, uniformly bounded, spatially compact inputs satisfies every hypothesis, while the bilinear output has an \(L^2\) norm growing at least as the square root of the number of selected scales and both right-hand norms remain bounded. The appendix’s treatment of products with zero output frequency does not justify the required square-function bound. The proposition is used directly in the core heat-flux proof, so this is one Major finding. No counterexample to a solution of the coupled convection equations or to the final physical upper bound is claimed. A replacement argument has not been verified.
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review of
Sharp bounds on the Nusselt number in Rayleigh–Bénard convection and a bilinear estimate by Coifman–Meyer
# Identity, version and coverage

The assigned article is Sagun Chanillo and Andrea Malchiodi, Sharp bounds on the Nusselt number in Rayleigh–Bénard convection and a bilinear estimate by Coifman–Meyer, M25-0066, Inventiones mathematicae 240 (2025), 633–660, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01326-z [paper]. The reviewed original is the acquired publisher version of record, 28 pages. Printed page \(p\) corresponds to one-based PDF page \(p-632\).

All 1561 lines of the native PDF extraction were read continuously, including the full appendix and references. Twenty-one original PDF pages were visually inspected: \[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,12,13,15,16,17,18,20,21,23,24,25,26.\] This includes every figure page, 8, 13, 18 and 24. The exact hypotheses of Proposition 2.3, its application on p. 648, and the appendix on pp. 656–658 were checked in the page images. Selected passages of the supplied arXiv:2001.01662v4 TeX were inspected statically as related author-source evidence, without treating that earlier manuscript as the journal source. All nine manifest-listed files were hash checked.

The principal audit followed the normalization, boundary conditions, Green-kernel reduction, localization, bilinear estimate and final dependency chain. It did not independently reconstruct all cited PDE regularity results, all asymptotic derivative calculations, or every Fourier correction formula. No author code was executed, and no fluid simulation was performed.
# Scope of the claimed theorem and the analytic input

The physical setting is the infinite-Prandtl-number Boussinesq system with horizontal periodicity, no-slip velocity at the two plates, and fixed temperatures one and zero. The rescaled height is \(H=\mathrm{Ra}^{1/3}\), with \(H\gg1\). Theorem 1.2, p. 635, claims a uniform bound on the rescaled Nusselt number; Corollary 1.3 converts it to \(\mathrm{Nu}_{\mathrm{phys}}\le C_0\mathrm{Ra}^{1/3}\). The theorem does not cover arbitrary finite Prandtl number or supply the numerical constant discussed in the introduction.

The temperature fluctuation \(\theta\) has zero horizontal mean and \(|\theta|\le1\) under the maximum-principle bound. The vertical velocity is obtained from a clamped fourth-order equation. The proof separates the forcing into lower and upper half-strips, represents the lower part by a half-space kernel, and corrects its upper boundary values by a biharmonic function. The near-bottom correlation bound is the essential point: Proposition 3.2 invokes Proposition 2.3 to eliminate dependence on the number of scales between the boundary and the height \(H\).

The finding below concerns the independently stated functional inequality. Its hypotheses require no heat equation, no harmonicity of the second input in the scale variable, and no common underlying function across scales. Those distinctions are decisive.
# Problem 1: the scale-dependent bilinear estimate is false
## Source claim and location

Equation reference: claimed. Proposition 2.3, printed p. 640 (PDF p. 8), uses \[P_t(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{t}{(t^2+|x|^2)^{3/2}},
 \qquad Q_tf=\psi_t*f=t\nabla(P_t*f).\] For \(\rho\in\mathrm{BMO}(\mathbb R^2)\), bounded compactly supported \(F\) on \(\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\), and measurable \(|m|\le1\), it asserts \[
 \left\|\int_0^\infty Q_t\rho\cdot Q_tF^t\,m(t)\,\frac{dt}{t}\right\|_2
 \le C\|\rho\|_{\mathrm{BMO}}\,\|N(Q_tF^t)\|_2 ,\] with \(C\) independent of all inputs. Here \(NF(x)=\sup_{|z-x|<t}|F(z,t)|\), as defined in (17), p. 639. The paragraph below Remark 2.4 explicitly identifies arbitrary \(t\)-dependence as the extension beyond the original setup.
## Construction and verification of every hypothesis

Equation reference: inputs. Use angular frequencies \(q_j=5^j\), \(1\le j\le N\), and disjoint intervals \[I_j=[q_j^{-1},2q_j^{-1}].\] Let \[E=[0,2\pi]^2,\qquad Q=[-2\pi,4\pi]^2,\qquad
 g_N(x_1)=\sum_{j=1}^N\cos(q_jx_1),\qquad
 r_N(x_1)=\operatorname{sgn}g_N(x_1).\] The value at zeros may be set to zero. Define \[
 \rho_N(x)=\mathbf1_Q(x)r_N(x_1),\qquad
 F_N(x,t)=
 \begin{cases}
 \mathbf1_Q(x)\cos(q_jx_1),&t\in I_j,\\
 0,&t\notin\bigcup_{j=1}^NI_j,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad m(t)=1.\] These are real measurable functions. Both inputs have absolute value at most one, and \(\|\rho_N\|_{\mathrm{BMO}}\le2\). In fact \(\rho_N\) is spatially compact as well, although the proposition does not require that. The support of \(F_N\) lies in \[Q\times[5^{-N},2/5],\] a compact subset of the open upper half-space for each finite \(N\). Its approach to \(t=0\) as \(N\) grows violates no stated hypothesis: the claimed constant is independent of \(F\).

Equation reference: kernel, maximal. The vector kernel is \[
 \psi_t(y)=-\frac{3}{2\pi}\frac{t^2y}{(t^2+|y|^2)^{5/2}},
 \qquad \|\psi_t\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb R^2)}=1.\] Consequently \(|Q_tF_N^t|\le1\). It vanishes for \(t\) outside the selected intervals. Write \(a=(\pi,\pi)\). When \(|x-a|\) is larger than a fixed radius containing \(Q\), \(t\le2/5\) and \(|z-x|<t\) imply \[|Q_tF_N^t(z)|\le C_Q|x-a|^{-4}.\] Indeed, the integration is over the fixed square \(Q\) and [kernel] (#kernel) is bounded by a constant times \(t^2|z-y|^{-4}\) there. Combining this with the bound one on a fixed disk gives \[
 \|N(Q_tF_N^t)\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}\le C_Q,\] uniformly in \(N\). Thus the entire right-hand side of [claimed] (#claimed) is bounded by \(2CC_Q\).
## Exact lower bound for the left-hand side

Equation reference: mean. Let \(\mathbb E\) denote normalized integration over \(E\) for functions periodic in \(x_1\) and constant in \(x_2\). Temporarily omit both spatial cutoffs and write \(\overline B_N\) for the corresponding bilinear expression with first input \(r_N\) and second input \(\cos(q_jx_1)\) on \(I_j\). For the paper’s Poisson normalization, \[P_t*\cos(q_jx_1)=e^{-tq_j}\cos(q_jx_1).\] Periodic integration, or the skew-adjointness of horizontal differentiation, therefore gives \[\mathbb E\big[Q_tr_N\cdot Q_t\cos(q_jx_1)\big]
 =(tq_j)^2e^{-2tq_j}\mathbb E[r_N\cos(q_jx_1)].\] Hence \[
 \mathbb E\overline B_N
 =A\,\mathbb E[r_Ng_N]
 =A\,\mathbb E|g_N|,
 \qquad
 A=\int_1^2u e^{-2u}\,du=\frac{3e^{-2}-5e^{-4}}4>0.\] The use of the full vector kernel causes no cancellation here: the periodic comparison functions depend only on \(x_1\), so their second derivative components vanish.

Equation reference: L1. There are no non-pairing signed four-term relations among the frequencies \(5^j\). To see this, a largest frequency occurring once cannot be balanced by three smaller ones; two occurrences with the same sign cannot be balanced by two smaller ones; and three occurrences cannot be balanced by one smaller frequency. The remaining possibilities are opposite pairs. Orthogonality thus yields the exact moments \[\mathbb Eg_N^2=\frac N2,\qquad
 \mathbb Eg_N^4=\frac{3N^2}{4}-\frac{3N}{8}\le\frac{3N^2}{4}.\] Hölder interpolation between \(L^1,L^2,L^4\) gives \[
 \mathbb E|g_N|\ge
 \frac{(\mathbb Eg_N^2)^{3/2}}{(\mathbb Eg_N^4)^{1/2}}
 \ge\sqrt{\frac N6}.\]

This is an analytic counterexample family, not an extrapolation from numerical samples. Independent exact Fourier-moment checks for thirteen values of \(N\), up to \(64\), corroborate the moment calculation. The output records \(A=0.0786069138165418\). Small-grid quadrature is explicitly labeled illustrative.
## Where the appendix’s extension fails

The appendix distinguishes the separated input \(F(x,t)=f(x)m(t)\) in (55), p. 657, from the more general input it wants to admit. The support argument preceding (59) is valid for a product whose output spectrum stays away from zero. That does not cover the interaction of opposite frequencies in the present family.

The multiplier \(\widehat\psi_3\) on p. 657 is allowed to be supported in a ball or a proper annulus. On p. 658, immediately after (59), the first factor is bounded by a constant times \(\|h\|_2\): \[\left(\int_0^\infty\|\psi_{3,t}*h\|_2^2\,\frac{dt}{t}\right)^{1/2}
 \lesssim\|h\|_2.\] If the multiplier is one near zero, then \(\psi_{3,t}*h\to h\) in \(L^2\) as \(t\downarrow0\), and this integral diverges for every nonzero \(h\in L^2\). An annular multiplier avoids that divergence but cannot preserve a product’s nonzero constant-frequency contribution. The general reduction must control this resonant case by additional information; merely retaining the support inclusion does not do so. The counterexample proves that the proposed final extension cannot hold.
## Counterevidence, impact and repair boundary

Several possible restrictions do not remove the example. Both inputs are bounded by one, \(\rho_N\) is also compactly supported, all scale integrals are over a finite interval bounded away from zero for each \(N\), and the non-tangential maximal function has a uniform integrable tail. The proposition assumes no smoothness. If desired, for each fixed \(N\) one can smooth the spatial and temporal cutoffs and the bounded sign function, retaining uniform bounds and passing to the displayed finite-scale integrals; the obstruction is not a singularity of the inputs.

The kernel used in the application on p. 648 is \(t\nabla P_{t/2}\). The same argument works for it: the positive scale coefficient becomes \(\int_1^2u e^{-u}\,du=2e^{-1}-3e^{-2}\), and all cutoff and maximal-function constants remain uniform. Changing this normalization cannot repair the estimate.

The core dependency is explicit: \[\begin{aligned}
 &\text{Proposition 2.3}\ \longrightarrow\
 \text{(37), Proposition 3.2}\\
 &\hspace{2em}\longrightarrow\
 \text{Proposition 3.3}\ \longrightarrow\
 \text{Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.3}.
\end{aligned}\] Equation (37), p. 648, is the direct invocation. Proposition 3.3, p. 649, is then used in the proof of Theorem 1.2 on p. 655. The later biharmonic boundary correction does not supply a substitute for the failed bilinear bound. This establishes a Major defect in a core derivation.

The family is not asserted to solve the coupled temperature–velocity evolution. It therefore does not disprove the long-time physical Nusselt bound. Restricting the scale dependence to a fixed underlying function would remove the freedom used here, but the temperature slices in the application do not have that form. No corrected proposition sufficient for the application has been proved in this review. A repair needs a different analytic estimate or additional PDE structure that controls the accumulating interactions.
# Overall assessment and other checked material

The Poisson normalization, kernel homogeneity, half-space/strip separation, spatial localization and role of the no-slip boundary correction were followed. The local integrability near the Green-kernel singularity and the distinction between the critical cubic far-field term and its integrable remainder were checked at the level used in Lemma 3.1. These parts do not resolve Problem 1.

The report does not elevate isolated sign, coefficient or typesetting discrepancies in the displayed Fourier formulas into additional findings. In particular, zero horizontal mean suppresses the zero mode in the actual forcing, and a global sign convention does not repair or negate an absolute-value bilinear counterexample. An independent rederivation of every boundary-correction coefficient is outside the completed scope.

The arXiv record [arxiv] reports that an early version was withdrawn over a scaling argument and a previous Proposition 3.1. The current journal article acknowledges a problem pointed out in a previous version. This historical attribution is retained; it is not evidence that the present counterexample was previously identified or corrected. The acquired v4 source contains the same scale-dependent proposition and the corresponding appendix argument at the inspected passages. The publisher and arXiv records and a limited correction search did not identify a later correction of this claim at consultation; that search was not exhaustive.
Item | Disposition
Issue judgment | One Major: Proposition 2.3 fails for bounded compact inputs.
Supported impact | A required estimate in the core proof is invalid; the physical theorem itself is not refuted here.
Repair verification | No replacement sufficient for the application verified.
Adoption | Not requested; no author contact.
Remaining work | Independent assessment of the counterexample and a valid replacement heat-flux argument.
Scientific decision | Pending; human reviews remain empty.
