=(2^{-10}u\mathbb Z)\times(2^{-10}v\mathbb Z)\times(2^{-10}w\mathbb Z)\] and the rectangle family \(\mathcal R_{u\times v\times w}\) centered on this fixed lattice. For \(R=R_{u_0\times u_0w_0\times w_0}(\omega_0)\), Section 3.4 defines \[\psi_R(a,b,c)=
\left(\frac{a-a_0}{u_0},
\frac{b-b_0-c_0(a-a_0)}{u_0w_0},
\frac{c-c_0}{w_0}\right).\] Lemma 3.3 on printed p. 1068 (PDF p. 24) correctly states a phase-space isometry, then claims that \(\psi_R^{-1}\) bijects the fixed rectangle families. Its last proof paragraph explicitly claims the corresponding bijection of \(\mathcal C\) lattices. The shear term prevents that last assertion.
All scales strictly negative dyadic powers; all required triples admissible; outer and inner centers on specified grids and in Omega.
analysis:
Take outer scales and center \[u_0=w_0=\tfrac12,\quad v_0=u_0w_0=\tfrac14,\quad
\omega_0=(0,0,2^{-11}).\] These are admissible dyadic scales. The center belongs to \(\mathcal C_{1/2\times1/4\times1/2}\), since its third coordinate is one third-coordinate lattice step. Take inner scales \(u=v=w=1/2\), also admissible, and center \[q=(2^{-11},0,0)\in\mathcal C_{1/2\times1/2\times1/2}.\] Direct inversion gives \[\psi_R^{-1}(q)=(2^{-12},2^{-23},2^{-11}).\] The claimed target scale is \[uu_0\times vu_0w_0\times ww_0=\tfrac14\times\tfrac18\times\tfrac14.\] Its lattice steps are \(2^{-12},2^{-13},2^{-12}\). Dividing the three coordinates of \(\psi_R^{-1}(q)\) by these steps gives \[(1,\;2^{-10},\;2).\] The middle ratio is not an integer. Thus the image center is not in the target lattice. All centers used here lie in \(\Omega\); no endpoint convention concerning \(2^{-\mathbb N}\) is involved because every chosen scale is a strictly negative power of two. An affine map takes the center of a centrally symmetric rectangle to its center, which is unique. Consequently the claimed bijection of the fixed rectangle families fails as well.

The rescaling assertion supplies the transport of canonical covering and concentration counts from \(X\cap R\) to \(\psi_R(X\cap R)\). This transport is used when Lemma 3.11, printed pp. 1078–1079 (PDF pp. 34–35), applies the weak-uniformity estimate of Lemma 3.7 to the rescaled set. Lemma 3.11 then proves closure of the limiting branching functions under the blow-up \(f\mapsto f_Q\). The regular-rectangle blow-up in the proof of Theorem 1.4, printed pp. 1088–1090, uses this rescaling framework. The false fixed-grid assertion therefore lies in a derivation tied to the core incidence method. Supported severity: Major.

The weaker cover comparison proved above explains the repair boundary. Lemma 3.11 needs comparisons up to multiplicative factors; an additional universal factor contributes only \(O(1/|\log\delta|)\) to normalized logarithms. This establishes a local replacement and does not exhibit a failure of the limiting exponents. Full propagation through uniform extraction and every subsequent use has not been certified here. Repairability is separate from the severity of the invalid printed transport argument.
result:
Direct substitution in [eq:phase] (#eq:phase) does prove \[d_{u\times v\times w}(\psi_R(\omega_1)\to\psi_R(\omega_2))
=d_{uu_0\times vu_0w_0\times ww_0}(\omega_1\to\omega_2).\] For the middle term, the numerator becomes \((b_2-b_1-c_1(a_2-a_1))/(u_0w_0)\). The other two terms rescale directly. Thus the failure concerns the chosen grids, not the geometric isometry.

A valid local replacement compares the two covers up to a uniform constant. To see this, pull the canonical inner cover back by \(\psi_R^{-1}\) and compare it to the canonical target cover. Both cover space by rectangles of the same target shape and volume, and both have uniformly bounded overlap. The isometry transfers the inner overlap bound. The approximate triangle and symmetry bounds in Lemma 3.1 imply that any rectangle of either family meeting a fixed rectangle of the other lies inside a fixed enlargement of it. Integrating overlap multiplicity over that enlargement bounds the number of meeting rectangles by a universal constant: volume of the enlargement divided by the common rectangle volume, multiplied by the overlap bound. The argument works in both directions.

Hence for any finite bounded set \(Y\), the numbers of rectangles meeting \(Y\) in these two covers are comparable by uniform constants. The maximal point counts in a rectangle are likewise comparable, because each rectangle is covered by a bounded number from the other family. This proves the cover comparison needed in place of an exact lattice bijection.

Impact: Invalid fixed-grid transport in the rescaling derivation used by Lemma3.11 and limiting branching-function blow-ups; local bounded-factor repair verified, principal incidence exponents not refuted.

report: Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Formal initial review: M25-0072
Orbit equivalences of pseudo-Anosov flows
# Scope and outcome

The inspected object is the 52-page author manuscript and its bound author-source tree. The DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01332-1 identifies the associated journal publication; it does not establish that this manuscript equals the 2025 version of record. None of the findings below is attributed to an uninspected journal text.

The manuscript develops rigidity of Anosov-like actions on bifoliated planes, applies it to orbit equivalence of pseudo-Anosov flows, and studies the necessity of transitivity. The full extracted text was read, with direct image inspection of 26 selected source pages. The review concentrates on quantified hypotheses, the continuity extension of the conjugacy, the construction in Section 7, and the proposed axioms in Section 8. Long geometric arguments and external classification results have not all been independently reproved.

Initial outcome: Major. Two demonstrated defects occur in arguments tied to central claims: a convergence criterion used in extending the conjugacy, and the stated obstruction to reversing the auxiliary flow in the sharpness construction. Two additional defects affect examples or a proposed definition. This is a judgment about the inspected derivations, not a counterexample to the main classification theorem and not scientific acceptance or rejection of the paper.
No. | Confirmed issue in v1 | Severity / scope
1 | Corollary 5.8 includes common-leaf sequences for which its criterion fails; Remark 5.22 widens subsequent use | Major: extension proof
2 | A proper attractor without any repeller cannot supply the asserted obstruction on the closed auxiliary manifold | Major: Theorem 7.1 proof
3 | The affine example contains translations violating Axiom (A1) | Minor: example and remark
4 | Conditions (2) and (3) of Definition 8.1 are mutually incompatible | Minor: proposed definition

There is no issue quota. Clerical formulas and unresolved external dependencies were not promoted to confirmed scientific defects. No acquired computational implementation required execution; that absence is not a defect.
# Conventions

Page numbers are one-based PDF pages, equal to the printed page numbers. Total linkedness has the inclusive definition of Definition 4.1 (p. 22): both transverse-leaf intersections exist. In particular, two points on the same leaf are totally linked. A non-corner fixed point is abbreviated NC. Only reviewer-written checking code was run.
# Problem 1. The common-leaf case is missing from the convergence argument

Locations. Definition 4.1, p. 22; Observation 5.6, pp. 31–32; Corollary 5.8, p. 33; Lemma 5.21 and Remark 5.22, p. 38; Corollary 5.24, p. 39; Proposition 5.44, p. 46, and completion of Theorem 1.4, p. 47.

Claim and quantifiers. Corollary 5.8 takes a pairwise totally linked sequence \(z_n\to z\in P\cup\partial P\) and a positive NC fixed point \(w\) of \(g\), totally linked with every \(z_n\). It asserts that condition \((*)\) holds if and only if \(z\in\mathcal F^-(w)\). Its pertinent first clause says that for every sufficiently large \(i\), there exists \(K\) such that for every \(k>K\), \[g^{-k}z_i \text{ is not totally linked with }z_j
                    \quad\text{for every }j\leq i.\] The second clause requires eventual total linking with the tail of the sequence. Observation 5.6 explicitly assumes \(z_n\notin\mathcal F^-(w)\) and \(z\ne w\). The corollary omits these restrictions.

Counterexample with all displayed corollary hypotheses. Fix such a \(w\). Choose an embedded compact arc \(\iota:[1,2]\to\mathcal F^-(w)\setminus\{w\}\), and set \[z=\iota(1),\qquad z_n=\iota(1+1/n).\] These points are distinct, converge in \(P\), and their limit differs from \(w\). They, and \(w\), are pairwise totally linked: whenever \(a,b\) lie on the same negative leaf, \(\mathcal F^+(a)\) meets that leaf at \(a\), and \(\mathcal F^+(b)\) meets it at \(b\). Since \(g\) fixes \(w\) and preserves the foliations, it preserves \(\mathcal F^-(w)\). Thus \[g^{-k}z_i\mathrel{\mathrm{TL}}z_j
                    \quad\text{for every }i,j,k .\] The first clause of \((*)\) fails for every possible threshold. Nevertheless \(z\in\mathcal F^-(w)\). This disproves the corollary as stated without a constant sequence, an ideal boundary point, or a singular limit.

Core dependency and counterevidence. Lemma 5.21 invokes Observation 5.6 to produce \((*)\), transports it through total-linkedness preservation, and invokes Corollary 5.8 to confine accumulation points to a negative leaf. For distinct NC fixed points, the common-leaf obstruction is restricted: the earlier fixed-point structure prevents a different NC fixed point on the same invariant leaf. This is material counterevidence against treating the example as a refutation of that restricted lemma.

However, Remark 5.22 explicitly removes the fixed-point restriction and asserts that the same proof works in any subsequently enlarged domain of \(H\). After extension to intersections of NC leaves (Corollary 5.24), sequences on \(\mathcal F^-(w)\) are allowed, while the displayed invocation of Observation 5.6 cannot apply. Proposition 5.44 uses Lemma 5.21 in the enlarged domain to control accumulation before proving continuity. The claimed uniform extension of this proof thus has an unhandled case on the route to Theorem 1.4. This demonstrated dependency, rather than the false sentence alone, motivates Major.

Repair and limits. An off-leaf restriction removes the explicit counterexample from Corollary 5.8. It does not by itself prove Remark 5.22. A repair must handle common-leaf, constant, and mixed subsequences at each extension stage, or replace the criterion. Order preservation on a leaf may help, but the required global argument has not been completed here. No failure of the ultimate conjugacy or classification statement has been proved.
# Problem 2. The auxiliary flow cannot have the stated attractor–repeller asymmetry
Locations. Theorem 7.1 and its first proof paragraph, p. 49; the construction of \(N'\) on that page; the final contradiction, p. 50. Compare Proposition 2.38, p. 17.

Suspect step. The proof requires the auxiliary Anosov flow \(\phi_{N'}\) to have no direction-reversing self-orbit equivalence. It says this is ensured by giving it an attracting set but no repelling set. The construction removes a neighborhood of one periodic orbit from each of two closed manifolds and glues their torus boundaries. Thus \(N'\) is closed, rather than an open plug with an unglued escape boundary. The final paragraph uses the asserted impossibility of direction reversal to conclude non-equivalence of the two flows.

Compact-flow obstruction. For a complete continuous flow on a compact space, a proper attractor with a proper forward-trapping neighborhood \(U\) has a nonempty dual repeller. Choose \(U\) proper and a trapping time \(T>0\), so that its basin is \[B(A)=\bigcup_{n\geq0}\phi_{-nT}(U),\] an increasing union of open sets. If \(B(A)\) were the whole compact manifold, a finite subcover and the largest index would give \(\phi_{-NT}(U)=N'\). A time map is a bijection, so this forces \(U=N'\), a contradiction. Therefore \[R=N'\setminus B(A)\ne\varnothing .\] This is the compact invariant dual repeller: the complement of a trapping neighborhood is backward trapping, and its maximal backward-time invariant subset yields \(R\). The usual attractor/repeller meanings for closed Anosov flows thus rule out the stated premise.

This also agrees with the manuscript’s use of an attractor and a repeller for a nontransitive closed Anosov flow in Proposition 2.38. The argument does not forbid an attracting-only plug; it applies to the closed \(N'\) constructed here.

Impact. The premise offered to rule out a reversing self-equivalence is impossible in the stated setting. The later claim that this impossibility has already been established lacks the supplied justification. That obstruction is needed for the asserted non-orbit-equivalence in Theorem 7.1, which supplies the advertised necessity of transitivity. This is a Major defect of that proof. The classification theorem does not depend on this sharpness construction, so the finding is not propagated backwards to every main result.

Counterevidence and repair limits. Having both an attractor and a repeller does not imply that a reversing equivalence exists. A flow may forbid reversal through a verified asymmetry of basic pieces, their topology, or incidence. Neither Theorem 7.1 itself nor the existence of nonreversible Anosov flows is disproved. A correction needs an actual choice of auxiliary flow or plugs, and a proof that any self-orbit equivalence preserves enough structure to rule out reversal. Deleting the impossible premise alone leaves the step unproved. A substitute construction and its compatibility with the later gluings have not been independently established here.
# Problem 3. The displayed affine action violates its defining axiom
Locations. Axiom (A1), p. 5; Example 1, p. 6; related faithfulness and normal-form assertions in Remark 2.8, p. 7.

The example generates an action on the trivially bifoliated plane using \[\tau_1(x,y)=(x+1,y),\quad \tau_2(x,y)=(x,y+1),\quad
 D_\lambda(x,y)=(\lambda x,\lambda^{-1}y).\] Axiom (A1) requires that a nonidentity element preserving a leaf have a fixed point on that leaf, with the stipulated transverse hyperbolic behavior. But \(\tau_1\) preserves every horizontal leaf and has no fixed point anywhere. The vertical translation similarly violates the axiom. This holds for every choice of the dilation parameters. The first-coordinate action is also not faithful, since \(\tau_2\) acts trivially there.

Counterevidence. Generic or algebraically independent dilation parameters cannot remove the explicit translations from the generated group. The phrase about algebraic independence of a list containing \(1\) may be a clerical error, but correcting it does not resolve the axiom violation. The defect is therefore not merely typographical.

Impact and severity. This is not an Anosov-like action under the paper’s definition, so it cannot establish the asserted example or associated failure of rigidity in the trivial-plane class. The principal rigidity theorem excludes trivial planes. No dependency of its proof on this invalid example has been established. The severity is Minor.

Validated substitute with a different generating set. A coupled translation repairs the example’s main role. This is a reviewer-supplied replacement, not a construction attributed to the authors. Choose \(a,b,c>1\) algebraically independent over \(\mathbb Q\). For the pair \((a,b)\), use \[\tau(x,y)=(x+1,y+1),\quad D_a,\quad D_b .\] Every group element has the form \[(x,y)\longmapsto
 \left(qx+p(a,b),\ q^{-1}y+p(a^{-1},b^{-1})\right),
 \quad q=a^m b^n,\quad p\in\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1},s^{\pm1}].                 \tag{R}\] Composition gives the semidirect product of the additive Laurent-polynomial group by \(\mathbb Z^2\). Algebraic independence makes this normal form faithful. We have \(q=1\) only for \(m=n=0\); a nonzero \(p\) is nonzero at both parameter pairs in (R). Every nontrivial pure translation therefore moves both leaf spaces and preserves no leaf. When \(q\ne1\), the element has a unique fixed point, expands in one coordinate and contracts in the other; each preserved leaf contains that point. This proves (A1).

Density. The translation subgroup contains \(v_k=(a^k,a^{-k})\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\). If their additive subgroup had proper closure in \(\mathbb R^2\), the elementary structure of closed subgroups would give a nonzero character \((u,v)\) with \(w_k=u a^k+v a^{-k}\in\mathbb Z\) for all \(k\). But \[w_{k+1}+w_{k-1}=(a+a^{-1})w_k .\] Since \(a+a^{-1}\) is irrational, all \(w_k\) must vanish. The equations at \(k=0,1\) force \(u=v=0\), a contradiction. Thus the translation subgroup is dense.
# Completion of the substitute in Problem 3

Dense translations give dense point orbits, proving (A2). The conjugates \(T_vD_aT_v^{-1}\) fix the dense translation vectors \(v\), proving (A3). There are no singular leaves, making (A4) vacuous; both leaf spaces are Hausdorff, making (A5) vacuous. Every horizontal leaf intersects every vertical leaf, so there are no perfect fits or forbidden totally ideal quadrilaterals, establishing (A6).

The pairs \((a,b)\) and \((a,c)\) realize the same abstract semidirect-product group. In either action a nonidentity element has a fixed point precisely when its dilation exponent pair \((m,n)\) is nonzero. Their fixed-element sets agree. Any equivariant homeomorphism must commute with the common \(\tau,D_a\), hence with every \(v_k\)-translation, and by density with all translations. It is therefore \(h(z)=z+d\). Commutation with \(D_a\) forces \(d=0\). The identity cannot conjugate \(D_b\) to \(D_c\), since \(b\ne c\). This proves failure of equivariant rigidity for the repaired trivial-plane actions.

Reviewer-written SymPy checks verify affine composition, the fixed point of \(T_vD_aT_v^{-1}\), and the recurrence. These symbolic identities supplement the analytic arguments; they do not prove density by finite sampling.
# Problem 4. The proposed everywhere-hyperbolic class is empty as written
Locations. Definition 8.1, p. 50, conditions (2) and (3); motivation and Remark 8.2, pp. 50–51.

Condition (2) considers any pairwise distinct \(g_n\) with \(g_nx\to y\), any foliated box \(V\) about \(y\), and any compact sets \(K^\pm\subset\mathcal F^\pm(x)\). It requires eventually exactly one image \(g_nK^\pm\) to be contained in \(V\). Choose the permitted sets \(K^+=K^-=\{x\}\). Then both images equal \(\{g_nx\}\subset V\) eventually. Neither alternative holds. Thus (2) prohibits every convergent distinct-element orbit sequence.

This is not vacuous. Condition (3) supplies \(g_n^+\) such that \(g_n^+x\to y^+\) and every compact subset of \(\mathcal F^+(x)\) is eventually mapped into every neighborhood of \(y^+\). Take \(u\ne x\) on this leaf and the compact set \(\{x,u\}\). Both \(g_n^+x\) and \(g_n^+u\) converge to \(y^+\). The sequence must contain infinitely many distinct elements: otherwise some \(h\) recurs infinitely, forcing \(h(x)=h(u)=y^+\), contrary to injectivity. A pairwise distinct subsequence still has a convergent orbit at \(x\), contradicting (2) with the singleton compact sets. Conditions (2) and (3) are therefore incompatible.

Impact, counterevidence, repair. This invalidates the proposed class as a source of examples; it does not invalidate (A1)–(A6) or the main theorem. Severity is Minor. A necessary repair excludes degenerate compact sets and specifies suitable nondegenerate leaf segments. Whether a revised condition captures the intended dynamics remains unproved. That restriction is a necessary change, not a verified characterization theorem.
# Positive checks, exclusions, and coverage

The NC fixed-point assignment is consistent conditional on the earlier fixed-point and common-spectrum results: stabilizers at one NC point commute after the appropriate leaf-preserving passage, and their images must share their unique NC fixed point. Final equivariance follows on the dense fixed-point set from conjugation of stabilizers and extends if continuity is established. These checks isolate Problem 1 to the continuity justification.

Section 6 distinguishes the dynamics on the ideal boundary, rather than relying only on a count of four fixed points. Free elements with four boundary fixed points therefore do not alone refute that argument. Signs are assigned to the relevant orbits of scalloped trees, not independently to arbitrary lozenges.

The 52 pages of extracted text were read in full. Direct image inspection covered \[1\!-\!7,\ 17,18,\ 22,\ 25,26,\ 31,32,33,\ 35,36,\ 38,39,\
45,46,47,48,49,50,51.\] These checks verified formulas, quantifiers, relevant diagrams, and precise statement/proof locations. Other pages were read as extracted text and are not recorded as image-inspected.

Sections 3–4 | Boundary and linking arguments read; shared-endpoint qualifications checked against later use. Long lozenge-chain geometry not fully reconstructed.

Sections 6–8 | Boundary reduction read; compact-flow obstruction and incompatible quantifiers proved. DA/gluing theorem not independently reconstructed.

A scope issue in Lemma 4.3 at a chain corner was compared with Proposition 4.8, whose proof separates shared ideal endpoints before the relevant application; no core defect was inferred. External pseudo-Anosov extensions near Proposition 2.38 remain a verification limitation, not a confirmed error.

The classification theorem does not depend on this sharpness construction, so the finding is not propagated backwards to every main result.

Counterevidence and repair limits. Having both an attractor and a repeller does not imply that a reversing equivalence exists. A flow may forbid reversal through a verified asymmetry of basic pieces, their topology, or incidence. Neither Theorem 7.1 itself nor the existence of nonreversible Anosov flows is disproved. A correction needs an actual choice of auxiliary flow or plugs, and a proof that any self-orbit equivalence preserves enough structure to rule out reversal. Deleting the impossible premise alone leaves the step unproved. A substitute construction and its compatibility with the later gluings have not been independently established here.
result: Impact: The stated reason required for the final contradiction proving non-orbit-equivalence fails; classification result does not depend backwards on sharpness.

paragraphs: Construct and verify a different asymmetry, including compatibility with subsequent gluings.

problems.title: The displayed affine action violates its defining axiom
problems.source_location: A1 p5 Example1 p6 Remark2.8 p7
claim: Independent coordinate translations and diagonal dilations give Anosov-like affine actions
analysis: Locations. Axiom (A1), p. 5; Example 1, p. 6; related faithfulness and normal-form assertions in Remark 2.8, p. 7.

The example generates an action on the trivially bifoliated plane using \[\tau_1(x,y)=(x+1,y),\quad \tau_2(x,y)=(x,y+1),\quad
 D_\lambda(x,y)=(\lambda x,\lambda^{-1}y).\] Axiom (A1) requires that a nonidentity element preserving a leaf have a fixed point on that leaf, with the stipulated transverse hyperbolic behavior. But \(\tau_1\) preserves every horizontal leaf and has no fixed point anywhere. The vertical translation similarly violates the axiom. This holds for every choice of the dilation parameters. The first-coordinate action is also not faithful, since \(\tau_2\) acts trivially there.

Counterevidence. Generic or algebraically independent dilation parameters cannot remove the explicit translations from the generated group. The phrase about algebraic independence of a list containing \(1\) may be a clerical error, but correcting it does not resolve the axiom violation. The defect is therefore not merely typographical.

Impact and severity. This is not an Anosov-like action under the paper’s definition, so it cannot establish the asserted example or associated failure of rigidity in the trivial-plane class. The principal rigidity theorem excludes trivial planes. No dependency of its proof on this invalid example has been established. The severity is Minor.

Validated substitute with a different generating set. A coupled translation repairs the example’s main role. This is a reviewer-supplied replacement, not a construction attributed to the authors. Choose \(a,b,c>1\) algebraically independent over \(\mathbb Q\). For the pair \((a,b)\), use \[\tau(x,y)=(x+1,y+1),\quad D_a,\quad D_b .\] Every group element has the form \[(x,y)\longmapsto
 \left(qx+p(a,b),\ q^{-1}y+p(a^{-1},b^{-1})\right),
 \quad q=a^m b^n,\quad p\in\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1},s^{\pm1}].                 \tag{R}\] Composition gives the semidirect product of the additive Laurent-polynomial group by \(\mathbb Z^2\). Algebraic independence makes this normal form faithful. We have \(q=1\) only for \(m=n=0\); a nonzero \(p\) is nonzero at both parameter pairs in (R). Every nontrivial pure translation therefore moves both leaf spaces and preserves no leaf. When \(q\ne1\), the element has a unique fixed point, expands in one coordinate and contracts in the other; each preserved leaf contains that point. This proves (A1).

Density. The translation subgroup contains \(v_k=(a^k,a^{-k})\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\). If their additive subgroup had proper closure in \(\mathbb R^2\), the elementary structure of closed subgroups would give a nonzero character \((u,v)\) with \(w_k=u a^k+v a^{-k}\in\mathbb Z\) for all \(k\). But \[w_{k+1}+w_{k-1}=(a+a^{-1})w_k .\] Since \(a+a^{-1}\) is irrational, all \(w_k\) must vanish. The equations at \(k=0,1\) force \(u=v=0\), a contradiction. Thus the translation subgroup is dense.
result: Impact: Example and trivial-plane nonrigidity illustration fail; main rigidity theorem excludes trivial planes.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use a coupled translation (1,1), faithful Laurent-polynomial module, and independent dilations. Report verifies all axioms, density, equal spectra and nonconjugacy.

problems.title: The proposed everywhere-hyperbolic class is empty as written
problems.source_location: Definition8.1 conditions2-3 p50 Remark8.2 p51
claim: Everywhere-hyperbolic dynamics proposed as a useful class
analysis: Locations. Definition 8.1, p. 50, conditions (2) and (3); motivation and Remark 8.2, pp. 50–51.

Condition (2) considers any pairwise distinct \(g_n\) with \(g_nx\to y\), any foliated box \(V\) about \(y\), and any compact sets \(K^\pm\subset\mathcal F^\pm(x)\). It requires eventually exactly one image \(g_nK^\pm\) to be contained in \(V\). Choose the permitted sets \(K^+=K^-=\{x\}\). Then both images equal \(\{g_nx\}\subset V\) eventually. Neither alternative holds. Thus (2) prohibits every convergent distinct-element orbit sequence.

This is not vacuous. Condition (3) supplies \(g_n^+\) such that \(g_n^+x\to y^+\) and every compact subset of \(\mathcal F^+(x)\) is eventually mapped into every neighborhood of \(y^+\). Take \(u\ne x\) on this leaf and the compact set \(\{x,u\}\). Both \(g_n^+x\) and \(g_n^+u\) converge to \(y^+\). The sequence must contain infinitely many distinct elements: otherwise some \(h\) recurs infinitely, forcing \(h(x)=h(u)=y^+\), contrary to injectivity. A pairwise distinct subsequence still has a convergent orbit at \(x\), contradicting (2) with the singleton compact sets. Conditions (2) and (3) are therefore incompatible.

Impact, counterevidence, repair. This invalidates the proposed class as a source of examples; it does not invalidate (A1)–(A6) or the main theorem. Severity is Minor. A necessary repair excludes degenerate compact sets and specifies suitable nondegenerate leaf segments. Whether a revised condition captures the intended dynamics remains unproved. That restriction is a necessary change, not a verified characterization theorem.
result: Impact: Proposed class is empty as written.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Exclude degenerate compact sets and specify nondegenerate segments; adequacy of the revised definition remains unproved.

report: Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Formal initial review: M25-0073
Minimal hypersurfaces for generic metrics in dimension 8
# Scope and outcome
The primary object is the acquired 111-page publisher PDF. DOI:

All 111 pages were read as extracted text. Thirty-one selected source pages were additionally inspected as actual page images. The associated source tree is the older author version arXiv:2205.01047v1 (2 May 2022); it is not the exact source of the journal PDF. All four findings below are established directly against the publisher PDF.

Initial outcome: Major. The global compactness assertion used to obtain the countable covering in Theorem 3.4 lacks uniform positivity of the ambient metrics. A sequence satisfying the stated bounds and remaining outside the excluded higher-multiplicity neighborhood disproves that assertion. This is a demonstrated failure of a step in the principal proof, even though a countable ellipticity exhaustion repairs this step. It does not disprove Theorem 1.2. Three further statements have local scope defects for which no damage to the main conclusion was established.
No. | Confirmed issue in the bound version | Severity / scope
1 | The global bounded family need not have a Riemannian limit | Major: countable-cover argument
2 | A two-sided lift does not determine a unique ambient double cover | Minor: preliminary assertion
3 | The first Dirichlet eigenspace need not be simple on disconnected \(\mathcal U\) | Minor: Lemma D.3(i)
4 | Lemma D.6 includes nonsingular invertible examples for which its set is empty | Minor: auxiliary lemma scope

The main theorem concerns connected embedded locally stable minimal hypersurfaces (LSMHs), with its specified area and singular-set conditions. It is not read here as a claim about arbitrary stationary varifolds. The paper’s one-sided index convention is the index of the two-sided cover. These conventions were retained.

Page convention. Locations below give printed journal pages; the one-based PDF page is the printed number minus 1192. Verification describes only the stated check, not all arguments of the paper. No issue quota was imposed.
# Problem 1. The exhaustion used for global compactness omits uniform positivity

Location and exact claim. Section 9.1, p. 1253 (PDF 61), defines \[\mathcal M^{k,\alpha}(M;\Lambda,I)=
 \{(g,\Sigma)\in\mathcal M^{k,\alpha}(M):
 \|g\|_{C^{k,\alpha}}\leq\Lambda,\ 
 \mathcal H^7_g(\Sigma)\leq\Lambda,\ \operatorname{index}(\Sigma,g)\leq I\}.\] The set \(\mathcal M_{>1}^{k,\alpha}(M;\Lambda,I,\delta)\) consists of pairs in these bounds within \(\delta\), in the metric-factor \(C^{k-1,\alpha}\) distance plus varifold \(\mathbf F\) distance, of \((\widetilde g,m|\widetilde\Sigma|)\) for some bounded pair and integer \(m\geq2\). The text asserts that its complement in the bounded family is compact for every \(\delta>0\), citing Theorem G.1, and uses this for the finite cover (76). Theorem G.1, p. 1299 (PDF 107), assumes \(g_i\to g\) in \(C^3\) with \(g\) a Riemannian metric.

Counterexample: all geometric assumptions. Let \(M=S^1_{2\pi}\times T^7\), where \(T^7=\mathbb R^7/\mathbb Z^7\) has its flat unit-volume metric \(h\). Set \[\rho(s)=2-\cos s,\qquad
 g_* = ds^2+\rho(s)^2h,\qquad \Sigma=\{0\}\times T^7 .\] This is a smooth closed eight-manifold and a smooth connected embedded two-sided hypersurface. Since \[\rho(0)=1,\quad \rho'(0)=0,\quad \rho''(0)=1,
 \qquad A_\Sigma=0,\qquad
 \operatorname{Ric}_{g_*}(\partial_s,\partial_s)|_\Sigma=-7,\] \(\Sigma\) is minimal, has area one, and its Jacobi operator is \(L=\Delta_h-7\). In the article’s convention, \[Q(u,u)=\int_{T^7}(|\nabla u|^2+7u^2)\,d\mu_h>0
 \quad (u\ne0).\] It is strictly stable, hence locally stable and of index zero. Its singular set is empty; all stated measure conditions are satisfied.

Put \(H(t)=e^{-1/t}\) for \(t>0\), \(H(t)=0\) for \(t\leq0\), and \[\chi(s)=\frac{H(\cos s-\tfrac12)}
 {H(\cos s-\tfrac12)+H(\tfrac34-\cos s)},\quad
 q_\varepsilon=\chi+\varepsilon(1-\chi),\quad
 g_\varepsilon=q_\varepsilon g_*,\quad 0<\varepsilon\leq1.\] The denominator is positive everywhere. The smooth function \(\chi\) equals one on a fixed neighborhood of \(0\) and zero near \(\pi\). Every \(g_\varepsilon\) is positive definite and equals \(g_*\) near \(\Sigma\). Thus \(\Sigma\) retains area one and index zero.

For any fixed background tensor norm the \(C^{k,\alpha}\) norms of \(g_\varepsilon\) are uniformly bounded, because \(g_\varepsilon=\chi g_*+\varepsilon(1-\chi)g_*\). Choose an integer \(\Lambda\) above this bound and above one, and \(I=1\). All pairs satisfy the displayed bounds. Yet \(g_{1/j}\to\chi g_*\) in \(C^\infty\), and the limit vanishes on an open set. No subsequence has a Riemannian limit, even in \(C^0\).
# Problem 1 continued: the excluded set and the repair

The higher-multiplicity exclusion does not remove the sequence. There is a single \(\delta_0>0\) for which all pairs \((g_\varepsilon,\Sigma)\), \(0<\varepsilon\leq1\), avoid \(\mathcal M_{>1}^{k,\alpha}(M;\Lambda,I,\delta_0)\). Otherwise choose \(\varepsilon_j\), metrics \(\widetilde g_j\), connected LSMHs \(\widetilde\Sigma_j\), and integers \(m_j\geq2\) with \[\|\widetilde g_j-g_{\varepsilon_j}\|_{C^{k-1,\alpha}}
       +\mathbf F(m_j|\widetilde\Sigma_j|,|\Sigma|)\longrightarrow0.\] On a fixed tubular neighborhood \(U\) of \(\Sigma\) all \(g_{\varepsilon_j}=g_*\). Hence \(\widetilde g_j\to g_*\) in \(C^3\) on \(U\), while the integral stationary varifolds \(V_j=m_j|\widetilde\Sigma_j|\) converge there to the smooth multiplicity-one varifold \(|\Sigma|\).

Choose a regular point \(x\) of \(\Sigma\). The local geometric bounds are uniform. Local monotonicity gives upper semicontinuity of densities at points \(x_j\to x\). Such \(x_j\) can be chosen in the regular part of \(\widetilde\Sigma_j\), since the limit has positive mass in every ball about \(x\). Consequently, \[2\leq m_j=\Theta(V_j,x_j),\qquad
 \limsup_j\Theta(V_j,x_j)\leq\Theta(|\Sigma|,x)=1,\] a contradiction. Equivalently, Allard regularity at the smooth multiplicity-one limit excludes such integer multiplicities. Only the fixed positive geometry on \(U\) is used; degeneration outside \(U\) is irrelevant.

Take \(\delta=\delta_0/2\) (or \(1/J<\delta_0\)). The entire noncompact sequence belongs to the precise complement claimed to be compact. This verifies the exclusion condition rather than merely exhibiting arbitrary degenerating metrics.

Counterevidence. The local canonical neighborhoods in Definition 3.1, pp. 1211–1212, also impose closeness to a fixed positive metric. That condition supplies positivity and does not suffer from this example. Remark 3.1 uses the coarser \(C^{k-1,\alpha}\) topology; the example fails even there. No convention incorporating a bound on \(g^{-1}\) was found in the global definition or surrounding argument. Such a convention or an explicit bound is needed.

Impact. The invalid inference precedes (76), the countable cover (77), the refinement (78), and Theorem 3.4 on p. 1255. Theorem 3.4 and Theorem 3.3 yield Corollary 3.5 (pp. 1213–1214), used in Theorem 1.2 (pp. 1215–1219). This explicit dependency supports Major under the prescribed calibration. It is a defect in the supplied derivation, not a refutation of generic regularity.

Repair and limit. Fix a smooth reference metric \(g_{\rm ref}\) and add \(g\geq L^{-1}g_{\rm ref}\) to each bounded family, \(L\in\mathbb N\). The metric limit is now positive. Bounded \(C^{k,\alpha}\) norms give \(C^{k-1,\alpha}\) precompactness, and Theorem G.1 applies. A higher-multiplicity limit would put the original pairs in the excluded \(\delta\)-set eventually, so the complementary stratum is compact. Every positive metric on compact \(M\) satisfies such a bound for some integer \(L\); this extra countable index preserves countability. This repairs the identified compactness step. It is not a reproof of all later tree refinements or the main theorem.
# Problem 2. The ambient double cover is not unique

Location and claim. Section 2, p. 1200 (PDF 8), immediately before (1), asserts that for a connected one-sided \(\Sigma\subset M\) there is a unique ambient double cover \(\widehat M\to M\) whose inverse image of \(\Sigma\) is connected and two-sided.

Complete example. Take \[M=\mathbb{RP}^8\#(S^1\times S^7),\qquad
 \Sigma=\mathbb{RP}^7\subset\mathbb{RP}^8,\] with the connected sum performed in a ball disjoint from \(\Sigma\). Choose a metric round near this standard projective hyperplane and extend it smoothly across the connected sum. The hypersurface is closed, connected, smooth, embedded, one-sided and totally geodesic. It is minimal and locally stable: on sufficiently small intrinsic balls the Dirichlet gradient term dominates the bounded second-variation potential. At points off \(\Sigma\), small balls miss it. Its area is finite and its singular set empty, so it is an LSMH.

Van Kampen gives \(\pi_1(M)=\langle a,b\mid a^2=1\rangle=\mathbb Z_2*\mathbb Z\). The two characters \[\chi_0(a)=1,\quad\chi_0(b)=0,\qquad
 \chi_1(a)=1,\quad\chi_1(b)=1
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z_2\] are surjective and have distinct kernels. They define inequivalent connected double covers over \(M\). Both restrict nontrivially to \(\pi_1(\Sigma)=\langle a\rangle=\mathbb Z_2\). For either cover the full inverse image of \(\Sigma\) is its connected cover \(S^7\). The normal line bundle of \(\mathbb{RP}^7\) in \(\mathbb{RP}^8\) has nontrivial orientation character on \(a\), which is killed on \(S^7\); hence both lifts are two-sided. Pullback metrics preserve minimality and local stability. The lift of a \(b\)-loop distinguishes the ambient covers.

Counterevidence, impact and repair. The intrinsic normal orientation double cover of \(\Sigma\) is canonical. That does not make the ambient cover unique. Subsequent sign and lifted Jacobi arguments need an appropriate cover, not uniqueness among all ambient covers. No failure of those arguments was established. Specify a choice, for example the cover determined by the mod-two class dual to \(\Sigma\), or state the canonical property for the intrinsic cover alone. The example does not dispute existence. The impact is local; severity Minor.
# Problem 3. Simplicity of the first eigenspace needs connectedness

Location. Appendix D allows an arbitrary precompact open \(U\subset M\) with \(\partial U\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma)=\varnothing\) (p. 1273, PDF 81), and sets \(\mathcal U=U\cap\Sigma\). Lemma D.3(i), p. 1275 (PDF 83), asserts \(\dim E_1=1\) and a positive first eigenfunction, without requiring \(\mathcal U\) connected.

Use \((M,g_*,\Sigma)\) from Problem 1. Choose \(U\) as two disjoint small product neighborhoods whose intersections with \(T^7\) are isometric Euclidean balls \(B_r^{(1)},B_r^{(2)}\), and take the lemma’s potential \(h=0\). All stated conditions hold. The Dirichlet space and operator split as a direct sum. If \(\phi\) is the first Dirichlet eigenfunction of \(-\Delta+7\) on \(B_r\), then \((\phi,0)\) and \((0,\phi)\) are independent first eigenfunctions with the same lowest eigenvalue. Thus \(\dim E_1=2\).

Require \(\mathcal U\) connected for simplicity, or state the result componentwise. The main uses on connected \(\Sigma\) and near a single isolated conical singularity do not yield a demonstrated central failure from this example. The spectral decomposition itself survives. Severity Minor.
# Problem 4. Lemma D.6 must exclude the nonsingular invertible case

Location and quantifiers. Lemma D.6, p. 1283 (PDF 91), takes a two-sided LSMH and a finite group \(G\) acting freely on \(M\), preserving the geometric data. It claims that \[\mathcal F_G^{k,\alpha}=
 \{f\in C^{k,\alpha}(M)^G:
 L_{\Sigma,g}u=\nu(f)
 \text{ has no slower-growth $G$-invariant solution}\}\] contains an open dense subset of \(C^{k,\alpha}(M)^G\). There is no assumption \(\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma)\ne\varnothing\).

Counterexample and all hypotheses. Use the same smooth closed warped product \((M,g_*,\Sigma)\) from Problem 1 and \(G=\{\mathrm{id}\}\). This is a finite free action, exactly the trivial-group case also used on p. 1291. The hypersurface is two-sided and an LSMH. Its Jacobi operator is \(L=\Delta_h-7\) and is invertible. For every \(f\in C^{k,\alpha}(M)\) set \(b=\nu(f)|_\Sigma\). In Fourier variables on \(T^7\) the unique solution is \[\widehat u(m)=-\frac{\widehat b(m)}
                      {4\pi^2|m|^2+7},\qquad m\in\mathbb Z^7.\] Elliptic regularity gives the required local regularity and \(u\in L^2(\Sigma)\). Since \(\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma)=\varnothing\), Definition 2.5 on p. 1206 (PDF 14) explicitly says that every \(L^2\) function satisfies its slower-growth condition. Therefore every \(f\) has such a solution: \(\mathcal F_{\{\mathrm{id}\}}^{k,\alpha}=\varnothing\). It cannot contain an open dense subset of the nonempty function space.

Counterevidence and core use. The proof of D.6 constructs functions at singular points. Its intended application is Theorem 2.6, which explicitly assumes a nonempty singular set on p. 1206. That theorem’s proof on p. 1291 (PDF 99) invokes D.6 under the same assumptions. Thus the example invalidates the wider lemma but does not invalidate that application. Add \(\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma)\ne\varnothing\) to D.6. This check validates the necessity and compatibility of the restriction; it does not reconstruct every step of the restricted lemma. Severity Minor.
# Candidates not counted as scientific findings

The actual image of Lemma 7.1, p. 1228 (PDF 36), shows condition (b) ending after the word and without the expected density display. The older v1 source, lines 1370–1374, supplies density pinching and equality of the two singular densities. That older formula is version-specific explanatory evidence, not silently inserted into the journal text. Density assumptions are also visible in later journal statements. This typesetting omission is not counted under the assigned scientific scope.

There is a squared-norm convention mismatch between the integral in (32), p. 1222, and the norm scaling in (44), p. 1229. Taking the square root restores the scaling, and monotonicity is unchanged under the positive square root. Author v1 explicitly defines the square of \(J\) as the integral in its local growth lemma. This notational matter is not promoted to a further scientific defect. Unresolved questions about singular sheeting constants or external min–max applications remain coverage limits.
# Independent positive checks and proof-chain audit

Logarithmic cone mode (Appendix A). For the repeated-root case, write \(a=2\alpha'\), \(X=K^a\), \(L_0=\log K\), and \(z=\log r\). Evaluating the defining integral gives a positive factor \(r^a\) times \[Az^2+2Bz+C,\qquad
 A=\frac{(X-1)^3}{a},\quad
 B=\frac{3XL_0(X-1)^2}{a}-\frac{(X-1)^3}{a^2}.\] The independently expanded finite difference and determinant give \[B^2-AC=\frac{(X-1)^4}{a^2}
 \left(3XL_0^2-\frac{(X-1)^2}{a^2}\right).\] Both identities were checked symbolically against the defining integral, without running author code. With \(x=a\log K\), the sign condition is \(3x^2<4\sinh^2(x/2)\). It holds for \(|x|\geq6\): \(\sinh t/t\) increases for \(t>0\), and \(\sinh3>3+3^3/6>3\sqrt3\). Thus \(K\geq\max(3,e^{3/\sigma})\) suffices when \(|a|\geq2\sigma\). This verifies the uniform large-\(K\) step for the logarithmic mode, including negative \(a\), not every nonlinear growth estimate.

Critical compactness barrier (Appendix E). At \(n=7\), the two powers in the radial barrier are \(-3\) and \(-49/24\), exactly the roots of \[a(a-1)+\frac{145}{24}a+\frac{49}{8}=0.\] The error margin \(1/24-1/196-1/70=131/5880\) is positive. The independent script verifies these rational identities. The critical Hardy case was not dismissed by assuming all tangent cones strictly stable.

Lipschitz Sard argument. Lemma 8.5, pp. 1243–1244 (PDF 51–52), defines critical points by all limiting normalized secants landing in a proper subspace. Lipschitz boundedness makes the image of a sufficiently small relative ball lie in an arbitrarily thin slab around that subspace. Its \(n\)-volume is at most a constant times slab thickness times \(r^n\). The disjoint-ball covering and fivefold enlargement in the proof yield zero image measure as thickness tends to zero. This supports the measure step; it does not alone prove the geometric slice parametrization.

Main dependency and boundary cases. The definitions of slower growth, semi-nondegeneracy, canonical neighborhoods and the one-sided index were traced into Sections 3–4. The index induction uses the integer-valued singular capacity, finitely many maximizers, and a strict capacity drop. The four multiplicity/index alternatives on p. 1218 were read individually: a higher-multiplicity limit has index zero by G.1; regular strong nondegeneracy excludes certain limits; the singular stable case uses the strict capacity drop. The countable intersection over area and index bounds on p. 1219 is compatible with these quantifiers, conditional on the component theorems.

The positive-Jacobi-field argument on p. 1300 was checked using \(Q(gh,gh)=\int h^2|\nabla g|^2\) for a positive solution \(h\). The one-sided case uses the cover and the paper’s index convention. Problem 1 is an applicability defect for G.1, not a counterexample to G.1 under its own assumptions.

There is a single \(\delta_0>0\) for which all pairs \((g_\varepsilon,\Sigma)\), \(0<\varepsilon\leq1\), avoid \(\mathcal M_{>1}^{k,\alpha}(M;\Lambda,I,\delta_0)\). Otherwise choose \(\varepsilon_j\), metrics \(\widetilde g_j\), connected LSMHs \(\widetilde\Sigma_j\), and integers \(m_j\geq2\) with \[\|\widetilde g_j-g_{\varepsilon_j}\|_{C^{k-1,\alpha}}
       +\mathbf F(m_j|\widetilde\Sigma_j|,|\Sigma|)\longrightarrow0.\] On a fixed tubular neighborhood \(U\) of \(\Sigma\) all \(g_{\varepsilon_j}=g_*\). Hence \(\widetilde g_j\to g_*\) in \(C^3\) on \(U\), while the integral stationary varifolds \(V_j=m_j|\widetilde\Sigma_j|\) converge there to the smooth multiplicity-one varifold \(|\Sigma|\).

Choose a regular point \(x\) of \(\Sigma\). The local geometric bounds are uniform. Local monotonicity gives upper semicontinuity of densities at points \(x_j\to x\). Such \(x_j\) can be chosen in the regular part of \(\widetilde\Sigma_j\), since the limit has positive mass in every ball about \(x\). Consequently, \[2\leq m_j=\Theta(V_j,x_j),\qquad
 \limsup_j\Theta(V_j,x_j)\leq\Theta(|\Sigma|,x)=1,\] a contradiction. Equivalently, Allard regularity at the smooth multiplicity-one limit excludes such integer multiplicities. Only the fixed positive geometry on \(U\) is used; degeneration outside \(U\) is irrelevant.

Take \(\delta=\delta_0/2\) (or \(1/J<\delta_0\)). The entire noncompact sequence belongs to the precise complement claimed to be compact. This verifies the exclusion condition rather than merely exhibiting arbitrary degenerating metrics.

Counterevidence. The local canonical neighborhoods in Definition 3.1, pp. 1211–1212, also impose closeness to a fixed positive metric. That condition supplies positivity and does not suffer from this example. Remark 3.1 uses the coarser \(C^{k-1,\alpha}\) topology; the example fails even there. No convention incorporating a bound on \(g^{-1}\) was found in the global definition or surrounding argument. Such a convention or an explicit bound is needed.

Impact. The invalid inference precedes (76), the countable cover (77), the refinement (78), and Theorem 3.4 on p. 1255. Theorem 3.4 and Theorem 3.3 yield Corollary 3.5 (pp. 1213–1214), used in Theorem 1.2 (pp. 1215–1219). This explicit dependency supports Major under the prescribed calibration. It is a defect in the supplied derivation, not a refutation of generic regularity.

Repair and limit. Fix a smooth reference metric \(g_{\rm ref}\) and add \(g\geq L^{-1}g_{\rm ref}\) to each bounded family, \(L\in\mathbb N\). The metric limit is now positive. Bounded \(C^{k,\alpha}\) norms give \(C^{k-1,\alpha}\) precompactness, and Theorem G.1 applies. A higher-multiplicity limit would put the original pairs in the excluded \(\delta\)-set eventually, so the complementary stratum is compact. Every positive metric on compact \(M\) satisfies such a bound for some integer \(L\); this extra countable index preserves countability. This repairs the identified compactness step. It is not a reproof of all later tree refinements or the main theorem.

problems.title: The ambient double cover is not unique
problems.source_location: Printed1200/PDF8 before(1)
claim: Unique ambient double cover with connected two-sided lift.
analysis: Location and claim. Section 2, p. 1200 (PDF 8), immediately before (1), asserts that for a connected one-sided \(\Sigma\subset M\) there is a unique ambient double cover \(\widehat M\to M\) whose inverse image of \(\Sigma\) is connected and two-sided.

Complete example. Take \[M=\mathbb{RP}^8\#(S^1\times S^7),\qquad
 \Sigma=\mathbb{RP}^7\subset\mathbb{RP}^8,\] with the connected sum performed in a ball disjoint from \(\Sigma\). Choose a metric round near this standard projective hyperplane and extend it smoothly across the connected sum. The hypersurface is closed, connected, smooth, embedded, one-sided and totally geodesic. It is minimal and locally stable: on sufficiently small intrinsic balls the Dirichlet gradient term dominates the bounded second-variation potential. At points off \(\Sigma\), small balls miss it. Its area is finite and its singular set empty, so it is an LSMH.

Van Kampen gives \(\pi_1(M)=\langle a,b\mid a^2=1\rangle=\mathbb Z_2*\mathbb Z\). The two characters \[\chi_0(a)=1,\quad\chi_0(b)=0,\qquad
 \chi_1(a)=1,\quad\chi_1(b)=1
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z_2\] are surjective and have distinct kernels. They define inequivalent connected double covers over \(M\). Both restrict nontrivially to \(\pi_1(\Sigma)=\langle a\rangle=\mathbb Z_2\). For either cover the full inverse image of \(\Sigma\) is its connected cover \(S^7\). The normal line bundle of \(\mathbb{RP}^7\) in \(\mathbb{RP}^8\) has nontrivial orientation character on \(a\), which is killed on \(S^7\); hence both lifts are two-sided. Pullback metrics preserve minimality and local stability. The lift of a \(b\)-loop distinguishes the ambient covers.

Counterevidence, impact and repair. The intrinsic normal orientation double cover of \(\Sigma\) is canonical. That does not make the ambient cover unique. Subsequent sign and lifted Jacobi arguments need an appropriate cover, not uniqueness among all ambient covers. No failure of those arguments was established. Specify a choice, for example the cover determined by the mod-two class dual to \(\Sigma\), or state the canonical property for the intrinsic cover alone. The example does not dispute existence. The impact is local; severity Minor.
result: Impact: Preliminary uniqueness statement only; no demonstrated core damage.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Specify mod2 dual-class cover or restrict uniqueness to intrinsic normal orientation cover.

problems.title: Simplicity of the first eigenspace needs connectedness
problems.source_location: Printed1273/PDF81 setup and LemmaD.3(i) printed1275/PDF83
claim: First Dirichlet eigenspace simple for arbitrary UcapSigma.
analysis: Location. Appendix D allows an arbitrary precompact open \(U\subset M\) with \(\partial U\cap\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma)=\varnothing\) (p. 1273, PDF 81), and sets \(\mathcal U=U\cap\Sigma\). Lemma D.3(i), p. 1275 (PDF 83), asserts \(\dim E_1=1\) and a positive first eigenfunction, without requiring \(\mathcal U\) connected.

Use \((M,g_*,\Sigma)\) from Problem 1. Choose \(U\) as two disjoint small product neighborhoods whose intersections with \(T^7\) are isometric Euclidean balls \(B_r^{(1)},B_r^{(2)}\), and take the lemma’s potential \(h=0\). All stated conditions hold. The Dirichlet space and operator split as a direct sum. If \(\phi\) is the first Dirichlet eigenfunction of \(-\Delta+7\) on \(B_r\), then \((\phi,0)\) and \((0,\phi)\) are independent first eigenfunctions with the same lowest eigenvalue. Thus \(\dim E_1=2\).

Require \(\mathcal U\) connected for simplicity, or state the result componentwise. The main uses on connected \(\Sigma\) and near a single isolated conical singularity do not yield a demonstrated central failure from this example. The spectral decomposition itself survives. Severity Minor.
result: Impact: Auxiliary spectral statement over disconnected domains.

problems.title: Lemma D.6 must exclude the nonsingular invertible case
problems.source_location: LemmaD.6 printed1283/PDF91; Definition2.5 printed1206/PDF14; actual use printed1291/PDF99
claim: The set of f for which Lu=nu(f) has no slower-growth invariant solution contains open dense subset, without requiring singularities.
analysis:
Location and quantifiers. Lemma D.6, p. 1283 (PDF 91), takes a two-sided LSMH and a finite group \(G\) acting freely on \(M\), preserving the geometric data. It claims that \[\mathcal F_G^{k,\alpha}=
 \{f\in C^{k,\alpha}(M)^G:
 L_{\Sigma,g}u=\nu(f)
 \text{ has no slower-growth $G$-invariant solution}\}\] contains an open dense subset of \(C^{k,\alpha}(M)^G\). There is no assumption \(\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma)\ne\varnothing\).

Counterexample and all hypotheses. Use the same smooth closed warped product \((M,g_*,\Sigma)\) from Problem 1 and \(G=\{\mathrm{id}\}\). This is a finite free action, exactly the trivial-group case also used on p. 1291. The hypersurface is two-sided and an LSMH. Its Jacobi operator is \(L=\Delta_h-7\) and is invertible. For every \(f\in C^{k,\alpha}(M)\) set \(b=\nu(f)|_\Sigma\). In Fourier variables on \(T^7\) the unique solution is \[\widehat u(m)=-\frac{\widehat b(m)}
                      {4\pi^2|m|^2+7},\qquad m\in\mathbb Z^7.\] Elliptic regularity gives the required local regularity and \(u\in L^2(\Sigma)\). Since \(\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma)=\varnothing\), Definition 2.5 on p. 1206 (PDF 14) explicitly says that every \(L^2\) function satisfies its slower-growth condition. Therefore every \(f\) has such a solution: \(\mathcal F_{\{\mathrm{id}\}}^{k,\alpha}=\varnothing\). It cannot contain an open dense subset of the nonempty function space.

Counterevidence and core use. The proof of D.6 constructs functions at singular points. Its intended application is Theorem 2.6, which explicitly assumes a nonempty singular set on p. 1206. That theorem’s proof on p. 1291 (PDF 99) invokes D.6 under the same assumptions. Thus the example invalidates the wider lemma but does not invalidate that application. Add \(\operatorname{Sing}(\Sigma)\ne\varnothing\) to D.6. This check validates the necessity and compatibility of the restriction; it does not reconstruct every step of the restricted lemma. Severity Minor.
result: Impact: Overbroad auxiliary lemma, not a demonstrated failure of its singular application.

Title: Formal initial review: M25-0074
The Smale conjecture and min-max theory
# Scope and initial outcome

The acquired primary PDF is the 38-page author manuscript identified above. The journal DOI is https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01334-z. The publisher landing page identifies an article published on 4 April 2025 in Inventiones mathematicae 241, 1–34; the journal full text was not acquired or established to coincide with this manuscript. All findings here concern v3 only. PDF and printed page numbers coincide.

Initial outcome: Major. The explicit homotopy used in Proposition 7.2 can leave its prescribed target. A smooth relative family satisfying the normalization in the proof gives an exact counterexample. This invalidates a displayed construction in the principal proof chain. A range-preserving replacement for that local construction is proved below; the main theorem is not disproved. Four other literal statements have local scope or orientation defects, with counterevidence restricting their impact.
No. | Confirmed statement or step | Assessment
1 | Collar homotopy, p. 33, between (7.13) and (7.14) | Major; core construction
2 | Uniform absolute projection-area estimate (6.1), p. 22 | Minor; excess direction unnecessary in the main use
3 | Boundary equality in Lemma 6.4, p. 27 | Minor; missing boundary hypothesis
4 | All essential embeddings versus an oriented target, pp. 30–32 | Minor; excess component in Proposition 7.2
5 | Connected identity-orbit quotient versus two points, pp. 6–7 | Minor; incompatible target definitions

All 38 pages were read as extracted text, including references and the appendix. Eighteen source pages were inspected as actual images. The acquired TeX/bibliography tree was parsed completely for structure, dependencies, and execution tokens; critical passages were also read directly. No author code or author TeX was executed. Absence of computational code is not a defect.

The argument reviewed runs from the diffeomorphism/embedding pair reduction, through genus-one min–max and the near-minimal relative cycle, to removal of thin protrusions, collar retraction, and the final relative homotopy vanishing. The external classification and min–max theorems were checked for the roles assigned to their hypotheses, but not independently reproved in full. Detailed coverage limits appear on the last page.
# Problem 1. The displayed collar homotopy exits the tube

Location and claim. Proposition 7.2, pp. 32–33; specifically the unnumbered formula following (7.13) and used to define (7.14). In product coordinates, a collar \(e:T^2\times[-r,0]\to T^2\times[-r,r]\) has bottom height \(-r\), and is normalized by \(\partial_\rho e^2(y,-r)=1\). The proposed homotopy, for \(t>0\), is \[e_t(y,\rho)=\left(e^1(y,t(\rho+r)-r),
-r+\frac{e^2(y,t(\rho+r)-r)+r}{t}\right).\] The proof treats this as a path in the same collar space.

Complete counterexample. Put \(u=(\rho+r)/r\) and \[F(u)=u+\frac{16}{5}u^2-\frac{49}{20}u^3,\qquad
 e(y,\rho)=(y,-r+rF(u)).\] Here \(F(0)=0\), \(F'(0)=1\), \(F(1)=7/4\), and \[F'(u)=1+\frac{32}{5}u-\frac{147}{20}u^2.\] This last polynomial is concave; its endpoint values on \([0,1]\) are \(1\) and \(1/20\). Thus it is strictly positive throughout the interval. Consequently \(e\) is a smooth collar embedding, maps its lower boundary onto the lower boundary of the tube, has the required bottom derivative, and has image heights in \([-r,3r/4]\). Its top is an essential, positively oriented torus in the intended isotopy class.

This is also a relative-family counterexample. For \(x\in[-1,1]\), let \(\lambda(x)=1-x^2\) and \[F_x(u)=u+\lambda(x)\bigl(F(u)-u\bigr).\] Then \(F'_x=(1-\lambda)+\lambda F'>0\), \(F_x(1)\le 7/4\), and the bottom conditions hold for every \(x\). At both boundary parameters \(x=\pm1\), the collar is exactly \((y,\rho)\), belonging to the standard minimal collar family. At \(x=0\), the preceding violation remains. For a higher-dimensional parameter disk use \(\lambda(x)=1-\|x\|^2\). Thus the relative boundary requirement does not exclude the example.

Counterevidence and impact. The formula works for a linear vertical collar, and its limit as \(t\to0\) is correct. Neither fact gives a bound for intermediate \(t\). No global inequality controlling \(e^2+r\) by \(\rho+r\) is imposed at this point; normalizing the derivative only at the bottom does not impose one. Shrinking \(r\) does not fix this scale-invariant counterexample. The defect is independent of the orientation issue in Problem 4.

Proposition 7.2 supplies the contractions in Proposition 7.4 (p. 34), which finishes Theorem 7.3 and Claims 4.1–4.2, hence Theorem 2.8. This is a demonstrated failure of a core construction, warranting Major under the review calibration even though a local repair exists. It is not a counterexample to the Smale conjecture.
# Problem 1 continued: a verified local replacement

Here is a continuous relative-family repair of the range defect. For a compact normalized family \(e_x\), set, for \(t>0\), \[A_{x,t}(y,\rho)=
 \frac{e_x^2(y,t(\rho+r)-r)+r}{t},\qquad
 M_{x,t}=\max_{(y,\rho)\in T^2\times[-r,0]}A_{x,t}(y,\rho),\] \[\ell_{x,t}=\min(1,r/M_{x,t}).\] Since the collar is contained in the original tube, \(A_{x,t}\ge0\). It is not identically zero because the normalized derivative is one; hence \(M_{x,t}>0\). These maxima are continuous in the compact family parameters. Uniform Taylor expansion at the bottom gives \[A_{x,t}\longrightarrow \rho+r,\qquad M_{x,t}\longrightarrow r,\qquad
 \ell_{x,t}\longrightarrow1\] as \(t\to0\), with the first convergence in every spatial \(C^j\) norm.

First deform \(e_x\) by vertical contraction about height \(-r\), using the scalar \(b_{x,s}=(1-s)+s\ell_{x,1}>0\): \[e^{\mathrm{pre}}_{x,s}(y,\rho)
 =\bigl(e_x^1(y,\rho),-r+b_{x,s}(e_x^2(y,\rho)+r)\bigr).\] This is an embedding, fixes the lower boundary, and remains in the tube. Then, with \(t\) decreasing from one to zero, use \[\widetilde e_{x,t}(y,\rho)=
 \bigl(e_x^1(y,t(\rho+r)-r),-r+\ell_{x,t}A_{x,t}(y,\rho)\bigr).\] At \(t=1\) this is the endpoint of the preliminary contraction. For \(t>0\), it is a restriction and reparametrization of an embedding, followed by a positive vertical affine rescaling; hence it remains an embedding. Its height lies in \([-r,0]\), because \(\ell_{x,t}A_{x,t}\le r\). At zero define \[\widetilde e_{x,0}(y,\rho)=(e_x^1(y,-r),\rho).\] The bottom restriction is a diffeomorphism of \(T^2\), so this limit is also an embedding. The Taylor expansion proves continuity into the smooth spatial mapping space, uniformly on the compact parameter set.

For a standard minimal collar, \(e^2=\rho\) and \(e^1\) is independent of \(\rho\). Then \(M_{x,t}=r\), \(\ell_{x,t}=1\), and both homotopies fix that collar. Thus the repair is relative to the same boundary family. The maximum need not be differentiable in parameters; a continuous parameterized homotopy is all that is used here.

Repair limits. This verifies the replacement for the displayed scaling step after the paper’s bottom-derivative normalization. It does not supply the preceding normalization argument, settle all mapping-class components, or certify the later gluing automatically. The intended orientation component must be specified as in Problem 4. No claim of full acceptance of Proposition 7.2 or of the entire theorem follows from this local repair.

Independent computation. Reviewer-written SymPy checks evaluated the polynomial endpoints, derivatives, concavity, relative boundary values, convex-combination identity, and \(47/45\) exactly. The actual interpreter output is retained in `independent_checks.json`. These algebra checks support, and do not replace, the embedding and continuity proof above.
# Problem 2. Equation (6.1) has no uniform absolute error

Location. Section 6, p. 22, (6.1); subsequent use on p. 23 in (6.4)–(6.6). The asserted bound is \[\bigl|\operatorname{Area}(\Gamma)-\|p_\#\Gamma\|\bigr|\le \Lambda r^2\] for every smooth closed surface \(\Gamma\subset N_r(\Sigma)\), with \(\Lambda\) depending only on the ambient manifold. No area or slope bound is included in that assertion.

Complete counterexample. Use the standard genus-one Heegaard splitting of \(S^3\). Choose a smooth Riemannian metric which is \(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2\) on a collar of the splitting torus \(\Sigma=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2\times\{0\}\). Such a positive smooth metric extends over the two solid tori. The surface remains a Heegaard torus and has area one. Fix a sufficiently small \(r>0\), set \(a=r/2\), and take \[\Gamma_N=\{(x,y,a\sin(2\pi Nx)):x,y\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\},
 \qquad N\in\mathbb N.\] Each is a connected smooth embedded closed torus in the prescribed tube. Projection has degree one and \(\|p_\#\Gamma_N\|=1\), whereas \[\operatorname{Area}(\Gamma_N)=
 \int_0^1\sqrt{1+(2\pi Na\cos(2\pi Nx))^2}\,dx
 \ \ge\ 4aN.\] Therefore the absolute difference is at least \(4aN-1\), unbounded for fixed \(r\). Taking \(N>(\Lambda r^2+1)/(4a)\) violates the assertion. This checks all assumptions of the standalone estimate. It does not assert that these highly oscillatory graphs satisfy the later small-\(\mathbf F\) hypothesis of Proposition 6.1.

Counterevidence: the main application needs less. The use in (6.4) needs a lower area bound arising from projection degree, not a uniform upper bound for the graph’s area excess. For a round Clifford torus \(C\), Fermi coordinates give the metric \[ds^2+\cos^2(\pi/4+s)\,d\alpha^2+
       \sin^2(\pi/4+s)\,d\beta^2.\] The two-dimensional Jacobian of projection on any tangent two-plane is at most \(\sec(2r)\) for \(|s|\le r<\pi/4\). Indeed, its maximum is on the tangent plane of the parallel torus, whose area-density ratio to \(C\) is \(\cos(2s)\); planes with a normal component cannot increase that Jacobian. Thus \[\|p_\#\Gamma\|\le\sec(2r)\operatorname{Area}(\Gamma).\] When the projection has degree one, this gives precisely \[\operatorname{Area}(\Gamma)\ge\cos(2r)\operatorname{Area}(C)
 =\operatorname{Area}(C)-O(r^2).\] This proves the needed one-sided estimate in the main round-Clifford application, without a slope restriction.

Impact and repair limits. Replace (6.1) by the appropriate Jacobian inequality. For a general nonminimal Heegaard surface the analogous distortion is usually \(1+O(r)\), so the full generality of Proposition 6.1 still needs an adjusted smallness argument. No counterexample to that proposition was established. The confirmed false part of (6.1) is an overstrong auxiliary estimate whose unneeded direction can be removed in the main application; it is classified Minor.
# Problem 3. Lemma 6.4 lacks a boundary membership hypothesis

Location and claim. Page 27, Lemma 6.4 asks for a map \(g:X\to\mathcal T(\Sigma,M)\) agreeing with the oriented image of \(f(x)\) on \(\partial X\), but assumes only that \(f\) is sufficiently \(\mathbf F\)-close to that isometric orbit.

Counterexample with all assumptions. Let \(X=[0,1]\), \(M=L(3,1)\) with its round metric, and let \(\Sigma=C\) be a Clifford torus. Take \(f\) constant, equal to a parametrization of the parallel torus \(C_s\), where \(s\ne0\) is arbitrarily small. This is an embedding in the required global component and \(\mathbf F(C_s,C)\to0\). It satisfies any prescribed positive closeness tolerance by choosing \(s\) sufficiently small. However, \(\operatorname{Area}(C_s)=\cos(2s)\operatorname{Area}(C)<\operatorname{Area}(C)\). Every member of the isometric orbit \(\mathcal T(\Sigma,M)\) has area \(\operatorname{Area}(C)\). Thus \(C_s\) is not in that orbit, and the required equality \(g(0)=C_s\) is impossible.

Repair and counterevidence. Add \(f(\partial X)\subset\mathcal T(\Sigma,M)\), interpreting the image with the chosen orientation. Set \(g=f\) on the boundary before performing the relative small-cell extension. Proposition 6.5 on the same page already includes this extra boundary hypothesis, so its stated application is compatible with the intended version. The contradiction is to the lemma as written, not to the main theorem. This is a Minor scope defect. A complete independent construction of all the parameter-dependent local extensions was not undertaken.
# Problem 4. Proposition 7.2 includes an opposite orientation component

Location and claim. Page 30 defines \(\operatorname{Emb}_0(T^2,N_r(C_q))\) using the global component in \(M\) and essential images in the tube. The target \(\mathcal T_{\min}(q)\) fixes the orientation of \(q\). Proposition 7.2, p. 32, includes \(k=0\) and asserts surjectivity onto all path components of this domain.

Counterexample. Take \(M=L(3,1)=S^3/\mathbb Z_3\), with central deck action, \(q=f_0\) the standard Clifford embedding, and \(\sigma(z,w)=(w,z)\). This matrix lies in the connected group \(U(2)\) and commutes with the deck action; a path in \(U(2)\) descends to a path of isometries from the identity to \(\sigma\). Hence \(E=\sigma\circ f_0\) lies in the global component \(\operatorname{Emb}_0(T^2,M)\). Its image is exactly \(C_q\), hence essential in every small tube. Swapping the two angular coordinates has determinant \(-1\), so \(E\) represents \(-[C_q]\) in \(H_2(N_r(C_q);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\). Every element of \(\mathcal T_{\min}(q)\) represents \(+[C_q]\). Homotopies through maps into the tube preserve this homology class; there can be no such path from \(E\) to the claimed target.

Impact, counterevidence, and repair. Restrict the domain to projection degree \(+1\), with compatible oriented parametrizations. The proof invokes an oriented Goeritz group and cannot use its triviality for an isometry swapping the handlebodies. The preceding construction of the near-minimal family uses oriented \(\mathbf F\)-closeness, which supports the intended restricted version. A failure of the final theorem has not been shown; preservation of this restriction through every extension still requires an explicit trace. This is classified Minor, as an extra-component defect outside the intended oriented application, separately from the core range failure of Problem 1.
# Problem 5. The defined orbit cannot be a two-point space

Location. Page 6 defines \(\overline{\mathcal T}_{\min}=\operatorname{isom}(M)/\operatorname{isom}^+(M,T)\), where \(\operatorname{isom}(M)\) is explicitly the identity component. Proposition 2.3(3), p. 7, assigns cardinality two to this space for \(q\ne1,\ p>2\). The next paragraph describes the connected space \(\mathcal T_{\min}\cong\operatorname{isom}(M)\) as a \(T^2\)-bundle over it.

Verification. The continuous image of a connected group under its quotient map is connected. It cannot consist of two distinct points. Concretely, for \(L(5,2)\), the identity isometry group is the two-torus of coordinate rotations. Every such rotation preserves the standard Clifford torus and its orientation, so the stabilizer \(\operatorname{isom}^+(M,T)\) is the whole group and the quotient is one point. This also excludes a surjective bundle from the connected \(\mathcal T_{\min}\) to a two-point base.

Counterevidence and repair. The space of both formal orientations of the single unoriented Clifford torus does have two points. That is a different space from the defined identity-component orbit in this case. Use a one-point base for this orbit, or explicitly define a larger oriented moduli space and separate its two components from the chosen parametrized component. The main relative argument concerns the component of \(f_0\); no false main conclusion follows merely from the extra formal orientation. This definitional incompatibility is Minor. A repaired convention should be used consistently in Sections 5–7.
# Positive checks and rejected suspicions

Relative Hurewicz, p. 13. The general relative Hurewicz theorem uses coinvariants (the quotient by relations \(\gamma a-a\), with normal closure in degree two), not an arbitrary orbit set. The paper’s orbit wording alone is not a sufficient general argument. In this particular application, however, there is a direct justification for trivial action. In the pair \((G,H)=(\operatorname{diff}(M),\operatorname{isom}(M))\), take a loop \(\gamma\) in \(H\) and a relative representative \(f\). The homotopy \(F_t(x)=\gamma(t)f(x)\) moves the basepoint along \(\gamma\), keeps the relative boundary in \(H\), and starts and ends at \(f\). Thus the basepoint action is trivial. Transfer through the relative isomorphism (2.11) gives the same result for \((\mathcal T,\mathcal T_{\min})\). The coinvariant quotient is then the original relative group. With the inductive connectivity hypothesis, the desired Hurewicz step is justified. This is recorded as a resolved point, not a confirmed failure of the application.

Genus and multiplicity. The genus-one sweepouts are separating. Positive Ricci curvature rules out stable two-sided closed minimal surfaces, so the stated one-sided alternative with stable connected double cover is excluded in the width contradiction. A minimal sphere in a nontrivial lens space lifts to disjoint minimal spheres in \(S^3\), contradicting Frankel. A connected lifted minimal torus has Euler characteristic zero and is covered by the stated Brendle classification. These checks support the contradiction in (4.12)–(4.16).

Relative chains. The signs in (5.17)–(5.18) are consistent: the bottom face cancels, and the product boundary rule leaves \(\partial I^k\times\{0\}\). The separate \(k=1\) path argument avoids replacing reduced \(H_0\) by an inappropriate unreduced statement. No computational code is needed for these topological arguments.
