problems.title: The displayed collar homotopy exits the tube
problems.source_location: p.33, unnumbered homotopy after (7.13), before (7.14); Proposition 7.2
claim: Normalized collar scaling remains in T^2 x [-r,r]
analysis:
Location and claim. Proposition 7.2, pp. 32–33; specifically the unnumbered formula following (7.13) and used to define (7.14). In product coordinates, a collar \(e:T^2\times[-r,0]\to T^2\times[-r,r]\) has bottom height \(-r\), and is normalized by \(\partial_\rho e^2(y,-r)=1\). The proposed homotopy, for \(t>0\), is \[e_t(y,\rho)=\left(e^1(y,t(\rho+r)-r),
-r+\frac{e^2(y,t(\rho+r)-r)+r}{t}\right).\] The proof treats this as a path in the same collar space.

Complete counterexample. Put \(u=(\rho+r)/r\) and \[F(u)=u+\frac{16}{5}u^2-\frac{49}{20}u^3,\qquad
 e(y,\rho)=(y,-r+rF(u)).\] Here \(F(0)=0\), \(F'(0)=1\), \(F(1)=7/4\), and \[F'(u)=1+\frac{32}{5}u-\frac{147}{20}u^2.\] This last polynomial is concave; its endpoint values on \([0,1]\) are \(1\) and \(1/20\). Thus it is strictly positive throughout the interval. Consequently \(e\) is a smooth collar embedding, maps its lower boundary onto the lower boundary of the tube, has the required bottom derivative, and has image heights in \([-r,3r/4]\). Its top is an essential, positively oriented torus in the intended isotopy class.

This is also a relative-family counterexample. For \(x\in[-1,1]\), let \(\lambda(x)=1-x^2\) and \[F_x(u)=u+\lambda(x)\bigl(F(u)-u\bigr).\] Then \(F'_x=(1-\lambda)+\lambda F'>0\), \(F_x(1)\le 7/4\), and the bottom conditions hold for every \(x\). At both boundary parameters \(x=\pm1\), the collar is exactly \((y,\rho)\), belonging to the standard minimal collar family. At \(x=0\), the preceding violation remains. For a higher-dimensional parameter disk use \(\lambda(x)=1-\|x\|^2\). Thus the relative boundary requirement does not exclude the example.

Counterevidence and impact. The formula works for a linear vertical collar, and its limit as \(t\to0\) is correct. Neither fact gives a bound for intermediate \(t\). No global inequality controlling \(e^2+r\) by \(\rho+r\) is imposed at this point; normalizing the derivative only at the bottom does not impose one. Shrinking \(r\) does not fix this scale-invariant counterexample. The defect is independent of the orientation issue in Problem 4.

Proposition 7.2 supplies the contractions in Proposition 7.4 (p. 34), which finishes Theorem 7.3 and Claims 4.1–4.2, hence Theorem 2.8. This is a demonstrated failure of a core construction, warranting Major under the review calibration even though a local repair exists. It is not a counterexample to the Smale conjecture.

Here is a continuous relative-family repair of the range defect. For a compact normalized family \(e_x\), set, for \(t>0\), \[A_{x,t}(y,\rho)=
 \frac{e_x^2(y,t(\rho+r)-r)+r}{t},\qquad
 M_{x,t}=\max_{(y,\rho)\in T^2\times[-r,0]}A_{x,t}(y,\rho),\] \[\ell_{x,t}=\min(1,r/M_{x,t}).\] Since the collar is contained in the original tube, \(A_{x,t}\ge0\). It is not identically zero because the normalized derivative is one; hence \(M_{x,t}>0\). These maxima are continuous in the compact family parameters. Uniform Taylor expansion at the bottom gives \[A_{x,t}\longrightarrow \rho+r,\qquad M_{x,t}\longrightarrow r,\qquad
 \ell_{x,t}\longrightarrow1\] as \(t\to0\), with the first convergence in every spatial \(C^j\) norm.

First deform \(e_x\) by vertical contraction about height \(-r\), using the scalar \(b_{x,s}=(1-s)+s\ell_{x,1}>0\): \[e^{\mathrm{pre}}_{x,s}(y,\rho)
 =\bigl(e_x^1(y,\rho),-r+b_{x,s}(e_x^2(y,\rho)+r)\bigr).\] This is an embedding, fixes the lower boundary, and remains in the tube. Then, with \(t\) decreasing from one to zero, use \[\widetilde e_{x,t}(y,\rho)=
 \bigl(e_x^1(y,t(\rho+r)-r),-r+\ell_{x,t}A_{x,t}(y,\rho)\bigr).\] At \(t=1\) this is the endpoint of the preliminary contraction. For \(t>0\), it is a restriction and reparametrization of an embedding, followed by a positive vertical affine rescaling; hence it remains an embedding. Its height lies in \([-r,0]\), because \(\ell_{x,t}A_{x,t}\le r\). At zero define \[\widetilde e_{x,0}(y,\rho)=(e_x^1(y,-r),\rho).\] The bottom restriction is a diffeomorphism of \(T^2\), so this limit is also an embedding. The Taylor expansion proves continuity into the smooth spatial mapping space, uniformly on the compact parameter set.

For a standard minimal collar, \(e^2=\rho\) and \(e^1\) is independent of \(\rho\). Then \(M_{x,t}=r\), \(\ell_{x,t}=1\), and both homotopies fix that collar. Thus the repair is relative to the same boundary family. The maximum need not be differentiable in parameters; a continuous parameterized homotopy is all that is used here.

Repair limits. This verifies the replacement for the displayed scaling step after the paper’s bottom-derivative normalization. It does not supply the preceding normalization argument, settle all mapping-class components, or certify the later gluing automatically. The intended orientation component must be specified as in Problem 4. No claim of full acceptance of Proposition 7.2 or of the entire theorem follows from this local repair.

Independent computation. Reviewer-written SymPy checks evaluated the polynomial endpoints, derivatives, concavity, relative boundary values, convex-combination identity, and \(47/45\) exactly. The actual interpreter output is retained in `independent_checks.json`. These algebra checks support, and do not replace, the embedding and continuity proof above.
result: Impact: Displayed core retraction invalid; Prop7.4 -> Thm7.3 -> Claims4.1/4.2 -> Thm2.8 uses it.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Precontract vertically and use ell_x,t=min(1,r/max A_x,t) in scaled homotopy; embedding, range, continuous extension and relative boundary are proved in report.

problems.title: Equation (6.1) has no uniform absolute error
claim: Absolute area-projected-mass difference <= Lambda r^2 for any smooth closed surface in tube
analysis: Location. Section 6, p. 22, (6.1); subsequent use on p. 23 in (6.4)–(6.6). The asserted bound is \[\bigl|\operatorname{Area}(\Gamma)-\|p_\#\Gamma\|\bigr|\le \Lambda r^2\] for every smooth closed surface \(\Gamma\subset N_r(\Sigma)\), with \(\Lambda\) depending only on the ambient manifold. No area or slope bound is included in that assertion.

Complete counterexample. Use the standard genus-one Heegaard splitting of \(S^3\). Choose a smooth Riemannian metric which is \(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2\) on a collar of the splitting torus \(\Sigma=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2\times\{0\}\). Such a positive smooth metric extends over the two solid tori. The surface remains a Heegaard torus and has area one. Fix a sufficiently small \(r>0\), set \(a=r/2\), and take \[\Gamma_N=\{(x,y,a\sin(2\pi Nx)):x,y\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\},
 \qquad N\in\mathbb N.\] Each is a connected smooth embedded closed torus in the prescribed tube. Projection has degree one and \(\|p_\#\Gamma_N\|=1\), whereas \[\operatorname{Area}(\Gamma_N)=
 \int_0^1\sqrt{1+(2\pi Na\cos(2\pi Nx))^2}\,dx
 \ \ge\ 4aN.\] Therefore the absolute difference is at least \(4aN-1\), unbounded for fixed \(r\). Taking \(N>(\Lambda r^2+1)/(4a)\) violates the assertion. This checks all assumptions of the standalone estimate. It does not assert that these highly oscillatory graphs satisfy the later small-\(\mathbf F\) hypothesis of Proposition 6.1.

Counterevidence: the main application needs less. The use in (6.4) needs a lower area bound arising from projection degree, not a uniform upper bound for the graph’s area excess. For a round Clifford torus \(C\), Fermi coordinates give the metric \[ds^2+\cos^2(\pi/4+s)\,d\alpha^2+
       \sin^2(\pi/4+s)\,d\beta^2.\] The two-dimensional Jacobian of projection on any tangent two-plane is at most \(\sec(2r)\) for \(|s|\le r<\pi/4\). Indeed, its maximum is on the tangent plane of the parallel torus, whose area-density ratio to \(C\) is \(\cos(2s)\); planes with a normal component cannot increase that Jacobian. Thus \[\|p_\#\Gamma\|\le\sec(2r)\operatorname{Area}(\Gamma).\] When the projection has degree one, this gives precisely \[\operatorname{Area}(\Gamma)\ge\cos(2r)\operatorname{Area}(C)
 =\operatorname{Area}(C)-O(r^2).\] This proves the needed one-sided estimate in the main round-Clifford application, without a slope restriction.

Impact and repair limits. Replace (6.1) by the appropriate Jacobian inequality. For a general nonminimal Heegaard surface the analogous distortion is usually \(1+O(r)\), so the full generality of Proposition 6.1 still needs an adjusted smallness argument. No counterexample to that proposition was established. The confirmed false part of (6.1) is an overstrong auxiliary estimate whose unneeded direction can be removed in the main application; it is classified Minor.
result: Impact: Overstrong auxiliary estimate false; required main-use direction has independent proof.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use projection Jacobian inequality; general nonminimal surface may have O(r) distortion.

problems.title: Lemma 6.4 lacks a boundary membership hypothesis
problems.source_location: p.27 Lemma6.4
claim: Boundary equality with g into isometric orbit under only F-closeness
analysis: Location and claim. Page 27, Lemma 6.4 asks for a map \(g:X\to\mathcal T(\Sigma,M)\) agreeing with the oriented image of \(f(x)\) on \(\partial X\), but assumes only that \(f\) is sufficiently \(\mathbf F\)-close to that isometric orbit.

Counterexample with all assumptions. Let \(X=[0,1]\), \(M=L(3,1)\) with its round metric, and let \(\Sigma=C\) be a Clifford torus. Take \(f\) constant, equal to a parametrization of the parallel torus \(C_s\), where \(s\ne0\) is arbitrarily small. This is an embedding in the required global component and \(\mathbf F(C_s,C)\to0\). It satisfies any prescribed positive closeness tolerance by choosing \(s\) sufficiently small. However, \(\operatorname{Area}(C_s)=\cos(2s)\operatorname{Area}(C)<\operatorname{Area}(C)\). Every member of the isometric orbit \(\mathcal T(\Sigma,M)\) has area \(\operatorname{Area}(C)\). Thus \(C_s\) is not in that orbit, and the required equality \(g(0)=C_s\) is impossible.

Repair and counterevidence. Add \(f(\partial X)\subset\mathcal T(\Sigma,M)\), interpreting the image with the chosen orientation. Set \(g=f\) on the boundary before performing the relative small-cell extension. Proposition 6.5 on the same page already includes this extra boundary hypothesis, so its stated application is compatible with the intended version. The contradiction is to the lemma as written, not to the main theorem. This is a Minor scope defect. A complete independent construction of all the parameter-dependent local extensions was not undertaken.
result: Impact: Standalone lemma scope false; intended use compatible with missing condition.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Add f(boundary X) in target and extend relatively.

problems.title: Proposition 7.2 includes an opposite orientation component
problems.source_location: p.30 domain definition and p.32 Prop7.2 k=0
claim: All globally isotopic essential embeddings in tube connect to fixed oriented target
analysis: Location and claim. Page 30 defines \(\operatorname{Emb}_0(T^2,N_r(C_q))\) using the global component in \(M\) and essential images in the tube. The target \(\mathcal T_{\min}(q)\) fixes the orientation of \(q\). Proposition 7.2, p. 32, includes \(k=0\) and asserts surjectivity onto all path components of this domain.

Counterexample. Take \(M=L(3,1)=S^3/\mathbb Z_3\), with central deck action, \(q=f_0\) the standard Clifford embedding, and \(\sigma(z,w)=(w,z)\). This matrix lies in the connected group \(U(2)\) and commutes with the deck action; a path in \(U(2)\) descends to a path of isometries from the identity to \(\sigma\). Hence \(E=\sigma\circ f_0\) lies in the global component \(\operatorname{Emb}_0(T^2,M)\). Its image is exactly \(C_q\), hence essential in every small tube. Swapping the two angular coordinates has determinant \(-1\), so \(E\) represents \(-[C_q]\) in \(H_2(N_r(C_q);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\). Every element of \(\mathcal T_{\min}(q)\) represents \(+[C_q]\). Homotopies through maps into the tube preserve this homology class; there can be no such path from \(E\) to the claimed target.

Impact, counterevidence, and repair. Restrict the domain to projection degree \(+1\), with compatible oriented parametrizations. The proof invokes an oriented Goeritz group and cannot use its triviality for an isometry swapping the handlebodies. The preceding construction of the near-minimal family uses oriented \(\mathbf F\)-closeness, which supports the intended restricted version. A failure of the final theorem has not been shown; preservation of this restriction through every extension still requires an explicit trace. This is classified Minor, as an extra-component defect outside the intended oriented application, separately from the core range failure of Problem 1.
result: Impact: Extra-component claim false; main intended oriented application not refuted.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Restrict positive-degree compatible oriented component.

problems.title: The defined orbit cannot be a two-point space
problems.source_location: pp.6-7 definition of Tbar_min and Prop2.3(3)
claim: Connected identity group quotient is two points when q!=1
analysis: Location. Page 6 defines \(\overline{\mathcal T}_{\min}=\operatorname{isom}(M)/\operatorname{isom}^+(M,T)\), where \(\operatorname{isom}(M)\) is explicitly the identity component. Proposition 2.3(3), p. 7, assigns cardinality two to this space for \(q\ne1,\ p>2\). The next paragraph describes the connected space \(\mathcal T_{\min}\cong\operatorname{isom}(M)\) as a \(T^2\)-bundle over it.

Verification. The continuous image of a connected group under its quotient map is connected. It cannot consist of two distinct points. Concretely, for \(L(5,2)\), the identity isometry group is the two-torus of coordinate rotations. Every such rotation preserves the standard Clifford torus and its orientation, so the stabilizer \(\operatorname{isom}^+(M,T)\) is the whole group and the quotient is one point. This also excludes a surjective bundle from the connected \(\mathcal T_{\min}\) to a two-point base.

Counterevidence and repair. The space of both formal orientations of the single unoriented Clifford torus does have two points. That is a different space from the defined identity-component orbit in this case. Use a one-point base for this orbit, or explicitly define a larger oriented moduli space and separate its two components from the chosen parametrized component. The main relative argument concerns the component of \(f_0\); no false main conclusion follows merely from the extra formal orientation. This definitional incompatibility is Minor. A repaired convention should be used consistently in Sections 5–7.
result: Impact: Definitions and connected-bundle description incompatible; no main-theorem counterexample.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use one-point identity orbit or distinguish full oriented moduli and chosen component.

Title: Formal initial review: M25-0075
Bordifications of the moduli spaces of tropical curves and abelian varieties, and unstable cohomology of \(\mathrm{GL}_g(\mathbb Z)\) and \(\mathrm{SL}_g(\mathbb Z)\)
# Scope and initial outcome

All 118 PDF pages were read, including the Appendix and references. Printed page numbers are PDF page numbers plus 34. The separately acquired TeX is arXiv:2309.12753v3 (28 February 2025); it was inspected statically and at relevant passages, but is not asserted to be the exact source of this journal PDF. No author code or author TeX was executed.

Initial outcome: Major. Explicit low-dimensional counterexamples invalidate a general algebraic boundary formula and two unrestricted algebraic statements in the Appendix. These affect advertised geometric structure and supporting constructions. They do not by themselves refute the unstable cohomology injections. Two other false intermediate identities admit complete local corrections.
ID | Confirmed statement or step | Assessment
F1 | Proposition 5.10, final boundary formula, pp. 66–67; related quotient-coordinate step, p. 59 | Major
F2 | Global Gram-map morphisms (A.25)–(A.27), p. 145; domain in (A.31), p. 146 | Major
F3 | Closed exceptional loci identified with open products, (A.28), p. 146; Theorem A.2, p. 131 | Major
F4 | Footnote 3: maximal coordinate arrangement minimizes to core arrangement, p. 76 | Minor
F5 | Ambient kernel equality in Lemma 9.4, p. 89 | Minor

The principal chain was followed from polyhedral configurations and wonderful blow-ups, through graph and perfect-cone diagrams, determinant separation and extension of canonical forms, to relative cohomology, duality, inflation and the motivic pairing. Fourteen exact reviewer-written checks support the calculations below. Finite computations do not replace the general arguments or certify every external dependency.
# F1. The algebraic boundary formula fails for an oversized center

Location. Proposition 5.10, final displayed formula after (5.12), printed pp. 66–67 (PDF 32–33). Definition 4.6 and the paragraph following it, pp. 58–59, expressly allow the center to be larger than the Zariski span of the face it meets.

Claim under test. If no smaller member of \(\mathcal B\) contains \(\sigma_W\), the proposition asserts \[L^\mathcal B\cap E_W^\mathcal B
 =(L_{\sigma_W}^{\mathcal B_W}\times P^{\mathcal B_{/W}})
 \cup(P^{\mathcal B_W}\times L_{\sigma_{/W}}^{\mathcal B_{/W}}).\] Here \(L^\mathcal B\) is the union of the Zariski closures of the facets of the blown-up polytope. This assertion concerns the ambient algebraic boundary, and is stronger than the asserted product of real polytopes.

Example satisfying the hypotheses. Take \(V=\mathbb Q^4\), let \(\sigma\) be the standard projective three-simplex, and set \[C=\mathbb R_{\geq0}^4,\qquad
 W=\langle e_1,e_2-e_3\rangle,\qquad \mathcal B=\{\mathbb P(W)\}.\] The arrangement is intersection-closed. A vector in \(C\cap W\) has the form \((a,b,-b,0)\), so \(b=0\) and \(a\geq0\). Thus \(\sigma_W=\{[e_1]\}\) is a nonempty face, and there is no smaller member of \(\mathcal B\). The quotient map \[q(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=(u,v)=(x_2+x_3,x_4)\] has kernel \(W\) and maps \(C\) onto \(\mathbb R_{\geq0}^2\). Hence the normal polytope is an interval in \(\mathbb P^1\), whose boundary consists of \([1:0]\) and \([0:1]\). The arrangements on both factors are empty. The proposed right-hand side is \[\mathbb P(W)\times\{[1:0],[0:1]\},\] because the intrinsic boundary of the point \(\sigma_W\) is empty.

Actual blow-up calculation. In the affine chart \(x_1=1\), put \(z=x_2\), so \(x_3=u-z\). The center has ideal \((u,v)\). In the blow-up chart \(v=ut\), the coordinates are \((u,z,t)\), the exceptional divisor is \(E=\{u=0\}\), and the strict transforms of the three relevant original facets are \[\widetilde H_2=\{z=0\},\qquad
 \widetilde H_3=\{u-z=0\},\qquad
 \widetilde H_4=\{t=0\}.\] Each is the closure of an actual two-dimensional facet. The point \(P=(0,0,1)\) belongs to \(E\cap\widetilde H_2\cap\widetilde H_3\), and therefore to \(L^\mathcal B\cap E\). It is also in the lifted polytope: the interior points \((u,z,t)=(\varepsilon,\varepsilon/2,1)\), \(\varepsilon>0\), approach it. Under \(E\simeq\mathbb P(W)\times\mathbb P(V/W)\) its coordinates are \(([e_1],[1:1])\). This point is absent from the proposed right-hand side.

Conclusion. The final algebraic boundary formula is false with all its stated hypotheses. The real product \(\sigma^\mathcal B\cap E=\sigma_W\times\sigma_{/W}\) is not contradicted by this example; indeed it is consistent with the calculation.
# F1 continued: cause, counterevidence and repair limits

The proof treats hyperplanes cutting out the point inside the larger \(\mathbb P(W)\) as if they were intrinsic boundary hyperplanes of that point. Their intersections with \(E\) contain \(\{[e_1]\}\times\mathbb P^1\), including normal directions in the interior of the interval. This is precisely the component missed by the displayed formula.

The same center also exposes the quotient-coordinate step in Lemma 4.7 (p. 59; PDF 25). Of the three independent facet equations \(x_2,x_3,x_4\) through \([e_1]\), only \(x_4\) annihilates \(W\): their values on \(e_2-e_3\) are \(1,-1,0\). Thus one cannot choose \(p=\dim(V/W)=2\) of them as coordinates on \(V/W\), as that proof proposes.

Complete local correction of Lemma 4.7. Its convexity conclusion is nevertheless true. If \(q(a)=-q(b)\) for \(a,b\in C\), then \(a+b\in C\cap W\). Since \(C\cap W\) is a face of \(C\), both \(a\) and \(b\) belong to that face and hence to \(W\). Thus \(q(C)\) contains no nonzero line. It is a finitely generated rational cone, so its projective link is a polyhedron. This proves the needed pointedness without any descent of the original facet equations.

Impact and repair boundary. The failure of Proposition 5.10 enters the general face and boundary formalism, including the following corollary. Replacing the assertion by a formula restricted to the actual face span, or imposing appropriate span hypotheses, requires a fresh argument. A blanket assumption \(W=V_{\sigma_W}\) cannot simply be inserted throughout the paper: Remark 10.8 (p. 96) explicitly requires larger centers, and the wheel example on pp. 109–110 exhibits them. The determinant factorization and the real polytope product may survive. This review has not established a complete replacement of the algebraic boundary formalism for all later applications. Severity is Major because the false formula is a structural assertion in the main geometric construction.
# F4. The stated minimality of the core arrangement is false
Location. Footnote 3, printed p. 76 (PDF 42), read with Definition 5.13 and Proposition 5.14, pp. 69–70.

For a coordinate simplex, different coordinate subspaces meet the simplex in different faces. Each such subspace is already the unique smallest member of the maximal coordinate arrangement having that intersection. Consequently \((\mathcal B^{G,\max})^{\min}=\mathcal B^{G,\max}\), not in general \(\mathcal B^{G,\mathrm{core}}\).

For a concrete stable graph, take \(G=K_4\) and a two-edge path \(\gamma=\{12,23\}\). The coordinate center defined by \(x_{12}=x_{23}=0\) is a \(\mathbb P^3\) in \(\mathbb P^5\), belongs to the maximal arrangement, and is minimal for its face. It is absent from the core arrangement, because the path is not bridgeless. At a relative interior point of this face, no core center passes through it: no nonempty subset of the two zero edges is core. The core blow-up is locally unchanged there, whereas the maximal blow-up has an interval of positive normal directions. This is not an extraneous modification.

Counterevidence and correction. The comparison morphism from the maximal blow-up to the core blow-up still follows from inclusion of arrangements and Proposition 5.2(ii). The core construction was defined directly. Delete the false minimality assertion and use that proposition for the comparison; no failure of the graph bordification is proved. This peripheral, unnecessary justification is Minor.
# F2. The global algebraic Gram map has an unresolved base point

Location. Appendix A.5, (A.25)–(A.27), printed p. 145 (PDF 111), and the unrestricted domain in (A.31), p. 146 (PDF 112). The morphisms are used to construct the map in Theorem A.16, an input to Theorem A.2.

Exact algebraic counterexample. Take \(V=\mathbb Q^2\) and the flag \(0\subset\mathbb Qe_2\subset V\). The affine space \(\mathcal P_F\) consists of lower triangular matrices \[M=\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\u&b\end{pmatrix}.\] On its projectivization the proposed map is \[[a:u:b]\longmapsto[a^2+u^2:ub:b^2]\in\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V)).\] After the legitimate base change to \(\mathbb Q(i)\), the point \(N=[i:1:0]\) is in the stated domain and has \(M^TM=0\). It even belongs to \(\mathcal P_F^\circ\), since each of the two row components is nonzero. This is a failure of an algebraic morphism over \(\mathbb Q\); a morphism over \(\mathbb Q\) would remain defined after base change.

The base point is nonremovable. Along \([i+r:1:0]\) the target tends to \([1:0:0]\), whereas along \([i:1:r]\) it tends to \([0:1:0]\): \[M_1(r)^TM_1(r)=
 \begin{pmatrix}2ir+r^2&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 M_2(r)^TM_2(r)=
 \begin{pmatrix}0&r\\r&r^2\end{pmatrix}.\] These are distinct projective limits as \(r\to0\). The source blow-up specified in (A.26) has center \(\mathbb P(\mathcal P_0)=\{[1:0:0]\}\). It is an isomorphism near \(N\) and therefore cannot resolve this indeterminacy. Thus the universal-property argument does not produce the stated global morphism (A.26).

There is a separate elementary domain obstruction to (A.31) as printed. The real matrix \[R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathcal P_F^\circ
 \quad\hbox{has}\quad R^TR=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] On the open monoid stratum \(\lambda_i\ne0\), its image is singular, contrary to the asserted target \(\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V))\setminus\operatorname{Det}\). Nonzero row components do not imply invertibility.

Counterevidence. The topological space \(X(P)\) is formed from invertible real parabolic matrices. The two counterexamples are not elements of that group. Equation (A.24) already uses a determinant-complement restriction, and the explicit positive-block calculation (A.32) is consistent with the intended real map. The topological embedding is not disproved.

Impact and repair limits. The advertised unrestricted algebraic construction, and the derivation of the real map from it, are invalid as written. One should restrict to a suitable algebraic open neighborhood of the relevant real locus and prove extension over the monoid boundary using block coordinates and the pullbacks of the blow-up ideals. Merely invoking the universal property, or merely changing the order of the transpose, does not do this. The complete construction on overlapping flags has not been re-established here. This is Major for the Appendix’s central algebraic construction, with the impact confined as stated.
# F3. Closed exceptional loci retain deeper boundary strata

Location. Equation (A.28), printed p. 146 (PDF 112); the closed-locus product and \(f(e(P))=f(X^{\rm BS})\cap E_P(\mathbb R)\) in Theorem A.2, p. 131 (PDF 97); the assertion about intersections of exceptional strata in A.6.1, p. 149 (PDF 115).

The notation immediately preceding (A.28) identifies \(E_{F'}\) with a product of iterated blow-ups, namely a closed exceptional locus. It then removes only the strict transform of \(\operatorname{Det}\) and replaces those factors by unblown determinant complements. This loses deeper exceptional strata. Removing a strict transform does not remove every exceptional divisor over the original hypersurface.

Finite rank-three verification. Let \(V_1=\langle e_2,e_3\rangle\), \(V_2=\langle e_3\rangle\), and blow up \(\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V/V_1))\) followed by the strict transform of \(\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V/V_2))\). In the affine chart \(q_{11}=1\), first take \(q_{22}=z\) as the normal coordinate to the rank-one center. For the second blow-up take the new \(q_{33}/z\) coordinate as \(w\). A genuine chart is \[Q(z,w,b,c,e)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&zb&zwc\\
 zb&z&zwe\\
 zwc&zwe&zw
 \end{pmatrix}.\] The two exceptional divisors have equations \(z=0\) and \(w=0\). Direct expansion gives \[\det Q=z^2w
 \bigl(1-zb^2-we^2+2zwbce-zwc^2\bigr).\] The strict transform of \(\operatorname{Det}\) is the vanishing of the parenthesized factor. At \(z=w=b=c=e=0\) that factor equals \(1\). Thus the two closed exceptional divisors intersect outside the strict determinant locus. The point is approached by the positive definite matrices \(\operatorname{diag}(1,z,zw)\) with \(z,w>0\).

For the coarser flag \(F':0\subset V_1\subset V\), blow-down of the second modification sends this point to a normal quadratic form whose restriction to \(V_1\) is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\). That point is excluded by the determinant-complement factor on the right of (A.28), but is present on its stated left. The claimed canonical identification through blow-down therefore fails. The same corner belongs to the full-flag boundary stratum, not to the open stratum \(e(P_{F'})\) alone; the closed intersection in Theorem A.2 cannot isolate the latter.

Counterevidence and repair. The paper explicitly distinguishes \(S_I\) and \(S_I^\circ\) in (A.17) and (A.23). For the corresponding open exceptional stratum, one removes all additional exceptional divisors; the product of unblown determinant complements is then the appropriate local description. In the displayed chart, the coarser open stratum has \(z=0,w\ne0\), and the corner has \(z=w=0\). This confirms the intended stratified picture rather than contradicting existence of the intended embedding.

Impact. Revise the closed/open loci consistently in (A.28), Theorem A.2 and the injectivity argument. Distinct open strata are disjoint by definition; closed exceptional intersections are not forced into \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Det}}\). The incorrect algebraic identification is central to the Appendix’s boundary description, hence Major under the review standard. No counterexample to the cohomology injections or to the appropriately corrected topological correspondence is claimed.
# F5. An ambient kernel identity needs the positivity restriction
Location. Lemma 9.4, first paragraph of the proof, printed p. 89 (PDF 55). For \(f_v(Q)=Q(v,v)\), it asserts \(\ker f_v=\mathcal Q(V/\mathbb Qv)\) on the entire vector space of quadratic forms.

Take \(V=\mathbb Q^2\), \(v=e_1\) and \[Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(Q(v,v)=0\), but \(Qv=e_2\ne0\). The kernel of the scalar linear functional \(f_v\) has dimension \(2\), while \(\mathcal Q(V/\mathbb Qv)\) has dimension \(1\). Thus the ambient equality is false.

Complete correction and counterevidence. The lemma itself only concerns a positive polyhedron. If \(Q\) is positive semidefinite, write \(Q=B^TB\) over \(\mathbb R\); then \(Q(v,v)=\|Bv\|^2=0\) implies \(Bv=0\) and hence \(Qv=0\). Consequently the correct equality is \[\sigma\cap\mathbb P(\ker f_v)
 =\sigma\cap\mathbb P\bigl(\mathcal Q(V/\mathbb Qv)\bigr).\] Choose a basis \(v_1,\ldots,v_d\) of \(K\). Each \(f_{v_i}\) is nonnegative on \(\sigma\), so its zero locus on \(\sigma\) is a face or empty. Their intersection equals \(\sigma\cap\mathbb P(\mathcal Q(V/K))\), using the just-proved restricted identity. A nonempty intersection of faces is a face. This proves the stated lemma. The indefinite matrix above refutes only the ambient identity, not the positive-semidefinite conclusion. The defect is Minor and the local repair is complete.
# Positive checks and boundaries of the findings
The following checks found no additional defect in the indicated step, subject to the dependencies and limits stated on the next page.

For positive semidefinite matrices and positive coefficients, \(\ker(\sum_i\lambda_iQ_i)=\bigcap_i\ker Q_i\) follows by summing their nonnegative quadratic values. This supports the essential-envelope arguments and corrects the proof of Lemma 9.4. In the blow-up block model, the initial determinant is \(z^{\dim K}\det(Q_K)\det(Q_C)\). Both rank-three splits \(\dim K=1,2\) were expanded exactly.

The wheel matrix on pp. 109–110 was reconstructed as \(H^T\operatorname{diag}(x_1,\ldots,x_6)H\) from the three listed cycles. Setting \(x_1=x_2=x_4=x_5=0\) gives \(\operatorname{diag}(0,x_6,x_3)\). Its two-dimensional linear span is properly contained in the three-dimensional space \(\mathcal Q(V/\mathbb Qh_1)\), confirming the paper’s own explanation of why oversized centers occur.

For odd \(g=2m+1\), \(\sum_{k=1}^m(4k+1)=g(g+1)/2-1\). Complementary exterior monomials pair in this top degree. The orientation character on symmetric matrices is \((\det h)^{g+1}\): a reflection changes the signs of precisely \(g-1\) off-diagonal coordinates. This agrees with the odd/even distinction in Lemma 15.10. The compact-support shift by one for \(\mathbb R_{>0}\) and the additional inflation shift give the stated low-rank degrees: \(H^3(\mathrm{SL}_4(\mathbb Z))\), and two degree-five contributions plus degree ten for \(\mathrm{SL}_6(\mathbb Z)\). These checks concern degrees and mechanisms, not a computation of the complete cohomology rings.

report: Author: Scientific review performed in this conversation
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Formal initial review: M25-0076
The Assouad dimension of Kakeya sets in \(\mathbb R^3\)
# Scope and initial outcome

All 48 pages of the bound author manuscript were read, including references. Page numbers below are both the printed and one-based PDF numbers. The acquired `main.tex` was parsed completely for structure and dependencies and read directly at the principal disputed passages. The report applies to this v2 author manuscript. The journal reference attached to its metadata does not establish identity with the publisher’s version of record.

Initial outcome: Major. Two finding groups are established. First, the unrestricted twisted-projection argument in Section 7 exceeds the domains on which its geometric reduction and cinematic-function input are valid. There is an explicit horizontal-tube counterexample to the unrestricted Proposition 7.1 and Lemma 7.12, and an independent polynomial check of the unnormalized cinematic-family claim. Second, the parameter choice in the proof of Theorem 1.4 does not force the claimed contradiction. A complete local correction of that deduction is given below, conditional only on the stated Theorem 1.5.
ID | Confirmed claim or inference | Assessment
F1 | Proposition 7.1, p. 39; Lemma 7.12, pp. 42–44: direction-domain and cinematic-normalization restrictions are absent from the stated/generalized argument. | Major
F2 | Theorem 1.4 proof, p. 46: the measure-error exponent is too large for the stated dimension gap; the final exponent comparison is invalid. | Major

These findings do not constitute a counterexample to the main Kakeya dimension conclusions. The horizontal construction fails the stronger Convex Wolff Axioms used for the main theorem. It is excluded by an explicit transversality convention. The measure argument has a direct repair. What remains is to state the correct restricted projection input and verify that the main proof supplies its hypotheses, with the necessary quantitative losses.

The proof chain was traced through the two extremal parameters, the four-way structural alternative, plank enlargement, the generalized sticky Kakeya argument, twisted projections, and the final dimension deductions. Fifteen reviewer-written checks support specific calculations. They do not replace an all-scale proof or certify every imported result.
# F1(a). Horizontal tubes refute the unrestricted projection claim

Locations. Proposition 7.1, p. 39; Lemma 7.12 and (7.2), p. 42; the refinement-and-rotation reduction to lines \((a+ct,b+dt,t)\), p. 43. The tube definition on pp. 3 and 6 allows arbitrary directions. The restatement on p. 33 specifies a thickened line in a cube and does not explicitly impose a lower bound for its \(z\) component.

Construction. Fix a sufficiently large absolute integer \(M\). For arbitrarily small \(\delta\), take \(a,b\) in the \(M\delta\) lattice inside \([-1/8,1/8]\), and set \[v_b=\left(\frac{1-b^2}{1+b^2},\frac{2b}{1+b^2},0\right),\qquad
 L_{a,b}=\{(0,a,0)+t v_b:-1/2\leq t\leq1/2\}.\] Let \(T_{a,b}=N_\delta(L_{a,b})\) and \(Y(T)=T\). The vector \(v_b\) has norm one. Thus these are genuine unit-segment tubes. Their centers have norm at most \(1/8\), so the segments lie in \(B(0,5/8)\) and the tubes lie in \(B(0,1)\) for small \(\delta\). There are \(N\asymp\delta^{-2}\) tubes. Taking \(M\) large ensures essential distinctness, although Proposition 7.1 does not separately require it.

All-scale Tube Wolff check. For \(\delta\leq r\ll1\), if an \(r\)-tube contains one of these unit segments, its axis must be within \(O(r)\) in angle of the segment direction. On this compact, almost-horizontal chart, intersection with \(x=0\) and direction are uniformly bi-Lipschitz coordinates for the lines. Consequently, all pairs \((a,b)\) whose tubes are contained in a fixed \(r\)-tube lie in a parameter rectangle with side lengths \(O(r)\). The lattice count is \[\#\{T:T\subset T_r\}
 \leq C\left(1+\frac r{M\delta}\right)^2
 \leq C_0 r^2 N
 \leq C_1 |T_r|N.\] For \(r\) bounded below the same estimate follows by increasing \(C_1\). For \(r<\delta\), containment is impossible because each \(\delta\)-tube contains a ball of radius \(\delta\). The constants are independent of \(\delta\). For any proposed \(\eta>0\), choose \(\delta\) so small that \(C_1\leq\delta^{-\eta}\). The full shading is uniformly 1-dense. Thus every substantive hypothesis of the unrestricted Proposition 7.1 holds.

Projection. Choose \(f(z)=z\), so \(f'=1\) and \(f''=0\). All tubes lie in \(|z|\leq\delta\), with bounded \(x,y\). Therefore \[\bigcup_T\pi_f(Y(T))\subset[-1,1]\times[-\delta,\delta],
 \qquad \left|\bigcup_T\pi_f(Y(T))\right|\leq4\delta .\] For \(\varepsilon=1/2\) and sufficiently small \(\delta\), this is less than \(\delta^\varepsilon\), contrary to Proposition 7.1.

The same construction refutes Lemma 7.12 as unrestricted. For any nonempty projected subshading \(E\) inside this strip and \(r\gg\delta\), Fubini gives \[|E|\leq 2\delta\,|\operatorname{proj}_1E|,
 \qquad |N_rE|\geq r\,|\operatorname{proj}_1E|,
 \qquad |E|/|N_rE|\leq2\delta/r.\] Here the second bound follows by including the vertical interval \([-r/2,r/2]\) above each first coordinate, since \(\delta<r/2\). If \(r>\delta^{1-\varepsilon^2}\) and \(0<\varepsilon<1\), then \(2(\delta/r)^{1-\varepsilon}\to0\), contradicting (7.2). Positive shading density ensures a positive-area projection.
# F1 continued: counterevidence, normalization and repair limits

Counterevidence and precise scope. The horizontal example does not satisfy the Convex Wolff Axioms with small error: a slab of volume \(O(\delta)\) contains every tube. It is therefore not a counterexample to Proposition 6.8 or Theorem 1.5. The earlier sticky-Kakeya paper explicitly uses a restricted line chart with final direction component at least \(1/2\). If that full convention is intended to be inherited here, it must be stated and propagated; the counterexample is outside that revised domain.

A general rotation cannot justify the p. 43 reduction for a fixed \(\pi_f(x,y,z)=(x+f(z)y,z)\). Rotating a horizontal family to a vertical one changes its relation to the distinguished \(z\) coordinate and changes the projection problem. Tube Wolff non-concentration alone does not supply the missing transversality.

Repair boundary. State a projection lemma for a fixed transverse chart, for example \(|\operatorname{dir}(T)\cdot e_3|\geq c>0\), bounded line parameters, and a normalized, bounded slope function. Track any change of coordinates in both the tube family and the projection. Then establish that the extremal family delivered by Section 6 has these properties in those same coordinates. The prior restricted theorem is relevant counterevidence and a plausible repair route; it is not a proof of the larger statement as printed. A complete quantitative reconstruction of that interface, including all transferred refinements, was not completed here.

Impact. These domain errors occur in the advertised generalization used to close the generalized sticky-Kakeya argument. They are Major under the review standard even if the intended restricted route can be recovered. No assertion is made that the principal dimension conclusions are false.
# F2. The measure-error exponent does not yield a contradiction
Location. Proof of Theorem 1.4, p. 46: the choice \(\varepsilon=(3-\alpha)/4\), \(\eta_1=(3-\varepsilon)\eta/6\), and the last display. The identical choices occur in the acquired TeX.

Exact calculation. Write \(d=3-\varepsilon-\alpha=3\varepsilon>0\) and temporarily write \(\kappa\) for the measure-error exponent. The covering-number and two-sided measure estimates give, after the usual fixed enlargements of balls, \[(r/\rho)^{3-\varepsilon}\rho^{\alpha+\kappa}
 \lesssim r^{\alpha-\kappa},
 \qquad
 (r/\rho)^d\lesssim(r\rho)^{-\kappa}.\] Since \(\delta\leq\rho\leq\delta^\eta r\) and \(r\geq\delta\), the available comparison is \[\delta^{-\eta d}\lesssim\delta^{-2\kappa}.\] A contradiction requires \(\eta d>2\kappa\). For the printed choice this margin is \[\eta(3-\varepsilon-\alpha)-\frac{\eta(3-\varepsilon)}3
 =\eta\left(\frac{10\varepsilon}{3}-1\right).\] It is negative whenever \(\varepsilon<3/10\), which includes the dimension range near 3 that the argument must exclude.

For a concrete numerical check take \[\alpha=\frac52,\quad \varepsilon=\frac18,\quad
 d=\frac38,\quad \kappa_{\rm printed}=\frac{23\eta}{48}.\] The two exponents are \(\eta d=3\eta/8\) and \(2\kappa_{\rm printed}=23\eta/24\). The claimed contradiction is unavailable. For example \(\rho=\delta\), \(r=\delta^{1-\eta}\), with \(\eta=1/10\), meets the scale conditions and makes the preceding mass comparison compatible. This is a countercheck to the inference, not a proposed Kakeya set.

The first equality in the last display is also false: \(d=3-\varepsilon-\alpha\) is generally not \((3-\varepsilon)/2\). The power of \(r/\rho\) arising from rearrangement is \(+d\), not the printed \(-\eta d\). Correcting those display errors alone does not fix the overly large value of \(\eta_1\).

Complete local repair, conditional on Theorem 1.5. Keep \(\varepsilon=(3-\alpha)/4\), obtain \(\eta\) from Theorem 1.5, and choose \[\kappa=\frac{\eta(3-\varepsilon-\alpha)}4=\frac{3\eta\varepsilon}{4}>0.\] Definition 1.3 permits this arbitrarily small error exponent. Choose its measure first, then a positive-measure direction subset with a uniform positive line-intersection length. The associated tube shading has fixed positive density, and its Convex Wolff constant is fixed; both meet Theorem 1.5 once \(\delta\) is small enough.

To apply the measure bounds at legitimate centers, choose a separated subset of \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\) within \(O(\rho)\) of the points supplied by the \(\rho\)-neighborhood estimate. A fixed-factor thinning gives \(\gtrsim(r/\rho)^{3-\varepsilon}\) separated support points in an enlarged \(O(r)\) ball. Their small balls are disjoint, and the two-sided measure bounds yield exactly the comparison above, with fixed constants. Consequently \[\delta^{-\eta d}\lesssim\delta^{-2\kappa}
 =\delta^{-\eta d/2},\] which is impossible as \(\delta\downarrow0\). Thus the local deduction of Theorem 1.4 is repaired without strengthening its hypotheses.
Assessment. Major for the invalid final inference in a stated main theorem; repair complete at this local interface. This does not certify the independent proof of Theorem 1.5 or resolve F1.
# Coverage and positive verification
PDF pages | Scope actually read and checked
1–5 | Dimension notions, stable equality, quantifier order, measurable shadings, scale separation and the main proof architecture.
6–9 | Regularization, convex versus tube non-concentration, uniform partitioning covers, rescaling and the distinction between all-scale and self-similar conditions.
10–12 | Supremum/limsup definitions of \(\omega\) and \(\alpha\), monotonicity and existence of near-extremal pairs.
13–24 | Robust broadness, localization, transverse plank intersections, \(L^2\) overlap sums, enlargement, slab bound, and transfer back to tubes.
25–31 | Multiscale regularization, four-way alternative, elimination of richer counterexamples, anisotropic density transfer, and the reduction to Theorem 5.2.
32–38 | Imported sticky-Kakeya structure, balanced covers, local/global grains, slope regularity and the replacement of direction separation by slab non-concentration.
39–45 | Twisted projections, Frostman/Katz–Tao conversions, uniform refinement, scale merging, translated copies, cinematic input and iteration. F1.
45–48 | Assouad deduction, stable-equality measure argument (F2), two-scale corollary, and reference correspondence.

Overlap and rescaling checks. For a fixed \(s\times1\times1\) slab the dyadic overlap sum is \(\lesssim Ks^2N\log(1/s)\). Summing over all \(N\) slabs and applying Cauchy–Schwarz to total shading mass \(K^{-1}sN\) gives \(|E|\gtrsim K^{-3}/\log(1/s)\), as required in Lemma 4.4. The repeated \(N\) factor omitted in the typeset intermediate identity is not treated as an independent scientific defect.

The inverse tube rescaling has Jacobian \(\rho^2\). A ball of radius \(r_2\) has preimage dimensions \(\rho r_2,\rho r_2,r_2\). The regular-shading argument loses a positive density factor \(\delta^\eta\), in agreement with (5.8), rather than gaining \(\delta^{-\eta}\) as printed in (5.6). These dimensional corrections preserve the intended exponent-slack mechanism; a new global proof is not claimed.
# Limits, interpretation and evidence

External-input inspection. Selected passages of Wang–Zahl, Sticky Kakeya sets and the sticky Kakeya conjecture, https://arxiv.org/html/2210.09581v2, were read: the restricted line convention, the projection lemma for AD sets, the grain-to-slab argument, and the cinematic definition, estimate and normalized-family proof. That accessible v2 is dated 7 October 2025, later than the bound manuscript. It is supporting comparison evidence, not a verified substitute for the exact earlier version cited here. Attempts to retrieve the earlier v1 failed.

Not fully verified. The full external grain-structure and radial-projection proofs, all scale-merging inputs, and the cinematic maximal estimate were not independently re-proved. The exact constants and nesting construction in Lemma 2.13, and the weighted selection/truncation details in the proof of Corollary 1.7, require a fuller reconstruction. Local geometric suspicions about these steps are not recorded as additional confirmed defects. problems.title: Unrestricted twisted-projection generalization without transverse line chart and normalized f
problems.source_location: Proposition7.1 p39; Lemma7.12 and(7.2)p42; rotation p43; cinematic import p44
claim: Unrestricted twisted-projection generalization without transverse line chart and normalized f
analysis: Locations. Proposition 7.1, p. 39; Lemma 7.12 and (7.2), p. 42; the refinement-and-rotation reduction to lines \((a+ct,b+dt,t)\), p. 43. The tube definition on pp. 3 and 6 allows arbitrary directions. The restatement on p. 33 specifies a thickened line in a cube and does not explicitly impose a lower bound for its \(z\) component.

Construction. Fix a sufficiently large absolute integer \(M\). For arbitrarily small \(\delta\), take \(a,b\) in the \(M\delta\) lattice inside \([-1/8,1/8]\), and set \[v_b=\left(\frac{1-b^2}{1+b^2},\frac{2b}{1+b^2},0\right),\qquad
 L_{a,b}=\{(0,a,0)+t v_b:-1/2\leq t\leq1/2\}.\] Let \(T_{a,b}=N_\delta(L_{a,b})\) and \(Y(T)=T\). The vector \(v_b\) has norm one. Thus these are genuine unit-segment tubes. Their centers have norm at most \(1/8\), so the segments lie in \(B(0,5/8)\) and the tubes lie in \(B(0,1)\) for small \(\delta\). There are \(N\asymp\delta^{-2}\) tubes. Taking \(M\) large ensures essential distinctness, although Proposition 7.1 does not separately require it.

All-scale Tube Wolff check. For \(\delta\leq r\ll1\), if an \(r\)-tube contains one of these unit segments, its axis must be within \(O(r)\) in angle of the segment direction. On this compact, almost-horizontal chart, intersection with \(x=0\) and direction are uniformly bi-Lipschitz coordinates for the lines. Consequently, all pairs \((a,b)\) whose tubes are contained in a fixed \(r\)-tube lie in a parameter rectangle with side lengths \(O(r)\). The lattice count is \[\#\{T:T\subset T_r\}
 \leq C\left(1+\frac r{M\delta}\right)^2
 \leq C_0 r^2 N
 \leq C_1 |T_r|N.\] For \(r\) bounded below the same estimate follows by increasing \(C_1\). For \(r<\delta\), containment is impossible because each \(\delta\)-tube contains a ball of radius \(\delta\). The constants are independent of \(\delta\). For any proposed \(\eta>0\), choose \(\delta\) so small that \(C_1\leq\delta^{-\eta}\). The full shading is uniformly 1-dense. Thus every substantive hypothesis of the unrestricted Proposition 7.1 holds.

Projection. Choose \(f(z)=z\), so \(f'=1\) and \(f''=0\). All tubes lie in \(|z|\leq\delta\), with bounded \(x,y\). Therefore \[\bigcup_T\pi_f(Y(T))\subset[-1,1]\times[-\delta,\delta],
 \qquad \left|\bigcup_T\pi_f(Y(T))\right|\leq4\delta .\] For \(\varepsilon=1/2\) and sufficiently small \(\delta\), this is less than \(\delta^\varepsilon\), contrary to Proposition 7.1.

The same construction refutes Lemma 7.12 as unrestricted. For any nonempty projected subshading \(E\) inside this strip and \(r\gg\delta\), Fubini gives \[|E|\leq 2\delta\,|\operatorname{proj}_1E|,
 \qquad |N_rE|\geq r\,|\operatorname{proj}_1E|,
 \qquad |E|/|N_rE|\leq2\delta/r.\] Here the second bound follows by including the vertical interval \([-r/2,r/2]\) above each first coordinate, since \(\delta<r/2\). If \(r>\delta^{1-\varepsilon^2}\) and \(0<\varepsilon<1\), then \(2(\delta/r)^{1-\varepsilon}\to0\), contradicting (7.2). Positive shading density ensures a positive-area projection.

Counterevidence and precise scope. The horizontal example does not satisfy the Convex Wolff Axioms with small error: a slab of volume \(O(\delta)\) contains every tube. It is therefore not a counterexample to Proposition 6.8 or Theorem 1.5. The earlier sticky-Kakeya paper explicitly uses a restricted line chart with final direction component at least \(1/2\). If that full convention is intended to be inherited here, it must be stated and propagated; the counterexample is outside that revised domain.

A general rotation cannot justify the p. 43 reduction for a fixed \(\pi_f(x,y,z)=(x+f(z)y,z)\). Rotating a horizontal family to a vertical one changes its relation to the distinguished \(z\) coordinate and changes the projection problem. Tube Wolff non-concentration alone does not supply the missing transversality.

Repair boundary. State a projection lemma for a fixed transverse chart, for example \(|\operatorname{dir}(T)\cdot e_3|\geq c>0\), bounded line parameters, and a normalized, bounded slope function. Track any change of coordinates in both the tube family and the projection. Then establish that the extremal family delivered by Section 6 has these properties in those same coordinates. The prior restricted theorem is relevant counterevidence and a plausible repair route; it is not a proof of the larger statement as printed. A complete quantitative reconstruction of that interface, including all transferred refinements, was not completed here.

Impact. These domain errors occur in the advertised generalization used to close the generalized sticky-Kakeya argument. They are Major under the review standard even if the intended restricted route can be recovered. No assertion is made that the principal dimension conclusions are false.
result: Impact: False supporting statements in generalized sticky-Kakeya input as written; arbitrary rotation does not preserve fixed projection.

problems.title: Printed exponent selection forces contradiction from two-sided measure bounds
problems.source_location: Theorem1.4 proof p46 parameter eta1=(3-eps)eta/6 and last display
claim: Printed exponent selection forces contradiction from two-sided measure bounds
analysis: Location. Proof of Theorem 1.4, p. 46: the choice \(\varepsilon=(3-\alpha)/4\), \(\eta_1=(3-\varepsilon)\eta/6\), and the last display. The identical choices occur in the acquired TeX.

Exact calculation. Write \(d=3-\varepsilon-\alpha=3\varepsilon>0\) and temporarily write \(\kappa\) for the measure-error exponent. The covering-number and two-sided measure estimates give, after the usual fixed enlargements of balls, \[(r/\rho)^{3-\varepsilon}\rho^{\alpha+\kappa}
 \lesssim r^{\alpha-\kappa},
 \qquad
 (r/\rho)^d\lesssim(r\rho)^{-\kappa}.\] Since \(\delta\leq\rho\leq\delta^\eta r\) and \(r\geq\delta\), the available comparison is \[\delta^{-\eta d}\lesssim\delta^{-2\kappa}.\] A contradiction requires \(\eta d>2\kappa\). For the printed choice this margin is \[\eta(3-\varepsilon-\alpha)-\frac{\eta(3-\varepsilon)}3
 =\eta\left(\frac{10\varepsilon}{3}-1\right).\] It is negative whenever \(\varepsilon<3/10\), which includes the dimension range near 3 that the argument must exclude.

For a concrete numerical check take \[\alpha=\frac52,\quad \varepsilon=\frac18,\quad
 d=\frac38,\quad \kappa_{\rm printed}=\frac{23\eta}{48}.\] The two exponents are \(\eta d=3\eta/8\) and \(2\kappa_{\rm printed}=23\eta/24\). The claimed contradiction is unavailable. For example \(\rho=\delta\), \(r=\delta^{1-\eta}\), with \(\eta=1/10\), meets the scale conditions and makes the preceding mass comparison compatible. This is a countercheck to the inference, not a proposed Kakeya set.

The first equality in the last display is also false: \(d=3-\varepsilon-\alpha\) is generally not \((3-\varepsilon)/2\). The power of \(r/\rho\) arising from rearrangement is \(+d\), not the printed \(-\eta d\). Correcting those display errors alone does not fix the overly large value of \(\eta_1\).

Complete local repair, conditional on Theorem 1.5. Keep \(\varepsilon=(3-\alpha)/4\), obtain \(\eta\) from Theorem 1.5, and choose \[\kappa=\frac{\eta(3-\varepsilon-\alpha)}4=\frac{3\eta\varepsilon}{4}>0.\] Definition 1.3 permits this arbitrarily small error exponent. Choose its measure first, then a positive-measure direction subset with a uniform positive line-intersection length. The associated tube shading has fixed positive density, and its Convex Wolff constant is fixed; both meet Theorem 1.5 once \(\delta\) is small enough.

To apply the measure bounds at legitimate centers, choose a separated subset of \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\) within \(O(\rho)\) of the points supplied by the \(\rho\)-neighborhood estimate. A fixed-factor thinning gives \(\gtrsim(r/\rho)^{3-\varepsilon}\) separated support points in an enlarged \(O(r)\) ball. Their small balls are disjoint, and the two-sided measure bounds yield exactly the comparison above, with fixed constants. Consequently \[\delta^{-\eta d}\lesssim\delta^{-2\kappa}
 =\delta^{-\eta d/2},\] which is impossible as \(\delta\downarrow0\). Thus the local deduction of Theorem 1.4 is repaired without strengthening its hypotheses.
Assessment. Major for the invalid final inference in a stated main theorem; repair complete at this local interface. This does not certify the independent proof of Theorem 1.5 or resolve F1.
result: Impact: Invalid final contradiction for a main theorem, independently of display typos.

paragraphs: Set kappa=eta*d/4. Use support-centered separated subset, fixed ball enlargement/thinning and uniform positive shading density. Then delta^(-eta*d)<=C delta^(-eta*d/2), impossible as delta tends0.

Title: Formal initial review: M25-0077
Carleson’s \(\varepsilon^2\) conjecture in higher dimensions
# Scope and initial outcome

All 101 pages of the acquired publisher PDF were read, including the references. Locations use one-based PDF page / printed page; printed page equals PDF page plus 206. The related arXiv:2310.12316v3 source was parsed in full for structure, dependency declarations, and dimension conventions. It is a related author version, not the publisher TeX; its additional appendix is not attributed to the publisher PDF.

Initial outcome: Major. A complete planar construction refutes the \(n=1\) case of Theorem B as printed. It satisfies the precise logarithmic capacity density condition, has \(\mathcal A=0\) at every point of a line, and has no true tangent at any of those points. This does not refute Theorem A, the qualitative large-piece rectifiability mechanism, or the \(n\ge2\) case of Theorem B. Two further core proof steps have separate problems: the scale uniformity asserted in Lemma 9.1 and the preservation of a \(99\%\) mass conclusion under Claim 13.1.
No. | Confirmed claim or inference | Judgment
1 | Theorem B, 6/212: planar CDC does not imply the asserted true-tangent characterization. | Major
2 | Lemma 9.1, 50–51/256–257: its useful small-parameter assertion fails for half-spaces. | Major
3 | Claim 13.1, 69/275: localization does not retain the original \(99\%\) mass target. | Major
4 | Remark 2.6(ii), 13/219: an unweighted spherical coarea identity is false. | Minor
5 | Lemma 3.3, 17/223: the displayed linear tail cannot have a dimension-only constant. | Minor
6 | Rigidity after (1.5), 5/211: equality requires a capacity-zero qualification. | Minor
7 | Proposition 15.1, 89/295: the slicing-center set \(G\) needs localization. | Minor
Finite calculations supplement the analytic arguments below; they do not certify all imported lemmas or the whole paper.
# Problem 1: a planar counterexample to Theorem B

Locations and claim. Theorem B, 6/212, explicitly assumes \(n\ge1\), two disjoint open subsets \(\Omega^\pm\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\), and the CDC for their union. It asserts, up to an \(\mathcal H^n\)-null set, that \(\mathcal A(x)<\infty\) is equivalent to a true tangent. The definition on 3/209 tests the union \(\partial\Omega^+\cup\partial\Omega^-\) against every sufficiently narrow double cone. Definition 2.2, 11/217, specifies logarithmic capacity when \(n=1\): \[\operatorname{Cap}_L(B(z,r)\setminus(\Omega^+\cup\Omega^-))\ge c r
 \quad(z\in\partial(\Omega^+\cup\Omega^-),\ 0<r<\operatorname{diam}(\Omega^+\cup\Omega^-)).\]
## Construction and all geometric hypotheses

Let \(C\subset[0,1]\) be the middle-third Cantor set, and put \(d=\log2/\log3\in(0,1)\). Its standard probability measure has a bound \(
u(B(t,ho))\le Aho^d\) for \(0<ho<1\): choose basic Cantor intervals of length \(3^{-m}\) comparable to \(ho\); an interval of length \(2ho\) meets at most a fixed number, each of mass \(2^{-m}\). Consequently, \[\iint\log^+ rac1{|u-v|}\,d
u(u)d

 =\int_0^\infty(

u)\{|u-v|<e^{-t}\}\,dt
 \le A\int_0^\infty e^{-dt}\,dt<\infty .\] Thus \(q:=\operatorname{Cap}_L(C)>0\). Translation and dilation give \(\operatorname{Cap}_L(a+\ell C)=\ell q\).

For \(j\ge1\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\), define \[h_j=2^{-j},\quad
 K_{j,k}=\bigl(kh_j+(h_j/4)C\bigr)\times\{h_j\},\quad
 F=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup\bigcup_{j,k}K_{j,k}.\] Set \(\Omega^-=\{y<0\}\) and \(\Omega^+=\{y>0\}\setminus F\). Above any positive height, the family is locally finite; its only new accumulation points as \(j\to\infty\) lie on the included horizontal axis. Hence \(F\) is closed. It has empty interior, so the sets are open and disjoint, their union is \(\mathbb R^2\setminus F\), and its boundary is exactly \(F\). Every \(K_{j,k}\) belongs to \(\partial\Omega^+\), and the entire axis belongs to \(\partial\Omega^+\cap\partial\Omega^-\). The union has infinite diameter.
## Uniform CDC, including every center and scale

At an axis point, a closed horizontal segment of length \(r\) lies in \(F\cap B(z,r)\) and has logarithmic capacity \(r/4\). At \(z\in K_{j,k}\), write \(h=h_j\) and \(\ell=h/4\). For \(0<r<\ell\), choose the basic Cantor cylinder containing \(z\) whose length \(L=\ell3^{-m}\) first becomes at most \(r/2\). Then \(r/6<L\le r/2\), the entire cylinder lies in \(B(z,r)\), and its capacity is \(qL>qr/6\). For \(\ell\le r\le2h\), a first-generation cylinder containing \(z\) has length \(\ell/3<r\); its capacity is \(q h/12\ge qr/24\). For \(r>2h\), the axis segment of length \(r\) centered below \(z\) lies in \(B(z,r)\), since its maximum distance is \(\sqrt{h^2+(r/2)^2}<r\), and has capacity \(r/4\). Monotonicity proves the required CDC with \(c=\min(q/24,1/4)>0\), for every \(z\in F\) and \(r>0\). All comparison subsets lie strictly inside the balls.
## The square function vanishes

Fix \(x=(a,0)\). The radii for which \(S(x,r)\) hits an off-axis piece form \[D_x=\bigcup_{j,k}\{|y-x|:y\in K_{j,k}\}.\] Each distance map is Lipschitz, so each image has Hausdorff dimension at most \(d<1\). The countable union has Lebesgue measure zero. For \(r\notin D_x\), the spherical sections are complementary open semicircles. The unit semicircle has first Dirichlet eigenvalue \(1\); the relation \(\lambda=\alpha(n-1+\alpha)\) at \(n=1\) gives \(\alpha^+=\alpha^-=1\). Therefore \[\min(1,\alpha^+(x,r)+\alpha^-(x,r)-2)=0
 \ \text{for almost every }r>0,\qquad \mathcal A(x)^2=0.\] The exceptional set is also null for \(dr/r\) on \((0,1)\), by first restricting to \([1/m,1]\). The integrand is bounded by one even at exceptional radii.
## There is no true tangent

Since the complete axis lies in the boundary union, a normal with a nonzero horizontal component has axis points in some double cone at every scale. Any possible tangent must thus be horizontal, with vertical normal. Choose \(k_j\) nearest to \(a/h_j\). Since \(0\in C\), \(z_j=(k_jh_j,h_j)\in K_{j,k_j}\), \(z_j\to x\), and \[\frac{|(z_j-x)\cdot e_2|}{|z_j-x|}
 \ge\frac1{\sqrt{1+(1/2)^2}}=\frac2{\sqrt5}>\frac12.\] The cone \(X_{1/2}(x,e_2)\) contains boundary points arbitrarily close to \(x\). The true-tangent definition fails on the entire axis, not an \(\mathcal H^1\)-null set.
## Counterevidence, dependency, and repair limit

The example is compatible with the measure-theoretic results. The off-axis sets have area zero and \(\mathcal H^1\) measure zero. At axis centers \(\varepsilon_1\) and the smooth half-space coefficient are zero; the axis is rectifiable and has its expected \(L^1\) tangent. The failure is the upgrade to the topological true tangent.

The Jordan-domain theorem on 3/209 has stronger hypotheses. Our punctured upper domain is not Jordan, and Theorem B does not assume it is. Changing the sets on null sets is no response: the true-tangent definition sees these boundary points, and the added sets have positive logarithmic capacity.

The proof’s dimension obstruction is explicit. Proposition 15.1 requires \(s>1\) (89/295), whereas in dimension one the attempted application in Lemma 16.1 uses a CDC exponent \(s\in(0,1)\) (93/299 and 97/303). The spherical thick-point definition on 12/218 treats \(n\ge3\) and \(n=2\), not \(n=1\). Defining a negative-index quantity cannot remove the example.

A necessary correction is to remove \(n=1\) from this CDC-only claim, or to supply a stronger planar hypothesis and a separate proof. The construction does not decide the \(n\ge2\) theorem. Restricting dimension removes this counterexample only; it does not complete the verification of the remaining proof. Adoption and acceptance remain pending.
# Problem 2: a scale-dependent Gaussian translation

Locations. Lemma 9.1 and Remark 9.2, 50/256; the last estimate and (9.3), 51/257. The useful assertion is that, for each small \(\lambda>0\), one can choose a small \(\epsilon\) and then \(\delta\) so that \[\mathfrak a^\pm(x,r)<\lambda\quad
 (x\in N_{2\epsilon r_0}(L_{B_0})\cap B_0,\quad
 10\epsilon r_0\le r\le r_0).\] Its assumption is a small square function on \(E\). Remark 9.2 requires \(\epsilon\ll\lambda\), and the proof takes \(10\epsilon<\lambda\).

Complete check. Take \(n=1\), \(B_0=B(0,1)\), \(E=[-0.9,0.9]\times\{0\}\), \(\mu=\frac12\mathcal H^1|_E\), and \(c_0=0.1\). The growth bound is \(\mu(B(z,r))\le r\) and \(\mu(B_0)=0.9\ge c_0\). The center lies in \(E\), which also meets the outer annular region when required. Let \(\Omega^\pm\) be the complementary open upper and lower half-planes. Every coefficient in (9.1) vanishes on \(E\) at every radius, so the assumption holds for every \(\delta>0\). The minimizing line is the horizontal axis.

For any \(0<\epsilon\le0.1\), choose \(x=(0,\epsilon)\) and \(r=10\epsilon\). Both restrictions hold. Direct Gaussian integration in general dimension gives \[r^{-(n+1)}\int_{\{y_{n+1}>0\}}e^{-|x-y|^2/r^2}\,dy
 =\frac{\pi^{(n+1)/2}}2
 \left(1+\operatorname{erf}\frac{x_{n+1}}r\right).\] Hence, for both signs, \[\mathfrak a^\pm(x,r)=\frac{\pi^{(n+1)/2}}2\operatorname{erf}(1/10).\] At \(n=1\) this is \(0.176656335382\ldots\), independently of \(\epsilon\). Taking \(\lambda=0.05\) contradicts the asserted nonvacuous small-\(\epsilon\) conclusion, despite the zero input square function.

Definition convention. The calculation uses \(\mathfrak a^i=\mathfrak a_\psi^i\) with the constant \(c_\psi=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}\psi\) defined in Section 3.2 (16/222). The subsequent display on 18/224 also writes the reference integral over \(\mathbb R^{n+1}_+\) with a kernel centered at \(x\). If that half-space is read literally as the fixed coordinate half-space, the same example instead gives \(\mathfrak a^+(x,r)=0\) and \(\mathfrak a^-(x,r)=\pi^{(n+1)/2}\operatorname{erf}(1/10)\). The minus coefficient still violates (9.2). Thus neither reading removes the counterexample; the equal values for both signs above use the explicit constant-reference definition.

Alternative reading. The bare existential wording permits \(\epsilon>0.1\), making the radius interval empty. Such an isolated vacuous reading is not refuted, but it is incompatible with Remark 9.2, (9.3), and the stated useful application. The finding concerns that explicitly intended regime.

Fault and supported local correction. The limiting translation estimate on 51/257 omits the scale normalization. For \(K_r(y)=r^{-(n+1)}e^{-|y|^2/r^2}\), \[\|K_r(\cdot-x)-K_r(\cdot-x')\|_1
 \le\|\nabla K_r\|_1|x-x'|=C_n|x-x'|/r.\] Thus displacement \(O(\epsilon r_0)\) costs \(O(\epsilon r_0/r)\), not uniformly \(O(\epsilon)\). A separate fixed minimum scale \(r\ge\eta r_0\) gives \(C_n\epsilon/\eta\), small after \(\epsilon\ll\lambda\eta\). Alternatively the strip must shrink with \(\lambda\) relative to the minimum radius.

Section 10 uses this input for domain splitting in Main Lemma I, which feeds the rectifiability proof. Its macroscopic test radii suggest a repair by separating the parameters and revising their order. The full downstream replacement has not been verified. The half-plane example does not refute the main rectifiability conclusion.
# Problem 3: localization loses the \(99\%\) target

Locations and dependency. Theorem A*, 5/211, and Lemma 11.1, 59–60/265–266, require a single Lipschitz graph with \(\mu(\Gamma)\ge0.99\mu(B_0)\). Claim 13.1, 69/275, replaces \(\mu\) by \(\mu|_{B_1}\) and \(B_0\) by \(\widetilde B_1/100\). The selected \(B_1\) is only guaranteed to have a fixed positive fraction of the original mass. Section 14.3, 88/294, finishes with \(99\%\) of the new measure on the new \(E_0\).

Logical check. The restricted conclusion is \[(\mu|_{B_1})(\Gamma)\ge0.99\mu(B_1).\] From \(\mu(B_1)\ge c(c_0)\mu(B_0)\) this gives only \(\mu(\Gamma)\ge0.99c(c_0)\mu(B_0)\). Adjusting \(c_0\) does not change the denominator in the target.

An explicit witness satisfying the original assumptions illustrates the lost implication. Use the half-planes, \(B_0\), \(E\), \(\mu\), and \(c_0\) from Problem 2. Flatness and half-space splitting are exact. The reflection coefficient \(\mathfrak g\) in Lemma 11.1 vanishes for every center in \(E\) and every radius. Its assumptions hold for arbitrarily small positive \(\theta\) and \(\varepsilon\).

Take \(B_1=B((-1/2,0),10^{-4})\) and \(B_2=B((1/2,0),10^{-4})\). They are centered in \(E\), with equal positive radii, and \(\operatorname{dist}(B_1,B_2)=0.9998\ge1000\,10^{-4}\). Their radii and masses are fixed positive fractions of the original quantities, as in the claimed comparability conditions. The smallest ball concentric with \(B_1\) containing \(B_2\) has radius \(1.0001\), giving new base radius \(0.010001\). The restricted support lies in that base ball; the center of \(B_2\) lies in its \(99\)–\(100\) annulus. The new mass lower bound holds with \(c_0'=0.001\). All flatness and symmetry assumptions persist.

Let \[I=[-0.5002,-0.4998],\qquad
 \Gamma=\{(t,0.01\,\operatorname{dist}(t,I)):t\in\mathbb R\}.\] This graph has slope at most \(0.01<0.1\) and contains \(E\cap B_1\). It satisfies the restricted conclusion, whereas \[\mu(B_0)=0.9,\quad\mu(B_1)=10^{-4},\quad
 \mu(\Gamma)=\tfrac12|I|=0.0002<0.891=0.99\mu(B_0).\] These numbers illustrate the transfer failure; they are not asserted to be the unique balls selected by the cited selection lemma.

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The horizontal axis covers the entire measure in this example. This refutes the stated transfer of a graph’s restricted conclusion, not existence of a suitable global graph. A union of local graphs need not be one graph with the required slope.

A positive-mass graph suffices for the qualitative contradiction argument in Theorem A. The unsupported strength is the near-total mass statement in Theorem A* and Lemma 11.1. A repair must retain the original mass, or provide global selection/gluing that preserves both the fraction and the single-graph constraint. Weakening the target to a fixed positive fraction changes the statement. No complete repair of the stronger claim is supplied.
# Two local analytic problems
## Problem 4: spherical coarea and a complete measurability repair
Location. Remark 2.6(ii), 13/219, equates an unweighted integral of latitude-section measures to upper-hemisphere surface measure outside \(\Omega^+\). The tangential coarea Jacobian is missing.

On \(S^2\), take the allowed Borel set \(\Omega^+=\varnothing\). A latitude of height \(h\in(0,1)\) has length \(2\pi\sqrt{1-h^2}\), so \[\int_0^1 2\pi\sqrt{1-h^2}\,dh=\frac{\pi^2}{2}
 \ne2\pi=\mathcal H^2(S^2_+).\] The correct height coarea factor is \((1-h^2)^{-1/2}\). If a finite-measure set of centers is needed in the surrounding discussion, a compact patch containing this center suffices; the mismatch is pointwise.

The intended measurability assertion has a direct proof. For a unit vector \(u\), put \[A(x,r,u)=\int_{S^n}\!
 \left[{\bf1}_{\omega\cdot u>0}{\bf1}_{(\Omega^+)^c}(x+r\omega)
 +{\bf1}_{\omega\cdot u<0}{\bf1}_{(\Omega^-)^c}(x+r\omega)\right]d\sigma(\omega).\] The integrand and its parameter integral are jointly Borel. For fixed \((x,r)\), changing \(u\) to \(v\) changes this integral by at most the measure of the hemisphere symmetric differences. That bound tends to zero as \(v\to u\), independently of \(\Omega^\pm\). Thus \(A(x,r,\cdot)\) is continuous. If \((u_m)\) is countable and dense, \[\varepsilon_n(x,r)=\inf_m A(x,r,u_m).\] This gives joint Borel measurability. Integrating the nonnegative square against \(dr/r\) gives square-function measurability. The \(r^{-n}\) factor is already canceled by the unit-sphere parametrization. This is a complete local repair without the false coarea identity or a fixed-radius section argument. The defect is peripheral: Minor.
## Problem 5: the kernel tail has the wrong homogeneity

Location. Lemma 3.3, 17/223. Its first constant may depend on \(\psi\), but its displayed linear tail has a dimension-only coefficient. Write \[I=\int_0^R\mathfrak a_\psi(x,r)^2\frac{dr}{r},\quad
 J=\int_0^{MR}\varepsilon_n(x,r)^2\frac{dr}{r},\quad
 T_\phi=\int_M^\infty\phi(t)t^n\sqrt{\log^+(t/M)}\,dt.\] The proof gives \(\sqrt I\le A_\phi\sqrt J+C_nT_\phi\), which supports \[I\le2A_\phi^2J+2C_n^2T_\phi^2,\] not the claimed uniformly linear tail.

For a complete test, take \(x=0\), \(M=R=1\). Inside \(B(0,1)\) let \(\Omega^\pm\) be complementary half-balls; outside assign all points to \(\Omega^+\) and none to \(\Omega^-\). The sets are disjoint Borel. For \(r<1\), \(\varepsilon_n(0,r)=0\), so \(J=0\). Choose nonzero nonnegative \(\phi_0\in C_c^\infty((2,3))\) and put \(\phi=A\phi_0\), \(\psi(y)=\phi(|y|)\). Every stated kernel integrability condition holds for all \(A>0\). For \(1/2\le r\le1\) the kernel is supported outside the unit ball. With \(c_{\psi_0}=\frac12\int\psi_0>0\), both signs satisfy \(\mathfrak a_\psi^\pm(0,r)=A c_{\psi_0}\). Thus \[I\ge A^2c_{\psi_0}^2\log2,\qquad T_\phi=A T_{\phi_0}.\] No dimension-only constant bounds this quadratic lower bound by the printed linear tail as \(A\to\infty\). The first coefficient cannot help, since it multiplies \(J=0\).

The squared-tail estimate above is verified. A kernel-dependent linear coefficient also follows by bounding one factor of the squared tail by the fixed weighted kernel norm. The later fixed Gaussian and normalized kernel are not refuted by this amplitude test. Assessment: Minor.
# Two local scope problems
## Problem 6: spectral equality is insensitive to polar punctures
Location. The rigidity assertion after (1.5), 5/211, is made for arbitrary disjoint open subsets of \(S^n\) and identifies equality with exact complementary hemispheres.

Take \(n=3\), complementary open hemispheres \(H^\pm\subset S^3\), and north pole \(p\). Let \(V^+=H^+\setminus\{p\}\) and \(V^-=H^-\). They are open and disjoint, but not exact complementary hemispheres. A cutoff zero on \(B(p,\rho)\), one outside \(B(p,2\rho)\), with gradient \(O(\rho^{-1})\), has energy \(O(\rho^{3-2})=O(\rho)\). Multiplying smooth compactly supported test functions on \(H^+\) by this cutoff approximates them in \(H^1\). Density gives \[H_0^1(H^+\setminus\{p\})=H_0^1(H^+).\] The first eigenvalue remains \(3\) and hence \(\alpha^+=\alpha^-=1\) by \(\lambda=\alpha(2+\alpha)\). Equality holds despite the puncture.

This does not dispute the inequality. Equality must be described modulo sets of zero Sobolev capacity, or under extra regularity excluding such punctures. The capacity discussion in Allen–Kriventsov–Neumayer [3] supports this distinction. No core failure is inferred from this local rigidity overstatement. Assessment: Minor.
## Problem 7: unrestricted slicing centers

Locations. Proposition 15.1 and Lemma 15.2, 89/295; their proof, 90/296; the use in Lemma 16.1, 97/303. The proposition permits any compact \(G\subset\Gamma\), without restricting \(G\) to \(B(0,r_0)\), yet bounds an expression containing \(\mathcal H^n(G)^2/r_0^n\).

Fix \(n=2\), \(s=3/2\), \(r_0=1\), \(\tau=10^{-3}\), and \(\Gamma=\mathbb R^2\times\{0\}\). Take \(B=B((0,0,1/2),1/20)\) and \(F=\overline B((0,0,1/2),1/40)\). Then \(B\subset B(0,1)\), its radius is below \(1/10\), \(\operatorname{dist}(B,\Gamma)=0.45\ge100\tau\), and \(F\subset B\) is compact. Normalized volume measure on \(F\) has finite \(s\)-energy since \(s<3\), so \(\operatorname{Cap}_s(F)>0\). Let \(G_T\) be the radius-\(T\) closed disk in \(\Gamma\), allowed for every \(T\).

Write \(d=\operatorname{diam}F=1/20\). For \(K\subset F\), the energy definition gives \(\operatorname{Cap}_{s-1}(K)\le d^{s-1}\), since every pairwise distance is at most \(d\). For each \(z\), radii whose spheres hit \(F\) occupy an interval of length at most \(d\). Consequently \[\int_0^\infty\operatorname{Cap}_{s-1}(F\cap S(z,r))\,dr\le d^s.\] The asserted inequality would give \[\operatorname{Cap}_s(F)(\pi T^2)^2\le C(\tau)d^s\pi T^2
 \quad\text{for every }T,\] impossible as \(T\to\infty\).

The missing restriction also enters the comparison \(|z-x|+|z-y|\asymp r_0\) and the bounded strip-measure claim for the graph. The eventual application uses \(G=E\cap\frac14B_0\) and therefore has a bounded center range. Adding an appropriate localization removes this obstruction and matches that use; every localized transversality constant has not been verified here. This is a Minor overscope of the auxiliary proposition, not a counterexample to its localized application.

For a radial smooth kernel, the multiplier scaling in Lemma 12.2 is \[\int_0^\infty|\widehat\phi(r\xi)-\widehat\phi(0)|^2\,\frac{dr}{r^3}
 =C_\phi|\xi|^2.\] Evenness gives a numerator \(O(r^4|\xi|^4)\) near zero, and the integrand is \(O(r^{-3})\) at infinity. The change of variables is legitimate; the zero frequency contributes zero.
