problems.title: a planar counterexample to Theorem B
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: # Problem 1: a planar counterexample to Theorem B
claim: TheoremB n=1
analysis:
Locations and claim. Theorem B, 6/212, explicitly assumes \(n\ge1\), two disjoint open subsets \(\Omega^\pm\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\), and the CDC for their union. It asserts, up to an \(\mathcal H^n\)-null set, that \(\mathcal A(x)<\infty\) is equivalent to a true tangent. The definition on 3/209 tests the union \(\partial\Omega^+\cup\partial\Omega^-\) against every sufficiently narrow double cone. Definition 2.2, 11/217, specifies logarithmic capacity when \(n=1\): \[\operatorname{Cap}_L(B(z,r)\setminus(\Omega^+\cup\Omega^-))\ge c r
 \quad(z\in\partial(\Omega^+\cup\Omega^-),\ 0<r<\operatorname{diam}(\Omega^+\cup\Omega^-)).\]

Let \(C\subset[0,1]\) be the middle-third Cantor set, and put \(d=\log2/\log3\in(0,1)\). Its standard probability measure has a bound \(
u(B(t,ho))\le Aho^d\) for \(0<ho<1\): choose basic Cantor intervals of length \(3^{-m}\) comparable to \(ho\); an interval of length \(2ho\) meets at most a fixed number, each of mass \(2^{-m}\). Consequently, \[\iint\log^+ rac1{|u-v|}\,d
u(u)d
u(v)
 =\int_0^\infty(
u	imes
u)\{|u-v|<e^{-t}\}\,dt
 \le A\int_0^\infty e^{-dt}\,dt<\infty .\] Thus \(q:=\operatorname{Cap}_L(C)>0\). Translation and dilation give \(\operatorname{Cap}_L(a+\ell C)=\ell q\).

For \(j\ge1\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\), define \[h_j=2^{-j},\quad
 K_{j,k}=\bigl(kh_j+(h_j/4)C\bigr)\times\{h_j\},\quad
 F=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup\bigcup_{j,k}K_{j,k}.\] Set \(\Omega^-=\{y<0\}\) and \(\Omega^+=\{y>0\}\setminus F\). Above any positive height, the family is locally finite; its only new accumulation points as \(j\to\infty\) lie on the included horizontal axis. Hence \(F\) is closed. It has empty interior, so the sets are open and disjoint, their union is \(\mathbb R^2\setminus F\), and its boundary is exactly \(F\). Every \(K_{j,k}\) belongs to \(\partial\Omega^+\), and the entire axis belongs to \(\partial\Omega^+\cap\partial\Omega^-\). The union has infinite diameter.

At an axis point, a closed horizontal segment of length \(r\) lies in \(F\cap B(z,r)\) and has logarithmic capacity \(r/4\). At \(z\in K_{j,k}\), write \(h=h_j\) and \(\ell=h/4\). For \(0<r<\ell\), choose the basic Cantor cylinder containing \(z\) whose length \(L=\ell3^{-m}\) first becomes at most \(r/2\). Then \(r/6<L\le r/2\), the entire cylinder lies in \(B(z,r)\), and its capacity is \(qL>qr/6\). For \(\ell\le r\le2h\), a first-generation cylinder containing \(z\) has length \(\ell/3<r\); its capacity is \(q h/12\ge qr/24\). For \(r>2h\), the axis segment of length \(r\) centered below \(z\) lies in \(B(z,r)\), since its maximum distance is \(\sqrt{h^2+(r/2)^2}<r\), and has capacity \(r/4\). Monotonicity proves the required CDC with \(c=\min(q/24,1/4)>0\), for every \(z\in F\) and \(r>0\). All comparison subsets lie strictly inside the balls.

Fix \(x=(a,0)\). The radii for which \(S(x,r)\) hits an off-axis piece form \[D_x=\bigcup_{j,k}\{|y-x|:y\in K_{j,k}\}.\] Each distance map is Lipschitz, so each image has Hausdorff dimension at most \(d<1\). The countable union has Lebesgue measure zero. For \(r\notin D_x\), the spherical sections are complementary open semicircles. The unit semicircle has first Dirichlet eigenvalue \(1\); the relation \(\lambda=\alpha(n-1+\alpha)\) at \(n=1\) gives \(\alpha^+=\alpha^-=1\). Therefore \[\min(1,\alpha^+(x,r)+\alpha^-(x,r)-2)=0
 \ \text{for almost every }r>0,\qquad \mathcal A(x)^2=0.\] The exceptional set is also null for \(dr/r\) on \((0,1)\), by first restricting to \([1/m,1]\). The integrand is bounded by one even at exceptional radii.

Since the complete axis lies in the boundary union, a normal with a nonzero horizontal component has axis points in some double cone at every scale. Any possible tangent must thus be horizontal, with vertical normal. Choose \(k_j\) nearest to \(a/h_j\). Since \(0\in C\), \(z_j=(k_jh_j,h_j)\in K_{j,k_j}\), \(z_j\to x\), and \[\frac{|(z_j-x)\cdot e_2|}{|z_j-x|}
 \ge\frac1{\sqrt{1+(1/2)^2}}=\frac2{\sqrt5}>\frac12.\] The cone \(X_{1/2}(x,e_2)\) contains boundary points arbitrarily close to \(x\). The true-tangent definition fails on the entire axis, not an \(\mathcal H^1\)-null set.
result: The example is compatible with the measure-theoretic results. The off-axis sets have area zero and \(\mathcal H^1\) measure zero. At axis centers \(\varepsilon_1\) and the smooth half-space coefficient are zero; the axis is rectifiable and has its expected \(L^1\) tangent. The failure is the upgrade to the topological true tangent.

The Jordan-domain theorem on 3/209 has stronger hypotheses. Our punctured upper domain is not Jordan, and Theorem B does not assume it is. Changing the sets on null sets is no response: the true-tangent definition sees these boundary points, and the added sets have positive logarithmic capacity.

The proof’s dimension obstruction is explicit. Proposition 15.1 requires \(s>1\) (89/295), whereas in dimension one the attempted application in Lemma 16.1 uses a CDC exponent \(s\in(0,1)\) (93/299 and 97/303). The spherical thick-point definition on 12/218 treats \(n\ge3\) and \(n=2\), not \(n=1\). Defining a negative-index quantity cannot remove the example.

A necessary correction is to remove \(n=1\) from this CDC-only claim, or to supply a stronger planar hypothesis and a separate proof. The construction does not decide the \(n\ge2\) theorem. Restricting dimension removes this counterexample only; it does not complete the verification of the remaining proof. Adoption and acceptance remain pending.

problems.title: a scale-dependent Gaussian translation
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: # Problem 2: a scale-dependent Gaussian translation
claim: Lemma9.1 useful small-epsilon regime
analysis:
Locations. Lemma 9.1 and Remark 9.2, 50/256; the last estimate and (9.3), 51/257. The useful assertion is that, for each small \(\lambda>0\), one can choose a small \(\epsilon\) and then \(\delta\) so that \[\mathfrak a^\pm(x,r)<\lambda\quad
 (x\in N_{2\epsilon r_0}(L_{B_0})\cap B_0,\quad
 10\epsilon r_0\le r\le r_0).\] Its assumption is a small square function on \(E\). Remark 9.2 requires \(\epsilon\ll\lambda\), and the proof takes \(10\epsilon<\lambda\).

Complete check. Take \(n=1\), \(B_0=B(0,1)\), \(E=[-0.9,0.9]\times\{0\}\), \(\mu=\frac12\mathcal H^1|_E\), and \(c_0=0.1\). The growth bound is \(\mu(B(z,r))\le r\) and \(\mu(B_0)=0.9\ge c_0\). The center lies in \(E\), which also meets the outer annular region when required. Let \(\Omega^\pm\) be the complementary open upper and lower half-planes. Every coefficient in (9.1) vanishes on \(E\) at every radius, so the assumption holds for every \(\delta>0\). The minimizing line is the horizontal axis.

For any \(0<\epsilon\le0.1\), choose \(x=(0,\epsilon)\) and \(r=10\epsilon\). Both restrictions hold. Direct Gaussian integration in general dimension gives \[r^{-(n+1)}\int_{\{y_{n+1}>0\}}e^{-|x-y|^2/r^2}\,dy
 =\frac{\pi^{(n+1)/2}}2
 \left(1+\operatorname{erf}\frac{x_{n+1}}r\right).\] Hence, for both signs, \[\mathfrak a^\pm(x,r)=\frac{\pi^{(n+1)/2}}2\operatorname{erf}(1/10).\] At \(n=1\) this is \(0.176656335382\ldots\), independently of \(\epsilon\). Taking \(\lambda=0.05\) contradicts the asserted nonvacuous small-\(\epsilon\) conclusion, despite the zero input square function.

Definition convention. The calculation uses \(\mathfrak a^i=\mathfrak a_\psi^i\) with the constant \(c_\psi=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^{n+1}}\psi\) defined in Section 3.2 (16/222). The subsequent display on 18/224 also writes the reference integral over \(\mathbb R^{n+1}_+\) with a kernel centered at \(x\). If that half-space is read literally as the fixed coordinate half-space, the same example instead gives \(\mathfrak a^+(x,r)=0\) and \(\mathfrak a^-(x,r)=\pi^{(n+1)/2}\operatorname{erf}(1/10)\). The minus coefficient still violates (9.2). Thus neither reading removes the counterexample; the equal values for both signs above use the explicit constant-reference definition.

Alternative reading. The bare existential wording permits \(\epsilon>0.1\), making the radius interval empty. Such an isolated vacuous reading is not refuted, but it is incompatible with Remark 9.2, (9.3), and the stated useful application. The finding concerns that explicitly intended regime.

Fault and supported local correction. The limiting translation estimate on 51/257 omits the scale normalization. For \(K_r(y)=r^{-(n+1)}e^{-|y|^2/r^2}\), \[\|K_r(\cdot-x)-K_r(\cdot-x')\|_1
 \le\|\nabla K_r\|_1|x-x'|=C_n|x-x'|/r.\] Thus displacement \(O(\epsilon r_0)\) costs \(O(\epsilon r_0/r)\), not uniformly \(O(\epsilon)\). A separate fixed minimum scale \(r\ge\eta r_0\) gives \(C_n\epsilon/\eta\), small after \(\epsilon\ll\lambda\eta\). Alternatively the strip must shrink with \(\lambda\) relative to the minimum radius.

Section 10 uses this input for domain splitting in Main Lemma I, which feeds the rectifiability proof. Its macroscopic test radii suggest a repair by separating the parameters and revising their order. The full downstream replacement has not been verified. The half-plane example does not refute the main rectifiability conclusion.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Bare existential epsilon>.1 makes interval empty; finding concerns explicitly required epsilon<<lambda. Main rectifiability not refuted. Section3.2 uses constant c_psi; the shifted-reference halfspace display on PDF18 read literally yields a_plus=0 and a_minus=pi^((n+1)/2)erf(0.1), so the conclusion still fails for the minus sign. Equal values for both signs refer to Section3.2.

claim: Claim13.1 mass-preserving reduction
analysis: Locations and dependency. Theorem A*, 5/211, and Lemma 11.1, 59–60/265–266, require a single Lipschitz graph with \(\mu(\Gamma)\ge0.99\mu(B_0)\). Claim 13.1, 69/275, replaces \(\mu\) by \(\mu|_{B_1}\) and \(B_0\) by \(\widetilde B_1/100\). The selected \(B_1\) is only guaranteed to have a fixed positive fraction of the original mass. Section 14.3, 88/294, finishes with \(99\%\) of the new measure on the new \(E_0\).

Logical check. The restricted conclusion is \[(\mu|_{B_1})(\Gamma)\ge0.99\mu(B_1).\] From \(\mu(B_1)\ge c(c_0)\mu(B_0)\) this gives only \(\mu(\Gamma)\ge0.99c(c_0)\mu(B_0)\). Adjusting \(c_0\) does not change the denominator in the target.

An explicit witness satisfying the original assumptions illustrates the lost implication. Use the half-planes, \(B_0\), \(E\), \(\mu\), and \(c_0\) from Problem 2. Flatness and half-space splitting are exact. The reflection coefficient \(\mathfrak g\) in Lemma 11.1 vanishes for every center in \(E\) and every radius. Its assumptions hold for arbitrarily small positive \(\theta\) and \(\varepsilon\).

Take \(B_1=B((-1/2,0),10^{-4})\) and \(B_2=B((1/2,0),10^{-4})\). They are centered in \(E\), with equal positive radii, and \(\operatorname{dist}(B_1,B_2)=0.9998\ge1000\,10^{-4}\). Their radii and masses are fixed positive fractions of the original quantities, as in the claimed comparability conditions. The smallest ball concentric with \(B_1\) containing \(B_2\) has radius \(1.0001\), giving new base radius \(0.010001\). The restricted support lies in that base ball; the center of \(B_2\) lies in its \(99\)–\(100\) annulus. The new mass lower bound holds with \(c_0'=0.001\). All flatness and symmetry assumptions persist.

Let \[I=[-0.5002,-0.4998],\qquad
 \Gamma=\{(t,0.01\,\operatorname{dist}(t,I)):t\in\mathbb R\}.\] This graph has slope at most \(0.01<0.1\) and contains \(E\cap B_1\). It satisfies the restricted conclusion, whereas \[\mu(B_0)=0.9,\quad\mu(B_1)=10^{-4},\quad
 \mu(\Gamma)=\tfrac12|I|=0.0002<0.891=0.99\mu(B_0).\] These numbers illustrate the transfer failure; they are not asserted to be the unique balls selected by the cited selection lemma.

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The horizontal axis covers the entire measure in this example. This refutes the stated transfer of a graph’s restricted conclusion, not existence of a suitable global graph. A union of local graphs need not be one graph with the required slope.

A positive-mass graph suffices for the qualitative contradiction argument in Theorem A. The unsupported strength is the near-total mass statement in Theorem A* and Lemma 11.1. A repair must retain the original mass, or provide global selection/gluing that preserves both the fraction and the single-graph constraint. Weakening the target to a fixed positive fraction changes the statement. No complete repair of the stronger claim is supplied.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Global horizontal graph exists in example; no counterexample to existence theorem or qualitative rectifiability. Illustrative balls need not be unique selection.

problems.title: spherical coarea and a complete measurability repair
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: ## Problem 4: spherical coarea and a complete measurability repair
claim: Remark2.6(ii) coarea
analysis: Location. Remark 2.6(ii), 13/219, equates an unweighted integral of latitude-section measures to upper-hemisphere surface measure outside \(\Omega^+\). The tangential coarea Jacobian is missing.

On \(S^2\), take the allowed Borel set \(\Omega^+=\varnothing\). A latitude of height \(h\in(0,1)\) has length \(2\pi\sqrt{1-h^2}\), so \[\int_0^1 2\pi\sqrt{1-h^2}\,dh=\frac{\pi^2}{2}
 \ne2\pi=\mathcal H^2(S^2_+).\] The correct height coarea factor is \((1-h^2)^{-1/2}\). If a finite-measure set of centers is needed in the surrounding discussion, a compact patch containing this center suffices; the mismatch is pointwise.

The intended measurability assertion has a direct proof. For a unit vector \(u\), put \[A(x,r,u)=\int_{S^n}\!
 \left[{\bf1}_{\omega\cdot u>0}{\bf1}_{(\Omega^+)^c}(x+r\omega)
 +{\bf1}_{\omega\cdot u<0}{\bf1}_{(\Omega^-)^c}(x+r\omega)\right]d\sigma(\omega).\] The integrand and its parameter integral are jointly Borel. For fixed \((x,r)\), changing \(u\) to \(v\) changes this integral by at most the measure of the hemisphere symmetric differences. That bound tends to zero as \(v\to u\), independently of \(\Omega^\pm\). Thus \(A(x,r,\cdot)\) is continuous. If \((u_m)\) is countable and dense, \[\varepsilon_n(x,r)=\inf_m A(x,r,u_m).\] This gives joint Borel measurability. Integrating the nonnegative square against \(dr/r\) gives square-function measurability. The \(r^{-n}\) factor is already canceled by the unit-sphere parametrization. This is a complete local repair without the false coarea identity or a fixed-radius section argument. The defect is peripheral: Minor.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Measurability itself is true; local proof route false.

claim: Lemma3.3 tail constant
analysis:

 J=\int_0^{MR}\varepsilon_n(x,r)^2\frac{dr}{r},\quad
 T_\phi=\int_M^\infty\phi(t)t^n\sqrt{\log^+(t/M)}\,dt.\] The proof gives \(\sqrt I\le A_\phi\sqrt J+C_nT_\phi\), which supports \[I\le2A_\phi^2J+2C_n^2T_\phi^2,\] not the claimed uniformly linear tail.

For a complete test, take \(x=0\), \(M=R=1\). Inside \(B(0,1)\) let \(\Omega^\pm\) be complementary half-balls; outside assign all points to \(\Omega^+\) and none to \(\Omega^-\). The sets are disjoint Borel. For \(r<1\), \(\varepsilon_n(0,r)=0\), so \(J=0\). Choose nonzero nonnegative \(\phi_0\in C_c^\infty((2,3))\) and put \(\phi=A\phi_0\), \(\psi(y)=\phi(|y|)\). Every stated kernel integrability condition holds for all \(A>0\). For \(1/2\le r\le1\) the kernel is supported outside the unit ball. With \(c_{\psi_0}=\frac12\int\psi_0>0\), both signs satisfy \(\mathfrak a_\psi^\pm(0,r)=A c_{\psi_0}\). Thus \[I\ge A^2c_{\psi_0}^2\log2,\qquad T_\phi=A T_{\phi_0}.\] No dimension-only constant bounds this quadratic lower bound by the printed linear tail as \(A\to\infty\). The first coefficient cannot help, since it multiplies \(J=0\).

The squared-tail estimate above is verified. A kernel-dependent linear coefficient also follows by bounding one factor of the squared tail by the fixed weighted kernel norm. The later fixed Gaussian and normalized kernel are not refuted by this amplitude test. Assessment: Minor.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Later fixed kernels not refuted; could absorb fixednorm into kernel-dependent constant.

problems.title: spectral equality is insensitive to polar punctures
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: ## Problem 6: spectral equality is insensitive to polar punctures
claim: Rigidity after1.5
analysis: Location. The rigidity assertion after (1.5), 5/211, is made for arbitrary disjoint open subsets of \(S^n\) and identifies equality with exact complementary hemispheres.

Take \(n=3\), complementary open hemispheres \(H^\pm\subset S^3\), and north pole \(p\). Let \(V^+=H^+\setminus\{p\}\) and \(V^-=H^-\). They are open and disjoint, but not exact complementary hemispheres. A cutoff zero on \(B(p,\rho)\), one outside \(B(p,2\rho)\), with gradient \(O(\rho^{-1})\), has energy \(O(\rho^{3-2})=O(\rho)\). Multiplying smooth compactly supported test functions on \(H^+\) by this cutoff approximates them in \(H^1\). Density gives \[H_0^1(H^+\setminus\{p\})=H_0^1(H^+).\] The first eigenvalue remains \(3\) and hence \(\alpha^+=\alpha^-=1\) by \(\lambda=\alpha(2+\alpha)\). Equality holds despite the puncture.

This does not dispute the inequality. Equality must be described modulo sets of zero Sobolev capacity, or under extra regularity excluding such punctures. The capacity discussion in Allen–Kriventsov–Neumayer [3] supports this distinction. No core failure is inferred from this local rigidity overstatement. Assessment: Minor.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Inequality itself valid; equality may conventionally be meant modulo capacity.

analysis: Locations. Proposition 15.1 and Lemma 15.2, 89/295; their proof, 90/296; the use in Lemma 16.1, 97/303. The proposition permits any compact \(G\subset\Gamma\), without restricting \(G\) to \(B(0,r_0)\), yet bounds an expression containing \(\mathcal H^n(G)^2/r_0^n\).

Fix \(n=2\), \(s=3/2\), \(r_0=1\), \(\tau=10^{-3}\), and \(\Gamma=\mathbb R^2\times\{0\}\). Take \(B=B((0,0,1/2),1/20)\) and \(F=\overline B((0,0,1/2),1/40)\). Then \(B\subset B(0,1)\), its radius is below \(1/10\), \(\operatorname{dist}(B,\Gamma)=0.45\ge100\tau\), and \(F\subset B\) is compact. Normalized volume measure on \(F\) has finite \(s\)-energy since \(s<3\), so \(\operatorname{Cap}_s(F)>0\). Let \(G_T\) be the radius-\(T\) closed disk in \(\Gamma\), allowed for every \(T\).

Write \(d=\operatorname{diam}F=1/20\). For \(K\subset F\), the energy definition gives \(\operatorname{Cap}_{s-1}(K)\le d^{s-1}\), since every pairwise distance is at most \(d\). For each \(z\), radii whose spheres hit \(F\) occupy an interval of length at most \(d\). Consequently \[\int_0^\infty\operatorname{Cap}_{s-1}(F\cap S(z,r))\,dr\le d^s.\] The asserted inequality would give \[\operatorname{Cap}_s(F)(\pi T^2)^2\le C(\tau)d^s\pi T^2
 \quad\text{for every }T,\] impossible as \(T\to\infty\).

Title: Formal initial review: M25-0078
The spectrum of excisive functors
# Scope and initial outcome

All 102 pages of the acquired publisher PDF were read, including the appendix and references. Locations below use one-based PDF page / printed page; printed page equals PDF page plus 362. Related author source arXiv:2402.04244v2 was parsed in full for structure and dependencies. It is not identified with the publisher’s TeX. All findings below concern the bound publisher PDF.

Initial outcome: Major. Two central proofs use an invalid intermediate inference: the passage from relative openness to ambient openness in Theorem 11.22, and the replacement of a proper-family Tate construction by ordinary cyclic Tate cohomology in Theorem 12.27. The first has a complete local repair. For the second, a direct elementary-abelian argument supplies the missing nonvanishing mechanism. Neither finding is a counterexample to the stated main classification. Four additional auxiliary assertions require restrictions or corrections.
No. | Confirmed assertion or inference | Judgment
1 | Theorem 11.22, 84/446: a finite relative open need not be ambient open. | Major
2 | Theorem 12.27, 96–97/458–459: the cyclic target is the wrong Tate construction. | Major
3 | Proposition 2.38, 18/380: arbitrary limit shapes do not give a smashing localization. | Minor
4 | Remark 2.28, 17/379: compact objects require stable, not only finite-colimit, generation. | Minor
5 | Corollary 8.13, 58/420: the first unital presentation omits \(x_1=1\). | Minor
6 | Definition 10.27 and Example 10.28, 76–77/438–439: non-\(p\)-local scope is inconsistent. | Minor
The severity reflects the role of the defective inference, not a claim that a repair is impossible. Finite computations supplement the proofs below and do not certify every imported theorem.
# Problem 1: relative openness in the geometric blueshift proof

Exact location. Theorem 11.22, paragraph following (11.25), 84/446; setup (11.24) on 83/445 and subsequent use on 84–85/446–447. Write \(X=\operatorname{Spc}(\mathrm{Exc}_d(\mathrm{Sp}^c,\mathrm{Sp})^c)\). The truncated spectrum is a finite subspace \(V=V_{\le h+n}\) of \(X\). The proof takes \[W=V\setminus(\overline{\{P_d([l],p,h)\}}\cap V)\] and asserts that its finiteness and relative openness make it open in \(X\), then chooses a compact \(z\) with \(\operatorname{supp}(z)=X\setminus W\). The second assertion requires ambient quasi-compact openness.
## A legal instance where ambient openness fails

Take \(d=2\), \(l=1\), \(p=2\), \(h=1\). The partition \(2\) has length one, so \(\delta_2(2,1)=1\) and the proof uses \(n=0\). Here \[V=\{P_2([1],0,1),P_2([2],0,1)\}.\] Proposition 11.7 excludes an inclusion between the two primes at equal finite height. Thus \(W=\{P_2([2],0,1)\}\).

Under the embedding \(\operatorname{Spc}(\partial_2):\operatorname{Spc}(\mathrm{Sp}^c)\to X\) from Proposition 7.7, the inverse image of this \(W\) is the singleton \(\{C_{0,1}\}\). That singleton is not open in the integral finite-spectrum Balmer spectrum. Indeed, a basic open \(U(a)\) containing \(C_{0,1}\) means that the finite spectrum \(a\) is rationally acyclic. Its integral homology is finite torsion in finitely many degrees, so only finitely many primes occur. For every other prime \(q\), \(a_{(q)}=0\). Consequently \(U(a)\) also contains the \(q\)-primary chromatic points. Every open neighborhood of \(C_{0,1}\) contains such a basic neighborhood, and cannot be the singleton. Continuity therefore proves that \(W\) is not open in \(X\). In particular \(X\setminus W\) cannot be the closed support claimed in the printed proof.
## Complete repair of the support-selection step

The actual argument only needs (11.25), not equality of the support with \(X\setminus W\). Since \(W\) is relatively open, choose an ambient open \(O\) with \(O\cap V=W\). For each \(w\in W\), choose a basic quasi-compact open \(B_w\) with \(w\in B_w\subset O\). The union \[U=\bigcup_{w\in W}B_w\] is a finite union of quasi-compact opens, and \(U\cap V=W\). Balmer’s Proposition 2.14 [Balmer] gives a compact \(z\) with \(U=X\setminus\operatorname{supp}(z)\). Hence \[\operatorname{supp}(z)\cap V=V\setminus W
 =\overline{\{P_d([l],p,h)\}}\cap V,\] exactly (11.25). If \(W\) is empty, take the tensor unit instead.

Downstream check and limits. The derivative tests in (11.27)–(11.29) only use this intersection identity, compactness, and dualizability. The triangle-inequality contradiction for \(\delta_p\) is unchanged. The Tate-vanishing step on the truncated category can use the right-adjoint identity in Remark 6.17. The support-splitting criterion used on 85/447 is [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition 2.29]{PSW}], whose hypothesis is a compact object and a Thomason subset; those hypotheses hold after the finite localization. When \(h+n=1\), the relevant Tate derivatives vanish directly by Theorem 10.33, avoiding an unnecessary height-zero prime comparison. Thus the replacement repairs this specific gap. It is not a new independent proof of every earlier categorical construction.

Impact and counterevidence. This is a false inference in the core lower-bound proof, hence Major under the review standard. The support object actually needed does exist; the main theorem is not refuted. Working in an explicitly \(p\)-localized ambient category could also alter the openness issue, but the printed setup names the integral category and does not make that replacement.
# Problem 2: ordinary and proper-family Tate constructions

Exact location. Proof of Theorem 12.27, 96–97/458–459, the computation after (12.28) and the ring map on 97/459 attributed to Theorem 10.33. Compare the actual construction on 78/440, and Definitions 10.16–10.17.

For a nontrivial cyclic \(p\)-group \(C\), the restriction constructed in Theorem 10.33 has target \[(H\mathbb F_p)^{t\mathcal P(C)}
 =\Phi^C\bigl(\text{Borel-completed }H\mathbb F_p\bigr),\] where \(\mathcal P(C)\) is the family of all proper subgroups. The proof of Theorem 12.27 instead writes \((H\mathbb F_p)^{tC}\) and asserts nonvanishing using ordinary Tate cohomology. The two constructions coincide for \(C=C_p\), but not for higher prime-power order. The distinction is explicit in the paper’s own family notation and in [Retained latex: \cite[Definition 3.3]{BHN}].
## The actual target is zero for a permitted cyclic group

Take \(k=d=4\), \(l=1\), \(p=2\), \(\lambda=(4)\). The long-cycle subgroup is \(C=C_4\subset\Sigma_4\). Its proper subgroups are \(e\) and \(C_2\), both nontransitive, so the restricted family is precisely \(\mathcal P(C_4)\).

The reduced real regular representation is a sign line plus a real rotation plane: \(\bar\rho=\epsilon\oplus\eta\). Let \(v\in H^1(BC_4;\mathbb F_2)\) be the parity homomorphism. It satisfies \(v^2=0\). This can be checked without a cohomology-ring lookup: for representatives \(a=0,1,2,3\), put \(b(a)=\lfloor a/2\rfloor\bmod2\). With trivial coefficients, \[\delta b(a,c)=b(c)-b(a+c\bmod4)+b(a)
             =(a\bmod2)(c\bmod2).\] All sixteen pairs were also checked exactly in the independent script. Thus the mod-two Euler class of \(\bar\rho\) satisfies \[e(\bar\rho)=v\,w_2(\eta),\qquad e(\bar\rho)^2=0.\] The representation-sphere model of Example 10.10 and Lemma 10.24, together with the mod-two Thom isomorphism, identifies the homotopy groups of the proper-family construction with the localization of \(H^*(BC_4;\mathbb F_2)\) at this Euler class. Equivalently, its direct-system maps multiply by \(e(\bar\rho)\). Every element becomes zero after at most two such maps. Therefore \[(H\mathbb F_2)^{t\mathcal P(C_4)}=0.\] In contrast, ordinary \((H\mathbb F_2)^{tC_4}\) is nonzero: the complete periodic cyclic resolution has alternating maps \(g-1\) and \(1+g+g^2+g^3\), both zero on the trivial \(\mathbb F_2\) module. The asserted nonzero target cannot be the target constructed earlier.

What this does and does not disprove. It disproves the cited nonvanishing argument for a legal partition. It does not show that the \(\Sigma_4\) family factor vanishes, or that the prime inclusion in Theorem 12.27 is false. Indeed, restriction to the regular subgroup \(C_2^2\) gives the Euler class \(xy(x+y)\) in \(\mathbb F_2[x,y]\), which is nonnilpotent. That provides the required nonzero target in this instance.
## A repair using elementary abelian groups

For any \(p\)-power partition \(\lambda=(p^{e_1},\ldots,p^{e_l})\) with \(l<k\), use \[E=\prod_{i=1}^l E_i,\qquad E_i=(C_p)^{e_i},\] with the regular permutation action of \(E_i\) on its block. The restriction of the representation in Lemma 10.24 is \(V=\bigoplus_i\bar\rho_{E_i}\), inflated to the product. Its Euler class is a product of nonzero linear forms in the polynomial part of \(H^*(BE;\mathbb F_p)\), up to nonzero scalar factors. For \(p=2\) these are the nontrivial real characters in degree one. For odd \(p\), the nontrivial characters pair into oriented real planes; their Euler classes are nonzero degree-two linear forms. Blocks of size one contribute the unit.

The polynomial part is an integral domain. For odd \(p\), the full cohomology is free over that polynomial part with an exterior basis. Consequently \(e(V)\) is not nilpotent and \[H^*(BE;\mathbb F_p)[e(V)^{-1}]\ne0.\] The representation-sphere model and restriction give a unital ring map from \((H\mathbb F_p)^{t\mathcal F_{\rm nt}(\lambda)}\) to this nonzero construction. It follows that the factor is nonzero. Proposition 10.26 then gives nonzero \(\partial_l t_k i_k(H\mathbb F_p)\). This is a general argument; the finite polynomial calculations are only supporting checks.
## Coefficient exchange should also be made explicit

The printed calculation on 96/458 invokes Proposition 6.14 to commute free \(H\mathbb Z\) extension with a Tate construction. The Tate assertion there has a closed-monoidal hypothesis; it is not justified merely by a strong monoidal left adjoint. This review does not count a separate counterexample to that particular exchange.

One can avoid the unestablished exchange. First pass to the \(k\)-excisive truncation, which preserves compactness and the derivatives of degrees at most \(k\). Let \(U\) be the forgetful functor from \(H\mathbb Z\)-module-valued functors to spectrum-valued functors. It preserves limits and colimits, hence commutes with the derivative construction. The right-adjoint formula of Remark 6.17, applied to \(t=i_k(S/p)\), identifies \[U\bigl(t_k^\mathbb Zi_k^\mathbb Z(H\mathbb F_p)\bigr)
       \simeq t_k i_k(H\mathbb F_p).\] Here free extension sends \(i_k(S/p)\) to \(i_k^\mathbb Z(H\mathbb F_p)\), and \(t\otimes U1\) is \(i_k(H\mathbb F_p)\). Thus \(M=\partial_l^\mathbb Zt_k^\mathbb Zi_k^\mathbb Z(H\mathbb F_p)\) is a nonzero \(H\mathbb F_p\)-module by the elementary-abelian argument.

For the compact object \(x\) in (12.28), dualizability and \(\partial_k^\mathbb Z(i_k^\mathbb Z(H\mathbb F_p)\mathbin{\circledast}x)=0\) give \[0=M\otimes_{H\mathbb Z}\partial_l^\mathbb Zx
   \simeq
 M\otimes_{H\mathbb F_p}
       \bigl(H\mathbb F_p\otimes_{H\mathbb Z}\partial_l^\mathbb Zx\bigr).\] Tensor product with a nonzero complex over the field \(\mathbb F_p\) detects zero: choose nonzero homology classes in both factors and use the field Künneth formula. Hence \(H\mathbb F_p\otimes_{H\mathbb Z}\partial_l^\mathbb Zx=0\). This proves the required inclusion for a single \(p\)-power partition; the partition-chain argument handles the remaining congruent pairs.

Impact and repair limits. The coefficient-spectrum classification has a Major proof gap as printed. The above replacement gives its missing algebraic nonvanishing and uses an explicit right-adjoint comparison. The full coherence of the surrounding Day-convolution and module category constructions has not been reconstructed from first principles here; no scientific acceptance is inferred from this repair.
# Problem 3: arbitrary limit shapes in Proposition 2.38

Location. Proposition 2.38 and its proof, 18/380, with the unrestricted small family of diagrams in Remark 2.37. The argument uses left exactness of filtered colimits to assert closure of the local objects under filtered colimits. Left exactness only controls finite limit shapes.
## Counterexample satisfying the stated tensor stability

Fix a prime \(p\). For every finite spectrum \(X\), include in \(J\) the inverse tower \[\cdots\xrightarrow{p}X\xrightarrow{p}X\] with cone vertex \(0\) and zero cone maps. Use an essentially small skeleton and its tensor closure. This is a small set of diagrams, closed under postcomposition with tensoring by any finite spectrum.

For \(j\ge1\) let \(F_j(X)=H(\mathbb Z/p^j)\otimes X\). These are reduced, linear functors. On \(H(\mathbb Z/p^j)\) the \(j\)-fold composite in the inverse \(p\)-tower is zero. Its inverse limit and derived inverse limit vanish; explicitly the tower is pro-zero, and the Milnor sequence gives a contractible homotopy limit. Tensoring with a finite \(X\) preserves that limit because \(X\) is dualizable. Therefore every \(F_j\) sends every diagram in \(J\) to a limit diagram.

The maps \(\mathbb Z/p^j\to\mathbb Z/p^{j+1}\), \(a\mapsto pa\), induce a filtered system with colimit \[F(X)=H(P)\otimes X,\qquad P=\mathbb Z[1/p]/\mathbb Z.\] At \(X=S\), the inverse \(p\)-tower on \(P\) has a nonzero compatible element \[x_n=p^{-(n+1)}+\mathbb Z,\qquad p x_{n+1}=x_n.\] Because \(\pi_1 HP=0\), the Milnor sequence identifies \(\pi_0\operatorname{holim}(\cdots HP\xrightarrow p HP)\) with \(\lim_p P\), which contains this nonzero element. Thus \(F\) is not \(J\)-local.

Consequence. The inclusion of local objects does not preserve this filtered colimit, so the localization endofunctor is not smashing in Definition 2.34. This does not challenge the existence of the localization or tensor compatibility alone.

Repair and counterevidence. Restrict the allowed shapes to finite limit diagrams, in particular finite poset cubes. Colimits in spectra commute with finite limits; the local subcategory is then colimit closed. The actual Goodwillie-excision application in Theorem 2.39 uses finite cubes, so that application survives this restriction. The finding concerns auxiliary generality and is Minor. An assumption ensuring colimit closure by another argument would also suffice; tensor stability of \(J\) alone does not.
# Problem 4: finite colimits do not generate all compact objects
Location. Remark 2.28, 17/379. It characterizes compact functors as retracts of finite colimits of corepresentable functors \(h_X=\Sigma^\infty\operatorname{Map}(X,-)\).

Each \(h_X\) is objectwise connective. Spectra that are connective stay connective under finite colimits and retracts, and these operations in the functor category are objectwise. But \(\Sigma^{-1}h_S\) is compact: corepresentables are compact and suspension is an autoequivalence preserving compactness. At \(S\) its \(\pi_{-1}\) is \(\pi_0 h_S(S)\ne0\), since the stable degree components of \(\operatorname{Map}(S,S)\) give nontrivial reduced zeroth homology. It cannot lie in the stated finite-colimit/retract closure.

Repair and limits. Use the thick stable closure of the corepresentables, or finite colimits and retracts of all their integer suspensions. Compact generation, dualizability, and closure under the objectwise smash product then extend through this stable closure. The cited Ching Lemma 4.14 was checked and uses the same abbreviated finite-colimit wording; this report does not attribute a missing qualification to that reference or claim the wording originated here. The explicit closure characterization needs the correction, but no main classification is refuted. Judgment: Minor.
# Problem 5: the missing unit relation in Corollary 8.13
Location. First presentation and proof of Corollary 8.13, 58/420; relations (8.11) on 57/419.

Let \(B=\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_d]/I\), with \(I\) generated only by the displayed multiplication relations \[x_i x_j=\sum_l\mu(i,j,l)x_l .\] Evaluation at all \(x_i=0\) is a unital map \(B\to\mathbb Z\), so these relations cannot imply \(x_1=1\). Already for \(d=1\), \[B=\mathbb Z[x_1]/(x_1^2-x_1)\cong\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z,
 \qquad A(1)=\mathbb Z.\] This is a counterexample to the first presentation, not merely a failure of its proof.

More generally the product rules give \(x_1x_i=x_i\), and all positive degree monomials reduce to integer combinations of the \(x_i\). There is an explicit isomorphism \[B\longrightarrow \mathbb Z\times A(d),\qquad
 1\longmapsto(1,1),\quad x_i\longmapsto(0,x_i).\] Surjectivity follows using \(1-x_1\) and the \(x_i\). For injectivity reduce any polynomial to \(a_0+\sum_i a_i x_i\) and use the given free abelian basis of \(A(d)\): the first coordinate determines \(a_0\), and then the second determines all \(a_i\). Thus the omitted relation adds a whole extra factor.

Repair and counterevidence. Add \(x_1-1\) to \(I\), or use the paper’s second presentation over \(\mathbb Z[x_2,\ldots,x_d]\) with \(x_1\) interpreted as \(1\). The actual construction of \(A(d)\) by its mark embedding and the identification \(R(d)\cong A(d)\) through the derivative marks remain valid. The separate malformed product display in Theorem 9.25 is an evident index/typesetting error whose intended rule is fixed by its proof; it is not counted as another finding. Judgment: Minor.
# Problem 6: nonlocal spectra in the height convention
Locations. Definition 10.27, Example 10.28 and Remark 10.29, 76–77/438–439; \(C_{p,0}=\mathrm{Sp}^c_{(p)}\) in Example 6.5, 41/403.

The definition takes the infimum over \(h\in\mathbb N\cup\{-1,\infty\}\) such that \(M\otimes C_{p,h+1}=0\). Example 10.28 then asserts that every spectrum which is not \(p\)-local has infinite \(p\)-height. Choose a distinct prime \(q\) and \(M=H\mathbb F_q\). For every finite \(p\)-local spectrum \(X\), multiplication by \(q\) is invertible on \(X\) and zero on \(H\mathbb F_q\). Therefore \(H\mathbb F_q\otimes X=0\). The \(h=-1\) condition holds, and the literal definition gives \[\operatorname{height}_p(H\mathbb F_q)=-1.\] Yet this nonzero spectrum is not \(p\)-local. It also cannot satisfy \(M\simeq L^f_{p,h}M\) for any listed \(h\): at \(h=-1\) the target is zero, and for other \(h\) it is \(p\)-local. The rewritten infimum in Remark 10.29 therefore gives infinity.

Repair and limits. Restrict the definition and equivalence to \(p\)-local \(M\), replacing the sphere example by \(S_{(p)}\), or explicitly define the height of arbitrary \(M\) through \(M_{(p)}\) and rewrite the subsequent criterion accordingly. The spectra \(L^f_{p,h}S\) and their Tate derivatives used in Theorem 10.33 are \(p\)-local, so this counterexample does not refute that theorem. It concerns the advertised scope of the definition and is Minor.
# Positive checks, proof dependencies, and coverage
## Definitions, monoidal structures, and generators

The functors are reduced; Day convolution is distinguished from objectwise smash throughout this review. The source is finite spectra, with finitary extension where used. The \(d\)-excisive localization and the finite derivative family were tracked through the recollement, compact generation, and prime classification. The Boolean cross-effect idempotents were checked algebraically: with \(\psi_U\psi_V=\psi_{U\cap V}\), \[c_U=\sum_{V\subset U}(-1)^{|U|-|V|}\psi_V\] are mutually orthogonal and sum to the identity. Exact finite checks cover up to five inputs. The empty-subset convention in one product rewrite does not alter the first or third defining formula or the subsequent arguments; it is not counted as a substantive finding.

For the generators \(P_dh_S(i)\), the derivative formula uses \(|\operatorname{surj}(k,i)|\) copies of the sphere, with the appropriate vanishing for \(k<i\). The tensor product formula counts subsets of \([i]\times[j]\) projecting onto both factors. Independent enumeration for \(i,j\le3\) agrees with the inclusion-exclusion formula. The surjection-product identity was checked for \(k\le12\). For the integral mark matrix, \[M_{ki}=i!\,\left\{\begin{matrix}k\\i\end{matrix}\right\},
 \qquad M=L\,\operatorname{diag}(1!,\ldots,d!),\] the Stirling matrix \(L\) is lower triangular and unimodular. This justifies the cokernel factors \(\mathbb Z/i!\), rather than inferring them from a triangular diagonal alone. Smith forms were checked through \(d=8\). Mark-prime congruences were checked for \(d=20\) and primes at most 19. The trace generators in Section 9 and the \(d!\) transfer argument were checked against this mark description.
## Tate derivatives, height, and partition chains

Proposition 10.26 was followed through its partition indexing, Young subgroup, and representation-sphere family. The vanishing direction uses a Sylow subgroup contained in the nontransitive family and a prime-to-\(p\) index. For Theorem 10.33, ordinary Tate vanishing supplies the upper bound. For the lower bound the diagonal cyclic subgroup has order the largest block size. Every proper subgroup fails transitivity on a block of maximal size; this is the needed reason the restricted family consists of all proper subgroups. It need not fail transitivity on every smaller block. The abelian-group height theorem cited there concerns the finite-local sphere and gives a drop by the cyclic group’s \(p\)-rank one [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 1.5]{BHN}]. It does not justify substituting ordinary \(H\mathbb F_p\) Tate cohomology in Problem 2.

The base-\(p\) digit sum, splitting/carrying operations and the two-step partition construction were checked analytically. Dynamic programming independently enumerated partition lengths and shortest chains for \(1\le l\le k\le128\) at \(p=2,3,5,7,11\): 41,280 pairs, including 720 two-step cases. They agree with \[\delta_p(k,l)=
 \begin{cases}
 0 & k=l,\\
 1 & k>l,\ k\equiv l\pmod{p-1},\ l\ge s_p(k),\\
 2 & k>l,\ k\equiv l\pmod{p-1},\ l<s_p(k),\\
 \infty & \text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}\] This finite enumeration is not a substitute for the general proof. The height shifts, the distinction between equal finite heights and infinite height, and the restriction \(p=q\) away from height one were checked in the prime-inclusion statement.
## Applications and boundaries of the audit

Thomason subsets, admissible type functions, and the order of the correspondence were traced through Section 12. The type uses nonvanishing Morava \(K\)-homology; the original page image confirms the nonzero symbol that extraction can lose. The Smith/Floyd discussion uses the appropriate compactness, idempotent actions, and field dimensions; the separate caveat on multiplicative Morava theories at the prime two was read. The coefficient classification, noetherian description, and stratification/costratification/telescope applications were followed through their stated dependencies. Appendix A and all references were read.

Not fully reconstructed are all infinity-categorical coherences of Day convolution, Kan extension and module comparisons; full external nilpotence/chromatic and stratification theorems; and every detail of the external Smith-to-Floyd idempotent-filtration argument. Those limitations are recorded as remaining scientific work, not converted into confirmed defects. Isolated index or extraction errors with an unambiguous correct argument were excluded.

problems.title: relative openness in the geometric blueshift proof
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: # Problem 1: relative openness in the geometric blueshift proof
claim: Ambient openness in Theorem11.22
analysis: Exact location. Theorem 11.22, paragraph following (11.25), 84/446; setup (11.24) on 83/445 and subsequent use on 84–85/446–447. Write \(X=\operatorname{Spc}(\mathrm{Exc}_d(\mathrm{Sp}^c,\mathrm{Sp})^c)\). The truncated spectrum is a finite subspace \(V=V_{\le h+n}\) of \(X\). The proof takes \[W=V\setminus(\overline{\{P_d([l],p,h)\}}\cap V)\] and asserts that its finiteness and relative openness make it open in \(X\), then chooses a compact \(z\) with \(\operatorname{supp}(z)=X\setminus W\). The second assertion requires ambient quasi-compact openness.

Take \(d=2\), \(l=1\), \(p=2\), \(h=1\). The partition \(2\) has length one, so \(\delta_2(2,1)=1\) and the proof uses \(n=0\). Here \[V=\{P_2([1],0,1),P_2([2],0,1)\}.\] Proposition 11.7 excludes an inclusion between the two primes at equal finite height. Thus \(W=\{P_2([2],0,1)\}\).

Under the embedding \(\operatorname{Spc}(\partial_2):\operatorname{Spc}(\mathrm{Sp}^c)\to X\) from Proposition 7.7, the inverse image of this \(W\) is the singleton \(\{C_{0,1}\}\). That singleton is not open in the integral finite-spectrum Balmer spectrum. Indeed, a basic open \(U(a)\) containing \(C_{0,1}\) means that the finite spectrum \(a\) is rationally acyclic. Its integral homology is finite torsion in finitely many degrees, so only finitely many primes occur. For every other prime \(q\), \(a_{(q)}=0\). Consequently \(U(a)\) also contains the \(q\)-primary chromatic points. Every open neighborhood of \(C_{0,1}\) contains such a basic neighborhood, and cannot be the singleton. Continuity therefore proves that \(W\) is not open in \(X\). In particular \(X\setminus W\) cannot be the closed support claimed in the printed proof.

The actual argument only needs (11.25), not equality of the support with \(X\setminus W\). Since \(W\) is relatively open, choose an ambient open \(O\) with \(O\cap V=W\). For each \(w\in W\), choose a basic quasi-compact open \(B_w\) with \(w\in B_w\subset O\). The union \[U=\bigcup_{w\in W}B_w\] is a finite union of quasi-compact opens, and \(U\cap V=W\). Balmer’s Proposition 2.14 [Balmer] gives a compact \(z\) with \(U=X\setminus\operatorname{supp}(z)\). Hence \[\operatorname{supp}(z)\cap V=V\setminus W
 =\overline{\{P_d([l],p,h)\}}\cap V,\] exactly (11.25). If \(W\) is empty, take the tensor unit instead.

Downstream check and limits. The derivative tests in (11.27)–(11.29) only use this intersection identity, compactness, and dualizability. The triangle-inequality contradiction for \(\delta_p\) is unchanged. The Tate-vanishing step on the truncated category can use the right-adjoint identity in Remark 6.17. The support-splitting criterion used on 85/447 is [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition 2.29]{PSW}], whose hypothesis is a compact object and a Thomason subset; those hypotheses hold after the finite localization. When \(h+n=1\), the relevant Tate derivatives vanish directly by Theorem 10.33, avoiding an unnecessary height-zero prime comparison. Thus the replacement repairs this specific gap. It is not a new independent proof of every earlier categorical construction.

Impact and counterevidence. This is a false inference in the core lower-bound proof, hence Major under the review standard. The support object actually needed does exist; the main theorem is not refuted. Working in an explicitly \(p\)-localized ambient category could also alter the openness issue, but the printed setup names the integral category and does not make that replacement.

problems.title: ordinary and proper-family Tate constructions
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: # Problem 2: ordinary and proper-family Tate constructions
claim: Ordinary vs proper-family Tate in Theorem12.27
analysis: Exact location. Proof of Theorem 12.27, 96–97/458–459, the computation after (12.28) and the ring map on 97/459 attributed to Theorem 10.33. Compare the actual construction on 78/440, and Definitions 10.16–10.17.

For a nontrivial cyclic \(p\)-group \(C\), the restriction constructed in Theorem 10.33 has target \[(H\mathbb F_p)^{t\mathcal P(C)}
 =\Phi^C\bigl(\text{Borel-completed }H\mathbb F_p\bigr),\] where \(\mathcal P(C)\) is the family of all proper subgroups. The proof of Theorem 12.27 instead writes \((H\mathbb F_p)^{tC}\) and asserts nonvanishing using ordinary Tate cohomology. The two constructions coincide for \(C=C_p\), but not for higher prime-power order. The distinction is explicit in the paper’s own family notation and in [Retained latex: \cite[Definition 3.3]{BHN}].

Take \(k=d=4\), \(l=1\), \(p=2\), \(\lambda=(4)\). The long-cycle subgroup is \(C=C_4\subset\Sigma_4\). Its proper subgroups are \(e\) and \(C_2\), both nontransitive, so the restricted family is precisely \(\mathcal P(C_4)\).

The reduced real regular representation is a sign line plus a real rotation plane: \(\bar\rho=\epsilon\oplus\eta\). Let \(v\in H^1(BC_4;\mathbb F_2)\) be the parity homomorphism. It satisfies \(v^2=0\). This can be checked without a cohomology-ring lookup: for representatives \(a=0,1,2,3\), put \(b(a)=\lfloor a/2\rfloor\bmod2\). With trivial coefficients, \[\delta b(a,c)=b(c)-b(a+c\bmod4)+b(a)
             =(a\bmod2)(c\bmod2).\] All sixteen pairs were also checked exactly in the independent script. Thus the mod-two Euler class of \(\bar\rho\) satisfies \[e(\bar\rho)=v\,w_2(\eta),\qquad e(\bar\rho)^2=0.\] The representation-sphere model of Example 10.10 and Lemma 10.24, together with the mod-two Thom isomorphism, identifies the homotopy groups of the proper-family construction with the localization of \(H^*(BC_4;\mathbb F_2)\) at this Euler class. Equivalently, its direct-system maps multiply by \(e(\bar\rho)\). Every element becomes zero after at most two such maps. Therefore \[(H\mathbb F_2)^{t\mathcal P(C_4)}=0.\] In contrast, ordinary \((H\mathbb F_2)^{tC_4}\) is nonzero: the complete periodic cyclic resolution has alternating maps \(g-1\) and \(1+g+g^2+g^3\), both zero on the trivial \(\mathbb F_2\) module. The asserted nonzero target cannot be the target constructed earlier.

What this does and does not disprove. It disproves the cited nonvanishing argument for a legal partition. It does not show that the \(\Sigma_4\) family factor vanishes, or that the prime inclusion in Theorem 12.27 is false. Indeed, restriction to the regular subgroup \(C_2^2\) gives the Euler class \(xy(x+y)\) in \(\mathbb F_2[x,y]\), which is nonnilpotent. That provides the required nonzero target in this instance.

The printed calculation on 96/458 invokes Proposition 6.14 to commute free \(H\mathbb Z\) extension with a Tate construction. The Tate assertion there has a closed-monoidal hypothesis; it is not justified merely by a strong monoidal left adjoint. This review does not count a separate counterexample to that particular exchange.

One can avoid the unestablished exchange. First pass to the \(k\)-excisive truncation, which preserves compactness and the derivatives of degrees at most \(k\). Let \(U\) be the forgetful functor from \(H\mathbb Z\)-module-valued functors to spectrum-valued functors. It preserves limits and colimits, hence commutes with the derivative construction. The right-adjoint formula of Remark 6.17, applied to \(t=i_k(S/p)\), identifies \[U\bigl(t_k^\mathbb Zi_k^\mathbb Z(H\mathbb F_p)\bigr)
       \simeq t_k i_k(H\mathbb F_p).\] Here free extension sends \(i_k(S/p)\) to \(i_k^\mathbb Z(H\mathbb F_p)\), and \(t\otimes U1\) is \(i_k(H\mathbb F_p)\). Thus \(M=\partial_l^\mathbb Zt_k^\mathbb Zi_k^\mathbb Z(H\mathbb F_p)\) is a nonzero \(H\mathbb F_p\)-module by the elementary-abelian argument.

For the compact object \(x\) in (12.28), dualizability and \(\partial_k^\mathbb Z(i_k^\mathbb Z(H\mathbb F_p)\mathbin{\circledast}x)=0\) give \[0=M\otimes_{H\mathbb Z}\partial_l^\mathbb Zx
   \simeq
 M\otimes_{H\mathbb F_p}
       \bigl(H\mathbb F_p\otimes_{H\mathbb Z}\partial_l^\mathbb Zx\bigr).\] Tensor product with a nonzero complex over the field \(\mathbb F_p\) detects zero: choose nonzero homology classes in both factors and use the field Künneth formula. Hence \(H\mathbb F_p\otimes_{H\mathbb Z}\partial_l^\mathbb Zx=0\). This proves the required inclusion for a single \(p\)-power partition; the partition-chain argument handles the remaining congruent pairs.

Impact and repair limits. The coefficient-spectrum classification has a Major proof gap as printed. The above replacement gives its missing algebraic nonvanishing and uses an explicit right-adjoint comparison. The full coherence of the surrounding Day-convolution and module category constructions has not been reconstructed from first principles here; no scientific acceptance is inferred from this repair.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Sigma4factor is nonzero via regularC2²; maincoefficient theorem not refuted.

problems.title: arbitrary limit shapes in Proposition 2.38
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: # Problem 3: arbitrary limit shapes in Proposition 2.38
claim: Smashing for arbitrary diagram shapes in Proposition2.38
analysis: Location. Proposition 2.38 and its proof, 18/380, with the unrestricted small family of diagrams in Remark 2.37. The argument uses left exactness of filtered colimits to assert closure of the local objects under filtered colimits. Left exactness only controls finite limit shapes.

Fix a prime \(p\). For every finite spectrum \(X\), include in \(J\) the inverse tower \[\cdots\xrightarrow{p}X\xrightarrow{p}X\] with cone vertex \(0\) and zero cone maps. Use an essentially small skeleton and its tensor closure. This is a small set of diagrams, closed under postcomposition with tensoring by any finite spectrum.

For \(j\ge1\) let \(F_j(X)=H(\mathbb Z/p^j)\otimes X\). These are reduced, linear functors. On \(H(\mathbb Z/p^j)\) the \(j\)-fold composite in the inverse \(p\)-tower is zero. Its inverse limit and derived inverse limit vanish; explicitly the tower is pro-zero, and the Milnor sequence gives a contractible homotopy limit. Tensoring with a finite \(X\) preserves that limit because \(X\) is dualizable. Therefore every \(F_j\) sends every diagram in \(J\) to a limit diagram.

The maps \(\mathbb Z/p^j\to\mathbb Z/p^{j+1}\), \(a\mapsto pa\), induce a filtered system with colimit \[F(X)=H(P)\otimes X,\qquad P=\mathbb Z[1/p]/\mathbb Z.\] At \(X=S\), the inverse \(p\)-tower on \(P\) has a nonzero compatible element \[x_n=p^{-(n+1)}+\mathbb Z,\qquad p x_{n+1}=x_n.\] Because \(\pi_1 HP=0\), the Milnor sequence identifies \(\pi_0\operatorname{holim}(\cdots HP\xrightarrow p HP)\) with \(\lim_p P\), which contains this nonzero element. Thus \(F\) is not \(J\)-local.

Consequence. The inclusion of local objects does not preserve this filtered colimit, so the localization endofunctor is not smashing in Definition 2.34. This does not challenge the existence of the localization or tensor compatibility alone.

Repair and counterevidence. Restrict the allowed shapes to finite limit diagrams, in particular finite poset cubes. Colimits in spectra commute with finite limits; the local subcategory is then colimit closed. The actual Goodwillie-excision application in Theorem 2.39 uses finite cubes, so that application survives this restriction. The finding concerns auxiliary generality and is Minor. An assumption ensuring colimit closure by another argument would also suffice; tensor stability of \(J\) alone does not.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: ActualGoodwillieapplicationfinitecubes survives.

problems.title: finite colimits do not generate all compact objects
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: # Problem 4: finite colimits do not generate all compact objects
claim: Compact finite-colimit characterization in Remark2.28
analysis: Location. Remark 2.28, 17/379. It characterizes compact functors as retracts of finite colimits of corepresentable functors \(h_X=\Sigma^\infty\operatorname{Map}(X,-)\).

Each \(h_X\) is objectwise connective. Spectra that are connective stay connective under finite colimits and retracts, and these operations in the functor category are objectwise. But \(\Sigma^{-1}h_S\) is compact: corepresentables are compact and suspension is an autoequivalence preserving compactness. At \(S\) its \(\pi_{-1}\) is \(\pi_0 h_S(S)\ne0\), since the stable degree components of \(\operatorname{Map}(S,S)\) give nontrivial reduced zeroth homology. It cannot lie in the stated finite-colimit/retract closure.

Repair and limits. Use the thick stable closure of the corepresentables, or finite colimits and retracts of all their integer suspensions. Compact generation, dualizability, and closure under the objectwise smash product then extend through this stable closure. The cited Ching Lemma 4.14 was checked and uses the same abbreviated finite-colimit wording; this report does not attribute a missing qualification to that reference or claim the wording originated here. The explicit closure characterization needs the correction, but no main classification is refuted. Judgment: Minor.

problems.title: the missing unit relation in Corollary 8.13
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 5: # Problem 5: the missing unit relation in Corollary 8.13
claim: Unital presentation in Corollary8.13
analysis: Location. First presentation and proof of Corollary 8.13, 58/420; relations (8.11) on 57/419.

Let \(B=\mathbb Z[x_1,\ldots,x_d]/I\), with \(I\) generated only by the displayed multiplication relations \[x_i x_j=\sum_l\mu(i,j,l)x_l .\] Evaluation at all \(x_i=0\) is a unital map \(B\to\mathbb Z\), so these relations cannot imply \(x_1=1\). Already for \(d=1\), \[B=\mathbb Z[x_1]/(x_1^2-x_1)\cong\mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z,
 \qquad A(1)=\mathbb Z.\] This is a counterexample to the first presentation, not merely a failure of its proof.

More generally the product rules give \(x_1x_i=x_i\), and all positive degree monomials reduce to integer combinations of the \(x_i\). There is an explicit isomorphism \[B\longrightarrow \mathbb Z\times A(d),\qquad
 1\longmapsto(1,1),\quad x_i\longmapsto(0,x_i).\] Surjectivity follows using \(1-x_1\) and the \(x_i\). For injectivity reduce any polynomial to \(a_0+\sum_i a_i x_i\) and use the given free abelian basis of \(A(d)\): the first coordinate determines \(a_0\), and then the second determines all \(a_i\). Thus the omitted relation adds a whole extra factor.

Repair and counterevidence. Add \(x_1-1\) to \(I\), or use the paper’s second presentation over \(\mathbb Z[x_2,\ldots,x_d]\) with \(x_1\) interpreted as \(1\). The actual construction of \(A(d)\) by its mark embedding and the identification \(R(d)\cong A(d)\) through the derivative marks remain valid. The separate malformed product display in Theorem 9.25 is an evident index/typesetting error whose intended rule is fixed by its proof; it is not counted as another finding. Judgment: Minor.

problems.title: nonlocal spectra in the height convention
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: # Problem 6: nonlocal spectra in the height convention
claim: Non-p-local height convention
analysis: Locations. Definition 10.27, Example 10.28 and Remark 10.29, 76–77/438–439; \(C_{p,0}=\mathrm{Sp}^c_{(p)}\) in Example 6.5, 41/403.

The definition takes the infimum over \(h\in\mathbb N\cup\{-1,\infty\}\) such that \(M\otimes C_{p,h+1}=0\). Example 10.28 then asserts that every spectrum which is not \(p\)-local has infinite \(p\)-height. Choose a distinct prime \(q\) and \(M=H\mathbb F_q\). For every finite \(p\)-local spectrum \(X\), multiplication by \(q\) is invertible on \(X\) and zero on \(H\mathbb F_q\). Therefore \(H\mathbb F_q\otimes X=0\). The \(h=-1\) condition holds, and the literal definition gives \[\operatorname{height}_p(H\mathbb F_q)=-1.\] Yet this nonzero spectrum is not \(p\)-local. It also cannot satisfy \(M\simeq L^f_{p,h}M\) for any listed \(h\): at \(h=-1\) the target is zero, and for other \(h\) it is \(p\)-local. The rewritten infimum in Remark 10.29 therefore gives infinity.

Repair and limits. Restrict the definition and equivalence to \(p\)-local \(M\), replacing the sphere example by \(S_{(p)}\), or explicitly define the height of arbitrary \(M\) through \(M_{(p)}\) and rewrite the subsequent criterion accordingly. The spectra \(L^f_{p,h}S\) and their Tate derivatives used in Theorem 10.33 are \(p\)-local, so this counterexample does not refute that theorem. It concerns the advertised scope of the definition and is Minor.

Title: Formal initial review: M25-0079
The \(D\)-equivalence conjecture for hyper-Kähler varieties via hyperholomorphic bundles
# Scope and initial outcome

All 15 PDF pages, including the references, were read continuously and all 15 original page images were actually inspected. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed numbers. The acquired `main.tex` belongs to the same pinned arXiv revision; all 887 lines were parsed for structure, inputs and execution tokens. The author source was not compiled or executed.

Outcome: Major, one confirmed core proof-step error. Lemma 2.1 asserts that a particular set of orthogonal transformations is Zariski open. The assertion fails at transformations for which the restricted linear functional is zero. A smaller nonempty open set gives a complete repair, with precisely the divisor class needed later. This is not a counterexample to Lemma 2.1 or to Theorems 0.2 and 0.3.

The main construction was checked through its arithmetic and geometric interfaces: the choice of a positive transcendental representative, divisibility-one classes, the isotropic Mukai vector, the dual-fiber calculation, both Brauer signs, the MBM square bound and the final divisibility contradiction. Eight groups of independent symbolic and integer checks passed. They supplement the general arguments; they do not independently reconstruct all imported hyperholomorphic deformation theory.

# Confirmed issue: the openness assertion in Lemma 2.1

Location and quantifiers. At the bottom of p. 9 and top of p. 10, put \(P=\operatorname{Pic}(X)\otimes\mathbb C\), \(V=\Lambda\otimes\mathbb C\) and \(w=(W,-)|_P\). The proof asserts that \[S=\{g\in O(V):\ker((g\delta,-)|_P)
e\ker w\}\] is Zariski open. Here \(X\) is projective, \(\operatorname{rk}\operatorname{Pic}(X)\ge2\), \(W^2<0\), and \(\delta^2=2-2n
e0\) for \(n\ge2\). By the Hodge index signature, \(P\) is nondegenerate and \(w
e0\).
## Counterevidence under these hypotheses

Write \(d_0=\delta^2\). The nondegenerate space \(P^\perp\) has complex dimension at least two. Choose \(v\in P^\perp\) with \(v^2=d_0\) and \(g_0\in O(V)\) with \(g_0\delta=v\). Then the restricted functional is zero: \(\ker((v,-)|_P)=P\ne\ker w\), so \(g_0\in S\).

Choose an analytic function \(c(z)\) near zero such that \(c(0)=1\) and \(c(z)^2=1-z^2W^2/d_0\). On the nondegenerate plane spanned by \(v,W\), define \[R(z)v=c(z)v+zW,\qquad
 R(z)W=-z\frac{W^2}{d_0}v+c(z)W,\] and extend \(R(z)\) by the identity on its orthogonal complement. The displayed identity for \(c(z)\) proves directly that \(R(z)\) is orthogonal. Thus \(g(z)=R(z)g_0\) is a curve in \(O(V)\) with \(g(0)=g_0\). For every sufficiently small nonzero \(z\), \[(g(z)\delta,-)|_P=z\,w,\qquad
 \ker((g(z)\delta,-)|_P)=\ker w.\] Consequently \(g(z)\notin S\). The set \(S\) is not even analytically open at \(g_0\), and hence is not Zariski open. This tests the zero-functional boundary that is omitted in the printed openness justification.
## Complete repair and downstream effect

Use instead \[U=\{g\in O(V):((g\delta,-)|_P)\wedge w\ne0\}.\] This is a Zariski open set, defined by nonvanishing of at least one two-by-two minor. It is nonempty: choose \(p\in P\) for which \((p,-)|_P\) is independent of \(w\), then choose \(v'\in P^\perp\) with \((v')^2=d_0-p^2\). Over \(\mathbb C\) such a vector exists. The nonzero-norm vector \(p+v'\) is the image of \(\delta\) under an orthogonal transformation, which belongs to \(U\).

The integral orthogonal group is Zariski dense as used in the paper, so choose \(g\in O(\Lambda)\cap U\). The rational hyperplane \(g(\delta)^\perp\cap\operatorname{Pic}(X)_\mathbb Q\) is not contained in \(W^\perp\). Choose a rational vector there with nonzero pairing with \(W\), clear denominators and take its primitive part \(A\). Both lattice intersections are saturated, so \(A\) remains in the intersection. The lattice \(g(\delta)^\perp\) is a unimodular K3 lattice, hence a primitive vector there has divisibility one in \(\Lambda\). This proves exactly \((A,W)\ne0\) and \(\operatorname{div}(A)=1\).

Impact and repair limit. The false openness assertion is the stated justification for applying integral orthogonal-group density to obtain the divisibility-one class used in Proposition 2.2. That class feeds the Mukai construction in Section 2.2, the wall-avoidance argument of Proposition 2.4, and Theorem 0.3. This is a Major error in a core proof step, even though the nonempty open subset \(U\) above supplies a complete repair. The corrected argument preserves the later constants, Brauer classes and Fourier–Mukai construction. No counterexample to Lemma 2.1 or the derived-equivalence theorem is asserted; integral-group density and global Torelli remain imported inputs.
# Definitions, moduli components and wall reduction

The paper works over \(\mathbb C\), with projective varieties in the main theorems and possibly nonprojective intermediate marked manifolds. Theorem 0.3 quantifies over every Brauer class and gives the naturally corresponding class on a birational partner. Theorem 0.2 is its zero Brauer-class case. For \(n=1\), birational K3 surfaces are isomorphic. For Picard rank one, the absence of a birational wall gives the same trivial case; the construction in Section 2 therefore legitimately assumes an algebraic negative wall class and Picard rank at least two.
## A moduli component check

The space \(\mathcal M_\phi\) requires the rational Hodge isometry to send some Kähler class to a Kähler class. Equality of periods alone is not sufficient. Lemma 1.1 uses the componentwise surjectivity in Markman’s Lemma 5.7 [Markman]. Lemma 1.2 can be justified without assuming that every path lifts merely because a projection is surjective.

Indeed, let \(C,C'\) be the components containing its two quadruples. Their first projections are the same marked-manifold component. Choose a point of Picard rank zero in that component and use surjectivity to find a quadruple over it in each of \(C,C'\). The second projections lie in the same component because the original second factor is the same. Their periods are prescribed by \(\phi\). At Picard rank zero the marked partner of this period in that component is unique by the relevant Torelli statement; the Kähler compatibility is automatic for these quadruples. Thus the two quadruples coincide, so \(C=C'\). Markman’s proof also constructs appropriate generic twistor paths. The manuscript’s abbreviated path argument is not counted as a separate confirmed defect.
## Brauer representatives and walls

For a projective hyper-Kähler manifold, the rational Picard and transcendental spaces split orthogonally. The exponential-sequence description used in (2)–(3) therefore lets a Brauer class be written \([-B/d]\) with integral \(B\in T(X)\) and \(d>0\). Since \(T(X)_\mathbb R\) has two positive directions, a positive integral vector \(v\) exists. Replacing \(B\) by \(B+dNv\) for sufficiently large integer \(N\) preserves the Brauer class and makes \(B^2=2e>0\). Thus the positivity assumption on p. 9 does not restrict the theorem.

The birational Kähler cone is convex within the positive cone. A compact segment between interior points meets finitely many walls by local finiteness; a small perturbation avoids wall intersections. It therefore suffices to treat adjacent chambers. If \(\phi^{-1}W\) is not proportional to an MBM class, its hyperplane does not coincide with a wall on the partner. On a small open part of the separating facet, local finiteness allows a point avoiding those walls. A partner Kähler chamber then meets the images of both adjacent chambers. Its birational model \(Y''\) supplies the two quadruples used in Section 1.6. Lemma 1.2 keeps both in the initial component.

Projectivity is preserved here because the rational Hodge isometry transports a positive rational \((1,1)\) class. The two transported twisted equivalences can therefore be composed. The Brauer classes on \(Y''\) agree because their defining rational classes and marking agree. Inverting one equivalence uses the dual kernel with the appropriate shift; this does not obstruct existence of the composition.

e0\).

The printed prime argument is valid for a sufficiently large prime \(q=|1+tb|>|c|\): a common divisor of \(q\) and \(tc\) divides \(c\) since \(\gcd(q,t)=1\). The final divisibility by \(c\) is not an independent assumption. There is also an elementary infinite choice: take \(t=|c|j\), \(j>0\). Then \(\gcd(1+tb,tc)=1\), so \(\operatorname{div}(A+t\omega)=1\), while its square tends to infinity. This also applies to choosing a suitable \(t\) in \(D+4gtdB\).
## Section 2.2, pp. 10–12

Set \[q=4td^2,\quad r=gq^2=16gt^2d^4,\quad
 s=1+4gt^2d^4(n-1)+16gt^2d^2e,\quad H^2=2gs.\] Then \(m=\epsilon q\), \(\epsilon=\pm1\), and \(m^2H^2=2rs\), so \((r,mH,s)\) is isotropic. Every prime dividing \(r\) divides \(2gtd\); the nonconstant terms of \(s\) are divisible by that prime. Hence \(\gcd(r,s)=1\), giving primitivity and the fine-moduli condition.

The classes \(H-2gtd^2\delta\) and \(D+4gtdB\) have the same square: \[2gs+(2gtd^2)^2(2-2n)=2g+32g^2t^2d^2e.\] Both have divisibility one. The primitive polarization \(H\) has divisibility one in the unimodular K3 lattice; the other class was chosen with that property. The cited primitive-lattice and monodromy criterion therefore gives the parallel transport in (10), allowing the orientation sign \(\epsilon\).

For the local-freeness criterion, divide the rank and first Chern class by their common factor \(q\). The primitive pair has rank \(gq\) and first Chern class \(\epsilon H\). Since \(g>1\), \[gq\nmid H^2/2+1=gs+1.\] Rank one of the Picard group makes \(H\) general in the sense used in Yoshioka’s Lemma 1.2(2) [Yoshioka]. That lemma, whose statement and proof were checked, gives both slope stability and local freeness. Thus the actual bundles satisfy the required stability hypothesis.

Yoshioka’s Theorem 2.2 gives primitive isotropic dual fibers. His Appendix A gives \(\widehat H^2=H^2\) here because \(\gcd(r,s)=1\). Writing their vector as \((r,k\widehat H,\widehat s)\), isotropy yields \(\widehat s=s(k/q)^2\in\mathbb Z\). As \(\gcd(s,q)=1\), prime valuations imply \(q\mid k\). Write \(k=q\ell\). Primitivity forces \(\gcd(r,\ell)=1\), since a prime dividing both divides all three entries. Consequently \[\gcd(r,k)=q,\qquad \frac r{\gcd(r,qk)}=g.\] These identities, including either sign of \(k\), are the exact arithmetic input for Proposition 2.4.
# Brauer sign and exclusion of a second wall
## The prescribed twist, p. 12
## Proposition 2.4, pp. 12–13

Suppose \(\phi^{-1}W=(b/a)W'\) for coprime nonzero integers \(a,b\) and a primitive MBM class \(W'\). If \(u=-W^2\) and \(v=-(W')^2\), isometry gives \(ub^2=va^2\). Coprimality implies \(a^2\mid u\), \(b^2\mid v\), whence \[a^2<C_0,\qquad b^2<C_0\] by the MBM square bound in Theorem 1.5. Transport to the base point preserves the lattice and the deformation-invariant MBM property. Write \(\rho^{-1}W=W_{\rm K3}+\lambda\delta\).

The block decomposition (5) implies \(\phi_U^{-1}(aW_{\rm K3})\) is integral. In Buskin’s Chern-character calculation [Buskin], the only possibly nonintegral mixed contribution is the rank denominator: for \(c_1(U)=mH+k\widehat H\) it is proportional to \((\gamma,H)mk/r\). The K3 intersection form is even, so the remaining Chern-character contribution is integral. Thus integrality requires \[\frac r{\gcd(r,mk)}\mid (H,aW_{\rm K3}).\] Here \(m=\epsilon q\) and the calculation on the preceding page makes the divisor exactly \(g\). The sign convention normalizing the rational Hodge isometry does not affect this integral subgroup.

Equation (10) and \((B,W)=0\) now give \[(H,aW_{\rm K3})=\epsilon aC_1+
     2gtd^2a\,(\rho(\delta),W),
 \qquad g\mid aC_1.\] Since \(a\ne0\), this implies \(g\le |a|C_1\le a^2C_1<C_0C_1\), contradicting \(g>C_0C_1\). This also covers negative \(a\). The proof establishes exactly the wall-avoidance condition needed in Section 1.6. The main result is not refuted by the local openness finding.
