Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Verification of Murmurations
# Identity, recovery basis, and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Nina Zubrilina, Murmurations, Inventiones mathematicae 241 (2025), 627–680, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01347-8 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01347-8). The primary input is the acquired 54-page publisher Version of Record. PDF p. means its one-based PDF page; printed page equals PDF page plus 626. The separate companion arXiv:2310.07681v2 is used only for a static comparison of the cited formulas. Whole-document equivalence is not asserted.

This continuation recovers the substantive report and mathematical checks produced by the predecessor recovery. Its analytic arguments, exact checks, source extraction, and numerical output are retained with their original attribution. The present recovery checks the cited source correspondence and completes the missing verification record; it does not repeat a whole-paper review.

The substantive scope comprises the definitions and main statements in Theorems 1–3 and 5–6 and Corollary 4; the displayed error estimate leading to Proposition 3.1; the Poisson/Bessel reduction in Section 5; and Lemma 7.3 with its use in Section 7.3. Section 8’s computational sign argument was examined for its evidence requirements. The detailed class-number analysis throughout Section 3.3, every intermediate lemma, and the complete proofs in the later repair preprint have not been independently re-proved. No claim of whole-paper correctness is made.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

Equation reference: eq:qbound. Fix an even integer \(k\ge2\). The density \(\mathcal M_k(y)\), for \(y>0\), is defined in Theorem 1. Its weights in Theorem 3 are \[A_p=p^4-2p^2-p+1,\qquad
 Q(d)=\mu^2(d)\prod_{p\mid d}\frac{p^2}{A_p}.\] The constants \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) have the paper’s normalization. In particular \(\alpha>0\), \(Q(1)=1\), \(Q(d)\ge0\), and \[
 Q(d)\ll d^{-2},\] because \(\prod_p p^4/A_p\) converges: every factor is positive and \(1+O(p^{-2})\). None of the arguments below changes the normalization of the standard Bessel function \(J_\nu\).

For the conditional argument, RH has exactly the meaning used in Lemma 7.3: the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function have real part \(1/2\). Theorem 6 additionally assumes fixed \(c>1\) and even \(k\ge6\). For Proposition 3.1, \(P>2\) is prime, \(X\to\infty\), and \(Y=o(X)\); the decisive test below takes \(X=P\) along primes and \(Y=X^{3/4}\), within the actual parameter range of Theorem 1.
# Supported findings

Problem 1 (Incorrect leading normalization in Theorem 3).  The stated asymptotic coefficient differs from the one implied by the exact Bessel representation by the factor \(2\sqrt{\pi}\). Its effect is a leading-order discrepancy, not an error absorbed by the stated \(O(1)\).
## Source and decisive calculation

Equation reference: eq:exact. Theorem 3, PDF p. 5 (printed p. 631), states \[
 \mathcal M_k(y)=\alpha\sqrt y\sum_{d,s\ge1}\frac{Q(d)}s
 J_{k-1}\left(\frac{4\pi s\sqrt y}{d}\right).\] Its next display has the coefficient \(\alpha(-1)^{k/2-1}\sqrt{2/\pi}\) in front of the universal cosine series times \(y^{1/4}\). Section 5, PDF pp. 42–43, derives [eq:exact] (#eq:exact); its last two displays also introduce a sign discrepancy.
## Verification of the remainder and of a counterexample sequence

To demonstrate actual incompatibility of the two asymptotic statements, let \[B=\zeta(3/2)\sum_{d\ge1}Q(d)\sqrt d\in(0,\infty).\] Absolute convergence permits dominated convergence along \(T_n=n!\). For each fixed \(d,s\), eventually \(d\mid n!\), so \[F(n!)\longrightarrow-B/\sqrt2.\] All assumptions of Theorem 3 hold with fixed \(k=2\) and \(y_n=(n!)^2\to\infty\). Formula [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) yields \[\frac{\mathcal M_2((n!)^2)}{\sqrt{n!}}\longrightarrow
            -\frac{\alpha B}{2\pi},\] whereas the printed formula would yield \(-\alpha B/\sqrt\pi\). These limits differ since \(\alpha B>0\). The contradiction is analytic and does not depend on numerical Bessel evaluation or finite sampling.
## Counterevidence, impact, and verified repair

A normalization change cannot reconcile the two displays while preserving their common \(\alpha\), standard \(J_\nu\), and common argument. The phase in the theorem statement is correct; the proof page’s \((-1)^{k/2}\) must instead be \((-1)^{k/2-1}\). The replacement [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) and the split-range proof above repair this asymptotic step, conditional only on the checked Bessel representation. This is Major under the specified calibration because it changes a main theorem’s leading asymptotic. The demonstrated consequence is the normalization error. The order \(y^{1/4}\), universal oscillatory series, and qualitative parity dependence survive. It does not refute the original modular-form correlation result or certify the computational sign-change claim.

Problem 2 (An impossible remainder in Lemma 7.3: known issue reproduced).  The remainder \(R(T)\ll_\varepsilon T^{-2+\varepsilon}\) is incompatible with RH. Theorem 6’s printed proof depends on that remainder.
## Source and noncancellation proof

Equation reference: eq:dirichlet. Lemma 7.3 appears at PDF p. 46 (printed p. 672); its contour argument and Euler product are on PDF p. 47. Write \(B_p=2p^2+p-1\). The exact local identity \(A_p+B_p=p^4\) gives \[
 L(s)=\sum_{d\ge1}Q(d)d^{-s}
     =\frac{\zeta(s+2)}{\zeta(2s+4)}H(s),\qquad
 H(s)=\prod_p\left(1+\frac{B_p}{A_p(1+p^{s+2})}\right).\] Indeed, multiply one \(H\)-factor by \(1+p^{-s-2}\). The result is \(1+p^{2-s}/A_p\), the local factor of \(L(s)\).

On every compact subset of \(\Re s>-2\), the correction in each \(H\)-factor is \(O(p^{-\sigma_0-4})\) for some \(\sigma_0>-2\). Thus the product is locally uniformly absolutely convergent and holomorphic there. Its denominators are nonzero since \(|p^{s+2}|>1\). Assume RH and choose any nontrivial zeta zero \(\rho=\frac12+i\gamma\). At \[s_0=(\rho-4)/2=-\frac74+\frac{i\gamma}{2},\] the denominator in [eq:dirichlet] (#eq:dirichlet) vanishes. The numerator is \(\zeta(\rho/2)\), nonzero under RH because its real part is \(1/4\). An \(H\)-factor could vanish only if \[A_p p^{s_0+2}+p^4=0.\] Taking absolute values and fourth powers would give \(A_p^4=p^{15}\), contrary to \(A_p\equiv1\pmod p\). Every local factor is nonzero at \(s_0\); absolute convergence proves \(H(s_0)\ne0\). Therefore \(L(s)\) has a genuine pole there, without any assumption that \(\rho\) is simple.
## Why the asserted remainder is false

An integer-only interpretation of \(T\) does not help: replacing \(x\) by \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) changes \(\Delta/x\) by \(O(x^{-2})\). Likewise \(d<T\) versus \(d\le T\) changes an endpoint by \(Q(T)=O(T^{-2})\). The argument holds for any fixed \(\Delta\), so the variable misprint in its displayed Euler product is immaterial.
## Dependence, prior correction, and supported judgment

The Euler-factor cancellations in the Poisson/Bessel reduction were checked against PDF pp. 42–43. The companion TeX contains the same normalization, contour, and cutoff problems; this is a local comparison.

report: Abstract: This report examines the published paper’s hypotheses, selected descent and derived-length arguments, and the final rationality/ruledness reductions. One quantified auxiliary proposition fails for the trivial algebraic group. A second, local boundary problem occurs in the stated branch-polynomial construction in dimension two. Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of group theoretical characterizations of rationality
# Paper identity and scope

The reviewed work is Andriy Regeta, Christian Urech, and Immanuel van Santen, Group theoretical characterizations of rationality, Inventiones mathematicae 241 (2025), 681–716, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01348-7 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01348-7) [paper]. The source is the acquired 36-page publisher Version of Record. PDF page \(j\) corresponds to printed page \(680+j\). Statements below concern those exact bytes.

The full extracted article was read to map the argument. Detailed checks concerned the characteristic-zero interpolation in Proposition 4.2, the countable-index and dimension argument leading to Theorem 1.3, Proposition 6.7 and its applications, the boundary construction in Corollary 1.4, and the divisibility obstruction in Proposition 6.9. The Rosenlicht construction and the geometric descent machinery were read as dependencies but not independently re-proved in their entirety. In particular, this review does not independently establish the paper’s imported results on algebraic families, regularization, or rational additive-group actions.
# Definitions and checks of the principal reductions

The standing base field in Sections 5–6 is algebraically closed, uncountable, and of characteristic zero (PDF p. 4 and the relevant section openings). A subgroup is not, by convention, required to be nontrivial: the paper explicitly adds that requirement in statements such as Theorem 6.1. Derived length means the least \(i\) for which the \(i\)-th derived subgroup is trivial, so the identity group has length zero.
## Descent in Proposition 4.2

On PDF pp. 15–16 (printed pp. 695–696), a rational additive action defined over a finite Galois extension is descended by evaluating its rational comorphism at integer times. Let \(F=k(X)\) and let \(L(X)/F\) be that extension. After multiplying a denominator by its conjugates, one obtains \(q(t)\in F[t]\). If \(p(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{m}p_jt^j\) takes values in \(F\) at \(m+1\) consecutive sufficiently large integers, then the coefficient vector lies in \(F^{m+1}\), because \[\det\big((N+i)^j\big)_{0\le i,j\le m}
   =\prod_{0\le i<j\le m}(j-i)\ne0.\] Characteristic zero is essential to this computation and is assumed. The finite set of denominator zeros can be avoided. Thus the interpolation step itself does not hide a positive-characteristic extrapolation. The converse also uses that an additive action whose time-one element fixes \(k(Y)\) fixes it at all integer times and hence identically, by the same rational-function identity principle. This checks the descent mechanism, conditional on the cited correspondence between rationally integrable derivations and rational additive actions.
## Derived length and the equality case

Lemmas 5.5–5.8 and the proof of Theorem 1.3 are on PDF pp. 19–21. The use of uncountability is explicit: an irreducible parameter variety cannot be partitioned into countably many proper closed coset preimages. Countable-index subgroups are consequently dense, allowing the derived-length comparison.

Writing \(d=\dim X-\dim Y\) for the generic-fibre dimension, the induction gives \[\operatorname{len}(G)\le \operatorname{len}(H^\circ)+\operatorname{len}(G/H^\circ)
 \le 2d+2\dim Y=2\dim X.\] If equality holds, both summands attain their individual bounds. Conjugation on the self-centralizing commutative algebraic group on the generic fibre then gives \(2d\le 1+d\); since \(d>0\), this forces \(d=1\). The subsequent additive-group descent and triangular reduction use this one-dimensional case. Closure bars that disappear in plain-text extraction were checked against the rendered source, especially on PDF p. 21. No contradiction in this chain was established.
## The divisibility obstruction

Proposition 6.9 (PDF p. 31) states that for \(\dim X>0\) some \(f\in k(X)^\times\) has no positive power divisible by every positive integer. For a transcendence basis, put \(F=k(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\) and \(D=[k(X):F]\). Given \(l\ge1\), choose a prime \(p>l\) with \(p\nmid D\). The \(t_1\)-adic valuation rules out a \(p\)-th root of \(t_1^l\) in \(F\); the cited Kummer lemma then gives degree \(p\) for such a root. It cannot lie in an extension of degree \(D\). This verifies the specific obstruction used in Case 2 of Theorem 1.1. The existence of divisible powers in the auxiliary closed affine algebraic subgroup is imported by the paper from its reference [33], and was not independently proved here.
# Local findings

Problem 1 (The trivial group violates Proposition 6.7).  The statement of Proposition 6.7 on PDF p. 29 (printed p. 709) asserts that \(\operatorname{rRepl}_X(G)\) is self-centralizing for a connected commutative affine algebraic subgroup \(G\subseteq\operatorname{Bir}(X)\), without excluding \(G=\{1\}\).
## Exact counterexample and hypotheses

Take \(k=\mathbb C\), \(X=\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb C}\), and \(G=\{\mathrm{id}_X\}\). The variety is irreducible and the base field satisfies every standing assumption. The one-point algebraic group is affine, connected, commutative, and is an algebraic subgroup of \(\operatorname{Bir}(X)\). Its inclusion is faithful.

By Definition 6.5 on PDF p. 28, a rational replica comes from a \(G\)-invariant rational map \(X\dashrightarrow G\). There is exactly one such map, and it induces the identity. Therefore \[\operatorname{rRepl}_X(G)=\{\mathrm{id}_X\},\qquad
 \operatorname{Cent}_{\operatorname{Bir}(X)}(\operatorname{rRepl}_X(G))=\operatorname{Bir}(X).\] The map \(z\mapsto z+1\) lies in the right-hand group and is not the identity. The asserted equality is consequently false for an input satisfying the written hypotheses. This is an exact group-theoretic counterexample; no numerical or author-code execution is involved.
## Counterevidence, repair, and impact

The proof of Claim 3 on PDF p. 30 chooses a morphism to \(G'\) that separates two points of \(Y\). That step cannot work when \(G'=\{1\}\). The counterexample therefore identifies an actual missing hypothesis, rather than a rendering problem. A precise repair is to assume \(G\ne\{1\}\) in Proposition 6.7. In its proof, a nontrivial connected group acting faithfully on an irreducible variety has a positive-dimensional generic orbit; the resulting \(G'\) is nontrivial. Rational maps to its split additive or multiplicative factors can then separate the specified points after shrinking the domain. This supplies the needed nondegeneracy for Claim 3; it is not a new proof of the imported quotient theorem.

The applications in Theorem 1.1 use a nontrivial vector group \(U\) containing the nontrivial image of translations in its replica group, and a positive-dimensional torus \(D\). Theorem 1.2 uses \(U=\mathbb G_a\) and \(D=\mathbb G_m\) explicitly (PDF pp. 33–34). The displayed counterexample does not reach these applications. The defect is therefore Minor: a false boundary instance of an auxiliary proposition, with no demonstrated damage to the principal conclusions.

Problem 2 (The branch-polynomial choice excludes \(n=2\)).  Corollary 1.4 includes every \(n\ge2\) (PDF p. 3). Its proof on PDF p. 23 (printed p. 703) begins by choosing a homogeneous irreducible polynomial \(F\in k[x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}]\) of degree \(2n\) with smooth projective zero locus.
## Boundary check and a valid replacement

For \(n=2\), this would be an irreducible binary quartic over an algebraically closed field. Every binary homogeneous polynomial of degree four factors into four linear forms, counted with multiplicity: dehomogenize at \(x_0=1\), factor the resulting univariate polynomial, and include any missing degree as a power of \(x_0\). Thus the requested irreducible polynomial does not exist. This prevents the written construction from starting in that dimension; it does not disprove the corollary.

A concrete repair for this boundary case is the squarefree quartic \[F(x_0,x_1)=x_1(x_1-x_0)(x_1-2x_0)(x_1-3x_0).\] Its branch divisor in \(\mathbb P^1\) consists of four distinct finite points; \(x_0\) is not a factor, so the original projective hypersurface gains no extra component at infinity. Its dehomogenization is \(f(y)=y(y-1)(y-2)(y-3)\), which is not a square in \(k(y)\), since its valuation at \(y=0\) is one. The double cover \(z^2=f(y)\), completed over \(\mathbb P^1\), is smooth and has \[2g-2=2(-2)+4=0,\qquad g=1.\] It is therefore non-ruled. The matrices defining \(T_f(\mathbb A^1)\) have determinant \(a^2-b^2f\ne0\) for \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\), because \(f\) is not a square. Hence the nonsquare and non-ruled conditions actually used later in the construction survive this replacement.
## Counterevidence and impact boundary

The article already identifies \(n=2\) as a previously proved case, citing its reference [20] both in the introduction and surrounding discussion. Reading the new construction as intended only for \(n\ge3\) therefore supplies a second resolution: state that restriction and retain the cited two-dimensional result. That earlier paper was not independently audited here.

The supported finding is the local incompatibility of the written construction with its endpoint, not a new counterexample to the existence of nonstandard Borel subgroups. The corrected squarefree construction was checked above; the higher-dimensional construction is not challenged by this argument. Its impact is Minor, limited to presentation of the already known two-dimensional endpoint.
# Overall assessment

The two findings concern different boundaries: the identity group in a general auxiliary proposition, and an impossible irreducible branch polynomial at an endpoint dimension. The checked applications of Proposition 6.7 avoid the first boundary. The paper itself cites prior treatment of the second, and an explicit squarefree replacement retains the required geometry. Neither finding establishes an invalid rationality or ruledness theorem, nor does either warrant a Major assessment.

analysis: The statement of Proposition 6.7 on PDF p. 29 (printed p. 709) asserts that \(\operatorname{rRepl}_X(G)\) is self-centralizing for a connected commutative affine algebraic subgroup \(G\subseteq\operatorname{Bir}(X)\), without excluding \(G=\{1\}\).

Take \(k=\mathbb C\), \(X=\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb C}\), and \(G=\{\mathrm{id}_X\}\). The variety is irreducible and the base field satisfies every standing assumption. The one-point algebraic group is affine, connected, commutative, and is an algebraic subgroup of \(\operatorname{Bir}(X)\). Its inclusion is faithful.

By Definition 6.5 on PDF p. 28, a rational replica comes from a \(G\)-invariant rational map \(X\dashrightarrow G\). There is exactly one such map, and it induces the identity. Therefore \[\operatorname{rRepl}_X(G)=\{\mathrm{id}_X\},\qquad
 \operatorname{Cent}_{\operatorname{Bir}(X)}(\operatorname{rRepl}_X(G))=\operatorname{Bir}(X).\] The map \(z\mapsto z+1\) lies in the right-hand group and is not the identity. The asserted equality is consequently false for an input satisfying the written hypotheses. This is an exact group-theoretic counterexample; no numerical or author-code execution is involved.
result: The proof of Claim 3 on PDF p. 30 chooses a morphism to \(G'\) that separates two points of \(Y\). That step cannot work when \(G'=\{1\}\). The counterexample therefore identifies an actual missing hypothesis, rather than a rendering problem. A precise repair is to assume \(G\ne\{1\}\) in Proposition 6.7. In its proof, a nontrivial connected group acting faithfully on an irreducible variety has a positive-dimensional generic orbit; the resulting \(G'\) is nontrivial. Rational maps to its split additive or multiplicative factors can then separate the specified points after shrinking the domain. This supplies the needed nondegeneracy for Claim 3; it is not a new proof of the imported quotient theorem.

The applications in Theorem 1.1 use a nontrivial vector group \(U\) containing the nontrivial image of translations in its replica group, and a positive-dimensional torus \(D\). Theorem 1.2 uses \(U=\mathbb G_a\) and \(D=\mathbb G_m\) explicitly (PDF pp. 33–34). The displayed counterexample does not reach these applications. The defect is therefore Minor: a false boundary instance of an auxiliary proposition, with no demonstrated damage to the principal conclusions.

claim: The standing base field in Sections 5–6 is algebraically closed, uncountable, and of characteristic zero (PDF p. 4 and the relevant section openings). analysis: Corollary 1.4 includes every \(n\ge2\) (PDF p. 3). Its proof on PDF p. 23 (printed p. 703) begins by choosing a homogeneous irreducible polynomial \(F\in k[x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}]\) of degree \(2n\) with smooth projective zero locus.

For \(n=2\), this would be an irreducible binary quartic over an algebraically closed field. Every binary homogeneous polynomial of degree four factors into four linear forms, counted with multiplicity: dehomogenize at \(x_0=1\), factor the resulting univariate polynomial, and include any missing degree as a power of \(x_0\). Thus the requested irreducible polynomial does not exist. This prevents the written construction from starting in that dimension; it does not disprove the corollary.

A concrete repair for this boundary case is the squarefree quartic \[F(x_0,x_1)=x_1(x_1-x_0)(x_1-2x_0)(x_1-3x_0).\] Its branch divisor in \(\mathbb P^1\) consists of four distinct finite points; \(x_0\) is not a factor, so the original projective hypersurface gains no extra component at infinity. Its dehomogenization is \(f(y)=y(y-1)(y-2)(y-3)\), which is not a square in \(k(y)\), since its valuation at \(y=0\) is one. The double cover \(z^2=f(y)\), completed over \(\mathbb P^1\), is smooth and has \[2g-2=2(-2)+4=0,\qquad g=1.\] It is therefore non-ruled. The matrices defining \(T_f(\mathbb A^1)\) have determinant \(a^2-b^2f\ne0\) for \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\), because \(f\) is not a square. Hence the nonsquare and non-ruled conditions actually used later in the construction survive this replacement.
result: The article already identifies \(n=2\) as a previously proved case, citing its reference [20] both in the introduction and surrounding discussion. Reading the new construction as intended only for \(n\ge3\) therefore supplies a second resolution: state that restriction and retain the cited two-dimensional result. That earlier paper was not independently audited here.

The supported finding is the local incompatibility of the written construction with its endpoint, not a new counterexample to the existence of nonstandard Borel subgroups. The corrected squarefree construction was checked above; the higher-dimensional construction is not challenged by this argument. Its impact is Minor, limited to presentation of the already known two-dimensional endpoint.

report: Abstract: This report checks selected determinant, spinor-norm, and mapping-torus arguments in the acquired author manuscript. A fully realized genus-two mapping torus shows that the discriminant specified in equation (C.2) can be zero under the written hypotheses. The determinant must instead be taken on the generalized \(1\)-eigenspace, as the manuscript’s earlier formula already indicates. The correction leaves the ordinary fixed-space dimension in the torsion sign unchanged. The supported assessment is Minor, with no demonstrated refutation of the main theorems. A finite-characteristic divided-derivative concern is resolved by explicit counterevidence in the source. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of symplectic \(L\)-functions and symplectic Reidemeister torsion
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed source is Amina Abdurrahman and Akshay Venkatesh, Symplectic \(L\)-functions and symplectic Reidemeister torsion (mod squares), arXiv:2303.13436v1, dated 23 March 2023, 98 pages [paper]. PDF and printed page numbers agree. The associated journal DOI in the acquisition metadata is 10.1007/s00222-025-01349-6, but the journal Version of Record was not acquired. No equivalence between that version and the reviewed v1 is assumed.

The checks concern the hypotheses of Theorems 2.1 and 3.1; the normalized Frobenius and central-value conventions in Section 3; the spinor formula (B.31); and the mapping-torus computation in Appendix C. The full topological \(K\)-theory argument, arithmetic variation, Hilbert–Siegel construction, determinant-category foundations, and Appendix D numerical examples were not reconstructed. Mechanical extraction and lexical searches are not treated as whole-paper reading.

For Theorem 2.1 (p. 10), the coefficient field has characteristic different from two and the local system on a three-manifold is symplectic. The arithmetic theorem on p. 31 has additional admissibility and congruence assumptions, including geometric surjectivity. The counterexample below concerns the characteristic-zero corollary (C.2), not a local system asserted to satisfy those stronger arithmetic hypotheses.
# A realized counterexample to the printed discriminant

Problem 1 (Ordinary invariants in equation (C.2)).  On p. 87, Lemma C.2.1 assumes \(H^0(S,\rho)=0\) and characteristic zero. Writing \(T\) for the induced action on \(H^1(S,\rho)\) and \(h=\dim\ker(T-I)\), it identifies \[(-1)^{h/2}\operatorname{RT}(M_t,\rho)=\operatorname{spinor}(T).\] The following equation (C.2) replaces the right side by \[\det{}'(1-T)\,\delta.\] Here \(\det{}'\) removes the generalized \(1\)-eigenspace, whereas the next line defines \(\delta\) on the ordinary fixed space \(H^1(S,\rho)^{T=1}\). That latter restriction can be degenerate.
## All hypotheses are realized

Let \(S\) be the closed oriented genus-two surface with presentation \[\pi_1(S)=\langle a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2\mid[a_1,b_1][a_2,b_2]=1\rangle.\] Over \(\mathbb Q\), take a rank-two local system with fiber form \[J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \rho(a_1)=-I_2,\quad \rho(b_1)=\rho(a_2)=\rho(b_2)=I_2.\] The matrices are symplectic and satisfy the surface relation. Since \(-I_2\) fixes no nonzero vector, \(H^0(S,\rho)=0\); duality gives \(H^2(S,\rho)=0\).

Choose \(t\) fixing \(a_1,b_1,a_2\) and sending \(b_2\) to \(b_2a_2\). This is the inverse of the explicitly displayed Dehn twist \(T_4\) on p. 86; it is an orientation-preserving mapping class. The identity \([a_2,b_2a_2]=[a_2,b_2]\) also verifies preservation of the relator. We have \(\rho\circ t=\rho\), so equation (C.1) holds with intertwining matrix \(M=I_2\). The representation therefore extends to the mapping torus \(M_t\).

Write the values of a cocycle on the four generators as \((x_1,y_1,u,v)\). The cocycle relation gives \(-2y_1=0\), and the coboundaries are \((-2w,0,0,0)\). Consequently \[H^1(S,\rho)\simeq\mathbb Q^2\oplus\mathbb Q^2,\qquad [\phi]\longleftrightarrow(u,v).\] This agrees with (C.5) on p. 88. The actual cocycle action on p. 89 is \(T(\phi)=M^{-1}\phi\circ t\), and hence \[T(u,v)=(u,v+u),\qquad
 T=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&0\\ I_2&I_2\end{pmatrix}.\] The additional eigenvalue condition used later on p. 89 to obtain the computational shortcut (C.6) is not a hypothesis of (C.2); no such shortcut is used here.
## Pairing and the decisive computation

The cohomology can be represented on the second handle, where the local system is constant. More explicitly, cutting along the separating circle gives an isomorphism from the first handle’s \(H^1\) to the circle’s \(H^1\), induced by \(-2y_1\), while the constant second handle has zero boundary restriction in degree one and an isomorphism in degree zero. Mayer–Vietoris thus identifies the global \(H^1\) with the second handle’s \(H^1\). Relative representatives on that handle give \[B((u,v),(u',v'))=u^{\mathsf T}Jv'-v^{\mathsf T}Ju',
 \qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&J\\-J&0\end{pmatrix}.\] An overall orientation sign does not alter the following degeneracy or determinant conclusions. Direct exact arithmetic gives \[B^{\mathsf T}=B,\quad \det B=1,\quad T^{\mathsf T}BT=B,\quad \det T=1.\] With \(N=T-I\), \[N^2=0,\qquad \operatorname{rank}N=2,\qquad
 \ker N=\operatorname{im}N=\{(0,v):v\in\mathbb Q^2\}.\] The ordinary fixed space is therefore two-dimensional and its Gram matrix is zero. This is also coordinate-free: invariance implies \[B(Nx,y)=B(x,T^{-1}y)-B(x,y)=0\qquad(y\in\ker N).\] Since \(\operatorname{im}N=\ker N\), the restriction to the entire fixed space vanishes.

In contrast, the generalized \(1\)-eigenspace is all of \(\mathbb Q^4\), with determinant \(1\). Its complement is zero-dimensional, so \(\det{}'(1-T)=1\). The printed right side of (C.2) is thus \(1\cdot0=0\), which is not even an element of the asserted group \(\mathbb Q^\times/\mathbb Q^{\times2}\).

For an independent square-class check, set \(R=I+N/2\). Exact multiplication verifies \(R^{\mathsf T}BR=B\), \(\det R=1\), and \(R^2=T\). The spinor norm is a homomorphism to a group of exponent two, so \[\operatorname{spinor}(T)=\operatorname{spinor}(R)^2=1.\] Thus the expression in (C.2) fails on an input satisfying its written hypotheses. This is an exact algebraic and topological example, not a numerical approximation.
## Alternative readings, correction, and impact

The distinction cannot be removed by an unstated global notation convention. On p. 82 the manuscript explicitly distinguishes \(V^+\), the generalized \(1\)-eigenspace, from \(V^1\), the ordinary eigenspace. On p. 83 it explicitly interprets superscript \(1\) as invariants and treats unipotent blocks. No semisimplicity hypothesis is imposed in Lemma C.2.1. The later optional assumption on \(\rho(b_1)\) does not retroactively restrict that lemma.

The precise correction is \[\delta=\operatorname{disc}\!\left(H^1(S,\rho)_{\mathrm{gen},\,1}\right),
 \qquad h=\dim\ker(T-I)\ \text{unchanged}.\] This repair follows from the manuscript’s own (B.31). In its orthogonal decomposition \(V=V^+\oplus V^-\oplus W\), that formula gives \(\operatorname{spinor}(T)=\det(1-T)|_W\,\operatorname{disc}(V^+)\). Adding \(V^-\) to the determinant complement contributes \(2^{\dim V^-}\), a square because \(T\in SO(V)\) and \(\dim V^-\) is even. This yields the corrected \(\det{}'\) expression. In the example the corrected discriminant is \(1\). The ordinary dimension is \(h=2\), whereas the generalized dimension is four; replacing \(h\) as well would incorrectly change the torsion sign.

The assessment is Minor: a false local determinant reformulation with a verified limited correction. The valid generalized-space formula is already present, and semisimple-at-one or acyclic cases do not exhibit this discrepancy. The counterexample does not refute Lemma C.2.1, Theorems 2.1 or 3.1, or the existence of the nonsquare example used in Appendix C. A complete audit of every downstream use was not performed; no broader damage or author adoption is asserted.
# Further checks and rejected concerns
## The half-Euler sign

Under \(H^0(S,\rho)=H^2(S,\rho)=0\), the Wang sequence gives \(H^0(M_t,\rho)=0\) and \(H^1(M_t,\rho)=\ker(T-I)\). Thus the semicharacteristic used on p. 10 is \(\chi_{1/2}(M_t,\rho)=-h\). Its factor \((-1)^{\chi_{1/2}/2}\) equals \((-1)^{h/2}\), since \(h\) is even. The checked sign is consistent; the established problem is the space defining \(\delta\).
## Divided derivatives in finite characteristic

Equation (3.4), p. 28, uses a divided-derivative notation. Literal division by \(h!\) in the coefficient field would be undefined when its characteristic divides \(h!\). For example, over \(\mathbb F_7\), the ordinary eighth derivative of \((1-t)^8\) and \(8!\) both vanish, while the coefficient of \((t-1)^8\) is \(1\).

This calculation alone does not establish an error in the intended formula. On p. 44, the manuscript expressly identifies the notation with the leading Taylor coefficient. That coefficient, equivalently a Hasse derivative, remains defined. Moreover (3.4) itself defines the quantity by the spinor norm and correctly uses a generalized fixed space. The source therefore supplies a coherent interpretation; this concern is not counted as a second finding.
## Characteristic and dependency limits

Lemma C.2.1 is stated in characteristic zero, whereas its mapping-torus interpretation is used with finite coefficient fields in Lemma 5.2.1 (pp. 41–42). The preserved bounded helper analysis gives a conditional extension: pass to a cyclic cover of odd degree \(p^a\) to kill the unipotent part of \(T\); the spinor norm and the corrected torsion, interpreted through Theorem 2.1, are unchanged under that odd cover. The semisimple case separates nondegenerate fixed and acyclic summands and uses (B.31). This is conditional on the topological theorem and its torsion formalism, not an independent reproof of them. No failure of the finite-field application was established, and the visible characteristic restriction alone is not graded as a proved error.
# Overall assessment and evidential limits

One demonstrated local formula defect is supported in the acquired v1. The admissible example, precise source locations, coordinate-free degeneracy argument, counterevidence, and generalized-space repair fix its mathematical scope. The arithmetic theorem has stronger assumptions, and no counterexample to it has been supplied. The result is an initial technical assessment, not a certificate of all 98 pages or an independent acceptance.

Same-conversation native helpers supplied bounded matrix/cochain checks and a separate challenge; their actual roles, exact computation records, and limitations are preserved. No author code was executed, and absence of code is not a mathematical defect. Scientific decision is pending, with no human review recorded.
# Supporting checks

The acquired author TeX was consulted statically. The exact rational matrices, cocycle ranks, surface-word check, current TeX/PDF, retained compiler/dependencies, actual build logs, coverage/findings/provenance, and all used source-page and report-page inspection bindings accompany the report. Earlier rendering-time records retain their original uninspected state; subsequent receipts record actual viewing. No later-version or erratum audit was performed, and no correction in the journal version is assumed.

report: Abstract: This report examines four selected argument chains: the \(p\)-subgroup condition and additive quotient for modular fixed points, the normalizer step in point classification, the finite topological colimit, and the cyclic \(p\)-group boundary cases. The inspected steps retain their necessary normality, characteristic, finiteness, and prime-domain assumptions. Exact finite diagnostics agree with the corresponding elementary calculations. No substantive defect was established within this declared scope. This conclusion does not certify the full conservativity, stratification, or twisted-cohomology arguments, and is restricted to the acquired author manuscript. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of the geometry of permutation modules
# Identity and mathematical setting

The reviewed work is Paul Balmer and Martin Gallauer, The geometry of permutation modules, arXiv:2307.04398v2, with a PDF version stamp of 21 July 2025, 76 pages [paper]. PDF page numbers agree with the printed numbers used here. The journal DOI associated with the acquisition record is 10.1007/s00222-025-01350-z. The journal Version of Record was not acquired, and textual equivalence to it is not assumed.

The domain is a finite group \(G\) and a field \(k\) of characteristic \(p>0\). The compact tensor triangulated category is the idempotent completion of the bounded homotopy category of finite permutation modules, denoted \(\mathcal K(G)\). Write \(G/\!/H=N_G(H)/H\) for the Weyl group. The modular fixed-point functor \(\Psi^H\), the ordinary fixed-vector functor, and the geometric localization have different meanings; replacing one by another would change the assertions being checked.

A same-conversation native helper supplied bounded proof analysis, static author-TeX excerpts, and independently written finite computations. The introduction and selected proof passages were read; full text extraction is not counted as full reading. Neither the author source nor author software was executed.
# The \(p\)-subgroup condition and the additive quotient
## Necessity in Warning 5.1

On p. 17 the manuscript explains why a tensor functor satisfying \[\Psi^H(kX)\simeq k(X^H)\] on finite \(G\)-sets cannot have arbitrary \(H\). Let \(P\) be a Sylow \(p\)-subgroup. The coaugmentation and augmentation \[k\longrightarrow k(G/P)\longrightarrow k\] have composite \([G:P]\), invertible in \(k\). Thus the tensor unit is a retract of \(k(G/P)\). A unital additive tensor functor to the stated nonzero target cannot send \(k(G/P)\) to zero. The fixed-set formula therefore forces \((G/P)^H\ne\varnothing\). An \(H\)-fixed coset \(gP\) gives \(g^{-1}Hg\le P\), so \(H\) is a \(p\)-group.

For the excluded extension, \(G=H=C_3\) over \(\mathbb F_2\) already exhibits the obstruction: \(k\) is a retract of \(kG\), but the regular \(G\)-set has no \(G\)-fixed point. This is a check of the necessity of the paper’s restriction, not a counterexample to its actual theorem.
## The vanishing lemma retains normality

Lemma 5.3 (p. 18) assumes a normal \(p\)-subgroup \(N\trianglelefteq G\), \(N\le H\), and \(N\nleq K\). After the stated double-coset reduction, a map \(k(G/H)\to k(G/K)\to k\) is determined by the transfer index \[[H:L],\qquad L=H\cap gKg^{-1}.\] The \(N\)-action on \(H/L\) has no fixed point. Indeed, a fixed coset would imply a conjugate of \(N\) lies in \(L\); normality in \(G\) then implies \(N\le K\), a contradiction. Every orbit consequently has size divisible by \(p\). Thus \(p\mid[H:L]\), and the map is zero over \(k\). Both normality and the characteristic hypothesis are used in the displayed proof.
## Faithfulness and idempotent completion

Proposition 5.4 on the same page identifies the permutation category for \(G/N\) with the additive quotient that kills modules \(k(G/K)\) with \(N\nleq K\). Inflation is fully faithful before quotienting. To check that the quotient introduces no new kernel between surviving objects, use rigidity to turn a factorization \(A\to B\) through the killed ideal into a factorization \(A\otimes B^\vee\to k\). Surviving transitive factors have stabilizers containing \(N\); a tensor product involving a killed stabilizer decomposes into factors still failing to contain \(N\). Lemma 5.3 kills each such factorization.

Every transitive module either survives as an inflated \(G/N\)-module or becomes zero. Full faithfulness lifts the remaining idempotents, which split in the completed source. This verifies the stated essential-surjectivity step. Equation (5.13) and Corollary 5.16 on p. 20 are consistent with this quotient and its inflation section. No defect was established in these steps. The general double-coset and Mackey formulas were used as mathematical dependencies, not re-audited from their original references.
# Point classification and the normalizer step
## Conservativity-to-nilpotence reduction

Proposition 7.1 (p. 26) considers a conservative coproduct-preserving tensor functor between big tensor triangulated categories. Rigidity reduces a morphism with compact source to one from the unit. Its tensor-power telescope maps to a sequential homotopy colimit of zero maps after applying the functor, and is therefore zero there. Conservativity makes the original telescope zero; compactness of the unit then forces vanishing at a finite stage. This verifies the specific telescope step. The full Conservativity Theorem 6.12 and the external spectrum-surjectivity theorem remain unproved dependencies of the classification.
## Support direction and uniqueness

The point \(\mathcal P_G(H,\mathfrak p)\) is the inverse image of a cohomological prime for \(G/\!/H\), as defined on p. 26. Lemma 5.21 (p. 22) gives the two alternatives behind Lemma 7.12 (pp. 27–28): \[\operatorname{kos}_G(K)\in\mathcal P_G(H,\mathfrak p)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 H\ \text{is subconjugate to }K.\] When \(H\) is not subconjugate to \(K\), the fixed-point image has the tensor unit as a direct summand and cannot belong to a proper prime. In the other case it is acyclic and becomes zero in the derived category used to define the point. Consequently \[\mathcal P_G(H,\mathfrak p)\subseteq\mathcal P_G(H',\mathfrak p')
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad H'\ \text{is subconjugate to }H.\] Evaluating the test object with \(K=H\) checks this direction. Equality forces conjugacy, as Corollary 7.13 states.

For Proposition 7.14 (p. 28), set \(N=N_G(H)\). Corollary 4.9 (p. 16), invoked as a descent input, represents equal images by a prime over an intersection of conjugates of \(N\). Classification and naturality express that prime through a subgroup \(L\), with both \(L\) and its relevant conjugate \(N\)-conjugate to \(H\). Since \(H\trianglelefteq N\), these subgroups are exactly \(H\); the conjugating element must normalize \(H\), hence lies in \(N\). The comparison then occurs within \(N\), where inner conjugation acts trivially on the spectrum. Finally the section supplied by inflation in Corollary 5.16 gives equality of the original cohomological primes.

This checks the fusion step used for the uniqueness assertion of Theorem 7.16. The proof does not assume \(H\trianglelefteq G\), nor does it assert that unrestricted restriction maps or all modular fixed-point maps are injective. It uses the cohomological open and normality inside the normalizer. No missing normality assumption or reversed support inclusion was established in this chain.
# The topology of the finite colimit

Proposition 7.32 (p. 31) explicitly gives a set partition by locally closed strata. Recollection 10.7 (p. 41) then states the problem of attaching these strata topologically. The coproduct symbol in the partition is not a claim that the spectrum is a topological disjoint union.

Construction 11.1 and the maps in (11.5)–(11.8), pp. 41–42, use the category \(\mathcal E_p(G)\) of elementary abelian \(p\)-sections \((H,K)\), with \(K\trianglelefteq H\) and \(H/K\) elementary abelian. Quotient-type arrows are explicitly included. They are essential: the arrow \((H,L)\to(H,K)\), for \(K\le L\le H\), need not be an inclusion \(H/L\to H/K\).

The closed-map step in Theorem 11.10 (p. 43) is justified by finiteness. There are only finitely many objects \((H,K)\) because \(G\) is finite. If \(X\) is the topological colimit and \(C\subset X\) is closed, its inverse image \(C_a\) in each component is closed. Lemma 11.9 gives a closed component map \(\varphi_a\). Therefore \[\varphi(C)=\bigcup_{a\in\operatorname{Ob}\mathcal E_p(G)}\varphi_a(C_a)\] is a finite union of closed sets. The argument would not be valid for an arbitrary infinite family, but that is outside the theorem’s hypotheses.

The injectivity reduction also stays inside the indexing category. A point represented by \(\mathcal P_{H/K}(L/K,\mathfrak p)\) can be represented at \((H,L)\), since the quotient \(H/L\) is again elementary abelian. Equality of the global primes forces the kernel subgroups to be conjugate by Theorem 7.16. After identifying them, the invoked Quillen/descent relation in \(N_G(K)/K\) produces a common elementary abelian section of the form \((H\cap gH'g^{-1},K)\). Its conjugation/restriction arrows identify the two points already in the colimit. Together with the invoked surjectivity, this yields a continuous closed bijection and hence a homeomorphism.

The original Quillen and separable-descent theorems were not independently re-proved. The checked argument is the internal reduction, admissibility of its sections, and closed-map inference; it does not certify all later local ring presentations.
# Cyclic \(p\)-groups and finite diagnostics

For \(G=C_{p^n}\), Notation 8.1 and Proposition 8.3 (pp. 31–32) label \(N_j\) by its index \(p^j\), so \(N_0=G\) and \(N_n=1\). The quotient \(G/N_0\) contributes one cohomological point and each nontrivial cyclic quotient contributes two. The point count is therefore \(2n+1\); when \(n=0\), the space is a singleton.

For \(1\le i\le n\), put \(M_i=k(G/N_{i-1})\). Its \(N_j\)-fixed set is empty for \(j<i-1\), and is the whole coset set for \(j\ge i-1\). In the latter case the resulting \(k(C_{p^j})\)-module has the form \[k[t]/(t^{p^{i-1}})\quad\text{over}\quad k[t]/(t^{p^j}).\] It is regular and perfect at \(j=i-1\). At \(j>i-1\), its nonzero dimension is smaller than \(p^j\), so it cannot be free over the local group algebra. Self-injectivity rules out finite projective dimension for this nonprojective module. This gives precisely the support formula used on p. 32: \[\operatorname{supp}(M_i)=\{m_j:j\ge i-1\}\ \cup\ \{\mathfrak p_j:j\ge i\}.\] Combining it with the subgroup-order restriction gives \(\overline{\{\mathfrak p_i\}}\subseteq\{m_{i-1},\mathfrak p_i,m_i\}\). The within-stratum specialization to \(m_i\) is already known. Omitting the remaining edge to \(m_{i-1}\) would disconnect the finite specialization graph. The cited rigid-category splitting principle would then give a nontrivial idempotent in \(\operatorname{End}(\mathbf1)=k\), impossible for a field. This verifies the boundary and connectivity argument conditional on the cited splitting principle and cyclic cohomology input.

# Assessment and remaining coverage

The supported assessment is No Issue Found within the declared scope. Four inspected chains retain their needed hypotheses, and no admissible counterexample or invalid implication was established. No correction is proposed. The finite tests, source-page checks, and exact arguments support this bounded result, not a statement that every theorem in the paper is correct.

The full conservativity proof in Section 6, stratification in Section 9, and twisted-cohomology constructions, presentations, closure calculations, and larger examples in Sections 12–18 were not fully verified. External references were not independently audited. No journal-final comparison, later-version/erratum search, author-code reproduction, or author adoption is asserted. The result is an initial AI technical review with native bounded assistance; it is not independent acceptance or a human decision. Scientific decision remains pending.

Abstract: One Major issue is established in the acquired publisher version: the universal string-and-reduction criterion in Proposition 5.6 is false at \(r=2\). A normalized stable formal series satisfies every written hypothesis but fails a required weight-two constraint. The proof uses a weight-two annihilation relation that its preceding induction does not supply at this endpoint. This criterion is used in the paper’s route to a principal integrability conclusion. The counterexample does not refute the particular Brezin–Gross–Witten identification; the paper itself cites full \(r=2\) constraints that may supply a separate proof. Three additional checks support the stated rank and normalization calculations, the unmarked top-degree exception, and finite coefficients of the displayed \(\kappa\)-series. All conclusions have the explicit coverage limits below. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of relations on moduli spaces and the negative \(r\)-spin Witten conjecture
# Source identity and scope

The reviewed work is Nitin Kumar Chidambaram, Elba Garcia-Failde, and Alessandro Giacchetto, Relations on \(\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}\) and the negative \(r\)-spin Witten conjecture, Inventiones mathematicae 241 (2025), 929–997, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01351-y [paper]. The acquired 69-page PDF is the publisher Version of Record. Throughout this report, PDF page \(p\) is printed page \(p+928\); both locators are given for the decisive issue. No later correction, author adoption, or equivalence to another version is asserted.

The principal domain is an integer \(r\ge2\), stable pairs \((g,n)\) with \(2g-2+n>0\), and positive primary labels \(1\le a_i\le r-1\) for the \(\Theta\) theory. The auxiliary \(\Upsilon\) construction also uses zero primary labels. Theorem E/5.5 states the full \(W\)-constraints, whereas the general \(r\)-KdV/BGW identification is Conjecture F/5.17; Theorem G/5.20 proves the stated \(r=2,3\) cases. The review does not attribute an all-\(r\) integrability theorem to the authors.

The existing same-conversation native helper `/root/check_0090` supplied bounded source checks and independently written exact symbolic calculations. A second existing helper, `/root/check_0089`, challenged the hypotheses, normal ordering, and downstream scope of the proposed counterexample analytically. This is an initial technical review, not independent acceptance. Author software was not executed.
# Major: the \(r=2\) endpoint of Proposition 5.6
## Claim, operators, and exact source locations
## A formal series meeting every stated hypothesis

Equation reference: eq:Zzero. Set \(r=2\) and take the binomial expansion at the origin \[
 Z_0=(1-t_1)^{-1/8},\qquad
 \log Z_0=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{t_1^n}{8n}.\] Define \[\Phi_{1,n}[1,\ldots,1]=\frac{(n-1)!}{8}\quad(n\ge1),
 \qquad \Phi_{g,n}[a_1,\ldots,a_n]=0\] in every other case. Substitution into [eq:stable] (#eq:stable) gives precisely [eq:Zzero] (#eq:Zzero): the factor \(1/n!\) leaves \(1/(8n)\), and \(\hbar^{g-1}=1\). The arrays are symmetric; all indices are positive. Every nonzero term has \(g=1\), \(n\ge1\), and \(2g-2+n=n>0\). There is no \(n=0\) term, and \(Z_0(0)=1\). Thus neither instability nor an arbitrary multiplicative normalization explains the example. Formal expansion at the origin is sufficient; no analytic branch continuation is used.

Even the geometric dimension selection rule would not discard these coefficients: at \(r=2\), all \(a_i=1\), the class degree is \(D=2g-2+n\), so the total descendant degree must be \(g-1\). The nonzero terms in [eq:Zzero] (#eq:Zzero) have genus one and all descendant indices zero. This observation does not assume that \(Z_0\) arises from a CohFT, which is not a written hypothesis of Proposition 5.6.
## A required constraint fails exactly
Theorem 5.5, equation (5.15), on PDF p. 51/printed p. 979 requires \(H_k^iZ^{\Theta^r}=0\) for \(1\le i\le r\) and \(k\ge-i+2\). In particular \(H_1^2Z^{\Theta^2}=0\).

Equation reference: eq:nonzero. For \(Z_0\), all normally ordered terms of [eq:Htwo] (#eq:Htwo) at \(r=2,k=1\) vanish except \(p_1=p_2=1\). A negative index forces its partner to be at least \(3\), whose derivative annihilates \(Z_0\); zero-index terms vanish because \(J_0=0\). The surviving coefficient is \(-1/2\), and the central term is zero. Consequently \[
 H_1^2Z_0=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2}\partial_{t_1}^2Z_0
 =-\frac{9\hbar^2}{128}(1-t_1)^{-17/8}\ne0.\] At all times zero the value is already \(-9\hbar^2/128\). This is an exact formal coefficient, not a numerical discrepancy. It proves that \(Z_0\) cannot be the descendant potential characterized by the full constraints, despite satisfying every written premise of Proposition 5.6. The retained reviewer-written SymPy calculation confirms [eq:Hzero] (#eq:Hzero)–[eq:nonzero] (#eq:nonzero); the finite expansion is supplementary to the analytic identity.
## Proof failure, core impact, and counterevidence

At \(r=2\), the range in (5.19) contains only conformal weight \(i=1\). It does not provide \(H_k^2Z=0\) for positive \(k\). The next commutator paragraph on PDF p. 53/printed p. 981 nevertheless sets \([H_k^2,H_0^2]Z=0\) using the preceding constraints. From \(H_0^2Z=\mu Z\) alone this does not follow: the second term involves \(H_0^2(H_k^2Z)\), for which the required annihilation has not been established. The coefficient \(k(1-r)-r+2\) also becomes \(-k\) and vanishes at \(k=0\). Fixing \(\mu=0\) cannot repair the sufficiency claim, because the explicit example already has that value.

Proposition 5.18 on PDF pp. 62–63/printed pp. 990–991 explicitly invokes Proposition 5.6 to reduce identification of the BGW function to the string equation. The proof of Theorem 5.20 on PDF p. 63/printed p. 991 then invokes Proposition 5.18. Thus the false endpoint criterion is a stated proof bridge to a principal conclusion, which supports the Major assessment under the assigned mathematical standard.

The demonstrated failure has a narrower scope than falsity of that conclusion. No claim is made that \(Z_0\) is a KP or KdV tau function, that the particular BGW function fails a constraint, or that the BGW equality is false. The paper states on PDF pp. 10 and 63 that full \(r=2\) Virasoro constraints were already established in its references [5,33]. Those external proofs were not independently audited here. They are material counterevidence against interpreting this proof defect as a refutation of the final equality.

A defensible repair route is to exclude \(r=2\) from the stated universal criterion and treat that endpoint separately using verified full Virasoro constraints and the uniqueness in Theorem 5.5. The remaining \(r\ge3\) proof and the cited replacement dependencies require their own verification; this report does not certify them. Adding only \(Z(0)=1\), the genus expansion, the dimension selection rule, or \(\mu=0\) is insufficient, since the example satisfies all four.
# Additional checks and their boundaries
## Selection, rank, and stable domain

Definitions 2.2 and 2.4, equations (2.10)–(2.12) and (2.21)–(2.24), and Proposition 2.3 occur on PDF pp. 12–14/printed pp. 940–942. The root condition is \[|a|\equiv-(2g-2+n)\pmod r.\] In the operative nonnegative-primary domain, on a smooth curve, \[\deg L=-\frac{2g-2+n+|a|}{r}<0.\] Hence \(h^0(L)=0\), and Riemann–Roch gives \[D=h^1(L)=g-1+\frac{2g-2+n+|a|}{r}
   =\frac{(r+2)(g-1)+n+|a|}{r}.\] The root congruence makes this rank integral. If the congruence fails, the corresponding root component is empty. At \(r=2,a_i=1\), the specialization is \(D=2g-2+n\), in agreement with the dimension calculation used above. This is a smooth-curve rank and domain check. It does not independently reconstruct local freeness and base change over every compactified nodal stratum, and does not claim vanishing for arbitrary negative primary labels.
## Deformation degree, node matching, and modified unit

Definition 2.5 and Proposition 2.6, PDF pp. 15–16/printed pp. 943–944, add \(m\) zero-primary markings and then forget them. Before forgetting, the rank is \(D+m/r\); pushforward lowers degree by \(m\), leaving \[D-\frac{r-1}{r}m.\] This explains finiteness and why \(m>0\) cannot alter the degree-\(D\) term. The rendered source on PDF p. 16 reads \(D+m/r\). An earlier extraction lost the denominator and appeared to read \(D+m\); actual image inspection rejects that apparent discrepancy as an extraction artifact.

For the nonseparating node with labels \(b,c\), the child rank is \[D+\frac mr-1+\frac{b+c}{r}.\] The inverse Chiodo pairing permits \(b+c=r\) or \(b=c=0\). The first case has the required degree; in the second case the rank is one smaller and the relevant higher Chern component vanishes. The child’s normalization is \(r\) times the parent’s; expressing the raw child class in normalized form cancels the inverse-pairing factor \(r\).

Appending a primary label \(r-1\) raises rank by one. The normalization in (2.21) changes by \(-r\), while (2.19) at \(s=-1\) contributes \(-\psi/r\); their product is \(+\psi\), as in the modified-unit equation (2.28). These checked degrees and signs yield no substantive issue. A complete separating-node and stack-theoretic reconstruction was not undertaken.
## Unmarked exception and finite \(\kappa\)-coefficients

Theorem B and Corollary C, PDF pp. 5–7/printed pp. 933–935, retain an unmarked top-degree exception. In the homogeneity comparison of Theorem 3.13 and Proposition 3.15, PDF pp. 26–28/printed pp. 954–956, equality of the one-marked expressions gives, for stable \(n=0\) and thus \(g\ge2\), \[[\delta(g-1)-d]\bigl(\Omega_{g,0}^{d}
                   -\widetilde\Omega_{g,0}^{d}\bigr)=0.\] Division is justified only away from \(d=\delta(g-1)\). For \(\delta=3\), this is precisely \(d=3g-3\), preserved in Corollaries 3.24–3.25 on PDF pp. 32–33/printed pp. 960–961. The review does not promote the stated cohomological relations to a Chow-ring or Pixton-relation conclusion.

Independently, exact rational expansion of \[-\log\left(\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k(2k+1)!!\,u^k\right)
 =\sum_{m\ge1}s_m u^m\] gives \[(s_1,s_2,s_3,s_4,s_5)
 =\left(3,-\frac{21}{2},69,-\frac{2529}{4},
                        \frac{36243}{5}\right).\] Exponentiating \(\sum s_m\kappa_m u^m\) agrees with all displayed weighted-degree components zero through five on PDF pp. 6–7. For example, the first nonconstant components are \[3\kappa_1,\qquad
 \frac32(3\kappa_1^2-7\kappa_2),\qquad
 \frac32(3\kappa_1^3-21\kappa_1\kappa_2+46\kappa_3).\] All six components and the exact calculation are retained. This finite algebraic check does not prove the geometric vanishing relations, Teleman’s theorem, all-degree identities, or the unmarked Euler-characteristic integral.
# Coverage, evidence, and disposition

The actual primary source-image inspection covers PDF pages 1, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 26, 27, 28, 32, 33, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 62, and 63. The decisive evidence for the single finding is the eight source pages \(48\)–\(53\), \(62\), and \(63\), the exact operator calculation, and the separately attributed native challenge. Their current bytes and hashes are bound in the evidence inventory. Mechanical extraction and a programmatic heading scan are not counted as full-paper reading.

The compactified spin geometry, full \(R\)-matrix/vacuum construction, stable-graph expansion, Airy asymptotics, complete topological-recursion correspondence, and all Kac–Schwarz and external-reference arguments were not independently reconstructed. The report establishes the stated counterexample and local positive checks, not an exhaustive certification of the 69-page article. No lack of author code is classified as a mathematical defect.

The delivery consists of the source PDF and manifest, this English TeX/PDF report, coverage and findings records, per-issue evidence, exact calculation files, actual build and render logs, page-inspection bindings, and an inventory of current support files. The final build record distinguishes real cache warm-up from the stable `–only-cached` build; successful rendering alone is not recorded as visual inspection. Backend model identity is not inferred from a user-interface label. Provenance preserves the runtime’s declared identity, the controller’s recorded UI observation, and the native helpers’ bounded roles separately.

The assessment is Major, for the false \(r=2\) universal implication and its use in a core proof route. This is not a rejection decision or independent acceptance: `scientific_decision=pending` and `human_reviews=[]`. The proposed repair is a reviewer suggestion, with no assertion of author adoption.

Title: Initial review of Riesz means asymptotics on Lipschitz domains
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed work is Rupert L. Frank and Simon Larson, Riesz means asymptotics for Dirichlet and Neumann Laplacians on Lipschitz domains, Inventiones mathematicae 241 (2025), 999–1079, DOI `10.1007/s00222-025-01352-x` [1]. The bound source is the acquired publisher version of record, file `papers/0091/0091.pdf`, 81 PDF pages, 1,868,420 bytes. Throughout, PDF page \(p\) means the one-based file page; its printed page is \(998+p\).

The main checks concern Theorems 1.1–1.2 (PDF pp. 4–5), the integration of local estimates in Section 3 (pp. 25–29), the Dirichlet–Neumann comparison and quantified transfer in Section 4 (pp. 30–35), interpolation in Section 5 (pp. 35–37), and Proposition 7.1 and its proof (pp. 43–48). The hypotheses of Proposition 8.1 (p. 49) and relevant convex-geometric estimates (pp. 73–76) were checked against their uses. Introductory and definitional pages 1–11, 24, and statements on p. 50 were also read. Remark 9.10 on pp. 72–73 was inspected for historical attribution. These 38 source pages were visually inspected as rendered pages.

This is not an independent verification of every proof in the 81-page article. In particular, the detailed local spectral/heat-kernel proofs on pp. 12–23, further applications on pp. 38–42, and technical Tauberian proofs on pp. 51–71 were not audited. The final continuation on p. 77 and bibliography pages were not independently inspected. No computational author code or essential computational supplement was identified in the supplied manifest; no author code was executed. Missing optional code is not a defect.
# Definitions, hypotheses, and dependencies

Theorem 1.2 assumes convexity and gives bounds for every \(\lambda>0\). Its auxiliary parameter is \(\alpha=1\) for \(\gamma\ge1\), and any \(0<\alpha<\gamma\) for \(0<\gamma<1\). It does not claim the endpoint \(\alpha=\gamma\) in the latter range or uniformity as \(\gamma\downarrow0\). Constants depending on \(\gamma\), \(\alpha\), or the domain must not be read as uniform across those parameters.

The proof uses the local estimate in Theorem 2.1 and near-boundary bounds in Propositions 2.2–2.4; the \(\gamma=1\) Dirichlet result from the article’s reference [27]; Brown’s heat-trace theorem as stated in Theorem 4.1; the companion heat-trace estimate cited as [31]; and a Tauberian argument. The present review checks how these inputs are used, but does not independently certify all their original proofs. This qualification is material to the scope of the outcome.
# Verified reasoning and boundary checks
## Integration of the local remainder

In Section 3, the boundary-strip quantity is \[\Theta_\Omega=\sup_{s>0}s^{-1}
 |\{x\in\Omega:d_\Omega(x)\le s\}|.\] The layer-cake calculation in equation (16), PDF p. 26, gives \[\int_\Omega\min\{\lambda^{(1+\gamma)/2},d_\Omega^{-1-\gamma}\}\,dx
 \le (1+\gamma)\Theta_\Omega
 \int_{\lambda^{-1/2}}^\infty s^{-1-\gamma}\,ds
 =\frac{1+\gamma}{\gamma}\Theta_\Omega\lambda^{\gamma/2}.\] Multiplication by the pointwise prefactor \(\lambda^{(\gamma+d-1)/2}\) gives \(\lambda^{\gamma+(d-1)/2}\), exactly the required order. The integral requires \(\gamma>0\); its divergence at \(\gamma=0\) explains why Proposition 3.6 instead has a logarithm. No passage to the excluded endpoint is needed.

The Neumann proof splits according to whether \(r_{\mathrm{in}}(\Omega)\ge\lambda^{-1/2}\) (PDF pp. 26–27). This prevents a bulk estimate from being applied when the bulk region is empty. For convex domains, equation (18), pp. 28–29, uses disjoint \(\ell\)-balls, a covering by \(2\ell\)-balls, and bounds on inner and outer boundary layers. The comparison of \(\ell^d/|\Omega\cap B_\ell(x)|\) with the radius-\(4\ell\) expression is applied only at \(x\in\Omega\), where Lemma A.5 supplies the needed monotonicity. The interior layer is bounded by \(2\ell S\) and the exterior layer by \(C_d\ell S[1+(\ell/r_{\mathrm{in}})^{d-1}]\). These give the two terms in the stated convex Neumann estimate.
## The first-order Neumann boundary coefficient

On PDF pp. 31–32, put \(f=R_1^{\mathrm N}-R_1^{\mathrm D}\). The variational principle gives \(N_{\mathrm N}(\mu)\ge
N_{\mathrm D}(\mu)\), so \(f'(\mu)\ge0\) almost everywhere. Thus the positive measure needed for the Tauberian step is the derivative of this difference. Its transform is \[\int_0^\infty e^{-t\lambda}\,df(\lambda)
 =t^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}e^{t\Delta_\Omega^{\mathrm N}}
              -\operatorname{Tr}e^{t\Delta_\Omega^{\mathrm D}}\bigr)
 \sim \frac{S}{2(4\pi)^{(d-1)/2}}t^{-(d+1)/2}.\] The resulting coefficient is \(\tfrac12 L_{1,d-1}S\lambda^{(d+1)/2}\). Adding the Dirichlet boundary coefficient \(-\tfrac14L_{1,d-1}S\) therefore produces \(+\tfrac14L_{1,d-1}S\), as required. Equation (19), p. 30, extends this to \(\gamma>1\) by a beta integral: for a single spectral value with \(a>0\), \(\gamma(\gamma-1)\int_0^a t^{\gamma-2}(a-t)\,dt=a^\gamma\). The normalization agrees with the definition of \(L_{\gamma,d}\).
## Interpolation down to every positive order

The proof of Proposition 7.1 (PDF pp. 44–48) was followed through the semigroup identity, the real-valued mean-value argument of Lemma 7.2, the split at \(\Lambda_1\), the two competing powers of \(\Lambda-\Lambda_1\), and the discrete interpolation for orders greater than one. The equal-endpoint case in Lemma 7.2 is satisfied directly by taking \(\lambda_0=\lambda_1\); it need not use the intermediate density construction. No obstruction was found in the real-valued application used in Section 5.
## Quantified convex bounds and the zero mode

For \(0<\alpha<\gamma<1\), taking \(\kappa=(\gamma-\alpha)/(1-\alpha)\) gives \(0<\kappa<\gamma\) and \(\theta=\alpha\). This accounts for the open range of \(\alpha\) and the Dirichlet exponent \(-\alpha/11\). In Section 4.2, the measure correction for Proposition 8.1 has exponent \(\nu=(d+1)/2\ge1\) and its Riesz order is \(\gamma-1\); hence its error is \(k^{-\gamma}\). Choosing \(k\) proportional to \(\log(r_{\mathrm{in}}\sqrt\lambda)\) with coefficient smaller than \(1/11\) yields the stated large-parameter logarithmic decay (PDF pp. 33–35). The small-parameter range is handled separately.
# Independent computation, alternative readings, and outcome

For the unit square, all original geometric assumptions hold. Separation of variables gives the exact cancellation identity \[R_\gamma^{\mathrm N}(\lambda)-R_\gamma^{\mathrm D}(\lambda)
 =\lambda^\gamma+2\sum_{n\ge1}(\lambda-\pi^2n^2)_+^\gamma.\] The boundary prediction is \(2L_{\gamma,1}\lambda^{\gamma+1/2}\) since \(S=4\). An independently written Python calculation, using no author code, gave the following ratios of the exact finite spectral sum to that prediction: \[\begin{array}{c|cc}
\gamma&\lambda=10^4&\lambda=10^6\\ \hline
0.1&0.993429121&1.000347518\\
0.5&0.999054013&1.000029589\\
1.0&0.999960462&1.000000699
\end{array}\] This checks normalization and the zero mode on a valid example. Finite floating-point results do not prove a uniform asymptotic theorem. SymPy simplifications of [exponent] (#exponent), the parameter conversion for \(\alpha\), and the small-energy exponent each returned exactly zero residual.

No substantive concern met the evidence threshold. Apparent endpoint objections are resolved by the explicit strict inequalities on \(\gamma\), \(\kappa\), and \(\alpha\); objections based on a signed second-order counting remainder do not apply to the nonnegative comparison measure actually used. The historical issue discussed in Remark 9.10 concerns Safarov’s earlier work and its odd-extension argument. It is not recorded as a new defect in this article; the earlier source and proposed historical repair were not independently re-verified.

Title: Initial review of regularity of the singular set in optimal transportation
# Identity and exact scope

The reviewed source is Shibing Chen and Jiakun Liu, Regularity of singular set in optimal transportation, arXiv:2210.13841v4, revised 20 July 2025 [1]. It has 43 PDF pages; PDF and printed page numbers agree. The bound file is `papers/0092/0092.pdf`. The associated journal record is Inventiones mathematicae 242 (2025), 1–44, DOI `10.1007/s00222-025-01353-w`, published 30 July 2025 [2]. The journal version of record was not acquired; no equivalence with that version is asserted.

Pages 1–19 and 39–42 were read in extracted text and actually viewed as page images (23 pages). The focus was Theorems 1.1–1.2, Lemmas 3.1–3.5, the beginning of Section 4 through Lemma 4.3, and Lemma 5.2. The statement and beginning of Lemma 4.4 were read, but its complete proof was not reviewed. Pages 20–38, containing much of the decisive obliqueness analysis, and page 43 were not scientifically inspected. Indexing the entire PDF is not counted as reviewing it.
# Hypotheses, quantifiers, and dependencies

The source and target are bounded open sets with probability densities bounded above and below by positive constants. The target has two convex components separated by a hyperplane. The source is not assumed convex. The convex transport potential \(u\) has branches \(u_i\), defined by restricted Legendre duality, and the interface is \[{\mathcal{F}}=\{u_1=u_2\}\cap\Omega .\] The claims are local inside \(\Omega\), including closures of branch regions at \(\mathcal F\), not assertions of regularity at an arbitrary exterior source boundary. Theorem 1.1 gives \(C^{1,\beta}\) regularity for some \(\beta\in(0,1)\). Theorem 1.2 additionally assumes \(C^2\) uniformly convex target components, \(f\in C^\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)\) and \(g\in C^\alpha(\overline{\Omega^*})\), with \(0<\alpha<1\), and concludes \(C^{2,\alpha}\) regularity.

Centered and tangent sections are different objects. Their comparison in (4.7) is needed in the width estimates. Lemma 3.5 gives Alexandrov measure inequalities, not merely almost-everywhere determinant bounds.

The checked chain is: compactness of the zero set and exposed points give localized sections (Lemmas 3.1–3.3); differentiability puts nearby subgradients inside the source (Lemma 3.4); images of exterior target points then lie in the Lipschitz interface, a null set, proving absence of exterior Alexandrov mass (Lemma 3.5). Quantitative convexity and Legendre duality give branch \(C^{1,\beta}\) estimates. The nonzero gradient jump in (1.5) determines the interface normal. Existing results cited as [4], [5], [7], and [14] in the paper remain external dependencies.
# Problem 1: an invalid affine-invariance step in Lemma 3.4
## Exact location and geometric check

Let \[S=\{(x_1,x_2):x_1^2/4+x_2^2<1\},\quad
 L=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1),\quad p=(0,1-\delta),\quad 0<\delta<1.\] This bounded convex centered section shape maps to the unit disk, with \(L0=0\). The distance from \(p\) to the ellipse boundary is \(\delta\): parametrizing a boundary point as \((2\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) gives squared distance \[4-3s^2-2(1-\delta)s+(1-\delta)^2,\qquad s=\sin\theta\in[-1,1].\] This concave polynomial has its minimum at an endpoint; \(s=1\) gives \(\delta^2\), smaller than \((2-\delta)^2\). The original quotient is therefore \(\delta/4\) and the transformed quotient is \(\delta/2\). At \(\delta=1/100\), these are exactly \(1/400\) and \(1/200\).
This example tests only the affine geometric identity. It does not purport to satisfy every transport assumption of Theorems 1.1–1.2 and is not a counterexample to either theorem.
## Complete replacement and impact

The comparison of (3.22) and (3.23) requires only this \(C_n/M\) bound; its large-\(M\) contradiction survives. Replace the literal equality by [good] (#good). The paper explicitly invokes ordinary affine invariance of the Euclidean distance ratio; John normalization in (3.19) imposes no similarity condition and no pullback metric is defined. Chord-ratio invariance proves the replacement inequality, not the displayed equality.

This is a Major error in a core proof step. The false equality is used to obtain (3.20), hence (3.23), the contradiction establishing Lemma 3.4, and then (3.24), Lemma 3.5 and (3.25) in the proof of Theorem 1.1. The complete repair above uses the existing endpoints and adds no transport hypothesis. The geometric counterexample disproves the invoked affine principle; it is not a constructed transport solution satisfying every hypothesis of the regularity theorem. Neither theorem falsity nor author adoption is asserted.
# Further checks and counterevidence
## Localization

In Lemma 3.1, a ray in the zero set forces subgradients into a half-space by monotonicity; the positive source density near the normalized interior point rules this out. Lemmas 3.2–3.3 use exposedness and compact section limits. In Lemma 3.5, (3.24) puts an exterior target point’s subgradient in \(\Omega\). An interior branch point would send that gradient back into the corresponding target component by strict convexity and duality. The remaining subgradients lie in \(\mathcal F\), whose Lipschitz regularity makes its Lebesgue measure zero. The local ball avoids the other target component. No source convexity is assumed.
## Small exponents

In Lemma 5.2, choose \(\varepsilon=\beta/[8(1+\beta)]\). Then \[(1/2-\varepsilon)(1+\beta)-(1/2+\beta/4)=\beta/8>0,\qquad
 \beta/4-\varepsilon>0.\] The graph-height threshold is asymptotically smaller than the section’s positive axial radius. The convex-segment argument places the upper cap inside \(\Omega_1\), and John normalization gives a fixed positive volume fraction for small \(h\). Convexity of \(\Omega_1\) is not needed.
## Forward references and higher regularity

The use of Lemma 5.4 in Case III on p. 39 is not by itself evidence of circularity: the relevant branch is already oblique in that case, and the estimates of Section 5 are branchwise once that branch’s obliqueness and the earlier interface regularity are available. A complete audit of Case I/II dependencies was not performed.

For care with the displayed powers there, conjugating an upper bound of exponent \(2-\eta\) yields a lower growth exponent \((2-\eta)/(1-\eta)>2\), rather than the same \(2-\eta\). The weaker resulting lower bound still dominates a power \(3+\varepsilon\) for sufficiently small \(\eta\), which is the comparison needed in that paragraph. This is not a transport counterexample and is not promoted to a confirmed substantive defect. The \(C^{2,\alpha}\) perturbation step on p. 42 invokes [10, Section 4]; that external proof and its full transfer were not independently audited.
# Outcome and remaining work

One Major proof-step error is established within the inspected scope: the affine-invariance assertion in Lemma 3.4. Its required replacement bound is proved, preserving the localization argument after correction. A targeted primary-source check found arXiv v4 as the listed latest version and the journal publication record; no article-specific correction was located in that limited search. This is not proof that no correction exists.
