Title: Initial review of character extensions in type D
# Identity, version, and coverage

The bound work is Britta Späth, Extensions of characters in type D and the inductive McKay condition, II, Inventiones mathematicae 242 (2025), 45–122, DOI `10.1007/s00222-025-01354-9` [1]. The acquired publisher version of record has 78 PDF pages and 2,208,737 bytes. PDF page \(p\) corresponds to printed page \(44+p\); page references below use PDF numbering unless explicitly marked printed.

The actual text and image inspection covers pp. 1–9, 12–17, 23–24, 50–54, 68–69, and 73–77: 29 pages. The selected claims are Theorems A–C, Condition 2.1 and Hypothesis 2.2, Lemmas 3.2, 3.5–3.6, the architecture of Theorem 3.3 and Proposition 3.11, Theorem 3.19, the reduction in Proposition 6.4, the trace calculation in Proposition 6.6, Lemma 7.1 and the final use of Proposition 7.7. Reading a theorem’s dependency statement is not counted as verifying the dependency’s entire proof.
# Definitions and exact claims

Here \(G=\mathbf G^F\) is the specified universal cover of a simple group of Lie type, with regular embedding into \(\widetilde G\) and graph-field automorphism group \(E(G)\). The introductory restriction on exceptional universal covers is explicit (p. 3); their separate character-table treatment is not checked here. The diagonal action factors through the finite abelian group \[\mathcal Z_F=\widetilde G/(GZ(\widetilde G)).\] Condition \(A'(\infty)\) asserts an \(E(G)\)-stable diagonal transversal. Condition \(A(\infty)\) additionally asks each chosen representative \(\chi\) to extend to \(G E(G)_\chi\). It does not say that every diagonal conjugate extends to the same graph-field subgroup. That distinction matters in the two-character orbits of Proposition 7.7.

Theorem B asserts an equivariant bijection with conjugacy classes of pairs \((s,\phi)\), including unipotent characters of possibly disconnected finite centralizers. Orbit sums, irreducible characters, rational series and geometric series must remain distinct. Theorem C concerns every finite group and the prime \(3\), and uses both the new global condition and previously established local conditions. It is not an assertion here of all-prime McKay solely from Theorem A.
# Checked equivariant and extension arguments
## Lifting orbit bijections

Lemma 3.2 (p. 12) requires three separate inputs: stable transversals, equality of stabilizer subgroups in \(Z\), and an equivariant bijection of \(Z\)-orbit sets. Choose stable transversals \(T_I,T_J\) and the induced map \(j:T_I\to T_J\). Defining \[J(zx_0)=zj(x_0),\qquad z\in Z,\ x_0\in T_I,\] is well-defined because two choices of \(z\) differ by \(Z_{x_0}=Z_{j(x_0)}\). The same condition gives injectivity and surjectivity on each orbit. For \(e\in E\), \[J(e(zx_0))=J(e(z)\,ex_0)=e(z)j(ex_0)=e(z)e(j(x_0))=e(J(zx_0)).\] This verifies full \(ZE\)-equivariance. Equality of orbit sizes alone would not justify this construction.

In Theorem 3.19 (pp. 23–24), the stabilizers on both sides are identified with the same inverse image under \(\widehat\omega_s\) of an annihilator subgroup. This is the appropriate subgroup equality, not merely a cardinality comparison. Its input from Proposition 3.17(c) remains an unaudited dependency here. Proposition 3.11 (pp. 16–17) supplies the second stable transversal using an invariant extension from Corollary 3.9 and Clifford correspondence.

The Clifford step needs only a twist by a linear character trivial on \(C=C_{\mathbf H}^{\circ}(s)^F\). If two extensions on the inertia group differ by a character of its quotient by \(C\), that character extends to the abelian component quotient and induction gives the required twist. This spells out the standard reading sufficient for the orbit argument; no stronger kernel condition is needed.
## Central kernels and wreath products

Lemma 3.5 (pp. 13–14) uses \(N\cap C_G(N)=Z(N)\leq\ker\chi\). Therefore \[NC_G(N)/C_G(N)\cong N/Z(N)\] carries \(\chi\), and an extension through the image of \(G_\chi\) in \(A_\chi\) inflates to the desired extension. The central-kernel hypothesis is essential and is present.

For Lemma 3.6 (p. 15), conjugating the factors first makes characters in the same \(Y\)-orbit equal. The stabilizer splits along equal-character blocks. On one block, an extension represented on \(V\) gives the tensor product representation on \(V^{\otimes n}\); permutation of tensor factors implements \(\mathcal S_n\) and satisfies the semidirect-product relations. Its restriction to \(X^n\) is the specified irreducible tensor character, so it is an extension. The general case is the product over blocks. This checks the elementary wreath-product step without assuming extension from invariance alone.

Theorem 3.3 uses algebraic components and automorphisms arising from them, not an unrestricted automorphism assertion about arbitrary small finite groups. Malle’s extension theorem and the unipotent identifications invoked there are still external prerequisites, including small-field cases.
# Counting and the two-extension alternative
## The signed trace

Set \(N=|\operatorname{Irr}(G^F)^D|\), let \(b\) be the number of those characters without extension to \(G^F D\), and set \(M=|\operatorname{Irr}(G^{F_0})^{\langle\gamma\rangle}|\). In Proposition 6.6 (pp. 53–54), the chosen basis contributes \(+1\) for an extendible invariant character and \(-1\) for a nonextendible invariant character. A pair exchanged by \(\gamma\) has trace zero. Consequently \[\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma_1)=N-2b=M,\qquad
 b=\frac{N-M}{2},\qquad N-b=\frac{N+M}{2}.\] Both signs and the factor \(1/2\) are consistent. The equality of traces through Shintani descent is assumed from the cited construction; it was not computationally reproduced. Given a subset of nonextendible characters with cardinality \((N-M)/2\), finite-set inclusion and equal size prove that it is the complete exceptional set. Cardinality alone, without nonextendibility, would not suffice.
## Lemma 7.1

The quotient in Lemma 7.1 (pp. 68–69) is the stated abelian \(2\)-group with independent cyclic factors generated by the images of \(d,f,c\); the images of \(d,c\) are involutions. Let \(\varphi\) extend \(\chi\) to \(\langle X,fangle\). Since this quotient over \(X\) is cyclic, extensions differ by its linear characters, and conjugation by \(c,d\) acts trivially on those linear characters. The noninvariance hypothesis for extensions to \(\langle X,dangle\) forces \[\varphi^d=\varphi
u,\qquad 
u^2=1,\quad 
u
eq1.\] Conjugation by \(c\) gives either \(\varphi^c=\varphi\) or \(\varphi^c=\varphi
u\). Thus exactly one of \(c\) and \(dc\) fixes \(\varphi\). The corresponding next quotient is cyclic, so an invariant \(\varphi\) extends. Twisting \(\varphi\) cannot change either invariance test; hence the other subgroup admits no extension of \(\chi\). This last observation justifies the nonexistence assertion for all extensions, not only for a selected one.

An independent exact calculation tested both alternatives in groups of order 16. On tuples \((z,d,c,f)\in\mathbf F_2^4\), use \[x y=(z+Z+f(D+aC),\,d+D,\,c+C,\,f+F),\qquad a\in\{0,1\},\] where \(y=(Z,D,C,F)\). The central subgroup \(X=\langle z\rangle\) has character \(\chi(z)=-1\), and the quotient is \(C_2^3\). In both cases \([d,f]=z\), so \(f\) interchanges the two extensions to \(\langle X,d\rangle\). For \(a=0\), there are four linear extensions to \(\langle X,f,c\rangle\) and none to \(\langle X,f,dc\rangle\); for \(a=1\) the counts reverse. Associativity was checked on all 4096 triples in each group. These finite examples illustrate the lemma; the preceding analytic argument supplies the general check.
# Scope question and main-theorem dependence

Proposition 6.4(ii.2), p. 52 (printed p. 96), assumes \(|\operatorname{Irr}(\bar\chi)^D|=2\). Its last proof case explicitly adds \(|\operatorname{Irr}(\bar\chi)|=2\) and then uses the order-two diagonal stabilizer on p. 53. These are different predicates. This review has not established the remaining general case where the full orbit is larger but exactly two points are \(D\)-fixed, nor produced a character of the specified Lie-type groups refuting the proposition. The general wording is therefore an unresolved scope question, not a confirmed defect.

There is decisive counterevidence to inferring failure of Theorem A from that question: the application on p. 76 invokes Proposition 7.7 to obtain a full two-element orbit whenever a nonextendible character occurs, and otherwise every invariant character extends. Thus this application uses precisely the stronger alternative treated in the proof. No unsupported case is required at that interface, conditional on the cited construction of the exceptional sets.

The rank induction in the proof of Theorem A (p. 76) starts at \(l=4\), where the smaller-rank hypothesis is empty. The induction hypothesis covers every smaller rank and every field exponent required by Hypothesis 2.2; Theorem 6.1 supplies the untwisted case, followed by the twisted case through Theorem 5.1. Mentioning dependence between twisted and untwisted arguments does not alone establish a circular proof. The complete internal verification of those descent arguments remains outside this review.

For Theorem B, Theorem A supplies \(A'(\infty)\) and Theorem 3.19 supplies the equivariant bijection. For Theorem C (pp. 76–77), the text separately invokes the reduction theorem, the non-Lie-type results, and \(A(1),B(1),A(2),B(2)\). Those external results were not independently audited.

Title: Initial review of the quasilinear Schrödinger flow
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed work is Mihaela Ifrim and Daniel Tataru, Global solutions for 1D cubic dispersive equations, part III: the quasilinear Schrödinger flow, Inventiones mathematicae 242 (2025), 221–304, DOI `10.1007/s00222-025-01356-7` [1]. This report is bound to the acquired publisher version of record, 84 pages and 1,928,821 bytes. PDF page \(p\) is printed page \(220+p\). Unless stated otherwise, locations below use PDF page numbers.

Text and page-image inspection covers pp. 1–9, 12–24, 39–47, 64–66, and 69–81, a total of 47 pages. The main checked chain is the formulation of Theorems 2–8, the independent linear flow in (4.2), Theorem 9 and its proof, its use in Section 8, and the final long-time/global argument in Section 9. Reading a cited estimate at an interface does not certify its uninspected proof. The full paradifferential expansions, most of the density-flux construction, the wave-packet parametrix in Section 7, and the adaptation to DQNLS have not been completely reproduced.

The source manifest has the original PDF and publisher HTML. No author source code, author TeX, or essential missing computational supplement was identified in those inputs. The work is analytic; absence of optional code is not a defect.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and boundaries

The QNLS equation is \[i u_t+g(u)u_{xx}=N(u,u_x),\] with a real metric, smooth coefficients, and \(N\) at most quadratic in \(u_x\). The normalized metric has \(g(0)=1\); the cubic convention concerns the nonlinear perturbation of that constant. DQNLS additionally allows derivative dependence in the metric. The local thresholds are strictly \(s>1\) and \(s>2\), respectively (Theorem 2, p. 5). The endpoints are explicitly open, and generic optimality is Conjecture 3, not a proved ill-posedness theorem. Rough uniqueness is formulated for uniform limits of regular solutions, not arbitrary distributional solutions.

For long-time results the cubic symbol \(c(\xi_1,\xi_2,\xi_3)\) is phase compatible and conservative: \[c(\xi,\xi,\xi),\quad \partial_{\xi_j}c(\xi,\xi,\xi)\in\mathbb R.\] Defocusing additionally requires the positive lower bound in Definition 1.4; for QNLS it is \(c(\xi,\xi,\xi)\gtrsim\langle\xi\rangle^2\). This is stronger than mere reality or positivity at one frequency. Scattering on p. 3 is explicitly the weak sense of global spacetime estimates, not convergence to a linear solution.

Theorem 6 propagates energy to \(T\ll\epsilon^{-8}\), but its long-time \(L^6\) and bilinear bounds are on subintervals of length \(\epsilon^{-6}\). Theorem 7 supplies such bounds on the entire interval under defocusing. Keeping these two time quantifiers separate is necessary for the energy argument.
# Problem 1: a false frequency gain in the core linear estimate
## Claim and location

Equation reference: bad. Theorem 9, p. 40 (printed p. 260), equation (6.5), asserts, for \(\mu\approx\lambda\), \[
 \|\partial_x(v_\lambda\overline{v_\mu^{x_0}})\|_{L^2_{t,x}}
 \lesssim d_\lambda d_\mu\lambda^{-1/2}(1+\lambda|x_0|).\] Here the functions solve the independent paradifferential equations (4.2), p. 24, and \[d_\lambda^2=\|v_\lambda(0)\|_2^2+
       \sup_{x_0}\|v_\lambda f_\lambda^{x_0}\|_{L^1_{t,x}}\] by (6.1). Theorem 9 imposes the small-solution assumptions on the background \(u\), not a relation \(v_\lambda=P_\lambda u\). Page 40 explicitly allows independent \(v_\lambda\); p. 41 even allows normalization \(d_\lambda=1\).
## Counterexample with every hypothesis checked

Fix any smooth cubic QNLS with \(g(0)=1\), for example \(g(u)=1+|u|^2\) and \(N(u,u_x)=|u|^2u\). Take the background \(u\equiv0\), any \(s>1\), and sufficiently small fixed \(\epsilon>0\). This is a smooth exact solution. Every background estimate (3.1)–(3.4) is zero on the left, for any admissible envelope. Fix \(T=1\); it satisfies \(T\ll\epsilon^{-4}\) after decreasing \(\epsilon\). At the zero background, \(g_{[<\lambda]}=1\) for all sufficiently large \(\lambda\).

Choose a nonzero \(\widehat\phi\in C_c^\infty\) supported in a sufficiently narrow compact subinterval of a unit dyadic annulus. Its width is fixed to fit the paper’s fixed step \(\mathfrak c>1\); no assumption that the step is two is used. Normalize \(\|\phi\|_2=1\), and set \[w(\tau,y)=e^{i\tau\partial_y^2}\phi(y),\qquad
 v_\lambda(t,x)=\lambda^{1/2}w(\lambda^2t,\lambda x),
 \quad \lambda=\mathfrak c^k\longrightarrow\infty.\] These are smooth exact solutions of \(i\partial_t v_\lambda+\partial_x^2v_\lambda=0\). Their Fourier supports remain inside the corresponding annuli of size \(\lambda\). Set \(f_\lambda=0\), so all source regularity assumptions hold and \(d_\lambda=1\) exactly. Set \(\mu=\lambda\) and \(x_0=0\); the balanced-frequency and translation hypotheses are then satisfied.

Define the fixed positive finite constant \[A=\|\partial_y|w|^2\|_{L^2([0,1]\times\mathbb R)}.\] Finiteness follows from the Schwartz regularity on a compact time interval. Positivity needs no numerical assumption: if \(\partial_y|\phi|^2\) were identically zero, its Schwartz decay would force \(\phi=0\). Continuity in time therefore gives \(A>0\).

Equation reference: counter. The change of variables \(\tau=\lambda^2t\), \(y=\lambda x\) gives \[\partial_x|v_\lambda|^2
       =\lambda^2(\partial_y|w|^2)(\lambda^2t,\lambda x),
 \qquad dt\,dx=\lambda^{-3}\,d\tau\,dy.\] Consequently, \[
 \|\partial_x|v_\lambda|^2\|_{L^2([0,1]\times\mathbb R)}
 \ge
 \|\partial_x|v_\lambda|^2\|_{L^2([0,\lambda^{-2}]\times\mathbb R)}
 =\lambda^{1/2}A.\] Equation [bad] (#bad) would instead bound this by \(K\lambda^{-1/2}\), with \(K\) independent of the dyadic frequency. It would imply \(A\lambda\le K\) for every \(k\), a contradiction. The initial data are square-integrable Schwartz packets; a nonintegrable plane wave is not being offered as a theorem counterexample.
## Where the proof fails and what its own estimates support

The last paragraph of Section 6, p. 46 (printed p. 266), claims that (6.12), (6.14), and (6.17) imply (6.5). At \(x_0=0\) and \(\mu=\lambda\), the cited boundary and source bounds have size \[\lambda d_\lambda^2d_\mu^2,\] and (6.14)–(6.15) identify the leading spacetime expression with the squared differentiated bilinear norm. Taking a square root gives \(\lambda^{1/2}d_\lambda d_\mu\), not \(\lambda^{-1/2}d_\lambda d_\mu\).

The printed bootstrap also cannot justify the stated continuation. On p. 41, (6.9) has right-hand side \(C^2\epsilon d_\lambda d_\mu\lambda^{-1/2}(1+\lambda|x_0|)\), and the unbalanced bootstrap (6.10) likewise has a negative half-power and an extra \(\epsilon\). Improving to a bound of the form (6.5) with constant independent of \(\epsilon\) does not recover the smaller bootstrap for \(\epsilon\ll_C1\). The free-flow family above shows directly why a uniform continuation of the printed (6.9) cannot be true.

This is a demonstrated quantitative failure and invalid inference in a main proof input, rather than a finding based only on the appearance of an unusual exponent. Section 8, pp. 64–66, invokes Theorem 9 both for \(v_\lambda=u_\lambda\) and for the linearized flow. Under the prescribed core-contribution calibration, the supported impact is Major for this estimate and its stated bootstrap argument.
## Counterevidence and repair limits

There is strong evidence for an intended weaker, correctly scaled result. Theorem 8 on p. 22 and (3.2), (3.6) on p. 20 have the positive half-power. The Morawetz identity in the proof also has exactly that scaling. In the unbalanced case, converting a product estimate to a differentiated-product estimate introduces one frequency, as the first display on p. 46 explicitly shows.

For the balanced estimate, the candidate replacement is \[\|\partial_x(v_\lambda\overline{v_\mu^{x_0}})\|_2
 \lesssim d_\lambda d_\mu\lambda^{1/2}(1+\lambda|x_0|).\] It agrees with the counterexample scaling and the algebra of the displayed Morawetz estimates. The bootstrap must also consistently distinguish differentiated from undifferentiated products and remove an unsupported small factor for the \(v,v\) pair. Correcting only the theorem statement does not repair the printed continuation argument.

This review does not claim that Theorems 2–4 are false. The weaker estimate already matches the bounds they use at the theorem interfaces. Nor does it certify a full variable-coefficient repair: every later occurrence in Sections 6–8 must be audited after a consistent correction. A typographical origin is plausible from the counterevidence, but does not make the quantitative assertion [bad] (#bad) valid. The recorded impact is restricted to the disproved core estimate and the invalid derivation as printed; no failure of global existence or optimal-regularity well-posedness has been demonstrated.
# Other checks and limitations
## Resonance and interpolation

With \(\xi_4=\xi_1-\xi_2+\xi_3\), \[\xi_1^2-\xi_2^2+\xi_3^2-\xi_4^2
 =-2(\xi_1-\xi_2)(\xi_3-\xi_2).\] Thus the resonance description on p. 15 follows, including the double diagonal. The alternating conjugation convention on pp. 16–17 agrees with this computation.

The energy accumulation on pp. 73–74 uses at most \(O(1+T\epsilon^6)\) blocks of length comparable to \(\epsilon^{-6}\). An \(O(\epsilon^4)\) error per block gives \(O(\epsilon^4+T\epsilon^{10})\), which is small relative to \(\epsilon^2\) for \(T\ll\epsilon^{-8}\). The displayed block count \(T\epsilon^{-6}\) on p. 74 has the opposite sign, but the corrected count directly restores the asserted lifespan. This isolated counting transcription is retained as a clarification, not a separate substantive finding.

For the defocusing argument, Lemma 9.2 is the stated input identifying the positive diagonal sixth-order symbol. If that input and the density-flux construction hold, its one-third-order multiplier gives the factor \(\lambda^2\) in the sixth power, converting \(\lambda^{1-4s}\) into \(\lambda^{-1-4s}\) as required by (3.5). The underlying symbol calculation, deferred to the earlier paper, was not fully reproduced.
## The introductory model and an unresolved estimate

For the model on p. 7, \[iu_t+(1+a|u|^2)u_{xx}=bu|u_x|^2+cu|u|^2,\] the cubic right-hand side after moving the metric perturbation is \(-a|u|^2u_{xx}+bu|u_x|^2+cu|u|^2\). In the paper’s Fourier convention its symmetrized symbol has diagonal \[c_{\rm model}(\xi,\xi,\xi)=(a+b)\xi^2+c.\] Thus the printed sign test \(a-b,c>0\) must be replaced by \(a+b,c>0\) for this displayed model. For example \((a,b,c)=(0,-1,1)\) passes the printed test but has diagonal \(1-\xi^2\), equal to \(-3\) at \(\xi=2\); \((0,1,1)\) has the positive diagonal \(1+\xi^2\) despite the printed focusing label. The coefficients are smooth, real where required, cubic and phase compatible, with real symbol derivatives. This is a check of the classification of a model, not a small-data counterexample to Theorem 4: the first model fails Theorem 4’s actual defocusing hypothesis. It is recorded as a local sign clarification, without an additional severity count.

A separate unresolved point is the final estimate for four balanced factors in Lemma 8.3, p. 69. The first displayed Hölder bound contains \(T^{1/2}\); direct insertion of the stated norms gives an \(\epsilon^2T^{1/2}\) factor, whereas the next displayed bound no longer contains \(T\). On \(T\ll\epsilon^{-4}\) this directly gives a small interval constant, not uniformly the claimed \(\epsilon^2\) gain. No function satisfying all the equation and \(X_\lambda\) constraints has been constructed here to refute the lemma, and no full alternative estimate has been verified. This is a Needs Evidence item for a focused follow-up, not a second confirmed defect.

The frequency-envelope construction of rough solutions on pp. 69–71 is conditional on the corrected linear estimates and the higher-regularity bounds. Its use of the square-summable envelope tail is appropriate for convergence. External high-regularity existence, continuous-dependence machinery, and all omitted source-term estimates remain dependencies.
# Disposition

The supported finding is Problem 1, with the scope and counterevidence stated above. The symbolic computation checks scaling exponents, resonance, the model diagonal and long-time bookkeeping; it does not solve a nonlinear PDE or independently validate all estimates. A limited publisher/title/DOI correction search did not locate a specific erratum. That negative search is not proof that no correction exists. No later author manuscript was silently substituted for the bound publisher PDF.

Taking a square root gives \(\lambda^{1/2}d_\lambda d_\mu\), not \(\lambda^{-1/2}d_\lambda d_\mu\).

The printed bootstrap also cannot justify the stated continuation. On p. 41, (6.9) has right-hand side \(C^2\epsilon d_\lambda d_\mu\lambda^{-1/2}(1+\lambda|x_0|)\), and the unbalanced bootstrap (6.10) likewise has a negative half-power and an extra \(\epsilon\). Improving to a bound of the form (6.5) with constant independent of \(\epsilon\) does not recover the smaller bootstrap for \(\epsilon\ll_C1\). The free-flow family above shows directly why a uniform continuation of the printed (6.9) cannot be true.

This is a demonstrated quantitative failure and invalid inference in a main proof input, rather than a finding based only on the appearance of an unusual exponent. Section 8, pp. 64–66, invokes Theorem 9 both for \(v_\lambda=u_\lambda\) and for the linearized flow. Under the prescribed core-contribution calibration, the supported impact is Major for this estimate and its stated bootstrap argument.
result: There is strong evidence for an intended weaker, correctly scaled result. Theorem 8 on p. 22 and (3.2), (3.6) on p. 20 have the positive half-power. The Morawetz identity in the proof also has exactly that scaling. In the unbalanced case, converting a product estimate to a differentiated-product estimate introduces one frequency, as the first display on p. 46 explicitly shows.

For the balanced estimate, the candidate replacement is \[\|\partial_x(v_\lambda\overline{v_\mu^{x_0}})\|_2
 \lesssim d_\lambda d_\mu\lambda^{1/2}(1+\lambda|x_0|).\] It agrees with the counterexample scaling and the algebra of the displayed Morawetz estimates. The bootstrap must also consistently distinguish differentiated from undifferentiated products and remove an unsupported small factor for the \(v,v\) pair. Correcting only the theorem statement does not repair the printed continuation argument.

This review does not claim that Theorems 2–4 are false. The weaker estimate already matches the bounds they use at the theorem interfaces. Nor does it certify a full variable-coefficient repair: every later occurrence in Sections 6–8 must be audited after a consistent correction. A typographical origin is plausible from the counterevidence, but does not make the quantitative assertion [bad] (#bad) valid. The recorded impact is restricted to the disproved core estimate and the invalid derivation as printed; no failure of global existence or optimal-regularity well-posedness has been demonstrated.
Impact: Invalid quantitative core input and claimed derivation/continuation used in Section 8. Major calibration restricted to this guarantee, not whole-paper refutation.

Title: Initial scientific review: M25-0095
Compatibility of canonical \(\ell\)-adic local systems
on adjoint Shimura varieties
# Version, scope and main claims

The bound article is Christian Klevdal and Stefan Patrikis, Inventiones mathematicae 242 (2025), 305–335, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01357-6, publisher Version of Record, published online 25 August 2025. The original PDF has 31 pages and 1,462,931 bytes. All references below use PDF page numbers; printed page equals PDF page plus 304. All 31 pages were read as full extracted text and actually viewed as page images. Reading the references is not verification of all cited works.

The source manifest contains the original PDF and publisher HTML, with no author TeX or released code identified. Both manifest files were hash-checked. This absence is not a defect. No author code was executed. The review’s calculations are small exact checks written independently by the reviewer.

Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 (pp. 3, 5), and the more general Theorem 3.10 and Corollary 3.12 (pp. 25–28), require a neat level, discreteness of \(Z_G(\mathbb Q)\) in \(Z_G(\mathbb A_f)\), and real rank at least two for every \(\mathbb Q\)-simple adjoint factor. The uniform exceptional integer is chosen before \(\ell,\ell'\) and the closed point. After specializing to a number-field point, a further integer may depend on that point. The conclusion concerns semisimple geometric conjugacy classes in the adjoint GIT quotient. It does not provide a rational representative in \(G^\mathrm{ad}(\mathbb Q)\), compatibility in the full central extension \(G\), or the missing motives. The qualifications in Remarks 1.2, 1.4, 1.5 and 3.14 were preserved. Results of subsequent papers cited there were not used to certify the present proof.
# Checks of the proof chain
## Adjointness and descent

Lemma 2.1 (p. 8) is correct by uniqueness of conjugators. Zariski density gives \[C_H(\rho(\Pi'))=Z(H)=1.\] For \(x,y\in\Pi\), the element \(h_xh_y\) conjugates \(\rho\) to \(\rho^{xy}\), so uniqueness gives \(h_{xy}=h_xh_y\). For \(x\in\Pi'\) it gives \(h_x=\rho(x)\). Applying every element of \(\operatorname{Gal}(K^s/K)\) gives \(h_x\in H(K)\). This also identifies exactly why the extension argument cannot simply be copied to a group with center: central characters of \(\Pi/\Pi'\) can produce distinct extensions.

In Proposition 2.3 (pp. 9–11), the hypothesis \(F(\lambda)=F\) is essential and is not proved for arbitrary rigid systems. Canonical models supply a common field in the Shimura application (p. 18). The use of \(N'=\gcd_\lambda N_\lambda\) is consistent: a prime outside this gcd is good for at least one coefficient place, and that place cannot lie over the same rational prime because its own coefficient prime was included in \(N_\lambda\).

The companion is pulled back by tame specialization, not by an asserted inverse to specialization. Its geometric Zariski closure is a normal subgroup \(H\) of the adjoint semisimple group. The quotient \(G/H\) is densely generated by a single Frobenius and is therefore commutative. A quotient of the adjoint semisimple group that is commutative is trivial. This verifies the density step needed for superrigidity. After geometric factorization, inertia centralizes the dense geometric image; adjointness makes inertia trivial. The final extension across the fiber still depends on the cited ramification detection and Hilbert irreducibility results. Their full proofs were not reproduced.
## Removing the outer ambiguity

Proposition 2.8 (pp. 12–13) correctly needs a Frobenius element fixed by no automorphism with nontrivial outer class. Equality of the semisimple classes says that a lift \(\widetilde\tau\) of the outer class carries a representative \(t\) to a conjugate. Choosing \(g\) with \((\operatorname{inn}(g)\widetilde\tau)(t)=t\) and transporting to the coefficient field produces an actual automorphism fixing \(t_\lambda\). Assumption 2.7(2) then forces the outer class to vanish. Merely knowing equality of characteristic polynomials in one representation would not suffice for this step.

Proposition 3.3 (pp. 16–17) reduces the dense representation to a product of arithmetic subgroups. The finite index of that product ensures density is retained. Commuting normal images in a simple adjoint target leave one nontrivial source factor per target factor. The resulting surjective algebraic endomorphism has finite central kernel, hence is an automorphism because the source is adjoint. Its agreement on the normal finite-index subgroup extends to the whole group by the trivial centralizer argument. For the final descent one may first enlarge the auxiliary field to an algebraically closed overfield; then invariance under automorphisms over the algebraically closed base gives descent. Alternatively, the unique conjugator is the unique geometric point of the conjugacy equations, which are defined over the base. This supplies the routine field-descent detail without assuming that an arbitrary field extension has a large automorphism group. Margulis’s external theorem itself remains an input.
## Canonical systems and the special-point formula

The right action, opposite automorphism group and base-point choices in pp. 14–18 were checked together. The topological inclusion is sent to \(a^{-1}\gamma a\), as shown by \([\gamma^{-1}x,a]_K=[x,\gamma a]_K\). The convention of geometric Frobenius agrees with the reciprocity convention on p. 8. Lemma 3.2 gives \[r_x(\alpha)=q\,a k_0(\sigma)a^{-1},\qquad qx=x.\] When the centralizer is the torus, the component away from the support of the uniformizer yields Equation (6), \[k_{0,\ell}(\operatorname{Frob}_w)=a_\ell^{-1}q^{-1}a_\ell.\] The inverse is necessary. The same rational \(q\) works for the coefficient primes, which is the required horizontal compatibility, subject to the torus and integrality inputs.

In Lemma 3.6 and Proposition 3.7 (pp. 19–22), the full Weyl-group action and transitive action on absolutely simple factors give irreducibility of the rational character representation. The local prescriptions at \(p\), at infinity and at finitely many pairwise auxiliary primes are finite in number. The twisting argument preserves the local torus isomorphism types outside one auxiliary prime. Its use of Brauer–Nesbitt and Chebotarev concerns rational character representations, not integral lattices. The Hasse principle, existence of the cohomology class and weak approximation for the variety of tori remain external inputs.
## Frobenius closure and rationality

For a rational element \(t\) of a \(\mathbb Q\)-irreducible torus, infinite order implies that the identity component of the \(\mathbb Q\)-Zariski closure of \(\langle t\rangle\) is a nonzero subtorus, hence the whole torus. With pairwise non-isogenous irreducible factors, a connected subtorus projecting onto all factors is their full product: its character quotient has no diagonal identification between distinct irreducible rational modules. This is the precise input required on p. 27; the distinction in the next section matters.

An automorphism fixing a maximal torus pointwise fixes its characters and roots. Over an algebraically closed field it acts on the one-dimensional root spaces by compatible scalars, and is conjugation by an element of that torus. Thus the final elimination of outer automorphisms is valid once the full-torus closure has been obtained. The base-change assertion in footnote 9 is appropriate because the powers of \(t\) are rational.

Finally, compatibility over all coefficient embeddings is used before descent from \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\) to \(\mathbb Q\). For a finite field of definition, invariance under the decomposition groups for almost all rational primes forces invariance under the entire finite Galois group by Chebotarev. This proves rationality in the quotient, not rational conjugacy in \(G^\mathrm{ad}\). Corollary 3.12 then follows because an \(F\)-rational point determines a Galois-stable geometric component, whose field of definition is contained in \(F\).
# Clarifications and unresolved scope
## U1: non-isomorphic versus non-isogenous tori
Location. Proposition 3.7(3), p. 20; its local choice on p. 21; the first paragraph of the proof of Lemma 3.9, p. 23; the closure argument in Theorem 3.10, p. 27.

Exact concern. The stated property is that the irreducible \(\mathbb Q\)-tori \(T_i\) are pairwise non-isomorphic. The proof on p. 23 then treats \(X^*(T_i)_\mathbb Q\) as pairwise non-isomorphic. In general, rational character modules classify tori up to isogeny, not isomorphism. The full-product conclusion requires non-isogeny, or a further argument ruling out diagonal subgroups.

Here is an exact lattice test of the logical distinction. Let the signed permutation group on two coordinates act on \[L_0=\mathbb Z^2,\qquad
 L_1=\{(m,n)\in\mathbb Z^2:m+n\equiv0\pmod2\}.\] Both rationalizations are the same irreducible representation. A basis matrix for \(L_1\) is \[B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad |\det B|=2.\] The common commutant of the sign change \(\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\) and coordinate swap in \(M_2(\mathbb Q)\) consists only of scalars. An equivariant lattice isomorphism would therefore be scalar. Equality on each coordinate axis would force its absolute scalar to be \(2\), but \(2\mathbb Z^2\) does not contain \((1,1)\in L_1\). Thus the integral modules are not isomorphic although the rational ones are. A signed-permutation Galois action realizes the same distinction for tori. This calculation tests the inference; it is not a construction of a Shimura datum satisfying every hypothesis of Lemma 3.9.

Counterevidence and local repair. The construction on p. 21 can explicitly choose, for every pair \((i,j)\), a prime at which both ambient groups split, and take a split maximal torus on one side and an anisotropic maximal torus on the other. The cited existence input already used there permits these choices. Local split rank is invariant under isogeny; these two tori are therefore not isogenous. The local twisting preserves their types at that prime. Keeping this stronger property throughout gives pairwise non-isomorphic rational character modules, and the semisimple-module argument on pp. 23 and 27 then works.

Scope and disposition. This verifies a concrete strengthening of the construction sufficient for the main argument, conditional on the same external existence inputs. It does not prove that the standalone weaker hypotheses of Lemma 3.9 always imply the intermediate assertion printed on p. 23. That question is Needs Evidence; no all-hypothesis counterexample to the lemma or main theorem is claimed. The report does not infer a Major or Minor finding solely from the abstract lattice example.
## U2: the torus inside a fixed hyperspecial subgroup

Location. Lemma 3.9, last paragraph of p. 24 and first paragraph of p. 25. The equality \[G_{\mathbb Z_p}(\mathbb Z_p)\cap T_x(\mathbb Q_p)=T_x(\mathbb Q_p)^0\] is used to infer that the special-point field is unramified, and then to take the uniformizer to be \(p\).

Exact check. An unramified torus as an abstract local group need not be in good integral position relative to a prescribed reductive model. For \(p=5\), in \(\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Q_5)\) let \(D\) be the diagonal torus, \[u=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/5\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=uDu^{-1}.\] This is a split, hence unramified, maximal torus, contained in a rational Borel. Its maximal compact subgroup contains \[u\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}u^{-1}
 =\begin{pmatrix}1&1/5\\0&2\end{pmatrix},\] which is not in \(\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z_5)\). The printed general inference therefore needs an integral embedding condition. The author’s public 2022 draft of the cited Getz–Hahn book states Lemma A.5.2 for a torus and Borel subgroup scheme of the reductive integral model. That draft is supplementary evidence only; equivalence with every detail of the 2024 edition was not assumed.

This example verifies the local distinction, but has not been embedded here in a full higher-rank Shimura datum with all the global irreducibility and level conditions. Accordingly it is not presented as a counterexample to Lemma 3.9’s infinite-order conclusion.

Scope and disposition. The norm-valuation replacement is checked and preserves the needed infinite-order conclusion once the preceding torus and reciprocity steps hold. The separate assertion that the special-point field is unramified under exactly the printed assumptions remains Needs Evidence. A complete uniform correction of all preparatory claims and all external inputs was not certified. No failure of the main compatibility conclusion was established.
## A small product-group clarification

In the first sentence of the proof of Lemma 3.6 (p. 19), an arbitrary open subgroup of a product need not itself decompose as the product of its projections. For example, inverse images of a diagonal subgroup under finite quotient maps give open subgroups with coupled factors. What is sufficient is to choose a product of open subgroups contained in \(K_v\). Such a product exists by the product topology. Applying the factorwise argument to that smaller product gives conjugators in the original \(K_v\). This is a local proof clarification with a complete repair and no change to the lemma’s conclusion.

Title: Initial scientific review: M25-0096
Counting pseudo-Anosovs as weakly contracting isometries
# Bound version and inspected scope

This review concerns Inhyeok Choi’s arXiv:2408.00603v3, submitted 12 October 2025; the bound PDF is dated 14 October 2025 and has 38 pages and 646,186 bytes. The journal identity is DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01358-5, Inventiones mathematicae 242 (2025), 337–386, published online 22 August 2025. The journal Version of Record was not acquired. Neither metadata linkage nor the repository’s description of v3 as accepted establishes equality with the journal text.

All locations below are author-version PDF page numbers. Full extracted text on pp. 1–36 was read. Pages 1–3 and 7–36 (33 pages) were additionally actually viewed as original page images, including every main theorem, formal proof section, and Appendix A. Pages 4–6 were text-reviewed but not visually inspected; pp. 37–38 were not independently reviewed. The full 170,741-byte author TeX was parsed statically, with targeted mathematical source contexts compared to the PDF. Parsing an index or source inventory is not scientific review. No author source was compiled or executed.

The eight manifest files were verified against their recorded sizes and SHA-256 values. Author TeX, bibliography and archive are typesetting material, not released computational code. Absence of released code is not a defect. An independently written normal-form calculation was actually executed and retained; the general counterexample proof below does not depend on finite numerical sampling.
# Claims, hypotheses and dependency audit

Theorem A (p. 2) and Theorem 5.3 (p. 18) fix an arbitrary finite generating set of the mapping class group of the specified finite-type hyperbolic surface, excluding the three-punctured sphere. The stronger statement controls the union of the small curve-complex translation-length event and the event \(\tau_S(g)\le0.33R\). Constants may depend on the generating set. They are not uniform over all generating sets. Word-ball counting is not interchangeable with random-walk counting or counting ambient-metric balls.
## Projection and concatenation, pp. 7–18 and 34–36

The fixed pseudo-Anosov has a geodesic axis in the curve complex, with \(D_C>0\), and the orbit map is Lipschitz. Fact 2.2 uses two different inputs: non-elementarity supplies bounded connecting letters, while WPD turns long overlapping oriented axis segments into finitely many possibilities in the word metric. This distinction matters in Finding F1: WPD alone does not supply non-elementarity.

Lemma 2.4 follows by choosing an orbit point near the projected point and using the comparison \(d_S(a,b)\le(D_S/D_C)d_C(ax_0,bx_0)\) along the chosen orbit. Proposition 2.3 is an external weak-contraction input; its original subsurface-projection proof was not reconstructed here. The alignment convention in Definition 3.2 controls terminal and initial projections in the prescribed orientation. Facts 3.3–3.5, Lemmas 3.6–3.7 and the Appendix A projection estimates were traced, including the requirement that interior segments exceed the alignment-error thresholds.

Proposition 4.1 chooses a crossing component of a word-geodesic whose curve-complex projections lie near the axis midpoint. If the component stays far away in the word metric, weak contraction forces many long steps before the projected crossing can finish. Its choice \(T=103K_{\mathrm{map}}^3/D_C\) satisfies the displayed comparison; the previously reported numerical adjustment is withdrawn below. Proposition 4.3 then distributes errors with weights \(30^{-j}\). The induction’s left and right coefficient gaps dominate the extra contribution from the newly chosen first point. In Corollary 4.5, \[2\sum_{j\ge1}30^{-j}=\frac2{29}<\frac1{14};\] the ordered points on the word-geodesic therefore give the required bound on the sum of distances to the orbit midpoints.

Corollary 4.6 combines linear progress of the aligned segments with the fact that the two relevant word-geodesic pieces concatenate to a geodesic. For the range used in the fibre argument, summing \(D_i+D_i'\ge 2K_{\mathrm{map}}(i-L')\) gives a quadratic lower bound. The displayed sum proves this directly when the number of segments is at least \(L'\). For smaller numbers, the fibre estimate is already bounded by a constant; one should use the positive part \((n-L')_+^2\) in a universally stated lower bound. This audit does not claim that the printed stronger small-\(n\) bound has been independently established.
## Counting and translation-length bounds, pp. 18–24

Fekete’s lemma applies to the submultiplicative word-ball counts, and positive exponential growth is essential for the inner-ball ratio. For a fixed positive growth exponent \(\lambda\), choose the upper growth-rate error sufficiently smaller than \((1-0.99)\lambda\); then \(|B_S(0.99n)|/|B_S(n)|\) decays exponentially.

In Lemma 5.5, an aligned orbit near one quarter of the word length either iterates to produce positive translation length, or yields a conjugacy expression with conjugator length at most \(0.31n\) and conjugated element length at most \(0.57n\). The conjugator is counted once, not twice: it also determines its inverse. Thus \(0.31+0.57<1\) makes the latter set exponentially negligible. The retained exact arithmetic check gives \[0.86(0.99-0.6-0.001)-0.334=\frac{27}{50000}>0,\qquad
0.334\cdot0.99-0.33=\frac{33}{50000}>0.\] These margins remove a superficial concern about the non-strict inequalities at the translation-length cutoff. The lower distance in the definition of \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{thick}}\) is \(0.25\|g\|_S\), not necessarily \(0.25n\); the later estimates can and do retain the former bound.

The insertion map \(F_n\) removes a fixed-length block and replaces it by \(s\phi^{L_{\mathrm{map}}}t\), so its image remains in \(B_S(n)\). Overlapping trimmed intervals on \([x_0,Ux_0]\) are clustered by WPD, with a number of word choices independent of \(n\). A maximal disjoint family is aligned. If its last segment aligns with the translated endpoint, the original input lies in \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{thick}}\), contrary to the domain definition. Otherwise Corollary 4.6 bounds the disjoint family by \(O(\sqrt n)\). There are \(\Theta(n)\) insertion positions, so the double count gives an \(O(n^{-1/2})\) exceptional proportion. The fixed constants and the finitely many small radii can be absorbed into the theorem’s \(K\).
## Two insertions and extensions

Lemmas 6.1–6.2 count a last-stage prefix/block/suffix triple and then its possible predecessors, each with \(O(\sqrt n)\) possibilities. The midpoint case split in Lemma 6.2 uses the original geodesic word and the original input’s exclusion from \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{thick}}\); an arbitrary intermediate word is not automatically another valid input. This is why a complete multi-stage induction needs to retain those data. The two-insertion argument gives an \(O(n^{-1})\) bound after correcting a harmless counting coefficient below. The proof of Theorem 6.3 explicitly writes out only \(k=2\); verification of the all-\(k\) step is recorded separately as U1.

The HHG and quasi-isometry extensions require the external results on maximal hyperbolic spaces, Morse detection, and weak contraction. Lemma 7.8 transports projections through quasi-isometries; the constants must be enlarged together so that the additive errors are absorbed. For the CAT(0) extension, geometric action gives word/ambient metric comparison and properness gives WPD; the rank-one/strong-contraction equivalence is an external input. These external theorems were not re-proved.

For braids, the argument first counts cosets of the center. If \(A=\max_{s\in S}|\rho(s)|\) for exponent sum \(\rho\), then \(|\rho(g)|\le A\|g\|_S\), and \(\rho(\Delta^2)\ne0\) bounds each central coset’s intersection with \(B_S(R)\) by \(O(R)\). Quotient word balls are images of the original word balls. Thus a quotient exceptional bound \(O(R^{-q})\) yields \(O(R^{1-q})\) upstairs, and an arbitrary polynomial exponent is needed to deduce the final superpolynomial statement. The literal phrase that word norm only decreases under homomorphisms must be read with the appropriate generating-set Lipschitz constant. No claim that a braid itself is a Morse element is required.
# F1: confirmed Major — missing non-virtually-cyclic hypothesis
## Exact location and claim

Theorem C, p. 3 (author TeX lines 167–172), allows every group quasi-isometric to a well-behaved HHG containing Morse elements. Theorem 7.4, pp. 28–29 (TeX lines 1471–1476), assumes a finitely generated group with a WPD loxodromic isometry weakly contracting by means of the hyperbolic space. Neither statement excludes virtually cyclic groups. Theorem C claims an \(O(R^{-1/2})\) non-Morse proportion; Theorem 7.4 claims superpolynomial genericity of loxodromics.

The displayed numerator of Theorem 7.4 counts loxodromics instead of non-loxodromics. That sign-of-event error is not the basis of this finding: the counterexample below defeats the intended genericity conclusion even after the numerator is corrected.
## Full counterexample and every hypothesis

Let \[G=D_\infty=\langle r,s\mid s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle,\qquad
S=\{r,s\},\qquad X=\mathbb R.\] Use the action \(r(x)=x+1\), \(s(x)=-x\) and basepoint \(0\). The space is geodesic and \(0\)-hyperbolic, and the action is isometric. Every element has a unique normal form \(r^m s^\epsilon\), \(m\in\mathbb Z\), \(\epsilon\in\{0,1\}\). The orbit of \(\phi=r\) is the integer line, hence a geodesic orbit and loxodromic.

For WPD, the condition \(d_X(0,h0)<L\) already forces \(|m|<L\) and permits only two values of \(\epsilon\). It gives a finite bound independent of the second condition, so any positive \(N\), with sufficiently large \(M\), works in Definition 7.3. This verifies WPD directly, rather than inferring non-elementarity from it.

For weak contraction as Definition 7.2 states it, put \[\pi_\gamma(r^m s^\epsilon)=r^m,\qquad \gamma=\{r^j:j\in\mathbb Z\}.\] This projection fixes \(\gamma\), and its image under the orbit map is exactly the nearest projection of \(h0=m\) to the integer orbit. It is therefore a valid projection by means of \(X\). Also \[d_S(r^m s^\epsilon,\gamma)=\epsilon\le1.\] Taking the weak-contraction threshold \(K'=2\) makes the required condition for points farther than \(K'\) vacuous. The orbit is nevertheless an actual geodesic. The theorem has no requirement that the complement of the orbit have unbounded distance, so this is a legitimate instance of all its assumptions.

The word length is exactly \[\|r^m s^\epsilon\|_S=|m|+\epsilon.\] The upper bound is its normal form. For the lower bound, each \(r^{\pm1}\) changes the integer coordinate by at most one, and a word representing \(\epsilon=1\) must contain at least one \(s\). For every integer \(n\ge1\) there are \(2n+1\) translations with \(|m|\le n\) and \(2n-1\) reflections with \(|m|\le n-1\). The nonzero translations are loxodromic; every reflection squares to the identity, and the identity is also non-loxodromic. Hence \[|B_S(n)|=4n,\qquad
|\{g\in B_S(n):g\text{ is non-loxodromic}\}|=2n,\qquad
\frac{2n}{4n}=\frac12.\] The ratio cannot be at most \(K n^{-k/2}\) for any fixed \(K\) and any \(k>0\) at all large \(n\). The literal loxodromic numerator also has ratio \(1/2\). Actual independent enumeration of balls of radii 1–20 agrees with these formulas; the formulas above prove the assertion for every \(n\).

For Theorem C, choose \(H=\mathbb Z\) with its single-domain HHG structure: the top hyperbolic space is its Cayley line and the projection is the identity. This is normalized; bounded-domain dichotomy holds; unbounded products imposes no condition because there is no proper domain. The top space has a cobounded isometry group and uniform bi-infinite geodesics, so it is well-behaved in the cited Definition 6.9. The definition and the proper-domain restriction were checked in the 2023 primary preprint of Goldsborough–Hagen–Petyt–Sisto, pp. 20, 23 (with Russell’s appendix). No equality with its later journal version is assumed.

The generator of \(\mathbb Z\) is Morse, since its orbit is the whole Cayley line and quasi-geodesics in a line stay within a bound depending only on their quasi-geodesic constants. Finally, \[f:D_\infty\longrightarrow\mathbb Z,\qquad f(r^m s^\epsilon)=m\] is surjective and changes distances by at most one: \(d_S(r^m s^\epsilon,r^l s^\eta)=|m-l|+(\epsilon\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}\eta)\). Thus \(G\) is quasi-isometric to this well-behaved \(H\). Reflections and the identity have bounded cyclic orbits and are not Morse elements. Nonzero translations have geodesic, coarsely dense orbits in the quasi-line, and are Morse. The non-Morse proportion is again exactly \(1/2\), contradicting Theorem C’s bound.
## Counterevidence, impact and repair limits

Theorem 7.6 (p. 29), Theorem 7.9 (p. 31; TeX line 1541), Theorem 7.13 (p. 32) and Theorem 7.15 (p. 33) explicitly require the relevant group to be non-virtually cyclic. This is strong internal evidence of the intended restriction. The non-elementarity argument in Fact 2.2(1), p. 8, and positive growth exponent in Lemma 5.1, p. 18, also identify exactly why the proof cannot be transferred to this example.

Add the non-virtually-cyclic hypothesis to Theorem C and Theorem 7.4, and correct Theorem 7.4’s exceptional event. For Theorem C this makes its scope agree with Theorem 7.9. This is a restriction of an advertised theorem, not a proof of its unrestricted form. The counterexample does not address the mapping-class-group result, the non-virtually-cyclic CAT(0) cases, or the correctly restricted Theorem 7.9. It also does not independently verify the general multi-insertion step or the external HHG machinery. Severity is Major because a principal quantitative genericity statement is false on an allowed class, even though the scope repair is short.
# Reconstructed estimates and unresolved verification
## Local numerical corrections, without an additional core-failure claim

In Proposition 4.1, p. 12, write \(A=K_{\mathrm{map}}\). The source chooses \(T=103A^3/D_C\), as confirmed directly in both the original PDF page image and author TeX line 596. The comparison is valid: \[\begin{aligned}
(10^6-1)A^6-6000A^3(1+D_CT)
&=A^3(381999A^3-6000)>0
\end{aligned}\] for \(A\ge1\); at \(A=1\) the margin is \(375999\). Also \[D_CT-A=103A^3-A\ge102A^3.\] No change of \(T\) is required. The previous numerical criticism and proposed \(T=150A^3/D_C\) repair resulted from reading \(103\) as \(1000\) and are withdrawn. This correction does not affect Finding F1. Discrete word-geodesic steps can be rounded down while retaining the original projected-traversal slack \(103A^3-A\) before weakening the bound; this is separate bookkeeping, not a defect in the source’s choice of \(T\).

In (5.4), p. 23, Proposition 4.1 gives \(0.01(d_S(\mathrm{id},q)+d_S(q,p))\) and the final lower bound retains a factor \(0.98\) on both terms. The useful conclusion survives: \[d_S(\gamma_1,\gamma_M)
\le\left(\frac{0.28}{0.98}-0.27\right)n
=\frac{11}{700}n<0.016n.\] For the subsequent lower distance to the translated endpoint, \(0.274n-0.016n-O(1)=0.258n-O(1)\) suffices to exceed \(0.25\|g_1\|_S\) at large \(n\); the displayed stronger \(0.26n\) is unnecessary. Distances and diameters of these fixed-length orbit segments differ by \(O(1)\), which must be retained before taking large \(n\).

In the two-cut index set on p. 24, let \(m\) be the number of available consecutive integers and let \(D=2K_{\mathrm{map}}L_{\mathrm{map}}+3\). The actual number of pairs with \(j-i>D\) is \[\frac{(m-D-1)(m-D)}2 \quad (m>D+1).\] Thus the coefficient-one product printed in the last display on p. 27 is not the literal count. It remains \(\Theta(n^2)\) for fixed \(D\), which is all the stated \(O(n^{-1})\) argument needs. These repairs concern local bookkeeping; they are not additional counterexamples to the main genericity theorem.
## U1: Needs Evidence — the arbitrary-number-of-insertions step

Locations: the opening of Section 6, p. 24; Theorem 6.3 and its proof, p. 27; transfer to Corollary 7.20, p. 34. The proof explicitly treats \(k=2\) and states that the same idea gives the general case. The natural desired extension has \(\Theta(n^k)\) separated choices and an \(O_k(n^{k/2})\) fibre bound. To certify it one needs intermediate records retaining the original geodesic, removed blocks, fixed suffixes and the original exclusion from \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{thick}}\), with the analogue of both cases of Lemma 6.2 at every stage.

The two-insertion construction provides substantial positive evidence for such an induction, and no all-hypotheses counterexample to the superpolynomial assertion was found. This review did not complete that induction with all alignments and endpoint constants. Accordingly U1 is an unresolved verification item, not a confirmed Major or Minor defect and not evidence that the superpolynomial theorem is false. Its relevance is substantive: the \(O(R)\) central-fibre loss in the braid argument requires an exponent beyond the explicitly written \(k=2\) case.
# Supporting checks

The actual calculations used reviewer-written Python normal forms and exact rational arithmetic, with exit code zero; no author code was run. The complete author TeX static record reports 1,793 lines, 40 parsed theorem-like environments and 92 labels, its package/bibliography commands, and targeted theorem contexts. Those counts only describe the inspection input. The source images and page-specific observations are retained separately.

The repository record independently confirms v3 and states that it includes corrections based on a referee report. A limited title/DOI correction search did not identify a separate article-specific erratum; this is not proof that no correction exists. The external definition check used https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.07013, v1, via the University of Bristol primary preprint copy, Definition 6.9 and the definitions at the start of Section 6. Only those definitions were checked for F1; the full external paper was not audited.

The final report is compiled from the current TeX using the authorized local Tectonic 0.17.0. Source and the complete cached dependency set must have identical pre/post hashes; the produced PDF, compiler, logs and inspected page images are hash-bound by provenance and delivery state. Page rendering alone does not count as inspection.

analysis: Theorem C, p. 3 (author TeX lines 167–172), allows every group quasi-isometric to a well-behaved HHG containing Morse elements. Theorem 7.4, pp. 28–29 (TeX lines 1471–1476), assumes a finitely generated group with a WPD loxodromic isometry weakly contracting by means of the hyperbolic space. The displayed numerator of Theorem 7.4 counts loxodromics instead of non-loxodromics. That sign-of-event error is not the basis of this finding: the counterexample below defeats the intended genericity conclusion even after the numerator is corrected.

Let \[G=D_\infty=\langle r,s\mid s^2=1,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle,\qquad
S=\{r,s\},\qquad X=\mathbb R.\] Use the action \(r(x)=x+1\), \(s(x)=-x\) and basepoint \(0\). The space is geodesic and \(0\)-hyperbolic, and the action is isometric. This verifies WPD directly, rather than inferring non-elementarity from it.

It is therefore a valid projection by means of \(X\). Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review: M25-0097
Singular algebraic curves and infinite symplectic staircases

Version and disposition. Dusa McDuff and Kyler Siegel, arXiv:2404.14702v3, submitted 15 July 2025, supplied PDF dated 16 July 2025 (75 pages). Associated DOI: 10.1007/s00222-025-01359-4. This report binds to the author version; equality with the journal Version of Record is not established. Two Major proof-interface findings and two Minor scope findings are confirmed. No counterexample to the main theorems as intended is established. Human reviews remain empty and the scientific decision is pending.
# Claims, definitions, and positive checks

The paper links singular rational curves in del Pezzo surfaces to ellipsoid-embedding staircases. Upper bounds use inflation after cusp resolution; lower bounds use index-zero unicuspidal curves. Constructions use Orevkov twists and toric degenerations with \(T\)-singularities.

The conventions are material: curves are reduced and irreducible; \((p,1)\) permits a smooth distinguished point; sesquicuspidal curves can have ordinary double points away from the cusp, and weak algebraic variants allow further singularities. The normalization \([\omega]=c_1\) gives line area \(3\) in \(\mathbb{CP}^2\). The embedding function is an infimum. Theorem A uses \(c'>c\), not attainment at the limiting boundary. Stabilized lower bounds require the stated semipositivity input, satisfied in the monotone applications.
## Twists and outer corners

Sections 1–2, pp. 1–22, were checked for the definitions, index formula, seed curves, anticanonical boundaries, and recurrence. Blowing up a node preserves the reduced total anticanonical boundary. The chain has the required \(-2\) components and terminal \(-1\) component. The complementary birational isomorphism and positivity against the boundary support the Nakai argument; the parity argument distinguishes the degree-eight del Pezzo surfaces. The specific transformed exceptional-class Chern-number calculation on p. 17 was not independently expanded in homology.

For a well-placed cusp the two local intersections are \(p,q\), giving \(c_1(C)=p+q\) and index zero. The twist \[(p,q)\mapsto(Kp-q,p),\qquad K=c_1(M)^2-2,\] has determinant one, preserves coprimality, and preserves positivity for \(p>q\), \(K\geq3\). Its ratios agree with Table 2.4.1. The reflection \(R(x)=K+1/(x-K)\) is an involution on its domain. The boundary seed \(p=q=1\) needs the elementary first-step construction rather than a literal invocation of a proposition assuming \(p>q\). The plane conic supplies the other initial branch. In Lemma 2.4.3 the Hessian condition becomes the square of a mixed quadratic coefficient after a pure coefficient vanishes; the resulting linear conditions and Bézout exclusion were traced. No substantive issue is asserted in this part.
## Inflation

In Section 3, Euclidean cusp-resolution weights satisfy \(\sum w_i^2=pq\) and \(\sum w_i=p+q-1\). For the first stage of a multiple Puiseux cusp they are multiplied by \(k\), giving a self-intersection drop \(k^2pq\). Reviewer calculations checked 773 coprime cases, including weights \((3,2,1,1)\) for \((5,3)\); these support the Euclidean argument and are not a proof by finite sampling. Resolving the cusp and smoothing positive nodes gives nonnegative self-intersection, the inflation hypothesis. After contraction the cohomology factor is \(1+sc\), while the ellipsoid parameter is \[\frac{\epsilon+ks}{1+cs}\longrightarrow\frac{k}{c}.\] This explains the strict \(c'>c\) in the upper bound. A special two-Puiseux lemma invoked in the more general case needs the first-stage weight argument. The full local analytic normalization, inflation theorem, and relative contraction theorem were not independently reproved.
## Toric curves, classification, and stabilization

Sections 4–5 depend on the distinction between a dual Fano polygon and a polygon with the same fan. Balanced exponent vectors make the product parametrization extend at infinity; coprime boundary data rule out a multiple cover. Boundary contact orders give the indicated exponents. The logarithmic derivative has numerator degree at most the number of punctures minus two. In the three-puncture case the rank-two torus map makes the pair of pants immersed. The cited automatic-transversality and deformation inputs were checked at their interfaces, not fully reconstructed. Contact order \(k\) after blowdowns yields \((kq;kp,kp+1)\).

In Section 6, for sufficiently small nonzero \(t\), the selected component \(y=0\), \(w^r=\zeta z^a\), \(\zeta^m=-t\), has the required local \((r,a)\) behavior and avoids the other singular chart. The later algebraic-to-symplectic comparison uses F1 below. The first-Hirzebruch-surface classification imports the cited classification of perfect exceptional classes; it was not independently rebuilt. Its explicit index-zero condition is important.

In Section 7 the Fibonacci degree/cusp formulas give exactly one residual node by the genus calculation; nine recurrence stages were checked exactly. The degree-three seed still relies on the cited enumerative count and degeneration arguments. Stabilized folding results and conjectural extensions were not treated as new unproved theorems of this paper.
# F1 — Major: the non-Gorenstein smoothing interface
Locations. Eq. (4.1.3), pp. 32–33; Proposition 4.2.7 and proof, pp. 41–42; its application in Theorem 6.1.7, pp. 63–64. Author TeX lines 1752–1757 and 2244–2256.
## Missing deformation direction

The claimed miniversal base is \(\mathbb C^{m-1}\) and the polynomial begins \[xy=z^{rm}+C_{m-2}z^{r(m-2)}+\cdots+C_0.\] For \(r>1\) the \(z^{r(m-1)}\) coefficient cannot generally be removed by translating \(z\), since translation breaks the nontrivial \(\mu_r\) action. Set \(m=1,r=2,a=1\). The singularity \(\frac14(1,1)\) has a nontrivial smoothing \[X_t=\{xy=z^2+t\}/\mu_2,\qquad (x,y,z)\mapsto(-x,-y,-z).\] The central quotient is \(\mathbb C^2/\mu_4\) with scalar action: use \((x,y,z)=(u^2,v^2,uv)\) and the residual action induced by multiplication by \(i\) on \((u,v)\). For \(t\ne0\) the cover is smooth and the involution is free. Indeed, a zero gradient or a fixed point forces \(x=y=z=0\), hence \(t=0\). Flatness follows from the hypersurface family and taking invariants of a finite group in characteristic zero. The index-one cover gives a \(\mathbb Q\)-Gorenstein deformation of index two. Thus an actual parameter exists when the printed base has dimension zero.

As a primary cross-check, Hacking–Prokhorov, Smoothable del Pezzo surfaces with quotient singularities, arXiv:0808.1550v2, Remark 2.5 and Eq. (1), pp. 4–5, gives the one-dimensional \(\frac14(1,1)\) case and the full range \[xy=z^{dn}+t_{d-1}z^{(d-1)n}+\cdots+t_0.\] The elementary example supplies an independent check.
## The total-space assumption excludes the intended fibers

Proposition 4.2.7 assumes the total space \(\mathcal X\) is a complex manifold. Flatness over a disk makes the central fiber a Cartier hypersurface in a smooth threefold, hence Gorenstein. But \[\operatorname{index}\left(\frac1{mr^2}(1,mra-1)\right)
=\frac{mr^2}{\gcd(mr^2,mra)}=r.\] A central singularity with \(r>1\) cannot occur under that hypothesis. In the example, eliminating \(t\) gives total space \(\mathbb C^3/\{\pm1\}\), singular at the origin. This is not a counterexample to the proposition under its own assumptions: it proves that the proposition does not justify its intended non-Gorenstein applications.

Counterevidence and impact. Eq. (4.1.5) has a valid product-form smoothing, and the chart in Section 6.3 has a genuine smoothing parameter. These and the known local geometry suggest repair. Section 2’s independent twist construction is unaffected. Nevertheless Theorem 6.1.7 explicitly uses this comparison, hence the corresponding Theorems D/F route contains a demonstrated invalid core proof interface. This warrants Major without asserting that the conclusions are false.

Repair and limits. Restore the full equivariant miniversal family. Formulate and prove the comparison for a normal \(\mathbb Q\)-Gorenstein total space with local quotient models. Transport away from singular loci must still give the claimed boundary identifications, extension, tameness, and symplectic class. Replacing the word manifold alone does not verify those steps. A complete repaired comparison theorem is not claimed here.
# F2 — Major: scaling in Theorem E breaks the invoked hypotheses

Locations. Theorem 5.3.1, pp. 50–51; proof of Theorem E, p. 51; author TeX lines 2786–2789. The theorem requires a dual Fano lattice \(T\)-polygon with coprime affine edge lengths. The proof chooses the least \(s>0\) such that \(sQ\) is a lattice polygon, asserts these hypotheses for \(sQ\), and derives \(k=1\) in triangular cases.

Take \[Q=\operatorname{conv}\{(-1,-1),(5,-1),(-1,\tfrac12)\}.\] Its primitive inequalities \(x\geq-1\), \(y\geq-1\), \(x+4y\leq1\) all have support height one, so it is dual Fano. The bottom vertices are Delzant; the top has type \(\frac14(1,1)\), a \(T\)-vertex. It is the monotone plane triangle illustrated in Figure 5.1.1, p. 45. Its area is \(9/2\) and the lengths adjacent to the lower-left smooth vertex are \(6\) and \(3/2\), giving inner-corner data \(p/q=4\), \(y=2/3\), also obtained from Table 2.4.1.

The minimum scaling about the displayed origin is \(s=2\): the coordinates force \(s\) integral and the half-integral vertex forces it even. But \(2Q\) has affine edge lengths \(12,3,3\), whose gcd is \(3\), and primitive support heights \(2\). It is neither dual Fano nor primitive in edge lengths. The proof’s formula also gives \[k=s/(qy)=2/(2/3)=3,\] not \(1\). This is a concrete failure of the asserted applicability and normalization.

Counterevidence and impact. The intended conclusion survives in this example: a conic has self-intersection \(4=pq\) and index \(6\cdot2-2\cdot4-2\cdot1=2\). Translate the smooth vertex to zero and scale by \(2/3\) to obtain vertices \((0,0),(4,0),(0,1)\) and primitive lengths. This diagnoses a possible normalization repair, but the new triangle is still not dual Fano. The underlying toric-curve construction may extend under a weaker assumption on the fan, but that extension is not the stated theorem. Proposition 5.1.2’s visible embeddings remain unaffected.

Repair and limits. State and prove a version for translated/scaled lattice \(T\)-polygons with the appropriate fan and deformation properties. Normalize relative to the smooth vertex and primitive lengths, track the rescaled symplectic class, and check the asserted \(k\) in each case. The invalid application lies on the main inner-corner proof route, hence Major. No nonexistence of inner-corner curves is asserted.
# F3 — Minor: an additional exceptional pencil parameter

Locations. Eq. (6.3.1), p. 59; Proposition 6.3.3, p. 60; global-parameter extensions on pp. 61–63. Author TeX lines 3161–3163 and 3186–3206. Choose \(m=1,r=2,a=3\), positive with \(\gcd(r,a)=1\). The setup’s triangle has vertices \((0,0),(0,5),(4,0)\), a Delzant distinguished vertex, an adjacent singularity \(\frac14(1,5)=\frac14(1,1)\), and the third singularity \(\frac15(1,4)\). Even the stronger \(T\)-triangle condition holds. In \(\mathbb{CP}(1,5,2,3)\) the pencil is \[(1+t)xy=w^2+t z^3.\] The denominator in the printed formula is undefined at \(t=-1\). In the natural projective pencil closure the fiber is \(w^2=z^3\). On the smooth chart \(x=1\) its equation is independent of \(y\) and its gradient vanishes along \(z=w=0\). It is singular along \([1:y:0:0]\), including \([1:0:0:0]\), contrary to the assertion that every \(t\ne0,\infty\) has only the designated singularity at \([0:1:0:0]\).

Counterevidence, repair, and scope. Lemma 6.4.2 and the proof of Theorem 6.1.7 explicitly use \(t\) sufficiently close to zero, avoiding \(-1\). Exclude \(-1\) from the generic-fiber assertions, or restrict to a small disk near zero. The same global projective pencil cannot have the asserted description at \(-1\). The demonstrated error is auxiliary global scope; no damage to the local construction is proved, so this finding is Minor.
# F4 — Minor: missing index zero in the plane warmup
Location. Lemma 6.5.1, p. 64, author TeX lines 3387–3392. It states that Theorem 2.1.3 gives all data for rational unicuspidal plane curves with one Puiseux pair, without an index condition.

The irreducible rational cubic \[C=\{X^3=Y^2Z\},\qquad [s:t]\mapsto[s^2t:s^3:t^3],\] has gradient \((3X^2,-2YZ,-Y^2)\) and its only singularity is \([0:0:1]\), locally of type \((3,2)\). All literal curve hypotheses hold, but degree \(3\) is absent from the odd Fibonacci degrees \(1,2,5,13,\ldots\) in Theorem 2.1.3. Its index is \(6\cdot3-2\cdot3-2\cdot2=8\).

Counterevidence, repair, and scope. Theorem 1.2.2(a) already includes this family. The paragraph before the lemma explicitly intends the index-zero list in Theorem 1.2.2(d); Theorem F and the perfect-class definition impose index zero. Insert that condition in the lemma and in the cited symplectic-classification application. This is a false auxiliary scope statement with a precise local repair, not a counterexample to Theorem F, hence Minor.
# Coverage, reproducibility, and remaining limits

Full scientific text on PDF pp. 1–71 was read. The source-image inspection record lists the pages actually opened, including all finding locations and decisive counterevidence. References pp. 72–75 and other source images were not reviewed. The supplied author TeX was statically parsed in full (153 labels and retained targeted contexts); author programs and author TeX were not executed. Missing computational code is not treated as a defect.

Reviewer-owned exact computations checked the quotient-smoothing example, singular pencil fiber, cubic, polygon normalization, Euclidean weights, reflection, inflation factor, and Fibonacci genus identities. The all-hypothesis mathematical checks are given above. These do not independently certify external enumerative geometry, automatic transversality, perfect-class classification, or the full analytic deformation and transport arguments.

Repository metadata and a limited correction search were checked; exhaustive absence of corrections is not asserted. Primary model cross-check: Hacking–Prokhorov, arXiv:0808.1550v2, pp. 4–5. Accompanying records bind the actual version, current source, unchanged build dependencies, compiler, PDF, and inspection of every final report page.

For \(t\ne0\) the cover is smooth and the involution is free. Indeed, a zero gradient or a fixed point forces \(x=y=z=0\), hence \(t=0\). Flatness follows from the hypersurface family and taking invariants of a finite group in characteristic zero. The index-one cover gives a \(\mathbb Q\)-Gorenstein deformation of index two. Thus an actual parameter exists when the printed base has dimension zero.

As a primary cross-check, Hacking–Prokhorov, Smoothable del Pezzo surfaces with quotient singularities, arXiv:0808.1550v2, Remark 2.5 and Eq. (1), pp. 4–5, gives the one-dimensional \(\frac14(1,1)\) case and the full range \[xy=z^{dn}+t_{d-1}z^{(d-1)n}+\cdots+t_0.\] The elementary example supplies an independent check.

Proposition 4.2.7 assumes the total space \(\mathcal X\) is a complex manifold. Flatness over a disk makes the central fiber a Cartier hypersurface in a smooth threefold, hence Gorenstein. But \[\operatorname{index}\left(\frac1{mr^2}(1,mra-1)\right)
=\frac{mr^2}{\gcd(mr^2,mra)}=r.\] A central singularity with \(r>1\) cannot occur under that hypothesis. In the example, eliminating \(t\) gives total space \(\mathbb C^3/\{\pm1\}\), singular at the origin. This is not a counterexample to the proposition under its own assumptions: it proves that the proposition does not justify its intended non-Gorenstein applications.

Counterevidence and impact. Eq. (4.1.5) has a valid product-form smoothing, and the chart in Section 6.3 has a genuine smoothing parameter. These and the known local geometry suggest repair. Section 2’s independent twist construction is unaffected. Nevertheless Theorem 6.1.7 explicitly uses this comparison, hence the corresponding Theorems D/F route contains a demonstrated invalid core proof interface. This warrants Major without asserting that the conclusions are false.

Repair and limits. Restore the full equivariant miniversal family. Formulate and prove the comparison for a normal \(\mathbb Q\)-Gorenstein total space with local quotient models. Transport away from singular loci must still give the claimed boundary identifications, extension, tameness, and symplectic class. Replacing the word manifold alone does not verify those steps. A complete repaired comparison theorem is not claimed here.

claim: The paper links singular rational curves in del Pezzo surfaces to ellipsoid-embedding staircases. Upper bounds use inflation after cusp resolution; lower bounds use index-zero unicuspidal curves. Constructions use Orevkov twists and toric degenerations with \(T\)-singularities.

The conventions are material: curves are reduced and irreducible; \((p,1)\) permits a smooth distinguished point; sesquicuspidal curves can have ordinary double points away from the cusp, and weak algebraic variants allow further singularities. The normalization \([\omega]=c_1\) gives line area \(3\) in \(\mathbb{CP}^2\). The embedding function is an infimum. Theorem A uses \(c'>c\), not attainment at the limiting boundary. Stabilized lower bounds require the stated semipositivity input, satisfied in the monotone applications.
Minimal s giving lattice sQ satisfies dual Fano and primitive edge assumptions, k=1 in triangle case.
analysis: Locations. Theorem 5.3.1, pp. 50–51; proof of Theorem E, p. 51; author TeX lines 2786–2789. The theorem requires a dual Fano lattice \(T\)-polygon with coprime affine edge lengths. The proof chooses the least \(s>0\) such that \(sQ\) is a lattice polygon, asserts these hypotheses for \(sQ\), and derives \(k=1\) in triangular cases.

Take \[Q=\operatorname{conv}\{(-1,-1),(5,-1),(-1,\tfrac12)\}.\] Its primitive inequalities \(x\geq-1\), \(y\geq-1\), \(x+4y\leq1\) all have support height one, so it is dual Fano. The bottom vertices are Delzant; the top has type \(\frac14(1,1)\), a \(T\)-vertex. It is the monotone plane triangle illustrated in Figure 5.1.1, p. 45. Its area is \(9/2\) and the lengths adjacent to the lower-left smooth vertex are \(6\) and \(3/2\), giving inner-corner data \(p/q=4\), \(y=2/3\), also obtained from Table 2.4.1.

The minimum scaling about the displayed origin is \(s=2\): the coordinates force \(s\) integral and the half-integral vertex forces it even. But \(2Q\) has affine edge lengths \(12,3,3\), whose gcd is \(3\), and primitive support heights \(2\). It is neither dual Fano nor primitive in edge lengths. The proof’s formula also gives \[k=s/(qy)=2/(2/3)=3,\] not \(1\). This is a concrete failure of the asserted applicability and normalization.

Counterevidence and impact. The intended conclusion survives in this example: a conic has self-intersection \(4=pq\) and index \(6\cdot2-2\cdot4-2\cdot1=2\). Translate the smooth vertex to zero and scale by \(2/3\) to obtain vertices \((0,0),(4,0),(0,1)\) and primitive lengths. This diagnoses a possible normalization repair, but the new triangle is still not dual Fano. The underlying toric-curve construction may extend under a weaker assumption on the fan, but that extension is not the stated theorem. Proposition 5.1.2’s visible embeddings remain unaffected.

Repair and limits. State and prove a version for translated/scaled lattice \(T\)-polygons with the appropriate fan and deformation properties. Normalize relative to the smooth vertex and primitive lengths, track the rescaled symplectic class, and check the asserted \(k\) in each case. The invalid application lies on the main inner-corner proof route, hence Major. No nonexistence of inner-corner curves is asserted.
result: Impact: Core theorem application invalid, not nonexistence of inner-corner curves.
