Author: Reviewing assistant
Date: 26 October 2026
Title: Initial review: Liouville property for groups and conformal dimension
# Identity, scope, and conclusions

The reviewed work is by Nicolás Matte Bon, Volodymyr Nekrashevych, and Tianyi Zheng, Liouville property for groups and conformal dimension, M25-0098. The bound source is arXiv: 2305.14545v4, submitted 5 August 2025, with PDF dated 6 August 2025, 42 pages. Page references below are PDF pages, agreeing with printed pagination. DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01360-x identifies the associated journal article; equality with the journal version has not been established. These findings belong only to the bound author version.

Theorem 1.1 (p. 2) asserts that a finitely generated contracting self-similar group whose limit space has Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension \(\alpha<2\) has the Liouville property for every symmetric measure with finite \(\beta\)-moment for some \(\beta>\alpha\). Theorem 1.3 (p. 3) gives \[\operatorname{Cr}_{\rm Liouv}(G)\le p_c(G,\mathfrak B)\le\operatorname{ARdim}\mathcal J_G.\] The audit followed definitions, contraction coefficients, portrait estimates, tile overlap, capacities, entropy encoding, long-jump decomposition, and applications. All 42 pages were read as text; selected original pages were also inspected as images, as listed in the coverage record. Reading references is not independent verification of all cited theorems.

The decisive distinctions are between an abstract self-similar biset and a faithful group of tree automorphisms, and between an arbitrary Ahlfors-regular metric and one quasisymmetric to a visual metric. Both appear in the preliminaries but are lost in statements used later.
# Problem 1: faithfulness missing from the principal scope (Major)
## Location and source claim

Theorem 1.1, p. 2; Theorem 1.3, p. 3; the general definition in §2.1, pp. 7–8; portrait determination on p. 19; Proposition 5.5, p. 26; Theorem 5.9 and Corollary 5.10, pp. 29–32. The definition on p. 7 allows a \(G\)-biset with free right action and finitely many right orbits. Page 8 defines the faithful quotient separately. No global faithfulness requirement was found in the full text or complete source search. Proposition 5.5, in contrast, explicitly assumes a group of rooted-tree automorphisms.
## Counterexample and all hypotheses

Let \(G=F(a,b)\) be free of rank two, \(X=\{0,1\}\), and \[\mathfrak B=X\times G,\qquad
 (x,h)\cdot k=(x,hk),\qquad g\cdot(x,h)=(x,h).\] The actions commute; the right action is free and has two orbits. This is a self-similar group in the explicitly stated biset sense. For the basis \(\{(0,1),(1,1)\}\) its wreath recursion sends every \(g\) to \((\operatorname{id};1,1)\). Every nonempty section is the identity. The group is finitely generated and contracting with nucleus \(\mathcal N=\{1\}\). Its associated tree action and faithful quotient are trivial. For all \(p>0\) and \(n\ge1\), \(\eta_{p,n}=0\), hence \(\eta_p=0\) and \(p_c=0\).

Asymptotic equivalence on \(X^{-\omega}\) identifies only equal sequences, since the nucleus is trivial. Thus \(\mathcal J_G\) is binary Cantor space. If \(L(\xi,\zeta)\) is common terminal-prefix length, then for any \(s>0\), \[d_s(\xi,\zeta)=e^{-sL(\xi,\zeta)}\] off the diagonal is a visual ultrametric. Bernoulli measure has mass \(2^{-n}\) on length-\(n\) cylinders, giving Ahlfors regularity of dimension \(\log2/s\). These metrics are positive powers of each other, hence quasisymmetric. Therefore \(\operatorname{ARdim}\mathcal J_G=0<2\).

Let \(\mu\) be uniform on \(a,a^{-1},b,b^{-1}\). It is symmetric, generating, finitely supported, and has every positive word-length moment. Its Cayley graph is the four-regular tree. The probability of returning to the root from a neighbor is \(q=1/3\): radial distance has probabilities \(1/4\) towards and \(3/4\) away from the root, and the decaying hitting-probability solution is \(q^r\). The walk is transient and has an almost sure limiting end.

Let \(f(g)\) be the probability that this end lies in the branch beginning with \(a\). The Markov property makes \(f\) bounded and \(\mu\)-harmonic. Symmetry and the return probability give \[f(1)=\tfrac14,\qquad
 f(a)=1-\tfrac13+\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac34.\] At depth \(r\) in that branch, \(f=1-\frac34\,3^{-r}\); in another branch, \(f=\frac14\,3^{-r}\). The formulas satisfy the mean-value equation at every vertex, including the root. Thus \(f\) is nonconstant on \(\langle\operatorname{supp}\mu\rangle=G\), violating exactly the stated Liouville definition. Amenability also fails: a nonempty finite vertex set \(F\) has at most \(|F|-1\) internal tree edges and at least \(2|F|+2\) boundary edges.
## Proof obstruction, counterevidence, and repair

Tree permutations and sections determine an element of a faithful group, but need not determine an element of an abstract nonfaithful biset group. Here every element has identical trivial positive-level data. Proposition 5.5 therefore controls the image group only; it cannot bound the entropy of the original free group. The assertion after Proposition 4.5 that labeled portraits uniquely determine \(g\) has the same obstruction.

The preliminaries begin with a faithful action before giving the general biset definition. Conventional informal usage of self-similar group often means a faithful automorphism group. Section 6.1 explicitly says faithful, and iterated monodromy groups are defined as faithful quotients. These are strong indications of the intended meaning, but do not add the missing condition to the broader written definition used in Theorems 1.1 and 1.3.

A precise repair is to require the associated action on \(X^*\) to be faithful in the Liouville, entropy, and growth statements, or to state those conclusions for the faithful quotient with its induced measure. The latter does not imply the original claim for \(G\): the kernel can be the entire free group. Further kernel assumptions would require another theorem. This is Major because the central universal guarantee is false under the printed definition, even if repair is a short scope restriction. It does not refute the intended faithful theorem or Corollary 6.4 for iterated monodromy groups.
# Problem 2: regularity alone does not give exponential energy decay (Minor)
## Location and missing hypothesis

Equation reference: eq:energy. Proposition 5.6, p. 27, assumes only an Ahlfors-regular metric \(d\) on \(\mathcal J_G\) of Hausdorff dimension \(\alpha\), together with \(\beta>\alpha\) and \(p>p_c\). It concludes, uniformly in \(g\) and the left-infinite tail, \[
 \sum_{v\in X^n}d(\ldots x_2x_1g(v),\ldots x_2x_1v)^\beta
 \le C\lambda^n l(g)^p,\qquad 0<\lambda<1.\] Its proof uses Proposition 3.8, p. 16, which requires a quasi-conformal metric. Ahlfors regularity alone does not imply this.
## Faithful counterexample

Use the faithful binary adding machine \(G=\mathbb Z=\langle a\rangle\), with \(a=\sigma(1,a)\) and generating set \(\{a,a^{-1}\}\). It is contracting with nucleus \(\{1,a,a^{-1}\}\) and limit circle. At level \(n\), the section exponents of \(a^k\) are \(\lfloor(k+j)/2^n\rfloor\), \(0\le j<2^n\), up to permutation. Letting \(|k|\to\infty\) proves \[\eta_{p,n}=2^{n(1/p-1)},\qquad \eta_p=2^{1/p-1},\qquad p_c=1.\] On \([0,1]/(0=1)\) with ordinary arc metric \(d_0\), define a circle homeomorphism by \[h(0)=0,\qquad h(x)=\frac1{1-\log_2x}\ (0<x\le\tfrac12),
 \qquad h(x)=x\ (\tfrac12\le x\le1).\] It is continuous and strictly increasing, with matching formulas at \(1/2\) and the identified endpoints. The metric \(d(x,y)=d_0(h(x),h(y))\) is isometric to the ordinary circle. Its Hausdorff measure is the pullback of arc length, so it is Ahlfors regular with \(\alpha=1\) and the original topology.

Set \(\beta=p=2\), \(g=a\), and take the zero left-infinite tail. The word \(0^n\) represents \(0\) and its image \(10^{n-1}\) represents \(2^{-n}\) in the limit circle. For \(n\ge2\), \[d(0,2^{-n})=\frac1{n+1}.\] A single summand in [eq:energy] (#eq:energy) is \((n+1)^{-2}\). Because \(l(a)=1\), the claimed estimate would imply \((n+1)^{-2}\le C\lambda^n\) for all \(n\), impossible since the logarithm of this ratio divided by \(n\) tends to \(-\log\lambda>0\).

All printed hypotheses hold, including faithfulness, \(\beta>\alpha\), and \(p>p_c\). The metric is not quasisymmetric to a visual circle metric: the points \(\varepsilon\) and \(1-\varepsilon\), equally far from \(0\) in \(d_0\), have \(d\)-distance ratio comparable to \(1/(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon))\).
## Counterevidence, repair, and impact

Add the quasi-conformal hypothesis to obtain exactly the input required by Proposition 3.8. In Theorem 5.7, choosing \(\alpha<\beta\) from the definition of \(\operatorname{ARdim}\) already permits a metric in this conformal gauge. The repair is therefore available in the core application. This is Minor: it falsifies an overbroad auxiliary statement, without showing another failure of the intended core theorem.
# Proof clarifications and positive checks
## Basepoint change in Corollary 5.8

The proof’s opening paragraph (p. 29; author TeX line 1405) asserts that contraction makes the word sets \(U_{z,n}\) exactly independent of basepoint for all sufficiently large \(n\). Convergence of locations does not imply equality of membership in a fixed neighborhood.

Use the adding-machine model on \(\mathbb R\), with translations by \(\mathbb Z\) and \(I_x(\xi)=(\xi+x)/2\), \(x=0,1\). Give the graph vertices \(\frac12\mathbb Z\) and edges length one. The quotient has two vertices and circumference two, with no adjacent vertices in the same orbit. The radius-\(1/3\) neighborhood of \(0\) is the ordinary circle interval of radius \(1/6\). Level-\(n\) images from basepoints \(0\) and \(1\) are respectively \[j/2^n,\quad (j+1)/2^n,\qquad 0\le j<2^n.\] The word sets differ for every \(n\ge3\): a nonempty proper cyclic interval is not invariant under a one-step cyclic shift. Exact rational checks for \(3\le n\le12\) give symmetric difference two; the interval argument proves the infinite statement.

A complete repair preserves the capacity conclusion. Enlarge each neighborhood to a closed ball of radius \(5/12\). Balls about distinct vertices remain disjoint since centers have distance at least one. Uniform contraction makes images of two fixed basepoints less than \(1/12\) apart at large levels. The original sets are thus contained in the enlarged sets computed from a basepoint in the image of \(\mathcal X_G\). The enlarged sets are preimages of disjoint closed subsets of \(\mathcal J_G\), so Theorem 5.7 applies. Capacity is monotone increasing in either prescribed plate; it bounds the smaller original plates. Finitely many earlier levels are absorbed into the constant. The main theorem can alternatively choose the convenient basepoint from the outset. This is a verified proof clarification with a complete repair, not an additional counterexample to the core theorem.
## Contraction, dimension, and entropy

For Proposition 4.3 (pp. 18–19), enlarge the generators to contain the nucleus and all generator sections. Truncated length vanishes below a threshold; block iteration gives exponential decay, and a bounded number of extra levels moves every short section into the nucleus. This checks uniformity in \(g,n\). Counting nonnucleus sections extends the portrait estimate to \(p>0\); the identity must be treated separately or the root bound use \(1+l(g)^p\). The printed \(p\ge1\) in Proposition 4.5 alone does not justify its later \(p<1\) use, but Proposition 4.3 supplies the same counting argument.

For Theorem 4.6 (pp. 19–21), the essential factor is \(M_n^{\beta-\alpha}\) from tile diameter decay and \(\beta>\alpha\). Summing over \(m\) increments gives \(m^\beta\), not the intermediate displayed \(m^{\beta-1}\) on p. 20; the final bound already has the correct \(m^\beta\) order. Tile overlap is applied after permuting suffixes by partial products. First take \(l(g)\to\infty\) to remove the additive level-dependent term, then choose a block with coefficient below one and use submultiplicativity. No interchange of these limits is required.

For Proposition 5.6 with the repaired metric hypothesis, choose \[0<\varepsilon<\frac{-\log\eta}{\log|X|-\log\eta},
 \qquad |X|^\varepsilon\eta^{1-\varepsilon}<1.\] This controls short suffixes; bounded overlap and exponential tile decay control long suffixes. In Theorem 5.9, capacity decay bounds expected traverses; large jumps are pulled back a fixed number \(k\) of levels and bounded using sections outside the nucleus and the finite \(p\)-moment. The resulting estimate is \[\mathbb E\sum_{v\in X^n}l(g_t|_v)
 \le C|X|^n+C'(\lambda^n+\eta^{n-k})t.\] The entropy argument takes \(t\to\infty\) first, then \(n\to\infty\), for faithful actions. The \(p_c<1\) case uses a smaller exponent below one and the cited growth/entropy theorem, not independently reproved here. The literal traverse definition on p. 13 omits the first intermediate time from its exclusion condition. Correcting that index, or allowing the resulting bounded multiplicity in the expectation estimate, preserves the bound; the exact event identity needs the corrected convention.
## Boundary cases and examples

The Liouville definition uses constancy on the support-generated subgroup, so the identity-supported measure is not a counterexample. Symmetry is needed for the counting-measure Dirichlet form. A length-\(N\) cycle with nearest-neighbor probabilities \(1/2\) has antipodal capacity \(2/N\), consistent with the ordered-energy factor \(1/2\); this was also checked exactly.

The Thurston matrix on p. 23 has eigenvalues \(1,-1/2,(-1\pm i\sqrt7)/4\), giving spectral radius one. The carpet inequality \(2\cdot3^{1-p}<1\) gives \(p>\log6/\log3\); lower and upper bounds are approximately \(1.63093\) and \(1.89279\). The intermediate printed sign does not change the correct final bound.

In Proposition 6.5 (pp. 39–40), the projected masses printed on p. 40 sum to \(8/9\). For the uniform measure on nine generators, the corrected masses are \(1/9\) on each of \(a_0,\ldots,a_7,1\): one fragmented generator acts as \(a_0\) and the other as the identity at an orbit point, with both fixing the distinguished point when appropriate. This restores a probability measure and the same transient comparison. The normalization error alone is not scored as substantive. Nontriviality of the limiting tail event and the complete topological identification were not independently reconstructed.

Corollary 6.4 uses a finitely generated section-closed enlargement of the given subgroup. Each generator has finitely many sections by contraction; adjoining the common nucleus preserves contraction and the limit space. Ambient word length is bounded by a constant times subgroup word length, preserving the finite second moment. The cited quasiconformal conjugacy and strict Julia dimension bounds remain external dependencies.

Problem 2 | Minor, scope | Require a metric in the conformal gauge, available in the downstream choice.

No global faithfulness requirement was found in the full text or complete source search. Proposition 5.5, in contrast, explicitly assumes a group of rooted-tree automorphisms.

Let \(G=F(a,b)\) be free of rank two, \(X=\{0,1\}\), and \[\mathfrak B=X\times G,\qquad
 (x,h)\cdot k=(x,hk),\qquad g\cdot(x,h)=(x,h).\] The actions commute; the right action is free and has two orbits. This is a self-similar group in the explicitly stated biset sense. For the basis \(\{(0,1),(1,1)\}\) its wreath recursion sends every \(g\) to \((\operatorname{id};1,1)\). Every nonempty section is the identity. The group is finitely generated and contracting with nucleus \(\mathcal N=\{1\}\). Its associated tree action and faithful quotient are trivial. For all \(p>0\) and \(n\ge1\), \(\eta_{p,n}=0\), hence \(\eta_p=0\) and \(p_c=0\).

Asymptotic equivalence on \(X^{-\omega}\) identifies only equal sequences, since the nucleus is trivial. Thus \(\mathcal J_G\) is binary Cantor space. If \(L(\xi,\zeta)\) is common terminal-prefix length, then for any \(s>0\), \[d_s(\xi,\zeta)=e^{-sL(\xi,\zeta)}\] off the diagonal is a visual ultrametric. Bernoulli measure has mass \(2^{-n}\) on length-\(n\) cylinders, giving Ahlfors regularity of dimension \(\log2/s\). These metrics are positive powers of each other, hence quasisymmetric. Therefore \(\operatorname{ARdim}\mathcal J_G=0<2\).

Let \(\mu\) be uniform on \(a,a^{-1},b,b^{-1}\). It is symmetric, generating, finitely supported, and has every positive word-length moment. Its Cayley graph is the four-regular tree. The probability of returning to the root from a neighbor is \(q=1/3\): radial distance has probabilities \(1/4\) towards and \(3/4\) away from the root, and the decaying hitting-probability solution is \(q^r\). The walk is transient and has an almost sure limiting end.

Let \(f(g)\) be the probability that this end lies in the branch beginning with \(a\). The Markov property makes \(f\) bounded and \(\mu\)-harmonic. Symmetry and the return probability give \[f(1)=\tfrac14,\qquad
 f(a)=1-\tfrac13+\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac34.\] At depth \(r\) in that branch, \(f=1-\frac34\,3^{-r}\); in another branch, \(f=\frac14\,3^{-r}\). The formulas satisfy the mean-value equation at every vertex, including the root. Thus \(f\) is nonconstant on \(\langle\operatorname{supp}\mu\rangle=G\), violating exactly the stated Liouville definition. Amenability also fails: a nonempty finite vertex set \(F\) has at most \(|F|-1\) internal tree edges and at least \(2|F|+2\) boundary edges.

Tree permutations and sections determine an element of a faithful group, but need not determine an element of an abstract nonfaithful biset group. Here every element has identical trivial positive-level data. Proposition 5.5 therefore controls the image group only; it cannot bound the entropy of the original free group. The assertion after Proposition 4.5 that labeled portraits uniquely determine \(g\) has the same obstruction.

The preliminaries begin with a faithful action before giving the general biset definition. Conventional informal usage of self-similar group often means a faithful automorphism group. Section 6.1 explicitly says faithful, and iterated monodromy groups are defined as faithful quotients. These are strong indications of the intended meaning, but do not add the missing condition to the broader written definition used in Theorems 1.1 and 1.3.

A precise repair is to require the associated action on \(X^*\) to be faithful in the Liouville, entropy, and growth statements, or to state those conclusions for the faithful quotient with its induced measure. The latter does not imply the original claim for \(G\): the kernel can be the entire free group. Further kernel assumptions would require another theorem. This is Major because the central universal guarantee is false under the printed definition, even if repair is a short scope restriction. It does not refute the intended faithful theorem or Corollary 6.4 for iterated monodromy groups.
result: Impact: Central guarantee false for printed general-biset scope; intended faithful and IMG cases not refuted.

problems.title: regularity alone does not give exponential energy decay (Minor)
problems.source_location: Proposition 5.6 p27 contrasted with Proposition 3.8 p16
claim: Every Ahlfors-regular metric yields uniform exponential displacement energy.
analysis:
Equation reference: eq:energy. Proposition 5.6, p. 27, assumes only an Ahlfors-regular metric \(d\) on \(\mathcal J_G\) of Hausdorff dimension \(\alpha\), together with \(\beta>\alpha\) and \(p>p_c\). It concludes, uniformly in \(g\) and the left-infinite tail, \[
 \sum_{v\in X^n}d(\ldots x_2x_1g(v),\ldots x_2x_1v)^\beta
 \le C\lambda^n l(g)^p,\qquad 0<\lambda<1.\] Its proof uses Proposition 3.8, p. 16, which requires a quasi-conformal metric. Ahlfors regularity alone does not imply this.

Use the faithful binary adding machine \(G=\mathbb Z=\langle a\rangle\), with \(a=\sigma(1,a)\) and generating set \(\{a,a^{-1}\}\). It is contracting with nucleus \(\{1,a,a^{-1}\}\) and limit circle. At level \(n\), the section exponents of \(a^k\) are \(\lfloor(k+j)/2^n\rfloor\), \(0\le j<2^n\), up to permutation. Letting \(|k|\to\infty\) proves \[\eta_{p,n}=2^{n(1/p-1)},\qquad \eta_p=2^{1/p-1},\qquad p_c=1.\] On \([0,1]/(0=1)\) with ordinary arc metric \(d_0\), define a circle homeomorphism by \[h(0)=0,\qquad h(x)=\frac1{1-\log_2x}\ (0<x\le\tfrac12),
 \qquad h(x)=x\ (\tfrac12\le x\le1).\] It is continuous and strictly increasing, with matching formulas at \(1/2\) and the identified endpoints. The metric \(d(x,y)=d_0(h(x),h(y))\) is isometric to the ordinary circle. Its Hausdorff measure is the pullback of arc length, so it is Ahlfors regular with \(\alpha=1\) and the original topology.

Set \(\beta=p=2\), \(g=a\), and take the zero left-infinite tail. The word \(0^n\) represents \(0\) and its image \(10^{n-1}\) represents \(2^{-n}\) in the limit circle. For \(n\ge2\), \[d(0,2^{-n})=\frac1{n+1}.\] A single summand in [eq:energy] (#eq:energy) is \((n+1)^{-2}\). Because \(l(a)=1\), the claimed estimate would imply \((n+1)^{-2}\le C\lambda^n\) for all \(n\), impossible since the logarithm of this ratio divided by \(n\) tends to \(-\log\lambda>0\).

All printed hypotheses hold, including faithfulness, \(\beta>\alpha\), and \(p>p_c\). The metric is not quasisymmetric to a visual circle metric: the points \(\varepsilon\) and \(1-\varepsilon\), equally far from \(0\) in \(d_0\), have \(d\)-distance ratio comparable to \(1/(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon))\).
result: Add the quasi-conformal hypothesis to obtain exactly the input required by Proposition 3.8. In Theorem 5.7, choosing \(\alpha<\beta\) from the definition of \(\operatorname{ARdim}\) already permits a metric in this conformal gauge. The repair is therefore available in the core application. This is Minor: it falsifies an overbroad auxiliary statement, without showing another failure of the intended core theorem.
Impact: Overbroad auxiliary statement; no demonstrated additional failure of intended main theorem.

Title: Initial scientific review of M25-0099
On Cheeger constants of hyperbolic surfaces
# Version, claim, and scope

Thomas Budzinski, Nicolas Curien and Bram Petri, On Cheeger constants of hyperbolic surfaces, Inventiones mathematicae 242 (2025), 511–530, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01361-w. The reviewed object is the manifest-bound publisher Version of Record, 20 PDF pages; PDF page \(p\) has printed page \(510+p\). All 20 pages were read as text and actually inspected as page images. No arXiv text is substituted for this version.

For a closed orientable curvature \(-1\) surface \(S\) of genus \(g\geq2\), put \(V=|S|=4\pi(g-1)\). Theorem 1 (PDF p. 2, printed p. 512) asserts \[\limsup_{g\to\infty}\ \sup_{S\in\mathcal M_g}h(S)\leq \frac2\pi .\] This is an asymptotic supremum bound, not a bound \(h(S)\leq2/\pi\) for each finite genus and not a claim of sharpness. The definition on p. 1 takes the infimum of boundary length divided by positive area over smooth subsurfaces of area at most \(V/2\).

The essential dependencies are Lemma 2 (area concentration), Proposition 3 (uniform expected Voronoi boundary length), Lemmas 4–7 used in that proposition, and the coloring/Markov argument in Section 3.4. Definitions, quantifiers, degeneration of the injectivity radius, and limiting operations were checked along this chain. Background comparisons with random surfaces, spectral gaps, and graphs were read but their cited theorems were not independently reproved. Statements about ideal tessellations are motivation rather than a dependency of this proof.
# Area concentration: hypotheses and probability identities

The construction on pp. 7–8 uses a Poisson process of intensity \(\lambda\) relative to area and independent fair colors for its Voronoi cells. When there are no nuclei, the convention is the single cell \(S\). The chosen \(A_\lambda\) is the smaller of the unions of the two colors; it need not be a single connected component. This formal definition resolves the looser introductory component language.

Let \(X\) be the total black area and let the cell areas be \(v_i\). Conditional on the tessellation, \[\mathbb E(X\mid\mathrm{Vor})=\frac V2,\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathrm{Vor})=\frac14\sum_i v_i^2.\] The conditional mean is deterministic, including the zero-nucleus convention. Thus there is no missing between-tessellation variance term, and \[\operatorname{Var}X
 =\frac14\int_{S^2}\mathbb P(x,y\hbox{ lie in the same cell})\,dx\,dy .\] This verifies the normalization in Lemma 2, pp. 8–9. Exhaustive independent-color enumeration for four cells of areas \(1,2,3,4\) gives mean \(5\) and variance \(15/2\), exactly the formula above.

The lower ball-growth estimate uses \(h(S)\geq\delta\) only while \(|B_r(x)|\leq V/2\). Coarea gives \(B_r'\geq\delta B_r\) almost everywhere in that range. The wording on p. 9 should retain this restriction; its actual application chooses the genus large enough that the universal hyperbolic upper bound for \(|B_{r_1}|\) is below \(V/2\), so the required range is valid.

For clarity, the thin-area estimate concerns truncated thin collars, not maximal standard collars. Choose \(r_0\) smaller than the collar-disjointness threshold. For a core geodesic of length \(\ell\leq2r_0\), the normal displacement formula gives \[\cosh R\leq \frac{\sinh r_0}{\sinh(\ell/2)},\qquad
 2\ell\sinh R\leq 4\sinh r_0.\] At most \(3g-3\) disjoint short cores contribute. Hence the area with injectivity radius at most \(r_0\), divided by \(V\), is bounded by \(3\sinh(r_0)/\pi=O(r_0)\) uniformly in the surface. Taking a smaller \(r_0\) is allowed and supplies the desired \(\delta^3\) bound.

For thick \(x\), the ball of radius \(r_0\) has its full hyperbolic area. Choose \(r_1=r_1(\lambda,\delta)\) so its subsequent exponential growth makes \(\exp(-\lambda|B_{r_1}(x)|)<\delta^3/2\). If \(x,y\) are thick and \(d(x,y)>2r_1\), a common nearest nucleus cannot coexist with a nucleus in each of the two disjoint \(r_1\)-balls. The union bound therefore gives same-cell probability at most \(\delta^3\). Pairs with a thin endpoint occupy at most \(2\delta^3 V^2\), and pairs at distance at most \(2r_1\) occupy at most \(V\,2\pi(\cosh(2r_1)-1)\). Consequently \[\operatorname{Var}X\leq \tfrac34\delta^3 V^2+O_{\lambda,\delta}(V)
 <\delta^3 V^2\] for sufficiently large genus. Chebyshev gives the stated probability bound. The genus threshold may depend strongly on \(\lambda,\delta\); the theorem requires no quantitative control of that dependence.
# Perimeter estimate and uniformity
## Angular optimization and Poisson conditioning

Lemma 4 (pp. 10–11) bounds the angular kernel \(K(t)=|\sin(t/2)|\). With Fourier normalization \((2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}\), \[\widehat K(0)=\frac2\pi,\qquad
 \widehat K(n)=-\frac{2}{\pi(4n^2-1)}\quad(n\ne0).\] All nonconstant coefficients are negative, which proves the asserted maximum \(2/\pi\) for probability measures, attained by uniform measure. Smooth approximation extends the density calculation to arbitrary probability measures because the kernel is bounded and continuous. The coefficients for \(n=0,\ldots,8\) were independently integrated symbolically. For the test density \((1+t\cos(m\theta))/(2\pi)\) the integral is \(2/\pi-t^2/[\pi(4m^2-1)]\), consistent with the sign and normalization.

For fixed \(S\), Voronoi boundaries form finitely many geodesic segments almost surely. Their \(\varepsilon\)-tube area divided by \(2\varepsilon\) converges to total boundary length. Fatou’s lemma has the correct direction for the desired expectation upper bound. The nearest-nucleus integral in (11), p. 13, includes the empty-ball factor \(e^{-\lambda|B_r(x)|}\) and a second-nucleus factor \(1-e^{-\lambda|A^\varepsilon_S(x,y)|}\). The latter region is outside the open nearest-nucleus ball, so independent Poisson increments apply. Null distance ties do not change the integral. Replacing \(1-e^{-u}\) by \(u\) gives (12).

A bisector meeting the small ball need not itself be an exposed Voronoi face. Nevertheless, the segment from \(x\) to that bisector either stays in the nearest cell up to its boundary, or exits earlier through another cell boundary. This justifies the event interpretation used for the upper bound. The zero-nucleus event creates no boundary.
## Thin annuli and changes of lift

Lemma 5 (pp. 11–12) gives \(o(\varepsilon)\) intersection area for two thin annuli when their centers are separated by \(1/K\) and their radii are at most \(K\). Hyperbolic cosine law restricts the angle to an interval in the cosine coordinate of size \(O_K(\varepsilon)\), so the angular measure is \(O_K(\sqrt\varepsilon)\) even at tangency. Multiplication by radial thickness gives \(O_K(\varepsilon^{3/2})\).

The preliminary inference printed as \(a\geq1/(2K)\) from nonempty intersection is slightly too strong: it only gives \(a\geq1/(2K)-\varepsilon\). Requiring \(\varepsilon<1/(4K)\) gives \(a\geq1/(4K)\), which is all that is needed to bound the hyperbolic-law denominator away from zero. This repairs the argument with changed constants, not changed hypotheses or conclusion.

In Lemma 6 (pp. 13–14), competing deck translates give intersections of such annuli. For a fixed compact surface their centers are separated by its positive systole, their radii are bounded by its diameter, and only finitely many translates are relevant, uniformly in \(x,y\). Thus the accumulated error is \(o_S(\varepsilon)\). This is not an error uniform over moduli space and need not be: the proof first takes \(\varepsilon\to0\) for each fixed \(S\). The bound left after that limit has constants depending only on \(\delta,\lambda\). No positive uniform systole is assumed.

Lemma 6 is a one-sided estimate. Accordingly the second line of the last display on p. 16 can be read with \(\leq o_S(\varepsilon)+\cdots\), rather than the printed equality. Every subsequent step is an upper bound and remains valid.
## The angle-sensitive displacement estimate

The calculation in Lemma 7 (pp. 14–16) yields, with \(r'\geq r\), \[(\cosh r'-\cosh r)^2
 \leq \varepsilon^2(\sinh r'-\sinh r)^2+
 4\varepsilon^2\sin^2\!\frac{\theta'-\theta}{2}\sinh r\,\sinh r'.\] Here \((\sinh r'-\sinh r)/(\cosh r'-\cosh r)
=\coth((r+r')/2)\leq\coth r_0\), and \(r'\leq r+2\varepsilon\). Choose \(\varepsilon_0\) so \[\varepsilon_0^2\coth^2r_0
 <1-(1+\delta/2)^{-2},\qquad
 e^{\varepsilon_0\coth r_0}
 <\frac{1+\delta}{1+\delta/2}.\] These inequalities justify absorption and the remaining square-root ratio, giving \[r'-r\leq2(1+\delta)\varepsilon
 \left|\sin\frac{\theta'-\theta}{2}\right|.\] Thus the last step uses both a large \(r_0\) and a small \(\varepsilon_0\); increasing \(r_0\) alone would not make a fixed \(\varepsilon\) ratio tend to one. The lemma already allows both choices. Independent parameter checks gave a common sufficient choice for several \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\).

The Dirichlet domain is star-shaped at its center, so its allowed angle sets \(I_r\) decrease with \(r\). This gives the inclusion used in the polar-area estimate and \[B'_r=|I_r|\sinh r,\qquad
 B_r\geq |I_r|(\cosh r-1),\qquad
 B'_r\leq(1+\delta)B_r\quad(r\geq r_0).\] The derivative identities hold almost everywhere; ball area is absolutely continuous, which is sufficient for integration.
# A verified finite-volume correction, with its effect

The last evaluation on p. 17 (printed p. 527), immediately after (17), drops the terminal term at \(r=\infty\). On a compact surface \(B_r\to V\), not infinity. The exact value is \[\lambda^2\int_0^\infty B'_r B_r e^{-\lambda B_r}\,dr
 =\lambda^2\int_0^V u e^{-\lambda u}\,du
 =1-(1+\lambda V)e^{-\lambda V}\leq1.\] It is strictly less than \(1\) for finite positive \(\lambda V\). Independent symbolic integration verifies the identity; its derivative in \(x=\lambda V\) is \(xe^{-x}>0\), and its limits are \(0\) and \(1\).

This is recorded as a verified proof clarification, with exact location, correction, and effect, rather than a new substantive Major or Minor defect. It neither falsifies the proposition nor requires an additional geometric hypothesis. Likewise, the introductory ball-growth display on p. 4 has an extraneous additive \(1\); the usual differential inequality gives \(B_r\geq B_{r_0}e^{h(S)(r-r_0)}\) over its permitted range. That background slip is not used in the new proof.
# Final implication, boundary cases, and disposition

Fix \(0<\delta<1/2\). Surfaces with \(h(S)\leq\delta\) need no further argument. For the rest choose \(\lambda=\lambda(\delta)>0\) so the expected total Voronoi boundary is at most \((2/\pi)(1+\delta)V\). A side separating distinct cells belongs to the two-color interface with probability \(1/2\) conditional on the tessellation. Therefore \[\mathbb E|\partial A_\lambda|\leq \frac{1+\delta}{\pi}V,\qquad
 \mathbb P\!\left(|\partial A_\lambda|\leq
 \frac{(1+\delta)^2}{\pi}V\right)\geq\frac{\delta}{1+\delta}.\] The sidewise expectations require no independence between distinct sides.

Apply Lemma 2 with tolerance \(\delta^2\); \(h(S)>\delta\) implies its required \(h(S)\geq\delta^2\). Its area event has probability greater than \(1-\delta^2\) and gives \(|A_\lambda|\geq V(1/2-\delta^2)\geq(1-\delta)V/2\). The intersection with the perimeter event has positive probability, since \[\frac{\delta}{1+\delta}-\delta^2
 =\frac{\delta(1-\delta-\delta^2)}{1+\delta}>0.\] No area/perimeter independence and no expectation-of-a-ratio identity is being used. The smaller-color choice ensures area at most \(V/2\). Finitely many polygonal corners can be rounded with changes tending to zero in area and length; taking the smaller complementary side if necessary respects the smooth-boundary definition. Hence \[h(S)\leq\frac2\pi\,\frac{(1+\delta)^2}{1-\delta}.\] For each fixed \(\delta\) the genus threshold is uniform in \(S\); letting \(\delta\downarrow0\) proves precisely the stated limsup bound.
## Limits of this initial review

No confirmed substantive defect remains in the checked central chain. This does not certify every result cited in the introduction or the full external collar/Poisson-process literature. Those external theories were used in their standard stated forms; the specific collar-area bound and conditional calculations needed here were reconstructed above. No empirical computation is part of the theorem, and absence of released author code is not a defect. There was no author source package in this two-file manifest, so no author-code execution or source compilation was attempted.

Title: Initial scientific review of M25-0100
Group actions on contractible 2-complexes I
# Bound version, claims, and conventions

Iván Sadofschi Costa, Group actions on contractible 2-complexes I, arXiv:2102.11458v2, 21 August 2025, 27 PDF pages. All page numbers below refer to this PDF and agree with its printed numbering. All 27 pages were read as text and actually viewed as page images. The manifest associates the work with DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01362-9, Inventiones mathematicae 242 (2025), 531–562. The journal text was not acquired; no identity of its wording with v2 is asserted. The findings belong only to the bound v2 PDF and its accompanying typesetting source.

Theorem A asserts the fixed-point property for finite-group actions on finite contractible two-dimensional complexes. The operative notion is the admissible \(G\)-CW action specified in Section 2, not an arbitrary unstructured topological action. The stronger intermediate conclusion is that a fixed-point-free finite acyclic \(G\)-complex has a nontrivial unitary representation of its fundamental group. Theorem B supplies this for \(\operatorname{PSL}_2(2^n)\), \(n\geq2\); \(\operatorname{PSL}_2(3^n)\), odd \(n\geq3\); the stated prime-power cases \(q\equiv11,19\pmod{24}\); and \(\operatorname{Sz}(2^n)\), odd \(n\geq3\). Theorem C is an external result from Part II for \(q>5\), \(q\equiv5,13\pmod{24}\). The exceptional \(q=5\) is covered through \(\operatorname{PSL}_2(5)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(4)\). This review does not independently certify Part II.

The internal chain examined is the reduction in Theorem 3.8, Brown’s extension and the representation quotient in Section 5, the character and centralizer construction in Section 7, the dimension and differential arguments in Sections 8–9, the degree computation in Section 10, and the final representation-extension argument in Section 11. The calculations below use \([R,S]=RS-SR\) for a matrix commutator, not the multiplicative group commutator.
# Problem 1: Suzuki centralizers in the selected basis

Classification: Major; demonstrated invalid core proof calculation, with a verified local repair. The location is Proposition 7.10, Suzuki case, p. 21, especially the displayed \(C\) and the following displayed formula for \(C_{\mathrm U(m)}(\rho_0(G_{v_1}))\); the author TeX has the relevant construction at lines 1490–1518, including \(C\) at line 1510 and the centralizer calculation at lines 1513–1518. Parts (ii)–(v) are used by Propositions 10.1–10.3 on pp. 24–25, and thus by Theorem 11.1 and Theorem B on p. 26.
## All parameters and the false equality

Set \[q=2^n,\quad n\geq3\text{ odd},\qquad r=\sqrt{2q},\quad
 h=r/2,\quad s=q/2-1,\quad N=sh,\quad m=(q-1)h=2N+h.\] Here \(h\geq2\). In the source \(J_d\) is the scalar antidiagonal permutation matrix of size \(d\), not a reversal of blocks that preserves coordinates inside each block.

The selected dihedral representative is \[X=\rho_0(x)=
 \operatorname{diag}(\xi I_h,\xi^2 I_h,\ldots,\xi^{q-2}I_h,I_h),
 \qquad Y=\rho_0(y)=J_{2N}\oplus(-I_h),
 \quad \xi=e^{2\pi i/(q-1)} .\]

These matrices have exactly the character used in the proof and satisfy the dihedral relations. In particular all \(q-1\) eigenvalues of \(X\) are distinct as blocks. Write \[A=2^{-1/2}
 \begin{pmatrix}I_N&J_N\\ I_N&-J_N\end{pmatrix}\oplus I_h .\] The printed centralizer of \(\langle X,Y\rangle\) consists of matrices \[\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_s,a_s,\ldots,a_1,b),
 \qquad a_i,b\in\mathrm U(h).
 \tag{1}\] This is false in the displayed basis: the internal \(J_h\) conjugations have been omitted.

For an admissible instance take \(q=8\), \(r=4\), \(h=2\), \(N=6\), and \(m=14\). Choose \(a_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) and \(a_2=a_3=b=I_2\). The matrix \[H_{\rm bad}=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,I_2,I_2,I_2,I_2,a_1,I_2)\] belongs to (1) and commutes with \(X\), but \[[H_{\rm bad},Y]_{1,12}=2\ne0.\] For clarity, \(Y_{1,12}=1\), whereas the relevant diagonal entries of \(H_{\rm bad}\) are \(1\) and \(-1\). This is a direct counterexample to the printed centralizer equality in the actual allowed Suzuki parameters. It is not a counterexample to a fixed-point theorem.

There is also a dimensional error in the printed \(C=A^{-1}(I_N\oplus J_N\oplus I_1)A\): its middle matrix has size \(2N+1\), whereas \(A\) has size \(2N+h\). For \(q=8\) these are 13 and 14. This dimensional slip alone is not the basis of the Major classification; the false commutant formula and its use in the core calculation are substantive.
## Complete repair of the required block calculation

The actual centralizer is \[H=C_{\mathrm U(m)}(\langle X,Y\rangle)
 =\{\operatorname{diag}(P,J_NPJ_N,b):
       P=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_s),\ a_i,b\in\mathrm U(h)\}.
 \tag{2}\] Indeed commuting with \(X\) first forces block diagonality with \(h\)-dimensional blocks. Commuting with \(J_{2N}\) then identifies the opposite blocks by conjugation by \(J_h\), exactly (2). The last block is unrestricted because \(Y\) is \(-I_h\) there.

Replace \(C\) by \[D=I_N\oplus J_N\oplus I_h,\qquad C=A^{-1}DA.
 \tag{3}\] Both \(A\) and \(C\) are unitary. Direct multiplication gives \[AYA^{-1}=I_N\oplus(-I_{N+h}).\] Since \(D\) commutes with this diagonal matrix, \(C\) commutes with \(Y\), proving (iv). If \(K=C_{\mathrm U(m)}(X)=\mathrm U(h)^{q-1}\), the block splitting at \(N=sh\) gives \(K\subseteq\mathrm U(N)\times\mathrm U(N+h)\). Thus \(A^{-1}KA\subseteq C_{\mathrm U(m)}(Y)\), proving (iii).

For (v) we have \[AC=DA=2^{-1/2}
 \begin{pmatrix}I_N&J_N\\ J_N&-I_N\end{pmatrix}\oplus I_h .
 \tag{4}\] The upper right block of \((AC)\operatorname{diag}(P,J_NPJ_N,b)\) is \(PJ_N/\sqrt2\), and its lower left block is \(J_NP/\sqrt2\); the same blocks occur in the reverse product. The diagonal blocks also agree. Hence (4) commutes with every member of the full centralizer (2), as required. Finally, \[\dim H=(s+1)h^2=q^2/4,\qquad
 \dim K=(q-1)h^2=(q-1)q/2,\qquad
 \dim K-\dim H=q(q-2)/4>0.\] This proves (ii) with the original strict inequality. The Borel irreducibility used for (i) is unaffected: the character-norm computation from Proposition 7.8 equals one. All of these repairs hold for every originally allowed \(q\), not only \(q=8\).
## Impact, counterevidence, and limits

The proof on p. 25 expressly invokes (v) to produce the equivariant homotopy from \(Y_0\) to \(Z\). The original displayed centralizer is therefore part of the main degree argument. This dependency supports Major under the supplied core-contribution standard, even though the repair is local and complete at this step. The abstract group type and its dimension were correct, and the errors do not refute Proposition 7.10’s existential conclusion or Theorems A/B. Equations (2)–(4) repair the needed construction without narrowing \(q\) or changing the representation character. They do not independently reprove the external character classification on which the construction relies. Exact reviewer-written SymPy calculations checked the \(q=8\) commutator, all 28 basis elements of the cyclic commutant algebra, and all 16 basis elements of the corrected dihedral commutant algebra; the preceding general proof supplies the unbounded statement.
# Problem 2: edge slides require different edge orbits

Classification: Minor; false auxiliary lemma in its stated generality. Lemma 3.9, p. 7, author TeX lines 564–572, assumes a finite \(G\)-graph with adjacent edges \(e=\{u,v\}\), \(e'=\{v,w\}\) and \(G_{e'}\subseteq G_e\). It claims that removing \(G\cdot e'\) and attaching an orbit of edges from \(u\) to \(w\) preserves the \(G\)-homotopy type. No different-orbits hypothesis appears.

Let \(G=C_4\) act by rotation on the four-cycle with vertices \(v_i\) and distinct edge cells \(e_i\) from \(v_i\) to \(v_{i+1}\), indices modulo four. This is a finite admissible \(G\)-CW graph. Set \(u=v_0\), \(v=v_1\), \(w=v_2\), \(e=e_0\), \(e'=e_1\). All edge stabilizers are trivial, so the stated inclusion holds; the adjacent vertices and edge cells are distinct. However \(G\cdot e=G\cdot e'\) consists of all four edges. After removing that orbit, the prescribed new free orbit has four distinct cells from \(v_i\) to \(v_{i+2}\). Two parallel cells join \(v_0\) to \(v_2\), and two join \(v_1\) to \(v_3\). Consequently the original graph is connected and the new graph has two components: \[\operatorname{rank}H_0(X^1;\mathbb Z)=1,\qquad
 \operatorname{rank}H_0(Y^1;\mathbb Z)=2.\] They are not even nonequivariantly homotopy equivalent. The proposed homotopy in the proof travels along \(e\), which has been removed in this example.

A sufficient repair is to require \(G\cdot e\ne G\cdot e'\). Then the entire orbit of \(e\) remains in \(X^1-G\cdot e'\). Move the first attaching endpoint from \(v\) to \(u\) along this retained edge and keep \(w\) fixed. Since \(G_{e'}\subseteq G_e\), that path is fixed by \(G_{e'}\) and extends to a well-defined \(G\)-homotopy on the attaching orbit. Equivariant attachment along homotopic maps gives the claimed equivalence.

The use in Proposition 3.10, pp. 7–8, concerns rearranging distinct edge orbits; even in the Suzuki case its two orbits of the same stabilizer type are different orbits. No failure of that application or of Theorem B has been established. Thus this supported scope defect is Minor. The repair changes the lemma’s hypotheses and cannot justify the false same-orbit case.
# Problem 3: an unstated path-component condition

Classification: Minor; false first assertion of an auxiliary homotopy lemma. Lemma 5.9, p. 14, author TeX lines 1012–1017, first claims that the maps on \(\mathcal M\) induced by \(ww'\) and \(w i_v(g)w'\) are homotopic for a general target Lie group \(\mathcal G\). Its proof chooses a path from \(1\) to \(\rho_0(g)\) without a hypothesis guaranteeing that path. The connected double-centralizer condition is stated only for the subsequent quotient assertion.

Take \(G=C_2\) acting trivially on a one-edge tree \(X^1\), with root vertex \(v_0\). Every vertex and edge stabilizer is \(G\), and Brown’s extension has \(\Gamma=G\). Choose the compact zero-dimensional Lie group \(\mathcal G=\{1,-1\}\) and the nontrivial representation \(\rho_0:G\to\mathcal G\). Then \(\mathcal M=C_{\mathcal G}(\rho_0(G))=\{1,-1\}\) is nonempty. The normalized vertex gauge group is also \(\{1,-1\}\), acts freely, and has a one-point quotient, so the preceding moduli setup causes no obstruction. For \(w=w'=1\) and nonidentity \(g\in G_{v_0}\), the two maps on \(\mathcal M\) are respectively the constant maps \(1\) and \(-1\). They cannot be homotopic: restricting a proposed homotopy to any point of \(\mathcal M\) would produce a path between distinct points of a discrete space.

For the first assertion it suffices to add \(\rho_0(g)\in\mathcal G^\circ\), or to assume \(\mathcal G\) connected. For the quotient assertion the chosen path must lie in the identity component of the double centralizer; the lemma’s printed connectedness hypothesis already ensures this. This is not a counterexample to that second conditional assertion.

All uses in the main degree proof have \(\mathcal G=\mathrm U(m)\). This target and its subgroup centralizers, including the double centralizers, are connected; the finite-dimensional commutant decomposition gives products of unitary groups. Theorem 4.5 is therefore adequate for the application in Proposition 10.5. No main-theorem failure follows from this general-Lie-group overstatement. The repair does not assert that arbitrary disconnected targets have the claimed homotopies.
# Checks of the remaining proof chain
## Reduction, representations, and quotient

The definitions in Sections 2–3 specify the family of solvable stabilizers and admissible cells. For Theorem 3.8, the reverse induction on nontrivial stabilizers removes excess cells in \(X^H\) while retaining the Oliver–Segev tree. Cells outside that tree have exact stabilizer \(H\), so the residual \(N_G(H)/H\) action on them is free. Equivariant extension of the retraction over their zero-, one-, and two-cells is possible because the target tree is contractible. Conjugate fixed sets intersect in already retained higher-stabilizer sets, so the retractions glue. The pushout preserves homology, while the retraction on the one-skeleton supplies the needed epimorphism on \(\pi_1\). An isomorphism of fundamental groups is neither proved nor required. The orbit Euler characteristic then yields \(k+1\) free two-cell orbits after \(k\) extra free one-cell orbits.

The relations in Theorem 5.2 are consistent with the ordered products defining \(\tau_v\) and with the inverses in the edge formula. Root normalization in Theorem 5.3 makes the compact gauge action free; equality of its orbits is equality of the represented homomorphisms, not merely equality of conjugacy classes. The unitary centralizers give compact connected smooth factors and an orientable quotient. In Proposition 5.5 every group element fixes a vertex: its cyclic subgroup is solvable, and the required fixed graph is nonempty. Hence a universal representation has the same character as \(\rho_0\). Irreducibility at the root Borel subgroup makes the intertwiner scalar and gives the unique universal point in the normalized quotient.
## Characters, dimensions, and differentials

Lemma 8.1 uses the split exact cellular chain sequence over \(\mathbb C\) for a finite group and the resulting identity of permutation characters. Frobenius reciprocity gives Corollary 8.2. The real dimension of a unitary centralizer is the sum of the squares of character multiplicities, so there is no complex-versus-real dimension mismatch. The dimensions of the global and root-Borel centralizers are both one and cancel; the \(k+1\) free two-cell orbits then give \(\dim\overline{\mathcal M}_k=(k+1)m^2\).

For Lemma 9.1, acyclicity implies surjectivity of the integral cellular coboundary into degree two. Applying the group-ring involution to the resulting identity gives \[1=\sum_e s_eN(G_e)x_e,\qquad
 N(G_e)=\sum_{h\in G_e}h .\] On any representation this implies \(V=\sum_es_eV^{G_e}\). No division in the integral group ring is assumed. Applied to the real adjoint representation, the identity gives surjectivity of the differential in Proposition 9.2 through the explicit derivative formula in Theorem 5.7. The latter follows by differentiating the ordered product; the signs and adjoint transports telescope as stated. Lemma 5.8 gives \(dX=A\,dW\) because commutator derivatives vanish at a representation trivial on \(N\). The quotient map is a submersion; together with equal dimensions this transfers regularity to Corollary 9.4.
## Degree, nontriviality, and Theorem A

In Proposition 10.1, dropping the first edge factor and the corresponding vertex gauge factor leaves a quotient whose dimension is smaller than \(\dim\mathrm U(m)\) by the positive gap just calculated. The remaining compact gauge action is free, and Sard’s theorem gives nonsurjectivity. In Proposition 10.2 the substitution \(\widehat\tau_{\eta_1}=\tau_{\eta_1}C^{-1}A^{-1}\tau_{\eta_0}A\) belongs to the required centralizer by (iii)–(iv); the matrix order in Table 5, including the conjugation tail when \(q\equiv11\pmod{24}\), agrees with \(T(\widehat\tau)=Z(\tau)\). With Problem 1 repaired, (v) and connected double centralizers supply the equivariant homotopy in Proposition 10.3.

The actual source and target of every degree argument are compact oriented connected manifolds without boundary of equal dimension. The informal general degree paragraph omits some of these qualifications, but they hold in its applications. The free-edge factors give \(\overline{\mathcal M}_k=\overline{\mathcal M}_0\times\mathrm U(m)^k\). The first factor has degree zero, so the product has degree zero regardless of the orientation signs of inversion on the other factors. Lemma 5.9, with its valid unitary hypotheses, removes vertex constants by homotopy, not by an equality of group words. Thus Proposition 10.5 obtains degree zero for the required word map.

Theorem 11.1 correctly needs only one regular preimage of the identity. If it were the sole preimage, the identity would be a regular value with signed degree \(1\) or \(-1\), contradicting degree zero. The second point is nonuniversal by Proposition 5.5 and yields a nontrivial representation of the kernel quotient. Acyclicity supplies the normal-generation condition modulo \([N,N]\).

Finally \(Y=X^N\) in the proof of Theorem A is an acyclic subcomplex with an essential action of \(G/N\). A lower-dimensional finite acyclic graph would be a tree and have a fixed point, so it cannot create an unhandled fixed-point-free case. Theorem B and the external Theorem C cover the classified groups. Proposition 11.2 gives a balanced relative presentation with nonsingular exponent-sum matrix; the relative acyclic chain complex explains that condition. Gerstenhaber–Rothaus applies to the compact connected unitary target and extends the nontrivial representation of \(\pi_1(Y)\) to \(\pi_1(X)\). Injectivity of \(\pi_1(Y)\to\pi_1(X)\) is not assumed: nontriviality of its represented restriction suffices. A finite prime-power enumeration through \(10000\) checked 632 admissible cases as a supplementary residue check, not as a proof of the unbounded classification.
# Evidence, coverage, and unresolved limits

The main author TeX has 1871 lines. Static parsing read and hashed all six extracted source files, indexed all 77 labels, and exposed 14 targeted contexts; the complete resulting record was read, and the finding-related contexts were checked against the PDF. This does not claim a semantic review of every style or bibliography line. No author code or author TeX was executed. Reviewer-written graph and exact-matrix calculations were actually run with SymPy 1.13.3; their script, results, and static-source record are retained with this review.

The author-hosted Oliver–Segev primary text was consulted for its principal classification statements and Examples 3.4, 3.5, and 3.7, rather than independently re-proving that classification. The original Gerstenhaber–Rothaus theorem was checked through accessible article text in an author-uploaded copy: nonsingular exponent matrix gives nonzero degree and solvability for compact connected Lie targets. Publisher/PMC direct full-text attempts encountered access obstacles and are not represented as successful full-text reads. Part II, all external character tables, and all proofs of background results were not independently re-audited. A limited identity/erratum search found no correction used here; that is not evidence that no correction exists.

All 27 original pages were actually viewed. The bound source package and manifest were checked for size and SHA-256. Rendering or indexing alone is not counted as visual or scientific review. Scientific decision remains pending; the human-review list is empty.

problems.title: Suzuki centralizers in the selected basis
problems.source_location: Proposition7.10 Suzuki case, PDF p21; author TeX1490-1518, especially1510 and1513-1518. Core dependencies Proposition10.1-10.3 pp24-25 and Theorem11.1/B p26.
claim: In the chosen global-antidiagonal basis the dihedral centralizer is printed as diag(a1,...,as,as,...,a1,b), and C has final identity block I1.
analysis: Classification: Major; demonstrated invalid core proof calculation, with a verified local repair. The location is Proposition 7.10, Suzuki case, p. 21, especially the displayed \(C\) and the following displayed formula for \(C_{\mathrm U(m)}(\rho_0(G_{v_1}))\); the author TeX has the relevant construction at lines 1490–1518, including \(C\) at line 1510 and the centralizer calculation at lines 1513–1518. Parts (ii)–(v) are used by Propositions 10.1–10.3 on pp. 24–25, and thus by Theorem 11.1 and Theorem B on p. 26.

Set \[q=2^n,\quad n\geq3\text{ odd},\qquad r=\sqrt{2q},\quad
 h=r/2,\quad s=q/2-1,\quad N=sh,\quad m=(q-1)h=2N+h.\] Here \(h\geq2\). In the source \(J_d\) is the scalar antidiagonal permutation matrix of size \(d\), not a reversal of blocks that preserves coordinates inside each block.

The selected dihedral representative is \[X=\rho_0(x)=
 \operatorname{diag}(\xi I_h,\xi^2 I_h,\ldots,\xi^{q-2}I_h,I_h),
 \qquad Y=\rho_0(y)=J_{2N}\oplus(-I_h),
 \quad \xi=e^{2\pi i/(q-1)} .\]

These matrices have exactly the character used in the proof and satisfy the dihedral relations. In particular all \(q-1\) eigenvalues of \(X\) are distinct as blocks. Write \[A=2^{-1/2}
 \begin{pmatrix}I_N&J_N\\ I_N&-J_N\end{pmatrix}\oplus I_h .\] The printed centralizer of \(\langle X,Y\rangle\) consists of matrices \[\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_s,a_s,\ldots,a_1,b),
 \qquad a_i,b\in\mathrm U(h).
 \tag{1}\] This is false in the displayed basis: the internal \(J_h\) conjugations have been omitted.

For an admissible instance take \(q=8\), \(r=4\), \(h=2\), \(N=6\), and \(m=14\). Choose \(a_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) and \(a_2=a_3=b=I_2\). The matrix \[H_{\rm bad}=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,I_2,I_2,I_2,I_2,a_1,I_2)\] belongs to (1) and commutes with \(X\), but \[[H_{\rm bad},Y]_{1,12}=2\ne0.\] For clarity, \(Y_{1,12}=1\), whereas the relevant diagonal entries of \(H_{\rm bad}\) are \(1\) and \(-1\). This is a direct counterexample to the printed centralizer equality in the actual allowed Suzuki parameters. It is not a counterexample to a fixed-point theorem.

There is also a dimensional error in the printed \(C=A^{-1}(I_N\oplus J_N\oplus I_1)A\): its middle matrix has size \(2N+1\), whereas \(A\) has size \(2N+h\). For \(q=8\) these are 13 and 14. This dimensional slip alone is not the basis of the Major classification; the false commutant formula and its use in the core calculation are substantive.

The actual centralizer is \[H=C_{\mathrm U(m)}(\langle X,Y\rangle)
 =\{\operatorname{diag}(P,J_NPJ_N,b):
       P=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_s),\ a_i,b\in\mathrm U(h)\}.
 \tag{2}\] Indeed commuting with \(X\) first forces block diagonality with \(h\)-dimensional blocks. Commuting with \(J_{2N}\) then identifies the opposite blocks by conjugation by \(J_h\), exactly (2). The last block is unrestricted because \(Y\) is \(-I_h\) there.

Replace \(C\) by \[D=I_N\oplus J_N\oplus I_h,\qquad C=A^{-1}DA.
 \tag{3}\] Both \(A\) and \(C\) are unitary. Direct multiplication gives \[AYA^{-1}=I_N\oplus(-I_{N+h}).\] Since \(D\) commutes with this diagonal matrix, \(C\) commutes with \(Y\), proving (iv). If \(K=C_{\mathrm U(m)}(X)=\mathrm U(h)^{q-1}\), the block splitting at \(N=sh\) gives \(K\subseteq\mathrm U(N)\times\mathrm U(N+h)\). Thus \(A^{-1}KA\subseteq C_{\mathrm U(m)}(Y)\), proving (iii).

For (v) we have \[AC=DA=2^{-1/2}
 \begin{pmatrix}I_N&J_N\\ J_N&-I_N\end{pmatrix}\oplus I_h .
 \tag{4}\] The upper right block of \((AC)\operatorname{diag}(P,J_NPJ_N,b)\) is \(PJ_N/\sqrt2\), and its lower left block is \(J_NP/\sqrt2\); the same blocks occur in the reverse product. The diagonal blocks also agree. Hence (4) commutes with every member of the full centralizer (2), as required. Finally, \[\dim H=(s+1)h^2=q^2/4,\qquad
 \dim K=(q-1)h^2=(q-1)q/2,\qquad
 \dim K-\dim H=q(q-2)/4>0.\] This proves (ii) with the original strict inequality. The Borel irreducibility used for (i) is unaffected: the character-norm computation from Proposition 7.8 equals one. All of these repairs hold for every originally allowed \(q\), not only \(q=8\).

The proof on p. 25 expressly invokes (v) to produce the equivariant homotopy from \(Y_0\) to \(Z\). The original displayed centralizer is therefore part of the main degree argument. This dependency supports Major under the supplied core-contribution standard, even though the repair is local and complete at this step. The abstract group type and its dimension were correct, and the errors do not refute Proposition 7.10’s existential conclusion or Theorems A/B. Equations (2)–(4) repair the needed construction without narrowing \(q\) or changing the representation character. They do not independently reprove the external character classification on which the construction relies. Exact reviewer-written SymPy calculations checked the \(q=8\) commutator, all 28 basis elements of the cyclic commutant algebra, and all 16 basis elements of the corrected dihedral commutant algebra; the preceding general proof supplies the unbounded statement.

Title: Initial verification of
Group actions on contractible 2-complexes II
# Identity and review scope

Paper M25-0101 is by Kevin Iván Piterman and Iván Sadofschi Costa, with journal DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01363-8. The reviewed file is the seven-page arXiv version dated 21 August 2025 [paper]. Page numbers below are the PDF’s one-based pages, identical to its printed pages. All seven pages were read and visually inspected; page 7 contains affiliations rather than an argument.

Theorem C concerns finite acyclic, fixed-point-free, two-dimensional \(G\)-complexes, where \(G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(q)\), \(q>5\), and \(q\equiv5\) or \(13\pmod {24}\). Here \(q\) is a prime power, as required by the group notation. Its conclusion is the existence of a nontrivial unitary representation of the fundamental group. The passage to the fixed-point theorem for arbitrary finite groups uses Part I and the structural reductions cited there. The present review does not replace a review of that entire dependency chain.
# Verified reasoning
## Simultaneous centralizer bound

Lemma 2.1 (p. 2) does not assert that two arbitrary group elements commute. Instead it diagonalizes their images separately, using the same choice on isomorphic irreducible summands. In an isotypic decomposition, these diagonalizing operators act on representation factors and commute with the multiplicity-space operators. Thus \(A_1^{-1}A_2\) commutes with the original representation’s centralizer.

In the resulting common coordinate basis let \(r_{\lambda,\mu}\) count the coordinates with the indicated pair of eigenvalues. Then \(\sum r_{\lambda,\mu}=m\). The intersection of the two diagonal centralizers contains \(\prod_{\lambda,\mu}U(r_{\lambda,\mu})\), so \[\dim_{\mathbb R}(C_1\cap C_2)\geq\sum_{\lambda,\mu}r_{\lambda,\mu}^2
 \geq\frac{m^2}{n_1n_2}.\] The last inequality is Cauchy–Schwarz, with zero-sized blocks allowed. This verifies the bound and the compatibility condition later needed for the homotopy.
## The character calculations omitted in Proposition 4.2
## Central extension and differential

For \(\widehat G=\mathrm{SL}_2(q)\), write \(z=-I\). In Lemma 6.1 (pp. 4–5), the homomorphism \(\mathbb C[\widehat G]\to\mathbb C[G]\) has kernel generated by \(1-z\). Every lifted edge stabilizer has twice the order of its image, hence \[\pi\bigl(N(\widehat G_e)\bigr)=2N(G_e).\] The factor \(1/2\) used to lift the coefficients is consequently required and correct. Applying the resulting group-ring identity to a representation gives the stated spanning relation.

For the adjoint representation on \(\mathfrak u(m)\), \(\rho_0(z)=-I\) acts trivially. The \((1-z)\) term disappears, giving the spanning of the tangent space by the images of the centralizer tangent spaces. Although the displayed group-ring identity uses complex coefficients, it may be applied to \(\mathfrak u(m)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C\); full rank of this complexification implies full rank of the original real differential. Thus this change of coefficient field does not supply a counterexample.

The differential formula in Part I, Theorem 5.7, was checked in its versioned HTML [part1]. Its common minus sign does not affect surjectivity. The graph action is an admissible \(G\)-CW action; it is not an unrestricted action on a topological space.
## Quotients and the degree-zero arguments

For Proposition 7.2 (p. 6), the cyclic edge groups have orders 6 and 4, so their numbers of eigenvalues are at most 6 and 4. These are the compatibility conditions in Part I, Proposition 5.11; its connected-double-centralizer condition holds for unitary centralizers [part1].

Abstract: This report checks labeled-shape definitions, stabilizer quotients, normalization, and selected geometric inputs in the publisher version of Arana–Herrera and Calderon’s paper. An exact finite ribbon graph gives a genus-three witness against the full-stabilizer invariance asserted for arbitrary labeled-shape weights. The defect enters the construction and unfolding used for the principal equidistribution statement. The later oriented formulation identifies consistent repairs, whose definitions and counting identities are verified here. A second explicit hyperbolic family refutes the general center-stability assertion in Lemma 4.8; a verified estimate with both inradii bounded repairs its compact-surface application. # Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is Francisco Arana–Herrera and Aaron Calderon, The shapes of complementary subsurfaces to simple closed hyperbolic multi-geodesics, Inventiones mathematicae 242 (2025), 571–626, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01364-7.
