# Definitions and essential dependencies

In Section 1.1, curves are unoriented free homotopy classes, and \(s(X,\gamma,L)\) counts their mapping-class orbit up to length \(L\). In Section 2.6, \(\mathcal{MRG}_{h,b}\) has distinctly labeled boundary components. Cutting a nonseparating curve in genus \(g\) gives type \((g-1,2)\). Write \[Z=\mathcal{MRG}_{g-1,2}(1,1),\qquad \tau:Z\longrightarrow Z\] for the involution exchanging its boundary labels. An orientation of the curve distinguishes its sides. The full stabilizer \(\operatorname{Stab}(\gamma)\) contains orientation-reversing-on-the-curve mapping classes, whereas \(\operatorname{Stab}_0(\gamma)\) preserves that orientation.

The realization of positive ribbon graphs uses the fixed-boundary spine homeomorphism stated in Theorem 2.4 (p. 582). The measure argument uses Theorem 2.7, the polynomial total-volume asymptotic, and earthquake-flow ergodicity. The finite calculation below does not replace these background results. Necessary external source statements and their applicable hypotheses are separately bound in the dependency checks.
# A labeled shape does not descend through the full stabilizer

Problem 1 (Core definition and descent defect; Major).  For arbitrary nonnegative \(h\in C_c(Z)\), the measure in (5.1) is asserted to be \(\operatorname{Stab}(\gamma)\)-invariant and is then pushed locally to \(\mathcal T_g/\operatorname{Stab}(\gamma)\). This is false under the paper’s explicit labeled-boundary convention.
## Source and core dependency

The relevant statements are the unoriented convention on p. 573; the single Dirac mass \(\delta_{\operatorname{RSC}_\alpha(X)}\) and Theorem 1.1 on p. 574; the labeled target on p. 578; and the invariance assertion immediately after (5.1) on p. 597. Proposition 6.6 (pp. 610–611) uses the same quotient when replacing the count by a coset sum and unfolding. The issue therefore affects a required step of the main proof, rather than only an auxiliary description.
## An explicit positive metric graph

Take the cube graph with the following edge order: \[(01),(02),(04),(13),(15),(23),(26),(37),(45),(46),(57),(67).\] Specify its ribbon structure by these cyclic neighbor orders: \[\begin{array}{c|cccccccc}
v&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
\text{order}&124&035&036&127&056&147&742&653 .
\end{array}\] For example, \(124\) means \((1,2,4)\). The boundary permutation sends \((u,v)\) to \((v,w)\), where \(w\) follows \(u\) at \(v\). Its two cycles, listed by successive vertices and then closed, are \[\begin{split}
 F_1&=(0,1,3,2,6,7,5,1,0,2,3,7,6,4),\\
 F_2&=(2,0,4,5,7,3,1,5,4,6).
\end{split}\] They exhaust all 24 directed edges. Since \(V=8\), \(E=12\), and \(b=2\), the thickened graph satisfies \(2-2h-b=V-E=-4\), so \(h=2\).

In the stated edge order assign \[w=(1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128,2081,512,1024,2048).\] All lengths are positive. With \(C=2+4+8+16+64+128+512+1024=1758\), the two perimeters are \[P_1=C+2(1+32+2048)=5920,\qquad
 P_2=C+2(2081)=5920.\] Division by 5920 gives \(G\in\mathcal{MRG}_{2,2}(1,1)\). Any ribbon-graph automorphism preserves the number of directed edges in a boundary cycle, but here the counts are 14 and 10. Hence \(G\ne\tau G\). Independently, the distinct lengths force every metric automorphism to fix all edges, and then all trivalent vertices.

The saved independent program `checks/labels/boundary_label_witness.py` calculated the cycles and perimeters with exact rational arithmetic and verified positivity. Its JSON output records the full witness. This is a finite combinatorial check followed by an analytic construction.
## Hypotheses and failure of invariance

Set the ambient genus to \(g=3\). The fixed-length spine homeomorphism realizes \(G\) as a compact hyperbolic \(Y\) of genus two with two geodesic boundaries of length one. This application was checked in Luo’s published Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.4 [Luo]: all fundamental-cycle sums are positive because every coordinate is positive, and each boundary-cycle sum is one with multiplicity. The coordinate formula and canonical-spine interpretation in Mondello’s Definition 2.8 and Theorem 2.14 [Mondello] confirm that these are the full boundary-projection widths, with no factor of two. Gluing them by an orientation-reversing isometry gives a closed oriented genus-three hyperbolic surface \(X\). The glued geodesic \(\gamma\) is essential, simple, has length one, and is nonseparating because cutting it recovers connected \(Y\).

Choose an orientation of the reference curve to define a labeled cut on Teichmüller space. A mapping class \(\phi\in\operatorname{Stab}(\gamma)\setminus\operatorname{Stab}_0(\gamma)\) reverses that orientation and exchanges its sides. Thus \[\operatorname{RSC}_\gamma(\phi X)=\tau\operatorname{RSC}_\gamma(X).\] Choose a relatively compact neighborhood \(U\) of \(G\) in its trivalent cell, with \(U\cap\tau U=\varnothing\), and a nonnegative \(h\in C_c(U)\) equal to one near \(G\). Then \[h(G)=1,\qquad h(\tau G)=0,\qquad
 \int_Zh\,d\eta_{\operatorname{Kon}}>0.\] The last assertion uses the positive volume form on the cell. For cutoff \(L=2\), the length indicators in (5.1) at \(X\) and \(\phi X\) both equal one, whereas the weighted densities equal one and zero. This difference persists on an open Teichmüller neighborhood of positive Weil–Petersson measure, by continuity of length and the labeled spine. Since the Weil–Petersson measure and length cutoff are \(\phi\)-invariant, the weighted measure is not. The claimed full-stabilizer descent fails for an allowed \(h\).

An arbitrary single-label choice per unoriented curve does not repair Theorem 1.1. For every curve choose a labeling outside \(U\); such a choice always exists because \(U\cap\tau U=\varnothing\). The resulting \(h\)-weighted count is zero for every \(L\), while the claimed limiting integral is positive. This tests a continuous compactly supported function. It does not infer failure of vague convergence from total mass alone.
## Counterevidence and verified repair scope

Section 7.3 (p. 614) explicitly identifies the orientation obstruction and introduces ordered oriented curves and \(\operatorname{Stab}_0\). Remark 7.6 also expressly discusses the larger oriented orbit. These passages provide substantial evidence for the intended repair.

For one nonseparating curve, ordering has no effect and \[s_{\rm or}(X,\vec\gamma,L)=2s_{\rm un}(X,\gamma,L).\] For \(g\ge3\), Definition 7.3 and the scaling degree imply \[m_{\vec\gamma}=\frac{c_g}{6g-6}
       =2\,\frac{c_g}{12g-12}=2c(\gamma).\] The literal unoriented definition of \(s\) in Section 7.6 must therefore be reconciled with the oriented interpretation of Theorem 7.5 and the oriented numerator in Theorem 7.7. This linked convention correction is not counted as a separate Major.
Three definitions remove the demonstrated obstruction:
1. Use \(Z/\langle\tau\rangle\) for the unoriented cut, with limiting probability \(q_*(\eta_{\operatorname{Kon}}/c_g)\).
2. Assign \(\tfrac12(\delta_{G_\alpha}+\delta_{\tau G_\alpha})\) to each unoriented curve in the labeled target. This measure is independent of the initial labeling and has total mass \(s_{\rm un}\).

3. Count oriented curves, use \(\operatorname{Stab}_0\) throughout, and normalize by \(s_{\rm or}\). For a general multicurve use its actual stabilizer index, rather than assuming a universal \(2^k k!\).

The second formulation tests \(h_{\rm av}=(h+h\circ\tau)/2\). For arbitrary labeled \(h\), the oriented horoball pushforward equals twice the unoriented pushforward weighted by \(h_{\rm av}\); the unaveraged formula in Remark 7.9 requires this qualification.

These repairs have been verified for definitions, descent, and exact counting identities. A full reproof of the corrected convergence theorem is not claimed. The Major classification rests on the demonstrated false invariance and its direct use in the core construction and unfolding, independently of the survival of the intended geometric phenomenon.
# The general center-stability bound is false

Problem 2 (Uniform geometric lemma used in the core proof; Major).  Lemma 4.8 (p. 593) asserts that an \(e^\varepsilon\)-bi-Lipschitz map moves the center of three pairwise disjoint, mutually nonseparating geodesics a distance bounded by \(D(r,\varepsilon)\) from the center of the straightened image triple, where \(r\) is the input inradius. This bound fails without a bound on the target inradius.

The proof bounds the distance of \(f(u)\) from all three image geodesics and then asserts the same bound for their center \(u'\). An equidistant center need not minimize the maximum distance to the three lines. The following counterfamily addresses all the stated geometric and mapping hypotheses.
## A triple whose center escapes

Use the hyperboloid model with form \(\langle x,y\rangle=-x_0y_0+x_1y_1+x_2y_2\). Fix \(a=2\), \(S=\sinh a\), and \(h_*=\log S\). For \(h\in(h_*,a]\), take geodesics with spacelike unit normals \[n_1=(S,\cosh a,0),\quad n_2=(S,-\cosh a,0),\quad
 n_3(h)=(\sinh h,0,\cosh h),\] and central halfplanes \(\langle x,n_i\rangle<0\). The normal products are \[\langle n_1,n_2\rangle=-\cosh(2a)<-1,\qquad
 \langle n_j,n_3(h)\rangle=-S\sinh h<-1.\] Indeed the least limiting product magnitude is \((S^2-1)/2>1\). The lines are ultraparallel. Each line’s two companions lie in its central halfplane, so none separates the others.

Their central equidistant point and inradius are \[u_h=(\cosh t_h,0,-\sinh t_h),\qquad
 t_h=\operatorname{artanh}\frac{S-\sinh h}{\cosh h},
 \qquad r_h=h+t_h .\] The fraction belongs to \([0,1)\). Direct substitution gives \[d(u_h,g_1)=d(u_h,g_2)
   =\operatorname{arsinh}(S\cosh t_h)=h+t_h=d(u_h,g_3(h)).\] All central sign conditions hold, so the closed ball of radius \(r_h\) is contained in the central region and tangent to all three lines. In particular, these are genuine finite inscribed circles. Since \(e^{h_*}=S\), one has \(t_h\to\infty\) as \(h\downarrow h_*\).
## Uniformly bi-Lipschitz maps, including arbitrarily small distortion

In the Poincaré disk, a line at distance \(d\) from the origin, in direction \(\beta\), has ideal endpoints \(\beta\pm\theta_d\), where \(\theta_d=\arccos(\tanh d)\). Here \(\theta_{h_*}=2\theta_a\) and \(3\theta_a<\pi/2\).

As \(h_0\downarrow h_*\), both \(m_*,M_*\to1\). Thus for any prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) one can fix \(h_0\) so that all \(F_n\) are \(e^\varepsilon\)-bi-Lipschitz. The radius \(r_{h_0}\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but is fixed independently of \(n\), as the lemma requires. The south-pointing ray is fixed pointwise, so \[F_n(u_{h_0})=u_{h_0},\qquad
 d(F_n(u_{h_0}),u_{h_n})=t_{h_n}-t_{h_0}\longrightarrow\infty.\] Straightening the images gives exactly the specified target triple. This contradicts \(D(r_{h_0},\varepsilon)<\infty\), even for an arbitrarily small prescribed positive \(\varepsilon\).

The saved reviewer program checks the basic family \(h_0=a\), the normal products, angular slope bounds, and equal-radius identity. For \(h_n=h_*+(a-h_*)/n\), its center distances at \(n=10^2,10^4,10^6,10^8\) are approximately \(2.50729,4.81188,7.11449,9.41707\), with bi-Lipschitz bound below two. The divergence and the small-distortion strengthening are analytic arguments, rather than conclusions inferred from this numerical table.
## A verified bound for the actual application

This defect matters because Proposition 4.2 invokes Lemma 4.8 on pp. 594–595 to control corresponding spine vertices and hence edge weights. The principal averaging argument subsequently uses that estimate. The Major classification concerns this false general lemma and the missing hypothesis in the invoked proof; it does not assert a counterexample to Proposition 4.2 itself.

A sufficient replacement is \[d(f(u),u')\le
 2\max(e^\varepsilon r+\delta(\varepsilon),r'),\] where \(r'\) is the target inradius and \(\delta\) is the two-sided Morse bound. To prove it, both points lie in the intersection of the \(C\)-neighborhoods of the target lines, for the displayed maximum \(C\). That intersection has diameter at most \(2C\). If points \(x,y\) in it were more than \(2C\) apart, each of the three lines would meet their disjoint \(C\)-balls and hence cross the perpendicular bisector of \([x,y]\). The middle of three disjoint lines crossing a common transversal separates the other two, contradicting the hypothesis. This proves the required form of Claim 4.9 directly.

For the compact-surface application, fix \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(s_0=e^{-\varepsilon_0}s\). Compactness of the \(s_0\)-thick part in fixed genus gives a finite diameter bound \(R\). Every point is within \(R\) of the nonempty multicurve, so both source and target spine inradii are at most \(R\). Choose a common Morse bound \(\delta_0\) for \(0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0\), and put \[C_0=e^{\varepsilon_0}R+\delta_0,\qquad
 E_0=(e^{\varepsilon_0}+1)R+2C_0 .\] Matched boundary basepoints are within \(E_0\) after applying \(f\). The two endpoint errors and the bi-Lipschitz inequalities give \[e^{-\varepsilon}|e|_X-2E_0
 \le |e|_{X'}\le e^\varepsilon|e|_X+2E_0 .\] Taking \(K_2>\!K_1\) and \(K_2\ge2E_0\) restores the required uniform estimate. Lemma 4.1’s short-arc matching is justified by the separate coarse bounds below. The counterfamily’s target inradii diverge, so it is consistent with this corrected estimate.
# A ratio-one short-arc asymptotic fails

Problem 3 (Quantitative preliminary; Minor).  Lemma 2.5 (p. 583) asserts \[|e|_Y\sim\log(1/\ell_Y(a)),\] and explicitly defines \(\sim\) as ratio tending to one. A symmetric pair of pants gives ratio two.

Equation reference: eq:seam. For \(T>0\), take the hyperbolic pair of pants \(Y_T\) with all three boundary lengths \(2T\). Its spine is a theta graph with every edge weight \(T\), as follows by solving its three perimeter equations. The dual perpendicular seam has length \(a_T\). The right-angled hexagon identity gives \[\cosh a_T
 =\frac{\cosh T+\cosh^2T}{\sinh^2T}
 =\frac{\cosh T}{\cosh T-1},\] or, equivalently, \[
 a_T=2\operatorname{arsinh}\!\left(\frac{1}{2\sinh(T/2)}\right)
     \sim2e^{-T/2}.\] All boundary lengths and spine weights are positive; \(a_T\) is the shortest orthogeodesic in its class. Both limiting regimes in the lemma hold. Nevertheless, \[\log(1/a_T)=T/2-\log2+o(1),\qquad
 \frac{|e|_{Y_T}}{\log(1/a_T)}\longrightarrow2.\] This is an analytic counterexample, supplemented by the independently executed calculations in `checks/geometry/`. No universal corrected ratio is inferred from this one family.
## Downstream dependence and a bounded correction

The demonstrated defect is a false sharp preliminary, but the required coarse downstream bounds can be supplied from the cited dependency. No failure of Proposition 3.1, Lemma 4.1, or Proposition 4.2 is established. The Minor assessment follows this checked dependence, not simply the ease of repair.
# Other checked arguments and resolved technical details

Write \(d=6g-6>0\). The complementary fixed-boundary slice has dimension \(d-2\). Conditional on a correctly defined invariant weight, Proposition 5.4 has twist factor \(\ell\) and symmetry factor \(1/2\): \[\frac12\int_0^L\ell^{d-1}\,d\ell=\frac{L^d}{2d}.\] The \(\sqrt L\) split controls the short part by \(O(L^{d/2})\), and convergence of the normalized integrand controls the long part uniformly in its tail. This yields \(1/(12g-12)\). The paper’s separate total-volume polynomial argument justifies the constant-weight case and the comparison in Corollary 5.8 without extending \(C_c\) convergence to the constant function without justification.

The measure check traces invariance, absolute continuity, and nonescape through the earthquake-flow endgame. Finite approximation of the open cover avoids interchanging an infinite sum with a \(\limsup\). The hypotheses of the necessary horosphere dependency were actually checked for \(n=0,k=1,a_1=1,f=\chi_{[0,1]}\); that source explicitly allows the bounded Borel length cutoff. Its whole proof was not independently reproduced.

The same-facet envelopes used in Section 6 need not be declared continuous to close the averaging argument. On the marked locally finite filling-arc structure, extend the positive edge coordinates by zero to all arc classes, use their sup norm, and take the infimum over mapping classes to define a quotient metric. It is nondegenerate: if the distance between two fixed orbits were zero, sufficiently close representatives would have identical supports, leaving only finitely many permutations of the fixed positive weights. A filling support has finitely many completions, so this metric induces the stated topology and is locally compact. Since the fixed perimeters imply \(\sum_e|e|=1\), the neighborhood \(N_{2\varepsilon,\delta}(x)\) lies in a metric ball of radius \(\rho=e^{2\varepsilon}-1+\delta\). For a nonnegative \(f\in C_c(Z)\), choose a compact neighborhood of its support and a continuous compactly supported cutoff \(\chi\) equal to one on it. For sufficiently small \(\rho\), if \(\omega_f(\rho)\) is a modulus of continuity, the continuous functions \[H^+=(f+\omega_f(\rho)\chi),\qquad
 H^-=(f-\omega_f(\rho))_+\] bound the same-facet supremum and infimum. Their integrals converge to \(\int f\,d\eta_{\operatorname{Kon}}\). Substituting these continuous bounds legitimately applies the stated \(C_c\) results. For fixed \(\varepsilon,\delta\), first let \(L\to\infty\); only then let \(\varepsilon,\delta\to0\), so that each weight is fixed when applying equidistribution. The full support and metric details are retained in the bounded envelope check; no RSC Borel-weight extension is assumed.

Local transcription inconsistencies are recorded without creating additional substantive Problems: the missing \(b\) in the exterior degree in Section 2.7, the reciprocal mass ratio in Lemma 5.9’s proof, and missing \(h\) subscripts in the final Section 5 endgame. Explicit comparison calculations and the correctly stated neighboring results resolve their intended use.

The coordinate formula and canonical-spine interpretation in Mondello’s Definition 2.8 and Theorem 2.14 [Mondello] confirm that these are the full boundary-projection widths, with no factor of two. Gluing them by an orientation-reversing isometry gives a closed oriented genus-three hyperbolic surface \(X\). The glued geodesic \(\gamma\) is essential, simple, has length one, and is nonseparating because cutting it recovers connected \(Y\).

Choose an orientation of the reference curve to define a labeled cut on Teichmüller space. A mapping class \(\phi\in\operatorname{Stab}(\gamma)\setminus\operatorname{Stab}_0(\gamma)\) reverses that orientation and exchanges its sides. Thus \[\operatorname{RSC}_\gamma(\phi X)=\tau\operatorname{RSC}_\gamma(X).\] Choose a relatively compact neighborhood \(U\) of \(G\) in its trivalent cell, with \(U\cap\tau U=\varnothing\), and a nonnegative \(h\in C_c(U)\) equal to one near \(G\). Then \[h(G)=1,\qquad h(\tau G)=0,\qquad
 \int_Zh\,d\eta_{\operatorname{Kon}}>0.\] The last assertion uses the positive volume form on the cell. For cutoff \(L=2\), the length indicators in (5.1) at \(X\) and \(\phi X\) both equal one, whereas the weighted densities equal one and zero. This difference persists on an open Teichmüller neighborhood of positive Weil–Petersson measure, by continuity of length and the labeled spine. Since the Weil–Petersson measure and length cutoff are \(\phi\)-invariant, the weighted measure is not. The claimed full-stabilizer descent fails for an allowed \(h\).

An arbitrary single-label choice per unoriented curve does not repair Theorem 1.1. For every curve choose a labeling outside \(U\); such a choice always exists because \(U\cap\tau U=\varnothing\). The resulting \(h\)-weighted count is zero for every \(L\), while the claimed limiting integral is positive. This tests a continuous compactly supported function. It does not infer failure of vague convergence from total mass alone.
result: Section 7.3 (p. 614) explicitly identifies the orientation obstruction and introduces ordered oriented curves and \(\operatorname{Stab}_0\). Remark 7.6 also expressly discusses the larger oriented orbit. These passages provide substantial evidence for the intended repair.

For one nonseparating curve, ordering has no effect and \[s_{\rm or}(X,\vec\gamma,L)=2s_{\rm un}(X,\gamma,L).\] For \(g\ge3\), Definition 7.3 and the scaling degree imply \[m_{\vec\gamma}=\frac{c_g}{6g-6}
       =2\,\frac{c_g}{12g-12}=2c(\gamma).\] The literal unoriented definition of \(s\) in Section 7.6 must therefore be reconciled with the oriented interpretation of Theorem 7.5 and the oriented numerator in Theorem 7.7. This linked convention correction is not counted as a separate Major.
Three definitions remove the demonstrated obstruction:
1. Use \(Z/\langle\tau\rangle\) for the unoriented cut, with limiting probability \(q_*(\eta_{\operatorname{Kon}}/c_g)\).
2. Assign \(\tfrac12(\delta_{G_\alpha}+\delta_{\tau G_\alpha})\) to each unoriented curve in the labeled target. This measure is independent of the initial labeling and has total mass \(s_{\rm un}\).

3. Count oriented curves, use \(\operatorname{Stab}_0\) throughout, and normalize by \(s_{\rm or}\). For a general multicurve use its actual stabilizer index, rather than assuming a universal \(2^k k!\).

The second formulation tests \(h_{\rm av}=(h+h\circ\tau)/2\). For arbitrary labeled \(h\), the oriented horoball pushforward equals twice the unoriented pushforward weighted by \(h_{\rm av}\); the unaveraged formula in Remark 7.9 requires this qualification.

These repairs have been verified for definitions, descent, and exact counting identities. A full reproof of the corrected convergence theorem is not claimed. The Major classification rests on the demonstrated false invariance and its direct use in the core construction and unfolding, independently of the survival of the intended geometric phenomenon.

Recorded evidence: Counterexample: The exact cube witness has equal perimeters 5920 before normalization and unequal boundary dart counts. An orientation-reversing element of Stab(gamma) swaps its labels, giving h(G)=1 and h(tau G)=0 on an open positive-WP-measure set. The length cutoff is unchanged. Therefore the asserted weighted measure is not invariant.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Section7.3 expressly introduces ordered oriented curves and Stab_0 and acknowledges the labeling obstruction. This supports an intended oriented formulation, not the literal earlier descent.
Limits: Exact definitions, descent/count identities and the counterexample are checked; the whole corrected global convergence theorem is not reproved.

problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (Uniform geometric lemma used in the core proof; Major).
claim: In Section 1.1, curves are unoriented free homotopy classes, and \(s(X,\gamma,L)\) counts their mapping-class orbit up to length \(L\). In Section 2.6, \(\mathcal{MRG}_{h,b}\) has distinctly labeled boundary components. Cutting a nonseparating curve in genus \(g\) gives type \((g-1,2)\). Write \[Z=\mathcal{MRG}_{g-1,2}(1,1),\qquad \tau:Z\longrightarrow Z\] for the involution exchanging its boundary labels. An orientation of the curve distinguishes its sides. The full stabilizer \(\operatorname{Stab}(\gamma)\) contains orientation-reversing-on-the-curve mapping classes, whereas \(\operatorname{Stab}_0(\gamma)\) preserves that orientation.
Recorded check: Lemma4.8 has no bound depending only on the input inradius and bi-Lipschitz constant
analysis: Lemma 4.8 (p. 593) asserts that an \(e^\varepsilon\)-bi-Lipschitz map moves the center of three pairwise disjoint, mutually nonseparating geodesics a distance bounded by \(D(r,\varepsilon)\) from the center of the straightened image triple, where \(r\) is the input inradius. This bound fails without a bound on the target inradius.

The proof bounds the distance of \(f(u)\) from all three image geodesics and then asserts the same bound for their center \(u'\). An equidistant center need not minimize the maximum distance to the three lines. The following counterfamily addresses all the stated geometric and mapping hypotheses.

Use the hyperboloid model with form \(\langle x,y\rangle=-x_0y_0+x_1y_1+x_2y_2\). Fix \(a=2\), \(S=\sinh a\), and \(h_*=\log S\). For \(h\in(h_*,a]\), take geodesics with spacelike unit normals \[n_1=(S,\cosh a,0),\quad n_2=(S,-\cosh a,0),\quad
 n_3(h)=(\sinh h,0,\cosh h),\] and central halfplanes \(\langle x,n_i\rangle<0\). The normal products are \[\langle n_1,n_2\rangle=-\cosh(2a)<-1,\qquad
 \langle n_j,n_3(h)\rangle=-S\sinh h<-1.\] Indeed the least limiting product magnitude is \((S^2-1)/2>1\). The lines are ultraparallel. Each line’s two companions lie in its central halfplane, so none separates the others.

Their central equidistant point and inradius are \[u_h=(\cosh t_h,0,-\sinh t_h),\qquad
 t_h=\operatorname{artanh}\frac{S-\sinh h}{\cosh h},
 \qquad r_h=h+t_h .\] The fraction belongs to \([0,1)\). Direct substitution gives \[d(u_h,g_1)=d(u_h,g_2)
   =\operatorname{arsinh}(S\cosh t_h)=h+t_h=d(u_h,g_3(h)).\] All central sign conditions hold, so the closed ball of radius \(r_h\) is contained in the central region and tangent to all three lines. In particular, these are genuine finite inscribed circles. Since \(e^{h_*}=S\), one has \(t_h\to\infty\) as \(h\downarrow h_*\).

In the Poincaré disk, a line at distance \(d\) from the origin, in direction \(\beta\), has ideal endpoints \(\beta\pm\theta_d\), where \(\theta_d=\arccos(\tanh d)\). Here \(\theta_{h_*}=2\theta_a\) and \(3\theta_a<\pi/2\).

As \(h_0\downarrow h_*\), both \(m_*,M_*\to1\). Thus for any prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) one can fix \(h_0\) so that all \(F_n\) are \(e^\varepsilon\)-bi-Lipschitz. The radius \(r_{h_0}\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but is fixed independently of \(n\), as the lemma requires. The south-pointing ray is fixed pointwise, so \[F_n(u_{h_0})=u_{h_0},\qquad
 d(F_n(u_{h_0}),u_{h_n})=t_{h_n}-t_{h_0}\longrightarrow\infty.\] Straightening the images gives exactly the specified target triple. This contradicts \(D(r_{h_0},\varepsilon)<\infty\), even for an arbitrarily small prescribed positive \(\varepsilon\).

The saved reviewer program checks the basic family \(h_0=a\), the normal products, angular slope bounds, and equal-radius identity. For \(h_n=h_*+(a-h_*)/n\), its center distances at \(n=10^2,10^4,10^6,10^8\) are approximately \(2.50729,4.81188,7.11449,9.41707\), with bi-Lipschitz bound below two. The divergence and the small-distortion strengthening are analytic arguments, rather than conclusions inferred from this numerical table.

This defect matters because Proposition 4.2 invokes Lemma 4.8 on pp. 594–595 to control corresponding spine vertices and hence edge weights. The principal averaging argument subsequently uses that estimate. The Major classification concerns this false general lemma and the missing hypothesis in the invoked proof; it does not assert a counterexample to Proposition 4.2 itself.

A sufficient replacement is \[d(f(u),u')\le
 2\max(e^\varepsilon r+\delta(\varepsilon),r'),\] where \(r'\) is the target inradius and \(\delta\) is the two-sided Morse bound. To prove it, both points lie in the intersection of the \(C\)-neighborhoods of the target lines, for the displayed maximum \(C\). That intersection has diameter at most \(2C\). If points \(x,y\) in it were more than \(2C\) apart, each of the three lines would meet their disjoint \(C\)-balls and hence cross the perpendicular bisector of \([x,y]\). The middle of three disjoint lines crossing a common transversal separates the other two, contradicting the hypothesis. This proves the required form of Claim 4.9 directly.

For the compact-surface application, fix \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(s_0=e^{-\varepsilon_0}s\). Compactness of the \(s_0\)-thick part in fixed genus gives a finite diameter bound \(R\). Every point is within \(R\) of the nonempty multicurve, so both source and target spine inradii are at most \(R\). Choose a common Morse bound \(\delta_0\) for \(0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0\), and put \[C_0=e^{\varepsilon_0}R+\delta_0,\qquad
 E_0=(e^{\varepsilon_0}+1)R+2C_0 .\] Matched boundary basepoints are within \(E_0\) after applying \(f\). The two endpoint errors and the bi-Lipschitz inequalities give \[e^{-\varepsilon}|e|_X-2E_0
 \le |e|_{X'}\le e^\varepsilon|e|_X+2E_0 .\] Taking \(K_2>\!K_1\) and \(K_2\ge2E_0\) restores the required uniform estimate. Lemma 4.1’s short-arc matching is justified by the separate coarse bounds below. The counterfamily’s target inradii diverge, so it is consistent with this corrected estimate.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterexample: Hyperboloid normals n1=(sinh2,cosh2,0), n2=(sinh2,-cosh2,0), n3(h)=(sinh h,0,cosh h), h*=log(sinh2). Centers t(h)=atanh((sinh2-sinh h)/cosh h) escape as h decreases to h*. Choose one source h0 sufficiently close to h*, and angular maps with all slopes in [exp(-epsilon),exp(epsilon)]. They fix the source center on the south ray while the target center escapes.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: In the actual fixed-genus thick-surface application, the target inradius is independently bounded. The counterfamily lacks that additional bound and does not refute Proposition4.2.

Limits: False general lemma and actual missing proof hypothesis are confirmed; no counterexample to the paper's main convergence theorem is claimed. Analytic small-epsilon strengthening is not misrepresented as a new numerical run.

report: Abstract: This report examines the voracious projection and geodesic-language proof in Osajda and Przytycki’s arXiv version 2. An exact example in \((C_2\times C_2)*C_2\) shows that the lexicographic complexity printed in the projection-existence argument need not decrease. Adding its omitted height-zero coordinate gives a complete termination correction. The invalid termination step is a Major defect in the core projection proof; the verified repair does not assert a counterexample to biautomaticity. The review separately traces bounded projection steps, both fellow-traveller estimates, finite-state recognition, and the hypotheses of the building transfer. Conclusions are restricted to the assigned author manuscript; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Voracious projections and biautomaticity:
a version-specific proof audit
# Exact source and scope

The reviewed source is Damian Osajda and Piotr Przytycki, Coxeter groups are biautomatic, arXiv:2206.07804v2, 26 June 2022, ten PDF pages [OP]. Page numbers in this report refer to that exact file. Its SHA256 is

The associated journal article is Inventiones mathematicae 242 (2025), 627–637, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01365-6. The journal PDF was not obtained or compared, so this report does not assert that a preprint-level textual issue persists in the journal.

The official arXiv history inspected during this review lists versions 1 and 2. The publisher records a 2 October 2025 update concerning a missing author affiliation and cites a 2025 alternative treatment. Those metadata do not establish mathematical equivalence of the ten-page preprint and the eleven-page journal article.

All ten source pages were read as extracted text, and the mathematically relevant evidence images were separately inspected as recorded in the verification files. The audit checks specified proof paths and dependencies; it does not independently reconstruct every external theorem or constitute human acceptance.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and the proof chain

Section 2 explicitly uses a finite Coxeter generating set \(S\). Thus the Main Theorem is read under the paper’s finite-rank convention. The group element represented by a word \(v\) has length \(\ell(v)\); prefixes are held constant after the endpoint when testing fellow travelling.

For \(g\in W\), let \(\mathcal W(g)\) be the separating walls closest to \(g\) in the separation order, and define \[P(g)=\{p:p\preceq g,\ 
       \text{no wall in }\mathcal W(g)\text{ separates }p\text{ from }\operatorname{id}\}.\] The order \(p\preceq g\) means that \(p\) is on a geodesic from \(\operatorname{id}\) to \(g\). Theorem 2.1 gives a largest element \(p(g)\) of \(P(g)\). For \(g\ne\operatorname{id}\), it is strictly below \(g\).

The recursive language \(\mathcal V\) attaches any minimal word for \(p(g)^{-1}g\) to an allowed word for \(p(g)\). The strict length decrease makes the recursion well founded. Since \[\ell(g)=\ell(p(g))+\ell(p(g)^{-1}g),\] induction proves that its words are geodesic and that every element has a representative. Finite \(S\) then implies finitely many representatives per element. The empty word is the only allowed representative of \(\operatorname{id}\). No assertion about infinitely generated Coxeter systems is required.
The principal dependency chain is:
1. Theorem 2.1 and the rank-three wall lemma establish the projection.
2. Proposition 4.1 bounds every final block by one constant \(C(W)\).
3. Section 5 establishes synchronous right and left fellow travelling for every pair of allowed representatives, not merely selected words.
4. Section 6 supplies finite-state recognition; finite-to-one geodesicity then permits the stated biautomaticity criterion.
5. Invariance under automorphisms preserving \(S\) is the additional input for the external building-transfer result.
# A missing coordinate in the termination complexity

Problem 1 (Invalid termination step in the projection proof; Major).  The proof of Theorem 2.1 on p. 6 defines the complexity of its embedded path as \((n_1,\ldots,n_{\ell(g)})\), where \(n_j\) counts height-\(j\) vertices. Its prescribed valley replacement need not decrease this tuple when the valley is the identity.
## A fully specified example

Take \[W=\langle s,t,u\mid s^2=t^2=u^2=1,\ st=ts\rangle
   =(C_2\times C_2)*C_2,\qquad g=stu .\] There are no further relations involving \(u\) with \(s\) or \(t\). The Cayley graph consists of squares joined by \(u\)-edges. The only reduced words for \(g\) are \(stu\) and \(tsu\), so \[[\operatorname{id},g]=\{\operatorname{id},s,t,st,stu\}.\] The three walls separating \(g\) from \(\operatorname{id}\) are \(W_s,W_t,stW_u\). The last wall is the midpoint of the final bridge and separates \(g\) from each of the first two. Hence \[\mathcal W(g)=\{stW_u\},\qquad P(g)=\{\operatorname{id},s,t,st\}.\] This verifies the hypotheses on the endpoints and the whole path, rather than presenting an arbitrary sequence of heights.

The geodesic \(\pi=(s,\operatorname{id},t)\) is an allowed path in \(P(g)\). The rank-two residue is the commuting square; the prescribed second path is \(\pi'=(s,st,t)\). Their printed complexities are \[(n_1,n_2,n_3)(\pi)=(2,0,0),\qquad
 (n_1,n_2,n_3)(\pi')=(2,1,0).\] The new tuple is larger in lexicographic order.

The original reviewer program `checks/main/complexity_witness.py` represents the two finite factors by exact normal forms, computes the weak interval, checks separating reflections and the nearest-wall set, and then evaluates the tuples. Its actual output agrees with the displayed calculation. This is not author code and is not a computation over an unverified finite truncation of a general Coxeter group.
## Complete local correction and impact

Use instead \[\kappa(\pi)=(n_0,n_1,\ldots,n_{\ell(g)}).\] For the example this changes \[(1,2,0,0)\longmapsto(0,2,1,0),\] which strictly decreases. In general a valley at height \(j\) removes one height-\(j\) vertex; the internal vertices of the opposite rank-two path have strictly greater height. Counts at smaller heights are unchanged. Erasing a resulting loop cannot increase any coordinate, so the strict decrease survives.

All vertices remain in the finite interval \([\operatorname{id},g]\) and the path is made embedded after each replacement. Thus only finitely many corrected count tuples occur, proving termination. A path without an interior down-then-up step has an up-then-down height profile; its peak lies above both endpoints. The directedness argument then gives the largest point of the finite set \(P(g)\).

This correction retains the geometric content of Lemma 3.2 and the rank-two replacement. The example does not contradict the existence of \(p(g)\); indeed \(p(g)=st\) in the example. The original termination argument is invalid in Theorem 2.1, which supplies the projection used by the core normal-form construction. Its original proof impact is therefore Major. The complete verified repair and survival of the intended conclusion are recorded separately.
# Rank-three reduction and the projection invariant

The reflection subgroup in Lemma 3.2 has rank at most three, not automatically exactly three from the rank bound alone. The disjoint wall supplies an infinite reflection product. An infinite rank-two Coxeter group is infinite dihedral and cannot contain the given finite, noncommuting reflection pair. Thus the rank is exactly three. After choosing an ambient chamber in the specified acute sector, that pair consists of ambient simple generators. The canonical reflection-subgroup construction retains them as simple generators. Dyer’s author-hosted thesis, Theorem 1.8, Remark 3.14 and Corollary 3.16, was checked for precisely these assertions [Dyer].

Write the three finite or ideal triangle angles as \(\alpha=\pi/m,\ \beta=\pi/n,\ \gamma=\pi/k\), with \(m<\infty\), and put \(x=\cos\alpha,\ y=\cos\beta,\ z=\cos\gamma\). For the dihedral walls, the positive roots are \[v_i=a_i r+b_i q,\qquad
 a_i=\frac{\sin((i+1)\alpha)}{\sin\alpha},\quad
 b_i=\frac{\sin(i\alpha)}{\sin\alpha}.\] The generic branch of Figure 1 follows by checking \(y a_i+z b_i\ge1\) for every nonexceptional \(i\). For \(n,k\ge3\), use \(y,z\ge1/2\) and \(a_i+b_i\ge1+2x\ge2\). If \(k=2\), the finite-\(n\) exceptions are precisely those separated out in the paper; when \(n=\infty\), \(y=1\) and \(a_i\ge1\) suffice. In the \(n=3,k=2\) branch, infinitude forces \(m\ge6\), and \(\sin(3\alpha)/\sin\alpha=4x^2-1\ge2\).

For the exceptional cutting walls, the relevant inner products include \[1-2x^2-2y^2\le-1,\qquad
 -8x^4+6x^2-1\le-1.\] The equality cases are parallel or asymptotic walls, and remain disjoint in the required sense. The intermediate wall in Figure 2 has inner product \(-2x(2x^2-1)\); its intersecting subcase is \(m=6\). The bounded check also verifies wall sides and the complete two-, three-, four-, and six-chamber caps, so a disjointness calculation is not being substituted for the separation conclusion. The last reflection identity is \[r(srqrW_s)=srqW_r .\] An original exact polynomial calculation checks the reflection and cap-boundary identities. A separate finite numerical sweep is recorded as supporting evidence only; the all-parameter conclusions use the displayed inequalities and the explicit chamber reconstruction.

For the parabolic application in Theorem 2.1, set \(h=p^{-1}g\) at a valley \(p\). Both adjacent generators \(a,b\) are left descents of \(h\). Every positive root of the standard subsystem on \(\{a,b\}\) is therefore mapped by \(h^{-1}\) to a negative root. This embeds that subsystem’s positive roots in the finite inversion set of \(h\), forcing the subsystem to be finite. Inversion-set inclusion then puts every element of its standard parabolic group below \(h\) in weak order. Translating by \(p\) puts the whole residue on geodesics to \(g\).

Both initial residue walls are inversion walls excluded from \(\mathcal W(g)\); the wall lemma excludes every additional residue wall. Consequently the replacement stays in \(P(g)\). Its initial geodesic also stays there, since \(P(g)\) is an intersection of the relevant wall halfspaces. These facts close the invariant used in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:zero)’s correction. The exact cited Ronan page was not acquired; the preceding specific consequence was independently derived from the root and inversion framework, rather than inferred from an unverified citation.
# Bounded steps and the fellow-traveller constants

The uniformity required is in \(g\) and the separating wall, for one fixed finite Coxeter system. A bounded radius meets only finitely many walls because the Cayley graph has finite degree. The Parallel Wall Theorem consequently bounds \(|\mathcal W(g)|\) by one \(N(W)\). Its cited source, Brink–Howlett Theorem 2.8, states finiteness of elementary roots [BH]. The translation was checked: domination is inclusion of the negative halfspaces, so a non-elementary root has an intervening wall. For a positive root \(\rho\), \[d(\operatorname{id},U_\rho)=\operatorname{dp}(\rho)-\tfrac12.\] Taking the largest depth among the finitely many elementary roots and then left translating gives the uniform parallel-wall constant \(Q\). This accounts for the difference between the literal root statement and the wall formulation.

The geometric bound in Lemma 4.3 uses the finitely many shapes of spherical Coxeter cells. A vertex is a positive distance from each wall section not containing it, so the minimum relevant angle is strictly positive. With the source’s notation, the CAT(0) comparison gives \[c_2\sin\alpha\le d,\qquad
 c\le\operatorname{diam}(\sigma)+d/\sin\alpha .\] Here is the missing geometric detail made explicit. The first exit face of the initial Coxeter cell is a parabolic coset \(wW_U\) not containing the initial vertex. A first letter of its shortest representative starts every reduced face-vertex word, so its simple wall separates the initial vertex from that face. The initial straight segment must cross that wall before exiting. Convexity of fixed-point walls excludes a transverse crossing of any other simple wall; thus the wall is \(W_s\). For a fixed cell, its relevant positive vertex-to-wall distances and bounded diameter give a positive angle bound. Reflecting the geodesic tail in \(W_s\), then applying CAT(0) convexity of distance, yields the displayed inequality. This argument requires no global assertion that the geodesic never touches another wall.

For the at-most-\(N\) iteration, an unpassed wall of \(\mathcal W(g)\) must remain eligible at the current weak-order predecessor. A hypothetical new wall between that predecessor and the original wall would also separate \(g\) from the original wall, contradicting membership in \(\mathcal W(g)\). This supplies the needed preservation condition; previously passed walls stay passed under further weak-order descent. The resulting point is in \(P(g)\), and maximality gives \[d(g,p(g))\le C_0N=:C.\]

The right-fellow-traveller proof interleaves the \(p\)-iterates for adjacent endpoints. In either alternating interval of prefix lengths, both prefixes are within \(C\) of a suitable projection anchor. The second path need not literally contain that anchor: the intervening weak-order segment has exactly the length difference needed for the same bound. The resulting constant is \(2C\).

For left multiplication by \(s\), the case where \(W_s\) is not a nearest wall gives \(p(sg)=sp(g)\), permitting induction on \(\ell(g)\). In the other case the reflection displacement is at most \(2Q\). Chaining the right-fellow-traveller estimate along a generator path of length at most \(C+2Q\), then adding the displacement, gives \[C'=2C(C+2Q)+2Q .\] The padded tail case also has a direct bound \(2C\): the two remaining geodesic tails have lengths at most \(C\) and \(C-1\) when \(\ell(sg)=\ell(g)+1\). These checks retain the distinction between right adjacency and left translation.
# Finite-state recognition and the building implication

The state set is the power set of the finite set of elementary walls near the identity. Condition \(p(w)=\operatorname{id}\), together with Proposition 4.1, bounds the transition block length by \(C\); finite \(S\) therefore makes both the candidate block set and the collections of minimal word labels finite. A finite word-labeled automaton can be expanded into an ordinary letter-labeled automaton by adding finitely many states.

The identity block produces only an empty-word loop at the initial empty state. At a nonempty state, condition (b) rules it out because its walls were defined to have no wall separating them from the identity. Removing empty initial loops makes the last block of every nonempty accepted word nonempty, justifying strict word-length induction. If more than one block gives the same ordered pair of states, the finite label collections can be united on that arrow; no actual collision is asserted without evidence.

Here are the recognition implications with their invariant stated. At a reachable state \(a=p^{-1}\mathcal W(p)\), every old inversion wall is either in \(\mathcal W(p)\) or shielded by one of those walls. Condition (a) therefore gives \(p\preceq pw=g\), and condition (b) hides every old wall from \(g\). Hence \(\mathcal W(g)=p\mathcal W(w)\). In the forward direction, \(p=p(g)\) has these properties. If \(q=p(w)\), then \(pq\in P(g)\), so maximality of \(p(g)\) forces \(q=\operatorname{id}\). In the reverse direction, (a) and (b) give \(p\in P(g)\). Writing \(p(g)=pq\) then gives \(q\in P(w)\), and condition (c) forces \(q=\operatorname{id}\). The final block is therefore exactly the recursive block. The empty-loop observation above makes the induction strict whenever the word is nonempty.

Amrhein’s Theorem 6 requires a regular onto language whose evaluation map has finite fibers over a finite inverse-closed generating alphabet [Amrhein]. All these hypotheses hold here. To connect the paper’s separate conditions (ii) and (iii) to that criterion, insert a representative of \(a\bar v\) when comparing \(avb\) with another representative of the same element. A left prefix shifts time by one step, and a final generator costs one further step; a finite bound follows from the two established fellow-traveller constants. If both added letters are empty, compare both representatives with one of \(\bar v s\), using the right estimate twice. The empty generating-set case is trivial. Thus neither equal endpoints nor padded tails leave a gap.

An automorphism of \(W\) preserving \(S\) preserves the wall data and weak order. Uniqueness gives equivariance of \(p(g)\); allowing all minimal final-block words makes \(\mathcal V\) invariant. This algebraic invariance supplies the extra hypothesis of Świątkowski’s Theorem 6.7 [Swi]. Theorem 6.1 assumes a simplicial building action with finite panel residues, finitely many chamber orbits, and finite chamber stabilizers. Its remark identifies these conditions with proper discontinuity and cocompactness on the Davis realization. Theorem 6.7 removes type preservation when the geodesic (bi)automatic language is invariant under the induced subgroup of \(\operatorname{Sym}(W,S)\). The language here is invariant under the whole group, so the stated corollary follows under that action convention. Both numbered statements and the intervening remark were actually read in the author-uploaded journal HTML; an official earlier DVI copy was also retained. No journal PDF image inspection is claimed for this dependency.

The explicit complexity error is confirmed in the assigned arXiv v2, with a complete local correction. No conclusion about its presence in the journal text follows. The three bounded checks and their counterevidence have been integrated. One Major defect in the original termination argument is confirmed, with a complete verified repair. claim: Section 2 explicitly uses a finite Coxeter generating set \(S\). Thus the Main Theorem is read under the paper’s finite-rank convention. The group element represented by a word \(v\) has length \(\ell(v)\); prefixes are held constant after the endpoint when testing fellow travelling.

For \(g\in W\), let \(\mathcal W(g)\) be the separating walls closest to \(g\) in the separation order, and define \[P(g)=\{p:p\preceq g,\ 
       \text{no wall in }\mathcal W(g)\text{ separates }p\text{ from }\operatorname{id}\}.\] The order \(p\preceq g\) means that \(p\) is on a geodesic from \(\operatorname{id}\) to \(g\). Theorem 2.1 gives a largest element \(p(g)\) of \(P(g)\). For \(g\ne\operatorname{id}\), it is strictly below \(g\).

The recursive language \(\mathcal V\) attaches any minimal word for \(p(g)^{-1}g\) to an allowed word for \(p(g)\). The strict length decrease makes the recursion well founded. Since \[\ell(g)=\ell(p(g))+\ell(p(g)^{-1}g),\] induction proves that its words are geodesic and that every element has a representative. Finite \(S\) then implies finitely many representatives per element. The empty word is the only allowed representative of \(\operatorname{id}\). No assertion about infinitely generated Coxeter systems is required.

analysis: The proof of Theorem 2.1 on p. 6 defines the complexity of its embedded path as \((n_1,\ldots,n_{\ell(g)})\), where \(n_j\) counts height-\(j\) vertices. Its prescribed valley replacement need not decrease this tuple when the valley is the identity.

Take \[W=\langle s,t,u\mid s^2=t^2=u^2=1,\ st=ts\rangle
   =(C_2\times C_2)*C_2,\qquad g=stu .\] There are no further relations involving \(u\) with \(s\) or \(t\). The Cayley graph consists of squares joined by \(u\)-edges. The only reduced words for \(g\) are \(stu\) and \(tsu\), so \[[\operatorname{id},g]=\{\operatorname{id},s,t,st,stu\}.\] The three walls separating \(g\) from \(\operatorname{id}\) are \(W_s,W_t,stW_u\). The last wall is the midpoint of the final bridge and separates \(g\) from each of the first two. Hence \[\mathcal W(g)=\{stW_u\},\qquad P(g)=\{\operatorname{id},s,t,st\}.\] This verifies the hypotheses on the endpoints and the whole path, rather than presenting an arbitrary sequence of heights.

The geodesic \(\pi=(s,\operatorname{id},t)\) is an allowed path in \(P(g)\). The rank-two residue is the commuting square; the prescribed second path is \(\pi'=(s,st,t)\). Their printed complexities are \[(n_1,n_2,n_3)(\pi)=(2,0,0),\qquad
 (n_1,n_2,n_3)(\pi')=(2,1,0).\] The new tuple is larger in lexicographic order.

The original reviewer program `checks/main/complexity_witness.py` represents the two finite factors by exact normal forms, computes the weak interval, checks separating reflections and the nearest-wall set, and then evaluates the tuples. Its actual output agrees with the displayed calculation. This is not author code and is not a computation over an unverified finite truncation of a general Coxeter group.

Use instead \[\kappa(\pi)=(n_0,n_1,\ldots,n_{\ell(g)}).\] For the example this changes \[(1,2,0,0)\longmapsto(0,2,1,0),\] which strictly decreases. In general a valley at height \(j\) removes one height-\(j\) vertex; the internal vertices of the opposite rank-two path have strictly greater height. Counts at smaller heights are unchanged. Erasing a resulting loop cannot increase any coordinate, so the strict decrease survives.

All vertices remain in the finite interval \([\operatorname{id},g]\) and the path is made embedded after each replacement. Thus only finitely many corrected count tuples occur, proving termination. A path without an interior down-then-up step has an up-then-down height profile; its peak lies above both endpoints. The directedness argument then gives the largest point of the finite set \(P(g)\).

This correction retains the geometric content of Lemma 3.2 and the rank-two replacement. The example does not contradict the existence of \(p(g)\); indeed \(p(g)=st\) in the example. The original termination argument is invalid in Theorem 2.1, which supplies the projection used by the core normal-form construction. Its original proof impact is therefore Major. The complete verified repair and survival of the intended conclusion are recorded separately.

Title: Strict comparison and quantitative group arguments:
a version-specific proof audit

Review status. The bounded proof checks and primary-dependency checks described below are complete. Scientific decision is pending; human reviews are empty. The accompanying verification files record the independent focused checks and their completion status.
# Exact source, conventions and scope

The reviewed paper is T. Amrutam, D. Gao, S. Kunnawalkam Elayavalli and G. Patchell, Strict comparison in reduced group \(C^*\)-algebras, Inventiones mathematicae 242 (2025), 639–657, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01366-5 [main]. It is the assigned nineteen-page publisher PDF. Its SHA256 is

Printed page numbers are used below; PDF page number is printed number minus \(638\). The full extracted text and all reference pages were read, with selected mathematical pages separately inspected as images.

The official arXiv page currently lists v4, dated 27 August 2025, and the publisher records publication on 18 September 2025. The preprint was not substituted for the assigned PDF. A bounded metadata lookup found no entry under the searched correction/history headings; this is not a claim of an exhaustive correction search.

Theorem A concerns finite integers \(n\ge2\). Theorem B assumes finite generation, acylindrical hyperbolicity, trivial finite radical and rapid decay. Exactness is an additional explicit hypothesis for Theorem C and the trace-based applications; it is not inferred merely from rapid decay.

In Definition 3.1, group selflessness requires retractions \(\phi_n:G*\langle a\rangle\to G\), injective on the radius-\(n\) ball, whose image there lies in a ball of radius \(f(n)\), with \[\liminf_{n\to\infty} f(n)^{1/n}=1.\] The liminf quantifier is weaker than a subexponential upper bound at every sufficiently large integer. It matters in Problem Problem 3 (#prob:liminf).

The proof chain separates into a group-theoretic construction, a rapid-decay norm estimate, a diagonal map into a norm ultrapower, and Robert’s selflessness criterion. Theorem B obtains its group-theoretic input from Theorem 3.3 and Appendix A. For free groups there is also the elementary free-product argument of Proposition 3.2. This separation is essential when evaluating the impact of the following findings.
# A non-quasi-geodesic path in the quantitative appendix

Problem 1 (Major: invalid input to the quantitative proof).  On p. 652 the orbit polygon \[\gamma=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}[g^ko,g^{k+1}o]\] is asserted to be a \((\lambda,0)\)-quasi-axis for \(\lambda=d(go,o)/\tau(g)\), in the explicit sense that every subpath has length at most \(\lambda\) times its endpoint distance. This fails even for the conjugate elements used in Theorem 3.3, acting on a free-group Cayley tree.
## An exact witness satisfying the hypotheses

Let \(G=F(a,b)\), let \(X\) be its unit-edge Cayley tree, and take \(o=\operatorname{id}\). This action is free, acylindrical and \(0\)-hyperbolic. For every \(N\ge1\), put \[g_N=b^Na b^{-N}.\] Reduced words give \[|g_N|=2N+1,\qquad
 |g_N^k|=2N+k\quad(k\ge1),\qquad
 \tau(g_N)=1.\] Thus the proposed constant is \(\lambda=2N+1\), and the stable length is fixed throughout the family.

At the junction of the geodesics \([\operatorname{id},g_N]\) and \([g_N,g_N^2]\), the polygon contains the subpath \[g_Nb\ \longrightarrow\ g_N\ \longrightarrow\ g_Nb .\] Its length is \(2\), while its endpoint distance is \(0\). No finite multiplicative constant can satisfy the asserted inequality. For \(N=1\), this is the concrete path \[ba\ \longrightarrow\ bab^{-1}\ \longrightarrow\ ba .\] The original reviewer program `orbit_path_counterexample.py` carries out exact reduced-word multiplication and checks this example for several \(N\). The normal-form identity above proves it for all \(N\); the conclusion is not based on finite numerical testing.

The failure concerns the actual concatenated path, not its orbit vertices. For orbit vertices the printed estimate is valid: \[|k-\ell|\,d(g_No,o)
       \le \lambda\,d(g_N^ko,g_N^\ell o).\] It does not control subpaths that cross a junction and backtrack. As a set, the union also has hanging branches, rather than being an embedded axis, so treating the displayed union as an unparametrized set does not establish the claimed path property.
## Why this matters to the proof

The appendix uses this continuous \((\lambda,0)\) control to invoke the quantitative Morse lemma, pass to contracting families and apply Yang’s admissible-path result. On p. 654 it explicitly sets the additive quasi-geodesic constant to zero. The precise Yang definitions require control of rectifiable subpaths; an inequality only at orbit vertices is insufficient.

This is a substantive gap in the stated route to Theorem 3.3 and hence the given proof of Theorem B. The example does not contradict the nontrivial-product conclusion of Theorem A.4, nor the strict-comparison statement of Theorem B. It invalidates a claimed input actually used by their proof.

A repair could replace the orbit polygons by suitable genuine quasi-axes or by geodesic long pieces, and account for the connecting segments and additive constants. Such a replacement must prove the needed projection, contraction, overlap and length bounds uniformly in the varying conjugate element. An unquantified assertion that the paths stay near an axis does not establish the degree-six threshold. No complete replacement proof of that threshold is claimed here.
## A separate boundary in the axis setup

The appendix also says that the infimum displacement is attained. This need not hold under its stated hypotheses. Here is an explicit geodesic hyperbolic example. Let \(T\) be the unit-edge Cayley tree of \(F(a,b)\), let \(S\) be the bilateral shift of real \(\ell^2(\mathbb Z)\), and put \[C=\{v\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z):v_k\ge0,\ 0<\|v\|<1\},\qquad
 X=T\times C\] with the Euclidean product metric. The set \(C\) is convex: a convex combination of nonzero nonnegative vectors is nonzero, and its norm is less than \(1\). It has diameter at most \(2\). Consequently \(X\) is geodesic and its triangles are \(2\)-thin: the tree coordinate of each point on one side occurs on another side, and the two fibre coordinates are at distance at most \(2\).

Let \(\chi(a)=1,\chi(b)=0\), and let \(h(t,v)=(ht,S^{\chi(h)}v)\). This is an isometric action. For each displacement bound \(r\), the number of group elements moving any given tree point by at most \(r\) is uniformly bounded by a finite word ball (replace the point by a nearest vertex). The same bound holds in \(X\), so this action is acylindrical. For \(g=a\), no nonzero square-summable vector is fixed by \(S\); hence \[d_X((t,v),a(t,v))
 =\sqrt{d_T(t,at)^2+\|Sv-v\|^2}>1.\] On the tree axis, taking \(v=\epsilon e_0\) and \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) shows that \([a]=1\), but no point realizes this infimum. Also \(\tau(a)=1\), since the fibre displacement is bounded and the tree displacement of \(a^m\) grows as \(m\). The example is not complete or proper; neither condition is required by the source assertion. Scaling tree edges to any \(M>200\) keeps the hyperbolicity bound \(2\) and gives \([a]=\tau(a)=M\), still without attainment.

Delzant’s checked Proposition 5 assumes both a sufficiently large minimal displacement and a point realizing that displacement; it does not prove universal attainment [Delzant]. A suitable graph action or a controlled near-minimizing axis could avoid this boundary in the actual group application. This example is therefore a defect in the general setup, not a counterexample to Theorem B.
## The degree ledger and relevant counterevidence

There is a second bookkeeping issue within the same argument. The p. 653 bound is stated as \(T=O(\lambda^3)\), giving \(\nu(U)=2U+O(\lambda^3)\). With the other displayed bounds, direct substitution into p. 654 yields \[B=O(|g|^3),\quad R=O(|g|^3),\quad
 \Lambda=O(|g|^4),\quad D=O(|g|^7),\quad
 \lambda D=O(|g|^8),\] rather than the printed degrees \(2,2,3,5,6\). This calculation identifies what follows from the bounds written there; it does not show that an improved degree-six argument is impossible.

In fact, there is relevant counterevidence to treating this degree issue as a separate theorem counterexample. For the actual conjugate family, the minimal displacement \([g_N]\) is constant. More generally, the checked hyperbolic-isometry comparison \(\lvert\tau(g)-[g]\rvert\le16\delta\) bounds \([g]\) when \(\tau(g)\) is fixed. Thus the earlier factor \(Q_2(\lambda)(1+[g])\) can have degree two rather than three. This can repair that part of the degree ledger, conditional on a valid quasi-axis and the required quantitative projection transfer. It does not remove the backtracking obstruction in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:axis).

For a short connecting geodesic, the checked projection estimate is bounded by its length plus \(2\mu+\epsilon\), not just its length. With the improved \(T=O(\lambda^2)\), these terms still permit the conditional degree-six ledger. The passage from contraction to quasiconvexity also needs an excursion argument, rather than merely showing that one point is close: each component outside a prescribed neighbourhood has endpoints controlled by contraction, giving \(\sigma(U)=2\max\{U,\mu\}+\epsilon/2\), up to harmless slack. The exponent threshold must exceed \((\lambda D+c)/\tau(g)\), with an integer ceiling and a strict margin.

The primary-source checks are material here. Yang’s rectifiable-path definitions, Proposition 3.3 and Corollary 3.4 were read in arXiv:1301.5623v2 [Yang]; the corollary literally states \((\Lambda,0)\), with \(\Lambda=\lambda(6R+1)+3c\). It supplies no exception for backtracking between orbit vertices. Wan–Yang’s Definitions 2.1–2.2 and Lemmas 2.8, 2.23 were checked in v3 [WanYang]. Bestvina–Fujiwara’s contraction statements concern geodesic segments and a valid transfer to quasi-geodesics [BF]. The corrected Gouëzel–Shchur Morse theorem retains the quadratic bound \(92\lambda^2(C+\delta)\) [GS]; the historical gap in an earlier proof is not evidence that the target’s Lemma A.1 is false. None of these citations eliminates the explicit loop above.
## The group-theoretic chain and the conditional repair

The actual DGO and Osin statements were checked, rather than inferring their hypotheses from titles [DGO, Osin]. Osin’s Theorem 1.2 and DGO’s Theorem 6.14 supply a hyperbolically embedded \(F_2\times K(G)\); the finite radical here is trivial. DGO’s Theorem 4.31 and Proposition 4.35 give undistortion and transitivity. Free factors are hyperbolically embedded by the relative Cayley graph normal form. Osin’s Theorem 1.4 supplies one fixed acylindrical action in which the chosen element is loxodromic. DGO’s WPD and elementary-subgroup statements, together with almost malnormality, identify \(E(g_n)=\langle g_n\rangle\) for the primitive conjugates \(g_n=b^nab^{-n}\). Conjugacy preserves their stable length. These checks close the group-theoretic prerequisites, but do not replace the missing quantitative path argument.

There is also a complete local correction to the normal-form use in Theorem 3.3, conditional on a valid uniform polynomial big-powers threshold \(P\). Fix undistortion constants \(C,D\ge1\) so that \(|h|_{\{a,b\}}\le C|h|_G\) and \(|h|_G\le D|h|_{\{a,b\}}\) on the free subgroup. For an integer \(N\ge1\), take \[n_N=\left\lceil\max\{2CN^2,C^2D/2\}\right\rceil,\qquad
 q_N=\left\lceil P_+\bigl(D(2n_N+1)\bigr)\right\rceil+1 ,\] where \(P_+\) is an increasing nonnegative polynomial envelope for the conditional threshold. A nonzero power of \(g_{n_N}\) has free-group length \(2n_N+|k|\), hence \(G\)-length greater than \(4N^2\). Therefore no nontrivial connector of length at most \(2N\) lies in \(E(g_{n_N})\).

Map the new generator to \(g_{n_N}^{q_N}\). To prove injectivity on the radius-\(N\) ball, apply the kernel argument to words of length at most \(2N\) and cyclically reduce them. A pure \(G\)-word stays nontrivial; a pure power of the new generator maps to a nonzero loxodromic power. In a mixed cyclically reduced word all connecting \(G\)-syllables and all generator exponents are nonzero, so the conditional big-powers assertion applies. Allowing arbitrary identity connectors before cyclic reduction would be false, as the two powers \(g^k,g^{-k}\) show. This correction proves the needed normal-form step, including small \(N\) and integer thresholds. If \(P\) has degree \(d\), the image-ball radius is \(O(N^{2d+3})\): degrees \(6\) and \(8\) give \(15\) and \(19\), respectively, both sufficient for the subexponential requirement. The degree discrepancy by itself is therefore not an additional Major finding.
# Proper powers invalidate the scope of Theorem 3.10

Problem 2 (Minor: a stated theorem fails for proper powers).  Theorem 3.10 on p. 651 allows any nonidentity \(a\in F_n\) in \[G=F_n*_{\langle a\rangle}(\langle a\rangle\times\mathbb Z)\] and concludes that \(G\) is existentially \(C^*\)-residually-\(F_n\). For a proper power this is not, in general, an extension over the maximal centralizer, and the displayed conclusion is false.
## A norm obstruction, not only a noninjective group map

Take \(F_2=\langle x,y\rangle\) and \(a=x^2\). With \(t\) the new commuting generator, the displayed group is \[G=\langle x,y,t\mid[x^2,t]=1\rangle
   =K*\langle y\rangle,\qquad
 K=\langle x,t\mid[x^2,t]=1\rangle.\] Let \(w=[x,t]=xtx^{-1}t^{-1}\). The amalgamated-product normal form in \[K=\langle x\rangle*_{\langle x^2\rangle}
             (\langle x^2\rangle\times\langle t\rangle)\] shows that every positive power of \(w\) remains reduced: the \(x^{\pm1}\) and \(t^{\pm1}\) syllables lie outside the amalgam. Consequently \(w\) has infinite order. Normal forms in \(K*\langle y\rangle\) then show that \[u=w,\qquad v=ywy^{-1}\] freely generate a rank-two free subgroup.

Any homomorphism \(\phi:G\to F_2\) fixing the original \(F_2\) satisfies \[\phi(t)\in C_{F_2}(x^2)=\langle x\rangle.\] It therefore sends both \(u\) and \(v\) to the identity. Set \[z=\tfrac14(u+u^{-1}+v+v^{-1})\in\mathbb CG.\] These are four distinct basis elements, so \(\|z\|_1=1\), whereas \[\|\lambda_{F_2}(\phi(z))\|=1.\] The subgroup inclusion preserves reduced norms. On its four-regular Cayley tree, the adjacency operator has norm at most \(2\sqrt3\), giving \[\|\lambda_G(z)\|\le\frac{\sqrt3}{2}<1 .\] For completeness, this upper bound follows from the weighted Schur test with positive weight \(3^{-d(o,\cdot)/2}\). At a nonroot vertex the weighted row sum is \(2\sqrt3\); at the root it is \(4/\sqrt3\le2\sqrt3\). Thus no exact spectral-radius formula is needed.

Choose any \(0<\varepsilon<1-\sqrt3/2\) in Definition 3.4 and the fixed support of \(z\). Every homomorphism fixing \(F_2\) violates the required norm inequality. This directly disproves the conclusion as stated, even though that definition does not require the group homomorphism to be injective.
## Correct scope and unaffected applications

The actually checked published Louder–Magee Definition 3.1 requires extension over a maximal abelian subgroup; its p. 11 construction retains this hypothesis [Louder]. Proposition 1.8 and Lemma 3.4 support the valid construction. The published norm-lifting statement is Theorem 1.7, whereas the target cites Theorem 1.6 for this role. A reference-number correction alone does not fix the missing maximality assumption. Restricting \(a\) to a generator of its maximal cyclic centralizer removes the specific obstruction above. The proper-power case cannot be retained without changing the displayed group or the claimed conclusion.

The actual subsequent application takes \(a=y\), which is primitive. It does not use the false proper-power generality. Nor is its generator \(txt\), as printed, an erroneous missing inverse. To check this, in \[\langle x\rangle*(\langle y\rangle\times\langle t\rangle)\] take the index-two kernel of the parity of the exponent of \(t\). It has free-product form \[\langle x\rangle*\langle u=txt^{-1}\rangle*
          \langle y,v=t^2\mid[y,v]=1\rangle .\] The substitution \(u\mapsto uv\), fixing \(x,y,v\), is a free-product automorphism. It carries the free subgroup \(\langle x,y,u\rangle\) to \(\langle x,y,txt\rangle\), so the latter is indeed \(F_3\).

The defect is a false proper-power extension of the cited auxiliary theorem. The actual primitive application does not use this additional generality, and no core conclusion has been shown to depend on the failing proper-power case. Its demonstrated impact is therefore Minor. This classification concerns the dependency scope, not the shortness of a possible repair.
# The rapid-decay selection and the trivial-group boundary

Problem 3 (Major: liminf does not justify sampling a progression).  In Theorem 3.5, p. 649, the condition \(\liminf f(n)^{1/n}=1\) is used to choose \(m\) with \(P(f(2mR))^{1/(2m)}<1+\varepsilon/3\). A liminf over all integers does not ensure this on the progression \(2mR\).

This is not merely a concern about an arbitrary irrelevant function. For the valid free-product construction on \(F_2=\mathbb Z*\mathbb Z\), one can take the image-radius bound \(q(n)=n(4n+3)\). Keeping the same retractions, enlarge this bound to \[f(n)=
 \begin{cases}
 q(n),&n\ \text{odd},\\
 2^nq(n),&n\ \text{even}.
 \end{cases}\] It still witnesses Definition 3.1. For integer \(R\ge1\), every \(2mR\) is even. Enlarge any valid rapid-decay polynomial, if necessary, so that \(P(r)\ge r\). Then \[P(f(2mR))^{1/(2m)}\ge 2^R ,\] and the printed selection need not be possible.

There is a complete correction preserving the stated definition. Choose integers \(n_j\to\infty\) such that \(\log f(n_j)/n_j\to0\), choose an integer \(R\ge1\) containing the given finite support, and set \[m_j=\left\lfloor\frac{n_j}{2R}\right\rfloor .\] Use \(\phi_{n_j}\), not \(\phi_{2m_jR}\). For large \(j\), \(m_j\ge1\), and \[\operatorname{supp}(a_i^*a_i)^{m_j}\subset B(2m_jR)\subset B(n_j).\] Injectivity still gives exact equality of the relevant \(\ell^2\) norms. Polynomial growth and \(2m_j\sim n_j/R\) give \[\frac{\log P(f(n_j))}{2m_j}\longrightarrow0.\] One sufficiently large \(j\) works for every point of the finite net. The two remaining \(\varepsilon/3\) errors are controlled by \(\ell^1\)-contractivity of the group-ring maps and \(\|\lambda(a)\|\le\|a\|_1\). This proves the required conclusion under the original hypotheses. The invalid selection is used in Theorem 3.5, which explicitly feeds the proof of Theorem B on p. 651. Its original proof impact is therefore Major. The complete subsequence repair establishes the stated conclusion under unchanged hypotheses; this repair status is recorded separately.
Problem 4 (Minor: the trivial group in Corollary 3.8).  Corollary 3.8 does not exclude \(G=\{\operatorname{id}\}\), although its selflessness assertion needs that exclusion.

For this group, \(G*\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z\). The unique retraction is evaluation at \(1\) on \(C_r^*(\mathbb Z)=C(\mathbb T)\), which is contractive. It satisfies Definition 3.4 exactly. But \(C_r^*(G)=\mathbb C\) is excluded by Robert’s selflessness definition; equivalently, there is no injective map \(C(\mathbb T)\to\mathbb C^{\mathcal U}=\mathbb C\). The strict-comparison conclusion for \(\mathbb C\) remains true. Adding \(G\ne\{\operatorname{id}\}\) supplies the needed free-product simplicity in the argument. Every group-selfless application in this paper is infinite and already satisfies the correction.
# Norm-ultrapower and application checks

A countable exhaustion of \(\Gamma\), together with tolerances tending to zero, supplies the sequence in Proposition 3.7. The uniform finite-support inequality and \(\ell^1\)-contractivity extend it to all group-ring elements. Coordinatewise multiplication and involution then give a bounded unital star homomorphism on the reduced completion, fixing the diagonal copy of \(C_r^*(G)\). This is an argument about the norm ultrapower, not only trace moments. Injectivity is supplied separately by simplicity of the nontrivial reduced free product. For \(G\ne\{1\}\), the free product \(G*\mathbb Z\) is \(C^*\)-simple and has a unique trace by the checked de la Harpe–Préaux criterion [dHP]. The map just constructed is unital and nonzero, so simplicity makes it injective. Composing it with the ultrapower trace gives a tracial state on \(C_r^*(G*\mathbb Z)\); uniqueness identifies that state with the canonical trace. Thus the embedding is state preserving, as required by Robert’s criterion [Robert]. The argument does not assert that every star homomorphism, including the zero map, is injective.

For Proposition 3.2, the middle conjugated syllables remain nontrivial \(H\)-syllables, or start and end with such syllables, because the chosen \(h_n\) is longer than the intervening word. At the two endpoints only the inward-facing syllable is needed. The printed assertion that every parenthesized term begins and ends in \(H\) is unnecessarily strong at those endpoints; the normal-form noncancellation argument still works with the appropriate one-sided assertion.

Theorem C requires the hypotheses of Robert’s embedding result: a unital simple nonelementary algebra, stable rank one, a unique normalized quasitrace, and strict comparison. Gerasimova–Osin’s Theorem 1.1 gives stable rank one for a countable acylindrically hyperbolic group with trivial finite radical, without an RD or exactness assumption [GO]. Simplicity and infinitude give nonelementarity; BKKO’s published Theorem 1.3 gives the unique trace [BKKO]. Haagerup’s Theorem 5.11 converts quasitraces to traces under the explicit exactness hypothesis [Haagerup]. These match Robert’s Proposition 6.3.1, actually read in arXiv:1007.1964v3, including the unique normalized 2-quasitrace condition [Robert2012]. The target need not be nuclear. The conclusion is existence of a unital embedding of \(\mathcal Z\), unique up to pointwise approximate unitary equivalence; it is not actual unitary conjugacy or Jiang–Su absorption. For groups covered only through Theorem B, the application remains dependent on a correct proof of its group-theoretic input.
## An unambiguous zero convention for the Cuntz semigroup

The p. 644 discussion first identifies the strictly positive lower-semicontinuous affine functions with \((0,\infty]\), but later displays \(V(A)\sqcup[0,\infty]\) and \(\mathbb N\sqcup[0,\infty]\). If \(V(A)\) includes its usual zero and the union is literally disjoint, the latter notation would add another zero-rank element. Faithfulness rules out a nonzero positive class with zero dimension: after rescaling a nonzero positive element to a contraction, its dimension dominates its positive trace.

There is relevant counterevidence to declaring a new substantive theorem failure from this notation alone: Robert’s cited source uses the same closed-endpoint shorthand, and the placement or identification of the common zero can be a convention. The appropriate correction is to specify the model and its operations explicitly. With zero in the projection summand, the free-group model is \[\operatorname{Cu}(C_r^*(F_2))=\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\sqcup(0,\infty].\] Writing \(n\) for a compact projection class and \(r\) for a positive soft class, addition within each part is usual and \(n+r\) is the soft class of numerical value \(n+r\). The mixed order is \[n\le r \iff n<r,\qquad
      r\le n \iff r\le n\] where the right-hand comparisons are numerical. Thus the integer class \(n\) and the soft class of value \(n>0\) are distinct. The only zero is the compact class \(0\). This is a minor notation clarification, not an additional counterexample to the intended classification.
## Rank realization, comparison and projection classes

The checked Brown–Toms Theorem 2.6 assumes exactness and surjectivity of the finite-matrix rank map \(W(A)_+\to\mathrm{LAff}_b(T(A))^{++}\) [BrownToms]. It is not legitimate to drop that premise or replace it silently with a statement about \(\operatorname{Cu}(A)\). For the present exact monotracial application the following direct stabilized argument supplies the needed conclusion instead.

Antoine–Perera–Thiel–Vilalta’s Theorem 5.13 and Example 5.14 give pureness, hence almost divisibility, for the exact infinite \(C^*\)-simple groups under strict comparison [Pure]. Put \(u=[1]\). Almost divisibility gives \(kx_k\le u\le(k+1)x_k\), so \[\frac1{k+1}\le d_\tau(x_k)\le\frac1k .\] Integer multiples of these positive numbers meet any prescribed positive interval once \(k\) is sufficiently large. Given \(t>0\), choose classes \(y_j\) whose dimensions increase strictly to \(t\). Strict comparison makes \(y_j\le y_{j+1}\). Then \(y_t=\sup_jy_j\) has dimension \(t\) and is not compact: compactness would put it below some \(y_j\), contradicting \(d_\tau(y_j)<t\). The class \(\sup_jj[1]\) supplies infinity.

Brown–Toms Lemma 2.2 has no rank-surjectivity premise. It approximates each nonprojection class by increasing finite-matrix classes of strictly increasing dimensions; Proposition 2.5 and strict comparison then identify soft classes with the same dimension. For the mixed order, compactness of \(n[1]\) and this approximation give \(n[1]\le y_t\) only if \(n<t\). Conversely \(n<t\) gives strict comparison. If \(t\le n\), all the strictly smaller-rank approximants lie below \(n[1]\), hence \(y_t\le n[1]\); the converse follows from the dimension functional. A sum with a soft term cannot be compact: otherwise compactness and the same approximants would force its dimension below its own value. This proves the addition and mixed-order rules stated above.

Finally, Pimsner–Voiculescu’s published Corollary 3.2, inspected on the scanned printed p. 152, gives \(K_0(C_r^*(F_n))=\mathbb Z[1]\) [PV]. Stable rank one gives projection cancellation, so \(V(A)\) injects into \(K_0(A)\). Faithfulness of the normalized trace forces nonzero projection coordinates to be positive integers; direct sums of units realize every nonnegative integer. Thus the compact summand is precisely \(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). Absence of nontrivial projections in \(A\) alone would not establish this stabilized conclusion.

The broader introductory formula for arbitrary nonexact algebras and quasitrace simplexes is not independently proved here. The completed derivation concerns the exact monotracial applications, and it does not conflate stabilized rank surjectivity with the finite-matrix premise of the cited theorem.
# Disposition and verification limits

The orbit-path assertion and the proper-power generalization have explicit obstructions under their literal hypotheses. The rapid-decay subsequence selection and the trivial-group boundary have complete local corrections. None is evidence that every main theorem is false. In particular the free-product route to Theorem A is separately checked, with the repaired rapid-decay selection, and the primitive centralizer application survives the proper-power counterexample.

The bounded checks, counterevidence and citation-hypothesis mapping are complete within the stated scope. External classification, contraction and group-embedding theorems are used at their checked statements; their entire original proofs are not claimed to have been independently reproduced. Scientific decision remains pending, human reviews are empty, and no author adoption is claimed. The accompanying verification files record the independent focused checks. The lack of author code is not a defect; only original reviewer calculations were executed.

The main reviewer integrates the English report, compiles its exact current TeX and inspects every final report page. The native helpers have bounded geometric, norm-theoretic and application assignments.
