report: Abstract: This report examines arXiv:2311.15765v2, dated 5 December 2023. A principal-order Hilbert-conjugation error changes the degenerate Fourier block; correcting it reveals a periodic translation mode for every orbit parameter. The displayed approximate solution also retains a fourth-order residual, and the Nash–Moser induction does not justify its required uniform high norm. Each issue is tied to the relevant existence-proof input, with explicit calculations and counterevidence. Positive checks of point dynamics, geometric constraints and measure estimates are recorded separately. The conclusions concern this exact author version and do not assert that the nonlinear existence theorem is false or that the 2025 journal version contains the same defects.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Planar Euler leapfrogging:
verification of the assigned author manuscript
# Identity, outcome and scope

Paper. Zineb Hassainia, Taoufik Hmidi and Nader Masmoudi, Rigorous derivation of the leapfrogging motion for planar Euler equations, arXiv:2311.15765v2, 5 December 2023 [V2]. The assigned PDF has 81 pages; all page references below use its printed page numbers, equal to PDF page numbers. The source SHA256 is recorded in Appendix 9 (#app:evidence). The journal association is DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01368-3, Inventiones mathematicae 242 (2025), 725–825. That 101-page publication is a different version. Its public metadata and subscription preview were checked, but a complete journal text was not compared with the assigned manuscript.

The full assigned text, including Appendix A and references, was read. The principal review checks cover the point-vortex Hamiltonian and period, the contour equation and leading derivative, both coordinate changes, the degenerate monodromy, the tame inverse, the induction exponents and the final parameter-measure argument. Actual source images resolve signs and coefficients that plain-text extraction obscures. Bounded native checks were integrated by the report writer; their scopes, numerical limitations and dependency versions are preserved in the evidence records.

Problems 1–3 establish distinct invalid steps in the central proof. The first is structural: a corrected leading periodic operator has a kernel throughout the parameter interval, so the displayed discrete-exception argument cannot supply its inverse. The second admits an explicit correction to the constructed approximation. The third admits a sufficient strengthened regularity choice and revised loss bookkeeping, conditional on a valid inverse. A separate stability-lemma issue is assessed below with its application limits. These are judgments of the supplied arguments, not a claim of nonexistence of leapfrogging patches. No author adoption is claimed: `scientific_decision=pending`; `human_reviews=[]`. The accompanying verification files record the independent focused checks and their completion status.
# Quantifiers, spaces and the proof dependence

Fix \(y_0>0\) and a compact interval \[O=[\xi_*,\xi^*],\qquad
  0<\xi_*<\xi^*<y_0/\sqrt2.\] Theorem 1.1 (p. 4) asserts that for every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(C_\varepsilon\subset O\) with \(|C_\varepsilon|\to |O|\), and for every \(\xi_0\in C_\varepsilon\) there is a four-patch Euler solution for all real time. The two upper patches have vorticity \(\varepsilon^{-2}\); their complex reflections have the opposite vorticity. Writing \(D_{t,k}^\varepsilon=z_k(t)+\varepsilon O_{t,k}^\varepsilon\), the normalized domains satisfy \[O_{t,2}^\varepsilon=O_{t+T(\xi_0)/2,1}^\varepsilon,\qquad
 O_{t+T(\xi_0),1}^\varepsilon=O_{t,1}^\varepsilon.\] The centers follow the translating point-vortex configuration. The theorem does not assert that the physical patches are periodic in a fixed laboratory frame, or include the collision and separatrix endpoints.

Use \(\varphi=\omega_0t\), \(\omega_0=2\pi/T\), and \(z_1-z_2=\sqrt q\,e^{i\Theta}\). The rotating radial parametrization is \[\gamma_1(\varphi,\theta)
  =e^{i\Theta(\varphi)}R(\varphi,\theta)e^{i\theta},
 \qquad R=\sqrt{1+2\varepsilon r}.\] The space \(H_0^s(\mathbb T^2)\) imposes zero \(\theta\)-average for each \(\varphi\); it imposes no centroid or first-harmonic constraint. The delay in the second upper patch is a shift by \(\pi\) in \(\varphi\), with the rotation sign treated in (3.12)–(3.18). The Hilbert convention on p. 23 is \[\mathcal He^{ij\theta}=i\operatorname{sign}(j)e^{ij\theta},\qquad j\ne0.\] All circle integrals below use normalized Haar measure. The notation \(a\leq_C b\) denotes \(a\leq Cb\) for a positive constant uniform in the small parameters under the stated hypotheses.
# Principal-order conjugation and the periodic kernel

Problem 1 (Major: the Hilbert conjugation changes the degenerate block).  The first identity on p. 40 and (4.31), propagated into Proposition 4.3, (5.4) and the monodromy analysis, use an incorrect factor and sign for the density pullback.
## Exact identity and an independent Fourier check

Equation reference: eq:exactH. For an orientation-preserving circle diffeomorphism \(f(\theta)=\theta+b(\theta)\), put \(p=f^{-1}\) and \(\mathcal Bh=f'(h\circ f)\), exactly as in (4.1). The stated Hilbert convention gives \[\mathcal Hh(\theta)
  =-2\partial_\theta\int_\mathbb T
     \log|e^{i\theta}-e^{i\eta}|\,h(\eta)\,d\eta.\] Changing variables in the integral and applying the inverse density pullback yields the exact formula \[
 (\mathcal B^{-1}\mathcal H\mathcal B-\mathcal H)h
  =-2\partial_\theta\int_\mathbb T
   \log\left|
    \frac{e^{ip(\theta)}-e^{ip(\eta)}}
         {e^{i\theta}-e^{i\eta}}\right|h(\eta)\,d\eta.\] The manuscript has \(+1\) in front of the same derivative and logarithm. The discrepancy is not a normalization ambiguity: both its explicit Fourier multiplier and its singular-kernel definition fix the sign and factor.
## Propagation in the actual orbit-dependent change

Let \[\widehat\Theta=\Theta-\varphi,\quad
 a_2=\frac1q-\frac{e^{2i\Theta}}{w_3^2}
                  -\frac{e^{2i\Theta}}{w_4^2},\quad
 A=a_2e^{-2i\widehat\Theta}.\] Here \(w_3=i\sqrt q\sin\Theta+iy_0\) and \(w_4=\sqrt q\cos\Theta+iy_0\). The second harmonic in the actual first transformation is \(\varepsilon^2\Im(Ae^{2i\theta})\), after removing its spatially constant rotation. The manuscript’s own logarithmic expansion is \[K_0=-\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}
        \Re\{A(e^{i\theta}+e^{i\eta})^2\}
          +O(\varepsilon^{2+\mu}).\] Write \(\widehat H_0h=\int_\mathbb T\Re(Ae^{i(\theta+\eta)})h(\eta)\,d\eta\). Zero mean removes one pure term and differentiation removes the other. Formula [eq:exactH] (#eq:exactH) gives \[\mathcal B^{-1}\mathcal H\mathcal B-\mathcal H
       =2\varepsilon^2\partial_\theta\widehat H_0
            +O(\varepsilon^{2+\mu}),\] whereas (4.31) gives \(-\varepsilon^2\partial_\theta\widehat H_0\). Therefore the finite-rank operator in the conjugated linearization must be \[\mathcal Q_{\rm correct}=\mathcal Q_{\rm rot}+\widehat H_0,
 \qquad\hbox{rather than}\qquad
 \mathcal Q_{\rm printed}=\mathcal Q_{\rm rot}-\tfrac12\widehat H_0.\] This changes the principal \(\varepsilon^2\) block. At \(\varphi=0\), \(\Theta=\pi/2\), \(q=\xi_0^2\), \[a_2(0)=\xi_0^{-2}-(y_0+\xi_0)^{-2}-y_0^{-2}>0
       \quad (0<\xi_0<y_0/\sqrt2);\] the disputed coefficient is nonzero on the relevant orbits. Under the later scaling, \(\varepsilon^{2+\mu}+\varepsilon^6/\lambda=o(\varepsilon^2)\). It cannot be absorbed into the stated remainder.
## The corrected block has a periodic translation mode

Set \[S_w=w_3^{-2}+w_4^{-2},\qquad
 d=e^{-2i\widehat\Theta}/q,\qquad
 A=d-e^{2i\varphi}S_w.\] For the real function \(h=\cos(\varphi+\theta)\), its Fourier coefficients are \(h_1=e^{i\varphi}/2\), \(h_{-1}=e^{-i\varphi}/2\), and each changes sign under \(\varphi\mapsto\varphi+\pi\). Combining the delayed and undelayed kernels gives for the positive-frequency amplitude of \(\mathcal Q_{\rm correct}h\), after removing a common factor of \(1/2\), \[S_w h_1+(A-d)h_{-1}
  =S_w\frac{e^{i\varphi}}2
      -e^{2i\varphi}S_w\frac{e^{-i\varphi}}2=0.\] Also \((\partial_\varphi-\partial_\theta)h=0\). Thus the corrected order-\(\varepsilon^2\) operator on the degenerate subspace annihilates this nonzero, \(2\pi\)-periodic, real, spatial-zero-mean function for every \(\xi_0\in O\).

This is consistent with common horizontal translation of the four patches. Such a translation preserves the reflected-pair geometry and half-period relation. Neither \(H_0^s\) nor \(X^s\) removes it. An invertible periodic coordinate change cannot remove its Floquet multiplier \(1\). For the corrected unperturbed periodic system, \(\det(M_0(2\pi)-\operatorname{Id})=0\) throughout the interval; discarding a discrete set as in Lemma 5.2 cannot remedy this.
## Counterevidence, impact and required work

The calculation \(\det(e^{2\pi A_0}-\operatorname{Id})\simeq0.12126170473544845\) is reproducible for the printed constant matrix, with frequencies \(\sqrt{15}/4\) and \(\sqrt7/4\). It is not evidence for the corrected block. The corrected limiting characteristic polynomial is \(z^2(z^2+1)\). Independent orbit integration at five admissible parameters corroborates the translation mode, but the exact kernel calculation, not a floating-point near-zero determinant, establishes the issue.

The primary Hilbert-conjugation source [BM] uses a pure composition operator and the opposite Hilbert sign. Its smoothing statement cannot supply the manuscript’s density coefficient without rederivation. The explicit derivative check above does that rederivation.

This invalidates the displayed nonresonance route from Proposition 4.3 to the approximate inverse used in Section 6. It does not disprove nonlinear existence. A repair would require a correctly constrained phase space and the associated solvability conditions, or another treatment of the neutral mode, followed by a new inverse and iteration analysis. No such complete repair is claimed here. The kernel and conjugation error are one dependent issue, not two separately counted Major findings.
# The residual of the displayed approximate solution

Problem 2 (Major: the stated construction leaves an order-\(\varepsilon^4\) term).  In Lemma 3.3, equations (3.49)–(3.53), the definition of \(A_1\) at the top of p. 32 omits a term needed for the asserted \(O(\varepsilon^5)\) residual and the initialization (6.5).

Equation reference: eq:A1. Put \(D_0=(\partial_\theta-\mathcal H)/2\). The construction chooses \(r_0=g+\varepsilon B_0\), with no first harmonic, so that the circle-state forcing is canceled. Expansion using the correctly printed final derivative (3.21) gives the order-\(\varepsilon^4\) coefficient \[
 A_{1,\rm correct}
  =\omega_0\partial_\varphi g
     -\omega_0\dot\Theta\,\partial_\theta g
     -\tfrac34\partial_\theta(g^2).\] The middle term is missing from \(A_{1,\rm printed}\). The \(B_1\) on p. 32 contains the rotation coefficient multiplying \(B_0\), which contributes at the next order; it does not contain the missing term multiplying \(g\).

For a completely admissible parameter test take \(y_0=1\), \(\xi_0=1/2\) in, for example, \(O=[0.45,0.55]\). At \(\varphi=0\), \[q=\tfrac14,\quad \Theta=\tfrac\pi2,\quad
 a_2=\tfrac{23}{9},\quad
 \omega_0\dot\Theta=4+\tfrac43=\tfrac{16}{3}.\] The last equality follows directly from the point-vortex ODE; it does not approximate the frequency. At \(\theta=\pi/4\), \(g=(23/9)\cos2\theta\), so \[-\omega_0\dot\Theta\,\partial_\theta g
       =\frac{736}{27}\ne0.\] The construction printed in the proof sets \(D_0r_1=-\varepsilon A_{1,\rm printed}\) and \(r_\varepsilon=r_0+\varepsilon r_1\). It therefore leaves \[\mathcal G(\varepsilon r_\varepsilon)(0,\pi/4)
       =\frac{736}{27}\varepsilon^4+O(\varepsilon^5),\] in place of the claimed fifth-order bound.
## An explicit verified local correction

All terms in [eq:A1] (#eq:A1) have even spatial modes. On the second harmonics, \(D_0g=\partial_\theta g/4\). Replacing the printed \(r_1\) by \[r_{1,\rm corrected}
      =r_{1,\rm printed}+4\varepsilon\omega_0\dot\Theta\,g\] gives \(D_0r_{1,\rm corrected}=-\varepsilon A_{1,\rm correct}\). Equivalently, add \(4\varepsilon^2\omega_0\dot\Theta\,g\) to \(r_\varepsilon\). This preserves its zero mean, absence of first harmonics, smooth parameter dependence and stated size; substituting it into the Taylor expansion cancels exactly the missing fourth-order term. The unchanged higher-order bounds then give the asserted fifth-order residual for this corrected approximation.
## Why the error is material despite this correction

Without the correction, \(\mathcal F(0)\) has order \(\varepsilon^{2-\mu}\), not \(\varepsilon^{3-\mu}\) as in (6.5). Multiplication by the stated inverse scale \(\lambda^{-1}=\varepsilon^{-2-\delta}\) gives \(\varepsilon^{-\mu-\delta}\), instead of the small initial size \(\varepsilon^{1-\mu-\delta}\). Thus the printed object does not supply the small-data input advertised for the core Nash–Moser construction. The finding concerns that invalid construction, not falsity of the existential assertion of Lemma 3.3. The explicit correction is counterevidence against a broader nonexistence claim; its simplicity does not erase the demonstrated dependence on the incorrect residual. It also does not fix Problem 1.
# Closing the high norm in the induction

Problem 3 (Major: the inverse’s high-norm hypothesis is not obtained).  The interpolation and summation on p. 56 do not establish the uniform norm required by (5.49). The parameter restrictions (6.4) force the displayed interpolated exponent to be positive. The subsequent use of a smaller derivative loss in (6.31) also requires replacement.

Let \[L=2s_0+2\tau+3,\qquad
 R_*=2s_0+2\tau+4+\tfrac32\mu_2,\qquad
 A_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{b_0}/\lambda=\varepsilon^{1-\mu-\delta}.\] The induction supplies increments of size \(A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{-a_2}\) in \(H^L\), while the \(H^{b_1}\) norm of the iterates is permitted to grow as \(A_\varepsilon N_{n-1}^{\mu_1}\). The inverse needs \(\left\lVert \rho_n\right\rVert_{R_*}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}\le1\). Page 56 uses half-weight interpolation and obtains \[\left\lVert u_k\right\rVert_{R_*}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}
   \mathrel{\leq_C}A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{(\mu_1-a_2)/2}.\] It then sums this upper bound as though it decayed. However, (6.4) gives \[\mu_1>\frac6\delta>
       \frac{6(a_1+2)}{1-\mu}>6a_1>9a_2 .\] The exponent is strictly positive for every permitted choice.
## An explicit test of the implication used on p. 56

Take \[(s_0,\tau,\mu,a_2,a_1,\mu_2,\delta,\mu_1,b_1)
   =(4,2,\tfrac14,4,60,41,\tfrac1{100},630,1400).\] Every strict inequality in (6.4) holds: \(4>3\), \(60>57\), \(41>40\), \[\tfrac1{100}
 <\min\{\tfrac14,\tfrac3{248},\tfrac3{56}\},\qquad
 630>627,\qquad 1400>\max\{1315,149\}.\] Here \(L=15\), \(R_*=155/2\), and the printed exponent is \(313\). The \(4\mu_1/3\) term in the source gives the lower bound \(1315\). The earlier retained witness with \(b_1=900\) was therefore inadmissible and is superseded by the present parameters; its historical computation is not evidence of an admissible example.

For fixed small \(\varepsilon\), let \(m_k=\lfloor N_{k-1}^{1/4}\rfloor\), ignoring finitely many initial repetitions if needed, and let \(w_m=\cos(m\theta)\) normalized to have \(H^{15}\) norm one. Set \[u_1=0,\qquad
 u_k=A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{-4}w_{m_k}\ (k\ge2),\qquad
 \rho_n=\sum_{k=2}^n u_k.\] These are real, spatial-zero-mean trigonometric polynomials. They are independent of the parameter and of \(\varphi\), so their Lipschitz seminorm vanishes. Their frequency support satisfies \(\rho_n\in E_{n-1}\). Their low norms are summable, and \[\left\lVert u_k\right\rVert_{1400}\asymp
       A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{1369/4},\qquad
 \left\lVert u_k\right\rVert_{155/2}\asymp
       A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{93/8}.\] The superexponentially spaced high-norm sum is bounded by a constant times \(A_\varepsilon N_{n-1}^{1369/4}\le A_\varepsilon N_{n-1}^{630}\). Thus the low/high bounds and localization used in that interpolation argument hold. But distinct Fourier modes are orthogonal, and \(\left\lVert \rho_n\right\rVert_{155/2}\) is unbounded.

This is a counterexample to the displayed implication from those bounds, not an asserted Euler solution or a sequence satisfying the separate nonlinear residual condition (P2). The page-56 argument does not invoke (P2) to obtain its high-norm conclusion. Any alternative use of the nonlinear structure must actually be supplied.
## Sufficient repair conditions and the genuine losses

Equation reference: eq:b1. Since the authors can choose \(b_1\), a valid interpolation can be arranged by strengthening its lower bound. Set \[\vartheta=\frac{R_*-L}{b_1-L},\qquad
 \kappa=a_2-\vartheta(\mu_1+a_2).\] Interpolation of the actual low increment bound and the high increment bound gives \[\left\lVert u_k\right\rVert_{R_*}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}
       \mathrel{\leq_C}A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{-\kappa}.\] Both the supremum norm and the one-derivative-lower difference norm interpolate with the same \(\vartheta\). The sufficient condition \[
 b_1>L+2\frac{\mu_1+a_2}{a_2}(R_*-L)\] ensures \(\kappa>a_2/2>0\), so the increments sum in \(H^{R_*}\). For the same remaining parameters, \(b_1=20000\) gives \(\vartheta=25/7994\) and \(\kappa=8063/3997>2\). The available upper regularity \(S\) must be selected to include this \(b_1\) and the finite losses, for example \(S\ge b_1+4\tau+6\) for the displayed bounds used here. No fixed-\(\varepsilon\) infinite-smoothness conclusion is inferred from this finite-regularity argument.

The actual inverse estimate (6.6) is \[\left\lVert T_nh\right\rVert_s\mathrel{\leq_C}\lambda^{-1}
 \bigl(\left\lVert h\right\rVert_{s+2\tau}
       +\left\lVert \rho_n\right\rVert_{s+4\tau+5}\left\lVert h\right\rVert_{s_0+2\tau}\bigr).\] Equation (6.31) replaces \(s+4\tau+5\) by \(s+2\tau\); that general replacement is unjustified. After [eq:b1] (#eq:b1), low-order use can instead exploit \[R_*-(L+4\tau+5)=\tfrac32\mu_2-4\tau-4>0.\] For \(s\le L\) this gives \[\left\lVert u_{n+1}\right\rVert_s
   \mathrel{\leq_C}A_\varepsilon
          N_n^{s-s_0+2\tau-\frac23a_1}.\] At \(s=b_1\), retain \(N_{n-1}^{4\tau+5}\left\lVert \rho_n\right\rVert_{b_1}\) and combine it with the residual decay \(N_{n-1}^{-a_1}\). The resulting two high-growth exponents are bounded by \[\tfrac23\mu_1+\tfrac43\tau+\tfrac73+\tfrac2\delta,
 \qquad
 \tfrac23\mu_1+2\tau+\tfrac23(4\tau+5-a_1),\] both strictly below \(\mu_1\) under (6.4). The original reviewer calculation record gives the complete inequality chain.

The apparent loss of \(2\tau\) in (6.22) has a bounded explanation: retaining the required \(H^{s_0+2\tau+2}\) norm yields a factor \(N_n^{-\frac32\mu_2+2\tau+2}\), which is at most \(N_n^{-\mu_2+2}\) because \(\mu_2\ge4\tau+3\). Its final weaker exponent can survive, although its intermediate display needs correction. The small powers \[1-\mu-\delta,\quad \mu-\delta,\quad
 2+\mu-\delta(1+\mu_2),\quad
 1-\mu-\delta(a_1+2)\] are all positive for the specified choices.

This supplies a precise route for the affected regularity and loss estimates, conditional on the nonlinear and inverse inputs. It does not make the printed half-weight summation valid or establish the claimed freedom to use every choice satisfying only (6.4). The uniform high norm is required before invoking the inverse and again when evaluating the limiting frequency coefficient. Its absence is therefore a core proof gap. Neither this conditional repair nor a larger \(b_1\) repairs the neutral-mode obstruction in Problem 1.
# The normalized transport-stability statement

Problem 4 (Major in the stated stability bridge; application not refuted).  Proposition A.9(4), p. 72, gives a state-difference estimate for the normalized correction \(c\) with the scaling of a full transport speed. With the proof’s definition \(c_0=0\), a constant-coefficient example contradicts that estimate. The bridge to (4.26) requires a corrected statement and explicit difference hypotheses.

The homological forcing has no nonconstant Fourier modes. The recurrence (A.26) gives \(\beta=0\) and \(c=r\) exactly after the first mean update. Consequently [eq:A9literal] (#eq:A9literal) would require \[|r_1-r_2|\mathrel{\leq_C}t^4|r_1-r_2|,\] which is impossible with a uniform constant. This is an exact test of the stated normalized lemma and its construction, not a numerical approximation to the patch solution.

Two plausible intended readings limit the conclusion. If \(c_0\) in part (4) meant \(\langle f_0\rangle\), the constant test would no longer contradict it; however, that is not the \(c_0=0\) defined by this proof and needs a new definition. If the left side meant the full speed \(c_{-1}+\epsilon_2c\), the factor \(\epsilon_2\) would have the expected scale. That reading changes the displayed quantity. Moreover, (A.10)–(A.11) give absolute state norms, not the state-difference assumptions needed for a general \(\Delta\rho\) conclusion.

The source invoked for the omitted proof, Hmidi–Roulley [HR21], Proposition 6.2 and (6.30), estimates differences of the full transport coefficient. Its parameter regularity and frequency cutoffs also differ from those in A.9. The actual primary statement was inspected; a citation to it does not resolve these normalization and hypothesis changes by itself.

In the specific application, (4.6)–(4.7) provide additional difference controls. A corrected estimate for the full coefficient could therefore still yield (4.26). The constant example does not disprove (4.26). The material issue is that the general lemma stated as its justification is false under its explicit normalization, and the necessary adapted stability proof is not supplied. Section 6.2 uses (4.26) to compare the limiting and finite-step Cantor inequalities, so this is a core dependency rather than an unrelated appendix assertion. A complete corrected stability lemma has not been verified here; its exact hypotheses, loss indices and parameter factors require restatement and proof.
# Positive checks, counterevidence and local corrections
## Point dynamics and the compact parameter range

For \(Y=y_0\), the reduced Hamiltonian is \[H(\eta,\xi)=\tfrac12\log
       \frac{(Y^2-\xi^2)(Y^2+\eta^2)}{\eta^2+\xi^2}.\] Direct differentiation reproduces (2.4) with \(\dot\eta=\partial_\xi H\), \(\dot\xi=-\partial_\eta H\). If \(\alpha=\xi_0^2/Y^2\), \(v=1-2\alpha\), \(x=\xi^2/Y^2\) and \(z=\eta^2/Y^2\), its level set gives \[x(1+\alpha z)=\alpha-vz,\qquad
 \frac{\eta^2+\xi^2}{Y^2}
       =\frac{\alpha(1+z)^2}{1+\alpha z}.\] Hence \(\xi_0^2\le\eta^2+\xi^2\le\xi_0^2/v\) and \(|\xi|\le\xi_0<Y/\sqrt2\). The regular compact reduced orbit is noncolliding and periodic; the centroid has bounded horizontal velocity. These facts establish complete relative-periodic point trajectories, not laboratory-frame boundedness.

For \[K(\alpha,u)=
 \frac{(1-\alpha)(v+\alpha u)^2}
      {v(v+\alpha^2u)^{3/2}},\qquad
 T=4\xi_0^2\int_0^1\frac{K(\alpha,s^2)}{\sqrt{1-s^2}}\,ds ,\] the denominators remain positive on compact parameter intervals. Dominated analytic differentiation justifies analyticity of \(T\) and \(\omega_0\). Writing \(A=v+\alpha u\), \(B=v+\alpha^2u\), the numerator of \((1-\alpha)vAB\,\partial_\alpha\log K\) is \[\alpha v^2(1-u)^2+
 2v(1-\alpha)(1-\alpha/2+\alpha^2)u(1-u)
 +2(1-\alpha)^4u^2>0.\] Also \[\partial_u\log K
   =\frac{\alpha[(4-3\alpha)v+\alpha^2u]}{2AB}>0 .\] It follows that \[2\pi\xi_0^2\le T\le\frac{2\pi\xi_0^2}{v},\qquad
 T'\ge4\pi\xi_0,\qquad
 |\omega_0'|\ge\frac{2v^2}{\xi_0^3}.\] This supplies the needed twist on every fixed compact \(O\). The record also derives the angular estimates independently.

The reviewer checked physical-time orbit integration, quadrature and the correctly normalized elliptic formula at \(\xi_0=0.02,0.1,0.3,0.5,0.65\), \(Y=1\). The largest relative orbit/quadrature period difference was \(2.253\times10^{-12}\). These finite checks corroborate the analytic argument; they are not interval bounds or a simulation of patch existence. Behring–Goodman [BG] was checked with its coordinate and time rescalings. Its neutral and transverse stability directions cannot be confused with an existence obstruction for the present symmetric ansatz.

The p. 13 elliptic parameter must be \(\alpha=\xi_0^2/Y^2\); the names of the two standard complete elliptic integrals are reversed there. The derivative bracket on p. 15 also needs the ratio \(A/B\) rather than the printed product. The positive derivative identities above verify that the period/twist conclusions survive these local formula corrections. They are not additional Major findings. The unavailable original Love PDF and the cited table entries were not represented as read; the required claims were derived independently.
## Contour, geometry and non-rigidity

Direct differentiation of the quadratic cross-interaction kernels agrees with the leading delayed and reflected terms in (3.24). The actual final formula (3.21) contains \(-\varepsilon^2g/2\); its coefficient is correct despite ambiguous text extraction. The intermediate (3.44) loses a half that the final formula restores. The delayed kernel in p. 34’s definition of \(K_{0,1}^\varepsilon\) should be \(K_3^\varepsilon\), without the extra \(1/\varepsilon\). These local displays are distinguished from the incorrect principal conjugation in Problem 1. The transport change itself can be checked by the chain rule, and its density factor preserves the spatial integral. A spatially constant, non-small rotation does not require the small-diffeomorphism lemma when separated from the small \(\theta\)-dependent part.

Conditional on a valid small solution, zero spatial mean gives \(|O_{t,k}^\varepsilon|=\pi\) exactly and hence circulations \(\pm\pi\). The point-center distances are uniformly bounded below by \[d_*=\min\{\xi_*,\,y_0-\xi^*\}>0.\] For \(R\le2\), \(4\varepsilon<d_*\) makes all four patches disjoint for all time. The same smallness ensures \(R^2>0\). The rescaled bound \(\rho=O(\varepsilon^{1-\mu-\delta})\), with \(\delta<1-\mu\), is consistent with the leading \(\varepsilon^2\) shape term and the stated \(O(\varepsilon^{2+\mu})\) remainder.

A separate exact check supports leading non-rigidity throughout the admissible interval. Put \(s=\xi_0/y_0\). At the two vertical-axis crossings, the second-harmonic coefficients, apart from \(y_0^{-2}\), are \[a_+=s^{-2}-(1+s)^{-2}-1,\qquad
 a_-=s^{-2}-(1-s)^{-2}-1.\] At a horizontal-axis crossing, set \(Q=s^2/(1-2s^2)\). The squared amplitude is \[H_*=\left[Q^{-1}+1-\frac{Q-1}{(Q+1)^2}\right]^2
                   +\frac{4Q}{(Q+1)^4}.\] The reduced numerator polynomials of \(a_+^2-a_-^2\) and \(H_*-a_+^2\) have greatest common divisor one; the saved exact calculation verifies a Bezout identity. All denominators are nonzero on \(0<s<1/\sqrt2\), so the three amplitudes cannot all agree at any admissible parameter. For example, at \(s=1/2\), \(a_+=23/9\), \(H_*=97/9\), and \(H_*-a_+^2=344/81\). This is a positive shape check conditional on construction, not a substitute for the missing inverse.
## Normal modes, extension and parameter measure

The cutoff inverse on \(|j|\ge2\) has the asserted \(\lambda^{-1}\) size with a \(2\tau\) spatial loss in the weighted Lipschitz norm. In (5.34), the term \(\Pi_{N_n}^{\perp}D_1T_n\) is zero by its Fourier support; the remaining high-frequency projector has the stated decay. An incorrect sign in the preceding decomposition does not change this support calculation. The actual higher coefficient losses are tracked in Problem 3.

Extension from a closed subset of a real parameter interval can be performed by affine interpolation across complementary gaps, and constant continuation at outside endpoints. The same linear construction preserves all relevant Hilbert norms and the Lipschitz bounds. Thus no incompatibility between separate Sobolev extensions needs to be presumed from the brief Kirszbraun citation.
# Overall judgment and remaining work

The main existence argument in this assigned version is not verified by the presented proof. Problem 1 requires a substantive reanalysis of neutral directions, range conditions and the approximate inverse. Problem 2 has a verified change of the approximate solution. Problem 3 has sufficient additional regularity conditions and conditional replacements for the affected induction estimates. Problem 4 identifies a false normalized stability statement and an incompletely specified application bridge; it does not establish that the desired application estimate is false. Local formula and norm corrections with valid replacements are not promoted to separate core failures.

The review does not claim the 2025 journal text is unchanged. The official version/correction lookup conducted for this review did not return a separate correction; that limited search is not evidence that no correction exists. A journal-version comparison and a revised neutral-mode proof remain outside the completed bounded checks. The current independent acceptance is recorded separately in the verification files. No empirical experiment or author-code execution is needed to validate the exact countercalculations above, and absence of code is not a defect in this mathematical paper.

claim: The conjugated order-epsilon^2 finite-rank operator supplies an invertible degenerate periodic block outside a discrete parameter set.
analysis: The first identity on p. 40 and (4.31), propagated into Proposition 4.3, (5.4) and the monodromy analysis, use an incorrect factor and sign for the density pullback.

Equation reference: eq:exactH. For an orientation-preserving circle diffeomorphism \(f(\theta)=\theta+b(\theta)\), put \(p=f^{-1}\) and \(\mathcal Bh=f'(h\circ f)\), exactly as in (4.1). The stated Hilbert convention gives \[\mathcal Hh(\theta)
  =-2\partial_\theta\int_\mathbb T
     \log|e^{i\theta}-e^{i\eta}|\,h(\eta)\,d\eta.\] Changing variables in the integral and applying the inverse density pullback yields the exact formula \[
 (\mathcal B^{-1}\mathcal H\mathcal B-\mathcal H)h
  =-2\partial_\theta\int_\mathbb T
   \log\left|
    \frac{e^{ip(\theta)}-e^{ip(\eta)}}
         {e^{i\theta}-e^{i\eta}}\right|h(\eta)\,d\eta.\] The manuscript has \(+1\) in front of the same derivative and logarithm. The discrepancy is not a normalization ambiguity: both its explicit Fourier multiplier and its singular-kernel definition fix the sign and factor.

Let \[\widehat\Theta=\Theta-\varphi,\quad
 a_2=\frac1q-\frac{e^{2i\Theta}}{w_3^2}
                  -\frac{e^{2i\Theta}}{w_4^2},\quad
 A=a_2e^{-2i\widehat\Theta}.\] Here \(w_3=i\sqrt q\sin\Theta+iy_0\) and \(w_4=\sqrt q\cos\Theta+iy_0\). The second harmonic in the actual first transformation is \(\varepsilon^2\Im(Ae^{2i\theta})\), after removing its spatially constant rotation. The manuscript’s own logarithmic expansion is \[K_0=-\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}
        \Re\{A(e^{i\theta}+e^{i\eta})^2\}
          +O(\varepsilon^{2+\mu}).\] Write \(\widehat H_0h=\int_\mathbb T\Re(Ae^{i(\theta+\eta)})h(\eta)\,d\eta\). Zero mean removes one pure term and differentiation removes the other. Formula [eq:exactH] (#eq:exactH) gives \[\mathcal B^{-1}\mathcal H\mathcal B-\mathcal H
       =2\varepsilon^2\partial_\theta\widehat H_0
            +O(\varepsilon^{2+\mu}),\] whereas (4.31) gives \(-\varepsilon^2\partial_\theta\widehat H_0\). Therefore the finite-rank operator in the conjugated linearization must be \[\mathcal Q_{\rm correct}=\mathcal Q_{\rm rot}+\widehat H_0,
 \qquad\hbox{rather than}\qquad
 \mathcal Q_{\rm printed}=\mathcal Q_{\rm rot}-\tfrac12\widehat H_0.\] This changes the principal \(\varepsilon^2\) block. At \(\varphi=0\), \(\Theta=\pi/2\), \(q=\xi_0^2\), \[a_2(0)=\xi_0^{-2}-(y_0+\xi_0)^{-2}-y_0^{-2}>0
       \quad (0<\xi_0<y_0/\sqrt2);\] the disputed coefficient is nonzero on the relevant orbits. Under the later scaling, \(\varepsilon^{2+\mu}+\varepsilon^6/\lambda=o(\varepsilon^2)\). It cannot be absorbed into the stated remainder.

Set \[S_w=w_3^{-2}+w_4^{-2},\qquad
 d=e^{-2i\widehat\Theta}/q,\qquad
 A=d-e^{2i\varphi}S_w.\] For the real function \(h=\cos(\varphi+\theta)\), its Fourier coefficients are \(h_1=e^{i\varphi}/2\), \(h_{-1}=e^{-i\varphi}/2\), and each changes sign under \(\varphi\mapsto\varphi+\pi\). Combining the delayed and undelayed kernels gives for the positive-frequency amplitude of \(\mathcal Q_{\rm correct}h\), after removing a common factor of \(1/2\), \[S_w h_1+(A-d)h_{-1}
  =S_w\frac{e^{i\varphi}}2
      -e^{2i\varphi}S_w\frac{e^{-i\varphi}}2=0.\] Also \((\partial_\varphi-\partial_\theta)h=0\). Thus the corrected order-\(\varepsilon^2\) operator on the degenerate subspace annihilates this nonzero, \(2\pi\)-periodic, real, spatial-zero-mean function for every \(\xi_0\in O\).

This is consistent with common horizontal translation of the four patches. Such a translation preserves the reflected-pair geometry and half-period relation. Neither \(H_0^s\) nor \(X^s\) removes it. An invertible periodic coordinate change cannot remove its Floquet multiplier \(1\). For the corrected unperturbed periodic system, \(\det(M_0(2\pi)-\operatorname{Id})=0\) throughout the interval; discarding a discrete set as in Lemma 5.2 cannot remedy this.
result: The calculation \(\det(e^{2\pi A_0}-\operatorname{Id})\simeq0.12126170473544845\) is reproducible for the printed constant matrix, with frequencies \(\sqrt{15}/4\) and \(\sqrt7/4\). It is not evidence for the corrected block. The corrected limiting characteristic polynomial is \(z^2(z^2+1)\). Independent orbit integration at five admissible parameters corroborates the translation mode, but the exact kernel calculation, not a floating-point near-zero determinant, establishes the issue.

The primary Hilbert-conjugation source [BM] uses a pure composition operator and the opposite Hilbert sign. Its smoothing statement cannot supply the manuscript’s density coefficient without rederivation. The explicit derivative check above does that rederivation.

This invalidates the displayed nonresonance route from Proposition 4.3 to the approximate inverse used in Section 6. It does not disprove nonlinear existence. A repair would require a correctly constrained phase space and the associated solvability conditions, or another treatment of the neutral mode, followed by a new inverse and iteration analysis. No such complete repair is claimed here. The kernel and conjugation error are one dependent issue, not two separately counted Major findings.

Impact: Core leading inverse in Proposition5.1 and the subsequent approximate inverse is not established by the printed nonresonance calculation. Corrected monodromy has multiplier1 on the entire interval.

problems.title: Printed approximate solution retains a fourth-order residual required to be fifth order
claim: The constructed r_epsilon satisfies G(epsilon r_epsilon)=O(epsilon^5).
analysis: In Lemma 3.3, equations (3.49)–(3.53), the definition of \(A_1\) at the top of p. 32 omits a term needed for the asserted \(O(\varepsilon^5)\) residual and the initialization (6.5).

Equation reference: eq:A1. Put \(D_0=(\partial_\theta-\mathcal H)/2\). The construction chooses \(r_0=g+\varepsilon B_0\), with no first harmonic, so that the circle-state forcing is canceled. Expansion using the correctly printed final derivative (3.21) gives the order-\(\varepsilon^4\) coefficient \[
 A_{1,\rm correct}
  =\omega_0\partial_\varphi g
     -\omega_0\dot\Theta\,\partial_\theta g
     -\tfrac34\partial_\theta(g^2).\] The middle term is missing from \(A_{1,\rm printed}\). The \(B_1\) on p. 32 contains the rotation coefficient multiplying \(B_0\), which contributes at the next order; it does not contain the missing term multiplying \(g\).

For a completely admissible parameter test take \(y_0=1\), \(\xi_0=1/2\) in, for example, \(O=[0.45,0.55]\). At \(\varphi=0\), \[q=\tfrac14,\quad \Theta=\tfrac\pi2,\quad
 a_2=\tfrac{23}{9},\quad
 \omega_0\dot\Theta=4+\tfrac43=\tfrac{16}{3}.\] The last equality follows directly from the point-vortex ODE; it does not approximate the frequency. At \(\theta=\pi/4\), \(g=(23/9)\cos2\theta\), so \[-\omega_0\dot\Theta\,\partial_\theta g
       =\frac{736}{27}\ne0.\] The construction printed in the proof sets \(D_0r_1=-\varepsilon A_{1,\rm printed}\) and \(r_\varepsilon=r_0+\varepsilon r_1\). It therefore leaves \[\mathcal G(\varepsilon r_\varepsilon)(0,\pi/4)
       =\frac{736}{27}\varepsilon^4+O(\varepsilon^5),\] in place of the claimed fifth-order bound.

All terms in [eq:A1] (#eq:A1) have even spatial modes. On the second harmonics, \(D_0g=\partial_\theta g/4\). Replacing the printed \(r_1\) by \[r_{1,\rm corrected}
      =r_{1,\rm printed}+4\varepsilon\omega_0\dot\Theta\,g\] gives \(D_0r_{1,\rm corrected}=-\varepsilon A_{1,\rm correct}\). Equivalently, add \(4\varepsilon^2\omega_0\dot\Theta\,g\) to \(r_\varepsilon\). This preserves its zero mean, absence of first harmonics, smooth parameter dependence and stated size; substituting it into the Taylor expansion cancels exactly the missing fourth-order term. The unchanged higher-order bounds then give the asserted fifth-order residual for this corrected approximation.

Without the correction, \(\mathcal F(0)\) has order \(\varepsilon^{2-\mu}\), not \(\varepsilon^{3-\mu}\) as in (6.5). Multiplication by the stated inverse scale \(\lambda^{-1}=\varepsilon^{-2-\delta}\) gives \(\varepsilon^{-\mu-\delta}\), instead of the small initial size \(\varepsilon^{1-\mu-\delta}\). Thus the printed object does not supply the small-data input advertised for the core Nash–Moser construction. The finding concerns that invalid construction, not falsity of the existential assertion of Lemma 3.3. The explicit correction is counterevidence against a broader nonexistence claim; its simplicity does not erase the demonstrated dependence on the incorrect residual. It also does not fix Problem 1.
result: Impact: F(0) becomes O(epsilon^(2-mu)); multiplying by lambda^-1 gives epsilon^(-mu-delta), so the printed Nash–Moser initialization loses its smallness.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Replace r1 by r1+4 epsilon omega0 Theta_dot g, equivalently r_epsilon by r_epsilon+4epsilon^2 omega0 Theta_dot g. D0g=partial_theta g/4 cancels the missing coefficient; all sizes/even modes preserved.

problems.title: High Sobolev input is not obtained by the printed interpolation and loss bookkeeping
problems.source_location: pp55–56(6.4),P1,P3 and high-norm summation p61(6.31) p53(5.49)
claim: Every choice satisfying(6.4) closes the inverse high-norm input and induction.
analysis: The interpolation and summation on p. 56 do not establish the uniform norm required by (5.49). The parameter restrictions (6.4) force the displayed interpolated exponent to be positive. The subsequent use of a smaller derivative loss in (6.31) also requires replacement.

Let \[L=2s_0+2\tau+3,\qquad
 R_*=2s_0+2\tau+4+\tfrac32\mu_2,\qquad
 A_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{b_0}/\lambda=\varepsilon^{1-\mu-\delta}.\] The induction supplies increments of size \(A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{-a_2}\) in \(H^L\), while the \(H^{b_1}\) norm of the iterates is permitted to grow as \(A_\varepsilon N_{n-1}^{\mu_1}\). The inverse needs \(\left\lVert \rho_n\right\rVert_{R_*}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}\le1\). Page 56 uses half-weight interpolation and obtains \[\left\lVert u_k\right\rVert_{R_*}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}
   \mathrel{\leq_C}A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{(\mu_1-a_2)/2}.\] It then sums this upper bound as though it decayed. However, (6.4) gives \[\mu_1>\frac6\delta>
       \frac{6(a_1+2)}{1-\mu}>6a_1>9a_2 .\] The exponent is strictly positive for every permitted choice.

Take \[(s_0,\tau,\mu,a_2,a_1,\mu_2,\delta,\mu_1,b_1)
   =(4,2,\tfrac14,4,60,41,\tfrac1{100},630,1400).\] Every strict inequality in (6.4) holds: \(4>3\), \(60>57\), \(41>40\), \[\tfrac1{100}
 <\min\{\tfrac14,\tfrac3{248},\tfrac3{56}\},\qquad
 630>627,\qquad 1400>\max\{1315,149\}.\] Here \(L=15\), \(R_*=155/2\), and the printed exponent is \(313\). The \(4\mu_1/3\) term in the source gives the lower bound \(1315\). The earlier retained witness with \(b_1=900\) was therefore inadmissible and is superseded by the present parameters; its historical computation is not evidence of an admissible example.

For fixed small \(\varepsilon\), let \(m_k=\lfloor N_{k-1}^{1/4}\rfloor\), ignoring finitely many initial repetitions if needed, and let \(w_m=\cos(m\theta)\) normalized to have \(H^{15}\) norm one. Set \[u_1=0,\qquad
 u_k=A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{-4}w_{m_k}\ (k\ge2),\qquad
 \rho_n=\sum_{k=2}^n u_k.\] These are real, spatial-zero-mean trigonometric polynomials. They are independent of the parameter and of \(\varphi\), so their Lipschitz seminorm vanishes. Their frequency support satisfies \(\rho_n\in E_{n-1}\). Their low norms are summable, and \[\left\lVert u_k\right\rVert_{1400}\asymp
       A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{1369/4},\qquad
 \left\lVert u_k\right\rVert_{155/2}\asymp
       A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{93/8}.\] The superexponentially spaced high-norm sum is bounded by a constant times \(A_\varepsilon N_{n-1}^{1369/4}\le A_\varepsilon N_{n-1}^{630}\). Thus the low/high bounds and localization used in that interpolation argument hold. But distinct Fourier modes are orthogonal, and \(\left\lVert \rho_n\right\rVert_{155/2}\) is unbounded.

This is a counterexample to the displayed implication from those bounds, not an asserted Euler solution or a sequence satisfying the separate nonlinear residual condition (P2). The page-56 argument does not invoke (P2) to obtain its high-norm conclusion. Any alternative use of the nonlinear structure must actually be supplied.

Equation reference: eq:b1. Since the authors can choose \(b_1\), a valid interpolation can be arranged by strengthening its lower bound. Set \[\vartheta=\frac{R_*-L}{b_1-L},\qquad
 \kappa=a_2-\vartheta(\mu_1+a_2).\] Interpolation of the actual low increment bound and the high increment bound gives \[\left\lVert u_k\right\rVert_{R_*}^{\operatorname{Lip}(\lambda)}
       \mathrel{\leq_C}A_\varepsilon N_{k-1}^{-\kappa}.\] Both the supremum norm and the one-derivative-lower difference norm interpolate with the same \(\vartheta\). The sufficient condition \[
 b_1>L+2\frac{\mu_1+a_2}{a_2}(R_*-L)\] ensures \(\kappa>a_2/2>0\), so the increments sum in \(H^{R_*}\). For the same remaining parameters, \(b_1=20000\) gives \(\vartheta=25/7994\) and \(\kappa=8063/3997>2\). The available upper regularity \(S\) must be selected to include this \(b_1\) and the finite losses, for example \(S\ge b_1+4\tau+6\) for the displayed bounds used here. No fixed-\(\varepsilon\) infinite-smoothness conclusion is inferred from this finite-regularity argument.

The actual inverse estimate (6.6) is \[\left\lVert T_nh\right\rVert_s\mathrel{\leq_C}\lambda^{-1}
 \bigl(\left\lVert h\right\rVert_{s+2\tau}
       +\left\lVert \rho_n\right\rVert_{s+4\tau+5}\left\lVert h\right\rVert_{s_0+2\tau}\bigr).\] Equation (6.31) replaces \(s+4\tau+5\) by \(s+2\tau\); that general replacement is unjustified. After [eq:b1] (#eq:b1), low-order use can instead exploit \[R_*-(L+4\tau+5)=\tfrac32\mu_2-4\tau-4>0.\] For \(s\le L\) this gives \[\left\lVert u_{n+1}\right\rVert_s
   \mathrel{\leq_C}A_\varepsilon
          N_n^{s-s_0+2\tau-\frac23a_1}.\] At \(s=b_1\), retain \(N_{n-1}^{4\tau+5}\left\lVert \rho_n\right\rVert_{b_1}\) and combine it with the residual decay \(N_{n-1}^{-a_1}\). The resulting two high-growth exponents are bounded by \[\tfrac23\mu_1+\tfrac43\tau+\tfrac73+\tfrac2\delta,
 \qquad
 \tfrac23\mu_1+2\tau+\tfrac23(4\tau+5-a_1),\] both strictly below \(\mu_1\) under (6.4). The original reviewer calculation record gives the complete inequality chain.

The apparent loss of \(2\tau\) in (6.22) has a bounded explanation: retaining the required \(H^{s_0+2\tau+2}\) norm yields a factor \(N_n^{-\frac32\mu_2+2\tau+2}\), which is at most \(N_n^{-\mu_2+2}\) because \(\mu_2\ge4\tau+3\). Its final weaker exponent can survive, although its intermediate display needs correction. The small powers \[1-\mu-\delta,\quad \mu-\delta,\quad
 2+\mu-\delta(1+\mu_2),\quad
 1-\mu-\delta(a_1+2)\] are all positive for the specified choices.

This supplies a precise route for the affected regularity and loss estimates, conditional on the nonlinear and inverse inputs. It does not make the printed half-weight summation valid or establish the claimed freedom to use every choice satisfying only (6.4). The uniform high norm is required before invoking the inverse and again when evaluating the limiting frequency coefficient. Its absence is therefore a core proof gap. Neither this conditional repair nor a larger \(b_1\) repairs the neutral-mode obstruction in Problem 1.
result: Impact: The inverse cannot be invoked from the displayed induction hypotheses; limiting frequency also needs this high regularity.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Require b1>L+2(mu1+a2)(R-L)/a2, choose S sufficiently large and use theta=(R-L)/(b1-L). At b1=20000 kappa=8063/3997>2. Retain rho_(s+4tau+5), use high-norm smallness at low s and residual decay at high s. Missing2tau in(6.22) is absorbed by mu2>=4tau+3.

problems.title: Normalized stability lemma has wrong parameter scale and lacks the adapted state-difference bridge
problems.source_location: pp71–72(A.10)–(A.13),PropositionA.9(4) pp74–77 recurrence(A.26) p38(4.26) p65 limiting-frequency inclusion
claim: Normalized c satisfies Delta c<=C(Delta c0+epsilon2 Delta rho) with proof c0=0.
analysis: Proposition A.9(4), p. 72, gives a state-difference estimate for the normalized correction \(c\) with the scaling of a full transport speed. With the proof’s definition \(c_0=0\), a constant-coefficient example contradicts that estimate. The bridge to (4.26) requires a corrected statement and explicit difference hypotheses.

The homological forcing has no nonconstant Fourier modes. The recurrence (A.26) gives \(\beta=0\) and \(c=r\) exactly after the first mean update. Consequently [eq:A9literal] (#eq:A9literal) would require \[|r_1-r_2|\mathrel{\leq_C}t^4|r_1-r_2|,\] which is impossible with a uniform constant. This is an exact test of the stated normalized lemma and its construction, not a numerical approximation to the patch solution.

Two plausible intended readings limit the conclusion. If \(c_0\) in part (4) meant \(\langle f_0\rangle\), the constant test would no longer contradict it; however, that is not the \(c_0=0\) defined by this proof and needs a new definition. If the left side meant the full speed \(c_{-1}+\epsilon_2c\), the factor \(\epsilon_2\) would have the expected scale. That reading changes the displayed quantity. Moreover, (A.10)–(A.11) give absolute state norms, not the state-difference assumptions needed for a general \(\Delta\rho\) conclusion.

The source invoked for the omitted proof, Hmidi–Roulley [HR21], Proposition 6.2 and (6.30), estimates differences of the full transport coefficient. Its parameter regularity and frequency cutoffs also differ from those in A.9. The actual primary statement was inspected; a citation to it does not resolve these normalization and hypothesis changes by itself.

In the specific application, (4.6)–(4.7) provide additional difference controls. A corrected estimate for the full coefficient could therefore still yield (4.26). The constant example does not disprove (4.26). The material issue is that the general lemma stated as its justification is false under its explicit normalization, and the necessary adapted stability proof is not supplied. Section 6.2 uses (4.26) to compare the limiting and finite-step Cantor inequalities, so this is a core dependency rather than an unrelated appendix assertion. A complete corrected stability lemma has not been verified here; its exact hypotheses, loss indices and parameter factors require restatement and proof.
result: Impact: The general lemma invoked to justify the necessary limiting-frequency stability is invalid under its explicit normalization; primary[48] controls full speed under different norms/cutoffs and does not supply the adapted bridge.

report: Abstract: This report examines the exact author manuscript arXiv:2302.07794v5 of Willie Rush Lim. An almost-tiling selection is impossible as literally stated, the initial-level construction of first-return domains degenerates, and a scale cutoff is off by one. Explicit bounded corrections preserve the quantitative conclusions examined. A prescribed-return-time transition and a geometric width comparison require proof supplements, which are distinguished from their original formulations. No counterexample to the principal theorems was established. The impossible selection is a Major defect in the core amplification proof; the other two findings have bounded local impact. Verified repairs and the remaining dependency limits do not certify the complete paper. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted mathematical review
Title: Technical verification of bounded-type Herman-ring estimates
# Identity, source, and scope

The paper is Willie Rush Lim, A priori bounds and degeneration of Herman rings with bounded type rotation number, arXiv:2302.07794v5, 9 September 2025, 59 PDF pages, [Lim], associated with DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01369-2 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01369-2). All locations below refer to this exact author’s PDF. Its printed page numbers agree with the PDF page indices. The journal’s typeset version was not obtained; neither textual equivalence nor the persistence of these observations in that version is asserted.

The available record comprises a complete reading of the source and bounded checks of its extremal-width, amplification, compactness, realization, and first-return arguments. This report integrates those preserved checks with targeted recovery of the outstanding proofs and page evidence. The coverage ledger distinguishes reading, verified derivation, externally invoked results, and incomplete independent reconstruction. The external results cited below were checked only in the documented relevant ranges; their complete foundational proofs were not reproduced. No author code was run. Missing author code is irrelevant to the mathematical assessments made here.
# Definitions and operative hypotheses

The principal family has fixed local degrees \(d_0,d_\infty\geq2\) at the superattracting fixed points \(0,\infty\), total degree \(d=d_0+d_\infty-1\), and an invariant separating Herman ring of rotation number \(\theta\). Every remaining critical point lies on its two boundaries. The rotation is of bounded type; write \(B=\sup_j a_j<\infty\) for its continued-fraction bound. Theorems for this family are not statements about arbitrary rational Herman rings.

Use the source conventions \(q_{-1}=0\), \(q_0=1\), \(q_n=a_nq_{n-1}+q_{n-2}\) and \(l_n=|q_n\theta-p_n|\). Lengths on the distinguished invariant set are measured in the rotation coordinate. Constants described as absolute may depend on \(d_0,d_\infty,B\). A quasicircle, a closed thick ring, and a boundary circle at the Siegel scale are different geometric cases. In particular, the latter scale requires the interval length to be no greater than the ring modulus.

The extremal width \(\mathcal W\) is the reciprocal of extremal length. For canonical horizontal types \(A,B\) the weighted quantity is \(Z=\mathcal W(A)+2\mathcal W(B)\), so \(\mathcal W\leq Z\leq2\mathcal W\). For positive numbers write \(a\oplus b=ab/(a+b)\). The distinction between total covering degree and local degree over a marked collar is essential: thresholds can depend on the former, whereas the multiplicative gain used for uniform amplification must use the latter.
# An impossible narrow-gap selection

Problem 1 (Almost-tiling pieces cannot always satisfy the stated gap window).  In the deep-case proof of Theorem 5.1, pp. 23–24, the source chooses \(N=\lfloor\lambda/(3\tau^2)\rfloor\) level-\(n\) almost-tiling pieces with consecutive gaps in \(((\tau-1)l_n,\tau l_n]\), where \(\tau=10\). The same narrow-window selection is used in Lemma 6.2, p. 28. For golden-mean rotation and every even \(n\geq8\), a chain meeting this literal condition contains at most four pieces.
## Exact certificate and its assumptions

Put \(\theta=(\sqrt5-1)/2\) and \(\varphi=1/\theta\). For even \(n\), let \(q=q_n\), \(p=q_{n-1}\), \(Q=q+p=q_{n+1}\), and \(r=p/q\). The allowed initial points are \(c+i\theta\), \(0\leq i<Q\), and the pieces have positive angular length \(l_n\). Translation of \(c\) changes none of the following differences. The recurrence gives \[\frac35\leq r\leq\frac58,\qquad
  q_n\theta-p_n=l_n,\qquad
  q_{n-1}\theta-p_{n-1}=-\varphi l_n.\] The interval for \(r\) is invariant under the two-step update \(r\mapsto(1+r)/(2+r)\).

A permitted forward difference of initial points lies in \((10l_n,11l_n]\). If \(k\) is its time-index difference, then \(|k|<Q\). Unimodularity of consecutive convergents gives unique integers \(a,b\) with \[(k,m)=a(q_n,p_n)+b(q_{n-1},p_{n-1}),\quad
 E=a-b\varphi\in(10,11],\quad
 k/q=E+b(\varphi+r).\] If \(b\geq-3\), this last expression is greater than \(13/4>1+r\); if \(b\leq-6\), it is less than \(-11/5<-(1+r)\). Thus \(b=-4\) or \(-5\). The respective integer values are \(a=4\) and \(2\). There are exactly two possible steps, \[A=4q-4p,\qquad B_*=2q-5p.\] The admissible starting bands are \[L_+=[0,-3q+5p-1],\qquad L_-=[-2q+5p,Q-1].\] Step \(A\) sends \(L_+\) into \(L_-\). An \(A\) step followed by \(B_*\) lands in \([6q-9p,3q-4p-1]\), strictly between the two starting bands. Step \(B_*\) cannot land in \(L_-\). Consequently every chain has at most three steps, hence four pieces.

This conclusion also covers circular shortest-distance readings. A large forward difference would be at least \(1-11l_n\). A five-piece ordered chain can have at most one such gap; that gap and the other three differences, each greater than \(10l_n\), would total more than one. Thus the large-gap alternative does not evade the certificate. Endpoint conventions do not help, since both permitted errors are strictly inside the specified interval.

This is an analytic argument at arbitrarily deep even levels, not extrapolation from numerical experiments. For any fixed arbitrarily large \(\lambda\) with \(N\geq5\), \(n\) can be chosen beyond the finite deep-case thresholds. The independently written exact finite checks at \(n=14,20,28\) agree with it. For example, \(q=514229\), \(p=317811\) at \(n=28\), and the maximal chain \(560597\to0\to785672\to225075\) has only four vertices. Full exact arithmetic and the parameter-binding certificate are retained as evidence E1.
## Counterevidence, correction, and impact

This certificate refutes the intermediate combinatorial selection. It does not exhibit a rational map satisfying an arbitrarily large-width hypothesis and therefore is not a counterexample to Theorem 5.1.

A greedy replacement chooses the first subsequent piece with gap greater than \((\tau-1)l_n\). Adjacent initial-point separations are less than \(2l_n\), so the new upper gap bound is \((\tau+1)l_n\). The selected cluster has length \(L<(\tau+2)Nl_n\). The separation of the \(\tau\)-neighborhoods is unchanged. Moreover \(\tau P\subset\lambda I_j\) follows from \((\tau+1)L\leq\lambda l_n\), because at \(\tau=10\) \[(\tau+1)(\tau+2)N\leq 132\lambda/300<\lambda .\] Thus the same \(N\) and the same quasi-additivity gain \(\sqrt{N/2}\,K\) are available. The level offset remains \(O_B(\log\lambda)\), with no dependence on the modulus. The analogous fixed constants in Lemma 6.2 can be enlarged without changing their independence from \(\lambda\).

The supported assessment is Major. Theorem 6.1 and Proposition 4.2 feed the deep-case gain of Theorem 5.1; the impossible selection is an input to its Quasi-Additivity argument. That gain is then used in Theorem 8.1, Corollary 8.2 and the proof of Theorem A (pp. 44–46). This is an invalid derivation in a core proof. The verified wider-window repair retains the same gain and parameter dependence; repair status is recorded separately and no counterexample to Theorem A is asserted. The selection should be corrected at both source locations.
# The initial first-return construction

Here \(f=f_\theta\) is a unicritical boundary realization selected by Theorem C. Its unique free critical point is \(c_0=1\), with local degree \(d\), and \(c_j=f^j(c_0)\) lies on the invariant curve. These additional hypotheses, rather than the general multicritical family alone, justify the single-cycle covering argument below.

Problem 2 (The displayed enlarged interval degenerates at initial levels).  Theorem 10.2, p. 51, states a pointed first-return construction for every \(n\). Its proof uses enlarged-interval endpoints \(c_{q_n-q_{n-1}}\) and \(c_{q_{n-1}}\). For golden-mean combinatorics, \(q_0=q_1=1\), \(q_2=2\). At \(n=2\) both endpoints are \(c_1\); at \(n=1\) the proposed target \(c_{q_1}\) is an endpoint. The displayed construction therefore does not provide the asserted nondegenerate pointed collar at these levels.

These are exact integer equalities under the source’s own recurrence, verified against pp. 13 and 51. They are not extraction errors, roundoff, or an allegation that the stated first-return map cannot exist. A shortest-arc ambiguity can also occur at \(n=3\). Here is a repair with the required uniform dependence. For \(n\leq3\), put \(Q_0=(B+1)^3\), so \(q_n\leq Q_0\). The bounded-type estimate \[\|k\theta\|_{\mathbb R/\mathbb Z}\geq((B+2)|k|)^{-1}\] uniformly separates the finitely many relevant orbit points. Use the normalized uniform quasiconformal conjugacy supplied by the limiting family, fixing \(0,\infty\) and taking the invariant curve to the unit circle. Choose two concentric disks about the image of \(c_{q_n}\) with small radii \(r,2r\) depending only on \(B\). Their inverse images \(V,\widetilde V\) avoid all other critical values of \(f^{q_n}\) and have a uniform collar.

The component \(\widetilde U\) of the preimage containing \(c_0\) has degree \(d\): the only critical-value monodromy in the target disk is the \(d\)-cycle at \(c_0\); connectedness excludes extra fixed sheets in that component. Riemann–Hurwitz gives a disk. In Riemann coordinates the map is a rotated \(z^d\). Pulling back the smaller target disk and applying Koebe distortion yields bounded pointed shape. The full argument, including the normalization that keeps \(0,\infty\) separated, is retained in E2.

The assessment is Minor: the defect concerns a finite prefix of the specific construction. The repaired statement retains the uniform dependence, and the subsequential rescaled limit in Corollary 10.3 is unaffected by deleting a finite prefix. No existence or compactness theorem is refuted. For the latter corollary, degree preservation was checked separately by writing each normalized map in Riemann coordinates as \(e^{i\alpha_n}z^d\); bounded pointed domains give nonconstant limiting Riemann maps. Bounded shape alone was not treated as a general no-degree-loss theorem.
# A boundary between the two scale regimes

Problem 3 (The Siegel-scale range starts one level too early).  Equation (8.1), p. 45, defines \(M\) by \(l_{M+1}\leq\mu<l_M\), but the subsequent text treats every \(n\geq M\) as Siegel scale. At \(n=M\) the interval length is \(l_M>\mu\), contrary to the earlier scale hypothesis.

This is a concrete mismatch of applicability, rather than a numerical counterexample to the final a priori bound. Set \(S=M+1\). Then the Herman range ends at \(n<S\) and the Siegel range starts at \(n\geq S\). In Lemma 8.3 the undefined cutoff \(N_1\) should likewise be replaced by the actual threshold \(S\). The passage through the transition band is then \(S\leq n_1<S+tm\). Since \(\mu<l_{S-1}\), the same bounded-type estimates give \(\mu/l_{n_1+1}\leq C^{tm+1}\). The fixed transition losses and the order of choices are preserved. Evidence E3 verifies pp. 45–46 and this substitution.

The assessment is Minor, supported by the one-level range correction and unchanged quantitative transition argument. Isolated incorrect interval labels elsewhere were not counted as additional substantive findings.
# Proof supplements and unresolved limits
## From a stopping time to the specified denominator

Proposition 7.2, p. 33, requests small horizontal width at the prescribed time \(q_{n+m_2}\). Its printed proof on p. 43 produces a time \(a=tq_{n+m}\), \(1\leq t\leq\bar t\). A small width at that stopping time does not by itself state the prescribed-time bound; a multiple of a convergent denominator need not be a convergent denominator.

For the proper disk covers and disjoint full marked continua used in Section 7, the finite-cover middle-cut argument supplies the needed supplement under its actual hypotheses. If \(a+b\leq q_{n+k}\) for fixed \(k\), the marked continua have local degree at least two, and the finite topology is controlled, it gives \[Z^{a+b}\leq Z^a+C(k,\lambda).\] The type-\(A\) once/type-\(B\) twice crossing argument, peripheral rectangles, and bounded canonical-restriction loss must be retained. For sufficiently large fixed \(k_0\), \(b\geq q_{n+k_0}\) ensures the required precritical encounters in the marked intervals. Choose the stopping offset \(m\geq k_0\) at the outset, and run the stopping argument with \(\eta=\delta/8\). Choose \(m_2\) with \(q_{n+m_2}\geq(\bar t+1)q_{n+m}\), using \(q_{j+2}\geq2q_j\). Then \(b=q_{n+m_2}-a\) is large enough, and \[\mathcal W(F^{q_{n+m_2}})\leq Z^a+C\leq2\eta K+C<\delta K\] after the permitted enlargement of \(K\). The order is \(\Delta,\delta\), then \(\eta,M,m,\nu,\bar t,m_2\), then \(C(\lambda,m_2)\), then \(K\). It preserves independence of \(m_1,m_2\) from \(\lambda\).

This is a proof-completeness clarification with a bounded supplement, not a verified false proposition. The step feeds Lemma 6.6 and Theorem 6.1 and should be written explicitly. Evidence E3 distinguishes the original stopping proof from the reconstructed bridge. No unrestricted monotonicity of widths under arbitrary branched maps is being assumed.
## The literal domain inclusion and the inequality actually used

The cut construction on p. 30 does not by itself certify the literal inclusion (6.3). No rational-map counterexample to that inclusion was obtained. For the required p. 32 width inequality, a direct replacement suffices: the new full, disjoint marked continua are compactly contained in the new disk and contain the old ones. A type-\(A\) leaf has an essential horizontal or vertical first-transition segment. A type-\(B\) leaf that hits the opposite enlarged continuum or leaves the new disk also has such a first-transition segment. Otherwise, nonzero winding in the complement of the opposite marked continuum forces a segment between different lifted copies of its own marked continuum. Overflow, the parallel law, and canonical maximality then give the desired horizontal-plus-vertical width bound with an absolute topological loss. This argument does not assert the disputed literal inclusion. Its full hypotheses and proof are in E3.

The geometric canonical-restriction statement in Appendix A.12 was also checked separately from the wording of Kahn’s weighted-arc-diagram corollary [Kahn]. A strip metric bounds the discarded bad-segment width by four per noncrossing arc class, giving a topology-dependent total loss. The stronger geometric statement was not silently attributed to a weaker external formula.
## A dependency that remains only partially reconstructed

The additional peripheral \(E\)-absorption and canonical reidentification in Section 7.1 was read in context, but its complete surgery with quantitative buffers was not independently rederived. The established restriction lemma does not, by itself, prove that additional operation. A separate stronger outer-buffer assertion on pp. 19–20, retaining a subfamily of an arbitrary original lamination, also remains uncertified: the checked rectangular-wave replacement supplies the width needed downstream but does not establish that its new vertical leaves belong to the original family. No counterexample to that stronger wording was constructed. These are limits of the audit, not confirmed mathematical defects. The principal conclusions also depend on external quasiconformal, realization, and extremal-length theorems that were invoked with checked hypotheses, rather than re-proved in their entirety.
# Positive checks and overall dependence

The recovered analytic checks support several potentially delicate parts of the argument. In particular, \[\bigl((a+c)\oplus(b+e)\bigr)-(a\oplus b)-(c\oplus e)
 =\frac{(ae-bc)^2}{(a+b)(c+e)(a+b+c+e)}\geq0\] for positive parameters, verifying the aggregation direction in (7.2). The scalar contraction in Lemma 7.14 satisfies \[1-\nu'=\frac{81}{10(20\kappa+29)}>0,\qquad\kappa>1 .\] These are exact identities, not empirical checks.

The global amplification choices are noncircular: fix the gain \(\chi\) first, then \(\Xi=2/\chi\) and its spreading constant, then \(\lambda\), and finally the large-width threshold. The fixed-map finite width bound is sufficient for the contradiction proving a uniform threshold; uniformity is not assumed at the start. The thick-ring transition preserves this logic with a finite band of levels.

For the degeneration argument, zero–pole separation prevents loss of degree. Uniform attracting neighborhoods exclude the free Julia critical points from colliding with \(0\) or \(\infty\); collisions among free critical points are allowed. For a zero-modulus limit, the postcritical set is the invariant curve together with the two attractors. The rotation-domain boundary theorem [McMullen] then excludes an additional rotation domain without assuming that its rotation is of bounded type. The realization input uses an explicit reviewer-constructed topological model together with the checked obstruction and surgery hypotheses of Zhang, Wang, and Shishikura [Zhang2, Wang, Shishikura]; Wang’s obstruction criterion alone was not quoted as arbitrary-tuple existence. Zhang’s quantitative proof was traced to obtain the required uniform dependence on a bound for the continued-fraction entries, instead of silently changing a literal \(K(d,\theta)\) statement to \(K(d,B)\) [Zhang]. The relevant Log Rule and local-versus-total-degree collar estimates were also checked in their primary formulation [DL].

Finally, for the unicritical family with \(m=d_0\), \(n=d_\infty\), \(d=m+n-1\), set \[Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}(-1)^j{d\choose j}z^j,\qquad
 P(z)=\sum_{j=m}^{d}(-1)^j{d\choose j}z^j .\] Since \(P+Q=(1-z)^d\) and \(Q(1)=(-1)^{m-1}{d-1\choose m-1}\ne0\), the formula \(F_c=-cP/Q\), \(c\in\mathbb C^*\), has no cancellation. The identity \[dQ+(1-z)Q'=(-1)^{m-1}\frac{d!}{(m-1)!(n-1)!}z^{m-1}\] gives the exact critical pattern and ramification total \(2d-2\). This does not imply that every \(c\) has a Herman curve. Conjecture D and parameter-plane illustrations were not treated as proved theorems.

analysis: In the deep-case proof of Theorem 5.1, pp. 23–24, the source chooses \(N=\lfloor\lambda/(3\tau^2)\rfloor\) level-\(n\) almost-tiling pieces with consecutive gaps in \(((\tau-1)l_n,\tau l_n]\), where \(\tau=10\). The same narrow-window selection is used in Lemma 6.2, p. 28. For golden-mean rotation and every even \(n\geq8\), a chain meeting this literal condition contains at most four pieces.

Put \(\theta=(\sqrt5-1)/2\) and \(\varphi=1/\theta\). For even \(n\), let \(q=q_n\), \(p=q_{n-1}\), \(Q=q+p=q_{n+1}\), and \(r=p/q\). The allowed initial points are \(c+i\theta\), \(0\leq i<Q\), and the pieces have positive angular length \(l_n\). Translation of \(c\) changes none of the following differences. The recurrence gives \[\frac35\leq r\leq\frac58,\qquad
  q_n\theta-p_n=l_n,\qquad
  q_{n-1}\theta-p_{n-1}=-\varphi l_n.\] The interval for \(r\) is invariant under the two-step update \(r\mapsto(1+r)/(2+r)\).

A permitted forward difference of initial points lies in \((10l_n,11l_n]\). If \(k\) is its time-index difference, then \(|k|<Q\). Unimodularity of consecutive convergents gives unique integers \(a,b\) with \[(k,m)=a(q_n,p_n)+b(q_{n-1},p_{n-1}),\quad
 E=a-b\varphi\in(10,11],\quad
 k/q=E+b(\varphi+r).\] If \(b\geq-3\), this last expression is greater than \(13/4>1+r\); if \(b\leq-6\), it is less than \(-11/5<-(1+r)\). Thus \(b=-4\) or \(-5\). The respective integer values are \(a=4\) and \(2\). There are exactly two possible steps, \[A=4q-4p,\qquad B_*=2q-5p.\] The admissible starting bands are \[L_+=[0,-3q+5p-1],\qquad L_-=[-2q+5p,Q-1].\] Step \(A\) sends \(L_+\) into \(L_-\). An \(A\) step followed by \(B_*\) lands in \([6q-9p,3q-4p-1]\), strictly between the two starting bands. Step \(B_*\) cannot land in \(L_-\). Consequently every chain has at most three steps, hence four pieces.

This conclusion also covers circular shortest-distance readings. A large forward difference would be at least \(1-11l_n\). A five-piece ordered chain can have at most one such gap; that gap and the other three differences, each greater than \(10l_n\), would total more than one. Thus the large-gap alternative does not evade the certificate. Endpoint conventions do not help, since both permitted errors are strictly inside the specified interval.

This is an analytic argument at arbitrarily deep even levels, not extrapolation from numerical experiments. For any fixed arbitrarily large \(\lambda\) with \(N\geq5\), \(n\) can be chosen beyond the finite deep-case thresholds. The independently written exact finite checks at \(n=14,20,28\) agree with it. For example, \(q=514229\), \(p=317811\) at \(n=28\), and the maximal chain \(560597\to0\to785672\to225075\) has only four vertices. Full exact arithmetic and the parameter-binding certificate are retained as evidence E1.
result: This certificate refutes the intermediate combinatorial selection. It does not exhibit a rational map satisfying an arbitrarily large-width hypothesis and therefore is not a counterexample to Theorem 5.1.

A greedy replacement chooses the first subsequent piece with gap greater than \((\tau-1)l_n\). Adjacent initial-point separations are less than \(2l_n\), so the new upper gap bound is \((\tau+1)l_n\). The selected cluster has length \(L<(\tau+2)Nl_n\). The separation of the \(\tau\)-neighborhoods is unchanged. Moreover \(\tau P\subset\lambda I_j\) follows from \((\tau+1)L\leq\lambda l_n\), because at \(\tau=10\) \[(\tau+1)(\tau+2)N\leq 132\lambda/300<\lambda .\] Thus the same \(N\) and the same quasi-additivity gain \(\sqrt{N/2}\,K\) are available. The level offset remains \(O_B(\log\lambda)\), with no dependence on the modulus. The analogous fixed constants in Lemma 6.2 can be enlarged without changing their independence from \(\lambda\).

The supported assessment is Major. Theorem 6.1 and Proposition 4.2 feed the deep-case gain of Theorem 5.1; the impossible selection is an input to its Quasi-Additivity argument. That gain is then used in Theorem 8.1, Corollary 8.2 and the proof of Theorem A (pp. 44–46). This is an invalid derivation in a core proof. The verified wider-window repair retains the same gain and parameter dependence; repair status is recorded separately and no counterexample to Theorem A is asserted. The selection should be corrected at both source locations.

report: Abstract: The reviewed source is the 152-page author manuscript arXiv:2405.10732v3. Seven substantive concerns are established within the inspected scope. They include an admissible counterexample to the full Sobolev-exponent claim of Theorem B, a sharp matrix counterexample to Lemma 2.6, failures of two advertised coefficient-field examples, an incorrect independent-sum tail bound, and two invalid proof dependencies. The report supplies explicit assumptions, calculations, counterevidence, and bounded repairs where proved. These findings support Major revision of the reviewed version; they do not establish that the uniformly elliptic homogenization theorem or the complete renormalization program is false. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

# Assumptions that govern the checks

The coefficient field is allowed to be nonsymmetric and microscopically degenerate. Its symmetric and skew parts are \(\mathbf s=(\mathbf a+\mathbf a^t)/2\) and \(\mathbf k=\mathbf a-\mathbf s\). The ambient space on p. 7 requires \[\mathbf s,\quad \mathbf s^{-1},\quad
 \mathbf k^t\mathbf s^{-1}\mathbf k\in L^1_{\rm loc},\] with positive symmetric part, up to irrelevant null-set representatives. Theorem B assumes \(\mathbb Z^d\) stationarity (P1), coarse ellipticity (P2) with \(\gamma\in[0,1)\), and the concentration condition (P3) with \(\nu>\gamma\). The sum in (1.17) is an average; the convention is explicit on p. 15. Treating it as an unnormalized sum would create a spurious objection.

The weighted solution spaces \(H^1_{\mathbf a}\) in (2.2)–(2.5) need not embed in ordinary \(H^1\). In contrast, the \(H^{-s}\) norms in (1.20) are ordinary fractional Sobolev dual norms, volume-normalized as in (1.32)–(1.33). This distinction is essential in Problem 1. For the matrix checks, coarse \(\mathbf k(U)\) is not required to be skew-symmetric; this is stated on p. 17 and allowed in Lemma 2.6.
# A principal conclusion with an inadmissibly broad exponent range

Problem 1 (P01: Theorem B, Dirichlet estimate (1.20); Major).  On p. 10, Theorem B asserts its gradient and flux error estimate for every \(s\in(0,\tfrac12)\). That quantifier is false under (P1)–(P3).
## An admissible field

Take \(d=2\), \(\alpha=4/5\), \(\gamma=9/10\), \(\nu=1\), and \(\beta=0\). Define the one-periodic function \[w(t)=\bigl(2\operatorname{dist}(t,\mathbb Z)\bigr)^\alpha\quad(t\notin\mathbb Z),
 \qquad w(t)=1\quad(t\in\mathbb Z),
 \qquad
 \mathbf a(x)=\operatorname{diag}(w(x_1),1).\] Changing the values on the integer planes changes no integral or weak equation. The field is bounded, symmetric, positive definite with this representative, and its inverse is locally integrable because \(\alpha<1\). It belongs to \(\Omega\) and has \(\mathbf k=0\), so \(H^1_{\mathbf a}=H^1_{\mathbf s}\).

Let the law be the Dirac measure at this field. It is \(\mathbb Z^2\)-stationary. Every centered random variable is zero almost surely, so (P3) holds with the parameters above and \(\Psi(t)=\exp(t^2)\), \(K_\Psi=3\). The additional measurability and sensitivity requirements only restrict which centered variables are tested; they do not affect this observation.
## A smooth datum with a singular weighted solution

Set \(L=1/4\), \(U=(-L,L)^2\), \(q=\pi/(2L)\), \(b(x_2)=\cos(qx_2)\), and \(g(x)=x_1b(x_2)\). The function \(g\) is smooth on \(\overline U\). Every ellipsoid \(E_1\) in Theorem A contains the unit Euclidean ball, since \(\overline{\mathbf s}\ge\bar\lambda I\); therefore \(U\subset E_1\).

Equation reference: eq:volterra. Fix any \(\varepsilon>0\) and put \(w_\varepsilon(t)=w(t/\varepsilon)\). On \([0,L]\) solve \[
 v(t)=\int_0^t\frac{F(r)}{w_\varepsilon(r)}\,dr,\qquad
 F(t)=c+q^2\int_0^t v(r)\,dr.\] The coefficient \(w_\varepsilon^{-1}\) is integrable, so this linear Volterra system has a unique absolutely continuous solution. For \(c=1\), \(v(L)>0\). By linearity choose \(c=L/v_{c=1}(L)>0\), so that \(v(L)=L\). Extend \(v\) oddly and \(F\) evenly. Then \[-(w_\varepsilon v')'+q^2v=0,\qquad v(\pm L)=\pm L,
 \qquad u^\varepsilon(x)=v(x_1)b(x_2)\] solves the required equation and has boundary data \(g\).

The weighted energy is finite because \(\int w_\varepsilon(v')^2=\int F^2/w_\varepsilon<\infty\). Here is also a direct check of the precise zero-boundary closure. Write \(z=v-t\). Approximate \(z'\) in \(L^2(w_\varepsilon\,dt)\) by smooth compactly supported \(p_n\) on \((-L,L)\), first excluding the finitely many zero points. This implies \(L^1\) convergence by Cauchy–Schwarz and \(\int w_\varepsilon^{-1}<\infty\). For a fixed smooth compactly supported \(\chi\) of integral one, replace \(p_n\) by \(r_n=p_n-(\int p_n)\chi\). Then \(\int r_n=0\) and \(r_n\to z'\) in weighted \(L^2\). The primitives \(z_n(t)=\int_{-L}^t r_n\) are smooth, vanish at both endpoints, and converge uniformly to \(z\). The functions \(z_n(x_1)b(x_2)\in H^1_0(U)\) converge to \(u^\varepsilon-g\) in weighted energy and \(L^1\). Approximation of each by \(C_c^\infty(U)\) in ordinary \(H^1\) also converges in weighted energy, since \(\mathbf a^\varepsilon\le I\). A diagonal sequence proves \(u^\varepsilon-g\in H^1_{\mathbf a^\varepsilon,0}(U)\). The usual energy identity proves uniqueness in that weighted class.
