# A false large-contrast matrix bound
Problem 2 (P02: Lemma 2.6, (2.81)–(2.82); Major).  The stated linear-in-contrast upper bounds are false under the explicit algebraic hypotheses of Lemma 2.6, pp. 35–36.
## An exact admissible family

By [eq:rankone] (#eq:rankone), one eigenvalue of \(E_{*,1}^{-1/2}E_1E_{*,1}^{-1/2}\) in each scalar block is \(1\). The determinant ratio is \(t^2\), so the other eigenvalue is \(t^2\). Its distance from the identity is therefore \(t^2-1\), not bounded by \(6(t-1)\) when \(t>5\). For \(t=10\), the two false inequalities read \[81\le18,\qquad 99\le54.\] All entries and determinant identities have also been checked by the saved reviewer-authored exact-rational script. No numerical spectral approximation is needed.
## Failed step and a bounded repair

On p. 36 the relevant congruence has top-left term \(4s_*^{-1/2}k\,s_*^{-1}k\,s_*^{-1/2}\) after removing the skew part of \(k\). The proof substitutes \(s_1^{-1}\) for the middle \(s_*^{-1}\) and invokes (2.85). Since \(s_1\succeq s_*\), that substitution reduces a positive term and does not give an upper bound for the original expression.

Equation reference: eq:quadraticrepair. For a general pair satisfying the lemma’s assumptions, put \(t=\left\lVert s_*^{-1/2}s_1s_*^{-1/2}\right\rVert\). The valid quadratic estimate (2.86) instead yields \[\left\lVert s_*^{-1/2}(k+k^t)s_*^{-1/2}\right\rVert^2\le(t-1)^2.\] It also gives the sharp replacement \[
 t-1\le
 \left\lVert E_*^{-1/2}EE_*^{-1/2}-I\right\rVert
 \le t^2-1.\] Indeed, after the same congruence, the positive semidefinite gap has diagonal-block norms bounded by \(t(t-1)\) and \(t-1\). For a positive semidefinite block matrix, block Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its norm by the sum of those two norms. This proves the upper bound; the family above attains it. The \(t=1\) case follows by continuity or directly from the positive block inequality. In particular, the printed linear bound still follows for \(1\le t\le5\). This is a verified algebraic repair, not a reproof of every downstream homogenization estimate.
## Impact and counterevidence

The source uses (2.82) in Lemma 2.7, p. 37, and invokes Lemma 2.6 in the comparison leading to (2.98), p. 39. These are quantitative inputs to the renormalization argument. The failure therefore affects a supporting estimate tied directly to the main proof framework. Correcting one inverse while retaining the lemma’s conclusions is insufficient.

The matrix family need not be realized as the coarse matrix of a stationary field: realization is not a hypothesis of Lemma 2.6. Conversely, it would be unjustified to claim that this family refutes every subsequent field-dependent conclusion. In particular, the intrinsic contrast \(\Theta\) used in (2.98) differs from \(\widetilde\Theta_1\): for this family it is \((t+1)^2/4\). The example does not refute a bound linear in that larger quantity. The remaining task is to audit each invocation with the correct contrast and regime. Evidence: P02, the exact matrix certificate, and source images of pp. 35–36.
# The printed Poisson field is not elliptic

Problem 3 (P03: (1.28), Proposition 1.1, and Appendix D.1; Major).  The additive counting formula in (1.28), p. 13, need not have positive coefficients, even at arbitrarily small positive inclusion intensity.

For ordinary convolution with a Poisson point measure, \(N_r(x)=(1_{B_r}*\omega_2)(x)\) counts points in \(B_r(x)\). Set \(d=2\), \(\rho_1=0\), \(\Lambda=1\), and \(\lambda=1/2\). The printed coefficient becomes \[\mathbf a(x)=\bigl(1-\tfrac12N_r(x)\bigr)I,\] where \(r=1\) in (1.28) and \(r=1/3\) in (D.1), p. 135. Let \(\rho_2>0\) be arbitrarily small. The event of exactly three points in \(B_{r/2}\) and no other points in \(B_{3r/2}\) has probability \[\exp(-\rho_2|B_{3r/2}|)\,
 \frac{(\rho_2|B_{r/2}|)^3}{6}>0.\] On that event, every \(x\in B_{r/2}\) sees exactly these three points within distance \(r\), apart from null boundaries. Consequently \(\mathbf a=-I/2\) on a set of positive measure. This violates both the ambient positivity requirement and the claimed uniform lower bound. A small-intensity restriction cannot remove an event of positive probability. Positive high-inclusion counts likewise need not obey the claimed upper bound \(\Lambda\).

Appendix D.1 explicitly changes only the radius, not counting to occupancy. Its use of \(\mathbf a\le\Lambda\) and of the inverse field on pp. 137–138 therefore cannot validate the printed model. A possible revised model replaces each count by its occupancy indicator \(1_{\{N_r>0\}}\). Its values are \(1,\Lambda,\lambda,\Lambda+\lambda-1\), all in \([\lambda,\Lambda]\). This repairs that elementary ellipticity failure, but changes the defined random field; the full stated coarse-ellipticity and tail estimates for the revised model have not all been rederived here. The objection concerns the claimed example, not the conditional abstract homogenization theorem. Evidence: P03 and the Poisson-event certificate; source pp. 13, 135, 137.
# Matrix exponentiation does not provide the claimed ellipticity

Problem 4 (P04: Proposition 1.3 and Proposition D.3; Major).  The unrestricted nonsymmetric matrix-exponential examples are invalid, and the uniform ellipticity estimate fails even within the positive symmetric-part class.
## Failure of the Gaussian example

On p. 15 the source explicitly allows a nonsymmetric real matrix-valued Gaussian field \(g\) and defines \(\mathbf a=\exp(hg)\). Let \[J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad J^2=-I,
 \qquad g=F(I+J),\] where \(F\) is one nondegenerate mollified fractional Gaussian field with one of the stated Hurst parameters. Every matrix entry is \(F\) or \(-F\), with the required marginal law; the assumptions do not demand independent entries. Then \[\mathbf a=e^{hF}\bigl(\cos(hF)I+\sin(hF)J\bigr),\qquad
 \operatorname{sym}\mathbf a=e^{hF}\cos(hF)I.\] At a fixed point, \(F\) is a nondegenerate real Gaussian variable, so \(\cos(hF)<0\) has positive probability. By stationarity and Tonelli’s theorem, the expected measure of the negative set in any bounded region of positive volume equals that volume times the positive one-point probability. Thus there is positive probability of a positive-measure negative set. The failure cannot be removed by changing values on a null set; no continuity assumption is needed for this argument.
## A counterexample that already belongs to \(\Omega\)

The double-variable matrix \(A\) in (2.8), p. 20, has lower-right block \(\sec\theta\,I\). The bounds (2.22), p. 22, squeeze the coarse matrix of a constant field to that same pointwise \(A\) on every domain. Taking \(n=m\) in (P2\(\dagger\)), (2.71), p. 33, shows that any finite minimal scale must eventually give \(A(\square_m)\preceq E_0\). But Proposition D.3 claims \(E_0=C\exp(18h^2)I\), with \(C=C(d)\) independent of \(\theta\). As \(\theta\uparrow\pi/2\), \(\sec\theta\) is unbounded. No finite universal \(C\) works, and delaying the scale cannot improve a constant matrix. The asserted tail bound forces the scale to be finite, so it does not remove this contradiction.

The specific estimate used near p. 149, \(\left\lVert A\right\rVert\le(1+\left\lVert\mathbf a\right\rVert^2)\left\lVert\mathbf a^{-1}\right\rVert\), also fails: the right side is \(2\) for this orthogonal rotation, whereas \(\left\lVert A\right\rVert\ge\sec\theta\).
## Impact and repair boundary

Invertibility and bounded singular values of \(\exp(g)\) do not control its symmetric part. The negative example addresses the stated class; the positive rotation family addresses the quantitative claim even after positivity is imposed. Both are relevant counterevidence to a mere implicit-ellipticity defense. Symmetric \(g\) would make \(\exp(g)\) positive definite, with inverse bounds controlled by \(e^{\left\lVert g\right\rVert}\); a sufficiently quantitative sector condition is another possible starting point. Neither observation certifies the source’s full probabilistic statement, constants, or mixed-entry dependence under such a revision. Evidence: P04, the rotation certificate, and pp. 15, 145, 149.
# A false tail bound for independent sums
Problem 5 (P05: Lemma C.2, (C.15); Major).  For \(1<\sigma<2\), the large-deviation term in (C.15), p. 129, omits essential dependence on the number of summands.

Let \(\sigma=3/2\), \(m=100\), and \(t=10^8\). Take independent \(X_i=\epsilon_iV_i\), where \(\epsilon_i\) are independent Rademacher signs and \(\mathbb P(V_i>u)=\exp(-u^{3/2})\) for \(u\ge0\). Then \(\mathbb EX_i=0\) and \(\mathbb P(|X_i|>u)=\exp(-u^{3/2})\), so every required weak Orlicz bound holds with scale one.

The event \(X_i>t/m\) for all \(i\) implies \(\sum_iX_i>t\) and has logarithm \[-100\log2-10^{11}>-100000000100.\] The two quantities inside the maximum on the right of (C.15) have logarithms \[-\frac{t^2}{40m}=-2500000000000,\qquad
 \log1024-\frac{t^{3/2}}3
 <10-\frac{10^{12}}3.\] Both are strictly smaller than the logarithm of the exhibited event. Thus the claimed upper bound is false. These comparisons use exact integer bounds and \(\log2<1\); no floating-point evaluation of exponentially small probabilities is involved.

The source starts with the correct Chernoff product (C.17), but on p. 131 inserts a one-variable moment-generating-function bound without retaining its \(m\)th power. The same all-positive event, at general \(m\), has leading logarithm \(-m^{1-\sigma}t^\sigma\). A uniform large-deviation exponent cannot be independent of \(m\) in the claimed way.

This is a substantive error in an explicit probabilistic ingredient of the quantitative framework. It does not by itself refute the weaker normalized Orlicz estimate (C.16), all of Appendix C, or Theorem A. Those conclusions would require a valid independent-sum argument, including its actual constants. A corrected Chernoff calculation must retain the product and optimize at the appropriate \(t/m\) scale. A full replacement with the printed numerical constants has not been verified here. Evidence: P05 and the exact tail certificate, source pp. 129–131.
# The renormalization reduction does not meet its stated premises

Problem 6 (P06: scale selection in Section 3.1; Major proof dependency).  The determinant argument and its application on p. 54 have incompatible normalizations and scale budgets. A further strengthened hypothesis is used on pp. 55–57 without following from the stated one.
## Determinant normalization and the missing scale factor

The source defines \(\Xi_j=\det(\overline A_j)^{1/d}\) in (2.107), p. 41. If \(B\succeq C>0\) but \(B\npreceq(1+\delta_1)C\), at least one eigenvalue of \(C^{-1/2}BC^{-1/2}\) exceeds \(1+\delta_1\), and all are at least one. The determinant ratio therefore gives only \[\bigl(\det C/\det B\bigr)^{1/d}
 \le(1+\delta_1)^{-1/d},\] whereas Lemma 3.4 uses \((1+\delta_1)^{-1}\). The discrepancy is witnessed exactly in the same block-algebraic class. Take \(d=2\), \(\delta_1=\sigma=1/2\), \(h=1\), \(N=3\), \(r=25/16\), and \[\overline A_j=\operatorname{diag}(r^{3-j},1,1,1),\qquad 0\le j\le3.\] These matrices are decreasing and have the prescribed block form with \(k=0\) and \(s\succeq s_*=I\). The printed count \(N\ge\lceil4\log2\rceil=3\) holds. Every required consecutive Loewner-closeness alternative fails, since \(r>3/2\), but \(\Xi_3/\Xi_0=r^{-3/2}=64/125>1/2\). This refutes the matrix inference used by the proof. It is not a claim that this finite sequence has been realized by an admissible random coefficient field.

A sufficient matrix-only repair is \[N\ge h\left\lceil2d\,\delta_1^{-1}|\log\sigma|\right\rceil,\] using \(\log(1+\delta_1)\ge\delta_1/2\). The application (3.9) has a second problem: it sets \(\delta_1=\delta\sigma^2/2\) and \(h=2n\), but takes \[N/h=\left\lceil2\delta^{-1}|\log\sigma|\right\rceil.\] Even the printed lemma requires \(\lceil4\delta^{-1}\sigma^{-2}|\log\sigma|\rceil\); the repaired matrix argument requires \(\lceil4d\delta^{-1}\sigma^{-2}|\log\sigma|\rceil\). For \(d=2\) and \(\delta=\sigma=1/2\), the three counts are respectively \(3\), \(23\), and \(45\). The missing \(\sigma^{-2}\) cannot be absorbed into a universal constant as \(\sigma\downarrow0\).
## The strengthened hypothesis is not automatic

The first term of (3.5), p. 54, is \(\Pi3^{-(1-\beta)\ell/4}\). The purported repeat (3.11), p. 55, instead uses \[\frac{K_{\Psi_{\mathcal S}}^{3\gamma}}{1-\gamma}
 \Pi3^{-(1-\beta)\ell/4},\] and that stronger estimate is used on p. 57. Here is a complete parameter check that survives arbitrarily small \(\delta\). Let \(q\ge1\) be any integer and set \[\begin{gathered}
 d=2,\quad\beta=7/8,\quad\gamma=1/2,\quad\nu=1,\quad
 \Pi=2,\quad K_\Psi=3,\quad K_{\Psi_{\mathcal S}}=3^{100},\\
 \delta=3^{-q},\qquad \sigma=1/2,\qquad
 \ell=3296+32q,\qquad m=100\ell.
 \end{gathered}\] The four terms in (3.5) are \[2\,3^{-103-q},\quad
 2\,3^{-95-q},\quad
 256\,3^{-96-32q},\quad
 2\,3^{-1648-16q}.\] Each is at most \(\delta\sigma^2=\tfrac14\,3^{-q}\). The strengthened first term in (3.11) is instead \(4\,3^{47-q}\), whose ratio to that threshold is \(16\,3^{47}>1\).

These parameters are consistent with an actual law: take the constant field \(\mathbf a=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), a Dirac measure, \(E_0=\operatorname{diag}(2,1,1/2,1)\), \(\mathcal S=0\), and \(\Psi=\Psi_{\mathcal S}=\exp(t)\). The allowed growth constants need not be minimal, so \(K_{\Psi_{\mathcal S}}=3^{100}\) is admissible. The contrast is \(\Theta=1\), \(\Pi=2\), and (3.6) holds exactly. For any positive \(\delta_0(d)\), choose \(q\) large enough. The strengthened premise still fails. ## Impact, a surviving iteration, and repair limits

These steps are the reduction to the central one-step estimate. The direct block-count repair introduces a \(\sigma^{-2}|\log\sigma|\) cost. It does not by itself recover the displayed uniform-in-\(\sigma\) scale in Proposition 3.2. The strengthening of (3.5) also needs a corresponding scale choice.

There is useful counterevidence to an overbroad negative conclusion. At a fixed target \(\sigma_0(d)>0\), the extra factors are dimensional constants. Conditional on the other one-step hypotheses, the logarithmic-in-contrast step cost and logarithmic iteration count still have the order needed for an \(\exp(C\log^2\text{contrast})\) scale.

The shifted-product iteration on pp. 72–73 can also be made rigorous in its needed range by a positive part. If decreasing \(x_j,y_j\ge1\) satisfy \[\min\{(x_{j+1}-1)/x_j,\ y_{j+1}/y_j\}\le\sigma,\qquad
 0<\sigma\le1/2,\] set \(u_j=(x_j-1-2\sigma)_+\). Either the first alternative gives \(u_{j+1}\le\sigma u_j\), or the second gives \(u_{j+1}y_{j+1}\le\sigma u_jy_j\) by monotonicity. Thus \(u_ky_k\le\sigma^k x_0y_0\le\sigma^k\Theta^2\). For \(k\ge\lceil2\log_2\Theta\rceil+1\), this yields \(x_k\le1+3\sigma\). The unnecessary untruncated product estimate is not being accepted as a proof outside that stopping regime.

This is a material proof-closure concern, with exact local repairs and a precise limit on the preserved asymptotic claim. No proof is given here of a false Theorem A or of the full arbitrary-\(\sigma\) replacement. Evidence: P06, the two exact arithmetic certificates, and source pp. 41, 54–55, 57, 72–73.
# The stated finite-range decomposition is not constructed

Problem 7 (P07: Appendix D.2.2, (D.18)–(D.22); Major proof dependency).  The printed cutoffs cannot exist, and the subsequent heat-convolution definition does not produce the finite-range fields required by the example-verification argument.

On pp. 142–143 the annuli \(B_{3^n}\setminus B_{3^{n-1}}\), \(n\in\mathbb Z\), tile punctured space apart from boundaries. The requirements \[1_{B_{3^n}\setminus B_{3^{n-1}}}\le\eta_n,\qquad
 \eta_n\ge0,\qquad \sum_n\eta_n=1\] force \(\eta_n=1\) inside its own annulus and zero inside every other one. Approaching an annular boundary from the two sides gives a jump. No continuous, and hence no smooth compactly supported, family satisfies the stated conditions.

Even for the intended product kernels, use of the same white noise does not make entire fields at different scales independent. Translate one nonzero kernel so that it overlaps a positive open part of another. Their cross-covariance is then positive. Disjoint centered annuli could at most supply a fixed-center observation. Cross-scale independence is fortunately not an assumption of Propositions D.2 and D.4, so it need not be restored.
## A valid local construction and its boundary

Choose a smooth radial nonincreasing \(\chi\) equal to one on \(B_1\) and zero outside \(B_{3/2}\), and set \[\eta_n(x)=\chi(3^{-n}x)-\chi(3^{1-n}x),\qquad
 \widetilde F_{\sigma,n}(x)
 =\int k_\alpha(y-x)\eta_n(y-x)\,W(dy).\] The cutoffs are nonnegative and smooth, sum to one off the origin, and have the required dilation relation; the impossible indicator lower bound is removed. Each product kernel is supported in \(B_{(3/2)3^n}\), so the field has dependence range at most \(3^{n+1}\). White-noise scaling gives \[\widetilde F_{\sigma,n}\ \stackrel{\rm law}{=}\
 3^{-n\sigma}\widetilde F_{\sigma,0}(3^{-n}\,\cdot).\] The field and gradient variance scales are respectively \(3^{-2n\sigma}\) and \(3^{-2n(1+\sigma)}\).

For a Schwartz test function, the convolved partial kernels converge in \(L^2\) to \(k_\alpha*\psi\): the singularity is locally integrable because \(\sigma<d/2\), and the decay at infinity is square-integrable because \(\sigma>0\). Dominated convergence and white-noise isometry give the distributional decomposition. No cross-scale independence is asserted.

This proves a qualitative replacement with finite range, scaling, and distributional convergence. It does not certify all uniform dependence on \(\sigma\) in the subsequent supremum estimates, nor the mixing assertions referred to external work. The original construction fails to supply a necessary premise for the Gaussian-field application, which is the reason for its substantive classification. The finding is not a counterexample to Proposition 1.2 itself. Evidence: P07, source pp. 142–143, and the saved reconstruction.

problems.title: Theorem B (1.20) fails for its full Sobolev-exponent range
problems.source_location: p10 Theorem B first bullet,(1.20) pp7-9 (P1)-(P3) p16 (1.32)-(1.33) pp110-111 proof
claim: Recorded check: Theorem B (1.20) fails for its full Sobolev-exponent range
analysis: On p. 10, Theorem B asserts its gradient and flux error estimate for every \(s\in(0,\tfrac12)\). That quantifier is false under (P1)–(P3).

Take \(d=2\), \(\alpha=4/5\), \(\gamma=9/10\), \(\nu=1\), and \(\beta=0\). Define the one-periodic function \[w(t)=\bigl(2\operatorname{dist}(t,\mathbb Z)\bigr)^\alpha\quad(t\notin\mathbb Z),
 \qquad w(t)=1\quad(t\in\mathbb Z),
 \qquad
 \mathbf a(x)=\operatorname{diag}(w(x_1),1).\] Changing the values on the integer planes changes no integral or weak equation. The field is bounded, symmetric, positive definite with this representative, and its inverse is locally integrable because \(\alpha<1\). It belongs to \(\Omega\) and has \(\mathbf k=0\), so \(H^1_{\mathbf a}=H^1_{\mathbf s}\).

Let the law be the Dirac measure at this field. It is \(\mathbb Z^2\)-stationary. Every centered random variable is zero almost surely, so (P3) holds with the parameters above and \(\Psi(t)=\exp(t^2)\), \(K_\Psi=3\). The additional measurability and sensitivity requirements only restrict which centered variables are tested; they do not affect this observation.

Set \(L=1/4\), \(U=(-L,L)^2\), \(q=\pi/(2L)\), \(b(x_2)=\cos(qx_2)\), and \(g(x)=x_1b(x_2)\). The function \(g\) is smooth on \(\overline U\). Every ellipsoid \(E_1\) in Theorem A contains the unit Euclidean ball, since \(\overline{\mathbf s}\ge\bar\lambda I\); therefore \(U\subset E_1\).

Equation reference: eq:volterra. Fix any \(\varepsilon>0\) and put \(w_\varepsilon(t)=w(t/\varepsilon)\). On \([0,L]\) solve \[
 v(t)=\int_0^t\frac{F(r)}{w_\varepsilon(r)}\,dr,\qquad
 F(t)=c+q^2\int_0^t v(r)\,dr.\] The coefficient \(w_\varepsilon^{-1}\) is integrable, so this linear Volterra system has a unique absolutely continuous solution. For \(c=1\), \(v(L)>0\). By linearity choose \(c=L/v_{c=1}(L)>0\), so that \(v(L)=L\). Extend \(v\) oddly and \(F\) evenly. Then \[-(w_\varepsilon v')'+q^2v=0,\qquad v(\pm L)=\pm L,
 \qquad u^\varepsilon(x)=v(x_1)b(x_2)\] solves the required equation and has boundary data \(g\).

The weighted energy is finite because \(\int w_\varepsilon(v')^2=\int F^2/w_\varepsilon<\infty\). Here is also a direct check of the precise zero-boundary closure. Write \(z=v-t\). Approximate \(z'\) in \(L^2(w_\varepsilon\,dt)\) by smooth compactly supported \(p_n\) on \((-L,L)\), first excluding the finitely many zero points. This implies \(L^1\) convergence by Cauchy–Schwarz and \(\int w_\varepsilon^{-1}<\infty\). For a fixed smooth compactly supported \(\chi\) of integral one, replace \(p_n\) by \(r_n=p_n-(\int p_n)\chi\). Then \(\int r_n=0\) and \(r_n\to z'\) in weighted \(L^2\). The primitives \(z_n(t)=\int_{-L}^t r_n\) are smooth, vanish at both endpoints, and converge uniformly to \(z\). The functions \(z_n(x_1)b(x_2)\in H^1_0(U)\) converge to \(u^\varepsilon-g\) in weighted energy and \(L^1\). Approximation of each by \(C_c^\infty(U)\) in ordinary \(H^1\) also converges in weighted energy, since \(\mathbf a^\varepsilon\le I\). A diagonal sequence proves \(u^\varepsilon-g\in H^1_{\mathbf a^\varepsilon,0}(U)\). The usual energy identity proves uniqueness in that weighted class.

The source’s proof already exposes the restriction: p. 110 starts with \(s>\gamma/2\); (5.4), p. 86, requires a choice \(\gamma<\rho<2s\). The subsequent choices \(\rho=(1+s)/2\) and \(s=(1+\gamma)/2\) do not supply the stated full range. The printed sign in \((\rho-2s)^{-1}\) and the passage from decay of \(\mathcal E^2\) to decay of \(\mathcal E\) also require correction, but the counterexample does not depend on those textual mistakes.

This is a false principal conclusion for the reviewed version. It does not refute Theorem A, whose uniform ellipticity hypothesis excludes the example, or all other conclusions of Theorem B. A repair must restrict the exponent/topology or strengthen microscopic regularity. The written route suggests \(s>\gamma/2\) with \(\rho\in(\gamma,2s)\) and with the resulting dependence on the gap \(2s-\gamma\) tracked. That is a necessary proof-design boundary, not a certification of a replacement theorem with all original tail constants and quantifiers. Evidence: P01 and the complete saved periodic-counterexample proof, including the bounded helper’s coefficient-space and density cross-check.
result: Recorded evidence: Proof: Complete analytic coefficient, law, coarse-ellipticity, weighted-density, Volterra-solution and dual-test proof; no finite computation substitutes for the universal conclusion.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The example satisfies Omega, all stochastic hypotheses, U subset E1, smooth g and the exact weighted closure; Theorem A's uniform ellipticity is absent, so Theorem A is not refuted.

problems.title: Lemma 2.6 large-contrast algebraic bounds are false
claim: Recorded check: Lemma 2.6 large-contrast algebraic bounds are false
analysis: The stated linear-in-contrast upper bounds are false under the explicit algebraic hypotheses of Lemma 2.6, pp. 35–36.

By [eq:rankone] (#eq:rankone), one eigenvalue of \(E_{*,1}^{-1/2}E_1E_{*,1}^{-1/2}\) in each scalar block is \(1\). The determinant ratio is \(t^2\), so the other eigenvalue is \(t^2\). Its distance from the identity is therefore \(t^2-1\), not bounded by \(6(t-1)\) when \(t>5\). For \(t=10\), the two false inequalities read \[81\le18,\qquad 99\le54.\] All entries and determinant identities have also been checked by the saved reviewer-authored exact-rational script. No numerical spectral approximation is needed.

On p. 36 the relevant congruence has top-left term \(4s_*^{-1/2}k\,s_*^{-1}k\,s_*^{-1/2}\) after removing the skew part of \(k\). The proof substitutes \(s_1^{-1}\) for the middle \(s_*^{-1}\) and invokes (2.85). Since \(s_1\succeq s_*\), that substitution reduces a positive term and does not give an upper bound for the original expression.

Equation reference: eq:quadraticrepair. For a general pair satisfying the lemma’s assumptions, put \(t=\left\lVert s_*^{-1/2}s_1s_*^{-1/2}\right\rVert\). The valid quadratic estimate (2.86) instead yields \[\left\lVert s_*^{-1/2}(k+k^t)s_*^{-1/2}\right\rVert^2\le(t-1)^2.\] It also gives the sharp replacement \[
 t-1\le
 \left\lVert E_*^{-1/2}EE_*^{-1/2}-I\right\rVert
 \le t^2-1.\] Indeed, after the same congruence, the positive semidefinite gap has diagonal-block norms bounded by \(t(t-1)\) and \(t-1\). For a positive semidefinite block matrix, block Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its norm by the sum of those two norms. This proves the upper bound; the family above attains it. The \(t=1\) case follows by continuity or directly from the positive block inequality. In particular, the printed linear bound still follows for \(1\le t\le5\). This is a verified algebraic repair, not a reproof of every downstream homogenization estimate.

The source uses (2.82) in Lemma 2.7, p. 37, and invokes Lemma 2.6 in the comparison leading to (2.98), p. 39. These are quantitative inputs to the renormalization argument. The failure therefore affects a supporting estimate tied directly to the main proof framework. Correcting one inverse while retaining the lemma’s conclusions is insufficient.

The matrix family need not be realized as the coarse matrix of a stationary field: realization is not a hypothesis of Lemma 2.6. Conversely, it would be unjustified to claim that this family refutes every subsequent field-dependent conclusion. In particular, the intrinsic contrast \(\Theta\) used in (2.98) differs from \(\widetilde\Theta_1\): for this family it is \((t+1)^2/4\). The example does not refute a bound linear in that larger quantity. The remaining task is to audit each invocation with the correct contrast and regime. Evidence: P02, the exact matrix certificate, and source images of pp. 35–36.
result: Recorded evidence: Proof: Exact rank-one positive difference and generalized spectrum1,t^2; actual exact-rational certificate.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: No coefficient-field realization is needed for this algebraic lemma. Intrinsic Theta=(t+1)^2/4 differs from tildeTheta=t, so (2.98) and all later field-dependent results are not thereby refuted.

problems.title: The additive Poisson model can be negative
problems.source_location: p13 (1.28) p14 Proposition1.1 p135 (D.1) pp137-138 proof
claim: Recorded check: The additive Poisson model can be negative
analysis: The additive counting formula in (1.28), p. 13, need not have positive coefficients, even at arbitrarily small positive inclusion intensity.

For ordinary convolution with a Poisson point measure, \(N_r(x)=(1_{B_r}*\omega_2)(x)\) counts points in \(B_r(x)\). Set \(d=2\), \(\rho_1=0\), \(\Lambda=1\), and \(\lambda=1/2\). The printed coefficient becomes \[\mathbf a(x)=\bigl(1-\tfrac12N_r(x)\bigr)I,\] where \(r=1\) in (1.28) and \(r=1/3\) in (D.1), p. 135. Let \(\rho_2>0\) be arbitrarily small. The event of exactly three points in \(B_{r/2}\) and no other points in \(B_{3r/2}\) has probability \[\exp(-\rho_2|B_{3r/2}|)\,
 \frac{(\rho_2|B_{r/2}|)^3}{6}>0.\] On that event, every \(x\in B_{r/2}\) sees exactly these three points within distance \(r\), apart from null boundaries. Consequently \(\mathbf a=-I/2\) on a set of positive measure. This violates both the ambient positivity requirement and the claimed uniform lower bound. A small-intensity restriction cannot remove an event of positive probability. Positive high-inclusion counts likewise need not obey the claimed upper bound \(\Lambda\).

Appendix D.1 explicitly changes only the radius, not counting to occupancy. Its use of \(\mathbf a\le\Lambda\) and of the inverse field on pp. 137–138 therefore cannot validate the printed model. A possible revised model replaces each count by its occupancy indicator \(1_{\{N_r>0\}}\). Its values are \(1,\Lambda,\lambda,\Lambda+\lambda-1\), all in \([\lambda,\Lambda]\). This repairs that elementary ellipticity failure, but changes the defined random field; the full stated coarse-ellipticity and tail estimates for the revised model have not all been rederived here. The objection concerns the claimed example, not the conditional abstract homogenization theorem. Evidence: P03 and the Poisson-event certificate; source pp. 13, 135, 137.
result: Recorded evidence: Proof: Analytic Poisson event and exact count arithmetic.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Arbitrarily low positive intensity does not remove the event. No saturation convention is defined; AppendixD1 only changes radius.

problems.title: Nonsymmetric matrix exponentiation does not give the claimed ellipticity
problems.source_location: p15 Proposition1.3 p145 PropositionD3,(D.26) p149 pointwise bound pp20,22,33 (2.8),(2.22),(2.71)
claim: Recorded check: Nonsymmetric matrix exponentiation does not give the claimed ellipticity
analysis: The unrestricted nonsymmetric matrix-exponential examples are invalid, and the uniform ellipticity estimate fails even within the positive symmetric-part class.

On p. 15 the source explicitly allows a nonsymmetric real matrix-valued Gaussian field \(g\) and defines \(\mathbf a=\exp(hg)\). Let \[J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad J^2=-I,
 \qquad g=F(I+J),\] where \(F\) is one nondegenerate mollified fractional Gaussian field with one of the stated Hurst parameters. Every matrix entry is \(F\) or \(-F\), with the required marginal law; the assumptions do not demand independent entries. Then \[\mathbf a=e^{hF}\bigl(\cos(hF)I+\sin(hF)J\bigr),\qquad
 \operatorname{sym}\mathbf a=e^{hF}\cos(hF)I.\] At a fixed point, \(F\) is a nondegenerate real Gaussian variable, so \(\cos(hF)<0\) has positive probability. By stationarity and Tonelli’s theorem, the expected measure of the negative set in any bounded region of positive volume equals that volume times the positive one-point probability. Thus there is positive probability of a positive-measure negative set. The failure cannot be removed by changing values on a null set; no continuity assumption is needed for this argument.

The double-variable matrix \(A\) in (2.8), p. 20, has lower-right block \(\sec\theta\,I\). The bounds (2.22), p. 22, squeeze the coarse matrix of a constant field to that same pointwise \(A\) on every domain. Taking \(n=m\) in (P2\(\dagger\)), (2.71), p. 33, shows that any finite minimal scale must eventually give \(A(\square_m)\preceq E_0\). But Proposition D.3 claims \(E_0=C\exp(18h^2)I\), with \(C=C(d)\) independent of \(\theta\). As \(\theta\uparrow\pi/2\), \(\sec\theta\) is unbounded. No finite universal \(C\) works, and delaying the scale cannot improve a constant matrix. The asserted tail bound forces the scale to be finite, so it does not remove this contradiction.

The specific estimate used near p. 149, \(\left\lVert A\right\rVert\le(1+\left\lVert\mathbf a\right\rVert^2)\left\lVert\mathbf a^{-1}\right\rVert\), also fails: the right side is \(2\) for this orthogonal rotation, whereas \(\left\lVert A\right\rVert\ge\sec\theta\).

Invertibility and bounded singular values of \(\exp(g)\) do not control its symmetric part. The negative example addresses the stated class; the positive rotation family addresses the quantitative claim even after positivity is imposed. Both are relevant counterevidence to a mere implicit-ellipticity defense. Symmetric \(g\) would make \(\exp(g)\) positive definite, with inverse bounds controlled by \(e^{\left\lVert g\right\rVert}\); a sufficiently quantitative sector condition is another possible starting point. Neither observation certifies the source’s full probabilistic statement, constants, or mixed-entry dependence under such a revision. Evidence: P04, the rotation certificate, and pp. 15, 145, 149.
result: Recorded evidence: Proof: Matrix exponential identity; stationarity/Tonelli; exact constant-coarse sandwich and sec(theta) divergence.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The positive rotation family belongs to Omega, so an implicit positivity restriction does not rescue the uniform D3 estimate.

problems.title: Independent-sum tail (C.15) loses sample-size dependence
problems.source_location: p124 weak Orlicz definition p129 LemmaC2,(C.15)-(C.17) p131 Chernoff substitution
claim: Recorded check: Independent-sum tail (C.15) loses sample-size dependence
analysis: For \(1<\sigma<2\), the large-deviation term in (C.15), p. 129, omits essential dependence on the number of summands.

Let \(\sigma=3/2\), \(m=100\), and \(t=10^8\). Take independent \(X_i=\epsilon_iV_i\), where \(\epsilon_i\) are independent Rademacher signs and \(\mathbb P(V_i>u)=\exp(-u^{3/2})\) for \(u\ge0\). Then \(\mathbb EX_i=0\) and \(\mathbb P(|X_i|>u)=\exp(-u^{3/2})\), so every required weak Orlicz bound holds with scale one.

The event \(X_i>t/m\) for all \(i\) implies \(\sum_iX_i>t\) and has logarithm \[-100\log2-10^{11}>-100000000100.\] The two quantities inside the maximum on the right of (C.15) have logarithms \[-\frac{t^2}{40m}=-2500000000000,\qquad
 \log1024-\frac{t^{3/2}}3
 <10-\frac{10^{12}}3.\] Both are strictly smaller than the logarithm of the exhibited event. Thus the claimed upper bound is false. These comparisons use exact integer bounds and \(\log2<1\); no floating-point evaluation of exponentially small probabilities is involved.

The source starts with the correct Chernoff product (C.17), but on p. 131 inserts a one-variable moment-generating-function bound without retaining its \(m\)th power. The same all-positive event, at general \(m\), has leading logarithm \(-m^{1-\sigma}t^\sigma\). A uniform large-deviation exponent cannot be independent of \(m\) in the claimed way.

This is a substantive error in an explicit probabilistic ingredient of the quantitative framework. It does not by itself refute the weaker normalized Orlicz estimate (C.16), all of Appendix C, or Theorem A. Those conclusions would require a valid independent-sum argument, including its actual constants. A corrected Chernoff calculation must retain the product and optimize at the appropriate \(t/m\) scale. A full replacement with the printed numerical constants has not been verified here. Evidence: P05 and the exact tail certificate, source pp. 129–131.
result: Recorded evidence: Proof: Exact rational/integer comparisons of logarithms; actual reviewer-authored script exit0.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: This does not refute the weaker normalized(C.16) or the separate(C.31) argument; their exact constants were not re-proved.

problems.title: Renormalization scale selection does not supply its stated premises
claim: Recorded check: Renormalization scale selection does not supply its stated premises
analysis: The determinant argument and its application on p. 54 have incompatible normalizations and scale budgets. A further strengthened hypothesis is used on pp. 55–57 without following from the stated one.

The source defines \(\Xi_j=\det(\overline A_j)^{1/d}\) in (2.107), p. 41. If \(B\succeq C>0\) but \(B\npreceq(1+\delta_1)C\), at least one eigenvalue of \(C^{-1/2}BC^{-1/2}\) exceeds \(1+\delta_1\), and all are at least one. The determinant ratio therefore gives only \[\bigl(\det C/\det B\bigr)^{1/d}
 \le(1+\delta_1)^{-1/d},\] whereas Lemma 3.4 uses \((1+\delta_1)^{-1}\). The discrepancy is witnessed exactly in the same block-algebraic class. Take \(d=2\), \(\delta_1=\sigma=1/2\), \(h=1\), \(N=3\), \(r=25/16\), and \[\overline A_j=\operatorname{diag}(r^{3-j},1,1,1),\qquad 0\le j\le3.\] These matrices are decreasing and have the prescribed block form with \(k=0\) and \(s\succeq s_*=I\). The printed count \(N\ge\lceil4\log2\rceil=3\) holds. Every required consecutive Loewner-closeness alternative fails, since \(r>3/2\), but \(\Xi_3/\Xi_0=r^{-3/2}=64/125>1/2\). This refutes the matrix inference used by the proof. It is not a claim that this finite sequence has been realized by an admissible random coefficient field.

A sufficient matrix-only repair is \[N\ge h\left\lceil2d\,\delta_1^{-1}|\log\sigma|\right\rceil,\] using \(\log(1+\delta_1)\ge\delta_1/2\). The application (3.9) has a second problem: it sets \(\delta_1=\delta\sigma^2/2\) and \(h=2n\), but takes \[N/h=\left\lceil2\delta^{-1}|\log\sigma|\right\rceil.\] Even the printed lemma requires \(\lceil4\delta^{-1}\sigma^{-2}|\log\sigma|\rceil\); the repaired matrix argument requires \(\lceil4d\delta^{-1}\sigma^{-2}|\log\sigma|\rceil\). For \(d=2\) and \(\delta=\sigma=1/2\), the three counts are respectively \(3\), \(23\), and \(45\). The missing \(\sigma^{-2}\) cannot be absorbed into a universal constant as \(\sigma\downarrow0\).

The first term of (3.5), p. 54, is \(\Pi3^{-(1-\beta)\ell/4}\). The purported repeat (3.11), p. 55, instead uses \[\frac{K_{\Psi_{\mathcal S}}^{3\gamma}}{1-\gamma}
 \Pi3^{-(1-\beta)\ell/4},\] and that stronger estimate is used on p. 57. Here is a complete parameter check that survives arbitrarily small \(\delta\). Let \(q\ge1\) be any integer and set \[\begin{gathered}
 d=2,\quad\beta=7/8,\quad\gamma=1/2,\quad\nu=1,\quad
 \Pi=2,\quad K_\Psi=3,\quad K_{\Psi_{\mathcal S}}=3^{100},\\
 \delta=3^{-q},\qquad \sigma=1/2,\qquad
 \ell=3296+32q,\qquad m=100\ell.
 \end{gathered}\] The four terms in (3.5) are \[2\,3^{-103-q},\quad
 2\,3^{-95-q},\quad
 256\,3^{-96-32q},\quad
 2\,3^{-1648-16q}.\] Each is at most \(\delta\sigma^2=\tfrac14\,3^{-q}\). The strengthened first term in (3.11) is instead \(4\,3^{47-q}\), whose ratio to that threshold is \(16\,3^{47}>1\).

These parameters are consistent with an actual law: take the constant field \(\mathbf a=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), a Dirac measure, \(E_0=\operatorname{diag}(2,1,1/2,1)\), \(\mathcal S=0\), and \(\Psi=\Psi_{\mathcal S}=\exp(t)\). The allowed growth constants need not be minimal, so \(K_{\Psi_{\mathcal S}}=3^{100}\) is admissible. The contrast is \(\Theta=1\), \(\Pi=2\), and (3.6) holds exactly. For any positive \(\delta_0(d)\), choose \(q\) large enough. The strengthened premise still fails. The proposition’s conclusion is true for this constant field; the example proves a failed implication between proof premises, not a false homogenization conclusion.

These steps are the reduction to the central one-step estimate. The direct block-count repair introduces a \(\sigma^{-2}|\log\sigma|\) cost. It does not by itself recover the displayed uniform-in-\(\sigma\) scale in Proposition 3.2. The strengthening of (3.5) also needs a corresponding scale choice.

There is useful counterevidence to an overbroad negative conclusion. At a fixed target \(\sigma_0(d)>0\), the extra factors are dimensional constants. Conditional on the other one-step hypotheses, the logarithmic-in-contrast step cost and logarithmic iteration count still have the order needed for an \(\exp(C\log^2\text{contrast})\) scale.

The shifted-product iteration on pp. 72–73 can also be made rigorous in its needed range by a positive part. If decreasing \(x_j,y_j\ge1\) satisfy \[\min\{(x_{j+1}-1)/x_j,\ y_{j+1}/y_j\}\le\sigma,\qquad
 0<\sigma\le1/2,\] set \(u_j=(x_j-1-2\sigma)_+\). Either the first alternative gives \(u_{j+1}\le\sigma u_j\), or the second gives \(u_{j+1}y_{j+1}\le\sigma u_jy_j\) by monotonicity. Thus \(u_ky_k\le\sigma^k x_0y_0\le\sigma^k\Theta^2\). For \(k\ge\lceil2\log_2\Theta\rceil+1\), this yields \(x_k\le1+3\sigma\). The unnecessary untruncated product estimate is not being accepted as a proof outside that stopping regime.

This is a material proof-closure concern, with exact local repairs and a precise limit on the preserved asymptotic claim. No proof is given here of a false Theorem A or of the full arbitrary-\(\sigma\) replacement. Evidence: P06, the two exact arithmetic certificates, and source pp. 41, 54–55, 57, 72–73.
result: Recorded evidence: Proof: Analytic determinant comparison, exact rational matrix sequence, exact q-family scalar bounds, and a positive-part iteration repair.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The finite matrix sequence is not claimed realized by a random field. The constant-field witness satisfies Proposition3.3's conclusion. Fixed tolerance/exponents can retain log-squared contrast order conditional on the other steps.

problems.title: The printed fractional-field finite-range construction is invalid
claim: Recorded check: The printed fractional-field finite-range construction is invalid
analysis: The printed cutoffs cannot exist, and the subsequent heat-convolution definition does not produce the finite-range fields required by the example-verification argument.

On pp. 142–143 the annuli \(B_{3^n}\setminus B_{3^{n-1}}\), \(n\in\mathbb Z\), tile punctured space apart from boundaries. The requirements \[1_{B_{3^n}\setminus B_{3^{n-1}}}\le\eta_n,\qquad
 \eta_n\ge0,\qquad \sum_n\eta_n=1\] force \(\eta_n=1\) inside its own annulus and zero inside every other one. Approaching an annular boundary from the two sides gives a jump. No continuous, and hence no smooth compactly supported, family satisfies the stated conditions.

Even for the intended product kernels, use of the same white noise does not make entire fields at different scales independent. Translate one nonzero kernel so that it overlaps a positive open part of another. Their cross-covariance is then positive. Disjoint centered annuli could at most supply a fixed-center observation. Cross-scale independence is fortunately not an assumption of Propositions D.2 and D.4, so it need not be restored.

Choose a smooth radial nonincreasing \(\chi\) equal to one on \(B_1\) and zero outside \(B_{3/2}\), and set \[\eta_n(x)=\chi(3^{-n}x)-\chi(3^{1-n}x),\qquad
 \widetilde F_{\sigma,n}(x)
 =\int k_\alpha(y-x)\eta_n(y-x)\,W(dy).\] The cutoffs are nonnegative and smooth, sum to one off the origin, and have the required dilation relation; the impossible indicator lower bound is removed. Each product kernel is supported in \(B_{(3/2)3^n}\), so the field has dependence range at most \(3^{n+1}\). White-noise scaling gives \[\widetilde F_{\sigma,n}\ \stackrel{\rm law}{=}\
 3^{-n\sigma}\widetilde F_{\sigma,0}(3^{-n}\,\cdot).\] The field and gradient variance scales are respectively \(3^{-2n\sigma}\) and \(3^{-2n(1+\sigma)}\).

For a Schwartz test function, the convolved partial kernels converge in \(L^2\) to \(k_\alpha*\psi\): the singularity is locally integrable because \(\sigma<d/2\), and the decay at infinity is square-integrable because \(\sigma>0\). Dominated convergence and white-noise isometry give the distributional decomposition. No cross-scale independence is asserted.

This proves a qualitative replacement with finite range, scaling, and distributional convergence. It does not certify all uniform dependence on \(\sigma\) in the subsequent supremum estimates, nor the mixing assertions referred to external work. The original construction fails to supply a necessary premise for the Gaussian-field application, which is the reason for its substantive classification. The finding is not a counterexample to Proposition 1.2 itself. Evidence: P07, source pp. 142–143, and the saved reconstruction.
result: Recorded evidence: Proof: Boundary jump contradiction, positive convolution covariance, translated-kernel overlap; explicit corrected cutoff/product construction with finite range, scaling and distributional convergence.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Cross-scale independence is not required byD2/D4. A valid qualitative replacement exists. Proposition1.2 itself is not refuted.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the exact acquired 31-page publisher PDF of Kra, Moreira, Richter, and Robertson. It identifies a false density assertion in the motivating weak-mixing example and two missing-hypothesis problems in the stated uniformity estimates. Explicit counterexamples establish the failures. The required restricted uses are examined separately: the weak-mixing example retains progressiveness, normalized estimates retain the zero-seminorm argument, and the actual multiple-average coefficients are distinct. The report also records positive checks of the correspondence, progressive-measure construction, recurrence reduction, and final pronilfactor argument. No counterexample to the density finite sums theorem is established. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Review of
The Density Finite Sums Theorem
# Identity, version, and review boundary

The paper is The density finite sums theorem, by Bryna Kra, Joel Moreira, Florian K. Richter, and Donald Robertson, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01371-8 [paper]. Every source location below refers to the acquired publisher PDF, whose printed and PDF page numbers agree. Its first page reads Inventiones mathematicae (2025), 243:1–31, and records online publication on September 24, 2025. The publisher’s current landing page instead assigns the issue to January 2026 [record]. This bibliographic year difference is recorded without changing the supplied 2025 assignment or asserting equivalence to a newly downloaded file. The exact source hash, rather than a year label, identifies the reviewed object.

The preserved index contains only four target source/identity/manifest entries and no recoverable substantive report for this paper. The present work is therefore its necessary initial review. It is not an independent acceptance review. All 31 page texts were read in the root scientific conversation; bounded native helpers additionally checked the structural, uniformity, and final-progression arguments. Actual source images were used to resolve formulas and extraction artifacts. The scope is broader than an abstract-only assessment, but it is not an independent reconstruction of the complete Host–Kra structure theory or of every cited theorem.
# Quantifiers and the proof architecture

Theorem 1.1, p. 2, fixes an arbitrary finite \(k\). It produces a strictly increasing positive sequence \(b\) and a shift \(t\geq0\) such that every sum of \(m\) distinct selected terms, \(1\leq m\leq k\), lies in \(A-t\). Neither a single sequence working for all \(k\) nor an unshifted conclusion is claimed. For example, odd integers already rule out the unshifted conclusion when \(k\geq2\). No repeated-index sum is part of the assertion.

The dynamical statement requires full measure on the forward orbit closure of \(a\). Its reduction uses a Følner sequence in \(\mathbb N\) along which \(a\) is generic. This does not mean that \(a\) must be generic along the initial intervals, or that every open-set return sequence has density one. These distinctions matter in Problem 1.

The essential chain is Theorem 1.1 \(\leftarrow\) Theorem 1.2 \(\leftarrow\) Theorem 2.4 \(\leftarrow\) Theorem 3.3. Proposition 3.2 extracts an Erdős progression from a progressive measure concentrated on \(\{a\}\times X^k\). Theorems 4.8 and 4.9 provide, respectively, positive mass in a common shifted target and progressiveness. The latter uses Theorems 6.1 and 6.2. The uniformity estimates discussed below enter the proof of Theorem 6.2.
# A false density assertion in the weak-mixing example

Problem 1 (P01: Example 4.2, p. 11; Minor).  The displayed inclusion and the ensuing claim that the recurrence-time set has full density along every Følner sequence omit the distinguished zeroth coordinate of \(\sigma=\delta_a\otimes\mu^{\otimes k}\).

Equation reference: eq:mass. Put \(U_0=U_{k+1}=X\), as in the source. Direct evaluation gives \[\begin{aligned}
&\sigma\bigl((X\times U_1\times\cdots\times U_k)
 \cap T_\Delta^{-n}(U_1\times\cdots\times U_k\times X)\bigr) \notag\\
&\hspace{12mm}=
 \mathbf 1_{U_1}(T^n a)\,\mu(U_k)
 \prod_{i=1}^{k-1}\mu(U_i\cap T^{-n}U_{i+1}). \end{aligned}\] The condition \(\mu(U_0\cap T^{-n}U_1)>0\) on the source’s right-hand side is automatic when \(\mu(U_1)>0\); it cannot replace \(T^n a\in U_1\).
## An admissible counterexample

Take the two-sided fair Bernoulli shift \(X=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}\), with product probability \(\mu\) and the left shift \(T\). Disjoint-coordinate cylinder functions are independent once their supports are sufficiently separated; approximation by cylinder functions proves mixing, hence weak mixing. Choose a point \(a\) generic for \(\mu\) along \(\Phi_N=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), and put \[k=2,\qquad U_1=U_2=\{x:x(0)=1\}.\] Such generic points exist by the ergodic theorem. For every \(n\geq1\), \[\mu(U_1\cap T^{-n}U_2)=\frac14,\qquad
 \mu(T^{-n}U_1)=\mu(U_2)=\frac12 .\] Consequently the right-hand intersection printed in Example 4.2 is all of \(\mathbb N\). By [eq:mass] (#eq:mass), the left-hand positivity set is exactly \(\{n:a(n)=1\}\), since the measure there is \(\frac18\mathbf 1_{\{a(n)=1\}}\). That set has density \(1/2\), not one. This disproves the inclusion and the strong density claim under valid hypotheses. The same missing pointwise condition is visible already when \(k=1\).
## Complete local repair and impact

For general \(k\), write \[H=\{n:T^n a\in U_1\},\qquad
 D_i=\{n:\mu(U_i\cap T^{-n}U_{i+1})>0\},\quad 1\leq i<k.\] The positivity set is \(H\cap\bigcap_iD_i\). Weak mixing gives density one for each \(D_i\) along every Følner sequence. Along the particular sequence \(\Phi\) for which \(a\) is generic, the Portmanteau inequality for open \(U_1\) gives \[\liminf_N\frac{|H\cap\Phi_N|}{|\Phi_N|}\geq\mu(U_1)>0.\] Removing finitely many zero-density complements preserves this positive lower bound. Since \(|\Phi_N|\to\infty\), there are infinitely many admissible times. Thus \(\sigma\) is progressive, as intended. Moreover, \(\sigma(X\times(T^{-t}E)^k)=\mu(E)^k>0\) for every \(t\).

The correction restores the example’s required conclusion using its generic-point hypothesis. The false statement concerns an auxiliary full-density strengthening; it is not used as a replacement for the general proof of Theorem 4.9. The Minor classification follows from that verified dependency and local repair, not merely from the existence of some possible correction. Evidence is in P01, including the exact product calculation and the actually inspected p. 11 image.
# Missing normalization in the quantitative estimate

Problem 2 (P02: Theorem 6.6, p. 20, equation (6.6); Minor).  The estimate is stated for arbitrary bounded functions, while its constant depends only on \(k\) and its right-hand side is only homogeneous of degree one in the functions.

For \(k=3\), take a one-point probability system, with its identity transformation, and let \(\tau\) be the unique measure on its fourth power. This system is ergodic, \(\tau\) has the required invariance, and \(\tau_i=\mu\leq i\mu\) for \(i=1,2\). Set \(b(n)=1\) and \(f_1=f_2=M>0\). Every Følner average on the left of (6.6) equals \(M^2\). Every uniformity seminorm of a positive constant \(M\) equals \(M\), by the recursive definition. The claimed inequality is therefore \[M^2\leq C_3 M
 \qquad\hbox{for every }M>0,\] which is impossible for a constant \(C_3\) independent of \(M\). For \(k\geq3\), the same construction compares degrees \(k-1\) and one. This objection does not apply to the single-function case \(k=2\).
## The normalized and homogeneous versions
## Dependency and severity

Theorem 6.2 begins with \(\|f_i\|_\infty\leq1\) and uses this estimate to discard terms containing \(f_i-\mathbb E(f_i\mid Z_{k-1})\), whose supremum norm is at most two and whose \(U^k\) seminorm is zero. Dividing that difference by two, or applying [eq:homogeneous] (#eq:homogeneous), gives exactly the required zero limit. It does not create an uncontrolled constant in a nonzero error estimate. The tensor argument of Lemma 6.10 and the normalized version of Theorem 6.9 supply the remaining bound, subject to the restricted-coefficient correction in Problem 3.

The printed uniform estimate is false. Its actual use in the core proof requires only the normalized zero-seminorm conclusion, and that use survives the demonstrated homogeneous correction. This specific boundary supports a local Minor classification; no failure of Theorem 6.2 is deduced from scaling. Evidence is in P02.
# The multiple-average lemma needs coefficient restrictions

Problem 3 (P03: Lemma 6.7(iii), p. 21; Minor).  The lemma permits arbitrary positive integers \(c_1,\ldots,c_k\) and all \(k\geq1\). Its asserted \(U^k\) control fails both for repeated coefficients and, independently, for the stated one-function endpoint.
## Repeated coefficients

Use the two-sided fair Bernoulli shift on \(\{-1,1\}^{\mathbb Z}\) and let \(f(x)=x(0)\). This system is ergodic and \(|f|=1\). For every \(h\geq1\), \[\int (T^h f)f\,d\mu=0.\] Ergodicity and the definition of \(U^2\) give \[\|f\|_{U^2}^4
 =\lim_{H\to\infty}\frac1H\sum_{h=1}^H
       \left|\int(T^hf)f\,d\mu\right|^2=0.\] Take \(k=2\), \(c_1=c_2=1\), and \(f_1=f_2=f\). Every term of the average is \((T^nf)^2=1\). Its \(L^2\) norm is one, whereas the proposed upper bound is zero, for every finite \(C\). All unit-ball hypotheses hold. The obstruction is a repeated linear form, not a missing numerical constant.
## The one-function endpoint

Take the two-point space \(\{0,1\}\) with uniform measure and \(T(x)=x+1\pmod2\). It is ergodic. For \(f(0)=1\), \(f(1)=-1\), \[\|f\|_{U^1(\mu,T)}=\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|=0.\] With \(k=1\) and \(c_1=2\), however, \(T^{2n}f=f\) for every \(n\). The average has \(L^2\) norm one. The correct one-function limit is \(\|\mathbb E(f\mid\mathcal I_{T^{c_1}})\|_2\), which need not be controlled by \(U^1(\mu,T)\).
## Repair boundary and actual application

For \(k\geq2\), the bound needed here is valid for pairwise distinct nonzero coefficients, with a limsup if existence of the norm limit is not separately invoked. Host’s Proposition 1 [host] bounds the average, for each distinguished \(i\), by the box seminorm with directions \(c_i\) and \(c_j-c_i\) for \(j
e i\). All these directions are nonzero. The power comparison in Frantzikinakis–Kuca, Lemma 3.1 [fk], gives \[\|\cdot\|_{	ext{box}(c_i,(c_j-c_i)_{j
e i})}
 \leq R_i^{1/2^k}\|\cdot\|_{U^k(T)},\qquad
 R_i=|c_i|\prod_{j
e i}|c_j-c_i|.\] The cited comparison is valid on general measure-preserving systems for degree at least two. Real/imaginary expansion, if needed, loses only a finite factor depending on \(k\). The interval estimate transfers to arbitrary one-dimensional Følner sets by decomposing them into consecutive runs: the proportion in runs of length below \(L\) is at most \(L\) times the boundary-to-volume ratio. First choose large \(L\), then let \(N\) increase. This proves the restricted bound used downstream, with a constant depending only on the fixed coefficients and \(k\). For \(k=1\), one may use \(c_1=1\), or retain the invariant-factor norm for \(T^{c_1}\); replacing it by the \(T\)-invariant norm without further hypotheses is invalid. The FK dependency checked here is its specified author manuscript, not an asserted copy of its journal final version.

In Theorem 6.9, pp. 22–23, the coefficients are \(c_i=c/i\), where \(c=\operatorname{lcm}(1,\ldots,k)\). They are positive, integral, and pairwise distinct. Its \(k=1\) case can be proved directly: \(\nu_1\leq\mu\) and equality of total masses imply \(\nu_1=\mu\), and the mean ergodic theorem gives the required \(U^1\) norm. Thus the actual application falls within the valid restricted statement. In turn, Theorem 6.6 uses Theorem 6.9 for \(k-1\) functions; its smallest case is covered by that direct one-function argument.

These counterexamples disprove the lemma as printed, including a unit-bounded example with zero right-hand side. The impact is confined here to overbroad auxiliary hypotheses because the specific downstream coefficients and endpoint have been checked. The Minor assessment does not rest on a rule that a supporting lemma must overturn the main theorem to be serious; it rests on the verified applicability of the corrected version to this proof. Evidence is in P03.
# Positive checks and boundaries of the reconstruction
## Correspondence and positive-time genericity

For Theorem 2.3, pp. 6–7, a two-sided symbolic shift with the positive coordinates of \(a\) equal to \(\mathbf 1_A\) gives the exact return set to the clopen cylinder \(E=\{x:x(0)=1\}\). Weak-star limits of orbit averages on long intervals of positive \(A\)-density are invariant: translating an interval changes only its endpoints. They give \(\mu(E)>0\) and are supported on the forward orbit closure. The ergodic-component reduction retains positive mass on \(E\).

The claimed genericity along some positive Følner sequence can also be seen directly. Choose an ergodic generic point \(y\) in that orbit closure. For longer and longer initial orbit segments of \(y\), continuity allows a forward translate of \(a\) to shadow the averages of finitely many continuous test functions. A diagonal choice over a countable dense family gives intervals in \(\mathbb N\) on which \(a\) is generic for that ergodic component. This validates the forward-time requirement without assuming that \(a\) is a typical initial-segment generic point.
## Extraction from a progressive measure

In Lemma 2.2, the recursive neighborhoods remain neighborhoods of their specified points; the common convergence subsequence meets every finite set of requirements. Peeling the selected indices in descending order places each distinct-term sum in its prescribed target. In Proposition 3.2, the actual p. 9 image contains the closure bars on the nested sets and their intersection. Their loss in extracted text is not an error in the paper. Using a max product metric gives product balls, so the rectangular definition of progressiveness applies. Positive-mass open intersections meet the support, and smaller balls with compactly nested closures give the limiting progression.
## Disintegration, recurrence, and nilpotent structure

The marginal estimate in Lemma 4.6 has a direct explanation. If \(\xi_i\) is \(T^i\)-invariant, then \(i^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}T_*^j\xi_i\) is \(T\)-invariant and therefore equals the unique invariant measure of the ergodic pronilsystem. Positivity gives \(\xi_i\leq i m_{k-1}\). This also ensures that the integrals of conditional expectations in Definition 4.5 are independent of their almost-everywhere representatives. Disintegration then defines a positive probability measure \(\sigma\) with the stated marginals. Equivariance gives Lemma 4.7.

The use of a continuous topological factor includes intertwining on the relevant orbits, in particular at \(a\). Mere continuity of an almost-everywhere equivariant measurable map, without the topological factor property, would not justify evaluation at an exceptional point. The inspected lifting construction [sumsets] takes an orbit closure inside the product of the original system and its pronilfactors. The factor maps are coordinate projections and intertwine everywhere, including at the lifted point. The measurable graph map is used to identify the invariant measure and its ergodicity. Restricting the base to the orbit closure of \(a\) supplies the transitivity hypothesis. This validates the intended application without turning a purely almost-everywhere interpretation into an unproved finding.

In Theorem 6.3, setting \(c=\operatorname{lcm}(v_1,\ldots,v_k)\) and \(w_i=cu_i/v_i\) reduces the required rectangular intersection to a multiple-recurrence intersection for the measure-preserving map \(T_v\). For an arbitrary Følner sequence, residue classes have asymptotic proportion \(1/c\), and \(\Psi_N=\{n:cn\in\Phi_N\}\) is eventually nonempty and Følner. The factor \(1/c\) therefore preserves positivity. Furstenberg’s theorem applies without an ergodicity assumption on that system. The product-set hypothesis is essential; Example 6.4 correctly exhibits its failure for a nonrectangular subtorus.
## The final approximation argument

In Theorem 6.2, unit-bounded tensor products approximate a continuous \(G\) by finite linear combinations. A uniform approximation error \(\delta\) contributes at most \(2\delta\) to the difference of the two averages, without requiring \(\sigma\) to be \(T_\Delta\)-invariant. Conditional-expectation differences have zero \(U^k\) seminorm. The normalized forms discussed in Problems 2–3 consequently remove the unstructured factors. Marginal domination controls the continuous approximations to the remaining conditional expectations.

The pointwise-in-\(y\) estimate of Lemma 6.11 is particularly useful. For the quantity \(Z_N(y)\) in (6.24), it gives \(\limsup_N|Z_N(y)|\leq\varepsilon\) for every \(y\), and \(|Z_N(y)|\leq2\). Reverse Fatou applied to the squares yields \[\limsup_N\|Z_N\|_{L^2(\xi)}^2
 \leq\int\limsup_N |Z_N(y)|^2\,d\xi(y)
 \leq\varepsilon^2.\] This bypasses the p. 29 estimate that would otherwise need a factor two when bounding an \(L^2\) square by an \(L^1\) norm. The resulting error still tends to zero; no additional substantive problem is counted.

For (6.22), expand the square and use two copies of the nilpotent orbit space, with commuting actions corresponding to the two averaging variables and their common progression variable. Unique ergodicity of the joint orbit closure makes the joint Følner limit independent of order. For fixed progression parameter, the translation \(n\mapsto n-m\) changes a Følner average by a vanishing boundary error, so the inner difference tends to zero. For each fixed outer index, the needed inner limit exists: in the progression variable by orbit unique ergodicity, and in the averaging variable by the just-described vanishing. Uniform convergence when both indices are large then identifies both iterated limits, as in the bounded-Fubini principle of [bl]. This gives the required limit exchange and vanishing. The existence and structure of these pronilsystems remain explicit external inputs; their entire theory is not claimed re-proved here.

For \(k=1\), set \(\sigma=\delta_a\otimes\mu\) directly. Genericity sends the scalar average \(G(T^na)\) to \(\int G\,d\mu\), and the Følner mean ergodic theorem sends the other average to the same constant in \(L^2(\mu)\). This proves Theorem 6.2 at that endpoint without applying Theorem 6.6 outside its stated range.
# Conclusion

The reviewed version needs local correction of three mathematical statements. Problems P01–P03 are supported by exact counterexamples and specific repairs. Their uses in the main argument have been traced: no failure of the asserted density finite sums conclusion has been established within this scope. This is not a certification that no other issue exists.

report: Abstract: This initial review concerns the supplied 84-page publisher PDF of the article by Arul Shankar, Anders Södergren and Nicolas Templier. It establishes a prime-level hypothesis missing from the cited subconvexity argument, an incorrect extension of secondary residue weights to prime powers, a noncongruence obstruction for the stated all-order local-specification indicator, and a counterexample to the border-range estimate within the parameter range actually used in its proof. These are substantial defects in essential inputs; they do not constitute counterexamples to the article’s main nonvanishing conclusions. # Mathematical framework and checked dependencies

The article studies \(L(s,\rho_K)=\zeta_K(s)/\zeta_{\mathbb Q}(s)\) for cubic fields, where \(\rho_K\) is the two-dimensional standard Artin representation. For a non-Galois cubic field it is irreducible, the finite conductor is \(D_K=|\operatorname{Disc}(K)|\), and \(L(1/2,\rho_K)\) is real. Since \(\zeta_{\mathbb Q}(1/2)<0\), positive \(L(1/2,\rho_K)\) corresponds to negative \(\zeta_K(1/2)\). The sign follows, for example, from \(\zeta(s)=\eta(s)/(1-2^{1-s})\) and \(\eta(s)>0\) for real \(0<s<1\). This sign conversion was checked rather than inferred from a numerical sample.

Binary cubic forms are acted on by the twisted action \(g\cdot f(x,y)=(\det g)^{-1}f((x,y)g)\). Discriminants are homogeneous of degree four in the coefficients. Integral orbits parametrize cubic orders; maximality, the generic \(\mathbb Q_p\)-algebra, and the splitting type of a possibly nonmaximal reduction are different conditions. The distinction is essential in Problems 2 and 3.

The finite calculations supporting the positive local checks included all 144 entries of the relevant Fourier-table tests at \(p=2,5,7,11\), and direct maximality/lift enumerations modulo \(p^2\) at \(p=2,3,5\). Problem 1 (P01: the cited subconvexity theorem has an unmet prime-level hypothesis).  Severity: Major.
## Original claim and exact location

Equation reference: eq:subconv. Theorem 4.1, p. 57 (PDF 25), asserts, for every cubic field \(K\), \[
 |L(1/2+it,\rho_K)|
 \ll_{\varepsilon}(1+|t|)^{O(1)}D_K^{1/4-1/128+\varepsilon}.\] For the \(S_3\) case its proof identifies a weight-zero or weight-one automorphic form of level \(D_K\) and invokes Blomer–Khan, Theorem 1. The inspected theorem in the Blomer–Khan arXiv version [BK] assumes a prime level \(q\) and a primitive central character. The article gives no reduction from arbitrary cubic discriminants to prime level. The claimed numerical savings are then used in the later \(\delta\)-dependent bounds and the numerical lower bounds of Theorem 3, pp. 35–36 (PDF 3–4).
## A concrete failure of the invocation

Let \(K=\mathbb Q(\theta)\), where \[f(T)=T^3-5T+1.\] The only possible rational roots are \(\pm1\), and \(f(1)=-3\), \(f(-1)=5\). Thus \(f\) is irreducible. Its discriminant is \[-4(-5)^3-27=473=11\cdot43.\] It is squarefree, so \(\mathbb Z[\theta]\) is maximal and \(D_K=473\). It is positive and nonsquare, so \(K\) is a totally real non-Galois cubic field. The associated Artin conductor is therefore the composite integer 473. It does not satisfy the prime-level hypothesis of the theorem invoked.

This example also lies in the type of \(S_3\) family used in the article: modulo 2, \(T^3+T+1\) has no root and is irreducible; modulo 3, \[T^3-5T+1=(T-1)(T^2+T+2),\] and the quadratic factor has nonsquare discriminant 2. Consequently the field has inert type \((3)\) at 2 and mixed type \((12)\) at 3. The obstruction is not removed by the later use of two auxiliary splitting conditions.

This proves a failure of the cited theorem’s applicability. It does not disprove the estimate [eq:subconv] (#eq:subconv): one field cannot by itself contradict a uniform asymptotic bound with an unspecified constant. Nor does the check establish that no alternative theorem could supply the requested saving. It establishes that the proof given has not supplied it. The cyclic case, handled separately by a Burgess-type estimate, does not repair the missing \(S_3\) argument.

Problem 3 (P03: the stated generic-algebra indicator is not a fixed congruence function on all orders).  Severity: Major.
## Original claim and exact location

On p. 78 (PDF 46), before Corollary 6.7, \(\chi_\Sigma\) is defined on all integral or \(p\)-adic forms by the condition \(R_f\otimes\mathbb Q_p\in\Sigma_p\). The text then treats it as a function factoring through \(V(\mathbb Z/r_\Sigma\mathbb Z)\) and asserts the requisite \(S_3\) support property. No maximality restriction at the specified primes is inserted in that definition. Corollary 6.7 and the subsequent counts apply finite-congruence estimates to this function.
## A counterexample to every fixed modulus

Take \(\Sigma_7\) to consist of the unramified cubic extension, \(\Sigma_{11}\) to consist of \(\mathbb Q_{11}\) times its unramified quadratic extension, and \(\Sigma_\infty=\{\mathbb R\times\mathbb C\}\); impose no other conditions. This is an \(S_3\)-collection. Let \[g(x,y)=x^3-2y^3,\qquad h(x,y)=x^3-15y^3.\] The first is Eisenstein at 2 and the second at 3. Their discriminants are \(-108\) and \(-6075\), respectively, both negative and nonsquare, so each defines a non-Galois cubic field. At 7, 2 is a noncube in \(\mathbb F_7^\times\), whereas \(15\equiv1\) and \(T^3-1\) has three distinct roots. At 11, cubing is bijective on \(\mathbb F_{11}^\times\), so each polynomial has one simple root and an irreducible quadratic factor. Both discriminants are units at 7 and 11. Thus \(\chi_\Sigma(g)=1\) and \(\chi_\Sigma(h)=0\).

For every positive integer \(M\), the twisted action of \(M I_2\) sends \(f\) to \(Mf\). This matrix is invertible over \(\mathbb Q\) and every \(\mathbb Q_p\); hence it preserves the generic algebra. Therefore \[\chi_\Sigma(Mg)=1,\qquad \chi_\Sigma(Mh)=0,
 \qquad Mg\equiv Mh\equiv0\pmod M.\] No fixed congruence modulus can distinguish them. The witnesses remain irreducible and nondegenerate, so exclusion of singular or reducible forms does not remove the obstruction. For a modulus containing 7, the zero reduction also contradicts the asserted inert finite-level support condition.
## Impact and precise limits of a repair

The statement is false on the domain on which it is defined. Its use affects Corollary 6.7, Theorem 6.10 and the weighted counts in Sections 8–9. One may define a different finite-level extension agreeing with the desired local algebra on the maximal locus, or impose maximality at the finitely specified primes and sieve only elsewhere. Either route changes the weights on nonmaximal orders. The switching argument, overlaps at the fixed primes and the corresponding residue functionals must then be checked explicitly.

Even on maximal orders, arbitrary ramified specifications cannot in general be encoded solely by the mod-\(p\) splitting type. For instance, over \(\mathbb Q_7\) the Eisenstein cubics \(T^3-7\) and \(T^3-14\) give distinct tame cubic extensions but the same reduction \(T^3\). The field \(\mathbb Q_7\) contains the cube roots of unity, and the Kummer classes of 7 and 14 generate different lines since 2 is not a cube. Both local orders are maximal. This observation limits a proposed repair; it is not counted as an additional finding.

The ability to choose a corrected extension on the maximal locus is counterevidence against declaring the main field-counting conclusion false. It is not a proof of the printed all-order congruence assertion, or a completed repair of its downstream uses.

Problem 5 (P05: the Euler product uses global density coefficients as normalized local factors).  Severity: Minor, with the analytic conclusion locally restored.
## Original claim and exact location

The definition on p. 80 (PDF 48) uses additive Haar integrals over the maximal locus, with \(\operatorname{vol}(V(\mathbb Z_p))=1\). On p. 90 (PDF 58) the article sets \(t_\Sigma(n)=\mathcal A^{\max}(\lambda_n\chi_\Sigma)\). Proposition 8.4, p. 91 (PDF 59), then asserts multiplicativity, uses reciprocal finite-orbit cardinalities as local weights, and places \(t_\Sigma(p^j)\) inside every Euler factor. Under the actual definition, \[t_\Sigma(1)=D_\Sigma,\] the global density of the specified maximal locus, and generally \(0<D_\Sigma<1\). For the fixed inert/mixed family above this strict inequality holds. The displayed product over prime powers exactly dividing \(n\) is empty at \(n=1\) and equals 1, already contradicting the definition. Reciprocal orbit cardinality is not the additive Haar mass of the orbit.
## Correct normalization and complete analytic check

Define the genuinely local quantities \[a_p(j)=\int_{V(\mathbb Z_p)^{\max}}
       \chi_{\Sigma,p}(f)\lambda_{p^j}(f)\,df,\qquad
 m_p=a_p(0),\qquad D_\Sigma=\prod_p m_p.\] The local specification here is imposed only on the maximal locus; this definition does not assert the false all-order extension from Problem 3. Nonempty admissible local conditions have \(m_p>0\). Away from finitely many primes, \(m_p=(1-p^{-2})(1-p^{-3})\). The exact coefficient formula is \[t_\Sigma(n)=D_\Sigma\prod_{p^j\parallel n}\frac{a_p(j)}{m_p},
 \qquad
 T_\Sigma(s)=D_\Sigma\prod_p F_p(s),
 \quad
 F_p(s)=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{a_p(j)}{m_p}p^{-js}.\] Thus \(t_\Sigma/D_\Sigma\), not \(t_\Sigma\), is normalized multiplicative.

For an unspecified prime \(p\), Proposition 3.9 supplies the raw moments \[a_p(1)=\frac{(p-1)(p^2-1)}{p^4},\qquad
 a_p(2)=\frac{(p^2-1)^2}{p^4}.\] Dividing by \(m_p\) gives \[\frac{a_p(1)}{m_p}=\frac{p}{p^2+p+1},
 \qquad
 \frac{a_p(2)}{m_p}=\frac{p(p+1)}{p^2+p+1}.\] The first is \(O(p^{-1})\) and the second is \(1+O(p^{-2})\). Since \(|\lambda_{p^j}|\le j+1\), for \(\sigma=\Re s>1/3\), \[(1-p^{-2s})F_p(s)
 =1+O\!\left(p^{-1-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}+p^{-3\sigma}\right),\] locally uniformly. Therefore \[T_\Sigma(s)=D_\Sigma\zeta(2s)H_\Sigma(s),\] where \(H_\Sigma\) is holomorphic for \(\Re s>1/3\). The finitely specified local factors are holomorphic there: their Artin denominators have no zero for \(|p^{-s}|<1\).

At \(s=1/2\), each \(F_p\) is positive. Indeed, putting \(x=p^{-1/2}\in(0,1)\), it is the normalized positive average of the local factors \[(1-x)^{-2},\quad(1-x^2)^{-1},\quad
 (1+x+x^2)^{-1},\quad(1-x)^{-1},\quad1.\] The absolutely convergent corrected product consequently gives \[R_\Sigma:=\operatorname{Res}_{s=1/2}T_\Sigma(s)
 =\frac{D_\Sigma}{2}\prod_p(1-p^{-1})F_p(1/2)>0.\] This restores Proposition 8.4’s analytic assertion. It preserves the implicitly defined \(C_\Sigma=\alpha^\pm R_\Sigma\) in (54) and the derivative constant in the Mellin expansion of Proposition 8.5, since it is a correct representation of the original Dirichlet series.
## Why the printed residue recipe is false

With the actual global coefficients, \[\sum_{j\ge0}t_\Sigma(p^j)p^{-j/2}=D_\Sigma F_p(1/2).\] The printed finite products would therefore be \[\frac12\prod_{p\le P}\left[(1-p^{-1})
      \sum_{j\ge0}t_\Sigma(p^j)p^{-j/2}\right]
 =\frac{D_\Sigma^{\pi(P)}}2
      \prod_{p\le P}(1-p^{-1})F_p(1/2).\] They tend to zero when \(0<D_\Sigma<1\), in contradiction with \(R_\Sigma>0\) above.

Problem 6 (P06: unrestricted unweighted switching neglects automorphism orbits).  Severity: Minor on the verified downstream path.
## Original claim and exact location

Proposition 6.1, p. 73 (PDF 41), and Theorem 6.5, p. 75 (PDF 43), state unweighted sums over cubic-form orbit sets before the \(S_3\) restriction of Section 6.2. The intermediate bijection of Lemma 6.2 is a bijection of isomorphism classes of pairs. The roots of a representative must themselves be divided by its automorphism action when such pairs are counted as isomorphism classes.
## An exact discriminant-four counterexample

Set \(q=2\). Choose a nonnegative smooth \(\Psi\) supported in a sufficiently small interval about 4 containing no other positive integer, with \(\Psi(4)=1\). In the right-hand side of Proposition 6.1, the terms with the \(2^4\) scaling require a discriminant near \(1/4\) and vanish. The term with the \(2^2\) scaling comes from \(\mathbb Z^3\), of discriminant 1, represented by \(xy(x-y)\). It has three projective roots over \(\mathbb F_2\), so the right side is 3.

For completeness, every nonmaximal-at-2 ring \(R\) of discriminant 4 has index \(j\ge2\) in its maximal order \(O\) and \(4=j^2\operatorname{Disc}(O)\). Positivity and integrality force \(j=2\) and \(\operatorname{Disc}(O)=1\). A cubic field of discriminant 1 is impossible: Minkowski’s ideal bound would produce an integral ideal of norm at most \((3!/3^3)\sqrt1=2/9<1\). A product of \(\mathbb Q\) and a quadratic field cannot have discriminant 1 by the quadratic discriminant formula. Hence the only possible maximal algebra is \(\mathbb Q^3\) and \(O=\mathbb Z^3\).

An index-two subring of \(\mathbb Z^3\) contains \(2\mathbb Z^3\). It corresponds to a two-dimensional unital subalgebra of \(\mathbb F_2^3\). There are exactly three, defined by equality of one pair of coordinates. The group \(S_3=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb Z^3)\) permutes these transitively. There is therefore one isomorphism class on the left side, represented by \(xy(x-2y)\) of discriminant 4. The displayed identity would give \(1=3\).

The automorphism orders are 2 for this subring and 6 for \(\mathbb Z^3\). With reciprocal-automorphism weights both sides are \(1/2\). This agrees with the pair-mass proof in Problem 2 and is corroborated by a direct exact enumeration of the three subalgebras and their single \(S_3\) orbit.
## Impact, counterevidence and repair

Reciprocal stabilizer weights restore the identity. Alternatively, the statement can be restricted to invariant support on which all stabilizers are trivial. The later \(S_3\) applications have precisely that property, so this specific defect does not invalidate their switching step. The original cited switching literature uses its own weighted/irreducible counting convention [BST]; it does not justify the unrestricted unweighted extension. Minor severity follows from this verified downstream restriction, rather than from a general rule that repairable defects are minor.

 c=-\gamma^-\mathcal C_n^{(q)}(\phi)>0.\] Their signs follow from the nonempty local type sets, their positive Haar masses and table values, and \(\gamma^-<0\).
