Every nonzero integral discriminant has absolute value at least 1, so the left side is identically zero for every \(M\). The stated main terms are \[M\left(a\int_0^\infty\Psi(x)\,dx
       -c\int_0^\infty x^{-1/6}\Psi(x)\,dx\right)
 <-Ma\int_0^\infty\Psi(x)\,dx.\] The asserted error is independent of \(M\), since \(n,q,d,\Psi\) and \(\phi_{n/d}\) are fixed. Letting \(M\to\infty\) is a contradiction. This proof tests the literal coefficients and uniformity. It does not assume that the secondary functional criticized in Problem 2 is a correct residue.
## Impact and exact repair boundary

The switching formula requires multiplication of the error by \(|\phi_d(1^21)|\), or an explicit bound on that scalar. This restores the missing homogeneity; it does not repair the independent residue issue. For the ordinary \(\lambda_{p^j}\) applications at type \((1^21)\), the removed factor is 1. Thus this omission, by itself, does not enlarge that application’s bound. The proved limitation of its downstream effect is the basis for Minor severity. General tensor functions still require the stated norm correction.
# Checks that constrain the interpretation
## Section 10 conditional implications

The end of the paper is not rejected merely because it depends on earlier defective inputs. Its sign argument and exponent algebra were checked on their own terms. An arbitrary finite family can be refined at two previously unrestricted primes to impose inert and mixed splitting, and at infinity if necessary. A lower count for that subfamily is a lower count for the original family.

The identity \(|x|=2\max(x,0)-x\) for real \(x\) underlies the two-case argument. The count denoted \(P_A(Y)\) is over the interval \([Y/2,3Y]\); where the subsequent prose uses a cutoff \(Y\), the appropriate comparison is with the positive-value count up to \(3Y\). Replacing the cutoff by this fixed multiple preserves the logarithmic exponents, and \(3Y<X\) eventually in the indicated range \(Y\le X^{3/4+\nu}\). This correction is local and does not alter the asserted asymptotic power.

The choices of auxiliary \(\varepsilon,
u,\mu\) must be in that order of smallness, as in the preserved derivation. A claimed exponent with an \(o(1)\) loss requires a diagonal choice when \(
u	o0\), rather than treating a fixed positive \(
u\) as zero. The fixed-\(
u\) argument still supplies the required positive power margin. These checks delimit what survives conditionally; they do not repair the earlier essential inputs.
## External sources and unsuccessful retrievals

The primary source search located the target publisher page, the target arXiv version history, the Blomer–Khan arXiv PDF and author correction list, Wu’s version-5 PDF, and the primary PDFs used for the residue and counting comparisons. Direct access to the Blomer–Khan journal page was blocked, and the eGrove repository PDF endpoint returned HTTP 405. The inspected arXiv theorem and the official publisher-indexed statement both show the prime-level restriction. No claim of bytewise identity with an unavailable final journal PDF is made. The inspected entry of the author’s correction list did not supply the missing general-level statement. The bounded search found no applicable correction to the target claims; it was not an exhaustive assertion that no correction exists.

The Wu bound is used only in the precise form of the inspected Corollary 1.5. # Conclusion

The evidence supports a Major initial-review assessment because the proof as written uses several essential inputs with demonstrated defects. The counterexamples concern the stated intermediate claims and the indicated used parameter ranges. They do not establish falsity of the main nonvanishing theorem. The supplied weaker subconvex input, local residue corrections, normalization correction and aggregate square-power estimates have different scopes and cannot be combined into an unproved declaration that the complete argument is repaired.

problems.title: Theorem 4.1 invokes a prime-level theorem for arbitrary cubic discriminants
problems.source_location: Theorem4.1, printed57/PDF25 Theorem3 and numerical exponents, printed35-36/PDF3-4 Section10, printed109-112/PDF77-80
claim:
Equation reference: eq:subconv. Theorem 4.1, p. 57 (PDF 25), asserts, for every cubic field \(K\), \[
 |L(1/2+it,\rho_K)|
 \ll_{\varepsilon}(1+|t|)^{O(1)}D_K^{1/4-1/128+\varepsilon}.\] For the \(S_3\) case its proof identifies a weight-zero or weight-one automorphic form of level \(D_K\) and invokes Blomer–Khan, Theorem 1. The inspected theorem in the Blomer–Khan arXiv version [BK] assumes a prime level \(q\) and a primitive central character. The article gives no reduction from arbitrary cubic discriminants to prime level. The claimed numerical savings are then used in the later \(\delta\)-dependent bounds and the numerical lower bounds of Theorem 3, pp. 35–36 (PDF 3–4).
analysis: Severity: Major.

Let \(K=\mathbb Q(\theta)\), where \[f(T)=T^3-5T+1.\] The only possible rational roots are \(\pm1\), and \(f(1)=-3\), \(f(-1)=5\). Thus \(f\) is irreducible. Its discriminant is \[-4(-5)^3-27=473=11\cdot43.\] It is squarefree, so \(\mathbb Z[\theta]\) is maximal and \(D_K=473\). It is positive and nonsquare, so \(K\) is a totally real non-Galois cubic field. The associated Artin conductor is therefore the composite integer 473. It does not satisfy the prime-level hypothesis of the theorem invoked.

This example also lies in the type of \(S_3\) family used in the article: modulo 2, \(T^3+T+1\) has no root and is irreducible; modulo 3, \[T^3-5T+1=(T-1)(T^2+T+2),\] and the quadratic factor has nonsquare discriminant 2. Consequently the field has inert type \((3)\) at 2 and mixed type \((12)\) at 3. The obstruction is not removed by the later use of two auxiliary splitting conditions.

This proves a failure of the cited theorem’s applicability. It does not disprove the estimate [eq:subconv] (#eq:subconv): one field cannot by itself contradict a uniform asymptotic bound with an unspecified constant. Nor does the check establish that no alternative theorem could supply the requested saving. It establishes that the proof given has not supplied it. The cyclic case, handled separately by a Burgess-type estimate, does not repair the missing \(S_3\) argument.
The Section 10 exponent algebra, considered conditionally on its other inputs, then gives the following exact values:
\(\delta\) | liminf lower bound | limsup lower bound

The formulas are \(2/(3-4\delta)\) and \(3/4+\delta\). Only the last row is the article’s numerical choice. This local substitution does not restore the residue, congruence or border-range inputs treated below.

The issue is Major because a stronger uniform subconvex input is used to deduce the article’s quantitative improvements, and the named theorem does not establish that input for the family at hand. A valid unrestricted discriminant theorem, with its exact hypotheses and uniformity checked, would be a repair. Otherwise the numerical conclusions must be weakened and all dependent exponents revisited. No conclusion that the main nonvanishing theorem is false is drawn.

problems.title: Prime-level residue weights are incorrectly pulled back to prime powers and maximality loci
problems.source_location: Eq35 and Proposition5.2, printed66-67/PDF34-35 Theorem5.6 and Theorem6.6 Nonmaximal/maximal functionals, printed76,80/PDF44,48
analysis: Severity: Major.

Take \(p=5\), \(n=p^2\), and \(\phi(f)=\mathbf1_{\{f\equiv0\pmod{p^2}\}}\). This is a permitted invariant function. The printed definition gives \[\mathcal C_{p^2}(\phi)=p^{-8}p^{2/3}=p^{-22/3}.\] On the other hand, multiplication by \(p^2\) is an exact bijection from integral cubic forms to the forms in its support, compatible with \(\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)\)-orbits and preserving stabilizers. Since \(\operatorname{Disc}(p^2g)=p^8\operatorname{Disc}(g)\), the actual Shintani series satisfies \[\xi^\pm(\phi,s)=p^{-8s}\xi^\pm(1,s).\] Its residue at \(5/6\) is therefore \[\gamma^\pm p^{-20/3},\] which differs from the asserted \(\gamma^\pm p^{-22/3}\). Here \(\gamma^\pm\ne0\): the gamma factor is nonzero, and \(\zeta(1/3)<0\) by the alternating-series identity already used above.

The contradiction is exact and does not depend on fitting a finite numerical count. For a fixed smooth nonnegative test function whose Mellin transform at \(5/6\) is nonzero, the coefficient discrepancy has order \(X^{5/6}\). It cannot be absorbed into Theorem 5.6’s error for this fixed modulus. To stay on an \(S_3\) support, multiply the indicator by an inert condition and a mixed condition at two different primes other than \(p\). Scaling by \(p^2\) is an invertible scalar at those primes and preserves their types. Their secondary factors are positive. The same discrepancy then occurs on an \(S_3\) support in the \(q=1\) case of Theorem 6.6.

The prime-level table itself is not rejected: the failure is its unchanged use at higher level and on a locus whose content affects the residue. The scaling test is already decisive without any assumed formula for the entire corrected sieve. The correct one-prime value [eq:true-nm] (#eq:true-nm) supplies an additional independent comparison. A repair requires the actual level-dependent orbital residue functionals, followed by corrected nonmaximal and maximal factors and their uniform error estimates. Only the scaling identity and the one-prime comparisons above have been restored here. The error changes a secondary term and affects an essential counting input; it is Major even though it does not by itself disprove the final sign theorem.

problems.title: Generic local algebra on all orders cannot be encoded by a fixed congruence modulus
problems.source_location: Definition before Corollary6.7, printed78/PDF46 Corollary6.7/Theorem6.10 and nonmaximal-order applications
claim: On p. 78 (PDF 46), before Corollary 6.7, \(\chi_\Sigma\) is defined on all integral or \(p\)-adic forms by the condition \(R_f\otimes\mathbb Q_p\in\Sigma_p\). The text then treats it as a function factoring through \(V(\mathbb Z/r_\Sigma\mathbb Z)\) and asserts the requisite \(S_3\) support property. No maximality restriction at the specified primes is inserted in that definition. Corollary 6.7 and the subsequent counts apply finite-congruence estimates to this function.
analysis: Severity: Major.

Take \(\Sigma_7\) to consist of the unramified cubic extension, \(\Sigma_{11}\) to consist of \(\mathbb Q_{11}\) times its unramified quadratic extension, and \(\Sigma_\infty=\{\mathbb R\times\mathbb C\}\); impose no other conditions. This is an \(S_3\)-collection. Let \[g(x,y)=x^3-2y^3,\qquad h(x,y)=x^3-15y^3.\] The first is Eisenstein at 2 and the second at 3. Their discriminants are \(-108\) and \(-6075\), respectively, both negative and nonsquare, so each defines a non-Galois cubic field. At 7, 2 is a noncube in \(\mathbb F_7^\times\), whereas \(15\equiv1\) and \(T^3-1\) has three distinct roots. At 11, cubing is bijective on \(\mathbb F_{11}^\times\), so each polynomial has one simple root and an irreducible quadratic factor. Both discriminants are units at 7 and 11. Thus \(\chi_\Sigma(g)=1\) and \(\chi_\Sigma(h)=0\).

For every positive integer \(M\), the twisted action of \(M I_2\) sends \(f\) to \(Mf\). This matrix is invertible over \(\mathbb Q\) and every \(\mathbb Q_p\); hence it preserves the generic algebra. Therefore \[\chi_\Sigma(Mg)=1,\qquad \chi_\Sigma(Mh)=0,
 \qquad Mg\equiv Mh\equiv0\pmod M.\] No fixed congruence modulus can distinguish them. The witnesses remain irreducible and nondegenerate, so exclusion of singular or reducible forms does not remove the obstruction. For a modulus containing 7, the zero reduction also contradicts the asserted inert finite-level support condition.

The statement is false on the domain on which it is defined. Its use affects Corollary 6.7, Theorem 6.10 and the weighted counts in Sections 8–9. One may define a different finite-level extension agreeing with the desired local algebra on the maximal locus, or impose maximality at the finitely specified primes and sieve only elsewhere. Either route changes the weights on nonmaximal orders. The switching argument, overlaps at the fixed primes and the corresponding residue functionals must then be checked explicitly.

Even on maximal orders, arbitrary ramified specifications cannot in general be encoded solely by the mod-\(p\) splitting type. For instance, over \(\mathbb Q_7\) the Eisenstein cubics \(T^3-7\) and \(T^3-14\) give distinct tame cubic extensions but the same reduction \(T^3\). The field \(\mathbb Q_7\) contains the cube roots of unity, and the Kummer classes of 7 and 14 generate different lines since 2 is not a cube. Both local orders are maximal. This observation limits a proposed repair; it is not counted as an additional finding.

The ability to choose a corrected extension on the maximal locus is counterevidence against declaring the main field-counting conclusion false. It is not a proof of the printed all-order congruence assertion, or a completed repair of its downstream uses.

claim:
Proposition 9.11, pp. 100–102 (PDF 68–70), writes \(n=n_1\ell_1\), with \((\ell_1,q_1)=1\) and \(n_1\) supported on primes dividing \(q_1\), and defines \(\ell=\operatorname{rad}(\ell_1)\).  \qquad
 \mathcal C_{\ell_1}(\lambda_{\ell_1})\ll \ell^{-1/3},\] citing Lemma 5.9. That lemma concerns the first prime coefficient \(\lambda_p\). The coefficient \(\lambda_{p^2}\) instead has a positive mean of order one. analysis: Severity: Major.

Equation reference: eq:border-parameters. Fix the totally real specification at infinity, inert type at 7, mixed type at 11, and no other restrictions. Let \(\Psi\ge0\) be a fixed smooth function supported in \([1,2]\) with integral one. Choose a sufficiently small fixed \(\kappa=\kappa_1\in(0,1/100)\) and put \[a=\kappa/10,\qquad \varepsilon=\kappa/100.\] Let \(Q\) run through primes other than 7 and 11, set \(X=Q^8\), and choose another prime \(p\asymp X^a\). Bertrand’s postulate suffices for this last choice; for large \(Q\) it is different from \(Q,7,11\). Set \[
\begin{aligned}
 q=q_1=Q,\quad m=m_1=1,\quad k=Q^2,\quad n=p^2,\\
 n_1=1,\quad\ell_1=p^2,\quad\ell=p,\quad Y=X/Q^2=X^{3/4}.
\end{aligned}\] The integer 1 is powerful; \(q_1\) is squarefree and all required coprimalities hold. The choice \(q=X^{1/8}\) is in every stated border interval. The integer \(k\) is cubefree, has the article’s \(k_2=1\), is supported on \(mq\), and is divisible by \(q_1\). Finally, \(n=p^2\le X^{1/2+\varepsilon}/k\) for all large \(X\) since \(a<1/8\). Thus this is a retained term of the later sum.

Every \(f\in\mathcal U_Q(\Sigma)\) has a maximal overorder of index \(Q\). Lemma 9.8 and (62), pp. 98–99 (PDF 66–67), give \(E_Q(s,f)\in\{1-Q^{-s},1+Q^{-s},1\}\). With \(x=Q^{-s}\), the local coefficient definition gives \[\sum_j e_{Q,j}(f)Q^{j/2}x^j
 =Qx^2\frac{E_Q(1/2-s,f)}{E_Q(1/2+s,f)}.\] For \(E_Q(s)=1\pm Q^{-s}\), the right-hand side is \(Qx(x\pm Q^{-1/2})/(1\pm Q^{-1/2}x)\), whose \(x^2\) coefficient is \(Q-1\). For \(E_Q=1\) the coefficient is \(Q\). Hence \[e_{Q,2}(f)\in\{1-1/Q,1\}>0.\] At the different prime \(p\), \(f\) is maximal. Expanding the five local Artin factors gives, in the order \((111),(12),(3),(1^21),(1^3)\), \[\lambda_{p^2}(f)=3,1,0,1,0.\] All are nonnegative. On the support of \(\Psi\) the kernel argument is \[\frac{p^2Q^2}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Disc}(f)}}=O(X^{2a-1/4})\longrightarrow0.\] The normalized kernel satisfies \(V^+(y)\to1\). Its real part is therefore at least \(1/2\) uniformly for sufficiently large \(X\). This also covers any initially permitted complex auxiliary smoothing choice; alternatively one can fix an allowed real choice. There is no negative real contribution from the remaining summands.

 \sum_K\Psi(D_K/Y)
 =c_{Q,p}Y+
 O\!\left(Y^{5/6}+(Qp)^{2/3}Y^{2/3+\tau}\right),
 \qquad c_{Q,p}\ge c>0.\] The fixed conditions at 7, 11 and infinity are absorbed into \(c\) and the implicit constant. The totally split local main density is \(Q^2/[6(Q^2+Q+1)]\), and similarly at \(p\); the secondary densities are bounded. The variable-prime error factors are \((Qp)^{2/3}\). The second error in [eq:btt] (#eq:btt) has \(X\)-exponent \(7/12+2a/3+3\tau/4<3/4\) for a sufficiently small fixed \(\tau>0\). The count is consequently \(\gg Y\).

Each such \(S_3\) field has three index-\(Q\) suborders: they are the preimages of the three pair-equality subalgebras of \(\mathbb F_Q^3\). They are distinct as isomorphism classes because \(\operatorname{Aut}(K)=1\). For each, \(\lambda_{p^2}=3\), \(e_{Q,2}=1-1/Q\), and \(\operatorname{Disc}(f)=Q^2D_K\). Writing \(\mathcal S\) for the left-hand side of Proposition 9.11, we obtain \[|\mathcal S|\ge\Re\mathcal S
 \ge \frac92(1-1/Q)\sum_K\Psi(D_K/Y)
 \gg X^{3/4}.\] The external counting theorem is an identified input whose statement, uniformity and local factors were checked. Its full proof is not claimed as a new derivation here. Crucially, this argument does not use the reviewed article’s disputed congruence counts or secondary residues.

For [eq:border-parameters] (#eq:border-parameters), the printed \(H\) reduces to \[H=\frac{X^{3/4}}p+
    \frac{X^{5/8+\kappa/3}}{p^{1/3}}+
    pX^{1/4+9\kappa}+X^{3/4-\kappa}.\] After multiplication by \(X^\varepsilon\), the four exponents are \[\frac34-a+\varepsilon,\quad
 \frac58+\frac{\kappa}3-\frac a3+\varepsilon,\quad
 \frac14+a+9\kappa+\varepsilon,\quad
 \frac34-\kappa+\varepsilon.\] Every one is strictly less than \(3/4\) for the choices above. Thus the asserted upper bound is \(o(X^{3/4})\), contradicting the proved lower bound. This is an asymptotic counterexample satisfying the application range, not a numerical experiment or an unproved conjecture about central values.

The estimate is used directly in (64), Proposition 9.13, Proposition 9.14, Theorem 9.15 and Corollary 9.16, and hence in the proof of Theorem 9.1 under either hypothesis and in the Section 10 argument. Its wrong savings are therefore essential to the proof as written.

claim: The definition on p. 80 (PDF 48) uses additive Haar integrals over the maximal locus, with \(\operatorname{vol}(V(\mathbb Z_p))=1\). analysis: Severity: Minor, with the analytic conclusion locally restored.

Define the genuinely local quantities \[a_p(j)=\int_{V(\mathbb Z_p)^{\max}}
       \chi_{\Sigma,p}(f)\lambda_{p^j}(f)\,df,\qquad
 m_p=a_p(0),\qquad D_\Sigma=\prod_p m_p.\] The local specification here is imposed only on the maximal locus; this definition does not assert the false all-order extension from Problem 3. Nonempty admissible local conditions have \(m_p>0\). Away from finitely many primes, \(m_p=(1-p^{-2})(1-p^{-3})\). The exact coefficient formula is \[t_\Sigma(n)=D_\Sigma\prod_{p^j\parallel n}\frac{a_p(j)}{m_p},
 \qquad
 T_\Sigma(s)=D_\Sigma\prod_p F_p(s),
 \quad
 F_p(s)=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{a_p(j)}{m_p}p^{-js}.\] Thus \(t_\Sigma/D_\Sigma\), not \(t_\Sigma\), is normalized multiplicative.

For an unspecified prime \(p\), Proposition 3.9 supplies the raw moments \[a_p(1)=\frac{(p-1)(p^2-1)}{p^4},\qquad
 a_p(2)=\frac{(p^2-1)^2}{p^4}.\] Dividing by \(m_p\) gives \[\frac{a_p(1)}{m_p}=\frac{p}{p^2+p+1},
 \qquad
 \frac{a_p(2)}{m_p}=\frac{p(p+1)}{p^2+p+1}.\] The first is \(O(p^{-1})\) and the second is \(1+O(p^{-2})\). Since \(|\lambda_{p^j}|\le j+1\), for \(\sigma=\Re s>1/3\), \[(1-p^{-2s})F_p(s)
 =1+O\!\left(p^{-1-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}+p^{-3\sigma}\right),\] locally uniformly. Therefore \[T_\Sigma(s)=D_\Sigma\zeta(2s)H_\Sigma(s),\] where \(H_\Sigma\) is holomorphic for \(\Re s>1/3\). The finitely specified local factors are holomorphic there: their Artin denominators have no zero for \(|p^{-s}|<1\).

At \(s=1/2\), each \(F_p\) is positive. Indeed, putting \(x=p^{-1/2}\in(0,1)\), it is the normalized positive average of the local factors \[(1-x)^{-2},\quad(1-x^2)^{-1},\quad
 (1+x+x^2)^{-1},\quad(1-x)^{-1},\quad1.\] The absolutely convergent corrected product consequently gives \[R_\Sigma:=\operatorname{Res}_{s=1/2}T_\Sigma(s)
 =\frac{D_\Sigma}{2}\prod_p(1-p^{-1})F_p(1/2)>0.\] This restores Proposition 8.4’s analytic assertion. It preserves the implicitly defined \(C_\Sigma=\alpha^\pm R_\Sigma\) in (54) and the derivative constant in the Mellin expansion of Proposition 8.5, since it is a correct representation of the original Dirichlet series.

With the actual global coefficients, \[\sum_{j\ge0}t_\Sigma(p^j)p^{-j/2}=D_\Sigma F_p(1/2).\] The printed finite products would therefore be \[\frac12\prod_{p\le P}\left[(1-p^{-1})
      \sum_{j\ge0}t_\Sigma(p^j)p^{-j/2}\right]
 =\frac{D_\Sigma^{\pi(P)}}2
      \prod_{p\le P}(1-p^{-1})F_p(1/2).\] They tend to zero when \(0<D_\Sigma<1\), in contradiction with \(R_\Sigma>0\) above.

The error affects a displayed multiplicativity claim and an explicit residue recipe. The complete normalization correction retains the global density once, uses \(a_p(j)/m_p\) in the Euler factors and uses actual Haar masses at the finitely specified primes. Minor classification rests on the proved preservation of the analytic assertion and the implicitly defined leading and derivative constants. It does not rest on the error being repairable or on its failure to overturn a whole theorem. The independent counting and border-range problems remain outside this correction.

problems.title: Unweighted switching over all orbit classes neglects automorphism action
problems.source_location: Proposition6.1, printed73/PDF41 Theorem6.5, printed75/PDF43
claim: Proposition 6.1, p. 73 (PDF 41), and Theorem 6.5, p. 75 (PDF 43), state unweighted sums over cubic-form orbit sets before the \(S_3\) restriction of Section 6.2. The intermediate bijection of Lemma 6.2 is a bijection of isomorphism classes of pairs. The roots of a representative must themselves be divided by its automorphism action when such pairs are counted as isomorphism classes.
analysis: Severity: Minor on the verified downstream path.

Set \(q=2\). Choose a nonnegative smooth \(\Psi\) supported in a sufficiently small interval about 4 containing no other positive integer, with \(\Psi(4)=1\). In the right-hand side of Proposition 6.1, the terms with the \(2^4\) scaling require a discriminant near \(1/4\) and vanish. The term with the \(2^2\) scaling comes from \(\mathbb Z^3\), of discriminant 1, represented by \(xy(x-y)\). It has three projective roots over \(\mathbb F_2\), so the right side is 3.

For completeness, every nonmaximal-at-2 ring \(R\) of discriminant 4 has index \(j\ge2\) in its maximal order \(O\) and \(4=j^2\operatorname{Disc}(O)\). Positivity and integrality force \(j=2\) and \(\operatorname{Disc}(O)=1\). A cubic field of discriminant 1 is impossible: Minkowski’s ideal bound would produce an integral ideal of norm at most \((3!/3^3)\sqrt1=2/9<1\). A product of \(\mathbb Q\) and a quadratic field cannot have discriminant 1 by the quadratic discriminant formula. Hence the only possible maximal algebra is \(\mathbb Q^3\) and \(O=\mathbb Z^3\).

An index-two subring of \(\mathbb Z^3\) contains \(2\mathbb Z^3\). It corresponds to a two-dimensional unital subalgebra of \(\mathbb F_2^3\). There are exactly three, defined by equality of one pair of coordinates. The group \(S_3=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb Z^3)\) permutes these transitively. There is therefore one isomorphism class on the left side, represented by \(xy(x-2y)\) of discriminant 4. The displayed identity would give \(1=3\).

The automorphism orders are 2 for this subring and 6 for \(\mathbb Z^3\). With reciprocal-automorphism weights both sides are \(1/2\). This agrees with the pair-mass proof in Problem 2 and is corroborated by a direct exact enumeration of the three subalgebras and their single \(S_3\) orbit.

Reciprocal stabilizer weights restore the identity. Alternatively, the statement can be restricted to invariant support on which all stabilizers are trivial. The later \(S_3\) applications have precisely that property, so this specific defect does not invalidate their switching step. The original cited switching literature uses its own weighted/irreducible counting convention [BST]; it does not justify the unrestricted unweighted extension. Minor severity follows from this verified downstream restriction, rather than from a general rule that repairable defects are minor.

report: Abstract: The acquired nine-page arXiv version was read in full. A regularity mismatch is demonstrated in the transfer of the sharp whole-plane upper estimate to the half-plane: odd reflection of admissible nonzero boundary data need not belong to the Sobolev class used in that estimate. This is a proof-level concern for the quantitative optimality conclusion, not a counterexample to the growth theorem. The geometric lower-growth construction was also checked, including a corrected normal-velocity comparison derived from its existing constants.
Date: 25 October 2026

Title: Verification report M25-0111
Sharp vorticity growth on the half-plane
# Identity and scope

The reviewed work is Andrej Zlatoš, Maximal Double-Exponential Growth for the Euler Equation on the Half-Plane, arXiv:2507.04198v2, dated 30 September 2025 [source]. It is associated with DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01374-5 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01374-5). The journal version was not acquired, and textual equivalence is not established. All source page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, identical to the printed numbers 1–9. Every source page was visually inspected after rendering; all nine pages were also read as extracted text.

The checked chain comprises Theorems 1.1–1.2, the kernel estimates in Section 2, and the barrier construction in Section 3. Theorem 1.3’s extension to general uniformly smooth domains is explicitly left to the reader in the source and was not independently reconstructed. The imported proof of Lemma 2.1 from reference [14] was not re-proved in full. No numerical fluid simulation or author code was executed; none is needed to test the reflection regularity below.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and dependencies

Write \(H=\mathbb R	imes(0,\infty)\). The equation is \[\partial_t\omega+u\cdot
abla\omega=0,\qquad
u=
abla^\perp\Delta_D^{-1}\omega,\qquad

abla^\perp=(\partial_2,-\partial_1).\] The Dirichlet condition is imposed on the stream function; it gives impermeability of the boundary, not a zero boundary value for vorticity. Theorem 1.2 quantifies over every \(\omega_0\in W^{1,\infty}(H)\cap L^1(H)\) with \(\left\lVert\omega_0ightVert_\infty=1\), as well as the corresponding whole-plane class (p. 3). It asserts the upper logarithmic growth rate \(2/\pi\). Theorem 1.1 supplies an example attaining that rate.

The whole-plane argument first controls the instantaneous rate of approach of two particles. Its improvement for separations below the gradient scale uses \[|\omega(y_1,y_2)-\omega(-y_1,y_2)|
 \le 2\left\lVert\nabla\omega\right\rVert_\infty |y_1|.\] Translation and rotation then produce a gradient differential inequality with leading coefficient \(2/\pi\), on p. 5. This Lipschitz input is the relevant hypothesis in the transfer to \(H\).
# Problem 1: the reflection transfer loses its regularity hypothesis
## Source claim and precise suspect step

At the bottom of p. 5, immediately after the whole-plane differential inequality, the source invokes odd reflection in \(x_2\) to assert the same bound on \(H\), with the \(L^1\) mass doubled. Odd reflection does preserve the velocity representation and bounded-vorticity weak evolution. It does not, for the entire class in Theorem 1.2, preserve the finite Sobolev gradient used in the preceding argument.
## An admissible test of the inference

Equation reference: eq:gaussian. Consider the explicit initial datum \[
 \omega_0(x,y)=e^{-x^2-y^2},\qquad (x,y)\in H .\] It is smooth up to the boundary. Its essential supremum is one, its \(L^1(H)\) norm is \(\pi/2\), and \[|\nabla\omega_0|=2r e^{-r^2},\qquad
 \left\lVert\nabla\omega_0\right\rVert_\infty=\sqrt{2/e}<\infty .\] The maximum occurs at \(r=1/\sqrt2\), which is attained within \(H\). Thus every stated initial-data hypothesis of the half-plane part of Theorem 1.2 is satisfied. The associated Dirichlet stream-function prescription is the one in the paper; no extra vorticity boundary condition has been added.

These calculations are a counterexample to preservation of the proof hypothesis, not a counterexample to the long-time growth bound. No claim about the actual long-time gradient of [eq:gaussian] (#eq:gaussian) is needed or made.
## Alternative readings and counterevidence

The odd extension still belongs to \(L^\infty\cap L^1\), with mass \(\pi\), and is a valid device for constructing the half-plane velocity. Thus the basic Biot–Savart reflection in the introduction is not the problem. The coarse separation estimate, which needs only boundedness and mass, also remains available.

Reading the gradient as the classical derivative away from the reflection line does not repair the invoked \(W^{1,\infty}\) argument: the distributional jump and the displayed cross-line difference quotients remain. After the rotation used on p. 5, a pair of reflected points in the proof can straddle that line. Conversely, if zero boundary trace were separately assumed, odd extension would preserve the Lipschitz class. Such a restriction is absent from Theorem 1.2 and would not justify its stated full quantifier.

A direct half-plane strain estimate may recover the claimed rate by exploiting cancellation at the flat boundary. This report has not supplied that estimate. Consequently the conclusion is a demonstrated gap in the stated proof, with the theorem itself unresolved by this test.
## Dependency, severity, and repair status

This step supplies the sharp upper bound on the half-plane. The exact limit in Theorem 1.1 and its asserted quantitative maximality combine that upper bound with the lower bound in Section 3. The concern therefore reaches a core contribution. Under the assigned calibration it is Major at the proof level. It neither disproves the lower-growth construction nor establishes that the sharp rate is false.

A valid repair must establish the same finite gradient estimate for nonzero boundary traces, or give another upper-growth proof under the original hypotheses. Imposing a zero trace only repairs a restricted statement. No full repair of this general transfer is claimed here.
# A checked local correction in the lower-bound argument

The first display on p. 8 compares \(-2C'v_s s\alpha\) with \(-3C'v_s s_0\alpha\) for all \(s\in[s_0,e^{-1}]\). The strict comparison written there requires \(2s<3s_0\) and does not follow on the full interval. For example \(s=2s_0\) is allowed for every \(s_0\le e^{-4}\), and gives the reverse comparison. This test respects the full stated range of \(s_0\); it does not choose an \(s_0\) that might violate its earlier smallness condition.

However, the exact normal velocity gives the required stronger estimate with the constants already defined in the source. Let \[q=\sqrt{|\log s|},\quad q_0=\sqrt{|\log s_0|},\quad
 g(s)=s e^q,\quad \rho_0=\frac{s_0}{2q_0}.\] For \(s\in[s_0,e^{-1}]\), \(1\le q\le q_0\), and direct differentiation yields \[g'(s)=e^q(1-\tfrac1{2q}),\qquad
 \frac{g(s)}{g'(s)}-s=\frac{s}{2q-1}
 \ge \frac{s}{2q_0}=\frac{s\rho_0}{s_0}.\] Equation (3.9) states \(\alpha'\le-3C's_0\rho_0^{-1}\alpha<0\). The moving boundary normal speed is therefore \[V_n=\alpha'v_s\left(\frac{g}{g'}-s\right)
 \le-3C'v_s s\alpha
 <-2C'v_s s\alpha
 \le u\cdot n.\] This proves the desired barrier comparison, including the endpoints of the interval, without altering (3.8), \(\rho_0\), or the limiting rate. It is recorded as a verified local correction, not counted as a second substantive defect: the necessary information already occurs in the adjacent calculation. Author adoption has not been requested.

The remaining rate check is consistent: the angular integral is \((4/\pi)\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta=2/\pi\); \(g(s)/s\to\infty\) while \(|\log g(s)|/|\log s|\to1\). Thus the leading term in the differential inequality for \(-\log\varepsilon\) has coefficient tending to \(2/\pi\), while its square-root and constant corrections are lower order. Equation (3.11) supplies the corresponding lower rate. This check does not resolve Problem 1.
# Overall outcome and remaining work

The demonstrated concern applies to the exact acquired arXiv version. The arXiv landing page inspected during this review still identified v2 as the latest version. A title-based correction search and the publisher landing page did not identify a correction; this limited search does not establish that no correction exists. The publisher full text was not obtained or compared. The source’s general-domain extension and its cited kernel lemma remain external dependencies of the review.
Item | Judgment | Repair / remaining work
Odd reflection | Major proof-level gap | General-trace upper bound unresolved
Curved barrier | Local correction verified | Exact normal-speed calculation above
Lower-rate coefficient | No issue in checked calculation | Imported kernel lemma not re-proved
Journal-final version | Not compared | Exact-version limitation retained
Scientific acceptance and any author adoption remain pending independent human/expert review. Fresh empirical experiments are not required to settle the identified analytical gap.
# Supporting checks
Evidence consists of the assigned PDF and its source manifest, the actual rendered source pages 1–9, and the explicit analytical calculations above.

The manifest SHA-256 and all acquired file bindings are preserved in the accompanying provenance and input-audit JSON. Extraction used the existing Windows Poppler `pdftotext -layout -enc UTF-8`; rendering used `pdftoppm` at 120 dpi. Rendering alone was not counted as inspection.

The current environment’s model self-description is GPT-6 Astra Pro; it is recorded separately and does not independently establish the backend route or equivalence of labels. The controller performed logistical dispatch, not the scientific checks reported here. No human verification or author agreement is claimed.

The exact report source is compiled with the pre-existing authorized Tectonic 0.17.0 executable using its untrusted mode, with no shell escape. Actual command, compiler/source/PDF hashes, dependency record, build output, and final page inspection are recorded in the accompanying build and provenance files; those records govern completion status.

Title: Initial mathematical review:
On the monotonicity of the Fisher information for the Boltzmann equation

Authors: Cyril Imbert, Luis Silvestre and Cédric Villani. Source: arXiv:2409.01183v1, submitted 2 September 2024; supplied PDF dated 4 September 2024, 35 pages. Assigned journal DOI: `10.1007/s00222-025-01376-3`. All page references are one-based PDF pages, equal to printed pages. This review does not certify an unexamined journal revision.
# Scope and outcome

One Major proof-level gap was established in the full-range global-regularity deduction of Theorem 1.6. The interpolation on p. 29 cannot supply the required continuation exponent for some kernels allowed by the theorem. Below are a kernel/parameter example satisfying the stated hypotheses and a smooth positive family disproving the relevant norm implication. Neither is a blow-up example for the Boltzmann equation.

The conditional Fisher-information argument was checked through the product lifting, radial square completion and angular constants, with no issue found in that chain. All 35 pages were read as extracted text and decisive evidence pages were inspected visually. This is a claim-focused initial review, not an independent reproof of every lemma or imported theorem.
# Definitions and core proof checks

Equation reference: eq:key, eq:rad. For \(B(|v-w|,\cos\theta)=\alpha(|v-w|/2)b(\cos\theta)\), define \(\mathcal Bf(\sigma)=\int(f(\sigma')-f(\sigma))b(\sigma'\cdot\sigma)\,d\sigma'\). Theorem 1.2 (p. 3) uses the best constant \(\Lambda_b\) in \[
 \int f\,\Gamma^2_{\mathcal B,\Delta}(\log f,\log f)\,d\sigma
 \geq\Lambda_b\iint\frac{(f'-f)^2}{f'+f}b(\sigma'\cdot\sigma)\,d\sigma'\,d\sigma\] for positive even functions on \(S^{d-1}\), and assumes \[
 r|\alpha'(r)|/\alpha(r)\leq2\sqrt{\Lambda_b}.\] For \(\alpha=r^\gamma\), this is \(|\gamma|\leq2\sqrt{\Lambda_b}\). Section 2.2 (p. 8) restricts the differentiations to smooth, positive, sufficiently decaying solutions; there is no unqualified weak-solution assertion here.

Equation reference: eq:square. For \(F=f\otimes f\), exchange symmetry becomes angular evenness under \(v=z+r\sigma,\ w=z-r\sigma\). The product/marginal identity is \(\langle i'(f),q(f)\rangle=\tfrac12\langle I'(F),Q(F)\rangle\). For \(S=F+F'>0\), \(D=F'-F\), \(X=\partial_r\log F-\partial_r\log F'\), the radial calculation on pp. 10–11 is the valid identity \[
 -\frac{\alpha S}{2}X^2+\alpha'XD
 =-\frac{\alpha S}{2}\left(X-\frac{\alpha'D}{\alpha S}\right)^2
 +\frac{(\alpha')^2D^2}{2\alpha S}
 \leq\frac{(\alpha')^2D^2}{2\alpha S}.\] On p. 16, angular dissipation has coefficient \(4\alpha r^{d-3}\) multiplying the left side of [eq:key] (#eq:key), and the radial remainder has coefficient \((\alpha')^2r^{d-1}/\alpha\). Thus [eq:rad] (#eq:rad), including its factor 2, is sufficient. Common positive coordinate normalization factors do not change this sign comparison.

Equation reference: eq:frac. The constants on p. 23 give \(2c_K/C_P=d-2\). For subordinate kernels, pp. 25–28 give \[c_K=\tfrac12\int_0^\infty\omega(t)(1-e^{-2\Lambda_{\rm local}t})\,dt,\qquad
 C_P=\tfrac1d\int_0^\infty\omega(t)(1-e^{-2dt})\,dt.\] These yield the stated final ratio \(2c_K/C_P\). For the fractional kernel, Corollary 9.10 gives \[
 \Lambda_{b_s}\geq\Lambda_{\rm local}^{\,s}d^{1-s},
 \qquad \Lambda_{\rm local}=d+3-\frac1{d-1}.\] The imported projective-space estimate in Theorem 9.4 was not independently reproved. Evenness is essential, and the general \(d-2\) estimate gives no positive lower bound in dimension two.
# Problem 1: an unavailable continuation exponent
Major — proof gap. Evidence: Theorem 1.6, p. 5; Theorem 2.1, p. 8; Section 10, pp. 28–29; kernel conditions and constants, pp. 4,25–26,28,30.

Equation reference: eq:int, eq:crit, eq:range. In dimension three, \(i(f)=4\|\nabla\sqrt f\|_2^2\) controls \(f\) in \(L^3\). Interpolation with a moment of order \(k_2\) yields \[
 \int\langle v\rangle^{k_2(3-p)/2}f^p\,dv
 \leq
 \left(\int\langle v\rangle^{k_2}f\,dv\right)^{(3-p)/2}
 \left(\int f^3\,dv\right)^{(p-1)/2},\qquad 1\leq p\leq3.\] The two powers must be nonnegative. Higher moments increase a velocity weight, not the maximum admissible \(p\). The continuation criterion in Theorem 2.1 requires \[
 p_1>\frac3{3+\gamma+2s},\qquad k_1=1-\frac{3(\gamma+2s)}{2s}.\] The choice \(p=3/(3+\gamma+2s)+\) on p. 29 is possible in [eq:int] (#eq:int) only if \[
 \gamma+2s>-2.\] Equality fails too because the continuation inequality is strict. Theorem 1.6 does not assume [eq:range] (#eq:range).
## The Fisher hypothesis does not exclude the problematic range

Set \(d=3,\ s=1/8,\ \gamma=-5/2\). Let \(b_s\) be the fractional Laplace–Beltrami kernel and let \(b(c)=(b_s(c)+b_s(-c))/2\). The even-function constant is unchanged by symmetrization (p. 4). The fractional-kernel endpoint asymptotic discussed on p. 30 gives \(b(\cos\theta)\asymp|\sin\theta|^{-2-2s}\), including both endpoints after symmetrization. Angular integrability holds since \(s<1\). By [eq:frac] (#eq:frac), \[\Lambda_b\geq(11/2)^{1/8}3^{7/8}>3,\qquad
 |\gamma|=5/2<2\sqrt3<2\sqrt{\Lambda_b}.\] All the displayed kernel/range and Fisher assumptions of Theorem 1.6 hold, but \[\gamma+2s=-9/4,\qquad p_1>4,\qquad k_1=28 .\]
## A direct counterexample to the norm implication

Equation reference: eq:fam. Choose \(\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)\), \(0\leq\psi\leq1\), equal to 1 on \(B_1\) and zero outside \(B_2\). For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), let \[
 f_\varepsilon(v)=\psi(v)^2(|v|^2+\varepsilon^2)^{-2/5}+e^{-|v|^2}.\] Each is smooth, strictly positive and individually belongs to every polynomially weighted \(L^\infty\) space. Every fixed mass moment is uniformly bounded: the compactly supported part is bounded by \(|v|^{-4/5}\) off the origin.

Equation reference: eq:div. Fisher information is uniformly bounded as well. Pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(I(a+b)\leq I(a)+I(b)\), with the continuous interpretation at zeros. The square root of the first term is \(\psi(v)(|v|^2+\varepsilon^2)^{-1/5}\). Apart from a bounded cutoff contribution, its Dirichlet integral is bounded by \[C\int_0^2r^4(r^2+\varepsilon^2)^{-12/5}\,dr
 \leq C\int_0^2r^{-4/5}\,dr<\infty .\] The Gaussian contribution is fixed. The \(L^3\) norm is also uniformly bounded since its limiting radial exponent is \(2-12/5=-2/5>-1\). On \(|v|\leq\varepsilon\), however, \[
 \int f_\varepsilon^p\,dv\geq
 \frac{4\pi}{3}\,2^{-2p/5}\varepsilon^{\,3-4p/5}\longrightarrow\infty
 \quad(p>15/4).\] In particular this diverges for every \(p>4\), and the required weight \(\langle v\rangle^{28}\geq1\) cannot help. Bounded positive normalization factors can enforce a common mass.

This family refutes the stated norm inference, not global existence: the functions are not asserted to solve Boltzmann. Additional dynamical estimates might repair the full theorem, but are not supplied by the interpolation on p. 29.
## Impact and limited repair

The full-range global-regularity deduction is affected. The conditional Fisher theorem is not disproved. For the physical three-dimensional inverse-power-law relation \(\gamma=(q-5)/(q-1),\ s=1/(q-1),\ q>2\), one has \(\gamma+2s\in(-1,1)\); this particular obstruction does not arise.

A restricted repair adds [eq:range] (#eq:range), chooses \[\max\{1,3/(3+\gamma+2s)\}<p<3,\qquad
 k_2>\max\{2,2k_1/(3-p)\},\] and assumes sufficient initial polynomial decay for that moment and the imported local theory. Then [eq:int] (#eq:int) supplies the weighted continuation norm. This verifies a restricted proof, not the original full-range claim. Author adoption has not been sought.
# Numerical support and code

Appendix A, pp. 30–32, tabulates numerical comparisons with subordinate kernels; the introduction expressly calls the difficult comparison empirical. The continuum-wide interpretation must retain that qualification. No numerical contradiction was established.
The supplied repository `luissilvestre/collisionkernel` is pinned at:

The README, all 140 lines of `collisionkernels.jl`, and all 303 lines of `subordinate.jl` were read statically. They use quadrature, iterative inversion, a fixed finite-difference step \(h=0.001\), finite sampling and truncated spectral reconstruction. No interval certificate covering all angles and all physical parameters was identified in these modules.

A rigorous upgrade requires error control for those operations, angular endpoints and continuous parameter coverage. This is a Needs Evidence scope qualification, not an observed numerical failure. The notebooks and two-dimensional module were not audited; author code was not run. The pinned commit is not asserted to be the historical run producing the tables.

Claim | Review result
Theorem 1.2 | Symmetry, square completion and angular comparison checked; no issue found in this chain.
Angular estimates | General constant ratio and fractional specialization checked; imported projective-space theorem not independently reproved.
Theorem 1.6 | Major proof gap for allowed parameters requiring \(p>3\); explicit admissible example requires \(p>4\).
Appendix A | Empirical comparison with partial static code audit; no numerical reproduction.
Other dependencies | Text screened, without a complete independent audit of every spectral lemma, approximation or imported existence result.
Recommended disposition: Major revision of the full-range global-regularity deduction. The exact theorem and proof need reconciliation. Independent scientific acceptance is pending.
# Supporting checks

Evidence images inspected: pages 1, 3–5, 8–11, 16, 23, 25–26, 28–32. All manifest identities, sizes and hashes were checked. The delivered TeX is compiled with the authorized portable Tectonic 0.17.0; accompanying provenance binds the exact TeX, dependencies, compiler, PDF and page images.

They are recorded separately, with no independent backend-routing verification. All science and page inspection were performed by the current assistant, without another scientific model or subagent. No author-code execution, shell escape or new compiler installation was used.
Official arXiv metadata consulted on 26 October 2026 displayed only v1. A limited correction search found none; that does not establish absence, and journal full text was not compared.

Title: Initial mathematical review:
Kähler compactification of \(\mathbb C^n\) and Reeb dynamics

Authors: Chi Li and Zhengyi Zhou. Version: supplied publisher PDF, published online 7 October 2025, DOI `10.1007/s00222-025-01377-2`, 28 pages, printed pp. 181–208. Below, PDF page \(j\) means printed page \(180+j\).
# Outcome and scope

A concrete error was found in the isotropy-group indexing preceding Proposition 3.3. The asserted unique predecessor need not exist, and choosing one arbitrarily can produce a false Morse–Bott family in the first page of the spectral sequence. This is classified as a Major proof-level correction because that first page is an input to the general orbifold argument. A direct period-and-component replacement is given below, and the lowest-degree survival argument can be checked with this replacement. No counterexample to a main theorem is claimed. In particular the regular, free-circle-action case used for smooth-divisor compactification does not exhibit this obstruction.

All 28 PDF pages were read as text. The principal hypotheses, grading shifts, local cyclic-orbit formula, spectral survival argument and final index calculation were audited. Imported analytic compactification, Floer foundations, algebraic discrepancy results and metric rigidity theorems are dependencies, not independently reproved results of this review. Fifteen evidence pages were also inspected visually.
# Hypotheses and normalization checks

Theorem 1.1 assumes the compact complex manifold and smooth Kähler complement divisor setup from the introduction; it is not a statement for arbitrary noncompact \(X\). Theorem 1.3(2) retains the smooth-link assumption and, in general dimension, Shokurov’s conjecture. The unconditional dimensional conclusion in the paper is \(n\leq3\). The homological formula in Theorem 1.4 additionally requires a Liouville filling with \(c_1^\mathbb Q(W)=0\); its first, orbit-theoretic formula does not require that filling (PDF pp. 2–3).

Equation reference: eq:shift, eq:principal. The paper’s \(\operatorname{md}\) is discrepancy, so its value at a smooth \(n\)-dimensional point is \(n-1\), not the log-discrepancy value \(n\). Its lower SFT degree is \[
 \operatorname{lSFT}(\gamma)=\mu^\mathbb Q_{\rm LCZ}(\gamma)+n-3,\qquad
 \mu_{\rm LCZ}=\mu_{\rm RS}-\tfrac12\dim\ker(\phi(1)-I).\] For a principal orbit of the regular action, \(R(M)=r\), and for its \(\ell\)-fold cover (PDF pp. 17–18) \[
 \mu_{\rm RS}=2\ell r,\quad
 \mu_{\rm LCZ}=2\ell r-(n-1),\quad
 \operatorname{lSFT}=2\ell r-2.\] For the Hopf sphere, \(r=n\); the simple-orbit values are \(n+1\) and \(2n-2\), respectively. These agree with the first nonzero equivariant positive symplectic-homology degree \(n+1\) in Proposition 3.6 and with \(2\operatorname{md}(0,\mathbb C^n)=2n-2\). Thus the two relevant shifts pass this normalization test.

Equation reference: eq:local. The local calculation in Proposition 3.4 (PDF pp. 19–20), for a cyclic chart of order \(m\), yields \[
 \operatorname{lSFT}(\gamma)
 =\frac2m\left(rw_1+\sum_{j=2}^{n}w_j\right)-2.\] Indeed the local trivialization has \(\operatorname{lSFT}^\tau(\gamma)=-2\), including the zero normal weights through the nullity term. On the \(m\)-fold iterate the local value is \(-2\sum_{j=2}^nw_j-2\), while the global value is \(2w_1r-2\). Dividing their difference by \(m\) gives [eq:local] (#eq:local). This matches the weights and the final minus one in Proposition 2.16’s discrepancy formula. This check accepts that algebraic formula as a dependency rather than validating every valuation argument in its proof.
# Problem 1: the isotropy poset need not have unique predecessors
Major proof-level indexing defect. Source: PDF p. 17 (printed p. 197), the paragraph defining \(G^-\) and Proposition 3.3(1); the dependent first-page formula is on PDF p. 21 (printed p. 201).

The text considers the finite set \(S\) of isotropy subgroups, ordered by inclusion, and assigns to each nonminimal \(G\) a unique maximal smaller member \(G^-\). Such uniqueness does not follow from the subgroups being cyclic.

Equation reference: eq:action. Take the effective weighted circle action on \(S^5\subset\mathbb C^3\) \[
 t\cdot(z_1,z_2,z_3)
 =(e^{2\pi i2t}z_1,e^{2\pi i3t}z_2,e^{2\pi i6t}z_3),
 \qquad t\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z.\] This is a positive quasi-regular Reeb action in the standard Sasaki cone, with smooth link and \(c_1(\xi)=0\). Concretely, if the standard contact form is normalized by \(\alpha_0(R_a)=H>0\), where \(R_a\) generates [eq:action] (#eq:action) and \(H=2|z_1|^2+3|z_2|^2+6|z_3|^2\), then \(\alpha_0/H\) has Reeb field \(R_a\), up to the common period normalization. The identities \(R_a(H)=0\) and \(\iota_{R_a}d\alpha_0=-dH\) verify the Reeb equations directly.

The stabilizer at a point is the group of order equal to the greatest common divisor of the weights of its nonzero coordinates. Hence \[S=\{\{e\},\mathbb Z_2,\mathbb Z_3,\mathbb Z_6\}.\] Both \(\mathbb Z_2\) and \(\mathbb Z_3\) are maximal proper members below \(\mathbb Z_6\), and neither contains the other. The proposed \((\mathbb Z_6)^-\) is undefined.

This is not just a choice of notation. At the indicated times the full fixed-point sets are \[\begin{array}{c|c|c}
T&N_T=\operatorname{Fix}(\phi_T)&\text{topology}\\ \hline
1/6&\{z_1=z_2=0\}\cap S^5&S^1\\
1/3&\{z_1=0\}\cap S^5&S^3\\
1/2&\{z_2=0\}\cap S^5&S^3\\
1&S^5&S^5
\end{array}\] If one selects \(G^-=\mathbb Z_3\) for \(G=\mathbb Z_6\), the paper’s set \(G\setminus G^-\) includes \(k=3\). It then labels the period-\(1/2\) family by \(M^{\mathbb Z_6}=S^1\), although the actual family is \(N_{1/2}=S^3\); the latter is also counted under \(\mathbb Z_2\). Choosing \(G^-=\mathbb Z_2\) creates the analogous error at period \(1/3\). The smaller circle is not an independent Morse–Bott family at those periods: the kernel of the return map includes the additional fixed coordinate direction. Thus family dimension, nullity correction and multiplicity of the written first-page terms can be wrong.
## A direct correction and its mathematical extent

Equation reference: eq:page. Index by each positive period \(T\) and each connected component \(N_{T,i}\) of the full fixed-point set \(\operatorname{Fix}(\phi_T)\). Put \(B_{T,i}=N_{T,i}/S^1\). Count a component once at that period, including orbits that are iterates of shorter orbits; do not add a second copy for a proper fixed submanifold. In this notation the intended first page has the form \[
 E^1_{p,q}=
 \bigoplus_{\substack{T=p/N\\i}}
 H_{p+q-\mu_{\rm LCZ}(T,i)}(B_{T,i};\mathbb Q),\] with the same common period denominator \(N\) and the orientation conventions of the paper’s cited Morse–Bott construction.

The clean fixed-point property follows from the compact circle action: an invariant metric linearizes it normally, and \(\ker(d\phi_T-I)=T N_{T,i}\). The contact nullity is \(2\dim_\mathbb CB_{T,i}\), giving the stated lower-index shift. In the normal complement the nontrivial complex eigenvalues give positive real determinant for \(I-d\phi_T\); the mod-two lower index is therefore still \(n-1\). Thus the parity input to Proposition 3.8 is retained under this corrected indexing.

In the explicit example, one may equivalently remove the union of both proper subgroups when listing the \(\mathbb Z_6\) terms; only residues 1 and 5 remain. The period/component formulation avoids assuming a globally tree-like isotropy poset. This is a verified correction of the enumeration and of the abstract survival argument below; it is not a complete new construction of equivariant Floer theory. Author adoption and independent acceptance remain pending.
# Lowest-degree survival and final deductions

The proof on PDF p. 23 chooses a bottom \(H_0(B_{T,i};\mathbb Q)\) class \(\alpha\) with minimum rational degree \(a\), then maximum period among those classes. Since \(R(M)>0\), adding a full principal period raises degree by \(2R(M)>0\); finitely many period types suffice, so that maximum exists.

An outgoing differential would have total degree \(a-1\), which is absent. If an incoming differential kills \(\alpha\), some source \(\beta\) at a strictly larger period has degree \(a+1\) and the opposite mod-two degree. Every bottom class has parity \(n-1\); consequently \(\beta\) lies in an odd, positive homology degree \(j\geq1\) of its block. The bottom class of that block then has degree \(a+1-j\leq a\), contradicting either the minimal degree or the maximal-period choice. This checks the algebraic survival argument when the blocks are the correctly enumerated families in [eq:page] (#eq:page).

For the compactification filling, the source supplies a homology ball and a Liouville cobordism to the standard sphere (PDF pp. 8,11). The unital transfer and exact/Gysin sequences give nonzero degrees \(n+1+2m\), \(m\geq0\) (PDF pp. 20–21). Combining the lowest degree with [eq:shift] (#eq:shift) gives \[2\operatorname{md}=(n+1)+(n-3)=2n-2.\] In the smooth divisor case the local quotient terms disappear, so \(\operatorname{md}=r-1\), hence \(r=n\). This is the required maximal Fano index for a manifold of dimension \(n-1\), consistent with the invoked Kobayashi–Ochiai criterion. The weighted example does not contradict this regular-case deduction.

For the metric conclusion, the stated conditionality on Shokurov and the smooth-link condition must be retained. The volume functional on positive weights obeys \[\frac{(w_1+\cdots+w_n)^n}{w_1\cdots w_n}\geq n^n\] by arithmetic–geometric mean, with equality only for equal weights. The external cone classification and metric rigidity inputs in PDF p. 24 are not independently reproved.
# Supporting checks

The report requests correction of Proposition 3.3’s indexing and the dependent first-page formula. The demonstrated defect is in a core general-orbifold proof input, even though its replacement is concrete. No main theorem is shown false; the regular-case normalization and final index deduction pass the checks above. Remark 3.9’s extension using linearized contact homology is explicitly accompanied by a foundation caveat in the source; it is not treated here as an established substitute for the filling hypothesis of Theorem 1.4.

No released author code or separate supplement was identified in the manifest; neither absence is a defect for this theoretical paper. This review does not certify all analytic estimates, all quotient valuation constructions, the full Floer transversality/orientation machinery, or every cited external theorem.

report: Abstract: Two explicit suspension calculations expose an inconsistent normalization in the family Frøyshov invariant used in the proof of the main theorem. The printed definition changes by two under a trivial real two-dimensional suspension, whereas Lemma 5.15 predicts no change. A separate complex-line test changes the proposed boundary invariant by four while preserving its stable presentation. These establish one Major defect in the core derivation as printed; they do not refute the asserted infinite-order Dehn twist. The higher-coherence step of Lemma 3.3 remains a separate Needs Evidence item.

Title: Grading and proof audit of
Exotic Dehn twists and homotopy coherent group actions
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is by Sungkyung Kang, JungHwan Park, and Masaki Taniguchi, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01378-1 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01378-1) [KPT]. The source is the supplied 33-page publisher PDF, first published online on 10 October 2025. Throughout, PDF p. \(r\) means the \(r\)-th page of that exact file; its printed page is \(208+r\). The frozen identifier is M25-0114.

All 33 pages of the extracted source text were read in this continuation. The detailed checks concern theorem hypotheses, the collar construction and finite-order reduction, the definitions and suspension behavior in Sections 5.2–5.5, and their use in the final contradiction. Reading the analytic construction in Section 4 is recorded as a dependency review, not a fresh proof of its Fredholm, compactness, or Conley-index results. The external gauge-theoretic and lattice theorems cited by the authors were not independently reproved.

Theorem 1.1 (PDF p. 2, printed p. 210) assumes a smooth compact positive-definite filling \(X\) of the oriented Brieskorn homology sphere \(Y\ne S^3\), with \(b_1(X)=0\). Its conclusion concerns infinite order in \(\pi_0\operatorname{Diff}^+(X,\partial X)\). Simple connectivity is an additional hypothesis of the exoticness conclusion in Corollary 1.2 (PDF p. 3), not a substitute for the weaker hypothesis in Theorem 1.1.
# Problem 1: incompatible grading conventions in a core invariant
## Source statements and exact locations

Equation reference: eq:raw. Definition 5.3 and Definition 5.5 occur on PDF p. 24 (printed p. 232), with the Thom-class explanation continuing on p. 25. Write the quantity in the displayed Definition 5.5 as \[
 d^{\mathrm{raw}}_{j,n}(X)
 =\min\{i:\text{an admissible class lies in }H^i_{S^1}(X,s(B))\}-2j .\] Admissibility means that restriction to the fixed-point sphere bundle has the stated leading term \(S^jU^k\) times its Thom generator, modulo the displayed ideal. There is no subtraction of the fixed-point level in [eq:raw] (#eq:raw). The equivariant definition on PDF p. 23 likewise uses an ordinary cohomological degree.

Equation reference: eq:printedshift. For \(E=E_{\mathbb R}\oplus E_{\mathbb C}\), Lemma 5.15 (PDF p. 27, printed p. 235) asserts \[
 d_{j,n}(\Sigma^E X)
 =\dim_{\mathbb R}E_{\mathbb C}+d_{j,n}(X).\] Here \(S^1\) acts trivially on \(E_{\mathbb R}\) and by scalar multiplication on \(E_{\mathbb C}\). Its proof displays a Thom isomorphism shifting total degree by \(\dim_{\mathbb R}E\), which does not by itself yield [eq:printedshift] (#eq:printedshift) under [eq:raw] (#eq:raw).
## Check A: a fully specified counterexample to the real-suspension formula

Equation reference: eq:example. Fix \[p=3,\qquad n=2,\qquad B=(B\mathbb Z_3)_2,\qquad j=0,\] and take \[
 X=B\times S^0,\qquad E_{\mathbb R}=B\times\mathbb R^2,\qquad E_{\mathbb C}=0.\] Use the point at infinity as section and give \(X\) and \(E_{\mathbb R}\) the trivial circle action.

The two-skeleton used by the paper has finitely many cells, so \(B\) is a compact connected finite CW complex. The projection of \(X\) is a fiber bundle with finite CW fiber. Its fixed-point bundle is \(B\times S^0\), the compactification of the rank-zero bundle. The complement of the fixed points is empty, and hence satisfies the required freeness condition. The bundle \(E_{\mathbb R}\) is oriented. The suspended family \(\Sigma^E X=B\times S^2\), with its infinity section, satisfies the same conditions with fixed-point level two. Thus every assumption used in Definition 5.3 and Lemma 5.15 holds.

Equation reference: eq:value0, eq:value2. Set \(A=H^*(B\times BS^1;\mathbb F_3)\). For the first family, \[H^*_{S^1}(X,s(B);\mathbb F_3)\cong A.\] The fixed-point restriction is the identity. The degree-zero unit is admissible for \(j=k=0\); there are no negative-degree classes. Consequently, \[
 d^{\mathrm{raw}}_{0,2}(X)=0.\] For the suspended family the Thom isomorphism gives \[H^*_{S^1}(\Sigma^E X,s(B);\mathbb F_3)\cong A[-2].\] The Thom generator has degree two and unit coefficient, and restriction is again the identity. Therefore \[
 d^{\mathrm{raw}}_{0,2}(\Sigma^E X)=2.\] In contrast, the right-hand side of [eq:printedshift] (#eq:printedshift) is \(0+0=0\). Equations [eq:value0] (#eq:value0)–[eq:value2] (#eq:value2) are an analytic counterexample to the lemma with the printed degree convention. The argument uses \(j=0\), so it is unaffected by truncation of high powers of the base class \(S\). The same degree calculation works over either field appearing in the surrounding printed notation; the field label itself is not being counted as a substantive finding.
## Check B: the boundary normalization fails a stable-presentation test

Equation reference: eq:Dplus. On PDF p. 13 (printed p. 221), repeated on p. 22, the stable Floer presentation is \[SWF(Y,t,g_Y)=\Sigma^{-V_\lambda^0(g_Y)}I_\lambda^\mu(g_Y).\] The definition at the top of PDF p. 30 (printed p. 238) uses a plus sign: \[
 D(I,V)=d_{j,n}(I)-2c+\dim_{\mathbb R}V,
 \qquad c=n(Y,t,g_Y).\] It is immediately followed by a claim of independence of the spectral cutoffs and by Corollary 5.19 comparing it with the equivariant invariant.

Equation reference: eq:four. There is a direct formal compatibility test. Take \(j=0\), keep \(c\) fixed, and let \(W=\mathbb C\) have circle weight one and trivial \(\mathbb Z_3\)-action. Compare the presentations \[(I,V)=(S^0,0),\qquad (I',V')=(S^{\mathbb C},\mathbb C),\] with the trivial families over \(B=(B\mathbb Z_3)_2\). Both represent the same stable object: \[\Sigma^{-\mathbb C}S^\mathbb C\simeq S^0.\] The equivariant Thom generator of \(S^\mathbb C\) has degree two, and its fixed-point restriction is its Euler class \(U\). Thus \(d_{0,2}(I')=2\), whereas \(d_{0,2}(I)=0\). Both fixed-point levels are zero, so subtracting the fixed-point level would not change this test. Formula [eq:Dplus] (#eq:Dplus) gives \[
 D(I',V')-D(I,V)=2+2=4.\] The sign is therefore incompatible with invariance of the stable presentation. Interpreting the dimension term as complex dimension would give a change of three, not zero.

This calculation is a formal suspension test of the displayed normalization. It is not a numerical reconstruction of a particular three-manifold’s spectral cutoffs. No actual gauge-theoretic spectrum has been computed or attributed to the authors.
## Alternative readings, local repairs, and their limits

An intended level-normalized convention \[\bar d_{j,n}(X)=d^{\mathrm{raw}}_{j,n}(X)
                -\operatorname{level}(X)\] removes the discrepancy in Check A. Under the printed raw convention, the trivial real two-dimensional suspension instead has to contribute two. Both statements follow from the explicit Thom calculation. Neither convention is supplied by the displayed Definition 5.5.

For Check B, replacing the plus sign by a minus sign cancels the tested complex-line shift: \[[d_{0,2}(I')-\dim_{\mathbb R}V']-
 [d_{0,2}(I)-\dim_{\mathbb R}V]=2-2=0.\] This is a verified local repair for that test only. A coordinated repair still has to state one grading convention, reconcile the equivariant and family definitions, and carry it through the Bauer–Furuta map and the comparison theorem. This report does not assert that those global repairs have been completed.

There is related degree bookkeeping in Proposition 5.18 (PDF pp. 28–29): the proof sets \(k=d_j(X)\) and places the defining class in degree \(k\), although [eq:raw] (#eq:raw) puts it in degree \(d_j(X)+2j\). For fixed \(j\), choosing a skeleton above the actual class degree addresses that local mismatch. This observation is part of the same grading finding, not a separate claim that eventual comparison is false.
## Core dependence and severity

Theorem 5.20 on PDF p. 30 explicitly invokes Lemmas 5.15 and 5.17 and then Corollary 5.19 to establish the family Frøyshov inequality. Lemma 6.1 on PDF p. 31 uses that inequality, and the concluding contradiction on PDF p. 32 uses Lemma 6.1 to prove Theorem 1.1. Thus the faulty normalization is directly inside the core proof chain. The supported judgment is Major: an invalid core derivation under the definitions as printed. The evidence does not establish falsity of the infinite-order or exoticness conclusions.
# Problem 2: higher coherence requires additional evidence

Lemma 3.3 (PDF p. 11, printed p. 219) constructs the two-simplex homotopies from a collar diffeomorphism \(\tau\) and a path \(H_t\) satisfying \[\tau^p=\Phi,\qquad H_0=\Phi,\qquad H_1=\operatorname{id},\qquad
 H_t\tau=\tau H_t.\] The displayed three-simplex comparison follows by strict commutation. The passage to all higher simplices is attributed to contractibility of the interval-reparametrization space.

The stated algebraic relations alone do not guarantee that extension for arbitrary topological groups. To see the distinction, take a topological-group model \(G\simeq\Omega S^2\), put \(\tau=1\), and choose \(H\) as a loop generating \(\pi_1(G)\cong\mathbb Z\). The cyclic carry rule for the two-simplex homotopies represents the generator \(t\in H^2(B\mathbb Z_p;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/p\). If that assignment extended to \(f:B\mathbb Z_p\to BG\simeq S^2\), it would pull the generator \(u\in H^2(S^2;\mathbb Z)\) back to \(t\). But \[0=f^*(u^2)=t^2,\] whereas \(t^2\ne0\) in \(H^4(B\mathbb Z_p;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/p\). Thus a general inference from the commuting relation to all higher fillers is insufficient.

This diagnostic is deliberately outside the paper’s manifold class: it is not a four-manifold counterexample. The particular collar construction may provide additional geometry that resolves the obstruction. The unresolved item is an explicit compatible higher extension for those collar data, or a theorem establishing it. The judgment is Needs Evidence, with no confirmed-error severity assigned. Its dependency is Lemma 3.3 to Proposition 3.5 and then to the final finite-order contradiction.
# Checks that do not support additional defects
## Finite order, prime choice, and monodromy

The collar calculation in Lemma 3.1 commutes strictly: the first isotopy and \(\tau\) are circle rotations on each collar fiber; the second isotopy has support disjoint from that of \(\tau\). For a hypothetical finite positive order \(d\), choose an odd prime \(p\) large enough for the cited Floer calculation and coprime both to \(d\) and to the Seifert multiplicity product. Choose \(d'=kd\) with \(d'\equiv1\pmod p\). Reparametrizing the circle action by \(d'\) leaves its \(\mathbb Z_p\) generator unchanged and replaces the boundary twist by \(\Phi^{d'}\), which is relatively isotopic to the identity. This verifies the reduction in Remark 3.6 (PDF p. 12). The ordinary isotopy of \(\tau\) to the identity is not required to fix the boundary, so the monodromy conclusion of Lemma 3.4 is consistent.
## Cyclic Spin\(^c\) lifting

The cohomology-isomorphism hypothesis printed in Corollary 2.5 (PDF pp. 8–9) is not an available hypothesis for the main fillings. However, the needed cyclic lifting can be obtained directly from Lemma 2.4. With \(b_1(X)=0\), the gauge group is homotopy equivalent to the constant \(S^1\) gauges. These constants are central, so the obstruction has untwisted coefficients and lies in \(H^3(B\mathbb Z_p;\mathbb Z)=0\). The lift torsor is \(H^2(B\mathbb Z_p;\mathbb Z)\), and restriction to the homology-sphere boundary induces the identity on the constant gauges. One can therefore adjust the interior lift to the chosen boundary lift. This supplies a direct explanation for the cyclic application; the citation mismatch is not treated as a failed main conclusion. The broader wording of Theorem 5.20, which does not repeat every Section 4 assumption, has not been separately disproved.
## Orientation and finite skeletons

A positive-definite filling enters the negative-definite cobordism argument with reversed orientation. With that convention, the sign of the characteristic square in Lemma 6.1 is consistent. The form on the free quotient is unimodular for a homology-sphere boundary; finite torsion does not itself invalidate the lattice step. The external characteristic-vector bound and equivariant Floer values remain cited dependencies.

Proposition 5.18 requires a skeleton threshold for each fixed \(j\). The final argument does not need one threshold uniform in \(j\). Likewise, the obstruction prime may be chosen after the hypothetical finite order is specified. Neither quantifier was found to create an additional contradiction.
# Version checks, conclusion, and remaining work

The current publisher landing page and a targeted title search were consulted for correction notices. No correction notice was located in those checks. The arXiv record inspected lists v2, dated 26 September 2024 [KPTarxiv]; it is earlier than the supplied publisher PDF. No unexamined author version is being used to certify a repair.

report: Abstract: The inspected shooting argument supports the stated radial, subcritical, \(n\ge3\) scope.
