Title: A scope and shooting-proof audit of
Uniqueness of bound states
# Identity, scope, and outcome

This report concerns Moxun Tang’s Uniqueness of bound states to \(\Delta u-u+|u|^{p-1}u=0\) in \(\mathbb R^n\), \(n\ge3\), DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01379-0 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01379-0) [Tang]. The exact supplied publisher PDF has 47 pages, printed 245–291; PDF page \(r\) means printed page \(244+r\). The record was first published online on 10 October 2025.

A bound state is defined here to be a sign-changing radial solution. The main equation has \(n\ge3\) and \(1<p<(n+2)/(n-2)\); uniqueness is up to translation and change of sign. It is not a uniqueness claim for arbitrary nonradial sign-changing solutions. The finite-ball conclusion is also radial. Theorems 1–2 and their hypotheses are on PDF pp. 4–5.

The primary reviewer checked the preliminary energy identities, the conditional shooting reduction, selected phase and tail calculations, and the dimension counterexample. The ledger distinguishes text reading, analytic checks, image inspection, and externally cited dependencies. No numerical shooting or author code was executed. The outcome is one Minor finding in a broader preliminary assertion, with no additional substantive defect established in the inspected main-model proof. Independent scientific acceptance remains pending.
# Problem 1: strict positivity exceeds the stated dimensional range
## Claim and locations

Equation reference: eq:ivp, eq:P2. Section 2 explicitly allows the dimension to be a real variable in \((1,\infty)\) (PDF p. 6, printed p. 250). It studies \[
 u''+\frac{n-1}{r}u'+f(u)=0,\qquad u(0)=\alpha>0,\quad u'(0)=0.\] The definition on PDF p. 12, equation (2.20), is \[
 P_2(r)=r^n\left((u')^2+\frac{n-2}{n}uf(u)\right)
             +(n-2)r^{n-1}uu'.\] Under (C1)–(C3) and (C7), Proposition 2.5(iii) on PDF p. 13 claims \(P_2(r)>0\) and \(-[P(r)/r^n]'>0\), for all \(r>0\) for a ground/bound state, and up to the largest zero for a nodal solution. The proof on PDF p. 14 uses \[nP_2(c_i)=(n-2)c_i^n u(c_i)f(u(c_i))>0\] at a nonzero critical point. This strict sign needs \(n>2\).
## All assumptions of a counterexample

Equation reference: eq:choice. Set \[
 n=2,\qquad f(s)=s^3-s,\qquad
 F(s)=\frac{s^4}{4}-\frac{s^2}{2}.\] Then \(f\) is smooth and odd, negative for \(0<s<1\), and positive for \(s>1\), as required by (C1). Its unique positive primitive-zero is \(\alpha_*=\sqrt2>1\), giving (C2); \(-f'(0)=1>0\) gives (C3). Moreover \[h_2(s)=(n+2)f(s)-(n-2)sf'(s)=4(s^3-s),\] so (C7) holds with threshold \(\widetilde\alpha=1\). Condition (C4), although not needed in the displayed statement, also holds: \(f'(1)=2>0\).

Equation reference: eq:limit, eq:explicit. For completeness, the initial datum can be fixed analytically, rather than chosen from an uncertified numerical shooting plot. Let \(w_0\) be the unique regular solution of \[
 w_0''+\frac1t w_0'+w_0^3=0,\qquad w_0(0)=1,\quad w_0'(0)=0.\] Let \(c_-\) be its first negative minimum and \(c_+\) its following positive maximum. Both are finite, as proved below. Define \[
 T=c_+,\quad m=\min\{-w_0(c_-),w_0(c_+)\}>0,\quad
 \varepsilon=\min\left\{\frac14,\frac{3m}{4(e^{3T^2}-1)}\right\},
 \quad \alpha=\varepsilon^{-1/2}.\] These formulas specify a positive real initial datum in terms of a fixed, parameter-free ODE. No decimal value of \(\alpha\) is asserted.

Equation reference: eq:counter-u. Let \(w_\varepsilon\) solve \[w_\varepsilon''+\frac1t w_\varepsilon'
       +w_\varepsilon^3-\varepsilon w_\varepsilon=0,\qquad
 w_\varepsilon(0)=1,\quad w_\varepsilon'(0)=0.\] Then \[
 u(r)=\alpha w_\varepsilon(\alpha r)\] solves [eq:ivp] (#eq:ivp) with [eq:choice] (#eq:choice). The construction below proves that \(u\) has at least two simple zeros and only finitely many zeros. Thus it has a largest zero \(z_k\), and a critical point \(c\) strictly between its first two zeros lies inside the precise range \((0,z_k]\) in Proposition 2.5.
## Existence and nodal properties of the specified solution

The energy for [eq:limit] (#eq:limit) decreases: \[\left(\frac{(w_0')^2}{2}+\frac{w_0^4}{4}\right)'
       =-\frac{(w_0')^2}{t}.\] Hence the regular solution is global and \(|w_0|\le1\). While it is positive, the flux \(tw_0'\) is strictly decreasing because \((tw_0')'=-tw_0^3\). If it stayed positive forever, after any fixed positive time \(w_0'\le-a/t\) for some \(a>0\), forcing a zero by logarithmic divergence. That zero is simple by ODE uniqueness.

After this zero, if \(w_0'\) never became zero, \(w_0\) would remain below a fixed negative value and \((tw_0')'\ge b^3t\) for some \(b>0\); this forces \(w_0'>0\), a contradiction. Thus the negative minimum \(c_-\) is finite. After the minimum the positive flux similarly forces a second zero. Following that zero, a persistently positive derivative is impossible because \((tw_0')'\le-b^3t\) once \(w_0\) has a fixed positive lower bound. The positive maximum \(c_+\) is therefore finite. The relevant extrema are strict and have the signs used in [eq:explicit] (#eq:explicit).

Equation reference: eq:gronwall. For \(0<\varepsilon\le1/4\), decreasing energy with potential \(s^4/4-\varepsilon s^2/2\) also gives \(|w_\varepsilon|\le1\) globally. The Volterra formula is \[w_\varepsilon(t)=1-\int_0^t s\log(t/s)
              \bigl(w_\varepsilon(s)^3-\varepsilon w_\varepsilon(s)\bigr)\,ds.\] For \(D(t)=|w_\varepsilon(t)-w_0(t)|\), use \(|a^3-b^3|\le3|a-b|\) for \(|a|,|b|\le1\), and \(s\log(t/s)\le T\) when \(0<s<t\le T\). Gronwall’s inequality gives \[
 D(t)\le\frac{\varepsilon}{3}(e^{3Tt}-1)\le\frac m4
       \qquad(0\le t\le T).\] Thus \(w_\varepsilon(c_-)<0\) and \(w_\varepsilon(c_+)>0\). Together with \(w_\varepsilon(0)=1\), this supplies two distinct zeros. They are simple, since a simultaneous zero of the solution and its derivative at positive time would force the solution to vanish identically.

The finite-zero conclusion used here is the cubic \(n=2\) instance of the energy argument in Proposition 2.4(ii), PDF pp. 9–11. That instance can be checked without the strict-positivity claim under review. If there were infinitely many zeros, decreasing energy would have a limit \(E_\infty\ge0\). When \(E_\infty>0\), consecutive extrema have uniformly bounded separation: the speed on the central crossing is bounded below, and outside \(|u|\le\sqrt2\) the cubic satisfies \(|f(u)|\ge f(\sqrt2)>0\). Each crossing dissipates a fixed positive multiple of \(1/r\); the resulting harmonic series contradicts finite total energy loss.

When \(E_\infty=0\), extrema approach absolute height \(\sqrt2\). For \(\widehat E=r^2E\), \(\widehat E'=2rF(u)\). The intervals above height \(\sqrt2\) have bounded length and their maximum \(F\)-value tends to zero. Each central passage through \(1/2\le|u|\le1\) has a length bounded below, since \(|u'|\) is bounded, and there \(F\le F(1/2)<0\). Over successive zero-to-zero intervals, these estimates give \(\Delta\widehat E\le-d r_i\) for some \(d>0\) and large \(i\). This forces \(\widehat E<0\), contrary to \(E>0\) under the infinite-zero hypothesis. All signs used here are valid at \(n=2\), where the weight exponent \(2n-3\) is \(1\). Thus the solution in [eq:counter-u] (#eq:counter-u) meets the largest-zero qualification of Proposition 2.5.
## Stated and actual values, impact, and local repair

At the critical point \(c\) between the first two zeros, [eq:P2] (#eq:P2) becomes \[P_2(c)=c^2(u'(c))^2=0,\] whereas the proposition asserts \(P_2(c)>0\). The identity (A.8), PDF p. 41, also gives \[-\left(\frac{P(r)}{r^2}\right)'
     =\frac{2(u'(r))^2}{r},\] so its asserted strict sign likewise becomes equality at \(c\).

At \(n=2\), the exact replacement is nonnegativity, with equality at critical points. These statements follow directly from the definitions and are a verified local correction. Retaining \(n>2\) for the strict statement excludes this demonstrated boundary failure; this report does not thereby certify every other generalization in Section 2.

The alternative reading that the original \(n\ge3\) restriction remains implicit is understandable, and would remove this example from scope. However, Section 2 explicitly enlarges the dimensional range, and no restriction is restated before Proposition 2.5. The supported severity is Minor: the broader preliminary strict-positivity assertion is false as written, while the main uniqueness theorem and Section 5 already restrict to \(n\ge3\). No core failure at the main theorem’s parameters follows from this test.
# Main-model checks and resolved concerns
## Conditional shooting reduction

Lemma 3.1 (PDF pp. 16–18) reduces the result to the ordering of zeros of \(v=\partial_\alpha u\), and its eventual divergence for a bound state. At a node \(z_i(\alpha)\), the checked sign \(u'v>0\) yields \[z_i'(\alpha)=-v(z_i(\alpha),\alpha)/u'(z_i(\alpha),\alpha)<0.\] Continuity and a strictly negative energy value beyond the last zero give the local constancy of the node count for oscillatory solutions. For a bound state, the diverging variation gives the one-sided jump through the maximum-principle comparison on a tail where \(f'<0\). The existence of prescribed-node solutions and the large-initial-value zero-radius limit remain the external existence/asymptotic dependencies cited in that section; they were not independently reproved here.
## The apparent singular endpoint in Lemma 4.2

On PDF p. 20, the first-zero argument for \(M\) involves \(T_1=Q-g_1(u)M\), although \(g_1(u)\) is singular at a node. For the actual model, this endpoint has a valid limiting justification. If both \(u(z_1)\) and \(v(z_1)\) vanish, put \(a=u'(z_1)<0\), \(b=v'(z_1)>0\), and \(s=z_1-r\). Then \(u=-as+O(s^2)\), \(v=-bs+O(s^2)\), and \[M'=(p-1)r^{n-1}u^pv=O(s^{p+1}),\qquad M=O(s^{p+2}).\] Since \(g_1(u)=O(s^{1-p})\), its product with \(M\) tends to zero. Consequently \(T_1\to Q(z_1)=z_1^nab<0\), contradicting the established positivity before the node. This resolves the apparent endpoint problem for every \(p>1\) in the main range.
## Phase bridge and tail

The identities \[Q'=2r^{n-1}f(u)v,\qquad
 M'=r^{n-1}(uf'(u)-f(u))v,\qquad
 B_a'=-\frac{2F_a(u)Q_n}{r(u')^2}\] were independently differentiated on their stated open intervals. They support the bridge in Lemma 4.3 (PDF pp. 21–22): at a hypothetical first \(Q_1\)-zero \(q\), positive energy gives \(B_0(q)=-2q^{n-1}(v/u')E(q)<0\), whereas monotonicity gives \(B_0(q)>B_0(z_1)=Q(z_1)>0\).

The Section 5 audit checked the phase-parity signs, the separate \(n=3,\ 1<p<2\) case, and the final induction to Lemma 3.1. It did not identify an omitted exponent range. In the tail argument on PDF pp. 38–39, assuming \(v\) bounded allows a direct estimate from \((r^{n-1}v')'=-r^{n-1}f'(u)v\): \[|r^{n-1}v'(r)|
 \le |R^{n-1}v'(R)|+\frac{CM}{n}(r^n-R^n).\] Thus \(v'=O(r)\). Exponential decay of \(u,u'\) implies \(Q\to0\); also \(F(u)=O(u^2)\) and \(u'/u\to-1\) imply \(B_0-Q\to0\). This contradicts the positive increasing tail of \(B_0\). These are analytic checks, not numerical reproductions. Isolated symbol slips whose intended values are fixed by the defining identities are not counted as substantive findings.

The current publisher page and targeted correction search revealed no correction notice in the checks performed. The arXiv history inspected lists v2 dated 3 October 2025, earlier than publication [arxiv]; no equivalence of uninspected version bytes is assumed. A later two-dimensional preprint is not needed for the counterexample, whose existence argument is given above.

report: Abstract: Two deterministic tests show that the curvature/profile conditions in the central Section 3 reduction are impossible as printed. They are grouped as one Major proof-interface finding. The local curvature proof elsewhere uses the consistent constant, providing specific evidence for a repair; no counterexample to the final characterization is established. Title: A proof-interface and normalization audit of
Strong Characterization for the Airy Line Ensemble
# Identity, theorem scope, and result

This report concerns Amol Aggarwal and Jiaoyang Huang, Strong Characterization for the Airy Line Ensemble [AH], assignment M25-0116. The inspected document is arXiv:2308.11908v2, 10 October 2025, 263 PDF pages. Page references below are PDF pages; the numbered text from page 3 uses the same numbers. The assignment’s journal DOI is 10.1007/s00222-025-01381-6 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01381-6). The journal PDF was not obtained, and equivalence to that version has not been established. A targeted primary-source check found the same v2 record and no separate correction notice; this is not an exhaustive absence claim.

Set \(a=2^{-1/2}\). Assumption 2.8 and Theorem 2.9 (p. 30) concern a continuous, \(\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\times\mathbb R\)-indexed Brownian Gibbs ensemble \(L\) satisfying \[\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists K(\varepsilon)<\infty\
 \forall t\in\mathbb R:\quad
 \mathbb P\{|L_1(t)+at^2|\le\varepsilon t^2+K(\varepsilon)\}
 \ge1-\varepsilon.\] The probability bound is pointwise in \(t\), uniformly with the same constant; it is not a single simultaneous event for all \(t\). The asserted conclusion is \(L_j(t)=S_j(t)+lt+c\), with \((l,c)\) independent of the scaled parabolic Airy ensemble \[S_j(t)=a(A_j(t)-t^2).\] Stationarity and extremality are additional hypotheses for the deterministic-shift specialization.

The outcome is one Major and one Minor finding. The Major rating records a failed central intermediate claim and its actual use in the proof, not a demonstrated false main theorem. The inspected local proof strongly suggests coordinated corrections. The scope is a dependency audit with explicit analytic tests, not a complete independent reconstruction of every estimate in 263 pages. Independent scientific acceptance remains pending.
# Problem 1: incompatible core curvature and profile conditions
## A deterministic contradiction in Lemma 3.21

Equation reference: eq:incompatible. On p. 38, Lemma 3.21(3), equation (3.18), requires, for fixed \(\delta\in(0,1/4)\) and sufficiently large \(n\), a twice-differentiable \(h:[-T,T]\to\mathbb R\), where \[T=\delta^{-1}n^{1/3},\qquad b=2^{-7/6}(3\pi)^{2/3},\] satisfying, among its requirements, \[
 \sup_{|t|\le T}|h''(t)+a|\le\delta,\qquad
 \sup_{|t|\le T}|h(t)+at^2+bn^{2/3}|
       \le\frac{\delta n^{2/3}}2.\] The original page image confirms the negative exponent in the curvature constant. The same constant appears in the related Theorem 3.16, Assumption 3.18, and the application on p. 42.

Take the allowed value \(\delta=1/8\), and any integer \(n\ge\max\{2,N_0(\delta)\}\). Put \(g(t)=h(t)+at^2+bn^{2/3}\). The first bound in [eq:incompatible] (#eq:incompatible) implies \(g''\ge a-\delta>0\). Thus \(g(t)-(a-\delta)t^2/2\) is convex, and its midpoint inequality gives \[g(T)+g(-T)-2g(0)\ge(a-\delta)T^2.\] The second bound instead gives \[g(T)+g(-T)-2g(0)\le2\delta n^{2/3}.\] Consequently \[a\le\delta+2\delta^3=\frac{33}{256},\] impossible since \(a=1/\sqrt2>1/2\). The argument only uses twice differentiability, exactly as stated; continuity of \(h''\) has not been added. It is deterministic and does not invoke an unproved stochastic rigidity estimate.

The underlying ensemble hypotheses are nonempty. Take the paper’s standard \(L=S\). Lemma 2.5 (p. 29) supplies its unit-variance Brownian Gibbs property, and Lemma 2.6 (p. 30) makes \(S_1(t)+at^2\) stationary. A finite quantile of \(|S_1(0)|\) supplies \(K(\varepsilon)\) uniformly for each fixed \(t\). Thus this is an admissible instance of Assumption 2.8. Nevertheless no \(h\) can satisfy the two requirements, so the event asserted to have probability at least \(1-\delta=7/8\) is empty. The additional approximation requirement involving \(L_{n+1}\) cannot rescue that event.
## The Airy-gap hypothesis has an empty profile event

Equation reference: eq:profile. On p. 37, equation (3.16) in Assumption 3.18 prints \[
 \mathcal F_n(t)=
 \left\{\max_{1\le j\le n}
 \left|x_j(t)-b\bigl(n^{2/3}-j^2\bigr)-f_n(t)\right|
 \le\delta_n n^{2/3}\right\}.\] Both the ordinary image and a higher-resolution inspection confirm \(j^2\), rather than \(j^{2/3}\). Under the nonintersecting bridge law above the finite lower boundary \(f_n\), one has \(x_n(0)>f_n(0)\) almost surely. The \(j=n\) term therefore exceeds \(b(n^2-n^{2/3})\). For sufficiently large \(n\), this is greater than \(\delta_n n^{2/3}\), because \(0<\delta_n<1/4\). Hence \(\mathcal F_n(0)\) is empty. Equation (3.17), requiring its probability to be at least \(1-\delta_n\), cannot hold.

This is a failure of satisfiability of the stated hypothesis and of its claimed verification. It is not a counterexample to a theorem under satisfiable hypotheses. The profile consistent with the global law and Lemma 3.21 is \(b(n^{2/3}-j^{2/3})\). At \(j=n\) that corrected profile vanishes and creates no conflict with the lower boundary.
## Core dependency, counterevidence, and repair limits

The proof on pp. 38–42 uses curvature approximation and Lemma 3.23 to obtain Lemma 3.21, then verifies Assumption 3.18 and applies the Airy-gap theorem (Theorem 3.19). Together with Proposition 3.20, these are inputs to Theorem 2.9. The incompatible bounds occur in the main proof reduction. This supports the Major classification of one combined interface defect, rather than two independent issue counts or a list of harmless isolated symbol errors.

There is substantial counterevidence against interpreting the finding as a false final characterization. Proposition 17.2, equation (17.2) on p. 189, bounds \(h''+2^{1/2}\). The gluing estimate on p. 191 retains this constant. Equation (17.36) on p. 199 differentiates the quadratic profile and obtains curvature \(-2^{1/2}\) exactly. The comparison calculation on p. 209 and the gap-scale limit in Lemma 19.4 on pp. 210–211 agree with that normalization.

Replacing \(+2^{-1/2}\) by \(+2^{1/2}\) in the second-derivative conditions removes the first contradiction: the exact quadratic \(h_0(t)=-at^2-bn^{2/3}\) has the corrected curvature and zero profile error. Replacing \(j^2\) by \(j^{2/3}\) removes the second contradiction. Intermediate gap factors must also agree with \[\sqrt2(S_j-S_{j+1})=A_j-A_{j+1};\] some displays on pp. 38–39 use the reciprocal factor, whereas the stated gap theorem and the final conclusion use \(\sqrt2\).

These are verified local consistency repairs. They do not show that \(h_0\) approximates the required random curve, prove all probability estimates, or certify every corrected application in the manuscript. The demonstrated defect is the printed central derivation; a counterexample to Theorem 2.9 has not been obtained. Author adoption and a correction of the journal version are not recorded.
# Problem 2: the KPZ corollary states a different limiting law

Corollary 25.1 (p. 255) states convergence to \(2^{-1/2}S^{(q)}\), with \(q=2^{-1/6}\), whereas its proof concludes convergence to \(S^{(q)}\). Definition (2.3) gives \[S_j^{(q)}(t)=q^{-1}S_j(q^2t)
       =2^{-1/3}A_j(2^{-1/3}t)-\frac{t^2}{2}.\] Thus \(S_1^{(q)}(0)=2^{-1/3}X\), where \(X=A_1(0)\) has the nondegenerate Tracy–Widom GUE law.

At \(t=0\), the paper’s own equation (25.1) gives the limiting distribution function \(F_{\rm TW}(2^{1/3}z)\), exactly that of \(S_1^{(q)}(0)\). The extra factor in the corollary instead gives \(2^{-5/6}X\) and distribution function \(F_{\rm TW}(2^{5/6}z)\). These distributions differ: a finite, nonzero, nondegenerate real random variable cannot have the same law as a nontrivial positive contraction of itself, since iteration would concentrate its law at zero. The discrepancy changes a stated application.

The local correction is to remove the prefactor \(2^{-1/2}\). The centering signs in (25.1) and (25.2), on pp. 255–256, also need to be consistent with the negative parabola: the centered variables use \(+t^2/2\) and \(+2^{-1/2}q^3t^2\), respectively. The \(t=0\) contradiction above is independent of these sign slips. This is a Minor finding in a secondary application; the main characterization does not depend on it. The correction agrees with the proof’s stated limit. The model-dependent log-gamma scale has not been independently rederived from its external references.
# Positive checks and bounded proof qualifications
## No hidden moment hypothesis for affine shifts

An arbitrary almost surely finite random pair \((l,c)\), independent of \(S\), is compatible with the main top-curve assumption. Choose quantiles \(M,N\) so that \[\mathbb P\{|l|>M\text{ or }|c|>M\}<\varepsilon/2,\qquad
 \mathbb P\{|S_1(0)|>N\}<\varepsilon/2.\] For each fixed \(t\), with probability at least \(1-\varepsilon\), \[|S_1(t)+at^2+lt+c|
 \le N+M+M|t|
 \le\varepsilon t^2+N+M+\frac{M^2}{4\varepsilon}.\] No moment of the shifts is used. Affine addition preserves the Brownian bridge specification, and independent mixtures preserve that same specification.

The transformation \(q^{-1}S(q^2t)\) retains Brownian variance one, since \(q^{-2}q^2=1\); its quadratic coefficient is \(q^3/\sqrt2\). This verifies \(q=2^{1/6}\sigma^{1/3}\) in Corollary 2.11. The sharper sublinear bound forces \(l=\ell\) almost surely: after division by \(t\), the stationary finite marginal and \(c\) vanish in probability. Stationarity similarly forces \(l=0\). Extremality removes a random intercept. The bounded function \(c\mapsto\mathbb E[\arctan(S_1(0)+c)]\) is strictly increasing, so a nontrivial split of the intercept law gives two distinct stationary Gibbs mixtures, contradicting extremality.

The step removing an independent intercept from \(X+c\stackrel d=X\) is valid without moments. The characteristic function of \(X\) is nonzero near zero, forcing that of \(c\) to equal one there and hence \(c=0\) almost surely.
## Curvature, constants, and conditioning

The curvature gluing has sufficient asymptotic room: with \(\varpi=n^{-13/15}\) and \(\eta=\exp(-\sqrt{\log n})\), \(n^{2/3}\varpi=n^{-1/5}\), and \(\varpi\eta^{-2}\) is smaller than every negative power of \(\log n\). Fixed multiples of \(\delta^{1/6}+(\log n)^{-1/3}\) can be absorbed in \(\delta^{1/8}+(\log n)^{-1/4}\) after the appropriate choices.

Two further local qualifications have explicit repairs. The application on p. 205 claims a full-domain \(C^{50}\) bound from the \(C^{45}\) bound in Definition 17.9. The general variant following Lemma 8.29 (p. 98), with \(m=44\) and \(\gamma=1/20000<1/(5m^2)\), instead needs precisely \(C^{45}\); its exponent \(2/44-1+1/20000\) beats the required \(-9/10\) budget, including the stated rescaling of particle number. On p. 42 the tolerance must be chosen after \(B=B'(\delta)+C_3(\delta)\), small enough for \(c(B)\); an unspecified positive \(c(B)\) need not exceed \(\delta^{20}\). An auxiliary tolerance below both \(c(B)/2\) and \((\delta/4)^8\) is compatible with the global-law theorem.

Conditioning on the exterior makes bridge data deterministic. The sequential formulation of Theorem 3.19 supplies uniformity over admissible configurations by contradiction and diagonal selection. Lemma 4.27 explicitly provides uniformity in initial data. Lemma 19.4 yields \(\sigma_{\nu;t}\to\sqrt2\); fixing a tolerance, sending \(n\) to infinity, and then decreasing that tolerance is a valid order.
## Affine limits and independence

In Section 20, \(N=n^{15}\), \(T=n^{1/3}\), and the endpoint normalization \((\xi_n,\zeta_n)\) is exterior-measurable. The deterministic sequential convergence of Proposition 20.1 likewise gives uniform conditional convergence for each bounded continuous test function on a fixed compact restriction.

The Cauchy argument on p. 216 needs a union of the two endpoint failure events, rather than their printed intersection. For fixed \(n\), convergence as the comparison index tends to infinity and the Airy concentration bound give a summable error \(C_\delta e^{-c_\delta n}\). Applying the union bound first over a finite tail of indices, and then taking limits, controls the supremum of all pairwise tail differences. This proves almost-sure Cauchy convergence of \((\xi_n,\zeta_n)\), rather than merely convergence in probability.

For bounded continuous \(F,G\), uniform conditional convergence gives \[\left|\mathbb E[F(L^n)G(\xi_n,\zeta_n)]
 -\mathbb E[F(S)]\,\mathbb E[G(\xi_n,\zeta_n)]\right|
 \le \|G\|_\infty\varepsilon_n+
 2\|F\|_\infty\|G\|_\infty\,\mathbb P(E_n^c),\] with both errors tending to zero. Dominated convergence then factorizes the limiting law. Taking \(S=L-\ell_\infty t-c_\infty\) on the same probability space gives the simultaneous pathwise decomposition and independence from the pair \((\ell_\infty,c_\infty)\). It does not assert that the two coefficients are independent of each other.

The coverage ledger records other locally repairable range and display mismatches in pp. 40 and 213–221, including the available stronger error bound in Lemma 20.2. They do not establish an independent obstruction to this mechanism. These bounded checks do not replace a full corrected proof.

report: Abstract: No substantive mathematical defect was confirmed in the audited definitions, main reductions, regularization limits, Gaussian constant, or application scopes. The report gives explicit checks of the noncompact Gaussian limit and of the passage to even log-concave majorants. A direct trace argument independently verifies the Kolesnikov–Werner Gaussian constant, including its distinct two-input and multiple-input equality cases. These are bounded positive checks, not a certification of every cited external result.

Title: A mathematical audit of
A generalized Legendre duality relation and Gaussian saturation
# Source, scope, and outcome

The reviewed article is Shohei Nakamura and Hiroshi Tsuji, A generalized Legendre duality relation and Gaussian saturation, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01382-5 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01382-5) [NT]. The exact supplied publisher PDF has 49 pages, printed 607–655, and records online publication on 20 October 2025. PDF page \(r\) below corresponds to printed page \(606+r\). The primary source and source manifest were hash-verified. A targeted publisher/arXiv correction lookup found no separate correction notice; this is not an exhaustive absence claim.

Theorem 1.1 (PDF pp. 6–7) takes \(c_i>0\), an orthogonal block decomposition \(\mathbb R^N=\bigoplus_i\mathbb R^{n_i}\), an arbitrary symmetric matrix \(Q\), and nonnegative even integrable functions satisfying \[\prod_i f_i(x_i)^{c_i}\le e^{-x^TQx}\quad\hbox{for every }x.\] It bounds the product of their integrals by the supremum over centered Gaussians with the same constraint. This supremum may be infinite. Theorem 1.3 (PDF pp. 11–12), concerning the inverse Brascamp–Lieb functional, additionally requires log-concavity. It is proved for positive exponents and the stated coordinate projections; a theorem for arbitrary linear maps or negative exponents is not being asserted.

The outcome is no confirmed substantive finding. Gaussian saturation identifies the optimal constant; it does not, by itself, classify every functional equality case. The paper proves the exponential-kernel case \(\rho(t)=e^{-t/(m-1)}\) of the more general Kolesnikov–Werner functional conjecture, as explicitly qualified on PDF pp. 5–6. It does not claim the full arbitrary-\(\rho\) result. Independent scientific acceptance remains pending.
# Regularized inverse inequality: checks of the main mechanism
## Compactness and extended-valued cases

The fixed lower envelope makes the regularized inverse constant strictly positive. In the convolution proof one should separate the case where it is infinite: then the Gaussian constant is also infinite because the Gaussian class is a subclass. Cancellation is needed only in the finite positive case. This supplies the harmless extended-value qualification to the argument.
## Self-convolution and the Gaussian limit

For fixed \(x_i\), the paired function \[y_i\longmapsto
 f_i((x_i+y_i)/\sqrt2)\,f_i((x_i-y_i)/\sqrt2)\] is even in \(y_i\), positive, and retains both curvature bounds. The \(45^\circ\) change of variables preserves \(x^TQx+y^TQy\) and the joint Jacobian. Integration of the paired function gives \(2^{n_i/2}(f_i*f_i)(\sqrt2x_i)\), a normalized density. These checks verify the factors and inequality direction in Proposition 2.4 (PDF pp. 17–19).

The rescaled convolution remains in the same curvature class, as shown in Appendix Lemma A.2 (PDF p. 46). The initial even density has mean zero, finite covariance, and nondegenerate covariance because of the Gaussian envelopes. The normalized repeated convolutions therefore have a centered Gaussian limit. The use of almost-everywhere convergence after \(L^1\) convergence can be made precise by taking one common subsequence for the finitely many inputs; convergence of the entire sequence almost everywhere is unnecessary. The same envelopes and curvature bounds persist, so the limit belongs to the permitted Gaussian class. Fatou’s lemma then has the correct direction for the infimum.
## Removing regularization

The order of limits in Lemma 2.7 is significant: first \(\Lambda\to\infty\), then the additional lower-curvature parameter tends to zero. The preliminary quartic cutoff \(f_i e^{-\varepsilon_0|x_i|^4}\) preserves evenness and log-concavity. Its removal uses monotone convergence and \(c_i>0\).
# The duality reduction and its boundary cases
## Uniformity in the Gaussian limit

Lemma 3.1 (PDF pp. 24–25) uses \(c_i(p)=(d_i+p)/p\), \(Q_p=Q/p\), and \(d_i>0\). Writing \(M=\sup_x e^{x^TQx}\prod_i f_i(x_i)^{d_i}\), the regularized bound gives \[e^{x^TQ_px}\prod_i f_i(x_i)^{c_i(p)}
 \le M^{1/p}\prod_i f_i(0)\,e^{-\lambda|x|^2/2}.\] Taking the \(p\)-th power of the integral removes the fixed Gaussian factor as \(p\downarrow0\). This avoids an unjustified \(L^p\)-to-\(L^\infty\) limit on an infinite-measure space.

The potentially noncompact case \(\Lambda=\infty\) in Lemma 3.2 also has a direct justification. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(A_i)\), \(A_i\ge\lambda I\), and \[C_p=\operatorname{diag}((d_i+p)I_{n_i})-2A^{-1/2}QA^{-1/2}.\] For the finite Gaussian integral, \(C_p>0\). Exact integration gives \[\mathrm{BL}(A)^p
 =(2\pi)^{-\sum_i d_i n_i/2}\,
 p^{Np/2}\prod_i(\det A_i)^{d_i/2}
 (\det C_p)^{-p/2}.\] For \(0<p\le1\), \(C_p\le CI\), with \(C\) independent of \(A,p\). Hence the final factor together with \(p^{Np/2}\) is bounded below by \((p/C)^{Np/2}\to1\), uniformly.

If the liminf under consideration is finite, near minimizers have bounded \(\prod_i(\det A_i)^{d_i/2}\). Because \(A_i\ge\lambda I\) and every \(d_i>0\), each \(A_i\) then has bounded eigenvalues. A subsequence converges, and (35) passes to \(\operatorname{diag}(d_iA_i)-2Q\ge0\). Continuity of the determinant yields the claimed limiting infimum. If no bounded near-minimizer values exist, the lower-bound statement is immediate. Thus the monotone feasible-set observation can be completed without assuming compactness when \(\Lambda=\infty\). The isolated inverse-matrix symbol in the final sentence on PDF p. 26 is inconsistent with (35); the consistent constraint is the one just displayed. It does not create a separate substantive finding.
## Even log-concave envelopes and damping

In the nontrivial case of Theorem 1.1, each diagonal block \(Q_{ii}\) can be taken positive semidefinite. If it has a negative direction, choose a Gaussian precision tending to zero in that direction and fixed sufficiently large precisions on the complementary directions and blocks. The matrix constraint still has slack, while the Gaussian integral product diverges. The claimed upper bound is then infinite.

For \(Q_{ii}\ge0\), taking the infimum of the ratio defining the \(i\)-th dual envelope amounts, after a negative logarithm, to \(x_i^TQ_{ii}x_i\) plus a supremum of affine functions of \(x_i\). It is therefore convex. Simultaneously reflecting the other coordinates verifies evenness. Each replacement enlarges that input and preserves the joint pointwise constraint; induction preserves both properties for the final tuple.

Assume the original integral product is nonzero, since otherwise the inequality is immediate. Choosing positive values of the other inputs and also their simultaneous reflections bounds each envelope above by a finite constant. It is measurable and log-concave; zero values outside its support are permitted. Multiplication by \(e^{-\varepsilon|x_i|^2}\) ensures integrability and preserves the constraint. Monotone convergence removes this damping before comparing with the original inputs. Thus integrability of an undamped envelope need not be assumed.
## Elementary scope tests

For \(m=1\) and \(Q>0\), the constraint is exactly \(f(x)\le e^{-x^TQx/c}\); its Gaussian bound is immediate. For \(Q=0\), the dual supremum is infinite, as the paper allows. The inverse functional equals one when every \(c_i=1\); if some \(c_i\ne1\), its Gaussian infimum is zero by changing that block’s scale.

Evenness cannot simply be discarded from the stated dual inequality. In dimension one, take \[f_1(x)=e^{-(x-a)^2/2},\qquad
 f_2(y)=e^{-y^2/2-ay},\quad a\ne0.\] The exact Legendre inequality gives \(f_1(x)f_2(y)\le e^{-xy}\), but their integral product is \(2\pi e^{a^2/2}>2\pi\). This is a check of an essential hypothesis, not a counterexample to the theorem as stated.
# Independent verification of the Gaussian constant

For the Kolesnikov–Werner datum, PDF p. 33 gives the constraint \(M(A)\ge0\), with diagonal blocks \(A_i>0\) and off-diagonal blocks \(-I/(m-1)\). The following direct calculation verifies the optimization target without assuming an extremizer exists.

Put \(B_i=A_i^{-1/2}\), and test the block quadratic form on \(x_i=B_i z\). Taking the trace of the resulting inequality yields \[\sum_{i\ne j}\operatorname{tr}(B_iB_j)\le mn(m-1).\] Although \(B_iB_j\) need not be symmetric, it is similar to a positive definite symmetric matrix. Applying \(s\ge1+\log s\) to its positive eigenvalues gives \[\operatorname{tr}(B_iB_j)\ge n+\log\det(B_iB_j).\] Summing and using \[\sum_{i\ne j}\log\det(B_iB_j)
   =-(m-1)\sum_i\log\det A_i\] therefore proves \(\sum_i\log\det A_i\ge0\). Equivalently \(\prod_i\det A_i^{-1}\le1\). The choice \(A_i=I\) is feasible, so the supremum is exactly one. This recovers the constant \((2\pi)^{mn/2}\) in Theorem 4.1.

If equality holds, every scalar eigenvalue inequality above is an equality, so \(B_iB_j=I\) for all \(i\ne j\). For \(m\ge3\), this forces \(A_i=I\) for every \(i\). For \(m=2\), it gives \(A_2=A_1^{-1}\), retaining the expected linear invariance. This classifies the equality cases of this Gaussian matrix problem only. It is not an assertion about all non-Gaussian functional extremizers.

The direct certificate above independently verifies their target constant and bypasses reliance on the external equality argument for that target. It does not certify every assertion made in the cited transport literature.
# Applications and limits of the audit

The Minkowski-functional substitution in Corollary 4.2 has the correct factor \(1/2\) and reproduces the claimed volume product. Theorem 4.3 (PDF p. 29) deliberately uses two different conditions: the condition on \(\sum_i V_i\) for \(0\le\lambda\le1/2\), and the condition on \(\sum_i V_i^*\) for \(1/2\le\lambda\le1\). This distinction is necessary. Taking \(V_i=a|x|^2/2\), \(a>1\), satisfies the first condition but gives product affine surface area \((2\pi)^{mn/2}a^{mn(\lambda-1/2)}\), which exceeds the claimed bound if one incorrectly extends that condition to \(\lambda>1/2\). The printed theorem avoids that extension. The range \(p\in[0,n]\) in Corollary 4.4 agrees with \(\lambda=p/(n+p)\in[0,1/2]\).

Theorem 4.5 concerns symmetric measures in \(\mathcal P_2\) and equal weights \(1/m\). If any relative entropy is infinite, the bound is immediate. Finite entropy gives absolute continuity, and finite second moments are already part of \(\mathcal P_2\). The multimarginal cost identity verifies the coefficient \((m-1)/m^2\). For finite entropy, symmetrized Kantorovich potentials with \[\sum_i\phi_i(x_i)\le
 \frac{1}{2(m-1)}\sum_{i<j}|x_i-x_j|^2\] give even inputs \(f_i=e^{\phi_i-|x_i|^2/2}\) for Theorem 4.1. Its conclusion and entropy duality yield the barycentric inequality. One can first truncate to symmetric balls, use compact dual potentials extended by \(-\infty\), and then pass to the limit using entropy convergence and \(W_2\) convergence. This handles potential integrability without assuming an unproved global bound. At \(m=2\), the coefficient reduces exactly to the symmetric two-measure Talagrand inequality.

Title: A mathematical audit of
Resolvent estimates in \(L^\infty\) for the Stokes operator in nonsmooth domains
# Source, scope, and principal conclusions

The reviewed source is Jun Geng and Zhongwei Shen, Resolvent estimates in \(L^\infty\) for the Stokes operator in nonsmooth domains, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01383-4 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01383-4) [GS]. The supplied publisher PDF has 45 pages, printed 657–701, and records online publication on 23 October 2025. PDF page \(r\) below means printed page \(656+r\). The exact source and manifest were hash-verified. A targeted publisher/arXiv lookup found no separate correction notice; this is not an exhaustive absence claim.

The problem is \[-\Delta u+\nabla p+\lambda u=F,\qquad
 \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad u|_{\partial\Omega}=0,
 \quad
 \lambda\in\Sigma_\theta
 =\{z\ne0:|\arg z|<\pi-\theta\},\] where \(0<\theta<\pi/2\). The space \(L^\infty_\sigma\) requires both distributional zero divergence and zero normal boundary trace. Theorem 1.1 concerns bounded \(C^1\) domains for \(d\ge3\) and bounded Lipschitz domains for \(d=2\). It proves \[|\lambda|\|u\|_\infty\le C\|F\|_\infty.\] The \(L^\infty\) gradient estimate is separately restricted to \(C^{1,\alpha}\) domains. Theorem 1.6 treats the corresponding exterior domains only for \(|\lambda|>\lambda_0\), with bounded weak velocity and pressure bounded at infinity. The solution’s velocity is unique; pressure retains its additive constant unless a gauge is fixed.

# 0118-F1: excessive regularity in Theorem 9.5
## Exact claim and why the proof does not establish it

On PDF p. 39, Theorem 9.5 takes any bounded Lipschitz \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^2\), any \(1<q<\infty\), and \(F\in L^q_\sigma(\Omega)\). It asserts a solution in \(W^{1,q}_0(\Omega)\times L^q(\Omega)\), with mean-zero pressure, as well as the velocity estimate (9.13). Its proof interpolates the \(L^2\) and \(L^\infty\) velocity estimates and then uses duality. That reasoning does not supply the asserted gradient or pressure membership. The following construction shows that the extra membership is actually false.

Classification: Minor. The failure concerns a secondary regularity assertion. The example’s velocity is bounded and does not violate (9.13), Theorem 9.4, or Theorem 1.1. A correction should state the velocity resolvent realization separately and restrict gradient/pressure regularity to the domain-dependent range near \(2\), or strengthen the boundary regularity. Interpolating velocity bounds must not be presented as proving gradient bounds.
# 0118-F2: the arbitrary-graph Poincare assertion

Take \(d=2\), \(R=1\), and \[\psi(x)=\max\{0,\,3-12|x-\tfrac12|\}.\] It is globally Lipschitz with \(\psi(0)=0\). For \(0.45<x<0.55\), \(\psi(x)\ge2.4\), so this entire vertical strip misses \(D_2\). There are positive-area components of \(D_2\) on both sides. Choose smooth \(\chi\) equal to zero for \(x\le0.45\) and one for \(x\ge0.55\), changing only inside that strip. For \(\zeta\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb R^2)\) equal to one near \(\overline{B_2}\), let \(\eta(x,y)=\chi(x)\zeta(x,y)\). It is an admissible homogeneous Sobolev test function, and \(\nabla\eta=0\) everywhere in \(D_2\). However, \(\beta\in(0,1)\), and \(I_1\) contains positive-length segments with \(\eta=0\) and with \(\eta=1\). The claimed inequality has positive left side and zero right side, for example for \(q'=3/2\).

Classification: Minor; explicit local repair. The example lies outside Theorem 2.2’s small-slope assumption. For a graph with Lipschitz constant \(M\), use instead the connected graph box \[P_R=\{(x',x_d):|x'|<4R,\quad
               \psi(x')<x_d<(4M+4)R\}.\] Its geometry is controlled by \(M\), and it contains the relevant \(D_{2R}\) and graph patches. Choose the same \(\beta\) as its average throughout the localization calculation. Poincare and trace inequalities on this box give the required bounds with \(C(M)\), the same powers of \(R\), and \(\|\nabla\eta\|_{L^{q'}(P_R)}\) on the right.

The dual test in Section 2 already satisfies \(\|\nabla\eta\|_{L^{q'}(\mathbb H_\psi)}\le1\). Changing its averaging box therefore requires no additional values of \(u\) or \(F\) outside their existing localization supports. The cancellation \(\int g=0\) permits subtracting this new constant. This repairs the arbitrary-slope use needed in the planar argument; it does not justify the false fixed-ball assertion itself.
# 0118-F3: missing flux compatibility in Theorem A.1

On PDF pp. 39–40, Theorem A.1 quantifies over every \(f\in W^{1,q}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb R^d)\), for \(q\) near \(2\), and claims a divergence-free \(v\) with boundary trace \(f\). It omits \[\int_{\partial\Omega} f\cdot n\,d\sigma=0.\] For the unit disk, \(q=2\), and \(f(x)=x\) on the unit circle, every printed geometry and regularity hypothesis holds, but \[0=\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}v
   =\int_{\partial\Omega}f\cdot n=2\pi\] would be required. Thus the theorem as stated is false.

Classification: Minor. Adding the displayed zero-flux hypothesis repairs this obstruction. The explicit Appendix A application has \(f=-w\), with \(\operatorname{div}w=0\), and is compatible. This example therefore does not invalidate that application or the main resolvent estimate.
# Checks of the main proof and the exterior solution class
## Localization, pressure scales, and absorption

The localized divergence is \(g=\operatorname{div}(u\varphi)\). Its compact support and zero trace imply \(\int g=0\), which is essential to the homogeneous negative Sobolev pairing. The boundary scaling \[(Nr)^{(d-1)/q}(Nr)^{-1/q'}=(Nr)^{d/q-1}\] matches the localization estimate. A common pressure constant can be subtracted from the interior and boundary terms.

For \(C^1\) charts one fixes \(q>d\), chooses a uniform small-slope radius, and then chooses the large parameter \(N\). The condition \(|\lambda|>16r_0^{-2}N^4\), with \(r=2N|\lambda|^{-1/2}\), ensures \(2Nr<r_0\). There is no circular choice of the frequency threshold. The complementary bounded-frequency range is handled by (3.25). For planar Lipschitz domains, Theorem 9.3 and the boundary regularity interval allow a common \(q>2\) sufficiently close to \(2\). This is enough to make \(2/q-1<0\) in (9.12). The main argument does not need Theorem 9.5’s false all-\(q\) gradient membership.

The truncated boundary quantity \(M_q(g)(t)\) takes suprema over radii at least \(t\). The pressure proofs use near patches at scale \(r\ge t\), larger dyadic annuli, and a fixed-scale far remainder. Their terms have summable factors \(2^{-j\sigma}\) or \(j2^{-j\sigma}\). They do not require gradient control at arbitrarily smaller radii. Away from the boundary, an occasional notation \(M_q(g)(\delta(x))\) beyond its defined upper cutoff is read through the fixed-scale/global boundary bound already supplied by the proof.

The tangential operator \(n_i\partial_j-n_j\partial_i\) has zero integral on the closed boundary. It supplies the Neumann compatibility and integration by parts in Sections 4–6. On interior approximating boundaries, the pressure data retain the necessary term \(h_\ell=-\lambda u\cdot n_\ell\); one cannot set it to zero before taking the limit. In an exterior domain, its total flux is exactly zero by applying the divergence theorem to the bounded collar. This removes the planar logarithmic obstruction. The exterior pressure mean is controlled through Lemma 5.3, rather than freely discarded after fixing its value at infinity.
## A finite-\(q\) completion of exterior uniqueness

Theorem 1.6, PDF p. 7, uses \[u\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\overline\Omega)\cap L^\infty,
 \qquad p\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\overline\Omega).\] The uniqueness paragraph on PDF p. 35 instead starts with \(u\in W^{1,\infty}_0\). A bounded gradient is not a consequence of the stated \(C^1\) boundary hypothesis. The connection can nevertheless be supplied with the finite-\(q\) estimates already used in the paper:

For a homogeneous bounded weak solution, rewrite the stationary forcing as \(-\lambda u\in L^\infty\). The local estimate underlying (3.12) gives \(W^{1,q}\) velocity and \(L^q\) pressure on boundary patches, with finite \(q>d\) for \(C^1\) domains or \(2<q<2+\varepsilon\) in the planar Lipschitz case. The potential decomposition in Lemma 3.5 and (3.13) give finite-\(q\) boundary gradient control. The trace argument (A.4)–(A.8) provides the needed nontangential traces and convergence on approximating boundaries.

Since \(q>d\), the zero velocity trace gives \(\sup_{\partial\Omega_\ell}|u|\to0\). A finite cover of the compact physical boundary suffices; no global \(W^{1,q}\) norm on the unbounded domain is assumed. The condition that \(p\) is bounded at infinity, together with harmonicity and Lemma 5.1, gives \(p\to\beta\). Subtract \(\beta\), retain the collar’s exact zero-flux condition, and pass to the finite-\(q\) exterior pressure estimates. The local bounds at \(t=|\lambda|^{-1/2}\) control the boundary gradient quantities by \(C|\lambda|^{1/2}\|u\|_\infty\). The same high-frequency absorption as in (8.1), now with \(F=0\), forces \(u=0\).

Thus there is a proof-class clarification to make, with a concrete completion using weaker estimates. It is not evidence of nonuniqueness and is not counted as an additional independent substantive defect.
## Semigroup scope and verification limits

The bounded-domain semigroup conclusion explicitly distinguishes the \(C_0\) semigroup on \(C_{0,\sigma}\) from the non-\(C_0\) analytic semigroup on \(L^\infty_\sigma\). On compactly supported solenoidal data, the resolvent identity \(\lambda R_\lambda F-F=R_\lambda\Delta F\) verifies the large-\(\lambda\) approximation used with density. For exterior domains, PDF p. 8 explicitly states that uniform semigroup boundedness has not been established from the available high-frequency estimates. This report does not extend that conclusion.

The audit checked the main hypotheses, local scaling, boundary-pressure interfaces, planar exponent selection, and the three explicit counterexamples above. The cited external resolvent and boundary-regularity theorems, and every interpolation-space identification in Appendix B, were not independently reconstructed in full. No author code or numerical root computation was used. Coverage records distinguish text reads from actual source-image inspection, and positive checks from unproved global certification.

Assumption 1.1 requires a finite symmetric force set \(F\subset\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}\), integer span \(\mathbb Z^2\), and at least two modes of different lengths. All coefficients \(c_k\) are nonzero and viscosity is fixed positive. The velocity initially belongs to \(H^5_{\mathrm{sol},0}(\mathbb T^2)\). For a fixed mean-zero \(\phi_0\in L^2\), Theorem 1.2 asserts, for every \(p>0\), an exponentially decaying \(H^{-1}\) bound with a random prefactor \(K(p,\phi_0,u_0)\) having a uniform \(p\)-th moment. # 0119-F1: the weighted cost is not logarithmic near the diagonal
## The exact construction and its core dependency

Proposition 4.3, particularly p. 29, constructs \[f(u,x,y)=|x-y|^{-1}e^{V(u)},\qquad
 W(z)=\min_{1\le n\le T}a^{-n}\mathbb E_z[f(Z_n)^{p_0}],
 \tag{1}\] for some \(p_0>0\), \(a\in(0,1)\), and finite integer \(T\). Theorem 4.10, p. 32, uses the cost \[d(z,z')=
 \sqrt{d^\beta(z,z')\,[1+W(z)+W(z')]},\qquad
 d^\beta=1\wedge\beta^{-1}d_V,
 \tag{2}\] where \(d_V\) is the path metric from Definition 4.4. Its proof asserts \[d(\delta_{u,0,e_1},\delta_{u,x,y})
 \le Ce^{V(u)}\log|x-y|^{-1}.
 \tag{3}\] It then invokes a triangle inequality and integrates to obtain (2.8). Proposition 2.7 uses (2.8) to pass from two-point Markov mixing to scalar mixing; Theorem 1.2 is deduced immediately after this argument. Thus (3) occurs in a core proof interface.
## A lower bound contradicting the asserted estimate

Fix \(u_0=0\), \(x_0=0\), \(y_0=\varepsilon e_1\), with \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\). These are permissible initial conditions for any force set satisfying Assumption 1.1. Let \[I_n=\int_0^n\|\nabla u_s\|_\infty\,ds.\] The spatial flow is Lipschitz for the torus geodesic distance, so \(|x_n-y_n|\le\varepsilon e^{I_n}\). Since \(V\ge0\), \[\mathbb E[f(Z_n)^{p_0}]
 \ge \varepsilon^{-p_0}\mathbb E e^{-p_0I_n}
 \ge \varepsilon^{-p_0}e^{-p_0\mathbb E I_n}.
 \tag{4}\] Corollary 2.6 bounds \(\mathbb E I_n\) for the finitely many \(n\le T\), uniformly in the initial spatial points when \(u_0=0\). Taking the finite minimum in (1) therefore yields \[W(0,0,\varepsilon e_1)\ge c\varepsilon^{-p_0}.
 \tag{5}\]

The path norm controls spatial displacement even if a path changes its velocity coordinate. Indeed, with \(D=\operatorname{diam}\mathbb T^2\), \[|v_x|+|v_y|
 \le |v_x+v_y|+|v_x-v_y|
 \le \max(1,D)\|v\|_{H^5,2},\] and \(e^{V/2}\ge1\). The distance \(d^\beta\) between \(z_*=(0,0,e_1)\) and \(z_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon e_1)\) is consequently bounded below by a positive constant as \(\varepsilon\to0\). Dirac measures have only one coupling. From (2) and (5), \[d(\delta_{z_*},\delta_{z_\varepsilon})
 \ge c\varepsilon^{-p_0/2}.
 \tag{6}\] This cannot be bounded by \(C\log(1/\varepsilon)\). The contradiction remains if one adds a constant to the logarithm or makes the local waiting-time parameter correction discussed below. It is not a missing-symbol issue.
## A complete replacement for the required integrated bound

The pointwise assertion (3) is unnecessary. Choose the exponent \(b\) in the upper bound of Proposition 4.3 with \(0<b\le1\), so that \[W(u,x,y)\le C|x-y|^{-b}e^{bV(u)}.\] Let \(\pi=\mu^b\times\mathrm{Leb}\), where the superscript in \(\mu^b\) denotes the base-process invariant measure, not the exponent \(b\). Use normalized spatial Lebesgue measure. As \(d^\beta\le1\), Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[\begin{split}
 d(\delta_z,\pi)^2
 &=\left(\int d(z,z')\,\pi(dz')\right)^2\\
 &\le\int d(z,z')^2\,\pi(dz')
 \le1+W(z)+\pi(W).
\end{split}
 \tag{7}\] The quantity \(\pi(W)\) is finite: the diagonal singularity \(|x-y|^{-b}\) is integrable in two relative dimensions for \(b<2\), and the base invariant measure has the required exponential moment. Integrating (7) over \(x,y\) gives \[\int d(\delta_{u,x,y},\pi)^2\,dx\,dy
 \le Ce^{bV(u)}\le Ce^{V(u)},
 \tag{8}\] which is precisely the required form of (2.8). No triangle inequality for the weighted coupling cost is used.

Classification: Major, invalid core derivation. Equations (4)–(6) disprove the printed bound with the paper’s actual construction. Equations (7)–(8) repair this particular interface using its existing Lyapunov bound, conditional on the other Harris inputs. They do not repair the independent controllability defects below and do not constitute a new proof of the entire paper.
# 0119-F2: the proposed control recipes do not establish their claims
## A four-shear path that never winds around the circle

Lemma B.6, Step 4, p. 73, claims that four shear segments, with parameters \(T,T,-T,-T\), wind the tangent direction around \(S^1\) and therefore reach every target direction. The printed formula also has phase and elapsed-time slips. Grant the natural corrections that make the shears fix the origin and vary continuously within each segment; the winding claim still fails.

Take the admissible force set \[F=\{\pm(1,0),\pm(0,1),\pm(1,1)\},\qquad c_k=1.\] It is symmetric, spans \(\mathbb Z^2\), and contains lengths \(1\) and \(\sqrt2\). Choose \(k_0=(1,0)\), \(k_1=(0,1)\). The origin-fixing shears available from cosine vorticity modes have physical maps \[f_{0,t}(x,y)=(x,y+t\sin x),\qquad
 f_{1,t}(x,y)=(x-t\sin y,y).\] For row tangent vectors their derivative matrices at zero are \[S_0(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 S_1(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-t&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Start at \(v_0=(1,0)\). For \(s\in[0,T]\), the four successive unnormalized tangent segments are \[\begin{array}{ll}
 (1,s),&
 (1-sT,T),\\[2pt]
 (1-T^2,\ T-s(1-T^2)),&
 (1-T^2+sT^3,\ T^3).
\end{array}
 \tag{9}\] For every \(T>0\), their second coordinates are positive except at the initial point. In the third segment the second coordinate lies between \(T\) and \(T^3\), both positive. After normalization, the path never enters the lower semicircle and never reaches \((0,-1)\). Its final vector is \((1-T^2+T^4,T^3)\), in the first quadrant. Thus neither the continuous path nor the endpoint obtained by varying \(T>0\) has the asserted winding property. This is a counterexample to the specific recipe, not to reachability by other controls.
## A concrete replacement for this projective step

Two nonparallel origin-fixing shears become, after a fixed change of basis and nonzero parameter rescaling, the elementary matrices \[U(a)=\begin{pmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 L(b)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\b&1\end{pmatrix}.\] For an oriented angle \(\theta\in[-\pi,\pi]\), put \(a=\tan(\theta/4)\), \(b=-\sin(\theta/2)\). Direct multiplication gives \[U(a)L(b)U(a)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \cos(\theta/2)&\sin(\theta/2)\\
 -\sin(\theta/2)&\cos(\theta/2)
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{10}\] Repeating this three-shear block gives the desired rotation. The coordinate-direction map from a fixed invertible change of basis is a bijection of the oriented circle. Therefore this construction also reaches any oriented target for nonorthogonal shear axes. Six shears suffice, with bounded parameters, including for antipodal targets.

Each shear can be realized over positive physical time by a smooth single-mode velocity amplitude \(a_j(t)\) with zero endpoints and prescribed integral. The corresponding forcing derivative is proportional to \(a_j'(t)+\nu|k_j|^2a_j(t)\). Stretching the time interval makes it satisfy the control bound; negative parameters use negative amplitudes. Every segment fixes the origin and returns the velocity to zero. The bounded parameters give a common finite duration; zero-velocity padding makes it an integer if needed. The support/stability argument then gives positive-probability approximation. This supplies a valid replacement for the failed Step 4, without asserting that all remaining appendix steps are thereby proved.
## The two-point case split also fails for an admissible force set

Lemma B.8 defines on p. 73 \[R_k=\left\{y:|\sin(k\cdot y)|
       \ge\frac1{100\max_{k'\in F}|k'|}\right\}.\] Step 3 on p. 75 claims that, when \(y_0\) lies in none of these sets and meets the specified separation from zero, the integer-span assumption yields an independent pair with \(\cos(k_2\cdot y_0)<-1/2\).

Take \[F=\{\pm(2,1),\pm(3,1)\},\quad
 K=\sqrt{10},\quad a=\frac1{200K},\quad y_0=(-2a,5a).
 \tag{11}\] Choose nonzero coefficients, for example all equal to one, and \(u_0=0,x_0=0\). The positive modes have unequal lengths \(\sqrt5,\sqrt{10}\) and determinant \(-1\), so every condition in Assumption 1.1 holds. Moreover, \[|y_0|=\sqrt{29}\,a>2a=\frac1{100K},\] and \(y_0\) is a nonzero torus point in the usual coordinate chart. Its mode phases are \[(2,1)\cdot y_0=a,\qquad (3,1)\cdot y_0=-a.\] For every signed mode in \(F\), \[|\sin(k\cdot y_0)|=\sin a<a<2a,
 \qquad \cos(k\cdot y_0)=\cos a>\tfrac12.
 \tag{12}\] Thus \(y_0\) is in none of the \(R_k\), yet no required negative-cosine mode exists. This disproves the stated implication independently of the phase slips in the shear notation. The configuration lies in the class Step 3 explicitly purports to handle.
## Dependency, severity, and bounded consequence

Lemma B.6 is used for projective-process irreducibility in Corollary 2.11 and to exclude invariant finite line families in Theorem 3.6, p. 26. Lemma B.8 supplies the common-target control in Proposition 4.9, p. 31. That proposition is the small-set input to Theorem 4.10, which in turn feeds Theorem 1.2. Appendix placement does not make these steps peripheral.

Classification: Major, invalid core controllability derivations. The examples verify the force-set, state-space, and target conditions. They invalidate the asserted recipes and case split, not the general controllability or mixing conclusions. Equation (10) repairs the projective winding step. A complete replacement for the general two-point construction, with its uniform time and probability bounds, was not established in this audit and should be supplied rather than presumed. The two related failures are consolidated into one finding.
# Bounded positive checks and explicit local completions
## Continuous invariant families and positive-exponent logic

The measure iteration in Proposition 3.3, pp. 23–24, closes with \(\beta=1/4\), a contraction exponent \(\delta<1\), \(\eta=(1-\delta)\beta\), and then sufficiently small smoothing parameter and sufficiently large induction constant. The parameter order is consistent.

The infinite-dimensional base is not locally compact. Nevertheless, pointwise subsequential convergence follows by diagonalizing over a countable dense subset, using compactness of \(\mathcal P(S^1)\) and the uniform local Lipschitz bounds. Those bounds extend convergence to the whole base. Dominated convergence against each fixed transition kernel passes the invariant-family relation.

The backward-shift construction in Proposition 3.1 has the correct stationary marginal laws and twisted pushforward identity. In the actual two-dimensional application, \(\|A^{-1}\|=\|A\|\) for \(A\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb R)\) in the Euclidean operator norm. For the general-dimensional formulation, equality of the exponents is unnecessarily strong: \(\|A^{-1}\|\le\|A\|^{d-1}\) suffices to transfer a zero top exponent. The application has the needed log-integrability.

Compactness of invariant-measure approximations requires one-time parabolic regularization at an order above the state-space norm; bounded \(H^5\) balls alone are insufficient. The estimates of Proposition 2.3 supply that regularization. Uniform integrability suffices for the expected stretching limit; the argument need not assume the stronger displayed exponential tail for \(\|\nabla u\|_\infty\). These are bounded completions of the analytic interfaces; the control defects in Section 3 remain separate.
## Lyapunov construction and the weak Harris inputs

In Proposition 4.3, the sublevel of \(V\) is compact in \(H^1\), the topology actually used for the finite-cover argument, because it bounds the velocity in \(H^5\). The short-distance secant comparison can be made in a common torus lift up to the injectivity scale. Exponential moments of the integrated Lipschitz norm control the exceptional event where this scale is exceeded.

The variable waiting-time argument needs the local correction \(a=(1-p_0/2)^{1/T}\), so that \(a^n\ge1-p_0/2\) for \(n\le T\). This supplies the factor required by Lemma 4.1. If \(W(z)\le K\), its minimizing time may depend on \(z\). The estimate \(P_kf^{p_0}\le C_Tf^{p_0}\) for \(k\le T\) gives \(P_Tf^{p_0}(z)\le C_TK\), and hence a common-time event with bounded \(V\) and inverse separation. No compactness in the full \(H^5\) topology is being assumed.

Definition B.1 places the common time and positive probability before the quantifier over initial states. A valid Lemma B.8 would therefore give exactly the uniform small-set input required in Proposition 4.9. The issue is its proof, not an altered quantifier in this deduction.
## Malliavin estimates and the anisotropic derivative norm

The Section 5 audit found no additional substantiated substantive failure in the assigned estimates. Qualitative covariance nondegeneracy \(g(\varepsilon)\to0\) suffices for Lemma 5.28: split the layer-cake integral into a bounded interval, controlled by that nondegeneracy, and a tail controlled by the uniform eighth moment. The needed fourth-moment smallness does not require polynomial inverse-covariance tails.

The high-frequency input tail can be bounded directly through the semigroup decomposition \[J_{1/2,1}\Pi_{\ge R}
 =J_{3/4,1}J_{1/2,3/4}\Pi_{\ge R}.\] The \(L^2\)-to-\(H^n\) smoothing bound and \(\|\Pi_{\ge R}\|_{H^n\to L^2}\le R^{-n}\), followed by Holder’s inequality, give an \(R\)-independent moment constant. This addresses the abbreviated coupled-system justification in Lemma 5.27.

Footnote 5 on p. 48 explicitly says that derivatives are measured in the dual norms. This resolves the apparent reversed inequalities involving the near-diagonal tangent norm \[\|(\xi,v_x,v_y)\|_{H^5,2}
 =\|\xi\|_{H^5}+|v_x+v_y|+\frac{|v_x-v_y|}{|x-y|}.\] The tangent-process control transfers to the two-point process using the stated first-derivative comparison. It is not valid to apply the tangent weights directly to an ordinary Euclidean gradient without this dual interpretation.
## Scalar reduction and all positive moments

The Fourier summation in Proposition 2.7 uses \(\sum_{k\ne0}|k|^{-3}<\infty\) in dimension two, yielding an \(H^{-2}\) second-moment estimate and then the \(H^{-1}\) estimate by interpolation with conserved \(L^2\). The actual path metric controls spatial displacement globally, including between different velocities, which supplies the Lipschitz bound for the Fourier observables used here.

Use a strictly positive burn-in time \(T\in t_0\mathbb N\), with \(T\ge t_0+C\log(2+\|u_0\|_{H^1})\), and condition on the full past at \(T\). This avoids requiring high-norm regularization at time zero and permits a random transported scalar at the restart. Uniform-in-time control follows from the integrated velocity-gradient moments.

For clarity, let the resulting normalized estimate be \[X_t\le\min\{1,K_0e^{-ct}(1+U)^A\},
 \quad \mathbb EK_0\le C,\quad A\ge1,\quad U=\|u_0\|_{H^1}.\] For any desired moment \(p>0\), take \(\vartheta=\min\{1,(Ap)^{-1}\}\). Then \(\vartheta p\le1\), \(A\vartheta\le1/p\), and \[X_t\le K_0^\vartheta e^{-c\vartheta t}(1+U)^{1/p},
 \qquad \mathbb E K_0^{\vartheta p}\le C'.\] This verifies the all-\(p\) conversion without making the prefactor uniform over all \(L^2\) initial scalars. The zero initial scalar is handled separately. For the universal \(H^1\) result, the summable Fourier weights in Proposition 2.12 and operator interpolation are consistent.
# Normalization checks, limits, and acceptance status

Corollary 1.4 on p. 3 prints Batchelor variance bounds linear in \(\|g\|_2\). The isometry calculation on p. 17 and Proposition 2.13 use the mathematically consistent \(\|g\|_2^2\). Indeed, with zero initial scalar, \(\phi^{ag}=a\phi^g\) pathwise, so the projected variance scales as \(a^2\). The quadratic form, with \(N\ge N_0(g)\), is the supported normalization. The dependence of \(N_0\) on \(g\) cannot restore a uniform linear-amplitude law: apply the asserted bounds to \(g\) and \(ag\) at a common \(N\) above both thresholds and let \(a\) be large. Because the proof consistently identifies the quadratic quantity, this is recorded as a normalization correction, rather than added as a standalone finding based on omitted superscripts.

For its lower-bound argument, choose the Fourier cutoff so that \(\|\Pi_{>R}g\|_2\le\|g\|_2/4\), instead of inferring that tail bound from \(\|\Pi_{\le R}g\|_2\ge3\|g\|_2/4\). For example the stronger squared low-frequency mass \(15/16\) suffices. Then \[\|\Pi_{\le N}\Phi_{s,t}g\|_2^2
 \ge \frac{13}{32}\|g\|_2^2
 -\frac{R^2}{2N^2}
       \|\Phi_{s,t}\|_{H^1\to H^1}^2\|g\|_2^2.\] On a sufficiently short logarithmic time window this gives a positive fixed fraction of \(\|g\|_2^2\). Integrating and taking \(N\ge R^2\) recovers the intended logarithmic lower rate with adjusted constants. The independent scalar Brownian forcing permits the stochastic isometry after conditioning on the entire velocity path; no anticipative integral with respect to that Brownian motion is required.

The paper treats zero scalar diffusivity. It expressly defers uniform positive-diffusivity mixing and the corresponding Batchelor result, and presents OU-tower forcing as a proposed extension. None is credited here as a proved theorem. Isolated inverse, phase, time-index, and exponent-label slips with identifiable local corrections were not separately counted. The full external weak Harris and Furstenberg theorems were not independently reproved, and the general replacement for the two-point control construction remains an open requirement of the reviewed proof.

Title: M25-0120
Scientific Review of
Rotation-invariant web bases from hourglass plabic graphs
# 1. Identity, scope, and assessment
Authors. Christian Gaetz, Oliver Pechenik, Stephan Pfannerer, Jessica Striker, and Joshua P. Swanson.
Reviewed source. The preserved 84-page author manuscript arXiv:2306.12501v6 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.12501v6), submitted 8 May 2026; its title page is dated 12 May 2026. The exact PDF SHA256 is
00000TOKEN

The journal record is Inventiones Mathematicae 243, 703–804 (2026), DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01385-2 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01385-2), first published online 10 November 2025. The journal PDF was not obtained. This review makes no assertion of equivalence to that version. All source page numbers below refer to the preserved manuscript, whose printed and PDF page numbers agree.

Assessment. Two substantive proof defects are confirmed by explicit finite graph constructions. The first concerns the characterization of full reducedness by boundary-started trip strands. The second concerns the immediate-decrease assertion in the reduction algorithm’s termination proof. Neither construction is a counterexample to the principal web-basis conclusion.
ID | Severity | Supported conclusion
F1 | Major | Proposition 3.21 and the literal monotonicity converse in Corollary 3.33 miss a closed straight trajectory, even in a connected graph.
F2 | Major | Algorithm 7.1(4) and Theorem 7.2’s next-iteration reduction claim fail on a graph requiring two preparatory benzene moves.

Under the supplied rubric, a demonstrated invalid derivation closely tied to a core result is Major even when a repair is available. This classification does not assert that the main theorem is false. Typographical slips and missing citations alone are outside the finding count. No additional issue has been upgraded merely because an external computation was not rerun.

The central claims examined are the graph/tableau bijection of Theorem 6.1, the leading-term result of Theorem 6.4, and the rotation-invariant basis of Theorem 6.10. The quantum statement is over \(\mathbb C(q)\) for \(U_q(\mathrm{sl}_4)\); the semistandard extension in Section 9.3 is at \(q=1\) and \(r=2,3,4\). Rotation invariance is understood in the paper’s stated sense, allowing scalar multiples and the corresponding rotation of the boundary type.

Recovery scope. This report completes M25-0120 within the authorized seven-paper recovery. There was no substantive earlier report for this paper to repair; preserved sources and acquisition evidence were reused. Independent scientific acceptance remains pending.
# 2. F1 — Closed trajectories escape the stated criterion

Locators. Definitions 3.1 and 3.4 (p. 14); Definitions 3.14, 3.16, and 3.19 (pp. 16–17); Proposition 3.21 (p. 18); Definition 3.30 and Corollary 3.33 (pp. 22–23). These statements were checked in rendered source pages.

Take two internal vertices \(v,w\), three distinct parallel simple edges \(a,b,c\) joining them, and boundary edges \(pv,wq\). The clockwise orders are \[v:(p,a,b,c),\qquad w:(q,c,b,a).\] Here \(p\) or \(q\) in a cyclic order denotes the incident boundary edge. Color \(v,q\) black and \(w,p\) white. # 3. F1 — Core dependency, repair, and bounded checks

> Initially every dangling wire has one original boundary endpoint. An X crosses two wires without joining their straight trajectories, so every surviving dangling wire still has one distinct original endpoint. A cap joins two such wires into a completed boundary-to-boundary trajectory and removes them. Induction therefore excludes every closed straight trajectory in the final linearized diagram.

## Other checks in Sections 2–4

The labeling and tableau arguments were checked with their actual signed and generalized-rectangle conventions. A generalized rectangle may terminate at \(k(1,1,1,1)\); total signed size need not be zero. Proper-labeling incidence counts give the same signed boundary count for every label, because each internal vertex sees each label once and internal edges cancel. This supplies the balancedness used in Theorem 4.24.

Removing a balanced consecutive substring shifts all later prefix vectors by a scalar multiple of \((1,1,1,1)\), leaving adjacent-row slacks unchanged. Concatenating the rectangular lattice words used in the proof likewise preserves the inequalities. Neither argument requires the false assertion that arbitrary nonrectangular lattice words can be freely concatenated.

Oscillization uses increasing row order for positive skew columns and removes lower rows first for negative columns. The comparison with promotion uses \(|c_1|\) elementary steps, matching the corresponding number of boundary rotations. The exceptional case in which cutting does not decrease the number of internal vertices is expressly handled by Lemma 4.25 (pp. 35–37).

Theorem 2.9’s coefficient formula has a useful noncancellation consequence. For a fixed boundary word, every proper labeling contributes the same sign times a Laurent monomial in \(q\). Thus equality of web invariants cannot hide an earlier boundary word by cancellation; a coefficient \(\pm q^a\) entails a unique contributing labeling. This supports the square-move transfer in Theorem 6.4. These positive checks do not eliminate F1.
# 4. F2 — A web needing two preparatory benzene moves

# 5. F2 — Termination, scope of impact, and other interfaces

The invalid inference. The principal same-face term of the benzene relation after the first flip in the example still has no forbidden square. It therefore cannot undergo Step (2) on the next iteration. The existence of lower-face side terms in the skein relation does not change that fact about this principal term. The written semistandard spanning argument on p. 80 also invokes Algorithm 7.1. The principal proof in Sections 5–6 does not depend on this immediate-decrease assertion; its separate criterion issue is addressed by F1.

A revised procedure could select a finite preparatory witness sequence and control both its remaining length and the face count, while treating lower-face skein side terms by an appropriate induction. Such a procedure must justify the permitted preliminary square and contraction moves and prove well-founded progress in every recursive branch. This report has not completed that general replacement proof.

The leading terms in Theorem 6.4 are distinct, have coefficients \(\pm q^a\), and hence give linear independence over \(\mathbb C(q)\). The dimension comparison uses rectangular fluctuating tableaux. The common-neighbor property used for descents passes between contracted representatives.
