report: Abstract: This claim-focused initial review establishes that the component-quotient assertion of Lemma 3.2 is false in its stated generality. An explicit diamond quotient has a connected underlying space although the action on source components is not transitive. The lemma is the stated justification of Proposition 3.12, which is used in the central implication of Theorem 6.1. This supports a qualified Major finding about a core proof dependency, without a counterexample to the actual shtuka assertions or the main component formula. A separate converse argument in Proposition 6.6 remains a Needs Evidence item. Scientific adjudication and independent acceptance are pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Verification of
The Connected Components of Affine Deligne–Lusztig Varieties
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Ian Gleason, Dong Gyu Lim and Yujie Xu, The connected components of affine Deligne–Lusztig varieties, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01386-1 [GLX]. The canonical source is the acquired publisher version of record, 57 PDF pages, printed pages 805–861. It was published online on 12 November 2025 and assigned to volume 243 (2026). Throughout this report, unqualified page numbers are printed pages; physical PDF page \(j\) is printed page \(804+j\).

The review checks the main theorem’s hypotheses and reduction structure, the component-quotient lemma and its exact uses, the ad-isomorphism reduction, coarsening of parahoric level, and the final component-stabilizer argument. The long geometric constructions in Sections 4–5 and the integral-model applications are not independently rederived. Nineteen source pages supporting these checks were inspected as rendered images; the coverage ledger distinguishes this from other extracted-text reading.

The acquired arXiv source is v3 of arXiv:2208.07195 (10 November 2025); it is supporting author material, not a replacement for the version of record. No separately applicable supplement or computational code was identified in the bounded source search. Code absence is not a mathematical defect. A live title/DOI search did not identify a formal correction; this is a bounded search result, not proof that none exists.
# Definitions, hypotheses and dependencies

Equation reference: eq:published. Immediately before Lemma 3.2 (p. 820), the paper defines \(\pi_0(F)\) as the connected components of the underlying topological space \(|F|\), equipped with the quotient topology. Lemma 3.2 assumes that \(K\) is locally profinite, \(F,G\) are small \(v\)-sheaves, and \(G=F/\underline K\). It asserts \[
 |G|=|F|/K,\qquad \pi_0(G)=\pi_0(F)/K.\] It does not assume a compact group, a proper action, quasiseparatedness, or local spatiality.

The main geometric applications have additional structure. In particular, actual infinite-level shtuka spaces and their period maps are not arbitrary small \(v\)-sheaves, and the Iwahori and Galois groups occurring in several quotient steps are compact. The counterexample below must be evaluated against the written lemma, while these additional structures limit what it says about those applications.

The relevant core dependency is explicit. Proposition 3.12 (p. 828) invokes Lemma 3.2 to deduce transitivity of \(G(\mathbf Q_p)\) on shtuka components from connectedness of the admissible locus. Proposition 6.11 (pp. 854–855) invokes Proposition 3.12 to identify that component set with a homogeneous space \(G(\mathbf Q_p)/H_t\). Lemmas 6.12–6.14 then use this description in the central \((4)\Rightarrow(5)\) implication of Theorem 6.1. This is a concrete dependency in the proof.
# Confirmed substantive finding

Problem 1 (The component-quotient assertion in Lemma 3.2).  The second equality in [eq:published] (#eq:published) fails for an actual free action of a locally profinite group on an affinoid perfectoid space, with a diamond as quotient.
## A counterexample satisfying the stated assumptions

Equation reference: eq:example. Set \(p=2\). Let \(C\) be an algebraically closed complete perfectoid field of characteristic \(2\), for example the completion of an algebraic closure of \(\mathbf F_2((t))\), and let \(C^+=\mathcal O_C\). Put \[
\begin{split}
 S&=\mathbf Z_2,\qquad K=\mathbf Z_{\mathrm{discrete}},\\
 F&=\underline S\times\operatorname{Spa}(C,\mathcal O_C)
   =\operatorname{Spa}\!\left(C^0(S,C),C^0(S,\mathcal O_C)\right).
\end{split}\] The profinite-product construction is an affinoid perfectoid space with underlying space \(S\); see [Retained latex: \cite[Example 11.12 and Example 11.16]{Scholze}]. Thus \(F\) is a small \(v\)-sheaf and every component of \(|F|=\mathbf Z_2\) is a singleton. The group \(K\) is locally profinite: the trivial subgroup is an open profinite subgroup. Compactness was not required.

Let \(n\in\mathbf Z\) translate the \(S\)-coordinate by \(n\) and fix the coefficient-field coordinate. Pullback of continuous functions induces automorphisms of the displayed perfectoid space. This acts on the index space \(\mathbf Z_2\), not by addition in the characteristic-\(2\) coefficient field. The action is free because \(\mathbf Z\hookrightarrow\mathbf Z_2\) is injective. Its equivalence relation is \[R=\coprod_{n\in\mathbf Z}F \rightrightarrows F,
 \qquad s(n,x)=x,\quad t(n,x)=x+n.\] Both projections are pro-étale, being isomorphisms on each summand. The relation is representable and its map into \(F\times F\) is a monomorphism. Therefore \(Y=F/R=F/\underline K\) is a diamond and hence a small \(v\)-sheaf [Retained latex: \cite[Definition 11.1, Proposition 11.3, Definition 12.1 and Remark 12.2]{Scholze}]. Quasiseparatedness is not required by that diamond definition.

Equation reference: eq:orbit. The quotient-topology result for a diamond presentation gives \[
 |Y|=\mathbf Z_2/\mathbf Z\] as an orbit set with its ordinary quotient topology [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition 11.13 and Definition 11.14]{Scholze}]. This is not a Hausdorff or \(T_0\) reflection.

Direct calculation of the two sides. Let \(V\) be a nonempty open subset of \(\mathbf Z_2/\mathbf Z\). Its inverse image \(U\) is a nonempty open \(\mathbf Z\)-invariant subset of \(\mathbf Z_2\), so it contains \(a+2^m\mathbf Z_2\) for some \(a,m\). Integer translation runs through all residue classes modulo \(2^m\), so \[\bigcup_{n\in\mathbf Z}(a+n+2^m\mathbf Z_2)=\mathbf Z_2.\] Invariance gives \(U=\mathbf Z_2\). Thus the quotient is indiscrete and connected.

Equation reference: eq:contradiction. There are nevertheless at least two distinct orbits. Both \(0\) and \(1/3\) belong to \(\mathbf Z_2\), but they do not differ by an integer: \(1/3=n\in\mathbf Z\) would imply \(3n=1\) in \(\mathbf Z_2\), hence in \(\mathbf Z\) by injectivity, an impossibility. Consequently \[
 \pi_0(Y)=\{*\},\qquad
 \pi_0(F)/K=\mathbf Z_2/\mathbf Z,\qquad
 \#(\mathbf Z_2/\mathbf Z)>1.\] The claimed equality fails even as a bijection of sets. The first equality of [eq:published] (#eq:published) holds in this example. ◻
## The invalid inference

The proof on p. 820 treats \(\pi_0\) as commuting with the relevant topological coequalizer. Applying \(\pi_0\) to the example’s action diagram leaves \(\mathbf Z\times\mathbf Z_2\rightrightarrows\mathbf Z_2\). Its coequalizer in topological spaces is the nonsingleton indiscrete space \(\mathbf Z_2/\mathbf Z\), whereas the component space of the quotient is a singleton. An adjunction into a suitable category of component objects would preserve colimits in that target category; it does not identify those colimits with ordinary orbit quotients in all topological spaces. The calculation directly isolates the failed inference.
## Counterevidence and exact impact

The quotient \(Y\) is not locally spatial: its nonsingleton indiscrete topology is not \(T_0\). The relation is not quasicompact and \(K\) is not compact. These properties do not violate the written lemma. They prevent claiming that this example occurs among the paper’s actual shtuka spaces or compact-level quotients.

In particular, the Iwahori quotient in formula (1.12), p. 813, and formula (6.17), p. 853, has a compact acting group. Galois-group quotient uses also involve compact groups. They are not refuted by the example. The specialization bijection equation (3.12), p. 826, belongs to Theorem 3.9 and is locally justified by rich smelted kimberlites and unibranchness. It must not be confused with Proposition 3.12 on p. 828; this review does not refute that specialization bijection.

The demonstrated error is a false general theorem used as the stated bridge to core component transitivity. The inspected proof supplies no replacement theorem with verified hypotheses for that bridge. Its use through Proposition 6.11 in Theorem 6.1 supports Major as a core proof-support defect. This does not assert that actual transitivity or the main theorem is false. Potential repairability does not make the demonstrated inference valid or automatically lower its severity.

A defensible correction must prove a component-transitivity result applicable to the particular period torsor, or give an independent argument for Proposition 3.12, and revisit affected uses. Adding local spatiality alone is not a repair established here. No universal replacement lemma is proposed.
# A bounded unresolved check
## Proposition 6.6(2): converse under an ad-isomorphism

Proposition 6.6, pp. 850–851, includes a torsor equivalence. Write \(A=G(\mathbf Q_p)\), \(B=H(\mathbf Q_p)\), \(N=\operatorname{im}G^{\mathrm{sc}}(\mathbf Q_p)\), and \(M=f(N)\). Subject to the component induction formula, the forward computation \[(A/N)\times^A B \simeq B/M\] is valid. Conversely, if a transitive \(A\)-set has stabilizer \(C\), its induced \(B\)-set has stabilizer \(f(C)\). Knowing the induced set is a \(B/M\)-torsor gives \(f(C)=M\), which alone does not give \(C=N\). Triviality of the simply connected action in the passage from (6.8) to (6.10) is immediate under the forward assumption; it does not by itself prove the converse.

There is substantial counterevidence to a confirmed defect. In an isotropic simply connected reduction with the required determinant control, one can obtain \(C\subset N\) and \(N=C(N\cap\ker f)\). A finite central intersection gives finite index, and the no-proper-finite-index-subgroup property can force \(C=N\). The general anisotropic situation and all geometric stabilizer hypotheses were not resolved here. No actual shtuka counterexample has been constructed.

This is Needs Evidence, not a second established Major or Minor finding. It asks for an explicit converse under the exact hypotheses and does not raise the supported severity or claim that every subsequently needed direction fails.
# Checks without a separate issue

The coarsening diagram in Section 6.3, p. 852, gives the claimed implication conditional on the stated vertical surjections and lower bijection: lift two points from the coarser level, use their common lower image, and invoke injectivity at the finer level. The set-theoretic deduction is valid.

The tori calculation in Lemma 6.5, p. 849, and the parahoric determinant calculation in Proposition 6.9, p. 854, are consistent with their smooth connected special-fiber and Lang-surjectivity inputs. Their formal roles were checked; external group-scheme results were not re-proved.

Discreteness in Lemma 6.13, p. 856, is compatible with openness of the normalizer: it contains the relevant open derived stabilizer and the center, and the central-times-derived map has open image in the \(p\)-adic group. Abbreviation of this explanation is not a separate finding. The anisotropic discussion in Theorem 6.2, p. 858, has additional geometry and is not itself disproved by the general counterexample.

Title: Verification of the curvature criterion for Lipschitz inextendibility
# Identity and inspected scope

The source is Jan Sbierski, Lipschitz inextendibility of weak null singularities from curvature blow-up, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01387-0 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01387-0), the acquired publisher PDF, 31 physical pages, printed pp. 961–991. Throughout, PDF page numbers are one-based; their printed page numbers are larger by 960. The separately acquired arXiv:2409.18838v2 source is not asserted to be identical to the publisher version.

The principal scope comprises Theorem 3.14 (PDF p. 13), Proposition 3.6 (pp. 11–13), Remark 3.22 and the three proof steps (pp. 15–25), and Examples 4.1, 4.5, 4.7 and 4.8 (pp. 26–29). The preserved scientific checkpoint records a full text reading and specific analytic checks by the interrupted predecessor. This continuation reuses those supported checks and supplies actual source-image inspection and the report. External theorems invoked by the paper are dependencies, not independently reproved results of this report.
# Assumptions, quantifiers and endpoint scope

Write \(v=\underline u\) for the second null coordinate. The spacetime has \(M=(-1,1)\times(-1,0)\times\mathbb S^2\), a \(C^2\) Lorentzian metric in the double-null gauge (2.1), and the stipulated continuous nondegenerate extension to \(v=0\). Proposition 3.6 bounds the indicated coefficients \(\underline\omega,\eta,\underline\eta,\underline\chi\), while the supremum of \(|\chi|\) is integrable in \(v\). Condition (3.15) likewise gives an \(L^1_v\) bound on the supremum of angular derivatives of the shift. These hypotheses do not say that all connection coefficients stay bounded.

Equation reference: eq:blowup. The curvature hypothesis is local at every boundary point and every open neighbourhood \(W\). Inside \(W\), it requires a boundary point \(q\), a compact neighbourhood \(\overline V\) with the stated manifold-with-corners cutoffs, continuous fields \(X_1,\ldots,X_4\), and \(\epsilon_0>0\), such that every continuous quadruple within \(\epsilon_0\) satisfies \[
 \left|\int_{\overline V\cap\{v<v_k\}}
 R(\widehat X_1,\widehat X_2,\widehat X_3,\widehat X_4)\,\operatorname{vol}\right|
 \longrightarrow\infty\] along a sequence \(v_k\to0\). The sequence may depend on the quadruple. The absolute value encloses the signed integral.

The conclusion excludes a locally Lipschitz extension admitting a limit endpoint of an affinely parameterized, future-directed and future-inextendible timelike geodesic with \(v\to0\) and limiting \(u<1\). It does not by itself exclude every extension through other regions or establish global strong cosmic censorship. Remark 3.20 makes this distinction explicitly (PDF p. 15).
# Verification of the proof mechanism
## Energy estimate and boundary flow

For \(E=2\Omega^2\dot v+2\dot u\), timelikeness controls the angular frame velocities. Equations (3.10)–(3.13) give \[E'\le C(E^2+E\dot v\,|\chi|).\] Dividing by \(E>0\) gives \[(\log E)'\le C E+C\dot v\,\sup_{u,\theta}|\chi(u,v,\theta)|.\] The integral of \(E\) is bounded by finite changes in the null coordinates, using the bounds on \(\Omega^2\). Changing variables from affine parameter to \(v\) in the other term invokes exactly the \(L^1_v\) hypothesis. Thus the bounded-energy conclusion uses the stated integrability with the correct coefficient (PDF pp. 12–13), not an uncontrolled global Riccati estimate.

In Remark 3.22 (PDF pp. 15–16), the difference of two coordinate flow curves satisfies the underlying ODE estimate \[|(|\delta|)'|\le L(v)|\delta|,\quad L\in L^1,\qquad
 |\delta(v)|\ge|\delta(v_0)|\exp\!\left(-\int_{v_0}^{v}L(s)\,ds\right).\] Distinct curves cannot acquire the same endpoint. The printed one-sided inequality is an abbreviated presentation of this ODE argument, not an established defect in injectivity.
## Connecting curves and identification of extensions

The connectors in (3.23) deliberately move backward and forward in \(v\), with slopes of absolute value one (PDF pp. 17–18). The integrable coefficient is therefore integrated over a shrinking \(v\)-interval. A connector constrained to a fixed \(v\)-slice would not justify this bound; the paper does not use such a connector.

In Step 2 (PDF pp. 19–23), uniformly integrable connection matrices along the space-filling family and bounded parallel frames give \[\sup_z|d(s_2,z)-d(s_1,z)|
 \le C\int_{s_1}^{s_2}\sup_z|A(s,z)|\,ds .\] This uniform Cauchy estimate supports continuous extension of the frames. Their inner products and the nondegenerate limiting metric preserve invertibility. The subsequent \(C^1\) identification invokes Proposition 5.11 of the paper’s reference [34]; Step 1 invokes Proposition 5.1 there. These external results are retained as proof dependencies. The parameter shifts in (3.30)–(3.31) do not establish a substantive defect after consistent translation of the affine parameters.
## Smoothing and the signed Stokes estimate

Step 3 (PDF pp. 23–25) pushes the continuous \(X_i\) through the \(C^1\) identification, smooths them on a compact neighbourhood in the hypothetical extension, and pulls them back. This produces one fixed admissible quadruple. The universal quadruple quantifier in [eq:blowup] (#eq:blowup) supplies its diverging sequence; a sequence uniform over all quadruples is unnecessary.

The fixed smooth fields and their derivatives are bounded on the compact set. The locally Lipschitz extension metric bounds its Christoffel symbols in the smooth interior, so the lower-order terms in (3.36) are bounded. Stokes’ theorem is applied to compact interior cutoffs. The fixed side boundary has finite piecewise \(C^1\) measure, and the moving face pulls back to the density \[\sqrt{-\det\widetilde g}\,|\widehat X_i^v|\,du\,d\theta^1\,d\theta^2.\] Its integrand and coordinate domain are uniformly bounded. This contradicts [eq:blowup] (#eq:blowup). The estimate bounds the absolute value of the signed curvature integral; it is not an \(L^1\) bound on absolute curvature.
# Examples and the volume factor

For Example 4.1, \[g=-2(du\otimes dv+dv\otimes du)+r(v)^2g_{\mathbb S^2},\qquad
 |\operatorname{vol}|=2r^2\sin\theta\,du\,dv\,d\theta\,d\phi.\] The convention in (4.2)–(4.4) gives \(R(\partial_v,\partial_\theta,\partial_\theta,\partial_v)=rr''\) and \(|\chi|=\sqrt2|r'|/r\).

In Example 4.5 (PDF pp. 27–28), set \(L=1-\log|v|\) and \(r=1+L^{-(p-1)}\), \(p>1\). Differentiation gives \[r'=\frac{p-1}{vL^p},\qquad
 r''=\frac{p-1}{v^2}(-L^{-p}+pL^{-p-1}).\] For \(L\ge2p\), \(r''\) is negative and comparable to \(-1/(v^2L^p)\). The first derivative is integrable, whereas the negative second-derivative integral diverges. Positive volume factors on the compact angular patch are bounded above and below; the leading sign survives sufficiently small allowed perturbations. This is consistent with the theorem.

Example 4.7 (PDF pp. 28–29) takes \(r''=\sin(1/v)/v\). Oscillatory integration bounds \(r'\), permitting a Lipschitz extension, although \(\int |r''|\,dv=\int^\infty|\sin x|\,dx/x\) diverges. The actual signed-integral hypothesis is stronger and is not contradicted.

Equation reference: eq:ibp. Example 4.8 (PDF p. 29) has \(r'=-\cos(-1/v)\), \(r\ge1\), and \(r''=\sin(-1/v)/v^2\). The fields in (4.9) give \(R=r''(1-v\sin(1/v))\). The volume factor must be retained. The first relevant term is bounded: \[
 \int r^2r''\,dv=r^2r'-2\int r(r')^2\,dv .\] Here \(r,r'\) are bounded on a finite interval. With \(x=-1/v\), the other term is, up to a fixed positive angular factor, \[-\int^\infty r(-1/x)^2\frac{\sin^2x}{x}\,dx\longrightarrow-\infty .\] Thus the divergence survives the volume weight. Replacing the first and fourth fields near the boundary by \(\partial_v\), with a cutoff away from the boundary, is an arbitrarily small continuous perturbation and leaves only the bounded expression [eq:ibp] (#eq:ibp). The example correctly demonstrates why one unperturbed quadruple is insufficient. This is a consistency clarification, not a defect or a proposed repair.
# Outcome and limits

No substantive problem is established in the stated scope. The checked estimates and examples support the internal use of the curvature hypothesis. No global correctness certificate, nonlinear Kerr curvature-blow-up proof, or independent verification of external extension-identification theorems is claimed. Remark 3.37’s lower-regularity direction is not treated as an established theorem.

Title: Local normalization and proof-scope verification for relative Langlands duality
# Source identity, scope and mathematical status

The source is Zhengyu Mao, Chen Wan and Lei Zhang, Relative Langlands duality for some strongly tempered spherical varieties, the acquired 35-page author-hosted PDF at https://sites.rutgers.edu/chen-wan/wp-content/uploads/sites/518/2025/04/BZSV.pdf. It has no intrinsic revision date establishing a journal-final identity. All locations below refer to this exact acquired manuscript; physical PDF and printed page numbers coincide. No equivalence to the journal version is asserted. The full source hash, manifest, recovery lineage, exact computations and image bindings accompany this report.

Theorem 1.13 (p. 10) is the principal proved local result: fundamental-lemma and smooth-transfer assertions for the six specified split models over nonarchimedean local fields. Its detailed statements and restrictions are in Sections 3–5. In particular, Theorem 5.9(2), p. 26, assumes unramified additive character and residual characteristic different from two for its spherical formula. Conjectures 1.1, 1.5, 1.7, 1.8, 2.1 and 2.3 are not promoted to theorems. The global relative trace formula requires the acknowledged regularization; Remarks 1.2 and 1.6 suppress specified zeta, global or ramified factors. The calculations below do not resolve these global conjectures.

The coverage comprises the main definitions and claim hierarchy, the local range and germ argument, selected unfolding and Fourier steps for Models 1–6, the complete Model 1 adjoint branching, and the Section 6 symplectic branching and formal period comparison. General Jordan integrations, every root-coordinate identification, and the external proofs cited by the manuscript were not all independently reconstructed. This report is consequently a bounded technical review, not a certification of the whole manuscript.
# Problem 1: incorrect volume multipliers in two local constructions
## Exact claim and first occurrence

Equation reference: eq:Jordan. The first occurrence is the first proof paragraph of Theorem 4.4(1), p. 18; the defining integral follows Proposition 4.2 on p. 17: \[
 I(a,\phi)=\int_{J(F)}\phi(a,A)
 \psi\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{tr}A-N_J(A)}{a}\right)\,dA,\qquad a\in F^\times.\] The proof chooses \(B=a_0+\varpi^m\mathcal O_F\), with \(|a|=|a_0|\) on \(B\), and a small compact open \(K\subset J(F)\) so that the phase is trivial. It instructs multiplication of the indicator of \(B\times K\) by the volume of the set, and claims \(I(a,\phi)=1_B(a)\).

Equation reference: eq:scalar. For \(\phi=c\,1_B1_K\) under the stipulated phase condition, direct integration gives \[
 I(a,\phi)=c\,\operatorname{vol}(K)\,1_B(a).\] The variable \(a\) is a parameter, not an integration variable. The required coefficient is therefore \(\operatorname{vol}(K)^{-1}\), without a factor involving \(\operatorname{vol}(B)\).

For a fully admissible instance, take Model 1, \(F=\mathbb Q_5\), \(J=\mathrm{Mat}_3(F)\), \(\psi\) of conductor \(\mathbb Z_5\), and product self-dual measure with \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathbb Z_5)=1\). For any integer \(m\ge1\), put \[a_0=1,\qquad B=1+5^m\mathbb Z_5,\qquad
 K=5^m\mathrm{Mat}_3(\mathbb Z_5).\] All \(a\in B\) are units, \(\operatorname{tr}A\in5^m\mathbb Z_5\), and \(\det A\in5^{3m}\mathbb Z_5\). Thus the character in [eq:Jordan] (#eq:Jordan) is identically one on the proposed support, and all compactness and local-constancy requirements hold. Since \(\operatorname{vol}(B)=5^{-m}\) and \(\operatorname{vol}(K)=5^{-9m}\), the literal coefficient \(c=\operatorname{vol}(B\times K)\) gives \[I(a,\phi)=5^{-19m}1_B(a)\ne1_B(a).\] Reading the coefficient as \(\operatorname{vol}(K)\) instead yields \(5^{-18m}\), which also fails. Taking \(m\) arbitrarily large excludes an implicit sufficiently-small-support exception. The corrected function \[\phi(a,A)=\operatorname{vol}(K)^{-1}1_B(a)1_K(A)\] has the claimed integral and has both singular values \(\phi(0,I)\) and \(\phi(0,-I)\) equal to zero.
## Second occurrence and exact countercalculation

Equation reference: eq:wrong39. Take \(F=\mathbb Q_3\), an unramified \(\psi\), normalized product measure, and \[B=1+3^M\mathbb Z_3,\quad K=(3^M\mathbb Z_3)^{15},\quad
 K'=(3^M\mathbb Z_3)^4,\qquad M\ge1.\] The four phase terms have respective valuations at least \(M,3M,2M,2M\). Both \(a\) and \(2\) are units. Hence the phase in [eq:FJ] (#eq:FJ) is integral throughout the support and the character is one. Write \(b=3^{-M}\), \(k=3^{-15M}\), \(k'=3^{-4M}\). The literal volume multipliers \(bk\) for \(\phi\) and \(k'\) for \(\phi'\) give \[
 I(a,\phi,\phi')=(bk)k'\,kk'\,1_B(a)
 =3^{-39M}1_B(a)\ne1_B(a).\] At \(M=1\), the scalar is exactly \(1/4052555153018976267\). Independent rational arithmetic reproduced this value. If the first multiplier means \(k\) alone, the scalar is instead \(3^{-38M}\), still incorrect.
## Verified repair, counterevidence and impact

Equation reference: eq:repair. For any \(f\in C_c^\infty(F^\times)\), its support is compact and bounded away from zero. Consequently the coefficients containing \(a^{-1}\) and \(a^{-2}\) in [eq:FJ] (#eq:FJ) are uniformly bounded on that support. Choose common sufficiently small \(K,K'\) about zero so that the character is identically one there for every \(a\in\operatorname{supp}(f)\). Then \[
 \phi(a,A)=f(a)\frac{1_K(A)}{\operatorname{vol}(K)},\qquad
 \phi'(Y)=\frac{1_{K'}(Y)}{\operatorname{vol}(K')}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I(a,\phi,\phi')=f(a).\] This proves the required realization by a single pair, without assuming that an arbitrary sum of pure tensors is itself pure. Dividing by \(\operatorname{vol}(B\times K)\) would not be the correct repair: it would leave an unwanted factor \(\operatorname{vol}(B)^{-1}\).

The established defect is the false exact identity for the stated test functions. Its assessment is Minor. This classification rests on the actual proof dependency: the local argument needs the image to contain \(C_c^\infty(F^\times)\); the printed witnesses already yield nonzero multiples of the required indicators, and linearity gives this image in Section 4. Formula [eq:repair] (#eq:repair) directly supplies it in Section 5. The germ computation and basic-function fundamental lemma are separate calculations. No failure of the required range, transfer exponent, or singular distribution follows from the wrong multiplier. The classification is not based merely on the repair being short, and it is not a claim that a Major issue would require an irreparable or globally false theorem.
# Positive local checks and their limits
## Character orthogonality and matching germs

For the unramified character and self-dual measure in (4.2), p. 18, \[\int_{\varpi^m\mathcal O_F}\int_{\varpi^m\mathcal O_F}
 \psi(bxy)\,dx\,dy=|b|^{-1}\qquad (|b|>q^{2m}).\] Indeed the inner integral is \(q^{-m}\) exactly when \(y\in b^{-1}\varpi^{-m}\mathcal O_F\). The stated inequality makes this ball a subset of \(\varpi^m\mathcal O_F\); its volume is \(|b|^{-1}q^m\). This verifies the identity analytically.

Definition 3.1 and Proposition 3.3 (p. 15) normalize the Kuznetsov function as \(|a|J(a)\), while Theorem 4.4 uses \(|a|^{(1-n)/2}I(a)\). Equality of these expressions gives exactly \(I(a)=|a|^{(n+1)/2}J(a)\). The two singular coefficients must both be matched. The chosen condition \(|2|>|\varpi^m|\) separates the neighbourhoods of \(I\) and \(-I\), including dyadic characteristic-zero fields after increasing \(m\). Independent local bump functions prescribe the two values. After their germs agree, the difference vanishes near zero and is boundedly supported, so the away-from-zero range result supplies the remaining correction.

For Model 1, the stationary equation for \(\operatorname{tr}A-\det A\) is \(\operatorname{adj}(A)=I\). It forces \(A=\det(A)I\) and \(\det(A)^2=1\), hence \(A=\pm I\). Off these points, a nonzero coordinate derivative and separate affine dependence of the determinant permit character-orthogonality cancellation on small balls. This validates the inspected nonstationary step in that model. The corresponding Jordan calculations in every other model and the full general basic-function computation remain dependencies on the manuscript’s cited work [21].
## Finite fundamental-lemma checks
\(p\) | Matrix phase counts | Scaled difference

The differences are multiples of the relevant cyclotomic relations. These checks support the normalization for the specified fields and single valuation only; they do not prove the general fundamental lemma. They are concrete counterevidence against attributing its failure to Problem 1.
## Fourier–Jacobi factors in Model 5

On p. 27, Fourier integration in \(Y'\simeq F^4\) forces \(A_i\in a\mathcal O_F\) for \(i=2,\ldots,5\). When the residual characteristic is not two, the remaining quadratic phase is integral, justifying the stated restriction. The four paired integrations in (5.15), p. 28, contribute \(|a|^4\). On p. 29 the four Fourier restrictions contribute \(q^{-4m}\), and \(A_i=aB_i\) contributes \(|a|^4\), agreeing with the progression \(|a|^3\) to \(|a|^7\). The earlier \(|a|^3\) reduction imported from [21] was not independently reconstructed.

For a sufficiently large ball \(D=\varpi^{-m}\mathcal O_F\), \[\int_D\int_D\psi(-xy/2)\,dx\,dy
 =\operatorname{vol}(D)\operatorname{vol}(D\cap 2\varpi^m\mathcal O_F)=|2|.\] The four-variable quadratic factor on p. 30 consists of two such pairs, hence equals \(|4|\). Completing the bilinear products translates by fixed centres contained in \(D\) for sufficiently large \(m\). Exact finite character-orthogonality checks at \(p=2,3,5\), \(m=1,2\), gave the four-variable factors \(1/4,1,1\), respectively. The Model 5 factor \(|4|\) is therefore supported, including at the checked dyadic place. This is consistent with the germ coefficients \(c_\pm=|4|I^\pm\) in Theorem 5.9(3) and the transfer factor in Conjecture 5.8.
# Representation bookkeeping and conjectural scope
## Model 1 in Table 3

Equation reference: eq:table. This is a scope clarification, not an additional substantive Problem. On p. 2 the decomposition is defined for the full adjoint representation. The Model 1 nilpotent on p. 12 has root vectors \(E_{31},E_{42},E_{53},E_{64}\), with two Jordan chains of length three. Thus, over the complex representation category relevant here, \[V=U\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^2W,\qquad \dim U=\dim W=2.\] The multiplicity-space action induces \(H_0=\mathrm{PGL}_2\). Put \(A=\operatorname{Ad}_{\mathrm{PGL}_2}\), of dimension three. The full decomposition is \[
 \mathfrak{sl}_6
 =(A\otimes\mathbf1)
 \oplus((A\oplus\mathbf1)\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^2W)
 \oplus((A\oplus\mathbf1)\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^4W).\] Its dimension is \(3+4\cdot3+4\cdot5=35\). Exact matrix ranks \(4,2,0\) for the first three nilpotent powers and an independent comparison of every torus weight verified this calculation.

On its most favourable reading, the first row of Table 3 (p. 13) lists the nontrivial \(H_0\)-isotypic part, of dimension \(27\). The omitted eight dimensions are \(\mathbf1\otimes(\operatorname{Sym}^2W\oplus\operatorname{Sym}^4W)\). Restoring them introduces precisely \(\zeta_k(2)\zeta_k(3)\) in Conjecture 2.3 (p. 14). Remark 1.2 expressly permits suppression of Dedekind zeta factors, so this does not contradict the conjecture at its stated normalization precision. Both readings retain only the indices \(0,2,4\), preserving the relevant parity assumption. An explicit nontrivial-isotypic convention, or the full coefficients in [eq:table] (#eq:table), would remove the ambiguity. No damage to the local main theorem was established.
## Section 6 branching and the formal comparison

In Section 6.2 (p. 31), the standard representation of \(\mathrm{SO}_{4n+1}(\mathbb C)\) restricts as \((V\otimes W)\oplus\mathbf1\), with \(V\) the \(2n\)-dimensional symplectic standard module and \(W\) the two-dimensional \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) module. The exterior-square identity gives \[\operatorname{Ad}_{\mathrm{SO}_{4n+1}}
 =\operatorname{Ad}_{\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}}\otimes\mathbf1
 \oplus V\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^1W
 \oplus\Lambda^2V\otimes\operatorname{Sym}^2W.\] The dimensions sum to \(n(2n+1)+4n+3n(2n-1)=8n^2+2n\), as required. The odd coefficient is \(V\), and the denominator shifts in Conjecture 6.1 are consequently \(1,3/2,2\), matching the displayed formula. Formally multiplying the normalized squared-period expressions in Conjectures 6.1 and 6.2 gives the stated \(L(1/2)^2/L(1,\operatorname{Ad})^2\) pattern, at the declared precision of suppressed factors. This algebra does not prove either conjecture or an unnormalized equality of periods. Proposition 6.4 (pp. 33–34) retains the external root-exchange and vanishing dependencies [9] and [10]; those proofs were not independently re-established.
# Unresolved checks and final assessment

Remark 5.6 (p. 25) specifies the Model 6 spaces \(J=\mathrm{Mat}_{1\times1}\times\mathrm{Asym}_{4\times4}\) and a two-dimensional \(Y'\), but leaves its pairings to analogous definitions. The proof after Theorem 5.9 (p. 26) explicitly treats the \(\mathrm{Spin}_{11}\) case. The explicit Model 6 quadratic-phase coefficient and coordinate/Haar comparison needed for an independent dyadic scalar calculation were not reconstructed here. A naive one-pair substitution yielding \(|2|\) would assume precisely the unverified normalization. It is therefore not an admissible counterexample and is recorded only as an unresolved verification item.

The proved finding is one repeated local normalization error, with a checked repair and a demonstrated boundary on its effect. No additional substantive defect is established in the inspected claims. Full external Jordan and Weil calculations, all Model 2–4 analogues, and the Model 6 dyadic normalization remain outside completed verification. Absence of author code is not a mathematical deficiency.

report: Abstract: The acquired publisher version of Gorodetski, Kleptsyn and Monakov is examined through its cutoff-energy, transport and contraction arguments. Two local discrepancies are established: a missing dimension factor in an explicit energy constant, and an overbroad monotonicity lemma, for which an exact counterexample is supplied. Their repairs preserve the parameter range and existential conclusions of the main theorems. The normalized Hilbert-space argument, compact-family limit, iteration and moment-boundary example receive positive bounded checks. The report assessment is Minor; scientific adjudication and independent acceptance remain pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Kernel constants, quantifiers and the proof of Hölder regularity of stationary measures
# Identity, assumptions and conclusion scope

The inspected source is A. Gorodetski, V. Kleptsyn and G. Monakov, Hölder regularity of stationary measures, Inventiones mathematicae 243 (2025), 1037–1077, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01389-y (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01389-y). It is the acquired publisher version of record, 41 physical pages. Below, PDF pages are one-based and printed page numbers equal PDF page numbers plus 1036. The separately acquired arXiv:2209.12342v1 source is not assumed equivalent to the publisher text.

For a smooth closed \(k\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold \(M\), put \(\mathcal L(f)=\max(\operatorname{Lip}(f),\operatorname{Lip}(f^{-1}))\). Theorems 1.1 and 2.3 (PDF pp. 2, 5–6) require a positive moment \(\int\mathcal L(f)^\gamma\,d\mu(f)<\infty\), and absence of a common invariant probability measure. The finite-measure wording of Theorem 2.3 is understood as nonzero finite measures after normalization, consistently with Theorem 1.1. Their conclusion is an upper mass bound \[\nu(B_r(x))\le C r^\beta\] for all stationary probability measures, with uniform positive \(\beta,C\). It does not assert uniqueness, absolute continuity, a lower Ahlfors bound, or exact dimensionality.

Theorem 2.6 (PDF p. 6) concerns arbitrary initial probability measures and averaged \(n\)-step images, only at radii \(r>\kappa^n\). Finite-time atomic images are compatible with it. Theorem 2.8 (PDF p. 7) permits arbitrary independent step distributions in a weakly compact family, with a uniform positive moment and the stronger absence of deterministic images: no pair of probability measures \(m,m'\) satisfies \(f_*m=m'\) for almost every \(f\) under any law in that family. These quantifiers and the distinction between stationary and nonstationary hypotheses are essential.

This review checks the principal internal dependencies in Sections 2, 4–6 and Appendix A. It does not certify all external results cited in the introductory discussion. Source acquisition and index parsing are recorded as provenance, not as scientific proof verification.
# Problem 1: missing dimension factor in the energy ceiling
## Decisive calculation and admissible instance

Equation reference: eq:correctmax. The error occurs in Lemma 4.7 and the subsequent proof of Corollary 4.8, PDF p. 16 / printed p. 1052. Definition 4.1, PDF p. 13, sets \[\varphi_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(r)=
 \begin{cases}
 r^{-(k+\alpha)/2},&r\ge\varepsilon,\\
 \varepsilon^{-\alpha}r^{-(k-\alpha)/2},&0<r<\varepsilon.
 \end{cases}\] The Euclidean convolution kernel satisfies \(U_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(0)=\int_{\mathbb R^k}
\varphi_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(|x|)^2\,dx\). Writing \(V_k=\operatorname{vol}_{\mathbb R^k}(B_1)\), direct radial integration yields \[\begin{aligned}
 U_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(0)
 &=kV_k\left[
 \varepsilon^{-2\alpha}\int_0^\varepsilon r^{\alpha-1}\,dr
 +\int_\varepsilon^\infty r^{-\alpha-1}\,dr\right]\notag\\
 &=\frac{2kV_k}{\alpha}\varepsilon^{-\alpha}. \end{aligned}\] The source instead defines \(L=2V_k\) and states \(U_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(0)=(L/\alpha)\varepsilon^{-\alpha}\). Its own preceding radial-integration line retains \(k\), so the discrepancy is visible in the actual PDF and is not a text-extraction artefact.

Take \(k=2\), \(\alpha=1/4\), \(\varepsilon=1\), within the operative range \(0<\alpha<1/2\). Formula [eq:correctmax] (#eq:correctmax) gives \(16\pi\), whereas the stated constant gives \(8\pi\). For the admissible probability measure \(\nu=\delta_x\) on any closed two-dimensional Riemannian manifold, \[\mathcal E_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(\delta_x)=U_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(0).\] Thus the specific choice \(C''_\alpha=L/\alpha\) in Corollary 4.8’s proof is too small. The existential assertion that some finite \(C''_\alpha\) works remains true.
## Repair and actual downstream effect

Equation reference: eq:holder. The exact repair is \[L=2kV_k,\qquad C''_\alpha=\frac{2kV_k}{\alpha}.\] The proof of Theorem 2.6 explicitly reuses \(C''_\alpha=L/\alpha\) at PDF pp. 24–25 / printed pp. 1060–1061, so this is an affected bound, not merely an unused coefficient. With the corrected value, the same recurrence gives \[\mathcal E_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(\nu_n)
 \le\max\{\lambda^n C''_\alpha\varepsilon^{-\alpha},\widetilde C\}.\] Setting \(\varepsilon=\lambda^{n/\alpha}\) still yields a uniform ceiling and, by Lemma 4.9, \[
 \nu_n(B_r(x))
 \le
 \left(\frac{2^\alpha\max\{2kV_k/\alpha,\widetilde C\}}{c'_\alpha}\right)^{1/2}
 r^{\alpha/2},\qquad r>\lambda^{n/\alpha}.\] The cutoff rate and Hölder exponent are unchanged. Only the explicit finite ceiling and resulting prefactor require enlargement. The initial assessment is Minor, based on this verified dependency boundary. The Dirac example refutes the printed energy bound; it is not asserted to refute a stationary or iterated Hölder bound under the main theorem’s hypotheses.
# Problem 2: an exact counterexample to the all-positive-\(\alpha\) lemma
## Source claim and calculation

Lemma 6.6, PDF p. 27 / printed p. 1063, claims that \(U_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(r)\) is non-increasing in \(r\) for every \(\alpha,\varepsilon>0\). Its proof invokes radial monotonicity of \(\varphi_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\), which need not hold when \(\alpha>k\).
## Sufficient correction and scope of impact

Restricting the lemma to \(0<\alpha\le k\) makes both pieces of \(\varphi_{\alpha,\varepsilon}\) non-increasing. The source’s layer-cake argument using intersections of balls then proves the desired radial monotonicity. This is a sufficient repaired range; no maximal range is claimed.

Proposition 4.6 and all required main-theorem applications already impose \(0<\alpha<1/2\), contained in that repaired range for positive integer dimension \(k\). Thus the broad auxiliary assertion is false, while the operative small-\(\alpha\) dependency is valid. The initial assessment is Minor. This counterexample is not presented as a counterexample to the main theorem.

Lemma 6.8 has a separate broad-\(\alpha\) wording issue in its proof: its displayed uncut-kernel majorant requires \(\alpha<k\). The comparison was verified here in the operative range, but no counterexample to the broader Lemma 6.8 was established. That unverified extension is not conflated with Problem 2.
# Verification of the central proof mechanism
## Finite cutoff, energy comparison and positive moments

For fixed \(\alpha,\varepsilon>0\), the radial exponents of \(\varphi_{\alpha,\varepsilon}^2\), after the volume element, are \(\alpha-1\) near zero and \(-\alpha-1\) at infinity. Hence its Euclidean \(L^2\) norm is finite. The cutoff also gives finite manifold energies for every probability measure, including atoms. This addresses the infinite-energy obstruction expressly identified in Section 3; an inequality of the form \(\mathcal E(\nu)\le\lambda\mathcal E(\nu)+C\) alone would not rule out infinite energy.

Tonelli justifies the three-variable kernel representation. The scaling identities in Lemma 6.1 give \[U_{\alpha,\lambda\varepsilon}(\lambda r)
 =\lambda^{-\alpha}U_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(r).\] In the operative range, the convolution limit as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) is locally integrable because \(\alpha<k\), and its tail is integrable because \(\alpha>0\). The power-law lower bound and radial monotonicity then yield \[\mathcal E_{\alpha,\varepsilon}(\nu)
 \ge c'_\alpha(2r)^{-\alpha}\nu(B_r(x))^2,\qquad r>\varepsilon,\] with exactly the square-root exponent in [eq:holder] (#eq:holder).

Proposition 4.10 compares the Euclidean interaction energy \(\mathcal E\) with the manifold \(L^2\) energy \(\widetilde{\mathcal E}\) at high energy, uniformly in the cutoff. The normal-coordinate proof is valid after making its near/far split explicit: separated pairs have a uniformly bounded kernel in the small-\(\alpha\) range; close pairs lie in a common normal chart, where the two kernel factors and volume Jacobian are uniformly controlled. The chart tails are bounded using the uncut majorant, without imposing an extra upper restriction on \(\varepsilon\). Finite additive constants are absorbed by the high-energy threshold.

u]\). The cutoff makes the required second moments finite and the normalizing denominators positive. The Hilbert identity gives \[\mathbb E\|g_f-g\|_2^2
 =\mathbb E\widetilde{\mathcal E}(f_*
u)-\widetilde{\mathcal E}(\mu*
u).\] Under the noncontraction assumption in Proposition 5.1, this is at most \(2\delta\widetilde{\mathcal E}(
u)\), while \(\|g\|_2^2\ge(1-\delta)\widetilde{\mathcal E}(
u)\).

For normalized \(h_f=g_f/\|g_f\|_2\) and \(\bar h=g/\|g\|_2\), \[\|h_f-\bar h\|_2\le
 \frac{2\|g_f-g\|_2}{\|g\|_2},\qquad
 \operatorname{TV}(h_f^2\,dy,\bar h^2\,dy)\le\|h_f-\bar h\|_2.\] The source uses half the \(L^1\) difference as total variation. Therefore \[\mathbb E\operatorname{TV}^2\le\frac{8\delta}{1-\delta}\le16\delta
 \quad(\delta\le1/2),\] and Markov gives probability at most \(4\sqrt\delta\) above the threshold \(2\delta^{1/4}\). The Wasserstein estimate follows from \(W_1\le\operatorname{diam}(M)\operatorname{TV}\). This reproduces Lemma 5.3 (PDF pp. 22, 36–37). The repeated \(f_*\nu\) in both printed TV arguments in the later proof is an evident notation slip: the explicitly defined \(\bar h\) and the lemma statement identify the second density as that of \(\mu*\nu\).

Proposition 4.21’s approximate equivariance is obtained by comparing the normalized energy measure with the first-coordinate marginal of its three-variable measure. Most mass lies near the diagonal at high energy. The first-coordinate marginal is supported on the original measure’s support, and kernel comparison controls its push-forward for \(\mathcal L(f)\le R\). The triangle inequality and the Lipschitz push-forward bound then give the stated \(W_1\) conclusion. Unspecified constants can absorb the displayed diameter factor, and the small tolerance can be chosen at most one.
## Compactness, uniformity and iteration

The order of choices in the contradiction argument is the tolerance, the distortion cutoff \(R\), sufficiently small \(\alpha\), and then a sufficiently large energy threshold. The counterexample measure and cutoff are chosen last. The moment bound supplies the required uniform tail control; for example, if \(\alpha\le\gamma/2\), \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L^\alpha 1_{\{\mathcal L>R\}}\big]
 \le C_0R^{-\gamma/2}.\] The resulting normalized measures \(m_j,m'_j\) have subsequential weak limits. In the compact-family case, the laws \(\mu_j\) also converge within the family. The bounded function \[(f,m,m')\longmapsto W_1(f_*m,m')\] is jointly continuous in the \(C^1\) and weak measure topologies on compact \(M\). Its expectation tends to zero by the quantitative exceptional-set estimate. Passing to the limit yields \(\int W_1(f_*m,m')\,d\mu(f)=0\), hence a deterministic image for almost every map, contradicting exactly the assumed condition. No common null set across varying laws is needed.

Low-energy control and high-energy contraction combine to give a max recurrence uniform in \(\varepsilon\). Its iteration is valid because \(0<\lambda<1\). Formula [eq:holder] (#eq:holder) follows with the corrected constant; the energy exponent is renamed after taking its square root. Stationarity then removes the shrinking cutoff for every fixed positive radius.

For the weaker stationary hypothesis, Proposition 2.12 (PDF p. 9) supplies a finite block length with no deterministic images. If arbitrarily long deterministic chains existed, their time averages would satisfy \[f_* ar
u_\ell- ar
u_\ell
 = rac{
u_{\ell,\ell}-
u_{\ell,0}}{\ell}\] on a common full-measure set of maps. Compactness would give a common invariant probability measure. Fixed-length blocking preserves a positive moment by submultiplicativity of \(\mathcal L\). Remainders in \(n\) are absorbed in the arbitrary initial distribution and a finite adjustment of constants and cutoff rate. For a compact family, nested closed sets of laws admitting deterministic block images yield a uniform block length. This also supports the uniformity in Remark 2.4.
# Boundary settings and the necessity example
## Manifolds with boundary

Remarks 2.9 and 5.7 (PDF pp. 7, 25) extend the argument to embeddings of a compact manifold with boundary into itself. An arbitrary such map need not be silently assumed to extend to a diffeomorphism of a chosen ambient closed manifold.

A precise adaptation uses the double \(\widetilde M\) and a Lipschitz folding retraction \(P:\widetilde M\to M\). Define the energy densities on the double and use \(\eta(\nu)=P_*\theta(\nu)\) as the probability measure in the final contradiction. The first-coordinate proxy remains supported on \(M\); pushing its comparison with \(\theta\) through \(P\) changes only fixed Lipschitz constants. The kernel ratio uses \(f\) only on \(M\), and the pullback is only on \(f(M)\), so the embedding is sufficient. Total variation contracts under \(P\), preserving the variance estimate. The two compact metrics are uniformly bi-Lipschitz equivalent, so the moment bounds change by a fixed geometric factor. This supports the extension with an explicit adaptation; no global ambient diffeomorphism extension is claimed.
## Appendix A: checking the moment boundary

With the clockwise projective coordinate, the attracting directions lie in \(I=[0,2/5]\), an invariant cone interval. The attracting directions of \(A_2,A_3\) lie in its interior and their repellers differ. Every point therefore enters that interior under a suitable power of one of these two maps. Compactness supplies a finite cover and a uniform positive finite-block hitting probability; forward invariance and stationarity force all stationary mass into \(I\).

On this interval, \[|f'_n(x)|\le q_n:=100\,2^{-2n^2},\qquad
 \nu(B(s_n,q_n^j))\ge p_n^j\] for sufficiently large \(n\). For any integer \(m\ge1\), choose \(n=m+4\). Then \(p_n^m>q_n\), because \(2n^2-mn=m^2+12m+32>7\) and \(2^7>100\). Letting \(j\) grow contradicts any Hölder bound with exponent \(1/m\), and hence any positive exponent. Exact rational computations checked representative values in addition to this analytic proof. The example supports the necessity of the stronger moment assumption; it does not satisfy that assumption and is not a counterexample to the main theorem.
# Assessment and limits

Two local mathematical claims require correction: the explicit dimension-dependent constant and the unrestricted monotonicity quantifier. Both have decisive calculations, source locations and verified repairs. Their core dependencies remain valid after the stated corrections, supporting an overall Minor initial assessment.

The broader \(\alpha\)-range of Lemma 6.8 was not resolved, and external introductory literature was not independently re-proved. The completed small-\(\alpha\) checks, boundary adaptation and Appendix A calculations do not imply a universal certification of the paper. No author code is required for these analytic claims, and none was executed. Author adoption of the corrections has not been requested or verified. Scientific decision: pending; human reviews: none; independent acceptance: not performed.

report: Abstract: The acquired publisher version of Galashin, Lam and Sherman-Bennett is examined through its Deodhar geometry, deletion–contraction argument, braid moves and cohomological application. A rank-one counterexample refutes Proposition 3.14, a used general criterion; a stronger factorial criterion adequate for the braid application is proved here. Independently, a type A3 braid variety is a two-dimensional torus on which the specified form vanishes, refuting the stated Lefschetz conclusion even after correcting its dimension indices. Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Deletion–contraction, orientation and the specified Lefschetz class in braid variety cluster structures
# Identity, definitions and review scope

The inspected work is P. Galashin, T. Lam and M. Sherman-Bennett, Braid variety cluster structures, II: general type, Inventiones mathematicae 243 (2025), 1079–1127, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01390-5 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01390-5). The acquired publisher version of record has 49 physical pages. Throughout, PDF pages are one-based; printed page numbers equal PDF page numbers plus 1078. The acquired arXiv:2301.07268v3 source is a separately identified artifact; equivalence with the publisher version is not assumed.

The working group in [1, PDF p. 2] is complex, simple and simply connected, with a fixed pinning and opposite Borel subgroups. A double word \(\beta=i_1\cdots i_m\) has letters in \(\pm I\) and Demazure product \(w_0\). Weighted flags are points of \(G/U_+\); strict relative position must be distinguished from relative position allowing a torus factor. The quotient \(\mathring R_\beta\) is asserted smooth, affine, factorial and irreducible, of complex dimension \[D=d(\beta)=m-\ell(w_0).\] The rightmost positive distinguished subexpression runs backwards from \(u_m=w_0\). Its solid positions form \(J_\beta\), with \(|J_\beta|=D\). The Deodhar torus has character variables \(x_e\), determined by their orders on the boundary divisors. A solid index is mutable when the corresponding almost-positive subexpression has initial value \(\mathrm{id}\). Frozen boundary divisors lie outside the open braid variety, and the frozen variables are units there.

Theorem 1.1 identifies \(\mathbb C[\mathring R_\beta]\) with the cluster algebra of the constructed seed. This statement is distinct from the general criterion in Proposition 3.14 and from the particular cohomological conclusion in Theorem 6.8. A seed on an affine variety, as defined on PDF p. 18, requires its initial torus to be an open dense subset. It does not already require every mutated variable to be regular on that variety.

The review covers the principal internal definitions, valuations, quotient and torus constructions, deletion–contraction hypotheses, induction ordering, selected braid calculations, folding dependencies and the exact Lefschetz assertion. Bounded native checks supplement the primary analysis. External algebraic-group, local-acyclicity and cohomological results remain identified dependencies where their proofs were not retrieved. Neither source indexing nor hash verification is counted as scientific validation.
# Problem 1: the ring containment in Proposition 3.14 does not produce embedded cluster tori
## Claim and exact counterexample

Proposition 3.14 [1, PDF pp. 21–22; printed pp. 1099–1100] states that if \(X\) is affine, factorial and irreducible, \(\Sigma\) is an integral sink-recurrent seed on \(X\), and \(\mathbb C[X]\subset U(\Sigma)\), then \(\mathbb C[X]=A(\Sigma)\). The proof first treats the cluster tori as embedded in \(X\), and then invokes a codimension-two complement. The stated containment does not supply those embeddings.

Equation reference: eq:rankone. Set \[X=\mathbb A^1\times\mathbb G_m,\qquad R=\mathbb C[x,y,y^{-1}],
 \qquad T=(\mathbb G_m)^2\subset X.\] Take \(x\) mutable, \(y\) frozen, \(d=(1,1)\), and exchange column \(\widetilde B=(0,1)^t\). A full skew matrix is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), with \(\omega=-\operatorname{dlog}x\wedge\operatorname{dlog}y\). Mutation gives \[
 xt=1+y,\qquad t=x'=(1+y)/x .\] The ring \(R\) is a localization of a polynomial unique factorization domain, so every geometric hypothesis on \(X\) holds. The seed is integral. Its mutable graph has one vertex and no arrows, hence it is sink-recurrent. Its exchange rows even span \(\mathbb Z\), so it is really full rank. The special frozen-row condition in the standing Assumption 3.11 also holds: the frozen row is \(+1\) and there is no other mutable column. Thus neither that standing assumption nor full rank eliminates the example.

There are only two alternating rank-one clusters, since mutation returns \(x\). Consequently \[U(\Sigma)=
 \mathbb C[x^{\pm1},y^{\pm1}]\cap\mathbb C[t^{\pm1},y^{\pm1}]
 \quad\hbox{inside }\mathbb C(x,y).\] Every generator of \(R\) belongs to both Laurent rings: in the second one, \(x=(1+y)/t\). Therefore \(R\subset U(\Sigma)\), exactly as required.

Nevertheless, \(t\) is a cluster generator and is not regular on \(X\). At the admissible point \((x,y)=(0,1)\), a regular extension of [eq:rankone] (#eq:rankone) would imply \(0=2\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{ord}_{\{x=0\}}t=-1\). Hence \(R\ne A(\Sigma)\). This is a counterexample to the proposition, with all its hypotheses verified, rather than merely an unfilled proof step.

The induced mutated-torus morphism is \[\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[t^{\pm1},y^{\pm1}]\longrightarrow X,\qquad
 (t,y)\longmapsto((1+y)/t,y).\] It sends every \((t,-1)\), \(t\ne0\), to \((0,-1)\). It is therefore not an open immersion. Together with the initial torus it still misses \(\{x=0,\ y\ne-1\}\), a codimension-one set. Exact reviewer-written arithmetic independently checked two distinct preimages and the nonzero numerator at \((0,1)\); the ring argument above establishes the general discrepancy. See the saved `aux_induction/exact_counterexample_checks.json`.
## Dependency and a sufficient repair

Theorem 3.13 explicitly ends by invoking Proposition 3.14 [1, PDF p. 21]. This is a used dependency in the central deletion–contraction route to Theorem 1.1. In addition, Theorem 3.13 assumes only normality, whereas Proposition 3.14 assumes factoriality. The counterexample does not satisfy every stronger deletion–contraction hypothesis of Theorem 3.13, and is not claimed to refute that theorem itself.
The following replacement suffices for the actual factorial braid setting.

Proposition 1.  Let \(R=\mathbb C[X]\) be factorial and let \(\Sigma\) be integral, full rank and sink-recurrent on \(X\). Assume \(R\subset U(\Sigma)\), all initial variables and all one-step mutated variables belong to \(R\), and every frozen variable is a unit of \(R\). Then \(R=A(\Sigma)\).

Proof. Retain the paper’s local-acyclicity consequence \(A=U\) for sink-recurrent seeds. Every unit of \(A\) is a unit of the initial Laurent ring, hence a constant Laurent monomial. On mutating at a mutable index \(i\), the exchange polynomial \(P_i=M_++M_-\) is not a Laurent unit in the remaining variables: full rank excludes a zero exchange column, so the two monomials are distinct. Requiring both the unit and its inverse to remain Laurent forces its \(x_i\)-exponent to be zero. Thus units of \(A\) are precisely constant frozen Laurent monomials.

If an initial mutable \(x_i=ab\) in \(A\), the two factors are Laurent monomials on the initial torus. Mutation at \(j\ne i\) forces each factor’s \(x_j\)-exponent to vanish. Mutation at \(i\) forces its two exponents to be nonnegative and sum to one. One factor is therefore a frozen Laurent unit. The same proof applies to each adjacent seed, since full rank is mutation invariant. Initial mutable variables are pairwise nonassociate; \(x_i\) and \(x_i'\) are also nonassociate, since their exchange polynomial cannot equal a frozen monomial times \(x_i^2\).

These irreducibility and nonassociation assertions descend from \(A\) to \(R\): the functions are regular by hypothesis, and all units of \(A\) just identified are already units of \(R\). Factoriality makes the relevant irreducibles prime. For each initial or adjacent cluster, the inclusion \(R\subset U\) and regularity of its variables identify the localization of \(R\) at those variables with its Laurent ring. These are now actual principal-open tori in \(X\).

Every height-one prime is covered. If it contains an initial mutable variable \(x_i\), it cannot contain another initial mutable \(x_j\) or the nonassociate prime \(x_i'\); frozen variables are units. Thus the adjacent \(i\)-torus contains its generic point. The union of these tori has complement of codimension at least two. Normality gives \(U\subset R\), and hence \(R=U=A\). ◻

For braid varieties, factoriality is supplied by Proposition 2.5, and initial regularity and frozen units by Corollary 2.24. In the preceding argument of Theorem 3.13, adjacent regularity can be made explicit. The complement \(V=\{x_s=0\}\) is irreducible by its product description. For \(j\ne s\), the denominator \(x_j\) is nonzero at the generic point of \(V\), so \(x_j'=P_j/x_j\) has no pole there; it is already regular on the open deletion stratum. Normality extends it across \(X\). The special \(x_s'\) is regular by hypothesis. The product description also supplies the missing inverse on the exchange locus: the other torus coordinates specify the contraction point and \(x_s'\) specifies its affine-line coordinate.

This is a verified sufficient repair for the factorial application, conditional on the consistently oriented deletion–contraction hypotheses discussed next and on the cited \(A=U\) result. It does not independently settle the general normal, nonfactorial scope of Theorem 3.13. The finding is Major because a false criterion is explicitly used in a central derivation; a short stronger replacement does not erase that dependency.
# Problem 2: the induction uses a source as a sink under the printed convention

The graph convention on PDF p. 18 is \(i\to j\) when \(B_{ij}>0\). The sink criterion freezes a sink together with its incoming neighbors. Theorem 4.10 [1, PDF pp. 31–33; printed pp. 1109–1111] applies this construction to the leading mutable crossing of \(\beta=ii\beta'\).

Equation reference: eq:orientation. Take type \(A_1\), \(G=SL_2\), and \(\beta=1111\). Its Demazure product is the longest reflection. Writing \(\mathrm{id}=0\), \(s=1\), the positive distinguished sequence is \[(u_0,\ldots,u_4)=(0,0,0,0,1),\qquad J_\beta=\{1,2,3\}.\] The almost-positive sequences are \[(1,0,0,0,1),\quad(0,1,0,0,1),\quad(0,0,1,0,1).\] Hence vertex \(1\) is frozen and \(2,3\) are mutable. The vanishing-order criterion and simple diagonal zeros give, for the unique simple-root minors, \[\Delta_0=x_1,\quad\Delta_1=x_2,\quad\Delta_2=x_3,\quad\Delta_3=1.\] Using the internally consistent half-sum normalization of (2.26), discussed below, \(L_c=\operatorname{dlog}\Delta_c\). Equation (2.27) therefore gives \[
 \omega_\beta=\operatorname{dlog}x_1\wedge\operatorname{dlog}x_2+
                 \operatorname{dlog}x_2\wedge\operatorname{dlog}x_3,\qquad
 B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\-1&0&1\\0&-1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Thus the mutable graph is \(2\to3\): vertex \(2\) is a source, not a sink. Its incoming-neighbor set is empty. Freezing \(\{2\}\cup N_2^{\mathrm{in}}\) leaves vertex \(3\) mutable, whereas \(\beta'=11\) has one frozen variable and no mutable variable. The contraction identification used in the proof therefore has the wrong mutable rank under the literal convention.

The exchange relation gives the geometric reason: \[x_2x_2'=x_1+x_3.\] On the contraction divisor \(x_2=0\), one has \(x_3=-x_1\), a unit. It is the outgoing neighbor \(3\) that must become frozen. The distinguished recurrences, skew matrix and neighbor sets were independently computed exactly in `aux_induction/a1_orientation_check.json`.

A consistent correction reverses the declared graph convention globally, or uses the source/outgoing-neighbor version throughout the recurrence and application. The exchange matrix and exchange algebra need not change: reversing the quiver exchanges the two monomials in the symmetric exchange sum, and the corresponding local-acyclicity argument is mirrored. This removes the demonstrated local obstruction. It does not turn the literal contraction statement into a valid statement without that correction.

This is a substantive convention error at a used central induction step, with an explicit rank discrepancy, and is assessed Major for that derivation. It is not a counterexample to the resulting cluster-coordinate-ring identification. The correction is separate from the extra regularity hypotheses needed in Problem 1.
# Problem 3: the specified class in Theorem 6.8 can vanish on a two-dimensional torus
## Exact source assertion and the index discrepancy

Equation reference: eq:printedlefschetz. Section 6.4 [1, PDF p. 44; printed p. 1122] explicitly sets \(d=d(\beta)\), the full complex dimension. For even \(d\), it defines the curious Lefschetz property with respect to the particular class \([\omega_\beta]\) by \[
 [\omega_\beta]^{d-p}:
 H^{p+s,(p,p)}(\mathring R_\beta,\mathbb C)
 \longrightarrow H^{2d-p+s,(2d-p,2d-p)}(\mathring R_\beta,\mathbb C).\] Theorem 6.8 on the next page asserts this property for every even-dimensional double braid variety, and asserts the associated curious Poincare symmetry also in odd dimensions. The source images confirm both the dimension definition and the specified class; neither is an extraction artifact.

For a complex two-dimensional torus, [eq:printedlefschetz] (#eq:printedlefschetz) with \(p=s=0\) would map the nonzero \(H^0\) isomorphically to \(H^4=0\). The dimension center has been doubled. With full dimension denoted \(D\), the expected even-dimensional indexing would instead use exponent \(D/2-p\) and target \[H^{D-p+s,(D-p,D-p)}.\] The printed Poincare symmetry has the same center discrepancy. Correcting those indices alone, however, does not repair the specified-class theorem.
## An admissible braid with \(\omega_\beta=0\)

Let \[G=SL_4,\qquad
 \beta=(1,3,1,2,1,3,2,1)=13\cdot121321 .\] The last six letters form a reduced expression of \(w_0\): right multiplication gives \[1234,\ 2134,\ 2314,\ 3214,\ 3241,\ 3421,\ 4321 .\] Thus \(\delta(\beta)=w_0\), \(m=8\), \(\ell(w_0)=6\) and \(D=2\), within every group and word assumption of the theorem.

The backwards distinguished recursion uses all six suffix letters and has \(u_2=u_1=u_0=\mathrm{id}\). Thus \(J_\beta=\{1,2\}\). At the first solid position, the almost-positive initial value is \(s_1\). At the second it is \(s_3\): indeed \(\min(s_3,s_3s_1)=s_3\), since \(1\) and \(3\) commute. Both solid positions are frozen. Proposition 2.19 consequently excludes every torus-boundary divisor from the open variety, giving \[\mathring R_\beta=T_\beta\cong(\mathbb C^\times)^2 .\]

Equation reference: eq:zeroform. Lemma 2.8 gives \[h_2^+=1,\qquad
 h_1^+=\alpha_3^\vee(t_2),\qquad
 h_0^+=\alpha_1^\vee(t_1)\alpha_3^\vee(t_2),\] and all later \(h_c^+=1\). The simple roots \(1\) and \(3\) are orthogonal: \(a_{13}=a_{31}=0\). Hence in the first local term of (2.27), \(L_{1,1}=0\); in the second, \(L_{2,3}=0\). Every hollow contribution vanishes by Corollary 2.27. Therefore \[
 \omega_\beta=0 .\] This conclusion is unaffected by the factor-of-two convention in (2.26).

Now \(H^0((\mathbb C^\times)^2,\mathbb C)\cong\mathbb C\) and \(H^{2,(2,2)}((\mathbb C^\times)^2,\mathbb C)\cong\mathbb C\). Even with the corrected dimension center, multiplication by \([\omega_\beta]\) from the former to the latter is zero and is not an isomorphism. The counterexample refutes the theorem with its specified class, beyond its indexing discrepancy.

Two bounded native checks independently reconstructed the Weyl permutations, frozen tests and zero wedge coefficients. The executed integer/rational calculations are saved in `aux_geometry/low_rank_checks.json` and `aux_folding/lefschetz_counterexample.json`. They implement reviewer-written checks of the definitions, not author code.
## Repair boundary and surviving conclusions

On this particular torus, \(\eta=\operatorname{dlog}t_1\wedge\operatorname{dlog}t_2\) has a nonzero cohomology class and supplies the corrected-dimensional map \(H^0\to H^2\). Replacing a prescribed possibly degenerate form by a suitable nondegenerate one is a substantive change of statement. No general existence or compatibility theorem for such a replacement has been independently verified here. The cited external Lefschetz source has not been used as authority for the false assertion about an arbitrary specified \(\omega_\beta\).

The main coordinate-ring theorem survives this example: the all-frozen rank-zero seed gives exactly the Laurent ring \(\mathbb C[t_1^{\pm1},t_2^{\pm1}]\). Mixed Tate cohomology also holds for the torus. Corrected-center Poincare symmetry is not refuted by [eq:zeroform] (#eq:zeroform); the printed-center version is refuted by the degree calculation. The Major assessment concerns the explicit cohomological application, not a claim that the entire cluster construction fails.
# Problem 4: one folded mutation word does not project from its listed lift

Table 1 [1, PDF p. 41; printed p. 1119], panels (b) and (f), gives the \(G_2\) case with hollow expanded positions \([8,11]\). The listed lifted word is \[\mu_{\mathrm{lift}}=\mu_{(5,6,7,12,5,6,7)},\] whereas the corresponding folded word is printed as \(\mu_{\mathrm{fold}}=\mu_{(6,3,6)}\). The expanded word and orbit map in the table caption give \[\lambda^{-1}(3)=\{5,6,7\},\qquad \lambda^{-1}(6)=\{12\}.\] Consequently this lift consists of orbit mutations \((3,6,3)\), not \((6,3,6)\). The assertion immediately before Proposition 6.4, and the literal use in Corollary 6.5 (PDF p. 42), require the two descriptions to correspond.

The discrepancy is not removed by reversing composition: both orbit words are palindromes. Commuting the three mutations inside the first orbit likewise does not change its order relative to the second orbit. Nor are the two folded mutation maps identical. With variables \((x_3,x_6)=(2,5)\), trivial coefficients and \[B=\begin{pmatrix}0&-3\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\] the two final ordered pairs are respectively \[\mu_{(3,6,3)}:(2,5)\mapsto(11/5,28/5),\qquad
 \mu_{(6,3,6)}:(2,5)\mapsto(7/5,52/25).\] These follow directly from \(x_3'=(1+x_6)/x_3\) and \(x_6'=(1+x_3^3)/x_6\), with matrix mutation between steps; all denominators are nonzero. The exact rational calculation and source transcription are preserved in `aux_folding/table_resolution.json`.

Changing this row of \(\mu_{\mathrm{fold}}\) to \((3,6,3)\) restores the projection from the listed lift. The independent principal-coefficient check of that lift against the braid sequence passed. This is assessed Minor as a demonstrated local table defect: the valid listed lift supplies counterevidence against concluding that the long-braid equivalence itself fails. The check does not certify a complete revised Table 1.
# Positive checks, alternative readings and bounded coverage
## Geometry and low-rank boundaries

The opposite weighted-flag pair has trivial stabilizer, but freeness alone would not prove affineness of a unipotent quotient. The proof has the stronger regular opposite-cell slice: after fixing \(X_0\), write the opposite flag \(Y_0=u w_0hU_+\), and use the unique \(u\in U_+\) to obtain the slice. The isolated \(Y_m\) in the slice sentence of Proposition 2.5 (PDF p. 7) must be \(Y_0\). For \(\beta=-i\) in rank one, \(Y_m=X_m=X_0\), making the literal index impossible, while the corrected slice works. The surrounding argument already identifies \(Y_0\); this indexing correction is recorded without a separate substantive Problem.

The chamber minor near a boundary has the form \((p+t)\Delta_{\omega_i,\omega_i}(h)\), with the second factor nonzero. This gives a simple diagonal zero and an integral unitriangular valuation matrix. The prescribed divisor orders consequently determine a character basis, rather than only a rational basis. Normality extends functions with no codimension-one poles. Frozen divisors are outside the open variety, explaining invertibility there. The general order criterion distinguishes zero from positive order; a universal \(0/1\) assertion was not imported from the separately stated \(SL_n\) case.

For \(SL_2\), direct determinant calculations give \[R_i\cong\{\mathrm{pt}\},\qquad R_{ii}\cong\mathbb C^\times,\qquad
 R_{iii}\cong\{(a,d)\in\mathbb C^2:1+ad\ne0\}.\] On the last surface, \(h=(1+ad)^{-1}\), \(x_1=-h,\ x_2=-ha,\ x_2'=-d\), and \(x_2x_2'=1+x_1\). Exact rational evaluations included the mutable boundary. The analytic determinant derivation, rather than those finitely many evaluations alone, establishes the formula.

Equation (2.26), PDF p. 16, equates a full logarithmic derivative with a half-sum. Later (4.6) and (4.15) explicitly use the half-root convention, which gives the rank-one exchange just checked. Taking the first expression literally instead multiplies the two-form by four and produces the wrong exchange exponent. The report uses the consistent half-sum throughout; the supplied alternative reading is therefore resolved by later source formulas, rather than promoted into a claim that the intended seed fails.
## Moves, induction and external dependencies

In the solid-special move, the minor identity reduces to \(A=B+1\), so \(\operatorname{dlog}A\wedge\operatorname{dlog}B=0\). In the nonspecial case, the difference of local forms is a multiple of \(d_j a'-d_i a=0\), by the invariant root pairing. The rank-two polynomial identity \[z_1(a)z_2(b)z_1(c)=z_2(c)z_1(ac-b)z_2(a)\] has both sides equal to \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}ac-b&-a&1\\c&-1&0\\1&0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\); this directly supports the change of parameters in Proposition 4.9. These are analytic checks. They are not reported as executions of the author’s implementation.

Theorem 4.2 is conditional on an already established cluster-variety presentation. Its use of irreducibility in the final part of the move argument is therefore not itself circular. For a nonreduced positive word, the Coxeter exchange condition and braid equivalence expose a repeated letter; the deletion and contraction calls shorten the word. When the second leading crossing is hollow, the proof uses a product with \(\mathbb C^\times\) and only the first shorter word. It does not require an undefined empty-suffix variety in the minimal rank-one case. When both are solid, the genuine contraction applies.

The really-full-rank extension is an integral pivot-row calculation, using the special frozen coefficient \(\pm1\). Quasi-equivalence changes the character basis by an integral unimodular matrix, preserving the row lattice. Proposition 3.4’s unqualified irreducibility wording needs care for frozen units and zero exchange columns: in rank one with zero column, \(xx'=2\) makes \(x\) a unit over \(\mathbb C\). The actual full-rank range excludes this boundary case, and Proposition Proposition 1 (#prop:repair) proves the required irreducibility there.

The proof ordering through Sections 5–7 was checked explicitly. The simply-laced main theorem precedes its use in folding; Proposition 7.2 assumes the main results, and Remark 7.3 explains that only its already established simply-laced instance is used in the multiply-laced proof. Its recursive argument increases the relevant Bruhat lengths until a terminal value, providing termination. This removes a superficial circularity objection. It does not independently re-prove every external generalized-minor, folding or local-acyclicity result.
## Folding computations and a remaining labeling limitation

The folding check distinguished orbit invariance from admissibility, retained the restriction to coefficients coming from the fixed-point embedding, and tracked frozen-variable rescaling separately from mutation. The reduction in Proposition 6.4 to framed restricted quivers was inspected in the source, including the use of the already proved simply-laced algorithm.

A reviewer-written exact calculation reconstructed the six nontrivial restricted-quiver cases displayed in Table 2: one \(B_2/C_2\) case and five \(G_2\) cases. It tracked principal-coefficient \(F\)-polynomials, gradings and exchange matrices. Five printed braid/lift comparisons passed. For the all-solid \(G_2\) case, the implemented right-to-left convention agreed after interchanging output labels \(11,12\); the printed exact labeling did not agree. Inverting both printed permutations did not resolve that discrepancy. Alternative left-to-right expansions reached the declared 30,000-term bound and were not completed.

The last result remains a bounded labeling concern requiring evidence, not an established additional failure of the general theorem. Mutation equivalence up to mutable relabeling is explicitly allowed in Proposition 6.6. No universal Table 1 certification is claimed. Inputs, exact outputs, convention trials and the preserved computation limit are saved in `aux_folding/table_mutation_checks.json` and `aux_folding/table_resolution.json`. These scientific computations are distinct from the manifest and hash audits.
# Overall impact and state

Problems 1 and 2 concern used dependencies of the coordinate-ring proof. The first is repaired for the actual factorial setting by added regularity and unit hypotheses; the second requires a consistent graph orientation. Their evidence does not show that Theorem 1.1 is false. Problem 4 is a local folded-word transcription mismatch with a verified projection correction. Problem 3 is a counterexample to the particular Lefschetz-class claim itself. Correcting its dimension center is necessary but insufficient; a general replacement class or extra hypothesis remains to be justified.

No author correction was independently acquired or adopted in this recovery. The report does not claim priority of discovery. Its demonstrated counterexamples and verified local repairs are distinguished from the unresolved normal-only criterion and any general replacement cohomological theorem.
