problems.title: Proposition 3.14 does not follow from coordinate-ring containment
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 21 Pdf pages: 22 Printed pages: 1099 Printed pages: 1100 Labels: Proposition3.14 Labels: Theorem3.13
claim: The working group in [1, PDF p. 2] is complex, simple and simply connected, with a fixed pinning and opposite Borel subgroups. A double word \(\beta=i_1\cdots i_m\) has letters in \(\pm I\) and Demazure product \(w_0\). Weighted flags are points of \(G/U_+\); strict relative position must be distinguished from relative position allowing a torus factor. The quotient \(\mathring R_\beta\) is asserted smooth, affine, factorial and irreducible, of complex dimension \[D=d(\beta)=m-\ell(w_0).\] The rightmost positive distinguished subexpression runs backwards from \(u_m=w_0\). Its solid positions form \(J_\beta\), with \(|J_\beta|=D\). The Deodhar torus has character variables \(x_e\), determined by their orders on the boundary divisors. A solid index is mutable when the corresponding almost-positive subexpression has initial value \(\mathrm{id}\). Frozen boundary divisors lie outside the open braid variety, and the frozen variables are units there.

Theorem 1.1 identifies \(\mathbb C[\mathring R_\beta]\) with the cluster algebra of the constructed seed. This statement is distinct from the general criterion in Proposition 3.14 and from the particular cohomological conclusion in Theorem 6.8. A seed on an affine variety, as defined on PDF p. 18, requires its initial torus to be an open dense subset. It does not already require every mutated variable to be regular on that variety.

Proposition 3.14 [1, PDF pp. 21–22; printed pp. 1099–1100] states that if \(X\) is affine, factorial and irreducible, \(\Sigma\) is an integral sink-recurrent seed on \(X\), and \(\mathbb C[X]\subset U(\Sigma)\), then \(\mathbb C[X]=A(\Sigma)\). The proof first treats the cluster tori as embedded in \(X\), and then invokes a codimension-two complement. The stated containment does not supply those embeddings.

Equation reference: eq:rankone. Set \[X=\mathbb A^1\times\mathbb G_m,\qquad R=\mathbb C[x,y,y^{-1}],
 \qquad T=(\mathbb G_m)^2\subset X.\] Take \(x\) mutable, \(y\) frozen, \(d=(1,1)\), and exchange column \(\widetilde B=(0,1)^t\). A full skew matrix is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), with \(\omega=-\operatorname{dlog}x\wedge\operatorname{dlog}y\). Mutation gives \[
 xt=1+y,\qquad t=x'=(1+y)/x .\] The ring \(R\) is a localization of a polynomial unique factorization domain, so every geometric hypothesis on \(X\) holds. The seed is integral. Its mutable graph has one vertex and no arrows, hence it is sink-recurrent. Its exchange rows even span \(\mathbb Z\), so it is really full rank. The special frozen-row condition in the standing Assumption 3.11 also holds: the frozen row is \(+1\) and there is no other mutable column. Thus neither that standing assumption nor full rank eliminates the example.

There are only two alternating rank-one clusters, since mutation returns \(x\). Consequently \[U(\Sigma)=
 \mathbb C[x^{\pm1},y^{\pm1}]\cap\mathbb C[t^{\pm1},y^{\pm1}]
 \quad\hbox{inside }\mathbb C(x,y).\] Every generator of \(R\) belongs to both Laurent rings: in the second one, \(x=(1+y)/t\). Therefore \(R\subset U(\Sigma)\), exactly as required.

Nevertheless, \(t\) is a cluster generator and is not regular on \(X\). At the admissible point \((x,y)=(0,1)\), a regular extension of [eq:rankone] (#eq:rankone) would imply \(0=2\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{ord}_{\{x=0\}}t=-1\). Hence \(R\ne A(\Sigma)\). This is a counterexample to the proposition, with all its hypotheses verified, rather than merely an unfilled proof step.

The induced mutated-torus morphism is \[\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[t^{\pm1},y^{\pm1}]\longrightarrow X,\qquad
 (t,y)\longmapsto((1+y)/t,y).\] It sends every \((t,-1)\), \(t\ne0\), to \((0,-1)\). It is therefore not an open immersion. Together with the initial torus it still misses \(\{x=0,\ y\ne-1\}\), a codimension-one set. Exact reviewer-written arithmetic independently checked two distinct preimages and the nonzero numerator at \((0,1)\); the ring argument above establishes the general discrepancy. See the saved `aux_induction/exact_counterexample_checks.json`.
analysis: Theorem 3.13 explicitly ends by invoking Proposition 3.14 [1, PDF p. 21]. This is a used dependency in the central deletion–contraction route to Theorem 1.1. In addition, Theorem 3.13 assumes only normality, whereas Proposition 3.14 assumes factoriality. The counterexample does not satisfy every stronger deletion–contraction hypothesis of Theorem 3.13, and is not claimed to refute that theorem itself.
The following replacement suffices for the actual factorial braid setting.

Proposition 1.  Let \(R=\mathbb C[X]\) be factorial and let \(\Sigma\) be integral, full rank and sink-recurrent on \(X\). Assume \(R\subset U(\Sigma)\), all initial variables and all one-step mutated variables belong to \(R\), and every frozen variable is a unit of \(R\). Then \(R=A(\Sigma)\).

Proof. Retain the paper’s local-acyclicity consequence \(A=U\) for sink-recurrent seeds. Every unit of \(A\) is a unit of the initial Laurent ring, hence a constant Laurent monomial. On mutating at a mutable index \(i\), the exchange polynomial \(P_i=M_++M_-\) is not a Laurent unit in the remaining variables: full rank excludes a zero exchange column, so the two monomials are distinct. Requiring both the unit and its inverse to remain Laurent forces its \(x_i\)-exponent to be zero. Thus units of \(A\) are precisely constant frozen Laurent monomials.

If an initial mutable \(x_i=ab\) in \(A\), the two factors are Laurent monomials on the initial torus. Mutation at \(j\ne i\) forces each factor’s \(x_j\)-exponent to vanish. Mutation at \(i\) forces its two exponents to be nonnegative and sum to one. One factor is therefore a frozen Laurent unit. The same proof applies to each adjacent seed, since full rank is mutation invariant. Initial mutable variables are pairwise nonassociate; \(x_i\) and \(x_i'\) are also nonassociate, since their exchange polynomial cannot equal a frozen monomial times \(x_i^2\).

These irreducibility and nonassociation assertions descend from \(A\) to \(R\): the functions are regular by hypothesis, and all units of \(A\) just identified are already units of \(R\). Factoriality makes the relevant irreducibles prime. For each initial or adjacent cluster, the inclusion \(R\subset U\) and regularity of its variables identify the localization of \(R\) at those variables with its Laurent ring. These are now actual principal-open tori in \(X\).

Every height-one prime is covered. If it contains an initial mutable variable \(x_i\), it cannot contain another initial mutable \(x_j\) or the nonassociate prime \(x_i'\); frozen variables are units. Thus the adjacent \(i\)-torus contains its generic point. The union of these tori has complement of codimension at least two. Normality gives \(U\subset R\), and hence \(R=U=A\). ◻

For braid varieties, factoriality is supplied by Proposition 2.5, and initial regularity and frozen units by Corollary 2.24. In the preceding argument of Theorem 3.13, adjacent regularity can be made explicit. The complement \(V=\{x_s=0\}\) is irreducible by its product description. For \(j\ne s\), the denominator \(x_j\) is nonzero at the generic point of \(V\), so \(x_j'=P_j/x_j\) has no pole there; it is already regular on the open deletion stratum. Normality extends it across \(X\). The special \(x_s'\) is regular by hypothesis. The product description also supplies the missing inverse on the exchange locus: the other torus coordinates specify the contraction point and \(x_s'\) specifies its affine-line coordinate.

This is a verified sufficient repair for the factorial application, conditional on the consistently oriented deletion–contraction hypotheses discussed next and on the cited \(A=U\) result. It does not independently settle the general normal, nonfactorial scope of Theorem 3.13. The finding is Major because a false criterion is explicitly used in a central derivation; a short stronger replacement does not erase that dependency.
result: Result: Proposition3.14 false; ring inclusion does not make mutated tori open immersions; codimension-one complement remains.
Impact: Theorem3.13 explicitly invokes false3.14 at its last step, a central induction dependency. Normal-only scope also lacks factoriality.

analysis: The graph convention on PDF p. 18 is \(i\to j\) when \(B_{ij}>0\). The sink criterion freezes a sink together with its incoming neighbors. Theorem 4.10 [1, PDF pp. 31–33; printed pp. 1109–1111] applies this construction to the leading mutable crossing of \(\beta=ii\beta'\).

Equation reference: eq:orientation. Take type \(A_1\), \(G=SL_2\), and \(\beta=1111\). Its Demazure product is the longest reflection. Writing \(\mathrm{id}=0\), \(s=1\), the positive distinguished sequence is \[(u_0,\ldots,u_4)=(0,0,0,0,1),\qquad J_\beta=\{1,2,3\}.\] The almost-positive sequences are \[(1,0,0,0,1),\quad(0,1,0,0,1),\quad(0,0,1,0,1).\] Hence vertex \(1\) is frozen and \(2,3\) are mutable. The vanishing-order criterion and simple diagonal zeros give, for the unique simple-root minors, \[\Delta_0=x_1,\quad\Delta_1=x_2,\quad\Delta_2=x_3,\quad\Delta_3=1.\] Using the internally consistent half-sum normalization of (2.26), discussed below, \(L_c=\operatorname{dlog}\Delta_c\). Equation (2.27) therefore gives \[
 \omega_\beta=\operatorname{dlog}x_1\wedge\operatorname{dlog}x_2+
                 \operatorname{dlog}x_2\wedge\operatorname{dlog}x_3,\qquad
 B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\-1&0&1\\0&-1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Thus the mutable graph is \(2\to3\): vertex \(2\) is a source, not a sink. Its incoming-neighbor set is empty. Freezing \(\{2\}\cup N_2^{\mathrm{in}}\) leaves vertex \(3\) mutable, whereas \(\beta'=11\) has one frozen variable and no mutable variable. The contraction identification used in the proof therefore has the wrong mutable rank under the literal convention.

The exchange relation gives the geometric reason: \[x_2x_2'=x_1+x_3.\] On the contraction divisor \(x_2=0\), one has \(x_3=-x_1\), a unit. It is the outgoing neighbor \(3\) that must become frozen. The distinguished recurrences, skew matrix and neighbor sets were independently computed exactly in `aux_induction/a1_orientation_check.json`.

A consistent correction reverses the declared graph convention globally, or uses the source/outgoing-neighbor version throughout the recurrence and application. The exchange matrix and exchange algebra need not change: reversing the quiver exchanges the two monomials in the symmetric exchange sum, and the corresponding local-acyclicity argument is mirrored. This removes the demonstrated local obstruction. It does not turn the literal contraction statement into a valid statement without that correction.

This is a substantive convention error at a used central induction step, with an explicit rank discrepancy, and is assessed Major for that derivation. It is not a counterexample to the resulting cluster-coordinate-ring identification. The correction is separate from the extra regularity hypotheses needed in Problem 1.

problems.title: The specified Lefschetz class vanishes on an admissible two-dimensional torus
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 44 Pdf pages: 45 Printed pages: 1122 Printed pages: 1123 Labels: Section6.4 Labels: Theorem6.8
claim: The working group in [1, PDF p. 2] is complex, simple and simply connected, with a fixed pinning and opposite Borel subgroups. A double word \(\beta=i_1\cdots i_m\) has letters in \(\pm I\) and Demazure product \(w_0\). Weighted flags are points of \(G/U_+\); strict relative position must be distinguished from relative position allowing a torus factor. The quotient \(\mathring R_\beta\) is asserted smooth, affine, factorial and irreducible, of complex dimension \[D=d(\beta)=m-\ell(w_0).\] The rightmost positive distinguished subexpression runs backwards from \(u_m=w_0\). Its solid positions form \(J_\beta\), with \(|J_\beta|=D\). The Deodhar torus has character variables \(x_e\), determined by their orders on the boundary divisors. A solid index is mutable when the corresponding almost-positive subexpression has initial value \(\mathrm{id}\). Frozen boundary divisors lie outside the open braid variety, and the frozen variables are units there.

Theorem 1.1 identifies \(\mathbb C[\mathring R_\beta]\) with the cluster algebra of the constructed seed. This statement is distinct from the general criterion in Proposition 3.14 and from the particular cohomological conclusion in Theorem 6.8. A seed on an affine variety, as defined on PDF p. 18, requires its initial torus to be an open dense subset. It does not already require every mutated variable to be regular on that variety.
Every even-dimensional double braid variety satisfies the curious Lefschetz property with respect to [omega_beta] as defined with d=d(beta).
analysis:
Equation reference: eq:printedlefschetz. Section 6.4 [1, PDF p. 44; printed p. 1122] explicitly sets \(d=d(\beta)\), the full complex dimension. For even \(d\), it defines the curious Lefschetz property with respect to the particular class \([\omega_\beta]\) by \[
 [\omega_\beta]^{d-p}:
 H^{p+s,(p,p)}(\mathring R_\beta,\mathbb C)
 \longrightarrow H^{2d-p+s,(2d-p,2d-p)}(\mathring R_\beta,\mathbb C).\] Theorem 6.8 on the next page asserts this property for every even-dimensional double braid variety, and asserts the associated curious Poincare symmetry also in odd dimensions. The source images confirm both the dimension definition and the specified class; neither is an extraction artifact.

For a complex two-dimensional torus, [eq:printedlefschetz] (#eq:printedlefschetz) with \(p=s=0\) would map the nonzero \(H^0\) isomorphically to \(H^4=0\). The dimension center has been doubled. With full dimension denoted \(D\), the expected even-dimensional indexing would instead use exponent \(D/2-p\) and target \[H^{D-p+s,(D-p,D-p)}.\] The printed Poincare symmetry has the same center discrepancy. Correcting those indices alone, however, does not repair the specified-class theorem.

Let \[G=SL_4,\qquad
 \beta=(1,3,1,2,1,3,2,1)=13\cdot121321 .\] The last six letters form a reduced expression of \(w_0\): right multiplication gives \[1234,\ 2134,\ 2314,\ 3214,\ 3241,\ 3421,\ 4321 .\] Thus \(\delta(\beta)=w_0\), \(m=8\), \(\ell(w_0)=6\) and \(D=2\), within every group and word assumption of the theorem.

The backwards distinguished recursion uses all six suffix letters and has \(u_2=u_1=u_0=\mathrm{id}\). Thus \(J_\beta=\{1,2\}\). At the first solid position, the almost-positive initial value is \(s_1\). At the second it is \(s_3\): indeed \(\min(s_3,s_3s_1)=s_3\), since \(1\) and \(3\) commute. Both solid positions are frozen. Proposition 2.19 consequently excludes every torus-boundary divisor from the open variety, giving \[\mathring R_\beta=T_\beta\cong(\mathbb C^\times)^2 .\]

Equation reference: eq:zeroform. Lemma 2.8 gives \[h_2^+=1,\qquad
 h_1^+=\alpha_3^\vee(t_2),\qquad
 h_0^+=\alpha_1^\vee(t_1)\alpha_3^\vee(t_2),\] and all later \(h_c^+=1\). The simple roots \(1\) and \(3\) are orthogonal: \(a_{13}=a_{31}=0\). Hence in the first local term of (2.27), \(L_{1,1}=0\); in the second, \(L_{2,3}=0\). Every hollow contribution vanishes by Corollary 2.27. Therefore \[
 \omega_\beta=0 .\] This conclusion is unaffected by the factor-of-two convention in (2.26).

Now \(H^0((\mathbb C^\times)^2,\mathbb C)\cong\mathbb C\) and \(H^{2,(2,2)}((\mathbb C^\times)^2,\mathbb C)\cong\mathbb C\). Even with the corrected dimension center, multiplication by \([\omega_\beta]\) from the former to the latter is zero and is not an isomorphism. The counterexample refutes the theorem with its specified class, beyond its indexing discrepancy.

Two bounded native checks independently reconstructed the Weyl permutations, frozen tests and zero wedge coefficients. The executed integer/rational calculations are saved in `aux_geometry/low_rank_checks.json` and `aux_folding/lefschetz_counterexample.json`. They implement reviewer-written checks of the definitions, not author code.
result: Result: Specified-class theorem false even after correcting dimension center; printed curious Poincare symmetry also has doubled center.
Impact: Material failure of an explicit cohomological application, not of main cluster-coordinate-ring identification.

A double word \(\beta=i_1\cdots i_m\) has letters in \(\pm I\) and Demazure product \(w_0\). Weighted flags are points of \(G/U_+\); strict relative position must be distinguished from relative position allowing a torus factor. The quotient \(\mathring R_\beta\) is asserted smooth, affine, factorial and irreducible, of complex dimension \[D=d(\beta)=m-\ell(w_0).\] The rightmost positive distinguished subexpression runs backwards from \(u_m=w_0\). Its solid positions form \(J_\beta\), with \(|J_\beta|=D\). The Deodhar torus has character variables \(x_e\), determined by their orders on the boundary divisors. A solid index is mutable when the corresponding almost-positive subexpression has initial value \(\mathrm{id}\). Frozen boundary divisors lie outside the open braid variety, and the frozen variables are units there.

Theorem 1.1 identifies \(\mathbb C[\mathring R_\beta]\) with the cluster algebra of the constructed seed. This statement is distinct from the general criterion in Proposition 3.14 and from the particular cohomological conclusion in Theorem 6.8. A seed on an affine variety, as defined on PDF p. 18, requires its initial torus to be an open dense subset. It does not already require every mutated variable to be regular on that variety.
Table1(f)'s lifted orbit-mutation sequence lifts the corresponding Table1(b) folded sequence, as used in Corollary6.5.
analysis: Table 1 [1, PDF p. 41; printed p. 1119], panels (b) and (f), gives the \(G_2\) case with hollow expanded positions \([8,11]\). The listed lifted word is \[\mu_{\mathrm{lift}}=\mu_{(5,6,7,12,5,6,7)},\] whereas the corresponding folded word is printed as \(\mu_{\mathrm{fold}}=\mu_{(6,3,6)}\). The expanded word and orbit map in the table caption give \[\lambda^{-1}(3)=\{5,6,7\},\qquad \lambda^{-1}(6)=\{12\}.\] Consequently this lift consists of orbit mutations \((3,6,3)\), not \((6,3,6)\). The assertion immediately before Proposition 6.4, and the literal use in Corollary 6.5 (PDF p. 42), require the two descriptions to correspond.

The discrepancy is not removed by reversing composition: both orbit words are palindromes. Commuting the three mutations inside the first orbit likewise does not change its order relative to the second orbit. Nor are the two folded mutation maps identical. With variables \((x_3,x_6)=(2,5)\), trivial coefficients and \[B=\begin{pmatrix}0&-3\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\] the two final ordered pairs are respectively \[\mu_{(3,6,3)}:(2,5)\mapsto(11/5,28/5),\qquad
 \mu_{(6,3,6)}:(2,5)\mapsto(7/5,52/25).\] These follow directly from \(x_3'=(1+x_6)/x_3\) and \(x_6'=(1+x_3^3)/x_6\), with matrix mutation between steps; all denominators are nonzero. The exact rational calculation and source transcription are preserved in `aux_folding/table_resolution.json`.

report: Abstract: The acquired publisher version of Alpöge, Bhargava, Ho and Shnidman is examined through its Selmer, prime-equation and rank-descent arguments. The proposed equal-squareclass simplification at dyadic ramified primes is demonstrably obstructed in a permitted field. A replacement using quadratic characters is proved for all relevant local conductors. A missing normalization in the displayed singular series is also identified; the separately cited affine-prime-pattern route remains applicable. The Selmer and Diophantine-definability dependencies receive positive bounded checks, and the infinitude argument is completed using the existing freedom to enlarge an exponent. The overall assessment is Major for the affected universal-construction step, with a verified repair; no counterexample to the main theorem is established.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Local admissibility and the proof of rank stability in quadratic extensions
# Identity, exact scope and logical structure

The source is L. Alpöge, M. Bhargava, W. Ho and A. Shnidman, Rank stability in quadratic extensions and Hilbert’s tenth problem for the ring of integers of a number field, Inventiones mathematicae 243 (2025), 1129–1139, DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01392-3 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01392-3). The acquired publisher version has 11 physical pages. PDF page numbers below are one-based; printed page numbers equal PDF page numbers plus 1128. The separately acquired arXiv:2501.18774v1 source is not presumed equivalent to the publisher text.

Theorem 1.1 [1, PDF p. 2] quantifies over every quadratic extension \(K/F\) of number fields and asserts existence of an abelian variety \(A/F\) with \[0<\operatorname{rank}A(F)=\operatorname{rank}A(K).\] It does not require a uniform variety, an elliptic curve, rank one, equality of the full point groups, or an effective procedure selecting \(A\). Corollary 1.2 concerns existential definability of \(\mathbb Z\) in \(\mathcal O_K\), and undecidability of polynomial solvability over that ring. It makes no corresponding assertion about solvability over the fraction field \(K\).

After a cyclotomic base change, the proof assumes that an odd prime \(\ell\) has \(\mu_\ell\subset F\), that \(K=F(\sqrt q)\) is quadratic and unramified above \(\ell\), and that \[C_n:y^2=x^\ell+n,\quad n\ne0,\qquad J_n=\operatorname{Jac}(C_n),
 \qquad \phi=1-\zeta_\ell.\] Yu’s input supplies \(r\in\mathcal O_F\setminus\{0\}\), a unit at primes ramifying in \(K/F\), with \(\operatorname{Sel}_\phi(J_{q^\ell r^2})=0\). The finite set \(S\) consists of the primes in \(S'\) above \(\ell\) or split in \(K\), where \(S'\) contains the primes dividing \(\ell!\) or the conductor of that Jacobian. Put \(\Sigma=S\cup S_{\mathrm{inert}}\).

The critical arithmetic step, Proposition 2.5, requires infinitely many classes \[t=a^{(\ell-1)/2}b\pmod{F^{\times\ell}},\qquad
 a,b\in\mathcal O_{F,\Sigma}^{\times},\quad a+2rb=1,
 \quad t\in F_{ p}^{\times\ell}\ ( p\in S).\] Lemma 2.4 preserves zero Selmer rank for the corresponding companion twists. Lemma 2.6 and Proposition 2.7 give positive rank on all but finitely many of their quadratic twists. The rational eigenspace decomposition then yields the required stable rank. Thus the local admissibility in Proposition 2.5 is a used step in the universal main theorem.

All principal sections of the short publisher paper were read, and all 11 source pages were actually viewed. The cited Yu, Kai and Mazur–Rubin–Shlapentokh inputs were checked in precisely identified preprint versions and selected passages. Their entire proofs, and every other background theorem, are not certified here.
# Problem 1: equal squareclasses do not remove the dyadic obstruction
## Location, hypotheses and a permitted counterexample to the argument

Equation reference: eq:conic. In the ramified case of the proof of Proposition 2.5 [1, PDF p. 9; printed p. 1137], the authors must prescribe inert-prime residue classes compatible with \[p_1+\beta p_2=p_3,\qquad \beta=2r\gamma^{n\ell}.\] Here \(\gamma\) has prime support exactly \(S\), and \(n\) may be made large. At primes dividing the relative conductor \(m\), both \(r\) and \(\gamma\) are units. The source reduces compatibility to \[
 t_1x^2+\beta t_2y^2=t_3z^2\pmod{ m}\] and asserts that setting \(t_1=t_3\) removes the obstruction at dyadic primes. The prime residues \(t_ix^2,t_iy^2,t_iz^2\) in this construction must be units; allowing a zero or nonunit coordinate would not give the required prime congruences.

Take the permitted cyclotomic setting \[\ell=3,\qquad F=\mathbb Q(\zeta_3),\qquad K=F(i).\] It arises from the initial quadratic extension \(\mathbb Q(i)/\mathbb Q\) by the paper’s allowed base change. The extension \(K/F\) is unramified above \(3\). At its dyadic prime, \(F_{ p}\) is the unramified quadratic extension of \(\mathbb Q_2\), with residue field \(\mathbb F_4\), and the local conductor of adjoining \(i\) is \(4\). Consequently \[v_{ p}(2)=1,\qquad
 v_{ p}(r)=v_{ p}(\gamma)=0,\qquad
 v_{ p}(\beta)=1\] for every \(r\) allowed by Lemma 2.3 and every \(n\). This example does not depend on guessing a particular rank-zero twist.

Suppose \(t_1=t_3\) and all the displayed parameters and coordinates in [eq:conic] (#eq:conic) are units. Reduction modulo \(2\) forces \(x^2=z^2\), hence \(x=z\) in \(\mathbb F_4\). Therefore both \(x-z\) and \(x+z\) are divisible by \(2\), and \[x^2-z^2\in4\mathcal O_{F_{ p}}.\] But \(\beta t_2y^2/t_1\) has valuation one. Equation [eq:conic] (#eq:conic) is impossible modulo \(4\). This refutes the supplied equal-squareclass justification within the paper’s actual field assumptions; a \(\mathbb Q_2\)-only example would not have sufficed.

Reviewer-written finite-ring arithmetic independently used \(\mathbb Z[z]/(z^2+z+1,4)\). For each of the three possible nonzero residues \(2u\) with \(u\) a unit, it found no unit solution with \(t_1=t_3\), but found twelve triples when only the required inert quadratic characters were imposed. The exact inputs and counts are in `aux_primes/exact_local_checks.json`. The general obstruction is the valuation argument above.
## A replacement valid for every relevant ramified local character

The needed condition is equality of quadratic characters of the three prime residues. It is stronger than necessary to require equality of their full squareclasses. The following gives the required local freedom.

Lemma 1.  Let \(L\) be a dyadic local field containing \(\mu_\ell\) for an odd prime \(\ell\), and let \(\chi:L^\times\to\{\pm1\}\) be a ramified quadratic character. If \(\beta=2u\) with \(u\in\mathcal O_L^\times\), there is \(v\in\mathcal O_L^\times\) such that \[\chi(v)=\chi(1+\beta v)=1.\]

Proof. Write \(e=v_L(2)\), let \(c\) be the conductor exponent of \(\chi\), and put \(U^j=1+ p^j\). The last nontrivial character on \(U^{c-1}/U^c\) is an additive residue-field character. The residue field has at least four elements: reduction preserves the odd-order roots of unity, so \(\ell\mid(\#k_L-1)\).

If \(c\le e\), take \(v=1\). If \(c=e+1\), the function on residues induced by \(\chi(1+\beta v)\) is a nonzero additive character, after a unit scaling. Its kernel contains a nonzero residue because \(\#k_L\ge4\). Choose a unit lift \(v\) of such a residue. Multiplying \(v\) by a suitable element of \(U^e\) arranges \(\chi(v)=1\). This does not change \(\chi(1+\beta v)\): the induced multiplicative change belongs to \(U^{2e}\subset U^{e+1}\).

If \(c\ge e+2\), start with any unit \(v\), and replace it by \(v(1+w)\), where \(w\in p^{c-e-1}\). The ratio of the new and old expressions \(1+\beta v\) is \[1+\frac{\beta v}{1+\beta v}\,w .\] Its image runs over \(U^{c-1}/U^c\), so one can arrange \(\chi(1+\beta v)=1\). Now multiply \(v\) by an element of \(U^{c-1}\) to arrange \(\chi(v)=1\). The corresponding change of \(1+\beta v\) lies in \(U^{e+c-1}\subset U^c\), leaving its character unchanged. ◻

Choose a unit \(a\) with any prescribed character \(\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}\) and set \[b=av,\qquad d=a(1+\beta v).\] Then \(a+\beta b=d\), and all three characters equal \(\varepsilon\). At an odd ramified prime, \(\beta\) is a unit and the residue field has size \(Q\ge7\), since it contains \(\mu_\ell\) and the prime is not above \(\ell\). The conic \(z^2-\beta y^2=1\) has \(Q-\chi_k(\beta)\) affine points; excluding \(y=0\) or \(z=0\) removes at most four. A remaining point gives \(v=y^2\) with both required characters equal to one. Hensel lifting supplies the local unit conditions.

Choose signs at the ramified places whose product under the quadratic ray character is \(-1\). The preceding construction gives three local units with these same signs. The Chinese remainder theorem combines them with the disjoint \(S\)-congruences. This supplies compatible inert-prime residue classes without the false requirement \(t_1=t_3\).
## Impact and counterevidence

The dyadic sentence is the given justification for a local condition in the ramified branch of Proposition 2.5. That proposition feeds the positive-rank construction and hence the assertion for every quadratic extension. The finding is Major for this demonstrated invalid derivation in the core chain. The existence of the preceding local repair does not make the printed derivation valid.

At the same time, the repair proves precisely the missing local compatibility in the stated setting. The example is not a counterexample to Proposition 2.5, Theorem 1.1 or the Hilbert-tenth corollary. The stronger equality of squareclasses fails; equality of the actual quadratic characters can be obtained. The independent analytic prime theorem and the rest of the construction remain explicit dependencies.
# Problem 2: the displayed singular-series count is unnormalized

For \(p\nmid\beta\), reduction modulo \(p\) leaves \((Q-1)(Q-2)\) pairs. Each pair has \(Q^{2(j-1)}\) lifts, so [eq:baddensity] (#eq:baddensity) diverges. For example, at \(Q=7\) the first three displayed factors are \[35/36,\qquad1715/36,\qquad84035/36 .\] Thus the formula is not the finite local density needed in a singular series.

This is assessed Minor. It is a real error in a displayed calculation, but the paper also gives an independent prime-pattern proof of Proposition 3.1. Kai’s Theorem 13.1 in the consulted arXiv:2306.16983v3, PDF pp. 67–68 [3], permits affine-linear forms taking values in an ideal and supplies an asymptotic under the relevant local-admissibility condition. Its full analytic proof was not reverified.

For that alternative application, the source’s \(W\) is an affine coset, rather than a subgroup. Since \(I\) and \((C)\) are coprime, choose a residue lift \((a_1,a_2)\in I^2\) and write \[W=(a_1,a_2)+(CI)^2.\] The three maps become affine forms with linear parts \((1,0),(0,1),(1,\beta)\), pairwise independent over \(F\). At primes dividing \(C\), the prescribed unit residues give admissibility. At other primes, two nonzero residues can avoid \(x+\beta y=0\); if the residue field has two elements, \(\beta\in2\mathcal O_F\) makes that last form equal to \(x\). This verifies the needed local compatibility. The affine-coset correction is a clarification, not a failure of the theorem allowed by Kai’s statement.
# Completing infinitude of the power classes

The final paragraph of Proposition 2.5 [1, PDF p. 9] uses \[t=(p_1^k p_2 p_3^k),\qquad k=(\ell-1)/2,
 \qquad (a^k b)= t\,(\gamma^n p_3^{-1})^\ell .\] The intended conclusion is that infinitely many varying primes occur with exponents between \(1\) and \(\ell-1\). A shared residual prime in all three \((p_i)=I q_i\) would instead have exponent \(2k+1=\ell\). Infinite homogeneous triples alone also need not give infinitely many distinct ratios. These points can be resolved using the already allowed sufficiently large \(n\), rather than asserted as new defects.

Fix \(r,\gamma\) and let \(S_0\) contain the prime support of \(2r\gamma\). If \(q_1= q_2= q_3\), then \(a=p_1/p_3\) is an ordinary unit and \(b=\gamma^{n\ell}(p_2/p_3)\) is \(\gamma^{n\ell}\) times an ordinary unit. The pairs \((a,2rb)\) solve a fixed finite-\(S_0\) unit equation. By the same Siegel–Mahler finiteness invoked in the source, there are only finitely many such pairs. Since \(S\) contains primes above \(\ell\), \(\gamma\) is a nonunit. At any \(p\mid\gamma\), \[v_{ p}(b)=n\ell\,v_{ p}(\gamma),\] so only finitely many \(n\) can occur in this common-prime case. Choose \(n\) beyond these exceptions and beyond the local-power thresholds.

Outside the fixed prime support of \(2r\gamma I\), equality of two residual primes forces equality of the third by \(p_1+\beta p_2=p_3\), which has now been excluded. Every large residual prime consequently has exponent \(k\) or \(1\) in \(t\), strictly between zero and \(\ell\).

Finally, two triples with the same \((a,b)\) differ by common scaling. For distinct residual primes, comparison of their principal divisors forces the scaling to be a unit. Thus infinitely many triples modulo common units yield infinitely many pairs. Finite total prime support would contradict the \(S\)-unit theorem for those pairs. This proves the required infinitude of ideal power classes, hence of element power classes. It is a verified completion of an omitted step, compatible with the source’s choice of \(n\), and is not listed as another Problem.
# Positive checks of the remaining proof chain
## Selmer conditions, torsion and rational points

The kernel \(J_n[\phi]\) has order \(\ell\), generated by the class of \((0,\sqrt n)-\infty\), and carries the quadratic character of \(F(\sqrt n)/F\). At a nonsplit prime away from \(\ell\), its local invariants and dual invariants vanish. Local duality and the Euler characteristic give \(H^1=0\), including ramified primes of residue characteristic two. The exclusion of primes above \(\ell\) is necessary; they remain in the controlled set \(S\).

The Kummer injection gives \(J(F)/\phi J(F)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Sel}_\phi(J)\). For the torsion-free \(\mathbb Z[\zeta_\ell]\)-module of Mordell–Weil points, reduction at \(1-\zeta_\ell\) detects its rank. Thus Selmer vanishing implies rank zero without assuming finiteness of the Tate–Shafarevich group.

Yu’s Theorem 4 [2, PDF p. 3] applies after interchanging the affine coordinates: \(X^\ell=Y^2-q^\ell\), with a separable degree-two polynomial whose Galois group is \(S_2\). The odd prime \(\ell\) does not divide that degree. The rank-lowering proof in Proposition 4.2, pp. 15–16, uses a parameter supported at a new prime and congruent to one at the protected ray modulus. This supports the extra requirement that \(r\) be a unit at all ramified primes. The inverse twist convention converts by \(r=d^{(\ell-1)/2}\). These are checks of applicability and the relevant local control, not a re-proof of Yu’s full machinery.

In Lemma 2.4, the local cases exhaust all places. On \(S\), the twist is locally an \(\ell\)-th power. At other nonsplit primes the ambient cohomology vanishes. At the remaining split primes, both Jacobians have good reduction and the same unramified Kummer image. The common quadratic kernel character is unchanged by the square twist parameters.

For fixed \(n\), torsion points of the twists become height-zero points of \(J_n\) of degree at most \(\ell\); Northcott gives finitely many possibilities. If one non-kernel point occurred on two distinct twist classes, comparison of their twisting characters would force it to be fixed by a nontrivial power of \(\zeta_\ell\), and hence by \(\zeta_\ell\), a contradiction. This validates the finite exceptional set in Lemma 2.6.

The Fermat covering has the exact identity \[\begin{split}
 U&=a x y^{-2},\qquad
 V=a^{(\ell-1)/2}(y^{-\ell}-rb),\\
 V^2-U^\ell-r^2a^{\ell-1}b^2
 &=a^{\ell-1}y^{-2\ell}(1-a x^\ell-2rb y^\ell).
\end{split}\] At \(x=y=1\), the equation \(a+2rb=1\) gives the stated rational point with first coordinate \(a\ne0\). The Abel–Jacobi embedding is injective for this positive-genus curve and is equivariant under \(\zeta_\ell\); therefore this point is not in \(J[\phi]\). Outside the finite exceptional twists, it is not torsion. The saved reviewer-written Laurent-polynomial checks at \(\ell=3,5,7,11\) complement this arbitrary-\(\ell\) identity.
## Descent and the Diophantine conclusion

The initial choice of \(\ell\) outside the absolute discriminant of \(K\) makes \(K\) disjoint from \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_\ell)\): every nontrivial subfield of the latter is ramified at \(\ell\). The compositum over \(F(\zeta_\ell)\) is therefore still quadratic. Weil restriction identifies its two relevant point groups with those over the original \(F,K\), preserving ranks while allowing a higher-dimensional variety.

For a quadratic extension, the rational Mordell–Weil space splits into the two involution eigenspaces. This proves \[\operatorname{rank}A(K)=\operatorname{rank}A(F)+\operatorname{rank}A^q(F).\] The constructed positive-rank Jacobian has zero-rank companion \(J_{q^\ell r^2a^{\ell-1}b^2}\), so this gives the required equality once Proposition 2.5 is supplied with the preceding local repair and infinitude completion.

Theorem 3.1 of Mazur–Rubin–Shlapentokh [4, PDF p. 7] requires exactly equal positive abelian ranks. Its Theorem 4.8, pp. 10–11, reduces definability over all number rings to that for quadratic extensions. The reduction uses a Galois closure and intersections of complex-conjugation fixed fields, whose intersection is totally real; it does not require a tower of quadratic extensions. Equal ranks imply only a finite torsion quotient, which is sufficient. Existential choices for each fixed field suffice; no uniform selection algorithm is needed.

Their Lemma 4.1 also reconciles finite systems with the single-equation wording. Over a number ring, choose an integral nonsquare \(u\); \(f^2-u g^2=0\) is equivalent to \(f=g=0\). Iteration combines a finite system. The deeper definability theorem and the totally-real input remain external dependencies. The separate introductory extension to all finitely generated infinite \(\mathbb Z\)-algebras was not checked.
# Overall impact and review state

The core defect established here is the invalid dyadic equal-squareclass argument, not the conclusion that suitable inert-prime congruences exist. Lemma Lemma 1 (#lem:local) and the odd-prime argument restore that compatibility in the stated range. The corrected local-density factor repairs the displayed singular series, while the separately inspected affine-prime-pattern theorem supplies another route to Proposition 3.1. The common-prime issue is resolved by a permitted large-\(n\) refinement.

With those distinctions, no counterexample to rank stability or to the ring-of-integers corollary is established. The positive checks are conditional on the explicitly retained analytic, duality and definability theorems. No author correction or adoption of the proposed repairs was independently acquired.

This does not change \(\chi(1+\beta v)\): the induced multiplicative change belongs to \(U^{2e}\subset U^{e+1}\).

If \(c\ge e+2\), start with any unit \(v\), and replace it by \(v(1+w)\), where \(w\in p^{c-e-1}\). The ratio of the new and old expressions \(1+\beta v\) is \[1+\frac{\beta v}{1+\beta v}\,w .\] Its image runs over \(U^{c-1}/U^c\), so one can arrange \(\chi(1+\beta v)=1\). Now multiply \(v\) by an element of \(U^{c-1}\) to arrange \(\chi(v)=1\). The corresponding change of \(1+\beta v\) lies in \(U^{e+c-1}\subset U^c\), leaving its character unchanged. ◻

Choose a unit \(a\) with any prescribed character \(\varepsilon\in\{\pm1\}\) and set \[b=av,\qquad d=a(1+\beta v).\] Then \(a+\beta b=d\), and all three characters equal \(\varepsilon\). At an odd ramified prime, \(\beta\) is a unit and the residue field has size \(Q\ge7\), since it contains \(\mu_\ell\) and the prime is not above \(\ell\). The conic \(z^2-\beta y^2=1\) has \(Q-\chi_k(\beta)\) affine points; excluding \(y=0\) or \(z=0\) removes at most four. A remaining point gives \(v=y^2\) with both required characters equal to one. Hensel lifting supplies the local unit conditions.

Choose signs at the ramified places whose product under the quadratic ray character is \(-1\). The preceding construction gives three local units with these same signs. The Chinese remainder theorem combines them with the disjoint \(S\)-congruences. This supplies compatible inert-prime residue classes without the false requirement \(t_1=t_3\).

The dyadic sentence is the given justification for a local condition in the ramified branch of Proposition 2.5. That proposition feeds the positive-rank construction and hence the assertion for every quadratic extension. The finding is Major for this demonstrated invalid derivation in the core chain. The existence of the preceding local repair does not make the printed derivation valid.

At the same time, the repair proves precisely the missing local compatibility in the stated setting. The example is not a counterexample to Proposition 2.5, Theorem 1.1 or the Hilbert-tenth corollary. The stronger equality of squareclasses fails; equality of the actual quadratic characters can be obtained. The independent analytic prime theorem and the rest of the construction remain explicit dependencies.

report: Abstract: The acquired author manuscript of Boxer and Pilloni is examined through its support formalism, fixed-weight construction, interpolation and comparison theorems. The stated bilinear duality over the full weight algebra is incompatible with its central-character specialization and requires an involution on the second factor. Two further errors affect explicit steps in the core construction: the displayed support window is empty, and a Weyl-shift placement gives an incorrect ordinary-normalization exponent. Exact replacements are derived. Auxiliary boundedness, dyadic quotient and stratum-range defects have narrower effects. The overall assessment is Major for the specified structural statement and derivations; the existence of higher Hida complexes and the corrected control and comparison statements are not disproved.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Duality, support conditions and normalization in higher Hida theory
# Paper identity, scope and principal claims

The reviewed paper is George Boxer and Vincent Pilloni, Higher Hida theory for Siegel modular forms, associated with Inventiones mathematicae (2025), DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01393-2 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01393-2). The exact source is the 65-page manuscript acquired from the Imperial College author page [1]. Its intrinsic revision date was not established. All page references below are one-based physical PDF pages; they agree with the printed page numbers. No equivalence with the publisher’s version is asserted.

The central objects are indexed by the minimal representatives \({}^{M}W\) of \(W_M\backslash W\) for \(G=\operatorname{GSp}_{2g}\). Write \(d=g(g+1)/2\), and retain the paper’s opposite-Siegel-parabolic and Borel conventions. The complex \(\operatorname{R\Gamma}_w(K^p)\) is an ordinary part of a cohomology with partial support on an Igusa tower. A canonical theory before taking that ordinary part is not claimed. The tame level is neat, and the family construction uses the cofinal decomposable compact subgroups of §5.1. At \(p=2\), decomposability expressly includes a semidirect-product requirement.

The main assertions must be kept separate. Theorem 1.4.3 gives admissibility, fixed-weight control, and a Cousin spectral sequence. Its integral amplitude statement is proved for \(g=1,2\), while the all-\(g\) assertion remains Conjecture 5.6.1. The general amplitude result is rational. Classicality is obtained when \(C(\kappa)\) has one element; singular weights retain a spectral sequence. Comparison with higher Coleman theory is a normalized slope-zero comparison. The arithmetic-group vanishing of Theorem 1.5.1 is over \(\mathbb Q_p\), not an integral vanishing statement.

Selected source pages were actually viewed, and reviewer-written exact checks supplement the arguments below. The deep solid-category, toroidal, degree-theoretic and earlier Coleman inputs remain named dependencies. This is not a claim to have reconstructed every external theorem.
# Problem 1: full-weight duality requires an involution
## The incompatible formulations

Equation reference: eq:printedpair. Theorem 1.4.8 [1, p. 5] explicitly asserts a perfect \(\Lambda\)-bilinear pairing \[
 M_w^\bullet\otimes_\Lambda M_{w',\mathrm{cusp}}^\bullet
 \longrightarrow\Lambda[-d],
 \qquad w'=w_{0,M}ww_0,\quad
 \Lambda=\mathbb Z_p[[T(\mathbb Z_p)]],\] with adjoint \(t\mapsto w_0(t^{-1})\). Theorem 5.5.2, p. 57, repeats the pairing. The preceding definitions, pp. 55–57, use the same full torus and weight algebra for every \(w\), with \[M_w^\bullet=\operatorname{RHom}_{T(\mathbb Z_p)}
 \bigl(1,\operatorname{R\Gamma}_w(K^p)\widehat\otimes_{\mathbb Z_p}\Lambda\bigr).\] The preceding \(w\)-twist of the torus action fixes its center. No involution on the second \(\Lambda\)-action is specified in these definitions.

Equation reference: eq:dualweight. By contrast, the fixed-weight Theorem 5.5.1 correctly pairs \[\kappa \quad\hbox{with}\quad
 \kappa'=-w_{0,M}\kappa-2\rho_{\mathrm{nc}},
 \qquad \chi\quad\hbox{with}\quad w_0\chi^{-1}.\] With the common specialization parameter \[\nu=-w^{-1}w_{0,M}(\kappa+\rho)-\rho,\] a direct calculation gives \[
 \nu'=-w_0\nu.\] Indeed \(w_{0,M}\rho_{\mathrm{nc}}=\rho_{\mathrm{nc}}\), \(w_{0,M}\rho=2\rho_{\mathrm{nc}}-\rho\), and \(w_0\rho=-\rho\). Substitution in the formula for \(w'\) proves [eq:dualweight] (#eq:dualweight). The map \(-w_0\) is the identity on the derived symplectic character space, but negates the scalar-center character. The full \(GSp\) torus in §3.1 therefore matters.
## An admissible nonzero fiber

Take \(g=1\), \(p=5\), \(w=1\). In the paper’s coordinates \(ho=(-1;0)\), and Remark 4.3.3, p. 47, identifies the Hodge line with weight \((1;-1)\). Thus \[\kappa=(4;-4),\qquad 
u=(-2;4),\qquad
 \kappa'=(-2;4),\qquad 
u'=(-2;-4).\] The parameter \(
u\) is dominant in the convention \(0\geq
u_1\). At the same \(\Lambda\)-point \(-
u\), the \(w'=w_0\) factor instead has weight \((-2;-4)\). Its central component differs from the required Serre partner.

There is a nonzero ordinary first fiber. Let \[E_4(q)=1+240\sum_{n\geq1}\sigma_3(n)q^n,\qquad
 f(q)=E_4(q)-5^3E_4(q^5).\] The classical Eisenstein series and its degeneracy pullback are modular of weight four. Their combination has constant coefficient \(-124\), hence is nonzero. The identity \[\sigma_3(5n)=(1+5^3)\sigma_3(n)-5^3\sigma_3(n/5)\] with the last term zero when \(5\nmid n\), proves \(U_5f=f\) coefficient by coefficient. Pullback to sufficiently small neat tame level preserves this nonzero class. Modularity of \(E_4\) is the standard classical input; checking finitely many Fourier coefficients would not prove it.

Under the diagonal-invariant construction of \(M_w^\bullet\), an inherited unit-torus operator \(u\) acts as \([u]^{-1}\). At specialization \(-\nu\), choose \(u=6I_2\). Then \(u\) acts by \(6^4\), whereas its prescribed adjoint \(w_0(u^{-1})=u^{-1}\) on the second factor at that same point acts by \(6^{-4}\). A bilinear pairing \(P\) satisfying the asserted adjoint relation must obey \[(6^4-6^{-4})P=0,\qquad
 6^4-6^{-4}=\frac{1679615}{1296}\ne0.\] Over \(\mathbb Q_5\) it is zero, contradicting perfectness at the nonzero fiber. A uniform inverse convention for the regular \(\Lambda\)-action changes both factors together and does not remove this incompatibility. The exact weight arithmetic and coefficients \(0\)–\(20\) are saved in `aux_families/exact_duality_checks.json`; the all-coefficient identity is the proof.
## Correction and impact

Equation reference: eq:correctpair. Define the algebra involution \[\iota:\Lambda\longrightarrow\Lambda,\qquad
 [t]\longmapsto[w_0(t^{-1})].\] The compatible formulation uses \[
 M_w^\bullet\otimes_\Lambda
 \iota^*M_{w',\mathrm{cusp}}^\bullet\longrightarrow\Lambda[-d],\] or states explicitly that the original pairing is \(\iota\)-sesquilinear. The twist changes the second specialization to \(-\nu'\), as required by [eq:dualweight] (#eq:dualweight). It is an exact repair of the character and adjoint obstruction. The fixed-weight Serre pairing, transposition of support and finite-level perfectness supply the corresponding construction; their background duality remains a dependency. The character correction and its specializations are verified here; a complete new proof of the global twisted perfect pairing, including every transition-map compatibility, is not claimed.

A relevant countercheck is the authors’ earlier modular-curve paper [2, pp. 17–18], which explicitly changes the weight-algebra action before forming its \(\Lambda\)-linear Serre pairing. Its one-variable parametrization differs from the full-torus formula here, so it is supporting evidence for the need to specify a twist, not a claim that the two formulas are identical.

This is Major: [eq:printedpair] (#eq:printedpair), with the displayed actions, is a false main structural guarantee at an allowed nonzero fiber. The corrected duality can coexist with the construction, control and amplitude theorems. No failure of their existence statements follows. A silently intended twist would be a substantive clarification of the statement, not a validation of the untwisted formula.
# Problem 2: the displayed support window is empty

For a concrete allowed case take \(g=1\), depth \(n=1\), and the longest representative, for which \(w_1=0\). Both indices in [eq:emptywindow] (#eq:emptywindow) are \(1\), so the space is empty. The corresponding ordinary étale stratum is not empty. The smooth curve \(y^2=x^3-x\) over \(\mathbb F_5\) has eight points and Frobenius trace \(-2\), hence is ordinary. Over an algebraic closure it admits the required étale subgroup and neat prime-to-five level. The saved exact count is an independent finite witness; the ordinary-stratum description comes from the stated moduli problem.

An empty scheme cannot be a compactification of that stratum. Thus the base case of Lemma 4.4.2, invoked by Proposition 4.4.4 and then by the definitions of the fixed-weight and family complexes, is invalid as printed.
## A verified replacement

Replace the second endpoint by \(w_i-1\): \[Y_w=\bigcap_i
 \bigl(\operatorname{supp}Z_{i,<w_i+1}\cap\operatorname{supp}Z_{i,>w_i-1}\bigr).\] At endpoints use full-special-fiber support for \(Z_{i,>-1}\) and \(Z_{i,<i+1}\). These conventions agree with the extreme positive or negative parts of \(Z_i-njV(p)\), since \(0\leq Z_i\leq niV(p)\). The corrected \(Y_w\) is closed in the proper special fiber. Removing \(D_{w,+}\cup D_{w,-}\) gives the ordinary \(w\)-chart by Proposition 4.1.13. If density is required, take its closure, as in Proposition 4.4.4.

It is necessary to verify strict dynamics, rather than infer it from pointwise monotonicity. The degree inequalities of 4.2.10–4.2.11 supply the local relation \[a=q b,\qquad a=p_1^*f_+,\quad b=p_2^*f_+,\quad
 q\in\sqrt{(a)}\] on the corrected window. The two boundary supports for a fixed index are disjoint. On a finite cover choose a common \(N\) with \(q^N=u a\). Then, without cancelling a possible zero divisor, \[a^N=q^Nb^N=u q b^{N+1}.\] Thus \((a)^N\subseteq(b)^{N+1}\), which is exactly \[p_2^*D_+\leq \frac{N}{N+1}p_1^*D_+\] in the paper’s ideal-power ordering. The other sign gives strict contraction of \(D_-\); finite sums admit a common strict bound. The nilpotent-thickening lemma then gives the higher reductions modulo \(p^s\).

In Corollary 4.4.3 the support containment needed for the factorization is sufficient; the printed stronger equality need not hold. On \(Y_w\), the excess divisor contains the support of \(p_1^*D_++p_2^*D_+\), since outside the excess one is on an ordinary correspondence chart, and the window selects only the \(w\)-chart. The source’s square-and-glue argument consequently supplies the required global map.

The assessment is Major for this explicit invalid construction in the core chain \(4.4.2\to4.4.4\to5.1.4\to5.2\). The replacement above verifies the missing local input, conditional on the named degree and compactification results. It does not claim that higher Hida theory itself is false.
# Problem 3: the ordinary-normalization exponent has the wrong shift

Remark 4.3.12 [1, p. 48] gives an exponent comparing the global normalization with the local \(w'\)-normalization and asserts strict positivity for \(w'\notin C(\kappa)\). Its displayed difference puts the extra \(\rho\) inside both Weyl actions. That placement changes the calculation.

Equation reference: eq:correctexponent. Put \(A=w_{0,M}(\kappa+ho)\). Proposition 4.3.9, on the same page, gives the correct normalization character \[
u_w=-w^{-1}A-ho.\] Therefore the ratio of the global normalization, with \(w\in C(\kappa)\), to the \(w'\)-normalization is the character \[
u_w-
u_{w'}=(w')^{-1}A-w^{-1}A.\] Its valuation is \[
 n_{w'}= igl\langle (w')^{-1}A-w^{-1}A,\ v(t) igrangle.\] The common \(-ho\) cancels before the Weyl actions. For \(t=\lambda(p)\) the ratio is \(p^{n_{w'}}\); for general \(t\), retain the character ratio, including its unit factor. This unit has no effect on the ordinary projector.

Take \(g=1\), \(\kappa=(2;0)\), \(\rho=(-1;0)\), \(w=1\), \(w'=s\), and \(t=\operatorname{diag}(1,p)\in T^{++}\). Then \(C(\kappa)=\{1\}\), \(A=(1;0)\), \(\nu_1=(0;0)\), and \(\nu_s=(2;0)\). The character \((2;0)\) evaluates on \(t\) as \(p^{-1}\). The correct ratio is \(p\), so \(n_s=1\). In the printed expression the inner weight is \(\kappa+2\rho=0\), producing zero. It therefore contradicts the stated positivity in this permitted example. The exact calculation is saved in `aux_fixed/exact_checks.json`.

Formula [eq:correctexponent] (#eq:correctexponent) also restores the general argument: \(w^{-1}A\) is the anti-dominant orbit representative. Pairing with a strictly dominant cocharacter is uniquely minimized there, modulo the stabilizer. The difference is positive precisely for \(w'\notin C(\kappa)\). Multiplication by \(p^{n_{w'}}\) then removes those terms from the ordinary part. This is the normalization step that selects the \(C(\kappa)\)-terms in Theorem 4.5.2 and its regular-weight classicality consequence.

The assessment is Major for the invalid essential calculation, not for an alleged failure of the corrected positivity theorem. The neighboring Proposition 4.3.9 is strong counterevidence against broader damage and directly supplies the verified repair.
# Problem 4: coherent cohomology alone does not ensure finiteness

Lemma 2.10.1(4) [1, p. 29] allows an arbitrary complex \(F\) in the displayed derived category, assumes coherent cohomology and proper \(Z\), and concludes finite cohomology for \(\operatorname{R\Gamma}_Z(Y,F)=\operatorname{R\Gamma}(Z,i^!F)\). No lower boundedness is imposed.

Let \(k=\mathbb F_2\), \(A=k[e]/(e^2)\), \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}A\), \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}k\), and \[F=\bigoplus_{n\geq0} k[n].\] Each \(H^{-n}(F)=k\) is coherent, and \(Z\) is proper over \(k\). A bounded-above free resolution of \(k\) is \[\cdots\xrightarrow{e}A\xrightarrow{e}A\xrightarrow{e}A\longrightarrow k.\] Multiplication by \(e\) has kernel equal to image. In the Hom complex into \(F\), every differential vanishes, while degree zero is \[H^0\operatorname{RHom}_A(k,F)=\prod_{n\geq0}k.\] This is not finite-dimensional. Thus every stated hypothesis holds and the asserted finiteness fails. Finite truncations \(F_N\) give dimensions \(N+1\); exact binary-ring checks for \(0\leq N\leq8\) corroborate the explicit infinite-product argument.

Adding \(F\in D^+_{\mathrm{coh}}(Y)\), in the surrounding noetherian setting, repairs the assertion: a fixed total degree receives only finitely many coherent Ext contributions, and proper coherent cohomology is finite. A use involving derived pullback must preserve this boundedness or impose the appropriate finite Tor-dimension.

This is Minor. The fixed-weight applications use locally free automorphic bundles, boundary twists, and nebentypus bundles invertible on the relevant ordinary charts; their required pullbacks are bounded. No failure of the main Hida construction is established by this unbounded-complex example. The concern is the unrestricted auxiliary lemma.
# Problem 5: the dyadic Levi quotient need not be the intersection

On p. 37, §3.4 defines \(U_K=K\cap U_P(\mathbb Q_p)(1)\) and \(M_K=K\cap M(\mathbb Q_p)\). It proves \(K=M_K\ltimes U_K\) when \(p>2\), but then uses, without that restriction, \[1\longrightarrow U_K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow M_K\longrightarrow1\] and identifies the group in Proposition 3.4.9(5) with \(M_K\). At \(p=2\) the Levi projection can be larger than this intersection.

Here is an explicit genus-one compact. Write the lower parabolic in coordinates \(U(u)\operatorname{diag}(a,d)\), whose Levi action on \(u\) is \(d/a\). For \(a,d\in\mathbb Z_2^\times\) put \(\epsilon(a)=(a-1)/2\bmod2\), and define \[K=\{(a,d,u):u\in\tfrac12\mathbb Z_2,\quad 2u\bmod2=\epsilon(a)\}.\] The function \(\epsilon\) is a multiplicative-group character into \(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\). Every \(d/a\) is odd and acts trivially on \(\tfrac12\mathbb Z_2/\mathbb Z_2\). These facts prove closure under multiplication and inversion. The subgroup is compact and open, and is stable under the Galois action multiplying \(u\) by the odd cyclotomic character. It therefore has exactly the descent required in §3.4.5.

Its unipotent intersection is \(\mathbb Z_2\). Its Levi projection is all \((\mathbb Z_2^\times)^2\), whereas its Levi intersection requires \(a\equiv1\pmod4\). For example \((-1,-1,\tfrac12)\in K\), but \((-1,-1,0)\notin K\). The natural map from \(K\cap M\) to \(K/U_K\) is not surjective. The reviewer-written quotient calculation modulo four has eight group elements and projection/intersection sizes four and two, respectively; the analytic construction above proves the full claim.

Replace the quotient by \(\operatorname{pr}_M(K)\), or restrict this assertion to split compacts. The later §5.1 explicitly imposes the latter condition, even at two, and uses a cofinal collection of such compacts. Thus the family control theorem does not rely on the false general intersection identity. The assessment is Minor for the unrestricted finite-level formulation; no failure of the smooth quotient or of the later decomposable tower is established.
# Problem 6: stratum assertions need their positive-level and special-fiber ranges
## Depth zero

Section 4.1 [1, pp. 40–41] starts with \(n\geq0\), then defines strata by requiring certain graded subgroups \(\operatorname{Gr}_i\) of order \(p^n\) to be multiplicative and asserts that they lie in the ordinary locus. At \(n=0\) all these groups are trivial, hence multiplicative. The condition selects the entire special fiber.

For example the smooth elliptic curve \(y^2=x^3+1\) over \(\mathbb F_5\) has six points and trace zero, so it is supersingular. It nevertheless satisfies all the depth-zero graded-group conditions. The exact point count and discriminant check are saved with the ordinary example in `aux_fixed/exact_checks.json`. Restrict this Iwahori-stratum construction to \(n\geq1\). Positive depths are cofinal in the family tower, so the resulting limit construction is unaffected.
## Whole schemes versus special fibers

Proposition 4.1.13(2), p. 42, states that \[\bigcap_{i=1}^k
 \bigl(Z_{i,>j_i}^{\,c}\cap Z_{i,<j_i}^{\,c}\bigr)\] is empty unless every increment \(j_i-j_{i-1}\) is zero or one. As an assertion about the whole scheme, it is false. Take \(g=2\), \(n=1\), \(j_1=0,j_2=2\). Both indices satisfy \(0\leq j_i\leq i\), and the sequence is increasing, but its second increment is two. Every displayed divisor is vertical: it is a positive or negative part of \(Z_i-nj_iV(p)\), with \(Z_i\) supported over \(p=0\). The complementary open therefore contains the entire nonempty generic fiber, unchanged by these vertical blow-ups.

The empty-stratum assertion belongs to the special fiber or its formal completion. This correction leaves the valid zero/one-increment charts and Corollary 4.1.14 available. Both range defects are Minor: they are explicit false auxiliary assertions at the stated boundary, with no demonstrated damage to the positive-level formal construction.
# Positive checks, local corrections and dependency limits
## Support formalism and interpolation

The distinction between ideal-power inequalities, set inclusion and topological compactness in §2 is essential. The support limits are not freely interchanged. Strict contraction supplies the off-diagonal maps in 2.5.3–2.5.4; after taking the ordinary part, their composites become invertible and give the comparison equivalences. The Artinian hypotheses are used for finite direct factors.

Base-change and perfectness in §2.6 retain flatness of the coefficient sheaf. The finite-group version uses an actual finite étale torsor and group-ring flatness, not division by the group order. The transposed-correspondence duality of 2.7.4 retains smoothness, local freeness and the Artinian base. Flatness of both correspondence maps is used in the iteration argument. The Cousin spectral sequence comes from a finite filtration and retains its total degree \(a+b\).

In §3 the cyclotomic base extension reconciles the multiplicative and constant Tate-module level structures. The manuscript explicitly warns that the chosen integral models need not commute with this base change. The ordinary models, rather than arbitrary deep-level integral models, provide the smooth local input.

In 5.2.6–5.2.7 the order \(\lim_m\operatorname{colim}_n\) modulo \(p^m\) produces continuous functions. The finite \(p\)-group rings used for minimal complexes are local; the final quotient \(T(\mathbb F_p)\) has order prime to \(p\), including \(p=2\). The shift \(-w^{-1}w_{0,M}\rho-\rho\) in the control theorem is absorbed by the normalized trace and must not be dropped.
## Comparison, slopes and vanishing

The source image on p. 59 confirms the closure condition \(T(\overline U)\subset U\) in Definition 6.1.3. Its omission in plain-text extraction was not a paper defect. That condition supplies the compactness reduction in Lemma 6.1.5. The two kinds of neighborhoods in 6.1.10–6.1.11 contract to the same ordinary stratum; their finite-slope comparison is the bridge to Coleman theory.

The integral comparison preserves a lattice on each finite-slope part. It does not assert that all overconvergent cohomology is finite-dimensional. In 6.2.14, the bound on poles is independent of the reduction exponent before passing to the inverse limit.

The passage from strict to weak dominance in 6.2.10 and 6.2.16 can be completed precisely. For \(t\in T^+\), fix \(s\in T^{++}\); then \(t^ns\in T^{++}\) for every positive \(n\). On any common finite-slope eigencharacter \(\lambda\), \[n\,v(\lambda(t))+v(\lambda(s))\geq0\quad(n\geq1)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v(\lambda(t))\geq0.\] Group generation alone would not give this inequality, but the available all-strict-element bounds do. This is a verified omitted-step completion, not another asserted defect.

The bounded external checks of [2] and [3] concern the stated duality and vanishing dependencies. More precisely, [3, Theorem 6.7.3, p. 162] gives locally analytic finite-slope amplitudes \([0,\ell(w)]\) for cusp coefficients and \([\ell(w),d]\) otherwise. It imposes no regular-weight or strongly-small-slope hypothesis for these ranges; a domain hypothesis belongs only to its additional torsion-free conclusion. Selecting slope zero through [1, 6.2.15] therefore supports its rational amplitude assertion.

For the arithmetic application, [3, Theorem 5.12.11 and Remark 5.12.12, p. 132] permits the strongly-small-slope condition to be weakened after proving its Conjecture 5.9.2. That is the bound supplied by [1, 6.2.10]. Trivial coefficients are allowed: in [3, Definition 5.11.2, p. 126], put \(\kappa_w=-w_{0,M}w\rho-\rho\). For \(v\ne w\), the excluded threshold is \(\rho-v^{-1}w\rho\), a nonzero sum of positive roots. The zero slope does not dominate that threshold. The opposite-sign condition follows from [3, Proposition 5.11.3, p. 127]. Non-neat principal levels may be treated rationally by pullback and trace at an auxiliary neat tame level; this does not give integral torsion vanishing.

The complete earlier proofs, the solid six-functor foundations, Fargues’ degree theory, Raynaud quotient theory, toroidal comparison, and the lowest-weight-kernel input from Pilloni’s earlier work were not independently reconstructed. Those limits are retained in the coverage ledger.
## Localized notation

Several further slips can be corrected from adjacent formulas without creating additional substantive Problems. On p. 2, \(M_\mu\) must be the Levi, as correctly defined on pp. 33 and 36. On p. 34 the minimal-representative test is \(w^{-1}\Phi_M^+\subset\Phi^+\), with Levi positive roots, not the displayed non-Levi set \(\Phi^{+,M}\). The line-bundle map in 2.5.3 needs its negative \(D_-\) sign; the ensuing formula has it. The induced-representation action in 4.3.1 should read \((m'\cdot f)(m)=f((m')^{-1}m)\). The singleton-\(C(\kappa)\) corollaries 4.5.4–4.5.5 follow for \(M\)-dominant weights from their preceding theorem, despite the narrower printed dominance label. analysis:
Equation reference: eq:printedpair. Theorem 1.4.8 [1, p. 5] explicitly asserts a perfect \(\Lambda\)-bilinear pairing \[

 \longrightarrow\Lambda[-d],

 \kappa'=-w_{0,M}\kappa-2\rho_{\mathrm{nc}},

 \nu'=-w_0\nu.\] Indeed \(w_{0,M}\rho_{\mathrm{nc}}=\rho_{\mathrm{nc}}\), \(w_{0,M}\rho=2\rho_{\mathrm{nc}}-\rho\), and \(w_0\rho=-\rho\). Substitution in the formula for \(w'\) proves [eq:dualweight] (#eq:dualweight). The map \(-w_0\) is the identity on the derived symplectic character space, but negates the scalar-center character. The full \(GSp\) torus in §3.1 therefore matters.

Take \(g=1\), \(p=5\), \(w=1\). In the paper’s coordinates \(ho=(-1;0)\), and Remark 4.3.3, p. 47, identifies the Hodge line with weight \((1;-1)\). Thus \[\kappa=(4;-4),\qquad 
u=(-2;4),\qquad

u'=(-2;-4).\] The parameter \(
u\) is dominant in the convention \(0\geq
u_1\). At the same \(\Lambda\)-point \(-

There is a nonzero ordinary first fiber. Let \[E_4(q)=1+240\sum_{n\geq1}\sigma_3(n)q^n,\qquad
 f(q)=E_4(q)-5^3E_4(q^5).\] The classical Eisenstein series and its degeneracy pullback are modular of weight four. Their combination has constant coefficient \(-124\), hence is nonzero. The identity \[\sigma_3(5n)=(1+5^3)\sigma_3(n)-5^3\sigma_3(n/5)\] with the last term zero when \(5\nmid n\), proves \(U_5f=f\) coefficient by coefficient. Pullback to sufficiently small neat tame level preserves this nonzero class. Modularity of \(E_4\) is the standard classical input; checking finitely many Fourier coefficients would not prove it.

Under the diagonal-invariant construction of \(M_w^\bullet\), an inherited unit-torus operator \(u\) acts as \([u]^{-1}\). At specialization \(-\nu\), choose \(u=6I_2\). Then \(u\) acts by \(6^4\), whereas its prescribed adjoint \(w_0(u^{-1})=u^{-1}\) on the second factor at that same point acts by \(6^{-4}\). A bilinear pairing \(P\) satisfying the asserted adjoint relation must obey \[(6^4-6^{-4})P=0,\qquad
 6^4-6^{-4}=\frac{1679615}{1296}\ne0.\] Over \(\mathbb Q_5\) it is zero, contradicting perfectness at the nonzero fiber. A uniform inverse convention for the regular \(\Lambda\)-action changes both factors together and does not remove this incompatibility. The exact weight arithmetic and coefficients \(0\)–\(20\) are saved in `aux_families/exact_duality_checks.json`; the all-coefficient identity is the proof.

Equation reference: eq:correctpair. Define the algebra involution \[\iota:\Lambda\longrightarrow\Lambda,\qquad
 [t]\longmapsto[w_0(t^{-1})].\] The compatible formulation uses \[
 M_w^\bullet\otimes_\Lambda
 \iota^*M_{w',\mathrm{cusp}}^\bullet\longrightarrow\Lambda[-d],\] or states explicitly that the original pairing is \(\iota\)-sesquilinear. The twist changes the second specialization to \(-\nu'\), as required by [eq:dualweight] (#eq:dualweight). It is an exact repair of the character and adjoint obstruction. A relevant countercheck is the authors’ earlier modular-curve paper [2, pp. 17–18], which explicitly changes the weight-algebra action before forming its \(\Lambda\)-linear Serre pairing. Its one-variable parametrization differs from the full-torus formula here, so it is supporting evidence for the need to specify a twist, not a claim that the two formulas are identical.

analysis: For a concrete allowed case take \(g=1\), depth \(n=1\), and the longest representative, for which \(w_1=0\). Both indices in [eq:emptywindow] (#eq:emptywindow) are \(1\), so the space is empty. The corresponding ordinary étale stratum is not empty. The smooth curve \(y^2=x^3-x\) over \(\mathbb F_5\) has eight points and Frobenius trace \(-2\), hence is ordinary. Over an algebraic closure it admits the required étale subgroup and neat prime-to-five level. The saved exact count is an independent finite witness; the ordinary-stratum description comes from the stated moduli problem.

An empty scheme cannot be a compactification of that stratum. Thus the base case of Lemma 4.4.2, invoked by Proposition 4.4.4 and then by the definitions of the fixed-weight and family complexes, is invalid as printed.

Replace the second endpoint by \(w_i-1\): \[Y_w=\bigcap_i
 \bigl(\operatorname{supp}Z_{i,<w_i+1}\cap\operatorname{supp}Z_{i,>w_i-1}\bigr).\] At endpoints use full-special-fiber support for \(Z_{i,>-1}\) and \(Z_{i,<i+1}\). These conventions agree with the extreme positive or negative parts of \(Z_i-njV(p)\), since \(0\leq Z_i\leq niV(p)\). The corrected \(Y_w\) is closed in the proper special fiber. Removing \(D_{w,+}\cup D_{w,-}\) gives the ordinary \(w\)-chart by Proposition 4.1.13. If density is required, take its closure, as in Proposition 4.4.4.

It is necessary to verify strict dynamics, rather than infer it from pointwise monotonicity. The degree inequalities of 4.2.10–4.2.11 supply the local relation \[a=q b,\qquad a=p_1^*f_+,\quad b=p_2^*f_+,\quad
 q\in\sqrt{(a)}\] on the corrected window. The two boundary supports for a fixed index are disjoint. On a finite cover choose a common \(N\) with \(q^N=u a\). Then, without cancelling a possible zero divisor, \[a^N=q^Nb^N=u q b^{N+1}.\] Thus \((a)^N\subseteq(b)^{N+1}\), which is exactly \[p_2^*D_+\leq \frac{N}{N+1}p_1^*D_+\] in the paper’s ideal-power ordering. The other sign gives strict contraction of \(D_-\); finite sums admit a common strict bound. The nilpotent-thickening lemma then gives the higher reductions modulo \(p^s\).

In Corollary 4.4.3 the support containment needed for the factorization is sufficient; the printed stronger equality need not hold. On \(Y_w\), the excess divisor contains the support of \(p_1^*D_++p_2^*D_+\), since outside the excess one is on an ordinary correspondence chart, and the window selects only the \(w\)-chart. The source’s square-and-glue argument consequently supplies the required global map.

The assessment is Major for this explicit invalid construction in the core chain \(4.4.2\to4.4.4\to5.1.4\to5.2\). The replacement above verifies the missing local input, conditional on the named degree and compactification results. It does not claim that higher Hida theory itself is false.

claim: ProperZ and coherentcohomologyofF implyfinitecohomologyofRΓ_Z(Y,F), no boundedness.

analysis: Lemma 2.10.1(4) [1, p. 29] allows an arbitrary complex \(F\) in the displayed derived category, assumes coherent cohomology and proper \(Z\), and concludes finite cohomology for \(\operatorname{R\Gamma}_Z(Y,F)=\operatorname{R\Gamma}(Z,i^!F)\). No lower boundedness is imposed.

Let \(k=\mathbb F_2\), \(A=k[e]/(e^2)\), \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}A\), \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}k\), and \[F=\bigoplus_{n\geq0} k[n].\] Each \(H^{-n}(F)=k\) is coherent, and \(Z\) is proper over \(k\). A bounded-above free resolution of \(k\) is \[\cdots\xrightarrow{e}A\xrightarrow{e}A\xrightarrow{e}A\longrightarrow k.\] Multiplication by \(e\) has kernel equal to image. In the Hom complex into \(F\), every differential vanishes, while degree zero is \[H^0\operatorname{RHom}_A(k,F)=\prod_{n\geq0}k.\] This is not finite-dimensional. Thus every stated hypothesis holds and the asserted finiteness fails. Finite truncations \(F_N\) give dimensions \(N+1\); exact binary-ring checks for \(0\leq N\leq8\) corroborate the explicit infinite-product argument.

Adding \(F\in D^+_{\mathrm{coh}}(Y)\), in the surrounding noetherian setting, repairs the assertion: a fixed total degree receives only finitely many coherent Ext contributions, and proper coherent cohomology is finite. A use involving derived pullback must preserve this boundedness or impose the appropriate finite Tor-dimension.

This is Minor. The fixed-weight applications use locally free automorphic bundles, boundary twists, and nebentypus bundles invertible on the relevant ordinary charts; their required pullbacks are bounded. It proves \(K=M_K\ltimes U_K\) when \(p>2\), but then uses, without that restriction, \[1\longrightarrow U_K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow M_K\longrightarrow1\] and identifies the group in Proposition 3.4.9(5) with \(M_K\). Here is an explicit genus-one compact. Write the lower parabolic in coordinates \(U(u)\operatorname{diag}(a,d)\), whose Levi action on \(u\) is \(d/a\). For \(a,d\in\mathbb Z_2^\times\) put \(\epsilon(a)=(a-1)/2\bmod2\), and define \[K=\{(a,d,u):u\in\tfrac12\mathbb Z_2,\quad 2u\bmod2=\epsilon(a)\}.\] The function \(\epsilon\) is a multiplicative-group character into \(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\).
