report: Abstract: The acquired revised manuscript of Fraczyk, Hurtado and Raimbault is examined from its arithmetic collar lemma through orbital growth, thin-volume estimates and the bounded-degree nerve construction. The introductory collar theorem lacks an essential irreducibility restriction. The rank-one spectral-gap calculation and the final nerve-degree argument contain explicit errors in core derivations. Several narrower algebraic and tube-counting statements also require correction. Counterexamples, exact checks and local replacement arguments are supplied, including a factorwise supplement for the main theorem. The overall assessment is Major for the specified claims and derivations. These findings do not establish that the corrected topological-complexity or torsion-homology conclusions are false.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Scope, spectral estimates and the good-cover argument for arithmetic locally symmetric spaces
# Identity, exact version and mathematical scope

The reviewed paper is Mikołaj Frączyk, Sebastian Hurtado and Jean Raimbault, Topological complexity of arithmetic locally symmetric spaces, associated with Inventiones mathematicae (2025), DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01394-1 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01394-1). The actual source is arXiv:2202.13619v2, dated 2 February 2026, 23 pages [1]. No equivalence with the publisher’s version is asserted. References to the source below use physical PDF pages, equal to its printed page numbers. The accompanying `mainrev.tex`, `macros.tex` and bibliography were read as source text; they were not executed.

For a fixed symmetric space \(X\), Theorem A asserts that every closed arithmetic locally \(X\)-manifold has a homotopy-equivalent simplicial complex with both its total number of simplices and its vertex incidences controlled: the former is linear in volume, the latter uniform in the manifold. Theorem B bounds the logarithm of integral homology torsion for finite-volume arithmetic manifolds. The noncompact topological case is an earlier Gelander input, not newly proved in this manuscript. The new compact argument passes through the degree-dependent arithmetic Margulis lemma, orbital growth, a polynomial overlap estimate and an adaptive good cover.

Write \(d=[k:\mathbb Q]\), \(n=\dim X\), and use the ordinary geometric convention \[\operatorname{inj}_M(x)=\frac12\inf_{\gamma\ne1}d_X(\widetilde x,\gamma\widetilde x)\] for a torsion-free effective lattice quotient. For orbifolds this expression measures proximity to the singular locus. The source’s first injectivity-radius display on p. 8 has a factor inconsistent with its following \(B(2R)\) display; its intended standard convention is used here. Accordingly tubes defined by displacement \(<R\) correspond to injectivity radius \(<R/2\). Constant rescaling reconciles the later volume estimates.

All six principal sections and the exact author TeX were read in this initial review; the primary session actually inspected source images pp. 1–21. Selected passages of the primary dependencies [2]–[6] were also read and viewed. Their complete proofs, the full arithmetic-lattice classification, the flat torus theorem, Jordan’s theorem and the quoted uniform triangularization results remain named external inputs.
# Problem 1: the introductory collar theorem needs irreducibility
## The quantifier failure

Theorem C [1, p. 3] says that for any arithmetic lattice in the fixed group, elements moving a point by at most \(\varepsilon_X d\) generate a virtually nilpotent subgroup. It does not impose irreducibility. The actual Theorem 3.1, p. 9, does impose it.

Take \(G=\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\times\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\). In its first factor use the arithmetic lattice \(\Gamma_1=\Gamma(2)/\{\pm I\}\), containing \[a=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad b=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Their nonzero powers act by ping-pong on the projective-line regions \(\{|x|<1\}\) and \(\{|x|>1\}\), respectively; hence \(\langle a,b\rangle\) is a nonabelian free group. In the curvature \(-1\) normalization, both move \(i\in\mathbb H^2\) by \(\operatorname{arcosh}(3)\), since \[\cosh d(i,gi)=\frac{a_g^2+b_g^2+c_g^2+d_g^2}{2}.\] A different fixed normalization of \(X\) merely changes this fixed displacement.

Choose totally real fields \(F_j\) of unbounded degree and quaternion algebras over \(F_j\) split at exactly one real place. The standard norm-one order construction gives arithmetic Fuchsian lattices \(\Gamma_j'\) with invariant, equivalently adjoint, trace field \(F_j\); the construction and field identification are explicitly recorded in [2, p. 534]. For degree greater than one these may be chosen cocompact. Set \(\Gamma_j=\Gamma_1\times\Gamma_j'\). This is an arithmetic lattice in the same fixed \(G\). Its adjoint trace field is \(F_j\): traces on the direct-sum Lie algebra add, the first factor has rational adjoint traces, and \(\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Ad}(1,\gamma)=3+\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Ad}(\gamma)\).

For every proposed \(\varepsilon_X>0\), sufficiently large \(j\) makes \(\varepsilon_X[F_j:\mathbb Q]\) exceed the fixed displacement of \(a\) and \(b\). The short-element subgroup at \((i,x_j)\) then contains \(\langle(a,1),(b,1)\rangle\cong F_2\). A virtually nilpotent group cannot contain this subgroup. Every condition in Theorem C as printed is met; its conclusion fails.
## Repair and impact

Add irreducible to Theorem C, as already required by Theorem 3.1, or formulate a factorwise radius using the individual irreducible degrees. A single full product trace degree cannot replace these separate parameters. This is Major for a prominently stated technical guarantee central to the paper’s method. It does not refute Theorem 3.1. The proof of Theorem A on p. 18 also applies irreducible degree estimates to an unrestricted lattice without explaining that reduction; a valid factorwise completion is given in Section 8 (#sec:completion) below.

For the irreducible compact case, the height-gap mechanism itself checks out after the local height correction in Problem 3. The small-displacement set is finite, contains the identity, and its word displacements are bounded by word length times the original bound. Breuillard’s actual Corollary 1.7 [3, p. 1061] supplies the stated uniformly short word with an eigenvalue of positive height. The anisotropic solvable-subgroup argument then gives virtual abelianness. The nonuniform rational-structure sentence should be read with its cited Gelander Lemma 5.2 [4, physical pp. 20–21]; a naive objection based only on a presentation over a larger number field was rejected after that passage was checked.
# Problem 2: the orbital-growth proof uses an incorrect spectral calculation
## A decisive rank-one test

Lemma 4.2 [1, p. 11] assigns critical exponents \(m,m,2m\) to its three listed real and complex hyperbolic subgroup cases. Its spectral formula uses \(\dim\partial X\) as the entropy parameter. Already the first case is inconsistent with the desired conclusion. Take \(G=\operatorname{SO}^0(2,1)\), \(H=\operatorname{SO}^0(1,1)\), the centralizer of a hyperbolic element, and a cyclic uniform lattice \(\Lambda\) in \(H\). The orbit of \(\Lambda\) grows linearly along a geodesic, so its critical exponent is zero. The printed assignment has \(m=1\), hence critical exponent one. Together with \(\dim\partial\mathbb H^2=1\), the displayed second branch gives \(\lambda_0=1(1-1)=0\), not a positive lower bound. This is an admissible centralizer, not an excluded endpoint.

These corrected values are strictly below \(h_X\) for every listed proper noncompact subgroup, with only finitely many relevant dimensions for fixed \(G\). Compact centralizers are handled by the regular-representation spectral bound. Thus the corrected formula supplies the intended positive uniform gap. The property-\((T)\) branch is separate; one can choose the averaging kernel as a convolution square to ensure positivity of the self-adjoint averaging operator.
## The compact-factor restriction

Theorems E and 4.1 [1, pp. 4, 10] also state their exponential orbital-growth assertion for arbitrary semisimple \(G\) with finite center. Lemma 4.2 excludes compact factors. This discrepancy has a literal counterexample. Let \[G=G_0\times\operatorname{SO}(3),\qquad
 \Gamma=\Gamma_0\times F,
 \qquad \gamma=(1,u),\] where \(\Gamma_0\) is a uniform lattice in the noncompact \(G_0\), \(F\) is the finite tetrahedral rotation group, and \(u\) is an order-three rotation noncentral in both \(F\) and \(\operatorname{SO}(3)\). Then \(\Gamma\) is uniform and \(\gamma\) is noncentral. The compact factor acts trivially on \(X=G/K\), so every conjugate of \(\gamma\) has displacement zero. Its orbital integral over \(G_\gamma\backslash G\) is the same finite positive compact-orbit volume for every positive radius. The asserted inequality would force \(1<C e^{-\delta R_2}\) for arbitrarily large \(R_2\), which is impossible.

Restrict the theorem to groups without compact factors, or require a noncentral projection to the effective noncompact quotient. The earlier no-compact-factor phrase on p. 5 is explicitly local to its paragraph; it does not repair the independently restated broader theorems. Replace the strict inequality by a non-strict one at zero orbital mass.
## Core dependency and counterevidence

The spectrum calculation is Major as an invalid derivation of the uniform gap used in \[\mathrm{Lemma}\ 4.2\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{Theorem}\ 4.1\
 \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{Theorem}\ 5.7\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{Theorem}\ A.\] The compact-factor counterexample also refutes the literal orbital-growth guarantee. Neither finding disproves its corrected effective version. Once a genuine gap is supplied, the p. 12 convolution argument is sound: convolution expands displacement support from \(R\) to \(R+2\), preserves the integral, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[\mathcal O(\gamma,1_{B(R)})\le e^{-2\delta}\mathcal O(\gamma,1_{B(R+2)}).\] Iteration and monotonicity yield the required exponential growth, with a uniform prefactor.
# Problem 3: the auxiliary splitting-field bound is false

In the proof of Proposition 2.2 [1, p. 8], the manuscript asserts \[[k(\Phi(\gamma)):k]\le n,\qquad n=\dim\mathbf G,\] where \(k(\Phi(\gamma))\) is generated by all adjoint root values. Individual eigenvalue degrees have a dimension bound, but their common splitting field need not.

Take \(G=\operatorname{PGL}_5(\mathbb R)\), the arithmetic lattice given by the image of \(\operatorname{SL}_5(\mathbb Z)\), \(k=\mathbb Q\), and the companion matrix of \(f(t)=t^5-t-1\). It has determinant one and distinct roots, so its image is an allowed semisimple element. Exact polynomial division gives irreducibility modulo three and the square-free factorization \[f(t)\equiv(t^2+t+1)(t^3+t^2+1)\pmod2.\] Thus the Galois group is transitive of prime degree five and contains a permutation of cycle type \((2)(3)\), whose cube is a transposition. A primitive group containing a transposition is the full symmetric group: the graph of its conjugate transpositions has components forming a block system. Consequently the splitting field has degree \(120\).

Its root ratios generate that whole field. An automorphism fixing every ratio scales every root by a common \(\zeta\); the nonzero fourth and fifth elementary symmetric functions force \(\zeta^4=\zeta^5=1\), hence \(\zeta=1\). Therefore \[[\mathbb Q(\Phi(\gamma)):\mathbb Q]=120>24=\dim\operatorname{PGL}_5.\] The exact modular tests are preserved in `aux_height/exact_checks.json`; the Galois and ratio-field arguments are the proof, not a numerical extrapolation.

There is a direct repair requiring no splitting-field bound. Let \(L=k(\Phi(\gamma))\). For an archimedean embedding \(\sigma\) of \(k\), set \[S_\sigma=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\log^+|\tau(\alpha(\gamma))|,\] where \(\tau\) is any extension to \(L\). Galois invariance of the root-value multiset makes \(S_\sigma\) independent of that choice. Each \(\sigma\) has exactly \([L:k]\) extensions; this multiplicity cancels the denominator in Weil height. If one representative is used per complex conjugate pair, the exact relation is \[[k:\mathbb Q]h(\gamma)=
 \sum_{\sigma\ \mathrm{real}}S_\sigma+
 2\sum_{\sigma\ \mathrm{complex\ pairs}}S_\sigma.
 \tag{4.1}\] Thus, writing \(S\) for the corresponding unweighted representative sum, \(S\le[k:\mathbb Q]h(\gamma)\le2S\); the p. 8 displayed inequality has the wrong direction when complex-place contributions occur. Together with the preceding displacement comparison, (4.1) restores Proposition 2.2 with constants depending only on \(X\). For zero height, state it multiplicatively instead of using an undefined \(0/0\) quotient. The false extra field-degree bound is Minor: it is unnecessary, and the already available multiset invariance supplies the full intended comparison.
# Problem 4: the overlap bound loses its necessary uniform prefactor
Proposition 5.1 [1, p. 13] bounds the number of small-displacement tubes through a point by \(d^m\), with no multiplicative constant. At \(d=1\) this is exactly one, independent of \(m\).

Consider \[q=x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2-7x_4^2,\qquad
 \Gamma=\operatorname{SO}^+(q,\mathbb Z).\] The form is anisotropic over \(\mathbb Q\). In a primitive integral solution of \(q=0\), an odd \(x_4\) would express seven modulo eight as a sum of three squares; an even \(x_4\) forces all three other coordinates even, contradicting primitivity by descent. The standard anisotropic arithmetic-lattice criterion therefore gives a uniform lattice in the real simple group of signature \((3,1)\). Its adjoint trace field is \(\mathbb Q\).

The integral rotation \(r\) through \(90^\circ\) in the first two coordinates preserves \(q\), has order four, and fixes a geodesic in hyperbolic three-space. Both \(r\) and \(r^2\) have zero displacement on that axis. Their positive-radius tubes are genuinely distinct: in curvature \(-1\), \[\sinh\!\left(\frac{d(x,r_\theta x)}2\right)
 =|\sin(\theta/2)|\sinh d(x,\mathrm{axis}),\] so \(S_{r^2}^{R}\subsetneq S_r^{R}\). Thus every positive radius gives at least two distinct tubes through an axis point, contradicting \(d^m=1\). The exact residue and matrix checks are saved in `aux_thin/exact_checks.json`. The criterion establishing arithmetic cocompactness is a named standard input, not inferred from finite enumeration.

Replace the bound by \(C(d+1)^m\), or \(Cd^m\) with the small-degree cases treated explicitly. This is a Minor boundary defect in the stated overlap bound; its proof itself already produces multiplicative constants, and the required large-degree polynomial scale is unchanged.

Several supporting proof steps on pp. 13–16 also need precise completion. Lemma 5.2’s hypothesis implies that every element is semisimple: a positive power belongs to its semisimple abelian finite-index subgroup, and in characteristic zero this forces the original unipotent Jordan part to vanish. Hence the alternative uniform triangularization argument already given in Remark 5.3 applies, conditional on its stated external inputs. It avoids the unjustified identification of the chosen torsion-free subgroup with the entire diagonal intersection.

For the flat action, normalizing a translation subgroup does not preserve an arbitrary flat selected from its minimum set. Choose a normal abelian subgroup of bounded index, then a characteristic torsion-free finite-index subgroup \(L_0\). The transverse factor in \(\operatorname{Min}(L_0)=Y\times E\) has a fixed point under the finite quotient. This selects a \(\Delta\)-invariant flat. Its action kernel is finite, and Jordan’s theorem together with bounds on algebraic roots of unity bounds that kernel polynomially in \(d\). The useful elementary bound is \(\varphi(N)\ge\sqrt{N/2}\), not the printed \(\sqrt N\), which fails for \(N=2,6\).

The translation lattice of the projected group need not be exactly \(\pi(L_0)\). For any projected nonzero translation, equivariant nearest-point projection to the chosen flat shows that its translation length equals that of its lift on \(X\). The nonelliptic systole bound therefore applies directly. At bounded degree use a positive constant, or write the coarse bound with \(\log(d+2)\). The rank-zero case is just a finite-group bound.

Finally, the successive-minima vectors in Lemma 5.5 need not form a lattice basis. For \[L=\mathbb Z^4+\mathbb Z(1/2,1/2,1/2,1/2)\] the four standard unit vectors attain all successive minima but generate an index-two sublattice. The printed fundamental-domain assertion therefore fails. A direct replacement is simpler: in each coset of the translation lattice, orbit points are separated by its minimum length \(\ell\). Disjoint balls of radius \(\ell/2\) give \[\#\{g:d(gx,x)\le R\}\le A(r)(1+2R/\ell)^r,
 \qquad r=\dim E,
 \tag{5.1}\] where the finite point-group bound \(A(r)\) depends only on \(r\). This covers \(R<\ell\) as well. Together these completions recover the intended polynomial overlap estimate, with explicit external Jordan, flat-torus and triangularization dependencies.
# Problem 5: the tube-volume comparison is false in the nonuniform range

Corollary 5.6 [1, p. 16] omits the uniformity assumption of Proposition 5.1. It claims that a finite polynomial in \(d\) controls the sum of volumes of all conjugacy-class tubes by the thin-part volume. No finite constant can make that assertion true for every nonuniform arithmetic lattice.

For every \(R>0\), including every sufficiently small allowed radius, (6.1) yields a divergent harmonic class sum. The modular surface has finite area, so its thin part has finite area. The asserted lower comparison therefore fails.

Restrict Corollary 5.6 to uniform lattices and retain the prefactor from Problem 4. For a rigorous unfolding, count fibers over \(\Gamma\backslash G\), normalize Haar measure on \(K\), and then descend to \(\Gamma\backslash X\). The literal map displayed to \(X\) has continuous \(K\)-fibers and is not finite-to-one. Also use displacement \(2R\) when the thin radius is defined by the usual injectivity radius.

This is Minor in its established impact: the false nonuniform extension is auxiliary to the new compact-manifold argument, which uses uniform lattices. The bounded-degree nonuniform range of Theorem 5.7 can be obtained separately from monotonicity by increasing its constant. That observation does not prove the strictly smaller-than-one fraction asserted in Theorem D; this distinction is retained below.
# Problem 6: the good-cover proof does not count the adjacent vertices
## The essential wrong set

In the final paragraph proving Proposition 6.1 [1, p. 20], the degree bound counts centers \(q\in B(p,\varepsilon_p/6)\). Adjacency in the nerve instead means \[B(p,\varepsilon_p/6)\cap B(q,\varepsilon_q/6)\ne\varnothing.\] The latter does not require that \(q\) lie in the first ball. Equal radii \(1/6\) and center distance \(1/4\) give a direct local example. The two centers also satisfy the required net separation. Thus the displayed count omits allowed neighbors and does not establish the claimed vertex degree. This is the final essential step supplying the bounded-incidence conclusion of Proposition 6.1 and Theorem A.

There is a complete replacement. The radius function \(\varepsilon_x=\min(1,\operatorname{inj}_M(x))\) is 1-Lipschitz. Writing \(s=d(p,q)\), intersecting balls imply \[6s<\varepsilon_p+\varepsilon_q
 \le2\varepsilon_p+s.\] Hence \[s<2\varepsilon_p/5,\qquad
 \varepsilon_q>\varepsilon_p-s>3\varepsilon_p/5.
 \tag{7.1}\] All neighbor centers therefore lie in \(B(p,2\varepsilon_p/5)\) and, by the net condition, are \(\varepsilon_p/60\)-separated. The corrected packing bound below gives \[\deg(p)\le C_X(49).\] Every simplex incident to \(p\) is determined by a subset of its neighbors, so the number of incident simplices is at most \(2^{\lceil C_X(49)\rceil}\). This restores precisely the missing uniform bound.
## Two quantitative corrections needed in the same construction

Lemma 6.2, p. 18, claims \(|P|<C_X(\delta/\eta)\) for an \(\eta\)-separated set in a \(\delta\)-ball. The correct packing argument lifts the centers to \(X\); their disjoint \(\eta/2\)-balls fit in the ball of radius \(\delta+\eta/2\). It gives \[|P|\le C_X(2\delta/\eta+1).
 \tag{7.2}\] The stated smaller constant is actually false. In curvature-\(-1\) \(\mathbb H^2\), choose \(\eta=1/10\), \(\delta=11/100\) and points at distances \(3/40\) on opposite sides of a geodesic midpoint. There are two separated points in the required ball, but \[C_{\mathbb H^2}(11/10)\le(3520/3079)^2<2.\] This rational estimate follows from \(\sinh(ru)/\sinh u\le r\cosh(ru)\) for \(0<u<1/4\), together with \(\cosh(11/40)\le(1-121/3200)^{-1}\). The exact arithmetic and the repaired constants are recorded in `aux_nerve/exact_constant_checks.json`. For any fixed rescaling of the metric, continuity as \(\delta/\eta\) tends to one gives the same failure.

The function \(F_p\) in Lemma 6.3, pp. 18–19, has support radius \(\varepsilon_p/4\) but normalization denominator \(\operatorname{vol}B(p,\varepsilon_p/2)\). Consequently \[\int_M F_p=
 \frac{\operatorname{vol}B(p,\varepsilon_p/4)}{\operatorname{vol}B(p,\varepsilon_p/2)}
 <1,\] contrary to the printed equality. Use instead \(\int F_p\ge C_X(2)^{-1}\). Formula (7.2) changes the multiplicity bound for \(H_p(x)\) to \(C_X(73)\). The argument then gives \[|S|\le C_X(2)^2C_X(73)
 \int_M\operatorname{vol}B(x,\varepsilon_x/2)^{-1}\,dx
 \ll_X\int_M\varepsilon_x^{-n}\,dx.
 \tag{7.3}\] The embedded-ball volume is comparable to \(\varepsilon_x^n\), with its inverse comparable to \(\varepsilon_x^{-n}\).
## What the construction does establish

Maximality of the separated net does give coverage: using the Lipschitz property in the failed separation inequality yields \(d(x,p)\le\varepsilon_p/35<\varepsilon_p/6\). Compactness ensures a finite net. The source’s lift argument rules out distinct lifts intersecting the same small ball, because their center separation would be below the injectivity bound. All finite intersections then lift to convex ball intersections in \(X\), so the cover is good. The nerve theorem supplies the homotopy equivalence.

The assessment is Major for the wrong-set degree argument in a core construction, with the normalization and packing corrections as additional local defects. The replacement (7.1)–(7.3) verifies the intended bounded-degree nerve conclusion. A short and successful repair is not evidence that the original derivation was valid.
# Completion of the main reduction and remaining dependencies
## Irreducible large and small degrees

After the corrected uniform overlap and orbital-growth arguments, the thin-volume comparison gives \[\frac{\operatorname{vol}(M_{\le\eta d})}{\operatorname{vol}M}\le C d^m e^{-ad}.\] For sufficiently large \(d\), this is at most \(e^{-a'd}\) for a fixed \(0<a'<a\). Ensure also \(1\le\eta d\) before using it to estimate the 1-thin part. Combining it with the nonelliptic length bound gives \[e^{-a'd}\log(d+2)^{3n}=O_{X,n}(1).\] For bounded degree, the eigenvalue degrees are uniformly bounded and non-roots of unity have a positive uniform height lower bound; equivalently use the bounded-degree part of the systole argument. Thus the compact torsion-free case has a uniform positive injectivity lower bound in that range. No statement that a positive-radius thin estimate is vacuous is needed.
## The reducible case, including projected torsion

Use the standard decomposition of a lattice into discrete irreducible projection blocks. For the connected effective group, write \(\Gamma\subset\prod_i\Gamma_i\) with finite index, allowing torsion in the cocompact projected lattices \(\Gamma_i\). No uniform bound on that index is assumed.

For \(M_i=\Gamma_i\backslash X_i\) define the nonelliptic radius \[\rho_i(x_i)=
 \min\!\left(1,\frac12
 \inf_{\gamma_i\ \mathrm{of\ infinite\ order}}
 d_{X_i}(\widetilde x_i,\gamma_i\widetilde x_i)\right).
 \tag{8.1}\] Take the empty infimum as \(+\infty\). Every nonidentity element of the torsion-free \(\Gamma\) has an infinite-order projection: a finite tuple of finite-order elements has finite order. For the product metric, its displacement is at least that in this component. It follows that \[\varepsilon_M(x)\ge\min_i\rho_i(x_i),
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_M(x)^{-n}\le\sum_i\rho_i(x_i)^{-n}.
 \tag{8.2}\] Because each factor function descends to its orbifold quotient, finite-cover and product integration give exactly \[\frac1{\operatorname{vol}M}\int_M\rho_i(x_i)^{-n}\,dx
 =
 \frac1{\operatorname{vol}M_i}\int_{M_i}\rho_i(x_i)^{-n}\,dx_i.
 \tag{8.3}\] The covering index cancels.

At bounded factor degree, the positive nonelliptic systole bounds (8.1) away from zero, including near orbifold singularities. At large degree, \(\{\rho_i<1\}\) is contained in the usual 1-thin part, so the large-degree exponential bound and the logarithmic systole bound give a uniform upper bound for the right side of (8.3). Equations (8.2)–(8.3) and the corrected Proposition 6.1 therefore supply the general compact conclusion, conditional on the named standard lattice decomposition. This handles projected torsion; blindly using the ordinary orbifold injectivity radius would instead introduce zeros at singular strata.

If disconnected effective isometries are allowed, put \(\Gamma_0=\Gamma\cap\operatorname{Isom}(X)^0\) and \(f=[\Gamma:\Gamma_0]\). The component count bounds \(f\) solely in terms of \(X\). For every \(\gamma\ne1\), torsion-freeness gives \(\gamma^f\ne1\) in \(\Gamma_0\), and \[d(x,\gamma^f x)\le f\,d(x,\gamma x).\] Hence \(\varepsilon_\Gamma\ge\varepsilon_{\Gamma_0}/f\). Normalized integration over the \(f\)-sheeted cover increases the bound by at most \(f^n\), still uniform in \(M\). For connected effective groups the discrete irreducible projection decomposition itself needs no preliminary cover. These reductions replace the unjustified use of one product trace degree; they do not assume a uniform index in the product of the projected lattices.
## Torsion and other claims

For the compact case of Theorem B, the repaired nerve has \(O_X(\operatorname{vol}M)\) simplices. Each simplicial boundary column in degree \(i+1\) has Euclidean norm \(\sqrt{i+2}\). Hadamard’s determinant bound controls the torsion of its cokernel exponentially in the number of columns. The kernel of the next boundary is primitive, so this is also the relevant homology torsion bound. The noncompact case retains the previous Gelander topological result as a dependency.

Two ranges remain explicitly unresolved in this bounded review. First, §5.1, p. 17, does not establish the full bounded-degree nonuniform version of Theorem D: absorbing \(Cd^m\) works for large degree, and bounded degree alone does not make its strictly subunit volume fraction automatic. Monotonicity repairs Theorem 5.7 with a prefactor but does not supply this stronger assertion. This is recorded as Needs Evidence, without claiming a counterexample to Theorem D.

Second, the intended lower bound in Proposition 6.4 concerns \(C\simeq M\), as its proof states; the printed \(C\simeq X\) is an isolated target-symbol error. The consulted Lafont–Schmidt straightening [6, pp. 133, 135–137] has the required face compatibility and compatible equivariant homotopies. These justify gluing and preservation of the fundamental class within its scope. Its bounded-Jacobian theorem, however, excludes every local \(\mathbb H^2\) or \(\operatorname{SL}_3(\mathbb R)/\operatorname{SO}(3)\) factor. The present manuscript explicitly discusses the exceptional whole spaces but does not supply the mixed-factor bounded-image argument. A complete exceptional/product extension was not verified here; the bounded attempts to acquire the cited Bucher text failed and are recorded. This dependency remains Needs Evidence, not an asserted false lower-bound theorem. The remarks about adaptive Delaunay triangulation also retain their external construction as a dependency; no triangulation algorithm was executed.
# Impact and review state

The unsupported generality of the introductory collar theorem and orbital-growth theorem is separated from their corrected effective, irreducible uses. The spectral-gap and nerve-degree calculations are demonstrated invalid core derivations. The exact counterexamples to the height estimate, unit-prefactor overlap bound and nonuniform tube comparison have narrower impact. The replacement arguments above support the main compact-complexity chain without pretending that every cited external proof, every version of Theorem D, or the mixed-factor lower-bound extension has been independently reconstructed.

For degree greater than one these may be chosen cocompact. Set \(\Gamma_j=\Gamma_1\times\Gamma_j'\). This is an arithmetic lattice in the same fixed \(G\). Its adjoint trace field is \(F_j\): traces on the direct-sum Lie algebra add, the first factor has rational adjoint traces, and \(\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Ad}(1,\gamma)=3+\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Ad}(\gamma)\).

For every proposed \(\varepsilon_X>0\), sufficiently large \(j\) makes \(\varepsilon_X[F_j:\mathbb Q]\) exceed the fixed displacement of \(a\) and \(b\). The short-element subgroup at \((i,x_j)\) then contains \(\langle(a,1),(b,1)\rangle\cong F_2\). A virtually nilpotent group cannot contain this subgroup. Take \(G=\operatorname{PGL}_5(\mathbb R)\), the arithmetic lattice given by the image of \(\operatorname{SL}_5(\mathbb Z)\), \(k=\mathbb Q\), and the companion matrix of \(f(t)=t^5-t-1\). It has determinant one and distinct roots, so its image is an allowed semisimple element. Exact polynomial division gives irreducibility modulo three and the square-free factorization \[f(t)\equiv(t^2+t+1)(t^3+t^2+1)\pmod2.\] Thus the Galois group is transitive of prime degree five and contains a permutation of cycle type \((2)(3)\), whose cube is a transposition. A primitive group containing a transposition is the full symmetric group: the graph of its conjugate transpositions has components forming a block system. Consequently the splitting field has degree \(120\).

Its root ratios generate that whole field. An automorphism fixing every ratio scales every root by a common \(\zeta\); the nonzero fourth and fifth elementary symmetric functions force \(\zeta^4=\zeta^5=1\), hence \(\zeta=1\). Therefore \[[\mathbb Q(\Phi(\gamma)):\mathbb Q]=120>24=\dim\operatorname{PGL}_5.\] The exact modular tests are preserved in `aux_height/exact_checks.json`; the Galois and ratio-field arguments are the proof, not a numerical extrapolation.

For an archimedean embedding \(\sigma\) of \(k\), set \[S_\sigma=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\log^+|\tau(\alpha(\gamma))|,\] where \(\tau\) is any extension to \(L\). Galois invariance of the root-value multiset makes \(S_\sigma\) independent of that choice. Each \(\sigma\) has exactly \([L:k]\) extensions; this multiplicity cancels the denominator in Weil height. If one representative is used per complex conjugate pair, the exact relation is \[[k:\mathbb Q]h(\gamma)=
 \sum_{\sigma\ \mathrm{real}}S_\sigma+
 2\sum_{\sigma\ \mathrm{complex\ pairs}}S_\sigma.
 \tag{4.1}\] Thus, writing \(S\) for the corresponding unweighted representative sum, \(S\le[k:\mathbb Q]h(\gamma)\le2S\); the p. 8 displayed inequality has the wrong direction when complex-place contributions occur. analysis: Proposition 5.1 [1, p. 13] bounds the number of small-displacement tubes through a point by \(d^m\), with no multiplicative constant. At \(d=1\) this is exactly one, independent of \(m\).

Consider \[q=x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2-7x_4^2,\qquad
 \Gamma=\operatorname{SO}^+(q,\mathbb Z).\] The form is anisotropic over \(\mathbb Q\). In a primitive integral solution of \(q=0\), an odd \(x_4\) would express seven modulo eight as a sum of three squares; an even \(x_4\) forces all three other coordinates even, contradicting primitivity by descent. The standard anisotropic arithmetic-lattice criterion therefore gives a uniform lattice in the real simple group of signature \((3,1)\). Its adjoint trace field is \(\mathbb Q\).

The integral rotation \(r\) through \(90^\circ\) in the first two coordinates preserves \(q\), has order four, and fixes a geodesic in hyperbolic three-space. Both \(r\) and \(r^2\) have zero displacement on that axis. Their positive-radius tubes are genuinely distinct: in curvature \(-1\), \[\sinh\!\left(\frac{d(x,r_\theta x)}2\right)
 =|\sin(\theta/2)|\sinh d(x,\mathrm{axis}),\] so \(S_{r^2}^{R}\subsetneq S_r^{R}\). Thus every positive radius gives at least two distinct tubes through an axis point, contradicting \(d^m=1\). The exact residue and matrix checks are saved in `aux_thin/exact_checks.json`. The criterion establishing arithmetic cocompactness is a named standard input, not inferred from finite enumeration.

Replace the bound by \(C(d+1)^m\), or \(Cd^m\) with the small-degree cases treated explicitly. This is a Minor boundary defect in the stated overlap bound; its proof itself already produces multiplicative constants, and the required large-degree polynomial scale is unchanged.

Several supporting proof steps on pp. 13–16 also need precise completion. Lemma 5.2’s hypothesis implies that every element is semisimple: a positive power belongs to its semisimple abelian finite-index subgroup, and in characteristic zero this forces the original unipotent Jordan part to vanish. Hence the alternative uniform triangularization argument already given in Remark 5.3 applies, conditional on its stated external inputs. It avoids the unjustified identification of the chosen torsion-free subgroup with the entire diagonal intersection.

For the flat action, normalizing a translation subgroup does not preserve an arbitrary flat selected from its minimum set. Choose a normal abelian subgroup of bounded index, then a characteristic torsion-free finite-index subgroup \(L_0\). The transverse factor in \(\operatorname{Min}(L_0)=Y\times E\) has a fixed point under the finite quotient. This selects a \(\Delta\)-invariant flat. Its action kernel is finite, and Jordan’s theorem together with bounds on algebraic roots of unity bounds that kernel polynomially in \(d\). The useful elementary bound is \(\varphi(N)\ge\sqrt{N/2}\), not the printed \(\sqrt N\), which fails for \(N=2,6\).

The translation lattice of the projected group need not be exactly \(\pi(L_0)\). For any projected nonzero translation, equivariant nearest-point projection to the chosen flat shows that its translation length equals that of its lift on \(X\). The nonelliptic systole bound therefore applies directly. At bounded degree use a positive constant, or write the coarse bound with \(\log(d+2)\). The rank-zero case is just a finite-group bound.

Finally, the successive-minima vectors in Lemma 5.5 need not form a lattice basis. For \[L=\mathbb Z^4+\mathbb Z(1/2,1/2,1/2,1/2)\] the four standard unit vectors attain all successive minima but generate an index-two sublattice. The printed fundamental-domain assertion therefore fails. A direct replacement is simpler: in each coset of the translation lattice, orbit points are separated by its minimum length \(\ell\). Disjoint balls of radius \(\ell/2\) give \[\#\{g:d(gx,x)\le R\}\le A(r)(1+2R/\ell)^r,
 \qquad r=\dim E,
 \tag{5.1}\] where the finite point-group bound \(A(r)\) depends only on \(r\). This covers \(R<\ell\) as well. Together these completions recover the intended polynomial overlap estimate, with explicit external Jordan, flat-torus and triangularization dependencies.

report: Abstract: The acquired version of Coiculescu and Palasek’s construction is examined through its critical initial data, alternating principal flows, residual correction and final solution class. Two core derivations require correction: the support and cutoff construction does not provide the containments it uses, and the stated linearized derivative estimate is contradicted by an admissible Fourier family. Explicit replacement arguments are supplied. Three further findings concern local heat estimates, a time-integral comparison and the auxiliary energy inequality. The overall assessment is Major for these specified derivations. The evidence does not establish that the main non-uniqueness conclusion is false.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Support, semigroup estimates and non-uniqueness from critical data
# Identity, exact version and scope

This report concerns Non-Uniqueness of Smooth Solutions of the Navier–Stokes Equations from Critical Data, by Matei P. Coiculescu and Stan Palasek, identifier M25-0129, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01396-z. The reviewed source is the 54-page arXiv:2503.14699v2 PDF, whose margin gives 21 July 2025 and whose title page gives 18 March 2025 [CP]. Physical and printed page numbers coincide. Equivalence with the journal version has not been established. The canonical SHA256 is

Theorem 1.2, p. 2, claims two distinct global solutions on the length-\(2\pi\) torus, smooth for positive time, bounded in \(\operatorname{BMO}^{-1}\), and continuous at the common initial datum in \(\dot W^{-1,p}\) for every finite \(p\) in the usual Sobolev range. The proof explicitly treats \(1<p<\infty\); the endpoint \(p=1\) follows by finite-volume inclusion. It claims neither finite-energy Leray–Hopf non-uniqueness nor the corresponding whole-space or two-dimensional results; Remarks 1.5 and 1.7 expressly delimit those questions.

The main construction uses \[M_k\simeq A^{b^k},\qquad N_k\simeq M_k^\gamma,\qquad
 b>5\vee(1-8\alpha)^{-1},\qquad
 (1-4\alpha)^{-1}<\gamma<(4\alpha+b^{-1})^{-1},\] with \(0<\alpha<1/8\) and constants independent of the final large parameter \(A\). The dependence order matters: fixed geometric and regularity parameters are chosen before \(A\). The two principal flows alternate heat-dominated and inverse-cascade-dominated modes, and the perturbations are intended to correct a small residual.

The preserved intake has no recoverable substantive report or core verification files for this paper. Accordingly, this is a necessary initial review of the acquired materials. The report identifies two Major and three Minor findings, with the two local heat assertions grouped in Problem 3. Their number is not a severity criterion. Major means an invalid step in a core derivation, even where an explicit repair is available. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
# Problem 1: support and cutoff assertions in the critical-data construction
## Locations and consequence

Definition 3.1, pp. 14–15; Lemma 3.2(3), p. 15; Lemma 3.3, pp. 15–17; Definition 3.4, p. 17; Proposition 3.7 and (3.17), pp. 19–21; Remark 3.12, p. 23. These assertions feed the amplitude recursion, Proposition 3.8’s \(\operatorname{BMO}\) estimate, and the equality of the two initial traces.
## Decisive discrepancies

Let \(S_{j,k}=\operatorname{supp}\Psi_{j,k}\). It is nonempty and invariant under translations by \((2\pi/M_k)\mathbb Z^3\), since \(N_k/M_k\) is integral. Translates of any one point of \(S_{j,k}\) have covering radius at most \(\sqrt3\pi/M_k\). The literal fixed \(\delta_0\)-neighborhood in Definition 3.1 is therefore all of \(\mathbb T^3\) once \[M_k>\sqrt3\pi/\delta_0.\] The admissible choice of arbitrarily large \(A\) makes this true already at \(k=0\). Both intersections in that definition then equal the torus, whereas Lemma 3.3 at \(k=1\) requires \(|\widetilde\Omega_1|\leq|\mathbb T^3|/2\). This is a direct contradiction. The \(M_k^{-1}\) factor in Lemma 3.2’s separation formula is strong internal evidence for the intended radii \[\rho_k=\delta_0/M_k,\qquad 2\rho_k.\]

Restoring that factor is necessary but insufficient. The bump on p. 16 is one only on the base supports and zero outside their \(\delta_0\)-neighborhood. It cannot majorize the indicator of their \(2\delta_0\)-neighborhood: a point in the intervening annulus has indicator one and bump zero. In addition, the plateau required of \(\chi_k\) is \(\Omega_{k-1}\), not the entire new pipe \(\Omega_{j,k}\) used on p. 20. The choice \(x=x_j\) does not make \(\widetilde\varphi_j(M_kx)=1\).

Equation reference: trace-identity. Most consequentially, the definitions and the Nash identity give exactly \[
 \overline v_k(0)=\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\!\left(\chi_{k+1}^{\,2}\mathcal D\psi_k^0\right).\] The scalar multiple of \(\operatorname{Id}\) disappears under \(\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\). The desired value \(\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}\psi_k^0\) follows if \(\chi_{k+1}=1\) on \(\operatorname{supp}\mathcal D\psi_k^0\). Definition 3.4 does not supply this property after transition regions and convolution have enlarged the support. The first power of \(\chi_{k+1}\) printed on p. 23 is an additional algebraic slip; replacing it by its square does not supply the missing containment.
## An explicit compatible repair

Use the corrected radii and put \(S_m=\bigcup_jS_{j,m}\). Write \[\ell_m=N_{m+1}^{-1/3}N_m^{-2/3}\] for the mollifier support radius. Increase \(A\) so that, for every \(m\), \[\ell_m<\rho_m/4,\qquad
 \sum_{r\geq m+1}\ell_r\leq\rho_m/4,\qquad
 M_{m+1}/M_m\geq4.\] These conditions are compatible with the stated superlacunary scales. For \(k>m\), set \[d_{m,k}=\rho_m2^{-(k-m+2)},\qquad
 a_{m,k}=\rho_m+\sum_{r=m+1}^{k-1}(d_{m,r}+\ell_r).\] Choose \(0\leq h_{m,k}\leq1\), equal to one on the closed \(a_{m,k}\)-neighborhood of \(S_m\) and zero outside the \((a_{m,k}+d_{m,k})\)-neighborhood, with derivatives bounded by \(C_qd_{m,k}^{-q}\). Define \(\chi_k=\prod_{m<k}h_{m,k}\).

The sums of transition widths and later mollifier radii are each at most \(\rho_m/4\). Thus \(\chi_k=1\) on \(\Omega_{k-1}\) and is supported inside \(\widetilde\Omega_{k-1}\). Moreover, \[\sum_{m<k}d_{m,k}^{-1}
 =\frac4{\delta_0}\sum_{m<k}2^{k-m}M_m
 \leq C M_{k-1},
 \qquad
 \|\nabla^q\chi_k\|_\infty\leq C_qM_{k-1}^q.\] Hence the stated derivative scale (3.9) is retained, with constants independent of \(A\).

This choice also accounts for convolution. For every old index \(m<k\), the support of the unmollified \(k\)th potential lies in the \((a_{m,k}+d_{m,k})\)-neighborhood of \(S_m\). After convolution its radius is at most \[a_{m,k}+d_{m,k}+\ell_k=a_{m,k+1}.\] For the new index \(m=k\), its distance from \(S_k\) is at most \(\ell_k<\rho_k\). Consequently \(\chi_{k+1}=1\) on the entire support of \(\psi_k\), including its derivatives, and \(\operatorname{supp}\psi_k\subset\widetilde\Omega_k\). The base step follows from \(\operatorname{supp}\psi_0\subset N_{\ell_0}(S_0)\). Formula [trace-identity] (#trace-identity) now gives the required common initial data.

Finally, the amplitude lower bound can be recovered by choosing a point at the correct scale. Inductively, \(\Omega_{k-1}\) contains a ball of radius \(\rho_{k-1}/2\). A point \(y=(x_j+2\pi z)/M_k\) lies within \(\sqrt3\pi/M_k\) of its center. For large \(A\), the ball of radius \(\rho_k/2\) around \(y\) remains in the old ball and in the new pipe neighborhood. Moving by at most \(\pi/(N_k|\eta_j|)\) in the \(\eta_j\) direction sets the cosine to one, keeps \(\chi_k=1\), and leaves \(\widetilde\varphi_j(M_kx)\geq1/2\). The positive Nash coefficient then gives the needed lower bound for \(I_1\). The mollifier and profile errors are smaller by positive powers of the scale ratios. The same argument at \(k=0\) makes the base upper and lower bounds uniform in \(A\).
## Assessment

Major. The printed construction fails at claims directly used to obtain critical data and equal initial traces. The repair above supplies the missing choices and estimates for this bounded part of the proof; it is more than a typographical replacement. It does not show the final non-uniqueness theorem false. Author adoption is not established. The monotonicity of the actual supports asserted in Remark 1.6 is unnecessary: the corrected nested enclosing sets suffice for smoothness outside their measure-zero intersection.
# Problem 2: the linearized derivative estimate is false uniformly in the scale
## Locations
## An admissible counterexample family

Equation reference: ratio. Fix \[\alpha=\frac1{32},\quad b=6,\quad \gamma=2,\quad
 \kappa=\frac1{16},\quad \epsilon=\frac1{64}.\] All printed restrictions hold. For integers \(L\to\infty\), choose \[A=L^{17},\qquad N_0=L^{34},\qquad
 n=L^{16},\qquad s=L^{-34}=n^{-2(1+\kappa)},\qquad
 t=L^{-32}=n^{-2}.\] Integer scales avoid any rounding issue. Let \(\eta\) be a fixed smooth bump supported in \((1/2,2)\), with \(\eta(1)=1\). Take the symmetric tensor whose only nonzero entries are \[a_{12}(r,x)=a_{21}(r,x)=s^{-1+\alpha}\eta(r/s)\sin(nx_1).\] It has \(\|a\|_Y\leq C\) uniformly in \(L\): the gradient term contributes \(s^{1/2}n^{1+\kappa}=1\). Also \[\mathbb P\operatorname{div}a(s)=s^{-1+\alpha}n\cos(nx_1)e_2.\] For the heat evolution, since \(n^2(t-s)=1-L^{-2}\), the weighted derivative norm is at least \(c\,s^{-1+\alpha}n^{1+\kappa}\). The right side of [false-semigroup] (#false-semigroup) is at most \(C\,s^{-1+\alpha}n^{1+2\kappa\epsilon}\). Their ratio tends to infinity as \[
 n^{\kappa(1-2\epsilon)}=L^{31/32}.\]
## Repair and impact on the fixed point

Major. A false uniform operator bound is used directly in the core perturbation argument. The weaker bound plus the additional parameter restriction repairs this step. No counterexample to the main theorem is claimed. At the time diagonal, arbitrary \(Y\) data give only \(C^\kappa\) initial vector fields; the derivative statement should be made for \(0<s<t\), using smoothing approximation for nonsmooth initial vectors.
# Problem 3: two local heat assertions need corrected scope and scaling
## The zero-gap endpoint, p. 13 after (2.7)

The homogeneous Hölder–Zygmund estimate itself is consistent. The subsequent blanket replacement of an output \(\mathcal C^0\) norm by \(L^\infty\) excludes too few endpoints. For \[f_J(x)=\sum_{j=1}^J2^{-j}\sin(2^jx_1),\qquad t_J=4^{-J},\] dyadic finite overlap gives \(\|f_J\|_{\mathcal C^1}\leq C\), whereas \[\partial_1e^{t_J\Delta}f_J(0)
 =\sum_{j=1}^Je^{-4^{j-J}}\geq J/e.\] Thus the advertised case \(m=1,s_1=0,s_2=1\) cannot have a uniform constant. The examples are smooth and mean zero; \(f_Je_2\) is divergence free and fixed by \(\mathbb P\). This is not the single Leray endpoint already excluded in the text.

Keep (2.7), and require a strictly positive smoothing gap for this general output-\(L^\infty\) replacement, or a summable Besov input at zero gap. Classical valid \(L^\infty\) heat endpoints can be stated separately. The inspected core applications have positive gaps or positive Hölder regularity.
## The pointwise kernel, p. 49, Appendix C.3

At \(t=0\), the inverse transform of \(m_n(\xi)=\pi(\xi/n)\) is \[\check m_n(x)=n^3\check\pi(nx).\] Choose \(x_*\) with \(\check\pi(x_*)\neq0\) and put \(x=x_*/n\). The left side grows as \(n^3\), while the printed bound is uniformly bounded by its minimum with \(1\). A compatible corrected estimate is \[|\check m_n(x)|
 \leq Cn^3\min\!\left\{1,
       \left(\frac{1+n^2t}{n|x|}\right)^{10}\right\}e^{-cn^2t}.\] Integration cancels the spatial factor \(n^3\); the remaining polynomial in \(1+n^2t\) is absorbed by a weaker exponential. This restores the uniform \(L^1\) kernel estimate.

Minor. These are false local assertions with explicit counterexamples. They do not refute Lemma 2.2’s operator bounds or the main construction. The following multiplier argument on p. 50 supplies further counterevidence to any claim that the heat theory itself fails.
# Problem 4: the final time-integral comparison in Proposition 3.13

On pp. 25–26, the quantity denoted \(III\) is \[III=\sum_k\int_{t_1}^{t_2}
          N_k^{1+\beta_1}e^{-N_{k+1}^2r}r^{-1/2}\,dr.\] Page 26 bounds it by a constant times \(t_1^{1/2-(1+\beta_1)/(2b)}\). Fix \(A\) and \(t_2=1\). The \(k=0\) summand has a strictly positive limit as \(t_1\downarrow0\), while the proposed upper bound tends to zero since \(1+\beta_1<b\). Its preceding intermediate bound has a \(k=0\) term proportional to \(t_1^{-1/2}\) and cannot imply the displayed positive power either.
Minor. The displayed comparison is false, but the corrected integral proves exactly the required bound. The slow logarithmic loss used in the linearized argument survives.
# Problem 5: the auxiliary energy bound loses dependence on the initial data

Proposition B.1, p. 44, gives after Grönwall an upper bound \[\|w^0\|_2^2+8\exp\!\left(\|v\|_{L^2_tL^\infty_x}^2\right)\] for the squared energy supremum plus a nonnegative gradient term. The additive allowance cannot control energy growth for a homogeneous linear equation under arbitrary scaling of \(w^0\).

On \([0,1]\times\mathbb T^3\), take \[v=\sin(x_2)e_1,\qquad
 w^0=c e_2,\qquad
 w(t)=c e_2-c(1-e^{-t})\cos(x_2)e_1.\] Both fields are smooth and divergence free. Direct differentiation verifies (B.1), with pressure zero. The span of \(e_2\) and \(\cos(x_2)e_1\) is invariant, so this is also an exact Fourier Galerkin example. At time one, \[\|w(1)\|_2^2-\|w^0\|_2^2
 =\frac{c^2(2\pi)^3}{2}(1-e^{-1})^2,
 \qquad \|v\|_{L^2_tL^\infty_x}^2=1.\] Taking \(c=100\) contradicts the allowance \(8e\) even if spatial volume is normalized; in that convention the gain is approximately \(1997.882\), versus \(21.746\).

A valid bound, with inessential constants, is \[\sup_{t_0\leq t\leq T}\|w(t)\|_2^2
       +\frac12\int_{t_0}^T\|\nabla w\|_2^2
 \leq2\|w^0\|_2^2
       \exp\!\left(8\int_{t_0}^T\|v\|_\infty^2\right).\] This is uniform in the Galerkin cutoff. It restores existence, and its application to a difference supplies uniqueness. One should use an \(L^2\)-orthonormal divergence-free basis complete in the relevant Sobolev space, and correct the factor \(2\) and sign in the later weak and forced-Stokes formulas. Smoothness of \(v\) on each finite interval is sufficient; integrability on the entire half-line is unnecessary.
Minor. The displayed bound is refuted, but a standard energy argument repairs the auxiliary linear existence proof. This does not furnish a counterexample to the final solutions.
# Positive checks, counterevidence and completion of the claimed solution class
## Residual algebra and parameter margins

The residual proof in Section 4.1 was checked through all four contributions. The lower-case \(a_{j,k}\) printed as the leading coefficient of \(\mathcal N_{k,1}\) on p. 28 must be \(A_{j,k}\): both \(\mathcal N_{k,2}\) and \(\overline R_k\) identify that coefficient. With this local correction, the stress decomposition and \(\partial_t\overline R_k+\mathcal N_{k+1,1}=0\) are exact. The error terms have scales \[N_k^{4/3}N_{k+1}^{-1/3},\quad M_k^2/N_k,\quad M_k,\quad N_{k-1},\] all controlled by \(M_k\) under the prescribed restrictions. The mixed products and stationary-phase sums have positive margins. In particular, the available margins include \[\frac{1-\gamma^{-1}-2\kappa}{4}>\alpha,\qquad
 \frac{1-\beta}{4\gamma}-\frac1{4b}>\alpha,\qquad
 \frac{1-\kappa-c_1}{2}-\frac{1-c_1}{2b}>\alpha\] with the paper’s choices of \(\beta,c_1\). A suspected defect in the first residual estimate was withdrawn because a different positive split extracts the needed \(A\)-smallness. The normalization and phase slips in the Fourier coefficients on p. 32 leave the absolute coefficient bounds intact.

The six-vector Nash decomposition in Appendix A was checked exactly for the constant term and each of the six independent symmetric entries. All seven identities pass. The squared coefficients remain positive on the prescribed ball; the anti-divergence identity follows by cancellation in its displayed symbol. The actual use of the stationary-phase lemma has a nonzero integral frequency and the required Hölder range. Its external cited proofs were not independently reproduced.

For Lemmas B.2–B.3, the nonnegative-\(a\) edge case follows by replacing \(a\) with \(a+\delta\) and passing to the limit. The fractional Grönwall exponents sum to one, the beta integral is finite for \(p>2\), and the application at \(p=3\) with positive initial time is consistent. The multiplier periodization, lattice split and Young interpolation in Appendix C have the stated powers once Problem 3’s pointwise scaling is corrected.
## Trace, separation and global continuation

After Problem 1’s support repair, the potential series has \(\|\operatorname{curl}\psi_k^0\|_p\leq C_p2^{-k/p}\) for every finite \(p\geq1\). The two time-dependent trace differences are dominated by these summable bounds; the finite low-frequency contribution is \(O(t^{1/2})\). The heat-part limit on p. 39 must retain its parity index set until the complementary part is added. Formula [trace-identity] (#trace-identity) supplies the necessary equality of each pair of initial modes.

The perturbation trace follows from the heat Duhamel formula and interpolation: the mixed product has \(C^{\alpha/2}\) size \(O(t^{-1+\alpha/4})\), while the quadratic perturbation and residual contribute \(O(t^{-1+3\alpha/4})\). Thus \(\|w(t)\|_{\mathcal C^{-1+\alpha/2}}\lesssim t^{\alpha/4}\to0\). Problem 2’s restricted \(\kappa\) retains the same \(X\) bounds needed here.

At \(t_0=N_0^{-2}\), the lowest principal mode has size at least \(cN_0\), the tails are smaller, and \(\|w^{(i)}(t_0)\|_\infty\leq\epsilon_1N_0^{1-\alpha}\). The displayed separation inequality on p. 40 should therefore have \(\|u^{(1)}(t_0)-u^{(2)}(t_0)\|_\infty\) on its left; the subtracted perturbation terms already give precisely this conclusion. Likewise the final continuation on p. 41 must use \(u^{(i)}(1)=v^{(i)}(1)+w^{(i)}(1)\). The first term is exponentially small, and the second is small in \(C^{1,\kappa}\) and hence in \(H^{1/2}\). The ordinary small-data continuation applies to the full solution.
## Uniform critical bounds require an explicit bridge
The following is a reviewer-supplied completion, conditional on the corrected support and perturbation estimates. It is not represented as an argument written out in Section 5.

For the heat component \(H=\sum v_k\) over its parity class, put \(E_k=\widetilde\Omega_k\). The pointwise bounds and weighted Cauchy–Schwarz imply \[|H(t,x)|^2\leq Ct^{-1/2}
          \sum_kN_ke^{-cN_k^2t}\mathbf1_{E_k}(x).\] For a cube \(Q\) of side \(R\leq1\), integration up to \(R^2\) bounds its local energy by \[C\sum_k\min(1,RN_k)|Q\cap E_k|.\] Let \(q=k(Q)\). For \(k\leq q-2\), the sum is bounded by \(CRN_{q-2}|Q|\leq C|Q|\), since \(\gamma<b\) and \(M_{q-1}<C_0/R\). The index \(q-1\) contributes one bounded term, and \(k\geq q\) is a geometric tail by the corrected local volume estimate. Empty low blocks when \(q=0,1\) cause no problem. This proves the local Carleson bound for \(H\). The inverse-cascade part is bounded by \(Ct^{-(1+\beta_1)/(2b)}\), with \((1+\beta_1)/b<1\), and \(w\) by \(\epsilon_1t^{-1/2+\alpha/2}\), so both have integrable squared \(L^\infty\) norms near zero. Periodicity handles large balls on \([0,1]\); the zero-mean smooth small solution has finite subsequent spacetime energy by the energy identity and Poincaré inequality. The pointwise bound and subsequent small-data decay give the other term in \(X_{KT}\).

The uniform \(\operatorname{BMO}^{-1}\) bound follows from the same cube split applied to the heat potentials and to the tensors \(N_{k+1}^{-2}a_{j,k+1}^2\) with their bounded exponential factors. Their amplitudes are bounded, their derivatives cost \(N_k\), and their supports lie in \(E_k\). The periodic Leray multiplier is bounded on \(\operatorname{BMO}\) modulo constants, and divergence removes the zero mode. Finally \(\mathcal C^{-1+\alpha/2}\) embeds into \(\operatorname{BMO}^{-1}\) by taking a positive-Hölder potential. This proves the required boundedness after the specified repairs; it does not assert norm continuity in \(\operatorname{BMO}^{-1}\) at zero.

The unnormalized introductory heat formula on p. 4 needs the missing spatial-volume factor. The standard definition on p. 12 and the normalized path norm on p. 2 identify the intended space. The author-hosted Koch–Tataru source was inspected: its theorem gives uniqueness of a small solution in its path space, not unrestricted uniqueness among all positive-time smooth solutions [KT]. Periodic comparisons with local \(bmo^{-1}\) also require the zero-mode qualification, satisfied by this construction. These clarifications are not additional Major findings.
# Supporting checks

All 1695 lines of the acquired author `main.tex` were read in the primary session, with a truncated output reread before proceeding. The canonical text and source images were cross-checked. Three pages of the separately acquired Koch–Tataru author PDF were also rendered and viewed. That file bears 26 December 2007 and is not silently identified with the typeset 2001 article.

Their saved checkpoints, actual page observations and hash records identify those roles. Their union of source views supplements the primary inspection. They are not separate independently verified GPT-6/Pro sessions or an acceptance panel. The semigroup counterexample and parameter repair also received a separate bounded countercheck.

Executed reviewer-written checks cover the rational parameter inequalities, seven Nash matrix identities, the semigroup exponent \(31/32\), the repaired exponent \(1/128\), the exact shear residual, and finite evaluations of the endpoint series. The first endpoint diagnostic contained a reviewer-written exponential-sign error; its script and output are retained and superseded by the corrected run. The analytic counterexample uses the correct negative sign throughout. No author code, numerical Navier–Stokes solver or shell escape was executed. Index parsing and hashes are provenance checks, not scientific proofs.

The overall assessment is Major, confined to the two demonstrated core failures and their stated dependencies. The report supplies compatible local repairs and several completion arguments. It does not certify every external theorem, the journal version, or the repaired paper as a whole. No unresolved conjecture is used as confirmed evidence. Repair verification, author adoption and independent acceptance are distinct: only the specified reviewer derivations have been checked.
The acquired source manifest and preserved snapshot trace are retained. The UI account/model observations belong to the external controller; backend verification has not been independently performed.

Mechanical delivery completion requires the actual successful build and inspection of every final report page. Scientific decision remains pending, with `human_reviews=[]`; this is initial review completion, not independent acceptance.

problems.title: Support scales and recursive cutoff containments in critical initial data
problems.source_location: Definition3.1 pp14–15; Lemma3.3 pp15–17; Definition3.4 p17; Proposition3.7 pp19–21; Remark3.12 p23
claim: Support envelopes shrink, amplitude lower bounds hold, and χk+1=1 on mollifiedψk support gives common initial data.
Fixedδ0, arbitrarily largeA, Mk-periodic nonempty supports; exact stated cutoff plateau and convolution radius.
analysis: Definition 3.1, pp. 14–15; Lemma 3.2(3), p. 15; Lemma 3.3, pp. 15–17; Definition 3.4, p. 17; Proposition 3.7 and (3.17), pp. 19–21; Remark 3.12, p. 23. These assertions feed the amplitude recursion, Proposition 3.8’s \(\operatorname{BMO}\) estimate, and the equality of the two initial traces.

Let \(S_{j,k}=\operatorname{supp}\Psi_{j,k}\). It is nonempty and invariant under translations by \((2\pi/M_k)\mathbb Z^3\), since \(N_k/M_k\) is integral. Translates of any one point of \(S_{j,k}\) have covering radius at most \(\sqrt3\pi/M_k\). The literal fixed \(\delta_0\)-neighborhood in Definition 3.1 is therefore all of \(\mathbb T^3\) once \[M_k>\sqrt3\pi/\delta_0.\] The admissible choice of arbitrarily large \(A\) makes this true already at \(k=0\). Both intersections in that definition then equal the torus, whereas Lemma 3.3 at \(k=1\) requires \(|\widetilde\Omega_1|\leq|\mathbb T^3|/2\). This is a direct contradiction. The \(M_k^{-1}\) factor in Lemma 3.2’s separation formula is strong internal evidence for the intended radii \[\rho_k=\delta_0/M_k,\qquad 2\rho_k.\]

Restoring that factor is necessary but insufficient. The bump on p. 16 is one only on the base supports and zero outside their \(\delta_0\)-neighborhood. It cannot majorize the indicator of their \(2\delta_0\)-neighborhood: a point in the intervening annulus has indicator one and bump zero. In addition, the plateau required of \(\chi_k\) is \(\Omega_{k-1}\), not the entire new pipe \(\Omega_{j,k}\) used on p. 20. The choice \(x=x_j\) does not make \(\widetilde\varphi_j(M_kx)=1\).

Equation reference: trace-identity. Most consequentially, the definitions and the Nash identity give exactly \[
 \overline v_k(0)=\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\!\left(\chi_{k+1}^{\,2}\mathcal D\psi_k^0\right).\] The scalar multiple of \(\operatorname{Id}\) disappears under \(\mathbb P\operatorname{div}\). The desired value \(\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}\psi_k^0\) follows if \(\chi_{k+1}=1\) on \(\operatorname{supp}\mathcal D\psi_k^0\). Definition 3.4 does not supply this property after transition regions and convolution have enlarged the support. The first power of \(\chi_{k+1}\) printed on p. 23 is an additional algebraic slip; replacing it by its square does not supply the missing containment.

Use the corrected radii and put \(S_m=\bigcup_jS_{j,m}\). Write \[\ell_m=N_{m+1}^{-1/3}N_m^{-2/3}\] for the mollifier support radius. Increase \(A\) so that, for every \(m\), \[\ell_m<\rho_m/4,\qquad
 \sum_{r\geq m+1}\ell_r\leq\rho_m/4,\qquad
 M_{m+1}/M_m\geq4.\] These conditions are compatible with the stated superlacunary scales. For \(k>m\), set \[d_{m,k}=\rho_m2^{-(k-m+2)},\qquad
 a_{m,k}=\rho_m+\sum_{r=m+1}^{k-1}(d_{m,r}+\ell_r).\] Choose \(0\leq h_{m,k}\leq1\), equal to one on the closed \(a_{m,k}\)-neighborhood of \(S_m\) and zero outside the \((a_{m,k}+d_{m,k})\)-neighborhood, with derivatives bounded by \(C_qd_{m,k}^{-q}\). Define \(\chi_k=\prod_{m<k}h_{m,k}\).

The sums of transition widths and later mollifier radii are each at most \(\rho_m/4\). Thus \(\chi_k=1\) on \(\Omega_{k-1}\) and is supported inside \(\widetilde\Omega_{k-1}\). Moreover, \[\sum_{m<k}d_{m,k}^{-1}
 =\frac4{\delta_0}\sum_{m<k}2^{k-m}M_m
 \leq C M_{k-1},
 \qquad
 \|\nabla^q\chi_k\|_\infty\leq C_qM_{k-1}^q.\] Hence the stated derivative scale (3.9) is retained, with constants independent of \(A\).

This choice also accounts for convolution. For every old index \(m<k\), the support of the unmollified \(k\)th potential lies in the \((a_{m,k}+d_{m,k})\)-neighborhood of \(S_m\). After convolution its radius is at most \[a_{m,k}+d_{m,k}+\ell_k=a_{m,k+1}.\] For the new index \(m=k\), its distance from \(S_k\) is at most \(\ell_k<\rho_k\). Consequently \(\chi_{k+1}=1\) on the entire support of \(\psi_k\), including its derivatives, and \(\operatorname{supp}\psi_k\subset\widetilde\Omega_k\). The base step follows from \(\operatorname{supp}\psi_0\subset N_{\ell_0}(S_0)\). Formula [trace-identity] (#trace-identity) now gives the required common initial data.

Finally, the amplitude lower bound can be recovered by choosing a point at the correct scale. Inductively, \(\Omega_{k-1}\) contains a ball of radius \(\rho_{k-1}/2\). A point \(y=(x_j+2\pi z)/M_k\) lies within \(\sqrt3\pi/M_k\) of its center. For large \(A\), the ball of radius \(\rho_k/2\) around \(y\) remains in the old ball and in the new pipe neighborhood. Moving by at most \(\pi/(N_k|\eta_j|)\) in the \(\eta_j\) direction sets the cosine to one, keeps \(\chi_k=1\), and leaves \(\widetilde\varphi_j(M_kx)\geq1/2\). The positive Nash coefficient then gives the needed lower bound for \(I_1\). The mollifier and profile errors are smaller by positive powers of the scale ratios. The same argument at \(k=0\) makes the base upper and lower bounds uniform in \(A\).

Major. The printed construction fails at claims directly used to obtain critical data and equal initial traces. The repair above supplies the missing choices and estimates for this bounded part of the proof; it is more than a typographical replacement. It does not show the final non-uniqueness theorem false. Author adoption is not established. The monotonicity of the actual supports asserted in Remark 1.6 is unnecessary: the corrected nested enclosing sets suffice for smoothness outside their measure-zero intersection.
result: Result: Literal support-decay claim false and core containments not supplied even after scale correction.
Impact: Directly affects BMO data, amplitude recursion and common trace; not a proof that mainnonuniqueness isfalse.

 w(t)=c e_2-c(1-e^{-t})\cos(x_2)e_1.\] Both fields are smooth and divergence free. Direct differentiation verifies (B.1), with pressure zero. The span of \(e_2\) and \(\cos(x_2)e_1\) is invariant, so this is also an exact Fourier Galerkin example. At time one, \[\|w(1)\|_2^2-\|w^0\|_2^2
 =\frac{c^2(2\pi)^3}{2}(1-e^{-1})^2,
 \qquad \|v\|_{L^2_tL^\infty_x}^2=1.\] Taking \(c=100\) contradicts the allowance \(8e\) even if spatial volume is normalized; in that convention the gain is approximately \(1997.882\), versus \(21.746\).

A valid bound, with inessential constants, is \[\sup_{t_0\leq t\leq T}\|w(t)\|_2^2
       +\frac12\int_{t_0}^T\|\nabla w\|_2^2
 \leq2\|w^0\|_2^2
       \exp\!\left(8\int_{t_0}^T\|v\|_\infty^2\right).\] This is uniform in the Galerkin cutoff. It restores existence, and its application to a difference supplies uniqueness. One should use an \(L^2\)-orthonormal divergence-free basis complete in the relevant Sobolev space, and correct the factor \(2\) and sign in the later weak and forced-Stokes formulas. Smoothness of \(v\) on each finite interval is sufficient; integrability on the entire half-line is unnecessary.

report: Abstract: The acquired publisher version of Koval’s local Birkhoff and spectral uniqueness paper is examined through its geometric preservation functionals, finite-dimensional nondegeneracy, analytic continuation, nonlinear approximation and spectral isolation. Two core derivations require correction. The printed coordinate conventions give a nonzero first-order preservation functional on translated ellipses, and the row scaling uses a basis index where the selected caustic denominator is required. Four further local findings concern exact Fourier coefficients, uniformity of an asymptotic estimate and spectral separation formulas. Concrete repairs and their limits are described. The overall assessment is Major for the identified derivations; no counterexample to the final local uniqueness conclusions is established.

Title: Coordinates, operator scaling and local uniqueness of ellipses
# Identity, version and mathematical scope

This report concerns Local strong Birkhoff conjecture and local spectral uniqueness of almost every ellipse, by Illya Koval, identifier M25-0130, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01397-y [K]. The canonical input is the acquired 78-page publisher PDF, printed pp. 221–298. Its title page gives publication on 11 December 2025. Its SHA256 is

All page citations below use these printed numbers; the physical PDF page is the printed number minus 220. The accompanying arXiv:2111.12171v2 source has a different title, using rigidity. It is retained as historical source material and is not equated with the publisher text.

Definitions 1.1–1.3, pp. 223–224, concern smooth convex rational caustics whose invariant curves consist of periodic points. Theorem 1 is local near a noncircular, nondegenerate ellipse, assumes a bounded \(C^k\) norm with \(k\geq39\) and small \(C^1\) distance, and excludes a locally finite eccentricity set. Theorem 2 additionally assumes \(C^\infty\) smoothness and small \(C^{10}\) distance, and excludes a small set whose accumulation set is locally finite. The spectral discussion concerns Dirichlet or Neumann conditions, as specified in Section 8.1. These statements do not assert an unconditional global Birkhoff theorem or global Laplace uniqueness.

Cutoffs, bounds and neighborhoods may depend on the fixed ellipse, the regularity bound and the caustic cutoff. They are not uniform as eccentricity approaches \(1\) or an exceptional value. A larger rational-integrability cutoff imposes a weaker requirement and can be chosen when only near-boundary caustics are needed. The degenerate circular limit used in the rescaling argument is not itself an assertion of invertibility at \(e=0\).

The preserved snapshot and current intake contain no recoverable substantive report or core scientific verification for this paper. This report is therefore a necessary initial review. Two Major and four Minor findings are reported. Major denotes an invalid step in a core derivation; a concrete repair does not require the whole theorem to be false. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
# Problem 1: incompatible coordinate origins invalidate the printed preservation functional
## Locations
Equations (2.1), (2.4) and (2.7)–(2.8), pp. 237–238; the weights in (5.24) and (5.27), pp. 260–261; the vanishing assertion (6.34), p. 269; (6.46), p. 272; Proposition 7.1 and (7.1), p. 273.
## A geometric discrepancy

Write the ellipse as \[r(\phi)=(a\cos\phi,b\sin\phi),\qquad
 c^2=a^2-b^2,\qquad e=c/a.\] With \(a=1\), its speed is \(v(\phi)=\sqrt{1-e^2\cos^2\phi}\) and its curvature radius is \(v(\phi)^3/b\). Thus the Lazutkin density defined by (2.8) is proportional to \[(1-e^2\cos^2\phi)^{-1/2}.\] The limit \(\lambda=0\) of the printed (2.7), under the definition of \(F\) in (2.4), instead has density proportional to \((1-e^2\sin^2\phi)^{-1/2}\). The ratios of the densities at \(0\) and \(\pi/2\) are \(1/b\) and \(b\), respectively. An additive origin or scalar normalization of the same printed formula cannot reconcile them for \(e>0\).
## A genuine integrable deformation contradicts (7.1)

Equation reference: translation, wrong-pairing. Translate the ellipse by \((t,0)\) and express its boundary in the original elliptic coordinates. Since \[r_\mu=(b\cos\phi,a\sin\phi),\qquad
 r_\phi=(-a\sin\phi,b\cos\phi),\qquad r_\mu\cdot r_\phi=0,\] the deformation has the expansion \[
 \mu_t(\phi)
 =t\,\frac{b\cos\phi}{a^2-c^2\cos^2\phi}+O_{C^{39}}(t^2).\] For \(a=1\), put \(H(\phi)=\cos\phi/(1-e^2\cos^2\phi)\). The printed functional for \(p/q=1/3\) is \[c^\phi_{1,3}(\phi)=\theta'(\phi)\cos(3\theta(\phi)),
 \qquad
 \theta(\phi)=\frac{\pi F(\phi,k)}{2K(k)}.\] The small-modulus expansion and the rotation relation give \[\theta=\phi-\frac{k^2}{8}\sin2\phi+O(k^4),
 \qquad k^2=4e^2+O(e^4).\] Consequently \[c^\phi_{1,3}
 =\cos3\phi+\frac{k^2}{16}\cos\phi
              -\frac{5k^2}{16}\cos5\phi+O(k^4),\] and direct integration yields \[
 \int_0^{2\pi}H(\phi)c^\phi_{1,3}(\phi)\,d\phi
 =\frac{\pi e^2}{2}+O(e^4)\neq0\] for sufficiently small fixed positive \(e\). The two order-\(e^2\) contributions are each \(\pi e^2/4\).

Every translated ellipse retains every rational elliptic caustic. Nevertheless, [translation] (#translation) and [wrong-pairing] (#wrong-pairing) make the left side of (7.1) equal to a nonzero constant times \(t+O(t^2)\), while the asserted right side is \(O_e(t^2)\). Its size restriction \(3<c(e)\|\mu_t\|_{C^1}^{-1/8}\) holds for all sufficiently small nonzero \(t\). The \(C^5\) norms remain bounded. This is an admissible counterexample to the printed preservation estimate, not a deformation that loses integrability.

The exact coefficient calculation was checked independently by the primary reviewer and the analytic auxiliary. Numerical evaluations at \(e=.01,.02,.05\) give the normalized pairing divided by \(\pi e^2\) approximately \(.500062504\), \(.500250060\), and \(.501564844\). They illustrate the Taylor argument; they are not interval-certified proofs.
## A coherent repair and its boundary

Equation reference: correct-angle. Keeping the physical parametrization (2.1), use \[
 \Theta(\phi)=\frac{\pi}{2K(k)}
 \bigl(F(\phi+\pi/2,k)-K(k)\bigr).\] This is the correct action-angle origin, not merely a correction at zero rotation. One can verify it with the Jacobi addition identities [DLMF]. For \[R(u)=(a\operatorname{sn}u,b\operatorname{cn}u),\qquad
 \operatorname{sn}v=\lambda/b,\qquad k^2=c^2/(a^2-\lambda^2),\] the chord through \(R(u-v)\) and \(R(u+v)\) lies on \[\frac{\operatorname{sn}u\,\operatorname{dn}v}{a}\,x+\frac{\operatorname{cn}u}{b}\,y=\operatorname{cn}v .\] The support condition for the confocal caustic reduces to \[\left(1-\frac{\lambda^2}{a^2}\right)\operatorname{sn}^2u\,\operatorname{dn}^2v+
 \left(1-\frac{\lambda^2}{b^2}\right)\operatorname{cn}^2u=\operatorname{cn}^2v .\] Using the stated relations verifies this identity. The incoming and outgoing tangent chords obey the reflection law. Thus the orbit advances by \(2v\) in \(u\), with rotation number \(v/(2K)\), and [correct-angle] (#correct-angle) follows after the fixed reflection and origin change.

There is also an exact geometric check of the restored infinitesimal functional. At a vertex on a caustic-tangent orbit, the normal component of the incoming minus outgoing unit vectors is \(2\lambda/\sqrt{a^2-c^2\cos^2\phi}\), while the elliptic radial vector has the corresponding length \(\sqrt{a^2-c^2\cos^2\phi}\). Thus the first variation of the polygon perimeter is \[\delta L=2\lambda\sum_\ell\mu(\phi_\ell).\] A translation changes no perimeter, so its tangent vector has zero sum on every such periodic orbit. Fourier decomposition in the corrected angle gives exact annihilation of the infinitesimal translation by both preservation functionals. Finite deformation graphs still have quadratic remainders; this calculation does not independently prove the full uniform \(q^8\) estimate.

All weights must be changed together. In physical coordinates the motion weights have the form \[H_i(\phi)=\frac{e_i(\phi)}{1-e^2\cos^2\phi},
 \qquad
 J_{\mathrm{corr}}=\frac{2K(e)}{\pi}
                   \sqrt{1-e^2\cos^2\phi},
 \qquad h_i^{\mathrm{corr}}=J_{\mathrm{corr}}H_i .\] In \(\psi=\phi+\pi/2\), their denominator becomes \(1-e^2\sin^2\psi\) and their five numerators are a signed permutation of \(1,\cos\psi,\sin\psi,\cos2\psi,\sin2\psi\). Each paired harmonic and each paired preservation functional undergoes an invertible two-dimensional change of basis. The finite nondegeneracy argument therefore survives this coordinated change. The opposite signs in the corrected Taylor expansion cancel [wrong-pairing] (#wrong-pairing), as independently checked.

This does not show that the originally mixed operator is already conjugate to the corrected operator. Its weights, Jacobians, elliptic-motion subspace and exact preservation formulas require consistent revision. Severity: Major, because the printed core functional fails on actual translated ellipses. The evidence supports a repair of the coordinate conventions; it does not refute local rigidity.
# Problem 2: row-slot scaling does not produce the claimed invertible limit
## Locations and distinction of indices
Lemma 4.1 and the scalings (4.1), (4.33), pp. 245–246 and 252; definition (6.11), p. 264; Lemma 6.8, especially (6.26), p. 268, (6.31), p. 269, and the limit (6.36), p. 270.

A row of the preservation operator is attached to a selected caustic denominator \(q_n\). Its slot in the paired Fourier enumeration is \(n\), whose nominal frequency is \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\). These numbers need not agree: the construction omits low denominators and uses several numerators for some denominators. The finite-dimensional rescaling requires the eccentricity factor \[e^{j-q_n}\] in the entry for column frequency \(j\). The left and right factors printed in (6.26) instead combine to \[e^{q_1-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\,e^{j-q_1}
 =e^{j-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}.\] The other prefactors, which depend on the actual caustic and parity, are finite and nonzero at \(e=0\); they do not remove this discrepancy.
## A zero-row obstruction

Choose the allowed cutoff \(q_0=3\). Lemma 4.1 uses \(p_n/q_n<1/3\), so every selected denominator satisfies \(q_n>3\). For the first nonelliptic row, \(n=6\), the printed scaling gives \[e^{j-3} A_{p_6,q_6,j}(e)
 =O\!\left(e^{\,j-3+|q_6-j|}\right)
 \longrightarrow0,\qquad 3\leq j\leq q_1 .\] Opposite-parity entries vanish identically. For \(j\leq q_6\) the displayed exponent is \(q_6-3>0\); for \(j>q_6\) it is even larger. The entire finite row tends to zero. Hence it cannot tend to the corresponding row of the invertible matrix \(\widehat A\) asserted in (6.36). This obstruction remains after the coordinate correction in Problem 1. Relabelling the rows cannot assign a nonexistent selected denominator \(3\) to this slot.
## Repair and effect on the tail estimates

For each nonelliptic row replace its left eccentricity factor by \[(S^\ell)_n=C_n e^{q_1-q_n},
 \qquad
 (S^r)_i=D_i e^{j_i-q_1},\] retaining the parity-dependent nonzero constants from (4.1) or (4.33). Then the product is the required \(e^{j_i-q_n}\). Since \(q_n\leq q_1\), the corrected left exponents remain nonnegative. The finite-to-high-frequency block \(C\) still tends to zero: each selected functional tends to a harmonic of frequency at most \(q_1\), and the corrected factor is bounded. The high-to-finite block \(B\) is unaffected, because its rows have left factor one. Its bound in (6.43)–(6.44) remains a convergent geometric tail for sufficiently small \(e\). The \(D-\operatorname{Id}\) estimate follows from the square-summable \(j^{-1}\) errors.

There is a separate harmless normalization in the limiting motion block. With the usual normalized constant mode \(e_1=1/\sqrt{2\pi}\) and printed \(h_1(0)=1\), its first entry is \(\sqrt2\), not \(1\). Normalize that mode consistently or use \(\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt2,1,1,1,1)\) instead of the first identity block. Both are invertible.

Severity: Major. The stated invertible limit is the nondegeneracy input for analytic continuation and the nonlinear theorem. The literal scaling does not establish it. Correcting the actual row denominator restores the intended mechanism, subject to the other coordinated corrections; the final conclusion is not disproved.
# Problem 3: the exact sine and cosine coefficients differ

Thus Lemmas 3.1–3.2 retain the same leading asymptotic separately in the two branches. The universal leading coefficient also follows directly from \[\exp\!\left(\sigma j\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{z^n}{n}\right)
