# Problem 4: the uniform coefficient bound needs a rotation ceiling
## Locations and quantifier
Theorem 4 and (1.6), p. 228; the use of \(k_{p/q}<k_{1/3}\) on p. 245.

Specify \(p/q\leq\omega_{\max}<1/2\) and let both \(C\) and the small-eccentricity threshold depend on \(\omega_{\max}\). Then \(k_{p/q}\leq k_{\omega_{\max}}=O_{\omega_{\max}}(e)\) supplies the required uniformity. The printed \(k_{1/3}\) comparison is valid only for rotations at most \(1/3\). If dependence on \(p/q\) was intended by the phrase some constant, it must be made explicit; that interpretation does not supply an absolute uniform bound.
Severity: Minor. The main construction can increase its cutoff and retain a fixed rotation ceiling. In particular, the infinite \(p=1\) tail in Problem 2 has the required uniform estimate.
# Problem 5: the lower spectral separation bound is false
## Locations
Equation (8.52), p. 285, and its use to rule out perimeter multiples in Section 8.7, pp. 289–290.

The printed assertion is \[t_{p,q}(\Omega)\geq\frac{2p-1}{p}\,\ell(\Omega).\] For \(p=1\) it requires a finite inscribed polygon to have length at least the perimeter. In a smooth strictly convex domain, every chord is strictly shorter than its corresponding boundary arc. Summing around a one-winding polygon gives \(T_{1,q}<\ell\). An ellipse has such rational caustics for arbitrarily large \(q\), so no choice of \(q_0\) remedies this contradiction.

Equation reference: separation. The required replacement is \[
 (p-\tfrac12)\ell<t_{p,q}\leq T_{p,q}<p\ell.\] The upper bound is the chord–arc comparison already used in Lemma 8.6. For the finitely bounded numerators \(p\leq7\), (8.33), bounded \(c_{2,p}\) and a positive lower bound on \(\ell\) give the lower bound after increasing \(q_0\). This excludes all integer perimeter multiples, including the intermediate multiples that the printed expression would not exclude when \(p\geq3\).

Independent evaluations at \(e=1/2\), \(p=1\), \(q=4,10,50,100\) give perimeter deficits about \(.578346\), \(.095296\), \(.003832\), \(.000958\). These are diagnostic illustrations, not the proof of [separation] (#separation). Severity: Minor; the corrected bound supplies the local spectral separation actually needed.
# Problem 6: normalization in the identification of the spectral coefficient
## Locations and correction
Lemma 8.12 and (8.59)–(8.61), pp. 288–289; the prior common-coefficient assumption (8.54), p. 286.

Put \(c_0=c_{2,1}(\mathcal E)\) and \(c=c_{2,1}(\Omega)\). The printed \(g(\ell-x)=c_0^{-1/2}x^{-1/2}\) sends \(\ell-c_0/q^2\) to \(q/c_0\), whereas (8.60) requires \(q\). The corrected formula and deformed center are \[g(\ell-x)=\sqrt{c_0}\,x^{-1/2},
 \qquad
 g(\ell-c/q^2)\sim\lambda q,\qquad
 \lambda=\sqrt{c_0/c}.\] The ratio in (8.61) must therefore also be inverted.
## A noncircular interval argument

The reference to (8.56) should explicitly mean an interval construction using each domain’s own coefficient. A literal invocation of the already common-coefficient intervals would presuppose the conclusion. The author’s instruction to follow the preceding ideas, and the separate coefficients in (8.61), provide evidence for the intended valid reading. A possible stronger circularity allegation was therefore withdrawn.

First exclude all \(p>1\) lengths from a neighborhood of the common perimeter, using non-incidence, fixed-type continuity, the large-\(p\) estimate and bounded-\(p\) asymptotics. For Laplace-isospectral domains the perimeter is a heat invariant. If only equality of the relevant singular-support germs is assumed, its unique nearby accumulation point supplies the same identification.

Equality of singular supports matches that endpoint to an ellipse length indexed by an integer \(n(q)\). Even using the weaker remainder from (8.55), rather than the \(O(q^{-4})\) displayed in (8.33), one obtains \[|n(q)-\lambda q|\leq C\varepsilon+C'/q .\] Choose \(\varepsilon\) so that \(|\lambda-1|<1/10\) and, for all sufficiently large \(q\), the right side is below \(\eta<1/5\). Then \[|n(q+1)-n(q)-1|<2\eta+1/10<1/2 .\] Every integer gap is exactly one. Thus \(n(q)=q+d\) on the entire tail, and division by \(q\) gives \(\lambda=1\). The argument needs every sufficiently large integer \(q\), not an unspecified subsequence.
Severity: Minor. Correct the two reciprocal factors and state the own-coefficient construction. The coefficient-identification conclusion survives this explicit repair.
# Positive checks, boundary cases and proof dependencies
## Finite algebra and analytic continuation

The odd and even finite-rank mechanisms were checked independently of the erroneous operator scaling. For a new prime \(Q\), the preceding denominators give a cyclotomic field of conductor coprime to \(Q\). The real \(Q\)th-root cosine has degree \((Q-1)/2\) over that field: a smaller degree, followed by adjoining its imaginary partner, would contradict the degree of the compositum. Conjugating vanishing minors and retaining the requisite rank lower bound justifies the kernel argument. The numerator ratios form the required subgroup; a primitive root makes it the whole group.

The even-mode terminal determinant has powers \(1,\ldots,Q-1\). Removing the nonzero factor \(1+\cos(\pi p/Q)\) from each row gives an ordinary Vandermonde on distinct nodes. Five exact determinant calibrations were performed; positivity and distinctness, not those finite examples, justify the general conclusion. The noncoprime rows are higher-harmonic conditions on the same rational caustic and are legitimate.

The primitive-root input is Heath-Brown’s cited theorem for three distinct prime bases, not the full Artin conjecture [HB]. Its bibliographic identity was verified. The complete original proof was not available in this review and is not claimed to have been rechecked. No recent claimed resolution of Artin’s conjecture is used.

The analytic construction has the correct functional-analytic structure after the preceding corrections: a square-summable \(j^{-1}\) Fourier error gives a Hilbert–Schmidt perturbation, bounded holomorphic matrix elements give a holomorphic operator family, and analytic Fredholm theory yields locally finite singular points once one nonsingular eccentricity is established. Finiteness on an entire selected strip requires working in a compactly contained smaller strip, not merely invoking local discreteness. The notation for \(G_e\) in (5.3), p. 255, uses \(1-e_{\max}\) where the figure and subsequent argument use \(e_{\max}\); the neighborhood must contain the intended real interval consistently.

The resulting basis is a Riesz basis because its synthesis map is bounded and invertible. Hence the analysis inequality (7.8) is valid even though the functions are not orthogonal. No orthogonality of the complete basis is needed.
## The nonlinear exponent

Let \(\delta=\|\mu\|_{C^1}\) and take \(J=\delta^{-1/9}\). Once the corrected preservation functionals annihilate the elliptic tangent subspace, the low-frequency squared contribution is \[C\delta^4\sum_{j\leq J}j^{16}
 =O(\delta^{19/9}),\] while the high-frequency contribution is \(C\delta^2\sum_{j>J}j^{-2}=O(\delta^{19/9})\). The finite exceptional list of denominators is absorbed by making \(\delta\) smaller. The condition in Proposition 7.1 holds because \(\delta^{-1/9}=o(\delta^{-1/8})\). Thus \(\|\mu^\perp\|_{L^2}\leq C\delta^{19/18}\). Interpolation between \(L^2\) and the bounded \(H^{39}\) norm, followed by \(H^2\hookrightarrow C^1\) in one dimension, gives \[\frac{19}{18}\frac{37}{39}=\frac{703}{702}>1 .\] The claimed improvement exponent is therefore consistent. Local boundedness of the inverse away from the exceptional set permits the nearby-ellipse argument. This verifies the quantitative step; it does not remove the need to correct Problems 1 and 2 first.
## Hyperbolic onset and the exceptional set

Holomorphy only away from the onset of a hyperbolic orbit family would not alone exclude zeros accumulating at that onset. A completion of the argument in Lemma 5.9 and Section 8.7 is available. Put \[e_0=\cos(\pi\widetilde\omega),\qquad
 m=k^{-2},\qquad
 \phi(m,e)=\arcsin\frac{\sqrt{1-e^2}}{\sqrt{1-e^2m}},\] and \(W(m,e)=F(\phi(m,e)\mid m)/(2K(m))\), where the vertical bar denotes the elliptic parameter convention. Near \((0,e_0)\) these functions are analytic and \[W(0,e)=\frac{\arccos e}{\pi},\qquad
 W_m(0,e)=\frac{e\sqrt{1-e^2}}{4\pi}>0 .\] The analytic implicit-function theorem gives \(m(e)\) across the onset. Although \(\sqrt m\) has a branch there, the integrals in (2.16) depend analytically on \(m\); the length therefore extends. This supplies the endpoint control needed for isolated incidence zeros. The inconsistent lower-bound notation in (5.31) should use the onset \(\cos(\pi\widetilde\omega)\).
## Spectral visibility and conditional global uniqueness

The spectral proof partitions competing orbits into large winding, bounded winding with large period, and finitely many remaining types. The KAM barriers supply the needed exclusion of grazing for each fixed type. Nonprimitive periods are explicitly handled in the normal-form calculation. The \(C^{10}\) input in Lemma 8.1 supports \(C^9\) closeness of the billiard map; the intervening \(C^{11}\) claim for its generating function should be \(C^{10}\). The inverse-coordinate estimate concerns its difference from the identity, and the perimeter normalizer is \(1+O(\varepsilon)\).

Appendix B’s final no-cancellation argument is sound under its stated smooth loop parametrix and positive principal symbol. In the nondegenerate case, after the common Maslov factor is removed, the summands have positive amplitudes times \(\exp(\pm i\pi/4)\), so their real parts cannot cancel. In the degenerate case, smoothness would force the oscillatory integral to be \(O(\lambda^{-1})\), contradicting the stated weighted \(L^2\) obstruction for an exponent below \(1/2\). The complete external KAM, normal-form and microlocal theorems were not rederived from first principles; their uses and boundaries, rather than an independent certification of those works, were examined.

Proposition A.1, pp. 292–293, is expressly conditional on the stated strong global Birkhoff conjecture. Its argument compares a superpolynomial splitting of two endpoint lengths with the ellipse’s adjacent \(q^{-3}\) spacing near a perimeter multiple. After both domains are known to be ellipses, equality of the two tail sets identifies the \(q^{-2}\) coefficient: matching indices have the form \(n(q)=\lambda q+O(q^{-1})\). Consecutive integer gaps make \(\lambda\) an integer, and reverse matching makes its reciprocal an integer. Hence \(\lambda=1\). No conjectural premise has been promoted to a theorem.

The last identification of ellipses by their first and third beta coefficients is supported by Proposition 1 of Sorrentino’s explicitly retrieved arXiv version [S]. Its statement and proof on p. 28, and the rational-caustic criterion on p. 8, were actually inspected. For completeness, set \(r=E(\sqrt m)/K(\sqrt m)\). The derivative sign of \((1-m)K(\sqrt m)^3/E(\sqrt m)\) is the sign of \[P(r)=3r^2-(4-2m)r+1-m .\] The weighted-mean formula gives \(1-m<r<1-m/2\). The convex quadratic is negative at both endpoints: \(P(1-m)=-m(1-m)\) and \(P(1-m/2)=-m^2/4\). This verifies strict monotonicity, hence uniqueness of eccentricity and then scale.
## Scope clarifications

Theorem 3, p. 226, introduces an exceptional set but omits the condition \(e\notin\mathcal Z\). The paper’s own near-perimeter route should state this restriction or explicitly explain an alternative all-eccentricity argument. Appendix A attributes an all-ellipse local full-length-spectrum result to its reference [18]; this report does not turn the omission into a counterexample at an exceptional eccentricity. Full length-spectrum information and only its germ near perimeter multiples must be distinguished.

Theorem 5 assumes beta equality on an open interval. To apply a definition that includes its right endpoint, take a strictly larger cutoff and the corresponding exceptional set. Sign conventions for beta do not affect equality or the caustic criterion, but should be consistent. Theorem 5 remains local and Proposition A.1 remains conditional.
# Supporting checks

The canonical input, its complete source manifest and the preserved snapshot inventory were parsed and actually rehashed. Forty-two materialized inputs for this paper matched their bindings. That intake establishes identity, not scientific correctness. Existing acquired materials were reused; no earlier substantive scientific report was replaced.

The primary session read the main statements, the operator and nonlinear arguments, the decisive spectral formulas and both appendices, and integrated the bounded native reviews of Sections 2–4, Sections 5–7, and Section 8 with Appendix B. Thirty-four selected canonical evidence pages were actually displayed in the primary session. A fourth bounded check by the same algebra auxiliary tested the translated-ellipse objection and the exact coordinated action-angle repair. These are native contributions to an initial review, not independent acceptance or human review.

Reviewer-authored exact computations checked the Fourier convolution, determinant factors, translation pairing, interpolation exponent, interval-separation polynomial and invariant-ratio algebra. Numerical elliptic-integral evaluations are labelled diagnostic. problems.title: Incompatible angular origins invalidate the preservation functional
claim: Elliptic tangent weights annihilate printed caustic-preservation functionals and caustic-preserving graphs obey a quadratic bound.
Fixed sufficiently small positive e, a1, x-translation t->0, p1q3; all caustics remain, bounded C5/C39 norms and stated smallness threshold.
analysis: Equations (2.1), (2.4) and (2.7)–(2.8), pp. 237–238; the weights in (5.24) and (5.27), pp. 260–261; the vanishing assertion (6.34), p. 269; (6.46), p. 272; Proposition 7.1 and (7.1), p. 273.

Write the ellipse as \[r(\phi)=(a\cos\phi,b\sin\phi),\qquad
 c^2=a^2-b^2,\qquad e=c/a.\] With \(a=1\), its speed is \(v(\phi)=\sqrt{1-e^2\cos^2\phi}\) and its curvature radius is \(v(\phi)^3/b\). Thus the Lazutkin density defined by (2.8) is proportional to \[(1-e^2\cos^2\phi)^{-1/2}.\] The limit \(\lambda=0\) of the printed (2.7), under the definition of \(F\) in (2.4), instead has density proportional to \((1-e^2\sin^2\phi)^{-1/2}\). The ratios of the densities at \(0\) and \(\pi/2\) are \(1/b\) and \(b\), respectively. An additive origin or scalar normalization of the same printed formula cannot reconcile them for \(e>0\).

Equation reference: translation, wrong-pairing. Translate the ellipse by \((t,0)\) and express its boundary in the original elliptic coordinates. Since \[r_\mu=(b\cos\phi,a\sin\phi),\qquad
 r_\phi=(-a\sin\phi,b\cos\phi),\qquad r_\mu\cdot r_\phi=0,\] the deformation has the expansion \[
 \mu_t(\phi)
 =t\,\frac{b\cos\phi}{a^2-c^2\cos^2\phi}+O_{C^{39}}(t^2).\] For \(a=1\), put \(H(\phi)=\cos\phi/(1-e^2\cos^2\phi)\). The printed functional for \(p/q=1/3\) is \[c^\phi_{1,3}(\phi)=\theta'(\phi)\cos(3\theta(\phi)),
 \qquad
 \theta(\phi)=\frac{\pi F(\phi,k)}{2K(k)}.\] The small-modulus expansion and the rotation relation give \[\theta=\phi-\frac{k^2}{8}\sin2\phi+O(k^4),
 \qquad k^2=4e^2+O(e^4).\] Consequently \[c^\phi_{1,3}
 =\cos3\phi+\frac{k^2}{16}\cos\phi
              -\frac{5k^2}{16}\cos5\phi+O(k^4),\] and direct integration yields \[
 \int_0^{2\pi}H(\phi)c^\phi_{1,3}(\phi)\,d\phi
 =\frac{\pi e^2}{2}+O(e^4)\neq0\] for sufficiently small fixed positive \(e\). The two order-\(e^2\) contributions are each \(\pi e^2/4\).

Every translated ellipse retains every rational elliptic caustic. Nevertheless, [translation] (#translation) and [wrong-pairing] (#wrong-pairing) make the left side of (7.1) equal to a nonzero constant times \(t+O(t^2)\), while the asserted right side is \(O_e(t^2)\). Its size restriction \(3<c(e)\|\mu_t\|_{C^1}^{-1/8}\) holds for all sufficiently small nonzero \(t\). The \(C^5\) norms remain bounded. This is an admissible counterexample to the printed preservation estimate, not a deformation that loses integrability.

The exact coefficient calculation was checked independently by the primary reviewer and the analytic auxiliary. Numerical evaluations at \(e=.01,.02,.05\) give the normalized pairing divided by \(\pi e^2\) approximately \(.500062504\), \(.500250060\), and \(.501564844\). They illustrate the Taylor argument; they are not interval-certified proofs.

Equation reference: correct-angle. Keeping the physical parametrization (2.1), use \[
 \Theta(\phi)=\frac{\pi}{2K(k)}
 \bigl(F(\phi+\pi/2,k)-K(k)\bigr).\] This is the correct action-angle origin, not merely a correction at zero rotation. One can verify it with the Jacobi addition identities [DLMF]. For \[R(u)=(a\operatorname{sn}u,b\operatorname{cn}u),\qquad
 \operatorname{sn}v=\lambda/b,\qquad k^2=c^2/(a^2-\lambda^2),\] the chord through \(R(u-v)\) and \(R(u+v)\) lies on \[\frac{\operatorname{sn}u\,\operatorname{dn}v}{a}\,x+\frac{\operatorname{cn}u}{b}\,y=\operatorname{cn}v .\] The support condition for the confocal caustic reduces to \[\left(1-\frac{\lambda^2}{a^2}\right)\operatorname{sn}^2u\,\operatorname{dn}^2v+
 \left(1-\frac{\lambda^2}{b^2}\right)\operatorname{cn}^2u=\operatorname{cn}^2v .\] Using the stated relations verifies this identity. The incoming and outgoing tangent chords obey the reflection law. Thus the orbit advances by \(2v\) in \(u\), with rotation number \(v/(2K)\), and [correct-angle] (#correct-angle) follows after the fixed reflection and origin change.

There is also an exact geometric check of the restored infinitesimal functional. At a vertex on a caustic-tangent orbit, the normal component of the incoming minus outgoing unit vectors is \(2\lambda/\sqrt{a^2-c^2\cos^2\phi}\), while the elliptic radial vector has the corresponding length \(\sqrt{a^2-c^2\cos^2\phi}\). Thus the first variation of the polygon perimeter is \[\delta L=2\lambda\sum_\ell\mu(\phi_\ell).\] A translation changes no perimeter, so its tangent vector has zero sum on every such periodic orbit. Fourier decomposition in the corrected angle gives exact annihilation of the infinitesimal translation by both preservation functionals. Finite deformation graphs still have quadratic remainders; this calculation does not independently prove the full uniform \(q^8\) estimate.

All weights must be changed together. In physical coordinates the motion weights have the form \[H_i(\phi)=\frac{e_i(\phi)}{1-e^2\cos^2\phi},
 \qquad
 J_{\mathrm{corr}}=\frac{2K(e)}{\pi}
                   \sqrt{1-e^2\cos^2\phi},
 \qquad h_i^{\mathrm{corr}}=J_{\mathrm{corr}}H_i .\] In \(\psi=\phi+\pi/2\), their denominator becomes \(1-e^2\sin^2\psi\) and their five numerators are a signed permutation of \(1,\cos\psi,\sin\psi,\cos2\psi,\sin2\psi\). Each paired harmonic and each paired preservation functional undergoes an invertible two-dimensional change of basis. The finite nondegeneracy argument therefore survives this coordinated change. The opposite signs in the corrected Taylor expansion cancel [wrong-pairing] (#wrong-pairing), as independently checked.

This does not show that the originally mixed operator is already conjugate to the corrected operator. Its weights, Jacobians, elliptic-motion subspace and exact preservation formulas require consistent revision. Severity: Major, because the printed core functional fails on actual translated ellipses. The evidence supports a repair of the coordinate conventions; it does not refute local rigidity.
result: Result: Nonzero term linear in t contradicts printed O(t²) preservation estimate.
Impact: Core linearization and projection transfer fail as printed; no counterexample to final local rigidity theorem.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use quarter-period-corrected F, physical cos-squared motion weights and corresponding Jcorr, both Fourier sectors; exact first variation restores tangent annihilation. Quantitative uniform q8 theorem must be carried through consistently.

problems.title: Row-slot index is incorrectly used in finite operator scaling
claim: Scaled operator tends to a block matrix with invertible finite Ahat.
Allowed q0=3; selected positive rational rotations strictly below1/3; finite row n6 and all column frequencies3..q1.
analysis: Lemma 4.1 and the scalings (4.1), (4.33), pp. 245–246 and 252; definition (6.11), p. 264; Lemma 6.8, especially (6.26), p. 268, (6.31), p. 269, and the limit (6.36), p. 270.

A row of the preservation operator is attached to a selected caustic denominator \(q_n\). Its slot in the paired Fourier enumeration is \(n\), whose nominal frequency is \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\). These numbers need not agree: the construction omits low denominators and uses several numerators for some denominators. The finite-dimensional rescaling requires the eccentricity factor \[e^{j-q_n}\] in the entry for column frequency \(j\). The left and right factors printed in (6.26) instead combine to \[e^{q_1-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\,e^{j-q_1}
 =e^{j-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}.\] The other prefactors, which depend on the actual caustic and parity, are finite and nonzero at \(e=0\); they do not remove this discrepancy.

Choose the allowed cutoff \(q_0=3\). Lemma 4.1 uses \(p_n/q_n<1/3\), so every selected denominator satisfies \(q_n>3\). For the first nonelliptic row, \(n=6\), the printed scaling gives \[e^{j-3} A_{p_6,q_6,j}(e)
 =O\!\left(e^{\,j-3+|q_6-j|}\right)
 \longrightarrow0,\qquad 3\leq j\leq q_1 .\] Opposite-parity entries vanish identically. For \(j\leq q_6\) the displayed exponent is \(q_6-3>0\); for \(j>q_6\) it is even larger. The entire finite row tends to zero. Hence it cannot tend to the corresponding row of the invertible matrix \(\widehat A\) asserted in (6.36). This obstruction remains after the coordinate correction in Problem 1. Relabelling the rows cannot assign a nonexistent selected denominator \(3\) to this slot.
result: Result: Entire finite row is zero in the claimed limit, independently of coordinate defect.
Impact: Invalidates stated near-circle invertibility input to analytic Fredholm and nonlinear argument; final theorem not disproved.

problems.title: Printed lower spectral-separation bound contradicts strict chord length
problems.source_location: Printed285 (8.52), used289–290 Section8.7
claim: t_pq >= (2p-1)ell/p for all relevant large periods.
Smooth strictly convex ellipse; p1 and arbitrarily large rational q.
analysis: Equation (8.52), p. 285, and its use to rule out perimeter multiples in Section 8.7, pp. 289–290.

The printed assertion is \[t_{p,q}(\Omega)\geq\frac{2p-1}{p}\,\ell(\Omega).\] For \(p=1\) it requires a finite inscribed polygon to have length at least the perimeter. In a smooth strictly convex domain, every chord is strictly shorter than its corresponding boundary arc. Summing around a one-winding polygon gives \(T_{1,q}<\ell\). An ellipse has such rational caustics for arbitrarily large \(q\), so no choice of \(q_0\) remedies this contradiction.

Equation reference: separation. The required replacement is \[
 (p-\tfrac12)\ell<t_{p,q}\leq T_{p,q}<p\ell.\] The upper bound is the chord–arc comparison already used in Lemma 8.6. For the finitely bounded numerators \(p\leq7\), (8.33), bounded \(c_{2,p}\) and a positive lower bound on \(\ell\) give the lower bound after increasing \(q_0\). This excludes all integer perimeter multiples, including the intermediate multiples that the printed expression would not exclude when \(p\geq3\).

Independent evaluations at \(e=1/2\), \(p=1\), \(q=4,10,50,100\) give perimeter deficits about \(.578346\), \(.095296\), \(.003832\), \(.000958\). These are diagnostic illustrations, not the proof of [separation] (#separation). Severity: Minor; the corrected bound supplies the local spectral separation actually needed.

problems.title: Reciprocal normalization in spectral-coefficient identification
claim: Printed reciprocal map sends ellipse tail to integers and yields stated ratio.
c0,c>0, common perimeter and near-ellipse smallness; endpoints visible on every sufficiently large q.

Put \(c_0=c_{2,1}(\mathcal E)\) and \(c=c_{2,1}(\Omega)\). The printed \(g(\ell-x)=c_0^{-1/2}x^{-1/2}\) sends \(\ell-c_0/q^2\) to \(q/c_0\), whereas (8.60) requires \(q\). The corrected formula and deformed center are \[g(\ell-x)=\sqrt{c_0}\,x^{-1/2},
 \qquad
 g(\ell-c/q^2)\sim\lambda q,\qquad
 \lambda=\sqrt{c_0/c}.\] The ratio in (8.61) must therefore also be inverted.

The reference to (8.56) should explicitly mean an interval construction using each domain’s own coefficient. A literal invocation of the already common-coefficient intervals would presuppose the conclusion. The author’s instruction to follow the preceding ideas, and the separate coefficients in (8.61), provide evidence for the intended valid reading. A possible stronger circularity allegation was therefore withdrawn.

First exclude all \(p>1\) lengths from a neighborhood of the common perimeter, using non-incidence, fixed-type continuity, the large-\(p\) estimate and bounded-\(p\) asymptotics. For Laplace-isospectral domains the perimeter is a heat invariant. If only equality of the relevant singular-support germs is assumed, its unique nearby accumulation point supplies the same identification.

Equality of singular supports matches that endpoint to an ellipse length indexed by an integer \(n(q)\). Even using the weaker remainder from (8.55), rather than the \(O(q^{-4})\) displayed in (8.33), one obtains \[|n(q)-\lambda q|\leq C\varepsilon+C'/q .\] Choose \(\varepsilon\) so that \(|\lambda-1|<1/10\) and, for all sufficiently large \(q\), the right side is below \(\eta<1/5\). Then \[|n(q+1)-n(q)-1|<2\eta+1/10<1/2 .\] Every integer gap is exactly one. Thus \(n(q)=q+d\) on the entire tail, and division by \(q\) gives \(\lambda=1\). The argument needs every sufficiently large integer \(q\), not an unspecified subsequence.

report: Abstract: This initial review concerns the 88-page author manuscript arXiv:2209.04046v4. It examines the definitions, main theorem dependencies, regularity and positivity criteria, finite-map transformation rule, and applications. One major proof gap is established in the global geometric application: the specified \(p\)-adically completed graded absolute integral closure cannot receive the asserted map from the completed cone. A separate minor calculation error affects two normalized-length constants; their correct values still supply the required positive bounds. Neither finding is a counterexample to a main theorem. The local fundamental-group argument is not shown to fail. External foundational results are used as cited dependencies, with the limits of this review stated below. Scientific adjudication is pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Review of Perfectoid Signature
and Perfectoid Hilbert–Kunz Multiplicity
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Perfectoid signature, perfectoid Hilbert–Kunz multiplicity, and an application to local fundamental groups, by Hanlin Cai, Seungsu Lee, Linquan Ma, Karl Schwede, and Kevin Tucker [paper]. Its journal identifier is DOI `10.1007/s00222-025-01399-w`. The inspected object is specifically arXiv version 4, dated 3 July 2025, not an asserted copy of the journal version of record. All page numbers below are physical PDF pages, which agree with printed pages in this 88-page manuscript.

The bounded review covered the mathematical text of Sections 1–8 through the source files and PDF text, with deeper reconstructions of the normalized-length arguments, regularity characterization, BCM positivity, rational signature, finite-map transformation, and Section 7 applications. Page-image inspections are separately recorded. This is not a claim that every external cited theorem or every sentence has been independently proved. The derived and prismatic foundations, existence and weak functoriality of perfectoid big Cohen–Macaulay algebras, and several cited local-cohomology and cover-comparison results remain accepted dependencies.

No separate supplement or original computational implementation was obtained in the bounded acquisition search. This is a theoretical paper; absence of code is not a mathematical finding. The acquisition manifests identify the exact files consulted. A bounded primary-source search did not identify an author correction for the two findings; this does not establish novelty or absence of a correction elsewhere.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and principal checks

Let \((R,\mathfrak m,k)\) be a complete Noetherian local domain of mixed characteristic \((0,p)\), dimension \(d\), with perfect residue field. The paper fixes a finite coefficient-ring inclusion \[A=W(k)\mathopen{[\![}x_2,\ldots,x_d\mathclose{]\!]}\subset R,
 \qquad
 A_n=A[p^{1/p^n},x_2^{1/p^n},\ldots,x_d^{1/p^n}],\] and its \(p\)-adically completed tower \(A_\infty\). Normalized length on a finite-level module is scaled by \(p^{-nd}\). The relevant algebra is \(B=(R\otimes_A A_\infty)_{\mathrm{perfd}}\), not its image in a chosen absolute integral closure. For an \(\mathfrak m\)-primary ideal \(J\) and the non-splitting ideal \(I_\infty\subset B\), the invariants are \[e_{\mathrm{perfd}}^{\underline{x}}(J)=\lambda_\infty(B/JB),
 \qquad
 s_{\mathrm{perfd}}^{\underline{x}}(R)=\lambda_\infty(B/I_\infty).\] Their dependence on the chosen tower is retained throughout. Parameter independence is posed as Conjecture 8.1, not established by this paper. In particular, the class-group bound in Theorem 7.0.12 uses some choices of parameters; it must not be read as proving independence for arbitrary choices.

The regularity checks reconstructed the chain from the rank/multiplicity comparison and parameter limit closure to \(e_{\mathrm{perfd}}^{\underline{x}}(R)\geq1\), the equality criterion, and the implication \(s_{\mathrm{perfd}}^{\underline{x}}(R)=1\Rightarrow R\) regular. The final regularity argument relies on the cited homological criterion; its external proof was not re-audited. The distinction between \(B\) and its image is essential even for ramified regular rings and is correctly emphasized in the source.

For positive signature, the converse implication is quantified as \[\forall\,0\ne g\in R,\quad \exists e,\quad
 \forall\,\text{perfectoid BCM }R^+\text{-algebras }C:
 \quad R\xrightarrow{\,1\mapsto g^{1/p^e}\,}C
 \text{ is pure}.\] The exponent can depend on \(g\); it is not one exponent for all \(g\). The domination lemma and essential socle of the injective hull support uniformity over \(C\). The forward implication from BCM-regular pairs retains the effective boundary and log-\(\mathbb Q\)-Cartier assumptions. For rational signature, the stabilized tail-span argument in Theorem 5.4.10 supplies a positive valuation threshold uniform over all socle injections. Pointwise positivity alone would not justify the infimum. Problem 2 changes its numerical lower bound, not that uniformity.

The finite-map check retained normality, splitting, quasi-étaleness, the compatible tower, and the residue-field factor in Theorem 6.0.1. Trace adjunction and the two-sided normalized-length estimates give the stated transformation under these assumptions. Lemma 7.0.1 supplies splitting and ascent of weak BCM-regularity; together with Theorem 6.0.1 it supports the local cover-degree and fundamental-group bound in Theorem 7.0.2. These local arguments are not shown to be affected by the gap below. No stronger result without those hypotheses is inferred.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The completed cone does not map to the specified target).  The natural factorization used in Claim 7.0.5, p. 75, is impossible for the algebra \(T\) defined there. This is a major proof gap in the derivation of the global geometric application, Theorem 7.0.4.
## Claim, hypotheses, and dependency

Theorem 7.0.4 concerns a normal integral scheme \(Y\), projective over \(R=H^0(Y,\mathcal O_Y)\), with equidimensional fibers. Here \(R\) is a complete Noetherian local domain with algebraically closed residue field. An effective \(\mathbb Q\)-divisor \(\Delta\) satisfies \(-(K_Y+\Delta)\) ample, and for every effective Cartier divisor \(D>0\) there is \(\epsilon>0\) such that \((Y,\Delta+\epsilon D)\) is globally \(+\)-regular. The conclusion is finiteness of the étale fundamental group of every open subset with complement of codimension at least two.

Equation reference: eq:badmap. In the proof, the chosen section ring \(S'\) is finite over \[A''=A'[x_0,\ldots,x_r],\qquad
 A'=W(k)\mathopen{[\![}y_1,\ldots,y_s\mathclose{]\!]}.\] Write \(\mathfrak n\) for its homogeneous maximal ideal and \(S=\widehat{S'}_{\mathfrak n}\). Claim 7.0.5 asserts BCM-regularity of \((S,\Delta_S)\) and hence positive perfectoid signature. After another graded finite extension and completion \(S_1\), the proof asserts a natural factorization \[
 S\longrightarrow S_1\longrightarrow
 T:=\widehat{S'^{+,\mathrm{GR}}}^{\,p}.\] It explicitly defines the last completion as \(p\)-adic. This factorization supplies the tensor product and local-cohomology map used to invoke Proposition 5.2.3. The subsequent reduction of covers of \(Y\) to covers of \(S\) needs the resulting positive signature.
## Exact obstruction

Equation reference: eq:residue. Put \(C=S'^{+,\mathrm{GR}}\). Under the stated definition, \(C\) is an integral extension of \(S'\), so it is integral over \(A''\). Consider the maximal ideal \[\mathfrak a=(p,y_1,\ldots,y_s,x_0-1,x_1,\ldots,x_r)
 \subset A'' .\] It is proper: its quotient is \(k\). Lying over gives a prime \(\mathfrak q\subset C\) contracting to \(\mathfrak a\). Consequently \(p\in\mathfrak q\) and \(1-x_0\in\mathfrak q\). There is a unital map to a nonzero ring \[
 T=\varprojlim_m C/p^mC\longrightarrow C/pC
 \longrightarrow C/\mathfrak q .\] Thus the image of \(1-x_0\) in \(T\) is not a unit.

By contrast, \(x_0\in\mathfrak n\), so \(1-x_0\) is a unit in the complete local ring \(S\); its inverse is the convergent \(\mathfrak n\)-adic series \(\sum_{j\geq0}x_0^j\). Every unital \(S'\)-algebra map \(S\to T\) would preserve this unit and its inverse, contradicting [eq:residue] (#eq:residue). Therefore the natural \(S'\)-algebra map required by [eq:badmap] (#eq:badmap) does not exist. The argument uses precisely the finite integral extension and completion specified in the proof. It does not assume failure of global \(+\)-regularity or require a counterexample to the geometric theorem.
## Alternative readings and counterevidence

The PDF image on p. 75 explicitly distinguishes completion at the homogeneous maximal ideal from the \(p\)-adic completion defining \(T\). The source TeX agrees; this is not an OCR substitution. The same paper does not define \(S'^{+,\mathrm{GR}}\) here to include prior localization at \(\mathfrak n\). A localization or a suitable completion after base change could remove this particular unit obstruction, but would change the target and require justification of the properties used next. Merely assuming that a formal power series converges \(p\)-adically does not fix the problem: \(x_0\) is not \(p\)-adically topologically nilpotent, as the quotient in [eq:residue] (#eq:residue) also shows.

The cone construction and the local fundamental-group theorem may still yield the intended result with an appropriate auxiliary algebra. This possibility is counterevidence against concluding that Theorem 7.0.4 is false; it does not validate its displayed factorization.
## Impact and repair status

The failure is in a necessary map for Claim 7.0.5, so the stated local-cohomology injection cannot be used with this \(T\). The affected chain is Claim 7.0.5 \(\Rightarrow\) the cone positivity step \(\Rightarrow\) Theorem 7.0.4, including the proof-based relaxation in Remark 7.0.6. Problem 2 (Total-degree volume is missing from normalized length).  The proof of Lemma 4.0.13, p. 32, uses an incorrect monomial-count lower bound. The final display of Theorem 5.4.11, p. 60, similarly assigns an incorrect scalar to a valuation-ideal quotient. This is a minor local calculation error, with a verified correction preserving both qualitative conclusions.
## Claim and assumptions

Definition 4.0.11, p. 31, extends the \(\mathfrak m_A\)-adic order to the tower by total monomial degree, with \(v(p)=v(x_i)=1\). For \(\epsilon>0\), the lemma sets \(I_n=\{a\in A_n:v(a)\geq\epsilon\}\) and uses \[\operatorname{length}_A(A_n/I_n)\geq p^{nd}\epsilon^d.\] At the end of Theorem 5.4.11, the paper instead calculates \(\lambda_\infty(A_\infty/\{v\geq p^{-e_0}\})=p^{-e_0}\). ## Independent exact calculation

Equation reference: eq:binomial, eq:volume. Let \(q=p^n\) and \(\mathfrak m_n=(p^{1/q},x_2^{1/q},\ldots,x_d^{1/q})\). The ring \(A_n\) is regular local with residue field \(k\), and \(v|_{A_n}=q^{-1}\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak m_n}\). For \(a>0\), put \(I_a=\{b\in A_\infty:v(b)\geq a\}\). Then \[
 I_a\cap A_n=\mathfrak m_n^{\lceil qa\rceil},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{length}_A\bigl(A_n/(I_a\cap A_n)\bigr)
   =\binom{\lceil qa\rceil+d-1}{d}.\] Indeed, degree-\(j\) monomials in \(d\) regular parameters number \(\binom{j+d-1}{d-1}\), and summing for \(0\leq j<\lceil qa\rceil\) gives [eq:binomial] (#eq:binomial).  \lambda_\infty(A_\infty/I_a)
 =\lim_{n\to\infty}p^{-nd}
     \binom{\lceil p^n a\rceil+d-1}{d}
 =\frac{a^d}{d!}.\] For any \(a>0\), choose an integer \(N\geq a\). Then \(p^N A_\infty\subseteq I_a\). The uncompleted tower and its completion agree modulo \(p^N\), so completion does not change the quotient or this calculation.

In dimension one the printed scalars agree with the correct formula. For \(d>1\), neither a change from floor to ceiling nor a different reading of the exponent removes the simplex-volume factor. The PDF images and the TeX agree on the disputed expressions. The valuation is explicitly total degree, not a coordinatewise minimum or a rescaled volume.

   \geq \frac{p^{-de_0}}{d!}>0.\] Together with the type bound, the relative signature is at least \(p^{-de_0}/(t\,d!)\) when \(t\) is the Cohen–Macaulay type. The exponent \(e_0\) is uniform over socle injections by Theorem 5.4.10, so taking the infimum remains valid.

The erroneous numerical values are auxiliary constants in proofs; the main theorem statements assert qualitative vanishing/positivity equivalences, not those numerical lower bounds. The corrected calculation restores the exact needed implications under unchanged hypotheses. Minor is assigned on that demonstrated dependency and bounded impact, not merely because the repair is short. No author adoption is documented.

The highest supported assessment is Major, restricted to the invalid target-map construction in the global geometric application. The count issue is separately Minor. Neither is a proved false theorem, and the review does not establish wholesale invalidity of the paper. The inspected local fundamental-group and transformation arguments retain their stated assumptions. Unexamined external dependencies limit any positive conclusion about the whole manuscript.

 \subset A'' .\] It is proper: its quotient is \(k\). Lying over gives a prime \(\mathfrak q\subset C\) contracting to \(\mathfrak a\). Consequently \(p\in\mathfrak q\) and \(1-x_0\in\mathfrak q\). There is a unital map to a nonzero ring \[
 T=\varprojlim_m C/p^mC\longrightarrow C/pC
 \longrightarrow C/\mathfrak q .\] Thus the image of \(1-x_0\) in \(T\) is not a unit.

It is not asserted to damage Theorems A–G, the local fundamental-group bound, or the torsion class-group argument.

A repair must construct a target receiving \(S_1\), establish the required perfectoid structure and compatible roots, and prove that the splitting/local-cohomology information from the graded covers survives the intervening operations. No complete replacement argument has been verified in this review. Author adoption is unknown.
result: The PDF image on p. 75 explicitly distinguishes completion at the homogeneous maximal ideal from the \(p\)-adic completion defining \(T\). The source TeX agrees; this is not an OCR substitution. The same paper does not define \(S'^{+,\mathrm{GR}}\) here to include prior localization at \(\mathfrak n\). A localization or a suitable completion after base change could remove this particular unit obstruction, but would change the target and require justification of the properties used next. Merely assuming that a formal power series converges \(p\)-adically does not fix the problem: \(x_0\) is not \(p\)-adically topologically nilpotent, as the quotient in [eq:residue] (#eq:residue) also shows.

The cone construction and the local fundamental-group theorem may still yield the intended result with an appropriate auxiliary algebra. This possibility is counterevidence against concluding that Theorem 7.0.4 is false; it does not validate its displayed factorization.
Result: The specified factorization is impossible and the local-cohomology tensor product cannot use the asserted algebra structure. This is not a counterexample to the theorem conclusion.

Impact: Major at the claim level because the failed map is the necessary bridge to an explicitly advertised global geometric theorem. The local fundamental-group theorem, class-group bound and signature constructions are not shown to fail.

report: Abstract: The acquired author manuscript is reviewed for its definitions, period-space constructions and bi-analytic Ax–Lindemann argument. One local error is established: Lemma 9.3.3 identifies two inequivalent conditions on an arbitrary subdiamond. An explicit neutral admissible family on two points has empty Hodge-generic locus, whereas restriction to the entire base leaves its motivic Galois group unchanged. The pointwise criterion actually used in the main theorem remains valid. The supported assessment is Minor, with scientific adjudication pending. No counterexample to the principal theorem is established.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Verification of
Admissible Pairs and \(p\)-adic Hodge Structures II
# Paper identity and review scope

The paper is by Sean Howe and Christian Klevdal, Admissible pairs and \(p\)-adic Hodge structures II: the bi-analytic Ax-Lindemann theorem, associated with DOI 10.1007/s00222-025-01400-6 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00222-025-01400-6). This report concerns exactly arXiv:2308.11064v2, dated 28 February 2025, a 68-page author manuscript [paper]. Equivalence to the journal version of record has not been established. Locations below are one-based PDF pages; the internal page numbers agree at the cited mathematical passages.

Definitions and dependencies were traced, selected arguments were reconstructed, and the cited source pages were visually checked. This does not certify every external theorem or every sentence of the paper. Particular attention was given to one-sided weight conditions, nonreductive groups, admissibility, Hodge loci, basic duality, the constant-rank argument and generic points. No separate supplement or original computational repository was identified in the bounded availability checks. Their absence is not a mathematical finding.
# Definitions and operative hypotheses

The main theorem, Theorem 9.1.3, concerns the two analytic structures on a basic infinite-level space. The Newton cocharacter must be central in the full group \(G\), not merely in its reductive quotient. The analytic closure is defined using finite-level rigid analytic subspaces over \(\overline L\); the text does not prove the corresponding unrestricted \(C\)-analytic assertion. For non-minuscule cocharacters the Hodge and Hodge–Tate notions of special subvariety have different one-sided adjoint-weight conditions. These distinctions are retained in this review.

The Hodge-generic locus in Definition 9.3.2 is the complement in \(|S|\) of the union of all proper Hodge loci of rank-one sub-isocrystals in representations of \(G\). Section 9.3 expressly returns to an arbitrary locally spatial diamond \(S\) over \(\operatorname{Spd}\breve{\mathbb Q}_p\) before stating Lemma 9.3.3. No connectedness or irreducibility assumption is imposed on \(S\) or on the subdiamond \(T\) in that lemma. Neutral admissible pairs have a common isocrystal and a varying \(\mathbb B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+\)-lattice on that isocrystal; the definition permits disconnected bases.
# A local error in the generic-locus criterion

Problem 1 (An arbitrary subdiamond need not contain a generic point).  Lemma 9.3.3, PDF p. 59, asserts, in paraphrase, that \(T\subseteq S\) meets the Hodge-generic locus if and only if \[\operatorname{MG}(\mathcal G|_T,y)=\operatorname{MG}(\mathcal G,y)\] for a geometric point \(y\) of \(T\). The proof establishes instead that group equality is equivalent to \(T\) not being contained in any single proper Hodge locus. It does not exclude a covering of \(T\) by several such loci.
## Construction and verification of all hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:filtrations. Fix a prime \(p\), put \(K=\breve{\mathbb Q}_p\), and choose a completed algebraic closure \(C\) of \(K\). On \[W=K e_0\oplus K e_1\oplus K e_2\] take the semilinear Frobenius \(\varphi(e_0)=e_0\), \(\varphi(e_1)=p e_1\), \(\varphi(e_2)=p e_2\). Set \(N=0\). Consider the two decreasing filtrations with \(F_i^0=W\), \(F_i^2=0\), and \[
 F_1^1=\langle e_1+e_0,e_2\rangle_K,\qquad
 F_2^1=\langle e_1,e_2+e_0\rangle_K .\] They are defined over \(\mathbb Q_p\), and hence over \(K\). Both have \(t_H(W)=2=t_N(W)\).

Equation reference: eq:wa. We check every subobject inequality, rather than a sample of lines. By slope decomposition, any Frobenius-stable sub-isocrystal \(D\subseteq W\) decomposes as \(D_0\oplus D_1\), where \(D_0\) has slope zero and \(D_1\) has slope one. The planes in [eq:filtrations] (#eq:filtrations) have zero intersection with \(K e_0\). Projection to the slope-one summand is therefore injective on \(D\cap F_i^1\). Consequently \[
 t_H(D)=\dim_K(D\cap F_i^1)
       \leq \dim_K D_1=t_N(D).\] Thus both filtered isocrystals are weakly admissible. Theorem A of Colmez–Fontaine, in the author-hosted version whose p. 2 explicitly allows a complete discretely valued field of characteristic zero with perfect residue field, makes them admissible [cf]. With \(N=0\) they are crystalline. We use the good-reduction comparison and its lattice convention in Part I, Definition 5.4.1, Theorem 5.5.1 and Remark 5.5.2 [parti]; we do not claim to reprove those external comparison theorems.

Equation reference: eq:lattices. Let \[S=\operatorname{Spd}C\ \coprod\ \operatorname{Spd}C .\] The two objects have the same isocrystal \(W\), so they give a neutral rank-three admissible family on this locally spatial diamond. Via the standard representation it has \(G=\operatorname{GL}_3\) structure. Its lattices are \[
 \mathcal L_i=W\otimes_K\mathbb B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+(C)
       +t^{-1}F_i^1\otimes_K\mathbb B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+(C).\] These good filtrations also give the exact tensor structure in all representations. The common Frobenius supplies a \(b\)-rigidification if one is requested. Basicness is not an assumption of Lemma 9.3.3.
## Evaluation and discrepancy
For the slope-one lines \(\ell_1=K e_1\) and \(\ell_2=K e_2\), direct intersection with [eq:lattices] (#eq:lattices) gives the following table. Here \(B^+=\mathbb B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+(C)\).
Line | First component | Second component

For example \(e_2\notin F_2^1\), because cancelling its \(e_0\) coefficient in a combination of \(e_1,e_2+e_0\) forces the \(e_2\) coefficient to vanish. This gives the lower-right entry. The other entries follow by the same coordinate check.

For either line the Newton number is one. The \(t^{-1}\) lattice has Hodge number one and is an admissible rank-one subobject; the \(B^+\) lattice has Hodge number zero and is not admissible. It follows that \[|\operatorname{Hdg}(\ell_2)|=|\text{first component}|,\qquad
 |\operatorname{Hdg}(\ell_1)|=|\text{second component}|.\] Both loci are proper, and together they cover \(|S|\). The Hodge-generic locus is empty. Now take \(T=S\), which is permitted by the displayed non-strict inclusion in the lemma. For every geometric point \(y\) of \(S\), restriction to \(T\) changes nothing, so \(\operatorname{MG}(\mathcal G|_T,y)=\operatorname{MG}(\mathcal G,y)\) tautologically. The claimed implication to a nonempty intersection is false.
## Counterevidence, impact and exact repair

The printed PDF and the released TeX agree on the arbitrary-\(T\) wording. This is not an extraction error. The next paragraph explicitly allows the generic locus to be empty. Conversely, the pointwise criterion is valid: a single point lies in a union precisely when it lies in at least one member. Theorem 9.1.3 uses the lemma at a geometric point. The source also states that the generic-density argument does not depend on this lemma. The geometrically irreducible hypothesis of Lemma 9.3.1 and the smooth connected setting of Lemma 9.3.5 exclude the disconnected counterexample above.

The supported assessment is therefore Minor: the auxiliary statement has unused excess generality, and no central dependency is shown to fail. This assessment is based on the traced uses, not on the length of a repair. Either of the following corrected statements is supported:
1. For a geometric point \(T=\{y\}\), the point is Hodge generic if and only if its motivic Galois group equals that of the family.
2. For arbitrary nonempty \(T\), retain the group equality but replace the intersection assertion by: \(T\) is not contained in any single proper Hodge locus.
The first suffices for the traced use in the principal theorem. No author adoption of this correction has been established.
# Other checked reasoning and remaining limits

The core proof reduces the structure group to the generic motivic Galois group and uses the Part I open-image input. For a general \(L\), one may pass inside \(C\) to the completed maximal unramified extension to apply the strict-field form of that input; its open Galois image is contained in the original Galois image. A compact open \(p\)-adic orbit, a local constant-rank argument and Griffiths transversality then force the relevant period map to have full rank. The step that an analytic function vanishing on a \(\mathbb Q_p\)-open ball vanishes locally follows by successive one-variable identity arguments; it is not a counterexample arising from the difference between \(\mathbb Q_p\) and \(C\). Closedness and full dimension then give the required connected component. This reconstruction accepts the cited comparison, openness and rigid-geometric foundations within their stated interfaces.

The nonreductive Bialynicki–Birula comparison was checked against the one-sided weight bound; the basic duality is used only in the basic case. The abbreviated passage from smooth to seminormal bases can be supplied by resolution on irreducible branches, agreement of type at common fibers and descent. The general-field form of the external Liu–Zhu comparison remains an accepted dependency, not an independent verification of that foundational theorem.

In the generic-density argument, the current version’s compact-open decomposition of the parameter set of proper Hodge loci repairs the previously acknowledged omission. No finding is based on the earlier proof. A field containing \(\breve{\mathbb Q}_p\) need not have algebraically closed residue, although its residue is infinite. Infinitude already suffices for the Gauss-point approximation used here: finitely many nonzero reductions of polynomials cannot vanish on all residue-field points. This supplies the needed weaker hypothesis for that elementary step. Section 10’s distinctions between local bi-analytic results and global bi-algebraic questions are preserved; the future global statements are not treated as theorems proved in this paper.

report: Abstract: The acquired journal version is reviewed through its uniform integral Tate condition, Galois-orbit lower bound, integral norm comparison and independence arguments. A core proof-applicability gap is established: Proposition 5.7 invokes a comparison theorem requiring connected stabilizers, whereas its full centralizer stabilizer can remain disconnected at every good prime, including in a faithful adjoint representation. This is a localized Major finding about the derivation; it is not a counterexample to the principal theorem. The required fixed-centralizer comparison is repaired below by a finite-component quotient without changing its weight constant. Four auxiliary defects are separately assessed as Minor after tracing their actual uses. Exact counterexamples, counterevidence and repair boundaries are given below. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Verification of the Generalised
André–Pink–Zannier Conjecture
for Shimura Varieties of Abelian Type
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Rodolphe Richard and Andrei Yafaev, Generalised André-Pink-Zannier conjecture for Shimura varieties of Abelian type, Publications Mathématiques de l’IHÉS 141 (2025), 249–331, DOI 10.1007/s10240-025-00154-4 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10240-025-00154-4) [paper]. The canonical input is the 83-page publisher version of record. A separately acquired 2023 arXiv source archive was not substituted for the journal text. Below, a PDF page is a one-based physical page; its printed page number is larger by 248.

The coverage ledger distinguishes full text reading, reconstructed arguments, actual selected image inspection and accepted external inputs. This is not a certification of every proof in the cited literature. No separate original supplement or computational repository was identified in the bounded availability checks. Lack of code is not a mathematical defect.

The principal strategy combines the uniform integral Tate property with a Galois-orbit lower bound and the earlier height/o-minimal argument. The exact published companion [height], rather than an assumed matching preprint, was consulted at the decomposition, reciprocity and main-proof interfaces. Its Lemma 6.12 corresponds to the older numbering cited in the reviewed paper.
# Definitions and quantifiers that govern the review

Definition 2.1 concerns a compact subgroup \(U\subset M(\widehat{\mathbb Z})\), with \(M\subset G\subset\operatorname{GL}_n\) connected reductive groups. The rational condition requires the appropriate connected Zariski closures, semisimplicity and centralizer equality. The residual condition is eventual and uniform in bounded index: for every fixed bound \(D\), a threshold \(M_U(D)\) controls all subgroups of the relevant residual image of index at most \(D\). It imposes no condition at every individual small prime.

The centralizer \(Z_G(M)\) is the full group scheme, not automatically its identity component. The abelianization \(M^{\mathrm{ab}}\), the full center \(Z(M)\), and the connected center are different objects. Likewise, stability under integral points \(G(\mathbb Z_p)\) is weaker than stability under the coaction of the integral group scheme \(G_{\mathbb Z_p}\). These distinctions are decisive in Problems 1, 2 and 4.
# A disconnected stabilizer in the core norm-comparison invocation

Problem 1 (Theorem 6.1 is invoked outside its connected-stabilizer hypotheses).  Proposition 5.7, PDF pp. 31–32 (printed pp. 279–280), uses Theorem 6.1 to prove equation (37). Its stabilizer is \(F=Z_G(M)\). Section 6.1, equation (49) and footnote 12, PDF p. 45 (printed p. 293), explicitly require the special fibers of both \(F\) and \(G\) to be connected reductive groups. Theorem 6.1 on the next page uses that setup and the full scheme stabilizers of its vectors. Definition 2.1 does not imply the required connectedness.
## A model satisfying the operative group hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:disconnected. Let \(W\) be a split four-dimensional quadratic space, put \(V=W\oplus\langle-1\rangle\), and take \[G=\operatorname{SO}(V)\simeq\operatorname{SO}_5,\qquad M=\operatorname{SO}(W)\simeq\operatorname{SO}_4\] with \(M\) fixing the last line. Over characteristic zero and every odd characteristic, the \(M\)-module \(W\) is absolutely irreducible and nontrivial. A commuting endomorphism of \(V\) therefore has the form \(\operatorname{diag}(aI_4,b)\). Preserving the quadratic form and determinant gives \[a^2=b^2=1,\qquad a^4b=1.\] Consequently \[
 Z_G(M)=\{\operatorname{diag}(I_4,1),\operatorname{diag}(-I_4,1)\}\simeq\mu_2.\] This has two geometric components at every odd prime.

Choose the product of the full integral local groups at good primes, with an arbitrary compact open integral subgroup at the finitely many remaining primes. Every local factor is Zariski dense in connected \(M_{\mathbb Q_p}\); the characteristic-zero representations are semisimple. For the residual clause, fix \(D\) and let \(q>\max(D,5)\). An index-at-most-\(D\) subgroup of \(M(\mathbb F_q)\) contains every element of order \(q\): the action on its cosets takes such an element to the identity in a symmetric group on fewer than \(q\) letters. It therefore contains \[\Omega_4^+(\mathbb F_q)
   =\operatorname{im}\bigl(\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_q)\times\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_q)
                          \longrightarrow \operatorname{SO}_4(\mathbb F_q)\bigr).\] The four-dimensional representation is the tensor product of the two standard two-dimensional representations; it is absolutely irreducible. Together with the trivial last line it is semisimple, and its commuting endomorphisms are exactly the two scalar blocks used above. Intersecting this commutant with \(G\) gives the same scheme-theoretic centralizer \(\mu_2\). This verifies the residual semisimplicity and centralizer conditions, uniformly for each fixed \(D\). Finally \(M^{\mathrm{ab}}=1\), so the additional abelian-image condition in Theorem 5.1 is automatic.

Passing to an adjoint representation does not remove the obstruction: \(G=\operatorname{SO}_5\) is adjoint and its adjoint representation is faithful. Moreover, \(\operatorname{Lie}G=\operatorname{Lie}M\oplus W\), and the nonidentity element of [eq:disconnected] (#eq:disconnected) acts as \(-1\) on \(W\). The uniform Tate property passes through the faithful representation change used in the paper; alternatively, at large \(q\) the summands are the two simple three-dimensional adjoint modules and their four-dimensional tensor module, and the same residual check applies. Thus this obstruction to the literal connectedness hypothesis survives the adjoint image and exclusion of finitely many primes. The product group constructed here verifies the abstract theorem assumptions; it is not asserted to be the Galois image of a particular Shimura point.
## Counterevidence and bounded impact

The geometric auxiliary role also checked the related adjoint example \(\mathrm{PGL}_2\subset\mathrm{PGSp}_4\), obtained from two copies of the standard two-dimensional representation. Its centralizer is \(\mathrm{GO}_2/\mathbb G_m\), with two components. The detailed integral Tate verification is retained in the evidence files; the simpler model above already proves the missing implication.
## A verified finite-component repair

The fixed centralizer in this application admits the required extension after excluding finitely many primes. This keeps the full stabilizer \(F\), rather than substituting \(F^0\) in the orbit problem.

Put \(R=\mathbb Z_p\). Since \(F=Z_G(M)\) is fixed over \(\mathbb Q\), outside a finite set of primes its integral model is smooth, \(F^0_R\) is connected reductive, and \(Q=F_R/F^0_R\) is finite etale. Exclude also the prime divisors of its order \(m\). The connected quotient results in §7.3 and Lemma 7.11 [1, PDF pp. 56–58, 61] then give \[B=R[G]^{F^0_R},\qquad Y=\operatorname{Spec}B,
 \qquad Y_k=G_k/F^0_k\] for geometric fibers \(k\), with \(B\) of finite type and \(Y\) smooth. Right translation defines a \(Q\)-action on \(Y\). Set \[A=B^Q=R[G]^{F_R},\qquad X=\operatorname{Spec}A.\] After a finite etale base change making \(Q\) constant, the averaging operator \(m^{-1}\sum_{q\in Q}q\) is an idempotent onto the invariants. Thus invariants commute with passage to the residue and fraction fields. The orbit polynomial \(\prod_{q\in Q}(T-qb)\) shows that \(B\) is integral over \(A\); the finite-group invariant argument gives finite generation of \(A\) and finiteness of \(B\) over \(A\). These properties descend from the etale cover. Moreover \(A\subset R[G]\) is torsion-free, hence flat over the discrete valuation ring \(R\).

The action of \(Q_k\) on \(G_k/F^0_k\) is free: a component fixing \(gF^0_k\) must be the identity component. Its finite etale quotient is therefore smooth and \[X_k=(G_k/F^0_k)/Q_k=G_k/F_k .\] Finite presentation, flatness and geometrically smooth fibers imply that \(X/R\) is smooth. The same fiber criterion, applied to \(G\to X\), makes that morphism smooth and surjective. These are precisely the quotient inputs needed below.

For completeness, the normalization step also retains the full \(F\). Let \(S\) be the schematic orbit closure for a vector satisfying the other hypotheses of Theorem 7.1. In Lemma 7.10 [1, PDF pp. 59–61], \(X\) is normal, and \(X\to S\) is quasi-finite: its generic fiber is an isomorphism, and its special fibers have equal dimensions and the transitive orbit description just obtained. The normalization \(\widetilde S\) has a genuine \(G_R\)-action. Indeed the action lifts through normalization because \(G\times_R\widetilde S\) is normal by smooth base change; uniqueness gives the action law. Thus the corrected coaction hypothesis of Problem 4 applies. The proof of claim (3) of Lemma 7.10 uses Lemma 7.4, Corollary 7.5, stabilizer dimensions and connectedness of \(G\), with no further connectedness requirement on \(F\). It makes the special fiber of \(\widetilde S\) one geometric orbit. Zariski’s Main Theorem then identifies \(X\) with \(\widetilde S\), so \(X\to S\) is integral.

Proposition 7.15 [1, PDF p. 63] now gives the same integral-point criterion (67), over the integral closure \(\overline{\mathbb Z}_p\subset\overline{\mathbb Q}_p\) used in the paper. Smoothness and geometric surjectivity of \(G\to X\) also give the lifting step of Proposition 7.14. No assertion of surjectivity on \(\mathbb F_p\)-rational points is needed. In §6.3 [1, PDF p. 47], Cartan decomposition uses only the hyperspecial model of \(G\), and the two zero sets are exactly \[h_v(g)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 gF\in X(\overline{\mathbb Z}_p)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h_{v'}(g)=0.\] The convex zero sets therefore coincide. Corollary 8.3 uses the unchanged representation weights, so the same constant \(C(\Sigma(\rho))\) works and no additive constant is introduced.

This finite exclusion is allowed: Proposition 5.7 states \(p\gg0\), and §5.1.3 [1, PDF p. 21] requires the uniform estimate only at almost all primes, with separate treatment of the remaining ones. The repair is verified for that actual fixed-centralizer application, using the stated connected quotient and normalization foundations. It is additional reasoning, not a claim that the authors supplied or adopted it.
## Impact and assessment

Equation (37) feeds Corollary 5.8 and the remaining local-height cases, then Theorems 5.4 and 5.1 and the Section 3 strategy for Theorem 1.4. The original invocation still fails an explicit hypothesis at this core step. Its assessment remains Major under the claim-level standard for a demonstrated invalid central derivation. The complete finite-component repair is recorded separately: the inequality and final theorem are not refuted, and the bridge is no longer an unresolved repair in this review.
# The equality endpoint in the residual index assertion

Problem 2 (Index \(p\) does not preserve the dagger subgroup).  Remark 2.1.3(2), PDF p. 5 (printed p. 253), asserts in paraphrase that \([U:U']\le p\) preserves the subgroup generated by residual unipotents: \(U'(p)^\dagger=U(p)^\dagger\). The equality endpoint is false.

Equation reference: eq:index. Fix a prime \(p_0\ge5\), take \(M=G=\operatorname{GL}_2\), and let \[C=\{I+aE_{12}:a\in\mathbb F_{p_0}\}.\] Set \(U_{p_0}\) equal to its full inverse image under reduction \(\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z_{p_0})\to\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_{p_0})\), and set \(U_q=\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z_q)\) at other primes. In the product \(U\), replace the \(p_0\)-factor by \(1+p_0M_2(\mathbb Z_{p_0})\) to obtain \(U'\). Then \[
 [U:U']=p_0,\qquad U(p_0)^\dagger=C,\qquad U'(p_0)^\dagger=1.\] All local factors are open and Zariski dense in \(\operatorname{GL}_2\). For a fixed \(D\), choose \(q>\max(p_0,D,3)\). The same coset-action argument forces every index-at-most-\(D\) residual subgroup to contain \(\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_q)\), which acts absolutely irreducibly with scalar commutant. Thus Definition 2.1 is satisfied; the exceptional prime \(p_0\) is permitted by its quantifiers.

The corrected hypothesis is \([U:U']<p\). A unipotent of \(p\)-power order acts trivially on fewer than \(p\) cosets, so all such elements lie in the smaller residual group and the dagger groups agree. This proves the corrected statement. Actual source images confirm the printed non-strict inequality; the example is not based on OCR.

The traced Section 5 uses have fixed index bounds followed by sufficiently large primes, so their cutoffs can impose \(p>D\); no essential use of the equality endpoint was found. The assessment is Minor, based on this dependency check and the proved strict-index assertion, not merely on the small size of the correction.
# The subgroup constructed in Lemma 5.12

Problem 3 (A kernel-intersection witness has a larger projective centralizer).  Lemma 5.12, PDF pp. 37–39 (printed pp. 285–287), seeks a bounded-index \(U'\subset U\) with \[Z_{M^{\mathrm{ad}}}(\operatorname{ad}U')=Z_M(U')/Z(M).\] Its proof specifies \(U[e]\), the intersection of the kernels of all homomorphisms \(U\to\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z\), for a suitable \(e\). That specified subgroup need not satisfy the displayed equality.

Take \(M=\operatorname{SL}_2\) over \(\mathbb F_{17}\), \(e=2\), and \[g=\operatorname{diag}(2,9),\quad U=\langle g\rangle\simeq C_8,\quad
 h=g^2=\operatorname{diag}(4,13).\] Here \(e\) is divisible by the order of \(Z(M)(\overline{\mathbb F}_{17})\), and the prescribed subgroup is \(U[2]=\langle h\rangle\simeq C_4\). For \[w=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\] direct calculation gives \(whw^{-1}=-h\). Thus \(\operatorname{ad}(w)\) centralizes \(\operatorname{ad}(U[2])\), although \(w\), and every centrally modified lift of it, fails to centralize \(h\). Since \(h\) has distinct eigenvalues, \(Z_M(U[2])\) is the diagonal torus; the projective centralizer has an additional Weyl component.

An independently written finite-field enumeration retained in `native_galois_cyclic_calculation.json` checks the same matrix equalities and counts 16 elements in the \(\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_{17})\) centralizer of \(h\), against 32 in the inverse image of the projective centralizer. The direct matrix witness proves the discrepancy without identifying rational points of a quotient with a quotient of rational points.

Equation reference: eq:weaker. The commutator argument does prove the weaker statement \[
 Z_{M^{\mathrm{ad}}}(\operatorname{ad}U)
       \subseteq \operatorname{im}\bigl(Z_M(U[e])\to M^{\mathrm{ad}}\bigr).\] Indeed, for a lift of an element on the left, its commutators with \(U\) form a homomorphism into the finite central group; the kernel intersection kills its cyclic coordinates. This argument keeps \(U\) on the left. It does not permit replacing it there by \(U[e]\).

The existential assertion of Lemma 5.12 is not refuted by this example: \(U'=1\), of index 8, works in this individual case. Its general strong form remains unverified in this review. In the actual use in Lemma 5.11, however, [eq:weaker] (#eq:weaker) is enough: the Tate property identifies the centralizer of the selected bounded-index subgroup with \(Z(M)\), forcing the projective centralizer of the original subgroup to be trivial. Thus the assessment is Minor: the proposed witness and stronger proof assertion fail, whereas the required downstream implication has a complete weaker replacement.
# Integral-point stability versus a group-scheme action

Problem 4 (Proposition 7.2 assumes too little stability).  Proposition 7.2, PDF pp. 51–52 (printed pp. 299–300), assumes a finitely generated \(G(\mathbb Z_p)\)-stable subalgebra of \(\mathbb Z_p[G]\) and concludes an equivariant integral representation/orbit realization. Pointwise stability does not supply the required scheme action.

Equation reference: eq:coaction. Let \(G=\mathbb G_m\) and \[A=\mathbb Z_p[pt,t^p-t]\subset\mathbb Z_p[t,t^{-1}].\] This meets the stated finite-generation and smooth reductive group hypotheses. For every \(u\in\mathbb Z_p^	imes\), \[u(pt)=u\,pt,\qquad
 u(t^p-t)=u^p(t^p-t)+ rac{u^p-u}{p}\,pt ,\] so \(A\) is stable under all integral points. On the other hand, \(t
otin A\): modulo \(p\), the image of \(A\) is \(\mathbb F_p[t^p-t]\), whose nonconstant elements have degree divisible by \(p\). The scaling coaction satisfies \[
 \delta(t^p-t)=(t^p-t)s^p+t(s^p-s).\] Its coefficient of \(s\) is \(-t
otin A\), so \(\delta(t^p-t)
otin A[s,s^{-1}]\). The specified generic action cannot extend to this integral algebra. Normality or an equality of generic fibers is not a hypothesis of the printed proposition.

A sufficient repair is to require stability under the \(G_{\mathbb Z_p}\)-coaction. The actual applications have this stronger property. In Lemma 7.6, \(A=\mathbb Z_p[G]^F\); left and right translations commute, and flat base change preserves the kernel defining invariants, giving the genuine left coaction. In Lemma 7.10, the action on a schematic orbit closure lifts uniquely to its normalization: the product with the smooth group is normal, and the dominant action factors through the normalization. Uniqueness gives the group law. The normalization interfaces are supported by the precise primary statements in [stacks].

The assessment is Minor: the general auxiliary proposition is false, while the two traced applications satisfy the corrected hypothesis. This coaction repair is also used in the normalization step of the finite-component extension proved in Problem 1.
# The conjugacy-finiteness prelude to Lemma B.5

Problem 5 (Semisimple embeddings have infinitely many Frobenius twists).  The first preliminary bullet before Lemma B.5, PDF p. 72 (printed p. 320), asserts boundedly many \(\operatorname{GL}_n(\overline{\mathbb F}_p)\)-conjugacy classes of semisimple algebraic subgroups for fixed \(n\), uniformly in \(p\). Even at one fixed prime and dimension, the unrestricted assertion is false.

Fix \(p\ge5\), \(n=4\), and for every \(r\ge1\) let \[S_r=\{\operatorname{diag}(g,\operatorname{Frob}^{r}(g)):g\in\operatorname{SL}_2\}.\] This is an \(\mathbb F_p\)-defined closed connected semisimple subgroup, isomorphic to \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) by its first projection. Its Lie algebra is \(\operatorname{diag}(\mathfrak{sl}_2,0)\). The common fixed space of that Lie algebra is the second two-dimensional block, and the span of its images is the first block. Any conjugacy \(S_r\to S_s\) must therefore be block diagonal, say \(\operatorname{diag}(a,b)\). Its induced equations, applied to \(g=I+tE_{12}\), imply \[I+t^{p^r}N_1=I+t^{p^s}N_2\] for nonzero constant matrices \(N_1,N_2\). Polynomial degrees force \(r=s\). Thus the groups are pairwise nonconjugate even over the algebraic closure.

The actual printed conjugating field is \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p\); the review does not use the incorrect OCR reading \(\mathbb F_p\). There is also relevant mathematical counterevidence: \(S_r(\mathbb F_p)\) is always diagonal \(\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_p)\), so its Nori envelope is diagonal \(\operatorname{SL}_2\), not \(S_r\). The displayed family does not contradict the narrower Nori-group setting actually needed.

More directly, the two structural bounds used in Lemma B.5 do not need finiteness of embeddings. A semisimple subgroup of \(\operatorname{GL}_n\) has rank at most \(n\). There are finitely many semisimple root data of that bounded rank, including the finitely many central-isogeny types. Their centers have uniformly bounded order, and their outer automorphism groups are bounded by automorphisms of the corresponding based root data. Taking maxima gives the required constants. This proves the needed replacement without the false embedding-finiteness assertion.
The assessment is Minor, limited to an unnecessarily strong auxiliary assertion. No counterexample to Lemma B.5 or Theorem B.1 is established.

Section 4’s specialization and finite-type-field independence arguments were checked at the stated interfaces. The general-field independence input is supplied by the exact Gajda–Petersen result [gp]; a number-field-only objection is not retained. The auxiliary role consulted the relevant Noot and Serre passages [noot, serre], without claiming a full audit of all external proofs.

Several candidates were discharged. The torus in Section 6.1 can be chosen to fit the hyperspecial point; footnote 13 and the freedom of choice support that interpretation. An arbitrary badly positioned torus need not have a reductive closure, but that observation is not an additional finding against the required choice. In Lemma B.10, the \(e\)-power map has derivative \(e\,\mathrm{id}\) over \(\mathbb Q_p\). Its image contains an identity neighborhood, so a subgroup containing all \(e\)-th powers is open; taking its normal core makes the stated restricted-Burnside step applicable. The global projection/pure-factor argument can use the subsequent independent cyclic extraction argument in an earlier order. Actual images retain the closure bars lost by text extraction.

The isolated description of the full center as a torus in Appendix B.1 should read a smooth group of multiplicative type, with torus identity component: \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) has full center \(\mu_2\) at odd primes.
