analysis: Proposition 5.7, PDF pp. 31–32 (printed pp. 279–280), uses Theorem 6.1 to prove equation (37). Its stabilizer is \(F=Z_G(M)\). Section 6.1, equation (49) and footnote 12, PDF p. 45 (printed p. 293), explicitly require the special fibers of both \(F\) and \(G\) to be connected reductive groups. Theorem 6.1 on the next page uses that setup and the full scheme stabilizers of its vectors. Definition 2.1 does not imply the required connectedness.

Equation reference: eq:disconnected. Let \(W\) be a split four-dimensional quadratic space, put \(V=W\oplus\langle-1\rangle\), and take \[G=\operatorname{SO}(V)\simeq\operatorname{SO}_5,\qquad M=\operatorname{SO}(W)\simeq\operatorname{SO}_4\] with \(M\) fixing the last line. Over characteristic zero and every odd characteristic, the \(M\)-module \(W\) is absolutely irreducible and nontrivial. A commuting endomorphism of \(V\) therefore has the form \(\operatorname{diag}(aI_4,b)\). Preserving the quadratic form and determinant gives \[a^2=b^2=1,\qquad a^4b=1.\] Consequently \[
 Z_G(M)=\{\operatorname{diag}(I_4,1),\operatorname{diag}(-I_4,1)\}\simeq\mu_2.\] This has two geometric components at every odd prime.

Choose the product of the full integral local groups at good primes, with an arbitrary compact open integral subgroup at the finitely many remaining primes. Every local factor is Zariski dense in connected \(M_{\mathbb Q_p}\); the characteristic-zero representations are semisimple. For the residual clause, fix \(D\) and let \(q>\max(D,5)\). An index-at-most-\(D\) subgroup of \(M(\mathbb F_q)\) contains every element of order \(q\): the action on its cosets takes such an element to the identity in a symmetric group on fewer than \(q\) letters. It therefore contains \[\Omega_4^+(\mathbb F_q)
   =\operatorname{im}\bigl(\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_q)\times\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_q)
                          \longrightarrow \operatorname{SO}_4(\mathbb F_q)\bigr).\] The four-dimensional representation is the tensor product of the two standard two-dimensional representations; it is absolutely irreducible. Together with the trivial last line it is semisimple, and its commuting endomorphisms are exactly the two scalar blocks used above. Intersecting this commutant with \(G\) gives the same scheme-theoretic centralizer \(\mu_2\). This verifies the residual semisimplicity and centralizer conditions, uniformly for each fixed \(D\). Finally \(M^{\mathrm{ab}}=1\), so the additional abelian-image condition in Theorem 5.1 is automatic.

Passing to an adjoint representation does not remove the obstruction: \(G=\operatorname{SO}_5\) is adjoint and its adjoint representation is faithful. Moreover, \(\operatorname{Lie}G=\operatorname{Lie}M\oplus W\), and the nonidentity element of [eq:disconnected] (#eq:disconnected) acts as \(-1\) on \(W\). The uniform Tate property passes through the faithful representation change used in the paper; alternatively, at large \(q\) the summands are the two simple three-dimensional adjoint modules and their four-dimensional tensor module, and the same residual check applies. Thus this obstruction to the literal connectedness hypothesis survives the adjoint image and exclusion of finitely many primes. The product group constructed here verifies the abstract theorem assumptions; it is not asserted to be the Galois image of a particular Shimura point.

The fixed centralizer in this application admits the required extension after excluding finitely many primes. This keeps the full stabilizer \(F\), rather than substituting \(F^0\) in the orbit problem.

Put \(R=\mathbb Z_p\). Since \(F=Z_G(M)\) is fixed over \(\mathbb Q\), outside a finite set of primes its integral model is smooth, \(F^0_R\) is connected reductive, and \(Q=F_R/F^0_R\) is finite etale. Exclude also the prime divisors of its order \(m\). The connected quotient results in §7.3 and Lemma 7.11 [1, PDF pp. 56–58, 61] then give \[B=R[G]^{F^0_R},\qquad Y=\operatorname{Spec}B,
 \qquad Y_k=G_k/F^0_k\] for geometric fibers \(k\), with \(B\) of finite type and \(Y\) smooth. Right translation defines a \(Q\)-action on \(Y\). Set \[A=B^Q=R[G]^{F_R},\qquad X=\operatorname{Spec}A.\] After a finite etale base change making \(Q\) constant, the averaging operator \(m^{-1}\sum_{q\in Q}q\) is an idempotent onto the invariants. Thus invariants commute with passage to the residue and fraction fields. The orbit polynomial \(\prod_{q\in Q}(T-qb)\) shows that \(B\) is integral over \(A\); the finite-group invariant argument gives finite generation of \(A\) and finiteness of \(B\) over \(A\). These properties descend from the etale cover. Moreover \(A\subset R[G]\) is torsion-free, hence flat over the discrete valuation ring \(R\).

The action of \(Q_k\) on \(G_k/F^0_k\) is free: a component fixing \(gF^0_k\) must be the identity component. Its finite etale quotient is therefore smooth and \[X_k=(G_k/F^0_k)/Q_k=G_k/F_k .\] Finite presentation, flatness and geometrically smooth fibers imply that \(X/R\) is smooth. The same fiber criterion, applied to \(G\to X\), makes that morphism smooth and surjective. These are precisely the quotient inputs needed below.

For completeness, the normalization step also retains the full \(F\). Let \(S\) be the schematic orbit closure for a vector satisfying the other hypotheses of Theorem 7.1. In Lemma 7.10 [1, PDF pp. 59–61], \(X\) is normal, and \(X\to S\) is quasi-finite: its generic fiber is an isomorphism, and its special fibers have equal dimensions and the transitive orbit description just obtained. The normalization \(\widetilde S\) has a genuine \(G_R\)-action. Indeed the action lifts through normalization because \(G\times_R\widetilde S\) is normal by smooth base change; uniqueness gives the action law. Thus the corrected coaction hypothesis of Problem 4 applies. The proof of claim (3) of Lemma 7.10 uses Lemma 7.4, Corollary 7.5, stabilizer dimensions and connectedness of \(G\), with no further connectedness requirement on \(F\). It makes the special fiber of \(\widetilde S\) one geometric orbit. Zariski’s Main Theorem then identifies \(X\) with \(\widetilde S\), so \(X\to S\) is integral.

Proposition 7.15 [1, PDF p. 63] now gives the same integral-point criterion (67), over the integral closure \(\overline{\mathbb Z}_p\subset\overline{\mathbb Q}_p\) used in the paper. Smoothness and geometric surjectivity of \(G\to X\) also give the lifting step of Proposition 7.14. No assertion of surjectivity on \(\mathbb F_p\)-rational points is needed. In §6.3 [1, PDF p. 47], Cartan decomposition uses only the hyperspecial model of \(G\), and the two zero sets are exactly \[h_v(g)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 gF\in X(\overline{\mathbb Z}_p)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h_{v'}(g)=0.\] The convex zero sets therefore coincide. Corollary 8.3 uses the unchanged representation weights, so the same constant \(C(\Sigma(\rho))\) works and no additive constant is introduced.

This finite exclusion is allowed: Proposition 5.7 states \(p\gg0\), and §5.1.3 [1, PDF p. 21] requires the uniform estimate only at almost all primes, with separate treatment of the remaining ones. The repair is verified for that actual fixed-centralizer application, using the stated connected quotient and normalization foundations. It is additional reasoning, not a claim that the authors supplied or adopted it.

Equation (37) feeds Corollary 5.8 and the remaining local-height cases, then Theorems 5.4 and 5.1 and the Section 3 strategy for Theorem 1.4. The original invocation still fails an explicit hypothesis at this core step. Its assessment remains Major under the claim-level standard for a demonstrated invalid central derivation. The complete finite-component repair is recorded separately: the inequality and final theorem are not refuted, and the bridge is no longer an unresolved repair in this review.

analysis: Remark 2.1.3(2), PDF p. 5 (printed p. 253), asserts in paraphrase that \([U:U']\le p\) preserves the subgroup generated by residual unipotents: \(U'(p)^\dagger=U(p)^\dagger\). The equality endpoint is false.

Fix a prime \(p_0\ge5\), take \(M=G=\operatorname{GL}_2\), and let \[C=\{I+aE_{12}:a\in\mathbb F_{p_0}\}.\] Set \(U_{p_0}\) equal to its full inverse image under reduction \(\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z_{p_0})\to\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_{p_0})\), and set \(U_q=\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z_q)\) at other primes. In the product \(U\), replace the \(p_0\)-factor by \(1+p_0M_2(\mathbb Z_{p_0})\) to obtain \(U'\). Then \[
 [U:U']=p_0,\qquad U(p_0)^\dagger=C,\qquad U'(p_0)^\dagger=1.\] All local factors are open and Zariski dense in \(\operatorname{GL}_2\). For a fixed \(D\), choose \(q>\max(p_0,D,3)\). The same coset-action argument forces every index-at-most-\(D\) residual subgroup to contain \(\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_q)\), which acts absolutely irreducibly with scalar commutant. Thus Definition 2.1 is satisfied; the exceptional prime \(p_0\) is permitted by its quantifiers.

The corrected hypothesis is \([U:U']<p\). A unipotent of \(p\)-power order acts trivially on fewer than \(p\) cosets, so all such elements lie in the smaller residual group and the dagger groups agree. This proves the corrected statement. Actual source images confirm the printed non-strict inequality; the example is not based on OCR.

The traced Section 5 uses have fixed index bounds followed by sufficiently large primes, so their cutoffs can impose \(p>D\); no essential use of the equality endpoint was found. The assessment is Minor, based on this dependency check and the proved strict-index assertion, not merely on the small size of the correction.

analysis: Lemma 5.12, PDF pp. 37–39 (printed pp. 285–287), seeks a bounded-index \(U'\subset U\) with \[Z_{M^{\mathrm{ad}}}(\operatorname{ad}U')=Z_M(U')/Z(M).\] Its proof specifies \(U[e]\), the intersection of the kernels of all homomorphisms \(U\to\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z\), for a suitable \(e\). That specified subgroup need not satisfy the displayed equality.

Take \(M=\operatorname{SL}_2\) over \(\mathbb F_{17}\), \(e=2\), and \[g=\operatorname{diag}(2,9),\quad U=\langle g\rangle\simeq C_8,\quad
 h=g^2=\operatorname{diag}(4,13).\] Here \(e\) is divisible by the order of \(Z(M)(\overline{\mathbb F}_{17})\), and the prescribed subgroup is \(U[2]=\langle h\rangle\simeq C_4\). For \[w=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\] direct calculation gives \(whw^{-1}=-h\). Thus \(\operatorname{ad}(w)\) centralizes \(\operatorname{ad}(U[2])\), although \(w\), and every centrally modified lift of it, fails to centralize \(h\). Since \(h\) has distinct eigenvalues, \(Z_M(U[2])\) is the diagonal torus; the projective centralizer has an additional Weyl component.

An independently written finite-field enumeration retained in `native_galois_cyclic_calculation.json` checks the same matrix equalities and counts 16 elements in the \(\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_{17})\) centralizer of \(h\), against 32 in the inverse image of the projective centralizer. The direct matrix witness proves the discrepancy without identifying rational points of a quotient with a quotient of rational points.

Equation reference: eq:weaker. The commutator argument does prove the weaker statement \[
 Z_{M^{\mathrm{ad}}}(\operatorname{ad}U)
       \subseteq \operatorname{im}\bigl(Z_M(U[e])\to M^{\mathrm{ad}}\bigr).\] Indeed, for a lift of an element on the left, its commutators with \(U\) form a homomorphism into the finite central group; the kernel intersection kills its cyclic coordinates. This argument keeps \(U\) on the left. It does not permit replacing it there by \(U[e]\).

The existential assertion of Lemma 5.12 is not refuted by this example: \(U'=1\), of index 8, works in this individual case. Its general strong form remains unverified in this review. In the actual use in Lemma 5.11, however, [eq:weaker] (#eq:weaker) is enough: the Tate property identifies the centralizer of the selected bounded-index subgroup with \(Z(M)\), forcing the projective centralizer of the original subgroup to be trivial. Thus the assessment is Minor: the proposed witness and stronger proof assertion fail, whereas the required downstream implication has a complete weaker replacement.

A sufficient repair is to require stability under the \(G_{\mathbb Z_p}\)-coaction. The actual applications have this stronger property. In Lemma 7.6, \(A=\mathbb Z_p[G]^F\); left and right translations commute, and flat base change preserves the kernel defining invariants, giving the genuine left coaction. In Lemma 7.10, the action on a schematic orbit closure lifts uniquely to its normalization: the product with the smooth group is normal, and the dominant action factors through the normalization. Uniqueness gives the group law. The normalization interfaces are supported by the precise primary statements in [stacks].

The assessment is Minor: the general auxiliary proposition is false, while the two traced applications satisfy the corrected hypothesis. This coaction repair is also used in the normalization step of the finite-component extension proved in Problem 1.

The centralizer \(Z_G(M)\) is the full group scheme, not automatically its identity component. The abelianization \(M^{\mathrm{ab}}\), the full center \(Z(M)\), and the connected center are different objects. analysis: The first preliminary bullet before Lemma B.5, PDF p. 72 (printed p. 320), asserts boundedly many \(\operatorname{GL}_n(\overline{\mathbb F}_p)\)-conjugacy classes of semisimple algebraic subgroups for fixed \(n\), uniformly in \(p\). Even at one fixed prime and dimension, the unrestricted assertion is false.

Fix \(p\ge5\), \(n=4\), and for every \(r\ge1\) let \[S_r=\{\operatorname{diag}(g,\operatorname{Frob}^{r}(g)):g\in\operatorname{SL}_2\}.\] This is an \(\mathbb F_p\)-defined closed connected semisimple subgroup, isomorphic to \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) by its first projection. Its Lie algebra is \(\operatorname{diag}(\mathfrak{sl}_2,0)\). The common fixed space of that Lie algebra is the second two-dimensional block, and the span of its images is the first block. Any conjugacy \(S_r\to S_s\) must therefore be block diagonal, say \(\operatorname{diag}(a,b)\). Its induced equations, applied to \(g=I+tE_{12}\), imply \[I+t^{p^r}N_1=I+t^{p^s}N_2\] for nonzero constant matrices \(N_1,N_2\). Polynomial degrees force \(r=s\). Thus the groups are pairwise nonconjugate even over the algebraic closure.

The actual printed conjugating field is \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p\); the review does not use the incorrect OCR reading \(\mathbb F_p\). There is also relevant mathematical counterevidence: \(S_r(\mathbb F_p)\) is always diagonal \(\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_p)\), so its Nori envelope is diagonal \(\operatorname{SL}_2\), not \(S_r\). The displayed family does not contradict the narrower Nori-group setting actually needed.

More directly, the two structural bounds used in Lemma B.5 do not need finiteness of embeddings. A semisimple subgroup of \(\operatorname{GL}_n\) has rank at most \(n\). There are finitely many semisimple root data of that bounded rank, including the finitely many central-isogeny types. Their centers have uniformly bounded order, and their outer automorphism groups are bounded by automorphisms of the corresponding based root data. Taking maxima gives the required constants. This proves the needed replacement without the false embedding-finiteness assertion.
The assessment is Minor, limited to an unnecessarily strong auxiliary assertion. No counterexample to Lemma B.5 or Theorem B.1 is established.

Title: Technical Verification of
\(C^*\)-Rigidity of Bounded Geometry Metric Spaces
# Paper identity, version and scope

The paper is Diego Martínez and Federico Vigolo, \(C^*\)-rigidity of bounded geometry metric spaces, Publications Mathématiques de l’IHÉS 141 (2025), 333–348, DOI 10.1007/s10240-025-00155-3 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10240-025-00155-3) [paper]. This report concerns the acquired 16-page publisher version of record, published online on 4 March 2025. The separately acquired arXiv:2501.03128v1 author source is not asserted equivalent to that version. A physical PDF page is one-based; its printed number is larger by 332.

The root reviewer read the complete extracted canonical text. The principal checks concern definitions and quantifiers, Proposition 3.2, Theorems A and B, Proposition 4.3 and Theorem 4.5. Full text reading is distinguished from independent reproof of every external dependency. No separate supplement or original computational repository was identified in the bounded source checks; no defect is inferred from their absence. There are no manufactured numbered Problems.
# Operative definitions and external interfaces

Throughout the operative arguments, \(X,Y\) are uniformly locally finite ordinary metric spaces. Thus nonempty bounded balls are finite, and each nonempty space is countable by exhaustion about a fixed point. The main Roe and controlled-propagation algebras use \(H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)\); the uniform Roe algebra uses \(H=\mathbb C\). The zero Hilbert space is not an alternative coefficient choice for the main rigidity assertion.

Write \(P_A\) for the projection onto \(\ell^2(A;H)\). Weak approximate control means that for every propagation bound \(r\) and error \(\varepsilon>0\), one propagation bound \(R\) works for all contractions of propagation at most \(r\). In particular it controls the projections \(P_A\), even when these are not locally compact for infinite-dimensional \(H\).

The spatiality interface in Theorem 2.14 can be recovered from the compact operators: they form the unique minimal nonzero ideal in either algebra, and an isomorphism on that ideal is spatial. Multiplying by rank-one operators then shows that the same unitary implements the entire isomorphism. This argument does not require separability.

The exact author version of Braga–Vignati [bv] was consulted for the uniform-approximation and multiplier interfaces. Its Theorems 3.4–3.5 do not require property A, despite the title of that paper. For the Roe interface, control initially stated on the Roe algebra extends to every bounded finite-propagation contraction: compress by diagonal finite-rank finite-support projections, use the uniform bound, and take a weak-operator limit of bounded approximants. Propagation constraints and the closed error ball persist under that limit. The bounded auxiliary notes also supply a separable reducing-space argument for arbitrary \(H\); the main coefficient choices already lie within the directly consulted scope.
# The concentration estimate and coarse inverse maps

Equation reference: eq:energy, eq:corner. Consider Proposition 3.2, PDF pp. 7–8 (printed pp. 339–340). Let \(U:\ell^2(X;H)\to\ell^2(Y;H)\) be unitary, choose a unit vector \(h\in H\), and set \[v=U^*(\delta_y\otimes h),\qquad B=B_Y(y;R),\qquad
 w_x=(I-P_B)UP_xv .\] Under its hypothesis \(\|P_BU P_x\|\le\delta\), \[
 \sum_x\|w_x\|^2
 \ge (1-\delta^2)\sum_x\|P_xv\|^2
 =1-\delta^2.\] The original family \(P_xv\) is orthogonal. Its signed sums converge unconditionally, uniformly in the signs on tails. Applying the bounded operator \((I-P_B)U\) proves the same convergence needed for \(w_x\). Finite Rademacher averaging followed by this limit therefore gives \[\mathbb E\Bigl\|\sum_x\epsilon_xw_x\Bigr\|^2
       =\sum_x\|w_x\|^2 .\] Moreover \(\sum_xw_x=(I-P_B)Uv=0\). With \(A=\{x:\epsilon_x=1\}\), the signed sum equals \(2\sum_{x\in A}w_x\). For any \(0<\varepsilon<\frac12\sqrt{1-\delta^2}\), choose \(\eta<1-\delta^2-4\varepsilon^2\). The averaging argument then supplies signs for which \[
 \|P_{Y\setminus B}UP_AU^*P_y\|
 \ge \Bigl\|\sum_{x\in A}w_x\Bigr\|
 >\varepsilon.\] Local finiteness of \(Y\) ensures \(d_Y(y,Y\setminus B)>R\), so [eq:corner] (#eq:corner) contradicts \(\varepsilon\)-\(R\)-quasi-locality. This verifies the constant \(1/2\), the quantifiers and the strict error margin.

The general wording of Lemma 3.1 needs the usual almost-everywhere or finite-partial-sum interpretation: square-summable norms alone do not make every signed series converge, as \(v_n=h/n\) illustrates. Its actual application above has the stronger unconditional convergence, so that wording does not leave a gap in Proposition 3.2. Likewise, in Lemma 2.13 one can choose witness vectors with norms strictly greater than half the asserted lower bound, or use error \(\delta^2/8\). The printed weak inequalities do not obstruct the required strict contradiction.

For Theorem A, weak approximate control gives a single \(R\) for all \(UP_AU^*\). The contrapositive of Proposition 3.2 then chooses \(g(y)\) with \(\|P_{B(y;R)}UP_{g(y)}\|>\delta\). Apply Lemma 2.13 to \(U^*\), which implements the inverse isomorphism, and to \(B(y;R)\cup B(y';R)\). Its diameter is at most \(2R+d_Y(y,y')\), giving uniform control of \(g\). The symmetric construction gives \(f\).

To check \(g\circ f\), use \(U^*\), the domain ball \(B(f(x);R)\), and output sets \(\{g(f(x))\}\) and \(B(x;R)\). The two norm bounds in the proof give a uniform bound on the distance between these sets; adding \(R\) bounds \(d_X(g(f(x)),x)\). The other composition is symmetric. This reconstruction retains the uniform constants and does not interchange pointwise and uniform choices.
# The refinement and the outer automorphism group

Theorem 4.5, PDF pp. 10–12, assumes infinite-dimensional \(H\). For a finite-rank diagonal projection \(p=\sum_i p_{x_i}\), Claim 4.6 chooses fiber unitaries so that the unwanted output tails have orthogonal ranges as well as orthogonal initial supports. Only finitely many finite-dimensional constraints occur at each step; infinite-dimensionality supplies the needed room. The norm of the sum of those tails is therefore their maximum norm, rather than a bound depending on the number of fibers.

The product-approximation step can require contractive approximants without changing propagation: first approximate a contraction with error \(\varepsilon/4\), then rescale by \(\max(1,\|s\|)\). The resulting error is at most \(\varepsilon/2\). This justifies the stated product error with a uniform support radius.

Here is a direct justification of the final closure step, also valid for nets. Let \(S_R\) be the linear subspace of operators supported within radius \(R\) of \(f\). Its defining zero matrix blocks make it weak-operator closed. If \[T_\lambda=S_\lambda+E_\lambda,\qquad
 S_\lambda\in S_R,\quad \|E_\lambda\|\le\varepsilon,\quad
 T_\lambda\longrightarrow T\ \hbox{strongly},\] take a weak-operator convergent subnet of the errors in their compact ball, with limit \(E\). Then \(S_\lambda\to T-E\) weakly, so \(T-E\in S_R\) and \(\|E\|\le\varepsilon\). Thus the fixed-radius error neighborhood is strongly closed. No assertion that every strongly convergent net is uniformly norm bounded is needed.

Proposition 4.3 preserves local compactness using finite-set tails. For finite \(A\), Lemma 2.13 gives finite neighborhoods \(N_R(B)\) such that \(\|(I-P_{N_R(B)})U^*P_A\|\to0\). For every locally compact \(t\) on the whole space, \(tP_{N_R(B)}\) is compact because that neighborhood is finite. Hence \(UtU^*P_A\) is a norm limit of compact operators; the left condition follows similarly. This supplies the argument with the correct whole-space operator domain.

For Theorem B, let \(T_n\to U\) in norm with every \(T_n\) coarsely supported on \(f\), and choose a unitary cover \(W\) of \(f\). Each \(T_nW^*\) has finite propagation: any nonzero block factors through an input point whose two output points are within the two support radii of its image under \(f\). Consequently \[UW^*=\lim_nT_nW^*\in C^*_{\mathrm{cp}}(X)\] is unitary. This proves surjectivity modulo multiplier innerness.

Injectivity also has a short direct check. If the cover \(U_f\) induces an inner automorphism, it differs from a unitary in \(C^*_{\mathrm{cp}}(X)\) by a scalar, since the commutant of all compact operators is scalar. Choose finite-propagation \(S\) with \(\|U_f-S\|<1\). If \(d(f(x),x)\) exceeded the sum of the support radius of \(U_f\) and \(\operatorname{Prop}(S)\), the images of the \(x\)-fiber under \(U_f\) and \(S\) would be orthogonal. This would force \(\|(U_f-S)P_x\|\ge1\), a contradiction. Thus \(f\) is close to the identity. Covers of close maps and compositions obey the same support estimates, giving the stated canonical homomorphism.
# Clarifications, limitations and conclusion

The proof uses \(Y\) for output complements and \(B(\ell^2(X;H),\ell^2(Y;H))\) for operators between the two spaces. The local \(X/Y\), tensor-order and whole-space/domain slips in the printed formulas are uniquely resolved by those types and do not invalidate the reconstructed estimates. Implementing unitaries are understood modulo their scalar ambiguity, or as normalizers before taking that quotient.

The countable basis in the displayed covering-unitary construction is appropriate to the main coefficient \(H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)\). For other infinite Hilbert dimensions, use the actual basis index set; multiplication by a finite nonzero cell cardinality leaves that infinite cardinality unchanged. Empty-space wording in the elementary identity and finite-dimension remarks is a convention boundary. For the main nonzero coefficients, an isomorphism with one empty space forces both spaces to be empty, where the conclusion is immediate.

The review retains the externally proved uniform-approximation and multiplier inputs at their identified interfaces. It does not claim to reprove all of their foundations or the broader arbitrary-proper-space results reserved for another paper. No empirical or author-code verification is relevant to these exact arguments.

Title: Technical Verification of
\(p\)-Adic Hodge Parameters in the
Crystabelline Representations of \(\mathrm{GL}_n\)
# Paper identity and review scope

The paper is Yiwen Ding, \(p\)-Adic Hodge parameters in the crystabelline representations of \(\mathrm{GL}_n\), Publications Mathématiques de l’IHÉS 142 (2025), 1–74, DOI 10.1007/s10240-025-00156-2 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10240-025-00156-2) [paper]. The reviewed source is the acquired 74-page publisher version of record, published online on 10 July 2025. Physical PDF and printed page numbers coincide. The separately acquired arXiv:2407.21237v2 source (12 June 2025) was used to clarify notation; its description as a final author version does not identify it with the publisher PDF.

The root role read the introduction, central construction and reconstruction, the finding locations and their interfaces. Together these reads cover the complete canonical text, including the references. Selected original pages were actually viewed. This is not a claim to have independently reproved every cited result or viewed every source page. The coverage ledger records exact ranges, external interfaces, exclusions and actual image observations.

The substantive checks include genericity and noncriticality at every refinement, deformation quotients, the higher-intertwining criterion, the map \(t_D\), recovery of Hodge parameters, universal extensions, and the hypotheses in the patched and unpatched applications. The source checks did not identify a separate supplement or original computational implementation. No mathematical defect is inferred from that bounded absence.
# Assumptions and notation that matter

Let \(K/\mathbb Q_p\) be finite, \(d=[K:\mathbb Q_p]\), and let the coefficient field \(E\) contain all embeddings of \(K\). The smooth characters \(\phi_i\) are generic: the ratio of any two distinct ordered parameters is neither \(1\) nor \(|\cdot|_K\). The Hodge–Tate weights are strictly decreasing at every embedding. Every refinement is noncritical; noncriticality of only one selected refinement would not support the argument.

The category \(\Phi\Gamma_{\mathrm{nc}}(\phi,\mathbf h)\) includes crystabelline \((\varphi,\Gamma)\)-modules that are not étale. An example in this category must not silently be called a Galois representation. The Galois applications separately assume that \(D=D_{\mathrm{rig}}(\rho)\) and impose their stated automorphic hypotheses.

On the Galois side, the bar has a precise meaning: \[\overline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1_?(D,D)=\operatorname{Ext}^1_?(D,D)/\operatorname{Ext}^1_0(D,D),\qquad
 \operatorname{Ext}^1_0(D,D)=\operatorname{Ker}\kappa_w .\] Lemma 2.11 makes the last kernel independent of \(w\). Writing \(c=n(n-1)/2\) and \(b=n(n+1)/2\), the dimension checks give \[\begin{aligned}
 \dim\operatorname{Ext}^1(D,D)&=1+n^2d,&
 \dim\operatorname{Ext}^1_0(D,D)&=1+cd-n,\\
 \dim\overline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1(D,D)&=bd+n,&
 \dim\overline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1_w(D,D)&=n(d+1).\end{aligned}\] For \(K\ne\mathbb Q_p\), the representation determines the flattened single-embedding objects \(D_\sigma\), not necessarily all relative filtrations of \(D\). The stronger full-\(D\) conclusion is correctly restricted to \(K=\mathbb Q_p\).
# Two confirmed local problems

Equation reference: eq:wrongdim. Problem 1 (Wrong sign in the quotient dimension).  In the proof of Corollary 2.14, p. 19, the dimension comparison used to prove that (2.19) is bijective prints \[
 \dim_E\overline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1_{\mathcal F_P}(D,D)
   =d\dim(B\cap L_P)-n
   =\sum_i\dim_E\overline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1(M_i,M_i).\] The middle expression must have \(+n\).

Equation reference: eq:rightdim. Direct calculation and hypotheses. Let \(L_P=\prod_{i=1}^r\mathrm{GL}_{n_i}\), with \(\sum_i n_i=n\), and set \(b_L=\sum_i n_i(n_i+1)/2\). The paper’s Proposition 2.13 and (2.14) give \[\begin{aligned}
 \dim_E\overline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1_{\mathcal F_P}(D,D)
 &= (1+d\dim P)-(1+dc-n)\notag\\
 &=d(\dim P-c)+n
 =db_L+n\notag\\
 &=\sum_i\left(d\,\frac{n_i(n_i+1)}2+n_i\right).
 \end{aligned}\] Here \(\dim P-c=b_L\), an identity for the block upper triangular parabolic. Equation [eq:rightdim] (#eq:rightdim) equals the target dimension by (2.16) applied to the \(M_i\).

For a concrete allowed case take \(n=2\), \(K=\mathbb Q_5\), \(P=B\), distinct Frobenius eigenvalues \(1,2\), and weights \(1>0\). A filtration whose nontrivial line is \(E(1,1)\) is transverse to both coordinate lines, hence every refinement is noncritical. The generic ratios avoid \(1\) and \(5^{\pm1}\). The filtered-module construction gives an object of the paper’s \((\varphi,\Gamma)\)-module category; no weak-admissibility assertion is needed. Then \(\dim\operatorname{Ext}^1_0=0\), the source dimension is \(4\), and the two rank-one target factors each have dimension \(2\). The printed middle value in [eq:wrongdim] (#eq:wrongdim) is \(2-2=0\).

Counterevidence, impact and correction. The minus sign is visible in the original PDF, so this is not an extraction error. The preceding formulas and the target calculation already force the corrected value. The error affects the explicit auxiliary numerical equality; it does not refute Corollary 2.14. The map is surjective as established before that equality, and [eq:rightdim] (#eq:rightdim) proves equal source and target dimensions. Thus its bijectivity follows with no changed hypotheses or conclusion. This is a Minor calculation defect with its complete local repair verified. An exact diagnostic checked [eq:rightdim] (#eq:rightdim) for all ordered block compositions of \(1\le n\le7\) and \(d=1,2,3\) (381 cases); the displayed algebra proves the general formula.

Problem 2 (The locally algebraic part is larger than the socle).  The proof of Theorem 4.5, p. 63, asserts \(\widetilde\pi^{\mathrm{lalg}}\simeq\pi_{\mathrm{alg}}(\phi,\mathbf h)\), citing Lemma 4.2(2). The cited lemma controls the multiplicity of the simple representation in a Hom space. It does not exclude nonsplit locally algebraic selfextensions, and such an extension occurs inside \(\widetilde\pi\).

Equation reference: eq:twist. A selfextension satisfying the operative conditions. Put \(A=\pi_{\mathrm{alg}}(\phi,\mathbf h)\), and normalize \(v_K(\varpi_K)=1\). Define an \(E\)-representation on \(V=A\otimes_E E[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)\) by \[
 g\cdot(a\otimes u)
   =(g\cdot a)\otimes
     \bigl(1+\epsilon\,v_K(\det g)\bigr)u .\] It fits into \(0\to A\to V\to A\to0\). The additional factor is smooth, since \(v_K\circ\det\) is locally constant. As \(A\) is smooth tensored with algebraic, every vector of \(V\) is locally algebraic.

This extension is nonsplit. The central element \(z=\varpi_K I_n\) acts on \(A\) by its nonzero central scalar \(\chi_A(z)\), whereas on \(V\) it acts by \[\chi_A(z)
 \begin{pmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\] in a suitable order of the two factors. The coefficient \(n\) is nonzero in the characteristic-zero field \(E\). A split sum of two copies of \(A\) would have scalar action at \(z\).

Why this extension is present in the actual object. Fix a refinement \(w\) and put \(B_w=\mathrm{PS}_1(w(\phi),\mathbf h)\). Its quotient by \(A\) has the nonalgebraic simple constituents listed in Section 3.1.2 and no copy of \(A\). Consequently \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{GL}_n(K)}(A,B_w/A)=0\), and the long exact sequence makes \[\operatorname{Ext}^1(A,A)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}^1(A,B_w)\] injective. Push out \(V\) along \(A\hookrightarrow B_w\). The resulting nonzero extension \(V_w\) contains \(V\) as a subrepresentation. Proposition 3.6(2) identifies this pushout with the smooth character direction used in the principal-series construction.

Counterevidence and the conclusion actually needed. The disputed superscript is visibly \(\mathrm{lalg}\) in the publisher PDF. The surrounding argument excludes all nonalgebraic simple subrepresentations and needs only \(\operatorname{soc}_{\mathrm{GL}_n(K)}\widetilde\pi\simeq A\). Lemma 4.2(2) gives \[\dim_E\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{GL}_n(K)}
   \bigl(A,\Pi_\infty^{R_\infty\text{-an}}[\mathfrak a_x]\bigr)=1 .\] An existing copy of \(A\) lies in \(\widetilde\pi\). Together with the preceding exclusion of the other possible simple constituents, this proves exactly the required socle assertion. Replace the false equality by this Hom-dimension argument. The subsequent multiplicity and universal-extension steps then retain their stated inputs. The confirmed defect is the unnecessarily strong local assertion, not a demonstrated failure of Theorem 4.5 or its compatibility corollaries. Its assessment is Minor; the weaker sufficient statement is already proved by the cited lemma, and its use has been traced explicitly.
# Central proof checks and resolved candidates
## Higher intertwining and single-embedding recovery

The reconstruction in Section 2 distinguishes the dimension-\(d\) cup-product kernel for full \(D\) from the dimension-one kernel after flattening away from a single embedding. For \(K=\mathbb Q_p\), the extension class therefore spans the kernel; for general \(K\), this argument applies to \(D_\sigma\). The rank and Hom arguments use genericity and strict weight separation.

The last equivalence in Theorem 2.32 can be made explicit. After twisting to set \(\kappa_{\mathcal F,2}=0\), restriction \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(D,D_1)\to\operatorname{Ext}^1(D_1,D_1)\) has kernel dimension \((n-1)d-1\). By Proposition 2.29, the inverse image of the specified intertwining subspace has dimension \[[1+(n-1)(n-2)d]+[(n-1)d-1]=(n-1)^2d .\] It contains the injective image of \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(C_1,D_1)\), which has that same dimension. Hence the two spaces agree, supplying the converse rather than only the forward inclusion.
## Spanning in Theorem 3.21

Equation (3.43), p. 49, is written as a direct sum of character spaces of maximal-Levi centres \(Z_j\), together with the full centre \(Z\). Each \(Z_j\) has rank two, so that literal direct sum has dimension \((2n-1)(d+1)\), whereas \(\operatorname{Hom}(T(K),E)\) has dimension \(n(d+1)\). The proof’s next step requires only the spanning assertion, which holds.

Indeed, put \(H=\operatorname{Hom}(K^\times,E)\), so \(\operatorname{Hom}(T(K),E)=H^n\). Characters of the two blocks of \(L_j\), pulled back by their determinants, include \[(h,\ldots,h,0,\ldots,0),\qquad h\in H,\] with \(j\) initial entries. Together with the all-entries diagonal characters, these vectors span \(H^n\), by taking consecutive differences. They belong to the subspaces used in (2.21). The block Weyl element in the proof fixes the corresponding block characters. The two known endpoint cases therefore extend to every refinement exactly as required on p. 50. The overstated direct-sum notation is recorded as a clarification; the necessary spanning step has been verified and no dimension argument in the construction relies on directness.
## The spaces in the reconstruction diagram

Theorem 3.34, p. 56, uses barred automorphic Ext symbols in (3.53)–(3.54), while the explicitly cited (3.52) supplies parabolic-image spaces. Treating the bars as ordinary full Ext would give incorrect dimensions. The following contextual reconstruction makes the needed domain precise.

Equation reference: eq:correctdiagram. Write \(A=\pi_{\mathrm{alg}}(\phi,\mathbf h)\), \(B=\pi_{1,\sigma}(\phi,\mathbf h)\), and \[\mathcal E=\operatorname{Ext}^1_\sigma(A,B),\quad
 \mathcal E_{\mathcal F},\mathcal E_{\mathcal G}\subset\mathcal E,\quad
 \mathcal K=\operatorname{Ker}t_{D_\sigma},\quad
 \mathcal K_{\mathcal F}=\mathcal K\cap\mathcal E_{\mathcal F},
 \quad
 \mathcal K_{\mathcal G}=\mathcal K\cap\mathcal E_{\mathcal G}.\] The tautological connecting maps identify the parabolic images in \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_\sigma(A,\pi^-)\) and \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_\sigma(A,\pi^+)\) with \(\mathcal E_{\mathcal F}/\mathcal K_{\mathcal F}\) and \(\mathcal E_{\mathcal G}/\mathcal K_{\mathcal G}\). Proposition 3.20 gives the surjection \[
 \frac{\mathcal E_{\mathcal F}}{\mathcal K_{\mathcal F}}
 \oplus
 \frac{\mathcal E_{\mathcal G}}{\mathcal K_{\mathcal G}}
 \longrightarrow\frac{\mathcal E}{\mathcal K}.\] Its kernel is determined by the common representation data. Diagram (3.52) identifies its source with \(V(D_{1,\sigma},C_{1,\sigma})_\sigma\). After the induction hypothesis identifies \(D_{1,\sigma}\) and \(C_{1,\sigma}\), the middle map is unchanged for \(D\) and \(D'\). The same kernel therefore gives the same two Galois graph subspaces; Corollary 2.38 recovers \(D_\sigma\).

For \(n=3\), the two restricted source dimensions are \(7\) and \(7\), the target dimension is \(9\), and the kernel dimension is \(5\). Full Ext spaces would instead give \(20\) in the middle. The undefined extra bar admits the parabolic-image reading specified by (3.52), and [eq:correctdiagram] (#eq:correctdiagram) completes that argument. Accordingly the full-Ext dimension objection is not graded as a proved defect in the reconstruction theorem.
# Overall impact and limits

The main construction has kernel dimension \((2^n-n(n+1)/2-1)d\); its single-embedding kernels have dimension \(2^n-n(n+1)/2-1\) and form the direct sum in Corollary 3.31. These dimensions and the rank-one and rank-two boundary cases are consistent. In the global argument, the first-order algebra action, annihilator description of \(\pi_{\min}(D)\), and the multiplicity argument are distinct from the false local equality in Problem 2.

The unpatched application is conditional on Hypotheses 4.10 and 4.15 and the stated automorphic setup; it is not an unconditional local Langlands construction for all representations. The review checks the interfaces used to pass to the specified tangent subspace and the stated multiplicity, while retaining the external patching, adjunction, triangulation and Selmer-vanishing theorems as external inputs. The exact versions and interface pages actually consulted are listed in the evidence ledger. Full reproof of those foundations is not claimed. The original low-degree spectral-sequence interface of Schraen [schraen] was inspected, but the separately linked author erratum could not be retrieved from the tried primary URLs. Its complete text and effect on the adopted interface therefore remain unverified; no defect is inferred from that access failure.

The two numbered defects have verified local corrections. Neither establishes central damage after the corrected arguments. This assessment does not use repairability alone to downgrade a core error: in Problem 1 the necessary isomorphism is independently obtained from the already stated dimensions; in Problem 2 the required socle assertion follows directly from the already proved Hom statement. The ambiguities and isolated indexing slips resolved by the surrounding definitions are not promoted to additional substantive problems. No author adoption is known from the bounded version checks.

Generic crystabelline all-refinements noncritical D, regular weights, standard parabolic blocks n_i. Test K=Q5,n2,P=B,phi eigenvalues1,2,weights1>0,line(1,1). No etaleness assumed.
analysis:
In the proof of Corollary 2.14, p. 19, the dimension comparison used to prove that (2.19) is bijective prints \[
 \dim_E\overline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1_{\mathcal F_P}(D,D)
   =d\dim(B\cap L_P)-n
   =\sum_i\dim_E\overline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1(M_i,M_i).\] The middle expression must have \(+n\).

Equation reference: eq:rightdim. Direct calculation and hypotheses. Let \(L_P=\prod_{i=1}^r\mathrm{GL}_{n_i}\), with \(\sum_i n_i=n\), and set \(b_L=\sum_i n_i(n_i+1)/2\). The paper’s Proposition 2.13 and (2.14) give \[\begin{aligned}
 \dim_E\overline{\operatorname{Ext}}^1_{\mathcal F_P}(D,D)
 &= (1+d\dim P)-(1+dc-n)\notag\\
 &=d(\dim P-c)+n
 =db_L+n\notag\\
 &=\sum_i\left(d\,\frac{n_i(n_i+1)}2+n_i\right).
 \end{aligned}\] Here \(\dim P-c=b_L\), an identity for the block upper triangular parabolic. Equation [eq:rightdim] (#eq:rightdim) equals the target dimension by (2.16) applied to the \(M_i\).

For a concrete allowed case take \(n=2\), \(K=\mathbb Q_5\), \(P=B\), distinct Frobenius eigenvalues \(1,2\), and weights \(1>0\). A filtration whose nontrivial line is \(E(1,1)\) is transverse to both coordinate lines, hence every refinement is noncritical. The generic ratios avoid \(1\) and \(5^{\pm1}\). The filtered-module construction gives an object of the paper’s \((\varphi,\Gamma)\)-module category; no weak-admissibility assertion is needed. Then \(\dim\operatorname{Ext}^1_0=0\), the source dimension is \(4\), and the two rank-one target factors each have dimension \(2\). The printed middle value in [eq:wrongdim] (#eq:wrongdim) is \(2-2=0\).

Counterevidence, impact and correction. The minus sign is visible in the original PDF, so this is not an extraction error. The preceding formulas and the target calculation already force the corrected value. The error affects the explicit auxiliary numerical equality; it does not refute Corollary 2.14. The map is surjective as established before that equality, and [eq:rightdim] (#eq:rightdim) proves equal source and target dimensions. Thus its bijectivity follows with no changed hypotheses or conclusion. This is a Minor calculation defect with its complete local repair verified. An exact diagnostic checked [eq:rightdim] (#eq:rightdim) for all ordered block compositions of \(1\le n\le7\) and \(d=1,2,3\) (381 cases); the displayed algebra proves the general formula.
result: Result: Printed auxiliary dimension false by2n; corrected general equality verified.
Impact: Supported local calculation defect; existing surjection plus independently corrected equal dimensions proves same bijectivity, with no central damage demonstrated.

problems.title: Locally algebraic part is larger than simple socle in Theorem4.5 proof
problems.source_location: Pdf page: 63 Printed page: 63 Locator: Theorem4.5 first proof paragraph after exclusion of other simple constituents.
claim: tildeπ^lalg≅πalg by Lemma4.2(2).
Full Section4.1 patched setup, including inherited hypotheses of Ref23, generic noncritical D and Lemma4.3 embeddings. Construction works in every such setup.
analysis: The proof of Theorem 4.5, p. 63, asserts \(\widetilde\pi^{\mathrm{lalg}}\simeq\pi_{\mathrm{alg}}(\phi,\mathbf h)\), citing Lemma 4.2(2). The cited lemma controls the multiplicity of the simple representation in a Hom space. It does not exclude nonsplit locally algebraic selfextensions, and such an extension occurs inside \(\widetilde\pi\).

Equation reference: eq:twist. A selfextension satisfying the operative conditions. Put \(A=\pi_{\mathrm{alg}}(\phi,\mathbf h)\), and normalize \(v_K(\varpi_K)=1\). Define an \(E\)-representation on \(V=A\otimes_E E[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)\) by \[
 g\cdot(a\otimes u)
   =(g\cdot a)\otimes
     \bigl(1+\epsilon\,v_K(\det g)\bigr)u .\] It fits into \(0\to A\to V\to A\to0\). The additional factor is smooth, since \(v_K\circ\det\) is locally constant. As \(A\) is smooth tensored with algebraic, every vector of \(V\) is locally algebraic.

This extension is nonsplit. The central element \(z=\varpi_K I_n\) acts on \(A\) by its nonzero central scalar \(\chi_A(z)\), whereas on \(V\) it acts by \[\chi_A(z)
 \begin{pmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\] in a suitable order of the two factors. The coefficient \(n\) is nonzero in the characteristic-zero field \(E\). A split sum of two copies of \(A\) would have scalar action at \(z\).

Why this extension is present in the actual object. Fix a refinement \(w\) and put \(B_w=\mathrm{PS}_1(w(\phi),\mathbf h)\). Its quotient by \(A\) has the nonalgebraic simple constituents listed in Section 3.1.2 and no copy of \(A\). Consequently \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{GL}_n(K)}(A,B_w/A)=0\), and the long exact sequence makes \[\operatorname{Ext}^1(A,A)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}^1(A,B_w)\] injective. Push out \(V\) along \(A\hookrightarrow B_w\). The resulting nonzero extension \(V_w\) contains \(V\) as a subrepresentation. Proposition 3.6(2) identifies this pushout with the smooth character direction used in the principal-series construction.

Counterevidence and the conclusion actually needed. The disputed superscript is visibly \(\mathrm{lalg}\) in the publisher PDF. The surrounding argument excludes all nonalgebraic simple subrepresentations and needs only \(\operatorname{soc}_{\mathrm{GL}_n(K)}\widetilde\pi\simeq A\). Lemma 4.2(2) gives \[\dim_E\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{GL}_n(K)}
   \bigl(A,\Pi_\infty^{R_\infty\text{-an}}[\mathfrak a_x]\bigr)=1 .\] An existing copy of \(A\) lies in \(\widetilde\pi\). Together with the preceding exclusion of the other possible simple constituents, this proves exactly the required socle assertion. Replace the false equality by this Hom-dimension argument. The subsequent multiplicity and universal-extension steps then retain their stated inputs. The confirmed defect is the unnecessarily strong local assertion, not a demonstrated failure of Theorem 4.5 or its compatibility corollaries. Its assessment is Minor; the weaker sufficient statement is already proved by the cited lemma, and its use has been traced explicitly.
result: Result: Actual tildeπ contains length-two locally algebraic selfextension, contradicting equality to simple A.

Impact: False unnecessary local strengthening. Existing Hom multiplicity1 plus exclusion of other simple constituents gives exact required socle A; no failure of4.5/compatibility corollaries established.

report: Abstract: The acquired publisher version is checked through the weighted elliptic identities, frequency estimates, propagation of almost splitting, quadratic rigidity and gauge iteration. A core propagation argument invokes a relative endpoint estimate without establishing its required hypothesis. A scalar diagnostic confirms that the displayed input bounds alone cannot give the asserted decay. Retaining a boundary term yields a weaker estimate on a smaller expanded region; its positive exponential rate is sufficient for the subsequent qualitative iteration. Separately, a Gaussian Hermite polynomial disproves the precise integrated estimate (4.5), whose correction preserves the polynomial degree. These are respectively a Major proof defect and a Minor quantitative defect. Neither is a counterexample to cylindrical shrinker rigidity. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Verification of
Singularities of Ricci Flow and Diffeomorphisms
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The paper is Tobias Holck Colding and William P. Minicozzi II, Singularities of Ricci flow and diffeomorphisms, Publications Mathématiques de l’IHÉS 142 (2025), 75–152, DOI 10.1007/s10240-025-00157-1 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10240-025-00157-1) [paper]. The reviewed source is the acquired 78-page publisher version of record, published online on 22 September 2025. Physical PDF page \(p\) corresponds to printed page \(p+74\). The separately acquired arXiv:2109.06240v4 author source, dated 19 September 2025, is a distinct version and is not asserted identical to the publisher PDF.

The bounded checks cover Sections 2–5, Sections 6, 8–9, and Sections 7, 10 and the reference list, with overlapping root checks of the operative statements and proof interfaces. Critical source pages were actually viewed, separately from text reading and rendering. This is an initial technical review, not independent acceptance or a complete reproof of every cited foundation. No separate supplement or original code repository was identified in the bounded availability checks; absence of code is not a mathematical defect.
# Definitions, quantifiers and proof architecture

The model is \(\Sigma=N^\ell\times\mathbb R^{n-\ell}\), with \(N\) closed, \(\operatorname{Ric}_N=g_N/2\), and \(\bar f=|x|^2/4+\ell/2\). Condition \((\star)\) in Section 6 is a spectral gap on trace-free \(N\)-tensors with a constant \(C_{N,n}\). It is not a statement that every positive Einstein manifold is admissible or that all constants are uniform over all \(N\). For round shrinking spheres the operative normalization is radius \(\sqrt{2(\ell-1)}\), \(\ell\ge2\), as fixed by the Ricci equation and curvature formula.

Theorem 7.1 extends the strong weighted closeness \((\star_R)\) to the weaker uniform closeness \((\dagger_{(1+\beta)R})\). Theorem 10.1 improves \((\dagger_\rho)\) to \((\star_{\theta\rho})\), for any fixed \(0<\theta<1\). Choosing \(\theta(1+\beta)>1\) gives expanding scales. The precise tangent-flow result is Theorem 10.8, which assumes the compactness and shrinking-limit conclusions of Mantegazza–Müller Theorem 1.4 [mm]; closed Type I flows are an included case. The unrestricted introductory wording is not substituted for those operative hypotheses. In the exact author version consulted, Theorem 1.4(2) allows arbitrary blow-up sequences with a fixed adjoint heat-kernel potential. It therefore supplies subsequences at the exit times used in Section 10; continuity of a time-dependent choice of entropy minimizer is not required. The potential normalization must also be aligned by its additive entropy constant. The common limiting entropy discussed there permits the same shift for the compared limits. The noncompact extension mentioned in its remarks is not treated here as a proved unrestricted theorem.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The relative endpoint hypothesis is missing in the core propagation step).  The deduction of (7.20) from Proposition 4.16, in the proof of Proposition 7.2, is invalid from the bounds established there. This is a Major defect in the displayed derivation of almost splitting.
## Original claim and exact location

Equation reference: eq:relative. Proposition 4.16, PDF pp. 34–35 (printed pp. 108–109), assumes \(\langle\mathcal Lu,u\rangle\ge-\lambda|u|^2\) on \(r_1\le b\le L\), with \(r_1\) sufficiently large, and the relative endpoint condition \[
 D(L)\le \exp\!\left(\frac{2L-1}{6}\right)I(r_1).\] It then bounds \(I(r)\) by a fixed power of \(r/r_1\) times \(I(r_1)\) for \(r\le L-1\).

In the proof of Proposition 7.2, PDF p. 49 (printed p. 123), set \(u=\operatorname{Hess}v_i\) and \(L=(1+\alpha_0)R-R^{-1}\). The displayed inputs are a polynomial bound on \(I_u,D_u\) up to \(L\), the local differential inequality (7.19), and \[I_u(s)\le C_s e^{-R^2/8}
 \quad\hbox{for each fixed sufficiently large }s.\] The text then invokes Proposition 4.16 to assert \[I_u(r)\le CR^m e^{-R^2/8}\qquad(r\le L-1),\] and derives the pointwise Hessian estimate (7.20). A polynomial upper bound on \(D_u(L)\) and a small upper bound on \(I_u(s)\) do not establish [eq:relative] (#eq:relative). In particular, no lower bound on \(I_u(s)\), or corresponding small relative bound on \(D_u(L)\), is supplied.
## An exact diagnostic of the insufficient inputs

This diagnostic addresses that inference, not all geometric hypotheses of Proposition 7.2. On the one-dimensional Gaussian shrinker, let \[f(x)=x^2/4,\qquad
 w_L(x)=\chi_L(x)e^{(x^2-L^2)/4},\] where \(0\le\chi_L\le1\) is smooth, equals one on \([-L,L]\), and vanishes outside \([-L-1,L+1]\). On every interval \(s\le |x|\le L\), \[\mathcal Lw_L=\tfrac12w_L,\qquad
 I(r)=2e^{(r^2-L^2)/2},\qquad
 D(r)=r^2e^{(r^2-L^2)/2}.\] Thus the required differential inequality holds for any positive \(\lambda\), and \(I,D\) are polynomially bounded up to \(L\). At any fixed inner radius \(s\) exceeding the required threshold, \(I(s)\) is exponentially small in \(L^2\), but \[D(L)=L^2,\qquad I(L-1)=2e^{-L+1/2}.\] The ratio \(D(L)/I(s)\) grows as \(e^{L^2/2}\), so [eq:relative] (#eq:relative) fails for all sufficiently large \(L\).
## A proved boundary-term correction

Equation reference: eq:boundary. The proof of Proposition 4.16 supplies a useful replacement. Fix \(0<\delta<\min\{1,2\lambda\}\), set \[a=2\lambda+\delta,\qquad q=2a,\qquad K=D-aI,\] and choose \(s\) above the fixed threshold in the differential estimates. The same inequality used in that proof gives \(K'(t)\ge tK(t)/3\) wherever \(K(t)>0\). Absolute continuity implies that a positive value cannot cross down through zero. Consequently \[K_+(t)\le e^{-(L^2-t^2)/6}D_+(L),\qquad s\le t\le L.\] Combining this with \(I'\le2D/t=qI/t+2K/t\) and integrating gives \[\begin{aligned}
 I(r)&\le \left(\frac rs\right)^q I(s)
 +2r^q D_+(L)\int_s^r
       t^{-q-1}e^{-(L^2-t^2)/6}\,dt\\
 &\le \left(\frac rs\right)^q
 \left\{I(s)+\frac2qD_+(L)e^{-(L^2-r^2)/6}\right\}.
 \end{aligned}\] This proof does not assume [eq:relative] (#eq:relative). It exposes the missing boundary contribution.

At \(r=L-1\), that term has only \(e^{-O(L)}\) decay. Instead restrict to \(r\le(1+\alpha_0/2)R\). For large \(R\), the established polynomial endpoint bound and [eq:boundary] (#eq:boundary) give \[I(r)\le CR^M e^{-cR^2},\qquad
 0<c\le\min\!\left\{\frac18,
 \frac{(1+\alpha_0)^2-(1+\alpha_0/2)^2}{12}\right\}.\] Thus a smaller expansion factor and a model-dependent positive exponential rate can be recovered. This does not recover the printed fixed rates \(1/8\) and \(1/16\) on their stated domains.
## Impact, counterevidence and repair range

Proposition 7.2 supplies the almost parallel fields used throughout Theorem 7.1, which is one of the two iteration steps in Theorem 10.2. The missing hypothesis is therefore tied directly to the core contribution. Its severity concerns that demonstrated derivation, not a claim that the qualitative theorem is false.

There is substantial positive counterevidence to a broader failure. Local elliptic estimates, square roots, interpolation and integration of the almost parallel fields lose only polynomial factors and fixed fractions of a positive exponent. On a further reduced expansion factor \(\beta>0\), they give \(CR^M e^{-c_1R^2}\) uniform errors for some \(c_1>0\). Choosing \(a_0<c_1/[2(1+\beta)^2]\) and enlarging the starting radius gives the \((\dagger_{(1+\beta)R})\) needed by Theorem 7.1. Section 10 requires only \(a_0>0\), with no positive lower threshold.

For completeness, the apparent global flow/completeness assertion on p. 51 can be localized. Let \(G_{ij}=\langle
abla u_i,
abla u_jangle\) and \(X_i=\sum_j(G^{-1})_{ij}
abla u_j\), so \(du_j(X_i)=\delta_{ij}\). Flowing from the central zero section along \(\sum_i x_iX_i\) gives \(u(H(q,tx))=tx\) exactly. The almost parallel estimates imply \(f(H(q,tx))=f(q)+t^2|x|^2/4+O(\varepsilon R^2)\). Choose the target radius strictly below the coordinate boundary and that boundary strictly inside the controlled region. The flow remains inside that region, the restricted map is a proper local diffeomorphism, and its degree is one because its zero-section fiber is unique. This supplies the required local product map without assuming the uncontrolled exterior already has product topology.

Finally, in the improvement step choose \[\frac1{1+\beta}<\theta<1,\qquad
 0<\epsilon<\min\{1/2,\,2(1-\theta^2)\}.\] Then \(1-\epsilon/2>\theta^2\). The Gaussian shell errors in Theorem 9.1 dominate all polynomial losses and give \((\star_{\theta\rho})\); the new scale multiplier is \(\theta(1+\beta)>1\). The weaker positive-rate repair therefore supports the qualitative extension/improvement mechanism. The original sharp propagation rate remains unverified, and no author adoption of this repair is known.
Problem 2 (The integrated frequency bound has the wrong exponential coefficient).  Theorem 4.1, equation (4.5), PDF p. 21 (printed p. 95), is false as printed. This is a Minor quantitative defect.
## Claim, hypotheses and complete counterexample

Equation reference: eq:printed. The theorem assumes \(u,\mathcal Lu\in L^2(e^{-f})\), the weight identities, \(\langle\mathcal Lu,u\rangle\ge-\lambda|u|^2\), and that \(u\) does not vanish identically outside a compact set. It states, for every \(\epsilon>0\) and all sufficiently large \(r_2>r_1\), \[
 I(r_2)\le I(r_1)(r_2/r_1)^{4\lambda}
 e^{(\bar\mu+\epsilon)(r_1^{-2}-r_2^{-2})},
 \qquad \bar\mu=2n+4\max\{\lambda-1,0\}.\]
## Correction and bounded impact

Lemma 4.7 gives \((\log I)'\le2U/r\). Integrating the preceding correct bound \(U(r)\le2\lambda[1+(\bar\mu+\epsilon)/r^2]\) yields \[I(r_2)\le I(r_1)(r_2/r_1)^{4\lambda}
 e^{\,2\lambda(\bar\mu+\epsilon)(r_1^{-2}-r_2^{-2})}.\] The missing factor is \(2\lambda\). The original image and the proof on p. 30 confirm that this is not an extraction error. For \(\lambda=1/2\) the coefficients coincide, and for other parameters the correction does not change the polynomial degree \(4\lambda\). Later estimates with a fixed multiplicative constant, or a positive power loss, can absorb it by increasing the starting radius. This defect does not itself damage the qualitative propagation or rigidity argument.
# Other checked mechanisms and honest limits

The principal symbol of \(\mathcal P\) is \(\tfrac12(|\xi|^2\operatorname{Id}+\xi\otimes\xi)\), hence positive definite. Weighted cutoff arguments control the boundary terms at infinity; properness and the weighted concentration estimate combine with local Rellich compactness to give the discrete spectral argument. The forcing in Theorem 5.5 is orthogonal to the Killing kernel, and division by positive eigenvalues gives the stated solution on its orthogonal complement.

The Section 6 Jacobi decomposition was checked with its spectral hypotheses. For \(v=x^{\top}Ax-2\operatorname{Tr}A\), where \(A\) is real symmetric, normalized Gaussian expectation with covariance \(2I\) gives \[\mathbb E[v^2]=8\operatorname{Tr}(A^2),\qquad
 q=|\nabla v|^2-\Delta|\nabla v|^2,\qquad
 \mathbb E[q^2]=128\operatorname{Tr}(A^4).\] Thus the quadratic obstruction cannot disappear through a trace-free or indefinite choice of \(A\). An independent warped-product calculation for \(g_t=(1+tu)g_N+g_{\mathbb R^{n-\ell}}\), \(f_t=\bar f+t\ell u/2\), gives \[\phi''_N(0)=-|\nabla u|^2g_N,\qquad
 \phi''_E(0)=-\ell u\,\operatorname{Hess}u-\tfrac\ell2\,du\otimes du.\] This verifies (8.2) using only \(\operatorname{Ric}_N=g_N/2\), without assuming constant sectional curvature. Symbolic residuals and twelve exact Gaussian matrix cases were saved in the native calculation record; the general argument, rather than those finite tests alone, supports the conclusion.

The gauge iteration is bounded in \(C^{5,\alpha}\) and contracting in \(C^{4,\alpha}\). Compactness and lower semicontinuity preserve the stronger bound in the limit. The center-of-mass adjustment treats the translation kernel, and the Gaussian cutoff-shell errors provide the improvement used above. The weighted \(L^1\) residual term must be retained from Theorem 9.1 and the preceding derivation; its omission in the last display (9.36) is not used to infer an additional defect.

Several local signs, radius labels and norm exponents are uniquely corrected by their immediately adjacent identities. They are not counted as independent Problems. Two claims remain bounded Needs Evidence items: the exact forcing coefficient in (5.9), which is stronger than the direct application of Theorem 4.2 records, and the unrestricted geometric scope of Proposition 5.8’s uniform elliptic estimates. The cylinder instance needed in Section 10 has the required geometric control. No counterexample to either broader statement was established, and these open items do not increase the report’s assessment.
# Overall impact and state

The highest supported assessment is Major because the missing relative endpoint hypothesis affects the core almost-splitting derivation. The boundary-term correction and parameter choices above support a weaker propagation estimate and the qualitative iteration. They do not certify the original fixed rate, a complete revised manuscript, or author adoption. The separate false integrated estimate has a fully verified local correction and is Minor. No central rigidity counterexample has been established.

analysis: The deduction of (7.20) from Proposition 4.16, in the proof of Proposition 7.2, is invalid from the bounds established there. This is a Major defect in the displayed derivation of almost splitting.

This diagnostic addresses that inference, not all geometric hypotheses of Proposition 7.2. On the one-dimensional Gaussian shrinker, let \[f(x)=x^2/4,\qquad
 w_L(x)=\chi_L(x)e^{(x^2-L^2)/4},\] where \(0\le\chi_L\le1\) is smooth, equals one on \([-L,L]\), and vanishes outside \([-L-1,L+1]\). On every interval \(s\le |x|\le L\), \[\mathcal Lw_L=\tfrac12w_L,\qquad
 I(r)=2e^{(r^2-L^2)/2},\qquad
 D(r)=r^2e^{(r^2-L^2)/2}.\] Thus the required differential inequality holds for any positive \(\lambda\), and \(I,D\) are polynomially bounded up to \(L\). At any fixed inner radius \(s\) exceeding the required threshold, \(I(s)\) is exponentially small in \(L^2\), but \[D(L)=L^2,\qquad I(L-1)=2e^{-L+1/2}.\] The ratio \(D(L)/I(s)\) grows as \(e^{L^2/2}\), so [eq:relative] (#eq:relative) fails for all sufficiently large \(L\).

Equation reference: eq:boundary. The proof of Proposition 4.16 supplies a useful replacement. Fix \(0<\delta<\min\{1,2\lambda\}\), set \[a=2\lambda+\delta,\qquad q=2a,\qquad K=D-aI,\] and choose \(s\) above the fixed threshold in the differential estimates. The same inequality used in that proof gives \(K'(t)\ge tK(t)/3\) wherever \(K(t)>0\). Absolute continuity implies that a positive value cannot cross down through zero. Consequently \[K_+(t)\le e^{-(L^2-t^2)/6}D_+(L),\qquad s\le t\le L.\] Combining this with \(I'\le2D/t=qI/t+2K/t\) and integrating gives \[\begin{aligned}
 I(r)&\le \left(\frac rs\right)^q I(s)
 +2r^q D_+(L)\int_s^r
       t^{-q-1}e^{-(L^2-t^2)/6}\,dt\\
 &\le \left(\frac rs\right)^q
 \left\{I(s)+\frac2qD_+(L)e^{-(L^2-r^2)/6}\right\}.
 \end{aligned}\] This proof does not assume [eq:relative] (#eq:relative). It exposes the missing boundary contribution.

At \(r=L-1\), that term has only \(e^{-O(L)}\) decay. Instead restrict to \(r\le(1+\alpha_0/2)R\). For large \(R\), the established polynomial endpoint bound and [eq:boundary] (#eq:boundary) give \[I(r)\le CR^M e^{-cR^2},\qquad
 0<c\le\min\!\left\{\frac18,
 \frac{(1+\alpha_0)^2-(1+\alpha_0/2)^2}{12}\right\}.\] Thus a smaller expansion factor and a model-dependent positive exponential rate can be recovered. This does not recover the printed fixed rates \(1/8\) and \(1/16\) on their stated domains.

Proposition 7.2 supplies the almost parallel fields used throughout Theorem 7.1, which is one of the two iteration steps in Theorem 10.2. The missing hypothesis is therefore tied directly to the core contribution. Its severity concerns that demonstrated derivation, not a claim that the qualitative theorem is false.

There is substantial positive counterevidence to a broader failure. Local elliptic estimates, square roots, interpolation and integration of the almost parallel fields lose only polynomial factors and fixed fractions of a positive exponent. On a further reduced expansion factor \(\beta>0\), they give \(CR^M e^{-c_1R^2}\) uniform errors for some \(c_1>0\). Choosing \(a_0<c_1/[2(1+\beta)^2]\) and enlarging the starting radius gives the \((\dagger_{(1+\beta)R})\) needed by Theorem 7.1. Section 10 requires only \(a_0>0\), with no positive lower threshold.

For completeness, the apparent global flow/completeness assertion on p. 51 can be localized. Let \(G_{ij}=\langle
abla u_i,
abla u_jangle\) and \(X_i=\sum_j(G^{-1})_{ij}
abla u_j\), so \(du_j(X_i)=\delta_{ij}\). Flowing from the central zero section along \(\sum_i x_iX_i\) gives \(u(H(q,tx))=tx\) exactly. The almost parallel estimates imply \(f(H(q,tx))=f(q)+t^2|x|^2/4+O(\varepsilon R^2)\). Choose the target radius strictly below the coordinate boundary and that boundary strictly inside the controlled region. The flow remains inside that region, the restricted map is a proper local diffeomorphism, and its degree is one because its zero-section fiber is unique. This supplies the required local product map without assuming the uncontrolled exterior already has product topology.

Finally, in the improvement step choose \[\frac1{1+\beta}<\theta<1,\qquad
 0<\epsilon<\min\{1/2,\,2(1-\theta^2)\}.\] Then \(1-\epsilon/2>\theta^2\). The Gaussian shell errors in Theorem 9.1 dominate all polynomial losses and give \((\star_{\theta\rho})\); the new scale multiplier is \(\theta(1+\beta)>1\). The weaker positive-rate repair therefore supports the qualitative extension/improvement mechanism.
