report: Abstract: The acquired publisher version is reviewed through its stratification, surface-pairing and Springer-action arguments. One local computational defect is established: the closed formula in Proposition 2.21 reconstructs incorrect compact-support Hodge numbers even for a two-dimensional torus. The primitive-block inversion is valid, and the correct geometric sum restores that proposition. The preceding sum in the printed proof is already correct; no dependence of the main curious Lefschetz argument on the erroneous closed form was found. The supported assessment is Minor. Integral lattice saturation, affine shifts, the Springer sign convention and flatness on the weight-graded cohomology were checked at their stated interfaces. This initial review does not constitute independent acceptance; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Verification of
Toric Stratifications of Character Varieties
# Identity, exact version and scope

The paper is Anton Mellit, Toric stratifications of character varieties, Publications Mathématiques de l’IHÉS 142 (2025), 153–240, DOI 10.1007/s10240-025-00158-0 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10240-025-00158-0) [paper]. This report concerns the acquired 88-page publisher version of record, published online on 25 September 2025. Physical PDF page \(p\) has printed number \(p+152\). The separately acquired arXiv:1905.10685v1 source, dated 25 May 2019 and titled Cell decompositions of character varieties, is linked from the author’s publication entry. It is an earlier related version; neither equality with the publisher text nor identity as its typesetting source is asserted.

The review reconstructs the main proof dependencies and selected calculations, with actual source-image inspection of the formulas and diagrams used as evidence. Complete text reading does not mean that every external theorem was independently reproved or that every source page was visually inspected. The coverage and source-page records retain those distinctions. No separate supplement, computational release or correction was identified in the bounded publisher, author-page and arXiv checks. Their absence is not treated as a mathematical defect.
# Definitions and main proof dependencies

The operative genericity condition is Definition 4.9, PDF p. 40: \(\prod_i\det C_i=1\), and for every \(1\le r<n\), every choice of \(r\) eigenvalues from each \(C_i\) has total product different from one. A common invariant proper subspace would violate this condition by taking determinants on that subspace. It therefore excludes reducible representations, rather than merely imposing a condition on the full determinant. The introductory omission of \(r=1\), and the repeated subscript in the determinant product, are resolved by the body definition and are not additional Problems.

The smoothness and scalar-stabilizer interface in Theorem 4.10 agrees with the explicitly consulted author version of Hausel–Letellier–Rodriguez-Villegas [hlrv], Definition 2.1.1, Proposition 2.1.4 and Theorem 2.1.5, PDF pp. 16–18. Nonemptiness is kept separate from smoothness of a possibly empty variety. At \(k=0\), the genericity condition excludes \(n>1\); when \(n=1\), the resulting space is \((\mathbb C^*)^{2g}\). Thus Theorem 8.13 does not assert an unrestricted result for all untwisted higher-rank character varieties.

Equation reference: eq:middle. For a regular semisimple last puncture, set \(r=\binom n2\) and \(d=\dim_{\mathbb C}X\). Theorem 1.2 gives a rank-\(r\) vector bundle over \(X\), with strata \[(\mathbb C^*)^{d-2i}\times\mathbb C^{i+r}.\] The center of the compact-support curious Lefschetz symmetry on each stratum is \[
 (d-2i)+2(i+r)=d+2r.\] The affine-bundle isomorphism shifts cohomological degree and weight by \(2r\), recovering center \(d\) for \(X\). Consequently Proposition 2.19 is applied with a common center on all strata. The long exact compact-support sequence is compatible with cup product, and strictness of mixed Hodge structures makes its weight-graded rows exact. The five-lemma argument then preserves the asserted isomorphisms.
# A local defect in Hodge-number reconstruction

Problem 1 (The geometric sum in Proposition 2.21 has the wrong ratio).  In Proposition 2.21, PDF p. 21 (printed p. 173), both the statement and the last closed-form step in its proof use a geometric sum with ratio \(uv\). A primitive Lefschetz step raises both the cohomological degree and the Hodge index by two, so the ratio must be \(u^2v^2\).
## Claim and hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:inversion, eq:printed. Write \(N=\cup\omega\), assume that \(X\) is Tate, \(\omega\in F^2H^2(X)\), and \(N\) satisfies curious Lefschetz with middle weight \(2d\). The proposition defines \[g_a(u)=\sum_k u^k\dim\ker\bigl(N^a:H_c^k(X)\longrightarrow
 H_c^{k+2a}(X)\bigr)\quad(a>0),\qquad g_a=0\quad(a\le0),\] and \[
 f_i(u)=(1+u^2)g_{i+1}(u)-g_i(u)-u^2g_{i+2}(u).\] Its claimed output is \[
 \operatorname{MH}_X(u,v)=\sum_{i\ge0}v^{d-i}f_i(u)
       \frac{(uv)^{i+1}-1}{uv-1},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{MH}_X(u,v)=\sum_{k,j}u^kv^j\dim H_c^k(X)^{j,j}.\] The quotient is a finite polynomial sum, so the issue is unrelated to substitution at \(uv=1\).
## A counterexample satisfying every hypothesis

Take \(X=(\mathbb C^*)^2\) and \(\omega=d\log x\wedge d\log y\). This smooth variety is Tate, and the nonzero class of \(\omega\) lies in \(F^2H^2(X)\). Its compact-support groups are \[H_c^2(X)=\mathbb C(0),\qquad
 H_c^3(X)=\mathbb C(-1)^{\oplus2},\qquad
 H_c^4(X)=\mathbb C(-2).\] Poincaré duality shows that \(N:H_c^2\to H_c^4\) is an isomorphism; all other positive-degree maps are zero for degree reasons. Thus curious Lefschetz holds with middle weight \(2\), so \(d=1\). This example is also a rank-one genus-one character variety.

Equation reference: eq:wrongoutput, eq:trueoutput. The actual kernel polynomials are \[g_1=2u^3+u^4,\qquad
 g_a=u^2+2u^3+u^4\quad(a\ge2).\] Equation [eq:inversion] (#eq:inversion) correctly yields \(f_0=2u^3,\ f_1=u^2\), and \(f_i=0\) for \(i\ge2\). However, substitution in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) gives \[
 \operatorname{MH}_{\rm printed}=2u^3v+u^2(1+uv)=u^2+3u^3v,\] whereas the actual answer is \[
 \operatorname{MH}_X=u^2+2u^3v+u^4v^2.\] The printed output assigns dimension three to \(H_c^3\) of type \((1,1)\), and zero to the nonzero top group \(H_c^4\). These are incorrect numerical invariants, not merely alternative notations. The exact calculation and its input hypotheses are saved in `verification/0137/root_prop221_exact.json`.
## General correction and its verification

Equation reference: eq:correct. Let \(F_m(u)\) be the graded polynomial of primitive vectors in blocks of length \(m+1\). With \(\Delta g_a=g_a-g_{a-1}\), direct inspection of a nilpotent block gives \[\Delta g_a=\sum_{m\ge a-1}u^{2(m-a+1)}F_m,\qquad
 \Delta g_{i+1}-u^2\Delta g_{i+2}=F_i.\] This proves [eq:inversion] (#eq:inversion). A primitive vector with Hodge index \(d-i\) contributes its successive powers under \(N\) at indices \(d-i,d-i+2,\ldots,d+i\). Therefore the corrected statement is \[
 \operatorname{MH}_X(u,v)
 =\sum_{i\ge0}v^{d-i}f_i(u)\sum_{j=0}^i(u^2v^2)^j
 =\sum_{i\ge0}v^{d-i}f_i(u)
       \frac{(uv)^{2(i+1)}-1}{(uv)^2-1}.\] The finite-sum interpretation applies also at \((uv)^2=1\). This derivation verifies the correction for every primitive block under the original assumptions, and hence for their direct sum. The saved exact symbolic checks additionally reproduce the torus counterexample and the kernel inversion on 35 finite blocks.
## Counterevidence, impact and classification

The strongest counterevidence is on the same page: the preceding double sum in the printed proof already contains \(v^{d-i+2j}u^{2j}f_i(u)\), which is correct. The primitive decomposition and kernel inversion also remain valid. The error is therefore consistent with a transcription mistake. No subsequent use of the incorrect closed form was found in the canonical text, and the main stratification and curious Lefschetz proofs use other propositions.

This report retains one Minor finding because the independently stated numerical reconstruction, when used as printed, produces the wrong Hodge numbers on a fully admissible input. It does not count unrelated typographical slips as findings. The supported consequence is confined to Proposition 2.21’s closed formula. Neither a failure of the main Lefschetz theorem nor a defect in its primitive-block mechanism is established. Equation [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) restores the stated numerical reconstruction; author adoption and any prior discovery remain unverified.
# Geometric and representation-theoretic checks

The bounded checks of Sections 5–6 include the braid relations, the up/down/stay stratification, the local surface gluings and the identification of the logarithmic two-form with the intersection pairing on the capped surface, up to its fixed nonzero normalization. The overline in \(H_1(\overline\Sigma)\) in Corollary 6.9 is present in the actual image; its absence in extracted text is not a mathematical defect.

Two integral points in the quotient argument deserve explicit treatment. For Proposition 6.10, the boundary map \[H_1(\Sigma,A;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H_0(A;\mathbb Z)\] has image \(\ker(H_0(A;\mathbb Z)\to H_0(\Sigma;\mathbb Z))\), a saturated lattice. Its integral dual controls the stabilizer. This excludes a hidden finite stabilizer, which a dimension count alone would not exclude. For Proposition 6.13, the nonzero coordinate weights are differences of the torus coordinates attached to cycles of the braid permutation. Freeness makes the associated graph connected; a spanning tree supplies an integral character basis. Those coordinates give the asserted Zariski local trivialization. A general free torus representation would not justify choosing such a subset without this root-weight structure.

Theorem 6.14 has the common center \[\dim H_1(\overline\Sigma)+2|U_p|
   =2-n+|S_p|-c(\pi)+2|U_p|
   =2-n+\ell(\beta)-c(\pi).\] Here \(|S_p|+2|U_p|=\ell(\beta)\). The genericity condition rules out disconnected surfaces. The genus contributions and affine shifts in Section 7 were checked against this center and the dimension of the character variety. As a finite positive control, the rank-two four-puncture example has four connected walks at braid length six and one at length four. With the three choices at length four this gives seven strata and \[E_c(X;q)=(q-1)^2+6q=q^2+4q+1.\] This verifies the stated finite combinatorics and additive invariant, without asserting a new proof of the geometric stratification.

The descent of the two-form uses equality on the full action groupoid, which includes horizontality, rather than invariance under constant group elements alone. The torus splitting argument and strictness give its \(F^2\) property. The consulted author version of Guruprasad–Huebschmann–Jeffrey–Weinstein [ghjw], Theorems 7.1 and 8.3, supplies the nondegenerate parabolic pairing interface. Its invariant bilinear form has a normalization choice. For example, Mellit’s rank-one genus-one formula is \(2\,d\log a\wedge d\log b\); this corresponds to scaling the trace pairing. A nonzero scalar affects neither nondegeneracy nor curious Lefschetz. Literal identity of all conventions in the two published versions is not claimed.
# The general-puncture passage

Proposition 8.7 is checked on the full generic open set \(V\), including the repeated-eigenvalue fiber at one. After the affine cover, each relevant stratum factors over \(V\) as an affine space times a torus times \(V\). The saturated boundary lattice supplies the required splitting of the torus map. Compact-support pushforwards of the pieces are constant; successive extensions give locally constant cohomology sheaves. Strict weight filtrations retain the corresponding conclusion for the associated graded. Constancy of individual Hodge subspaces is not assumed.

For the Springer convention, the exact author version arXiv:1304.2642v2 of Achar–Henderson–Juteau–Riche [ahjr], Lemmas 4.3, 4.6 and 4.7, identifies the restriction/Grothendieck action on the top flag cohomology as the sign character. Its differently defined compact-support action must not be substituted. For \(\operatorname{GL}_n\), translation \(g\mapsto g-I\) identifies the relevant group neighborhood with an open subset of the Lie algebra, preserving stable flags and the regular-semisimple covering. This supplies the group-to-Lie-algebra interface.

Let \(N=\dim(G/B)\) in this paragraph. The sign summand in Proposition 8.5 is supported at the identity and is \(i_*\mathbb C[-2N]\); integration along the flag variety selects it. The zero-map assertion can be justified by \(\operatorname{Hom}(A,i_*V)=\operatorname{Hom}(i^*A,V)\). It does not require the false general principle that every derived morphism vanishing on all stalk cohomology groups is zero. Corollary 8.11 shifts both degree and weight by \(2N\), as required.

Section 8.5 needs flatness only after passing to \(\operatorname{Gr}^W_4H^2\). The displayed derivative is represented by \(2\sum_i d\log t_i\otimes c_1(L_i)\). Individual flag quotients may require a scalar-gauge choice. Intrinsically, the ratios \(R_i=L_i\otimes L_1^{-1}\) descend, and \(\sum_i d\log t_i=0\) on \(\det t=1\) gives \[\nabla[\omega]=
 2\sum_{i\ge2}d\log t_i\otimes c_1(R_i).\] Its values lie in \(W_2\). Thus the weight-graded cup operator is parallel and commutes with the relevant Weyl action. Projection to the sign part preserves Lefschetz isomorphisms, and the center shifts by \(2N\); the difference of fiber dimensions is exactly \(n^2-n=2N\). These checks support the stated general-puncture argument within the declared reference interfaces.
# Conclusion and limits

One local numerical reconstruction defect is supported, with a complete admissible example and a general algebraic correction. No substantive failure of Theorems 1.2, 1.5, 1.6, 7.5 or 8.13 was established in the inspected scope. The review retains mixed Hodge theory, Grothendieck–Springer theory and the cited smooth-quotient results as identified external inputs; it is not a recursive verification of all their foundations. claim: The operative genericity condition is Definition 4.9, PDF p. 40: \(\prod_i\det C_i=1\), and for every \(1\le r<n\), every choice of \(r\) eigenvalues from each \(C_i\) has total product different from one. A common invariant proper subspace would violate this condition by taking determinants on that subspace. It therefore excludes reducible representations, rather than merely imposing a condition on the full determinant. The introductory omission of \(r=1\), and the repeated subscript in the determinant product, are resolved by the body definition and are not additional Problems.

The smoothness and scalar-stabilizer interface in Theorem 4.10 agrees with the explicitly consulted author version of Hausel–Letellier–Rodriguez-Villegas [hlrv], Definition 2.1.1, Proposition 2.1.4 and Theorem 2.1.5, PDF pp. 16–18. Nonemptiness is kept separate from smoothness of a possibly empty variety. At \(k=0\), the genericity condition excludes \(n>1\); when \(n=1\), the resulting space is \((\mathbb C^*)^{2g}\). Thus Theorem 8.13 does not assert an unrestricted result for all untwisted higher-rank character varieties.

Equation reference: eq:middle. For a regular semisimple last puncture, set \(r=\binom n2\) and \(d=\dim_{\mathbb C}X\). Theorem 1.2 gives a rank-\(r\) vector bundle over \(X\), with strata \[(\mathbb C^*)^{d-2i}\times\mathbb C^{i+r}.\] The center of the compact-support curious Lefschetz symmetry on each stratum is \[
 (d-2i)+2(i+r)=d+2r.\] The affine-bundle isomorphism shifts cohomological degree and weight by \(2r\), recovering center \(d\) for \(X\). Consequently Proposition 2.19 is applied with a common center on all strata. The long exact compact-support sequence is compatible with cup product, and strictness of mixed Hodge structures makes its weight-graded rows exact. The five-lemma argument then preserves the asserted isomorphisms.

Equation reference: eq:inversion, eq:printed. Write \(N=\cup\omega\), assume that \(X\) is Tate, \(\omega\in F^2H^2(X)\), and \(N\) satisfies curious Lefschetz with middle weight \(2d\). The proposition defines \[g_a(u)=\sum_k u^k\dim\ker\bigl(N^a:H_c^k(X)\longrightarrow
 H_c^{k+2a}(X)\bigr)\quad(a>0),\qquad g_a=0\quad(a\le0),\] and \[
 f_i(u)=(1+u^2)g_{i+1}(u)-g_i(u)-u^2g_{i+2}(u).\] Its claimed output is \[
 \operatorname{MH}_X(u,v)=\sum_{i\ge0}v^{d-i}f_i(u)
       \frac{(uv)^{i+1}-1}{uv-1},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{MH}_X(u,v)=\sum_{k,j}u^kv^j\dim H_c^k(X)^{j,j}.\] The quotient is a finite polynomial sum, so the issue is unrelated to substitution at \(uv=1\).
X=(C*)² smooth Tate,ω=dlogx∧dlogy inF²H² nonzero; Hc²=C(0),Hc³=C(-1)^2,Hc4=C(-2); cupωHc²→Hc4 isomorphism byPoincare duality;CHLmiddle2,d1.
analysis: In Proposition 2.21, PDF p. 21 (printed p. 173), both the statement and the last closed-form step in its proof use a geometric sum with ratio \(uv\). A primitive Lefschetz step raises both the cohomological degree and the Hodge index by two, so the ratio must be \(u^2v^2\).

Take \(X=(\mathbb C^*)^2\) and \(\omega=d\log x\wedge d\log y\). This smooth variety is Tate, and the nonzero class of \(\omega\) lies in \(F^2H^2(X)\). Its compact-support groups are \[H_c^2(X)=\mathbb C(0),\qquad
 H_c^3(X)=\mathbb C(-1)^{\oplus2},\qquad
 H_c^4(X)=\mathbb C(-2).\] Poincaré duality shows that \(N:H_c^2\to H_c^4\) is an isomorphism; all other positive-degree maps are zero for degree reasons. Thus curious Lefschetz holds with middle weight \(2\), so \(d=1\). This example is also a rank-one genus-one character variety.

Equation reference: eq:wrongoutput, eq:trueoutput. The actual kernel polynomials are \[g_1=2u^3+u^4,\qquad
 g_a=u^2+2u^3+u^4\quad(a\ge2).\] Equation [eq:inversion] (#eq:inversion) correctly yields \(f_0=2u^3,\ f_1=u^2\), and \(f_i=0\) for \(i\ge2\). However, substitution in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) gives \[
 \operatorname{MH}_{\rm printed}=2u^3v+u^2(1+uv)=u^2+3u^3v,\] whereas the actual answer is \[
 \operatorname{MH}_X=u^2+2u^3v+u^4v^2.\] The printed output assigns dimension three to \(H_c^3\) of type \((1,1)\), and zero to the nonzero top group \(H_c^4\). These are incorrect numerical invariants, not merely alternative notations. The exact calculation and its input hypotheses are saved in `verification/0137/root_prop221_exact.json`.

Equation reference: eq:correct. Let \(F_m(u)\) be the graded polynomial of primitive vectors in blocks of length \(m+1\). With \(\Delta g_a=g_a-g_{a-1}\), direct inspection of a nilpotent block gives \[\Delta g_a=\sum_{m\ge a-1}u^{2(m-a+1)}F_m,\qquad
 \Delta g_{i+1}-u^2\Delta g_{i+2}=F_i.\] This proves [eq:inversion] (#eq:inversion). A primitive vector with Hodge index \(d-i\) contributes its successive powers under \(N\) at indices \(d-i,d-i+2,\ldots,d+i\). Therefore the corrected statement is \[
 \operatorname{MH}_X(u,v)
 =\sum_{i\ge0}v^{d-i}f_i(u)\sum_{j=0}^i(u^2v^2)^j
 =\sum_{i\ge0}v^{d-i}f_i(u)
       \frac{(uv)^{2(i+1)}-1}{(uv)^2-1}.\] The finite-sum interpretation applies also at \((uv)^2=1\). This derivation verifies the correction for every primitive block under the original assumptions, and hence for their direct sum. The saved exact symbolic checks additionally reproduce the torus counterexample and the kernel inversion on 35 finite blocks.
result: The strongest counterevidence is on the same page: the preceding double sum in the printed proof already contains \(v^{d-i+2j}u^{2j}f_i(u)\), which is correct. The primitive decomposition and kernel inversion also remain valid. The error is therefore consistent with a transcription mistake. No subsequent use of the incorrect closed form was found in the canonical text, and the main stratification and curious Lefschetz proofs use other propositions.

This report retains one Minor finding because the independently stated numerical reconstruction, when used as printed, produces the wrong Hodge numbers on a fully admissible input. It does not count unrelated typographical slips as findings. The supported consequence is confined to Proposition 2.21’s closed formula. Neither a failure of the main Lefschetz theorem nor a defect in its primitive-block mechanism is established. Equation [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) restores the stated numerical reconstruction; author adoption and any prior discovery remain unverified.
Result: Printed numerical reconstruction misstates Hc³ dimension3 instead2 and omits nonzero topHc4.
Impact: Local supported computational defect inProposition2.21, no demonstrated centraldamage ormainCHLcounterexample; notMajor.

report: Abstract: The acquired publisher version is reviewed through the quaternionic construction, global period conditions, elliptic existence argument and final deformation step. Three local defects are established: periodicity of the parameter does not force the same period for its signed analytic square root; the unrestricted cylinder theorem asserts a translation period absent for permitted nonperiodic parameters; and the discrete transform can collapse an edge at a nonzero parameter. The actual spherical family and the stated angle perturbations satisfy stronger period conditions, and the discrete closure identity survives. The highest supported assessment is Minor. The rank-three assertion and the exclusion of all ambient identifications in the final deformation argument remain Needs Evidence; no failure of that rank or counterexample to the main existence theorems is claimed. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Verification of
Compact Bonnet Pairs: Isometric Tori
with the Same Curvatures
# Identity, exact version and scope

The paper is Alexander I. Bobenko, Tim Hoffmann and Andrew O. Sageman-Furnas, Compact Bonnet pairs: isometric tori with the same curvatures, Publications Mathématiques de l’IHÉS 142 (2025), 241–293, DOI 10.1007/s10240-025-00159-z (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10240-025-00159-z) [paper]. The reviewed object is the acquired 53-page publisher version of record; physical PDF page \(p\) has printed number \(p+240\). The separately acquired arXiv:2110.06335v2 source, dated 27 December 2023, is an author version. Its identity as the publisher’s production source is not asserted.

The review checks the forward quaternion construction, its domains and periods, the planar/spherical interfaces, the elliptic closing argument, the deformation linearization, the discrete construction and Appendix A. The companion classification [companion] was consulted in its exact arXiv:2312.14956v2 author version at the admissibility and fundamental-piece interface. Its complete classification proof, the Kamberov–Pedit–Pinkall converse, and all cited historical results were not recursively reproved. Complete text reading is distinguished from selected proof reconstruction and actual image inspection.
# Operative assumptions and positive checks

Equation reference: eq:metric. Write \(z=u+iv\), and use the quaternion convention \(XY=-\langle X,Y\rangle+X\times Y\) for imaginary quaternions. For an isothermic immersion with metric \(e^{2h}(du^2+dv^2)\), \[\alpha=df^*=e^{-2h}(f_u\,du-f_v\,dv).\] The curvature-line equations give \(f_{uv}=h_vf_u+h_uf_v\), hence \(d\alpha=0\). Moreover \(df\wedge\alpha=\alpha\wedge df=0\). These identities imply \[d(f\alpha f)=0,\qquad d[\alpha,f]=0.\] Consequently the three terms in \[df^\pm=-f\alpha f+\epsilon^2\alpha
             \pm\epsilon[\alpha,f]\] are closed. For \(\epsilon\ne0\), quaternion norm multiplicativity gives \[
 ds_\pm^2=(\epsilon^2+|f|^2)^2 e^{-2h}(du^2+dv^2).\] Thus the forward construction is immersive and isometric. The diagonal second fundamental forms agree, giving equal oriented mean curvature. This checks the construction under its prescribed correspondence; it does not classify all other parametrizations of the images.

Equation reference: eq:frame. The explicit cylinders use a rhombic modulus \(\tau=\frac12+i b\), \(0<b<b_0\), with \(b_0\approx0.3547\), and the critical \(\omega\in(0,\pi/4)\) satisfying \(\vartheta_2'(\omega)=0\). Definition 1, PDF p. 17, requires \(w:\mathbb R\to(0,2\pi b)\) real analytic and an analytic real function \(a\) with \[a^2=1-(w')^2.\] Remark 6 explicitly permits \(a\) to change sign. The surface and frame are \[
 f=\Phi^{-1}\gamma(u,w)j\Phi,\qquad
 \Phi' =a(v)W_1(w(v))k\Phi,\qquad
 W_1(w)=\frac{i\vartheta_1'(0)\vartheta_2(\omega-iw)}
                    {2\vartheta_2(\omega)\vartheta_1(iw)}.\] The orthogonal terms in the frame have squared coefficients \(a^2+(w')^2=1\); a zero of \(a\) is not a loss of immersion.

Equation reference: eq:generic. The generic-plane condition can be retained in both examples below. Put \(F(w)=W_1(w)k\) and \(m=\Phi^{-1}i\Phi\). Direct differentiation gives \[
 \det(m,m',m'')=4a^2w'\det(i,F,F_w).\] There are open intervals on which the last determinant is nonzero. After removing their common phase \(e^{i\pi/8}\), the relevant theta Fourier coefficients are real, and \(W_1(w)\sim1/(2w)\) at zero. Thus constant phase on an interval, followed by analytic continuation, would force the normalized \(\vartheta_2(\omega-iw)\) to be real and all odd derivatives of \(\vartheta_2\) at \(\omega\) to vanish. Evenness about both \(0\) and \(\omega\) would give the extra real period \(2\omega\), incompatible with its nonconstant theta Fourier series and \(0<2\omega<\pi/2\). Choose the parameter interval there. At points where \(aw'\ne0\), the plane normals span \(\mathbb R^3\), so the examples do not rely on a degenerate family of parallel planes or a common plane axis.
# Local period statements

Problem 1 (The fundamental-piece lemma needs the signed root’s period).  Lemma 1, PDF p. 20 (printed p. 260), infers periodic coefficients in [eq:frame] (#eq:frame) from periodicity of \(w\) alone. Definition 2 requires \(w(v+\mathcal V)=w(v)\) and that one piece does not already close; it does not impose \(a(v+\mathcal V)=a(v)\).
## A permitted analytic counterexample

Set \[g(x)=\frac{4\cos x+\cos2x}{5},\qquad
 G(x)=\frac45\sin x+\frac1{10}\sin2x.\] Then \(G'=g\), \(g\in[-3/5,1]\), and \[A(x)=\frac{2\sqrt2}{5}\sin(x/2)
       \sqrt{(\cos x+3)((\cos x+1)^2+1)}\] is real analytic, satisfies \(A^2=1-g^2\), and is antiperiodic: \(A(x+2\pi)=-A(x)\). It is positive on \((0,2\pi)\). Choose \(w_0\) in an interval described above, with \(W_1(w_0)\ne0\), and, for small \(\lambda>0\), define \[w_\lambda(v)=w_0+\lambda G(v/\lambda),\qquad
 a_\lambda(v)=A(v/\lambda),\qquad \mathcal V=2\pi\lambda.\] The image lies strictly inside \((0,2\pi b)\), \(w_\lambda'=g(v/\lambda)\), and every admissibility condition holds. Formula [eq:generic] (#eq:generic) supplies the generic-plane condition at suitable phases.

Equation reference: eq:monodromy. Normalize \(\Phi(0)=1\). In the variable \(x=v/\lambda\), its ODE is \[\Phi_x=\lambda A(x)W_1(w_0+\lambda G(x))k\Phi.\] Analytic dependence on \(\lambda\), on the fixed interval \(0\le x\le4\pi\), yields \[
 \Phi(\mathcal V)=1+\lambda C+O(\lambda^2),\qquad
 \Phi(2\mathcal V)=1+O(\lambda^2),\qquad
 C=\left(\int_0^{2\pi}A(x)\,dx\right)W_1(w_0)k\ne0.\] The first-order term over two periods cancels by antiperiodicity. For some \(u\), the profile point \(q=\gamma(u,w_0)j\) does not commute with \(C\): the regular closed planar profile is not contained in the line through \(C\). Therefore \(f(u,\mathcal V)\ne f(u,0)\) for sufficiently small \(\lambda\), as Definition 2 requires.

Lemma 1 with \(k=2,v=0\) predicts, for \(R=\Phi(\mathcal V)\), \(f(u,2\mathcal V)=R^{-2}qR^2\). The actual and predicted quantities are respectively \[q+O(\lambda^2),\qquad
 q+2\lambda[q,C]+O(\lambda^2),\] which differ. This is an admissible failure of the asserted monodromy formula, not an ambiguity about a principal square root.
## Counterevidence, repair and bounded impact

Require \(\mathcal V\) to be a common period of \(w\) and its chosen analytic root \(a\). Then the coefficient in [eq:frame] (#eq:frame) is periodic, and the usual ODE uniqueness proof gives \(\Phi(v+\mathcal V)=\Phi(v)\Phi(0)^{-1}\Phi(\mathcal V)\), restoring the lemma. For a nonzero analytic root of a periodic analytic function, the shift by \(\mathcal V\) changes that root by a constant sign; thus \(2\mathcal V\) is always a common period. The rotational angle must then be recomputed over that common period. If the doubled interval already closes the surface, it is a full period and its zero-angle case must be treated separately.

The actual spherical family has \(a=(s-s_1)(s-s_2)/(\delta s_w)\) on the chosen real branch, so \(a\) has the same period as \(s\) and \(w\). Section 7.3 also uses a winding angle \(\psi(v+\mathcal V)=\psi(v)+2\pi\), making both \(a=\sin\psi\) and \(w'=\cos\psi\) periodic. These are strong operative special-case safeguards. The general lemma needs correction, but this counterexample does not invalidate those actual construction families. The supported impact is Minor. The exact identity and complete native analysis are retained in `verification/0138/root_exact_checks.json` and `verification/0138/native_elliptic_check.md`.

Problem 2 (Arbitrary admissible cylinders need not have a translation period).  Theorem 5, PDF p. 21 (printed p. 261), and Theorem 10, PDF p. 47 (printed p. 287), assert \(v\)-direction translation periods, opposite for the two transforms, for an arbitrary cylinder of Theorem 3. That hypothesis allows nonperiodic \(w\).
## A nonperiodic metric on fully admissible input

Set \(\epsilon=1\). Theorem 4 gives \(|f(\omega,v)|=|R(\omega)|\), so [eq:metric] (#eq:metric) has \(u\)-coefficient \[H(v)=\frac{(1+R(\omega)^2)^2}{E(w(v))^2}.\] Its two limits at \(v=\pm\infty\) are distinct. If either transformed surface satisfied \(f^\pm(u,v+T)=f^\pm(u,v)+c\) for \(T>0\) and constant vector \(c\), differentiating in \(u\) would imply \(H(v+T)=H(v)\). A continuous periodic function with a limit at infinity is constant, contradicting these limits. Thus neither surface has the claimed translation period.
## Repair and actual dependency

The explicit formulas and \(2\pi\)-periodicity in \(u\) remain valid. To assert opposite \(v\)-translation periods, require the generating surface \(f\) to be a torus with the corresponding periodic differential data. Its explicit inverse and Christoffel symmetries make the \(\mathcal A\)-period vanish; the remaining \(\mathcal B\)-periods then have opposite signs. The paragraph immediately following Theorem 5 explicitly introduces this torus setting, and the subsequent closing argument uses it. Periodic \(w\) alone is not an adequate substitute for frame closure. The supported defect is local to the theorem’s overbroad period conclusion, with no demonstrated failure of the torus-specific existence argument: Minor. The analytic proof and a separate 70-digit diagnostic are retained in `verification/0138/p0138_foundations.md` and its calculation record.
# The elliptic existence argument and explicit formulas

Equation reference: eq:axial. Write \(a_0=U_1'(\omega)\), \(b_0=U_2(\omega)\), \(c_0=U'(\omega)\), \(d_0=U(\omega)^2\). The axial coefficient in equation (93) simplifies to \[
 \mathcal A(x,y)=(x+y)(a_0xy-c_0)-b_0xy-d_0.\] For large \(x\) with \(a_0x>0\), its roots have leading terms \[y_1=\frac{c_0}{a_0x}+O(x^{-2}),\qquad
 y_2=-x+\frac{b_0}{a_0}+O(x^{-1}).\] These give the required signs of \(Q_3(x)\) and \(Q_3(y)\), a real nonzero axis norm, and the two nondegeneracy conditions in Lemma 8. In particular \(\partial_y\mathcal A=a_0x(x+2y)-b_0x-c_0\). The fixed-interval substitution removes the moving square-root endpoints of the elliptic integrals, justifying the analytic extension of the axial integral divided by \(\delta^2\). The nonzero leading angular coefficient along its zero branch then permits rational angles. These checks support the Lemma 8–Lemma 9–Theorem 8 existence route. The displayed factor \(2\) in the small-root expression (98) is inconsistent with [eq:axial] (#eq:axial), but does not alter these signs or existence conclusions; it is not a separate substantive finding.

The incorrect reciprocal exponent and sign in the preparatory quaternion displays on PDF p. 13 are likewise resolved by the closedness calculation above. The endpoint \(\epsilon=0\) gives coincident transforms and is excluded for a noncongruent Bonnet pair; the text’s rescaling by \(\epsilon\) makes its intended regime clear. These clarifications are not additional numbered Problems.
# A discrete nondegeneracy qualification

Problem 3 (The discrete transform can collapse an allowed edge).  Section 8, PDF p. 44, defines a discrete net to have nonzero edges. Proposition 7, PDF p. 46 (printed p. 286), calls the outputs of (119) discrete nets for every real \(\epsilon\). The formulas need an additional edge nondegeneracy condition for that conclusion.
## Exact global example

Take the square net and its Christoffel dual \[f(n,m)=(2n-1)i+2mj,\qquad
 f^*(n,m)=\tfrac n2 i-\tfrac m2 j.\] Every horizontal and vertical edge is nonzero. On every square the cross-ratio in (116) is \((2i)(2j)^{-1}(2i)(2j)^{-1}=(-k)^2=-1\), so the input meets the stated isothermic-net definition. For \(\epsilon=1\), the edge from \((0,0)\) to \((1,0)\) has endpoints \(-i,i\) and dual difference \(i/2\). Its two transformed quaternions are \[(1+i)(i/2)(1+i)=-1,\qquad
 (-1+i)(i/2)(-1+i)=1.\] Both imaginary parts vanish, giving zero output edges despite nonzero \(\epsilon\) and nonzero original endpoints.

Equation reference: eq:edge. More generally, for imaginary endpoints \(a,b\) and \(d=b-a\ne0\), quaternion norm multiplicativity gives \[
 \left|\operatorname{Im}_{\mathbb H}\frac{(\epsilon-a)d(\epsilon+b)}{|d|^2}\right|^2
 =\frac{(\epsilon^2+a\cdot b)^2+|a\times b|^2}{|d|^2}.\] Thus an edge collapses exactly when \(a\times b=0\) and \(a\cdot b=-\epsilon^2\). The vertical-edge sign and the choice of Bonnet branch do not alter this criterion. Excluding these conditions on every edge restores the nonzero-edge conclusion; a finite net has only finitely many forbidden values of \(\epsilon\).
## Counterevidence and scope

The quad closure identity immediately following (119) remains true. If the proposition is read only as integration to vertex maps, its algebraic assertion is valid. The defect concerns the previously defined immersive-net conclusion and subsequent geometric label. The counterexample even has explicit polynomial integrated maps, saved with exact rational quaternion calculations in `verification/0138/native_0138_discrete_nondegeneracy.md` and `verification/0138/native_discrete_edge_exact_check.json`. No collapse was established for the paper’s displayed compact examples, and the smooth transform has a different immersion mechanism. This local defect is Minor and does not refute the smooth existence theorem.
# Outstanding evidence in the final deformation step
## Fixed-period rank: Needs Evidence

For the base spherical example, Section 7.3 fixes \(\mathcal V\) and perturbs \(\psi=\psi_0+\eta\phi\), with \(\phi\) periodic analytic and vanishing at the two specified zeros. Set \(w=w_0(0)+\int_0^v\cos\psi(t)\,dt\). The constraints are a fixed rational monodromy angle \(\theta\), zero axial period \(b\), and \(c=\int_0^\mathcal V\cos\psi\,dv=0\). The last condition is needed for \(w\) itself to be periodic.

The ODE linearization is valid. For the chosen nontrivial monodromy, \(\theta_0\notin2\pi\mathbb Z\). If \(M=M_0(1+\eta G+o(\eta))\), quaternion multiplication gives \[\delta\theta=2\langle A_0,G\rangle,\quad
 \delta A=\cot(\theta_0/2)
       (G-\langle A_0,G\rangle A_0)+A_0\times G.\] Fubini and the correct commutator variation give analytic integral densities \(\widehat a,\widehat b,-\sin\psi_0\) for the three differentials. The detailed kernels are retained in `verification/0138/native_0138_endpoint_map.md`. This verifies the existence of the densities, not their independence.

PDF p. 43 asserts their linear independence and then chooses three test functions to make the \(3\times3\) derivative matrix invertible. Once that assertion holds, the ensuing finite-dimensional analytic implicit function theorem is appropriate. Vanishing at finitely many points does not itself obstruct the integral functionals: analytic test functions with those zeros are sufficiently rich to detect any nonzero continuous density. The spherical-family rank in Lemma 8 is relevant support, but its period varies, so it is not automatically the required fixed-period rank statement with \(w(0)\) fixed.

This review has neither proved the asserted independence nor found a dependence. A completion would provide three allowed test functions with a rigorously nonzero determinant at one exact closing base, or another proof of surjectivity. This is a material unresolved proof interface, recorded as Needs Evidence rather than a demonstrated invalid derivation or a false Theorem 9.
## All ambient identifications: Needs Evidence

Remark 11 explains why the initial spherical examples are mirror images. The final paragraph before Theorem 9 argues that a generic parameter lacking that reflection symmetry produces images related by no ambient isometry. Breaking the indicated parameter reflection does not, without a further argument, classify all identifications that may include a different domain parametrization. The prescribed Bonnet correspondence being noncongruent is a weaker statement.

A possible completion would characterize every ambient identification through the conformal or anti-conformal automorphisms of the parameter torus and the metric and curvature data, and then show that the chosen perturbation avoids all such symmetry conditions. Functional freedom is supporting evidence, but that exclusion has not been established in this bounded review. No actual ambient congruence of the claimed perturbed examples was found. Rounded numerical parameters and figures illustrate the claim without providing an exact closure or symmetry certificate.
# Conclusion and source availability

The three demonstrated defects concern overbroad local statements. The actual common-period safeguards, the torus-specific period argument, and the discrete closure identity delimit their impact. The highest supported assessment is Minor; the two unresolved Theorem 9 interfaces do not raise that assessment. This is not a certification of all main conclusions, nor a counterexample to either main existence theorem.

The paper’s figure-data link was followed to the public Compact Bonnet Pairs gallery entry [gallery]. Its 26 OBJ meshes and 12 PNG figures were acquired and hashed. The entry cites the 2021 preprint; no identity with the 2025 production calculations is inferred. Mesh data and figures do not supply exact period or symmetry proofs. The separately acquired Julia visualization repository is pinned to its recorded commit and is not identified as the original Mathematica implementation. No original Mathematica source was identified in the bounded search; no author code was executed, and missing code is not a mathematical defect.

 G(x)=\frac45\sin x+\frac1{10}\sin2x.\] Then \(G'=g\), \(g\in[-3/5,1]\), and \[A(x)=\frac{2\sqrt2}{5}\sin(x/2)
       \sqrt{(\cos x+3)((\cos x+1)^2+1)}\] is real analytic, satisfies \(A^2=1-g^2\), and is antiperiodic: \(A(x+2\pi)=-A(x)\). It is positive on \((0,2\pi)\). Choose \(w_0\) in an interval described above, with \(W_1(w_0)\ne0\), and, for small \(\lambda>0\), define \[w_\lambda(v)=w_0+\lambda G(v/\lambda),\qquad
 a_\lambda(v)=A(v/\lambda),\qquad \mathcal V=2\pi\lambda.\] The image lies strictly inside \((0,2\pi b)\), \(w_\lambda'=g(v/\lambda)\), and every admissibility condition holds. Formula [eq:generic] (#eq:generic) supplies the generic-plane condition at suitable phases.

Equation reference: eq:monodromy. Normalize \(\Phi(0)=1\). In the variable \(x=v/\lambda\), its ODE is \[\Phi_x=\lambda A(x)W_1(w_0+\lambda G(x))k\Phi.\] Analytic dependence on \(\lambda\), on the fixed interval \(0\le x\le4\pi\), yields \[
 \Phi(\mathcal V)=1+\lambda C+O(\lambda^2),\qquad
 \Phi(2\mathcal V)=1+O(\lambda^2),\qquad
 C=\left(\int_0^{2\pi}A(x)\,dx\right)W_1(w_0)k\ne0.\] The first-order term over two periods cancels by antiperiodicity. For some \(u\), the profile point \(q=\gamma(u,w_0)j\) does not commute with \(C\): the regular closed planar profile is not contained in the line through \(C\). Therefore \(f(u,\mathcal V)\ne f(u,0)\) for sufficiently small \(\lambda\), as Definition 2 requires.

Lemma 1 with \(k=2,v=0\) predicts, for \(R=\Phi(\mathcal V)\), \(f(u,2\mathcal V)=R^{-2}qR^2\). The actual and predicted quantities are respectively \[q+O(\lambda^2),\qquad
 q+2\lambda[q,C]+O(\lambda^2),\] which differ. This is an admissible failure of the asserted monodromy formula, not an ambiguity about a principal square root.
result: Require \(\mathcal V\) to be a common period of \(w\) and its chosen analytic root \(a\). Then the coefficient in [eq:frame] (#eq:frame) is periodic, and the usual ODE uniqueness proof gives \(\Phi(v+\mathcal V)=\Phi(v)\Phi(0)^{-1}\Phi(\mathcal V)\), restoring the lemma. For a nonzero analytic root of a periodic analytic function, the shift by \(\mathcal V\) changes that root by a constant sign; thus \(2\mathcal V\) is always a common period. The rotational angle must then be recomputed over that common period. If the doubled interval already closes the surface, it is a full period and its zero-angle case must be treated separately.

The actual spherical family has \(a=(s-s_1)(s-s_2)/(\delta s_w)\) on the chosen real branch, so \(a\) has the same period as \(s\) and \(w\). Section 7.3 also uses a winding angle \(\psi(v+\mathcal V)=\psi(v)+2\pi\), making both \(a=\sin\psi\) and \(w'=\cos\psi\) periodic. These are strong operative special-case safeguards. The general lemma needs correction, but this counterexample does not invalidate those actual construction families. The supported impact is Minor. The exact identity and complete native analysis are retained in `verification/0138/root_exact_checks.json` and `verification/0138/native_elliptic_check.md`.
Result: Fully admissible analytic input violates the stated arbitrary-period monodromy formula; not a principal-root convention artifact.
Impact: Local overbroad monodromy lemma; actual employed spherical and psi construction families satisfy strongercondition. No demonstrated central existence failure; Minor not based on easeofrepair.

Take the square net and its Christoffel dual \[f(n,m)=(2n-1)i+2mj,\qquad

Title: Technical Verification of
Marked Length Spectrum Rigidity for Anosov Surfaces
# Identity, version and inspected scope

The paper is Colin Guillarmou, Thibault Lefeuvre and Gabriel P. Paternain, Marked length spectrum rigidity for Anosov surfaces, associated with Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), 131–157, DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0022 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0022). The exact reviewed document is arXiv:2303.12007v5 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12007v5), dated 6 September 2024, with 22 PDF pages [paper]. Equivalence to the journal version has not been established. All locations below use this author PDF’s physical page numbers, which agree with its printed page numbers.

Actual source-image inspections cover all 22 pages across those roles. Reading and image inspection do not mean that every external theorem has been independently reproved. The principal inspected claims are Theorem 1.1, Lemmas 2.4–2.8, Propositions 3.1–3.7, Lemma 3.8 and the separate Remark 3.9/Lemma 3.10. Corollaries 1.2–1.3 and the unused higher-mode and algebra remarks have the narrower dependency coverage recorded below. No separate supplement or original computational repository was identified in bounded checks; their absence is not a mathematical defect. No numbered substantive Problem is manufactured.
# Definitions and the smooth analytic chain

The operative setting is a closed connected oriented surface with an Anosov geodesic flow. Its genus is at least two. The marked length spectrum is understood on nontrivial free homotopy classes; the trivial class can instead be assigned length zero if the codomain is adjusted. This harmless convention is needed for the positive-length notation on p. 1.

Write \(X\) for the geodesic field, \(V\) for positive fiber rotation and \(H=[V,X]\). The dual coframe \((\lambda,\beta,\psi)\) satisfies \[d\lambda=\psi\wedge\beta,\qquad
 \mu=-\lambda\wedge d\lambda=\lambda\wedge\beta\wedge\psi.\] The operators \(\eta_\pm=(X\mp iH)/2\) change Fourier degree by \(\pm1\). In isothermal coordinates \(g=e^{2\rho}|dz|^2\), \[\eta_-\bigl(ae^{in\theta}\bigr)
 =e^{-(n+1)\rho}\bar\partial(ae^{n\rho})e^{i(n-1)\theta}.\] This verifies the holomorphic-bundle identification including its metric factor. For a distribution \(f\in\mathcal A_+\), the \(-1\) and zero modes of \(Xf=0\) give \(\eta_-f_0=\eta_-f_1=0\). Base elliptic regularity makes these coefficients smooth; compactness makes \(f_0\) constant. No initial smoothness of an arbitrary distribution’s Fourier coefficients is presumed.

The first-mode extension has the required hypotheses. In the exact consulted version of Paternain–Salo–Uhlmann [psu], Theorem 5.6, p. 18, supplies \[w=\sum_{k\ge1}w_k\in L_x^2H_\theta^{-1},\qquad
 Xw=0,\qquad w_1=a_1\] for any \(\eta_-a_1=0\) on a smooth Anosov surface. It imposes no negative-curvature or nonhyperelliptic restriction. With the paper’s adjoint convention \(\pi_{1*}\pi_1^*=2\pi\operatorname{Id}\), set \(a_1=(2\pi)^{-1}\pi_1^*\omega\). This produces \(\pi_{1*}w=\omega\). A choice on a finite complex basis gives a complex-linear right inverse \(e_1\), with no uniqueness requirement. The stronger higher-mode remark can use the solenoidal extension of [gui], Corollary 3.8, together with its surface injectivity Theorem 3.12 and a parity/truncation argument. Its kernel-orthogonality hypothesis is not silently dropped, and that stronger result is not needed for the main first-mode proof.

For the Anosov splitting write \(Y^s=H+r_-V\), \(Y^u=H+r_+V\), with \(r_+>r_-\). The inequality follows from the positive transverse Jacobi coefficients and their Wronskian; it does not assume curvature is everywhere negative. In the characteristic plane \(\xi(X)=0\), put \[\xi_s=\psi-r_-\beta,\qquad \xi_u=\psi-r_+\beta.\] Both evaluate to one on \(V\). Their lifted-flow factors are positive and have opposite exponential behaviour. A negative coefficient on either ray eventually exits \(\{\xi(V)\ge0\}\) in one time direction. Consequently its maximal two-sided invariant subset is precisely the positive cone generated by these rays. This supplies the central step in Lemma 2.5. Every nonzero covector in that cone has positive vertical component, so fiber push-forward makes every Fourier coefficient smooth.

An exact smooth time-preserving conjugacy preserves \(X\), the individual stable and unstable bundles, and therefore \(\lambda\) and contact volume. The leaf-space circle on the universal cover has degree \(+1\) under the identity-isotopy condition in Proposition 3.2. It fixes the transverse orientation; contact orientation then fixes the two individual ray signs. Thus pullback carries the positive cone to the positive cone, not its negative. For \(f'=\phi^*f\), the negative Szegö projection is smooth and \[X_2(S^-f')=\eta_+f'_0+\eta_+f'_{-1}.\] Only degrees zero and one occur. Degree-one tensor tomography makes \(S^-f'=f'_0\), eliminating all negative modes. The inverse conjugacy gives the inverse map on \(\mathcal A_+\). The needed Szegö statement includes its horizontal, zero-vertical kernel directions; these do not intersect the strict positive cone. The argument does not require a falsely diagonal-only kernel description.
# Pairing, marking and the conformal conclusion
## The constant and the local sign clarification

Equation reference: eq:pair. At angle \(\theta\) over an oriented geodesic, the coordinate tangent is \(T_\tau=\cos\theta\,X-\sin\theta\,H\). Thus the consistent orientation is \((\cos\theta\,\lambda-\sin\theta\,\beta)\wedge\psi\). The two corresponding plus signs preceding Lemma 2.7 on p. 11 are local display slips: that printed form evaluates to \(\cos(2\theta)\) on the actual coordinate basis. With the corrected signs, \[d\lambda=\sin\theta\,d\tau\wedge d\theta,\qquad
 \int_0^{2\pi}e^{ik\theta}\sin\theta\,d\theta
 =i\pi(\delta_{k1}-\delta_{k,-1}).\] For \(f\in\mathcal A_+\) the negative first mode vanishes, and the adjoint normalization therefore gives exactly the formula actually used: \[
 2i\int_{S^1\gamma}f\,d\lambda
 =-\int_{[\gamma]}\pi_{1*}f .\] The final sign and factor in Lemma 2.8 survive the clarification. Ten exact symbolic controls, including modes \(-4,\ldots,4\), support this calculation; the displayed Fourier identity is the all-integer analytic argument.

The conormal to the parametrized circle bundle annihilates \(V\), whereas the admissible wavefront cone has strictly positive vertical component. Thus its distributional pullback exists. Self-intersecting geodesics are handled as immersed cycles with multiplicity, or one can use simple representatives of a symplectic homology basis. Passing from smooth functions to distributions uses wavefront-controlled regularization, not unrestricted weak convergence.
## Why homology suffices

The form \(f\,d\lambda\) is closed because \(Xf=0\). For a direct smooth-category justification of the de Rham step on pp. 16–17, choose an auxiliary smooth metric, its harmonic projector \(\mathcal{H}\) and Green operator \(G\). For a closed current \(T\), \[T=\mathcal{H}T+d(d^*GT),\qquad
 \operatorname{WF}(d^*GT)\subseteq\operatorname{WF}(T).\] The identity follows from Hodge decomposition and \(dT=0\); the wavefront inclusion follows from the pseudodifferential nature of \(d^*G\). It gives a smooth closed representative plus a primitive whose traces are defined on both relevant cycles. Stokes’ formula then makes the pairing depend only on their homology. Together with \(\phi^*\lambda_1=\lambda_2\), this proves that \[F=\pi_{1*}\phi^*e_1:
 H^0_{J_1}(\Sigma,K)\longrightarrow H^0_{J_2}(\Sigma,K)\] preserves all periods. A holomorphic one-form with zero periods is zero, so \(F\) is injective and hence an isomorphism in genus \(g\). Normalized \(a\)-period bases therefore give identical period matrices.

Torelli yields an unmarked biholomorphism at this point. The paper correctly retains the mapping-class ambiguity. The exact author version of Alvarez–Brum–Martínez–Potrie with Wolff’s appendix [abmp], Theorem C on pp. 37–38, applies to every simple closed geodesic, including a separating one. It gives a finite cover with a degree-one lift of that curve and all other simple closed geodesics longer than any prescribed \(K\).

If two marked hyperbolic metrics differ, choose a simple class \(\alpha\) with unequal lengths. Compactness gives a uniform ratio bound \(C\) for the lengths of all free homotopy classes. Choose \(K/C>\max(\ell_1(\alpha),\ell_2(\alpha))\). The isolated lift is then the systole for both lifted metrics, with different lengths. The lifts cannot lie in the same mapping-class orbit. The comparison must include nonsimple projected curves; the proof explicitly does. Applying the period/Torelli conclusion on every finite cover proves Proposition 3.7.

Finally suppose the marked conformal representatives satisfy \(g_2=e^{2f}g_1\). Contact conjugacy gives equality of area, \(A_1=A_2\). Each \(g_1\)-closed geodesic has \(g_2\)-length at least the \(g_2\)-minimum in its free homotopy class, which equals its \(g_1\)-length. Periodic-orbit approximation of Liouville measure yields \[\int_\Sigma e^f\,dA_1\ge A_1,\qquad
 \left(\int_\Sigma e^f\,dA_1\right)^2
 \le A_1\int_\Sigma e^{2f}\,dA_1=A_1A_2=A_1^2.\] Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz makes \(e^f\) constant, and equal area makes that constant one. This checks the final conformal closing step under the established conjugacy and standard Anosov periodic-approximation interface.
# Finite regularity and remaining dependency limits

Lemma 3.10, pp. 19–20, has a valid endpoint trace estimate under its stated conormal wavefront condition. In local coordinates split Fourier space at \(|\xi_1|=A|\xi'|\). Inside the cone, the integration interval has length \(O(\langle\xi'\rangle)\) and \(\langle\xi\rangle\asymp\langle\xi'\rangle\). Cauchy–Schwarz gives the \(H^s\to H^{s-1/2}\) estimate for every real \(s\); the rapidly decreasing normal-cone remainder has smooth trace. The weight comparison is made while retaining that cone restriction. This avoids an invalid unrestricted weighted-integral comparison.

A distinct endpoint remains to be completed in Remark 3.9. The exact consulted Gogolev–Rodriguez Hertz version [gr] states conjugacy regularity \(C^{r_*}\), with \(r_*=r\) for nonintegral \(r\) and \(C^{r_*}=C^{r-1,\mathrm{Lip}}\) at an integer. For a \(C^4\) metric its flow is \(C^3\), so this citation directly gives \(C^{2,\mathrm{Lip}}\), whereas the remark says \(C^3\). This difference alone is not a counterexample to either regularity improvement or the \(C^4\) rigidity conclusion.

The weaker endpoint may suffice: it has the relevant bounded weak derivatives, and \(H^{-1}\) distributional pullback is well-defined. A finite Sobolev wavefront argument can split off an \(H^2\) remainder, whose trace is \(H^{3/2}\); the main admissible trace is \(H^{-3/2}\) and can be paired with \(C^2\) coefficients. However, this review does not complete the required endpoint microlocal covariance and propagation under \(C^{2,\mathrm{Lip}}\) coordinate changes, nor the entire low-regularity Pestov argument. The requested completion is a precise endpoint lemma and its application, or an independent stronger conjugacy result. This is retained as Needs Evidence, with the smooth result separately supported. No unsupported Minor or Major finding is assigned.

Corollary 1.2 uses positive Livšic and the geodesic-current volume comparison argument cited by the authors. The ordering and equality implications were traced at their interfaces; the full Croke–Dairbekov/Lopes–Thieullen proofs were not independently reproduced. A bounded author-site retrieval returned HTTP 403. Corollary 1.3 concerns a smooth, time-preserving conjugacy. The center of the unit-tangent-bundle fundamental group identifies the fiber subgroup, so the conjugacy induces a base-surface automorphism. After realizing its mapping class and applying Theorem 1.1, one reduces to a self-conjugacy with trivial base marking. The universal-cover endpoint description fixes each oriented geodesic; on a dense orbit, time preservation fixes a single shift, and continuity gives the same shift everywhere. Time reversal is outside this corollary’s hypothesis.

Classical Torelli, the orbit-equivalence construction, the complete smooth-conjugacy and tensor-tomography foundations, and the unused general-geometry algebra statement remain external inputs. Specific extension and finite-cover interfaces were consulted in exact author versions, without asserting equality to their later journal files.
# Assessment and state

No substantive defect is established in the inspected smooth main argument. The local orientation signs are clarified with the operative pairing unchanged. The \(C^4\) endpoint and the expressly bounded external proof coverage remain visible limitations.

Title: Technical Verification of
Maximal Parahoric Arithmetic Transfers,
Resolutions and Modularity
# Identity, version and scope

The paper is Zhiyu Zhang, Maximal parahoric arithmetic transfers, resolutions and modularity, associated with Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), 1–129, DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0023 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0023). The exact reviewed file is arXiv:2112.11994v3 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.11994v3), 9 May 2024, with the internal date 10 May 2024 [paper]. It is the accepted author manuscript; equivalence to the publisher’s version has not been established. All page locations below are physical pages of this 106-page PDF, whose printed numbering agrees. Journal page numbers are not substituted.

The root covered pp. 1–13 and 90–106, with additional direct checks of the findings; the auxiliary assignments covered pp. 14–30, 31–60 and 61–89. The p. 61 end of Section 9 was also checked by the local-geometry role. Hash-bound image records distinguish actual inspections from rendering. The coverage ledger identifies external interfaces not independently reproved. The acquired author TeX was read as a source witness, not executed. No separate supplement or original computational repository was identified in bounded primary-source checks; absence of code is not a defect.
# Assumptions and checks that survive

For arithmetic transfer \(F/F_0\) is unramified quadratic and the residue characteristic is odd. A vertex lattice has \(L\subseteq L^\vee\subseteq\varpi^{-1}L\), rank \(n\), and type \(0\le t\le n\). The original hermitian space \(V\) and the special-homomorphism space \(\mathbb V\) have opposite determinant parity. For \(L=L^\flat\oplus O_Fe\), \(i=v((e,e))\) is zero or one and \(t(L^\flat)=t-i\). The intermediate-type main theorem additionally requires \(F_0/\mathbb Q_p\) unramified; the extreme types retain the broader odd-residue-characteristic scope. Part 1’s Jacquet–Rallis transfer includes \(p=2\), separately from the arithmetic assertion.

The product-node resolution has, after removal of Rees-chart torsion, charts \[x_1=x_0u,\quad y_0=uy_1,\quad x_0uy_1=\varpi,
 \qquad
 x_0=x_1v,\quad y_1=vy_0,\quad x_1vy_0=\varpi.\] These are regular strict semistable charts, with a projective-line exceptional fiber over the double linking locus. The graph lifts in Proposition 5.17 use a Cartier pullback of the center; they do not need the excessive generality criticized below. The unit-denominator Lemma 6.10 is preserved and used in Problem 1.

The Weil/Fourier-transfer interface in the paper’s reference [67], Theorem A.1, was checked in the 2021 typeset version [weil], physical pp. 107–109, printed pp. 969–971. Its local-field formulation imposes no \(p\ne2\) restriction and retains \(\eta(\det V)\). Its underlying local trace formula was not independently reproved. Finite-etale descent in Proposition 3.19 supplies the dyadic integral Hilbert 90 step. The separate \(p>2\) explanation does not justify a trace-zero integral basis at \(p=2\). Slips in \(\delta,\sqrt\delta\) and a sign in that alternative explanation are clarifications. The assigned checks also verify orthogonal-basis construction by residue trace, integral transitivity, volume-one stabilizer unfolding, and the two-root-group argument in the double uncertainty principle.
# Central reduction and modularity findings

Problem 1 (The given Cayley pair changes under the scalar twist).  Theorem 6.15(1), p. 45, asserts \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Int}}(G)=\widetilde{\operatorname{Int}}^{\mathcal Z}(c_U(G))\) for any relative regular semisimple \(G\), with the original untwisted pair. Its proof twists \(G\) to obtain a unit denominator, changing the right-hand side. Assessment: Major.
## Every hypothesis and the explicit input

Equation reference: eq:G, eq:cayley. Take \(F_0=\mathbb Q_3\), \(F=\mathbb Q_3(\iota)\), \(\iota^2=-1\). This extension is unramified. Hensel lifting gives \(r\in\mathbb Q_3\) with \(r^2=-2\), and \(a=r+\iota\) satisfies \(a\bar a=-1\). Take an original split rank-two space with self-dual \(L=L^\flat\oplus O_Fe\), \((e,e)=1\). Thus \(n=2,t=0,i=0\). In its nearby space use \(f,e_0\) with Gram matrix \(J=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\). Put \[
 G=\begin{pmatrix}-2&a\\-3\bar a&-2\end{pmatrix}.\] Exact multiplication gives \(G^*JG=J\), \(\det G=1\). The vectors \(e_0,Ge_0\) are independent, with determinant \(-a\); \(T^2+4T+1\) has distinct roots. Relative regular semisimplicity holds. The reduced vector is nonzero, so its rank-one pair is also regular semisimple. Here \(d=-2,\ 1-d=3\). Formula (6.9), p. 43, gives \[
 c_U(G)=(-1,af/3),\qquad (af/3,af/3)=-1/3.\] By Proposition 5.7(3) this special divisor is empty, so the claimed right-hand side is zero.
## An actual derived intersection of length one

The moduli input exists: in the rank-one nearby space choose the special pair \(A=B=3^{-1}O_{\breve F}f\), with \(A^\vee=B^\vee=O_{\breve F}f\). It satisfies Proposition 7.6, and \(af\in B^\vee\) gives an integral special-fiber homomorphism by (7.14). Principal polarizations make its adjoint integral, with \(u^*u=uu^*=-3\). Thus [eq:G] (#eq:G) is a genuine polarized automorphism of the framed product.

The central scalar \(-1\) acts trivially on Rapoport–Zink moduli: multiplication by \(-1\) on the object identifies the two framings. Hence \(\Gamma_G=\Gamma_{-G}\), whereas \[1-d(-G)=-1\in O_F^\times,\qquad c_U(-G)=(-1,af).\] Apply the correctly restricted Lemma 6.10 to \(-G\), without using the disputed theorem. For \(D=\delta(\mathcal N^\flat)=\mathcal Z(e_0)\), \[(D\times D)\cap\Gamma_G
 \simeq\mathcal Z(af)\subseteq\mathcal N^\flat=\mathcal N_1^{[0]}.\] Proposition 9.2, p. 56, gives \(\mathcal Z(af)=\operatorname{Spf}(O_{\breve F}/(3))\), since \(v(-3)=1\).

Equation reference: eq:onezero. At type zero the resolution is the identity. The ambient \(\mathcal N_2^{[0]}\) is a regular formal surface and \(D,GD\) are horizontal Cartier divisors. The first-factor graph pullback is Tor-independent. The remaining equation restricts to \(3\) times a unit on the DVR \(D\simeq\operatorname{Spf}O_{\breve F}\). It is a nonzerodivisor, so no higher Tor term cancels the ordinary length. Thus \[
 \widetilde{\operatorname{Int}}(G)=1,\qquad \widetilde{\operatorname{Int}}^{\mathcal Z}(c_U(G))=0.\] The rank-one canonical-lifting formula is the explicitly retained base-theory interface; a new proof of all canonical-lifting theory is not claimed.
## Counterevidence, impact and correction

The twist preserves the left side but changes the reduced norm from \(-1/3\) to \(-3\). The correct unit-denominator lemma is consistent with the example. One can impose \(1-d\in O_F^\times\), or explicitly choose the twist and redefine the pair afterward. This repairs the statement; every repaired general reduction has not been verified here. The identity is a central Section 6 bridge, cited in the boundary induction on p. 103. Theorem 6.15(3) may survive a correctly stated twisted reduction. No counterexample to that implication or the main arithmetic transfer identity is asserted.

Problem 2 (The maximal-order sum includes nonexistent fixed components).  Theorem 9.10, p. 59, sums over every algebra factor, omitting the signature/type admissibility in Theorem 9.6. This false formula is explicitly used to prove Theorem 9.14, p. 61. Assessment: Major.

Take the same \(F_0,F\), \(n=2,t=0\), and \[\mathbb V=\langle1,3\rangle,\qquad
 g=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1),\qquad u=(3,1).\] The first line is split and the second nonsplit. Since the eigenvalue difference \(2\) is a unit, \(O_F[g]=O_F\times O_F\) is an etale maximal order. Also \(\det[u,gu]=-6\ne0\). Both components are integral; no nonintegral inactive-component ambiguity is needed.

At total type zero every \(t_i\) is zero. Theorem 9.6 allows only \(i_0=2\): an active split line would require odd type. Thus \(\operatorname{Fix}(g)\) is one copy of \(\operatorname{Spf}O_{\breve F}\). The inactive \(u_1=3\) lifts everywhere between the canonical signature-\((0,1)\) factors. The active component has norm \(3\). Proposition 9.2 gives length one, and Corollary 9.7 identifies the modified derived fixed cycle with the ordinary smooth fixed scheme. Consequently \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Int}}^{\mathcal Z}(g,u)=1\). The printed formula instead gives \[\sum_{j=1}^{2}\max\{0,(v((u_j,u_j))+a_j)/2\}
 =\frac{2+0}{2}+\frac{1+1}{2}=2.\] The extra one comes from the nonexistent \(i_0=1\) component.
## Independent analytic control

Equation reference: eq:orb. A matching triple is \(\gamma=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), \(b=(1,1)\), \(c=(9,3)\); its moments agree with those of \((g,u)\). The transfer factor is \(\eta(\det[b,\gamma b])=\eta(-2)=1\); the cyclic reference lattice is \(O_F^2\). Integral idempotents force stable lattices to be \(3^{s_1}O_F\oplus3^{s_2}O_F\). Support is exactly \(s_1\in\{-2,-1,0\},\ s_2\in\{-1,0\}\). With the volume-one stabilizer normalization, the six cosets give \[
 \operatorname{Orb}(z)=(3^{2z}-3^z+1)(1-3^z),\qquad
 \partial\operatorname{Orb}(0)=-\log3.\] This agrees with the actual geometric length one. The exact enumeration is separately recorded. Corollary 9.13 gives the same value: it retains the admissible active index, and the inactive rank-one orbital integral at zero is one.
## Dependence and repair boundary

Theorem 9.14 explicitly cites Theorem 9.10, Corollary 9.13 and the rank-one calculation. Those inputs do not agree as printed. Section 9 supplies a maximal-order input to global modification and induction. This establishes an invalid derivation tied to the core argument, although [eq:orb] (#eq:orb) verifies the desired transfer identity in this example. A repaired sum must retain admissible components and inactive-factor integrality conditions. The complete general corrected formula is not established here. A single local field factor is not contradicted; global irreducibility alone does not force local irreducibility.

Problem 3 (The Y-series has the wrong prescribed constant).  Equation (13.5), p. 86, and Theorem 13.9, p. 89, identify the arithmetic series with a theta series for both test functions. For the Y-family the constant identification contradicts Theorem 8.7. Assessment: Major for the exact modularity claim.
## The local discrepancy

Equation reference: eq:ZY. Take \(n=2,t=1\) and a type-zero component \(C=\mathbb P^1_\Lambda\). It is very special by Definition 12.14. Equation (8.11), p. 54, gives, for \(u\ne0\), \[
 (\mathcal Z(u),C)=1_\Lambda(u),\qquad
 (\mathcal Y(u),C)=-q1_\Lambda(u).\] The unique locally constant extensions at zero have values \(1,-q\). The factor is deliberate and compatible with Theorem 8.1’s Fourier relation.

Equation reference: eq:constant. The global test functions have the same away-from-\(v_0\) part and local factors \(1_L,1_{L^\vee}\), both one at zero. Proposition 11.18, p. 73, identifies their nonzero coefficients with \(\mathcal Z,\mathcal Y\). Equation (13.5) prescribes the same constant \(-\phi_i(0)c_1(\widehat\omega)\) for both. Proposition 13.7 computes \(\deg(\omega|_C)=-1\). Retaining a common nonzero arithmetic degree factor \(\kappa\), the prescribed constants are both \(\kappa\); the theta constants are \(\kappa,-q\kappa\). For the arithmetic Fourier series \(F_Z,F_Y\), all nonconstant coefficients therefore cancel in \[
 F_Y+qF_Z=(q+1)\kappa\ne0.\] A nonzero constant is not a holomorphic modular form of positive parallel weight: a congruence element with nonzero lower-left entry has a nonconstant weight factor. Intersecting the two levels makes this the same modularity test. It rules out simultaneous exact modularity and the exact Y theta identity.

For a type-two component, (8.12) instead reads \[(\mathcal Z(u),C)=-q1_\Lambda(u),\qquad
 (\mathcal Y(u),C)=1_{\Lambda^\vee}(u).\] The zero limits are \(-q,1\). The two identities in Proposition 13.7 would force \(\deg\omega=q\) and \(q\deg\omega=1\), hence \(q^2=1\). Thus a uniform scalar change of the degree cannot repair that proposition on both kinds of component.
## An admissible global instance

The discrepancy can remain nonzero in \(\mathbb R_\Delta\). Take \[F_0=\mathbb Q(\sqrt5),\quad F=F_0(\iota),\quad
 V=\operatorname{diag}(1,11\sqrt5),\quad L=O_F^2.\] Choose the CM type sending \(\iota\) to \(+i\) at both real embeddings, with distinguished embedding \(\sqrt5<0\). Set \(\Delta=\{v:v\mid2\text{ or }v\mid5\}\), and choose sufficiently small level there. The signatures are \((1,1)\), \((2,0)\). The Galois CM field gives total reflex field \(E=F\). Ramification over \(2\) permits the paper’s nonempty CM datum. The prime \(11\) splits in \(F_0\), while \(-1\) is nonsquare modulo \(11\). At either place above \(11\), \(F_{0,v}=\mathbb Q_{11}\), the quadratic extension is unramified and \(L_v\) has type one. Propositions 12.15–12.19 provide basic projective-line components. Choose the common away-from-\(v_0\) Schwartz factor to have value one at zero. The resulting nonzero degree factor is a rational multiple of \(\log11\), outside the rational span of \(\log2,\log5\). Thus [eq:constant] (#eq:constant) is nonzero in the required quotient.
## Counterevidence and limited impact

Theorem 13.5(1) asserts modularity only up to a constant; this example does not refute it. The vertical-annihilator version in Theorems 13.4 and 13.5(2) has a separate generic-fiber argument. Section 15 also uses nonzero coefficients of the genuinely defined theta series, and those coefficients remain correct. The bad constant alone does not disprove the final transfer identity. A repair must supply a suitable Y-family extension or vertical correction and reconcile both kinds of component. No complete global repair or author adoption is certified. The exact basic-locus theta/modularity theorem is a central claimed ingredient, so its established failure remains Major.
# Additional defects with bounded local impact

Problem 4 (A fixed Cayley parameter does not give every target norm).  Proposition 3.2 and Corollary 3.4, p. 18, and the reverse implication in Theorem 3.26, p. 25, omit an image constraint for fixed \(d\ne1\). Assessment: Minor.

For \(h=(e,e)\) and \(G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}t&u\\w&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), unitarity requires \((u,u)=h(1-d\bar d)\). Thus arbitrary \(g,u,d\ne1\) cannot be reconstructed. For a relative-regular witness over the same unramified \(\mathbb Q_3\) extension, take \(V^\flat=\langle1\rangle,h=1,d=0\), and \((g,u_1)=(1,2)\). The target pair is regular semisimple, but its required last column \((2,0)\) has norm four, not one. Passing to orbits does not remove this invariant obstruction.

The corrected condition is, for \(\alpha=(u_1,u_1)/h,\ z=(1-d)^{-1}\), \[\operatorname{Tr}_{F/F_0}z=1+\alpha.\] If \(\alpha\) is integral, every finite-field trace fiber contains a nonzero element, including at \(q=2\). Surjectivity of the unramified integral trace lifts it to a unit \(z\) with the prescribed trace. This chooses \(d\) with unit denominator. Writing \(s=1-d\) and \(w_1(x)=(gx,u_1)/h\), the reconstruction is \[G=\begin{pmatrix}g-su_1w_1&su_1\\sw_1&d\end{pmatrix}.\] The trace condition makes its mixed pairings zero and its last-column norm \(h\), giving the correct inverse on the compatible locus. The supported lattice condition \(u_1\in\Lambda\cap h\Lambda^\vee\) makes \(\alpha\) integral. If \(\alpha\) is nonintegral, no conjugate can meet this lattice support, so the relevant matching integrals vanish. For integral \(\alpha\), choose the unit \(z\) as above. This variable-\(d\) and support split repairs the intended reverse transfer argument. A charitable reading of Corollary 3.4 as an isomorphism onto its image does not validate the explicit unrestricted inverse assertion. No central transfer conclusion is refuted by this local defect.

Problem 5 (Scalar normalization is stated for too many inputs and tests).  The paragraph after (3.3), p. 20, quantifies over every regular semisimple orbit and every Schwartz test function. Both require restrictions. Assessment: Minor.

For \(J_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), let \[H=\begin{pmatrix}5/3&4/3\\4/3&5/3\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(H^*J_0H=J_0,\det H=1\), and \(e_2,He_2\) are independent. Its \(d=5/3\) has valuation \(-1\). Every norm-one scalar \(\xi\) is a unit, so \(v(1-\xi d)=-1\). None makes the denominator a unit. Independently, scalar twisting does not preserve every Schwartz test: the invariant \(d\) separates the relative orbits of \(H,\xi H\) when \(d\ne\xi d\). A nonnegative compact locally constant bump near one orbit, supported in a small separated \(d\)-neighborhood, has a positive orbital integral there and zero on the other. In this example the conjugating \(U(1)\) is compact, so positivity and convergence present no difficulty.

The actual lattice-stabilizer characteristic functions are invariant under central norm-one units. A negative-valuation \(d\) is outside their support. One may first discard those zero contributions, then normalize the integral \(d\) cases and recompute the twisted Cayley pair. These restrictions restore the intended application; unrestricted Schwartz invariance is not a valid general theorem.

Problem 6 (Strict transform does not preserve every local dimension).  Proposition 5.14(2), p. 37, allows any closed formal subscheme \(Y\), without purity or a surviving-component condition. Assessment: Minor.

Let \(k\) be the residue field, \(X=\mathbb A_k^3,\ Z=V(z),\ Y=V(z)\cup V(x,y)\), with reduced ideal \((xz,yz)\). These are locally formally of finite type over \(O_{\breve F}\) through \(k\). Blowing up the ambient Cartier plane is the identity. The strict transform is the closure of \(Y\setminus Z\), the \(z\)-axis. It is nonempty, but at the origin its local dimension is one and \(\dim_0Y=2\). Regular/pure graph applications instead use Cartier pullback and Proposition 5.17; the checked Hecke applications use their smooth or etale projections. No actual construction is refuted. An appropriate surviving-pure-component condition is needed; a fully general replacement theorem is not certified.

Problem 7 (The single-incidence local model has excessive dimension).  The proof of Theorem 10.8, p. 66, retains only a line \(\ell\), a hyperplane \(H\), and \((\ell,H)=0\). This is not the claimed model. Assessment: Minor.

The text uses a vector space over \(W(k)[1/p]\) with test rings where \(p\) is nilpotent. Even correcting the scalar ring to an integral lattice leaves a substantive problem. For \(n=3,t=2\), reduction of \(\operatorname{diag}(p,p,1)\) has a two-dimensional radical \(R\). Every line in \(R\) and every hyperplane satisfy the sole condition, giving \[\mathbb P(R)\times(\mathbb P^2)^\vee
 \simeq\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^2\] of dimension three, versus claimed relative dimension two. At the stated linking point \(\ell=\langle e_1\rangle,H=R\) the same excess persists locally.

Proposition 5.9, explicitly cited as the proof’s model, keeps both polarized lattice maps \(\lambda,\lambda^\vee\), with composite \(\varpi\). Theorem 10.5 also supplies a separate semistability interface. These are counterevidence against treating the naive model as the actual integral model. Repair requires the correct linked-lattice deformation problem or justified flat closure and a local-ring calculation; changing only \(W(k)[1/p]\) to \(W(k)\) is insufficient. No counterexample to the actual semistability conclusion is established.
# Double induction and unresolved interfaces
## Completing the relevant Lemma 15.1 argument

Theorem 15.7 uses \(B=\{v_0\}\), \(k_1=-c,k_2=-c+1\), so \(k_1+k_2+2c=1\), and boundary valuations zero and minus one. The Fourier support argument makes the enlarged-unipotent difference \(f_i(hn(b))-f_i(h)\) constant. For this single-place application, Fourier uniqueness on the compact adelic unipotent quotient suffices; the printed absolute-convergence assertion for every continuous function is unnecessary. After all nonzero coefficients vanish, archimedean unipotent invariance and its conjugate by a rational lower unipotent in the level group give archimedean invariance. Strong approximation then gives constancy.

The cyclotomic example on p. 98 gives \(F_0=\mathbb Q\) for \(q=3,5\). A totally real extension split at \(p\) preserves the local field, e.g. \(\mathbb Q(\iota,\sqrt{13})/\mathbb Q(\sqrt{13})\) at \(3\), or \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3},\sqrt{11})/\mathbb Q(\sqrt{11})\) at \(5\). This repairs the example-level \(F_0\ne\mathbb Q\) requirement and does not disprove globalization.
## Needs Evidence: modification normalization

Put \(A=	au(Z^{\mathbb Q})[E:F]\). Equations (14.16), (15.5), (15.6), pp. 94,100, divide geometric and archimedean terms by \(A\), while (15.7) adds a bare theta sum. Theorem 15.6, p. 101, writes \(\Theta(\xi,\phi'_{C_
u})=(\widehat Z^B(\xi,\phi_i),C_
u)\) without that denominator. For \(T=\sum_
u(\widehat Z^B(\xi,\phi_i),C_
u)\), the auxiliary-cycle identity makes the displayed modified difference equal the original normalized difference plus \[(1-A^{-1})T.\] No explicit rescaling convention for these theta functions or cycles was found. The printed volume definition also suppresses the compact level present in (11.14). An unstated normalization may remove this residual; this is a precise question for reconciliation, not another established Major finding.
## Needs Evidence: intermediate-type irreducibility

Proposition 12.24, pp. 82–83, adapts external arguments for \(1<t<n-1\). The exact cited van Hoften version [vh], arXiv:2010.10496v1, was consulted at its setup and Theorem 3.7.1/Lemma 3.7.4. Besides properness and adjoint simplicity, that argument uses a quasi-split/tame setup and noncompact \(J_b\)-factors. Its auxiliary union of strata of dimension at most one is not literally the whole basic intersection named in the target proof. A connected subspace meeting every closure component can suffice, so a terminology difference alone is no counterexample. The target acknowledges quasi-split qualifications on p. 84.

The asserted adaptation, all group hypotheses and its two further external interfaces were not fully verified. This remains a bounded dependency limitation, not a claim that Proposition 12.24 is false. The \(n=2,t=1\) constant-term example uses the separate projective-line description, not this adaptation.
# Overall impact and state

Problems 1–3 establish central intermediate claims or derivations that are invalid in the reviewed version, independently of the unresolved normalization question. Problems 4–7 are local defects without demonstrated central damage. The explicit maximal-order example verifies the desired transfer identity using its actual geometric length. The Y-series finding leaves modularity up to a constant, the vertical-annihilator argument and nonzero theta coefficients as surviving statements. These distinctions do not certify fully repaired proofs of all main results.

For \(h=(e,e)\) and \(G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}t&u\\w&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), unitarity requires \((u,u)=h(1-d\bar d)\). Thus arbitrary \(g,u,d\ne1\) cannot be reconstructed. The target pair is regular semisimple, but its required last column \((2,0)\) has norm four, not one. Passing to orbits does not remove this invariant obstruction.

The corrected condition is, for \(\alpha=(u_1,u_1)/h,\ z=(1-d)^{-1}\), \[\operatorname{Tr}_{F/F_0}z=1+\alpha.\] If \(\alpha\) is integral, every finite-field trace fiber contains a nonzero element, including at \(q=2\). Writing \(s=1-d\) and \(w_1(x)=(gx,u_1)/h\), the reconstruction is \[G=\begin{pmatrix}g-su_1w_1&su_1\\sw_1&d\end{pmatrix}.\] The trace condition makes its mixed pairings zero and its last-column norm \(h\), giving the correct inverse on the compatible locus. If \(\alpha\) is nonintegral, no conjugate can meet this lattice support, so the relevant matching integrals vanish. For integral \(\alpha\), choose the unit \(z\) as above.
