report: Abstract: A claim-focused examination of the author manuscript identifies three substantive issues. The unrestricted six-dimensional distance estimate in Corollary 1.6 fails for an explicit positive multiple of one bubble whose residual is exactly one. The decomposition used in Lemma 6.2 does not have the asserted orthogonality and therefore does not justify its spectral-gap argument. The final unweighted estimate in Lemma 6.5 does not give a little-oh interaction remainder in dimensions at least twelve. A conditional globalization correction and a local weighted replacement for the last estimate are provided. The findings concern the identified author manuscript and the stated proof steps; they do not establish that the local sharp stability theorem is false.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Verification of the quantitative Struwe decomposition
# Identity, reviewed material, and scope

This report concerns Sharp quantitative estimates of Struwe’s decomposition, by Bin Deng, Liming Sun, and Jun-cheng Wei, associated with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0026 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0026). The primary source is the 59-page author-hosted manuscript dated January 3, 2024 [DSW24]. All source page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, which agree with the printed pages. The publisher’s version of record was not acquired or compared. The preserved arXiv v2 source is dated 2021 and is a separate version [DSW21].

The review checks the statements in the introduction, the closing argument of Section 2, the energy and remainder estimates in Section 6, the relevant sharpness argument in Section 7, and the weight bounds needed for a local correction. The lengthy bubble-tree and neck-region estimates in Sections 3–5 are not independently certified in full. No missing optional code is treated as a mathematical defect. The supported assessment is Major: the first finding disproves a stated quantitative corollary, and the other two identify invalid steps used in the proof of the central theorem.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

Equation reference: eq:rate. The manuscript uses \[p=\frac{n+2}{n-2},\qquad
U[z,\lambda](x)=(n(n-2))^{(n-2)/4}
 \left(\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda^2|x-z|^2}\right)^{(n-2)/2}.\] These satisfy \(-\Delta U=U^p\) and have parameter-independent \(\dot H^1\) norm. The residual is \(\Gamma(u)=\|\Delta u+u|u|^{p-1}\|_{H^{-1}}\). We first use the dual of the homogeneous energy norm, consistent with the source’s \(\dot H^1\) framework. The rate in source equation (1.8), p. 4, is \[
 \zeta_n(t)=
 \begin{cases}t\sqrt{|\log t|},&n=6,\\
 t^{p/2},&n\ge7,\end{cases}\qquad t>0.\] Theorem 1.4 assumes proximity to a weakly interacting family of bubbles. Corollary 1.6 instead assumes positivity and an energy shell, without an explicit small-residual condition. Constants may depend on \(n\) and the fixed number \(\nu\) of bubbles. For \(\nu\ge2\), the interaction parameter is \[Q=\max_{i\ne j}\left(\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_j}+\frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_i}
       +\lambda_i\lambda_j|z_i-z_j|^2\right)^{-(n-2)/2}.\] It tends to zero along the separated configurations considered below.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The unrestricted six-dimensional corollary vanishes at a nonzero residual).  Corollary 1.6, p. 5, together with equation (1.8), p. 4, is false as written for \(n=6\).
## Original assertion

For every nonnegative \(u\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^n)\) satisfying \[(
u-	frac12)S^n\le\|
abla u\|_2^2\le(
u+	frac12)S^n,\] the corollary asserts a distance to a sum of \(
u\) normalized bubbles at most \(C\zeta_n(\Gamma)\). Here \(S\) is normalized by \(S\|u\|_{2^*}\le\|
abla u\|_2\). The proof on p. 13 consists of a reference to the proof of a corollary in the cited Figalli–Glaudo work.
## Exact check

Equation reference: eq:bubble. Set \(n=6\), \(\nu=1\), and \[
 U(x)=\frac{24}{(1+|x|^2)^2},\qquad
 A=\|\nabla U\|_2=\sqrt{\frac{1152\pi^3}{5}},\qquad
 c=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4/A}}2,\qquad u=cU.\] The identity \(-\Delta U=U^2\) gives \[A^2=\int_{\mathbb R^6}U^3
 =24^3\pi^3\int_0^\infty\frac{r^5}{(1+r^2)^6}\,dr
 =\frac{1152\pi^3}{5}=S^6.\] Thus \(u>0\) and \(u\in\dot H^1\). Since \(A>5\) and \(c-1=1/(Ac)<1/5\), we have \(1/2<c^2<36/25<3/2\). Every energy hypothesis is satisfied.

Equation reference: eq:residual, eq:distance. Integration by parts and Cauchy–Schwarz show \(\|U^2\|_{\dot H^{-1}}\le A\), with equality on the test function \(U/A\). Consequently, \[
 \Gamma(u)=\|(c^2-c)U^2\|_{\dot H^{-1}}=Ac(c-1)=1.\] For every normalized bubble \(V=U[z,\lambda]\), \(\|V\|_{\dot H^1}=A\). The reverse triangle inequality and the choice \(V=U\) give the exact distance \[
 \inf_{z,\lambda}\|cU-U[z,\lambda]\|_{\dot H^1}=(c-1)A=\frac1c>0.\] The claimed right-hand side is \(C\zeta_6(1)=0\), a contradiction for every finite \(C\). The pair-interaction assertion is vacuous when \(\nu=1\).
## Alternative readings and correction boundary

Equation (1.8) expressly defines the rate for all positive arguments, and the source only says it is increasing near zero. The proximity assumption of Theorem 1.4 cannot silently be appended to the separately stated corollary. This example does not challenge the sufficiently small-residual asymptotic rate.

Even interpreting \(H^{-1}\) as the usual inhomogeneous dual does not remove the defect. Put \(B=\|U^2\|_{H^{-1}}\) and replace \(A\) by \(B\) in the definition of \(c\). Since \(\|U\|_2^2=96\pi^3\), testing against \(U\) gives \(B\ge A\sqrt{12/17}>5\). Then \(\Gamma=1\) and the same energy and positive-distance argument applies.

A precise local correction is to require \(0\le\Gamma\le\epsilon(n,\nu)<1\), sufficiently small for Struwe compactness to place the function in the local theorem’s regime. Alternatively replace the six-dimensional rate by \(\widetilde\zeta_6(t)=t\sqrt{1+|\log t|}\), with value zero at \(t=0\). This preserves the small-residual order. For \(t\ge\epsilon\) the modified rate is at least \(\epsilon\), while the energy shell bounds the distance to any fixed family of \(\nu\) bubbles. Increasing \(C\) then extends a valid local estimate to this remaining range; a fixed sufficiently separated family also bounds the pair interactions. This verifies the globalization mechanism conditional on the local theorem. The proof issues below must be addressed independently.

Problem 2 (The coefficients in the spectral decomposition are not projection coordinates).  Source equations (6.4)–(6.6), p. 46, do not imply the orthogonality used in the proof of Lemma 6.2 on p. 47.
## Source step and complete algebraic check

Equation reference: eq:gram. The source sets \[\rho_1=\sum_i\beta_iU_i+\rho_2,\qquad
 \beta_i=\langle \rho_1,U_i\rangle_{\dot H^1},\] and asserts \(\langle \rho_2,U_k\rangle_{\dot H^1}=0=\langle \rho_2,Z_k^a\rangle_{\dot H^1}\). Write \(G_{ki}=\langle U_i,U_k\rangle_{\dot H^1}\) and \(b_k=\langle \rho_1,U_k\rangle_{\dot H^1}\). The actual identity is \[
 (\langle \rho_2,U_k\rangle_{\dot H^1})_k=(I-G)b.\] The diagonal entries of \(G\) equal \(A_n^2=\|\nabla U\|_2^2\), not one, and its off-diagonal entries are positive interaction integrals. Furthermore, the initial tangent orthogonality of \(\rho_1\) only implies \[\langle \rho_2,Z_k^a\rangle_{\dot H^1}=-\sum_i b_i\langle U_i,Z_k^a\rangle_{\dot H^1},\] whose cross terms need not vanish.

Equation reference: eq:badgap. There is an exact arbitrarily small one-bubble diagnostic. Take \(n=6\), \(u=(1+t)U\), \(0<|t|\ll1\), with \(U\) as in [eq:bubble] (#eq:bubble). The closest normalized bubble is \(U\), so \(\rho=tU\). The interaction forcing is zero and \(\rho_0=0\) solves the projected correction equation; hence \(\rho_1=tU\). Parameter invariance of \(\|U\|_{\dot H^1}\) gives \(\langle U,Z^a\rangle_{\dot H^1}=0\), as required. The printed definitions yield \[\beta=tA^2,\qquad
 \rho_2=t(1-A^2)U,\qquad
 \langle \rho_2,U\rangle_{\dot H^1}=t(1-A^2)A^2\ne0.\] This is an algebraic test of the asserted decomposition; it does not depend on assigning a value to a maximum over an empty set of bubble pairs. For this \(\rho_2\) the spectral quotient is exactly \[
 \frac{p\int U^{p-1}\rho_2^2}{\int|\nabla\rho_2|^2}=p=2.\] It therefore cannot satisfy the bound with \(\widetilde c<1\) displayed at the bottom of p. 47.

The problem also persists for arbitrarily weakly interacting multiple bubbles. In the orthogonal complement of all tangent modes, project \(U_1\) onto that complement and multiply it by a small scalar. As separation tends to infinity, the tangent Gram matrix tends to invertible single-bubble blocks and the cross terms tend to zero. For this admissible \(\rho_1\), the vector \(b\) tends to a nonzero multiple of the first coordinate vector, while \(G\to A_n^2I\). Equation [eq:gram] (#eq:gram) is then nonzero whenever \(A_n^2\ne1\), including \(n=6\). Thus the diagnostic does not arise solely from the one-bubble endpoint.
## Dependence, counterevidence, and repair

Lemma 6.2 uses the asserted orthogonality both to eliminate multiplier terms and to invoke a second-variation gap. It feeds Lemma 6.3, Proposition 6.4 (p. 49), and the closing proof of Theorem 1.4 (p. 13). This is a core proof defect; equation [eq:badgap] (#eq:badgap) does not disprove the conclusion of Lemma 6.2 or Theorem 1.4.

An intended genuine projection would resolve the elementary algebra but is not the displayed definition. Even dividing by \(A_n^2\) leaves the off-diagonal and tangent terms. Solving \(G\beta=b\) enforces only bubble orthogonality. A complete revision must either project onto the joint bubble-and-tangent span, or project the bubble directions within the tangent-orthogonal subspace, and then rederive the multiplier cancellation and coefficient estimates. That full repair has not been verified here. The source normalization and formulas were checked directly on the rendered pages.

Problem 3 (The last unweighted remainder estimate fails in dimensions at least twelve).  The last display of the proof of Lemma 6.5, at the top of p. 50, does not follow from Proposition 6.1 in the full claimed dimensional range.
## Exponent and sharpness check

The source bounds the weighted integral through the global energy norm and then asserts \[\|
ablaho_0\|_2^p+\|
ablaho_1\|_2^p
 \lesssim o(Q)+\|f\|_{H^{-1}}^p.\] Proposition 6.1 gives \(\|
ablaho_0\|_2\lesssim\zeta_n(Q)\). For \(n\ge7\) this only supplies \[\zeta_n(Q)^p=Q^{p^2/2}.\] It is \(o(Q)\) precisely when \(p^2/2>1\). The integer-dimensional threshold is \(7\le n\le11\); at \(n=12\), \[p= rac75,\qquad  rac{p^2}{2}= rac{49}{50}<1,\qquad
  rac{Q^{49/50}}{Q}=Q^{-1/50}\longrightarrow\infty.\] The exponent decreases thereafter. For \(n=6\), the corresponding \(Q^2|\log Q|\) is indeed \(o(Q)\).

This is not cured by claiming an unstated improvement of the global norm. The two-bubble construction in Section 7 has \(\|f\|_{H^{-1}}\lesssim Q\) by (7.3), p. 50. The displayed lower bound on p. 52, before replacing \(Q\) by the residual, gives \(\|\nabla\rho_0\|_2\gtrsim\zeta_n(Q)\) after fixing \(L\) and increasing \(R\). In dimension twelve its \(p\)th power is bounded below by a multiple of \(Q^{49/50}\), whereas both \(o(Q)\) and \(O(Q^p)\) are \(o(Q)\). Thus the stated unweighted intermediate estimate is incompatible with that sharpness bound. The weighted integral in Lemma 6.5 can still have the required order.
## A verified local replacement

Equation reference: eq:weightedfix. Keep the weight instead of discarding it. For the affected range \(n\ge12\), Proposition 5.4, p. 44, the bound preceding (5.39), p. 45, and the integral estimate on p. 43 from Lemma B.1 give \[|\rho_0|\lesssim W,\qquad
 W^p\lesssim R^{-4(p-1)}V,\qquad
 \int VU_k\lesssim Q,\qquad |Z_k^{n+1}|\lesssim U_k.\] Consequently, \[
 \int |\rho_0|^p|Z_k^{n+1}|
 \lesssim R^{-4(p-1)}\int VU_k
 \lesssim R^{-4(p-1)}Q=o(Q).\] The remaining component is bounded, conditional on Proposition 6.4, by \[\int|\rho_1|^p|Z_k^{n+1}|
 \lesssim\|\nabla\rho_1\|_2^p
 \lesssim Q^{2p}+\|f\|_{H^{-1}}^p.\] Since \(p>1\), \(Q^{2p}=o(Q)\) and the last term is \(O(\|f\|_{H^{-1}})\) for small residual. Together with \(|\rho_0+\rho_1|^p\le2^{p-1}(|\rho_0|^p+|\rho_1|^p)\), this restores precisely the weighted estimate needed. It does not fix the decomposition in Problem 2 or certify every upstream estimate. The affected dependency is Lemma 6.5 to the interaction bound in Lemma 2.3 and then Theorem 1.4. The short available repair does not change that core dependency.
# Overall conclusion

The three findings distinguish a false unrestricted corollary from invalid arguments for a local theorem. The small-residual rates and the conceptual two-bubble sharpness mechanism are not refuted by the counterexample. Full verification of the repaired main theorem requires a corrected spectral decomposition and its downstream estimates, together with checking the remaining pointwise analysis. No empirical reruns are required for the analytic findings made here.

A bounded current search of the author/repository and publisher records did not locate an explicit correction to these exact passages; this is not an absence or priority claim. Conclusions about the unexamined journal-final text remain open.
# Supporting checks

problems.title: Unrestricted six-dimensional corollary at residual one
problems.source_location: PDF/printed pp4-5, equation(1.8), Corollary1.6; proof p13
claim:
Equation reference: eq:rate. The manuscript uses \[p=\frac{n+2}{n-2},\qquad
U[z,\lambda](x)=(n(n-2))^{(n-2)/4}
 \left(\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda^2|x-z|^2}\right)^{(n-2)/2}.\] These satisfy \(-\Delta U=U^p\) and have parameter-independent \(\dot H^1\) norm. The residual is \(\Gamma(u)=\|\Delta u+u|u|^{p-1}\|_{H^{-1}}\). We first use the dual of the homogeneous energy norm, consistent with the source’s \(\dot H^1\) framework. The rate in source equation (1.8), p. 4, is \[
 \zeta_n(t)=
 \begin{cases}t\sqrt{|\log t|},&n=6,\\
 t^{p/2},&n\ge7,\end{cases}\qquad t>0.\] Theorem 1.4 assumes proximity to a weakly interacting family of bubbles. Corollary 1.6 instead assumes positivity and an energy shell, without an explicit small-residual condition. Constants may depend on \(n\) and the fixed number \(\nu\) of bubbles. For \(\nu\ge2\), the interaction parameter is \[Q=\max_{i\ne j}\left(\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_j}+\frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_i}
       +\lambda_i\lambda_j|z_i-z_j|^2\right)^{-(n-2)/2}.\] It tends to zero along the separated configurations considered below.
Every nonnegative u in the specified energy shell has distance at most C Gamma sqrt(|log Gamma|) in dimension6.
analysis: Corollary 1.6, p. 5, together with equation (1.8), p. 4, is false as written for \(n=6\).

For every nonnegative \(u\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^n)\) satisfying \[(
u-	frac12)S^n\le\|
abla u\|_2^2\le(
u+	frac12)S^n,\] the corollary asserts a distance to a sum of \(
u\) normalized bubbles at most \(C\zeta_n(\Gamma)\). Here \(S\) is normalized by \(S\|u\|_{2^*}\le\|
abla u\|_2\). The proof on p. 13 consists of a reference to the proof of a corollary in the cited Figalli–Glaudo work.

Equation reference: eq:bubble. Set \(n=6\), \(\nu=1\), and \[
 U(x)=\frac{24}{(1+|x|^2)^2},\qquad
 A=\|\nabla U\|_2=\sqrt{\frac{1152\pi^3}{5}},\qquad
 c=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4/A}}2,\qquad u=cU.\] The identity \(-\Delta U=U^2\) gives \[A^2=\int_{\mathbb R^6}U^3
 =24^3\pi^3\int_0^\infty\frac{r^5}{(1+r^2)^6}\,dr
 =\frac{1152\pi^3}{5}=S^6.\] Thus \(u>0\) and \(u\in\dot H^1\). Since \(A>5\) and \(c-1=1/(Ac)<1/5\), we have \(1/2<c^2<36/25<3/2\). Every energy hypothesis is satisfied.

Equation reference: eq:residual, eq:distance. Integration by parts and Cauchy–Schwarz show \(\|U^2\|_{\dot H^{-1}}\le A\), with equality on the test function \(U/A\). Consequently, \[
 \Gamma(u)=\|(c^2-c)U^2\|_{\dot H^{-1}}=Ac(c-1)=1.\] For every normalized bubble \(V=U[z,\lambda]\), \(\|V\|_{\dot H^1}=A\). The reverse triangle inequality and the choice \(V=U\) give the exact distance \[
 \inf_{z,\lambda}\|cU-U[z,\lambda]\|_{\dot H^1}=(c-1)A=\frac1c>0.\] The claimed right-hand side is \(C\zeta_6(1)=0\), a contradiction for every finite \(C\). The pair-interaction assertion is vacuous when \(\nu=1\).
result: Equation (1.8) expressly defines the rate for all positive arguments, and the source only says it is increasing near zero. The proximity assumption of Theorem 1.4 cannot silently be appended to the separately stated corollary. This example does not challenge the sufficiently small-residual asymptotic rate.

Even interpreting \(H^{-1}\) as the usual inhomogeneous dual does not remove the defect. Put \(B=\|U^2\|_{H^{-1}}\) and replace \(A\) by \(B\) in the definition of \(c\). Since \(\|U\|_2^2=96\pi^3\), testing against \(U\) gives \(B\ge A\sqrt{12/17}>5\). Then \(\Gamma=1\) and the same energy and positive-distance argument applies.

A precise local correction is to require \(0\le\Gamma\le\epsilon(n,\nu)<1\), sufficiently small for Struwe compactness to place the function in the local theorem’s regime. Alternatively replace the six-dimensional rate by \(\widetilde\zeta_6(t)=t\sqrt{1+|\log t|}\), with value zero at \(t=0\). This preserves the small-residual order. For \(t\ge\epsilon\) the modified rate is at least \(\epsilon\), while the energy shell bounds the distance to any fixed family of \(\nu\) bubbles. Increasing \(C\) then extends a valid local estimate to this remaining range; a fixed sufficiently separated family also bounds the pair interactions. This verifies the globalization mechanism conditional on the local theorem. The proof issues below must be addressed independently.

Impact: False unrestricted dimension6 distance conclusion; n>=7 and small-residual logarithmic asymptotics not refuted.

beta_i=<rho1,Ui> and rho2=rho1-sum beta_i Ui imply rho2 orthogonal to Ui and Zi.

analysis: Source equations (6.4)–(6.6), p. 46, do not imply the orthogonality used in the proof of Lemma 6.2 on p. 47.

Equation reference: eq:gram. The source sets \[\rho_1=\sum_i\beta_iU_i+\rho_2,\qquad
 \beta_i=\langle \rho_1,U_i\rangle_{\dot H^1},\] and asserts \(\langle \rho_2,U_k\rangle_{\dot H^1}=0=\langle \rho_2,Z_k^a\rangle_{\dot H^1}\). Write \(G_{ki}=\langle U_i,U_k\rangle_{\dot H^1}\) and \(b_k=\langle \rho_1,U_k\rangle_{\dot H^1}\). The actual identity is \[
 (\langle \rho_2,U_k\rangle_{\dot H^1})_k=(I-G)b.\] The diagonal entries of \(G\) equal \(A_n^2=\|\nabla U\|_2^2\), not one, and its off-diagonal entries are positive interaction integrals. Furthermore, the initial tangent orthogonality of \(\rho_1\) only implies \[\langle \rho_2,Z_k^a\rangle_{\dot H^1}=-\sum_i b_i\langle U_i,Z_k^a\rangle_{\dot H^1},\] whose cross terms need not vanish.

Equation reference: eq:badgap. There is an exact arbitrarily small one-bubble diagnostic. Take \(n=6\), \(u=(1+t)U\), \(0<|t|\ll1\), with \(U\) as in [eq:bubble] (#eq:bubble). The closest normalized bubble is \(U\), so \(\rho=tU\). The interaction forcing is zero and \(\rho_0=0\) solves the projected correction equation; hence \(\rho_1=tU\). Parameter invariance of \(\|U\|_{\dot H^1}\) gives \(\langle U,Z^a\rangle_{\dot H^1}=0\), as required. The printed definitions yield \[\beta=tA^2,\qquad
 \rho_2=t(1-A^2)U,\qquad
 \langle \rho_2,U\rangle_{\dot H^1}=t(1-A^2)A^2\ne0.\] This is an algebraic test of the asserted decomposition; it does not depend on assigning a value to a maximum over an empty set of bubble pairs. For this \(\rho_2\) the spectral quotient is exactly \[
 \frac{p\int U^{p-1}\rho_2^2}{\int|\nabla\rho_2|^2}=p=2.\] It therefore cannot satisfy the bound with \(\widetilde c<1\) displayed at the bottom of p. 47.

The problem also persists for arbitrarily weakly interacting multiple bubbles. In the orthogonal complement of all tangent modes, project \(U_1\) onto that complement and multiply it by a small scalar. As separation tends to infinity, the tangent Gram matrix tends to invertible single-bubble blocks and the cross terms tend to zero. For this admissible \(\rho_1\), the vector \(b\) tends to a nonzero multiple of the first coordinate vector, while \(G\to A_n^2I\). Equation [eq:gram] (#eq:gram) is then nonzero whenever \(A_n^2\ne1\), including \(n=6\). Thus the diagnostic does not arise solely from the one-bubble endpoint.

Lemma 6.2 uses the asserted orthogonality both to eliminate multiplier terms and to invoke a second-variation gap. It feeds Lemma 6.3, Proposition 6.4 (p. 49), and the closing proof of Theorem 1.4 (p. 13). This is a core proof defect; equation [eq:badgap] (#eq:badgap) does not disprove the conclusion of Lemma 6.2 or Theorem 1.4.

An intended genuine projection would resolve the elementary algebra but is not the displayed definition. Even dividing by \(A_n^2\) leaves the off-diagonal and tangent terms. Solving \(G\beta=b\) enforces only bubble orthogonality. A complete revision must either project onto the joint bubble-and-tangent span, or project the bubble directions within the tangent-orthogonal subspace, and then rederive the multiplier cancellation and coefficient estimates. That full repair has not been verified here. The source normalization and formulas were checked directly on the rendered pages.
result: Result: Invalid algebraic orthogonality and invalid invocation of strict spectral gap
Impact: Lemma6.2 -> Lemma6.3 -> Proposition6.4 -> Lemma6.5/Lemma2.3 -> Theorem1.4. The theorem is not disproved.

report: Abstract: The characteristic-two length argument is consistent under the explicit finite-length, nonzero-homology hypotheses of Theorem 4.1. The acquired manuscript nevertheless defines the codimension of total homology using a maximum. With that definition its central extension to short complexes is false: a minimal complex over a regular local ring of dimension three has total rank six while satisfying the printed shortness condition. Replacing the maximum by the codimension of the total support excludes this example and explains the intended localization. A separate omission of nonzero homology affects introductory and subsidiary formulations. These findings concern the acquired author manuscript; they do not establish a failure of the finite-length module theorem or of the intended corrected result.
Author: AI-assisted initial scientific review

Title: Technical review of
The total rank conjecture in characteristic 2
# Identity, scope, and notation

This report concerns Keller VandeBogert and Mark E. Walker, The total rank conjecture in characteristic 2, arXiv:2305.09771v2, 11 April 2024, 19 PDF pages, associated with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0027. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed pagination. The publisher version was not available for comparison. The primary PDF SHA256 begins `31af4cce625fcb39`; its complete digest, the acquired TeX digest, and all input checks are recorded in the accompanying provenance.

The full manuscript text was read. Detailed checks concentrated on the definition of shortness, the symmetric/exterior-square exact sequences, the equality statement in Theorem 3.2, the asymptotic inequalities and positivity in Theorem 4.1, and the reduction in Theorem 5.1. The background theorems on Dold–Kan, Dutta limits, the New Intersection Theorem, and characteristic-zero transfer are dependencies; this review is not an independent proof of those theorems.

Write \(H(P)=\bigoplus_jH_j(P)\). Over a local ring, \(\beta(P)\) denotes the sum of the ranks of a minimal free representative, as in Notation 1.13. A complex with all differential entries in the maximal ideal is already minimal.
# A false domain for the short-complex extension

Problem 1 (Major: maximum codimension in Definition 1.5).  Definition 1.5, p. 2, defines a short complex supported in degrees \(0,\ldots,c\) by \[c=\operatorname{codim}_R(H(P)):=\max_j\{\operatorname{codim}_R H_j(P)\}.\] Conjecture 1.6, p. 3, then asserts the total rank bound \(2^c\); Theorem 5.1, p. 16, asserts this conjecture for all Noetherian algebras over a field. The printed maximum admits the following counterexample.

Let \(k=\mathbf F_2\), \(R=k[x,y,z]_{(x,y,z)}\), and take \[P=\bigl(0\longrightarrow R
       \xrightarrow{\,0\,}R
       \xrightarrow{\,0\,}R^3
       \xrightarrow{\,[\,x\ y\ z\,]\,}R
       \longrightarrow0\bigr),\] in degrees \(3,2,1,0\). The ring is a connected, Noetherian, regular local field algebra of dimension three. All four terms are nonzero and free, all compositions vanish, and the complex is minimal. Its homology is \[H_0(P)=k,\qquad
 H_1(P)=\ker[\,x\ y\ z\,],\qquad
 H_2(P)=H_3(P)=R.\] The kernel in degree one is nonzero, since it contains \((y,x,0)\). It is a submodule of a free module over a domain and has zero annihilator. Consequently the four homology codimensions are \(3,0,0,0\), respectively. In particular, \[\max_{0\le j\le3}\operatorname{codim}_RH_j(P)=3,\qquad
 \sum_j\operatorname{rank}_RP_j=\beta(P)=6<8=2^3.\] All homology groups in the displayed interval are nonzero. Here the printed maximum is read over that interval, equivalently over the nonzero homology groups in this example. If all zero groups outside the interval are included with codimension \(+\infty\), Definition 1.5 instead assigns no finite \(c\) to a bounded complex and itself requires clarification. Under the finite interpretation, this nonexact complex meets the printed shortness condition. Neither minimality nor a requirement that the endpoint terms be nonzero removes the counterexample.
## Dependency and counterevidence

The first sentence of the proof of Theorem 5.1 localizes at a prime of height \(c\) in the support and claims to obtain a tiny complex. For this example, localization at the maximal ideal leaves the positive-rank homology in degrees \(1,2,3\); these modules do not have finite length. Thus the displayed reduction does not apply to the class defined using the maximum.

There is strong evidence for a different intended definition. Page 3 identifies tiny complexes with complexes having finite-length homology, and Section 2.2, p. 10, restates that finite-length, nonzero-homology condition explicitly. The operative Theorem 4.1, p. 13, also requires finite-length, nonzero homology. The counterexample above violates those finite-length hypotheses and therefore does not refute that theorem, nor the original total rank conjecture for finite-length modules.
## Correction boundary

For a nonzero total homology module, the codimension of its support is \[\operatorname{codim}_R\!\left(\bigoplus_j H_j(P)\right)
 =\min_{H_j(P)\ne0}\operatorname{codim}_R H_j(P).\] Replacing the maximum by this minimum excludes the example: its total support has codimension zero. Localizing at a minimal prime of that support of height \(c\) then makes every surviving homology module finite length over the local ring of dimension \(c\), which is the reduction used on p. 16. This is a concrete correction of the domain, not a proof that the uncorrected assertion holds. The corrected result still depends on the subsequent tiny-complex and transfer arguments. The Major classification concerns a demonstrated false central statement under its printed definition; it does not assert irreparability.
# Nonzero homology in subsidiary formulations

Problem 2 (Minor: omitted nonzero hypothesis).  Introductory Theorem 1.7, p. 3, and Theorem 4.10, pp. 15–16, omit \(H(P)\ne0\). The latter divides by \(h^\infty(P)\). Notation 1.13, p. 6, permits exact objects in \(\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{fl}}(R)\), so membership in that category does not supply the missing condition.

Set \(R=\mathbf F_2[[x,y]]\), \(d=2\), and let \(P\) be the contractible complex \(R\xrightarrow{1}R\) in degrees \(1,0\), extended by zero to the displayed intervals of these theorems. This ring is complete and has perfect residue field. Every Frobenius iterate is again contractible, and \[H(P)=0,\quad \beta(P)=h^\infty(P)=h_1^\infty(P)
       =\chi^\infty(P)=0,\qquad
 \sum_j\operatorname{rank}_RP_j=2.\] The literal inequality in Theorem 1.7 would say \(2\ge4\). The ratio in Theorem 4.10 is \(0/0\), while its subsequent assertion for \(\chi^\infty(P)=0\) would give \(0=\beta(P)\ge2\). The zero complex is an even simpler boundary case.

Requiring nonzero homology excludes these examples and supplies the positivity needed in the proof. Theorem 4.1 already states this requirement. The surrounding discussion of total rank conjectures also concerns nontrivial homology, which supports this repair. The issue is classified as Minor because it concerns omitted domain restrictions in these formulations and does not defeat the explicitly restricted central characteristic-two theorem. The analogous nontriviality convention should also be stated when formulating the Section 6 conjecture and applications.
# Checks supporting the retained core argument
## Exact sequences and equality

The two sequences in Lemma 2.16, pp. 9–10, were checked with the characteristic-two Frobenius twist: the map \(x\mapsto x^2\) is linear with that twist. The absolute values in (3.3), p. 12, are present in the page image. They yield the lower bound used in (3.6), p. 13, rather than an unsupported signed equality.

For Theorem 3.2 the hypotheses include a nonzero finite-length module of finite projective dimension over a quasi-Roberts ring. The checked inequalities give \[\ell(M)\beta(M)\ge h(P\otimes P)
 \ge 2^d\ell(M)+2\ell(\Lambda^2M).\] If \(\beta(M)=2^d\), then \(\Lambda^2M=0\). Reduction modulo the maximal ideal forces \(M\) to be cyclic. Equality in the first bound forces the differential of \(P\otimes M\) to vanish, and hence \(I/I^2\) is free for \(M=R/I\). The concluding use of the Ferrand–Vasconcelos criterion requires finite projective dimension, which is available here. That cited criterion itself was not reproved.
## The asymptotic inequality

For the proof of Theorem 4.1, write \[a_j=h_j^\infty(\widetilde\Lambda^2P),\qquad
 s_j=h_j^\infty(\widetilde S^2P).\] The long exact sequence and Theorem 2.26 give \(a_j=s_j\) for \(j\ge3\). Equations (4.8)–(4.9), p. 15, then give \[\begin{aligned}
 2^d h^\infty(P)&\le a_1+s_0-a_0+s_1+a_2-s_2,\\
 h^\infty(P\otimes P)&\ge s_0+\sum_{j\ge0}|a_j-s_{j+1}|\\
 &\ge s_0-a_0+a_1+s_1+a_2-s_2.\end{aligned}\] For the last inequality, use \(s_1-a_0\) in the first absolute value, \(a_1-s_2\) in the second, and telescope the finite tail from \(j=2\). This checks the signs and the tail endpoint explicitly. Lemma 4.4 supplies \[h^\infty(P\otimes P)\le h^\infty(P)\beta(P).\] A minimal representative remains minimal under Frobenius, so its Betti sum is unchanged; the bounded spectral sequence gives the required length bound. Under Theorem 4.1’s nonzero-homology assumption, the Hilbert–Kunz argument when \(H_0(P)\ne0\), and the tiny-complex reduction when \(H_0(P)=0\), justify \(h^\infty(P)>0\).

For Theorem 4.10, the asymptotic argument needs only \(a_3\ge s_3\), obtained from the long exact sequence and asymptotic vanishing. The stronger finite-iterate injection mentioned on p. 16 is unnecessary for this inference. No additional defect is inferred merely from that stronger wording.
# Assessment and limits

The principal finding is the false short-complex domain in Definition 1.5 and its use in Theorem 5.1. A separate nonzero-homology restriction is needed in the formulations identified above. These conclusions are exact algebraic examples, not numerical evidence or an inference from missing code.

The full text was inspected, but the full proofs of cited background theorems were not independently reproduced. No issue was established in the checked finite-length characteristic-two inequality or in the checked equality deduction, subject to their stated external dependencies. The publisher version may differ and has not been adjudicated.

This is an initial scientific review. The scientific decision remains pending; there are no human reviews, no author response, and no independent acceptance. They were not separate human reviewers or independently verified alternative models. The external controller’s UI observations are recorded as such.

       \longrightarrow0\bigr),\] in degrees \(3,2,1,0\). The ring is a connected, Noetherian, regular local field algebra of dimension three. All four terms are nonzero and free, all compositions vanish, and the complex is minimal. Its homology is \[H_0(P)=k,\qquad
 H_1(P)=\ker[\,x\ y\ z\,],\qquad
 H_2(P)=H_3(P)=R.\] The kernel in degree one is nonzero, since it contains \((y,x,0)\). It is a submodule of a free module over a domain and has zero annihilator. Consequently the four homology codimensions are \(3,0,0,0\), respectively. In particular, \[\max_{0\le j\le3}\operatorname{codim}_RH_j(P)=3,\qquad
 \sum_j\operatorname{rank}_RP_j=\beta(P)=6<8=2^3.\] All homology groups in the displayed interval are nonzero. Here the printed maximum is read over that interval, equivalently over the nonzero homology groups in this example. If all zero groups outside the interval are included with codimension \(+\infty\), Definition 1.5 instead assigns no finite \(c\) to a bounded complex and itself requires clarification. Under the finite interpretation, this nonexact complex meets the printed shortness condition. Neither minimality nor a requirement that the endpoint terms be nonzero removes the counterexample.

The first sentence of the proof of Theorem 5.1 localizes at a prime of height \(c\) in the support and claims to obtain a tiny complex. For this example, localization at the maximal ideal leaves the positive-rank homology in degrees \(1,2,3\); these modules do not have finite length. Thus the displayed reduction does not apply to the class defined using the maximum.

There is strong evidence for a different intended definition. Page 3 identifies tiny complexes with complexes having finite-length homology, and Section 2.2, p. 10, restates that finite-length, nonzero-homology condition explicitly. The operative Theorem 4.1, p. 13, also requires finite-length, nonzero homology. The counterexample above violates those finite-length hypotheses and therefore does not refute that theorem, nor the original total rank conjecture for finite-length modules.

For a nonzero total homology module, the codimension of its support is \[\operatorname{codim}_R\!\left(\bigoplus_j H_j(P)\right)
 =\min_{H_j(P)\ne0}\operatorname{codim}_R H_j(P).\] Replacing the maximum by this minimum excludes the example: its total support has codimension zero. Localizing at a minimal prime of that support of height \(c\) then makes every surviving homology module finite length over the local ring of dimension \(c\), which is the reduction used on p. 16. This is a concrete correction of the domain, not a proof that the uncorrected assertion holds. The corrected result still depends on the subsequent tiny-complex and transfer arguments. The Major classification concerns a demonstrated false central statement under its printed definition; it does not assert irreparability.

report: Abstract: The inspected author manuscript contains three demonstrable local construction problems: a missing valuation factor in the explicit Cox-ring map, and a normalization assertion that fails for choices of generators permitted by the text. A further boundary example obstructs the regular toric perturbation asserted in Lemma 4.3. The examples do not refute the Craw–Ishii theorem. Title: Technical review of
Moduli of \(G\)-constellations and crepant resolutions II:
the Craw–Ishii conjecture
# Source and scientific scope

The paper is Ryo Yamagishi, Moduli of \(G\)-constellations and crepant resolutions II: the Craw–Ishii conjecture, arXiv:2209.11901v3, 19 April 2024, 48 pages, associated with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0028. All locations below refer to this PDF, whose printed and PDF page numbers coincide. Its SHA256 begins `53fb0add706f80d7`; full input hashes are retained.

A 49-page institutional deposit was additionally acquired from Kyushu University. The repository labels it an accepted manuscript, and it has a cover followed by 48 article pages. Sampled text passages align with the assigned manuscript, with extraction differences in ligatures and mathematical glyphs. Neither complete mathematical identity nor publisher-final identity is asserted. The findings are pinned to the assigned arXiv version.

The main theorem concerns projective crepant resolutions of \(\mathbf C^3/G\), with \(G\) finite in \(\mathrm{SL}_3(\mathbf C)\), and a generic stability parameter for \(G\)-constellations. The checked dependency chain is the toric embedding (Theorem 3.5), the contraction criterion (Lemma 4.3), the Type 0 wall analysis (Lemmas 4.5–4.12 and Proposition 4.13), and the final flop argument (pp. 42–43). Proposition 4.14 was checked separately at the algebraic deduction level. The large explicit quiver examples were not fully recomputed, and the external BKR, BCHM, and flop-connectivity theorems were not independently reproved.
# An explicit Cox-ring formula

Problem 1 (Minor: the valuation factor in (3.4)).  Equation (3.4), p. 17, gives \[\phi_C(h)=\phi(h)\prod_k t_k^{-r_k\operatorname{ord}_{E_k}(h)},\] where the following sentence defines \(\operatorname{ord}_{E_k}(h)\) as the coefficient of \(E_k\) in the zero divisor \(D_h\). This conflicts with the associated lift in (3.1), p. 10, and with the degree of a weight-zero invariant.

Take \(G=\langle\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,1)angle\), and take the resolution \(X\) given by the minimal resolution of the \(A_1\) surface singularity times \(\mathbb A^1\). There is one exceptional divisor \(E\), with \(r=2\) and \[
u(x)=
u(y)=1,\qquad 
u(z)=0.\] The length-two \(x\)-cycle \(h=x_0x_1\) in the McKay quiver is an invariant of weight zero. Thus \(\phi(h)=x^2\), and the coefficient of \(E\) in its pullback zero divisor is \(
u(x^2)/2=1\).

Set \(a=xt\) and \(e=t^{-2}\), using the coordinates of (3.1). The geometric definition of \(\phi_C\) sends \(h\) to the degree-zero element \[x^2=a^2e.\] The printed formula instead gives \(x^2t^{-2}=a^2e^2\). Since \(e\) has degree \([E]\), this changes the degree and adds an exceptional component to the divisor. It is therefore not simply a choice of a nonzero scalar representative.
# Compatibility of the chosen generators

Problem 2 (Minor: Lemma 3.3 for the permitted choices).  The construction on p. 18 chooses Cox generators \(f_i\), then semi-invariant generators \(h_j\) whose images have specified monomial presentations in the \(f_i\). Lemma 3.3, pp. 18–19, identifies the resulting map \(\overline Y_W\to Y_W\) with normalization. The stated choices do not ensure this.

Let \(G=\{1\}\), so \(W=X=\mathbb A^3\), \(\Theta=0\), \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)=0\), and there are no exceptional divisors. Choose \[(f_1,f_2,f_3,f_4)=(x,y,z,x+y),\qquad
 (h_1,h_2,h_3)=(x,y,z),\] with the presentations \(\phi(h_i)=f_i\) for \(i=1,2,3\). These are homogeneous generating systems of the required rings. Minimality of the Cox generators is not imposed; the remark on p. 14 only adds a neatness property when they are minimal.

The cone \(\sigma_W=\sigma_A\) is the positive orthant in \(\mathbb R^4\). In the notation of pp. 18–19, \[S_W=\mathbb N^4,\qquad
 S'_W=\mathbb N^3\times\{0\}.\] Consequently \(\overline Y_W=\mathbb A^4\), \(Y_W=\mathbb A^3\), and the alleged normalization map is the coordinate projection \(\mathbb A^4\to\mathbb A^3\). It is neither finite nor birational. The polynomial ring in three variables is already integrally closed; adjoining an independent fourth variable is not its integral closure.

The proof on p. 19 tests regularity after restriction to \(\overline W\). Here the fourth ambient coordinate restricts to \(x+y\), which is regular on \(W\). That fact cannot establish the required equality of ambient semigroup rings: the restriction has forgotten a relation. Thus the example also isolates the failure of that inference.

Adding \(h_4=x+y\) with the presentation \(\phi(h_4)=f_4\) repairs this example, as does choosing the compatible minimal systems. It does not by itself prove the general saturation assertion or the claim that normalization preserves the specified closed immersion. A revised construction should specify compatible generators and prove the asserted integral-closure and quotient properties. This is a counterexample to the unrestricted auxiliary construction, not to the existential embedding theorem or the Craw–Ishii conclusion.
# The perturbation in Lemma 4.3 at a boundary face

Problem 3 (Minor: the claimed regular toric perturbation need not exist).  Lemma 4.3, pp. 31–32, allows any face \(F\) with \(\operatorname{relint}(F)\cap\overline C\ne\varnothing\) and \(\psi_C(F)\) not full-dimensional. Its proof moves an exceptional ray to a general ray in \(\sigma_k\), asserting that the resulting regular toric morphism still induces the same quotient isomorphism. The following allowed boundary case prevents those properties from holding simultaneously.

For \(G=\frac12(1,1,0)\), use \[W=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf C[a,b,c,d,z]/(ad-bc),
 \qquad \mathrm{wt}(a,b,c,d,z)=(1,1,-1,-1,0).\] The positive chamber quotient is the \(A_1\) resolution times \(\mathbb A^1\). Its Cox coordinates \(u,v,w,z\) have degrees \(1,1,-2,0\), and the positive-chamber map is \[(a,b,c,d,z)=(u,v,uw,vw,z).\] At the zero-section point represented by \((a,b,c,d,z)=(1,0,0,0,1)\), the orbit cone is the positive ray. Its face \(F=\{0\}\) satisfies both hypotheses of the lemma: it meets \(\overline C\), and \(\psi_C(F)=\{0\}\) has dimension zero in the one-dimensional Picard space.

The two exceptional ray valuations on \((a,b,c,d)\) are \[\tau_+=(0,0,1,1),\qquad \tau_-=(1,1,0,0).\] The proof’s general ray in their cone has strictly positive values on all four coordinates. A regular toric morphism gives integral orders of vanishing; thus each is at least one along \(w=0\). Every generator of the quotient singular-locus ideal \[I=(ac,ad,bd)\subset
 \mathbf C[ac,ad,bd,z]/((ac)(bd)-(ad)^2)\] would then pull back with order at least two. But the original Cox quotient pulls this ideal back to \[(u^2w,uvw,v^2w),\] of order exactly one along the prime divisor \(w=0\). An isomorphism of the quotient preserves its singular-locus ideal, so it cannot produce this change of order. Allowing an automorphism of the quotient does not remove the contradiction. Using a fractional interior ray instead would not define the asserted integral regular toric map.

The lemma’s conclusion is true in this example: the zero section contracts to the \(A_1\) singular locus. Omitting the unnecessary perturbation at \(F=0\) handles this case. The classification is local because this group supplies no flop contradicting the main application. A compatible construction for the faces used in the general flop argument still requires proof. The example establishes a failure of the proposed auxiliary construction, not a failure of the Craw–Ishii theorem.
# Core proof obligations not resolved by this review
## Reducedness in Lemma 4.5

The proof on p. 34 uses a coordinate ideal \(I_S\), generated by arrows from \(R_1\) to \(R_2\), and asserts that \[f^m\in I_N+I_S\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f_0^m\in I_N,\] where \(f_0\) deletes terms containing those arrows. Commutativity relations alone do not justify this inference.

An exact test can be made within a McKay representation space. Let \(G=\langle\operatorname{diag}(\zeta,\zeta^{-1},1)\rangle\), \(\zeta^3=1\), and index a regular-representation basis by \(0,1,2\). Take \(X\) to be cyclic shift, \(Y=X^{-1}\), and \(Z=0\); these commute and describe a free orbit. Split \(R_1=\langle e_0,e_1\rangle\), \(R_2=\langle e_2\rangle\). Deleting the forbidden entries \(X_{21},Y_{20}\) gives \[X'=E_{10}+E_{02},\qquad Y'=E_{01}+E_{12},
 \qquad [X',Y']=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,0).\] More explicitly, the \((0,0)\) commutator relation is \(p=X_{02}Y_{20}-Y_{01}X_{10}\). Its surviving part \(p_0=-Y_{01}X_{10}\) belongs to \(I_N+I_S\), but takes the value \(-1\) at the original commuting point and hence does not belong to \(I_N\). The asserted inference already fails at \(m=1\) for this coordinate split.

This split has not been shown to arise from a Type 0 wall. In fact this surface-quotient product does not supply the compact unstable divisors needed for that use. The computation therefore does not refute Lemma 4.5 in its actual wall setting. It does show that the stated general polynomial mechanism is insufficient: a Type 0-specific argument or a different proof of reducedness is needed. Ambient smoothness alone does not ensure reducedness of a coordinate section. An attracting-locus argument would also have to control the limiting split representation, which need not remain in the smooth stable locus.
## Product structure and the subsequent \(K\)-group argument

Lemma 4.10, pp. 38–39, uses \[G\text{-}\operatorname{Ext}^1(S,Q)
 \simeq G\text{-}\operatorname{Ext}^1(Q,S)\simeq\mathbf C,\] then passes from the tangent-space calculation and the map of Lemma 4.9 to a product of curves. The preceding discussion explicitly allows nonprimitive or decomposable factors. The review did not complete the justification of these Ext dimensions in that generality, the scheme-level product identification, or the independently selectable contractions of the two factors. Lemma 4.12, p. 41, further needs a global splitting statement for the particular bundles on the Dynkin trees; splitting on individual \(\mathbb P^1\) components alone does not establish it.

These are recorded as Needs Evidence, not as counterexamples. Once the stated geometric and pairing inputs are assumed, the checked \(K\)-group calculation is consistent: \(\chi(E,E)=0\) makes \[T_E=I-E\otimes\chi(-,E),\qquad
 T_E^{-1}=I+E\otimes\chi(-,E),\qquad \det T_E=1.\] The image-collinearity and divisor-independence argument in Proposition 4.13 then gives connectedness, and the elementary-transform identities give the claimed rank-one action. Thus a failure of this conditional linear algebra is not alleged.
## Toric perturbation and prescribed sections

The perturbation in Lemma 4.3, pp. 31–32, requires compatible lattice maps, preservation of the equations defining \(W\), and the asserted quotient identification. Preservation of projected cones alone does not verify all of these requirements. The bounded check did not finish that construction. The local coordinate-stratum descriptions also require care: an orbit cone can correspond to a union of coordinate strata, and a chosen locally closed stratum need not be closed in the semistable locus.

In Proposition 4.14, p. 43, the existence of a homogeneous section with the specified scheme-theoretic zero divisor is the remaining geometric obligation. Normality by itself is not a general section-surjectivity theorem. The particular toric contraction may supply the needed property, but that step was not independently established here. Conditional on the asserted section \(f\) with \(\phi_C(f)=\widetilde f_i\), the final algebraic generation deduction is valid: expand \(f\) in the homogeneous generators \(h_j\), and use the corrected formula to express every \(\phi_C(h_j)\) as its associated lift times nonnegative powers of the exceptional generators. General valuation cancellation is therefore not a counterexample to that final deduction.
# Supporting checks

The highest supported assessment is Minor, with three confirmed local construction findings and separate Needs Evidence items. No counterexample satisfying the hypotheses of Theorem 4.1 was found. The reducedness, product, and toric-map obligations above prevent this initial review from certifying the entire proof chain.

Detailed page and claim ledgers distinguish text reading from proof checking. A reviewer-authored exact calculation of the junior powers \(1,2,4,5,7\) for the example \(\frac1{10}(1,3,6)\) agrees with all five valuation triples in (3.2). The six-resolution enumeration and the 400-generator example were not reproduced. No author code was run; unavailable code is not treated as a mathematical defect.
The scientific decision remains pending, with no human reviews and no independent acceptance. The external controller’s interface observation was not independently verified by this executor.

Title: Scientific initial review of
Counting negative eigenvalues for the magnetic Pauli operator
# Source, scope and principal statement

This report concerns S. Fournais, R. L. Frank, M. Goffeng, A. Kachmar and M. Sundqvist, Counting negative eigenvalues for the magnetic Pauli operator, arXiv:2307.16079v1, 29 July 2023, 29 pages [paper]. The assigned journal identifier is DOI `10.1215/00127094-2024-0029`. The final journal text was not acquired; the findings below concern this exact author version. Page numbers refer to its PDF, whose printed pagination agrees.

For a smooth bounded connected planar domain with \(d+1\) boundary components, the paper studies the scalar component \(H_{A,g}=(-i\nabla-A)^2-B\) with the specified inward Robin condition. Write \(\Phi_j=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\Gamma_j}A_\tau\,\mathrm ds\) and \(\Phi_{g,j}=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\Gamma_j}g\,\mathrm ds\), with the boundary orientations fixed in the paper. Theorem 1.1, p. 5, states \[N(H_{A,g},0)\ \geq\ -d+\sum_{j=0}^{d}
          \lceil\Phi_j-\Phi_{g,j}\rceil ,\] where \(N(\,\cdot\,,0)\) counts strictly negative eigenvalues. Equality is asserted on a disk for \(g=0\) and a nonnegative radial field that is nonincreasing in the radius.

All 29 pages were read as text. The definitions, quadratic-form identity, radial argument, boundary spectra, adjoint boundary condition, relative-index calculation, conformal reduction and Hardy-space argument received claim-focused checks. Selected source pages were also inspected as rendered images. This is an initial review, not an independent acceptance or a human review.
# Established problems

Problem 1 (Major: the unweighted extension does not give a negative trial space).  In Section 7.2, p. 26, immediately before and in the proof of (7.2), the holomorphic extension \(E(e^{ims})=z^m\) is used to assert \[q_{A,g}(Ev)=\langle P_+D_VP_+v,v\rangle<0,
 \qquad V=g-A_\tau,\] for a vector in the negative spectral subspace of \(P_+D_VP_+\). The ensuing proposed space is the image of that subspace under \(E\). This assertion fails for admissible data.

Decisive calculation. Take the unit disk, \(B=\beta>8\), \(g=0\), and \[\phi(z)=\frac{\beta}{4}(|z|^2-1),\qquad
 A=\frac{\beta}{2}(-x_2,x_1).\] These are smooth data in the hypotheses, \(\phi=0\) on the boundary, \(\operatorname{curl}A=\beta\), and \(V=-\beta/2\). The boundary vector \(v=1\) is a strictly negative eigenvector, of eigenvalue \(-\beta/2\), and \(Ev=1\). Direct integration gives \[\langle D_V1,1\rangle=-\pi\beta,\qquad
 q_{A,0}(1)=\int_{D(0,1)}(|A|^2-\beta)\,\mathrm dx
             =\frac{\pi\beta^2}{8}-\pi\beta .\] For example, at \(\beta=16\), the asserted boundary value is \(-16\pi\) while the actual bulk value is \(16\pi>0\). Hence the proposed trial space contains a positive-form vector and is not negative definite. No numerical approximation or limiting regularity issue is involved.

Dependency and repair. Proposition 3.1, p. 11, and (5.2), p. 15, have the nonnegative bulk term \[4\|e^{-\phi}\partial_{\bar z}(e^\phi u)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2 .\] Ordinary holomorphicity of \(u=Ev\) does not annihilate this term. The required extension is \[E_\phi v=e^{-\phi}Ev .\] For every vector in the finite negative boundary spectral subspace this is an \(H^1\) function, its trace is \(v\), and \(e^\phi E_\phi v=Ev\) is holomorphic. The form identity therefore yields \[q_{A,g}(E_\phi v)=\langle D_Vv,v\rangle<0 .\] Multiplication by the smooth positive factor preserves injectivity. Glazman’s lemma now applies and proves (7.2) with the corrected space.

Counterevidence and severity boundary. Remark 3.3, p. 12, already uses \(e^{-\phi}z^m\); Section 5.1 and (5.3), p. 16, also explicitly contain the correct weight. Thus the missing ingredient is present elsewhere in the manuscript. The demonstrated defect is in a step directly establishing the principal bound by the advertised second proof, which warrants Major under the review contract’s core-derivation criterion. It does not show that Theorem 1.1, (7.2), or Lemma 7.3 is false. The local repair above is complete for this step, and the independent APS route remains available.

Problem 2 (Minor: the radial field in Remark 2.2 does not give the displayed value).  On p. 10, Remark 2.2 takes \(R=1\), \(m=-1\), and \(B(r)=(r-\tfrac12)^2+\delta\), and assigns the potential at \(r=1\) the value \(1-4/(1+12\delta)^2\), claimed negative for \(0<\delta<1/12\). The actual substitution gives a positive value.

Exact substitution. Using the definition \(a(r)=r^{-1}\int_0^r B(\rho)\rho\,\mathrm d\rho\), \[a(1)=\frac1{24}+\frac{\delta}{2},\qquad
 \left(-1-a(1)\right)^2-B(1)
       =\frac{481}{576}+\frac{\delta}{24}+\frac{\delta^2}{4}>0 .\] For \(\delta=1/24\), the actual value is \(643/768\); the printed expression is \(-7/9\). Exact symbolic arithmetic independently confirms these fractions.

Repair and impact. Introducing the omitted scale \(B_\beta(r)=\beta[(r-\tfrac12)^2+\delta]\) gives instead \[V_{-1}(1)=1-\frac{\beta}{6}
             +\frac{\beta^2(1+12\delta)^2}{576}.\] Its minimum occurs at \(\beta=48/(1+12\delta)^2\) and equals precisely the printed expression. Alternatively, the smooth Cartesian radial field \(B(r)=12r^4\) gives \(a(1)=2\) and \(V_{-1}(1)=9-12=-3\). Either corrected illustration shows failure of pointwise potential positivity without monotonicity. A negative potential at one point does not itself establish a negative eigenvalue; the original remark also distinguishes these questions. This is an erroneous local illustration, not a counterexample to the radial equality theorem.
# Checks supporting the principal argument
## Boundary spectra, orientation and the APS route

For \(D_V=-i\partial_s+V\) on a component of length \(L\), solving the periodic first-order equation gives \(\mu_m=2\pi(m+\Phi_V)/L\), \(m\in\mathbb Z\). The normal-phase conjugation in Proposition 4.4 has the curvature shift \(V-\kappa\); integration by parts consequently produces the adjoint condition \(\gamma_0u\in(E_{V-\kappa})^\perp\) in Proposition 6.1, p. 19. Strict negativity in \(E_V\) and nonnegativity in its complement are consistent at a zero eigenvalue.

The relative-cutoff count in Proposition 6.4, p. 21, contributes \(\lceil-\Phi_{V_j}\rceil\), including at integer flux. The baseline disk index is zero, and the formula \[\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_\Gamma\kappa\,\mathrm ds-\frac{1+d}{2}=-d\] uses \(2\pi\) on the outer component and \(-2\pi\) on each inner component (pp. 22–23). A direct annulus Fourier check gives zero kernel and a one-dimensional cokernel, represented by \(1/\bar z\), hence index \(-1\). These checks support the signs and topology term in the main estimate. For a fixed elliptic boundary space, a smooth change in the bulk magnetic potential is a compact zeroth-order perturbation from \(H^1\) to \(L^2\); this also checks index invariance without assuming that different holonomies are gauge equivalent.

There is a local sign slip in Remark 4.2(2), p. 13: on the outer boundary the mean of \(g-A_\tau-\kappa\) is \(\Phi_g-\Phi-1\), not \(\Phi_g-\Phi+1\). The actual shifted eigenvalue computation on p. 15 and the subsequent disk and general-domain calculations use the correct sign. It is not promoted here to an additional mathematical Problem. The general Fredholm and APS theorems invoked by the paper have not been reproved in this review.
## The radial equality and threshold cases

For \(m=-k<0\), the radial potential can be written \[\frac{k^2}{r^2}+a^2+\frac{2(k-1)a}{r}
                     +\left(\frac{2a}{r}-B\right),\qquad
 \frac{2a}{r}-B(r)
   =\frac{2}{r^2}\int_0^r[B(\rho)-B(r)]\rho\,\mathrm d\rho .\] It is nonnegative for a nonnegative nonincreasing field. For \(m\geq0\) and the scaled field \(\beta B\), put \(f=r^m e^{-\beta\phi}\), where \(\phi'=a\). The ground-state identity is \[q_m^\beta[u]=
 \int_0^R r f^2\left|(u/f)'\right|^2\,\mathrm dr
       +(m-\beta\Phi)|u(R)|^2 .\] It follows first on the regular core and then on the form domain. If \(m\geq\beta\Phi\), the form is nonnegative. If \(m<\beta\Phi\), \(u=f\) gives a negative direction, whereas the codimension-one trace-zero subspace is nonnegative; there is exactly one negative eigenvalue in that mode. Thus the total is \(\lceil\beta\Phi\rceil\). At an integer flux the threshold mode is zero and is excluded. The zero-field case is nonnegative and is handled separately, without division by \(\Phi=0\). These identities check the conclusion independently of an informal eigenvalue-crossing argument.
## Semiclassical consequences

For the magnetic Neumann operator \(\mathcal L_h\) in Theorem 1.4, p. 6, the identity \(\mathcal L_h-h=h^2H_{A/h,0}\) supplies the lower estimate \[N(\mathcal L_h,h)\geq |\Omega|/(2\pi h)+O(1).\] Combined with the cited semiclassical upper estimate, this gives the stated leading term. Corollary 1.6 follows from \[\sum_{e_j<h}e_j=hN(\mathcal L_h,h)-\sum_{e_j<h}(h-e_j).\] The quoted Riesz sum is of order \(h^{1/2}\). On a disk the exact ceiling count makes the error in \(hN\) only \(O(h)\), giving the stated negative \(h^{1/2}\) correction. The external Riesz asymptotic and upper bound were treated as dependencies, not independently reproduced.
# Hardy transfer: a domain completion and an external dependency

The conformal change in Lemma 7.1, pp. 25–26, preserves the magnetic, bulk-field and Robin forms when \(\widetilde A=(DF)^T(A\circ F)\), \(\widetilde B=|F'|^2B\circ F\), and \(\widetilde g=|f'|g\circ f\). The required conclusion is invariance of the negative index under an invertible \(H^1\) map, rather than equality of \(L^2\) norms.

On p. 27 the Cayley correspondence explicitly assumes both \(\psi\in L^2(S^1)\) and \(\Psi(t)=\psi((i-t)/(i+t))\in L^2(\mathbb R)\). Thus \(\psi=1\), whose composition is not in \(L^2(\mathbb R)\), does not refute the printed conditional statement. It does reveal why a form-domain argument is needed to transfer arbitrary negative subspaces. One can supply it explicitly. Set \[H_N=\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac1k,\qquad
 p_N(z)=1-\frac1{H_N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{(-z)^k}{k}.\] Then \(p_N(-1)=0\), and, with normalized circle measure, \[\|p_N-1\|_2^2=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{N}k^{-2}}{H_N^2}\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad |p_N-1|_{\dot H^{1/2}}^2=\frac1{H_N}\longrightarrow0.\] Multiplication by a fixed analytic polynomial is continuous in \(H^{1/2}\). Analytic polynomials vanishing at \(-1\) therefore form a dense core in the Hardy form domain. Their Cayley compositions decay as \(O(t^{-1})\), belong to the line Hardy space, and preserve the derivative form and the potential form with \[W(t)=\frac{2}{1+t^2}V\!\left(\frac{i-t}{i+t}\right),\qquad
 \int_{S^1}V|\psi|^2\,\mathrm ds=\int_\mathbb RW|\Psi|^2\,\mathrm dt .\] The last potential identity in the source interchanges \(V\) and \(W\); the formula above is the consistent one. Finite-dimensional strict negativity persists under form-norm approximation. In the reverse direction, the standard weighted unitary Cayley map identifies the Hardy \(L^2\) spaces, and the unweighted inverse composition has an additional bounded factor \(1+z\); conformal invariance of analytic Dirichlet energy controls the derivative form. This establishes both inequalities between the negative indices. It is a completion of the domain justification, not a separate counterexample to Lemma 7.3.

For constant \(V=-a\), the circle Hardy eigenvalues are \(m-a\), \(m\geq0\), so the strict negative count is \(\max\{\lceil a\rceil,0\}\). No extra unit is present at integer \(a\). The scattering identity quoted from Kaup–Matsuno in the proof of Lemma 7.3 has a nonnegative integral correction; if valid with its required hypotheses, it implies the claimed ceiling lower bound. Its full Equation (113) was not independently accessible and verified. Selected primary-source scattering definitions and decay assumptions were checked, but this is not a proof of that identity. The Cayley potential decays as \(O(t^{-2})\); compatibility with a weighted space alone does not settle every scattering hypothesis.

Author: M25-0145 Initial scientific review

Title: Scientific initial review of
The characteristic gluing problem for the Einstein equations and applications
# Identity, version and scope

The reviewed paper is S. Aretakis, S. Czimek and I. Rodnianski, The characteristic gluing problem for the Einstein equations and applications, arXiv:2107.02441v1, 6 July 2021, 31 pages [overview]. The assigned journal DOI is `10.1215/00127094-2024-0030`. The journal PDF was not obtained; no equivalence with its final text is asserted. All page references below are PDF pages, agreeing with printed pagination.

All 31 pages of the author manuscript were read as text. The bounded checks concerned the null-data definitions, linear obstruction count, gauge maps, nonlinear proof dependency, Kerr parameter matching, localized charge correction, radial iteration and geometric passage to spacelike data. The paper explicitly refers detailed linear and nonlinear estimates to its reference [10]. The corresponding arXiv:2107.02449v1, 102 pages [linear], was acquired and inspected only at selected definitions and proof steps needed for the gauge-map question. It was not subjected to a separate whole-paper review. Their actual roles and inspected material are recorded in the evidence bundle.

Theorem 1.1 concerns \(C^2\) gluing up to ten charges and gauge perturbations. Theorem 1.2 uses two null hypersurfaces and an auxiliary sphere for higher transverse regularity. These are different statements: the one-hypersurface result does not claim unrestricted higher-order transverse matching. Theorems 1.3–1.4 and Corollary 1.5 use Kerr parameter matching; Theorems 1.9–1.10 use localized correction and a rescaled iteration.
# Established problems

A sequence within the prescribed parameter domain. On the round sphere, choose a real spherical harmonic \(A_n\) of degree and azimuthal order \(n\), normalized by \(\|A_n\|_{H^6}=1\). Its sine partner is orthogonal with the same norm. Put \[a_n=\frac{A_n}{n},\qquad
 f_n|_S=0,\quad (f_n)_u|_S=2a_n,\quad
 (f_n)_{uu}|_S=(f_n)_{uuu}|_S=0.\] These are smooth jets, realized, for example, by \(f_n(u,\theta)=2u
a_n(\theta)\) near \(u=0\), with a fixed smooth cutoff in \(u\). Thus \(\|f_n\|_{\mathcal Y_f}=2/n\). Let \(j_n\) represent the smooth azimuthal rotation \(R_{1/n}\); \(\|j_n\|_{\mathcal Y_j}=O(n^{-1})\). Sobolev embedding makes \(1+2a_n\) positive for large \(n\), so the coordinate change is admissible. The target characteristic data, the initial sphere data and the unknown unperturbed null data can all be held equal to the exact smooth Minkowski data.

The precise proof dependency. Section 3.1 of [overview], p. 15, reduces nonlinear gluing to an implicit-function theorem and points to [linear] for the detailed setup. Proposition 2.22 of that companion, p. 36, asserts the same smooth map. Its matching map \(\mathcal M\), Definition 2.11, p. 28, retains the entire lapse component. Definition 5.1, p. 63, contains \[F(x_{0,1},\widetilde x,x,f,j)
  =\bigl(x|_{S_{0,1}}-x_{0,1},\
       \mathcal M(x|_{S_{0,2}})-\mathcal M(P_jP_f(\widetilde x)),\
       (C_i(x))_i\bigr)\] and asserts full smoothness in an open Hilbert-space neighborhood. Holding the other variables at Minkowski leaves precisely the lapse remainder above. Thus the charge projection does not remove the counterexample, and giving the original target the stronger \(\mathcal X^+\) regularity does not resolve composition of the two free gauge parameters.

Counterevidence, impact and repair boundary. On pp. 64–65 the companion restricts \(F\) to the orthogonal complement of the kernel of its formal linearization. Rigid rotations are among the kernel directions. The sequence above has not been proved to lie in that complement, and does not independently disprove differentiability of the restricted map. The demonstrated defect is the false full-smoothness premise from which the text obtains the restricted smoothness needed for its implicit-function argument. This is directly tied to the nonlinear codimension-ten construction, hence Major under the contract’s core-derivation criterion.

A valid proof could establish the required regularity on a carefully chosen slice, change the gauge parametrization/order, or use a functional setup that handles derivative loss. Raising a norm alone also requires rechecking the bounded right inverse and all matching estimates. No complete such repair was established here. Neither Theorem 1.1 nor the subsequent existence theorems are declared false.

Problem 2 (Minor: the displayed localized momentum-charge prescription has the wrong normalization).  In Lemma 6.2, p. 23, equation (6.4) specifies a perturbation \(W\) with prescribed charges. Write \(r=1+2c\) and \(h=\Omega\operatorname{tr}\underline\chi\). For a target with \(\dot E_0=\dot L_0=\dot G_0=0\), \(\dot P_0^m=p\ne0\), the displayed formula sets \[\eta=0,\qquad h^{(1m)}=\frac{16\pi}{r^2\sqrt{4\pi}}p.\] The preceding charge formula instead gives \[\dot P^m(W)=\frac{\sqrt{4\pi/3}}{16\pi}r^2h^{(1m)}
                =\frac{p}{\sqrt3}\ne p.\]

This input is allowed: the required scalar moments can be realized by a smooth function supported in any fixed nonempty open transition region, as shown below. It is a counterexample to the explicit right-inverse prescription, not merely a normalization preference.
# Positive checks and rejected objections
## Linear charges and radial moments

The gauge-invariant sector consists of the electric and magnetic degree-one vector modes of \(Q_0\), giving six components, and the degree-zero and degree-one scalar modes of \(Q_2\), giving four. This matches \(E,P,L,G\) on pp. 14, 16–17.

The shear moments used in (3.2)–(3.6) have distinct radial weights \(r^{-2},1,r^{-3},r^{-4}\). These functions are linearly independent on an open radial interval. Choosing a smooth positive interior weight \(w\), the moment Gram matrix \[G_{ij}=\int w(r)\,r^{p_i+p_j}\,\mathrm dr,
       \qquad (p_i)=( -2,0,-3,-4),\] is positive definite: its quadratic form is the integral of the square of a nonzero linear combination. This gives independent compactly supported controls for these finite moment conditions. The angular low-mode exceptions in the displayed elliptic operators agree with the separate conserved-charge treatment. This verifies the moment mechanism, not every inhomogeneous estimate or every higher-order commutator in the companion.
## Kerr degree calculation

A potential objection based on nonvanishing \(O(1)\) angular errors is incorrect. The source defines distinct \(O\) and little-\(o\) notation on p. 11; (4.7), p. 21, has \(o(1)\) in the last two components. For the parameter deviations define \[T_R(\delta E,P,\delta L,\delta C)
       =(\delta E,P,\delta L,\delta C-3RP).\] If the error in (4.7) is \(e=(O(R^{-1}),O(R^{-3/2}),o(1),o(1))\), then \[T_R^{-1}e=(e_E,e_P,e_L,e_G+3Re_P).\] After applying the ellipsoid weights \(\operatorname{diag}(R^{1/2},R^{1/2}I_3,I_3,I_3)\), all four components tend to zero, including the shear contribution \(3Re_P=O(R^{-1/2})\). Hence the degree argument is consistent, conditional on the stated uniform remainder estimates and on the positive-timelike Kerr parameter regime.

The strong spacelike decay \(k=O(r^{-5/2})\) implies zero limiting ADM momentum. Corollary 1.5 explicitly assumes positive ADM energy, so its limiting vector is timelike. Definitions (2.4)–(2.5) also allow \(M=0\), while the Kerr parameter construction in Section 4.2 assumes \(M>0\). The treatment of general zero-mass characteristic families is a remaining scope question; no impossibility example was proved. The detailed ADM/Kerr expansions and the spacelike existence theorem remain dependencies.
## Supported moments and iteration

For low scalar harmonics \(Y_i\) and a nonnegative smooth bump \(\chi\) supported in a fixed nonempty transition open set, the matrix \[B_{ij}=\int\chi\,Y_iY_j\,\mathrm d\mu\] is positive definite. A nonzero degree-at-most-one harmonic cannot vanish on an open set. Thus \(f=\chi\sum_i(B^{-1}v)_iY_i\) realizes arbitrary prescribed low moments. The same argument applies to the six analytic degree-one vector harmonics. Constants depend on the fixed open set; uniform bounds as its size shrinks are not asserted by this verification.

Put \(q=1+2c>1\). The exact charge recurrence in Section 7.2 has \[A_n=q^{-1}A_{n-1}+O(q^{-2n+2}R^{-2}).\] Multiplication by \(q^{n-1}\) makes the accumulated errors a convergent geometric sum. Therefore \(A_n=q^{-n+1}(A_1+O(R^{-2}))\), as actually parenthesized in (7.11). The \(L,G\) recurrence has coefficient \(q^{-2}\); its possible factor \(nq^{-2n}\) is bounded by a constant times \(q^{-n}\). There is no arbitrary \(C^n\) amplification in these exact recurrences. These are conditional checks of the iteration algebra, assuming the nonlinear local estimates and their uniformity.

For the causal calculation, a light-cone section is a ball of radius \(\rho c\), centered a distance \(\rho(1+c)\) from the origin. Its angular half-width is \(\arcsin(c/(1+c))\), independent of the annular scale \(\rho\). A fixed strict angular margin, followed by sufficiently large \(R\), is consistent with the domain-of-dependence construction. The characteristic well-posedness estimates were not independently reproved.
# Other proof obligations and conventions

Lemma 6.1, p. 23, claims that the solution orthogonal to the zero-endpoint kernel is supported in the angular support of its endpoint data. Its cutoff proof requires angular cutoff of free data to preserve zero endpoint data. The endpoint formulas contain angular differential operators, which generally have nonzero commutators with a cutoff. A justification specialized to this kernel and to the chosen orthogonal solution is still needed. No complete counterexample satisfying all bifurcate constraints and the orthogonality hypothesis was constructed. This remains Needs Evidence, not a proved false lemma.

The annular derivative norm in Section 7.3, p. 29, should be written using the current radius \(r_n=q^nR\): \[\sum_{\ell\leq m+1}r_n^\ell\|\partial^\ell(\widetilde g-e)\|_\infty
 +\sum_{\ell\leq m}r_n^{\ell+1}\|\partial^\ell\widetilde k\|_\infty
      \leq C r_n^{-1}.\] This implies the claimed \(r^{-1-\ell}\) and \(r^{-2-\ell}\) decay. The literal fixed-\(R\) weights printed there do not by themselves imply the second decay: \(k(r)=1/(Rr)\) meets that weaker annular estimate. This scalar example concerns the norm implication only, and is not vacuum initial data. The source’s preceding rescaling mechanism indicates the appropriate correction. Its first display with \(R\) in place of \(R^{-1}\) is merely weaker for \(R\geq1\), not an independent false inequality.

Two additional local conventions were checked to avoid building an argument on transcription errors. The geometric Schwarzschild expansions in the stated double-null convention are \(\Omega\operatorname{tr}\chi=2\Omega_M^2/r_M\) and \(\Omega\operatorname{tr}\underline\chi=-2\Omega_M^2/r_M\); the reference tuple on p. 13 prints different entries, including the wrong incoming sign already at \(M=0\). The later linearized formulas use the expected incoming sign. Also, the coordinate sentence \(u'=u+f\) on p. 15 is opposite to the pullback formulas on p. 16; the companion’s equation (2.46), p. 34, fixes the old coordinate as new coordinate plus \(f\). These require correction, but no separate false gluing theorem is inferred from them.

problems.title: the full gauge-matching map is not Fréchet differentiable in the stated norms
problems.source_location: Primary Section3.2 p16 and implicit-function reduction p15; bounded dependency check of companion2107.02449v1 Proposition2.22 p36, Definition2.11 p28, Definition5.1 p63, restriction/IFT pp64–65
claim: Gauge action and full composed matching map are smooth between the specified finite-Sobolev Hilbert spaces in an open neighborhood of Minkowski.

Fixed target, initial and null data exactly Minkowski; independent smooth f jets f0=0,fu=2a_n,fuu=fuuu=0 with a_n=A_n/n where degree/order-n real spherical harmonic A_n has H6 norm1; angular parameter is rotation by1/n. Yf=H8⊕H6⊕H4⊕H2, Yj=H7; total increment O(1/n); lapse positive for large n.
analysis:
A sequence within the prescribed parameter domain. On the round sphere, choose a real spherical harmonic \(A_n\) of degree and azimuthal order \(n\), normalized by \(\|A_n\|_{H^6}=1\). Its sine partner is orthogonal with the same norm. Put \[a_n=\frac{A_n}{n},\qquad
 f_n|_S=0,\quad (f_n)_u|_S=2a_n,\quad
 (f_n)_{uu}|_S=(f_n)_{uuu}|_S=0.\] These are smooth jets, realized, for example, by \(f_n(u,\theta)=2u
a_n(\theta)\) near \(u=0\), with a fixed smooth cutoff in \(u\). Thus \(\|f_n\|_{\mathcal Y_f}=2/n\). Let \(j_n\) represent the smooth azimuthal rotation \(R_{1/n}\); \(\|j_n\|_{\mathcal Y_j}=O(n^{-1})\). Sobolev embedding makes \(1+2a_n\) positive for large \(n\), so the coordinate change is admissible. The target characteristic data, the initial sphere data and the unknown unperturbed null data can all be held equal to the exact smooth Minkowski data.

The precise proof dependency. Section 3.1 of [overview], p. 15, reduces nonlinear gluing to an implicit-function theorem and points to [linear] for the detailed setup. Proposition 2.22 of that companion, p. 36, asserts the same smooth map. Its matching map \(\mathcal M\), Definition 2.11, p. 28, retains the entire lapse component. Definition 5.1, p. 63, contains \[F(x_{0,1},\widetilde x,x,f,j)
  =\bigl(x|_{S_{0,1}}-x_{0,1},\
       \mathcal M(x|_{S_{0,2}})-\mathcal M(P_jP_f(\widetilde x)),\
       (C_i(x))_i\bigr)\] and asserts full smoothness in an open Hilbert-space neighborhood. Holding the other variables at Minkowski leaves precisely the lapse remainder above. Thus the charge projection does not remove the counterexample, and giving the original target the stronger \(\mathcal X^+\) regularity does not resolve composition of the two free gauge parameters.

Counterevidence, impact and repair boundary. On pp. 64–65 the companion restricts \(F\) to the orthogonal complement of the kernel of its formal linearization. Rigid rotations are among the kernel directions. The sequence above has not been proved to lie in that complement, and does not independently disprove differentiability of the restricted map. The demonstrated defect is the false full-smoothness premise from which the text obtains the restricted smoothness needed for its implicit-function argument. This is directly tied to the nonlinear codimension-ten construction, hence Major under the contract’s core-derivation criterion.

A valid proof could establish the required regularity on a carefully chosen slice, change the gauge parametrization/order, or use a functional setup that handles derivative loss. Raising a norm alone also requires rechecking the bounded right inverse and all matching estimates. No complete such repair was established here. Neither Theorem 1.1 nor the subsequent existence theorems are declared false.
result: Impact: False full-smoothness premise directly used to obtain restricted smoothness and apply the nonlinear implicit-function theorem. Major concerns that proof derivation, not impossibility of gluing.
