Title: Scientific initial review of
Growth in linear groups
# Identity, summary, and scope

The paper is by Sean Eberhard, Brendan Murphy, László Pyber, and Endre Szabó, associated with Duke Mathematical Journal (2025), DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0031 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0031). The reviewed artifact is the 39-page author manuscript arXiv:2107.06674v3, dated 26 April 2024 [paper]; all page references below are its one-based PDF pages, which agree with its printed numbering. The journal typesetting was not independently obtained. The arXiv record identifies v3 as incorporating referees’ corrections; this does not establish byte-level agreement with the journal edition.

Assessment: Major. The most substantial finding is a counterexample to the prime-field tensor decomposition required by Theorem 9.6. It also occurs for the precise module used in the diameter proof. Consequently that proof has a false structural input, although no counterexample to the diameter conclusion is established. A separate rank-one counterexample contradicts the stated step bound in Theorem 1.2. Two local failures arise because symmetry is explicitly defined without requiring the identity: the affine conjugating lemma has an odd-power obstruction, and Proposition 8.5 can miss a singleton nontrivial root image.

The full manuscript text and supplied TeX were available. The review concentrated on definitions, the finite-field reduction, normality of the resulting subgroups, the soluble-to-nilpotent argument, and the diameter application. External classification, representation, and linearization theorems were not completely rederived. Positive checks and unresolved steps are separated below.
# Necessary conventions

A symmetric set means \(A=A^{-1}\), not \(1\in A\), by Section 4.1, p. 10. The notation \(A^r\) denotes products of exactly \(r\) elements, whereas \(A^{\pm r}\) allows the identity and inverses. A section is \(H/N\); its trace is the image of \(A\cap H\), not an arbitrary projection from a larger group (p. 7). Lower central series are indexed from \(\gamma_1\), and Remark 1.3(a), p. 3, permits \(H=\gamma_n(\Gamma)\). Quasirandomness is measured by the least dimension of a nontrivial complex representation. These distinctions are operative in the counterexamples.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Major: the prime-field bounded-chain assertion is false).  Definition 9.4(c), p. 34, requires every irreducible constituent \(W\) of a bounded chain to have the form \[W\simeq X_1\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}\cdots\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}X_l,\] with \(X_i\) an irreducible \(\mathbb F_pS_i\)-module for the quasisimple factors of \(G/O_p(G)\). Theorem 9.6, on the same page, asserts the existence of such a chain for every \(G\)-invariant section of every normalized \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{GL}_n(F)\), once \(\deg_{\mathbb C}G\) is sufficiently large in terms of \(n\).
#### Admissible family.

Let \(p\ge5\) be prime, \(q=p^2\), and set \[L=\operatorname{SL}_2(q)\times\operatorname{SL}_2(q),\qquad
 P=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}I_2&X\\0&I_2\end{pmatrix}:X\in M_2(\mathbb F_q)\right\}.\] Embed \(L\) block diagonally in \(\operatorname{GL}_4(q)\), and put \(G=P\rtimes L\). Then \(P\) is an elementary abelian \(p\)-group of dimension \(8\) over \(\mathbb F_p\), and \(G\) acts on its additive matrix coordinate by \(X\mapsto aXb^{-1}\). Conjugation by \(P\) itself is trivial. Thus this is a normalized \(p\)-subgroup within exactly the ambient dimension \(n=4\) required by the theorem.
#### Irreducibility over the stated field.

The \(\mathbb F_p\)-algebra generated by \(\operatorname{SL}_2(q)\) in \(M_2(\mathbb F_q)\) contains \[(I+tE_{12})-I=tE_{12},\qquad
 (I+tE_{21})-I=tE_{21}\quad(t\in\mathbb F_q).\] Products give \(tE_{11}\) and \(tE_{22}\), so it contains all of \(M_2(\mathbb F_q)\). An invariant \(\mathbb F_p\)-subspace of \(P=M_2(\mathbb F_q)\) is therefore stable under all left and right multiplications by matrices over \(\mathbb F_q\). In particular it is \(\mathbb F_q\)-linear and a two-sided ideal of the simple matrix algebra. It is consequently either zero or \(P\). Both factors of \(L\) act nontrivially.

It follows that \(O_p(G)=P\), \(\operatorname{Sol}(G)=PZ(L)\), and \([G,\operatorname{Sol}(G)]=[P,L]=P\). Here \([P,L]\ne0\), and irreducibility makes it all of \(P\); \(L\) is perfect. In particular \(G\) is perfect and the section \(P/[P,P]\) used on p. 36 is precisely this module.
#### No tensor product of the prescribed dimensions.

Every nontrivial representation of \(\operatorname{SL}_2(p^2)\) over \(\mathbb F_p\) has dimension at least \(3\). One elementary verification in dimensions at most \(2\) is as follows. The upper unipotent subgroup \(U\simeq C_p^2\) has image in a \(p\)-subgroup of \(\operatorname{GL}_2(p)\), whose order is at most \(p\). Its kernel therefore contains a nonidentity \(u(t)\). Diagonal conjugation gives all \(u(s^2t)\), \(s\ne0\). Squares span \(\mathbb F_q\) additively when \(p\) is odd: for instance \(x=((x+1)/2)^2-((x-1)/2)^2\). Hence the kernel contains \(U\), then its opposite by normality, and hence all of \(\operatorname{SL}_2(q)\). The one-dimensional case also follows from perfectness.

If \(P\) had the decomposition in Definition 9.4(c), both tensor factors would be nontrivial, so \[8=\dim_{\mathbb F_p}P=\dim_{\mathbb F_p}X_1\,\dim_{\mathbb F_p}X_2\ge 3\cdot3=9,\] a contradiction. Because \(P\) is irreducible, refining the chain cannot remove the obstruction. It fails for every value of the proposed boundedness constant.
#### Arbitrarily strong quasirandomness.

The example cannot be excluded by increasing \(K(4)\). A nontrivial complex representation of \(\operatorname{SL}_2(q)\) is nontrivial on \(U\), since conjugates of \(U\) generate the group. A nontrivial \(U\)-character has a diagonal-torus orbit of size \((q-1)/2\), so the representation has dimension at least this large. Every nontrivial representation of \(G=P\rtimes L\) restricts nontrivially to \(L\): killing \(L\) would also kill \([P,L]=P\). Thus \(\deg_{\mathbb C}G\ge(q-1)/2\to\infty\), with \(n=4\) fixed.
#### Faulty step, impact, and repair boundary.

The proof on p. 35 passes from tensor products over an algebraic closure to tensor products of irreducible modules over \(\mathbb F_p\). Restriction of scalars does not preserve that asserted tensor factorization. The dimension calculation above is a direct obstruction, not an OCR issue: the rendered definition and proof both specify \(\mathbb F_p\). Theorem 9.6 is invoked on p. 36 for \(P/[P,P]\); the present semidirect family makes this dependency explicit. This is a demonstrated invalid derivation closely tied to the diameter contribution.

A reformulation over appropriate endomorphism fields or with coupled Frobenius constituents would need a new bounded-chain statement and a revised growth argument. Merely changing a tensor subscript does not verify the remaining steps. In particular the proof of Lemma 9.7 on p. 36 also asserts that each vector of an isotypic module generates one simple copy. For \(S=\operatorname{SL}_2(p)\), \(X=\mathbb F_p^2\), and \(a=(e_1,e_2)\in X\oplus X\), the generated module is all of \(X\oplus X\): the matrix algebra generated by \(S\) sends the ordered basis to arbitrary ordered pairs. This refutes that proof sentence, but does not itself refute Lemma 9.7. The trivial-factor branch also uses generators only of \(G/O_p(G)\) as though they generated \(G\). For the natural action on \(V=\mathbb F_p^3\) of \[G=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\v&1\end{pmatrix}:a\in\operatorname{SL}_2(p),\
 v\in\mathbb F_p^{1\times2}\right\},\] the chain \(0<\mathbb F_pe_3<V\) satisfies the definition with \(B=1\), and \(V=[V,G]\). Lifts chosen in \(\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{SL}_2(p),1)\) generate the quotient, but their commutator images lie in \(\mathbb F_pe_1+\mathbb F_pe_2\), so the displayed equality with \(V\) on p. 36 fails. This is another invalid proof step, not a counterexample to the lemma’s final bound. No replacement proof of the diameter theorem is certified here.

Problem 2 (Major, confined to the admitted rank-one boundary).  Theorem 1.2, pp. 2–3, allows \(n=1\), gives nilpotency step at most \(n-1\), and says \(H=1\) in characteristic zero. These requirements are incompatible with its uniform coset-covering bound.

Take \(F=\mathbb Q\) and \[A_N=\{2^j:-N\le j\le N\}\subset\operatorname{GL}_1(\mathbb Q).\] This set is finite, nonempty, symmetric, and even contains the identity. Its cardinalities are \[|A_N|=2N+1,\qquad |A_N^3|=6N+1<3|A_N|.\] Thus \(K=3\) is fixed. The characteristic-zero clause gives \(H=1\), while step at most zero gives \(\Gamma/H=1\), hence \(\Gamma=1\). Covering \(A_N\) requires \(2N+1\) singleton cosets, contradicting \(3^{O_1(1)}\) as \(N\to\infty\).

No \(n\ge2\) exclusion was located, and Remark 1.3(a) rules out interpreting a nontrivial abelian group as step zero. The finite-field reduction on p. 14 uses \(e_{12}\), and Section 8.3 uses \(\gamma_n(T)=1\) for an abelian torus; both also reveal the intended \(n\ge2\) regime. Restricting the theorem to \(n\ge2\), or replacing the step bound by \(\max(1,n-1)\), addresses this boundary. In rank one the latter correction is verified directly by taking \(\Gamma=\langle A\rangle\), \(H=1\). The counterexample does not disprove the asserted \(n\ge2\) structure theorem. Its Major classification concerns a false quantified guarantee in the main theorem, not an alleged failure throughout the intended range.

Problem 3 (Minor: exact odd powers in the affine conjugating lemma).  Lemma 1.8, p. 6, restated as Lemma 7.11, pp. 21–22, claims \(A^{7d}\supseteq[V,G]\) for a symmetric \(G\)-invariant generating set of an abelian \(V\), under the tripling and quasirandomness hypotheses.

Let \(V=C_2\) additively, \(G=1\), \(d=1\), \(K=2\), and \(A=\{v\}\) for the nonzero element \(v\). The trivial group is generated by its identity and has \(\deg_{\mathbb C}G=\infty\), as defined on p. 11. Every hypothesis holds, but \(A^7=\{v\}\) does not contain \([V,G]=\{0\}\).

In the p. 22 proof, \(B=AG\) need not contain \(G\). The inference placing a commutator in \(B^6B\) therefore uses an absent hypothesis. Since \(G\subseteq B^2\), the already established conjugate inclusion instead puts each commutator in \(B^6B^2\cap V=A^8\). Rhemtulla’s displayed identity then gives \(A^{8d}\supseteq[V,G]\). This is a verified local repair; alternatively \(1\in A\) restores the printed \(7d\) argument. Later adjustable exponents must be changed accordingly. No new main-theorem counterexample follows from this parity defect alone.

Problem 4 (Minor: singleton nontrivial root images evade Proposition 8.5).  Proposition 8.5, p. 26, assumes symmetry and \(\langle A^\pi\rangle=T\), but not \(1\in A\). It concludes either a nontrivial root image of cardinality strictly greater than one and at most a specified bound, or uniformly bounded-power coverage of \(\langle(A^2\cap V)^T\rangle\).

For odd primes \(p>7\), take the affine group \(\Sigma=\mathbb F_p\rtimes\{\pm1\}\subset\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_p)\), with \(U=V=\mathbb F_p\) the translations and \(T=\{\pm1\}\). Then \([V,U]=1\) and \(C_V(T)=1\). Let \[A=\{x\mapsto -x+b:b=-1,0,1\}.\] Each element is an involution, so \(A\) is symmetric; its projection generates \(T\). Moreover \(|A|=3\), \(|A^3|=7\), so \(K=3\) is valid. The unique nontrivial root has \(\chi(A)=\{-1\}\), of cardinality one, so alternative (a) fails.

The set \(A^2\) contains translation by \(1\), whence \(\langle(A^2\cap V)^T\rangle=V\). An odd power contains only reflections; an even \(m\)-th power has at most \(2m+1\) translations. No uniform exponent can cover all \(p\) translations as \(p\to\infty\). Alternative (b) fails as well.

Adding \(1\in A\) prevents a singleton nontrivial root image when \(A^\pi\) generates \(T\), and restores the relevant initial inference in the proof. Proposition 8.8 already includes \(1\in A\), and its uses of this lemma therefore supply the missing condition. This is a local false auxiliary statement, without demonstrated damage to that downstream application.
# Other checks and remaining uncertainty

The finite-field reduction’s finite pigeonhole argument over the possible normal closures of \(A^6\cap\Gamma\) was checked; its role is to make the subgroup independent of the finite test set, rather than merely to obtain unrelated finite approximations. The distinction between an arbitrary soluble section and a section covered by a trigonalizable subgroup is used explicitly in Section 6. The characteristic-intersection construction and bounded Weyl action were traced, subject to the cited finite-linear-group theorems.

In Section 8, the pushforward of uniform measure under an invariant bilinear map gives \(\widehat\mu(\chi)=[U:U_\chi]^{-1}\). The large-composition-factor condition therefore supplies the Fourier gap needed in Proposition 8.7. The central, abelian, and lower-central-series stages of Proposition 8.8 were followed, as were the comparison \(H_1=H_2\), the subsequent normalizer argument, and the finite intersection of conjugates in Section 8.5. These checks do not certify every imported theorem.

Two other proof details merit separate treatment rather than an additional claimed theorem counterexample. On p. 21, projection of \(B^3\) onto retained simple factors is used to infer coverage of the section \(\Gamma_1/\operatorname{Sol}(\Gamma)\); the defined trace requires intersection with \(\Gamma_1\). A complete justification under the special hypotheses was not supplied by this review. On p. 31, the coprime-action identity is stated for arbitrary subgroups \(L\le V\), although it requires \(T\)-invariance. This local step is repaired by taking \(L_T=\langle\operatorname{tr}(A^2,V)^T\rangle\): the trace lies in the \(T\)-stable image of \(U_1\), and \(C_V(T)=1\) gives \(L_T=[L_T,T]\le\operatorname{im}[U_1,T]\), which is the inclusion actually needed. This local repair is not a complete independent proof of the theorem.

The high-rank and non-finitely-generated examples in Section 3 were used as counterevidence against imposing stronger conclusions than the paper claims. Missing computational code is not a mathematical defect here. No author correction addressing the findings was established by the version search; this is not a claim of first discovery.
# Conclusion and review state

The main rank-one bound and the bounded-chain input to the diameter proof are false as stated in the reviewed version. The remaining structural theorem for \(n\ge2\) and the diameter theorem itself are not refuted by the examples. A satisfactory revision should repair the rank domain, supply a valid replacement for the prime-field descent and the affected orbit argument, and make the identity hypotheses or exponents consistent.

Every nontrivial representation of \(G=P\rtimes L\) restricts nontrivially to \(L\): killing \(L\) would also kill \([P,L]=P\). Thus \(\deg_{\mathbb C}G\ge(q-1)/2\to\infty\), with \(n=4\) fixed.

The proof on p. 35 passes from tensor products over an algebraic closure to tensor products of irreducible modules over \(\mathbb F_p\). Restriction of scalars does not preserve that asserted tensor factorization. The dimension calculation above is a direct obstruction, not an OCR issue: the rendered definition and proof both specify \(\mathbb F_p\). Theorem 9.6 is invoked on p. 36 for \(P/[P,P]\); the present semidirect family makes this dependency explicit. This is a demonstrated invalid derivation closely tied to the diameter contribution.

A reformulation over appropriate endomorphism fields or with coupled Frobenius constituents would need a new bounded-chain statement and a revised growth argument. Merely changing a tensor subscript does not verify the remaining steps. In particular the proof of Lemma 9.7 on p. 36 also asserts that each vector of an isotypic module generates one simple copy. For \(S=\operatorname{SL}_2(p)\), \(X=\mathbb F_p^2\), and \(a=(e_1,e_2)\in X\oplus X\), the generated module is all of \(X\oplus X\): the matrix algebra generated by \(S\) sends the ordered basis to arbitrary ordered pairs. This refutes that proof sentence, but does not itself refute Lemma 9.7. The trivial-factor branch also uses generators only of \(G/O_p(G)\) as though they generated \(G\). For the natural action on \(V=\mathbb F_p^3\) of \[G=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\v&1\end{pmatrix}:a\in\operatorname{SL}_2(p),\
 v\in\mathbb F_p^{1\times2}\right\},\] the chain \(0<\mathbb F_pe_3<V\) satisfies the definition with \(B=1\), and \(V=[V,G]\). Lifts chosen in \(\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{SL}_2(p),1)\) generate the quotient, but their commutator images lie in \(\mathbb F_pe_1+\mathbb F_pe_2\), so the displayed equality with \(V\) on p. 36 fails. This is another invalid proof step, not a counterexample to the lemma’s final bound. No replacement proof of the diameter theorem is certified here.
result: Result: No B-bounded invariant chain exists. The actual diameter-proof section [G,Sol(G)]/its derived subgroup is exactly P.
Impact: False structural theorem is applied to exact counterexample family in the core diameter proof.

claim: Theorem1.2 allows n=1 and forces H=1 in char0 and Gamma/H of class<=n-1 while covering A by K^{O_n(1)} cosets.

analysis: Theorem 1.2, pp. 2–3, allows \(n=1\), gives nilpotency step at most \(n-1\), and says \(H=1\) in characteristic zero. These requirements are incompatible with its uniform coset-covering bound.

Take \(F=\mathbb Q\) and \[A_N=\{2^j:-N\le j\le N\}\subset\operatorname{GL}_1(\mathbb Q).\] This set is finite, nonempty, symmetric, and even contains the identity. Its cardinalities are \[|A_N|=2N+1,\qquad |A_N^3|=6N+1<3|A_N|.\] Thus \(K=3\) is fixed. The characteristic-zero clause gives \(H=1\), while step at most zero gives \(\Gamma/H=1\), hence \(\Gamma=1\). Covering \(A_N\) requires \(2N+1\) singleton cosets, contradicting \(3^{O_1(1)}\) as \(N\to\infty\).

No \(n\ge2\) exclusion was located, and Remark 1.3(a) rules out interpreting a nontrivial abelian group as step zero. The finite-field reduction on p. 14 uses \(e_{12}\), and Section 8.3 uses \(\gamma_n(T)=1\) for an abelian torus; both also reveal the intended \(n\ge2\) regime. Restricting the theorem to \(n\ge2\), or replacing the step bound by \(\max(1,n-1)\), addresses this boundary. In rank one the latter correction is verified directly by taking \(\Gamma=\langle A\rangle\), \(H=1\). The counterexample does not disprove the asserted \(n\ge2\) structure theorem. Its Major classification concerns a false quantified guarantee in the main theorem, not an alleged failure throughout the intended range.

problems.title: singleton nontrivial root images evade Proposition 8.5
problems.source_location: Pages: 26 Pages: 27 Pages: 28 Pages: 29
claim: Proposition8.5 forces small root image cardinality>1 or bounded-power coverage under symmetry only.
analysis: Proposition 8.5, p. 26, assumes symmetry and \(\langle A^\pi\rangle=T\), but not \(1\in A\). It concludes either a nontrivial root image of cardinality strictly greater than one and at most a specified bound, or uniformly bounded-power coverage of \(\langle(A^2\cap V)^T\rangle\).

For odd primes \(p>7\), take the affine group \(\Sigma=\mathbb F_p\rtimes\{\pm1\}\subset\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb F_p)\), with \(U=V=\mathbb F_p\) the translations and \(T=\{\pm1\}\). Then \([V,U]=1\) and \(C_V(T)=1\). Let \[A=\{x\mapsto -x+b:b=-1,0,1\}.\] Each element is an involution, so \(A\) is symmetric; its projection generates \(T\). Moreover \(|A|=3\), \(|A^3|=7\), so \(K=3\) is valid. The unique nontrivial root has \(\chi(A)=\{-1\}\), of cardinality one, so alternative (a) fails.

The set \(A^2\) contains translation by \(1\), whence \(\langle(A^2\cap V)^T\rangle=V\). An odd power contains only reflections; an even \(m\)-th power has at most \(2m+1\) translations. No uniform exponent can cover all \(p\) translations as \(p\to\infty\). Alternative (b) fails as well.

Adding \(1\in A\) prevents a singleton nontrivial root image when \(A^\pi\) generates \(T\), and restores the relevant initial inference in the proof. Proposition 8.8 already includes \(1\in A\), and its uses of this lemma therefore supply the missing condition. This is a local false auxiliary statement, without demonstrated damage to that downstream application.
result: Result: Neither alternative holds uniformly as p tends to infinity.
Impact: Local false auxiliary statement; downstream application not refuted.

report: Author: Assigned scientific review unit: M25-0147
Date: Initial review; adjudication pending

Title: Scientific initial review of
Convex polytopes from fewer points
# Identity and summary

The reviewed paper is Convex polytopes from fewer points, by Cosmin Pohoata and Dmitrii Zakharov, associated with Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), 449–471, DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0034 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0034). The actual source is the 15-page author manuscript arXiv:2208.04878v1, dated 9 August 2022 [paper]. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with the printed numbers. The journal version was not acquired, so the findings are not attributed to its text.

Assessment: Major, concerning the displayed main derivation. The half-space construction in Proposition 3.1 excludes the point groups it is meant to contain. The subsequent cap assembly uses undefined or repeated endpoint triples and does not retain the claimed vertex count if those endpoints are merely removed. Explicit local corrections are verified below, and the corrected counting argument still yields the qualitative \(2^{o(n)}\) conclusion, conditional on the preliminary geometry. No counterexample to Theorems 1.1–1.3 is established.

A separate, local counterexample disproves Proposition 2.3 under its printed projection hypotheses. Its downstream application has additional projection structure excluding this example. The positive-fraction argument was checked for the stronger conclusion of separation of whole convex hulls, and its counting exponents are consistent after two local proof clarifications.
# Scope and operative hypotheses

The entire manuscript text was read. Actual source images and exact reviewer-written calculations were used to check the findings. These agents are recorded as AI assistants within this initial review, not as independent acceptance reviewers or different verified models.

General position means no four points are coplanar in \(\mathbb R^3\). It does not by itself guarantee that projection onto the first two coordinates is injective or in planar general position. A \(C\)-free set has every line through two of its points disjoint from \(C\); a \(C\)-cap has each point outside the convex hull of \(C\) together with the other points. A collection in convex position has each entire convex hull disjoint from the convex hull of all the other sets (pp. 2, 4). These distinctions matter.

The cited planar support-region prerequisite was compared with Suk’s Theorem 2.4, pp. 2–3 of arXiv:1604.08657v2 [suk]. Taking its parameter \(r=k+1\) gives \(k\) consecutive regions of density \(2^{-32(k+1)}\ge2^{-40k}\) for \(k\ge4\), covering the large-\(k\) application here. This substitution alone does not certify the separately stated \(k=3\) endpoint. The Four Color Theorem, the general Ramsey theorem, and the full original proofs of the imported geometric theorems were not re-proved.
# Problems and evidence

Problem 1 (Major: the constructed half-spaces have the wrong containments).  Proposition 3.1, pp. 8–9, requires \(Z_1\cup Z_3\subset P_J^1\) and \(Z_2\cup Z_4\subset P_J^2\). The proof orients \(H_1\) with \(Z_1\subset H_1^+\) and \(H_2\) with \(Z_2\subset H_2^+\), then defines \[P_J^1=H_0^-\cap H_1^+\cap H_2^+,\qquad
 P_J^2=H_0^-\cap H_1^-\cap H_2^-.\] These definitions conflict with the preceding separation requirements.

Indeed, \(H_2\) separates \(Z_1\cup Z_3\cup X_{j_2}\) from \(Z_2\cup Z_4\). With the printed orientation, the former group is on its negative side. Thus nonempty \(Z_1\) or \(Z_3\) is excluded from the proposed \(P_J^1\); the analogous problem occurs for \(P_J^2\).

Here is an exact geometric witness to the construction failure. Take singleton clusters \(X_i=\{(t,t^2,t^3)\}\), for \(t=-2,-1,0,1,2\) in order, and \(J=\{2,3,4\}\). All four-point affine determinants are nonzero by the Vandermonde formula; the planar projections are consecutive points on a parabola, and the above/below orientation of interlacing chords is consistent. Define the positive half-spaces by \(f_i\ge0\), where \[f_0=\tfrac12-y,\quad
 f_1=-z+\tfrac12y+\tfrac94x-\tfrac98,\quad
 f_2=z+\tfrac12y-\tfrac94x-\tfrac98.\] Their exact signs, without floating-point tolerance, are as follows: \[\begin{array}{c|rrrrr}
 t&-2&-1&0&1&2\\ \hline
 2f_0&-7&-1&1&-1&-7\\
 8f_1&35&-15&-9&5&-21\\
 8f_2&-21&5&-9&-15&35
\end{array}\] Consequently all the required preconstruction separations and printed orientations hold, while \(X_1,X_4\not\subset P_J^1\) and \(X_2,X_5\not\subset P_J^2\). The sign table and general-position determinants were independently evaluated in the saved exact-calculation record.
#### Impact and verified repair.

These polyhedra are used immediately in the chain/antichain coloring and then to certify convexity of the union of caps. Their containments are therefore part of the core derivation, rather than an unused label. This is the basis for the Major assessment; it is not a claim that the existence proposition or the final theorem is false.

Reversing the stated \(H_2\) orientation restores the intended point containments, but is insufficient for the asserted separation: the manuscript defines \(H^\pm\) to be closed half-spaces (p. 6). In the witness above, the two orientation-corrected polyhedra share the line \(y=9/4,\ z=9x/4\). In particular, \((0,9/4,0)\) belongs to both, and its line to the middle point \((0,0,0)\) meets all three sets.

A verified repair adds a positive margin. Put \(A=Z_1\cup Z_3\), \(B=Z_2\cup Z_4\), and \(C=\operatorname{conv}(X_{j_2})\). Choose affine defining functions \(h_0,h_1,h_2\) for the strictly separating planes, oriented so that their sign triples on \(C,A,B\), respectively, are \[(+,-,+),\qquad(-,+,+),\qquad(-,-,-).\] By finiteness of the input, choose \(\eta>0\) smaller than every absolute value of these functions at the input points. Define \[Q_1=\{h_0\le-\eta,\ h_1\ge\eta,\ h_2\ge\eta\},
 \qquad
 Q_2=\{h_0\le-\eta,\ h_1\le-\eta,\ h_2\le-\eta\}.\] Then \(A\subset\operatorname{int}Q_1\) and \(B\subset\operatorname{int}Q_2\). The inequalities for \(h_0,h_1,h_2\), respectively, strictly separate \(C\) from \(\operatorname{conv}(Q_1\cup Q_2)\), \(Q_1\) from \(\operatorname{conv}(Q_2\cup C)\), and \(Q_2\) from \(\operatorname{conv}(Q_1\cup C)\). Hence a line cannot meet all three sets: one of its three intersection points would lie between the other two, contradicting the corresponding strict separation. Each \(Q_i\) still uses three half-spaces, so the bounded truncation and asymptotic estimates below apply to these strengthened polyhedra. In the displayed witness, \(h=(f_0,f_1,-f_2)\) and \(\eta=1/4\) work. This repair does not independently settle every other preliminary lemma.

Problem 2 (Major: endpoint triples do not support the cap count).  On p. 9 the proof uses \(\{j_{l-1},j_l,j_t\}\) for every \(l\in[t]\), then forms the union of odd-indexed caps of size \(2n/t\). The triple is undefined at \(l=1\) and has a repeated index at \(l=t\), so the corresponding color and cap cannot be invoked.

Merely deleting the invalid endpoints can also delete the required cardinality. For instance, with \(t=5\), the printed odd indices are \(1,3,5\); only index \(3\) is valid, and a cap of size \(2n/5\) does not supply \(n\) vertices. This is a defect in the actual concluding inference, not a counterexample to the existence of a convex \(n\)-set by other means.
#### A complete local index correction.

Let \[I=\{2,4,\ldots\}\cap\{2,\ldots,t-1\},\qquad
 m=|I|=\left\lfloor\frac{t-1}{2}\right\rfloor,\qquad
 a=\left\lceil\frac nm\right\rceil.\] For a red clique use \(\{j_{l-1},j_l,j_t\}\) for \(l\in I\). Every other selected cluster lies in the associated \(P_J^1\), because selected indices are nonadjacent and interior. For a blue clique use \(\{j_1,j_l,j_{l+1}\}\); the analogous containment is in \(P_J^2\). A relative cap of size \(a\) in each selected cluster therefore gives a convex union with \(ma\ge n\) vertices. Every triple now has three distinct indices.

The manuscript applies Proposition 2.1, stated for a polytope, to an unbounded intersection of three half-spaces. A sufficient local justification is to intersect each such set with a large box containing the entire finite input. The resulting bounded three-dimensional polytope has at most nine facets and at most \(3\cdot9-6=21\) edges. Freeness persists under taking a subset; all other selected caps remain inside the truncation. A cap relative to this truncation consequently suffices for the union argument. This correction replaces the displayed exponent \(3\) by an absolute constant, without changing the qualitative conclusion.
#### Quantifiers and asymptotic counterevidence.

Choose an integer \(k_0\) asymptotic to \(n^{1/4}\). The initial loss is \(2^{40k_0+k_0^3}=2^{o(n)}\); for fixed \(\epsilon>0\), cluster sizes are at least \(|X|^{1-\delta}\), with \(\delta\to0\). The two fixed Ramsey inversions give \(t\to\infty\). With the corrected cap size and the truncation bound, a sufficient estimate for large \(n\), \(\delta\le1/2\), is \[\frac{\log_2|X|}{n}
 \le
 \frac{84\log_2 21}{n}+
 84\left(\frac1m+\frac1n\right)
 \log_2\!\bigl(e(m+1)\bigr)
 \longrightarrow0.\] Thus the local repair preserves the contradiction with \(|X|\ge2^{\epsilon n}\), conditional on the relative-cap proposition and the other preceding inputs. The exact \(n/\log_{(5)}n\) refinement in the p. 10 remark was not certified by this check; the qualitative theorem does not require it.

Problem 3 (Minor: Proposition 2.3 allows endpoint projection collisions).  Proposition 2.3, pp. 5–6, assumes four disjoint sets in spatial general position and that every segment \(x_1x_3\) lies above \(x_2x_4\). It concludes that \(\operatorname{conv}(X_1\cup X_3)\) and \(\operatorname{conv}(X_2\cup X_4)\) are disjoint. The definition of above on p. 5 allows a projected intersection at a common endpoint; projected general position is not imposed.

Take \[\begin{split}
 X_1&=\{(0,0,101)\},\qquad X_2=\{(0,0,-103)\},\\
 X_3&=\{(1,1,0),(5,2,1),(2,6,3),(4,5,8)\},\\
 X_4&=\{q\},\qquad q=(3,7/2,3).
\end{split}\] All seven points are distinct, and all \(35\) four-point affine determinants are nonzero; the minimum absolute value is \(51/2\). The saved exact rational calculation verifies these statements.

For each \(v\in X_3\), the segments from \((0,0)\) to \(\pi(v)\) and to \(\pi(q)\) meet only at \((0,0)\): their two-dimensional determinants are respectively \(1/2,23/2,-11,-1\). At this projected intersection the two spatial heights differ by \(204>0\). Thus every required above relation holds, with a unique projected intersection and disjoint spatial segments.

Nevertheless \[q=\tfrac14\bigl((1,1,0)+(5,2,1)+(2,6,3)+(4,5,8)\bigr),\] so \(q\in\operatorname{conv}(X_3)\). Both convex hulls in the asserted conclusion contain \(q\). This is a counterexample to the standalone proposition.
#### Boundary and correction.

The proof’s inference that the four projected sets are in convex position fails here. Requiring the nondegenerate, properly crossing projected configuration used in the subsequent application excludes this witness. Corollary 2.4 starts with points whose projections are consecutive vertices of a convex polygon, and Section 3 begins with a generic projection. Accordingly this example does not refute that application or the main theorem. A corrected general statement should make the projection condition explicit; a full unrestricted replacement is not certified.
# Preliminary geometry requiring further justification

In Proposition 2.1, p. 4, spatial general position does not ensure that the relation defined by an edge-parallel projection is antisymmetric. For \[P=\operatorname{conv}(0,e_1,e_2,e_3),\quad
 X=\{(2,2,0),(2,2,1),(3,2,0),(2,3,0)\},\] every pair-line misses \(P\), and the four-point determinant is \(1\). Projection along \([0,e_3]\) identifies the first two points, making each related to the other. The relation is a preorder on that fiber. Resolving projection fibers by an ordered refinement is a possible local remedy, but it should be stated.

Nor does a projected antichain automatically satisfy planar general position. Replacing \(X\) by \[\{(2,2,0),(3,2,1),(4,2,0),(2,3,0)\}\] gives a \(P\)-free spatially general set, determinant \(2\), whose projection is an antichain with three collinear points. Thus the planar Theorem 2.1 cannot be applied to that projected set without a degeneracy argument.

For compact full-dimensional \(P\), these projection issues admit a bounded repair. Refine the preorder by ordering each equivalence class; incomparable pairs are unchanged. For each pair-line choose the manuscript’s strictly separating witness edge direction, which is not parallel to that line. Its projected line has positive distance from the compact projected \(P\). Perturb the finitely many directions sufficiently little to preserve every assigned strict separation, while avoiding pair collisions and projected collinear triples. This retains \(E=e(P)\) orders and the \(|X|^{1/E}\) antichain bound.

A weaker relative-cap estimate can also be proved explicitly. Put \(B=\binom{a+b-4}{a-2}\), with \(a,b\ge2\). For a planar-general-position antichain \(S\) and compact polygon \(C\), partition \(S\) by a strictly violated facet inequality. Within one part every segment misses \(C\); if a full pair-line met \(C\) beyond an endpoint, that pair would be comparable. Thus all pair-lines avoid \(C\). Fix \(c\in C\). All of \(C\) has the same strict orientation signs as \(c\) against these lines; triangle membership then shows that a \(c\)-cap in this part is a \(C\)-cap. In coordinates \(c=0\) and \(x>0\) on the part, the projective map \[(x,y)\longmapsto (y/x,1/x)\] turns \(c\)-caps into lower cups and preserves convex position in this chart. The ordinary cups/caps theorem applies. Since the projected polygon has at most \(E\) facets, this proves the sufficient modified threshold \[|X|>(E B)^E\] for compact full-dimensional \(P\), after the preceding projection correction. All assumptions are needed; a projective map alone does not remove collinearity. For the main-proof truncations \(E\le21\), the added factor contributes only \(84\log_2(21)/n\) to the normalized exponent displayed above. This gives substantive counterevidence against a claimed failure of the qualitative main asymptotic. The sharper printed threshold \(B^E\), and degenerate-polytope extensions, are not certified; no counterexample to that existence assertion is established.
# Positive-fraction proof: checked reasoning and limits

Write \(M=\operatorname{ES}_3(8n)\), \(N=|\mathcal X|\). The double count of convex \(8n\)-subsets, the independent set obtained from the planar polytope graph, and the common \(6n\)-point core lead to the visibility-cell count in Section 4. The resulting lower bound for an assigned fiber is \[\frac{N^{2n}}{M^{8n}}\,
 \frac{n^{4n}}{(3^{10}e^{20})^n}.\] For the numerical factor alone, the coarse constant \(3^{30}\) and \(n\ge6561\) suffice. The threshold for all other arguments is kept separate.

Two statements in this chain should be read with their valid weaker replacements. On p. 11 the formula \(\binom{dt}{t}/((d-1)t+1)\) is not the exact count of rooted subtrees in the \(d\)-regular tree: at \(d=2,t=3\) the actual count is \(3\), whereas the formula gives \(5\). It counts the rooted \(d\)-ary comparison tree and therefore supplies the required upper bound. On p. 13, the assigned fiber injects into the product of the visibility cells, giving \[|\text{fiber}|\le \prod_{i=1}^{2n}|\mathcal X\cap R(P,S_i)|.\] Equality is unnecessary and is not established by arbitrary recombination, which need not preserve the prior assignment or every vertex of the fixed core. This inequality is in precisely the direction needed for the subsequent product lower bound.

The conclusion is strong convex-hull separation. For each selected nonempty, pairwise disjoint visibility set \(S_i\), choose a facet \(F_i\in S_i\). Its supporting functional is strictly positive on the whole cell \(R(P,S_i)\cap\mathcal X\) and nonpositive on every other selected cell. It separates their entire convex hulls. The product lower bound and the upper bound \(N\) on each cell imply at least \(n\) cells of size \(N/M^8\).

For Theorem 1.3 the exceptional small \(n\) are handled by \[\epsilon_n=\operatorname{ES}_3\!\left(8\max(n,n_0)\right)^{-8}.\] If \(n<n_0\), use Theorem 1.2 at \(n_0\) for sufficiently large inputs, and otherwise use \(n\) convex singletons. A generic projection from \(\mathbb R^d\) to \(\mathbb R^3\) preserves cardinality and four-point affine independence under the paper’s general-position convention. An intersection of original convex hulls would project to an intersection, so projected separation lifts. This verifies the stated dimension-independent choice and the \(2^{-o(n)}\) behavior, conditional on Theorem 1.1.
# Conclusion and state

The displayed construction and endpoint assembly need correction. Their dependence on the main argument is explicit, and the local repairs preserve its qualitative asymptotic mechanism. The standalone above/below proposition requires an additional projection hypothesis. No false final theorem is claimed. The unverified exact relative-cap threshold and sharp iterated-log refinement remain separate from the established findings. The bounded-loss repair above covers the full-dimensional truncations needed for the qualitative main argument.

Endpoint cap assembly | Major | Interior indices and count checked | Not requested | Preliminary dependencies

Proposition 3.1, pp. 8–9, requires \(Z_1\cup Z_3\subset P_J^1\) and \(Z_2\cup Z_4\subset P_J^2\). The proof orients \(H_1\) with \(Z_1\subset H_1^+\) and \(H_2\) with \(Z_2\subset H_2^+\), then defines \[P_J^1=H_0^-\cap H_1^+\cap H_2^+,\qquad
 P_J^2=H_0^-\cap H_1^-\cap H_2^-.\] These definitions conflict with the preceding separation requirements.

Indeed, \(H_2\) separates \(Z_1\cup Z_3\cup X_{j_2}\) from \(Z_2\cup Z_4\). With the printed orientation, the former group is on its negative side. Thus nonempty \(Z_1\) or \(Z_3\) is excluded from the proposed \(P_J^1\); the analogous problem occurs for \(P_J^2\).

Here is an exact geometric witness to the construction failure. Take singleton clusters \(X_i=\{(t,t^2,t^3)\}\), for \(t=-2,-1,0,1,2\) in order, and \(J=\{2,3,4\}\). All four-point affine determinants are nonzero by the Vandermonde formula; the planar projections are consecutive points on a parabola, and the above/below orientation of interlacing chords is consistent. Define the positive half-spaces by \(f_i\ge0\), where \[f_0=\tfrac12-y,\quad
 f_1=-z+\tfrac12y+\tfrac94x-\tfrac98,\quad
 f_2=z+\tfrac12y-\tfrac94x-\tfrac98.\] Their exact signs, without floating-point tolerance, are as follows: \[\begin{array}{c|rrrrr}
 t&-2&-1&0&1&2\\ \hline
 2f_0&-7&-1&1&-1&-7\\
 8f_1&35&-15&-9&5&-21\\
 8f_2&-21&5&-9&-15&35
\end{array}\] Consequently all the required preconstruction separations and printed orientations hold, while \(X_1,X_4\not\subset P_J^1\) and \(X_2,X_5\not\subset P_J^2\). The sign table and general-position determinants were independently evaluated in the saved exact-calculation record.

These polyhedra are used immediately in the chain/antichain coloring and then to certify convexity of the union of caps. Their containments are therefore part of the core derivation, rather than an unused label. This is the basis for the Major assessment; it is not a claim that the existence proposition or the final theorem is false.

Reversing the stated \(H_2\) orientation restores the intended point containments, but is insufficient for the asserted separation: the manuscript defines \(H^\pm\) to be closed half-spaces (p. 6). In the witness above, the two orientation-corrected polyhedra share the line \(y=9/4,\ z=9x/4\). In particular, \((0,9/4,0)\) belongs to both, and its line to the middle point \((0,0,0)\) meets all three sets.

A verified repair adds a positive margin. Put \(A=Z_1\cup Z_3\), \(B=Z_2\cup Z_4\), and \(C=\operatorname{conv}(X_{j_2})\). Choose affine defining functions \(h_0,h_1,h_2\) for the strictly separating planes, oriented so that their sign triples on \(C,A,B\), respectively, are \[(+,-,+),\qquad(-,+,+),\qquad(-,-,-).\] By finiteness of the input, choose \(\eta>0\) smaller than every absolute value of these functions at the input points. Define \[Q_1=\{h_0\le-\eta,\ h_1\ge\eta,\ h_2\ge\eta\},
 \qquad
 Q_2=\{h_0\le-\eta,\ h_1\le-\eta,\ h_2\le-\eta\}.\] Then \(A\subset\operatorname{int}Q_1\) and \(B\subset\operatorname{int}Q_2\). The inequalities for \(h_0,h_1,h_2\), respectively, strictly separate \(C\) from \(\operatorname{conv}(Q_1\cup Q_2)\), \(Q_1\) from \(\operatorname{conv}(Q_2\cup C)\), and \(Q_2\) from \(\operatorname{conv}(Q_1\cup C)\). Hence a line cannot meet all three sets: one of its three intersection points would lie between the other two, contradicting the corresponding strict separation. Each \(Q_i\) still uses three half-spaces, so the bounded truncation and asymptotic estimates below apply to these strengthened polyhedra. In the displayed witness, \(h=(f_0,f_1,-f_2)\) and \(\eta=1/4\) work. This repair does not independently settle every other preliminary lemma.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: With Z2 in H2+, Z1 union Z3 lies in H2- and is excluded from P1. Exact moment-curve five-point witness satisfies general position and preconstruction separations; all sign evaluations are rational. The earlier orientation-only report repair leaves y=9/4,z=9x/4 in both closed polyhedra. Positive margins remove that intersection and give all three strict convex-hull separations.

problems.title: endpoint triples do not support the cap count
problems.source_location: PDF pp9-10, Section3 concluding cap assembly
claim: Every l in [t] supports the triple {j_(l-1),j_l,j_t} and odd caps of size2n/t yield n vertices
analysis: On p. 9 the proof uses \(\{j_{l-1},j_l,j_t\}\) for every \(l\in[t]\), then forms the union of odd-indexed caps of size \(2n/t\). The triple is undefined at \(l=1\) and has a repeated index at \(l=t\), so the corresponding color and cap cannot be invoked.

Merely deleting the invalid endpoints can also delete the required cardinality. For instance, with \(t=5\), the printed odd indices are \(1,3,5\); only index \(3\) is valid, and a cap of size \(2n/5\) does not supply \(n\) vertices. This is a defect in the actual concluding inference, not a counterexample to the existence of a convex \(n\)-set by other means.

Let \[I=\{2,4,\ldots\}\cap\{2,\ldots,t-1\},\qquad
 m=|I|=\left\lfloor\frac{t-1}{2}\right\rfloor,\qquad
 a=\left\lceil\frac nm\right\rceil.\] For a red clique use \(\{j_{l-1},j_l,j_t\}\) for \(l\in I\). Every other selected cluster lies in the associated \(P_J^1\), because selected indices are nonadjacent and interior. For a blue clique use \(\{j_1,j_l,j_{l+1}\}\); the analogous containment is in \(P_J^2\). A relative cap of size \(a\) in each selected cluster therefore gives a convex union with \(ma\ge n\) vertices. Every triple now has three distinct indices.

The manuscript applies Proposition 2.1, stated for a polytope, to an unbounded intersection of three half-spaces. A sufficient local justification is to intersect each such set with a large box containing the entire finite input. The resulting bounded three-dimensional polytope has at most nine facets and at most \(3\cdot9-6=21\) edges. Freeness persists under taking a subset; all other selected caps remain inside the truncation. A cap relative to this truncation consequently suffices for the union argument. This correction replaces the displayed exponent \(3\) by an absolute constant, without changing the qualitative conclusion.

Choose an integer \(k_0\) asymptotic to \(n^{1/4}\). The initial loss is \(2^{40k_0+k_0^3}=2^{o(n)}\); for fixed \(\epsilon>0\), cluster sizes are at least \(|X|^{1-\delta}\), with \(\delta\to0\). The two fixed Ramsey inversions give \(t\to\infty\). With the corrected cap size and the truncation bound, a sufficient estimate for large \(n\), \(\delta\le1/2\), is \[\frac{\log_2|X|}{n}
 \le
 \frac{84\log_2 21}{n}+
 84\left(\frac1m+\frac1n\right)
 \log_2\!\bigl(e(m+1)\bigr)
 \longrightarrow0.\] Thus the local repair preserves the contradiction with \(|X|\ge2^{\epsilon n}\), conditional on the relative-cap proposition and the other preceding inputs. The exact \(n/\log_{(5)}n\) refinement in the p. 10 remark was not certified by this check; the qualitative theorem does not require it.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: At l1 the predecessor is undefined; at lt the triple repeats jt. Deleting invalid endpoints loses the asserted count, e.g t5 retains only K3.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: m grows, and the revised exponent remains o(n); this does not refute the main theorem.

problems.title: Proposition 2.3 allows endpoint projection collisions
problems.source_location: PDF pp5-6, Proposition2.3 and definition of above
claim: Above relations alone under spatial general position imply disjoint joined hulls
analysis: Proposition 2.3, pp. 5–6, assumes four disjoint sets in spatial general position and that every segment \(x_1x_3\) lies above \(x_2x_4\). It concludes that \(\operatorname{conv}(X_1\cup X_3)\) and \(\operatorname{conv}(X_2\cup X_4)\) are disjoint. The definition of above on p. 5 allows a projected intersection at a common endpoint; projected general position is not imposed.

Take \[\begin{split}
 X_1&=\{(0,0,101)\},\qquad X_2=\{(0,0,-103)\},\\
 X_3&=\{(1,1,0),(5,2,1),(2,6,3),(4,5,8)\},\\
 X_4&=\{q\},\qquad q=(3,7/2,3).
\end{split}\] All seven points are distinct, and all \(35\) four-point affine determinants are nonzero; the minimum absolute value is \(51/2\). The saved exact rational calculation verifies these statements.

For each \(v\in X_3\), the segments from \((0,0)\) to \(\pi(v)\) and to \(\pi(q)\) meet only at \((0,0)\): their two-dimensional determinants are respectively \(1/2,23/2,-11,-1\). At this projected intersection the two spatial heights differ by \(204>0\). Thus every required above relation holds, with a unique projected intersection and disjoint spatial segments.

Nevertheless \[q=\tfrac14\bigl((1,1,0)+(5,2,1)+(2,6,3)+(4,5,8)\bigr),\] so \(q\in\operatorname{conv}(X_3)\). Both convex hulls in the asserted conclusion contain \(q\). This is a counterexample to the standalone proposition.

The proof’s inference that the four projected sets are in convex position fails here. Requiring the nondegenerate, properly crossing projected configuration used in the subsequent application excludes this witness. Corollary 2.4 starts with points whose projections are consecutive vertices of a convex polygon, and Section 3 begins with a generic projection. Accordingly this example does not refute that application or the main theorem. A corrected general statement should make the projection condition explicit; a full unrestricted replacement is not certified.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: Seven exact points with X1=(0,0,101), X2=(0,0,-103), X3 four listed tetrahedron vertices, X4 their barycenter. All35 four-point determinants nonzero, minimum51/2; projected segments intersect only at common origin with height gap204. Both asserted hulls contain X4.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Corollary2.4 convex polygon projections and Section3 generic projection exclude endpoint collision.

Title: Scientific initial review of
Syzygies of adjoint linear series on projective varieties
# Identity, scope, and assessment

The paper is Syzygies of adjoint linear series on projective varieties, by Purnaprajna Bangere and Justin Lacini, associated with Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), 473–499, DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0035 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0035). The source actually reviewed is the 20-page author manuscript arXiv:2302.02517v1, dated 6 February 2023 [paper]. References to pages below mean its one-based PDF pages, agreeing with its printed pagination. The author publication list confirms the journal identity; the publisher article and public download endpoints did not provide the journal text. No equivalence with the journal proof is asserted.

Assessment: Major, a demonstrated failure of a core proof step. The claimed invariant isomorphism on p. 15 is false for the canonical Galois action in an example satisfying the main hypotheses. Branchwise transport of a canonical-form section need not glue at ramification. The manuscript uses this construction first for Lemma 5.10 and then for the higher-diagonal lifting in Theorems 5.11 and 5.12. This interrupts the displayed route from enlarged diagonals to the actual diagonals.

The example does not disprove Lemma 5.10 or either main theorem. In fact, unrestricted lifting is explicitly surjective in the example. The algebra of tree-shaped diagonal ideals and the enlarged-diagonal vanishing estimates have substantial positive checks, recorded below. The assessment concerns the specified author-version proof, not an assertion that its final results are false or irreparable.
The entire manuscript text was read. They are AI assistants within this initial review; no independent acceptance, human review, or independently verified different-model identity is claimed.
# Operative definitions and dependency chain

Throughout, \(X\) is smooth and projective over \(\mathbb C\), \(A\) is ample and globally generated, and \(L_m=\mathcal O_X(K_X+mA)\). Theorem 1.2 states \(N_p\) for \(m\ge n+1+p\); Theorem 1.4 states Koszulness for \(m\ge n+2\). Section 2 explicitly permits \(N_p\) for globally generated line bundles without requiring an embedding. Consequently \(X=\mathbb P^n,A=\mathcal O(1),m=n+1\), where \(L_m=\mathcal O\), is not a counterexample to the stated \(N_0\) convention.

A basepoint-free subspace of dimension \(n+1\) gives a finite flat map \(\alpha:X\to\mathbb P^n\). The enlarged diagonal is \(\Gamma_X=X\times_{\mathbb P^n}X\); it contains \(\Delta_X\), and its extra components meet the ordinary diagonal over the branch locus. The star arrangement \(\Delta^1\) uses edges \((1,j)\); the chain arrangement \(\Delta^2\) uses edges \((j-1,j)\). These are different ideals and serve different criteria.

The proof establishes vanishing for the enlarged arrangements in Theorem 5.8, with thresholds \(m\ge n+r-1\) for stars and \(m\ge n+2\) for chains. It then needs surjectivity of restrictions from enlarged to ordinary arrangements. The invariant construction on p. 15 and its reuse on p. 17 are the bridge to this required surjectivity; they are not consequences of Theorem 5.8 alone.
# Problem and decisive evidence

Problem 1 (Major: canonical Galois transport does not preserve branch gluing).  In Section 5.4, p. 15, let \(Y\) be the Galois closure and let \(G\) act on the second factor. For \[F=(\omega_Y\otimes\beta^*\mathcal O_X(mA))
       \boxtimes(\omega_Y\otimes\beta^*\mathcal O_X(mA)),\] the manuscript asserts that the injection into restrictions to the graph components induces an isomorphism \[(F|_{\Gamma_{Y_0}})^G
 \ \cong\
 \left(\bigoplus_{g\in G} F|_{g^*\Delta_{Y_0}}\right)^G.\] It deduces surjectivity onto the diagonal and subsequently extends sections by the Galois action in the p. 17 induction. The displayed invariant isomorphism fails at ramification.
## An admissible global example

Take \[X=Y=\mathbb P^1,\qquad
 \alpha:[z_0:z_1]\longmapsto[z_0^2:z_1^2],\qquad
 A=\alpha^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(2),\qquad m=2.\] Here \(n=1\), the space spanned by \(z_0^2,z_1^2\) is basepoint free, \(\alpha\) is finite flat and Galois, \(\beta\) is the identity, and \[L=\omega_{\mathbb P^1}\otimes\alpha^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(2)=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(2).\] Thus all main assumptions and \(m\ge n+1\) hold. The involution is \(g(z)=-z\). The smooth locus is all of \(Y\); on a curve the required removal of a codimension-at-least-two set cannot discard the ramification points \(0,\infty\).
## Local computation at a branch point

On affine charts write the two coordinates as \(u,v\). The fiber product has ring \[R=\mathbb C[u,v]/(u^2-v^2).\] Its two graph components are \(v=u\) and \(v=-u\), meeting at \((0,0)\). The restriction injection is \[R\hookrightarrow \mathbb C[u]\oplus\mathbb C[u],\qquad
 h\longmapsto(h(u,u),h(u,-u)).\] Its image consists exactly of pairs with equal value at zero.

Let \(e\) be the local frame \(du\boxtimes dv\), including the frames of the pulled-back base line bundles. Those latter frames are invariant. The canonical second-factor action sends \(v\) to \(-v\) and \(e\) to \(-e\). Writing \(h=a(u)+v b(u)\), invariance of \(he\) requires \(a=0\). Its component values are therefore \[(u b(u),-u b(u))e.\] On the direct sum of graph restrictions, however, all pairs \((s(u),-s(u))e\) are invariant. The invariant pair \((1,-1)e\) is not in the restriction image, because \(1\ne-1\) at the node. Equivalently, the induced map on invariant modules is \[u\,\mathbb C[u]\ \hookrightarrow\ \mathbb C[u],\] with nonzero cokernel. Taking invariants is exact in characteristic zero; it does not force this cokernel’s invariant part to vanish.

This also identifies the obstruction to the proposed canonical identification of the two pulled-back canonical bundles by the ramification formula. The identification coming from the base differential has component values \(+1\) and \(-1\); it does not extend as a regular unit through the node. This statement does not exclude other, noncanonical isomorphisms of the abstract line bundles.
## Global section count

The discrepancy is visible in global sections as well. In the affine frame, \(H^0(L)\) consists of \(p(z)\,dz\) times the base frame, with \(\deg p\le2\), and \[g\cdot p(z)\,dz=-p(-z)\,dz.\] Its invariant subspace is one-dimensional, spanned by \(z\,dz\). Hence \(H^0(\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1,F)^G\) has dimension \(3\).

The divisor \(\Gamma\) has bidegree \((2,2)\), while \(F=\mathcal O(2,2)\). The exact sequence \[0\longrightarrow\mathcal O(0,0)\longrightarrow\mathcal O(2,2)
       \longrightarrow F|_\Gamma\longrightarrow0\] has \(H^1(\mathcal O(0,0))=0\). Its one-dimensional kernel is anti-invariant, represented locally by \((u^2-v^2)\,du\,dv\). It follows that \[\dim H^0(\Gamma,F)^G=3,\qquad
 \dim\left(\bigoplus_{g\in G}H^0(g^*\Delta,F)\right)^G
       =h^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(4))=5.\] The first invariant space maps to the diagonal sections vanishing at both ramification points. In a degree-four polynomial basis these are the two independent endpoint conditions on the constant and leading coefficients. Exact polynomial and rational linear-algebra calculations in the verification record check the character dimensions and rank-two compatibility condition; the displayed module argument gives the general local reason.
## Impact, counterevidence, and repair boundary

The affected step supplies the Galois case of Lemma 5.10 (pp. 15–16). The general case then uses it in the trace diagram, and the p. 17 proof invokes the same Galois extension to patch higher unions. Thus the invalid isomorphism concerns the central derivation of both \(N_p\) and Koszulness. This explicit dependence, together with an admissible counterexample to the asserted map, supports the Major assessment.

There is decisive counterevidence against calling the final restriction claim false. For this example, \[H^0(\mathcal O(2))\otimes H^0(\mathcal O(2))\longrightarrow H^0(\mathcal O(4))\] is surjective: every monomial of degree at most four is a product of two monomials of degree at most two. A global section of \(F\) on the product restricts first to \(\Gamma\) and then to \(\Delta\). Therefore the unrestricted map \(H^0(\Gamma,F)\to H^0(\Delta,F)\) is surjective despite the invariant construction’s failure. The same polynomial multiplication verifies the required powers in this test case.

A repair must construct regular lifts satisfying the compatibility conditions on intersecting graph components, and must show that these lifts have the prescribed restrictions on the mixed unions used in the induction. Simply deleting the branch locus is insufficient because it is a divisor. Merely choosing another linearization in this cyclic example does not prove a uniform replacement compatible with the canonical trace construction. No complete general repair is certified here; no counterexample to Theorems 1.2 or 1.4 is asserted.
# Positive checks and limits of coverage
#### Products, diagonal ideals, and trace.

The separate-factor Tor vanishing in Lemmas 3.1–3.3 follows by flat extension over the ground field. The displayed identification \(A/\mathfrak m=\mathbb C\) should be restricted to the intended closed-point setting; the vanishing itself still follows with an arbitrary residue field, which is flat over \(\mathbb C\).

The star/chain statements in Corollary 3.5 admit a direct algebraic justification beyond the phrase change of coordinates. For a new leaf factor write \(R=B\otimes_\mathbb CA_{\rm new}\). Quotienting by its attaching diagonal gives \(B\), free over the old factor \(B\). A free resolution of an old ideal, extended to \(R\), stays exact after this quotient. The associated Tor vanishing gives product/intersection and tensor-product identifications inductively. Thus singular-coordinate concerns do not supply a counterexample to the forest-diagonal assertions. Likewise the normalized trace in characteristic zero splits \(\mathcal O_X\) from \(f_*\mathcal O_Y\); dualizing this split supports Section 3.5. This legitimate trace splitting is distinct from the false invariant isomorphism in the Problem.
#### Koszul criteria.

The star criterion of Theorem 3.6 was checked using the joint kernel of multiplication maps and its alternating part, which is the usual Koszul cycle space. Adding a star diagonal and using the stated \(H^1\)-vanishing supplies a lift; antisymmetrization gives the Koszul boundary in characteristic zero. For Theorem 3.8, the chain ideals give the intersection of adjacent multiplication kernels in \(H^0(L)^{\otimes j}\). Adding the last diagonal and using the stated vanishing proves exactness degree by degree of the corresponding linear free complex. These checks support the criteria in the main connected-projective setting. The full original Green and Inamdar–Mehta papers were not acquired; the historical correction claimed in Remark 3.7 was not independently adjudicated.
#### Vanishing and endpoint arithmetic.

For \(m\ge n+1\), \(L_m\) is globally generated, hence nef: Kodaira vanishing gives the required Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity relative to the finite map \(\alpha\). Consequently \[L_m^{\,k}\otimes\mathcal O(lA)
 =\omega_X\otimes\bigl(L_m^{\,k-1}\otimes\mathcal O((m+l)A)\bigr)\] has vanishing higher cohomology when \(m+l\ge1\). This supplies the implicit nefness behind Lemma 5.2.

The exterior-power evaluation sequence yields both inductions in Lemma 5.3. In Lemma 5.4, if all nonzero cohomology degree is on the first factor, then \(i\ge d-r+2\) and \(i\le n\) imply \(d\le n+r-2<m\). Lemmas 5.5–5.6 force either a vanishing factor or an impossible strictly increasing exponent sequence; deletion of zero-degree endpoint factors preserves the needed inequality. The induction on zero complex degrees in Lemma 5.7 shifts the required cohomology degree by at least \(j-1\), exactly matching its bound. Theorem 5.8 consequently has the thresholds needed by the star and chain criteria. These checks do not replace the subsequent diagonal-lifting obligation.

There are minor endpoint clarifications. Lemma 5.1 includes \(s=1\), for which the empty tensor is \(\mathcal O\) in degree zero and is not an exact augmented complex; restricting the assertion to \(s\ge2\) covers the main uses. The index range in the first line of Lemma 5.6’s proof should run through \(r\), not \(n\). These local issues are not promoted to failures of the main vanishing theorem.
#### Higher lifting and powers.

The chain induction has a valid combinatorial stabilization: when replacing the edge \((s,s+1)\), act on factor \(s\). Earlier edges are enlarged \(\Gamma\)-conditions invariant under the action, while later ordinary diagonals avoid that factor. Thus a supposed failure merely because one factor meets two neighboring chain edges is not established. The ramified section-gluing problem remains.

The final proof must cover every \(k\ge1\) required in Theorems 3.6 and 3.8. Sections 5.4–5.5 display \(F\) with first powers, whereas Lemma 5.10 and the criteria involve unequal powers. Tensoring a sheaf map with a line bundle does not automatically preserve surjectivity on global sections. A replacement lifting argument must explicitly handle these powers as well as mixed-union compatibility; this is a specified remaining obligation, not a separate claimed counterexample.
# Conclusion and state

The report identifies one demonstrated core proof defect and gives both local and global evidence under the main hypotheses. The successful enlarged-diagonal vanishing and the positive unrestricted test case are retained as counterevidence. General lifting at ramification remains to be justified.

Enlarged vanishing | Positive bounded check | Indices and thresholds checked | None | Does not imply lifting
Unused endpoints | Minor clarification | \(s\ge2\); index through \(r\) | Not requested | Correct local wording
All powers and unions | Needs Evidence | Test case succeeds | None | General replacement proof

The review records distinguish complete text reading, selected source-image inspection, bounded proof checks, exact reviewer calculations, and unverified external dependencies. Manifest parsing and hashing are not counted as scientific verification. No author code was run.
