Let \(e\) be the local frame \(du\boxtimes dv\), including the frames of the pulled-back base line bundles. Those latter frames are invariant. The canonical second-factor action sends \(v\) to \(-v\) and \(e\) to \(-e\). Writing \(h=a(u)+v b(u)\), invariance of \(he\) requires \(a=0\). Its component values are therefore \[(u b(u),-u b(u))e.\] On the direct sum of graph restrictions, however, all pairs \((s(u),-s(u))e\) are invariant. The invariant pair \((1,-1)e\) is not in the restriction image, because \(1\ne-1\) at the node. Equivalently, the induced map on invariant modules is \[u\,\mathbb C[u]\ \hookrightarrow\ \mathbb C[u],\] with nonzero cokernel. Taking invariants is exact in characteristic zero; it does not force this cokernel’s invariant part to vanish.

This also identifies the obstruction to the proposed canonical identification of the two pulled-back canonical bundles by the ramification formula. The identification coming from the base differential has component values \(+1\) and \(-1\); it does not extend as a regular unit through the node. This statement does not exclude other, noncanonical isomorphisms of the abstract line bundles.

The discrepancy is visible in global sections as well. In the affine frame, \(H^0(L)\) consists of \(p(z)\,dz\) times the base frame, with \(\deg p\le2\), and \[g\cdot p(z)\,dz=-p(-z)\,dz.\] Its invariant subspace is one-dimensional, spanned by \(z\,dz\). Hence \(H^0(\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1,F)^G\) has dimension \(3\).

The divisor \(\Gamma\) has bidegree \((2,2)\), while \(F=\mathcal O(2,2)\). The exact sequence \[0\longrightarrow\mathcal O(0,0)\longrightarrow\mathcal O(2,2)
       \longrightarrow F|_\Gamma\longrightarrow0\] has \(H^1(\mathcal O(0,0))=0\). Its one-dimensional kernel is anti-invariant, represented locally by \((u^2-v^2)\,du\,dv\). It follows that \[\dim H^0(\Gamma,F)^G=3,\qquad
 \dim\left(\bigoplus_{g\in G}H^0(g^*\Delta,F)\right)^G
       =h^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(4))=5.\] The first invariant space maps to the diagonal sections vanishing at both ramification points. In a degree-four polynomial basis these are the two independent endpoint conditions on the constant and leading coefficients. Exact polynomial and rational linear-algebra calculations in the verification record check the character dimensions and rank-two compatibility condition; the displayed module argument gives the general local reason.

The affected step supplies the Galois case of Lemma 5.10 (pp. 15–16). The general case then uses it in the trace diagram, and the p. 17 proof invokes the same Galois extension to patch higher unions. Thus the invalid isomorphism concerns the central derivation of both \(N_p\) and Koszulness. This explicit dependence, together with an admissible counterexample to the asserted map, supports the Major assessment.

There is decisive counterevidence against calling the final restriction claim false. For this example, \[H^0(\mathcal O(2))\otimes H^0(\mathcal O(2))\longrightarrow H^0(\mathcal O(4))\] is surjective: every monomial of degree at most four is a product of two monomials of degree at most two. A global section of \(F\) on the product restricts first to \(\Gamma\) and then to \(\Delta\). Therefore the unrestricted map \(H^0(\Gamma,F)\to H^0(\Delta,F)\) is surjective despite the invariant construction’s failure. The same polynomial multiplication verifies the required powers in this test case.

A repair must construct regular lifts satisfying the compatibility conditions on intersecting graph components, and must show that these lifts have the prescribed restrictions on the mixed unions used in the induction. Simply deleting the branch locus is insufficient because it is a divisor. Merely choosing another linearization in this cyclic example does not prove a uniform replacement compatible with the canonical trace construction. No complete general repair is certified here; no counterexample to Theorems 1.2 or 1.4 is asserted.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: H0(O2) tensor H0(O2)->H0(O4) is onto by all monomials. Therefore unrestricted Gamma->Delta is onto in this example; it is not a theorem or Lemma5.10 counterexample.

report: Abstract: The acquired author manuscript contains a consequential arithmetic error in its nonspin kernel table and incompatible generator relations in its presentation theorem. An admissible complete intersection of degrees \((2,3)\) gives an exact order-\(21\) characteristic-number class where the printed table gives order \(3\). The quintic likewise exposes the incorrect presentation orders and missing relations. Two impossible relative dual-class identifications occur in the geometric calculation underlying the kernel description. Local corrections to a characteristic number, a genus-zero splitting clause, and an integral symplectic homology table are also established. Counterevidence and the limits of proposed repairs are retained. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical Verification of
Mapping Class Group of Manifolds Which Look Like
3-Dimensional Complete Intersections
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The paper is by Matthias Kreck and Yang Su, with journal identifier 10.1215/00127094-2024-0036 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0036). The scientific object inspected is [KS], arXiv:2009.08054v3, 11 June 2024, 62 pages. All page references below are its one-based PDF pages, which agree with its printed numbering. The primary PDF has 576,226 bytes. Its matching source archive and extracted `source.tex` were available and verified. The manuscript’s description as a final version does not establish byte-level equivalence with the publisher’s article. The publisher endpoint did not yield an independently inspected article, so the findings are confined to this author version.

The complete manuscript text was read. Detailed checks addressed the variation lattice and extension, characteristic-number conventions, the spin and nonspin relation lattices, explicit generators, the relative-to-absolute kernel argument, low-genus boundaries, lower homology, and the bordism appendix. Exact integer calculations supplement the arguments below. Selected primary dependencies were acquired and inspected at the stated locations; a complete reconstruction of all cited surgery, embedding, and arithmetic-group results is not claimed. Source inventory parsing and hashing are separate from scientific checking.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

The standing class consists of smooth, oriented, closed, simply connected six-manifolds \(M\) with \(H_2(M;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\), a chosen generator \(x\in H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\), and \(d=\langle x^3,[M]\rangle>0\). Write \(x^2=dy\), with \(y\) the corresponding generator of \(H^4(M;\mathbb Z)\), and \(H=H^3(M;\mathbb Z)\), a free symplectic lattice of rank \(2g=b_3(M)\). In the spin case, \[p_1(TM)=4ky,\qquad k=d+6l.\] In the nonspin case, \[d=2\delta,\qquad p_1(TM)=(4k-d)y=(d+48l)y,\qquad
 k=\delta+12l.\] Here \(l\in\mathbb Z\). The Torelli group \(\mathcal I(M)\) is the kernel of the action on \(H\). The variation takes values in \[L_{d,k}=(H\oplus H)/\Delta_{d,k},\qquad
 \Delta_{d,k}=\{(du,ku):u\in H\},\] and \(\mathcal K(M)\) is its kernel. The special Torelli group \(\mathcal J(M)\) acts trivially on \(\pi_3(M)\) and fits into \(1\to\mathcal K(M)\to\mathcal J(M)\to H\to0\). A fixed disk gives the relative group \(\mathcal K(M,D)\).

Normal and tangent Pontryagin classes are distinguished throughout. In particular, for a spin bordism, \(p_1(\nu W)=-p_1(TW)\). The relative characteristic numbers require actual preimages of the specified absolute classes. Replacing such a preimage by a class with different absolute evaluations is not an allowable choice ambiguity.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Major: the nonspin table loses a factor of seven).  Theorem 6.1(2), pp. 26–27, and its reduction in Section 10.4, pp. 51–52, disagree with the original geometric relation lattice (10.5), p. 49, on a smooth complete intersection satisfying every standing hypothesis.
## Decisive calculation

Let \(M=X_{2,3}\subset\mathbb {CP}^5\) be a smooth complete intersection of degrees \(2\) and \(3\). It is a simply connected complex threefold with \(H_2(M;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\). The hyperplane class is primitive, and the tangent/normal sequence gives \[\begin{gathered}
 d=6,\qquad c_1(TM)=(6-2-3)x=x,\\
 p_1(TM)=(6-2^2-3^2)x^2=-7x^2=-42y .
 \end{gathered}\] Thus \(w_2(M)\ne0\), \(\delta=3\), \(k=-9\), and \(l=-1\). This is an actual complete intersection, not a formal parameter pair.

Equation reference: eq:21. Put \(h=d+24l\). The columns of (10.5) are \[\begin{aligned}
 c_1&=(0,0,-224),&c_2&=(6,-6,8),&c_3&=(1,-3,8),\\
 c_4&=(d^2,-d(h-1),(h-1)^2-1),\\
 c_5&=(2d^2,-2dh,2h^2),&
 c_6&=(-2d,3d+24l,-4h).
\end{aligned}\] For this \(M\), the last three columns are \[(36,114,360),\quad (72,216,648),\quad (-12,-6,72).\] The geometric generator \(N_{-1}\) in Section 10.4 has original characteristic vector \(v=(1,-1,0)\): its \((\mu/4,\lambda)\) coordinates are \((-1,-2)\), as on p. 51. Its order modulo the original column lattice is exactly \(21\). Indeed, \[
 21v=9c_3-c_6.\] Every column has second coordinate divisible by \(3\), whereas \(v_2=-1\). Also the functional \[\phi(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3)=2\sigma_1+\sigma_2+\sigma_3\pmod7\] annihilates every column and satisfies \(\phi(v)=1\). Hence the order is divisible by both \(3\) and \(7\), and [eq:21] (#eq:21) gives the matching upper bound. Exact determinant computations independently give indices \(336\) and \(16\) before and after adjoining \(v\).

The source of the discrepancy is directly visible. Applying the printed definition \(\mu=6\sigma_1+10\sigma_2+3\sigma_3\) to \(c_5\) gives \[\frac{\mu(c_5)}4=-2(\delta^2+48\delta l-432l^2).\] The transformed table on p. 51 instead has \(-2(\delta^2+96\delta l-864l^2)\). At \((\delta,l)=(3,-1)\) these values are \(1134\) and \(2286\), respectively. The latter incorrectly kills the seven-primary class. Theorem 6.1 assigns \(a=0,b=1,c=0\), hence \(\mathcal K(M)\cong\mathbb Z/3\).
## Geometric verification, impact, and repair

The original columns were checked from \(\alpha=x^2-dy\) and \(\beta=(p_1(\nu W)-x^2)/2+hy\). For example, on \(\mathbb {CP}^2\times S^4\), \(\beta=-2x^2+hy\), giving \((-2d,3d+24l,-4h)\). On \(S^4\times S^4\), \(x=0\), \(y=a+b\), and \(\langle y^2,[W]\rangle=2\), giving \(c_5\). On \(\mathbb {HP}^2\) with its positive generator \(y\), \(\beta=(h-1)y\); subtracting the constant-map \(\mathbb {HP}^2\) gives \(c_4\). The \(\mathbb {CP}^2\times\mathbb {CP}^2\) and \(\mathbb {CP}^4\) calculations give \(c_2,c_3\). The nonspin sphere-bundle construction at \(m=-1\) gives \((1,-1,0)\) directly. Thus the discrepancy is not merely a comparison of two unmotivated tables.

The invariant homomorphism and the gluing comparison of Proposition 10.2 and Lemma 10.4 identify this class with the cyclic kernel generator. Within that framework, the answer is \(21\), not \(3\). At minimum the original lattice, its claimed simplification, and the theorem cannot all be correct; the explicit arithmetic and geometric column calculations locate the error in the simplification. The full external bordism-generation and modified-surgery theorems have not been reproved from first principles.

The corrected seven-primary condition from this lattice is \(\delta\equiv4l\pmod7\), equivalently \(d\equiv l\pmod7\), rather than \(d\equiv l\equiv0\pmod7\). The \(c_6\) coordinate is \(3(\delta-4l)\); when it vanishes modulo \(7\), all other relevant \(\mu/4\) coordinates vanish as well. A separate discrepancy in the \(\lambda(c_4)\) coefficient is a multiple of \(4\) and is harmless under the fixed \(\lambda\) relation. The quadric parameters \((d,l)=(2,0)\) give the same trivial kernel in both calculations. Repair requires correcting the transformation, the seven-primary statement, and its dependent applications; it does not require discarding every entry of the table.

Problem 2 (Major: Theorem 2.16 does not present the stated group).  The generator orders in Theorem 2.16, p. 10, repeated on p. 43, are incompatible with (8.1) and the paper’s quintic result. Changing only individual orders would still omit necessary joint relations.

For the quintic \(X_5\), the verified parameters are \((d,k,l)=(5,-25,-5)\), and (8.1) becomes the column lattice of \[C=\begin{pmatrix}
 -28&0&0&325&625&0\\
 0&12&0&140&275&-30\\
 0&0&2&-255&-500&50
 \end{pmatrix}.\] Its index is \(2\), with Hermite basis \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1&1\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). The character \((a,b,c)\mapsto a+b+c\pmod2\) kills every column and is nonzero on each coordinate vector. Each coordinate therefore represents the same nonzero element of \(\mathbb Z/2\).

The classes \(f_c,u,z\) are identified on p. 43 with these three coordinate vectors. Their orders are consequently \((2,2,2)\), whereas the printed formulas give \((7,6,1)\). This also contradicts Theorem 2.5, p. 4, which explicitly makes the disk-supported class nontrivial in the quintic’s \(\mathbb Z/2\) center. For an exact upper certificate, if \(e_i\) denotes the \(i\)th coordinate vector, then \[2e_1=C(91,-95,1035,4,2,-1)^t,\qquad
 2e_2=C(25,-24,265,6,-2,0)^t,\qquad 2e_3=c_3.\] These equalities and the parity character avoid reliance on numerical linear algebra.

The independent boundary example \(\mathbb {CP}^3\), with \((d,k,l)=(1,1,0)\), gives coordinate orders \((4,4,1)\) rather than \((7,12,1)\). The nonspin quadric gives a trivial kernel, whereas the nonspin order formula in Theorem 2.16 gives \(168\). For these genus-zero examples \(\mathcal J=\mathcal K\), so the contradiction cannot be attributed to an infinite quotient of \(\mathcal J\).

This is a defect in an explicit principal conclusion. Even substituting the correct quintic orders leaves a presentation with extra independent central generators: the actual relations include \(f_c=u=z\). A valid repair must recover the full relation lattice among the central generators and its interaction with the commutators, not just swap exponents or replace three orders. The abstract spin table agrees with the tested relation lattices; the incorrect presentation does not itself disprove that abstract table or the quintic description.

Problem 3 (Major: impossible relative dual classes in core calculations).  Section 7.3, pp. 36–37, and the proof of Proposition 8.1, pp. 39–40, use relative classes whose stated absolute images are incompatible with their intersection matrices. These steps feed the twist invariants and the surjectivity in Lemma 8.4 used to determine the kernel.

On p. 36 let \(e=[S_b^4]\) be the actual zero-section sphere and \(f=[Y]\). Their intersection form is \(Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\chi&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Page 37 simultaneously requires \(j^*\bar\alpha=x^2\) and \(D\bar\alpha=e\). These assertions imply \[\langle x^2,e\rangle=e\cdot e=\chi .\] But \(H^2(S^4;\mathbb Z)=0\), so the restriction of \(x\) to the zero-section vanishes and \(\langle x^2,e\rangle=0\). The permitted twist parameter \(\chi=1\), used for \(\epsilon\), is decisive. This contradiction is independent of the tangent-versus-normal sign convention.

There is useful repair evidence, but it is not a completed replacement of the geometry. In Section 7, if the Hopf evaluation is normalized by \(\langle x^2,Y\rangle=1\), the compatible dual is \(e-\chi f\). At the chosen framing \(A=0\), the stated normal class has dual \((2b-\chi)f\). Hence \[\bar\alpha^2=-\chi,\qquad
 \bar\alpha\bar\beta=2b-\chi,\qquad s_2/2=b-\chi .\] The last value is the negative of the printed one, but \(\rho\) still generates the cyclic order-\(12\) factor and \(\epsilon\) still has its order-\(2\) coordinate. The corresponding nonspin endpoint agrees with \(\mu/4=5b-4\chi\) on p. 52.

Two associated p. 37 inferences also require correction. Multiplication by the displayed matrix gives \(\bar\beta^2=A((2-A)\chi-4b)\), the opposite of the printed sign. Divisibility by \(8\) for all \(\chi,b\) forces \(A\) to be even, not \(A\equiv2\pmod4\): \(A=0\) is a direct counterexample to that inference. Evenness suffices for the stated reframing. For p. 40, the relative-image condition and the displayed radical force \(\alpha=0\) at the algebraic level. Moreover the spin characteristic property of \(p_1/2\) forces \(A\) even when \(Y^2=0\), so the proposed normalization \(A\in\{0,1\}\) would leave only \(A=0\). These observations suggest a shorter corrected calculation. They do not certify the required attaching maps, framing freedom, or normal extension. A new proof of these steps and propagation through Lemma 8.4 is needed. No additional counterexample to the final twist-generator theorem is asserted.
Problem 4 (Minor: the sphere-bundle invariant in (5.4)).  For the explicitly constructed \(N_m=S(\xi_m)\) on pp. 25–26, equation (5.4) omits \(8\) from \(s_1(N_m)\).

Here \(e(\xi_m)=x^2\), \(p_1(\xi_m)=(3+4m)x^2\), and \(p_1(T\mathbb {CP}^2)=3x^2\). Thus on the disk bundle \(p_1(\nu W)/2=-(2m+3)x^2\), and the Thom self-pairing is \(1\). The prescribed connected sum with \(\overline{\mathbb {HP}^2}\) makes the signature zero and subtracts \(1\) from the Pontryagin square. Therefore \[s_1(N_m)=(2m+3)^2-1=4m(m+3)+8,
 \quad s_2(N_m)=-2(m+1),\quad s_3(N_m)=-(2m+3).\] At \(m=0\), \(s_1=8\), rather than \(0\), in \(\mathbb Z/224\). The sign difference in \(s_3\) disappears modulo \(2\). The \(8\) difference is genuine for the unreduced invariant, but disappears modulo \(8\) after quotienting by homotopy spheres. Lemma 7.8 on p. 35 uses precisely that quotient. Thus this correction does not invalidate its reduced generation argument or, by itself, Theorem 7.9.
Problem 5 (Minor: the genus-zero nonsplitting boundary).  The residual nonsplitting clause of Theorem 4.6, p. 21, includes \(b_3(M)=0\), although the extension then splits.

The standing assumptions allow \(\mathbb {CP}^3\), for which \(H=0\). The Torelli group is the whole mapping class group, the variation target vanishes, and \(\mathcal K=\mathcal I=\operatorname{MCG}\). Both the kernel and quotient in (4.4) are trivial, so the extension splits. This needs no classification of \(\operatorname{MCG}(\mathbb {CP}^3)\). Include genus zero among the split cases and restrict the remaining nonsplitting cases to \(b_3\ge4\), as the proof’s actual case division does. Theorem 2.4 itself makes no contrary nonsplitting assertion at genus zero.

Problem 6 (Minor: missing genus-three integral torsion).  The table for \(E^2_{2,0}\) in Section 11.2, p. 55, incorrectly gives \(H_2(\operatorname{Sp}(2g,\mathbb Z);\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\) for every \(g\ge3\).

The directly cited primary [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 6.11 and the following table,
pp.~14--15]{BCRR}] gives \[H_2(\operatorname{Sp}(6,\mathbb Z);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z/2,
 \qquad H_2(\operatorname{Sp}(2g,\mathbb Z);\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\quad(g\ge4).\] The genus-three summand must be retained in an integral spectral sequence. The later naturality argument factors the differential through zero coinvariants, so it kills this torsion as well. Rational rank is unchanged. This local correction does not itself refute the asserted integral surjectivity or rational dimension.
# Unresolved scope and affirmative checks
## Corollary 2.10: Needs Evidence

Corollary 2.10, p. 7, states \(\dim H_2(B\operatorname{Diff}_0(M);\mathbb Q)\ge2\) without an additional restriction. Its proof on p. 57 uses dimensions \(2\) for \(H_2(B\operatorname{MCG};\mathbb Q)\) and \(4\) for \(H_2(B\operatorname{Diff};\mathbb Q)\). The former is established here only for \(b_3\ge6\). The cited [Retained latex: \cite[Section 5.3, pp.~19, 23--24]{GRW}] treats hypersurfaces \(V_d\subset\mathbb {CP}^4\) in degrees \[*\le (d^4-5d^3+10d^2-10d+4)/4=g(V_d)/2 .\] Its degree-two calculation supplies the needed input for these hypersurfaces with \(d\ge3\), not automatically for arbitrary standing \(M\) or low genus. Given the two input dimensions, the homology spectral sequence does yield the lower bound: the kernel in degree two is a quotient of fiber coinvariants. The issue is the scope of the inputs. An extension of the cited result or an additional argument is needed. No counterexample to the unrestricted corollary is asserted.
## Checks that constrain the conclusions

The exact sequence \(0\to H\to L_{d,k}\to H/d\to0\) and the injective doubling map \([a,b]\mapsto[a,2b]\) were checked directly, including possible torsion in \(L_{d,k}\). The quintic section \(v\mapsto[v,-5v]\) is well defined. The right-cocycle convention for the quadratic refinement was verified algebraically and by exact finite-field checks; this does not replace the external integral extension-class theorem.

The image-parity step has a direct supporting argument. For an oriented closed seven-manifold, instability gives \(v_4=0\), hence \(w_4=w_2^2\). For a spin mapping torus, \(q_1=p_1/2\) is therefore even; in the nonspin case the same holds for the spin bundle \(TM_f\oplus\eta\). The Wang sequence then makes the second variation even for every Torelli element. An alleged image gap is consequently not retained.

The intermediate center calculation on p. 57 omits \(d=1\), where \((H/d)\rtimes\operatorname{Sp}\) is \(\operatorname{Sp}\) and has central \(-I\). The paper’s next argument repairs this case: a lift of \(-I\) has commutator \(-2b\) with \(b\) in the free \(H\) kernel and cannot be central. The final center assertion is not disproved by this omission. The standard-module statements used here were checked in [Retained latex: \cite[Appendix A, pp.~32--34]{Krannich}].

The total-degree-seven terms of the untwisted bordism spectral sequence give the stated upper bound \(24\). In the twisted sequence, the apparent objection from \(Sq^2b+xb=xb\) is invalid: \(xb=Sq^1(xa)\) is a Bockstein class and annihilates reduction of integral \(H_8\). The integral-row reduction in the differential matters; the relevant primary rule was checked in [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~750--751]{Teichner}]. No counterexample to the appendix’s splitting was established.
# Conclusion

The nonspin kernel calculation and the presentation theorem require substantive correction. The explicit dual-class calculations also require replacement before their dependent geometric arguments can be accepted as written. Several broader constructions survive the particular tests reported here; this report does not infer wholesale failure from local errors.

 c_4&=(d^2,-d(h-1),(h-1)^2-1),\\
 c_5&=(2d^2,-2dh,2h^2),&
 c_6&=(-2d,3d+24l,-4h).
\end{aligned}\] For this \(M\), the last three columns are \[(36,114,360),\quad (72,216,648),\quad (-12,-6,72).\] The geometric generator \(N_{-1}\) in Section 10.4 has original characteristic vector \(v=(1,-1,0)\): its \((\mu/4,\lambda)\) coordinates are \((-1,-2)\), as on p. 51. Its order modulo the original column lattice is exactly \(21\). Indeed, \[
 21v=9c_3-c_6.\] Every column has second coordinate divisible by \(3\), whereas \(v_2=-1\). Also the functional \[\phi(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3)=2\sigma_1+\sigma_2+\sigma_3\pmod7\] annihilates every column and satisfies \(\phi(v)=1\). Hence the order is divisible by both \(3\) and \(7\), and [eq:21] (#eq:21) gives the matching upper bound. Exact determinant computations independently give indices \(336\) and \(16\) before and after adjoining \(v\).

The source of the discrepancy is directly visible. Applying the printed definition \(\mu=6\sigma_1+10\sigma_2+3\sigma_3\) to \(c_5\) gives \[\frac{\mu(c_5)}4=-2(\delta^2+48\delta l-432l^2).\] The transformed table on p. 51 instead has \(-2(\delta^2+96\delta l-864l^2)\). At \((\delta,l)=(3,-1)\) these values are \(1134\) and \(2286\), respectively. The latter incorrectly kills the seven-primary class. Theorem 6.1 assigns \(a=0,b=1,c=0\), hence \(\mathcal K(M)\cong\mathbb Z/3\).

The original columns were checked from \(\alpha=x^2-dy\) and \(\beta=(p_1(\nu W)-x^2)/2+hy\). For example, on \(\mathbb {CP}^2\times S^4\), \(\beta=-2x^2+hy\), giving \((-2d,3d+24l,-4h)\). On \(S^4\times S^4\), \(x=0\), \(y=a+b\), and \(\langle y^2,[W]\rangle=2\), giving \(c_5\). On \(\mathbb {HP}^2\) with its positive generator \(y\), \(\beta=(h-1)y\); subtracting the constant-map \(\mathbb {HP}^2\) gives \(c_4\). The \(\mathbb {CP}^2\times\mathbb {CP}^2\) and \(\mathbb {CP}^4\) calculations give \(c_2,c_3\). The nonspin sphere-bundle construction at \(m=-1\) gives \((1,-1,0)\) directly. Thus the discrepancy is not merely a comparison of two unmotivated tables.

The invariant homomorphism and the gluing comparison of Proposition 10.2 and Lemma 10.4 identify this class with the cyclic kernel generator. Within that framework, the answer is \(21\), not \(3\). At minimum the original lattice, its claimed simplification, and the theorem cannot all be correct; the explicit arithmetic and geometric column calculations locate the error in the simplification. The full external bordism-generation and modified-surgery theorems have not been reproved from first principles.

The corrected seven-primary condition from this lattice is \(\delta\equiv4l\pmod7\), equivalently \(d\equiv l\pmod7\), rather than \(d\equiv l\equiv0\pmod7\). The \(c_6\) coordinate is \(3(\delta-4l)\); when it vanishes modulo \(7\), all other relevant \(\mu/4\) coordinates vanish as well. A separate discrepancy in the \(\lambda(c_4)\) coefficient is a multiple of \(4\) and is harmless under the fixed \(\lambda\) relation. The quadric parameters \((d,l)=(2,0)\) give the same trivial kernel in both calculations. Repair requires correcting the transformation, the seven-primary statement, and its dependent applications; it does not require discarding every entry of the table.

analysis: The generator orders in Theorem 2.16, p. 10, repeated on p. 43, are incompatible with (8.1) and the paper’s quintic result. Changing only individual orders would still omit necessary joint relations.

For the quintic \(X_5\), the verified parameters are \((d,k,l)=(5,-25,-5)\), and (8.1) becomes the column lattice of \[C=\begin{pmatrix}
 -28&0&0&325&625&0\\
 0&12&0&140&275&-30\\
 0&0&2&-255&-500&50
 \end{pmatrix}.\] Its index is \(2\), with Hermite basis \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1&1\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). The character \((a,b,c)\mapsto a+b+c\pmod2\) kills every column and is nonzero on each coordinate vector. Each coordinate therefore represents the same nonzero element of \(\mathbb Z/2\).

The classes \(f_c,u,z\) are identified on p. 43 with these three coordinate vectors. Their orders are consequently \((2,2,2)\), whereas the printed formulas give \((7,6,1)\). This also contradicts Theorem 2.5, p. 4, which explicitly makes the disk-supported class nontrivial in the quintic’s \(\mathbb Z/2\) center. For an exact upper certificate, if \(e_i\) denotes the \(i\)th coordinate vector, then \[2e_1=C(91,-95,1035,4,2,-1)^t,\qquad
 2e_2=C(25,-24,265,6,-2,0)^t,\qquad 2e_3=c_3.\] These equalities and the parity character avoid reliance on numerical linear algebra.

The independent boundary example \(\mathbb {CP}^3\), with \((d,k,l)=(1,1,0)\), gives coordinate orders \((4,4,1)\) rather than \((7,12,1)\). The nonspin quadric gives a trivial kernel, whereas the nonspin order formula in Theorem 2.16 gives \(168\). For these genus-zero examples \(\mathcal J=\mathcal K\), so the contradiction cannot be attributed to an infinite quotient of \(\mathcal J\).

This is a defect in an explicit principal conclusion. Even substituting the correct quintic orders leaves a presentation with extra independent central generators: the actual relations include \(f_c=u=z\). A valid repair must recover the full relation lattice among the central generators and its interaction with the commutators, not just swap exponents or replace three orders. The abstract spin table agrees with the tested relation lattices; the incorrect presentation does not itself disprove that abstract table or the quintic description.

analysis: Section 7.3, pp. 36–37, and the proof of Proposition 8.1, pp. 39–40, use relative classes whose stated absolute images are incompatible with their intersection matrices. These steps feed the twist invariants and the surjectivity in Lemma 8.4 used to determine the kernel.

On p. 36 let \(e=[S_b^4]\) be the actual zero-section sphere and \(f=[Y]\). Their intersection form is \(Q=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\chi&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Page 37 simultaneously requires \(j^*\bar\alpha=x^2\) and \(D\bar\alpha=e\). These assertions imply \[\langle x^2,e\rangle=e\cdot e=\chi .\] But \(H^2(S^4;\mathbb Z)=0\), so the restriction of \(x\) to the zero-section vanishes and \(\langle x^2,e\rangle=0\). The permitted twist parameter \(\chi=1\), used for \(\epsilon\), is decisive. This contradiction is independent of the tangent-versus-normal sign convention.

There is useful repair evidence, but it is not a completed replacement of the geometry. In Section 7, if the Hopf evaluation is normalized by \(\langle x^2,Y\rangle=1\), the compatible dual is \(e-\chi f\). At the chosen framing \(A=0\), the stated normal class has dual \((2b-\chi)f\). Hence \[\bar\alpha^2=-\chi,\qquad
 \bar\alpha\bar\beta=2b-\chi,\qquad s_2/2=b-\chi .\] The last value is the negative of the printed one, but \(\rho\) still generates the cyclic order-\(12\) factor and \(\epsilon\) still has its order-\(2\) coordinate. The corresponding nonspin endpoint agrees with \(\mu/4=5b-4\chi\) on p. 52.

Two associated p. 37 inferences also require correction. Multiplication by the displayed matrix gives \(\bar\beta^2=A((2-A)\chi-4b)\), the opposite of the printed sign. Divisibility by \(8\) for all \(\chi,b\) forces \(A\) to be even, not \(A\equiv2\pmod4\): \(A=0\) is a direct counterexample to that inference. Evenness suffices for the stated reframing. For p. 40, the relative-image condition and the displayed radical force \(\alpha=0\) at the algebraic level. Moreover the spin characteristic property of \(p_1/2\) forces \(A\) even when \(Y^2=0\), so the proposed normalization \(A\in\{0,1\}\) would leave only \(A=0\). report: Abstract: The explicit formula in Theorem 3.26 does not have the nonnegative integral coefficients required of the stated counting function. Title: Technical Verification of
Exact Enumeration of Fullerenes
# Paper identity, conventions, and review boundary

This report concerns only M25-0150: Philip Engel and Peter Smillie, Exact enumeration of fullerenes, with an appendix by Jan Goedgebeur, Duke Mathematical Journal 174(3) (2025), 575–613, DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0037 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0037). The controlling input is the 39-page journal-typeset PDF deposited at NSF PAR, record 10642973. Journal page \(p\) is PDF page \(p-574\). The separately acquired arXiv:2304.01655v3 PDF and its TeX source were used for version comparison. The findings below are confined to these hash-pinned inputs, not to an unexamined later correction.

All 39 journal pages were read in extracted text. Relevant formula, proof, table, and dependency pages were also inspected as rendered images. The complete 14-file input manifest was parsed and its byte lengths and SHA256 hashes checked. Native session auxiliaries performed bounded geometry, enumeration, and modular-form checks; their actual roles and separate records are preserved. They were not independent human referees or independently verified model instances.

The paper counts oriented fullerenes with \(2n\) vertices: mirror images are distinct unless related by an orientation-preserving equivalence. Euler’s formula gives twelve pentagons and \(n-10\) hexagons, hence \(\mathrm{BB}_n=0\) for \(n<10\). In the dual triangulation \(q^n\) records \(2n\) triangles. We use the paper’s normalization \[E_2(q)=-\frac1{24}+\sum_{n\ge1}\sigma_1(n)q^n,\qquad
 E(q)=\frac16+\sum_{n\ge1}\left(\sum_{d\mid n}\chi_3(d)\right)q^n,\] where \(\chi_3(1)=1,\ \chi_3(2)=-1,\ \chi_3(0)=0\). For higher Eisenstein series, the divisor sums and generalized Bernoulli constants were checked against Definition 3.25 and the primary normalization reference [Retained latex: \cite[Section 5]{Stein}]. Positive-degree counterexamples below do not depend on a choice of additive constant.
# Problems with decisive evidence
Problem 1 (Major: the main explicit generating series).  Location. Theorem 3.26, journal pp. 605–606 (PDF pp. 31–32); arXiv v3 PDF p. 25; pinned TeX lines 1672, 1689–1690.

Evidence. The denominator of the \(E_4(q^3)\) term is typeset with only the first digit of \(11\) in the exponent of \(2\). The source is literally `2^11`, rather than `2^{11}`. Read literally, its denominator is \(2\cdot1\cdot3^9\cdot5\), and the displayed series has \[[q^3]\mathrm{BB}_{\rm literal}(q)=-\frac{911198717}{67184640}.\] The source’s commented coefficient vector instead gives denominator \(201553920=2^{11}3^9 5\), supporting restoration of the missing braces.

Equation reference: eq:bad. Even after making this favorable restoration, the formula still fails. Let \(F\) denote that exponent-restored series, with all other printed coefficients unchanged, and put \[R=F-\frac1{64}E_2(q^9)-\frac2{27}E_2(q^{12}).\] Exact rational arithmetic applied to the other 43 terms gives \[[q^9]R=-\frac1{18},\qquad [q^{12}]R=\frac{47}{48}.\] Consequently, \[
 [q^9]F=-\frac1{18}+\frac1{64}=-\frac{23}{576},
 \qquad
 [q^{12}]F=\frac{47}{48}+\frac2{27}=\frac{455}{432}.\] The first violates the elementary vanishing condition \(n<10\); the second is not an integer. These are decisive failures of the stated theorem, irrespective of the correctness of the appendix’s numerical counts. Two separately written reviewer calculations, based on independent transcriptions, agree. The full per-term sums are retained.

Repair and its boundary. In addition to restoring \(2^{11}\), replace \[\frac1{64}E_2(q^9)+\frac2{27}E_2(q^{12})
 \quad\text{by}\quad
 \frac1{18}E_2(q^9)+\frac1{48}E_2(q^{12}).\] The resulting series \(F^\ast\) agrees exactly with all 201 supplied table entries \(0\le n\le200\), including its zero constant term. Before these two changes, the exponent-restored formula differs at 34 of these indices. This comparison uses the published table; it is not a fresh generation of all fullerene graphs.

The difference is \[F^\ast-F=\frac{23}{1728}\bigl(3E_2(q^9)-4E_2(q^{12})\bigr).\] The parenthesis equals one third of \[\bigl(E_2(q)-12E_2(q^{12})\bigr)
 -\bigl(E_2(q)-9E_2(q^9)\bigr),\] so it is a weight-two modular form on \(\Gamma_0(36)\), contained in the claimed ambient space \(\Omega\). Section 4 (#sec:positive) independently verifies coefficient injectivity on \(\Omega\). Thus, conditional on the inclusion \(\mathrm{BB}\in\Omega\) and the accuracy of the supplied initial counts, the repaired candidate is the unique generating series in that space with those counts. No author adoption of these corrections is claimed.

Counterevidence limiting the impact. The embedded commented Sage appendix contains coefficient vectors compatible with the proposed changes; its original Sage basis ordering was not regenerated. The correction is supported only at indices divisible by \(9\) or \(12\), apart from the constant. Example 3.27’s restricted polynomial and Example 3.28’s count \[\mathrm{BB}_{5000}=1203397779055806181762759\] survive the two weight-two changes. Their survival does not repair the formula for general \(n\). The severity is Major because an explicit principal theorem gives impossible counts, even though a short correction appears sufficient.
Problem 2 (Minor: exponent of the discriminant group is not the Weil level).  Location. Proposition 3.9 and its explanation, journal p. 598 (PDF p. 24).

The counterexample invalidates the unrestricted formulation, not the needed levels for the actual Eisenstein lattices. Independent Gram-matrix calculations give quadratic levels \(3,2,3,1\) for \(A_2,D_4,E_6,E_8\). Taking negatives and isotropic subquotients does not enlarge their least-common-multiple level. Keeping the quadratic forms in the complement and saturation argument therefore supports the levels \(1,2,3,6\) used in Theorems 3.13 and 3.16. Replace the general hypothesis and make this application explicit; enlarging every asserted level merely because the discriminant group was misdescribed is not warranted.

There is a related, readily repairable hypothesis mismatch in Proposition 3.18 (p. 602) and its use in Theorem 3.20 (p. 603): the former assumes \(d\mid N\), although some applications take \(d=|G|\) without that divisibility. The same argument works for every positive integer \(d\). If \(h\) is modular for \(\Gamma(N)\) and has a \(q^{1/d}\)-expansion, then it is invariant under \(T^d\). For \[M=\begin{pmatrix}1+aN&bd\\cN&1+eN\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det M=1,\] one has \(M=T^{bd}K\) with \(K\in\Gamma(N)\). Conjugation by \(\operatorname{diag}(d,1)\) yields \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1+aN&b\\cdN&1+eN\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\Gamma(N,d)\). Problem 3 (Minor: the stratum description needs action and collision data).  Location. Proposition 2.14 and the criterion after Definition 2.15, p. 585; Proposition 2.19, pp. 587–588. Relevant corrective evidence occurs in Table 2, pp. 590–593, and Example 3.30, pp. 607–608.

Conjugacy of inertia is finer than the abstract automorphism group together with the upstairs curvature multiset. Consider \(G=C_2\) and upstairs profile \((2,2,1^8)\). Table 2 distinguishes quotient profiles \[(3^e,3^e;2,1,1,1,1),\qquad (4,4;1,1,1,1),\] of dimensions four and three. Generic cone configurations invariant under \(z\mapsto-z\) realize the first with curvature-two points at \(\pm1\), and the second with curvature-two points at \(0,\infty\); the eight remaining curvature-one points form four generic pairs. Both have full automorphism group \(C_2\). In the first case the involution exchanges the two \(C_3\) collision factors, producing nonabelian inertia. In the second it fixes the collision lines and centralizes their order-three reflections; the central kernel has cyclic quotient, hence the inertia is abelian. The two inertia types cannot be conjugate. The action on collision data, not just a jump in group order, matters.

The numerical criterion for a nonempty exact bistratum also needs exclusion of forced extra symmetry. For \(G=C_1\) and profile \((4,4,4)\), the three equal cone angles give the doubled equilateral triangle with full \(D_3\) symmetry. The later table explicitly marks the repetition. Finally, Proposition 2.19’s bijection with unmarked completed triangulations is too coarse: Example 3.30 exhibits two collision branches of the same \((5,5,2)\) triangulation, according as the original curvature-two point remains separate or joins a curvature-five cluster. Thurston’s completion retains such partitions [Thurston, p. 528].

These distinctions should be included in the statement: use the ramification action and the normalization with marked collision data, then sum inverse stabilizer orders over its finite fibres. The quotient by \(N_H(G)/G\) handles residual automorphisms of an actual \(G\)-quotient. The paper’s detailed table and worked example already retain the needed refinements, and the resulting conversion remains rational and triangular with the appropriate exact-stratum diagonal. No counterexample to that refined inversion has been established. A complete \(96\times96\) transition matrix was not independently computed.
Problem 4 (Minor: the exponent unit in a zero-dimensional stratum).  Location. Example 2.22, p. 589 (PDF p. 15), compared with Definition 2.21 and p. 604.

The parameter \(r\) in \(E(q^r)\) must be half the minimum number of triangles, since \(q^n\) records \(2n\) triangles. The doubled equilateral triangle has two triangles and gives \(E(q)\), not \(E(q^2)\). Likewise the icosahedral quotient has \(20/60=1/3\) triangle, hence \(r=1/6\); pullback gives \(E(q^{10})\), as required. # Analytic evidence still needed

Problem 7 (Needs Evidence: regularization at a noncompact weight-two cusp).  Location. Definition 3.7 and the sketch of Theorem 3.8, p. 597 (PDF p. 23). The definition gives an ordinary theta integral also for signature \((1,1)\); the sketch calls its noncompact case conditionally convergent.

There is a direct obstruction to that literal convergence assertion. Put \(\mathcal O=\mathbb Z[\zeta_6]\), \(\alpha=1+\zeta_6\), and take the Hermitian lattice \[\Lambda=\mathcal Oe+\mathcal Of,\qquad
 \star=\begin{pmatrix}0&\alpha\\\overline\alpha&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Its underlying form \((2/3)\operatorname{Re}\star\) is even, unimodular, and of signature \((2,2)\): in the indicated Eisenstein basis the off-diagonal integral block is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). It has an isotropic sublattice \(\mathcal Oe\). At \(\tau=iy\), all terms of the theta kernel are positive. At cusp height \(H\), the terms indexed by \(\beta e\) have the form \[\exp(-Cy|\beta|^2/H),\qquad C>0.\] There are at least \(cH\) Eisenstein integers with \(|\beta|\le\sqrt H\), so the kernel is bounded below by \(c_yH\). Integration over a cusp strip with invariant measure proportional to \(dx\,dH/H^2\) therefore dominates \[c'_y\int_{H_0}^{\infty}\frac{dH}{H}=\infty.\] A positive divergent integral is not conditionally convergent. This boundary occurs in the paper’s \((5,5,1,1)\) profile: its \(E_8\oplus E_8\) root complement in \(\mathrm{II}_{2,18}\) leaves \(\mathrm{II}_{2,2}\).

The cited earlier construction explicitly assumes \(s>1\) in [Retained latex: \cite[Definition 4.4, p.~13]{ES}]. Its isotropic sum in Lemma 4.10 is proportional to \(\sum_{\beta\ne0}|\beta|^{-2s}\), which diverges at \(s=1\). Thus that reference does not directly supply the missing ordinary integral.

Required evidence and limit. Specify a truncation or regularized lift, its subtraction convention, and the derivative or holomorphic-part operation; justify both the transformed weight-two completion and the stated positive Fourier coefficients. The leading divergent term after the \(y\)-prefactor can be independent of \(\tau\), so differentiation may remove it in a correctly defined construction. The paper itself recognizes the exceptional case and a nonholomorphic correction. No counterexample to the resulting quasimodularity is asserted here. The demonstrated defect is in the unregularized route; the status of the required regularized argument is Needs Evidence.
# Affirmative checks and core dependencies
## Independent dimension and coefficient injectivity

Propositions 3.22–3.23 were checked beyond repeating their software claim. Let \(\chi_3\) be as above. The nine modular summands of \(\Omega\), after identifying the \(-I\) cosets of the paper’s groups, have the following descriptions: \[\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
\text{weight}&10&9&8&7&6&5&4&3&2\\ \hline
\text{level}&1&3&6&6&12&12&72&72&72\\
\text{character}&1&\chi_3&1&\chi_3&1&\chi_3&1&\chi_3&1\\
\text{dimension}&1&4&9&8&13&11&44&32&20
\end{array}\] The level row denotes \(\Gamma_0(N)\) with the displayed character. The dimensions sum to 142. The two additional \(E_2\) series, seven dilates \(E(q^t)\), \(t\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6,10\}\), and a constant give an upper bound of 152.

For \(N=6,12,72\), the torsion-free modular curves have respectively \[(\mu,c,g)=(12,4,0),\ (24,6,0),\ (144,16,5).\] The character is trivial on the primitive cusp parabolics. The weight-one character line bundle \(L\) has \(L^2=K(D_{\rm cusp})\), hence degrees \(1,2,12\). In all weights used here, Riemann–Roch gives \(\dim H^0(L^k)=k\deg L+1-g\). At level three, the weight-three character bundle has trivial elliptic stabilizer and degree one on a genus-zero curve, so its cube has four sections. The weight-ten level-one dimension is one by the valence bound. These are explicit upper bounds independent of a software dimension command.

For lower bounds and injectivity, reviewer code constructed integral Fourier series \[\Theta_t=1+6\sum_{n\ge1}\sum_{a\mid n}\chi_3(a)q^{tn},
 \qquad
 B=\sum_{n\ge1}\sum_{a\mid n}\chi_3(n/a)a^2q^n.\] Here \(\Theta_t\) is a dilated \(A_2\) theta series of weight one and \(B\) a weight-three level-three Eisenstein series. Adjoining the ten extra series gives a \(200\times152\) coefficient matrix for \(q^0,\ldots,q^{199}\).

A separately written root-executor row elimination checked this saved minor directly. The largest selected coefficient index is 168. This establishes both dimension 152 and injectivity at the stated precision without using the printed answer or fullerene counts. The appendix’s \(q^{200}\) value is an additional check, not an off-by-one failure.
## Geometry, normalization, and finite computations

The bounded quotient-data enumeration produces 116 covering-group labels; removing the 20 repetitions explicitly identified in the table leaves 96. Every label passes the upstairs total-curvature-twelve condition. This checks the finite catalogue arithmetic under its stated classification; it does not construct every stratum or a complete transition matrix.

The period-integrality argument, the face and edge period superlattices, the cyclic-to-dihedral enlargement for orders four through six, and the reciprocal-stabilizer interpretation were examined. The positive-vector orbital integral in [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 4.8, pp.~14--15]{ES}] gives the stated inverse-stabilizer coefficient after differentiation. Independent rational arithmetic verified the formula witnesses, constant cancellation after repair, the actual root-lattice levels, and the worked mass example. A separate enumeration auxiliary compared all 201 table entries. Explicit 20- and 24-vertex examples and their preserving/reversing automorphism counts were checked by reviewer code; these establish examples and the orientation convention, not classification of all graphs. problems.title: Theorem 3.26 gives impossible fullerene counts
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: Problem 1 (Major: the main explicit generating series). Location. Theorem 3.26, journal pp. 605–606 (PDF pp. 31–32); arXiv v3 PDF p. 25; pinned TeX lines 1672, 1689–1690.
claim: Recorded check: Theorem 3.26 gives impossible fullerene counts
analysis: Location. Theorem 3.26, journal pp. 605–606 (PDF pp. 31–32); arXiv v3 PDF p. 25; pinned TeX lines 1672, 1689–1690.

Evidence. The denominator of the \(E_4(q^3)\) term is typeset with only the first digit of \(11\) in the exponent of \(2\). The source is literally `2^11`, rather than `2^{11}`. Read literally, its denominator is \(2\cdot1\cdot3^9\cdot5\), and the displayed series has \[[q^3]\mathrm{BB}_{\rm literal}(q)=-\frac{911198717}{67184640}.\] The source’s commented coefficient vector instead gives denominator \(201553920=2^{11}3^9 5\), supporting restoration of the missing braces.

Equation reference: eq:bad. Even after making this favorable restoration, the formula still fails. Let \(F\) denote that exponent-restored series, with all other printed coefficients unchanged, and put \[R=F-\frac1{64}E_2(q^9)-\frac2{27}E_2(q^{12}).\] Exact rational arithmetic applied to the other 43 terms gives \[[q^9]R=-\frac1{18},\qquad [q^{12}]R=\frac{47}{48}.\] Consequently, \[
 [q^9]F=-\frac1{18}+\frac1{64}=-\frac{23}{576},
 \qquad
 [q^{12}]F=\frac{47}{48}+\frac2{27}=\frac{455}{432}.\] The first violates the elementary vanishing condition \(n<10\); the second is not an integer. These are decisive failures of the stated theorem, irrespective of the correctness of the appendix’s numerical counts. Two separately written reviewer calculations, based on independent transcriptions, agree. The full per-term sums are retained.

Repair and its boundary. In addition to restoring \(2^{11}\), replace \[\frac1{64}E_2(q^9)+\frac2{27}E_2(q^{12})
 \quad\text{by}\quad
 \frac1{18}E_2(q^9)+\frac1{48}E_2(q^{12}).\] The resulting series \(F^\ast\) agrees exactly with all 201 supplied table entries \(0\le n\le200\), including its zero constant term. Before these two changes, the exponent-restored formula differs at 34 of these indices. This comparison uses the published table; it is not a fresh generation of all fullerene graphs.

The difference is \[F^\ast-F=\frac{23}{1728}\bigl(3E_2(q^9)-4E_2(q^{12})\bigr).\] The parenthesis equals one third of \[\bigl(E_2(q)-12E_2(q^{12})\bigr)
 -\bigl(E_2(q)-9E_2(q^9)\bigr),\] so it is a weight-two modular form on \(\Gamma_0(36)\), contained in the claimed ambient space \(\Omega\). Section 4 (#sec:positive) independently verifies coefficient injectivity on \(\Omega\). Thus, conditional on the inclusion \(\mathrm{BB}\in\Omega\) and the accuracy of the supplied initial counts, the repaired candidate is the unique generating series in that space with those counts. No author adoption of these corrections is claimed.

Counterevidence limiting the impact. The embedded commented Sage appendix contains coefficient vectors compatible with the proposed changes; its original Sage basis ordering was not regenerated. The correction is supported only at indices divisible by \(9\) or \(12\), apart from the constant. Example 3.27’s restricted polynomial and Example 3.28’s count \[\mathrm{BB}_{5000}=1203397779055806181762759\] survive the two weight-two changes. Their survival does not repair the formula for general \(n\). The severity is Major because an explicit principal theorem gives impossible counts, even though a short correction appears sufficient.
result: Impact: The principal explicit theorem fails both elementary vanishing and integrality. Major does not require the entire theory to be false or irreparable.

problems.title: Quadratic discriminant level and the dilation quantifier
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (Minor: exponent of the discriminant group is not the Weil level). Location. Proposition 3.9 and its explanation, journal p. 598 (PDF p. 24).
claim: Recorded check: Quadratic discriminant level and the dilation quantifier
analysis: Location. Proposition 3.9 and its explanation, journal p. 598 (PDF p. 24).

The counterexample invalidates the unrestricted formulation, not the needed levels for the actual Eisenstein lattices. Independent Gram-matrix calculations give quadratic levels \(3,2,3,1\) for \(A_2,D_4,E_6,E_8\). Taking negatives and isotropic subquotients does not enlarge their least-common-multiple level. Keeping the quadratic forms in the complement and saturation argument therefore supports the levels \(1,2,3,6\) used in Theorems 3.13 and 3.16. Replace the general hypothesis and make this application explicit; enlarging every asserted level merely because the discriminant group was misdescribed is not warranted.

There is a related, readily repairable hypothesis mismatch in Proposition 3.18 (p. 602) and its use in Theorem 3.20 (p. 603): the former assumes \(d\mid N\), although some applications take \(d=|G|\) without that divisibility. The same argument works for every positive integer \(d\). If \(h\) is modular for \(\Gamma(N)\) and has a \(q^{1/d}\)-expansion, then it is invariant under \(T^d\). For \[M=\begin{pmatrix}1+aN&bd\\cN&1+eN\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det M=1,\] one has \(M=T^{bd}K\) with \(K\in\Gamma(N)\). Conjugation by \(\operatorname{diag}(d,1)\) yields \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1+aN&b\\cdN&1+eN\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\Gamma(N,d)\). Removing the unnecessary divisibility assumption repairs this invocation; it gives no counterexample to the final level bound.
result: Impact: General Proposition3.9 is false as stated; Proposition3.18 has a removable hypothesis restriction. Actual application-level conclusions are not refuted.

report: Abstract: This claim-focused review identifies an invalid minimum-distance inference in the proof of the main transport–Stokes limit, an explicit counterexample to the stated unrestricted parameter range of the two general-kernel mean-field theorems, and local errors in two Stokes-field formulas. The first finding is a core proof gap, not a counterexample to the physical limit theorem. The second does not apply to the Oseen kernel. All conclusions concern the acquired arXiv version 5; correspondence with the journal version has not been established. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical verification of
Sedimentation of particles with very small inertia I
# Identity, version, and checked scope

The reviewed work is Richard M. Höfer and Richard Schubert, Sedimentation of particles with very small inertia I: Convergence to the transport-Stokes equation, associated with Duke Mathematical Journal DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0038 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0038). The actual input is arXiv:2302.04637v5, submitted 9 January 2025, whose title page is dated 10 January 2025. It has 59 PDF pages. Throughout this report, page numbers are one-based physical PDF pages, which coincide with the printed numbering.

The review traced Theorem 1.1 through the energy estimate, resistance estimates, separation estimate, and bootstrap; examined the assumptions and finite-\(p\) estimates of Section 2; checked Sections 4–5 and the binary and rotational adaptations in Appendices B–C. These are analytical and static-source checks. External results about Stokes well-posedness, solenoidal extension, and convergence of reflections were not reproved from first principles. No author code, particle simulation, or empirical reproduction was run. Detailed coverage and independently written checks accompany this report.

The repository page still identifies v5 as its latest version in the check performed for this review. Its note calls v4 an accepted version and describes v5 as correcting an abstract typo. No paper-specific erratum was located in the bounded repository/author-record search. These observations do not establish identity with the unacquired publisher PDF or absence of other corrections.
# The mathematical setting and positive checks

The physical theorem assumes \(\gamma_N=NR\) bounded above and below, \(q>3\), convergence of the initial empirical measure in \(\mathcal W_2\) coupled to the minimum distance as in (H2), the initial relative-velocity condition \[|V_i^0-V_j^0|\le 3\pi\gamma_N\lambda_N |X_i^0-X_j^0|,\] and the energy/maximum-velocity bound (H4). In particular (H2) forces \(\lambda_N\to\infty\). The continuum comparison uses \(\gamma_N\), rather than a fixed limiting value, so omission of a separate \(\gamma_N-\gamma_\ast\) error is intentional.

With the unnormalized Euclidean norm, \(|\bar g|=\sqrt N\), the equilibrium velocity is \(\widetilde V=\mathcal R^{-1}\bar g/N\). For \(E=|V-\widetilde V|^2/(2N)\), direct differentiation gives the dissipative coefficient \(\lambda_N N c_{\mathcal R}\). Under the bootstrap estimates \(c_{\mathcal R}\gtrsim N^{-1}\) and \(\|\nabla\mathcal R^{-1}\bar g\|\lesssim N\), Proposition 3.1 yields a normalized velocity error of order \[N^{-1/2}|V-\widetilde V|(0)e^{-c\lambda_Nt}
       +\min\{t,\lambda_N^{-1}\}.\] Its time integral has the order used in (3.37)–(3.41). The extra square on a gradient norm in one intermediate display of the proof is not needed: integrating the preceding differential inequality gives the stated linear dependence directly. It is not treated as an additional substantive problem.

The variational resistance scaling \(c_{\mathcal R}\gtrsim R/(1+RS_1)\), \(C_{\mathcal R}\lesssim R\), and the powers in the force-average errors are consistent after the local field corrections below. The finite-\(p\) interpolation exponents in Lemma 2.4 were checked on their stated domain \(0<\beta<d\), \(q>d/(d-\beta)\). These checks do not remove the separation gap.
# Findings
Problem 1 (The minimum-distance bootstrap uses an invalid lower-bound inference).
## Source claim and exact dependence

Equation reference: eq:lower. Lemma 3.4, (3.18), p. 26, claims \[
 d_{\min}(t)\ge \tfrac12d_{\min}(0)
 -C\int_0^t d_{\min}(s)A(s)\,ds,
 \quad A=|F|_\infty S_2+R^3S_2S_6^{1/2}|F|_2.\] Its proof ends on p. 44 after (5.16). On p. 29, Step 3 substitutes the force bounds into [eq:lower] (#eq:lower) and invokes Gronwall to infer (3.44), an \(N\)-uniform exponential lower bound. Step 4, p. 30, explicitly uses (3.44) in (3.45)–(3.46) to close the bootstrap for every fixed time interval. This is a direct dependency of the proof of Theorem 1.1, including its separation conclusion (1.11).
## Complete check of the suspect steps

Equation reference: eq:pair. For a fixed pair, Duhamel’s formula and (5.7) give \[
 d_{ij}(t)\ge \tfrac12d_{ij}(0)
       -C\int_0^t d_{ij}(s)A(s)\,ds.\] Choosing a pair that minimizes distance at the final time does not justify replacing its historical distances \(d_{ij}(s)\) by \(d_{\min}(s)\). Since the integral is subtracted, that replacement raises the lower bound. A pair minimizing at time \(t\) need not minimize earlier. The displayed proof supplies no further comparison that establishes this step.

Even accepting [eq:lower] (#eq:lower), a lower integral inequality with a negative integral is not the usual lower differential Gronwall inequality. A complete scalar counterexample has precisely the factor one-half in [eq:lower] (#eq:lower). Set \[y(t)=2-t^2,\quad b(t)=1,\quad a=\tfrac12y(0)=1,
 \qquad 0\le t\le 7/5.\] The function \(y\) is smooth, positive, and nonincreasing. The margin in \(y(t)\ge a-\int_0^t b(s)y(s)\,ds\) equals \[g(t)=1+2t-t^2-t^3/3.\] Since \(g''(t)=-2-2t<0\), its minimum on the interval occurs at an endpoint; the endpoint values are \(1\) and \(347/375>0\). Nevertheless \[y(7/5)=1/25<e^{-7/5}=0.2465969639\ldots .\] More generally \(y_\varepsilon(t)=2-(2-\varepsilon)t^2\), \(0<\varepsilon<1\), on \([0,1]\) satisfies the same integral premise with the same initial value and \(b=1\), while \(y_\varepsilon(1)=\varepsilon\). The integral premise therefore supplies no uniform positive terminal lower bound, even allowing a different fixed constant in the exponential. The exact polynomial calculations were independently checked in `native_resistance/independent_checks.json`.
## Counterevidence, impact, and repair boundary

This is a counterexample to the inference, not to the particle–Stokes system. The original relative dynamics contain information lost in [eq:pair] (#eq:pair). For instance, writing \(r=X_i-X_j\), \(a_N=6\pi\gamma_N\lambda_N\), one has \[r''+a_Nr'=a_N b,\qquad b=(u)_i-(u)_j.\] If \(|b|\le L|r|\) with a uniform \(L\le a_N/4\), then the upper Dini derivative of \(z=|r'|/|r|\) obeys \[D^+z\le z^2-a_Nz+a_NL.\] The cone \(z\le a_N/2\), initially guaranteed by (H3), is invariant, and gives \[|r(t)|\ge |r(0)|\exp[-2z(0)/a_N-2Lt].\] This is a valid conditional repair route. The paper’s displayed coefficient is only bounded by \(C(1+|V^0|_\infty e^{-\gamma_N\lambda_Nt})\). Assumption (H4) bounds \(|V^0|_\infty/\lambda_N\) by an arbitrary finite constant, not the small constant needed for that cone argument. Thus this review has not verified a repair under the original (H1)–(H4).

Appendix B, Step 4, p. 49, repeats the pair-minimum and lower-integral inference for the binary system. There a uniform Lipschitz coefficient \(L\) on the intended bootstrap permits the cone argument for \(\lambda_N>4L\), yielding \(d_{\min}(t)\ge d_{\min}(0)e^{-1-2Lt}\). That conditional local repair does not resolve the separate parameter-domain failure below, and cannot simply be imported into the Stokes initial layer.

Assessment: Major, a demonstrated invalid derivation in a core proof chain. Theorem 1.1 has not been disproved. A valid separation argument through the initial layer is still required; the unaffected conditional energy and Wasserstein estimates remain useful.
Problem 2 (The stated general-kernel domain admits nonconvergent quadratic shear).
## Claim, assumptions, and source locations

Theorem 2.1, pp. 13–14, assumes \[|K(x)|+|x||\nabla K(x)|\le C|x|^{-\alpha},\qquad
 \operatorname{div}K=0,\qquad \alpha<d-1,\] and imposes no lower bound on \(\alpha\), no uniform support bound, and no higher-moment condition beyond the selected Wasserstein distance. Under (2.3), it asserts \(\mathcal W_p(\sigma_N(t),\sigma(t))\le e^{Ct}\mathcal W_p(\sigma_N(0),\sigma^0)\). Theorem 2.3, pp. 14–15, inherits this kernel domain and asserts the corresponding vanishing-inertia estimate under (D1)–(D3).
## An admissible family and its exact evolution

Take \(d=3,\alpha=-2,p=1,q=2\), and \[K(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(x_2^2,0,0),\qquad
 \sigma^0=\mathbf 1_{[0,1]^3}.\] The kernel is smooth and divergence free, \(K(0)=0\), and \(|K(x)|+|x||\nabla K(x)|\le3|x|^2\). Also \(q=2>3/4=d/(d-\alpha-1)\). The continuum solution is the volume-preserving shear \[(x,y,z)\longmapsto (x+t(y^2-y+1/3),y,z).\] It exists globally and preserves both total mass and its \(L^2\) norm, equal to one.

For \(N=n^3\), start from the midpoint \(n^3\) grid in the unit cube. Move one grid point with second coordinate \(y_0=1-1/(2n)\) to height \(L_N=N^{3/4}\), keeping its first and third coordinates unchanged. All other points remain fixed initially. Coupling each cube cell to its midpoint and then moving this one atom gives \[\eta_N(0)=\mathcal W_1(\sigma_N^0,\sigma^0)
 \le \frac{\sqrt3}{2n}+\frac{L_N-y_0}{N}\longrightarrow0 .\] The initial minimum distance is \(1/n=N^{-1/3}\). With \(q'=2\), the exponent in (2.3) is \(4/5\), and its second factor is \(1+d_{\min}(0)N^{1/3}=2\). Thus the full smallness condition holds.

Write \(m_{k,N}=N^{-1}\sum_i y_i^k\). Direct summation gives \[m_{1,N}=\tfrac12+\frac{L_N-y_0}{N},\quad
 m_{2,N}=\tfrac13-\frac1{12n^2}+\frac{L_N^2-y_0^2}{N}.\] Every particle keeps its second and third coordinates. Its first-coordinate velocity is the constant \(y_i^2-2m_{1,N}y_i+m_{2,N}\). There are no collisions: particles with distinct \((y,z)\) remain separated in those coordinates, and particles with identical \((y,z)\) have equal velocities and retain their initial first-coordinate separation.

Equation reference: eq:shear. The empirical first-coordinate barycenter has velocity \(2(m_{2,N}-m_{1,N}^2)\), whereas the continuum barycenter has velocity \(1/6\). Initial first-coordinate barycenters agree. The Kantorovich dual test function \(x\mapsto x_1\) therefore yields \[
 \mathcal W_1(\sigma_N(t),\sigma(t))
 \ge t\left|2(m_{2,N}-m_{1,N}^2)-\tfrac16\right|
 =2tN^{1/2}(1+o(1))\] for every fixed \(t>0\). This contradicts the claimed bound whose right side tends to zero.

To define a sequence for every integer \(N\), use any \(N\) points of the \(\lceil N^{1/3}\rceil^3\) midpoint grid, omitting only the excess \(O(N^{2/3})\) points, and move one retained point in the same way. The omission and weight normalization have \(\mathcal W_1\) cost \(O(N^{-1/3})\) before the outlier is moved. Separation remains comparable to \(N^{-1/3}\), the bounded-coordinate moments change by \(O(N^{-1/3})\), and the same diverging outlier contribution persists. The exact cube subsequence alone already exhibits the contradiction along this complete family.

For Theorem 2.3 choose \(V_i^0=0\) and \(\lambda_N=N\). Conditions (D2) and (D3) are immediate; (D1) is \((\eta_N(0)+N^{-1})^{4/5}/2\to0\) on the cube subsequence. The first-coordinate displacement is \[h_N(t)(y_i^2-2m_{1,N}y_i+m_{2,N}),\qquad
 h_N(t)=t-\frac{1-e^{-Nt}}N.\] Hence the barycenter discrepancy is \(2h_N(t)(m_{2,N}-m_{1,N}^2)-t/6\), again diverging as \(2tN^{1/2}\). Collision avoidance remains exact. Both universal conclusions fail on their written domain.
## Checks, counterevidence, and impact

The independent rational-moment script computes, for \(N=4096\), an initial-distance upper bound \(0.178891\) and a time-one lower bound \(127.718231\). These finite evaluations corroborate the formulas; the contradiction is the analytic \(N\to\infty\) argument, not a simulation.

The Oseen kernel in the physical theorem has \(\alpha=1\), so this example does not refute Theorem 1.1. Interpreting the general-kernel theorems as intended only for \(0\le\alpha<d-1\) excludes the example and agrees with the positive-singularity estimates used in the proof. That is a substantive restriction of the stated domain. The report verifies that it excludes this failure mechanism; it does not certify every endpoint or every part of a revised theorem. Alternatively, treating growing kernels requires additional growth/moment control and a new proof.

Assessment: Major for the false general-kernel guarantees, which are presented as an independent methodological contribution. The effect is bounded to their stated generality, separately from Problem 1.
Problem 3 (Two explicit auxiliary Stokes fields do not satisfy their defining properties).

In Section 4, p. 34, and (4.6), p. 35, the exterior single-sphere field is written as \[(\Phi-R^2\Delta\Phi/6)G,\qquad
 \Phi(x)=\frac{I/|x|+xx^{T}/|x|^3}{8\pi},\] with interior value \(G/(6\pi R)\). Taking \(G=e_1\), the exterior trace at \(x=Re_1\) is \(e_1/(3\pi R)\), whereas changing the minus sign to a plus gives \(e_1/(6\pi R)\). The wrong sign produces a nonzero jump on an open boundary patch, so the piecewise field is not in \(\dot H^1\). The plus sign is already used in (3.6), p. 23. It restores the correct surface-force solution and leaves the decay orders used in the estimates unchanged.

In the proof of Lemma 5.1, p. 40, set \[\Psi[W]=\left( rac{3r}{2|x|}- rac{r^3}{2|x|^3}ight)
                  rac{W	imes x}{2},\quad
 U=
abla	imes\Psi,\quad
 P_{m bad}=r
abla(|x|^{-1})\cdot W .\] The claimed exterior Stokes equation fails. At the admissible point \(x=2re_1\), with \(r>0\) and \(W=e_1\), exact differentiation gives \[-\Delta U+
abla P_{m bad}= rac{5}{8r^2}e_1
e0.\] This is not a constant pressure gauge discrepancy. The compatible pressure is \[P_{m good}= rac{3r(W\cdot x)}{2|x|^3}
            =- rac{3r}{2}
abla(|x|^{-1})\cdot W .\] Symbolic differentiation gives zero exterior residual for this corrected pair. It has \(U=W\) on the sphere and the required traction \(-\sigma[U,P_{m good}]n=3W/(2r)\). The correction must also be used in the cut-off pressure and weight construction on p. 41. Choosing the cut-off equal to one on \(B_{d/2}\), possible since \(d\ge4r\), places its derivatives in the prescribed annulus. The reciprocal identity then gives the intended normalized weight.

Assessment: Minor, supported local construction defects. These errors change equations and boundary traces, so they are not merely cosmetic. The independently defined weak solutions and the scaling estimates survive the checked local corrections. No additional failure of the resistance propositions or of the physical limit is established by these formulas.
# Overall dependence and remaining work

Problem 1 interrupts the supplied route to the main theorem’s separation estimate and bootstrap closure; it does not falsify the theorem. Problem 2 falsifies two subsidiary general-kernel statements on an explicitly admitted range, while leaving the physical kernel outside the counterexample. Problem 3 has verified local corrections and should not be used to inflate the impact of Problems 1–2.

The rotational refinement in (1.10) and (1.12) uses \(R^2(\Omega-\widetilde\Omega)\), while the displayed Appendix C energy controls \(R(\Omega-\widetilde\Omega)\). Rotlet scaling offers a plausible extra power of \(R\) in translational and local-\(L^2\) effects. No admissible counterexample to that refinement was established, and a complete sharper block-coupling estimate was not verified. This remains an explicitly unverified aspect, not an additional confirmed error. The finite-\(q\) local-fluid estimates in Step 6 likewise were not completely reconstructed after all interpolations. Neither unresolved item raises severity.

The continuum solution is the volume-preserving shear \[(x,y,z)\longmapsto (x+t(y^2-y+1/3),y,z).\] It exists globally and preserves both total mass and its \(L^2\) norm, equal to one.

For \(N=n^3\), start from the midpoint \(n^3\) grid in the unit cube. Move one grid point with second coordinate \(y_0=1-1/(2n)\) to height \(L_N=N^{3/4}\), keeping its first and third coordinates unchanged. All other points remain fixed initially. Coupling each cube cell to its midpoint and then moving this one atom gives \[\eta_N(0)=\mathcal W_1(\sigma_N^0,\sigma^0)
 \le \frac{\sqrt3}{2n}+\frac{L_N-y_0}{N}\longrightarrow0 .\] The initial minimum distance is \(1/n=N^{-1/3}\). With \(q'=2\), the exponent in (2.3) is \(4/5\), and its second factor is \(1+d_{\min}(0)N^{1/3}=2\). Thus the full smallness condition holds.

Write \(m_{k,N}=N^{-1}\sum_i y_i^k\). Direct summation gives \[m_{1,N}=\tfrac12+\frac{L_N-y_0}{N},\quad
 m_{2,N}=\tfrac13-\frac1{12n^2}+\frac{L_N^2-y_0^2}{N}.\] Every particle keeps its second and third coordinates. Its first-coordinate velocity is the constant \(y_i^2-2m_{1,N}y_i+m_{2,N}\). There are no collisions: particles with distinct \((y,z)\) remain separated in those coordinates, and particles with identical \((y,z)\) have equal velocities and retain their initial first-coordinate separation.

Equation reference: eq:shear. The empirical first-coordinate barycenter has velocity \(2(m_{2,N}-m_{1,N}^2)\), whereas the continuum barycenter has velocity \(1/6\). Initial first-coordinate barycenters agree. The Kantorovich dual test function \(x\mapsto x_1\) therefore yields \[
 \mathcal W_1(\sigma_N(t),\sigma(t))
 \ge t\left|2(m_{2,N}-m_{1,N}^2)-\tfrac16\right|
 =2tN^{1/2}(1+o(1))\] for every fixed \(t>0\). This contradicts the claimed bound whose right side tends to zero.

To define a sequence for every integer \(N\), use any \(N\) points of the \(\lceil N^{1/3}\rceil^3\) midpoint grid, omitting only the excess \(O(N^{2/3})\) points, and move one retained point in the same way. The omission and weight normalization have \(\mathcal W_1\) cost \(O(N^{-1/3})\) before the outlier is moved. Separation remains comparable to \(N^{-1/3}\), the bounded-coordinate moments change by \(O(N^{-1/3})\), and the same diverging outlier contribution persists. The exact cube subsequence alone already exhibits the contradiction along this complete family.

For Theorem 2.3 choose \(V_i^0=0\) and \(\lambda_N=N\). Conditions (D2) and (D3) are immediate; (D1) is \((\eta_N(0)+N^{-1})^{4/5}/2\to0\) on the cube subsequence. The first-coordinate displacement is \[h_N(t)(y_i^2-2m_{1,N}y_i+m_{2,N}),\qquad
 h_N(t)=t-\frac{1-e^{-Nt}}N.\] Hence the barycenter discrepancy is \(2h_N(t)(m_{2,N}-m_{1,N}^2)-t/6\), again diverging as \(2tN^{1/2}\). Collision avoidance remains exact. Both universal conclusions fail on their written domain.

The independent rational-moment script computes, for \(N=4096\), an initial-distance upper bound \(0.178891\) and a time-one lower bound \(127.718231\). These finite evaluations corroborate the formulas; the contradiction is the analytic \(N\to\infty\) argument, not a simulation.

The Oseen kernel in the physical theorem has \(\alpha=1\), so this example does not refute Theorem 1.1. Interpreting the general-kernel theorems as intended only for \(0\le\alpha<d-1\) excludes the example and agrees with the positive-singularity estimates used in the proof. That is a substantive restriction of the stated domain. The report verifies that it excludes this failure mechanism; it does not certify every endpoint or every part of a revised theorem. Alternatively, treating growing kernels requires additional growth/moment control and a new proof.

Assessment: Major for the false general-kernel guarantees, which are presented as an independent methodological contribution. The effect is bounded to their stated generality, separately from Problem 1.
