report: Abstract: An explicit ascending HNN extension contradicts the finite-orbit and universal-periodicity assertions of Proposition 6.5 in the generality expressly admitted in Section 6. The weaker existence statement needed downstream is not refuted by this example, but requires a valid replacement proof. Three additional local corrections concern compactness in the normal-form theorem, regularity of cyclic covers, and the terminal complexity value. The latter corrections preserve the intended finite-complex applications. Conclusions are limited to arXiv version 3 and do not certify the unacquired journal text. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical verification of
One-relator hierarchies
# Identity and scope

The reviewed work is Marco Linton, One-relator hierarchies, associated with Duke Mathematical Journal DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0040 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0040). The actual input is arXiv:2202.11324v3, dated 27 June 2024, 35 PDF pages. All page references use that PDF’s physical, one-based numbering, which agrees with its printed numbering. The repository lists v3 as its latest version and describes it as the version to appear in Duke; that metadata is not a textual comparison with the journal article.

The review traced the main implications through the hierarchy construction, normal forms, stability, and cyclic-stabilizer arguments. Their notes are incorporated with explicit limits. The primary review checked the disputed hypotheses, reconstructed the counterexamples, and examined the cited source-page images. No author code was executed. An independently written script checked the finite edge paths used in Problem 2 for \(m=1,\ldots,12\); the infinite family is proved analytically below.
# Claims and positive checks

Theorem 7.1, p. 31, concerns a specified one-relator hierarchy: a hyperbolic quasiconvex hierarchy, an acylindrical hierarchy, and a \(\mathbb Z\)-stable hierarchy without Baumslag–Solitar subgroups are equivalent, with virtual specialness and quasiconvexity of the indicated subcomplex images. It does not assert that every one-relator group without a Baumslag–Solitar subgroup is hyperbolic. Theorem 7.2 adds negative immersions, using Corollary 6.9 to obtain stability.

The reduced-rank estimate of Theorem 2.11, p. 8, can be organized consistently. Write \(A_0=\pi_1(A)\), \(B_0=\pi_1(B)\), \(E=A_0\cap B_0\). For \(C<A_0\), \(D<B_0\), choose representatives \(b\) for \(D\backslash B_0/E\), followed by representatives \(a\) for \((E\cap D^b)\backslash A_0/C\). Then \[C\cap D^{ba}=C\cap(E\cap D^b)^a.\] Successive applications of strong inertia give the required bound by \(\operatorname{rr}(D)\). Intersections outside \(B_0A_0\) are cyclic or trivial under the cited intersection theorem and contribute zero reduced rank. Connectedness of the Magnus-subgraph intersection has a real role in this identification.

For regular cyclic covers, the interval condition on translates of a \(\mathbb Z\)-domain gives the contractible fibers used in the horizontal-map argument. The hierarchy terminates after the correction in Problem 4. In the normal-form proof, the two thin-triangle cases provide a polynomial endpoint bound; a direct correction of its final subpath estimate appears in Problem 2.

The external Louder–Wilton paper was checked at the statement level: Theorem 1.2 relates negative immersions to the two-generator subgroup condition, Theorem A gives coherence, and Theorem B gives the co-Hopf and finite-conjugacy-class properties used in the descending-chain application. Those external proofs were not reconstructed. The final isomorphism and subgroup-hyperbolicity corollaries also retain their cited external dependencies.
# Findings
Problem 1 (Finite segment-orbit bounds do not imply Proposition 6.5).
## Location and claim

Proposition 6.5, p. 25, claims that if \(s_{\mathbb Z}(\psi)=\infty\), there are at most \(\operatorname{rr}(A)\) \(H\)-orbits of biinfinite geodesics through \(H\) all of whose finite subsets have noncyclic stabilizer. It further claims that every such line is preserved by a hyperbolic element. Its proof infers the finite-orbit statement from Lemma 6.4 by a pigeonhole argument.

Section 6, pp. 23–24, admits strongly inert subgroups of Magnus subgroups; Remark 6.2 explicitly includes a free base group with trivial relation, with the whole base group regarded as a Magnus subgroup. These stated allowances are essential to the example.
## Counterexample with all hypotheses checked

Let \[H=F(a,b),\quad A=H,\quad B=\langle a^2,b^2\rangle,\qquad
 \psi(a)=a^2,\quad\psi(b)=b^2,\] and \[G=\langle a,b,t\mid tat^{-1}=a^2,\ tbt^{-1}=b^2\rangle .\] A nonempty reduced word remains nonempty under this substitution, so \(\psi:A\to B\) is an isomorphism. Both edge groups are strongly inert: \(A=H\) trivially is, and \(B\) has rank two, a class explicitly listed on p. 6. For this particular \(B\), its folded core is two subdivided loops sharing their only vertex of valence greater than two; the fiber-product degree bound gives the same conclusion. The subgroup \(B\) is proper, since its abelianized image is \(2\mathbb Z^2\), and has infinite index: finite index \(d\) in \(F_2\) would give rank \(d+1=2\), hence \(d=1\), a contradiction.

For every \(n\), the recursively defined collection contains \[[\psi^n(H)]=[\langle a^{2^n},b^{2^n}\rangle].\] These groups have rank two. Thus \(s_{\mathbb Z}(\psi)=\infty\) and \(\operatorname{rr}(A)=1\).

In the Bass–Serre tree, a vertex \(gH\) has one edge in one direction and infinitely many in the other. Choose the direction in which its children are \(ghtH\), with \(h\) ranging over \(H/B\). Their stabilizers satisfy \[\operatorname{Stab}(ghtH)=ghBh^{-1}g^{-1}
       \subset gHg^{-1}=\operatorname{Stab}(gH).\] The child stabilizer is also a conjugate of \(H\), hence is noncyclic of rank two. The pointwise stabilizer of every finite directed segment is therefore its terminal vertex stabilizer and has rank two.

Every infinite forward ray from \(H\) extends uniquely backwards to a biinfinite directed line. Choosing just two children at each stage gives continuum many such lines. Every finite subset lies in a finite directed segment, and hence has the stipulated noncyclic stabilizer. Since \(H\) is countable, each \(H\)-orbit is countable. There are continuum many orbits, contradicting the asserted upper bound one. The countable group \(G\) also has at most countably many axes of hyperbolic elements, so most of these lines cannot be preserved by any hyperbolic element.
## Impact and repair boundary

The example is compatible with Lemma 6.4: orbit bounds at every finite length do not supply a single group element identifying entire infinite lines. Elements identifying longer prefixes need not stabilize as the prefix grows.

Theorem 6.8, pp. 26–27, uses Proposition 6.5 to obtain a periodic line and then a bounded-rank descending chain. Corollary 6.9 and the negative-immersions application use that theorem. The defective proposition is therefore a substantive proof dependency. Nevertheless, this example has the standard \(t\)-axis \[\cdots,t^{-1}H,H,tH,t^2H,\cdots .\] It does not disprove the weaker existential consequence actually needed in Theorem 6.8. Its total group is not asserted here to be a counterexample to the main one-relator theorem. A sufficient repair would establish that weaker existence statement in the required class, or provide another route to stability. Deleting the universal wording without a new proof does not establish the repair. The finite-\(s_{\mathbb Z}\) hypothesis of Theorem 6.14 excludes this example.
Problem 2 (Compactness is missing from the general normal-form theorem).
## Location and construction

Theorem 5.7, p. 19, assumes hyperbolicity of the vertex cover, acylindricity on the Bass–Serre tree, and prefix-closed relative quasigeodesic normal forms. Its proof invokes Theorem 3.4, p. 10, which additionally requires a compact total graph of spaces. The general setup does not impose this requirement.

For \(n\in\mathbb Z\), take two boundary lines with vertices \(A_n,B_n\), consecutive edges \(a_n,b_n\), and rungs \(r_n\) from \(A_n\) to \(B_{2n}\). Fill each pentagon \[A_n,A_{n+1},B_{2n+2},B_{2n+1},B_{2n},A_n.\] This is a contractible, locally finite strip \(X\). Give every edge length one. The function \(q(A_n)=n\), \(q(B_n)=n/2\) is 1-Lipschitz; the \(A\)-boundary is isometric to a line and every vertex is within two of it. Thus \(X^{(1)}\) is hyperbolic.

Take the edge space \(C\) to be an integer line with embeddings \(c_n\mapsto A_n\), \(c_n\mapsto B_n\), over a one-loop underlying graph. All vertex and edge groups are trivial, so the total group is \(\mathbb Z\), acting freely, and hence acylindrically, on its Bass–Serre line.

Use unique tree paths in \[T_A=A\cup\{r_n:n\in\mathbb Z\}\cup\{b_{2n}:n\in\mathbb Z\},
 \qquad T_B=B\cup\{r_n:n\in\mathbb Z\}\] as \(\eta_A,\eta_B\), and put \(\eta_X=\eta_A\). Each omitted edge has a tree detour of length four. Every subpath has length at most \(4d+5\), including endpoints inside edges, so these are uniformly 5-quasigeodesic normal forms. Tree paths are prefix-closed. Cancellation of their common tail gives the full relative-normal-form condition, since \(A\) and \(B\) are subtrees of their respective trees. Equivariance holds because \(\pi_1(X)=1\).
## Correction and compact applications

Adding compactness to Theorem 5.7 restores the missing premise of Theorem 3.4. The finite complexes and domains in Theorem 5.9, pp. 22–23, possess it, so the example does not refute the intended hierarchy application.

There is also a repairable estimate on p. 21: comparing \(f(d(u,v))+f(d(v,z))\) with \(f(d(u,z))\) has no justification for an arbitrary intermediate \(v\). But the normal-form identity already proved gives \(\eta(u,z)=\eta_X(u,v)*\mathrm{tail}\). For the corresponding subpath \(h'\), taking \(K\ge1\) yields \[|h'|\le K|\eta_X(u,v)|+K+|\mathrm{tail}|
       \le K|\eta(u,z)|+K
       \le K f(d(u,z))+K.\] This polynomial bound suffices for the invoked subexponential-detour theorem. Thus the displayed arithmetic error does not by itself defeat the compact case.
Problem 3 (The definition of a \(\mathbb Z\)-cover needs regularity).

Section 4, p. 10, defines a \(\mathbb Z\)-cover only by connectedness and deck group isomorphic to \(\mathbb Z\). Proposition 4.6, p. 13, claims a finite \(\mathbb Z\)-domain for every such cover of a finite CW-complex. This formal scope is too broad.

Let \(X\) be the three-petal rose and set \[G=F(a,b,c)=K*\langle c\rangle,\quad K=\langle a,b\rangle,
 \qquad L=\ker(K\to\mathbb Z),\ a\mapsto1,\ b\mapsto0 .\] For the connected cover corresponding to \(L<G\), malnormality of the free factor \(K\) and \(L\ne1\) imply \(N_G(L)=K\). Its deck group is therefore \(K/L\cong\mathbb Z\), as required. But the deck quotient is the intermediate \(K\)-cover of \(X\), a noncompact locally finite graph: the cosets \(Kc^n\) are distinct. A finite domain \(D\) satisfying \(\mathbb ZD=Y\) would surject onto that quotient and make it compact, a contradiction.

The covers actually chosen from epimorphisms onto \(\mathbb Z\) are regular. Inserting regular in the definition excludes the example and matches the proof’s use of regularity. This is a local scope correction, not a counterexample to the intended hierarchy.
Problem 4 (The terminal complexity is \((0,-1)\)).

The complexity definition and Proposition 4.12’s proof, p. 15, use \[c(X)=\bigl(|\lambda|/\deg(\lambda)-|X_\lambda^{(0)}|,\ -\chi(X)\bigr).\] For \(\langle a\mid a^m\rangle\), \(m\ge1\), the first coordinate is zero and \(\chi(X)=1\), so \(c(X)=(0,-1)\), although the proof calls the terminal value \((0,0)\). Conversely, \(\langle a,b\mid a^m\rangle\) has complexity \((0,0)\) and admits a cyclic cover through \(a\mapsto0,b\mapsto1\).

For a connected underlying graph of rank \(r\ge1\), the second coordinate is \(r-2\ge-1\); the first is a nonnegative integer. The lexicographic order on \(\mathbb N_0\times\{-1,0,1,\ldots\}\) is well founded. At \(r=1\) the group is finite cyclic and the complexity is \((0,-1)\). At \(r\ge2\), abelianization has rank at least \(r-1\), hence a quotient \(\mathbb Z\). Proposition 4.11’s strict decrease therefore still gives finite termination. This local arithmetic correction has a complete repair.
# Assessment and limits

Assessment: Major. Problem 1 disproves a substantive auxiliary proposition used on the route to the main negative-immersions result. Its impact is a required replacement argument, not an established counterexample to the main theorem. Problems 2–4 are local corrections; the compact, regular-cover hierarchy applications survive the specific counterexamples above.

The cited results on Magnus intersections, combinations of hyperbolic spaces, subexponential detours, virtual specialness, and the isomorphism algorithm were not independently reproved. The cyclic-stabilizer and Grushko arguments were traced, but every subsidiary combinatorial choice was not certified. These findings are not claimed exhaustive. A bounded search found no paper-specific correction; absence of a retrieved correction is not evidence that none exists. Only the acquired author version is assessed.
This is an initial technical review. The recorded scientific decision is `pending`; the human-review list is empty. It is not independent acceptance or a human journal recommendation.

Every subpath has length at most \(4d+5\), including endpoints inside edges, so these are uniformly 5-quasigeodesic normal forms. Tree paths are prefix-closed. Cancellation of their common tail gives the full relative-normal-form condition, since \(A\) and \(B\) are subtrees of their respective trees. Equivariance holds because \(\pi_1(X)=1\).

Adding compactness to Theorem 5.7 restores the missing premise of Theorem 3.4. The finite complexes and domains in Theorem 5.9, pp. 22–23, possess it, so the example does not refute the intended hierarchy application.

There is also a repairable estimate on p. 21: comparing \(f(d(u,v))+f(d(v,z))\) with \(f(d(u,z))\) has no justification for an arbitrary intermediate \(v\). But the normal-form identity already proved gives \(\eta(u,z)=\eta_X(u,v)*\mathrm{tail}\). For the corresponding subpath \(h'\), taking \(K\ge1\) yields \[|h'|\le K|\eta_X(u,v)|+K+|\mathrm{tail}|
       \le K|\eta(u,z)|+K
       \le K f(d(u,z))+K.\] This polynomial bound suffices for the invoked subexponential-detour theorem. Thus the displayed arithmetic error does not by itself defeat the compact case.
result: Impact: False at stated noncompact generality; finite main applications are compact.

problems.title: The definition of a \(\mathbb Z\)-cover needs regularity
problems.source_location: Section4 definition p10; Definition4.1 p11; Proposition4.6 p13
claim: Deck(p)=Z alone gives finite Z-domain for cover of finite complex.
analysis: Section 4, p. 10, defines a \(\mathbb Z\)-cover only by connectedness and deck group isomorphic to \(\mathbb Z\). Proposition 4.6, p. 13, claims a finite \(\mathbb Z\)-domain for every such cover of a finite CW-complex. This formal scope is too broad.

Let \(X\) be the three-petal rose and set \[G=F(a,b,c)=K*\langle c\rangle,\quad K=\langle a,b\rangle,
 \qquad L=\ker(K\to\mathbb Z),\ a\mapsto1,\ b\mapsto0 .\] For the connected cover corresponding to \(L<G\), malnormality of the free factor \(K\) and \(L\ne1\) imply \(N_G(L)=K\). Its deck group is therefore \(K/L\cong\mathbb Z\), as required. But the deck quotient is the intermediate \(K\)-cover of \(X\), a noncompact locally finite graph: the cosets \(Kc^n\) are distinct. A finite domain \(D\) satisfying \(\mathbb ZD=Y\) would surject onto that quotient and make it compact, a contradiction.

The covers actually chosen from epimorphisms onto \(\mathbb Z\) are regular. Inserting regular in the definition excludes the example and matches the proof’s use of regularity. This is a local scope correction, not a counterexample to the intended hierarchy.
result: Impact: Local definition/scope defect.

problems.title: The terminal complexity is \((0,-1)\)
problems.source_location: Complexity definition and Proposition4.12 p15
claim: Terminal complexity (0,0) characterizes finite cyclic endpoint.
analysis: The complexity definition and Proposition 4.12’s proof, p. 15, use \[c(X)=\bigl(|\lambda|/\deg(\lambda)-|X_\lambda^{(0)}|,\ -\chi(X)\bigr).\] For \(\langle a\mid a^m\rangle\), \(m\ge1\), the first coordinate is zero and \(\chi(X)=1\), so \(c(X)=(0,-1)\), although the proof calls the terminal value \((0,0)\). Conversely, \(\langle a,b\mid a^m\rangle\) has complexity \((0,0)\) and admits a cyclic cover through \(a\mapsto0,b\mapsto1\).

For a connected underlying graph of rank \(r\ge1\), the second coordinate is \(r-2\ge-1\); the first is a nonnegative integer. The lexicographic order on \(\mathbb N_0\times\{-1,0,1,\ldots\}\) is well founded. At \(r=1\) the group is finite cyclic and the complexity is \((0,-1)\). At \(r\ge2\), abelianization has rank at least \(r-1\), hence a quotient \(\mathbb Z\). Proposition 4.11’s strict decrease therefore still gives finite termination. This local arithmetic correction has a complete repair.
result: Impact: Arithmetic error in induction base.

report: Abstract: The paper connects geometric canonical heights, analytic rigidity of entropy measures, and arithmetic equidistribution to obtain uniform and relative dynamical Bogomolov statements. This review establishes a counterexample to the all-points height inequality in Theorem 4.10, an invalid measure identity in the central proof of Lemma 5.2, and a counterexample to the unequal-degree extension in Theorem 3.1. A further local conjugacy inference requires correction. The height inequality has a sufficient dense-open replacement for its later generic-sequence use. A complete local replacement for Lemma 5.2 is supplied using the already cited Yuan–Zhang theorem. These findings do not disprove the principal uniform or relative Bogomolov theorems. The assessment is Major: revision of statements and proofs required; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: Scientific initial-review execution unit
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Initial mathematical review of
On the dynamical Bogomolov conjecture
for families of split rational maps
Paper. Niki Myrto Mavraki and Harry Schmidt, Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), no. 5, 803–856; DOI: 10.1215/00127094-2024-0041. Assignment: M25-0153.

Reviewed versions. The principal input is arXiv:2201.10455v4 (1 July 2024), including its supplied TeX. An independently obtained Warwick accepted manuscript was compared at the three principal problem anchors. Its extra cover page shifts physical page numbers by one. Unless indicated otherwise, page numbers below are both printed and physical pages of the arXiv version. The publisher’s final text was not acquired; conclusions about unchanged journal text are not asserted.
# Scope and principal dependencies

The review examined the definitions and quantifiers in the introduction, the normalization of heights and pulled-back measures, the ordinary and exceptional branches of Section 3, the geometric-height arguments of Section 4, the equidistribution and slicing chain of Section 5, Section 6, and the specialization appendix. They were not separate external referees or an independent acceptance panel.

The principal chain is geometric nondegeneracy, followed by equidistribution, equality of measures on a fibre product, slicing, and the equal-degree analytic rigidity theorem. The passage from relative non-density to uniform fibre counts permits deletion of finitely many base parameters. That permission resolves the apparent exceptional-fibre objection to the generically finite counting argument on pp. 29–30. The normalized pullback weights in Theorem 1.10 and the use of the fundamental inequality in Corollary 1.5 are consistent.

The primary statements of Yuan–Zhang used in the repair below were checked in their v6 manuscript, which predates the reviewed revision. The height-coincidence input of Mavraki–Schmidt–Wilms was checked for its function-field hypotheses and exceptional set. The complete proofs of Yuan–Zhang, the external local Julia-symmetry rigidity results, Ax-type results, and the cited dynamical Manin–Mumford theorems were not independently reproved. This is a substantial initial proof audit, not certification of every external dependency.
# Problem 1: an isotrivial zero-height section survives the stated exceptional locus

Assessment: Major. Location: Theorem 4.10 and its preceding one-sentence deduction, p. 23; the exceptional-locus definition, p. 6; Definition 1.7, p. 4; the reused induction, pp. 22–23. The accepted manuscript retains the same Theorem 4.10 on physical p. 24.

Theorem 4.10 claims a positive lower bound \[\widehat h_\Phi(P)\ge c_1h_{\mathcal N}(\pi(P))-c_2
 \quad\text{for every }P\in\mathcal C^{\Phi,\star}(\overline{\mathbb Q})\] when at least one coordinate is isotrivial, with an additional non-isotriviality condition on the curve if both coordinates are isotrivial. The displayed exceptional locus does not remove every horizontal section of geometric canonical height zero.

Take \(B=\mathbb P^1\), \(K=\overline{\mathbb Q}(t)\), \(B_0=\mathbb A^1\), and \[\Phi=(f_1,f_2)=(z^2,z^2+t),\qquad
 \mathbf C:\ y=\frac1{x-2},\qquad P_t=(2,\infty).\] Both maps have degree two. The first is isotrivial. The second is not: the two finite fixed-point multipliers satisfy \(u^2-2u+4t=0\), and the multiplier at infinity is zero. Their second elementary symmetric function \(4t\) is a nonconstant conjugacy invariant. Thus the additional both-isotrivial hypothesis is inapplicable.

The curve is the graph of a Möbius transformation, so both projections are isomorphisms. In coordinates \(x=[X:Z]\), \(y=[Y:W]\), its closure is \[Y(X-2Z)=ZW.\] Its only point above \(y=\infty\) is \((2,\infty)\); above \(x=\infty\) it has \((\infty,0)\). Since a polynomial has no finite preimage of infinity, the only point of \(\Phi^n(\mathbf C)\) above \(y=\infty\) is \((2^{2^n},\infty)\). These points are distinct, so \(\mathbf C\) is not preperiodic. The section \(P_t\) is not preperiodic either.

Under the paper’s stated preperiodic/torsion-coset convention this section belongs to \(\mathcal C^{\Phi,\star}\). In this pair \(f_2\) is ordinary: Remark 4.5 identifies a non-isotrivial exceptional map with a flexible Lattès map of square degree, excluding degree two. Thus the exceptional torsion-coset alternative is unavailable. The curve itself is not special; the non-preperiodic point is not a special point-component. The definition removes components of special subvarieties contained in \(\mathcal C\), not arbitrary intersections with an ambient preperiodic curve such as \(\mathbb P^1\times\{\infty\}\). No convention removing all non-preperiodic constant points of isotrivial coordinates is supplied in the manuscript.

For every algebraic \(t\), \[\widehat h_{\Phi_t}(P_t)
 =\widehat h_{z^2}(2)+\widehat h_{z^2+t}(\infty)=\log 2.\] With \(\mathcal N=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)\), positive integer parameters have unbounded base height. The claimed inequality is impossible for fixed \(c_1>0,c_2\). Shrinking \(B_0\) cannot remove this contradiction, and adding dominance of both projections cannot repair it.

Cause and impact. The generic section has geometric canonical height zero, since its first coordinate is constant and the second is fixed. In an isotrivial coordinate, geometric height zero does not imply preperiodicity. The base case of Theorem 1.11 uses non-isotriviality precisely to obtain that implication; it cannot be reused unchanged. Theorem 4.10 is a false height statement used in Proposition 4.13 and hence in the mixed-isotrivial route to the uniform theorem. The example does not violate the isotrivial-free hypotheses of Theorem 1.11.

Repair boundary. For the dominant curves in cases (2)–(3) of Proposition 4.12, Theorem 4.3 gives positive geometric curve height and Appendix A.1 gives the required inequality on a nonempty Zariski open subset \(U\). A generic sequence in the sense of Definition 4.11 meets the fixed proper closed complement only finitely often. The bound on base heights needed in Proposition 4.13 therefore follows after discarding finitely many terms. This repairs that downstream use, but does not restore the all-points assertion on the original \(\mathcal C^{\Phi,\star}\). A stronger corrected theorem must explicitly enlarge the removed locus or supply a different valid hypothesis. Dependence of the slope on the fixed choice of \(\mathcal N\) must also be allowed.
# Problem 2: finite pushforward does not determine its source measure

Assessment: Major; a local repair is verified below. Location: Lemma 5.2, p. 26, between (5.5) and the concluding display; diagram (5.2), p. 25. The same inference occurs on physical p. 27 of the accepted manuscript.

The proof asserts \[\pi_i^*\pi_{i*}\pi_{\mathcal C*}P
   =\deg(\pi_i)\pi_{\mathcal C*}P\] because \(\pi_i\) is finite. This is not a finite-map identity. For \(\pi(z)=z^2\), let \(m\) be Haar probability measure on the unit circle and put \(\mu=(1+\varepsilon\cos	heta)m\), where \(0<\varepsilon<1\). The two inverse branches cancel the cosine term under pushforward, giving \[\pi_*\mu=m,\qquad \pi^*\pi_*\mu=2m
e2\mu.\] Testing against \(\cos	heta\) gives respectively \(0\) and \(\varepsilon\). These are positive nonatomic measures. The universally valid degree identity has the opposite order, \(\pi_*\pi^*
u=\deg(\pi)
u\). The same obstruction persists after taking a product with a base measure.

This disproves the stated justification, not Lemma 5.2 under all its dynamical hypotheses. Its particular limiting measure can have the required symmetry, but that symmetry must be proved. The step is central: Lemma 5.2 supplies the equality sliced in the proof of Theorem 1.8, which is then used for Theorem 1.4.
## A replacement using the cited equidistribution theorem

Write \[Y=\mathcal C\times_{B_0}\mathcal X,\quad
 Z=\mathbb P^1\times\mathcal X,\quad
 a_i=\deg(\widetilde\pi_i)=\deg(\pi_i),\quad r=\dim Y.\] After the permitted shrinking of \(B_0\), the coordinate projections are finite. Let \(\overline L_i\) be the invariant adelic line bundle for \(f_i\times_{B_0}\Psi\) restricted to \(Z\), and set \(\overline M_i=\widetilde\pi_i^*\overline L_i\). The following facts justify applying equidistribution on the source \(Y\).

First, \(\overline L_i\) is nef by Yuan–Zhang [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 6.1.1, pp.~191--192]{YZ}]; finite pullback preserves nefness. Second, the earlier nondegeneracy argument gives \(v_i=\int_Z\nu_i>0\), where \(\nu_i=\widehat T_{f_i\times\Psi}^{\,r}\wedge[Z]\). The finite projection formula [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition 4.1.2, p.~111]{YZ}] gives positive geometric top degree \(a_iv_i\) for \(\overline M_i\), with the compatible normalizations. Third, the original generic small sequence \(z_n\) on \(Y\) satisfies \[0\le h_{\overline M_i}(z_n)
 =\widehat h_{f_i\times\Psi}(\widetilde\pi_i(z_n))
 \le \widehat h_{\Phi\times\Psi}(z_n)\longrightarrow0.\] Finally, nefness and the fundamental inequality [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 5.3.3, p.~170]{YZ}] give \[0\le h_{\overline M_i}(Y)
 \le\lambda_1(Y,\overline M_i)=0.\] Thus smallness is convergence to the normalized variety height, as the general theorem requires.

Yuan–Zhang [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 5.4.3, p.~177]{YZ}] now applies to each \((Y,\overline M_i)\). Uniqueness of the weak limit of the same Galois-orbit measures gives the stronger assertion \[P= rac1{a_iv_i}\widetilde\pi_i^*
u_i.\] Pushing forward through the Cartesian square yields \[\pi_{\mathcal C*}P
   = rac1{a_iv_i}\pi_i^*p_*
u_i,\qquad
 \pi_1^*p_*
u_1
   = rac{a_1v_1}{a_2v_2}\pi_2^*p_*
u_2,\] which proves the desired lemma with the intended positive constant. For this base-change identity one may work off the branch locus, where the finite map is a union of local biholomorphisms. Products of Green currents with continuous local potentials charge no proper analytic subsets; the equality consequently extends across that locus. This avoids applying the separate submersion lemma outside its hypotheses.

The replacement is complete at this local step, conditional on the paper’s earlier nondegeneracy inputs and the cited theory. It does not claim an independent proof of that theory. The original invalid central derivation remains a Major correction even though its replacement is available; the corrected lemma and principal relative theorem have not been counterexampled.
# Problem 3: equal entropy measures need not imply commensurable degrees

Assessment: Minor, confined to the advertised unequal-degree extension. Location: Theorem 3.1, p. 11; the exceptional branch, pp. 15–16. The theorem’s statement is identical at the inspected accepted-manuscript physical p. 12.

Take \(f_1(z)=z^2\), \(f_2(z)=z^3\), and \(C=\Delta\subset(\mathbb P^1)^2\). The diagonal is smooth and irreducible, and both projections have degree one. Both entropy measures are the same Haar measure \(m\) on \(S^1\). Indeed \((z^d)^*m=dm\), and \(m\) is the atomless balanced probability measure. Thus the normalized pullback measures agree and their supports intersect. However, no positive integers \(\ell,k\) satisfy \(2^\ell=3^k\). The equivalence asserted in Theorem 3.1 is therefore false.

These are exceptional maps associated with \(\mathbb G_m\), and the diagonal is a subgroup. The proof obtains degree commensurability in its ordinary branch; the exceptional coset argument cannot imply it. The repair must distinguish an ordinary alternative involving suitable iterates from an exceptional coset alternative without a universal commensurability requirement. Since the paper defines weak specialness for polarized pairs, the latter alternative must be stated explicitly or accompanied by an extended definition. A full rewritten generalized theorem has not been certified here.

A related local algebra error occurs in the torus converse on p. 16: \(x^{k_1}y^{k_2}=\theta\), \(|\theta|=1\), does not imply \(k_1\log^+|x|=k_2\log^+|y|\). For \(xy=1\), \(x=2\), \(y=1/2\), the two sides are \(\log2\) and \(0\). The desired measure conclusion is nevertheless correct in this example: \[\log^+|t|-\log^+|t^{-1}|=\log|t|\] is harmonic on \(\mathbb C^*\), so applying \(dd^c\) gives equality. More generally a torus coset parametrized by \((at^m,bt^n)\) has pulled-back circle measures of masses \(|m|\), \(|n|\); intersecting supports force the same support radius, and normalization by projection degree gives equality.

Impact boundary. Theorem 1.10 assumes equal degrees. Proposition 3.6 and the arithmetic proof invoke that theorem, not the false extra unequal-degree conclusion. The example therefore does not refute the equal-degree rigidity theorem or the principal arithmetic results. The local classification here reflects that verified dependency boundary, not a claim that a false theorem is merely a typographical issue.
# Problem 4: nonconstant conjugacies can preserve the diagonal
Assessment: Minor. Location: Section 6, p. 31, the isotrivial case of the proof of Theorem 1.3 (source lines 1478–1483).

The proof infers that \((M_1,M_2)(\Delta)\) is not constant from nonconstancy of at least one \(M_i\). Let \[M_t(z)=z+t,\qquad f_t(z)=(z+t)^2-t,\qquad
 g_t(z)=(z+t)^2+1-t.\] Both maps vary, both are conjugate to fixed maps through \(M_t\), and \((M_t,M_t)(\Delta)=\Delta\). Hence the inference fails.

This is not confined to a weakly special diagonal. The fixed map \(g_0=z^2+1\) has an infinite critical orbit of \(0\), so it is ordinary; moreover \(\Delta\) is not preperiodic for \((z^2,z^2+1)\): if its image curves were eventually periodic, infinitely many orbit points of \((1,1)\) would lie on one image curve above first coordinate \(1\). That curve has finite projection to the first factor, whereas \(g_0^n(1)\) is strictly increasing. This is impossible.

The uniform conclusion still follows in this case because simultaneous conjugacy identifies the common-preperiodic sets with those of a fixed pair, so their intersection cardinality is independent of \(t\). The proof should distinguish a constant transformed diagonal from a varying one. This is a local logical correction, not a counterexample to Theorem 1.3.
# Overall assessment and revision state

The two central corrections justify the overall Major assessment. The all-points height assertion and the unequal-degree analytic extension require revised statements. This review did not disprove the main uniform or relative conclusions. The affected downstream steps have explicit replacement arguments, with their necessary hypotheses identified.

u_i.\] Pushing forward through the Cartesian square yields \[\pi_{\mathcal C*}P
   = rac1{a_iv_i}\pi_i^*p_*
u_i,\qquad
 \pi_1^*p_*
u_1
   = rac{a_1v_1}{a_2v_2}\pi_2^*p_*
u_2,\] which proves the desired lemma with the intended positive constant. For this base-change identity one may work off the branch locus, where the finite map is a union of local biholomorphisms. Products of Green currents with continuous local potentials charge no proper analytic subsets; the equality consequently extends across that locus. problems.title: Unequal-degree exceptional maps invalidate universal commensurability
problems.source_location: arXiv p11 Theorem3.1 pp15–16 exceptional proof accepted physicalp12
claim: Recorded check: Unequal-degree exceptional maps invalidate universal commensurability
analysis: Assessment: Minor, confined to the advertised unequal-degree extension. Location: Theorem 3.1, p. 11; the exceptional branch, pp. 15–16. The theorem’s statement is identical at the inspected accepted-manuscript physical p. 12.

Take \(f_1(z)=z^2\), \(f_2(z)=z^3\), and \(C=\Delta\subset(\mathbb P^1)^2\). The diagonal is smooth and irreducible, and both projections have degree one. Both entropy measures are the same Haar measure \(m\) on \(S^1\). Indeed \((z^d)^*m=dm\), and \(m\) is the atomless balanced probability measure. Thus the normalized pullback measures agree and their supports intersect. However, no positive integers \(\ell,k\) satisfy \(2^\ell=3^k\). The equivalence asserted in Theorem 3.1 is therefore false.

These are exceptional maps associated with \(\mathbb G_m\), and the diagonal is a subgroup. The proof obtains degree commensurability in its ordinary branch; the exceptional coset argument cannot imply it. The repair must distinguish an ordinary alternative involving suitable iterates from an exceptional coset alternative without a universal commensurability requirement. Since the paper defines weak specialness for polarized pairs, the latter alternative must be stated explicitly or accompanied by an extended definition. A full rewritten generalized theorem has not been certified here.

A related local algebra error occurs in the torus converse on p. 16: \(x^{k_1}y^{k_2}=\theta\), \(|\theta|=1\), does not imply \(k_1\log^+|x|=k_2\log^+|y|\). For \(xy=1\), \(x=2\), \(y=1/2\), the two sides are \(\log2\) and \(0\). The desired measure conclusion is nevertheless correct in this example: \[\log^+|t|-\log^+|t^{-1}|=\log|t|\] is harmonic on \(\mathbb C^*\), so applying \(dd^c\) gives equality. More generally a torus coset parametrized by \((at^m,bt^n)\) has pulled-back circle measures of masses \(|m|\), \(|n|\); intersecting supports force the same support radius, and normalization by projection degree gives equality.

Impact boundary. Theorem 1.10 assumes equal degrees. Proposition 3.6 and the arithmetic proof invoke that theorem, not the false extra unequal-degree conclusion. The example therefore does not refute the equal-degree rigidity theorem or the principal arithmetic results. The local classification here reflects that verified dependency boundary, not a claim that a false theorem is merely a typographical issue.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Theorem1.10 requires equaldegree and is not refuted; arithmetic dependency trace retained.

problems.title: Nonconstant conjugacies may keep diagonal constant
problems.source_location: arXiv p31 Section6 isotrivial case source lines1478–1483
claim: Recorded check: Nonconstant conjugacies may keep diagonal constant
analysis: Assessment: Minor. Location: Section 6, p. 31, the isotrivial case of the proof of Theorem 1.3 (source lines 1478–1483).

The proof infers that \((M_1,M_2)(\Delta)\) is not constant from nonconstancy of at least one \(M_i\). Let \[M_t(z)=z+t,\qquad f_t(z)=(z+t)^2-t,\qquad
 g_t(z)=(z+t)^2+1-t.\] Both maps vary, both are conjugate to fixed maps through \(M_t\), and \((M_t,M_t)(\Delta)=\Delta\). Hence the inference fails.

This is not confined to a weakly special diagonal. The fixed map \(g_0=z^2+1\) has an infinite critical orbit of \(0\), so it is ordinary; moreover \(\Delta\) is not preperiodic for \((z^2,z^2+1)\): if its image curves were eventually periodic, infinitely many orbit points of \((1,1)\) would lie on one image curve above first coordinate \(1\). That curve has finite projection to the first factor, whereas \(g_0^n(1)\) is strictly increasing. This is impossible.

The uniform conclusion still follows in this case because simultaneous conjugacy identifies the common-preperiodic sets with those of a fixed pair, so their intersection cardinality is independent of \(t\). The proof should distinguish a constant transformed diagonal from a varying one. This is a local logical correction, not a counterexample to Theorem 1.3.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: M_t=z+t; f_t=(z+t)²−t,g_t=(z+t)²+1−t; (M_t,M_t)(Delta)=Delta.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: No theorem1.3 counterexample; nonweak-special example checked.

paragraphs: Separate constant transformed diagonal; simultaneous conjugation gives fixed common-preperiodic intersection.

report: Abstract: The Floquet decomposition, trace-class continuation, elliptic determinant argument, global analytic branches, and nonflat spectral-band structure were examined under the paper’s exact smoothness assumption. An explicit trial-subspace construction in Lemma 8.4 is invalid: a translated trial vector can have negative quadratic form even though the first vector has positive form. An exact counterexample and a complete replacement construction are given below. This lemma supports the central Mathieu–Hankel examples, including infinitely many flat bands and coexistence of flat and nonflat bands. The assessment is Major for that invalid derivation. The repair restores the lemma; the example does not disprove the spectral conclusions or the general Theorems 1.2 and 1.4. Several additional local formula corrections have no demonstrated substantive effect and are recorded separately.

Title: Initial mathematical review of
Hankel operators with band spectra and elliptic functions
Paper. Alexander Pushnitski and Alexander Sobolev, Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), no. 4, 685–746, DOI: 10.1215/00127094-2024-0043. Assignment: M25-0154.

Version. The principal input is arXiv:2307.09242v2, 14 June 2024, with its supplied TeX and figure files. The corresponding UCL accepted manuscript was separately acquired and the defective proof on p. 45 was compared directly. Printed and physical page numbers agree in both consulted PDFs. The publisher’s final PDF was not acquired, so this report makes no unverified assertion about the journal’s final wording.
# Scope, assumptions, and verified proof structure

The available figures were considered with their associated arguments; the supplied source was read as mathematical text, not executed. External monographs cited for analytic perturbation, trace ideals, and Laplace representations were not fully reread. Their specific input hypotheses were checked at the uses described in the evidence notes.

The operator is \(\mathbf Hf(t)=\int_0^\infty h(t+s)f(s)\,ds\), with \(h(t)=p(\log t)/t\), \(p\) real and \(T\)-periodic, \(T>0\), and \[\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb Z}|\widetilde p_\ell|
       \langle\ell\rangle^{1/2}<\infty,\qquad \omega=2\pi/T.\] The conclusions are not being extended to arbitrary bounded, rough log-periodic kernels. Theorem 1.4 lists only nonzero fibre eigenvalues; zero and the kernel require separate consideration.
## Floquet fibres and elliptic continuation

Theorem 4.1, pp. 21–25, correctly retains a constant-determinant alternative. Thus the zero operator and flat eigenvalue parameters are not counterexamples to its elliptic assertion. For a nonconstant determinant, the two simple poles in the \(\omega\)-by-\(2i\) cell give total order two; its derivative has total pole order four. Evenness and the periods provide four distinct half-period zeros, which are consequently all simple. This is the actual reason the critical-point count is valid.
## Global branches and spectral multiplicity

Removing the gamma phases gives \(H_*(k)=G(k)H(0)G(k)\), where \[g_n(k)=
 \sqrt{\frac{\cosh(\pi\omega n)}{\cosh(\pi(\omega n+k))}},
 \qquad \|G'(k)f\|\le\frac{\pi}{2}\|G(k)f\|.\] For either sign of a nonzero eigenvalue branch, \[|E'(k)|\le\pi|E(k)|,\qquad
 |E(k_*)|e^{-\pi|k-k_*|}
 \le |E(k)|\le |E(k_*)|e^{\pi|k-k_*|}.\] This prevents reaching zero at a finite real continuation endpoint. Compactness then reduces continuation to a finite isolated spectral cluster. The phase derivative itself is not incorrectly assumed bounded.

The flat factors must be removed before counting zeros of the residual determinant. Holomorphic division at a flat value is justified by its constant multiplicity and analytic continuation. The residual is not identically zero. Its order-two zero count yields nonflat simplicity in the open half-cell, strict monotonicity, the endpoint extremum or transverse crossing alternatives, and the separation from reflected nonflat bands (Sections 6.2–6.3). The two half-cell multiplication representations then give absolutely continuous multiplicity two. A nonzero kernel is infinite-dimensional by nonatomic direct integration, or because a finite-dimensional eigenspace would give an eigenvector of a dilation, which has none in \(L^2(\mathbb R_+)\).

The Carleman check \(p=1\) gives \(E_n(k)=\pi/\cosh(\pi(k+\omega n))\), recovering \([0,\pi]\) with touching bands and multiplicity two. It also confirms why individual analytic branches need not themselves be periodic. The Gronwall bound makes convergence of an infinite band list to zero uniform on a compact half-cell. The alternation argument in Section 7 is consistent with these checks.
# Problem 1: translation of the trial vectors destroys positivity

Assessment: Major, with a complete repair. Location: Lemma 8.4, pp. 44–46, specifically the definition of \(F_j\) and the quadratic-form calculation on p. 45. The same construction appears on p. 45 of the acquired UCL accepted manuscript.

Section 8 uses the normalized symbol \(s(\xi)=A+\cos(\omega\xi)\), so \[H(k;A)=D^*S(A)D,\qquad
 D=\operatorname{diag}(\gamma_n),\qquad
 \gamma_n=\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac12+i(\omega n+k)\right),\] where \(S(A)\) has diagonal \(A\) and two off-diagonals \(1/2\). For \(A>-1\), the proof chooses \(N>(1+A)^{-1}\), sets \[f_n=\begin{cases}\gamma_n^{-1},&1\le n\le N,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
 \qquad [F_j]_n=f_{n-(j-1)(N+2)},\] and claims that the span of any \(M\) such vectors is positive for \(H(k;A)\). It computes the form only for \(F_1\), obtaining \((1+A)N-1>0\). The weighted operator \(D^*S(A)D\) is not translation invariant, so this computation does not transfer to \(F_j\).
## An exact counterexample to the claimed positive subspace

Take \[A=-\tfrac14,\qquad \omega=1,\qquad k=-\tfrac72,\qquad
 N=2,\qquad j=2.\] These satisfy \(A>-1\), \(T=2\pi>0\), and \(N=2>4/3=(1+A)^{-1}\). Lemma 8.4 and its construction explicitly allow every real \(k\). The corresponding symbol is a trigonometric polynomial and hence meets all smoothness assumptions.

Put \[a=\gamma_5=\Gamma(\tfrac12+\tfrac32i),\qquad
 b=\gamma_6=\Gamma(\tfrac12+\tfrac52i).\] Then \(\gamma_1=\overline b\) and \(\gamma_2=\overline a\). The prescribed translation is by \(N+2=4\), so \(F_2\) is supported on \(5,6\), and \[(DF_2)_5=\frac a{\overline b},\qquad
 (DF_2)_6=\frac b{\overline a}.\] Its off-diagonal contribution is exactly \(1\), since \(\overline{(a/\overline b)}(b/\overline a)=1\). Writing \[r=\frac{|a|^2}{|b|^2}
   =\frac{\cosh(5\pi/2)}{\cosh(3\pi/2)},\] the gamma reflection identity therefore gives \[\langle H(k;-\tfrac14)F_2,F_2\rangle
    =1-\frac14(r+r^{-1})<0.\] Indeed \(r>e^\pi/2>4\). In contrast, \(\langle H(k;-\tfrac14)F_1,F_1\rangle=1/2>0\). Thus the asserted two-dimensional positive subspace is not positive. This is an exact sign contradiction, independent of finite-precision gamma evaluation. Separate high-precision computations corroborate it and are retained with their parameters and outputs.

The alternative interpretation that only the supports are translated while the weights are recomputed is precisely the repair below; it is not the displayed definition of \(F_j\). Disjoint supports do eliminate cross terms, but cannot change the negative diagonal quadratic form of \(F_2\).
## Complete correction

For \(d_j=(j-1)(N+2)\), replace the vectors by \[[\widetilde F_j]_n=
 \begin{cases}
 \gamma_n^{-1},&d_j+1\le n\le d_j+N,\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}\] Every vector has finite support and belongs to \(\ell^2(\mathbb Z)\); the gamma function is finite and nonzero at these real-\(k\) arguments. No bounded inverse for the full diagonal operator \(D\) is needed. Now \(D\widetilde F_j\) is exactly the indicator of its own block, giving \[\langle H(k;A)\widetilde F_j,\widetilde F_j\rangle
   =(N-1)+AN=(1+A)N-1>0\] for every \(j\). The gaps between blocks exceed the tridiagonal coupling range, so the cross forms vanish. Consequently every nonzero linear combination satisfies \[\left\langle H(k;A)\sum_{j=1}^M c_j\widetilde F_j,
                  \sum_{j=1}^M c_j\widetilde F_j\right\rangle
 =\big((1+A)N-1\big)\sum_{j=1}^M|c_j|^2>0.\] The vectors are linearly independent. Since \(M\) is arbitrary, the min–max principle gives infinitely many positive eigenvalues. The \(A<1\) negative-eigenvalue conclusion follows by the same sign symmetry used in the paper. The \(A\ge1\) and \(A\le-1\) semidefinite cases were already valid. Thus the correction restores the full statement of Lemma 8.4.
## Impact and surviving results

Lemma 8.4 supplies infinitude in Theorem 8.1 (p. 44) and the positive and negative band lists used in the coexistence proof of Theorem 8.6 (pp. 47–48). The invalid positive-subspace construction therefore belongs to the proof of a prominently claimed example phenomenon; it is more than a harmless sign in descriptive prose. Its short replacement does not erase that original dependency. The replacement above restores the lemma and the affected inputs. There is no counterexample here to Theorems 8.1 or 8.6, and the general Theorems 1.2 and 1.4 do not depend on this construction.

The all-gap statement in Theorem 8.5 also survives scrutiny. Fibre simplicity first gives even, periodic individual branches. For two nonflat branches, equality at different quasimomenta reduces to equality at the same quasimomentum by Theorem 6.3(v) and these symmetries. A flat value lying in a nonflat band’s range would likewise create a same-fibre degeneracy. Both possibilities contradict simplicity. This supplies the details needed beyond the terse reference to Remark 6.6(ii).
# Local corrections and limits
The following observations are retained separately from the substantive Problem. They do not change the essential spectral calculations.

In the atomic-measure example of Section 2.8, p. 16, the declared Fourier convention gives \(\widetilde s_\ell=T^{-1}e^{-i\alpha\omega\ell}\). Changing the printed positive phase to this negative phase produces diagonally unitarily equivalent fibre matrices, so the rank-one, single-band, and infinite-kernel conclusions are unchanged. In the discrete-sum comparison on p. 20, an endpoint term should be replaced by \(1\); the corrected comparison gives the same strip-dependent weight and trace-class estimate. In (7.11), p. 41, the numerator consistent with (7.8) is \(\beta(\lambda)-\Delta^\#(s_0;\lambda)\). Entireness and reality are unaffected, and the subsequent alternation calculation uses \(\alpha^2\).

The sentence following Theorem 8.9, p. 51, about sufficiently fast decay of \(\widetilde s_n\) requires a nonzero symbol if read literally: the zero operator has a nontrivial kernel. For a nonzero continuous symbol the argument is valid because the gamma-weighted Fourier series is analytic and vanishes on an open set where the symbol is nonzero. The actual Mathieu symbol is always nonzero.

Figure 3’s numerical value \(A_*\approx0.48\) is compatible with an independent computation at \(\omega=1\). The proof establishes existence for fixed \(\omega>0\), not a universal numerical crossing parameter. The displayed figure should specify its chosen \(\omega\). Numerical diagnostics do not replace the exact existence proof, and absence of the author’s plotting code is not classified as a mathematical defect. The external source search located the author revision and the accepted manuscript; it did not establish author adoption of any correction.
# Conclusion and state

The overall assessment is Major, limited to the invalid Lemma 8.4 trial-subspace derivation and its demonstrated role in the Mathieu–Hankel examples. A full local correction is verified. The broad spectral results were not disproved; the remaining inspected chains are supported by the checks and limitations stated above.

Title: Initial mathematical review of
The equivalence of lattice and Heegaard Floer homology
Paper. Ian Zemke, The equivalence of lattice and Heegaard Floer homology, Duke Mathematical Journal (2025), DOI: 10.1215/00127094-2024-0044. Assignment: M25-0155.

Version. The principal input is arXiv:2111.14962v4, 18 July 2024, 46 pages, with its supplied TeX and figures. The arXiv record identifies it as an accepted manuscript. An additional NSF repository manuscript was acquired; its extracted text agrees character for character after removal of whitespace and the arXiv stamp. That comparison is an identity check, not a proof check. Neither copy is being represented as the publisher’s final PDF. Page numbers below refer to the supplied manuscript.
# Claim, hypotheses, and scope

Theorem 1.1, p. 2, concerns finite integrally weighted plumbing trees of disk bundles over \(S^2\). All coefficients are in \(\mathbb F=\mathbb Z/2\). It asserts \[\mathbb{HF}(G)\cong \boldsymbol{HF}^{-}(Y(G))\] as \(\mathbb F[[U]]\)-modules, where the right side is completed in \(U\) and the lattice complex uses the product completion specified on p. 9. Negative definiteness is not a hypothesis. The relative-grading assertion is restricted to \(b_1(Y(G))=0\). An integral-coefficient theorem, a general extension to graphs with cycles or positive-genus vertices, and compatibility with the exterior homology action are not asserted here. The last compatibility remains Conjectures 1.2 and 7.2.

The primary conversation concentrated on the main reduction in Section 6, its hypotheses, the older lattice/surgery identification, and degenerate examples. The auxiliary checks covered the bordered algebra and Hopf models, the homology actions, and the finite-generation argument. Their actual roles and source-page observations are separately recorded. The foundational analytic construction of Heegaard Floer theory and the entirety of the lengthy external surgery-formula papers were not re-proved. In particular, the geometric left/right arc and twist conventions remain imported from the pairing theory. The final argument allows either factor: it selects a null-homologous factor when \(b_1=0\), and eliminates the correction on either finite factor when \(b_1>0\). A left/right label discrepancy alone does not demonstrate a failure of that argument.
# The main reduction and its critical steps
## The vertex complexes and the coefficient ring

Proposition 2.3, p. 11, identifies the cube obtained from vertex homology and induced length-one maps with \(\mathbb{CF}(G)\). The cited Ozsváth–Stipsicz–Szabó result was checked directly in [OSS], Lemma 4.2 and Proposition 4.4, pp. 10 and 12–14. The former supplies the completed rank-one vertex homology for plumbing links; the latter identifies the two edge maps and their powers of \(U\). The framing-independence comparison in its Lemmas 4.5–4.7 matters: this input is not restricted to the negative-definite framings used in an intermediate computation.

There is a genuine extension issue if one only proves collapse of a spectral sequence. The discussion in [Retained latex: \cite[Section 4.2]{OSS}] explicitly acknowledges it. Zemke’s Proposition 6.3 constructs a chain homotopy equivalence over the retained variable \(U_1\), rather than deducing a module isomorphism from spectral-sequence collapse. Thus that possible objection does not apply to the proof given here.
## The contraction and completion

For fixed cube coordinate \(\varepsilon\) and Alexander grading \(\mathbf s\), the uncompleted complex in (6.1), pp. 40–41, has Hopf levels \[\mathcal F^\ell\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\mathcal F^1,
 \qquad H_*\cong\mathbb F[U_1],\] with homology generated at the lowest level. Over \(\mathbb F[U_1]\) the homology and the intervening kernels are free, so the exact sequences split. The splitting can be chosen homogeneous: the differential and the modules are graded, and homogeneous lifts and a homogeneous basis of the graded submodules give the required sections. With \(\mathcal F^i=L^i\oplus R^i\), the restriction \[\partial:R^{i+1}\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }L^i\] defines \(h^i\) by inversion. Extend it by zero on the other summands. This gives \[\pi i=\mathrm{id},\qquad i\pi=\mathrm{id}+\partial h+h\partial,\qquad
 h^2=\pi h=hi=0.\] In particular, no equivariance in all variables \(U_j\) is claimed for this splitting.

The continuation to the completion on p. 41 has an applicable continuity argument. At fixed \((\varepsilon,\mathbf s)\) there are finitely many polynomial generators, each \(U_j\) has grading \(-2\), and the grading filtration and \((U_1,\ldots,U_\ell)\)-adic filtration are cofinal. The homogeneous maps therefore extend continuously. Taking the product of these coordinate maps respects the product over Alexander gradings. This does not replace that product by a direct sum or assume an arbitrary ungraded splitting to be continuous.
## Why higher arrows disappear

The mixed alpha–beta Hopf model is essential. In (3.5) and Propositions 3.9–3.10, pp. 23–25, the bottom generators are \(a,d\) and the upper generators are \(b,c\). The length-one maps preserve these levels. In the mixed model, the term \(c\mapsto d\,\mathcal V_1^{\lambda_1-1}\mathcal V_2^{\lambda_2}\) is deleted; the remaining length-two terms raise the level. The alternate model retains a lowering term and would not justify the last step. Remark 6.4 correctly distinguishes the two models.

This property propagates through a merge. For a map involving the merged root, its length is \[r=r_1+r_2-1.\] If \(r=1\), both factors have length one and preserve the total Hopf level. If \(r\ge2\), at least one factor has higher length and raises that level, while the other does not lower it. Nonroot maps inherit the property from one tensor factor.

In Lemma 6.1 each path is strictly increasing in a finite cube, so all perturbation sums are finite. Every summand transferring a higher-length map either contains an \(h\) or already contains a higher-length arrow. It consequently raises Hopf level before reaching \(\pi\), which is supported only at the bottom. It vanishes. Exactly the induced length-one differential remains. This verifies the mechanism needed for Proposition 6.3; it is stronger than a numerical test or a dimension comparison.
## The two gluing cases

Lemma 6.5, p. 42, follows because one knot surgery changes first Betti number by at most one. If the final plumbing is a rational homology sphere, the sum of the Betti numbers of the branch manifolds is at most one. At each relevant merge at least one knot is rationally null-homologous. Corollary 4.10 can therefore be applied to the appropriate left or right pair-of-pants model. The explicit homotopies in this case respect the relative grading used in Section 6.3.

For positive \(b_1\), the paper does not reuse that null-homology argument without its hypothesis. It invokes Propositions 5.1 and 5.3 instead. The finite-generation input can also be checked in [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 9.1]{General}], including partial fillings; it imposes no additional negative-framing or rational-homology-sphere restriction. The algebraic simplification is examined next. The resulting proof supports the ungraded completed-module claim; Remark 6.6 expressly leaves stronger grading compatibility open.
# Additional algebraic checks and boundary cases
## Finite generation and the Euler derivation

The coefficient ring relevant to the \(h\)-map in Section 5 is \[S=\mathbb F((\mathcal V^{-1}))[[\mathcal U]],
 \qquad U=\mathcal U\mathcal V,\] a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer associate to \(U\). It is not an arbitrary two-variable Laurent power-series ring. For a finite free complex over \(S\), the square-zero differential splits into one-step summands and two-step summands with differential \(U^j\).

The apparent extra \(\mathbb Z/2\) grading hypothesis in Lemma 5.5 is not an obstruction to the application in Corollary 5.6. Even without an assigned parity, \(\operatorname{im}\partial\) is free, so \(0\to\ker\partial\to C\to\operatorname{im}\partial\to0\) splits. Smith normal form for the inclusion \(\operatorname{im}\partial\subset\ker\partial\) then yields the same decomposition.

The formal derivation \(E=\mathcal U\partial_{\mathcal U}+\mathcal V\partial_{\mathcal V}\) satisfies \[E(U^j)=2jU^j=0\] in characteristic two. Differentiating a change-of-basis chain equation gives the conjugating chain homotopy. Thus \(\mathcal U\Phi+\mathcal V\Psi\) is null-homotopic over precisely the enlarged coefficient ring allowed for the \(h\)-map. This supplies the extra-term elimination in Proposition 5.1. It is not a claim that the analogous action vanishes over every smaller coefficient ring.
## Homology actions

The torsion argument in Lemma 4.1 uses an integer-valued function on the Alexander lattice with prescribed increments. It does not divide by the order of a torsion class in \(\mathbb F\), which would be invalid for even torsion. Section 7 admits the same translation to characteristic vectors.

The exterior relations can also be checked directly. Write \[a_v(K,E)=g(K,E-v)-g(K,E).\] For distinct \(v,w\), the exponent in \(A_vA_w\) telescopes to \(g(K,E-\{v,w\})-g(K,E)\), independently of the order. The mixed terms with the other half of the lattice differential telescope in the same way, using the shifted characteristic vector. Thus \(A_v\) is a chain map, distinct actions commute in characteristic two, and \(A_v^2=0\) because a vertex cannot be deleted twice. As in the differential itself, the expression is zero when \(v\notin E\). These checks support well-definedness of the lattice action, without proving the expressly conjectural compatibility under Theorem 1.1.
## A degenerate one-vertex check

For the single vertex of weight zero, write \(K(v)=2n\). The two targets of the lattice differential coincide, and the coefficient is \[U^{\max(0,-n)}+U^{\max(0,n)}.\] For \(n\ne0\) it is \(1+U^{|n|}\), a unit in \(\mathbb F[[U]]\); that component is contractible. For \(n=0\) it vanishes, leaving one copy of \(\mathbb F[[U]]\) in each of the two cube levels. This gives \(\mathbb F[[U]]\oplus\mathbb F[[U]]\), as required for the completed theory of \(S^1\times S^2\). Completion is essential to the unit argument. The retained auxiliary calculations also examine positive weight and a three-vertex zero-weight tree, where the positive-\(b_1\) gluing argument is needed. These examples test boundary assumptions and do not replace the general proof.
# Local clarifications and assessment

The following are local corrections, not numbered substantive Problems. In Section 3.2, p. 16, the first displayed \(\tau\mathcal V\) relation should read \(\tau\mathcal V=\mathcal U\mathcal V^2\tau\), as follows from the immediately following \(\phi^\tau(\mathcal V)=U\mathcal V\) and the symmetric-variable description. In the merge formula of Section 3.6 the output of the \(\tau,\tau\) operation should have idempotent \(i_1\), consistently with the balanced tensor product. The caption of Figure 3.1 reverses the alpha/beta order of the two input arcs stated in the surrounding text; the pairing hypothesis requires opposite types. Finally, on p. 41 the inverse defining \(h^i\) is the inverse of \(\partial|_{R^{i+1}}\), not of its zero restriction to \(L^{i+1}\); the displayed splitting diagram already specifies the correct map. No downstream use of these literal misprints producing a substantive failure was established.

Abstract: The reviewed source is the 25-page arXiv manuscript 2302.07069v1. An explicit smooth complete intersection refutes the prescribed-fiber lifting assertion in Claim 25.2. Title: Technical Verification of
Stable Maps of Curves and Algebraic Equivalence of 1-Cycles
# Identity, version and scope

The paper is by János Kollár and Zhiyu Tian, published in Duke Mathematical Journal 174(5) (2025), 911–947, DOI `10.1215/00127094-2024-0045`. The scientific source inspected here is arXiv:2302.07069v1, dated 14 February 2023 [KT]. All page references below refer to its printed pages, which agree with PDF pages 1–25. The assigned PDF, TeX source and source archive were hash-checked. Author and institutional pages confirm identity; the publisher endpoints returned a security-check page. The journal body was not obtained and is not assumed to coincide with this manuscript.

The review read the manuscript and traced the principal dependencies: the elementary changes in Sections 2–4, the assembly and descent in Section 5, the comb construction in Section 6, the arithmetic applications in Section 7, and the loop and residue-field statements in Sections 8–9. The strongest direct checks are the two constructions below, the index/Euler-characteristic calculation, and the descent bookkeeping. External semistable-reduction, Bertini and deformation-theory results were not all re-proved from their original sources. This is an initial review, not independent acceptance.
# Definitions and operative hypotheses

Theorem 1 concerns finitely many maps from nodal curves to a smooth projective variety over an algebraically closed field, whose pushforward cycles are algebraically equivalent. It appends mutually isomorphic curve maps and asks for deformation equivalence of the resulting maps. Theorem 2 adds a perfect ground field and equality of Euler characteristics. Its endpoints descend to the specified extension field, and its common tail descends to the ground field; Remark 3 explicitly does not descend the entire connecting family.

In Paragraph 25, for \(n=\dim X\), an \(H^{ci}\)-curve is \[L=H_1\cap\cdots\cap H_{n-1}\cap H_n^*
 \subset X\times\mathbb P^1,\qquad
 H_i\in p_1^*|H|,\quad H_n^*\in|p_1^*H+p_2^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(2)|.\] It must be smooth, and a length-two subscheme \(T\subset L\) is marked. The linear system \(H=mA\), \(A\) very ample and \(m\geq2\), is explicitly allowed. Claim 25.2 purports to lift an arbitrary reduced base curve in the marked length-two Hilbert scheme with arbitrary prescribed values in this family at finitely many base points.

In Theorem 44 the ambient variety is smooth projective of dimension at least three over a perfect field. Its bounded locally closed set \(W\) of nodal handles is not required to parametrize connected curves. A comb with \(r\) teeth is balanced when every irreducible handle component has at least \(r/(2c)\) teeth, where \(c\) is the number of components. Definition 42 further requires freeness and the vanishing of \(H^1\) after a divisor of degree at most \(d\) on every handle subcurve.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Prescribed-fiber lifting fails when projected marks coalesce).  Assessment: Major. The affected assertions are the projective-bundle description in Paragraph 25 and Claim 25.2, p. 11. Corollary 26 on the same page invokes that claim directly.
## A complete admissible input

Work over \(\mathbb C\), put \(X=\mathbb P^2\), and take \(H=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(2)\). On \(B=\mathbb A^1_t\) mark the two points \[((0,0),[1:0]),\qquad ((t,0),[0:1])\] in the affine chart \(Z=1\) of \(X\times\mathbb P^1\). They remain distinct even at \(t=0\), so they define an honest morphism \(g:B\to\operatorname{Hilb}_{(2)}(X\times\mathbb P^1)\); designate the first point as the marked one.

Equation reference: eq:L, eq:binary. At \(0\) prescribe the conic \(Q_0=(XZ+Y^2=0)\) and the intersection \(L_0\) of \(Q_0\times\mathbb P^1\) with the divisor \[
 X^2S^2+Z^2SW+(YZ+X^2)W^2=0.\] This divisor has bidegree \((2,2)\), as required. Parametrizing \(Q_0\) by \([X:Y:Z]=[-u^2:uv:v^2]\) gives \[
 u^4S^2+v^4SW+(uv^3+u^4)W^2=0.\] The coefficients do not vanish simultaneously, so the projection to \(Q_0\) is finite of degree two. Its discriminant is \(\Delta=v^8-4u^5v^3-4u^8\). It is nonzero at infinity and is squarefree: a common root of \(1-4z^5-4z^8\) and its derivative would satisfy \(z^3=-5/8\) and \(z^5=2/3\), giving incompatible values of \(z^{15}\). Thus \(L_0\) is smooth. At \([u:v]=[0:1]\), equation [eq:binary] (#eq:binary) is \(SW=0\), so \(L_0\) contains both prescribed marks. This verifies, rather than assumes, that the specified fiber belongs to the source’s \(H^{ci}\)-family.
## The obstruction

If the asserted lift existed, the pulled-back conics \(Q_t\) would form a family regular near \(0\), specializing to \(Q_0\), and passing through \((0,0)\) and \((t,0)\). Write its affine equation as \[q_t(x,y)=a_{20}(t)x^2+a_{11}(t)xy+a_{02}(t)y^2
              +a_{10}(t)x+a_{01}(t)y+a_{00}(t).\] Choose a local projective coefficient chart containing \(Q_0\). The incidence conditions imply \[a_{00}(t)=0,\qquad t a_{10}(t)+t^2a_{20}(t)=0.\] Over the punctured base, \(a_{10}(t)+t a_{20}(t)=0\), hence regularity forces \(a_{10}(0)=0\). But \(q_0=x+y^2\) has \(a_{10}(0)\neq0\). This contradiction rules out even a rational lift defined at the prescribed point. A dominant ramified base change does not remove it: replace \(t\) by the nonzero local base parameter function and cancel it in the same identity.

The source’s bundle argument overlooks the rank jump in conditions imposed on \(p_1^*H\): two distinct projections impose two value conditions, whereas two points over the same \(x\) impose only one. Their limiting incidence nevertheless remembers a tangent direction. The extra \(\mathbb P^1\)-coordinate keeps the marks distinct but does not make the pulled-back divisors separate them.
## Counterevidence, dependency and repair boundary

This uses the most favorable reading of the forgetful map in Claim 25.2; its notation is not the objection. No stated condition excludes two different points in a common \(p_1\)-fiber. Increasing the degree does not remove the same first-order restriction. On a locus where the projections impose independent constant-rank conditions, the projective-bundle interpolation argument can work.

The explicit dependency is Claim 25.2 \(\to\) Corollary 26 \(\to\) the proof of Theorem 29 (p. 12) \(\to\) Theorem 31 (p. 13) \(\to\) Proposition 34 (pp. 14–15) \(\to\) Paragraphs 35–36 proving Theorems 1–2. These proofs require a justified gluing construction in place of the false unrestricted lifting assertion. This demonstrated invalid step is closely tied to the central contribution, which supports Major severity. It does not show that Theorems 1–2, or their arithmetic consequences, are false.

Using sufficiently ample divisors on \(X\times\mathbb P^1\) in every factor would remove this particular failure of length-two separation. It also changes the curve family and its double-cover description; the interpolation, moving and later teeth properties would need to be re-established. Another possible repair is to allow additional components of the base contracted to a bad marked point, varying the connector first inside a fixed incidence fiber. Theorem 29 permits base changes that may leave room for this maneuver. Such components are absent from fixed-base Claim 25.2, and the required construction at arbitrary pivots and branches is not supplied by its proof. Neither repair route is claimed to be a complete replacement proof here.

Problem 2 (The comb theorem omits connectedness of the handles).  Assessment: Minor. Theorem 44, p. 19, asserts that a single \(r>0\) gives both connected fibers and surjectivity on extension-field points. Its proof in Paragraph 47 moves teeth across nodes, without a connected-handle hypothesis.
## A counterexample to the existential choice of \(r\)

Let \(Y=\mathbb P^3_{\mathbb C}\), \(d=1\), and let \(W\) consist of two points: one represents \(C_2\), a union of two disjoint lines; the other represents \(C_3\), a union of three disjoint lines. This is a bounded locally closed subset of \(\operatorname{Hilb}^{nodal}_1(Y)\). Take all pointed lines as the teeth. The tangent-direction map is the isomorphism with \(\mathbb P(TY)\); its fibers are geometrically irreducible. For a fixed marked point \(x\), evaluation away from it identifies the universal line with \(Y\setminus\{x\}\). Finally \(N_{\ell/Y}=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)^{\oplus2}\), so the vanishing required in (39.5) holds. All hypotheses on the teeth are satisfied.

For transverse teeth meeting just their designated handle and avoiding one another, these combs are free and 1-free along every handle subcurve. One can check this without assuming Theorem 44: the normal restriction on a handle line is a positive elementary modification of \(\mathcal O(1)^{\oplus2}\); on a tooth it is \(\mathcal O(1)\oplus\mathcal O(2)\). The latter evaluates surjectively at its unique node and remains globally generated after vanishing there. The normalization sequence, using the teeth independently at their nodes, gives \(H^1(N(-D))=0\) for every allowed divisor of degree at most one. The same argument proves global generation and applies after removing any handle components; detached teeth cause no obstruction.

If \(r=1\), there is no balanced comb on \(C_2\). If \(r=2\), there is no balanced comb on \(C_3\). Thus (44.3) fails in these cases. For every integer \(r\geq3\), balanced combs on \(C_2\) have allocations \[m_1+m_2=r,\qquad m_i\geq \lceil r/4\rceil .\] There are \(r-2\lceil r/4\rceil+1\geq2\) such allocations, each realized by the free combs just described. Within the fiber over the fixed disconnected handle, the number of attachment points on each open and closed component is locally constant. The distinct allocations therefore lie in disjoint nonempty open and closed pieces. Consequently (44.1) fails for every remaining \(r\). The two-element choice of \(W\) is essential: a singleton handle at its smallest feasible tooth number would not refute the existential quantifier.
## Impact and boundary

The manuscript does not globally define curves to be connected; it explicitly introduces connectedness when needed, for example in Lemma 37. Allowing triple nodes does not connect two disjoint handle components. A corrected connected-handle hypothesis removes the obstruction exhibited here and matches the tooth-sliding argument. The intended main applications first arrange connected handles. No central damage from this separate omission is established, hence Minor rather than Major severity for this problem. A complete re-proof of all uniformity and field-point statements of a corrected Theorem 44 is not asserted.

Problem 3 (A union of free curves need not be free).  Assessment: Minor. Claim 38.3, p. 17, says that if \(C_1,C_2\) are free and \(C_1+C_2\) is locally unobstructed, their union is free. There is no restriction on the number of intersection points.

In the plane \(W=0\) of \(\mathbb P^3_{\mathbb C}\), take \[C_1=(XZ-Y^2=0),\qquad C_2=(X^2+Y^2+Z^2=0).\] Both are smooth conics. Under the parametrization \([X:Y:Z]=[u^2:uv:v^2]\) of \(C_1\), the second equation becomes \(u^4+u^2v^2+v^4=0\). It has four distinct roots, so their union \(C\) is a connected nodal plane quartic and has locally unobstructed singularities. Each conic has \(N_{C_i/\mathbb P^3}=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(4)\oplus\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(2)\), hence is free. But \(C\) is the complete intersection of degrees \(1,4\), and therefore \[N_{C/\mathbb P^3}=\mathcal O_C(1)\oplus\mathcal O_C(4),\qquad
 \omega_C=\mathcal O_C(1),\qquad
 H^1(C,\mathcal O_C(1))\simeq H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)^*\simeq\mathbb C.\] Thus \(H^1(C,N_{C/\mathbb P^3})\ne0\), contradicting freeness as defined immediately before the claim. Local unobstructedness of the nodes does not remove this global cohomology group.

This refutes the unrestricted union assertion, including its displayed normal-sheaf justification. It does not show failure of the specialized operation of attaching one tooth at one point; that operation can be checked using normal restrictions and the normalization sequence, as done independently in Problem 2. The full intended tooth-sliding and triple-node argument still needs its appropriate local justification. No additional central damage from this generalization alone is established, so the classification is Minor.

Problem 4 (The degree and counting strengthenings of Lemma 60 are false).  Assessment: Minor. In Lemma 60, p. 24, part (60.1) requires infinitely many residue degrees when the perfect field is infinite, and part (60.2) requires at least \(q^d/2\) closed points of degree \(d\) for every \(d\) in an infinite set when \(k=\mathbb F_q\). Both fail already for the identity morphism of the affine line.

For \(k=\mathbb C\), every closed point of \(\mathbb A^1_k\) has degree one. Thus no infinite subset of degrees can satisfy (60.1). For \(k=\mathbb F_q\), let \(N_d\) count degree-\(d\) closed points of \(\mathbb A^1_k\). Each contributes \(d\) distinct \(\mathbb F_{q^d}\)-points, so \(dN_d\leq q^d\). For every \(d>2\) this contradicts the asserted \(N_d\geq q^d/2\); an infinite permissible degree set is impossible. These inputs satisfy perfectness and the nonconstant-morphism hypothesis.

Poonen’s qualitative equal-residue-field assertion is compatible with both examples. In the descent construction, applying it on successive nonempty opens avoids finitely many forbidden attachment points. Thus the proof need not use either false strengthening. The infinite-degree assertion is not repaired merely by inserting a missing factor \(1/d\) into the finite-field count: the degree set itself must also be qualified for infinite fields. The statement requires correction, but the present evidence establishes only a local Minor defect. No replacement uniform counting theorem for all bounded families in (60.3) is certified.
# Other checks and limits

The normalization contribution to Euler characteristic in Paragraph 50 is supported on a zero-cycle and is divisible by the index. The canonical divisor gives \(\operatorname{ind}(X)\mid2\chi(C)\). These checks explain why the invariant \(2\chi(C)/\operatorname{ind}(X)\bmod2\), rather than an unqualified integer genus, controls the possible order-two kernel. The descent bookkeeping of Theorem 2 is conditional on the earlier geometric construction: equal-residue-field attachment points allow one to add Galois orbits of tails while retaining distinct nodes. Poonen’s Corollary 2 [Poo] supplies that qualitative point-existence input over a perfect field.

Several observations were not promoted to additional substantive Problems. The sign of the node term in Example 9 does not change its congruence obstruction. Lemma 52’s construction must be read for effective cycles; unrestricted negative coefficients cannot be pushforwards of curves. Positive/negative decomposition supplies effective inputs in its intended application. These local presentation corrections do not establish an additional failure of the principal conclusions.

Paragraph 55 also invokes the perfect-field criterion (6.2) over the fraction field of a Henselian DVR with perfect residue field. Such a fraction field need not be perfect in equal positive characteristic. An extension of the criterion or a descent reduction needs checking; this review has not supplied one and does not turn that unresolved point into a counterexample. The loop construction was checked as a dependency trace, not as an independent proof bypassing Problems 1–2. No missing author code was treated as a mathematical defect.
# Conclusion and state

The highest supported assessment for the reviewed version is Major, from Problem 1. Problems 2–4 are separate local Minor defects. No published-version correction or author adoption was established by the source search.
