analysis: Assessment: Major. The affected assertions are the projective-bundle description in Paragraph 25 and Claim 25.2, p. 11. Corollary 26 on the same page invokes that claim directly.

Work over \(\mathbb C\), put \(X=\mathbb P^2\), and take \(H=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(2)\). On \(B=\mathbb A^1_t\) mark the two points \[((0,0),[1:0]),\qquad ((t,0),[0:1])\] in the affine chart \(Z=1\) of \(X\times\mathbb P^1\). They remain distinct even at \(t=0\), so they define an honest morphism \(g:B\to\operatorname{Hilb}_{(2)}(X\times\mathbb P^1)\); designate the first point as the marked one.

Equation reference: eq:L, eq:binary. At \(0\) prescribe the conic \(Q_0=(XZ+Y^2=0)\) and the intersection \(L_0\) of \(Q_0\times\mathbb P^1\) with the divisor \[
 X^2S^2+Z^2SW+(YZ+X^2)W^2=0.\] This divisor has bidegree \((2,2)\), as required. Parametrizing \(Q_0\) by \([X:Y:Z]=[-u^2:uv:v^2]\) gives \[
 u^4S^2+v^4SW+(uv^3+u^4)W^2=0.\] The coefficients do not vanish simultaneously, so the projection to \(Q_0\) is finite of degree two. Its discriminant is \(\Delta=v^8-4u^5v^3-4u^8\). It is nonzero at infinity and is squarefree: a common root of \(1-4z^5-4z^8\) and its derivative would satisfy \(z^3=-5/8\) and \(z^5=2/3\), giving incompatible values of \(z^{15}\). Thus \(L_0\) is smooth. At \([u:v]=[0:1]\), equation [eq:binary] (#eq:binary) is \(SW=0\), so \(L_0\) contains both prescribed marks. This verifies, rather than assumes, that the specified fiber belongs to the source’s \(H^{ci}\)-family.

If the asserted lift existed, the pulled-back conics \(Q_t\) would form a family regular near \(0\), specializing to \(Q_0\), and passing through \((0,0)\) and \((t,0)\). Write its affine equation as \[q_t(x,y)=a_{20}(t)x^2+a_{11}(t)xy+a_{02}(t)y^2
              +a_{10}(t)x+a_{01}(t)y+a_{00}(t).\] Choose a local projective coefficient chart containing \(Q_0\). The incidence conditions imply \[a_{00}(t)=0,\qquad t a_{10}(t)+t^2a_{20}(t)=0.\] Over the punctured base, \(a_{10}(t)+t a_{20}(t)=0\), hence regularity forces \(a_{10}(0)=0\). But \(q_0=x+y^2\) has \(a_{10}(0)\neq0\). This contradiction rules out even a rational lift defined at the prescribed point. A dominant ramified base change does not remove it: replace \(t\) by the nonzero local base parameter function and cancel it in the same identity.

The source’s bundle argument overlooks the rank jump in conditions imposed on \(p_1^*H\): two distinct projections impose two value conditions, whereas two points over the same \(x\) impose only one. Their limiting incidence nevertheless remembers a tangent direction. The extra \(\mathbb P^1\)-coordinate keeps the marks distinct but does not make the pulled-back divisors separate them.
result: This uses the most favorable reading of the forgetful map in Claim 25.2; its notation is not the objection. No stated condition excludes two different points in a common \(p_1\)-fiber. Increasing the degree does not remove the same first-order restriction. On a locus where the projections impose independent constant-rank conditions, the projective-bundle interpolation argument can work.

The explicit dependency is Claim 25.2 \(\to\) Corollary 26 \(\to\) the proof of Theorem 29 (p. 12) \(\to\) Theorem 31 (p. 13) \(\to\) Proposition 34 (pp. 14–15) \(\to\) Paragraphs 35–36 proving Theorems 1–2. These proofs require a justified gluing construction in place of the false unrestricted lifting assertion. This demonstrated invalid step is closely tied to the central contribution, which supports Major severity. It does not show that Theorems 1–2, or their arithmetic consequences, are false.

Using sufficiently ample divisors on \(X\times\mathbb P^1\) in every factor would remove this particular failure of length-two separation. It also changes the curve family and its double-cover description; the interpolation, moving and later teeth properties would need to be re-established. Another possible repair is to allow additional components of the base contracted to a bad marked point, varying the connector first inside a fixed incidence fiber. Theorem 29 permits base changes that may leave room for this maneuver. Such components are absent from fixed-base Claim 25.2, and the required construction at arbitrary pivots and branches is not supplied by its proof. Neither repair route is claimed to be a complete replacement proof here.
Result: All original hypotheses verified; no rational lift regular at0 exists. Exact polynomial gcd=1 and commonroot contradiction retained.

problems.source_location: Theorem44 and proof47,p19; Definitions39–42,pp17–18
claim:
In Paragraph 25, for \(n=\dim X\), an \(H^{ci}\)-curve is \[L=H_1\cap\cdots\cap H_{n-1}\cap H_n^*
 \subset X\times\mathbb P^1,\qquad
 H_i\in p_1^*|H|,\quad H_n^*\in|p_1^*H+p_2^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(2)|.\] It must be smooth, and a length-two subscheme \(T\subset L\) is marked. The linear system \(H=mA\), \(A\) very ample and \(m\geq2\), is explicitly allowed. Claim 25.2 purports to lift an arbitrary reduced base curve in the marked length-two Hilbert scheme with arbitrary prescribed values in this family at finitely many base points.

In Theorem 44 the ambient variety is smooth projective of dimension at least three over a perfect field. Its bounded locally closed set \(W\) of nodal handles is not required to parametrize connected curves. A comb with \(r\) teeth is balanced when every irreducible handle component has at least \(r/(2c)\) teeth, where \(c\) is the number of components. Definition 42 further requires freeness and the vanishing of \(H^1\) after a divisor of degree at most \(d\) on every handle subcurve.
For anyboundedlocallyclosednodalW, somepositiveinteger r gives connected combfibers and surjectivityonfieldpoints.
Y=P3_C,d=1,W={C2,C3},whereCn isunionofn disjointlines; allpointedlinesasteeth satisfy39.2–5.
analysis: Assessment: Minor. Theorem 44, p. 19, asserts that a single \(r>0\) gives both connected fibers and surjectivity on extension-field points. Its proof in Paragraph 47 moves teeth across nodes, without a connected-handle hypothesis.

Let \(Y=\mathbb P^3_{\mathbb C}\), \(d=1\), and let \(W\) consist of two points: one represents \(C_2\), a union of two disjoint lines; the other represents \(C_3\), a union of three disjoint lines. This is a bounded locally closed subset of \(\operatorname{Hilb}^{nodal}_1(Y)\). Take all pointed lines as the teeth. The tangent-direction map is the isomorphism with \(\mathbb P(TY)\); its fibers are geometrically irreducible. For a fixed marked point \(x\), evaluation away from it identifies the universal line with \(Y\setminus\{x\}\). Finally \(N_{\ell/Y}=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)^{\oplus2}\), so the vanishing required in (39.5) holds. All hypotheses on the teeth are satisfied.

For transverse teeth meeting just their designated handle and avoiding one another, these combs are free and 1-free along every handle subcurve. One can check this without assuming Theorem 44: the normal restriction on a handle line is a positive elementary modification of \(\mathcal O(1)^{\oplus2}\); on a tooth it is \(\mathcal O(1)\oplus\mathcal O(2)\). The latter evaluates surjectively at its unique node and remains globally generated after vanishing there. The normalization sequence, using the teeth independently at their nodes, gives \(H^1(N(-D))=0\) for every allowed divisor of degree at most one. The same argument proves global generation and applies after removing any handle components; detached teeth cause no obstruction.

If \(r=1\), there is no balanced comb on \(C_2\). If \(r=2\), there is no balanced comb on \(C_3\). Thus (44.3) fails in these cases. For every integer \(r\geq3\), balanced combs on \(C_2\) have allocations \[m_1+m_2=r,\qquad m_i\geq \lceil r/4\rceil .\] There are \(r-2\lceil r/4\rceil+1\geq2\) such allocations, each realized by the free combs just described. Within the fiber over the fixed disconnected handle, the number of attachment points on each open and closed component is locally constant. The distinct allocations therefore lie in disjoint nonempty open and closed pieces. Consequently (44.1) fails for every remaining \(r\). The two-element choice of \(W\) is essential: a singleton handle at its smallest feasible tooth number would not refute the existential quantifier.

The manuscript does not globally define curves to be connected; it explicitly introduces connectedness when needed, for example in Lemma 37. Allowing triple nodes does not connect two disjoint handle components. A corrected connected-handle hypothesis removes the obstruction exhibited here and matches the tooth-sliding argument. The intended main applications first arrange connected handles. No central damage from this separate omission is established, hence Minor rather than Major severity for this problem. A complete re-proof of all uniformity and field-point statements of a corrected Theorem 44 is not asserted.
result: Result: No r satisfiesallconclusions. Two-elementWclosesexistentialquantifierloophole.

analysis: Assessment: Minor. Claim 38.3, p. 17, says that if \(C_1,C_2\) are free and \(C_1+C_2\) is locally unobstructed, their union is free. There is no restriction on the number of intersection points.

In the plane \(W=0\) of \(\mathbb P^3_{\mathbb C}\), take \[C_1=(XZ-Y^2=0),\qquad C_2=(X^2+Y^2+Z^2=0).\] Both are smooth conics. Under the parametrization \([X:Y:Z]=[u^2:uv:v^2]\) of \(C_1\), the second equation becomes \(u^4+u^2v^2+v^4=0\). It has four distinct roots, so their union \(C\) is a connected nodal plane quartic and has locally unobstructed singularities. Each conic has \(N_{C_i/\mathbb P^3}=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(4)\oplus\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(2)\), hence is free. But \(C\) is the complete intersection of degrees \(1,4\), and therefore \[N_{C/\mathbb P^3}=\mathcal O_C(1)\oplus\mathcal O_C(4),\qquad
 \omega_C=\mathcal O_C(1),\qquad
 H^1(C,\mathcal O_C(1))\simeq H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)^*\simeq\mathbb C.\] Thus \(H^1(C,N_{C/\mathbb P^3})\ne0\), contradicting freeness as defined immediately before the claim. Local unobstructedness of the nodes does not remove this global cohomology group.

This refutes the unrestricted union assertion, including its displayed normal-sheaf justification. It does not show failure of the specialized operation of attaching one tooth at one point; that operation can be checked using normal restrictions and the normalization sequence, as done independently in Problem 2. The full intended tooth-sliding and triple-node argument still needs its appropriate local justification. No additional central damage from this generalization alone is established, so the classification is Minor.

analysis: Assessment: Minor. In Lemma 60, p. 24, part (60.1) requires infinitely many residue degrees when the perfect field is infinite, and part (60.2) requires at least \(q^d/2\) closed points of degree \(d\) for every \(d\) in an infinite set when \(k=\mathbb F_q\). For \(k=\mathbb C\), every closed point of \(\mathbb A^1_k\) has degree one. Thus no infinite subset of degrees can satisfy (60.1). For \(k=\mathbb F_q\), let \(N_d\) count degree-\(d\) closed points of \(\mathbb A^1_k\). Each contributes \(d\) distinct \(\mathbb F_{q^d}\)-points, so \(dN_d\leq q^d\). Title: Initial mathematical review: M25-0157
On the Balmer spectrum of the Morel–Voevodsky category
Authors: Peng Du and Alexander Vishik. Publication identity: Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), no. 6, 1013–1044; DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0051 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0051).
Reviewed version: arXiv:2309.09077v3, 28 July 2024, 28 PDF pages. All page references below are to that manuscript, with its printed pagination.

Initial assessment: Major. Two printed derivations supporting the main theorem use false auxiliary assertions: the infinite-height bridge to conservativity, and annihilation of a local projector in the field-equivalence argument. Both required intermediate conclusions admit the repairs proved below; no counterexample to Theorem 7.6 is established. A separate finite-generation assertion also fails at infinite height, outside its actual downstream use. Severity is assigned to the demonstrated proof dependencies, separately from survival of the repaired conclusions. This is an initial review under frozen contract 0.7.1; the scientific decision remains `pending`, and `human_reviews=[]`. It is not an independent acceptance decision.
# Scope and central argument

The paper constructs prime tensor ideals \(\mathfrak a_{(p,m),E}\) of the compact Morel–Voevodsky category over a characteristic-zero field. Here \(p\) is prime, \(1\le m\le\infty\), and \(E/k\) is an arbitrary field extension, considered up to the stated \(K(p,m)\)-equivalence. Theorem 7.6 asserts primality, the exact coincidence criterion for these ideals, and compatibility at \(m=\infty\) with isotropic motivic points. The use of a flexible closure, compactness, and the infinite-height convention are substantive hypotheses, not cosmetic notation.

The entire assigned text was read, and the following chain was examined: anisotropy and its coefficient-ideal criterion (Section 2); the two localizations and the compact-object description (Section 3); the bounded weight structure and numerical heart (Section 4); invariant annihilator radicals (Section 5); semisimplicity and the tensor weight complex (Section 6); the finite-height annihilator argument, primality, and the infinite-height endpoint (Section 7); and local categories, conservativity, separation of fields and heights, and examples (Section 8). They were collaborators within this initial review, not independent adjudicators.

The exact coefficient convention matters: \[\mathbb L_{(p)}=BP[x_i:i\ne p^r-1],\qquad
 P(m)=BP/(p,v_1,\ldots,v_{m-1}).\] At infinite height \(P(\infty)=\mathbb F_p\), but \(P(\infty)[x]=\mathbb F_p[x]\) still has the non-\(p\)-typical polynomial variables. The target of the Morava coefficient change is \(K(p,\infty)=\mathbb F_p\).
# Problem 1: finite generation fails at infinite height
Location. Proposition 5.2, p. 12, and its finite-presentation argument on p. 13; compare Proposition 4.3, p. 11, and the separate infinite-height case in Proposition 7.4, p. 17.

Claim and decisive test. Proposition 5.2 states that the radical of the coefficient annihilator of a compact object is finitely generated. It does not restrict \(m\) to finite height. Take a flexible characteristic-zero field, for example \(k=\mathbb C(t_1,t_2,\ldots)\), and take the compact localized unit in \(\widehat{\mathrm{SH}}_{(p,\infty)}(k/k)\). This is the first localization, before the further quotient in Definition 3.1. Its \(\mathrm{MGL}\)-motive is the unit in the numerical heart of Proposition 4.3. The graded coefficient endomorphisms of that unit are \(\mathbb F_p[x]\). Numerical equivalence introduces no additional relation on the point: pairing a nonzero coefficient with \(1\) detects it. Consequently, after \(p\)-localization, \[J=\operatorname{Ann}_{\mathbb L_{(p)}}(\widehat M^{\mathrm{MGL}}(\mathbf1))
   =(p,v_1,v_2,\ldots)\mathbb L_{(p)} .\] This ideal is radical, since the quotient is the polynomial domain \(\mathbb F_p[x]\).

It is not finitely generated. Any finite family of elements of \(J\) involves only finitely many of the variables \(v_i\). For a sufficiently large \(N\), that family belongs to \((p,v_1,\ldots,v_N)\). Its generated ideal therefore cannot contain \(v_{N+1}\): the latter survives in the polynomial quotient by \((p,v_1,\ldots,v_N)\). This is an algebraic counterexample under the paper’s own flexible-field and compactness hypotheses. Finite generation before localization would imply finite generation after localization, so working \(p\)-locally does not evade the claim.

Failed proof step. For the one-term weight complex of this unit, the endomorphism module is \(\mathbb F_p[x]\) as an \(\mathbb L_{(p)}\)-module. It has infinitely many independent defining relations \(p,v_1,v_2,\ldots\). The finite-presentation assertion used on p. 13 is therefore unavailable at \(m=\infty\).

Impact, counterevidence, and repair boundary. Restrict Proposition 5.2 and the finite-presentation argument to \(m<\infty\), with the flexible-field hypothesis used in the proof made explicit. The demonstrated counterexample does not affect finite height. More importantly, Proposition 7.4 explicitly separates \(m=\infty\) and uses conservativity there, rather than this finite-generation argument. The downstream main-theorem damage is thus not established. The defect is assessed as Minor, based on this actual dependency boundary. The unit counterexample itself is fully verified; a uniform theorem over nonflexible fields is not supplied by this review.

There is also a harmless logical convention to state in Proposition 5.3: if the \(\mathrm{MGL}\)-motive is zero, its annihilator is the whole ring. The proper-prime description applies to the nonzero case; the zero case in Proposition 7.4 is immediate. This qualification is recorded without promoting it to a separate Problem.
# Problem 2: the infinite-height functor is not an equivalence

Location. The coefficient-change functor displayed immediately before Proposition 7.1, p. 15, and the first sentence of its proof, p. 16. Its required downstream use is the last sentence of Proposition 7.4, p. 17.

Decisive evidence. At \(m=\infty\) this functor is induced by \[R=\mathbb F_p[x]\longrightarrow \mathbb F_p,\qquad x_i\longmapsto0.\] It is not faithful, even on the heart, and hence cannot be an equivalence. For instance, take \(p=2\). The allowed variable \(x_2\) is a nonzero coefficient morphism \(\mathbf1(2)[4]\to\mathbf1\) in numerical \(R\)-motives. It survives numerical equivalence over the point, but maps to zero after coefficient change. Viewed as a morphism between one-term complexes, it gives the same failure in the bounded homotopy category. Thus the asserted equivalence cannot be justified by passing to complexes.

The needed weaker assertion and its repair. The argument needs conservativity, not faithfulness. Here is a bounded proof of that weaker assertion. Numerical correspondences for the polynomial extension of \(CH/p\) are numerical \(CH/p\) correspondences tensored with \(R\): numerical triviality is tested coefficient by coefficient by the degree pairing. In the presentation inherited from \(\mathbb L_{(p)}=BP[x]\), an orientation change gives the same correspondence category; its Todd factors are invertible and do not remove the polynomial variables.

Let \(V\) be a fixed finite direct sum of twisted smooth projective motives, and put \(J_x=(x)\). The kernel of \[\operatorname{End}(V)\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}(V\otimes_R R/J_x)\] is nilpotent. Each factor in a product from this kernel contributes positive coefficient degree. In a fixed source–target correspondence group, the compensating Chow codimension is bounded by the dimensions and the fixed twists. A sufficiently long product therefore vanishes. Reduction on Hom groups is surjective, and these properties pass to idempotent summands.

Now let a bounded complex \(C\) become zero in the target homotopy category. Choose a contracting homotopy there and lift its components to a degree \(-1\) map \(h\) on \(C\). The chain endomorphism \(q=dh+hd\) reduces to \(\operatorname{id}\). The error \(\delta=\operatorname{id}-q\) lies in the preceding nilpotent kernel on the finite direct sum of the terms of \(C\). Hence \[q^{-1}=\operatorname{id}+\delta+\cdots+\delta^{N-1}\] exists for some \(N\), commutes with \(d\), and \(hq^{-1}\) contracts \(C\). This proves conservativity. Combining it with conservativity of the bounded weight complex yields exactly the infinite-height implication needed in Proposition 7.4.

Impact and classification. The nonfaithful Tate map alone refutes only the stronger equivalence assertion. The core proof problem is more specific: bounded-weight conservativity applies first to the weight complex over \(\mathbb F_p[x]\), whereas Proposition 7.4 needs conservativity after further reduction to \(\mathbb F_p\). The false equivalence on p. 16 is the manuscript’s stated bridge across this loss of coefficients; the final sentence on p. 17 invokes the resulting conservativity without a separate justification. That route feeds Proposition 7.5 and Theorem 7.6(1),(3) at infinite height. The contraction argument above supplies the essential missing bridge. Under contract 0.7.1, the demonstrated invalid derivation directly supporting this part of the main contribution is Major. Its repairability does not lower that assessment. The repaired conservativity is true, and no counterexample to Proposition 7.4 or Theorem 7.6 is claimed.
# Problem 3: the bare local projector need not be killed by \(p\)

Location. Proof of Proposition 8.5, p. 24, after the first correspondence diagram: the assertion that the identity of \(\widetilde{\mathcal X}_{Q}\) is killed by \(p\). Here \(Q\) comprises smooth projective varieties whose function fields strictly dominate the chosen field under the \(K(p,m)\)-order. The actual subsequent maps also contain \(M^{\mathrm{MGL}}(R)\) or \(M^{\mathrm{MGL}}(P)\) as tensor factors.

Counterexample to the stated intermediate assertion. Take \(p=2\), finite \(m\ge1\), \[k=\mathbb Q(t_1,t_2,\ldots),\qquad E=F=k(\sqrt2),\qquad
 P=R=\operatorname{Spec}E .\] This satisfies the flexible-base and finitely generated equivalent-extension conditions in the proof. For every integral component \(Q_j\) of the defining union, \(k(Q_j)\ge_{(2,m)}E\) forces \(E\subset k(Q_j)\). Indeed, the quadratic finite scheme \(\operatorname{Spec}E\) over \(k(Q_j)\) is \(K(2,m)\)-isotropic only if it splits. Normality extends this field inclusion to an \(E\)-structure on \(Q_j\).

Strict domination means that \((Q_j)_E\) is \(K(2,m)\)-anisotropic. Every closed point of \(Q_j\), as an \(E\)-variety, consequently has even degree: an odd-degree point would have nonzero pushforward in characteristic two. Every closed-point degree over \(k\) is therefore divisible by four. Conversely, the defining union includes \(\operatorname{Spec}E(\sqrt{t_1})\), which has degree four over \(k\) and strictly dominates \(E\). Its index ideal over \(k\) is thus exactly \(4\mathbb Z\).

Apply the monoidal change from \(\mathrm{MGL}\)-modules to integral motives. For the complementary Čech projector, the degree-zero homology sequence gives \[H_{0,0}\bigl(\widetilde M(\check C(Q));\mathbb Z\bigr)
 \cong \mathbb Z/\operatorname{im}\bigl(H_{0,0}(M(\check C(Q)))\to\mathbb Z\bigr)
 =\mathbb Z/4 .\] The image is precisely the degree ideal; negative degree-zero-weight homology of the effective Čech complex vanishes. Its unit class is not killed by \(2\). Thus \(2\operatorname{id}\) cannot vanish on the bare projector in \(\mathrm{MGL}\)-modules either: vanishing would survive change of coefficients.

Required tensor factors and repair. The needed assertions are \[p\,\operatorname{id}_{M^{\mathrm{MGL}}(R)\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal X}_Q}=0,
 \qquad
 p\,\operatorname{id}_{M^{\mathrm{MGL}}(P)\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal X}_Q}=0 .\] Choose the degree-\(p\) extension \(L/k\) in the proof, remaining anisotropic over both function fields. The finite covers \(R_L\to R\) and \(P_L\to P\) have degree \(p\), and their function fields strictly dominate the respective fields. Their motives are killed by the complementary projector. Pullback followed by pushforward along either cover is multiplication by \(p\), proving the displayed tensor-factor versions. On these objects multiplication by an integer prime to \(p\) is invertible. This is sufficient to remove the integer \(l\) in the two factorization maps on p. 24.

Impact and repair boundary. The bare-projector statement is explicitly used to remove \(l\) and obtain the two \(v_m\)-factorizations. These factorizations establish equality of kernels in Proposition 8.5, which supplies the field-equivalence part of Theorem 7.6(2). Thus the false assertion is an operative justification in a core derivation, not an unused stronger aside. This meets the Major criterion in contract 0.7.1. Both maps in fact contain the required \(P\) or \(R\) factor, so the replacement transfer argument proves their needed form and restores this step. The correction is local in extent, but its brevity does not change the severity of the printed derivation. The counterexample is not a counterexample to equality of the two kernels or to Theorem 7.6.
# Checks supporting the unaffected argument

At finite height, the compactness in Proposition 3.3 is essential: a compact object in the localizing ideal generated by the compact cone of \(v_m\) lies in its thick closure, and hence is killed by a finite power of \(v_m\). Conversely a nilpotent action makes the object a retract of a cone construction. The review found no reversal of this implication.

The finite-height proof of Proposition 7.1 was checked separately from the defective endpoint sentence. Localization in \(v_m\) kills the higher Landweber factors and leaves finite free modules. Lemma 7.2 is the determinant-trick annihilator argument; in Lemma 7.3 an annihilator acting trivially on Tor and as a unit after coefficient change forces Tor to vanish. In the spectral sequence on p. 17, the induction starts at the lowest nonzero homology degree. Incoming differentials to the edge term originate in already vanishing lower rows, and outgoing differentials have negative first index. This makes the stated induction valid.

The primality argument in Proposition 6.6 uses semisimplicity of numerical Morava motives and the absence of tensor zero divisors. The numerical pairing detects products over the coefficient domain; bounded complexes split into shifted cohomology objects. The strong tensor weight complex, rather than an arbitrary weak complex, is the appropriate bridge. The relevant statements of Aoki and Sosnilo were checked, and the bounded-weight kernel-nilpotence input of Bondarko was inspected. Landweber’s original paper was not obtained as a readable full text; that classical input remains an explicitly identified external reliance.

The quantifiers in the order on arbitrary field extensions were checked against the finitely generated reductions. The local-to-isotropic conservativity statement in Proposition 8.3 is used on the image of compact objects from the base field, not asserted for every object without that restriction. The cited torsion-space results supply the test objects separating heights; their invariance under field extension is essential. Norm-variety examples give the stated direction of height separation. A reversed isotropy implication in the prose before Example 8.9 is not used to invalidate the correctly directed conclusion and is not counted as a separate scientific Problem.

These checks are targeted mathematical audits. They do not amount to reconstructing all of the cited literature, a formal verification of motivic category foundations, or proof of every ancillary example. No unsupported defect is inferred from absent code.

problems.title: Infinite-height annihilator radical is not finitely generated
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 12 Pdf pages: 13 Printed pages: 12 Printed pages: 13 Claim: Proposition5.2 Tex label: J-f-g Tex lines: 754–795
claim: sqrt J(U) is finitely generated, without a finite-m restriction.
Flexible characteristic-zero k=C(t1,t2,...), any prime p, m=infinity; U is the compact localized unit in the first anisotropy quotient.
analysis: Location. Proposition 5.2, p. 12, and its finite-presentation argument on p. 13; compare Proposition 4.3, p. 11, and the separate infinite-height case in Proposition 7.4, p. 17.

Claim and decisive test. Proposition 5.2 states that the radical of the coefficient annihilator of a compact object is finitely generated. It does not restrict \(m\) to finite height. Take a flexible characteristic-zero field, for example \(k=\mathbb C(t_1,t_2,\ldots)\), and take the compact localized unit in \(\widehat{\mathrm{SH}}_{(p,\infty)}(k/k)\). This is the first localization, before the further quotient in Definition 3.1. Its \(\mathrm{MGL}\)-motive is the unit in the numerical heart of Proposition 4.3. The graded coefficient endomorphisms of that unit are \(\mathbb F_p[x]\). Numerical equivalence introduces no additional relation on the point: pairing a nonzero coefficient with \(1\) detects it. Consequently, after \(p\)-localization, \[J=\operatorname{Ann}_{\mathbb L_{(p)}}(\widehat M^{\mathrm{MGL}}(\mathbf1))
   =(p,v_1,v_2,\ldots)\mathbb L_{(p)} .\] This ideal is radical, since the quotient is the polynomial domain \(\mathbb F_p[x]\).

It is not finitely generated. Any finite family of elements of \(J\) involves only finitely many of the variables \(v_i\). For a sufficiently large \(N\), that family belongs to \((p,v_1,\ldots,v_N)\). Its generated ideal therefore cannot contain \(v_{N+1}\): the latter survives in the polynomial quotient by \((p,v_1,\ldots,v_N)\). This is an algebraic counterexample under the paper’s own flexible-field and compactness hypotheses. Finite generation before localization would imply finite generation after localization, so working \(p\)-locally does not evade the claim.

Failed proof step. For the one-term weight complex of this unit, the endomorphism module is \(\mathbb F_p[x]\) as an \(\mathbb L_{(p)}\)-module. It has infinitely many independent defining relations \(p,v_1,v_2,\ldots\). The finite-presentation assertion used on p. 13 is therefore unavailable at \(m=\infty\).

Impact, counterevidence, and repair boundary. Restrict Proposition 5.2 and the finite-presentation argument to \(m<\infty\), with the flexible-field hypothesis used in the proof made explicit. The demonstrated counterexample does not affect finite height. More importantly, Proposition 7.4 explicitly separates \(m=\infty\) and uses conservativity there, rather than this finite-generation argument. The downstream main-theorem damage is thus not established. The defect is assessed as Minor, based on this actual dependency boundary. The unit counterexample itself is fully verified; a uniform theorem over nonflexible fields is not supplied by this review.

There is also a harmless logical convention to state in Proposition 5.3: if the \(\mathrm{MGL}\)-motive is zero, its annihilator is the whole ring. The proper-prime description applies to the nonzero case; the zero case in Proposition 7.4 is immediate. This qualification is recorded without promoting it to a separate Problem.
result: Result: Explicit admitted counterexample; finite presentation fails for the same unit's one-term complex.
Impact: No core dependency on the false infinity instance demonstrated; local scope error.

problems.title: False equivalence supplies an unsupported core infinity conservativity bridge
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 15 Pdf pages: 16 Pdf pages: 17 Pdf pages: 18 Printed pages: 15 Printed pages: 16 Printed pages: 17 Printed pages: 18 Claim: Opening of Proposition7.1 proof, then last sentence of Proposition7.4 and Theorem7.6(1),(3) Tex label: Ann-b Tex line: 959
claim: The coefficient-change functor is an equivalence at infinity; later its composite with the weight functor is invoked as conservative.
m=infinity, R=Fp[x] to K(p,infinity)=Fp; bounded numerical-motive complexes over flexible characteristic-zero k.
analysis: Location. The coefficient-change functor displayed immediately before Proposition 7.1, p. 15, and the first sentence of its proof, p. 16. Its required downstream use is the last sentence of Proposition 7.4, p. 17.

Decisive evidence. At \(m=\infty\) this functor is induced by \[R=\mathbb F_p[x]\longrightarrow \mathbb F_p,\qquad x_i\longmapsto0.\] It is not faithful, even on the heart, and hence cannot be an equivalence. For instance, take \(p=2\). The allowed variable \(x_2\) is a nonzero coefficient morphism \(\mathbf1(2)[4]\to\mathbf1\) in numerical \(R\)-motives. It survives numerical equivalence over the point, but maps to zero after coefficient change. Viewed as a morphism between one-term complexes, it gives the same failure in the bounded homotopy category. Thus the asserted equivalence cannot be justified by passing to complexes.

The needed weaker assertion and its repair. The argument needs conservativity, not faithfulness. Here is a bounded proof of that weaker assertion. Numerical correspondences for the polynomial extension of \(CH/p\) are numerical \(CH/p\) correspondences tensored with \(R\): numerical triviality is tested coefficient by coefficient by the degree pairing. In the presentation inherited from \(\mathbb L_{(p)}=BP[x]\), an orientation change gives the same correspondence category; its Todd factors are invertible and do not remove the polynomial variables.

Let \(V\) be a fixed finite direct sum of twisted smooth projective motives, and put \(J_x=(x)\). The kernel of \[\operatorname{End}(V)\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}(V\otimes_R R/J_x)\] is nilpotent. Each factor in a product from this kernel contributes positive coefficient degree. In a fixed source–target correspondence group, the compensating Chow codimension is bounded by the dimensions and the fixed twists. A sufficiently long product therefore vanishes. Reduction on Hom groups is surjective, and these properties pass to idempotent summands.

Now let a bounded complex \(C\) become zero in the target homotopy category. Choose a contracting homotopy there and lift its components to a degree \(-1\) map \(h\) on \(C\). The chain endomorphism \(q=dh+hd\) reduces to \(\operatorname{id}\). The error \(\delta=\operatorname{id}-q\) lies in the preceding nilpotent kernel on the finite direct sum of the terms of \(C\). Hence \[q^{-1}=\operatorname{id}+\delta+\cdots+\delta^{N-1}\] exists for some \(N\), commutes with \(d\), and \(hq^{-1}\) contracts \(C\). This proves conservativity. Combining it with conservativity of the bounded weight complex yields exactly the infinite-height implication needed in Proposition 7.4.

Impact and classification. The nonfaithful Tate map alone refutes only the stronger equivalence assertion. The core proof problem is more specific: bounded-weight conservativity applies first to the weight complex over \(\mathbb F_p[x]\), whereas Proposition 7.4 needs conservativity after further reduction to \(\mathbb F_p\). The false equivalence on p. 16 is the manuscript’s stated bridge across this loss of coefficients; the final sentence on p. 17 invokes the resulting conservativity without a separate justification. That route feeds Proposition 7.5 and Theorem 7.6(1),(3) at infinite height. The contraction argument above supplies the essential missing bridge. Under contract 0.7.1, the demonstrated invalid derivation directly supporting this part of the main contribution is Major. Its repairability does not lower that assessment. The repaired conservativity is true, and no counterexample to Proposition 7.4 or Theorem 7.6 is claimed.
result: Result: The printed only stated bridge to the composite conservativity is false. This feeds7.4 infinity->7.5->7.6(1),(3), a demonstrated invalid core derivation.
Impact: Major under0.7.1 for the explicit main-theorem proof dependency, not for a counterexample to the theorem.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use coefficientwise numerical CH/p polynomial extension, finite-object positive-degree kernel nilpotence, surjectivity on Hom, lift a target contracting homotopy h, invert q=dh+hd=1-delta via nilpotence, contract by hq^{-1}. This proves conservativity exactly where required.

problems.title: False bare-projector p-annihilation is used in the core field-equivalence derivation
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 24 Pdf pages: 25 Printed pages: 24 Printed pages: 25 Claim: Proposition8.5 proof after first diagram; application to7.6(2)
claim: p kills the identity of the bare complementary Cech projector Xtilde_Q, so prime-to-p l can be removed.
p=2, any finite m>=1, flexible k=Q(t1,t2,...), E=F=k(sqrt2), P=R=Spec E; Q comprises varieties whose function fields strictly dominate E.
analysis: Location. Proof of Proposition 8.5, p. 24, after the first correspondence diagram: the assertion that the identity of \(\widetilde{\mathcal X}_{Q}\) is killed by \(p\). Here \(Q\) comprises smooth projective varieties whose function fields strictly dominate the chosen field under the \(K(p,m)\)-order. The actual subsequent maps also contain \(M^{\mathrm{MGL}}(R)\) or \(M^{\mathrm{MGL}}(P)\) as tensor factors.

Counterexample to the stated intermediate assertion. Take \(p=2\), finite \(m\ge1\), \[k=\mathbb Q(t_1,t_2,\ldots),\qquad E=F=k(\sqrt2),\qquad
 P=R=\operatorname{Spec}E .\] This satisfies the flexible-base and finitely generated equivalent-extension conditions in the proof. For every integral component \(Q_j\) of the defining union, \(k(Q_j)\ge_{(2,m)}E\) forces \(E\subset k(Q_j)\). Indeed, the quadratic finite scheme \(\operatorname{Spec}E\) over \(k(Q_j)\) is \(K(2,m)\)-isotropic only if it splits. Normality extends this field inclusion to an \(E\)-structure on \(Q_j\).

Strict domination means that \((Q_j)_E\) is \(K(2,m)\)-anisotropic. Every closed point of \(Q_j\), as an \(E\)-variety, consequently has even degree: an odd-degree point would have nonzero pushforward in characteristic two. Every closed-point degree over \(k\) is therefore divisible by four. Conversely, the defining union includes \(\operatorname{Spec}E(\sqrt{t_1})\), which has degree four over \(k\) and strictly dominates \(E\). Its index ideal over \(k\) is thus exactly \(4\mathbb Z\).

Apply the monoidal change from \(\mathrm{MGL}\)-modules to integral motives. For the complementary Čech projector, the degree-zero homology sequence gives \[H_{0,0}\bigl(\widetilde M(\check C(Q));\mathbb Z\bigr)
 \cong \mathbb Z/\operatorname{im}\bigl(H_{0,0}(M(\check C(Q)))\to\mathbb Z\bigr)
 =\mathbb Z/4 .\] The image is precisely the degree ideal; negative degree-zero-weight homology of the effective Čech complex vanishes. Its unit class is not killed by \(2\). Thus \(2\operatorname{id}\) cannot vanish on the bare projector in \(\mathrm{MGL}\)-modules either: vanishing would survive change of coefficients.

Required tensor factors and repair. The needed assertions are \[p\,\operatorname{id}_{M^{\mathrm{MGL}}(R)\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal X}_Q}=0,
 \qquad
 p\,\operatorname{id}_{M^{\mathrm{MGL}}(P)\otimes\widetilde{\mathcal X}_Q}=0 .\] Choose the degree-\(p\) extension \(L/k\) in the proof, remaining anisotropic over both function fields. The finite covers \(R_L\to R\) and \(P_L\to P\) have degree \(p\), and their function fields strictly dominate the respective fields. Their motives are killed by the complementary projector. Pullback followed by pushforward along either cover is multiplication by \(p\), proving the displayed tensor-factor versions. On these objects multiplication by an integer prime to \(p\) is invertible. This is sufficient to remove the integer \(l\) in the two factorization maps on p. 24.

Impact and repair boundary. The bare-projector statement is explicitly used to remove \(l\) and obtain the two \(v_m\)-factorizations. These factorizations establish equality of kernels in Proposition 8.5, which supplies the field-equivalence part of Theorem 7.6(2). Thus the false assertion is an operative justification in a core derivation, not an unused stronger aside. This meets the Major criterion in contract 0.7.1. Both maps in fact contain the required \(P\) or \(R\) factor, so the replacement transfer argument proves their needed form and restores this step. The correction is local in extent, but its brevity does not change the severity of the printed derivation. The counterexample is not a counterexample to equality of the two kernels or to Theorem 7.6.
result: Result: Explicit counterexample to the printed operative assertion, with every flexibility/finite-extension/equivalence condition satisfied.
Impact: The false assertion explicitly removes l to produce two vm-factorizations; these give8.5 kernel equality and thus7.6(2). Major under core-derivation criterion; no theorem counterexample.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Replace bare-projector annihilation by p id=0 on M(P) tensor Xtilde_Q and M(R) tensor Xtilde_Q; finite-cover pullback/pushforward supplies it and permits removal of l.

report: Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Initial mathematical review: M25-0158
Twisted generating functions and the nearby Lagrangian conjecture

Authors: Mohammed Abouzaid, Sylvain Courte, Stéphane Guillermou, and Thomas Kragh. Publication identity: Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), no. 5, 949–1011; DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0052 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0052).
Reviewed source: arXiv:2011.13178v3, 29 July 2024, 53 pages. Printed and PDF page numbers agree. The journal body was not acquired or compared.

Initial assessment: Major. The displayed derived local system in the proof of Theorem 3.26 has an incorrect shift, already for the zero section of \(T^*S^1\). It therefore does not satisfy the hypothesis of the lemma used to obtain the fiber homology needed for tube generation. This is a demonstrated invalid derivation in the core argument, with a cohomological repair described below. Four further bounded defects concern strict cocycles, global indexing, and a missing properness hypothesis in auxiliary constructions. No counterexample to the main geometric conclusions is established. The scientific decision remains `pending`, with `human_reviews=[]`; this package is an initial review, not independent acceptance.
# Scope and proof structure

The main claims concern closed exact embedded Lagrangians \(L\subset T^*M\) with \(M\) closed. Theorem A gives vanishing of the induced maps on all homotopy groups of the stable Gauss map. It does not assert nullhomotopy for every \(M\). Theorem E obtains nullhomotopy for a homotopy sphere. Theorem C characterizes the existence of twisted generating functions for Legendrian immersions by factorization of the stable Gauss map through \(\pi:L\to M\). Theorem D supplies the additional tube-type control for nearby Lagrangians.

The central route is: the external homotopy equivalence \(\pi\); the twisted Giroux–Latour construction; a doubled generating function linear at infinity; contact-isotopy continuation; a difference-function homology calculation; stable recognition of tubes; and the tube-space lift of the Gauss class. The integral conclusion in the last step uses both Bökstedt’s rational result and the injectivity of the \(J\)-homomorphism in the two torsion congruence classes. Omitting the latter would misrepresent the paper.

The entire assigned manuscript, including Appendix A and Figure 1, was read as text. The checks below are exact algebraic, geometric, and derived-category tests. Foundational Floer, sheaf-theoretic, and algebraic \(K\)-theory results were checked at selected primary statements, not reconstructed in full.

The monoid \(\mathcal Q\) consists of actual quadratic forms with eigenvalues \(\pm1\), with ordered direct sum. It is not a commutative monoid. A \(\mathcal Q\)-twisted map to \(\mathbb N\) or \(\mathbb Z\) requires, on every relevant intersection, \[n_j=n_i+\dim q_{ij},\qquad q_{ij}\oplus q_{jk}=q_{ik}\] as strict equalities. Equality up to an unspecified permutation or homotopy does not satisfy the given definition.
# Problem 1: the derived local system has the wrong shift

Location. Theorem 3.26, proof on pp. 37–38, especially the displayed formula for \(G\) and its immediate application of Lemma 3.27. The latter lemma is on p. 36; \(D\) and its actual critical values appear on pp. 28–29 and in Figure 1.

The asserted construction. Writing \(k=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\) and \(\pi\) for projection to \(M\), the paper specifies \[G=\operatorname{RHom}\!\left(R\pi_*
 k_{\{-A<F(x,-)\le-4s_1\}},\,k_M[\dim M+d]\right).
 \tag{1}\] Here \(d\) has already been chosen by the Morse–Bott relation \(H_{*+d}(F\le-4s_1,F\le-\infty)\simeq H_*(M)\). The proof then applies Lemma 3.27 to conclude \(G\simeq k_M\). That lemma requires \(R\Gamma(M;G)\simeq R\Gamma(M;k_M)\), as well as constant cohomology sheaves.

An admitted test case. Take \(M=S^1\), take \(L\) to be its zero section, and choose the Legendrian lift with \(z=0\). All closedness, exactness, and embedding hypotheses hold; \(\pi:L\to M\) is the identity. Take the untwisted, base-independent generating function \(f(w)=D(w)\) used by the paper, and set \(s_1=2/3\). Since \(D(w)=w^3-3w\) near its critical points, its critical values are \(-2\) and \(2\), exactly \(\pm3s_1\). Its difference function is \[F(w,w')=D(w)-D(w').\] Below the threshold \(-4s_1=-8/3\), the only critical point in each fiber is \((1,-1)\), with value \(-4\) and Hessian \[\operatorname{Hess}_{(1,-1)}F=
 \begin{pmatrix}6&0\\0&6\end{pmatrix}.\] The associated global critical manifold is \(S^1\), with negative normal index \(d=0\). It is orientable. No covering or grading convention for a nonzero index is involved.

For \(A>4\), the fiber sublevel pair acquires a single index-zero handle in this band. Equivalently, its relative cohomology is \(k\) in degree zero. The family is a product over \(S^1\), so, with the extension-by-zero convention for the displayed locally closed band, \[H:=R\pi_*k_{\{-A<F\le-8/3\}}\simeq k_{S^1}.\] The unbounded part contributes the unchanged lower sublevel pair; the difference-function gradient control gives the usual relative Morse calculation. Formula (1) now gives \[G=\operatorname{RHom}(k_{S^1},k_{S^1}[1])\simeq k_{S^1}[1],
 \tag{2}\] rather than \(k_{S^1}\). In standard cohomological grading, \(R\Gamma(S^1;G)\) has nonzero groups in degrees \(-1,0\), whereas \(R\Gamma(S^1;k)\) has them in degrees \(0,1\). Thus the hypothesis of Lemma 3.27 fails. This discrepancy does not depend on the sign convention for \(d\), since \(d=0\).

A cohomological repair. Keep the relative-cohomology local system \[H=R\pi_*k_{\{-A<F\le-4s_1\}},\qquad \widetilde G=H[d],
 \tag{3}\] instead of the dual in (1). The controlled sublevel family gives locally constant finite-dimensional cohomology. After making the negative normal bundle orientable, the Thom identification gives \(R\Gamma(M;H)\simeq R\Gamma(L;k)[-d]\). The projection homotopy equivalence therefore gives \(R\Gamma(M;\widetilde G)\simeq R\Gamma(M;k)\). One may also pass to an orientation cover of \(M\) and to a finite cover trivializing the finitely many cohomology local systems: their monodromy groups lie in finite general linear groups over \(k\). Lemma 3.27 then applies to \(\widetilde G\).

This establishes the required rank-one fiber cohomology, hence the corresponding homology over the field. The argument can be repeated for each prime; the finite cover need not be uniform in \(p\). The finitely generated integral Morse complexes then permit the tensor-product argument in Lemmas 3.22 and 3.28. This repair uses the same controlled-sublevel and Thom inputs; it does not validate formula (1).

Impact. The faulty application is the step that supplies the fiber homology for Proposition 3.25, hence Theorem 3.26 and Theorem D. Tube generation then supplies the lift used for Theorems A and E. Under contract 0.7.1 this demonstrated invalid core derivation is Major, even though (3) repairs its normalization. The example does not refute tube generation or the Gauss-map conclusions: the zero section plainly satisfies them.
# Problem 2: the reordering cylinder requires negative dimensions
Location. Lemma 3.7, pp. 26–27, specifically its final sketch of equivalence of the underlying \(\mathcal Q\)-twisted maps. The application is Theorem 3.9, pp. 27–28.

Valid input and the failed construction. Let the base be a point, with three identical open sets, ordered \(1<2<3\). Take \[(n_1,n_2,n_3)=(0,1,1),\qquad
 q_{12}=q_{13}=u^2,\quad q_{23}=0.\] Use \(f_1=D\), \(f_2=D\oplus_b u^2\), and \(f_3=f_2\), with \(b\) a sufficiently large common bound. These are valid functions linear at infinity and generate the same two-point Legendrian immersion. The cocycle and dimension conditions hold.

For the adjacent swap \(i=1\), the proof sets \(m=2(n_2-n_1)=2\) and obtains \[(n'_1,n'_2,n'_3)=(2,1,3).\] The prescribed cylinder order on p. 27 is \[1<2<2'<1'<3<3'.\] At a middle parameter value all six cylinder charts intersect. The associated dimensions in this order are \(0,1,1,2,1,3\). Thus the edge \(1'\to3\) would require a quadratic form of dimension \(1-2=-1\). No element of \(\mathcal Q\) has that dimension. Independently, the prescription \(q_{3,3'}=0\) has dimension zero, whereas this edge requires dimension two. Filling in unspecified transition forms or permuting their coordinates cannot fix either obstruction while keeping these data.

Counterevidence and bounded impact. The preceding formulas (3.4)–(3.5) for the reordered functions and their cocycle pass the dimension and gluing tests; they still generate the same immersion. The defect is in the asserted cylinder proving equivalence of twisting classes. A general replacement cylinder was not completed in this review, so full repair of that subclaim is not asserted.

The existence part needed for the nearby-Lagrangian tube construction is not invalidated by this test. Moreover, for a nearby Lagrangian, \(\pi\) is a homotopy equivalence and the Gauss-map factorization can independently identify the twisting class of the generated component. The review therefore records a Minor defect in this auxiliary class-preservation proof, with its general correction outstanding, rather than using it to claim failure of Theorem D. This boundary is distinct from Problem 1’s actual homological application.
# Problem 3: the translation homotopy is not a strict cocycle

Location. Lemma 2.23 and its proof, p. 17. Definitions 2.7 and 2.9 are on pp. 7–8; strict bundle and twisted-map conditions are in Appendix A, pp. 48–49. The v3 version explicitly records that this proof was changed after an omission in an earlier version; the test here concerns the actual v3 construction.

Cocycle failure. The proposed doubled cover keeps the old forms within each copy and defines cross terms by \(q_{i'j''}=q\oplus q_{ij}\) for a fixed \(q\in\mathcal Q_1\). On the triple \(i'<j'<j''\), with \(q_{jj}=0\), the cocycle condition would require \[q_{ij}\oplus q=q\oplus q_{ij}.\] Take \(q=u^2\) and \(q_{ij}=-u^2\). The two matrices are \(\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\) and \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\); at \((1,0)\) their values are \(-1\) and \(1\). Both forms satisfy the normalized eigenvalue condition. They are isometric, but they are not equal as required. The additional rule declaring every first-copy index less than every second-copy index also asks for \(q_{ij}\) when \(j<i\), and can demand a negative dimension.

This is not cured by choosing a special representative of the universal identity map. If \(q=[\varepsilon]\), \(\varepsilon=\pm1\), the necessary identity \(A\oplus[\varepsilon]=[\varepsilon]\oplus A\) forces \(A=\varepsilon I\) by comparison of matrix entries. All transitions would then lie in the definite-form submonoid, isomorphic to \(\mathbb N\), whose space \(|B(\mathbb N,\mathbb N)|\) is contractible. Such data cannot represent the identity of \(X=|B(\mathbb N,\mathcal Q)|\): the two edges \(0\to1\) given by \(u^2\) and \(-u^2\) form a loop detected nontrivially by the additive index map to \(B\mathbb Z\). Thus \(X\) is noncontractible independently of Lemma 2.23.

What is and is not damaged. The printed proof does not establish either its full translation argument or the asserted inclusion equivalence by that argument. No counterexample to those conclusions is supplied. A coherent block-interchange construction would require actual compatibility data; merely saying that direct sum is homotopy commutative is not a completed repair.

The stronger claim is not essential in the places initially suggesting a main-theorem dependency. In diagrams (2.50)–(2.51), the map from \(B(\mathbb N,\mathcal Q)\) to \(B(\mathbb Z,\mathcal Q)\) need not itself be an equivalence to deduce the Gauss-map factorization. The later explicit translation use in Theorem 3.9 is by \(2m\), and even translations on the full stabilized model follow from left multiplication by the stabilizing hyperbolic form and Theorem 2.21. Freely chosen auxiliary dimensions in the existence construction can be chosen even. This prevents rating an unneeded full \(+1\) argument as an established main-theorem obstruction. The issue is Minor; the complete broader proof remains to be supplied.
# Problem 4: the refinement relation can contain a cycle
Location. Definitions A.2–A.3, p. 43, and the proposed order on \(I\sqcup J\) in the proof of Lemma A.10, p. 47.

Counterexample within the stated hypotheses. Let \(X=\{0,1\}\) be discrete. Let \(I=\{a<b\}\), \(U_a=\{0\}\), \(U_b=\{1\}\); let \(J=\{c<d\}\), \(V_c=\{1\}\), \(V_d=\{0\}\); and set \(\sigma(c)=b\), \(\sigma(d)=a\). These are directed covers. The map \(\sigma\) is an allowed refinement because its restriction to each \(J_x\) is a map from a singleton and hence is nondecreasing. Global monotonicity is not required by Definition A.3.

The stated cross rules yield \(a<c\) because \(a<\sigma(c)=b\), and \(d<a\) because \(\sigma(d)=a\le a\). Together with \(c<d\) they give \[a<c<d<a .\] Consequently the displayed relation is not a partial order and cannot index the claimed directed cylinder cover.

Verified order repair and impact. First retain in \(J\) only comparisons supported by nonempty intersections \(V_j\cap V_{j'}\), then take their transitive closure. This remains a suborder of the old order and makes \(\sigma\) globally nondecreasing. Every local order on \(J_x\) and every nonempty MV simplex is unchanged. Next take the transitive closure of the indicated cross rules together with the orders on \(I\) and the modified \(J\).

This generated relation is acyclic. Along a cross path the image in \(I\) is nondecreasing, and every \(I\to J\) edge makes a strict increase. A cycle crossing between the two parts is therefore impossible; cycles within a part are already excluded. New comparisons within \(J\) either concern disjoint sets or agree with the existing local total order. Thus the endpoints, nonempty MV simplices, cocycle data, and resulting classifying maps are unchanged. One may identify the identical MV blow-ups when applying the definition of equivalence.

This is a Minor defect in the global indexing description, with a complete correction of that description. No additional failure of the classifying maps or of the main geometric calculation is established. The grading rests on the unchanged mathematical data, not simply on the length of the correction.
# Problem 5: compactly supported lifting needs proper critical data

Location. Theorem 3.6, pp. 25–26, read with the unrestricted generating-function definition on pp. 5–6. The statement permits a manifold without boundary and a family of Legendrian immersions, but gives no compactness or properness condition on their critical preimages.

Take \(M\) to be a point and the constant family \(f^t(v)=\sin v\) on \(\mathbb R\). Its critical set is the countable discrete zero-manifold \(L=\{\pi/2+k\pi:k\in\mathbb Z\}\), and \(f'\) vanishes transversely there. It generates a Legendrian immersion into \(J^1(\mathrm{pt})=\mathbb R\), with values \(1\) and \(-1\). Thus it is allowed by the printed unrestricted definition, although \(L\) is not compact.

Choose a compactly supported contact isotopy of \(\mathbb R\) which translates neighborhoods of both critical values by \(1/4\) at its final time. Such an increasing diffeomorphism is obtained from a compactly supported vector field equal to \(1/4\) along the two short trajectories. The target critical values are then \(5/4\) and \(-3/4\).

For every finite stabilization and compactly supported correction \(\eta\), the function \[\sin v+x_1y_1+\cdots+x_my_m+\eta(v,x,y)\] still has critical points \((\pi/2+k\pi,0,0)\) for sufficiently large \(|k|\). They lie outside the support of \(\eta\) and retain values \(1\) and \(-1\). It therefore cannot generate the stated translated immersion. This directly refutes the unrestricted lifting assertion, without executing author code.

The actual application in Theorem 3.9 has functions linear at infinity and a proper critical locus over the compact base support of the contact isotopy. It excludes the example. A properness condition over that support, together with the parametric control used by the generating-family lifting theorem, is needed in Theorem 3.6. No extension to arbitrary nonproper families is justified here. This is a Minor statement-scope defect; it does not refute the compact application or Theorem D.
# Checks supporting the remaining argument and limitations

The right-\(\mathcal Q\) equivariance in Lemma 2.17’s quadratic generating-family construction was checked against the formulas, including the linear change of variables. The codimension estimate underlying Lemma 2.20 gives at least \(m+1\) for the nontransversality locus. The stable Gauss-map construction retains both compactness and the difference from the vertical Lagrangian distribution. In Definition 2.9 one must use the actual local singular-set cover when some charts omit branches; the stronger displayed equality with every full inverse-image chart does not follow from one-sided domain inclusion. Using that local cover as a refinement avoids treating this observation as a further theorem counterexample.

The cutoff gradient estimate in Lemma 3.4 uses \(\|\nabla q(u)\|=2\|u\|\), which explains the normalized eigenvalues in v3. For the difference operation in Definition 3.16, consistency with \(F=\cdots+\epsilon-\epsilon'\) and the unit action forces a minus sign on the second cutoff term. With that normalization, the separate gradient-error bounds combine in squared norm and the claimed control is valid for general normalized \(Q\). This uniquely determined formula correction is not counted as another independent Problem.

The difference-function tensor-product calculation uses finite free Morse complexes. Lemma 3.28 should be understood with finitely generated cohomology, as in its actual application. Mere finite rational rank would admit, for example, \(A=\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Q\) and \(B=\mathbb Z\), whose derived reductions modulo every prime are rank one although \(A\) is not a shift of \(\mathbb Z\). This scope qualification does not invalidate the finite Morse-complex use. The contact-isotopy lifting statement is likewise used with a compact/proper critical locus; a claim without such control for arbitrary noncompact immersed critical sets is not inferred.

Proposition 3.25’s stabilization allows both simple connectivity and the dimension range for disk embeddings and \(h\)-cobordism. Those hypotheses were tracked. The finite-field local-system argument, once normalized as in (3), legitimately uses finite covers that may depend on the prime.

For Section 4, the bar construction requires the homotopy-fiber conclusion supplied by a quasifibration; the primary Hatcher statement is sufficient for its exact sequence. The rational equivalence of the rigid-tube map implies injectivity on the free homotopy groups of \(BO\). In degrees \(1,2\bmod8\), the factorization through \(BG\) and the cited injective \(J\)-map handle the \(\mathbb Z/2\) groups. The separate index component handles \(\pi_0\) of the relevant fiber. Hence Corollary 4.7 is not an unjustified conversion of rational vanishing into integral vanishing. Nullhomotopy for a homotopy sphere follows from the homotopy-group statement and \(\pi:L\to M\); no blanket nullhomotopy for an arbitrary manifold is claimed.

The primary Bökstedt preview states the rational equivalence in its \(G/O\) and Whitehead-space formulation. The full Waldhausen comparison with tubes and the full proof were not rederived. The same limit applies to the full Floer/sheaf proof that \(\pi\) is a homotopy equivalence, and to all foundations of generating families and stable spherical fibrations. problems.title: The local-system dual has the wrong shift for Lemma 3.27
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: # Problem 1: the derived local system has the wrong shift
claim: Theorem 3.26, displayed G on p.38, invoking Lemma 3.27
analysis: Location. Theorem 3.26, proof on pp. 37–38, especially the displayed formula for \(G\) and its immediate application of Lemma 3.27. The latter lemma is on p. 36; \(D\) and its actual critical values appear on pp. 28–29 and in Figure 1.

The asserted construction. Writing \(k=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\) and \(\pi\) for projection to \(M\), the paper specifies \[G=\operatorname{RHom}\!\left(R\pi_*
 k_{\{-A<F(x,-)\le-4s_1\}},\,k_M[\dim M+d]\right).
 \tag{1}\] Here \(d\) has already been chosen by the Morse–Bott relation \(H_{*+d}(F\le-4s_1,F\le-\infty)\simeq H_*(M)\). The proof then applies Lemma 3.27 to conclude \(G\simeq k_M\). That lemma requires \(R\Gamma(M;G)\simeq R\Gamma(M;k_M)\), as well as constant cohomology sheaves.

An admitted test case. Take \(M=S^1\), take \(L\) to be its zero section, and choose the Legendrian lift with \(z=0\). All closedness, exactness, and embedding hypotheses hold; \(\pi:L\to M\) is the identity. Take the untwisted, base-independent generating function \(f(w)=D(w)\) used by the paper, and set \(s_1=2/3\). Since \(D(w)=w^3-3w\) near its critical points, its critical values are \(-2\) and \(2\), exactly \(\pm3s_1\). Its difference function is \[F(w,w')=D(w)-D(w').\] Below the threshold \(-4s_1=-8/3\), the only critical point in each fiber is \((1,-1)\), with value \(-4\) and Hessian \[\operatorname{Hess}_{(1,-1)}F=
 \begin{pmatrix}6&0\\0&6\end{pmatrix}.\] The associated global critical manifold is \(S^1\), with negative normal index \(d=0\). It is orientable. No covering or grading convention for a nonzero index is involved.

For \(A>4\), the fiber sublevel pair acquires a single index-zero handle in this band. Equivalently, its relative cohomology is \(k\) in degree zero. The family is a product over \(S^1\), so, with the extension-by-zero convention for the displayed locally closed band, \[H:=R\pi_*k_{\{-A<F\le-8/3\}}\simeq k_{S^1}.\] The unbounded part contributes the unchanged lower sublevel pair; the difference-function gradient control gives the usual relative Morse calculation. Formula (1) now gives \[G=\operatorname{RHom}(k_{S^1},k_{S^1}[1])\simeq k_{S^1}[1],
 \tag{2}\] rather than \(k_{S^1}\). In standard cohomological grading, \(R\Gamma(S^1;G)\) has nonzero groups in degrees \(-1,0\), whereas \(R\Gamma(S^1;k)\) has them in degrees \(0,1\). Thus the hypothesis of Lemma 3.27 fails. This discrepancy does not depend on the sign convention for \(d\), since \(d=0\).

A cohomological repair. Keep the relative-cohomology local system \[H=R\pi_*k_{\{-A<F\le-4s_1\}},\qquad \widetilde G=H[d],
 \tag{3}\] instead of the dual in (1). The controlled sublevel family gives locally constant finite-dimensional cohomology. After making the negative normal bundle orientable, the Thom identification gives \(R\Gamma(M;H)\simeq R\Gamma(L;k)[-d]\). The projection homotopy equivalence therefore gives \(R\Gamma(M;\widetilde G)\simeq R\Gamma(M;k)\). One may also pass to an orientation cover of \(M\) and to a finite cover trivializing the finitely many cohomology local systems: their monodromy groups lie in finite general linear groups over \(k\). Lemma 3.27 then applies to \(\widetilde G\).

This establishes the required rank-one fiber cohomology, hence the corresponding homology over the field. The argument can be repeated for each prime; the finite cover need not be uniform in \(p\). The finitely generated integral Morse complexes then permit the tensor-product argument in Lemmas 3.22 and 3.28. This repair uses the same controlled-sublevel and Thom inputs; it does not validate formula (1).

Impact. The faulty application is the step that supplies the fiber homology for Proposition 3.25, hence Theorem 3.26 and Theorem D. Tube generation then supplies the lift used for Theorems A and E. Under contract 0.7.1 this demonstrated invalid core derivation is Major, even though (3) repairs its normalization. The example does not refute tube generation or the Gauss-map conclusions: the zero section plainly satisfies them.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: The band has one index-zero fiber critical point (1,-1), value -4 and Hessian diag(6,6). Thus H=Rpi_*k_band=k_M. Printed RHom(H,k_M[dim M+d])=k_M[1], with RΓ nonzero in degrees -1,0, not degrees 0,1 of RΓk_M. Lemma 3.27 cannot be applied as written.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The zero section already has tube generation and satisfies the geometric conclusions; it is a counterexample to the printed derived normalization, not to the main theorem. The delta-action sign correction is explicitly granted.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use H[d] directly. For each finite field pass to a finite cover orienting the base and negative bundle and killing finitely many finite monodromy groups. Thom plus L~M yields RΓ(H[d])~RΓk_M. Lemma 3.27 then gives H[d]=k_M; finite-generation and tensor-product lemmas yield integral rank-one fiber homology.

problems.title: The translation construction is not a strict Q-cocycle
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: # Problem 3: the translation homotopy is not a strict cocycle
claim: Lemma 2.23, doubled cover proof on p.17
analysis: Location. Lemma 2.23 and its proof, p. 17. Definitions 2.7 and 2.9 are on pp. 7–8; strict bundle and twisted-map conditions are in Appendix A, pp. 48–49. The v3 version explicitly records that this proof was changed after an omission in an earlier version; the test here concerns the actual v3 construction.

Cocycle failure. The proposed doubled cover keeps the old forms within each copy and defines cross terms by \(q_{i'j''}=q\oplus q_{ij}\) for a fixed \(q\in\mathcal Q_1\). On the triple \(i'<j'<j''\), with \(q_{jj}=0\), the cocycle condition would require \[q_{ij}\oplus q=q\oplus q_{ij}.\] Take \(q=u^2\) and \(q_{ij}=-u^2\). The two matrices are \(\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\) and \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\); at \((1,0)\) their values are \(-1\) and \(1\). Both forms satisfy the normalized eigenvalue condition. They are isometric, but they are not equal as required. The additional rule declaring every first-copy index less than every second-copy index also asks for \(q_{ij}\) when \(j<i\), and can demand a negative dimension.

This is not cured by choosing a special representative of the universal identity map. If \(q=[\varepsilon]\), \(\varepsilon=\pm1\), the necessary identity \(A\oplus[\varepsilon]=[\varepsilon]\oplus A\) forces \(A=\varepsilon I\) by comparison of matrix entries. All transitions would then lie in the definite-form submonoid, isomorphic to \(\mathbb N\), whose space \(|B(\mathbb N,\mathbb N)|\) is contractible. Such data cannot represent the identity of \(X=|B(\mathbb N,\mathcal Q)|\): the two edges \(0\to1\) given by \(u^2\) and \(-u^2\) form a loop detected nontrivially by the additive index map to \(B\mathbb Z\). Thus \(X\) is noncontractible independently of Lemma 2.23.

What is and is not damaged. The printed proof does not establish either its full translation argument or the asserted inclusion equivalence by that argument. No counterexample to those conclusions is supplied. A coherent block-interchange construction would require actual compatibility data; merely saying that direct sum is homotopy commutative is not a completed repair.

The stronger claim is not essential in the places initially suggesting a main-theorem dependency. In diagrams (2.50)–(2.51), the map from \(B(\mathbb N,\mathcal Q)\) to \(B(\mathbb Z,\mathcal Q)\) need not itself be an equivalence to deduce the Gauss-map factorization. The later explicit translation use in Theorem 3.9 is by \(2m\), and even translations on the full stabilized model follow from left multiplication by the stabilizing hyperbolic form and Theorem 2.21. Freely chosen auxiliary dimensions in the existence construction can be chosen even. This prevents rating an unneeded full \(+1\) argument as an established main-theorem obstruction. The issue is Minor; the complete broader proof remains to be supplied.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: Triple i'<j'<j'' requires q_ij⊕q=q⊕q_ij. For q=+u² and q_ij=-u² the matrices diag(-1,1) and diag(1,-1) differ. All-first/all-second ordering also asks for old q_ij with j<i. For the universal identity representative, commuting A with the one-dimensional ε block forces A=εI; this factors through the contractible definite-form submonoid and cannot represent the noncontractible identity.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The conclusion is not disproved. Core factorization only needs the inclusion map, not its equivalence. Freely selected auxiliary dimensions can be even; the explicit shift in Theorem 3.9 is 2m. Even translations in the full stabilized model follow from left h action and Theorem 2.21, bypassing the bad full +1 argument.
