Title: Initial mathematical review: M25-0159
The monodromy of families of subvarieties on abelian varieties

Authors: Ariyan Javanpeykar, Thomas Krämer, Christian Lehn, and Marco Maculan. Publication: Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), no. 6, 1045–1149; DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0053 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0053).

Reviewed source: the exact 105-page journal typeset PDF obtained from Maculan’s author website. Printed page numbers are used below; physical PDF page \(p\) has printed number \(1044+p\). The separately retained arXiv:2210.05166v3 PDF and TeX, dated 18 March 2025, are ancillary sources, not presumed to be the journal’s typesetting source.

Initial assessment: Major. The signed-cycle definitions omit the permutation normalization required by their asserted degrees and by Claim 8.9. An admissible eight-point cycle gives the exact coefficient discrepancy \(552\ne0\). This affects the cycle-to-spin-representation bridge used in the main classification; the paper itself later displays the correct factor, and the normalized calculation can be repaired. Separately, the unexcluded zero-dimensional case contradicts the stated main monodromy equivalence and simplicity criterion. Three local defects concern arithmetic twists, line-valued pairings, and the \(r=1\) endpoint of an auxiliary wedge-power theorem. These findings do not refute the intended positive-dimensional classification after the identified corrections. The scientific decision remains `pending`; `human_reviews=[]`.
# Scope, assumptions, and the proof chain

The monodromy theorem concerns a smooth proper family \(\mathcal X\subset A\times S\) with connected fibers, where \(A\) is constant and the characteristic is zero. The stated dimension range is \(d<(g-1)/2\), with explicit Euler-characteristic exclusions for exceptional and certain half-spin representations. The theorem is an equivalence: geometric nonconstancy, nondivisibility, and the absence of product or symmetric-power decompositions are equivalent to big monodromy for most torsion tuples of characters. Most excludes a finite union of torsion translates of proper character subtori. It is not a claim about every character.

The Tannaka formulation concerns the derived group of the connected component, rather than the entire group. The chain is generic vanishing and Galois detection; characteristic cycles and their weight interpretation; simplicity; classification of minuscule representations; reconstruction of wedge powers from curves; and exclusion of spin representations in the stated range. The distinction between a finite Gauss map, mere nondegeneracy, and an ample normal bundle was retained. General singular statements were not silently replaced by smooth ones.

The primary reviewer read the introduction and Section 2 in full, checked the numerical and geometric interfaces, and independently examined the affected later statements. Thus the journal text was covered collectively, while the detailed proof audit remains the bounded one documented in the coverage records. Selected primary dependencies were retrieved and inspected. Deep generic-vanishing, microlocal Tannakian, and classification foundations were not all re-proved.
# Problem 1: ordered signed cycles have the wrong multiplicities

Location. Definition 5.21 and Lemma 5.22, pp. 1106–1107; the definitions in Section 8.3, pp. 1132–1133; the degree assertions on p. 1130; and Claim 8.9, p. 1134. The affected bridge is Theorem 8.5, used in the proof of Theorem 8.3 on p. 1132.

The definitions and their numerical consequence. Let \(\Lambda_Z\) be a reduced symmetric clean cycle of Gauss degree \(2n\), with a general fiber \[\{p_1,-p_1,\ldots,p_n,-p_n\}.\] The source defines \(\Lambda_{Z,S}^{[r]}\) inside \(A^r\times\mathbb P_A\), by removing the big diagonal and antidiagonal from the ordered fiber product. Its elements are ordered tuples, not unordered subsets. Section 8.3 then defines \[\Lambda_{Z,S}^{\alpha}:=\sigma_{\alpha *}\Lambda_{Z,S}^{[r]},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Alt}_S^r\Lambda_Z:=\Lambda_{Z,S}^{(1^r)}
 \tag{1}\] without the factor \(1/N(\alpha)\) used elsewhere. Definition 5.21 likewise omits that factor for the parity pieces.

For \(\alpha=(1^r)\), there are \(r!\) orderings of each signed subset. Consequently (1) has Gauss degree \[r!\,2^r\binom nr,
 \tag{2}\] not the stated \(2^r\binom nr\). When \(r=n\) and the Gauss monodromy is even, each parity piece has degree \(n!2^{n-1}\) rather than \(2^{n-1}\). Pushforward multiplicities are not discarded when two sums coincide; such coincidences cannot fix the total degree discrepancy.

A complete counterexample to Claim 8.9. Let \(E/\mathbb C\) be an elliptic curve, let \(p\in E(\mathbb C)\) have infinite order, and set \(A=E^4\). Let \(p_i\) have coordinate \(p\) in position \(i\) and zero in the other three positions. Then \[\sum_{i=1}^4 a_i p_i=0,\quad a_i\in\mathbb Z
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_1=\cdots=a_4=0.\] Take the reduced effective zero-cycle \(Z=\sum_{i=1}^4([p_i]+[-p_i])\). Its conormal cycle is eight disjoint copies of \(\mathbb P_A\). The Gauss map is finite of degree eight, with trivial, hence even, monodromy. Here \(n=4\), \(m=2\), and both parity-sum supports have dimension zero. Thus the hypothesis \(m-1>\min_\epsilon\dim\operatorname{Alt}_{S,\epsilon}^nZ\) in Lemma 8.8 is satisfied.

Let \[S_\pm=\sum_{\substack{a_i\in\{\pm1\}\\\prod a_i=\pm1}}
       [a_1p_1+\cdots+a_4p_4]\] denote the multiplicity-one fiber cycles. Under the printed ordered-tuple definitions, the fiber of \(\Lambda_\pm:=\operatorname{Alt}_{S,\pm}^4\Lambda_Z\) is \(24S_\pm\).

Claim 8.9 asserts \[\Lambda_+\circ\Lambda_+-[2]_*\Lambda_+
 =
 \Lambda_-\circ\Lambda_--[2]_*\Lambda_-.
 \tag{3}\] Evaluate the fiber cycles at \(q=2(p_1+p_2+p_3+p_4)\). Independence of the \(p_i\) forces both sign vectors in any sum yielding \(q\) to be \((+,+,+,+)\). Therefore the coefficient of \([q]\) on the left of (3) is \[24^2-24=552,\] whereas on the right it is zero. The witness satisfies the cycle, finiteness, parity, and dimension assumptions. It is not a floating-point diagnostic or a hypothetical representation without a geometric cycle. The retained reviewer-written finite calculation reproduces these coefficients exactly.

Counterevidence and repair. The intended normalization is unusually well evidenced within the paper. Definition 5.19 uses \(1/N(\alpha)\), the ordinary wedge definition on p. 1120 uses \(1/r!\), and the proof on p. 1140 explicitly writes \(1/N(\alpha)\) with \(\alpha=(1^n)\). Thus the problem is an inconsistency among actual definitions and calculations, not an allegation that the intended signed-weight identity is false.

Insert \(1/N(\alpha)\) into the affected definitions; for the spin application this is \(1/n!\). The quotient by permutations of equal-weight entries explains integrality: on the diagonal-free tuple locus the corresponding permutation group acts freely, and the sum map factors through its quotient. The normalized parity cycles have fibers \(S_\pm\) and degrees \(2^{n-1}\).

For these normalized cycles, (3) is valid. Its off-diagonal terms are paired by changing the first coordinate in which the two sign vectors differ. This reverses both parities, preserves their sum, and is an involution. The diagonal terms are exactly \([2]_*S_\pm\). This proves the repaired identity for every \(n\), rather than only the finite samples. Positive rescaling leaves support and dimension arguments unchanged, while the restored multiplicities also restore the stated starting degrees in the Segre-class recursion. With \(s=s(\Lambda_+)\), that recursion must use \(\delta=s(\Lambda_-)-s(\Lambda_+)\) to obtain \((2s+\delta)*\delta=[2]_*\delta\); the definition on p. 1135 reverses this sign. This uniquely determined sign correction is recorded with the normalization repair, without counting another Problem.

Impact. The raw cycle cannot be identified with the multiplicity-one spin-weight cycle as asserted in Theorem 8.5, and Claim 8.9 is false with the printed definitions. These are calculations in the exclusion of spin groups, hence in Theorem C and the main Tannaka classification. This is a Major invalid core derivation under contract 0.7.1, even though a specific normalization repair is available. The repaired counts, parity identity, and unchanged support calculations are verified here; an unconditional independent certification of every other geometric and Tannakian input is not claimed.

The type-\(D\) orbit formula on p. 1106 has a separate local wording issue: when the weight has length \(\ell<n\), an unused zero coordinate can absorb the sign parity, so the nonzero entries are not restricted to even sign changes. The \(\ell<n\) branch of Lemma 5.22 already uses the full signed cycle. This clarification is not counted as another core defect.

A further certification limit concerns the first reducedness conclusion of Lemma 5.22, p. 1107. Abstractly, sending \(\epsilon_4\) to zero and \(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon_3\) to independent lattice elements keeps all eight even all-ones weights distinct, while the standard weights \(\pm\epsilon_4\) coincide. A parity-compensating subgroup can still act transitively on those eight weights. Thus the quotient-lattice interface and abstract transitivity alone do not supply the type-\(B\) collision argument in this full-length type-\(D\) case. No perverse-sheaf or conormal realization satisfying all geometric hypotheses has been constructed here. This is an unclosed limitation, not a counterexample or an additional Problem; the verified normalization repair is not a certification of that separate assertion. For general signed type-\(D\) coefficients, a complete edited definition must also state the absolute-value and parity-relabeling convention.
# Problem 2: the zero-dimensional case contradicts the stated equivalences

Location. The setup on p. 1046, big-monodromy definition on p. 1048, and main monodromy theorem on p. 1049; Theorem A on p. 1053 and Theorem 6.1 on p. 1108. Lemma 2.12 on p. 1064 reflects the same missing restriction.

Take any complex abelian variety \(A\) of dimension \(g\ge3\), let \(S\) be a smooth connected variety, and set \[\mathcal X=\{0\}\times S\subset A\times S.\] This is a closed smooth proper family with connected fibers of dimension \(d=0\). The normal bundle of a fiber is the vector space \(T_0A\) on a point and is ample: its projectivization carries the ample bundle \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{g-1}}(1)\). The bound \(0<(g-1)/2\) holds. Its Euler characteristic is \(1\), and all conditional exclusions in Assumption 1.1 are vacuous. The source’s conventions on p. 1056 do not require a variety to have positive dimension; later statements explicitly impose that condition when needed.

The geometric generic fiber is constant up to translation, so condition (1) of the main monodromy theorem is false. On the other hand, for every character, \[V_\chi=R^0f_*\pi^*L_\chi\] is the trivial rank-one local system. The point is symmetric with translating section zero, and \(d\) is even. Hence the group used in the definition is \(\operatorname{SO}_1=\{1\}\). Its product for any tuple is a normal subgroup of the trivial monodromy group. Condition (2) is true for every torsion tuple. This directly contradicts the printed equivalence.

For the same fiber, \(\delta_{\{0\}}\) is the tensor unit. Its Tannaka group and derived group are trivial, with zero Lie algebra. Section 6.1 defines simplicity through a simple Lie algebra, so the derived group is not simple. Yet a point cannot be a product of two positive-dimensional smooth varieties. This also contradicts Theorem 6.1, not just an informal description in the introduction. Finally, Lemma 2.12 would give \(1=|e_X|\ge g\); its proof assumes \(H^1(X,\mathbb C)\ne0\), which fails for the point.

Repair, impact, and boundary. An explicit restriction \(d>0\) in the monodromy and simplicity statements, and in the relevant numerical lemma, excludes this example. The corresponding nontriviality restriction should also be stated when calling the representation minuscule. These are manifestations of one missing boundary hypothesis, not separate counted errors.

The finding is Major at the level of the stated main equivalence and its simplicity input: admissible parameters give opposite truth values for the two sides. Its scope is exactly the omitted zero-dimensional case. It establishes no failure of the intended positive-dimensional theorem, and adding \(d>0\) is not represented as a new proof of all the remaining cases.
# Problem 3: an arithmetic character twist need not preserve the tensor unit
Location. Lemma 3.12, p. 1077, with the non-algebraically-closed-field conventions of Section 3, p. 1067.

The character group there is defined using the étale fundamental group \(\pi_1(A,0)\), while the section explicitly permits arbitrary characteristic-zero fields. With that arithmetic fundamental group, the assertion that twisting by \(L_\chi\) is a tensor equivalence, and hence preserves the Tannaka group, needs a normalization at the identity.

Let \(k=\mathbb R\), let \(A/k\) be any abelian variety, and let \(\chi\) be the nontrivial character of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb C/\mathbb R)\), pulled back along \(\pi_1(A,0)\to\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb C/\mathbb R)\). Take coefficients in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) and \(P=\delta_0\). Then \[G(P)=1,\qquad P\otimes L_\chi=i_{0*}(\mathrm{sgn}),\qquad
 G(P\otimes L_\chi)=\mu_2.\] Both skyscraper sheaves have geometric Euler characteristic one, so passage to the negligible quotient does not identify them. The second object is a nontrivial invertible object of order two. In particular, the twist sends the tensor unit to a nontrivial object and cannot be a strong tensor equivalence.

The corrected hypothesis is that the restriction \(e^*L_\chi\) at the identity section be the trivial Galois representation, with the normalized multiplicative structure. Then \[m^*L_\chi\simeq \operatorname{pr}_1^*L_\chi
                    \otimes\operatorname{pr}_2^*L_\chi\] and tensoring with \(L_\chi\) respects both convolution and the unit; twisting by \(L_{\chi^{-1}}\) is its inverse. Over an algebraically closed base the arithmetic obstruction is absent.

This normalization is explicitly present in Definition 2.4 of the exact cited Lawrence–Sawin arXiv v4. The characters actually used after passage to the function field in Theorem 4.10 descend from an algebraically closed constant base and have trivial identity restriction. Thus the displayed counterexample establishes a Minor defect in the general lemma, without invalidating that normalized application.
# Problem 4: a line-valued pairing gives a similitude group
Location. The pairing and ensuing upper bound on pp. 1047–1048, together with the assertion on p. 1048 that a family constant up to translation has finite algebraic monodromy.

The pairing has values in the line local system \(a^*L_\chi\): \[V_\chi\otimes V_\chi\longrightarrow a^*L_\chi.
 \tag{4}\] Compatibility with monodromy means preservation with the character of this target line as multiplier. It does not imply preservation of a fixed scalar-valued bilinear form.

For an explicit positive-dimensional example, let \(C\) be a hyperelliptic curve of genus four and \(A=J(C)\). Embed \(C\) using a Weierstrass basepoint, so \(C=-C\). Over \(S=A\), consider the translating family \(X_t=C+t\). It is smooth and proper, and its symmetry section is \(a(t)=2t\). Multiplicativity of the normalized character local system gives \[V_\chi\simeq H^1(C,L_\chi|_C)\otimes L_\chi
 \quad\text{on }S.\] For a nontrivial character \(\chi\) of order three, \(H^0\) and \(H^2\) on \(C\) vanish and \(\dim H^1=6\). The monodromy contains \(\zeta I_6\), where \(\zeta^3=1\) and \(\zeta\ne1\). Its multiplier in the alternating pairing is \(\zeta^2\ne1\). Thus even a torsion character gives a full monodromy group not contained in the asserted symplectic group.

For an analytic character with infinite cyclic image generated by \(2\in\mathbb C^\times\), the same computation gives scalar algebraic monodromy \(\mathbb G_m\). The family is constant up to translation, but its monodromy is not finite. Finiteness of this scalar character is restored by the torsion restriction.

Correction and bounded impact. The unrestricted upper bound is the appropriate similitude group. For torsion \(\chi\), the multiplier has finite image and becomes trivial after a finite étale cover; for arbitrary \(\chi\), every derived subgroup kills the multiplier character. The definition of big monodromy requires the special orthogonal or symplectic group as a normal subgroup, which is compatible with a similitude ambient group. Therefore this is a Minor error in the introductory full-group statements, not a counterexample to the intended positive-dimensional main equivalence.
# Problem 5: the wedge reconstruction statement includes \(r=1\)
Location. Theorem 7.6, p. 1119; its use immediately below, and the end of its proof on p. 1127.

The theorem permits \(e,r\ge1\) and asserts that \(Z\) is a curve if \[\operatorname{Alt}^r\Lambda_Z=\Lambda_{[e](X)},\qquad r\dim Z<\dim A,
 \tag{5}\] with \(X\) smooth and nondivisible and both Gauss maps finite. For \(r=e=1\), (5) is the identity \(\Lambda_Z=\Lambda_X\) and imposes no curve condition.

For a concrete positive-dimensional witness, take a smooth plane quartic \(C\), let \(A=J(C)\), and set \(X=Z=\Theta\simeq\operatorname{Sym}^2C\). The source itself discusses this smooth genus-three theta surface in Proposition 2.9(2). The theta divisor is ample and principal. Its normal bundle is ample, so its Gauss map is finite by Theorem 2.8. Its stabilizer is trivial: a translation preserving \(\Theta\) belongs to the kernel of its principal polarization. Thus every hypothesis of Theorem 7.6 holds with \[e=r=1,\qquad \dim Z=2<3=\dim A,\] but \(Z\) is a surface.

The actual classification theorem, Theorem 7.3, uses \(1<r\le n/2\), and the final curve deduction uses the smoothness criterion for symmetric powers of exponent at least two. Requiring \(r\ge2\) in Theorem 7.6 excludes the example and matches that application. This is a Minor endpoint error in the auxiliary statement; no failure of the actual \(r>1\) reconstruction is established.
# Positive checks, counterevidence, and limitations

The conormal and numerical arguments in Section 2 were checked with their hypotheses. In the proof that a finite Gauss map implies nondegeneracy, both strict dimension inequalities are needed: one gives a positive-dimensional fiber of a quotient map, while the other supplies a nonzero conormal covector common to that fiber. The isogeny pushforward coefficient is the generic degree; nondivisibility forces this degree to be one.

For complete intersections of \(r=g-d\) ample divisors, the Chern-class computation gives \[|e_X|=\sum_{\substack{a_i\ge1\\\sum a_i=g}}D_1^{a_1}\cdots D_r^{a_r}
 \ge g!\binom{g-1}{d}.\] The mixed-intersection inequality supplies the lower bound term by term. When \(d\ge1\), some \(a_i\ge2\), and factorial divisibility in integral cohomology proves evenness. These checks support the stated exclusion of \(27\) and \(56\) in the actual positive-dimensional complete-intersection range. They do not justify extending Lemma 2.12 to points.

Debarre’s original Theorem 4.5 was inspected for the exact relative-cohomology range used in Proposition 2.9. Ein–Ilic–Lazarsfeld’s Proposition 2.4 was checked with \(n=d\) and bundle rank \(g-d\), including its convention \(\delta(t)=2^{\lfloor\sqrt t\rfloor}\) and the nef-cotangent hypothesis. Thus the square-root exponent in Lemma 2.12 is not an OCR or rounding error. The full classical foundations behind these theorems were not reconstructed.

The Galois/monodromy check traced observability and fixed-part inputs to the retrieved primary papers. In the exact Lawrence–Sawin v4, several results cited with Section 5 numbers occur in Section 4; the matching statements, rather than an unsupported citation-number match, were checked. The normalized geometric characters used in the main application avoid Problem 3. Nondivisibility supplies the relevant irreducibility of the connected derived action.

The symplectic wedge range was also stress-tested. For a positive-dimensional nondegenerate support, the identity relating \(\operatorname{Alt}^{n+1}V\) and \(\operatorname{Alt}^{n-1}V\) for \(\dim V=2n\), together with support dimensions, rules out \((n+1)d<g\). This explains why the primitive-wedge argument is used in its permissible range. An intermediate generic degree described as exactly two need only be at least two; no separate substantive issue is inferred from that overstatement.

The independent finite weight checks reproduce the normalized parity identity and the exceptional minuscule orbit sizes \(27,27,56\). They check those counts and duality properties, not the completeness of the classification of simple Lie algebras. In the spin exclusion, the possible Euler characteristic eight is ruled out using parity and the surface bound: the relevant dimensions force a surface and the bounds exceed eight. No missing low-rank exception was established.

The support-union formula on p. 1130 needs its stated range restricted to \(r\le n\), or its lower summation index changed to \(\max(0,r-n)\). The subsequent use is at \(r=2\le n\), so this out-of-range wording does not supply another main-theorem failure. The negative-valued second branch in Example 7.8 is similarly a transparent formula correction, not a separately counted Problem.

Appendix A’s field-reduction interfaces and Appendix B’s symmetric-power and birational arguments were checked in their stated characteristic-zero settings. The full external theories of constructible sheaves, microlocal characteristic cycles, generic vanishing, and Tannakian duality remain imported. No missing author code is treated as a mathematical defect, and no search is claimed to prove first discovery or the absence of corrections.

Take any complex abelian variety \(A\) of dimension \(g\ge3\), let \(S\) be a smooth connected variety, and set \[\mathcal X=\{0\}\times S\subset A\times S.\] This is a closed smooth proper family with connected fibers of dimension \(d=0\). Its Euler characteristic is \(1\), and all conditional exclusions in Assumption 1.1 are vacuous. The source’s conventions on p. 1056 do not require a variety to have positive dimension; later statements explicitly impose that condition when needed.

The geometric generic fiber is constant up to translation, so condition (1) of the main monodromy theorem is false. On the other hand, for every character, \[V_\chi=R^0f_*\pi^*L_\chi\] is the trivial rank-one local system. The point is symmetric with translating section zero, and \(d\) is even. Hence the group used in the definition is \(\operatorname{SO}_1=\{1\}\). Its product for any tuple is a normal subgroup of the trivial monodromy group. Condition (2) is true for every torsion tuple. This directly contradicts the printed equivalence.

For the same fiber, \(\delta_{\{0\}}\) is the tensor unit. Its Tannaka group and derived group are trivial, with zero Lie algebra. Section 6.1 defines simplicity through a simple Lie algebra, so the derived group is not simple. Yet a point cannot be a product of two positive-dimensional smooth varieties. This also contradicts Theorem 6.1, not just an informal description in the introduction. Finally, Lemma 2.12 would give \(1=|e_X|\ge g\); its proof assumes \(H^1(X,\mathbb C)\ne0\), which fails for the point.

Repair, impact, and boundary. An explicit restriction \(d>0\) in the monodromy and simplicity statements, and in the relevant numerical lemma, excludes this example. The corresponding nontriviality restriction should also be stated when calling the representation minuscule. These are manifestations of one missing boundary hypothesis, not separate counted errors.

The finding is Major at the level of the stated main equivalence and its simplicity input: admissible parameters give opposite truth values for the two sides. Its scope is exactly the omitted zero-dimensional case. It establishes no failure of the intended positive-dimensional theorem, and adding \(d>0\) is not represented as a new proof of all the remaining cases.
result: Impact: Literal main equivalence is false at admissible parameters; the central simplicity criterion also fails at the same endpoint. The numerical lemma would assert1≥g.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: State d>0/nontriviality in the affected theorems, minuscule statement and numerical lemma, or handle the unit object separately.

problems.title: Unnormalized arithmetic twists need not preserve the tensor unit
problems.source_location: Section3 field/character conventions p1067 Lemma3.12 p1077 Normalized main application pp1083–1086
claim: Recorded check: Unnormalized arithmetic twists need not preserve the tensor unit
analysis: Location. Lemma 3.12, p. 1077, with the non-algebraically-closed-field conventions of Section 3, p. 1067.

The character group there is defined using the étale fundamental group \(\pi_1(A,0)\), while the section explicitly permits arbitrary characteristic-zero fields. With that arithmetic fundamental group, the assertion that twisting by \(L_\chi\) is a tensor equivalence, and hence preserves the Tannaka group, needs a normalization at the identity.

Let \(k=\mathbb R\), let \(A/k\) be any abelian variety, and let \(\chi\) be the nontrivial character of \(\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb C/\mathbb R)\), pulled back along \(\pi_1(A,0)\to\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb C/\mathbb R)\). Take coefficients in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) and \(P=\delta_0\). Then \[G(P)=1,\qquad P\otimes L_\chi=i_{0*}(\mathrm{sgn}),\qquad
 G(P\otimes L_\chi)=\mu_2.\] Both skyscraper sheaves have geometric Euler characteristic one, so passage to the negligible quotient does not identify them. The second object is a nontrivial invertible object of order two. In particular, the twist sends the tensor unit to a nontrivial object and cannot be a strong tensor equivalence.

The corrected hypothesis is that the restriction \(e^*L_\chi\) at the identity section be the trivial Galois representation, with the normalized multiplicative structure. Then \[m^*L_\chi\simeq \operatorname{pr}_1^*L_\chi
                    \otimes\operatorname{pr}_2^*L_\chi\] and tensoring with \(L_\chi\) respects both convolution and the unit; twisting by \(L_{\chi^{-1}}\) is its inverse. Over an algebraically closed base the arithmetic obstruction is absent.

This normalization is explicitly present in Definition 2.4 of the exact cited Lawrence–Sawin arXiv v4. The characters actually used after passage to the function field in Theorem 4.10 descend from an algebraically closed constant base and have trivial identity restriction. Thus the displayed counterexample establishes a Minor defect in the general lemma, without invalidating that normalized application.
result: Impact: False general lemma; actual constant algebraically closed base characters in Theorem4.10 meet the missing normalization.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Require e*Lχ trivial as Galois representation with normalized multiplicative structure, or restrict the lemma to an algebraically closed field.

problems.title: Line-valued pairings and translating families require similitude/scalar qualifications
problems.source_location: Pairing p1047 Full group bound and translation-constant finiteness p1048
claim: Recorded check: Line-valued pairings and translating families require similitude/scalar qualifications
analysis: Location. The pairing and ensuing upper bound on pp. 1047–1048, together with the assertion on p. 1048 that a family constant up to translation has finite algebraic monodromy.

The pairing has values in the line local system \(a^*L_\chi\): \[V_\chi\otimes V_\chi\longrightarrow a^*L_\chi.
 \tag{4}\] Compatibility with monodromy means preservation with the character of this target line as multiplier. It does not imply preservation of a fixed scalar-valued bilinear form.

For an explicit positive-dimensional example, let \(C\) be a hyperelliptic curve of genus four and \(A=J(C)\). Embed \(C\) using a Weierstrass basepoint, so \(C=-C\). Over \(S=A\), consider the translating family \(X_t=C+t\). It is smooth and proper, and its symmetry section is \(a(t)=2t\). Multiplicativity of the normalized character local system gives \[V_\chi\simeq H^1(C,L_\chi|_C)\otimes L_\chi
 \quad\text{on }S.\] For a nontrivial character \(\chi\) of order three, \(H^0\) and \(H^2\) on \(C\) vanish and \(\dim H^1=6\). The monodromy contains \(\zeta I_6\), where \(\zeta^3=1\) and \(\zeta\ne1\). Its multiplier in the alternating pairing is \(\zeta^2\ne1\). Thus even a torsion character gives a full monodromy group not contained in the asserted symplectic group.

For an analytic character with infinite cyclic image generated by \(2\in\mathbb C^\times\), the same computation gives scalar algebraic monodromy \(\mathbb G_m\). The family is constant up to translation, but its monodromy is not finite. Finiteness of this scalar character is restored by the torsion restriction.

Correction and bounded impact. The unrestricted upper bound is the appropriate similitude group. For torsion \(\chi\), the multiplier has finite image and becomes trivial after a finite étale cover; for arbitrary \(\chi\), every derived subgroup kills the multiplier character. The definition of big monodromy requires the special orthogonal or symplectic group as a normal subgroup, which is compatible with a similitude ambient group. Therefore this is a Minor error in the introductory full-group statements, not a counterexample to the intended positive-dimensional main equivalence.
result: Impact: Incorrect full-group and unrestricted finiteness assertions; derived-group and torsion formulations used for the main theorem remain protected.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use the appropriate similitude group; qualify finiteness by torsion and distinguish full from derived monodromy.

claim: Recorded check: Wedge reconstruction incorrectly permits r=1
analysis: Location. Theorem 7.6, p. 1119; its use immediately below, and the end of its proof on p. 1127.

The theorem permits \(e,r\ge1\) and asserts that \(Z\) is a curve if \[\operatorname{Alt}^r\Lambda_Z=\Lambda_{[e](X)},\qquad r\dim Z<\dim A,
 \tag{5}\] with \(X\) smooth and nondivisible and both Gauss maps finite. For \(r=e=1\), (5) is the identity \(\Lambda_Z=\Lambda_X\) and imposes no curve condition.

For a concrete positive-dimensional witness, take a smooth plane quartic \(C\), let \(A=J(C)\), and set \(X=Z=\Theta\simeq\operatorname{Sym}^2C\). The source itself discusses this smooth genus-three theta surface in Proposition 2.9(2). The theta divisor is ample and principal. Its normal bundle is ample, so its Gauss map is finite by Theorem 2.8. Its stabilizer is trivial: a translation preserving \(\Theta\) belongs to the kernel of its principal polarization. Thus every hypothesis of Theorem 7.6 holds with \[e=r=1,\qquad \dim Z=2<3=\dim A,\] but \(Z\) is a surface.

The actual classification theorem, Theorem 7.3, uses \(1<r\le n/2\), and the final curve deduction uses the smoothness criterion for symmetric powers of exponent at least two. Requiring \(r\ge2\) in Theorem 7.6 excludes the example and matches that application. Title: Initial mathematical review: M25-0160
A Schiffer-type problem for annuli with applications to stationary planar Euler flows

Authors: Alberto Enciso, Antonio J. Fernández, David Ruiz, and Pieralberto Sicbaldi. Publication identity: Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), no. 6, 1151–1208; DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0054 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0054).

Reviewed version: arXiv:2309.07977v2, dated 12 August 2024, 50 pages, with its matching deposited TeX and two figures. All page numbers below refer to this author manuscript; printed and physical PDF page numbers coincide. The publisher version of record was not acquired, so the findings are not attributed to its text.

Initial assessment: Major, at the level of two stated proof derivations. The passage from a local Euler solution to the global weak equation drops a nonzero pressure term on the hole and the compensating boundary flux. An explicit admissible test field makes the displayed intermediate integral nonzero. In the infinite-spectrum rigidity argument, the vector used after (6.10) omits the absolute inverse-square-root weights; the asserted linear rewriting is false. Both steps directly prove advertised contributions, Theorem 1.3 and Theorem 6.1, respectively. Both admit explicit repairs verified below. No counterexample to either repaired theorem, or to the principal large-angular-mode bifurcation construction, was established. The scientific decision remains `pending`; `human_reviews=[]`.
# Scope and logical structure

The main construction seeks a nonconstant Neumann eigenfunction satisfying \[\Delta u+\mu u=0\quad\hbox{in }\Omega,\qquad
 \nabla u=0\quad\hbox{on }\partial\Omega.\] Its boundary value may differ between connected components. This distinction from the classical Schiffer problem is essential. The domains are small analytic perturbations of an annulus, and the nonradial conclusion concerns the nontrivial branch, with the radial annulus retained at the bifurcation parameter zero.

The proof first identifies a crossing of the second nonconstant radial Neumann eigenvalue \(\mu_{0,2}\) with the first angular-mode-\(l\) Dirichlet eigenvalue \(\lambda_{l,0}\). It proves nonresonance in a dihedral symmetry class, establishes transversality for sufficiently large \(l\), and applies the Crandall–Rabinowitz theorem in anisotropic Hölder spaces. A separate numerical appendix treats \(l=4\). The resulting eigenfunction yields a Pompeiu-type integral identity and a compactly supported stationary Euler flow. Section 6 gives two additional rigidity theorems.

The primary reviewer read the introduction, the crossing and nonresonance argument, the complete applications section, and the decisive curvature passage. Three actual native scientific assistants checked the full spectral section; the functional setting, bifurcation proof and pullback appendix; and the rigidity section with the numerical appendix. Thus reading coverage is collective and the proof checks are bounded by the retained ledger. Selected original dependencies were inspected. The full external theories of analytic perturbation, elliptic regularity, stationary phase and nodal geometry were not all independently rebuilt.
# Problem 1: the weak Euler calculation omits the hole pressure

Location and claim. Theorem 1.3, p. 5; the definition of a stationary weak solution and the pressure formula, p. 33; and the first displayed calculation on p. 34, concluding its proof. The test class is explicitly every \(w\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2,\mathbb R^2)\), not only divergence-free tests.

Write \(\Omega'\) for the bounded hole, \(\Gamma_1\) for the outer boundary and \(\Gamma_2=\partial\Omega'\) for the inner boundary. The source has \(u|_{\Gamma_j}=c_j\), \(\nabla u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\), and defines \[v=\begin{cases}(u_{x_2},-u_{x_1})&\text{in }\Omega,\\0&\text{outside }\Omega,\end{cases}\] together with the continuous pressure \[p=\begin{cases}
 0&\text{in the unbounded complementary component},\\
 -\frac12\bigl(|\nabla u|^2+\mu u^2-\mu c_1^2\bigr)&\text{in }\Omega,\\
 p_h:=-\frac{\mu}{2}(c_2^2-c_1^2)&\text{in }\Omega'.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{1}\] For \[I_D(w):=\int_D\bigl(v_i v_j\partial_iw_j+p\,\operatorname{div}w\bigr)\,\mathrm dx,\] the display on p. 34 asserts \[I_{\mathbb R^2}(w)=I_\Omega(w)
 =-\int_\Omega\bigl((v\cdot\nabla)v+\nabla p\bigr)\cdot w\,\mathrm dx=0.
 \tag{2}\] Both intermediate reductions in (2) fail for the defined pressure.

The pressure on the hole is nonzero. The radial Neumann branch used in the construction satisfies \[\psi''+\frac1r\psi'+\mu\psi=0,\qquad \psi'(a)=\psi'(1)=0.\] Its energy obeys the exact identity \[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dr}
 \left(\frac{(\psi')^2}{2}+\frac{\mu\psi^2}{2}\right)
 =-\frac{(\psi')^2}{r}.
 \tag{3}\] The eigenfunction is nonconstant and \(\mu>0\), so integration gives \(\psi(a)^2>\psi(1)^2\). Neither endpoint value vanishes, by uniqueness for the ODE. The second nonconstant radial eigenfunction has two interior zeros and therefore its endpoint values have the same sign.

The branch retains these radial boundary values: in the formula for \(\widetilde w_s\) on p. 31, both \(v_s\) and \(\overline\psi_{a(s)}'\) vanish on the boundary. Consequently \(c_2^2>c_1^2\) and \(p_h<0\). Alternatively, strict inequality at the radial point and continuity already suffice for small nonzero branch parameters. Thus the omitted term is not identically zero under the application’s hypotheses.

An admissible test and a decisive discrepancy. Choose a smooth compactly supported vector field \(w\) equal to \(x\) on a neighborhood of \(\overline{\Omega'}\) and zero near \(\Gamma_1\). Such a cutoff exists because the two boundary curves are disjoint compact sets. Then \[\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}w\,\mathrm dx=2|\Omega'|,
 \qquad
 \int_{\Gamma_2}w\cdot\nu_\Omega\,\mathrm dS=-2|\Omega'|.
 \tag{4}\] The normals of \(\Omega\) and \(\Omega'\) on their common interface are opposite.

Inside \(\Omega\), the pointwise equation is correct. Direct differentiation gives \[(v\cdot\nabla)v+\nabla p
 =-(\Delta u+\mu u)\nabla u=0.
 \tag{5}\] Since \(v=0\) on both boundary components, the kinetic boundary flux vanishes. However, the pressure flux on \(\Gamma_2\) does not. Integration by parts therefore gives \[I_\Omega(w)=p_h\int_{\Gamma_2}w\cdot\nu_\Omega\,\mathrm dS
          =-2p_h|\Omega'|\ne0.
 \tag{6}\] The hole contributes \[I_{\Omega'}(w)=p_h\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}w\,\mathrm dx
           =2p_h|\Omega'|.
 \tag{7}\] Thus the source’s assertion \(I_\Omega(w)=0\) is false, and the equality \(I_{\mathbb R^2}(w)=I_\Omega(w)\) is false as well. This is an exact flux calculation for an allowed test, not a numerical residual or a counterexample that violates the test class. The coordinate identity (5), the energy identity (3), and the cancellation in (6)–(7) were also checked with reviewer-written symbolic code.

Complete repair and counterevidence. The actual pair \((v,p)\) in (1) is a global weak solution. For an arbitrary test \(w\), the correct calculation is \[\begin{aligned}
 I_{\mathbb R^2}(w)
 &=I_\Omega(w)+p_h\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}w\,\mathrm dx\\
 &=-\int_\Omega\bigl((v\cdot\nabla)v+\nabla p\bigr)\cdot w\,\mathrm dx\\
 &\quad+p_h\left(
   \int_{\Gamma_2}w\cdot\nu_\Omega\,\mathrm dS+
   \int_{\partial\Omega'}w\cdot\nu_{\Omega'}\,\mathrm dS\right)=0.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{8}\] The outer pressure is zero and the two inner fluxes cancel. Equivalently, the stress tensor \(v\otimes v+pI\) has matching normal traces. In fact it is globally \(C^1\): from \(u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)\) and \(\nabla u=0\) on the boundary, one has \(\nabla p=-(D^2u+\mu uI)\nabla u\to0\), and the first derivatives of \(v_iv_j\) also tend to zero. Direct integration by parts on the whole plane therefore gives another complete repair. The pressure was already defined correctly in the source; it is the displayed integration argument that fails.

An interpretation using divergence-free tests would avoid the pressure integral, but it does not match the explicit quantifier on p. 33. An interpretation in which \(\Omega\) includes its hole contradicts the domain notation and the separate definition of \(p\) on \(\Omega'\). Neither reading makes (2) true as written.

Impact and classification. The invalid calculation is the step that turns the constructed annular eigenfunction into the whole-plane weak Euler solution promised in the title, abstract and Theorem 1.3. Under contract 0.7.1, this is a Major invalid derivation tied directly to an advertised core application. Its short repair and the survival of the actual construction do not change what the original calculation asserts. The finding does not invalidate the bifurcation theorem, the Pompeiu corollary, or the repaired Euler solution. No further hypothesis or new computation is needed for repair (8).
# Problem 2: the rigidity proof changes its curvature weights

Location and dependency. Theorem 6.1, p. 34; the parallel-curve relation (6.5), p. 37; the stationary-phase reduction (6.10), p. 39; and the definition of \(V\) leading to (6.11), p. 40. The theorem asserts that a smooth bounded planar domain admitting infinitely many orthogonal Neumann eigenfunctions locally constant on the boundary must be a disk or an annulus.

At the decisive point, the proof has distinct constants \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\), with \(C_1=0\), and a nonzero curvature \(k(s)\) on a small interval where \(1+C_\ell k(s)\ne0\). Equation (6.10) is \[\sum_{\ell=1}^m\widetilde\delta_\ell
 \left|\frac{k(s)}{1+C_\ell k(s)}\right|^{-1/2}=o(1).
 \tag{9}\] Taking a nonvanishing real or imaginary part and normalizing supplies unit vectors \(A_r\) and a subsequential limit \(A\) of norm one. The source then states that (9) can be rewritten using \[V(s)=\left(
 \frac{k(s)}{1+C_1k(s)},\ldots,
 \frac{k(s)}{1+C_mk(s)}
 \right)
 \tag{10}\] as \(A_r\cdot V(s)=o(1)\) and hence \(A\cdot V(s)=0\).

The actual vector determined by (9) is \[W(s)=\left(
 \left|\frac{k(s)}{1+C_1k(s)}\right|^{-1/2},\ldots,
 \left|\frac{k(s)}{1+C_mk(s)}\right|^{-1/2}
 \right).
 \tag{11}\] A linear relation among the components of \(W\) does not become the same linear relation among the components of \(V\).

Exact algebraic witness. Take regular values \[m=2,\qquad k=1,\qquad C_1=0,\quad C_2=3,\qquad
 A=\frac1{\sqrt5}(2,-1).\] All denominators are nonzero and the constants are distinct. Then \[W=(1,2),\qquad V=(1,\tfrac14),\qquad
 A\cdot W=0,\quad A\cdot V=\frac7{4\sqrt5}\ne0.
 \tag{12}\] Thus the proposed rewriting is not a linear-algebra identity, even at a single regular curvature value with a normalized nonzero coefficient vector. This is a counterexample to the displayed rewriting, not a constructed domain satisfying the spectral hypotheses of Theorem 6.1. The latter theorem is not claimed false.

A full repair of the curvature step. Retain \(W\) in the subsequence argument. The conclusion is then \(A\cdot W(s)=0\). Multiplying by \(\sqrt{|k(s)|}\) gives \[\sum_{\ell=1}^m A_\ell f_\ell(k(s))=0,\qquad
 f_\ell(k):=\sqrt{|1+C_\ell k|}.
 \tag{13}\] On a regular interval the signs of the linear factors are fixed. For any point \(k_0\) of that interval, \[f_\ell^{(j)}(k_0)
 =f_\ell(k_0)
   \left(\tfrac12\right)_{\!j}
   \left(\frac{C_\ell}{1+C_\ell k_0}\right)^j,
 \qquad 0\le j\le m-1,
 \tag{14}\] where \((\frac12)_j=\frac12(\frac12-1)\cdots(\frac12-j+1)\) is the falling factorial, with value one for \(j=0\).

Put \(q_\ell=C_\ell/(1+C_\ell k_0)\). The Wronskian determinant factors as \[\det\bigl[f_\ell^{(j)}(k_0)\bigr]_
       {\substack{0\le j<m\\1\le\ell\le m}}
 =
 \left(\prod_{\ell=1}^m f_\ell(k_0)\right)
 \left(\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\left(\tfrac12\right)_{\!j}\right)
 \prod_{i<\ell}(q_\ell-q_i).
 \tag{15}\] Every factor is nonzero. Indeed, \[q_\ell-q_i=
 \frac{C_\ell-C_i}{(1+C_\ell k_0)(1+C_i k_0)}\ne0.\] This also includes \(C_1=0\); no division by \(C_1\) is used.

If \(k(s)\) were nonconstant, its continuous image would contain a nondegenerate interval. Equation (13) would give a fixed linear relation among the \(f_\ell\) on that interval, contradicting (15) because \(|A|=1\). Therefore \(k\) is constant. The subsequent circular-boundary and unique-continuation argument can then proceed with the intended conclusion.

Counterevidence and limits of the repair. The inverse-square-root factor in (9) is the stationary-phase amplitude and agrees with the preceding displayed formulas. Thus changing the definition of \(V\) to \(W\) is strongly supported by the source. Merely replacing the symbol in (10), however, does not prove the asserted noncontainment in a hyperplane; (13)–(15) provide the needed argument for the correct vector.

The common-phase calculation on p. 39 also contains local \(\xi/\eta\) and phase-sign inconsistencies. Correcting the derivative to \(p_1(s)\cdot\widetilde\eta(s)\) and absorbing the appropriate constant phase restores a common factor of modulus one. These are recorded with the proof clarification, not counted as independent Problems.

The stationary-phase grouping upstream of (9) was stress-tested separately. For each fixed \(s\), finitely many fixed imaginary shifts give a Vandermonde system in the distinct numbers \(\exp(b)\). Keeping the bounded coefficients \(\sigma_{n,\ell}\) until after this separation avoids an unsupported interchange with a growing exponential factor. This supplies counterevidence against an additional asserted failure upstream. The exact large-imaginary-shift theorem cited from Berenstein was not retrieved from the subscription-only primary source; the fixed-shift argument does not claim to certify that particular formulation.

Impact and classification. The claimed \(A\cdot V=0\) is the decisive input to curvature constancy and hence to Theorem 6.1. Its derivation from (9) is invalid. This is a Major defect in that rigidity derivation under contract 0.7.1, with the dependency explicit. The corrected Wronskian calculation restores this local step. It does not establish that every other imported part of the rigidity proof has been independently certified, and no failure of the main nonradial existence theorem follows from this issue.
# Positive checks and bounded clarifications
## Crossing, nonresonance and the large-parameter calculation

The derivative of a radial Neumann eigenfunction obeys the angular-mode-one Dirichlet equation. Sturm oscillation gives the index shift \[\mu_{0,n}(a)=\lambda_{1,n-1}(a),\qquad n\ge1.\] For fixed \(l\), the thin-annulus limits with \(h=(1-a)/\pi\) give \(\mu_{0,2}\sim4h^{-2}\) and \(\lambda_{l,0}\sim h^{-2}+l^2\). At the disk end, the relevant limits are \(j_{1,2}^2\) and \(j_{l,1}^2\), with the required strict inequality starting at \(l=4\). The official Bessel-zero interlacing formula [DLMF] and independent numerical values were inspected. Continuity supplies a crossing. The proof of nonresonance separately handles higher multiples of \(l\), higher radial indices, and the radial mode; it does not assume that the full unsymmetrized spectrum is simple.

The spectral checker reconstructed the first-order corrections and the second-order coefficients. With the source’s notation, the explicit functions \[\Phi_{10}(x)=(2x-\pi)\sin x+\frac32x(\pi-x)\cos x,
 \qquad
 \widetilde\Psi_{10}(x)=
 \left(\frac x2-\frac\pi4\right)\cos2x-\frac14\sin2x\] give \(\Lambda_{20}=-16\) and \(\widetilde\nu_{20}=3/4\). These are exact symbolic checks, distinct from numerical corroboration. The fixed-domain simple eigenbranches depend analytically on the common parameters, which supplies control of differentiated Taylor remainders. In particular the independent first-order calculation gives \[\mu'_{0,2}(a_l)-\lambda'_{l,0}(a_l)
 =\frac{2l^3}{\sqrt3\,\pi}+O(l^2)>0\] for sufficiently large \(l\). No invalid differentiation of a merely pointwise big-\(O\) estimate was established.
## Functional setting, branch symmetry and analyticity

The anisotropic space, following the framework in [FMW], controls an additional radial derivative. Its role is to keep the nonlinear pullback map and the boundary reconstruction in compatible spaces. The check traced the kernel, the weighted range orthogonality, the Fredholm index and the eigenvalue-derivative form of transversality through the bifurcation argument. The original Crandall–Rabinowitz statement [CR] was checked against the actual one-dimensional kernel and codimension-one range.

The first-order inner-radius expression in Theorem 1.1 also needs \(a'(0)=0\). This follows from a justified symmetry: rotation by \(\pi/l\) preserves the dihedral function space and changes the sign of its kernel vector. Using the kernel projection as the local parameter and an invariant complement, local uniqueness gives \(a(-s)=a(s)\). Thus the constant radial drift is \(o(s)\), and the stated leading cosine is consistent.

Spatial analyticity is distinct from analyticity in the bifurcation parameter. Near each boundary, \(u=c_i\ne0\) and \(\nabla u=0\); for \(z=u-c_i\) the equation is \(\Delta z+\mu z+\mu c_i=0\). The nonzero constant term supplies the nondegeneracy required by the inspected Kinderlehrer–Nirenberg free-boundary theorem [KN]. The source asserts a \(C^1\) parameter curve and analytic spatial boundaries, not an analytic parameter dependence.
## Applications, rigidity and the numerical appendix

The Pompeiu-type gluing has matching values and first derivatives across both interfaces. Its compactly supported function satisfies \[(\Delta+\mu)w=\mathbf{1}_{\Omega}-c\,\mathbf{1}_{\Omega'},
 \qquad c=c_2/c_1-1>0,\] in the distributional sense. Entire Helmholtz solutions therefore annihilate this source. The rigid-motion line has an inverse-convention slip, repaired by the standard change of variables; the universal integral identity survives.

For the Euler field, analyticity and nonconstancy imply that the gradient cannot vanish on an open subset, so \(\operatorname{supp}v=\overline\Omega\). The nonzero boundary values also explain the jump in the normal derivative of the velocity, while the velocity itself remains continuous. These properties are compatible with the weak, rather than \(C^1\), formulation. If the analytic field were radial on a nonempty open piece, its rotational derivative about that center would vanish analytically throughout the connected annular domain. The boundary would then lie on circles where the radial derivative vanishes. The noncircular branch therefore cannot be assembled from locally radial pieces.

The low-eigenvalue rigidity argument was checked separately from the infinite-spectrum theorem. It uses the derivatives generated by translations and rotations as Dirichlet eigenfunctions, eigenvalue comparison with multiplicities, and nodal topology. Its hypotheses and zero-based indexing were retained; no additional counterexample was established. The full cited Filonov/Friedlander and Reichel originals were not all retrieved; their role here is a checked statement and applicability interface, not a newly certified foundation.

Independent floating-point calculations for Appendix A give \[\begin{aligned}
 a_4&=0.1409893318207135179162\ldots,\\
 \mu_{0,2}(a_4)=\lambda_{4,0}(a_4)
     &=57.585155069669585459\ldots,\\
 \mu'_{0,2}(a_4)&=105.970673822067813524\ldots,\\
 \lambda'_{4,0}(a_4)&=0.1206696801319745464\ldots .
 \end{aligned}\] The reported derivative formulas agree with independent implicit differentiation and convergent centered differences. The numerical mode count gives 18 eigenvalues below the target, counting angular multiplicities, consistent with \(\mu_{18}\). Two printed index labels on p. 46 are transposed: the value \(44.0466317110\ldots\) belongs to \(\mu_{2,1}\) and \(64.1201718634\ldots\) to \(\mu_{3,1}\). Correcting those labels preserves the count.

The appendix itself distinguishes these computations from a computer-assisted proof. The present recomputation likewise supplies no certified interval enclosure. problems.title: The weak Euler integration chain discards nonzero hole pressure and inner boundary flux
problems.source_location: Theorem 1.3, p. 5 Weak-solution test class and pressure definition, p. 33 First display on p. 34, concluding the proof of Theorem 1.3 Deposited TeX, approximately lines 1815–1832
claim: For every compactly supported smooth vector test w, the global stress integral equals its annular restriction, which equals the negative local Euler-residual integral and hence zero.
analysis: Location and claim. Theorem 1.3, p. 5; the definition of a stationary weak solution and the pressure formula, p. 33; and the first displayed calculation on p. 34, concluding its proof. The test class is explicitly every \(w\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2,\mathbb R^2)\), not only divergence-free tests.

Write \(\Omega'\) for the bounded hole, \(\Gamma_1\) for the outer boundary and \(\Gamma_2=\partial\Omega'\) for the inner boundary. The source has \(u|_{\Gamma_j}=c_j\), \(\nabla u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\), and defines \[v=\begin{cases}(u_{x_2},-u_{x_1})&\text{in }\Omega,\\0&\text{outside }\Omega,\end{cases}\] together with the continuous pressure \[p=\begin{cases}
 0&\text{in the unbounded complementary component},\\
 -\frac12\bigl(|\nabla u|^2+\mu u^2-\mu c_1^2\bigr)&\text{in }\Omega,\\
 p_h:=-\frac{\mu}{2}(c_2^2-c_1^2)&\text{in }\Omega'.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{1}\] For \[I_D(w):=\int_D\bigl(v_i v_j\partial_iw_j+p\,\operatorname{div}w\bigr)\,\mathrm dx,\] the display on p. 34 asserts \[I_{\mathbb R^2}(w)=I_\Omega(w)
 =-\int_\Omega\bigl((v\cdot\nabla)v+\nabla p\bigr)\cdot w\,\mathrm dx=0.
 \tag{2}\] Both intermediate reductions in (2) fail for the defined pressure.

The pressure on the hole is nonzero. The radial Neumann branch used in the construction satisfies \[\psi''+\frac1r\psi'+\mu\psi=0,\qquad \psi'(a)=\psi'(1)=0.\] Its energy obeys the exact identity \[\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dr}
 \left(\frac{(\psi')^2}{2}+\frac{\mu\psi^2}{2}\right)
 =-\frac{(\psi')^2}{r}.
 \tag{3}\] The eigenfunction is nonconstant and \(\mu>0\), so integration gives \(\psi(a)^2>\psi(1)^2\). Neither endpoint value vanishes, by uniqueness for the ODE. The second nonconstant radial eigenfunction has two interior zeros and therefore its endpoint values have the same sign.

The branch retains these radial boundary values: in the formula for \(\widetilde w_s\) on p. 31, both \(v_s\) and \(\overline\psi_{a(s)}'\) vanish on the boundary. Consequently \(c_2^2>c_1^2\) and \(p_h<0\). Alternatively, strict inequality at the radial point and continuity already suffice for small nonzero branch parameters. Thus the omitted term is not identically zero under the application’s hypotheses.

An admissible test and a decisive discrepancy. Choose a smooth compactly supported vector field \(w\) equal to \(x\) on a neighborhood of \(\overline{\Omega'}\) and zero near \(\Gamma_1\). Such a cutoff exists because the two boundary curves are disjoint compact sets. Then \[\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}w\,\mathrm dx=2|\Omega'|,
 \qquad
 \int_{\Gamma_2}w\cdot\nu_\Omega\,\mathrm dS=-2|\Omega'|.
 \tag{4}\] The normals of \(\Omega\) and \(\Omega'\) on their common interface are opposite.

Inside \(\Omega\), the pointwise equation is correct. Direct differentiation gives \[(v\cdot\nabla)v+\nabla p
 =-(\Delta u+\mu u)\nabla u=0.
 \tag{5}\] Since \(v=0\) on both boundary components, the kinetic boundary flux vanishes. However, the pressure flux on \(\Gamma_2\) does not. Integration by parts therefore gives \[I_\Omega(w)=p_h\int_{\Gamma_2}w\cdot\nu_\Omega\,\mathrm dS
          =-2p_h|\Omega'|\ne0.
 \tag{6}\] The hole contributes \[I_{\Omega'}(w)=p_h\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}w\,\mathrm dx
           =2p_h|\Omega'|.
 \tag{7}\] Thus the source’s assertion \(I_\Omega(w)=0\) is false, and the equality \(I_{\mathbb R^2}(w)=I_\Omega(w)\) is false as well. This is an exact flux calculation for an allowed test, not a numerical residual or a counterexample that violates the test class. The coordinate identity (5), the energy identity (3), and the cancellation in (6)–(7) were also checked with reviewer-written symbolic code.

Complete repair and counterevidence. The actual pair \((v,p)\) in (1) is a global weak solution. For an arbitrary test \(w\), the correct calculation is \[\begin{aligned}
 I_{\mathbb R^2}(w)
 &=I_\Omega(w)+p_h\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}w\,\mathrm dx\\
 &=-\int_\Omega\bigl((v\cdot\nabla)v+\nabla p\bigr)\cdot w\,\mathrm dx\\
 &\quad+p_h\left(
   \int_{\Gamma_2}w\cdot\nu_\Omega\,\mathrm dS+
   \int_{\partial\Omega'}w\cdot\nu_{\Omega'}\,\mathrm dS\right)=0.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{8}\] The outer pressure is zero and the two inner fluxes cancel. Equivalently, the stress tensor \(v\otimes v+pI\) has matching normal traces. In fact it is globally \(C^1\): from \(u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)\) and \(\nabla u=0\) on the boundary, one has \(\nabla p=-(D^2u+\mu uI)\nabla u\to0\), and the first derivatives of \(v_iv_j\) also tend to zero. Direct integration by parts on the whole plane therefore gives another complete repair. The pressure was already defined correctly in the source; it is the displayed integration argument that fails.

An interpretation using divergence-free tests would avoid the pressure integral, but it does not match the explicit quantifier on p. 33. An interpretation in which \(\Omega\) includes its hole contradicts the domain notation and the separate definition of \(p\) on \(\Omega'\). Neither reading makes (2) true as written.

Impact and classification. The invalid calculation is the step that turns the constructed annular eigenfunction into the whole-plane weak Euler solution promised in the title, abstract and Theorem 1.3. Under contract 0.7.1, this is a Major invalid derivation tied directly to an advertised core application. Its short repair and the survival of the actual construction do not change what the original calculation asserts. The finding does not invalidate the bifurcation theorem, the Pompeiu corollary, or the repaired Euler solution. No further hypothesis or new computation is needed for repair (8).
result: Impact: A demonstrated invalid derivation directly supports a named core application in the title, abstract and Theorem 1.3. The severity concerns that derivation, not falsity of the theorem.

problems.title: The infinite-spectrum rigidity proof replaces inverse-square-root curvature weights by raw curvatures
problems.source_location: Theorem 6.1, p. 34 Parallel-curve relation (6.5), p. 37 Stationary-phase relation (6.10), p. 39 Definition of V and relation (6.11), p. 40 Deposited TeX, approximately lines 2075–2120
claim: Equation (6.10) can be rewritten with the same normalized coefficients as A_r·V(s) = o(1), where V_l = k/(1 + C_l k), and then implies curvature constancy.
analysis: Location and dependency. Theorem 6.1, p. 34; the parallel-curve relation (6.5), p. 37; the stationary-phase reduction (6.10), p. 39; and the definition of \(V\) leading to (6.11), p. 40. The theorem asserts that a smooth bounded planar domain admitting infinitely many orthogonal Neumann eigenfunctions locally constant on the boundary must be a disk or an annulus.

At the decisive point, the proof has distinct constants \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\), with \(C_1=0\), and a nonzero curvature \(k(s)\) on a small interval where \(1+C_\ell k(s)\ne0\). Equation (6.10) is \[\sum_{\ell=1}^m\widetilde\delta_\ell
 \left|\frac{k(s)}{1+C_\ell k(s)}\right|^{-1/2}=o(1).
 \tag{9}\] Taking a nonvanishing real or imaginary part and normalizing supplies unit vectors \(A_r\) and a subsequential limit \(A\) of norm one. The source then states that (9) can be rewritten using \[V(s)=\left(
 \frac{k(s)}{1+C_1k(s)},\ldots,
 \frac{k(s)}{1+C_mk(s)}
 \right)
 \tag{10}\] as \(A_r\cdot V(s)=o(1)\) and hence \(A\cdot V(s)=0\).

The actual vector determined by (9) is \[W(s)=\left(
 \left|\frac{k(s)}{1+C_1k(s)}\right|^{-1/2},\ldots,
 \left|\frac{k(s)}{1+C_mk(s)}\right|^{-1/2}
 \right).
 \tag{11}\] A linear relation among the components of \(W\) does not become the same linear relation among the components of \(V\).

Exact algebraic witness. Take regular values \[m=2,\qquad k=1,\qquad C_1=0,\quad C_2=3,\qquad
 A=\frac1{\sqrt5}(2,-1).\] All denominators are nonzero and the constants are distinct. Then \[W=(1,2),\qquad V=(1,\tfrac14),\qquad
 A\cdot W=0,\quad A\cdot V=\frac7{4\sqrt5}\ne0.
 \tag{12}\] Thus the proposed rewriting is not a linear-algebra identity, even at a single regular curvature value with a normalized nonzero coefficient vector. This is a counterexample to the displayed rewriting, not a constructed domain satisfying the spectral hypotheses of Theorem 6.1. The latter theorem is not claimed false.

A full repair of the curvature step. Retain \(W\) in the subsequence argument. The conclusion is then \(A\cdot W(s)=0\). Multiplying by \(\sqrt{|k(s)|}\) gives \[\sum_{\ell=1}^m A_\ell f_\ell(k(s))=0,\qquad
 f_\ell(k):=\sqrt{|1+C_\ell k|}.
 \tag{13}\] On a regular interval the signs of the linear factors are fixed. For any point \(k_0\) of that interval, \[f_\ell^{(j)}(k_0)
 =f_\ell(k_0)
   \left(\tfrac12\right)_{\!j}
   \left(\frac{C_\ell}{1+C_\ell k_0}\right)^j,
 \qquad 0\le j\le m-1,
 \tag{14}\] where \((\frac12)_j=\frac12(\frac12-1)\cdots(\frac12-j+1)\) is the falling factorial, with value one for \(j=0\).

Put \(q_\ell=C_\ell/(1+C_\ell k_0)\). The Wronskian determinant factors as \[\det\bigl[f_\ell^{(j)}(k_0)\bigr]_
       {\substack{0\le j<m\\1\le\ell\le m}}
 =
 \left(\prod_{\ell=1}^m f_\ell(k_0)\right)
 \left(\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\left(\tfrac12\right)_{\!j}\right)
 \prod_{i<\ell}(q_\ell-q_i).
 \tag{15}\] Every factor is nonzero. Indeed, \[q_\ell-q_i=
 \frac{C_\ell-C_i}{(1+C_\ell k_0)(1+C_i k_0)}\ne0.\] This also includes \(C_1=0\); no division by \(C_1\) is used.

If \(k(s)\) were nonconstant, its continuous image would contain a nondegenerate interval. Equation (13) would give a fixed linear relation among the \(f_\ell\) on that interval, contradicting (15) because \(|A|=1\). Therefore \(k\) is constant. The subsequent circular-boundary and unique-continuation argument can then proceed with the intended conclusion.

Counterevidence and limits of the repair. The inverse-square-root factor in (9) is the stationary-phase amplitude and agrees with the preceding displayed formulas. Thus changing the definition of \(V\) to \(W\) is strongly supported by the source. Merely replacing the symbol in (10), however, does not prove the asserted noncontainment in a hyperplane; (13)–(15) provide the needed argument for the correct vector.

The common-phase calculation on p. 39 also contains local \(\xi/\eta\) and phase-sign inconsistencies. Correcting the derivative to \(p_1(s)\cdot\widetilde\eta(s)\) and absorbing the appropriate constant phase restores a common factor of modulus one. These are recorded with the proof clarification, not counted as independent Problems.

The stationary-phase grouping upstream of (9) was stress-tested separately. For each fixed \(s\), finitely many fixed imaginary shifts give a Vandermonde system in the distinct numbers \(\exp(b)\). Keeping the bounded coefficients \(\sigma_{n,\ell}\) until after this separation avoids an unsupported interchange with a growing exponential factor. This supplies counterevidence against an additional asserted failure upstream. The exact large-imaginary-shift theorem cited from Berenstein was not retrieved from the subscription-only primary source; the fixed-shift argument does not claim to certify that particular formulation.

Impact and classification. The claimed \(A\cdot V=0\) is the decisive input to curvature constancy and hence to Theorem 6.1. Its derivation from (9) is invalid. This is a Major defect in that rigidity derivation under contract 0.7.1, with the dependency explicit. The corrected Wronskian calculation restores this local step. It does not establish that every other imported part of the rigidity proof has been independently certified, and no failure of the main nonradial existence theorem follows from this issue.
result: Impact: The invalid transformation supplies the decisive curvature step in an advertised rigidity contribution. It does not enter the main large-l construction.

paragraphs: Retain W, multiply the limiting relation by √|k|, and prove linear independence of f_l(k) = √|1 + C_l k|.

report: Abstract: A claim-focused examination of the variance reduction, overlap estimates and GCD-graph argument identifies one local defect: the strict quality-increment alternative in Lemma 10.1 fails when the permitted measure has zero-weight vertices. An explicit counterexample and a positive-support repair are given. The repair preserves the graph quantities and restores the high-degree subgraph lemma used downstream. No failure of Theorems 1 or 2 is established. The separate passage from a variance asymptotic to almost-everywhere sharpness requires an additional argument if Section 16 is intended as a standalone proof. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of an almost sharp quantitative Duffin–Schaeffer theorem
# Identity, reviewed version and scope

This report concerns Dimitris Koukoulopoulos, James Maynard and Daodao Yang, An almost sharp quantitative version of the Duffin–Schaeffer conjecture, assigned identifier M25-0161. The exact reviewed source is arXiv:2404.14628v2, bearing the arXiv date 20 September 2024 and an internal date of 23 September 2024 [source]. Its 41 PDF pages have printed page numbers 1–41; all page references below are one-based PDF pages, equal to the printed numbers. The assignment links the article to DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0055 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0055). The acquired author manuscript is not asserted to be the journal version of record.

The examination covered the statements and dependency chain in Sections 1–16, with independent algebraic reconstruction of the dyadic variance argument, the anatomical estimates, the main graph-quality inequalities and the prime-supported variance calculation. Three native in-chat assistants checked disjoint portions of Sections 8–16; the lead reviewer independently checked the reported defect and its repair. The retained coverage ledger distinguishes direct checks, helper checks and external results not re-proved. In particular, cited sieve and multiplicative-function theorems and the historical central limit theorem were not independently verified from their original publications. No separate supplement or released repository was available in the assigned source package. No author code was run.
# Claims and checks

Let \(0\leq\psi(q)\leq 1/2\), and set \[\Psi(Q)=2\sum_{q\leq Q}\frac{\varphi(q)\psi(q)}q,\qquad
 N(\alpha;Q)=\#\{(a,q)\in\mathbb Z\times\mathbb N:
 q\leq Q,\ (a,q)=1,\ |\alpha-a/q|<\psi(q)/q\}.\] Theorem 1 assumes \(\Psi(Q)\to\infty\) and gives the almost-everywhere error \(O_\varepsilon(\Psi(Q)^{1/2+\varepsilon})\). Theorem 2 bounds the second centered moment by \(\Psi(Q)+O_\varepsilon(\Psi(Q)^{1+\varepsilon})\). The review did not find a counterexample to either statement.
## Normalization and the variance-to-pointwise reduction
## Overlap, anatomical estimates and dyadic sums

For Lemma 5.1, the triangular weight has integral \(2\delta\Delta\) and total variation \(2\delta\). Hence the Riemann-sum error in (5.3) is uniformly \(O(\delta)\). The coprimality relaxation to the \(t\)-smooth part, the square-free divisor expansion and the estimate \(\prod_{p>t}(1-1/p)^{-1}\leq
\exp(2\sum_{p>t}1/p)\) give the stated overlap upper bound, conditional on the initial exact overlap-counting identity.

The exponential moments in Lemmas 6.2–6.3 are compatible with Lemma 6.1: one chooses a fixed divisor-function order large enough to dominate the prime-power values. The large-prime contribution is bounded using \(t\sum_{p>t}p^{-2}=O(1)\); the small-prime moment grows at most as a fixed power of \(\log(2t)\), absorbed into the spare factor \(t\). These bounds explain the two exceptional-pair savings.

The Section 7 sums have the required decay: \(2^{i(\varepsilon/2-1)}2^{i(1-\varepsilon)}
=2^{-i\varepsilon/2}\), and the anatomical exceptional classes have summable exponential or geometric tails. At \(\Psi(Q)<1\), the large-\(D\) remainder may be bounded directly by \(\Psi(Q)^2\); this closes the small-mass case without reversing the order of powers of a number below one. When \(1/2\leq D<1\), replacing the sieve cutoff \(D^2\) by 1 leaves the relevant prime sums unchanged.
## Graph reductions

The graph checks followed the modified exponent \(2+\tau\), with \(0<\tau<1/100\), through the quality ratios, density restrictions, anatomical pruning and small-/large-prime iteration. The finite sets of unaccounted gcd primes provide a termination measure. Several compressed arguments can be reconstructed with the changed exponent rather than assumed from the older graph argument. The local zero-weight defect below must be addressed when using maximality to deduce pointwise degree bounds. Exact prime valuations in Proposition 8.1(e) and Lemma 13.2(v) are interpreted on the output vertex sets; the preceding discussion and construction support that reading. No separate substantive finding is assigned to that notation.
# A local defect and its verified repair

Problem 1 (Zero-weight vertices invalidate Lemma 10.1 as stated).  Definition 1(a), page 13, permits a measure on \(\mathbb N\) with finite singleton masses, including zero. Lemma 10.1, pages 22–23, asserts that every GCD graph of positive edge density either has the stated positive weighted degree at every vertex or admits a subgraph with the same multiplicative data and strictly larger quality. These alternatives need not exhaust the allowed graphs.
## Complete counterexample

Take \(\tau=1/200\), \(\mu(\{1\})=1\), and \(\mu(\{n\})=0\) for \(n\ne1\). Let \[V=\{1,2\},\qquad W=\{1\},\qquad
 E=\{(1,1)\},\qquad P=\varnothing,\] with both multiplicity functions empty. The vertex sets are finite positive integers; \(E\subseteq V\times W\); all singleton masses are finite; and the prime constraints are vacuous. Furthermore \[\mu(V)=\mu(W)=\mu(E)=1,\qquad \delta(G)=1,\qquad q(G)=1.\] Thus every hypothesis of the lemma holds. The neighborhood of \(2\in V\) is empty, so \[\mu(\Gamma_G(2))=0<
 \frac{1+\tau}{2+\tau}\delta(G)\mu(W)
 =\frac{201}{401}.\] Alternative (a) fails.

Any subgraph with the same multiplicative data either retains the sole positive-weight edge \((1,1)\), in which case its density and quality are both 1, or has zero edge measure and quality 0. Therefore no such subgraph has quality larger than 1, and alternative (b) also fails. This is an exact finite argument, not a floating-point test. The independent finite enumeration retained with the helper evidence agrees with it.
## Where the proof fails

On page 23 the proof multiplies the strict low-degree inequality by \(\mu(v)\) and continues with a strict inequality. That operation preserves strictness only for \(\mu(v)>0\). For the counterexample vertex \(v=2\), deleting it leaves both edge measure and quality unchanged. This is not an extraction artifact: the definition, lemma and strict inequalities were checked on rendered source pages.
## Repair and exact downstream scope

Restrict the initial graph to \[V_+=\{v\in V:\mu(v)>0\},\qquad
 W_+=\{w\in W:\mu(w)>0\},\qquad
 E_+=E\cap(V_+\times W_+).\] All removed edges have product measure zero. Consequently \(\mu(V_+)=\mu(V)\), \(\mu(W_+)=\mu(W)\), \(\mu(E_+)=\mu(E)\), and both density and quality are unchanged. The GCD constraints and multiplicative data are inherited. Now choose a maximal subgraph of this positive support. The strict-increment proof applies to every remaining vertex and yields the degree conclusion of Lemma 8.6, with quality at least the original quality, exactly as that lemma requires.

For completeness, write \(x=\mu(v)/\mu(V)\in(0,1)\) and \(c=(1+\tau)/(2+\tau)\). Removing a vertex whose degree is below the threshold gives \[\frac{q(G')}{q(G)}>
 \frac{(1-cx)^{2+\tau}}{(1-x)^{1+\tau}}>1,\] because the logarithm on the right vanishes at \(x=0\) and has derivative \[(1+\tau)\left(\frac1{1-x}-\frac1{1-cx}\right)>0.\] This verifies the repaired strict-increment argument. An equivalent formulation allows a proper vertex deletion with nondecreasing quality, using decreasing vertex count for termination.
## Impact

The supported impact is Minor: the printed auxiliary dichotomy is false on an allowed degenerate input. The retained positive-support repair restores the downstream high-degree subgraph existence result without changing any weighted quantity. The counterexample does not invalidate the bilinear estimates, the variance theorem or the almost-everywhere counting theorem. The classification reflects that bounded consequence, rather than the length of the repair.
# Scope of the separate sharpness argument

Section 16, pages 38–39, correctly reduces the prime-supported choice \(\psi(q)=1_{q\ {\rm prime}}/q\) to pair-correlation errors \(O(\max(q,r)^{-2})\). Their sum over distinct primes is bounded, as is \(\sum_q\lambda(A_q)^2\). This gives the stated \(\operatorname{Var}N(\alpha;Q)=\Psi(Q)+O(1)\).

The introductory assertion that this alone proves almost-everywhere optimality needs an additional passage from second moments to sample behavior. Divergent second moments can be concentrated on shrinking exceptional sets. This remains true for nondecreasing indicator counts: Appendix A gives an exact countermodel. It is a countermodel to that general inference, not a Duffin–Schaeffer counterexample.

The source separately invokes a central limit theorem on page 2. That is relevant counterevidence against any claim that the paper’s sharpness conclusion is false. The historical theorem was not independently checked here. Accordingly this review records the standalone implication in Section 16 as Needs Evidence, and does not raise the supported severity of the paper or assert failure of its main theorem.

# A countermodel to the second-moment implication

Set \(T_1=a_1=1/2\). For \(n\geq2\), define \[x_n=n-a_{n-1},\quad
 T_n=x_n-\sqrt{x_n^2-1}
     =\frac1{x_n+\sqrt{x_n^2-1}},\quad
 a_n=a_{n-1}+T_n.\] Inductively \(x_n\geq(n+1)/2>1\), the tails \(T_n\) decrease to zero, and \(a_n=O(\log n)\). Let \(K\) be a nonnegative integer random variable with \(\Pr(K\geq n)=T_n\), and put \[N_n=(n-K)_+=\sum_{j=1}^n1_{\{K<j\}},\qquad
 \Psi_n=\mathbb EN_n=n-a_n.\] These are nondecreasing integer counts of events and \(\Psi_n\to\infty\). Writing \(Y_n=\min(K,n)\), the tail formulas give \(\mathbb EY_n=a_n\) and \(\mathbb EY_n^2=\sum_{j=1}^n(2j-1)T_j\). Hence, for \(n\geq2\), \[\operatorname{Var}(Y_n)-\operatorname{Var}(Y_{n-1})
 =(2x_n-1)T_n-T_n^2=1-T_n
 =\Psi_n-\Psi_{n-1},\] where \(2x_nT_n-T_n^2=1\). Since \(\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)=1/4=\Psi_1-1/4\), it follows that \[\operatorname{Var}(N_n)=\Psi_n-\tfrac14
 \quad\hbox{for every }n.\] Yet \(K<\infty\) almost surely and, eventually, \(N_n-\Psi_n=a_n-K=O(\log n)\) almost surely. Thus even this variance asymptotic, expectation normalization and monotone counting structure do not by themselves establish a square-root almost-sure lower fluctuation. No arithmetic realization of this model is asserted.

problems.title: Zero-weight vertices invalidate Lemma 10.1 as stated
problems.source_location: Definition1 p13, Definition2 pp13–14, Lemma10.1 pp22–23, Lemma8.6 p23
claim: Every positive-density GCD graph either has the stated degree bound at every vertex or has a same-data subgraph of strictly greater quality.
analysis: Definition 1(a), page 13, permits a measure on \(\mathbb N\) with finite singleton masses, including zero. Lemma 10.1, pages 22–23, asserts that every GCD graph of positive edge density either has the stated positive weighted degree at every vertex or admits a subgraph with the same multiplicative data and strictly larger quality. These alternatives need not exhaust the allowed graphs.

Take \(\tau=1/200\), \(\mu(\{1\})=1\), and \(\mu(\{n\})=0\) for \(n\ne1\). Let \[V=\{1,2\},\qquad W=\{1\},\qquad
 E=\{(1,1)\},\qquad P=\varnothing,\] with both multiplicity functions empty. The vertex sets are finite positive integers; \(E\subseteq V\times W\); all singleton masses are finite; and the prime constraints are vacuous. Furthermore \[\mu(V)=\mu(W)=\mu(E)=1,\qquad \delta(G)=1,\qquad q(G)=1.\] Thus every hypothesis of the lemma holds. The neighborhood of \(2\in V\) is empty, so \[\mu(\Gamma_G(2))=0<
 \frac{1+\tau}{2+\tau}\delta(G)\mu(W)
 =\frac{201}{401}.\] Alternative (a) fails.

Any subgraph with the same multiplicative data either retains the sole positive-weight edge \((1,1)\), in which case its density and quality are both 1, or has zero edge measure and quality 0. Therefore no such subgraph has quality larger than 1, and alternative (b) also fails. This is an exact finite argument, not a floating-point test. The independent finite enumeration retained with the helper evidence agrees with it.

On page 23 the proof multiplies the strict low-degree inequality by \(\mu(v)\) and continues with a strict inequality. That operation preserves strictness only for \(\mu(v)>0\). For the counterexample vertex \(v=2\), deleting it leaves both edge measure and quality unchanged. This is not an extraction artifact: the definition, lemma and strict inequalities were checked on rendered source pages.

The supported impact is Minor: the printed auxiliary dichotomy is false on an allowed degenerate input. The retained positive-support repair restores the downstream high-degree subgraph existence result without changing any weighted quantity. The counterexample does not invalidate the bilinear estimates, the variance theorem or the almost-everywhere counting theorem. The classification reflects that bounded consequence, rather than the length of the repair.
result: Impact: Local false auxiliary dichotomy; no demonstrated failure of bilinear estimates or main theorems.
