report: Abstract: The reviewed author manuscript contains a false global uniqueness assertion for lifts: strict inequality between the top exponent on the given subspace and the quotient cocycle average does not exclude intermediate critical directions. A four-dimensional diagonal example satisfies every stated condition and has a continuum of stationary ergodic lifts. This supports Major impact for that classification guarantee, while leaving the stated existence criterion and the filtration-based classification unrefuted. Three narrower issues concern the hypothesis of a recurrence lemma, a positive-recurrence assertion, and passage from projective compactness to linear compactness. Their actual downstream scopes and precise local corrections are distinguished. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of stationary probability measures on projective spaces: the critical case
# Identity and inspected scope

The paper is Richard Aoun and Cagri Sert, Stationary probability measures on projective spaces 2: The critical case, assignment M25-0162. The exact source is arXiv:2305.02879v2, stamped 15 May 2023, 15 pages [source]. One-based PDF and printed page numbers agree. The assignment associates the article with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0056 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0056); this report does not assert that the acquired author manuscript is the journal version of record.

Sections 1–4 were read with attention to theorem quantifiers, return-time reduction, the random projection construction, invariant complements, cocycle averages and lift uniqueness. Native helpers checked disjoint proof portions; the lead reviewer independently verified each counterexample below and viewed the decisive source pages. The ledger records the exact division of work and source-page evidence. External results of Furstenberg–Kifer, Atkinson and others were examined through their use in this source, not independently re-proved from the original publications. The earlier paper cited by the source as reference [1] was not acquired. No author code or empirical experiment was used.

Write \(\Gamma_\mu\) for the closed semigroup generated by \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\) and \(H_\mu\) for its Zariski closure. A stationary lift of \(\bar\nu\) from \(\mathbb P(V/W)\) is a stationary probability on \(\mathbb P(V)\setminus\mathbb P(W)\) projecting to \(\bar\nu\). The top Lyapunov exponent \(\lambda_1(W)\) is distinct from the smallest Furstenberg–Kifer–Hennion exponent \(\beta_{\min}(W)\). That distinction is decisive in Problem 1.
# The lift uniqueness guarantee

Problem 1 (A strict top-exponent gap does not imply uniqueness).  Remark 4.4(1), page 14, retains the hypotheses of Theorem 1.5 and an invariant \(W'\) whose intersection with \(W\) has slower expansion. It asserts that \(\lambda_1(W)>\alpha(\bar\nu)\) gives a unique stationary lift on the full \(\mathbb P(V)\setminus\mathbb P(W)\). The introductory paragraph below Theorem 1.5 on page 4 makes the same distinction between the strict and critical cases. The global uniqueness assertion is false.
## Input and verification of every condition

In the standard basis of \(V=\mathbb R^4\), take \[g=\operatorname{diag}(2,1,1,1/2),\qquad \mu=\delta_g,\qquad
 W=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_4),\qquad W'=\operatorname{span}(e_3,e_4).\] The first moment is finite: \(\int\log\max(\|g\|_2,\|g^{-1}\|_2)\,d\mu=\log2\). All the displayed subspaces are \(\Gamma_\mu\)- and \(H_\mu\)-invariant, because they are coordinate subspaces of a diagonal action. The quotient \(V/W\) is the line generated by \(e_3+W\); let \(\bar\nu=\delta_{[e_3+W]}\). This measure is stationary and ergodic, and \[\alpha(\bar\nu)=\lambda_1(V_{\bar\nu})=0
 <\lambda_1(W)=\log2.\] Moreover, \[W'\cap W=\mathbb Re_4,\qquad
 \lambda_1(W'\cap W)=-\log2<0,\qquad
 W'/(W'\cap W)\simeq\mathbb R(e_3+W).\] Thus the existence condition in Theorem 1.5 and the extra premise of Remark 4.4 are both satisfied, including the exact quotient support-span requirement.
## Stated result versus actual result

For every \(c\in\mathbb R\), define \[\nu_c=\delta_{[e_3+ce_2]}.\] Since \(g(e_3+ce_2)=e_3+ce_2\), each \(\nu_c\) is stationary. A Dirac probability at a fixed point is an extreme stationary probability, hence ergodic. Its point lies outside \(\mathbb P(W)\), and its quotient is always \([e_3+W]\). Distinct \(c\)’s yield distinct projective points. Consequently there are continuously many stationary ergodic lifts, whereas Remark 4.4(1) asserts exactly one. No limiting argument or numerical approximation enters this example.

The mechanism is the invariant direction \(e_2\subset W\) with exponent zero. The strict inequality for the top exponent on \(W\) does not remove this critical direction. Here the FKH exponents of \(W\) are \(\log2,0,-\log2\); replacing all of them by their maximum loses information needed for uniqueness.
## Alternative readings, impact and a bounded replacement

The counterexample is consistent with Theorem 1.5’s existence criterion: a lift does exist. It is also consistent with Theorem 1.3, whose unique lifts are taken across the specific FKH filtration, and with Corollary 1.6, which claims uniqueness on each individual \(H_\mu\)-orbit. In this example each \([e_3+ce_2]\) is its own orbit. These surviving statements do not supply global uniqueness for an arbitrary given \(W\).

The supported impact of Problem 1 is Major: an explicit uniqueness guarantee in the paper’s central classification of lifts is false within its stated hypotheses. The finding does not assert that the critical semisimplicity theorem or every classification result fails.

A precise restricted replacement is: for a fixed invariant \(W'\) satisfying \(\lambda_1(W'\cap W)<\alpha( ar
u)\), there is at most one stationary lift concentrated on \(\mathbb P(W')\setminus\mathbb P(W'\cap W)\), conditional on existence. Appendix A supplies the uniqueness argument. This statement does not claim uniqueness on the larger ambient complement. For the example, that fixed carrier is the affine chart \([e_3+ye_4]\), on which \(g\) acts by \(y\mapsto y/2\). Its only stationary probability is \(\delta_0\), since \(\Pr(|Y|>t)=\Pr(|Y|>2^nt)	o0\). Thus only \(
u_0\) lies in this \(W'\). The stronger assertion in the remark that the lift spans all of \(W'\) also fails here: its span is only \(\mathbb Re_3\). A verified restricted statement uses \(V_
u\subseteq W'\), with equality requiring a minimal-carrier condition.
# Other proof and hypothesis issues

Problem 2 (Lemma 3.6 assumes irreducibility of the wrong acting group).  Lemma 3.6, page 9, assumes that \(\rho,\rho'\) are strongly irreducible representations of a topological group \(G\), that their pushforwards of \(\mu\) have finite first moments and the same top exponent, and concludes a positive lower bound along a subsequence for \(\|\rho(b_1\cdots b_n)\|/\|\rho'(b_1\cdots b_n)\|\). The statement does not require the support-generated action to be strongly irreducible.

Take \[G=\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb R),\quad
 \rho=\mathrm{Std},\quad \rho'=\operatorname{Sym}^2(\mathrm{Std}),\quad
 \mu=\delta_u,\qquad u=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Both representations of \(G\) are irreducible. For \(\operatorname{Sym}^2\), the diagonal torus separates the three monomial weights and the two unipotent one-parameter subgroups connect them, so any nonzero invariant subspace contains all three weight spaces. Connectedness of \(G\) then makes both representations strongly irreducible: a finite invariant union would give a finite permutation action of a connected group and hence an invariant individual subspace. Both point-mass pushforwards have finite first moment. For the unique sample path, \[\rho(u^n)=\begin{pmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \rho'(u^n)=
 \begin{pmatrix}1&n&n^2\\0&1&2n\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\] in the monomial basis. With Euclidean coordinate norms, \[0<
 \frac{\|\rho(u^n)\|_2}{\|\rho'(u^n)\|_2}
 \leq \frac{\sqrt{n^2+2}}{n^2}\longrightarrow0.\] The logarithms of both norms divided by \(n\) tend to zero, so their top Lyapunov exponents are equal to zero. All stated assumptions hold, but every infinite subsequence has infimum zero, contradicting (3.6).

The missing condition concerns \(\rho(\Gamma_\mu)\) and \(\rho'(\Gamma_\mu)\), not only their ambient representations. The proof’s stationary-measure and norm-comparison arguments require that support-generated irreducibility. In the actual application in Proposition 3.7, \(G\) is the connected Zariski closure \(H_\mu\), and the representations are irreducible quotients of its module. Zariski density then provides the stronger condition. This is Minor for the stated overgeneralization: the counterexample lies outside the actual application’s stronger scope. Adding that condition excludes the example and matches the proof’s requirements; a complete independent proof of the repaired general recurrence lemma would still require its cited external results.

Problem 3 (The support reduction invokes a false recurrence assertion).  The first paragraph of page 7 claims that every neighborhood \(O\) of every \(g\in\Gamma_\mu\cap H_\mu^\circ\) is visited infinitely often with positive probability by \(b_n\cdots b_1\).

Let \(V=\mathbb R\), \(\mu=\delta_2\), \(g=2\), and \(O=(3/2,5/2)\). The moment is \(\log2<\infty\), the only nonzero invariant subspace has exponent \(\log2\), and the projective space is a singleton, so its probability is stationary, ergodic and nondegenerate. The Zariski closure of the infinitely many scalars \(2^n\) is \(\operatorname{GL}_1\), which is Zariski-connected, and the return time to its identity component is \(\tau=1\). Yet \(2^n\in O\) only for \(n=1\), and therefore \[\Pr\!\left(\limsup_n\{b_n\cdots b_1\in O\}\right)=0,\] rather than a positive number.

The intended equality \(\Gamma_{\mu^\tau}=\Gamma_\mu\cap H_\mu^\circ\) survives. For its reverse inclusion, approximate an element of the right-hand side by finite products of support elements. Since the identity component is relatively open in the finite component quotient, the approximating products may be chosen in it. Split each finite word at successive first returns to the identity coset. Each block product belongs to \(\operatorname{supp}\mu^\tau\): neighborhoods of its factors have positive product probability, and the finite coset itinerary is locally constant. Taking products and then closure gives the required inclusion. The other inclusion is immediate. This is a verified algebraic replacement for the incorrect probabilistic assertion. Its supported impact is Minor; the support identity and the main reduction are not contradicted.

Problem 4 (Projective compactness is replaced by linear compactness).  In Section 3.4(i), page 12, the sandwich set \(\pi(O\cap\Gamma_\mu)\pi\) is called a compact subgroup of \(\operatorname{GL}(\operatorname{Im}\pi)\). Proposition 3.7, pages 10–11, instead provides compact closure of the projective image of its generated semigroup. The literal linear-compactness assertion is false.

Take \(V=\mathbb R^2\), \(\mu=\delta_{2I}\), any line \(W\), and the rotation-invariant probability on \(\mathbb P(\mathbb R^2)\). The measure is stationary and nondegenerate; moments are finite; all subspace exponents equal \(\log2\); \(H_\mu\) is the connected algebraic scalar group; and \(W\) is irreducible. The cone \(C(\Gamma_\mu)\) consists of nonnegative scalar matrices, so its only nonzero idempotent is \(\pi=I\). A nonempty Zariski-open subset of the scalar group omits at most finitely many scalars. Thus \(\pi(O\cap\Gamma_\mu)\pi\) contains unbounded \(2^nI\)’s, while its projective image is the identity.

The needed complete reducibility nevertheless follows from the actual proposition. Normalize each real invertible map on the \(d\)-dimensional image by \[A\longmapsto |\det A|^{-1/d}A.\] This is multiplicative and preserves every invariant subspace. The normalized inverse image of a compact projective group is compact: projective compactness bounds singular-value ratios, and determinant modulus one bounds each singular value away from zero and infinity. Average an inner product over the compact normalized closure. The orthogonal complement of an invariant subspace is invariant, and scalar rescaling preserves this fact for the original semigroup. This supplies exactly the complement used in (3.10)–(3.11). The supported impact is Minor, with the downstream complement step analytically restored.
# Remaining checks and dependence

The finite component quotient is an irreducible finite Markov chain, so its return time has finite expectation; periodicity does not prevent this. If \(M(g)=\log\max(\|g\|,\|g^{-1}\|)\), then \[M(b_\tau\cdots b_1)\leq\sum_{j\leq\tau}M(b_j),\qquad
 \mathbb E\sum_{j\leq\tau}M(b_j)
 =\mathbb E\tau\,\mathbb E M(b_1)<\infty.\] The induced first-moment condition and the return-time scaling of exponents are therefore compatible with the reduction. In Lemma 2.2 one should choose an ergodic component of the constructed stationary extension; its projection remains the given ergodic base measure and its finite-group marginal remains uniform.

The projective-limit construction was checked in the form actually used: normalized-product limits, the two nonzero quotient images, simultaneous eigenvalue-phase approximation, the idempotent limit, measure-preserving sandwich semigroup and its compact projective closure. With the normalization above, the invariant subspace transfer and the finite-dimensional quotient induction recover the intended complement argument. The broader wording of Lemma 3.5(3) for arbitrary \(\pi\in\Pi_b\) is not fully proved by the displayed argument, which treats normalized-product limits; no counterexample to that broader wording was established.

Theorem 1.5’s FKH-layer reduction and the orbit-closure argument in Corollary 1.6 were examined conditional on the stated external contracting-lift and semisimple-orbit results. No contrary example was found for those conclusions. Appendix A independently checks the cocycle-average identity used in Lemma 4.3.

# Two direct checks for lifts

Let \(q:V\to V/W\) be the quotient map with its quotient norm. On the complement of \(\mathbb P(W)\), set \(f([v])=\log(\|v\|/\|qv\|)\geq0\). The difference of the ambient and quotient norm cocycles is \(f(g[v])-f([v])\), whose absolute value is at most \(2M(g)\). For a stationary lift, the bounded truncations \(f_m=\min(f,m)\) satisfy \(\int(f_m(gx)-f_m(x))\,d\mu(g)d\nu(x)=0\). Their increments are dominated by \(|f(gx)-f(x)|\). Dominated convergence therefore gives equality of ambient and quotient cocycle averages without assuming \(f\) itself integrable. This verifies Lemma 4.3’s conclusion directly.

For uniqueness on a fixed carrier \(W'\), put \(Z=W'\cap W\). Given two stationary lifts on \(\mathbb P(W')\setminus\mathbb P(Z)\) of the same ergodic \( ar
u\), couple their conditional probabilities over \( ar
u\), and average this coupling under the common random action. A stationary limit exists on the compact product of projective spaces. Its marginals are the original stationary measures, hence give zero mass to \(\mathbb P(Z)\); it lies in the closed relation \(qu\wedge qv=0\). Choose representatives with \(qu=qv
e0\), so \(u-v\in Z\). For common products \(L_n\), projective distance is bounded by \[d([L_nu],[L_nv])
 \leq  rac{2\|L_n|_Z\|\,\|u-v\|}{\| ar L_n qv\|}.\] Under \(\lambda_1(Z)<\alpha( ar
u)\), the numerator and denominator exponents make this tend to zero almost surely, using the stationary ergodic cocycle growth in the source. Stationarity forces the coupling to be diagonal. Its marginals therefore coincide. This proves conditional uniqueness on \(W'\), and says nothing about lifts on other carriers.

Take \(V=\mathbb R^2\), \(\mu=\delta_{2I}\), any line \(W\), and the rotation-invariant probability on \(\mathbb P(\mathbb R^2)\). The measure is stationary and nondegenerate; moments are finite; all subspace exponents equal \(\log2\); \(H_\mu\) is the connected algebraic scalar group; and \(W\) is irreducible. The cone \(C(\Gamma_\mu)\) consists of nonnegative scalar matrices, so its only nonzero idempotent is \(\pi=I\). A nonempty Zariski-open subset of the scalar group omits at most finitely many scalars. Thus \(\pi(O\cap\Gamma_\mu)\pi\) contains unbounded \(2^nI\)’s, while its projective image is the identity.

The needed complete reducibility nevertheless follows from the actual proposition. Normalize each real invertible map on the \(d\)-dimensional image by \[A\longmapsto |\det A|^{-1/d}A.\] This is multiplicative and preserves every invariant subspace. The normalized inverse image of a compact projective group is compact: projective compactness bounds singular-value ratios, and determinant modulus one bounds each singular value away from zero and infinity. Average an inner product over the compact normalized closure. The orthogonal complement of an invariant subspace is invariant, and scalar rescaling preserves this fact for the original semigroup. This supplies exactly the complement used in (3.10)–(3.11). The supported impact is Minor, with the downstream complement step analytically restored.
result: Impact: Literal GL compact subgroup assertion false, but needed invariant complement follows from projective compactness.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Normalize A by |det A|^(-1/d). Normalized projective compact closure has bounded singular values and inverse, is compact group; average inner product; scalar rescaling preserves invariant complements.

report: Abstract: The inspected manuscript reverses the two positive shear maps when identifying its discrete map with the inverse time-one flow. An explicit point separates the maps for every even amplitude. Coordinate exchange supplies an exact conjugacy, including diffusion and arbitrary kicks, so the stated decay conclusions survive a bounded repair. A ball-scale comparison has the wrong inequality direction, and a continuous-time correlation step requires a Lipschitz approximation argument. These are local issues with verified corrections; no counterexample to the optimal logarithmic dissipation timescale or exponential mixing conclusion was established. The highest supported impact is Minor. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical verification of optimal enhanced dissipation and mixing for alternating Lipschitz shears
# Exact source and scope

The paper is Tarek M. Elgindi, Kyle Liss and Jonathan C. Mattingly, Optimal enhanced dissipation and mixing for a time-periodic, Lipschitz velocity field on \(\mathbb T^2\), M25-0163. The exact source is arXiv:2304.05374v1, 37 pages, stamped 11 April 2023 and internally dated 12 April 2023 [source]. Physical PDF and printed page numbers agree. The assignment associates the article with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0057 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0057); identity with the journal-final text is not asserted.

Sections 1–4 and Appendix A were reviewed: definitions and quantifiers, Doeblin minorization, the pulsed-to-continuous energy comparison, hyperbolic cones and cutting estimates, area formula, Jacobian factors, and correlations. Native scientific helpers examined disjoint portions; the lead independently checked the findings and central calculations. Detailed coverage and actual image-view evidence accompany the report. The hypotheses and statement of the external Demers–Liverani theorem were checked in an author-hosted preprint [DL]; its full proof was not independently re-proved. No author code, journal-final comparison or later-version search forms part of this review.
# The inverse flow and the analyzed map

Problem 1 (The shear composition is reversed).  Page 2 defines \(u_\alpha\) as the negative vertical shear first and negative horizontal shear second. Page 7 sets \(T=\phi_1^{-1}\). Page 22 defines positive vertical and horizontal shears \(T_1,T_2\) but asserts \(T=T_2\circ T_1\). These definitions are inconsistent.

Write, modulo \(\mathbb Z^2\), \[V_+(x,y)=(x,y+\alpha|x-\tfrac12|),\qquad
 H_+(x,y)=(x+\alpha|y-\tfrac12|,y),\] and let \(V_-,H_-\) denote their inverses. Each half-period has duration \(1/2\), while the velocity coefficient is \(2\alpha\). Therefore \[\phi_1=H_-\circ V_-,\quad
 T_{\rm actual}=V_+\circ H_+,\quad T_{\rm printed}=H_+\circ V_+.\] For every even \(\alpha\ge2\), set \(z=(1/(2\alpha^2),0)\). Then \[T_{\rm actual}z=\left(\frac1{2\alpha^2},1-\frac1{2\alpha}\right),
 \qquad
 T_{\rm printed}z=\left(\frac12+\frac1{2\alpha^2},1-\frac1{2\alpha}\right)
 \pmod1.\] Thus one cannot retain both definitions as identical. The matrices on pages 7 and 23 concern the printed map, with a nearly horizontal unstable cone, rather than the actual inverse map.
## Verified repair and impact

For \(S(x,y)=(y,x)\), one has \(T_{\rm actual}=S T_{\rm printed}S\). The identity extends to arbitrary kicked words: \[(T_{\rm actual})_\xi^n=S(T_{\rm printed})_{S\xi}^nS,
 \qquad S\xi=(S\xi_1,S\xi_2,\ldots).\] The map \(S\) preserves grids, Lebesgue measure and \(L^p\) norms. The pullback \(U_Sf=f\circ S\) commutes with heat, giving \[\Phi_{\nu,{\rm actual}}=U_S\Phi_{\nu,{\rm printed}}U_S.\] Thus Sections 3–4 apply to the printed map and their estimates transfer to the actual map before using Lemma 2.4.

Equivalently, the velocity \(w_\alpha(t,z)=S u_\alpha(t,Sz)\) has flow \(S\phi_tS\) and printed inverse time-one map. Its advection–diffusion evolution is unitarily conjugate to that of \(u_\alpha\), preserving diffusion, the Lipschitz bound, mean-zero data and decay constants. Correlations transfer in the same way. This is a complete bounded repair; the supported impact is Minor. The counterexample refutes the identification, not the main rates.
# Two local comparison issues

Problem 2 (Remark 2.3 reverses the ball-radius inequality).  Remark 2.3, page 19, claims that dyadic mixing at scale \(h=2^{-N}\) implies (39) for every \(0<\epsilon\le Ch\), with a fixed tolerance strictly below one. This is false.

Take \(f_m(x,y)=\sin(2\pi2^m x)\), \(\kappa'=1/2\), \(m\ge0\). At level \(N=m\), every dyadic square average is zero. At level \(m+1\), some averages have magnitude \(2/\pi>1/2\). The largest absolute dyadic conditional average cannot decrease under refinement, by averaging children to recover a parent. Hence \(\operatorname{mix}_{1/2}(f_m)=2^{-m}\) exactly. At a point where \(f_m=1\), continuity gives \[\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}\frac1{m(B_\epsilon(z))}\int_{B_\epsilon(z)}f_m\,dm=1.\] For any \(\kappa<1\) and \(C>0\), a sufficiently small \(\epsilon\le C2^{-m}\) contradicts (39).

The correct comparison uses a radius larger than the grid scale by a fixed factor. If each \(h\)-square average is bounded by \(\kappa'\|f\|_\infty\), squares wholly inside a ball of radius \(r\ge4\sqrt2h\), below the injectivity radius, occupy at least half its area: their union contains \(B_{r-\sqrt2h}\). The remaining boundary strip contributes at most \(\|f\|_\infty\), so \[\left|\frac1{m(B_r)}\int_{B_r}f\,dm\right|\le\frac{1+\kappa'}2\|f\|_\infty.\] For coarser scales, the whole torus and zero mean provide the comparison after an absolute adjustment of the constant. This suffices to transfer exponential decay of the dyadic scale to the usual ball-based scale. Theorem 4’s dyadic statement and the dissipation proof do not require the false all-smaller-radii assertion. Impact: Minor.

Problem 3 (A Lipschitz flow need not preserve \(C^1\)).  Theorem 2’s proof, page 22, inserts \(g\circ\phi_s\) into a \(C^1\) correlation estimate using only a Lipschitz bound for \(\phi_s\). The composition need not be \(C^1\).
For \(0<s<1/2\), \(\phi_s(x,y)=(x,y-2\alpha s|x-1/2|)\). Taking \(g(x,y)=\sin(2\pi y)\), the one-sided \(x\)-derivatives of the composition at \((1/2,0)\) are opposite nonzero numbers.

To repair the step, mollify a Lipschitz observable periodically. The approximants converge uniformly, with \(C^1\) norms bounded by its supremum norm plus Lipschitz constant. Apply Lemma 2.7 and pass to the limit in the correlation integral. Its bound then holds for Lipschitz observables. Since \(\|g\circ\phi_s\|_{\rm Lip}\le C_\alpha\|g\|_{C^1}\) uniformly on \(0\le s\le1\), the stated continuous-time exponential estimate follows. Impact: Minor, with verified repair.
# Substantive estimates and boundary checks
## Minorization and energy comparison

The one-step density is \(G_
u(z_0-T^{-1}z)\), with gradient bound \(C_\alpha
u^{-3/2}\). A dyadic approximation of mesh at most \(
u^2\) has error \(O(C_\alpha\sqrt
u)\). Lemma 2.1 supplies cell mass at least \(\lambda/2\) times area after \(O(|\log
u|)\) steps. The final heat step on a square of side \(2^{-N+1}\), \(2^{-N}\le\sqrt
u<2^{-N+1}\), gives density at least \(\lambda/(32\pi e^2)\). To keep the approximation threshold independent of \(\alpha\), condition instead on the first Gaussian before applying \(T\); its gradient bound is amplitude-independent and the subsequent maps form an allowed kicked word.

Doeblin contraction gives \(L^\infty\) decay. The \(L^2\) step uses both kernel normalization and Lebesgue invariance: \[\|\Phi_
u^nf\|_2^2\le
 2\|f\|_2^2\sup_z\int|p_n(z,z')-1|\,dz'.\] Reversibility is not needed. The comparison with continuous diffusion is \[\|F_d(2n)-f(n)\|_2^2\le
 C\epsilon

Small actual dissipation and \(\epsilon=\delta\) would make the two solutions too close to permit the pulsed factor \(1/2\), a contradiction. For general \(L^2\) data, the first unit interval either dissipates a fixed fraction or ensures the scaled gradient condition for \(f(1)\). One iterates at intervals \(n_0+1\), using monotonicity between them. The omitted square on a gradient norm on page 18 and the occurrence of \(n_0\) for \(n_0+1\) on page 15 do not alter this argument.
## Geometry and Jacobians

Branch determinants are one. The forward/backward cone bounds prevent cancellation for arbitrary matrix products and translations. The never-long ancestry term is bounded using \(4^n/(\delta_1\alpha^2)^n\). The application to \(I_k\) on page 28 requires \(\alpha^{-3k/2}\), not \(\alpha^{-3(n-k)/2}\); the final finite sum is unchanged by reindexing. The final segment enlargement loses \(O(1/\alpha)\) of preimage length.

Equation (47) gives ordinary slopes \(dy/dx=\pm\alpha\). The \(\pm1/\alpha\) on page 24 are their reciprocal slopes \(dx/dy\). The actual singularity equations give the required at-most-four component bound for a short unstable segment. In the area formula, the application uses nonnegative indicators and an almost everywhere positive Jacobian.

For odd iterates, use half-lengths \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) and \(\lceil n/2\rceil\). The two complexity bounds and the same matrix calculation hold with unequal lengths. Uniformity in large \(\alpha\) is recovered by retaining the actual ancestry factor \[\frac{[4/(\delta_1\alpha^2)]^m}{8\alpha|W|}.\] It is enough that \([4/(\delta_1\alpha^2)]^m\le4|W|\). Subdividing an initially long segment into lengths comparable to \(\alpha^{-1}\) costs only boundedly many iterates; for length \(2^{-N}\), a uniform \(O(N)\) bound suffices. These completions address parity and amplitude dependence without claiming a counterexample to Lemma 2.1.

Remark 1.4 also needs the second-half time shift: use a smooth nonnegative profile on \([0,1/2]\), compactly supported in its interior, with integral \(\alpha/2\); place it in the vertical half-period and its translate in the horizontal half-period. Since \(H_1,V_1\) have coefficient \(2\), this preserves the original integrated shear. Integral \(\alpha\) instead yields effective amplitude \(2\alpha\), which still gives the asserted existence of a smooth-in-time example. The printed formula does not literally preserve the parameter without this normalization.

The continuous-time step for Theorem 4 also requires attention to order: \(\phi_{n+s}=\phi_s\circ\phi_1^n\), so the partial-period composition cannot in general be moved to the initial observable. Instead, for a dyadic square \(R\) of side \(L\), its preimage under \(\phi_s\) has area \(L^2\) and boundary length at most \(4L\operatorname{Lip}(\phi_s^{-1})\). The part not covered by complete \(h\)-grid cells has area at most \(C L\operatorname{Lip}(\phi_s^{-1})h+Ch^2\). Taking \(L\) a sufficiently large fixed multiple of \(h\), uniformly for \(s\in[0,1]\), leaves at least half the area in complete cells. The tolerance becomes \((1+\kappa)/2<1\), preserving exponential geometric mixing with adjusted constants. This supplies the omitted composition-order argument.
## Correlation decay and optimality

For a step function on a square grid, the geometric lower bound gives a doubly stochastic matrix with a fixed positive constant component. The remaining part is an \(L^2\) contraction, proving (44). Approximation yields ergodicity of every power.

For [DL], the required piecewise smooth branches and finite singularity curves are present; the images of the singularities are transverse to the stable cone. Expansion dominates the bounded one-step intersection count, with a sufficiently small exponent in condition (P1). Its Theorem 2.8(5) gives exponential correlations from total ergodicity. Lebesgue measure is invariant here. This verifies the use of that external theorem, not its entire proof.

The lower-bound scaling is also consistent: for fixed smooth data, \(\|
abla f(t)\|_2^2\le e^{Ct}\|
abla f(0)\|_2^2\). The energy identity then prevents a fixed fractional loss before a constant times \(|\log
u|\). No faster uniform rate is inferred.
# Assessment and limitations

Problems 1–3 have local, verified repairs. The additional index, slope, domain and constant corrections do not establish a failure of the principal rates. The supported assessment is Minor. Scientific adjudication remains pending and human reviews are empty.

These conclusions apply only to the exact v1 inspected. No author adoption, later correction, journal-final status or independent backend-model verification is claimed. No author code was executed; unavailable code is not a mathematical defect. The checks are analytic.

report: Abstract: The general scaling statement in Theorem 6 loses a factor of the time-scale parameter in the noise strength. An exact occupation-coordinate calculation and a bounded Gaussian test show that its asserted coupled mean limit is false when that parameter differs from one. The natural corrected strength is beta times rho. This is a Major issue in the stated general theorem; the counterexample does not refute the rho equals one specialization or its KPZ interpretation. A separate Major proof defect occurs in the high-probability truncation used for the central convergence argument: the printed uncentered bridge cutoff is empty at large drift. The fixed-cutoff repair and its limits are stated explicitly. Other auxiliary formulas also require correction: classical divergence normalization and domain, a polymer heat-kernel denominator, Gaussian pair counting, and local-time scaling and truncation bounds. Explicit counterexamples and the limits of the repairs are given below. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical verification of KPZ fluctuations in the planar stochastic heat equation
# Exact source and scope

The source is Jeremy Quastel, Alejandro Ramírez and Bálint Virág, KPZ fluctuations in the planar stochastic heat equation, M25-0164, arXiv:2210.13607v3, 10 April 2024, 69 pages [source]. Physical PDF and printed page numbers agree on inspected pages. The assignment associates the article with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0058 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0058); no identity with a journal-final version is asserted.

The review covers Sections 1–7: the \(L^1\) divergence definition, finite projections and uniqueness, randomized shifts and their convergence, occupation moments, intersection local times, truncated exponential estimates, and assembly of the main results. Native scientific helpers examined disjoint sections; the lead checked the findings and the central normalization calculations. Coverage, exact file hashes, and actual page-view records accompany this report. Calculations are analytic. No unavailable author program is treated as a mathematical defect. The bibliography was not independently re-proved; the one external normalization comparison used below is identified precisely.
# The general scaling theorem has the wrong noise strength
Problem 1 (Major: Theorem 6, pages 8–9 and 66).  With the parameters and common-noise coupling stated in Theorem 6, the limiting noise strength is \(\beta\rho\), whereas the theorem prints \(\beta\).

Equation reference: eq:rho. Let the target time interval have length \(s>0\). The planar bridge runs for \(N\rho s\), and the scaled basis is \[e_{N,j}(x,y)=N^{-1}e_j(N^{-1/2}x,N^{-3/2}y).\] At time \(N\rho r\), its coordinates have the representation \[B_N(N\rho r)=
 \bigl(N^{1/2}b_{\rm sp}(t+r),\,
       N^{3/2}(t+r)+N^{1/2}b_{\rm ti}(t+r)\bigr),
 \quad 0\le r\le s,\] where the spatial bridge has variance parameter \(\nu\rho\), and the centered transverse bridge has variance parameter \(\rho\). Consequently its occupation coordinate, including the noise coefficient, is exactly \[\begin{aligned}
 m_{N,j}
 &=\beta\int_0^{N\rho s} e_{N,j}(B_N(u))\,du \notag\\
 &=\beta\rho\int_0^s
 e_j\bigl(b_{\rm sp}(t+r),t+r+N^{-1}b_{\rm ti}(t+r)\bigr)\,dr.
 \end{aligned}\] The change of variable on page 9 omits \(\rho\). For bounded continuous \(e_j\), the limiting coordinate is thus \(\beta\rho\int_0^s e_j(b_{\rm sp}(t+r),t+r)\,dr\). The deterministic heat-kernel normalization in the theorem does not remove this factor.
## A bounded-test contradiction to the printed \(L^1\) limit

Take \(\rho=2\), \(\nu=\beta=s=1\), and both spatial endpoints and the initial time equal to zero. Choose as the first orthonormal basis function \[e_1(x,r)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\exp(-x^2-r^2).\] It has \(L^2(\mathbb R^2)\) norm one and can be extended to an orthonormal basis of bounded continuous functions, by Gram–Schmidt applied to a dense family containing it. Write \(M=\|e_1\|_\infty=\sqrt{2/\pi}\) and \[m=\int_0^1 e_1(b_{\rm sp}(r),r)\,dr.\] Every continuous bridge path gives \(0<m\le M\), and [eq:rho] (#eq:rho) gives \(m_{N,1}\to2m\), with \(|m_{N,1}|\le2M\).

Divide the rescaled solution by its deterministic limiting spatial heat kernel, and denote the resulting mean-one partition function by \(Z_N\). The randomized-shift identity, (65) or (85) in the source, gives for \(a=\pi/(8M)\) \[\mathbb E_P[Z_N\sin(a\xi_1)]
 =e^{-a^2/2}\mathbb E_Q[\sin(a m_{N,1})]
 \longrightarrow e^{-a^2/2}\mathbb E_Q[\sin(2am)].\] The partition function \(Z_*\) of the printed target \(z_{2,1}\) instead satisfies \[\mathbb E_P[Z_*\sin(a\xi_1)]
 =e^{-a^2/2}\mathbb E_Q[\sin(am)].\] Since \(0<am\le\pi/8\), the first limiting expectation is strictly larger. A bounded test must have convergent expectations under \(L^1(P)\) convergence. This proves a contradiction to the exact printed theorem, without assuming uniform second moments or invoking a merely formal chaos expansion.
## Repair, boundaries, and effect

Replace the target \(z_{\nu\rho,\beta}\) by \(z_{\nu\rho,\beta\rho}\), with the same correction in the polymer coupling, or replace the planar noise coefficient by \(\beta/\rho\). This is the necessary algebraic repair. The deterministic prefactor \(N\sqrt{2\pi\rho s}\exp(N^2s/(2\rho))\) is consistent with the remaining spatial heat kernel. The counterexample uses strictly positive admissible parameters, not a degenerate endpoint. At \(\rho=1\) the missing factor disappears, so Theorem 5 is not refuted. A full convergence proof still requires the local-time and truncated-exponential inputs discussed in Section 5 (#sec:ilt); correcting one coefficient alone is not presented as a new proof of every statement of Theorem 6.
# Classical divergence and mild-equation normalization

Problem 2 (Minor: Section 2.5, pages 19–23).  The tensor conventions in (36)–(37) do not give the claimed comparison with Definition 8. The displayed divergence norm and full-domain description on page 21 are also false.

The paper uses unnormalized symmetrization \(\operatorname{Sym}g=\sum_{\sigma}g\circ\sigma\). In one dimension (36) therefore gives \(I_k(e^{\otimes k})=H_k(\xi)/k!\). For \(G=H_2(\xi)=\xi^2-1\), its kernel in that convention is \(g=2e^{\otimes2}\). Formula (37) yields \[I_3\bigl(\operatorname{Sym}(2e^{\otimes3})\bigr)=2H_3(\xi),\] whereas Definition 8 and Gaussian integration by parts give \(\delta G=\xi G-G'=H_3(\xi)\). This discrepancy survives the admissible bounded test \(F(\xi)=\sin\xi\): \[\mathbb E[H_3(\xi)\sin\xi]
 =\mathbb E[H_2(\xi)\cos\xi]=-e^{-1/2},\] while the printed candidate gives twice this value. All terms are finite polynomials with every finite moment.

There is a separate obstruction to the asserted norm equality. On a two-coordinate Gaussian space let \(G=(\xi_2,-\xi_1)\). Then \(\delta G=0\), while the claimed weighted chaos norm is \((1+1)\mathbb E\|G\|^2=4\). Symmetrization can have a kernel. The weighted condition (41) is sufficient, but is not the full domain. Indeed, for \(k\ge1\), put \[v_k=
 \frac{(H_{k-1}(\xi_1)\xi_2,\,-H_k(\xi_1))}
 {\sqrt{(k-1)!+k!}} .\] These mutually orthogonal vector fields have norm one, lie in chaos \(k\), and satisfy \(\delta v_k=0\). Thus \(G=\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-1}v_k\) is in \(L^2\) and in the classical divergence domain with divergence zero, but \[\sum_{k\ge1}(k+1)\mathbb E\|\pi_kG\|^2
 =\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{k+1}{k^2}=\infty.\] Closed Gaussian adjoint duality, or the convergent divergence chaos series, justifies the domain assertion in this example.

A consistent repair uses averaged symmetrization and standard Wiener integrals throughout. For kernels \(f_k\in H^{\odot k}\otimes H\), the actual condition is \(\sum_{k\ge0}(k+1)!\|\widetilde f_k\|^2<\infty\), and \(\mathbb E|\delta G|^2\) equals that sum. If the paper’s rescaled \(I_k\) convention is retained, (37) needs a factor \(1/k!\), and the occupation-coordinate formulas must be adjusted consistently.
## Function integrability versus coordinate integrability

Lemma 25 must also distinguish Definition 8 from Definition 10. The deterministic function \(g(x)=(1+|x|)^{-3/4}\) on \(\mathbb R\) has \(\int g^2=4\), so its classical Wiener integral exists, but \(\int |g|=\infty\). It does not satisfy Definition 10’s finite absolute-mass hypothesis. The coordinate interpretation can be correct; the function interpretation needs that additional hypothesis.

The needed PDE comparison can be obtained without the false tensor norm identity. Finite Hermite integration by parts gives the Gaussian adjoint relation. Correct \(L^2\) chaos summation extends it to the divergence domain. For predictable step integrands, integration by parts in an independent future increment identifies this divergence with the Itô integral; step approximation and Itô isometry extend the identity on the predictable \(L^2\) class.
## The missing heat factor and the missing endpoint integral

In Example 28, already at first chaos, the mild kernel is \[g_1(y;t,x)=\int_0^t p(x-y,t-r)p(y,r)\,dr.\] A probability bridge’s expected occupation density is \(g_1(y;t,x)/p(x,t)\). Thus (46) needs the deterministic factor \(p(x,t)\), consistently with the chronological heat products in (47).

Equation (49), pages 23–24, incorrectly equates a fixed-endpoint heat convolution with the full \(L^1\) norm. With \(t=1\), \(v(y,r)=p(y,r)\) and \(x=0\), its sides are \(p(0,1)=1/(2\pi)\) and \(1\). The sufficient estimate is instead, with \[A(x,t)=\mathbb E\int_{\mathbb R^2}\int_0^t
 p(x-y,t-r)|u(y,r)|\,dr\,dy,\] \[\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R^2} A(x,t)\,dx\,dt
 =\int_0^T(T-r)\mathbb E\|u(\cdot,r)\|_1\,dr
 \le T\|u\|_{L^1(dx\,dr\,dP)}.\] Tonelli therefore gives the required finite absolute mass and coordinate integrability at almost every endpoint. This repairs the Fubini steps used in Propositions 29–30 and 33 under their stated \(L^1\) hypothesis.
# Randomized shifts and polymer masses
Problem 3 (Minor: Proposition 39(c), Example 47, and Lemma 87).  Three auxiliary normalizations need correction. Their effects are distinct from the missing time-scale factor in Theorem 6.
## Gaussian pair counting
## The circle illustration

Example 47, page 35, combines covariance \(2\log|e^{i\omega}-e^{i\omega'}|^{-1}\) with the exponential \(\exp(\gamma\zeta-\gamma^2\mathbb E\zeta^2/2)\), but states the subcritical range \(\gamma<2\). With that covariance and exponential, the range is \(\gamma<1\). In the explicitly checked comparison [Remy], page 2, (1.2)–(1.3), the range \(<2\) uses the coefficient \(\gamma/2\) in front of the same field. Substituting \(2\gamma\) gives the correction. The source’s \(L^2\) threshold \(1/\sqrt2\) is consistent with its actual exponential. This is an ancillary example, not an input to the Brownian-bridge construction.
## A deterministic denominator in Lemma 87

The reference bridge law \(Q\) is a probability measure, and the random measure \(M\) defined by (85) has \(\mathbb E_P M=Q\), hence \(\mathbb E_P M(\Omega)=1\). In Lemma 87, page 65, the displayed finite-time density should be \[\mathbb E_M\varphi
 =\frac{1}{q(x_{k+1}-x_0,s_{k+1}-s_0)}
 \int_{\mathbb R^k}\varphi(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
 \prod_{i=0}^k z(x_i,s_i;x_{i+1},s_{i+1})\,dx_1\cdots dx_k .\] The source omits the denominator. Its own (118) is correct: multiplying the segment partition functions under the probability bridge produces the bridge density \(\prod_i q_i/q_{\rm total}\).

For an exact contradiction take \(k=1\), intermediate time \(1/2\), endpoints \((0,0),(0,1)\), and \(\varphi=1\). The expectation of the left side is \(1\). Independence of the two time-noise slabs, \(\mathbb Ez=q\), and the heat semigroup identity give expectation \(q(0,1)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}\) on the printed right side. Restoring the denominator also gives the familiar normalized polymer density \(\prod_i z_i/z_{\rm total}\). It does not invalidate the existence of the random measure.
## The meaning of the convergence criterion

Proposition 52(2) concerns convergence of nonnegative martingale limits. Its limiting cutoff condition should not be silently read as existence of a mean-one randomized-shift density for every approximating model. This distinction matters when invoking the random measures in Proposition 60.

For clarity, a concrete boundary example is available. Let \(U\) be uniform on \([0,1]\), independently of a fair infinite binary path. Index the nonempty tree nodes \(v\), and put \(h_v=2\,1_{\{v\text{ is a prefix}\}}\). Two independent paths share a prefix of length \(L\) with \(\mathbb P(L\ge n)=2^{-n}\); their intersection sum is \(4L\), with all finite polynomial moments. The depth-\(n\) partition martingale \(W_n\) satisfies \[\mathbb EW_n^{1/2}\le(\sqrt2e^{-1/2})^n\longrightarrow0,\] by subadditivity of the square root, so its limit has lost all mass. Let \(\varepsilon_\ell=(\ell+1)^{-1}\) and \(m_\ell=1_{\{U\le\varepsilon_\ell\}}h\), with limit \(m=0\). The coordinates converge almost surely, the second intersection moments tend to zero, and for each \(p<1\) the cutoffs \(A_\ell=\{U>\varepsilon_\ell\}\) eventually have probability \(>p\) and zero intersection on their product. Nevertheless, every martingale limit is the constant \(1-\varepsilon_\ell\), not a mean-one density. These constants do converge to \(1\) in \(L^1\); thus this example does not refute Proposition 52’s convergence assertion. Existence of the individual GMCs must be supplied where they are used. The Brownian applications have separate uniform-integrability arguments.
# Intersection-local-time estimates

Problem 4 (Major: the large-drift truncation used in Theorem 6).  The high-probability truncation needed in the main convergence proof is not established by the printed argument. Several local-time formulas also require correction; weaker corrected bounds suffice for the stated limiting application.
## Occupation mass is quadratic in the time change

In Lemma 76, page 53, \(\widehat X=tX\circ L^{-1}\). Bilinearity gives \[\alpha(\widehat X,\widehat X')
 =\frac{t^2}{|\det L|}\alpha(X,X'),\] not \(t/|\det L|\). For the deterministic path \(B(r)=r\) on \([0,1]\), in dimension one, take \(L=1\) and \(t=2\). The original occupation density is \(1_{[0,1]}\), the new one is \(2\,1_{[0,1]}\), and their self-intersection values are \(1\) and \(4\), not \(1\) and \(2\). This exact finite-density example satisfies the definition without any singular limiting issue.

In Proposition 74(2), page 52, duplication of the gamma function reduces the exact displayed moment to \[\mathbb E\alpha^k=t^{k/2}\Gamma(1+k/2).\] Stirling’s formula gives order \(\sqrt{k}\,(tk/(2e))^{k/2}\), not the printed upper bound with \(1/\sqrt{k}\). The all-exponential-moments conclusion nevertheless survives: \(\mathbb E\alpha^{2m}=t^m m!\) gives \(\mathbb E\cosh(\gamma\alpha)\le e^{\gamma^2t}\).

For Lemma 78, page 55, the bridge bound \(e^{10\gamma}\) should be \(e^{10\gamma t}\), and the drift second-moment numerator should be \(ct^2\), not \(ct\). These are genuine failures for unrestricted \(t\). At zero drift, planar intersection local time scales as \(\alpha_t\stackrel d=t\alpha_1\). Thus \(\mathbb E\alpha_t^2=t^2\mathbb E\alpha_1^2\) cannot be bounded by \(ct\) for all \(t\). For bridges, take \(\gamma=1/t\); the permitted condition \(\gamma t=1\) holds, but the left side is the fixed number \(\mathbb Ee^{\alpha_1}>1\), whereas \(e^{10/t}\to1\). The proof at \(t=1\) and correct Brownian scaling yield the repaired forms. Lemma 82 already prints the correct \(t^2\) numerator.
## Proposition 77: the quantity being limited

The definition (102) omits a square: the proof and (103) concern \(\phi(
u,y)=\mathbb E[\alpha(B^{
u,y},(B^{
u,y})')^2]\). At \(
u=0,y=0,t=1\), Proposition 74 gives \(\mathbb E\alpha=\sqrt{\pi}/2\) and \(\mathbb E\alpha^2=1\), so the distinction is substantive. The Gaussian integral on page 54 also has \(2\pi
u^{-2}\sqrt{\det C}\) in the denominator where \(2\pi
u^2\sqrt{\det C}\) is required. After these corrections, the remaining step is a singular approximate identity limit near the paired time diagonals; it needs control of endpoint and collision neighborhoods, not only pointwise passage under a Fourier integral.

On a bridge prefix ending at \(v<1\), the pair Radon–Nikodym bound relative to drifted motions is \((1-v)^{-2}\). Splitting at \(1/2\), using time reversal and moment-density Cauchy–Schwarz for mixed halves, proves \(\sup_{\nu\le1}M_\nu(0)<\infty\). For endpoint windows \(E_a=[0,a]\cup[1-a,1]\), the same bound gives \(\mathbb E\alpha(X_{E_a},X'_{E_a})^2\le Ca\) after the anisotropic factor \(N^2\). Applying Cauchy–Schwarz twice shows that all four-time terms having at least one endpoint time in \(E_a\) contribute at most \(Ca^{1/4}\).

After excluding these regions, \(C\) is uniformly positive definite. The substitution \(t=s+
u w\) has an integrable Gaussian majorant, so dominated convergence gives density \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{\det(2G(s))})\). First send \(
u	o0\), then \(h	o0\), and then \(a	o0\). The full limiting integral is \[ rac1{2\pi}\int_{0<u<v<1}
 [u(v-u)(1-v)]^{-1/2}\,du\,dv=1.\] Thus the intended \(M_
u(y)	o1\) is verified for every fixed \(y\), after the two printed corrections. The companion proof record gives the cutoff details; neither the literal first-moment definition nor the later exponential bound is validated by this calculation.
## Proposition 84 cannot have the printed uniform prefactor

In Proposition 84, page 61, fix \(N=1\) and both starting points at zero. Let \(A_r\) be its stated centered-strip event and let \(m=\mathbb E\alpha(B,B')>0\). Gaussian maximal tails give \(\mathbb P((A_r\times A_r)^c)\le C e^{-r^2/8}\), and integrability gives \(\mathbb E[\alpha1_{A_r\times A_r}]\to m\). Set \(\gamma=r^{-2}\), which satisfies \(\gamma\le\pi/(8r)\) for all sufficiently large \(r\). Since \(e^x\ge1+x\), \[\mathbb E[e^{\gamma\alpha}1_{A_r\times A_r}]
 \ge1-Ce^{-r^2/8}+\frac{m}{2r^2},
 \qquad
 e^{c\gamma^2}=1+O(r^{-4}).\] No fixed \(c\) makes the printed inequality true for all \(r\). The factor \(2\) in the paper’s (115) cannot be absorbed into \(e^{c\gamma^2}\) uniformly as \(\gamma\downarrow0\).

A sufficient repair retains a prefactor \(C_0>1\). The interval covering also needs slack: \(|s-t|\le r/N\) on the strip does not ensure that a pair belongs to one of two half-shifted grids of windows of length \(r/N\). Windows of length \(2r/N\), with shift \(r/N\), supply such a cover, at the cost of a smaller universal constant in the admissible bound \(\gamma r<c_0\). The Gaussian weight must also use the actual block duration: at duration \(r/N\) it is \(\exp[-NY_i^2/(8r)]\), rather than the \(\exp[-Y_i^2/(8r)]\) printed near (115). Only the former becomes a fixed-parameter Gaussian weight after normalizing the increments to a standard random walk. These changes do not justify retaining every printed numerical constant.
## What the large-drift application actually needs

The event \(H\) in Proposition 85 uses the uncentered norm from (107). For a bridge from \(0\) to \((0,N)\), \(\|B\|_\kappa\ge N\), so that event is empty when \(N>r/2\). It cannot be the high-probability cutoff needed for the limit.

On page 66, the proof of Theorem 6 explicitly invokes Proposition 85 to supply the hypothesis of Proposition 52(2): for every \(p<1\), there must be path sets \(A_N\) with \(Q(A_N)>p\) and a finite limiting upper bound on the truncated exponential moments. That page fixes \(\nu=\rho=\beta=s=1\) and \(x=t=0\). The printed empty bridge event cannot provide those sets. After centering, the covering and exponential estimates still require the corrections and conditional argument below. Thus the displayed proof does not establish a necessary uniform control in the central convergence argument, including its standard-parameter specialization. This is a Major proof defect, not a counterexample to that limit. This operative dependency determines the assessment of this group; the other local coefficient and scaling errors are not each thereby classified as Major.

Use instead \[H_r=\{\|B-(0,N)\,\cdot\|_\kappa\le r/2\}.\] Its probability can be made arbitrarily close to one independently of \(N\). This centered event is also what implies the increment conditions \(G_i\) used on page 62.

After choosing fixed \(r,\gamma,\kappa\), select a finite \(m\) large enough that the corrected short-block bound applies, and then \(N\) large enough for the separation of the blocks. The conditional block bound needs an additional argument because each increment cutoff is centered at its own starting position. For two such independent path measures \(X,Y\), with respective cutoffs \(G,G'\), moment-density Cauchy–Schwarz at each order and then Cauchy–Schwarz in the nonnegative exponential series give \[\mathbb E[e^{\theta\alpha(X,Y)}1_G1_{G'}]
 \le\left(
 \mathbb E[e^{\theta\alpha(X,X')}1_G1_{\widetilde G}]\,
 \mathbb E[e^{\theta\alpha(Y,Y')}1_{G'}1_{\widetilde G'}]
 \right)^{1/2}.\] The zeroth term is the product of cutoff probabilities. For every positive order, the moment densities are in \(L^2\) by the untruncated Brownian moment bounds. The self terms are identical up to a common translation, because the increment cutoff is translation covariant. Each can therefore use the corrected strip bound. No independent translation of the two paths inside a cross intersection local time is being assumed. The retained prefactor costs \(C_0^m\), which is finite and independent of \(N\). The resulting bound is \[\sup_{N\ge N_0(r,\gamma,\kappa)}
 \mathbb E[e^{\gamma N\alpha(B,B')}1_{H_r\times H_r}]
 <\infty .\] For motions, one may take \(m\) larger than a fixed multiple of \(1+(\gamma r)^{1/\kappa}\) and \(N\) larger than a fixed multiple of \(rm\). For bridges, the overlapping two-thirds prefixes and their pair Radon–Nikodym factor \(9\), followed by time reversal and Cauchy–Schwarz, preserve a finite bound depending on the fixed cutoff parameters. This weaker bound is the one needed by the cutoff convergence criterion. The displayed choice \(m=\lceil(16\gamma r/\pi)^{1/\kappa}\rceil\) does not by itself establish the printed cubic threshold in \(N\) for every \(\kappa<1/2\). That numerical threshold is not certified here; no counterexample to it is claimed.

Two further proof completions are bounded. In Lemma 83, the chosen \(a=4\gamma e^{\lambda/2}/\sqrt{k}\) need not be at most one under the stated \(k\ge\gamma^2\). For \(k\ge16e^\lambda\gamma^2\) the argument applies; below that threshold the trivial estimate \(\exp(\gamma\sqrt{k})\le\exp(4e^{\lambda/2}\gamma^2)\) is covered by the claimed right side. In Proposition 79, the grid-measurable occupation cutoff must remain in the conditional estimate through (108)–(111). Dropping it before invoking its bound on the number of pairs is not justified. Keeping it gives the finite exponential bound used by Corollary 81.
# Verified dependence and limits of the conclusion

The identification in Lemma 67 need not rely on pointwise convergence of raw Dirichlet Fourier sums from continuity alone. Heat-kernel regularizations of the convolution have a second-moment inner product controlled by the \(L^2\) occupation moment densities. Strong continuity of heat convolution makes them Cauchy in \(L^2\); the defining rectangle-test identity identifies the limit with \(\alpha\). For a realized finite convolution measure whose density is continuous near zero, the positive heat approximate identity converges to that density value. These two limits prove the identification used in the paper.

The finite-dimensional construction in Section 3 can be checked directly from Definition 8. On a finite time interval, \(|m(r)|\le r(\sum_{j\le n}\|e_j\|_\infty^2)^{1/2}\); the Wick exponential and its needed Gaussian derivatives therefore have uniform integrable bounds. Bridge disintegration and the correct Tonelli estimate prove existence. Fourier tests in the Gaussian coordinates reduce uniqueness to an \(L^1\) heat equation with bounded potential. An \(L^1\) Gronwall argument proves uniqueness; using rational Fourier parameters first and then continuity handles the common-null-set issue.

For Proposition 33, \(\mathbb E|u_n(x,t)|\le P_t|\varsigma|(x)\). Pointwise \(L^1(P)\) convergence is consequently dominated in the full space–time product \(L^1\) norm. Conditional expectations of the limiting kernel agree with the finite projected kernels, so Corollary 14 applies. These arguments do not depend on the false classical norm equality.

The randomized-shift identity follows from finite Gaussian completion of the square. Mean-one martingale uniform integrability, the cutoff Cauchy argument of Proposition 45, the coordinate moment bounds of Propositions 48–50, and the \(L^2\) part of Proposition 52 were checked. For an already existing random measure \(M\), finite-coordinate approximations satisfy \(M_n(F)=\mathbb E_P[M(F)\mid\mathcal F_n]\) for every bounded path test \(F\). Conditional-expectation convergence and tightness from \(\mathbb EM_n=Q\) give weak convergence in probability on the Polish path space. This supplies the approximation step without assuming that a convergence criterion creates every individual GMC.

Two Major assessments are supported: the explicit false general parameter limit in Theorem 6, and the missing high-probability uniform exponential control in its printed tightness proof. The latter also affects the standard-parameter derivation on page 66; the verified centered fixed-cutoff repair restores the needed hypothesis, without proving the stronger printed constants or cubic threshold. It is not a counterexample to the standard-parameter limit. The remaining auxiliary issues have the specified local effects. The exact sharp constants and all formulations of the repaired auxiliary statements are not claimed as independently optimized. No journal-final comparison, author-code reproduction, or comprehensive later-literature search was performed. The local evidence and the necessary corrections are tied to the exact supplied version.

claim: The limiting noise coefficient is beta*rho, not beta.
analysis: With the parameters and common-noise coupling stated in Theorem 6, the limiting noise strength is \(\beta\rho\), whereas the theorem prints \(\beta\).

Equation reference: eq:rho. Let the target time interval have length \(s>0\). The planar bridge runs for \(N\rho s\), and the scaled basis is \[e_{N,j}(x,y)=N^{-1}e_j(N^{-1/2}x,N^{-3/2}y).\] At time \(N\rho r\), its coordinates have the representation \[B_N(N\rho r)=
 \bigl(N^{1/2}b_{\rm sp}(t+r),\,
       N^{3/2}(t+r)+N^{1/2}b_{\rm ti}(t+r)\bigr),
 \quad 0\le r\le s,\] where the spatial bridge has variance parameter \(\nu\rho\), and the centered transverse bridge has variance parameter \(\rho\). Consequently its occupation coordinate, including the noise coefficient, is exactly \[\begin{aligned}
 m_{N,j}
 &=\beta\int_0^{N\rho s} e_{N,j}(B_N(u))\,du \notag\\
 &=\beta\rho\int_0^s
 e_j\bigl(b_{\rm sp}(t+r),t+r+N^{-1}b_{\rm ti}(t+r)\bigr)\,dr.
 \end{aligned}\] The change of variable on page 9 omits \(\rho\). For bounded continuous \(e_j\), the limiting coordinate is thus \(\beta\rho\int_0^s e_j(b_{\rm sp}(t+r),t+r)\,dr\). The deterministic heat-kernel normalization in the theorem does not remove this factor.

 =e^{-a^2/2}\mathbb E_Q[\sin(a m_{N,1})]
 \longrightarrow e^{-a^2/2}\mathbb E_Q[\sin(2am)].\] The partition function \(Z_*\) of the printed target \(z_{2,1}\) instead satisfies \[\mathbb E_P[Z_*\sin(a\xi_1)]
 =e^{-a^2/2}\mathbb E_Q[\sin(am)].\] Since \(0<am\le\pi/8\), the first limiting expectation is strictly larger. A bounded test must have convergent expectations under \(L^1(P)\) convergence. claim: Ordered Gaussian pairs lack1/2; circle example uses incompatible critical convention; polymer cylinder formula lacks deterministic heat denominator.
analysis: Three auxiliary normalizations need correction. Their effects are distinct from the missing time-scale factor in Theorem 6.

Example 47, page 35, combines covariance \(2\log|e^{i\omega}-e^{i\omega'}|^{-1}\) with the exponential \(\exp(\gamma\zeta-\gamma^2\mathbb E\zeta^2/2)\), but states the subcritical range \(\gamma<2\). With that covariance and exponential, the range is \(\gamma<1\). In the explicitly checked comparison [Remy], page 2, (1.2)–(1.3), the range \(<2\) uses the coefficient \(\gamma/2\) in front of the same field. Substituting \(2\gamma\) gives the correction. The source’s \(L^2\) threshold \(1/\sqrt2\) is consistent with its actual exponential. This is an ancillary example, not an input to the Brownian-bridge construction.

The reference bridge law \(Q\) is a probability measure, and the random measure \(M\) defined by (85) has \(\mathbb E_P M=Q\), hence \(\mathbb E_P M(\Omega)=1\). In Lemma 87, page 65, the displayed finite-time density should be \[\mathbb E_M\varphi
 =\frac{1}{q(x_{k+1}-x_0,s_{k+1}-s_0)}
 \int_{\mathbb R^k}\varphi(x_1,\ldots,x_k)
 \prod_{i=0}^k z(x_i,s_i;x_{i+1},s_{i+1})\,dx_1\cdots dx_k .\] The source omits the denominator. Its own (118) is correct: multiplying the segment partition functions under the probability bridge produces the bridge density \(\prod_i q_i/q_{\rm total}\).

For an exact contradiction take \(k=1\), intermediate time \(1/2\), endpoints \((0,0),(0,1)\), and \(\varphi=1\). The expectation of the left side is \(1\). Independence of the two time-noise slabs, \(\mathbb Ez=q\), and the heat semigroup identity give expectation \(q(0,1)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}\) on the printed right side. Restoring the denominator also gives the familiar normalized polymer density \(\prod_i z_i/z_{\rm total}\). It does not invalidate the existence of the random measure.

Proposition 52(2) concerns convergence of nonnegative martingale limits. Its limiting cutoff condition should not be silently read as existence of a mean-one randomized-shift density for every approximating model. This distinction matters when invoking the random measures in Proposition 60.

For clarity, a concrete boundary example is available. Let \(U\) be uniform on \([0,1]\), independently of a fair infinite binary path. Index the nonempty tree nodes \(v\), and put \(h_v=2\,1_{\{v\text{ is a prefix}\}}\). Two independent paths share a prefix of length \(L\) with \(\mathbb P(L\ge n)=2^{-n}\); their intersection sum is \(4L\), with all finite polynomial moments. The depth-\(n\) partition martingale \(W_n\) satisfies \[\mathbb EW_n^{1/2}\le(\sqrt2e^{-1/2})^n\longrightarrow0,\] by subadditivity of the square root, so its limit has lost all mass. Let \(\varepsilon_\ell=(\ell+1)^{-1}\) and \(m_\ell=1_{\{U\le\varepsilon_\ell\}}h\), with limit \(m=0\). The coordinates converge almost surely, the second intersection moments tend to zero, and for each \(p<1\) the cutoffs \(A_\ell=\{U>\varepsilon_\ell\}\) eventually have probability \(>p\) and zero intersection on their product. Nevertheless, every martingale limit is the constant \(1-\varepsilon_\ell\), not a mean-one density. These constants do converge to \(1\) in \(L^1\); thus this example does not refute Proposition 52’s convergence assertion. Existence of the individual GMCs must be supplied where they are used. The Brownian applications have separate uniform-integrability arguments.

problems.source_location: Props74/77/84/85 and Lemmas76/78/82/83, pp52-62; explicit application in Theorem6 proof p66
claim: Time-mass scaling and several constants/powers are wrong; Prop84 cannot be uniform with prefactor1; Prop85 needs centered cutoff and additional conditional-bound argument.
analysis: The high-probability truncation needed in the main convergence proof is not established by the printed argument. Several local-time formulas also require correction; weaker corrected bounds suffice for the stated limiting application.

In Lemma 76, page 53, \(\widehat X=tX\circ L^{-1}\). Bilinearity gives \[\alpha(\widehat X,\widehat X')
 =\frac{t^2}{|\det L|}\alpha(X,X'),\] not \(t/|\det L|\). For the deterministic path \(B(r)=r\) on \([0,1]\), in dimension one, take \(L=1\) and \(t=2\). The original occupation density is \(1_{[0,1]}\), the new one is \(2\,1_{[0,1]}\), and their self-intersection values are \(1\) and \(4\), not \(1\) and \(2\). This exact finite-density example satisfies the definition without any singular limiting issue.

In Proposition 74(2), page 52, duplication of the gamma function reduces the exact displayed moment to \[\mathbb E\alpha^k=t^{k/2}\Gamma(1+k/2).\] Stirling’s formula gives order \(\sqrt{k}\,(tk/(2e))^{k/2}\), not the printed upper bound with \(1/\sqrt{k}\). The all-exponential-moments conclusion nevertheless survives: \(\mathbb E\alpha^{2m}=t^m m!\) gives \(\mathbb E\cosh(\gamma\alpha)\le e^{\gamma^2t}\).

For Lemma 78, page 55, the bridge bound \(e^{10\gamma}\) should be \(e^{10\gamma t}\), and the drift second-moment numerator should be \(ct^2\), not \(ct\). These are genuine failures for unrestricted \(t\). At zero drift, planar intersection local time scales as \(\alpha_t\stackrel d=t\alpha_1\). Thus \(\mathbb E\alpha_t^2=t^2\mathbb E\alpha_1^2\) cannot be bounded by \(ct\) for all \(t\). For bridges, take \(\gamma=1/t\); the permitted condition \(\gamma t=1\) holds, but the left side is the fixed number \(\mathbb Ee^{\alpha_1}>1\), whereas \(e^{10/t}\to1\). The proof at \(t=1\) and correct Brownian scaling yield the repaired forms. Lemma 82 already prints the correct \(t^2\) numerator.

The definition (102) omits a square: the proof and (103) concern \(\phi(
u,y)=\mathbb E[\alpha(B^{
u,y},(B^{
u,y})')^2]\). At \(
u=0,y=0,t=1\), Proposition 74 gives \(\mathbb E\alpha=\sqrt{\pi}/2\) and \(\mathbb E\alpha^2=1\), so the distinction is substantive. The Gaussian integral on page 54 also has \(2\pi
u^{-2}\sqrt{\det C}\) in the denominator where \(2\pi
u^2\sqrt{\det C}\) is required. After these corrections, the remaining step is a singular approximate identity limit near the paired time diagonals; it needs control of endpoint and collision neighborhoods, not only pointwise passage under a Fourier integral.

On a bridge prefix ending at \(v<1\), the pair Radon–Nikodym bound relative to drifted motions is \((1-v)^{-2}\). Splitting at \(1/2\), using time reversal and moment-density Cauchy–Schwarz for mixed halves, proves \(\sup_{\nu\le1}M_\nu(0)<\infty\). For endpoint windows \(E_a=[0,a]\cup[1-a,1]\), the same bound gives \(\mathbb E\alpha(X_{E_a},X'_{E_a})^2\le Ca\) after the anisotropic factor \(N^2\). Applying Cauchy–Schwarz twice shows that all four-time terms having at least one endpoint time in \(E_a\) contribute at most \(Ca^{1/4}\).

After excluding these regions, \(C\) is uniformly positive definite. The substitution \(t=s+
u w\) has an integrable Gaussian majorant, so dominated convergence gives density \(1/(2\pi\sqrt{\det(2G(s))})\). First send \(
u	o0\), then \(h	o0\), and then \(a	o0\). The full limiting integral is \[ rac1{2\pi}\int_{0<u<v<1}
 [u(v-u)(1-v)]^{-1/2}\,du\,dv=1.\] Thus the intended \(M_
u(y)	o1\) is verified for every fixed \(y\), after the two printed corrections. The companion proof record gives the cutoff details; neither the literal first-moment definition nor the later exponential bound is validated by this calculation.

In Proposition 84, page 61, fix \(N=1\) and both starting points at zero. Let \(A_r\) be its stated centered-strip event and let \(m=\mathbb E\alpha(B,B')>0\). Gaussian maximal tails give \(\mathbb P((A_r\times A_r)^c)\le C e^{-r^2/8}\), and integrability gives \(\mathbb E[\alpha1_{A_r\times A_r}]\to m\). Set \(\gamma=r^{-2}\), which satisfies \(\gamma\le\pi/(8r)\) for all sufficiently large \(r\). Since \(e^x\ge1+x\), \[\mathbb E[e^{\gamma\alpha}1_{A_r\times A_r}]
 \ge1-Ce^{-r^2/8}+\frac{m}{2r^2},
 \qquad
 e^{c\gamma^2}=1+O(r^{-4}).\] No fixed \(c\) makes the printed inequality true for all \(r\). The factor \(2\) in the paper’s (115) cannot be absorbed into \(e^{c\gamma^2}\) uniformly as \(\gamma\downarrow0\).

A sufficient repair retains a prefactor \(C_0>1\). The interval covering also needs slack: \(|s-t|\le r/N\) on the strip does not ensure that a pair belongs to one of two half-shifted grids of windows of length \(r/N\). Windows of length \(2r/N\), with shift \(r/N\), supply such a cover, at the cost of a smaller universal constant in the admissible bound \(\gamma r<c_0\). The Gaussian weight must also use the actual block duration: at duration \(r/N\) it is \(\exp[-NY_i^2/(8r)]\), rather than the \(\exp[-Y_i^2/(8r)]\) printed near (115). Only the former becomes a fixed-parameter Gaussian weight after normalizing the increments to a standard random walk. These changes do not justify retaining every printed numerical constant.

The event \(H\) in Proposition 85 uses the uncentered norm from (107). For a bridge from \(0\) to \((0,N)\), \(\|B\|_\kappa\ge N\), so that event is empty when \(N>r/2\). It cannot be the high-probability cutoff needed for the limit.

On page 66, the proof of Theorem 6 explicitly invokes Proposition 85 to supply the hypothesis of Proposition 52(2): for every \(p<1\), there must be path sets \(A_N\) with \(Q(A_N)>p\) and a finite limiting upper bound on the truncated exponential moments. That page fixes \(\nu=\rho=\beta=s=1\) and \(x=t=0\). The printed empty bridge event cannot provide those sets. After centering, the covering and exponential estimates still require the corrections and conditional argument below. Thus the displayed proof does not establish a necessary uniform control in the central convergence argument, including its standard-parameter specialization. This is a Major proof defect, not a counterexample to that limit. This operative dependency determines the assessment of this group; the other local coefficient and scaling errors are not each thereby classified as Major.

Use instead \[H_r=\{\|B-(0,N)\,\cdot\|_\kappa\le r/2\}.\] Its probability can be made arbitrarily close to one independently of \(N\). This centered event is also what implies the increment conditions \(G_i\) used on page 62.

After choosing fixed \(r,\gamma,\kappa\), select a finite \(m\) large enough that the corrected short-block bound applies, and then \(N\) large enough for the separation of the blocks. The conditional block bound needs an additional argument because each increment cutoff is centered at its own starting position. For two such independent path measures \(X,Y\), with respective cutoffs \(G,G'\), moment-density Cauchy–Schwarz at each order and then Cauchy–Schwarz in the nonnegative exponential series give \[\mathbb E[e^{\theta\alpha(X,Y)}1_G1_{G'}]
 \le\left(
 \mathbb E[e^{\theta\alpha(X,X')}1_G1_{\widetilde G}]\,
 \mathbb E[e^{\theta\alpha(Y,Y')}1_{G'}1_{\widetilde G'}]
 \right)^{1/2}.\] The zeroth term is the product of cutoff probabilities. For every positive order, the moment densities are in \(L^2\) by the untruncated Brownian moment bounds. The self terms are identical up to a common translation, because the increment cutoff is translation covariant. Each can therefore use the corrected strip bound. No independent translation of the two paths inside a cross intersection local time is being assumed. The retained prefactor costs \(C_0^m\), which is finite and independent of \(N\). The resulting bound is \[\sup_{N\ge N_0(r,\gamma,\kappa)}
 \mathbb E[e^{\gamma N\alpha(B,B')}1_{H_r\times H_r}]
 <\infty .\] For motions, one may take \(m\) larger than a fixed multiple of \(1+(\gamma r)^{1/\kappa}\) and \(N\) larger than a fixed multiple of \(rm\). For bridges, the overlapping two-thirds prefixes and their pair Radon–Nikodym factor \(9\), followed by time reversal and Cauchy–Schwarz, preserve a finite bound depending on the fixed cutoff parameters. This weaker bound is the one needed by the cutoff convergence criterion. The displayed choice \(m=\lceil(16\gamma r/\pi)^{1/\kappa}\rceil\) does not by itself establish the printed cubic threshold in \(N\) for every \(\kappa<1/2\). That numerical threshold is not certified here; no counterexample to it is claimed.

Two further proof completions are bounded. In Lemma 83, the chosen \(a=4\gamma e^{\lambda/2}/\sqrt{k}\) need not be at most one under the stated \(k\ge\gamma^2\). For \(k\ge16e^\lambda\gamma^2\) the argument applies; below that threshold the trivial estimate \(\exp(\gamma\sqrt{k})\le\exp(4e^{\lambda/2}\gamma^2)\) is covered by the claimed right side. In Proposition 79, the grid-measurable occupation cutoff must remain in the conditional estimate through (108)–(111). Dropping it before invoking its bound on the number of pairs is not justified. Keeping it gives the finite exponential bound used by Corollary 81.
result: Impact: Major is assigned specifically to the missing high-probability uniform exponential control in the central convergence proof. The other local coefficient/scaling errors do not individually become Major by grouping. The printed bridge bound is vacuous at largeN, not itself contradicted by the empty-event observation.
