report: Abstract: The general hierarchy criteria admit an explicit compact zero-dimensional counterexample. In the Brownian application, the natural measure is almost surely not doubling, and the bad-tile covering argument contains an almost-sure counterexample to an actual intermediate assertion. The false all-generation flatness assertion in the carpet proof is also a Major defect in a core derivation. These issues do not establish that the main Brownian conformal-dimension conclusion is false. A replacement modulus argument removes the doubling requirement, but further gaps in the good-set, compact-core, and weighted-averaging arguments remain. The uniform-fiber carpet and continuous-graph results have explicit repairs, which are distinguished from the unresolved Brownian proof. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of Conformal dimension of the Brownian graph
# Exact source and review scope

The reviewed source is Ilia Binder, Hrant Hakobyan and Wen-Bo Li, Conformal dimension of the Brownian graph, M25-0165, arXiv:2309.02350v2, 15 October 2024, 54 pages [source]. The assignment associates it with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0059 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0059). No identity with the journal-final article, or with a later corrected version, is asserted. Page references below are one-based physical PDF pages; they agree with the printed numbers on inspected pages.

Sections 1–7 were covered by the lead and native scientific helpers with disjoint section assignments. The checks include all stated hierarchy hypotheses, local-radius quantifiers in the modulus argument, symbolic and boundary measures in the carpets, Brownian occupation and stopping-time constructions, the compact-core selection, and the positive-modulus step. The lead independently checked the principal counterexamples and repairs. Exact hashes, source-view records, and helper scopes accompany the report. These records distinguish extraction from scientific reading and source-page viewing from report-page viewing.

The assessment is Major because a principal general criterion is false as stated and the core Brownian proof uses demonstrably false intermediate claims. No counterexample to Theorem 1.1 itself is claimed. The carpet conclusions are assessed separately, since their more rigid geometry supplies repairs unavailable from the printed Brownian argument.
# The general hierarchy theorems are false as stated

Problem 1 (Major: Theorems 3.4, 3.6 and 3.7, pages 16–23).  The definitions do not require hierarchy cells to shrink. All their printed hypotheses can hold on a compact metric space of conformal dimension zero.

Let \(E=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\). For distinct \(a,b\), let \(k(a,b)\) be the first differing coordinate and set \[d(a,b)=2^{-k(a,b)^2}.\] This compact ultrametric space has diameter \(1/2\). Its ordinary length-\(n\) prefix cylinders give a cover with total \(s\)-content at most \[2^n\bigl(2^{-(n+1)^2}\bigr)^s
 =2^{n-s(n+1)^2}\longrightarrow0
 \qquad(s>0).\] Thus \(\dim_H E=\dim_C E=0\).

The hierarchy used for the counterexample is different from these ordinary cylinders. Let \(c(b)=\sum_{j\ge1}2b_j3^{-j}\), the continuous bijection onto the ternary Cantor set. If \(a\) has an asymptotic frequency of ones \(p(a)\) in that Cantor set, put \(q(a)=c^{-1}(p(a))\); otherwise put \(q(a)=0^\infty\). The map \(q\) is Borel: the convergence set of the Cesàro means is Borel, their limit is Borel there, and \(c^{-1}\) is continuous. Every fiber \(q^{-1}(b)\) is dense and nonempty. Indeed, after any prescribed finite prefix, append the sequence \(\lfloor np\rfloor-\lfloor(n-1)p\rfloor\), with \(p=c(b)\).

For a binary word \(w\) of length \(i\), define \[E_{i,w}=q^{-1}([w]).\] Each generation is a Borel partition of \(E\); each cell has exactly two children, one parent and one sibling. Every infinite branch has nonempty intersection \(q^{-1}(b)\). Every cell is dense and has diameter \(1/2\), and every pair of siblings has distance zero. Therefore (3.6) and (3.7) hold with relative distance zero and \(L=1\).

Every proper ball in this ultrametric is clopen and contains no dense hierarchy cell. A ball equal to \(E\) contains each cell together with its parent. Hence the cardinality in the printed flatness condition on page 16 is always zero. In particular a uniform flatness constant exists. The conclusion \(\dim_C E\ge1\) of Theorem 3.4 is nevertheless false. Taking the constant family \(E^n=E\), with the same cells for every \(n\), also satisfies the nesting, boundedness, uniform-flatness, ratio and iterated-limit conditions of Theorems 3.6 and 3.7 and refutes their conclusions.

The stopping-cell cover on page 19 implicitly assumes that each point eventually lies in a cell contained in a given small ball. That is exactly what fails here. A vanishing-mesh hypothesis excludes this example, but is not by itself a complete repair: the proof also transfers original-metric flatness to image-space balls without proof, uses an inclusion of a closure into the original set, and reverses the inside/outside directions of a decreasing sequence. The limiting arguments in 3.6–3.7 require further localization and mass retention. For example, finite measures on a bounded noncompact space need not have a nonzero weak limit there.

The cylinder-weight algebra of Lemma 3.5 was checked separately. It does not supply the missing ball cover, and the example above is not offered as a counterexample to its intended normalized cylinder bound. A complete corrected general hierarchy theorem is not certified. Nor does this example describe the particular carpets or Brownian sets.
# The Brownian measure is not doubling
Problem 2 (Major proof-level issue: page 38 and the use of Theorem 3.2).  The measure defined by (6.1) is almost surely not doubling, even on the compact set used in the application.

Let \[X=\Gamma(W)\cap([0,T_6]\times[0,1]),\qquad z_0=(0,0).\] The space-time occupation identity identifies the integral of level local times in (6.1) with the pushforward of \(dt\) to the graph. One may use, for example, (2.5) of [occupation]; a common local-time normalization constant cancels in all ratios below.

For \(c=1,2\), define, before the terminal-time truncation, \[m_c(r)=\int_0^{cr}
 \chi_{\{0<W_t<r\sqrt{c^2-(t/r)^2}\}}\,dt .\] For all sufficiently small \(r\), almost surely, \(m_c(r)=\mu_X(B(z_0,cr))\), since \(2r<T_6\), \(2r<1\), and the times at level zero have zero Lebesgue measure. Brownian scaling, with \(\varepsilon=\sqrt r\), gives the joint law \[r^{-3/2}m_c(r)\ \stackrel{\rm law}{=}\
 \varepsilon^{-1}\int_0^c
 \chi_{\{0<B_u<\varepsilon f_c(u)\}}\,du,
 \qquad f_c(u)=\sqrt{c^2-u^2}.\] On one fixed Brownian path \(B\), joint continuity of local time and the occupation formula imply \[\varepsilon^{-1}\int_0^c
 \chi_{\{0<B_u<\varepsilon f_c(u)\}}\,du
 \longrightarrow V_c:=\int_0^c f_c(u)\,dL_u^0 .
 \tag{1}\] For completeness, a constant step height \(a\) on \((u,v]\) gives \(\varepsilon^{-1}\int_0^{\varepsilon a}
(L_v^x-L_u^x)\,dx\to a(L_v^0-L_u^0)\). Uniform upper and lower step approximations of the continuous \(f_c\) then prove (1).

We have \(V_1\ge(\sqrt3/2)L_{1/2}^0>0\) almost surely. Moreover \(V_2/V_1\) has unbounded support. For every \(\epsilon>0\), \[\mathbb P\{L_1^0\le\epsilon,\ L_{3/2}^0-L_1^0\ge1\}>0.\] The first condition has positive probability. Conditional on the finite position \(B_1\), there is positive probability to reach zero by time \(5/4\) and then accumulate at least one unit of local time by \(3/2\). On this event, \(V_1\le\epsilon\) and \(V_2\ge\sqrt7/2\).

Equality of a level local time with a gauge Hausdorff measure does not imply measure doubling, nor does approximating levels by dyadics. The upper mass estimate (6.2) is different: joint local-time Hölder continuity on a fixed compact time/height region does yield \(\mu_X(B(x,r))\le C_{\epsilon,X}r^{3/2-\epsilon}\) uniformly in \(x\). Thus the upper bound survives (2). A replacement for the modulus step is provided in Section 6 below.
# The bad-tile cover fails on actual Brownian paths
Problem 3 (Major: Proposition 6.2 proof, pages 41–43).  Assertion (1) in the proof, and the resulting covering estimate (6.5), are false almost surely for all sufficiently fine generations.

Put \[a_n=2^{-n},\qquad
 \delta_n=\frac{a_n}{2(n+1)\log2}.\] The set \(S'_n\) on page 42 consists of times \(t\le T_6\) for which the path stays within \(a_n\) of \(W_t\) for longer than \(\delta_n\).

Nevertheless bad tiles exist at every sufficiently fine level. Almost surely, Brownian maxima on all rational compact intervals are unique, interior, and have non-dyadic heights. After the first hit of \(1/2\), choose a rational interval before the path leaves \((0,1)\); it lies before \(T_6\). Its maximizer \(\tau\) has height \(h\in(0,1)\), not dyadic, and some \(\delta>0\) satisfies \[W_s<h\quad(0<|s-\tau|\le\delta).\] The tile \(E_n\) containing \((\tau,h)\) has a dyadic height band \((a_n^*,b_n^*]\) with \(b_n^*>h\). The construction on pages 39–41 makes each tile project onto its whole band, so it contains a point \((s_n,b_n^*)\). Necessarily \(|s_n-\tau|>\delta\). Hence \[\operatorname{diam}\pi_x(E_n)>\delta>
 \frac{2^{-n}}{n\log2}\] for all sufficiently large \(n\): these are bad tiles. They cannot meet the empty \(S'_n\). Likewise the left side of (6.5) counts squares meeting a nonempty bad tile, while its right side is zero. This is an actual counterexample to the covering step.

There is also a direct geometric error on page 43. Already the first upcrossing from zero to \(1/2\), after the height restriction, has time projection \(\{0<t\le T_{1/2}:W_t>0\}\). Immediate positive and negative oscillations give infinitely many components. It is not one interval or a union of two intervals; appending the final crossing piece does not remove the initial oscillations.

These facts do not disprove \(\dim_H A'\le1/2\) or \(\mu(A')=0\). The strict local maxima used above form a countable set, compatible with both estimates. They demonstrate that a new proof of those estimates is needed before the subsequent lemmas can use them. The range in Lemma 5.6 is \(2/3<\alpha\le2\), as confirmed on the source image; decreasing \(\alpha\) toward one is allowed. The difficulty here is the comparison of tiles with slow exit times, not that parameter range.
# Two further Brownian deductions need new arguments
## The compact-core selection

On page 46, compact subsets \(F_{n,j}\subset E_{n,j}\) are chosen only subject to \[\operatorname{diam}F_{n,j}\ge \operatorname{diam}E_{n,j}-128^{-n}.
 \tag{4}\] This does not ensure compatibility across generations, surviving branches, or the claimed almost-full vertical projection after taking infinite intersections.

A deterministic model shows the failure of this inference. Take \(E=(0,1]\) on a vertical line with its dyadic cells. In every level-\(n\) cell choose only the two points at distance \(\epsilon_n=2^{-(7n+2)}\) from its endpoints. Their diameter is \(2^{-n}-2\epsilon_n\ge2^{-n}-128^{-n}\), so (4) holds. Each such point has reduced dyadic denominator exactly \(2^{7n+2}\). The unions \(F_n\) for different \(n\) are therefore disjoint. Their liminf and all common tails are empty. This also defeats the intended tail version of \(K^N\), whose printed indexing on page 46 is inconsistent. It does not prove that no better Brownian compact-core construction exists.
## The averaging step uses unproved mass ratios

The proof on pages 48–49 copies the minimum-average selection used for uniform-fiber carpets, but Brownian child masses are not equal. The claimed monotonicity is not a formal consequence of minimum parent averages. Consider two parents in one height band: \[\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
 &P_{\rm lower}&P_{\rm upper}&Q_{\rm lower}&Q_{\rm upper}\\
\hline
 \mu&1&99&9900&1\\
 \rho&100&0&2&2
\end{array}\] Parent \(P\) has average one, whereas \(Q\) has average two. Copying the selected \(P\)-average to the band gives integral \(10001\), below the original \(19902\). Refining \(P\) and copying its lower and upper child averages gives instead \[100(1+9900)+0(99+1)=990100,\] which exceeds the original integral. Multiplying all masses by a common constant does not repair this algebra. Adding one to the density and every copied average preserves the selection and the failed monotonicity, while ensuring admissibility when the fiber measures are probabilities.

This is a finite mass-tree countermodel to the inference, not an assertion that these four exact masses occur in the specified Brownian construction. A Brownian-specific relation between child masses, or a different selection/disintegration argument, is required. The carpet proof has exactly such an equal-mass relation; the source does not establish it here.
## Conditional steps that do work

If Proposition 6.2 were independently proved, (6.1) and \(\mu(A')=0\) would immediately give \(l^a(A')=0\) outside one Lebesgue-null set of heights. This is stronger than the half-mass claim in Remark 6.5 and avoids inferring a local-time estimate from an unweighted count of bad tiles.

For non-dyadic heights outside \(\pi_y(A')\), the selected nested fiber sections are compact and nonempty; their excluded time endpoints have dyadic heights. Their intersection gives a point of \(A\). At a point of \(A\), all sufficiently fine cells are good and have diameter at most \[2^{-n}\sqrt{1+(n\log2)^{-2}}\longrightarrow0.\] This supplies the eventual, rather than all-level, shrinking used for injectivity of \(\pi_y\) in Lemma 6.6. The Borel injective projection then has a Borel inverse on its image, so the pullback Lebesgue measure is meaningful. A good descendant with height \(h\in(r/3,2r/3]\) lies inside the radius-\(r\) ball and has \(\lambda_E\)-mass \(h\); this gives the local bound in Lemma 6.8. These conditional checks leave the bad-set estimate, compatible compact cores and positive modulus unresolved.
# A replacement modulus argument removes doubling

Remark 3.3 points toward [bhw]. Its Theorem 4.1 and Remark 4.6 use upper regularity and a supremum density, without a doubling measure. The published global lower-radius hypotheses are not the pointwise hypotheses here. The following independent localization supplies the needed compact finite-measure version.

Assume \(X\) is compact, \(\mu(X)<\infty\), and \(\mu(B(x,r))\le C_0r^q\) uniformly for small \(r\). Suppose every \(E\) has conformal dimension at least one and, for each \(s>1\), a common \(c_s>0\) satisfies \(\lambda_E(B(x,r))\ge c_sr^s\) for \(x\in E\) at a possibly \(E,x\)-dependent small radius. If \(\operatorname{Mod}_p\{\lambda_E\}>0\) for \(1\le p<q\), then \(\dim_C X\ge q\).

Suppose otherwise and choose a quasisymmetry \(f\) and numbers \[\max(p,\dim_H f(X))<\alpha<q,\qquad
 0<t<1,\quad \dim_H f(X)<\alpha t,\qquad
 1<s<q/\alpha .\] Let \(E_N\) contain those points of \(E\) where the lower estimate holds for every \(r<1/N\). Since \(E=\bigcup_NE_N\) and \(\dim_H f(E)\ge1\), some \(E_N\) has dimension greater than \(t\). Stratify the family by pairs \((N,j)\) for which \(\mathcal H^t_{1/j}(f(E_N))\ge1\). It suffices to give each stratum zero \(p\)-modulus.

Fix such a stratum. Cover the union of its \(f(E_N)\) by image balls \(B_i'\), centered in that union, with radii \(\sigma_i\) and \(\sum_i\sigma_i^{\alpha t}<\varepsilon\). All radii may be arbitrarily small. If \(x_i\) is the preimage center and \(R_i=\sup\{d(x_i,x):f(x)\in B_i'\}\), take \(r_i=2R_i\) and \(B_i=B(x_i,r_i)\). A comparison with a point at distance at least \(R_i/2\) gives \[B_i'\subset f(B_i),\qquad
 f(10B_i)\subset B(f(x_i),\eta(40)\sigma_i).\] Isolated centers can instead use arbitrarily small singleton balls. Uniform continuity on the compact space makes \(2r_i<1/N\), \(r_i<1\), and \(2\eta(40)\sigma_i<1/j\). Define \[g=\sup_i\frac{\sigma_i^t}{r_i^s}\chi_{2B_i}.\] For a fixed \(E\), retain balls \(B_i\) meeting \(E_N\). A \(5r\) selection yields disjoint \(2B_j\) whose \(10B_j\) cover \(E_N\). At a good point in \(B_j\cap E_N\), \(B(x,r_j)\subset2B_j\), so \[\int g\,d\lambda_E
 \ge c_s\sum_j\sigma_j^t
 \ge c_s[2\eta(40)]^{-t}.\] Thus a fixed multiple of \(g\) is admissible. On the other hand, \[\int g^\alpha\,d\mu
 \le \sum_i\sigma_i^{\alpha t}r_i^{-\alpha s}\mu(2B_i)
 \le C_0 2^q\sum_i\sigma_i^{\alpha t}r_i^{q-\alpha s}
 \le C\varepsilon .\] Hölder on the finite measure space gives energy tending to zero also in exponent \(p\). Countable subadditivity over \((N,j)\) contradicts positive \(p\)-modulus.

The supporting checkpoint gives the additional finite-neighborhood localization for noncompact spaces. For the Brownian application, the compact upper mass bound is available. This repair therefore removes the doubling obstruction. It does not supply minimal vertical sets or positive modulus when the independent constructions of Sections 4–5 above remain unproved.
# The uniform-fiber carpet conclusions can be repaired

Theorem 4.3 and Corollary 1.4 have more structure than the general hierarchy theorem. The following direct checks provide a replacement for the false flatness step, together with several bounded local corrections.

For \(2\le\ell<m\) and \(k\) retained columns in each row, let \(q=1+\log_m k\). Give every child symbolic mass \(1/(k\ell)\). The vertical marginal is Lebesgue measure; at a non-\(\ell\)-adic height the horizontal conditional measure gives mass \(k^{-n}\) to each allowed \(n\)-prefix. Integrating its Frostman bound gives \(\mu(B(x,r))\le Cr^q\). For the reverse bound, fix an address of \(x\), its first \(n\) row digits, and its first \(p=\lfloor n\log\ell/\log m\rfloor\) horizontal choices. The resulting approximate cell has mass \(\ell^{-n}k^{-p}\) and diameter at most \(\sqrt{m^2+1}\ell^{-n}\). Choosing this scale below \(r\) gives \(\mu(B(x,r))\ge cr^q\). This repairs the axis alignment and boundary explanation on page 29, including \(k=1\), when mass may lie on a vertical grid boundary.

Each vertical set \(E\) has one child in every row. Its level-\(n\) cylinders have diameter between \(\ell^{-n}\) and \(\sqrt2\ell^{-n}\), and their adjacent relative gaps tend uniformly to zero. The cylinder-weight construction in Lemma 4.5 gives, for \(0<\alpha<1\), a probability \(\nu\) with \[\nu(f(E_{n,j}))\le C_\alpha
 \left(\frac{\operatorname{diam}f(E_{n,j})}{\operatorname{diam}f(E)}\right)^\alpha .
 \tag{5}\] The image scale factor must be retained. Symbolic probabilities give a rigorous measure: cylinder diameters shrink, individual codes have zero mass, and at most two codes meet at a boundary point.

Problem 4 (Major: the flatness step leading to Lemma 4.6, page 29).  The asserted flatness constant \(A\le2\) fails within the stated carpet class. Take \(\ell=2,m=3,k=2\), retaining the left and right columns in every row, and choose the left column at every stage. Then \(E=\{0\}\times[0,1]\) is an allowed vertical set with its dyadic hierarchy. In the ball whose height interval is \((1/3,1/2)\), infinitely many cylinders \[I_j=\left[\frac13+\frac1{6\cdot4^j},
           \frac13+\frac1{6\cdot4^{j-1}}\right],
 \quad j\ge2,\] lie inside the ball while their parents do not. Thus no finite flatness constant works. The page-29 deduction of (4.12) invokes this false premise and Theorem 3.4; it is then used in Lemma 4.6, Theorem 4.3 (the carpet conclusion of Theorem 1.2), and Corollary 1.4. This is a failure of that core derivation, not a numerical adjustment to the constant. A separate proof is required.

A fixed-generation cover supplies that replacement proof: for \(S=f^{-1}(B(f(x),r))\) put \(R=\sup_{y\in S}d(x,y)\), and choose \(R/\ell<\ell^{-n}\le R\). At most \(2\ell+2\) level-\(n\) cylinders meet \(S\). Comparison with a point of \(S\) at distance at least \(R/2\) shows that each selected image cylinder has diameter at most \(2\eta(2+2\sqrt2)r\). Summing (5) proves the required image ball bound. Singleton and large-radius cases follow from atomlessness and the root cylinder. Thus \(\dim_C E=1\), without Theorem 3.4.

There is also an exact positive-modulus argument. At every parent and row choose one of the \(k\) retained children uniformly and independently. This produces a random vertical set. For almost every height, its horizontal address has exactly the conditional law of \(\mu\), and hence \[\mathbb E_E\lambda_E=\mu,\qquad
 \int\rho\,d\mu=\mathbb E_E\int\rho\,d\lambda_E\ge1\] for every admissible nonnegative Borel density. The constant density one is admissible, so the modulus is exactly one; the printed strict inequality \(>1\) is false. The same calculation identifies why the minimum-average argument works here: all \(k\ell\) child masses are equal. Applying the repaired compact modulus criterion proves carpet minimality for \(k\ge2\). For \(k=1\), \(K=E\) and the preceding vertical-set proof handles the endpoint directly.

Finally, the three graph types on pages 31–33 have endpoint pairs \((0,0),(0,1),(1,0)\). The displayed blocks match adjacent column endpoints and define a contraction with vertical factor \(1/\ell\) on triples of continuous functions. Their fixed points are continuous graphs and retain \(k\) cells per row. Exact rational checks of both printed examples supplement this general argument.

The restriction \(1\le r<s\) in \(k=2^r,\ \ell=2^s\) yields only \(1+r/(r+s)<3/2\), contrary to the claimed density in \([1,2]\). Allow arbitrary positive \(r,s\); the construction still has \(m=k\ell>\ell\) and yields a dense subset of \((1,2)\). Use a constant function for dimension one. For dimension two, take \(r_i=i,s_i=1\). The final scaled union has domain \([0,1)\), so add \((1,0)\). Its piece heights are at most \(2^{-i}\), proving continuity at that endpoint. Hausdorff dimension is the supremum of the piece dimensions, while every quasisymmetry restricts to each minimal piece. This proves the corrected existence conclusion for every dimension in \([1,2]\), without assuming countable stability of conformal dimension. The false flatness step is classified separately as Major because it breaks the original core derivation. The scale, measure-boundary, strict-modulus, parameter-range and endpoint corrections are Minor with the explicit local repairs above. The replacement proof supports the specialized conclusions; it does not make the original flatness assertion true or complete the Brownian proof.
# Remaining evidentiary limits

The unresolved Brownian work is specific: replace the false bad-tile covering estimate; construct compatible compact cores with the claimed projection and geometric bounds; and prove positive modulus with the actual nonuniform local-time masses. A replacement for the doubling-dependent modulus step alone does not complete these tasks. No error is inferred from the conjectures in Section 7, which are presented as conjectures.

Only the cited portions of the external occupation, germ-law and modulus references were checked. Attempts to retrieve the Mörters–Peres book did not produce its full text; its quoted Theorems 6.19 and 6.43 are not represented as independently verified. No author code was supplied or executed, and that absence is not a mathematical defect. Supporting analytic proofs, exact finite checks, and actual source/report page records are bound to the reviewed files. Scientific decision is pending, human reviews are empty, and author adoption of any repair is unknown.

Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of Rationality of proper holomorphic maps between bounded symmetric domains of the first kind
# Exact source, hypotheses and scope

The reviewed source is Sung-Yeon Kim, Rationality of proper holomorphic maps between bounded symmetric domains of the first kind, M25-0166, arXiv:2305.01875v1, 3 May 2023, 33 pages [source]. The assignment’s title uses type one and associates the paper with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0060 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0060). This review does not identify the supplied author manuscript with the journal-final text or any later correction. Page references are one-based physical PDF pages; printed numbers agree on all inspected pages.

Write \[D_{p,q}=\{Z\in M_{p,q}(\mathbb C):I_q-Z^*Z>0\},\qquad p\ge q.\] The rank-\(r\) boundary orbit \(S_r\) has \(r\) strictly negative directions and \(q-r\) null directions in its Grassmannian realization. Thus \(S_0\) is the Shilov boundary; for \(p=q\) it is \(U(q)\). Theorem 1.2 assumes \(q,q'\ge2\), properness, and only a local \(C^2\) extension near a Shilov point with local Shilov-boundary preservation. It asserts a totally geodesic product factorization with a proper rational factor and a nonproper factor, and rationality of the whole map for \(p>q\). Corollary 1.3 assumes global smooth boundary regularity, \(q\ge3\), and \(q'\le2q-1\).

All scientific sections were read collectively by the lead and three native helpers with disjoint section assignments. The review checks the incidence definitions and dimensions, finite-jet and rational moduli arguments, adapted frames, CR and contact types, transversality, osculation, parallelism, product properness, and the final theorem dependencies. The lead independently verified the principal counterexample and the key source formulas. Exact local hashes and actual source-page views are recorded separately. Programmatic extraction is not counted as scientific reading.
# A counterexample to the core osculation assertion

Problem 1 (Major: page 22 and its use on page 28).  The asserted containment of the nullspace image in its affine second-order osculating space is false, even for a polynomial proper map preserving the entire Shilov boundary.

Take \[f:D_{2,2}\longrightarrow D_{8,8},\qquad f(Z)=Z^{\otimes3}.
 \tag{1}\] The operator-norm identity \(\|f(Z)\|=\|Z\|^3\) proves that it maps the source into the target and is proper: any sequence approaching the source boundary has image norm tending to one. The map is polynomial, extends smoothly across the closure, and sends unitary matrices to unitary matrices. It therefore satisfies every relevant hypothesis of Theorem 1.2 and Proposition 5.1. The generic characteristic-direction rank used later is also seven: for invertible \(Z\), factor \(df_Z(A)\) by \(Z^{\otimes3}\) and put \(B=Z^{-1}A\). For rank-one \(A\) with \(\operatorname{tr}B\ne0\), \(B\) is similar to \(\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{tr}B,0)\). The sum of its actions in three tensor slots has a one-dimensional kernel.

Put \(P=I_2\), \(\lambda=-1/10\), and, for real \(|t|<1/2\), set \[v(t)=(1,t)^t,\quad w(t)=(-t,1)^t,\quad H(t)=v(t)v(t)^*,
 \qquad Z(t)=I_2+\lambda H(t).\] Here \(Z(t)\) has eigenvalues \(a(t)=1+\lambda(1+t^2)\) and \(1\), with \(0<a(t)<1\). It lies on \(S_1(D_{2,2})\) in the family of boundary components through \(P\). Define the two curves appearing in the page-22 argument by \[\begin{split}
 x(t)&=f(Z(t)),\\
 y(t)&=I_8+\lambda\,df_{I_2}(H(t))\\
 &=I_8+\lambda\bigl(H(t)\otimes I_2\otimes I_2+
 I_2\otimes H(t)\otimes I_2+I_2\otimes I_2\otimes H(t)\bigr).
 \end{split} \tag{2}\] The eigenvalues of \(x(t)\) are \(a(t)^k\), and those of \(y(t)\) are \(1+\lambda k(1+t^2)\), for \(k=0,1,2,3\), with multiplicities \(\binom3k\). Every eigenvalue except the \(k=0\) eigenvalue lies strictly between zero and one. Consequently both curves lie in \(S_7(D_{8,8})\) and have the same null line. In the identification of \(V_{I_8}\) with \(\mathbb C^8\), that line is \[Z_0(x(t))=Z_0(y(t))
 =\mathbb C\,w(t)^{\otimes3},\qquad
 w(t)^{\otimes3}
 =(-t^3,t^2,t^2,-t,t^2,-t,-t,1)^t.
 \tag{3}\] Thus this is also a test of the claimed equality of the two nullspace curves, not an example violating an earlier prerequisite.

The last coordinate in (3) is one. In the corresponding big Schubert cell of \(\operatorname{Gr}(1,V_{I_8})=\mathbb P^7\), the nullspace curve is \[\kappa(t)=(-t^3,t^2,t^2,-t,t^2,-t,-t).\] Both \(\kappa'(0)\) and \(\kappa''(0)\) have first coordinate zero, whereas \(\kappa(t)\) has first coordinate \(-t^3\). Hence \[\kappa(t)\notin
 \kappa(0)+\operatorname{span}\{\kappa'(0),\kappa''(0)\}\quad(t\ne0).
 \tag{4}\] The full complex null-base family is the cubic Veronese curve \([\omega]\mapsto[\omega^{\otimes3}]\) on \(\mathbb P^1\). Its tangent plus second fundamental form in this affine chart has dimension two. It does not contain the curve. This directly refutes the last displayed containment on page 22, including its stated flat-connection interpretation.
## The earlier differential inference is also invalid

A quadratic curve on a nonlinear Schubert variety need not have ambient acceleration tangent to that variety. Already for the identity map of \(D_{2,2}\), the same \(y(t)=I_2+\lambda H(t)\) lies on \[W_P=\{Y:\operatorname{rank}(Y-I_2)\le1\}.\] At \(y(0)=I_2+\lambda\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\), its tangent space requires the \((2,2)\) entry of an increment to vanish. But \(y''(0)=2\lambda\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\) is not tangent. Thus the page-22 inclusion \(\operatorname{span}\{y'(0),y''(0)\}\subset T_{y(0)}W_P\) is itself false. Moreover a nonlinear projection of a quadratic curve need not be quadratic: the second derivative of a composition includes the Hessian of the projection. Equation (3) demonstrates the actual failure, rather than merely pointing out a missing chain-rule term.

The preceding page-21 justification of tangent parallelism along an entire target boundary component also needs correction. For the proper linear map \(f(Z)=\operatorname{diag}(Z,Z)\) from \(D_{2,2}\) to \(D_{4,4}\), its null-base family through \(I\) is \(A\mapsto A\oplus A\). At \(A=\mathbb Ce_1\), order the target as \((A\oplus A)\oplus(A^\perp\oplus A^\perp)\) and write a leaf point as \(Y_B=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,B)\). Differentiating \(A_\chi=\mathbb C(e_1+\chi e_2)\) shows that the complex span of the saturated-family tangent has off-diagonal blocks \(a(I_2-B)\) and \(b(I_2-B)\), with \(a,b\in\mathbb C\), and an arbitrary lower-right block. For \(B=0\) and \(B=\operatorname{diag}(0,1/2)\) these off-diagonal lines differ although the leaf is the same. Ambient block parallelism therefore does not imply this smaller tangent space is parallel. For the particular linear example the chosen first-order and true image points can coincide; the example refutes the general justification, while (3)–(4) separately refute the final containment.
## The downstream dimension equality fails for the same map

Replacing second order by a universal fixed order cannot suffice: \(Z\mapsto Z^{\otimes d}\) gives the degree-\(d\) Veronese null curve for every \(d\). A different argument using stabilized higher osculating spans might be possible; none is supplied or certified here.
## Counterevidence against overstating the conclusion

The map (1) is rational and is consistent with the main theorem. Indeed, the symmetric tensor subspace and its orthogonal complement are reducing subspaces for every \(Z^{\otimes3}\), since the operators and their adjoints commute with tensor permutations. A fixed unitary basis therefore gives a block decomposition \[f(Z)=F_1(Z)\oplus F_2(Z),\qquad
 F_1=\operatorname{Sym}^3 Z\in D_{4,4},\quad F_2\in D_{4,4}.\] A maximizing singular vector \(u\) gives the symmetric tensor \(u^{\otimes3}\), so \(\|F_1(Z)\|=\|Z\|^3\); \(F_1\) is proper and polynomial. Along \(Z_\epsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1-\epsilon,0)\), \(F_2(Z_\epsilon)=0\), so \(F_2\) is nonproper. The standard block product is totally geodesic. Thus the counterexample refutes the central derivation, not Theorem 1.2 or Corollary 1.3.
# Two arguments that can be repaired completely
## Rationality from the singleton condition: Lemma 3.1
Assume the cited rationality of \(g=f_1^\sharp\). The lemma’s finite singleton condition then gives a direct proof of rationality without the problematic chain-avoidance step on pages 12–13.

For target interval subgrassmannians \([A_j,B_j]_{q'}\) containing a common \(q'\)-plane, put \(A=\sum A_j\) and \(B=\bigcap B_j\). Their intersection is \([A,B]_{q'}\). In exterior coordinates their minimal linear spans are described by \[a\wedge\omega=0\ (a\in A_j),\qquad
 \iota_\phi\omega=0\ (\phi\in\operatorname{Ann}B_j).\] Combining these equations replaces \(A_j\) by \(A\) and \(\operatorname{Ann}B_j\) by \(\operatorname{Ann}B\). If the intersection is a singleton, either \(\dim A=q'\) or \(\dim B=q'\); the intersection of the exterior linear spans is exactly its one-dimensional Plücker line. There is no arbitrary-linear-section counterexample to this particular inference.

Choose a source chart \(V_x=\operatorname{graph}Z\) centered at \(x_0\), and set \(T_Z=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&0\\Z&I\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). For the finitely many prescribed flags \(\sigma_j=(C_j,D_j)\) through \(x_0\), the flags \(\sigma_j(x)=(T_ZC_j,T_ZD_j)\) are algebraic sections through those exact flags. On a small neighborhood inside the source, \(f(x)\in X'_{g(\sigma_j(x))}\); all \(g(\sigma_j(x))\) are defined after shrinking because the original flags lie in its domain. Their Plücker spans give a rational linear system \(M(x)u=0\). At \(x_0\) it has rank \(N'\) in \(N'+1\) homogeneous unknowns. Signed maximal minors give a rational projective point equal to \(f(x)\) on a nonempty open set. The Plücker equations then hold identically, so this is a rational map from \(X\) to \(X'\). Connectedness gives agreement with \(f\) on its original domain.

The printed generic-chain argument does not by itself show that all flags can avoid the bad set while retaining a prescribed endpoint. The construction above bypasses that issue and avoids taking jets of \(f\) outside its known domain. Lemma 2.3’s finite-jet argument is valid on the connected parameter locus actually needed: analyticity turns vanishing of all jets into an identity, and finite-dimensional linear algebra selects finitely many rows. A disconnected parameter manifold needs this qualification.

The moduli-map premise is corroborated by Lemmas 6.1–6.2 of the later primary version [KMS], whose Section 6 assumes properness but no small rank gap. The exact cited 2022 preprint and the full Mok–Tsai Proposition 2.6 proof were not retrieved. This remains an identified external dependency, not a fully reproduced external proof.
## Transversality: Proposition 5.1

The Taylor expansion on pages 18–19 omits a factor \(1/2\). With \(h=A_0+rA_1+r^2A_2+o(r^2)\), the displayed differential identity yields \[A_2\cdot\overline{A_0}=\tfrac12\|A_1\|^2,\qquad
 \|h\|^2=1+2\|A_1\|^2r^2+o(r^2),\] rather than coefficients one and three. Its sign contradiction survives. The following proof also removes the need to select a point simultaneously for all rotated target bases.

On a Shilov disc let \(F=f\circ\varphi\). For each unit \(u\in\mathbb C^{q'}\), \(F(\zeta)u\) lies in the unit ball inside the disc and has norm one on the available boundary arc. The nonnegative superharmonic function \(1-\|F(\zeta)u\|^2\) is strictly positive inside. The Hopf lemma gives a strictly positive outward derivative of \(\|F(\zeta)u\|^2\) at every point of that arc. After normalizing \(F(P)=(I_{q'},0)^t\), the radial derivative of its upper block is Hermitian by differentiation along the boundary. Its quadratic form is positive on every nonzero \(u\), so it is positive definite and has rank \(q'\). This proves the asserted full-rank direction and, by nonvanishing of the corresponding minor, full rank for general directions. Only the local boundary arc is needed. This repair does not imply the false osculation statement.
# Bounded geometric and frame corrections
These issues are grouped as Minor; their particular intended conclusions have local repairs, unlike the osculation step.

For arbitrary \(M=[V_M,W_M]_q\), the parameter space in Lemma 2.1 has second factor \(\operatorname{Gr}(p+r-\dim W_M,H/W_M)\), not an undefined \(r-s\). In Lemma 2.2, \(\dim(A^*/V_P)=r\), so the second factor is \(\operatorname{Gr}(r,H/V_P)\), not \(\operatorname{Gr}(q-r,H/V_P)\). For example \(q=3,r=1\) gives a line, not a two-plane. The Hermitian form identifies \(A\mapsto A^*/V_P\) anti-holomorphically between the two factors in tube type; its graph is maximally totally real. The lemma’s intended conclusion is preserved. Empty flag intersections must be excluded when defining the nonempty boundary-component orbits.

The fixed-coordinate complementary-vector assertion on page 7 is false. Set \(b=1/2\), \(Z_t=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&b\\0&t\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), and use the fixed flag \[A=\mathbb Ce_1,\qquad B=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2+b e_3,e_4).\] The characteristic subgrassmannian has constant tangent \(\mathbb CE_{22}\) in the graph chart, but its complementary characteristic vector for the compact canonical metric is, up to scale, \[v_t=\begin{pmatrix}1+b^2&0\\bt&0\end{pmatrix}.\] This follows by moving \(e_1\) toward \(B^\perp=\mathbb C(e_3-b e_2)\) and restoring the identity upper graph block. Its directions at \(t=0,1/2\) differ. The weaker constancy of the tangent space of a fixed interval subgrassmannian is correct, because its graph-chart incidence conditions are affine linear.

Definition 4.1(i), page 14, lacks a quadratic correction ensuring that the transformed \(Y\)-vectors remain null. In the scalar block take \(W_0=V_0=\widetilde W=1\), \(W_u^\beta=t\) and \(V_\alpha^v=-t\) with real \(t\ne0\). All printed constraints hold, but \(Y'=Y-t\widetilde Z\) has norm \(-t^2\) and \(\langle Y',\widetilde Z+tZ\rangle=2t\). Thus adding a quadratic term alone does not fix the printed signs. For this real scalar block the complete Gram-preserving replacement is \[Z'=Z,\qquad \widetilde Z'=\widetilde Z+tZ,\qquad
 Y'=Y+t\widetilde Z+\tfrac12t^2Z .\] Indeed \(\langle Z',Y'\rangle=1\), \(\|\widetilde Z'\|^2=-1\), \(\|Y'\|^2=0\), and \(\langle\widetilde Z',Y'\rangle=0\); all other pairings remain as prescribed. The general change must likewise preserve the full Gram matrix. In Lemma 4.2, page 15, \(\|Z_\alpha+c_\alpha Y_\alpha\|^2=2\Re c_\alpha\); the asserted null vector requires purely imaginary \(c_\alpha\), not arbitrary real \(c_\alpha\), in the printed normalization. The curvature-nullspace conclusion has the direct complementary-block proof. Lemmas 4.3–4.4 agree with linearized Schubert rank conditions.

The strictly increasing pivot indices on page 24 must allow empty blocks. For the identity of \(D_{q,q}\) with \(q\ge3\), \(r=J_1=1\) and \(q'-r=q-1\); there cannot be \(q-1\) strictly positive increments ending at one. Nondecreasing indices give the usual row-kernel elimination. The type separation used in (5.12) is valid: the relevant \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\) components are independent.

With only \(C^2\) regularity, the second-jet expansion on page 25 has an \(o(t^2)\) remainder, not necessarily \(O(t^3)\). That weaker remainder suffices for the second-derivative identities. If the coefficients \(C_\alpha^u\) vary, their differentiated terms lie in the already known first-order span; exact constancy needs a gauge choice but is unnecessary modulo that span.

On page 26, \(V=\widetilde Z-X\) and \(\widehat V=\widetilde Z+X\) imply \(X=(\widehat V-V)/2\), with the opposite sign to that printed. Consequently the coefficient of \(\widehat V_W\) in \(dV_u\) is \[\tfrac12(\widetilde\Omega_u^W-\Omega_u^W+
             \Delta_u^W-\overline{\Delta_u^W}),\] and the vanishing relation corresponding to (5.18) must use this combination. After substitution, the subsequent expression \(dV_u=\sum_W(\widetilde\Omega_u^W-\overline{\Delta_u^W})V_W
\pmod Z\) survives. These sign repairs do not establish (5).
# Remaining obligations and final theorem assembly

The factor-properness argument in Corollary 5.5, pages 29–30, needs additional evidence even if the preceding geometric construction is replaced. From properness of \((f_1,f_2)\), a failure of properness of \(f_1\) gives a boundary-approaching sequence on which \(f_2\) approaches its boundary. It does not alone show that \(f_2\) is proper on every boundary-approaching sequence. The printed contradiction step needs a global propagation argument, especially under only a local \(C^2\) extension. The proof then invokes Corollary 5.5 itself for \(f_2\), without an explicit induction or a separately established weaker decomposition statement.

There is a partial noncircular repair. If a fixed global product has already been obtained and \(M_P=\{A_P\}\times M\) is defined by the span of the actual nullspaces in (5.19), then block diagonality gives \(Z_0(f(y))=Z_0(f_1(y))\oplus Z_0(f_2(y))\). Retaining the entire second factor in \(M_P\) forces the second nullspace component to vanish for all nearby \(y\) in the family. A proper \(f_2\), continuous at these boundary points, would have a nonzero nullspace there, a contradiction. This can exclude properness of \(f_2\) without citing the corollary recursively. It does not prove the missing implication that \(f_1\) is proper. No counterexample to that intended conclusion is claimed.

Local boundary hypotheses are not automatically fatal to the global factorization. In tube coordinates the Shilov edge is the space of Hermitian matrices. A holomorphic defining function that vanishes on a local edge patch also vanishes inside: along \(W=A+\zeta I\), use one-variable zero-boundary reflection/uniqueness, then uniqueness on the translated maximal real slice. Holomorphic identity extends a resulting fixed product constraint over the connected source. Nearby unitary points can also be joined by rank-one phase steps using a spectral decomposition, all within a small germ. These observations can localize the chain argument once correct parallelism and product constraints exist; they do not prove those missing premises.

For the non-tube argument in Lemma 6.1, the rank-one boundary component is a ball of dimension \(p-q+1\ge2\). A smooth CR map from its sphere to the totally real Shilov boundary of a tube factor is constant: its differential kills complex tangent directions, their brackets span the remaining tangent direction, and local holomorphic uniqueness applies. This part of the mechanism is valid. The product to which it is applied still depends on the unproved geometric reduction.

In Corollary 1.3, \(m\ge1\) and \(r>m\) imply \(q'-r\le2q-3<2(q-1)\), as required by the displayed numerical comparison. The exact rigidity application needs the stated embedding and transversality hypotheses matched to its boundary stratum. The accessible primary preprint [KimCR] distinguishes a local transversal CR embedding theorem from a global corollary with an additional numerical condition. The published 2021 version cited in the source was not retrieved, so no published numbering mismatch or false corollary is asserted.

Finally, an established standard isometric factor would imply Kobayashi isometry of the graph map: projection to that factor gives a holomorphic left inverse, and the two distance-contraction inequalities give equality. The retraction and isometry results in [Mok] support this step. They do not supply the earlier factorization.
# Assessment and required revision

The supported assessment is Major. The decisive evidence is the exact counterexample (1)–(5) to a central derivation, not the number of typographical corrections. A revision needs a replacement for the second-order containment and the page-28 span argument, followed by a noncircular proof of the proper rational factor. The bounded corrections and the two independent repairs above should be incorporated and the local-to-global uses made explicit.

No conclusion that the main theorem is false is supported. No author code was supplied or executed, and its absence is not a mathematical defect. The exact reviewed version, the limited external-reference checks, and the collective scientific coverage are explicit. Native helpers were not human reviewers, their serving backends were not independently verified, author adoption is unknown, and scientific adjudication remains pending.

Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of A topological gap theorem for the pi-two systole of positive scalar curvature three-manifolds
# Exact source and assessment

The source is Kai Xu, A topological gap theorem for the \(\pi_2\)-systole of positive scalar curvature 3-manifolds, M25-0167, arXiv:2307.01922v3, 27 October 2024, 13 pages [source]. The assignment associates it with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0061 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0061). The supplied author version is the exact object reviewed; identity with the journal-final article or a later revision is not asserted. All page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages and agree with the printed numbering.

The lead read the complete supplied text and actually inspected all 13 source pages. Three native helpers independently covered weak-flow preliminaries, the main topology and decomposition, and the doubling and gluing construction. This includes every stated theorem, claim, definition and proof, with explicit checks of covering invariance, orientability, initial-data conditions, weak time regularity, the terminal time, long-neck constants and the smoothing parameters. The external works were checked only in the specific scopes stated in Section 6, not represented as full independent reviews.

The supported assessment is Minor: the principal new theorems remain supported after bounded clarifications. The confirmed counterexample concerns the introductory rigidity formulation, not the topological gap. The paper itself leaves sharpness, equality and further gaps open; this review does not turn those open questions into defects.
# The main topological and flow argument

Let \(A_0=\operatorname{sys}_{\pi_2}(M,g)\) and \(\lambda=\min_M R_g\). If \(\lambda\le0\), the desired upper bound is immediate; only \(\lambda>0\) requires the positive-scalar-curvature classification. The oriented closed three-manifold is then a connected sum of spherical space forms and \(S^2\times S^1\). The finite fundamental-group case has \(\pi_2=0\). The infinite virtually cyclic cases are \(S^2\times S^1\) and \(\mathbb{RP}^3\#\mathbb{RP}^3\), both excluded by the topological covering hypothesis. The remaining free products have exponential growth. This is the growth input to the proper weak-flow existence theorem, not a geometric assumption on an arbitrary universal cover. More explicitly, the normal-cover consequence in [proper] gives isoperimetric lower bounds \(cv^{2/3}\) for small volume and \(cv^{1/2}\) for large volume. These make the reciprocal profile integrable at zero and the profile divergent at infinity, exactly the existence theorem’s hypotheses. Infinite deck translates of a small ball also verify the infinite-volume assumption.
## Covering and the initial sphere

Every sphere map lifts through a covering, and the induced map on based \(\pi_2\) is an isomorphism. Local isometries preserve the area of each lift, so systoles agree even though the corresponding sets of free homotopy classes need not be in bijection.

The instruction to remove all \(\mathbb{RP}^3\) factors by one double cover can be made explicit. Send the generator of every \(\mathbb Z/2\) free-product factor to the nonzero element of \(\mathbb Z/2\), and send all other factors and free generators to zero. The kernel has index two and intersects every conjugate of those \(\mathbb Z/2\) factors trivially. Kurosh decomposition and prime uniqueness give a cover with no \(\mathbb{RP}^3\) prime factor. An embedded projective plane in an oriented three-manifold has a regular neighborhood equal to a punctured \(\mathbb{RP}^3\); it would give such a factor. The Meeks–Yau minimizer can therefore be taken to be an embedded sphere, rather than a twofold projective plane. Its lift \(\widetilde\Sigma\) separates the simply connected universal cover.

Both sides of that sphere are noncompact. Otherwise one side \(W\) is compact and simply connected with boundary \(S^2\). Relative duality and the cohomology exact sequence give \(H_2(W;\mathbb Z)=H^1(W,\partial W;\mathbb Z)=0\); Hurewicz then makes its boundary null-homotopic in the universal cover, a contradiction.
## Excision and outward minimization

Start the proper weak flow with a one-sided collar in the unused side of \(\widetilde\Sigma\), restrict it to the other side, and cap off the initial sphere by a disk \(D\). The metric extends smoothly over the cap and the resulting manifold is complete. The variational definition is local outside the initial set, so the restriction, extended negatively in \(D\), is a proper solution with \(E_0=D\). No scalar-curvature lower bound is needed inside this arbitrary cap.

A bounded least-area envelope of the original collar gives an envelope of the capped disk. This follows by replacing its part on the retained side with any competing set and comparing perimeters; the collar fixes the trace at the separating sphere. If the envelope differs from \(D\), its boundary is stable minimal and represents \([\widetilde\Sigma]\) in the universal cover. Its components are two-sided and orientable. Stability with constant test function and \(\lambda>0\) gives \[0<\frac{\lambda}{2}|\Gamma|
 \le \int_\Gamma K=2\pi\chi(\Gamma),\] so each is spherical. Nonzero total homology forces at least one component to be nonzero in \(\pi_2\), with area at least \(A_0\). The original disk is therefore outward minimizing. This justifies the exact area law \[|\Sigma_t|=e^t A_0.
 \tag{1}\]
## The homological control of every spherical component

The flow’s connected sublevel sets and absence of compact exterior components give \[H_3(N\setminus E_0,\Sigma_t;\mathbb Z)=0.\] To see the two contributions separately, relative duality gives \(H^0(\overline E_t\setminus E_0,\Sigma_0;\mathbb Z)=0\), since every component meets the initial boundary, and \(H_c^0(N\setminus E_t;\mathbb Z)=0\), since no exterior component is compact. Excision and the exact sequence then make \(H_2(\Sigma_t;\mathbb Z)\to H_2(N\setminus E_0;\mathbb Z)\) injective. Noncompactness of the unused side similarly makes \[H_2(\widetilde M_2;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H_2(\widetilde M;\mathbb Z)\] injective. A spherical component is therefore nontrivial in \(\pi_2(\widetilde M)\), by Hurewicz. Although the weak flow gives \(C^{1,\alpha}\) surfaces, smooth isotopic approximation with convergent areas transfers the smooth immersion definition of systole to these spheres.

Each sphere consequently has area at least \(A_0\). Equation (1) shows there is at most one when \(t<\log2\). Every other orientable component has nonpositive Euler characteristic, hence \[\chi(\Sigma_t)\le2\qquad(0<t<\log2).
 \tag{2}\] This direct count also covers the case in which the first splitting time \(T\) defined on page 8 is infinite. The proof need not assume that its defining set is nonempty or that the infimum is attained.
# The weak time calculation and the constant

Put \(\mathcal H(t)=\int_{\Sigma_t}H^2\). Dropping nonnegative dissipation terms in the Geroch inequality gives \[\mathcal H(t_2)\le\mathcal H(t_1)+
 \int_{t_1}^{t_2}
 \left(4\pi\chi(\Sigma_s)-\lambda A_0e^s
                         -\tfrac12\mathcal H(s)\right)\,ds.
 \tag{3}\] The applicable weak-flow result [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 5.7]{HI}] allows the initial minimal surface and does not require a connected evolving surface, asymptotic flatness, or nonnegative scalar curvature inside the cap.

The paper correctly avoids differentiating \(\mathcal H\). For fixed \(t\), define the absolutely continuous function \(F(s)=\int_s^t\mathcal H(r)\,dr\). Rearranging (3) with \(t_1=s,t_2=t\) yields, almost everywhere, \[\frac{d}{ds}(e^{s/2}F(s))
 \le 4\pi e^{s/2}\int_s^t\chi(\Sigma_r)\,dr
 -\lambda A_0e^{s/2}(e^t-e^s)-e^{s/2}\mathcal H(t).\] Fubini and integration give the coefficient \((4/3)e^{3t/2}-2e^t+2/3\) in (2.5). Substitution into (3) proves \[\mathcal H(t)\le e^{-t/2}\mathcal H(0)
 +4\pi e^{-t/2}\int_0^t e^{s/2}\chi(\Sigma_s)\,ds
 -\frac23\lambda A_0(e^t-e^{-t/2}).\] Thus the factor \(2/3\), all signs and the exponential weights in Corollary 2.5 are correct.

The initial sphere is minimal, so \(\mathcal H(0)=0\). Using (2) and \(\mathcal H(t)\ge0\), for \(0<t\le\log2\) one obtains \[0\le16\pi(1-e^{-t/2})
       -\frac23\lambda A_0(e^t-e^{-t/2}).\] The single endpoint value of the Euler characteristic does not affect the integral. With \(x=e^{t/2}\) this simplifies to \[\lambda A_0\le\frac{24\pi}{x^2+x+1}.\] The right side decreases with \(t\); at \(t=\log2\) it is \[\frac{24\pi}{3+\sqrt2}
 =\frac{24\pi(3-\sqrt2)}7
 =24\pi\frac{2-\sqrt2}{4-\sqrt2},
 \tag{4}\] exactly the claimed approximately \(5.44\pi\). As \(t\downarrow0\), the same expression tends to \(8\pi\). This is a check of the stated bound and its optimization within the available time interval, not a proof of sharpness.
# The local theorem and its bounded bookkeeping repairs

For each stable minimal boundary sphere with metric \(h\), let \(\phi>0\) be the first stability eigenfunction. The Jacobi operator can be written \[-\Delta_h+K_h-\tfrac12(R+|A|^2).\] Its nonnegative lowest eigenvalue implies \(\Delta_h\phi\le(K_h-\lambda/2)\phi\). The translation-invariant neck metric \(g_i=h_i+\phi_i^2dt^2\) therefore satisfies \[R_{g_i}=2K_{h_i}-2\phi_i^{-1}\Delta_{h_i}\phi_i\ge\lambda.\] Its slices are totally geodesic. Gluing two copies of the punctured sphere by the \(k\) necks gives \(N=\#^{\,k-1}(S^2\times S^1)\), with \(k-1\ge2\). A neck slice is nonseparating because the other necks still connect the two copies; it is nontrivial in \(\pi_2(N)\). The least-area such slice gives \(\operatorname{sys}_{\pi_2}(N)\le A_0\). The free fundamental group has no projective-plane obstruction, so a systolic minimizer is an embedded sphere.
## Uniform neck exclusion

A minimal sphere entering a neck is either a horizontal slice or crosses every height. Otherwise its height range has an interior extremum and the maximum principle against the minimal slices forces coincidence. Equivalently the height satisfies the appropriate weighted harmonic equation on the surface. The local monotonicity estimate supplies a positive area \(c_0\) in a fixed-width slab, independently of neck length.

The displayed index range on page 10 includes possible end slabs outside the permitted interior range. A precise replacement is: choose an integer \[m>A_0/c_0+2,\qquad T=4m,\] and use the \(2m-1\) centers \(t=4j\), \(|j|\le m-1\). The slabs \((t-2,t+2)\) lie inside the neck, are disjoint up to endpoints, and each contributes at least \(c_0\). A crossing minimizer would have area \((2m-1)c_0>A_0\), contradicting the comparison slice. Alternatively one can first reduce \(c_0\) and enlarge the printed \(T\); its precise value is not part of the theorem. The reference to Claim 1 in this count should be to Claim 3.

A minimizer avoiding all necks lies in one punctured \(S^3\) piece. If its class were zero there, it would bound a ball and be trivial in the double. Its nonzero absolute homology class has an area-minimizing integral representative in that piece. The minimal boundary is a barrier; any interior component is stable, and hypothesis (ii) makes its homology class zero. Removing it lowers area. Thus the minimizing representative consists of boundary components with nonzero multiplicity and has area at least \(A_0\).
## Smoothing with explicit parameter budgets

The conformal perturbation \(g'=e^{2u}g\), with \(u=0\) and \(\partial_\nu u>0\) on the boundary, preserves the boundary tensor and makes its outward mean curvature positive. A collar parametrized with normal speed \(\phi_i\) makes the extended neck metric equal to \(g'\) as a full tensor at the seam; it is totally geodesic on the neck side. The hypotheses of the Brendle–Marques–Neves gluing theorem [BMN] are therefore met. The normal collar can be chosen using the original metric, since \(u=0\) makes \(g'=g\) at the seam; thus the smooth structure can be fixed independently of the small perturbation.

Its construction also permits arbitrary \(C^0\) closeness to \(g'\). Writing the boundary difference as \(\widetilde g-g'=\rho T\), the outer perturbation is \(O(\Lambda^{-1})T\), while the inner perturbation is bounded by \[\|T\|_\infty
 \bigl(e^{-\Lambda^2}+\Lambda e^{-2\Lambda^2}\bigr).\] Both tend to zero. This verifies the additional \(C^0\) clause used by this paper; it is not an unsupported strengthening.

The two displayed bounds of size \(\varepsilon^3\) on pages 10–11 do not literally sum to \(\varepsilon^3\). Choose each \(C^0\) perturbation at most \(\varepsilon^3/4\) instead, accounting for the uniformly equivalent tensor norms. Choose the conformal scalar loss and the gluing loss each at most \(\varepsilon/2\). These choices give a smooth metric equal to \(g_i\) on every neck, with \[\|g_N'-g_N\|_{C^0(g_N)}\le\varepsilon^3,\qquad
 R_{g_N'}\ge\lambda-\varepsilon.\] For a two-dimensional surface, this tensor bound gives area distortion at most \((1-\varepsilon^3)^{-1}<1+\varepsilon^2\) when \(0<\varepsilon<1/100\). Consequently \(\operatorname{sys}_{\pi_2}(N,g_N')\ge(1-\varepsilon)A_0\). Take also \(\varepsilon<\lambda\), apply Theorem 1.1, and let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Theorem 1.2 follows with the same (4).
# The introductory rigidity equivalence needs correction
Problem 1 (Minor: equation (1.2), page 1).  Equality in the old \(8\pi\) bound does not imply a Riemannian covering by a compact round product \(S^2\times S^1\).
The primary result [BBN] instead identifies the universal cover with a round \(S^2\times\mathbb R\), up to scale.

Here is a counterexample to the stronger wording in this version. Let \(R_\theta\) be a sphere rotation with \(\theta/(2\pi)\notin\mathbb Q\), and take the quotient of the unit round \(S^2\times\mathbb R\) by \[\gamma(x,t)=(R_\theta x,t+L),\qquad L>0.\] This is a closed oriented manifold diffeomorphic to \(S^2\times S^1\) with scalar curvature two. The sphere area form descends to a closed form of comass one. Any nonzero \(\pi_2\) map lifts to the universal cover and its sphere projection has nonzero integer degree \(d\); thus its area is at least \(4\pi|d|\). A slice attains \(4\pi\), so \(\operatorname{sys}_{\pi_2}\,\min R=8\pi\).

A covering from a compact round product would have finite degree. On the universal cover, every isometry preserves the positive and zero Ricci eigendistributions, hence is a product isometry. It cannot conjugate a pure translation into \(\gamma^n(x,t)=(R_{n\theta}x,t+nL)\) for any \(n\ge1\). Irrationality makes every such rotation nontrivial. This disproves precisely the claimed compact-product covering.

The correction does not affect Theorem 1.1: this example is topologically \(S^2\times S^1\) and is excluded by its hypothesis. The invariant \(w(M)\) discussion on page 4 also needs the convention \(\operatorname{sys}_{\pi_2}=+\infty\) for \(\pi_2=0\) if it is to include spherical space forms; the original definition was restricted to nonzero \(\pi_2\).
# Alternative decomposition and verification limits

Remark 3.2 is consistent with the main result after clarifying its compressed steps. A finite-index free subgroup is obtained by mapping the finite free-product factors to their direct product; Kurosh and prime decomposition give a finite cover \(\#^k(S^2\times S^1)\). Small bumpy perturbations preserve positive scalar curvature. The stability area bound and compactness prevent an infinite disjoint family of essential stable spheres for a bumpy metric: an accumulating family would produce a Jacobi field, contrary to bumpiness. Systole is continuous under uniform metric comparison, so the perturbation can be removed at the end.

To exclude a punctured piece with a remaining \(S^2\times S^1\) factor, choose an absolute \(H_2\) class whose image in \(H_2(U,\partial U)\) is nonzero and minimize among closed cycles. Boundary components vanish in the relative group, so a minimizer must have an interior component. This supplies the contradiction with maximality without relying on an unspecified relative minimizer that might have free boundary. A piece with one boundary component would be a ball and make that cutting sphere inessential. If every piece had at most two, all would be cylinders and the connected gluing graph a cycle, yielding \(S^2\times S^1\). Therefore a piece with at least three boundary components exists. The word triviality in the last contradiction of Step 2 on page 12 should be nontriviality.

The specific primary checks were the Huisken–Ilmanen growth formula and its treatment of the initial minimal surface and arbitrary endpoints (printed pages 405–408), Xu’s properness theorem and normal-cover example in arXiv:2307.00725v2 (16 September 2024), the Brendle–Marques–Neves Theorem 5 and its cutoff construction, and the Bray–Brendle–Neves rigidity statement and minimizer proposition. The original Coulhon–Saloff-Coste PDF did not yield readable content in the available retrieval; the inspected normal-cover consequence in Xu’s primary article suffices for the existence application. These are bounded reference checks; the full analytic proofs of every cited theorem, the entire bibliography, and later developments were not independently reproduced. The covering, homological, weak-time and constant calculations, the explicit rigidity counterexample, and the local repairs above were independently worked out.
