report: Abstract: Three statements are false with their printed hypotheses: the general interval-label criterion, the restricted systolic-presentation theorem, and the positive-square theorem. Explicit torsion examples establish these failures. The special positive-germ construction has stronger properties than the defective background definition; the Artin-group conclusions are not disproved by these examples. Local corrections to the lattice and support arguments, a checked unmarked complex identification in the homotopy argument, exact finite Coxeter checks, and the remaining standard-theorem dependencies are given below. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of New Garside structures and applications to Artin groups
# Exact source, scope and assessment

The reviewed object is Thomas Haettel and Jingyin Huang, New Garside structures and applications to Artin groups, M25-0168, arXiv:2305.11622v2, stamped 16 October 2024 and internally dated 17 October 2024, 50 pages [source]. The assignment associates it with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0062 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0062). Identity with the journal-final article or a subsequent correction is not asserted. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages, agreeing with printed numbers.

The lead read the complete supplied text, including all definitions, proofs, examples and references. Three native helpers independently checked Section 3, Section 5, and Section 6 with their dependencies. The lead actually viewed 31 source pages; combined actual source-image coverage is all 50 pages. The checks distinguish simple-generator length, reflection length, partial-product divisibility and ambient absolute order, and include identity cases, empty supports, repeated letters, parabolic intersections and the scope of geometric consequences.

The supported impact is Major: Theorems 3.13 and 3.15 admit explicit counterexamples under their printed hypotheses. The overbroad background criterion, Theorem 2.9, also has a counterexample, but its effect is Minor here: the actual positive-germ construction has the additional nondegeneracy and interval structure needed for the valid standard theorem. This does not assert that the Artin-group main theorems are false. Their positive-germ route survives these examples, subject to the repairs and scoped standard dependencies below.
# The arbitrary interval-label criterion

Problem 1 (Minor background qualification; Definitions 2.6–2.8 and Theorem 2.9, pp.15–17).  A group-like balanced labeling of a finite graded lattice, in the literal sense defined here, need not have a Garside interval group.

Take \(P=\{0<1<2<3\}\), with \[\lambda(i,j)=j-i\pmod 2\quad\hbox{in }C_2=\{z,x\},\] where \(z\) is the identity label. This is a bounded finite graded lattice. Labels on every weak three-point chain multiply in \(C_2\); cancellation makes any two corresponding labels determine the third. The bottom-label, top-label and complete label sets all equal \(\{z,x\}\). Both strengthened balanced equalities therefore hold.

Definition 2.7 identifies all vertices. The edge labels are \(z,x\), and the four strict three-point chains give \[x^2=z,\qquad xz=x,\qquad zx=x.\] The top three-cell does not change the fundamental group. Hence \[G_P=\langle x,z\mid x^2=z,\ xz=x,\ zx=x\rangle=C_2.\] Separately collapsing the identity-labeled edge leaves the same group. A nontrivial finite group cannot satisfy Definition 2.5: a nonidentity generator has finite order and yields arbitrarily long positive expressions for the identity, contrary to condition (2).

The original framework extends edge labels to languages of edge words in intervals [mcc05]. The arbitrary map in this manuscript discards that information. The assertion that every labeling in Definition 2.8 defines the required Noetherian germ is consequently false. Moreover, Digne’s Proposition 2.4(ii) requires cancellation against arbitrary words of the universal monoid, not just one local product [digne]. A correction must restore a nondegenerate interval-language/germ framework and its global theorem. Repeating the balanced equalities cannot suffice.
# The systolic example theorem
Problem 2 (Major; Definition 3.12, Theorem 3.13 and Corollary C, pp.2–3 and 28–29).  The two printed restricted-systolic conditions allow torsion.

Consider \[G=\langle a,b,c\mid aa=b,\ bb=c,\ cc=a\rangle.\] Eliminating \(b=a^2,c=a^4\) gives \(G=C_7\). The images of \(S=\{a,b,c\}\) are \(\{1,2,4\}\) modulo seven; their positives and negatives are all six nonzero residues, without repetitions. The unoriented Cayley graph is \(K_7\), without loops or multiple edges. Its flag completion is a six-simplex, hence simply connected, and every vertex link is a simplex and is 6-large. All defining relators have the required form \(st r^{-1}\), with repeated letters permitted. Both printed hypotheses hold.

But \(G\times\mathbb Z\) has order-seven torsion and cannot be Garside. For the standard torsion-free consequence, left divisibility extends to a lattice on a Garside fraction group. If \(g^m=1\), left multiplication by \(g\) permutes \(\{1,g,\ldots,g^{m-1}\}\); it fixes their join \(j\), and \(gj=j\) implies \(g=1\).

The construction fails explicitly at partial associativity: in \(U=\{1,a,b,c\}\), \((a*a)*b=b*b=c\) exists, whereas \(a*b=a^3\) is absent. Associativity of an ambient group does not imply Definition 3.1’s strong existence requirements. The genuine restricted-triangular framework includes \(stu\in S\Rightarrow st,tu\in S\) and its other presentation and local conditions [soergel]. Restoring those hypotheses excludes the example and narrows the statement. Torsion-freeness alone does not fix the proof: the free presentation \(\langle a,b,c,p,q\mid ab=p,\ pc=q\rangle\) has a systolic two-triangle flag complex, but \((a*b)*c\) exists while \(b*c\) does not. This latter observation refutes the germ inference, not the Garside-product conclusion for a free group.
# The positive-square theorem
Problem 3 (Major; Definition 3.14 and Theorem 3.15, pp.29–30).  The three link exclusions allow positive-square groups with torsion.

Use distinct \(a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h,x,y\) and eight further letters \(t_v\), \(v\in V=\{a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h\}\). Put \(H(v)=x\) on \(\{a,d,e,f\}\), and \(H(v)=y\) on \(\{b,c,g,h\}\), and impose \[ab=cd,\qquad ef=gh,\qquad t_vv=t_vH(v)\quad(v\in V).\] Repeated letters are expressly allowed in Definition 3.14. Cancellation and Tietze elimination give \[G\cong\langle x,y\mid xy=yx,\ x^2=y^2\rangle*F_8
   \cong(\mathbb Z\oplus C_2)*F_8.\] The element \(xy^{-1}\) has order exactly two: its nontriviality is detected by \(x\mapsto1,y\mapsto0\) in \(C_2\).

For \(pq=rs\), the link corner edges, with multiplicity retained, are \[\{p^+,r^+\},\quad\{q^-,s^-\},\quad
 \{p^-,q^+\},\quad\{r^-,s^+\}.\] The two main relations give outgoing edges \(a^+c^+,e^+g^+\), incoming edges \(b^-d^-,f^-h^-\), and mixed edges \(a^-b^+,c^-d^+,e^-f^+,g^-h^+\). A clone gives a loop at \(t_v^+\), an incoming edge \(v^-H(v)^-\), and mixed edges \(t_v^-v^+,t_v^-H(v)^+\). There are no parallel nonloop outgoing or incoming pairs. The endpoints of either outgoing nonloop edge have no common incoming neighbor. For every incoming edge, the endpoints have no common outgoing neighbor: the hubs \(x^-,y^-\) and the endpoints of the two main incoming edges have no mixed neighbors. The mixed graph is a forest of subdivided stars with incoming leaves attached. It contains no alternating embedded four-cycle. The loops are not any expressly excluded type. Exact independent enumeration retains all 40 corners and eight loops and finds zero forbidden patterns. Thus all hypotheses hold, whereas \(G\times\mathbb Z\) has torsion.

Banning loops or non-reduced relators alone is insufficient. For each clone introduce five fresh \(p_v,q_v,r_v,s_v,t_v\) and replace its equation by \[p_vv=q_vr_v,\qquad q_vr_v=s_vt_v,\qquad s_vt_v=p_vH(v).\] These equations give \(v=H(v)\); eliminating \(r_v=q_v^{-1}p_vv\) and \(t_v=s_v^{-1}p_vv\) leaves \(p_v,q_v,s_v\) free. The group becomes \((\mathbb Z\oplus C_2)*F_{24}\). Each gadget has an outgoing triangle on \(p_v^+,q_v^+,s_v^+\), an incoming path \(v^-,r_v^-,t_v^-,H(v)^-\), and mixed edges \(p_v^-v^+,p_v^-H(v)^+\) together with duplicated \(q_v^-r_v^+\) and \(s_v^-t_v^+\). Only mixed pairs are parallel, a type the theorem permits. The mixed simple graph is still a forest; same-type edges have no common opposite-type neighbor. All relators are cyclically reduced and no link loop occurs. An independent enumeration of 50 generators, 26 relations and 104 corners again gives zero forbidden patterns.

A sufficient narrowed formulation would require every nontrivial length-two equivalence class to be an isolated pair \(\{ab,cd\}\), with different first and last letters and no side shared by another relation, together with the printed link conditions. The resulting three-level germ has no nonidentity triple products; cancellation, atomic joins and the rectangle condition follow directly from the excluded configurations. This is a sufficient restriction, not a proposed characterization. The examples expose a substantive equivalence-chain obstruction.
# The general construction and valid examples

The doubled poset in Section 3 has properties absent from the counterexample in Section 2. Write its elements \(u_0,\bar u_1\). Its minimum is \(e_0\), its maximum is \(\Delta=\bar e_1\), and \(u_0\le\bar v_1\) means \(v*u\) exists. Both partial-associativity implications prove transitivity; positivity and cancellation prove antisymmetry. The identity case \(U=\{e\}\) is allowed. The three possible label relations give inverse maps \[G_E\longleftrightarrow G_U\times\mathbb Z,\qquad
 u_0\mapsto(u,0),\quad\bar u_1\mapsto(u^{-1},1).\] Indeed \(u_0\bar u_1=\Delta=\bar u_1u_0\), so \(\Delta\) is central and all upper generators equal \(u_0^{-1}\Delta\). Proposition 3.6 does not require a prior embedding of \(U\).

Proposition 3.7 incorrectly treats an arbitrary upper bowtie endpoint as minimal. A complete local repair is available. For lower \(u_0,v_0\) and upper \(w_0,\bar a_1\), take \(j=u\vee_Lv\le_Lw\); assumption (3) gives \(a*j\), so \(j_0\) is intermediate. The reversed distribution uses a right join and assumption (4), with the order reversed in the upper copy. For two endpoints in each copy, the rectangle hypothesis gives one of the needed joins and the multiplication hypotheses make it intermediate. Pure-copy cases use the corresponding meet. These exhaust the distributions. Bounded height ensures that a pair with an upper bound in a meet-semilattice has a join: a minimal upper bound \(j\) has \(j\wedge z=j\) for every other upper bound \(z\).

For this specific \(E\), \(\lambda(e_0,z)=z\), only degenerate intervals have identity label, and translation gives a label-preserving order isomorphism \[[x,\Delta]\longrightarrow[e_0,\partial x],\qquad
 y\mapsto\lambda(x,y),\qquad
 \partial u_0=\bar u_1,\quad\partial\bar u_1=u_0.\] Both directions follow from strong associativity and cancellation. All interval factorizations and atom-word languages are transported. Writing \(x\backslash y=\lambda(x,x\vee y)\) and \(J=x\vee y\vee z\), join transport gives \[(x\backslash y)\backslash(x\backslash z)
 =\lambda(x\vee y,J)
 =(y\backslash x)\backslash(y\backslash z).\] The opposite multiplication has the mirror identity. Positivity, nondegeneracy, bounded factorization height and these translations place \(E\) within the genuine interval-germ framework. Global cancellation, normal forms, fractions and asphericity remain the standard theorem dependency [mcc05, digne]; local cancellation is not a substitute. With this qualification, no counterexample to Theorems 3.8–3.9 is established.

In the \(T(5)\) branch, proper subwords are not newly identified and full-side classes cannot extend, proving strong associativity. Different first and last letters give cancellation. Bowties, multiplication of joins and rectangles respectively produce forbidden parallel corners, triangles and alternating squares. Identity, equality and comparability cases must be separated before asserting distinct signed vertices. Unused generators are adjoined as isolated atoms, including the zero-relator free-group case. The source’s sentence about proper subwords must exempt literally identical words. For the surface examples, elimination recovers the standard relations; their links have lengths \(6g-4\) for orientable \(g\ge2\), and \(2g\) for nonorientable \(g\ge3\). The sphere, torus, Klein bottle and free boundary cases also satisfy the conclusion; the excluded projective plane has torsion. These checks support Theorem 3.10 and Corollary 3.11.
# Reflection germs and the Salvetti comparison

The sentence after Lemma 4.1 identifying induced orders with restricted absolute order needs additional closure. In \(W(A_2)=\langle s,t\rangle\), let \(U=\{1,s,t,st\}\). The displayed factor conditions using \(R_U=\{s,t\}\) hold, but \(t\le_{\rm abs}st\) has no partial complement in \(U\), since \(tst\notin U\). All actual Artin applications use unions of full compatible spherical intervals and possess the needed closure. The general statement should use germ orders throughout, or explicitly impose that closure.

In Proposition 4.2, joins of covers \(vr_1,vr_2\) arise from \(r_1\vee r_2\) and atomic multiplication compatibility. The nested induction extending multiplication to longer elements works because a nonidentity remainder strictly increases the outer parameter. For the rectangle induction, \(a=e\) or \(b=e\) already gives a right join, and \(u=e\) or \(v=e\) a left join. Otherwise the positive remainder gives \(|a'x|>|x|\). The concluding \(aw=wu_1w''\) should be \(aw=au_1w''\). At the start of Section 4, reflection decomposition means a product in \(R\), not \(S\).

The proposed objection to Theorem 4.3’s complex identification is withdrawn. The natural marked poset map \(\bar u_1\mapsto u^{-1}\delta_Ts_0\) twists upper labels by conjugation, but page 34 asserts coincidence of the complexes, without prescribing this marking or the image of the top loop. There is an explicit unmarked cellular isomorphism.

Write \(U=U_T\), and let \(z\) be the positive generator of the new infinite cyclic Artin factor. The product dual interval is \(D=U\times\{1,z\}\); \(z\) projects to the Coxeter involution \(s_0\), but is not itself an involution in the interval group. On one-cells send \[u_0\longmapsto u,\qquad
 \bar v_1\longmapsto(vz)^{-1}.\] The second map reverses the orientation of the edge labeled \(vz\). In particular \(\Delta_E=\bar e_1\) maps to \(z^{-1}\), not to \(\delta_Tz\); the alleged centrality obstruction disappears.

For a mixed chain \[u_{0,0}<\cdots<u_{r,0}<\bar v_{0,1}<\cdots<\bar v_{s,1},\] the group vertices are \(u_i\) and \(v_j^{-1}z^{-1}\). Left translate by \(v_0z\) and cyclically reorder the vertices. The result is the chain in \(D\) \[1=v_0v_0^{-1}<\cdots<v_0v_s^{-1}
       <(v_0u_0)z<\cdots<(v_0u_r)z .\] The lower terms and upper terms belong to \(U\) because \(v_j\le_Rv_0\) and \(v_0*u_i\) exists. Their cross differences are \(v_j*u_i\), which are defined by the mixed-chain conditions. Consequently this is a simplex of the product dual interval.

Conversely a mixed chain \(a_0<\cdots<a_r<b_0z<\cdots<b_sz\) in \(D\) gives the chain in \(E_T\) \[(b_0^{-1}b_0)_0<\cdots<(b_0^{-1}b_s)_0
 <\overline{a_0^{-1}b_0}_1<\cdots<
       \overline{a_r^{-1}b_0}_1 .\] All displayed differences are in \(U\): the left terms are successive factors of the \(b\)-chain, the right terms are right factors of \(a_0^{-1}b_0\), and each mixed product equals \(a_i^{-1}b_j\). Applying the forward construction recovers the original simplex after left translation by \(a_0^{-1}\). The reverse composite similarly recovers the original \(E_T\) simplex. One-layer chains reduce to chains in \(U\). Deleting a vertex gives the same face, possibly with a different base vertex; that change is precisely a common left translation, which preserves all interval labels. Thus these simplex maps respect face identifications and descend to inverse cellular maps on the interval complexes.

This proves the unmarked identification used locally in Theorem 4.3. The formula is compatible with inclusions of spherical subsets. The global Salvetti homotopy conclusion still uses the compatible parabolic intersections and standard naturality-and-gluing result of [ps21]. Those are identified dependencies, not a newly established error in the source’s coincidence assertion. Asphericity of the Salvetti product implies that of the original Salvetti complex, as Corollary 4.4 requires.
# Cyclic Artin groups: support and finite checks

Lemmas 5.1–5.2 have the needed support content. A word equal to the identity cannot contain a unique occurrence of a simple generator. If \(s\notin\operatorname{Supp}(w)\) and \(sw=ws\), track its unique occurrence through braid moves between the reduced words \(sw,ws\). Before a noncommuting letter reaches its left, no first noncommuting braid involving \(s\) is possible. Thus \(s\) commutes with all of \(\operatorname{Supp}(w)\).

Lemma 5.3 needs a reducedness justification before strong exchange. The induction makes \(h=s_2\cdots s_n\cdots s_2\) reduced of length \(2n-3\); since \(s_1\) is outside its support, \(\ell(s_1h)=2n-2\). If \(s_1hs_1\) is nonreduced, its length is exactly \(2n-3\). The deletion word has this length and is reduced. Strong exchange and the singleton-letter argument then apply.

Lemma 5.4 first restricts to the connected union of the two reflection supports. Order reversal corresponds to inverting the product and reverses a possible counterexample. The generic intersection argument uses parabolic subgroups: a proper finite parabolic containing a specified codimension-one parabolic must equal it. This conclusion would not hold for arbitrary reflection subgroups. In the exceptional \(F_4\) case, the three full-support reflections of its \(B_3\) subgroup are \[s_1s_2s_3s_2s_1,\quad s_1s_3s_2s_3s_1,\quad
 s_2s_3s_2s_1s_2s_3s_2.\] Their displayed factorizations and conjugate-subgroup intersections were checked exactly; the decisive intersection orders are eight and two. Corollary 5.5 follows by selecting a reflection factor whose support crosses the endpoint of the predecessor-containing factor and applying ordered reflection rewriting [mcc15].

Exact arithmetic over \(\mathbb Q\) and \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)\) checked both path orientations for \(A_2\)–\(A_5\), \(B_2\)–\(B_5\), \(H_2,H_3,H_4,F_4\): 11,548 ordered reflection-pair implications, including 486 substantive predecessor/noncontainment candidates. All passed. These computations supplement the all-rank proof; finite sampling is not claimed to establish an infinite family.

Table 1 was checked analytically. For at least four vertices, labels at least six fail a proper three-vertex Gram test. Four vertices allow \(3333,3334,3335,3434,3435,3535\) up to symmetry; five allow \(33333,33334\). At least six vertices permit only three: a proper five-vertex path with an interior four already has nonpositive Gram determinant. Exact enumeration for four through eight vertices gives \(6,2,1,1,1\) classes. For the full cycle, the all-ones quadratic form is \(n-2\sum_e\cos(\pi/m_e)\le0\), proving nonsphericity. Connectedness gives irreducibility, including the affine cases.

In Proposition 5.6, omitted-vertex intervals intersect in the principal interval of their common spherical generators; their joins therefore agree on overlaps. In (4), membership of \(aw\) follows with length additivity. If \(a'=(au)\vee(av)=aww_0\), then \[|a|+|w|+|w_0|=|a'|
 \le |aw|+|w_0|\le |a|+|w|+|w_0|.\] Hence \(aw\le a'\le\delta_i\). Support containment alone would not prove this membership.

The proof of (6) has a definite but repairable factor-order error. Using the predecessor of \(\min I_u\) on \(au\) reverses Lemma 5.4’s left-factor hypothesis. Assume instead \(I_a\cup I_b=I_u\cup I_v=S\), and choose the predecessor of \(\min I_a\). It lies in \(I_u\) or \(I_v\). The correctly ordered lemma gives \(I_a\subset I_u\) or \(I_a\subset I_v\), contradicting \(bu\in U\) or \(bv\in U\), respectively. Thus one pair has proper support union and the required join. The cyclic conclusion survives this repair.
# Combination and geometric consequences

For Lemma 6.1, every oriented spherical Dynkin forest admits a linear extension. Compatible extensions differ by commuting swaps, hence give one Coxeter element. Deleting generators and reflection rewriting give nested intervals. For Lemma 6.2, cut the relevant tree at the edge between the selected support differences. A wrong orientation makes both \(r_1r_2\) and \(r_2r_1\) rank-two upper bounds in the finite interval and forces equality. Their positive root normals have a strictly negative inner product across the cut, so the independent reflections cannot commute. This also handles reducible ambient spherical diagrams.

Global atomic joins in Theorem 6.3 are computed in the finite carrier of the support union; principal-interval intersections make them independent of the carrier. For multiplying a join, the total support is complete and has the specified cyclic-by-spherical decomposition. The exact mixed case (2) on p.46 is empty: if only \(u\) lies in the cyclic factor, its entire nonspherical vertex set would equal \(\operatorname{Supp}(a_1)\cup\operatorname{Supp}(u)\), contained in the spherical support of \(au\in U\). An initially considered example using a larger ambient factor decomposition actually lies in the all-spherical case; it was rejected before assessment and is not a finding.

For the final rectangle, a complete same-side support union gives a join by a finite carrier or the cyclic criterion. Otherwise choose nonadjacent \(s,t\) in the first pair and nonadjacent \(s_u,s_v\) in the second. The four complete cross unions place these vertices in the exact support differences needed by Lemma 6.2. All cross edges have label two or point toward \(s_u,s_v\). The four-cycle hypothesis forces one of the two deliberately absent diagonals, a contradiction. This checks the distinctness and difference-set quantifiers in the final abbreviated argument.

Both Figure 1 examples were actually inspected and independently parsed from the source vector data. They have, respectively, seven vertices/seventeen edges/two maximal cliques and fourteen vertices/forty-two edges/six maximal cliques. All maximal cliques have the stated cyclic types, their commuting complements are empty, and neither graph has an induced four-cycle. These finite checks support the examples, not the general theorem.

Theorem 2.15 and the Bestvina paragraph need a centrality qualification: \(\langle\Delta\rangle\) need not be normal. In \(B_3\), classical \(\Delta=aba\) maps to a transposition changed by conjugation by \(a\). Normality, combined with exponent sum, would force \(a\Delta a^{-1}=\Delta\), a contradiction. Use a central power or assume centrality. The paper’s \(\Delta_E=(1,1)\) is already central.

For Theorem D’s generic direct-factor step, let \(H=G\times\mathbb Z\) be Garside, let \(d\) be a central Garside power and \(z\) generate the displayed split factor. For large \(N\), \(D=d^Nz\) is positive and central and contains the old simple divisors. Atomicity makes its divisor set finite; it is a Garside element for the same monoid. Choose \(N\) so its \(\mathbb Z\)-coordinate is nonzero. Then \(G\) injects with finite index into \(H/\langle D\rangle\), and the quotient geometric action restricts geometrically. Translation-number claims need the specified combinatorial metric, not arbitrary rescalings of arbitrary actions.

The external metric statements checked are injectivity for the Garside complex’s piecewise \(\ell^\infty\) orthoscheme metric [hae24] and the central-power CUB quotient statement [hae22]. Helly is asserted for \(A_\Gamma\times\mathbb Z\), CUB for \(A_\Gamma\); no general CAT(0) conclusion is proved. For the cyclic center corollary, the verified irreducibility and nonsphericity supply Jankiewicz–Schreve’s no-spherical-factor hypothesis after the checked \(K(\pi,1)\) argument [js23]. It does not extend to all joins with spherical factors.

report: Abstract: The entropy submartingale in Proposition 48 is false: an explicit three-state example has a strictly positive, rigorously certified reversal of the claimed convexity. The variance assertion survives. A different conditional-entropy functional supplies a valid annealing statement under a stronger endpoint hypothesis and repairs the product-endpoint Ising applications. A separate correlation-matrix argument contains an invalid operator-norm step. Several technical inequalities and definitions need corrected constants or hypotheses. The hardcore endpoint citation does not supply the stated entropy implication. These findings concern the exact supplied author version; they do not establish that its final mixing theorems are false. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of Localization schemes: A framework for proving mixing bounds for Markov chains
# Exact source, scope and assessment

The reviewed object is Yuansi Chen and Ronen Eldan, Localization schemes: A framework for proving mixing bounds for Markov chains, M25-0169, arXiv:2203.04163v2, 6 June 2022, 62 pages [source]. The assignment associates this paper with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0063 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0063). Identity with the journal-final article or any subsequent correction is not asserted. All source page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages, agreeing with the printed pages.

The retained initial-review records document a complete reading of the supplied text and actual viewing of 34 source pages by that review’s lead; three native helpers supplied the remaining source-image coverage, for a recorded union of all 62 pages. The present independent acceptance has separately rechecked every reported issue and its proof dependencies, using the targeted text and actual-image coverage recorded with this revision. Checks include boundary supports, zero conditional variances, matrix normalization, stochastic quantifiers, entropy homogeneity, time integration and uniformity in external fields.

The highest supported impact is Major. The counterexample to Proposition 48 invalidates the printed proof of the general entropy annealing theorem, an organizing result of the paper. This is an explicit false intermediate assertion, not merely a missing citation. The separate failure of equation (67) leaves the first stability branch unproved by the supplied argument. No counterexample to Theorems 44, 47, 49, 60 or 62 is asserted. Complete local repairs, modified statements and unresolved proof obligations are distinguished below.
# The kernel and conservation identities that do work

For a localization martingale \(
u_t\), the kernel \[
u(dx)P(x,dy)=\mathbb E[
u_	au(dx)
u_	au(dy)]\] has the stated invariant measure and is reversible. In particular, \[\langle\varphi,P\varphiangle_
u
   =\mathbb E[
u_	au(\varphi)^2]\ge0.\] Thus these kernels are positive semidefinite. The variance decomposition proves Proposition 19’s spectral-gap identity. Jensen’s inequality proves its entropy lower bound \[\operatorname{Ent}_
u f-\operatorname{Ent}_
u(Pf)\ge \mathbb E[\operatorname{Ent}_{
u_	au}f].\] The distinction between a lower bound and an equality is essential later. Functions with zero entropy or variance are omitted from the corresponding quotients; nonnegative functions are handled with \(0\log0=0\), and finite-entropy truncations justify limiting steps.

For a fixed partition \(\Sigma\), the quadratic quantity \[\sum_{A\in\Sigma}\frac{\mu(\varphi\chi_A)^2}{\mu(A)}\] is convex in \(\mu\). Averaging over a partition law independent of \(\mu\) retains convexity. This verifies the variance half of Proposition 48 and the variance annealing mechanism of Theorem 46. At a zero-mass cell the closed convex perspective is assigned the value zero when its numerator also vanishes. This extension is continuous along the cell measures for bounded \(\varphi\), since \(|\mu(\varphi\chi_A)|\le\|\varphi\|_\infty\mu(A)\); it is not jointly continuous for arbitrary numerator and denominator. Bounded stopping times follow directly; extension to a stopping time requires the usual integrability or truncation justification, rather than an unqualified appeal to optional stopping.

The coordinate and Brownian conservation calculations have the expected structure: entropy loss is controlled by the mean displacement of the normalized tilted measure \(d\mu=f\,d\nu/\nu(f)\). Coordinate reveal gives the sum of binary marginal divergences divided by the number of remaining coordinates. For Brownian localization the instantaneous quadratic variation uses the actual noise matrix \(C_t\) on both sides of the covariance. The negative-fields entropy calculation in Appendix A.2 uses the globally valid upper scalar inequality discussed below, so it does not depend on the defective lower inequality.
# A counterexample to entropy submartingality

Problem 1 (Major; Proposition 48, p.33, and Appendix A.1, pp.53–54).  The asserted submartingale \(\int (P^{(t)}f)\log(P^{(t)}f)\,d\nu_t\) fails for a Doob localization with a fixed, measure-independent partition law.

On \(\Omega=\{0,1,2\}\), choose each of \[\Sigma_1=\{\{0,1\},\{2\}\},\qquad
 \Sigma_2=\{\{0\},\{1,2\}\}\] with probability \(1/2\). The associated kernel acts by \(P_\mu f=\frac12\mathbb E_\mu[f\mid\Sigma_1]
+\frac12\mathbb E_\mu[f\mid\Sigma_2]\). Set \[a=(1/5,1/10,7/10),\quad b=(3/5,3/10,1/10),\quad
 m=(a+b)/2=(2/5,1/5,2/5),\quad f=(10,0,1).\] All measure coordinates are strictly positive, and direct rational calculation gives \[\begin{array}{c|ccc}
 & (P_\mu f)_0 &(P_\mu f)_1 &(P_\mu f)_2\\ \hline
a&25/3&181/48&15/16\\
b&25/3&83/24&5/8\\
m&25/3&11/3&5/6
\end{array}\] For \(F(\mu)=\sum_i\mu_i(P_\mu f)_i\log(P_\mu f)_i\), the first coordinate cancels in the midpoint difference. Exactly, \[\begin{split}
 F(m)-\tfrac12(F(a)+F(b))
  ={}&\tfrac{11}{15}\log\tfrac{11}{3}
       +\tfrac13\log\tfrac56
       -\tfrac{181}{960}\log\tfrac{181}{48}\\
    &-\tfrac{21}{64}\log\tfrac{15}{16}
       -\tfrac{83}{160}\log\tfrac{83}{24}
       -\tfrac1{32}\log\tfrac58\\
  \in{}&(0.0339892404532605,\,0.0339892404532606).
\end{split}\] This is a strict reversed Jensen inequality. It is not based on floating-point sign detection. Each rational logarithm was reduced by a power of two to \([1,2]\), and evaluated using \[\log q=2\sum_{j=0}^{59}\frac{z^{2j+1}}{2j+1}+R,\qquad
 z=\frac{q-1}{q+1},\qquad
 |R|\le\frac{2|z|^{121}}{121(1-z^2)}.\] All interval arithmetic was exact rational arithmetic, followed by outward decimal rounding. The independent script and certificate are retained. Continuity also gives a strictly positive \(f\) example by replacing its zero coordinate with a sufficiently small positive number, if \(\mathbb R_+\) is read as excluding zero.

This midpoint split is an admissible initial localization: start from \(m\), reveal a fair choice of \(a\) or \(b\), and then sample from that conditional law and reveal the resulting point. For the final Doob scheme, first sample \(X\sim\mu\) and choose \(\Sigma\) independently. At time one reveal \(\Sigma\) and its cell containing \(X\); at time two reveal \(X\) itself. The partition law is independent of \(X\) and of the starting measure \(\mu\). Thus the time-one conditional law is precisely \(\mu(\,\cdot\mid A_\Sigma(X))\), giving the displayed kernel. Consequently the example satisfies the structural hypotheses, including eventual localization, and contradicts Proposition 48.

The error on p.53 is the replacement of entropy of an average conditional expectation by average entropy of the conditional expectations. These are generally related by Jensen, not equality. That display also subtracts \(\mu(f)\log\mu(f)\) on only one side; constant \(f\) already detects this normalization error. Removing that subtraction does not cure the midpoint counterexample.
## A valid replacement and its precise scope

Define the average conditional-entropy functional \[D_\mu(f)=\operatorname{Ent}_\mu f-

# Quantifiers, normalization and domain repairs
These issues are mostly local or concern overgeneralized preliminary statements; their existence is not evidence against every application.

Fact 13, p.16, needs a simultaneous almost-sure excitation condition. Let \(U\) be a uniformly random line known at time zero in \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(\nu=N(0,I)\), and take \[C_t=P_{U^\perp}+e^{-t}P_U.\] Every \(C_t\) is positive definite. For each fixed deterministic unit vector \(\theta\), almost surely \(\int_0^\infty|C_t\theta|^2dt=\infty\). Nevertheless the Gaussian posterior covariance along \(U\) tends to \((1+\int_0^\infty e^{-2t}dt)^{-1}=2/3\); localization fails. Require a common full-probability event on which the excitation diverges in every direction, equivalently here divergence of the least eigenvalue of the integrated information matrix. The fixed identity and fixed positive-definite controls used in the applications satisfy the stronger condition.

The Brownian calculation in Section 3.1.1, p.24, confuses \(C_t\) with its square root and loses a squared norm. A one-dimensional test is decisive: for \(\nu=N(0,1)\), \(C_t=c>1\) and \(\varphi(x)=x\), the actual variance is \((1+c^2t)^{-1}\). Equation (20)’s printed rate instead yields the larger claimed lower bound \((1+c^2t)^{-1/c}\). The correct covariance rate is \(\|C_t\operatorname{Cov}(\nu_t)C_t\|_{\rm OP}\). Even after that correction, the passage from a random integrating factor to the particular reciprocal-expectation bound is not established by a generic drift inequality alone. No counterexample to that corrected SDE-specific assertion was found. A deterministic upper envelope proves the bounds needed in the applications and should be stated explicitly, also in Proposition 39.

Proposition 18, pp.18 and 55–56, overstates uniqueness without specifying its generator. When \(v\equiv0\) and \(\nu\) is uniform on two points, both the constant process and a process that reveals a random sign at an independent exponential time are martingales with the printed zero conditional mean increment. The latter’s reveal is a pinning. Specify that an unpinned coordinate jumps only to \(-\operatorname{sign}v_i'\), with the rates given in Appendix A.2, and exclude additional jumps. The driving curve also needs locally integrable variation, for example \(C^1\) regularity: the differentiable curve \(v(t)=t^2\sin(t^{-4})\), \(v(0)=0\), has nonintegrable \(|v'|\) near zero, so the displayed hazard gives a first jump at zero rather than the asserted strictly later time. All actual straight-line applications meet the corrected regularity.

The sentence asserting Dirac convergence under every pinning process also fails: the uniform measure on \(\{(+,-),(-,+)\}\) is unchanged by the tilt \(v(t)=(t,t)\) with no pinnings. For the specified generator, convergence follows instead from the bounded measure martingale and the fact that a nondegenerate limiting marginal, together with diverging driving variation, would have infinite integrated pinning hazard. This is a construction scope repair, not a finding that the intended negative-fields localization does not exist.

The maximum-entropy principle on p.25 needs its actual domain. Fact 30 is false for arbitrary real-valued \(g\). For masses \(9/20,1/10,9/20\) on \(-1,0,1\) and \(g\equiv-1\), its two infima are \(-\log10\) and \(-\log(20/9)\). At a boundary mean, the minimizing measure also need not be a finite exponential tilt. Lemma 31, with no continuity condition on its nonnegative cost, is false: for the uniform two-point law, let \(\psi(x,y)=\chi_{\{x=1,y=0\}}\). Every finite tilt has zero cost, so any \(\alpha>0\) satisfies Definition 29; but \(\mu=\delta_1,\alpha=1/2\) violates Lemma 31. For the actual finite-support continuous quadratic and binary-divergence costs, minimize entropy at relative-interior means and approximate \(\mu\) by \((1-t)\mu+t\nu\). Continuity, or appropriate lower semicontinuity, then passes to the boundary. Degenerate affine directions must first be removed. Lemma 33’s assumption of invertible covariance alone does not ensure that all exponential tilts exist: a symmetric heavy-tailed law with finite nonzero variance is an immediate obstruction. Compact support, or appropriate exponential-integrability and Legendre-domain hypotheses, restores the uses made here.

The influence convention needs one consistent factor. For \(\{-1,1\}\)-valued coordinates, \[\mathbb E[X_i\mid X_j=1]-\mathbb E[X_i\mid X_j=-1]
      =\frac{2\operatorname{Cov}_{ij}}{1-b_j^2}.\] Thus (17) has diagonal two and is twice the matrix used on p.9, in Fact 23 and in Section 6. Inserting \(1/2\) in (17) yields the intended covariance convention. This factor is distinct from the invalid similarity-to-operator-norm inference. The Appendix A proof of Lemma 36 likewise needs \(\operatorname{diag}\int xx^{\top}d\nu=I\) and \(\operatorname{diag}\operatorname{Cov}=\operatorname{diag}(1-x_i^2)\); the full matrix identities printed there are false. With those diagonal corrections, the inverse-Hessian comparison and the continuous-cost limiting argument give the intended all-tilts implication.

# Applications: retained bounds and remaining obligations
## Ising models

The general Theorem 49 inherits Theorem 47’s unresolved entropy hypothesis. Its product-endpoint specialization is supported by the corrected conditional-entropy argument. With \(C_t=(2J)^{1/2}\), the quadratic interaction decreases to zero at time one. Deterministic covariance envelopes give the entropy-conservation factor, and product tensorization supplies \(D\ge\operatorname{Ent}/n\) at the endpoint. This establishes the route used by Corollaries 51 and 54 without the false Proposition 48.

The ferromagnetic susceptibility reduction additionally uses the stated external covariance comparison [dss] and nonnegativity, then entrywise comparison with a nonnegative matrix. That theorem is a named dependency, not independently reproved here. The localization integration and product endpoint are consistent with Corollary 54.

For graphical Ising, the identities on p.37 require repair. The matrix \((D+A)/2\) does not encode the displayed edge-agreement energy with the asserted factor; it is not generally positive definite, nor equal to the claimed normalized-Laplacian expression. Here \(D\) and \(A\) are the degree and adjacency matrices. For either sign of the interaction parameter \(\beta\), use \[J=|\beta|(D\mathbin{\pm}A)/4+I/8,\] with the matching sign. It is strictly positive definite and encodes the original energy up to a constant. The interpolating interaction is \((1-t)\beta\), so uniqueness is preserved.

The external influence bound must also be translated with its zero-diagonal probability convention. Definition 1.2 and Lemma 8.3 of [cfyz] directly give the sufficient covariance bound \(1+2/\delta\); it is unnecessary to identify their matrix literally with this manuscript’s inconsistent \(\Psi\). Since \(\|J\|\le|\beta|\Delta/2+1/8\), uniqueness gives \[2\|J\|(\delta+2)
 \le (|\beta|\Delta+1/4)(\delta+2)
 <6\log3+3/4<8.\] For the middle estimate, the function \((\delta+2)\log((\Delta-\delta)/(\Delta-2+\delta))\) decreases in \(\delta\), and \(\Delta\log(\Delta/(\Delta-2))\le3\log3\) for \(\Delta\ge3\). Thus the product-endpoint argument still yields \(e^{-8/\delta}/n\), the constant stated in Corollary 56, using only the checked weaker covariance conversion. The case \(\beta=0\) is a product measure.
## The restricted Gaussian oracle
## Negative fields and hardcore

Problem 3 (Confirmed proof defects; Theorem 60 and Lemma 66, pp.39–43).  The general duration is omitted from entropy conservation, and the cited endpoint result controls a different entropy functional.

Theorem 60 permits arbitrary \(s>0\), but its integration drops that duration. This cannot be a valid uniform conservation assertion. For one uniform sign, \(v(t)=-t\) and \(f=\chi_{\{+\}}\), the no-pin probability is \((1+e^{-2t})/2\); on that event the positive probability is \((1+e^{2t})^{-1}\). Therefore \[\mathbb E\operatorname{Ent}_{\nu_t}f
     =\tfrac12e^{-2t}\log(1+e^{2t})\longrightarrow0.\] The spectral and tameness parameters can be kept bounded uniformly in this example. Correct integration includes \(s\) in the exponent. This refutes the proof’s conservation assertion, not the final theorem’s conclusion by itself.

With the repaired second stability branch, \(C=K\) gives a sufficient general exponent of order \(sK^5\eta\), whereas the printed \(K^4\eta\) dependence has not been recovered. For the hardcore application \(s=2\) and \(K\) is an absolute constant, so these two changes alone would preserve the form \(e^{c/\delta}\). They do not settle the endpoint issue.

Lemma 66 claims the manuscript’s one-step coefficient is at least \(1/(4n)\), citing Proposition 51 of [ajk] and Fact 3.5 of [clv]. The former uses the Dirichlet/continuous-time MLSI constant. The latter assumes approximate tensorization and derives both that constant and one-step entropy contraction as separate consequences; it does not infer tensorization or one-step contraction from a Dirichlet MLSI. The underlying Ricci result [ehmt] likewise concerns continuous time. The distinction is explicit in [ajk]’s discussion of the easier measure. The cited implication is therefore incomplete. A direct proof of the appropriate endpoint conditional-entropy inequality, or another valid annealing mechanism, is needed. Neither Lemma 66 nor the final hardcore mixing bound is declared false on this basis.

The combinatorial marginal estimates in Lemma 64 work for a free vertex \(u_v=0\). The printed lower bound without that qualification fails when \(v\) is pinned negative; pinned positive vertices also invalidate the general upper bound. For an explicit admissible example take the star \(K_{1,3}\), \(\lambda=1\), and \(\delta=1/2\). Here \(\Delta=3\) and \(\lambda\le(1-\delta)\lambda_3=2\). Pin only the center \(v\), leaving all its neighbors unpinned (\(u_a=0\) for \(a\in N_v\)), exactly as allowed in the statement. Both pinning events have positive probability. Pinning \(v=+1\) makes the displayed upper bound \(1\le1/2\) false; pinning \(v=-1\) makes the first lower bound \(1/16\le0\) false. Already forced coordinates are removed before applying the estimates. On the remaining graph, the injection deleting an occupied vertex proves the upper bound, sequential conditioning of its neighbors proves the lower bound, and negative tilting replaces fugacity by \(\lambda e^{-2t}\). The degree estimate at the endpoint includes \(\Delta=3\): \(9e^{-3}<1/2\) at \(t=2\), despite the proof’s strict \(\Delta>3\) wording. These combinatorial checks do not resolve the missing entropy implication.

The external hardcore spectral estimate also uses a derivative gap and a zero-diagonal influence convention [cfyzall]. For branching number \(d\ge2\), its critical-fugacity ratio is \[\frac{\lambda_{c,s}(d)}{\lambda_{c,0}(d)}
   =(1-s)(1+s/(d-1))^{-(d+1)}\ge1-4s.\] Thus relative fugacity slack \(\delta\) safely permits \(s=\delta/4\). The degree-one threshold \((1-s)/s^2\) also exceeds the required fugacity range. The cited \(144/s\) estimate, followed by adding the diagonal and comparing signed influence with its absolute-value matrix, gives a sufficient correlation bound \(577/\delta\). This verifies the required order with a universal constant; the printed \(144/\delta\) under unchanged conventions was not separately certified and is not declared false.
## Uniform starting states

The repeated appeal to Fact 2 alone leaves an apparent dependence on the smallest stationary mass, which may be arbitrarily small with external fields or fugacity. It can be removed without asserting that the mixing conclusions are false.

For hardcore, condition on a fixed scan sequence that updates every vertex at least once. For a specified final independent set \(x\), its occupied vertices must all succeed at their last updates, each with conditional probability at most \(q=\lambda/(1+\lambda)\). Order these last-update events chronologically and use iterated conditional expectations. Thus the output law satisfies \(\mu(x)\le q^{|x|}\), and \[\mu(x)/\nu(x)\le Z/(1+\lambda)^{|x|}
       \le Z\le(1+\lambda)^n\le5^n\] in the stated uniqueness range. Random scan fails to cover all vertices by \(n\log(2n/\epsilon)\) steps with probability at most \(\epsilon/2\). Conditioning on coverage changes the scan law, not the update randomness. The conditional output has relative entropy at most \(n\log5\); any subsequently justified \(c_\delta/n\) entropy contraction gives the desired order of mixing independently of tiny \(\lambda\).

For Ising, compare each last-update probability with its external-field-only product marginal \(p_i\); their ratio is at most \(\exp(4\sum_{j\ne i}|J_{ij}|)\). Multiplication over chronological last updates and comparison of the target with that product measure give warmness at most \[\exp\{4\sum_{i\ne j}|J_{ij}|+n\|J\|_{\rm OP}\}
       \le\exp\{C\|J\|_{\rm OP}n^{3/2}\}.\] The logarithm of its relative-entropy bound is \(O(\log n)\) for bounded interaction norm. This supplies the needed warmup uniformly in arbitrary external fields, followed by the supported Ising entropy contraction. This argument repairs a uniformity omission; it does not repair an unproved contraction coefficient.

report: Abstract: Two quantitative steps in the isoperimetric application fail under the printed definitions. A family of flat tori with truncated distances disproves uniform dependence on the listed local geometric data. A smooth ellipsoid disproves the fixed dilation asserted in the proof: local constancy need not give one multiplicity on a disconnected metric ball. An explicit global volume parameter and a larger dilation repair the argument. The fundamental-class and surface constructions survive the checks, with local endpoint and proof-writing repairs. These findings concern the supplied author version. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical verification of Geometric and analytic structures on metric spaces homeomorphic to a manifold
# Exact source, scope and assessment

The reviewed paper is Giuliano Basso, Denis Marti and Stefan Wenger, Geometric and analytic structures on metric spaces homeomorphic to a manifold, M25-0170, arXiv:2303.13490v2, 22 September 2023, 36 pages [source]. The assignment associates it with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0064 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0064). Identity with the journal-final text is not asserted. Source page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages, agreeing with the printed pages.

The lead read the complete supplied text, including all definitions, proofs and references, and viewed 30 source pages. Three native helpers checked disjoint mathematical scopes: the fundamental class, the lower-measure and Sobolev surface arguments, and the isoperimetric application. Combined actual image coverage is all 36 source pages. Checks included orientations, degree quantifiers, mass and support, dimension-one and zero-measure endpoints, small and large metric balls, and the distinction between ordinary and Busemann mass.

The highest supported impact is Major. The uniform dependence claimed after Theorem 1.5 is false for the printed Ahlfors definition. Independently, equation (7.1) is false and its local-constancy argument is invalid on general metric balls. Both are on the proof path to a principal application. The counterexamples do not disprove the existence of an isoperimetric constant for each fixed space, nor the fundamental-class or Lipschitz-volume-rigidity theorems. A corrected quantitative statement is proved below; its added datum must not be silently omitted.
# Definitions and dependencies that matter

Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 construct a cycle \(T\) with \(\varphi_\#T=\deg(\varphi)[\![M]\!]\) for every Lipschitz \(\varphi:X\to M\). Since \(\mathcal H^{n+1}(X)=0\), top-dimensional integral homology is the group of cycles, without nonzero higher-dimensional boundaries. Theorem 1.1 supplies a quantitative lower mass density; the surface theorem obtains existence without LLC. The isoperimetric proof uses this cycle, minimal fillings in the compact injective hull, a controlled continuous retraction, and topological constancy after Lipschitz approximation. The rigidity application instead needs the Hausdorff/Busemann mass of a suitable cycle.
# The missing global scale in the advertised data

Problem 1 (Major; Theorem 1.5 and its following paragraph, p.4; the doubling inference, p.26).  Under definition [eq:ahlfors] (#eq:ahlfors), the constants in [eq:iso] (#eq:iso) cannot be bounded by \(n,\alpha,\Lambda\) alone.
## A family satisfying every printed hypothesis

For each \(L\ge4\), take the flat torus \[X_L=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)\times(\mathbb R/4\mathbb Z),\qquad
 d(x,y)=\min\{d_0(x,y),1\},\] where \(d_0\) is its Riemannian distance. This is a metric, since \(\min\{a+b,1\}\le\min\{a,1\}+\min\{b,1\}\). It induces the same topology and agrees with \(d_0\) at small distances. In particular, the Hausdorff measures agree: their covers of diameter less than any fixed \(\delta<1\) are identical. Thus \[D=1,\qquad \mathcal H^2_d(X_L)=4L.\] These are compact, connected, oriented smooth topological two-manifolds of finite measure.

The flat injectivity radius is at least \(2\). For every \(0<r<1\), \(B_d(x,r)\) is an embedded Euclidean disk, and \[\mathcal H^2_d(B_d(x,r))=\pi r^2.\] Consequently \(\alpha=\pi\) works in [eq:ahlfors] (#eq:ahlfors) for every \(L\). Each such ball contracts inside itself by Euclidean radial contraction, so \(\Lambda=1\) also works uniformly. These are even the smallest allowed upper Ahlfors and LLC constants in this example.
## The claimed and actual bounds

Let \(B=B_d(p,2)=X_L\), and take the closed half-cylinder \[E=[0,L/2]\times(\mathbb R/4\mathbb Z).\] Then \[\mu(E)=\mu(X_L\setminus E)=2L.\] For \(0<t<1\), the exterior \(t\)-neighborhood adds a strip of width \(t\) along each of the two boundary circles, each of length \(4\). Equivalently, its long-coordinate interval has length \(L/2+2t\). Hence \[\mu(E_t)=2L+8t,\qquad
 \mathcal M_-(E\mid\lambda B)=8\quad\hbox{for every }\lambda\ge1.\] The asserted uniform conclusion is therefore \[2L\le64\,C(2,\pi,1),\qquad\text{or}\qquad
 C(2,\pi,1)\ge L/32.\] As \(L\) is arbitrary, no such finite uniform constant exists. Increasing the dilation has no effect because \(\lambda B=X_L\).

The same family diagnoses the proof’s uniform-doubling inference. For example, \[\frac{\mu(B_d(p,3/2))}{\mu(B_d(p,3/4))}
       =\frac{64L}{9\pi}.\] Each individual torus is doubling; a bound from the three listed data does not follow.
## Alternative reading and precise impact

If Ahlfors regularity was intended to include a bound on the total measure at the diameter scale, this family would be excluded. The supplied definition explicitly restricts the upper bound to \(r<D\), while the theorem concerns every open ball. Interpreting data dependence as permitting an arbitrary larger Ahlfors constant chosen using total volume would hide the missing datum. The ordinary quantitative interpretation must apply to the valid common choice \(\alpha=\pi\).

This is a counterexample to the stated uniform dependence. It is not a counterexample to the existence of some finite \(C\) for a fixed \(X_L\). The source’s qualitative existence conclusion can be retained with the additional parameter described in Section 5 (#sec:repair).
# The fixed dilation and disconnected balls

Problem 2 (Major; equation (7.1), p.26; local constancy and Lemma 7.3, p.29; concluding inference, p.30).  The stronger claim with the fixed dilation \(\lambda=6\) is false, even for a smooth compact ellipsoid with explicit global geometric bounds. Local constancy gives one integer per connected component, which need not be one common integer on the target metric ball.
## An explicit metric two-sphere

Let \[X=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3:(x^2+y^2)/10000+z^2=1\}\] with the restricted Euclidean distance. Put \(F(u)=\operatorname{diag}(100,100,1)u\) for \(u\in S^2\), where \(S^2\) has its chordal metric. Then \[|u-v|\le|F(u)-F(v)|\le100|u-v|,\qquad D=200.\] This is a compact connected oriented smooth metric sphere.

For a chordal cap on the unit sphere, the area is \(\pi s^2\) for \(0<s\le2\). The above distance comparisons give \[\frac{\pi r^2}{10000}\le\mathcal H^2(B_X(Fu,r))
       \le10000\pi r^2,\qquad 0<r<200.\] For the upper bound when \(r>2\), use \(\mathcal H^2(X)\le10000\mathcal H^2(S^2)=40000\pi\le10000\pi r^2\). Thus \(\alpha=10000\pi\) satisfies both sides of the source definition.

The LLC condition holds with \(\Lambda=200\). Indeed, if \(r<1\), the preimage of \(B_X(Fu,r)\) lies in the chordal cap \(B_{S^2}(u,r)\). Contract this cap to \(u\) by normalized straight-line contraction. The homotopy stays in that cap, so its image under \(F\) lies in \(B_X(Fu,100r)\subset B_X(Fu,200r)\). Since \(D/\Lambda=1\), this checks every required radius and center.
## A positive left side and a zero right side

Equation reference: eq:positive. Take \[p=(0,0,1),\qquad B=B_X(p,3),\qquad E=X\cap\{z\ge0\}.\] Both graphs \[z=\pm\sqrt{1-(x^2+y^2)/10000},\qquad x^2+y^2<1,\] lie in \(B\): their squared distance to \(p\) is less than \(5<9\). Orthogonal projection onto the planar unit disk is \(1\)-Lipschitz. It follows that \[
 \min\{\mathcal H^2(E\cap B),\mathcal H^2(B\setminus E)\}\ge\pi.\]

For \(q=(x,y,z)\in6B\) with \(z<0\), we have \(x^2+y^2<18^2\); therefore \[z^2>1-\frac{18^2}{10000}
       =\frac{2419}{2500}>
          \left(\frac{49}{50}\right)^2.\] For every \(e\in E\), \(|q-e|\ge|z|>49/50\). Consequently \[E_t\cap6B=E\cap6B\quad(0<t<49/50),\qquad
 \mathcal M_-(E\mid6B)=0.\] Equation (7.1) asserts that the positive quantity in [eq:positive] (#eq:positive) is at most zero, for every finite \(C\). The verification is exact and does not rely on a plot or numerical surface approximation.
## The invalid inference and its scope

The source obtains \(\operatorname{spt}(\partial Q)\subset\rho(X\setminus2B)\), then writes \[Q\mathbin{\vert}\rho(B)
       =c[\![M]\!]\mathbin{\vert}\rho(B)\] with one integer \(c\). Constancy only provides such a constant on each connected component of \(\rho(2B)\). In this example, \(B\) meets two caps in distinct components of \(2B\), and even of \(6B\). The northern-hemisphere current has multiplicity \(1\) on the upper cap and \(0\) on the lower cap, with its boundary near the remote equator. The two alternatives used in Lemma 7.3 cannot be selected by a single global choice of \(c=0\) or \(c\ne0\).

This issue survives adding a global volume bound. Conversely, it does not disprove an estimate with a dilation depending on LLC: the statement of Theorem 1.5 already permits that dependence. The correct local-to-global step is given next.
# A corrected quantitative statement and proof

Equation reference: eq:global. Retain the hypotheses of Theorem 1.5 and make explicit the additional bound \[
 \mathcal H^n(X)\le A_0D^n,\qquad D>0.\] For a fixed compact \(X\), \(A_0=\mathcal H^n(X)/D^n\) is finite: finitely many balls of radius less than \(D\) cover \(X\). Problem 1 shows that \(A_0\) cannot be bounded by the printed local data alone.

Proposition 1.  With [eq:global] (#eq:global), the source’s construction yields [eq:iso] (#eq:iso) with \(\lambda=9\Lambda\) and \(C=C(n,\alpha,\Lambda,A_0)\). If [eq:global] (#eq:global) is required with \(A_0\le\alpha\), the advertised dependence on \(n,\alpha,\Lambda\) is recovered.

Proof. First, the missing global control now follows quantitatively. At radii \(r<D/2\), the measure-doubling ratio is at most \(2^n\alpha^2\). For \(D/2\le r<D\), total mass and the local lower bound give a ratio at most \(2^nA_0\alpha\). The endpoint \(r=D\) follows by comparison with \(D/2\), and \(r>D\) is trivial. Thus a bound \[2^n\max\{\alpha^2,A_0\alpha,1\}\] suffices. The usual disjoint-ball packing argument gives a uniform metric doubling constant and hence the finite Nagata data needed in the source. Moreover, \(\mu(B(x,r))\le\max\{\alpha,A_0\}r^n\) at every positive radius.

Fix a target ball \(B_0=B(x_0,R)\). Define a separate working radius \[q=
 \begin{cases}
   \Lambda R,&R<D/\Lambda,\\
   3D/2,&R\ge D/\Lambda.
 \end{cases}\] Then \(q<2D\), \(q\le3\Lambda R/2\), and \(B_0\subset B(x_0,q)\). In the first case the LLC contraction places all of \(B_0\) in one connected component \(O\) of \(B(x_0,2q)\). In the second case this larger ball is \(X\), so take \(O=X\). These components are open because \(X\) is a topological manifold. Also, \[B(x_0,6q)\subset B(x_0,9\Lambda R).\]

Run the filling construction on pp.27–30 with working radius \(q\) and \(P_0=\mathcal M_-(E\mid B(x_0,6q))\). Keep \(B_0\) as the target of the final two volume terms. If \(P_0>\varepsilon_0 q^{n-1}\), the desired estimate follows immediately from the global upper bound on \(\mu(B(x_0,q))\). Otherwise choose \(0<\delta<\min\{C_2\varepsilon_0q^{n-1},1\}\) and a regular distance level \(r>0\) with \[V=\partial(T\mathbin{\vert}E_r),\qquad
 \|V\|(B(x_0,6q))\le C_2P_0+\delta,\qquad
 \mu(B_0\setminus E)\le2\mu(B_0\setminus E_{3r}).\] Closure of \(E\) changes no relevant measure when \(P_0<\infty\). Slicing and the defining liminf allow these simultaneous choices with \(r\) arbitrarily small.

Choose \(R'\in(5q,6q)\), fill the boundary of \(V\mathbin{\vert}B(x_0,R')\) minimally by \(U\), and then fill \(W=V\mathbin{\vert}B(x_0,R')-U\) minimally by \(S\). Exactly as in (7.4)–(7.8), \[\operatorname{M}(U)\le C_2P_0+\delta,\quad
 \operatorname{M}(W)\le2(C_2P_0+\delta),\quad
 \operatorname{M}(S)\le D_*\operatorname{M}(W)^{n/(n-1)}.\] Here \(D_*\) is the filling constant, distinct from the diameter. The source’s smallness choice for \(\varepsilon_0\) keeps the fillings in the controlled retraction neighborhood because \(q<2D\), and keeps \(U\) outside \(B(x_0,4q)\). The zero-dimensional filling used when \(n=2\) is covered by Theorem 3.3’s explicit convention.

Let \(Q=\varphi_\#(T\mathbin{\vert}E_r-S)\) as in the source. Its boundary is outside \(\rho(B(x_0,2q))\). Apply constancy on \(\rho(O)\), which contains \(\rho(B_0)\). There is now legitimately one integer \(c\) on the target. The proof of Lemma 7.3, restricted to \(B_0\), gives \[B_0\cap E_{r-h}\subset N_h(\pi(\operatorname{spt}S))
 \quad\hbox{or}\quad
 B_0\setminus E_{3r}\subset N_h(\pi(\operatorname{spt}S)).\]

The source’s covering and minimal-filling density argument in Lemmas 7.2 and 7.4 is used at radius \(q\). For completeness, with \(r_j=d(y_j,A)\), the relevant indices satisfy \[r_j\le d(y_j,\operatorname{spt}\partial S),\qquad
 \sum_{d(y_j,x_0)\le3q}r_j^n
   \le L_*(D_*/a)^n\operatorname{M}(S).\] The small balls have multiplicity at most \(L_*\); the remaining cover of \(A\) has sum of \(n\)-th powers of radii at most \(\delta\). The controlled retraction and the global upper bound on ball measure therefore give \[\mu\bigl(N_h(\pi(\operatorname{spt}S))\cap2B_q\bigr)
       \le C_3\bigl(P_0^{n/(n-1)}+\delta\bigr)\] through the finite covering set \(A^*\) of the source. Since \(B_0\subset2B_q\), the preceding alternative implies \[\min\{\mu(B_0\cap E),\mu(B_0\setminus E)\}
       \le2C_3\bigl(P_0^{n/(n-1)}+\delta\bigr).\] Let \(\delta\downarrow0\), choosing \(r,h\) as above. This includes \(P_0=0\), without dividing by it.
Finally, \(\mathcal M_-(E\mid U)\) is monotone in \(U\): its numerator is \(\mu((E_t\setminus E)\cap U)\). Thus \(P_0\le\mathcal M_-(E\mid9\Lambda B_0)\), proving the proposition. ◻

This repair preserves the qualitative existence assertion for each \(X\) by allowing its finite \(A_0\), and proves a quantitative version with the stated added datum. It does not establish the false original uniform dependence or the fixed dilation \(6\). Combining the repaired estimate with the ball-volume upper bound gives the strong relative inequality \(\min\{\mu(E\cap B),\mu(B\setminus E)\}\le C'R\mathcal M_-(E\mid\lambda B)\). The source’s cited doubling-space characterization then gives its qualitative weak \(1\)-Poincare conclusion. That external characterization is retained as a dependency.
# A local zero-measure endpoint

Problem 3 (Minor; Lemma 4.2, equation (4.1), p.15).  The asserted approximation by a finite complex with zero displacement when \(\mathcal H^{n-1}(S)=0\) is not available in that literal form. The lemma itself has a direct repair.

Take \(n=2\), a round two-sphere \(X\), and an infinite middle-thirds Cantor set \(S\) embedded in a short smooth arc. It is closed and has \(\mathcal H^1(S)=0\), so it satisfies the small-measure hypothesis for every positive \(c,r\). Equation (4.1) would give a finite zero-dimensional simplicial complex \(K\) and a map \(f:S\to K\) with \(\|x-f(x)\|\le c_1\mathcal H^1(S)=0\). Hence \(f(x)=x\) and \(S\subset K\), impossible because a finite zero-complex has finitely many points.

The cited filling result explicitly retains a positive tolerance at zero Hausdorff content [llnr]. More directly, handle this case before the finite-complex construction: \(\mathcal H^{n-1}(S)=0\) implies \(\dim_{\rm top}S\le n-2\). Take \(Z=S\), \(f=\mathrm{id}_S\), and \(g\) the inclusion into \(X\); the constant homotopy proves Lemma 4.2 in this case. For positive measure the approximation argument proceeds. Thus neither Lemma 4.2 nor Theorem 4.1 is refuted. For nonorientable manifolds in Theorem 4.1, the cited separator lemma uses mod-\(2\) cohomology and requires no doubling hypothesis [kinneberg].
# Verified constructions and boundary repairs
## Fundamental class and uniqueness

The degree construction in Section 5 is consistent after the routine choices are made explicit. A controlled extension of each bi-Lipschitz chart has local degree \(+1\) or \(-1\) almost everywhere: composition with a Lipschitz extension of the inverse has derivative the identity at density points. The finite-fiber area formula then turns the oriented current into the sum of local degrees. Bate approximation eliminates the purely unrectifiable image, so the total degree of a map to \(\mathbb R^n\) is zero and \(\partial T=0\). The same calculation and uniform Lipschitz approximation into \(M\) give the degree identity. Finite mass justifies summation and continuity in the first test function.

The thin-filling uniqueness argument of Lemma 5.6 uses a finite-dimensional linear contraction \(\psi\) approximating the identity on compact \(C\). Deformation gives \(\psi_\#S=0\). A straight-line homotopy, with orientation chosen to have boundary \(S\), gives the correct estimate \[\operatorname{M}(R)\le(n+1)\varepsilon\operatorname{M}(S).\] The intervening \(\operatorname{M}(S')\) in the printed p.20 display is incorrect after \(S'=\psi_\#S=0\). Deleting it restores the argument: evaluation of \(S=\partial R\) against a fixed Lipschitz test tuple tends to zero with \(\varepsilon\). This is a verified local correction, not evidence that uniqueness fails.

The proof of Proposition 5.7 uses \(1/(n-1)\) and should separate \(n=1\). Here is the missing endpoint. Proposition 5.9 independently gives \(\operatorname{spt}T=X\). For almost every \(r<D/8\), if \(\partial(T\mathbin{\vert}B(x,r))=0\), Proposition 5.5 makes this restriction \(mT\). Its proper support forces \(m=0\), contradicting full support. The slice is therefore a nonzero integral zero-cycle with total coefficient zero, and has mass at least \(2\). Slicing yields \(\|T\|(B(x,r))\ge2r\) in this range. Monotonicity extends the bound to \(r\le D\), for example with constant \(1/4\). No singular exponent is needed. For \(n\ge2\), the small-ball proof extends to all scales by decreasing its constant by a factor \(8^n\).

The density-point estimate in Lemma 5.3 is valid if the nearby point \(w'\in K\) is chosen so that \[|w-w'|\le
   \frac{|w-z|}{2L(C+L^{-1})}.\] Then \(L^{-1}|z-w'|-C|w-w'|\ge|w-z|/(2L)\). Density permits this stronger choice. These proof-writing corrections do not constitute additional substantive Problem sections.
## Sobolev pushforward and the surface theorem

For \(n>1\), Proposition 6.1’s uniform convergence is justified even at the critical exponent. Put \(A_k=\{h\le k\}\) and \(\varepsilon_k=\int_{M\setminus A_k}h^n\). The source has \(\mathcal H^n(M\setminus A_k)\le\varepsilon_k/k^n\) and \(\varepsilon_k\to0\). A uniform lower volume bound for small balls on the compact Riemannian domain gives \[k\,\sup_{z\in M}d(z,A_k)\le C_M\varepsilon_k^{1/n}\longrightarrow0.\] Indeed, a ball of radius less than \(d(z,A_k)\) is contained in the bad set. The \(2k\)-Lipschitz extensions and uniform continuity of \(\rho\) now imply \[\sup_M d(\rho_k,\rho)
 \le 4k\,s_k+\omega_\rho(2s_k)\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad s_k=\sup_M d(\,\cdot\,,A_k).\] This uses the controlled bad-set estimate; it is not an untrue general continuous embedding of \(W^{1,n}\). If \(s_k=0\), the two continuous maps agree on the dense good set, so they agree everywhere. For \(n=1\), strong \(L^1\) boundedness of a maximal function must not be assumed. Instead, if \(g\in L^1\) is the curve gradient and \(h=C\mathcal{M}g\), weak type \((1,1)\) and truncating \(g\) give \(k\mathcal H^1(\{h>k\})\to0\). Use \(\eta_k=k\mathcal H^1(M\setminus A_k)\) in place of \(\varepsilon_k\); the remainder bound is \(2\eta_k\), and the same uniform-convergence argument works. Integrability of \(g\) controls the omitted-domain volume. The surface theorem uses \(n=2\), where the displayed \(L^n\)-tail argument applies directly.

The remainder mass is at most \(2^n\varepsilon_k\). Agreement on the nested good sets makes the pushforward cycles Cauchy in mass; integral closure and shrinking support place the limit in \(X\), with zero boundary. The uniformization theorem used on p.25 applies to non-length metric surfaces [nrnonlength]. Its monotone map has singleton fibers for target-almost every point by the separately applicable Lemmas 7.5 and 7.8 of [nrpoly]. Applying the area formula on the Lipschitz good sets suffices; a global Lusin \(N\) assumption is not silently needed. The uniqueness argument uses compactness and \(\mathcal H^3(X)=0\), without importing LLC back into Theorem 1.3.
## Lipschitz-volume rigidity

In Lemma 8.2, surjectivity, the \(1\)-Lipschitz bound and equality of total finite Hausdorff measures force measure preservation and multiplicity one almost everywhere. On the rectifiable charts of a nonzero cycle \(S\), the area formula and \(\varphi_\#S=k[\![M]\!]\) give \(|\theta_i|=|k|\) almost everywhere. Degenerate Jacobians cannot carry positive chart measure under measure preservation. Thus \(k\ne0\), \(T=S/k\) remains an integral cycle, and \[\operatorname{spt}T=\operatorname{spt}S,\qquad \varphi_\#T=[\![M]\!],\qquad
 \operatorname{M}^{b}(T)\le\mathcal H^n(X).\] This is the required Busemann mass comparison, rather than the weaker ordinary-mass upper bound of Theorem 1.1.

The hypotheses of Züst’s Theorem 1.2 were checked in the later external version [zuest]: a closed Riemannian target is an infinitesimally Euclidean essential length space; its boundary condition is empty; and Busemann volume is Euclidean rigid. Together with full support, these hypotheses match the application. The alternative surface proof’s compactness and degree argument prevents a zero limiting cycle. At the \(n=1\) endpoint of Theorem 1.4, a finite-length metric circle has an oriented arclength parametrization giving the needed cycle directly; this avoids invoking the LLC theorem without LLC.
# Dependence, limits and conclusion

Problems 1 and 2 affect the quantitative isoperimetric application and its printed proof. Problem 1 requires either a global hypothesis or an explicit extra parameter. Problem 2 requires a connected region for constancy and a compatible enlargement of the localization ball. The corrected proposition addresses both. Problem 3 has a local zero-measure repair and does not damage the lower-measure or fundamental-class result.

analysis: Under definition [eq:ahlfors] (#eq:ahlfors), the constants in [eq:iso] (#eq:iso) cannot be bounded by \(n,\alpha,\Lambda\) alone.

For each \(L\ge4\), take the flat torus \[X_L=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)\times(\mathbb R/4\mathbb Z),\qquad
 d(x,y)=\min\{d_0(x,y),1\},\] where \(d_0\) is its Riemannian distance. This is a metric, since \(\min\{a+b,1\}\le\min\{a,1\}+\min\{b,1\}\). It induces the same topology and agrees with \(d_0\) at small distances. In particular, the Hausdorff measures agree: their covers of diameter less than any fixed \(\delta<1\) are identical. Thus \[D=1,\qquad \mathcal H^2_d(X_L)=4L.\] These are compact, connected, oriented smooth topological two-manifolds of finite measure.

The flat injectivity radius is at least \(2\). For every \(0<r<1\), \(B_d(x,r)\) is an embedded Euclidean disk, and \[\mathcal H^2_d(B_d(x,r))=\pi r^2.\] Consequently \(\alpha=\pi\) works in [eq:ahlfors] (#eq:ahlfors) for every \(L\). Each such ball contracts inside itself by Euclidean radial contraction, so \(\Lambda=1\) also works uniformly. These are even the smallest allowed upper Ahlfors and LLC constants in this example.

Let \(B=B_d(p,2)=X_L\), and take the closed half-cylinder \[E=[0,L/2]\times(\mathbb R/4\mathbb Z).\] Then \[\mu(E)=\mu(X_L\setminus E)=2L.\] For \(0<t<1\), the exterior \(t\)-neighborhood adds a strip of width \(t\) along each of the two boundary circles, each of length \(4\). Equivalently, its long-coordinate interval has length \(L/2+2t\). Hence \[\mu(E_t)=2L+8t,\qquad
 \mathcal M_-(E\mid\lambda B)=8\quad\hbox{for every }\lambda\ge1.\] The asserted uniform conclusion is therefore \[2L\le64\,C(2,\pi,1),\qquad\text{or}\qquad
 C(2,\pi,1)\ge L/32.\] As \(L\) is arbitrary, no such finite uniform constant exists. Increasing the dilation has no effect because \(\lambda B=X_L\).

The same family diagnoses the proof’s uniform-doubling inference. For example, \[\frac{\mu(B_d(p,3/2))}{\mu(B_d(p,3/4))}
       =\frac{64L}{9\pi}.\] Each individual torus is doubling; a bound from the three listed data does not follow.
result: If Ahlfors regularity was intended to include a bound on the total measure at the diameter scale, this family would be excluded. The supplied definition explicitly restricts the upper bound to \(r<D\), while the theorem concerns every open ball. Interpreting data dependence as permitting an arbitrary larger Ahlfors constant chosen using total volume would hide the missing datum. The ordinary quantitative interpretation must apply to the valid common choice \(\alpha=\pi\).

This is a counterexample to the stated uniform dependence. It is not a counterexample to the existence of some finite \(C\) for a fixed \(X_L\). The source’s qualitative existence conclusion can be retained with the additional parameter described in Section 5 (#sec:repair).
Impact: Uniform dependence false. Each fixed torus still admits finite constants; qualitative theorem not disproved.

report: Abstract: This review identifies six concerns in the specified author manuscript: an incorrect objectwise calculation for an augmented complex, a false exterior-power formula, an invalid step in the proof of flag surjectivity, a reversed filtration convention, omitted degenerate relaxation cases, and a scalar-field mismatch in the determinant differential. Explicit examples establish the affected claims and constructions. Complete replacement arguments are supplied for flag surjectivity and rational determinant normalization; more limited repairs are distinguished from them. The maximization theorem itself is not refuted by the augmented-complex example. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
