Title: Technical Verification of
Categorical Valuative Invariants of Polyhedra and Matroids
# Identity, conventions, and scope

The reviewed paper is by Ben Elias, Dane Miyata, Nicholas Proudfoot, and Lorenzo Vecchi, Categorical valuative invariants of polyhedra and matroids [paper], specifically arXiv:2401.06869v4, dated 22 October 2024. The assignment links it to DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0065 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0065). The acquired 56-page PDF is an author manuscript; correspondence with the journal version of record has not been established. Page references are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed pagination.

The lead review and native helpers read the source across all 56 pages. Proof reconstruction was deepest for the six concerns below, which received explicit hypothesis checks and independent calculations. Other arguments received claim and dependency checks. External results cited by the paper were not all independently re-proved, including the external Chow-basis, stellahedral, and skew-Specht results. Separate supplements and released author code were unavailable in the acquired inputs; their absence is not a mathematical defect. No author code was executed. No later-version or erratum correspondence, author adoption, or first-discovery claim is established here.

We retain the paper’s conventions. A morphism \(M\to M'\) on one ground set means that every basis of \(M'\) is a basis of \(M\); the ranks agree and \(\operatorname{rk}_{M'}(S)\leq\operatorname{rk}_M(S)\) for every \(S\) (p. 15). Write \(d(M)=\dim P(M)\), distinct from matroid rank. For a decomposition \(\mathcal Q\) of a \(d\)-dimensional polyhedron \(P\), \(C_\bullet^\Omega(\mathcal Q)\) includes both the internal-cell terms and an augmentation \(P\) in degree \(d+1\) (pp. 10, 17). The notation \(X[-i]\) places \(X\) in degree \(i\) (p. 7). Exact finite complexes of \(\mathbb Q\)-vector spaces are split exact; this does not identify exactness with contractibility in an arbitrary additive category.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The augmented complex contradicts Lemma 6.9).  Assessment: Major. On p. 29, \(C(F)_\bullet=\Delta_\psi(C_\bullet^\Omega(\mathcal Q))^F\) contains all copies of \(F\) in the full augmented complex. For \(F\) internal in \(\mathcal Q_\psi\), Lemma 6.9 (p. 30) claims \[C(F)_\bullet\simeq F[-\dim P+\dim P_\psi-\dim F].\] An allowed trivial decomposition contradicts this claim.

Take \(V=\mathbb R\), \(P=[0,1]\), \(\psi(x)=x\), and \(\mathcal Q=\{\{0\},\{1\},[0,1]\}\). This finite collection is face-closed, has intersections that are common faces, and covers \(P\); Remark 3.1 explicitly permits it. The functional is nonconstant and bounded above. Moreover \(P_\psi=F=\{1\}\) and \(\mathcal Q_\psi=\{\{1\}\}\), whose sole zero-dimensional cell is internal relative to \(P_\psi\).

Equation reference: eq:aug. Here \(\mathcal Q_1=\mathcal Q_2=\{P\}\) and \(\mathcal Q_0=\varnothing\). With agreeing orientations the source complex is \(P\) in degree \(2\) mapped by \(\mathrm{id}\) to \(P\) in degree \(1\). By the definition of \(\Delta_\psi\) (p. 26), \[
 C(F)_\bullet=(F\text{ in degree }2
       \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}_F}F\text{ in degree }1)=\operatorname{Null}(F,2).\] Taking \(h_1=\mathrm{id}_F\) contracts it. After the trivial vector-space functor \(\tau\), all homology vanishes, whereas Lemma 6.9 predicts \(F[-1]\), with \(H_1=\mathbb Q\).

The same failure occurs for the nontrivial subdivision of \([0,2]\) at \(1\): the full image complex is \(\operatorname{Null}(\{2\},2)\oplus\operatorname{Null}(\{1\},1)\). The augmentation maps isomorphically to the cell ending at \(2\); the cell ending at \(1\) maps isomorphically to the internal vertex. The maximizing-face block again has zero homology.

Theorem 6.3’s proof (p. 31) uses Lemma 6.9 to determine a minimal complex \(D_\bullet\) for the full image complex. In the trivial example this minimum is zero, yet the proof identifies its shift, as a graded object, with the nonzero two-term augmented \(C_\bullet(\mathcal Q_\psi)\). This stronger identification is also false. The artificial \(P\) term cannot silently be discarded: the full and truncated complexes are separately defined, and p. 29 requires all copies of \(F\). The one-object calculation [eq:aug] (#eq:aug) is unaffected by the order repair in Problem Problem 4 (#prob:order).

Theorem 6.3 is explicitly the technical heart (p. 26). Its use in Lemma 7.4 leads to Theorem 7.3 and categorical convolution in Corollary 7.7, so this is a central invalid derivation. Theorem 6.3 itself is not refuted: its asserted homotopy equivalence holds in these examples because both augmented complexes are contractible. Replacing the blocks by those of \(\Delta_\psi(C_{\leq d}^\Omega(\mathcal Q))\) fixes these local calculations, but a general proof must then transport and verify the augmentation before taking its cone. That complete repair has not been established here.

Problem 2 (Corollary 9.8 has the wrong exterior-power degree).  Assessment: Major. Corollary 9.8 (p. 52) uses \(\bigwedge^k V_{[h-1,1]}\) in the Orlik–Solomon relaxation formula, where \(k=\operatorname{rk}M\) and \(h=|H|\). Lemma 9.7 on the same page uses \(\bigwedge^{k-1}V_{[h-1,1]}\). The corollary’s formula gives an incorrect graded dimension.

Let \(\Gamma=\{1\}\), \(E=\{1,2,3\}\), \(H=\{1,2\}\), and \[M=U_{1,\{1,2\}}\sqcup U_{1,\{3\}},\qquad k=2,\quad h=2.\] The bases are \(13,23\). The set \(H\) is a rank-one flat since adjoining \(3\) raises its rank. Its restriction and contraction are \(U_{1,2}\) and \(U_{1,1}\), respectively, so it is stressed under p. 13’s definition. Its cusp is \(\{12\}\) and relaxation gives \(\widetilde M=U_{2,3}\). The group, orbit, induction, and restriction factors are trivial.

The circuit \(12\) gives \(u_2-u_1=0\) in \(\operatorname{OS}(M)\), leaving dimensions \((1,2,1)\). For \(U_{2,3}\) the boundary of the only circuit \(123\) gives one relation among three degree-two monomials, yielding \((1,3,2)\). Equivalently, for \(1<2<3\) the no-broken-circuit sets are \(\varnothing,1,3,13\) and \(\varnothing,1,2,3,12,13\), respectively. Consequently \[\pi_{\widetilde M}(t)-\pi_M(t)=t+t^2.\] Since \(V_{[1,1]}\) is one-dimensional, \(\bigwedge^2V_{[1,1]}=0\), and the printed corollary predicts zero difference. Independent finite enumeration confirms these basis, flatness, and dimension calculations [checks].

Equation reference: eq:wedgefix. The supported local correction replaces \(k\) by \(k-1\) in the exterior power: \[
 \operatorname{OS}(\widetilde M)=\operatorname{OS}(M)+
 \operatorname{Ind}_{\Gamma_H}^{\Gamma}
 \left(\operatorname{Res}_{\Gamma_H}^{S_h}\bigwedge\nolimits^{k-1}V_{[h-1,1]}\right)
 \otimes\bigl(\mathbb Q(1-k)\oplus\mathbb Q(-k)\bigr).\] Here restriction means pullback along \(\Gamma_H\to S_h\). Where Proposition 9.6 and Lemma 9.7 apply, substitution gives [eq:wedgefix] (#eq:wedgefix), and it restores the displayed example. This does not separately settle all exceptional orbits in Problem Problem 5 (#prob:relax). The false quantitative formula is an explicitly advertised application (p. 4), and the ease of editing its exponent does not remove that impact. This example does not invalidate categorical valuativity or the corrected formula.

Problem 3 (Proposition 8.19 assumes a false intersection rank).  Assessment: Major. The induction proving Whitney-map surjectivity (p. 43) asserts that a source lift \(F_2\) with \(\operatorname{cl}_{M'}(F_2)=F'_2\) makes \(F'_1\cap F_2\) a rank-\(k_1\) flat of \(M'|F_2\). That rank does not follow from the induction hypothesis.

Take \[M=U_{3,4},\qquad
 M'=U_{2,\{1,2,3\}}\sqcup U_{1,\{4\}}.\] Every \(M'\)-basis (\(124,134,234\)) is an \(M\)-basis, so the identity map is an allowed rank-preserving weak map. The target flag \(F'_1=\{3\}\subset F'_2=\{1,2,3\}\) has ranks \(1,2\). The source flat \(F_2=\{1,2\}\) has rank two and \(\operatorname{cl}_{M'}(F_2)=F'_2\), but \(F'_1\cap F_2=\varnothing\) has rank zero. Thus an arbitrary valid inductive lift need not have the asserted compatibility with the lower flag. A different lift, such as \(\{1,3\}\), would work; the final existence claim is not refuted. The invalid step feeds directly into Corollary 8.20, a main monotonicity result highlighted on p. 5.
Verified replacement argument 1.  Every Whitney map \(\Phi_{\boldsymbol k}(M)\to\Phi_{\boldsymbol k}(M')\) associated with the paper’s weak maps is surjective.

Proof. Identify the ground sets. For a target flag \(F'_1\subset\cdots\subset F'_r\), choose nested bases \(B_1\subset\cdots\subset B_r\), with \(B_i\) a basis of \(F'_i\) in \(M'\). An \(M'\)-independent set extends to an \(M'\)-basis, hence is also \(M\)-independent. Put \(F_i=\operatorname{cl}_M(B_i)\). These are nested source flats of ranks \(k_i\), strictly nested for strictly increasing \(k_i\).

If \(x\in F_i\), then \[k_i=\operatorname{rk}_{M'}(B_i)
 \leq\operatorname{rk}_{M'}(B_i\cup\{x\})
 \leq\operatorname{rk}_M(B_i\cup\{x\})=k_i.\] Hence \(x\in\operatorname{cl}_{M'}(B_i)=F'_i\) and \(B_i\subseteq F_i\subseteq F'_i\). Taking closure in \(M'\) gives \(\operatorname{cl}_{M'}(F_i)=F'_i\), so the source flag maps to the prescribed target flag. For rank zero, take the empty basis; the same argument uses the source and target loop flats. ◻

This proves the exact proposition without a new assumption. The direct sums of shifted Whitney functors then give Corollary 8.20. For the ordinary Chow functor a looped target has zero space, and a weak map from a looped source to a loopless target cannot occur; the remaining cases use those direct sums. The augmented functor is handled directly. This is a complete analytic repair, separate from the valuativity proof issues elsewhere.

Problem 4 (The objectwise filtration uses the opposite order).  Assessment: Minor. Section 2.4 (p. 9) defines \(X\leq Y\) by an arrow \(X\to Y\), then uses lower-object collections for subcomplexes \(C^{\leq X}\) and \(C^{<X}\). Their quotient need not contain only copies of \(X\).

In the thin category with \(a<b\) and one nonidentity arrow \(f:a\to b\), take the bounded complex \(C_1=a\xrightarrow{f}C_0=b\) in its additive \(\mathbb Q\)-linear closure. A termwise-split subcomplex supported only on \(a\) is zero: otherwise \(f\) would land in the excluded \(b\) term. Thus \(C^{\leq a}=C^{<b}=0\) and \(C^{\leq b}=C\), making the paper’s \(C^b\) the full two-object complex. It is minimal in the stated sense, since the differential joins distinct objects, but its differential is nonzero. This contradicts the asserted triviality of the differential of a minimal objectwise part.

Use upper sets \(C^{\geq X},C^{>X}\) and quotient \(C^{\geq X}/C^{>X}\) instead, or reverse the order convention consistently. Upper sets are closed under arrows; the quotient contains only the object class \(X\), whose minimal complex has zero differential. This completely repairs the local filtration statement and does not refute minimal-complex uniqueness. It cannot repair the independent one-object counterexample in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:aug).

Problem 5 (Relaxation statements omit degenerate configurations).  Assessment: Minor. The exceptional branch of Theorem 3.10 (p. 14) identifies simultaneous orbit relaxation with one single-flat relaxation when \(M=\Pi\). Theorem 3.8 also misclassifies internal faces when a stressed flat has empty cusp, a case allowed by the printed definition.

For the orbit case take \(F=\{1,2\}\), \(F'=\{3,4\}\), and \[M=U_{1,F}\sqcup U_{1,F'}=\Pi_{1,2,F,E},\qquad
 \Gamma=\langle(13)(24)\rangle.\] The two blocks are rank-one flats with uniform restriction and contraction; \(\Gamma\) preserves \(M\) and swaps them. Their cusps are \(\{12\}\) and \(\{34\}\), so \[\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal B(M)&=\{13,14,23,24\},\\
 \mathcal B(\Lambda_F)&=\mathcal B(M)\cup\{12\},\\
 \mathcal B(\Lambda_{F'})&=\mathcal B(M)\cup\{34\},\\
 \mathcal B(\widetilde M)&=\binom E2.
 \end{aligned}\] Thus \(\widetilde M=U_{2,4}\) has six bases, while \(\Lambda_F\) has five. Its octahedron is divided into two maximal square pyramids by \(x_1+x_2=1\), with internal common square \(P(M)\). The point \((1/2,1/2,1/2,1/2)\) witnesses internality. Theorem 3.10’s asserted trivial decomposition of \(\Lambda_F\) is false; Example 3.11 (p. 15) expressly admits this orbit.

For the empty-cusp case take \(M=U_{2,3}\), \(F=\{1\}\). It is a rank-one flat with uniform restriction \(U_{1,1}\) and contraction \(U_{1,2}\). But no two-element set contains two elements of \(F\), so the cusp is empty and \(\widetilde M=M\). Here \(\Pi=\Lambda\) has bases \(12,13\), whereas \(M\) also has basis \(23\). Although \(M\ne\Pi\), \(P(\Pi)\) is the boundary edge \(x_1=1\) of the triangle \(P(M)\), and the only internal face is \(M\). This contradicts Theorem 3.8’s second branch; p. 13 supplies no nonempty-cusp exclusion.

An orbit-singleton condition makes the first asserted trivial identification valid, while a nonempty-cusp condition excludes the second example. A complete classification of all degenerate orbits is not supplied here. The same incorrect shortcut \(\widetilde M=\Lambda_F\) opens the proof of Proposition 9.6 (p. 50), but its formula survives the square example. Writing \(\varepsilon\) for the sign character of \(C_2\), the actual determinant-twisted subdivision gives \[\Phi(U_{2,4})=\operatorname{Ind}_1^{C_2}\Phi(\Lambda_F)-\Phi(M)\otimes\varepsilon.\] The identity \(\operatorname{Ind}_1^{C_2}\operatorname{Res}_1^{C_2}\Phi(M)=\Phi(M)\otimes(1\oplus\varepsilon)\) makes this agree with Proposition 9.6’s printed formula. Thus these examples establish a false exceptional classification and proof shortcut, but not a false final representation identity.

Problem 6 (A unit normal need not be a rational morphism).  Assessment: Major. Sections 9.2–9.3 (pp. 48–49) define the rational spaces \[V(N)=\operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb R}\{x-y:x,y\in P(N)\}\cap\mathbb Q^E,\qquad
 L(N,N')=\bigwedge^{d(N)-d(N')}(V(N)/V(N')).\] The differential is specified as the class of an outward unit normal. That real class need not belong to the rational morphism line.

Split \(P=P(U_{2,5})=\{x\in[0,1]^5:\sum x_i=2\}\) at \(x_1+x_2=1\). Let \(H=\{1,2\}\). The upper cell \(N_+\) has all two-element bases meeting \(H\); the lower \(N_-\) has all pairs except \(12\); the common cell is \(N_0=U_{1,\{1,2\}}\sqcup U_{1,\{3,4,5\}}\). These are rank-two matroids: \(N_+\) has parallel class \(\{3,4,5\}\), \(N_-\) has parallel class \(\{1,2\}\), and \(N_0\) has the displayed two parallel classes. Basis exchange was also independently enumerated.

Their polytopes are the two closed half-hypersimplices and the common cut, as follows directly from the rank-two parallel-class inequalities. Equivalently, the cut creates no new nonintegral vertices, since \(x_1+x_2\) changes by at most one along a hypersimplex edge. Including all faces gives a matroid subdivision. The point \((1/2,1/2,1/3,1/3,1/3)\) lies in the relative interior of the cut and of \(P\), so \(N_0\) is internal. The dimensions are \(4,4,3\).

The maximal-cell tangent space is \(V=\{v\in\mathbb Q^5:\sum v_i=0\}\) and \[V(N_0)=\{v\in\mathbb Q^5:v_1+v_2=0,\ v_3+v_4+v_5=0\}.\] An orthogonal normal in \(V\) is \(n=(3,3,-2,-2,-2)\) with \(\|n\|^2=30\); the outward unit normals are \(\pm n/\sqrt{30}\). The rational functional \(\delta_H(v)=v_1+v_2\) annihilates \(V(N_0)\) and is rational-valued on the rational quotient. On the proposed unit-normal class it instead gives \(\pm6/\sqrt{30}\), an irrational number. That class is not a morphism in the specified category. This is a scalar-field defect, independent of a real-field check of \(d^2=0\).

A coherent rational repair uses \(\Lambda_N=V(N)\cap\mathbb Z^E\). For a facet \(N'\), take the outward primitive generator of the rank-one lattice \(\Lambda_N/\Lambda_{N'}\). The sublattice is saturated, so the quotient is free, and the determinant isomorphism for \[0\longrightarrow\Lambda_{N'}\longrightarrow\Lambda_N
 \longrightarrow\Lambda_N/\Lambda_{N'}\longrightarrow0\] takes primitive generators to primitive generators. Orienting these determinant lattices identifies the differentials with ordinary incidence coefficients \(\pm1\). For a codimension-two incidence the two facet paths give opposite primitive generators of the same determinant line and cancel. The augmentation uses the common tangent lattice of parent and maximal cells, so its diagonal maps remain identities. Coordinate permutations preserve both the lattices and outward rays, establishing equivariance.

This verifies the replacement differential and Proposition 9.2’s orientation comparison: primitive oriented determinant bases identify the corrected complex with the ordinary oriented decomposition complex. Merely omitting the word unit would not prescribe coherent scalars. The original undefined rational complex is central to the orientation-independent machinery of Corollary 9.3, supporting Major. The rational replacement restores that construction for a valuative functor; it does not refute the virtual-character identity or resolve Problem Problem 1 (#prob:aug).

Title: Technical Verification of
Symplectic Capacities of Domains Close to the Ball and
Banach–Mazur Geodesics in the Space of Contact Forms
# Identity, conventions, and scope

This review concerns Alberto Abbondandolo, Gabriele Benedetti, and Oliver Edtmair, Symplectic capacities of domains close to the ball and Banach–Mazur geodesics in the space of contact forms [paper], arXiv:2312.07363v1, dated 12 December 2023, a 70-page author manuscript. The assignment associates it with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0066 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0066). Equality with the journal version of record has not been established. All page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with the printed numbers on the inspected pages.

The lead reviewer and three native helpers read the source across all 70 pages. The deepest independent reconstructions concern the three problems below, the Hamiltonian suspension identities, the capacity sandwiches, and the metric argument. The normal-form theorem imported from [AB23], symplectic-field-theory compactness, and the Gromov–Witten input are used as named external results rather than independently re-proved in this review. The appendix received argument and parameter checks, not an independent reconstruction of every external Anosov–Katok result. Acquired inputs contain no separate author code or supplement whose absence establishes a mathematical defect. No author code was executed. No claim is made about later versions, errata, author adoption, or priority of these observations.

We use the manuscript’s convention \(\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH\) and its extrinsic capacities, whose monotonicity is required for ambient symplectomorphisms. A compatible almost complex structure satisfies that \(\omega(\,\cdot\,,J\,\cdot\,)\) is symmetric positive definite. On the symplectization in \(\alpha\)-coordinates, \(\omega=d(e^a\alpha)\). The class \(\mathcal J(\alpha)\) permits arbitrary compatible structures in a compact middle region; adjustment to \(\alpha\) is required only at the two ends (pp. 47–48).
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Major: the global radial stretch need not preserve compatibility).  The proof of Theorem 10.1 on p. 49 asserts that \(f_r(a,p)=(ra,p)\) induces a bijection \(f_r^*:\mathcal J(r\alpha)\longrightarrow\mathcal J(\alpha)\). This is false for the class defined on p. 48, although the end adjustment transforms correctly.
## Exact check

Equation reference: eq:badmatrix. Work at \(a=0\) in symplectic tangent coordinates \((a,R_\alpha,x,y)\), with \(\Omega=\operatorname{diag}(W,W)\) and \(W=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). For \(r=2\), set \[J_b=\operatorname{diag}
 \left(\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\1/2&0\end{pmatrix},
       \begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\right),
 \qquad
 S=\begin{pmatrix}
 1&0&0&0\\0&1&0&-1\\1&0&1&0\\0&0&0&1
 \end{pmatrix}.\] Here \(S^T\Omega S=\Omega\) and \(J=S J_bS^{-1}\) is compatible. For example, the leading principal minors of the symmetric matrix \(\Omega J\) are \(3/2,3,1,1\), all positive. With \(D=df_2=\operatorname{diag}(2,1,1,1)\), however, \[\Omega(D^{-1}JD)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 3&0&-1&0\\
 0&1&0&1\\
 -2&0&1&0\\
 0&2&0&3
 \end{pmatrix},
 \] which is not symmetric. Thus \(f_2^*J\) is not compatible.

This is an admissible middle-region example, not an inadmissible end condition. Start with a \(2\alpha\)-adjusted structure and implant the displayed compatible value in a small interior chart, keeping the structure fixed outside that chart. One may use a symplectic frame and a smooth path from the identity to \(S\) with a bump function. Equivalently, the local quadratic Hamiltonian \(a y\) has the shear \(S\) as its linearized time-one map; a cutoff realizes it locally. Compatibility is preserved by symplectic conjugation and the two ends remain adjusted. The four-dimensional example also embeds as a direct summand in higher dimensions. Exact rational matrix calculations were independently run and retained with exit status zero.
## Verified replacement

For each given \(J\in\mathcal J(r\alpha)\) choose a compact interval containing its entire non-adjusted region. Choose a smooth increasing diffeomorphism \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) which is the identity on that interval and has derivative \(r\) outside a larger interval. Its transition regions can be placed entirely where \(J\) is adjusted. Put \(F(a,p)=(f(a),p)\).

On the identity region \(F^*J=J\). In either adjusted transition region, write the tangent splitting as \(\langle\partial_a,R_\alpha\rangle\oplus\xi\). Then \[(F^*J)\partial_a=\frac{f'}r R_\alpha,
 \qquad (F^*J)R_\alpha=-\frac r{f'}\partial_a.\] Since \(f'>0\), this block is compatible with \(da\wedge\alpha\), and the \(\xi\)-block remains compatible with \(d\alpha\). The positive factor \(e^a\) does not change compatibility. At both ends \(f'=r\), so \(F^*J\) is \(\alpha\)-adjusted and belongs to \(\mathcal J(\alpha)\).

The diffeomorphism \(F^{-1}\) gives an exact bijection between the corresponding holomorphic curves with transformed point constraints. It preserves nonconstant components, punctured-sphere domains and the existence of a negative end. The affine reparameterizations at infinity preserve finite energy and asymptotic geometric orbits; on the compact transition band the relevant positive energy norms are uniformly comparable. Their positive actions satisfy \(A^+_{r\alpha}(u)=r A^+_\alpha(F^{-1}u)\). For each original auxiliary datum this gives an infimum bounded by \(r c_k(\alpha)\). Taking the supremum yields \(c_k(r\alpha)\le r c_k(\alpha)\); the same construction with \(1/r\) gives the reverse inequality. This proves scaling without the false fixed-map bijection.

The severity concerns an invalid derivation of a structural property used for continuity, degenerate extensions and the lower bound in Theorem 5 (p. 58). The replacement repairs this scaling step. It does not independently establish the other analytic properties of Theorem 10.1 or refute its final scaling conclusion.

Problem 2 (Major: the parameter limit in the spectral identification is reversed).  In Section 11, p. 59 defines \(\beta_t=((1-t)S+t)\alpha_0\) and claims that its short closed orbits are independent of \(t\in(0,1]\). Page 60 then invokes Proposition 10.4 for small positive \(t\) on the ground that this coefficient is \(C^2\)-close to \(1\). These are the wrong endpoint and limit for the displayed family.

Equation reference: eq:norm. For nonconstant invariant \(S\), at \(t=1\) the form is \(\alpha_0\) and every Zoll fiber is an orbit. For \(t<1\), a fiber through a point with \(dS\ne0\) is not a Reeb orbit of \(\beta_t\); the short fibers are the critical fibers. Also, exactly, \[\|((1-t)S+t)-1\|_{C^2}=(1-t)\|S-1\|_{C^2}.
 \] The available normal-form control at this step is \(C^1\)-closeness of \(S\). Taking \(t\) near zero does not provide the required \(C^2\) control. This is the step identifying \(c_0(\alpha),c_1(\alpha)\) with the minimum and maximum short periods, hence it is directly used in Theorem 5, not an unrelated notation issue.
## Verified replacement for this step

Write \(T_0=\operatorname{sys}(\alpha_0)\) and use \(0\le t<1\). The normal-form relations \(dS=-B[V]\), with \(V\) small in \(C^1\), and the short-orbit argument of Proposition 4.3 and Lemma 4.4 apply uniformly to \(V_t=(1-t)V\). They identify the short orbits with the critical fibers of \(S\) for every \(t<1\), with actions \(((1-t)S(\gamma)+t)T_0\).

Problem 3 (Major for the unrestricted sharpness claims: dimension one must be excluded).  Page 7 explicitly allows contact dimension \(2n-1\) with \(n\ge1\). Proposition 3 on p. 9 has no exclusion of \(n=1\) and asserts a strict increase of the systolic ratio near every Zoll form. Proposition 1 on p. 4 likewise states the strict capacity inequality without excluding the planar case.

On the circle, any positive form \(\alpha=f(\theta)d\theta\) has \(R_\alpha=f^{-1}\partial_\theta\). Its minimal period and contact volume both equal \(\int_{S^1}\alpha\), so \[\rho_{\rm sys}(\alpha)
 =\frac{\operatorname{sys}(\alpha)}{\int_{S^1}\alpha}=1.\] In particular \(\alpha_0=d\theta\) is Zoll and admits no strict improvement whatsoever. This directly contradicts Proposition 3 in an expressly included dimension, independently of any regularity or limiting argument.

For completeness, Proposition 1 also fails in dimension two of the ambient symplectic space. A planar smooth star-shaped domain \(D\) has boundary \(I=b(\theta)>0\) in action-angle coordinates \(I=r^2/2\), with \(\omega=dI\wedge d\theta\) and area \(A=\int_0^{2\pi}b(\theta)d\theta\). Choose a circle diffeomorphism \(g\) with \(g'=2\pi b/A\). The annular map \[(I,\theta)\longmapsto \bigl(I/g'(\theta),g(\theta)\bigr)\] preserves \(dI\wedge d\theta\) and sends the boundary to \(I=A/(2\pi)\). It extends to an ambient compactly supported Hamiltonian diffeomorphism: interpolate the lifts by \(g_t=(1-t)\operatorname{id}+tg\), whose derivatives stay positive; write \(\eta_t=\dot g_t\circ g_t^{-1}\) and use \(H_t=-I\eta_t(\theta)\). Its vector field is \(-I\eta_t'\partial_I+\eta_t\partial_\theta\). Cut off this Hamiltonian on an annulus containing all boundary trajectories, with cutoff identically one on a neighborhood of those trajectories and zero near the origin and infinity. The boundary map is unchanged, and the bounded component maps to the disk of area \(A\). Normalization and ambient invariance give \(c(D)=A\) for every normalized capacity; Stokes gives \(\operatorname{sys}(D)=A\). The claimed strict inequality is impossible.

The verified correction is to restrict these strict sharpness statements to \(n\ge2\). Section 2 uses a nonempty displaceable open set in the transverse ball in \(\mathbb C^{n-1}\) (pp. 18–20), which requires that restriction. The positive capacity coincidence and local systolic results are not contradicted in dimension one; on a connected circle the latter is equality. Related dimension-free claims of arbitrarily large systolic ratio need the same restriction. This is a false boundary case of the asserted sharpness, not evidence against the higher-dimensional construction.
# Other checks and remaining scope

The Hamiltonian suspension formulas were checked with the stated sign convention: \(\Phi^*\lambda_0=(\pi+s)dt+\widehat\lambda_0\), \(\iota_{X_{\widetilde H}}(ds\wedge dt+\widehat\omega_0)=d(H-s)\), and \(n!\operatorname{vol}D(H)=\pi^n+n\operatorname{Cal}(\varphi)\). The absolute-value bars in the action bound (2.2) on p. 19 are present in the actual PDF; their loss in text extraction is not a source error. The scaled short/long period estimates and the displaceable-set construction are consistent in positive transverse dimension.

The local normal-form, generating-function and Moser steps were checked against their stated derivative estimates. The homogeneous contact lift and cutoff used for the capacity embeddings were checked for ambient extendibility. Theorem 4(ii)’s length assertion follows directly from \(d(\gamma(s),\gamma(t))\le|t-s|\operatorname{osc}f\) and the endpoint equality; separation of points by the pseudo-metric is unnecessary. The appendix’s rational approximants can be chosen with distinct ratios and increasing denominators, so this selectable detail was not promoted to a false existence claim. These checks do not amount to a formal certification of every proof.
# Conclusion

The assessment is Major for the exact reviewed version: two core derivations need the displayed replacement arguments and the unrestricted sharpness claims need a dimension hypothesis. Repair status is separate from scientific adjudication and author adoption.

The strongest independent checks concern the counterexamples below, their local repairs, pressure and sampling quantifiers, the scaled Hölder sums, and finite specification concatenation. Those are explicit external inputs, not purportedly reproduced computations. No author code was executed; absence of separately supplied code is not treated as a defect. No assertion is made about subsequent versions, errata, priority, or author adoption.

Write \(f_t\) for the flow, \(x_t=f_t(x)\), and \(E\oplus F\) for the normal stable/center-unstable splitting. The quantities \(d_E,d_F\) are the manuscript’s fake-leaf lengths. A sectional-hyperbolic estimate with a fixed multiplicative constant does not imply the same estimate with constant one at every positive real time. This distinction is material even when the total good-segment length is an integer.
# Core findings

Problem 1 (Major: Lemma 7.4 fails at arbitrary real times).  Lemma 7.4(b), p. 61, asserts that outside \(W_r\), initial \(d_F\ge d_E\) implies a ratio at least \(\lambda_R^t\) after time \(t\), with \(\lambda_R>1\) and no prefactor. Its proof invokes time-one domination. The stated real-time assertion is false under those hypotheses.
## A smooth, admissible dynamical counterexample

Equation reference: eq:metric. Let \(A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(\lambda=(3+\sqrt5)/2\), and \(\mu=\log\lambda\). Take the unit-roof mapping torus of \(A\) with its suspension flow. Its stable line is \(E^{ss}\), and its flow and unstable directions span \(F^{cu}\). Give the flow unit speed, make the three directions orthogonal, and in suspension coordinates use the norm weights \[w_s(\theta)=e^{-\mu\theta},\qquad
 w_u(\theta)=e^{\mu\theta+h(\theta)},\qquad
 h(\theta)=-6\sin(2\pi\theta).
 \] These define a smooth global metric: at \(\theta+1\) the weights are respectively \(\lambda^{-1}\) and \(\lambda\) times their values at \(\theta\), precisely as required by the \(A\) identification. All derivatives match because \(h\) is smooth and periodic.

Every time-one stable norm is \(\lambda^{-1}<1/2\); the time-one sectional area factor on \(F^{cu}\) is \(\lambda>1\); the normal unstable/stable ratio gains \(\lambda^2\). At general times the bounded factor involving \(h\) supplies the allowed fixed constants in sectional hyperbolicity and domination. Thus the flow satisfies the stated type of hypotheses. It has no singularities, so \(W_r\) is empty. The whole manifold is an Anosov attractor; if a proper attractor is desired, take its product with a contracting normal direction and use the invariant sink slice.

At each phase of this periodic orbit the time-one normal return is hyperbolic. The locally invariant fake leaves have tangents equal to its stable and unstable eigendirections. Choose an arbitrarily small transverse displacement whose initial fake-leaf ratio tends to \(11/10\). Its terminal ratio tends to \((11/10)G<1\), since \(e^{2/5}>1+2/5>11/10\). The strict inequality persists for sufficiently small nonzero displacement. Shrinking it also puts it in any specified Bowen ball for this fixed finite time. Initially \(d_F>d_E\), but finally \(d_F<d_E\), contradicting the claimed bound \(\lambda_R^{13/12}>1\). This uses actual leaf lengths through their tangents, not a different definition of \(d_E,d_F\).
## Impact and repair boundary

Pages 54–55 explicitly restrict fake-foliation invariance to integer iterates. Page 62 applies Lemma 7.4 on intervals between singular exits and entries. These have arbitrary real lengths even if the full good segment has integer length. The resulting preservation of a large \(F\)-coordinate is used in Proposition 7.2, the Bowen property in Theorem 5.1, and the route to Theorem C and its applications.

A discrete proof with bounded end-interval factors, or a suitably adapted continuous-time geometry, may repair this route. Such a repair has not been completed here. Simply adding a constant to the exponential estimate does not establish the repeated threshold \(d_F\ge d_E\) needed at the next passage. The finding is a false core intermediate assertion and invalid use of it, not a counterexample to Theorems A–C or the final Bowen property.

Problem 2 (Major: the Pliss conclusion uses the wrong sampling grid).  Definitions 10 and 11 (pp. 31, 33) sample backward from a possibly real endpoint \(t\). Lemma 4.7 (p. 35) nevertheless demands selected times in \([0,t]\cap\mathbb N\). Its argument produces times \(t-j\), which need not be integers.

Use a roof-two suspension of a hyperbolic toral automorphism, taking a suitable power for the prescribed time-one bounds. Start at phase zero, and let \[W=\{\theta\pmod2:0.8<\theta<1.2\},\qquad t=N+\tfrac12 .\] There are no singularities, so this is an open neighborhood of \(\operatorname{Sing}(X)\cap\Lambda\) as allowed by the lemma. Both endpoints lie outside \(W\), and every backward sample \(t-j\) has phase \(1/2\) or \(3/2\), so its \(W\) frequency is zero. For any \(\beta_0<1/2\), however, an odd positive integer endpoint lies in \(W\) and fails recurrence; an even positive integer endpoint has frequency \(1/2\) in its last two samples and also fails. Time zero is not an admissible positive-length Pliss time under the definitions. No positive integer candidate exists, however large \(N\) is. The other Pliss condition need not be tested once every candidate fails recurrence.

The local correction selects candidates on the common endpoint grid \((t-\mathbb Z)\cap(1,t]\) and retains strict slack in the large-\(N\) counts. There is a further interface to repair: \(\mathcal G_B\) on p. 37 is defined for integer durations, whereas the first-exit time \(p(x,t)\) on p. 41 is real. Consequently the core duration \(s-p(x,t)\) used on p. 42 need not be an integer. Choosing all later endpoints on the grid of \(\widetilde s(x,t)\) aligns suffix increments but does not make the core duration integer. A Bowen result for the resulting real-time collection and a coherent decomposition are still required. The bare Lemma 4.8. on p. 35 also needs its intended statement. Integer-grid concatenation follows by splitting the backward products and counts at the join; it does not justify arbitrary phase changes.
A local phase correction is established, while a complete combined repair of Sections 5 and 7 is not. The defect directly affects the good/bad decomposition used by the uniqueness criterion.

Problem 3 (Major: Lemma 5.9 cannot hold for every empirical limit).  The pressure on p. 42 is a limsup over real times. Lemma 5.9 (p. 43) bounds it by the measure pressure of any limit point of the integer-indexed empirical measures. Appendix A (pp. 78–79) incorrectly replaces growth along an arbitrary subsequence by the full limsup.

Take two distinct periodic orbits \(\gamma_0,\gamma_1\) of a transitive Anosov suspension and a smooth potential \(\varphi\) equal to \(0\) and \(1\), respectively, on them. Such examples lie in the same sectional-hyperbolic setting; singularity assumptions are vacuous. For each \(t>0\) let \(\mathcal C_t\) be a singleton on \(\gamma_0\) when \(\lfloor t\rfloor\) is odd and on \(\gamma_1\) when it is even. Every separated partition sum is exactly \(1\) or \(e^t\), hence \(P(\mathcal C,\varphi,\delta)=1\). Along odd integers the empirical limit is the invariant measure on \(\gamma_0\), with entropy zero and potential integral zero. The asserted inequality reads \(1\le0\).

Even replacing the arbitrary limit by an integer subsequence is insufficient for arbitrary \(\mathcal C\): put the singleton on \(\gamma_0\) at every integer and on \(\gamma_1\) at every noninteger. The real-time pressure is still one, but every integer empirical limit has measure pressure zero. No closure under time truncation was imposed on the stated arbitrary collection.
## Verified replacement for the variational step

First choose real times \(t_j\to\infty\) realizing the pressure limsup, with the near-maximizing separated sets and exponential weights of (5.13). Then take a weak limit of their empirical measures. Put \(n_j=\lceil t_j\rceil\) and \(\psi(x)=\int_0^1\varphi(f_sx)\,ds\). A \((t_j,\delta)\)-separated set remains \((n_j,\delta)\)-separated. Choose a finite partition of diameter less than \(\delta\) for the time-one flow metric, with boundary of zero measure for the limiting discrete empirical measure \(\mu^1\). Its \(n_j\)-join separates the set, and Gibbs weights give the entropy identity \[H_{\nu_j}(\mathcal A^{n_j})
   +\int\Phi(x,t_j)\,d\nu_j=\log Z_{t_j}.\] Replacing \(\Phi(x,t_j)\) by \(S_{n_j}\psi(x)\) costs at most \(\|\varphi\|_\infty\). The entropy block inequality, first letting \(j\to\infty\) and then the block size tend to infinity, yields \[P(\mathcal C,\varphi,\delta)
 \le h_{\mu^1}(f_1)+\int\psi\,d\mu^1.\] No assertion that \((x,n_j)\in\mathcal C\) is needed.

The continuous empirical limit is \(\mu=\int_0^1(f_s)_*\mu^1\,ds\): the averaging lengths differ by at most one, hence their bounded-test-function discrepancy is \(O(t_j^{-1})\). Translating a long averaging interval also proves flow invariance. Entropy affinity and conjugacy under the commuting maps \(f_s\) give \(h_\mu(f_1)=h_{\mu^1}(f_1)\); the potential integrals agree. This proves the required existence statement for a maximizing real-time subsequence. Pressure \(-\infty\) is trivial; otherwise use unbounded nonempty times. The missing exponential in the first weight display on p. 78 must be restored consistently with (5.13).
## The occupation estimate needed downstream

The inference on p. 44 from discrete \(W_r\) counts to continuous occupation needs a quantitative loss and the union \(W_r\cup U_{\operatorname{Sing}}\), since a prefix can lie in \(U_{\operatorname{Sing}}\setminus W_r\). Conditional on a consistent grid and the asserted discrete counts, this step has a local repair. Near a singularity, \(|X(z)|\le L\operatorname{dist}(z,\sigma)\). A complete visit from radius \(r_0\) to radius \(r\) and back lasts at least \(2L^{-1}\log(r_0/r)\). Decrease \(r\) before fixing the later scales so each such visit lasts at least four. If its length is \(\ell\) and it contains \(K\) unit-grid samples, then \(K\le\ell+1\le5\ell/4\). Occupation is at least \(4/5\) of the discrete count. A larger cutoff absorbs floor errors and retains at least \(0.6\beta_1\) mass in \(W_r\cup U_{\operatorname{Sing}}\), including the prefix and suffix. The bound \(\beta_1/1000\) for the unwanted part of \(U_{\operatorname{Sing}}\) leaves more than \(\beta_1/2\) in the singular balls, sufficient for Lemma 5.4. Weak limits use the corresponding closed neighborhoods.

This repairs the local conversion with the available strict margin. It is conditional on the grid/decomposition correction in Problem 2 and does not solve Problem 1. The pressure-gap proof cannot be declared complete solely from the corrected Lemma 5.9.

Problem 4 (Major: the unconditional lower bounds in Lemma 6.1 are false).  For the orthogonal coordinate splitting on p. 49, Lemma 6.1 asserts \(|y^2|-L_0\alpha|y^1|\le |y^F|\) and its symmetric counterpart. Appendix B drops a nonzero second-order term in (B.7)–(B.8), p. 80.

Equation reference: eq:cones. In \(\mathbb R^2\) take \(E\) horizontal, \(F\) vertical, and any \(a=\alpha>0\): \[y=(0,1),\quad
 u=y^F=\left(\frac{a}{1+a^2},\frac1{1+a^2}\right),\quad
 v=y-u=\left(\frac{-a}{1+a^2},\frac{a^2}{1+a^2}\right).
 \] Both cone hypotheses hold with equality: \(|u_E|=a|u_F|\) and \(|v_F|=a|v_E|\). The normalizations \(|y|=1\) and \(|u|\le1\) also hold. Yet \(y^1=0\), \(|y^2|=1\), and \(|u|=1/\sqrt{1+a^2}<1\), contradicting the bound for every \(L_0\) and arbitrarily small \(a\). Swapping \(E,F\) gives the other failure.

Equation reference: eq:correctcone. Write \(f=|u_F|\), \(e=|v_E|\). The cone conditions give \(f\le |y^2|+ae\), \(e\le |y^1|+af\), and \(|y^2|\le f+ae\). For \(0<a<1\), valid general bounds are \[\frac{|y^2|-a|y^1|}{1+a^2}
 \le |u|
 \le \frac{\sqrt{1+a^2}}{1-a^2}(|y^2|+a|y^1|),
 \] with symmetric bounds for \(v\). A negative lower numerator is harmless. The omitted term is of order \(a^2|y^2|\) and cannot be absorbed into \(a|y^1|\) when \(y^1=0\).
## The conditional cases used later can be restored

Suppose \(A=|u|\ge C_0B\), where \(B=|v|\) and \(C_0>0\) is fixed. Projection estimates directly give \[\left(\frac1{\sqrt{1+a^2}}-\frac a{C_0}\right)A
 \le |y^2|\le(1+a/C_0)A,\qquad
 |y^1|\le(a+C_0^{-1})A .\] For small enough \(a\) the lower coefficient is positive. Inverting proves \(A=(1+O_{C_0}(a))|y^2|\); division by the last bound gives \(|y^2|\ge C_0(1-O_{C_0}(a))|y^1|\). These are the required conditional comparisons. The symmetric argument proves Case (2); the zero case is immediate.

Lemma 6.4, p. 51, uses these conditional cases and the graph length estimate of Lemma 6.3. Its needed coordinate comparison therefore has this independent repair. The Major classification concerns a false intermediate assertion and its use in deriving a core coordinate tool; it does not mean that the conditional conclusion or equilibrium theorem has been refuted.
# Local normalization and boundary corrections

Problem 5 (Minor: absolute value in the time-change potential).  Footnote 5 on p. 11 writes \(|c\varphi|\) for a constant speed change. For \(g_t=f_{ct}\), \(c>0\), the correct potential is \(c\varphi\), because \[h_\mu(g_1)+\int c\varphi\,d\mu
 =c\left(h_\mu(f_1)+\int\varphi\,d\mu\right).\] Pressure and the singular pressure gap scale by \(c\). An absolute value generally changes equilibrium measures.

Use an Anosov suspension of finite topological entropy \(H\) and two periodic orbits. Choose a smooth \(\varphi\in[-B,0]\) equal to \(0\) and \(-B\) on them, with \(B>2H\). Any \(\varphi\) equilibrium has \(\int\varphi\ge-H\), since its pressure is at least zero. Any \(-\varphi\) equilibrium has \(\int\varphi\le H-B<-H\), since its pressure is at least \(B\). The sets are disjoint. Existence here follows from entropy upper semicontinuity. As \(|c\varphi|=-c\varphi\), the printed substitution fails. Removing the absolute value fully repairs this local normalization; it is not a new obstruction to Theorem C.

Problem 6 (Minor: finite endpoint counts need a weak inequality or slack).  Theorem 4.1, p. 30, permits \(A=b_2>b_1\), making its density \(\theta_0=1\), yet requires \(\ell>\theta_0N=N\) among \(N\) indices. This boundary case requires \(\ell\ge\theta_0N\) or a strictly smaller density. Lemma 4.6, p. 34, claims at least \(\kappa(\lfloor t\rfloor+1)\) positive candidates for every \(t\). At \(t=1\), \(W=\varnothing\), and \(\kappa>1/2\), this exceeds one although only the length-one candidate is admissible.

Use a count proportional to \(\lfloor t\rfloor\), or choose an intermediate density \(\kappa'>\kappa\) and enlarge the large-time cutoff. The later intersection argument has strict density slack, so these bounded losses are absorbable once the common grid is fixed. These finite failures do not disprove the asymptotic Pliss mechanism.

Problem 7 (Minor: Lemma 2.16 needs finite backward entrance).  On p. 23 the lemma quantifies over every \(x\in B_r(\sigma)\cap\Lambda\) and evaluates \(x_{-t_x}\) at the supremal backward stay time. For \(x=\sigma\) this time is infinite; the same occurs at local unstable points whose backward orbit stays in the ball. The displayed entrance point is then undefined.

Restrict the assertion to \(t_x<\infty\) and use \(\partial B_{r_0}(\sigma)\), not the printed \(\partial B_{r_0}(x)\). The intended compactness proof applies to finite entrance passages. Later good segments, with endpoints outside the singular neighborhood, use finite completed visits. This is a missing boundary hypothesis rather than a counterexample to the passage conclusion for those visits.
# Checks that survive and explicit remaining limits

Lemma 5.4 was checked using compactness, entropy upper semicontinuity, and affinity after separating singular point masses. Backward recurrence gives zero invariant mass to \(W^u(\sigma)\setminus\{\sigma\}\) in Lemma 5.5. The nested-neighborhood argument of Lemma 5.6 is consistent with these facts. The principal parameter order accommodates the extra long-residence choice before the final Bowen scale is fixed.

Conditional on valid scaled shadowing, the Hölder estimate on pp. 65–69 has the required summable terms \(\lambda_1^{\gamma(i-t)}\) and \(\lambda_E^{\gamma i}\), with \(\lambda_1>1\), \(0<\lambda_E<1\). The factor \(|X(x_i)|^{-1}\) from the projection derivative cancels the factor \(|X(x_i)|\) from the normal displacement bounds, preventing a spurious singular denominator in the Birkhoff-integral bound. In (7.16), p. 68, the initial stable leg must be from \(y^F_{\tau(0)}\) to \(y_{\tau(0)}\); the printed superscript \(E\) is an immediate label error. A nonzero point on the stable leaf makes the printed right side zero and left side positive. The corrected label restores that stable contraction step, conditional on its stated premises.

The finite specification construction admits a consistent choice of radii: choose the output radius in terms of the shadowing scale, then the bridge radius, and finally the long-time cutoff. No proportionality of the first radius to a later input radius is needed. On p. 76 the initial disk center should be the available intersection of the periodic orbit’s unstable manifold with the small stable plaque of \(x^1\); assumption (B1) does not state that \(x^1\) itself is in that unstable manifold. The hyperbolic-time disk lemma already allows a center on this plaque.

For the local branches \(F_j\) in (8.6), set \(z^k=y^k\) and \(z^j=F_j^{-1}(z^{j+1})\) successively. The exact orbit identity follows by induction, with each gap evaluated once at its actual preimage. The two flow-box time corrections are bounded per gap, not accumulated into one gap over all pieces. A positive minimum bridge time may be requested before the inclination construction to make the final gaps nonnegative. These are verified completions of finite gluing conditional on the cited quantitative disk and inclination inputs.

In Appendix C, the deep-visit duration tends uniformly to infinity as \(r\to0\), allowing fixed coordinate factors to be absorbed by a smaller exponential rate. The flow-speed ratio at entry and exit has a uniform positive lower bound on the fixed sphere of radius \(r_0\), using invertibility of \(DX(\sigma)\), not merely an upper Lipschitz estimate. That sphere also supplies a uniform normal-flow-box radius; an infimum over \(W_r^c\) need not stay positive as \(r\) shrinks. The written reduction of a real passage time to an integer and the off-attractor cone extensions are not fully reconstructed here. They must be integrated with the continuous-time repair in Problem 1.

The Lorenz linearization at the origin was checked exactly: its eigenvalues are \((-11\pm\sqrt{1201})/2\) and \(-8/3\). This local calculation is not a rerun of Tucker’s global verified return-map construction. The reductions of Theorems A and B from Theorem C were checked against their stated external Lorenz and periodic-manifold inputs; those reductions do not remove the internal proof issues above.
# Conclusion

The assessment for this exact version is Major. Four core auxiliary assertions have demonstrated failures. Some local tools can be repaired explicitly, but a complete continuous-time Bowen/decomposition repair is not established. None of these conclusions asserts that the main uniqueness theorems are false.

problems.title: General cone lower estimates are false
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: Problem 4 (Major: the unconditional lower bounds in Lemma 6.1 are false).
claim: Recorded check: General cone lower estimates are false
analysis: For the orthogonal coordinate splitting on p. 49, Lemma 6.1 asserts \(|y^2|-L_0\alpha|y^1|\le |y^F|\) and its symmetric counterpart. Appendix B drops a nonzero second-order term in (B.7)–(B.8), p. 80.

Equation reference: eq:cones. In \(\mathbb R^2\) take \(E\) horizontal, \(F\) vertical, and any \(a=\alpha>0\): \[y=(0,1),\quad
 u=y^F=\left(\frac{a}{1+a^2},\frac1{1+a^2}\right),\quad
 v=y-u=\left(\frac{-a}{1+a^2},\frac{a^2}{1+a^2}\right).
 \] Both cone hypotheses hold with equality: \(|u_E|=a|u_F|\) and \(|v_F|=a|v_E|\). The normalizations \(|y|=1\) and \(|u|\le1\) also hold. Yet \(y^1=0\), \(|y^2|=1\), and \(|u|=1/\sqrt{1+a^2}<1\), contradicting the bound for every \(L_0\) and arbitrarily small \(a\). Swapping \(E,F\) gives the other failure.

Equation reference: eq:correctcone. Write \(f=|u_F|\), \(e=|v_E|\). The cone conditions give \(f\le |y^2|+ae\), \(e\le |y^1|+af\), and \(|y^2|\le f+ae\). For \(0<a<1\), valid general bounds are \[\frac{|y^2|-a|y^1|}{1+a^2}
 \le |u|
 \le \frac{\sqrt{1+a^2}}{1-a^2}(|y^2|+a|y^1|),
 \] with symmetric bounds for \(v\). A negative lower numerator is harmless. The omitted term is of order \(a^2|y^2|\) and cannot be absorbed into \(a|y^1|\) when \(y^1=0\).

Suppose \(A=|u|\ge C_0B\), where \(B=|v|\) and \(C_0>0\) is fixed. Projection estimates directly give \[\left(\frac1{\sqrt{1+a^2}}-\frac a{C_0}\right)A
 \le |y^2|\le(1+a/C_0)A,\qquad
 |y^1|\le(a+C_0^{-1})A .\] For small enough \(a\) the lower coefficient is positive. Inverting proves \(A=(1+O_{C_0}(a))|y^2|\); division by the last bound gives \(|y^2|\ge C_0(1-O_{C_0}(a))|y^1|\). problems.title: Time-change potential must not be replaced by absolute value
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 5: Problem 5 (Minor: absolute value in the time-change potential).
claim: Recorded check: Time-change potential must not be replaced by absolute value
analysis:
Footnote 5 on p. 11 writes \(|c\varphi|\) for a constant speed change. For \(g_t=f_{ct}\), \(c>0\), the correct potential is \(c\varphi\), because \[h_\mu(g_1)+\int c\varphi\,d\mu
 =c\left(h_\mu(f_1)+\int\varphi\,d\mu\right).\] Pressure and the singular pressure gap scale by \(c\). An absolute value generally changes equilibrium measures.

Use an Anosov suspension of finite topological entropy \(H\) and two periodic orbits. Choose a smooth \(\varphi\in[-B,0]\) equal to \(0\) and \(-B\) on them, with \(B>2H\). problems.title: Finite Pliss count endpoint cases
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: Problem 6 (Minor: finite endpoint counts need a weak inequality or slack).
claim: Recorded check: Finite Pliss count endpoint cases
analysis: Theorem 4.1, p. 30, permits \(A=b_2>b_1\), making its density \(\theta_0=1\), yet requires \(\ell>\theta_0N=N\) among \(N\) indices. problems.title: Finite entrance hypothesis missing
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 7: Problem 7 (Minor: Lemma 2.16 needs finite backward entrance).
claim: Recorded check: Finite entrance hypothesis missing
analysis: On p. 23 the lemma quantifies over every \(x\in B_r(\sigma)\cap\Lambda\) and evaluates \(x_{-t_x}\) at the supremal backward stay time. Title: Technical Verification of
Kähler–Einstein Bergman Metrics on Pseudoconvex
Domains of Dimension Two
# Identity, conventions, and coverage

This review concerns Nikhil Savale and Ming Xiao, Kähler–Einstein Bergman metrics on pseudoconvex domains of dimension two [paper], arXiv:2309.10595v2, dated 23 March 2025, 22 pages. The assignment associates it with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0071 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0071). Equality with the journal version of record has not been verified. All locations below use one-based physical PDF pages; the inspected printed numbers coincide with them.

The lead reviewer read all 22 pages and independently checked the normalization witness, the valuation argument in Theorem 8, the logarithmic-power comparison, the final gamma-function reduction, and the two elementary preliminary corrections. A native in-chat helper independently reviewed the whole paper, including source-page images and the exact ellipsoid computation. The source text, page images and exact algebra calculations are distinguished in the associated evidence records.

We retain the paper’s Euclidean measure convention, its unit normal field \(U_0\) with \(U_0\rho=1\), its normal depth \(\rho=-\varepsilon^r\) on (3.4), and its polynomial \(p\) in (3.2). The full microlocal construction imported from Hsiao–Savale, the external spectral asymptotics and coefficient formulas, and the strongly pseudoconvex ball-uniformization results were used as stated inputs rather than independently re-proved from their original papers. The normalization correction below is not a complete new proof of that external machinery. No author code was run, and missing separate code is not treated as a mathematical defect.
# The leading coefficient and its verified correction

Problem 1 (Major: the critical tangent vector has the wrong scale).  Theorem 4, (3.7)–(3.8), pp. 8–9, uses the prefactor \((-2\rho)^{-2-(2+w'\cdot\alpha')/r}\) but evaluates the model coefficient at \(z_{1,V}\). For the prescribed path \(\widehat x=\varepsilon z_{1,V}+O(\varepsilon^2)\), \(\rho=-\varepsilon^r\), the corresponding evaluation point is \(2^{-1/r}z_{1,V}\).

Equation reference: eq:scale. The error is already visible in the leading diagonal term of (3.13). Its phase is \(e^{2\rho t}\) and its leading amplitude is \(t^{1+2/r}B_p(t^{1/r}\widehat x)\). Setting \(s=-2\rho t\) gives \[(-2\rho)^{2+2/r}K_D
 \ \sim\ \frac1\pi\int_0^\infty e^{-s}s^{1+2/r}
 B_p\left(s^{1/r}\frac{\widehat x}{(-2\rho)^{1/r}}\right)\,ds.
 \] The quotient in this formula tends to \(2^{-1/r}z_{1,V}\), not \(z_{1,V}\). The failure is not merely an informal concern about manipulating the parametrix: the following exact example tests the statement on a domain satisfying all of its hypotheses.
## A bounded finite-type witness

Equation reference: eq:norm, eq:ellipsoid. For an integer \(m\ge2\) let \[E_m=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^{2m}+|w|^2<1\}.\] It is bounded, smoothly bounded, pseudoconvex and of finite type. At \((0,1)\) the type is \(r=2m\). Coordinates whose tangential linear parts are \(\Re z,\Im z\) and whose normal is unit give \(p(z)=|z|^{2m}/2\). Monomial orthogonality and a beta integral yield, for \(a,b\ge0\) and \(q=(a+1)/m\), \[\|z^a w^b\|_{L^2(E_m)}^2
 =\frac{\pi^2}{m}
   \frac{\Gamma(b+1)\Gamma(q)}{\Gamma(b+q+2)}.
 \] Indeed, integrate first over the \(z\) disk of radius \((1-|w|^2)^{1/(2m)}\), then put \(u=|w|^2\) in the remaining radial integral. Summing the reciprocal monomial norms first in \(b\) and then in \(a\) gives the exact diagonal kernel \[K_{E_m}(z,w)=
 \frac{(m+1)-(m-1)u}
 {m\pi^2(1-|w|^2)^{2+1/m}(1-u)^3},
 \qquad
 u=\frac{|z|^2}{(1-|w|^2)^{1/m}}.
 \] The numerator follows from \(\sum_{a\ge0}(a+1)(a+m+1)u^a
=[(m+1)-(m-1)u]/(1-u)^3\).

Along the paper’s path, \(z=\varepsilon V+o(\varepsilon)\) and \[1-|w|^2=\varepsilon^{2m}(2+|V|^{2m})+o(\varepsilon^{2m}).\] To check the factor two, write \(F=|z|^{2m}+|w|^2-1\). On the boundary \(F=0\), and \(U_0F\to2\) near \((0,1)\). Moving normal time \(-\varepsilon^{2m}\) therefore gives \(F=-2\varepsilon^{2m}+o(\varepsilon^{2m})\). This calculation respects the prescribed unit normal; it is not a freely rescaled defining function.
## The related model-domain identity
Page 11 identifies \(\widetilde B_{p,0}(z)\) with \(K_{D_p}(z,i[1+p(z)])\), where \(D_p=\{\Im w>p(z)\}\). With the stated definitions the correct depth is \(1/2\).

Equation reference: eq:fourier. For clarity, Fourier decomposition in \(\Re w\) and \(\int_{p(z)}^\infty e^{-2ty}\,dy=e^{-2tp(z)}/(2t)\) give \[K_{D_p}(z,iy)
 =\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty t\,e^{-2t(y-p(z))}B_{tp}(z,z)\,dt,
 \] where \(B_{tp}\) here denotes the unweighted-space projector kernel for \(\overline\partial+ t\,\overline\partial p\), called \(B_t\) in (4.3). Homogeneity gives \(B_{tp}(z,z)=t^{2/r}B_p(t^{1/r}z)\). Putting \(y=p(z)+1/2\) in [eq:fourier] (#eq:fourier) is exactly the definition of \(\widetilde B_{p,0}\). At \(p=|z|^2/2\), one can also check without a general Fourier argument that \(B_p(z,z)=1/\pi\), so \(\widetilde B_{p,0}=2/\pi^2\). The corresponding Siegel kernel at \((0,i)\) is \(1/(4\pi^2)\), a factor eight smaller; its value at \((0,i/2)\) is \(2/\pi^2\). The discrepancy is a normal-depth normalization, not a convention that leaves the printed identification true.
## Repair and the interface with the main proof

Set \[\eta=\widehat x/(-2\rho)^{1/r}.\] Retain the prefactor in (3.7), but evaluate the differentiated model coefficient in (3.8) at \(\eta\to2^{-1/r}z_{1,V}\). The normal derivatives \((U_0/2)^{\alpha_0}\) contribute \(t^{\alpha_0}\) in the leading phase; the tangential derivatives contribute the corresponding derivatives of the model integral. This supplies the corrected leading coefficient under the same parametrix input.

The commutator term in the determinant must be scaled in the same variable. Since \(\Delta p\) is homogeneous of degree \(r-2\), \[\Delta p(\widehat x)
 =(-2\rho)^{(r-2)/r}\Delta p(\eta).\] Consequently its leading contribution \((\Delta p/2)\widetilde B_{p,1}\) has exactly the same total weight as \(\partial_\eta\partial_{\bar\eta}\widetilde B_{p,0}\). Factoring all entries in (5.1) gives equation (5.2) with every entry evaluated at \(\eta\), including \(\Delta p(\eta)\). Because \(2^{-1/r}z_{1,V}\) ranges over all of \(\mathbb C\) as \(V\) varies, the universal model identity (5.2) retains its printed form after renaming this variable. No new hypothesis on \(V\) is required.

This is a verified repair of the leading-scale mismatch and its determinant interface. Its Major severity concerns a false stated asymptotic theorem used in the central derivation; an explicit local correction does not erase that failure. The correction does not refute the ball characterization, and it does not independently reconstruct every remainder estimate in the imported all-orders parametrix.
# Two local preliminary corrections

Problem 2 (Minor: the Bergman kernel is not globally square integrable).  Page 3 places \(K_D(z,w)\) in \(L^2(D\times D)\). A bounded domain has an infinite-dimensional Bergman space, so its orthogonal projector is not Hilbert–Schmidt.

If \((e_j)\) is an orthonormal basis, the reproducing identity and Tonelli’s theorem give \[\int_D\int_D|K_D(z,w)|^2\,dw\,dz
 =\int_D K_D(z,z)\,dz
 =\sum_j\|e_j\|_{L^2(D)}^2=\infty.\] The polynomials already give infinitely many independent square-integrable holomorphic functions on a bounded domain. The correct local statement is \(K_D\in C^\infty(D\times D)
\subset L^2_{\rm loc}(D\times D)\), with its usual distributional Schwartz-kernel interpretation. The projector remains a bounded operator. This correction does not alter the later interior derivatives or boundary asymptotics.
Problem 3 (Minor: the general-dimensional frame formula omits a sign).  Equation (2.4) defines \(J(u)\) with the factor \((-1)^n\). The frame determinant in (2.5), p. 4, omits that factor.

In the coordinate frame take \(u=1-\sum_{j=1}^n|z_j|^2\). The block determinant is \((-1)^n(u+\sum_j|z_j|^2)=(-1)^n\), while \(J(u)=1\). For odd \(n\), including \(n=3\), (2.5) is therefore false. Insert \((-1)^n\) in that formula, or explicitly restrict it to the even-dimensional case being used. The main proof has \(n=2\), so its (5.1) has the correct sign.
# Independent checks of the surviving proof

The proof of Proposition 3 uses localization at a strongly pseudoconvex boundary point, the limiting Ricci constant \(-1\), and pluriharmonicity of \(\log B\). The maximum principle on attached analytic disks makes \(B\) constant on an interior open set; real analyticity and connectedness then extend the constant. The argument is coherent with its stated localization, disk-filling and boundary-asymptotic inputs.

The scaling identity (4.4) follows by a change of variables in the weighted holomorphic space. At points where \(\Delta p>0\), Proposition 6 imports the positive-curvature expansion. The passage from its scalar expansion to differentiated coefficients and the restriction to that open set were checked. The full external derivation of the coefficient \(b_3\) was not independently repeated here.

The logarithmic comparison on p. 19 is also decisive. Each entry of the \(3\times3\) determinant has at most first powers of \(\log t\) in its polyhomogeneous expansion, so the determinant has log degree at most three. On the right, the first possible \((\log t)^4\) term has coefficient proportional to \(b_3^4\). No higher-order logarithmic term can contribute at that same first order. Uniqueness of the expansions forces \(b_3=0\) where \(\Delta p>0\). The radial model then follows from Theorem 8 and the absence of pure holomorphic terms in \(p\).

For \(p=c|z|^r/2\), the monomial integral on the plane produces the orthonormal basis and series in Theorem 14. Its decomposition into the \(r/2\) residue classes and the incomplete-gamma differential equation have the stated solution with zero initial condition. The values and mixed derivatives at zero used on p. 20 also follow directly from the first two terms of this series, without requiring off-diagonal branch choices.

For \(r>2\), \(\Delta p(0)=0\). Substitution into (5.2) and the gamma recurrence give \[(1+4/r)(2+2/r)=\frac94(1+2/r)^2 .\] The difference of the two sides is exactly \[-\frac{(r-2)^2}{4r^2}.\] Thus \(r=2\) is the only positive solution, contradicting \(r>2\). The strongly pseudoconvex characterization then gives the ball, conditional on the cited Fu–Wong and Nemirovski–Shafikov results. The finite-type reduction for a bounded real-analytic boundary is likewise an external background input, not a new calculation in this review.
# Conclusion

The overall assessment is Major for the exact version because Theorem 4’s leading coefficient is false as written. A consistent leading-scale repair and its compatibility with the main determinant identity are supplied. The surviving algebraic chain was checked explicitly; the ball conclusion has not been refuted.

On a Question of Kwakkel and Markovic on Existence
of Wandering Domains with Bounded Geometry
# Exact version and review scope

The source is Sergei Merenkov, On a question of Kwakkel and Markovic on existence of wandering domains with bounded geometry [paper], arXiv:2405.02176v4, dated 22 March 2025, 22 pages. The assignment associates it with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0072 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0072). Identity with the journal version of record has not been established. Locations are one-based physical PDF pages, agreeing with the inspected printed labels.

The lead reviewer and a native in-chat helper each read all 22 pages. The review checked the bounded-geometry distortion argument, the Hilbert-space modulus construction, essential-intersection counts, both mapping-class branches, and the quantitative repairs below. The helper’s actual source-image views are attributed to that helper; they are not represented as views by a separate external referee. Exact rational calculations supplement, and do not replace, the analytic geometric argument.

Named external inputs include measurable conformal uniformization, quasiconformal absolute continuity and modulus theory, the maximal function estimate, Nielsen–Thurston classification and pseudo-Anosov length growth, and the single-curve Jenkins–Strebel theorem. Their complete original proofs were not independently re-proved. No author code was executed or needed to produce the counterexample; unavailable code is not itself a defect. No claim is made about later versions, author adoption, or priority.
# A false circular-projection estimate

Problem 1 (Major: one-Lipschitz projection does not give (14)).  In the proof of Lemma 5.4, pp. 16–17, the annular cover is projected orthogonally onto its closed geodesic axis \(\widehat\gamma\). Equation (14) asserts \[\ell(\widehat\gamma)\le
 \ell_{\widehat S}(\widehat\gamma')
 =
 \ell(\widehat\gamma'\cap\widehat S)
 +\sum_{\widehat D\cap\widehat\gamma'\ne\varnothing}
      \operatorname{diam}(\widehat D).\] The diameter is the ambient annular-cover diameter. A one-Lipschitz map controls diameter, but a connected subset of a circle can have length up to twice its circular diameter. Contractibility of the domain does not prevent its projection from covering the circle.
## A counterexample with all local hypotheses

Take the flat unit torus \(M=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2\) and the horizontal primitive geodesic \(\gamma\), of length one. Its annular cover is \((\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\times\mathbb R\). In the universal plane let \[K=\{(s,s/10):-1/100\le s\le101/100\},\qquad w=1/1000,\] and let \(D\) be the projection to \(M\) of the open \(w\)-neighborhood of \(K\).

The closed capsule is disjoint from every nontrivial integral translate. Its horizontal span is \(1.022<2\), and its vertical span is \[H=0.102+2w=13/125<1.\] Vertical translates are therefore disjoint. For the only possible nonzero horizontal translates, the containing parallel lines are separated by \(1/\sqrt{101}>2w\). Thus the projection is injective on the closed capsule, and \(\overline D\) is an embedded closed disk. At \(p=(1/2,1/20)\) the domain contains \(B(p,w)\) and lies in \(B(p,3/5)\): circular horizontal distance is at most \(1/2\) and vertical distance at most \(H/2\), so \[\frac14+(H/2)^2<(3/5)^2.\] It satisfies bounded geometry with constant \(600\). If an infinite collection is desired, add pairwise closure-disjoint round disks of shrinking radii in an open region disjoint from this domain and the curve below. Their geometry constant is one; the resulting complement \(S\) is compact. Density is not a hypothesis of Lemma 5.4.

Let \(\gamma'\) follow \((s,s/10)\) for \(0\le s\le1\) and then close by the vertical interval at \(x=0\) from \(y=1/10\) to \(0\) on the torus. It is a simple rectifiable curve in the horizontal primitive class. The slanted portion lies inside \(D\); the portion outside \(D\) has length at most \(1/10\). The complement of \(\overline D\) along the curve is one vertical open arc. Adding that arc to \(\overline D\) contains the essential horizontal loop, so there is exactly one essential intersection. No added round disk meets \(\gamma'\).
## Corrected estimate and modulus decay

Equation reference: eq:fixed. If \(A\) is connected in a geodesic circle, then \(\mathcal H^1(A)\le2\operatorname{diam}(A)\): an arc of length at most half the circumference has length equal to its diameter; a longer arc, or the whole circle, has diameter half the circumference. The projected domain lift is connected. Applying this fact and one-Lipschitz projection to the covering of the axis gives \[\ell(\widehat\gamma)\le
 \ell(\widehat\gamma'\cap\widehat S)
 +2\sum_{\widehat D\cap\widehat\gamma'\ne\varnothing}
       \operatorname{diam}(\widehat D).
 \] The continuous term needs no factor two.

Equation reference: eq:base. The source’s uniform lift-comparison constant \(c\in(0,1)\) and the at-most-\(N\) lift count now yield \[\ell(\gamma)\le
 \ell(\gamma'\cap S)+\frac{2N}{c}
     \sum_{D_k\cap\gamma'\ne\varnothing}\operatorname{diam}(D_k)
 \le\frac{2N}{c}\ell_S(\gamma').
 \] Let \(\rho\) be one on \(S\) and \(\rho(D_k)=\operatorname{diam}(D_k)\). Disjoint inner balls and bounded geometry imply \(\sum_k\operatorname{diam}(D_k)^2<\infty\), so \(\operatorname{mass}(\rho)<\infty\). The distribution \(2N\rho/(c\ell(\gamma))\) is admissible and gives \[\operatorname{mod}_S(\Gamma)\le
 \frac{4N^2\operatorname{mass}(\rho)}{c^2\ell(\gamma)^2}.\] This proves the stated conclusion of Lemma 5.4 with a changed constant. The constant remains independent of the iterated geodesic class. Pseudo-Anosov length growth therefore still forces the upper bound to zero, contradicting the fixed positive modulus given by conformality on \(S\).

An alternative repair retains diameters of universal-cover lifts throughout: their projection onto the axis line has length at most their diameter. The preceding paragraph of the original proof already provides the requisite uniform comparison. Either repair requires changing the printed reasoning.
## Why the same repair preserves the final variation

Equation reference: eq:qcompetitor. The second use is Proposition 7.2, pp. 20–21, in the quadratic differential metric. Its universal cover has cone angles at least \(2\pi\) and the usual nonpositive-curvature projection property. The same argument applies, with a uniform comparison constant \(c_q\) and axis length normalized to one. An admissible competitor can therefore be chosen as \[\rho_1|_S=|q|^{1/2},\qquad
 \rho_1(D_k)=\frac{2N}{c_q}\operatorname{diam}_q(D_k).
 \] Its discrete mass is finite because the \(q\) metric is bounded above by a constant times the smooth metric. The continuous part is unchanged. This matters: multiplying that part by two would not preserve the strict area comparison used in the proof. The corrected estimate [eq:fixed] (#eq:fixed) requires the factor only on the discrete weights and supplies exactly the needed competitor.
Thus the defect is an invalid central derivation with a verified local repair. The conclusions of Lemma 5.4, Proposition 7.2 and Theorem 1.4 have not been refuted.
# Norms, exceptional curves, and the final contradiction

Problem 2 (Minor: Lemma 7.3 needs squared norms and almost-everywhere admissibility).  Pages 20–21 identify \(L^2\) norms with mass or \(q\)-area, although the definition on p. 8 makes mass the squared norm. They also state the admissibility inequality for every horizontal trajectory, whereas the definition allows a family of classical 2-modulus zero.

The correct identities are \[\|\rho_1|_S\|_2^2=\operatorname{area}_q(S),\qquad
 \|\rho_0\|_2^2=\operatorname{mass}(\rho_0)\] when \(\rho_0\) is purely continuous. For example, a unit density on a set of area four has norm two and mass four. An \(L^2\) representative can be modified on one horizontal circle without changing its class; that circle has 2-modulus zero. Hence pointwise admissibility on every height does not follow from weak admissibility.

Here the required inequality has a full repair. Use the single-curve Jenkins–Strebel cylinder of circumference one and height \(b\); its complement is a critical graph of \(q\)-area zero. A family of horizontal circles indexed by heights in a measurable set \(E\) has 2-modulus \(|E|\), by circlewise Cauchy–Schwarz and the density equal to one on those circles. In particular a zero-modulus exceptional family has a null set of heights. The same conclusion for arbitrary exceptional height sets follows by enclosing them in the measurable superlevel sets of arbitrarily small-energy admissible densities.

Equation reference: eq:gap. Extend \(\rho_0\) by zero off \(S\), and express its density in the flat cylinder coordinates. For almost every height \(y\) its horizontal integral is at least one. Cauchy–Schwarz on the unit circle and Fubini give \[\operatorname{mass}(\rho_0)\ge b=\operatorname{area}_q(C_q)>\operatorname{area}_q(S)
   =\|\rho_1|_S\|_2^2 .
 \] The strict inequality uses a nonempty open complementary domain: \(q\) has only isolated zeros, so that domain has positive \(q\)-area. The full-area single-cylinder property is the specific Jenkins–Strebel input used here; it is stronger than merely having some closed trajectories.

Equation reference: eq:variation. Write \(\rho_0=(u,0)\) and \(\rho_1=(v,d)\) in \(L^2(S)\oplus\ell^2\). The exact variation is \[\begin{aligned}
 &\operatorname{mass}((1-t)\rho_0+t\rho_1)-\operatorname{mass}(\rho_0) \notag\\
 &\qquad=2t\bigl(\langle u,v\rangle-\|u\|^2\bigr)
  +t^2\bigl(\|v-u\|^2+\|d\|^2\bigr).
 \end{aligned}\] By [eq:gap] (#eq:gap), \(\langle u,v\rangle\le\|u\|\|v\|<\|u\|^2\). The quadratic coefficient is finite even after the discrete weights in [eq:qcompetitor] (#eq:qcompetitor) are doubled. For small positive \(t\) the variation is negative, contradicting extremality. Convex combinations remain admissible outside the union of their two zero-modulus exceptional families. This proves the needed contradiction with the corrected norm identities and quantifiers.

If \(S\) has area zero, a purely continuous distribution is already zero as a Hilbert-space element and contradicts positive transboundary modulus directly. No separate positive-area hypothesis is required.
# An unused numerical collar formula

Problem 3 (Minor: the displayed width can be nonreal).  On p. 15 the collar width is written \(d=\operatorname{arccosh}(\operatorname{coth}(\ell(\gamma))/2)\). For \(\ell(\gamma)=1\) the argument is less than one, so this is not a real positive width. More generally it is less than one whenever \(\ell(\gamma)>(\log3)/2\).

The proof needs no explicit width. A smooth simple closed geodesic has a sufficiently small embedded annular neighborhood. Choose one and then a relatively compact conformal subannulus, as the text already does. On that subannulus the required derivative bounds and uniform lengths hold. Deleting the incorrect numerical expression fully repairs this local use without changing Corollary 5.2.
# Other proof and boundary checks
## Distortion and invariant conformal structure

In Lemma 2.1 the rescaled limit \(\Omega\) contains a unit disk and lies in a disk of radius \(C\). Its image by \(A=D_pf^n\) contains a disk of radius \(r'\) and lies in a concentric disk of radius \(Cr'\). If \(a\ge b>0\) are the singular values of \(A\), comparison of widths gives \(a\le Cr'\) and \(r'\le Cb\), hence \(a/b\le C^2\). Taking the shrinking-domain limit separately for each fixed iterate is sufficient; the differentiability remainder need not be uniform over all iterates.

The Beltrami composition law acts by hyperbolic disk isometries. Countability of the group permits one common conull set, and the bounded orbit’s circumcenter transforms equivariantly. Measurability follows from finite-subset circumcenters and their limit. Extending the resulting form by zero and applying measurable uniformization produces conformality on the residual set. The quasiconformal conjugacy preserves bounded geometry through its quasisymmetry on the compact surfaces. An orientation-reversing map may first be replaced by its square; all wandering-domain conditions survive.
## Existence, uniqueness, and conformal invariance of modulus

The nonnegative cone in \(L^2\oplus\ell^2\) is weakly closed. Mazur combinations of a minimizing sequence converge strongly and remain weakly admissible after deleting a countable union of exceptional families. With error at most \(2^{-K}\), the tail densities \(\sum_{K\ge i}K|\rho_K-\rho|\) have norms tending to zero and control the bad limsup family in Proposition 3.1. That family contains no constant curve: for a point in a domain, the single coordinate error is eventually less than \(1/K\); at a point of \(S\) the length contribution is zero. Thus Corollary 3.6 applies with its nonconstant-curve hypothesis. Strict convexity yields uniqueness as a Hilbert-space element.

The transfer from classical to transboundary modulus in Lemma 3.4 uses the positive diameter lower bound as stated. Its disk enlargement estimate is applied to the disjoint inner balls, and compact-surface area bounds give the required squared-radius comparison. In Lemma 3.7 one removes the quasiconformal absolute-continuity exceptional family before pulling back line integrals. On \(S\), conformality gives \(|Df|^2=J_f\) almost everywhere, so change of variables preserves the continuous mass; the domain permutation preserves the discrete mass. Applying the same reasoning to the inverse proves equality of moduli.
## Topology and the two mapping-class branches

The essential-intersection count is controlled by a positive uniform neighborhood scale. Small domains use a common local contractibility scale; the finitely many large contractible closures use the minimum of their individual scales. Each essential excursion costs a fixed positive length. The cyclic lift may be based outside the domain, or counted directly in the annular cover, to avoid splitting a single block at the parameter endpoints. Homeomorphisms preserve the count, so the same \(N\) works for all iterates of the original collar family.

For the \(q\)-length-one trajectories in Section 7, apply that same compact-neighborhood/excursion proof directly in the \(q\) length metric. It induces the original topology and has only finitely many cone singularities. One must not infer a bound on smooth length by reversing the one-sided metric comparison on p. 18. This direct metric version supplies the required uniform \(N\).

The pseudo-Anosov branch uses the corrected modulus bound and the cited growth of shortest representatives. In the periodic or reducible branch, pass to an iterate fixing the selected curve class. The family \(\Gamma_N\) is invariant. Uniqueness of its extremal distribution and conformal pullback force each discrete weight to be constant along its domain orbit. Every such orbit is infinite, so square summability forces all discrete weights to vanish. The repaired variation [eq:variation] (#eq:variation) then rules out the remaining purely continuous extremal distribution.

The sphere is expressly excluded from Theorem 1.4. The dilation example does not contradict that theorem. The stated Denjoy-product boundary example uses the applicable \(C^{1+\alpha}\) range \(0<\alpha<1\) and loses bounded geometry; it is not a claim of a \(C^2\) circle Denjoy example. The review found no additional counterexample to the nonexistence conclusion.
# Conclusion

The assessment of the exact version is Major because (14) is a false intermediate estimate used in both main proof branches. Its complete local correction preserves the modulus decay and the strict first variation. The remaining two problem groups are local corrections, with no demonstrated failure of Theorem 1.4.

# Exact source, theorem, and scope

The source is Matthew Emerton, Robert Pollack, and Tom Weston, Explicit reciprocity laws and Iwasawa theory for modular forms [paper], arXiv:2210.02013v2, dated 9 October 2024, 52 pages. Theorem A concerns a fixed newform of weight \(k\geq2\), critical integers \(0\leq j\leq k-2\), local irreducibility, the no-pole hypothesis at \(j+1\), and the specified Euler-system image hypothesis.
