# The local inverse needs a specified germ

Problem 1 (Major: Proposition 6.4.1 is false for arbitrary Kirillov functions).  On pp. 21–22, absence of a pole of \(L(\pi,s)\) at \(s=1\) is said to give a unique smooth \(\xi\) such that its restrictions near zero are Kirillov functions and \[(1-P)\xi=\phi,\qquad (P\xi)(x)=\xi(px).\] The proposition imposes no global support condition on \(\xi\).

Counterexample, including the representation hypotheses. Take \(p=3\), and a nontrivial ramified quadratic character \(\eta:\mathbb Q_3^\times\to\mathbb C^\times\) with \(\eta(3)=1\). Put \[\chi_1=|\cdot|_p^{-1}\eta,\qquad
 \chi_2\ \text{unramified},\quad\chi_2(p)=2,\qquad
 \pi=\operatorname{Ind}_{\overline B}^{\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Q_p)}(\chi_1\otimes\chi_2),\] in the source’s unnormalized lower-Borel convention. The ratio \(\chi_1/\chi_2\) is ramified, hence is not an exceptional unramified reducibility ratio. Thus \(\pi\) is irreducible and infinite dimensional. Its only unramified Euler factor, in this convention, is \[L(\pi,s)=(1-2p^{1-s})^{-1};\] the denominator at \(s=1\) is \(-1\).

The Fourier realization on p. 19 is \(\phi_f(x)=|x|_p\chi_1(x)\widehat f(x)=\eta(x)\widehat f(x)\). For every integer \(m\), the compactly supported function \(f_m=p^{-m}1_{p^{-m}\mathbb Z_p}\) has Fourier transform \(1_{p^m\mathbb Z_p}\). Consequently \(\eta1_{p^m\mathbb Z_p}\) is a Kirillov function. The same realization includes every compactly supported locally constant function on \(\mathbb Q_p^\times\).

Now set \[\phi=\eta1_{\mathbb Z_p^\times},\qquad
 \xi_0=\eta1_{\{\operatorname{ord}_p(x)\leq0\}},\qquad
 \xi_1=\xi_0+\eta.\] Because \(\eta(px)=\eta(x)\), both differences are \[\xi_i(x)-\xi_i(px)
 =\eta(x)\bigl(1_{\{\operatorname{ord}_p(x)\leq0\}}-

# The prime-two algebraic boundary

Problem 2 (Major: Lemmas 9.2.2 and 9.2.3 fail in the stated full algebra).  Section 8.1, p. 37, defines \(\Lambda=\mathcal O_L[[\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\mu_{p^\infty})/\mathbb Q)]]\). No odd-prime restriction or integral character-component replacement is stated. Lemma 9.2.2 says that a finitely generated torsion module with no nonzero finite submodule has principal zeroth Fitting ideal. Lemma 9.2.3 says that \(I\subseteq A\), with \(A\) of finite index, implies \(I\subseteq\operatorname{Fitt}_\Lambda(A/I)\). Both assertions have counterexamples at \(p=2\).

Let \(\mathcal O/\mathbb Z_2\) be any finite extension, with uniformizer \(\varpi\) and finite residue field \(k\). The actual algebra is \[R=\mathcal O[[X,U]]/(U^2+2U),\qquad
 \mathfrak m=(\varpi,U,X),\] where \(1+U\) represents the order-two element and \(X\) the open procyclic factor \(1+4\mathbb Z_2\). This ring is free of rank two over \(\mathcal O[[X]]\), so \(\varpi\) is a non-zero-divisor.

First counterexample. The module \(Y=R/(\varpi,U)=k[[X]]\) is cyclic and is killed by the regular element \(\varpi\), so it is torsion. Its nonzero submodules are nonzero \(k[[X]]\)-ideals and are infinite. Nevertheless, \[\operatorname{Fitt}_R(Y)=(\varpi,U)\] is not principal. Indeed, \(U^2+2U\) belongs to the square of the maximal ideal before quotienting, since \(2\in\varpi\mathcal O\). The classes of \(\varpi,U,X\) are independent in \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\). For \(J=(\varpi,U)\), its two generators remain independent in \(J/\mathfrak mJ\), because \(\mathfrak mJ\subseteq\mathfrak m^2\). Nakayama’s lemma gives minimal generator number two. This directly contradicts the explicit principality conclusion, without relying on an ambiguous characteristic-ideal convention.

Equation reference: eq:relations. Second counterexample and a complete presentation. Take \(A=\mathfrak m\), \(I=\varpi R\). Then \(I\subset A\) and \(R/A=k\) is finite. The module \[M=A/I=(U,X)\subset
 S=k[[X,U]]/(U^2)\] has generators \([U],[X]\) and relation matrix \[\begin{pmatrix}
 \varpi&0&U+2&-X\\
 0&\varpi&0&U
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \] To check completeness, modulo \(\varpi\) write \(a=a_0+Ua_1\), \(b=b_0+Ub_1\), with coefficients in \(k[[X]]\). The relation \(aU+bX=0\) gives \(b_0X=0\) and \(a_0+b_1X=0\). Thus the syzygies over \(S\) are generated by \((U,0)\) and \((-X,U)\). Lifting adds exactly the two \(\varpi\)-relations in [eq:relations] (#eq:relations).

The maximal minors generate \[\operatorname{Fitt}_R(A/I)
 =(\varpi^2,\varpi U,\varpi(U+2),\varpi X)
 =\varpi\mathfrak m.\] But \(\varpi\notin\varpi\mathfrak m\): canceling the regular element \(\varpi\) would give \(1\in\mathfrak m\). Therefore \(I\not\subseteq\operatorname{Fitt}_R(A/I)\), as opposed to Lemma 9.2.3. Even the stronger no-finite-submodule property holds here: \(M=k[[X]]U\oplus Xk[[X]]\), and multiplication by \(X\) is injective.

Impact and limits of repair. Lemma 9.2.3 feeds Lemma 9.2.4; the proof of Theorem 9.1.1 on p. 42 uses both that lemma and the equality of characteristic and Fitting ideals from Lemma 9.2.2. These are false universal inputs in the explicitly allowed algebra, not merely unexplained notation.

For odd \(p\), the torsion factor has order \(p-1\), invertible in \(\mathcal O\), and the usual character components are two-dimensional regular power-series rings. In that setting the argument can be justified componentwise. For example, \(A/fR\) has no finite submodule on each nonzero component, agrees with \(R/fR\) at height-one primes, and therefore has Fitting ideal \((f)\). An explicit odd-prime restriction removes these counterexamples.

Retaining \(p=2\) requires a replacement argument, such as working over an open procyclic algebra and proving an integral comparison back to the full ring. Additional suitable projective-dimension hypotheses would also require proof for the actual arithmetic modules. The allowed scalar \(C\) may make a replacement possible; this report does not establish a uniform prime-two repair. These examples refute the algebraic lemmas, not Theorem A for an explicit modular form.
# Sign projections do not give formula (18)

Problem 3 (Major: the analytic definitions and interpolation use different normalizations).  On p. 42, writing \(\lambda(a)=\lambda(f,z^j,a,p^n)\), the source sets \[\lambda^\pm(a)=\lambda(a)\pm\lambda(-a),\qquad
 \phi(a)=\lambda^+(a)/\Omega^++\lambda^-(a)/\Omega^-.\] There is neither a factor \(1/2\) nor a factor \((-1)^j\). Formula (18) on p. 43 instead uses the period with sign \((-1)^j\chi(-1)\).

This is a substantive mismatch, not an assumption that an unspecified central \(L\)-value is nonzero. Nonvanishing examples for the even case are available at the highest critical point of any even weight \(k\geq4\): \(j=k-2\), \(s=k-1>(k+1)/2\). The Ramanujan bound used by the source gives an absolutely convergent, nonzero twisted Euler product there. A primitive character has nonzero Gauss sum, so \(S_\chi\ne0\) in this case.

Equation reference: eq:projector. Local correction and propagation. To obtain (18) with the displayed formula for \(\phi\), replace the projections by \[\lambda^\pm_j(a)
 =\frac{\lambda(a)\pm(-1)^j\lambda(-a)}2
 \] and choose the periods consistently with these projections. Then the finite-character calculation gives exactly \(S_\chi/\Omega^{(-1)^j\epsilon}\). The change is to the printed definitions; it must not be silently assumed in reviewing their present form.

A fixed factor two alone is harmless for the existence of some multiplier \(C\). That observation does not remove the parity error or validate the comparison on pp. 45–46 as written. The correction must be propagated through the cohomological periods, Kato periods, and comparison constants. The error lies in the central analytic-to-algebraic identification; it does not establish failure of the intended weak main theorem.

A separate normalization question remains unproved. The calculation in Proposition 10.2.3 displays ratios \[D_\pm=\langle e,\omega_f\rangle\,
           \Omega_f^\pm/\Omega_{f,K}^\pm,\] while the assertion uses a single scalar \(D\). The permitted choices of the two sign components of the Kato class were not reconstructed sufficiently to disprove that assertion. This is a request for a compatible normalization, classified NeedsEvidence, not a fourth demonstrated error. One may instead formulate a componentwise comparison and clear fixed denominators, but this alone is not the missing full prime-two proof.
# Other proof and boundary checks

Period rings, traces, and the local classes. The Frobenius divisibility argument uses all integer specializations, not just one. The trace compatibility produces the required inverse system. The component convention \(\iota_i^-=\iota_0^-\varphi^{-i}\) gives the support and stabilization directions used in the reciprocity statement. The differential pairing differs from the absolute de Rham pairing by \(p^{-n}\); the dual-exponential comparison contributes \(p^n\). Those factors cancel in Proposition 7.4.1, rather than disappearing without explanation.

In Lemma 7.3.1, a unipotent difference lowers the degree in \(e_2\), so \(j+1\) differences kill the degree-\(j\) vector. The factor \(a^{k-2-j}\) combined with \(\det^{2-k}\) gives \(a^{-j}\); the twist by \(j\) removes it. The resulting functional factors through the finite-level dual exponential. Local duality supplies the rational class, and orthogonality puts it in \(H_e\subseteq H_f\). The stronger equality \(H_e=H_f\) invoked under the no-pole hypothesis is a cited input; its every-base-change form was not separately proved.

The integral argument works in the image of \(H^1(T(1+j))\) in rational cohomology, not by assuming the integral cohomology is torsion-free. The correct torsion identity uses \(A_1=V(1+j)/T(1+j)\): \[H^1(T(1+j))_{\rm tors}
 =H^0(A_1)/\operatorname{im}H^0(V(1+j)).\] This is the discrete-module identity needed for the annihilator calculation; the printed \(H^0(T)\) expressions on p. 37 should be corrected accordingly. Once the integral pairing is supplied by the chosen local-Langlands lattice, the minimal-\(\varpi\)-valuation argument lowers a hypothetical positive denominator and proves the claimed integrality.

Newvectors, recurrences, and exceptional parameters. The local Birch sum must be applied in the twisted model. Its angular factor cancels the twisting character on units. The unmodified-model identity on p. 32 should retain the angular character; its later evaluation at powers of \(p\), with \(\chi(p)=1\), has the printed scalar value. The source explicitly distinguishes a \(p\)-deprived newvector from a primitive newvector when twisting removes ramification. The Dirichlet coefficient \(L\)-series in the global argument must retain that distinction.

The corestriction sum at \(n=0\) has \(p-1\) terms and yields \(a-\delta-1\); it is not the degree-\(p\) recurrence. The explicit crystalline calculation separately assumes distinct parameters and nonzero denominators. Coincident parameters in the general construction are handled by the Jordan formula above. The no-pole classification in Lemma 10.1.6 follows by comparing Euler-root absolute values, with the integral critical range \(0\leq j\leq k-2\) retained. Negative or half-integral values of its displayed candidates do not create extra admissible cases.

The global algebra after its scope is corrected. For odd \(p\), the reflexive hull is free componentwise. The finite control error \(B_n\) need not vanish: the finite Selmer dual is a quotient of the relevant middle module, which is the direction required by the Fitting-ideal estimate. The finite-level coinvariant argument uses the torsion-free quotient’s lack of invariants. The group-ring coefficient calculation gives the stated involution \(\sigma\mapsto\sigma^{-1}\). For a nontrivial coefficient extension, a compatible \(\mathcal O_L\)-linear dual into \(L/\mathcal O_L\), or a trace/dual-lattice convention, is needed for the printed \(\mathbb Z_p\)-valued pairings. This review does not independently reconstruct all those integral comparison conventions.

The final divisibility can be justified without canceling a possible zero divisor in a finite group ring. Write \(F=\operatorname{char}_\Lambda H_P^2\), and use the Euler-system input to write \(\alpha=Fb\) in \(\Lambda\). If \(P_n\) denotes the local pairing sum, then \[\iota(\theta^{\rm alg}_{n,j})=F_nP_n,\qquad
 D\iota(\theta^{\rm an}_{n,j})
   =\alpha_nP_n=b_nF_nP_n
   =b_n\iota(\theta^{\rm alg}_{n,j}).\] Thus no cancellation of \(F_n\) is necessary. For a valid scalar \(D\ne0\), the valuation-ring choice \(C=D\) if \(D\in\mathcal O_L\), and \(C=1\) otherwise, is correct. The underlying Kato divisibility and Selmer-complex duality remain the named external inputs.
# Conclusion

The assessment of the exact version is Major. There are demonstrated failures in universal local and algebraic statements, and an incompatible normalization in the interpolation used by the main comparison. The restricted newvector construction and analytic projections have concrete local repairs. The full \(p=2\) argument still needs replacement; the main constant-scaled theorem has not been disproved.

A fixed factor two alone is harmless for the existence of some multiplier \(C\). That observation does not remove the parity error or validate the comparison on pp. 45–46 as written. The correction must be propagated through the cohomological periods, Kato periods, and comparison constants. The error lies in the central analytic-to-algebraic identification; it does not establish failure of the intended weak main theorem.

A separate normalization question remains unproved. The calculation in Proposition 10.2.3 displays ratios \[D_\pm=\langle e,\omega_f\rangle\,
           \Omega_f^\pm/\Omega_{f,K}^\pm,\] while the assertion uses a single scalar \(D\). The permitted choices of the two sign components of the Kato class were not reconstructed sufficiently to disprove that assertion. This is a request for a compatible normalization, classified NeedsEvidence, not a fourth demonstrated error. One may instead formulate a componentwise comparison and clear fixed denominators, but this alone is not the missing full prime-two proof.

report: Abstract: The printed degree convention makes central filtered-module assertions false in rank one. A bounded admissible-lattice choice in Proposition 5.23 is also false, even for an acyclic rank-two pair satisfying all its bounds. Both have complete local repairs: a corrected degree and Harder–Narasimhan argument, and a direct use of the coherent-sheaf/BC equivalence, respectively. Nine further groups of local statement or formula corrections are documented. These findings concern the reviewed arXiv version; they do not provide a counterexample to the intended geometric comparison theorems. Scientific adjudication is pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Technical Verification of
On the Cohomology of \(p\)-adic Analytic Spaces, II:
The \(C_{\mathrm{st}}\)-Conjecture
# Exact source and scope

The source is Pierre Colmez and Wiesława Nizioł, On the cohomology of \(p\)-adic analytic spaces, II: The \(C_{\mathrm{st}}\)-conjecture [paper], arXiv:2108.12785v4, 61 pages. Its margin stamp reads 25 November 2024, while the title page is dated November 26, 2024. The assignment associates it with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0074 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0074); identity with the journal version has not been established. Page numbers below are one-based physical PDF pages and agree with the inspected printed labels.

The principal results prove comparison statements for the specified small dagger varieties with nonnegative de Rham slopes, including the classes in Theorem 8.1 and the conclusions of Theorems 9.3 and 9.8. Small means finite-dimensional de Rham cohomology. The terminology de Rham slopes \(\geq0\) is introduced for small varieties on p. 5; thus its use in Theorem 9.8 includes this restriction even though the word small is not repeated there. The general conjectures are not asserted proved. Over \(C\), the main recovery statement concerns period-ring modules; it does not recover the Hodge filtration, Frobenius, or monodromy in general.

A native in-chat helper read all 61 pages and inspected 30 source page images. The lead reviewer read the main statements, definitions, decisive arguments and their dependencies, reconstructed the findings and repairs, and inspected 18 source page images. Helper work is attributed to that actual helper; no independent external referee or independently verified backend model is claimed. Source and report page-view records are separate from mere rendering records.

We use the source’s stated inputs on the Fargues–Fontaine curve, the BC equivalence, admissibility, and comparison theory. Their full external proofs were not independently reproduced. All computations below are reviewer-authored; no author code was run. Unavailable code is not treated as a mathematical defect.
# Degree convention and the central \(K\)-side comparison

Problem 1 (Major: pp. 32–35, Definition 5.1, Lemmas 5.3–5.4, and Theorem 5.8).  The printed degree \(t_N-t_H\) conflicts with the HN convention and with the claimed relation between acyclicity and admissibility.
## A rank-one witness

Equation reference: eq:rankone. Page 14 defines semistability by \(\mu(E')\leq\mu(E)\) for strict subobjects. Page 32 defines degree as \(t_N-t_H\) and calls an object acyclic when its HN slopes are nonnegative. Take \(K=F=\mathbb Q_p\) and \[
 M=Fe,\qquad \varphi(e)=pe,\qquad N=0,\qquad
 \operatorname{Fil}^iM_K=
 \begin{cases}M_K&i\leq0,\\0&i\geq1.\end{cases}\] For the version with \(G_K\)-action, extend scalars to \(F^{\mathrm{nr}}\) and use the coefficient action. This is a legitimate rank-one filtered module, of printed degree \(1\), hence acyclic under Definition 5.1.

A filtration contained in this one has its unique jump \(h\leq0\). Weak admissibility in rank one requires \(h=t_N=1\). Thus Lemma 5.3(b) is impossible. This also contradicts Lemma 5.4 with \(r=1\): the Frobenius slope is in \([0,1]\), \(\operatorname{Fil}^0=M_K\), and \(\operatorname{Fil}^2=0\). There is no omitted endpoint hypothesis that excludes the example.

The consequence for Theorem 5.8 is substantive. The actual associated bundle is \(\mathcal O(-1)\); by (3.10), p. 15, its \(H^0\) is zero. Equivalently, an element contributing to \(V_{\mathrm{st}}\) is \(x=t^{-1}y\), where \(y\in B_e\cap tB_{\mathrm{dR}}^+\). Since \(B_e\cap B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+=\mathbb Q_p\), this intersection is zero. Thus \(V_{\mathrm{st}}=0\), whereas the asserted recovered module \(M^*\) is nonzero. This refutes the printed algebraic comparison assertion under its printed definition. It does not produce a geometric \(X\) violating a main comparison theorem.
## Complete local correction

Equation reference: eq:correct-degree. Use degree \[
 \delta(M)=t_H(M)-t_N(M)\] with the existing HN convention. The proof of Lemma 5.3 also needs its HN orientation repaired; changing only the displayed sign does not justify its choice of a largest slope-zero subobject.

Here is a complete replacement. If \(M\) has nonnegative HN slopes and positive degree, let \(P=M^{>0}\) be its positive HN subobject and \(Q=M/P\) its slope-zero quotient. Every nonzero quotient of \(P\) has positive integral degree, hence degree at least one. Choose a nonzero graded piece of the filtration on \(P_K\), and replace that filtration step by a hyperplane containing the next step. On every induced quotient filtration the Hodge degree falls by either zero or one; its Newton degree is unchanged. Every quotient therefore still has nonnegative degree. By the quotient criterion for HN slopes, the new \(P\) is acyclic.

Choose a splitting of the underlying filtered \(K\)-vector-space sequence \(0\to P_K\to M_K\to Q_K\to0\), replace only the filtration on \(P_K\), and keep that on \(Q_K\). This gives a contained filtration on \(M_K\), an extension of two nonnegative objects, and lowers \(\delta(M)\) by exactly one. Repeating finitely many times gives a nonnegative object of degree zero, hence a weakly admissible one. Conversely, enlarging a filtration increases the Hodge degree of every quotient, so a filtration containing a weakly admissible one is acyclic. This proves both directions.

For Lemma 5.4, the Frobenius slopes of \(P\) remain in \([0,r]\), so \(t_N(P)\geq0\). Since \(\delta(P)>0\), one has \(t_H(P)>0\) and hence \(\operatorname{Fil}^1P_K\ne0\). Cut the largest nonzero step \(i_0\geq1\). This preserves both \(\operatorname{Fil}^0=M_K\) and \(\operatorname{Fil}^{r+1}=0\) throughout the induction.

With this repair, choose a contained admissible filtration and write the exact sequence used in Theorem 5.8 as \(0\to V_1\to V\to W\to0\). Here \(V_1\) is finite-dimensional and \(W\) is a finite torsion \(B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+\)-module. Proposition 2.14 gives the required Galois-equivariant period-Hom vanishing for \(W\); the injections and dimension comparison in the source then give the desired isomorphisms. The filtration check uses the correctly printed dual rule \(\operatorname{Fil}^iM_K^*=(\operatorname{Fil}^{1-i}M_K)^\perp\). This repairs the local argument, subject to the cited weak-admissibility/admissibility and HN inputs.
# A false bounded lattice choice, and a direct repair

Problem 2 (Major: pp. 38–39, proof of Proposition 5.23).  The proof chooses a weakly admissible lattice \(N\) with \(L_0\subset N\subset L\), where \(L_0=M\otimes B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+\) and \(L=M_{\mathrm{dR}}^+\). Such a lattice need not exist under the proposition’s hypotheses.
## Counterexample satisfying the stated bounds

Equation reference: eq:lattices. Put \(R=B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+\), with uniformizer \(t\), and start with \(E=\mathcal O(1)\oplus\mathcal O\) on the Fargues–Fontaine curve. At \(\infty\), choose local bases \(e,f\) and let \[
 L=Re+Rf,\qquad L_0=R(e+tf)+R(t^2f).\] Let \(E_0\) agree with \(E\) away from \(\infty\) and have lattice \(L_0\) at \(\infty\). Its intersection with the first summand is \(\mathcal O(1)(-\infty)=\mathcal O\), and its projection onto the second summand is \(\mathcal O(-1)\). The resulting extension splits because \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathcal O(-1),\mathcal O)=H^1(\mathcal O(1))=0\). Hence \(E_0\simeq\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O(-1)\). Choose a \((\varphi,N)\)-module \(M\) with Frobenius slopes \(0,1\), \(N=0\), and standard bundle \(E_0\). No Galois-descent condition is imposed on these \(C\)-side pairs. The pair \((M,L)\) has bundle \(E\), whose slopes \(1,0\) are nonnegative, so it is acyclic. For \(r=2\), \[t^2L_0\subset t^2L\subset L_0,
 \qquad t^2e=t^2(e+tf)-t(t^2f).\] All hypotheses of Proposition 5.23 hold, with any \(k\geq4\).

But \(L/L_0\simeq R/(t^2)\), so it has a unique submodule of length one. Since \(\deg E_0=-1\), a degree-zero intermediate bundle would have to arise from that submodule. Its lattice is \(N=Re+Rtf\), and its bundle is \(\mathcal O(1)\oplus\mathcal O(-1)\), which is not semistable of slope zero. Thus there is no weakly admissible intermediate lattice. The acyclicity assumption applies to \(E\), not to \(E_0\); the example does not confuse these two bundles.
## The estimate itself survives, with a stronger bound

Equation reference: eq:full-faithfulness. The source already supplies enough theory to replace the invalid choice. Let \(L_r=t^rL\) and \(E_r=E(M\{-r\},L_r)\). Multiplication by \(t^r\) identifies \(E_r\) with the original nonnegative bundle. Remark 5.16 identifies \(V_{\mathrm{st}}^r\) with \(H^0(E_r)\). Theorem 3.12, p. 15, and the full embedding of BCs into VSs give \[\begin{aligned}

 \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{VS}}(V_{\mathrm{st}}^r,B_k)
 &\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Coh}_X}(E_r,i_{\infty,*}B_k)\\
 &\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_R(L_r,B_k),\qquad B_k=R/(t^k).\notag\end{aligned}\] Both objects are in the nonnegative part of the tilted category, so this is an ordinary sheaf Hom, not an incorrectly substituted derived Ext.

Equation reference: eq:restriction. The natural map in the proposition is now simply restriction \[
 \operatorname{Hom}_R(L_0,B_k)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_R(L_r,B_k).\] The inclusions \(t^rL_0\subset L_r\subset L_0\) give elementary divisors \(t^{a_j}\), \(0\leq a_j\leq r\). In suitable bases the restriction is multiplication by \(t^{a_j}\) on each \(R/(t^k)\) summand. Its kernel and cokernel are killed by \(t^{a_j}\), hence by \(t^r\). This proves the claimed \(t^{2r}\)-bound and in fact improves it. The proof works for all \(k\geq0\); \(k=0\) gives zero modules, and \(r=0\) gives an isomorphism.

For [eq:lattices] (#eq:lattices), the matrix of \(L_r\hookrightarrow L_0\) at \(r=2\) is \[\begin{pmatrix}t^2&0\\-t&1\end{pmatrix};\] restriction has the transpose matrix and elementary divisors \(1,t^2\). Exact finite-jet checks at \(k=4,5,8\) corroborate the kernel and cokernel calculation. The example refutes a proof step, while satisfying the repaired conclusion. Major severity reflects the invalid central auxiliary derivation, not a claim that Proposition 5.23 or the geometric theorems are false.
# Further local corrections
The following nine groups are Minor. Each has a direct local correction; none supplies an additional counterexample to a main geometric theorem.
## HN extension bounds: p. 14

The last bullet of §3.2.2 assumes only slopes of \(E_1\geq\lambda_1\) and slopes of \(E_2\leq\lambda_2\), yet concludes that an extension has slopes in \([\lambda_1,\lambda_2]\). The split extension \(\mathcal O(2)\oplus\mathcal O(-1)\), with \(\lambda_1=0,\lambda_2=1\), disproves this. Require both factors to have slopes in the interval. The nonnegative-slope extension closure used in the corrected argument above is valid.
## Slope inequality and multiplicities: p. 17

At the end of Lemma 3.16 the conclusion must be \(h>d\), as the proof initially states, rather than \(h<d\). An injection \(U_{h,d}\to\mathbb V^h\) has cokernel of Dimension \((h-d,-h)\). Its first coordinate is nonnegative; if zero, its height cannot be negative. Hence \(h>d\).

In §3.2.6(2), if \(\lambda_j=d_j/h_j\) and \(\lambda_1+\lambda_2=d/h\) are reduced, the tensor multiplicity is \(h_1h_2/h\), forced by rank, rather than the printed \((h_1/h_2)h\). The displayed Hom formula must likewise include the multiplicity for \(-\lambda_1,\lambda_2\). For \(\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1/2\), the endomorphism algebra has \(\mathbb Q_p\)-dimension four, whereas the printed Hom formula gives \(H^0(\mathcal O)=\mathbb Q_p\). The categorical equivalence itself is unaffected by correcting these recalled formulas.
## The binomial choice in Lemma 4.13: p. 24

For \(k=p^r\), the proposed \(i=p^r\) is excluded by \(1\leq i<k\). For \(k\geq2\), use \[i=\begin{cases}
 1,&p\nmid k,\\
 p^r,&k=p^rm,\ r\geq1,\ m>1,\ p\nmid m,\\
 p^{r-1},&k=p^r,\ r\geq1.
 \end{cases}\] Then \(v_p\binom{k}{i}=0,0,1\), respectively. The middle case follows from the lowest nonzero base-\(p\) digit; in the last case use \(\binom{k}{i}=(k/i)\binom{k-1}{i-1}\), whose second factor is a \(p\)-adic unit. Consequently \(a_k=\binom{k}{i}^{-1}b_{i,k-i}\) has the required uniform \(p^{-1}\) bound and tends to zero with \(k\). The later index \(b_{i,k-1}\) must also be \(b_{i,k-i}\). The freely chosen linear term can be zero. The analytic conclusion is preserved; 635 exact integer cases merely corroborate this general argument.
## The Ext statement of Lemma 4.24(i): p. 28

The second displayed isomorphism should read \(\operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathrm{TVS}}(U_d,W)=0\), not \(W\). The proof explicitly derives this vanishing and part (ii) uses it. For example take \(d=1\), \(W=B_1\ne0\); applying Hom to \(0\to\mathbb Q_pt\to U_1\to B_1\to0\), the connecting map onto \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(B_1,B_1)=B_1\) is surjective, giving zero for \(\operatorname{Ext}^1(U_1,B_1)\). Keep the first formula \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{TVS}}(U_d,W)\simeq W\).
## The specialization in Example 5.11: p. 35

The first formula omits the twist \(\{r\}\) already present in Corollary 5.10. Take rank-one \(M\) with \(\varphi e=pe\), \(\operatorname{Fil}^1M_K=M_K\), and \(r=1\). It is admissible and \(X_{\mathrm{st}}^1(M)=\mathbb Q_pe\). Its smooth Galois-equivariant Hom into \(B_{\mathrm{st}}\) has Frobenius slope zero, whereas \(M^*\) has slope \(-1\). The correct answer is \(M^*\{1\}\). In the second formula the natural answer is \(M_K^*\), not \(M_K\), for \(j\leq0\); for \(j\geq1\) it remains zero. Remark 9.2 retains the necessary twist in the actual final comparison.
## The positive-period kernel and lattice direction: p. 38

In Proposition 5.20, a map from full \(B_{\mathrm{st}}\)-invariants to a quotient of \(M\otimes B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+\) is not defined by the displayed natural period inclusion. Use \(B_{\mathrm{st}}^+\) there, or use full \(B_{\mathrm{dR}}/t^rL\) as target. The immediately following exact sequence and Remark 5.16 specify the intended object.

For the second Hom isomorphism, the admissible lattice must be contained in \(L\), rather than containing \(L\). Remark 5.14(iii) supplies precisely the contained lattice. Then its finite-dimensional period space \(V\) satisfies \(t^rV\subset V_{\mathrm{st}}^r(M,L)\); its period-ring span is all of \(M\otimes B_{\mathrm{st}}\), yielding the stated Hom conclusion by the argument of Proposition 5.18. When using that proposition, choose the admissible lattice inside \(t^{-r}L_0\) to obtain the required bounded positive periods; the nonnegative bundle at that maximal lattice allows this choice. No additional lower bound \(L_0\subset N\) is asserted here. That stronger, false demand is the separate Major problem above.
## The bicartesian sequence: (6.17), p. 43

Both arrows have plus signs, so their composite is twice the common period map. Already for a point and \(r=0\), the diagonal element \(1\) maps to \(2\ne0\). Replace the last map by \((x,y)\mapsto\iota_{\mathrm{HK}}(x)-\operatorname{can}(y)\), or put the minus sign in the first arrow. The bicartesian square (6.16) then gives its usual exact sequence.
## Finite type versus finite length: p. 51

In the proof of Theorem 8.1(c), the group \[H^i(F^rR\Gamma_{\mathrm{dR}}(X^\times/B_{\mathrm{dR}}^+))\] need not have finite length over \(R\). For the proper point, \(i=0\), it equals \(t^rR\), a nonzero free rank-one module. Finite type is the appropriate property. The diagram’s surjectivity deduction uses exactness of the upper row and the de Rham identifications, not the false finite-length claim, so this correction leaves that deduction intact.
## Which Künneth factor is perfect: p. 54

Lemma 8.13’s proof calls \(R\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(T,R\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mathbb Z_p))\) perfect. The hypothesis makes the proper-factor complex \(R\Gamma_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y,\mathbb Z_p)\) perfect, not necessarily this global-section complex. With \(Y\) a point and \(T\) a countable disjoint union of points, the latter already has an infinite-dimensional rational \(H^0\). Such \(T\) is smooth, separated, taut, and countable at infinity.

Replace the claim by perfectness of the proper-factor complex. A bounded finite-projective representative commutes with taking derived global sections on \(T\), giving the displayed projection formula and the same Künneth result. Proper base change and proper finiteness remain the cited inputs. No Künneth formula for two arbitrary nonproper factors is inferred.
# Proof coverage, boundary checks, and limits
The full review covered §§1–9, Appendix A, and the references, with the following decisive dependency checks.

In §2, the almost-\(C\)-representation review assumes finite \(K/\mathbb Q_p\), while the alternative argument in §2.3 addresses the more general base field used later. Period-Hom vanishing requires the stated continuity and Galois equivariance. Density is in the specified natural topology, not an assertion that \(K\) is dense for the \(t\)-adic topology.

In §§3–4, curvature and numerical height were kept distinct: torsion supported away from \(\infty\) can have positive curvature and height zero. The generating-image hypothesis in Lemma 3.23, the separability and sympathetic-algebra conditions, and the same-type hypotheses of Theorem 4.30 were retained. The cocycle estimate, Mittag–Leffler and Baire steps, finite-length dévissage, and density arguments were checked in the categories actually specified; no unrestricted higher-Ext assertion was substituted.

In §5, monodromy is removed by its finite nilpotent exponential. On a Frobenius block of slope \(a/h\leq r\), the resulting equation \(\varphi^h x=p^{rh-a}x\), the independent unramified embeddings, and the finite quotient needed by Nakayama give the generation used in Lemma 5.17. The zero-slope endpoint and the positive-period restrictions were checked separately.

For the proper comparison in §6 the auxiliary integer must satisfy \(s>r\), so that degree \(r+1\) lies within the comparison range; the argument does not presuppose the degeneration it proves. The Stein result retains the Fréchet/LB distinction, strictness, and the quotient by \(\ker d\); at \(r=0\), negative-degree forms are zero.

In §7, the snake-lemma kernels and cokernels are the adjacent \(H^1\)’s of the modified bundles. Each nonzero such \(H^1\) has strictly negative height, by (3.10), so the two error terms cannot cancel in the height identity. The group in degree \((r,r+1)\) on p. 48 is syntomic, as its footnote states; it was not replaced by pro-étale cohomology outside the valid truncation range. The noncanonical splitting of §7.3 is explicitly unused later.

For §8, the product argument preserves nonnegative vector-bundle slopes, with the remaining coherent torsion supported at infinity. The resolution must be an isomorphism over the complement being studied. The almost-proper comparison quoted from the bibliography is an external input, not independently proved here. Tube hypotheses and radii, the countable exhaustion, Artinian-BC Mittag–Leffler arguments, and the finite proper factor in the product were retained.

In §9, the key assertion is density of appropriate cycles, proved using the Banach basis and finite partial sums, rather than a general claim that completion commutes with cohomology. Continuity then gives the period-Hom vanishing. The \(K\)-side twist and the finite-length density step on the \(C\)-side were checked. Appendix A uses strictness in the quasi-abelian setting; splitting requires the stated spherical-completeness or separability condition.

The full external proofs of the curve classification, Le Bras’s equivalence, the equivalence between weak admissibility and admissibility, previous syntomic comparison theorems, proper base change, resolution, and the almost-proper input remain outside this independent reconstruction. These limitations are not classified as errors. No later arXiv revision or journal version was substituted.

Main conclusions | No counterexample to the intended geometric comparison theorems is established.
Author adoption | Unknown; no author response or later-version verification is claimed.
Remaining work | Integrate the corrections into the source, check their use throughout an author-controlled revision, and assess the cited external inputs and exact journal version.

Title: Technical Verification of
The Sharp Growth Rate in
Nonuniformly Elliptic Schauder Theory
# Exact source, statements, and scope

The reviewed source is Cristiana De Filippis and Giuseppe Mingione, The sharp growth rate in nonuniformly elliptic Schauder theory [paper], arXiv:2401.07160v3, dated 14 December 2024, 51 pages. The first page says Duke Math. J., to appear. The assignment associates it with DOI 10.1215/00127094-2024-0075 (https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0075); the journal version and later corrections were not compared. Locations below use one-based physical PDF pages, agreeing with inspected printed labels.

Equation reference: eq:gap. Theorem 1 is scalar and concerns local minimizers of the Lebesgue–Serrin–Marcellini relaxation \(\overline{\mathcal F}\), under \(n\geq2\), \(1<p\leq q\), \(0<\alpha\leq1\), the growth and ellipticity hypotheses (1.11), and the strict gap \[
 \frac qp<1+\frac{\alpha}{n}.\] It yields local Lipschitz regularity and some positive gradient Hölder exponent. The optimal exponent \(\alpha\) additionally requires \(\mu>0\), \(\alpha<1\), and the stated continuity modulus for \(D_{zz}F\) on bounded gradient sets. The \(\mu=0\) conclusion does not identify the exponent with \(\alpha\); no endpoint \(C^{1,1}\) conclusion is asserted.

Theorem 2 assumes the relaxed minimizer is locally bounded, \(p\leq n\), and \(q<p+\alpha\min\{1,p/2\}\). It gives every finite gradient integrability exponent, with constants depending on that exponent. The extension to original-functional minimizers requires the vanishing Lavrentiev gap on every relatively compact ball. The asserted sharpness for Theorem 2 is restricted to \(p\geq2\).

A native in-chat helper read all 51 pages, with eight detailed groups of proof checks, and inspected 22 source page images. The lead reviewer read the decisive hypotheses, approximation, higher-integrability and final absorption steps; independently reconstructed the counterexample, repair, and selected identities; and inspected 13 original source page images. These are actual native-helper contributions, not an external controller’s scientific assessment. No independent external referee or independently verified backend model is claimed. All numerical and symbolic checks were reviewer-authored.
# The auxiliary maximum estimate
## A fixed-data counterexample

Equation reference: eq:counter, eq:growth. Let \(B=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^2\), and fix \[p=q=2,\quad \alpha=1,\quad \mu=1,\quad
 L=\widetilde L=L_*=4.\] For \(M>0\), set \[
 F(x,z)=2|z+x/2|^2+2,\qquad
 u_*(x)=M,\qquad u(x)=M+\frac{1-|x|^2}{4}.\] The integrand is smooth, independent of \(M\), and satisfies more than the growth hypothesis required by Lemma 8.1. Writing \(H=|z|^2+1\), direct completion of squares gives \[\begin{aligned}

 F-H&=|z+x|^2+1-\tfrac12|x|^2\geq\tfrac12,\\
 4H-F&=2|z-x/2|^2+2-|x|^2\geq1.\notag\end{aligned}\] Thus \(H\leq F\leq4H\) on \(B\). For (7.1)\(_1\), the required lower bound is \((L_*^{-1}+\widetilde L^{-1})H=H/2\) and the upper bound is \(2\widetilde L H=8H\), so both hold. The original bound (1.11)\(_2\) holds as well. Also \[D_{zz}F=4I,\qquad D_zF(x,z)=4z+2x,\] which verifies both ellipticity bounds and the coefficient Hölder bound for these constants. The strict gap is \(1<1+1/2\). If a larger ambient domain is desired, the same hypotheses hold on \(B_{5/4}\), which contains \(\overline B\).

Equation reference: eq:energy. The zero-boundary difference \(u-u_*=(1-|x|^2)/4\) belongs to \(W_0^{1,2}(B)\), and \(Du=-x/2\). For every \(\eta\in W_0^{1,2}(B)\), \[
 \mathcal F(u+\eta,B)-\mathcal F(u,B)
 =2\int_B|D\eta|^2\,dx.\] Hence \(u\) is the unique minimizer in (8.15), not just a formal solution of its Euler equation.

Its essential supremum is \(M+1/4\). For any proposed structural constant \(c\), choose \(M>c\sqrt{\pi}\). The right side of [eq:false] (#eq:false) is then \(M\). All structural data, the integrand, and the ball remain fixed while \(M\) varies. This disproves the stated quantifier on \(c\), not merely a particular numerical value.

The source defines \(\lesssim\) separately on p. 8; (8.17) uses the literal \(\leq\), with \(c\) only in its second entry. Reading a constant outside the entire maximum would avoid this counterexample, but changes the printed statement. No condition \(D_zF(x,0)=0\) is assumed; imposing it would unnecessarily narrow the paper’s setting.
## Complete local repair and downstream use

Equation reference: eq:repair. On the unit ball the source chooses \[\kappa_\infty\geq\|u_*^+\|_\infty,\qquad
 \kappa_\infty\geq C\mu,\] and its level-set iteration concludes \(u_+\leq2\kappa_\infty\), as printed immediately after (8.18). Choose \(\kappa_\infty\) to be the maximum of those two bounds. Apply the same argument to \(-u\), and rescale. This proves the corrected statement \[
 \|u\|_{L^\infty(B)}
 \leq2\max\{\|u_*\|_{L^\infty(B)},\,C\mu|B|^{1/n}\}.\] The corresponding two one-sided statements have the same factor two. At \(\mu=0\), the original coefficient-one maximum principle already follows from (8.18) and Poincaré; no iteration is needed. Equation [eq:repair] (#eq:repair) remains valid at that endpoint. This repair uses exactly the argument in the source and requires no new assumption.

Equation reference: eq:downstream. In the approximation \(\operatorname{App}(B_\rho)\), (8.2) gives \[\|\widetilde u_\varepsilon\|_\infty
 \leq(1+\rho)\|u\|_\infty+\rho,\qquad
 0<\rho\leq1,\quad \mu_\delta\leq2.\] Applying [eq:repair] (#eq:repair) to \(u_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) gives \[
 \|u_{\varepsilon,\delta}\|_\infty
 \leq C\bigl(\|u\|_\infty+\rho\bigr),\] which is precisely the form of (8.12), p. 34. The structural constant can absorb the factor two. Consequently (8.13)–(8.14), the ordered limits, and the Theorem 2 estimate retain the same exponents and dependencies.

This is classified Minor because the false assertion is an overly precise constant in an auxiliary bound; the needed weaker estimate is already proved and is explicitly the form used downstream. Neither principal theorem is refuted.
# Main proof chain and checks that did not yield defects
## Basic calculus and relaxation

The \(V_\mu\)-metric estimates, including their distinct subquadratic form, match the primitive \(E_\mu=(H_\mu^{p/2}-\mu^p)/p\). The finite-difference integration by parts in Lemma 2.1 applies to the whole bounded composite flux; mollification on the larger ball and zero trace justify its limiting use without differentiating a merely bounded field.

The normalization in §2.3 changes the energy by an \(x\)-dependent term independent of the competitor, preserving minimality and shifting relaxed energies by the same integral. Lemma 6.1 uses coercivity and convex lower semicontinuity; the relaxation equals the original functional on \(W^{1,q}\). Strict convexity in gradients is supported by the quantitative ellipticity defect. For the bounded recovery in Lemma 6.2, truncation affects a set of vanishing measure; testing gradients against a fixed \(L^{p'}\) field justifies weak convergence. The replacement-gradient energy cost tends to zero.
## Higher integrability in all three \(p\)-regimes

The regularized problem has \(\mu>0\) and additional \(q\)-coercivity, which justify the initial smooth testing and finite powers. The final estimates avoid dependence on that added coercivity. The gap in [eq:gap] (#eq:gap) implies the three branch bounds in (7.9), including the common endpoints \(p=2\) and \(p=n\).

With \(g=p+\gamma-q-\kappa>0\), the improved exponent is \(m=t+2g\). The identities in (7.20) cancel the excess powers needed for the ordinary first-difference estimate. The cut-off gaps are at least \((\tau_2-\tau_1)/(24K)\), while \(|h|<(\tau_2-\tau_1)/(10^4K)\); double shifts and the seven-shift margin used in Lemma 3.2 fit inside the larger ball.

For \(p\geq2\), the ellipticity defect controls the \(p\)-power gradient difference, and the positive Hessian average permits the required Cauchy–Schwarz and Young absorption. The \(q=2\) zero-power Hölder case is omitted as required. For \(p>n\), the three interpolation quotients in (7.47) equal one and the remaining integration powers do not exceed \(t\). For \(1<p<2\), combining the flux terms before applying Lemma 2.1 avoids an invalid singular Hessian upper bound.

The resulting second-difference order satisfies \(1<\beta_0(t)<2\) for each finite \(t\). It approaches one only as \(t\to\infty\), so the forbidden endpoint of Lemma 3.2 is never used. Iteration advances by \(t_{i+1}=t_i+2g\). Every prescribed finite target needs finitely many steps; interpolation then removes the initial large norm with power \((t_*-p)/(t_{i+1}-p)<1\). This does not prove a uniform bound at target exponent infinity.
## Approximation and ordered limits

The weak limits retain the relevant zero-boundary differences. Lower semicontinuity, minimality of the assigned relaxed minimizer, and strict gradient convexity identify the final limit with that minimizer. Estimates are not transferred to an unspecified solution. The p. 34 sentence about gradients being bounded in \(W^{1,q}\) has the functions in view; the displayed bounds and subsequent weak convergence require only gradients bounded in \(L^q\). This wording does not introduce an additional substantive finding. The interior radius limit in Remark 8.1 avoids an assumed boundary \(C^1\) estimate.
## Fractional comparison and the sharp absorption

The main gap implies the autonomous-estimate range \(q/p<1+2/(n-1)\). The improved autonomous exponent is \[s=\frac{2q}{(n+1)p-(n-1)q}\] in dimensions two and at least four, with the strict enlargement specified in dimension three. Thus the Caccioppoli coefficient has power \(M^{s(q-p)}\), which must be retained quantitatively.

Equation reference: eq:absorb. For \(0<\alpha<1\), choose \(k\) near one and \(\delta\) near zero so that \[\frac{\alpha}{2}<\beta<\widetilde\alpha
 <\frac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}.\] Set \(R=q/p\), \(D=n+1-(n-1)R\). The exponent of the unknown Lipschitz norm in (10.29) is \[
 \mathfrak t=\frac{sn(R-1)}{4\beta}
 =\frac{R}{D}\frac{n(R-1)}{2\beta}<1.\] Indeed \(D-R=1-n(R-1)>0\), so the first factor is below one; the second is below \(\alpha/(2\beta)<1\). For \(n=3\), replace \(R/(4-2R)\) by \(R/(4-2R)+\epsilon\), choosing \(\epsilon>0\) small enough to keep it below one. This is allowed because \(R<4/3\). For \(q=p\), \(\mathfrak t=0\), and Young absorption is unnecessary. For \(\alpha=1\), choose \(\alpha'\in(n(R-1),1)\) and use the local \(\alpha'\)-Hölder bound. This gives the claimed Lipschitz and nonoptimal Hölder conclusions without asserting \(C^{1,1}\).

The nonlinear potential bound is applied strictly above its integrability threshold. Young’s inequality and the radius iteration then close the Lipschitz estimate. Constants may deteriorate as the strict gap closes. The final weak limits can be taken at each finite gradient exponent before passing to infinity, as the source’s footnote explicitly explains.
## Final minimality and Schauder transfer

Once \(Du\) is locally bounded, the Euler flux is locally bounded. Density extends the Euler equation from smooth tests to \(W_0^{1,1}\), and convexity proves minimality for all competitors in Definition 1. Restricting recovery sequences proves monotonicity of \(\overline{\mathcal F}(u,A)\) in the domain, so the energy on the larger ball controls the smaller comparison balls. The conditional Proposition 5.1 is applied with an initial exponent strictly below \(\min\{\alpha,\alpha_*\}\), on a strictly larger interior ball. Dependence on \(\mu\) and the derivative continuity modulus remains necessary.
# External dependencies and sharpness limits

The preceding checks cover the source’s internal proof chain, not fresh proofs of all imported estimates. The autonomous bounds in its references [9] and [79], the local-boundedness input [51], the \(p\geq2\) conditional Schauder argument and final Campanato transfer from [26], and the general embedding and relaxation results remain identified external inputs. Their stated application hypotheses were tracked, but their full original proofs were not all read independently.

The sharpness constructions in [32], [34], and the further fractal examples are also external. The quoted range \(p<n<n+\alpha<q\) implies \(q/p>1+\alpha/n\) and approaches the claimed universal threshold as \(p\uparrow n\), \(q\downarrow n+\alpha\). This is not a construction for every fixed pair above the threshold. Nor may an irregular original-functional minimizer be called a counterexample to the relaxed theorem without checking relaxed minimality. Equality in [eq:gap] (#eq:gap) is expressly left outside Theorem 1; special double-phase endpoint regularity is not contradictory.

The helper’s 18 symbolic identities and 288 finite rational cases, and the lead reviewer’s nine identities and eight additional cases, corroborate the written arguments. Finite sampling does not prove a universal inequality. No author code was executed, and code availability is not treated as a defect in this analytic paper.
# Assessment and remaining work
Assessment | Minor: the literal boundary coefficient in the auxiliary maximum estimate is false.
Repair status | Complete local repair: retain the factor two already obtained by the iteration. The approximation estimates and main theorem statements preserve their stated forms.
Main conclusions | No counterexample to Theorem 1 or Theorem 2 was established.
Author adoption | Unknown; no response, correction, or journal-version incorporation was checked.
Remaining work | Correct (8.16)–(8.17) in the source and verify the exact published version and the identified external regularity and sharpness inputs.
Decision | Pending; human reviews are empty and independent acceptance has not been performed.

Title: Technical Verification of
Suslin’s Cancellation Conjecture
in the Smooth Case
# Exact source, hypotheses, and review scope
The source is Suslin’s cancellation conjecture in the smooth case, by Jean Fasel [paper].
Reviewed version: arXiv:2111.13088v2, dated 10 December 2024; 39 pages. Assigned journal DOI:
The journal version and subsequent corrections were not compared. Locations in this report are one-based physical PDF pages; inspected printed page labels agree.

Theorem 2 (p. 3) states that for a smooth affine \(d\)-dimensional scheme over an algebraically closed field \(k\), with \(d\geq3\) and \(d!\in k^\times\), stabilization \[s_{d-1}:\mathcal V_{d-1}(X)\longrightarrow\mathcal V_d(X)\] is injective. The bundles have arbitrary determinant; they need not be stably free or oriented. The existing rank-\(d\) cancellation input then gives the stated equivalence between stable isomorphism and isomorphism. The characteristic condition means characteristic zero or characteristic greater than \(d\). Theorem 3.0.9 is read with the dimension convention established in the argument. Rank zero and rank one are separate elementary cases, not applications of the unstable range used here.

A native in-chat helper read all 39 source pages and supplied 18 proof checks and three detailed derivations. The lead reviewer read the decisive source passages on 22 pages, inspected 12 source page images, and independently reconstructed the weight correction, cohomology comparison, spectral-sequence bounds and two obstruction actions. Helper and lead page-view records are separate. A second native helper cross-checked the added cohomology argument. These are scientific assistance roles, not independent human review. Parsing manifests or rendering pages was not counted as reading or inspection.
The input PDF has SHA256
`dbb7172a4de3119c75d70a6c5709b52eaafdaac81ab09810d754cc0c939c5ed0`.
The checked source is fixed to these bytes. No author code was run, and code availability is not treated as a mathematical defect.
# Proof architecture and hypothesis checks
## Determinants and change of base point

The representability identification is an external input: \[[X_+,B\mathrm{GL}_n]_{\mathbb A^1}\simeq\mathcal V_n(X).\] For a prescribed bundle, the motivic Postnikov tower is based at its actual stable class. The translation in \(K_0\) changes the loop base point, and the resulting obstruction maps retain its Chern classes. Replacing that class by the trivial bundle would prove only a stably free special case; the source does not make that replacement.

The relative Eilenberg–Mac Lane construction in Lemma 2.2.2 uses a fixed torsor and maps over that torsor. Thus the relevant fiber is not mistakenly enlarged by taking an additional quotient by all torsor automorphisms. In Lemma 2.2.3 (pp. 12–13), squares in \(k^\times\) identify the last Rost–Schmid terms canonically. One must also identify the images of their incoming differentials. The source does so by normalizing each codimension-\((d-1)\) curve, using the 2-divisibility of its Picard group to make the pulled-back line bundle a square, and comparing finite pushforwards. This proves the top-cohomology untwisting needed later, not a global untwisting of all sheaves.

The first homotopy sheaf of \(\mathbb A^d\setminus0\) is \(\pi^{\mathbb A^1}_{d-1}(\mathbb A^d\setminus0)=\mathbf K_d^{MW}\). For the fiber \(F_{d-1}\) of \(B\mathrm{GL}_{d-1}\to B\mathrm{GL}\), the first sheaf is Milnor–Witt in odd \(d\) and Milnor in even \(d\). The vanishing of \(I^m(L)|_X\) for \(m\geq d+1\), in the stated characteristic, makes their restrictions agree with \(\mathbf K_d^M|_X\). This is the legitimate point at which determinant dependence disappears from this coefficient sheaf.
## The two obstruction actions

Equation reference: eq:chern. Writing \(\xi\) for the fixed stable class, equation (3.0.9) on p. 25 gives \[
 \Delta(M)=c_d(M)+\sum_{r=1}^{d-1}c_r(M)c_{d-r}(\xi).\] For the Suslin map \(S_d\), the lower Chern classes vanish and the top one is \((d-1)!\kappa_d\). Surjectivity of \(\kappa_d\), together with prime-to-characteristic divisibility of \(H^{d-1}(X,\mathbf K_d^M)\), makes the first action surjective. This works for every \(\xi\). In dimension three, only surjectivity as a map of pointed sets is needed at this step; one need not impose an unjustified stable cohomotopy group law.

For the next action (pp. 26–28), the target identifies with \(H^d(X,\mathbf K_{d+1}^M)\). It is a quotient of \(\bigoplus_{x\in X^{(d)}}k^\times\), hence is \(d!\)-divisible. Given \(\alpha\), choose \(\beta\) with \(d!\beta=\alpha\) and a preimage of \(\beta\) under \(\kappa_{d+1}\). The chosen \(S_{d+1}\)-loop lifts through the preceding stage: all its Chern classes of degrees at most \(d\) vanish, so [eq:chern] (#eq:chern) is zero. Its upper obstruction action is therefore \(\alpha\). Arbitrary stable loops are not asserted to lift. This verifies the quantifier needed for the second transitivity argument.

Only stages \(d-1\) and \(d\) can contribute on a smooth affine \(d\)-fold. For disconnected smooth schemes, the argument applies componentwise: on lower-dimensional components, rank \(d-1\) is already at least their dimension and the older cancellation theorem suffices.
# Divisibility, dimensions, and annihilation

All cohomology below is Nisnevich unless specified otherwise. The proof of Lemma 4.0.3 uses the coniveau spectral sequence with nonzero region \(0\leq a\leq b\leq d\). No differential can enter \(E_2^{d-1,d}\) or \(E_2^{d-2,d}\), because its source would have second index greater than \(d\). No differential can leave them, because its target would lie below \(a=b\). Their total degrees exceed the affine cohomological dimension. The only possible incoming differential at \((d-1,d-1)\) is \[d_2:E_2^{d-3,d}\longrightarrow E_2^{d-1,d-1};\] it is onto for the same total-degree reason.

Norm residue, the cited torsion description, and the cited compatibility with the coniveau differential turn these facts into the dotted-map surjectivity in (4.0.4). The final term of the Gersten complex for \({}_\ell\mathbf K_d^M\) is zero, since \({}_\ell K_0^M(k)={}_\ell\mathbb Z=0\). The diagram chase gives unique \(\ell\)-divisibility of \(H^{d-1}(X,\mathbf K_d^M)\), for \(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k\).

For Lemma 4.0.5, first lift a class along the surjective vertical map in the p. 34 diagram, then subtract a preimage from the upper dotted map to kill its horizontal obstruction. This does not change its image under multiplication by \(\ell\). It gives divisibility of \(H^{d-2}(X,\mathbf K_d^M)\). If \(0\to H\to G\to M\to0\), \(G\) is \(\ell\)-divisible and \(M\) has no \(\ell\)-torsion, an \(\ell\)-root in \(G\) of an element of \(H\) still lies in \(H\). This checks Corollary 4.0.4 and, with the preceding result, the extension argument in Proposition 4.0.6.
The Suslin first-row calculation has the following exact ranges. Here \(n\) is the dimension of the punctured affine space and \(m\) the homotopy degree; Lemma 2.4.1 requires \(2\leq m\leq2n-4\).
Use | \((n,m)\) | Required range | Annihilator
First row in Prop. 4.0.9 | \((d,d)\) | \(d\geq4\) | \((d-1)!\)
Kernel in Lemma 4.0.8 | \((d+1,d+1)\) | \(d\geq3\) | \(d!\)

The affine quadric projection is locally an affine-space bundle: on \(x_i\ne0\), solve for \(y_i\). Thus its use as a model for \(\mathbb A^n\setminus0\) is justified more specifically than by merely having affine fibers.

The Hermitian \(K\)-theory factorization in Proposition 4.0.9 and its cited top-cohomology vanishing make the stabilized Suslin image zero. The stabilization kernel bound and first-row composite then annihilate \(H^d(X,\pi^{\mathbb A^1}_d(\mathbb A^d\setminus0))\) by \(d!(d-1)!\). Its prime divisors are those of \(d!\); divisibility under the main theorem’s assumptions therefore forces this group to vanish.
# Minor correction: the weight in Lemma 4.0.7

Equation reference: eq:weight. On p. 35, the displayed identification following the two exact cohomology sequences uses \(\mathbf K_{d+1}^{MW}\), and then \(\mathbf K_{d+1}^M\), for the first nonzero homotopy sheaf of \(\mathbb A^{d+2}\setminus0\). The correct identification is \[
 \pi^{\mathbb A^1}_{d+1}(\mathbb A^{d+2}\setminus0)=\mathbf K_{d+2}^{MW}.\] It follows directly from the general formula on p. 14 with \(d\) replaced by \(d+2\); the printed index is one too small.

Equation reference: eq:symbol. This correction does not destroy the lemma. By Corollary 3.0.2, its restriction to \(X\) is \(\mathbf K_{d+2}^M\). The last Gersten term computing \(H^d(X,\mathbf K_{d+2}^M)\) is \(\bigoplus_{x\in X^{(d)}}K_2^M(k)\). For every positive integer \(N\) and symbol \(\{a,b\}\), algebraic closedness supplies \(c^N=a\), so \[
 \{a,b\}=N\{c,b\}.\] Thus this last term, and its cohomology quotient, are divisible. The argument uses divisibility, not unique divisibility. It is valid even if the characteristic divides \(N\).

If \(C\) is the first cokernel sheaf in the proof of Lemma 4.0.7, right exactness of top cohomology identifies \(H^d(X,C)\) with the relevant cokernel. Lemma 2.4.1 kills it by \((d+1)!\). It is also divisible as a quotient of the group just described, so it is zero. The second short exact sequence now gives the desired stabilization isomorphism. No new exclusion of characteristic \(d+1\) is needed.
This is a local index correction with a complete replacement for the affected sentence; the main vanishing and cancellation conclusions survive. Author adoption is unknown.
# Explicit completion of the kernel comparison
## The inference that needs explanation

Lemma 4.0.8 ends on p. 35 by passing from an exact sheaf segment \(B\to D\to E\) to a claim about the kernel of \(H^d(D)\to H^d(E)\). Such a segment alone does not make that cohomology kernel the image of \(H^d(B)\). One must compare the image sheaf with \(E\). This review supplies the comparison under the main theorem’s hypothesis \(N=d!\in k^\times\). This is a proof-completeness observation; no counterexample to the lemma is claimed.

For this comparison, work on a connected component of dimension \(d\geq4\), as in the source’s running convention. Lower-dimensional components are handled separately as above. Set, on the small Nisnevich site of \(X\), \[D=\pi^{\mathbb A^1}_d(\mathrm{GL}_d)|_X,\qquad
 E=\pi^{\mathbb A^1}_d(\mathrm{GL}_{d+1})|_X,\qquad
 A=\mathbf K_{d+1}^M|_X.\] The long homotopy sequence continues as \(D\to E\xrightarrow{r}A\). The Suslin map gives \(t:A\to E\) with \(rt=N\,\mathrm{id}\). Indeed the punctured affine space now has dimension \(d+1\); the first-row degree is \(d!\), and the homotopy degree \(d\) is in the permitted range.
## Divisibility needed for the comparison

For each prime \(\ell\mid N\), the generic field of an étale scheme over \(X\) has \(\ell\)-cohomological dimension at most \(d\). Norm residue gives \(K_{d+1}^M(F)/\ell=0\). Unramifiedness of the strictly \(\mathbb A^1\)-invariant quotient therefore gives \(A/\ell=0\) on this site.

We also need \(H^d(X,{}_\ell A)=0\). Contraction commutes with the kernel defining the torsion sheaf. Its final Rost–Schmid term is \(\bigoplus_{x\in X^{(d)}}\mu_\ell(k)\). The Milnor coefficient has trivial orientation action, so this computation has no residual line-bundle twist. Choose a primitive root \(\tau\). For each codimension-\((d-1)\) curve, the torsion symbol \(\{\tau,f\}\) has boundary \(\tau^{\operatorname{ord}(f)}\), with a consistent choice of residue sign. The resulting boundaries contain all rational-equivalence relations modulo \(\ell\). Hence \[\mathrm{CH}_0(X)/\ell\twoheadrightarrow H^d(X,{}_\ell A).\]

The group \(\mathrm{CH}_0(X)\) is divisible in this affine situation. Each closed point lies on an integral affine curve. Normalize that curve; the normalization is a smooth affine curve, finite over its image, with a \(k\)-point above the chosen point. Its Picard group is divisible: compactify, use a boundary \(k\)-point to remove the degree part, then use divisibility of the Jacobian’s \(k\)-points. Pushing forward an \(\ell\)-root of the point class gives an \(\ell\)-root in \(\mathrm{CH}_0(X)\). Closed points generate that group. Consequently the displayed target vanishes.

The exact sequence \(0\to{}_\ell A\to A\xrightarrow{\ell}A\to0\) then makes \(H^{d-1}(X,A)\) \(\ell\)-divisible. Iterating over the prime factors of \(N\) proves \(N\)-divisibility of both \(A\) and \(H^{d-1}(X,A)\). The relation \(rt=N\) now proves that both \(r\) and \(H^{d-1}(r)\) are onto.
## Recovering the desired kernel

Equation reference: eq:kernel. Put \(J=\ker r=\operatorname{im}(D\to E)\). From \(0\to J\to E\to A\to0\) and the preceding surjectivity, \(H^d(J)\to H^d(E)\) is injective. From \(0\to B\to D\to J\to0\) and cohomological dimension at most \(d\), \[H^d(B)\longrightarrow H^d(D)\longrightarrow H^d(J)
 \longrightarrow0\] is exact. Thus \[
 \ker[H^d(D)\to H^d(E)]
   =\operatorname{im}[H^d(B)\to H^d(D)].\] The preceding homotopy segment and Lemma 2.4.1 make \(H^d(B)\) \(d!\)-torsion, exactly as the source intended. This completes that use in the main proof.

Lemma 4.0.8 and Proposition 4.0.9 are placed under the wider running assumption \(\operatorname{char}k\ne2\). The completion above does not establish their full range when \(\operatorname{char}k\mid d!\). Additional characteristic-\(p\) input or a different comparison would be needed there. That uncompleted extension is recorded as Needs Evidence, not as a demonstrated false statement or a refutation of the main theorem.
# The dimension-three boundary and external dependencies

The inequality \(d\leq2d-4\) excludes \(d=3\) from the first-row annihilation proof. The source instead uses Proposition 4.0.10 (pp. 36–37): \[T_5\longrightarrow\pi^{\mathbb A^1}_3(\mathbb A^3\setminus0)
       \longrightarrow GW_4^3\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 0\longrightarrow I^6\longrightarrow T_5
       \longrightarrow\mathbf K_5^M/24\longrightarrow0.\] The \(I^6\) restriction vanishes. The final term for \(H^3(X,\mathbf K_5^M/24)\) is a sum of \(K_2^M(k)/24=0\), by [eq:symbol] (#eq:symbol). The cited \(H^3(X,GW_4^3)=0\) then gives the required vanishing. This argument does not silently reuse the invalid dimension-three stable range. Characteristic three is already excluded from the cancellation theorem by \(3!\), although the auxiliary statement is formulated more broadly.

The review checked how the following external inputs enter, without independently reproving their full source texts: affine representability and motivic Postnikov machinery; Morel’s homotopy-sheaf and Freudenthal results; the Suslin matrix and Chern-class formulas; Bertini and the threefold unimodular-row divisibility result; norm residue, the torsion description and the coniveau differential compatibility; and the Hermitian \(K\)-theory factorization and top-cohomology vanishing. The references and proposition labels are those cited in [paper]. Their full proofs are outside this review’s source set. No missing code or unretrieved reference has been relabeled as an error.
