Matroids, Feynman Categories,
and Koszul Duality
# Exact version, mathematical scope, and evidence
The source is Matroids, Feynman categories, and Koszul duality, by Basile Coron [paper].
Reviewed version: arXiv:2211.12370v3, dated 11 December 2024; 70 pages, 570554 bytes. Assigned journal DOI:

The exact supplied author manuscript was reviewed; the journal version and later corrections were not compared. Source locations below are one-based physical PDF pages, agreeing with inspected printed labels. The source SHA256 is

The main objects are finite geometric lattices with building sets. An irreducible built lattice means that \(\hat 1\in\mathcal G\); its underlying lattice need not be an indecomposable lattice. In particular, the Boolean examples below with top-containing building sets are permitted. The paper constructs a Feynman category, FY and OS (co)operadic structures, a quadratic presentation and Gröbner basis for \(\mathrm{FY}^\vee\), and two Koszul arguments: one through a Leray model, another through shuffle operads.

A native helper read all 70 pages, including the bibliography, and inspected 23 source images. Two other native helpers provided disjoint local cross-checks of the normal-form proof and the Leray correction. The lead reviewer read decisive passages on 27 pages, inspected 18 source images, reconstructed the examples and repairs, and ran an independent exact calculation. These roles are recorded separately; they are not human reviewers or external controllers. Full manifest parsing, hashing and rendering were not counted as scientific reading or image inspection. No author code was run.

The Major labels below concern invalid core derivations or definitions even when a short repair exists. Minor labels concern local statements whose needed replacements are available without changing the main mechanism. The sign concern in Section 8 (#sec:sign) is qualified separately. Author adoption of every proposed change is unknown.
# Major F1: the normal-form invariant does not descend
## A permitted composition with two invariant values

Lemma 3.20 (p. 27) assigns raw inclusion to structural arrows on all non-bottom interval elements, inverse underlying poset maps to isomorphisms, and then extends by composition. Checking relations (6) and (7) does not check the additional structural composition (3) with its source identification \(\Phi\) from Lemma 3.12.

Let \(L=B_3\) have atoms \(a,b,c\), write \(ab=a\vee b\), and put \(t=abc\). Take \[\mathcal G=\{a,b,c,t\},\qquad S=\{a,t\}.\] For a proper Boolean element, its maximal building factors are its atoms and their product is its lower interval. For \(t\), the unique maximal factor is \(t\) itself. Thus \(\mathcal G\) is a building set, and \((L,\mathcal G)\) is irreducible. The upper interval \([a,t]\) has induced building set \(\{ab,ac,t\}\). Refine it by \(T=\{ab,t\}\), and use the unit in \([0,a]\). Both local sets are spanning and nested. Since \(\operatorname{Comp}_a(ab)=b\), equation (3) gives the composite \(U=\{a,b,t\}\), which is nested because \(ab\notin\mathcal G\).

The iterated and direct sources are respectively \[W=[0,a]\otimes[a,ab]\otimes[ab,t],\qquad
 W'=[0,a]\otimes[0,b]\otimes[ab,t].\] On the middle factor the underlying poset map defining \(\Phi\) is \(j:[0,b]\to[a,ab]\), \(j(x)=a\vee x\). The categorical isomorphism is represented in the opposite direction, so the proposed invariant sends \(ab\) to \(b\) along \(\Phi\). The two structural inclusions instead leave \(ab\) unchanged. Thus two expressions for the same arrow give \[\iota(S)\iota(\mathrm{Id}\otimes T)(ab)=ab,\qquad
 \iota(U)\iota(\Phi)(ab)=b.\] The invariant is not well-defined. In the maximal building set, \(\operatorname{Comp}\) happens to be inclusion; that special case cannot justify the general statement.
## Complete replacement using building sets

Equation reference: eq:compmap. Associate to an object its building set, with tagged disjoint union for tensor products. For a structural arrow \(S\), use \[
 c_S:\coprod_{G\in S}\operatorname{Ind}_{[\tau_S(G),G]}(\mathcal G)\longrightarrow\mathcal G,
 \qquad Y\longmapsto\operatorname{Comp}_{\tau_S(G)}(Y).\] For an isomorphism use the inverse poset map restricted to building sets. The domain restriction matters: \(\operatorname{Comp}\) need not be defined on every non-bottom lattice element.

Equation reference: eq:compidentity. Here is the full composition check. For one block of a refinement put \[A=\tau_S(G_i),\quad H=[A,G_i],\quad
 B=\tau_{T_i}(K),\quad C=\operatorname{Comp}_A^L(K),\quad D=\tau_U(C).\] The interval identification is \(j:[D,C]\to[B,K]\), \(j(Z)=A\vee Z\). The pointwise identity proved in Lemma 3.13 (pp. 22–24) is \[
 \operatorname{Comp}_A^L\!\left(\operatorname{Comp}_B^H(Y)\right)
   =\operatorname{Comp}_D^L\!\left(j^{-1}(Y)\right)\] for every \(Y\) in the induced building set of \([B,K]\). It follows by joining the proposed value with \(D\) and using the maximality characterization of \(\operatorname{Comp}\); the building-factor product decomposition proves that every other candidate lies below it. This preliminary proof precedes the normal-form theorem. Equation [eq:compidentity] (#eq:compidentity) is exactly the missing structural compatibility.

The remaining relations hold as follows. A built-lattice isomorphism preserves the maximal defining fiber of \(\operatorname{Comp}\), so \(h\operatorname{Comp}_A(Y)=\operatorname{Comp}_{h(A)}h(Y)\), proving naturality. Permuting source factors permutes tagged blocks in [eq:compmap] (#eq:compmap). Units use \(\operatorname{Comp}_0(Y)=Y\). Disjoint union gives tensor interchange and symmetry. Inverse poset maps respect identity and composition. Together these checks define \(c\) on the category as presented; they do not assume the later generator-presentation theorem.

For uniqueness of normal forms, labelled source-factor tops map to the corresponding nodes of \(S\). They recover \(S\) and the factor assignment; the chosen order determines its permutation. If \(h_i:L_i\to[\tau_S(H_i),H_i]\) is the forward interval isomorphism, recover it on building elements by \[h_i(g)=\tau_S(H_i)\vee c_F(g).\] Every atom lies in the building set, and an atomic lattice is join-generated by its atoms. Thus \(h_i\), including its bottom, is determined everywhere. Simply restricting \(c_F\) without joining the lower endpoint would not recover \(h_i\). Existence follows by moving isomorphisms to the source, flattening structural composites, and sorting the factors. This proves the intended normal form without circularity. It repairs the proof used for the presentation and shuffle comparison; it does not demonstrate a false normal-form theorem.
# Major F2: a rank-one top interval is missing

Proposition 5.23 and Lemma 5.24 (p. 53) prohibit every rank-one interval in the spanning frame. Yet their proposed frame is \[\operatorname{fr}(S)
 =\{G\in S:\operatorname{rk}[\tau_S(G),G]>1\}\cup\{t\}.\] The appended top may have local rank one.

Already a rank-one irreducible arity has its nonzero FY class and trivial normal monomial, but has no allowed frame under the printed restriction. A positive-weight example is \(B_3\) with maximal building set and atom order \(a<b<c\). The nested set \(\{ab,t\}\) is normal: its lower node has rank two, whereas the quadratic leading terms on p. 54 have a nonminimal atom as lower node. Its top interval \([ab,t]\) has rank one. Rank additivity implies that a rank-three frame with every interval of rank at least two can have only its top node, so the printed parametrization misses this monomial.

The correction is to prohibit rank-one intervals only at non-top frame nodes. Keep the displayed frame formula. Removed rank-one nodes form clusters in the frame intervals; each is assigned to its unique nearest retained parent. A proper retained node has residual rank greater than one, so its cluster is proper. The top cluster may exhaust all but one unit of its interval rank. Accordingly the existing bounds \[k_G<\operatorname{rk}[\tau(G),G]-1\quad(G\ne t),\qquad
 k_t\leq\operatorname{rk}[\tau(t),t]-1\] remain correct; a rank-one top interval allows \(k_t=0\). The exponent correspondence \[\alpha_G=\operatorname{rk}[\tau(G),G]-k_G-1\] then gives positive proper-node exponents and a possibly zero top exponent, exactly the spanning version of the FY basis. The intrinsic frame criterion and unique local clusters give uniqueness. With the minimum argument in Section 7 (#sec:minor), the normal-cluster/EL-chain proof survives.

Exact enumeration in \(B_3\) gives six FY normal monomials, with half-degree Hilbert polynomial \(1+4z+z^2\). The printed frames give three; the corrected frames give six. Thus the printed basis-count step is false, but the corrected step supports the intended Gröbner conclusion.
# Major F3: cubical insertion must use the current interval

The formula on p. 57 joins the next node with earlier selected nodes strictly below it. That join does not change the node. For \(B_3\), \(\mathcal G=\{a,b,c,t\}\), and \(S=\{a,b,t\}\), insert \(a\) first. The current factors are \([0,a]\) and \([a,t]\). The printed next node \(b\) lies in neither factor. The needed induced node is \(ab\in[a,t]\), with \(\operatorname{Comp}_a(ab)=b\). The tensor generator asserted by the printed formula is therefore undefined.

Equation reference: eq:insert. A complete insertion rule is available. Start with \(T=\{t\}\). For each next original node \(G\), let \(P\) be the least element of \(T\) strictly above \(G\), and put \[
 A=\tau_T(P),\qquad H=A\vee G.\] Insert \(H\) in the factor \([A,P]\), then adjoin \(G\) to \(T\). The nested-factor decomposition gives \(A<H<P\), \(H\in\operatorname{Ind}_{[A,P]}(\mathcal G)\), and \(\operatorname{Comp}_A(H)=G\). Indeed \(G\leq A\) would put it below a smaller current parent; \(A\vee G=P\) would make a forbidden nested antichain with join in \(\mathcal G\). The factor characterization supplies the \(\operatorname{Comp}\) identity.

After the normal-form repair, chains modulo intermediate isomorphisms are precisely orderings of the non-top nodes. The rule [eq:insert] (#eq:insert) reconstructs every ordering. Permuting those orderings gives a free symmetric-group action, preserves the composite, and has exactly the degree-\(n\) composition fibers as its orbits. Concatenation gives the required compatibility. The target in Definition 6.1 should accordingly be the degree-\(n\) component \(\operatorname{Hom}_n(A,B)\). The least-atom convention also respects these interval identifications in the shuffle category. The intended cubicality is supported by this replacement; the old formula does not prove it.
# Major F4: the printed Leray differential is not defined
## A rank-two witness
Definition 6.4 (pp. 61–62) includes all \(e_G,x_G\), kills \(e_t\), and prescribes \(d(e_G)=x_G\) without a top exception. A differential on a quotient must preserve its defining ideal.

Use the flats of the simple connected matroid \(U_{2,3}\): bottom, atoms \(a,b,c\), and top \(t\), with maximal building set. A nested set contains at most one atom. The atom-linear relations give \(x_a=x_b=x_c=-h\), where \(h=x_t\). The nonnested relations give \(h^2=0\), \(e_i h=0\), and \(e_i e_j=0\) for distinct atoms. In the graded quotient by \(e_t\), \(h\) is nonzero: the algebra map \[x_t\mapsto h,\qquad x_a,x_b,x_c\mapsto-h,\qquad e_G\mapsto0
 \quad\text{to }\mathbb Q[h]/(h^2)\] respects every defining relation. But the prescribed differential sends the zero class \(e_t\) to this nonzero class. Thus the object used immediately for the comparison of complexes is not a DGA as printed.
## A well-defined correction and its projective map

Equation reference: eq:bpr. Define instead \[
 B_{\mathrm{pr}}
 =\left(\Lambda(e_G:G\in\mathcal G\setminus\{t\})
          \otimes\mathbb Q[x_G:G\in\mathcal G]\right)/J,\] where \(J\) has the same nonnested mixed-support relations and atom-linear relations. Keep every \(x_G\), including \(x_t\). Set \(de_G=x_G\) for proper \(G\) and \(dx_G=0\). The bidegrees remain \((0,1)\) and \((2,0)\); \(d\) has bidegree \((2,-1)\).

Differentiating a nonnested monomial replaces one \(e_G\) by \(x_G\), preserving its support, so every summand remains in \(J\). The atom-linear relations are closed. The odd derivation has square zero on generators and hence everywhere. This is a general DGA proof, not merely a calculation in rank two.

Write \(z=e_t\) in the affine model \(\widehat B\), where \(dz=x_t\). Adding top never changes whether a support is nested, so as graded algebras \(\widehat B=B_{\mathrm{pr}}\otimes\Lambda(z)\). The inclusion of \(B_{\mathrm{pr}}\) is a chain map; the graded projection \(q(z)=0\) generally is not.

Equation reference: eq:chain. For an atom \(H\), put \[\eta_H=\sum_{\substack{G\geq H\\G\ne t}}e_G,\qquad
 d\eta_H=-x_t.\] Let \(\phi_{\mathrm{aff}}\) be the affine algebra map used by the source, \(e_H\mapsto\sum_{G\geq H}e_G\), and let \(\phi_{\mathrm{pr}}=q\phi_{\mathrm{aff}}\) as a graded map. The derivation rule gives \[
 d\phi_{\mathrm{pr}}(\alpha)
   =-x_t\,\phi_{\mathrm{pr}}(\delta\alpha).\] Consequently its restriction to \(\overline{\mathrm{OS}}=\ker\delta\) is a chain map. An individual affine generator has differential \(-x_t\); it is not a projective element. Requiring every \(\eta_H\) to be closed would test the wrong domain.

There is also a precise conditional reduction of the quasi-isomorphism. Choose an atom \(H_0\), set \(v=z+\eta_{H_0}\), and observe \(dv=0\). Then \[\widehat B\simeq B_{\mathrm{pr}}\otimes\Lambda(v),\qquad
 \mathrm{OS}\simeq\overline{\mathrm{OS}}\otimes\Lambda(e_{H_0}).\] The second decomposition follows from \(\delta(e_{H_0})=1\): write \(\alpha=(\alpha-e_{H_0}\delta\alpha)+e_{H_0}\delta\alpha\). Under these decompositions, \(\phi_{\mathrm{aff}}=\phi_{\mathrm{pr}}\otimes\mathrm{id}\). Over \(\mathbb Q\), the external affine quasi-isomorphism therefore implies the corrected projective objectwise quasi-isomorphism. In rank one the proper exterior set is empty and the atom relation forces \(x_t=0\); the formula gives \(\mathbb Q\). The rank-zero tensor unit is treated separately.

In the \(U_{2,3}\) example, \(B_{\mathrm{pr}}\) has basis \(1,e_a,e_b,e_c,h\), and its only nonzero differential is \((-1,-1,-1):\mathbb Q^3\to\mathbb Qh\). Thus its cohomology dimensions are \(1,2,0\), as required for the projective OS algebra. Adding \(x_t=0\) instead would give three degree-one classes; it is not an adequate repair.

The local bar differential agrees with this correction: contracting a proper node inserts \(x_G\), as in \(\mathrm{FY}^{PD}([G])\) on p. 39, and moving that exterior generator to the contracted position gives the usual alternating sign. There is no projective top contraction. The underlying graded quotient is unchanged by [eq:bpr] (#eq:bpr), so the cited nested-set decomposition has the same indexing.

These checks fix the DGA and its objectwise projective map. They do not independently prove the external affine Leray theorem, the complete graded decomposition, every odd-cooperad compatibility, or the identification with the canonical quadratic-dual map. The atom choice above is not claimed to give a natural cooperadic splitting. Corollary 6.6 needs a synchronized corrected comparison. Its conclusion is not disproved, and Corollary 6.10 has a separate Gröbner route.
# Major F5b: the all-object projective OS assignment

On p. 58, the source assigns \(\overline{\mathrm{OS}}(L)[-1]\) to every built lattice, while the construction is supposed to be a strong monoidal cooperad. Let each of two irreducible rank-one factors be \(B_1\). Each assigned vector space is one-dimensional in shifted degree one, so their tensor is one-dimensional in degree two. The product lattice \(B_2\) has projective OS dimensions \(1,1\) in original degrees \(0,1\), hence dimensions \(1,1\) in shifted degrees \(1,2\). Its assigned total dimension is two, not one. The rank-zero unit likewise receives a shifted copy of the ground field instead of the tensor unit.

No choice of structural maps can repair this object-level dimension obstruction. Define the displayed value only on irreducible arities, extend to a product by tensoring the factor values, and send the empty product to the tensor unit. This is a complete repair of the object assignment. It leaves the separate braiding issue below to be checked. The classification is Major because the literal core cooperad definition cannot be strong monoidal, not because the intended aritywise construction is refuted.
# Five local issue groups
## F5a: projective FY presentations require irreducibility

Proposition 2.23 and the following top-degree assertion (pp. 14–15) are stated for every built lattice. For \(B_2\) with reducible building set \(\{a,b\}\), Definition 2.22 gives \[\mathrm{FY}=\mathbb Z[x_a,x_b]/(x_a,x_b)=\mathbb Z.\] The displayed projective presentation instead gives \(\mathbb Z[x_a,x_b]/(x_a-x_b)\simeq\mathbb Z[u]\), since all its subsets are nested. There is no top generator in this building set.

Restrict the projective elimination and its top generator to irreducible built lattices. For a product with \(m\) maximal building factors the top degree is \(2(\operatorname{rk}L-m)\), by tensoring the irreducible factor rings. The later generator theorem explicitly uses irreducible arities. This is a Minor scope correction.
## F6: use the least node greater than or equal to the input

The general \(\mathrm{FY}(S)\) formula on p. 32 selects \(G'=\min S_{>G}\). It is undefined for \(G=t\). For maximal \(B_3\), \(S=\{ab,t\}\), \(G=ab\), it also selects the wrong interval: its alleged index is the bottom \(ab\) of \([ab,t]\), whereas the elementary map puts \(h_{ab}\) in \([0,ab]\).

Replace \(>\) by \(\geq\). Spanning gives existence and the nested-factor property gives a unique least node. If \(G\leq\tau_S(G')\), the building-factor decomposition would place \(G\) below a smaller node, contradicting minimality. Thus \(\tau_S(G')\vee G\) is a valid non-bottom index. Equality \(G'=G\), including top, now works. The elementary maps on p. 31 and their relations independently define the cooperad, so this is a Minor closed-form correction.
## F7: only equality of fiber minima is needed

In Lemma 5.25 (p. 54), the second claimed fiber equality is too strong. Take \(U_{2,3}\oplus U_{1,1}\) on atoms \(a<b<c<d\), with maximal building set, and the increasing chain \(S=\{a,abc,t\}\). Put \(G_1=a\), \(G_2=abc\). Then \(H_{G_2}=b\), \(\tau_{S\setminus\{G_1\}}(G_2)=0\), and \(\tau_S(G_2)=a\). The two displayed fibers are respectively \(\{b\}\) and \(\{b,c\}\), not equal.

For the required repair, put \(u=\tau_{S\setminus\{G_1\}}(G_2)\), \(v=\tau_S(G_2)\), \(h=H_{G_2}\). The fiber \(u\vee H=u\vee h\) is contained in the fiber \(v\vee H=G_2\), and contains \(h\). Since \(h\) is the minimum of the latter fiber, their minima agree. That is all inequality (24) uses. The first fiber comparison follows from the nested product decomposition. The increasing-label conclusion survives; this is a Minor unnecessary auxiliary equality.
## F8: two outlook axioms need qualifications

Definition 7.1 (p. 66) omits rank monotonicity. On \(E=\{a,b\}\), set \(r(\varnothing)=0\), \(r(a)=r(b)=1\), \(r(E)=0\). Every printed submodular and one-element upper-increment inequality holds, but \(r(a)>r(E)\). Add monotonicity, equivalently the lower bound in \(0\leq r(A\cup\{x\})-r(A)\leq1\).

The equivalence following Definition 7.2 is also not injective as stated. On the genuine simple loopless matroid \(U_{2,3}\), let \(\nu\) be discrete on proper subsets and one-block on \(E\); let \(\nu'\) be one-block on every nonempty subset. Both satisfy refinement, the block idempotence condition and rank additivity. They agree on all flats, namely the empty set, singletons and \(E\). They give the same building set but differ on pairs.

Equation reference: eq:closure. For the asserted bijection, impose \[
 \nu(X)=\nu(\operatorname{cl}X)|_X.\] On a flat, rank-additive blocks give a direct-sum restriction, so the blocks are closed. Refinement shows that every one-block flat below it lies in one such block; those are exactly its maximal building factors. Conversely building factors partition each flat. Their intersections with a spanning subset span their respective factors, so the induced partitions satisfy block idempotence and rank additivity. Equation [eq:closure] (#eq:closure) determines every nonflat subset. This verifies the local bijection repair in the simple loopless setting. Alternatively the original decompositions can be described as richer data without claiming equivalence. Neither repair is a proof of the whole proposed future category. These outlook issues form one Minor group and are not used in the preceding geometric-lattice results.
## F9: the lower polymatroid branch has a wrong index

On p. 68, the lower branch sends \(h_{G'}\) to \(1\otimes h_G\) when \(G'\leq G\). In maximal \(B_3\), take \(G=ab\), \(G'=a\). The source has \(h_a=0\), while the printed image is \(1\otimes h_{ab}\ne0\) in the lower rank-two FY ring \(\mathbb Q[u]/(u^2)\). Thus the displayed algebra map is not well-defined even in the matroid special case. Replace the lower index by \(G'\), as in the earlier elementary FY formula. This is a Minor index correction; the whole polymatroid extension is not thereby certified.
# A qualified shifted-sign concern

This calculation uses the standard Koszul symmetry on graded vector spaces, consistent with the explicit graded-commutativity convention on p. 16. For \(B_3\), \(\mathcal G=\{a,b,c,t\}\), let \[\alpha=\delta(e_c e_b e_a)
       =e_b e_a-e_c e_a+e_c e_b\in\overline{\mathrm{OS}}(B_3).\] It is nonzero. Apply the displayed p. 58 maps literally. Cutting at \(a\) gives \((e_{ab}-e_{ac})\otimes1\); then cutting the upper factor at \(ab\) gives \(-1\otimes1\otimes1\). Cutting first at \(b\) gives \((e_{bc}-e_{ab})\otimes1\); the next cut at \(ab\) gives \(+1\otimes1\otimes1\). The final \(\sigma_{2,3}\) exchanges two shifted units of degree one, hence supplies another minus sign. The aligned composites are therefore equal and nonzero, where relation (27) requires them to be negatives.

An unsigned flip instead makes this particular relation hold. The source does not separately specify such a target symmetry in this construction. This report does not claim that changing the flip supplies a globally coherent repair, nor that every possible intended suspension convention fails. The exact calculation is a conditional failure of the displayed maps under the stated conventional interpretation. A fully specified symmetry/twist and recheck of all odd relations are needed. It is recorded as Needs Evidence for the intended convention, not counted as an additional convention-independent Major defect.
# Other proof checks and the two Koszul routes

The following positive checks delimit the findings. Building-factor decompositions justify induced intervals, the unique parent of a nonzero building element, and the maximality and injectivity of \(\operatorname{Comp}\). Nestedness ensures every structural local interval is nontrivial. Rank zero is the separately adjoined monoidal unit, not an irreducible structural arity. The proper grading can be checked directly as the number of source irreducible factors minus the number of target irreducible factors; it is additive under composition and tensor products.

The elementary FY maps preserve atom relations by semimodularity: an atom outside \(G\) joins \(G\) to an atom of the upper interval. Images of antichain relations reduce to the maximal image antichain, with additional factors multiplying an existing relation. Comparable cuts satisfy the three generator cases; nested incomparable cuts use the product-factor decomposition. The affine OS maps similarly kill circuit boundaries because either the lower subset is dependent or its upper contracted images are dependent. Affine OS is monoidal on product lattices, which does not imply the incorrect all-object projective assignment.

For Proposition 4.4, the coefficient-isolation induction has diagonal coefficient one. Read as a unitriangular integral argument, it gives a split injection on dual data and hence the required surjectivity. Mere injectivity of a dual map over \(\mathbb Z\) would not suffice; no torsion counterexample is inferred when this stronger argument is available. The degree identity \[\sum_{G\in S}\operatorname{rk}[\tau_S(G),G]=\operatorname{rk}L\] follows by peeling a minimal node and using the interval product. It checks the degree bounds and top-minus-one coefficient computations.

The shuffle construction uses the least atom in each join fiber, compatible with induced intervals. The geometric-lattice EL-chain property follows by greedily taking the least atom outside the current flat: delaying a smaller available atom forces a later decrease in labels. With corrected frames and fiber minima, this supplies the intended normal-monomial count in the Gröbner proof. The source’s reverse-prefix word order must be retained; substituting ordinary prefix lexicographic order changes its convention.

For Proposition 6.9 (p. 65), fix a decorated nested monomial. Quadraticity makes admissible contractions a condition on its adjacent edges. Normal-block decompositions form the augmented simplex on the admissible-edge set. If that set is nonempty, adjoining one fixed vertex gives a contracting homotopy. If it is empty, one fully split class remains on the quadratic diagonal. The filtration is bounded on each fixed finite arity/weight component relevant here. Thus this combinatorial mechanism supports Corollary 6.10 after the category and frame repairs. It does not use the ill-defined quotient differential of Definition 6.4.

The alternate Corollary 6.6 route needs the corrected DGA, the external Leray theorem, and synchronized cooperadic and suspension conventions. The two routes must not be conflated. Full proofs of the cited FY basis theorem, the Bibby–Denham–Feichtner Leray comparison, the Kaufmann–Ward/Ward bar–cobar framework, the Hodge results and geometric identifications were not independently retrieved or reproved. Their use and the local hypotheses were tracked in the review evidence. The general nonhomogeneous or infinite-dual extensions are not certified beyond the checked finite FY components. Unavailable code is not an error.
# Calculations, repair status, and assessment

The lead reviewer’s exact Python calculation verified the building axiom on all eight Boolean elements, all 29 node orderings for the two stated \(B_3\) building sets, the six-versus-three frame count, the nonzero Leray top class and differential rank, the two-element rank inequalities, both \(U_{2,3}\) partition systems, the unequal fibers, and the conditional OS signs. Exact augmented simplex boundary matrices for zero through five vertices satisfy \(d^2=0\) and have the stated homology, including the empty case. The process exited with status zero. These are finite checks supporting explicit examples; the general repairs are the arguments above, not extrapolations from enumeration.

The normal-form helper additionally checked 19 local refinements, 64 pointwise \(\operatorname{Comp}\)–\(\Phi\) identities and 186 naturality instances. The independent Leray helper supplied the general support-ideal proof and the conditional affine/projective splitting. All final mathematical evidence is tied to the exact source and reviewer files; author programs were not executed.

The conditional sign observation is additional and is not counted as a demonstrated convention-independent error. No example here disproves the intended final Koszulness conclusion. report: Abstract: This report examines the acquired third arXiv version, concentrating on the period construction, algebraic relations, height bounds and their stated dependencies. A scalar-matrix obstruction invalidates the homogeneous-tensor description of the period torsor used on a core proof path. A direct monodromy argument repairs the particular orbit-containment step needed for nontriviality of relations. Two further local defects concern a Jacobian-rank inference and the asserted simplicity of an orthogonal group. An additional quotient-incidence step remains unresolved. These conclusions concern specific statements and proofs; they do not establish that the main finiteness theorems are false. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical verification of
Geometric G-functions and Atypicality
# Identity, version and review scope

The reviewed work is David Urbanik, Geometric G-functions and Atypicality, arXiv:2301.01857v3, submitted on 26 July 2025, with printed title-page date 29 July 2025 [U]. Its frozen journal identity is Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), 2425–2512, DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2024-0079. The acquired author PDF has 72 pages; the journal pagination has 88 pages. The publisher’s full text was not acquired or certified equivalent. All page references below mean one-based pages of the acquired PDF; its printed Arabic page numbers agree.

The review followed the local log de Rham construction and realization in Sections 2–4; the algebra of relations and nontriviality argument in Sections 5–6; the point-counting reduction and idempotent bounds in Section 7; the dependence of the applications in Section 8; and the alternative comparison argument in Appendix B. The coverage ledger distinguishes direct inspection, bounded native checks and unverified external inputs. It does not assert a formal verification of every cited theorem. The released LaTeX was inspected as source text. No author program or author LaTeX was executed. A separate supplement or computational repository was not identified in the acquired materials; this absence is not a mathematical defect.
# Assumptions relevant to the conclusions

The period construction uses a projective family over a smooth curve, a simple normal-crossing degeneration, a local equation \(s=z_1\cdots z_\mu\), and cohomological degree \(w=\mu-1\). The height arguments further require the specified simplicity and CM conditions, two independent functionals where stated, relations at all relevant places, and functional nontriviality in the Hasse principle. CM is read with the paper’s algebraic Definition 1.4.

In Section 6 the connected algebraic monodromy group \(H\) is obtained as the identity component of the Zariski closure of monodromy, after the stated covering adjustment. The paper explicitly sets \[L^{a,b}=L^{\otimes a}\otimes(L^*)^{\otimes b}.\] Preserving a subspace setwise is distinct from fixing its vectors pointwise. This distinction is decisive for Problem 1.
# Established substantive findings

Problem 1 (A homogeneous-tensor stabilizer cannot give the claimed torsor).  The universal stabilizer assertion in Section 6.1, p. 38, is false under the displayed definition of \(L^{a,b}\). Consequently the stated justification of the \(H\)-torsor in equation (26), pp. 38–39, does not establish the construction used in Proposition 6.4.
## Claim, parameters and complete check

The source asserts that for every algebraic subgroup \(H\subset\operatorname{GL}(L)\) there are \(a,b\geq0\) and a line \(M\subset L^{a,b}\) whose setwise stabilizer is \(H\). Take \(L=\mathbb C^2\) and \(H=\operatorname{SL}_2\), which meet these hypotheses. For every \(a,b\) and every subspace \(M\), \[(\lambda I)|_{L^{a,b}}=\lambda^{a-b}I,\qquad
 (\lambda I)M=M\quad(\lambda\in\mathbb C^\times).\] Thus its stabilizer contains all scalar matrices. But \(\det(2I_2)=4\), so \(2I_2\notin\operatorname{SL}_2\). No choice permitted by the assertion can produce \(\operatorname{SL}_2\). Allowing higher-dimensional \(M\), as the following source paragraph does, cannot remove this obstruction.

The obstruction occurs in the actual local-system setting. On \(T=\mathbb P^1_\mathbb C\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\) assign its two free fundamental-group generators to \[U=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 V=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.\] The Zariski closures of their integral powers contain the upper and lower one-parameter unipotent groups: a polynomial vanishing on all integers vanishes identically. These groups generate \(\operatorname{SL}_2\). The resulting rank-two local system has connected algebraic monodromy \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) and fits the regular-singular Riemann–Hilbert setup invoked in Section 6.1.

For illustration, the natural determinant line \(M=\bigwedge^2L\subset L^{\otimes2}\) has setwise stabilizer \(\operatorname{GL}_2\). Putting that line into equation (26) gives fibre \(\operatorname{GL}_2\) at the basepoint, whereas parallel transport fixes a determinant tensor and lies in the determinant-one subvariety. The point \(2I_2\) is in the former fibre and outside the closure of the latter graph. This illustration is not presented as a line satisfying the impossible original assertion; it shows the consequence of substituting the natural invariant line into the displayed formula.
## Counterevidence, dependence and impact

The PDF confirms the single tensor bidegree and the setwise equation; this is not an extraction error. Material counterevidence appears in Section 7.4, p. 58: that paragraph allows a direct sum over tensor bidegrees and invokes pointwise-fixed tensors. Such a representation can distinguish scalars. For example, a line generated by \(1+t_1+\cdots+t_r\), with the tensors placed in separate summands, has setwise preservation forcing the coefficient of the trivial summand, and hence the individual tensors, to be fixed.

This later adjustment supplies a credible repair route, but does not make the explicit assertion on p. 38 true. The displayed dependence is Section 6.1 \(\longrightarrow\) Proposition 6.4 \(\longrightarrow\) Lemma 6.7 \(\longrightarrow\) Propositions 6.8–6.9 \(\longrightarrow\) Sections 6.5.2 and 6.6.2 \(\longrightarrow\) nontriviality in the Hasse-principle application. This is a demonstrated invalid derivation on a core proof path and supports Major under the supplied calibration. It is not a counterexample to Theorems 1.5 or 1.15. The separately adjusted Section 7.4 torsor has not been refuted.
## A verified repair of the needed orbit-containment step

The particular conclusion of Lemma 6.7 can be proved without that torsor. Let \(\widetilde R\) be the closed algebraic subset in Definition 6.6 containing the local flat graph \(\Gamma_1\). Continue the defining identities along each loop based at \(c\). They still hold, so \(\widetilde R_c\) contains the monodromy orbit of \(\alpha_1^*\). As \(\widetilde R_c\) is Zariski closed, it contains \(H(\mathbb C)\alpha_1^*\). With \(\widetilde R_c=V(Q)\) this is the required conclusion.

For a nonzero product of linear forms, irreducibility of a connected group orbit implies that one factor vanishes on the whole orbit. Its linear span is then a proper invariant subspace. When \(\alpha_1^*\) is \(E\)-defined, that span descends from the span of its \(E\)-monodromy orbit, contradicting the stipulated \(E\)-simplicity. This checks the specific nontriviality link, not every other input of the full height theorem.

Problem 2 (Uniqueness of a formal solution does not force the stated Jacobian rank).  In the proof of Lemma 4.3, the first paragraph of p. 32 infers full column rank of the matrix \(\boldsymbol M\) in equations (16)–(18) from uniqueness of the formal power-series solution. That inference is invalid.
## Complete counterexample

Set \(K=\mathbb Q\), \(\nu=\sigma=c=1\), \(q=0\), \(B_1(y)=y^3\) and \(C_1(x)=x^3\). These are the polynomials and initial condition permitted by Lemma 4.3 (p. 30). There is exactly one \(A\in\mathbb Q[[x]]\) with \(A(0)=0\) and \(A^3=x^3\). Indeed \(\operatorname{ord}_x(A)=1\), so \(A=xu\) and \(u^3=1\). Its rational constant term is \(1\), while \(u^2+u+1\) is a unit with constant term \(3\). Factoring \(u^3-1\) gives \(u=1\) and \(A=x\). Nevertheless, \[\boldsymbol M=(B_1'(0))=(0),\qquad
 \operatorname{rank}\boldsymbol M=0<1=\sigma .\] Later coefficient equations can constrain earlier apparent choices; a deficient matrix at each immediate recursion does not create infinitely many compatible full solutions.
## Boundary and restricted repair

The example is polynomial and does not refute the lemma’s convergence conclusion. The actual application in the preceding Lemma 4.2 has the stronger hypothesis that \(g:U\to V\) is étale. If a tangent vector annihilates the gradients of the equations defining \(U\), it lies in \(T_qU\); if it also annihilates \(dg\), étaleness makes it zero. Hence the combined Jacobian of the defining equations and \(g\) has full column rank independently of uniqueness. Using this rank fact repairs the recursion in that application. It does not prove the broader uniqueness-only lemma. The supported assessment is Minor, because the inspected core application has this independent justification and no material failure of the main realization theorem was demonstrated.

Problem 3 (The orthogonal rank-four case contradicts Lemma 7.21).  Lemma 7.21, p. 56, asserts that for a non-degenerate polarized Hodge structure the special isometry group is the \(\mathbb Q\)-simple special Mumford–Tate group of a point in the orbit. Its proof excludes only \(\operatorname{SO}_2\) as a possible non-simple case. A split \(\operatorname{SO}_4\) example meets the stated non-degeneracy hypothesis.
## Construction and verification

Let \(U_\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z^2\) with \(J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the weight-one Hodge structure whose \((1,0)\) part is the \(+i\) eigenspace of \(J\), and alternating polarization \(J\). Put \(W_\mathbb Z=U_\mathbb Z\otimes U_\mathbb Z\) with its tensor Hodge structure. Its Weil operator and symmetric polarization can be written \[C=J\otimes J,\qquad Q=J\otimes J,\qquad C^tQ=I_4.\] Thus \(Q(C-, -)\) is positive definite, while \(Q\) has signature \((2,2)\). The Hodge numbers are \((1,2,1)\), so \(\dim_\mathbb CF^1=3<4\); Definition 7.20 on p. 55 calls this non-degenerate. It is also realized by the Künneth summand \(H^1(E)\otimes H^1(E)\) of a product of elliptic curves.

The map \[\operatorname{SL}_2\times\operatorname{SL}_2\longrightarrow\operatorname{SO}(W,Q),\qquad
 (A,B)\longmapsto A\otimes B\] preserves \(Q\), has kernel \(\{(I,I),(-I,-I)\}\), and has six-dimensional image, the connected split special orthogonal group. The image of \(\operatorname{SL}_2\times\{I\}\) is a three-dimensional connected \(\mathbb Q\)-normal subgroup of this six-dimensional group. Consequently \(\operatorname{SO}(W,Q)\) is not \(\mathbb Q\)-simple. Changing the Hodge point cannot change this property of the fixed group.
## Impact and repair boundary

This refutes the simplicity clause and the proof’s classification. It does not by itself refute existence of generic full \(\operatorname{SO}(2,2)\) special Mumford–Tate group, nor Lemma 7.22(iii). The downstream abelian application in Proposition 7.27 expressly uses weight one, with symplectic factors. No core dependence on the false orthogonal simplicity assertion was demonstrated; the assessment is Minor. Restricting the invoked lemma to the weight-one setting avoids this example. Merely deleting an adjective has not been verified as a complete all-weight replacement.
# Unresolved point and checks that did not establish defects

In the proof of Corollary 7.17, p. 54, let \(A_j=\{g:gP_j\in I\}\). The source replaces the condition that \(gM(\mathbb C)P_j\) meet \(I\) by the condition \(gP_j\in I\). The former is invariant under right multiplication by \(M\); the latter need not be. The set-theoretically correct expression is \[q^{-1}(G_j)=A_jM(\mathbb C).\] Whenever a positive-dimensional orbit meets \(I\) in an isolated point, moving its representative slightly inside the orbit exhibits the distinction. Zero-dimensional orbits are counterevidence to a blanket objection. This review has not produced a complete geometric counterexample satisfying all global infinitude, height and Galois hypotheses of Corollary 7.17, nor verified a full replacement for the complex-analytic incidence argument preceding Lemma 7.18. This item is Needs Evidence; it is not used to raise the supported severity or to declare the corollary false.

Several initially suspicious steps have positive explanations. In Proposition 5.3 a largest cyclic block supplies a nonzero Krylov minor. For Proposition 5.4, if the characteristic and minimal polynomials of \(\tau\) agree, the nonzero polynomial \[D_\tau(x)=\det[x,\tau^*x,\ldots,(\tau^*)^{m-1}x]\] has degree \(m\), is defined over the base field, vanishes on noncyclic vectors, and factors into linear forms over a splitting field. It supplies a uniform relation for the relevant places. The two-functional argument in Section 6.6 uses the valid inequality \(\dim(E^2\cap W)\geq1\) for a codimension-one subspace \(W\).

For Lemma 7.25, the adjugate identity \[(\det\alpha)e=\operatorname{adj}(\alpha)e'\alpha\] shows that every coordinate denominator divides the isogeny degree when \(e'\) and \(\alpha\) are integral. Appendix A’s triangular support and symmetry argument yields \(\|s\eta s^{-1}\|_\infty\leq C D\), with \(D\) the largest coordinate denominator. Under the usual affine multiplicative height convention, one can use the common denominator to obtain \(H(s\eta s^{-1})\leq C'D^{m^2+1}\). This preserves the polynomial conclusion. The different possible matrix-height conventions are treated as a clarification, not as a claim that Proposition A.1 is false.

Finally, Appendix B, pp. 64–66, supplies an open-annulus decomposition and kernel description addressing the apparent splitting freedom in Section 3. The external comparison results remain dependencies rather than theorems independently re-proved in this review.
# Overall dependence and state

Problem 1 affects the displayed proof of a necessary nontriviality step in the height method. The direct monodromy repair above supports that step, while the mixed-tensor paragraph in Section 7.4 is essential counterevidence. Problems 2–3 concern stated auxiliary arguments beyond what their checked core uses require. No counterexample to the main height or finiteness conclusions has been established.

The arXiv version page and the author’s publication page checked for this review still identified v3; the bounded check did not identify a specific erratum resolving these findings. This is not an assertion of first discovery or absence of all later corrections. A source-by-source comparison with the publisher’s final text remains outside this report.

report: Abstract: This report examines the acquired third arXiv version. Explicit admissible examples disprove a Cartesian assertion used in the NS5 proof and the moment-map compatibility of a printed D5 resolution table. A separate co-separated example disproves the stated unnormalized one-term coefficient. Two local specification problems concern an attracting correspondence and change of group after full coefficient-field localization. The report records the correct constructions already present elsewhere in the paper, checks several coefficient and induction steps, and limits its conclusions to the acquired version. It does not establish that the normalized mirror identity is false. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical verification of
Bow varieties: Stable envelopes
and their 3d mirror symmetry
# Source identity, assumptions and coverage

The reviewed work is T. M. Botta and R. Rimányi, Bow varieties: Stable envelopes and their 3d mirror symmetry, arXiv:2308.07300v3, dated 11 November 2024 [BR]. The frozen journal identity is Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), 2651–2748, DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0002. The acquired PDF has 68 pages. The journal text was not acquired or certified equivalent; the frozen 2025 membership is unchanged. All page references below are to the acquired PDF, whose printed page numbers agree. Released LaTeX was read as source text and was not executed.

The review followed the bow-variety definitions and fixed-locus geometry, the elliptic stable-envelope axioms, the two resolution constructions, the reduction in Section 8, and Appendix A. Three native bounded checks were integrated with the primary analysis. The record distinguishes direct proof checks from imported theorems. In particular, the general existence theorem for stable envelopes and the previously proved full-flag and projective-space mirror results were used as dependencies, not independently reproved here.

The paper assumes throughout that the bow variety has an \(\mathbb A\)-fixed point (p. 8). The examples below satisfy this condition. The standard chamber, the specified good line bundle, and the distinction between full torus and intermediate subtori are retained. Theta-function identities are read meromorphically on their indicated parameter spaces; division by a vanishing factor is not justified by evaluation alone. The source’s convention \(\vartheta(u^{-1})=-\vartheta(u)\) is used consistently.

The current arXiv record explicitly says that v3 adds Lemma 7.11 to fill a gap in the proof of Theorem 7.9. That lemma is present and was read. The NS5 finding below concerns a different, explicitly false Cartesian assertion which is still used by the current proof. The historical absence of Lemma 7.11 is not listed as a defect.
# Findings on the geometric proof path
Problem 1 (The NS5 Cartesian square contains additional points).  Equation (46), p. 48, and the Cartesian assertion of Corollary 7.3 are false for an allowed elementary NS5 resolution.

Exact example and conventions. The source uses quotient flag dimensions (footnote 7, p. 47). Take \[X=T^*\operatorname{Fl}(1;3),\qquad \overline X=T^*\operatorname{Fl}(1,2;3).\] Thus the coarse flag is a two-dimensional kernel \(K\subset\mathbb C^3\); the refined flag consists of kernel subspaces \(F_1\subset F_2\subset\mathbb C^3\) of dimensions one and two. The separated bow is \(/1/3\backslash2\backslash1\backslash\). Splitting its final NS5 local charge \(2\) as \(1+1\) gives \(/1/2/3\backslash2\backslash1\backslash\). Every D5 local charge is one, so this is exactly the flag-variety case used in the proof of Proposition 7.2.

Let \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) be the standard basis and put \[F_1=\mathbb Ce_1,\qquad F_2=\mathbb Ce_1+\mathbb Ce_2,\qquad
 N=E_{12}.\] The refined cotangent conditions hold: \(N(F_1)=0\), \(N(F_2)\subset F_1\), and \(N(\mathbb C^3)\subset F_2\). Moreover \(N^2=0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}N=1\). It lies in the coarse Springer image \(Z_1\), since \(K=\ker N=\mathbb Ce_1+\mathbb Ce_3\) satisfies \(\operatorname{im}N\subset K\subset\ker N\). Consequently \((F_\bullet,N)\) lies in \(\overline X\times_{Z_2}Z_1\).

The incidence correspondence \(L\), however, requires the cotangent condition for the coarsened flag of the same point: \(N(F_2)=0\). Here \(N(e_2)=e_1\ne0\). Thus this point does not lie in \(j(L)\). This disproves the asserted Cartesian equality by an explicit point satisfying all the relevant flag and nilpotence conditions.

The affine square also fails. Footnote 8 observes that the affine bow quotient need not equal the Springer image. The following check does not assume such equality. In the refined NS5 quiver, take \[C_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
 D_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad D_1=0.\] The two choices \(C_1=(0,1)\) and \(C_1=(1,0)\) give, respectively, a bad point and a good point in the same flag-variety presentation; the remaining three-way data are unchanged. All moment equations hold: \(C_2D_2=0=D_1C_1\) and \(C_1D_1=0\). For both representatives \(D_2C_2=E_{12}\), so the unchanged three-way tail still satisfies the boundary moment equation. The surjective \(C\)-maps give the stable flag representatives. The condition for membership in \(j(L)\) is that \(D_2\) factor through \(C_1\). It fails for the bad point and holds for the good one with \(D=e_1\).

Scaling the first gauge space by \(t\ne0\) sends \(C_1\) to \(tC_1\) and fixes the other maps. Both representatives have the same limit \(C_1=0\) in the affine moment variety as \(t\to0\). Polynomial invariants therefore give them the same affine quotient point. Pairing the bad stable point with the \(L_0\)-image of the good point produces an element of the fibre product in Corollary 7.3 which does not come from \(L\). The issue persists with the actual affine quotient.

Dependence, counterevidence and repair boundary. Lemma 7.7 explicitly invokes Corollary 7.3, through the orbit argument of Lemma 6.11. Theorem 7.9 uses Lemma 7.7 for its support condition, equation (49); the nonresonance analysis in the added Lemma 7.11 also uses the lower-fixed-point containment. This is a demonstrated invalid premise on a core proof path and supports Major. No counterexample to the conclusion of Lemma 7.7 or the stable-envelope equality of Theorem 7.9 has been obtained.

The actual map \(j\) remains a closed incidence embedding in this example, and \(p\) remains a proper \(\mathbb P^1\) bundle. The extra linear condition on the coarsened flag proves closedness directly. Hence it would be incorrect to infer that Proposition 7.2’s properness or closedness is false. A replacement proof of the required orbit-chain containment may recover the argument. Neither the incorrect Cartesian statement nor its use in that containment proof is repaired merely by proving that \(j\) is closed.

Problem 2 (The printed D5 table does not preserve the moment equation).  The separated column of Table 1, p. 31, sends an admissible stable bow representation outside the target moment-zero locus. This contradicts the compatibility assertion in the proof of Proposition 6.3, pp. 32–33.

A full stable input. Use the separated diagram \(/1/2/3\backslash1\backslash\), with NS5 charges \((1,1,1)\) and D5 charges \((2,1)\), and split the first D5 charge as \(1+1\). For its first three-way part set \[B_-=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\-1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix},
 \quad B_+=0,\quad A=e_1,\quad a=e_2,\quad b=1.\] For the NS5 maps choose \[C_2=(1,0),\quad D_2=\binom01,\qquad
 C_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 D_3=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] The last D5 has \(W_-=\mathbb C\), \(W_+=0\), \(a=1\), and \(B_-=0\). Maps involving the zero end spaces are zero. Direct multiplication gives \[C_2D_2=0,\quad C_3D_3=D_2C_2,\quad -D_3C_3=B_-,
 \quad B_-A-AB_++ab=0.\] These are all the nontrivial moment equations. Condition (S1) holds because \(A\) is injective. Condition (S2) follows because \(A=e_1\), \(a=e_2\) and \(B_-a=e_3\) span \(\mathbb C^3\). The last framing vector generates the last one-dimensional space; \(A,a,B_-\) then generate \(\mathbb C^3\), and the surjective \(C\)-maps generate both remaining spaces. This verifies the stated graded-subspace criterion for GIT stability. The native evidence also records a semi-invariant frame check and exact integer products. A binary contingency table with the indicated row and column sums exists, so the paper’s nonempty-fixed-locus hypothesis is satisfied.

Counterevidence and bounded repair. Example 6.1, p. 31, draws \(a''=-1\), which fixes this right-hand residual. Its displayed left triangle also uses the coherent signs \[A'=(A,-a),\quad a'=-B_-a,\quad b'=(0,-1).\] Together with the displayed \(+b\) block of \(B_{\mathrm{mid}}\), these give both resolved moment equations equal to zero whenever the original equation holds. The surrounding prose instead mentions a \(-b\) block. The source therefore contains incompatible prescriptions; it also contains a correct elementary prescription. This material counterevidence is retained.

The printed table is the stated general construction and is cited for moment compatibility before the embedding, fusion and mirror-reduction arguments. Its failure supports Major for that construction and derivation. The coherent elementary signs give a verified local repair. This review does not certify all general splitting formulas or all co-separated table entries after a silent sign replacement, and does not refute the existence of the intended geometric embedding.
# An explicit normalization failure
Problem 3 (The co-separated one-term coefficient has the wrong range).  The uniform product in Corollary 6.14, p. 39, is false for a co-separated split with \(w'=1\) and \(w''=2\).

Take the source bow \(X=\backslash3/2/1/\), a point, and resolve its sole D5 local charge \(3\) as \(1+2\). Its global charges are zero; the zero \(3\times1\) contingency table gives its unique fixed point. Section 6.1 and Corollary 6.14 do not exclude this case. Use the coherent co-separated elementary map displayed in Example 6.1; this isolates the scalar issue from Table 1’s incompatible entries. The resolved component is \(F=\backslash1\backslash3/2/1/\). The original framing torus acts trivially on \(F\), so \(N_j^-=0\) for the original chamber and \(\operatorname{Stab}_X=1\). At the distinguished resolution \(f_\sharp\), the vertex characters are \[W_{\mathrm{mid}}=\{a'h\},\quad
 W_3=\{a'h,a''h,a''h^2\},\quad
 W_2=\{a''h,a''h^2\},\quad W_1=\{a''h^2\}.\] Subtracting the moment-equation and gauge characters from the representation characters gives exactly \[T_{f_\sharp}F=\frac{a''}{a'}+\frac{a'}{a''}h.\] For the chamber \(a'>a''\) the negative character is \(a''/a'\). The change of group in (33) is \((a',a'',h)=(a,ah,h)\), so the diagonal stable-envelope value is \(\vartheta(h)\).

The pullback at the image of the source point can be identified with this diagonal value without assuming that tautological characters determine every elliptic class. An explicit stable affine line joins the two points. In the resolved second triangle take \[A=e_1^*,\quad a=u,\quad b=e_2^*,\quad
 B_-=0,\quad B_+=uE_{12}+E_{23},\] and in its NS5 tail take \[D_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
 C_1=\begin{pmatrix}-u&0\\0&-1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
 \quad D_2=(0,1),\quad C_2=\binom{-1}{0}.\] The first triangle has \(b_0=1\) and \(B_0=0\). All moment equations hold for every \(u\). The three covectors \(b_0A,b,bB_+\) form the identity frame, which verifies (S1); the surjectivity of \(A\) verifies (S2). The tail and frame criterion verify stability throughout. The point \(u=1\) is the coherent resolution image and \(u=0\) is \(f_\sharp\). The parameter has character \((a'/a'')h\), which becomes one under \(\varphi\), so this affine line is fixed pointwise by the original \(T\). Equivariant homotopy invariance identifies the two restrictions. Thus the value \(\vartheta(h)\) is the relevant pullback.

The printed coefficient instead gives \(\vartheta(h)\vartheta(h^2)\). They are unequal: for an elliptic parameter \(0<q<1\), \(h=-1\) has \(\vartheta(h)\ne0\) and \(\vartheta(h^2)=\vartheta(1)=0\). The other parameters can be chosen generically. Equivalently the two explicit functions have different zero divisors, so this is not rescued by reading the formula meromorphically. The evidence records the admissible representative, its tangent-character cancellation, and the restriction to the distinguished point.

The source’s unprinted comment distinguishes the co-separated product through \(w'\). That comment is corroborating context; the tangent calculation and the stable-envelope diagonal axiom are the proof. In this example the product through \(w'=1\) is the correct value. A proof of a corrected formula for every split is not claimed here.

The one-term fusion identity is an advertised construction in the paper, and this is an explicit failure of its unnormalized statement. It supports Major at that scope. The normalized ratios used in the mirror identity can cancel a common factor. This counterevidence prevents promoting the example into a counterexample to Theorem 8.1.
# Two local specification problems

Problem 4 (The normalization correspondence is an attracting graph).  On p. 19 the paper identifies the stable-envelope kernel on \(F\times\operatorname{Attr}_{\mathfrak C}(F)\) with the Thom line of the inclusion of that whole product. The claimed identification fails when \(F\) has positive dimension.

Take the bow \(X=T^*\mathbb P^1\) and let \(A\) be the diagonal framing torus, which acts trivially. Use \(T=A\times\mathbb C_h^\times\), as allowed in Section 5.3. There is one fixed component \(F=X\), and \(\operatorname{Attr}(F)=X\). The printed map \(j\) is the identity on \(X\times X\), so \(N_j=0\) and \(\Theta(N_j)=\mathcal O\).

Here \(\mathcal L_{A,F}=\mathcal L_X\). By the source’s dual-kernel convention, the line \(\mathcal L_{A,F}^{\triangledown}\boxtimes\mathcal L_X\), restricted at a diagonal point \((f,f)\), is \(\Theta(T_fX)\). At a point of the zero section the two \(T\)-weights are \(1\) and \(h\). Thus this line has degree one along the elliptic \(h\) parameter, while \(\mathcal O\) has degree zero. They cannot be isomorphic. This example uses no residual framing-ratio parameter outside the chosen \(T\).

The correct correspondence is the graph of the attracting projection \(x\mapsto\lim_{t\to0}\sigma(t)x\). When \(A\) acts trivially, this is \(\Delta_X\) and its normal bundle is \(TX\), exactly supplying the missing Thom factor. Remark 5.5, p. 20, already states the correct \(\vartheta(N^-)[\Delta]\) restriction. The triangle and D5 proofs later use this diagonal normalization and the \(\Theta(TF)\) factor. For that reason the supported assessment is Minor: the printed specification is inconsistent, while the inspected core formulas explicitly use the corrected correspondence. This assessment is based on that counterevidence and dependency check, not merely on the brevity of a repair.

Problem 5 (Full coefficient-field localization does not commute with restriction).  The unrestricted change-of-group map used in Appendix A, pp. 64–65, does not exist on the fully localized coefficient fields displayed there.

Consider the allowed separated D5 split \(2=1+1\). In additive equivariant coordinates, (33) gives \[\varphi^*(u')=u-\eta,\qquad
 \varphi^*(u'')=u,\qquad \varphi^*(\eta)=\eta.\] The nonzero polynomial \(t=u''-u'-\eta\) is killed by \(\varphi^*\). After tensoring the source with \(\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb Q[u',u'',\eta]\), \(t\) is invertible. A unital extension would therefore imply \[1=\varphi^*(t\,t^{-1})=\varphi^*(t)\varphi^*(t^{-1})=0,\] a contradiction in the nonzero target coefficient field. The bow \(/1/2\backslash\) and its resolution \(/1/2\backslash1\backslash\) realize this torus map.

One may first change group on unlocalized equivariant cohomology and then localize at target coefficients, or localize the source only at elements whose images are nonzero. Regular stable-envelope classes can lie in such a valid domain. The proof’s phrase allowing arbitrary fully localized \(\alpha\) requires this restriction. The finding is Minor at the level of that overly broad map; no counterexample to Proposition A.1’s intended image statement or to the mirror identity has been established. A complete rewritten proof of the image statement is not asserted.
# Positive checks, rejected candidates and overall assessment

For Theorem 3.1, an extra torus weight block without framing would admit scalar automorphisms, contrary to freeness at a stable point. On an unframed three-way block, (S1) and (S2) force its \(A\)-map to be invertible. These observations support the two-factor fixed-locus decomposition and the charge bookkeeping.

The local \(K\)-theory identity of Proposition 3.6 can be checked directly. Writing \(x=\xi_1\), \(y=\xi_2\), \(z=\xi_3\), \(c=C_A\) and \(y'=x+z+c-y\), the local expressions are \[\alpha_{\rm before}=h y'y^*,\qquad
 \alpha_{\rm after}=h y'(y^*-c^*)+cx^*.\] Their difference is the stated \(\operatorname{Hom}(x,c)-h\operatorname{Hom}(c,y')\). The quadratic change \(-2h\sum t_i\) cancels the dynamical change \(+2h\sum t_i\), including the boundary interpretation modulo parameter-only terms.

The induction in Theorem 8.1 is finite: fully splitting one brane of charge \(w>1\) takes \(w-1\) elementary operations and reduces the number of nonunit branes by one. It is not necessary for every intermediate operation to reduce that number. The zero-charge step and the full-flag base result remain explicit dependencies.

The supported overall assessment is Major, with the separate scope and counterevidence stated for each item. The first three findings concern explicit geometric or fusion assertions; the last two concern local specifications with viable restricted interpretations. No counterexample to the normalized mirror formula has been established. The repairs verified here are bounded calculations, not certification of the complete revised paper.
# Evidence and review state

Source rendering and visual inspection are separately recorded. All current input, compiler, dependency/cache, log, PDF and image hashes are bound in the verification records. Failed attempts and earlier checkpoints are retained.

No author code or author TeX was executed. The acquired source package contains TeX and bibliography files; a separate computational release or supplement was not identified. That absence is not a mathematical defect. An author-hosted later PDF was reported inaccessible during acquisition and was not compared. The bounded version search does not claim that no later correction exists.
