analysis: Equation (46), p. 48, and the Cartesian assertion of Corollary 7.3 are false for an allowed elementary NS5 resolution.

Exact example and conventions. The source uses quotient flag dimensions (footnote 7, p. 47). Take \[X=T^*\operatorname{Fl}(1;3),\qquad \overline X=T^*\operatorname{Fl}(1,2;3).\] Thus the coarse flag is a two-dimensional kernel \(K\subset\mathbb C^3\); the refined flag consists of kernel subspaces \(F_1\subset F_2\subset\mathbb C^3\) of dimensions one and two. The separated bow is \(/1/3\backslash2\backslash1\backslash\). Splitting its final NS5 local charge \(2\) as \(1+1\) gives \(/1/2/3\backslash2\backslash1\backslash\). Every D5 local charge is one, so this is exactly the flag-variety case used in the proof of Proposition 7.2.

Let \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) be the standard basis and put \[F_1=\mathbb Ce_1,\qquad F_2=\mathbb Ce_1+\mathbb Ce_2,\qquad
 N=E_{12}.\] The refined cotangent conditions hold: \(N(F_1)=0\), \(N(F_2)\subset F_1\), and \(N(\mathbb C^3)\subset F_2\). Moreover \(N^2=0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}N=1\). It lies in the coarse Springer image \(Z_1\), since \(K=\ker N=\mathbb Ce_1+\mathbb Ce_3\) satisfies \(\operatorname{im}N\subset K\subset\ker N\). Consequently \((F_\bullet,N)\) lies in \(\overline X\times_{Z_2}Z_1\).

The incidence correspondence \(L\), however, requires the cotangent condition for the coarsened flag of the same point: \(N(F_2)=0\). Here \(N(e_2)=e_1\ne0\). Thus this point does not lie in \(j(L)\). This disproves the asserted Cartesian equality by an explicit point satisfying all the relevant flag and nilpotence conditions.

The affine square also fails. Footnote 8 observes that the affine bow quotient need not equal the Springer image. The following check does not assume such equality. In the refined NS5 quiver, take \[C_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
 D_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad D_1=0.\] The two choices \(C_1=(0,1)\) and \(C_1=(1,0)\) give, respectively, a bad point and a good point in the same flag-variety presentation; the remaining three-way data are unchanged. All moment equations hold: \(C_2D_2=0=D_1C_1\) and \(C_1D_1=0\). For both representatives \(D_2C_2=E_{12}\), so the unchanged three-way tail still satisfies the boundary moment equation. The surjective \(C\)-maps give the stable flag representatives. The condition for membership in \(j(L)\) is that \(D_2\) factor through \(C_1\). It fails for the bad point and holds for the good one with \(D=e_1\).

Scaling the first gauge space by \(t\ne0\) sends \(C_1\) to \(tC_1\) and fixes the other maps. Both representatives have the same limit \(C_1=0\) in the affine moment variety as \(t\to0\). Polynomial invariants therefore give them the same affine quotient point. Pairing the bad stable point with the \(L_0\)-image of the good point produces an element of the fibre product in Corollary 7.3 which does not come from \(L\). The issue persists with the actual affine quotient.

Dependence, counterevidence and repair boundary. Lemma 7.7 explicitly invokes Corollary 7.3, through the orbit argument of Lemma 6.11. Theorem 7.9 uses Lemma 7.7 for its support condition, equation (49); the nonresonance analysis in the added Lemma 7.11 also uses the lower-fixed-point containment. This is a demonstrated invalid premise on a core proof path and supports Major. No counterexample to the conclusion of Lemma 7.7 or the stable-envelope equality of Theorem 7.9 has been obtained.

The actual map \(j\) remains a closed incidence embedding in this example, and \(p\) remains a proper \(\mathbb P^1\) bundle. The extra linear condition on the coarsened flag proves closedness directly. Hence it would be incorrect to infer that Proposition 7.2’s properness or closedness is false. A replacement proof of the required orbit-chain containment may recover the argument. Neither the incorrect Cartesian statement nor its use in that containment proof is repaired merely by proving that \(j\) is closed.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: j remains closed and p proper in the example; all A-fixed points are in L; no counterexample to the conclusion of Lemma7.7, Theorem7.9 or normalized mirror duality.

problems.title: Printed D5 table fails moment compatibility
problems.source_location: PDF p.31 Table1 and Example6.1; Proposition6.3 pp.32–33.
claim: Recorded check: Printed D5 table fails moment compatibility
analysis: The separated column of Table 1, p. 31, sends an admissible stable bow representation outside the target moment-zero locus. This contradicts the compatibility assertion in the proof of Proposition 6.3, pp. 32–33.

A full stable input. Use the separated diagram \(/1/2/3\backslash1\backslash\), with NS5 charges \((1,1,1)\) and D5 charges \((2,1)\), and split the first D5 charge as \(1+1\). For its first three-way part set \[B_-=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\-1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix},
 \quad B_+=0,\quad A=e_1,\quad a=e_2,\quad b=1.\] For the NS5 maps choose \[C_2=(1,0),\quad D_2=\binom01,\qquad
 C_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 D_3=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] The last D5 has \(W_-=\mathbb C\), \(W_+=0\), \(a=1\), and \(B_-=0\). Maps involving the zero end spaces are zero. Direct multiplication gives \[C_2D_2=0,\quad C_3D_3=D_2C_2,\quad -D_3C_3=B_-,
 \quad B_-A-AB_++ab=0.\] These are all the nontrivial moment equations. Condition (S1) holds because \(A\) is injective. Condition (S2) follows because \(A=e_1\), \(a=e_2\) and \(B_-a=e_3\) span \(\mathbb C^3\). The last framing vector generates the last one-dimensional space; \(A,a,B_-\) then generate \(\mathbb C^3\), and the surjective \(C\)-maps generate both remaining spaces. This verifies the stated graded-subspace criterion for GIT stability. The native evidence also records a semi-invariant frame check and exact integer products. A binary contingency table with the indicated row and column sums exists, so the paper’s nonempty-fixed-locus hypothesis is satisfied.

Counterevidence and bounded repair. Example 6.1, p. 31, draws \(a''=-1\), which fixes this right-hand residual. Its displayed left triangle also uses the coherent signs \[A'=(A,-a),\quad a'=-B_-a,\quad b'=(0,-1).\] Together with the displayed \(+b\) block of \(B_{\mathrm{mid}}\), these give both resolved moment equations equal to zero whenever the original equation holds. The surrounding prose instead mentions a \(-b\) block. The source therefore contains incompatible prescriptions; it also contains a correct elementary prescription. This material counterevidence is retained.

The printed table is the stated general construction and is cited for moment compatibility before the embedding, fusion and mirror-reduction arguments. Its failure supports Major for that construction and derivation. The coherent elementary signs give a verified local repair. This review does not certify all general splitting formulas or all co-separated table entries after a silent sign replacement, and does not refute the existence of the intended geometric embedding.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The coherent negative signs in Example6.1 repair the elementary separated moment equations; existence of the intended geometric embedding is not disproved.

problems.title: Co-separated one-term fusion coefficient has the wrong range
problems.source_location: PDF p.39 Corollary6.14 equation(36); coherent elementary co-separated map Example6.1 p.31; Theorem6.13 p.38.
claim: Recorded check: Co-separated one-term fusion coefficient has the wrong range
analysis: The uniform product in Corollary 6.14, p. 39, is false for a co-separated split with \(w'=1\) and \(w''=2\).

Take the source bow \(X=\backslash3/2/1/\), a point, and resolve its sole D5 local charge \(3\) as \(1+2\). Its global charges are zero; the zero \(3\times1\) contingency table gives its unique fixed point. Section 6.1 and Corollary 6.14 do not exclude this case. Use the coherent co-separated elementary map displayed in Example 6.1; this isolates the scalar issue from Table 1’s incompatible entries. The resolved component is \(F=\backslash1\backslash3/2/1/\). The original framing torus acts trivially on \(F\), so \(N_j^-=0\) for the original chamber and \(\operatorname{Stab}_X=1\). At the distinguished resolution \(f_\sharp\), the vertex characters are \[W_{\mathrm{mid}}=\{a'h\},\quad
 W_3=\{a'h,a''h,a''h^2\},\quad
 W_2=\{a''h,a''h^2\},\quad W_1=\{a''h^2\}.\] Subtracting the moment-equation and gauge characters from the representation characters gives exactly \[T_{f_\sharp}F=\frac{a''}{a'}+\frac{a'}{a''}h.\] For the chamber \(a'>a''\) the negative character is \(a''/a'\). The change of group in (33) is \((a',a'',h)=(a,ah,h)\), so the diagonal stable-envelope value is \(\vartheta(h)\).

The pullback at the image of the source point can be identified with this diagonal value without assuming that tautological characters determine every elliptic class. An explicit stable affine line joins the two points. In the resolved second triangle take \[A=e_1^*,\quad a=u,\quad b=e_2^*,\quad
 B_-=0,\quad B_+=uE_{12}+E_{23},\] and in its NS5 tail take \[D_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
 C_1=\begin{pmatrix}-u&0\\0&-1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
 \quad D_2=(0,1),\quad C_2=\binom{-1}{0}.\] The first triangle has \(b_0=1\) and \(B_0=0\). All moment equations hold for every \(u\). The three covectors \(b_0A,b,bB_+\) form the identity frame, which verifies (S1); the surjectivity of \(A\) verifies (S2). The tail and frame criterion verify stability throughout. The point \(u=1\) is the coherent resolution image and \(u=0\) is \(f_\sharp\). The parameter has character \((a'/a'')h\), which becomes one under \(\varphi\), so this affine line is fixed pointwise by the original \(T\). Equivariant homotopy invariance identifies the two restrictions. Thus the value \(\vartheta(h)\) is the relevant pullback.

The printed coefficient instead gives \(\vartheta(h)\vartheta(h^2)\). They are unequal: for an elliptic parameter \(0<q<1\), \(h=-1\) has \(\vartheta(h)\ne0\) and \(\vartheta(h^2)=\vartheta(1)=0\). The other parameters can be chosen generically. Equivalently the two explicit functions have different zero divisors, so this is not rescued by reading the formula meromorphically. The evidence records the admissible representative, its tangent-character cancellation, and the restriction to the distinguished point.

The source’s unprinted comment distinguishes the co-separated product through \(w'\). That comment is corroborating context; the tangent calculation and the stable-envelope diagonal axiom are the proof. In this example the product through \(w'=1\) is the correct value. A proof of a corrected formula for every split is not claimed here.

The one-term fusion identity is an advertised construction in the paper, and this is an explicit failure of its unnormalized statement. It supports Major at that scope. The normalized ratios used in the mirror identity can cancel a common factor. This counterevidence prevents promoting the example into a counterexample to Theorem 8.1.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: General Theorem6.13 diagonal-factor form is not refuted. Common scalar cancellation can preserve normalized ratios and mirror duality.

problems.title: Normalization needs the attracting graph
problems.source_location: PDF pp.18–19 product inclusion and kernel specification; counterevidence Remark5.5 p.20, Proposition5.14 and Theorem6.13 proof.
claim: Recorded check: Normalization needs the attracting graph
analysis: On p. 19 the paper identifies the stable-envelope kernel on \(F\times\operatorname{Attr}_{\mathfrak C}(F)\) with the Thom line of the inclusion of that whole product. The claimed identification fails when \(F\) has positive dimension.

Take the bow \(X=T^*\mathbb P^1\) and let \(A\) be the diagonal framing torus, which acts trivially. Use \(T=A\times\mathbb C_h^\times\), as allowed in Section 5.3. There is one fixed component \(F=X\), and \(\operatorname{Attr}(F)=X\). The printed map \(j\) is the identity on \(X\times X\), so \(N_j=0\) and \(\Theta(N_j)=\mathcal O\).

Here \(\mathcal L_{A,F}=\mathcal L_X\). By the source’s dual-kernel convention, the line \(\mathcal L_{A,F}^{\triangledown}\boxtimes\mathcal L_X\), restricted at a diagonal point \((f,f)\), is \(\Theta(T_fX)\). At a point of the zero section the two \(T\)-weights are \(1\) and \(h\). Thus this line has degree one along the elliptic \(h\) parameter, while \(\mathcal O\) has degree zero. They cannot be isomorphic. This example uses no residual framing-ratio parameter outside the chosen \(T\).

The correct correspondence is the graph of the attracting projection \(x\mapsto\lim_{t\to0}\sigma(t)x\). When \(A\) acts trivially, this is \(\Delta_X\) and its normal bundle is \(TX\), exactly supplying the missing Thom factor. Remark 5.5, p. 20, already states the correct \(\vartheta(N^-)[\Delta]\) restriction. The triangle and D5 proofs later use this diagonal normalization and the \(\Theta(TF)\) factor. For that reason the supported assessment is Minor: the printed specification is inconsistent, while the inspected core formulas explicitly use the corrected correspondence. This assessment is based on that counterevidence and dependency check, not merely on the brevity of a repair.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The correct diagonal factor already appears in Remark5.5 and the inspected core proof calculations; this is the basis for Minor, not merely ease of repair.

problems.title: Full coefficient-field restriction is undefined
problems.source_location: AppendixA PDF pp.63–65; change-of-group map equation(33).
claim: Recorded check: Full coefficient-field restriction is undefined
analysis: The unrestricted change-of-group map used in Appendix A, pp. 64–65, does not exist on the fully localized coefficient fields displayed there.

Consider the allowed separated D5 split \(2=1+1\). In additive equivariant coordinates, (33) gives \[\varphi^*(u')=u-\eta,\qquad
 \varphi^*(u'')=u,\qquad \varphi^*(\eta)=\eta.\] The nonzero polynomial \(t=u''-u'-\eta\) is killed by \(\varphi^*\). After tensoring the source with \(\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb Q[u',u'',\eta]\), \(t\) is invertible. A unital extension would therefore imply \[1=\varphi^*(t\,t^{-1})=\varphi^*(t)\varphi^*(t^{-1})=0,\] a contradiction in the nonzero target coefficient field. The bow \(/1/2\backslash\) and its resolution \(/1/2\backslash1\backslash\) realize this torus map.

One may first change group on unlocalized equivariant cohomology and then localize at target coefficients, or localize the source only at elements whose images are nonzero. Regular stable-envelope classes can lie in such a valid domain. The proof’s phrase allowing arbitrary fully localized \(\alpha\) requires this restriction. The finding is Minor at the level of that overly broad map; no counterexample to Proposition A.1’s intended image statement or to the mirror identity has been established. A complete rewritten proof of the image statement is not asserted.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Unlocalized restriction and compatible multiplicative systems exist; intended regular stable classes may be in this domain. No counterexample to the image conclusion or mirror theorem established.

report: Abstract: The main determinant inequality in the acquired first arXiv version is supported by a direct coefficient argument, and its gradient formulation admits a separate verification. Four local findings concern radial derivatives, two assertions about general linear pullbacks, and the normalization of the Lagrangian eigenvalues. Explicit examples meet the relevant stated assumptions. The valid restricted constructions and their independence from the main proof are recorded. A proposed objection about completeness is rejected after checking the authors’ definition. The supported assessment is Minor; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical verification of
a determinant majorization theorem
# Identity, scope and conventions

This report concerns F. Reese Harvey and H. Blaine Lawson, Jr., A definitive determinant majorization result for nonlinear operators, arXiv:2407.05408v1 [HL]. The acquired PDF has 13 pages, an arXiv watermark dated 7 July 2024, and a printed date of 9 July 2024. Its title includes determinant although the arXiv landing title omits that word. The frozen journal identity is Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), 2749–2763, DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0003. The 15-page journal version was not acquired or certified equivalent. References to pages below mean one-based acquired PDF pages; printed page numbers agree.

All 13 PDF pages and the complete released TeX source were read. The review covers Definitions 1.1–1.2, Theorems 1.3 and 2.3, Proposition 1.6 and Corollary 1.7, the coefficient and hyperbolicity lemmas, and all the constructions in Section 3. Three native bounded checks were integrated into the primary analysis. Author TeX was inspected as text and was not executed.

The inner product on \(\mathcal S(n)\) is \(\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB)\). A Gårding–Dirichlet polynomial \(\mathfrak g\) has \(\mathfrak g(I)>0\), is hyperbolic in direction \(I\), and has a Gårding cone \(\Gamma\) containing every positive definite matrix. The central-ray condition is \(D_I\mathfrak g=kI\) with \(k>0\). These conditions, including the strict positivity of \(k\), are retained in the checks below.
# Verification of the main argument

Equation reference: eq:jensen. For a homogeneous diagonal restriction \(p(x)=\sum_{|\alpha|=N}a_\alpha x^\alpha\) with \(a_\alpha\geq0\), put \(w_\alpha=a_\alpha/p(e)\), where \(e=(1,\ldots,1)\). The central-ray condition and Euler’s identity give \[\sum_\alpha w_\alpha=1,\qquad
 \sum_\alpha w_\alpha\alpha_j=\frac{N}{n}.\] Consequently, for \(x_j>0\), concavity of the logarithm gives \[\log\frac{p(x)}{p(e)}
 \geq \sum_\alpha w_\alpha\log x^\alpha
 =\frac{N}{n}\sum_j\log x_j .
 \] This proves Basic Lemma 2.1 with exactly its stated constant. Equality occurs when \(\alpha\cdot\log x\) is constant on the positive coefficient support. No claim that equality forces a scalar matrix is justified or needed: \(\mathfrak g=\det\) has equality for every \(A>0\). The condition \(k>0\) excludes degree zero; degree one causes no difficulty in this argument.

For Lemma 2.5, the endpoint passage can be made precise by holding \(\epsilon>0\) fixed throughout the \(N\) directional derivatives in directions \(e_j+\epsilon e\). Repeated interlacing leaves, after \(N-1\) steps, a nonzero linear polynomial positive on the positive orthant. Its derivative in the last positive direction is positive. Taking the limit of this entire multilinear differential expression as \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) gives the desired nonnegative coefficient. One need not regard its penultimate coefficient vector as independent of \(\epsilon\). This clarifies a valid proof.

Orthogonal conjugation preserves the central-ray condition by \(D_I\mathfrak g_h=h^t(D_I\mathfrak g)h\). Every diagonal restriction of \(\mathfrak g_h\) has the nonnegative coefficients just proved. Diagonalizing \(A>0\) and applying [eq:jensen] (#eq:jensen) proves Theorem 1.3. Its constant is sharp at \(A=I\). Continuity also gives the corresponding nonnegative-matrix boundary inequality, although the stated theorem only quantifies over \(A>0\). The proof uses standard hyperbolicity-cone and interlacing properties; these foundational results are not independently reproved in full here.

There is a direct check of Proposition 1.6, so the equivalence need not rest solely on the cited forthcoming reference. Write \(f=\mathfrak g^{1/N}\) and \(H_B=D_Bf\) for \(B\in\Gamma\). Gårding concavity and degree-one homogeneity yield \(f(A)\leq\operatorname{tr}(H_BA)\) for \(A>0\). If \(f(A)\geq c(\det A)^{1/n}\), determinant-one positive matrices force \(H_B>0\): a negative eigenvalue makes the trace unbounded below, and a zero eigenvalue permits traces tending to zero after the remaining eigenvalues of \(A\) tend to zero. The matrix arithmetic–geometric mean identity then gives \[c\leq\inf_{\substack{A>0\\\det A=1}}\operatorname{tr}(H_BA)
       =n(\det H_B)^{1/n}.\] Conversely, \(H_A>0\) and \(\det H_A\geq\gamma\) imply, by Euler’s identity, \(f(A)=\operatorname{tr}(H_AA)\geq n\gamma^{1/n}(\det A)^{1/n}\). Thus the constant in Corollary 1.7 is \(\gamma=\mathfrak g(I)^{n/N}/n^n\), as printed.
# Local findings and bounded repairs

Problem 1 (Radial differentiation requires the missing hypotheses).  Proposition 3.1(2), p. 8, asserts that the radial derivative of a Gårding–Dirichlet polynomial is \(I\)-central, without requiring the input to be \(I\)-central. Its proof on p. 9 explicitly uses that condition.

On \(\mathcal S(2)\) let \(B=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\), \(\ell(A)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)\) and \(\mathfrak g(A)=\ell(A)^2\). Then \(\mathfrak g(I)=9\) and \(\mathfrak g(tI+A)=(3t+\ell(A))^2\) has only real roots. Its cone is \(\{\ell>0\}\) and contains all \(A>0\). The radial derivative is \(q(A)=6\ell(A)\), but \(D_Iq=6B\) is not a scalar multiple of \(I\). The claimed centrality therefore fails for an admissible input. If the conclusion were used to apply the main theorem to \(q\), it would give a false bound: for \(A=\operatorname{diag}(3/2,2/3)\), \[\det A=1,\qquad q(A)=17<18=q(I).\] There is also a degree endpoint. The \(I\)-central polynomial \(\mathfrak g(A)=\operatorname{tr}A\) on \(\mathcal S(2)\) has radial derivative \(2\), whose gradient is zero and hence does not meet Definition 1.2.

A precise valid version assumes an \(I\)-central input of degree \(N\geq2\). Set \(q(A)=d\mathfrak g(A+tI)/dt|_{t=0}\). Interlacing proves its Gårding–Dirichlet property, and differentiated Euler homogeneity gives \[D_Iq=(N-1)D_I\mathfrak g=(N-1)kI.\] Repeated radial differentiation must stop before reaching degree zero. The printed proof’s use of centrality and its stop at degree one are counterevidence showing the intended restricted construction. The finding is Minor: it concerns a supplementary closure statement and is absent from the verified main-theorem dependency path.

Problem 2 (A pullback does not test hyperbolicity outside its range).  Proposition 3.1(3)(a), p. 11, claims a two-way implication for arbitrary \(L\in\operatorname{End}(\mathcal S(n))\). A non-surjective \(L\) only tests directions in its range.

Take \(n=3\), \(\mathfrak g(A)=\det A\), \(J=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1)\), \(L(A)=\frac{\operatorname{tr}A}{3}J\), and \(B=I\). The original \(\mathfrak g\) is itself \(I\)-central and Gårding–Dirichlet. Since \(\det J=1\), \[\mathfrak g_L(A)=\left(\frac{\operatorname{tr}A}{3}\right)^3,\qquad
 \mathfrak g_L(tI+A)=\left(t+\frac{\operatorname{tr}A}{3}\right)^3.\] Thus \(\mathfrak g_L\) is \(I\)-hyperbolic and \(\mathfrak g_L(I)=1\). But, with \(C=E_{12}+E_{21}\), \[\det(tJ+C)=t(t^2+1),\] so \(\mathfrak g\) is not hyperbolic in direction \(L(I)=J\). All hypotheses of the displayed assertion are met; the positivity condition introduced separately in part (e) is not an assumption of part (a).

The implication from ambient hyperbolicity to pullback hyperbolicity is valid. The reverse implication becomes valid if \(L\) is surjective, because then every ambient test matrix is \(L(A)\). The eigenvalue and cone identities in (b)–(c) are valid under the ambient hyperbolicity assumption. The invertible congruences used in Lemma 2.4 meet it; hence this Minor error in the general extension does not invalidate that lemma or Theorem 1.3.

Problem 3 (Closed-cone preservation can annihilate the polynomial).  Proposition 3.1(3)(e), p. 11, assumes \(L(\mathcal P)\subset\overline{\Gamma(\mathfrak g)}\) and asserts that \(\mathfrak g_L\) is Gårding–Dirichlet. The closure bar was checked in the actual PDF. The proof on p. 12 instead uses strict positive definiteness of \(L(P)\).

On \(\mathcal S(2)\) take \(\mathfrak g=\det\) and \(L(A)=a_{11}E_{11}\). For every positive semidefinite \(P\), \(L(P)\) is positive semidefinite, so the stated closed-cone condition holds. Nevertheless \(\mathfrak g_L\equiv0\), and in particular \(\mathfrak g_L(I)=0\), contrary to Definition 1.1.

One sufficient repair is to retain closed-cone preservation and add \(L(I)\in\Gamma(\mathfrak g)\). For \(P>0\) choose \(\epsilon>0\) with \(P-\epsilon I\geq0\). Then \[L(P)=\epsilon L(I)+L(P-\epsilon I)
       \in\Gamma(\mathfrak g)+\overline{\Gamma(\mathfrak g)}
       \subset\Gamma(\mathfrak g).\] Hyperbolicity in direction \(L(I)\) and the valid forward pullback argument now give exactly the required conclusion. There is an important alternative reading: the introductory assertion that the pullback has degree \(N\) might be intended to impose \(\mathfrak g_L
ot\equiv0\) as an additional assumption. Under that reading the counterexample is excluded. Indeed, closed-cone preservation and \(\mathfrak g_L
ot\equiv0\) imply \(L(I)\in\Gamma\): choose \(P_0>0\) with \(\mathfrak g_L(P_0)
eq0\), hence \(L(P_0)\in\Gamma\), and then choose \(c>0\) with \(cI-P_0\geq0\). It follows that \(cL(I)\in\Gamma+\overline\Gamma\subset\Gamma\). Thus the finding is specifically the missing nondegeneracy condition in the stated construction for arbitrary \(L\), not a failure under that stronger interpretation. The later condition \(L(I)=kI\), \(k>0\), in part (f) would supply this missing condition if explicitly imposed on part (e). Moreover, the chain rule and trace-preserving argument of part (f) are valid. These are substantive restrictions on the counterexample’s scope. The assessment is Minor, since the faulty general construction is not used by the verified main proof.

Problem 4 (The Lagrangian factors are not normalized \(I\)-eigenvalues).  In the proof of Lemma 3.5, p. 10, equation (3.3) calls \(\Lambda_\pm(A)=\frac12\operatorname{tr}A\pm\lambda_1\pm\cdots\pm\lambda_n\) the \(I\)-eigenvalues on \(\mathcal S(2n)\).

For any homogeneous hyperbolic polynomial, \(\mathfrak g(tI+I)=\mathfrak g(I)(t+1)^N\), so every defined \(I\)-eigenvalue of \(I\) equals \(1\). The displayed \(\Lambda_\pm(I)\) instead equals \(n\), since the skew-Hermitian part of \(I\) vanishes. For \(n>1\) these cannot be the normalized \(I\)-eigenvalues.

The product factors obey \(\Lambda_\pm(tI+A)=nt+\Lambda_\pm(A)\). Thus the true \(I\)-eigenvalues are \(\Lambda_\pm(A)/n\), and their sum is \(2^{n-1}\operatorname{tr}A/n\). This remains a positive multiple of the ordinary trace, so the central-ray conclusion survives. The separately computed \(\mathfrak g(I)^{1/N}=n\) and the sharp inequality (3.2) are unchanged. The verified discrepancy is a Minor normalization error in the proof, not a failure of the stated Lagrangian determinant inequality.
# Counterevidence, dependence and assessment

The claim in Remark 3.2 about completeness was checked against the authors’ earlier definition [Retained latex: \cite[Appendix B]{HLprevious}]. It concerns all the variables in the underlying \(\mathbb R^n\), equivalently \(\mathcal P\cap E=\{0\}\) for the edge \(E\). It does not require the polynomial to have zero edge in the entire matrix space. The proposed trace-power objection is therefore rejected. Indeed, if \(0\neq P\geq0\) belonged to the edge, then \(D_I\mathfrak g(P)=0\) but centrality gives \(k\operatorname{tr}P>0\). The earlier source explicitly distinguishes this notion from regularity of the cone.

The product construction in Proposition 3.1(1) also passes: the hyperbolic roots combine, the cones intersect, and \(D_I(\mathfrak gh)=h(I)D_I\mathfrak g+\mathfrak g(I)D_Ih\) is a positive scalar multiple of \(I\). The nonhyperbolic example \(\|A\|^2\det A\) in Remark 3.3 satisfies the broader coefficient theorem in dimension at least two; it does not contradict the separate Gårding hypotheses.

The supported overall assessment is Minor. This rests on an explicit main-proof verification and dependency separation. It does not rest on the repairs being brief. No counterexample to Theorems 1.3 or 2.3, Corollary 1.7, or the sharp Lagrangian inequality has been found within this inspection. No general PDE existence or interior-regularity theorem is independently certified here.
Item | Judgment | Repair and remaining scope
Radial derivative | Minor | Central input and \(N\geq2\) verified sufficient.
Pullback converse | Minor | Forward implication valid; surjectivity restores converse.
Closed-cone map | Minor | Add \(L(I)\in\Gamma\); proof supplied.
Lagrangian roots | Minor | Divide by \(n\); sharp bound unchanged.
Completeness | Rejected | Existing definition and direct edge argument support the claim.

Author adoption is unknown and has not been requested. The current arXiv record lists v1; a bounded correction/material search identified no separate supplement or computational release. This is not an exhaustive claim about later corrections. The missing journal text and external PDE developments remain outside the version-specific conclusion.

problems.title: Radial derivative closure omits central input and positive output degree
problems.source_location: PDF8 Proposition3.1(2); proofPDF9; TeX1180 and1231–1241
claim: Recorded check: Radial derivative closure omits central input and positive output degree
analysis: Proposition 3.1(2), p. 8, asserts that the radial derivative of a Gårding–Dirichlet polynomial is \(I\)-central, without requiring the input to be \(I\)-central. Its proof on p. 9 explicitly uses that condition.

On \(\mathcal S(2)\) let \(B=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\), \(\ell(A)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)\) and \(\mathfrak g(A)=\ell(A)^2\). Then \(\mathfrak g(I)=9\) and \(\mathfrak g(tI+A)=(3t+\ell(A))^2\) has only real roots. Its cone is \(\{\ell>0\}\) and contains all \(A>0\). The radial derivative is \(q(A)=6\ell(A)\), but \(D_Iq=6B\) is not a scalar multiple of \(I\). The claimed centrality therefore fails for an admissible input. If the conclusion were used to apply the main theorem to \(q\), it would give a false bound: for \(A=\operatorname{diag}(3/2,2/3)\), \[\det A=1,\qquad q(A)=17<18=q(I).\] There is also a degree endpoint. The \(I\)-central polynomial \(\mathfrak g(A)=\operatorname{tr}A\) on \(\mathcal S(2)\) has radial derivative \(2\), whose gradient is zero and hence does not meet Definition 1.2.

A precise valid version assumes an \(I\)-central input of degree \(N\geq2\). Set \(q(A)=d\mathfrak g(A+tI)/dt|_{t=0}\). Interlacing proves its Gårding–Dirichlet property, and differentiated Euler homogeneity gives \[D_Iq=(N-1)D_I\mathfrak g=(N-1)kI.\] Repeated radial differentiation must stop before reaching degree zero. The printed proof’s use of centrality and its stop at degree one are counterevidence showing the intended restricted construction. The finding is Minor: it concerns a supplementary closure statement and is absent from the verified main-theorem dependency path.
result: Impact: Peripheral class-of-examples claim, with no demonstrated dependency into main theorem.

problems.title: Arbitrary pullback does not detect hyperbolicity outside its image
problems.source_location: PDF11 Proposition3.1(3)(a),TeX1327–1337 and1362–1373
claim: Recorded check: Arbitrary pullback does not detect hyperbolicity outside its image
analysis: Proposition 3.1(3)(a), p. 11, claims a two-way implication for arbitrary \(L\in\operatorname{End}(\mathcal S(n))\). A non-surjective \(L\) only tests directions in its range.

Take \(n=3\), \(\mathfrak g(A)=\det A\), \(J=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1)\), \(L(A)=\frac{\operatorname{tr}A}{3}J\), and \(B=I\). The original \(\mathfrak g\) is itself \(I\)-central and Gårding–Dirichlet. Since \(\det J=1\), \[\mathfrak g_L(A)=\left(\frac{\operatorname{tr}A}{3}\right)^3,\qquad
 \mathfrak g_L(tI+A)=\left(t+\frac{\operatorname{tr}A}{3}\right)^3.\] Thus \(\mathfrak g_L\) is \(I\)-hyperbolic and \(\mathfrak g_L(I)=1\). But, with \(C=E_{12}+E_{21}\), \[\det(tJ+C)=t(t^2+1),\] so \(\mathfrak g\) is not hyperbolic in direction \(L(I)=J\). All hypotheses of the displayed assertion are met; the positivity condition introduced separately in part (e) is not an assumption of part (a).

The implication from ambient hyperbolicity to pullback hyperbolicity is valid. The reverse implication becomes valid if \(L\) is surjective, because then every ambient test matrix is \(L(A)\). The eigenvalue and cone identities in (b)–(c) are valid under the ambient hyperbolicity assumption. The invertible congruences used in Lemma 2.4 meet it; hence this Minor error in the general extension does not invalidate that lemma or Theorem 1.3.
result: Impact: Auxiliarygeneralization;no main-theorem counterexample.

problems.title: Closed-cone construction needs nondegeneracy
problems.source_location: PDF11 Proposition3.1(3)(e);PDF12proof;TeX1343–1345,1398–1400
claim: Recorded check: Closed-cone construction needs nondegeneracy
analysis: Proposition 3.1(3)(e), p. 11, assumes \(L(\mathcal P)\subset\overline{\Gamma(\mathfrak g)}\) and asserts that \(\mathfrak g_L\) is Gårding–Dirichlet. The closure bar was checked in the actual PDF. The proof on p. 12 instead uses strict positive definiteness of \(L(P)\).

On \(\mathcal S(2)\) take \(\mathfrak g=\det\) and \(L(A)=a_{11}E_{11}\). For every positive semidefinite \(P\), \(L(P)\) is positive semidefinite, so the stated closed-cone condition holds. Nevertheless \(\mathfrak g_L\equiv0\), and in particular \(\mathfrak g_L(I)=0\), contrary to Definition 1.1.

One sufficient repair is to retain closed-cone preservation and add \(L(I)\in\Gamma(\mathfrak g)\). For \(P>0\) choose \(\epsilon>0\) with \(P-\epsilon I\geq0\). Then \[L(P)=\epsilon L(I)+L(P-\epsilon I)
       \in\Gamma(\mathfrak g)+\overline{\Gamma(\mathfrak g)}
       \subset\Gamma(\mathfrak g).\] Hyperbolicity in direction \(L(I)\) and the valid forward pullback argument now give exactly the required conclusion. There is an important alternative reading: the introductory assertion that the pullback has degree \(N\) might be intended to impose \(\mathfrak g_L
ot\equiv0\) as an additional assumption. Under that reading the counterexample is excluded. Indeed, closed-cone preservation and \(\mathfrak g_L
ot\equiv0\) imply \(L(I)\in\Gamma\): choose \(P_0>0\) with \(\mathfrak g_L(P_0)
eq0\), hence \(L(P_0)\in\Gamma\), and then choose \(c>0\) with \(cI-P_0\geq0\). It follows that \(cL(I)\in\Gamma+\overline\Gamma\subset\Gamma\). Thus the finding is specifically the missing nondegeneracy condition in the stated construction for arbitrary \(L\), not a failure under that stronger interpretation. The later condition \(L(I)=kI\), \(k>0\), in part (f) would supply this missing condition if explicitly imposed on part (e). Moreover, the chain rule and trace-preserving argument of part (f) are valid. These are substantive restrictions on the counterexample’s scope. The assessment is Minor, since the faulty general construction is not used by the verified main proof.
result: Impact: Missing nondegeneracy in asserted arbitrary-map construction; no failure under stronger nonzero interpretation, and no core dependency.

problems.title: Lagrangian factors are misnormalized as I-eigenvalues
problems.source_location: PDF10 Lemma3.5proof,equations3.3–3.4;TeX1284–1298
claim: Recorded check: Lagrangian factors are misnormalized as I-eigenvalues
analysis: In the proof of Lemma 3.5, p. 10, equation (3.3) calls \(\Lambda_\pm(A)=\frac12\operatorname{tr}A\pm\lambda_1\pm\cdots\pm\lambda_n\) the \(I\)-eigenvalues on \(\mathcal S(2n)\).

For any homogeneous hyperbolic polynomial, \(\mathfrak g(tI+I)=\mathfrak g(I)(t+1)^N\), so every defined \(I\)-eigenvalue of \(I\) equals \(1\). The displayed \(\Lambda_\pm(I)\) instead equals \(n\), since the skew-Hermitian part of \(I\) vanishes. For \(n>1\) these cannot be the normalized \(I\)-eigenvalues.

The product factors obey \(\Lambda_\pm(tI+A)=nt+\Lambda_\pm(A)\). Thus the true \(I\)-eigenvalues are \(\Lambda_\pm(A)/n\), and their sum is \(2^{n-1}\operatorname{tr}A/n\). This remains a positive multiple of the ordinary trace, so the central-ray conclusion survives. The separately computed \(\mathfrak g(I)^{1/N}=n\) and the sharp inequality (3.2) are unchanged. The verified discrepancy is a Minor normalization error in the proof, not a failure of the stated Lagrangian determinant inequality.
result: Impact: Local named-quantity normalization; no false Lagrangian determinant conclusion.

report: Abstract: The acquired paper is examined through its building models, invariant Steinberg pairing, bar constructions and stability applications. A rational three-dimensional example refutes the local product identification used in the semi-local connectivity proof. Two further core derivations require correction: the partial-order group comparison and the grading of the \(3\)-local argument for Steinberg homology. A further quantitative rank-filtration quotient is false. Local findings concern the ring pre-Bloch presentation and two Steinberg-module boundary assertions. The field-case divided-power calculation and the stated spectral-sequence ranges are supported within the inspected dependencies. Major is the supported overall assessment. This is an initial technical review, with scientific adjudication pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical verification of
\(E_\infty\)-cells and general linear groups
# Identity and scope

This report concerns Søren Galatius, Alexander Kupers and Oscar Randal-Williams, \(E_\infty\)-cells and general linear groups of infinite fields, arXiv:2005.05620v3 [GKRW]. The primary PDF has 82 pages, an arXiv watermark dated 18 January 2025 and a printed date of 22 January 2025. The frozen journal identity is Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), 2927–3046, DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0005. A separate Cambridge accepted manuscript [CAM] has 101 pages and is dated 17 January 2025. Neither acquired file is certified identical to the 120-page journal version.

The complete 5,027-line primary PDF extraction was read, with targeted checks against the actual PDF pages and the released source. The review covers Sections 1–10, the hypotheses and dependencies of Theorems A–H, the finite-rank and coefficient restrictions, and the figures describing low-degree homology. It does not reprove the full external theory of cellular \(E_k\)-algebras or every cited theorem. Native bounded checks were integrated into the primary analysis. All page references without a version prefix refer to one-based primary PDF pages; its printed numbering agrees. The accepted manuscript is cited by its own PDF pages.

The primary convention is that rings are commutative and that the semi-local applications require connectedness and infinite residue fields. The rank-zero part of the non-unital algebra is empty. A statement proved for infinite fields is not silently extended to finite fields. Group homology and algebraic \(K\)-theory use discrete groups unless a topological-ring comparison is expressly invoked.
# Supported parts of the argument

The Steinberg tensor-square coinvariant calculation in Section 2 uses the Lee–Szczarba relations and successive Jordan-block reductions. The pairing of a standard apartment with the one-block apartment is \(1\), so cyclicity together with the pairing gives the asserted integral isomorphism. In Section 6.3 the sign \(\epsilon(n)=n(n-1)/2\) obeys \[\epsilon(m+n)=\epsilon(m)+\epsilon(n)+mn.\] Consequently the apartment-product calculation gives \[\gamma_m(x)\gamma_n(x)=\binom{m+n}{m}\gamma_{m+n}(x).\] The factorial cancellation takes place over the torsion-free integral coinvariants, before base change; it does not divide by a factorial in an arbitrary coefficient ring. The prime-power boundary groups in Theorem B then agree with the indecomposables of this divided-power algebra. The case \(n=1\) is the free generator, handled separately.

For a field, two flags give a full two-dimensional lattice by taking intersections, so the global identification \(D^2(V)=D^1(V)\wedge D^1(V)\) in Proposition 6.3 is supported. Problem 1 concerns different, restricted subspaces indexed by a fixed simplex \(\sigma\); it does not contradict that global field statement.

Conditional on the asserted \(E_2\) vanishing, the passage to \(E_\infty\) vanishing preserves the line \(d<2n-2\). Indeed, in a further reduced bar construction of length \(p\), positive ranks \(n_1+\cdots+n_p=n\) contribute degree at least \(2n+p(k-1)\) before desuspending by \(k+1\). The resulting lower bound is \[2n-2+(p-1)(k-1)\geq 2n-2\qquad(k\geq2).\] For fixed \(n\), only \(1\leq p\leq n\) occurs. Thus the formal bar argument is not the source of the connectivity defect below.

The Harrison comparison in Section 9.3 has the announced thresholds \(n\geq5\) for semi-local rings and \(n\geq4\) for fields. The rational and mod-\(p\) minimal-degree arguments preserve their strict slopes \((4n-1)/3\), \(3n/2\) and \(5n/3\) under the stated inputs. The factorial range in Section 9.6 was checked separately from the exception \(n=3=\operatorname{char}(k)\); the paper explicitly imports the known low-rank result for that exception. These checks are conditional on the preceding inputs and do not erase the defects or the unresolved dependency recorded below.
# Confirmed problems

Equation reference: eq:local-product. Problem 1 (A local product isomorphism fails for compatible lattices).  Proposition 7.24, pp. 43–44, asserts for every simplex \(\sigma<E(M)\) a bijection \[
 D^2(M)^\sigma_{p,q}\longrightarrow
 D^1(M)^\sigma_p\wedge D^1(M)^\sigma_q.\] Definitions 7.14–7.15, pp. 38–39, require more than membership of each lattice entry in \(\operatorname{Sub}(M)_\sigma\): all the sums in equation (7.6) must belong to that set. Lemma 7.16 makes this distinction explicit.

Take the connected semi-local ring \(A=\mathbb Q\), the free module \(M=\mathbb Q^3\) with basis \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) and dual basis \(x,y,z\), and \[\sigma=\{x,y,z,x+y+z\}.\] Every member is a surjection to \(\mathbb Q\), and every subset has projective cokernel because it is a map of vector spaces. Thus \(\sigma\) is an actual simplex of \(E(M)\) under Definition 7.5, with no additional genericity assumption required. Put \[P=\ker x\cap\ker y=\mathbb Qe_3,\qquad
 Q=\ker z\cap\ker(x+y+z)=\mathbb Q(e_1-e_2).\] The flags \(0<P<M\) and \(0<Q<M\) both lie in \(D^1(M)^\sigma_2\). The only two-dimensional lattice with these boundary flags has \[\phi(1,1)=0,\quad \phi(1,2)=P,\quad
 \phi(2,1)=Q,\quad \phi(2,2)=M,\] and is zero when either coordinate is zero. It is a full lattice: \(P\cap Q=0\), and \(P+Q\) is a direct summand. For example, a decomposition as in Lemma 5.6 is obtained by putting \(P\) and \(Q\) in positions \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) and choosing a one-dimensional complement in position \((2,2)\).

At \(a=(1,1)\), however, equation (7.6) requires \(P+Q\in\operatorname{Sub}(M)_\sigma\). Its annihilator is \[(P+Q)^\perp=\mathbb Q(x+y).\] If \(P+Q\) were an intersection of kernels of a subset of \(\sigma\), that subset would span \(\mathbb Q(x+y)\). None of the four elements of \(\sigma\) belongs to this line. The empty subset spans zero, and no nonempty subset can span that line. This also gives an exact finite check over all 16 subsets. Thus the displayed pair of flags has no preimage in \(D^2(M)^\sigma_{2,2}\), disproving [eq:local-product] (#eq:local-product).

The proof on p. 43 verifies the lattice condition, but does not verify this stronger compatibility requirement. Lemma 7.10 only supplies projectivity of a relevant quotient; it does not put the sum back in \(\operatorname{Sub}(M)_\sigma\). The warning immediately before Lemma 7.16 that this set need not be closed under sums is consistent with the example.

Impact and repair boundary. The proof of Theorem 7.1(ii) on p. 44 starts with this claimed isomorphism and deduces \((2d-1)\)-connectivity. The proof of Theorem 7.6(7.2) on the same page also uses it. These feed the semi-local \(E_2\) calculation, Corollary 7.3 and Theorem A, and hence the semi-local applications. This is a Major invalid derivation closely tied to the main contribution. It is not a counterexample to Theorem A or to global field connectivity. Appendix A verifies a repair by changing the restricted pieces to require only entrywise membership and proving a new homotopy-colimit comparison. It restores this connectivity and resolution step under the original semi-local hypotheses. Lemmas 7.16–7.18 are not carried over to the changed pieces. This is a replacement argument; the original Proposition 7.24 remains false. The same original definitions and failed product claim occur on accepted pp. 47–49 and 53–54.

Problem 2 (The \(3\)-local proof uses incompatible degrees).  In the proof of Theorem 10.2, pp. 77–78, the model in (10.2) uses \(b\) of bidegree \((2,4)\) and a cell \(\rho_3\) of bidegree \((3,5)\) attached along \((\beta Q^1_3)_\mathbb Z(\sigma)-\sigma b\). After one bar construction, (10.3) and the next displays place \(\bar b\) in \((2,5)\) and the attached \(\bar\rho_3\) cell in \((3,6)\). The subsequent spectral sequence nevertheless treats \(\bar\rho_3\) as an exterior generator.

The earlier operation calculation, Lemma 9.2(ii) on p. 56, puts \(b\) in \(H_{2,3}(\mathbf R)\) and \((\beta Q^1_3)_\mathbb Z(\sigma)\) in \(H_{3,3}(\mathbf R)\). In the printed universal model, the two proposed attaching terms have different homological degrees, \(3\) and \(4\). They therefore do not define the stated homogeneous attaching map. Moreover a generator of the printed degree \(6\) is even, whereas the displayed Koszul pair uses it as odd. These discrepancies affect the actual differential and the cancellation of the low-slope polynomial generator; they are not changes to a citation or to a name alone.

A coherent correction has the following degrees: \[\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
 \text{object}&b&\rho_3\text{ cell}&\bar b&
       \beta Q^1_3(\bar\sigma)&\bar\rho_3\text{ cell}\\ \hline
 (n,d)&(2,3)&(3,4)&(2,4)&(3,4)&(3,5).
\end{array}\] The homology suspension raises degree \(3\) to \(4\). Writing \(u=\beta Q^1_3(\bar\sigma)\) and \(v=\bar\rho_3\), the relevant corrected differential graded factor over \(\mathbb F_3\) is \[\bigl(\Lambda_{\mathbb F_3}[\bar\sigma,v]\otimes\mathbb F_3[u],
        \ d v=u\bigr),\qquad |u|=(3,4),\quad |v|=(3,5).\] The factor \(\Lambda[v]\otimes\mathbb F_3[u]\) has homology \(\mathbb F_3\): multiplication by \(u\) is injective, and its cokernel is the constants. The remaining generators have slope at least \(3/2\) under the Dyer–Lashof degree estimates used in the source. Adding \(\bar b\) of degree \((2,4)\) preserves that bound. The motivating inequality also needs reversal: \((4k-1)/(3k-1)<3/2\) for \(k\geq2\), with equality for \(k=1\).

Impact and counterevidence. This supplies a corrected local calculation, conditional on the source’s cell-existence and connectivity inputs. The original degree-\(6\) exterior calculation is not that calculation. The affected argument proves the integral, including \(3\)-primary, range in Theorem 10.2, equivalently the named Theorem H. It is therefore Major as a demonstrated invalid core derivation, even though a coherent degree repair is available. No counterexample to the homology-vanishing conclusion is claimed. Both acquired PDF versions contain the incompatible degrees (accepted manuscript pp. 94–96).

Problem 3 (The partial-order comparison uses the wrong invariant module).  Proposition 5.13, pp. 21–22, proves a group-homology comparison by removing a maximal element \(t\) of a finite poset. The proof asserts \(f(M_t)\subset M_t\) and identifies a kernel with the full ambient group \(\operatorname{GL}(M,\operatorname{fix}M')\), where \(M'=\bigoplus_{x\ne t}M_x\).

Take \(A=\mathbb Q\), \(X=\{a,b,t\}\) with the only strict relation \(a<t\), and \(M_a=M_b=M_t=\mathbb Q\). These satisfy the Nesterenko–Suslin hypothesis. Under the paper’s convention that the matrix component \(M_x\to M_y\) is allowed when \(y\leq x\), the automorphism \(f=I+E_{a,t}\) belongs to \(\operatorname{GL}(M,\leq)\) but sends \(e_t\) to \(e_t+e_a\). Thus \(M_t\) is not invariant and the claimed induced action on \(M/M_t\) is not defined. In contrast, \(h=I+E_{b,t}\) fixes \(M'\) pointwise, so it belongs to the displayed ambient kernel group, but it does not belong to \(\operatorname{GL}(M,\leq)\) at all. The written sequence is not a sequence of the claimed subgroups.

Here is a repair with exactly the original hypothesis. The invariant module is \(M'\), and set \(U=\bigoplus_{x<t}M_x\), a direct summand preserved by \(G'=\operatorname{GL}(M',\leq)\). Restriction gives a split extension with kernel \[K=\operatorname{GL}(M_t)\ltimes\operatorname{Hom}_A(M_t,U).\] The associated-graded map is \[\operatorname{GL}(M,\leq)\longrightarrow G'\times\operatorname{GL}(M_t).\] Its map on kernels is the Nesterenko–Suslin comparison for \((P,Q)=(U,M_t)\). It is a homology isomorphism, equivariantly for \(G'\), whose action on \(\operatorname{GL}(M_t)\) is trivial. The comparison of extension spectral sequences gives the required homology isomorphism. Induction over the removed relations then proves Proposition 5.13.

The correction is verified at the group and extension level; it does not require that \(t\) be above every other element. Nevertheless the original derivation uses an undefined quotient action and an incorrect kernel. Theorem 5.18 directly invokes it to identify split and ordinary buildings, a central input to both the field and semi-local calculations. The affected derivation is Major under the core-dependency criterion; the repaired proposition is supported, and no false homology-equivalence theorem is asserted.

Problem 4 (A rank-filtration quotient is not the whole first layer).  Remark 8.4, p. 52 (accepted p. 64), identifies \(K_{2r}(A)/F_rK_{2r}(A)\) with the first quotient layer’s homotopy group, and then with \(H^{E_\infty}_{r+1,2r}(\mathbf R_\mathbb Z)\).

Choose the discrete field \(A=\mathbb C\) and \(r=1\). It is connected and semi-local with an infinite residue field, so it satisfies every ring hypothesis here. Corollary 6.12 gives \(H^{E_\infty}_{2,2}(\mathbf R_\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/2\). On the other hand Matsumoto’s theorem identifies \(K_2(\mathbb C)\) with Milnor \(K_2(\mathbb C)\); the paper itself recalls this on p. 64. For every integer \(m>0\), choose an \(m\)th root \(a^{1/m}\in\mathbb C\). Bilinearity of symbols gives \[\{a,b\}=m\{a^{1/m},b\}.\] Hence \(K_2(\mathbb C)\) is divisible. Every quotient of a divisible abelian group is divisible, while \(\mathbb Z/2\) is not. The stated equality is false.

Let \(C_r\) denote the cofiber of \(F_rK(A)\to K(A)\). The long exact sequence gives instead \[K_{2r}(A)/F_rK_{2r}(A)
 \ \cong\
 \ker\bigl(\pi_{2r}(C_r)\longrightarrow\pi_{2r-1}(F_rK(A))\bigr).\] The higher layers do not change \(\pi_{2r}(C_r)\) in the range under discussion, so this is a subgroup of the critical group, not necessarily the entire group. For \(\mathbb C,r=1\), the subgroup must be zero because it is both divisible and a subgroup of \(\mathbb Z/2\).

The weaker finiteness conclusion survives this correction. The adjacent Remark 8.5 expressly changes to topological rings and does not alter the discrete-field counterexample. The exact integral quotient is a quantitative application of the paper’s critical-group calculation to its central stable-rank-filtration question. The dependency is Theorem B, then the layer/Hurewicz identification, then the invalid replacement of a kernel by the whole layer. The claimed value changes from \(\mathbb Z/2\) to zero in the admissible example. This is Major for that application, even though Theorems A–B and the weaker finiteness consequence are not refuted.

Problem 5 (The ring pre-Bloch presentation admits inadmissible symbols).  Section 9.1.1, p. 53, defines \(\mathfrak p(A)\) with generators \(x\in A^\times\setminus\{1\}\). Equation (9.3), p. 55, then assigns a term \(x\wedge(1-x)\) in an exterior construction on \(A^\times\).

Let \(A=\mathbb Q[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)\) and \(x=1+\varepsilon\). The ring is connected and local with infinite residue field \(\mathbb Q\). The element \(x\) is a unit, with inverse \(1-\varepsilon\), and \(x\ne1\). Thus it is an allowed generator in the printed presentation, but \(1-x=-\varepsilon\) is not a unit. The displayed boundary expression is undefined.

This is not remedied by the five-term relations. When their stated parameters \(u,v,1-u,1-v,u-v\) are units, every argument appearing in the five terms has both itself and its complement invertible. Consequently the other generators never occur in a relation and form an additional free direct summand in the printed presentation. The required presentation uses \[W_A=\{x\in A: x\in A^\times,\ 1-x\in A^\times\}\] as its generator set. Over a field this coincides with the printed set.

The chain calculation with transverse rank-one summands already uses the admissible set, and the Milnor relations are correctly restricted to \(x,1-x\in A^\times\) in Section 9.2, p. 58. This is therefore a Minor mismatch in the stated ring presentation and boundary domain, with explicit consequences for the notation in Figure 1 and Theorem 9.1. It does not provide a counterexample to the standard admissible-symbol calculation or to the field stability theorems. The corrected domain must also be carried through the later presentations on pp. 61–62; simply applying the printed map to the additional generators is not possible. The same generator set is visible in the accepted version, p. 65.

Problem 6 (The finite-field extension of the adjoint argument is unsupported).  The paragraph introducing the proof of Corollary D and the proof itself, p. 11, use injectivity of the Steinberg pairing’s adjoint for a vector space over a field without an infinitude qualification. Theorem 2.4(iv), p. 10, only proves that injectivity for infinite fields, and Remark 2.5 explicitly warns against removing the assumption.

For the stated finite-field test take \(F=\mathbb F_2\), \(V=F^2\) and \(k=\mathbb F_3\). The coefficient ring is connected. There are three lines, so \[\operatorname{St}_k(V)=\ker(k^3\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}k).\] In the basis \(u=(1,-1,0)\), \(v=(0,1,-1)\), the restricted pairing has Gram matrix \[\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}.\] Its nonzero radical is spanned by \(u-v\). The \(k\)-linear endomorphism \(T(u)=u-v,\ T(v)=0\) is nonzero but is sent to the zero bilinear form. Thus the full \(\operatorname{Hom}_k\) injection used in the proof is false for these parameters.

This does not refute Corollary D. In this same example, the matrices of the two generating transpositions are \[\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] Their joint centralizer over \(\mathbb F_3\) consists of scalars. Thus the module is indecomposable and the equivariant endomorphism map remains injective here. The test map \(T\) is not equivariant. For infinite \(F\) the actual adjoint proof is valid, with the reference to part (iv). The finite-field extension needs another argument. This is a Minor scope defect outside the main infinite-field calculation; a false Corollary D is not established.

Problem 7 (The finite-dimensional-submodule assertion omits rank one).  The paragraph following Corollary D, p. 11, says that for a coefficient field with no nontrivial zero sum of squares, \(\operatorname{St}_k(V)\) has no finite-dimensional invariant submodules.

Take \(F=\mathbb Q\), \(V=\mathbb Q\) and \(k=\mathbb R\). The source explicitly allows nonzero finite-dimensional \(V\), including dimension one. Its reduced-homology convention gives \(\operatorname{St}_\mathbb R(\mathbb Q)=\mathbb R\); \(\operatorname{GL}_1(\mathbb Q)\) acts trivially. The whole module is therefore a nonzero one-dimensional invariant submodule. Even the infinite-base-field hypothesis is satisfied.

The displayed argument proves that such a finite-dimensional submodule is a direct summand. Indecomposability then makes it the whole module; it does not rule it out unless the whole Steinberg module is known to be infinite-dimensional. For infinite \(F\) and \(\dim V\geq2\), the apartment basis indexed by the upper-unipotent group supplies that missing fact. Adding these restrictions restores the intended argument. This local boundary assertion is Minor and does not affect Theorem C or the divided-power calculation.
# Clarifications and unresolved dependencies

The comparison displays in Theorem 5.20 and (6.1), p. 24, and again in Section 8, use \(d-k\) where the preceding suspension equivalence requires \(d+k\). At rank one, \(D^1(F)=S^1\) and \(H^{E_1}_{1,0}(\mathbf R_k)=k\), whereas the printed degree \(-1\) right side would be zero. Theorem 6.5’s actual proof already uses \(d+2\). This is recorded as a grading correction rather than a new independent failure of the vanishing theorem. The empty binomial-coefficient ideal at \(n=1\) is \((0)\), consistent with the correctly stated boundary group.

Lemma 7.32, p. 48, must refer to coinvariants in its generation claim. With \(A=\mathbb Q\) and rank two, fixing the first apartment \(a\) only produces elements in \(\mathbb Za\otimes\operatorname{St}(\mathbb Q^2)\), not all of \(\operatorname{St}(\mathbb Q^2)\otimes\operatorname{St}(\mathbb Q^2)\). For instance, a distinct apartment \(b\) with a nonzero coefficient on a third line gives \(b\otimes a\) outside that subgroup. The surrounding section and the subsequent applications expressly take coinvariants, where the stated reduction applies. The correction does not refute Corollary 7.33 or Proposition 7.34 in their intended scope.

Two items remain Needs Evidence. First, the Moore-complex maps used on p. 61 require torsion representatives, whereas the statement of Proposition 9.3 gives surjectivity onto \(\mathbb Z/2\) and \(\mathbb Z/3\). Surjectivity alone, as illustrated abstractly by \(\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/p\), does not supply such representatives. That abstract example is not a counterexample to the actual source construction; the operation construction may supply the missing lift, and no failure is confirmed. Second, Theorem 7.7 is phrased for any connected semi-local ring, while Section 7.5’s resolution argument assumes infinite residue fields. No finite-residue-ring counterexample was established. A section-wide implicit hypothesis is a possible reading, which must be made explicit before asserting an unrestricted extension.

The source’s Definition 7.9 says cokernel. A preliminary helper reading of that word as kernel was withdrawn after independent extraction and actual enlarged-page inspection. No version discrepancy or finding is based on that misreading.
# Overall impact and state

Problems 1–3 concern actual derivations on the route to the principal results. Their classification does not assert that all the resulting theorems are false, and the explicit repairs do not lower their core-dependency assessment. The field tensor-square and divided-power arguments survive the local compatible-piece counterexample. Problem 4 gives a false quantitative rank-filtration application even though its finiteness consequence remains valid. The remaining confirmed findings have the narrower scopes stated above.

# Replacement of the restricted local pieces

Retain the original hypotheses: \(A\) is connected and semi-local with infinite residue fields, and \(M\) is a finitely generated projective module of positive rank. For \(\sigma<E(M)\) define \(W^k_\sigma\) to consist of the basepoint and full lattices \(\phi\) for which \[\phi(a)\in\operatorname{Sub}(M)_\sigma\quad\text{for every }a.\] This is weaker than Definition 7.15. A surviving face or degeneracy only selects or repeats lattice entries, so these are multisimplicial subsets, natural under inclusion of \(\sigma\).

Fix a full lattice \(\phi\) and put \(V_a=\phi(a)^\perp\subset M^\vee\). These are finitely generated projective direct summands. The weak compatibility of a simplex \(\tau\) is equivalent to \[\operatorname{span}(\tau\cap V_a)=V_a\quad\text{for every }a.\] Indeed, the clean-evaluation condition makes the span of every subset of \(\tau\) a summand, so taking a double annihilator is legitimate. An adapted dual basis for a splitting of \(\phi\) gives at least one weakly compatible simplex.

Consider a finite nonempty collection of weakly compatible simplices \(\tau\). We construct a finite set \(S\) such that every \(\tau\cup S\) remains a simplex and \(S\) spans every \(V_a\) by its elements lying there. For each nonzero \(V_a\), choose \(\operatorname{rank}V_a\) vectors in it successively. For every face \(\rho\) of every current clean simplex \(\tau\cup S\), Lemma 7.11 applies with \(V=V_a\): the containing simplex \(\tau\cup S\) spans \(V_a\) because \(\tau\) already does. Thus only finitely many proper linear subspaces are forbidden modulo each maximal ideal. Also forbid the span of the previously chosen vectors for this \(V_a\), and zero. The residue fields are infinite and there are finitely many maximal ideals, so finite avoidance and the Chinese remainder theorem produce the next vector simultaneously. It is a unimodular functional and adjoining it preserves all required clean intersections. The chosen vectors form a basis modulo every maximal ideal, hence generate \(V_a\) by Nakayama’s lemma. The zero summands need no vectors.

At the end, \(\sigma=S\) and every \(\tau\cup\sigma\) are weakly compatible simplices. The inclusions \(\tau\subset\tau\cup\sigma\supset\sigma\) contract every finite subposet of weakly compatible simplices. Its realization is therefore weakly contractible. The fiber over a non-basepoint lattice in the levelwise homotopy colimit is precisely this realization; the basepoint fiber is controlled by the contractibility of \(E(M)\). Consequently \[\operatorname*{hocolim}_{\sigma<E(M)}W^k_\sigma
                      \simeq D^k(M).\]

For \(k=1\), \(W^1_\sigma=D^1(M)^\sigma\) with the source’s definition. For \(k=2\), the intersections of two such flags are kernels of unions of subsets of \(\sigma\). Lemma 7.10 makes the relevant sums summands, so the intersection diagram is a full lattice, and every entry belongs to \(\operatorname{Sub}(M)_\sigma\). Hence \[W^2_\sigma\cong
                D^1(M)^\sigma\wedge D^1(M)^\sigma.\] The original one-dimensional connectivity argument now gives \((2d-1)\)-connectivity of each \(W^2_\sigma\) and of their homotopy colimit. Replacing the local pieces by \(W^2_\sigma\) in the quotient comparison on p. 44 likewise restores the displayed resolution equivalence. This repair supplies the missing local-model argument; it does not claim that the strong-compatible pieces themselves have the asserted product decomposition.

problems.title: Strong-compatible local two-building product is false
problems.source_location: Primarypp38–40,43–44,Definitions7.14–7.15 andProposition7.24;acceptedpp47–49,53–54
claim: Recorded check: Strong-compatible local two-building product is false
analysis:
Proposition 7.24, pp. 43–44, asserts for every simplex \(\sigma<E(M)\) a bijection \[
 D^2(M)^\sigma_{p,q}\longrightarrow
 D^1(M)^\sigma_p\wedge D^1(M)^\sigma_q.\] Definitions 7.14–7.15, pp. 38–39, require more than membership of each lattice entry in \(\operatorname{Sub}(M)_\sigma\): all the sums in equation (7.6) must belong to that set. Lemma 7.16 makes this distinction explicit.

Take the connected semi-local ring \(A=\mathbb Q\), the free module \(M=\mathbb Q^3\) with basis \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) and dual basis \(x,y,z\), and \[\sigma=\{x,y,z,x+y+z\}.\] Every member is a surjection to \(\mathbb Q\), and every subset has projective cokernel because it is a map of vector spaces. Thus \(\sigma\) is an actual simplex of \(E(M)\) under Definition 7.5, with no additional genericity assumption required. Put \[P=\ker x\cap\ker y=\mathbb Qe_3,\qquad
 Q=\ker z\cap\ker(x+y+z)=\mathbb Q(e_1-e_2).\] The flags \(0<P<M\) and \(0<Q<M\) both lie in \(D^1(M)^\sigma_2\). The only two-dimensional lattice with these boundary flags has \[\phi(1,1)=0,\quad \phi(1,2)=P,\quad
 \phi(2,1)=Q,\quad \phi(2,2)=M,\] and is zero when either coordinate is zero. It is a full lattice: \(P\cap Q=0\), and \(P+Q\) is a direct summand. For example, a decomposition as in Lemma 5.6 is obtained by putting \(P\) and \(Q\) in positions \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) and choosing a one-dimensional complement in position \((2,2)\).

At \(a=(1,1)\), however, equation (7.6) requires \(P+Q\in\operatorname{Sub}(M)_\sigma\). Its annihilator is \[(P+Q)^\perp=\mathbb Q(x+y).\] If \(P+Q\) were an intersection of kernels of a subset of \(\sigma\), that subset would span \(\mathbb Q(x+y)\). None of the four elements of \(\sigma\) belongs to this line. The empty subset spans zero, and no nonempty subset can span that line. This also gives an exact finite check over all 16 subsets. Thus the displayed pair of flags has no preimage in \(D^2(M)^\sigma_{2,2}\), disproving [eq:local-product] (#eq:local-product).

The proof on p. 43 verifies the lattice condition, but does not verify this stronger compatibility requirement. Lemma 7.10 only supplies projectivity of a relevant quotient; it does not put the sum back in \(\operatorname{Sub}(M)_\sigma\). The warning immediately before Lemma 7.16 that this set need not be closed under sums is consistent with the example.

Impact and repair boundary. The proof of Theorem 7.1(ii) on p. 44 starts with this claimed isomorphism and deduces \((2d-1)\)-connectivity. The proof of Theorem 7.6(7.2) on the same page also uses it. These feed the semi-local \(E_2\) calculation, Corollary 7.3 and Theorem A, and hence the semi-local applications. This is a Major invalid derivation closely tied to the main contribution. It is not a counterexample to Theorem A or to global field connectivity. Appendix A verifies a repair by changing the restricted pieces to require only entrywise membership and proving a new homotopy-colimit comparison. It restores this connectivity and resolution step under the original semi-local hypotheses. Lemmas 7.16–7.18 are not carried over to the changed pieces. This is a replacement argument; the original Proposition 7.24 remains false. The same original definitions and failed product claim occur on accepted pp. 47–49 and 53–54.

problems.title: The prime3 cell construction is not homogeneous
problems.source_location: Primarypp77–78 Section10.2;Lemma9.2p56;acceptedpp94–96
claim: Recorded check: The prime3 cell construction is not homogeneous
analysis: In the proof of Theorem 10.2, pp. 77–78, the model in (10.2) uses \(b\) of bidegree \((2,4)\) and a cell \(\rho_3\) of bidegree \((3,5)\) attached along \((\beta Q^1_3)_\mathbb Z(\sigma)-\sigma b\). After one bar construction, (10.3) and the next displays place \(\bar b\) in \((2,5)\) and the attached \(\bar\rho_3\) cell in \((3,6)\). The subsequent spectral sequence nevertheless treats \(\bar\rho_3\) as an exterior generator.

The earlier operation calculation, Lemma 9.2(ii) on p. 56, puts \(b\) in \(H_{2,3}(\mathbf R)\) and \((\beta Q^1_3)_\mathbb Z(\sigma)\) in \(H_{3,3}(\mathbf R)\). In the printed universal model, the two proposed attaching terms have different homological degrees, \(3\) and \(4\). They therefore do not define the stated homogeneous attaching map. Moreover a generator of the printed degree \(6\) is even, whereas the displayed Koszul pair uses it as odd. These discrepancies affect the actual differential and the cancellation of the low-slope polynomial generator; they are not changes to a citation or to a name alone.

A coherent correction has the following degrees: \[\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
 \text{object}&b&\rho_3\text{ cell}&\bar b&
       \beta Q^1_3(\bar\sigma)&\bar\rho_3\text{ cell}\\ \hline
 (n,d)&(2,3)&(3,4)&(2,4)&(3,4)&(3,5).
\end{array}\] The homology suspension raises degree \(3\) to \(4\). Writing \(u=\beta Q^1_3(\bar\sigma)\) and \(v=\bar\rho_3\), the relevant corrected differential graded factor over \(\mathbb F_3\) is \[\bigl(\Lambda_{\mathbb F_3}[\bar\sigma,v]\otimes\mathbb F_3[u],
        \ d v=u\bigr),\qquad |u|=(3,4),\quad |v|=(3,5).\] The factor \(\Lambda[v]\otimes\mathbb F_3[u]\) has homology \(\mathbb F_3\): multiplication by \(u\) is injective, and its cokernel is the constants. The remaining generators have slope at least \(3/2\) under the Dyer–Lashof degree estimates used in the source. Adding \(\bar b\) of degree \((2,4)\) preserves that bound. The motivating inequality also needs reversal: \((4k-1)/(3k-1)<3/2\) for \(k\geq2\), with equality for \(k=1\).

Impact and counterevidence. This supplies a corrected local calculation, conditional on the source’s cell-existence and connectivity inputs. The original degree-\(6\) exterior calculation is not that calculation. The affected argument proves the integral, including \(3\)-primary, range in Theorem 10.2, equivalently the named Theorem H. It is therefore Major as a demonstrated invalid core derivation, even though a coherent degree repair is available. No counterexample to the homology-vanishing conclusion is claimed. Both acquired PDF versions contain the incompatible degrees (accepted manuscript pp. 94–96).

problems.title: Partial-order proof uses non-invariant quotient and wrong kernel
problems.source_location: Primarypp21–22 Proposition5.13
claim: Recorded check: Partial-order proof uses non-invariant quotient and wrong kernel
analysis: Proposition 5.13, pp. 21–22, proves a group-homology comparison by removing a maximal element \(t\) of a finite poset. The proof asserts \(f(M_t)\subset M_t\) and identifies a kernel with the full ambient group \(\operatorname{GL}(M,\operatorname{fix}M')\), where \(M'=\bigoplus_{x\ne t}M_x\).

Take \(A=\mathbb Q\), \(X=\{a,b,t\}\) with the only strict relation \(a<t\), and \(M_a=M_b=M_t=\mathbb Q\). These satisfy the Nesterenko–Suslin hypothesis. Under the paper’s convention that the matrix component \(M_x\to M_y\) is allowed when \(y\leq x\), the automorphism \(f=I+E_{a,t}\) belongs to \(\operatorname{GL}(M,\leq)\) but sends \(e_t\) to \(e_t+e_a\). Thus \(M_t\) is not invariant and the claimed induced action on \(M/M_t\) is not defined. In contrast, \(h=I+E_{b,t}\) fixes \(M'\) pointwise, so it belongs to the displayed ambient kernel group, but it does not belong to \(\operatorname{GL}(M,\leq)\) at all. The written sequence is not a sequence of the claimed subgroups.

Here is a repair with exactly the original hypothesis. The invariant module is \(M'\), and set \(U=\bigoplus_{x<t}M_x\), a direct summand preserved by \(G'=\operatorname{GL}(M',\leq)\). Restriction gives a split extension with kernel \[K=\operatorname{GL}(M_t)\ltimes\operatorname{Hom}_A(M_t,U).\] The associated-graded map is \[\operatorname{GL}(M,\leq)\longrightarrow G'\times\operatorname{GL}(M_t).\] Its map on kernels is the Nesterenko–Suslin comparison for \((P,Q)=(U,M_t)\). It is a homology isomorphism, equivariantly for \(G'\), whose action on \(\operatorname{GL}(M_t)\) is trivial. The comparison of extension spectral sequences gives the required homology isomorphism. Induction over the removed relations then proves Proposition 5.13.

The correction is verified at the group and extension level; it does not require that \(t\) be above every other element. Nevertheless the original derivation uses an undefined quotient action and an incorrect kernel. Theorem 5.18 directly invokes it to identify split and ordinary buildings, a central input to both the field and semi-local calculations. The affected derivation is Major under the core-dependency criterion; the repaired proposition is supported, and no false homology-equivalence theorem is asserted.
result: Impact: Invalid central split-building comparison step used in Theorem5.18 and subsequent core identifications.

problems.title: Stable-rank image quotient is incorrectly identified with a whole layer
problems.source_location: Primaryp52 Remark8.4;acceptedp64
claim: Recorded check: Stable-rank image quotient is incorrectly identified with a whole layer
analysis: Remark 8.4, p. 52 (accepted p. 64), identifies \(K_{2r}(A)/F_rK_{2r}(A)\) with the first quotient layer’s homotopy group, and then with \(H^{E_\infty}_{r+1,2r}(\mathbf R_\mathbb Z)\).

Choose the discrete field \(A=\mathbb C\) and \(r=1\). It is connected and semi-local with an infinite residue field, so it satisfies every ring hypothesis here. Corollary 6.12 gives \(H^{E_\infty}_{2,2}(\mathbf R_\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z/2\). On the other hand Matsumoto’s theorem identifies \(K_2(\mathbb C)\) with Milnor \(K_2(\mathbb C)\); the paper itself recalls this on p. 64. For every integer \(m>0\), choose an \(m\)th root \(a^{1/m}\in\mathbb C\). Bilinearity of symbols gives \[\{a,b\}=m\{a^{1/m},b\}.\] Hence \(K_2(\mathbb C)\) is divisible. Every quotient of a divisible abelian group is divisible, while \(\mathbb Z/2\) is not. The stated equality is false.

Let \(C_r\) denote the cofiber of \(F_rK(A)\to K(A)\). The long exact sequence gives instead \[K_{2r}(A)/F_rK_{2r}(A)
 \ \cong\
 \ker\bigl(\pi_{2r}(C_r)\longrightarrow\pi_{2r-1}(F_rK(A))\bigr).\] The higher layers do not change \(\pi_{2r}(C_r)\) in the range under discussion, so this is a subgroup of the critical group, not necessarily the entire group. For \(\mathbb C,r=1\), the subgroup must be zero because it is both divisible and a subgroup of \(\mathbb Z/2\).

The weaker finiteness conclusion survives this correction. The adjacent Remark 8.5 expressly changes to topological rings and does not alter the discrete-field counterexample. The exact integral quotient is a quantitative application of the paper’s critical-group calculation to its central stable-rank-filtration question. The dependency is Theorem B, then the layer/Hurewicz identification, then the invalid replacement of a kernel by the whole layer. The claimed value changes from \(\mathbb Z/2\) to zero in the admissible example. This is Major for that application, even though Theorems A–B and the weaker finiteness consequence are not refuted.

problems.title: Ring pre-Bloch generators omit complement-unit condition
problems.source_location: Primarypp53,55,61–62;acceptedpp65,68
claim: Recorded check: Ring pre-Bloch generators omit complement-unit condition
analysis: Section 9.1.1, p. 53, defines \(\mathfrak p(A)\) with generators \(x\in A^\times\setminus\{1\}\). Equation (9.3), p. 55, then assigns a term \(x\wedge(1-x)\) in an exterior construction on \(A^\times\).

Let \(A=\mathbb Q[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)\) and \(x=1+\varepsilon\). The ring is connected and local with infinite residue field \(\mathbb Q\). The element \(x\) is a unit, with inverse \(1-\varepsilon\), and \(x\ne1\). Thus it is an allowed generator in the printed presentation, but \(1-x=-\varepsilon\) is not a unit. The displayed boundary expression is undefined.

This is not remedied by the five-term relations. When their stated parameters \(u,v,1-u,1-v,u-v\) are units, every argument appearing in the five terms has both itself and its complement invertible. Consequently the other generators never occur in a relation and form an additional free direct summand in the printed presentation. The required presentation uses \[W_A=\{x\in A: x\in A^\times,\ 1-x\in A^\times\}\] as its generator set. Over a field this coincides with the printed set.

The chain calculation with transverse rank-one summands already uses the admissible set, and the Milnor relations are correctly restricted to \(x,1-x\in A^\times\) in Section 9.2, p. 58. This is therefore a Minor mismatch in the stated ring presentation and boundary domain, with explicit consequences for the notation in Figure 1 and Theorem 9.1. It does not provide a counterexample to the standard admissible-symbol calculation or to the field stability theorems. The corrected domain must also be carried through the later presentations on pp. 61–62; simply applying the printed map to the additional generators is not possible. The same generator set is visible in the accepted version, p. 65.

problems.title: Finite-field extension of adjoint proof uses false full-Hom injection
problems.source_location: Primarypp10–11 Theorem2.4/Remark2.5/CorollaryD proof
claim: Recorded check: Finite-field extension of adjoint proof uses false full-Hom injection
analysis: The paragraph introducing the proof of Corollary D and the proof itself, p. 11, use injectivity of the Steinberg pairing’s adjoint for a vector space over a field without an infinitude qualification. Theorem 2.4(iv), p. 10, only proves that injectivity for infinite fields, and Remark 2.5 explicitly warns against removing the assumption.

For the stated finite-field test take \(F=\mathbb F_2\), \(V=F^2\) and \(k=\mathbb F_3\). The coefficient ring is connected. There are three lines, so \[\operatorname{St}_k(V)=\ker(k^3\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}k).\] In the basis \(u=(1,-1,0)\), \(v=(0,1,-1)\), the restricted pairing has Gram matrix \[\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}.\] Its nonzero radical is spanned by \(u-v\). The \(k\)-linear endomorphism \(T(u)=u-v,\ T(v)=0\) is nonzero but is sent to the zero bilinear form. Thus the full \(\operatorname{Hom}_k\) injection used in the proof is false for these parameters.

This does not refute Corollary D. In this same example, the matrices of the two generating transpositions are \[\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] Their joint centralizer over \(\mathbb F_3\) consists of scalars. Thus the module is indecomposable and the equivariant endomorphism map remains injective here. The test map \(T\) is not equivariant. For infinite \(F\) the actual adjoint proof is valid, with the reference to part (iv). The finite-field extension needs another argument. This is a Minor scope defect outside the main infinite-field calculation; a false Corollary D is not established.
