Both macro files were read; source and archive members were checked by their actual bytes. Three native bounded checks cover the Epstein geometry, variation and gradient-flow arguments. The primary executor reconstructed the central counterexamples and mathematical dependencies and inspected their source pages. Author source was read as text and never compiled or executed.

Let \(\gamma\) bound \(\Omega\) and \(\Omega^*\), and let \(\rho_\Omega\) be the Poincaré metric of curvature \(-1\). The normal convention is \(B=-\nabla n\) and \(H=\operatorname{tr}(B)/2\). The symbol \(da\) is the signed area form determined by the lifted Epstein normal; it must not be replaced by the unsigned area measure at a fold. The main equality is \[\widetilde S(\gamma)=4V_R(\gamma),\qquad
 V_R=V-\frac12\int_{\Sigma_\Omega\cup\Sigma_{\Omega^*}}H\,da ,\] for \(C^{5,\alpha}\) curves, \(0<\alpha<1\). For general Weil–Petersson curves the source proves only \(\widetilde S\geq4V_R\) and expressly leaves equality open. That distinction is retained throughout this report.
# Checks that support the stated geometry

Write \(q=\|\mathcal S(f^{-1})\|_{\rho_\Omega}\). The eigenvalues of the shape operator at infinity are \(1\pm2q\). Inverting \(B=(1+\widehat B)^{-1}(1-\widehat B)\) gives, where the surface is immersed, \[da=(1-q^2)\,d\widehat a,\qquad
 H\,da=q^2\,d\widehat a,\qquad
 \det B\,da=-q^2\,d\widehat a .\] Thus the nonnegative mean-curvature integral is precisely the weighted Schwarzian \(A_2\) norm. The apparent poles of \(H\) at \(q=1\) cancel in \(H\,da\); the smooth form is the object that extends. The exceptional set has measure zero: \(q^2\) is real analytic, and \(q\equiv1\) on an open set would make \(\log|\mathcal S(f^{-1})|=\log\rho_\Omega\) there, contradicting harmonicity on the left and \(\Delta\log\rho_\Omega=2\rho_\Omega\) on the right. The circular case has \(q=0\) and a totally geodesic surface.

The disjointness argument in Proposition 4.2, p. 21, retains a genuine strictness test. After normalizing two distinct endpoints to \(0,\infty\), Grunsky’s inequality gives \(|g'(\infty)|\geq|f'(0)|\). Equality forces both nonnegative integrands to vanish, hence \(f'/f=g'/g=1/z\). The boundary must then be a circle. For a noncircle, the strict inequality separates the associated horospheres and therefore their Epstein points. No assumption that the entire Epstein surfaces are embedded is used here.

For smooth curves, the osculation calculation of Proposition 4.5 gives second-order agreement of the two boundary collars. In the coordinates \[G(s,a,b)=\gamma(s)+ia\gamma'(s)+jb,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{vol}_{\mathbb H^3}=\frac{1-a\,k(s)}{b^3}\,ds\,da\,db ,\] the gap \(a_{\Omega^*}-a_\Omega=O(b^3)\) makes the unsigned collar volume integrable. This is a geometric argument for suitably regular extensions. It does not supply the missing absolute integrability for every map allowed in Section 4.2, as Problem 2 shows.

The approximation argument in Section 5.5 has a one-sided conclusion. The equipotential actions increase to the limiting action, the two \(A_2\) Schwarzian norms converge in the Weil–Petersson topology, and the truncated signed volumes converge at a fixed positive height. With the controlled signed-volume definition, these yield the stated upper bound for \(V\) and hence \(\widetilde S\geq4V_R\). They do not establish continuity of the full volume or equality for all Weil–Petersson curves.
# Confirmed problems

Problem 1 (The one-form in Lemma 8.6 is not a divergence primitive).  On p. 45, Lemma 8.6 explicitly defines \[i_W(u)=\langle DE(u),W\rangle,\qquad W=\nabla_\xi n,\] and claims \[(\operatorname{div}W)\,E^*da=d i_W .
 \tag{*}\] Its proof identifies the exterior derivative of this metric-dual one-form with divergence times area. Equation (8.5), p. 46, then uses \[\operatorname{tr}\langle\nabla_\xi(B\cdot),DE(\cdot)\rangle E^*da
 =-d i_W-2\langle\xi,n\rangle E^*da .
 \tag{**}\] Both identities are false with the stated definition.

Consider the admissible \(C^\infty\) family \(\gamma_t=t+S^1\). Every curve has Euclidean length \(2\pi\). For its interior Epstein surface, use the source’s Example 3.15 (p. 20) and write, for \(u^2+v^2<1\), \[E=(X,Y,Z)=
 \left(\frac{2u}{1+r^2},\frac{2v}{1+r^2},
       \frac{1-r^2}{1+r^2}\right),\qquad r^2=u^2+v^2 .\] Then \(E_t=E+(t,0,0)\), \(n=Z(X,Y,Z)\) and \(\xi=(1,0,0)\). All these surfaces are totally geodesic, so \(B_t=0\). The upper-half-space connection gives \[W=\nabla_\xi n=(-Z,0,X),\qquad
 \phi=\langle\xi,n\rangle=\frac{X}{Z}=\frac{2u}{1-r^2}.\] The induced metric is \(\rho(du^2+dv^2)\) with \(\rho=4/(1-r^2)^2\). Direct differentiation gives \[W^\flat=-d\phi,\qquad dW^\flat=0,\qquad
 \Delta_{\mathbb H^2}\phi=2\phi,\qquad
 (\operatorname{div}W)\,da=-2\phi\,da .\] At \((u,v)=(1/2,0)\), \[\phi=\frac43,\qquad da=\frac{64}{9}\,du\wedge dv,\qquad
 (\operatorname{div}W)\,da=-\frac{512}{27}\,du\wedge dv\ne0.\] This contradicts \((*)\). In \((**)\) the left side is zero, since \(B_t=0\), whereas the right side is \(-512/27\) times \(du\wedge dv\). The test is on the immersed interior branch, so it does not exploit an undefined trace at a singular point. An exact symbolic and rational calculation verifies the connection, metric, normal, one-form and residual.

Equation reference: eq:correct-form. The appropriate replacement is the area-contraction one-form \[\alpha_W(u)=\operatorname{vol}_{\mathbb H^3}\bigl(n,W,DE(u)\bigr)
            =(\iota_W da)(DE(u)).
 \] With compatible orientation, \(d\alpha_W=(\operatorname{div}W)da\) on an immersed surface. Unlike the induced inverse metric, this ambient expression stays defined when \(DE\) loses rank. It is therefore also a suitable candidate for the smooth extension that Section 8 needs. The accompanying Stokes boundary term must use its conormal component; retaining the printed metric-dual form and merely changing the prose would not repair the argument.

There is specific counterevidence against a false main-theorem claim. For translating circles the total volume and action remain zero; the local residual does not create a nonzero global renormalized volume. The curvature-commutation formula of Proposition 8.4 is compatible with the corrected contraction form. The usual divergence theorem supplies exactly the missing rotation of the one-form. Nevertheless, the printed identity is an essential step in the nonimmersed Schläfli extension, then Theorem 5.2, the variation of \(V_R\), and Corollary 5.12. This is a Major defect in that supplied derivation. A local correction’s availability does not eliminate the core dependency.

Problem 2 (The printed extension class does not define a finite signed integral).  Section 4.2, pp. 22–23, permits any map \(\varphi\) continuous on the compactification, differentiable on the open \(\mathbb H^3\), with the prescribed Epstein boundary values and nonnegative Jacobian near \(\gamma\). It then concludes from compactness of the image above a cutoff that \(\int_{\mathbb H^3}\varphi^*\operatorname{vol}_\varepsilon\) is finite and independent of the chosen extension. These conditions do not ensure that the signed integral exists.

Take \(\gamma=S^1\). Put \(R^2=x^2+y^2\), \(D=R^2+z^2+1\), and \[F_0(x,y,z)=
 \left(\frac{2x}{D},\frac{2y}{D},
       \frac{\sqrt{D^2-4R^2}}{D}\right),\qquad z>0 .\] This is smooth in \(\mathbb H^3\), takes values in the upper unit hemisphere, and extends continuously to the compactification. At \(z=0\), its restriction is \[\left(\frac{2x}{1+R^2},\frac{2y}{1+R^2},
       \frac{|1-R^2|}{1+R^2}\right).\] These are precisely the interior and exterior circular Epstein boundary data. At the point at infinity it tends to \((0,0,1)\). Its Jacobian is identically zero.

For \(n\geq4\), take disjoint cubes centered at \(p_n=(0,0,2^{-n})\) with half-width \(h_n=2^{-n}/16\). They accumulate only at the boundary point \(0\), away from \(\gamma\). On the concentric inner cube use affine unit-cube coordinates \(U=(U_1,U_2,U_3)\in[0,1]^3\), and set \[a_n=\frac{2^{-n}}{100},\qquad m_n=2^{2n},\qquad Q=(0,0,1),\] \[P_n(U)=Q+a_n
 \bigl(\sin(2\pi m_nU_1),\sin(2\pi m_nU_2),\sin(2\pi m_nU_3)\bigr).\] A smooth cutoff equal to one on the inner cube and zero near the outer cube’s boundary interpolates between \(P_n\) and \(F_0\). Outside the outer cubes retain \(F_0\). The resulting map \(\varphi\) is smooth at every interior point, because the cubes are locally finite there. Since \(a_n\to0\) and \(F_0(p)\to Q\) as \(p\to0\), it is continuous at the sole accumulation point and hence on the compactification. It has unchanged boundary values and agrees with \(F_0\) near \(S^1\); its Jacobian is therefore nonnegative there. Its image on every altered cube stays above height \(1/2\).

This does not contradict the intended value \(V(S^1)=0\) obtained from the well-behaved extension \(F_0\). Nor does it show that a suitably defined geometric volume fails to exist. It disproves the stated finiteness and extension-independence assertion for the actual admissible class. Choosing an exhaustion that groups complete oscillatory cubes could conceal the divergent positive and negative parts; no such conditional regularization is specified in the source.

A sufficient correction is to require controlled smoothness up to the compactified boundary away from \(\gamma\), with an absolutely integrable Jacobian on each cutoff region, and to use homotopies with the same control. The collar positivity and subsequent geometric estimates can then address the limit near \(\gamma\). Alternatively, a precisely defined finite-mass current or boundary-based volume could replace the integral, but that requires its own agreement and independence proof. If the authors intended smoothness on the closure away from \(\gamma\), the counterexample is excluded; that is a substantive strengthening of the printed admissibility conditions.

The defect enters Definition 4.4 and the definition of \(V_R\), so it affects the formulation of the central object used in the volume identity and inequality. It is Major in that scope, without a claim that the intended geometrically controlled volume or the final identity is false.

Problem 3 (The displayed Ahlfors–Weill coefficient is unbounded).  The proof of Theorem 6.3, p. 38, takes \(q=\mathcal S(g_{\alpha(\tau)})\) with \(\|q\|_\infty<\delta/2\) and writes \[\widetilde\mu_{\rm print}(z)
 =-\frac{2}{\bar z^4}
       \left(\frac{q}{\rho_{\mathbb D^*}}\right)(1/\bar z).
 \tag{AW}\] It asserts that this is a Beltrami coefficient of supremum norm less than \(\delta\) and uses \([s\widetilde\mu_{\rm print}]\) to construct the short path required for the distance bound. Formula (AW) fails even for an explicitly realized analytic Jordan curve.

For each permitted \(0<\delta<1\), choose \(a=\delta\), put \(k=\sqrt{a/2}\), and set \[g(w)=k\cot(k/w),\qquad |w|>1,\qquad q(w)=\frac{a}{w^4}.\] The Schwarzian chain rule gives \(\mathcal S(g)=2k^2/w^4=q\). The function is univalent on a neighborhood of the closed exterior disk: two cotangent arguments with equal values differ by an integral multiple of \(\pi\), whereas their distance is less than \(2k<\pi\). The pole at \(w=\infty\) is simple, \(g(w)=w+O(w^{-1})\) there, and no other pole occurs in the exterior domain. The boundary is therefore an analytic Jordan curve and defines a Weil–Petersson point. Postcomposition by a Möbius map can impose the source’s three-point normalization without changing \(q\).

With the stated density \(\rho_{\mathbb D^*}(w)=4/(1-|w|^2)^2\), \[\|q\|_\infty=\frac a4<\frac\delta2,\qquad
 \|q\|_2^2
 =\frac{\pi a^2}{2}\int_1^\infty
       (r^2-1)^2r^{-7}\,dr
 =\frac{\pi a^2}{12}.\] Thus \(c=4\|q\|_2=2a\sqrt{\pi/3}\) satisfies the exact permitted range \(0<c<2\delta\sqrt{4\pi/3}\). All the smallness and finite-energy assumptions used at the path construction are met. Start the flow at this point: its allowed first hitting time is then \(\tau=0\), since \(\|V\|=c\) initially. But (AW) becomes \[\widetilde\mu_{\rm print}(z)
 =-\frac{a(1-|z|^2)^2}{2|z|^4},\] which is unbounded as \(z\to0\). In particular, \(s\widetilde\mu_{\rm print}\) fails to be a Beltrami coefficient for every \(s>0\). This is not just the separate factor-four overestimate of path length mentioned below.

The correct coefficient is \[\widetilde\mu_{\rm corr}(z)
 =-\frac{(1-|z|^2)^2}{2\bar z^4}\,q(1/\bar z)
 =-2\frac{z^2}{\bar z^2}
       \left(\frac{q}{\rho_{\mathbb D^*}}\right)(1/\bar z).\] Its modulus is \(2\|q(1/\bar z)\|_{\rho_{\mathbb D^*}}\). For the example it is simply \(-a(1-|z|^2)^2/2\) and is bounded by \(a/2<\delta\). The singularity of the displayed reflected formula at zero is interpreted by the holomorphic behavior of \(q\) at infinity; there is no unbounded coefficient.

A bounded repair preserves \(K=\sqrt2/(1-\delta)^2\). Define \[Jq(z)=\frac{\overline{q(1/\bar z)}}{z^4},\qquad
 \eta(w)=-2\,\frac{\overline{q(w)}}{\rho_{\mathbb D^*}(w)}.\] Reflection \(J\) preserves the normalized supremum and \(A_2\) norms. Inverse welding gives \(\beta(x^{-1})=Jq\) [Retained latex: \cite[Appendix A, pp.~49--50]{TTII}]. The Ahlfors–Weill section [TTI, p. 8] gives \[y(s)=[s\eta],\quad \beta(y(s))=sJq,\quad y(1)=x^{-1},
 \quad \|\eta\|_\infty<\delta,\quad \|\eta\|_2=c/2 .\] The supremum norm in [TTI] is four times the present normalized norm, so its radius-two section has precisely the needed range. Right-translate the velocity to the identity and apply the contracting harmonic projection. The direct right-translation estimate [Retained latex: \cite[Corollary 3.6, p.~29]{TTI}] gives \[\|\dot y(s)\|_{\mathrm{WP}}\leq
 \frac{\sqrt2}{(1-\|s\eta\|_\infty)^2}\|\eta\|_2\leq Kc/2 .\] Constant right translation and reversal of a path imply \(d_{\mathrm{WP}}(e,x)=d_{\mathrm{WP}}(e,x^{-1})\), without making inversion an isometry between arbitrary pairs. Hence \(d_{\mathrm{WP}}(e,x)\leq{\rm length}_{\mathrm{WP}}(y)\leq Kc/2<Kc\). The source’s energy and triangle inequalities yield its advertised weaker bound, including the initially-small-gradient case. This repair uses the actual right-translation bound, not the exact inverse-Bers norm asserted in Lemma 6.2. The inverse section has a factor two at the origin under these norms; the source’s existential choice of \(\delta\) prevents this observation alone from disproving that lemma. The distance theorem itself is not disproved. The printed essential construction of its short path, however, is not defined in the asserted class, so the defect is Major for Theorems 6.3 and 1.8.
# Additional verification and limitations

Finite total energy yields \(t_n\to\infty\) with \(\|V(\alpha(t_n))\|_{\mathrm{WP}}\to0\). The exterior Schwarzians tend to zero in \(A_2\), hence so do the standard Bers coordinates of the inverse weldings. The topological-group theorem [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem A.8, p.~65]{TTI}] gives \(\alpha(t_n)\to e\); continuity and monotonicity yield \(S(\alpha(t))\to0\). The energy-dependent quasicircle bound [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition 2.9, p.~9]{RW}] gives normalized quasiconformal compactness. Lower semicontinuity [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 2.12, p.~13]{RW}] makes every limit a zero-action circle; the three marked points identify it with \(S^1\). Carathéodory convergence makes the conformal-radius term tend to zero, so the remaining nonnegative integrals in \(S\) tend to zero. The pre-Schwarzian Hilbert chart [Retained latex: \cite[Corollary A.4, p.~49]{TTII}] then gives full WP convergence. These are bounded checks of the imported statements, not full independent reviews of those references.

The ambient all-\(T(1)\) flow assertion on p. 36 remains Needs Evidence. Bounded speed and completeness extend a locally well-posed field; they do not establish its local regularity. Indeed [Retained latex: \cite[Remark 2.3, p.~9]{TTI}] warns that right-translated fixed tangent vectors need not form a smooth field on full \(T(1)\). This does not show that the particular Schwarzian-dependent field fails to be smooth; its varying coefficient may compensate. No counterexample to that field was established. The bounded finite-type flow references checked by the audit do not provide the missing universal Banach-chart theorem.

For the distance estimate, \(\|V\|_{\mathrm{WP}}=c\) implies \(\|\mathcal S(g)\|_2=c/4\). The straight Schwarzian path therefore has \(A_2\) length \(c/4\), not the displayed \(c\) on p. 38. This overestimate is harmless for the weaker bound \(Kc\) used in Theorem 6.3. The exterior Bers coordinate must be compared using reflection and the inverse Teichmüller point; right invariance alone gives \(d_{\mathrm{WP}}(e,x)=d_{\mathrm{WP}}(e,x^{-1})\), without asserting that inversion is an isometry between arbitrary pairs.

Section 7 is independent of the volume proof. If the principal curvatures at infinity are greater than \(-1\) and have arithmetic mean \(e^{-2t}<1\), their product is less than one, giving the positive mean-curvature sign used for the barrier argument. For a minimal surface with principal curvatures \(\pm\lambda\), \(|\lambda|<1\), the visual metric has curvature \(-(1+\lambda^2)/(1-\lambda^2)\leq-1\); the stated Ahlfors–Schwarz comparison follows. The convex-hull estimate uses compactly contained round disks, the monotonicity of \((1-k)/(1+k)\) for \(k>-1\), and then a distance-\(t\) normal displacement to obtain the factor \(2t\). These arguments do not depend on the erroneous divergence primitive.

Some local displays require correction without generating additional independent findings. Naturality should read \(\operatorname{Ep}_\rho\circ h=h\circ\operatorname{Ep}_{h^*\rho}\); the source itself uses the correct composition in Lemma 3.7. The cutoff can be chosen monotone; alternatively Fatou’s lemma for infinite nonnegative mass and dominated convergence for finite mass establish the collar limit. Neither observation repairs the oscillatory interior counterexample. The proof of Theorem 5.9, p. 32, must differentiate \(H\,da\) as \(\delta H\,da+H\,\delta(da)\), with a plus. For \(f_a(z)=z+az^3\), \(0<a<1/3\), the printed sign gives \(-162a^3/(4-9a^2)\) at \(z=0\), whereas the correct density is zero. The immediately following at-infinity formula gives the correct zero; this is a display clarification, not a further independent core defect.

A second Needs Evidence item concerns Theorem 5.7, p. 30. Put \(h=1-r\). A nondegenerate cap of horizontal width \(O(h^3)\), affinely parametrized over the permitted interval of length \(1/r-r\asymp h\), has \(|E_s|=O(h^2)\). Its height is comparable to \(h\), so \[I_{ss}=O(h^2),\qquad (I^{-1})^{ss}\geq 1/I_{ss}=\Omega(h^{-2}),\] contrary to the printed inverse-metric estimate in these parameters. A fully documented global noncircle example satisfying both immersion hypotheses and the nondegenerate-cap conditions was not completed. The conditional calculation is therefore not a confirmed counterexample. In physical arclength and horizontal-distance coordinates the Euclidean metric is uniformly nondegenerate, and the hyperbolic inverse does have order \(h^2\). The moving coordinates and variation terms still need checking; no failed boundary limit is claimed.

The derivative-tail assertion on p. 31 has positive support. If the gap \(q=a_\Omega-a_{\Omega^*}\) is jointly \(C^{3,\alpha}\) and its boundary two-jets vanish, then \(\partial_tq=O(b^{2+\alpha})\), giving \[\int_0^\varepsilon b^{-3}|\partial_tq|\,db=O(\varepsilon^\alpha).\] A cubic remainder need not survive time differentiation. The moving ceiling has \(\partial_t b_r=O(h)\) and contributes \(O(h)\) using the original \(O(b^3)\) gap.

Each has an admissible example, a precise source location, counterevidence and a stated repair boundary. The two unresolved questions are excluded from that count. report: Abstract: This review concerns the acquired accepted-author arXiv version. The nonexistence argument is traced through brick partitions, discretization, weak amalgamation and robust winding cycles. The main obstruction has substantial positive support, but its supplied brick-discretization proof contains a false core–star equality. A demonstrated defect in the Appendix A measurability argument affects the supplied proof of the advertised interval and circle classification: its endpoint test accepts a root with no strictly monotone subchain, including on an infinite staircase, and rejects the endpoint of a genuine maximal strictly monotone subchain. An explicit Borel repair is provided. The purported converse to Hjorth’s turbulence theorem and two boundary conventions also need correction, with their limited impact separated from the main theorem. Several initially suspected failures are withdrawn or repaired by direct arguments. Two Major issues affect the core-partition proof and the classification measurability derivation. Explicit repairs do not remove the defects in the printed proofs, and neither example disproves the principal nonexistence or classification conclusion. Adjudication remains pending.

Theorem 1.2 requires a Peano continuum with no locally separating points and one of three additional hypotheses: a locally nonplanar open subset; a planar open subset containing a non-locally-separating simple closed curve; or a circular covering. The conclusions for compact surfaces preserve the exceptions \(S^2\) and \(\mathbb RP^2\). The generic-turbulence and nonclassification conclusions require the additional homogeneity assumptions. The Sierpiński-carpet appendix proves minimality but expressly leaves its generic turbulence unresolved. Neither the surface exceptions nor that open question are silently strengthened in this review.
# Positive checks of the main argument
## The closure-based stars and the chain dictionary

The source uses \(\operatorname{Star}(K,\mathcal W)=\{W:\operatorname{Cl}(W)\cap K\ne\varnothing\}\), rather than intersection with open bricks. This initially suggests extra boundary stars, but the alleged counterexample does not survive the prefix witnesses. If \[K\in O(P)=\{K:K\subseteq\bigvee P,\ K\cap W\ne\varnothing
                       \text{ for all }W\in P\},\] then \(\operatorname{Star}(K,\mathcal W)=P\) exactly. For a brick outside \(P\), its open set is disjoint from the closure of the union of \(P\), and its closure cannot meet the open regular join \(\bigvee P\). Conversely, every brick of \(P\) is met by \(K\). For two consecutive distinct first-visit prefixes, only one new brick is added. Any continuum between the corresponding witnesses in a nested chain has its star squeezed between those prefixes. Thus the equality of star families in Proposition 5.2 is supported, after correcting the prefix index noted below. The purported boundary-star defect is withdrawn.

Lemma 5.3 handles its two Hausdorff directions differently. In one direction equal stars give the mesh bound directly. In the other, the least chain member whose star contains the prescribed star either is the root or is the closure of its proper predecessors. The assumed inclusion of star families then puts those predecessors inside the prescribed union of brick closures. This supplies the reverse Hausdorff bound; mere density of the bricks would not suffice.

Theorem 5.8 must use connected, nonempty fibers and edge surjectivity, not merely a surjective vertex map. Its construction assigns core bricks first and attaches every remaining brick to a neighboring core. Conditional on the corrected core construction in Problem 5, connectedness of each fiber and the special paths across adjacent target bricks give precisely those two requirements. The forced-assignment property (5.7) is what makes the simultaneous prefix realization work. Theorem 5.9 then first refines sufficiently that distance two at the fine level projects to distance at most one. This is the needed loss allowance when the two closed-star neighborhoods meet; no exact amalgamation is asserted.
## Winding, robustness and the surface alternatives

For a spaced circular path of circular length at least four, the triangles in the local comparison in Lemma 3.5 have no nontrivial three-cycle. Their signed edge weights telescope, leaving just the two endpoint corrections, each of absolute value at most one. Monotone refinements add zero-weight stutters; backtracking on a spaced path cancels adjacent signed edge weights. These are the precise reasons for Lemmas 3.3–3.5, rather than an appeal to an undefined topological winding invariant for every graph.

In Theorem 6.4 the two-brick buffer around the robust cycle ensures that the final comparison occurs entirely inside the coarse cycle. Before that suffix, the projected competing walk is still in the stem; otherwise the buffer would be violated. The positive and negative long traversals consequently cannot be amalgamated within coarse distance one. Literal concatenation and endpoint bookkeeping require the clarifications discussed below; no counterexample to the resulting nonexistence conclusion was established.

For the three constructions of robust cycles, the hypotheses are used in different ways. Locally nonplanar pieces allow prescribed disjoint arcs. A non-locally-separating planar boundary curve allows the auxiliary path to be disjoined from a compatible circular partition. For a circular covering, the entire coarse nerve is a cycle, so the confinement condition is automatic. The path-doubling step in Theorem 6.12 should first upgrade the given walk to a path using Theorem 6.2, as done explicitly in the preceding two constructions. This preserves refinement of the original walk. The first large winding has positive sign because the initial spaced path already traverses the coarse cycle twice positively; the absolute-value stopping description alone is not the justification.

The final surface classification retains its topological distinction. The sphere and projective plane are excluded by unicoherence. The torus and Klein bottle carry circular coverings, and the connected-sum operation can be placed in the exclusive interior of one covering element. Surfaces with boundary use a boundary component in the planar alternative. The cited continuum-theoretic arc and brick-partition theorems remain imported dependencies; this audit does not independently reprove all those references.
# Confirmed mathematical problems

Problem 1 (A false endpoint test in the classification proof: Major).  Lemma A.2, p. 33, claims that conditions (a)–(c) characterize the maximum of a maximal nontrivial strictly monotone subchain. Condition (b) checks a southeast rectangle for horizontal or vertical pairs; condition (c) requires such a pair in every northwest rectangle. These conditions accept a vacuous rectangle at the root and exclude a legitimate maximum at the top of the chain.

In the triangle \(T=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq y\leq1\}\), consider \[\mathcal C_L=\{(x,\tfrac12):0\leq x\leq\tfrac12\}
       \cup\{(0,y):\tfrac12\leq y\leq1\},\qquad
 p=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12).\] This is a maximal chain of intervals, and it has no nontrivial strictly monotone subchain. Every nontrivial subarc contains a horizontal or vertical pair. Condition (a) holds at \(p\). For every \(n\geq1\), the southeast rectangle in (b) meets \(\mathcal C_L\) only at \(p\), so (b) holds vacuously. For every \(n\), choose \(m\geq\max\{n,2\}\) and the two points \[(\tfrac12,\tfrac12),\qquad
 (\tfrac12-\tfrac1m,\tfrac12).\] They satisfy the northwest bounds and the prescribed horizontal difference in (c). Thus the alleged equivalence gives a false positive.

The failure also occurs on the infinite-piece locus actually used in Theorem A.5. Begin at \(p\), join it horizontally to \(q_0=(1/4,1/2)\), and, for \(n\geq0\), join \[q_n=(2^{-n-2},1-2^{-n-1})
 \quad\hbox{horizontally to}\quad
 r_n=(2^{-n-3},1-2^{-n-1}),\] then vertically to \(q_{n+1}\). Include the limit \((0,1)\). This compact monotone staircase has infinitely many maximal horizontal and vertical pieces, and no nontrivial strictly monotone piece. Its parameter \(t=y-x\) runs continuously and bijectively from \(0\) to \(1\); hence it is a maximal chain, not just a partial collection of intervals. At its root, the same test works with \(m\geq\max\{n,4\}\). The source’s false predicate would therefore mark a nonexistent strict piece even on \(\Phi^\infty([0,1])\).

There is also a false negative. For \[\mathcal C_s=\{((1-t)/2,(1+t)/2):0\leq t\leq1\},\] the entire chain is a maximal strictly monotone subchain with maximum \((0,1)\). Every northwest rectangle at this point meets the triangle only at that point, so (c) fails.

These computations refute the stated characterization, not the Borelness of the genuine endpoint set. Theorem A.5, pp. 34–36, invokes precisely that Borel endpoint set to apply Lusin–Novikov and construct its countable invariant; Theorem A.6 then transfers classification to the circle. The false test is therefore an essential measurability step in the supplied derivation of an advertised result. Its impact is Major in that scope, even though a replacement is available. It does not affect the separate robust-cycle argument.

Here is an explicit Borel replacement. For every maximal interval chain \(\mathcal C\), let \(c_\mathcal C(t)=(x_\mathcal C(t),y_\mathcal C(t))\) be its unique member with \(y_\mathcal C(t)-x_\mathcal C(t)=t\), \(0\leq t\leq1\). This evaluation is jointly continuous in \((\mathcal C,t)\): every convergent subsequence of the selected points lies in the limiting chain and has the prescribed length, which determines it uniquely. Let \(S(\mathcal C,a,b)\) mean that both coordinates vary strictly in the appropriate directions on \([a,b]\). It suffices to check this on all rational pairs in \((a,b)\); monotonicity and continuity recover the endpoints. Thus \(S\) is Borel, including when an endpoint varies. For \(p=c_\mathcal C(t)\), \[\begin{aligned}
(\mathcal C,p)\in E^S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad&
\exists q\in\mathbb Q,\ 0\leq q<t:\ S(\mathcal C,q,t),\\
&\forall r\in\mathbb Q\cap(t,1],\ \neg S(\mathcal C,q,r).
\end{aligned}\] The rational test on the right is interpreted as vacuous when \(t=1\). Maximal extension to the left supplies the corresponding maximal subchain. This formulation excludes the root and accepts a strict piece ending at the top.

Problem 2 (The stated converse to Hjorth’s theorem: Minor).  Theorem 7.4, p. 28, asserts generic turbulence if and only if nonclassification by countable structures for an arbitrary continuous Polish action. The converse is false.

Take the translation action of the Polish group \(\ell^1\) on \(\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\) and adjoin one isolated fixed point \(*\). The translation action is turbulent: finitely supported translations give dense orbits, \(\ell^1\) is meager in the product space, and any sufficiently small convex cylinder is contained in the closure of a local orbit by splitting finitely supported translations into small increments. Hjorth’s forward theorem makes its orbit relation nonclassifiable by countable structures. A classification of the disjoint-union action would restrict to one of this translation action, so the union is also nonclassifiable. But it is not minimal, as the source’s definition of generic turbulence requires: the isolated point is a fixed invariant open component.

The repair is to retain the implication from generic turbulence to nonclassification. This is the only direction used for Corollary 7.9. The overstatement is therefore a real local theorem error, with no demonstrated damage to that downstream conclusion.

Problem 3 (The degenerate continuum is not excluded: Minor).  The explicit definition on p. 5 allows a one-point Peano continuum. Corollaries 1.5, 1.7, 1.8 and their Section 7 versions exclude the circle, sphere and projective plane, but do not exclude this case.

For \(X=\{p\}\), the homeomorphism group is trivial and the unique chain \(\{\{p\}\}\) has an open, comeager orbit. The space is homogeneous and strongly locally homogeneous: every relevant neighborhood and rigid-stabilizer orbit is \(\{p\}\). Its universal minimal flow is a singleton, and the chain equivalence relation has a constant countable-structure classification. Thus the unqualified corollaries fail on this boundary case. Requiring a nondegenerate continuum, or adding the singleton to the exceptions, repairs their stated range. The three additional alternatives in Theorem 1.2 already exclude it, so this is not a counterexample to the main theorem.

Problem 4 (The allowed two-edge circular walk has ambiguous weight: Minor).  On p. 7 a circular path need only have sequence length at least three. Thus \(\langle a,b,a\rangle\) is allowed in the two-vertex reflexive connected graph. In Definition 3.2, pp. 8–9, the pair \((a,b)\) satisfies both the \(+1\) and the \(-1\) cases, using respectively the two oriented steps of this circular path.

Consequently the assertion that the weight is well-defined is false for the stated domain. Require circular length at least three (sequence length at least four), or explicitly exclude this backtracking two-edge walk from the weight definition. The robust-cycle argument and Lemma 3.5 already impose circular length at least four. Their weights are unambiguous, so this correction does not challenge the core obstruction.

Problem 5 (A false core equality in the discretization proof: Major).  Proposition 5.7, pp. 14–15, defines its core-building seed as \(\operatorname{Star}(T_V\cap U,\mathcal W_0)\), but the following path argument uses \(\operatorname{Star}(T_V,\mathcal W_0)\). The resulting assertion \(\operatorname{Core}(V,\mathcal W)=\operatorname{Star}(T_V,\mathcal W)\) is false for the printed construction (source TeX lines 1141–1174). This equality supplies core connectedness for Theorems 5.8–5.9.

Proposition 5.7 assumes only that \(X\) is a Peano continuum and \(\mathcal U,\mathcal V\) are brick partitions. It does not require the absence of locally separating points. The following circle therefore lies within its actual hypotheses. On \(\mathbb R/12\mathbb Z\), take \(\mathcal U=\{(0,8),(8,12)\}\), \(\mathcal V=\{(6,14),(2,6)\}\), unit-arc refinement \(\mathcal W_0\), and trees \([7.5,12]\) and \([3.5,4.5]\). Write \(I_j=(j,j+1)\) modulo \(12\) and denote the two trees by \(T_0,T_1\). Each coarse and fine brick is connected, regular open and uniformly locally connected; each regular join of two bricks is uniformly locally connected. Both trees lie in their assigned \(V\) and meet every required coarse \(U\). The closure-based definition gives \[\begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{Star}(T_0,\mathcal W_0)&=\{I_0,I_7,I_8,I_9,I_{10},I_{11}\},\\
 \operatorname{Star}(T_1,\mathcal W_0)&=\{I_3,I_4\},\\
 \operatorname{Star}(\partial V_0,\mathcal W_0)
   &=\operatorname{Star}(\partial V_1,\mathcal W_0)=\{I_1,I_2,I_5,I_6\}.
\end{aligned}\] Thus the exact fineness requirement holds. The printed local seeds produce \(\mathcal C^{U_0,V_0}=\{I_7\}\), \(\mathcal C^{U_1,V_0}=\{I_8,I_9,I_{10},I_{11}\}\), \(\mathcal C^{U_0,V_1}=\{I_3,I_4\}\) and \(\mathcal C^{U_1,V_1}=\varnothing\). The remaining components in \(U_0\) are \(\{I_0,I_1,I_2\}\) and \(\{I_5,I_6\}\); none remain in \(U_1\). The printed seeds produce \(\mathcal W=\{(0,3),(3,5),(5,7),(7,8),(8,12)\}\). For \(V=(6,14)\) the core is \(\{(7,8),(8,12)\}\), but \(\operatorname{Star}(T_V,\mathcal W)\) also contains \((0,3)\), whose closure meets \(12=0\) and is not contained in \(V\). Thus the auxiliary equality fails with the displayed local seeds. The path argument fails at the same point: \(I_0\) is already in the global tree star but not in the local seed. Its one-vertex path to that star crosses no boundary-star brick. In this example the final core is nevertheless connected. The example refutes the stated equality and the supplied proof step, not the conclusion of Proposition 5.7.

Use \(\mathcal W_0(U\cap V)\cap\operatorname{Star}(T_V,\mathcal W_0)\) as the seed instead. Fineness puts every seed brick in the core. Each resulting core component meets the global tree star, whereas every remaining component meets the boundary star by the first-boundary-crossing argument. After amalgamation this proves \(\operatorname{Core}(V,\mathcal W)=\operatorname{Star}(T_V,\mathcal W)\) and its connectedness, together with adjacency of the remaining bricks to a core. Every global tree-star brick is now assigned to a core component, so no remaining component touches the tree. Conversely, every core component contains a seed and touches the tree. Finiteness of the amalgamation identifies the closure of each amalgam with the union of its constituent closures, giving the claimed equality. The graph star of a connected tree is connected, and the remaining components have neighbors among the core components. This restores exactly the input needed by Theorem 5.8.

The defect is Major because the false equality is the printed justification of core connectedness, an essential input to the monotone-epimorphism discretization and hence Theorem 5.9 and the main obstruction. The availability of this replacement construction does not make that proof step valid. No counterexample to the proposition’s existential conclusion or to the main theorem is claimed.
# Repaired proof steps and nonfindings

The generic-turbulence induction on p. 30 ends by applying Lemma 7.2 to a coarse walk \(u\), although that lemma assumes a spaced path and \(u\) was only chosen to cover the coarse partition. The conclusion can be justified without that application. The fine walk \(v\) is spaced. If \(D_j\) is its current prefix witness, the moved continuum \(h_j[D_j]\) joins the first and last fine-prefix bricks and stays in their regular join. Lemma 7.2 applied to this fine path supplies every already visited coarse-prefix witness.

For a later coarse first-visit set \(P\), take its original witness \(A_P\) in the current chain. It meets a brick not yet visited by \(D_j\), so chain ordering forces \(D_j\subseteq A_P\). The support of \(h_j\) lies in the newly visited coarse union, which is contained in \(\bigvee P\). Its image of \(A_P\) therefore stays in \(\bigvee P\), contains the new witness of all visited bricks, and retains the intersections with all future bricks outside the support. This verifies every coarse prefix and preserves membership in \(\mathbf O_{\mathcal U,u}\). The preliminary root adjustment can likewise be supported in a sufficiently small connected neighborhood inside \(u(0)\), ensuring membership in the prescribed identity neighborhood directly. These arguments fill the shortcut; they are not a counterexample to Theorem 7.7.

Appendix B uses a different mechanism: irrational separating circles cut the carpet into pieces which are again S-curves. The boundary-extension theorem is applied to three pieces with matching boundary maps, followed by the complementary piece. The maps send the root piece into \(U_0\), the selected later point into \(U_1\), and preserve the chosen larger component inside \(V\). The actual Figure 3 and the gluing domains on pp. 39–40 were checked. This supports the minimality construction subject to its cited Whyburn extension and carpet-characterization results.

Several displayed conventions should be corrected without being inflated into additional confirmed core defects. Definition 5.1 must test the nonempty prefixes \(1\leq i\leq\operatorname{lh}(w)\), rather than including \(i=0\) and omitting the last prefix. Repeated circular walks must suppress the duplicated joining endpoint, or consistently use a stutter convention. In Theorem A.6 the intersection defining the endpoint must omit \(C=S^1\); its inclusion contributes an empty set. For Proposition A.4, approximate a finite ordered list by nearby points on a strictly decreasing graph, allowing both coordinates to move. Holding \(x_i\) fixed cannot approximate two different \(y_i\) with the same \(x_i\); this does not prevent Hausdorff density. The infinite pasting step can use the order and density of domain and range to obtain continuity, rather than an unrestricted pasting lemma.

The literal joining-edge bounds in Claim 6.4.1 require separate bookkeeping: for ordinary concatenation, \[\operatorname{wd}(a^\frown b)=\operatorname{wd}(a)+\operatorname{weight}(a(-1),b(0))+\operatorname{wd}(b).\] The bounded calculation gives a projected circular word \(\langle0,3,0,1,2,3,0\rangle\) on the oriented four-cycle, with net weight \(N=4\) and maximal absolute prefix weight \(M_c=5\). A stem ending at label \(1\) has \(M_v=0\) and joins the initial \(0\) with weight \(-1\). For \(k=2\), the printed choice satisfies \(kN=8>3M_v+M_c+2=7\), but the complete concatenation has weight \(7\), not the strict bound \(>2M_v+M_c+2=7\) claimed in Claim 6.4.1(b0). Subdividing transitions with stutters yields a finite graph realization compatible with the distance buffer (6.3), without changing these numbers.

This is retained as Needs Evidence, not as a confirmed counterexample under every hypothesis. The bounded graph has not been realized as all the Peano-space brick partitions and robust-cycle witnesses required by the claim. The earlier concern about (a0)–(a1) is withdrawn: the definition of \(M_c\) already controls prefixes in both orientations and provides the necessary slack there. For a repaired proof, enlarge the stem allowance and choose \(k\) with an additional fixed margin, then include each joining edge explicitly. This indicates the repair boundary; it is not certification of a complete repaired topological argument.
# Supporting checks

The two confirmed Major issues concern the supplied measurability derivation for the interval/circle classification and the core-partition construction used by the main discretization argument. The three Minor issues are a false unused converse and two excluded boundary cases. No false-main-theorem claim follows from them. Positive repairs, rejected candidates and unavailable external proofs are retained in the supporting records.

report: Abstract: The acquired arXiv version is reviewed from its definitions through the height bound, Galois-orbit deduction and reduction for lines. The principal construction of a single relation valid at all relevant non-archimedean places is supported: the finite product is indexed by signed divisors of an isogeny degree, not by the number of places. Title: Technical verification of Zilber–Pink
under multiplicative degeneration
# Identity, scope and principal dependencies

The source is C. Daw and M. Orr, Zilber–Pink in a product of modular curves assuming multiplicative degeneration, arXiv:2208.06338v4, 3 March 2025, 42 pages [paper]. Its frozen journal identity is Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), no. 13, 2877–2926, DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0011. The acquired manuscript is an author preprint. The 50-page journal text was not acquired, and equivalence of the two versions is not asserted. All source page references below are both PDF and printed page numbers in the 42-page acquired version.

The complete PDF text and released mathematical TeX were examined through the primary review and three bounded native checks. The primary read all 1982 extraction lines and all 232 manifest lines, and actually inspected 37 selected source pages. All fourteen manifest-listed inputs, totaling 2,773,488 bytes, matched their current recorded sizes and hashes. The supporting coverage ledger distinguishes full primary text reading, assigned native TeX ranges, actual images and imported results. No author code or author TeX was executed.

Theorem 1.3 assumes an irreducible curve over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\), Hodge generic in \(Y(1)^n\), whose closure contains \((\infty,\ldots,\infty)\). The Galois bound excludes points with at least two CM coordinates, requires two distinct unordered coordinate pairs, and uses cyclic isogenies at its final arithmetic step. These qualifications are material. The non-strongly-special case, point counting and the final Pila–Zannier deduction are imported from Habegger–Pila; the present paper supplies the new height and orbit estimates. André’s G-function and normal-monodromy theorems, standard isogeny estimates, and the classical modular-polynomial facts remain named mathematical dependencies. They have not all been independently reproved in this review.
# Positive verification of the main construction
## Periods and isogeny relations

The symbolic normalization in Lemma 3.1, pp. 14–15, is consistent: \[\alpha^2=E_6/E_4,\qquad u=\alpha^{-1},\qquad
 \psi^*\omega=\alpha\,\widetilde\omega.\] The displayed initial coefficients of \(\alpha\) need correction, as discussed below, but the symbolic proof uses the correct ratio.

The regularity of the second period at the nodal limit can also be checked directly. In the coordinate change \[x=u^2\widetilde x+r,\qquad
 y=u^3\widetilde y+u^2s\widetilde x+t,\] comparison of \(a_1=1\), \(a_2=a_3=0\) on the two Weierstrass models gives \[s=(u-1)/2,\quad r=(u^2-1)/12,\quad t=-r/2.\] Consequently, for \(\eta=(x+1/12)\omega\), \[\psi^*\eta
 =u(\widetilde x+1/12)\widetilde\omega.\] Tate’s Laurent expansion on a fixed annulus has constant term \(-2\sum_{n\geq1}\sigma_1(n)q^n\) for \(\widetilde x\). Contour integration therefore gives the additional check \[G=\left(\frac{E_2}{12\alpha}\right)\circ\theta,\qquad G(0)=1/12,\] where \(E_2=1-24\sum_{n\geq1}\sigma_1(n)q^n\) and \(\theta\) is the inverse series of \(1/j\). This verifies holomorphy at zero and rational coefficients, rather than inferring absence of a pole only from a rational linear combination of \(F\) and \(F'\). The corresponding Tate formula and invariant differential were checked in the acquired primary reference [Tate].

For the complex calculation, the pullback matrix of an isogeny is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\0&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) with \(ad=M\); the homology matrix has determinant \(M\) as well. The Legendre relation yields \[-aG(s_2)F(s_1)+bF(s_2)F(s_1)+dF(s_2)G(s_1)=\frac r{2\pi i}.\] When \(r=0\), this is already a nonzero algebraic relation. Otherwise a second isogeny eliminates \(1/(2\pi i)\). The monomial with coefficient \(ra'\) remains nonzero even after \(Y_1=Y_3\), \(Z_1=Z_3\). This is precisely the noncollapse needed when the two coordinate pairs share one coordinate; it does not require four distinct coordinates.
## The covering construction and the global product

Lemma 5.1, pp. 26–27, uses a function with its only zero at the chosen degeneration point, takes a root to remove its ramification, and passes to a Galois closure. The resulting simple zeros of \(x\) and the automorphisms over \(x\) are essential: a point small in one embedding may be near a different zero than it is in another embedding.

In Lemma 5.5 the Taylor coordinates of all branches are algebraic. Their coefficient bounds and the separation of the finitely many zeros give radii positive everywhere and at least one almost everywhere. The constructed branches account for all \(\deg(x)\) preimages, which is the reason no extra branch is missed. Rational identities with a presentation denominator should be continued as meromorphic identities across removable zeros of that denominator. This supplies the intended equality even where a particular quotient presentation is \(0/0\).

There is a useful field-bookkeeping clarification in Lemma 5.8, pp. 35–36. For each \(k\), choose a field \(\widehat K_k/K(s)\) of degree at most \(144\) defining the two transported isogenies, and construct its factors over that field. Then place all factors in their compositum. One need not assert that a single field of degree \(144\) defines all the isogenies simultaneously. Every embedding of the compositum restricts to an embedding of each \(\widehat K_k\), so the appropriate factor still vanishes. The degree estimate is the sum of the individual bounds: \[\deg Q\leq
 288\ell[K(s):\mathbb Q]+2\ell\,d(MT^2).\] This preserves the stated estimate without a degree bound on the whole compositum.

Generic isogeny representatives do not merge distinct original coordinates for a fixed \(k\), because of Hodge genericity. Consequently each substituted factor is nonzero, including when one coordinate is shared by the exceptional pairs. The product is nonzero in a polynomial domain even when variables from different \(k\)’s coincide.
## Nontriviality and the height-to-orbit deduction

In Section 5.I, nonisotriviality and the normal-monodromy theorem give the full product \(\operatorname{SL}_2^\Lambda\), not a diagonal subgroup: a connected normal subgroup of the product having nontrivial projection to every simple factor must be the whole product. Analytic continuation of a period matrix along loops fills a Zariski-dense subset of its determinant torsor. It follows that the graph closure over the base is the product of that base with the torsors. Projection to the first columns is dominant, giving the claimed algebraic independence of the \(F_\lambda,G_\lambda\).

The substitution of the nonzero rational function \(H\) in Corollary 5.12 does not create a hidden zero polynomial. If the original polynomial is homogeneous of total degree \(d\), a fixed monomial in the \(Y_\lambda,Z_\lambda\) has a uniquely determined power of the extra variable \(W\). After \(W=H(X)\) that coefficient remains nonzero. This explains why homogeneity is required here.

For Lemma 5.7, basis-change coefficients over \(K(C_0)\) become algebraic functions of \(X\) and need not lie in \(K(X)\). Closure of G-functions under multiplication by algebraic functions supplies the intended conclusion; any finite Laurent pole in an intermediate coefficient is cleared before using the already established holomorphy. This correction is distinct from the false rank-two descent assertion in Problem 3.

Finally, put \(D=[K(s):K]\) and assume \(M\geq N\). The height estimate and isogeny bound give, after choosing \(\epsilon\) appropriately, \[M\leq M'\leq C\max\{D^a,M^{1/2}\}.\] Here \(M\leq M'\) follows because, for non-CM elliptic curves, \(\operatorname{Hom}(E_1,E_2)\) has rank one and a cyclic isogeny is primitive: a nontrivial integer multiple has a kernel containing full torsion and cannot be cyclic. If \(M>C^2\), the second term cannot dominate; the remaining case is absorbed into a constant since \(D\geq1\). This gives the required polynomial lower bound for \(D\). The finite covering degree controls descent to the original point. Points with a CM curve in either isogenous pair have two CM coordinates and are exactly excluded by \(\Sigma\).

For lines with constant coordinates, projection to nonconstant coordinates is injective on the line and its image intersects infinity. The residual mixed modular relations are the Habegger–Pila modular Mordell–Lang case. A constant CM coordinate or a relation among two constant coordinates would contradict the stated Hodge-generic hypothesis. The unequal degrees zero and positive in a constant/nonconstant pair permit the Habegger–Pila height comparison. Together with the mixed-pair orbit bound and cyclic minimality, the isogeny estimate also controls the second non-CM modular degree, as required for the full special complexity. The CM-coordinate cases belong to the imported non-strongly-special argument. The bounded primary-reference checks support these isogeny and modular-orbit inputs [GR, HP]; the complete point-counting theorem is an imported dependency.
# Confirmed local concerns

Problem 1 (A convergence boundary without convergence: Minor).  Lemma 2.1, p. 8, assumes only \(g\in K[[X]]\) and \(|x|\leq R^\dagger(g)\), and then evaluates \(g(x)\). These hypotheses do not ensure that the evaluation exists.

Take \(K=\mathbb Q_p\), \(g(X)=\sum_{n\geq0}X^n\), and \(x=1\). The coefficient definition on p. 7 gives \(R^\dagger(g)=R(g)=1\). Thus the printed closed inequality holds. But the summands at \(x=1\) do not tend to zero; successive partial sums differ by one, so the series is not Cauchy in \(\mathbb Q_p\). This is a direct failure of the evaluation domain, not a numerical violation inferred from analytic continuation.

Replace the closed condition by \(|x|<R^\dagger(g)\), or retain the boundary only with an explicit convergence assumption. In the strict interior, \[|b_nx^n|\leq (|x|/R^\dagger(g))^n\longrightarrow0,\] and the source’s coefficient estimate proves the stated inequality. If convergence is separately assumed on the boundary, the same estimate passes to the limit. The uses in Lemma 2.2 and Section 5 all have a strict radius inequality. Their actual required estimates survive, which limits this finding to the preliminary statement.

Problem 2 (The global-relation parameter can be infinite: Minor).  Lemma 5.8, p. 34, quantifies over all \(s\in C_0^*(\overline{\mathbb Q})\), but concludes that there is a global relation at \(x(s)\). The definition on p. 9 requires a finite algebraic parameter. The construction of \(C_0^*\) on p. 27 does not remove poles of \(x\).

Here is an example within the paper’s permitted geometry. Let \[(J_1,J_2,J_3)=
 \left(\frac{2048}{3},\frac{35152}{9},
                       \frac{28756228}{3}\right),\qquad
 \nu(t)=(J_1+t,J_2+t,J_3+t).\] Take \(C\) to be this line, \(C_4=\mathbb P^1_t\), and \(x=1/t\). All coordinates are nonconstant, the line meets full infinity, and no coordinate pair is identical. It is Hodge generic: a nontrivial classical modular correspondence is irreducible of degree greater than one in each coordinate and cannot contain a distinct affine line. The sole zero of \(x\) is the simple zero at infinity, and \(x:\mathbb P^1\to\mathbb P^1\) is Galois of degree one. These are exactly the requirements in Lemma 5.1.

At \(t=0\), the following smooth elliptic curves supply the exceptional isogenies: \[\begin{aligned}
 E_1&:y^2=z^3+z^2+z,\\
 E_2&:y^2=z^3-2z^2-3z,\\
 E_3&:y^2=z^3-14z^2+z.
\end{aligned}\] The quotient of \(E_1\) by \((0,0)\) is \(E_2\). After translating the point \((3,0)\) of \(E_2\) to the origin, its equation has coefficients \(A=7\), \(B=12\); the next degree-two quotient has \(A=-14\), \(B=1\). Thus there are isogenies \(E_1\to E_2\) of degree two and \(E_1\to E_3\) of degree four. The formulas \[c_4=16(A^2-3B),\quad
 \Delta=16B^2(A^2-4B),\quad
 j=256\frac{(A^2-3B)^3}{B^2(A^2-4B)}\] give exactly \(J_1,J_2,J_3\) above. None equals zero or \(1728\), and all are nonintegral rational numbers, hence non-CM. The \(1/j\) family fibers are isomorphic to these curves over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\), so the required isogenies exist for the actual families.

Therefore \(0\in C_0^*(\overline{\mathbb Q})\) and the distinct-pair hypotheses hold, while \(x(0)=\infty\). The promised relation at this parameter is not defined. An implicit reading that evaluates only finite parameters is precisely the missing restriction, not a consequence of the printed \(C_0^*\) definition.

Remove the poles of \(x\) before Lemma 5.8. There are finitely many, so their fixed heights can be treated separately in height bounds. For the non-CM cyclic-isogeny orbit bound, each fixed pair has at most one cyclic degree, so its finitely many exceptions can also be absorbed into the constants. If projective height is used, \(h(\infty)=0\) already handles the height assertion at a pole, but it does not define a G-function evaluation there. No failure of the nonexceptional global product or of the main finiteness conclusion follows.

Problem 3 (Rank-two descent in the effectivity remark: Minor).  Remark 5.14, p. 39, asserts that every column \((F_\lambda,G_\lambda)^{\mathsf T}\) satisfies a rank-two system over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}(X)\) because the differential forms are a basis over the function field of \(C_0\). A basis over \(K(C_0)\) does not imply descent to \(K(x)\). The asserted descent fails for an allowed cover.

Begin with the line \(C=\{(u,u+1,u+2)\}\) and set \[x_1(u)=\frac1{u(1-u)}.\] Its only zero is at \(u=\infty\), with order two. The normalization of the square-root base change used in Lemma 5.1 is explicitly \[C_4=\mathbb P^1_t,\qquad
 u=\frac1{1+t^2},\qquad x=t+t^{-1},\qquad x^2=x_1(u).\] This degree-two map \(x\) is Galois, with involution \(t\mapsto t^{-1}\). Its two zeros \(\pm i\) are simple and map to \(u=\infty\); take \(K=\mathbb Q(i)\). Thus this is an instance of the construction, not a different choice of base outside its hypotheses. The six possible \(j\) functions are \[u,\ u+1,\ u+2,\ 1-u,\ 2-u,\ 3-u.\] They are distinct affine functions of \(u\), so no two are generically isogenous by the same modular-correspondence argument. In particular the representative with \(j=u\) is present.

For this representative, the actual \(1/j\) family has invariants \[c_4=\frac{j}{j-1728},\qquad
 c_6=-\frac{j}{j-1728},\qquad
 \Delta=\frac{j^2}{(j-1728)^3}.\] At \(t=0\), \(j=u=1\) and the elliptic family is smooth; its local rank-two monodromy is the identity. At \(t=\infty\), put \(r=1/t\). Then \(j=r^2/(1+r^2)\), and the orders of \(c_4,c_6,\Delta\) are \(2,2,4\).

One can verify the latter monodromy without relying on a table of fiber types. Write the short Weierstrass equation as \(Y^2=Z^3+a(r)Z+b(r)\), with \(\operatorname{ord}(a)=
\operatorname{ord}(b)=2\) and nonzero leading coefficient of \(b\). After \(r=v^3\), \(Z=v^2Z_1\), \(Y=v^3Y_1\), the family has good limit \(Y_1^2=Z_1^3+b_0\) with \(b_0\ne0\). The deck transformation acts on this elliptic curve by \[(Z_1,Y_1)\longmapsto(\zeta_3 Z_1,Y_1),\] giving nontrivial order-three monodromy on its first cohomology.

Both \(t=0\) and \(t=\infty\) lie unramified above \(x=\infty\). A connection pulled back from a rank-two system over \(\mathbb C(x)\) would have conjugate local monodromies at these two branches. Identity and nontrivial order-three monodromy cannot be conjugate. Nor can the claimed equation hold accidentally only for the chosen period column: first-column algebraic independence over the algebraic extension \(\mathbb C(C_4)/\mathbb C(x)\) forces a rational coefficient matrix for that column to equal the actual Gauss–Manin matrix.

This refutes the rank-two shortcut in the optional effectivity remark. Proposition 5.13 itself applies Theorem 2.8 to G-functions, which does not require that shortcut. A correct rational system can be constructed by restriction of scalars: a rank-two differential module over \(K(C_4)\) gives rank \(2\deg(x)\) over \(K(x)\), with the corresponding algebraic multiples of the period functions. An effective treatment must supply this enlarged system and its relation ideal and singularities. This review does not claim to have computed all effective constants. The established impact is on the auxiliary rank and descent assertion, not the main height theorem.
# Further corrections and limits

The height-machine display on p. 39 needs an additive constant or the convention \(h^+=\max\{1,h\}\). This is visible within the isogeny example of Problem 2: keep its line and point \(t=0\), but choose \(x=1/(t+1)\). All the covering conditions still hold, and the same exceptional isogenies occur at \(x=1\). Then \(h(x)=0\) and \(h(J_1)=\log 2048>0\), so the displayed \[|h(x)-c_{22}h(j)|\leq c_{23}h(x)\] fails for every positive \(c_{22}\). The needed valid comparison is \(h(j(s))\leq A h(x(s))+B\) for constants fixed by the curve and the two nonconstant maps. The isogeny estimate already has \(D\geq1\) in its maximum, so this replacement supplies the same subsequent bound. The missing bounded-height convention is recorded explicitly, without asserting that the final exponent calculation fails.

Other corrections are retained as display or proof clarifications. The coefficient formula defining \(R^\dagger\) is the operative one; the alternative infimum on p. 7 has its scaling reversed and can also be affected by a discrete value group. It should not be repaired merely by reciprocating that infimum for every complete field. The strict growth bound at \(n=0\) in the G-function definition needs the customary harmless multiplicative constant. The correct initial expansion is \[\alpha=1-372q+10692q^2+\cdots;\] the printed \(1+372q+127692q^2+\cdots\) belongs to \(\alpha^{-1}\). The subsequent symbolic ratio and invariant differential calculation are consistent with the corrected \(\alpha\). The missing negation in the explanatory sentence about diagonal hyperplanes on p. 2 is likewise not used to reverse the actual Hodge-generic hypothesis in the theorem.

For Theorem 2.8, enlarge the finite exceptional set in its proof to include poles of the differential system. The homogeneous-ideal elimination in Lemma 2.9 is supported away from the finitely many leading-coefficient zeros. The theorem about global relations itself, including the vacuous-convergence case mentioned in Remark 2.7, remains an explicitly imported arithmetic result. No unproved transcendence statement is substituted for it.

The accessible source search confirmed arXiv v4 and found institutional accepted-manuscript listings. No separate correction or supplement resolving the above items was identified, and no distinct code release was found. This is a search limitation, not evidence of first discovery; absence of code is not a mathematical defect.
# Assessment and state

The three numbered concerns have local, demonstrated scope. The convergence boundary is unused in the strict-interior applications; poles are a finite parameter exception; and the false rank-two assertion belongs to an alternative effectivity argument rather than the invoked proof of the height theorem. These are the reasons for the Minor assessment. The length of a possible repair is not the severity criterion.

Title: Technical verification of a regular unimodular
triangulation of matroid base polytopes
# Identity and reviewed scope

The reviewed source is S. Backman and G. Liu, A Regular Unimodular Triangulation of the Matroid Base Polytope, arXiv:2309.10229v2, 4 April 2024, twelve pages [paper]. The frozen journal identity is Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), no. 14, 3047–3061, DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0015. The acquired author preprint has twelve pages; the fifteen-page journal version was not acquired. Equality of their mathematical contents is not assumed. All page numbers below refer to the acquired PDF, whose printed numbering agrees with its PDF numbering.

The review covers the definitions, Theorems 3.1 and 3.5, Corollaries 3.6 and 3.7, Remark 3.4 and Example 3.8. It distinguishes a unimodular triangulation from a flag one; the article does not claim to settle White’s conjecture. Unimodularity is measured in \(\operatorname{lin}(P)\cap\mathbb Z^n\), as in Definition 2.10. This relative lattice is essential for lower-dimensional polytopes and for the concern below.

The full PDF text, complete released TeX and bibliography were read. All twelve primary-source pages were actually inspected. The fourteen manifest inputs, totaling 1,239,502 bytes, matched their current recorded sizes and SHA-256 hashes. Three native bounded checks supplied lattice, genericity and extension arguments, with roles and actual page inspections separately recorded. The reviewed author TeX was read as evidence and was not executed.
# Verification of the principal construction
## Affine spans and saturated direction lattices

Lemma 2.6, p. 4, can be checked without a hidden full-dimensional assumption. Form a graph on \([n]\) whose edges are the pairs appearing in the edge directions of the polytope. If its connected components are \(C_1,\ldots,C_j\), its edge vectors span exactly \[V=\{z\in\mathbb R^n:z_{C_i}=0\text{ for every }i\}.\] For an integral vertex \(v\), the affine span is \(v+V\). Taking \(S_i=C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_i\) gives the asserted flag equations, with integral right-hand sides \(v_{S_i}\). Isolated graph vertices impose fixed-coordinate equations, so points, loops and coloops present no exception to this argument.

For each component, choose a spanning tree and a root. Every difference \(e_a-e_b\) in that component is an integral sum of oriented tree edges, and every integral vector with component sum zero is an integral sum of such differences. Thus any collection of type-\(A\) root directions generates the entire lattice in its real span. This gives Lemma 3.3, p. 6, including dependent pairs of direction spaces.

In Lemma 3.2 the intended independence condition is \(V\cap W=\{0\}\). For a rational subspace \(X\subset V\), the subgroup \(X\cap\mathbb Z^n\) is primitive in \(V\cap\mathbb Z^n\): if an integral multiple of an integral vector belongs to \(X\), the vector itself belongs to the real subspace \(X\). Its lattice basis can therefore be extended to one for \(V\cap\mathbb Z^n\). The same applies to \(Y\subset W\). Complementarity and independence make the two extended bases a basis of \((V+W)\cap\mathbb Z^n\). Uniqueness of its coordinates then proves that the two smaller bases generate \((X+Y)\cap\mathbb Z^n\). The source’s empty-set symbol in its independence definition is an evident typesetting error; the proof uses zero intersection.
## Genericity, refinement and the joining lattice

Let the two coordinate slices be \(P_0\) and \(P_1\). The initial height \(g\) is affine on each slice. A lower supporting affine function therefore cuts out a face \(F_i\) on each side, and its cell is their Cayley join. If \[L=\operatorname{lin}(F_0)\cap\operatorname{lin}(F_1)\] had positive dimension, Lemma 2.6 would make it a resonance flat. The linear part of the same supporting affine function restricts to both slice heights on \(L\). Consequently \((\ell_0-\ell_1)|_L\) would be constant, contrary to Definition 2.12. Hence \(L=\{0\}\). This verifies the decisive genericity step on p. 7.

The small-parameter choice can be made uniform. There are only finitely many candidate affine bases and support inequalities in the finite vertex configuration. For a height \(g+\epsilon h\), every relevant residual is \(\alpha+\epsilon\beta\). All nonzero \(\alpha\) retain their signs for one sufficiently small positive \(\epsilon\); zero residuals are resolved by \(h\). Equivalently, the perturbed height lies in a secondary cone whose closure contains \(g\). Its subdivision refines that of \(g\). The restrictions to the two coordinate faces are exactly the prescribed regular triangulations, because adding an affine function and multiplying by a positive scalar preserve them.

A maximal refined cell is thus \[T=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((T_0,0)\cup(T_1,1)\bigr),\] where each \(T_i\) is a unimodular simplex in \(F_i\). Independence of the two direction spaces makes this a simplex. Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 provide a basis \(B\) for the integral horizontal direction lattice using edges from \(T_0\) and \(T_1\). Take any joining vector \(w\) from level zero to level one. For \(z\in\operatorname{lin}(T)\cap\mathbb Z^n\), subtracting \(z_nw\) leaves an integral horizontal vector, hence an integral combination of \(B\). Thus \(B\cup\{w\}\) is a full lattice basis, proving unimodularity. If one side is empty, induction applies to the other side. A singleton, including the empty-ground-set matroid if it is allowed, has its unique zero-dimensional unimodular triangulation.

Theorem 3.5 follows by repeating these finite perturbations. For example, after an irrelevant common scaling, set \(\epsilon_k=t^k\). Each finite support residual is a polynomial in \(t\); its first nonzero coefficient fixes its sign for small positive \(t\). This supplies one compatible hierarchy for the finitely many branches.
## The unit-cube extension

Here is an explicit verification of the step in Corollary 3.6, p. 9. Write an integral generalized permutahedron as a base polytope for an integral submodular function \(f\), normalized at the empty set. In a nonempty unit-cube cell, put \(x=a+y\) with \(a\in\mathbb Z^n\) and \(0\le y_i\le1\), and set \(h(S)=f(S)-a_S\). Feasibility gives \(h(S)\ge0\). Define \[r(S)=\min_{T\subseteq[n]}\bigl(h(T)+|S\setminus T|\bigr).\] The function \(r\) is integral, normalized, monotone and submodular, and \(r(S)\le |S|\). For submodularity, take minimizing sets for two arguments and use submodularity of \(h\), together with the corresponding elementary inequality for the two set differences. For a feasible \(y\), the inequalities \(h(T)+|[n]\setminus T|\ge y_{[n]}=h([n])\) show that \(r([n])=h([n])\). These are the rank axioms of a matroid.

Moreover, the original cube cell is exactly \(B(r)\). The forward inclusion follows from \(y_S\le y_T+|S\setminus T|\le h(T)+|S\setminus T|\). Conversely, \(r(S)\le h(S)\) gives the original submodular inequalities, while monotonicity and \(r(\{i\})\le1\) give \(0\le y_i\le1\) for a vector of total sum \(r([n])\). This proves the required translated-matroid description.

One global height realizing the dicing is \[g(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2,\qquad z\in P\cap\mathbb Z^n.\] On \([a_i,a_i+1]\), the linear interpolation of \(z_i^2\) has slope \(2a_i+1\); the sum is convex and affine on each cube. The preceding integrality argument supplies its cell vertices. The common perturbation hierarchy in Corollary 3.6 therefore refines this regular subdivision and triangulates every cell compatibly. Only finitely many cells occur, so one set of small parameters works for all of them.

For Corollary 3.7, the map \[(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\longmapsto
 \bigl(r(E)-\textstyle\sum_i x_i,x_1,\ldots,x_n\bigr)\] has an integral inverse on its affine image. Its linear part identifies the relative lattices. The image of the independence polytope has only edge directions \(e_i-e_j\), including the directions \(e_i-e_0\) from adding an independent element, and has integral vertices. It is an integral generalized permutahedron. The map preserves regularity and unimodularity of the constructed triangulation.
# A confirmed auxiliary concern

Problem 1 (The lattice in Remark 3.4: Minor).  On p. 8, an alcoved polytope is placed in \(H=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\sum_i x_i=0\}\), while the surrounding definitions continue to use the ambient integer lattice. The remark claims integrality of intersections and unimodular triangulability of the two-polytope Cayley construction in that setting. These assertions fail with the stated lattice.

The facet directions in the remark are interpreted as the usual type-\(A\) facet normals; this is also the interpretation required by its subsequent assertion about \(\operatorname{lin}(P)^\perp\). Work in \(n=3\), and use the coordinates \[u=x_1-x_2,\qquad v=x_2-x_3.\] Their inverse on \(H\) is \[x=\left(\frac{2u+v}{3},\frac{v-u}{3},
             -\frac{u+2v}{3}\right).\] Thus the lattice \(\Lambda=H\cap\mathbb Z^3\) corresponds to \[\{(u,v)\in\mathbb Z^2:u+2v\equiv0\pmod3\},\] not to all of \(\mathbb Z^2\).

There is substantial counterevidence to a broader conclusion. The root-direction saturation in Lemma 3.3 is correct; it concerns edge directions of matroid polytopes. Theorem 3.1 and its extensions do not use Remark 3.4. The obstruction instead arises from carrying a statement about root normals into a different lattice realization.

A repair must specify the lattice as well as the real hyperplane. For example, the usual difference-coordinate realization uses the weight lattice \[\Lambda_{\mathrm w}
 =\{x\in H:x_i-x_j\in\mathbb Z\},\] which maps bijectively to \(\mathbb Z^2\) in the displayed coordinates. It contains \(\Lambda\) with index three. The fractional intersection vertex is a lattice point in \(\Lambda_{\mathrm w}\), and the displayed segments acquire additional lattice points there. Alternatively one may work in the usual coordinate realization with its stipulated integer lattice. These changes remove the counterexamples to the intended alcoved comparison, but they change the lattice used by the printed formulation. They cannot be suppressed as an unimodular coordinate change of \(\Lambda\). The ambient statement that \(\operatorname{lin}(P)^\perp\) is spanned by roots also needs its common diagonal direction or quotient convention specified: for a full-dimensional \(P\subset H\), \(\operatorname{lin}(P)^\perp=\mathbb R(1,1,1)\) in \(\mathbb R^3\).

The acquired primary reference confirms the convention behind this repair: Haase–Paffenholz–Piechnik–Santos, arXiv:1405.1687v3, p. 36, defines a type-\(\Gamma\) polytope using the lattice dual to the root lattice; Lemma 4.15 on pp. 72–73 then concerns that lattice and the canonical triangulations [HPPS]. Those pages were actually inspected. The acquired reference is an eighty-nine-page preprint, not an asserted copy of the 2021 published monograph. This comparison supports the lattice correction without treating the cited lemma as false.

The established impact is on the auxiliary comparison and its claimed alternative proof, not the article’s new triangulation theorem. That dependency distinction is the reason for the Minor assessment; the length of a possible repair is not the severity criterion.
# Exact example checks and clarifications

The sixteen basis triples in Example 3.8, p. 10, are exactly the spanning trees of \(K_4\) after correcting the repeated edge label \(v_0v_1=2\) to \(v_0v_2=2\). The four missing triples are \(\{0,1,2\}\), \(\{0,3,4\}\), \(\{1,3,5\}\) and \(\{2,4,5\}\), the four triangle circuits.

The forty-two listed six-vertex cells were checked with exact integer and rational arithmetic. Projecting away the last coordinate identifies the affine lattice \(\sum x_i=3\) with \(\mathbb Z^5\). For every listed cell, the determinant of its affine vertex matrix has absolute value one. Solving for its supporting height in each of the five \(\epsilon\) coefficients gives a strictly positive lexicographic residual at every other vertex. Thus each listed simplex is an actual lower facet for one sufficiently small common hierarchy. This computation uses the printed positive final coefficient in the functional; the all-negative interpretation also yields the same forty-two facets.

As an independent completeness check, the lattice-point counts for \(tP\), for \(t=0,\ldots,5\), are \[1,\ 16,\ 101,\ 396,\ 1167,\ 2848.\] They were enumerated using \(0\le x_i\le t\), \(\sum x_i=3t\), and the four triangle inequalities \(x_C\le2t\). The fifth finite difference is \(42\), hence the normalized volume is \(42\). The forty-two distinct unimodular lower simplices therefore exhaust the polytope’s volume; no further full-dimensional lower cell remains.

Genericity of the specified functionals was also checked in dimensions one through five. All independent collections of \(m-1\) nonzero zero–one normal vectors were tested using exact cofactor kernels. The numbers of independent collections were \(1,3,21,430,27990\); none had zero pairing with the printed coefficient vector. Every positive-dimensional flat contains a line flat, so this verifies the needed genericity in this example. It does not assert that one fixed exponential prescription works in every dimension.

This particular triangulation is not flag. For instance, the vertex indices \(\{0,6,8\}\) form a clique: each pair is an edge of a listed simplex, but no listed simplex contains the triple. This is a check of the exhibited triangulation only. It does not prove that all choices in Theorem 3.5 fail to be flag.

The introductory volume discussion on p. 1 needs consistent normalization. If \(d=\dim P\), the number of maximal unimodular simplices and \(h^*(1)\) equal \(\operatorname{Vol}_{\mathbb Z}(P)\), whereas \[[t^d]\,L_P(t)=\operatorname{Vol}_{\mathbb Z}(P)/d!.\] For \(P_{U_{1,3}}=\operatorname{conv}(e_1,e_2,e_3)\) there is one unimodular simplex and \(h^*=1\), but \(L_P(t)=\binom{t+2}{2}\) has leading coefficient \(1/2\). This is recorded as a normalization clarification. It changes none of the triangulation arguments. The misplaced \(f_1\) subscript on the \(P_0\) restriction on p. 7 likewise should be \(f_0\), as the defining height already says. These visible local corrections are not additional substantive findings.
# Assessment and state

The main proof and both extensions are supported within the reviewed version. Standard matroid base-polytope characterizations and finite regular-subdivision theory are identified dependencies; no complete formal verification of all cited literature is claimed. For the general face- and translation-closed families in Remark 3.4, the forward implications from lattice complementarity and the two-subspace duality have direct bounded proofs. The two arbitrary-family converse implications were not independently reconstructed in this review. This is a verification limit, not a claimed counterexample to those equivalences. The accessible search confirmed the pinned arXiv version. No separate correction, supplement or code release resolving the lattice issue was identified. The conference version and journal version are distinct bibliographic objects; no equality is inferred from their titles. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect.
