report: Abstract: The review follows the finite-jet and monodromy construction, the Serre–Tate calculation, the moving-divisor reduction, and the intersection argument over number and finite fields. Two local defects are established: reduction modulo four alone does not force full \(2\)-adic general linear monodromy, and inverse \(p\)-multiplication in multiplicative Serre–Tate coordinates requires inverse Frobenius on coefficients. The paper’s additional finite-quotient condition repairs the first inference; a uniform calculation on reduced formal branches shows why the second does not invalidate the required jet-preservation conclusion. Three further items require clarification or additional proof: the meaning of group constituents, reduced images versus correspondence cycles, and the Galois condition in Lemma 6.2. A precise reduced-image counterexample is given without claiming to refute the valid cycle interpretation. The highest established impact is Minor; unresolved items do not raise that assessment. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical verification of abelian varieties
not isogenous to Jacobians over global fields
# Identity, scope and quantifiers

The source is A. N. Shankar and J. Tsimerman, Abelian varieties not isogenous to Jacobians over global fields, arXiv:2105.02998v3, 5 March 2025, twenty-two pages [paper]. The frozen journal identity is Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), no. 18, 3535–3559, DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0016. The acquired twenty-two-page author version is labelled final by its arXiv metadata, but the twenty-five-page journal text was not acquired; their equivalence is not assumed. PDF and printed page numbers agree.

All six sections, the bibliography, and the actual source TeX were read. Material following `\end{document}` and commented alternative arguments were distinguished from the article. Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 concern \(F=\overline{\mathbb F_p(t)}\), the algebraic closure of the rational function field. Theorem 1.1 permits a divisor over \(F\), whereas Theorem 1.2 first treats a divisor defined over a finite field. Both assume \(g>1\). The Jacobian application uses the properness of the Torelli locus for \(g\geq4\); it is not a conclusion about every abelian variety of every dimension. Theorem 1.3 concerns a Hodge-generic point over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\). The finite-field assertion is \[\exists x\in\mathcal A_g(\overline{\mathbb F}_p)^{\rm ord}\quad
  \forall \tau\text{ prime to }p,\qquad \tau(x)\not\subset D .\] It does not say that the entire isogeny orbit is disjoint from \(D\).

The auxiliary odd prime \(r\ne p\) rigidifies the moduli problem. Maximal monodromy is understood relative to the group allowed by that fixed level. In characteristic zero its finite index in the full adelic similitude group must be absorbed into the constants; a full level structure does not give an arithmetic image literally equal to the unrestricted adelic group.
# Checks of the principal mechanism
## Finite jets and monodromy

The tame-ramification argument in Theorem 2.1 uses semistable reduction and unipotence of prime-to-\(p\) torsion. Lemma 3.2 is a finite-group argument: a subgroup meeting every conjugacy class is the whole finite group, and a rational point with trivial Frobenius image removes the arithmetic quotient. Its stated conclusion is modulo \(p^2\), not an automatic integral lifting result. Problem 1 isolates that distinction.

The simultaneous finite quotient \(H\times H'\) is important. After surjectivity to the separate infinite factors, Goursat’s lemma reduces entanglement to a common quotient. Factoring through \(H\) and \(H'\) then makes surjectivity onto their product force that quotient to be trivial. This extra hypothesis also supplies the missing characteristic-two argument below. The statement about density one of smooth hypersurface sections on page 9 is stronger than needed: at a fixed rational point of a smooth \(d\)-fold, the asymptotic probability that a random section vanishes with all first derivatives is \(q^{-(d+1)}>0\). The required existence should instead use Bertini with the finite local conditions imposed and positive density of smooth transverse sections. No failure of the required curve is inferred from that quantitative wording.
## Uniform preservation of the required formal jets

Proposition 4.1 has the correct matrix orientation \[Q'=(X^{T})^{-1}QY.\] Both the actual PDF on page 11 and the TeX have this formula. An apparent inverse-placement discrepancy in extracted text was rejected after inspection of the page. The lifting criterion in Katz, Theorem 2.1(4), is the compatibility \[q_A(e,\phi^\vee m')=q_B(\phi e,m'),\] which gives precisely \(QY=X^TQ'\) [katz]. Problem 2 concerns the definition of fractional multiplication, not this matrix orientation.

Equation reference: jet. Here is a complete version of the order calculation needed in Theorem 5.1. Choose the source parameter so that \(q'_{11}=1+t\) exactly. For \((i,j)\ne(1,1)\), the prescribed branch satisfies \(q'_{ij}=1+O(t^{m+1})\). For a Hecke type \(n\geq n_1\geq\cdots\geq n_g\geq0\), put \[c_{ij}=n-n_i-n_j,\qquad a=n-2n_1,\qquad
 d_{ij}=c_{ij}-a=2n_1-n_i-n_j\geq0.\] Over the perfect residue field let \(f^{[p^a]}\) mean coefficientwise Frobenius, allowing its inverse when \(a<0\). After the finite purely inseparable change needed to define the isogeny, and removal of a common inseparable parametrization, the reduced image has parameter \(u=t^{p^a}\) and coordinates \[
 R_{ij}(u)=\bigl(q_{ij}^{\prime\,[p^a]}(u)\bigr)^{p^{d_{ij}}}.\] This is obtained by substituting into \((q'_{ij}(t))^{p^{c_{ij}}}\). In particular, \[R_{11}=1+u,\qquad
 R_{ij}=1+O(u^{(m+1)p^{d_{ij}}})=1+O(u^{m+1})
 \quad ((i,j)\ne(1,1)).\] The first equality makes the reduced image formally smooth. The inequalities are uniform in the Hecke degree and valid for \(p=2\). Thus the requested primitive \(m\)-jet survives. The printed parameter need not itself be a uniformizer of the reduced image; the distinction is essential to this verification.

The hypersymmetric argument also has the required scope. An isogeny over \(\mathbb F_q\) to \(E^g\) makes Frobenius scalar on the rational Tate module and hence on its stable integral lattice. It preserves every finite \(p\)-subgroup and every rank-one cocharacter submodule. The resulting formal subtorus may be nonsplit over \(\mathbb F_q\); scalar descent, not split coordinates over \(\mathbb F_q\), is what is used.
## Density and the uniform jet bound

The proof of Proposition 5.3 is read in centered coordinates \(z_{ij}=q_{ij}-1\), with \(i\leq j\). A vector with all coordinates divisible by \(p\) does not itself generate a saturated line, but its parametrized image lies in the formal torus associated with the saturation. This removes the apparent primitivity obstruction in the chosen test family.

For completeness, a nonzero formal series has finitely many componentwise minimal exponent vectors, by Dickson’s lemma. For each such vector the substitution in the proof has weight \[W_N(\alpha)=\sum_{i\leq j}\alpha_{ij}p^{N^i+N^j}.\] For two distinct minimal vectors, the largest pair in the order determined by \(N^i+N^j\) eventually dominates their weight difference. There are finitely many pairs of minimal vectors, so for all sufficiently large \(N\) exactly one of them has least weight. Every other exponent dominates a minimal exponent and has strictly larger weight unless it is that exponent itself. Thus the substituted series cannot vanish. This argument includes characteristic two and does not replace the formal power series by a polynomial.

The passage from pointwise density to Proposition 5.4 additionally uses algebraicity of the finite-jet containment locus. Conditional on the cited formal-torus structure of the diagonal completion, the finite Igusa-level calculation must be truncated to the stated order. The finitely many rank-one jet directions then give a closed containment locus. These loci descend in a Noetherian space; their empty intersection, supplied by Proposition 5.3, implies that one finite order suffices. The original Chai reference was inaccessible from the attempted official hosts. Its indexed transcription is compatible with the cited structure, but it is not recorded as an inspected primary PDF. This dependency is an explicit verification limit.

Together with geometric irreducibility of Hecke translates, these checks support the constant-divisor mechanism. For the moving-divisor step, Lemma 5.6 is a uniform finite intersection assertion. Its uncountable-field argument can be made precise by choosing successively compatible prefixes from nested constructible subsets of the curve; Noetherian stabilization then gives the contradiction. The degree of the alternating cover must also be chosen at least as large as the bound in that lemma. No unrestricted inference that every finite extension preserves monodromy is used; see Problem 3.
# Numbered concerns

Problem 1 (Reduction modulo four does not alone force full \(2\)-adic monodromy).  Assessment: confirmed Minor. The standalone implication in the proof of Theorem 3.1, PDF page 9, TeX line 468, is false at \(p=2\) for every \(g>1\).

Let \(G=\operatorname{GL}_g(\mathbb Z_2)\) and set \[J_0=\{M\in G:\det M\bmod8\in\{1,7\}\}.\] This is a proper closed subgroup: \(\operatorname{diag}(3,1,\ldots,1)\) is excluded. Nevertheless \(J_0\) surjects onto \(\operatorname{GL}_g(\mathbb Z/4)\). Given any lift of an invertible matrix modulo four, multiplication by \(\operatorname{diag}(5,1,\ldots,1)\) preserves its reduction modulo four and switches its determinant to the required residue when necessary. The independent exact enumeration for \(g=2\) gives \[|\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z/8)|=1536,\quad |J_0\bmod8|=768,\quad
 |\operatorname{im}(J_0\bmod4)|=|\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z/4)|=96.\] The calculation is saved in `root_exact_checks_001.json`.

Counterevidence and complete repair from existing data. The constructed curve is also required to surject onto \(G/X\), where every element of \(X=X_{2,a}\) is a \(2^a\)-th power and \(a\geq1\). This is stronger than the hypothesis just refuted. Let \(J\) be the actual closed image, surjective modulo four. In \(G_8=\operatorname{GL}_g(\mathbb Z/8)\) the kernel of reduction to \(G_4\) is \(N=1+4M_g(\mathbb F_2)\). Squares of lifts of \(1+2E_{ij}\), for \(i\ne j\), give \(1+4E_{ij}\). Commutators of lifts of \(1+2E_{ij}\) and \(1+2E_{ji}\) give \(1+4(E_{ii}+E_{jj})\). Consequently \(J_8\cap N\) contains every trace-zero matrix. If \(J_8\) were proper, it would have index two in \(G_8\) and would contain all squares. It would therefore contain the image of \(X\). But \(J\to G/X\) is surjective, so \(JX=G\), contradicting properness modulo eight. Thus \(J\) surjects modulo eight. Repeated squaring of congruence lifts then gives surjectivity at every higher power of two, hence \(J=G\). For odd \(p\), the usual congruence-power argument starts from modulo \(p^2\).

The defect is local because the hypotheses already imposed in the paper prove the needed conclusion. The subgroup \(J_0\) is not presented as a geometric counterexample satisfying all those hypotheses, and Theorem 3.1 is not refuted.

Problem 2 (Inverse Frobenius is missing from fractional multiplication).  Assessment: confirmed Minor. Section 4.1, PDF page 10, TeX line 496, defines \(p^{-n}Q\) by replacing \(t\) with \(t^{1/p^n}\) while leaving coefficients unchanged. This does not extend the natural \(\mathbb Z_p\)-module structure on \(1+t k[[t]]\) to inverse \(p\)-multiplication.

Take \(p=2\), \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_2\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb F_4\) with \(\alpha^2+\alpha+1=0\). For the admissible multiplicative coordinate \(q=1+\alpha t\), the printed prescription gives \[q_{\rm printed}^{1/2}=1+\alpha t^{1/2},\qquad
  (q_{\rm printed}^{1/2})^2=1+(\alpha+1)t\ne q.\] The correct square root is \(1+(\alpha+1)t^{1/2}\). For \(g=2\), put this coordinate in \(q_{11}\) and set all other symmetric coordinates equal to one. This is a polarized ordinary deformation. With isogeny matrices \(X=2I_2\), \(Y=I_2\), the lifting criterion requires \((q'_{11})^2=q_{11}\). The printed scalar operation fails precisely that requirement; it is not a complaint about optional notation.

The explicit finite-field calculation and the Katz lifting criterion establish the discrepancy. Its demonstrated impact is a local coordinate operation. Formula [jet] (#jet) checks the entire order argument actually needed for Theorem 5.1 and shows that coefficient Frobenius preserves all its vanishing-order conditions. The core jet-preservation conclusion therefore survives for every type; the Minor assessment rests on that bounded impact, not merely on the shortness of the correction.

Problem 3 (The constituent condition in Lemma 5.5 needs a precise meaning).  Assessment: Needs Evidence / scope clarification. Lemma 5.5, PDF page 17, TeX lines 702–710, does not require \(\phi:\operatorname{Gal}_K\to H\) to be surjective and uses an undefined group-theoretic constituent condition.

Under the composition-factor reading, the assertion is false. Take \(K=\mathbb F_q\), \(L=\mathbb F_{q^2}\), \(G=C_2\), and \(H=A_5\). Map a Frobenius generator of \(\operatorname{Gal}_K=\widehat{\mathbb Z}\) to \((12)(34)\in A_5\). The groups \(C_2\) and \(A_5\) have no common simple composition factor, but \[\phi(\operatorname{Gal}_K)=C_2,\qquad \phi(\operatorname{Gal}_L)=1.\] Every field and continuity hypothesis holds. The proof incorrectly treats a quotient of a subgroup of \(H\) as if it had to be a quotient of \(H\).

There are two substantive counterreadings. If the constituent condition excludes the relevant simple sections of all subgroups of \(H\), the example is inadmissible. Alternatively, requiring \(\phi\) to be surjective makes the proof valid under the composition-factor condition: after passing to the normal closure, the image quotient is a common quotient of \(H\) and \(G\). The actual application starts with the surjective monodromy constructed for \(C_0\), so that repair supplies the necessary application. Because the terminology admits a stronger reading, this is not counted as an unqualified confirmed false lemma. The report requests an explicit definition or the surjectivity hypothesis, without claiming failure of Theorem 1.1.

Problem 4 (The degree argument must specify correspondence multiplicities).  Assessment: Needs Evidence. Lemma 6.1 and equations (6.1.1)–(6.1.2), PDF pages 19–21, use \(\deg\tau(C)=\deg(\tau)\deg(C)\) and count coincident Hecke targets by asserting that their image has distinct branches. These statements require a precise convention for \(\tau(C)\).

Let \(T\) be the Lagrangian \(7\)-isogeny correspondence. Its degree is \[d=(7+1)(7^2+1)=400.\] Since \(7\equiv1\pmod3\), the dual correspondence has compatible level structure and \(T\) is self-dual. The \(400\) targets of a generic point of \(B\) are distinct: two equivalent polarized quotient isogenies would, after composition with a dual, produce an endomorphism of a variety with endomorphism ring \(\mathbb Z\), forcing their kernels to agree. Counting all embeddings of \(K_1\) into \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\) replaces the use of \(\operatorname{Gal}(K_1/\mathbb Q)\) in Problem 4. # Overall impact and state

Problems 1 and 2 establish local failures of stated algebraic operations or implications, with explicit counterexamples and full checks of their relevance. Existing finite-quotient data repairs the first; the uniform reduced-branch calculation establishes the jet consequence needed despite the second. The principal function-field existence theorem has not been refuted.

Problems 3–5 retain their uncertainty. In particular, the reduced-image example must not be relabelled as a counterexample to a correspondence-cycle identity. The number-field proof can be organized around a weaker specialization lemma and counting on the Hecke cover, but the stated stronger lemma requires its own justification. No separate correction or associated executable code resolving these items was identified in the bounded search. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect.

problems.source_location: PDF9, proof of Theorem3.1; main__1_.tex468
claim: Surjectivity modulo p² alone implies full GL_g(Z_p) image.
p=2 and g>1 allowed; closed subgroup; the counterexample tests the isolated implication, not all geometric construction hypotheses.
analysis: Assessment: confirmed Minor. The standalone implication in the proof of Theorem 3.1, PDF page 9, TeX line 468, is false at \(p=2\) for every \(g>1\).

Let \(G=\operatorname{GL}_g(\mathbb Z_2)\) and set \[J_0=\{M\in G:\det M\bmod8\in\{1,7\}\}.\] This is a proper closed subgroup: \(\operatorname{diag}(3,1,\ldots,1)\) is excluded. Nevertheless \(J_0\) surjects onto \(\operatorname{GL}_g(\mathbb Z/4)\). Given any lift of an invertible matrix modulo four, multiplication by \(\operatorname{diag}(5,1,\ldots,1)\) preserves its reduction modulo four and switches its determinant to the required residue when necessary. The independent exact enumeration for \(g=2\) gives \[|\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z/8)|=1536,\quad |J_0\bmod8|=768,\quad
 |\operatorname{im}(J_0\bmod4)|=|\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z/4)|=96.\] The calculation is saved in `root_exact_checks_001.json`.

Counterevidence and complete repair from existing data. The constructed curve is also required to surject onto \(G/X\), where every element of \(X=X_{2,a}\) is a \(2^a\)-th power and \(a\geq1\). This is stronger than the hypothesis just refuted. Let \(J\) be the actual closed image, surjective modulo four. In \(G_8=\operatorname{GL}_g(\mathbb Z/8)\) the kernel of reduction to \(G_4\) is \(N=1+4M_g(\mathbb F_2)\). Squares of lifts of \(1+2E_{ij}\), for \(i\ne j\), give \(1+4E_{ij}\). Commutators of lifts of \(1+2E_{ij}\) and \(1+2E_{ji}\) give \(1+4(E_{ii}+E_{jj})\). Consequently \(J_8\cap N\) contains every trace-zero matrix. If \(J_8\) were proper, it would have index two in \(G_8\) and would contain all squares. It would therefore contain the image of \(X\). But \(J\to G/X\) is surjective, so \(JX=G\), contradicting properness modulo eight. Thus \(J\) surjects modulo eight. Repeated squaring of congruence lifts then gives surjectivity at every higher power of two, hence \(J=G\). For odd \(p\), the usual congruence-power argument starts from modulo \(p^2\).

The defect is local because the hypotheses already imposed in the paper prove the needed conclusion. The subgroup \(J_0\) is not presented as a geometric counterexample satisfying all those hypotheses, and Theorem 3.1 is not refuted.
result: Impact: False isolated inference, but existing hypotheses prove main curve monodromy; no geometric counterexample satisfying those hypotheses.

report: Abstract: The acquired author version contains a false effective square-representation assertion: \(441\) satisfies every relevant hypothesis of Theorem 2.6 for the numerator orbit starting at \((2,25)\), but its only possible matrix rows are nonprimitive. A family shows that replacing \(8xy\) by any universal constant times \(xy\) cannot repair this square bound. Neither the principal reciprocity phenomenon nor the continued-fraction counterexample is refuted by the findings. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical verification of reciprocity obstructions
in semigroup orbits in \(\operatorname{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\)
# Identity, scope and mathematical dependencies

The source reviewed is J. Rickards and K. E. Stange, Reciprocity obstructions in semigroup orbits in \(\operatorname{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\), arXiv:2401.01860v3, twenty-eight pages [paper]. Its arXiv watermark and submission metadata give 23 January 2025; the first page separately prints 27 January 2025. Both fields are retained. The frozen journal identity is Duke Mathematical Journal 174 (2025), no. 15, 3197–3244, DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0017. The forty-eight-page journal version was not obtained. All conclusions below are about the actual twenty-eight-page version; no equivalence with the journal text is assumed. Printed and PDF page numbers agree.

Write \[L=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \Psi=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in\Gamma_1(4)^{\geq0}:
                  \left(\frac{a}{b}\right)=1\right\}.\] Here the compact matrix notation in the source means \(a\equiv d\equiv1\pmod4\), \(c\equiv0\pmod4\), and determinant one; all four entries are nonnegative. The review consistently uses the usual Kronecker symbol, including its value zero for noncoprime arguments. The starting vector is primitive and nonnegative; the technical sufficient conditions of Section 4 assume both coordinates positive.

The paper has several logically distinct objectives. Proposition 2.2 characterizes \(\Psi\), and Theorem 2.5 excludes squares in specified orbits. Theorem 2.6 adds completeness and explicit bounds. Theorem 2.8 determines one orbit exactly. Theorem 2.10 constructs finitely generated semigroups with dimensions approaching one from below. Theorems 2.18 and 2.20 concern finite continued-fraction alphabets. The conjectures about \(\Psi_1\) and the large search in Table 2 are not presented here as proved theorems. Failure of one effective bound does not by itself refute these other assertions.
# Positive verification and controls
## Reciprocity, primitive rows and congruence

The analytical check of Section 3 follows the actual sign factors. For positive coordinates, Proposition 3.2’s seven reciprocity signs combine to \((-1)^{AB+AC+BC+AD}\); the exceptional valuations \(v_2(d)=1\), \(v_2(x)=1\) and \(v_2(cx+dy)=1\) give precisely the two printed \(\mu\) factors. Noncoprime input pairs yield zero on both sides, because an integral determinant-one matrix preserves the gcd. The denominator shift in Lemma 3.3 preserves the needed odd parts modulo four, and the finite CRT choice in Lemma 3.4 removes the positive-coordinate coprimality restriction.

The odd part of zero is not defined in the general formula. This is retained as a domain clarification, with direct endpoint proofs, rather than a counterexample to Proposition 2.2. If \(x=0\) in the coprime odd-denominator case, then \(y=1\) and the claim is the row/column identity of Lemma 3.1. If \(y=0\), then \(x=1\), and the corresponding identity follows directly. Zero entries in the matrix reduce to the triangular cases. The hypotheses of Theorem 2.5 themselves exclude zero coordinates. Its third case, \((x,y)\equiv(3,0)\pmod4\), excludes a square numerator by congruence; a hypothetical square denominator forces \[\left(\frac{ax+by}{cx+dy}\right)
   =\left(\frac{-1}{y}\right)\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)=-1,\] which is impossible for a square denominator and a primitive vector. Thus the exclusion theorem survives Problem 1.

Reviewer-authored diagnostics support, without replacing, these derivations: \(218\,304\) positive-coordinate evaluations of Proposition 3.2, including \(71\,120\) noncoprime pairs; \(20\,739\) cases of Lemma 3.4; \(19\,500\) character cases; and \(59\,798\) denominator shifts passed. Two independent symbol implementations agreed on \(17\,545\) signed inputs.

Lemma 4.1 is an exact useful criterion: a positive numerator \(n\) requires and is implied by a nonnegative row \((u,v)\) with \[u\equiv1\pmod4,\qquad ux+vy=n,\qquad \left(\frac{u}{v}\right)=1.
 \tag{2.1}\] The symbol condition enforces primitivity. A Bezout completion, followed by the prescribed congruence shift, produces a nonnegative matrix in \(\Psi\). The denominator version additionally imposes \(u\equiv0\) and \(v\equiv1\pmod4\).

The strong approximation proof in Section 8 was checked separately. The orders of \(L^4\) and \(R^4\) at coprime moduli allow CRT isolation of words. At odd moduli they generate the full special linear group. At \(2\)-power moduli, the elimination in Lemma 8.4 gives the complete preimage of \[\Psi_2/16=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1&4b\\4c&1\end{pmatrix}\pmod{16}:0\leq b,c\leq3\right\};\] the corresponding preimage for \(\Psi_1\) is determined modulo four. The quotient notation in Theorem 8.1 is understood as the assertion about reduction kernels, as its proof makes clear. These facts justify the congruence classifications independently of the faulty square-saturation bound.
## A finite-alphabet dimension certificate

The identities \(C_8C_4(C_4C_4)^{-1}=R^4\) and \((C_4C_4)^{-1}C_4C_8=L^4\), where \(C_a=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&a\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), give the stated congruence images and imply Zariski density of the even-word semigroup: its algebraic group closure contains both unipotent root groups. The transposition argument uses the functional \(3x+5y\) and the starting vector \((3,5)\). Thus the finite-alphabet counterexample retains a verified dimension threshold and the necessary square exclusion; it does not depend on repairing the near-one approximation in Problem 2.
# Confirmed findings

Problem 1 (Major: false square saturation and loss of primitivity).  Location. Theorem 2.6, PDF p. 5 and its proof on p. 19; Lemmas 4.3–4.6, pp. 13–17, especially (4.0.5) and the replacement of the square-denominator symbol by a constant. Source TeX lines 245–259, 686–946 and 1060–1087.

Take \((x,y)=(2,25)\) and \(n=441=21^2\). The starting coordinates are positive and coprime, \(y\) is odd, \(\left(\frac{2}{25}\right)=1\), and \(441\geq8xy=400\). Table 1 places no congruence or reciprocity obstruction on the numerator. Yet a putative matrix’s top row must satisfy \[2a+25b=441,\qquad a\equiv1\pmod4,\qquad a,b\geq0.\] All solutions are \[(a,b)=(33+100t,15-8t),\qquad t=0,1.\] Their gcds are respectively three and seven. Neither row can occur in any integral determinant-one matrix. Consequently \(441\) is absent even from the larger \(\Gamma_1(4)^{\geq0}\) orbit. This is a counterexample to the stated effective conclusion, with every hypothesis checked.

The common algebraic error is to replace \(\left(\frac{q}{m^2}\right)\) by one, or \(\left(\frac{q}{2m^2}\right)\) by \(\left(\frac{q}{2}\right)\), without retaining the condition \(\gcd(q,m)=1\). In the proof’s determinant-one change of coordinates, \[\gcd(cu+dv,n)=\gcd(u,v).\] Choosing \(d\) coprime to \(u\) does not make \((u,v)\) primitive. The exact factors are instead \[\left(\frac{q}{m^2}\right)=\mathbf1_{\gcd(q,m)=1},\qquad
 \left(\frac{q}{2m^2}\right)=\left(\frac{q}{2}\right)\,\mathbf1_{\gcd(q,m)=1}
 \quad(q\ \text{odd}).
 \tag{3.1}\] A denominator example is \((x,y,n)=(3,13,225)\): \(225\geq4xy\), \(\left(\frac{3}{13}\right)=1\), and the only permitted lower row is \((u,v)=(36,9)\). This refutes Lemma 4.4, though it is below the main theorem’s \(8xy\) threshold.

The twice-square numerator branch also fails: \((x,y,n)=(1,7,98)\) satisfies \(98\geq56\) and every congruence hypothesis of Lemma 4.5. All permitted rows are \[(21,11),\ (49,7),\ (77,3),
 \qquad\text{with symbols }-1,\ 0,\ -1.\] Equation (2.1) excludes \(98\) from this orbit. This small example does not refute the much larger nonsquare cutoff of Theorem 2.6; it refutes the intermediate lemma used to justify its twice-square branch.

A stronger repair boundary. No universal constant \(C\) can replace \(8\) in a square bound \(n\geq Cxy\). Choose an integer \(K\) with \(4K>C\) and put \[m=2t\prod_{j=0}^{K-1}(4j+3),\qquad n=m^2,\qquad x=1.\] For sufficiently large \(t\), the interval \((n/(4K+1),n/(4K))\) has length exceeding four. Choose \(y\equiv1\pmod4\) in that interval. Then \(n>Cxy\) and \(\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)=1\). Every nonnegative top row has \(a=n-yb\equiv1\pmod4\), hence \[b\in\{3,7,\ldots,4K-1\}.\] Each such \(b\) divides \(m\), so \(\gcd(a,b)=b>1\). This family varies the starting vector; it does not prove infinitely many exceptions for one fixed orbit.

Impact and counterevidence. The explicit central square bound is false, and its proof requires a primitive-point counting argument. It is therefore Major even though exact row criteria remain available. The square-exclusion theorem, the congruence classification and the finite-alphabet counterexample are unaffected. Qualitative eventual saturation for each fixed starting vector is not disproved by this family. The non-square, non-twice-square character-sign branch retains the zero values and does not suffer this particular cancellation.

Repair. Keep the indicators in (3.1), prove existence of a primitive row within the relevant sign class, and replace the effective square threshold by a justified bound with different dependence on the starting vector or additional arithmetic information. A pointwise demand for a primitive row is not a proof of the published uniform bound. The exact orbit in Theorem 2.8 has a separate verification described below; that verification does not repair the uniform statement. Author adoption is unknown.

Problem 2 (Major: parabolic maps invalidate the supplied dimension proof).  Location. Section 7.2, Lemma 7.4 and Proposition 7.6, PDF pp. 21–22; Theorem 2.10’s dependency on p. 23. Source TeX lines 1166–1281 and 1317–1320.

The actual admissible set \(\mathcal W=\{L,R^4\}\subset\Psi\) has disjoint closed images \([1/2,1]\) and \([0,1/5]\). Thus it satisfies the stated hypotheses of Lemma 7.4. Nevertheless \[T_{L^n}(t)=\frac{n+(1-n)t}{n+1-nt},\qquad
 T_{L^n}'(t)=\frac1{(n+1-nt)^2}.\] The endpoint derivative of \(T_L\) is one, so it is not a Lipschitz contraction with constant strictly below one on \([0,1]\). The distortion ratio of \(T_{L^n}\) is \((n+1)^2\). A finite bound for individual generators, which is what the displayed inequality in Section 7.2 literally quantifies, does not provide a uniform bound for their products.

The acquired author-hosted May 1995 preprint of Mauldin–Urbański [mu], checked on actual PDF pp. 1, 3, 5–7 and 22, requires a common contraction constant \(0<s<1\) in equation (2.1). Its open set condition includes invariance of the open set. The introduction explicitly distinguishes parabolic maps from this formalism and points to an induced-map approach. Equation (2.9) explicitly requires distortion control for every finite word, and Theorem 3.15 uses these same assumptions. The parabolic elements also persist in the paper’s construction: once a finite family contains \(L\) and \(R^4\), prefix reduction cannot discard either. The first has no proper nonidentity prefix; the proper prefixes \(R,R^2,R^3\) of the second are outside \(\Gamma_1(4)\). Consequently the direct invocation in Proposition 7.6 has not established the finite-approximation equality for the system used here.

Impact and repair boundary. The proof of Theorem 2.10 loses an essential dimension argument, so the finding is Major. No counterexample to its existence conclusion is asserted. An induced, uniformly contracting system, or a verified parabolic dimension theorem with its precise hypotheses, is required; its finite approximants must be related back to finitely generated subsemigroups of \(\Psi\). Simply deleting the parabolic maps can change both the limit set and the known congruence images, and is not a verified repair. The dimension-one argument for \(\Psi\) via finite partitions and the explicit indecomposable matrices in Lemma 7.7 are separate positive controls. The finite alphabet in Section 2 above is uniformly contracting and remains a valid example with dimension exceeding one half.

Problem 3 (Minor: an unjustified enlargement in the continued-fraction proof).  Location. Proof of Corollary 2.21, PDF p. 26, source TeX lines 1503–1507. The proof asserts that the full orbits \(\Psi\binom{3}{2+3k}\) never contain squares in either coordinate and that their numerators are always three modulo four.

For \(k=3\), the starting vector is \((3,11)\) and \(L^3=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) belongs to \(\Psi\): its determinant is one, its lower-left entry is zero, and \(\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)=1\). Nevertheless \[L^3\binom{3}{11}=\binom{36}{11}.
 \tag{3.3}\] The numerator is a square and is zero modulo four. All entries and the starting coordinates satisfy the actual nonnegativity and primitivity requirements. Thus the assertion about the enlarged semigroup is false.

The preceding continued-fraction argument only requires the smaller semigroup \(\Psi_2=\langle L^4,R^4\rangle\). Its matrices have both off-diagonal entries divisible by four and both diagonal entries one modulo four. On \(\Psi_2\binom{3}{2+3k}\) the numerator is indeed three modulo four. For \(k\equiv0,3\pmod4\) the denominator is respectively two or three modulo four. For \(k\equiv1\pmod4\), the odd denominator \(2+3k\) is five modulo twelve and \(\left(\frac{3}{2+3k}\right)=-1\). For \(k\equiv2\pmod4\), it is divisible by four and \(\left(\frac{3}{2+3k}\right)=-\left(\frac{-1}{2+3k}\right)\). The two remaining denominator cases are therefore covered by the proved reciprocity obstruction in Theorem 2.5. Keeping \(\Psi_2\) throughout supplies the required argument.

This verifies a local repair of the corollary’s proof. It does not validate the false assertion about \(\Psi\). The corollary’s continued-fraction conclusion and its congruence discussion survive; no central damage is demonstrated. The separate \((2,3)\) in the preceding transposition display should read \((3,5)\), consistently with the statement and the functional \(3x+5y\). That copy error is not counted independently.

The function `psi_rep` in both acquired copies of `semigroup.c`, lines 1055–1150, especially the consecutive tests on `vshiftm4` near lines 1123–1144. The repository documents this function as deciding numerator or denominator membership in \(\Psi\binom{x}{y}\) [code].

After imposing \(u\equiv0\pmod4\), the denominator branch tests whether the change in \(v\) is zero modulo four. It then starts a second independent conditional for the value two. The final `else` belongs to this second test:
Consequently the zero case also enters the final branch and quadruples a step that already preserves the required residue.

The exact control-flow trace for input \(\texttt{psi\_rep}(1,5,25,2)\) is decisive. The initial solution is \((u,v)=(0,5)\) and the intended step is \((20,-4)\). Problem 5 (Minor: the finite endpoints in the orbit equality).  Location. Corollary 2.17, PDF p. 7, source TeX lines 374–376, with its deduction on pp. 25–26. It identifies denominators of rationals in \((0,1)\) built from \(4\mathbb Z^+\) with the union of both coordinate sets of \(\Psi_2\binom{0}{1}\).

Such a rational has denominator at least four. The asserted union nevertheless contains zero and one. This does not rely on counting an empty word: \[R^4\binom{0}{1}=\binom{0}{1},\qquad L^4\binom{0}{1}=\binom{4}{1}.
 \tag{3.5}\] In particular the nonidentity matrix \(L^4\) supplies the forbidden denominator one. The exact equality therefore fails at its finite boundary.

The continued-fraction description in Proposition 9.1 gives the corrected equality after removing \(\{0,1\}\) from the union. For a nontrivial fraction below one, its coordinate ratio is a continued fraction with positive partial quotients in \(4\mathbb Z^+\); if the ratio exceeds one, take the reciprocal. Conversely the word description supplies every such denominator. Coordinates other than zero and one are at least four, so no other endpoint is introduced. This is a verified local correction. It does not change a Hausdorff dimension, a large-integer conclusion, or the reciprocity counterexample.

# Unscored clarifications and verification limits

Theorem 2.6 calls \(r\) the unique positive root of \[H(r)=\frac{\sqrt r}{\log r\log\log r}=7.542795xy.
 \tag{4.1}\] For positive integer \(xy\) there are two roots. Positive values of \(H\) require \(r>e\). With \(z=\log r\), \[\frac{d\log H}{dz}=\frac12-\frac1z-\frac1{z\log z}.\] This derivative increases strictly from a negative value to a positive limit. The function \(H\) tends to infinity at both ends of \((e,\infty)\) and has one minimum. Since \(H(e^2)=e/(2\log2)<3<7.542795xy\), it crosses the required level twice. The proof on p. 19 uses the increasing branch. Define \(r=r_+\) to be the larger root, equivalently the unique root beyond \(e^4\), and separate \(xy=0\) before using (4.1). For \(xy=6\), the computed upper root is about \(3\,404\,737.102082\), below \(3\,410\,000\). The reversed inequality on p. 20 is consistent with a local sign error; the conservative cutoff actually used is correct.

These facts specify the intended range, but no second core counterexample is inferred from the root wording. Because the proof itself supplies the large-root interpretation, this is recorded as an unscored scope clarification. Likewise, the odd part of zero and the positive-integer interpretation of Corollary 4.2 are retained as clarifications with direct endpoint checks.

The static continued-fraction routines also seed the value three as represented, whereas the displayed family with a positive tail parameter has smallest denominator five. This is a bounded source-level mismatch, not a certification that the original Table 2 aggregates were produced by these exact files or are incorrect. No rerun to \(2\times10^{13}\), CPU-hour replication, or verification of the terminal missing denominators was performed. The conjecture based on that experiment remains a conjecture.
# Independent verification of the explicit orbit
## The entire stated finite interval

Theorem 2.8 concerns the numerator orbit of \((2,3)\). A reviewer-authored exact sieve, using no author functions, checked every integer \[1\leq n\leq N=109\,120\,000.\] It uses the criterion \(2u+3v=n\), \(u\equiv1\pmod4\), \(\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)=1\).

For \(n\equiv2\pmod3\), the row \((1,(n-2)/3)\) always works. For \(n\equiv0\pmod3\), the sieve considers \(u=9,21,33,\ldots\); for \(n\equiv1\pmod3\), it considers \(u=5,17,29,\ldots\). A candidate is removed only when \(n\geq2u\) and the exact Jacobi symbol \(\left(\frac{v}{u}\right)\) is one. Since \(u\equiv1\pmod4\), reciprocity makes this exactly the required Kronecker condition. For a fixed \(u\), the lookup index \[\left(\frac{n\bmod(3u)+u}{3}\right)\bmod u
       =\left(\frac{n-2u}{3}\right)\bmod u\] is integral in the appropriate residue class. All intermediates fit in the specified unsigned integer type; no floating point is used for representation decisions.

The residue-zero class required forty-two rows through \(u=501\); the residue-one class required thirty rows through \(u=353\). The only survivors were the \(10\,446\) squares at most \(N\) and \[3,\ 6,\ 7,\ 10,\ 12,\ 15,\ 18,\ 19,\ 27,\ 31,\ 34,\ 55,\ 63,\ 99,\ 115.
 \tag{5.1}\] Every nonsquare survivor was then checked against all nonnegative congruence-compatible rows, with no positive symbol. The square exclusion also follows analytically from Theorem 2.5, because \(\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)=-1\). The saved execution result therefore reproduces the finite exception list by a different algorithm. It establishes a finite statement, not by itself the infinite theorem.
## A primitive-row repair for the large twice-squares

For \(n=2m^2\) in this particular orbit, write the eligible rows as \[u=u_0+12k,\qquad v=v_0-8k,\qquad
 0\leq k\leq n/24-u_0/12,\quad 0<u_0<12.\] Choose the auxiliary determinant-one change of coordinates used in Section 4 of the source, and let \(Q=cu+dv\). The correct character expression is \[\left(\frac{u}{v}\right)=s\left(\frac{Q}{2}\right)\,\mathbf1_{\gcd(Q,m)=1},
 \qquad s\in\{1,-1\},
 \tag{5.2}\] with \(s\) fixed. Here \(Q\) is odd, and the source’s \(\mu_2\) factor is one. Increasing \(k\) changes \(Q\) by \(-4\), so \(\left(\frac{Q}{2}\right)\) changes sign. Restrict to the parity \(k=\epsilon+2j\) that makes the sign in (5.2) positive. The allowed \(j\) form an interval of at least \[\ell=\left\lfloor m^2/24\right\rfloor\] consecutive integers: the amount subtracted from its upper endpoint is \((u_0/12+\epsilon)/2<1\).

As \(j\) increases, \(Q\) changes by \(-8\). Each odd prime divisor of \(m\) therefore forbids exactly one residue class of \(j\). If \(\omega\) is the number of these primes, CRT and inclusion–exclusion give at least \[\ell\prod_{p\mid m,\ p\ {\rm odd}}(1-1/p)-2^\omega
 \ \geq\ \ell/2^\omega-2^\omega\] primitive choices. Since the primes are distinct, \(4^\omega\leq(4/3)\operatorname{rad}(m_{\rm odd})\leq4m/3\). For \(m\geq34\), \[\left\lfloor m^2/24\right\rfloor
       >m^2/24-1>4m/3.\] The final inequality follows from \(m^2-32m-24>0\), already true at \(34\) and increasing thereafter. Thus every \(2m^2\geq2312\) in this orbit is represented. This repairs the large twice-square step needed here; it does not restore the general \(8xy\) assertion.
## The remaining analytic dependency

For nonsquares that are not twice-squares, the character-gap argument retains the full odd-part symbol, so a prescribed value \(\pm1\) also certifies primitivity. Rosser–Schoenfeld’s actual Theorem 15, printed pp. 71–72 [rs], verifies the uniform \(2.50637\) totient bound, including its exceptional integer. Robin’s Theorem 13 on printed p. 384 [robin] verifies the bound for \(\omega(n)\) with constant \(1.1714\) and range \(n\geq26\).

The Frolenkov–Soundararajan estimate quoted in Lemma 5.2 [fs] remains an imported dependency. Publisher and MathNet metadata were accessible, but the requested primary PDF returned HTML; no full-text page of that article was inspected. The consequent infinite propagation is explicitly conditional on the quoted bound, rather than presented as an independently proved character-sum theorem.

Eighty-decimal-digit calculations checked all six rounding margins used in Section 5. The final product is \(0.9428358919577<0.942836\), and the saved floor slack at \(N_0=3\,410\,000\) is greater than \(1.00714>1\). These are high-precision numerical checks with positive margins, not formal interval-arithmetic certificates. The analytical monotonicity is checked separately. With \(r_+\) specified, \(32\max(r_+,N_0)=N\) for \(xy=6\). The finite sieve, the primitive-row argument above, and this stated analytic dependency provide positive support for Theorem 2.8 while preserving the limits of the verification.
# Overall assessment and repair state

The overall assessment is Major, based on two demonstrated failures with different scopes. Problem 1 refutes a quantitative main-theorem assertion. Problem 2 invalidates essential derivations of a main existence theorem without refuting that theorem’s conclusion. Three supported local defects are Minor. Neither the number of problems nor the availability of some short corrections determines the two Major assessments.

The reciprocity identities, square avoidance, congruence classification and finite-alphabet counterexample receive positive checks. The exact orbit receives a full finite verification and a separate partial repair, with the remaining imported analytic dependency stated above. No author adoption has been established.

analysis: Location. Theorem 2.6, PDF p. 5 and its proof on p. 19; Lemmas 4.3–4.6, pp. 13–17, especially (4.0.5) and the replacement of the square-denominator symbol by a constant. Source TeX lines 245–259, 686–946 and 1060–1087.

Take \((x,y)=(2,25)\) and \(n=441=21^2\). The starting coordinates are positive and coprime, \(y\) is odd, \(\left(\frac{2}{25}\right)=1\), and \(441\geq8xy=400\). Table 1 places no congruence or reciprocity obstruction on the numerator. Yet a putative matrix’s top row must satisfy \[2a+25b=441,\qquad a\equiv1\pmod4,\qquad a,b\geq0.\] All solutions are \[(a,b)=(33+100t,15-8t),\qquad t=0,1.\] Their gcds are respectively three and seven. Neither row can occur in any integral determinant-one matrix. Consequently \(441\) is absent even from the larger \(\Gamma_1(4)^{\geq0}\) orbit. This is a counterexample to the stated effective conclusion, with every hypothesis checked.

The common algebraic error is to replace \(\left(\frac{q}{m^2}\right)\) by one, or \(\left(\frac{q}{2m^2}\right)\) by \(\left(\frac{q}{2}\right)\), without retaining the condition \(\gcd(q,m)=1\). In the proof’s determinant-one change of coordinates, \[\gcd(cu+dv,n)=\gcd(u,v).\] Choosing \(d\) coprime to \(u\) does not make \((u,v)\) primitive. The exact factors are instead \[\left(\frac{q}{m^2}\right)=\mathbf1_{\gcd(q,m)=1},\qquad
 \left(\frac{q}{2m^2}\right)=\left(\frac{q}{2}\right)\,\mathbf1_{\gcd(q,m)=1}
 \quad(q\ \text{odd}).
 \tag{3.1}\] A denominator example is \((x,y,n)=(3,13,225)\): \(225\geq4xy\), \(\left(\frac{3}{13}\right)=1\), and the only permitted lower row is \((u,v)=(36,9)\). This refutes Lemma 4.4, though it is below the main theorem’s \(8xy\) threshold.

The twice-square numerator branch also fails: \((x,y,n)=(1,7,98)\) satisfies \(98\geq56\) and every congruence hypothesis of Lemma 4.5. All permitted rows are \[(21,11),\ (49,7),\ (77,3),
 \qquad\text{with symbols }-1,\ 0,\ -1.\] Equation (2.1) excludes \(98\) from this orbit. This small example does not refute the much larger nonsquare cutoff of Theorem 2.6; it refutes the intermediate lemma used to justify its twice-square branch.

A stronger repair boundary. No universal constant \(C\) can replace \(8\) in a square bound \(n\geq Cxy\). Choose an integer \(K\) with \(4K>C\) and put \[m=2t\prod_{j=0}^{K-1}(4j+3),\qquad n=m^2,\qquad x=1.\] For sufficiently large \(t\), the interval \((n/(4K+1),n/(4K))\) has length exceeding four. Choose \(y\equiv1\pmod4\) in that interval. Then \(n>Cxy\) and \(\left(\frac{1}{y}\right)=1\). Every nonnegative top row has \(a=n-yb\equiv1\pmod4\), hence \[b\in\{3,7,\ldots,4K-1\}.\] Each such \(b\) divides \(m\), so \(\gcd(a,b)=b>1\). This family varies the starting vector; it does not prove infinitely many exceptions for one fixed orbit.

Impact and counterevidence. The explicit central square bound is false, and its proof requires a primitive-point counting argument. It is therefore Major even though exact row criteria remain available. The square-exclusion theorem, the congruence classification and the finite-alphabet counterexample are unaffected. Qualitative eventual saturation for each fixed starting vector is not disproved by this family. The non-square, non-twice-square character-sign branch retains the zero values and does not suffer this particular cancellation.

Repair. Keep the indicators in (3.1), prove existence of a primitive row within the relevant sign class, and replace the effective square threshold by a justified bound with different dependence on the starting vector or additional arithmetic information. A pointwise demand for a primitive row is not a proof of the published uniform bound. The exact orbit in Theorem 2.8 has a separate verification described below; that verification does not repair the uniform statement. Author adoption is unknown.

The acquired author-hosted May 1995 preprint of Mauldin–Urbański [mu], checked on actual PDF pp. 1, 3, 5–7 and 22, requires a common contraction constant \(0<s<1\) in equation (2.1). Its open set condition includes invariance of the open set. The introduction explicitly distinguishes parabolic maps from this formalism and points to an induced-map approach. Equation (2.9) explicitly requires distortion control for every finite word, and Theorem 3.15 uses these same assumptions. The parabolic elements also persist in the paper’s construction: once a finite family contains \(L\) and \(R^4\), prefix reduction cannot discard either. The first has no proper nonidentity prefix; the proper prefixes \(R,R^2,R^3\) of the second are outside \(\Gamma_1(4)\). Consequently the direct invocation in Proposition 7.6 has not established the finite-approximation equality for the system used here.

Impact and repair boundary. The proof of Theorem 2.10 loses an essential dimension argument, so the finding is Major. No counterexample to its existence conclusion is asserted. An induced, uniformly contracting system, or a verified parabolic dimension theorem with its precise hypotheses, is required; its finite approximants must be related back to finitely generated subsemigroups of \(\Psi\). Simply deleting the parabolic maps can change both the limit set and the known congruence images, and is not a verified repair. The dimension-one argument for \(\Psi\) via finite partitions and the explicit indecomposable matrices in Lemma 7.7 are separate positive controls. The finite alphabet in Section 2 above is uniformly contracting and remains a valid example with dimension exceeding one half.

Title: Initial Stability for Ricci Flow: A Claim-Focused Review
# Paper identity and scope

The paper is A. Deruelle, F. Schulze, and M. Simon, Initial stability estimates for Ricci flow and three dimensional Ricci-pinched manifolds [DSS]. The exact reviewed source is arXiv:2203.15313v2, submitted 17 March 2025, with 50 PDF pages. Its associated journal DOI is https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0018. The publisher PDF was not acquired; no identity of its text with this manuscript is asserted. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which agree with the manuscript’s printed page numbers.

The review covers the statements and dependencies of Theorems 1.2 and 1.3, the curvature and coordinate adjustments in Sections 2–4, the polynomial and exponential estimates in Sections 5–6, the rigidity/application chain in Sections 7–8, and the scaling and splitting mechanisms in Appendices A–B. It is a claim-focused initial review, not an independent reconstruction of every imported compactness, pseudolocality, Ricci-limit, or Alexandrov theorem. The coverage ledger distinguishes direct checks, bounded native AI assistance, and imported results not reproved. No computational experiment is needed for the mathematical statements under examination.
# Hypotheses and dependencies

The stability setting consists of smooth local Ricci flows for positive time, with \(|\operatorname{Rm}(g(t))|\leq c_0/t\) and \(\operatorname{Ric}(g(t))\geq-g(t)\), a common limiting distance up to isometry, Euclidean tangent cones, and sufficiently close-to-isometric distance coordinates. Completeness is not imposed on the local flows; the relative compactness assumptions used in the local distance and curvature arguments must be retained. The conclusion compares flows after harmonic-map gauges and on a smaller ball and time interval. An arbitrary comparison of ungauged metric components is not a test of this existential conclusion.

For Theorem 1.3, uniformly Ricci pinched explicitly includes \(\operatorname{Ric}\geq0\) together with \(\operatorname{Ric}\geq c\,\mathrm{R}g\) for some \(c>0\). A negatively curved Einstein metric does not satisfy this definition. Completeness, dimension three, and bounded initial curvature belong to the stated theorem. The higher-dimensional questions are not proved extensions.
# Checks supporting the argument
## Scaling and the initial gauge

Under \(\widehat g(t)=\lambda^2g(t/\lambda^2)\), \[t|\operatorname{Rm}(\widehat g(t))|
=(t/\lambda^2)|\operatorname{Rm}(g(t/\lambda^2))|.\] The lower Ricci bound improves by \(\lambda^{-2}\) in the rescaled metric. These are the scales required in Appendix A. The fixed-domain volume inequality used there also has the correct direction: if \(\mathrm{R}\geq-\eta\), then for a fixed measurable \(\Omega\) and \(r<s\), \[\operatorname{Vol}_{g(s)}(\Omega)
 \leq e^{\eta(s-r)}\operatorname{Vol}_{g(r)}(\Omega).\] A near-Euclidean lower bound at the later time therefore supplies the needed earlier-time lower bound.

The adjustment and harmonic-map steps precede comparison of metric tensors. Their scale-dependent derivative estimates and shrinking interior domains are consistent with the energy argument. A distance-space limit alone was not treated as tensor convergence. Literal index and constant slips were checked against subsequent use; no main-conclusion defect follows from those slips alone.
## Polynomial and exponential decay

Write \(h=\widetilde g_2-\widetilde g_1\) and \(u=t^{-C}|h|_\delta^2\). The Section 5 estimates supply decay faster than any fixed power after the required domain restriction. Thus the initial term vanishes when the localized divergence-form inequality for \(u\) is integrated from a positive time and that time tends to zero. The cutoff source is bounded and supported away from the observation ball.

For \(|x|<R_0/4\) and \(R_0/2\leq |y|<R_0\), the safe separation estimate is \(|x-y|\geq R_0/4\). The relevant Gaussian integral is therefore bounded by \[C\int_0^t s^{-n/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{aR_0^2}{16s}\right)\,ds .\] Substitution \(\tau=R_0^2/s\) gives a polynomial times an exponential tail. Fixed polynomial prefactors can be absorbed by reducing the positive exponential constant and time interval. The printed factor \(3/16\) on page 29 is not the geometric lower bound for the stated balls; replacing it by \(1/16\) preserves Theorem 6.2, whose exponent is unspecified. This establishes no failure of its qualitative rate.
## Splitting and the application

The product-space excess estimate in Appendix B admits a direct check. Put \(a=\delta/\varepsilon\), \(b=1/\delta\), and suppose \(R\geq20(a+b)\). The longitudinal distances satisfy \(s_\pm\geq19R/20\) and the transverse distances satisfy \(d_\pm\leq a+b\). Dropping the nonnegative transverse contribution from the subtracted long distance gives \[0\leq\mathcal E_R
 \leq\sum_\pm\bigl(\sqrt{s_\pm^2+d_\pm^2}-s_\pm\bigr)
 \leq\frac{40}{19R}(a^2+b^2).\] This gives the required vanishing excess with the selected \(R_i\). The opposite limiting Busemann functions are harmonic. Bochner’s formula and the maximum principle give unit parallel gradient; its contraction with Ricci vanishes. Since \(\partial_tg=-2\operatorname{Ric}\), the gradient vector field is independent of time, allowing a common product identification.

The compactness application depends on noncollapse, the three-dimensional Ricci-limit/cone structure, the comparison expander, and the almost-pinched rigidity result. Scaling from small time on an annulus to decay at infinity has been checked. The comparison transfers an exponentially small pinching error; it does not assert exact equality of the flows. The external asymptotic criterion in Deruelle’s Theorem 1.3 [Deruelle] was checked for applicability: \(f\asymp r^2\) and \(|\operatorname{Ric}|=O(e^{-f^\beta})\), \(\beta>0\), imply \(r^2|\operatorname{Ric}|\to0\), as that theorem requires. Its complete proof, and the other imported existence and structure results, were not independently reconstructed.
# Unresolved quantifier

Equation reference: eq:available. The fixed-order inference directly gives a bound of the form \[
 |D^kh(t)|_\delta\leq A_k t^{-m_k}e^{-a_k/t},
 \qquad A_k,a_k>0,\] on a suitable smaller spatial region. For each fixed \(k\), a reduced time interval absorbs \(A_kt^{-m_k}\). This does not itself show that those intervals contain a common positive time interval across every order.

A diagnostic of this logical distinction is \[f(x,t)=\frac{e^{-1/t}}{1-x},\qquad |x|<\tfrac12,\quad t>0.\] Each fixed derivative decays exponentially as \(t\downarrow0\), whereas \(D_x^kf(0,t)=k!e^{-1/t}\) is unbounded in \(k\) at each fixed positive time. Thus fixed-order exponential estimates do not generally imply [eq:printed] (#eq:printed), whose right-hand side is less than one. This scalar function is not a Ricci-flow counterexample and does not account for the theorem’s freedom of gauge.

The missing evidence is an argument controlling all derivative orders on the common interval, or clarification that the intended interval may depend on \(k\). An order-dependent prefactor as in [eq:available] (#eq:available), or separate \(T_k>0\), is consistent with the checked interpolation step. This observation does not disprove the geometric theorem, does not establish a Major or Minor error, and does not undermine the finite-order estimates needed for the curvature comparison in Section 8.
# Assessment

No substantive counterexample to local \(C^0\) exponential stability or the three-dimensional compact-or-flat conclusion was established. The exact all-orders/common-time phrasing remains Needs Evidence. Displayed sign and constant discrepancies were separated from demonstrated effects on the conclusions; no severity quota was used.

Analytic checks are distinct from numerical tests, author-code execution, and empirical reproduction; none of the latter is claimed. The source PDF, acquired TeX, coverage, native-helper notes, source-page images, exact report build, retained dependencies, and page-view receipts are bound by the verification records. Title: Green Functions on Hyperbolic Three-Space:
Review of the Acquired Author Manuscript
# Source identity and review scope

The reviewed paper is Special values of Green’s functions on hyperbolic 3-space, by S. Herrero, Ö. Imamoğlu, A.-M. von Pippich and M. Schwagenscheidt [paper], associated with DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0019. The exact source is the undated, 60-page ETH-hosted author PDF retrieved on 26 October 2026. Its production metadata is not treated as a submission date or version designation. The separately acquired 52-page arXiv:2405.01219v1, submitted 2 May 2024, and its TeX source are distinct artifacts. The publisher PDF was not acquired and textual equivalence with the version of record is not asserted. All source locations below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with the printed numbers on the inspected pages.

The checks cover the main hypotheses, the Eisenstein coefficient normalizations, the trace/theta-lift and splitting arguments, and the twisted formulas. Native AI helpers performed bounded proof and source-page checks; their exact coverage and limitations are retained separately. Imported Siegel–Weil, harmonic-Maass-form existence, and rationality theorems were not independently reproved in full. The findings below are supported by explicit calculations within the acquired source’s definitions.
# Hypotheses and checks that survive

Theorem 1.1 retains the prime-discriminant assumption, the vanishing plus cusp-space obstruction, even spectral parameter \(2n\), \(n\geq1\), and the nonsquare condition on \(mm'\). Theorem 1.5 has distinct even/odd and twisted/untwisted hypotheses; its partially twisted normalization is \(\pi(\sqrt{mm'})^{1+n}\), with only the square-root factor raised to \(1+n\). Replacing these hypotheses by a general claim about individual Green values would exceed the theorems.

For \(\rho>0\), the radial kernel in (1.2), page 3, is \[\varphi_s(\cosh\rho)=\frac{e^{-s\rho}}{\sinh\rho}.\] Direct differentiation gives \(f''+2\coth\rho\,f'=(s^2-1)f\), consistent with the stated nonnegative-Laplacian eigenvalue \(1-s^2\). The \(1/\rho\) singularity explains the distinct-orbit restriction.

If two positive forms of determinants \(m,m'\) define the same special point up to \(\Gamma\), conjugation reduces their relation to \(X=tY\). Their positive integral diagonal entries force \(t\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\), whence \(mm'=(tm')^2\). Thus the nonsquare hypotheses exclude singular pairs. For the primitive outer trace in Theorem 4.12 the more precise coefficient condition excludes all positive integer multiples of the fixed primitive form. In the determinant-\(4\) example, \(2I\) is excluded by primitivity; no unsupported diagonal subtraction is needed.

An independent finite calculation also confirms the stabilizers \(4\) and \(12\) in Example 1.3, page 5. For \[I,\qquad
 Y=\begin{pmatrix}1&(1+i)/2\\(1-i)/2&1\end{pmatrix},\] the corresponding \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z[i])\) stabilizers have orders \(8\) and \(24\). For \(2Y\), each row of a stabilizing matrix has squared Euclidean norm at most \(2/(2-\sqrt2)<4\), so an exhaustive search of integer real and imaginary entries in \(\{-1,0,1\}\) suffices. Quotienting by \(\{\pm I\}\) gives the stated orders and the factor \(48\) in the trace normalization. This does not purport to numerically evaluate the infinite Green sum.
# Individual cosets in the untwisted theta lift

Problem 1 (The positive trace loses its residue class under a sign change).  Theorems 4.2 and 4.3, pages 26–27, identify a component Poincaré theta lift with twice one positive-coset Green trace. The unfolded vector sum contains both signs. Replacing a negative vector by its negative changes the coset from \(\mu\) to \(-\mu\); the two positive traces need not coincide.
## Explicit data and an off-diagonal contradiction

Let \[D=-3,\qquad b=\frac1{\sqrt{-3}}=-\frac{i}{\sqrt3},
 \qquad \mu=b+\mathcal O_D,\qquad m=\frac23,\qquad n=1,\] and set \[X_+=\begin{pmatrix}1&b\\\bar b&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 X_-=\begin{pmatrix}1&-b\\-\bar b&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Both matrices are primitive, positive, and of determinant \(2/3\); their eigenvalues are \(1\pm1/\sqrt3\). The class \(\mu\) has order \(3\), so \(\mu\ne-\mu\). The source’s definition on page 25 uses positive definite matrices in the specified coset, not an average of the two cosets.

Page 24 states that \(\Gamma\) acts trivially on \(L'/L\). If a positive norm-\(m\) matrix in one coset defined the same point up to \(\Gamma\) as a matrix in the other, their positive rays and equal determinants would force equality after conjugation. This would imply \(\mu=-\mu\), a contradiction. Thus the two trace cycles have disjoint supports.

Put \(T_\pm(P)=\operatorname{tr}_{m,\pm\mu}(G_2(\,\cdot\,,P))\). The full-vector sum and gamma-duplication formula actually displayed on page 27 give, at \(n=1\), \(s=3/2\), \[\Phi(P)=4\sqrt m\,[T_+(P)+T_-(P)].\] The printed Theorem 4.3 instead gives \(\Phi(P)=8\sqrt m\,T_+(P)\). To exhibit failure away from every diagonal, take \[P(t)=\frac{i}{\sqrt3}+\sqrt{\frac23}e^t j,\qquad t>0.\] Its distance from the point of \(X_-\) is exactly \(t\). Every fixed-determinant positive form point has height \(\sqrt m/c\leq\sqrt m\), with \(c\in\mathbb N\), whereas \(P(t)\) has larger height. Thus \(P(t)\) is off both cycles for every \(t>0\). The opposite-coset trace is locally bounded near the limiting point because the cycles are disjoint and locally finite. Using \(\varphi_2(\cosh t)=t^{-1}+O(1)\) and cancellation of the stabilizer count against the trace weight, \[T_-(P(t))=\frac{\pi}{t}+O(1),\qquad T_+(P(t))=O(1).\] The actual value minus the printed right side is consequently \[4\pi\sqrt{\frac23}\,\frac1t+O(1),\] which is nonzero for all sufficiently small positive \(t\). This is an off-diagonal counterexample, not an evaluation at an undefined singular point.
## Scope, contrary evidence and supported correction

The central Weil action independently confirms the same obstruction: the relevant Poincaré series has principal part \(q^{-m}(e_\mu+e_{-\mu})\), and \(F_{1-2n,m,\mu}=F_{1-2n,m,-\mu}\). Its lift cannot equal an unsymmetrized trace with a different pole set.

The supported replacement in both component identities is \[2\operatorname{tr}_{m,\mu}\quad\longmapsto\quad
 \operatorname{tr}_{m,\mu}+\operatorname{tr}_{m,-\mu}.\] Equivalently, one may use the average of the two positive traces. Restricting to \(2\mu=0\) is another, narrower repair. The Gaussian examples with two-torsion discriminant group do not detect this error.

This is a Major defect in the claimed core component lift-to-trace identity, explicitly described as a main result of Section 4. Its impact is bounded by an important cancellation: the relevant modular coefficients satisfy \(a_\mu=a_{-\mu}\), so \[\sum_\mu a_\mu(T_\mu+T_{-\mu})
       =2\sum_\mu a_\mu T_\mu .\] The corrected component formula therefore gives the same fully summed expression used in Theorem 4.12. This counterexample does not refute that symmetric theorem or the introductory full-trace result. The subsequent individual-coset simplification in Remark 4.13(4), page 35, requires a fresh symmetry check; no separate counterexample to that specialization is claimed here.
# A false twisted splitting identity

Problem 2 (An exterior character forces an incorrect vanishing).  The first identity of Theorem 5.15, page 51, includes an exterior factor \(\chi_D(X_0)\) in the untwisted primitive outer trace of the twisted modified theta kernel. Under the stated hypotheses, that factor can vanish while the left side is nonzero.
## An admissible counterexample

Use \(D=-4\), \(m=1\), \(\mu=0\), and \(X_0=I\). The vector \(I\) is positive and primitive in \(L'\), and belongs to the specified determinant-\(1\), zero-coset set. Section 5.1, page 40, explicitly extends \(\chi_D\) by zero outside \[L_D=\{X\in L':Q(X)\in D\mathbb Z\}.\] Since \(Q(I)=1\notin4\mathbb Z\), the printed right side of the first identity is identically zero. The first identity does not assume \(\chi_D(X_0)\ne0\) or \(m\in |D|\mathbb Z\).

There is one class of positive integral binary Hermitian forms of determinant \(1\) over \(\mathbb Z[i]\). Here is a short verification. Choose a primitive shortest vector and complete it to an \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z[i])\) basis. The leading coefficient \(a\) is the minimum positive value, so \(c\geq a\). Reducing both components of \(b\) modulo \(a\) gives \(|b|^2\leq a^2/2\). Hence \(1=ac-|b|^2\geq a^2/2\), and the positive integer \(a\) equals \(1\). Now \(b\) can be reduced to zero and \(c=1\). Since \(|\Gamma_I|=4\), the claimed left side is \(\Theta^*_{L,\chi_{-4}}(\tau,j)/4\).
## A nonzero Fourier coefficient
## Impact, counterevidence and repair boundary

The example satisfies the prime-discriminant and primitive-vector conditions. It concerns a smooth theta identity, so a Green-function diagonal exclusion does not remove it. No choice of a nonzero global normalizing constant repairs zero versus nonzero.

The first identity is a central splitting step in the odd partially twisted evaluation. Theorem 5.20, page 53, repeats the exterior factor, and its proof on page 54 explicitly invokes Theorem 5.15. This is a Major issue in the exact identity and the printed derivation. The present counterexample does not independently refute Theorem 5.20 for an admissible weakly holomorphic input, nor the weaker rational-multiple-of-\(\pi\) conclusions of Theorem 5.21 and Theorem 1.5(2). Removing the exterior factor from the first identity is the natural repair suggested by the orbit integral; all constants, descent maps and the downstream formula still require rechecking. Its local form does not reduce the impact of the currently false principal identity.
# A class-number normalization

Equation reference: eq:classnumber. Problem 3 (Ordinary and narrow class numbers).  Remark 3.7(1), page 20, writes \[
 L(\chi_\Delta,1)=
 \frac{h(\Delta)\log\varepsilon_\Delta}{\sqrt\Delta}
 \qquad(\Delta>0).\] defines \(h(\Delta)\) as the class number of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt\Delta)\), and defines \(\varepsilon_\Delta\) as the smallest totally positive unit greater than \(1\). Under the ordinary ideal-class-number meaning, [eq:classnumber] (#eq:classnumber) is false.

The distinction can affect an actual nonzero coefficient: for the positive definite rank-three lattice \((\mathbb Z^3,Q=x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2)\), \(\gamma=0\), \(n=3\), the data in Theorem 3.6 give \(N_{0,3}(8)=96\) and \(c^+(3,0)=-6L(\chi_{12},1)/\pi\). Substitution of [eq:classnumber] (#eq:classnumber) with ordinary \(h(12)=1\) halves that coefficient. The representation count is retained as an exact finite calculation.

There is material counterevidence against a broader claim of damage. Theorem 3.6 itself retains the \(L\)-value. The worked coefficient on page 57 correctly uses \[-\frac{2L(\chi_{12},1)}{\pi}
 =-\frac{2\log(7+2\sqrt{12})}{\sqrt{12}\,\pi},\] and \(7+2\sqrt{12}=(2+\sqrt3)^2\). Thus that worked value is not refuted, and the rational logarithmic span is unchanged. The displayed real quadratic formula becomes correct if \(h\) means the narrow class number; the acquired text does not specify that convention. This is a Minor normalization/definition issue on the declared ordinary-field interpretation, with an explicit factor-two calculation and a bounded effect. Clarifying the narrow convention, or including the norm-dependent factor with ordinary class numbers, is the required repair.
# Assessment and evidence limits

The component trace and twisted splitting identities require correction. The latter problem must be resolved before the printed odd partially twisted evaluation can be accepted on the given derivation. The ordinary/narrow class-number convention also requires clarification. None of these findings is a claim that all Green-value or algebraicity results fail.

The nonzero cusp-space sign in the introduction’s proof sketch is contradicted by the correctly stated zero obstruction in the main argument and is not a separate substantive finding. The missing stabilizer weight in one display of the classical Siegel–Weil formula is bracketed by correctly weighted expressions. Other isolated indices were not converted into additional Problems without a demonstrated effect on a conclusion.

The zero-index justification in Remark 3.7(2) also needs a more careful argument: for \(\gamma=n=0\), the zero vector solves every congruence, so the representation counts cannot eventually vanish. For \(Q=x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2\) at \(p=2\), direct reduction modulo \(4\) gives \(N_0=1\), \(N_1=4\), and \(N_r=8N_{r-2}\) for \(r\geq2\). The local factor is nevertheless \[(1-4X)\sum_{r\geq0}N_rX^r
 =\frac{1-16X^2}{1-8X^2},\] and vanishes at \(X=1/4\), as the coefficient calculation requires. The retained note supplies the general anisotropic compactness estimate for this mechanism. This check corrects the stated justification without furnishing a counterexample to the zero-index coefficient or adding another core-theorem failure.

problems.title: Individual positive-coset trace is replaced incorrectly by its sign pair
problems.source_location: Theorems4.2–4.3, PDF/printed pp26–27; definitions pp24–25; Poincare symmetry p12.
claim: A component Poincare theta lift equals a constant times2 tr_(m,mu), despite its two-sided vector sum.
analysis: Theorems 4.2 and 4.3, pages 26–27, identify a component Poincaré theta lift with twice one positive-coset Green trace. The unfolded vector sum contains both signs. Replacing a negative vector by its negative changes the coset from \(\mu\) to \(-\mu\); the two positive traces need not coincide.

Let \[D=-3,\qquad b=\frac1{\sqrt{-3}}=-\frac{i}{\sqrt3},
 \qquad \mu=b+\mathcal O_D,\qquad m=\frac23,\qquad n=1,\] and set \[X_+=\begin{pmatrix}1&b\\\bar b&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 X_-=\begin{pmatrix}1&-b\\-\bar b&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Both matrices are primitive, positive, and of determinant \(2/3\); their eigenvalues are \(1\pm1/\sqrt3\). The class \(\mu\) has order \(3\), so \(\mu\ne-\mu\). The source’s definition on page 25 uses positive definite matrices in the specified coset, not an average of the two cosets.

Page 24 states that \(\Gamma\) acts trivially on \(L'/L\). If a positive norm-\(m\) matrix in one coset defined the same point up to \(\Gamma\) as a matrix in the other, their positive rays and equal determinants would force equality after conjugation. This would imply \(\mu=-\mu\), a contradiction. Thus the two trace cycles have disjoint supports.

Put \(T_\pm(P)=\operatorname{tr}_{m,\pm\mu}(G_2(\,\cdot\,,P))\). The full-vector sum and gamma-duplication formula actually displayed on page 27 give, at \(n=1\), \(s=3/2\), \[\Phi(P)=4\sqrt m\,[T_+(P)+T_-(P)].\] The printed Theorem 4.3 instead gives \(\Phi(P)=8\sqrt m\,T_+(P)\). To exhibit failure away from every diagonal, take \[P(t)=\frac{i}{\sqrt3}+\sqrt{\frac23}e^t j,\qquad t>0.\] Its distance from the point of \(X_-\) is exactly \(t\). Every fixed-determinant positive form point has height \(\sqrt m/c\leq\sqrt m\), with \(c\in\mathbb N\), whereas \(P(t)\) has larger height. Thus \(P(t)\) is off both cycles for every \(t>0\). The opposite-coset trace is locally bounded near the limiting point because the cycles are disjoint and locally finite. Using \(\varphi_2(\cosh t)=t^{-1}+O(1)\) and cancellation of the stabilizer count against the trace weight, \[T_-(P(t))=\frac{\pi}{t}+O(1),\qquad T_+(P(t))=O(1).\] The actual value minus the printed right side is consequently \[4\pi\sqrt{\frac23}\,\frac1t+O(1),\] which is nonzero for all sufficiently small positive \(t\). This is an off-diagonal counterexample, not an evaluation at an undefined singular point.
result: The central Weil action independently confirms the same obstruction: the relevant Poincaré series has principal part \(q^{-m}(e_\mu+e_{-\mu})\), and \(F_{1-2n,m,\mu}=F_{1-2n,m,-\mu}\). Its lift cannot equal an unsymmetrized trace with a different pole set.

The supported replacement in both component identities is \[2\operatorname{tr}_{m,\mu}\quad\longmapsto\quad
 \operatorname{tr}_{m,\mu}+\operatorname{tr}_{m,-\mu}.\] Equivalently, one may use the average of the two positive traces. Restricting to \(2\mu=0\) is another, narrower repair. The Gaussian examples with two-torsion discriminant group do not detect this error.

This is a Major defect in the claimed core component lift-to-trace identity, explicitly described as a main result of Section 4. Its impact is bounded by an important cancellation: the relevant modular coefficients satisfy \(a_\mu=a_{-\mu}\), so \[\sum_\mu a_\mu(T_\mu+T_{-\mu})
       =2\sum_\mu a_\mu T_\mu .\] The corrected component formula therefore gives the same fully summed expression used in Theorem 4.12. This counterexample does not refute that symmetric theorem or the introductory full-trace result. The subsequent individual-coset simplification in Remark 4.13(4), page 35, requires a fresh symmetry check; no separate counterexample to that specialization is claimed here.

Recorded evidence: Counterexample: D=-3, b=1/sqrt(-3), mu=b mod O_D of order3, m2/3,n1,s3/2; X±=[[1,±b],[±conj(b),1]] positive primitive. P(t)=i/sqrt3+sqrt(2/3)e^t j for t>0 is off every fixed-m cycle (height>sqrt(m)). Correct lift4sqrt(m)(T_mu+T_-mu) minus printed8sqrt(m)T_mu has asymptotic4pi sqrt(2/3)/t+O(1), nonzero for all sufficiently small t>0.

problems.title: Ordinary versus narrow class number in real quadratic L-value evaluation

claim: h(Delta) described as field class number, epsilon minimal totally positive unit, formulaL=h log(epsilon)/sqrtDelta. Wordordinary is not printed and interpretation is explicitly qualified.
analysis:
Remark 3.7(1), page 20, writes \[
 L(\chi_\Delta,1)=
 \frac{h(\Delta)\log\varepsilon_\Delta}{\sqrt\Delta}
 \qquad(\Delta>0).\] defines \(h(\Delta)\) as the class number of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt\Delta)\), and defines \(\varepsilon_\Delta\) as the smallest totally positive unit greater than \(1\). Under the ordinary ideal-class-number meaning, [eq:classnumber] (#eq:classnumber) is false.

The distinction can affect an actual nonzero coefficient: for the positive definite rank-three lattice \((\mathbb Z^3,Q=x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2)\), \(\gamma=0\), \(n=3\), the data in Theorem 3.6 give \(N_{0,3}(8)=96\) and \(c^+(3,0)=-6L(\chi_{12},1)/\pi\). There is material counterevidence against a broader claim of damage. Theorem 3.6 itself retains the \(L\)-value. The worked coefficient on page 57 correctly uses \[-\frac{2L(\chi_{12},1)}{\pi}
 =-\frac{2\log(7+2\sqrt{12})}{\sqrt{12}\,\pi},\] and \(7+2\sqrt{12}=(2+\sqrt3)^2\). Thus that worked value is not refuted, and the rational logarithmic span is unchanged. The displayed real quadratic formula becomes correct if \(h\) means the narrow class number; the acquired text does not specify that convention. This is a Minor normalization/definition issue on the declared ordinary-field interpretation, with an explicit factor-two calculation and a bounded effect. Clarifying the narrow convention, or including the norm-dependent factor with ordinary class numbers, is the required repair.
