report: Abstract: This review concerns the exact acquired arXiv version of the paper by Shlapentokh-Rothman and Van de Moortel. Four core dependencies fail as written: the reference spectral operator is assigned a domain that excludes every nonzero eigenfunction; the threshold-frequency freezing is incompatible with the claimed uniformity at the event horizon; and an Airy-to-oscillatory connection coefficient has the opposite leading phase from the one required by its own Wronskians; and a quadratic source quantity is used to bound a linear Fourier response. Each finding has a bounded analytic contradiction and is classified Major. The corrected Dirichlet operator, a modulated horizon amplitude, a consistent change of matching phase, and a source norm of the correct homogeneity offer distinct repair routes. The last also requires renewed checks of frequency weights and the downstream integral estimates. These calculations do not disprove the final physical decay theorem after such repairs. Several further normalization and scope issues are recorded separately. Scientific adjudication remains pending; current focused independent acceptance is documented in the companion provenance, without human-review or publication claims.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Klein–Gordon Decay on Reissner–Nordström:
Review of the Acquired Preprint
# Source identity and theorem scope

The reviewed work is Polynomial time decay for solutions of the Klein–Gordon equation on a subextremal Reissner–Nordström black hole, by Yakov Shlapentokh-Rothman and Maxime Van de Moortel [paper], associated with DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0020. The actual scientific source is the 76-page arXiv:2401.00048v1, submitted on 29 December 2023 and internally dated 2 January 2024. Its matching author TeX was read as source, not executed. The publisher PDF was not obtained through the attempted authorized route. The journal metadata lists a substantially longer, 134-page article; no equivalence with that version is asserted. The original assigned batch membership is retained. All locations below use one-based PDF pages, matching printed pagination on the inspected pages.

The background has fixed \(M>0\), \(0\leq |e|<M\), and \(m>0\). Theorem 1.2, page 2, claims pointwise decay on \(r_+\leq r\leq R\), including the horizon, for smooth compactly supported initial data. Its unconditional loss is \(1/23\); an arbitrarily small positive loss is conditional on the stated exponent-pair conjecture. The fixed-angular-mode asymptotic in Theorem 1.1 is imported from the authors’ previous work and is not a new uniform-in-mode estimate. The quasimodes of Theorem 1.4 move to \(r\gtrsim L^2\). Their logarithmic obstruction for polynomially localized data in moving large-radius regions does not contradict a decay statement for fixed compact observation regions and sufficiently localized data.

The proof chain runs from the separated radial equation through high- and intermediate-frequency estimates, three turning-point connections, a resonant Green formula, stationary phase, exponential sums, and angular Sobolev summation. The findings below concern specific links in that chain. Native AI helpers performed bounded section and source-page checks, whose roles, exact coverage and limitations are retained in the accompanying records. They are not human reviewers or independent acceptance agents.
# The reference spectral operator

Problem 1 (Two traces vanish at the regular endpoint).  Definition 4.2 and Lemma 4.7, page 20, assign the half-line Schrödinger operator \(Q\) the domain \(H^2_0((x_0,\infty))\) and assert self-adjointness. The preceding sentence explicitly defines \(H^k_0\) as the \(H^k\)-closure of compactly supported smooth functions. With this definition the domain is too small.
## An admissible contradiction

Choose \[M=m=1,\qquad e=0,\qquad x_0=2,\qquad
 \mathcal E_1=\mathcal E_2=0,\] and any sufficiently large integer \(L\). All the printed potential bounds are satisfied. The actual operator is then \[Qf=-f''+\left(-\frac2x+\frac{L(L+1)}{x^2}\right)f,\qquad
 D(Q)=H^2_0((2,\infty)).\] Continuity of the two endpoint trace maps on \(H^2\) implies \[f(2)=f'(2)=0\qquad(f\in D(Q)).\] If \(Qf=\lambda f\), the regular second-order equation \[f''=\left(-\frac2x+\frac{L(L+1)}{x^2}-\lambda\right)f\] has zero Cauchy data at \(2\). Uniqueness gives \(f\equiv0\). Thus this operator has no eigenfunctions, in direct contradiction to Lemma 4.8, page 21, which asserts infinitely many negative eigenvalues tending to zero.

Self-adjointness can also be refuted without any spectral calculation. Let \(g(x)=e^{-(x-2)}\). Both \(g\) and \[-g''+\left(-\frac2x+\frac{L(L+1)}{x^2}\right)g\] belong to \(L^2((2,\infty))\). Integration by parts against \(f\in H^2_0\) has no endpoint term because both traces of \(f\) vanish. Hence \(g\in D(Q^*)\). But \(g(2)=1\), so \(g\notin D(Q)\). Therefore \(Q\ne Q^*\).
## Core impact and the repair boundary

This is a Major defect in a core spectral dependency. The stated operator cannot provide the eigenfunctions, min–max principle, eigenvalue sequence or spectral resolvent used in Section 4.2 and the later frequency decomposition. In particular, the quantitative eigenvalue comparison of Lemma 4.11, pages 22–23, is not an estimate for the operator actually defined.

The source also gives strong evidence for the intended correction: the shifted sine-transform argument in Lemma 4.8 describes the Dirichlet realization. Its domain is \[D(Q_D)=H^2((2,\infty))\cap H^1_0((2,\infty)),\] which imposes \(f(2)=0\) but not \(f'(2)=0\). Equivalently, one can specify the Friedrichs operator associated with the \(H^1_0\) quadratic form. For this bounded real potential the Dirichlet realization is self-adjoint. It can have the Coulomb-type negative spectrum. The present counterexample does not refute the spectral estimates for that corrected operator; they must be stated and used for it consistently.

A related definition must be repaired in the frequency subdivision. Where distance to the spectrum is intended, the quantity is \[\inf_n|m^2-\omega^2+\lambda_n|.\] A signed infimum instead equals \(m^2-\omega^2+\lambda_1\) for an increasing eigenvalue sequence. Its sublevel set contains an interval of algebraic width, rather than only the intended small neighborhoods of the individual eigenvalues. The later lemmas use the absolute distance, whereas Section 6 uses the small-measure decomposition. This is recorded as an additional consistency requirement within the same spectral dependency, not as a separate constructed resolvent-growth counterexample.
# Uniformity of the threshold Green formula at the horizon

Problem 2 (Freezing an oscillatory horizon factor is not uniform).  Theorem 5.1(4), page 32, equation (5.10), evaluates the regular Green coefficients at \(\omega=m\). They contain \(u_H(m,s)\), while the error bounds explicitly hold for every \(s\leq s_{\max}\). The horizon normalization (5.5), page 31, makes these two requirements incompatible.
## An exact source within the theorem’s hypotheses

Fix a subextremal background and one sufficiently large \(L\); keep \(L\) fixed in the following threshold limit. Choose a real smooth cutoff \(\chi\) equal to \(1\) for \(s\leq0\) and \(0\) for \(s\geq1\). Define \[u(\omega,s)=\chi(s)u_H(\omega,s),\qquad
 H(\omega,s)=\chi''(s)u_H(\omega,s)
                 +2\chi'(s)\partial_su_H(\omega,s).\] Because \(u_H''=Vu_H\), one has \(u''-Vu=H\) exactly. Both \(H\) and \(\partial_\omega H\) are supported in \([0,1]\), and hence satisfy the theorem’s source support condition for any \(s_H>1\). On this fixed interval their norms are finite uniformly for \(m/2\leq\omega\leq m\), by the horizon Volterra construction away from zero frequency. In particular the printed quantity \(N[H]\) is finite at this fixed \(L\).

The solution is outgoing at the horizon and identically zero near infinity, an admissible decaying end condition for the inhomogeneous linear problem. A unit nonzero outgoing amplitude cannot be imposed on every inhomogeneous solution: it would exclude zero forcing and contradict the linear Green formula itself. If desired, a smooth frequency cutoff and conjugate reflection at negative frequencies give a real smooth physical source. The local theorem does not require time-compact support.

For \(s<0\), the two \(u^{\rm reg}_2\) integrals in (5.10) vanish. The two remaining regular terms depend on \(s\) only through \(u_H(m,s)\). Consequently the theorem implies \[u_H(\omega,s)=B_L(\omega)u_H(m,s)+R_L(\omega,s),
 \qquad
 \sup_{s<0}|R_L(\omega,s)|\leq C_LN[H]k^{-1/2},\] for some complex scalar \(B_L(\omega)\). Here \[k^{-2}=\frac{m^2-\omega^2}{(Mm^2)^2}.\] The constant \(C_L\) may be very large, but is finite and independent of \(\omega\) at fixed \(L\). Indeed the theorem states \[d_L:=1-|\Gamma(m,L)|>0,
 \qquad |1+\Gamma(m,L)e^{2i\vartheta}|\geq d_L.\] Thus the denominator and all bounded trigonometric factors can be absorbed into \(C_L\). No lower bound uniform in \(L\) is needed.
## The phase-circle contradiction

Equation (5.5) gives, for each fixed \(\omega\), \[u_H(\omega,s)=e^{-i\omega s}(1+o(1)),
 \qquad u_H(m,s)=e^{-ims}(1+o(1))
 \quad(s\longrightarrow-\infty).\] For every \(\omega\ne m\) and every \(B\in\mathbb C\), \[\limsup_{s\to-\infty}|u_H(\omega,s)-Bu_H(m,s)|
 =\max_{|z|=1}|z-B|=1+|B|\geq1.\] The phase \(e^{i(m-\omega)s}\) traverses the unit circle infinitely often. The two \(o(1)\) terms do not change this limit superior. But the claimed upper bound tends to zero as \(\omega\uparrow m\), since \(k\to\infty\). This is a contradiction with the theorem’s actual quantifiers.
## Propagation, contrary evidence and correction

The proof in Section 5.12, page 56, freezes all regular coefficients and invokes a frequency derivative bound. The unmodulated factor has a derivative whose leading term is \(-is e^{-i\omega s}\), which is not uniform on the stated half-line. Section 6 retains frozen factors multiplied by \(e^{i\omega p(s)}\). Near the horizon the residual factor is \(e^{i(\omega-m)s}\); multiplication by the horizon-penetrating Fourier phase does not remove the error.

This is a Major failure of the central uniform resolvent representation used for the announced decay up to the horizon. It is unaffected by Wronskian signs, by a correction of the action’s \(\pi\) normalization, or by keeping the source away from the horizon; the constructed source already has that support.

The appropriate regular object is \(e^{i\omega s}u_H(\omega,s)\), which tends to \(1\) at the horizon. The source uses such modulated derivatives elsewhere, providing evidence for an intended repair. One must retain \(e^{-i\omega s}\) and freeze only the regular amplitude, then re-establish both Green terms and the inverse-Fourier remainder estimates. Restricting \(s\) to a fixed bounded interval is a narrower repair that does not prove the claimed horizon-uniform result. No counterexample to the final physical decay rate is asserted.
# The second turning-point phase

Problem 3 (The inverse connection has the wrong leading phase).  Corollary 5.13, page 48, equation (5.45), gives a diagonal connection coefficient with phase \(e^{-i\pi/4}\). The forward expansion of Corollary 5.8, page 44, and the exact Wronskian normalization (5.36), page 42, require \(e^{+i\pi/4}\).
## A bounded Wronskian calculation

Write \[A=u_{Ai_2},\quad B=u_{Bi_2},\quad
 c=(Mm^2)^{1/2}\pi^{-1/2}\mathbb L^{-2/3},
 \quad F_+=A-iB,\quad F_-=A+iB.\] The paper’s convention is \(W(f,g)=f'g-fg'\). Its exact normalization is \(W(A,B)=c^2\), hence \[W(F_+,F_-)=2ic^2.\] The oscillatory solutions satisfy \(W(B_+,B_-)=2i\). Corollary 5.8 and the proof of Corollary 5.13 give \[F_-=c\,e^{i\pi/4}B_-+cR_-,
 \qquad
 W(B_+,R_-)=O(e^{-\kappa_+A_0}+\mathbb L^{-1}),\] where \(A_0\) denotes the paper’s large matching parameter, distinguished here from the Airy solution \(A\).
## Why the correction reaches the resonant formula

The same phase is carried into Lemma 5.16, page 50. With the source’s real-basis definitions, \[w_{\rm even}=\Re(e^{i\pi/4}w_{2,+}),\qquad
 w_{\rm odd}=-\Im(e^{i\pi/4}w_{2,+}),\] the corrected leading connection gives \[w_{\rm even}\sim c^{-1}B,\qquad
 w_{\rm odd}\sim-c^{-1}A,\] rather than the printed \(c^{-1}A,c^{-1}B\). The leading sine and cosine roles in Proposition 5.21, page 54, therefore rotate. The subsequent Wronskian and narrow-resonance formula must be recomputed with one consistent phase convention. A fixed \(\pi/2\) shift cannot be absorbed into the stated \(\phi_3=O(k^{-1})\).

This is a Major error in the central matching calculation. The bounded repair begins by conjugating the leading diagonal phases in (5.45), followed by propagation through the real basis, connection coefficients and resonant phase. A global basis convention could also be changed, but would require changing the already fixed Airy normalization and all dependent formulas consistently. The conserved flux calculation supplies useful contrary evidence: with a consistent basis, it still enforces the correct modulus gap \(1-|\Gamma|>0\). The existence of a gap and the general tunneling mechanism are not refuted by the phase error. Nor does this calculation alone determine that the final polynomial decay exponent changes.
# Homogeneity of the source-to-solution estimate

Problem 4 (A quadratic source quantity cannot bound a linear response).  Proposition 6.6, page 62, defines its quantity \(\mathcal D[H]\) as a supremum of weighted squared source integrals, without a square root. Its Fourier-response bound is linear in \(u\) but multiplies \(\mathcal D[H]\) once. There is no unit-source normalization or lower bound on \(\mathcal D\). The same mismatch occurs in Proposition 3.2, page 12, and Lemma 6.7, page 62.
## A nonzero response satisfying the source conditions

Both end amplitudes vanish, so \(u_0\) lies in the linear outgoing subspaces used by the paper’s Green formula. This convention is material: if the earlier symbol \(\sim\) were instead read as requiring unit amplitude at both ends for every inhomogeneous solution, it would conflict with that linear formula, the zero source and the final application to arbitrary initial data. The present construction uses the source-to-solution interpretation actually required in those applications, not a hidden unit-amplitude restriction.
## Actual dependence and limits of the repair

The final proof on pages 68–69 explicitly invokes Proposition 6.6 and Lemma 6.15 for the time-cutoff source \(F=2\nabla\chi\cdot\nabla\phi+(\Box\chi)\phi\). For actual compactly supported smooth initial data, a fixed smooth cutoff and finite propagation preserve linear scaling: \(\phi,F,H,u\) scale by \(\varepsilon\), whereas \(\mathcal D\) scales by \(\varepsilon^2\). A nonzero compact exterior single-mode solution at a fixed finite time can be chosen by finite-time Cauchy evolution. Its cutoff source is supported in a compact radial region during the transition, so its Fourier source has finite \(\mathcal D\). The outgoing and Fourier-inversion interpretation here is the one imported in the paper’s final proof; that external scattering theorem is not independently rederived in this review. The explicit construction above already refutes the stated general-source estimate. The final claim that the same quadratic \(\mathcal D\) is bounded by a first-power Sobolev norm also fails under large-amplitude scaling whenever \(\mathcal D>0\).

This is a Major defect in a core estimate, grouped as one problem across its repeated uses. Proposition 3.1 has a squared left side and supplies contrary evidence for the intended homogeneity. Taking a square root of the quadratic quantity restores necessary linear scaling, but does not certify the complete repair: frequency and angular weights and all subsequent estimates must be checked again. For example, the displayed \(\omega^8\) bound in Proposition 3.1, combined only with the \((1+\omega^{10})\) weight before taking square roots, gives a coarse \(\omega^{-1}\) derivative bound, insufficient by itself for the high-frequency \(L^1_\omega\) step in Lemma 6.7. Stronger weights or finer estimates are needed there. The final theorem has a first-power data norm and is not itself refuted by this scaling argument.
# Checks that survive and further bounded corrections
## The exponential-sum mechanism

The compensation between a narrow resonance and its prefactor survives an independent algebraic check. Let \(a\asymp1-r\), \(\rho=-\Gamma\), \(r=|\rho|<1\), and \(|1-\rho|\lesssim a\). If \[|b_q|\lesssim q^{1/3},\quad
 |b_{q+1}-b_q|\lesssim q^{-2/3},\quad
 |S_q|\leq Kq^{2/3},\] Abel summation gives \[a\left|\sum_{q\leq N}\rho^q b_qz_q\right|
 \lesssim K\left[
 aNr^N+a\sum_{q\geq1}r^q
       +a^2\sum_{q\geq1}qr^q\right]\lesssim K.\] Thus the large angular parameter need not destroy the sum estimate once the correct phase and amplitude hypotheses have been proved.

The dyadic exponent arithmetic also has a positive margin. For the two exponent pairs used in Appendix C, the competing exponents are \[E_1=\frac{1+884\alpha}{2745},
 \qquad E_2=\frac{13}{252}-\frac{4\alpha}{63}.\] Optimizing gives \(\alpha=3937/29632\) and the common value \(959/22224\). The difference from \(1/23\) is \(167/511152>0\), leaving room for sufficiently small losses. This checks the stated arithmetic mechanism; it neither proves the exponent-pair conjecture nor repairs the preceding analytic dependencies.
## Definitions and local normalizations

The coordinate displays on pages 10–11 need correction. The metric with \(f=1-2M/r+e^2/r^2\) requires \(ds/dr=f^{-1}\). For \(M=1,e=0\), the explicit printed coordinate is \(s=r+2\log[r(r-2)]\), so \[s'=\frac1f+\frac2r,
 \qquad s'(4)=\frac52\ne2=\frac1{f(4)}.\] The displayed radial operator \(f\partial_r(f^{-1}\partial_r)\) also differs from \(f\partial_r(f\partial_r)\). Applied to \(\psi=r\) at \(r=4\), the values are respectively \(-1/4\) and \(1/16\). The later analysis largely uses the intended tortoise-coordinate comparabilities. An additive normalization of the correct coordinate can preserve the displayed leading horizon constant \(C_+\). These observations establish the local errors, without separately refuting the subsequent decay inequalities.

The interpolation conditions on \(P\) in Definition 3.1, page 13, also need a low-frequency qualification: when \(M=1,e=0,m=1/2,\omega=1\), the asserted \(|\partial_s\log P|\lesssim S_\xi^{-1}\omega\log\omega\) forces a constant transition. Its prescribed outer value is \(3/4+1/(2r(2S_\xi))<1\) for large \(S_\xi\), whereas its inner value is \(1\). A different bounded-frequency interpolation is needed. This does not by itself refute the later large-frequency estimate.

Appendix A, page 69, uses an \(I_{i
u}-I_{-i
u}\) difference with the opposite sign from the standard \(K_{i
u}\) connection formula [dlmf]. Its small-argument sign agrees with that difference, but its positive large-argument leading term agrees with the standard \(K\). At \(
u=x=1\), the difference displayed in the paper is approximately \(-0.2894280370\), while \(K_i(1)\) is approximately \(+0.2894280370\). The exact connection identity, rather than this numerical illustration, proves the sign conflict. A consistent basis-sign correction is required; the modulus flux identity is not independently refuted.

Other recorded local corrections include the extra \(\pi^{-1}\) in (5.9) relative to the action definition in Proposition 5.22; and the derivative coefficients of the leading \(A^{2/3}\) phase in Section 6. The corrected derivative profile still has the shape needed for the exponent-pair argument. These remaining points retain their bounded uses. The source-norm homogeneity defect has instead been isolated as the core Problem 4.
## Quantifiers requiring clarification

Theorem 1.2 suppresses dependence on the support radius of the initial data, although the proved resolvent bounds explicitly depend on the support cutoff \(s_H\) or \(S_0\). The final proof does not supply a bound uniform as that cutoff tends to infinity. The source should either fix the support radius and display this dependence, introduce suitable spatial weights, or supply a uniform argument. No complete black-hole counterexample to that uniformity has been established here; this remains a request for evidence.

Similarly, the final statement about every coordinate derivative needs the appropriate dependence of the data regularity order on the derivative order. The argument only calls \(N\) sufficiently large. It should not be read as supplying one fixed finite Sobolev order for unbounded derivative orders without further proof. The dependence of the frequency cutoff exponent on the requested small loss must also be aligned with the final Sobolev-order quantifier.

A further bounded question concerns the geometric-tail derivative estimate (6.23), page 67. This concerns the genuine tail of the geometric expansion (6.19), with the summation index \(q\) restored in the subsequent exponential factors. Those factors, including the displayed definition of \(F\) preceding (6.23), omit \(q\) as printed and do not literally describe the same tail. After correcting the source homogeneity in Problem 4, consider the model tail \[F(\theta)=A_2\frac{(re^{i\theta})^{N+1}}{1-re^{i\theta}},\] its exact derivative at \(\theta=0\), with \(A_2,r\) fixed, has size \[|A_2|r^{N+1}|\theta'|
 \left[\frac{N+1}{1-r}+\frac{r}{(1-r)^2}\right].\] When \(|A_2|\asymp a\), \(1-r\asymp a\), and \(Na\ll1\), this can have size \(|\theta'|/a\). The stated geometric bounds alone therefore do not give the printed pointwise derivative gain. An actual lower bound for the data-dependent coefficient at a resonant frequency was not established here, so this is an inference diagnostic, not a counterexample to the physical solution. Phase averaging may instead prove the needed integrated estimate, since \(a\int_0^{2\pi}|1-re^{i\theta}|^{-2}\,d\theta=O(1)\). That repaired argument remains to be supplied.
# Assessment and verification limits

The four Major findings concern the operator domain, the horizon-uniform resolvent error, the turning-point connection phase, and the nonhomogeneous source-to-solution estimate. Each is supported by an explicit admissible calculation, the exact source location, a check of contrary evidence, and a bounded repair statement. None requires the entire paper to be false.

The acquisition record includes the available author source archive, metadata and unsuccessful publisher route. No paper-specific computational supplement or code was identified in the available searches; this is an access and reproducibility limitation, not a mathematical defect. No author code or author TeX was executed. External Olver, spectral-theoretic, prior fixed-mode scattering and number-theoretic inputs were not all independently reproved. This focused acceptance does not certify a corrected complete argument.

Source, TeX, dependencies, logs, resulting PDF and rendered page images are bound by actual hashes in the accompanying records. Actual page-inspection receipts are separate from render-only records. Native assistance is attributed by task and coverage; it is not represented as human review or as an independently observed backend model. Scientific decision remains pending and the human-review array is empty.

analysis: Definition 4.2 and Lemma 4.7, page 20, assign the half-line Schrödinger operator \(Q\) the domain \(H^2_0((x_0,\infty))\) and assert self-adjointness. The preceding sentence explicitly defines \(H^k_0\) as the \(H^k\)-closure of compactly supported smooth functions. With this definition the domain is too small.

Choose \[M=m=1,\qquad e=0,\qquad x_0=2,\qquad
 \mathcal E_1=\mathcal E_2=0,\] and any sufficiently large integer \(L\). All the printed potential bounds are satisfied. The actual operator is then \[Qf=-f''+\left(-\frac2x+\frac{L(L+1)}{x^2}\right)f,\qquad
 D(Q)=H^2_0((2,\infty)).\] Continuity of the two endpoint trace maps on \(H^2\) implies \[f(2)=f'(2)=0\qquad(f\in D(Q)).\] If \(Qf=\lambda f\), the regular second-order equation \[f''=\left(-\frac2x+\frac{L(L+1)}{x^2}-\lambda\right)f\] has zero Cauchy data at \(2\). Uniqueness gives \(f\equiv0\). Thus this operator has no eigenfunctions, in direct contradiction to Lemma 4.8, page 21, which asserts infinitely many negative eigenvalues tending to zero.

Self-adjointness can also be refuted without any spectral calculation. Let \(g(x)=e^{-(x-2)}\). Both \(g\) and \[-g''+\left(-\frac2x+\frac{L(L+1)}{x^2}\right)g\] belong to \(L^2((2,\infty))\). Integration by parts against \(f\in H^2_0\) has no endpoint term because both traces of \(f\) vanish. Hence \(g\in D(Q^*)\). But \(g(2)=1\), so \(g\notin D(Q)\). Therefore \(Q\ne Q^*\).

This is a Major defect in a core spectral dependency. The stated operator cannot provide the eigenfunctions, min–max principle, eigenvalue sequence or spectral resolvent used in Section 4.2 and the later frequency decomposition. In particular, the quantitative eigenvalue comparison of Lemma 4.11, pages 22–23, is not an estimate for the operator actually defined.

The source also gives strong evidence for the intended correction: the shifted sine-transform argument in Lemma 4.8 describes the Dirichlet realization. Its domain is \[D(Q_D)=H^2((2,\infty))\cap H^1_0((2,\infty)),\] which imposes \(f(2)=0\) but not \(f'(2)=0\). Equivalently, one can specify the Friedrichs operator associated with the \(H^1_0\) quadratic form. For this bounded real potential the Dirichlet realization is self-adjoint. It can have the Coulomb-type negative spectrum. The present counterexample does not refute the spectral estimates for that corrected operator; they must be stated and used for it consistently.

A related definition must be repaired in the frequency subdivision. Where distance to the spectrum is intended, the quantity is \[\inf_n|m^2-\omega^2+\lambda_n|.\] A signed infimum instead equals \(m^2-\omega^2+\lambda_1\) for an increasing eigenvalue sequence. Its sublevel set contains an interval of algebraic width, rather than only the intended small neighborhoods of the individual eigenvalues. The later lemmas use the absolute distance, whereas Section 6 uses the small-measure decomposition. This is recorded as an additional consistency requirement within the same spectral dependency, not as a separate constructed resolvent-growth counterexample.

problems.title: Freezing an oscillatory horizon factor is not uniform
problems.source_location: p31 eq5.5 p32 Theorem5.1(4),eq5.10 p56 Section5.12 pp63,66 frozenfactors
claim: Recorded check: Freezing an oscillatory horizon factor is not uniform
analysis: Theorem 5.1(4), page 32, equation (5.10), evaluates the regular Green coefficients at \(\omega=m\). They contain \(u_H(m,s)\), while the error bounds explicitly hold for every \(s\leq s_{\max}\). The horizon normalization (5.5), page 31, makes these two requirements incompatible.

Fix a subextremal background and one sufficiently large \(L\); keep \(L\) fixed in the following threshold limit. Choose a real smooth cutoff \(\chi\) equal to \(1\) for \(s\leq0\) and \(0\) for \(s\geq1\). Define \[u(\omega,s)=\chi(s)u_H(\omega,s),\qquad
 H(\omega,s)=\chi''(s)u_H(\omega,s)
                 +2\chi'(s)\partial_su_H(\omega,s).\] Because \(u_H''=Vu_H\), one has \(u''-Vu=H\) exactly. Both \(H\) and \(\partial_\omega H\) are supported in \([0,1]\), and hence satisfy the theorem’s source support condition for any \(s_H>1\). On this fixed interval their norms are finite uniformly for \(m/2\leq\omega\leq m\), by the horizon Volterra construction away from zero frequency. In particular the printed quantity \(N[H]\) is finite at this fixed \(L\).

The solution is outgoing at the horizon and identically zero near infinity, an admissible decaying end condition for the inhomogeneous linear problem. A unit nonzero outgoing amplitude cannot be imposed on every inhomogeneous solution: it would exclude zero forcing and contradict the linear Green formula itself. If desired, a smooth frequency cutoff and conjugate reflection at negative frequencies give a real smooth physical source. The local theorem does not require time-compact support.

For \(s<0\), the two \(u^{\rm reg}_2\) integrals in (5.10) vanish. The two remaining regular terms depend on \(s\) only through \(u_H(m,s)\). Consequently the theorem implies \[u_H(\omega,s)=B_L(\omega)u_H(m,s)+R_L(\omega,s),
 \qquad
 \sup_{s<0}|R_L(\omega,s)|\leq C_LN[H]k^{-1/2},\] for some complex scalar \(B_L(\omega)\). Here \[k^{-2}=\frac{m^2-\omega^2}{(Mm^2)^2}.\] The constant \(C_L\) may be very large, but is finite and independent of \(\omega\) at fixed \(L\). Indeed the theorem states \[d_L:=1-|\Gamma(m,L)|>0,
 \qquad |1+\Gamma(m,L)e^{2i\vartheta}|\geq d_L.\] Thus the denominator and all bounded trigonometric factors can be absorbed into \(C_L\). No lower bound uniform in \(L\) is needed.

Equation (5.5) gives, for each fixed \(\omega\), \[u_H(\omega,s)=e^{-i\omega s}(1+o(1)),
 \qquad u_H(m,s)=e^{-ims}(1+o(1))
 \quad(s\longrightarrow-\infty).\] For every \(\omega\ne m\) and every \(B\in\mathbb C\), \[\limsup_{s\to-\infty}|u_H(\omega,s)-Bu_H(m,s)|
 =\max_{|z|=1}|z-B|=1+|B|\geq1.\] The phase \(e^{i(m-\omega)s}\) traverses the unit circle infinitely often. The two \(o(1)\) terms do not change this limit superior. But the claimed upper bound tends to zero as \(\omega\uparrow m\), since \(k\to\infty\). This is a contradiction with the theorem’s actual quantifiers.

The proof in Section 5.12, page 56, freezes all regular coefficients and invokes a frequency derivative bound. The unmodulated factor has a derivative whose leading term is \(-is e^{-i\omega s}\), which is not uniform on the stated half-line. Section 6 retains frozen factors multiplied by \(e^{i\omega p(s)}\). Near the horizon the residual factor is \(e^{i(\omega-m)s}\); multiplication by the horizon-penetrating Fourier phase does not remove the error.

This is a Major failure of the central uniform resolvent representation used for the announced decay up to the horizon. It is unaffected by Wronskian signs, by a correction of the action’s \(\pi\) normalization, or by keeping the source away from the horizon; the constructed source already has that support.

The appropriate regular object is \(e^{i\omega s}u_H(\omega,s)\), which tends to \(1\) at the horizon. The source uses such modulated derivatives elsewhere, providing evidence for an intended repair. One must retain \(e^{-i\omega s}\) and freeze only the regular amplitude, then re-establish both Green terms and the inverse-Fourier remainder estimates. Restricting \(s\) to a fixed bounded interval is a narrower repair that does not prove the claimed horizon-uniform result. No counterexample to the final physical decay rate is asserted.

problems.source_location: p42 eq5.36 p44 Cor5.8 p48 Cor5.13,eq5.45 p50 Lemma5.16,eq5.51 p54 Prop5.21
claim: Recorded check: The inverse connection has the wrong leading phase
analysis: Corollary 5.13, page 48, equation (5.45), gives a diagonal connection coefficient with phase \(e^{-i\pi/4}\). The forward expansion of Corollary 5.8, page 44, and the exact Wronskian normalization (5.36), page 42, require \(e^{+i\pi/4}\).

Write \[A=u_{Ai_2},\quad B=u_{Bi_2},\quad
 c=(Mm^2)^{1/2}\pi^{-1/2}\mathbb L^{-2/3},
 \quad F_+=A-iB,\quad F_-=A+iB.\] The paper’s convention is \(W(f,g)=f'g-fg'\). Its exact normalization is \(W(A,B)=c^2\), hence \[W(F_+,F_-)=2ic^2.\] The oscillatory solutions satisfy \(W(B_+,B_-)=2i\). Corollary 5.8 and the proof of Corollary 5.13 give \[F_-=c\,e^{i\pi/4}B_-+cR_-,
 \qquad
 W(B_+,R_-)=O(e^{-\kappa_+A_0}+\mathbb L^{-1}),\] where \(A_0\) denotes the paper’s large matching parameter, distinguished here from the Airy solution \(A\).

The same phase is carried into Lemma 5.16, page 50. With the source’s real-basis definitions, \[w_{\rm even}=\Re(e^{i\pi/4}w_{2,+}),\qquad
 w_{\rm odd}=-\Im(e^{i\pi/4}w_{2,+}),\] the corrected leading connection gives \[w_{\rm even}\sim c^{-1}B,\qquad
 w_{\rm odd}\sim-c^{-1}A,\] rather than the printed \(c^{-1}A,c^{-1}B\). The leading sine and cosine roles in Proposition 5.21, page 54, therefore rotate. The subsequent Wronskian and narrow-resonance formula must be recomputed with one consistent phase convention. A fixed \(\pi/2\) shift cannot be absorbed into the stated \(\phi_3=O(k^{-1})\).

This is a Major error in the central matching calculation. The bounded repair begins by conjugating the leading diagonal phases in (5.45), followed by propagation through the real basis, connection coefficients and resonant phase. A global basis convention could also be changed, but would require changing the already fixed Airy normalization and all dependent formulas consistently. The conserved flux calculation supplies useful contrary evidence: with a consistent basis, it still enforces the correct modulus gap \(1-|\Gamma|>0\). The existence of a gap and the general tunneling mechanism are not refuted by the phase error. Nor does this calculation alone determine that the final polynomial decay exponent changes.

problems.title: A quadratic source quantity cannot bound a linear response
problems.source_location: p12 Proposition3.2 p62 Proposition6.6 and Lemma6.7 pp68-69 final Theorem1.2 proof
claim: Recorded check: A quadratic source quantity cannot bound a linear response
analysis: Proposition 6.6, page 62, defines its quantity \(\mathcal D[H]\) as a supremum of weighted squared source integrals, without a square root. Its Fourier-response bound is linear in \(u\) but multiplies \(\mathcal D[H]\) once. There is no unit-source normalization or lower bound on \(\mathcal D\). The same mismatch occurs in Proposition 3.2, page 12, and Lemma 6.7, page 62.

Both end amplitudes vanish, so \(u_0\) lies in the linear outgoing subspaces used by the paper’s Green formula. This convention is material: if the earlier symbol \(\sim\) were instead read as requiring unit amplitude at both ends for every inhomogeneous solution, it would conflict with that linear formula, the zero source and the final application to arbitrary initial data. The present construction uses the source-to-solution interpretation actually required in those applications, not a hidden unit-amplitude restriction.

The final proof on pages 68–69 explicitly invokes Proposition 6.6 and Lemma 6.15 for the time-cutoff source \(F=2\nabla\chi\cdot\nabla\phi+(\Box\chi)\phi\). For actual compactly supported smooth initial data, a fixed smooth cutoff and finite propagation preserve linear scaling: \(\phi,F,H,u\) scale by \(\varepsilon\), whereas \(\mathcal D\) scales by \(\varepsilon^2\). A nonzero compact exterior single-mode solution at a fixed finite time can be chosen by finite-time Cauchy evolution. Its cutoff source is supported in a compact radial region during the transition, so its Fourier source has finite \(\mathcal D\). The outgoing and Fourier-inversion interpretation here is the one imported in the paper’s final proof; that external scattering theorem is not independently rederived in this review. The explicit construction above already refutes the stated general-source estimate. The final claim that the same quadratic \(\mathcal D\) is bounded by a first-power Sobolev norm also fails under large-amplitude scaling whenever \(\mathcal D>0\).

This is a Major defect in a core estimate, grouped as one problem across its repeated uses. Proposition 3.1 has a squared left side and supplies contrary evidence for the intended homogeneity. Taking a square root of the quadratic quantity restores necessary linear scaling, but does not certify the complete repair: frequency and angular weights and all subsequent estimates must be checked again. For example, the displayed \(\omega^8\) bound in Proposition 3.1, combined only with the \((1+\omega^{10})\) weight before taking square roots, gives a coarse \(\omega^{-1}\) derivative bound, insufficient by itself for the high-frequency \(L^1_\omega\) step in Lemma 6.7. Stronger weights or finer estimates are needed there. The final theorem has a first-power data norm and is not itself refuted by this scaling argument.

report: Abstract: The acquired preprint proves a structural-coefficient version of Berthelot’s conjecture by a motivic realization and comparison with classical rigid cohomology. Three proof dependencies fail as written: a formal open immersion is used as an algebraic immersion, a formal-model indexing functor is asserted to be final despite a disconnected comma category, and an incorrect torus realization is used to justify stabilization. Explicit admissible examples and a split-cofiber calculation establish these Major proof defects. They do not constitute counterexamples to the final Berthelot theorem or to the intended pushforward compatibility. Two additional local assertions concerning dagger neighborhoods and a terminal object have bounded corrections. The scope of the all-frame comparison also requires clarification. Scientific adjudication remains pending; no human review is asserted.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Berthelot’s Conjecture via Homotopy Theory:
Review of the Acquired Preprint
# Exact source and scope of the claim

The work reviewed is Berthelot’s conjecture via homotopy theory, by Veronika Ertl and Alberto Vezzani [paper], associated with DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0021. The actual source is the 34-page arXiv:2406.02182v2 dated 1 April 2025. The corresponding author TeX was read as source, not executed. The publisher PDF was not obtained through the attempted authorized route. The journal metadata identifies a 54-page article; equivalence to that version is not assumed. All locations below refer to one-based pages of the acquired PDF, which agree with the printed pagination on the inspected pages.

Fix a perfect field \(k\) of characteristic \(p>0\) and \(K=W(k)[1/p]\). For a smooth proper morphism \(f:X\to S\), the main theorem on page 2 and Corollary 3.45 on page 25 claim that the structural-coefficient groups \[R^q f_{\mathrm{rig}*}\bigl(X/(T,\overline T,\mathfrak P)\bigr),
 \qquad q\geq0,\] as the proper frames over \(S\) vary, are realizations of a canonical overconvergent \(F\)-isocrystal. They are asserted to be vector bundles on every such frame, including frames not assumed smooth. The theorem does not establish preservation of arbitrary overconvergent coefficient objects. Remark 3.49, pages 25–26, explicitly postpones the classical comparison for coefficients of motivic origin; its proposed use of Proposition A.13 is conditional on a further equivalence of coefficient categories.

The main dependency chain is the dagger de Rham realization (Proposition 2.22), locally free cohomology of dualizable motives (Corollary 2.24), the Monsky–Washnitzer realization (Propositions 3.9–3.10), its Frobenius enhancement (Proposition 3.18 and Corollary 3.19), and the comparison with Berthelot’s complex (Propositions 3.33 and 3.39). The appendix investigates a separate pushforward compatibility. This distinction is essential when assessing the three Major findings.
# A formal open is not the asserted scheme immersion

Problem 1 (The algebraization step in Proposition 3.39).  Step 2 of Proposition 3.39, pages 22–23, takes \(\mathfrak T=\operatorname{Spf}A\subseteq\mathfrak T'=\operatorname{Spf}A'\) and a smooth \(A\)-algebra \[R=A[X_1,\ldots,X_M]/(f_1,\ldots,f_m).\] It then asserts that the chosen presentation gives an embedding \(\operatorname{Spec}R\subset\mathbb P^M_{A'}\), and uses its schematic closure to construct a geometric materialization. That embedding need not exist.
## A counterexample satisfying the local hypotheses

Take \(k=\mathbb F_p\) and \[A'=\mathbb Z_p\langle t\rangle,\qquad
 A=\mathbb Z_p\langle t,t^{-1}\rangle.\] The formal scheme \(\operatorname{Spf}A\) is the principal formal open \(D(\bar t)\) of \(\operatorname{Spf}A'\). Both are reduced, and \(A'\) is the ring of power-bounded functions on the rigid closed unit disc \(\mathfrak T'_{\mathbb Q_p}\). Thus the special hypotheses of Step 1, retained in Step 2, hold. Choose the identity smooth object over \(\mathfrak T\). It has \(R=A\), with no variables or relations, so \(M=0\). The claimed embedding becomes \[\operatorname{Spec}A\longrightarrow\mathbb P^0_{A'}=\operatorname{Spec}A'.\] This morphism is not an immersion.

Here is a direct algebraic verification. The convergent Laurent series \[z=\sum_{n\geq1}p^n t^{-n^2}\] belongs to \(A\). Suppose that \(z\in\operatorname{Frac}(A')\). There would then be a nonzero \(g=\sum_{j\geq0}g_jt^j\in A'\) with \(gz\in A'\). Put \[a=\min_j v_p(g_j),\qquad v_p(g_d)=a\] for some index \(d\). If \(2n>d+1\), the coefficient of \(t^{d-n^2}\) in \(gz\) is \[p^n g_d+\sum_{m>n}p^m g_{\,d-n^2+m^2}.\] All terms with \(m<n\) vanish because their \(g\)-index is negative. The first displayed term has valuation \(a+n\), whereas the remaining sum lies in \(p^{a+n+1}\mathbb Z_p\). This coefficient is therefore nonzero. For arbitrarily large \(n\) its exponent is negative. Consequently \(gz\) cannot belong to \(A'\), a contradiction.

Thus \[\operatorname{Frac}(A')\subsetneq\operatorname{Frac}(A).\] Both rings are domains and the generic point of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) maps to the generic point of \(\operatorname{Spec}A'\). An immersion induces an isomorphism on the residue field at each point of its image. The strict generic-field extension therefore excludes the asserted immersion.
## Impact, contrary evidence and repair boundary

This is a Major defect in the supplied comparison proof. The false embedding is the stated construction that realizes the local generators as geometric materializations. Step 3 then glues the comparisons obtained in Step 2, and Corollary 3.43 and the proof of Corollary 3.45 invoke this comparison. The issue affects an essential derivation of the principal result, even if a correct replacement can be supplied.

There is substantial contrary evidence to any stronger conclusion. The formal open immersion in the example is perfectly valid. It can have a different geometric materialization. Moreover, Remark 3.42 on page 24 supplies an alternative comparison route when the generic fiber is smooth, as it is in this example. The calculation does not disprove the comparison functor or the Berthelot conclusion.

A repair must distinguish completed formal localization from ordinary algebraic localization. One possible route is an appropriate weak algebraization or an algebraic model before completion, followed by a justified compactification. Another is an independent local comparison with its descent and pullback compatibilities proved. Merely replacing embedding by morphism does not establish that the stated schematic-closure construction has all the required geometric-materialization properties. The general reduced-base argument still needs an actual replacement.
# The formal-model functor is not final

Problem 2 (The projective-line branch of Proposition A.13).  The proof of Proposition A.13, page 31, asserts that, for \(X=\mathbb P^1_S\), the functor \[r:\mathrm{FSch}/S\longrightarrow\mathrm{FSch}/X,
 \qquad \mathfrak T\longmapsto\widehat{\mathbb P}^1_{\mathfrak T},\] is final. Here a formal model over \(X\) has a map of its reduced special fiber to \(X\), rather than a specified lift of that map to a formal projective line. This distinction makes the assertion false.
## An explicitly disconnected comma category

Set \[k=\mathbb F_p,\qquad S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_p,\qquad
 B=\operatorname{Spf}\mathbb Z_p,\qquad X=\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_p}.\] Let \(Y=B\) be an object of \(\mathrm{FSch}/X\) by sending its special fiber to \(\infty=[1:0]\). These formal schemes satisfy the paper’s conventions at the start of Section 3. For any formal \(\mathbb Z_p\)-scheme \(\mathfrak T\), let \[q_{\mathfrak T}:\widehat{\mathbb P}^1_{\mathfrak T}
       \longrightarrow\widehat{\mathbb P}^1_B\] be the structural map. An object of the comma category \((Y/r)\) is a map \(a:Y\to\widehat{\mathbb P}^1_{\mathfrak T}\) reducing to the prescribed special-fiber map. Attach to it the invariant \[h(\mathfrak T,a)=q_{\mathfrak T}\circ a.\] If \(b:(\mathfrak T,a)\to(\mathfrak T',a')\) is a comma morphism, then \(\widehat{\mathbb P}^1(b)\circ a=a'\), hence \[q_{\mathfrak T}\circ a
   =q_{\mathfrak T'}\circ\widehat{\mathbb P}^1(b)\circ a
   =q_{\mathfrak T'}\circ a'.\] The invariant is unchanged along every arrow and every zigzag.

Now take \(\mathfrak T=B\) and the two sections \[a_0=[1:0],\qquad a_p=[1:p].\] They both reduce to \(\infty\), but their invariants differ. On the formal chart with coordinate \(u=X_1/X_0\), they are the continuous homomorphisms \(\mathbb Z_p\langle u\rangle\to\mathbb Z_p\) sending \(u\) to \(0\) and \(p\), respectively. Thus the comma category has at least two connected components and its nerve is not contractible. In fact, within each fixed invariant \(h\), the object \((B,h)\) is terminal, since \(\mathfrak T\to B\) is the unique structural map. The defect is precisely the multiplicity of lifts.

This also checks the variance. The displayed coefficient diagrams are indexed contravariantly. Initiality of \(r^{\mathrm{op}}\), needed for their limit restriction, is equivalent to finality of \(r\). Taking the opposite of the disconnected comma category does not make its nerve contractible.
## Impact and the limit of the counterexample

This is a Major issue in the appendix’s algebraic pushforward comparison. The proof uses the asserted finality to assemble the projective-line calculation over formal bases and identify the resulting object in the limit category. A false categorical reduction cannot support that identification without an additional argument.

The example does not contradict the preceding rigid-analytic Proposition A.11: there the full map to the rigid projective line is already fixed. Nor does it contradict the étale branch of Proposition A.13, where formal étaleness supplies unique lifting. The two sections can be joined by the formal family \([1:pt]\). This is relevant evidence that a suitable homotopy-based proof may work, but it is not a zigzag of the asserted comma category. Localization inside the category of motives does not by itself prove finality of the ordinary formal-scheme indexing functor.

A valid repair could prove that the particular diagrams and comparison maps are invariant under those homotopies, or could work with chosen compatible lifts and then establish descent between them. The present computation does not show that the conclusion of Proposition A.13 is false. It also does not independently refute Corollary 3.45: that theorem is proved earlier without this appendix. The sole earlier reference to Proposition A.13 in Remark 3.49 concerns a future coefficient comparison with additional hypotheses.
# Further findings on dagger realization

Problem 3 (Smooth surjectivity does not remove the relative boundary).  Remark 2.7, page 5, asserts that a smooth surjective dagger morphism can be straightened with \(X_h=X_0\times_{S_0}S_h\), using \(\operatorname{Int}(X_0/K)=f_0^{-1}\operatorname{Int}(S_0/K)\).

Take the standard dagger closed unit disc over \(K=\mathbb C_p\) mapping to the point \(S=\operatorname{Spa}K\). This is a smooth surjective morphism of affinoid dagger varieties. The point has a cofinal constant presentation. The claimed formula would make its source presentation constant as well. But no fixed strict outer neighborhood of the closed unit disc is cofinal among its strict neighborhoods: if it contains a closed disc of radius \(\rho>1\), a smaller radius \(1<\rho'<\rho\) gives a strict neighborhood not containing that outer disc. Equivalently, the boundary of a closed outer disc does not lie in its interior over \(K\), although it lies in the inverse image of the interior of the point.

The cited Corollary A.11 of Vezzani [vezzani], actually checked in the acquired reference, instead contains \[\operatorname{Int}(X/S)=\operatorname{Int}(X/Y)\cap f^{-1}\operatorname{Int}(Y/S).\] The missing relative-interior factor cannot be discarded from smoothness alone. Partial properness is an appropriate condition for the boundary term to disappear, but an arbitrary smooth affinoid disc is not partially proper. This is Minor in the present dependency assessment: no essential later use of this false stationary straightening was identified, and Remark 2.20 retains shrinking source neighborhoods. Remove the assertion or give the required boundary hypothesis. The main realization is not disproved by this example.

Problem 4 (The unreduced torus does not realize to the unit).  In Step 2 of the proof of Proposition 2.22, page 9, the realization of the dagger torus \(\mathbb T^{1\dagger}\) is identified with the unit. The torus of Example 2.3 is the unreduced space, whereas the Tate object in Definition 2.14 is a cofiber.

Over \(\mathbb Q_p\), put \(A=\mathbb Q_p\langle T,T^{-1}\rangle^\dagger\). The complex is \[A\xrightarrow{\,d\,}A\,dT.\] Every exact form has residue zero, while \(dT/T\) has residue one. The kernel consists of constants. Conversely, a residue-zero overconvergent Laurent form has an overconvergent primitive after shrinking the annulus: division by a nonzero integer causes at most polynomial coefficient growth, which is absorbed by the available exponential decay. Thus \[H^0=\mathbb Q_p,\qquad H^1=\mathbb Q_p[dT/T],
 \qquad \operatorname{dR}(\mathbb T^{1\dagger})\simeq\mathbf1\oplus\mathbf1[-1].\] The cited Le Bras–Vezzani Corollary 4.37(6) gives this two-summand formula, not the displayed unit [lbv].

This is a Major defect in the supplied stabilization argument. Write \(M=\mathbb Q(\mathbb T^{1\dagger})\) and \(T_{\mathrm{red}}=\operatorname{cofib}(e:\mathbf1\to M)\). The unit section \(e\) has a retraction \(p:M\to\mathbf1\), with \(pe=\mathrm{id}\). Contravariant realization therefore identifies \(\operatorname{dR}(T_{\mathrm{red}})\) with \(\operatorname{fib}(\operatorname{dR}(e):\operatorname{dR}(M)\to\mathbf1)\). Under the printed equality \(\operatorname{dR}(M)\simeq\mathbf1\), this split epimorphism is an isomorphism over \(\operatorname{Spa}\mathbb Q_p\): its endomorphisms are scalars in \(\mathbb Q_p\). The resulting fiber would be zero, which is not tensor-invertible. Thus the stated computation cannot justify the ensuing extension to the stabilized category in Proposition 2.22. This proposition is an actual input to the main realization and comparison chain.

The corrected two-summand calculation instead gives \(\operatorname{dR}(T_{\mathrm{red}})\simeq\mathbf1[-1]\), which is tensor-invertible and supplies the required stabilization argument. This explicit repair is substantial counterevidence to any claim that the intended realization or the main theorem is false. It does not remove the core proof defect in the displayed argument or certify all the remaining comparison steps.

Problem 5 (Properness does not give the stated terminal object).  Remark 2.27, page 10, calls the canonical dagger structure of a proper rigid variety \(S\) terminal in \(\mathrm{Ad}^{\dagger}_{/S}\). Definition 2.25 allows an arbitrary analytic map from the completed source, which need not extend to a dagger map.

Take \(S=\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb Q_p}\), the dagger unit disc \(T^\dagger\), and the analytic map into the affine chart given by \[f(T)=\sum_{n\geq1}p^nT^{n!}.\] It converges on the closed unit disc, but its radius of convergence is exactly one, since \(p^{-n/n!}\to1\). A morphism to the alleged terminal object would extend \(f\) to a map from some larger closed disc to \(\mathbb P^1\). Such a map is a meromorphic function with finitely many poles on that affinoid disc: the inverse image of infinity is a proper zero-dimensional analytic subset of a one-dimensional affinoid. There are no poles on the unit disc. A slightly larger radius therefore avoids all poles and gives an analytic extension of \(f\), contradicting its convergence radius.

The ordinary rigid category \(\mathrm{Ad}_{/S}\) does have its identity as terminal object. The actual proof of Corollary 2.28 on page 11 begins with that ordinary category and then applies the forgetful restriction; it does not require the false dagger terminal assertion. This is therefore a Minor local categorical correction in the reviewed proof chain. Deleting Remark 2.27, or restricting the objects to maps admitting a dagger extension, resolves this particular obstruction.
# Positive checks and remaining boundaries

The definition immediately preceding Corollary 2.24 is important: \(\mathrm{Vect}\) consists of perfect complexes with locally free cohomology, not just objects in degree zero. Shifts of dualizable motives are therefore not counterexamples. For the actual mixed-characteristic application, the argument first obtains perfectness by monoidal duality, then invokes faithfully flat dagger completion and the locally free cohomology theorem of Le Bras–Vezzani. The latter’s Theorem 4.46 is explicitly stated over \(\mathbb Q_p\). The more general characteristic-zero formulation in Section 2 needs an extension of that cited input if equal-residue-characteristic zero is intended; this is a scope request, not a counterexample to its Witt-vector application.

The duality convention is also consistent: \[(f_*M)^\vee\simeq f_\sharp(M^\vee)\] for smooth proper \(f\). Consequently applying the dualized realization to \(f_*\mathbf1\) supplies the intended cohomological realization of \(f_\sharp\mathbf1\). The Frobenius construction uses invariance under universal homeomorphisms and the semilinear Witt-vector Frobenius. It does not require \(k=\mathbb F_p\) or an identity Frobenius on an arbitrary perfect field.

The proof does not silently assume that the underlying-module functor \(u\) is always \(t\)-exact. Remark 3.44 explicitly warns against that inference. In Corollary 3.45, local splitting of a perfect complex with projective cohomology is the stated justification for comparing the ordinary cohomology groups.

A separate Needs Evidence boundary remains: Proposition 3.39 assumes reduced formal schemes and a reduced generic fiber, and Corollary 3.43 is explicitly for proper reduced frames. Corollary 3.45 then says every proper frame. The review did not locate an explicit reduction or nilpotent base-change argument covering this change of scope. No admissible counterexample to the resulting rigid-cohomology claim has been established. A nonreduced base alone is insufficient to produce one: the identity smooth proper family still realizes the free rank-one module. The report therefore requests the missing reduction or the intended frame convention, rather than classifying the broad theorem as false.
# Assessment and verification limits

The three Major findings concern essential supplied derivations: the formal-to-algebraic construction in Proposition 3.39, the finality reduction in Proposition A.13, and the stabilization step in Proposition 2.22. Each has a proven bounded failure, an exact source location, counterevidence against a wider negative conclusion, and a specified repair boundary. The two Minor findings concern the relative-boundary and terminal-object assertions; no essential downstream use of those assertions was identified. Neither local repairability nor survival of the paper’s main conclusion is being used as a rule for downgrading a core defect.

Native AI helpers performed bounded readings of Section 2, Section 3 and Appendix A, together with actual source-page inspection and selected primary-reference checks. The initial primary reviewer checked the two original core counterexamples and the principal scope distinctions. The accompanying records distinguish these roles; no helper is represented as a human reviewer, an independently observed backend model, or independent acceptance.

The acquisition includes author TeX and available metadata. No paper-specific computational supplement or code was identified in the available searches. The publisher’s supplementary route could not be fully inspected after its access challenge. These are access limitations, not mathematical defects. No author code or author TeX was executed. The imported motivic, solid-module and classical rigid-cohomology theorems were not all independently reproved.

The current TeX, actual compiler, preserved dependencies, logs, PDF and page images are bound by real hashes in the delivery records. Render-only receipts retain their original false inspection status; actual image inspections are recorded separately. The scientific decision remains pending, the human-review array is empty, and this report does not certify a repaired proof.
