problems.title: The algebraization step in Proposition 3.39
problems.source_location: Proposition 3.39 Step 2, PDF pp22–23; exact embedding assertion p23
claim: Recorded check: The algebraization step in Proposition 3.39
analysis: Step 2 of Proposition 3.39, pages 22–23, takes \(\mathfrak T=\operatorname{Spf}A\subseteq\mathfrak T'=\operatorname{Spf}A'\) and a smooth \(A\)-algebra \[R=A[X_1,\ldots,X_M]/(f_1,\ldots,f_m).\] It then asserts that the chosen presentation gives an embedding \(\operatorname{Spec}R\subset\mathbb P^M_{A'}\), and uses its schematic closure to construct a geometric materialization. That embedding need not exist.

Take \(k=\mathbb F_p\) and \[A'=\mathbb Z_p\langle t\rangle,\qquad
 A=\mathbb Z_p\langle t,t^{-1}\rangle.\] The formal scheme \(\operatorname{Spf}A\) is the principal formal open \(D(\bar t)\) of \(\operatorname{Spf}A'\). Both are reduced, and \(A'\) is the ring of power-bounded functions on the rigid closed unit disc \(\mathfrak T'_{\mathbb Q_p}\). Thus the special hypotheses of Step 1, retained in Step 2, hold. Choose the identity smooth object over \(\mathfrak T\). It has \(R=A\), with no variables or relations, so \(M=0\). The claimed embedding becomes \[\operatorname{Spec}A\longrightarrow\mathbb P^0_{A'}=\operatorname{Spec}A'.\] This morphism is not an immersion.

Here is a direct algebraic verification. The convergent Laurent series \[z=\sum_{n\geq1}p^n t^{-n^2}\] belongs to \(A\). Suppose that \(z\in\operatorname{Frac}(A')\). There would then be a nonzero \(g=\sum_{j\geq0}g_jt^j\in A'\) with \(gz\in A'\). Put \[a=\min_j v_p(g_j),\qquad v_p(g_d)=a\] for some index \(d\). If \(2n>d+1\), the coefficient of \(t^{d-n^2}\) in \(gz\) is \[p^n g_d+\sum_{m>n}p^m g_{\,d-n^2+m^2}.\] All terms with \(m<n\) vanish because their \(g\)-index is negative. The first displayed term has valuation \(a+n\), whereas the remaining sum lies in \(p^{a+n+1}\mathbb Z_p\). This coefficient is therefore nonzero. For arbitrarily large \(n\) its exponent is negative. Consequently \(gz\) cannot belong to \(A'\), a contradiction.

Thus \[\operatorname{Frac}(A')\subsetneq\operatorname{Frac}(A).\] Both rings are domains and the generic point of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) maps to the generic point of \(\operatorname{Spec}A'\). An immersion induces an isomorphism on the residue field at each point of its image. The strict generic-field extension therefore excludes the asserted immersion.

This is a Major defect in the supplied comparison proof. The false embedding is the stated construction that realizes the local generators as geometric materializations. Step 3 then glues the comparisons obtained in Step 2, and Corollary 3.43 and the proof of Corollary 3.45 invoke this comparison. The issue affects an essential derivation of the principal result, even if a correct replacement can be supplied.

There is substantial contrary evidence to any stronger conclusion. The formal open immersion in the example is perfectly valid. It can have a different geometric materialization. Moreover, Remark 3.42 on page 24 supplies an alternative comparison route when the generic fiber is smooth, as it is in this example. The calculation does not disprove the comparison functor or the Berthelot conclusion.

A repair must distinguish completed formal localization from ordinary algebraic localization. One possible route is an appropriate weak algebraization or an algebraic model before completion, followed by a justified compactification. Another is an independent local comparison with its descent and pullback compatibilities proved. Merely replacing embedding by morphism does not establish that the stated schematic-closure construction has all the required geometric-materialization properties. The general reduced-base argument still needs an actual replacement.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterexample: Take A'=Z_p<t>, A=Z_p<t,t^-1>, R=A and M=0. These are reduced formal affinoids with Spf A the formal principal open in Spf A', and A'=O^+(T'_Qp). The series z=sum_(n>=1)p^n t^(-n^2) is in A. For any nonzero g=sum g_jt^j in A', choose a=min v_p(g_j), v_p(g_d)=a. For 2n>d+1 the coefficient of t^(d-n^2) in gz equals p^n g_d modulo p^(a+n+1), hence is nonzero. Thus gz has infinitely many negative exponents and cannot be in A'. Therefore z notin Frac(A'), and Spec A→Spec A' has a strict generic residue-field extension, impossible for an immersion.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The formal open exists, its identity object has a different materialization, and Remark3.42 provides an alternate smooth-generic-fiber route for this example. No false final theorem follows.

problems.title: The projective-line branch of Proposition A.13
problems.source_location: Proposition A.13 proof, PDF p31; FSch/S definition p13 and formal conventions p12
claim: Recorded check: The projective-line branch of Proposition A.13
analysis:
The proof of Proposition A.13, page 31, asserts that, for \(X=\mathbb P^1_S\), the functor \[r:\mathrm{FSch}/S\longrightarrow\mathrm{FSch}/X,
 \qquad \mathfrak T\longmapsto\widehat{\mathbb P}^1_{\mathfrak T},\] is final. Here a formal model over \(X\) has a map of its reduced special fiber to \(X\), rather than a specified lift of that map to a formal projective line. This distinction makes the assertion false.

Set \[k=\mathbb F_p,\qquad S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_p,\qquad
 B=\operatorname{Spf}\mathbb Z_p,\qquad X=\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_p}.\] Let \(Y=B\) be an object of \(\mathrm{FSch}/X\) by sending its special fiber to \(\infty=[1:0]\). These formal schemes satisfy the paper’s conventions at the start of Section 3. For any formal \(\mathbb Z_p\)-scheme \(\mathfrak T\), let \[q_{\mathfrak T}:\widehat{\mathbb P}^1_{\mathfrak T}
       \longrightarrow\widehat{\mathbb P}^1_B\] be the structural map. An object of the comma category \((Y/r)\) is a map \(a:Y\to\widehat{\mathbb P}^1_{\mathfrak T}\) reducing to the prescribed special-fiber map. Attach to it the invariant \[h(\mathfrak T,a)=q_{\mathfrak T}\circ a.\] If \(b:(\mathfrak T,a)\to(\mathfrak T',a')\) is a comma morphism, then \(\widehat{\mathbb P}^1(b)\circ a=a'\), hence \[q_{\mathfrak T}\circ a
   =q_{\mathfrak T'}\circ\widehat{\mathbb P}^1(b)\circ a
   =q_{\mathfrak T'}\circ a'.\] The invariant is unchanged along every arrow and every zigzag.

Now take \(\mathfrak T=B\) and the two sections \[a_0=[1:0],\qquad a_p=[1:p].\] They both reduce to \(\infty\), but their invariants differ. On the formal chart with coordinate \(u=X_1/X_0\), they are the continuous homomorphisms \(\mathbb Z_p\langle u\rangle\to\mathbb Z_p\) sending \(u\) to \(0\) and \(p\), respectively. Thus the comma category has at least two connected components and its nerve is not contractible. In fact, within each fixed invariant \(h\), the object \((B,h)\) is terminal, since \(\mathfrak T\to B\) is the unique structural map. The defect is precisely the multiplicity of lifts.

This also checks the variance. The displayed coefficient diagrams are indexed contravariantly. Initiality of \(r^{\mathrm{op}}\), needed for their limit restriction, is equivalent to finality of \(r\). Taking the opposite of the disconnected comma category does not make its nerve contractible.

This is a Major issue in the appendix’s algebraic pushforward comparison. The proof uses the asserted finality to assemble the projective-line calculation over formal bases and identify the resulting object in the limit category. A false categorical reduction cannot support that identification without an additional argument.

The example does not contradict the preceding rigid-analytic Proposition A.11: there the full map to the rigid projective line is already fixed. Nor does it contradict the étale branch of Proposition A.13, where formal étaleness supplies unique lifting. The two sections can be joined by the formal family \([1:pt]\). This is relevant evidence that a suitable homotopy-based proof may work, but it is not a zigzag of the asserted comma category. Localization inside the category of motives does not by itself prove finality of the ordinary formal-scheme indexing functor.

A valid repair could prove that the particular diagrams and comparison maps are invariant under those homotopies, or could work with chosen compatible lifts and then establish descent between them. The present computation does not show that the conclusion of Proposition A.13 is false. It also does not independently refute Corollary 3.45: that theorem is proved earlier without this appendix. The sole earlier reference to Proposition A.13 in Remark 3.49 concerns a future coefficient comparison with additional hypotheses.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterexample: Let k=F_p,S=Spec k,Y=B=Spf Z_p with special fiber at infinity in P1_k. For an object (T,a) of (Y/r), r(T)=formal P1_T, the composite h=q_T∘a:Y→formal P1_B is invariant under every comma arrow and zigzag. Sections [1:0] and [1:p] reduce to the same prescribed infinity and have distinct h. The comma nerve has ≥2 components. Opposites preserve this failure, so the contravariant-limit variance does not repair finality.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Fixed-map rigid A.11 and uniquely lifted etale branch are not contradicted. Cor3.45's main proof does not use A.13. [1:pt] is a formal homotopy, so an alternative localized proof may work.

problems.title: Smooth surjectivity does not remove the relative boundary
problems.source_location: Remark2.7 PDF p5
claim: Recorded check: Smooth surjectivity does not remove the relative boundary
analysis: Remark 2.7, page 5, asserts that a smooth surjective dagger morphism can be straightened with \(X_h=X_0\times_{S_0}S_h\), using \(\operatorname{Int}(X_0/K)=f_0^{-1}\operatorname{Int}(S_0/K)\).

Take the standard dagger closed unit disc over \(K=\mathbb C_p\) mapping to the point \(S=\operatorname{Spa}K\). This is a smooth surjective morphism of affinoid dagger varieties. The point has a cofinal constant presentation. The claimed formula would make its source presentation constant as well. But no fixed strict outer neighborhood of the closed unit disc is cofinal among its strict neighborhoods: if it contains a closed disc of radius \(\rho>1\), a smaller radius \(1<\rho'<\rho\) gives a strict neighborhood not containing that outer disc. Equivalently, the boundary of a closed outer disc does not lie in its interior over \(K\), although it lies in the inverse image of the interior of the point.

The cited Corollary A.11 of Vezzani [vezzani], actually checked in the acquired reference, instead contains \[\operatorname{Int}(X/S)=\operatorname{Int}(X/Y)\cap f^{-1}\operatorname{Int}(Y/S).\] The missing relative-interior factor cannot be discarded from smoothness alone. Partial properness is an appropriate condition for the boundary term to disappear, but an arbitrary smooth affinoid disc is not partially proper. This is Minor in the present dependency assessment: no essential later use of this false stationary straightening was identified, and Remark 2.20 retains shrinking source neighborhoods. Remove the assertion or give the required boundary hypothesis. The main realization is not disproved by this example.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterexample: The standard dagger closed disc over Spa C_p is smooth surjective. The base has constant cofinal presentation, but no fixed strict outer disc is cofinal among decreasing strict outer neighborhoods. Its boundary is excluded from Int(X0/K) but is in the inverse image of Int(point/K). The cited formula has additional factor Int(X/Y).
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Remark2.20 uses genuinely shrinking source neighborhoods, so no failure of the realization theorem is established.

problems.title: The unreduced torus does not realize to the unit
problems.source_location: Proposition2.22 proof Step2 PDF p9; Example2.3 p5 and Definition2.14 pp6–7
claim: Recorded check: The unreduced torus does not realize to the unit
analysis: In Step 2 of the proof of Proposition 2.22, page 9, the realization of the dagger torus \(\mathbb T^{1\dagger}\) is identified with the unit. The torus of Example 2.3 is the unreduced space, whereas the Tate object in Definition 2.14 is a cofiber.

Over \(\mathbb Q_p\), put \(A=\mathbb Q_p\langle T,T^{-1}\rangle^\dagger\). The complex is \[A\xrightarrow{\,d\,}A\,dT.\] Every exact form has residue zero, while \(dT/T\) has residue one. The kernel consists of constants. Conversely, a residue-zero overconvergent Laurent form has an overconvergent primitive after shrinking the annulus: division by a nonzero integer causes at most polynomial coefficient growth, which is absorbed by the available exponential decay. Thus \[H^0=\mathbb Q_p,\qquad H^1=\mathbb Q_p[dT/T],
 \qquad \operatorname{dR}(\mathbb T^{1\dagger})\simeq\mathbf1\oplus\mathbf1[-1].\] The cited Le Bras–Vezzani Corollary 4.37(6) gives this two-summand formula, not the displayed unit [lbv].

This is a Major defect in the supplied stabilization argument. Write \(M=\mathbb Q(\mathbb T^{1\dagger})\) and \(T_{\mathrm{red}}=\operatorname{cofib}(e:\mathbf1\to M)\). The unit section \(e\) has a retraction \(p:M\to\mathbf1\), with \(pe=\mathrm{id}\). Contravariant realization therefore identifies \(\operatorname{dR}(T_{\mathrm{red}})\) with \(\operatorname{fib}(\operatorname{dR}(e):\operatorname{dR}(M)\to\mathbf1)\). Under the printed equality \(\operatorname{dR}(M)\simeq\mathbf1\), this split epimorphism is an isomorphism over \(\operatorname{Spa}\mathbb Q_p\): its endomorphisms are scalars in \(\mathbb Q_p\). The resulting fiber would be zero, which is not tensor-invertible. Thus the stated computation cannot justify the ensuing extension to the stabilized category in Proposition 2.22. This proposition is an actual input to the main realization and comparison chain.

The corrected two-summand calculation instead gives \(\operatorname{dR}(T_{\mathrm{red}})\simeq\mathbf1[-1]\), which is tensor-invertible and supplies the required stabilization argument. This explicit repair is substantial counterevidence to any claim that the intended realization or the main theorem is false. It does not remove the core proof defect in the displayed argument or certify all the remaining comparison steps.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterexample: For A=Q_p<T,T^-1>^dagger, d:A→A dT has kernel Q_p, exact forms have residue zero, and dT/T has residue one. Residue-zero forms have primitives after shrinking by exponential-over-polynomial coefficient control. Hence H0=Q_p,H1=Q_p and dR(Torus)=1⊕1[-1], as LBV Cor4.37(6) confirms.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The correct two-summand torus realization gives R(Tred)=1[-1], which is invertible and repairs this stabilization step. Neither the intended stabilized realization nor the final Berthelot theorem is disproved; repairability does not downgrade an actual core proof defect.

problems.title: Properness does not give the stated terminal object
problems.source_location: Remark2.27 and Definition2.25 PDF p10; dagger map definition p5; actual Cor2.28 proof p11
claim: Recorded check: Properness does not give the stated terminal object
analysis: Remark 2.27, page 10, calls the canonical dagger structure of a proper rigid variety \(S\) terminal in \(\mathrm{Ad}^{\dagger}_{/S}\). Definition 2.25 allows an arbitrary analytic map from the completed source, which need not extend to a dagger map.

Take \(S=\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb Q_p}\), the dagger unit disc \(T^\dagger\), and the analytic map into the affine chart given by \[f(T)=\sum_{n\geq1}p^nT^{n!}.\] It converges on the closed unit disc, but its radius of convergence is exactly one, since \(p^{-n/n!}\to1\). A morphism to the alleged terminal object would extend \(f\) to a map from some larger closed disc to \(\mathbb P^1\). Such a map is a meromorphic function with finitely many poles on that affinoid disc: the inverse image of infinity is a proper zero-dimensional analytic subset of a one-dimensional affinoid. There are no poles on the unit disc. A slightly larger radius therefore avoids all poles and gives an analytic extension of \(f\), contradicting its convergence radius.

The ordinary rigid category \(\mathrm{Ad}_{/S}\) does have its identity as terminal object. The actual proof of Corollary 2.28 on page 11 begins with that ordinary category and then applies the forgetful restriction; it does not require the false dagger terminal assertion. This is therefore a Minor local categorical correction in the reviewed proof chain. Deleting Remark 2.27, or restricting the objects to maps admitting a dagger extension, resolves this particular obstruction.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterexample: The allowed analytic map from completed unit disc into P1_Qp given by F(T)=sum p^nT^(n!) has exact convergence radius1. Any dagger morphism to the alleged terminal object would extend it meromorphically to a larger closed disc. The inverse image of infinity is a proper zero-dimensional closed analytic subset of a one-dimensional affinoid, hence finite. No poles lie on the unit disc, so some radius>1 is pole-free and gives an impossible analytic extension.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Cor2.28 uses the ordinary Ad_/S identity and restriction, so its construction does not require this claim.

report: Abstract: The manuscript constructs a generic Hecke-module model intended to connect metaplectic Whittaker spaces with representations of quantum groups. Five substantive defects are established in the acquired 94-page author manuscript: incompatible coefficient-ring specializations, omitted affine-wall orbits, an invalid universal restricted-weight decomposition, an incorrect even-order quantum Frobenius prescription, and a nonunital spherical convolution formula. The counterexamples are explicit rank-one computations. Three groups of local formula corrections are also documented. The affected derivations are specified separately from the intended conclusions: neither the standard quantum Frobenius theorem nor every corrected metaplectic correspondence is disproved. The publisher version was not acquired, and no equivalence with it is assumed. Scientific adjudication and independent acceptance remain pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Metaplectic Covers of \(p\)-Adic Groups and Quantum Groups at Roots of Unity:
Review of the Acquired Author Manuscript
# Source, hypotheses, and proof architecture

This report concerns Valentin Buciumas and Manish M. Patnaik, Metaplectic covers of \(p\)-adic groups and quantum groups at roots of unity [paper], associated with DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0022. The exact primary is the undated, 94-page University of Alberta author-hosted PDF acquired on 26 October 2026. Its PDF metadata reports 24 November 2023; that field is not an authenticated author-stated revision date. The separately retained arXiv:2211.03724v1, dated 7 November 2022, has 63 pages, and its TeX is not the source of this primary. Journal metadata describes 115 pages, 3317–3431 in volume 174(16). The publisher access route returned a challenge. The findings below apply only to the actual 94-page snapshot.

All page numbers are one-based physical PDF pages, agreeing with the printed numbers on the inspected pages. The contents table is stale: Sections 2–8 begin on pages 20, 25, 50, 61, 68, 74, and 83. The full primary text, including references, was covered. The associated source manifests and files were checked against their actual bytes and hashes. No corresponding supplement or paper-specific computational repository was identified in the available metadata, source tree, PDF scan and saved searches; the inaccessible publisher supplement interface remains a limitation. The absence of code is not a mathematical defect.

The intended construction has three stages. First, affine parabolic Hecke modules and canonical bases are assembled into a model over a generic Gauss-parameter ring (Sections 3–4). Second, its \(p\)-adic specialization is identified with Iwahori and spherical Whittaker spaces (Sections 5–6). Third, quantum Frobenius and tensor-product theorems give an enriched Grothendieck-module interpretation (Section 7), from which Section 8 derives correspondences and applications.

The hypotheses require particular care. In Definition 3.2.1, page 27, simply-connected means that \(Y\) is freely generated by the simple coroots. The full coweight lattice is separately defined on page 28. The introduction and Section 8.1.3 require both \(\mathfrak D\) and \(\mathfrak D_{(Q,n)}\) to be simply-connected. Theorem 8.1.4, page 84, instead prints that \(\mathfrak D\) and the dual \((\mathfrak D_{(Q,l)})^\vee\) are simply-connected. These conditions are not identified in this review. In particular, the odd-degree \(A_1\) examples below satisfy the former conditions, but not the latter dual condition. The final theorem needs a coherent reconciliation with its preparatory constructions.

The tilting-basis identification in (7.32) and Section 8.1.6 is explicitly conditional/conjectural. It is not reviewed as a proved claim. Similarly, the prospective connections to metaplectic Macdonald polynomials and the principal-module coefficients in Sections 8.3.2 and 8.3.4 are not treated as established theorems.
# The generic parameters do not have the asserted specializations

Problem 1 (Coefficient-ring and Gauss-sum compatibility).  On page 21, (2.3)–(2.4) impose periodicity \(g_{k+n}=g_k\), \(g_0=-1\), and \(g_kg_{-k}=\tau^2\) for \(k\ne0\). The same page gives the \(p\)-adic Gauss sums using an unshifted character. These definitions do not support the specializations in Sections 2.3.2–2.3.3 as written.

For the literal coefficient ring, put \(k=n\ne0\). Periodicity gives \[1=g_ng_{-n}=\tau^2.\] A homomorphism sending \(\tau\) to an indeterminate cannot exist. Neither can a \(p\)-adic specialization sending \(\tau^2\) to \(q>1\). The intended exception is presumably \(k\not\equiv0\pmod n\), exactly the condition printed in the preceding numerical identity (2.2). This is strong evidence of the intended repair, but it is absent from the ring relation.

Even with that correction, the asserted free Laurent presentation in (2.5), with all \(g_1,\ldots,g_{n-1}\) independent, is false. For \(n=3\), the relation \(g_1g_2=\tau^2\) eliminates \(g_2\). For \(n=2\), the corrected ring has \[(g_1-\tau)(g_1+\tau)=0.\] Each factor is nonzero: evaluation at \(g_1=-\tau\) or at \(g_1=\tau\), respectively, proves this over \(\mathbb Z[\tau^{\pm1}]\). It is therefore not a Laurent polynomial domain. An odd-degree presentation must use one variable per inverse pair; an even degree retains the self-inverse residue relation, unless an additional quotient is explicitly chosen.

There is a separate, directly computable discrepancy in Section 2.2.4, on the same page. The measure has \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal O^\times)=q-1\), and \(\psi\) has conductor zero, so \(\psi|_{\mathcal O^\times}=1\). The text introduces \(\tau(u)=\psi(-\pi^{-1}u)\), but then defines \(g_k=g(\sigma,\psi)\), rather than \(g(\sigma,\tau)\). Take \(F=\mathbb Q_7\), \(n=3\), and the nontrivial cubic residue characters. These satisfy \(q\equiv1\pmod{2n}\). The literal definition gives \[(g_0,g_1,g_2)=(6,0,0),\] whereas (2.2) requires \(g_0=-1\) and \(g_1g_2=7\). The vanishing follows by summing a nontrivial multiplicative character over \(\mathbf F_7^\times\).

The intended shifted character restores those identities. For an exact check, choose a primitive twenty-first root \(z\), put \(\chi(3)=z^7\) on \(\mathbf F_7^\times\), and sum \[G_k=\sum_{u=1}^6\chi(u)^{-k}z^{-3u}.\] Reduction modulo \(\Phi_{21}(z)=z^{12}-z^{11}+z^9-z^8+z^6-z^4+z^3-z+1\) gives \(G_0=-1\) and \(G_1G_2=7\). The preserved calculation uses exact polynomial arithmetic.

This is a Major construction-level issue: the generic object and its two specialization maps are the central bridge between the three parts. The finding does not assert that the intended bridge is impossible. Section 3 also has constructions over the separate ring \(\mathbb Z_\tau\), which are not invalidated merely by this malformed presentation. A repair must state the actual coefficient ring, its units and relations, the shifted Gauss integral, and then recheck every specialization and bar operation over that ring.
# An affine-wall orbit is missing from the assembled modules

Problem 2 (The half-open negative alcove is not a fundamental domain).  The negative upper closure in (3.65)–(3.66), page 37, and its twisted dot version (3.74)–(3.75), page 38, omit the lower affine wall. The resulting all-weight decompositions in Sections 3.6, 4.2 and 6.2 are false.

Already without a shift, the rank-one affine Weyl group acts on the root coordinate \(z\) by \(z\mapsto\pm z+2k\). The orbit of \(z=1\), consisting of odd integers, has no representative in \((-1,0]\). Thus the strict lower inequality cannot be justified by removing duplicate representatives.

For an example satisfying the printed simply-connected lattice conditions, take \[Y=\mathbb Za^\vee,\qquad X=\tfrac12\mathbb Za,\qquad
 \langle a^\vee,a\rangle=2,\qquad Q(ma^\vee)=m^2,\qquad n=3.\] Then \(B(ma^\vee,ka^\vee)=2mk\), and \(\widetilde Y=3\mathbb Za^\vee\), with twisted simple coroot \(3a^\vee\). Both data are simply-connected under Definition 3.2.1. Use the intended usual \(\rho^\vee=a^\vee/2\), as specified by the pairing-one assertion after (3.15) and the introductory positive half-sum. The displayed half-sum in (3.15) itself omits the positive-root subscript; the unshifted argument above does not depend on repairing that typo.

The proposed integral representatives \(\eta=ma^\vee\) satisfy \[-3<2m+1\le0.\] Only \(m=-1\) is allowed. Its finite dot orbit is \(\{-a^\vee,0\}\), and translation by \(\widetilde Y\) covers only residues \(2,0\pmod3\). The dominant weight \(a^\vee\) is missing. Allowing real representatives does not recover it: the affine action preserves \(Y\), so any representative of an integral weight would itself be integral.

Put \(x=Y^{a^\vee}\). Over a consistent parameter specialization, for example \(\tau=1\), \(g_1=\tfrac12\), \(g_2=2\), the full polynomial module is \(R[x^{\pm1}]\), of rank three over \(R[x^{\pm3}]\). The proposed sum spans only \[x^{-1}R[x^{\pm3}]\oplus R[x^{\pm3}],\] of rank two. The monomial \(x\) is an explicit absent vector. This is the defect in the all-\(Y\) basis assertion of Section 3.6.5, page 44, and (4.38), page 56. The assertion in Section 6.2.4 that every weight has a corresponding finite-orbit-plus-translation expression fails for the same weight. Equations (6.24) and (6.28), page 73, explicitly inherit that decomposition.

The issue is Major: an entire component is absent from the modules and their claimed bases. It is not simply an incorrect name for a fundamental region. An earlier possible test using \(\eta=-2a^\vee\) was rejected: it lies on the excluded wall and cannot refute a statement quantified over admitted indices. The valid counterexample is the missing orbit.

A corrected closed-alcove construction must include the affine wall and its singular stabilizer, and align the negative alcove with the chosen affine simple system. Simply adding the missing label while retaining the old finite-stabilizer rank formula would not suffice. For the related local Shimura construction in Section 8.2.3, page 86, even the label \(-\rho^\vee=-a^\vee/2\) does not belong to \(Y\), so \(Y_{-\rho^\vee}\) is not a monomial of \(\mathbb C[Y]\). A shifted-coset or extended-lattice construction needs to be specified. In contrast, \(\widetilde\rho^\vee-\rho^\vee=(n-1)a^\vee/2\) is integral for odd \(n\); the spherical Steinberg formula (8.12) is therefore not disproved merely by the missing intermediate label.
# The restricted box does not cover the stated lattice

Problem 3 (Universal decomposition and its use in the tensor argument).  Equations (3.82)–(3.83), page 39, and the sentence following (7.17), page 79, assert that every dominant weight is uniquely a restricted weight plus a dominant modified-lattice weight. Existence already fails under the printed hypotheses.

Use the preceding \(A_1\) datum, now with \(n=5\). Then \[\widetilde Y=5\mathbb Za^\vee,\qquad
 \square=\{ma^\vee:0\le2m<5\}=\{0,a^\vee,2a^\vee\}.\] The dominant weight \(3a^\vee\) cannot equal \(\lambda_0+\eta\) with \(\lambda_0\in\square\) and \(\eta\in\widetilde Y_+\), since \(3\not\equiv0,1,2\pmod5\). This remains impossible if \(\eta\) is allowed in the whole modified lattice. The twisted fundamental coweight is \(5a^\vee/2\), outside \(\widetilde Y\), contrary to the integrality assertion in the proof and in (3.100). Simply-connectedness as defined in this manuscript does not supply all fundamental coweights.

This is a Major defect in the universal reduction. Proposition 3.9.1, page 48, and the quantum action calculation (7.25), page 81, use precisely this decomposition. Read as a conditional identity for a pair that actually exists, the Steinberg–Lusztig formula (7.18) is not refuted. The problem is the extension to every dominant weight and hence the proposed proof of an intertwiner on the entire module.

There is an additional bounded failure in the printed tensor-product proof. Section 3.9.4, page 49, uses the crystal for the twisted root datum but asserts in (3.146) that its nonhighest paths are paired by the original dot shift. For highest weight \(5a^\vee\), the rank-one crystal has weights \[5a^\vee,\quad0,\quad-5a^\vee.\] After deleting the highest path, the path of weight zero cannot be sent to a path of weight \(0\mathbin{\bullet}s=-a^\vee\), which is not in this crystal or even in \(\widetilde Y\). Using the twisted half-sum \(5a^\vee/2\) pairs zero with \(-5a^\vee\), as intended.

The same mismatch is visible in (3.154), page 50. For \(\lambda_0=0\), \(\lambda_0^\dagger=4a^\vee\), and \(\zeta=5a^\vee\), one has \(\mu=9a^\vee\), \(\langle\mu+\rho^\vee,a\rangle=19\), and residue \(4\pmod5\). The straightened weight \(\mu^{(1)}=5a^\vee\) has dot reflection \(-6a^\vee\). The printed terminal expression \(4a^\vee-5a^\vee-a^\vee\) is \(-2a^\vee\). Replacing the final subtraction by \(5a^\vee\) restores this particular calculation. These are proof-step counterexamples, not a disproof of the repaired conditional tensor identity.

A global correction must provide complete lattice representatives, or enlarge the lattice and then descend with the appropriate central-character conditions. Enlarging to the full coweight lattice changes the affine group and can require an extended affine Hecke algebra. Correcting the crystal shift alone does not repair the missing cosets; correcting the cosets alone does not supply the cancelled-path proof.
# The even-order Frobenius prescription is not multiplicative

Problem 4 (Root order versus divided-power divisor).  Section 7.3.1, page 77, permits \(\ell=5\), \(l=10\) and a primitive \(l\)-th root \(\zeta\). Sections 7.3.4–7.3.5, page 78, use \(l_i=l/\gcd(l,d_i)\) from (3.23), page 30, in the Frobenius formula (7.14). For \(A_1\), this gives \(l_i=10\), and the asserted algebra homomorphism fails.

In the rank-one integral divided-power algebra, \[E^{(a)}E^{(b)}=
 \begin{bmatrix}a+b\\a\end{bmatrix}_{u}E^{(a+b)}.\] At a primitive tenth root, the symmetric quantum binomial satisfies \[\begin{bmatrix}10\\5\end{bmatrix}_{\zeta}=-2.\] For a direct verification, write its factorial ratio as \[\frac{[6][7][8][9][10]}{[1][2][3][4][5]}.\] The first four corresponding ratios specialize to \(-1\); the last quotient is the Laurent polynomial \([10]/[5]=u^5+u^{-5}\), with value \(-2\). Equivalently, the saved exact integer calculation constructs \(u^{-25}{10\brack5}_{u^2}^{\rm Gaussian}\) and reduces it modulo \(\Phi_{10}(u)=u^4-u^3+u^2-u+1\), obtaining \(-2\).

The obstruction also respects the dotted algebra. For the adjoint dual \(A_1\) datum, write its root as \(\alpha\) and its character lattice as \(\mathbb Z\alpha\). Set \[x=E^{(5)}1_{5\alpha},\qquad y=E^{(5)}1_0.\] The idempotents match for multiplication, and \[xy=-2E^{(10)}1_0.\] The printed rule sends both \(x\) and \(y\) to zero, but sends \(E^{(10)}1_0\) to \(E'^{(1)}1_0\). This target element is nonzero: it acts nontrivially on the weight-zero vector in the three-dimensional rank-one quasi-classical representation. Consequently \[\operatorname{Fr}(x)\operatorname{Fr}(y)=0,\qquad
 \operatorname{Fr}(xy)=-2E'^{(1)}1_0\ne0.\]

This is Major for the quantum construction: the exact embedding (7.15)–(7.16), the tensor action (7.23), and the intertwining derivation (7.28)–(7.30) use this map. The elementary algebra obstruction precedes any Kazhdan–Lusztig or Coxeter-number restrictions.

The standard quantum Frobenius is not disproved. Its divisor in this example is the order of \(\zeta^2\), namely \(5\), not \(10\). Odd-order choices \(l=\ell\) are not contradicted by this test. Repair requires changing the divisor and reconciling the modified root datum, its quasi-classical group and the metaplectic degree. In this example the two modified character lattices happen to coincide, but their roots, \(5\alpha\) and \(10\alpha\), do not. Changing only the exponent in (7.14) is therefore insufficient. Alternatively, a consistently restricted odd-order theorem would require the surrounding range and applications to be rewritten and verified.
# The displayed spherical action fails the identity test

Problem 5 (Normalization of (6.1)–(6.2)).  Section 6.1.2, page 68, defines \(\widetilde J_\mu\) to take value one at \(\pi^\mu\). Section 5.3.3, page 66, normalizes spherical convolution by \(\operatorname{vol}(K)=1\). Nevertheless (6.1)–(6.2), page 69, multiply the output coefficient by \(q^{\langle\rho,\zeta\rangle}\).

Take the trivial cover of \(SL_2(\mathbb Q_7)\), \(n=1\), \(K=SL_2(\mathbb Z_7)\), and \(\mu=a^\vee\). These satisfy the stated Part II assumptions. The spherical identity is \(h_0=1_K\), and \(\langle\rho,\mu\rangle=1\). With \(\lambda=0\), the multiplication map \[U\pi^\mu K\times^K K\longrightarrow U\pi^\mu K\] is an isomorphism. Its fiber at \(\pi^\mu\) is one point, represented by \((\pi^\mu,1)\), with character value one. Thus (6.1) gives \[\widetilde J_\mu\star_K h_0=7\widetilde J_\mu.\] The same result follows from (6.2), since \[\int_U\psi(u)1_K(u)\,du
 =\int_{U(\mathbb Z_7)}1\,du=1.\] Actual convolution by \(1_K\) gives \(\widetilde J_\mu\). Even without assuming a unital-module convention, the displayed operation fails associativity with the idempotent \(h_0\): two applications yield \(49\widetilde J_\mu\), whereas \(h_0\star h_0=h_0\) requires \(7\widetilde J_\mu\).

This is a Major normalization defect in the claimed spherical module action. The right-hand side of (6.1) drops a tilde from \(J_\zeta\), but no differently normalized \(J\)-basis is defined there; the surrounding paragraph and Proposition 6.3.1, page 73, use the same value-one basis. A diagonal change of basis of a genuine module cannot make its identity act by the nonidempotent scalar \(7\).

There is useful contrary evidence: the averaging map (6.3)–(6.5), page 70, legitimately contains modular factors and explicitly rescales its Iwahori input by \(q^{-\langle\rho,\lambda\rangle}\). A normalization may have been transferred into the wrong formula. Removing the extra factor for value-one convolution, or supplying a fully consistent input/output identification, is a plausible repair. All dependent basis identifications must then be checked. This does not disprove the underlying correctly normalized Casselman–Shalika correspondence.
# Additional bounded formula corrections

The following three groups are Minor in this report. Their classification rests on nearby correct definitions and the limited role demonstrated by the counterexamples, rather than on a rule that every locally repairable error is Minor.
Problem 6 (Hecke and Satake normalization displays).  Several displayed identities contradict the defining rank-one Hecke algebra, while adjacent formulas identify the intended conventions.

On page 32, with \(t=\tau^{-2}\), \(T^2=t^{-1}+(t^{-1}-1)T\) gives \[T^{-1}=tT+(t-1).\] The printed expression with \(t^{-1}\) in both coefficients is false. At \(\tau=2\), \(t=1/4\), and scalar \(T=4\), it gives \(19\), whereas \(T^{-1}=1/4\). The factored normalized relation is \((H-\tau)(H+\tau^{-1})=0\); the second factor in (4.2), page 51, has the wrong sign. At \(\tau=1\), \(H=-1\), its printed polynomial is \(4\). Equation (4.36), page 55, correctly gives \(T^2=(\tau^2-1)T+\tau^2\), so the actual operator is not refuted by the erroneous equivalence.

For the antisymmetrizer on page 33, rank one gives \(\epsilon^-=H-\tau\) and \[(\epsilon^-)^2=-(\tau+\tau^{-1})\epsilon^-.\] Formula (3.41) instead produces the coefficient \(-(\tau-\tau^{-1})\). At \(\tau=1\), it predicts zero, whereas \((s-1)^2=-2(s-1)\) in \(\mathbb Z[W]\). The neighboring eigenrelation (3.40) also needs \(\epsilon^-\), not \(\epsilon^+\), on its right-hand side.

Finally, (3.91), page 40, at \(\mu=0\) in rank one gives \[S(h_0)=\frac{1+\tau^{-2}}{1+\tau^2}=\tau^{-2}.\] The numerator follows by adding \((1-\tau^{-2}x)/(1-x)\) and \((1-\tau^{-2}/x)/(1-1/x)\). But \(h_0=\epsilon^2=\epsilon\), and the defining Satake map sends \(\epsilon\) to one. This is a false displayed normalization, not a refutation of the abstract Satake isomorphism. These corrections require consistent tracking of \(T,H,t,\tau\), symmetrizers and measures; the nearby correct quadratic, inverse/bar relation and abstract maps prevent an inference that the corresponding Hecke modules cannot exist.
Problem 7 (The product rule and the \(\kappa\) inversion set).  Equations (4.12), page 52, and (4.40), page 56, fail under a parameter point satisfying even the literal ring relations.

Use \(A_1\), \(n=3\), \(\tau=1\), \(g_0=-1\), \(g_1=1/2\), \(g_2=2\), and \(x=Y^{a^\vee}\). Let \(f=x^{-1}\) and \(h=x^3\). The actual operator (4.10) gives \[(fh)H=2x^{-3},\qquad fH=2.\] Because \(\tau-\tau^{-1}=0\), the printed (4.12) identifies these two expressions, an explicit contradiction. Semilinearity (4.6) instead yields the consistent rule \[(fh)H=(fH)h^s+
 (\tau-\tau^{-1})f\,\frac{h-h^s}{1-Y^{-\widetilde a^\vee}}.\] Thus the intended operator can satisfy the proper Bernstein relation; the displayed product rule, and its later uses, need correction.

For the same parameters, take \(\eta=-a^\vee\). Definition (4.39) gives \(v_\eta=Y^\eta=x^{-1}\). But the positive-sign condition \(a\sigma^{-1}>0\) in the product (4.40), at \(\sigma=1\), gives \(\kappa(\eta)=g_2=2\). It would assert \(x^{-1}=2x^{-1}\). At \(\sigma=s\), the actual operator gives \(v_0=2\), while the printed empty product gives \(\kappa(0)=1\). An inversion-set condition with \(<0\) restores both values in this test.

The definition of \(v_\eta\), the first sentence of the proof and its induction supply contrary evidence to the printed product. Ratios of \(\kappa\)’s in the later basis and Littlewood–Richardson formulas must use the corrected values. The rank-one product \(\kappa(\lambda)\kappa(\lambda\bullet w_0)\) is unchanged by exchanging the two factors, so this example alone does not refute the bar formula or the abstract generic canonical-basis construction.

Problem 8 (A simple module replaces a tilting module in (7.19)).  The right-hand side of (7.19), page 79, prints \(L_{\lambda_0^\dagger}\) where the tilting tensor formula requires \(T_{\lambda_0^\dagger}\).
Take odd order \(l=\ell=5\) in \(A_1\) and \(\lambda_0=\eta=0\). Then \(\lambda_0^\dagger=4a^\vee\), ordinary \(SL_2\) highest weight \(8\). The printed formula asserts \(T_8=L_8\).

The Weyl module \(\Delta_8\) has dimension nine, with standard vectors \(v_0,\ldots,v_8\). For \(1\le r\le4\), both \(E^{(r)}v_4\) and \(F^{(r)}v_4\) have coefficient \({4+r\brack r}_\zeta=0\): the numerator contains \([5]_\zeta\), while the denominator contains no zero factor. For \(r\ge5\), the target index is outside \(0,\ldots,8\). Thus \(v_4\) spans a proper trivial submodule, and the simple highest-weight quotient has \(\dim L_8\le8\). A tilting module of highest weight eight has a Weyl filtration containing \(\Delta_8\), so \(\dim T_8\ge9\). Hence \(T_8\ne L_8\). The four vanishing coefficients were also checked by exact reduction modulo \(\Phi_5\).

Equation (7.26), page 81, already uses \(T\), giving the appropriate local repair. The main simple-basis matching uses the other tensor identity, and the later tilting identification is explicitly conditional. No failure of that conjectural identification is inferred from this local \(L/T\) error.
# Assessment, coverage, and limits

The five Major findings concern specific central dependencies: existence of specialization maps, completeness of module indices, coverage of the all-weight tensor reduction, multiplicativity of quantum Frobenius, and associativity of the displayed spherical action. Each has an exact admissible calculation and a bounded repair discussion. The findings do not require the entire paper to collapse. They also do not establish that the intended final results, after all definitions and hypotheses are consistently repaired, are false.

The elementary twist lattice and Weyl-invariance identities were checked; the rank-one twisted lattice agrees with (3.18)–(3.21). The admitted parabolic Hecke multiplication, the usual triangular/bar construction on such a module, and the dominance bound for \(\lambda_0^\dagger\) provide no additional demonstrated defect. They cannot recover an orbit that was omitted from the indexing set. The current proof does not justify replacing its two different simply-connected assumptions by one another.

The audit read definitions, quantifiers, theorem ranges, boundary cases and proof dependencies throughout the primary. The primary executor read the introduction and global synthesis, independently checked the explicit rank-one arguments, and prepared this report. Three named native helpers in this same conversation performed bounded checks of Sections 2–3, 4–6, and 7–8, respectively. They supplied complete assigned-text coverage and actual source-page inspection receipts; they are AI assistants, not human or independent reviewers. No model override or independently verified backend identity is asserted. The external controller’s observed UI selection and the runtime self-description are retained separately.

The work does not independently reprove all cited higher-rank braid relations, CPS parity-category results, Kazhdan–Lusztig character theorems, Ko’s results, or the imported metaplectic extension and local Shimura theorems. Their exact uses and restrictions were traced. In particular, an arbitrary distinguished-triangle argument was not used to allege a defect in a parity subcategory. Unproved possibilities and rejected counterexample candidates remain outside the confirmed findings.

All confirmed issues have source locations, preserved proof notes, actual source-image receipts and, where applicable, reproducible exact calculations written by the reviewers. No author code or author TeX was run. The current report is compiled with the existing approved compiler, and its exact source, dependency, log, PDF and rendered-image hashes are retained. Actual inspection of every report page is recorded separately after compilation; rendering alone is not counted as inspection. The 94-page source, its manifest, prior checkpoints and unsuccessful or false validation records are preserved.

The present outcome is confirmed issues requiring substantive revision of this acquired manuscript. It is an initial technical assessment. The machine delivery status is separate from scientific adjudication: `scientific_decision=pending`, `human_reviews=[]`, and no independent acceptance is claimed.

problems.title: Coefficient-ring and Gauss-sum compatibility
claim: Recorded check: Coefficient-ring and Gauss-sum compatibility
analysis: On page 21, (2.3)–(2.4) impose periodicity \(g_{k+n}=g_k\), \(g_0=-1\), and \(g_kg_{-k}=\tau^2\) for \(k\ne0\). The same page gives the \(p\)-adic Gauss sums using an unshifted character. These definitions do not support the specializations in Sections 2.3.2–2.3.3 as written.

For the literal coefficient ring, put \(k=n\ne0\). Periodicity gives \[1=g_ng_{-n}=\tau^2.\] A homomorphism sending \(\tau\) to an indeterminate cannot exist. Neither can a \(p\)-adic specialization sending \(\tau^2\) to \(q>1\). The intended exception is presumably \(k\not\equiv0\pmod n\), exactly the condition printed in the preceding numerical identity (2.2). This is strong evidence of the intended repair, but it is absent from the ring relation.

Even with that correction, the asserted free Laurent presentation in (2.5), with all \(g_1,\ldots,g_{n-1}\) independent, is false. For \(n=3\), the relation \(g_1g_2=\tau^2\) eliminates \(g_2\). For \(n=2\), the corrected ring has \[(g_1-\tau)(g_1+\tau)=0.\] Each factor is nonzero: evaluation at \(g_1=-\tau\) or at \(g_1=\tau\), respectively, proves this over \(\mathbb Z[\tau^{\pm1}]\). It is therefore not a Laurent polynomial domain. An odd-degree presentation must use one variable per inverse pair; an even degree retains the self-inverse residue relation, unless an additional quotient is explicitly chosen.

The measure has \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal O^\times)=q-1\), and \(\psi\) has conductor zero, so \(\psi|_{\mathcal O^\times}=1\). The intended shifted character restores those identities. A repair must state the actual coefficient ring, its units and relations, the shifted Gauss integral, and then recheck every specialization and bar operation over that ring.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Immediately preceding (2.2) uses the nonzero-mod-n exception; the shifted additive character is already introduced; the corrected Gauss sums satisfy the required identities by exact Phi21 reduction.

For highest weight \(5a^\vee\), the rank-one crystal has weights \[5a^\vee,\quad0,\quad-5a^\vee.\] After deleting the highest path, the path of weight zero cannot be sent to a path of weight \(0\mathbin{\bullet}s=-a^\vee\), which is not in this crystal or even in \(\widetilde Y\). Using the twisted half-sum \(5a^\vee/2\) pairs zero with \(-5a^\vee\), as intended.

The same mismatch is visible in (3.154), page 50. For \(\lambda_0=0\), \(\lambda_0^\dagger=4a^\vee\), and \(\zeta=5a^\vee\), one has \(\mu=9a^\vee\), \(\langle\mu+\rho^\vee,a\rangle=19\), and residue \(4\pmod5\). The straightened weight \(\mu^{(1)}=5a^\vee\) has dot reflection \(-6a^\vee\). The printed terminal expression \(4a^\vee-5a^\vee-a^\vee\) is \(-2a^\vee\). Replacing the final subtraction by \(5a^\vee\) restores this particular calculation. These are proof-step counterexamples, not a disproof of the repaired conditional tensor identity.

A global correction must provide complete lattice representatives, or enlarge the lattice and then descend with the appropriate central-character conditions. Enlarging to the full coweight lattice changes the affine group and can require an extended affine Hecke algebra. Correcting the crystal shift alone does not repair the missing cosets; correcting the cosets alone does not supply the cancelled-path proof.

problems.title: Root order versus divided-power divisor
claim: Recorded check: Root order versus divided-power divisor
analysis: Section 7.3.1, page 77, permits \(\ell=5\), \(l=10\) and a primitive \(l\)-th root \(\zeta\). Sections 7.3.4–7.3.5, page 78, use \(l_i=l/\gcd(l,d_i)\) from (3.23), page 30, in the Frobenius formula (7.14). For \(A_1\), this gives \(l_i=10\), and the asserted algebra homomorphism fails.

In the rank-one integral divided-power algebra, \[E^{(a)}E^{(b)}=
 \begin{bmatrix}a+b\\a\end{bmatrix}_{u}E^{(a+b)}.\] At a primitive tenth root, the symmetric quantum binomial satisfies \[\begin{bmatrix}10\\5\end{bmatrix}_{\zeta}=-2.\] For a direct verification, write its factorial ratio as \[\frac{[6][7][8][9][10]}{[1][2][3][4][5]}.\] The first four corresponding ratios specialize to \(-1\); the last quotient is the Laurent polynomial \([10]/[5]=u^5+u^{-5}\), with value \(-2\). Equivalently, the saved exact integer calculation constructs \(u^{-25}{10\brack5}_{u^2}^{\rm Gaussian}\) and reduces it modulo \(\Phi_{10}(u)=u^4-u^3+u^2-u+1\), obtaining \(-2\).

The obstruction also respects the dotted algebra. For the adjoint dual \(A_1\) datum, write its root as \(\alpha\) and its character lattice as \(\mathbb Z\alpha\). Set \[x=E^{(5)}1_{5\alpha},\qquad y=E^{(5)}1_0.\] The idempotents match for multiplication, and \[xy=-2E^{(10)}1_0.\] The printed rule sends both \(x\) and \(y\) to zero, but sends \(E^{(10)}1_0\) to \(E'^{(1)}1_0\). This target element is nonzero: it acts nontrivially on the weight-zero vector in the three-dimensional rank-one quasi-classical representation. Consequently \[\operatorname{Fr}(x)\operatorname{Fr}(y)=0,\qquad
 \operatorname{Fr}(xy)=-2E'^{(1)}1_0\ne0.\]

This is Major for the quantum construction: the exact embedding (7.15)–(7.16), the tensor action (7.23), and the intertwining derivation (7.28)–(7.30) use this map. The elementary algebra obstruction precedes any Kazhdan–Lusztig or Coxeter-number restrictions.

The standard quantum Frobenius is not disproved. Its divisor in this example is the order of \(\zeta^2\), namely \(5\), not \(10\). Odd-order choices \(l=\ell\) are not contradicted by this test. Repair requires changing the divisor and reconciling the modified root datum, its quasi-classical group and the metaplectic degree. In this example the two modified character lattices happen to coincide, but their roots, \(5\alpha\) and \(10\alpha\), do not. Changing only the exponent in (7.14) is therefore insufficient. Alternatively, a consistently restricted odd-order theorem would require the surrounding range and applications to be rewritten and verified.

problems.title: Normalization of (6.1)–(6.2)
claim: Recorded check: Normalization of (6.1)–(6.2)
analysis: Section 6.1.2, page 68, defines \(\widetilde J_\mu\) to take value one at \(\pi^\mu\). Section 5.3.3, page 66, normalizes spherical convolution by \(\operatorname{vol}(K)=1\). Nevertheless (6.1)–(6.2), page 69, multiply the output coefficient by \(q^{\langle\rho,\zeta\rangle}\).

Take the trivial cover of \(SL_2(\mathbb Q_7)\), \(n=1\), \(K=SL_2(\mathbb Z_7)\), and \(\mu=a^\vee\). These satisfy the stated Part II assumptions. The spherical identity is \(h_0=1_K\), and \(\langle\rho,\mu\rangle=1\). With \(\lambda=0\), the multiplication map \[U\pi^\mu K\times^K K\longrightarrow U\pi^\mu K\] is an isomorphism. Its fiber at \(\pi^\mu\) is one point, represented by \((\pi^\mu,1)\), with character value one. Thus (6.1) gives \[\widetilde J_\mu\star_K h_0=7\widetilde J_\mu.\] The same result follows from (6.2), since \[\int_U\psi(u)1_K(u)\,du
 =\int_{U(\mathbb Z_7)}1\,du=1.\] Actual convolution by \(1_K\) gives \(\widetilde J_\mu\). Even without assuming a unital-module convention, the displayed operation fails associativity with the idempotent \(h_0\): two applications yield \(49\widetilde J_\mu\), whereas \(h_0\star h_0=h_0\) requires \(7\widetilde J_\mu\).

Removing the extra factor for value-one convolution, or supplying a fully consistent input/output identification, is a plausible repair. All dependent basis identifications must then be checked. problems.title: Hecke and Satake normalization displays

problems.title: The product rule and the \(\kappa\) inversion set
claim: Recorded check: The product rule and the \(\kappa\) inversion set
analysis: Equations (4.12), page 52, and (4.40), page 56, fail under a parameter point satisfying even the literal ring relations.

problems.title: A simple module replaces a tilting module in (7.19)

report: Abstract: The acquired preprint derives local entropy rigidity from a microlocal Hessian estimate and solenoidal injectivity. Three essential steps fail as written. A concrete family of arbitrarily small solenoidal perturbations disproves the cubic absorption estimate at the advertised regularity, and an exact sphere-moment calculation disproves a scalar identity used in the complex-hyperbolic coercivity argument. A two-jet frame rotation also disproves the claimed intrinsic quaternionic operator. These calculations are not counterexamples to the final real or complex rigidity theorem or to the desired coercive inequality. Three groups of additional local corrections concern tensor conventions, projected symbols and the octonionic representative. Explicit contrary evidence and repair boundaries are given throughout. The assessment concerns arXiv:2409.11197v3 only; scientific adjudication and independent acceptance remain pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Katok’s Entropy Conjecture near Real and Complex Hyperbolic Metrics:
Review of the Acquired Preprint
# Exact source and mathematical scope

The work reviewed is Tristan Humbert, Katok’s entropy conjecture near real and complex hyperbolic metrics [paper], associated with DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0023. The actual primary is the 45-page arXiv:2409.11197v3 dated 20 October 2025. Its corresponding TeX was available and read, but was not compiled or executed. The publisher route returned an access interstitial. The journal metadata describes pages 135–184 in volume 175(1), with issue date 15 January 2026; the frozen batch-membership date is a separate metadata field. Neither the batch membership nor the acquired version is changed here, and content equivalence with the 50-page journal version is not asserted.

All references below are to physical, one-based PDF pages, which agree with the inspected printed page numbers. The full source text, including the references, was covered by the primary executor and three explicitly assigned native helpers in this conversation. All pages used as evidence have actual, hash-bound inspection receipts. The 19 manifest-bound files, totaling 2,310,088 bytes, had no intake integrity discrepancy. No separate supplement or computational repository was identified in the available bounded searches. The inaccessible publisher supplement interface is a limitation; missing code is not a mathematical defect.

For a closed negatively curved manifold, write \[\Phi(g)=\operatorname{Ent}_{\rm top}(g)
          -\operatorname{Ent}_{\rm Liou}(g)\ge0.\] Theorem 1, page 2, states that near a real or complex hyperbolic metric \(g_0\), equality of the two entropies forces homothety, in some sufficiently strong \(C^{N(n)}\) neighborhood. This existential regularity statement must be distinguished from Theorem 2, page 4, which specifies a \(C^{3n/2+7}\) neighborhood and a quantitative \(H^{3/2}\) estimate involving \(\Phi\) and the squared volume difference. The latter is restricted to the orthogonal complement of a finite-dimensional kernel in the solenoidal slice. Corollary 1 and Theorem 4, pages 5–6, also print the \(C^{3n/2+7}\) topology.

The proof uses the slice lemma, a pressure/variance expression for the Hessian, the ellipticity of a projected differential operator \(Q\), a volume estimate for its average, and a cubic-remainder absorption. Section 4 proves injectivity in the real and complex cases. Injectivity for the quaternionic and octonionic cases remains explicitly conjectural; this review does not turn that conjecture into a proved claim.
# The stated regularity does not permit the printed absorption

Problem 1 (Proposition 3.4, final display on page 35).  The proof uses \[\|S\|_{C^{5,\alpha}}^3
 \le C\|S\|_{H^{3/2}}^2\|S\|_{C^N},
 \qquad N>\tfrac32 n+6+6\beta,\quad \beta>\alpha,
 \tag{A}\] to absorb the Taylor remainder for \(S=\phi_g^*g-g_0\). This uniform inequality fails even for arbitrarily small perturbations in the exact solenoidal slice, at the regularity specified in Theorem 2.
## A concrete admissible family

Let \(g_0\) be a closed real hyperbolic metric in dimension \(n=4\), with \(\operatorname{Ric}(g_0)=-3g_0\). Use the geometric-sign Laplacian \(\Delta_{\rm geom}=\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Hess}\). For any smooth function \(u\), put \[S_u=\operatorname{Hess}u-(\Delta_{\rm geom}u)g_0+3u g_0.\] The identity \(\operatorname{div}\operatorname{Hess}u=d\Delta_{\rm geom}u+\operatorname{Ric}(\nabla u,\cdot)\) gives \(\operatorname{div}S_u=0\) exactly. This is the same kernel condition as \(D^*S_u=0\), regardless of the constant normalization of the adjoint.

Choose normal coordinates near a point, and a smooth compactly supported function \(\chi\), equal to one near the origin. For small \(\varepsilon>0\), define a global smooth function, extended by zero outside the chart, by \[u_\varepsilon(x)
 =A_\varepsilon\varepsilon^2
   \chi(x/\varepsilon)(x_1/\varepsilon)^7,
 \qquad A_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{14},
 \qquad S_\varepsilon=S_{u_\varepsilon}.\] The leading tensor is a fixed nonzero compactly supported profile of amplitude \(A_\varepsilon\) at scale \(\varepsilon\). Smooth bounded coordinate coefficients and Sobolev scaling give \[\|S_\varepsilon\|_{C^{13}}\le C A_\varepsilon\varepsilon^{-13}
       =O(\varepsilon),\qquad
 \|S_\varepsilon\|_{H^{3/2}}^2
       \le C A_\varepsilon^2\varepsilon.\] At the center, the vanishing of lower jets makes the leading derivative exact: \[\partial_1^5(S_\varepsilon)_{22}(0)
 =-5040 A_\varepsilon\varepsilon^{-5}.\] Comparison with a point outside the support at distance \(O(\varepsilon)\) therefore yields, for fixed \(0<\alpha<1\), \[\|S_\varepsilon\|_{C^{5,\alpha}}
 \ge c A_\varepsilon\varepsilon^{-5-\alpha}.\] Consequently \[\frac{\|S_\varepsilon\|_{C^{5,\alpha}}^3}
      {\|S_\varepsilon\|_{H^{3/2}}^2\,
       \|S_\varepsilon\|_{C^{13}}}
 \ge c\varepsilon^{-3-3\alpha}\longrightarrow\infty.
 \tag{B}\] The perturbations are smooth, solenoidal and tend to zero in \(C^{13}\). Thus \(g_0+S_\varepsilon\) remains positive definite and negatively curved for small \(\varepsilon\), and is already in the affine solenoidal slice. If orthogonality to the finite-dimensional smooth kernel is also imposed, subtract its fixed orthogonal projection. The projection coefficients are \(O(A_\varepsilon\varepsilon^4)\); the resulting smooth finite-rank correction is negligible in all the displayed norms and preserves solenoidality. Thus the stated kernel restriction does not rescue (A). For example, \(\alpha=1/24\), \(\beta=1/12\), \(N=13\) satisfy the printed threshold \(13>12+6\beta\). These are admissible parameters for the claimed estimate.

Indeed, \(\|S_\varepsilon\|_{C^{5,\alpha}}^3/
\|S_\varepsilon\|_{H^{3/2}}^2
\ge c\varepsilon^{-2-3\alpha}\). Smallness in \(C^{13}\) therefore does not itself make this particular cubic bound absorbable.
## Impact and repair boundary

This is Major for the supplied stability derivation. The last estimate is the step used to turn Hessian control into Theorem 2 at its explicit topology, and into the printed topologies of its applications. The counterexample respects the gauge condition; it is not an arbitrary nonsolenoidal test tensor.

The conclusion is deliberately bounded. It does not compute \(\Phi(g_0+S_\varepsilon)\), and hence does not disprove the entropy estimate or rigidity itself. A sharper, tame Taylor remainder might use fewer derivatives than the displayed \(C^{5,\alpha}\) bound. Theorem 1 only asserts the existence of a sufficiently large \(N(n)\), so increasing \(N\) could preserve that statement.

With the usual intended Sobolev embedding \(C^{5,\alpha}\leftarrow H^{n/2+5+\beta}\), interpolation between \(H^{3/2}\) and \(H^N\) gives a sufficient threshold \[N\ge\tfrac32 n+12+3\beta\] for the displayed cubic route, with a strict margin for embeddings. The malformed intermediate Sobolev exponent in the printed display is not used to create the counterexample: even granting the intended embedding, (A) fails. A repair must either strengthen the stated topology or prove a genuinely sharper remainder estimate at the existing one. The Banach-space differentiability needed for the Taylor remainder should also be cited with its precise regularity; its failure has not been established here.
# A scalar identity in the complex coercivity proof is false

Problem 2 (Equation (4.13), page 40).  The expansion of \(H_+Vf\) used to prove Lemma 4.3 has the opposite sign from the defining operators. The resulting scalar identity (4.13) fails for exactly solenoidal tensors on compact complex hyperbolic quotients.

Definition (2.41), page 20, gives \[\eta^\pm_+=\tfrac12(X_+\pm iH_+),\qquad
 H_+=-i(\eta^+_+-\eta^-_+).\] The latter sign is opposite to (2.42). For \(f=f_2+f_0+f_{-2}\), where \(Vf_j=ij f_j\), the definitions imply \[H_+Vf=
 2\eta^+_+f_2-2\eta^-_+f_2
 -2\eta^+_+f_{-2}+2\eta^-_+f_{-2}.\] The expansion on page 40 has its negative.

Here is an exact witness that also respects the solenoidal condition. On a compact complex hyperbolic four-manifold, \(\operatorname{Ric}=-6g_0\). With the positive Laplacian \(\Delta=-\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Hess}\), define \[S_u=\operatorname{Hess}u+(\Delta u+6u)g_0.\] Again \(\operatorname{div}S_u=0\) exactly. In a small chart choose a phase \(t\) with \(|dt|_{g_0}=1\) and a nonzero compactly supported cutoff \(\chi\), and set \(u_N=\chi\cos(Nt)\). The leading term of \(S_{u_N}\) is \[N^2\chi\cos(Nt)(g_0-dt^2).\] At a fiber choose an orthonormal frame with \(dt=e^1\), \(Je_1=e_2\), and write \(a=v_1,b=v_2\). After factoring out the common amplitude, the trace-free fiber polynomial and scalar trace part are \[f=\tfrac14|v|^2-a^2,\qquad h=\tfrac34.\] Let \(P_3\) denote harmonic projection of a cubic polynomial: \[P_3p=p-\frac{|v|^2\Delta_{\mathbb R^4}p}{12}.\] The principal actions are \(X=i a\), \(H=i b\), \(Vf=2ab\). Thus the leading fiber values in (4.13) are \[X_+f=-iP_3(a^3),\qquad
 X_+\mathcal Jf+H_+Vf=iP_3(ab^2).\] With normalized sphere measure on \(S^3\), \[\big\langle X_+\mathcal Jf+H_+Vf,X_+f\big\rangle
   =\frac1{192}.\] Writing \(z=a+ib\), one has \(f_2=-z^2/4\), and the two extreme raising terms each have squared norm \(1/256\). Also \(\|X_+f\|^2=1/64\). The printed right-hand side is therefore \[\frac1{64}-4\left(\frac1{256}+\frac1{256}\right)
 =-\frac1{64},\] which differs from the actual left-hand side by \(1/48\). These fractions follow from \[\mathbb E[a^2]=\tfrac14,\quad
 \mathbb E[a^4]=\tfrac18,\quad
 \mathbb E[a^2b^2]=\tfrac1{24},\quad
 \mathbb E[a^4b^2]=\tfrac1{64}.\] The preserved computation uses exact rational moments.

For the actual smooth fields \(S_{u_N}\), the discrepancy is \[\frac{N^6}{96}\int_M\chi^2\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g_0}
       +O(N^5),\] up to the common positive fiber-measure normalization. It is nonzero for all sufficiently large \(N\). Thus this is a family of genuine solenoidal counterexamples to the identity, not merely an arbitrary symbol comparison.
## The trace-sector identity also needs correction

The conversion (4.11), page 39, uses \(\Lambda_0^n\) as the coefficient of the trace part, although \(S=S_0+hg_0\). With ordinary tensor contraction it should be \(n\Lambda_0^n\); with the literal factorial-weighted norm on page 8, the coefficients are \(\Lambda_2^n/2\) and \(n\Lambda_0^n/2\).

The same principal packet gives \[Q_0S=-e^2\otimes e^2+\tfrac16e^1\otimes e^1,\quad
 \mathbb E[V_2f]=-\tfrac1{32},\quad
 \mathbb E[V_0h]=-\tfrac5{32}.\] Under the ordinary unnormalized-sphere convention used by the displayed \(\Lambda\)’s, their volume-adjusted values are \(\Lambda_2^4=12\), \(\Lambda_0^4=1\). Formula (4.11) therefore gives \(-17/32\). Actual tensor contraction is \(-1\), or \(-1/2\) under the literal page-8 norm. Neither agrees. Correct trace coefficients give exactly those respective answers.
## Core impact, contrary evidence and required repair

This is Major for the supplied complex-hyperbolic injectivity proof. Equations (4.11) and (4.13) feed (4.17)–(4.18), the bound (4.10), and hence Proposition 4.2 and the complex part of Proposition 4.1. The disputed identity supplies a cancellation used to retain a positive Weitzenbock margin.

There is significant contrary evidence to a stronger charge. The compact reconstruction formula (4.2), \(8p=-(X_+\mathcal Jf+H_+Vf)\), is algebraically correct under the defining \(\eta\)’s. An initial proposed reversal of that formula was rejected after direct expansion and is not a finding. The double twisted-derivative identity also retains its sign when both single-derivative signs are corrected. The final arithmetic turning the asserted (4.10) into the positive coefficient \(95n-198\), page 42, is consistent. None of these facts proves the missing estimate, but they locate the defect.

The examples above refute the printed identities, not the weaker inequality (4.10), the coercivity statement (4.5), or final rigidity. The repair must use one coherent sign and norm convention and rederive the estimates, including the smallest relevant real dimension \(n=4\). Changing a sign in the notation while leaving the subsequent scalar calculation unchanged does not provide that proof.
# The quaternionic differential operator depends on the frame

Problem 3 (Theorem 5, (3.4) and footnote 3, page 24).  With definition (2.29) on page 17, the expression \(\sum_{i=1}^3 D^{J_i}D^{J_i}S\) is not independent of the chosen smooth local quaternionic frame. The identification on page 29 that asserts this independence fails even for exactly solenoidal \(S\).

Write \(C_m(J)S=S(J\cdot,\ldots,J\cdot)\) on degree \(m\). Then \(C_m(J)^2=(-1)^m\operatorname{Id}\), including for a varying smooth \(J\), and the source defines \(D_m^J=C_{m+1}(J)D_mC_m(J)\). Consequently \[D_{m+1}^JD_m^J
   =(-1)^{m+1}C_{m+2}(J)D_{m+1}D_mC_m(J).\] The adjacent middle multiplication operators cancel before the next derivative acts. In particular, on two-tensors, \[A(S):=\sum_{i=1}^3D^{J_i}D^{J_i}S
      =-\sum_{i=1}^3 C_4(J_i)D^2C_2(J_i)S.\]

At a point \(p\), fix a quaternionic frame \(I,J,K=IJ\) and a unit vector \(v\). Make the valid local frame change \[I'=\cos\theta\,I+\sin\theta\,J,\qquad
 J'=-\sin\theta\,I+\cos\theta\,J,\qquad K'=K,\] where \(\theta(p)=0\), \(d\theta(p)=0\), and \(H=\operatorname{Hess}_p\theta\). The two frames have identical values and first derivatives at \(p\); any first-jet normalization therefore remains satisfied. Their second-jet difference gives, by direct differentiation, \[[A'(S)-A(S)](v,v,v,v)
   =-2\{H(Iv,Iv)+H(Jv,Jv)\}S(Kv,v).
 \tag{C}\] For example, let \(e_0=v,e_1=Iv,e_2=Jv,e_3=Kv\), take \(\theta=x_1^2/2\) near \(p\), and choose \[S(p)=e^0\otimes e^3+e^3\otimes e^0.\] The \(I'\) term contributes \(-2\), the \(J'\) term contributes zero, and \(K\) is unchanged. Thus (C) is \(-2\). This exact integer calculation is also preserved using the four-by-four quaternionic matrices.

The required tensor value is attained by a global smooth solenoidal field on the actual manifold. Since a quaternionic hyperbolic metric is Einstein, \(\operatorname{Ric}=\lambda g_0\), put \[S_u=\operatorname{Hess}u-(\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Hess}u)g_0-\lambda u g_0.\] Then \(\operatorname{div}S_u=0\). A quadratic polynomial times a cutoff can satisfy \(u(p)=du(p)=0\) and \(\operatorname{Hess}_pu=e^0\otimes e^3+e^3\otimes e^0\), whose trace vanishes. Hence \(S_u(p)\) is exactly the required tensor. A further bump away from \(p\) can fix its integral trace if a zero-volume tangent is desired without changing the local witness.

All other terms of (3.4) agree at \(p\) for the two frames: they are intrinsic or depend only on the frame values, which coincide. Its coefficient \(-1/8\) of \(A\) gives \[[Q'(S_u)-Q(S_u)](v,v,v,v)=\frac14.\] This is a frame dependence of the same operator on the same tensor and metric, not a change of the geometric data.

The defect is Major for Theorem 5’s quaternionic formula and the general stability framework using this \(Q\). Footnote 3 explicitly includes its global definition in the theorem. The proof on page 29 replaces an intrinsic covariant-Hessian contraction by this nonintrinsic iterated operator and expressly says that parallelness of \(J\) was not used.

There is a concrete repair boundary. The preceding expression \[F(S)(v,v,v,v)=
   \sum_{i=1}^3(\nabla^2_{J_i v,J_i v}S)(v,v)\] is intrinsic: it contracts the covariant Hessian over the quaternionic three-plane and uses only frame values. One can retain and symmetrize this expression, or derive the necessary quaternionic-connection correction terms. A second-jet frame convention would itself require a proof that the resulting construction is intrinsic.

The calculation does not show that the corrected Hessian identity is false, or that two possible patched expressions necessarily have different variance modulo coboundaries. The real case has no such frame choice and the complex case has its single parallel \(J\). Thus this defect does not refute the principal real/complex rigidity theorem.
# Three groups of local corrections
Problem 4 (Tensor conventions and the potential ambiguity).  The adjoint convention in Section 2.1.1 and the unrestricted uniqueness assertion in Lemma 2.2 need bounded corrections.

The pointwise scalar product on page 8 is \[\langle A,B\rangle_m=\frac1{m!}\sum A_{i_1\cdots i_m}
                                          B_{i_1\cdots i_m}.\] With the ordinary contraction \(\operatorname{tr}\), its adjoint is \[\operatorname{tr}^*B=(m+1)(m+2)\operatorname{Sym}(B\otimes g_0),\] rather than the \(L\) in (2.3). For \(B=1\) and \(A=e^1\otimes e^1\), \(\langle L1,A\rangle_2=1/2\), whereas \(\langle1,\operatorname{tr}A\rangle_0=1\). The corresponding formal adjoint of \(D\) on degree \(m\) also acquires a factor \(1/m\). The printed harmonic conformality constant (2.7) and the energy calculation for \(S=g_0\) on page 36 use the ordinary, unweighted contraction instead.

Removing \(1/m!\) reconciles those particular conventions; alternatively all adjoints and conformality constants must be changed. For \(S=g_0\), the page-36 energy is \(n(n-1)\operatorname{Vol}(M)/4\) with the literal norm, rather than the printed \(n(n-1)\operatorname{Vol}(M)/2\). Its positivity survives, so this is not a failure of the real-hyperbolic injectivity argument.

Finally, Lemma 2.2, page 13, asserts uniqueness of the potential \(p\) for all tensor degrees. For degree one, \(D(p+c)=Dp\); for degree three, \(D(p+c g_0)=Dp\). One must fix the component in \(\operatorname{Ker}D\), or state uniqueness of \(Dp\) and the solenoidal part. The actual degree-two gauge application has no such nonzero Killing one-form on a closed negatively curved manifold, so this general-degree ambiguity does not invalidate that application. These are Minor local corrections, with the separately demonstrated complex proof consequences already addressed above.
Problem 5 (A false commutation in the ellipticity proof).  On page 34, \(L\) is asserted to commute with \(D^*\) and with the principal solenoidal projection. It does not.

Take \(\xi=e^1\) and \(S=e^2\otimes e^2\). Then \(\iota_\xi S=0\), but \(\iota_\xi L(S)\ne0\), as can be seen from the \((1,1,2,2)\) component of \(\operatorname{Sym}(S\otimes g_0)\). Hence \(P_\xi^{(4)}L(S)\ne L(P_\xi^{(2)}S)\).

There is a complete principal-symbol repair. Identify symmetric tensors with homogeneous polynomials; orthogonal projection onto \(\operatorname{Ker}\iota_\xi\) is restriction to \(\xi^\perp\) followed by extension independent of the \(\xi\)-coordinate. For \(v\in\xi^\perp\), the complex or quaternionic projected symbol is \[\left(\frac{|\xi|^2|v|^2}{4}
       -\frac18\sum_i\langle J_i\xi,v\rangle^2\right)S(v,v).\] The \(J_i\xi\) are orthogonal, so the multiplier is at least \(|\xi|^2|v|^2/8\). If it vanishes as a tensor and \(S\in\operatorname{Ker}\iota_\xi\), then \(S=0\). The corresponding curvature bound supplies the same type of repair in the octonionic principal symbol. Thus this Minor proof correction does not refute the ellipticity conclusion; it replaces the false commutation by a valid projected calculation.
Problem 6 (The octonionic representative and its mean calculation).  The octonionic calculation drops a zero-order term when passing from (3.11) to (3.5) and the final display on page 30.

The initial expression contains \(-\tfrac12\pi_2^*S\), while the weighted trace computation contributes \(+\tfrac16\pi_2^*S\). Their sum is \(-\tfrac13\pi_2^*S\), not the \(+\tfrac16\pi_2^*S\) retained in (3.5). A direct admissible test is \(S=g_0\) on a closed octonionic hyperbolic quotient. The seven exponents of size two and eight of size one give, by (3.8), \[\operatorname{tr}(\nabla_\xi U)=\tfrac12(7\cdot2+8)=11.\] The printed \(Q(g_0)\), with \(\operatorname{Ric}=-36g_0\), gives \[\pi_4^*Q(g_0)=\tfrac16+\tfrac{16}{3}+6
             =\tfrac{23}{2}.\] Distinct constants cannot differ by an \(X\)-coboundary, since an invariant probability measure integrates \(Xu\) to zero. This refutes the asserted representative calculation.

Crucially, both constants have variance zero. This test therefore does not by itself refute the Hessian quadratic identity (3.1). The main real and complex formulas are not affected by this particular omitted term. This is classified as a Minor bounded formula correction, with a required recheck of the general octonionic Hessian assertion.

The related page-32 statement \(R^\circ(L(g_0))=-36g_0\) also has a degree mismatch. From (3.12) and the symmetrized product, \[[R^\circ L(g_0)](v,v,v,v)
   =\tfrac13\operatorname{Ric}(v,v)|v|^2=-12|v|^4.\] The fully symmetrized output is \(-12L(g_0)\), not a two-tensor. The integrated derivative term still vanishes against the appropriate parallel tensor. Thus the displayed coefficient error is not, on its own, a counterexample to the average bound.
# Assessment and remaining limits

The three Major findings concern actual essential derivations: fixed-regularity nonlinear absorption, complex-hyperbolic scalar cancellation, and the intrinsic definition of the quaternionic Hessian operator. Each has an explicit smooth, exactly solenoidal witness and a quantitative contradiction. They justify substantive revision of the supplied proof without asserting that every intended conclusion is false.

Several structural checks support the intended argument. The volume term correctly separates scaling from the zero-entropy gauge directions. Potential tensors yield geodesic coboundaries, while the mean augmentation of the X-ray operator detects constant metric tensors. In the real case, the curvature identities give \(R^\circ S_0=S_0\) and \(S_0\circ\operatorname{Ric}=-(n-1)S_0\); the Weitzenbock estimate therefore yields the positive \((n-2)/4\) margin for \(n\ge3\). The principal-symbol injectivity can be repaired as shown above. The final complex numerical margin is positive if its input estimate is established.

For the quaternionic case, the original mean calculation can be repaired separately by summing the frame-invariant tensor \(\sum_i S\circ J_i\) and integrating its derivatives against \(L(g_0)\); parallelness of each individual \(J_i\) is not needed for that integrated argument. This possible mean repair does not remove the demonstrated pointwise frame dependence. The full corrected quaternionic Hessian must be established with an intrinsic operator.

The thermodynamic Hessian and differentiability inputs, the general X-ray coercive theorem, and the external rigidity results used for the two applications were traced to their cited roles, not independently reproved in full. No defect is inferred merely from reliance on those references or from a conjectural remaining case.

The primary executor performed the synthesis, independently checked the bounded calculations, wrote the English report, used the existing approved compiler, and actually inspected every current report page. Native helpers `/root/m0191_rough_gauge`, `/root/m0191_rates`, and `/root/m0191_pinching` checked the assigned preliminary/real, Hessian/stability, and complex-geometric parts respectively. These are native AI roles in the same conversation, not human reviewers or independent acceptance. No independently verified backend identity is inferred from the external controller’s UI observation.

All calculations, corrected and rejected candidates, source-page observations, actual compiler/dependency bindings, logs, current PDF and image hashes are retained in the per-paper evidence package. Original render-only false records remain distinct from later actual views.
