problems.title: Proposition 3.4, final display on page 35
problems.source_location: p35 Proposition3.4 final norm display; p4 Theorem2; pp5–6 Corollary1/Theorem4
claim: Recorded check: Proposition 3.4, final display on page 35
analysis:
The proof uses \[\|S\|_{C^{5,\alpha}}^3
 \le C\|S\|_{H^{3/2}}^2\|S\|_{C^N},
 \qquad N>\tfrac32 n+6+6\beta,\quad \beta>\alpha,
 \tag{A}\] to absorb the Taylor remainder for \(S=\phi_g^*g-g_0\). This uniform inequality fails even for arbitrarily small perturbations in the exact solenoidal slice, at the regularity specified in Theorem 2.

Let \(g_0\) be a closed real hyperbolic metric in dimension \(n=4\), with \(\operatorname{Ric}(g_0)=-3g_0\). Use the geometric-sign Laplacian \(\Delta_{\rm geom}=\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Hess}\). For any smooth function \(u\), put \[S_u=\operatorname{Hess}u-(\Delta_{\rm geom}u)g_0+3u g_0.\] The identity \(\operatorname{div}\operatorname{Hess}u=d\Delta_{\rm geom}u+\operatorname{Ric}(\nabla u,\cdot)\) gives \(\operatorname{div}S_u=0\) exactly. This is the same kernel condition as \(D^*S_u=0\), regardless of the constant normalization of the adjoint.

Choose normal coordinates near a point, and a smooth compactly supported function \(\chi\), equal to one near the origin. For small \(\varepsilon>0\), define a global smooth function, extended by zero outside the chart, by \[u_\varepsilon(x)
 =A_\varepsilon\varepsilon^2
   \chi(x/\varepsilon)(x_1/\varepsilon)^7,
 \qquad A_\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{14},
 \qquad S_\varepsilon=S_{u_\varepsilon}.\] The leading tensor is a fixed nonzero compactly supported profile of amplitude \(A_\varepsilon\) at scale \(\varepsilon\). Smooth bounded coordinate coefficients and Sobolev scaling give \[\|S_\varepsilon\|_{C^{13}}\le C A_\varepsilon\varepsilon^{-13}
       =O(\varepsilon),\qquad
 \|S_\varepsilon\|_{H^{3/2}}^2
       \le C A_\varepsilon^2\varepsilon.\] At the center, the vanishing of lower jets makes the leading derivative exact: \[\partial_1^5(S_\varepsilon)_{22}(0)
 =-5040 A_\varepsilon\varepsilon^{-5}.\] Comparison with a point outside the support at distance \(O(\varepsilon)\) therefore yields, for fixed \(0<\alpha<1\), \[\|S_\varepsilon\|_{C^{5,\alpha}}
 \ge c A_\varepsilon\varepsilon^{-5-\alpha}.\] Consequently \[\frac{\|S_\varepsilon\|_{C^{5,\alpha}}^3}
      {\|S_\varepsilon\|_{H^{3/2}}^2\,
       \|S_\varepsilon\|_{C^{13}}}
 \ge c\varepsilon^{-3-3\alpha}\longrightarrow\infty.
 \tag{B}\] The perturbations are smooth, solenoidal and tend to zero in \(C^{13}\). Thus \(g_0+S_\varepsilon\) remains positive definite and negatively curved for small \(\varepsilon\), and is already in the affine solenoidal slice. If orthogonality to the finite-dimensional smooth kernel is also imposed, subtract its fixed orthogonal projection. The projection coefficients are \(O(A_\varepsilon\varepsilon^4)\); the resulting smooth finite-rank correction is negligible in all the displayed norms and preserves solenoidality. Thus the stated kernel restriction does not rescue (A). For example, \(\alpha=1/24\), \(\beta=1/12\), \(N=13\) satisfy the printed threshold \(13>12+6\beta\). These are admissible parameters for the claimed estimate.

Indeed, \(\|S_\varepsilon\|_{C^{5,\alpha}}^3/
\|S_\varepsilon\|_{H^{3/2}}^2
\ge c\varepsilon^{-2-3\alpha}\). Smallness in \(C^{13}\) therefore does not itself make this particular cubic bound absorbable.

This is Major for the supplied stability derivation. The last estimate is the step used to turn Hessian control into Theorem 2 at its explicit topology, and into the printed topologies of its applications. The counterexample respects the gauge condition; it is not an arbitrary nonsolenoidal test tensor.

The conclusion is deliberately bounded. It does not compute \(\Phi(g_0+S_\varepsilon)\), and hence does not disprove the entropy estimate or rigidity itself. A sharper, tame Taylor remainder might use fewer derivatives than the displayed \(C^{5,\alpha}\) bound. Theorem 1 only asserts the existence of a sufficiently large \(N(n)\), so increasing \(N\) could preserve that statement.

With the usual intended Sobolev embedding \(C^{5,\alpha}\leftarrow H^{n/2+5+\beta}\), interpolation between \(H^{3/2}\) and \(H^N\) gives a sufficient threshold \[N\ge\tfrac32 n+12+3\beta\] for the displayed cubic route, with a strict margin for embeddings. The malformed intermediate Sobolev exponent in the printed display is not used to create the counterexample: even granting the intended embedding, (A) fails. A repair must either strengthen the stated topology or prove a genuinely sharper remainder estimate at the existing one. The Banach-space differentiability needed for the Taylor remainder should also be cited with its precise regularity; its failure has not been established here.

C13 norm O(e),H1.5²<=C A²e, C5alpha>=c A e^-5-alpha, so cubic/(H1.5² C13)>=c e^-3-3alpha. Choosealpha1/24,beta1/12,N13 satisfyingprintedthreshold. problems.title: Equation (4.13), page 40
claim: Recorded check: Equation (4.13), page 40
analysis: The expansion of \(H_+Vf\) used to prove Lemma 4.3 has the opposite sign from the defining operators. The resulting scalar identity (4.13) fails for exactly solenoidal tensors on compact complex hyperbolic quotients.

Definition (2.41), page 20, gives \[\eta^\pm_+=\tfrac12(X_+\pm iH_+),\qquad
 H_+=-i(\eta^+_+-\eta^-_+).\] The latter sign is opposite to (2.42). For \(f=f_2+f_0+f_{-2}\), where \(Vf_j=ij f_j\), the definitions imply \[H_+Vf=
 2\eta^+_+f_2-2\eta^-_+f_2
 -2\eta^+_+f_{-2}+2\eta^-_+f_{-2}.\] The expansion on page 40 has its negative.

Here is an exact witness that also respects the solenoidal condition. On a compact complex hyperbolic four-manifold, \(\operatorname{Ric}=-6g_0\). With the positive Laplacian \(\Delta=-\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Hess}\), define \[S_u=\operatorname{Hess}u+(\Delta u+6u)g_0.\] Again \(\operatorname{div}S_u=0\) exactly. In a small chart choose a phase \(t\) with \(|dt|_{g_0}=1\) and a nonzero compactly supported cutoff \(\chi\), and set \(u_N=\chi\cos(Nt)\). The leading term of \(S_{u_N}\) is \[N^2\chi\cos(Nt)(g_0-dt^2).\] At a fiber choose an orthonormal frame with \(dt=e^1\), \(Je_1=e_2\), and write \(a=v_1,b=v_2\). After factoring out the common amplitude, the trace-free fiber polynomial and scalar trace part are \[f=\tfrac14|v|^2-a^2,\qquad h=\tfrac34.\] Let \(P_3\) denote harmonic projection of a cubic polynomial: \[P_3p=p-\frac{|v|^2\Delta_{\mathbb R^4}p}{12}.\] The principal actions are \(X=i a\), \(H=i b\), \(Vf=2ab\). Thus the leading fiber values in (4.13) are \[X_+f=-iP_3(a^3),\qquad
 X_+\mathcal Jf+H_+Vf=iP_3(ab^2).\] With normalized sphere measure on \(S^3\), \[\big\langle X_+\mathcal Jf+H_+Vf,X_+f\big\rangle
   =\frac1{192}.\] Writing \(z=a+ib\), one has \(f_2=-z^2/4\), and the two extreme raising terms each have squared norm \(1/256\). Also \(\|X_+f\|^2=1/64\). The printed right-hand side is therefore \[\frac1{64}-4\left(\frac1{256}+\frac1{256}\right)
 =-\frac1{64},\] which differs from the actual left-hand side by \(1/48\). These fractions follow from \[\mathbb E[a^2]=\tfrac14,\quad
 \mathbb E[a^4]=\tfrac18,\quad
 \mathbb E[a^2b^2]=\tfrac1{24},\quad
 \mathbb E[a^4b^2]=\tfrac1{64}.\] The preserved computation uses exact rational moments.

For the actual smooth fields \(S_{u_N}\), the discrepancy is \[\frac{N^6}{96}\int_M\chi^2\,d\operatorname{vol}_{g_0}
       +O(N^5),\] up to the common positive fiber-measure normalization. It is nonzero for all sufficiently large \(N\). Thus this is a family of genuine solenoidal counterexamples to the identity, not merely an arbitrary symbol comparison.

The conversion (4.11), page 39, uses \(\Lambda_0^n\) as the coefficient of the trace part, although \(S=S_0+hg_0\). With ordinary tensor contraction it should be \(n\Lambda_0^n\); with the literal factorial-weighted norm on page 8, the coefficients are \(\Lambda_2^n/2\) and \(n\Lambda_0^n/2\).

The same principal packet gives \[Q_0S=-e^2\otimes e^2+\tfrac16e^1\otimes e^1,\quad
 \mathbb E[V_2f]=-\tfrac1{32},\quad
 \mathbb E[V_0h]=-\tfrac5{32}.\] Under the ordinary unnormalized-sphere convention used by the displayed \(\Lambda\)’s, their volume-adjusted values are \(\Lambda_2^4=12\), \(\Lambda_0^4=1\). Formula (4.11) therefore gives \(-17/32\). Actual tensor contraction is \(-1\), or \(-1/2\) under the literal page-8 norm. Neither agrees. Correct trace coefficients give exactly those respective answers.

This is Major for the supplied complex-hyperbolic injectivity proof. Equations (4.11) and (4.13) feed (4.17)–(4.18), the bound (4.10), and hence Proposition 4.2 and the complex part of Proposition 4.1. The disputed identity supplies a cancellation used to retain a positive Weitzenbock margin.

There is significant contrary evidence to a stronger charge. The compact reconstruction formula (4.2), \(8p=-(X_+\mathcal Jf+H_+Vf)\), is algebraically correct under the defining \(\eta\)’s. An initial proposed reversal of that formula was rejected after direct expansion and is not a finding. The double twisted-derivative identity also retains its sign when both single-derivative signs are corrected. The final arithmetic turning the asserted (4.10) into the positive coefficient \(95n-198\), page 42, is consistent. None of these facts proves the missing estimate, but they locate the defect.

The examples above refute the printed identities, not the weaker inequality (4.10), the coercivity statement (4.5), or final rigidity. The repair must use one coherent sign and norm convention and rederive the estimates, including the smallest relevant real dimension \(n=4\). Changing a sign in the notation while leaving the subsequent scalar calculation unchanged does not provide that proof.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterexample: Exactly solenoidal S_phi=Hess phi+(Delta phi+6phi)g on CH2,phi_N=chi cosNt. Fiber f=r²/4-a²,h3/4 gives actual4.13 LHS1/192 versus printedRHS-1/64; global discrepancy N6/96 intchi²+O(N5). Exact normalized sphere moments are retained. Same packet gives printed4.11 -17/32 versus actual -1/2 under declared norm (-1 ordinary contraction).

claim: Recorded check: Tensor conventions and the potential ambiguity
analysis: The adjoint convention in Section 2.1.1 and the unrestricted uniqueness assertion in Lemma 2.2 need bounded corrections.

The pointwise scalar product on page 8 is \[\langle A,B\rangle_m=\frac1{m!}\sum A_{i_1\cdots i_m}
                                          B_{i_1\cdots i_m}.\] With the ordinary contraction \(\operatorname{tr}\), its adjoint is \[\operatorname{tr}^*B=(m+1)(m+2)\operatorname{Sym}(B\otimes g_0),\] rather than the \(L\) in (2.3). For \(B=1\) and \(A=e^1\otimes e^1\), \(\langle L1,A\rangle_2=1/2\), whereas \(\langle1,\operatorname{tr}A\rangle_0=1\). The corresponding formal adjoint of \(D\) on degree \(m\) also acquires a factor \(1/m\). The printed harmonic conformality constant (2.7) and the energy calculation for \(S=g_0\) on page 36 use the ordinary, unweighted contraction instead.

Removing \(1/m!\) reconciles those particular conventions; alternatively all adjoints and conformality constants must be changed. For \(S=g_0\), the page-36 energy is \(n(n-1)\operatorname{Vol}(M)/4\) with the literal norm, rather than the printed \(n(n-1)\operatorname{Vol}(M)/2\). Its positivity survives, so this is not a failure of the real-hyperbolic injectivity argument.

Finally, Lemma 2.2, page 13, asserts uniqueness of the potential \(p\) for all tensor degrees. For degree one, \(D(p+c)=Dp\); for degree three, \(D(p+c g_0)=Dp\). One must fix the component in \(\operatorname{Ker}D\), or state uniqueness of \(Dp\) and the solenoidal part. The actual degree-two gauge application has no such nonzero Killing one-form on a closed negatively curved manifold, so this general-degree ambiguity does not invalidate that application. These are Minor local corrections, with the separately demonstrated complex proof consequences already addressed above.

problems.title: A false commutation in the ellipticity proof
problems.source_location: p34 projected ellipticity proof
claim: Recorded check: A false commutation in the ellipticity proof
analysis: On page 34, \(L\) is asserted to commute with \(D^*\) and with the principal solenoidal projection. It does not.

Take \(\xi=e^1\) and \(S=e^2\otimes e^2\). Then \(\iota_\xi S=0\), but \(\iota_\xi L(S)\ne0\), as can be seen from the \((1,1,2,2)\) component of \(\operatorname{Sym}(S\otimes g_0)\). Hence \(P_\xi^{(4)}L(S)\ne L(P_\xi^{(2)}S)\).

There is a complete principal-symbol repair. Identify symmetric tensors with homogeneous polynomials; orthogonal projection onto \(\operatorname{Ker}\iota_\xi\) is restriction to \(\xi^\perp\) followed by extension independent of the \(\xi\)-coordinate. For \(v\in\xi^\perp\), the complex or quaternionic projected symbol is \[\left(\frac{|\xi|^2|v|^2}{4}
       -\frac18\sum_i\langle J_i\xi,v\rangle^2\right)S(v,v).\] The \(J_i\xi\) are orthogonal, so the multiplier is at least \(|\xi|^2|v|^2/8\). If it vanishes as a tensor and \(S\in\operatorname{Ker}\iota_\xi\), then \(S=0\). The corresponding curvature bound supplies the same type of repair in the octonionic principal symbol. Thus this Minor proof correction does not refute the ellipticity conclusion; it replaces the false commutation by a valid projected calculation.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterexample: xi=e1,S=e2² hasi_xiS=0 buti_xiL(S)nonzero,so projectedL doesnotcommute. Correctrestriction vperpxi gives symbol(|xi|²|v|²/4-sum<Ji xi,v>²/8)S(v,v),multiplier>=|xi|²|v|²/8.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Explicit correctedprojectedsymbol provesinjectivity; octonioniccurvaturebound suppliesanalogousrepair. Principal quaternionic symbol doesnot depend on frame derivatives, despiteP3lowerorderdefect.

problems.title: The octonionic representative and its mean calculation
problems.source_location: p24 (3.5); p27 (3.11); pp29–30 octonionic representative; p32 RcircleL calculation
claim: Recorded check: The octonionic representative and its mean calculation
analysis: The octonionic calculation drops a zero-order term when passing from (3.11) to (3.5) and the final display on page 30.

The initial expression contains \(-\tfrac12\pi_2^*S\), while the weighted trace computation contributes \(+\tfrac16\pi_2^*S\). Their sum is \(-\tfrac13\pi_2^*S\), not the \(+\tfrac16\pi_2^*S\) retained in (3.5). A direct admissible test is \(S=g_0\) on a closed octonionic hyperbolic quotient. The seven exponents of size two and eight of size one give, by (3.8), \[\operatorname{tr}(\nabla_\xi U)=\tfrac12(7\cdot2+8)=11.\] The printed \(Q(g_0)\), with \(\operatorname{Ric}=-36g_0\), gives \[\pi_4^*Q(g_0)=\tfrac16+\tfrac{16}{3}+6
             =\tfrac{23}{2}.\] Distinct constants cannot differ by an \(X\)-coboundary, since an invariant probability measure integrates \(Xu\) to zero. This refutes the asserted representative calculation.

Crucially, both constants have variance zero. This test therefore does not by itself refute the Hessian quadratic identity (3.1). The main real and complex formulas are not affected by this particular omitted term. This is classified as a Minor bounded formula correction, with a required recheck of the general octonionic Hessian assertion.

The related page-32 statement \(R^\circ(L(g_0))=-36g_0\) also has a degree mismatch. From (3.12) and the symmetrized product, \[[R^\circ L(g_0)](v,v,v,v)
   =\tfrac13\operatorname{Ric}(v,v)|v|^2=-12|v|^4.\] The fully symmetrized output is \(-12L(g_0)\), not a two-tensor. The integrated derivative term still vanishes against the appropriate parallel tensor. Thus the displayed coefficient error is not, on its own, a counterexample to the average bound.

report: Abstract: The manuscript combines a boundary-adapted local theory, two distinct ill-posedness constructions, and a moving-region argument for finite-time singularity. One auxiliary region in the central normal-velocity estimate is defined with a minimum where a maximum is required. Its printed tail integral is infinite, and the claimed positive lower bound is therefore false as written. This is a Major issue in that derivation, with an explicit repair that recovers the subsequent domains. Three Minor corrections concern an overbroad Euler endpoint, a missing critical logarithm, and an ill-posedness prefactor. None is a counterexample to the main theorems. The positive endpoint integral estimates and the repaired proof dependencies were checked. The review distinguishes the pinned 2023 preprint, the separately acquired unversioned author snapshot, and the unavailable journal version; adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Local Regularity and Finite Time Singularity for the Generalized SQG Equation on the Half-Plane:
Review of the Acquired Sources
# Sources, quantifiers and proof architecture

The work is Andrej Zlatoš, Local regularity and finite time singularity for the generalized SQG equation on the half-plane [primary], associated with DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0024. The primary actually reviewed is arXiv:2305.02427v2, 5 October 2023, 30 pages. Its matching TeX was read as source, not compiled or executed. A distinct 31-page author-hosted snapshot [alternate] was also acquired and compared. Its PDF metadata says 17 November 2025; that is not an authenticated revision date or a proof of journal equivalence. The publisher version, described by the acquired metadata as Duke Mathematical Journal 174(17), 3493–3533, 15 November 2025, was unavailable behind an access interstitial. The review does not transfer claims to unacquired journal bytes.

The 20 manifest-bound files total 2,415,863 bytes and had no intake size or hash discrepancy. The complete primary text and the corresponding scientific sections of the separate author snapshot were covered. No separate supplement or computational repository was located in the bounded searches; the publisher supplement inventory was inaccessible. This is an access limitation, not a mathematical objection.

Set \[X_\beta=L^1(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^+)\cap W^{1,\infty}_\beta,\qquad
 \|\theta\|_{\dot W^{1,\infty}_\beta}
 =\|\partial_1\theta\|_\infty+
   \|\min\{x_2^\beta,1\}\partial_2\theta\|_\infty.\] Theorem 1.1, primary page 4, assumes \(0<\alpha\le1/4\) and \(2\alpha\le\beta\le1-2\alpha\). It states existence, uniqueness, a norm-dependent lifespan and continuation criterion, followed by finite-time singularity for suitable smooth initial data. The definition of classical permits locally Lipschitz solutions satisfying the equation almost everywhere. Smooth data may be nonzero on the boundary; the theorem does not assume compact support strictly inside the open half-plane.

Theorem 1.2 must be read together with the opening of Section 3, page 9. For \(\beta<2\alpha\), the construction rules out a solution bounded in \(X_\beta\) on any positive time interval. For \(\beta>1-2\alpha\), it rules out the specified strong \(X_\beta\) continuous dependence for a convergent sequence of data. The latter is not a nonexistence assertion for each datum. The \(H^3\) or \(H^2\) patch-norm blow-up part of Theorem 1.3 is conditional on the corresponding local theory; the manuscript does not prove that entire patch local theory.

Section 2 uses the vertical coordinate map \(\Lambda_\beta(x)=(x_1,\lambda_\beta(x_2))\). The identities \(\lambda_\beta'=\kappa_\beta(\lambda_\beta)\), \(\kappa_\beta(s)=\min\{s^\beta,1\}\), convert the weighted norm into an ordinary Lipschitz norm. Section 3 uses boundary shearing at geometrically separated heights. Section 4 propagates a plateau \(\theta=1\) into a growing trapezoid, forcing its distance to the symmetry axis to vanish in finite time.
# The printed bad region makes the key integral diverge

Problem 1 (Primary pages 24–25, definition of \(B_*\) and (4.18)).  With \(a=x_*=x_1=x_2>0\), the manuscript defines \[B_*=\{(p,q):p>a,\ \min\{p,2a\}<q<p+2a\}.
 \tag{A}\] The asserted \(O(a)\) tail of its integral is false. Indeed, the left side of the normal-velocity lower bound (4.18) is \(-\infty\), even with symmetric truncation. The same minimum and tail assertion occur on page 25 of the acquired author snapshot.
## A direct admissible calculation

Fix \(0<a\le1/8\) and \(0<\alpha\le1/4\); \(a=1/100,\alpha=1/4\) is one concrete choice. For every \(p\ge1\), the interval \(p/2<q<p\) lies in (A). On this wedge, \[p-a\ge\tfrac78p,\qquad
 (p-a)^2+(q-a)^2\le2p^2.\] Consequently \[\int_{B_*\cap\{p\ge1\}}
       \frac{|p-a|}{[(p-a)^2+(q-a)^2]^{1+\alpha}}\,dp\,dq
 \ge \frac7{16}2^{-1-\alpha}
             \int_1^\infty p^{-2\alpha}\,dp
 =+\infty.
 \tag{B}\] This tests precisely the tail that the proof calls \(O(a)\). It uses admissible parameters and the actual printed domain.

In (4.18), the \(B_*\) integral enters with a negative sign. The reflected region \(\widetilde B_*\) enters in the first integral, but its numerator \(p-a\) is negative there. Thus the two divergent contributions have the same adverse sign. The good regions have bounded vertical width and finite integrals for \(\alpha>0\); the bounded rectangle is also integrable because \(\alpha<1/2\). There is no cancellation of opposite infinities. The displayed expression cannot be bounded below by \(Ca\) as claimed.
## Impact and a complete local repair

This is Major for the supplied finite-time-singularity derivation. Equation (4.18) supplies \(u_2\ge0\) on the slanted boundary of the moving trapezoid. Together with the negative \(u_1\) estimate, this excludes the first contact and closes the main blow-up argument. The failure is in an essential integral estimate, even though its repair is local.

For \(a<p<1\), reflecting the lower part of the original triangle across \(q=a\) gives the interval \((2a,p+2a)\). If \(p\ge2a\), this splits into \((2a,p)\), already in the upper part of the triangle, and \((p,p+2a)\), which is (C). If \(a<p<2a\), the whole interval is (C). These are exactly the pieces needed for the stated reflection cancellation, with no extra wedge.

The corrected strip has height at most \(2a\). Its tail is therefore bounded by \[C_\alpha a\int_1^\infty p^{-1-2\alpha}\,dp
 =O_\alpha(a).\] The subsequent rectangular cancellation adds only \[T=\{(p,q):a<p<2a,\ p<q<2a\}.\] The disjoint union \(B_*^{\rm corr}\cup T\) is \(\{p>a,\ p<q<p+2a\}\). Under \(z=((p-a)/a,(q-a)/a)\), it becomes precisely the printed domain \(B_0=\{z_1>0,z_1<z_2<z_1+2\}\). The reflected corrected strip becomes \[B_0^-=
 \{z_1<-2,\ \max\{-z_1-2,1\}<z_2<-z_1\},\] also precisely the domain in Lemma 4.3. Thus the later, correct maximum provides internal evidence for the repair, and the already stated final positivity lemma applies to it. No change of \(\alpha\), initial data or moving trapezoid is required. This review does not present (B) as a counterexample to the actual velocity inequality or to Theorem 1.1(ii).
# Three bounded local corrections

Problem 2 (The Euler endpoint in Lemma 2.2).  Both acquired texts, page 6, include \(\alpha=0\) in Lemma 2.2. Its estimate (2.3) then asserts \(\partial_1u_2=O(x_2)\) for all permitted data. That assertion is false.

Let \(\rho\) be an even nonnegative smooth cutoff, equal to one on \([-1,1]\) and supported in \((-2,2)\). Let \(\sigma\) be nonnegative and smooth on the closed half-line, equal to one on \([0,1]\) and supported in \([0,2)\). Put \[\theta(y_1,y_2)=|y_1|\rho(y_1)\sigma(y_2).\] This fixed function belongs to \(X_0\), and indeed to every \(X_\beta\) under consideration. Its cusp is allowed by the stated Lipschitz hypothesis.

Using the source’s kernel normalization and integrating the horizontal derivative through \(\theta\), at \(x=(0,r)\), \[\partial_1u_2(0,r)
 =\int_{y_2>0}y_1\partial_1\theta(y)
 \left\{\frac1{y_1^2+(r-y_2)^2}
        -\frac1{y_1^2+(r+y_2)^2}\right\}\,dy.
 \tag{D}\] On \([-1,1]\times[0,1]\), \(y_1\partial_1\theta=|y_1|\). The remaining contribution is \(O(r)\). Integrating in \(y_1\) shows that the leading part of (D) is \[\int_0^1\left[
 \log\frac{1+(t-r)^2}{1+(t+r)^2}
       +2\log\frac{t+r}{|t-r|}\right]dt
 =4r\log(1/r)+O(r).\] Thus \(r^{-1}|\partial_1u_2(0,r)|\to\infty\). The derivative is continuous for each \(r>0\), so this also contradicts the essential-supremum bound, not merely a value on a line of measure zero. An independent wedge estimate in the evidence package gives the lower bound \((128/841)r\log(1/(4r))-Cr\).

This is Minor with respect to the paper’s main claims because every main theorem requires \(\alpha>0\). The proof of (2.3) uses a radial integral that produces \(r^{1-2\alpha}\) for \(\alpha>0\), but \(r\log(1/r)\) for \(\alpha=0\). Restrict this estimate to positive \(\alpha\), or insert the logarithmic Euler boundary modulus. The separate estimate \(u_2=O(x_2)\), derived from \(\partial_2u_2\) and the zero normal boundary value, is not contradicted by this example.

Problem 3 (A missing logarithm immediately after (2.8)).  On page 8 of both texts, the proof bounds \[J_{\alpha,\beta}(r)
 =\int_{-2}^{2}|r-y|^{-\beta}|y|^{-2\alpha}\,dy
 \le C_{\alpha,\beta}\max\{r^{1-2\alpha-\beta},1\}.
 \tag{E}\] This fails when \(2\alpha+\beta=1\), including the main endpoint \(\alpha=1/4,\beta=1/2\).

For \(0<r<1/4\), at this endpoint the integral over \(2r<y<1\) alone is at least \(\int_{2r}^1dy/y=\log(1/(2r))\), whereas the right-hand maximum in (E) equals one. More precisely, \[J_{1/4,1/2}(r)
 =2\operatorname{arsinh}\sqrt{2/r}+\pi
  +2\operatorname{arcosh}\sqrt{2/r}
 =2\log(1/r)+O(1).\] The needed correction is a logarithmic middle case: bounded below the threshold, \(O(1+|\log r|)\) at it, and \(O(r^{1-2\alpha-\beta})\) above it.

The consequence needed for the theorem nevertheless survives. For fixed \(\alpha>0\), multiplication by \(r^{2\alpha}\) controls the critical logarithm; above the threshold it leaves \(r^{1-\beta}\), which is bounded since \(\beta<1\). Hence \(J_{\alpha,\beta}(r)\le C_{\alpha,\beta}r^{-2\alpha}\) for \(0<r\le1\), sufficient for (2.5). The stretched-velocity estimate remains valid when \(\beta\ge2\alpha\), including the closed main endpoint. This is a Minor correction to an intermediate estimate, with an explicit replacement argument.
Problem 4 (The prefactor after (3.17), page 13).  The last displayed equality in the first ill-posedness case uses an incorrect positive constant.

Since \(2\alpha-\beta>0\) in this case and the corrected constant is strictly positive, the lower bound still tends to infinity. Neither the crossing-time contradiction nor Theorem 1.2 is refuted. This is Minor; replace the prefactor while retaining the argument. The corresponding text of the author snapshot retains the same factor.

Two further algebraic slips can be corrected without changing their subsequent calculations. In the proof of Lemma 4.1 on primary page 21, the parenthetical \(-2y_2+2<0\) has the wrong sign for \(0<y_2<1\); the derivative estimate actually uses \(2y_2-2<0\). On primary page 29, remove the extra outer square in \(x_2^2+(x_2+2)^2=2((x_2+1)^2+1)^2\). At \(x_2=0\) the two printed sides are 4 and 8, whereas the correct right side is \(2((x_2+1)^2+1)\), as used in the next integral. These are local algebraic corrections, not additional failures of the positive integral lemmas.
# Checks supporting the intended conclusions
## Local theory and nonlinear uniqueness

The transformed velocity has bounded derivative when \(2\alpha\le\beta\le1-2\alpha\): the two off-diagonal terms require respectively \(\beta\ge2\alpha\) and \(\beta\le1-2\alpha\). The diagonal terms use the tangential derivative bound and \(u_2=O(x_2)\). Preservation of physical area gives constant \(L^1\) and \(L^\infty\) scalar norms and the Riccati-type gradient estimate (2.9). The logarithmic repair above preserves this reasoning.
## The two ill-posedness mechanisms

For the first case, the matching TeX confirms \[a_n=a\,2^{-8n/(1-2\alpha)^2};\] the denominator is squared. The decay of this sequence, the separated supports and the measure-preserving flow control the perturbative velocity terms. The crossing time is bounded by a constant times \(2^{-2(2\alpha-\beta)n/(1-\beta)}\to0\), while the transverse separation cannot exit its comparison interval that quickly. The corrected (F) still contradicts a uniform Lipschitz bound.

For the second case, the added \(1/n\) factor makes the truncated data converge in \(X_\beta\). Under the assumed convergence of their solutions, the background-cone and vertical-separation estimates hold uniformly in the truncation index. The crossing times are \[T_n=O\!\left(n^2
       2^{-4n(\beta+2\alpha-1)/(1-\beta)}\right)\to0.\] The concluding Lipschitz lower bound is \(n/3\), as confirmed from the actual page-18 image, not \(n^3\). Its divergence yields the stated failure of continuous dependence. Both exponents have the correct sign on their respective strict parameter ranges.
## The positive blow-up margins

The plateau construction is compatible with smooth initial data and odd symmetry. The moving boundary satisfies \(X'=-(50\alpha)^{-1}X^{1-2\alpha}\); the established tangential velocity bound uses \(-(45\alpha)^{-1}X^{1-2\alpha}\), leaving a strict first-contact margin. After the correction (C), the normal estimate is reduced to exactly the printed positive integral lemma.

The most delicate tangential integral is also supported by an analytic endpoint certificate. At \(\alpha=1/4\), let \(a_0=2^{1/4}\) and \[R=\frac{4+2^{3/4}-2^{3/2}}{4-2^{-1/4}}
   =\frac{4a_0+2-2a_0^3}{4a_0-1}.\] The elementary chord estimate on page 28 gives \[f(1)=\int_0^1(1+q^2)^{-1/4}\,dq\ge\frac{23}{25}.\] Exact rational fourth-power bounds \[\frac{1189207}{10^6}<a_0<\frac{1189208}{10^6}\] show \(R<271/300\): the equivalent polynomial \(116a_0+871-600a_0^3\) is negative at the lower rational endpoint and decreasing thereafter. Thus \(f(1)>R+1/60\), which yields the required \(I(1)>1/20\). The source’s monotonicity and its separate lower bound for \(I(1)+2g(1)\) then give the uniform \(1/(40\alpha)\) estimate. This check uses exact arithmetic and analytic inequalities, not a plot or unverified numerical quadrature.

The remaining normal integral simplifies to \[(2-2^{1-2\alpha})f(1)
 +2^{2-2\alpha}f(1/2)
 -\frac{2^{1-2\alpha}(1-2^{-\alpha})}{1-2\alpha}>0\] in the stipulated range. Its positive lower margin survives the noted algebraic typesetting correction.
# Version comparison, assessment and limits

The acquired author snapshot adds separate Lemmas 4.1 and 4.4 for the pointwise kernel majorant and minorant, and reorganizes the reflection argument. Primary Lemmas 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 correspond to its Lemmas 4.2, 4.3 and 4.5. This improves the exposition of the same mechanism; the comparison found no changed main parameter range. The critical minimum in \(B_*\), the two local endpoint issues and the prefactor remain in the acquired texts. This is a statement about those files, not the inaccessible journal version.

The assessment is one Major proof-step correction and three Minor local corrections. The severity of the first rests on its role in the central finite-time-singularity argument; the complete local repair is separately exhibited. No final theorem has been disproved. The strict ill-posedness ranges, positive integral margins and the weaker velocity consequences of the corrected bounds provide substantive supporting evidence.

The review uses the imported whole-plane kernel estimate, patch regularity results and continuation references in their stated roles; it does not claim to have independently reproved every cited theorem or the historical priority claims. The primary executor performed the scientific synthesis, checked the bounded calculations, wrote this report, compiled the current TeX with the existing approved compiler, and actually inspected every current report page. The native helpers `/root/m0191_rough_gauge`, `/root/m0191_pinching` and `/root/m0191_rates` checked respectively the local theory, ill-posedness constructions and blow-up integrals, with corresponding source-version comparisons. These are bounded AI roles in the same conversation, not human reviews or independent acceptance.

Exact source, TeX, compiler, preserved dependencies, logs, PDF and image hashes are bound in the evidence package. Raw render-only and failed-quality observations are preserved separately from actual usable inspections. UI observation and runtime self-description remain distinct; no independently verified backend identity is inferred. This is an initial review with `scientific_decision=pending`, `human_reviews=[]`, and no independent acceptance.

claim: Recorded check: The Euler endpoint in Lemma 2.2
analysis: Both acquired texts, page 6, include \(\alpha=0\) in Lemma 2.2. Its estimate (2.3) then asserts \(\partial_1u_2=O(x_2)\) for all permitted data. That assertion is false.

Let \(\rho\) be an even nonnegative smooth cutoff, equal to one on \([-1,1]\) and supported in \((-2,2)\). Let \(\sigma\) be nonnegative and smooth on the closed half-line, equal to one on \([0,1]\) and supported in \([0,2)\). Put \[\theta(y_1,y_2)=|y_1|\rho(y_1)\sigma(y_2).\] This fixed function belongs to \(X_0\), and indeed to every \(X_\beta\) under consideration. Its cusp is allowed by the stated Lipschitz hypothesis.

Using the source’s kernel normalization and integrating the horizontal derivative through \(\theta\), at \(x=(0,r)\), \[\partial_1u_2(0,r)
 =\int_{y_2>0}y_1\partial_1\theta(y)
 \left\{\frac1{y_1^2+(r-y_2)^2}
        -\frac1{y_1^2+(r+y_2)^2}\right\}\,dy.
 \tag{D}\] On \([-1,1]\times[0,1]\), \(y_1\partial_1\theta=|y_1|\). The remaining contribution is \(O(r)\). Integrating in \(y_1\) shows that the leading part of (D) is \[\int_0^1\left[
 \log\frac{1+(t-r)^2}{1+(t+r)^2}
       +2\log\frac{t+r}{|t-r|}\right]dt
 =4r\log(1/r)+O(r).\] Thus \(r^{-1}|\partial_1u_2(0,r)|\to\infty\). The derivative is continuous for each \(r>0\), so this also contradicts the essential-supremum bound, not merely a value on a line of measure zero. An independent wedge estimate in the evidence package gives the lower bound \((128/841)r\log(1/(4r))-Cr\).

This is Minor with respect to the paper’s main claims because every main theorem requires \(\alpha>0\). The proof of (2.3) uses a radial integral that produces \(r^{1-2\alpha}\) for \(\alpha>0\), but \(r\log(1/r)\) for \(\alpha=0\). Restrict this estimate to positive \(\alpha\), or insert the logarithmic Euler boundary modulus. The separate estimate \(u_2=O(x_2)\), derived from \(\partial_2u_2\) and the zero normal boundary value, is not contradicted by this example.

analysis:
On page 8 of both texts, the proof bounds \[J_{\alpha,\beta}(r)
 =\int_{-2}^{2}|r-y|^{-\beta}|y|^{-2\alpha}\,dy

report: Abstract: The fixed-separation theorem is supported by a coherent pruning, geometric and percolation argument. A separate construction in the concluding section does not, however, define the claimed infinite-lacunary direction set: with the printed order of the interval operators, the set is empty. This is a Major defect in that substantive example, with a precise correction and a proof of the intended separation limitation. One Minor correction concerns an impossible area comparison. It does not refute the main theorem; a uniform rectangular replacement is supplied. The displayed sticky map satisfies the required prefix conditions in both acquired PDFs and the obtained TeX. It also makes the independent choices in the percolation argument explicit. The author-hosted journal-layout reproduction is distinguished from publisher-original bytes and from the separately obtained preprint. Adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Probabilistic Construction of Kakeya-Type Sets in the Plane Associated to Separated Directions:
Review of the Acquired Sources
# Sources and the scope of the conclusions

This is the technical review of M25-0198: Paul Hagelstein, Blanca Radillo-Murguia and Alexander Stokolos, Probabilistic construction of Kakeya-type sets in \(\mathbb R^2\) associated to separated sets of directions [primary], DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0025. The primary is a 14-page author-hosted reproduction with journal pagination 185–198, Duke Mathematical Journal 175(2). It was retrieved from the author’s Baylor site; its Acrobat Distiller metadata dates the reproduction to 26 February 2026. Publisher-original byte identity has not been established. Its text layer is garbled, so the primary review used all fourteen actual page images.

The first page states first online publication on 21 December 2025. The frozen batch’s OpenAlex membership date, 22 December 2025, and the acquired Crossref print date, 1 February 2026, are distinct metadata fields. The separate arXiv:2405.17674v2 PDF, dated 10 July 2025, has thirteen pages [preprint]. The obtained TeX was fully read without execution. The two Table 1 entries checked directly in both acquired PDFs agree with that TeX. This local agreement does not establish global equivalence between the versions. The 25 manifest-bound source files total 4,069,508 bytes, with no intake size or hash anomaly. No separate supplement or released code was located in the bounded acquisition searches; the publisher supplement inventory was inaccessible. This is a source limitation, not a mathematical defect.

Theorem 1, primary printed page 189 (PDF page 5), assumes \[\exists\,\eta>0\quad\forall\,N\in\mathbb N:
 \quad \mathcal T_\Omega\text{ contains an }\eta\text{-separated
 subtree of lacunary order }N.
 \tag{1}\] The same \(\eta\) must work for all \(N\). The conclusion is unboundedness of the rectangular directional maximal operator on every \(L^p(\mathbb R^2)\), \(1\le p<\infty\). It does not assert unboundedness on \(L^\infty\), nor does it replace (1) by infinite lacunary value alone.

The tree uses closed dyadic intervals; a dyadic endpoint may give two rays. The manuscript explicitly acknowledges this and distinguishes its lacunary value from conventional lacunary order. Separation concerns two splitting descendants on opposite halves of a splitting ancestor, with distance at least \(\eta\) times the ancestor’s length. It is not a uniform separation of every pair of leaves.

The proof prunes to \(2^N\) terminal vertices at a common finite height and forms strips from sticky maps. Lemma 1 provides a near-slab area lower bound \(\gtrsim(\log N)/N\). Lemma 2 supplies a map with far-slab area \(\lesssim_\eta 1/N\). A directional maximal estimate then turns their ratio into unbounded operator norms. Theorem 2 separately gives a probability-one counterexample to a pointwise step in an earlier argument. The concluding section promises an infinite-lacunary set outside (1); that promise is the locus of the Major issue.
# The concluding direction set is empty as printed

Problem 1 (Section 5, printed page 197; PDF page 13).  For an interval \(I=[a,b]\), the source defines \[\rho_{j,1}(I)=
 \left[\frac{a+b}{2}-2^{-j}(b-a),\frac{a+b}{2}\right],
 \qquad
 \rho_{j,2}(I)=
 \left[\frac{a+b}{2},\frac{a+b}{2}+2^{-j}(b-a)\right].
 \tag{2}\] It defines \(\Omega\) by membership in infinitely many intervals \[\rho_{1,i_1}\rho_{2,i_2}\cdots\rho_{k,i_k}[0,1],
 \qquad i_j\in\{1,2\},
 \tag{3}\] and claims \(\lambda(\Omega)=\infty\). Under the composition convention used in the preceding section, (3) instead gives \(\Omega=\varnothing\).

These are operators on intervals, depending on each current midpoint and length. They cannot be replaced by fixed affine maps on points while retaining (3). Each \(\rho_{j,i}\) sends an interval into itself. Consequently every interval in the union \(U_k\) at level \(k\) is contained in the first interval acted upon: \[U_k\subset
 \left[\frac12-2^{-k},\frac12+2^{-k}\right].
 \tag{4}\] For \(k\ge3\), put \(\varepsilon=2^{-k}\). The innermost image is either \([1/2-\varepsilon,1/2]\) or \([1/2,1/2+\varepsilon]\). The next operation \(\rho_{k-1,i}\) places its image strictly inside that interval, at distance at least \[\varepsilon\left(\frac12-2^{-(k-1)}\right)>0
 \tag{5}\] from its endpoint \(1/2\). Every subsequent operation stays inside the current interval. Thus \(1/2\notin U_k\) for all \(k\ge3\).

Every fixed \(x\ne1/2\) is excluded from \(U_k\) for all large \(k\) by (4); the only possible remaining point is excluded by (5). There are only finitely many intervals at any fixed level, so no point belongs to infinitely many intervals in (3). This proves the assertion of emptiness, without a numerical or asymptotic assumption. An exact finite check gives \[U_3=[13/32,15/32]\cup[17/32,19/32].\] The source initially defines its directional objects for nonempty sets; on that convention the proposed example is inadmissible. Under the natural extension to the root-only tree, its splitting value is zero, never infinity.
## Counterevidence and impact

A left-to-right application convention would produce the intended forward recursion, but the source does not specify one. More decisively, Section 4, printed page 195, explicitly writes \(\rho_{a_k}\cdots\rho_{a_1}I_0\) for its forward recursive construction. The same ordinary convention makes (3) the reversed construction. Both obtained PDFs and the obtained TeX retain this discrepancy.

This is Major for the claimed Section 5 example: the construction supplies no infinite-lacunary direction set, and its stated model question concerns the wrong set. The example is a substantive claimed distinction, announced in the introduction, between infinite splitting value and the stronger hypothesis (1). Its failure is not merely an omitted explanatory sentence. The defect does not refute Theorem 1, Theorem 2, or the possibility of the intended example. Its severity is based on the failed mathematical conclusion, despite the short syntactic correction.
## A proved repair, including arbitrary subtrees

The nested compact unions define a nonempty compact set \(C\). Its splitting vertices are precisely the construction intervals, with unary paths between construction generations. Every finite number of generations gives a finite binary branching pattern, so \(\lambda(C)=\infty\).

Fix \(\eta>0\), and choose \(J\) with \(2^{-J}<\eta\). For a construction interval \(I\) of generation \(j\ge J\), all its points of \(C\) lie in the central union of its two children, whose total span is \[2L_{j+1}=2^{-j}L_j<\eta |I|.\] If a subtree has splitting descendants \(u,v\) in opposite halves of \(I\), their construction intervals satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(Q_u,Q_v)<\eta |I|\), contrary to separation. Therefore, in an \(\eta\)-separated subtree, all splitting vertices in each such late descendant region lie along one ray. Otherwise their least common ancestor would violate the preceding condition. Each tail has lacunary order at most one. The first \(J\) construction generations add at most \(J\) to that order, giving an upper bound \(J+1\) for the whole subtree. This includes subtrees that skip generations. Thus (6) has exactly the intended property, and the repair does not rely on an unproved assertion about a selected pruning.
# A local correction with preserved main estimates

Problem 2 (Reciprocal area, printed page 192; PDF page 8).  Put \(w=2^{-h(\mathcal P)}\) and \(L=(2\eta)^{-1}+1\). The proof says that a parallelogram is contained in a direction-adjusted parallelogram with \(1/L\) times its area. Since \(L>1\), positive-area containment makes that assertion impossible.

For example, \(\eta=1/4\) gives \(L=3\). The original parallelogram has area \(3w\); the alleged containing one would have area \(w\). This direct contradiction applies to the actual geometric claim. The preceding average identity is nevertheless correct: the far set is restricted to a unit-width \(x\)-slab, so its intersection with the given strip has area \(w\), and its average over the length-\(L\) parallelogram is \(1/L\).
## The displayed sticky map

Table 1, printed page 190 (PDF page 6), lists \(0101\mapsto1010\) and \(0110\mapsto1010\). Both entries are also present in the separate arXiv PDF and the obtained TeX. All sixteen displayed images preserve the common prefixes of their inputs, so the table does define a sticky map. The earlier alleged counterexample used incorrectly transcribed output strings and is withdrawn; no change to the authors’ table is indicated.
# Positive checks and proof dependencies

The separation estimate in Section 3 has the correct geometric scale. For a splitting interval \(I\) and two opposite splitting descendants, admissible slopes differ by at least \(\eta |I|\). At \(x>(2\eta)^{-1}\) their intercepts differ by more than \(|I|/2\), so they cannot both occur within the same half of a base interval of length \(|I|\). The restriction on the vertical boundary is harmless for the area integral.

For precision, the random sticky map can be generated using independent fair choices at input edges whenever the current target vertex splits. The phrase over all sticky maps should not be used to assume that uniform counting of the finite set of completed maps has that law. Completion counts can differ when target branching heights differ. Existence in Lemma 2 only requires the fair generative law, which is available.

Several candidate intervals inside the same input half share a single choice. They should be grouped under that half, rather than assigned fictitiously independent bits. The compatible half-intervals, joined by containment and with a virtual root, give a genuine independent percolation tree. If \[M_\eta=\left\lceil (2\eta)^{-1}+1\right\rceil+2,\] its level \(d\) contains at most \(M_\eta2^d\) vertices. This direct count avoids changing the far slab merely to make \(\eta\) dyadic.

Theorem 2 was checked at its exact level of assertion. Its intervals have length \(8^{-N}\), the offset \(2^{-100N}\) selects the intended finite dyadic tree, and the translated reflected child intervals lie in the same input half. The recursive choice therefore produces a strip containing the displayed point for every sticky map. The point lies \(8^{-(N+1)}\) below its top edge, strictly inside it. This disproves a universal pointwise probability bound. A single point of probability one does not, by itself, disprove the integral Claim 7(B) or the earlier final classification theorem. The source itself makes this distinction; the review retains it. The strict margin also gives a small common region at \(x>1\): if \(\varepsilon=8^{-(N+1)}\), then \(0\le x-1\le\varepsilon/4\) and \(|y-y_N|\le\varepsilon/4\) stay in every \(K_\sigma\). Its area is only \(\varepsilon^2/8\), so this strengthening still gives no contradiction to the integral bound.

The constant-ratio finite examples themselves contain separated subtrees after skipping generations: within an interval of length \(L\), the descendants labelled \(11\) and \(22\) are \([27/64,28/64]\) and \([36/64,37/64]\) in relative coordinates, with gap \(L/8\). Recursing on them verifies the opening remark of Section 5. This differs from the variable-ratio construction (2). The final question also differs between acquired versions: the primary asks about boundedness for some \(1<p<\infty\), whereas the preprint asks about every \(1<p\le\infty\). The review does not silently equate those formulations.
# Assessment and verification limits

The confirmed issues are one Major failure of the Section 5 example and one Minor defect in an intermediate area assertion. No defect is established in the illustrative table. The corrected direction set has the claimed separation limitation, and (7) restores the main directional estimate. The main fixed-separation theorem is not disproved by these findings. Nor does the review settle the concluding boundedness question for the corrected set.

The inherited near-slab lower bound and pruning are distinct dependencies from the disputed earlier pointwise upper bound. Their actual source and scope are recorded in the supporting dependency note; a separately retrieved 2007 preprint [bateman] is not represented as byte-identical to the 2009 journal article. Claims concerning all downstream applications or the current status of the broader classification theorem are outside this bounded review.

Three native helpers supplied bounded tree, probability and construction checks, with separate source and image hash receipts. They are assistance in the same initial review, not independent human acceptance. No author code or author TeX was executed. The delivery record retains compiler dependencies, failed or preliminary records and original render-only flags. The scientific decision remains pending, with an empty human-review list.

report: Abstract: The manuscript develops a substantial incidence method for smooth families with forbidden higher-order tangency. Its cellular estimates, several interpolation exponents, and the intended geometric applications have useful internal consistency. The acquired version nevertheless contains false quantitative statements at important points in the argument. # P1. Major: the uniform exponent in Proposition 2.27 is false
## Location and exact quantifier

Proposition 2.27, p. 22, asserts \(c=c(k)>0\), independently of the arbitrary positive two-ends/volume exponent \(\epsilon\). After choosing \(\eta,\delta_0\), it promises an extension with \(\delta\le\tau\le\delta^c\) capturing a fixed positive fraction of the curves incident to one small rectangle. Its proof is completed in Section 3.3, pp. 37–38, and the proposition is used to close the algebraic branch on p. 26.

Here is a counterexample for \(k=1\), including the norm, complexity, incomparability, prism, and all-interval hypotheses. If \(c>1\), the proposed interval of scales is empty. Fix any \(0<c\le1\), put \[\epsilon=c/4,\qquad A=\delta^\epsilon/4,\qquad
 h=\delta^2,\qquad b_0=1/4.\] For every proposed \(\eta>0\), choose \(\delta\) sufficiently small that \(A\ge128\delta\), \(h\le\delta/16\), and \(\delta^{-\eta}\ge8192\), as well as the fixed prism-padding conditions below.
## An admissible finite configuration

Take the affine functions \(f_{b,m}(x)=b+mx\), with \[b\in(b_0+h\mathbb Z)\cap[b_0,b_0+A],\qquad
 m\in h\mathbb Z\cap[A/8,A/4].\] They have degree one and, with the manuscript’s sum norm, \(\left\|f\right\|_{C^1}\le1/4+3A/2<1\). Let \(t_i=3i\delta\) with \(t_i+\delta\le1\), and \(q_l=b_0+A/2+4l\delta\) with \(4l\delta\le A/4\). Use rectangles \[R_{i,l}=[t_i,t_i+\delta]\times[q_l-\delta,q_l+\delta].\] They are pairwise incomparable in Definition 2.3. Different columns require horizontal span at least \(4\delta\), whereas a comparator has length \(2\delta\). Different rows in one column have vertical span at least \(6\delta\), whereas a comparator has height \(4\delta\).

For a fixed rectangle and slope, tangency means \[b\in[q_l-\delta-mt_i,\ q_l+\delta-m(t_i+\delta)].\] This interval lies in the allowed intercept range and has length between \(\delta\) and \(2\delta\). Consequently the original bipartite incidence graph has \[\#\mathcal R_0\le A/(16\delta^2),\quad
 \#F_0\le A^2/(2h^2),\quad
 E\ge A^2/(2048\delta h^2).\] Repeatedly delete a curve of degree below \(E/(4\#F_0)\) or a rectangle of degree below \(E/(4\#\mathcal R_0)\), using the original thresholds. Fewer than \(E/2\) edges can be lost. The nonempty retained graph satisfies \[\deg(f)\ge(4096\delta)^{-1},\qquad
 \deg(R)\ge A\delta/(128h^2).\] Define \(F(R)\) by its retained incidences. A curve meets at most one rectangle in each column. For every interval \(J\) of length \(j\ge\delta\), the fraction of its retained rectangles whose intervals lie in \(J\) is at most \(8192j\). Since \(j\le j^\epsilon\) on \([0,1]\), this is at most \(\delta^{-\eta}|J|^\epsilon\). For \(j<\delta\) the count is zero. Thus the required two-ends condition holds for every interval and every proposed \(\eta\).

For the fixed constant \(K\) in the prism definition, all prisms lie in the four-inequality box \[W=[0,1]\times[b_0+A/2-K\delta,\ b_0+3A/4+K\delta].\] It has volume \(A/4+2K\delta\le\delta^\epsilon\) and fixed complexity, so it obeys the volume and complexity hypotheses.
## Failure of every promised extension
## Impact and repair boundary

The exact failed input appears on p. 37: Proposition 3.11 requires \(|W|\le\rho\), but is applied with \(\rho=\delta^{1/(k+1)}\) when the stated input gives only \(|W|\le\delta^\epsilon\). For small \(\epsilon\) the latter does not imply the former. Choosing \(\rho\) using \(\epsilon\) loses the asserted uniformity.

This is a false core structural proposition, not merely an unproved estimate. There is meaningful contrary evidence against a stronger allegation: the actual p. 26 algebraic application supplies a volume power close to \(1/k\). A replacement proposition with a fixed stronger volume hypothesis, separated from the small two-ends exponent, may suffice. Merely changing \(c(k)\) to \(c(k,\epsilon)\) does not close the printed hierarchy: the application needs its two-ends exponent small relative to \(c\) times the square of an outer exponent. No counterexample to the final incidence theorem is asserted.
# P2. Major: covering numbers do not control curve multiplicity

Definition 4.2, p. 45, bounds \(E_\delta(E\cap B_r)\), the number of radius-\(\delta\) balls needed to cover a set, for \(r\ge\delta\). Theorem 1.11\('\), p. 49, sums the indicators of all individual curves but adds no separation hypothesis. The global notation on p. 13 does not add one.

Fix the uniformly smooth family of constants \(\mathcal F=\{f_a:a\in[1/4,1/3]\}\). It forbids first-order tangency with constant one. Take \(k=\alpha=\beta=1\), \(\epsilon=1/4\), a sufficiently small dyadic \(\delta\), and \(M=\delta^{-1}\) distinct constants \[a_j=1/4+\frac{j\delta}{100M}\quad(1\le j\le M).\] Their entire set fits in one \(C^1\) ball of radius \(\delta\). Thus it satisfies the curve covering-number bound for every \(r\ge\delta\), for any prescribed \(\eta>0\). Give every curve the same shading \[Y=[0,1]\times[1/4-\delta/4,\ 1/4+\delta/4].\] This lies in every Euclidean \(\delta\)-tube, has area \(\delta/2\), and obeys \(E_\delta(Y\cap B_r)\le4r/\delta\). Choose \(\delta^{-\eta}\ge4\). All the written hypotheses then hold, but (5.1) would imply \[M\sqrt{\delta/2}
 \le \delta^{-1/4}(\delta M)^{1/2}.\] The ratio of the left to right side is \(\delta^{-1/4}/\sqrt2\), tending to infinity.

The same example refutes discrete Lemma 8.2 on p. 59 through Definition 8.1 on p. 58. Its cardinality lower bound holds, and \(|Y|=\delta/2\ge\delta^{1+\eta}\) for sufficiently small \(\delta\). With \(E=Y\), the claimed bound \(|E|\ge\delta^\epsilon\) fails for any fixed \(\epsilon<1\). This is the same multiplicity defect, not a second finding.

The separated refinement in Step 1, p. 49, cannot preserve a fixed power fraction of an arbitrary cluster: choosing \(M=\delta^{-q}\) with \(q>\eta\) leaves at most one curve in a separated subfamily. The repair must impose \(\delta\)-separation or a point-count/mass condition on \(F\), and carry it through Definition 8.1. It should not impose discrete separation on the positive-area shadings. The original point-count Theorem 1.11 and the genuinely separated discretizations used in the continuous applications are not disproved.
# P3. Major: the ambient packing localization is invalid

Step 2 on p. 50 chooses a maximal disjoint family of radius-\(2t\) balls in ambient \(C^k\), and claims uniformly bounded overlap for their radius-\(8t\) enlargements by applying the forbidden-tangency inequality (1.11) to their centers. That inequality holds only for pairs in \(\mathcal F\).

Fix \(t=1/20\), and choose any number \(L\) of smooth, pairwise disjointly supported bumps \(b_j\) in \((1/4,3/4)\), normalized by \(\left\|b_j\right\|_{C^k}=1\). Set \(g_j=5t b_j\). Then \[\left\|g_j\right\|_{C^k}=5t<1,\qquad
 \left\|g_i-g_j\right\|_{C^k}\ge5t>4t\quad(i\ne j).\] Their radius-\(2t\) balls are disjoint and can be extended to a maximal admissible packing. All \(L\) corresponding radius-\(8t\) balls contain zero. Since \(L\) is arbitrary, the asserted multiplicity bound is false. The jets of all these centers at zero are identical, so the claimed jet separation fails directly, even when the underlying \(\mathcal F\) is the family of constants with tangency constant one.

This affects the summation of the local estimates in (5.12)–(5.13), not just an illustrative remark. Arbitrary centers also need not be polynomials, so the p. 51 subtraction does not preserve polynomiality. Division by \(4t\) does not normalize a radius-\(8t\) ball to unit norm.

A bounded repair is available in principle: take a maximal net centered in the actual finite polynomial family. Condition (1.11) then converts separation of those centers to separation of finite-dimensional jets and gives bounded overlap. Use consistent enlargement and division constants. Moreover, assign each spatial point to a net ball containing its whole active ball \(B(x)\), and use the corresponding ball-specific shadings. Otherwise restricting the denominator in (5.8) to an arbitrary ball does not preserve the two-ends inequality (5.10). These changes must be incorporated before the local estimates can be summed. They are substantial repairs to a core proof step; they do not demonstrate that the separated-family conclusion is false.

At p. 51 the invocation of Lemma B.3 is also unsuitable: it gives only derivatives below order \(k\), on its own short interval, rather than the needed global \(C^k\) distance from an arbitrary center. Lemma B.6 can instead be applied to the difference of two actual curves tangent to the same rectangle. It gives the required pairwise diameter \(\lesssim_c T^{-1}\) for \(k\ge2\); the \(k=1\) case follows from the corresponding derivative/sign argument. This supplies a repair route, not validation of the printed citation.
# P4. Major: the epsilon gains in (7.4) and (7.5) are false

On p. 56, Proposition 7.2 prints \[\left\|A_{\zeta,\phi}(P_kf)\right\|_p
 \le C\,2^{-((s+1)/p+\epsilon)k}\left\|f\right\|_p,
 \tag{5.1}\] and (7.5) prints the maximal analogue with exponent \(1/p+\epsilon\). The following admissible example disproves both gains for every positive \(\epsilon\), including arbitrarily small ones.

Take \(s=2\) and \[\zeta(w;t)=t^2/2+w_1t+w_2t^2/2+t^4/24.\] For \(T=(\zeta',\zeta'',\zeta''')\), \(\det[\partial_tT,\partial_{w_1}T,\partial_{w_2}T]=1\) identically. Choose a nonnegative smooth bump \(\phi\), supported sufficiently near the origin and positive on a smaller product neighborhood. Write \(\zeta_0(t)=\zeta(0;t)\). Take a compact smooth \(\chi(X)\) equal to one near the reflected integration support, with \(\left|\zeta_0'(-X)\right|<1/10\) on its support. For a nonzero \(b\ge0\) smooth and supported in \((1,1.1)\), put \[\psi(v)=\int b(\mu)e^{i\mu v}\,d\mu,\qquad
 f_\lambda(X,Y)=\chi(X)
       \psi\bigl(\lambda[Y+\zeta_0(-X)]\bigr),
 \qquad\lambda=2^k.\] An exact vertical change of variables gives \(\left\|f_\lambda\right\|_p=C_p\lambda^{-1/p}\). For \(\left|x\right|,\left|y\right|,\left|w\right|\le c/\lambda\), \[\lambda\{y-\zeta(w;t)+\zeta_0(t-x)\}=O(c)\] uniformly on the integration support. Since \(\Re\psi\) is positive near zero, a sufficiently small fixed \(c\) gives \(\Re A f_\lambda\ge c_0>0\) on an output box of volume comparable to \(\lambda^{-(s+2)}\). With \(w=0\) the same assertion holds on a two-dimensional box for the maximal operator. Thus \[\left\|Af_\lambda\right\|_p\gtrsim\lambda^{-(s+2)/p},
 \qquad
 \left\|Gf_\lambda\right\|_p\gtrsim\lambda^{-2/p}.
 \tag{5.2}\]

The frequency projection is accounted for. The \(Y\)-Fourier support is exactly \(\eta/\lambda\in[1,1.1]\). For such \(\eta\), the remaining transform is that of \(\chi(X)e^{i\eta\zeta_0(-X)}\). When \(\left|\xi\right|\ge\lambda/4\), the phase derivative is bounded below by a positive multiple of \(\left|\xi\right|+\lambda\). Repeated integration by parts gives arbitrarily rapid decay of these tails. A standard annular multiplier that equals one on \(\eta/\lambda\in[1,1.1]\), \(\left|\xi\right|\le\lambda/4\) therefore satisfies \[\left\|(I-P_k)f_\lambda\right\|_\infty=O_N(\lambda^{-N}).\] This error does not change (5.2). The alleged right sides become respectively \(C\lambda^{-(s+2)/p-\epsilon}\) and \(C\lambda^{-2/p-\epsilon}\), which are impossible.

The exact cited reference [CGY], v2, p. 6, Proposition 3.2, actually has \(2^{-dk/p+\epsilon k}\), an epsilon loss. Its normal-form reduction follows that proposition on pp. 6–7, rather than a Proposition 4.2. Changing to a loss and allowing the small Sobolev loss still gives positive maximal high-frequency decay after the total losses are chosen below \(1/p\). Thus the final interpolation on p. 57 may retain its intended \(p>s+1\) range. The Major classification concerns the false quantitative proposition and its claimed consequence, which are central analytic inputs; it is not a claim that this sign correction disproves Theorem 1.8.
# P5. Major: the advertised sharpness construction fails

Appendix A.1, p. 60, supplies the example supporting the sharpness claim on p. 4. Even after correcting its repeated \(w_2\), the proposed polynomial is \[h(x,y,w;t)=y+\sum_{j=1}^s w_j(t-x)^{j+1}.
 \tag{6.1}\] It satisfies \(h(x)=y\) and \(h'(x)=0\). A polynomial of degree at most \(s+1\) whose derivatives \(0,\ldots,s\) vanish at the fixed origin is \(ct^{s+1}\). The condition \(h'(x)=0\) then forces \(x=0\) or \(c=0\), and either case gives \(h(x)=0\). Hence (6.1) cannot produce the asserted contact for any output with \(y\) near one. Nor does it uniquely represent every polynomial: a nonconstant affine polynomial has no critical point, while other polynomials can have several. At \(t=x\), varying \(w_s\) preserves the first \(s+1\) jets and \((x,y)\), violating the stated transversality condition wherever that point lies in the chart.

This invalidates the supplied sharpness derivation. It does not show that the sharp threshold is wrong. For clarity, the following complete replacement verifies that the intended threshold can be recovered with a different admissible family.

Use \[h(u;t)=y+\sum_{j=1}^s w_j(t-x)^j+(t-x)^{s+2},
 \qquad \Phi(u)=(x,y),\qquad m=s+2.
 \tag{6.2}\] The Jacobian of jets \(0,\ldots,s+1\), in the parameters \((x,y,w_1,\ldots,w_s)\), has absolute determinant \[(s+2)!\prod_{j=1}^s j!>0.\] Indeed its last row has the sole nonzero entry \(-(s+2)!\) in the \(x\)-column, and the remaining Wronskian is triangular. A vector in the kernel of jets \(0,\ldots,s\) with \(dx=dy=0\) induces a polynomial of degree at most \(s\) with all those jets zero; it is zero. Thus \(\Phi\) has the required rank on the one-dimensional jet fiber.

Choose \(d\) near \(-1/2\), solve \(y=-(s+1)d^{s+2}\) on its smooth negative branch, and set \(t_0=x-d\). For outputs in a fixed small open rectangle \(U\) about \((0,-(s+1)(-1/2)^{s+2})\), the polynomial \[P(t)=(t-t_0)^{s+1}\{t-t_0-(s+2)d\}
 \tag{6.3}\] belongs exactly to (6.2): its leading coefficient is one, its coefficient of \((t-x)^{s+1}\) is zero, and \(P(x)=y\). The remaining Taylor coefficients give the \(w_j\). These parameters lie in one compact small set. For \(0<u=t-t_0<c_s\), uniformly on \(U\), \[t,P(t)\in[0,1],\qquad a_su^{s+1}\le P(t)\le b_su^{s+1}.\] Consequently \[f_\rho(X,Y)=(Y+\rho)^{-1/(s+1)}\mathbf1_{[0,1]^2}\] has \(L^{s+1}\) norm comparable to \((\log(1/\rho))^{1/(s+1)}\), whereas its curve integrals are at least \(c_s\log(1/\rho)-C_s\) throughout \(U\). For \(p<s+1\), the strip indicator \(\mathbf1_{[0,1]\times[0,\rho]}\) gives output \(\gtrsim\rho^{1/(s+1)}\) and input norm \(\rho^{1/p}\). These are the required divergent ratios. The output set may have negative vertical coordinate; the framework permits it. The compactness, jet rank, and projection conditions are all verified for the replacement. Its availability does not validate the printed family.

The following are five correction groups, P6–P10. Their individual bounded calculations and exact locations are also preserved in the accompanying evidence files. ## P6. Polynomial, slicing, and conic coordinates

On pp. 3 and 54, equality of jets of \(\sum u_jz^j\) at \(t\) means that the difference is divisible by \((z-t)^{s+1}\), rather than fixing its first \(s+1\) coefficients. For \(m=3,s=1,t=1/2\), the coefficient vector \((1/4,-1,1)\) gives \((z-1/2)^2\). The projected tangent is \((-2t,1)\), not a constant coordinate direction. The required projection is still injective on the jet kernel: a polynomial of degree at most \(s-1\) cannot have a zero of multiplicity \(s+1\).

On pp. 54–55, the slicing tangent space has dimension \(s+1\), and is transverse, generally not orthogonal, to the jet kernel. At \(t=1/1000\) in the preceding example, the kernel is spanned by \((t^2,-2t,1)\), whereas the slice tangent is \(\{du_2=0\}\). The direct-sum condition follows from invertibility of \(\pi D\Phi\) on the jet kernel and proves the needed sliced rank. The output-map uses of immersion should be submersion.

For the circle on p. 59, the actual fiber near \((x,y,r)=(0,0,1)\) is \(x=0,\ y+r=1\). The printed \((e,0,1-e)\) has value \(\sqrt{1-2e}\) and derivative \(e/\sqrt{1-2e}\) at zero, rather than value one and derivative zero. The correct tangent \((0,-1,1)\) projects nontrivially, so the circular example survives.

For the ellipse on p. 60, direct differentiation gives the jets \(0,\ldots,4\) determinant, in \((a,b,x,y,\theta)\), as \[\frac{18b^2(b^2-a^2)}{a^{13}}.\] It is zero at the circle \((a,b)=(1,1)\), where the source claims nonvanishing, but equals \(-27/4096\) at the intended noncircular base point \((2,1)\). Then \(\delta\sum|y_j|^2=1\), the stated dual normalization, but every displayed group is empty although the weighted curve sum is nonzero. Taking \(G_0=\{|y_j|<2\}\) restores the decomposition with a harmless factor two and the same logarithmic bounds. The associated small-loss sign and multiplicity transcriptions in Section 4 and the final sentence of Section 5 are separately listed with corrected exponents in the supporting notes; their intended estimates were checked rather than assumed.
# Proof dependencies, counterevidence, and remaining limits

The cellular branch’s exponent simplifies to \((2k-1-k\epsilon)\eta>0\) in the permitted small \(\epsilon\) range. The graph-curve cell-crossing bound follows directly by substituting a degree-\(D\) polynomial into the partition polynomial: a nonzero resulting polynomial has at most \(DE\) real roots; an identically zero one lies in the algebraic set. The Section 4 interpolation and anisotropic Jacobian cancel with the intended multiplicity power. In Section 5 the factor \((\delta/t)^{(\alpha-\beta)/k}\) is optimized at \(t=\delta\) if \(\alpha\ge\beta\), and at \(t=1\) otherwise. These checks support the architecture of the argument while leaving P1–P3 unresolved.

A separate candidate concerns Proposition 3.11’s chosen Gronwall interval. The source defines \(\rho_i=L_i^{-1/(\kappa n)}\), but proves a local estimate only on radius \(L_i^{-1}\), smaller than \(\rho_i^\kappa=L_i^{-1/n}\) when \(n>1\). The retained quartic diagnostic disproves the inference from those local data at that selected scale. It does not realize the universal bad-set hypotheses, and another allowed scale can succeed. It is therefore not counted as a counterexample to Proposition 3.11.

A compatible repair is recorded in full: write \(m=n+1\), \(a_i=(\kappa/(2m))^{i+1}\), \(L_i=\rho^{-a_i}\), and \(u_i=L_i^{-1/\kappa}\), for \(0<\kappa\le1\). Then the requested radius \(u_i^\kappa\) is exactly \(L_i^{-1}\); the volume recurrence and endpoint losses have positive powers controlled by \(a_n/m\). Use the correct ODE order \(n-i\), semialgebraic Lipschitz extensions, graph thickening including \(L_i\rho\), and the common refinement of all time membership intervals. For \(\kappa>1\), a repair at \(\kappa=1\) suffices. This addresses the local mechanism, conditional on the corrected closed-band decomposition, without resolving P1’s uniform-volume issue.

claim: Recorded check: Counterexample: For every proposed0<c<=1 set epsilon=c/4,A=delta^epsilon/4,h=delta².
analysis: Proposition 2.27, p. 22, asserts \(c=c(k)>0\), independently of the arbitrary positive two-ends/volume exponent \(\epsilon\). After choosing \(\eta,\delta_0\), it promises an extension with \(\delta\le\tau\le\delta^c\) capturing a fixed positive fraction of the curves incident to one small rectangle. Its proof is completed in Section 3.3, pp. 37–38, and the proposition is used to close the algebraic branch on p. 26.

Here is a counterexample for \(k=1\), including the norm, complexity, incomparability, prism, and all-interval hypotheses. If \(c>1\), the proposed interval of scales is empty. Fix any \(0<c\le1\), put \[\epsilon=c/4,\qquad A=\delta^\epsilon/4,\qquad
 h=\delta^2,\qquad b_0=1/4.\] For every proposed \(\eta>0\), choose \(\delta\) sufficiently small that \(A\ge128\delta\), \(h\le\delta/16\), and \(\delta^{-\eta}\ge8192\), as well as the fixed prism-padding conditions below.

Take the affine functions \(f_{b,m}(x)=b+mx\), with \[b\in(b_0+h\mathbb Z)\cap[b_0,b_0+A],\qquad
 m\in h\mathbb Z\cap[A/8,A/4].\] They have degree one and, with the manuscript’s sum norm, \(\left\|f\right\|_{C^1}\le1/4+3A/2<1\). Let \(t_i=3i\delta\) with \(t_i+\delta\le1\), and \(q_l=b_0+A/2+4l\delta\) with \(4l\delta\le A/4\). Use rectangles \[R_{i,l}=[t_i,t_i+\delta]\times[q_l-\delta,q_l+\delta].\] They are pairwise incomparable in Definition 2.3. Different columns require horizontal span at least \(4\delta\), whereas a comparator has length \(2\delta\). Different rows in one column have vertical span at least \(6\delta\), whereas a comparator has height \(4\delta\).

For a fixed rectangle and slope, tangency means \[b\in[q_l-\delta-mt_i,\ q_l+\delta-m(t_i+\delta)].\] This interval lies in the allowed intercept range and has length between \(\delta\) and \(2\delta\). Consequently the original bipartite incidence graph has \[\#\mathcal R_0\le A/(16\delta^2),\quad
 \#F_0\le A^2/(2h^2),\quad
 E\ge A^2/(2048\delta h^2).\] Repeatedly delete a curve of degree below \(E/(4\#F_0)\) or a rectangle of degree below \(E/(4\#\mathcal R_0)\), using the original thresholds. Fewer than \(E/2\) edges can be lost. The nonempty retained graph satisfies \[\deg(f)\ge(4096\delta)^{-1},\qquad
 \deg(R)\ge A\delta/(128h^2).\] Define \(F(R)\) by its retained incidences. A curve meets at most one rectangle in each column. For every interval \(J\) of length \(j\ge\delta\), the fraction of its retained rectangles whose intervals lie in \(J\) is at most \(8192j\). Since \(j\le j^\epsilon\) on \([0,1]\), this is at most \(\delta^{-\eta}|J|^\epsilon\). For \(j<\delta\) the count is zero. Thus the required two-ends condition holds for every interval and every proposed \(\eta\).

For the fixed constant \(K\) in the prism definition, all prisms lie in the four-inequality box \[W=[0,1]\times[b_0+A/2-K\delta,\ b_0+3A/4+K\delta].\] It has volume \(A/4+2K\delta\le\delta^\epsilon\) and fixed complexity, so it obeys the volume and complexity hypotheses.

The exact failed input appears on p. 37: Proposition 3.11 requires \(|W|\le\rho\), but is applied with \(\rho=\delta^{1/(k+1)}\) when the stated input gives only \(|W|\le\delta^\epsilon\). For small \(\epsilon\) the latter does not imply the former. Choosing \(\rho\) using \(\epsilon\) loses the asserted uniformity.

This is a false core structural proposition, not merely an unproved estimate. There is meaningful contrary evidence against a stronger allegation: the actual p. 26 algebraic application supplies a volume power close to \(1/k\). A replacement proposition with a fixed stronger volume hypothesis, separated from the small two-ends exponent, may suffice. Merely changing \(c(k)\) to \(c(k,\epsilon)\) does not close the printed hierarchy: the application needs its two-ends exponent small relative to \(c\) times the square of an outer exponent. No counterexample to the final incidence theorem is asserted.

claim: Recorded check: Counterexample: Atfixedt1/20 choosearbitrarilymany disjointsupportednormalizedsmoothbumps;gj=5t bj.
analysis: Step 2 on p. 50 chooses a maximal disjoint family of radius-\(2t\) balls in ambient \(C^k\), and claims uniformly bounded overlap for their radius-\(8t\) enlargements by applying the forbidden-tangency inequality (1.11) to their centers. That inequality holds only for pairs in \(\mathcal F\).

Fix \(t=1/20\), and choose any number \(L\) of smooth, pairwise disjointly supported bumps \(b_j\) in \((1/4,3/4)\), normalized by \(\left\|b_j\right\|_{C^k}=1\). Set \(g_j=5t b_j\). Then \[\left\|g_j\right\|_{C^k}=5t<1,\qquad
 \left\|g_i-g_j\right\|_{C^k}\ge5t>4t\quad(i\ne j).\] Their radius-\(2t\) balls are disjoint and can be extended to a maximal admissible packing. All \(L\) corresponding radius-\(8t\) balls contain zero. Since \(L\) is arbitrary, the asserted multiplicity bound is false. The jets of all these centers at zero are identical, so the claimed jet separation fails directly, even when the underlying \(\mathcal F\) is the family of constants with tangency constant one.

This affects the summation of the local estimates in (5.12)–(5.13), not just an illustrative remark. Arbitrary centers also need not be polynomials, so the p. 51 subtraction does not preserve polynomiality. Division by \(4t\) does not normalize a radius-\(8t\) ball to unit norm.

A bounded repair is available in principle: take a maximal net centered in the actual finite polynomial family. Condition (1.11) then converts separation of those centers to separation of finite-dimensional jets and gives bounded overlap. Use consistent enlargement and division constants. Moreover, assign each spatial point to a net ball containing its whole active ball \(B(x)\), and use the corresponding ball-specific shadings. Otherwise restricting the denominator in (5.8) to an arbitrary ball does not preserve the two-ends inequality (5.10). These changes must be incorporated before the local estimates can be summed. They are substantial repairs to a core proof step; they do not demonstrate that the separated-family conclusion is false.

At p. 51 the invocation of Lemma B.3 is also unsuitable: it gives only derivatives below order \(k\), on its own short interval, rather than the needed global \(C^k\) distance from an arbitrary center. Lemma B.6 can instead be applied to the difference of two actual curves tangent to the same rectangle. It gives the required pairwise diameter \(\lesssim_c T^{-1}\) for \(k\ge2\); the \(k=1\) case follows from the corresponding derivative/sign argument. This supplies a repair route, not validation of the printed citation.

analysis:
On p. 56, Proposition 7.2 prints \[\left\|A_{\zeta,\phi}(P_kf)\right\|_p
 \le C\,2^{-((s+1)/p+\epsilon)k}\left\|f\right\|_p,
 \tag{5.1}\] and (7.5) prints the maximal analogue with exponent \(1/p+\epsilon\). The following admissible example disproves both gains for every positive \(\epsilon\), including arbitrarily small ones.

Take \(s=2\) and \[\zeta(w;t)=t^2/2+w_1t+w_2t^2/2+t^4/24.\] For \(T=(\zeta',\zeta'',\zeta''')\), \(\det[\partial_tT,\partial_{w_1}T,\partial_{w_2}T]=1\) identically. Choose a nonnegative smooth bump \(\phi\), supported sufficiently near the origin and positive on a smaller product neighborhood. Write \(\zeta_0(t)=\zeta(0;t)\). Take a compact smooth \(\chi(X)\) equal to one near the reflected integration support, with \(\left|\zeta_0'(-X)\right|<1/10\) on its support. For a nonzero \(b\ge0\) smooth and supported in \((1,1.1)\), put \[\psi(v)=\int b(\mu)e^{i\mu v}\,d\mu,\qquad
 f_\lambda(X,Y)=\chi(X)
       \psi\bigl(\lambda[Y+\zeta_0(-X)]\bigr),
 \qquad\lambda=2^k.\] An exact vertical change of variables gives \(\left\|f_\lambda\right\|_p=C_p\lambda^{-1/p}\). For \(\left|x\right|,\left|y\right|,\left|w\right|\le c/\lambda\), \[\lambda\{y-\zeta(w;t)+\zeta_0(t-x)\}=O(c)\] uniformly on the integration support. Since \(\Re\psi\) is positive near zero, a sufficiently small fixed \(c\) gives \(\Re A f_\lambda\ge c_0>0\) on an output box of volume comparable to \(\lambda^{-(s+2)}\). With \(w=0\) the same assertion holds on a two-dimensional box for the maximal operator. Thus \[\left\|Af_\lambda\right\|_p\gtrsim\lambda^{-(s+2)/p},
 \qquad
 \left\|Gf_\lambda\right\|_p\gtrsim\lambda^{-2/p}.
 \tag{5.2}\]

The frequency projection is accounted for. The \(Y\)-Fourier support is exactly \(\eta/\lambda\in[1,1.1]\). For such \(\eta\), the remaining transform is that of \(\chi(X)e^{i\eta\zeta_0(-X)}\). When \(\left|\xi\right|\ge\lambda/4\), the phase derivative is bounded below by a positive multiple of \(\left|\xi\right|+\lambda\). Repeated integration by parts gives arbitrarily rapid decay of these tails. A standard annular multiplier that equals one on \(\eta/\lambda\in[1,1.1]\), \(\left|\xi\right|\le\lambda/4\) therefore satisfies \[\left\|(I-P_k)f_\lambda\right\|_\infty=O_N(\lambda^{-N}).\] This error does not change (5.2). The alleged right sides become respectively \(C\lambda^{-(s+2)/p-\epsilon}\) and \(C\lambda^{-2/p-\epsilon}\), which are impossible.

The exact cited reference [CGY], v2, p. 6, Proposition 3.2, actually has \(2^{-dk/p+\epsilon k}\), an epsilon loss. Its normal-form reduction follows that proposition on pp. 6–7, rather than a Proposition 4.2. Changing to a loss and allowing the small Sobolev loss still gives positive maximal high-frequency decay after the total losses are chosen below \(1/p\). Thus the final interpolation on p. 57 may retain its intended \(p>s+1\) range. The Major classification concerns the false quantitative proposition and its claimed consequence, which are central analytic inputs; it is not a claim that this sign correction disproves Theorem 1.8.
