claim: Recorded check: Counterexample: Printeddegree<=s+1familyhasP(x)=y,P'(x)=0.
analysis:
Appendix A.1, p. 60, supplies the example supporting the sharpness claim on p. 4. Even after correcting its repeated \(w_2\), the proposed polynomial is \[h(x,y,w;t)=y+\sum_{j=1}^s w_j(t-x)^{j+1}.
 \tag{6.1}\] It satisfies \(h(x)=y\) and \(h'(x)=0\). A polynomial of degree at most \(s+1\) whose derivatives \(0,\ldots,s\) vanish at the fixed origin is \(ct^{s+1}\). The condition \(h'(x)=0\) then forces \(x=0\) or \(c=0\), and either case gives \(h(x)=0\). Hence (6.1) cannot produce the asserted contact for any output with \(y\) near one. Nor does it uniquely represent every polynomial: a nonconstant affine polynomial has no critical point, while other polynomials can have several. At \(t=x\), varying \(w_s\) preserves the first \(s+1\) jets and \((x,y)\), violating the stated transversality condition wherever that point lies in the chart.

This invalidates the supplied sharpness derivation. It does not show that the sharp threshold is wrong. For clarity, the following complete replacement verifies that the intended threshold can be recovered with a different admissible family.

Use \[h(u;t)=y+\sum_{j=1}^s w_j(t-x)^j+(t-x)^{s+2},
 \qquad \Phi(u)=(x,y),\qquad m=s+2.
 \tag{6.2}\] The Jacobian of jets \(0,\ldots,s+1\), in the parameters \((x,y,w_1,\ldots,w_s)\), has absolute determinant \[(s+2)!\prod_{j=1}^s j!>0.\] Indeed its last row has the sole nonzero entry \(-(s+2)!\) in the \(x\)-column, and the remaining Wronskian is triangular. A vector in the kernel of jets \(0,\ldots,s\) with \(dx=dy=0\) induces a polynomial of degree at most \(s\) with all those jets zero; it is zero. Thus \(\Phi\) has the required rank on the one-dimensional jet fiber.

Choose \(d\) near \(-1/2\), solve \(y=-(s+1)d^{s+2}\) on its smooth negative branch, and set \(t_0=x-d\). For outputs in a fixed small open rectangle \(U\) about \((0,-(s+1)(-1/2)^{s+2})\), the polynomial \[P(t)=(t-t_0)^{s+1}\{t-t_0-(s+2)d\}
 \tag{6.3}\] belongs exactly to (6.2): its leading coefficient is one, its coefficient of \((t-x)^{s+1}\) is zero, and \(P(x)=y\). The remaining Taylor coefficients give the \(w_j\). These parameters lie in one compact small set. For \(0<u=t-t_0<c_s\), uniformly on \(U\), \[t,P(t)\in[0,1],\qquad a_su^{s+1}\le P(t)\le b_su^{s+1}.\] Consequently \[f_\rho(X,Y)=(Y+\rho)^{-1/(s+1)}\mathbf1_{[0,1]^2}\] has \(L^{s+1}\) norm comparable to \((\log(1/\rho))^{1/(s+1)}\), whereas its curve integrals are at least \(c_s\log(1/\rho)-C_s\) throughout \(U\). For \(p<s+1\), the strip indicator \(\mathbf1_{[0,1]\times[0,\rho]}\) gives output \(\gtrsim\rho^{1/(s+1)}\) and input norm \(\rho^{1/p}\). These are the required divergent ratios. The output set may have negative vertical coordinate; the framework permits it. The compactness, jet rank, and projection conditions are all verified for the replacement. Its availability does not validate the printed family.

claim: Recorded check: Counterexample: Momentm3s1t1/2vector(1/4,-1,1) keepsjetsbutchangeslowcoeffs;projectedtangent(-2t,1).
analysis: On pp. 3 and 54, equality of jets of \(\sum u_jz^j\) at \(t\) means that the difference is divisible by \((z-t)^{s+1}\), rather than fixing its first \(s+1\) coefficients. For \(m=3,s=1,t=1/2\), the coefficient vector \((1/4,-1,1)\) gives \((z-1/2)^2\). The projected tangent is \((-2t,1)\), not a constant coordinate direction. The required projection is still injective on the jet kernel: a polynomial of degree at most \(s-1\) cannot have a zero of multiplicity \(s+1\).

On pp. 54–55, the slicing tangent space has dimension \(s+1\), and is transverse, generally not orthogonal, to the jet kernel. At \(t=1/1000\) in the preceding example, the kernel is spanned by \((t^2,-2t,1)\), whereas the slice tangent is \(\{du_2=0\}\). The direct-sum condition follows from invertibility of \(\pi D\Phi\) on the jet kernel and proves the needed sliced rank. The output-map uses of immersion should be submersion.

For the circle on p. 59, the actual fiber near \((x,y,r)=(0,0,1)\) is \(x=0,\ y+r=1\). The printed \((e,0,1-e)\) has value \(\sqrt{1-2e}\) and derivative \(e/\sqrt{1-2e}\) at zero, rather than value one and derivative zero. The correct tangent \((0,-1,1)\) projects nontrivially, so the circular example survives.

For the ellipse on p. 60, direct differentiation gives the jets \(0,\ldots,4\) determinant, in \((a,b,x,y,\theta)\), as \[\frac{18b^2(b^2-a^2)}{a^{13}}.\] It is zero at the circle \((a,b)=(1,1)\), where the source claims nonvanishing, but equals \(-27/4096\) at the intended noncircular base point \((2,1)\). The correct local fiber of jets \((1,0,-1/4,0)\) is \(x=\theta=0,\ b=a^2/4,\ y=1-a^2/4\). Its tangent \((1,1,0,-1,0)\) has nonzero center projection. This verifies the intended elliptic application after correcting the base point and fiber. Symbolic determinants and reconstruction identities were actually computed; they agree with the displayed hand derivations.

claim: Recorded check: Counterexample: Two semialgebraic subitems only: W=[-1,1] x {-1} cannot be covered by strict one-sided bands with centers >=-1 and an exceptional base of measure O(1/L); for n=2…
analysis: Two literal semialgebraic statements need corrections that leave their intended applications available. For Proposition 3.1, p. 27, let \(W=[-1,1]\times\{-1\}\) and \(u=1\). The strict bands \(f_i(x)<z<f_i(x)+u\), with \(f_i\in[-1,1]\), cannot cover its bottom face. The exceptional base must have measure at least two, contradicting its \(O(M^{O(1)}/L)\) bound as \(L\) grows. The proof on p. 32 uses closed and centered bands; writing \(\left|z-f_i(x)\right|\le u\) repairs this obstruction.

For Proposition 3.6, p. 29, the stated \(n!L^n\) Lipschitz bound fails for small \(L\). With \(n=2,T=(0,1)^2,L=1/4,f=Lx_1\), the actual Lipschitz constant is \(L>2L^2\). The application can restrict to large \(L\); otherwise use a bound with \(\max(1,L)\).

The proposed long-interval ODE objection is withdrawn. The global convention on p. 13 restricts intervals to subsets of \([0,1]\), and Theorem 3.12 and Lemmas 3.13–3.14 do not state an exception. Thus the previous diagnostic on \([0,T]\) as \(T\to\infty\) does not satisfy their hypotheses.

In fact the displayed bounds hold in the stated scope. Put \(z=\mathcal J_{n-1}f-\mathcal J_{n-1}g\) and \(\ell=|I|\le1\). The shift part of the first-order jet system has Euclidean operator norm at most one. With one residual bounded by \(\rho\), \[|z'|\le(1+L)|z|+\rho,\qquad |z(t_0)|\le\rho .\] For \(d=|t-t_0|\le\ell\), forward or backward Gronwall gives \[|f(t)-g(t)|\le |z(t)|
 \le(1+d)e^{(1+L)d}\rho
 \le 2e\,e^{L|I|}\rho .\] This proves the claimed form in Theorem 3.12 and Lemma 3.13. Two residuals give the same conclusion with \(3e\) in Lemma 3.14. No ODE formulation defect is retained in P8. The separate selected-radius diagnostic for Proposition 3.11 below has a different scope and is not a theorem counterexample.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterexample: Two semialgebraic subitems only: W=[-1,1] x {-1} cannot be covered by strict one-sided bands with centers >=-1 and an exceptional base of measure O(1/L); for n=2, T=(0,1)^2, L=1/4 and f=L*x_1, the Lipschitz constant L exceeds n!*L^n=2L^2. Definition 3.3 allows L>=0.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The proof uses closed centered bands and the application permits large L. The long-interval ODE diagnostic is withdrawn: p.13 restricts I to [0,1], with no exception in Theorem 3.12 or Lemmas 3.13-3.14. The Euclidean jet system gives |z_prime| <= (1+L)|z| + rho and |z(t0)|<=rho, hence |f-g| <= 2e*exp(L*|I|)*rho on |I|<=1; two residuals give 3e in Lemma 3.14. This validates the claimed form in its actual scope.

For a fixed center, width and length, the admissible left endpoints for each degree-\(D\) polynomial form \(O(D+1)\) intervals. The exact prism-to-cube identity in Definition 2.18, p. 18, fails when the subtracted center is not its Taylor polynomial. report: Abstract: The manuscript develops a geometric automaton method for fixed-point properties of random groups, with small-cancellation and Rips-type applications. Several useful mechanisms survive detailed checking, including checkpoint separation, productive-language counting, fixed-point permanence, and the intended distinction between a fixed dimension and all dimensions. The acquired version nevertheless needs substantive corrections. Its growth definition admits an edgeless automaton, making a central simultaneous-intersection event have probability zero. A cube family disproves the uniform visible-clique growth bound used in the quantitative argument, although an action-dependent reading of the auxiliary lemma is true. The explicit empty-word conventions also give a counterexample to the advertised black-box criterion. In the reduced model, block rewiring alone does not justify the fixed-remainder transfer. Precise witnesses and bounded repairs are provided, together with five groups of local corrections. The Rips normality step remains a request for evidence under the full hypotheses, rather than a claimed counterexample to that corollary. No counterexample to the final fixed-ambient-dimension random-group theorems is established. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Random Groups Are Not \(n\)-Cubulated:
Review of the Acquired Version
# Identity, version, claims, and review scope

This is the initial scientific review of M25-0200, Zachary Munro, Random groups are not \(n\)-cubulated [Munro], DOI https://doi.org/10.1215/00127094-2025-0031. The reviewed source is the actual 36-page arXiv:2403.08522v2, dated 27 May 2025 in the first-page watermark. Its 1,054,594 bytes have SHA-256
The matching acquired TeX has 1,085 lines and 131,414 bytes; it was read, not executed. The 33 manifest-bound files total 3,286,701 bytes, with no intake byte or hash anomaly.

The publisher metadata identify Duke Mathematical Journal 174(18), 3615–3654, with print date 1 December 2025. That 40-page version was unavailable: the publisher request returned an access interstitial rather than article contents. No equivalence to it is assumed. No separate supplement or released computational repository was identified in the bounded available-source searches; the publisher’s supplemental inventory could not be inspected. These are access limitations, not mathematical defects. The source archive and its figures were obtained. All page references below refer to the acquired primary, whose physical and printed page numbers agree.

Theorem 1.2 concerns each fixed \(n\) and each fixed density \(d\in(0,1)\) in the plain-word model. Theorem 1.3 concerns the reduced-word model with a generator threshold \(k(n)\) independent of \(d\). The limit is relator length \(L\to\infty\). The argument constructs finite automata whose positive accepted words move a basepoint, then uses random relators to meet all required languages. It passes through a block presentation \(\widehat G_m\), a quotient onto \(H_m\), and fixed-point permanence. Theorem 5.10 is a separate arbitrary-presentation criterion. Theorem 1.5 constructs one finitely generated \(\mathrm{FW}_\infty\) group, and Corollary 1.6 asserts a Rips extension with a finitely generated \(\mathrm{FW}_n\) kernel.

The severity assessments concern the actual impact on these statements and deductions. A bounded repair does not by itself make a failure Minor. Conversely, an example violating an additional hypothesis is not presented as a counterexample to a stronger theorem.
# P1. Major: the asserted simultaneous probability is zero
## Exact location and witness

Definition 3.2, pp. 10–11, calls an automaton \(\lambda\)-large when some \(K>0\) makes every start path of length at least \(K\) terminate at a vertex with at least \(\lambda q\) outgoing edges, where \(q=|S^\pm|\). It does not require such a path to exist.

Let \(\Sigma_0\) have one vertex, designated as its start, and no edges. It is finite and deterministically labelled. Taking \(K=1\) satisfies the definition for every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). Its language is only the empty word; at every positive length it accepts zero words. Thus the growth-to-density assertion before Lemma 5.3, p. 27, and the automaton consequence of that lemma are false.

The effect in the main proof is exact. On p. 29, \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) is the set of all \(\lambda\)-large automata over the block alphabet of size \(Q=q^m\), with at most \((Qn+1)^n\) states. The one-state \(\Sigma_0\) belongs to this family. For \(L=m\widehat L+r\), \(0\le r<m\), \(L\ge m\), every block relator in \(\widehat R_{m,L}\) has formal block length \(2\widehat L>0\). Formal concatenation is not free reduction. Consequently, \[\widehat R_{m,L}\cap\mathcal L_{\Sigma_0}=\varnothing,
 \qquad
 \mathbb P\!\left\{\forall\Sigma\in\boldsymbol\Sigma,\
       \widehat R_{m,L}\cap\mathcal L_\Sigma\ne\varnothing\right\}=0.\] The displayed event in the proof is therefore impossible, rather than overwhelmingly probable. Excluding the empty word from accepted languages does not repair this issue: the language then becomes empty.
## The arbitrary-vertex assertion and a precise repair

Remark 5.9, p. 29, also needs a restriction. Over \(\{a,A,b,B\}\), take start edges \(s\to u\) labelled \(a\) and \(s\to v\) labelled \(b\); put all four loops at \(u\) and no edge at \(v\). This automaton has infinite start paths and is \(1\)-large with \(K=2\). Yet the accessible vertex \(v\) has no positive-length language. Removing unreachable vertices alone is insufficient.

Require deterministic labelling and a start path of length \(K\), in addition to the eventual branching condition. Then, for \(L\ge K\), \[\#\mathcal L_\Sigma(L)\ge
 \lceil\lambda q\rceil^{L-K}\ge(\lambda q)^{L-K}.\] Every vertex reached by a start path of length at least \(K\) has the same lower bound for all its continuations, and every outgoing endpoint remains in this eventual set. These are precisely the vertices required after the long prefix \(R_1\) in the source’s concatenation argument.

If a length-\(L\) language has at least \(c q^{d'L}\) words and \(d+d'>1\), independent uniform sampling of \(\lfloor q^{dL}\rfloor\) relators gives miss probability at most \[\exp\{-c' q^{(d+d'-1)L}\}\] for sufficiently large \(L\). For fixed alphabet and state bound there are finitely many deterministic automata up to state renaming: with at most \(B\) states their number is at most \(B^2(B+1)^{qB}\). A finite union bound, the eventual-state restriction, and the finitely many residue classes then justify this probabilistic step for a productive family.

This is a Major defect in a central deduction, not a counterexample to the final random-group conclusion. A repaired proof must show that its geometric construction always supplies members of the restricted productive family; it cannot infer that fact from the current definition.
# P2. Major: the required uniform visible-clique bound fails
## The quantifier distinction is essential

Lemma 4.8, p. 20, introduces \(\epsilon(n)>0\) and \(\alpha(\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1,n)>0\), using a bound on pairwise crossings only in the visible set \(\mathcal H\). Its proof, pp. 21–23, proposes \[\alpha(\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1,n)
   =\epsilon_0(1-\epsilon_1)D_n(n-1).\] Theorem 4.16, p. 26, explicitly needs a growth constant depending only on ambient dimension and its specified epsilon parameter. Its induction imports \(\alpha\) with the visible-clique index.

There is a genuine logical qualification. Lemma 4.8 begins by fixing the action and basepoint. If its functions are allowed to depend on those previously fixed data and on the alphabet, that weaker reading is true. Choose any nonbackward letter \(s\). The path \(ss^{-1}\) has safe prefix orbit points \(x,sx,x\) and terminal witness \(H\). Taking such paths gives a checkpoint tree with growth at least \(1/|S^\pm|\). The finding below concerns the uniform reading needed by the subsequent quantitative proof, not this weak existence assertion.
## A complete family of examples

Fix an integer \(h\ge3\), let \(M\) vary, and put \(D=hM+1\). Let \(X=[0,1]^D\), \(x=0\). Use \(M\) distinct formal generators \(b_\ell\), all acting by the coordinate-one flip, and \(D-1=hM\) generators \(t_j\), \(2\le j\le D\), acting by the transposition of coordinates \(1,j\). Their inverse symbols are distinct, although the assigned automorphisms are involutions. Faithfulness and distinct generator images are not hypotheses of the lemma.

Only the flip letters move \(x\). The visible set is the singleton \(\{H_1\}\), with \(H_1=\{z_1=1/2\}\), while every pair of distinct coordinate hyperplanes crosses. Writing \(N=|S^\pm|=2(h+1)M\), we have \[|\mathcal B(H_1)|=2M,\qquad
 |\mathcal B(H_1)|/N=r=\frac1{h+1}.\] The visible crossing bound is \(n=1\), independent of \(M\). If a uniform \(\epsilon(1)>0\) exists, choose \(h\) large enough that \(r\le\epsilon(1)\), and set \(\epsilon_0=\epsilon_1=r\).

Every word \(v\) acts on vertices as \(v(z)=a\mathbin{\oplus}Pz\), with \(a=v(x)\) and \(Pe_j=e_{\pi(j)}\). A progressing terminal word \(w\) must keep every prefix orbit point on the \(x\)-side of \(H_1\). Its only possible visible witness is \(H_1\). Since distinct coordinate hyperplanes cross, the terminal alternative reduces to \(\pi_w(1)=1\).

Consider the parent word \(v\) of a terminal leaf. Prefix safety gives \(a_1=0\). If \(\pi_v(1)=1\), a flip gives terminal first coordinate one and violates safety, whereas every swap sends \(H_1\) to a different coordinate hyperplane. There is no terminal child. If \(\pi_v(1)\ne1\), a flip cannot restore that index. Only the swap with \(j=\pi_v^{-1}(1)\), and its formal inverse, can terminate. Thus every possible terminal parent has at most two terminal children.

There is no one-letter progressing terminal word. Any checkpoint tree of positive growth therefore has a nonroot internal vertex of maximal depth, all of whose children are terminal. Its degree is at least two even under the source’s undirected-leaf convention. It follows that every such tree satisfies \[\alpha N\le2,\qquad
 \alpha\le\frac1{(h+1)M}\longrightarrow0.\] The bound is attained by taking swaps at the root and the two inverse-image swap symbols at each child. Thus the problem is not nonexistence of individual trees; their best growth tends to zero with fixed visible and epsilon parameters.
## Counterevidence, actual impact, and repair boundary

The same example works without hyperplane inversions. Subdivide every coordinate interval at \(1/2\) and use \(H=\{z_1=1/4\}\). It remains the only visible hyperplane. A signed permutation stabilizing a quarter-level hyperplane preserves its sides. A terminal image at level \(3/4\) would force first orbit coordinate one, contrary to safety; an image in another coordinate crosses \(H\). The preceding two-child bound is unchanged.

The example has a global fixed center and its corner is not a displacement minimizer. Neither exclusion appears in Lemma 4.8. Its ambient dimension also grows. It does not refute Theorem 4.16 under that theorem’s additional hypotheses, or the final fixed-dimension result. Both the epsilon threshold and alpha must be uniform for the family argument; allowing an action-dependent threshold can also protect the displayed formula on a shrinking domain.

The exact failed step on p. 23 is applying the visible crossing bound to the translates \(uH\), which need not be visible. Here \(t_jH_1=H_j\) already demonstrates this. The weak bound \(1/N\) cannot supply the later sufficient condition \(\lambda>N^{-d}\), \(0<d<1\).

A sufficient geometric repair uses a global crossing bound, such as ambient dimension, throughout the checkpoint lemma. Keep that ambient parameter fixed while the later induction decreases the visible-clique index. With the local corrections below, each relevant finite array entry can be made at least \(1/2\), giving growth \(\epsilon_0(1-\epsilon_1)/2>0\). A continuing path of length \(k\) gives \(k+1\) pairwise crossing translates, so continuing depth is at most \(n-1\). The final easy extension may add two edges; it must not be subjected to the continuing-tree bound. This gives a finite depth bound \(n+1\). It supports a revised uniform construction, but does not by itself verify every exact state bound or graph form printed later.
# P3. Major at the black-box statement: empty words

Section 2.1, p. 7, explicitly includes the empty word among every word’s prefixes. Section 3.1, p. 10, permits trivial paths, and Definition 3.1 accepts every path from the start. Thus every automaton accepts the empty word.

Definition 3.4(1), pp. 11–12, applied to the trivial start path requires \(x\ne x\). Definition 3.6, p. 13, similarly makes a starting progressing pair impossible by testing its empty prefix. The nontriviality conclusions in Lemmas 3.5 and 3.13 need corresponding restrictions.

This has a direct theorem-level witness, beyond notation. For any proposed family in Theorem 5.10, p. 30, take \(R=\{\varnothing\}\), the singleton containing the empty formal word. It meets every accepted language. Nevertheless, \[\langle S\mid\varnothing\rangle=F_S.\] For nonempty \(S\), its Cayley-tree action has no global fixed point. Taking the product with an \((n-1)\)-cube on which it acts trivially gives exactly dimension \(n\). The advertised arbitrary-presentation criterion is therefore false under the explicit conventions.

The repair is to use accepted positive-length words in the nontriviality criterion, require positive start paths, and omit the empty prefix only in conditions requiring movement of \(x\). The same-halfspace condition at an \(H\)-checkpoint may retain it. Positive random relator lengths make this convention repair compatible with the intended asymptotic argument. That counterevidence does not remove the actual counterexample to Theorem 5.10, so the final assessment is Major at that core statement. This differs from the bounded helper’s initial Minor proposal; the original proposal and the reason for the primary adjudication are preserved. P1 remains even after this repair, so the two findings are not duplicates.
# P4. Major: fixed remainders need endpoint control
## The missing reduced-model step

Theorem 1.3’s proof sketch, pp. 31–32, rewires states to prevent cancellation between blocks, retaining growth \(\lambda-1/q\). It then transfers the remainder of Theorem 1.2’s proof under the condition \(\lambda-1/q>0\). That proof, p. 29, uses a fixed word \(w\) of remainder length and the two languages \(\mathcal L_\Sigma^{s}w^{-1}\) and \(w\mathcal L_\Sigma^v\). Their seams are additional constraints.

Here is a finite witness satisfying more than merely positive abstract growth. Let \[\mathcal A=\{a,A,b,B,c,C,d,D\},\quad
 A=a^{-1},\ B=b^{-1},\ C=c^{-1},\ D=d^{-1},
 \quad m=2.\] There are \(N_m=8\cdot7=56\) reduced blocks. Put \(P=\{xa:x\in\mathcal A,\ x\ne A\}\) and \(E=P\sqcup P^{-1}\), so \(|E|=14\). Use one start edge labelled \(aa\), and fourteen states indexed by \(e\in E\). At state \(e\), put an \(f\)-edge to state \(f\) for every \(f\in E\setminus\{e^{-1}\}\). Every nonstart state has thirteen outgoing edges, so \(\lambda=1/6\) works. The original accepted block words are freely reduced. There are fifteen states, below the \(n=1\) bound \(N_m+1=57\), and \(\lambda-1/q=1/24>0\).

After rewiring, the reachable states are exactly the clones \((e,a)\), \(e\in P\). At each, the surviving labels are all seven members of \(P\), and each ends in \(a\). Induction gives \(7^{\ell-1}\) positive accepted words of block length \(\ell\), all ending in \(a\). For the permitted remainder \(w=a\), every \(R_1w^{-1}=R_1A\) has a terminal cancellation. At every length \(2\ell+1\), this fixed-remainder language contains zero freely reduced relators.
## Progression, limitations, and repair

After P3’s positive-word correction, this automaton is also progressing for an explicit action. Map the seven \(P\)-symbols of the block free group to a free basis of \(F_7\), map their inverses accordingly, and send the other 42 block symbols to the identity. Let \(X\) be the Cayley tree of \(F_7\). Declare every nonstart state \(e\) a checkpoint labelled by the visible midpoint \(H_{e^{-1}}\). For \(f\ne e^{-1}\), \(x\) and \(fx\) lie on the same side of \(H_{e^{-1}}\), whereas \(fH_{f^{-1}}\) is a distinct midpoint separating them. All relevant checkpoint tests reduce to these single edges. The start edge has the required separating witness. The identity vertex minimizes total displacement: fourteen nontrivial letters each move every vertex at least one edge, and equality is attained there.

This refutes the unrestricted fixed-remainder inference from the printed growth and rewiring assumptions. It does not say that \(q=8\) exceeds the theorem’s unspecified \(2k(1)\), or that every automaton the source might choose for this action fails. Indeed, its many fixed block letters permit a different fix-set construction, and other remainders may work. No counterexample to the final existential-\(k(n)\) theorem is asserted. The missing transfer is nevertheless part of the argument for a principal result, and requires a proof rather than an unchanged repetition of the plain model.

One sufficient repair retains the theorem’s quantifiers. For general \(q\), write \[N_m=q(q-1)^{m-1},\qquad \gamma=\lambda-\frac1q.\] A specified first or last letter occupies exactly \(N_m/q\) reduced blocks. Choose \(q>2/\lambda\). In addition to rewiring, impose the final-letter restriction on \(R_1\) and the first-letter restriction on \(R_2\) needed by the fixed remainder. Each costs at most \(N_m/q\) candidates at the affected block, leaving positive choices. Apply these restrictions at eventual productive states; the two paths still concatenate in the rewired automaton. Only fixed endpoint factors are lost.

The correct original-letter growth base is \[(\gamma N_m)^{1/m}
   =(q-1)\left(\frac{\gamma q}{q-1}\right)^{1/m}.\] Its exponent relative to \(q-1\) tends to one as \(m\to\infty\). For each fixed \(d>0\), choose \(m\) large enough to exceed the density threshold. The stronger lower bound on \(q\) depends only on the dimension-dependent \(\lambda\), while \(m\) may depend on \(d\). This repairs this step without changing the intended order of quantifiers.
# Local corrections with bounded impact
## P5. Minor: prefix safety in easy extensions

Lemma 4.3, pp. 17–18, and Corollary 4.5, pp. 18–19, need safety for every existing prefix, not just the endpoint. On the cubical line, let \(x=0\), \(a(t)=t+1\), \(H=\{1/2\}\), \(w=aA\), and \(s=A\). Then \(wx=0\) is in the carrier on the \(x\)-side, and \(wsx=-1\) is on that side outside the carrier, so \(s\in\mathcal A_w(H)\). But the prefix \(a\) crosses \(H\), and \((ws,H)\) is not progressing.

For the full corollary, let \(a,b\) both translate by one. Take root edges \(a,b\), followed respectively by \(A,B\). Every nonleaf has at least one outgoing edge, giving \(\lambda=1/4\) over four letters. At each terminal return to zero, \(|\mathcal A_w(H)|\ge2\). No extension can remove the earlier crossing, so the claimed general extension conclusion fails.

The actual continuing trees in the main construction use the crossing-parallel sets and do preserve prefix safety. State that hypothesis explicitly. The two-step branch must test \(|\mathcal B(H)|\), as in the corollary’s hypothesis, rather than \(|\mathcal B_w(H)|\), which can be empty there. The end of Lemma 4.3(3) must refer to \((wst,H)\), not \((ws,H)\), and the indexed parallel set is required in item (2). With these corrections the nearest-separator witnesses are valid. This is Minor because the intended application has the missing safety property; the general lemma’s printed scope is too broad.
## P6. Minor: rooted leaves and mixed-depth lifts

The leaf convention on p. 10 uses undirected degree one. A one-edge \(H\)-tree then has no nonleaf vertices, so Definition 3.8’s branching requirement is vacuous at its root. Lemma 3.11, pp. 14–15, uses that root’s branching.

After the positive-start convention is repaired, let \(a\) translate the line by one, and take \(H_\pm=\{\pm1/2\}\). Use start edges \(a,A\) with respective witnesses \(H_-,H_+\). Give \(T_{H_-}\) one \(a\)-edge and \(T_{H_+}\) one \(A\)-edge, each retaining its own hyperplane label. They satisfy the printed hyperplane progression conditions and are vacuously \(1\)-large under the undirected convention. Their realization accepts only \(a^L,A^L\) at positive length \(L\), and its long paths have one continuation instead of two. This is a conditional counterexample to the realization lemma after P3’s repair, not an example satisfying the unrepaired contradictory start definition.

Use rooted terminal vertices as leaves and require branching at every \(H\)-root and internal vertex. The Section 4 constructions have additional structure; the example does not establish their failure.

A separate scope problem occurs in Lemma 4.7, pp. 19–20. Let the prefix-closed vertex words be \[\{\varnothing,a,c,aa,ab,ac,aac\}.\] The subtree \(T_0\) on nonleaves is the path \(\{\varnothing,a,aa\}\), with the rooted-lift property. At its terminal vertex \(aa\), the outgoing set \(\{c\}\) is contained in all suffix-vertex outgoing sets, namely \(\{a,c\},\{a,b,c\},\{c\}\). Any root condition from the undirected convention is tautological. Nevertheless the edge from \(a\) to \(ab\), labelled \(b\), has no rooted lift. Require equal leaf depths, as in the intended continuing trees, or test every old vertex receiving a terminal edge. These hypotheses preserve the use made in the main construction, so no additional Major is inferred.
## P7. Minor: the finite array and parameter domains

On p. 26, the definition of \(\epsilon_0\) uses \(\epsilon_0\) inside the set whose supremum defines it, rather than the dummy variable \(x\). Writing \(z=\min\{1/5,\epsilon(n)\}\), choose \(\epsilon_1=(1+(1-4z)^n)/2\). If the defining set is nonempty, its supremum must be \(z\), where its displayed inequality is false. If it is empty it has no positive supremum in the specified range. Thus the literal prescription fails.

Even correcting the dummy variable leaves a domain issue. The resulting choice is \(\min\{z,(1-\epsilon_1^{1/n})/4\}\), which can exceed \(\epsilon_1\); take \(n=2,\epsilon_1=z/2\). Some alpha evaluations then lie outside the declared range \(\epsilon_1\ge\epsilon_0\). A sufficient replacement is \[\epsilon_0=\min\left\{\frac15,\epsilon(n),\frac{\epsilon_1}{2},
                      \frac{1-\epsilon_1^{1/n}}8\right\},
 \quad \lambda=1-2\epsilon_0,\quad \rho=1-4\epsilon_0,
 \quad \beta_i=\frac{\epsilon_1}{\rho^{n-i}}.\] Then \(\beta_i\in[\epsilon_1,1)\) and \(\beta_i\ge2\epsilon_0\). Keep ambient \(n\) in alpha and take \[\gamma(1)=1-\beta_1,\qquad
 \gamma(i)=\min\{\epsilon_0,\alpha(\epsilon_0,\beta_i,n),
                         \rho\gamma(i-1)\}.\] All are positive. The restriction step has the correct normalization \(\beta_i/\rho=\beta_{i-1}\). Lemma 4.15 also needs \(\lambda>1/2\), as this choice provides. These numerical repairs do not resolve P2 by themselves; they are recorded separately from its uniform geometric defect.
## P8. Minor: inversion of plain blocks

Definition 5.4, p. 27, asserts fixed-point-free inversion on all plain words of every length \(m>0\). For \(m=2r\), exactly \(q^r\) words are fixed: they are \(uu^{-1}\), \(|u|=r\). The smallest example is \(aA\). Such words cannot be partitioned into a set and its disjoint inverse image. For odd \(m\), a fixed word would have a central letter equal to its formal inverse, which is impossible.

Choose sufficiently large odd \(m\). This preserves every needed growth inequality and the finite residue-class argument. Indeed each original generator is represented by \(a(bB)^{(m-1)/2}\), so in the plain model \(H_m=G\) for odd \(m\). A nonempty reduced word is never fixed by formal inversion, for either parity. This correction does not change the main asymptotic conclusion or supply a counterexample to it.
## P9. Minor: dimension of the median fixed-set realization

The proof of Lemma 1.7, pp. 28–29, says the median realization \(X_Y\) is \(n\)-dimensional because \(X\) is. Take \(K=\mathbb Z/2\) reflecting an interval, with \(G=K\) and trivial quotient \(N\). After cubical subdivision the fixed vertices consist only of its midpoint. Thus \(\dim X_Y=0<1=\dim X\), under the stated extension hypotheses.

The preceding source paragraph correctly gives \(\dim X_Y\le n\), and that is sufficient. If \(\mathrm{FW}_n\) is defined using exactly dimension \(n\), pad a lower-dimensional action by a trivially acted-on cube. A fixed point in \(X_Y\) provides a finite orbit in its stabilized cube, hence a finite \(G\)-orbit in \(X\), and the CAT(0) fixed-point argument applies. The quotient and finite-index permanence arguments also check directly. No counterexample to extension closure was found.
# Applications, proof dependencies, and evidence still needed
## Rips normality is not yet verified under the full hypotheses

On p. 33, the displayed relations \(a_i b_j a_i^{-1}=B_{ij}\) prove only \(a_iKa_i^{-1}\subseteq K\). The inverse inclusion is not supplied by inverting this statement. For the general inference, the affine maps \(a(t)=2t\), \(b(t)=t+1\) satisfy \(aba^{-1}=b^2\), while \(a^{-1}ba\) translates by \(1/2\) and is outside \(\langle b\rangle\).

This affine example does not satisfy the manuscript’s full fixed-point and small-cancellation hypotheses. It is therefore evidence of an insufficient algebraic justification, not a certified counterexample to Corollary 1.6. The status of normality under the complete construction remains NeedsEvidence.

An explicit algebraic repair reserves distinct words for both conjugation signs \(a_i^{\pm1}b_j a_i^{\mp1}\). Then \(K\) is normal, the quotient is \(G\), and \(K\) is a quotient of the retained \(\mathrm{FW}_n\) presentation. Removing this larger but fixed finite number of random relators preserves density. To obtain the stipulated base \(C'(1/(2p))\) from Corollary 1.4, choose \(d<1/(4p)\); the earlier \(d<1/(2p)\) alone does not furnish that stronger condition. The existential application allows the smaller choice.

The p. 34 assertion that a new piece contains one old contiguous piece of length \(|w|-2C\) also requires a precise marker argument. Deleting short prefixes alone can leave multiple fragments. The actual distinction between the \(a\)-markers and long \(b\)-words, together with normalized distinct input relators, gives counterevidence to a generic fragmentation objection. No complete counterexample covering the actual cyclic, inverse, and symmetrized relator conditions was found. The revised two-sign construction needs this piece check explicitly; it is not silently certified here.
## The \(\mathrm{FW}_\infty\) construction and external imports

The ray construction on pp. 32–33 is locally finite: each vertex and edge meets only finitely many finite presentations and additional cells. Every adjacent group is meant to generate the same quotient, so a single resulting group inherits \(\mathrm{FW}_i\) for every \(i\). This does not exchange a probability limit with an infinite intersection.

The attachment \(s t^{-1}Qt\) gives the transported relation \(s=Q^{-1}\), while the text writes \(Q\). Inverting the selected word preserves the generation and quotient argument. At the first ray vertex the nonexistent left attachment must be omitted.

A sufficient way to make the piece estimates transparent is to choose the available stronger base \(C'(1/12)\) presentations and lengths \(L_i>36\). Use each reserved word once. A distinct new-cell piece cannot traverse the entire unique connector marker in both cells; otherwise it identifies the same occurrence. The remaining overlap has at most one old-word piece and at most three connector letters. When a long overlap exists, the common vertex alphabet has the same base length, and \[|{\rm piece}|<L_i/12+3<(L_i+3)/6.\] Other overlaps are bounded connector segments. Old/new overlaps obey the old perimeter bound. This describes a tightened construction, not an assertion that every original choice already has the needed slack.

Asphericity supplies geometric dimension at most two. Exact dimension additionally needs nontriviality and a lower-bound argument; it does not follow from asphericity alone. Small-cancellation normal-form reasoning and the nontrivial \(\mathrm{FW}_1\) condition are natural ways to supply these steps, with the appropriate dimension theorem stated explicitly. No full counterexample to Theorem 1.5 is established.

For a bounded citation check, the actual three-page Jankiewicz–Wise arXiv:2006.05297v1 [JW], 8 June 2020, was obtained, read, and visually inspected. Its p. 2 identifies Wise’s Theorem 10.5 and Corollary 10.7 as the local-finiteness and free-cubulation imports. This verifies the citation route, not those external theorems in full. The original Wise paper, the median-realization literature, and the general small-cancellation theorems were not independently reproved in this initial review.
## Positive checks and limits of the black-box repair

Checkpoint separation has a valid geometric mechanism after the stated conventions are fixed. If the new separator is parallel to the old one, visibility places the relevant point adjacent to the old hyperplane. The opposite adjacent vertex lies on the same side of the new separator. The old opposite halfspace is connected and disjoint from the new hyperplane, which gives the claimed continuing separation. This adjacency argument excludes a tempting but invalid arbitrary-point objection.

The \(\mathcal A,\mathcal B,\mathcal P\) partition and the visible-parallel equivalence check under their endpoint assumptions. In the corrected uniform-level trees, the suffix union bound is exactly the triangular recursion; positive lower bounds prevent premature leaves. The finite family argument needs deterministic transition maps, not arbitrary edge multiplicities.

Beyond P3, Theorem 5.10’s exact graph forms deserve an explicit construction: its \(c_1\) must be chosen below \(1/2\) for the stated theta argument, and growth measured in a restricted alphabet must be converted back to the full alphabet. Exact outgoing counts require an integer convention. These are recorded repair requirements, not additional confirmed theorem counterexamples. A final validation should supply the exact state bound and graph form after the global-dimension and productive family repairs.
# Supporting checks

The complete 1,085-line source, bibliography, and primary PDF were covered by the primary reviewer and three bounded native assistants in this same initial review. The assistants read Sections 3, the first part of Section 4, and the inductive construction through Theorem 5.10, respectively, with all assigned text remaining zero. The primary covered the introduction, preliminaries, all applications, returned proofs, quantifier challenges, and final synthesis. Their combined actual image coverage includes all 36 primary pages. The primary separately inspected all three pages of the obtained cited reference. Own exact calculations support the general proofs; finite enumeration is not substituted for an all-length or all-parameter argument.

This assessment records four Major findings and five groups of Minor corrections, with the distinct NeedsEvidence limitations stated above. The main random-group conclusions are not declared false. They require a revised proof carrying the corrected uniform parameters, productivity, word conventions, and reduced-remainder argument through the applications.

The native helpers used inherited configuration without a model override; neither human review nor an unverified backend identity is claimed. The external controller’s interface observation and the runtime self-description are stored separately. Original render-only false records, preliminary numbering, scope qualifications, and earlier calculations remain preserved. This is initial scientific delivery, not independent acceptance. problems.title: Recorded check: Counterexample: One-state edgeless deterministic automaton satisfies eventual growth vacuously with K=1, but has no positive-length word.
problems.source_location: Definition3.2 pp10–11 Section5.1 density assertion and Lemma5.3 p27 Remark5.9 and Theorem1.2 proof p29
claim: Recorded check: Counterexample: One-state edgeless deterministic automaton satisfies eventual growth vacuously with K=1, but has no positive-length word.
analysis: Definition 3.2, pp. 10–11, calls an automaton \(\lambda\)-large when some \(K>0\) makes every start path of length at least \(K\) terminate at a vertex with at least \(\lambda q\) outgoing edges, where \(q=|S^\pm|\). It does not require such a path to exist.

Let \(\Sigma_0\) have one vertex, designated as its start, and no edges. It is finite and deterministically labelled. Taking \(K=1\) satisfies the definition for every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). Its language is only the empty word; at every positive length it accepts zero words. Thus the growth-to-density assertion before Lemma 5.3, p. 27, and the automaton consequence of that lemma are false.

The effect in the main proof is exact. On p. 29, \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) is the set of all \(\lambda\)-large automata over the block alphabet of size \(Q=q^m\), with at most \((Qn+1)^n\) states. The one-state \(\Sigma_0\) belongs to this family. For \(L=m\widehat L+r\), \(0\le r<m\), \(L\ge m\), every block relator in \(\widehat R_{m,L}\) has formal block length \(2\widehat L>0\). Formal concatenation is not free reduction. Consequently, \[\widehat R_{m,L}\cap\mathcal L_{\Sigma_0}=\varnothing,
 \qquad
 \mathbb P\!\left\{\forall\Sigma\in\boldsymbol\Sigma,\
       \widehat R_{m,L}\cap\mathcal L_\Sigma\ne\varnothing\right\}=0.\] The displayed event in the proof is therefore impossible, rather than overwhelmingly probable. Excluding the empty word from accepted languages does not repair this issue: the language then becomes empty.

Remark 5.9, p. 29, also needs a restriction. Over \(\{a,A,b,B\}\), take start edges \(s\to u\) labelled \(a\) and \(s\to v\) labelled \(b\); put all four loops at \(u\) and no edge at \(v\). This automaton has infinite start paths and is \(1\)-large with \(K=2\). Yet the accessible vertex \(v\) has no positive-length language. Removing unreachable vertices alone is insufficient.

Require deterministic labelling and a start path of length \(K\), in addition to the eventual branching condition. Then, for \(L\ge K\), \[\#\mathcal L_\Sigma(L)\ge
 \lceil\lambda q\rceil^{L-K}\ge(\lambda q)^{L-K}.\] Every vertex reached by a start path of length at least \(K\) has the same lower bound for all its continuations, and every outgoing endpoint remains in this eventual set. These are precisely the vertices required after the long prefix \(R_1\) in the source’s concatenation argument.

If a length-\(L\) language has at least \(c q^{d'L}\) words and \(d+d'>1\), independent uniform sampling of \(\lfloor q^{dL}\rfloor\) relators gives miss probability at most \[\exp\{-c' q^{(d+d'-1)L}\}\] for sufficiently large \(L\). For fixed alphabet and state bound there are finitely many deterministic automata up to state renaming: with at most \(B\) states their number is at most \(B^2(B+1)^{qB}\). A finite union bound, the eventual-state restriction, and the finitely many residue classes then justify this probabilistic step for a productive family.

This is a Major defect in a central deduction, not a counterexample to the final random-group conclusion. A repaired proof must show that its geometric construction always supplies members of the restricted productive family; it cannot infer that fact from the current definition.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterexample: One-state edgeless deterministic automaton satisfies eventual growth vacuously with K=1, but has no positive-length word. It belongs to ALL bounded-state lambda-large automata, so the simultaneous block-relator intersection event is exactly probability0 for every L>=m. A productive start with a reachable short dead branch also disproves the arbitrary-vertex density assertion.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The final random-group theorem is not disproved. Eventual states after a long start path do have the required continuation growth once the family is made productive. Removing empty words alone does not repair the dead automaton.

problems.source_location: Lemma4.8 p20 Displayed alpha formula p21 Translated-hyperplane stopping argument p23 Theorem4.16 explicit theta dependence p26 Density threshold p27
claim: Recorded check: Counterexample: Cube family D=hM+1, M identical coordinate1 flips and hM coordinate swaps; visible set is a singleton and backward fraction r=1/(h+1) is fixed.
analysis:
Lemma 4.8, p. 20, introduces \(\epsilon(n)>0\) and \(\alpha(\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1,n)>0\), using a bound on pairwise crossings only in the visible set \(\mathcal H\). Its proof, pp. 21–23, proposes \[\alpha(\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1,n)
   =\epsilon_0(1-\epsilon_1)D_n(n-1).\] Theorem 4.16, p. 26, explicitly needs a growth constant depending only on ambient dimension and its specified epsilon parameter. Its induction imports \(\alpha\) with the visible-clique index.

There is a genuine logical qualification. Lemma 4.8 begins by fixing the action and basepoint. If its functions are allowed to depend on those previously fixed data and on the alphabet, that weaker reading is true. Choose any nonbackward letter \(s\). The path \(ss^{-1}\) has safe prefix orbit points \(x,sx,x\) and terminal witness \(H\). Taking such paths gives a checkpoint tree with growth at least \(1/|S^\pm|\). The finding below concerns the uniform reading needed by the subsequent quantitative proof, not this weak existence assertion.

Fix an integer \(h\ge3\), let \(M\) vary, and put \(D=hM+1\). Let \(X=[0,1]^D\), \(x=0\). Use \(M\) distinct formal generators \(b_\ell\), all acting by the coordinate-one flip, and \(D-1=hM\) generators \(t_j\), \(2\le j\le D\), acting by the transposition of coordinates \(1,j\). Their inverse symbols are distinct, although the assigned automorphisms are involutions. Faithfulness and distinct generator images are not hypotheses of the lemma.

Only the flip letters move \(x\). The visible set is the singleton \(\{H_1\}\), with \(H_1=\{z_1=1/2\}\), while every pair of distinct coordinate hyperplanes crosses. Writing \(N=|S^\pm|=2(h+1)M\), we have \[|\mathcal B(H_1)|=2M,\qquad
 |\mathcal B(H_1)|/N=r=\frac1{h+1}.\] The visible crossing bound is \(n=1\), independent of \(M\). If a uniform \(\epsilon(1)>0\) exists, choose \(h\) large enough that \(r\le\epsilon(1)\), and set \(\epsilon_0=\epsilon_1=r\).

Every word \(v\) acts on vertices as \(v(z)=a\mathbin{\oplus}Pz\), with \(a=v(x)\) and \(Pe_j=e_{\pi(j)}\). A progressing terminal word \(w\) must keep every prefix orbit point on the \(x\)-side of \(H_1\). Its only possible visible witness is \(H_1\). Since distinct coordinate hyperplanes cross, the terminal alternative reduces to \(\pi_w(1)=1\).

Consider the parent word \(v\) of a terminal leaf. Prefix safety gives \(a_1=0\). If \(\pi_v(1)=1\), a flip gives terminal first coordinate one and violates safety, whereas every swap sends \(H_1\) to a different coordinate hyperplane. There is no terminal child. If \(\pi_v(1)\ne1\), a flip cannot restore that index. Only the swap with \(j=\pi_v^{-1}(1)\), and its formal inverse, can terminate. Thus every possible terminal parent has at most two terminal children.

There is no one-letter progressing terminal word. Any checkpoint tree of positive growth therefore has a nonroot internal vertex of maximal depth, all of whose children are terminal. Its degree is at least two even under the source’s undirected-leaf convention. It follows that every such tree satisfies \[\alpha N\le2,\qquad
 \alpha\le\frac1{(h+1)M}\longrightarrow0.\] The bound is attained by taking swaps at the root and the two inverse-image swap symbols at each child. Thus the problem is not nonexistence of individual trees; their best growth tends to zero with fixed visible and epsilon parameters.
result: The same example works without hyperplane inversions. Subdivide every coordinate interval at \(1/2\) and use \(H=\{z_1=1/4\}\). It remains the only visible hyperplane. A signed permutation stabilizing a quarter-level hyperplane preserves its sides. A terminal image at level \(3/4\) would force first orbit coordinate one, contrary to safety; an image in another coordinate crosses \(H\). The preceding two-child bound is unchanged.

The example has a global fixed center and its corner is not a displacement minimizer. Neither exclusion appears in Lemma 4.8. Its ambient dimension also grows. It does not refute Theorem 4.16 under that theorem’s additional hypotheses, or the final fixed-dimension result. Both the epsilon threshold and alpha must be uniform for the family argument; allowing an action-dependent threshold can also protect the displayed formula on a shrinking domain.

The exact failed step on p. 23 is applying the visible crossing bound to the translates \(uH\), which need not be visible. Here \(t_jH_1=H_j\) already demonstrates this. The weak bound \(1/N\) cannot supply the later sufficient condition \(\lambda>N^{-d}\), \(0<d<1\).

A sufficient geometric repair uses a global crossing bound, such as ambient dimension, throughout the checkpoint lemma. Keep that ambient parameter fixed while the later induction decreases the visible-clique index. With the local corrections below, each relevant finite array entry can be made at least \(1/2\), giving growth \(\epsilon_0(1-\epsilon_1)/2>0\). A continuing path of length \(k\) gives \(k+1\) pairwise crossing translates, so continuing depth is at most \(n-1\). The final easy extension may add two edges; it must not be subjected to the continuing-tree bound. This gives a finite depth bound \(n+1\). It supports a revised uniform construction, but does not by itself verify every exact state bound or graph form printed later.

Recorded evidence: Counterexample: Cube family D=hM+1, M identical coordinate1 flips and hM coordinate swaps; visible set is a singleton and backward fraction r=1/(h+1) is fixed. Each terminal parent has at most2 possible terminal children, so best checkpoint growth is exactly2/N=1/((h+1)M). With uniform epsilon threshold and alpha this tends0 at fixed visible/epsilon parameters. A first subdivision removes hyperplane inversions without changing the obstruction.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The weak reading allowing action/alphabet-dependent epsilon and alpha is TRUE: safe ss^-1 trees give1/N growth. Both uniformities are essential. The counterfamily's ambient dimension grows, it has a global fixed center and nonminimal corner, and it does not refute the additional hypotheses or conclusion of Theorem4.16.

claim: Recorded check: Counterexample: Every automaton accepts the empty word.
analysis: Section 2.1, p. 7, explicitly includes the empty word among every word’s prefixes. Section 3.1, p. 10, permits trivial paths, and Definition 3.1 accepts every path from the start. Thus every automaton accepts the empty word.

Definition 3.4(1), pp. 11–12, applied to the trivial start path requires \(x\ne x\). Definition 3.6, p. 13, similarly makes a starting progressing pair impossible by testing its empty prefix. The nontriviality conclusions in Lemmas 3.5 and 3.13 need corresponding restrictions.

This has a direct theorem-level witness, beyond notation. For any proposed family in Theorem 5.10, p. 30, take \(R=\{\varnothing\}\), the singleton containing the empty formal word. It meets every accepted language. Nevertheless, \[\langle S\mid\varnothing\rangle=F_S.\] For nonempty \(S\), its Cayley-tree action has no global fixed point. Taking the product with an \((n-1)\)-cube on which it acts trivially gives exactly dimension \(n\). The advertised arbitrary-presentation criterion is therefore false under the explicit conventions.

The repair is to use accepted positive-length words in the nontriviality criterion, require positive start paths, and omit the empty prefix only in conditions requiring movement of \(x\). The same-halfspace condition at an \(H\)-checkpoint may retain it. Positive random relator lengths make this convention repair compatible with the intended asymptotic argument. That counterevidence does not remove the actual counterexample to Theorem 5.10, so the final assessment is Major at that core statement. This differs from the bounded helper’s initial Minor proposal; the original proposal and the reason for the primary adjudication are preserved. P1 remains even after this repair, so the two findings are not duplicates.

claim: Recorded check: Counterexample: q8,m2,N56; E={x a:x!=A} union inverses.15 states,13 outgoing labels excluding previous block inverse;lambda1/6, positive retained margin1/24.
analysis: Theorem 1.3’s proof sketch, pp. 31–32, rewires states to prevent cancellation between blocks, retaining growth \(\lambda-1/q\). It then transfers the remainder of Theorem 1.2’s proof under the condition \(\lambda-1/q>0\). That proof, p. 29, uses a fixed word \(w\) of remainder length and the two languages \(\mathcal L_\Sigma^{s}w^{-1}\) and \(w\mathcal L_\Sigma^v\). Their seams are additional constraints.

Here is a finite witness satisfying more than merely positive abstract growth. Let \[\mathcal A=\{a,A,b,B,c,C,d,D\},\quad
 A=a^{-1},\ B=b^{-1},\ C=c^{-1},\ D=d^{-1},
 \quad m=2.\] There are \(N_m=8\cdot7=56\) reduced blocks. Put \(P=\{xa:x\in\mathcal A,\ x\ne A\}\) and \(E=P\sqcup P^{-1}\), so \(|E|=14\). Use one start edge labelled \(aa\), and fourteen states indexed by \(e\in E\). At state \(e\), put an \(f\)-edge to state \(f\) for every \(f\in E\setminus\{e^{-1}\}\). Every nonstart state has thirteen outgoing edges, so \(\lambda=1/6\) works. The original accepted block words are freely reduced. There are fifteen states, below the \(n=1\) bound \(N_m+1=57\), and \(\lambda-1/q=1/24>0\).

After rewiring, the reachable states are exactly the clones \((e,a)\), \(e\in P\). At each, the surviving labels are all seven members of \(P\), and each ends in \(a\). Induction gives \(7^{\ell-1}\) positive accepted words of block length \(\ell\), all ending in \(a\). For the permitted remainder \(w=a\), every \(R_1w^{-1}=R_1A\) has a terminal cancellation. At every length \(2\ell+1\), this fixed-remainder language contains zero freely reduced relators.

After P3’s positive-word correction, this automaton is also progressing for an explicit action. Map the seven \(P\)-symbols of the block free group to a free basis of \(F_7\), map their inverses accordingly, and send the other 42 block symbols to the identity. Let \(X\) be the Cayley tree of \(F_7\). Declare every nonstart state \(e\) a checkpoint labelled by the visible midpoint \(H_{e^{-1}}\). For \(f\ne e^{-1}\), \(x\) and \(fx\) lie on the same side of \(H_{e^{-1}}\), whereas \(fH_{f^{-1}}\) is a distinct midpoint separating them. All relevant checkpoint tests reduce to these single edges. The start edge has the required separating witness. The identity vertex minimizes total displacement: fourteen nontrivial letters each move every vertex at least one edge, and equality is attained there.

This refutes the unrestricted fixed-remainder inference from the printed growth and rewiring assumptions. It does not say that \(q=8\) exceeds the theorem’s unspecified \(2k(1)\), or that every automaton the source might choose for this action fails. Indeed, its many fixed block letters permit a different fix-set construction, and other remainders may work. No counterexample to the final existential-\(k(n)\) theorem is asserted. The missing transfer is nevertheless part of the argument for a principal result, and requires a proof rather than an unchanged repetition of the plain model.

One sufficient repair retains the theorem’s quantifiers. For general \(q\), write \[N_m=q(q-1)^{m-1},\qquad \gamma=\lambda-\frac1q.\] A specified first or last letter occupies exactly \(N_m/q\) reduced blocks. Choose \(q>2/\lambda\). In addition to rewiring, impose the final-letter restriction on \(R_1\) and the first-letter restriction on \(R_2\) needed by the fixed remainder. Each costs at most \(N_m/q\) candidates at the affected block, leaving positive choices. Apply these restrictions at eventual productive states; the two paths still concatenate in the rewired automaton. Only fixed endpoint factors are lost.

The correct original-letter growth base is \[(\gamma N_m)^{1/m}
   =(q-1)\left(\frac{\gamma q}{q-1}\right)^{1/m}.\] Its exponent relative to \(q-1\) tends to one as \(m\to\infty\). For each fixed \(d>0\), choose \(m\) large enough to exceed the density threshold. The stronger lower bound on \(q\) depends only on the dimension-dependent \(\lambda\), while \(m\) may depend on \(d\). This repairs this step without changing the intended order of quantifiers.

analysis: Lemma 4.3, pp. 17–18, and Corollary 4.5, pp. 18–19, need safety for every existing prefix, not just the endpoint. On the cubical line, let \(x=0\), \(a(t)=t+1\), \(H=\{1/2\}\), \(w=aA\), and \(s=A\). Then \(wx=0\) is in the carrier on the \(x\)-side, and \(wsx=-1\) is on that side outside the carrier, so \(s\in\mathcal A_w(H)\). But the prefix \(a\) crosses \(H\), and \((ws,H)\) is not progressing.

For the full corollary, let \(a,b\) both translate by one. Take root edges \(a,b\), followed respectively by \(A,B\). Every nonleaf has at least one outgoing edge, giving \(\lambda=1/4\) over four letters. At each terminal return to zero, \(|\mathcal A_w(H)|\ge2\). No extension can remove the earlier crossing, so the claimed general extension conclusion fails.

The actual continuing trees in the main construction use the crossing-parallel sets and do preserve prefix safety. State that hypothesis explicitly. The two-step branch must test \(|\mathcal B(H)|\), as in the corollary’s hypothesis, rather than \(|\mathcal B_w(H)|\), which can be empty there. The end of Lemma 4.3(3) must refer to \((wst,H)\), not \((ws,H)\), and the indexed parallel set is required in item (2). With these corrections the nearest-separator witnesses are valid. claim: Recorded check: Counterexample: After positive-start repair, translation line with two start edges and one-edge H± trees makes the latter vacuously1-large under undirected leaf definition…
analysis: The leaf convention on p. 10 uses undirected degree one. A one-edge \(H\)-tree then has no nonleaf vertices, so Definition 3.8’s branching requirement is vacuous at its root. Lemma 3.11, pp. 14–15, uses that root’s branching.

After the positive-start convention is repaired, let \(a\) translate the line by one, and take \(H_\pm=\{\pm1/2\}\). Use start edges \(a,A\) with respective witnesses \(H_-,H_+\). Give \(T_{H_-}\) one \(a\)-edge and \(T_{H_+}\) one \(A\)-edge, each retaining its own hyperplane label. They satisfy the printed hyperplane progression conditions and are vacuously \(1\)-large under the undirected convention. Their realization accepts only \(a^L,A^L\) at positive length \(L\), and its long paths have one continuation instead of two. This is a conditional counterexample to the realization lemma after P3’s repair, not an example satisfying the unrepaired contradictory start definition.

Use rooted terminal vertices as leaves and require branching at every \(H\)-root and internal vertex. The Section 4 constructions have additional structure; the example does not establish their failure.

A separate scope problem occurs in Lemma 4.7, pp. 19–20. Let the prefix-closed vertex words be \[\{\varnothing,a,c,aa,ab,ac,aac\}.\] The subtree \(T_0\) on nonleaves is the path \(\{\varnothing,a,aa\}\), with the rooted-lift property. At its terminal vertex \(aa\), the outgoing set \(\{c\}\) is contained in all suffix-vertex outgoing sets, namely \(\{a,c\},\{a,b,c\},\{c\}\). Any root condition from the undirected convention is tautological. Nevertheless the edge from \(a\) to \(ab\), labelled \(b\), has no rooted lift. Require equal leaf depths, as in the intended continuing trees, or test every old vertex receiving a terminal edge. These hypotheses preserve the use made in the main construction, so no additional Major is inferred.

analysis: On p. 26, the definition of \(\epsilon_0\) uses \(\epsilon_0\) inside the set whose supremum defines it, rather than the dummy variable \(x\). Writing \(z=\min\{1/5,\epsilon(n)\}\), choose \(\epsilon_1=(1+(1-4z)^n)/2\). If the defining set is nonempty, its supremum must be \(z\), where its displayed inequality is false. If it is empty it has no positive supremum in the specified range. Thus the literal prescription fails.

Even correcting the dummy variable leaves a domain issue. The resulting choice is \(\min\{z,(1-\epsilon_1^{1/n})/4\}\), which can exceed \(\epsilon_1\); take \(n=2,\epsilon_1=z/2\). Some alpha evaluations then lie outside the declared range \(\epsilon_1\ge\epsilon_0\). A sufficient replacement is \[\epsilon_0=\min\left\{\frac15,\epsilon(n),\frac{\epsilon_1}{2},
                      \frac{1-\epsilon_1^{1/n}}8\right\},
 \quad \lambda=1-2\epsilon_0,\quad \rho=1-4\epsilon_0,
 \quad \beta_i=\frac{\epsilon_1}{\rho^{n-i}}.\] Then \(\beta_i\in[\epsilon_1,1)\) and \(\beta_i\ge2\epsilon_0\). Keep ambient \(n\) in alpha and take \[\gamma(1)=1-\beta_1,\qquad
 \gamma(i)=\min\{\epsilon_0,\alpha(\epsilon_0,\beta_i,n),
                         \rho\gamma(i-1)\}.\] All are positive. The restriction step has the correct normalization \(\beta_i/\rho=\beta_{i-1}\). claim: Recorded check: Counterexample: Evenm=2r has exactlyq^r formal inversion fixed wordsu u^-1;aa^-1 at m2 is simplest, so disjoint inverse pairing of all plain words fails.
analysis: Definition 5.4, p. 27, asserts fixed-point-free inversion on all plain words of every length \(m>0\). For \(m=2r\), exactly \(q^r\) words are fixed: they are \(uu^{-1}\), \(|u|=r\). report: Abstract: This review identifies a finite-rank counterexample to the lowest-index assertion of the abstract Toda theorem, a coordinate normalization error in the stated PNG equation, and a discontinuous approximation used in the backward-equation proof. A fourth, local issue concerns the distributional initial velocity in the narrow-wedge example. The first three issues affect a central theorem or a principal proof dependency and are classified Major; this classification does not assert that the intended PNG results are false or irreparable. The review concerns the identified publisher version and the explicitly documented portions of its proofs. It is an initial technical assessment, with scientific decision pending and no independent human acceptance.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Scientific initial review of
Polynuclear growth and the Toda lattice
# Article, version, and scope

The article is by Konstantin Matetski, Jeremy Quastel, and Daniel Remenik, DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1558. The reviewed PDF is the publisher version of record, Journal of the European Mathematical Society 28 (2026), no. 11, 4951–5021, published online on 3 January 2025. Its inclusion in this 2025 batch refers to the online-publication year, not the printed volume year. It has 71 PDF pages. Below, a page number without a PDF qualifier is the printed journal page; PDF page \(j\) is printed page \(4950+j\). The separate author source is arXiv:2209.02643v2, dated 18 August 2024. It was consulted for algebra and comparison, but equivalence of the two versions is not assumed.

The principal checks concern definitions and normalization in Sections 1–2; the indexed assumptions, resolvent identities, and PNG application in Section 3; and the state space, generator, approximation, and uniqueness step in Section 4. Selected portions of Appendix B were checked as possible counterevidence. The complete source inventory was read and hashed programmatically; this integrity operation is not mathematical verification. The review does not certify every estimate, cited theorem, or argument on all 71 pages. No author program was executed. The exact rational calculation below was written for this review and has a rigorous remainder bound.
# Objects and conventions

The paper studies PNG height probabilities \(F_r(t,x)=\mathbb P(h(t,x)\leq r)\) in the scalar case and their multipoint analogues. The abstract theorem uses trace-class kernels \(K_r\) on a finite direct sum of copies of \(\ell^2(\mathbb Z_{>0})\) and matrices \[Q_r=\big[(I-K_r)^{-1}\big](1,1).\] The abstract index \(r\) is a simultaneous shift of all height thresholds in its PNG application. This distinction matters at the lower endpoint. In Problem 2 only one spatial point is used, so no convention about differentiating a multipoint centre coordinate is needed. In Problems 3–4 the nucleation intensity is the paper’s intensity \(2\), and the deterministic lateral speed is \(1\).

Problem 1 (Major: the lowest interior index in Theorem 3.1).  Location. Theorem 3.1, p. 4974 (PDF 24), assumptions (1)–(3) and conclusion; the asserted mixed identity (3.4), p. 4975 (PDF 25); the application with three indices in Section 3.2, p. 4979 (PDF 29).

Equation reference: eq:toda. Claim being checked. The theorem assumes kernels indexed from \(\underline r\) to \(\overline r\), with \(\underline r<\overline r-1\), satisfying \[\begin{aligned}
K_{r+1}(u,v)&=K_r(u+1,v+1),\\
\partial_\eta K_r(u,v)&=K_{r-1}(u+1,v)-K_r(u+1,v),\\
\partial_\zeta K_r(u,v)&=K_{r-1}(u,v+1)-K_r(u,v+1).\end{aligned}\] The first identity is required up to \(r=\overline r-1\); the derivative identities start at \(r=\underline r+1\). With the stated trace-class, differentiability, and invertibility assumptions, the theorem claims, for every interior \(r\), \[
\partial_\zeta\big(\partial_\eta Q_r\,Q_r^{-1}\big)
 +Q_rQ_{r-1}^{-1}-Q_{r+1}Q_r^{-1}=0.\]

Decisive evidence. Take one copy of \(\ell^2(\mathbb Z_{>0})\), the open parameter set \(\mathbb R^2\), \(\underline r=0\), \(\overline r=2\), and \(P=|1\rangle\langle1|\). Set \[K_0=\tfrac12P,\qquad K_1=K_2=0\] at every parameter value. These are trace-class kernels, with trace norms \(1/2,0,0\). All parameter derivatives, including mixed derivatives, exist in trace norm and vanish. Every required shift or derivative relation holds: \(P(u+1,v)\), \(P(u,v+1)\), and \(P(u+1,v+1)\) vanish for positive integers \(u,v\). Moreover, \[(I-K_0)^{-1}=I+P,\qquad (I-K_1)^{-1}=(I-K_2)^{-1}=I,
\quad (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(2,1,1).\] Thus all required inverses exist, but the left side of [eq:toda] (#eq:toda) at \(r=1\) is \[0+\tfrac12-1=-\tfrac12.\] This is a counterexample to the theorem as quantified, not a numerical failure or a hypothetical objection.

The proof’s asserted identity \[\partial_\eta\partial_\zeta K_r=K_{r+1}-2K_r+K_{r-1}
\tag{3.4 in the article}\] would give \(0=\tfrac12P\) here. Deriving it by differentiating a first-order identity at the lowest interior index needs information on the derivative of \(K_{\underline r}\), which the theorem does not supply.

Impact and repair boundary. Section 3.2 applies the theorem with \(\underline r=-1\), \(\overline r=1\), at \(r=0\), exactly the affected endpoint. Restricting the theorem’s conclusion to \(r\geq\underline r+2\) avoids this particular logical step but leaves that three-kernel application empty. Adding the requisite mixed identity at the indices used is another possible repair. It must then be verified for the actual PNG kernels, including their forcing terms and trace-norm regularity. The rank-one example proves neither that a strengthened abstract theorem fails nor that the intended PNG probability identity is false. The remaining resolvent algebra was checked conditionally on the missing mixed identity; that conditional check does not repair the printed hypotheses.

Problem 2 (Major: a factor of four in the Toda coordinates).  Location. Definition of \(\zeta,\eta\), p. 4957 (PDF 7); Theorem 2.1 and equation (2.13), p. 4958 (PDF 8); the derivative statement preceding (2.19), p. 4959 (PDF 9); the kernel derivative calculation (3.15), p. 4979 (PDF 29). The narrow-wedge model and its Poisson/permutation description are on pp. 4954–4955 (PDF 4–5); the determinant-ratio identity is on p. 4980 (PDF 30).

Decisive chain-rule check. At a single point the printed coordinates are \[\zeta=(t-x)/2,\qquad \eta=(t+x)/2.\] Consequently \(t=\eta+\zeta\), \(x=\eta-\zeta\), and ordinary coordinate differentiation gives \[\partial_\eta=\partial_t+\partial_x,\qquad
\partial_\zeta=\partial_t-\partial_x,\qquad
\partial_\zeta\partial_\eta=\partial_t^2-\partial_x^2.\] The article instead writes the last operator with a factor \(1/4\). The kernel calculation and the scalar equation (2.18) use the half-sized vector fields. These conventions are inconsistent.

An explicit admissible test. The inconsistency affects the displayed equation, not merely a change of notation in an unused remark. Take narrow-wedge initial data \(h_0(0)=0\), \(h_0(x)=-\infty\) for \(x\ne0\), and \(|x|<t\). Write \(s=t^2-x^2\). The accessible Poisson area has mean \(s\), and \[F_k=e^{-s}G_k(s),\qquad
G_k(s)=\sum_{m\geq0}\frac{a_{m,k}}{(m!)^2}s^m,\] where \(a_{m,k}\) counts permutations of \(m\) letters whose longest increasing subsequence has length at most \(k\). Thus \[F_0=e^{-s},\quad
F_1=1-\frac{s^2}{4}+\frac{s^3}{9}+O(s^4),\quad
F_2=1-\frac{s^3}{36}+O(s^4),\quad
F_3=1+O(s^4).\] The threshold \(r=1\) is strictly above the deterministic height \(0\), as required. With \[Q_1=F_2/F_1,\qquad
U_1=F_2F_0/F_1^2,\qquad U_2=F_3F_1/F_2^2,\] the determinant-ratio identity also supplies the adjacent ratio at threshold \(0\), where the relevant determinants are positive. For any \(f(s)\), ordinary differentiation in the printed coordinates gives \[\partial_\zeta\partial_\eta f(s)=4\{f'(s)+sf''(s)\}.\] The residual of the scalar version of (2.13) is therefore \[\partial_\zeta\partial_\eta\log Q_1+U_1-U_2
=3s+O(s^2).\] It is nonzero for sufficiently small positive \(s\).

As a bounded quantitative check, independent exact rational arithmetic at \(t=1/10\), \(x=0\) proves \[\frac{29}{1000}
<
\partial_\zeta\partial_\eta\log Q_1+U_1-U_2
<
\frac{30}{1000}.\] The actual computed interval is approximately \([0.029628224985503042,\,0.02962822498558042]\); these decimal endpoints are only a display of a rational interval, not the basis of the assertion. Appendix A gives the count and tail method.

Impact and repair boundary. One coherent convention is \[D_\eta=\tfrac12(\partial_t+\partial_x),\qquad
D_\zeta=\tfrac12(\partial_t-\partial_x);\] at one point it corresponds to coordinates \(\eta=t+x\), \(\zeta=t-x\). Alternatively, retaining the printed coordinates requires a factor \(1/4\) on the mixed derivative in the corresponding scalar equation. All matrix and multipoint conventions must be reconciled consistently. This local normalization repair does not fix the missing endpoint hypothesis in Problem 1.

Problem 3 (Major: the spatially averaged indicator is not continuous).  Location. State-space topology and generator setup, pp. 4986–4989 (PDF 36–39); Proposition 4.6 and its proof, pp. 4996–4997 (PDF 46–47); the use in Proposition 4.8 and identification of the probability with the determinant, pp. 4998–4999 (PDF 48–49). Appendix B.1, p. 5012 (PDF 62), is relevant counterevidence.

Counterexample to continuity. Use \(n=1,x_1=r_1=0,\varepsilon=1\), and, for \(m\geq2\), define \[S_m=\bigcup_{j\in\mathbb Z}
\left[\frac{j}{m}-\frac{1}{2m^3},\,
      \frac{j}{m}+\frac{1}{2m^3}\right],
\qquad h_m=\mathbf 1_{S_m},\qquad h_* \equiv1 .\] Each \(S_m\) is closed and locally finite as a union of disjoint intervals. Each \(h_m\) is integer-valued and upper semicontinuous, with distinct locally finite jumps of heights \(+1\) and \(-1\); \(h_m(0)=h_*(0)=1\). In the stated topology \(h_m\to h_*\): every upper limit along \(x_m\to x\) is at most \(1\), and nearest grid points \(j_m/m\to x\) attain height \(1\). Nevertheless, \[|S_m\cap(-1,1)|=\frac{2}{m^2},
\qquad f_1(h_m)=1-\frac1{m^2}\longrightarrow1,
\qquad f_1(h_*)=0.\] Thus \(f_1\) is not continuous and cannot belong to the continuous-function domain used in the argument. Continuity on a stratum with a fixed list of jumps would not establish continuity on the declared state space.

A separate false convergence assertion in the same step. The proof also asserts uniform convergence of \(P_t f_\varepsilon\) to the point-evaluation probability. Fix \(t_0>0\) and initial data \(h(y)=\mathbf 1\{y\geq t_0\}\). At time \(t_0\), the deterministically expanding height-one step reaches \(0\), so \[F_0(t_0,z)=
\begin{cases}e^{-2t_0^2},&z<0,\\0,&z\geq0.\end{cases}\] Indeed for \(z<0\) the backward cone lies strictly below the initial step and has area \(t_0^2\); absence of intensity-two nucleations is exactly the event of height at most zero. Hence for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[P_{t_0}f_\varepsilon(h)=\tfrac12e^{-2t_0^2},
\qquad F_0(t_0,0)=0.\] Even pointwise convergence fails at this shock.

Adverse checks, impact, and repair boundary. The measure-zero shock argument and dominated-convergence discussion on p. 4997 can potentially replace the convergence assertion by a suitable almost-everywhere statement under the integration measure. They do not establish \(f_\varepsilon\in C_0\). Appendix B.1 explicitly distinguishes continuity from above from unrestricted continuity; it does not supply the missing premise for this sequence, which approximates from below. The later determinant-side regularity theorem does not independently prove the probability-side backward equation.

Proposition 4.8 explicitly uses (4.20) and (4.22) to obtain (4.25), leading to \(F=\widehat F\) on p. 4999 and then the general-initial-data statement of Theorem 2.3. The failed approximation therefore leaves a gap in a principal proof dependency. A valid repair could use a proved generator-domain approximation, or establish an appropriate weak/integrated backward equation directly. Such a replacement requires its own convergence and domain argument; none is certified here. This is a proof-gap finding, not a counterexample to the Fredholm formula.
Problem 4 (Minor: the narrow-wedge initial velocity needs a height restriction).  Location. The initial-velocity discussion on p. 4959 (PDF 9) and the narrow-wedge example on p. 4960 (PDF 10).

Decisive evidence. The narrow-wedge paragraph states an unqualified distributional velocity \(\partial_tF_r(0,x)=-2\delta_0\). In the same paragraph, the threshold-zero formula gives \(F_0(t,x)=e^{-(t^2-x^2)}\) on \(|x|\leq t\), and \(F_0=1\) outside. For a compactly supported smooth test function \(\varphi\), \[\left|\int_{\mathbb R}(F_0(t,x)-1)\varphi(x)\,dx\right|
\leq\|\varphi\|_\infty\int_{-t}^t(t^2-x^2)\,dx
=\tfrac43\|\varphi\|_\infty t^3.\] After division by \(t\) the limit is zero. For every \(r\geq0\), the inequality \(0\leq1-F_r\leq1-F_0\) proves the same zero derivative. For \(r<0\), \(F_r(t,x)=\mathbf 1\{|x|>t\}\), up to endpoints irrelevant to distributions, and the derivative is \(-2\delta_0\). The locally verified correction is \[\partial_t F_r(0,\cdot)=-2\mathbf 1\{r<0\}\delta_0.\]

The preceding jump-height expression also needs a scope restriction if it is meant to cover arbitrary integer jumps. For \(h_0(x)=2\mathbf 1\{x\geq0\}\) and threshold \(0\), \(F_0(t,x)=e^{-2t^2}\mathbf 1\{x<-t\}\), whose initial derivative is \(-\delta_0\), whereas weighting the threshold change by the jump height gives \(-2\delta_0\). The article introduces this discussion as applying in simple cases; if that phrase is intended to mean distinct unit jumps only, this latter example requests an explicit restriction rather than disproving that restricted claim. The narrow-wedge discrepancy does not depend on that interpretation.

claim: Theorem 3.1 claims non-Abelian Toda for every interior index under shift and first derivative hypotheses.
analysis: Location. Theorem 3.1, p. 4974 (PDF 24), assumptions (1)–(3) and conclusion; the asserted mixed identity (3.4), p. 4975 (PDF 25); the application with three indices in Section 3.2, p. 4979 (PDF 29).

Equation reference: eq:toda. Claim being checked. The theorem assumes kernels indexed from \(\underline r\) to \(\overline r\), with \(\underline r<\overline r-1\), satisfying \[\begin{aligned}
K_{r+1}(u,v)&=K_r(u+1,v+1),\\
\partial_\eta K_r(u,v)&=K_{r-1}(u+1,v)-K_r(u+1,v),\\
\partial_\zeta K_r(u,v)&=K_{r-1}(u,v+1)-K_r(u,v+1).\end{aligned}\] The first identity is required up to \(r=\overline r-1\); the derivative identities start at \(r=\underline r+1\). With the stated trace-class, differentiability, and invertibility assumptions, the theorem claims, for every interior \(r\), \[
\partial_\zeta\big(\partial_\eta Q_r\,Q_r^{-1}\big)
 +Q_rQ_{r-1}^{-1}-Q_{r+1}Q_r^{-1}=0.\]

Decisive evidence. Take one copy of \(\ell^2(\mathbb Z_{>0})\), the open parameter set \(\mathbb R^2\), \(\underline r=0\), \(\overline r=2\), and \(P=|1\rangle\langle1|\). Set \[K_0=\tfrac12P,\qquad K_1=K_2=0\] at every parameter value. These are trace-class kernels, with trace norms \(1/2,0,0\). All parameter derivatives, including mixed derivatives, exist in trace norm and vanish. Every required shift or derivative relation holds: \(P(u+1,v)\), \(P(u,v+1)\), and \(P(u+1,v+1)\) vanish for positive integers \(u,v\). Moreover, \[(I-K_0)^{-1}=I+P,\qquad (I-K_1)^{-1}=(I-K_2)^{-1}=I,
\quad (Q_0,Q_1,Q_2)=(2,1,1).\] Thus all required inverses exist, but the left side of [eq:toda] (#eq:toda) at \(r=1\) is \[0+\tfrac12-1=-\tfrac12.\] This is a counterexample to the theorem as quantified, not a numerical failure or a hypothetical objection.

The proof’s asserted identity \[\partial_\eta\partial_\zeta K_r=K_{r+1}-2K_r+K_{r-1}
\tag{3.4 in the article}\] would give \(0=\tfrac12P\) here. Deriving it by differentiating a first-order identity at the lowest interior index needs information on the derivative of \(K_{\underline r}\), which the theorem does not supply.

Impact and repair boundary. Section 3.2 applies the theorem with \(\underline r=-1\), \(\overline r=1\), at \(r=0\), exactly the affected endpoint. Restricting the theorem’s conclusion to \(r\geq\underline r+2\) avoids this particular logical step but leaves that three-kernel application empty. Adding the requisite mixed identity at the indices used is another possible repair. It must then be verified for the actual PNG kernels, including their forcing terms and trace-norm regularity. The rank-one example proves neither that a strengthened abstract theorem fails nor that the intended PNG probability identity is false. The remaining resolvent algebra was checked conditionally on the missing mixed identity; that conditional check does not repair the printed hypotheses.

analysis: Location. Definition of \(\zeta,\eta\), p. 4957 (PDF 7); Theorem 2.1 and equation (2.13), p. 4958 (PDF 8); the derivative statement preceding (2.19), p. 4959 (PDF 9); the kernel derivative calculation (3.15), p. 4979 (PDF 29).
