Decisive chain-rule check. At a single point the printed coordinates are \[\zeta=(t-x)/2,\qquad \eta=(t+x)/2.\] Consequently \(t=\eta+\zeta\), \(x=\eta-\zeta\), and ordinary coordinate differentiation gives \[\partial_\eta=\partial_t+\partial_x,\qquad
\partial_\zeta=\partial_t-\partial_x,\qquad
\partial_\zeta\partial_\eta=\partial_t^2-\partial_x^2.\] The article instead writes the last operator with a factor \(1/4\). The kernel calculation and the scalar equation (2.18) use the half-sized vector fields. These conventions are inconsistent.

An explicit admissible test. The inconsistency affects the displayed equation, not merely a change of notation in an unused remark. Take narrow-wedge initial data \(h_0(0)=0\), \(h_0(x)=-\infty\) for \(x\ne0\), and \(|x|<t\). Write \(s=t^2-x^2\). The accessible Poisson area has mean \(s\), and \[F_k=e^{-s}G_k(s),\qquad
G_k(s)=\sum_{m\geq0}\frac{a_{m,k}}{(m!)^2}s^m,\] where \(a_{m,k}\) counts permutations of \(m\) letters whose longest increasing subsequence has length at most \(k\). Thus \[F_0=e^{-s},\quad
F_1=1-\frac{s^2}{4}+\frac{s^3}{9}+O(s^4),\quad
F_2=1-\frac{s^3}{36}+O(s^4),\quad
F_3=1+O(s^4).\] The threshold \(r=1\) is strictly above the deterministic height \(0\), as required. With \[Q_1=F_2/F_1,\qquad
U_1=F_2F_0/F_1^2,\qquad U_2=F_3F_1/F_2^2,\] the determinant-ratio identity also supplies the adjacent ratio at threshold \(0\), where the relevant determinants are positive. For any \(f(s)\), ordinary differentiation in the printed coordinates gives \[\partial_\zeta\partial_\eta f(s)=4\{f'(s)+sf''(s)\}.\] The residual of the scalar version of (2.13) is therefore \[\partial_\zeta\partial_\eta\log Q_1+U_1-U_2
=3s+O(s^2).\] It is nonzero for sufficiently small positive \(s\).

As a bounded quantitative check, independent exact rational arithmetic at \(t=1/10\), \(x=0\) proves \[\frac{29}{1000}
<
\partial_\zeta\partial_\eta\log Q_1+U_1-U_2
<
\frac{30}{1000}.\] The actual computed interval is approximately \([0.029628224985503042,\,0.02962822498558042]\); these decimal endpoints are only a display of a rational interval, not the basis of the assertion. Appendix A gives the count and tail method.

Impact and repair boundary. One coherent convention is \[D_\eta=\tfrac12(\partial_t+\partial_x),\qquad
D_\zeta=\tfrac12(\partial_t-\partial_x);\] at one point it corresponds to coordinates \(\eta=t+x\), \(\zeta=t-x\). Alternatively, retaining the printed coordinates requires a factor \(1/4\) on the mixed derivative in the corresponding scalar equation. All matrix and multipoint conventions must be reconciled consistently. This local normalization repair does not fix the missing endpoint hypothesis in Problem 1.

claim: Prop4.6 spatial average f_epsilon belongs to C0 and its semigroup converges uniformly to the point probability.
analysis: Location. State-space topology and generator setup, pp. 4986–4989 (PDF 36–39); Proposition 4.6 and its proof, pp. 4996–4997 (PDF 46–47); the use in Proposition 4.8 and identification of the probability with the determinant, pp. 4998–4999 (PDF 48–49). Counterexample to continuity. Use \(n=1,x_1=r_1=0,\varepsilon=1\), and, for \(m\geq2\), define \[S_m=\bigcup_{j\in\mathbb Z}
\left[\frac{j}{m}-\frac{1}{2m^3},\,
      \frac{j}{m}+\frac{1}{2m^3}\right],
\qquad h_m=\mathbf 1_{S_m},\qquad h_* \equiv1 .\] Each \(S_m\) is closed and locally finite as a union of disjoint intervals. Each \(h_m\) is integer-valued and upper semicontinuous, with distinct locally finite jumps of heights \(+1\) and \(-1\); \(h_m(0)=h_*(0)=1\). In the stated topology \(h_m\to h_*\): every upper limit along \(x_m\to x\) is at most \(1\), and nearest grid points \(j_m/m\to x\) attain height \(1\). Nevertheless, \[|S_m\cap(-1,1)|=\frac{2}{m^2},
\qquad f_1(h_m)=1-\frac1{m^2}\longrightarrow1,
\qquad f_1(h_*)=0.\] Thus \(f_1\) is not continuous and cannot belong to the continuous-function domain used in the argument. Continuity on a stratum with a fixed list of jumps would not establish continuity on the declared state space.

A separate false convergence assertion in the same step. The proof also asserts uniform convergence of \(P_t f_\varepsilon\) to the point-evaluation probability. Fix \(t_0>0\) and initial data \(h(y)=\mathbf 1\{y\geq t_0\}\). At time \(t_0\), the deterministically expanding height-one step reaches \(0\), so \[F_0(t_0,z)=
\begin{cases}e^{-2t_0^2},&z<0,\\0,&z\geq0.\end{cases}\] Indeed for \(z<0\) the backward cone lies strictly below the initial step and has area \(t_0^2\); absence of intensity-two nucleations is exactly the event of height at most zero. Hence for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[P_{t_0}f_\varepsilon(h)=\tfrac12e^{-2t_0^2},
\qquad F_0(t_0,0)=0.\] Even pointwise convergence fails at this shock.

Adverse checks, impact, and repair boundary. The measure-zero shock argument and dominated-convergence discussion on p. 4997 can potentially replace the convergence assertion by a suitable almost-everywhere statement under the integration measure. They do not establish \(f_\varepsilon\in C_0\). Appendix B.1 explicitly distinguishes continuity from above from unrestricted continuity; it does not supply the missing premise for this sequence, which approximates from below. The later determinant-side regularity theorem does not independently prove the probability-side backward equation.

Proposition 4.8 explicitly uses (4.20) and (4.22) to obtain (4.25), leading to \(F=\widehat F\) on p. 4999 and then the general-initial-data statement of Theorem 2.3. The failed approximation therefore leaves a gap in a principal proof dependency. A valid repair could use a proved generator-domain approximation, or establish an appropriate weak/integrated backward equation directly. Such a replacement requires its own convergence and domain argument; none is certified here. This is a proof-gap finding, not a counterexample to the Fredholm formula.

Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Scientific initial review of
The eighth moment of the Riemann zeta function
# Identity, hypotheses, and scope

The reviewed work is by Nathan Ng, Quanli Shen, and Peng-Jie Wong, DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1568. The exact reviewed publisher PDF is Journal of the European Mathematical Society 28 (2026), no. 10, 4175–4237, published online on 9 January 2025. It has 63 pages. Printed page numbers are used below, with PDF page \(j\) corresponding to printed page \(4174+j\). The separate author source is arXiv:2204.13891v1, submitted 29 April 2022; its identity and text are not treated as identical to the publisher version.

Theorem 1.1, p. 4178 (PDF 4), assumes both the Riemann hypothesis and Conjecture 1, the smoothed quaternary additive divisor conjecture. Its conclusion is the leading asymptotic \[I_4(T)=\int_0^T|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|^8\,dt
\sim \frac{24024a_4}{16!}\,T(\log T)^{16}.\] It does not assert an unconditional theorem or a complete polynomial of lower-order terms. Conjecture 1 fixes a constant \(C>0\), admits small positive \(\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon'\), and requires the additive shift to satisfy \(1\le |r|\ll X^{1-\varepsilon'}\); its error is \(O(P^CX^{1/2+\varepsilon_0})\). These dependencies were retained in the checks.

Actual review concentrated on the statements and normalization, truncation and removal of smoothing, the application of the divisor conjecture, selected contour and Euler-product steps, and the leading residue arithmetic. The source inventory was also mechanically verified in full. That operation is not a scientific check. The report does not certify every derivative estimate, high-order remainder, external theorem, or argument on all 63 pages.
# Established problem

Problem 1 (Minor: the sign of the second Euler-factor coefficient).  Location. Proposition 6.5(ii), p. 4211 (PDF 37), with \(Y_p\) defined in (6.30); the remainder exponent on p. 4212 (PDF 38); the exact factor (6.29); and the proof on pp. 4227–4228 (PDF 53–54).

Equation reference: eq:printed. Claim. The proposition states \[
\mathcal I_p(u_1,u_2,u_3;s)
=1-Y_p p^{-2-4s}+O\!\left(p^{7\delta'+\vartheta(\sigma)}\right),
\qquad \sigma=\Re s,\] for \(|u_i|<\delta'\), \(0<\delta'<1/5\), and \(\sigma\ge-1/2+2\delta'\). In particular, \(\vartheta(\sigma)=-2-2\sigma\) when \(-1/4\le\sigma<0\).

Why the discrepancy is not hidden by the error term. Take \[u_1=u_2=u_3=0,\qquad \delta'=1/100,\qquad s=-1/10.\] All displayed assumptions hold. Here \(a=b=1\), \(Y_p=-9\), and \(W=p^{-4/5}\). From Lemma 2.3 and (6.29), \[G_4(1;p)=3-\frac3p+\frac1{p^2},\qquad
G_4(1;p^2)=6-\frac8p+\frac3{p^2},\] and \[\mathcal I_p(0,0,0;s)
=(1-W)^9
\left[1+\big(1-p^{2s-1}\big)
 \sum_{j\ge1}G_4(1;p^j)^2W^j\right].\] The \(j\ge3\) tail is \(O(W^3)\), since the coefficients grow at most polynomially in \(j\), uniformly for large \(p\). Therefore \[\mathcal I_p(0,0,0;-1/10)
=1-9p^{-8/5}+O(p^{-9/5}).\] In contrast, [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) would give \[\mathcal I_p(0,0,0;-1/10)
=1+9p^{-8/5}+O(p^{-173/100}).\] The difference \(18p^{-8/5}\) cannot be absorbed by \(O(p^{-173/100})\) as \(p\) tends to infinity through primes. This is an analytic specialization within the stated domain, not a floating-point experiment.

The proof’s sign and the leading-constant checks agree with the correction. No central failure of the eighth-moment asymptotic is established from this defect. It is classified Minor because its demonstrated effect is a local coefficient statement whose sign is not needed for the inspected convergence and leading-constant uses. The classification is not based merely on the brevity of the repair.
# Checks of the principal proof mechanism
## Truncation with an independent small-parameter constant

Proposition 3.1, pp. 4184–4186 (PDF 10–12), replaces the natural length parameter by \(U=T^{1-\varepsilon}\). For \(t\asymp T\), \[\left|\frac{t^{4i\tau}-U^{4i\tau}}{i\tau}\right|
\le4|\log(t/U)|\ll\varepsilon\log T\] once \(T\ge T_\varepsilon\). The bounded term \(\log(t/T)\) is absorbed by this permitted threshold; the resulting multiplicative constant need not depend on \(\varepsilon\).
## The range and cost of applying Conjecture 1

The normalization \(T^{-4\varepsilon_1}f_r\) and \(P=T^{1+\varepsilon_1}/T_0\) retain the derivative cost. After counting shifts, \[E_{M,N}\ll
(T/T_0)^{1+C}T^{(5+C)\varepsilon_1}M^{1/2+\varepsilon_0}.\] The stated parameter conditions \(\max(\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_1,C\varepsilon_1)\le\varepsilon/40\) leave room for \[(5+C)\varepsilon_1+2\varepsilon_0\le\varepsilon/5<\varepsilon/4.\] The dyadic geometric sum of \(M^{1/2}\) is \(O(U^{1+\varepsilon_2/4})=O(T^{1-3\varepsilon/4})\). Thus the claimed total \((T/T_0)^{1+C}T^{1-\varepsilon/2}\) is compatible with every counted loss. Extending the resulting explicit main-term expression in \(r\) does not mean that the conjecture was applied outside its stipulated range.
## A removable pole
## Leading coefficients and removal of smoothing

The diagonal coefficient in (4.8), p. 4191 (PDF 17), follows directly from the order-17 pole: \[2\,\frac{4^{16}}{2^{16}16!}=\frac{131072}{16!}
=\frac4{638512875}.\] The off-diagonal highest-degree coefficient was additionally checked by an independent, reviewer-written exact rational calculation; its retained program and actual output are provided with the report. The resulting coefficient is \(-107048/16!=-13381/2615348736000\). Thus the assembly in Propositions 3.2–3.3, p. 4187 (PDF 13), gives \[131072-107048=24024.\] The factor \((\log U)^{16}=(1-\varepsilon)^{16}(\log T)^{16}\) changes the leading expression by only \(O(\varepsilon(\log T)^{16})\).

For smoothing, fix \(0<\eta<1/2\) and set \(T_0=\eta T\). The remaining error \(O(T\eta^{-1-C})\), divided by \(T(\log T)^{16}\), vanishes as \(T\to\infty\) with \(\eta,\varepsilon\) fixed. Only afterwards are the small parameters sent to zero. The initial omitted dyadic interval is controlled by the RH moment bound and a further fixed parameter \(\eta_0\). The argument on pp. 4187–4189 (PDF 13–15) respects this order of limits; it does not require uniformity for an arbitrary shrinking \(\eta(T)\).
# Boundary of the assessment

Theorem 1.2 states a shifted bound for \(k\ge1/2\). The consulted published companion theorem states \(k\ge1\) with an additional bound on the sum of shifts. The present proof uses \(k=4\) and opposite shifts, which satisfy that version. Simple Hölder interpolation does not supply the sharper small-\(k\) exponent, but later work of Curran allows nonnegative moment exponents and provides a route to the wider bound. This is recorded as a citation-range clarification, not as evidence that the bound is false or that the main proof lacks its required input.

The article mentions Maple for involved residues. No author Maple program was identified in the frozen source files or bounded publisher/author-source checks, and none was executed. Code absence is not a mathematical defect. The retained rational check independently tests the leading coefficient only; it does not certify every lower-order term or analytic remainder.
No helper is labelled a separate web Pro session or a human reviewer. Backend identity was not independently verified.

Overall assessment: one established Minor problem; no further substantive issue established in the declared inspected main-theorem scope. Scientific decision and adjudication remain pending, with no human review or independent acceptance claimed.

Equation reference: eq:printed. Claim. The proposition states \[
\mathcal I_p(u_1,u_2,u_3;s)
=1-Y_p p^{-2-4s}+O\!\left(p^{7\delta'+\vartheta(\sigma)}\right),
\qquad \sigma=\Re s,\] for \(|u_i|<\delta'\), \(0<\delta'<1/5\), and \(\sigma\ge-1/2+2\delta'\). In particular, \(\vartheta(\sigma)=-2-2\sigma\) when \(-1/4\le\sigma<0\).

Why the discrepancy is not hidden by the error term. Take \[u_1=u_2=u_3=0,\qquad \delta'=1/100,\qquad s=-1/10.\] All displayed assumptions hold. Here \(a=b=1\), \(Y_p=-9\), and \(W=p^{-4/5}\). From Lemma 2.3 and (6.29), \[G_4(1;p)=3-\frac3p+\frac1{p^2},\qquad
G_4(1;p^2)=6-\frac8p+\frac3{p^2},\] and \[\mathcal I_p(0,0,0;s)
=(1-W)^9
\left[1+\big(1-p^{2s-1}\big)
 \sum_{j\ge1}G_4(1;p^j)^2W^j\right].\] The \(j\ge3\) tail is \(O(W^3)\), since the coefficients grow at most polynomially in \(j\), uniformly for large \(p\). Therefore \[\mathcal I_p(0,0,0;-1/10)
=1-9p^{-8/5}+O(p^{-9/5}).\] In contrast, [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) would give \[\mathcal I_p(0,0,0;-1/10)
=1+9p^{-8/5}+O(p^{-173/100}).\] The difference \(18p^{-8/5}\) cannot be absorbed by \(O(p^{-173/100})\) as \(p\) tends to infinity through primes. This is an analytic specialization within the stated domain, not a floating-point experiment.

The proof’s sign and the leading-constant checks agree with the correction. No central failure of the eighth-moment asymptotic is established from this defect. It is classified Minor because its demonstrated effect is a local coefficient statement whose sign is not needed for the inspected convergence and leading-constant uses. The classification is not based merely on the brevity of the repair.

Title: Technical review of
Rigidity of smooth finite-time blow-up for equivariant self-dual Chern–Simons–Schrödinger equation
# Identity and exact theorem scope

The reviewed article is by Kihyun Kim, DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1569, Journal of the European Mathematical Society 28 (2026), no. 12, 5469–5572. The exact 104-page publisher Version of Record is the primary source. Its first page gives receipt on 26 November 2022 and revision on 4 December 2023; the publisher landing page labels 3 January 2025 as Published. This date is recorded separately from the assigned issue year. The separately acquired author source is arXiv:2210.05412v2, dated 27 April 2024; it is not assumed to be the publisher production source or mathematically identical throughout. Below, PDF page \(j\) is printed page \(5468+j\).

Theorem 1.4, pp. 5475–5476 (PDF 7–8), concerns an \(m\)-equivariant \(H_m^3\) solution with \(m\ge1\) that blows up at a finite time \(T\). It gives an \(L^2\) decomposition \[u(t)-Q_{\ell(T-t),\gamma^*}\longrightarrow z^*,\qquad
\ell>0,\quad \gamma^*\in\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z),\] and a prescribed local structure for \(z^*\). It does not identify the entire solution with the explicit pseudoconformal solution: a nonzero radiation is allowed, without a near-threshold mass assumption. Corollary 1.5 requires the stronger weighted class \(H_m^{3,3}\) for its classification of global dynamics. Neither conclusion covers \(m=0\), nor does Remark 5.4’s proposed \(H^{3/2}\) extension constitute a proved theorem.
# Time-variable clarification

Location. Proof of Corollary 4.17, p. 5546 (PDF 78), the sentence immediately after (4.80); compare the definition of \(s\) on p. 5481 (PDF 13), the definition \(\mu=\lambda\sqrt{E[u]}\) on p. 5526 (PDF 58), and (4.74), (4.78)–(4.81), pp. 5545–5546 (PDF 77–78).

Printed claim and decisive evidence. The sentence says that (4.77) follows by integrating (4.80) using \[ds=\lambda^2\,dt.\] The defining relation is instead \(ds/dt=1/\lambda^2(t)\), so the correct differential is \[ds=\lambda^{-2}\,dt,\qquad
\mu^2\,ds=E[u]\,dt.                                      \tag{2.1}\] Both the defining page and the incorrect sentence were actually inspected as images, including a separate high-resolution rendering of PDF 78. This is not an inference from a lost minus sign in extracted text.

More explicitly, put \[G=\sqrt{1+\mathcal F}+\frac{b}{\mu^{3/4}}.\] Equation (4.80) gives \(G_s\le K''\mu^2G\). Equation (2.1) yields \[G(t)\le e^{K''E[u](t-t_0)}G(t_0),\] which is exactly the dependence displayed on the next line of the proof. In contrast, the printed positive power would give \(\mu^2ds=E[u]\lambda^4dt\), inconsistent with that change of variables. The spacetime integrals in (4.74) and (4.81) also correctly use \(dt/\lambda^2\).

Impact, counterevidence, and repair boundary. The written time-change identity is false for the paper’s time variable. Replace \(\lambda^2\) by \(\lambda^{-2}\) in that sentence. The surrounding estimate, its physical-time exponential, and the stated spacetime measure already use the corrected identity. The demonstrated discrepancy is therefore an isolated typesetting error, with no failed calculation established downstream. Under the substantive-error scope of this review, it is a clarification and is not counted as a confirmed Minor problem. No alteration to the hypotheses, energy bound, or blow-up classification is justified.
# Positive checks and rejected defect candidates
## Soliton normalization and the regularity boundary

From (1.9), p. 5472 (PDF 4), write \(n=m+1\) and \(z=r^{2n}\). Direct integration and differentiation give \[Q(r)=\sqrt8\,n\,\frac{r^{n-1}}{1+r^{2n}},\qquad
A_\theta[Q](r)=-\frac{2nz}{1+z},\qquad M[Q]=8\pi n.\] Indeed, \(Q'/Q=(m+A_\theta[Q])/r\), so the Bogomol’nyi equation holds, and \(m+A_\theta[Q](\infty)=-m-2\), consistent with the exterior effective negative equivariance used in Remark 4.4 (PDF 59). The self-dual energy has the nonnegative form \(\frac12\left\|\mathbf D_u u\right\|_2^2\). Its scaling is \(E[u_\lambda]=\lambda^{-2}E[u]\), while mass is invariant. Thus \(\mu=\lambda\sqrt{E[u]}\) has the stated scaling.

The pseudoconformal transform on PDF 4 contains \(-1/t\) and the phase \(e^{ir^2/(4t)}\); for the static soliton at \(t<0\) its phase is \(e^{-ir^2/(4|t|)}\). At fixed \(t\ne0\), the leading tail of the \(k\)-th radial derivative is proportional to \(r^kQ(r)\). Its squared radial integral behaves as \[\int^\infty r^{2k-2m-3}\,dr,\] which converges exactly when \(k<m+1\). Consequently the explicit solution is in \(H^1\) for \(m\ge1\) and in \(H^3\) only for \(m\ge3\). The zero-radiation explicit solutions for \(m=1,2\) therefore do not contradict the nonzero coefficient imposed on \(H_m^3\) blow-up solutions; this agrees with Remark 1.9 (PDF 10).
## Why the energy argument can precede the blow-up rate

For the conjugated operator, direct substitution into (2.21)–(2.22) gives \[\widetilde V_Q=m^2+\frac{4(m+1)}{1+r^{2m+2}},
\qquad -r\partial_r\widetilde V_Q=r^2Q^2\ge0 .\] Hence \(\widetilde V_Q\ge m^2\), and \(m\ge1\) supplies the positive Hardy term in Lemma 2.1 (PDF 23–24). This calculation supports the actual restriction on \(m\), not an extension to zero equivariance.
## Nondegeneracy, phase convergence, and parameter replacement

The refined variables in Lemma 5.2 (PDF 88) satisfy \[|\widehat b-b|+|\widehat\eta-\eta|\lesssim\mu^2,\quad
\left|\frac{\lambda_s}{\lambda}+\widehat b\right|
+|\gamma_s-(m+1)\widehat\eta|\lesssim\mu^2,\] and \[|\widehat b_s+\widehat b^2+\widehat\eta^2|
+|\widehat\eta_s|\lesssim\beta^3+\beta\mu^2+\mu^4.\] For a fixed blow-up solution, \(\mu\asymp_u\lambda\). With \(a=(\widehat b^2+\widehat\eta^2)^{1/2}/\lambda\), these estimates imply \[|a_t|\lesssim a+\lambda,\qquad
|\lambda_t|\lesssim a+\lambda.\] Thus \(h=a+\lambda>0\) satisfies \(|h_t|\lesssim h\). It is bounded by the coercivity estimates; its derivative is integrable up to \(T\), and two-sided Grönwall gives a strictly positive limiting value. Since \(\lambda\to0\), \(a\to\ell>0\). At a zero of the numerator one may use the absolute continuity of the vector norm; division by that norm is not essential.

There is no missing absolute-value hypothesis in Proposition 5.3 or Remark 5.4: the paper explicitly defines \(A\lesssim B\) to mean \(|A|\le CB\) for \(B\ge0\), on PDF 16–17. Next, in the order used on PDF 90–91, integration gives \(b\sim\ell^2(T-t)\), then almost decreasing \(\lambda\), then \(|\eta|\lesssim\lambda(T-t)\), and finally \(\lambda\sim\ell(T-t)\) and bounded \(\gamma_t\). Positivity of \(b\) is obtained at this stage. Theorem 1.4’s exact linear scale and fixed phase are permitted in the limiting \(L^2\) decomposition by strong continuity of the dilation and phase actions; they are not claims of exact finite-time modulation trajectories.
## The low-index profile and the origin

In (5.22)–(5.23), PDF 93–94, the leading profile terms rescale as \[\lambda^{-1}b^2(r/\lambda)=(b/\lambda)^2r,\qquad
\lambda^{-1}b^3(r/\lambda)^2=(b/\lambda)^3r^2 .\] The quoted modified-profile coefficients therefore give respectively \(-e^{i\gamma^*}\ell^2\sqrt2\,\chi(\ell r)r/8\) for \(m=1\), and \(ie^{i\gamma^*}\ell^3\sqrt2\,\chi(\ell r)r^2/64\) for \(m=2\). This verifies the rescaling of those coefficients, rather than independently reconstructing the entire profile expansion.

The change from \(\chi(\ell r)\) in the proof to \(\chi(r)\) in the theorem is harmless: their difference is smooth, compactly supported, and zero near the origin, so it can be absorbed into the regular part. Also, (1.16) does imply \(z_{\rm rg}^*=o(r^2)\). Put \(z_{\rm rg}^*(r)=r^2f(\log r)\). The weighted \(k=0,1\) conditions give \(f,2f+f'\in L^2((-\infty,c))\), hence \(f\in H^1\cap L^2\) and \(f(x)\to0\) as \(x\to-\infty\). The term singular here concerns the stronger weighted/exterior regularity; it should not be read as a claim that \(\chi(r)r^me^{im\theta}\) itself is nonsmooth in the original equivariance class.
# Assessment, coverage, and limitations

The assessment is No Issue Found within the inspected scope, with the time-variable clarification above. No substantive Major or Minor problem is established. No counterexample to Theorem 1.4 or Corollary 1.5 has been established. This statement is limited to the actual checks above.

The principal read the main statements and strategy, selected linear and nonlinear coercivity passages, the energy integration, and the final rigidity/profile argument; all source pages used as evidence here were actually inspected as images. The principal evaluated those checks, confirmed the misprint on the publisher images, authored this report, compiled it, and inspected every final report page. Native helpers were not represented as independently authenticated Pro instances or as independent acceptance.

The full construction of every modified-profile term in Section 3, every structural remainder in Sections 4.6–4.7, all Appendix B coercivity details, and the complete proof of the cited prior soliton-resolution theorem were not independently reconstructed. These are substantive coverage limits, not alleged defects. The publisher, author publication page, arXiv version page, and frozen source inventory were checked for supplementary material and corrections; no separate supplement or released program was identified in that bounded search. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect. No author code was executed.

The external controller’s UI observation is attributed separately from the runtime self-description; backend identity was not independently verified. The scientific decision is `pending`, and `human_reviews` is empty.

Abstract: The reviewed accepted-author version contains an inverted Gaussian target in its Wasserstein theorem, with an admissible counterexample to the printed rate. Three separate proof problems concern missing centering, a block normalization, and a uniform dependence hypothesis that fails at allowed bandwidths. Three local issues concern the denominator definition, finite-window dependence, and a constant quantified uniformly over all \(q\). These findings have different repair boundaries. They do not establish that the intended, correctly rescaled central limit theorems are false. The assessment is Major; scientific adjudication and human review remain pending.

Title: Scientific initial review of
Weak dependence and optimal quantitative self-normalized central limit theorems
# Identity, version, and scope

The author is Moritz Jirak. The journal association is DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1573. The exact primary input is the 41-page arXiv:2504.14403v1, uploaded 19 April 2025 and described on its arXiv landing page as a preprint of the accepted version. It is not the publisher Version of Record. The publisher landing page separately lists online-first publication in 2025, a Published date of 3 January 2025, submission on 12 December 2022, and acceptance on 30 September 2023. The publisher PDF was not accessible in the acquisition record. Findings below apply to the assigned author PDF; no equivalence with the unreviewed publisher PDF is asserted. PDF and printed page numbers coincide.

Assumption 2.1 (p. 6) requires a stationary centered causal process, \(p\ge6\), \(a>13/6\), finite \[\Theta_{a,p}=\left\|X_0\right\|_p+\sum_{\ell\ge1}\ell^a\theta_{\ell p},
\qquad
\theta_{\ell p}=\sup_k\left\|X_k-X_k^{(\ell,\prime)}\right\|_p,\] positive long-run variance \(\sigma^2=\sum_{h\in\mathbb Z}\mathbb EX_0X_h\), and \[b\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad b\le(n/\log^3n)^{1/4}.                 \tag{1.1}\] The coupling replaces one innovation at time \(k-\ell\), not an entire past. The empirical covariance in (2.6) is centered by \(\bar X_n\) and normalized by \(n\); throughout the results the lag weights are \(\omega\equiv1\). Write \[Q_n=\widehat\sigma_{nb}^{\,2}=\sum_{|h|\le b}\widehat\gamma_X(h),
\quad c_b=\sigma_b^2=\sum_{|h|\le b}\mathbb EX_0X_h .\] Theorem 2.3 (p. 7) uses the CDF \(\Phi(x\sigma_b/\sigma)\); the approximating variance is \(\sigma^2/\sigma_b^2\). Standard-normal approximation at the same rate requires the additional covariance-tail bias condition of Corollary 2.4. Theorem 2.6 (p. 9) requires \(p>6,a>4\), uses a lower-truncated denominator with \(\tau_n=C\sqrt{\log n}\), and claims an optimal \(W_1\) bound.
# Established problems

Problem 1 (Major: the linearized sums are not centered).  Location. Definitions (4.7)–(4.8), p. 18; (4.16)–(4.20), pp. 22–23; mean-zero hypothesis of Lemma 4.5, pp. 20–21; Proposition 4.10, p. 29; smoothed definitions and moments (4.46), (4.48)–(4.51), pp. 33–34.

An exact all-assumptions check is \(X_k\) iid \(N(0,1)\), with any admissible growing bandwidth. Then \(\sigma_{nb}=1\). For \(W_b=(\mathbf1_{\{|i-j|\le b\}})_{i,j=1}^n\), \(R_n(x)=S_n-xX^\top W_bX/(2\sqrt n)\). Odd Gaussian moments vanish, \(\operatorname{tr}W_b=n\), and \(\operatorname{tr}W_b^2=n(2b+1)-b(b+1)\). Therefore \[\mathbb ER_n(x)^2
=n+\frac{x^2n}{4}+\frac{x^2(2b+1)}2-\frac{x^2b(b+1)}{2n}.          \tag{2.2}\] At \(x=1\), the extra \(n/4\) contradicts (4.18)’s \(O((1+x^2)\sqrt n)\) error. In fact \(X^\top W_bX/n\to1\) in \(L^2\), so \(R_n(1)/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(-1/2,1)\). In (4.20) at \(x=1,\mu=0\), the probability tends to \(\Phi(3/2)\), whereas the displayed approximant tends to \(\Phi(2/\sqrt5)\). Their difference is nonzero.

Impact and repair. Mean-zero Lemma 4.5 is not applicable to the defined variables. The same omission enters the smoothed raw moments: a mean-zero coboundary does not remove this mean. Define centered variables and sums, replace raw moments by variances and central cumulants, and carry these changes through the event comparisons. Proposition 4.10 already estimates \(\mathbb E[(Y_k-\mathbb EY_k)(Y_0-\mathbb EY_0)]\), which supports a possible correction but cannot justify the present raw-moment calculation.

There is also an explicit boundary obligation: setting \(X_{k-h}=0\) for \(k-h\le0\) (p. 17) makes the defined \(Y_k\) nonstationary. Section 4.3 removes this convention only within that section. A repair must control the initial terms or use a suitable nonstationary approximation theorem. A subsidiary variance remainder immediately before (4.18) should be \(O(1)\), not generally \(O(n^{2-a})\): for the variance-one Gaussian AR(1) with covariance \(2^{-|h|}\), \(\mathbb ES_n^2=3n-4+4\,2^{-n}\). This smaller correction fits the subsequent \(O(\sqrt n)\) tolerance. These are failures of the written proof, not a counterexample to the intended centered CLT.

Problem 2 (Major: the concentration proof drops a block factor).  Location. Definition of \(W_k\) and Lemma 4.8, p. 26; blocks (4.30)–(4.31), p. 27; final paragraph of Lemma 4.9 and its use in Proposition 4.6, p. 29.

Evidence. The source sets \[W_k=2b^{-1/2}X_kB_{kb},\qquad
V_{\ell b}=\sum_{k\in I_{\ell b}}(b^{-1/2}X_k^2+W_k).\] On p. 29 it concludes from Lemma 4.8 and the block cardinality \(b\) that \(\left\|\sum_{k\in I_{\ell b}}(W_k-\mathbb EW_k)\right\|_q\lesssim1\). For iid standard Gaussian observations, choose the interior block \(I_{2b}=\{b+1,\ldots,2b\}\), so no initial zero boundary enters. These \(W_k\) are martingale differences, with \(\mathbb EW_k^2=4\). Thus \[\left\|\sum_{k\in I_{2b}}W_k\right\|_2=2\sqrt b,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(V_{2b})=2+4b.                                \tag{2.3}\] The second identity uses orthogonality of the diagonal and off-diagonal Gaussian quadratic monomials. Since \(L^q\) norms dominate \(L^2\) for \(q\ge2\), the claimed uniform block bound fails under the hypotheses used in the concentration proof.

Impact and repair boundary. This invalidates the written bounded-block step supplying the small-lag constants to the concentration argument. An additional normalization of the centered blocks by \(\sqrt b\), with consistent changes to the sum identity and tail thresholds, is a possible repair that must be carried out. The target \(\sqrt{b/n}\) fluctuation scale in Proposition 4.6 is not disproved by (2.3).

The coupling at the artificial sample origin must not be confused with a stationary block coupling. Under the literal zero-boundary convention, changing the innovation block \(\zeta_0\) does not affect iid positive-index blocks. We do not report a nonzero norm for that literal coupling. The decisive contradiction is the actually printed block-sum bound (2.3); restoring stationarity would require separate uniform relative-lag bounds.

Problem 3 (Major: the uniform Edgeworth hypothesis fails for allowed bandwidths).  Location. Lemma 4.2, pp. 19–20; Lemma 4.12(ii), p. 34; its application in the central region of the Wasserstein proof, p. 35; bandwidth assumption (A3), p. 6.

Evidence and quantifiers. Lemma 4.12 requires an exponent \(d>5/2\) and a constant independent of \(n\) bounding \[\sum_{k=1}^n k^d\sup_{\ell\ge k}\left\|Y_\ell-Y_\ell'\right\|_q .
                                                                    \tag{2.4}\] The assertion that \(a>4\) and Lemma 4.2 verify this misses the latter lemma’s explicit factor \(1+n^{-1/2}|x|b^{d+1}\).

This is a real obstruction, not just a loose upper estimate. Grant the favorable repairs of centering and stationarity from Problem 1, take iid standard Gaussian \(X_k=\varepsilon_k\), and fix \(x=1\). Replacing \(\varepsilon_0\) gives, for \(1\le\ell\le b\), \[Y_\ell^c-(Y_\ell^c)'=-n^{-1/2}\varepsilon_\ell
                        (\varepsilon_0-\varepsilon_0'),\] and gives zero for \(\ell>b\). Hence (2.4) equals a positive constant times \[n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^b k^d\asymp n^{-1/2}b^{d+1}.\] At \(b=\lfloor(n/\log^3n)^{1/4}\rfloor\), this diverges as \[n^{(d-1)/4}(\log n)^{-3(d+1)/4}\] for every \(d>5/2\). The original process satisfies the assumptions with, for example, \(p=8,a=5\). The independent smoothing coboundary only changes lag one; lags \(2,\ldots,b\) retain this obstruction. Under the literal initial zero convention the sequence is nonstationary, so that convention cannot instead validate the stationary lemma.

Impact and repair boundary. The claimed uniform Edgeworth input for Theorem 2.6 has not been established over the stated bandwidth range. It needs a theorem adapted to the actual triangular array or block structure, or a narrower bandwidth range with the bias tradeoff rechecked. This particular sufficient condition already requires \(b^{d+1}=O(\sqrt n)\) for fixed \(x\), substantially below the allowed \(n^{1/4}\) scale. Enlarging the original decay exponent \(a\) does not remove the iid obstruction. The calculation does not disprove the correctly targeted Wasserstein theorem. In contrast, the Kolmogorov lemma admits \(2/3<d<\min(1,a-3/2)\), so this obstruction should not be transferred to that weaker requirement.

Problem 4 (Major: the stated Wasserstein target has the reciprocal scale).  Location. Theorem 2.6, p. 9; the law notation and CDF identity in (4.53), p. 34; compare Theorem 2.3 and its variance explanation, p. 7.

Printed discrepancy. The named law is \(\mathcal L(G\sigma_b/\sigma)\), but the proof integrates against \(\Phi(x\sigma_b/\sigma)\), which is the CDF of \(\mathcal L(G\sigma/\sigma_b)\). The discrepancy can be much larger than \(n^{-1/2}\).

Admissible counterexample. Take the stationary variance-one Gaussian process \[X_k=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-j}\varepsilon_{k-j},
\qquad \varepsilon_j\ {\rm iid}\ N(0,1).\] All moment and weighted dependence assumptions hold with \(p=8,a=5\); \[\gamma(h)=2^{-|h|},\quad \sigma^2=3,\quad
c_b=3-2\cdot2^{-b}.\] Choose \(b=\lfloor\log\log n\rfloor\) for sufficiently large \(n\), using natural logarithms. It satisfies (1.1). To give the statement the benefit of an explicit real denominator, adopt the favorable repair \[R_n=\sqrt{Q_n\vee\tau_n^{-2}},\qquad T_n=S_n/(\sqrt n\,R_n).\] The following argument is independent of the disputed proof. Write \(P=I-\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top/n\), so \(Q_n=n^{-1}X^\top PW_bPX\). The covariance matrix \(\Gamma\) has \(\left\|\Gamma\right\|_{\rm op}\le3\), and the Gaussian quadratic-form formula gives \[\operatorname{Var}(Q_n)
=\frac2{n^2}\left\|\Gamma^{1/2}PW_bP\Gamma^{1/2}\right\|_F^2
\le\frac{18(2b+1)}n .\] The uncentered boundary bias is \(O(n^{-1})\); removing the sample mean changes the expectation by \(O(b/n)\), by the fixed-rank projection and \(\left\|W_b\right\|_{\rm op}\le2b+1\). Thus \(\left\|Q_n-c_b\right\|_2=O(\sqrt{b/n})\).

Let \(A_n=S_n/\sqrt n\). It is exactly Gaussian with \[\operatorname{Var}(A_n)=3-\frac4n(1-2^{-n}).\] The function \(g_n(u)=(u\vee\tau_n^{-2})^{-1/2}\) is globally Lipschitz with constant at most \(\tau_n^3/2\), including negative \(u\). Eventually \(g_n(c_b)=1/\sigma_b\), and Cauchy–Schwarz, without any independence assumption on \(A_n,Q_n\), gives \[\mathbb E|A_n(g_n(Q_n)-1/\sigma_b)|
\le\left\|A_n\right\|_2\frac{\tau_n^3}2\left\|Q_n-c_b\right\|_2
=O(\tau_n^3\sqrt{b/n}).\] It follows by coupling and the exact normal law of \(A_n\) that \[W_1(\mathcal L(T_n),\mathcal L(G\sigma/\sigma_b))
=O(\tau_n^3\sqrt{b/n}+n^{-1})=o(2^{-b}).\] On the other hand, for positive normal scales the distance is exactly the scale difference times \(\mathbb E|G|\), so \[W_1(\mathcal L(G\sigma/\sigma_b),\mathcal L(G\sigma_b/\sigma))
=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac{3-c_b}{\sqrt3\sqrt{c_b}}
\asymp2^{-b}\asymp(\log n)^{-\log2}.\] The triangle inequality therefore gives a lower bound \(c\,2^{-b}\gg n^{-1/2}\) against the printed target.

Impact and repair boundary. This refutes the actual quantitative target in Theorem 2.6, even after a natural denominator completion. Reverse the ratio in the named Gaussian laws; the CDF direction used in the proof is already correct. The Major classification reflects a false principal theorem statement at its asserted rate, despite a short textual correction. It neither disproves the intended reciprocal version nor repairs Problems 1–3.

Problem 5 (Minor: the random denominator needs a real-valued completion).  Location. Rectangular lag sum (1.6), p. 3; the choice \(\omega=1\) and (2.6), pp. 6–7; truncation (2.11), p. 9; good-event positivity (4.12)–(4.15), pp. 21–22.

Evidence. Let the observations be iid with probabilities \[\mathbb P(X=-2)=\tfrac14,\quad \mathbb P(X=0)=\tfrac12,\quad \mathbb P(X=2)=\tfrac14.\] They are centered, have \(\sigma^2=2\), all moments, and zero positive-lag dependence coefficients. For even \(n\) and odd \(b<n-1\), the two alternating samples \(0,2,0,2,\ldots\) and \(2,0,2,0,\ldots\) have total probability \(2^{1-3n/2}>0\). On this event \[\begin{aligned}
&\bar X_n=1,\quad S_n=n,\quad
\widehat\gamma_X(h)=(-1)^h(1-h/n),\\
&Q_n=-1+(b+1)/n<0.
\end{aligned}\] An odd sequence \(b=2\lfloor\log\log n/2\rfloor+1\) is admissible eventually. Thus the square root is not a real random variable on a positive-probability event at arbitrarily large admissible \(n\). Applying a maximum to the already undefined \(\widehat\sigma_{nb}\) does not supply a definition.

Impact and repair boundary. Specify the statistic on \(\{Q_n\le0\}\). For Wasserstein distance, write the squared-estimator floor explicitly, \(R_n=\sqrt{Q_n\vee\tau_n^{-2}}\). For the Kolmogorov result, an explicit measurable real completion has distributional cost at most the exceptional-event probability. The bounds asserted in (4.13) are of the appropriate order if their concentration proof is repaired. This is a local definition issue, not evidence that a reasonable completion destroys the rates. Arbitrarily large completions would not automatically preserve a Wasserstein bound.
Problem 6 (Minor: the finite-window coupling bound omits shifted coordinates).  Location. Proposition 3.1, (3.1)–(3.3), p. 10; single-innovation coupling (2.2), p. 5.

Evidence. Use \(\mathbb Y=\mathbb R\), a window of length two, and \(f(u,v)=\operatorname{clip}(v,-1,1)\). On all of \(\mathbb R^2\), this satisfies (3.1) with \(\alpha=1,\beta=0,C_f=2\), since \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le2\min(d(x,y),1)\). Take \(Y_k=\varepsilon_k\) iid Rademacher and \(p=q=6\). Then (3.2) gives \(X_k=\varepsilon_{k-1}\). At lag \(\ell=1\), \[\left\|X_k-X_k^{(1,\prime)}\right\|_6=2^{5/6}>0,\qquad
d(Y_k,Y_k^{(1,\prime)})=0.\] Thus the displayed right side of (3.3) vanishes while its left side is positive. The notation (3.2) explicitly lists the window coordinates; it has not redefined \(Y_k\) to be the whole window.

Impact and repair boundary. Replace that right side by a bound on the coupled window or a finite sum of shifted dependence coefficients, including lag zero where needed. A fixed finite window preserves weighted summability after these shifts, so the example does not itself refute the later examples or main CLT. It disproves the stated pointwise auxiliary inequality.

Problem 7 (Minor: the constant in Corollary 2.7 cannot be uniform in the written form).  Location. Corollary 2.7, p. 9: one constant depending only on \(\Theta_{a,p},p,\sigma^2\), followed by all \(q\ge1\), in \(\int|F_n-\Phi(\,\cdot\,\sigma_b/\sigma)|^q\le Cn^{-q/2}\).

Impact and repair boundary. This is a defect in the literal common-constant, common-\(n\)-range formulation. If a \(q\)-dependent threshold \(N(q)\) was intended, that is a different quantification requiring specification. Natural repairs are \(C^q n^{-q/2}\), a \(q\)-dependent constant, or the norm statement \(\left\|F_n-\Phi\right\|_q\le Cn^{-1/2}\). Indeed interpolation gives \(\left\|f\right\|_q^q\le\left\|f\right\|_\infty^{q-1}\left\|f\right\|_1\), naturally producing \(C^q\). No fixed-\(q\) convergence rate is disproved here.
# Positive checks, assessment, and limits

The square-root linearization (4.3)/(4.16) has the correct sign and remainder on its positive-denominator event; the error occurs in identifying its centered linear part with the defined sum. The ordinary dependence-exponent interval \(2/3<d<a-3/2\) is nonempty precisely when \(a>13/6\), and one can additionally choose \(d<1\). The displacement bound \[\sup_{|x|\le C\sqrt{\log n}}\frac{|x|b^2\log n}{n}
=O(n^{-1/2})\] is consistent with (A3). The deterministic \(c_b\) is eventually positive by covariance summability and \(\sigma^2>0\); this does not imply positivity of the random rectangular estimator. The smoothing perturbation telescopes to \(H_n-H_0\), and its sinc-power density has compact Fourier support. These checks support particular intended steps without establishing the missing uniform inputs.

Assessment: Major (four Major and three Minor Problems). The target-scale counterexample concerns a principal printed assertion. The centering, concentration, and Edgeworth issues affect indispensable proof inputs and have separate correction requirements. The remaining three issues have explicit local repair boundaries. Repairability does not make the first four inconsequential, and none warrants the broader claim that every intended theorem or application is false.

The principal read all 2,360 lines of the frozen PDF-derived text and inspected every cited source image, focusing on definitions, theorem quantifiers, linearization, covariance normalization, concentration blocks, and the Wasserstein proof. This is not a complete proof reconstruction or independent acceptance.

Not independently re-established were every martingale projection estimate in Lemmas 4.7–4.8, all fourth-order covariance decompositions in Proposition 4.10, all dynamical-system examples, or the external Berry–Esseen, Edgeworth, and maximal inequalities. The author TeX was used to corroborate selected formulas, not executed. The counterexamples above are analytical derivations, with no claimed simulation or author-code run. The supplied source inventory and bounded primary-page search identified no separate correction, supplement, or released program needed for these checks; this is not an exhaustive absence claim, and absence of code is not a mathematical defect.

claim: Recorded check: Uncentered linearized sums used in mean-zero approximation
analysis: Location. Definitions (4.7)–(4.8), p. 18; (4.16)–(4.20), pp. 22–23; mean-zero hypothesis of Lemma 4.5, pp. 20–21; Proposition 4.10, p. 29; smoothed definitions and moments (4.46), (4.48)–(4.51), pp. 33–34.

An exact all-assumptions check is \(X_k\) iid \(N(0,1)\), with any admissible growing bandwidth. Then \(\sigma_{nb}=1\). For \(W_b=(\mathbf1_{\{|i-j|\le b\}})_{i,j=1}^n\), \(R_n(x)=S_n-xX^\top W_bX/(2\sqrt n)\). Odd Gaussian moments vanish, \(\operatorname{tr}W_b=n\), and \(\operatorname{tr}W_b^2=n(2b+1)-b(b+1)\). Therefore \[\mathbb ER_n(x)^2
=n+\frac{x^2n}{4}+\frac{x^2(2b+1)}2-\frac{x^2b(b+1)}{2n}.          \tag{2.2}\] At \(x=1\), the extra \(n/4\) contradicts (4.18)’s \(O((1+x^2)\sqrt n)\) error. In fact \(X^\top W_bX/n\to1\) in \(L^2\), so \(R_n(1)/\sqrt n\Rightarrow N(-1/2,1)\). In (4.20) at \(x=1,\mu=0\), the probability tends to \(\Phi(3/2)\), whereas the displayed approximant tends to \(\Phi(2/\sqrt5)\). Their difference is nonzero.

Impact and repair. Mean-zero Lemma 4.5 is not applicable to the defined variables. The same omission enters the smoothed raw moments: a mean-zero coboundary does not remove this mean. Define centered variables and sums, replace raw moments by variances and central cumulants, and carry these changes through the event comparisons. Proposition 4.10 already estimates \(\mathbb E[(Y_k-\mathbb EY_k)(Y_0-\mathbb EY_0)]\), which supports a possible correction but cannot justify the present raw-moment calculation.

There is also an explicit boundary obligation: setting \(X_{k-h}=0\) for \(k-h\le0\) (p. 17) makes the defined \(Y_k\) nonstationary. Section 4.3 removes this convention only within that section. A repair must control the initial terms or use a suitable nonstationary approximation theorem. A subsidiary variance remainder immediately before (4.18) should be \(O(1)\), not generally \(O(n^{2-a})\): for the variance-one Gaussian AR(1) with covariance \(2^{-|h|}\), \(\mathbb ES_n^2=3n-4+4\,2^{-n}\). This smaller correction fits the subsequent \(O(\sqrt n)\) tolerance. These are failures of the written proof, not a counterexample to the intended centered CLT.
result: Impact: Written principal normal-approximation proof invalid; smoothed raw moments have same centering defect. Intended centered CLT not disproved.

problems.title: Concentration block proof loses sqrt(b)

claim: Recorded check: Concentration block proof loses sqrt(b)
analysis: Location. Definition of \(W_k\) and Lemma 4.8, p. 26; blocks (4.30)–(4.31), p. 27; final paragraph of Lemma 4.9 and its use in Proposition 4.6, p. 29.

Evidence. The source sets \[W_k=2b^{-1/2}X_kB_{kb},\qquad

problems.title: Uniform Edgeworth dependence hypothesis fails at allowed bandwidth
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 6 Pdf pages: 19 Pdf pages: 20 Pdf pages: 34 Pdf pages: 35 Details: A3; Lemma4.2; Lemma4.12(ii); central-region application
claim: Recorded check: Uniform Edgeworth dependence hypothesis fails at allowed bandwidth
analysis: Location. Lemma 4.2, pp. 19–20; Lemma 4.12(ii), p. 34; its application in the central region of the Wasserstein proof, p. 35; bandwidth assumption (A3), p. 6.

Evidence and quantifiers. Lemma 4.12 requires an exponent \(d>5/2\) and a constant independent of \(n\) bounding \[\sum_{k=1}^n k^d\sup_{\ell\ge k}\left\|Y_\ell-Y_\ell'\right\|_q .
                                                                    \tag{2.4}\] The assertion that \(a>4\) and Lemma 4.2 verify this misses the latter lemma’s explicit factor \(1+n^{-1/2}|x|b^{d+1}\).

This is a real obstruction, not just a loose upper estimate. Grant the favorable repairs of centering and stationarity from Problem 1, take iid standard Gaussian \(X_k=\varepsilon_k\), and fix \(x=1\). Replacing \(\varepsilon_0\) gives, for \(1\le\ell\le b\), \[Y_\ell^c-(Y_\ell^c)'=-n^{-1/2}\varepsilon_\ell
                        (\varepsilon_0-\varepsilon_0'),\] and gives zero for \(\ell>b\). Hence (2.4) equals a positive constant times \[n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^b k^d\asymp n^{-1/2}b^{d+1}.\] At \(b=\lfloor(n/\log^3n)^{1/4}\rfloor\), this diverges as \[n^{(d-1)/4}(\log n)^{-3(d+1)/4}\] for every \(d>5/2\). The original process satisfies the assumptions with, for example, \(p=8,a=5\). The independent smoothing coboundary only changes lag one; lags \(2,\ldots,b\) retain this obstruction. Under the literal initial zero convention the sequence is nonstationary, so that convention cannot instead validate the stationary lemma.

Impact and repair boundary. The claimed uniform Edgeworth input for Theorem 2.6 has not been established over the stated bandwidth range. It needs a theorem adapted to the actual triangular array or block structure, or a narrower bandwidth range with the bias tradeoff rechecked. This particular sufficient condition already requires \(b^{d+1}=O(\sqrt n)\) for fixed \(x\), substantially below the allowed \(n^{1/4}\) scale. Enlarging the original decay exponent \(a\) does not remove the iid obstruction. The calculation does not disprove the correctly targeted Wasserstein theorem. In contrast, the Kolmogorov lemma admits \(2/3<d<\min(1,a-3/2)\), so this obstruction should not be transferred to that weaker requirement.
result: Impact: Uniform Wasserstein proof input fails for allowed triangular array; correctly rescaled theorem not itself disproved.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: New structure-aware uniform Edgeworth theorem or narrower bandwidth plus bias analysis; larger original a alone cannot fix.

problems.title: Theorem2.6 Gaussian comparison law has inverse scale
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 7 Pdf pages: 9 Pdf pages: 34 Details: Theorem2.6; (4.53); contrast Theorem2.3
claim: Recorded check: Theorem2.6 Gaussian comparison law has inverse scale
analysis: Location. Theorem 2.6, p. 9; the law notation and CDF identity in (4.53), p. 34; compare Theorem 2.3 and its variance explanation, p. 7.

Printed discrepancy. The named law is \(\mathcal L(G\sigma_b/\sigma)\), but the proof integrates against \(\Phi(x\sigma_b/\sigma)\), which is the CDF of \(\mathcal L(G\sigma/\sigma_b)\). The discrepancy can be much larger than \(n^{-1/2}\).

Admissible counterexample. Take the stationary variance-one Gaussian process \[X_k=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-j}\varepsilon_{k-j},
\qquad \varepsilon_j\ {\rm iid}\ N(0,1).\] All moment and weighted dependence assumptions hold with \(p=8,a=5\); \[\gamma(h)=2^{-|h|},\quad \sigma^2=3,\quad
c_b=3-2\cdot2^{-b}.\] Choose \(b=\lfloor\log\log n\rfloor\) for sufficiently large \(n\), using natural logarithms. It satisfies (1.1). To give the statement the benefit of an explicit real denominator, adopt the favorable repair \[R_n=\sqrt{Q_n\vee\tau_n^{-2}},\qquad T_n=S_n/(\sqrt n\,R_n).\] The following argument is independent of the disputed proof. Write \(P=I-\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top/n\), so \(Q_n=n^{-1}X^\top PW_bPX\). The covariance matrix \(\Gamma\) has \(\left\|\Gamma\right\|_{\rm op}\le3\), and the Gaussian quadratic-form formula gives \[\operatorname{Var}(Q_n)
=\frac2{n^2}\left\|\Gamma^{1/2}PW_bP\Gamma^{1/2}\right\|_F^2
\le\frac{18(2b+1)}n .\] The uncentered boundary bias is \(O(n^{-1})\); removing the sample mean changes the expectation by \(O(b/n)\), by the fixed-rank projection and \(\left\|W_b\right\|_{\rm op}\le2b+1\). Thus \(\left\|Q_n-c_b\right\|_2=O(\sqrt{b/n})\).

Let \(A_n=S_n/\sqrt n\). It is exactly Gaussian with \[\operatorname{Var}(A_n)=3-\frac4n(1-2^{-n}).\] The function \(g_n(u)=(u\vee\tau_n^{-2})^{-1/2}\) is globally Lipschitz with constant at most \(\tau_n^3/2\), including negative \(u\). Eventually \(g_n(c_b)=1/\sigma_b\), and Cauchy–Schwarz, without any independence assumption on \(A_n,Q_n\), gives \[\mathbb E|A_n(g_n(Q_n)-1/\sigma_b)|
\le\left\|A_n\right\|_2\frac{\tau_n^3}2\left\|Q_n-c_b\right\|_2
=O(\tau_n^3\sqrt{b/n}).\] It follows by coupling and the exact normal law of \(A_n\) that \[W_1(\mathcal L(T_n),\mathcal L(G\sigma/\sigma_b))
=O(\tau_n^3\sqrt{b/n}+n^{-1})=o(2^{-b}).\] On the other hand, for positive normal scales the distance is exactly the scale difference times \(\mathbb E|G|\), so \[W_1(\mathcal L(G\sigma/\sigma_b),\mathcal L(G\sigma_b/\sigma))
=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac{3-c_b}{\sqrt3\sqrt{c_b}}
\asymp2^{-b}\asymp(\log n)^{-\log2}.\] The triangle inequality therefore gives a lower bound \(c\,2^{-b}\gg n^{-1/2}\) against the printed target.

Impact and repair boundary. This refutes the actual quantitative target in Theorem 2.6, even after a natural denominator completion. Reverse the ratio in the named Gaussian laws; the CDF direction used in the proof is already correct. The Major classification reflects a false principal theorem statement at its asserted rate, despite a short textual correction. It neither disproves the intended reciprocal version nor repairs Problems 1–3.
result: Impact: Principal quantitative assertion false as printed, even after favorable denominator completion.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Reverse ratio in named laws; separately repair P1-P3.

report: Abstract: The assigned author preprint presents a relative-entropy method for weak-strong uniqueness of planar multiphase mean curvature flow. This review identifies two Major problems: a scope inconsistency in the varifold extension and a curvature sign that obstructs the stated compatibility estimates used in the global calibration construction. Three Minor problems concern entropy bookkeeping, the hypotheses of a Fourier criterion, and a paired series. An admissible shrinking-circle example disproves the printed local implication in Lemma 22; the incompatible normal derivatives in Proposition 33 establish its consequential use in the proof chain. The integral positivity needed for the actual Read–Shockley profile admits a complete analytic repair. These findings do not disprove the principal weighted BV uniqueness theorem. The overall assessment is Major; scientific adjudication and human review remain pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 27 October 2026

Title: Scientific technical review of
The local structure of the energy landscape in multiphase mean curvature flow:
Weak-strong uniqueness and stability of evolutions
# Identity, version, and theorem scope

The authors are Julian Fischer, Sebastian Hensel, Tim Laux, and Theresa M. Simon. The journal association is DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1577. The exact assigned input is the 104-page arXiv:2003.05478v2, uploaded 27 September 2021. It is an author preprint, not the publisher Version of Record and not asserted here to be the accepted version. The publisher landing page separately records online-first publication in 2025, a Published date of 19 February 2025, submission on 13 December 2022, and acceptance on 26 December 2023. No equivalence with that later publisher text has been verified. PDF and printed page numbers coincide.

Theorem 1 (p. 11) concerns planar finite regular networks up to the strong solution’s lifetime. Definitions 14–16 (pp. 19–21) require regular interfaces, triple junctions, Herring balance, curvature and higher compatibility conditions, and a smooth family preserving the network structure. Constants on a fixed interval \(T<T_{\rm strong}\) are not claimed uniform at a topology change. Definition 9 (pp. 15–16) requires a symmetric tension matrix with positive off-diagonal entries, zero diagonal, and a nondegenerate Euclidean simplex realization \(\sigma_{ij}=|q_i-q_j|\). Strict triangle inequalities alone do not replace this requirement.

The BV competitors in Definition 13 (pp. 17–18) satisfy a transport identity, square-integrable normal velocities, a weighted first-variation identity, and a sharp global energy-dissipation inequality. The conclusion is not uniqueness among arbitrary Brakke flows. The abstract calibration implication (Theorem 3) and bulk-error estimate (Proposition 5) are conditional statements in \(d\ge2\); Theorem 6 and Lemma 8 construct the needed objects for the specified planar networks.

Write \[\xi_{ij}=\frac{\xi_i-\xi_j}{\sigma_{ij}},\qquad
 E_\sigma=\sum_{i\ne j}\sigma_{ij}\int_{I_{ij}}(1-n_{ij}\cdot\xi_{ij})\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}.\] The sums are over ordered pairs. The resulting double counting is intentional. Calibration coercivity gives \[|n-\xi|^2\le2(1-n\cdot\xi),\qquad
 0\le1-|\xi|^2\le2(1-n\cdot\xi),\] and controls the squared distance to the strong interface. Vanishing interface error gives containment; the signed transported weights in Definition 4 and their bulk error are also needed to identify the phases.
# Established problems

Problem 1 (Major: the varifold extension needs an explicit tension restriction).  Location. Definition 2(4a) and (5), pp. 12–13; Definitions 16 and 18, pp. 21, 23; (26), its following decomposition, and Theorem 19, p. 24; proof of Theorem 19, pp. 44–46, especially Step 4.

Evidence. Theorem 19 invokes the preceding strong solution and calibration without explicitly restricting the admissible \(\sigma_{ij}\) to unity. Definition 18 uses an unweighted integral-varifold mass \(\mu\). Its error functional is \[E_{\rm var}=2\mu(\mathbb R^d)-\sum_{i\ne j}\int_{I_{ij}}n_{ij}\cdot\xi_{ij}\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}.\] For \(\rho_i=d|D\chi_i|/d\mu\), the exact decomposition is \[E_{\rm var}
 =2\int\left(1-\frac12\sum_i\rho_i\right)d\mu
   +E_1,\qquad
 E_1=\sum_{i\ne j}\int_{I_{ij}}(1-n_{ij}\cdot\xi_{ij})\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}.       \tag{2.1}\] The text identifies the last term with the previously defined \(E_\sigma\). This is not an identity for general tensions. Problem 2 (Minor: two omissions in the entropy absorption step).  Location. Proposition 17(24), p. 22; definition of term II, p. 39; first display and (48), p. 40; Theorem 3(6), p. 13.

Evidence. Put \(w=V+\operatorname{div}\xi\). Replacing \(n\) by \(n-\xi\) in the mixed term involving \(I-\xi\otimes\xi\), as an equality, drops \[((I-\xi\otimes\xi)B)\cdot wn
 =((I-\xi\otimes\xi)B)\cdot w(n-\xi)
   +(1-|\xi|^2)(B\cdot\xi)w.                                  \tag{2.2}\] The last term need not vanish because a coercive calibration is short off its reference interface. The same page’s (48) also drops \(E_\sigma(0)\), present in Proposition 17. For distinct smooth concentric shrinking circles, \(E_\sigma(0)>0\) and \(E_\sigma(t)\) is continuous at zero. An estimate \(E_\sigma(T)+D(T)\le C\int_0^T E_\sigma(t)\,dt\), with nonnegative dissipation \(D\), cannot then hold as \(T\downarrow0\).

Problem 3 (Minor: the general Fourier criterion omits pointwise assumptions).  Location. Definition 9, pp. 15–16; (12)–(14) and Lemma 11, pp. 16–17; Fejér-limit argument, pp. 98–99.

Evidence. The generic part of Lemma 11 assumes a bounded profile \(f:[0,\pi/4]\to[0,1]\) and strict negativity of the nonzero Fourier coefficients of its even periodic squared extension. The proof later uses continuity of \(g=f^2\), absent from that statement. Define the continuous \(\pi/2\)-periodic function \[g_0(\theta)=\frac18\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}(1-\cos4k\theta),\qquad f_0=\sqrt{g_0}.\] Then \(0\le g_0\le1/4\), \(f_0(0)=0\), and its nonzero complex Fourier coefficients are \(\widehat g_0(k)=-2^{-|k|}/16<0\). Change only \(f(\pi/8)\) to zero, keeping \(f=f_0\) elsewhere on the defining interval, and extend evenly and periodically. The Fourier coefficients are unchanged. Two distinct orientations \(0,\pi/8\) nevertheless give \(\sigma_{12}=0\), violating strict off-diagonal positivity. The example already has zero diagonal.
If (12) is also to define the diagonal, a normalization is independently necessary: the continuous profile \(\sqrt{1/4+g_0}\) has the same strictly negative nonzero coefficients but \(f(0)=1/2\).

Repair and consequence. Require a continuous representative and \(f(0)=0\), or specify the zero diagonal separately. Fourier information alone is an almost-everywhere property and cannot control arbitrarily reassigned point values. With the pointwise hypotheses restored, the Fejér approximation and Vandermonde argument yield strict conditional negativity and the intended simplex realization. The actual Read–Shockley profile is continuous with \(f(0)=0\); this finding does not invalidate that subclass or Theorem 1, which independently assumes admissibility.

Problem 4 (Minor: an incorrect paired series in the Read–Shockley check).  Location. Equation (296), the two subsequent series, the \(500/11\) threshold, and the final numerical-integral assertion, p. 100.

Evidence. For \[I(\alpha)=\int_0^1(\log^2x+\log x-1)\cos(\alpha x)\,dx\] the unpaired series printed first gives \[I(\alpha)=\frac{5\alpha^2}{27}-\frac{7\alpha^4}{750}+O(\alpha^6).\] In the paired line the even-index numerator is printed \(4(2k)^2-6(2k)\); it must be \(4(2k)^2+6(2k)\). The printed expression instead has the coefficient \(-1/750\) at \(\alpha^4\). The correct first-pair positivity threshold is \(\alpha^2<1250/63\), not \(500/11\). Merely reversing the nearby malformed inequality does not bridge the resulting proof gap.

Complete analytic repair. In fact \(I(\alpha)>0\) for every \(\alpha>0\). Set \(w(x)=\log^2x+\log x-1\). Its integral is zero, and it changes sign once, from positive to negative, at \(r_0=\exp(-(1+\sqrt5)/2)\). For \(0<\alpha\le\pi\), the function \(\cos(\alpha x)\) strictly decreases on \((0,1)\).  J(a)=\int_0^a\frac{\operatorname{Si}(t)}t\,dt.\] Integration by parts, or termwise integration followed by integration of the sine integral, gives \[\alpha I(\alpha)=2J(\alpha)-\operatorname{Si}(\alpha)-\sin\alpha.              \tag{2.3}\] Pairing successive half periods of \(\sin t/t\) gives \(0<\operatorname{Si}(a)\le\operatorname{Si}(\pi)\) for \(a>0\); hence \(J\) is increasing. The bound \(\sin t\ge2t/\pi\) on \([0,\pi/2]\) gives \(J(\pi/2)\ge1\) and \(\operatorname{Si}(t)\ge1\) on \([\pi/2,\pi]\). Also \(\operatorname{Si}(\pi)\le\pi/2+\log2\), by splitting its integral at \(\pi/2\). Consequently, for \(\alpha\ge\pi\), \[\alpha I(\alpha)\ge2(1+\log2)-(\pi/2+\log2)-1
 =1+\log2-\pi/2>0.                                             \tag{2.4}\] For example, \(\log2>2/3\) and \(\pi<22/7\) make the last lower bound greater than \(2/21\).

Impact. The printed series argument is incorrect, but the required positivity and hence this ingredient of the actual Read–Shockley admissibility conclusion survive. The repair is analytic; no numerical integration or author program was executed or relied upon.

Problem 5 (Major: the tangential extension sign obstructs core compatibility estimates).  Location. Lemma 22, pp. 47–49, especially (65), (67), (75)–(76); (101)–(105), pp. 54–55; Proposition 33, (186)–(188) and Step 2, pp. 69–70; Construction 38, p. 83; Lemma 41, (268)–(269), pp. 87–89; Lemma 42, (271), (277), pp. 90–91.

Evidence. Use the source conventions \(\tau=J^\top n\), \(H=-\operatorname{div}_{\rm tan}n\), with \(H,n,\tau\) extended constantly in the normal direction, and \(B=Hn+\gamma\tau\). On the interface, \[\partial_\tau B=(\partial_\tau H+\gamma H)n
                  +(\partial_\tau\gamma-H^2)\tau,\qquad
 \partial_nB=(\partial_n\gamma)\tau .\] It follows that \[\nabla B:(n\otimes Jn+Jn\otimes n)
 =-(\partial_\tau H+\gamma H+\partial_n\gamma).                 \tag{2.5}\] To vanish there, as (76) requires, the right condition is \(\partial_n\gamma=-\gamma H-\partial_\tau H\). The printed (75) instead has \(+\gamma H-\partial_\tau H\), leaving the residual \(-2\gamma H\).

This is witnessed by a flow satisfying the local hypotheses, not merely arbitrary jets. Take two phases with unit tension and a shrinking circle \(R(t)=\sqrt{R_0^2-2t}>0\) on a closed interval before extinction. With the interior as the first phase, \[s=|x|-R(t),\quad n=e_r,\quad \tau=-e_\theta,\quad
 H=-1/R(t),\quad \gamma=\exp(-s/R(t)).\] These are smooth on a fixed sufficiently small tubular neighborhood. On the interface, \(\partial_n\gamma=\gamma H\) and \(\partial_\tau H=0\), so printed (75) holds. The first absolute-value term of (76) is \(2/R(t)>0\), the other is zero, and the claimed distance bound has right-hand side zero.

Actual core dependence. The error also prevents the stated matching between the curve and triple-junction velocity fields. Near an endpoint of the curve in Proposition 33, the cutoff in (188) is one. The interface value is therefore \(\gamma_c=\alpha\), where \(\alpha\) is the normally constant extension in (102). The triple-junction ansatz (101), with (105), has \[B^p=Hn+(\alpha+\beta s)\tau,\qquad
 \partial_n B^p=(-\alpha H-\partial_\tau H)\tau .\] But Proposition 33 expressly requires \(\gamma_c\) to satisfy the printed (75), and extends it by a normal Taylor expansion to do so. Thus \[\partial_n B^c=(+\alpha H-\partial_\tau H)\tau,\qquad
 \partial_n(B^p-B^c)=-2\alpha H\tau.                         \tag{2.6}\] At any point of the relevant interface segment where \(\alpha H\ne0\), this contradicts the \(O(\operatorname{dist})\) gradient estimate (187), whose right-hand side is zero on the interface. Along a normal segment it also gives \[B^p-B^c=-2\alpha Hs\tau+O(s^2),\] contrary to the \(O(\operatorname{dist}^2)\) estimate (186). The obstruction is not removed by choosing the tangential component to vanish identically: (104) imposes \(\partial_\tau\alpha=H^2\), so \(\alpha H\) cannot vanish throughout an open curved segment. The regular-network hypotheses do not require these segments to be flat. Step 2 on p. 70 identifies tangential values through (188), but equality on the interface does not supply the incompatible normal derivatives.

These estimates are actual inputs to the main construction. Construction 38 chooses the curve tangential component from Proposition 33 when the curve joins two triple junctions. Lemma 41 uses (186) to obtain (268), and uses (187) and (186) for the derivative estimate (269). Lemma 42 then explicitly invokes (269) in (277) and uses that identity to prove the global approximate transport estimate (271), required by the calibration condition (4c). This is a core proof defect as written, and its severity is Major even though a plausible correction is short. The bound used in that argument and the conclusion it was intended to prove must nevertheless be distinguished: the leading gradient discrepancy is \(-2\alpha H\,\tau\otimes n\), whose transpose annihilates \(n\). Thus this discrepancy alone does not refute the projected transport condition (271); a weaker projected estimate might suffice in a repaired proof.

Repair and limit. Reverse the sign of \(\gamma H\) in (75) and use the corresponding normal Taylor coefficient in Proposition 33. This agrees with the already printed \(\beta=-\alpha H-\partial_\tau H\) in (105), a substantive consistency check supporting the intended construction. A complete verification of the corrected global gluing argument is outside this focused acceptance. The shrinking circle is an actual counterexample to the local implication; the normal-jet calculation establishes the specified compatibility obstruction. Neither is asserted to be a counterexample to the corrected construction or to the main uniqueness theorem.
# Positive checks, dependencies, and limits

The entropy controls, the ordered-pair factors, and the bulk-weight sign identity were checked. If \(\vartheta_i\) is negative inside the strong phase and positive outside, then \(|\chi_i-\bar\chi_i||\vartheta_i|=(\chi_i-\bar\chi_i)\vartheta_i\). The strong-interface transport term is killed by \(\vartheta_i=0\) there. The remaining velocity and distance terms admit the advertised Young estimates. Both interface and bulk errors must vanish to obtain phase equality almost everywhere.

The local signed-distance transport identity \((\partial_t+B\cdot
abla)s=0\) yields \((\partial_t+B\cdot
abla)n+(
abla B)^	op n=0\). At a triple point with velocity \(p'\), the relations \(p'=H_i n_i+\alpha_i	au_i\), \(\partial_{	au_i}\alpha_i=H_i^2\), and (105) explain the matching first jets: \[
abla\widetilde\xi_i=	au_i\otimes Jp',
 \qquad
 
abla\widetilde B_i
 = eta_i(	au_i\otimes n_i-n_i\otimes	au_i)=- eta_iJ .\] The higher compatibility condition supplies a common \( eta_i\) at the junction. These checks support the construction’s mechanism; they are not a complete reconstruction of every interpolation and global gluing estimate. In particular the preliminary quadratic normal ansatz has squared length \(1+\alpha_i^4s_i^4/4\), so its later normalization cannot be silently omitted.

The transported weights need not be compactly supported to be integrable and strictly signed. The construction on pp. 95, 98 multiplies by \(\eta_R(x)=\kappa(e^{R-|x|})>0\), with \(|\nabla\eta_R|\le C\eta_R\). This resolves a potential concern about the exterior phase. The reduced-boundary/topological-boundary equality in Definition 14 deserves a closure or almost-everywhere convention at triple points; it is not counted as a separate theorem defect here.
# Assessment and actual review coverage

The assessment is Major, based on Problems 1 and 5. Problems 2–4 remain Minor with the explicit consequences and repairs established above. Problem 5 is Major because the incorrect extension enters the core calibration construction; the short form of its proposed correction does not reduce that impact. No claim is made that the main weighted BV uniqueness theorem is false. The exact reviewed version is older than the journal publication.

The initial-review principal checked the main definitions and theorem chain, entropy and bulk-error steps, the varifold cancellation, signed-distance and triple-point formulas, the transported-weight tail, and the Fourier/positivity argument. The initial review recorded actual inspection of thirty-six source evidence pages as rendered images: 1, 11–24, 39–46, 48–52, 54–55, 69, 94–95, and 98–100. The full 104-page proof was not independently reconstructed: substantial parts of Sections 3, 6.2, and 7, and the cited external existence/regularity results, remain dependencies rather than independently certified proofs. Text extraction and manifest parsing are not counted as scientific proof verification.

Their actual scopes and hashes are retained separately; they are not separately authenticated Pro reviewers or independent acceptance authorities. The external controller’s UI observation, this runtime’s self-description, and the absence of independent backend verification are recorded separately.

The initial review consulted the supplied same-version TeX and figures selectively. Public publisher/arXiv metadata and a bounded correction/supplement search were checked; no relevant correction or separate executable supplement was identified within that search. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect. No author code was run. The focused independent acceptance rechecked the five reported problems, their hypotheses, counterevidence, and consequences against the exact assigned source. It followed the additional dependency chain for Problem 5 through pp. 83 and 87–91, revised its severity and impact, and preserved the initial report. This is not a new complete review of all 104 pages. The current scientific status remains `scientific_decision=pending` and `human_reviews=[]`.

report: Abstract: The assigned author preprint proves uniqueness through a spectral ample–narrow decomposition. An explicit smooth epigraph construction shows that the basepoint-component eigenvalue used to define the preliminary narrow region need not be continuous, and that this region need not be open even under the stated spectral gap. This is a substantive gap in the written decomposition proof, not a counterexample to the uniqueness theorem. Three further local problems concern positive eigenfunctions on disconnected truncations, a Robin energy coefficient, and an upper parabolic envelope. The latter admit direct repairs. The assessment is Major; scientific adjudication and human review remain pending.
