Title: Scientific initial review of
The steady states of strong-KPP reactions in general domains
# Identity and exact mathematical scope

The authors are Henri Berestycki and Cole Graham. The journal association is DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1578. The assigned primary input is the 40-page arXiv:2212.06611v1, submitted 13 December 2022. This is an author preprint, not a verified copy of the publisher Version of Record. The publisher landing page separately records submission on 13 December 2022, acceptance on 21 April 2024, and publication on 13 January 2025, with an online-first 2025 citation. Findings below apply to the exact assigned author version; equivalence with the later publisher PDF has not been established. Printed and PDF page numbers agree.

The standing hypotheses (pp. 2–3) are a nonempty connected uniformly \(C^{2,\gamma}\) domain \(\Omega\), \(f\in C^{1,\gamma}([0,\infty))\), \(f(0)=f(1)=0\), \(f>0\) on \((0,1)\), \(f'(0)>0\), and \(f<0\) above 1. Strong KPP additionally requires \(s\mapsto f(s)/s\) strictly decreasing on \((0,1]\). Weak KPP only requires \(f(s)\le f'(0)s\). The equations and boundary convention are \[-\Delta u=f(u),\qquad
 \mathcal N_\rho u=\rho\partial_\nu u+(1-\rho)u=0,\quad 0\le\rho\le1.\] The conclusions concern positive bounded solutions. Dirichlet, Robin, and Neumann conditions correspond to \(\rho=0\), \(0<\rho<1\), and \(\rho=1\).

Definition 1.1 and Theorem 1.1 (p. 4) use the closure of the principal limit spectrum: \[f'(0)\notin\overline{\Sigma(\Omega,\rho)},\qquad
 \Sigma(\Omega,\rho)=\{\lambda(\Omega^*,\rho):\Omega^*\text{ is a connected limit}\}.\] Avoiding each isolated equality is not enough. Theorem 1.5 (p. 6) separates strict subcritical existence, weak-KPP strict supercritical nonexistence, and critical nonexistence in bounded or full-rank periodic domains under the stronger assumption. The general critical case and unconditional strong-KPP uniqueness remain conjectures in this version. Proposition 5.3 addresses a particular planar bulb with a critical half-strip, with the additional expansion \(f(s)=f'(0)s-Bs^2+O(s^3)\), \(B>0\).
# Established problems

Problem 1 (Major: the preliminary narrow region need not be open).  Location. Theorem 4.3 and Lemma 4.4, p. 21; (4.7), p. 22; definition of \(\Omega_+^0\), continuity claim, and application of Lemma 4.4, p. 23; connected-component convergence and (4.14), p. 24. Theorem 1.1 invokes this decomposition on p. 25.

Claim being tested. With \(R\) satisfying \(\lambda(B_1,0)R^{-2}<\delta\), the proof defines \[\Omega_+^0=
 \{z\in\Omega:\lambda(\operatorname{comp}_z(\Omega\cap B_{2R}(z)),\sigma)>\mu+\delta\}.
                                                                    \tag{2.1}\] It asserts continuity of the eigenvalue as a function of \(z\), infers openness, and applies the truncation lemma for an open set. Smoothness of the original domain does not prevent components of its ball intersection from joining through a newly opened passage.

Let \(\Omega=\{(x,y):y>h(x)\}\). It is connected and uniformly \(C^\infty\), a bounded perturbation of the upper half-plane. Let \[z_0=(0,0),\quad z_\varepsilon=(0,\varepsilon),\quad
 C_\varepsilon=\operatorname{comp}_{z_\varepsilon}
                  (\Omega\cap B_{20}(z_\varepsilon)).\] For \(\varepsilon=0\), the vertical sections at \(x=-1\) and \(x=1\) are empty. Hence \(C_0\subset(-1,1)\times\mathbb R\). The one-dimensional Dirichlet Poincaré inequality, applied to zero extensions and integrated in \(y\), gives \[\lambda(C_0,0)\ge\frac{\pi^2}{4}.                            \tag{2.3}\] For every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), the upper circle arc is \(g(x)+\varepsilon\); the former contact at \(x=1\) now has positive gap \(\varepsilon+(x-1)^2\). All vertical fibers for \(0\le x\le7\) are nonempty intervals, and their union connects \(z_\varepsilon\) to the fixed square \[Q=(3,7)\times(-2,2)\subset C_\varepsilon.\] The square lies strictly inside the ball for small \(\varepsilon\), and \(h=-3\) there. Domain monotonicity and a square test function yield \[\lambda(C_\varepsilon,0)\le\lambda(Q,0)
 =\frac{\pi^2}{8}.                                          \tag{2.4}\] Thus the claimed continuity fails. No numerical eigenvalue computation or assertion of a full thin-passage spectral limit is needed.

Impact and repair boundary. Lemma 4.4 cannot be applied to this set as written. The same component-switching phenomenon prevents the unqualified connected-component convergence asserted before (4.14); convergence of the smooth original domains does not supply convergence of these selected ball-intersection components. This invalidates indispensable steps in the written proof of Theorem 4.3, on which the general uniqueness argument depends.

A repair needs a stable localization construction, for example with appropriately proved radius buffers and open spectral labels, followed by new verification of the narrow-side Lieb bound, the ample-side coverage, and the limit inequalities. Merely citing continuity of eigenvalues on smoothly convergent bounded domains does not address the failed component convergence. A larger ball can retain some limiting connecting paths, but changing one fixed radius alone does not establish a general repair.

This is a counterexample to the auxiliary continuity/openness claim under its actual hypotheses, not to Theorems 4.3 or 1.1 themselves. Indeed this particular epigraph admits the trivial ample decomposition \(\Omega_-=\Omega,\Omega_+=\varnothing\). The Major classification concerns a central proof gap with a demonstrated failure, not a claim that the desired theorem is false or unrepairable.

Problem 2 (Minor: a disconnected truncation need not have a strictly positive principal eigenfunction).  Location. Disconnected-domain convention, p. 10; Proposition 2.1(iii)–(iv) and the normalized \(\varphi_R\) argument, pp. 11–12; related eigenfunction selection in the hair-trigger proof, p. 31.

Evidence. The source correctly defines the principal eigenvalue of a disconnected domain as the infimum of its component eigenvalues. It then takes \(\varphi_R>0\) on the whole \(\Omega\cap B_R\) at that eigenvalue and normalizes it at an arbitrarily fixed basepoint. These requirements can conflict. If two bounded Dirichlet components have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1>\lambda_2\), a positive eigenfunction at \(\lambda_2\) cannot exist on the first component. Testing against its positive first eigenfunction \(\psi_1\) gives \[(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)\int_{D_1}\varphi_R\psi_1=0,\] which contradicts positivity. Smooth connected domains with unequal components after a ball cut are allowed. The domain in Problem 1 already provides a basepoint component with eigenvalue at least \(\pi^2/4\) and another component containing \(Q\), whose eigenvalue is at most \(\pi^2/8\).

Repair. Let \(D_R\) be the connected component of \(\Omega\cap B_R(x)\) containing a fixed interior point, for large \(R\). These components increase and exhaust \(\Omega\): each compact subset can be connected to the point by finitely many interior paths, all contained in a sufficiently large ball. Normalize the positive eigenfunction on \(D_R\), not on all components. Its decreasing eigenvalues \(\mu_R\) have a limit. The local Harnack/compactness argument produces a positive generalized eigenfunction and gives \(\lambda(\Omega,\sigma)\ge\lim_R\mu_R\); domain monotonicity gives the reverse inequality. Finally, \[\lambda(\Omega,\sigma)\le\lambda(\Omega\mid B_R(x),\sigma)
 \le\mu_R\longrightarrow\lambda(\Omega,\sigma).\] This supplies the intended exhaustion conclusion. For a compactly supported nonlinear subsolution one can instead select a component with a sufficiently small eigenvalue and extend by zero, as the proof on p. 18 already does. The finding is a local proof-selection error, not a counterexample to Proposition 2.1’s intended connected-domain conclusions.
Problem 3 (Minor: the Robin energy is missing a factor one-half).  Location. Proof of Proposition 1.4, p. 29, energy display; comparison with the boundary operator (1.2), p. 3.

Evidence. For \(0<ho<1\), put \(a=(1-ho)/ho\). The displayed functional is \[E[v]=\int_\Omega\left( rac12|
abla v|^2-H(v)ight)
       +a\int_{\partial\Omega}v^2.\] Its first variation in direction \(\eta\) is \[DE[v]\eta
 =\int_\Omega(-\Delta v-h(v))\eta
   +\int_{\partial\Omega}(\partial_
u v+2av)\eta .\] Thus its critical points satisfy \(\partial_
u v+2av=0\), whereas (1.2) requires \(\partial_
u v+av=0\).

Repair and consequence. Replace the boundary coefficient by \(a/2\). The negative-energy construction can still be obtained by making the ignition reaction large; truncation to \([0,1]\), minimization, and subsequent sub/supersolution comparison retain their purpose. The error affects the displayed Robin variational argument. The Dirichlet case has no such boundary term, and this calculation does not refute the weak-KPP multiplicity proposition after the correction.

Problem 4 (Minor: the upper parabolic envelope must start at least at one).  Location. Proof of Proposition 1.8, p. 31, the choice \(M=\sup v(0,\cdot)\) and (4.24); positive-reaction versus strong-KPP hypotheses, pp. 7, 31–32; multiplicity construction, pp. 29–30.
Evidence. At this stage only positivity of \(f\), not uniqueness, has been assumed. The asserted identity \(\mathcal P_\infty M=\mathcal P_\infty1=u_+\) need not hold when \(M<1\).

For a concrete bounded setting within this stage’s assumptions, use a Robin example with \(0<\rho<1\) from the multiplicity construction, with its energy normalized as in Problem 3. It has a low solution \(u_L\), \(\sup u_L<1/2\), and a high solution \(u_H\), \(\sup u_H>1/2\). Hopf’s lemma and the Robin condition give \(m=\min_{\overline\Omega}u_L>0\). Take \[v(0,\cdot)=\epsilon u_L,\qquad
 0<\epsilon<\frac{m}{\|u_L\|_\infty}.\] Then the printed \(M=\epsilon\|u_L\|_\infty\) satisfies \(M<m\), so comparison gives \(\mathcal P_t M\le u_L\) for all \(t>0\). But \(\mathcal P_\infty1=u_+\ge u_H\), which exceeds \(u_L\) somewhere. Therefore the asserted equality is impossible, even without presuming existence of a limit for \(\mathcal P_tM\).

Repair and consequence. Use \(M=\max\{1,\sup v(0,\cdot)\}\). This constant is a supersolution, so its flow decreases to a bounded steady state. The latter is at most 1, while comparison with the flow from 1 gives equality with \(u_+\). The intended upper bound and, when uniqueness is available, the convergence conclusion survive. This is not a counterexample to the hair-trigger statement.
# Positive checks and remaining dependencies

The generalized eigenvalue and boundary conventions were checked against the Rayleigh formulation. Domain monotonicity is used with the partial order of Definition 2.1, which imposes Dirichlet conditions on artificial boundaries; ordinary Robin domain monotonicity is not assumed. In Lieb’s localization calculation (p. 14), integration in the translation variable cancels the cross gradient term and retains the correct Robin boundary contribution. Its actual error is \(O(R^{-2})\); the nearby informal scale \(\varepsilon^{-2}\) should be read as \(\varepsilon^{-1/2}\), without affecting the displayed theorem.

The weighted negative-part proof of the maximum principle (pp. 17–18) has the correct sign. With \(\zeta_\delta=\operatorname{sech}(\delta|x|)\), its key inequality is \[\bigl(\delta^2-\lambda(-\mathcal L,\Omega,\sigma)\bigr)
       \|\zeta_\delta w_-\|_2^2\ge0.\] Choosing \(\delta^2<\lambda\) forces \(w_-=0\). The bounded/periodic critical nonexistence argument correctly uses \(\int u f(u)<f'(0)\int u^2\). The Neumann zero eigenvalue argument (pp. 16–17) uses polynomial volume growth to rule out a uniformly positive shell-to-volume ratio.

Conditional on a valid ample–narrow decomposition, the sliding/comparison mechanism in pp. 25–27 was checked, including boundary approach and the difference quotient \(q\le f'(0)\). The last bound still holds when \(\mu u_2>1\): then \(f(\mu u_2)<0\le f(u_1)\), so the quotient is negative. There is no need to extend the strict ratio condition above 1. Quotients involving \(\sigma/\rho\) should of course be treated separately in the Dirichlet case.

Some auxiliary regularity steps remain dependencies. In particular, the normalized compactness assertion in Lemma 4.5 is not supplied merely by the usual Harnack inequality for an arbitrary supersolution. A finite-domain eigenvalue test offers a direct way to exclude vanishing supersolutions when the limit eigenvalue is strictly below \(f'(0)\). No additional counterexample to that lemma’s conclusion is established here. Nor is the informal uniform smoothing step of Lemma 4.4 fully rebuilt. These limitations are recorded separately from the demonstrated problems.
# Assessment and actual coverage

The assessment is Major because Problem 1 invalidates the written central decomposition step. Problems 2–4 have local repairs with bounded consequences. The review establishes no counterexample to the general uniqueness conclusion.

The principal actually read the complete supplied 40-page extracted text, including the appendix and references, and investigated the spectral definitions, exhaustion, localization, maximum principle, decomposition, sliding proof, multiplicity construction, parabolic envelope, and critical asymptotic constant. Complete textual reading is not a claim that all imported estimates or all proof details were independently reproved. Thirty-two source pages were actually inspected as images: 1–7, 10–12, 14, 16–19, 21–27, 29–38. The source-page receipt identifies the exact images and checks.

They did not compile, inspect images, execute author code, or act as independent acceptance reviewers. The principal evaluated the adopted arguments, wrote this English TeX, executed the retained build, and performed the source/report image inspections. External UI observations and runtime self-description are recorded separately; the backend was not independently verified.

The inventory of supplied same-version TeX and figures, publisher/arXiv records, and author publication page were checked within a bounded source search. The auxiliaries also consulted specified same-version TeX passages. No relevant correction or separate executable supplement was identified within that search. The publisher PDF remained a distinct unverified version. No author code or numerical spectral computation was executed, and absence of code is not a mathematical defect. The base \(K\) is a complete discretely valued field of mixed characteristic \((0,p)\), with perfect residue field, uniformizer \(\pi\), and Eisenstein polynomial \(E\). Write \(a=E'(\pi)\). Smooth formal schemes are separated and topologically of finite type by the convention on p. 9. Convention 1.19 assumes \(K_{\mathrm{cyc}}\cap K_\infty=K\); the examples below take \(p=3\), \(K=\mathbb Q_p\), and \(\pi=p\), within this convention. A small affine formal scheme has an étale toric framing and ring \(R^+\), with \(R=R^+[1/p]\).

The integral local equivalence in Theorem 4.3 depends on the framing (Remark 4.4). The global chart-independent correspondence in Theorem 6.4 is rational. The main categories have finite projective evaluations; an enhanced Higgs object includes the arithmetic operator \(\phi\), not just a Higgs field. With chart components \(\theta_i\), its conditions include \[P_m(\phi):=\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}(\phi+ia)\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 [\phi,\theta_i]=-a\theta_i,\qquad [\theta_i,\theta_j]=0.
 \tag{1.1}\] The Higgs field is nilpotent in the principal finite-rank category. Generalized representations are not silently identified with \(\mathbb Q_p\)-local systems, and the essential-image questions in Section 7 are not read as assertions of unrestricted essential surjectivity.
# Established problems

Problem 1 (Minor: the quasi-coherent extension lacks geometric convergence).  Location. Remark 4.6, pp. 29–30 (author TeX line 2254); required coefficient convergence on p. 35, (4.13) on p. 36, and (4.19)/Lemma 4.22 on p. 39.

The remark extends the target to \(p\)-complete modules with an integrable Higgs field and an arithmetic operator satisfying Definition 4.1(2), and asserts the same equivalence for quasi-coherent crystals. The finite-rank implication of geometric nilpotence is unavailable in this extension. We use the natural intended integral \(R^+\)-module meaning of the remark; its incidental notation \(R\)-modules is not the basis of this finding.

Set \(E(u)=u-p\), \(a=1\), \(R^+=\mathbb Z_p\langle T^{\pm1}\rangle\), and \[H=\widehat{\bigoplus}_{n\ge0}R^+e_n,\qquad
 \theta_0e_n=e_{n+1},\qquad \phi e_n=-ne_n,\qquad
 \theta=\theta_0\otimes\omega,\quad \omega=\frac{d\log T}{E(u)}.
 \tag{2.1}\] Thus \(H\) is the module of sequences tending \(p\)-adically to zero. It is separated, complete and \(p\)-torsion-free. Both operators are continuous, preserve \(p^rH\), and have norm at most one. Integrability is automatic in one variable, and \[[\phi,\theta_0]=-\theta_0,\qquad
 P_m(\phi)e_n=(-1)^m m!\binom nm e_n,\qquad
 P_m(\phi)H\subseteq p^{v_p(m!)}H.
 \tag{2.2}\] The arithmetic smallness holds uniformly as an operator. Nevertheless, \(\theta_0^m e_0=e_m\notin pH\) for every \(m\).

The coefficient recurrence of any putative PD stratification forces \(\phi_{0,m}=\theta_0^m\). After setting the arithmetic coordinate \(X=0\), it would give \[\varepsilon(e_0)=\sum_{m\ge0}e_mY^{[m]}.
 \tag{2.3}\] This is not an element of \(H\widehat\otimes_{R^+}R^+\{Y\}_{\mathrm{pd}}^\wedge\): modulo \(p\), that tensor product consists of finite sums in the basis \(e_nY^{[m]}\), whereas (2.3) has infinitely many coefficient-one terms. Thus the enlarged target contains an object that cannot arise from the required crystal.

Impact and repair boundary. The additional infinite-rank equivalence is false under the listed conditions. Remove or restrict the remark, or supply a topology-appropriate condition ensuring convergence of the full coefficients \(\theta^{\mathbf n}P_k(\phi)(x)\) as \(k+|\mathbf n|\to\infty\), together with the continuity needed for completed descent. No unrestricted quasi-coherent theorem is proved merely by proposing this necessary condition. This example does not refute the finite-rank main theorem: finite rank supplies the nilpotence used to reduce full convergence to (1.1). The limited supplementary scope supports the Minor classification.

Problem 2 (Minor: the geometric zeroth face has the wrong subscript).  Location. Proposition 4.13(1), p. 32, (4.2); the derivation on p. 33; author TeX lines 2326 and 2401. Compare the correct absolute formula (4.4), p. 33, and its use on p. 43.

The printed geometric formula is \(p_0(Y_{s,j})=Y_{s,j+1}-Y_{s,j}\). From the definition \[Y_{s,j}=\frac{T_{s,0}-T_{s,j}}{E(u_0)T_{s,0}}\] and the shift of tensor-factor indices under \(p_0\), the geometric reduction instead gives \[p_0(Y_{s,j})=Y_{s,j+1}-Y_{s,1}.                 \tag{2.4}\] There is a direct consistency test. Suppressing \(s\), the printed maps give \[p_0p_0(Y_1)=Y_3-2Y_2+Y_1,\qquad
 p_1p_0(Y_1)=Y_3-Y_2.
 \tag{2.5}\] Their difference \(Y_1-Y_2\) is nonzero in the free completed PD algebra, so the required cosimplicial identity fails.

Impact and repair boundary. Replace the final subscript \(j\) by \(1\) in (4.2) and the corresponding derivation. The adjacent ratio on p. 33 should be \(T_{s,0}/T_{s,1}=(1-E(u_0)Y_{s,1})^{-1}\); its reduction modulo \(E\) is still one. These are one local correction group. The correct absolute formula and subsequent calculations already use the reference coordinate \(Y_{s,1}\), providing counterevidence to a broader failure of the intended classification.

Problem 3 (Minor: incompatible normalizations in the cohomological construction).  Location. Construction 4.30, p. 41; its chain-map proof, p. 42; proof of Lemma 4.32, p. 43; compare Example 4.25, p. 40, and Construction 4.35, pp. 44–45. TeX anchors are 2780, 2787, 2813 and 2871–2872.

Differential base. The left-hand differential module is declared relative to \(\mathcal O_K\), but the displayed right-hand denominator is \(R^+\{X_i\}_{\mathrm{pd}}^\wedge\), which removes the base differentials. At \(m=n=0,q=1\) on the torus, the claimed identification becomes \[\widehat\Omega^1_{R^+/\mathcal O_K}\simeq\widehat\Omega^1_{R^+/R^+}=0,
 \tag{2.6}\] although the left side contains \(d\log T\). The base forms must be retained; the natural intended relative base on the right is \(\mathcal O_K\{X_i\}_{\mathrm{pd}}^\wedge\), with the compatible completed PD differential convention.

Breuil–Kisin basis. Construction 4.30 prints \(p_0^1(E(u))=(1-aX_1)^{-1}E(u)\), whereas the preceding example and following proof use the direct factor. The discrepancy breaks the asserted chain-map property, not merely a cosmetic convention. On the same torus with \(a=1\), take \[H=R^+e_0\oplus R^+e_1,\quad
 \phi=\operatorname{diag}(0,-1),\quad
 \theta_0e_0=e_1,\quad\theta_0e_1=0.
 \tag{2.7}\] All enhanced hypotheses hold: \(\theta_0^2=0\), \([\phi,\theta_0]=-\theta_0\), and \(P_2(\phi)=0\). Writing \(b=1-X_1\), the action \(b^{-\phi}\) fixes \(e_0\) and sends \(e_1\) to \(be_1\). The printed inverse action on \(E(u)\) sends \(\omega=d\log T/E(u)\) to \(b\omega\), so \[p_0^1d(e_0)=b^2e_1\omega,\qquad
 dp_0^1(e_0)=e_1\omega.                            \tag{2.8}\] The difference is nonzero. The corrected action \(E(u)\mapsto bE(u)\) sends \(\omega\mapsto b^{-1}\omega\) and restores equality.

Positive-index faces. In the \(k\ge1\) calculation on p. 43, the extra factor \(\exp(\sum_l\theta_lY_{l,1})\) conflicts with the identity action on \(H\) assigned to both positive-index faces. For (2.7), applying it to \(e_0\) gives \(e_0+Y_{1,1}e_1\), instead of \(e_0\). Remove it from both copied intermediate lines; the zeroth face legitimately retains it.

Impact and repair boundary. Align the differential base, direct \(E\)-factor and positive faces throughout this local construction. The surrounding proof already uses the corrected \(E\)-factor, so these tests do not establish that the cohomology comparison theorem is false. The cited PD homotopy and descent inputs still require their own hypotheses; this review does not claim to reconstruct those theories from the local corrections alone.
Problem 4 (Minor: finite orbit is not the Sen finite-vector condition).  Location. Theorem 7.4, its preceding prose and proof, and Theorem 7.5, p. 57; TeX lines 3462, 3468 and 3476.

The text defines \(W^{\mathrm{fin}}\) by requiring the orbit to be a finite set, then asserts \(W^{\mathrm{fin}}=W^{\mathrm{la}}\). Take the admissible rank-one semilinear representation at a point \[R=K=\mathbb Q_p,\quad W=\widehat K_{\mathrm{cyc}}e,\qquad
 g(ce)=g(c)\chi(g)e.
 \tag{2.9}\] The vector \(e\) is locally analytic because the cyclotomic character is analytic on a sufficiently small open subgroup. Its orbit \(\{\chi(g)e\}\) is infinite. Hence \(e\in W^{\mathrm{la}}\setminus W^{\mathrm{fin}}\) under the printed definition. No assertion that \(W^{\mathrm{fin}}\) is zero is needed.

Impact and repair boundary. The equality, the proof’s choice of a finite-vector basis, and the subsequent definition of \(D_{\mathrm{Sen},K_{\mathrm{cyc}}}\) are incompatible with the literal finite-set definition. Replace that definition consistently by the actual Sen decompleted module and justify its equality with locally analytic vectors. At a point the usual finiteness concerns the finite-dimensional \(K\)-span of an orbit. In the relative case the appropriate finite \(R\)-module span or finite-level decompletion must be stated precisely using Proposition 7.2. The example does not contradict the corrected decompletion theorem.

Problem 5 (Minor: the arithmetic Higgs commutator has the opposite sign).  Location. Definitions 7.15 and 7.16, p. 61; Construction 7.23 and Theorem 7.24, pp. 62–63; TeX 3644 versus 3647 and 3662 versus 3665. Compare Definition 6.2, pp. 48–49, and Theorem 7.13, p. 60.

Both arithmetic definitions print \([\Phi,\Theta]=-\Theta\), but their claimed equivalent first square says \[(\Phi-1)\Theta=\Theta\Phi,\quad\text{that is}\quad
 [\Phi,\Theta]=+\Theta.                           \tag{2.10}\] The explicit functor resolves which sign agrees with the rest of the paper. Set \(b=(\zeta_p-1)\lambda\). Construction 7.23 assigns \[\Phi=-\phi_H/a,\qquad \Theta=-b\theta_H.\] Using the enhanced relation \([\phi_H,\theta_H]=-a\theta_H\), one obtains \[[\Phi,\Theta]=(b/a)[\phi_H,\theta_H]
             =-b\theta_H=\Theta.                 \tag{2.11}\] The rank-two object (2.7) satisfies every enhanced condition. Its image has \(\Phi=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\) and nonzero \(\Theta=-bE_{21}\omega\), so it fails the printed negative relation in characteristic zero.

Impact and repair boundary. Change both displayed commutator conditions to \(+\Theta\), preserving the existing \(\Phi-j\) diagrams and the functor normalization. This is also the Sen shift associated with the Tate \((-1)\) twist. As printed the functor does not land in its declared target; the explicit compatible repair is local, and the example does not refute the correctly signed correspondence.

Problem 6 (Minor: the derivative of the analytic coordinate omits a factor).  Location. Construction 7.7 and the proof of Proposition 7.9(2), p. 58; TeX lines 3502 and 3533. Compare the Lie operators on p. 59.

Impact and repair boundary. Correct the derivative and the following constant-coefficient explanation. On the local analytic coordinate expansion, \(
abla_\gamma=-\alpha
abla_	au\), not \(-
abla_	au\). The scalar \(\alpha\) is nonzero: \(	au(\alpha)=\alpha+1\) rules out zero. It is therefore invertible in the coefficient field and locally analytically invertible after restricting the analytic neighborhood. The two derivatives have the same kernel, and characteristic-zero differentiation still yields the required constant coefficients. This defect does not refute Proposition 7.9’s kernel conclusion.
# Positive checks, dependencies and limits
## Finite-rank local classification

For finite rank in characteristic zero, \([\phi,\theta_i^m]=-ma\theta_i^m\) implies \(\operatorname{tr}(\theta_i^m)=0\). Newton identities and Cayley–Hamilton, or the paper’s Lie-theoretic argument, give nilpotence. Localizing in fraction fields and using projectivity over the reduced smooth algebra descends the identity. Commuting nilpotents are jointly nilpotent. This identifies exactly the finite-rank step absent from Problem 1.

The recurrence on pp. 35–36 forces the ordered coefficients \[\phi_{k,\mathbf n}=\theta^{\mathbf n}P_k(\phi)
                 =P_k(\phi+|\mathbf n|a)\theta^{\mathbf n}.
 \tag{3.1}\] Only finitely many geometric multi-indices survive in finite rank, reducing full convergence to \(P_k(\phi)\to0\). Independently, put \(S(X)=(1-aX)^{-\phi/a}\), interpreted by its integral PD series, and \(U(Y)=\exp(\sum_i\theta_iY_i)\). Then \[S(X_1)\theta_iS(X_1)^{-1}=(1-aX_1)\theta_i,\qquad
 (1-aX_1)\left(1-a\frac{X_2-X_1}{1-aX_1}\right)=1-aX_2.\] These identities verify the closed-form cocycle \[U(Y_1)S(X_1)
 U\!\left(\frac{Y_2-Y_1}{1-aX_1}\right)
 S\!\left(\frac{X_2-X_1}{1-aX_1}\right)=U(Y_2)S(X_2).
 \tag{3.2}\] The geometric exponential is finite and the arithmetic series converges by the hypothesis. This checks the intended absolute stratification without claiming an independent line-by-line reconstruction of every printed coefficient elimination.

The enhanced Higgs complex correctly uses \(\phi+qa\) in degree \(q\). The notation \(F(X,Z)=((1-aX)^{-Z/a}-1)/Z\) in Construction 4.35 denotes a series with polynomial coefficients; it does not require \(Z\) invertible. Its shifted coefficients converge by the rising-factorial Vandermonde identity and \(P_m((q+1)a)=a^m m!\binom{q+m}{m}\to0\). At relative dimension zero the intended cohomology complex is \([H\xrightarrow{\phi}H]\).
## Arithmetic action, Sen normalization and gluing

With \(b=(\zeta_p-1)\lambda\), write \(q_g=1+\pi ab\,c(g)\). Equation (6.1) gives \(g(b)=\chi(g)b/q_g\). Since \(c(gh)=c(g)+\chi(g)c(h)\), direct multiplication yields \[q_g\,g(q_h)=q_{gh}.                              \tag{3.3}\] Conjugation by \(q_g^{-\phi/a}\) multiplies \(\theta\) by \(q_g\); the scalar transformation of \(b\) and the Tate \((-1)\) factor cancel this. Treating \(b\) as Galois-fixed would incorrectly suggest a defect. Differentiating the actual Kummer action gives \(\nabla_\tau|_H=-\pi b\phi_H\), in agreement with pp. 51 and 60.

The remaining constant in Theorem 7.13 can also be checked directly. Write \(\widetilde\lambda=E(u)P(u)/E(0)\) near \(u=\pi\), where \(P\) is a unit, and \(\mathfrak t=t/(p\widetilde\lambda)\). The logarithmic derivative of \(P\) contributes zero after applying \(\theta\), since \(\theta(t)=0\). Thus \[p\,\theta(u\widetilde\lambda'\mathfrak t)
 =\pi a\,\theta(t/E(u))
 =\pi a(\zeta_p-1)\lambda.                        \tag{3.4}\] Here \(\theta(t/\xi)=\zeta_p-1\) and \(\lambda=\theta(\xi/E(u))\). The normalized Sen operator is therefore \(-\phi_H/a\). This verifies the sign and scalar, while retaining the imported period-ring existence and analytic-vector results as dependencies.

Proposition 6.11 invokes the later Sen calculation, but the examined proof of Theorems 7.12–7.13 uses the earlier explicit action, rather than the desired full faithfulness. No circular use was found in this dependency check. Full faithfulness then uniquely lifts the identity of the common Galois–Higgs realization between two framed constructions. Uniqueness supplies the triple-overlap cocycle before the étale stack descent on p. 55.
## Coverage and residual uncertainty

The principal read the complete extracted text, all 4,818 lines covering 65 PDF pages, and inspected the 41 source images enumerated in the evidence receipt. Reading text and parsing inventories are not represented as independent proofs of every assertion.

The main proof chain was followed through decompletion, the period-sheaf construction, local PD classification, perfect-prism comparison, global descent and the Sen comparison. The uniform annihilator/derived estimates in Sections 2–3, external Tate–Sen theorems, PD differential homotopies, and prismatic/analytic acyclicity inputs have not all been independently reproved. Lemma 2.21’s phrase finite étale covering could mean a finite covering family rather than a finite morphism; without settling the intended terminology and cited lemma, it is not elevated to an established Problem.

Their memoranda distinguish discovery, confirmation and unexamined dependencies. The principal evaluated the arguments and performed the actual image inspection, report authorship and compilation. The helpers are not independently authenticated Pro reviews or acceptance reviewers.

The publisher, arXiv and author pages were checked. The available same-version TeX was used as supplementary evidence. No separate correction or executable supplement for this exact paper was identified in that bounded search; absent code is not a mathematical defect. An author-page gap notice concerns a different earlier preprint, arXiv:2112.10140. This paper’s inspected reference [26] is arXiv:2311.07024; the older notice is not attributed to the present paper. Publisher-version comparison remains unavailable.
# Assessment

Six localized corrections are established, including a counterexample to the extra infinite-rank statement and explicit failures of printed formulas. Their scope and repairs are stated separately. No counterexample to the finite-rank principal correspondence has been established by this review; this is not a claim that every external dependency has been verified. The assessment is Minor revision. The delivery is an initial scientific review with `scientific_decision=pending` and `human_reviews=[]`.

report: Abstract: The assigned accepted author manuscript is reviewed through its lattice, planar-graph and four-manifold arguments. Five local correction groups are established: coordinate choices in the Hajós lemmas, graph statements with missing loop/bridge qualifications, two nonequivalent descriptions of an oriented cut, an incorrect reduced-diagram criterion, and a reversed positive-definite correction-term inequality. Each has an explicit small example and a bounded repair. The principal link classification is not refuted by these examples. The diagram-identification step in Proposition 5.1 and several imported topological inputs remain outside the completed verification. The assessment is Minor revision; scientific adjudication and human review remain pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Scientific initial review of
Alternating links, rational balls, and cube tilings
# Identity, version and mathematical scope

The authors are Joshua Evan Greene and Brendan Owens. The journal association is DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1580. The actual primary PDF is Glasgow repository item 303262, labelled Accepted Version, with manuscript date 11 May 2023 and deposit date 19 July 2023. Its first 35 PDF pages are the article and match the printed page numbers; PDF page 36 is the repository notice explicitly warning that the author version may differ from the published version. The repository records acceptance on 14 July 2023; EMS separately records submission on 16 December 2022, acceptance on 17 July 2023, and online publication on 27 January 2025. These source-specific dates are retained rather than reconciled by assumption.

The supplied arXiv:2212.06248v2 source archive is separately pinned to the revision uploaded 25 July 2023. Bounded passages were compared, but neither whole-document equivalence with the Glasgow PDF nor equivalence with the publisher Version of Record has been verified. All problems below are anchored in the actual Glasgow PDF.

The work is smooth. A \(\chi\)-slice link has nonzero determinant and bounds a properly embedded surface of Euler characteristic one with no closed components; orientability is not imposed. A \(\chi\)-ribbon surface has no index-two critical points. The standing link hypotheses are nonsplit and alternating. For the black Tait graph \(G(D)\), \[\Lambda(D)=\operatorname{Flow}(G(D)),\qquad
 \underline{\det}(\Lambda)=\frac{\det(\Lambda)}{4^{\operatorname{rk}\Lambda}}.
 \tag{1.1}\] Cubiquity requires every integral unit cube to meet the embedded lattice. Theorem 1 gives a necessary condition for a rational-ball filling. Its general converse remains Conjecture 2. Theorem 3 proves the equivalence with \(\chi\)-ribbonness under \(\underline{\det}(D)=\underline{\det}(L)=1\), while Theorem 4 concerns the stronger quasi-ribbon cobordism hypothesis, including surjectivity to \(H^2(Y_1;\mathbb Z)\). Theorem 7 has additional prime-diagram and normalized-determinant hypotheses. None of these is an assertion of the general slice–ribbon conjecture.
# Established problems

Problem 1 (Minor: Hajós coordinates and the last-column permutation).  Location. Lemma 2.4, pp. 9–10; Lemma 2.6 and its proof, p. 10. Compare Lemma 2.3 on p. 9 and the use in Proposition 4.1 on p. 20.

Lemma 2.4 asserts that the first nonzero entry of every vector of an arbitrary embedded 2-cube tiling lattice is even. This needs a specified Hajós coordinate order. The lattice \[\Lambda=\mathbb Z(1,2)+\mathbb Z(2,0)\subset\mathbb Z^2                 \tag{2.1}\] is the coordinate swap of the lattice with matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&0\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), hence is a 2-cube tiling lattice. Its vector \((1,2)\) has odd first entry. For a lattice already written \(\Lambda_H\), the intended parity proof is valid by lower triangularity.

There is a separate local error in the stated permutation in Lemma 2.6. Take \[H'=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad y=2e_1.\] The prescribed simultaneous transposition of the first and last rows and columns produces \[\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix},                 \tag{2.2}\] which is not a Hajós matrix. Instead, moving the first row and column to the end while preserving the relative order of the others gives \[\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\1&2&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}.                 \tag{2.3}\]

Impact and repair boundary. Specify \(\Lambda=\Lambda_H\) in Lemma 2.4, or explicitly choose coordinates first. In Lemma 2.6 move the pure column \(2e_i\) to the end by the stable permutation just described. The remaining principal submatrix stays lower triangular, and the new last row has permitted entries. If a sign change is needed for \(y\), reduce that last row modulo two by column operations afterwards. These repairs establish the intended last-column assertion; the examples refute the printed coordinate claim and the proposed operation, not the existence theorem.

Problem 2 (Minor: loops and bridges are missing from the graph qualifications).  Location. Definition of blocks and Proposition 3.2(a), p. 14; Proposition 3.3(a), p. 15; Proposition 3.8, p. 19; Lemma 4.3 proof and Theorem 4.4, pp. 23–24; algorithm, p. 25.

On p. 14, a 2-connected graph is explicitly loopless, and blocks are maximal induced 2-connected subgraphs. Proposition 3.2(a) nevertheless describes the full flow lattice of an arbitrary finite graph using only nontrivial such blocks. A graph with one vertex and one loop has \(\operatorname{Flow}(G)=\langle1\rangle\), but has no block under that definition. The universal condition that its blocks belong to the recursive class \(\mathcal G\) is vacuous, whereas its rank-one lattice has determinant one rather than four. It therefore also contradicts the unrestricted formulation of Theorem 4.4. The failure already occurs in its claimed one-edge base case.

Bridges cause the dual omission. For a graph consisting of one ordinary edge, the only block is declared trivial, but \[\operatorname{Cut}(G)=\mathbb Ze\ne0.                                \tag{2.4}\] Thus Proposition 3.3(a) cannot restrict to nontrivial blocks.

The \(d\)-invariant rigidity statement needs a related qualification. Let \(G\) be a triangle with an additional loop. It is connected and has no bridge, so is 2-edge-connected in the usual edge-deletion sense. Its flow lattice is \[\operatorname{Flow}(G)=\langle3\rangle\oplus\mathbb Z.\] The Euclidean factor has trivial discriminant group and \(d\)-invariant zero: its unique characteristic coset has minimum square one and rank one. Hence \[d_{\langle3\rangle\oplus\mathbb Z}\simeq d_{\langle3\rangle},
 \tag{2.5}\] but \(\langle3\rangle\) cannot be a stabilization of the rank-two lattice \(\operatorname{Flow}(G)\). This is an explicit boundary failure of Proposition 3.8 if loops are allowed.

Impact and repair boundary. State the needed loopless hypothesis for the rigidity and graph classification, or adopt a block convention that accounts for loops and rejects their norm-one flow factors. Include bridge \(\mathbb Z\)-summands in the cut decomposition. The general graph algorithm must reject loops before applying the recursive test. In Lemma 4.3(2), the claim that both factors are 2-connected blocks is unnecessary for the unrestricted case: the flow direct sum follows from their meeting at one vertex, even if the factors themselves have cut vertices.

These are local scope/convention repairs. A reduced alternating diagram has a loopless, bridgeless Tait graph. More generally a 2-cube tiling lattice has no norm-one vector, so its flow graph cannot contain a loop. The examples therefore do not disprove the intended reduced-link applications, and the full block convention should be repaired before transporting the statements to arbitrary diagrams.

Problem 3 (Minor: cut-lattice membership does not imply one directed bipartition cut).  Location. The two claimed equivalent descriptions of an oriented cut, p. 13; Proposition 3.3(b) and Lemma 3.4, pp. 15–16; cut reversal in Proposition 3.7, p. 18.

Consider the 4-cycle with vertices \(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3\) in cyclic order. Orient its edges as the two directed paths \(v_0\to v_1\to v_2\) and \(v_0\to v_3\to v_2\). Set the vertex potential to \(z=(2,1,0,1)\), using the convention of p. 16 that \((\partial^*z)\cdot(v,w)=z_v-z_w\). Then \[x=\partial^*z=(1,1,1,1)\in\operatorname{Cut}(G)                 \tag{2.6}\] in these oriented edge coordinates. It is the class of the entire oriented subgraph, and it is simple: for any integral decomposition \(x=y+w\), each coordinate satisfies \(y_iw_i=y_i(1-y_i)\le0\).

However this orientation is not \(E(A,V\setminus A)\) directed entirely out of one subset \(A\). The middle vertex \(v_1\) would have to be outside \(A\) because it receives the edge from \(v_0\), and inside \(A\) because it sends the edge to \(v_2\). This is impossible. The example is loopless and 2-connected, so removing graph degeneracies does not fix it.

Impact and repair boundary. If the first description, \([H]\in\operatorname{Cut}(G)\), is adopted as the definition, Proposition 3.3(b) is valid but the subsequent bipartition description is not equivalent. If the bipartition description is intended, Proposition 3.3(b) and the corresponding form of Lemma 3.4 are false. Use a simple cut-lattice vector, equivalently a compatible edge-disjoint union of directed cuts, throughout the latter arguments.

The acyclic-orientation conclusion in Proposition 3.7 has a direct repair. If an acyclic orientation \(O\) is reversed along such an \(H\) with \([H]\in\operatorname{Cut}(G)\), any directed cycle \(C\) in the result would satisfy \[[H]\cdot[C]=-\,|E(H)\cap E(C)|.\] Orthogonality to \(\operatorname{Flow}(G)\) makes this zero, so \(C\) uses no reversed edge and was already a directed cycle in \(O\), a contradiction. Thus the needed preservation of acyclicity survives the correction; no failure of the unique-short-characteristic argument is established.

Problem 4 (Minor: zero stabilization does not characterize reducedness).  Location. Introduction, p. 2, the assertion \(\Lambda(D')\simeq\Lambda(D)\oplus\mathbb Z^n\) with \(n=0\) if and only if \(D'\) is reduced. Compare the nugatory-crossing discussion and graph–diagram correspondence on p. 24.

Take \(D\) to be the crossing-free unknot and \(D'\) the one-crossing unknot whose black Tait graph is a single ordinary edge. This is the bridge-type nugatory crossing included among the recursive base diagrams in the paper. Then \[\Lambda(D)=0,\qquad \Lambda(D')=\operatorname{Flow}(\text{one edge})=0,
 \tag{2.7}\] so \(n=0\), although \(D'\) is not reduced.

Impact and repair boundary. Keep the valid stabilization statement and the implication that a reduced diagram has \(n=0\), but remove the converse. Bridge-type nugatory crossings do not affect the flow lattice; loop-type ones contribute norm-one factors. Thus \(n\) measures the latter contribution, not every failure of reducedness. The normalized-determinant equality in Theorem 3 excludes the loop contribution while allowing bridges, consistently with its recursive base diagrams. This does not refute Theorem 3.

Problem 5 (Minor: the positive-definite correction-term inequality is reversed).  Location. Section 6.1, p. 26, equation (1) and the final comparison with \(d_{\Lambda_X}\). Compare the minimum convention for \(d_\Lambda\), p. 19.

For a positive-definite filling the text prints \[d(Y,\mathfrak t)\ge\frac{c_1(\mathfrak s)^2-b_2(X)}4
 \quad\text{for every extension }\mathfrak s.      \tag{2.8}\] Take \(X=\mathbb{CP}^2\setminus\operatorname{int}B^4\) and \(Y=S^3\). The characteristic class \(3H\) is the first Chern class of a legitimate \(\operatorname{Spin}^c\) structure, \(H^2=1\), and its boundary structure is the unique one on \(S^3\). Thus \[d(S^3)=0,\qquad \frac{(3H)^2-1}{4}=2,             \tag{2.9}\] contradicting (2.8).

Impact and repair boundary. In the positive-definite convention used here the bound has direction \(\le\); the last paragraph must correspondingly read \(d(Y,\mathfrak t)\le d_{\Lambda_X}(\varphi(\mathfrak t))\). The equality condition defining a sharp extension is unchanged. The later cubiquity proof uses a sharp extension and the equality \(c_1^2=b_2\), not the erroneous inequality direction. The explicit example disproves the displayed universal bound, while leaving that equality argument available.
# Positive verification and proof dependencies
## Lattice and planar-graph mechanism

Proposition 2.1 is verified directly by translating the unit cube and choosing a representative of the coset \(-x+\Lambda\). Its finite set of \(2^n\) vertices supplies every coset, which forces full rank and \[[\mathbb Z^n:\Lambda]\le2^n,\qquad
 \det\Lambda=[\mathbb Z^n:\Lambda]^2\le4^n.               \tag{3.1}\] Equality makes the representatives unique. The associated half-open side-two cubes then give the tiling. The rank-zero case is the zero lattice, corresponding to a tree on the flow side; rank one at equality is \(\langle4\rangle\), corresponding to a 4-cycle.

In the Hajós induction, \(2e_i\) is primitive in the tiling lattice, since otherwise \(e_i\) would violate uniqueness in a unit cube. Orthogonal projection has kernel \(2\mathbb Ze_i\), so the index halves and the projected determinant is \(4^{n-1}\). This validates the reduction in Lemma 2.3, conditional on the cited Hajós theorem. A rank-two check is \[H=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\quad
 H^tH=\begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix},\quad
 \det(H^tH)=16.                                  \tag{3.2}\] A theta graph with path lengths \(2,2,3\) has these cycle pairings and \(2\cdot2+2\cdot3+2\cdot3=16\) spanning trees.

The irreducibility/rigidity calculation in Lemma 2.7 was checked in actual Hajós coordinates. The flow-lattice interpretation uses edge-disjoint decompositions of simple Eulerian subgraphs; sharing more than one vertex permits a new oriented cycle and prevents rigidity. In the planar argument, the pairwise-nesting and common-edge mechanism reduces an arbitrary 4-cycle to the decomposing configuration of Proposition 4.1. The overlap calculation gives inner product two with the last cycle; a conflicting overlap on both sides would produce an inner product at least three where the geometric intersection has only two edges. After correcting the coordinate permutation, no additional counterexample to this core step was established.

The composition deletes the two distinguished edges and introduces four new ones, so edge count rises by two. The flow rank is the sum of the factor ranks plus one. The lifted basis appends a last coordinate indicating whether a cycle used the distinguished edge, and the new cycle has square four. This is the block Hajós matrix construction in Lemma 4.3. The diagrammatic 0-handle/1-handle pair in Figure 3 has net Euler characteristic zero and supports the recursive \(\chi\)-ribbon construction. These are positive checks of the intended loopless classification, not an independent proof of the external Hajós or flyping theorems.
## Cobordism and rational-ball mechanism

For a cubiquitous embedding \(\Lambda_2\subset\Lambda_1\oplus\mathbb Z^n\) of index \(I\), determinant and rank give \[\underline{\det}(\Lambda_2)=\left(\frac I{2^n}\right)^2\underline{\det}(\Lambda_1).
 \tag{3.3}\] Equal normalized determinants imply \(I=2^n\), justifying the unique-point property \((\star)\) and the block-basis construction of Proposition 5.1.

The extension argument in Lemma 6.3 uses the actual quasi-ribbon surjectivity hypothesis: extend the incoming \(\operatorname{Spin}^c\) structure across the cobordism, choose a sharp outgoing extension, and glue. Rational homology cobordism preserves the appropriate correction term. The proof of Theorem 4 then uses an acyclic orientation to select a unique short characteristic vector in the graph factor. Within that characteristic coset, all short extensions differ only in the \(\{\pm1\}^n\) Euclidean coordinates, and translating by \((-1,\ldots,-1)\) and dividing by two gives the required \(\{0,1\}^n\) representatives. The corrected cut-reversal argument in Problem 3 preserves this step.

Lemma 7.2 also admits a direct homological check. Its stated handle decomposition has two 0-handles, \(n+1\) 1-handles and \(n\) 2-handles, giving \(\chi(W)=1\) and \(H_3(W;\mathbb Q)=0\). Since \(\partial W\) is a rational homology sphere, \[H_3(W;\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H_3(W,\partial W;\mathbb Q)
 \longrightarrow H_2(\partial W;\mathbb Q)\] forces the middle group to vanish. Duality gives \(b_1(W)=0\), and Euler characteristic then gives \(b_2(W)=0\). Connectedness and the handle indices give the claimed ribbon rational ball. The inverse braid words and the two band moves in Figure 7 are consistent with the displayed three-component unlink. Mutation preserves the double cover; this argument does not assert that the original link itself is \(\chi\)-slice. Proposition 7.1 expressly provides counterevidence to that stronger inference.
# Coverage, unresolved points and assessment

The principal read all 1,506 lines of the supplied text extraction and actually inspected all 36 PDF page images, including the eight numbered figures and the repository notice. Textual reading, inventory verification and visual inspection are separately recorded. They are not independent acceptance reviewers or independently authenticated Pro backends. The principal evaluated the evidence, wrote this report, executed the actual compiler, and inspected every final report page.

A specific unresolved point is retained in Proposition 5.1 (pp. 25–26). Its written induction discusses \(n=1\) and \(n>1\), without an explicit \(n=0\) case. At \(n=0\), cubiquity gives equality of the embedded lattices. At \(n=1\), the truncated Hajós matrix agrees with the initial one. The further identification with the specified diagram \(D_1\), rather than merely its flow lattice, needs a precise justification. General flow-lattice isometry does not by itself settle the planar diagram. This review has neither completed a uniqueness result within the recursive family nor verified a concrete pair that refutes Theorem 7. It is therefore a stated verification limit, not a fabricated counterexample or a completed certification of that theorem.

The cited Donaldson, Floer sharpness, lattice rigidity, flyping and branched-cover foundations have not all been independently reproved. Figure 8 was actually inspected, but every Kirby blow-down and framing update in its two large diagrams has not been independently reconstructed; the claimed census through twelve crossings was not rerun. The broad converse and expansion statements are labelled conjectures in the paper and remain so in this review.

Publisher, repository and arXiv metadata were checked, and a bounded correction/supplement search was performed. No separate correction or executable supplement for this exact version was identified. The available arXiv TeX was inspected only in stated portions, never executed or compiled. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect. The publisher PDF was not available as the reviewed input.

The established correction groups are assessed as Minor revision, with exact counterexamples to their printed local formulations and explicit repair boundaries. They do not establish that the principal link classification is false. The remaining limits, especially the diagram-identification step, preclude whole-proof certification. This is an initial review with `scientific_decision=pending` and `human_reviews=[]`.

If an acyclic orientation \(O\) is reversed along such an \(H\) with \([H]\in\operatorname{Cut}(G)\), any directed cycle \(C\) in the result would satisfy \[[H]\cdot[C]=-\,|E(H)\cap E(C)|.\] Orthogonality to \(\operatorname{Flow}(G)\) makes this zero, so \(C\) uses no reversed edge and was already a directed cycle in \(O\), a contradiction. Thus the needed preservation of acyclicity survives the correction; no failure of the unique-short-characteristic argument is established.
result: Impact: The claimed equivalence of definitions is false even for a loopless two-connected graph. Subsequent statements must specify the broad cut-lattice meaning.

report: Abstract: The assigned arXiv v1 is reviewed through its arithmetic characterization, distribution argument and conditional linearity proofs. Six local correction groups concern quotient conventions, the minimal abelian factor, the square-tiled terminology, a projection asserted to be an isomorphism, and two stages of the linearity argument. Explicit examples and bounded repairs are supplied. In particular, a weaker dimension inequality preserves the distribution contradiction without the asserted isomorphism. Later published nonlinear examples contradict Conjecture 2.7, rather than the conditional linearity theorems. The assessment is Minor revision for this exact author version. External foundational results are not all independently reproved, and scientific adjudication and human review remain pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Scientific initial review of
Abelian differentials and their periods:
The bi-algebraic point of view
# Identity, version and scope

The authors are Bruno Klingler and Leonardo A. Lerer. The journal association is DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1581. The actual reviewed input is the 28-page arXiv:2202.06031v1, uploaded on 12 February 2022; its PDF and printed page numbers agree. EMS records submission on 22 December 2022, acceptance on 26 February 2024 and online-first publication on 3 January 2025. The publisher PDF is subscription-restricted and was not the reviewed input. The separately supplied author-hosted Ax-AbelianDifferentialsv8.pdf has different bytes and no explicit version declaration. Its file creation metadata is not an acceptance date. Neither its equivalence with v1 nor equivalence of either author file with the Version of Record has been established.

The arithmetic condition uses \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\), not \(\mathbb Q\): both the algebraic differential up to scaling and its projective relative-period vector must be algebraic. The distinction is essential. For genus at least two and \(n\) zeros, the relative-cohomology rank is \(2g+n-1\), whereas the projectivized stratum has dimension \(2g+n-2\). The level structure and the finite cover labeling zeros must be respected when using local systems.

Theorem 2.2 involves the smallest abelian quotient \(A_{[\omega]}\) carrying the differential, its isotypic CM property, a central-CM-field eigenline, and torsion differences between images of zeros. Theorem 2.6 is a nondensity statement for invariant linear loci with the specified rank and field degree; it does not assert nondensity in every stratum. Theorem 2.8 concerns curves satisfying \((\star)\), while Theorem 2.9 concerns subvarieties in isoperiodic leaves. The constant-part case in which the projective differential varies is expressly left outside those two arguments. Conjecture 2.7 is therefore a separate assertion.
# Established local problems
Problem 1 (Minor: the quotient and projective-dimension conventions need correction).  Location. Section 1.2.2, p. 3; Section 3.5(i), p. 9; compare Section 6.1, p. 20.

The foliation on \(S_\alpha\) is described on p. 3 as having codimension \(2g\). In period coordinates it is given by \[\mathbb P V_\alpha\dashrightarrow\mathbb P V_\alpha^p,
 \qquad \dim\mathbb P V_\alpha^p=2g-1.\] The map is a submersion where the pure component is nonzero. Consequently the codimension is \(2g-1\) on \(S_\alpha\), and \(2g\) on \(H_\alpha\). For example, the minimal genus-two stratum \(S_2\) has dimension three and zero-dimensional isoperiodic leaves; codimension four is impossible. Likewise, a projective chart on an \(m\)-dimensional manifold requires \(\operatorname{rank}V_\mathbb Z=m+1\), not \(m\) as printed on p. 9.

There is also an omitted quotient in the Hurwitz-space discussion. With the stated meaning of covers to a fixed elliptic target, fix \(f:C\to E\) with \(g(C)\ge2\). The family \(t_a\circ f\), \(a\in E\), consists generically of distinct covers, since \(\operatorname{Aut}(C)\) is finite. Yet \[(t_a\circ f)^*\omega_E=f^*\omega_E\] for every \(a\). Thus the displayed map to projectivized differentials has a positive-dimensional fiber and cannot be an immersion.

Impact and repair boundary. Distinguish the two foliations and correct the projective rank. Define the Hurwitz space modulo target translations, or explicitly work with its image and an appropriate normalization; the unquotiented immersion assertion must be removed. These corrections preserve the intended isoperiodic image. The genus-one case should also be stated separately: the formulas \(4g-4\) and \(2g+n-2\) on p. 7, with positive zero orders and hence \(n=0\) at \(g=1\), do not describe the one-dimensional modular curve \(S_0\) used later. The elliptic case already has its own argument on pp. 12 and 14.
Problem 2 (Minor: the smallest factor is replaced by an entire isotypic block).  Location. Definition 2.1, p. 4; the identification \(A_{[\omega]}:=A_\nu^{k_\nu}\) in the proof of Theorem 2.2, p. 13.

Consider the smooth genus-two curve and elliptic curve \[C:\ y^2=x^6-1,\qquad E:\ Y^2=X^3-1.\] There are two maps, extending over the smooth projective models, \[f(x,y)=(x^2,y),\qquad
 h(x,y)=(x^{-2},iy/x^3).\] Their differential pullbacks are \[f^*(dX/Y)=2x\,dx/y,\qquad h^*(dX/Y)=2i\,dx/y.
 \tag{2.1}\] They are independent, so the induced map \(\operatorname{Jac}(C)\to E^2\) is an isogeny. For \(\omega=2x\,dx/y\), however, the minimal factor is \(A_{[\omega]}\sim E\), of dimension one. The full nonzero isotypic block of \(\operatorname{Jac}(C)\) is \(E^2\), of dimension two. The printed identification is therefore false.

Impact and repair boundary. Decompose the minimal quotient \(A_{[\omega]}\) itself, or retain the distinction between that quotient and the larger ambient isotypic block. Minimality, together with the period argument, then gives the required isotypy. The degree must remain the dimension of the minimal quotient. This example satisfies the intended CM characterization; it contradicts the intermediate identification, not Theorem 2.2.
Problem 3 (Minor: general CM elliptic covers are not all square-tiled in the stated sense).  Location. Remark 5.1(1) and the final paragraph of Section 5.1, pp. 15–16.

Use \(C,E,f,\omega\) from Problem 2. The degree-two map \(f\) ramifies only at the two points with \(x=0\); their images \((0,\pm i)\) on \(E\) are nonzero three-torsion points. Indeed the tangent lines \(Y=\pm i\) meet \(E\) to order three there. Hence the construction of Section 5.1 gives an arithmetic point of degree one.

It cannot, even after complex rescaling, have all its periods in \(\mathbb Q(i)\), as required by Remark 5.1(1). The rational span of its absolute periods is \(\Omega K\), where \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})\): the image of \(f_*H_1(C,\mathbb Z)\) has finite index in \(H_1(E,\mathbb Z)\). If a rescaling put this two-dimensional rational space inside \(\mathbb Q(i)\), it would equal \(\mathbb Q(i)\). The ratio of two independent periods would then force \[\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})=\mathbb Q(i),\] which is impossible.

Impact and repair boundary. Composing with \([N]:E\to E\) does collapse the finite torsion branch locus to the origin, and multiplies the differential by \(N\). It does not change the CM field or turn \(E\) into a square torus. Replace the last claim by the correct statement about covers of the same CM elliptic curve branched over one point; restrict to the \(\mathbb Q(i)\) case when using the stated square-tiled terminology. The density proof using \(\mathbb Q(i)\) remains valid, as does the degree-one arithmetic construction.
Problem 4 (Minor: Lemma 5.10 asserts an unnecessary isomorphism).  Location. Lemma 5.10, equations (5.9)–(5.12), p. 19.

The projection to the distinguished abelian factor need not recover the covering curve. A concrete test is the genus-two, three-square origami in \(H(2)\). Connected degree-three covers of a once-punctured torus with a three-cycle commutator are described by pairs \((h,v)\in S_3^2\), up to simultaneous conjugacy. There are exactly three classes, with cycle-order types \[A=(2,2),\qquad B=(2,3),\qquad C=(3,2).\] An independent finite enumeration found 18 pairs and these three conjugacy classes. The Nielsen operations \[S(h,v)=(v^{-1},h),\qquad T(h,v)=(h,vh)\] act as \(S=(BC)\) and \(T=(AB)\). They therefore belong to one Teichmüller curve and give a generically three-to-one map to the elliptic modular curve. Riemann–Hurwitz gives genus two and one zero of order two. Here \(k=d=1\), \(u=0\), \(n=1\), so the target in (5.8) is precisely the elliptic factor, without relative marked-point data.

This multiplicity is not automatically removed by the permitted level convention. For level five, \(T^5\) and \(ST^5S^{-1}\) lie in \(\Gamma(5)\) and still act transitively on the three classes. Adding level data to the genus-two curve refines a covering; it cannot identify these distinct generic differentials over the same elliptic data. The assertion of isomorphism is thus too strong. More generally, the claim that the whole mixed extension is recovered by the displayed projection needs an additional reconstruction argument; forgetting a complementary abelian factor does not supply one.
Problem 5 (Minor: the Ax–Schanuel iteration restricts the wrong inverse image).  Location. Proof of Proposition 6.3, p. 21, after the first application of Theorem 6.4.

From \(\sigma(Z)\subset a+B\), the proof infers that \(W=\operatorname{pr}^{-1}(V)\) is contained in a translate of \(L=\operatorname{Lie}B\). Only the lifted image of \(Z\) is so contained. The full inverse image \(W\) also contains all directions in \(\ker\operatorname{pr}\). Already for a point \(Z\), with \(r\ge2\), \(n=2\) and \(B=0\), this inverse image has dimension \(r-1\), whereas \(L=0\). The asserted containment does not follow even in this degenerate case allowed by the proposition.

Impact and repair boundary. Translate the lifted image into \(L\), and at the next stage use \[W_L=(\operatorname{pr}|_L)^{-1}(V)\subset L.\] If \(V\subsetneq\operatorname{pr}(L)\), then \(\dim W_L\le\dim L-1\). With \(N'=\dim L\) and \(s=\dim\overline{\sigma(Z)}\), the same computation gives \[\operatorname{codim}(\overline{\sigma(Z)}\times W_L)\ge N'-s+1,\quad
 \operatorname{codim}\Delta_B=N',\quad
 \operatorname{codim}U\le2N'-s.\] Ax–Schanuel again lowers the abelian dimension. Iteration ends with \(V\) equal to an affine image of a linear space. Bi-algebraicity supplies the required dimension equality between the original local image and its algebraic model. This fixes the written iteration without asserting a counterexample to Proposition 6.3 or Theorem 2.9.
Problem 6 (Minor: omitted hypotheses in the final linearity steps).  Location. Theorem 2.8, Step 2, p. 24; Lemma 6.7(2), p. 24; Proposition 6.9, pp. 25–26.

First, the existence of a dense orbit in \(\mathcal Y\) does not by itself imply that its linear span \(W\) is an irreducible representation. For instance, under \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) on \(\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C\), the affine plane \(\mathbb C^2\times\{1\}\) has a dense orbit and spans the reducible representation \(\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C\).

The actual argument has sufficient additional structure. Let \(K=\ker(W\to\mathcal Y^p)\subset W_0V_\alpha\). The connected semisimple group \(H'\) acts trivially on \(K\), since zero-label monodromy is finite. Complete reducibility gives \(W\simeq\mathcal Y^p\oplus K\). The orbit of a point \((v,k)\) with \(v\ne0\) is \((\mathcal Y^p\setminus\{0\})\times\{k\}\); its two-dimensional closure is all of the irreducible \(\mathcal Y\). Since \(\mathcal Y\) is a cone, \(k=0\). Since it spans \(W\), \(K=0\), proving the intended conclusion. These missing steps, rather than the false general inference, should be written.

Second, Lemma 6.7(2) uses \(\dim\widetilde{\mathrm{SO}}_{2n+1}\) although its parabolic belongs to \(\widetilde{\mathrm{SO}}_{2n}\). At \(n=3\), the printed difference is \(21-12=9\), whereas the claimed binomial value is three. The correct difference is \(15-12=3\). Use the even orthogonal group and consistently count projective highest-weight orbits in the preceding exclusions.

Third, the appeal to quasi-finiteness in Proposition 6.9 is made for the open set \(U\) of nonzero forms. Its period map forgetting scale has \(\mathbb C^*\)-fibers. Work on \(U/\mathbb C^*\), or use the direct genus-two monodromy argument: the cover labeling the two zeros, modulo scaling, is \(C\) minus its Weierstrass points. Moving one zero along a nonzero homology cycle \(c\) moves the other along its hyperelliptic conjugate, and changes a connecting relative path by \[\iota_*c-c=-2c\ne0.\] For generic \(\omega\), this yields the infinite period coset used on p. 26 and contradicts generic finiteness of a hypothetical two-dimensional algebraic graph.

Impact and repair boundary. Each correction supplies a local step using the existing hypotheses. The examples refute the printed inference or formula, while the repaired arguments preserve the stated conditional linearity and genus-two conclusions.
# Positive checks, later counterevidence and limits
## Arithmetic and distribution mechanisms

The CM eigenline criterion is compatible with the period decomposition: in the simple CM case, distinct embeddings have independent period lines, so an algebraic differential with a single projective algebraic period line must select one embedding. In an isotypic power the center, rather than a chosen individual copy, is the relevant action. The minimal quotient must be fixed first, as in Problem 2.

For the relative-period argument in Lemma 4.3, a relation between a relative period and a nonzero absolute period defines the algebraic hyperplane in \(\operatorname{Lie}(A\times A)\). The stated analytic subgroup theorem produces the requisite algebraic subgroup. In the simple case its nonzero first projection is an isogeny, yielding an endomorphism relation and then membership in the CM period \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\)-structure; the quoted torsion theorem finishes the implication. The full general-isotypic reduction and the imported transcendence theorems were not independently reproved. No false torsion conclusion was established. Conversely, torsion zero differences multiply relative paths into absolute cycles, so the CM eigenline condition supplies algebraic ratios of all relative periods.

The \(\mathbb Q(i)\)-coordinate density argument on pp. 14–15 has the correct local structure. Clearing denominators gives integration into a square torus; zeros map to the origin and the branched cover descends over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\). Projectivization removes the arbitrary complex normalization of the elliptic differential. Problem 3 changes the claimed exhaustive description, not this dense subset. For a finite cover \(f\), the rational cohomology pullback is injective and the minimal Hodge structure carrying \(f^*\omega\) is isomorphic to the original one; this supports the degree preservation in Lemma 5.2.

The example \(y^2=x^7-1\), \(\omega=x\,dx/y\), on p. 17 has divisor \((0,i)+(0,-i)+2\infty\). The function \(y-i\) has divisor \(7(0,i)-7\infty\), giving the stated torsion test. The CM simplicity and the non-Veech conclusion retain the cited external dependencies. For the exact-degree step in Theorem 2.6, the totally real field \(K_0\) acts on the minimal quotient carrying its eigendifferential. If that quotient has dimension \(a\), each real embedding of \(K_0\) gives a real summand of \(H_1\) preserved by the complex structure, so \(2a/d\) is even and \(d\mid a\). Together with \(a\le kd\), this gives \(a=d\) when \(k=1\), and \(a=kd\) under the higher-rank degree hypothesis. Arithmetic images and André–Oort then feed the special-locus dimension formula; the strict inequality in (2.2) verifies the final numerical obstruction for every \(d\ge2\), \(k\ge1\), \(u\ge0\).
## Conditional linearity

The pure-period model of a curve satisfying \((\star)\) is one-dimensional and has nontrivial semisimple monodromy action. Highest-weight orbit dimensions exclude all the stated weight-one representation types except the standard \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) case. For type \(A_n\), the projective orbit has dimension \(r(n+1-r)\); the spinor varieties have dimensions \(n(n+1)/2\) and \(n(n-1)/2\). For type \(C_n\) the projective orbit has dimension \(2n-1\); for the standard even-orthogonal highest-weight orbit it is \(2n-2\). The low-rank identifications must be treated before these counts. Multiple independent \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) factors or a nonzero trivial component would give an orbit too large for a curve. Problem 6 completes the passage from pure to relative periods.

For an isoperiodic algebraic locus the fixed-part theorem provides the constant abelian factor. The corrected Ax–Schanuel iteration makes its relative model affine, and the scaling cone over an affine fiber gives the projective linearity of Theorem 2.9. In genus two, the fixed factor is either elliptic, forcing projectively constant pure periods, or the entire abelian surface. Torelli then reduces the latter case to a fixed curve, where the relative-period monodromy in Problem 6 excludes bi-algebraicity.

The quartic \(Y^4=XZ(X-Z)(X-\lambda Z)\), \(\lambda\ne0,1\), in Section 6.4 is smooth of genus three. The vertical pencil has exactly the four stated total tangencies, each of intersection multiplicity four. The two-dimensional constant holomorphic part confines its projective periods to a line. This is consistent with the example and does not settle the unrestricted conjecture.
## Later evidence against the unrestricted conjecture

Deroin–Matheus [DM], Theorem 1 and pp. 1693–1696, give \[C_u:\ y^6=x(x-1)(x+1)(x-u),\qquad
 \omega_u=x^2dx/y^5,\qquad u
otin\{0,\pm1\}.\] This is a nonlinear bi-algebraic curve in the minimal genus-seven stratum. Finite monodromy supplies algebraicity. Their displayed Gauss–Manin calculation gives three independent vectors \(p_2,
abla p_2,
abla(6(1-u^2)
abla p_2)\). Recomputing its determinant gives \[- rac{35}{36(1-u^2)},\qquad
 \left.- rac{35}{36(1-u^2)}ight|_{u=2}= rac{35}{108}
e0.\] The principal checked this last value with exact rational arithmetic. These examples belong to the varying-differential fixed-part regime. They contradict Conjecture 2.7, not the \((\star)\) or isoperiodic theorems. A current account should cite this development. It postdates the reviewed February 2022 version; it is not evidence that the authors claimed a proved unrestricted theorem, nor evidence about uninspected changes in the 2025 publisher version.
## Coverage, attribution and assessment

The principal read all 1,737 lines of the supplied primary text extraction and inspected all 28 primary PDF pages. The 511-line extraction and all nine pages, including the cover, of the later Deroin–Matheus publisher PDF were also read and inspected. The principal evaluated and adopted the findings, wrote this report, ran the actual compiler, and inspected every final report page. The auxiliaries are not independent acceptance reviewers or independently authenticated Pro backends.

The exact finite \(S_3\) enumeration and rational determinant check were independently written review calculations. No author code or author TeX was executed. Same-version TeX passages were read only for source confirmation. The author-hosted alternative PDF was retained as a distinct input, without whole-version equivalence. A bounded publisher, arXiv, author-page and correction/supplement search identified the later nonlinear paper but no separate correction or executable supplement for this exact v1. Lack of code is not a mathematical defect.

The analytic subgroup, CM transcendence, André–Oort, full monodromy, Satake and fixed-part inputs remain external dependencies; reading the manuscript is not an independent reconstruction of all those results. Several auxiliary claims require the explicit corrections above, but the supplied repairs preserve the main routes within that dependency boundary. The assessment is Minor revision for this precise input, with six local problem groups and separately documented later counterevidence to a conjecture. This is an initial review with `scientific_decision=pending` and `human_reviews=[]`.

Replace the last claim by the correct statement about covers of the same CM elliptic curve branched over one point; restrict to the \(\mathbb Q(i)\) case when using the stated square-tiled terminology. The density proof using \(\mathbb Q(i)\) remains valid, as does the degree-one arithmetic construction.
