problems.title: Projection in Lemma5.10 need not be an isomorphism
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 5 Pdf pages: 18 Pdf pages: 19 Anchors: Lemma5.10 Anchors: (5.8)-(5.12)
claim: Recorded check: Projection in Lemma5.10 need not be an isomorphism
analysis: Location. Lemma 5.10, equations (5.9)–(5.12), p. 19.

The projection to the distinguished abelian factor need not recover the covering curve. A concrete test is the genus-two, three-square origami in \(H(2)\). Connected degree-three covers of a once-punctured torus with a three-cycle commutator are described by pairs \((h,v)\in S_3^2\), up to simultaneous conjugacy. There are exactly three classes, with cycle-order types \[A=(2,2),\qquad B=(2,3),\qquad C=(3,2).\] An independent finite enumeration found 18 pairs and these three conjugacy classes. The Nielsen operations \[S(h,v)=(v^{-1},h),\qquad T(h,v)=(h,vh)\] act as \(S=(BC)\) and \(T=(AB)\). They therefore belong to one Teichmüller curve and give a generically three-to-one map to the elliptic modular curve. Riemann–Hurwitz gives genus two and one zero of order two. Here \(k=d=1\), \(u=0\), \(n=1\), so the target in (5.8) is precisely the elliptic factor, without relative marked-point data.

This multiplicity is not automatically removed by the permitted level convention. For level five, \(T^5\) and \(ST^5S^{-1}\) lie in \(\Gamma(5)\) and still act transitively on the three classes. Adding level data to the genus-two curve refines a covering; it cannot identify these distinct generic differentials over the same elliptic data. The assertion of isomorphism is thus too strong. More generally, the claim that the whole mixed extension is recovered by the displayed projection needs an additional reconstruction argument; forgetting a complementary abelian factor does not supply one.
result: Impact: The literal isomorphism and automatic full-extension reconstruction are too strong; no theorem counterexample inferred.

problems.title: Ax-Schanuel iteration incorrectly contains the full inverse image in a smaller Lie space
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 20 Pdf pages: 21 Pdf pages: 22 Anchors: Proposition6.3 Anchors: Theorem6.4
claim: Recorded check: Ax-Schanuel iteration incorrectly contains the full inverse image in a smaller Lie space
analysis: Location. Proof of Proposition 6.3, p. 21, after the first application of Theorem 6.4.

From \(\sigma(Z)\subset a+B\), the proof infers that \(W=\operatorname{pr}^{-1}(V)\) is contained in a translate of \(L=\operatorname{Lie}B\). Only the lifted image of \(Z\) is so contained. The full inverse image \(W\) also contains all directions in \(\ker\operatorname{pr}\). Already for a point \(Z\), with \(r\ge2\), \(n=2\) and \(B=0\), this inverse image has dimension \(r-1\), whereas \(L=0\). The asserted containment does not follow even in this degenerate case allowed by the proposition.

Impact and repair boundary. Translate the lifted image into \(L\), and at the next stage use \[W_L=(\operatorname{pr}|_L)^{-1}(V)\subset L.\] If \(V\subsetneq\operatorname{pr}(L)\), then \(\dim W_L\le\dim L-1\). With \(N'=\dim L\) and \(s=\dim\overline{\sigma(Z)}\), the same computation gives \[\operatorname{codim}(\overline{\sigma(Z)}\times W_L)\ge N'-s+1,\quad
 \operatorname{codim}\Delta_B=N',\quad
 \operatorname{codim}U\le2N'-s.\] Ax–Schanuel again lowers the abelian dimension. Iteration ends with \(V\) equal to an affine image of a linear space. Bi-algebraicity supplies the required dimension equality between the original local image and its algebraic model. This fixes the written iteration without asserting a counterexample to Proposition 6.3 or Theorem 2.9.
result: Impact: The asserted intermediate containment is false; the dimension descent needs a restricted inverse image.

problems.title: Final linearity chain omits cone/kernel arguments and has two local normalization errors
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 8 Pdf pages: 22 Pdf pages: 23 Pdf pages: 24 Pdf pages: 25 Pdf pages: 26 Anchors: Theorem2.8 Step2 Anchors: Lemma6.7(2) Anchors: Proposition6.9
claim: Recorded check: Final linearity chain omits cone/kernel arguments and has two local normalization errors
analysis: Location. Theorem 2.8, Step 2, p. 24; Lemma 6.7(2), p. 24; Proposition 6.9, pp. 25–26.

First, the existence of a dense orbit in \(\mathcal Y\) does not by itself imply that its linear span \(W\) is an irreducible representation. For instance, under \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) on \(\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C\), the affine plane \(\mathbb C^2\times\{1\}\) has a dense orbit and spans the reducible representation \(\mathbb C^2\oplus\mathbb C\).

The actual argument has sufficient additional structure. Let \(K=\ker(W\to\mathcal Y^p)\subset W_0V_\alpha\). The connected semisimple group \(H'\) acts trivially on \(K\), since zero-label monodromy is finite. Complete reducibility gives \(W\simeq\mathcal Y^p\oplus K\). The orbit of a point \((v,k)\) with \(v\ne0\) is \((\mathcal Y^p\setminus\{0\})\times\{k\}\); its two-dimensional closure is all of the irreducible \(\mathcal Y\). Since \(\mathcal Y\) is a cone, \(k=0\). Since it spans \(W\), \(K=0\), proving the intended conclusion. These missing steps, rather than the false general inference, should be written.

Second, Lemma 6.7(2) uses \(\dim\widetilde{\mathrm{SO}}_{2n+1}\) although its parabolic belongs to \(\widetilde{\mathrm{SO}}_{2n}\). At \(n=3\), the printed difference is \(21-12=9\), whereas the claimed binomial value is three. The correct difference is \(15-12=3\). Use the even orthogonal group and consistently count projective highest-weight orbits in the preceding exclusions.

Third, the appeal to quasi-finiteness in Proposition 6.9 is made for the open set \(U\) of nonzero forms. Its period map forgetting scale has \(\mathbb C^*\)-fibers. Work on \(U/\mathbb C^*\), or use the direct genus-two monodromy argument: the cover labeling the two zeros, modulo scaling, is \(C\) minus its Weierstrass points. Moving one zero along a nonzero homology cycle \(c\) moves the other along its hyperelliptic conjugate, and changes a connecting relative path by \[\iota_*c-c=-2c\ne0.\] For generic \(\omega\), this yields the infinite period coset used on p. 26 and contradicts generic finiteness of a hypothetical two-dimensional algebraic graph.

Impact and repair boundary. Each correction supplies a local step using the existing hypotheses. The examples refute the printed inference or formula, while the repaired arguments preserve the stated conditional linearity and genus-two conclusions.
result: Impact: Three written intermediate steps require stated additional reasoning or corrections, with no demonstrated conditional main-theorem failure.

report: Abstract: The assigned arXiv v4 is examined through the two-bubble expansion and the compactness argument. The literal compactness statement of Theorem 1.2 is false without translations and dilations: a normalized minimizing sequence can be translated to have weak limit zero. This is a Major statement correction, even though compactness modulo these symmetries and the intended existence conclusion remain supported by a repair of the proof. A second Major issue concerns invalid limiting divisions in the balancing argument on the route to compactness; the explicit repair does not make that core proof gap peripheral. Four Minor groups concern the zero-function boundary and approximate identity, a dimension-dependent remainder, derivative constants, and an asymptotic spectral bound stated pointwise. Decisive examples and explicit repairs are given. The assessment is Major revision for this precise author version, with scientific adjudication and human review pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 26 October 2026

Title: Scientific review of
Stability for the Sobolev inequality:
Existence of a minimizer
# Identity, definitions and theorem scope

The author is Tobias König. The journal association is DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1582. The actual reviewed input is the 18-page author preprint arXiv:2211.14185v4, uploaded on 6 October 2023 and dated 5 October 2023 in the manuscript. The page numbers below are both PDF and printed page numbers. EMS records submission on 22 December 2022, acceptance on 30 September 2023, and online-first publication on 3 January 2025. The publisher PDF is subscription-restricted. No equivalence of the reviewed author file with the Version of Record has been established.

Put \[p=\frac{2d}{d-2s}>2,\qquad a=\frac{d-2s}{2}>0,\qquad
 H(f)=\|(-\Delta)^{s/2}f\|_2^2.\] The functional is \[\mathcal E(f)=\frac{H(f)-S_d\|f\|_p^2}{\operatorname{dist}(f,\mathcal M)^2},
 \qquad
 \mathcal M=\{c(a_0+|x-b_0|^2)^{-(d-2s)/2}:a_0>0,\ b_0\in\mathbb R^d,\ c\ne0\}.\] The different symbols \(a\) and \(a_0\) distinguish the exponent from the bubble parameter. The setting is real-valued functions; arbitrary complex phases or positivity of an eventual minimizer are not additional conclusions of the paper.

Theorem 1.1 asserts \(c_{\rm BE}(s)<2-2^{2/p}\) for every \(d\ge1\), \(0<s<d/2\). The existence argument uses in addition the strict spectral comparison \(c_{\rm BE}(s)<4s/(d+2s+2)\), cited from the author’s earlier paper, whose range is \(d\ge2\). Consequently no existence theorem in dimension one, endpoint statement at \(s=0,d/2\), explicit value of the best constant, or uniqueness of a minimizer follows here.
# Established problems and repair boundaries
Problem 1 (Major: Theorem 1.2 omits the noncompact symmetries).  Location. Theorem 1.2 and the preceding assertion on p. 4; the proof’s change of sequence at the bottom of p. 10 and top of p. 11.

The theorem states that every minimizing sequence with \(H(u_n)=1\) has a strongly convergent subsequence in \(\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)\). Its statement includes neither translations and dilations nor a centering condition. The proof, however, explicitly translates and rescales the sequence before extracting a nonzero weak limit. These are changes to the sequence, not subsequence extraction.

A counterexample to the literal statement does not require assuming that a minimizer already exists. Take any normalized minimizing sequence \(f_n\). Let \(\{\phi_j\}_{j\ge1}\) be a countable dense set in \(\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)\). For each fixed \(n,j\), \[\langle f_n(\,\cdot-y),\phi_j\rangle_{\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)}\longrightarrow0
 \quad\text{as }|y|\longrightarrow\infty.\] Indeed, the Fourier integrand \(\lvert\xi\rvert^{2s}\widehat f_n(\xi)\overline{\widehat\phi_j(\xi)}\) is integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz, so the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma applies. Choose \(y_n\) so that \[|\langle f_n(\,\cdot-y_n),\phi_j\rangle_{\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)}|\le n^{-1}
 \quad (j\le n),
 \qquad v_n=f_n(\,\cdot-y_n).\] Translation invariance gives \(H(v_n)=1\) and \(\mathcal E(v_n)=\mathcal E(f_n)\). Density of the test set and uniform boundedness imply \(v_n\rightharpoonup0\). Every subsequence has that same weak limit, whereas a strongly convergent subsequence would have a limit of norm one. Thus no such subsequence exists.

Impact and repair boundary. This contradicts a quantified conclusion of a main theorem. The required statement is that, after a subsequence, there are \(\lambda_n>0\) and \(x_n\in\mathbb R^d\) such that \[\lambda_n^{(d-2s)/2}u_n(\lambda_n\,\cdot+x_n)\longrightarrow u
 \quad\text{strongly in }\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d),\qquad H(u)=1,\quad \mathcal E(u)=c_{\rm BE}(s).\] The proof on pp. 10–15 is directed toward this corrected conclusion. Its use of \(L^p\) normalization can be converted back to energy normalization because the normalization factors have a positive limiting value. The existence conclusion is preserved by this repair, subject to the local proof corrections below and the cited compactness inputs. The Major classification concerns the false unqualified compactness assertion; it does not assert that the existence theorem is false or irreparable.
Problem 2 (Minor: the zero-function boundary and the approximate-identity proof).  Location. Definitions (1.2), (1.4)–(1.5), pp. 1,3; Lemma 2.2 and its last paragraph, pp. 6–7.

Because \(c=0\) is excluded from \(\mathcal M\), the stated domain \(\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)\setminus\mathcal M\) contains zero. At zero, the functional is \(0/0\). Also, \[\inf_{h\in\mathcal M}H(h)=0\] is not attained, contradicting the unconditional attainment assertion in Lemma 2.2. The supremum \(m(0)=0\) is attained by every normalized bubble; its corresponding coefficient is zero, and the resulting function is not in the stated \(\mathcal M\). The square-completion identity itself remains true as an identity of infima.

There is a separate error at the top of p. 7: the approximate-identity asymptotic has \(\lambda^{+(d-2s)/2}\), although p. 6 has the correct negative exponent. In fact, with \(K=B^{p-1}\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)\) and \(K_\lambda(x)=\lambda^dK(\lambda x)\), \[(f,B_{x,\lambda}^{p-1})=\lambda^{-a}(K_\lambda*f)(x).\] A positive power is already incompatible with the uniform Hölder bound \(\lvert(f,B_{x,\lambda}^{p-1})\rvert\le\|f\|_p\) at a point where the asserted leading coefficient is nonzero. The passage from continuous approximants to a pointwise asymptotic also needs an approximate-identity argument, rather than an unqualified exchange of the approximation and concentration limits.

Impact and repair boundary. Define \(\mathcal E\) on \(\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)\setminus(\mathcal M\cup\{0\})\), and restrict distance attainment to \(f\ne0\), or state an explicit convention using the closed cone \(\mathcal M\cup\{0\}\). For the needed positivity, no pointwise exchange is necessary: if \(m(f)=0\), then \(K_\lambda*f=0\) for every \(\lambda\); convergence in \(L^p\) to \((\int K)f\) implies \(f=0\). This proves \(m(f)>0\) for nonzero \(f\), and escape of bubble parameters then cannot maximize it. These corrections preserve the distance formula and all its uses for nonzero functions.

Problem 3 (Major: missing boundary cases in the balancing argument).  Location. Lemma 2.4, p. 7; the definitions of \(A,B,C,D\) and the limiting argument in Lemma 4.3, pp. 13–14; the quotient involving \(f\) before (4.14), p. 14.

The second strictness clause in Lemma 2.4 says that \(D<F\) alone makes \((A+C)/(B+D)>(A+E)/(B+F)\). Set \[A=B=C=D=1,\qquad E=F=2.\] Every hypothesis holds, including \(D<F\), but both displayed quotients and all three initial ratios equal one. This exact rational counterexample was also checked in an original calculation. The correct strictness condition is \[C/D>E/F
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 \bigl(D<F\ \text{and}\ A/B>C/D\bigr).\] The application on p. 13 does obtain the first condition, so this error alone does not invalidate that application.

The same passage needs two further corrections. First, \(B\) is printed as \(\lim[H(\widetilde g_n)-S_dm(\widetilde g_n)^2]\), whereas (2.3) and the immediately preceding denominator require \[B=\lim[H(\widetilde g_n)-S_dm(\widetilde g_n)].\] The quantity \(m\) is already a squared pairing. Second, being outside \(\mathcal M\) at every index does not make the limiting deficit and distance strictly positive: normalized perturbations of a bubble can have both limits zero. Thus \(A/B\) may be undefined. The separate treatment of a sequence lying exactly in \(\mathcal M\) does not address nonbubble sequences approaching it. In the reversed case, positivity of the energy alone does not justify a bounded rescaling to match the two \(m\)-values when the smaller one tends to zero. On p. 14 the weak limit \(f\) may itself be a bubble, again making the displayed quotient \(0/0\).

Severity and actual dependency. The unused strictness clause and the extra square in \(B\) are local errors. The limiting divisions are different: Lemma 4.3 supplies the balance of the two components used immediately in (4.14), and that estimate excludes residual mass in the proof of strong compactness and existence. Invoking strong convergence to exclude a bubble weak limit at this point would be circular. The written proof therefore has a Major gap in a core derivation. The examples diagnose the invalid inference, not a counterexample satisfying all hypotheses of the full minimizing-sequence argument. The repair below supports the intended conclusion without downgrading the original gap.

Impact and repair boundary. Work throughout with the continuous inequality \[H(v)-S_d\|v\|_p^2\ge c_{\rm BE}(s)\operatorname{dist}(v,\mathcal M)^2,\] which remains meaningful on a bubble. Write \(c=c_{\rm BE}(s)\). In the limiting notation of p. 13 it yields \(A\ge cB\) with \(A,B\ge0\). Since \(c(B+D)=A+C\), one gets \(C\le cD\). If the smaller component is enlarged so that \(F>D\) and \(E/F<C/D\), direct subtraction gives \[\begin{aligned}
 c(B+F)-(A+E)
 &=c(F-D)+C-E\\
 &>(F-D)(c-C/D)\ge0.
 \end{aligned}                                                    \tag{2.1}\] This is the desired strict decrease without dividing by \(A\) or \(B\).

The enlargement can be a fixed factor \(t>1\), sufficiently near one that the strict ordering of the two \(m\)-values is preserved. It need not continue all the way to equality. Strict increase of \[h(\eta)/\eta^2,\qquad h(\eta)=(1+\eta^p)^{2/p}-1,\] then supplies \(E/F<C/D\). This also avoids an unbounded scaling factor if the smaller limiting \(m\)-value is zero.

For completeness, in the reversed case the remainder cannot have vanishing \(L^p\) norm while retaining positive energy. If \(\|g_n\|_p\to0\), then \(m(g_n)\to0\). The splitting identities and the continuous stability inequality for \(f\) give \[\bigl[H(u_n)-S_d\|u_n\|_p^2\bigr]
 -c\,\operatorname{dist}(u_n,\mathcal M)^2
 \ge (1-c)H(g_n)+o(1).\] The left side tends to zero for a minimizing sequence, whereas the right side stays positive when \(H(g_n)\ge\delta>0\), because \(c<1\). Thus the remaining \(L^p\) mass is positive, and the fixed-factor comparison is strict. The same continuous inequality treats \(f\in\mathcal M\) when deriving (4.14). These steps repair the written limit argument and support its conclusion; they are not counterexamples to Lemma 4.3 or to existence.

Problem 4 (Minor: the quadratic remainder estimate misses two parameter regimes).  Location. Proof of Proposition 3.1(ii), p. 9, the display estimating \(\int_{B(0,\lambda^{-1/2})}B_\lambda^2B^{p-2}\).

Impact and repair boundary. Each line of (2.2) is still \(o(\lambda^{(d-2s)/2})\) for fixed \(0<s<d/2\). Replace the overly strong bound by the appropriate case, or prove just this common little-oh estimate. The first-order two-bubble expansion and its strictly negative correction remain intact over the stated parameter range. No uniform assertion as \(s\) approaches an endpoint is required.
Problem 5 (Minor: the exact derivative constants in Appendix A are incorrect).  Location. Lemma A.1, formula (A.1) and its derivation, pp. 15–16; use in (3.5), p. 10.

Retain \(a=(d-2s)/2\), and put \(b=(d+2s)/2\) and \(\omega_{d-1}=|\mathbb S^{d-1}|\). From definition (3.3), the actual normalized correlation is \[F(\mu)=c_d^p\omega_{d-1}\mu^b
 \int_0^\infty r^{d-1}(1+r^2)^{-a}(1+\mu^2r^2)^{-b}\,dr.\] Differentiating this expression, or using \(r^2/(1+r^2)\) with beta distribution of parameters \(d/2,d/2\), gives \[F'(1)=0,\qquad
 F''(1)=-\frac{ab}{d+1}
       =-\frac{d^2-4s^2}{4(d+1)}.\] Also, direct differentiation and dominated convergence, uniformly for \(\mu\) near one, give \[G_\lambda(\mu)=c_0\lambda^a\mu^{-a}+o(\lambda^a),
 \qquad G_\lambda'(1)=-a c_0\lambda^a+o(\lambda^a).\] Both constants printed in (A.1) are missing the common factor \(\omega_{d-1}b\). The intermediate differentiation formulas need correction as well: the radial surface measure and the derivative of \(\mu^b\) must be retained, and the coefficient inside the resulting bracket is \(1/a=2/(d-2s)\), rather than \(2/(d+2s)\).

An exact elementary case makes the discrepancy explicit. For \(d=3,s=1/2\), one has \(p=3\), \(c_d^3=4/\pi^2\), and \[F(\mu)=\frac{4\mu}{(1+\mu)^2},\qquad
 G_\lambda(\mu)=\frac{4\lambda\mu}{(\lambda+\mu)^2}.\] Hence \(F''(1)=-1/2\), \(c_0=4\), and \(G_\lambda'(1)=-4\lambda+o(\lambda)\). The printed constants are instead \(-1/(16\pi)\) and \(-1/(2\pi)\). The elementary radial integral and exact rational derivatives were independently checked; no author code was executed.

Impact and repair boundary. The actual constants still have the needed sign and size: \(F''(1)<0\) and \(G_\lambda'(1)=O(\lambda^a)\). Re-differentiating the correct normalized integral repairs the local maximum argument, including \(\mu(\lambda)-1=O(\lambda^a)\), and preserves Proposition 3.1(iii). The error concerns precise formulas, not an established failure of the two-bubble theorem.

Problem 6 (Minor: the spectral lower bound is asymptotic, not pointwise).  Location. Proof of Proposition 4.1, p. 11, the assertion \(\mathcal E(u_n)\ge4s/(d+2s+2)\) for sequences approaching \(\mathcal M\).

For the normalized sequences in question the needed statement is \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathcal E(u_n)\ge\kappa,
 \qquad \kappa=\frac{4s}{d+2s+2}.\] A pointwise inequality need not hold. The already cited earlier paper [sharp], Theorem 1 and pp. 3–5 of its arXiv v2, constructs perturbations \(U+\varepsilon\rho\) approaching a bubble with quotient strictly below \(\kappa\) for every sufficiently small positive \(\varepsilon\).

A concrete direction in the classical case \(d=3,s=1\) comes from the degree-two spherical harmonic \[v_2(\omega)=\omega_1\omega_2+\omega_2\omega_3+\omega_3\omega_1
 \quad\text{on }\mathbb S^3.\] Its cubic moment is \(6\int_{\mathbb S^3}\omega_1^2\omega_2^2\omega_3^2>0\). The corresponding normal perturbation has quotient \(\kappa-K\varepsilon+o(\varepsilon)\), \(K>0\). Dividing by its \(L^p\) norm preserves the quotient and gives the normalization used in Section 4, while the distance to \(\mathcal M\) tends to zero. Thus it also demonstrates the distinction within the relevant normalization.

Impact and repair boundary. Replace the pointwise assertion by the liminf bound. The strict comparison \(c_{\rm BE}(s)<\kappa\) then gives exactly the contradiction needed in Proposition 4.1. The underlying spectral and nearest-bubble inputs remain the stated external dependencies; a full independent reconstruction of those foundational results is not claimed.
# Positive checks and proof dependencies
## The two-bubble threshold.

The normalized bubble satisfies \(B^{p-1}\in L^1\), since its decay exponent is \(d+2s>d\); hence \(c_0>0\) is finite. The pairing identity from the Euler–Lagrange equation gives \[H(B+B_\lambda)=2S_d+2S_dc_0\lambda^a+o(\lambda^a).\] The inversion of radius \(\lambda^{-1/2}\) exchanges the two bubbles. Splitting the \(L^p\) integral at that radius, using the corrected remainder (2.2), yields \[\|B+B_\lambda\|_p^2
 =2^{2/p}+2^{2/p+1}c_0\lambda^a+o(\lambda^a).\] Positivity and radial decrease justify centering the maximizing comparison bubble at zero. The symmetry \(H_\lambda(\mu)=H_\lambda(\lambda/\mu)\) reduces scale optimization to \(\mu\ge\sqrt\lambda\). The estimates (3.4) keep maximizing scales in a compact interval away from zero; Hölder equality forces their limit to be one. Correct differentiation then gives \[m(B+B_\lambda)^{1/2}=1+c_0\lambda^a+o(\lambda^a).\] The first-order term in the distance cancels, so \[\operatorname{dist}(B+B_\lambda,\mathcal M)^2=S_d+o(\lambda^a),\qquad
 \mathcal E(B+B_\lambda)
 =2-2^{2/p}-(2^{2/p+1}-2)c_0\lambda^a+o(\lambda^a).\] The coefficient subtracted is strictly positive for every allowed \(p\). This verifies the mechanism of Theorem 1.1 after the stated local corrections, including dimension one.
## Splitting and exclusion of residual mass.

The energy identity follows from weak convergence in a Hilbert space. Local compactness followed by Brezis–Lieb gives the \(L^p\) mass identity after a subsequence. The maximum, rather than a sum, in Lemma 4.2 is essential and is supported by its two cases. A comparison bubble whose parameters remain compact pairs negligibly with \(g_n\rightharpoonup0\); a bubble whose parameters escape pairs negligibly with the fixed \(f\). Testing separately with optimizers for \(m(f)\) and \(m(g_n)\) gives the reverse inequality. This establishes \[m(f+g_n)=\max\{m(f),m(g_n)\}+o(1).\] The squared-pairing definition accommodates either sign of a component; no positivity assumption on a general minimizing sequence is needed.

With the corrected comparison in Problem 3, a nonvanishing remainder forces \(m(f)=m(g_n)+o(1)\). The larger \(L^p\) component may then be normalized to one, and the smaller has norm at most \(1+o(1)\). The continuous stability inequality for the larger component and strict increase of \(h(\eta)/\eta^2\) give the limiting form of (4.14), \[c_{\rm BE}(s)\ge
 1-\frac{S_d}{S(g_n)}(2^{2/p}-1)+o(1)
 \ge 2-2^{2/p}+o(1),\] because \(S(g_n)\ge S_d\). The positive gap in Theorem 1.1 excludes this possibility. A strong limit lies outside \(\mathcal M\) by the asymptotic spectral bound and its strict global comparison. These arguments support existence and compactness modulo translations and dilations, not the unqualified statement refuted in Problem 1.

The initial extraction of a nonzero profile uses the cited critical compactness theorem. The global fractional stability inequality, its local spectral expansion, and the compactness theorem are used as external inputs. The earlier strict spectral construction was read in its six-page arXiv v2 as a bounded dependency and counterevidence check; its cubic direction and dimension restriction were examined. Reading those six pages is not an independent proof of all their cited spectral or geometric results.

During the initial review, the principal read all 941 lines of the supplied primary text extraction and actually inspected all 18 primary PDF page images. analysis: Location. Theorem 1.2 and the preceding assertion on p. 4; the proof’s change of sequence at the bottom of p. 10 and top of p. 11.

The theorem states that every minimizing sequence with \(H(u_n)=1\) has a strongly convergent subsequence in \(\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)\). Its statement includes neither translations and dilations nor a centering condition. The proof, however, explicitly translates and rescales the sequence before extracting a nonzero weak limit. These are changes to the sequence, not subsequence extraction.

A counterexample to the literal statement does not require assuming that a minimizer already exists. Take any normalized minimizing sequence \(f_n\). Let \(\{\phi_j\}_{j\ge1}\) be a countable dense set in \(\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)\). For each fixed \(n,j\), \[\langle f_n(\,\cdot-y),\phi_j\rangle_{\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)}\longrightarrow0
 \quad\text{as }|y|\longrightarrow\infty.\] Indeed, the Fourier integrand \(\lvert\xi\rvert^{2s}\widehat f_n(\xi)\overline{\widehat\phi_j(\xi)}\) is integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz, so the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma applies. Choose \(y_n\) so that \[|\langle f_n(\,\cdot-y_n),\phi_j\rangle_{\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)}|\le n^{-1}
 \quad (j\le n),
 \qquad v_n=f_n(\,\cdot-y_n).\] Translation invariance gives \(H(v_n)=1\) and \(\mathcal E(v_n)=\mathcal E(f_n)\). Density of the test set and uniform boundedness imply \(v_n\rightharpoonup0\). Every subsequence has that same weak limit, whereas a strongly convergent subsequence would have a limit of norm one. Thus no such subsequence exists.

Impact and repair boundary. This contradicts a quantified conclusion of a main theorem. The required statement is that, after a subsequence, there are \(\lambda_n>0\) and \(x_n\in\mathbb R^d\) such that \[\lambda_n^{(d-2s)/2}u_n(\lambda_n\,\cdot+x_n)\longrightarrow u
 \quad\text{strongly in }\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d),\qquad H(u)=1,\quad \mathcal E(u)=c_{\rm BE}(s).\] The proof on pp. 10–15 is directed toward this corrected conclusion. Its use of \(L^p\) normalization can be converted back to energy normalization because the normalization factors have a positive limiting value. The existence conclusion is preserved by this repair, subject to the local proof corrections below and the cited compactness inputs. The Major classification concerns the false unqualified compactness assertion; it does not assert that the existence theorem is false or irreparable.
result: Impact: Refutes the literal quantified compactness assertion of a main theorem.

analysis: Location. Definitions (1.2), (1.4)–(1.5), pp. 1,3; Lemma 2.2 and its last paragraph, pp. 6–7.

Because \(c=0\) is excluded from \(\mathcal M\), the stated domain \(\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)\setminus\mathcal M\) contains zero. At zero, the functional is \(0/0\). Also, \[\inf_{h\in\mathcal M}H(h)=0\] is not attained, contradicting the unconditional attainment assertion in Lemma 2.2. The supremum \(m(0)=0\) is attained by every normalized bubble; its corresponding coefficient is zero, and the resulting function is not in the stated \(\mathcal M\). The square-completion identity itself remains true as an identity of infima.

There is a separate error at the top of p. 7: the approximate-identity asymptotic has \(\lambda^{+(d-2s)/2}\), although p. 6 has the correct negative exponent. In fact, with \(K=B^{p-1}\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)\) and \(K_\lambda(x)=\lambda^dK(\lambda x)\), \[(f,B_{x,\lambda}^{p-1})=\lambda^{-a}(K_\lambda*f)(x).\] A positive power is already incompatible with the uniform Hölder bound \(\lvert(f,B_{x,\lambda}^{p-1})\rvert\le\|f\|_p\) at a point where the asserted leading coefficient is nonzero. The passage from continuous approximants to a pointwise asymptotic also needs an approximate-identity argument, rather than an unqualified exchange of the approximation and concentration limits.

Impact and repair boundary. Define \(\mathcal E\) on \(\dot H^s(\mathbb R^d)\setminus(\mathcal M\cup\{0\})\), and restrict distance attainment to \(f\ne0\), or state an explicit convention using the closed cone \(\mathcal M\cup\{0\}\). For the needed positivity, no pointwise exchange is necessary: if \(m(f)=0\), then \(K_\lambda*f=0\) for every \(\lambda\); convergence in \(L^p\) to \((\int K)f\) implies \(f=0\). This proves \(m(f)>0\) for nonzero \(f\), and escape of bubble parameters then cannot maximize it. These corrections preserve the distance formula and all its uses for nonzero functions.
result: Impact: Incorrect domain/attainment boundary and local proof formula; nonzero distance identity remains valid.

analysis: Location. Lemma 2.4, p. 7; the definitions of \(A,B,C,D\) and the limiting argument in Lemma 4.3, pp. 13–14; the quotient involving \(f\) before (4.14), p. 14.

The second strictness clause in Lemma 2.4 says that \(D<F\) alone makes \((A+C)/(B+D)>(A+E)/(B+F)\). Set \[A=B=C=D=1,\qquad E=F=2.\] Every hypothesis holds, including \(D<F\), but both displayed quotients and all three initial ratios equal one. This exact rational counterexample was also checked in an original calculation. The correct strictness condition is \[C/D>E/F
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 \bigl(D<F\ \text{and}\ A/B>C/D\bigr).\] The application on p. 13 does obtain the first condition, so this error alone does not invalidate that application.

The same passage needs two further corrections. First, \(B\) is printed as \(\lim[H(\widetilde g_n)-S_dm(\widetilde g_n)^2]\), whereas (2.3) and the immediately preceding denominator require \[B=\lim[H(\widetilde g_n)-S_dm(\widetilde g_n)].\] The quantity \(m\) is already a squared pairing. Second, being outside \(\mathcal M\) at every index does not make the limiting deficit and distance strictly positive: normalized perturbations of a bubble can have both limits zero. Thus \(A/B\) may be undefined. The separate treatment of a sequence lying exactly in \(\mathcal M\) does not address nonbubble sequences approaching it. In the reversed case, positivity of the energy alone does not justify a bounded rescaling to match the two \(m\)-values when the smaller one tends to zero. On p. 14 the weak limit \(f\) may itself be a bubble, again making the displayed quotient \(0/0\).

Severity and actual dependency. The unused strictness clause and the extra square in \(B\) are local errors. The limiting divisions are different: Lemma 4.3 supplies the balance of the two components used immediately in (4.14), and that estimate excludes residual mass in the proof of strong compactness and existence. Invoking strong convergence to exclude a bubble weak limit at this point would be circular. The written proof therefore has a Major gap in a core derivation. The examples diagnose the invalid inference, not a counterexample satisfying all hypotheses of the full minimizing-sequence argument. The repair below supports the intended conclusion without downgrading the original gap.

Impact and repair boundary. Work throughout with the continuous inequality \[H(v)-S_d\|v\|_p^2\ge c_{\rm BE}(s)\operatorname{dist}(v,\mathcal M)^2,\] which remains meaningful on a bubble. Write \(c=c_{\rm BE}(s)\). In the limiting notation of p. 13 it yields \(A\ge cB\) with \(A,B\ge0\). Since \(c(B+D)=A+C\), one gets \(C\le cD\). If the smaller component is enlarged so that \(F>D\) and \(E/F<C/D\), direct subtraction gives \[\begin{aligned}
 c(B+F)-(A+E)
 &=c(F-D)+C-E\\
 &>(F-D)(c-C/D)\ge0.
 \end{aligned}                                                    \tag{2.1}\] This is the desired strict decrease without dividing by \(A\) or \(B\).

The enlargement can be a fixed factor \(t>1\), sufficiently near one that the strict ordering of the two \(m\)-values is preserved. It need not continue all the way to equality. Strict increase of \[h(\eta)/\eta^2,\qquad h(\eta)=(1+\eta^p)^{2/p}-1,\] then supplies \(E/F<C/D\). This also avoids an unbounded scaling factor if the smaller limiting \(m\)-value is zero.

For completeness, in the reversed case the remainder cannot have vanishing \(L^p\) norm while retaining positive energy. If \(\|g_n\|_p\to0\), then \(m(g_n)\to0\). The splitting identities and the continuous stability inequality for \(f\) give \[\bigl[H(u_n)-S_d\|u_n\|_p^2\bigr]
 -c\,\operatorname{dist}(u_n,\mathcal M)^2
 \ge (1-c)H(g_n)+o(1).\] The left side tends to zero for a minimizing sequence, whereas the right side stays positive when \(H(g_n)\ge\delta>0\), because \(c<1\). Thus the remaining \(L^p\) mass is positive, and the fixed-factor comparison is strict. The same continuous inequality treats \(f\in\mathcal M\) when deriving (4.14). These steps repair the written limit argument and support its conclusion; they are not counterexamples to Lemma 4.3 or to existence.

report: Abstract: This report examines the acquired author version of Shu and Wang’s generalized Erdős–Turán inequalities. An explicit bounded, even, lower-semicontinuous kernel satisfies every stated hypothesis of the energy stability theorem but has zero energy at a Dirac mass whose Wasserstein-infinity distance from the uniform measure is \(1/2\). A related construction disproves the stated \(L^\infty\) perturbation conclusion for arbitrary probability measures. These are two manifestations of one substantive issue: almost-everywhere kernel data do not determine energies of atomic measures. A separate local endpoint estimate in the multiplier proof requires a logarithm; the stated multiplier bound survives the repair. No counterexample to the principal Riesz-potential distance inequality is established. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Pointwise kernel values and atomic energies:
a technical verification report
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

The reviewed paper is Ruiwen Shu and Jiuya Wang, Generalized Erdős–Turán inequalities and stability of energy minimizers, arXiv:2110.03019v1, submitted 6 October 2021, 23 pages [paper]. Its associated journal record is Journal of the European Mathematical Society, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1583, published online on 3 January 2025 [journal]. This report concerns the exact acquired v1 PDF, not an established textual match to the subscription-restricted journal version. All page references below are one-based PDF pages; their printed numbers agree. The separately retained author-hosted PDF has not been substituted for this source.

The complete v1 text was read. Checks traced the transport characterization (Theorem 1.7), weighted Hall argument, regularized test-function construction, Fourier multiplier estimates, one-dimensional endpoint regimes, sharpness construction, and the energy applications. Particular attention was given to the quantification over all probability measures in \(\mathcal M(\mathbb T^d)\). External cited proofs and the particle simulation underlying Figure 1 were not independently reproduced. No article-specific executable code was found in the acquired source search; its absence is not a defect.
# Definitions and the affected proof chain

Equation reference: eq:energy, eq:h3, eq:spectral. The torus has normalized Lebesgue measure and its usual quotient metric. For an actual pointwise kernel \(W\), the paper defines \[
 \mathcal E_W[\rho]=\frac12\iint_{\mathbb T^d\times\mathbb T^d}
 W(x-y)\,d\rho(x)\,d\rho(y).\] The hypotheses on p. 4 require \(W\) to be integrable, even, lower semicontinuous and bounded below (H1), with zero mean and strictly positive nonzero Fourier coefficients (H2), and \[
 \frac1{|B(x;r)|}\int_{B(x;r)}(C_1+W(y))\,dy
 \le C(C_1+W(x))\] for some constants and every ball (H3). The additional lower bound is \(\widehat W(k)\ge c|k|^{-d+s}\), \(k\ne0\), with \(s<d\). Theorem 1.4 derives energy stability from the asserted identity \[
 \mathcal E_W[\rho]=\frac12\sum_{k\ne0}\widehat W(k)|\widehat\rho(k)|^2,\] which is equation (1.12) on p. 3. For \(d=1,s<0\), the conclusion is \(d_\infty(\rho,1)\lesssim \mathcal E_W[\rho]^{1/(2-s)}\). Theorem 1.6 on p. 5 then asserts the same control for any minimizer of \(\mathcal E_{\widetilde W}\), replacing the energy by \(\|W-\widetilde W\|_{L^\infty}\).
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Almost-everywhere kernel control does not control atomic energy).  The stated hypotheses do not justify [eq:spectral] (#eq:spectral) for arbitrary probability measures. Consequently Theorem 1.4(ii)(a) and the stated perturbation theorem admit explicit counterexamples in the reviewed version.
## A counterexample satisfying every energy-theorem hypothesis

Equation reference: eq:w. Take \(d=1,s=-1\), and let \[K(x)=2\pi^2\left(x^2-x+\frac16\right),\qquad 0\le x\le1,\] with periodic extension. It is continuous and even on \(\mathbb T\). Direct integration gives zero mean, and two integrations by parts give \(\widehat K(k)=k^{-2}\) for every nonzero integer \(k\). Moreover \[-\frac{\pi^2}{6}\le K(x)\le\frac{\pi^2}{3},
 \qquad K(0)=\frac{\pi^2}{3},\quad K(1/2)=-\frac{\pi^2}{6}.\] Define the actual pointwise function \[
 W(x)=K(x)\quad(x\ne0\text{ in }\mathbb T),\qquad W(0)=0.\] This bounded even function is lower semicontinuous: at zero its assigned value is below its limiting value, and elsewhere it is continuous. Thus (H1) holds. Changing one point leaves all Lebesgue Fourier coefficients unchanged, proving (H2) and the quantitative lower bound with \(c=1\).

For a fully explicit check of (H3), set \(C_1=1+\pi^2/6\) and \(C=1+\pi^2/2\). Pointwise, \[1\le C_1+W(x)\le C.\] Every ball average in [eq:h3] (#eq:h3) is therefore at most \(C\), whereas its right-hand side is at least \(C\). This verifies (H3) for all centers and radii, including the modified point. No unlisted regularity condition is needed.

Now take \(ho=\delta_0\), which is permitted by the definition of \(\mathcal M\) on p. 8. Equation [eq:energy] (#eq:energy) gives \[\mathcal E_W[\delta_0]= rac12W(0)=0,\qquad
 d_\infty(\delta_0,1)= rac12.\] The distance follows because the only coupling with first marginal \(\delta_0\) has the uniform second marginal, whose support reaches distance \(1/2\) from zero. Theorem 1.4(ii)(a) would require \[ rac12\le C\,0^{1/3}=0.\] The contradiction is independent of the implicit constant. The spectral expression instead equals \[ rac12\sum_{k
e0}k^{-2}= rac{\pi^2}{6},\] so the precise failed bridge is [eq:spectral] (#eq:spectral). The claim that the uniform measure minimizes this energy also fails: for \(
u=(\delta_0+\delta_{1/2})/2\), \[\mathcal E_W[
u]= rac14W(1/2)=- rac{\pi^2}{24}<0=\mathcal E_W[1].\]
## An independent failure of the perturbation estimate

Keep the unperturbed kernel equal to the continuous \(K\), and set \[\widetilde W(x)=K(x)\ (x\ne0),\qquad \widetilde W(0)=-\pi^2.\] This is again bounded, even and lower semicontinuous. In the usual Lebesgue meaning of \(L^\infty\), \(\|K-\widetilde W\|_{L^\infty}=0\). Since \(\widetilde W\ge-\pi^2\) pointwise, \(\mathcal E_{\widetilde W}[\rho]\ge-\pi^2/2\) for every probability measure, with equality at \(\delta_0\). Thus the measure in this counterexample is a genuine global minimizer, not an arbitrary competing measure. Theorem 1.6 would again bound its distance \(1/2\) by zero.

The uniform-measure comparison (1.18) remains valid. The decisive error is the use of the Lebesgue essential supremum in (1.19) against \(d\rho(x)d\rho(y)\): for the Dirac measure, the difference \(K(0)-\widetilde W(0)=4\pi^2/3\) is fully sampled. This failure persists even though the unperturbed kernel is canonical and continuous.
## Alternative readings, impact, and verified repair boundaries

No global convention in the read v1 text restricts \(\mathcal M\) to densities, forces general \(W\) to be continuous, or specifies a canonical pointwise representative. Atomic measures are explicitly used in Section 2. Reading \(L^\infty\) as a pointwise supremum would remove the second counterexample but does not remove [eq:w] (#eq:w), which already invalidates Theorem 1.4 without any perturbation norm.

This supports Major impact on the advertised energy applications: it disproves their stated guarantees within their quantified class. The main distance inequality in Theorem 1.1 and the canonical Riesz-kernel calculations do not depend on this invalid general energy identification. The examples do not challenge the numerical clustering pictures.

A precise restricted repair is available. If \(\rho=f\,dx\) with \(f\ge0\), \(\int f=1\), \(f\in L^2(\mathbb T^d)\), then \(W\in L^1\) gives absolute integrability of [eq:energy] (#eq:energy), by \(\||W|*f\|_2\le\|W\|_1\|f\|_2\). Parseval then proves [eq:spectral] (#eq:spectral); the original application of Theorem 1.1 yields Theorem 1.4 on this smaller measure class. If the perturbed minimizer is in this class and the uniform density remains an admissible competitor, the essential-supremum energy comparison is also valid. This proves a narrowed result, not the original assertion for atoms.

Alternatively, for a base kernel whose energy lower bound has been justified on all measures, imposing \(\widetilde W=W+V\) with \(|V(x)|\le\delta\) at every point gives \(|\mathcal E_{\widetilde W}[\rho]-\mathcal E_W[\rho]|\le\delta/2\). The minimizer comparison then gives \(\mathcal E_W[\rho]\le\delta\). This repairs the perturbation step only; the base kernel condition remains essential. No full repair for every singular kernel allowed by the original hypotheses is claimed.

Problem 2 (A missing logarithm in an intermediate multiplier estimate).  For the allowed parameter \(\beta=1\), the radial integral used in the last inequality of (3.26), p. 14, is not bounded by the displayed expression uniformly in \(|x|\).

Writing \(R=|x|>1\), the relevant nonnegative scalar integral is exactly \[\int_{R^{-1}<|\xi|\le1}|\xi|^{\beta-d-1}\,d\xi
 =|\mathbb S^{d-1}|\int_{R^{-1}}^1r^{\beta-2}\,dr.\] At \(\beta=1\) it equals \(|\mathbb S^{d-1}|\log R\), while the asserted bound is a constant multiple of \(R^{-(\beta-1)}+1=2\). This is a local invalid inequality in the proof, rather than a counterexample to Lemma 3.6.

Retaining the logarithm yields \(|u(x)|\le C R^{-d-1}(1+\log R)\) at this endpoint. It is still integrable at infinity. The periodization argument (3.27)–(3.28) therefore retains its \(L^1\) bound. The \(L^\infty\) bound follows directly from the absolutely summable Fourier coefficients and Schwartz decay: \[\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}|\widehat\psi(\epsilon k)|\,|k|
 \le C\epsilon^{-d-1}.\] Interpolation recovers exactly the bound of Lemma 3.6 at \(\beta=1\). The displayed decay estimate may admit a sharper proof, but the particular scalar-integral inequality in (3.26) cannot. The supported impact is Minor: the local derivation requires correction and the downstream multiplier estimate is restored without changing its statement.
# Other checked reasoning and remaining scope

The weighted transport argument accommodates irrational weights; a rational-weight approximation in \(d_\infty\) was not silently substituted. In Section 3 the crucial exponent is \[\frac{d-1}{d}-\frac1q=\frac1p-\frac1d\ge0
 \quad(1\le p\le d),\] and the regularized set and its complement contain balls at the relevant scale, yielding the stated \(r^{d+d/p-s}\) power. The one-dimensional Hilbert-transform step uses \(1<q<\infty\); the paper does not invoke its false \(L^1\) or \(L^\infty\) endpoint boundedness. The sharpness densities have zero perturbation mass and remain nonnegative; their moment cancellations give the asserted near- and far-field powers. These checks support the reported scope, not a formal verification of every cited theorem.

report: Abstract: The accepted manuscript of Gray and Kambites is examined through its Schützenberger-graph constructions and recursive-presentation arguments. The principal classification proofs can be followed within the dependencies stated in the paper. A precise boundary failure occurs in the idempotent specified for Theorem 5.3 when the finite set is empty: for a concrete two-element group its maximal subgroup is infinite, whereas the desired stabilizer has order two. This disproves the specified construction at that boundary, not the existential theorem. The nonempty-set construction and the principal applications survive. The supported finding is Minor; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Maximal subgroups of special inverse monoids:
a verification of the stabilizer construction
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is Robert D. Gray and Mark Kambites, Maximal subgroups of finitely presented special inverse monoids, the 25-page accepted manuscript in UEA repository record 94983 [paper]. Its filename identifies the accepted version of 18 April 2024. The internal PDF creation date, 11 October 2023, is a separate metadata field. The associated journal article is DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1585, published online on 7 January 2025 [journal]. The acquired arXiv v2 TeX, dated 26 April 2024, is retained separately and is not presumed identical to the accepted PDF or the journal version.

All 25 pages of the accepted PDF were read and visually inspected. Page references below are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed numbers. The checks cover definitions, quantifiers, the graph extension lemmas, the units construction, the nonempty finite-set stabilizer construction, recursive enumerability, the explicit infinitely generated example, and the finite-group application. The proofs of external results of Higman and Stephen, and the cited finite-generation theorem for units, were not independently re-proved from their original sources.
# Definitions and dependency chain

For an inverse monoid \(M\), the maximal subgroup at an idempotent \(e\) is its group \(\mathcal H\)-class \(H_e\). The group at \(1\) is the unit group \(U(M)\). These are distinct roles in the paper. An \(E\)-unitary inverse monoid has only idempotents in the kernel of its maximal group image; the paper uses the corresponding embedding of each Schützenberger graph into that group’s Cayley graph.

Theorem 4.1, pp. 10–15, characterizes the unit groups of finitely presented special inverse monoids as finitely generated recursively presented groups. The construction uses an embedding \(H\le G\), where \(G\) is finitely presented, and introduces \(p_i,z,d\). The maximum group image \(G*F(p_0,\ldots,p_k,z)\) proves that the \(G\)-Cayley graphs at \(p\)-vertices are genuinely embedded, rather than merely morphic images. The subgroup represented by \(zwz^{-1}\), \(w\in B^*\), is \(H\). The quotient to \(N\), followed by the bicyclic monoid, restricts the possible unit factors. The auxiliary graph \(\Omega\) then excludes the unwanted \(p_iap_i^{-1}\) factors by the absence of the required incoming \(a\)-edge. Only a morphism \(S\Gamma(1)\to\Omega\) is needed for that exclusion; an unproved isomorphism is not used.

Equation reference: eq:M. Theorem 5.3, pp. 16–20, starts from a group presentation \(G=\langle A\mid R\rangle\), a subgroup \(H\), and words \(B\) generating \(H\) as a monoid. It defines \[\begin{aligned}
 M=\operatorname{Inv}\langle A,y,z\mid {}&
 R,\ aa^{-1}=a^{-1}a=1\ (a\in A), \notag\\
 &zbz^{-1}zb^{-1}z^{-1}=1,\quad
 yby^{-1}yb^{-1}y^{-1}=1\ (b\in B)\rangle .
 \end{aligned}\] The maximum group image is \(G*F(y,z)\). The fundamental-idempotent relations preserve that group image. Lemma 3.5 consequently transfers \(E\)-unitarity from \(G*\operatorname{Inv}\langle y,z\rangle\) to \(M\); this is not an assertion that arbitrary quotients preserve \(E\)-unitarity.

Equation reference: eq:e. For a finite set \(X\subseteq G\), the proof specifies \[
 e_X=\prod_{x\in X}xz^{-1}zy^{-1}yx^{-1}\] and claims \(H_{e_X}\cong\operatorname{Stab}_G(XH)\). For nonempty \(X\), the vertices with both an incoming \(y\)-edge and an incoming \(z\)-edge identify the distinguished \(G\)-component. Its marked set is \(XH\). Lemma 3.1 extends its automorphisms uniquely; conversely the marked component forces every automorphism to arise this way.
# A verified local finding

Problem 1 (The empty-set idempotent does not realize the claimed stabilizer).  The statement of Theorem 5.3 on p. 16 permits every finite \(X\), including the empty set. The specific assertion about [eq:e] (#eq:e) on p. 17 and the final automorphism identification on p. 20 fail at this boundary.

Take \[G=H=C_2=\langle a\mid a^2=1\rangle,\qquad B=\{a\},\qquad X=\varnothing .\] All are allowed inputs to [eq:M] (#eq:M): \(G\) is finitely presented, \(H\) is finitely generated, and \(\{a\}\) is a monoid generating set for \(C_2\). The empty product in [eq:e] (#eq:e) is \(e_X=1\), whereas \[XH=\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{Stab}_G(XH)=G=C_2.\] In \(M\), \(a\) is a unit and \(a^{-1}=a\). Put \(u=yay^{-1}\). One defining relation in [eq:M] (#eq:M) is \[yay^{-1}ya^{-1}y^{-1}=1,\] so \(u^2=1\). Thus \(u\), and hence \(au\), is a unit of \(M\). Under the homomorphism to the maximum group image \(C_2*F(y,z)\), \[au\longmapsto ayay^{-1}.\] This is a cyclically reduced word of free-product syllable length four. For every positive integer \(n\), its \(n\)th power has syllable length \(4n\), and therefore is not the identity. Consequently \(au\) has infinite order in \(M\). In particular, \[|H_{e_X}|=|H_1|=|U(M)|=\infty
 \quad\hbox{but}\quad |\operatorname{Stab}_G(XH)|=2.\] This is an exact normal-form calculation, not a numerical experiment or a failure to locate a proof.

The logical cause is visible on pp. 18–20: preservation of an empty set of doubly marked vertices does not force preservation of a distinguished \(G\)-component. The extension direction alone supplies automorphisms from \(G\); it does not exclude the additional units just exhibited.
## Impact, counterevidence, and repair boundary

The example disproves the specified \(e_X\) construction, not the existential assertion that a suitable group \(\mathcal H\)-class exists somewhere in \(M\). Indeed, in this very example \(X=\{1\}\) in the nonempty construction gives a different idempotent realizing \(C_2\). This is decisive counterevidence to any stronger allegation that the whole theorem or the classification is false.

A verified restricted repair is to state and use the construction for nonempty finite \(X\). The nonempty marker restores the distinguished component argument. Theorem 5.4 uses \(\{1,t\}\); Corollary 5.8 can use \(\{1\}\); Corollary 5.12 uses a nonempty finite subgroup. Thus these applications do not require the failed empty-product case. If the original quantifier over all finite \(X\) is retained, a separate general argument realizing \(G=\operatorname{Stab}_G(\varnothing)\) in the same constructed monoid is still required. Such an argument has not been established here. The supported severity is Minor: a localized construction/proof boundary with a verified narrowing preserving the main applications. Author adoption and journal-final applicability are unknown.
# Additional checks and rejected apparent defects

The compressed prefix argument on p. 20 omits explicit mention of prefixes lying in \(G\). This need not be treated as a separate error: free-product normal forms provide the missing detail. Inside \(F=G*F(y,z)\), the relevant prefix monoid is \[P=\langle G,y,z,yHy^{-1},zHz^{-1}\rangle .\] For the homomorphism \(\phi:F\to\mathbb Z\), with \(\phi(G)=0\) and \(\phi(y)=\phi(z)=1\), its zero layer is \[P_0=L=G*(yHy^{-1})*(zHz^{-1}).\] If \(v\in G\) and \(vy^{-1}=xy^{-1}\ell\) for \(\ell\in L\), then \(\ell=yx^{-1}vy^{-1}\) lies in \(L\cap yGy^{-1}=yHy^{-1}\); hence \(v\in xH\). The alternative start \(xz^{-1}\) would require \(zx^{-1}vy^{-1}\in L\), excluded by reduced normal form. This explicitly accommodates the \(G\)-prefixes rather than incorrectly discarding them by the exponent map alone.

For Lemma 5.1, the two distinct cosets give an action into \(S_2\) with kernel \(K\cap tKt^{-1}\). If the cosets coincide, the stabilizer is directly \(K\), so no two-point action is needed. In Lemma 5.2 the HNN construction centralizing a recursively enumerable subgroup has an enumerable relation set. Britton’s lemma gives the intersection, and the stable-letter exponent excludes \(K\cap tKt\). The Higman embedding preserves both properties.

For Proposition 5.6, in \(F(a,b)\times\langle q\rangle\) the group \(U=\langle a,qb\rangle\) is the graph of the exponent homomorphism \(\operatorname{exp}_b\). Consequently \[\langle a,b\rangle\cap U=\ker(\operatorname{exp}_b)
 =\langle b^nab^{-n}:n\in\mathbb Z\rangle\] is free of infinite rank. This checks the claimed non-finite-generation mechanism without needing an undecidable membership computation. For Corollary 5.7, the equations \(vv^{-1}=e=v^{-1}v\) can be enumerated by positive derivations. Enumerating all resulting group relations supplies a recursive presentation; decidability is not asserted.

The parenthetical description of Higman’s universal group on p. 23 needs the recursive-presentation qualifier if phrased for finitely generated groups. The finite-group application only requires a finitely presented group containing every finite group. This scope clarification is recorded, without treating it as a second substantive problem. Questions 5.9–5.11 and 5.13 are explicitly questions, not unproved claims.

The subgroup represented by \(zwz^{-1}\), \(w\in B^*\), is \(H\). The quotient to \(N\), followed by the bicyclic monoid, restricts the possible unit factors. The auxiliary graph \(\Omega\) then excludes the unwanted \(p_iap_i^{-1}\) factors by the absence of the required incoming \(a\)-edge. Only a morphism \(S\Gamma(1)\to\Omega\) is needed for that exclusion; an unproved isomorphism is not used.

Equation reference: eq:M. Theorem 5.3, pp. 16–20, starts from a group presentation \(G=\langle A\mid R\rangle\), a subgroup \(H\), and words \(B\) generating \(H\) as a monoid. It defines \[\begin{aligned}
 M=\operatorname{Inv}\langle A,y,z\mid {}&
 R,\ aa^{-1}=a^{-1}a=1\ (a\in A), \notag\\
 &zbz^{-1}zb^{-1}z^{-1}=1,\quad
 yby^{-1}yb^{-1}y^{-1}=1\ (b\in B)\rangle .
 \end{aligned}\] The maximum group image is \(G*F(y,z)\). The fundamental-idempotent relations preserve that group image. Lemma 3.5 consequently transfers \(E\)-unitarity from \(G*\operatorname{Inv}\langle y,z\rangle\) to \(M\); this is not an assertion that arbitrary quotients preserve \(E\)-unitarity.

Equation reference: eq:e. For a finite set \(X\subseteq G\), the proof specifies \[
 e_X=\prod_{x\in X}xz^{-1}zy^{-1}yx^{-1}\] and claims \(H_{e_X}\cong\operatorname{Stab}_G(XH)\). For nonempty \(X\), the vertices with both an incoming \(y\)-edge and an incoming \(z\)-edge identify the distinguished \(G\)-component. Its marked set is \(XH\). Lemma 3.1 extends its automorphisms uniquely; conversely the marked component forces every automorphism to arise this way.

Recorded check: Empty product e=1, Stab_G(empty)=C2. a is a unit and a^-1=a. u=yay^-1 satisfies u²=1 from a defining relator. The unit au maps to the cyclically reduced word ay ay^-1 in C2*F(y,z); its nth power has free-product syllable length4n, so au has infinite order. H_1=U(M) is infinite.
G=H=C2=<a|a^2=1>, A={a}, B={a}, X=empty; satisfies finite presentation, finite generation and monoid-generating assumptions.
analysis: The statement of Theorem 5.3 on p. 16 permits every finite \(X\), including the empty set. The specific assertion about [eq:e] (#eq:e) on p. 17 and the final automorphism identification on p. 20 fail at this boundary.

Take \[G=H=C_2=\langle a\mid a^2=1\rangle,\qquad B=\{a\},\qquad X=\varnothing .\] All are allowed inputs to [eq:M] (#eq:M): \(G\) is finitely presented, \(H\) is finitely generated, and \(\{a\}\) is a monoid generating set for \(C_2\). The empty product in [eq:e] (#eq:e) is \(e_X=1\), whereas \[XH=\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{Stab}_G(XH)=G=C_2.\] In \(M\), \(a\) is a unit and \(a^{-1}=a\). Put \(u=yay^{-1}\). One defining relation in [eq:M] (#eq:M) is \[yay^{-1}ya^{-1}y^{-1}=1,\] so \(u^2=1\). Thus \(u\), and hence \(au\), is a unit of \(M\). Under the homomorphism to the maximum group image \(C_2*F(y,z)\), \[au\longmapsto ayay^{-1}.\] This is a cyclically reduced word of free-product syllable length four. For every positive integer \(n\), its \(n\)th power has syllable length \(4n\), and therefore is not the identity. Consequently \(au\) has infinite order in \(M\). In particular, \[|H_{e_X}|=|H_1|=|U(M)|=\infty
 \quad\hbox{but}\quad |\operatorname{Stab}_G(XH)|=2.\] This is an exact normal-form calculation, not a numerical experiment or a failure to locate a proof.

The logical cause is visible on pp. 18–20: preservation of an empty set of doubly marked vertices does not force preservation of a distinguished \(G\)-component. The extension direction alone supplies automorphisms from \(G\); it does not exclude the additional units just exhibited.

The example disproves the specified \(e_X\) construction, not the existential assertion that a suitable group \(\mathcal H\)-class exists somewhere in \(M\). Indeed, in this very example \(X=\{1\}\) in the nonempty construction gives a different idempotent realizing \(C_2\). This is decisive counterevidence to any stronger allegation that the whole theorem or the classification is false.

A verified restricted repair is to state and use the construction for nonempty finite \(X\). The nonempty marker restores the distinguished component argument. Theorem 5.4 uses \(\{1,t\}\); Corollary 5.8 can use \(\{1\}\); Corollary 5.12 uses a nonempty finite subgroup. Thus these applications do not require the failed empty-product case. If the original quantifier over all finite \(X\) is retained, a separate general argument realizing \(G=\operatorname{Stab}_G(\varnothing)\) in the same constructed monoid is still required. Such an argument has not been established here. The supported severity is Minor: a localized construction/proof boundary with a verified narrowing preserving the main applications. Author adoption and journal-final applicability are unknown.

report: Abstract: The 86-page accepted manuscript of Dartyge and Maynard is examined through its algebraic reduction, sieve parameters, and Type I/II estimates. A joint local-density calculation gives a counterexample to the constant in Lemma 9.5. The Type II argument also uses an invalid uniform lattice-index identification and an unsupported truncation of a minors gcd. These are Major issues in the presented proof, without a counterexample to the principal theorem. Two further Major proof defects concern the exponent saving and the prime reciprocal sum in the main Type I term. A Minor group concerns corrected discriminant identities and a restricted root-count boundary. Four Major groups and one Minor group are established. Explicit computations and the limits of the proposed repairs are given. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Local densities and lattice indices in the proof of large prime factors of quartic polynomial values
# Identity, scope, and proof structure

The reviewed work is Cécile Dartyge and James Maynard, On the largest prime factor of quartic polynomial values: the cyclic and dihedral cases, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1586. The scientific source is the 86-page Oxford Research Archive accepted author manuscript [paper], with repository acceptance date 12 October 2023 and deposit date 24 October 2023. The PDF’s internal creation date, 12 September 2023, is recorded separately. The journal page gives 31 January 2025 as publication date and restricts the journal PDF to subscribers [journal]. The acquired 84-page arXiv v1 of 7 December 2022 is a distinct version [arxiv]; neither its TeX nor its extracted text is treated as equivalent to the AAM.

During the initial review, the complete AAM text, including definitions, hypotheses, all proof sections, and references, was read. All source pages cited as decisive evidence below were also viewed as rendered images. The review checks the internal proof chain; it does not independently re-prove all results imported from the literature, in particular the full arguments of reference [14]. Source and report page receipts record exactly which images were viewed. All page numbers below refer to one-based AAM PDF pages, which match the printed numbers.

Theorem 1.1 (p. 3) asserts a positive-proportion lower bound \(P^+(P(n))\ge x^{1+c_P}\) on \(x<n\le2x\) for a monic irreducible quartic with Galois group \(C_4\) or \(D_4\). Lemma 3.1 and Propositions 3.2–3.3 (pp. 7–8) reduce this to \(S_0\gg1\) and \(S_1=o(X)\). Theorem 4.1 (pp. 9–11) is the central localized incomplete-norm-form estimate. Section 5 expresses a sextic auxiliary form as a quartic norm factor \(q_1\) times a quadratic factor \(q_2\); Sections 6–8 use its controlled factorization. Sections 9–11 supply the Type I/II estimates. The findings below distinguish failures of auxiliary assertions from failures of the final theorem.
# Joint local densities and the Type I constant

Problem 1 (Major: the constant in Lemma 9.5 is incorrect as stated).  Equation (9.3) and Lemma 9.4 are on p. 50; the Euler product (9.4) and Lemma 9.5 are on p. 51. The multiplicativity proved there assumes coprime norms. The ensuing product over individual prime ideals does not respect this restriction.

For an integral ideal \(\mathfrak d\), the definition is \[ho_v(\mathfrak d)=\mathrm N(\mathfrak d)^{-2}
 \#\{(a_1,a_2,a_3) mod\mathrm N(\mathfrak d):
 \mathfrak d\mid(a_1
u_1+a_2
u_2+a_3
u_3)\}.\] Take \(K=\mathbb Q(\zeta_5)\), \(v=(1,\zeta_5,\zeta_5^2,\zeta_5^3)\), \(m=1\), and \(I=\mathcal O_K\). These satisfy the stated quartic and basis hypotheses. At \(p=11\), the polynomial \(\Phi_5(T)=T^4+T^3+T^2+T+1\) has roots \(3,4,5,9\), and \((11)=\mathfrak p_1\mathfrak p_2\mathfrak p_3\mathfrak p_4\). Each degree-one factor has \(ho_v(\mathfrak p_i)=1\), whereas \[ho_v((11))=11,\] because divisibility by \((11)\) imposes divisibility of all three coefficients by 11. The normalization uses \(\mathrm N((11))=11^4\). This is not a counterexample to Lemma 9.4 itself: the norms of the four prime ideals are not coprime.

For a subset of \(k\) distinct roots, the simultaneous evaluation map on polynomials of degree at most two has rank \(\min(k,3)\). Direct enumeration of all \(11^3\) triples independently gives \[\begin{array}{c|rrrrr}
 k&0&1&2&3&4\\ \hline
 \text{solutions for each subset}&1331&121&11&1&1.
\end{array}\] Thus the actual squarefree Möbius local factor at \(s=1\) is \[A_p=1-\frac4p+\frac6{p^2}-\frac3{p^3},\] whereas independent multiplication over the four prime ideals gives \((1-p^{-1})^4\). At \(p=11\), these are respectively \(10010/14641\) and \(10000/14641\), with ratio \(1001/1000\).
## A global contradiction, not just a local mismatch
## Impact and repair boundary

Lemma 9.5 supplies the normalization for the approximation weights, and the same individual-prime-ideal separation appears in (10.17)–(10.20), pp. 64–66. This is a central proof dependency, so the supported severity is Major. The corrected joint local constant is explicit for \(m=1,I=\mathcal O_K\). A full repair must also establish the uniform formula for arbitrary \(m,I\), the associated \(h(J)\), and the Type I main term with the joint local factors. A multivariable local telescoping argument may retain the intended cancellation, but that complete repair is not proved here. Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 1.1 are not thereby disproved.
# The Type II lattice argument

Problem 2 (Major: restriction of congruences and a gcd truncation).  The proof of Lemma 11.7 on p. 76 identifies \(f_{\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2,p_1,p_2}=p_1p_2\) when \(p_1\ne p_2\). The justification proves nontriviality on the ambient four-dimensional space, not on the rank-two lattice to which the conditions are restricted. The preceding Lemmas 11.5–11.6, pp. 73–75, also use an invalid \(D_{\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2}\le B\) assertion.
## An exact restricted-index counterexample

Use \(K=\mathbb Q(\theta)\), \(\theta^4=-2\), with \(v=(1,\theta,\theta^2,\theta^3)\), and \(f(x)=x_1^2-5x_2^2\), \(D_f=20\). For \(b=(b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4)\), the fourth row of multiplication by \(b\) is \[T(b)=(b_4,b_3,b_2,b_1).\] Let \(p_1=41,p_2=61,s_1=13,s_2=26\), so \(s_i^2=5\bmod p_i\). The following explicit primitive pair was checked with integer arithmetic: \[\mathbf b_1=(250100001,1,0,0),\qquad
 \mathbf b_2=(250100367,-2501,3416,3294).\] Its norm residues modulo \(41,61\) are respectively \((3,3)\) and \((37,1)\); the two multiplication matrices are invertible modulo both primes. Writing \(M_i\) for these matrices, the two-row matrix \(T=(T(\mathbf b_1);T(\mathbf b_2))\) has rank two modulo each prime. The ranks after adjoining the relevant row \((1,s_i,0,0)M_i\) are \[\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &\operatorname{rank}T&\operatorname{rank}(T;(1,s_i,0,0)M_i)\\ \hline
 p_1=41&2&2\\
 p_2=61&2&3.
 \end{array}\] Since the rank-two row matrix has a unit minor at each prime, its integer kernel reduces onto the modular kernel. The first condition therefore has index one on \(\Lambda_{\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2}\), and the second has index 61. Hence the actual combined index is \[f_{\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2,41,61}=61\ne2501.\]

This phenomenon persists with growing primes. Choose distinct \(p_i\equiv1\pmod{20}\), put \(Q=p_1p_2\), take \(N\equiv1\pmod Q\), and let \(\mathbf b_1=(N,1,0,0)\). Choose \(\mathbf b_2=(M,-CQ,c_3,c_4)\), with fixed positive integer \(C\), so \[\mathbf b_2\equiv(-2,0,s_1,1+s_1)\pmod{p_1},\qquad
 \mathbf b_2\equiv(1,0,0,0)\pmod{p_2},\] \(M=N+O(Q)\), and \(c_3,c_4\in[Q,2Q)\). CRT permits these choices and, if needed, an additional condition \(\gcd(M,C)=1\); then the pair is primitive. The first new row equals \(T(\mathbf b_2)\bmod p_1\). Modulo \(p_2\), the original equations are \(a_3+a_4=a_4=0\), and the new one is \(a_1+s_2a_2=0\). Again the index is \(p_2\). The norm of \[-2+s\theta^2+(1+s)\theta^3
 =(s\theta^2+\theta^3)(1+\theta)\] is \(12(s^4+2)=324\bmod p_1\); thus the requisite norm coprimality holds.

The scale condition \(B\gg Q\) with a power margin follows from (4.11), since \(B=X^{S/4+o(1)}\), \(1<S<2\), and \(Q\le X^{2\tau'}\). The vectors approach the positive scalar direction, have norms \(N^4(1+O(Q/N))\), and can lie in a common permitted small box and a unit fundamental domain containing that direction. Choosing the sign \(-CQ\) also makes the real kernel compatible with positive first three product coordinates: \[a_4=-a_3/N,\qquad c_4a_1+c_3a_2=(CQ+M/N)a_3.\] Take \(C\) sufficiently large and \(a_2\asymp a_1/C\). The kernel equations give \(a_3\asymp a_1/C\) and \(a_4=-a_3/N\), so the \(\alpha\)-direction can also lie near the positive scalar ray. These observations exclude a mere fixed-small-prime or empty-real-region explanation for the local index error.

The calculation does not prove that the specific sieve weights \(g_{\mathbf b_1}g_{\mathbf b_2}\) are nonzero on this family, or that their total weighted contribution violates the final estimate. It refutes the uniform index assertion used to replace the summand. An exceptional-pair estimate or a different argument is required.
## The minors gcd need not be at most \(B\)

For the same power basis, take \[\mathbf b_1=(N,1,0,0),\qquad \mathbf b_2=(1,N-1,0,0),\qquad
 B=(N^4+2)^{1/4}.\] For \(N\ge7\), both norms \(N^4+2\) and \(1+2(N-1)^4\) lie in \([B^4,2B^4]\). Both vectors are primitive, but \[D_{\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2}=N(N-1)-1\asymp B^2.\] The common kernel is \(\mathbb Ze_1+\mathbb Ze_2\), of determinant one. At \(N=100\), \(D=9899\), and the vectors are nonproportional modulo 7. This directly invalidates the inference from individual primitivity to \(D\le B\) on p. 73. The ensuing sums truncate at \(d\le B\) on pp. 74–75 and again in the later reduction. For the example \(\|\mathbf b_1\wedge\mathbf b_2\|\asymp B^2\); the related determinant bound based on \(D\le B\) fails as well.

This is a counterexample to the intermediate geometric implication, not to the averaged bounds of Lemma 11.5 or 11.6. Membership of this second family in every particular fixed fundamental domain and in the full weight support is not asserted. A proof excluding or estimating \(D>B\) is still needed; simply extending the summation to \(B^2\) does not preserve the displayed error estimate. Together these issues leave the Type II proof incomplete as written.
# Further proof corrections

Problem 3 (Major: the exponent saving uses the wrong bound for \(q_{22}\)).  On p. 34, the bound for \(\theta_{22}\) is \((1+\alpha_0)/2-\theta_{21}\), but the second final condition substitutes \((1+\alpha_0)/4-\theta_{21}\).

The corrected condition is \[\theta_{21}>6\theta_0+10\alpha_0+
 512(2\eta_0+5\alpha_0/4).\] The p. 28 example has \(\alpha_0=10^{-5}\), \(\theta_{21}=0.001\); with \(\eta_0>\alpha_0\) its right side exceeds \(0.01674\). Thus that example cannot establish the required saving. A restricted, explicitly verified replacement is \[\alpha_0=10^{-7},\quad \theta_0=\tau_{ij}=10^{-10},
 \quad\eta_0=1.01\cdot10^{-7},\] with the original values \[(\theta_{11},\ldots,\theta_{16},\theta_{21})
 =(.1398,.1401,.1402,.21,.19,.1799,.001).\] Exact rational calculations verify (6.2)–(6.9), Lemma 7.1, the corrected three concluding conditions of Section 7, and the displayed condition of Lemma 8.1. The second corrected condition has margin \(0.0008315754\); (6.5) has margin \(4.94\cdot10^{-8}\). These positive margins allow the small epsilon losses in that calculation. This repair covers those explicit conditions, not every implicit choice later in the proof, and does not repair Problems 1–2.

Severity and actual dependency. The erroneous substitution is used on p. 34 to conclude \(S_1=o(X)\), the estimate required by Proposition 3.3. It therefore interrupts a core proof step, rather than merely misreporting an optional example. The explicit parameter repair is useful counterevidence to general infeasibility, but does not reduce the severity of the original derivation.
Problem 4 (Minor: the two representations of the discriminant factor).  Lemma 5.14 on p. 25 has an incorrect \(a_2^2\) coefficient and an incorrect representation in terms of \(q_2,q_3\).

An independent companion-matrix computation gives \(\Delta_{14}=-q_3h\), where \[\begin{aligned}
h={}&-4a_1^2+4c_3a_1a_2+(4c_2-3c_3^2)a_1a_3-c_3^2a_2^2\\
 &+(c_3^3-4c_1)a_2a_3+
 (-c_2c_3^2+4c_1c_3-4c_0)a_3^2\\
={}&-(c_3^2-4t_2)q_3-4q_2,\qquad
 t_2=(r_1+r_2)(r_3+r_4).\end{aligned}\] Thus \(-c_3a_2^2\) must be \(-c_3^2a_2^2\), and the last line of the printed identity must have the indicated sign and factor four. The exact symbolic differences are zero. Crucially, substitution of a root of \(q_1\) into this corrected \(h\) still gives the factorization (5.29). For odd primes satisfying the full coprimality and squarefreeness hypotheses of Lemma 5.16, the corrected formula retains the zero tests used there; the degenerate \(q_2\) branch is addressed separately below. This limits the impact of the displayed algebra error.

A related boundary deserves separate care. For the allowed \(D_4\) polynomial \(P(T)=T^4+2\), choose \(r_2=-r_1,r_3=ir_1,r_4=-r_3\). Then \(t_1=t_2=0\), contrary to Remark (ii) on p. 26. No subsequent division by \(t_1\) was found. More consequentially, \(c_3^2-4t_2=0\), so Lemma 5.16(ii) gives one \(B_{14}\) root at the \(q_2\)-primes, whereas the CRT calculation on p. 36 uniformly substitutes two. Increasing \(q_0\) cannot exclude divisors of zero. The accurate local factor uses \(\kappa_p\in\{1,2\}\) and \(1-\kappa_p/p\), which is at least \(1-2/p\). This suggests a lower-bound repair for the application, but the full weighted error analysis is not established here. No tuple satisfying every asymptotic condition of \(\mathcal J\) is claimed as a counterexample to the entire formula of Lemma 8.1.

Problem 5 (Major: normalization of the prime reciprocal sum in Type I).  The actual image of (10.22), p. 66, has \(\log(P_2/P_1)\). The corresponding main terms on pp. 59 and 61 carry the same expression.

Severity and actual dependency. The printed quantity is \((\tau'-\tau)\log X\), whereas the correct main term is bounded for fixed \(\tau,\tau'\). This is an error of asymptotic order in (10.22), propagated through Lemma 10.2 (p. 64), Proposition 9.13 (p. 59), and (9.28)–(9.30). The proof on pp. 59–60 explicitly derives Theorem 4.1 from Propositions 9.13 and 9.14. The already correct final logarithm is important counterevidence to a false final constant; it does not validate the printed Type I derivation. The core proof defect is Major even though partial summation identifies the necessary replacement.

There is also a finite-factor bookkeeping issue in (10.19)–(10.20): the ideals \(I\) in (9.20) exclude primes above \(m\). Formally writing \(r_e=\rho_v(\mathfrak P^e)/\mathrm N(\mathfrak P^e)\), \[h(\mathfrak P^e)=\frac{r_e-r_{e+1}}{1-r_1},\qquad
 1+\sum_{e\ge1}h(\mathfrak P^e)=\frac1{1-r_1}.\] Deleting factors above \(m\) cancels the earlier \(g((m'))\), since \(m'=mm_0\) and \(m_0\mid m^\infty\). This explains a possible cancellation of that finite factor, but it is only prime-local bookkeeping: Problem 1 prevents interpreting the formal calculation as a completed global repair.
# Counterevidence, remaining scope, and assessment

The general proof strategy is coherent at several important points. The quartic cofactor relation eliminates the \(a_0\)-dependence of the denominator; the factor \(q_1\) is represented as an incomplete quartic norm; the coprimality and squarefree hypotheses are used in the resultant argument. The corrected discriminant retains (5.29), and the smaller parameter package meets the explicit Section 7 constraints. The final scale requirements on p. 84, \[A<B^{3-\varepsilon},\qquad BP_2^2<A^{1-\varepsilon},\qquad
 P_2^{21}<B^{1-\varepsilon},\] are consistent with (4.10)–(4.11). These checks are counterevidence to an allegation of a general contradiction in the setup.
Item | Established result | Repair status
Problem 1 | Major; Lemma 9.5’s constant is refuted | Joint factors needed throughout Type I
Problem 2 | Major; uniform index and gcd implication fail | Exceptional-pair and large-gcd bounds remain
Problem 3 | Major; core exponent saving is unsupported | Replacement explicit inequalities verified
Problem 4 | Minor; discriminant displays are wrong | Correct identity and zero-test compatibility verified
Problem 5 | Major; Type I main-term order is wrong | Correct reciprocal-prime main term explicit

The revised assessment is Major, with four Major groups and one Minor group. This classification concerns substantive gaps in indispensable proof dependencies; it does not require that the paper be false or irreparable. No counterexample to the principal theorem is established, and no complete repair of the Type I/II argument is claimed. Scientific decision and adjudication remain pending, with no human reviews supplied.

Focused independent acceptance checked all five existing groups against the exact AAM, including the actual Type I/II dependencies and the limits of each counterexample. Problems 3 and 5 are raised from Minor to Major because their erroneous steps are used in core derivations; repairability is assessed separately. No new whole-paper initial review or independent proof of every imported result is claimed.

The bounded source search found no separate supplement or author code; absence of code is not a defect. The inspected current arXiv record lists only v1. No correction resolving these findings was identified on the checked primary records. Applicability to the subscription-only journal-final text remains unverified.

At \(p=11\), these are respectively \(10010/14641\) and \(10000/14641\), with ratio \(1001/1000\).

Lemma 9.5 supplies the normalization for the approximation weights, and the same individual-prime-ideal separation appears in (10.17)–(10.20), pp. 64–66. This is a central proof dependency, so the supported severity is Major. The corrected joint local constant is explicit for \(m=1,I=\mathcal O_K\). A full repair must also establish the uniform formula for arbitrary \(m,I\), the associated \(h(J)\), and the Type I main term with the joint local factors. A multivariable local telescoping argument may retain the intended cancellation, but that complete repair is not proved here. Theorem 4.1 and Theorem 1.1 are not thereby disproved.
result: Result: Strict counterexample to the constant of Lemma9.5, not to Lemma9.4 under its norm-coprime hypothesis.
