problems.title: TypeII restricted lattice index and minors-gcd truncation
problems.source_location: AAM pp70-71 lattice/index definitions; pp73-75 Lemmas11.5-11.6; p76 Lemma11.7 final paragraph; pp81-82 later d<=B truncation
claim: Recorded check: Norm residues(3,3),(37,1); row ranks T/augmented are2/2 at41,2/3 at61. Integer kernel reduces onto modular kernels via unit minors. Actual index61, not2501. General CRT family with p_i=1mod20,N=1modQ preserves index p2, primitivity and norm conditions at increasing scales. Separately b1=(N,1,0,0),b2=(1,N-1,0,0) has D=N(N-1)-1~B²,detLambda1, norms in[B⁴,2B⁴] forN>=7.
analysis: The proof of Lemma 11.7 on p. 76 identifies \(f_{\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2,p_1,p_2}=p_1p_2\) when \(p_1\ne p_2\). The justification proves nontriviality on the ambient four-dimensional space, not on the rank-two lattice to which the conditions are restricted. The preceding Lemmas 11.5–11.6, pp. 73–75, also use an invalid \(D_{\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2}\le B\) assertion.

Use \(K=\mathbb Q(\theta)\), \(\theta^4=-2\), with \(v=(1,\theta,\theta^2,\theta^3)\), and \(f(x)=x_1^2-5x_2^2\), \(D_f=20\). For \(b=(b_1,b_2,b_3,b_4)\), the fourth row of multiplication by \(b\) is \[T(b)=(b_4,b_3,b_2,b_1).\] Let \(p_1=41,p_2=61,s_1=13,s_2=26\), so \(s_i^2=5\bmod p_i\). The following explicit primitive pair was checked with integer arithmetic: \[\mathbf b_1=(250100001,1,0,0),\qquad
 \mathbf b_2=(250100367,-2501,3416,3294).\] Its norm residues modulo \(41,61\) are respectively \((3,3)\) and \((37,1)\); the two multiplication matrices are invertible modulo both primes. Writing \(M_i\) for these matrices, the two-row matrix \(T=(T(\mathbf b_1);T(\mathbf b_2))\) has rank two modulo each prime. The ranks after adjoining the relevant row \((1,s_i,0,0)M_i\) are \[\begin{array}{c|cc}
 &\operatorname{rank}T&\operatorname{rank}(T;(1,s_i,0,0)M_i)\\ \hline
 p_1=41&2&2\\
 p_2=61&2&3.
 \end{array}\] Since the rank-two row matrix has a unit minor at each prime, its integer kernel reduces onto the modular kernel. The first condition therefore has index one on \(\Lambda_{\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2}\), and the second has index 61. Hence the actual combined index is \[f_{\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2,41,61}=61\ne2501.\]

This phenomenon persists with growing primes. Choose distinct \(p_i\equiv1\pmod{20}\), put \(Q=p_1p_2\), take \(N\equiv1\pmod Q\), and let \(\mathbf b_1=(N,1,0,0)\). Choose \(\mathbf b_2=(M,-CQ,c_3,c_4)\), with fixed positive integer \(C\), so \[\mathbf b_2\equiv(-2,0,s_1,1+s_1)\pmod{p_1},\qquad
 \mathbf b_2\equiv(1,0,0,0)\pmod{p_2},\] \(M=N+O(Q)\), and \(c_3,c_4\in[Q,2Q)\). CRT permits these choices and, if needed, an additional condition \(\gcd(M,C)=1\); then the pair is primitive. The first new row equals \(T(\mathbf b_2)\bmod p_1\). Modulo \(p_2\), the original equations are \(a_3+a_4=a_4=0\), and the new one is \(a_1+s_2a_2=0\). Again the index is \(p_2\). The norm of \[-2+s\theta^2+(1+s)\theta^3
 =(s\theta^2+\theta^3)(1+\theta)\] is \(12(s^4+2)=324\bmod p_1\); thus the requisite norm coprimality holds.

The scale condition \(B\gg Q\) with a power margin follows from (4.11), since \(B=X^{S/4+o(1)}\), \(1<S<2\), and \(Q\le X^{2\tau'}\). The vectors approach the positive scalar direction, have norms \(N^4(1+O(Q/N))\), and can lie in a common permitted small box and a unit fundamental domain containing that direction. Choosing the sign \(-CQ\) also makes the real kernel compatible with positive first three product coordinates: \[a_4=-a_3/N,\qquad c_4a_1+c_3a_2=(CQ+M/N)a_3.\] Take \(C\) sufficiently large and \(a_2\asymp a_1/C\). The kernel equations give \(a_3\asymp a_1/C\) and \(a_4=-a_3/N\), so the \(\alpha\)-direction can also lie near the positive scalar ray. These observations exclude a mere fixed-small-prime or empty-real-region explanation for the local index error.

The calculation does not prove that the specific sieve weights \(g_{\mathbf b_1}g_{\mathbf b_2}\) are nonzero on this family, or that their total weighted contribution violates the final estimate. It refutes the uniform index assertion used to replace the summand. An exceptional-pair estimate or a different argument is required.

For the same power basis, take \[\mathbf b_1=(N,1,0,0),\qquad \mathbf b_2=(1,N-1,0,0),\qquad
 B=(N^4+2)^{1/4}.\] For \(N\ge7\), both norms \(N^4+2\) and \(1+2(N-1)^4\) lie in \([B^4,2B^4]\). Both vectors are primitive, but \[D_{\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2}=N(N-1)-1\asymp B^2.\] The common kernel is \(\mathbb Ze_1+\mathbb Ze_2\), of determinant one. At \(N=100\), \(D=9899\), and the vectors are nonproportional modulo 7. This directly invalidates the inference from individual primitivity to \(D\le B\) on p. 73. The ensuing sums truncate at \(d\le B\) on pp. 74–75 and again in the later reduction. For the example \(\|\mathbf b_1\wedge\mathbf b_2\|\asymp B^2\); the related determinant bound based on \(D\le B\) fails as well.

This is a counterexample to the intermediate geometric implication, not to the averaged bounds of Lemma 11.5 or 11.6. Membership of this second family in every particular fixed fundamental domain and in the full weight support is not asserted. A proof excluding or estimating \(D>B\) is still needed; simply extending the summation to \(B^2\) does not preserve the displayed error estimate. Together these issues leave the Type II proof incomplete as written.
result: Result: Two false intermediate assertions used in the displayed TypeII proof; no counterexample to final averaged bounds.
Impact: Replacing1/f by1/(p1p2) and truncating d<=B omit cases requiring estimates before Proposition9.14 is supported.

report: Abstract: The complete 42-page author manuscript of Bauer, Harms, and Michor, arXiv:2302.01631v3, is examined. Explicit counterexamples invalidate the joint-smoothness conclusion of Theorem 5.10(a) and the descent assertion of Proposition 5.12. The proof of the no-loss theorem uses a false inverse formula; a short-time repair is available, but its extension to the full interval is not established here. A further Major gap is the invalid boundedness inference used to construct the Banach model for differentiable elements; a fixed-order repair under the local-addition hypothesis is given. Several local jet, sign, and extension formulas require correction. The strong-metric Hopf–Rinow argument on the original group is assessed with its stated additional hypotheses intact. No counterexample to that result, or to the main differentiable- element theorem, is asserted. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Extensions, inverse regularity, and jet formulas in the theory of half-Lie groups
# Identity, scope, and dependencies

The reviewed work is Martin Bauer, Philipp Harms, and Peter W. Michor, Regularity and completeness of half-Lie groups, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1587. The primary scientific source is the author preprint arXiv:2302.01631v3, dated 7 January 2025 [paper]. During the initial review, its 42 pages, including all proofs and references, were read, and all 42 rendered source pages were actually viewed. Page references below are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed numbering.

The journal page records acceptance on 4 December 2023 and publication on 10 January 2025 [journal]. The author’s comment that v3 agrees with the published version is not an independent comparison. The subscription journal PDF was not acquired for a bytewise or pagewise comparison. The retained v3 TeX was read selectively to resolve formulas; it was not compiled or executed. No separate article-specific supplement or computational code was found in the bounded acquired-source search. Their absence is not a defect.

A right half-Lie group has continuous group operations and smooth individual right translations; joint smooth multiplication is not assumed (Definition 2.1, p. 3). Definition 3.1 (pp. 4–5) requires both \(L_x\) and \(L_{x^{-1}}\) to be \(C^k\). Theorem 3.4 and Lemma 3.7 construct \(G^k\) and the ILB Lie group \(G^\infty\) under a right-invariant local addition; their proofs run through Sections 9–10. Theorem 4.2 uses these spaces to integrate smooth controls. Definition 4.1 requires existence and uniqueness of evolution, not smooth dependence of the evolution map on the control. No extra Milnor-regularity condition is imposed.

Section 5 develops extension data and differentiable elements in extensions; Section 6 gives bundle examples. Theorem 7.7(a)–(d) concerns a connected group with a strong, smooth, right-invariant metric. Its geodesic-convexity conclusion (e) additionally assumes \(L^2\)-regularity and weak closedness of every endpoint fibre \(\mathcal A_x\). Its final assertion for the weaker metrics on \(G^k\) depends on the no-loss result 7.5–7.6. These dependencies are distinct.
# Substantive extension and proof issues
Problem 1 (Major: individual conjugation does not imply a jointly smooth action).
Location. Definitions 5.1–5.2 (pp. 8–9), Remark 5.8 (p. 11), Definition 5.9(b) and Theorem 5.10(a) (p. 12).

Let \(H=\ell^2(\mathbb C)\), viewed as a real Hilbert space, and set \[U_t(z_j)_{j\ge1}=(e^{ijt}z_j)_{j\ge1}.\] This is a strongly continuous unitary group. On \(E=\mathbb R\times H\) put \[(t,x)(s,y)=(t+s,U_{-s}x+y),\qquad
 (t,x)^{-1}=(-t,-U_tx).\] The group operations are continuous. For fixed \((s,y)\), right translation is a bounded affine smooth diffeomorphism. Thus \(E\) is a Banach right half-Lie group. Take the additive Banach Lie group \(N=H\), the quotient \(G=\mathbb R\), and \[i(n)=(0,n),\quad p(t,x)=t,\quad s(t)=(t,0),\quad r(t,x)=x.\] The split inclusion and projection have the required initial/final properties, and \(s,r\) are global smooth section and retraction. This is a smooth split extension, stronger than the assumptions of Theorem 5.10(a). For each fixed \(g=(t,x)\), \[g\,i(n)\,g^{-1}=i(U_tn)\] is a smooth bounded-linear automorphism of \(N\), as required by Definition 5.2. The flat local addition on the product vector space is right invariant, since right translations are affine.

Nevertheless the canonical section induces \[\alpha_t(n)=U_{-t}n,\qquad f(t,s)=0.\] Definition 5.9(b) requires \(\alpha:V\times N\to N\) to be jointly smooth on an identity neighbourhood \(V\). Take \(n_0=(1/j)_{j\ge1}\in H\). If \(t\mapsto U_{-t}n_0\) were differentiable at zero, its derivative would have every coordinate equal to \(-i\). This sequence is not in \(\ell^2\). Hence the orbit is not even \(C^1\). Since \(N\) is abelian, changing the section only introduces trivial inner conjugations and cannot remove the obstruction.

Impact and repair boundary. This is a counterexample to the actual implication in 5.10(a). Individual smooth conjugations, even with a smooth split extension and a right-invariant local addition, do not supply the required joint smoothness. One can restrict the classification to extensions with jointly smooth induced \(\alpha\), or weaken the datum and redo the atlas construction. The latter repair is not established here. The example does not refute the differentiable-vector theorem or Hopf–Rinow: its product flat strong metric is right invariant and complete.
Problem 2 (Major: a local addition respecting the kernel need not descend).
Location. Proposition 5.12 and its proof (pp. 14–15); the last quotient-local-addition step of Theorem 5.11 (p. 14).

Consider the split Lie-group extension \[0\longrightarrow\mathbb R\times\{0\}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^2,+)
 \xrightarrow{p}(\mathbb R,+)\longrightarrow0,\qquad p(a,b)=b.\] On \(V=\{(a,b;u,v):|u|<1/2,\ |v|<1\}\) define \[\tau_E(a,b;u,v)=\bigl(a+u,\ b+(1+u)v\bigr).\] This is a smooth right-invariant local addition. It fixes the zero section, its domain is invariant under tangent translations, and \((\pi,\tau_E)\) has the smooth inverse \[u=A-a,\qquad v=\frac{B-b}{1+A-a}\] on its open image. It maps \(TN\) to \(N\) and respects the tangent directions of every kernel coset. It is already normalized as in Remark 8.2: its vertical derivative at zero is the identity.

But \[p\tau_E(a,b;u,v)=b+(1+u)v,\qquad Tp(a,b;u,v)=(b,v).\] For fixed nonzero \(v\), varying \(u\) changes the first expression without changing the second. At \(v=1/2\), \(u=0\) and \(u=1/4\) give \(b+1/2\) and \(b+5/8\). The obstruction occurs for arbitrarily small nonzero \(u,v\). Therefore no \(\tau_G\) satisfies \(p\tau_E=\tau_G Tp\), even after shrinking to an open neighbourhood of the zero section.

Impact and repair boundary. The proof assumes separation of kernel and quotient directions that does not follow from respecting \(N\). Constancy of \(p\tau_E\) on the fibres of \(Tp\), or a separate compatible connection/local addition, is needed. Being totally geodesic is insufficient. This refutes descent of the given addition, not existence of another compatible one: the standard flat addition works here. The quotient step in 5.11 needs its own justification; its entire differentiable-element conclusion is not disproved.
Problem 3 (Major: the inverse step in the global no-loss argument is invalid).
Location. Theorem 7.5, especially its final proof lines (pp. 23–24); Definition 3.1 (pp. 4–5); Corollary 7.6 and the final assertion of 7.7 (pp. 24–26).

Writing \(\gamma(t)=\pi_G\operatorname{Fl}_t^S(X)\), the proof identifies the inverse of \(L_{\gamma(t)}\) with \(L_{\gamma(-t)}\). A second-order flow need not give a one-parameter subgroup. Even a right-invariant spray on \(G=(\mathbb R,+)\) supplies a counterexample: \[S(x,v)=(v,v^2),\quad X=(0,1),\quad
 \gamma(t)=-\log(1-t),\quad
 \gamma(1/2)+\gamma(-1/2)=\log(4/3)\ne0.\] This field is smooth, translation invariant, second order, and quadratic in velocity. The two translations are not inverses. Here \(G^k=G\), so this refutes the formula only, not the no-loss conclusion. The gap matters because Definition 3.1 explicitly requires inverse regularity and does not know it to follow from forward regularity alone.

A short-time repair is available. For fixed \(X\in TG^k\) set \[f_t(y)=\pi_G\operatorname{Fl}_t^S(T R_y X)=L_{\gamma(t)}(y).\] The valid part gives \(C^k\) dependence on \(y\), with \(D_e f_t\) continuous in \(t\). At zero this derivative is invertible. For small \(|t|\) it stays invertible, and right equivariance propagates invertibility to every point. The inverse function theorem and global bijectivity then give a \(C^k\) inverse.

Impact and repair boundary. This does not establish the entire flow interval: invertibility holds on an open set of times, but closedness requires further control. Uniform inverse-derivative bounds near finite boundary times would suffice, as would a separate inverse-regularity theorem for the specific group. Neither is established here. The global no-loss and \(G^k\)-completeness proof dependencies remain unresolved. The completeness statements for \(G\) itself have a separate argument and are not refuted by this example.
# The Banach model gap and local corrections
Problem 4 (Major: an invalid boundedness inference in the Banach model construction).
Location. Lemma 10.3 (pp. 34–35), its uses in 10.7 and 10.9 (pp. 35–37), and the model and chart constructions in 10.8–10.11 leading to Theorem 3.4 and Lemma 3.7 (pp. 36–39).

The proof infers boundedness in \(C^\infty(U,E)\) from pointwise bounded values. The functions \(f_n(x)=\sin(nx)\) on \((-1,1)\) are bounded by one, while \(f_n'(0)=n\). Thus the general function-space implication is false in the compact-open jet topology. This is not a half-Lie-group counterexample to 10.3.

Severity and actual dependency. Lemma 10.7 invokes 10.3 both to compare the identity-jet norm with the compact-open topology and to prove completeness. Lemma 10.8 uses that Banach model; 10.9 invokes 10.3 again, 10.10 uses 10.7 to identify the jet model, and 10.11 relies on 10.10. On p. 39, Theorem 3.4 follows explicitly from 10.8, 10.9, and 10.11, while Lemma 3.7 uses the charts of 10.8. The false inference is therefore part of the construction proving the main differentiable-element result. This is a Major proof gap. The new replacement below is counterevidence to irreparability, not evidence that the original argument was valid.

Under the local-addition hypothesis already in the main theorem, one can obtain the compact-parameter bounds needed for fixed \(k\). Normalize \(\tau\) and put \(\Omega(y,z)=\tau_y^{-1}(z)\). Then \[L_yv:=T_eR_yv=\Omega(y,\tau_e(v)y),\qquad
 L_y^{-1}w=\Omega(e,\tau_y(w)y^{-1}).\] These are jointly continuous in local tangent trivializations and linear in the tangent argument. Joint continuity at zero implies local operator-norm boundedness; finite covers give bounds on compact parameter sets. The relation \[R_y=\tau_y\circ L_y\circ\tau_e^{-1}\] bounds \(j_e^{k+1}R_y\) and \(j_y^kR_y^{-1}\) for \(y\) in a fixed compact set, using smoothness of \(\tau\). Together with the corrected polynomial jet bounds below, this supplies the estimate used in 10.7 to compare the full identity-jet norm with compact-open jets. Cauchy sequences have continuous derivative limits; integration along small segments identifies those limits as derivatives. Right invariance passes to the limit.

Boundary. This verifies replacement bounds under \(\tau\), not the stronger literal statement of 10.3 with one neighbourhood for all \(k\) and all compact sets, without that hypothesis. The norm in 10.7 includes the intermediate derivatives: its printed ellipsis was checked visually. For 10.8, use actual \(C^k\) diffeomorphisms as chart centres and shrink the model neighbourhood so that the identity derivative remains invertible. The inverse function theorem then provides \(C^k\) inverses of the resulting left translations. This avoids assuming an inverse is \(C^k\) for an arbitrary right-invariant \(C^k\) function. The fixed-\(k\) Banach model and these local charts can thus be supported, but the complete Banach/ILB proof is not claimed to have been rewritten.
Problem 5 (Minor: normalized jet evaluation and bundle transitions).
Location. Definitions 9.1 and 9.4, Lemma 9.5 (pp. 29–31), and Definition 9.11 (p. 34).

The normalization is \(p_j=D^jf/j!\). For \(1\le j\le k-1\), the normalized \(j\)th derivative of \(Tf\) is \[\left(p_j(\pi_H^j),\
 (j+1)p_{j+1}(\pi_H^j,X)
 +j p_j(\pi_H^{j-1},\pi_V)\right),\] with symmetrized mixed terms. The printed first term misses \(j+1\), in particular \(k\) in the last component. For \(f(x)=x^2\), \(k=2\), \(x=0\), one has \(Tf(x,X)=(x^2,2xX)\); the horizontal derivative is \((0,2X)\), whereas the printed formula gives \((0,X)\). The old constants in 9.5 cannot simply be retained after correction: at \(X=4\) the actual sum norm is \(12\), while its first displayed bound is \(11\).

For the same sum/product norms, sufficient corrected bounds are \[\begin{aligned}
 \|\sigma\odot\xi\|&\le
 \|\xi\|+k\|\sigma\|(1+\|\xi\|),\\
 \|\widetilde\sigma\odot\widetilde\xi-\sigma\odot\xi\|
 &\le k(1+\|\widetilde\xi\|)\|\widetilde\sigma-\sigma\|
 +(1+k\|\sigma\|)\|\widetilde\xi-\xi\|.\end{aligned}\] Collecting each \(p_j\) contribution proves these inequalities. The polynomial-control requirement in 10.6 survives. The original proof on p. 31 already lists the correct unnormalized derivatives, and 10.6 needs a fixed-order polynomial bound rather than the incorrect precise constants. These facts support the Minor scope.

Definition 9.11 freezes the base variable in a fibre coordinate change. On a trivial real line bundle take \(\psi(x,y)=y+x\). The zero section has first jet \((0,0,0)\) at zero. After changing coordinates the section is \(x\), with derivative one; freezing \(\psi(0,y)=y\) yields derivative zero. The transition must use the full jet \(j^k\psi\bullet j^k(\operatorname{Id},s)\). Also the right side of Lemma 9.3 must be \(g\circ f\) for \(j^kg\bullet j^kf\). These are local formula corrections, not counterexamples to the intended jet bundles or main group theorem.
Problem 6 (Minor: inconsistent bracket signs).
Location. Lemma 3.8(a)–(c) and proof (pp. 6–7); the related identity in Lemma 7.4 (p. 23).

On the positive affine group \((a,b)(c,d)=(ac,ad+b)\) take \[R_X=a\partial_a+b\partial_b,\qquad R_Y=\partial_b.\] Part (a) gives \(dR_Y\,X-dR_X\,Y=-Y\). But \((\operatorname{Fl}_t^{R_X})^*R_Y=e^{-t}R_Y\), so the negative derivative in (c) gives \(+Y\). Deleting that minus sign makes (c) agree with (a), (b), and the pullback calculation in the proof.

A consistent choice is also needed in 7.4: its identity \(-[R_X,R_Y]=R_{[X,Y]}\) uses the opposite convention to 3.8(a). Alternatively, retain the conventional Lie-algebra sign and negate 3.8(a)–(b), adjusting \(\operatorname{ad}\) consistently. This verifies the inconsistency, not an unqualified global sign substitution through all curvature and Eulerian formulas. The existence arguments do not depend on the convention chosen.
Problem 7 (Minor: an extension equivalence has the wrong direction).
Location. Theorem 5.10(d), final map (p. 12).

Let \(G=N=(\mathbb R,+)\), \(\alpha=\operatorname{Id}\), \(f=0\), and \(b(t)=t^2\). The printed transformation gives \(f_1(t,s)=-2ts\). The stated map \(E_f\to E_{f_1}\) is \(\phi(t,n)=(t,n+t^2)\), but \[\phi((1,0)(1,0))=(2,4),\qquad
 \phi(1,0)\mathbin{\cdot_{f_1}}\phi(1,0)=(2,0).\] The general discrepancy is \(4ts\). The correct forward map is \((t,n)\mapsto(t,n-t^2)\); in multiplicative notation it is \((x,n)\mapsto(x,b(x)^{-1}n)\). The printed map has the reverse direction. Substitution verifies this repair; it does not fix Problem 1.
Problem 8 (Minor: flatness gives a semidirect product here).
Location. Remark 6.3, final sentence (p. 18).

Use the trivial principal \(S^1\)-bundle over the compact simply connected manifold \(S^2\), with its flat connection. The homomorphic section is \(s(\varphi)(x,z)=(\varphi(x),z)\). The gauge kernel is the abelian group \(C^\infty(S^2,S^1)\). Conjugation acts by \(h\mapsto h\circ\varphi^{-1}\), generally nontrivially: take \(h(x)=e^{ix_3}\) and a rotation reversing \(x_3\). This distinguished kernel is not central, whereas it would be central in its direct product with \(\operatorname{Diff}(S^2)\). The section supplies a semidirect product. This refutes the direct-product assertion as an equivalence of these extensions, without asserting a stronger abstract non-isomorphism. Replacing direct by semidirect repairs this particular conclusion.
# Counterevidence, coverage, and limits

Theorem 7.7 on \(G\) itself has positive evidence with its exact hypotheses. A strong metric supplies Hilbert charts and local equivalence of metric and coordinate norms. Right translations are isometries, so a Cauchy sequence can be moved into a small fixed normal neighbourhood. Short paths cannot leave a larger normal ball; this supplies the local distance comparison in the proof. Metric completeness supports geodesic completeness.

For (e), the endpoint set is weakly closed by hypothesis; its intersection with an energy ball is weakly compact in \(L^2\). Weak lower semicontinuity gives a minimizer without requiring convexity of the endpoint set. Zero control handles equal endpoints. The strong metric also supplies continuous tangent right translation locally through \[T_xR_h(v)=t^{-1}\log_{xh}\bigl((\exp_x(tv))h\bigr)\] for small fixed \(t\). With the energy identity this justifies the \(H^1\)-path/\(L^2\)-control correspondence in the direct method. Local minimization and Gauss’ lemma yield a smooth geodesic. No defect in this argument on \(G\) with the extra conditions was established; the separate \(G^k\) dependency is Problem 3.

The initial review covered all 42 pages: definitions, differentiable elements and evolution, extensions and bundle examples, metrics and geodesics, local additions and jets, right-invariant mapping spaces, final proofs, and references. Exact page ranges are retained in coverage. External proofs on Sobolev groups, convenient calculus, and curvature were traced but not re-proved in full. The ILB definition does not require density; nondensity is not a defect. Finite-level uniqueness gives compatibility for the smooth inverse-limit evolution. No obligatory extra spatial derivative loss was established in Theorem 4.2.

Two reading artefacts were excluded. The near-minimizer formula on p. 26 has absolute-value bars and is correct; a text-only suggestion of a reversed inequality was withdrawn. The norm on p. 35 has an ellipsis for intermediate derivatives. Both were resolved by actual source-image inspection.

problems.title: Individual smooth conjugations do not supply jointly smooth extension data
problems.source_location: pp8-9 Definitions5.1-5.2; p11 Remark5.8; p12 Definition5.9(b),Theorem5.10(a)
claim: Recorded check: All hypotheses verified analytically. Alpha_t(n)=U_-t n, n=(1/j) has coordinate derivatives(-i) not in l2; abelian kernel makes section changes irrelevant.
H=l2(C) real Hilbert,U_t(z_j)=exp(ijt)z_j,E law(t,x)(s,y)=(t+s,U_-s x+y); split smooth section/retraction; each fixed conjugation smooth; flat right-invariant local addition.
analysis: Location. Definitions 5.1–5.2 (pp. 8–9), Remark 5.8 (p. 11), Definition 5.9(b) and Theorem 5.10(a) (p. 12).

Let \(H=\ell^2(\mathbb C)\), viewed as a real Hilbert space, and set \[U_t(z_j)_{j\ge1}=(e^{ijt}z_j)_{j\ge1}.\] This is a strongly continuous unitary group. On \(E=\mathbb R\times H\) put \[(t,x)(s,y)=(t+s,U_{-s}x+y),\qquad
 (t,x)^{-1}=(-t,-U_tx).\] The group operations are continuous. For fixed \((s,y)\), right translation is a bounded affine smooth diffeomorphism. Thus \(E\) is a Banach right half-Lie group. Take the additive Banach Lie group \(N=H\), the quotient \(G=\mathbb R\), and \[i(n)=(0,n),\quad p(t,x)=t,\quad s(t)=(t,0),\quad r(t,x)=x.\] The split inclusion and projection have the required initial/final properties, and \(s,r\) are global smooth section and retraction. This is a smooth split extension, stronger than the assumptions of Theorem 5.10(a). For each fixed \(g=(t,x)\), \[g\,i(n)\,g^{-1}=i(U_tn)\] is a smooth bounded-linear automorphism of \(N\), as required by Definition 5.2. The flat local addition on the product vector space is right invariant, since right translations are affine.

Nevertheless the canonical section induces \[\alpha_t(n)=U_{-t}n,\qquad f(t,s)=0.\] Definition 5.9(b) requires \(\alpha:V\times N\to N\) to be jointly smooth on an identity neighbourhood \(V\). Take \(n_0=(1/j)_{j\ge1}\in H\). If \(t\mapsto U_{-t}n_0\) were differentiable at zero, its derivative would have every coordinate equal to \(-i\). This sequence is not in \(\ell^2\). Hence the orbit is not even \(C^1\). Since \(N\) is abelian, changing the section only introduces trivial inner conjugations and cannot remove the obstruction.

Impact and repair boundary. This is a counterexample to the actual implication in 5.10(a). Individual smooth conjugations, even with a smooth split extension and a right-invariant local addition, do not supply the required joint smoothness. One can restrict the classification to extensions with jointly smooth induced \(\alpha\), or weaken the datum and redo the atlas construction. The latter repair is not established here. The example does not refute the differentiable-vector theorem or Hopf–Rinow: its product flat strong metric is right invariant and complete.
result: Result: Counterexample to Theorem5.10(a)'s required jointly smooth datum.
Impact: Stated extension classification includes extensions that fail its defining data regularity.

problems.title: Respecting the kernel does not imply descent of a local addition
problems.source_location: pp14-15 Proposition5.12; p14 final quotient-addition step of5.11
claim: Recorded check: Local diffeomorphism inverse u=A-a,v=(B-b)/(1+A-a); normalized vertical derivative identity; right invariant, preserves TN. Same Tp=(b,v) has different quotient endpoints when uv differs.
E=R2 additive,N=R x0,p(a,b)=b; tau(a,b;u,v)=(a+u,b+(1+u)v),|u|<1/2,|v|<1.
analysis: Location. Proposition 5.12 and its proof (pp. 14–15); the last quotient-local-addition step of Theorem 5.11 (p. 14).

Consider the split Lie-group extension \[0\longrightarrow\mathbb R\times\{0\}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^2,+)
 \xrightarrow{p}(\mathbb R,+)\longrightarrow0,\qquad p(a,b)=b.\] On \(V=\{(a,b;u,v):|u|<1/2,\ |v|<1\}\) define \[\tau_E(a,b;u,v)=\bigl(a+u,\ b+(1+u)v\bigr).\] This is a smooth right-invariant local addition. It fixes the zero section, its domain is invariant under tangent translations, and \((\pi,\tau_E)\) has the smooth inverse \[u=A-a,\qquad v=\frac{B-b}{1+A-a}\] on its open image. It maps \(TN\) to \(N\) and respects the tangent directions of every kernel coset. It is already normalized as in Remark 8.2: its vertical derivative at zero is the identity.

But \[p\tau_E(a,b;u,v)=b+(1+u)v,\qquad Tp(a,b;u,v)=(b,v).\] For fixed nonzero \(v\), varying \(u\) changes the first expression without changing the second. At \(v=1/2\), \(u=0\) and \(u=1/4\) give \(b+1/2\) and \(b+5/8\). The obstruction occurs for arbitrarily small nonzero \(u,v\). Therefore no \(\tau_G\) satisfies \(p\tau_E=\tau_G Tp\), even after shrinking to an open neighbourhood of the zero section.

Impact and repair boundary. The proof assumes separation of kernel and quotient directions that does not follow from respecting \(N\). Constancy of \(p\tau_E\) on the fibres of \(Tp\), or a separate compatible connection/local addition, is needed. Being totally geodesic is insufficient. This refutes descent of the given addition, not existence of another compatible one: the standard flat addition works here. The quotient step in 5.11 needs its own justification; its entire differentiable-element conclusion is not disproved.
result: Result: Explicit counterexample to p tauE=tauG Tp even after shrinking.
Impact: Given-addition descent and dependent quotient justification fail.

problems.title: False inverse formula leaves global no-loss proof incomplete
problems.source_location: pp23-24 Theorem7.5 proof final lines; pp4-5 Def3.1; pp24-26 dependent7.6/7.7
claim: Recorded check: gamma(t)=-log(1-t), gamma(1/2)+gamma(-1/2)=log(4/3), so printed left translations not inverses.
G=R additive,S(x,v)=(v,v²),X=(0,1),a smooth right-invariant spray.
analysis: Location. Theorem 7.5, especially its final proof lines (pp. 23–24); Definition 3.1 (pp. 4–5); Corollary 7.6 and the final assertion of 7.7 (pp. 24–26).

Writing \(\gamma(t)=\pi_G\operatorname{Fl}_t^S(X)\), the proof identifies the inverse of \(L_{\gamma(t)}\) with \(L_{\gamma(-t)}\). A second-order flow need not give a one-parameter subgroup. Even a right-invariant spray on \(G=(\mathbb R,+)\) supplies a counterexample: \[S(x,v)=(v,v^2),\quad X=(0,1),\quad
 \gamma(t)=-\log(1-t),\quad
 \gamma(1/2)+\gamma(-1/2)=\log(4/3)\ne0.\] This field is smooth, translation invariant, second order, and quadratic in velocity. The two translations are not inverses. Here \(G^k=G\), so this refutes the formula only, not the no-loss conclusion. The gap matters because Definition 3.1 explicitly requires inverse regularity and does not know it to follow from forward regularity alone.

A short-time repair is available. For fixed \(X\in TG^k\) set \[f_t(y)=\pi_G\operatorname{Fl}_t^S(T R_y X)=L_{\gamma(t)}(y).\] The valid part gives \(C^k\) dependence on \(y\), with \(D_e f_t\) continuous in \(t\). At zero this derivative is invertible. For small \(|t|\) it stays invertible, and right equivariance propagates invertibility to every point. The inverse function theorem and global bijectivity then give a \(C^k\) inverse.

Impact and repair boundary. This does not establish the entire flow interval: invertibility holds on an open set of times, but closedness requires further control. Uniform inverse-derivative bounds near finite boundary times would suffice, as would a separate inverse-regularity theorem for the specific group. Neither is established here. The global no-loss and \(G^k\)-completeness proof dependencies remain unresolved. The completeness statements for \(G\) itself have a separate argument and are not refuted by this example.
result: Result: Counterexample to proof identity only. No no-loss theorem counterexample.
Impact: Full ambient-time interval inverse regularity and inherited Gk geodesic completeness need additional proof.

paragraphs: Prove inverse-derivative bounds at possible finite boundary times or independent inverse-regularity principle.

problems.title: Invalid boundedness inference in the core Banach model construction
problems.source_location: pp34?35 Lemma10.3; pp35?39 Lemmas10.7?10.11; p39 proofs of main Theorem3.4 and Lemma3.7
claim: Recorded check: sin(nx) values bounded, derivatives at0 unbounded. Under tau, Omega identities give joint continuity of T_e R_y and its inverse, local operator bounds and compact-parameter fixed-k jet bounds.
Compact-open jet topology, fixed k; main theorem has smooth right-invariant local addition.
analysis: Location. Lemma 10.3 (pp. 34–35), its uses in 10.7 and 10.9 (pp. 35–37), and the model and chart constructions in 10.8–10.11 leading to Theorem 3.4 and Lemma 3.7 (pp. 36–39).

The proof infers boundedness in \(C^\infty(U,E)\) from pointwise bounded values. The functions \(f_n(x)=\sin(nx)\) on \((-1,1)\) are bounded by one, while \(f_n'(0)=n\). Thus the general function-space implication is false in the compact-open jet topology. This is not a half-Lie-group counterexample to 10.3.

Severity and actual dependency. Lemma 10.7 invokes 10.3 both to compare the identity-jet norm with the compact-open topology and to prove completeness. Lemma 10.8 uses that Banach model; 10.9 invokes 10.3 again, 10.10 uses 10.7 to identify the jet model, and 10.11 relies on 10.10. On p. 39, Theorem 3.4 follows explicitly from 10.8, 10.9, and 10.11, while Lemma 3.7 uses the charts of 10.8. The false inference is therefore part of the construction proving the main differentiable-element result. This is a Major proof gap. The new replacement below is counterevidence to irreparability, not evidence that the original argument was valid.

Under the local-addition hypothesis already in the main theorem, one can obtain the compact-parameter bounds needed for fixed \(k\). Normalize \(\tau\) and put \(\Omega(y,z)=\tau_y^{-1}(z)\). Then \[L_yv:=T_eR_yv=\Omega(y,\tau_e(v)y),\qquad
 L_y^{-1}w=\Omega(e,\tau_y(w)y^{-1}).\] These are jointly continuous in local tangent trivializations and linear in the tangent argument. Joint continuity at zero implies local operator-norm boundedness; finite covers give bounds on compact parameter sets. The relation \[R_y=\tau_y\circ L_y\circ\tau_e^{-1}\] bounds \(j_e^{k+1}R_y\) and \(j_y^kR_y^{-1}\) for \(y\) in a fixed compact set, using smoothness of \(\tau\). Together with the corrected polynomial jet bounds below, this supplies the estimate used in 10.7 to compare the full identity-jet norm with compact-open jets. Cauchy sequences have continuous derivative limits; integration along small segments identifies those limits as derivatives. Right invariance passes to the limit.

Boundary. This verifies replacement bounds under \(\tau\), not the stronger literal statement of 10.3 with one neighbourhood for all \(k\) and all compact sets, without that hypothesis. The norm in 10.7 includes the intermediate derivatives: its printed ellipsis was checked visually. For 10.8, use actual \(C^k\) diffeomorphisms as chart centres and shrink the model neighbourhood so that the identity derivative remains invertible. The inverse function theorem then provides \(C^k\) inverses of the resulting left translations. This avoids assuming an inverse is \(C^k\) for an arbitrary right-invariant \(C^k\) function. The fixed-\(k\) Banach model and these local charts can thus be supported, but the complete Banach/ILB proof is not claimed to have been rewritten.
result: Result: Generic bornology argument false; actual principal fixed-k boundedness step can be repaired under existing tau assumption.

Impact: Lemma10.7 uses the false 10.3 inference for topology and completeness; 10.8 uses the Banach model,10.9 uses10.3,10.10 uses10.7,10.11 uses10.10; p39 derives main Theorem3.4 and ILB Lemma3.7 through these constructions. This is a Major invalid core derivation despite the verified fixed-k replacement under tau.

report: Abstract: The 35-page v3 manuscript of Giacchetto, Kramer, Lewański, and Sauvaget and its nine-page computational supplement are examined. Finite calculations expose incompatible empty-partition and degree-zero conventions, an omitted central term in the Hodge operator, and an incorrect one-point recurrence. The printed degree-zero geometric formula also disagrees with the stated localization series. The connectedness of the principal statement and the positive-form proof of the conditional extension also require substantive correction. Local corrections concern operator signs and the scope of a Lie algebra projection. The supplement’s low-degree formulas and corrected recurrence receive independent exact checks. These findings do not establish that the intended positive-degree correspondence or BKP conclusion is false after repair. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Central terms, degree-zero conventions, and explicit formulas in the spin GW/Hurwitz correspondence
# Identity, reading scope, and dependency structure

The reviewed paper is A. Giacchetto, R. Kramer, D. Lewański, and A. Sauvaget, The spin Gromov–Witten/Hurwitz correspondence for \(\mathbb P^1\), DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1588. The primary scientific source is arXiv:2208.03259v3, 14 August 2025 [paper]. The initial review read the complete 35-page text and actually viewed every source page; it also read and viewed all nine pages of the author-linked Spin GW invariants of \(\mathbb P^1\): Calculations [supp]. Those retained facts are bound to unchanged source bytes. The present independent acceptance checks the eight reported Problems and their actual proof dependencies. Page references below refer to the primary PDF unless identified as supplemental.

The journal records acceptance on 8 October 2024 and publication on 6 January 2025 [journal]. Version 2, dated 17 October 2024, is labelled accepted on arXiv. Version 3 is later than publication; its authors report a correction to Lemma 2.11 and its proof. The v3 factor \(2^{-g}\) is actually present and is used in all calculations here. Its nonempty small cases are supported, not criticized. The retained v2 received only a targeted auxiliary comparison, not a second complete scientific review. The subscription journal PDF was not independently compared. The supplement has no independently established release date; its internal PDF metadata is not a publication date. Its older notation is not assumed identical to v3. No article-specific author code was found in the bounded acquired-source search. No author code was executed.

The proof route is: the neutral Clifford algebra and spin characters in Section 2; the spin ELSV theorem quoted there; the specialized localization calculation of Section 3; Hodge operators and their commutator in Section 4; the Fock-space GW formulas of Section 5; and dressing into the 2-BKP hierarchy in Section 6. Theorem E is explicitly conditional on Conjecture D, the proposed degeneration statement. It is not an unconditional theorem for every spin target curve. The cited spin ELSV, character theory, and hierarchy theorems have not been independently reproved here.

For clarity, suppress the superscript \(B\) on operators and set \[A=\alpha_1,\quad B=\alpha_{-1},\quad
 s(z)=2\sinh(z/2),\quad q_0(z)=\tfrac12\cosh(z/2),\quad
 c(z)=\frac{q_0(z)}{s(z)}=\tfrac14\coth(z/2).\] Thus \([A,B]=1/2\) and \(\mathcal E_0=\widehat{\mathcal E}_0+c\,\operatorname{Id}\). These definitions distinguish a scalar correction from a change in the nonzero-energy operators.
# Substantive normalization and boundary issues
Problem 1 (Major: completed cycles and removal of degree-zero terms are incompatible).
Location. Notation (p. 8), Definition 2.10 and (2.23) (p. 11), (2.24)–(2.27) (p. 12), Proposition 2.14, (2.31) (p. 13), the proof of Theorem C (p. 29), and Remark 5.7, (5.20) (p. 31).

The stated set of odd partitions includes \(\varnothing\). Equation (2.24) sums over it, and Lemma 2.11 gives \[\kappa_{k,\mu}
 =2^{-g}(k-1)!\frac{\prod_i\mu_i}{|\mu|!}
 [z^{2g}]S(2z)S(z)^{|\mu|-2}\prod_iS(\mu_i z),
 \qquad 2g=k+1-|\mu|-\ell(\mu).\] Since \(S(2z)/S(z)^2=(z/2)\coth(z/2)\), one obtains \[\kappa_{1,\varnothing}=\frac1{24},\quad
 \kappa_{1,(1)}=1,\qquad
 \kappa_{3,\varnothing}=-\frac1{1440},\quad
 \kappa_{3,(1)}=\frac16.\] In degree one, (2.23) gives \(H_1(\mathbb P^1;\varnothing)=H_1(\mathbb P^1;(1))=1\): the added-one binomial factor is one, and the unique degree-one cover has positive spin sign and trivial automorphism group. Consequently the literal completed-cycle expansion gives \[H_1(\overline c_1)=\frac{25}{24},\qquad
 H_1(\overline c_3)=\frac{239}{1440}.\] In contrast, the elementary Fock calculation \[\left\langle A\widehat{\mathcal E}_0(z)B\right\rangle=\tfrac12\sinh z\] makes (2.31) give \(1\) and \(1/6\), respectively. This contradiction already occurs in positive covering degree; it does not require a disputed genus convention for an empty source.

The proof (2.27) also uses an ordinary vacuum expectation where connected or inactive-sheet subtractions need to be specified. For example, with \(\mu=(1),k=1\) its ordinary expectation includes the same \(1/24\) vacuum contribution, although the final coefficient is \(1\). Changing \(\mathcal E_0\) to \(\widehat{\mathcal E}_0\) alone is not a proof of the required connected-cover extraction in general.

Impact and repair boundary. The comparison used to prove Theorem C needs one consistent definition of completed cycles, connected extraction, and allowed degree-zero components. Excluding the empty partition agrees with the centered operator in these tests; retaining it requires the corresponding scalar and disconnected terms. Neither choice alone is claimed here to repair the entire correspondence. Proposition 5.4 already explicitly excludes degree-zero components and is not refuted by this calculation. The new v3 factor is not the source of this discrepancy.
Problem 2 (Major: the stable degree-zero geometric boundary is not covered consistently).
Location. (1.5)–(1.6) (p. 3), Definition 3.1 and its unstable conventions (pp. 14–15), (3.14)–(3.16), Theorem 3.2 (pp. 16–18).

Connected positive-degree maps satisfy the required concavity; constant maps have \(H^0\neq0\) and \(R^1\) of rank \(g\), not \(g+d-1\). Restrict the geometric formula to its justified range and derive the degree-zero theory separately, or justify an explicit formal convention. The series alone does not establish the actual cosection-localized degree-zero value.

Independently, in the general \(\mathcal O(-k)\) formula (3.14), take a single degree-one edge with \(k=2,\alpha=1\). Its endpoint weights \([1,3]\) give \(\omega_{\mathbb P^1}\otimes\chi^2\), hence one-dimensional \(H^1\) of weight \(2\) and Euler class \(2t\). The printed product instead gives \[(1+2)(-t)+(1-2)t=-4t.\] The endpoint vertex factors are one. This does not refute the subsequent specialization \(k=1,\alpha=-1/2\): odd-edge signs cancel and even edges vanish. That specialized positive-degree calculation remains a separate question.
Problem 3 (Major: the Hodge operator omits a central term).
Location. Definition 4.1, (4.2), Proposition 4.2 (p. 20), its proof (pp. 21–22), and Theorem 4.7 (pp. 22–23).

The bound \(j\geq k'+1=(k+1)/2\) excludes \(k=j=0\). But \(\mathcal E_0(w)\) has leading scalar term \(1/(2w)\). At this index the Gamma quotient is \(1/z\), so the omitted contribution is the entire formal scalar \[\boxed{\frac{e^{uz^3/12}}{2z}\operatorname{Id}.}\] In particular the printed definition gives \(\mathcal B(1,0)=B\), whereas (4.3) gives \[e^A B e^{-A}=B+\tfrac12\operatorname{Id}.\] Theorem 4.7 at \(n=1,u^0\) likewise requires the nonzero unstable Hodge term \(1/(2z)\).

The printed \(u^1\) vacuum coefficient \(z(z+2)/24\) gains \(z^2/24\) from the missing scalar, giving \(H_1^\circ(z)=z(z+1)/12\). Restoring only \(1/(2z)\) therefore fails already at the next coefficient.

Impact and repair boundary. Scalar terms alter Hodge/GW expectations, not commutators. The proof on p. 22 drops \(k=0\). Restore the full scalar throughout; the two checked coefficients do not certify all-genus or central-lift identities.
# Statement errors and further proof restrictions
Problem 4 (Major: dimension and connectedness in the principal statements).
Location. (1.7), Theorem A (p. 3), Conjecture B (p. 4), Notation (p. 8), and the proofs on pp. 28–29.

Conjecture B prints \(\sum k_i=g-1+d(1-g(B))+n\). Each stationary insertion has codimension \(k_i+1\), so the \(n\) cancels against the localized virtual dimension. For \(\mathbb P^1\) the condition is \(\sum k_i=g-1+d\), precisely the condition actually used on p. 29. For example \(g=0,d=1,n=1,k_1=1\) satisfies the printed condition, but \(\psi_1\operatorname{ev}_1^*h\) has codimension two on the one-dimensional degree-one moduli space and integrates to zero. Using the literal completed-cycle convention of Problem 1, the stated corresponding expression is \(-\tfrac12H_1(\overline c_3)=-239/2880\neq0\). This example keeps that convention fixed throughout. Even using the centered coefficient \(1/6\) instead would give \(-1/12\), so the dimension conflict does not depend on retaining Problem 1’s empty-cycle contribution.

Equation (1.7) has no disconnected marker, although the notation declares an unmarked bracket connected. Set \(x=x^\star=0\). The connected \(d=2,g\geq0\) integrals without insertions vanish by their positive dimension \(g+1\). Theorem A’s operator expression instead equals \[\left\langle e^A(q/u)^H e^B\right\rangle=\exp(q/(2u)),\] whose \(q^2\) coefficient is \(1/(8u^2)\). An empty-curve convention can change the constant term but not this coefficient. The power \(u^{-2}\) cannot occur in a connected genus sum with \(g\geq0\); it represents two disconnected degree-one rational components. This refutes the literal principal statement without using any problematic inserted operator from Problems 1–3. Theorem 5.3 already has the proper bullet, which identifies the intended repair but does not validate Theorem A as stated. Use the disconnected potential with its arithmetic-genus range and delete the extra \(n\) from the dimension condition. The severity is Major because the asserted main result, not only auxiliary notation, changes.
Problem 5 (Minor: two operator signs disagree with their actual use).

The exponent in (2.12)–(2.13) is \(e^{(k+m/2)z}\). With the displayed indices \(k-m,k\), the centered exponent needed by the subsequent parity relation is \(e^{(k-m/2)z}\). Directly from the CAR, \[\mathcal E_{-1}^{\rm printed}(z)|0\rangle
 =e^{-z}\cosh(z/2)\phi_1\phi_0|0\rangle,\qquad
 \left\langle A\mathcal E_{-1}^{\rm printed}(z)\right\rangle
 =\tfrac12e^{-z}\cosh(z/2).\] Its derivative at zero is \(-1/2\), whereas (2.19) requires it to be even. Correcting the sign fixes this finite test; the proof on p. 21 already uses \(e^{w(l-k/2)}\).

The right exponential in each conjugated factor of (2.30) also needs a minus sign. For \(r=2,\mu=(1,1)\), put \(v_j=\phi_j\phi_0|0\rangle\). Then \(B|0\rangle=v_1\), \(Bv_1=v_2\), \(F_3v_j=j^3v_j\), and \(\left\langle e^A v_2\right\rangle=1/4\). Formula (2.29) has vacuum value \(e^{8u/3}/4\); printed (2.30) has \(e^{10u/3}/4\). With \(g=0,b=1\) the numbers are \(4/3\) and \(5/3\). The proof on p. 23 already uses the correct inverse exponential. Both findings are definition/use mismatches, with evidence of the intended local repair.
Problem 6 (Minor: the full parity projection is not a Lie homomorphism).
Location. Proposition 4.8 and its proof (pp. 23–24); the subsequent dressing argument (pp. 24–26).

Even after correcting the centering, the A-type relation gives \[[\mathcal E_2(0),\mathcal E_0(w)]=s(2w)\mathcal E_2(w),\qquad
 [\mathcal E_{2,0},\mathcal E_{0,2}]=2\mathcal E_{2,1}.\] The proposed \(p\) kills both inputs, since their index-plus-degree is even. It sends the bracket to \(2\mathcal E^B_{2,1}\neq0\). For a finite nonzero test, the vacuum component of \(\mathcal E^B_2(w)v_2\) is \(\tfrac12\sinh(w)|0\rangle\). Thus the coefficient of \(w\) does not vanish.

A narrower algebraic route is available. Let \(\tau\) be the anti-automorphism with \(\tau(S)=-S\), \(\tau(H)=-H\). The \(\tau\)-anti-invariant elements form a Lie subalgebra; the odd parity sector embeds correctly there. The actual operators \(D,\widetilde D,X,E\) of Lemma 4.9 are anti-invariant. For \(W'=WE/t\), \(W(0)=1\), one obtains \(\tau(W)=W^{-1}\) whenever this formal solution is defined, so its conjugation preserves the required subalgebra. This supplies a restricted route for the displayed calculations, not the asserted homomorphism from the full algebra. The choices of formal completion, central lift, and triangular normalization still require explanation. In particular the actual definition is \(Z=tS^2/(2u)\); it has not been silently replaced by its reciprocal. No counterexample to the commutator formula itself is asserted.
Problem 7 (Minor: the one-point recurrence and auxiliary energy are wrong).
Location. Corollary 5.5, (5.14)–(5.16) (p. 30); supplement, pp. 1–2, Corollary 2, Definition 4, Lemma 5.

With \(s=s(z),q_0=q_0(z)\), the printed recurrence starts at \((U_1,V_1)=(sq_0,q_0)\) and gives \[U_2=sq_0(s^2+4)=\tfrac12\sinh(2z)+\sinh z.\] The degree-two Fock space has the single strict partition \((2)\) with norm weight \(1/2\), hence \(U_2=\tfrac12\sinh(2z)\). For the valid parameters \(d=2,n=1,k=1,g=0\), (5.13) therefore gives \(-5/12\) from the printed recurrence, but \(-1/3\) from Corollary 5.6 and the actual operator expression.

Equation (5.16) defines \(V_d\) with total nonzero energy: \(\left\langle A^d\mathcal E_1(z)B^{d-1}\right\rangle=0\), contradicting \(V_1=q_0\). The supplement supplies the correctly balanced definition \(V_d=\left\langle A^{d-1}\mathcal E_1(z)B^d\right\rangle\) and the relations \[\begin{split}
 V_d&=sU_{d-1}+\frac{d-1}{2}V_{d-1}
       +\frac{(d-1)!}{2^{d-1}}q_0,\\
 U_d&=sV_d+\frac d2 U_{d-1}.
 \end{split}\] They follow by commuting \(A\) and \(B\), using \([A,B]=1/2\), \([A,\widehat{\mathcal E}_0]=s\mathcal E_1\), and \([\mathcal E_1,B]=s\widehat{\mathcal E}_0+q_0\). The corrected matrix and inhomogeneous term are thus \[\begin{pmatrix}s^2+d/2&(d-1)s/2\\s&(d-1)/2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \frac{(d-1)!}{2^{d-1}}q_0\binom{s}{1}.\] The initial review’s retained finite occupation-space implementation of the CAR verified these recurrences and all eight rows of the supplement’s Table 1 for \(1\leq d\leq8\). It also recovers the multipoint spectral sums \[\begin{split}
 d=1 &: \tfrac12\prod_i\sinh z_i,\\
 d=2 &: \tfrac12\prod_i\sinh(2z_i),\\
 d=3 &: \tfrac12\prod_i\sinh(3z_i)
       +\tfrac14\prod_i(\sinh(2z_i)+\sinh z_i).
 \end{split}\] These are counterevidence to any claim that all of the low-degree formulas are wrong. The recurrence can be corrected without discarding Proposition 5.4.
Problem 8 (Major: the conditional extension uses an undefined positive form).
Location. Section 5.2, (5.11)–(5.12) and the following conclusion (p. 29).

A possible proof would use a sufficiently large finite partition cutoff on each filtered finite-dimensional subspace, prove nondegeneracy of the resulting positive form, and justify (5.12) coefficient by coefficient. A unipotent isometry of a positive finite-dimensional form is the identity. The missing separation and identification steps have not been supplied here. The valid finite-dimensional isometry argument does not supply the missing Gram form or identity (5.12). These are the actual steps used to identify the two completed-cycle bases and prove Theorem E from Conjecture D. Their failure is therefore a Major gap in that conditional proof; no counterexample to Theorem E or Conjecture D is claimed.
# Coverage, checks, and assessment

The localization parity filter and its specialized positive-degree edge factors, the stable Hodge vertex expressions, and the global sign and parameter bookkeeping were traced with their hypotheses intact. The decomposition of the identity in Lemma 5.2 and the stated exclusion of degree-zero components in Proposition 5.4 were retained. The Section 6 divisor and string arguments and the BKP dependency on the dressing operators were read, without treating unproved central/degree-zero consistency as automatic. No independent counterexample to a fully corrected positive-degree correspondence or BKP theorem has been produced.

The initial-review executor’s retained Python/SymPy run exited zero. Its actual assertions check the completed-cycle coefficients, Hodge scalar, parity test, CAR recurrence through degree eight, and strict-partition norm weights. The present executor inspected the unchanged script and output and independently checked the analytic arguments. The conjugation numbers in Problem 5 and bracket in Problem 6 are only printed constants in that script; their justification is the explicit operator calculation above. The genus-one geometry in Problem 2 is likewise analytic. No author code or moduli-space computational package was run.

The original native cross-checks and source viewing belong to the initial review. A native read-only auxiliary also challenged these eight Problems during acceptance and checked the exact supplement and calculation bindings. Native assistance is neither human review nor independent backend verification.

Assessment: major revision required. Problems 1–4 and 8 are Major: they concern core normalization, a stable boundary formula, the Hodge operator, literal principal statements, and the conditional extension’s proof. Problems 5–7 remain Minor, with explicit local repairs and counterevidence from the actual downstream formulas. A possible repair does not reduce the severity of a core invalid statement or inference. No claim is made that every principal conclusion is false after consistent repair. Scientific adjudication is pending; no human reviews are recorded.

problems.title: One-point recurrence and V energy are incorrect
problems.source_location: p30 Cor5.5 Eq5.14-5.16 supplement pp1-2 Table1 Definition4 Lemma5
claim: Recorded check: One-point recurrence and V energy are incorrect
analysis: Location. Corollary 5.5, (5.14)–(5.16) (p. 30); supplement, pp. 1–2, Corollary 2, Definition 4, Lemma 5.

With \(s=s(z),q_0=q_0(z)\), the printed recurrence starts at \((U_1,V_1)=(sq_0,q_0)\) and gives \[U_2=sq_0(s^2+4)=\tfrac12\sinh(2z)+\sinh z.\] The degree-two Fock space has the single strict partition \((2)\) with norm weight \(1/2\), hence \(U_2=\tfrac12\sinh(2z)\). For the valid parameters \(d=2,n=1,k=1,g=0\), (5.13) therefore gives \(-5/12\) from the printed recurrence, but \(-1/3\) from Corollary 5.6 and the actual operator expression.

Equation (5.16) defines \(V_d\) with total nonzero energy: \(\left\langle A^d\mathcal E_1(z)B^{d-1}\right\rangle=0\), contradicting \(V_1=q_0\). The supplement supplies the correctly balanced definition \(V_d=\left\langle A^{d-1}\mathcal E_1(z)B^d\right\rangle\) and the relations \[\begin{split}
 V_d&=sU_{d-1}+\frac{d-1}{2}V_{d-1}
       +\frac{(d-1)!}{2^{d-1}}q_0,\\
 U_d&=sV_d+\frac d2 U_{d-1}.
 \end{split}\] They follow by commuting \(A\) and \(B\), using \([A,B]=1/2\), \([A,\widehat{\mathcal E}_0]=s\mathcal E_1\), and \([\mathcal E_1,B]=s\widehat{\mathcal E}_0+q_0\). The corrected matrix and inhomogeneous term are thus \[\begin{pmatrix}s^2+d/2&(d-1)s/2\\s&(d-1)/2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \frac{(d-1)!}{2^{d-1}}q_0\binom{s}{1}.\] The initial review’s retained finite occupation-space implementation of the CAR verified these recurrences and all eight rows of the supplement’s Table 1 for \(1\leq d\leq8\). It also recovers the multipoint spectral sums \[\begin{split}
 d=1 &: \tfrac12\prod_i\sinh z_i,\\
 d=2 &: \tfrac12\prod_i\sinh(2z_i),\\
 d=3 &: \tfrac12\prod_i\sinh(3z_i)
       +\tfrac14\prod_i(\sinh(2z_i)+\sinh z_i).
 \end{split}\] These are counterevidence to any claim that all of the low-degree formulas are wrong. The recurrence can be corrected without discarding Proposition 5.4.

report: Abstract: The 47-page second arXiv version of Hogancamp, Rose, and Wedrich is examined. The comparison in Theorem C with the full \(\mathfrak{gl}_2\) skein lasagna module is incompatible with the zero-framed unknot: its degree-zero dimension is infinite, whereas the total Kirby color gives dimension two. The fixed-class statement in Theorem 6.8 has a narrower scope. Other corrections concern finality and compact objects in general background statements, a reversed triangular inequality, a multiplicity and a grading shift in completed tensor products, and the displayed cabling limit. Several central finite algebra calculations and the filtered-colimit logic receive positive checks. The findings do not refute the Kirby object construction or the elementary handle-slide isomorphism. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Integer homology classes, completion, and grading conventions in a Kirby color for Khovanov homology
# Identity, scope, and proof structure

The reviewed work is M. Hogancamp, D. E. V. Rose, and P. Wedrich, A Kirby color for Khovanov homology, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1589. The actual primary source is arXiv:2210.05640v2, dated 25 October 2022, with 47 pages [paper]. The journal records submission on 6 February 2023, acceptance on 14 July 2024, and publication on 17 February 2025 [journal]. This review does not assert that the preprint and subscription journal PDF are equivalent. All 2,799 extracted-text lines and all 47 source pages were read and viewed. The retained author TeX was consulted for specific formulas, without compiling or executing author code. No article-specific computational supplement or executable code was located in the bounded source search; their absence is not a defect.

The paper first establishes graded category and completion conventions in Section 2, then the dotted Temperley–Lieb presentation, symmetrizers, quiver relations, and the faithful polynomial functor in Section 3. Section 4 constructs the Kirby ind-objects and handle-slide isomorphisms. Section 5 develops graphical rules, Hom representability, locally finite sums, and tensor-product decompositions. Section 6 extends colored Khovanov homology and compares it with skein lasagna modules. Section 7 describes further directions. This order matters: finite-dimensional polynomial checks do not by themselves establish coherence of all four-dimensional cobordism maps.

Throughout the calculations below, \(\mathbb K\) has characteristic zero, as assumed in the manuscript. Page numbers refer to the primary PDF. For the substantive comparison issue, the author-hosted 35-page Manolescu–Neithalath source [MN] was additionally obtained, and its first two pages were read and actually viewed. Only that bounded external dependency was checked; no complete review of that other paper is claimed.
# A substantive scope obstruction

Problem 1 (Major: Theorem C compares with too large a module).  Theorem C on p. 3 identifies the total-color invariant with the \(N=2\) skein lasagna module of the attached two-handlebody, without fixing an integer relative homology class. The preceding discussion specifies the \(\mathfrak{gl}_N\) theory. This is stronger than Theorem 6.8 on p. 42, whose index lies in \(\{0,1\}^r\) and denotes a particular class in \(H_2(B^4(L_2),L_1;\mathbb Z)\).

Take \(L_1=\varnothing\) and let \(L_2=U\) be the zero-framed unknot. Then \(B^4(U)=S^2\times D^2\). Proposition 4.6 (p. 23) and Example 6.7 (p. 41) give \[\operatorname{Kh}(U^{\omega_i})\cong\bigoplus_{n\geq0}q^{-2n}\mathbb K,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Kh}(U^\omega)\cong
 \bigoplus_{n\geq0}q^{-2n}(\mathbb K\oplus\mathbb K),
 \quad \omega=\omega_0\oplus\omega_1.\] In particular its homological and quantum degree \((0,0)\) has dimension \(2\).

In contrast, [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 1.2, p.~2]{MN}] states \[\mathcal S^2_{0,0,*}(S^2\times D^2;\varnothing)
 \cong \mathbb Z[A_1,A_0,A_0^{-1}],
 \qquad \deg_q A_1=-2,\quad \deg_q A_0=0.\] After extension to \(\mathbb K\), the vectors \(A_0^m\), \(m\in\mathbb Z\), are linearly independent in degree \((0,0)\). Thus that degree is countably infinite-dimensional. This contradicts the bigraded isomorphism in the literal full-module reading of Theorem C. Merely forgetting the integer homology grading does not identify different vectors or reduce this dimension.

The evidence against overextending this counterexample is also explicit in the manuscript. Example 6.7 first compares each \(\omega_i\) to a fixed-class calculation. Theorem 6.8 restricts the integer class to the chosen parity representatives. Remark 6.9 (p. 43) acknowledges that other integer classes can have grading shifts and that \(\mathfrak{gl}_2\) foams would remove the discrepancy. Remark 1.4 (p. 4) discusses a different \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) version with a \(\mathbb Z/2\) grading; it does not define the full \(\mathfrak{gl}_2\) module to be a mod-two quotient. None of these passages identifies all the Laurent monomials in the displayed external ring.

The necessary repair is to state exactly which module is being compared. One may retain the fixed-class conclusion of Theorem 6.8, with the normalization correction in Problem 6, and restrict the global conclusion accordingly. A genuinely mod-two or \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) version requires a precise definition and a comparison proof. Alternatively, a construction retaining all integer classes could target the full \(\mathfrak{gl}_2\) module. Simply changing its name is insufficient. Nor does the fixed-class comparison alone show that selecting the particular integer lifts \(0,1\) is canonical under all handle changes. The local handle-slide construction may have its own invariance argument; the invalid full-module identification cannot supply that missing implication. This is a central theorem-scope issue, not a counterexample to existence of \(\omega_i\).
# Background hypotheses and finite algebra

Problem 2 (Minor: the finality criterion omits a connectivity hypothesis).  Definition 2.18 (p. 8) omits nonemptiness from filteredness. Lemma 2.20 (p. 9) then states a finality criterion without assuming that its source indexing category \(I\) is filtered. Its two printed conditions are insufficient.

Let \(I\) consist of two isolated objects, \(J\) of one object, and \(F:I\to J\) be the unique functor. The first condition holds, and all relevant pairs of parallel maps in \(J\) are equal, so the second holds too. For the constant diagram \(\alpha(*)=\mathbb K\) in degree zero, the canonical comparison is \[\operatorname*{colim}_{I}\alpha F=\mathbb K\oplus\mathbb K
 \longrightarrow \operatorname*{colim}_{J}\alpha=\mathbb K,
 \qquad (a,b)\longmapsto a+b.\] It has the nonzero kernel vector \((1,-1)\) and is not an isomorphism. Thus \(F\) is not final.

Add nonemptiness to Definition 2.18, and assume \(I\) filtered in Lemma 2.20, or use the standard nonempty-connected comma-category criterion directly. With the filtered assumption, two arrows \(j\to F(i_1),j\to F(i_2)\) can first be moved to a common successor in \(I\); the second printed condition then equalizes them. This proves the needed connectedness. The tail inclusions used in Lemma 4.3 and the diagonal/cofinal sequences in Sections 4–5 already have nonempty filtered sources, so the counterexample does not invalidate those applications.

Problem 3 (Minor: compact objects require idempotent completion).  Remark 2.24 (p. 10) identifies an arbitrary graded linear category \(C\) with the compact objects of \(\operatorname{Ind}(C)\). This identification needs an idempotent-completeness hypothesis, or replacement of \(C\) by its Karoubi envelope.

Let \(C\) have a single object \(X\) with \(\operatorname{End}(X)=M_2(\mathbb K)\), concentrated in degree zero, and put \(e=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\). The ind-object \[E=\operatorname*{colim}(X\xrightarrow e X\xrightarrow e X
 \xrightarrow e\cdots)\] splits \(e\) and is a retract of the compact object \(X\), hence is compact. But \(\operatorname{End}(E)=eM_2(\mathbb K)e\cong\mathbb K\), so \(E\) cannot be isomorphic to the only original object \(X\). This is a failure of the asserted identification, not of compact generation. Convention 4.1 (p. 22) already takes the finite graded additive and Karoubi completions before forming the main ind-category. The intended main setting therefore has an available repair.

Problem 4 (Minor: triangular direction and two algebraic notations).  Proposition 3.26, especially (19) on p. 20, reverses the zero condition in its triangular pairing. Lemma 3.20 (p. 17) has an ill-typed index in one composition, and the proof of Corollary 3.23 (p. 19) prints a tensor product where a product is required.

For the first error use four boundary points and undotted caps \[d_{\mathrm{par}}=(1,2)(3,4),\qquad
 d_{\mathrm{nest}}=(1,4)(2,3).\] The manuscript’s monomials are \(\delta_{\mathrm{par}}^*=x_1x_3\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{nest}}^*=x_1x_2\). In the prescribed lexicographic order, the nested monomial is larger, but \[d_{\mathrm{nest}}(x_1x_3)=1.\] Thus the claim of vanishing for \(i>j\) is false. Ordering parallel before nested, the pairing matrix is \[\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.\] The correct condition is vanishing for \(i<j\). Indeed, a nonzero evaluation chooses exactly one endpoint of every undotted cap and no endpoint of a dotted cap. The ordered left endpoints are componentwise no larger than the chosen endpoints; their monomial is therefore lexicographically no smaller. Equality and the greedy reconstruction give the diagonal entries. This repairs the triangular proof and preserves faithfulness.

The two composition relations should be written separately: \[U_{n-2}D_n=-z_n^2\quad\hbox{in }\operatorname{End}(P_n),\qquad
 D_nU_{n-2}=-z_{n-2}^2\quad\hbox{in }\operatorname{End}(P_{n-2}).\] The proof already supplies the second correct subscript. For the center, the truncation is \(z_n^{n+1}\) rather than \(z_n^n\), and the even and odd inverse systems give \(\mathbb K[z]\times\mathbb K[z]\), not \(\mathbb K[z]\otimes\mathbb K[z]\). The correct map is \[(f,g)\longmapsto \frac{1+s}{2}f+\frac{1-s}{2}g
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb K[s,z]/(s^2-1).\] The printed tensor rule is not bilinear: \(f\otimes0=0\), but its proposed image is generally nonzero. The graded-limit convention in Remark 3.24 is sound; it gives polynomials, not an unrestricted power-series ring. These corrections leave the final center description intact.

There is positive evidence for the core finite algebra. Set \(y_a=(-1)^{a-1}x_a\) and \(z_n=\sum_a y_a\). The symmetrizer acts by ordinary permutations of the \(y_a\), and characteristic zero gives \[z_n^j=j!\,e_j(y_1,\ldots,y_n),\qquad
 \operatorname{Pol}(P_n)=q^{-n}\langle1,z_n,\ldots,z_n^n\rangle.\] With the specified dotted cup and cap normalization, \[U_m(z_m^j)=-\frac{z_{m+2}^{j+2}}{(m+1)(m+2)},\qquad
 D_{m+2}(z_{m+2}^j)=(m+1)(m+2)z_m^j,\] where powers beyond the truncation are zero. The two compositions are exactly the correctly indexed \(-z^2\). For \(n-m=2r\geq0\), \[(U_{n-2}\cdots U_m z_m^j)(1)
 =(-1)^r\frac{m!}{n!}z_n^{j+n-m},
 \qquad 0\leq j\leq m.\] These nonzero, distinct powers prove independence of the quiver spanning family. They support the stated Hom formula; they do not independently prove the external topological presentation of the annular category.
# Completion, cabling, and a boundary case

Problem 5 (Minor: multiplicity and grading in completed tensor products).  Section 5.4 (p. 35) twice writes \(\omega\otimes\omega\cong\bigoplus_{n\geq0}q^{-2n}\omega\). Proposition 5.27 has a separate extra shift in its proof on p. 38.

The degree-zero dimension of \(\operatorname{Pol}(\omega)\) is \(2\). Hence the degree-zero dimensions in the first displayed isomorphism are \(4\) and \(2\). Summing the four correct parity-component formulas in Corollary 5.25 gives instead \[\omega\otimes\omega
 \cong\bigoplus_{n\geq0}q^{-2n}(\omega\oplus\omega).\] This correction is consistent with the component formula.

In the proof of Proposition 5.27, the definition \(Y_n=q^{-i-j-2n}\omega'_{i+j}\) disagrees with the proposition’s \(q^{-2n}\omega'_{i+j}\). The merge followed by \(n\) pink dots has degree \(2n\), so into the printed shifted target its degree is \(-i-j\), whereas Definition 2.6 requires a degree-zero projection. For \((i,j)=(0,1)\) the left side has a one-dimensional degree-zero polynomial image, but the erroneously shifted right side has none. Remove the additional \(-i-j\) in \(Y_n\) and in the ensuing degree calculations. This is a repair of the proof’s normalization, not a refutation of the correctly stated proposition.

The convergence restriction on sums remains essential: Definition 5.21 permits a family only if its restriction along each canonical finite-stage inclusion has finite support. It does not allow arbitrary formal sums. Together with the finite-stage factorization in Lemma 5.20, this explains why composition of the admissible families is defined. The use of graded Hom also prevents replacing \(\operatorname{End}(\omega_i)=\mathbb K[z]\) by \(\mathbb K[[z]]\).

Problem 6 (Minor: the cabling colimit omits its grading shifts).  Equation (41), p. 42, omits the quantum shifts present in the construction, in Example 6.7, and in (42). It also prints \(i_r+n_r\) in the final cable exponent, where the indexing requires \(i_r+2n_r\).

Problem 7 (Minor: a future-direction vanishing claim includes identities).  Section 7.7 (p. 45) claims that all maps between its two-term complexes \(C_l\) and \(C_{l'}\) are null-homotopic when \(l\leq l'\), with \(P_l=0\) for negative indices. The equality case \(l=l'=0\) disproves this.

Here \(C_0\) is just \(P_0\) in degree zero. Its identity is nonzero because \(\operatorname{End}(P_0)=\mathbb K\). Both adjacent terms vanish, so every putative chain homotopy has \(dh+hd=0\) and cannot equal the identity. The statement must exclude equality or specify a different class of maps; this review does not claim that merely changing \(\leq\) to \(<\) proves every remaining case. The displayed arrow label also needs the source-compatible \(U_{l-2}\) under the earlier convention \(U_m:P_m\to P_{m+2}\). This future-direction error is not used in the main Kirby color construction.
# Checks that remain valid and limits of the assessment

The compact-test-object argument in Lemma 2.26 was checked: degreewise finiteness permits the sums, and the stipulated identity decomposition on compact generators identifies the biproduct. The elementary handle-slide argument uses an ind-object identity correctly. Composing the two finite slides gives a transition map, which becomes an isomorphism under the cofinal-tail identification; it need not be the identity on an unchanged finite stage.

The Hom representability argument extends from finite objects using duality and the polynomial tensor description, then converts filtered colimits into inverse limits. The graded dual convention is necessary here. Theorem 4.15 supplies a higher-categorical center construction as a proof sketch. This review has not independently rebuilt every two-dimensional cobordism relation or all higher coherence data. The introduction itself distinguishes handle-slide naturality from a direct Kirby-movie-coherent four-manifold functor. That acknowledged distinction is preserved rather than treated as an additional proved defect.

The reviewer’s retained exact-arithmetic script checked 15 cup columns, 25 cap columns, 40 composition columns, the four-endpoint triangular counterexample, and the finite Hilbert coefficients of the tensor-product identities. It terminated with exit code zero. The infinite-dimensional comparison uses the explicit Laurent basis and the cited ring theorem, not extrapolation from those finite computations. No author code was run. The external annular-presentation, colored-homology, and skein-lasagna theorems were not independently reproved in full.

Problem 1 warrants a major scientific revision of the comparison’s stated scope. Problems 2–7 admit narrower corrections or require a precise qualification. None establishes that all intended corrected results are false. Conversely, positive checks in selected dependencies do not certify the entire paper. These are initial-review findings; the formal scientific decision remains `pending`, and the human-review list is empty.

The external author-hosted PDF used only for pp. 1–2 is 588,540 bytes, SHA256

One checked Sections 2–3 and finite polynomial formulas; the other checked Sections 4–5 and the comparison scope. Their work was not an independent acceptance review. The controller’s reported UI selection and the runtime self-description are recorded separately; the backend has not been independently verified.

The accompanying records bind the exact source, TeX, compiler, dependencies, build logs, PDF, renders, actual page inspections, and the retained exact-check script. They preserve the unverified journal-version equivalence and the limited external-dependency scope.

claim: Finality criterion lacks sufficient connectivity assumption
analysis: Definition 2.18 (p. 8) omits nonemptiness from filteredness. Lemma 2.20 (p. 9) then states a finality criterion without assuming that its source indexing category \(I\) is filtered. Its two printed conditions are insufficient.

Let \(I\) consist of two isolated objects, \(J\) of one object, and \(F:I\to J\) be the unique functor. The first condition holds, and all relevant pairs of parallel maps in \(J\) are equal, so the second holds too. For the constant diagram \(\alpha(*)=\mathbb K\) in degree zero, the canonical comparison is \[\operatorname*{colim}_{I}\alpha F=\mathbb K\oplus\mathbb K
 \longrightarrow \operatorname*{colim}_{J}\alpha=\mathbb K,
 \qquad (a,b)\longmapsto a+b.\] It has the nonzero kernel vector \((1,-1)\) and is not an isomorphism. Thus \(F\) is not final.

Add nonemptiness to Definition 2.18, and assume \(I\) filtered in Lemma 2.20, or use the standard nonempty-connected comma-category criterion directly. With the filtered assumption, two arrows \(j\to F(i_1),j\to F(i_2)\) can first be moved to a common successor in \(I\); the second printed condition then equalizes them. This proves the needed connectedness. The tail inclusions used in Lemma 4.3 and the diagonal/cofinal sequences in Sections 4–5 already have nonempty filtered sources, so the counterexample does not invalidate those applications.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: I discrete two objects,J terminal,constant F satisfies printed conditions but K^2 -> K fold has kernel(1,-1). Empty category also meets printed filteredness axioms.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Actual index sequences are nonempty filtered.

problems.title: compact objects require idempotent completion
problems.source_location: Remark2.24 p10; Convention4.1 p22
claim: Compact objects in Ind(C) need idempotent completion
analysis: Remark 2.24 (p. 10) identifies an arbitrary graded linear category \(C\) with the compact objects of \(\operatorname{Ind}(C)\). This identification needs an idempotent-completeness hypothesis, or replacement of \(C\) by its Karoubi envelope.

Let \(C\) have a single object \(X\) with \(\operatorname{End}(X)=M_2(\mathbb K)\), concentrated in degree zero, and put \(e=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\). The ind-object \[E=\operatorname*{colim}(X\xrightarrow e X\xrightarrow e X
 \xrightarrow e\cdots)\] splits \(e\) and is a retract of the compact object \(X\), hence is compact. But \(\operatorname{End}(E)=eM_2(\mathbb K)e\cong\mathbb K\), so \(E\) cannot be isomorphic to the only original object \(X\). This is a failure of the asserted identification, not of compact generation. Convention 4.1 (p. 22) already takes the finite graded additive and Karoubi completions before forming the main ind-category. The intended main setting therefore has an available repair.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: One-object category End(X)=M2(K), e=diag(1,0); e-telescope compact retract E has End(E)=K and is not original X.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Main convention already takes finite additive/Karoubi completion.

problems.title: triangular direction and two algebraic notations
problems.source_location: Lemma3.20 p17; Corollary3.23 p19; Proposition3.26 Eq19 p20
claim: Finite algebra proof has reversed triangle, relation index, and product notation
analysis: Proposition 3.26, especially (19) on p. 20, reverses the zero condition in its triangular pairing. Lemma 3.20 (p. 17) has an ill-typed index in one composition, and the proof of Corollary 3.23 (p. 19) prints a tensor product where a product is required.

For the first error use four boundary points and undotted caps \[d_{\mathrm{par}}=(1,2)(3,4),\qquad
 d_{\mathrm{nest}}=(1,4)(2,3).\] The manuscript’s monomials are \(\delta_{\mathrm{par}}^*=x_1x_3\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{nest}}^*=x_1x_2\). In the prescribed lexicographic order, the nested monomial is larger, but \[d_{\mathrm{nest}}(x_1x_3)=1.\] Thus the claim of vanishing for \(i>j\) is false. Ordering parallel before nested, the pairing matrix is \[\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.\] The correct condition is vanishing for \(i<j\). Indeed, a nonzero evaluation chooses exactly one endpoint of every undotted cap and no endpoint of a dotted cap. The ordered left endpoints are componentwise no larger than the chosen endpoints; their monomial is therefore lexicographically no smaller. Equality and the greedy reconstruction give the diagonal entries. This repairs the triangular proof and preserves faithfulness.

The two composition relations should be written separately: \[U_{n-2}D_n=-z_n^2\quad\hbox{in }\operatorname{End}(P_n),\qquad
 D_nU_{n-2}=-z_{n-2}^2\quad\hbox{in }\operatorname{End}(P_{n-2}).\] The proof already supplies the second correct subscript. For the center, the truncation is \(z_n^{n+1}\) rather than \(z_n^n\), and the even and odd inverse systems give \(\mathbb K[z]\times\mathbb K[z]\), not \(\mathbb K[z]\otimes\mathbb K[z]\). The correct map is \[(f,g)\longmapsto \frac{1+s}{2}f+\frac{1-s}{2}g
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb K[s,z]/(s^2-1).\] The printed tensor rule is not bilinear: \(f\otimes0=0\), but its proposed image is generally nonzero. The graded-limit convention in Remark 3.24 is sound; it gives polynomials, not an unrestricted power-series ring. These corrections leave the final center description intact.

There is positive evidence for the core finite algebra. Set \(y_a=(-1)^{a-1}x_a\) and \(z_n=\sum_a y_a\). The symmetrizer acts by ordinary permutations of the \(y_a\), and characteristic zero gives \[z_n^j=j!\,e_j(y_1,\ldots,y_n),\qquad
 \operatorname{Pol}(P_n)=q^{-n}\langle1,z_n,\ldots,z_n^n\rangle.\] With the specified dotted cup and cap normalization, \[U_m(z_m^j)=-\frac{z_{m+2}^{j+2}}{(m+1)(m+2)},\qquad
 D_{m+2}(z_{m+2}^j)=(m+1)(m+2)z_m^j,\] where powers beyond the truncation are zero. The two compositions are exactly the correctly indexed \(-z^2\). For \(n-m=2r\geq0\), \[(U_{n-2}\cdots U_m z_m^j)(1)
 =(-1)^r\frac{m!}{n!}z_n^{j+n-m},
 \qquad 0\leq j\leq m.\] These nonzero, distinct powers prove independence of the quiver spanning family. They support the stated Hom formula; they do not independently prove the external topological presentation of the annular category.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: Ordered parallel/nested four-cap pairing [[1,0],[1,1]] violates zero for i>j; correct i<j. D_n U_(n-2) lies in End(P_(n-2)). Even/odd center gives product not tensor; proposed tensor map not bilinear; truncation n+1.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Corrected triangle determinant1; adjacent proof has correct index; graded center conclusion preserved.
