problems.title: multiplicity and grading in completed tensor products
problems.source_location: Section5.4 p35; Proposition5.27 proof pp38-39
claim: Total-color tensor square misses factor2; proof Y_n has extra -i-j
analysis: Section 5.4 (p. 35) twice writes \(\omega\otimes\omega\cong\bigoplus_{n\geq0}q^{-2n}\omega\). Proposition 5.27 has a separate extra shift in its proof on p. 38.

The degree-zero dimension of \(\operatorname{Pol}(\omega)\) is \(2\). Hence the degree-zero dimensions in the first displayed isomorphism are \(4\) and \(2\). Summing the four correct parity-component formulas in Corollary 5.25 gives instead \[\omega\otimes\omega
 \cong\bigoplus_{n\geq0}q^{-2n}(\omega\oplus\omega).\] This correction is consistent with the component formula.

In the proof of Proposition 5.27, the definition \(Y_n=q^{-i-j-2n}\omega'_{i+j}\) disagrees with the proposition’s \(q^{-2n}\omega'_{i+j}\). The merge followed by \(n\) pink dots has degree \(2n\), so into the printed shifted target its degree is \(-i-j\), whereas Definition 2.6 requires a degree-zero projection. For \((i,j)=(0,1)\) the left side has a one-dimensional degree-zero polynomial image, but the erroneously shifted right side has none. Remove the additional \(-i-j\) in \(Y_n\) and in the ensuing degree calculations. This is a repair of the proof’s normalization, not a refutation of the correctly stated proposition.

The convergence restriction on sums remains essential: Definition 5.21 permits a family only if its restriction along each canonical finite-stage inclusion has finite support. It does not allow arbitrary formal sums. Together with the finite-stage factorization in Lemma 5.20, this explains why composition of the admissible families is defined. The use of graded Hom also prevents replacing \(\operatorname{End}(\omega_i)=\mathbb K[z]\) by \(\mathbb K[[z]]\).

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Corollary5.25 component formula and Prop5.27 statement have correct normalization.

problems.title: a future-direction vanishing claim includes identities
problems.source_location: Section7.7 p45
claim: Null-homotopy assertion includes identity at equality
analysis: Section 7.7 (p. 45) claims that all maps between its two-term complexes \(C_l\) and \(C_{l'}\) are null-homotopic when \(l\leq l'\), with \(P_l=0\) for negative indices. The equality case \(l=l'=0\) disproves this.

Here \(C_0\) is just \(P_0\) in degree zero. Its identity is nonzero because \(\operatorname{End}(P_0)=\mathbb K\). Both adjacent terms vanish, so every putative chain homotopy has \(dh+hd=0\) and cannot equal the identity. The statement must exclude equality or specify a different class of maps; this review does not claim that merely changing \(\leq\) to \(<\) proves every remaining case. The displayed arrow label also needs the source-compatible \(U_{l-2}\) under the earlier convention \(U_m:P_m\to P_{m+2}\). This future-direction error is not used in the main Kirby color construction.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: l=l'=0 gives C0=P0 in one degree, End(P0)=K and no adjacent terms; identity cannot equal dh+hd=0.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Future direction not used in main construction.

report: Abstract: The 45-page publisher-typeset online-first article of Du, Gárriz, and Quirós is examined. Explicit weak solutions contradict two parameter regimes of the stated pressure gradient estimate. Differentiating the pressure equation reveals an omitted source term in the wave-speed calculation; a concrete admissible reaction contradicts its universal derivative bound. A separate energy inequality rules out the static subsolution used in the hair-trigger proof. Further corrections concern one-dimensional scope, tail normalization, and a missing logarithmic phase in a comparison function. These results identify false auxiliary statements and gaps in major proof dependencies. They do not establish that the intended asymptotic theorem, formulated using the actual wave-speed derivative, is false after repair. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Flux estimates, wave-speed differentiation, and comparison arguments for doubly nonlinear travelling waves
# Identity and mathematical scope

The reviewed article is Y. Du, A. Gárriz, and F. Quirós, Precise travelling-wave behaviour in problems with doubly nonlinear diffusion, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1590 [paper]. The actual source is the 45-page publisher-typeset online-first PDF deposited in the University of Granada repository. It displays the JEMS imprint, 2025 copyright, receipt on 12 February 2023, and revision on 14 December 2023. The publisher records acceptance on 21 April 2024 and publication on 17 January 2025 [journal]. The restricted current publisher download was not byte-compared with this institutional copy. An older, differently titled arXiv candidate was not assumed equivalent or used as the primary source. No exact-version author TeX archive or computational supplement was verified in the bounded acquisition search. No author code was executed.

All 2,403 extracted-text lines were read and all 45 PDF pages actually viewed, including the formulas discussed below. The problem is \[u_t=\Delta_p(u^m)+h(u),\qquad
 m>0,\quad p>1,\quad m(p-1)>1.\] Write \(\alpha=(p-1)^{-1}\) and \(v=m u^{m-\alpha}/(m-\alpha)\). The standing reaction assumptions are \(C^1\) regularity, the sign pattern (1.2), and \(h'(1)<0\); the positive weighted reaction integral in the bistable case is also required. The main precise asymptotics assume \(p\geq2\) and spreading. They do not assert that every bistable or combustion datum spreads. Lemma 3.1 explicitly uses a larger reaction class, including \(h\equiv0\).

The principal dependencies are the Section 3 flux estimate, the finite-wave and parameter analysis of Section 4, the spreading constructions in Section 5, and the barriers and eternal-solution argument in Section 6. The final convergence argument is largely transferred from cited porous-medium proofs. This review checks the internal chain and its displayed calculations; it does not claim to have independently reproved every external regularity, uniqueness, or eternal-solution theorem.
# Substantive problems

Problem 1 (Major: the pressure-gradient estimate has false regimes).  Lemma 3.1, pp. 10–11, especially (3.2), asserts \[|v_r|\leq
 \begin{cases}
 C M^{(m-\alpha)/p}(t^{-1}+H)^{1/p},&p\geq2,\\
 C M^{(m-\alpha)/2}(t^{-1}+H)^{1/2},&1<p<2,
 \end{cases}\] where \(C\) depends only on the constant convection parameter \(\gamma\), \(m\), and \(p\). The pure-diffusion case is expressly included. Both a nonzero-convection large-time limit and a singular-exponent short-time scaling contradict this claim.

First take \(p=m=2\), \(h=0\), \(\gamma>0\), and \(M>0\). For \(z>0\) set \[F(z)=M(1-e^{-\gamma z/2}),\qquad F(z)=0\quad(z\leq0),
 \qquad u(r,t)=F(r+\gamma Mt-R).\] On the positive branch, \[(F^2)'+\gamma F^2=\gamma MF.\] Differentiating proves \(u_t=(u^2)_{rr}+\gamma(u^2)_r\). The density and diffusive flux are continuous at the free boundary, with zero flux there, so this is a bounded weak solution of the auxiliary convection equation. Its pressure is \(v=2u\) and \[v_r=\gamma M e^{-\gamma z/2}\qquad(z>0).\] Given an arbitrarily large \(T\), choose \(R=\gamma MT+1\); then the front lies at \(r=1\) at time \(T\). At a fixed positive distance behind that increasing front, \(|v_r|\) is a positive constant independent of \(T\). The printed upper bound is \(CM^{1/2}T^{-1/2}\). Since \(C\) cannot depend on \(R\), the estimates are incompatible. This example addresses the stated bounded-solution class; it is not compactly supported on the whole line.

There is also a compactly supported, even counterexample to the \(1<p<2\) time exponent, with zero convection. Take \(p=3/2\), \(m=3\), \(\alpha=2\), \(h=0\), and \[B(x,s)=\left(s^{-1/2}-\frac{|x|^3}{36s^2}\right)_+ .\] In the positive set its flux is \[|(B^3)_x|^{-1/2}(B^3)_x=-\frac{xB}{2s}.\] Direct differentiation gives \(B_s=(-xB/(2s))_x\); the flux vanishes at the interface. Thus \(B\) is a weak solution. For \(\lambda>0\) put \[u_\lambda(x,t)=B\left(\frac{x}{\lambda},
                 1+\frac{t}{\lambda^{3/2}}\right).\] The initial supremum is \(M=1\), the data are even and compactly supported, and \(v_\lambda=3u_\lambda\). At \(x=\lambda\), \(t=\lambda^{3/2}\), \[|(v_\lambda)_x|=\frac{1}{16\lambda},
 \qquad
 CM^{1/2}t^{-1/2}=C\lambda^{-3/4}.\] No fixed \(C\) can satisfy this as \(\lambda\downarrow0\). This is an exact scaling contradiction, not a numerical approximation.

The proof exposes the corresponding defects. The Young inequality after (3.16), p. 17, applied to the convection term containing \(+1\), leaves a term that does not vanish with the spatial cutoff. That remainder is absent from (3.17), p. 18. On p. 19 the assertion that one may always arrange \(c_2S^{1-p}(t^{-1}+H)\geq1\) is impossible for \(H=0\) and unbounded \(t\). Moreover the maximum of its first power and its \(2/p\) power cannot generally be replaced by the selected branch in (3.2).

A valid replacement must retain the convection contribution and correct the time/scaling dependence. Corollary 3.2, pp. 19–20, invokes this derivation and therefore needs its own corrected argument. The weaker conclusion of Theorem 2.6 is only a bound for each fixed \(\tau>0\) and \(r\geq\rho>0\); these examples do not disprove that weaker statement. Nor does a counterexample with \(p<2\) directly refute the main asymptotic theorem, which assumes \(p\geq2\). Nevertheless, the advertised central technical estimate and its proof require substantive repair.

Problem 2 (Major: wave-speed differentiation loses a source term).  Lemma 4.15, pp. 30–32, asserts \(c'(\gamma)\in(-m,0)\). The displayed integral formula on p. 31 and (4.14) on p. 32 omit the contribution from differentiating \(\gamma|\mathcal P|^{p-2}\).

Here is a concrete counterexample to the joint differentiability-and-bound assertion. Take \(m=1\), \(p=3\), and, for \(a>0\), define \[h_a(u)=
 \begin{cases}
 a^3u^{3/2}(1-u)(4-3u),&0\leq u\leq1,\\
 -a^3(u-1),&u\geq1.
 \end{cases}\] This is \(C^1\), satisfies the monostable sign assumptions, and has \(h_a'(1)=-a^3\). At \(\gamma=0\) the finite profile is \[U(\xi)=\tanh^2(a\xi/2)\quad(\xi<0),\qquad
 U(\xi)=0\quad(\xi\geq0),\qquad c=a^2.\] Indeed \(U'=-a\sqrt U(1-U)\) and \(\phi(U)=a^2U(1-U)^2\) verify the wave equation exactly. Differentiate the trajectory equation (4.5) along the parameter branch whose regularity the lemma asserts. For \(Z=\partial_\gamma\phi\) this yields \[Z'=c'+a\sqrt U(1-U)
          +\frac{4-3U}{2(1-U)^2}Z .\] An integrating factor is \[\mu(U)=(1-U)^{3/2}
                  \exp\!\left(-\frac1{2(1-U)}\right).\] The asserted endpoint regularity implies vanishing boundary terms, and hence \[c'_a(0)=-a\,\frac{J}{I},\quad
 I=\int_0^1\mu(U)\,\mathrm dU,\quad
 J=\int_0^1\mu(U)\sqrt U(1-U)\,\mathrm dU.\] Using the whole interval for \(I\) and \([1/4,1/2]\) for \(J\), \[I\leq\frac25 e^{-1/2},\qquad
 J\geq\frac{e^{-1}}{32\sqrt2},\qquad
 \frac{J}{I}\geq\frac{5e^{-1/2}}{64\sqrt2}.\] Thus \(a=100\) forces \(c'_a(0)<-3\), contrary to \(c'(0)>-m=-1\). If the claimed regular parameter branch failed to exist, that would already violate the other part of the same lemma. The contradiction therefore does not presume the incorrect printed derivative formula.

The reaction scaling \(h\mapsto\lambda h\) provides a second check: \[c_\lambda(\gamma)=
 \lambda^{(p-1)/p}c_1(\gamma\lambda^{-1/p}),\qquad
 c'_\lambda(0)=\lambda^{(p-2)/p}c'_1(0).\] A nonzero negative derivative cannot have a universal lower bound \(-m\) for all \(\lambda\) when \(p>2\). The corrected formula can instead give a reaction-dependent bound involving \(\sup W^{p-2}\). The continuation estimate on p. 33 based on \(c(\gamma)\geq c(0)-m\gamma\) must also be revised.

This matters to the proof of the logarithmic shift, which uses parameter regularity and an inverse speed function. It does not by itself contradict the main asymptotic statement when \(c_\sharp\) is defined by the actual \(-c'(0)/c_*\). A corrected parameter analysis may still supply the local estimates that argument needs.

Problem 3 (Major: the hair-trigger proof uses an impossible static subsolution).  In Lemma 5.2, p. 34, the initial bump \(\underline u=\delta(1-|x|^\sigma)_+^\beta\) is claimed to satisfy \(-\Delta_p(\underline u^m)-\widehat h(\underline u)\leq0\) when \(\beta\) and \(\sigma\) are sufficiently large. The subsequent time-monotonicity argument depends on this assertion.

Take \(N=1\), \(p=m=2\), \(\delta=1/2\), so the Fujita exponent is \(q_F=4\). An explicit allowed reaction is \[\widehat h(u)=u^4\bigl[1-16(u-3/4)_+^2\bigr].\] It is \(C^1\), positive on \((0,1)\), negative on \((1,\infty)\), and \(\widehat h'(1)=-8\). It equals \(u^4\) on \([0,3/4]\). For every sufficiently regular choice of the proposed bump, put \(w=\underline u^2\). Then \(0\leq w\leq1/4\), \(w\not\equiv0\), and \(w\in H^1_0(-1,1)\). The alleged static-subsolution inequality would be \(-w''\leq w^2\). Testing by \(w\) gives \[\frac{\pi^2}{4}\int_{-1}^1w^2
 \leq\int_{-1}^1|w'|^2
 \leq\int_{-1}^1w^3
 \leq\frac14\int_{-1}^1w^2,\] an impossibility. Increasing \(\beta\) or \(\sigma\) cannot repair this fixed-support, fixed-amplitude construction.

The displayed \(C_2\geq C_3\) comparison overlooks the different powers of \(|x|\) in the positive and negative terms. An exact sample \(\sigma=4\), \(\beta=2\) gives \[-(\underline u^2)''(1/2)-\underline u(1/2)^4
 =\frac{122007938175}{68719476736}>0.\] The energy argument, rather than this one sample, rules out every proposed sufficiently regular large-exponent bump for the chosen parameters.

Lemma 5.1 only yields a limsup of the supremum. The invalid monotonicity step is what was intended to turn that information into the limit at the center and then into Theorem 2.2. An alternative hair-trigger argument is therefore required. The stated spreading conclusion may still be correct; this is a decisive failure of the present proof, not a counterexample to spreading itself.
# Scope, normalization, and comparison estimates

Problem 4 (Minor: Corollary 2.5(iii) needs a one-dimensional qualification).  The corollary on pp. 8–9 assumes \(p\geq2\) but not \(N\geq2\). For \(N=1\) its asserted region of uniform convergence to one is \(|x|\leq c_*t\), because the logarithmic retreat is multiplied by \(N-1\).

For any radial spreading solution covered by Theorem 2.4, that theorem gives \[u(c_*t,t)\longrightarrow U_{c_*}(-r_0)<1,\] since \(r_0\) is finite and the profile is strictly below one at every finite argument. Thus the two printed statements cannot both hold in dimension one. The Section 6.3 refinements do not impose an \(N\geq2\) restriction retroactively.

Restrict part (iii) to \(N\geq2\), or require an additional retreat \(w(t)\to\infty\) from the corrected front radius, with a nonempty comparison region. For \(N\geq2\), \((N-1)(c-c_\sharp)\log t\to\infty\) for \(c>c_\sharp\), which explains why the argument works. Parts (i)–(ii) are not refuted by this boundary case.

Problem 5 (Minor: a missing factor \(m\) changes the tail exponent).  Lemma 4.10(b), p. 28, and Lemma 4.14(b), p. 30, lose a factor \(1/m\) when converting the trajectory asymptotic to spatial or pressure-level coordinates.

For \(p\geq2\), (4.11) implies \[\phi(U)\sim C_{p,\gamma}(1-U)^{p-1},\qquad
 U'\sim-\frac{C_{p,\gamma}^{\alpha}}m(1-U).\] The exponential rate is therefore \(C_{p,\gamma}^{\alpha}/m\), not \(C_{p,\gamma}^{\alpha}\). Likewise, if \(Q=m/(m-\alpha)\), \[Q-q\sim m(1-U),\qquad
 \mathcal P(q;\gamma)\sim
 -\frac{C_{p,\gamma}^{\alpha}}m(Q-q).\] The later computation on p. 32 already uses the correctly normalized coefficient in the \(p>2\) case.

A concrete check is \(p=m=2\), \(\gamma=0\), \(h(u)=u(1-u)\): \[U(\xi)=1-e^{\xi/2}\quad(\xi<0),\qquad
 U(\xi)=0\quad(\xi\geq0),\qquad c_*=1.\] This is an exact finite wave. Here \(C_{2,0}=1\), but \(1-U(\xi)=e^{-|\xi|/2}\), which cannot be bounded by \(M e^{-(1-\varepsilon)|\xi|}\) for \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\). Restoring \(1/m\) repairs the stated rate; arguments requiring merely some positive exponential rate may still proceed.

Problem 6 (Major: the comparison function misses its logarithmic phase).  In Theorem 6.3, p. 39, set \(a=(N-1)c_\sharp\) and \(b=m(p-1)-1\). The printed comparison function has phase \(r-g(t)+C\), but its residual includes the extra term \(a/t\) that would come from differentiating \(a\log t\).

The specified ODE is \[g'=f^bc_*+(1-f^b)\frac at
 -\frac{\lambda\log(t-t_0)}{(t-t_0)^2}
 +\frac{\lambda}{(t-t_0)^2}.\] Consequently \(g'-c_*=O(\log t/t^2)\) and \(g-c_*t\) approaches a constant. It cannot already contain the required logarithmic shift. With the printed phase, the \(fU'\) coefficient is \(f^b(c_*-a/t)-g'\). The displayed residual instead has \(f^b(c_*-a/t)-g'+a/t\). The consistent repair is \[w(r,t)=f(t)U\!\left(r-g(t)+a\log t+C;\
                    \gamma(c_*-a/t)\right).\] It restores both the chain rule and the intended front location \(c_*t-a\log t+O(1)\). For \(N>1\), the omitted term in the actual printed subsolution residual is of order \(1/t\) and cannot be absorbed by the displayed \(O(\log t/t^2)\) terms. The actual residual exceeds the printed residual by \(-afU'/t>0\) at a fixed interior profile point when \(N>1\). Thus the printed comparison function does not establish the subsolution inequality used for Theorem 6.3 and the central logarithmic front-location estimate. This is a major defect in that proof dependency, even though the missing phase can be written explicitly. Restoring it repairs the chain rule; the full barrier still depends on resolving the parameter estimates in Problem 2. The additional formula corrections below are local and are not individually classified as major.

There are additional local formula corrections: Lemma 6.2 (p. 38) and both bounds in Theorem 6.3 (p. 39) print \(c_*\) where \(c_*t\) is required. The surrounding text and the ODE for \(g\) identify the intended expression. Lemma 4.12, (4.13) on p. 29, places both zero and nonzero derivative data at \(0\); the terminal nonzero-flux datum belongs at \(b\), with its derivative/flux normalization stated consistently. Lemma 4.6 (p. 25) reverses the ordering of trajectories with respect to the speed. The forward ODE (4.5) gives the larger trajectory for larger speed on their common positive interval, not the printed smaller one. For \(m=p=2\), \(h(U)=U(1-U)\), \(\gamma=0\) and \(c=3<4=d\), the maximal branches have slopes \(c,d\) at zero, contradicting the printed inequality.

Finally, the limit \(U^{(m-1)(p-1)}|U'|^{p-2}\to0\) at \(U\to1\), used on pp. 38 and 40, is \(1\) when \(p=2\). The argument there needs boundedness rather than vanishing, so replacing that assertion by the required boundedness avoids creating an artificial obstruction to the comparison.
# Positive checks and remaining proof obligations

The weak jump condition in the expanding compactly supported subsolution of Lemma 5.3 has the correct sign in the distributional inequality. Passing \(c_1\uparrow c\) gives the stated expanding-ball lower bound. The radial upper and lower comparisons explain the \(O(1)\) nonradial location conclusions of Corollary 2.5(i)–(ii), provided the radial asymptotics are established.

The cap-shaped subsolution in Lemma 6.1 has the appropriate power balance for \(p>2\): \[(n-1)(p-1)-1>n
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n>\frac p{p-2}.\] This supports the stated choice of a large spatial exponent. The \(p=2\) treatment is separately referred to prior work; the restriction \(p\geq2\) in the main result should not be discarded. The asymptotic finite-front law (2.2) and the identity \((u^m)_r=u^\alpha v_r\) are consistent with the explicit profiles above.

The parameter derivative should remain negative if the corrected positive-weight compatibility formula and endpoint controls are justified. Its bound must depend on the actual profile. Similarly, uniform flux bounds away from the initial time may be recoverable even though the stronger formula in (3.2) is false. These observations identify plausible repair boundaries; they are not completed replacements for the missing proofs.

Theorem 6.4 and the final subsequence-to-full-time argument in Theorem 2.4 are stated by adaptation of earlier results. Their entire external proofs were not independently reconstructed here. No counterexample to the correctly normalized final radial convergence theorem has been established by this review. Problems 1–3 and the missing phase in Problem 6 nonetheless affect central dependencies and warrant major scientific revision. The formal decision is `pending`, with an empty human-review list.

problems.title: the pressure-gradient estimate has false regimes
problems.source_location: Lemma3.1 pp10-11 Eq3.2; proof Eqs3.16-3.20 pp17-19; Cor3.2 pp19-20
claim: Pressure-gradient estimate false in stated convection and p<2 regimes
analysis:
Lemma 3.1, pp. 10–11, especially (3.2), asserts \[|v_r|\leq
 \begin{cases}
 C M^{(m-\alpha)/p}(t^{-1}+H)^{1/p},&p\geq2,\\
 C M^{(m-\alpha)/2}(t^{-1}+H)^{1/2},&1<p<2,
 \end{cases}\] where \(C\) depends only on the constant convection parameter \(\gamma\), \(m\), and \(p\). The pure-diffusion case is expressly included. Both a nonzero-convection large-time limit and a singular-exponent short-time scaling contradict this claim.

First take \(p=m=2\), \(h=0\), \(\gamma>0\), and \(M>0\). For \(z>0\) set \[F(z)=M(1-e^{-\gamma z/2}),\qquad F(z)=0\quad(z\leq0),
 \qquad u(r,t)=F(r+\gamma Mt-R).\] On the positive branch, \[(F^2)'+\gamma F^2=\gamma MF.\] Differentiating proves \(u_t=(u^2)_{rr}+\gamma(u^2)_r\). The density and diffusive flux are continuous at the free boundary, with zero flux there, so this is a bounded weak solution of the auxiliary convection equation. Its pressure is \(v=2u\) and \[v_r=\gamma M e^{-\gamma z/2}\qquad(z>0).\] Given an arbitrarily large \(T\), choose \(R=\gamma MT+1\); then the front lies at \(r=1\) at time \(T\). At a fixed positive distance behind that increasing front, \(|v_r|\) is a positive constant independent of \(T\). The printed upper bound is \(CM^{1/2}T^{-1/2}\). Since \(C\) cannot depend on \(R\), the estimates are incompatible. This example addresses the stated bounded-solution class; it is not compactly supported on the whole line.

There is also a compactly supported, even counterexample to the \(1<p<2\) time exponent, with zero convection. Take \(p=3/2\), \(m=3\), \(\alpha=2\), \(h=0\), and \[B(x,s)=\left(s^{-1/2}-\frac{|x|^3}{36s^2}\right)_+ .\] In the positive set its flux is \[|(B^3)_x|^{-1/2}(B^3)_x=-\frac{xB}{2s}.\] Direct differentiation gives \(B_s=(-xB/(2s))_x\); the flux vanishes at the interface. Thus \(B\) is a weak solution. For \(\lambda>0\) put \[u_\lambda(x,t)=B\left(\frac{x}{\lambda},
                 1+\frac{t}{\lambda^{3/2}}\right).\] The initial supremum is \(M=1\), the data are even and compactly supported, and \(v_\lambda=3u_\lambda\). At \(x=\lambda\), \(t=\lambda^{3/2}\), \[|(v_\lambda)_x|=\frac{1}{16\lambda},
 \qquad
 CM^{1/2}t^{-1/2}=C\lambda^{-3/4}.\] No fixed \(C\) can satisfy this as \(\lambda\downarrow0\). This is an exact scaling contradiction, not a numerical approximation.

The proof exposes the corresponding defects. The Young inequality after (3.16), p. 17, applied to the convection term containing \(+1\), leaves a term that does not vanish with the spatial cutoff. That remainder is absent from (3.17), p. 18. On p. 19 the assertion that one may always arrange \(c_2S^{1-p}(t^{-1}+H)\geq1\) is impossible for \(H=0\) and unbounded \(t\). Moreover the maximum of its first power and its \(2/p\) power cannot generally be replaced by the selected branch in (3.2).

A valid replacement must retain the convection contribution and correct the time/scaling dependence. Corollary 3.2, pp. 19–20, invokes this derivation and therefore needs its own corrected argument. The weaker conclusion of Theorem 2.6 is only a bound for each fixed \(\tau>0\) and \(r\geq\rho>0\); these examples do not disprove that weaker statement. Nor does a counterexample with \(p<2\) directly refute the main asymptotic theorem, which assumes \(p\geq2\). Nevertheless, the advertised central technical estimate and its proof require substantive repair.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: p=m2,h0,gamma>0 exact bounded increasing front has nondecaying pressure gradient with arbitrary initial translation; p3/2,m3,gamma0,h0 compact even Barenblatt scaling has |v_x|(lambda,lambda^1.5)=1/(16lambda) versus C lambda^-3/4.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: First example uses bounded noncompact class explicitly stated in Lemma; second is compact and even. Main asymptotics require p>=2; Theorem2.6 only needs unspecified bound at fixedtau,rho.

paragraphs: Retain convection remainder and correct time/scaling powers; redo radial derivation and limiting maximum argument.

problems.title: wave-speed differentiation loses a source term
problems.source_location: Lemma4.15 pp30-32, derivative formula p31, Eq4.14 p32 and continuation remark p33
claim: Variation source |P|^(p-2) missing; universal c' in(-m,0) false
analysis: Lemma 4.15, pp. 30–32, asserts \(c'(\gamma)\in(-m,0)\). The displayed integral formula on p. 31 and (4.14) on p. 32 omit the contribution from differentiating \(\gamma|\mathcal P|^{p-2}\).

Here is a concrete counterexample to the joint differentiability-and-bound assertion. Take \(m=1\), \(p=3\), and, for \(a>0\), define \[h_a(u)=
 \begin{cases}
 a^3u^{3/2}(1-u)(4-3u),&0\leq u\leq1,\\
 -a^3(u-1),&u\geq1.
 \end{cases}\] This is \(C^1\), satisfies the monostable sign assumptions, and has \(h_a'(1)=-a^3\). At \(\gamma=0\) the finite profile is \[U(\xi)=\tanh^2(a\xi/2)\quad(\xi<0),\qquad
 U(\xi)=0\quad(\xi\geq0),\qquad c=a^2.\] Indeed \(U'=-a\sqrt U(1-U)\) and \(\phi(U)=a^2U(1-U)^2\) verify the wave equation exactly. Differentiate the trajectory equation (4.5) along the parameter branch whose regularity the lemma asserts. For \(Z=\partial_\gamma\phi\) this yields \[Z'=c'+a\sqrt U(1-U)
          +\frac{4-3U}{2(1-U)^2}Z .\] An integrating factor is \[\mu(U)=(1-U)^{3/2}
                  \exp\!\left(-\frac1{2(1-U)}\right).\] The asserted endpoint regularity implies vanishing boundary terms, and hence \[c'_a(0)=-a\,\frac{J}{I},\quad
 I=\int_0^1\mu(U)\,\mathrm dU,\quad
 J=\int_0^1\mu(U)\sqrt U(1-U)\,\mathrm dU.\] Using the whole interval for \(I\) and \([1/4,1/2]\) for \(J\), \[I\leq\frac25 e^{-1/2},\qquad
 J\geq\frac{e^{-1}}{32\sqrt2},\qquad
 \frac{J}{I}\geq\frac{5e^{-1/2}}{64\sqrt2}.\] Thus \(a=100\) forces \(c'_a(0)<-3\), contrary to \(c'(0)>-m=-1\). If the claimed regular parameter branch failed to exist, that would already violate the other part of the same lemma. The contradiction therefore does not presume the incorrect printed derivative formula.

The reaction scaling \(h\mapsto\lambda h\) provides a second check: \[c_\lambda(\gamma)=
 \lambda^{(p-1)/p}c_1(\gamma\lambda^{-1/p}),\qquad
 c'_\lambda(0)=\lambda^{(p-2)/p}c'_1(0).\] A nonzero negative derivative cannot have a universal lower bound \(-m\) for all \(\lambda\) when \(p>2\). The corrected formula can instead give a reaction-dependent bound involving \(\sup W^{p-2}\). The continuation estimate on p. 33 based on \(c(\gamma)\geq c(0)-m\gamma\) must also be revised.

This matters to the proof of the logarithmic shift, which uses parameter regularity and an inverse speed function. It does not by itself contradict the main asymptotic statement when \(c_\sharp\) is defined by the actual \(-c'(0)/c_*\). A corrected parameter analysis may still supply the local estimates that argument needs.

problems.title: the hair-trigger proof uses an impossible static subsolution
problems.source_location: Lemma5.2 p34
claim: Static bump subsolution and ensuing temporal monotonicity proof invalid
analysis: In Lemma 5.2, p. 34, the initial bump \(\underline u=\delta(1-|x|^\sigma)_+^\beta\) is claimed to satisfy \(-\Delta_p(\underline u^m)-\widehat h(\underline u)\leq0\) when \(\beta\) and \(\sigma\) are sufficiently large. The subsequent time-monotonicity argument depends on this assertion.

Take \(N=1\), \(p=m=2\), \(\delta=1/2\), so the Fujita exponent is \(q_F=4\). An explicit allowed reaction is \[\widehat h(u)=u^4\bigl[1-16(u-3/4)_+^2\bigr].\] It is \(C^1\), positive on \((0,1)\), negative on \((1,\infty)\), and \(\widehat h'(1)=-8\). It equals \(u^4\) on \([0,3/4]\). For every sufficiently regular choice of the proposed bump, put \(w=\underline u^2\). Then \(0\leq w\leq1/4\), \(w\not\equiv0\), and \(w\in H^1_0(-1,1)\). The alleged static-subsolution inequality would be \(-w''\leq w^2\). Testing by \(w\) gives \[\frac{\pi^2}{4}\int_{-1}^1w^2
 \leq\int_{-1}^1|w'|^2
 \leq\int_{-1}^1w^3
 \leq\frac14\int_{-1}^1w^2,\] an impossibility. Increasing \(\beta\) or \(\sigma\) cannot repair this fixed-support, fixed-amplitude construction.

The displayed \(C_2\geq C_3\) comparison overlooks the different powers of \(|x|\) in the positive and negative terms. An exact sample \(\sigma=4\), \(\beta=2\) gives \[-(\underline u^2)''(1/2)-\underline u(1/2)^4
 =\frac{122007938175}{68719476736}>0.\] The energy argument, rather than this one sample, rules out every proposed sufficiently regular large-exponent bump for the chosen parameters.

Lemma 5.1 only yields a limsup of the supremum. The invalid monotonicity step is what was intended to turn that information into the limit at the center and then into Theorem 2.2. An alternative hair-trigger argument is therefore required. The stated spreading conclusion may still be correct; this is a decisive failure of the present proof, not a counterexample to spreading itself.

For \(p\geq2\), (4.11) implies \[\phi(U)\sim C_{p,\gamma}(1-U)^{p-1},\qquad

problems.title: the comparison function misses its logarithmic phase
problems.source_location: Theorem6.3 p39 residual; Lemma6.2 p38; local Lemmas4.6p25,4.12p29
claim: Missing logarithmic phase and associated local formula corrections
analysis: In Theorem 6.3, p. 39, set \(a=(N-1)c_\sharp\) and \(b=m(p-1)-1\). The printed comparison function has phase \(r-g(t)+C\), but its residual includes the extra term \(a/t\) that would come from differentiating \(a\log t\).

The specified ODE is \[g'=f^bc_*+(1-f^b)\frac at
 -\frac{\lambda\log(t-t_0)}{(t-t_0)^2}
 +\frac{\lambda}{(t-t_0)^2}.\] Consequently \(g'-c_*=O(\log t/t^2)\) and \(g-c_*t\) approaches a constant. It cannot already contain the required logarithmic shift. With the printed phase, the \(fU'\) coefficient is \(f^b(c_*-a/t)-g'\). The displayed residual instead has \(f^b(c_*-a/t)-g'+a/t\). The consistent repair is \[w(r,t)=f(t)U\!\left(r-g(t)+a\log t+C;\
                    \gamma(c_*-a/t)\right).\] It restores both the chain rule and the intended front location \(c_*t-a\log t+O(1)\). For \(N>1\), the omitted term in the actual printed subsolution residual is of order \(1/t\) and cannot be absorbed by the displayed \(O(\log t/t^2)\) terms. The actual residual exceeds the printed residual by \(-afU'/t>0\) at a fixed interior profile point when \(N>1\). Thus the printed comparison function does not establish the subsolution inequality used for Theorem 6.3 and the central logarithmic front-location estimate. This is a major defect in that proof dependency, even though the missing phase can be written explicitly. Restoring it repairs the chain rule; the full barrier still depends on resolving the parameter estimates in Problem 2. The additional formula corrections below are local and are not individually classified as major.

There are additional local formula corrections: Lemma 6.2 (p. 38) and both bounds in Theorem 6.3 (p. 39) print \(c_*\) where \(c_*t\) is required. The surrounding text and the ODE for \(g\) identify the intended expression. Lemma 4.12, (4.13) on p. 29, places both zero and nonzero derivative data at \(0\); the terminal nonzero-flux datum belongs at \(b\), with its derivative/flux normalization stated consistently. Lemma 4.6 (p. 25) reverses the ordering of trajectories with respect to the speed. The forward ODE (4.5) gives the larger trajectory for larger speed on their common positive interval, not the printed smaller one. For \(m=p=2\), \(h(U)=U(1-U)\), \(\gamma=0\) and \(c=3<4=d\), the maximal branches have slopes \(c,d\) at zero, contradicting the printed inequality.

Finally, the limit \(U^{(m-1)(p-1)}|U'|^{p-2}\to0\) at \(U\to1\), used on pp. 38 and 40, is \(1\) when \(p=2\). The argument there needs boundedness rather than vanishing, so replacing that assertion by the required boundedness avoids creating an artificial obstruction to the comparison.

report: Abstract: The 15 February 2024 author version of Kehle and Unger’s black-hole gluing paper is examined. A substantive gap occurs in the subsidiary interior-gluing argument: real characteristic pulses on a charged background generate complex transverse scalar derivatives, whereas the stated Borsuk–Ulam construction uses the dimension appropriate to a neutral real field. An exact covariant transport identity identifies the missing condition. Additional, locally repairable problems concern global seed-data existence, constrained electromagnetic jets, the printed gauge-group law, and several formula and parameter normalizations. The principal horizon-gluing construction uses the correct complex dimension and is not refuted by these observations. The finite-regularity, apparent-horizon, and trapped-surface quantifiers are retained throughout. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Characteristic data, complex transverse jets, and the scope of charged black-hole gluing
# Article, version, and review scope

The article is C. Kehle and R. Unger, Gravitational collapse to extremal black holes and the third law of black hole thermodynamics, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1591 [paper, journal]. The actual reviewed PDF is arXiv:2211.15742v2, dated 15 February 2024, with 49 pages including references. The repository labels it a final version. The publisher records online publication on 27 January 2025, after acceptance on 30 September 2023. No byte comparison with the restricted publisher PDF establishes version equivalence. All page references below concern the retained author PDF.

All 3,310 extracted-text lines and all 49 PDF pages were read or actually viewed as appropriate; the static author TeX was consulted at the relevant definitions and proof. The source archive and its listed members were checked as inputs, but author code and author-source compilation were not executed. No separate computational supplement was verified. Absence of such code is not a mathematical defect.

The system is the spherically symmetric Einstein–Maxwell charged massless scalar field system, with fixed nonzero coupling \(\mathfrak e\), complex scalar \(\phi\), and electromagnetic gauge \(A_v=0\). The black-hole charge \(e\) and the dimensionless ratio \(\mathfrak q=e/M\) must be distinguished from \(\mathfrak e\). Theorem 2A concerns neutral Minkowski-to-Schwarzschild gluing; Theorem 2B concerns gluing to an RN event horizon; Theorems 2C and \(2\mathrm C'\) concern general RN spheres and ingoing gluing. Theorem 1 uses 2A and 2B. Corollaries 2 and 3 use the more general construction.

The quantifier is that for each finite \(k\) there is a corresponding \(C^k\) example. It is not the existence of one \(C^\infty\) example; Remarks 1.6 and 1.8 explicitly discuss this limitation. The vacuum/extremal-Kerr statement on p. 4 is a conjecture. The massive-field extension in Remark 1.2 is not independently established by the present review.
# The substantive proof gap

Problem 1 (Major: the interior-gluing parameter count).  Section 4.3, p. 35, Gluing 3, uses \(k+1\) real pulses as in (4.1), imposes a mass condition, and invokes the Borsuk–Ulam argument. At nonzero background charge \(Q_f\), this does not supply the dimension needed to eliminate \(k\) complex transverse scalar jets. The static source confirms this wording (`final.tex`, lines 1663 and 1671).

Equation reference: covariant, imag. Here is an exact obstruction to treating the transverse jets as real. Along the gluing cone put \(\Omega^2=1\) and let \(\phi\) be real. Maxwell’s equation then makes \(Q=Q_f\) constant along that cone. Define \[\psi=r\phi,\qquad Z=D_u\psi=\partial_u\psi+i\mathfrak eA_u\psi .\] Combining (2.13), p. 18, with \(\partial_v A_u=-Q_f/(2r^2)\), equation (2.9), gives \[
 \partial_v Z=
 \left(-\frac{m}{2r^2}+\frac{Q_f^2}{4r^3}\right)\phi
       -\frac{i\mathfrak eQ_f}{4r}\phi .\] Indeed, the derivative of the gauge-potential term contributes \(-i\mathfrak eQ_f\phi/(2r)\); together with the positive imaginary term in (2.13), its net coefficient is the negative one in [covariant] (#covariant). If the scalar and its transverse derivative vanish at the initial endpoint, and the scalar vanishes at both endpoints, then \[
 \operatorname{Im}\!\left[r(1)\partial_u\phi(1)\right]
   =-\frac{\mathfrak eQ_f}{4}
       \int_0^1\frac{\phi(v)}{r(v)}\,\mathrm dv .\] The same obstruction holds with the transport initialized backwards at the final RN sphere. A nonnegative nonzero real pulse makes the right-hand side nonzero. Thus reality of the prescribed scalar along one characteristic does not preserve reality of its transverse derivative. An allowed residual gauge transformation cannot turn a nonzero endpoint scalar derivative into zero: where \(\phi=0\), that derivative is multiplied by a nonzero scale and phase.

There is also a strict counterexample to the printed two-pulse procedure when \(k=1\). Choose \(Q_f=R_f=M_f=M>0\), an allowed case for \(0<\mathfrak r\leq1\), and nonnegative, nonzero \(\chi_1,\chi_2\) with separated supports in that order. Let \(\phi=\alpha_1\chi_1+\alpha_2\chi_2\). Assume the claimed construction retains \(r>0\) and \(r_u<0\). The endpoint conditions give \(r_v(1)=0\); Raychaudhuri implies \(r_v\geq0\) and \(r\leq M\). The mass identity gives \(\varpi_v\geq0\) and \(\varpi\leq\varpi(1)=M\). Define \[H=\frac{2m}{r}-\frac{M^2}{r^2}.\] Using (2.14), direct differentiation yields \[H_v=4r(-r_u)|\phi_v|^2+
       \frac{3M^2-2mr}{r^3}r_v,\qquad
 3M^2-2mr=4M^2-2\varpi r\geq2M^2.\] If both amplitudes are nonzero, \(H\) is strictly increasing between the supports because the second pulse forces \(r_v>0\) there. Set \[J_j=\int_0^1\frac{\chi_j}{r}\,\mathrm dv>0,\qquad
 K_j=\int_0^1\frac{H\chi_j}{r}\,\mathrm dv .\] Then \(K_1/J_1<K_2/J_2\). Equation [covariant] (#covariant), with zero initial scalar jet, gives \[r(1)\phi_u(1)
   =-\tfrac14(\alpha_1K_1+\alpha_2K_2)
     -\frac{i\mathfrak eM}{4}(\alpha_1J_1+\alpha_2J_2).\] Vanishing imaginary part forces \(\alpha_1J_1=-\alpha_2J_2\); strict separation of the weighted averages then makes the real part nonzero. If only one amplitude is nonzero, the imaginary part already cannot vanish. The zero amplitude vector cannot supply the prescribed positive mass increment. Thus these allowed two nonnegative profiles admit no nonzero pulse parameters satisfying the advertised \(C^1\) matching within the construction’s positive-radius, negative-\(r_u\) class. This refutes that stated procedure for an allowed profile choice, not the existence assertion of Theorem 2C with a different family of pulses.

With \(k+1\) real amplitudes and one mass constraint, the described parameter surface has dimension \(k\). The required target is \(\mathbb C^k\simeq\mathbb R^{2k}\). Theorem 3 does not guarantee a zero for an odd map \(S^k\to\mathbb R^{2k}\); the coordinate inclusion itself is a zero-free odd example. Section 4.2 correctly uses \(2k+1\) amplitudes and a \(2k\)-dimensional target, so this problem does not apply to its horizon-gluing argument.

A concrete repair is available in principle: use \(2k+1\) real pulses in Gluing 3, construct the mass level as an antipodally invariant radial graph over \(S^{2k}\), and use all real and imaginary endpoint jets. Real pulses still keep the tangential charge constant. The relevant scale also appears compatible with this repair: for amplitude \(\beta\), \[\Delta\varpi
  =\beta^2\int_0^1 2r^2(-r_u)
       \left|\partial_v\sum_j\widehat\alpha_j\chi_j\right|^2\,\mathrm dv
  \asymp \beta^2 M_f^3.\] Since \(M_f-M'\asymp M_f\), this gives \(\beta^2\asymp M_f^{-2}\). These are repair requirements, not a completed replacement proof supplied here. The affected dependencies are 2C, \(2\mathrm C'\), and Corollaries 2–3; no counterexample to their existence conclusions, or to Theorem 1, is established.
# Local statements and formal data requiring correction

Problem 2 (Minor: unrestricted seed data need not exist on the whole interval).  Proposition 2.4, p. 21, asserts a globally regular \(A_u\) for every compatible seed, although the Raychaudhuri solution can reach zero. Its seed construction therefore needs a positive-radius restriction on the prescribed interval. Proposition 2.3 should make that restriction explicit; a classical interpretation of its rational constraint equations may already exclude zeros of their denominators.

Take \(k=1\), \(\mathfrak e=1\), \(v\in[0,\pi]\), \(\Omega^2=1\), and \[\phi(v)=e^{-iv},\qquad
 r(0)=1,\quad r_v(0)=0,\quad Q(0)=A_u(0)=0.\] The initial sphere jets can be completed using the constraints near \(v=0\): for example \(r_{vv}(0)=-1\), \(Q_v(0)=1\), \((A_u)_v(0)=0\), and \((A_u)_{vv}(0)=-1/2\). The paper’s convention is \(Q_v=\mathfrak er^2\operatorname{Im}(\phi\overline{\phi_v})\). The unique tangential solutions are \[r(v)=\cos v,\qquad Q(v)=\frac v2+\frac{\sin2v}{4}.\] At \(v=\pi/2\), \(r=0\) but \(Q=\pi/4\). Consequently \[\lim_{v\uparrow\pi/2}(\pi/2-v)^2(A_u)_v=-\frac{\pi}{8},\] so \(A_u\) cannot be \(C^2\) on the stated interval. This explicit seed counterexample refutes Proposition 2.4. It is not a separate counterexample to Proposition 2.3 when that proposition’s constraints are understood classically throughout the interval, nor to the small-pulse construction.

Require \(r>0\) and \(\Omega^2>0\) in Proposition 2.3, and restrict Proposition 2.4 to seeds whose Raychaudhuri solution remains strictly positive, or to the interval before its first zero. On a compact positive-radius interval the transport equations have the required regular coefficients. Also replace the lower integration limits \(0\) by \(v_1\) in the general statement. Lemma 4.4 and the preceding small-amplitude construction independently provide positive radius where the main argument needs it.

Problem 3 (Minor: RN data must retain their constrained Maxwell jets).  Definitions 3.4–3.5, pp. 24–25, prescribe nonzero charge and make all other components zero. Read literally, these are not elements of the sphere-data space \(\mathcal D_k\). Lemma 4.1, p. 26, also omits the lapse in its mass condition.

Definition 2.3(v) and (2.9) impose \[a_v^1=-\frac{q\omega}{2\varrho^2}.\] For the normalized charged RN sphere this is \(-e/(2\varrho^2)\ne0\). Higher dependent \(v\)-jets must likewise be obtained from the constraints. It is not possible to remove the nonzero electromagnetic field by a gauge choice. The definitions should specify the free components and fill the dependent components by the RN equations. The phrase in Lemma 4.2 that the charge vanishes to all orders must mean its positive-order derivatives; the charge itself is prescribed nonzero.

For Lemma 4.1, the invariant mass is \(\varrho(1+4\varrho_u^1\varrho_v^1/\omega)/2\), whereas the displayed hypothesis omits \(\omega\). Sphere data with \[\varrho=1,\quad \varrho_u^1=-\tfrac12,\quad
 \varrho_v^1=\tfrac12,\quad \omega=4,\quad q=\phi=0\] and zero remaining free jets satisfy the printed condition with \(M=0\), but have Hawking mass \(3/8\). Gauge transformations preserve that mass, so they cannot be equivalent to the asserted mass-zero sphere. Either require lapse-normalized input or restore the denominator. The actual applications on pp. 28 and 33 already use \(\omega=1\). These are exact formal inconsistencies with direct local repairs; they do not rule out gluing to actual RN data.

Problem 4 (Minor: the displayed gauge multiplication is not associative).  Definition 2.4, p. 20, prints the composition law \[((f_2,g_2),\chi_2)\cdot((f_1,g_1),\chi_1)
 =((f_2\circ f_1,g_2\circ g_1),\chi_2\circ f_1^{-1}+\chi_1).\] This law is incompatible with associativity for noncommuting coordinate changes.

Set \(f_1(u)=2u\), \(f_2(u)=u+u^3\), \(f_3(u)=u\), all \(g_i=\mathrm{id}\), \(\chi_1=\chi_2=0\), and \(\chi_3(u)=u\). These are allowed global increasing diffeomorphisms and smooth phases. The two associations give phases \[f_2^{-1}\circ f_1^{-1}(u)
    =\tfrac u2-\tfrac{u^3}{8}+O(u^5),\qquad
 f_1^{-1}\circ f_2^{-1}(u)
    =\tfrac u2-\tfrac{u^3}{2}+O(u^5),\] which differ. For the pullback transformations (2.15)–(2.19), a consistent left-action convention uses \((f_1\circ f_2,g_1\circ g_2)\) in this product and retains the printed phase expression. Alternatively, change the action convention consistently.
Problem 5 (Minor: local parameter, formula, and threshold corrections).  Several displayed formulas disagree with equations or quantifiers used elsewhere in the same proof.

On p. 32, the first two denominators of (4.18) should contain \(r\), not \(r^2\), as in (2.5). Lemma 4.8 actually uses the correct identity (2.12), which supports treating this as a local formula error. On p. 34, the listed final radius is \(2M_f\), although the construction imposes \(r_+=(1+\sqrt{1-\mathfrak q^2})M_f\); replace that copied Schwarzschild value.

Theorem 2C allows every real \(\mathfrak q\). Its proof’s reduction \(R_f\leq3M_f\) on p. 34 has no admissible radius if \((1+\mathfrak r)\mathfrak q^2>6\). In that regime it cannot be justified by extending from \(3M_f\), which can have nonpositive Hawking mass. Replace \(3\) by \(C(\mathfrak q,\mathfrak r)\geq
\max\{3,(1+\mathfrak r)\mathfrak q^2/2\}\). Beyond this admissible radius the RN lapse is positive, and the constants are already permitted to depend on these parameters. On p. 35, (4.25) gives \[M_f-M'\geq\frac{\mathfrak r}{2+2\mathfrak r}M_f,\] not the subsequently printed equality. This lower bound, with \(M_f-M'\leq M_f\), suffices for the intended scale.
# Proof-chain checks and counterevidence

The charge-surface construction in Section 4.2 has the right topological dimension. Disjointly supported pulses give a positive tangential charge density. The small amplitude bootstrap yields \(r\geq r_+/2\); the charge level is a smooth even radial graph, and the transverse scalar map is odd into \(\mathbb C^k\). The large \(|\mathfrak e|M/|\mathfrak q|\) condition also supplies the negative \(r_u\) margin. The neutral case is separated rather than dividing by \(\mathfrak q=0\). These checks explain why Problem 1 is confined to the subsidiary interior-gluing proof.

Section 5 constructs a spacetime first and then selects a spacelike, one-ended initial hypersurface with a regular center. It does not identify a characteristic cone with Cauchy data. The global conclusion relies on the cited maximal-development and future-boundary results, notably Kommemi’s theorem [kommemi]. Its repository metadata and abstract were checked, but its full proof, and the external local-existence and center-regularity proofs, were not independently reconstructed here. Uniform local-existence control when the final interior sphere approaches \(r_+\) remains part of the repair and verification required for Corollary 2.

The earlier Schwarzschild portion is an apparent-horizon segment behind the final global event horizon. Treating it as the earlier global event horizon would change the claim. Similarly, the theorem excludes strictly trapped closed surfaces wholly contained in a certain neighborhood \(U\) of the event horizon. It does not exclude every trapped surface that merely intersects \(U\); Remark B.1 explicitly makes that distinction. Persistent trapped spheres farther inside are therefore not contradictory evidence.

Appendix A gives a local stationary metric satisfying the dominant energy condition, not an asymptotically flat EMCSF collapse solution. For its explicit choice, \[g=u^3\,\mathrm dt^2-2\,\mathrm dt\,\mathrm du+(1-u)^2g_{\mathbb S^2},\] the displayed curvature calculation gives \[\theta=\frac{1-3u^2+4u^3}{(1-u)^2},\qquad
 \zeta=\frac{3u(2u-1)}{1-u}.\] Thus \(\theta(0)=1\), \(\zeta(0)=0\), and \(\theta>|\zeta|\) on a sufficiently small neighborhood, which is the stated energy-condition argument. The null-expansion comparison in Appendix B has the appropriate inequality direction. At a regular center, a spacelike surface cannot attain a local minimum of \(t-r\) or a local maximum of \(t+r\) there, supplying the briefly stated exclusion of a central contact point.

No independent counterexample was found to the central finite-\(k\) collapse construction after the local formal corrections. This is a bounded review conclusion, not a certificate of the complete external PDE and global causal theory.

report: Abstract: The retained 29 December 2023 version of Ron Mor’s linear-functional method for diagonal-flow entropy is examined. The main substantive difficulty is an incompatibility between the printed reductive Borel–Serre convergence convention and the labeling of cusp regions by dimensions of short subspaces. A three-dimensional diagonal lattice contradicts two boundary identifications used in passing from finite-scale bounds to boundary masses. Locally repairable issues concern a uniform time interval, the sign of a height increment, a window-dependent coding identity, and two adapted-basis estimates. The finite-scale covering strategy is not refuted by these examples, and no counterexample involving invariant-measure entropy is asserted. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

The article is Ron Mor, Bounding entropy for one-parameter diagonal flows on \(\mathrm{SL}_d(\mathbb R)/\mathrm{SL}_d(\mathbb Z)\) using linear functionals, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1592 [paper, journal]. Write \(G=\mathrm{SL}_d(\mathbb R)\), \(\Gamma=\mathrm{SL}_d(\mathbb Z)\), \(a_t=\exp(t\alpha)\), \(\sum_i\alpha_i=0\), and \(a=a_1\). For a standard upper block parabolic \(P\), the score is \[\chi_P(w)=h(P,a^w)-\phi\bigl(\pi_P(\alpha^w)\bigr),
 \qquad
 h(P,a^w)=\sum_{(i,j)\in E_P}
                   (\alpha_{w(i)}-\alpha_{w(j)})^+.\] Here \(\pi_P\) averages within blocks and the orientation is the double coset in \(\operatorname{stab}_W(a)\backslash W/W(T,P)\). The multiplicities of eigenvalues are not discarded.

Theorem 7.1 is the finite-scale entropy estimate. Theorems 1.1–1.2 translate it into a partition subordinate to boundary neighborhoods and a bound in terms of limiting boundary masses. Corollaries 1.3–1.4 concern total or stratum-specific escape of mass. Theorem 1.5 is a separate, explicit finite-scale consequence with \(\phi=0\). The optimized formulas and sharpness statements in Theorem 1.6 are attributed to subsequent work; they are not proved in this paper. Their external proofs have not been certified here.
# Proof structure and affirmative checks

The proof first controls diagonal trajectories of subspaces by grouping equal exterior-power weights. Its use of the Plücker relations addresses the fact that a dominant weight component need not itself be decomposable. Short rational subspaces are then isolated by gaps \(\eta_i=\lambda_i/\lambda_{i+1}\) in successive minima. The coding construction trims excursions at several scales, increasing the number of retained flag dimensions until it terminates after at most \(d\) steps.

Two estimates make the functional correction possible: the number of pieces is bounded by an arbitrarily small multiple of the observation time at suitably chosen cusp scales, and the sum of endpoint projection errors is \(O_a(rN)\). After discretization, the norm of the total \(\pi_P(\alpha^w)\) contribution is bounded by this error plus the difference between the endpoint heights. Adapted bases and parabolic Bowen-ball volume estimates supply a covering exponent. Birkhoff and Egorov then replace visiting frequencies by masses, with both endpoints in a large compact set. The entropy is affine under the discrete ergodic decomposition.

Several potential objections were explicitly checked and are not findings. The proof of Proposition 3.17 averages integer iterates and extends to an \(a\)-invariant measure, despite its stronger printed flow-invariance hypothesis. The subsequent Birkhoff and ergodic-decomposition arguments also concern \(T=a\). Lemma 7.3 is quoted with a stronger hypothesis and an omitted external proof; a matching discrete-time statement should be made explicit, but that wording difference alone is not a proved counterexample.

Negative individual values of \(\chi\) do not invalidate the visiting-frequency argument. Subtracting the global maximum leaves nonpositive coefficients, so frequency lower bounds give the required upper bound. Moreover the \(G\) score is \(h(G,a)\ge0\), as required in Proposition 4.9. For \(d=2\), \(\alpha=(1/2,-1/2)\) and \(\phi(h_1,h_2)=(h_1-h_2)/2\), both Borel orientation scores are exactly \(1/2\). The identity flow gives zero scores. These checks support the intended mechanism without resolving the boundary-identification problem below.
# Substantive boundary-identification problem

Problem 1 (Major: incompatible parabolic labels).  The convergence convention in §8.2, pp. 50–51, is incompatible with the short-gap labels used in the closure assertion on p. 52 and the set-limsup assertion on p. 54.

Decisive example. Let \(d=3\), let \(P_1=P_{(1,2)}\) and \(P_2=P_{(2,1)}\) be standard upper block parabolics, and set \[g_t=\operatorname{diag}(e^{2t},e^{-t},e^{-t}),\qquad x_t=g_t\mathbb Z^3.\] The printed convergence rule uses \(K M_P A_P N_P\) and requires \(\beta(a_j)\to\infty\) for every character in the adjoint action of \(A_P\) on \(\operatorname{Lie}N_P\). For \(P_1\), choose \(m_t=n_t=I\) and \(a_t=g_t\) in that decomposition. Both relevant characters equal \(e^{3t}\). Thus the printed rule gives \[x_t\longrightarrow y_\infty\in e_\infty(P_1),\] with fixed unit Levi data.

On the other hand, orthogonality of the rectangular lattice gives the exact successive minima \[(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)
       =(e^{-t},e^{-t},e^{2t}),\qquad
 (\eta_1,\eta_2)=(1,e^{-3t}).\] Consequently, for any fixed sufficiently small \(0<\delta<\delta'\), eventually \[x_t\in\mathcal N_{\delta,\delta'}(P_2,P_2)\subset Y_{P_2}.\] Neither \(P_1\subset P_2\) nor \(P_2\subset P_1\) holds. They are not \(\Gamma\)-conjugate, since their stabilized flag dimensions differ. Therefore \[y_\infty\in\overline{Y_{P_2}}\cap e_\infty(P_1)\] contradicts the p. 52 closure assertion. For any admissible sequence of scales tending to zero, the same fixed \(y_\infty\) belongs to every \(\overline{\mathcal N_{\delta_j,\delta'_j}(P_2,P_2)}\). Hence the p. 54 identification of their set-limsup with \(e_\infty(P_2)\) also fails under the printed convention.

Impact and repair boundary. The latter identification is the stated bridge from (8.3) to the boundary-weighted conclusion of Theorem 1.2. It is a substantive proof issue even if the final theorem admits a repair. It does not supply an invariant probability measure, a measure-theoretic entropy calculation, or a counterexample to the numerical inequality. Likewise, accumulation at a boundary point by itself does not rule out an open set containing \(Y_{P_2}\) and omitting that point; the example directly refutes the printed closed-set assertions, not the bare open-cover existence statement of Theorem 1.1.

A correction must reconcile the left/right quotient and opposite-parabolic conventions with the short-subspace flag. If the printed convergence convention is retained, the relevant short dimensions are reversed by \(i\mapsto d-i\), corresponding to reversed block sizes. If the convention is changed, the boundary action and quotient topology must also be checked. In either case the authors should prove the corrected closure limits and verify which \(\chi_P\) coefficient multiplies each boundary mass. Merely renaming a symbol without these checks does not finish the repair. The finite-scale statement in Theorem 7.1 and the \(\phi=0\) consequence in Theorem 1.5 do not use this boundary identification.
# Locally repairable findings

Problem 2 (Minor: uniform time interval at the endpoint).  Proposition 3.13, p. 16, quantifies over all \(0<\delta<\eta_0\) while claiming a uniform time interval \(|t|\ll_a|\log\delta|\) on which \(\eta_l(a_t x)<\eta_0\).

Take \(d=2\), \(a_t=\operatorname{diag}(e^t,e^{-t})\), and \(x=\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1})\mathbb Z^2\), with \[s^2=\eta_0e^{-2\varepsilon},\qquad
 \delta=\eta_0e^{-\varepsilon},\qquad t=2\varepsilon.\] For sufficiently small positive \(\varepsilon\), the short direction does not interchange, and \[\eta_1(x)=\eta_0e^{-2\varepsilon}<\delta,\qquad
 \eta_1(a_t x)=\eta_0e^{2\varepsilon}>\eta_0,
 \qquad
 \frac{t}{|\log\delta|}\longrightarrow0.\] This disproves the uniform endpoint quantifier. Restricting to sufficiently small \(\delta\), for example \(\delta\le\eta_0^2\) with a suitable time constant, or using a time bound proportional to \(\log(\eta_0/\delta)\), repairs this obstruction. The elementary singular-value estimate \(\eta_l(a_t x)\le e^{2\|\alpha\|_\infty|t|}\eta_l(x)\) explains the latter scale. The later asymptotic use \(\delta\to0\) is not refuted.

Problem 3 (Minor: sign of the projected height increment).  The estimate immediately before (4.4) and (4.4) itself, p. 23, have the opposite sign from the definition \(\operatorname{height}(x)=\operatorname{diag}(-\log\lambda_i(x))\) on p. 21.

Proposition 3.18 gives \[\Delta\operatorname{height}(U,P)=-|U|\pi_P(\alpha^w)+O(1).\] Thus the bounded expression is the sum of these two terms, not their difference. For a direct test take the preceding flow, \(x=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-L},e^L)\mathbb Z^2\), \(P=B\), and \(U=[0,L/2]\). For large \(L\) this whole segment has a fixed short direction and remains in the required cusp. Exactly, \(\Delta\operatorname{height}(U,B)=-|U|\alpha\); the printed residual has norm \(2|U|\|\alpha\|\), which is unbounded. Changing the two signs repairs the formulas. Corollaries 4.5 and 4.7 use the norm of the total sum, so their intended cancellation estimate survives the sign correction. No change to the sign of \(\phi\) in the final entropy score is forced by this local correction.

Problem 4 (Minor: translating a coding is not rerunning it).  The equality \(a_{-N}Z(C,\delta,\delta',r)=Z_+(C',\delta,\delta',r)\) in the proof of Lemma 6.4, p. 44, fails because the excursion algorithm depends on the observation window.

Here is an exact log-coordinate example. Let \(k\) be a sufficiently large positive integer, and set \[\begin{aligned}
 a_t&=\operatorname{diag}(e^{t/100},e^{-t/100}),&
 x&=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-474k},e^{474k})\mathbb Z^2,\\
 \delta&=e^{-1000k},&
 \delta'&=e^{-250k},\\
 r&=\frac{49}{50},&
 N&=1100k .\end{aligned}\] The parameters satisfy \(\delta'>\sqrt\delta\), \(r^3>1/4\), and \(N>|\log\delta|\); choosing \(k\) large also ensures \(\delta'<\eta_0\). On the original interval \([-N,N]\), \[\log\eta_1(a_t x)=-948k+t/50
                      \in[-970k,-926k].\] There is no hit of either \(\delta\) or \(\delta^r=e^{-980k}\) in this window. The two-dimensional algorithm therefore labels the whole window by \(G\).

Now let \(y=a_{-N}x\). Its enlarged window \([-2N,2N]\) corresponds to the old times \([-3300k,1100k]\), on which \[\log\eta_1\in[-1014k,-926k].\] This interval does hit \(\delta\), while it remains entirely inside one \(\delta'\) excursion. Both relevant excursion labels are now \(\{1\}\), and the new algorithm labels the entire enlarged window by \(B\). The prescribed translate \(C'\) of the old constant-\(G\) coding is still constant \(G\). Thus \(y\) belongs to the left-hand set of the asserted equality and not the right.

Definition 13 allows all label-valued functions, so \(C'\in\mathcal C_{2N}\) itself is not the problem. The covering conclusion can instead be proved by stating Lemma 6.3 for a given partition and its prescribed continuous-time cusp labels. Its induction only uses those properties. Translate the old partition and labels, apply that induction directly, and retain the original bounds on their number and exceptional durations. This is a local proof repair; the example does not disprove the covering exponent.
Problem 5 (Minor: two adapted-basis normalizations).  Equation (5.1), p. 38, and the fixed-radius step of Proposition 6.2, p. 42, require small corrections.

In (5.1), \(l\) is the block number, determined by \(\dim Z_{l-1}<j\le\dim Z_l\). The summation must begin at \(\dim Z_l+1\), not \(l+1\). For \(d=2\), \(P=G\), \(u=I\), \(l=1\) and \(j=2\), the printed sum includes the diagonal entry of \(u\) and gives \(2z_2\) instead of \(z_2\). The corrected block index gives the intended transverse-component estimate.

Proposition 5.3 bounds \(\|a_t^w u_2a_{-t}^w-I\|_F\) at the fixed \(\varepsilon_0\) scale. It does not make \(wu_2w^{-1}\) an element of a Bowen ball of radius \(O(\rho)\) as \(\rho\) tends to zero, as asserted on p. 42. For example \(u=I+cE_{21}\) and \(a_t=\operatorname{diag}(e^t,e^{-t})\) give transverse entry \(ce^{-2t}\) and supremum \(c\) on \(t\ge0\). Keep a fixed small radius \(C\varepsilon_0\), then cover that Bowen box by \(O_{\rho,\varepsilon_0}(1)\) smaller Bowen boxes. The coordinate contraction factors cancel in the volume ratio; the extra factor is independent of \(T\). This retains the exponential covering rate.

For completeness, the nonnegativity justification on p. 53 can be stated using the fact that averaging \(\pi_H(\alpha^w)\) over permutations gives zero. Choose an orientation with \(\phi(\pi_H(\alpha^w))\le0\) to obtain \(h-\phi\ge0\). The printed existence of an orientation with \(\phi\ge0\) is true but has the wrong sign for that justification.
# Supporting checks

The recommended initial assessment is major revision because the boundary-mass identification supporting Theorem 1.2 requires a coherent convention and a replacement argument. Four further findings above are local and have explicit repair directions. This assessment does not require the entire article to be false or irreparable. No invariant-measure entropy counterexample was obtained.

The full primary proof chain, definitions, quantifiers, repeated eigenvalues, zero flow, signs of the functional contribution, clipped-window behavior, and boundary limits were examined. Classical geometry-of-numbers results, the external entropy-covering lemma, and the full Borel–Ji construction were not independently reproved from their original books or papers. In particular, the boundary counterexample is an internal test of the conventions actually printed here. Theorem 1.6’s follow-up claims remain outside this manuscript’s proved contribution.

report: Abstract: The retained 13 July 2022 author version of Hamel and Rossi’s Fisher–KPP symmetry paper is examined in full. The truncation, reflection, and directional propagation arguments have a coherent mathematical structure, and no counterexample to Theorems 2.1–2.4 is obtained. A quantitative statement accompanying the counterexamples nevertheless exceeds the stated \(C^1\) hypotheses: an admissible logarithmic reaction term has a different front delay. The general-data extension also needs an explicit thickness condition; its two displayed distance conditions alone admit a counterexample. Four local proof corrections and a degenerate case of the final conjecture are identified. The distinction between a false quantitative assertion, an ambiguous extension scope, and the unrefuted main symmetry results is maintained. The initial recommendation is revision; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Asymptotic planar symmetry: geometric thickness and the scope of front-delay estimates
# Article, version, and hypotheses

The article is François Hamel and Luca Rossi, Asymptotic one-dimensional symmetry for the Fisher–KPP equation, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1593 [paper, journal]. The reviewed input is arXiv:2207.05147v2, 13 July 2022, with 34 PDF pages. The publisher records acceptance on 30 September 2023 and online publication on 21 January 2025. The author PDF has not been established to be byte-equivalent to that later publication. Every article page number below refers to the retained author PDF.

All 1,954 extracted-text lines, including references, were read. All 34 primary PDF pages were actually viewed. The 268-line manifest was read completely; its 14 listed inputs, totaling 1,396,516 bytes, were checked against their actual bytes and SHA256 values without discrepancy. Static source passages were consulted to resolve ambiguous extraction. The source archive was not executed. No separate computational supplement was verified, and absence of code is not treated as a defect.

The equation is \[u_t=\Delta u+f(u),\qquad u(0,x)=\mathbf1_U(x),
 \qquad N\ge2,\] where \(f\in C^1([0,1])\), \(f(0)=f(1)=0\), \(f>0\) on \((0,1)\), and \(s\mapsto f(s)/s\) is nonincreasing. Thus \(c^*=2\sqrt{f'(0)}>0\). The thickness assumption (2.1) is \[d_H(U,U_\delta)<\infty
 \quad\hbox{for some }\delta>0,\qquad
 U_\delta=\{x\in U:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial U)\ge\delta\}.\] Nearest points in (2.2) lie in \(\overline U\), as the actual source page and static TeX confirm. Consequently no closedness objection is inferred from an extraction that loses overbars. The opening condition (2.4) controls the maximal normalized scalar product between an outward nearest-point direction and chords into \(U\), uniformly as \(\operatorname{dist}(x,U)\) tends to infinity.

Theorems 2.1–2.2 assert that every translated large-time limit is one-dimensional and either constant or strictly monotone. Theorem 2.3 deduces uniform decay of the elementary symmetric Hessian polynomials of degrees at least two. Theorem 2.4 characterizes the possible decreasing directions by limits of distant projection directions. Corollary 2.5 specializes these statements to subgraphs with vanishing global mean increments. It does not claim convergence to one global profile uniformly over all translates.
# Proof structure and affirmative checks

Proposition 3.1 separates invasion inside expanding neighborhoods of the thick core from extinction beyond speed \(c^*\) measured from the initial support. The retracting supersolution in Lemma 3.2 uses a finite sum of traveling fronts and the subadditivity of the zero-extended KPP reaction. The coefficient two can be implemented by repeating each front twice; it does not require \(2\varphi\) to be an exact solution.

Lemma 4.1 removes the distant part of the initial support while keeping a uniformly small \(C^1\) error on a half-cylinder. Its exterior-distance estimate has a speed strictly larger than \(c^*\) when the auxiliary interior speed is chosen sufficiently close to \(c^*\). This leaves room for fixed spatial constants and one extra time unit. The use of a later \(L^\infty\) bound to control an earlier gradient is compatible with the nonnegative difference equation: Harnack controls an earlier neighborhood, and interior estimates then control its gradient.

After rotation about a nearest point, the opening condition places the relevant support inside a sufficiently flat cone. Truncation puts it inside a half-cylinder. A line in a nonzero transverse gradient direction avoids that cylinder, so a separating reflection plane and the Hopf lemma yield a contradiction. A second reflection establishes monotonicity; an entire-time limit and the strong maximum principle give strictness. Problems 3–5 below concern local formulas in this chain.

Lemma 4.3’s stability under finite Hausdorff distance survives a direct comparison of the two nearest-point directions and chord directions. The needed last estimate is a nonpositive upper limit; an unnecessary intermediate nonnegativity need not be used. The Gaussian estimate for the shrinking closed balls in Proposition 4.6 is also valid. The balls in (4.36) really are closed.

In the converse part of Theorem 2.4, a hypothetical uniformly small directional gradient allows a fixed positive seed to advance by \(1/(4\varepsilon)\) every fixed recovery time. That time is independent of \(\varepsilon\), which contradicts the finite propagation-speed bound. The selected indices must diverge: otherwise all selected points lie in finitely many compact segments, where invasion and parabolic estimates force gradients to zero. This implicit step can be supplied.

The long- and short-chord estimates in §6 use the uniform increment hypothesis (2.6). The scale in (6.8)–(6.9) is \(\sqrt[3]R\), not \(3\sqrt R\). The localization in Theorem 7.2 is directional, and its full vertical-line gradient conclusion uses equality in (7.1) when the vertical coordinate tends to \(-\infty\). Finally, the Hessian conclusion follows from compactness and the rank at most one of every limiting Hessian. The review does not infer the converse.
# A quantitative claim beyond the stated regularity

Problem 1 (Minor: the universal logarithmic phase is false).  On p. 21, immediately after (4.34), the paper states that the phase of the Heaviside solution satisfies \[\zeta(t)=c^*t-\frac{3}{c^*}\log t+x_\infty+o(1)\] under the standing \(C^1\) KPP assumptions. There are reaction terms allowed by (1.2) for which this phase cannot satisfy (4.34).

Admissible example. Set \(f(0)=0\) and, for \(0<s\le1\), let \[f(s)=s\bigl[1-(1-\log s)^{-2}\bigr].\] Writing \(q=1-\log s\), direct differentiation gives \[f'(s)=1-q^{-2}-2q^{-3},\qquad
 \left(\frac{f(s)}s\right)'=-\frac{2}{s q^3}<0.\] Thus \(f\in C^1([0,1])\), \(f'(0)=1\), \(f(1)=0\), \(f>0\) on \((0,1)\), and \(c^*=2\).

The precise external input is Bouin–Henderson [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 1.2(ii), p.~3]{bh}], with \(r=3\), \(A=1\), and Heaviside initial data, which meet their (1.4). Let \[\alpha=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\qquad
 \alpha(\alpha-1)=1,\qquad
 X(t)=2t-\left(\alpha+\frac12\right)\log t.\] Their (1.9) gives \[\lim_{L\to\infty}\limsup_{t\to\infty}
                  v(t,X(t)+L)=0.\] The solution \(v\) is nonincreasing in space by comparison. For the phase printed in the reviewed paper, \[\zeta_{\rm print}(t)-X(t)
       =(\alpha-1)\log t+x_\infty+o(1)\longrightarrow+\infty.\] For each fixed \(L\), therefore, \(v(t,\zeta_{\rm print}(t))\le v(t,X(t)+L)\) eventually. Taking the time upper limit and then \(L\to\infty\) proves \[v(t,\zeta_{\rm print}(t))\longrightarrow0.\] But (4.34), evaluated at that same spatial point, would give \(v(t,\zeta_{\rm print}(t))\to\varphi(0)>0\). This is a contradiction to the joint printed assertion, not just an objection about a citation.

Impact and repair boundary. The quantitative regularity claim needs correction. The nonplanar construction of Proposition 4.4 uses convergence with some phase, and Proposition 4.6 needs only its leading speed \(\zeta(t)\sim c^*t\); neither uses this exact logarithmic coefficient. No counterexample to either proposition or the main symmetry theorems is asserted. Delete the unsupported quantitative parenthesis, or state and verify additional near-zero assumptions for that claim. The bounded-support, higher-dimensional sharp asymptotic mentioned on p. 17 also deserves a hypothesis check, but the one-dimensional Heaviside example is not presented as its direct counterexample.

The first five pages of [bh], including the hypotheses and the decisive theorem, were actually read and viewed. Its whole proof was not independently reconstructed. The contradiction above is an analytic consequence of that explicit external theorem. Exact symbolic calculations check the parameter match and derivatives, not the PDE theorem.
# The general-data extension needs an explicit scope

Problem 2 (Minor: clarify the retained thickness hypothesis).  On p. 31, the sentence extending Corollary 2.5 lists \[d_H(\{u_0\ge h\},\operatorname{supp}u_0)<\infty,
 \qquad d_H(U,\operatorname{supp}u_0)<\infty,\] where \(U\) obeys (2.5)–(2.6). These two conditions alone are insufficient. The second condition of (8.1), the thickness of a high-level set, must remain in force.

A counterexample to the two-condition reading. Take \(N=2\), \(f(u)=u(1-u)\), \(H=\{x_2\le0\}\), and \[S=\bigcup_{\substack{k\in\mathbb Z^2\\k_2\le0}}
       \overline B_{\exp(-|k|^2)}(k),\qquad u_0=\mathbf1_S.\] The union is locally finite and closed, with positive-measure interior seeds. For any \(h\in(0,1]\) the high-level set and support both equal \(S\), and \(d_H(H,S)<\infty\). Thus both printed distances are finite, with the comparison subgraph \(H\) given by \(\gamma=0\). For each \(\delta>0\), however, \(S_\delta\) is bounded or empty: sufficiently remote balls are disjoint and have radii below \(\delta\). The omitted uniform thickness fails.

If every translated large-time limit depended only on \(x_2\), parabolic compactness would imply \(\|\partial_{x_1}u(t,\cdot)\|_\infty\to0\). Let \(K\ge1\) be a global large-time gradient bound. A value at least \(1/4\) gives a value at least \(1/8\) on a ball of radius \(1/(8K)\). KPP invasion then supplies a fixed recovery time \(\tau\) after which the center is at least \(1/2\). The fixed ball \(B_1(0)\subset S\) supplies the initial seed. Once \(|\partial_{x_1}u|\le\varepsilon\), each recovery permits a further displacement \(L=1/(4\varepsilon)\) along \(e_1\) while retaining a value at least \(1/4\). Choose \(\varepsilon<1/(8\tau)\). Iteration produces points moving at speed \(L/\tau>2\) whose values stay positive, contradicting the Gaussian propagation bound. Hence a nonvertical limiting profile exists.

Interpretive boundary and repair. The preceding paragraph of the article may intend to keep all of (8.1) implicit for this sentence. On that reading, the example is excluded and no counterexample to the intended extension is supplied. This is why the item is classified as a scope clarification rather than an unconditional refutation of the extension. Explicitly retain \(d_H(\{u_0\ge h\},\{u_0\ge h\}_\delta)<\infty\). The example demonstrates why it cannot simply be dropped, and does not use a null-set modification of the initial data.
# Local proof corrections

Problem 3 (Minor: the seed radius in Lemma 4.1).  On p. 11, the comparison solution is initialized by \(\mathbf1_{B_1}\), although the assumptions only provide \(B_\delta(x_0)\subset U\). For \(\delta=1/4\) and \(U=B_\delta(x_0)\), domination of the unit-ball initial value already fails in the intervening annulus. It also fails at suitable positive small times. Replace the initial datum by \(\mathbf1_{B_\delta}\). The waiting time already may depend on \(\delta\), so the lemma’s quantifiers and intended conclusion survive.

Problem 4 (Minor: an allowed zero denominator).  Theorem 4.2, Step 2, p. 15, ends its estimate with a constant containing \(|\beta'|/|\beta_N|\). Only \(\beta'\ne0\) is assumed, so \(\beta_N=0\) is allowed. Keep the constant supplied by direct substitution: \[\left(\frac{|\beta'|-\vartheta}{|\beta_N|+\vartheta}
                   +1\right)|\bar x|.\] For fixed \(\vartheta>0\) it is finite, and the coefficient of the large time variable remains positive after choosing \(\vartheta\) sufficiently small. This repairs the separation argument without changing its geometric conclusion.

Problem 5 (Minor: original and rotated coordinates are mixed).  In Step 6, p. 17, the limit is defined using \(u(t_n+t,x_n+M_nx)\), with \(M_ne_N=e_n\to e\). It follows that \[u_\infty(0,x)=\psi(Mx)=\Psi(x_N),\] whereas the printed text uses \(\Psi(x\cdot e)\) and then translates along \(e\) in the rotated coordinates. Use \(e_N\) consistently in this paragraph, or take the unrotated entire-time limit from its definition. The strong-maximum-principle argument then retains its strict-monotonicity conclusion.

Problem 6 (Minor: the support-to-level-set distance is missing).  In the general-data proof on p. 31, put \(A=\{u_0\ge h\}\) and \(S=\operatorname{supp}u_0\). The paper uses \(L=d_H(A,A_\delta)+1\), although the coordinate origin is a projection onto \(S\). The sufficient uniform choice is \[L>d_H(S,A)+d_H(A,A_\delta).\] Both terms are finite under the full (8.1). For a concrete failure of the printed choice, take two unit balls centered at \(0\) and \(100e_1\), assign values \(1\) and \(\varepsilon<h\) on them, and take \(\delta=1/4\). Then the printed \(L\) is \(5/4\). The projection \(100e_1+e_2\) of \(100e_1+2e_2\) onto \(S\) is at distance \(\sqrt{10001}-3/4\) from \(A_\delta\). Thus it cannot find the required core inside the stated \(L\)-ball. Adding the missing distance repairs this step.
# A boundary case of the final conjecture

Problem 7 (Minor: constant limits need not both occur).  Conjecture 8.1, p. 31, states without excluding degenerate supports that \[\Omega(u)=\{0,1,\varphi(x\cdot e+a):
                         e\in\mathcal E,\ a\in\mathbb R\}.\] Theorem 2.2 permits \(U=\mathbb R^N\). Here \(u\equiv1\), \(\mathcal E=\varnothing\), and \(\Omega(u)=\{1\}\), while the displayed right side contains zero as well. Likewise \(U=\varnothing\) gives only the zero function. More generally, nonempty relatively dense thick sets invade uniformly, so zero is not a limiting profile.

Restrict the conjecture to nonempty, non-relatively-dense supports, or include only the constant profiles that actually occur. This is an error in a conjecture’s boundary scope, not a counterexample to a proved main theorem. The bistable statements in the final section are treated according to their stated status as extensions or open questions, not as completed proofs.

Its actual process exit code is zero. It does not numerically solve the PDE, and neither the analytic counterexamples nor an external theorem are misrepresented as computer-certified proofs.
