report: Abstract: This review checks the explicit local distributions, their Palm normalization, and the final concentration-to-almost-sure-convergence implication in Martin, Sly and Zhang. One local error is established: the Bernoulli parameter in an alternative general-direction sampling representation is reversed. An exact correction is proved. The separate derivations of Propositions 1.5 and 1.6 agree with independent calculations. The complete geometric convergence argument is not certified.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Local distributions along exponential last-passage geodesics: a technical review
# Identity, version and scope

The reviewed article is James B. Martin, Allan Sly and Lingfu Zhang, Convergence of the environment seen from geodesics in exponential last-passage percolation, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 27 (2025), 877–970, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1594 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1594) [main]. The exact publisher PDF is the primary source; PDF page \(j\) corresponds to printed page \(876+j\). The supplied author manuscript arXiv:2106.05242v2, dated 16 December 2024, is a distinct source [preprint]; its page 29 was compared only for the alternative representation.

Detailed checks cover the geometric convention in (2.4)–(2.5), Lemmas 4.1–4.2, the calculations underlying Propositions 1.5–1.6, and the implication from Propositions 10.1–10.2 to Theorems 1.1–1.2. The introduction’s dependency map and the block argument in Section 10 were examined at the level described below. The coupling, ergodicity and geometric estimates in Sections 2–3 and 5–9 were not all re-proved. No whole-paper correctness claim follows.
# Definitions and checked dependencies

Fix \(p=\rho\in(0,1)\) and write \(q=1-p\), \(a=pq\) and \(D=p^2+q^2\). We use the paper’s positive-integer geometric convention, \[\Pr(X=k)=p q^{k-1},\qquad k=1,2,\ldots.\] The two Palm components \(\Psi^{(1)}\) and \(\Psi^{(2)}\) have mixture weights \(q^2/D\) and \(p^2/D\) (printed p. 908). Under either component, the next right and left waiting times are independent. Lemma 4.2 (p. 910) gives their survival functions. This conditional independence is essential: mixing the marginals first and then multiplying them would be unjustified.

Equation reference: eq:survival. Multiplying the two survival functions separately within each component gives \[S_1(h)=(1+ph)(1+ah)e^{-h},\qquad
 S_2(h)=(1+qh)(1+ah)e^{-h},\quad h\geq0.\] Consequently \[
 \frac{q^2S_1(h)+p^2S_2(h)}D
 =\left(1+\frac{a h}D\right)(1+ah)e^{-h},\] which reproduces Proposition 1.5. Differentiating yields the Gamma\((1,1)\), Gamma\((2,1)\) and Gamma\((3,1)\) mixture weights \[\frac{p^4+q^4}{D},\qquad 2pq,\qquad \frac{2p^2q^2}{D}.\] They are nonnegative and sum to one. Their mean equals \(1/D\), consistent with the Palm jump intensity \(D\) and the length-bias normalization in Lemma 4.1 (pp. 908–909).

For the corner calculation on p. 911, the first conditional crossing probability is \[\int_0^\infty (1+ah)e^{-qh}p^2h e^{-ph}\,dh
 =p^2(1+2a).\] The other is \(q^2(1+2a)\). Mixing gives \(2p^2q^2(1+2a)/D\), as in Proposition 1.6; the symmetric value is \(3/8\). These checks do not use the erroneous alternative representation below.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (Reversed Bernoulli parameter in the alternative representation).  On printed p. 911, under An alternative representation of the weights on geodesics, the article asserts, in paraphrase, that a positive-integer Geometric\((p)\) variable satisfies \(X-1\overset d=BX\) with an independent Bernoulli\((p)\) variable. It then uses that parameter in the general-\(p\) representation of \(L(0,1)\) and of its minimum with \(L(1,0)\). The parameter must be \(q=1-p\).
## Decisive check and original hypotheses

All assumptions can be met with \(p=1/3\) and an independent \(B\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\). Then \[\Pr(X-1=0)=p=\tfrac13,\qquad
 \Pr(BX=0)=1-p=\tfrac23.\] Both distributions are defined on the stated domains, so the claimed equality in distribution fails. An alternative convention does not resolve the discrepancy: equations (2.4)–(2.5) and their accompanying Bernoulli construction on p. 889 explicitly fix the convention.

Equation reference: eq:bern. The effect extends to the asserted continuous distribution. For independent \(E_3,E_4\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)\) and \(B\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(b)\), \[
 \Pr\{(E_3+B E_4)/p>h\}=(1+bph)e^{-ph}.\] The printed choice \(b=p\) produces \((1+p^2h)e^{-ph}\), whereas Lemma 4.2 requires \((1+pqh)e^{-ph}\). Setting \(p=1/3\) and \(h=1\) gives respectively \(10e^{-1/3}/9\) and \(11e^{-1/3}/9\).

# Convergence checks and limits

For each fixed bounded cylinder test function and tolerance, the exponential bounds in Propositions 10.1–10.2 are summable. report: Abstract: Three issues are established in the supplied publisher online-first article of Ruiz. The central nonlinear bifurcation construction uses incompatible notions of boundary mean; this invalidates a stated Banach-space mapping, although a fixed projection repairs that step without changing the desired solutions or linearization. Two local statements also require correction: differentiability of the radial family with values in \(C^4\), and a general spherical-harmonic multiplicity formula. Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Sign-changing overdetermined elliptic problems: a technical review
# Identity, version and coverage

The primary source is David Ruiz, Nonsymmetric sign-changing solutions to overdetermined elliptic problems in bounded domains, J. Eur. Math. Soc., publisher online-first version (2025), DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1595 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1595) [main]. Its 29 PDF pages are numbered 1–29. The first page records revision on 3 January 2024. The distinct supplied arXiv:2211.14014v2, dated 20 April 2023, was retained but not fully collated; findings below are attributed to the publisher file, not automatically to that manuscript.

The detailed review concerns the radial family and radial nondegeneracy in Section 3, the boundary operator and its linearization in Section 4, the variational sign-change mechanism and fixed-space bifurcation construction in Sections 5–6, and the invariant-space calculations in the Appendix. External PDE existence, elliptic regularity, unique continuation and degree-theoretic results are dependencies, not newly proved theorems here. This is a scoped initial review, not a certification of every proof or reference.
# The nonlinear range defect

Problem 1 (Major: the map used for inversion has the wrong range).  On p. 23, the proof of Theorem 2.1 asserts that \[S_\rho:w\longmapsto w-F(\rho,w)\] maps a neighborhood of zero in \(C^{2,\alpha}_{G,m}(\Sigma)\) into \(C^{1,\alpha}_{G,m}(\Sigma)\), and applies the inverse function theorem there. Formula [eq:F] (#eq:F) does not define such a map.
## A check within the actual PDE family

Equation reference: eq:mean. This is not just an example using an arbitrary boundary function. Put \(w=\varepsilon h\), where \(h\) is a nonzero smooth \(G\)-invariant function of fixed mean zero. Proposition 4.3 and (3.4), on pp. 17 and 9, give \[F(\rho,\varepsilon h)=-c_\rho\varepsilon H_\rho h+o(\varepsilon),
 \qquad c_\rho=u_\rho'(1)>0.\] Since \(J_{\varepsilon h}=1+(N-1)\varepsilon h+O(\varepsilon^2)\), the exact weighted-mean identity gives \[\begin{aligned}
\int_\Sigma F(\rho,\varepsilon h)\,d\theta
&=-\int_\Sigma F(\rho,\varepsilon h)(J_{\varepsilon h}-1)\,d\theta \notag\\
&=(N-1)c_\rho\varepsilon^2
       \int_\Sigma hH_\rho h\,d\theta+o(\varepsilon^2).
\end{aligned}\] Only the stated first differentiability of \(F\) is needed for this expansion.

Choose any \[\max\{\rho_0,\sigma^{-1}\}<\rho<\bar\lambda_2^{-1},\] an available interval because assumption (G) gives \(\sigma>\bar\lambda_2\). For the extension \(\psi_{\rho,h}\) of Proposition 3.4, Lemma 2.3 and (5.2)–(5.3), pp. 8 and 19, imply \[\rho\int_\Sigma hH_\rho h
 =Q_\rho(\psi_{\rho,h})
 \geq(\rho\sigma-1)\int_B\psi_{\rho,h}^2
       +(N-1)\rho\int_\Sigma h^2>0.\] For a concrete allowed symmetry, take \(N=2\), \(G=D_5\) and \(h(\theta)=\pi^{-1/2}\cos(5\theta)\). All symmetry, smoothness and mean conditions hold. For sufficiently small nonzero \(\varepsilon\), the domain remains valid and Proposition 4.1 supplies the actual solution. Equation [eq:mean] (#eq:mean) is strictly positive. Therefore \(\int_\Sigma S_\rho(\varepsilon h)\neq0\) arbitrarily close to the base point.
## Repair, counterevidence and scope

Let \(P_0f=f-|\Sigma|^{-1}\int_\Sigma f\) and replace \(F\) by \[\widehat F(\rho,w)=P_0q_w=P_0F(\rho,w).\] This lies in the fixed mean-zero space. Moreover, \[\widehat F=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ q_w\text{ is constant}
 \ \Longleftrightarrow\ F=0.\] Equation (4.6) states that \(H_\rho\) preserves fixed mean zero, so \(D_w\widehat F(\rho,0)=-c_\rho H_\rho\) on that space. Consequently \(\widehat S_\rho=w-\widehat F(\rho,w)\) has the range and linearization needed for the displayed inversion. The proposed correction changes neither the target overdetermined condition nor the spectrum used in the parity argument.

The linearization at the round ball was not itself contradicted: it misses the discrepancy, which starts at second order. Nor can a moving weighted function space silently resolve the printed proof, since p. 6 specifies fixed spaces and pp. 16–17 specify a radial pullback. The classification is Major because a core construction in the proof of Theorems 2.1 and 1.1 is not defined as claimed. A short repair and a plausible surviving theorem do not make that original construction valid. The verified repair is local to this defect; it is not an independent validation of the entire bifurcation proof.
# Regularity of the parameterized radial family

Problem 2 (Minor: \(C^1\) dependence with values in \(C^4\) fails).  Proposition 3.2(b), p. 12, asserts that \(U:(0,\bar\lambda_2^{-1})\to C^4(\overline B)\), \(U(\rho)=u_\rho\), is \(C^1\). The one-line inverse-function justification on p. 13 does not establish this regularity, and the claim is false at an explicit admissible parameter.
## Decisive nodal calculation

Take \(N=3\). The second radial Dirichlet eigenvalue is \(\bar\lambda_2=4\pi^2\). On the negative annulus \(p_\rho<r<1\), the function \(y(r)=r u_\rho(r)\) solves \[y''+\rho^{-1}y=0,\qquad y(p_\rho)=y(1)=0.\] Proposition 3.1(a) specifies exactly one interior node and a negative outer annulus. Hence \[p_\rho=1-\pi\sqrt\rho.\] At \(\rho_*=(16\pi^2)^{-1}\), one has \(p_{\rho_*}=3/4\) and \(p'_{\rho_*}=-2\pi^2\). The nodal slope \(a=u_{\rho_*}'(3/4)\) is negative and nonzero: zero value and zero slope would force the outer ODE solution to vanish identically.

Equation reference: eq:diff. If \(U\) were differentiable into \(C^4\), its derivative \(v=\partial_\rho u_\rho|_{\rho_*}\) would belong to \(C^4\) and differentiation of the nodal identity would give \[v(3/4)=-a p'_{\rho_*}=2\pi^2a\neq0.\] Differentiating the PDE would give \[
 -\Delta u_{\rho_*}-\rho_*\Delta v
   =\bigl(1-3(u_{\rho_*}^+)^2\bigr)v.\] The left side is \(C^2\) near \(r=3/4\). On the right, the second radial derivative has a jump of magnitude \(|6a^2v(3/4)|>0\): the contribution from \(-3(u^+)^2v\) on the positive side tends to \(-6a^2v(3/4)\), and on the negative side it is zero. This contradicts [eq:diff] (#eq:diff). The example satisfies the stated dimension, parameter interval and nodal conditions.
## A sufficient lower-regularity correction

For any fixed \(0<\alpha<1\), the defensible statement is local \(C^1\) dependence into \(C^{2,\alpha}_{0,r}(\overline B)\). Indeed, the map \[(\rho,u)\longmapsto-\rho\Delta u-u+(u^+)^3\] is \(C^1\) from the corresponding parameter–Hölder space into \(C^{0,\alpha}_r\). Its derivative in \(u\) is the radial linearized operator of (3.7), which is invertible by Proposition 3.2(a) and Schauder theory. The implicit function theorem, together with uniqueness of the radial family, gives that correction throughout the interval. It does not give a \(C^4\)-valued derivative.

Individual solutions may still be \(C^{4,\alpha}\), as stated in Proposition 3.1. That fact does not imply the stronger parameter regularity. The \(C^{2,\alpha}\) formulation is compatible with the normal-derivative construction in Section 4. Accordingly, this overstatement is classified as a local Minor issue; no additional failure of the existence conclusion is inferred.
# The four-dimensional multiplicity formula
## Representation-theoretic verification

Let \(Y'=2I\) be the binary icosahedral group and \(V_i=\operatorname{Sym}^i(\mathbb C^2)\). The full group and its action on spherical harmonics are \[G=(Y'\times Y')/\{(1,1),(-1,-1)\},\qquad
 \mathcal H_i(S^3;\mathbb C)\simeq V_i\otimes V_i^*.\] Thus \[\dim\mathcal H_i^G
   =\dim V_i^{Y'}\cdot\dim(V_i^*)^{Y'}
   =(\dim V_i^{Y'})^2.\] For even \(i\), the single-factor character average is exactly \(a_i\); for odd \(i\), the central element \(-1\) excludes invariants. This is also explicit in the article’s own reference [21]: Nelson–Widom [nw], printed pp. 123–124, equations (2.37), (2.42)–(2.48). In particular, their (2.47) contains the square before (2.48) gives the single-factor average.

Set \(i=60\), an allowed even degree. Each nonidentity character ratio in the displayed average equals 1, giving \[a_{60}=(61+20+12+12+15)/60=2,\qquad
 \dim\mathcal H_{60}^G=4.\] This exact example distinguishes the claimed dimension from the correct one. The correction is \(m(i)=a_i^2\) for even \(i\) and \(m(i)=0\) for odd \(i\); the factor \(1/60\) must be squared along with the bracket.

The values needed for (G) remain unchanged: \(a_2=a_4=a_6=a_8=a_{10}=0\) and \(a_{12}=1\). Consequently the first nontrivial invariant degree remains 12 with multiplicity one. This is a Minor error in an unnecessary general formula, not a disproof of the four-dimensional application.
# Surviving checks and remaining dependencies

The radial Morse-index argument in Proposition 3.2(a) uses the negative part \(u_\rho^-\), not \(u_\rho\): its zero quadratic-form value and lack of \(C^1\) regularity force a negative eigenvalue. If the second radial eigenvalue were nonpositive, a linear combination of the first two modes vanishing at \(p_\rho\) would have nonpositive form. The inner form is strictly positive unless the function vanishes, whereas the outer annular form is nonnegative with kernel proportional to \(u_\rho\). Matching at the node then gives a contradiction. This mechanism survives Problem 2.

The upper-parameter positive sign of the nonradial form follows from \(\rho\sigma>1\) as above. The Appendix’s low-degree invariant multiplicities were checked for the dihedral, icosahedral and 600-cell groups; the generally incorrect high-degree expression is not needed there. The sign-change and parity framework still depends on the analytic eigenvalue arguments, unique continuation, and the stated Krasnosel’skiı̆ theorem. Those imported results and every regularity assertion in their applications have not been independently certified. No author code or computer algebra notebook was executed.
# Conclusion
Item | State
Overall assessment | Major: invalid nonlinear fixed-space range in a central proof.
Other findings | Two Minor local statements, each with an exact analytic contradiction.
Repair status | Fixed projection, lower regularity, and squared multiplicity verified at the stated scope.
Main theorem | Not disproved; complete repaired proof not independently certified.
Author adoption | Unknown; no communication sent.
Scientific decision | Pending; human reviews empty.

Its derivative in \(u\) is the radial linearized operator of (3.7), which is invertible by Proposition 3.2(a) and Schauder theory. The implicit function theorem, together with uniqueness of the radial family, gives that correction throughout the interval. It does not give a \(C^4\)-valued derivative.

Individual solutions may still be \(C^{4,\alpha}\), as stated in Proposition 3.1. That fact does not imply the stronger parameter regularity. The \(C^{2,\alpha}\) formulation is compatible with the normal-derivative construction in Section 4. result: Result: C4-valued parameter differentiability fails at this admissible parameter.
Impact: Overstated parameter regularity; lower regularity suffices for the Section 4 construction, with no separate demonstrated failure of the main theorem.

problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 26 Pdf pages: 27 Labels: Section 7.3 Labels: displayed general even-degree m(i) formula Reference pdf: sources/0222/Nelson_Widom_1984.pdf Reference pages: 11 Reference pages: 12 Reference printed pages: 123 Reference printed pages: 124 Reference equations: 2.37 Reference equations: 2.42-2.48
claim: The displayed single-factor character average a_i equals dim H_i(S3)^G for all even i.
G is the full 7200-element rotation group specified in the article, G=(2I x 2I)/diag{+/-1}; i=60 is an allowed even degree.
analysis:
Let \(Y'=2I\) be the binary icosahedral group and \(V_i=\operatorname{Sym}^i(\mathbb C^2)\). The full group and its action on spherical harmonics are \[G=(Y'\times Y')/\{(1,1),(-1,-1)\},\qquad
 \mathcal H_i(S^3;\mathbb C)\simeq V_i\otimes V_i^*.\] Thus \[\dim\mathcal H_i^G
   =\dim V_i^{Y'}\cdot\dim(V_i^*)^{Y'}
   =(\dim V_i^{Y'})^2.\] For even \(i\), the single-factor character average is exactly \(a_i\); for odd \(i\), the central element \(-1\) excludes invariants. This is also explicit in the article’s own reference [21]: Nelson–Widom [nw], printed pp. 123–124, equations (2.37), (2.42)–(2.48). In particular, their (2.47) contains the square before (2.48) gives the single-factor average.

Set \(i=60\), an allowed even degree. Each nonidentity character ratio in the displayed average equals 1, giving \[a_{60}=(61+20+12+12+15)/60=2,\qquad
 \dim\mathcal H_{60}^G=4.\] This exact example distinguishes the claimed dimension from the correct one. The correction is \(m(i)=a_i^2\) for even \(i\) and \(m(i)=0\) for odd \(i\); the factor \(1/60\) must be squared along with the bracket.

report: Abstract: The specified arXiv version of Zhao’s paper contains a norm formula that does not define the asserted map of presheaves. A finite étale double cover gives an explicit failure of base-change naturality detected by a tame symbol. Three additional local statements require correction: a motivic-cohomology vanishing boundary, an omitted action in a Postnikov classification, and a global endomorphism assertion over a disconnected base. A later author-hosted manuscript removes or corrects the latter two passages, but retains the two comparison-section formulas examined here. These findings do not disprove the principal classification of étale metaplectic covers.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Étale metaplectic covers: a review of comparison maps and categorical hypotheses
# Source identity and scope

The primary source is Yifei Zhao, Étale metaplectic covers of reductive group schemes, arXiv:2204.00610v2, 21 February 2023, 78 pages [main]. The journal identity is J. Eur. Math. Soc., DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1596 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1596), online publication 21 January 2025. Publisher equivalence of the supplied author manuscript has not been verified. All unqualified page numbers below are one-based pages of that exact arXiv PDF, whose printed page numbers agree.

A separate 79-page PDF currently linked from the author’s website was retrieved [later]. The webpage labels the paper as updated in April 2026; the downloaded PDF has a distinct hash. This is a comparison source, not a replacement for the frozen primary input. The comparison here is limited to the four passages identified below, not a full collation or a claim about the publisher’s current text.

The detailed checks concern Sections 1.2 and 2.3, the self-cup-product and torus constructions in Sections 3–4, the strict quadratic-form and fiber-sequence structure in Section 5.1, Borel-choice dependence in Section 5.2, and dual-root and tensor-category constructions in Sections 6.1–6.4. Imported cohomology calculations, higher-categorical coherence and all applications are not independently re-proved.
# Failure of the prescribed norm construction

In Section 2.3.5, p. 20, the paper constructs \[\mathbb Z(n)[n]\longrightarrow \underline K_n \tag{2.16}\] from a purported presheaf map \(\mathbb Z_{\mathrm{tr}}(\mathbb G_m^{\times n})\to\underline K_n\). For an elementary finite correspondence \(Y_1\subset Y\times\mathbb G_m^n\) with coordinate units \(f_1,\ldots,f_n\), the rule takes the product of the separate norms \(\operatorname{Nm}(f_i)\) in \(K_n(Y)\).

Problem 1 (Major: separate norms do not give a natural map).  The rule in Section 2.3.5 fails naturality under a finite étale base change, already for \(n=2\) and smooth integral schemes over the perfect field \(\mathbb Q\).
## A correspondence satisfying the stated hypotheses

Set \[Y=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Q[s^{\pm1},t^{\pm1}],\qquad
 Z=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Q[u^{\pm1},t^{\pm1}],\qquad s=u^2.\] The map \(Z\to Y\) is finite étale of degree two. Inside \(Y\times\mathbb G_m^2\), with target coordinates \(x,y\), the equations \(x^2=s\), \(y=t\) define an integral closed correspondence finite and surjective over \(Y\), identified with \(Z\). Its two coordinate units are \(u,t\).

Use additive notation for \(K_2\), and write \(\{a,b\}\) for the product of two \(K_1\) units. The printed rule sends this correspondence to \[\{\operatorname{Nm}(u),\operatorname{Nm}(t)\}
       =\{-s,t^2\}.\] Pull back along \(Y'=Z\to Y\). Its image then becomes \[\{-u^2,t^2\}=2\{-u^2,t\}.\] However, the pulled-back correspondence splits as the sum of the two multiplicity-one graphs \[(u,t)\quad\text{and}\quad(-u,t).\] The factors \(x-u\) and \(x+u\) are comaximal because \(2u\) is invertible. Applying the additive rule directly after base change therefore gives \[\{u,t\}+\{-u,t\}=\{-u^2,t\}.\] The difference is \(\{-u^2,t\}\). It is nonzero: in \(\mathbb Q(u,t)\) its tame boundary at the valuation \(t=0\) is \(-u^2\neq1\) (or its inverse under the opposite convention). Thus the discrepancy is visible at the generic point and cannot disappear by Zariski sheafification. No singular correspondence, nonunit coordinate, inseparable extension or multiplicity ambiguity is involved.
## Impact and bounded repair

The invalid presheaf construction is used to specify (2.16), then (2.19), and hence the particular comparison asserted in Theorem 2.3.8. Section 2.3.11, p. 22, invokes that theorem to define the comparison with Brylinski–Deligne extensions. A complete repair must supply a transfer-compatible motivic-to-\(K_2\) morphism on all relevant finite correspondences, its descent to the complexes, and the compatibilities subsequently used. The displayed transfer fixes this example; it is not a newly certified construction of that entire functor.

A standard comparison may exist by other methods. The counterexample does not say that all comparison theorems are false, nor that the main classification in Sections 4–5 is false. The Major classification concerns the explicit construction of an important comparison map, which is not defined as claimed. The same separate-norm formula remains on p. 19 of the later author-hosted PDF.
# The boundary degree in motivic cohomology

Problem 2 (Minor: equation (2.22) excludes a nonzero boundary group).  Page 21 attributes to Kahn’s Theorem 1.6 the assertion \[H^i(X_{\mathrm{Zar}},\mathbb Z(2))=0\qquad(i\geq4)
 \tag{2.22}\] for connected smooth \(X\) over a perfect field. The case \(i=4\) is false.

Take \(X=\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb Q}\). Weight-two motivic cohomology in degree four is \[H^4(X_{\mathrm{Zar}},\mathbb Z(2))\simeq
 H^2(X_{\mathrm{Zar}},\underline K_2)
 \simeq\operatorname{CH}^2(\mathbb P^2_{\mathbb Q})\simeq\mathbb Z.\] The intersection of two rational lines is a point of degree one; the degree is invariant under rational equivalence, so this class cannot vanish. This example satisfies smoothness, connectedness and perfection of the ground field.

The cited primary reference was actually consulted: Kahn [kahn], printed p. 401, Theorem 1.6, includes \[H^i_{\mathrm{Zar}}(X,\Gamma_{\mathrm{Zar}}(2))
   \simeq H^{i-2}_{\mathrm{Zar}}(X,\underline K_2),
       \qquad 2\leq i\leq4.\] It states zero outside the listed degrees, not at degree four. The same page identifies the codimension-two Chow term; the projective-space calculation on printed p. 411 also exhibits the nonzero \(\mathbb Z\) term.

The positive-degree vanishing threshold in the quoted formula should be \(i>4\). One must also distinguish global hypercohomology from cohomology sheaves. Kahn’s Remark 1.5 states that the latter occur only in degrees 1 and 2. The paper’s preceding (2.21), and its section convention in 2.3.6, concern global hypercohomology, so interpreting (2.22) as a sheaf assertion does not rescue the printed wording.

The next paragraph deduces the fiber of \(\mathbb Z(2)[2]\to\underline K_2\) using (2.21)–(2.22). A corrected proof can use the actual cohomology-sheaf calculation, after a valid comparison map has been supplied. The boundary correction is local and does not by itself disprove Theorem 2.3.8; neither does it repair Problem 1. The later author-hosted PDF retains the same \(i\geq4\) assertion on p. 20.
# Missing monodromy in the preliminary classification

Problem 3 (Minor: Lemma 1.2.7 has an unrestricted target).  Section 1.2.6 and Lemma 1.2.7, p. 13, identify \(\operatorname{Maps}_{E_1}(H,B^{n+1}A)\) with all grouplike \(E_1\) objects having \(\pi_0=H\), \(\pi_n=A\), no other homotopy groups, and a convergent Postnikov tower. The target omits the action of \(H\) on \(A\).

Work on the terminal site, with \(n=1\), \(H=C_2\) and \(A=C_3\), written additively. Define a strict monoidal groupoid with objects \(h\in C_2\), no arrows between distinct objects, and automorphism group \(C_3\) at each object. Put \[h\otimes k=h+k,\qquad
 a\otimes b=a+(-1)^h b\] for arrows \(a\) at \(h\) and \(b\) at \(k\). The two parenthesizations of a triple give \(a+(-1)^h b+(-1)^{h+k}c\), so associativity holds; the identity and inverse conditions are immediate. This is a grouplike, 1-truncated object with exactly the required homotopy groups. Its Postnikov tower converges.

Conjugation by the nonidentity component of \(C_2\) acts on \(C_3\) by inversion. In contrast, an \(E_1\) map \(C_2\to B^2C_3\) deloops to \[BC_2\longrightarrow B^3C_3.\] Its homotopy fiber is a Postnikov extension with the constant, hence trivial, \(C_2\) action on \(C_3\). The displayed nontrivial action is invariant under an equivalence preserving the identified homotopy groups. It therefore excludes our groupoid from the image, disproving essential surjectivity. Since \(C_2\) is abelian, the \(k=1\) case of Remark 1.2.8(2) is affected as well.

One must restrict the target to trivial action, with the appropriate identification data, or retain an action \(\rho:H\to\operatorname{Aut}(A)\) and use a twisted Postnikov class. This review proves the missing-action obstruction and the point-site counterexample, not all coherences of a replacement statement over an arbitrary site.

There is counterevidence to treating this as a failure of the main geometric classification. Section 4.4.1 uses the forward construction from a map to its extension, which is valid. For the torus objects used there, geometric connectedness and finite locally constant coefficients exclude the displayed component action. Moreover, the later author-hosted PDF ends Section 1.2 at 1.2.5, then starts Section 1.3 (pp. 12–13): the old 1.2.6–1.2.8 passage is absent. This is an observed version change, not an assertion about the author’s reason for it.
# Global endomorphisms over a disconnected base

Problem 4 (Minor: Remark 6.3.7 needs connectedness or a sheaf formulation).  Page 63 asserts \(E\simeq\operatorname{End}(\mathbf1)\) for the category of global sections of the twisted representation stack. Section 6.0.1, p. 59, has not required the base scheme to be connected.

Let \(S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C\sqcup\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C\), take \(G=\mathbb G_m\), trivial coefficient group \(A\), zero cover \(\mu\), and any permitted coefficient field \(E\). The global category is the product of its two untwisted component categories. Thus \[\operatorname{End}(\mathbf1)=E\times E,
 \qquad E\longrightarrow E\times E,\quad a\longmapsto(a,a).\] The idempotent \((1,0)\) is not in the image. All the stipulated reductivity and coefficient assumptions hold.

The endomorphism sheaf is the constant sheaf \(E\); globally one obtains \(H^0(S,E)\). For a nonempty connected \(S\) this equals \(E\). Consequently the argument that checks the claim étale locally establishes the sheaf statement, not the unrestricted global statement. Section 6.4 already imposes connectedness, so the ensuing field-oriented construction is not contradicted by this example. The later author-hosted PDF, p. 64, explicitly uses the endomorphism-sheaf formulation and adds connectedness for the global Deligne-category conclusion. This local issue is therefore already corrected in that comparison source.
# Surviving computations and proof boundaries
Several potentially delicate points were checked without yielding further established defects.

For a strict quadratic form, write \(m=\langle\check\alpha,\lambda\rangle\). The defining relation on p. 45 gives \[Q(\lambda-m\alpha)
 =Q(\lambda)+m^2Q(\alpha)-m\,b(\alpha,\lambda)=Q(\lambda).\] It implies Weyl invariance. The converse need not follow with 2-torsion coefficients: for the cocharacter lattice of \(\mathrm{SL}_2\times\mathbb G_m\) and \(A=\mathbb Z/2\), the form \(Q(m,n)=mn\) is Weyl invariant but violates the strict mixed relation. This confirms the need for the paper’s stronger condition rather than refuting it.

The fiber sequence of Theorem 5.1.13, p. 48, is formally compatible with the exact lattice sequence \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{sc}}\to\Lambda\to\pi_1G\) and derived Hom into \(A[2]\). Rank-one checks for \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) and \(\mathrm{PGL}_2\) preserve the torsion contributed by \(\pi_1G\); replacing derived Hom by ordinary Hom would lose it. The requisite reductive-group cohomology calculation in Proposition 5.1.11 remains an imported dependency, not independently established here.

The cyclic calculation behind Proposition 3.3.5 and the 2-torsion correction in Proposition 3.4.2, pp. 26,28–29, is consistent: the cocycle \(c(a,b)=ab\) on \(C_N\) contributes \(\binom N2\) after lifting a generator \(N\) times, and \[-2\binom N2\equiv N\pmod{N^2}.\] This checks the displayed cancellation, not all canonical identifications in the descent proof. The torus argument on pp. 35–37 and the rank-one 2-torsion distinctions on pp. 40–42 were examined with the latter limitation.

On pp. 51–52, dependence on a Borel-conjugating element is measured by \(b\), and disappears only after restriction to its radical \(\Lambda^\sharp\). The proof does not assert unconditional independence on the original torus. On pp. 60–62, if \(n_\alpha\) is the order of \(Q(\alpha)\), the strict relation implies \(n_\alpha\alpha\in\Lambda^\sharp\) and integrality of \(\check\alpha/n_\alpha\) there. The reflected lattice action is unchanged. On \(\Lambda^\sharp\), the form \(Q\) is additive and \(2Q=0\), and \(Q(n_\alpha\alpha)=0\), as needed for the central 2-torsion sign. In rank one the parity of \(n_\alpha\) gives the expected dual root datum. These arithmetic checks do not certify every descent or higher-coherence assertion.

The finite-coefficient choices in Section 6.4 and the applications later in the paper were not fully independently verified. No author code was executed. A bounded title/supplement/correction search identified no dedicated code package or separate erratum; the later author PDF is recorded explicitly. Search incompleteness and lack of code are not counted as defects.

Repair status | Local corrections established; the complete replacement comparison functor is not certified.

Later author manuscript | Two passages removed/corrected; two comparison formulas retained.

report: Abstract: Four findings are established in the supplied author manuscript of Cadoret and Tamagawa. A quadratic Kummer system disproves the pointwise submodule conclusion of Proposition 5 when only a constant-field extension is allowed. An elementary finite-monodromy sheaf with a deleted stalk disproves the unrestricted Fourier-realization theorem in Appendix A. Two further local issues concern the hypotheses of a density lemma and the claimed uniqueness of conjugation between maximal tori. The examples do not refute the central maximality statement formulated in the almost category, or the geometric isogeny applications after appropriate corrections.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Ghosts of abelian schemes: pointwise descent, Fourier purity, and auxiliary hypotheses
# Identity, conventions and review scope

The reviewed file is Anna Cadoret and Akio Tamagawa, Ghosts and families of abelian varieties with a common isogeny factor, 26-page author-hosted manuscript [main]. Its revision date is undetermined. The journal identity is J. Eur. Math. Soc., DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1597 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1597), online first 27 January 2025. Equivalence of the author file with the publisher article has not been established. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, equal to the manuscript’s printed pages.

The paper explicitly distinguishes actual representations from the almost category obtained by restricting to open subgroups (p. 2). It also distinguishes arithmetic monodromy \(G_\ell\) from geometric monodromy \(\overline G_\ell\). These distinctions are essential to the first finding. The review follows the definitions, Hilbertian argument, density lemmas, ghost construction and gcd argument, abelian realization and Appendix. Detailed arithmetic checks are separated below from imported Tate, Honda–Tate, monodromy, companion, and weight theorems.
# Constant-field extension does not give every pointwise factor

Problem 1 (Major: the last assertion of Proposition 5 is too strong).  Proposition 5, p. 4, allows a finite extension of \(k\) and concludes that, for every closed point \(s\), \(a_s^*\Psi(V_\ell)\) is an actual submodule of \((s^*V_\ell)^{\mathrm{ss}}\). This conclusion fails for a rank-one pure rational compatible system.

Take \(k=\mathbb F_q\) with \(q\) odd, \(S=\mathbb G_m/k\), and the connected finite étale cover \[\mathbb G_m\longrightarrow\mathbb G_m,\qquad u\longmapsto u^2.\] For every \(\ell\ne p\), let \(V_\ell\) be its sign representation over \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). It has rank one, finite monodromy, rational characteristic polynomials \(T-1\) or \(T+1\) independent of \(\ell\), and weight zero. Its geometric algebraic monodromy is \(\mu_2\), whose maximal torus is trivial. Consequently \[\dim V_\ell^{\overline T_\ell}=1.\]

After any constant extension \(K=\mathbb F_{q^m}\), choose a square \(a\in K^\times\) and a nonsquare \(b\in K^\times\). They give two \(K\)-rational closed points of \(S_K\). The Frobenius eigenvalues of the sign sheaf at these points are respectively \(+1\) and \(-1\); inversion from arithmetic to geometric Frobenius makes no difference. If a one-dimensional \(\pi_1(K)\)-module \(W\) were an actual submodule at both points, then, since both points have degree one and both local representations have rank one, \[F_K|W=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad F_K|W=-1.\] This is impossible. The counterexample remains valid for every allowed constant-field extension, and satisfies all the purity and compatibility assumptions of the proposition.
## Location of the scope change and repair

Section 6.2.1, p. 12, passes to an arbitrary connected étale cover of \(S\) to obtain connected monodromy and a torsion-free group generated by Frobenius eigenvalues. Section 6.3.2, p. 13, uses those stronger hypotheses to put every semisimple Frobenius in a maximal torus and compare its action. Those reductions are appropriate for almost statements, but do not descend the asserted actual embedding to the original \(S\) after merely extending its constants.

There are two distinct possible corrections: retain the actual embedding only on a suitable finite étale cover of \(S\), with the reduction hypotheses explicitly incorporated; or formulate the original-base comparison as an almost submodule statement, with the needed descent argument. In this example the double cover trivializes the system, and at any fixed closed point the eigenvalue \(-1\) becomes \(+1\) after a quadratic residue-field extension. Thus the almost comparison survives.

The part of Proposition 5 quantified over conjugating elements \(g\) is not separately contradicted here: a nonidentity element of \(\mu_2\) cannot be conjugated into the trivial torus, so that conditional quantifier is empty at the relevant point. The decisive contradiction concerns the unconditional final assertion. This is a Major scope error in a central proposition, not a disproof of the existence of the ghost as an almost representation, Theorem 6’s almost maximality, or every geometric isogeny conclusion.
# An elementary Fourier transform with a weight-zero summand

Problem 2 (Major: Theorem 22 lacks a middle-extension or purity condition).  Appendix A, p. 23, assumes only that \(\mathcal F\) is elementary in the stated sense and has finite monodromy on a nonempty open set. It concludes that, on some nonempty open \(U_2\), its naive Fourier transform is a direct factor of \(R^1\pi_*\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\) for an abelian scheme. The conclusion is false even when the generic rank of \(\mathcal F\) is one.

Take \(k=\mathbb F_3\), \(\ell=2\), a nontrivial additive character \(\psi\) with values in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_2^\times\), and \[j:\mathbb G_m\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1,\qquad i:\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbb A^1,
 \qquad L=\mathcal L_{\psi(t^2)},\qquad \mathcal F=j_!j^*L.\] The generic monodromy has finite order three and is trivialized by an Artin–Schreier cover. The sheaf has no nonzero punctual sections, so it satisfies (Elem-1).

For every \(a\in\overline k\), \[H_c^2(\mathbb A^1_{\overline k},\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal L_{\psi(at)})
   =H_c^2({\mathbb G_m}_{\overline k},\mathcal L_{\psi(t^2+at)})=0.\] Indeed, the polynomial \(t^2+at\) has at infinity a pole of order two, prime to \(p=3\), and defines a geometrically nontrivial rank-one Artin–Schreier sheaf. A rational expression \(h^3-h\) with a pole has pole order divisible by three, so it cannot eliminate that pole. Poincaré duality identifies the indicated top compactly supported cohomology with the dual invariant space, which vanishes. Thus (Elem-2) holds for every \(a\), as required.

There is a short exact sequence \[0\longrightarrow\mathcal F\longrightarrow L
       \longrightarrow i_*\overline{\mathbb Q}_2\longrightarrow0.\] Tensor on \(\mathbb A^1_t\times\mathbb A^1_x\) with the Fourier kernel \(\mathcal L_{\psi(tx)}\) and apply \(Rp_{2!}\). The degree-zero compactly supported cohomology of the smooth rank-one sheaf \(\mathcal L_{\psi(t^2+xt)}\) is zero. The transform in degree zero of the punctual quotient is the constant sheaf. The long exact sequence therefore gives \[0\longrightarrow\overline{\mathbb Q}_2
    \longrightarrow \mathcal F_\psi(\mathcal F)
    \longrightarrow \mathcal F_\psi(L)\longrightarrow0.\] In particular, the Fourier transform contains a nonzero constant sub-local system on every nonempty open where it is lisse. At every closed point this contributes Frobenius eigenvalue \(1\).

For an abelian scheme \(\pi:A\to U_2\), the eigenvalues of geometric Frobenius on \((R^1\pi_*\overline{\mathbb Q}_2)_s\) have complex absolute value \(|k(s)|^{1/2}>1\). It cannot contain that constant subrepresentation, and hence cannot contain the proposed Fourier transform even as a subobject, much less as a direct factor. Shrinking \(U_2\) cannot remove a constant sub-local system.
## The cited purity theorem and the repair boundary

The proof on p. 23 infers generic Fourier purity of weight one from generic finite monodromy and the elementary conditions. On p. 25 that purity is used to kill the contribution of a weight-zero term before embedding in the cohomology of a proper curve. Our example exhibits exactly the term that the argument cannot discard.

Katz’s cited Theorem 7.3.8(5) was checked in the corrected author manuscript [katz], PDF pp. 211–213 (Chapter 7 local pp. 11–13). Its use of purity is governed by Definition 7.3.7, which requires a middle extension in addition to purity on a lisse open. Definition 7.3.5 likewise distinguishes Fourier sheaves from merely elementary ones. Here \(\mathcal F\) is not a middle extension: its stalk at zero is zero, while \(L_0=\overline{\mathbb Q}_2\). Thus the cited theorem does not supply the purity asserted in the paper.

A reasonable repair is to require the appropriate pure middle-extension hypothesis, or to formulate a result for a suitable weight-one quotient. The counterexample and the missing hypothesis are established; a complete corrected realization theorem, including splitting and arbitrary-rank details, is not independently proved in this review. In particular, the counterexample does not invalidate the specific pure middle-extension examples of Katz or the separately cited constructions of Bültel without an additional analysis of those examples.
# Two missing restrictions in the density lemma

Problem 3 (Minor: Lemma 9 needs analyticity and a positive-dimensional density setting).  Lemma 9(1), p. 9, identifies zero density with empty interior for every closed conjugacy-invariant subset of the compact image. This is false for arbitrary closed subsets. In addition, the stated setup on p. 7 allows \(\dim S=0\), where the density conclusions of Lemma 9 fail even for analytic subsets.
## A positive-dimensional counterexample with an actual density

Let \(k=\mathbb F_3\), \(S=\mathbb A^1/k\), \(\ell=2\), and let \[\rho:\pi_1(S)\longrightarrow\widehat{\mathbb Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb Z_2
   \longrightarrow\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Q_2),\qquad
 n\longmapsto u(n)=
 \begin{pmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\] where the arithmetic projection sends geometric Frobenius to \(1\). Its compact image is isomorphic to \(\mathbb Z_2\), and conjugacy in that image is trivial.

Define \[U=\bigcup_{j\geq1}\bigl(-j+2^{j+2}\mathbb Z_2\bigr),
 \qquad C=\mathbb Z_2\setminus U,\qquad \Phi=u(C).\] The negative integers are dense in \(\mathbb Z_2\), so \(U\) is open and dense. Hence \(\Phi\) is closed with empty interior. Its Haar measure satisfies \[\mu(C)\geq1-\sum_{j\geq1}2^{-j-2}=\frac34.\] A Haar-measure calculation alone would not establish the needed Frobenius density. Here it can be established directly. The least positive integer in the \(j\)th removed residue class is \(2^{j+2}-j\). Thus only \(O(\log x)\) classes meet \([1,x]\), and for fixed \(J\) the contribution of the classes with \(j>J\) is at most \[x\sum_{j>J}2^{-j-2}+O(\log x).\] Finite unions of residue classes have their Haar density. Letting first \(x\to\infty\) and then \(J\to\infty\) proves that \(D=C\cap\mathbb Z_{>0}\) has natural density \(d=\mu(C)\geq3/4\).

There are \(N_n=3^n/n+O(3^{n/2}/n)\) closed points of degree \(n\) on \(\mathbb A^1_{\mathbb F_3}\), and \(\rho(F_s)=u(n_s)\). With \(\varepsilon=(t-1)\log3\), the numerator in the paper’s density ratio is therefore \[\sum_{n\in D}\frac{e^{-\varepsilon n}}n+O(1),\] whereas the denominator is \(\sum_{n\geq1}e^{-\varepsilon n}/n+O(1)\). Partial summation from the natural density of \(D\) gives ratio tending to \(d\). Consequently \(\delta_S(\Sigma_\Phi)=d\geq3/4\) although \(\Phi\) has empty interior. This is a counterexample under the actual Frobenius density definition, not just an abstract topological objection.
## The zero-dimensional boundary

Independently take \(S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_3\) and the same arithmetic unipotent representation. There is one closed point, of degree one, and the paper’s ratio assigns \(|S|\) density one. Set \(\Phi=\{u(1)\}\). It is a closed analytic subset with empty interior, but \(\Sigma_\Phi=|S|\). Furthermore \(\Phi_{|S|}\) is a singleton, neither dense in \(u(\mathbb Z_2)\) nor Zariski dense in its connected algebraic closure \(\mathbb G_a\). This contradicts parts (1)–(3) of Lemma 9 under the printed zero-dimensional scope.
## Repair and surviving uses

For positive-dimensional \(S\), restrict the empty-interior equivalence to closed analytic subsets. Serre’s author lecture manuscript [serre], p. 81, states this hypothesis immediately before Theorem 6.11; p. 80 gives only the general closed-set upper-density bound by Haar measure. This 2011 author text is identified separately from the 2012 edition cited by the paper.

The actual subset used in the proof of Lemma 9(2) is explicitly closed analytic, so that positive-dimensional argument survives the restriction. The final assertion in (1), that positive upper density makes the topologically generated subgroup open, can also be obtained from the general Haar bound: the closed generated subgroup has positive Haar measure and hence finite index. It is not refuted by the example above. The zero-dimensional case should be removed from the density machinery and the original local-global questions handled directly when \(S=\operatorname{Spec}k\). These are bounded auxiliary corrections, not a disproof of the main positive-dimensional ghost argument.
# Normalizer ambiguity

Problem 4 (Minor: the conjugating map on zero weights is not canonical).  In the second functoriality bullet of Section 6.4, p. 14, a conjugating element \(g\) with \(\overline T'=g\overline T g^{-1}\) is claimed to be unique up to right multiplication by \(\overline T\). It is then asserted that the resulting map on invariant spaces is independent of \(g\). The ambiguity is the normalizer, not the centralizer.

For \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) and its adjoint representation, put \[T=\{\operatorname{diag}(a,a^{-1})\},\quad
 H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1),\quad
 w=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(V^T=\mathbb Q_\ell H\). Both \(1\) and \(w\) conjugate \(T\) to itself, but they induce \(H\mapsto H\) and \(H\mapsto-H\). Thus the asserted independence fails. This is the rank-one zero-weight situation of the adjoint representation; the large-geometric-monodromy example in Section 3.2, p. 6, produces the corresponding adjoint object when \(g=1\).

Choosing a particular conjugating element still induces an isomorphism natural in representations. Accordingly the earlier statement of independence up to natural isomorphism is not refuted. The repair is to remove the uniqueness assertion and record the Weyl-group ambiguity. At the pro-reductive level a proof must also arrange compatible choices in the relevant quotients; that coherence is not supplied merely by the displayed matrix calculation. This finding is local and does not change the ghost’s numerical dimension or its isomorphism class.
# Positive checks, dependencies and assessment
The following parts of the argument were checked at the stated scope.

In Section 2, pp. 5–6, an open specialized monodromy image suffices to transport an invariant injective map from a closed fiber to an open subgroup of the generic group. The Hilbertian specialization and Frattini input are invoked dependencies. The descent statement is geometric: the relevant field on p. 6 is \(\overline{k(s)}\), not \(k(s)\). The nonsemisimple Kummer example and the \(\operatorname{End}(V)/\mathbb Q_\ell\operatorname{Id}\) example in Section 3 correctly distinguish actual, almost and semisimplified assertions.

Lemma 10, p. 10, uses the convergent logarithm on \(1+\ell M\) (on \(1+4M\) at \(\ell=2\)) to recover a matrix from its positive power. Once that lemma and the corrected density hypothesis are available, Proposition 3’s finite union of closed characteristic-polynomial loci, irreducibility of \(G^\circ\), dominance of the power map at the identity, and semisimple character comparison form a consistent chain.

Under the connected and torsion-free reductions in Section 6.2, the finite central kernel in Section 6.3 lies in the geometric torus and acts trivially on its invariants. This explains lift independence, which is distinct from Problem 4’s Weyl ambiguity. In Section 6.5, torsion-freeness permits gcd to commute with taking powers of roots. The degrees of the normalized gcd polynomials decrease and stabilize. The finite set of initial closed points then supplies one common exponent for an almost factor, and Claim 1 yields Theorem 6’s maximality. The split-prime choice, the tracking of twists in Section 6.5.3.4, and the two cases in Claim 2 were examined; the invoked independence of zero-weight dimension, Frobenius-torus theorem, and open-image result were not re-proved.

Lemma 13 and Corollary 14, pp. 18–19, do not realize an arbitrary rational pure polynomial as an abelian variety. They take a gcd of actual Frobenius polynomials. If a simple Honda–Tate factor contributes \(\Pi_w^{n_w}\), the gcd exponent is \(n_w\min(m_1,m_2)\) and retains the required divisibility by \(n_w\). After a common constant extension, the normalized polynomials are those of actual base-changed fibers. This mechanism is consistent, conditional on the corrected ghost argument.

The implication from a nonzero minuscule weight to the absence of zero weights, and the Rosati argument in Lemma 21, p. 22, were checked. For types I–III the Rosati involution is trivial on the center, so the central subgroup in the polarization kernel satisfies \(h^2=1\) and is finite; this supports the one-dimensional-center and supersingularity conclusion. The characteristic-zero lifting and the specific Bültel/Katz monodromy constructions remain external dependencies. No author code was executed, and no numerical experiment is used as proof.

problems.title: Density lemma omits analyticity and positive-dimensional scope
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 7 Pdf pages: 9 Section: Section4 setup; Lemma9(1)-(3)
claim: The zero-density/empty-interior equivalence is asserted for every closed conjugacy-invariant set. The density-one topological and Zariski conclusions are stated in a setup that also allows dimension zero.
Part A: S=A^1 over F_3, ell=2, rho(F_s)=u(n_s) in u(Z_2). Part B: S=Spec F_3 with the same arithmetic unipotent representation.
analysis: Lemma 9(1), p. 9, identifies zero density with empty interior for every closed conjugacy-invariant subset of the compact image. This is false for arbitrary closed subsets. In addition, the stated setup on p. 7 allows \(\dim S=0\), where the density conclusions of Lemma 9 fail even for analytic subsets.

Let \(k=\mathbb F_3\), \(S=\mathbb A^1/k\), \(\ell=2\), and let \[\rho:\pi_1(S)\longrightarrow\widehat{\mathbb Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb Z_2
   \longrightarrow\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Q_2),\qquad
 n\longmapsto u(n)=
 \begin{pmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\] where the arithmetic projection sends geometric Frobenius to \(1\). Its compact image is isomorphic to \(\mathbb Z_2\), and conjugacy in that image is trivial.

Define \[U=\bigcup_{j\geq1}\bigl(-j+2^{j+2}\mathbb Z_2\bigr),
 \qquad C=\mathbb Z_2\setminus U,\qquad \Phi=u(C).\] The negative integers are dense in \(\mathbb Z_2\), so \(U\) is open and dense. Hence \(\Phi\) is closed with empty interior. Its Haar measure satisfies \[\mu(C)\geq1-\sum_{j\geq1}2^{-j-2}=\frac34.\] A Haar-measure calculation alone would not establish the needed Frobenius density. Here it can be established directly. The least positive integer in the \(j\)th removed residue class is \(2^{j+2}-j\). Thus only \(O(\log x)\) classes meet \([1,x]\), and for fixed \(J\) the contribution of the classes with \(j>J\) is at most \[x\sum_{j>J}2^{-j-2}+O(\log x).\] Finite unions of residue classes have their Haar density. Letting first \(x\to\infty\) and then \(J\to\infty\) proves that \(D=C\cap\mathbb Z_{>0}\) has natural density \(d=\mu(C)\geq3/4\).

There are \(N_n=3^n/n+O(3^{n/2}/n)\) closed points of degree \(n\) on \(\mathbb A^1_{\mathbb F_3}\), and \(\rho(F_s)=u(n_s)\). With \(\varepsilon=(t-1)\log3\), the numerator in the paper’s density ratio is therefore \[\sum_{n\in D}\frac{e^{-\varepsilon n}}n+O(1),\] whereas the denominator is \(\sum_{n\geq1}e^{-\varepsilon n}/n+O(1)\). Partial summation from the natural density of \(D\) gives ratio tending to \(d\). Consequently \(\delta_S(\Sigma_\Phi)=d\geq3/4\) although \(\Phi\) has empty interior. This is a counterexample under the actual Frobenius density definition, not just an abstract topological objection.

Independently take \(S=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_3\) and the same arithmetic unipotent representation. There is one closed point, of degree one, and the paper’s ratio assigns \(|S|\) density one. Set \(\Phi=\{u(1)\}\). It is a closed analytic subset with empty interior, but \(\Sigma_\Phi=|S|\). Furthermore \(\Phi_{|S|}\) is a singleton, neither dense in \(u(\mathbb Z_2)\) nor Zariski dense in its connected algebraic closure \(\mathbb G_a\). This contradicts parts (1)–(3) of Lemma 9 under the printed zero-dimensional scope.
result: Result: Part A refutes the general closed-set version of 9(1); part B separately refutes 9(1)–(3) in dimension zero.
Impact: The auxiliary lemma overstates its scope. The identified positive-dimensional uses admit bounded corrections.

paragraphs: Assume dim S>0 in the density machinery. Require closed analytic Phi in the empty-interior equivalence, or use the general Haar-measure bounds.

problems.title: Conjugating torus maps have Weyl ambiguity
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 6 Pdf pages: 14 Section: Section6.4 second functoriality bullet
claim: A conjugating element with T'=gTg^(-1) is unique modulo right multiplication by T, and hence the map on the zero-weight space is independent of g.
Connected semisimple SL_2, diagonal torus T and adjoint representation sl_2. No pointwise identification of the two tori is fixed in the claimed uniqueness statement.
analysis: In the second functoriality bullet of Section 6.4, p. 14, a conjugating element \(g\) with \(\overline T'=g\overline T g^{-1}\) is claimed to be unique up to right multiplication by \(\overline T\). It is then asserted that the resulting map on invariant spaces is independent of \(g\). The ambiguity is the normalizer, not the centralizer.

For \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) and its adjoint representation, put \[T=\{\operatorname{diag}(a,a^{-1})\},\quad
 H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1),\quad
 w=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(V^T=\mathbb Q_\ell H\). Both \(1\) and \(w\) conjugate \(T\) to itself, but they induce \(H\mapsto H\) and \(H\mapsto-H\). Thus the asserted independence fails. This is the rank-one zero-weight situation of the adjoint representation; the large-geometric-monodromy example in Section 3.2, p. 6, produces the corresponding adjoint object when \(g=1\).

Choosing a particular conjugating element still induces an isomorphism natural in representations. Accordingly the earlier statement of independence up to natural isomorphism is not refuted. The repair is to remove the uniqueness assertion and record the Weyl-group ambiguity. At the pro-reductive level a proof must also arrange compatible choices in the relevant quotients; that coherence is not supplied merely by the displayed matrix calculation. This finding is local and does not change the ghost’s numerical dimension or its isomorphism class.
result: Result: The asserted uniqueness and choice independence fail.
Impact: Local canonicality overstatement, not a counterexample to the numerical ghost theory.

paragraphs: Remove uniqueness, retain the normalizer/Weyl ambiguity, and arrange compatible choices at the pro-reductive level.

report: Abstract: The supplied manuscript contains a failure of choice independence in its local obstruction construction. An explicit example over \(\mathbb Q_3\), satisfying the stated global numerical conditions, gives two admissible decompositions with different obstruction values. A second explicit counterexample disproves a fixed-characteristic-polynomial realization statement in degree twenty. Four further findings concern a \(2\)-adic determinant quantifier, the abstract characterization of signature maps, dimensions in two constructions, and an omitted root hypothesis. These findings are distinguished from the geometric realization and finiteness arguments that remain compatible with the checks below. The assessment is Major; the scientific decision remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Local obstruction data and signature conditions in K3 realization
# Source identity and scope

The reviewed source is Eva Bayer-Fluckiger, Automorphisms of K3 surfaces, signatures, and isometries of lattices, arXiv:2209.06698v4, posted 1 May 2024, with internal date 2 May 2024, 59 pages [main]. The journal identity is DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1598 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1598), online first 30 January 2025 [publisher]. The author manuscript has not been established to be identical to the publisher version. All page references below are one-based PDF pages, equal to the printed page numbers.

The review reads the full manuscript, including definitions, local quadratic and hermitian forms, the obstruction argument, lattice surgery, K3 realization, examples and finiteness. It supplies exact counterexamples to specified statements, rather than a counterexample to every main result. Source images used for the findings and selected positive checks were actually viewed; their precise page list and hashes are in the accompanying provenance. Imported classification, Torelli and finiteness theorems are identified as dependencies, not represented as completely reproved here.
# The local obstruction is not independent of choices

Problem 1 (Major).  Notation 7.2 (p. 19) misses a possible local exchange. Consequently Proposition 8.1 and Lemma 8.3 (pp. 21–22) fail, and the ensuing definition of \(\epsilon^p\) is not independent of the chosen local data. This affects the obstruction used in Theorems 9.7 and 12.1 (pp. 25, 29).
## An input satisfying the numerical hypotheses

Set \[f(X)=X^2-7X+1,\qquad F(X)=f(X)^2(X+1)^4.\] Give the \(f\)-part signature \((2,2)\) and the \((-1)\)-part signature \((2,2)\), so the total signature is \((4,4)\). Then \[F(0)=1,\quad \deg F=8,\quad F(1)=400,\quad F(-1)=0.\] Thus both (C0) and (C1) hold. The determinant prescribed in Section 11 for the \((-1)\)-part is \[D_-=|f(-1)^2|=81=1\quad\text{in }\mathbb Q^\times/\mathbb Q^{\times2}.\] The field \(E_f=\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)\) is ramified only at \(5\), whereas \(f\bmod5=(X-1)^2\). Notation 7.2 therefore gives \[\Pi_{f,X+1}=\varnothing.\] For \(I=\{f,X+1\}\), its group \(C_0(I)\) permits the function \(c(f)=1,\ c(X+1)=0\).
## Two decompositions of the same local quadratic space

At \(p=3\), the extension \(E_f/\mathbb Q_3\) is unramified quadratic. Multiplication by \[\alpha=(7+3\sqrt5)/2\] reduces to \(-1\) on the natural integral basis. The trace forms of Notation 1.2 are \[b_\lambda(x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb Q_3(\sqrt5)/\mathbb Q_3}
       \bigl(\lambda x\sigma(y)\bigr)
       \simeq \langle2\lambda,-10\lambda\rangle.\] Consider \[\begin{array}{c|cc}
 & f\text{-part}&(-1)\text{-part}\\ \hline
 A&b_1\perp b_1&\langle1,1,1,1\rangle\\
 B&b_3\perp b_1&\langle3,3,1,1\rangle .
\end{array}\] On the \(f\)-part, let the generator act by multiplication by \(\alpha\) on each copy; on the other part let it act by \(-1\). Both characteristic polynomials are \(F\).

All four blocks have determinant squareclass \(1\). At \(3\), the Hasse invariant of each block in row \(A\) is zero. Row \(B\) changes each block’s Hasse invariant by \(1\): indeed \[(6,-30)_3=-1,\qquad (3,3)_3=-1,\] while the unit-coefficient contributions and the cross terms do not change the comparison. Therefore both total quadratic spaces have dimension eight, determinant \(1\) and Hasse invariant zero: both are \(H^4\) over \(\mathbb Q_3\).

The equivariant residue of row \(A\) is zero. In row \(B\) the nonzero residues come from the coefficients with odd \(3\)-adic valuation: \[\partial(b_3\perp b_1)=
      \langle-1,-1\rangle_{\chi_-},\qquad
 \partial\langle3,3,1,1\rangle=
      \langle1,1\rangle_{\chi_-}.\] They lie in the same \(\chi_-\) summand, because \(\alpha\equiv-1\bmod3\), and cancel. In particular both rows belong to the same set \(C^3_0\) used for \(\delta=0\). The class \(\langle1,1\rangle\) over \(\mathbb F_3\) is nonzero: \(x^2+y^2=0\) has no nonzero solution.

Relative to the reference forms of Sections 5–6, the two rows give \[a=(0,0),\qquad a'=(1,1)\in C^3_0.\] The function \(c\) above consequently satisfies \[\epsilon_a(c)=0,\qquad \epsilon_{a'}(c)=1.\] This is a direct contradiction to Lemma 8.3. It is not a failure confined to an arbitrary nonzero residue, an inadmissible signature, or an absent multiplicity: the example has \(\delta=0\), satisfies (C0)–(C1), and uses the allowed multiplicity \(n_f=2\).
## The reverse defect and the extent of repair

The stated edge condition can also add an impossible exchange. For a compact corroborating example, put \[g(Y)=Y^2+3Y+8,\quad
 h(X)=X^2g(X+X^{-1})=X^4+3X^3+10X^2+3X+1.\] The discriminant of \(g\) is \(-23\) and the norm of \(r^2-4\), for a root \(r\) of \(g\), is \(g(2)g(-2)=108\), not a rational square; hence \(h\) is irreducible. Over \(\mathbb Q_3\) the roots \(r_+,r_-\) of \(g\) near \(2,-2\) satisfy \[v_3(r_+-2)=2,\quad (r_+-2)/9\equiv1\pmod3,\qquad
 v_3(r_-+2)=1.\] Thus \(r_+^2-4\) is a square, while \(r_-^2-4\) has squareclass \(3\). The algebra is \(\mathbb Q_3\times\mathbb Q_3\times\mathbb Q_3(\sqrt3)\); its only ramified quadratic block has reduction \(\alpha=-1\). Yet \(h\bmod3=(X-1)^2(X+1)^2\). For \(h(X)(X-1)^4\), Notation 7.2 adds the edge to \(X-1\), although a Hasse change in the nonsplit block changes only the \(\chi_-\) residue. The \(+1\) block cannot cancel it. This also disproves the stability assertion in Proposition 8.1.

A repair must classify actual local residue exchanges, including nonsplit unramified blocks whose chosen generator reduces to \(\pm1\), and then reprove the orbit and choice-independence assertions. Merely requiring a ramified place with the matching sign removes the second example but does not repair the first. The obstruction group and its global use must be reconsidered accordingly.

There is strong counterevidence against interpreting the first example as a nonexistence result. On a global hyperbolic lattice, the integral isometry \(\operatorname{diag}(A,A^{-t})\), with \(A\) the unimodular companion matrix of \(f\), has characteristic polynomial \(f^2\). Adjoining \(-1\) on \(H^2\) realizes \(F\) globally. The demonstrated failure is the proposed obstruction construction, not nonexistence for this input, and not a proved failure of the Salem-realization theorems.
# An excessive determinant quantifier at \(2\)

Problem 2 (Minor).  Claim 2 in the proof of Proposition 2.6 (p. 9) allows arbitrary units \(u_+,u_-\) with \(u_+u_-=(-1)^n\), even when only one linear eigenspace exists. The determinant conclusion in that case is false.

Take \[F=(X-1)^2,\quad n=1,\quad n_+=2,\quad n_-=0,\quad
 F_1=1,\quad u_+=1,\quad u_-=-1.\] All stated numerical premises hold. The claim would supply an even unimodular rank-two \(\mathbb Z_2\)-lattice of determinant squareclass \(1\). Its Gram matrix would have the form \[\begin{pmatrix}2a&b\\b&2c\end{pmatrix},\qquad b\text{ odd}.\] Its determinant is \(4ac-b^2\equiv3\pmod4\), whereas a unit in squareclass \(1\) is \(1\bmod8\). This is impossible.

The same example disproves the sentence on p. 11 asserting that a nonzero linear eigenspace forces \(v_2(F_1(1))+v_2(F_1(-1))\) to be odd: here this sum is zero. The single-eigenspace choice on p. 9 also uses the exponent \(n_1\) where the asserted total determinant requires \(n\).

The ordinary existence conclusion survives this test: \(H\) with the identity is an even unimodular realization of \((X-1)^2\). In a single-eigenspace version, remove the arbitrary determinant prescription and choose the determinant compatible with the desired total form. Proposition 11.1 (p. 28) prescribes both component determinants only when both eigenspaces occur, so this example is not a counterexample to that proposition. The cited \(2\)-adic lattice criterion and the corrected single-eigenspace proof still require an explicit reconciliation.
# The abstract signature characterization
Problem 3 (Minor).  Proposition 3.7 (p. 13) overstates uniqueness in (a), and its listed conditions omit the hyperbolic constraint for nonreal reciprocal pairs off the unit circle.

For the identity on positive definite \(\mathbb R^4\), its signature map is \((4,0)\) on a polynomial vanishing at \(1\) and zero otherwise. Both \[(X-1)^4\quad\text{and}\quad(X-1)^2(X+1)^2\] are monic symmetric degree-four polynomials satisfying exactly the conditions stated in (a). Thus (a) alone does not give a unique polynomial, even with constant term \(1\). The multiplicity condition (d), applied jointly, selects the first polynomial.

There is also a distinct sufficiency issue. Let \[P=(X^2+4)(X^2+\tfrac14),\qquad
 \tau(u)=
 \begin{cases}(3,1)&P\mid u,\\(0,0)&P\nmid u.\end{cases}\] On nonzero real polynomials this satisfies the printed algebraic conditions (a)–(e). Condition (a) selects \(P\) uniquely. In (b), coprime symmetric factors cannot split the reciprocal pair \(X^2+4,\ X^2+\tfrac14\), so additivity holds. Taking the symmetric radical preserves divisibility by \(P\). Every irreducible symmetric real polynomial and every real reciprocal linear pair appearing in (d)–(e) has value zero and multiplicity zero.

However, an isometry annihilated by \(P\) on a nondegenerate four-dimensional space has the two reciprocal two-dimensional primary spaces totally isotropic. The form therefore has signature \((2,2)\), not \((3,1)\). The assertion is false even after the natural treatment of the zero polynomial; the example does not rely on the additional undefined expression \(\operatorname{rad}(0)\).

Move uniqueness after the joint multiplicity requirements, and add the hyperbolic multiplicity rule for all non-self-reciprocal factors, including nonreal quadratics. A complete reformulation should also specify the domain at the zero polynomial. The Salem-plus-cyclotomic applications have no off-circle nonreal quartet, so this example does not refute those applications.
# Two dimension inconsistencies
Problem 4 (Minor).  Two explicit constructions have dimensions incompatible with their claimed K3 signatures.

In the proof of Theorem 19.1, Case 1 (p. 42), for \(m=5\) or \(8\) the displayed choice is \[C=\Phi_m^2(X-1)^2.\] Since \(\varphi(5)=\varphi(8)=4\), this has degree \(10\), not the required \(12\). With \(\deg S=10\), the displayed \(SC\) has degree \(20\) and cannot be the polynomial of a signature map of maximum \((3,19)\). Replacing the final exponent by \(4\) repairs the degree and (C1): \(C(1)=0\), while \(C(-1)\) is respectively \(16\) or \(64\). The edge between \(S\) and \(\Phi_m\) is assumed; the usual ramified prime of \(\Phi_5\) or \(\Phi_8\) links it to \(X-1\) with multiplicity four. This checks the numerical correction, not every subsequent gluing assertion.

In the proof of Proposition 27.2 (p. 57), the complementary lattice is assigned signature \((1,22-\deg C)\). Its rank is then \(23-\deg C\), and its direct sum with the stated \((2,\deg C-2)\) lattice has signature \((3,20)\) and rank \(23\). In the branch \(\deg C\equiv4\bmod8\), the displayed complement does not even satisfy the necessary signature congruence. The required signature is \[(1,21-\deg C),\] giving rank \(22-\deg C\) and total signature \((3,19)\). This repair has the required congruence for \(\deg C\equiv4\bmod8\). Neither arithmetic error proves nonexistence of the intended automorphisms.
# A missing root hypothesis
Problem 5 (Minor).  Theorem 21.3 (p. 46) assumes only \(\delta\in\mathbb C^\times\) and \(|\delta|=1\), omitting \(S(\delta)=0\).

Choose any degree-four Salem polynomial, for example \[S=X^4-X^3-X^2-X+1.\] Its trace polynomial is \(Y^2-Y-3\), with one root \(>2\) and one in \((-2,2)\); irreducibility follows since the norm of \(r^2-4\) is \(-3\), not a square. Thus it satisfies the degree condition in part (a). Let \(\delta\) be a primitive \(29\)th root of unity. The printed hypotheses hold, but \(\delta\) cannot be an eigenvalue of an integral automorphism on the rank-\(22\) lattice \(H^2(X,\mathbb Z)\): its minimal polynomial has degree \(\varphi(29)=28\).

The introduction’s Theorem 3 (p. 2) and Notation 15.3 (p. 35) already contain the intended root restriction. Restoring \(S(\delta)=0\) aligns the local statement with them. This is a counterexample to the printed unrestricted quantifier, not to the introduction’s correctly restricted assertion.
# A fixed characteristic polynomial obstructed by the root chamber

Problem 6 (Major).  Theorem 24.1(a) (pp. 51–52), with the fixed polynomial \(F=S(X^2-1)\) specified immediately before it, is false. For the Salem polynomial below the discriminant action forced by the ambient unimodular lattice is incompatible with type (P).

Take \[S(X)=X^{20}+X^{19}-\sum_{j=3}^{17}X^j+X+1.\] Then \(S(1)=-11\) and \(S(-1)=1\), so the oddness, square-free and coprimality hypotheses hold. Here, as elsewhere in the theorem, square-free integers include \(1\).
## An exact certificate that \(S\) is Salem

Writing \(S(X)=X^{10}R(X+X^{-1})\) gives \[\begin{split}
R(Y)={}&Y^{10}+Y^9-10Y^8-10Y^7+34Y^6+33Y^5\\
 &-45Y^4-40Y^3+19Y^2+13Y-1.
\end{split}\] Exact integer Horner-equivalent evaluations, with denominators cleared by \(1000^{10}\), give a strict sign change on each of the following disjoint intervals; all endpoints shown are to be divided by \(1000\): \[\begin{array}{ccccc}
[-1973,-1972]&[-1777,-1776]&[-1519,-1518]&[-1170,-1169]&[-603,-602]\\
{}[70,71]&[750,751]&[1348,1349]&[1792,1793]&[2077,2078].
\end{array}\] There are ten intervals for a polynomial of degree ten, so they exhaust its roots. Nine roots lie in \((-2,2)\) and the remaining root exceeds \(2\).

For irreducibility, represent a polynomial over \(\mathbb F_2\) by the hexadecimal integer whose bit \(j\) is its \(X^j\) coefficient. The reduction of \(S\) is `1bfffb`. Exact modular squaring and Euclidean division give \[X^{2^{20}}\equiv X\pmod{\bar S},\qquad
 X^{2^{10}}\bmod\bar S=\mathtt{dfffd},\] and \[\gcd(\bar S,X^{2^{10}}-X)=
 \gcd(\bar S,X^{16}-X)=1.\] The prime divisors of \(20\) are \(2\) and \(5\), so these are the full irreducibility test over \(\mathbb F_2\). Thus \(S\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). Together with the trace-root intervals this proves that \(S\) is a Salem polynomial of degree \(20\). The complete integer endpoint values and modular remainders, independently recomputed by the primary reviewer using exact BigInt arithmetic, are saved in `exact_salem_check.json`. No floating-point approximation or author program enters this certificate.
## The discriminant and positivity contradiction

Suppose that the asserted realizable isometry \(t\) exists. Its cyclotomic lattice \[N=L\cap\ker(t^2-1)\] is even, negative definite and primitive of rank two. The orthogonal projection of the unimodular lattice \(L\) onto \(N\otimes\mathbb Q\) is \(N^*\). Since \(S(t)\) kills the Salem subspace, \[S(t)N^*\subset N.\] The determinant of \(S(t)\) on \(N\otimes\mathbb Q\) is \(S(1)S(-1)=-11\). Comparing indices therefore gives \[|\det N|\mid11.\] There is no even unimodular rank-two definite lattice, hence \(|\det N|=11\).

The positive lattice \(N(-1)\) is uniquely represented by \[B=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&6\end{pmatrix}.\] Indeed, write a reduced positive even binary form as \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2a&b\\b&2c\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) with \(|b|\le a\le c\). Then \(11=4ac-b^2\ge3a^2\), so \(a=1\), \(b=\pm1\) and \(c=3\). Its only roots are \(\pm e_1\), since \[x^2+xy+3y^2=(x+y/2)^2+\tfrac{11}{4}y^2=1\] forces \(y=0\). Type (P), together with characteristic polynomial \(X^2-1\), forces \(t(e_1)=e_1\) and hence \[t=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] On the discriminant group of order \(11\), generated by \((-e_1+2e_2)/11\), this acts by \(-1\).

On the other hand, reducing \(S\) modulo \(X^2-1\) gives \[S(t)=-5-6t.\] The containment \(S(t)N^*\subset N\) says that this expression acts as zero on the discriminant group. Modulo \(11\), it forces \(t=+1\), contradicting the required \(-1\) action. No realization with the theorem’s fixed polynomial and Salem signature exists.

The failure is at the final positivity assertion in the proof on p. 52, not merely at an unproved numerical irreducibility assertion. A repair must restrict the fixed-polynomial assertion, add the needed discriminant/chamber compatibility, or allow the cyclotomic polynomial to change. This counterexample does not disprove the general realizability of the Salem number after such a change, including the broader degree-\(20\) result attributed to Takada. The Weyl correction discussed below explains why that distinction matters.
# Positive checks, counterevidence and remaining limits
The following checks help delimit the findings.

First, the real Hasse comparison in Proposition 9.3 depends on the negative index modulo four, since \(w_2(\langle1^r,-1^s\rangle)\) is determined by \(\binom{s}{2}\bmod2\). This supports the stated invariance when the positive complex place of a fixed Salem factor is moved. It does not repair the finite-place obstruction in Problem 1.

Second, an apparent gap in passing from equal Witt residues to stability of a particular glued lattice is not by itself a counterexample to chamber realization. If an integral isometry \(t\) of \(L\) has negative definite cyclotomic part \(L_C\), each root \(r\in L_C\) gives the integral reflection \[s_r(x)=x+(x,r)r.\] It fixes the rational Salem part pointwise. The finite Weyl group acts transitively on the chambers of \(L_C\); choose \(w\) so that \(wt\) preserves a chosen chamber. Then \(wt\) still preserves \(L\), agrees with \(t\) on the Salem part, and has finite-order restriction to \(L_C\). It is semisimple and has the same Salem signature. This supplies a concrete existence mechanism when the cyclotomic polynomial may change, as allowed in Definition 15.5. A direct appeal to Proposition 16.1 for a product of different cyclotomic factors on p. 42 exceeds that proposition’s single-power premise; the reflection argument explains a way to avoid treating this compressed step as a proved nonexistence defect.

Third, Theorem 21.4 uses the positive period plane and the chamber condition. For a simple unit-circle root of the irreducible Salem factor, a rational vector in the Salem space orthogonal to that plane would generate, under \(\mathbb Q[t]\), the whole Salem space; that is incompatible with orthogonality to the nonzero plane. Hence the rational Picard part is the cyclotomic part as required. Positive entropy also makes the remaining orthogonal part negative definite in the nonprojective case, supporting semisimplicity in Proposition 20.6.

Fourth, the argument of Proposition 25.5 correctly uses the simple \(\delta\)-eigenline to recover \(H^{2,0}\) from the isometric structure. Weak Torelli identifies the surfaces; it need not identify the original chosen isometry with a cone-preserving automorphism. Finiteness still imports the integral isometric-structure theorem cited as [BM 79]. The finite cyclotomic possibilities follow from the fixed degree bound. The restrictions in Section 26 and the resultant-one splitting in Lemma 27.1 were traced, but numerical tables, complete root-system classifications and all cited global theorems were not independently reproduced.

No author program was executed. The degree-twenty certificate above was computed with an independently written exact-arithmetic calculation. Bounded searches of the publisher, arXiv and title-specific code/correction results found no article-specific supplementary code or erratum; unrelated K3 software is not treated as this paper’s code. Absence of code is not a defect. This review does not certify a corrected global obstruction theorem, every arithmetic example, or equivalence with the publisher text.
# Supporting checks

Three native helpers supplied bounded text checks: Part I, signature/surgery, and K3 realization/finiteness. Their precise actual reading ranges and limitations are preserved in the accompanying record; none is represented as an independent acceptance or as a verified separate scientific model. The controller’s UI observation is recorded separately from the runtime’s self-description. Source, TeX, compiler, dependencies, logs, PDF and image bytes and hashes, actual exit codes, and final report-page inspection are bound by the build and delivery records. The workflow state remains `scientific_decision=pending` with `human_reviews=[]`.
Conclusion.
