problems.title: Local residue exchanges are misclassified and epsilon is not choice independent
problems.source_location: PDF p19 Notation7.2; pp21–22 Proposition8.1, Lemma8.3 and epsilon^p definition; pp25,29 Theorems9.7,12.1
claim: Every admissible local datum gives the same epsilon pairing on C0(I).
F=f^2(X+1)^4, f=X^2−7X+1; signature(4,4), block signatures(2,2), D−=81 squareclass1; C0,C1 and delta=0 all hold.
analysis: Notation 7.2 (p. 19) misses a possible local exchange. Consequently Proposition 8.1 and Lemma 8.3 (pp. 21–22) fail, and the ensuing definition of \(\epsilon^p\) is not independent of the chosen local data. This affects the obstruction used in Theorems 9.7 and 12.1 (pp. 25, 29).

Set \[f(X)=X^2-7X+1,\qquad F(X)=f(X)^2(X+1)^4.\] Give the \(f\)-part signature \((2,2)\) and the \((-1)\)-part signature \((2,2)\), so the total signature is \((4,4)\). Then \[F(0)=1,\quad \deg F=8,\quad F(1)=400,\quad F(-1)=0.\] Thus both (C0) and (C1) hold. The determinant prescribed in Section 11 for the \((-1)\)-part is \[D_-=|f(-1)^2|=81=1\quad\text{in }\mathbb Q^\times/\mathbb Q^{\times2}.\] The field \(E_f=\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)\) is ramified only at \(5\), whereas \(f\bmod5=(X-1)^2\). Notation 7.2 therefore gives \[\Pi_{f,X+1}=\varnothing.\] For \(I=\{f,X+1\}\), its group \(C_0(I)\) permits the function \(c(f)=1,\ c(X+1)=0\).

At \(p=3\), the extension \(E_f/\mathbb Q_3\) is unramified quadratic. Multiplication by \[\alpha=(7+3\sqrt5)/2\] reduces to \(-1\) on the natural integral basis. The trace forms of Notation 1.2 are \[b_\lambda(x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb Q_3(\sqrt5)/\mathbb Q_3}
       \bigl(\lambda x\sigma(y)\bigr)
       \simeq \langle2\lambda,-10\lambda\rangle.\] Consider \[\begin{array}{c|cc}
 & f\text{-part}&(-1)\text{-part}\\ \hline
 A&b_1\perp b_1&\langle1,1,1,1\rangle\\
 B&b_3\perp b_1&\langle3,3,1,1\rangle .
\end{array}\] On the \(f\)-part, let the generator act by multiplication by \(\alpha\) on each copy; on the other part let it act by \(-1\). Both characteristic polynomials are \(F\).

All four blocks have determinant squareclass \(1\). At \(3\), the Hasse invariant of each block in row \(A\) is zero. Row \(B\) changes each block’s Hasse invariant by \(1\): indeed \[(6,-30)_3=-1,\qquad (3,3)_3=-1,\] while the unit-coefficient contributions and the cross terms do not change the comparison. Therefore both total quadratic spaces have dimension eight, determinant \(1\) and Hasse invariant zero: both are \(H^4\) over \(\mathbb Q_3\).

The equivariant residue of row \(A\) is zero. In row \(B\) the nonzero residues come from the coefficients with odd \(3\)-adic valuation: \[\partial(b_3\perp b_1)=
      \langle-1,-1\rangle_{\chi_-},\qquad
 \partial\langle3,3,1,1\rangle=
      \langle1,1\rangle_{\chi_-}.\] They lie in the same \(\chi_-\) summand, because \(\alpha\equiv-1\bmod3\), and cancel. In particular both rows belong to the same set \(C^3_0\) used for \(\delta=0\). The class \(\langle1,1\rangle\) over \(\mathbb F_3\) is nonzero: \(x^2+y^2=0\) has no nonzero solution.

Relative to the reference forms of Sections 5–6, the two rows give \[a=(0,0),\qquad a'=(1,1)\in C^3_0.\] The function \(c\) above consequently satisfies \[\epsilon_a(c)=0,\qquad \epsilon_{a'}(c)=1.\] This is a direct contradiction to Lemma 8.3. It is not a failure confined to an arbitrary nonzero residue, an inadmissible signature, or an absent multiplicity: the example has \(\delta=0\), satisfies (C0)–(C1), and uses the allowed multiplicity \(n_f=2\).

The stated edge condition can also add an impossible exchange. For a compact corroborating example, put \[g(Y)=Y^2+3Y+8,\quad
 h(X)=X^2g(X+X^{-1})=X^4+3X^3+10X^2+3X+1.\] The discriminant of \(g\) is \(-23\) and the norm of \(r^2-4\), for a root \(r\) of \(g\), is \(g(2)g(-2)=108\), not a rational square; hence \(h\) is irreducible. Over \(\mathbb Q_3\) the roots \(r_+,r_-\) of \(g\) near \(2,-2\) satisfy \[v_3(r_+-2)=2,\quad (r_+-2)/9\equiv1\pmod3,\qquad
 v_3(r_-+2)=1.\] Thus \(r_+^2-4\) is a square, while \(r_-^2-4\) has squareclass \(3\). The algebra is \(\mathbb Q_3\times\mathbb Q_3\times\mathbb Q_3(\sqrt3)\); its only ramified quadratic block has reduction \(\alpha=-1\). Yet \(h\bmod3=(X-1)^2(X+1)^2\). For \(h(X)(X-1)^4\), Notation 7.2 adds the edge to \(X-1\), although a Hasse change in the nonsplit block changes only the \(\chi_-\) residue. The \(+1\) block cannot cancel it. This also disproves the stability assertion in Proposition 8.1.

A repair must classify actual local residue exchanges, including nonsplit unramified blocks whose chosen generator reduces to \(\pm1\), and then reprove the orbit and choice-independence assertions. Merely requiring a ramified place with the matching sign removes the second example but does not repair the first. The obstruction group and its global use must be reconsidered accordingly.

There is strong counterevidence against interpreting the first example as a nonexistence result. On a global hyperbolic lattice, the integral isometry \(\operatorname{diag}(A,A^{-t})\), with \(A\) the unimodular companion matrix of \(f\), has characteristic polynomial \(f^2\). Adjoining \(-1\) on \(H^2\) realizes \(F\) globally. The demonstrated failure is the proposed obstruction construction, not nonexistence for this input, and not a proved failure of the Salem-realization theorems.
result: Result: The choice-independence assertion is false within the numerical and delta=0 range used downstream.
Impact: The prescribed obstruction is not well-defined as printed; its use in the main arithmetic criterion requires substantial repair.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Define exchanges from actual local residue images, including unramified nonsplit blocks reducing to±1, and reprove orbit/choice independence and global sufficiency.

problems.title: Claim2 allows an impossible determinant in a single linear eigenspace
problems.source_location: PDF pp9–11; downstream pp28–29
claim: Arbitrary units u+,u− with product(−1)^n can prescribe the extant component determinant.
analysis: Claim 2 in the proof of Proposition 2.6 (p. 9) allows arbitrary units \(u_+,u_-\) with \(u_+u_-=(-1)^n\), even when only one linear eigenspace exists. The determinant conclusion in that case is false.

Take \[F=(X-1)^2,\quad n=1,\quad n_+=2,\quad n_-=0,\quad
 F_1=1,\quad u_+=1,\quad u_-=-1.\] All stated numerical premises hold. The claim would supply an even unimodular rank-two \(\mathbb Z_2\)-lattice of determinant squareclass \(1\). Its Gram matrix would have the form \[\begin{pmatrix}2a&b\\b&2c\end{pmatrix},\qquad b\text{ odd}.\] Its determinant is \(4ac-b^2\equiv3\pmod4\), whereas a unit in squareclass \(1\) is \(1\bmod8\). This is impossible.

The same example disproves the sentence on p. 11 asserting that a nonzero linear eigenspace forces \(v_2(F_1(1))+v_2(F_1(-1))\) to be odd: here this sum is zero. The single-eigenspace choice on p. 9 also uses the exponent \(n_1\) where the asserted total determinant requires \(n\).

The ordinary existence conclusion survives this test: \(H\) with the identity is an even unimodular realization of \((X-1)^2\). In a single-eigenspace version, remove the arbitrary determinant prescription and choose the determinant compatible with the desired total form. Proposition 11.1 (p. 28) prescribes both component determinants only when both eigenspaces occur, so this example is not a counterexample to that proposition. The cited \(2\)-adic lattice criterion and the corrected single-eigenspace proof still require an explicit reconciliation.
result: Result: The printed universal single-component determinant claim is false.
Impact: Local proof needs a narrower quantifier and corrected determinant choice; the ordinary existence theorem is not disproved by this example.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Remove arbitrary determinant prescription for a sole linear eigenspace and choose total determinant consistently, using n where required; delete false parity inference.

problems.title: Signature-map characterization misses joint uniqueness and nonreal reciprocal blocks
problems.source_location: PDF p13 Proposition3.7 and p14 construction
claim: Conditions(a)–(e) characterize all semisimple real signature maps.
General real semisimple isometries, not only Salem-plus-cyclotomic spectra.
analysis: Proposition 3.7 (p. 13) overstates uniqueness in (a), and its listed conditions omit the hyperbolic constraint for nonreal reciprocal pairs off the unit circle.

For the identity on positive definite \(\mathbb R^4\), its signature map is \((4,0)\) on a polynomial vanishing at \(1\) and zero otherwise. Both \[(X-1)^4\quad\text{and}\quad(X-1)^2(X+1)^2\] are monic symmetric degree-four polynomials satisfying exactly the conditions stated in (a). Thus (a) alone does not give a unique polynomial, even with constant term \(1\). The multiplicity condition (d), applied jointly, selects the first polynomial.

There is also a distinct sufficiency issue. Let \[P=(X^2+4)(X^2+\tfrac14),\qquad
 \tau(u)=
 \begin{cases}(3,1)&P\mid u,\\(0,0)&P\nmid u.\end{cases}\] On nonzero real polynomials this satisfies the printed algebraic conditions (a)–(e). Condition (a) selects \(P\) uniquely. In (b), coprime symmetric factors cannot split the reciprocal pair \(X^2+4,\ X^2+\tfrac14\), so additivity holds. Taking the symmetric radical preserves divisibility by \(P\). Every irreducible symmetric real polynomial and every real reciprocal linear pair appearing in (d)–(e) has value zero and multiplicity zero.

However, an isometry annihilated by \(P\) on a nondegenerate four-dimensional space has the two reciprocal two-dimensional primary spaces totally isotropic. The form therefore has signature \((2,2)\), not \((3,1)\). The assertion is false even after the natural treatment of the zero polynomial; the example does not rely on the additional undefined expression \(\operatorname{rad}(0)\).

Move uniqueness after the joint multiplicity requirements, and add the hyperbolic multiplicity rule for all non-self-reciprocal factors, including nonreal quadratics. A complete reformulation should also specify the domain at the zero polynomial. The Salem-plus-cyclotomic applications have no off-circle nonreal quartet, so this example does not refute those applications.
result: Result: Literal uniqueness and general sufficiency fail.
Impact: General classification requires corrected conditions; practical Salem applications are not directly refuted by the quartet.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: State uniqueness after all multiplicity conditions; require balanced hyperbolic multiplicities for all non-self-reciprocal factors; define zero-polynomial convention.

problems.title: Two auxiliary constructions have the wrong dimension
problems.source_location: PDF p42 Theorem19.1 Case1; p57 Proposition27.2 proof
claim: The displayed polynomials and complementary lattices have total rank22 and signature(3,19).
m=5 or8 in Case1; degC≡4mod8 in Proposition27.2 branch.
analysis: Two explicit constructions have dimensions incompatible with their claimed K3 signatures.

In the proof of Theorem 19.1, Case 1 (p. 42), for \(m=5\) or \(8\) the displayed choice is \[C=\Phi_m^2(X-1)^2.\] Since \(\varphi(5)=\varphi(8)=4\), this has degree \(10\), not the required \(12\). With \(\deg S=10\), the displayed \(SC\) has degree \(20\) and cannot be the polynomial of a signature map of maximum \((3,19)\). Replacing the final exponent by \(4\) repairs the degree and (C1): \(C(1)=0\), while \(C(-1)\) is respectively \(16\) or \(64\). The edge between \(S\) and \(\Phi_m\) is assumed; the usual ramified prime of \(\Phi_5\) or \(\Phi_8\) links it to \(X-1\) with multiplicity four. This checks the numerical correction, not every subsequent gluing assertion.

In the proof of Proposition 27.2 (p. 57), the complementary lattice is assigned signature \((1,22-\deg C)\). Its rank is then \(23-\deg C\), and its direct sum with the stated \((2,\deg C-2)\) lattice has signature \((3,20)\) and rank \(23\). In the branch \(\deg C\equiv4\bmod8\), the displayed complement does not even satisfy the necessary signature congruence. The required signature is \[(1,21-\deg C),\] giving rank \(22-\deg C\) and total signature \((3,19)\). This repair has the required congruence for \(\deg C\equiv4\bmod8\). Neither arithmetic error proves nonexistence of the intended automorphisms.
result: Result: Both displayed constructions are dimensionally impossible as written.
Impact: Construction details require correction; no general nonexistence conclusion follows.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use Phi_m²(X−1)^4 and complementary signature(1,21−degC), then reconcile all later premises.

problems.title: Theorem21.3 omits S(delta)=0
problems.source_location: PDF p46 Theorem21.3; counterevidence p2 Theorem3 and p35 Notation15.3
claim: The stated realization holds for any complex delta with modulus1.
S=X4−X3−X2−X+1 is a degree4 Salem polynomial; delta is a primitive29th root.
analysis: Theorem 21.3 (p. 46) assumes only \(\delta\in\mathbb C^\times\) and \(|\delta|=1\), omitting \(S(\delta)=0\).

Choose any degree-four Salem polynomial, for example \[S=X^4-X^3-X^2-X+1.\] Its trace polynomial is \(Y^2-Y-3\), with one root \(>2\) and one in \((-2,2)\); irreducibility follows since the norm of \(r^2-4\) is \(-3\), not a square. Thus it satisfies the degree condition in part (a). Let \(\delta\) be a primitive \(29\)th root of unity. The printed hypotheses hold, but \(\delta\) cannot be an eigenvalue of an integral automorphism on the rank-\(22\) lattice \(H^2(X,\mathbb Z)\): its minimal polynomial has degree \(\varphi(29)=28\).

The introduction’s Theorem 3 (p. 2) and Notation 15.3 (p. 35) already contain the intended root restriction. Restoring \(S(\delta)=0\) aligns the local statement with them. This is a counterexample to the printed unrestricted quantifier, not to the introduction’s correctly restricted assertion.
result: Result: The unrestricted printed quantifier is false.
Impact: Local statement needs its intended hypothesis; the correctly restricted introduction is not refuted.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Add S(delta)=0.

problems.title: Theorem24.1(a) fails for its specified degree20 characteristic polynomial
problems.source_location: PDF p51 fixed F=S(X²−1), Theorem24.1(a); p52 final by-construction positivity assertion; p35 type(P)
claim: Odd, square-free coprime endpoint values suffice for a realizable isometry with the fixed F and Salem signature.
S=X20+X19−sum_{j=3}^{17}X^j+X+1; S(1)=−11,S(−1)=1. Both meet the endpoint hypotheses.
analysis: Theorem 24.1(a) (pp. 51–52), with the fixed polynomial \(F=S(X^2-1)\) specified immediately before it, is false. For the Salem polynomial below the discriminant action forced by the ambient unimodular lattice is incompatible with type (P).

Take \[S(X)=X^{20}+X^{19}-\sum_{j=3}^{17}X^j+X+1.\] Then \(S(1)=-11\) and \(S(-1)=1\), so the oddness, square-free and coprimality hypotheses hold. Here, as elsewhere in the theorem, square-free integers include \(1\).

Writing \(S(X)=X^{10}R(X+X^{-1})\) gives \[\begin{split}
R(Y)={}&Y^{10}+Y^9-10Y^8-10Y^7+34Y^6+33Y^5\\
 &-45Y^4-40Y^3+19Y^2+13Y-1.
\end{split}\] Exact integer Horner-equivalent evaluations, with denominators cleared by \(1000^{10}\), give a strict sign change on each of the following disjoint intervals; all endpoints shown are to be divided by \(1000\): \[\begin{array}{ccccc}
[-1973,-1972]&[-1777,-1776]&[-1519,-1518]&[-1170,-1169]&[-603,-602]\\
{}[70,71]&[750,751]&[1348,1349]&[1792,1793]&[2077,2078].
\end{array}\] There are ten intervals for a polynomial of degree ten, so they exhaust its roots. Nine roots lie in \((-2,2)\) and the remaining root exceeds \(2\).

For irreducibility, represent a polynomial over \(\mathbb F_2\) by the hexadecimal integer whose bit \(j\) is its \(X^j\) coefficient. The reduction of \(S\) is `1bfffb`. Exact modular squaring and Euclidean division give \[X^{2^{20}}\equiv X\pmod{\bar S},\qquad
 X^{2^{10}}\bmod\bar S=\mathtt{dfffd},\] and \[\gcd(\bar S,X^{2^{10}}-X)=
 \gcd(\bar S,X^{16}-X)=1.\] The prime divisors of \(20\) are \(2\) and \(5\), so these are the full irreducibility test over \(\mathbb F_2\). Thus \(S\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). Together with the trace-root intervals this proves that \(S\) is a Salem polynomial of degree \(20\). The complete integer endpoint values and modular remainders, independently recomputed by the primary reviewer using exact BigInt arithmetic, are saved in `exact_salem_check.json`. No floating-point approximation or author program enters this certificate.

Suppose that the asserted realizable isometry \(t\) exists. Its cyclotomic lattice \[N=L\cap\ker(t^2-1)\] is even, negative definite and primitive of rank two. The orthogonal projection of the unimodular lattice \(L\) onto \(N\otimes\mathbb Q\) is \(N^*\). Since \(S(t)\) kills the Salem subspace, \[S(t)N^*\subset N.\] The determinant of \(S(t)\) on \(N\otimes\mathbb Q\) is \(S(1)S(-1)=-11\). Comparing indices therefore gives \[|\det N|\mid11.\] There is no even unimodular rank-two definite lattice, hence \(|\det N|=11\).

The positive lattice \(N(-1)\) is uniquely represented by \[B=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&6\end{pmatrix}.\] Indeed, write a reduced positive even binary form as \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2a&b\\b&2c\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) with \(|b|\le a\le c\). Then \(11=4ac-b^2\ge3a^2\), so \(a=1\), \(b=\pm1\) and \(c=3\). Its only roots are \(\pm e_1\), since \[x^2+xy+3y^2=(x+y/2)^2+\tfrac{11}{4}y^2=1\] forces \(y=0\). Type (P), together with characteristic polynomial \(X^2-1\), forces \(t(e_1)=e_1\) and hence \[t=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] On the discriminant group of order \(11\), generated by \((-e_1+2e_2)/11\), this acts by \(-1\).

On the other hand, reducing \(S\) modulo \(X^2-1\) gives \[S(t)=-5-6t.\] The containment \(S(t)N^*\subset N\) says that this expression acts as zero on the discriminant group. Modulo \(11\), it forces \(t=+1\), contradicting the required \(-1\) action. No realization with the theorem’s fixed polynomial and Salem signature exists.

The failure is at the final positivity assertion in the proof on p. 52, not merely at an unproved numerical irreducibility assertion. A repair must restrict the fixed-polynomial assertion, add the needed discriminant/chamber compatibility, or allow the cyclotomic polynomial to change. This counterexample does not disprove the general realizability of the Salem number after such a change, including the broader degree-\(20\) result attributed to Takada. The Weyl correction discussed below explains why that distinction matters.
result: Result: No isometry with the specified polynomial and Salem signature can satisfy type(P) for this S.
Impact: A theorem statement with fixed characteristic polynomial is false; its final positivity inference needs substantive correction.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Restrict the fixed-polynomial assertion or add discriminant/chamber compatibility; alternatively allow the cyclotomic factor to change.

report: Abstract: The principal-triple slice used in Appendix B is not an isomorphism under the stated characteristic hypothesis. Explicit examples show failure even beyond the Coxeter number and under the paper’s sufficient banal-prime condition. This invalidates the given slice-based derivation of a determinant identity used in the unobstructedness argument, although the identity itself survives the examples. Four further findings have local repairs: an inertia-cohomology assertion, a finite-image adjustment, an exact sequence on the wrong site, and an inverted prime-set description. The assessment is Major for the proof dependency; the review does not establish that the main moduli-space conclusions are false. Independent scientific acceptance remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: A modular slice obstruction and local corrections
in moduli of Langlands parameters
# Identity, versions and scope

The primary source is J.-F. Dat, D. Helm, R. Kurinczuk and G. Moss, Moduli of Langlands parameters, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 27 (2025), 1827–1927, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1599 [main]. The 101-page publisher PDF records revision on 8 August 2024. The publisher records publication on 11 March 2025. The supplied arXiv:2009.06708v3 was posted on 29 February 2024; it is a distinct, earlier author version, and no equivalence or full collation is asserted.

All primary PDF text pages were read. References below use printed journal pages, with one-based PDF pages supplied for each finding; the conversion is printed page \(=\) PDF page \(+1826\). The checks track the tame construction, wild reduction, continuity, connectedness, unobstructed points, affine quotient and appendices. Selected source images, including every page carrying a reported defect, were actually viewed. External theorems and large classification tables were not all independently reproved. This is an initial mathematical review, not independent acceptance.
# The principal-triple slice in Appendix B

Problem 1 (Major).  Appendix B.4, pp. 1923–1924 (PDF 97–98), asserts that \[\mathfrak g^E\longrightarrow\mathfrak g/\!/\widehat G,\qquad
 X\longmapsto(F+X)\bmod\widehat G\tag{1}\] is an isomorphism when \(\widehat G\) is simple adjoint and the coefficient characteristic \(\ell\) does not divide its Weyl-group order. Here \((F,H,E)\) is the specified principal \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\)-triple with \(H=2\rho^\vee\). This assertion is false. Its failure affects the given derivation of Proposition B.5, used explicitly in Proposition 5.18, p. 1886 (PDF 60).
## A counterexample within the sufficient prime range

Work over an algebraically closed field \(L\) of characteristic \(7\), with \(\widehat G=\operatorname{PGL}_5\). Since \(5\) is invertible, identify \(\operatorname{Lie}(\operatorname{PGL}_5)\) with \(\mathfrak{sl}_5\). Write \(E_{ij}\) for matrix units and put \[E=E_{12}+E_{23}+E_{34}+E_{45},\quad
 F=4E_{21}+6E_{32}+6E_{43}+4E_{54},\quad
 H=\operatorname{diag}(4,2,0,-2,-4).\] Direct multiplication gives \([E,F]=H\), \([H,E]=2E\), and \([H,F]=-2F\). Thus these are the matrices prescribed by the principal triple. The centralizer of the regular Jordan block \(E\) in \(\mathfrak{sl}_5\) is \[\mathfrak g^E=L E\oplus L E^2\oplus L E^3\oplus L E^4 .\] For \(Y=F+xE+yE^2+zE^3+wE^4\), the only terms contributing to the trace of \(Y^3\) are the three cyclic arrangements of \(F,F,yE^2\). Consequently \[\operatorname{tr}(Y^3)=3y\,\operatorname{tr}(F^2E^2)
         =3y(4\cdot6+6\cdot6+6\cdot4)=252y=0\quad\text{in }L.       \tag{2}\] On the other hand, \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-2,0,0)\) is traceless and \(\operatorname{tr}(D^3)=-6=1\) in \(L\). The conjugation-invariant function \(\operatorname{tr}(A^3)\) therefore vanishes on the entire proposed slice but is nonzero on \(\mathfrak g/\!/\widehat G\). Map (1) is not surjective.

This example satisfies \(\ell\nmid |W|\), since \(|W|=120\), and \(\ell>h=5\). It also persists under the paper’s sufficient prime condition: take residue cardinality \(q=3\). The powers of \(3\) modulo \(7\) are \(3,2,6,4,5,1\), so its order is \(6>h\) and \(\chi_{\widehat G,1}^{*}(3)\ne0\) in \(L\). Merely imposing the stronger condition used for Theorem 5.7 does not restore this particular slice.
## Two further exact checks

For \(\operatorname{PGL}_4\) in characteristic \(5\), take the analogous matrices \[E=E_{12}+E_{23}+E_{34},\qquad
 F=3E_{21}+4E_{32}+3E_{43}.\] Here \(5\nmid24\) and \(5>h=4\). Nevertheless \(\operatorname{tr}((F+xE+yE^2+zE^3)^2)=20x=0\), while \(\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0,0)^2)=2\). An independent exact determinant calculation gives \[\det(TI-F-xE-yE^2-zE^3)
 =T^4-10xT^2-24yT+9x^2-36z.\] The missing \(T^2\) coefficient modulo \(5\) confirms the obstruction.

The preceding claim in B.4 that \(H=2\rho^\vee\) is always regular semisimple under \(\ell\nmid|W|\) also needs correction. In type \(C_2\) and characteristic \(3\), use the symplectic form with antidiagonal entries \((1,-1,1,-1)\). The same \(4\)-by-\(4\) triple has \[H=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,-1,0),\qquad F=E_{32}.\] Since \(|W(C_2)|=8\), this characteristic is permitted. The highest root \(2e_1\) vanishes on \(H\), so \(H\) is not regular. Moreover, \(\mathfrak g^E=L E\oplus L E^3\) and \[\det(TI-F-xE-yE^3)=T^2(T^2-x),\] so the proposed slice has identically zero determinant.
## Dependence, counterevidence and required repair

The actual Veldkamp reference [veldkamp], pp. 232, 234–236, uses its specified Chevalley sums \(X_+\) and \(X_-\) and defines the affine space \(X_-+\mathfrak g^{X_+}\). This does not by itself identify that space with the principal-triple expression in (1). The source’s precise choice matters; a name-level invocation of a section theorem does not justify the replacement.

The failure of (1) is not a counterexample to Proposition B.5’s final determinant identity. For example, for \(\operatorname{PGL}_n\) in the examples above, the basis \(E,\ldots,E^{n-1}\) has cocharacter weights \(2,4,\ldots,2n-2\). For the identity automorphism, its determinant is directly \[\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(t^{2j+2}-1)=\chi_{\operatorname{PGL}_n,1}(t^2),\] as B.5 requires. The corresponding type \(C_2\) weights are \(2,6\) and also give the expected formula.

A repair must provide a valid characteristic-sensitive proof of the graded, automorphism-equivariant centralizer identity needed for B.5, or a correctly chosen section with all those properties. The formulas just checked prove the identity only in the stated examples. They do not certify a replacement proof for every root system and outer automorphism. A blanket change to \(\ell>h\) is inadequate by (2). The Major assessment concerns this substantive dependency in the unobstructedness argument, not an established failure of flatness, connectedness, or all conclusions of Theorem 5.7.
# Four local corrections

Problem 2 (Minor: the cohomology group must be restricted).  In the proof of Corollary 4.20(1)(b), p. 1869 (PDF 43), the assertion \(H^1(I_F,T_{\phi^\ell}(L))=1\) does not follow from the action factoring through a cyclic \(\ell\)-group.

Take residue characteristic \(p=2\), coefficient characteristic \(\ell=3\), \(T=\mathbf G_m\), \(L=\overline{\mathbb F}_3\), and trivial action. A tame quotient \(I_F\twoheadrightarrow C_5\) and an embedding \(C_5\hookrightarrow\mu_5(L)\) give a nontrivial continuous cocycle. All coboundaries for trivial action are trivial, so this \(H^1\) is nonzero.

For the fixed-component lifting at issue, the obstruction factors through the finite cyclic \(\ell\)-group \(C\) acting on the full centralizer. The needed group is \(H^1(C,T(L))\), which vanishes because multiplication by \(|C|\) is an automorphism of \(T(L)\). Equivalently one can explicitly restrict to cocycles through \(I_F/I_F^\ell\). This repairs the local use; it does not disprove Corollary 4.20. The quotient notation used on the following page is compatible with this correction.

There is a related clarification in Lemma 4.28, p. 1876 (PDF 50): the fixed-point argument may use an abstract infinite cyclic group generating the same finite action, for which \(H^1\) is the group of coinvariants. The literal open subgroup of full inertia is not procyclic. This observation is not used here to claim a counterexample to Lemma 4.28.

Problem 3 (Minor: the finite-image adjustment needs an inverse).  In Lemma 4.24(2), p. 1873 (PDF 47), the text chooses \(t^r={}^{L}\phi(\operatorname{Fr})^r\) and claims that \(\phi^t\) has finite image, although the preceding definition multiplies its Frobenius value by \(t\).

For \(\widehat G=\mathbf G_m\) with trivial action, \(\phi(s)=1\) and \(\phi(\operatorname{Fr})=2\), each such \(t\) is \(2\zeta\) for a root of unity \(\zeta\), and the new Frobenius value is \(4\zeta\), still of infinite order. Thus the printed step fails even in rank one.

For a general repair, write \(g={}^{L}\phi(\operatorname{Fr})\) and let \(U\) be the relevant inertia-fixed torus normalized by \(g\). After increasing \(r\), arrange \(g^r\in(U^{\operatorname{Ad}g})^\circ\). Choose \(t\) in this torus with \(t^r=g^{-r}\). Then \(tg=gt\) and \((tg)^r=1\). The choice remains in the connected inertia centralizer, as required by the earlier deformation argument. Taking an arbitrary root without ensuring commutation would leave a gap. The corrected construction preserves the intended existence conclusion.

Problem 4 (Minor: the central-isogeny sequence requires the fppf site).  Lemma A.11(i), p. 1918 (PDF 92), describes its fixed-point/cohomology sequence as exact on the big étale site, although the central-isogeny kernel need not be smooth.

Take \(R=\mathbb Z[1/3]\), \(\Gamma=C_3\) acting trivially, and the central isogeny \[1\longrightarrow\mu_2\longrightarrow\operatorname{SL}_2\longrightarrow\operatorname{PGL}_2
 \longrightarrow1.\] These satisfy the printed assumptions. Since \(H^1(C_3,\mu_2)=1\), the displayed étale exactness would force \(\operatorname{SL}_2\to\operatorname{PGL}_2\) to be an étale-sheaf epimorphism. Over \(A=\mathbb F_2[u,u^{-1}]\), however, the class of \(\operatorname{diag}(u,1)\) can have a determinant-one representative only after adjoining a scalar \(a\) satisfying \(a^2u=1\). At the generic point this requires a purely inseparable square root, which no étale extension can supply.

The central-isogeny argument should first be made in the fppf topology. One can then return to the étale topology for the finite étale component-group objects. The invertibility of \(|\Gamma|\) is not the invertibility of the isogeny degree. The example refutes the stated site-exactness, not the final finiteness conclusion of A.11 or A.12.

Problem 5 (Minor: the introductory prime set is reversed).  On p. 1836 (PDF 10), immediately before and after Theorem 1.9, the description of \(M\) uses all \(^{L}G\)-banal primes rather than the non-banal primes.

The preceding page makes the banal set cofinite, so no positive integer can be divisible by every such prime. For the trivial-action torus and \(q=2\), the tame parameter scheme is just \(\mathbf G_m\), and every \(\ell\ne2\) is banal; the literal product is already impossible in this example. Proposition 6.2 and Remark 6.3, p. 1899 (PDF 73), give the intended finite exclusions: invert \(N_{\widehat G}\) and the non-banal primes, with the stated refinement in the unramified case. This is counterevidence against interpreting the introductory wording as a defect in the formal GIT theorem.
# Positive checks and proof coverage
## Tame geometry and wild reduction

For the trivial-action torus, the parameter ring is explicitly \[\mathbb Z[1/p][a^{\pm1},b^{\pm1}]/(b^{q-1}-1).\] It is flat and a complete intersection; its total space is reduced, while its characteristic-\(\ell\) fiber is nonreduced when \(\ell\mid(q-1)\). This directly tests the distinction maintained in Corollary 2.5 and Proposition 2.8. The tame proof allows nonreduced centralizers and uses the reduced strata for its dimension argument.

The wild restriction uses finite \(p\)-groups after \(p\) has been inverted. The averaging arguments in Appendix A therefore apply to the actual group orders. Theorem 3.4 guarantees preservation of a Borel pair; the stronger pinning statement has a separate smooth-center hypothesis in Theorem 3.12. The proof chain through torus-valued \(H^2\), finite-image lifts, valuation quotients and finite field extensions was traced with these hypotheses retained. The Bruhat–Tits and reductive fixed-point inputs remain external dependencies.
## Continuity and connectedness

The separatedness argument in Corollary 2.11 can be checked by a Noetherian ascending chain: if \(a=\ell^n a_n\ne0\) for every \(n\), stability of \((a_n)\) forces \(\ell\) to be invertible. In the situation at hand, an integral point in characteristic \(\ell\) rules that out. This separatedness makes the closed-subgroup descent of the extended \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) parameter valid: its defining equations vanish modulo every \(\ell^n\) and hence vanish.

For Theorem 4.8, a connected special fiber together with separatedness does imply connectedness of the affine total space. An idempotent reducing to zero satisfies \(e=e^n\in\ell^n R\) for every \(n\); hence \(e=0\). The same argument applied to \(1-e\) covers the other reduction. The canonical comparison in Theorem 4.18 uses the jointly faithful local completions to identify the two invariant subrings; it does not require their quotient to be a finitely generated \(\mathbb Z[1/p]\)-module.

General Borel-preserving connectedness remains explicitly conjectural. The proved pinning-preserving and smooth-center cases were not silently enlarged. Likewise, canonical independence of the affine quotient is distinct from the proposed equivalence for stack quotients.
## Unobstructedness and the quotient

The Euler-characteristic calculation in Lemma 5.1 yields \[\dim T_x Z^1=\dim\widehat G_L+
 \dim H^0(W_F^0,(\operatorname{Ad}\phi_x)^*\otimes\omega).\] Together with the established pure fiber dimension, this gives the smoothness criterion of Corollary 5.3. The later reductions distinguish good primes, very good primes, \(\ell>h\), and the stronger polynomial exclusions; they are not interchangeable. The classical-group weight calculation and the separate triality treatment were read. The exceptional cases use Lawther–Testerman tables, including private matrix information in the \(E_8\) case; these data were not independently reconstructed in full.

In Section 6 the restriction to finite inertia, the universal homeomorphism, the localization argument, the torus quotient and comparison with the Haines variety were traced. Theorem 6.8’s assertion about finite Weyl-type group orders was not separately proved in every root system. No failure of that assertion was established, and it is not entered as a finding.

problems.title: The principal-triple slice is not surjective in permitted characteristics
problems.source_location: Printed pages: 1886 Printed pages: 1923 Printed pages: 1924 Pdf pages: 60 Pdf pages: 97 Pdf pages: 98 Labels: Appendix B.4 Labels: Proposition B.5 proof Labels: Proposition 5.18 use
claim: X -> F+X from g^E to g//G is an isomorphism for simple adjoint G and ell not dividing |W|.
L algebraically closed, G=PGL5, ell=7, q=3, trivial action; |W|=120, h=5, ord_7(3)=6. Principal triple E=Jordan5, F subdiagonal(4,6,6,4), H=diag(4,2,0,-2,-4).
analysis:
Appendix B.4, pp. 1923–1924 (PDF 97–98), asserts that \[\mathfrak g^E\longrightarrow\mathfrak g/\!/\widehat G,\qquad
 X\longmapsto(F+X)\bmod\widehat G\tag{1}\] is an isomorphism when \(\widehat G\) is simple adjoint and the coefficient characteristic \(\ell\) does not divide its Weyl-group order. Here \((F,H,E)\) is the specified principal \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\)-triple with \(H=2\rho^\vee\). This assertion is false. Its failure affects the given derivation of Proposition B.5, used explicitly in Proposition 5.18, p. 1886 (PDF 60).

Work over an algebraically closed field \(L\) of characteristic \(7\), with \(\widehat G=\operatorname{PGL}_5\). Since \(5\) is invertible, identify \(\operatorname{Lie}(\operatorname{PGL}_5)\) with \(\mathfrak{sl}_5\). Write \(E_{ij}\) for matrix units and put \[E=E_{12}+E_{23}+E_{34}+E_{45},\quad
 F=4E_{21}+6E_{32}+6E_{43}+4E_{54},\quad
 H=\operatorname{diag}(4,2,0,-2,-4).\] Direct multiplication gives \([E,F]=H\), \([H,E]=2E\), and \([H,F]=-2F\). Thus these are the matrices prescribed by the principal triple. The centralizer of the regular Jordan block \(E\) in \(\mathfrak{sl}_5\) is \[\mathfrak g^E=L E\oplus L E^2\oplus L E^3\oplus L E^4 .\] For \(Y=F+xE+yE^2+zE^3+wE^4\), the only terms contributing to the trace of \(Y^3\) are the three cyclic arrangements of \(F,F,yE^2\). Consequently \[\operatorname{tr}(Y^3)=3y\,\operatorname{tr}(F^2E^2)
         =3y(4\cdot6+6\cdot6+6\cdot4)=252y=0\quad\text{in }L.       \tag{2}\] On the other hand, \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-2,0,0)\) is traceless and \(\operatorname{tr}(D^3)=-6=1\) in \(L\). The conjugation-invariant function \(\operatorname{tr}(A^3)\) therefore vanishes on the entire proposed slice but is nonzero on \(\mathfrak g/\!/\widehat G\). Map (1) is not surjective.

This example satisfies \(\ell\nmid |W|\), since \(|W|=120\), and \(\ell>h=5\). It also persists under the paper’s sufficient prime condition: take residue cardinality \(q=3\). The powers of \(3\) modulo \(7\) are \(3,2,6,4,5,1\), so its order is \(6>h\) and \(\chi_{\widehat G,1}^{*}(3)\ne0\) in \(L\). Merely imposing the stronger condition used for Theorem 5.7 does not restore this particular slice.

For \(\operatorname{PGL}_4\) in characteristic \(5\), take the analogous matrices \[E=E_{12}+E_{23}+E_{34},\qquad
 F=3E_{21}+4E_{32}+3E_{43}.\] Here \(5\nmid24\) and \(5>h=4\). Nevertheless \(\operatorname{tr}((F+xE+yE^2+zE^3)^2)=20x=0\), while \(\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,0,0)^2)=2\). An independent exact determinant calculation gives \[\det(TI-F-xE-yE^2-zE^3)
 =T^4-10xT^2-24yT+9x^2-36z.\] The missing \(T^2\) coefficient modulo \(5\) confirms the obstruction.

The preceding claim in B.4 that \(H=2\rho^\vee\) is always regular semisimple under \(\ell\nmid|W|\) also needs correction. In type \(C_2\) and characteristic \(3\), use the symplectic form with antidiagonal entries \((1,-1,1,-1)\). The same \(4\)-by-\(4\) triple has \[H=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,-1,0),\qquad F=E_{32}.\] Since \(|W(C_2)|=8\), this characteristic is permitted. The highest root \(2e_1\) vanishes on \(H\), so \(H\) is not regular. Moreover, \(\mathfrak g^E=L E\oplus L E^3\) and \[\det(TI-F-xE-yE^3)=T^2(T^2-x),\] so the proposed slice has identically zero determinant.

The actual Veldkamp reference [veldkamp], pp. 232, 234–236, uses its specified Chevalley sums \(X_+\) and \(X_-\) and defines the affine space \(X_-+\mathfrak g^{X_+}\). This does not by itself identify that space with the principal-triple expression in (1). The source’s precise choice matters; a name-level invocation of a section theorem does not justify the replacement.

The failure of (1) is not a counterexample to Proposition B.5’s final determinant identity. For example, for \(\operatorname{PGL}_n\) in the examples above, the basis \(E,\ldots,E^{n-1}\) has cocharacter weights \(2,4,\ldots,2n-2\). For the identity automorphism, its determinant is directly \[\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(t^{2j+2}-1)=\chi_{\operatorname{PGL}_n,1}(t^2),\] as B.5 requires. The corresponding type \(C_2\) weights are \(2,6\) and also give the expected formula.

A repair must provide a valid characteristic-sensitive proof of the graded, automorphism-equivariant centralizer identity needed for B.5, or a correctly chosen section with all those properties. The formulas just checked prove the identity only in the stated examples. They do not certify a replacement proof for every root system and outer automorphism. A blanket change to \(\ell>h\) is inadequate by (2). The Major assessment concerns this substantive dependency in the unobstructedness argument, not an established failure of flatness, connectedness, or all conclusions of Theorem 5.7.
result: Result: Exact counterexample to the stated intermediate isomorphism, including the body ell>h and sufficient chi-star(q) range.
Impact: The displayed section-based derivation of the graded equivariant centralizer identity used for unobstructedness requires substantive repair.

Title: Field families and local corrections
in holomorphic symplectic factorization
# Source, version and scope

The reviewed source is Josua Schott, Holomorphic factorization of mappings into the symplectic group, arXiv:2207.05389v2, posted 6 March 2023 [main]. Its title page retains the internal date 23 June 2022. These dates are distinct. The publisher identifies the article by DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1600 and records publication on 17 February 2025 [publisher]. The author manuscript has not been established equivalent to that later publication.

All 47 primary text pages were read and all 47 source page images were actually viewed. Page numbers below are both printed and one-based PDF page numbers. The review follows the definitions, parameter and null-homotopy quantifiers, Oka lifting, symplectic induction, critical loci, complete fields, saturation lemmas and the \(K=3,4,\ge5\) spanning arguments. External Oka and continuous factorization theorems were not independently reproved in full.
# The missing global base family

Problem 1 (Major).  Definition 3.19, p. 20, starts the union defining \(\mathcal V_K\) at \(L=3\). Together with Definition 3.35, p. 30, this makes the nested conclusion \(A_2\subset A_3\subset\mathcal Q_3=\Gamma(\mathcal V_3)\) in Theorem 3.36, p. 31, impossible. The base definition on p. 30 also needs regularization. The affected interfaces include Lemma 3.39, p. 32, and Lemma 3.42, pp. 33–34.

Use the transposed convention explicitly adopted on p. 11. For \(n=2\), set \[Z_1=\operatorname{diag}(0,1),\qquad Z_2=\operatorname{diag}(0,-1),\qquad Z_3=0.\] Then \[\Phi_1=(e_2,e_2),\qquad
 \Phi_2=(e_2,0),\qquad \Phi_3=(e_2,0).\] The two-factor fiber is generic, whereas the three-factor fiber is non-generic. Lemma 3.18, pp. 18–20, shows that every \(\varphi^3\) and \(\gamma^3\) vanishes where \(\widetilde P^2=P_s^2=0\). These are all the fields in \(\mathcal V_3\) as defined. Their complete flows fix each such point, and every pullback by the group they generate still vanishes there. Thus every element of \(\mathcal Q_3\) vanishes at the displayed point.

The generic two-factor fiber has dimension \(n(n-1)=2\). More concretely, Lemma 3.40, pp. 32–33, with \(j^*=2\), includes \[(P^1_2)^2\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{1,11}}
 =\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{1,11}}\] at this point. A family spanning that fiber cannot be a subset of a family all of whose values vanish. This is a contradiction to the claimed nesting, independently of any interpretation of a generic spanning claim away from this non-generic three-factor fiber.

A repair should define a regularized global base family first and include its coordinate lifts in every \(\mathcal V_K\). Its fields preserve \(\Phi_2\) and therefore all later \(\Phi_K\). This removes the explicit contradiction and supplies the missing old directions. The restrictions of generated fields and their flows in Lemmas 3.38–3.39 must then be reconciled with the revised family; it is not enough to assert that every newly listed conjugate vanishes on the non-generic stratum. The elementary repair ingredients are checked here, but a complete rewritten compatibility proof for the entire induction is not certified. This substantive dependency in the ellipticity argument motivates the Major assessment. No non-factorizable null-homotopic holomorphic map is established.
# Finite enlargement needs iterated pullbacks

Problem 2 (Major: invalid core spanning construction).  The construction in Lemma 3.30, pp. 28–29, takes only single-flow pullbacks of the original fields. Its resulting finite set need not span the claimed saturation. Lemma 3.31 inherits this proof step.

Take \(M=\mathbb C^3\), \(A=\{X,Y,Z\}\) with \[X=\partial_x,\qquad Y=x\partial_y,\qquad Z=y\partial_z,
 \qquad U=\{xy\ne0\}.\] All three fields are complete and span on \(U\). Every point can be moved into \(U\) by first translating \(x\) and then moving \(y\), so \(\mathcal C_A(U)=\mathbb C^3\). Under the usual pullback convention, \[(\alpha_s^X)^*Y=(x+s)\partial_y,\quad
 (\alpha_s^Y)^*Z=(y+sx)\partial_z,\quad
 (\alpha_s^Z)^*Y=x\partial_y-sx\partial_z.\] The other six single pullbacks are immediate. At the origin all nine types, for every time, lie in \(\operatorname{span}\{\partial_x,\partial_y\}\). Thus any collection of the form actually prescribed on p. 29 misses \(\partial_z\) there. In contrast, for \(\beta=\alpha_1^Y\circ\alpha_1^X\), \[\beta^*Z=(y+x+1)\partial_z\] is nonzero in that direction at the origin. A convention reversing pullbacks changes signs but not the single-step obstruction.

Here is a finite enlargement repair. Work on \(\Omega=\mathcal C_A(U)\), put \(B_0=A\), and let \(N_r\) be the analytic locus where \(B_r\) fails to span. For each irreducible component of \(N_r\), some original \(A\)-flow must leave \(N_r\) at a point of that component. Otherwise all these fields would be tangent to that component at its generic smooth points, their flows would preserve it, and its points could never reach \(U\). Choose one such point and field for each component. There are at most countably many components. For a fixed field, each chosen point has a discrete set of times returning to \(N_r\). A common time avoiding their countable union can therefore be chosen. Set \[B_{r+1}=B_r\cup
 \{(\alpha^V_{t_{r,V}})^*W:V\in A,\ W\in B_r\}.            \tag{3}\] Every irreducible component of \(N_r\) loses a point, and \(N_{r+1}\) is a proper analytic subset on every component. Its dimension decreases. After finitely many rounds, \(N_r\) is empty. Each \(B_r\) is finite and lies in \(\Gamma(A)\). This also applies to the vertical tangent bundle on the submersion saturation used in Lemma 3.31.

The two changes are essential: pull back the current family, allowing compositions, and use irreducible components in the dimension argument. This repairs the finite-enlargement lemma; the example is not a counterexample to its existence conclusion.

The dependency is part of the principal proof. Lemma 3.31, p. 29, imports this finite spanning construction. The paragraph following Theorem 3.36, p. 31, uses it to produce the generic spray, and Lemma 3.39, p. 32, uses the corresponding mechanism over the non-generic stratum. Corollary 3.32 and Remark 3.43, p. 34, transmit the step into the induction proving stratified ellipticity and the Oka lifting applications of Theorems 3.3 and 2.10, Corollary 2.11, and Theorem 2.12. The displayed construction therefore fails inside the core proof, which warrants Major even though an iterated repair is available. Neither the existence conclusion of Lemma 3.30 nor the final factorization theorem is disproved.
# Four further local corrections
Problem 3 (Minor: flow order).  Lemma 3.34, p. 30, gives the wrong order for its specified composition of flows.

Let \(f=y\) on \(\mathbb C^2\), \(N=\{y=0\}\), \(V_1=x\partial_y\) and \(V_2=\partial_x\). Then \(V_2V_1f=1\) everywhere on \(N\), but \[\alpha^{V_2}_{t_2}\circ\alpha^{V_1}_{t_1}(0,0)=(t_2,0)\] never leaves \(N\). The reversed composition gives \((t_2,t_1t_2)\) and does leave. Generally the mixed derivative of \(f(\alpha^{V_1}_{t_1}\circ\cdots\circ\alpha^{V_n}_{t_n}(x))\) at zero is \(V_n\cdots V_1f(x)\). Thus reversing the displayed flow order provides the intended assertion. The later saturation argument only needs a word in the generated group, so its escape mechanism survives.
Problem 4 (Minor: the approximation set).  Definition 2.7 and Theorem 2.8, p. 6, omit the requirement that \(K\) be an \(\mathcal O(X)\)-convex compact set.

Take the elliptic projection \(\mathbb C\to\{\mathrm{pt}\}\), \(X=\mathbb C\), one parameter, no interpolation subset, and \(K=\{|z|=1\}\). Define \[F_0(z)=
 \begin{cases}4\bar z,&|z|\le1/2,\\1/z,&|z|\ge1/2.\end{cases}\] This is continuous and holomorphic near \(K\). No entire function \(g\) can approximate it on \(K\) with error less than \(1\), since \[2\pi=\left|\int_{|z|=1}(1/z-g(z))\,dz\right|
 \le2\pi\sup_K|1/z-g|<2\pi\] would follow. Add holomorphic convexity and compactness, and the usual arbitrary accuracy quantifier. The lifting applications in Corollary 2.11 and Theorem 2.12 may take \(K=\varnothing\), so this omission does not refute those applications.
Problem 5 (Minor: block elimination).  The upper elementary factor in the elimination display on p. 10 has an extra minus sign.

In the notation of that display, write the remaining matrix as \[M=\begin{pmatrix}
 I_{n-1}&0&0&b\\
 -d^T&1&b^T&c\\
 0&0&I_{n-1}&d\\
 0&0&0&1
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 B=\begin{pmatrix}0&-b\\-b^T&-c-d^Tb\end{pmatrix}.\] The necessary right factor is \(U(B)\), where \(U(B)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&B\\0&I\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), whereas the text uses \(U(-B)\). With \(b=d=0,c=1\) the printed product is \(U(2E_{nn})\), although its claimed right-hand side is \(I\). Using \(U(B)\) gives the required elimination. The Whitehead identities on p. 9 and the null-homotopy of the smaller symplectic block survive this correction; the main existence assertion is not disproved.
Problem 6 (Minor: parity of critical values).  Lemma 3.16, p. 17, and its repetition in Remark 3.37, p. 31, omit the even/odd distinction.

For \(K\ge2\), the critical-value set following from Theorem 3.4 is \[\Phi_K(S_K)=
 \begin{cases}
 \{e_{2n}\},&K\ \text{even},\\
 \{(a,e_n):a\in\mathbb C^n\},&K\ \text{odd}.
 \end{cases}                                                   \tag{4}\] For even \(K\), every point of \(W_K^c\) has all the relevant odd blocks annihilating \(e_n\), so the recursion gives \(\Phi_K=e_{2n}\). For odd \(K\), only the last odd block can contribute, giving \((a,e_n)\); choosing the earlier even blocks zero realizes the critical values.

An explicit counterexample to the printed uniform condition is \(n=1,K=4,y=(1,1)\). Here \(S_4=\{z_1=z_2=z_3=0\}\) has image \((0,1)\). The fiber over \((1,1)\) is nonempty and smooth: after eliminating \(z_4\), its equation is \[z_1+z_3+z_1z_2z_3=1,\] whose gradient \((1+z_2z_3,z_1z_3,1+z_1z_2)\) never vanishes. Yet \(\pi_1(y)=1\). The sufficient-condition proof incorrectly infers vanishing of the odd blocks from the target’s second half alone. The even branch of Theorem 3.25 on p. 26 already uses the correct unique singular value. Smooth fibers still lie in \(W_K\), and the generic/non-generic partition by \(\pi_K\) remains valid.
# Positive checks, algebraic clarifications and limits

The insertion \((I_n,0,G_1-I_n,G_2,\ldots)\) on p. 8 preserves the complete product and places the continuous lift in \(W_L\). The Oka homotopy preserves the last row; the smaller symplectic block in pp. 9–10 starts at the identity, retaining the required null-homotopy. The uniform factor bound can be tracked by the existing uniform \(L(n,d)\) and the fixed Whitehead factor count. The final disjoint-union argument with varying parameter spaces is not independently certified as written, and the parametric \(n=1\) input remains an external boundary.

For every nonzero complex vector \(a\), \(Z\mapsto Za\) from symmetric matrices is surjective, without requiring \(a^Ta\ne0\). This verifies the three-step preimage construction in pp. 15–16, including isotropic vectors. The Jacobian recursion and low-order critical sets agree. The non-generic product decomposition and the connected-fiber projection argument were traced. Removing a positive-codimension subset from a connected singular space is not by itself sufficient to prove connectedness; the smooth-part argument on p. 26 should make explicit its projection over the connected complement of the exceptional affine subspace, with connected fibers and local openness.

Theorem 3.21’s completeness mechanism is valid. Its derivative columns are \(c_j+f_jv\); any cofactor containing two copies of \(v\) vanishes, so the vector field is affine in its active variables. The other coordinates remain fixed parameters. The eight sufficient field types and the forward complete-lifting mechanism of Lemma 3.18 were checked. This is not a proof of every global if and only if completeness formulation. The incomplete Riccati example is a different class and does not invalidate the listed sufficient types.

The complementary-bases assertion in pp. 38–40 can be checked directly. If a row \(u\) annihilates \(A_I\) and the basis columns \(B_J\), then \(uB=0\), while \(uA\) is supported in \(J\). From \(AB^T=BA^T\), \((uA)B^T=0\). Independence of \(B_J\) gives \(uA=0\); full rank of \([A\ B]\) then gives \(u=0\). Thus \([A_I\ B_J]\) is invertible.

The \(K=3,4,\ge5\) rank and escape calculations were read with their nonzero-component assumptions. Two displayed simplifications deserve explicit clarification. In Lemma 3.49, p. 45, put \(u=\widetilde P^{K-4}\), \(v=\widetilde P^{K-3}\). The actual determinant is \[\det B=\pm u_{i^*}^{\,n-k}v_{j^*}^{\,k}
 \det[(I+Z_{K-1}Z_{K-2})e_I\mid Z_{K-1}e_J].              \tag{5}\] The missing first factor is nonzero under the preceding reduction on p. 44, so the required nonvanishing survives. In the \(C_k\) steps on pp. 41 and 46, the exhibited motion in the previously zero \(i^*\)-diagonal direction raises the rank to \(k+1\); it can be routed directly to \(B_{k+1}\) instead of the stated intermediate \(B_k\setminus C_k\). Neither observation is a counterexample to the final rank-increase conclusion.

These checks do not certify a complete replacement of all interfaces after Problem 1. No failure of the final factorization theorem has been established. Absence of such a counterexample is not independent acceptance.

analysis: The construction in Lemma 3.30, pp. 28–29, takes only single-flow pullbacks of the original fields. Its resulting finite set need not span the claimed saturation. Lemma 3.31 inherits this proof step.

 (\alpha_s^Y)^*Z=(y+sx)\partial_z,\quad
 (\alpha_s^Z)^*Y=x\partial_y-sx\partial_z.\] The other six single pullbacks are immediate. At the origin all nine types, for every time, lie in \(\operatorname{span}\{\partial_x,\partial_y\}\).  \{(\alpha^V_{t_{r,V}})^*W:V\in A,\ W\in B_r\}.            \tag{3}\] Every irreducible component of \(N_r\) loses a point, and \(N_{r+1}\) is a proper analytic subset on every component. Title: Torsion detection and equivariant foundations
in complex K-theory of Higgs moduli
# Source and scope

The source is Michael Groechenig and Shiyu Shen, Complex K-theory of moduli spaces of Higgs bundles, arXiv:2212.10695v1, posted 20 December 2022, 49 pages [main]. The initial review read all 49 text pages and actually viewed all 49 source page images. Printed and one-based PDF page numbers agree. Publisher metadata identifies DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1601 and publication on 20 March 2025 [publisher]. The author manuscript has not been established equivalent to that later journal version; the findings below concern the acquired v1.

The review traced the relative K-theory comparison, spreading argument, Prym Fourier–Mukai construction, vanishing cycles, motivic torsion reduction, PGL torsion argument and the appendix’s equivariant definitions. The external autoduality, motivic and support theorems were not independently re-proved in full. Elementary examples below are reconstructed directly, retaining the difference between failure of a general lemma and failure of its intended geometric application.
# A finite cover with integral torsion

Problem 1 (Major).  Under an unrestricted reading of the covers defined by diagram (21), p. 23, Proposition 6.5, p. 25, is false. The proposition does not separately specify the parameters produced by the preceding motivic construction with \((d,n)=1\). Independently, the reverse induction on p. 27 applies Lemma 6.7 to a generally singular boundary, whereas that lemma requires a smooth closed subvariety.

Let \(C\) be a smooth projective genus-two curve, \(c_0\) a Weierstrass point, and \(\tau\) its hyperelliptic involution. Write \(J=\operatorname{Jac}(C)\) and \(\operatorname{AJ}(x)=\mathcal O_C(x-c_0)\). Then \(\tau(c_0)=c_0\) and \(\operatorname{AJ}(\tau x)=-\operatorname{AJ}(x)\). The positive parameters in the diagram-defined family \[n=2,\qquad l=(1,1),\qquad k=(1,1)\] give the smooth finite étale cover \[Y=\{(x,y,L)\in C^2\times J:2L=\operatorname{AJ}(x)+\operatorname{AJ}(y)\}.
                                                        \tag{1}\] It has degree 16. All indicated \(l_i,k_i\) are positive. The proposition does not explicitly quantify over all parameters or identify the actual admissible motivic subclass. This example tests the unrestricted reading; its membership in the coprime-degree motivic terms has not been shown.

Put \(\Pi=\pi_1(C,c_0)\), \(A=H_1(C,\mathbb Z/2)=(\mathbb Z/2)^4\) and \(K=\ker(\Pi\to A)\). The cover’s monodromy is the surjection \[\Pi\times\Pi\longrightarrow A,\qquad(u,v)\longmapsto\bar u+\bar v.\] Consequently \(Y\) is connected and \(\pi_1Y=\Gamma=\ker(\Pi^2\to A)\). Projection to the first factor yields \(1\to K\to\Gamma\to\Pi\to1\). It splits by \(u\mapsto(u,\tau_*u)\), induced by the actual section \(x\mapsto(x,\tau x,\mathcal O_C)\) of (1). Since \(\tau_*\) is an automorphism and inner conjugation by \(K\) is trivial on its abelianization, \[H_1(Y,\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^4\oplus H_1(K,\mathbb Z)_A.                       \tag{2}\]

The five-term group-homology sequence for \(1\to K\to\Pi\to A\to1\) is \[\mathbb Z=H_2(\Pi,\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H_2(A,\mathbb Z)
 \longrightarrow H_1(K,\mathbb Z)_A\longrightarrow\mathbb Z^4
 \longrightarrow A\longrightarrow0.\] By the integral Künneth formula, \(H_2(A,\mathbb Z)=\bigwedge^2 A=(\mathbb Z/2)^6\). With a symplectic basis \(a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2\), the surface fundamental class maps to \[\omega=\bar a_1\wedge\bar b_1+\bar a_2\wedge\bar b_2.\] This follows by factoring the classifying map through the abelianization \(\mathbb Z^4\); cup-product evaluation gives precisely the two symplectic pairs. The image has order 2. The kernel of \(\mathbb Z^4\to A\) is \(2\mathbb Z^4\). Hence \[0\longrightarrow(\mathbb Z/2)^5\longrightarrow H_1(K,\mathbb Z)_A
 \longrightarrow2\mathbb Z^4\longrightarrow0\] splits as abelian groups because its quotient is free. Equation (2) and the integral universal coefficient theorem now give \[H_1(Y,\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^8\oplus(\mathbb Z/2)^5,\qquad
 \boxed{\operatorname{Tor}H^2(Y,\mathbb Z)=(\mathbb Z/2)^5.}                        \tag{3}\] In particular the torsion subgroup has order 32; the rational first Betti number is 8 whereas the mod-2 first Betti number is 13.

The proof defect is visible independently. In Step 2 on p. 27, the complement of the product of affine symmetric powers is a union of coordinate divisors. Near an intersection of two coordinate divisors, the boundary has local equation \(xy=0\). Finite étale pullback preserves this crossing. Thus the boundary to which Lemma 6.7 is applied is not smooth. This crossing geometry is independent of any coprimality imposed on the numerical parameters. If the open set is instead read as the complement of only the lower product, the product-open definition and affine calculation in (25) no longer describe the same object. Neither reading supplies the missing hypothesis. Simply discarding smoothness cannot establish the unrestricted statement in view of (3).

The counterexample does not prove torsion in the actual fixed-determinant Higgs moduli space. Here \(\sum k_i l_i=2\) is not coprime to \(n=2\). The motivic computation may use a narrower parameter class; its exact restrictions and the torsion argument applicable to it must be stated and justified. No claim that an additional gcd condition alone suffices is certified. The displayed multi-factor reverse induction has an unmet smooth-boundary hypothesis in the proof used for Theorem 6.3. This is a core proof gap, not a counterexample to the actual coprime-degree Higgs-moduli conclusion.
# Finite monodromy does not detect all fiber torsion
Problem 2 (Major).  Lemma 6.18, p. 31, is false for its stated class of spectra, already for a one-dimensional torus. It is an explicit input to Theorem 6.11 on p. 32.

Fix a prime \(p\). In homological degrees 1 and 0, let \[C_1=\mathbb Z\{u,v\},\qquad C_0=\mathbb Z\{a,b\},\qquad
 d(u)=pb,\quad d(v)=0.\] For the associated Eilenberg–MacLane spectrum \(E=H(C)\), \(\pi_0E=\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z/p\), \(\pi_1E=\mathbb Z\), and all other groups vanish. Define the chain map \[N_0(a)=b,\quad N_0(b)=0,\qquad N_1(u)=v,\quad N_1(v)=0.\] It satisfies \(N^2=0\), so \(T=1+N\) is a chain automorphism with inverse \(1-N\). The degree-one homotopy \(h(a)=u\), \(h(b)=v\) obeys \[dh+hd=pN,\qquad T^p=1+pN\simeq1.                       \tag{4}\] The locally constant spectrum on \(S^1\) with monodromy \(T\) therefore becomes trivial on the degree-\(p\) cover. This uses only the classification of local systems on a circle by an automorphism up to homotopy.

Its global sections are \(\operatorname{hofib}(N)\). Write subscripts \(s,t\) for source and target in the mapping cone. The only nonzero degree-one boundary images are \[a_s\longmapsto b_t,\qquad u_t\longmapsto pb_t,\] and the degree-two differential sends \[u_s\longmapsto-pb_s+v_t,\qquad v_s\longmapsto0.\] The degree-one kernel has basis \(b_s,u_t-pa_s,v_t\). The image is generated by the primitive vector \(-pb_s+v_t\). Consequently \[H_0(\operatorname{Cone}N)=\mathbb Z,\quad
 H_1(\operatorname{Cone}N)=\mathbb Z^2,\quad
 H_2(\operatorname{Cone}N)=\mathbb Z.\] After the fiber shift, the only nonzero section groups are \[\pi_{-1}\Gamma=\mathbb Z,\qquad\pi_0\Gamma=\mathbb Z^2,\qquad
 \pi_1\Gamma=\mathbb Z.                                       \tag{5}\] There is no \(p\)-torsion, although the fiber has it and (4) satisfies the precise finite-cover hypothesis.

The erroneous step on p. 31 says that an automorphism preserves a chosen complementary torsion-free summand. In this example its action on \(\pi_0E\) is \((z,\bar t)\mapsto(z,\bar t+\bar z)\), which mixes such summands. An invariant torsion subgroup does not give an invariant chosen complement. Nor does nontrivial invariant torsion necessarily survive the extension in the homotopy-fiber exact sequence.

A repair must establish an appropriate torsion-detection theorem using additional structure of the actual geometric local system, or replace this step of the PGL argument. The chain-complex example refutes the general lemma; it is not asserted to arise as the particular Higgs-moduli K-theory spectrum. A helper’s stronger KU-module variant was not needed or independently certified for the adopted finding.
# The orbit site and stack fixed points
Problem 3 (Major).  The partial-domain morphisms in Definition A.4, p. 34, and the covering rule in Definition A.6, p. 35, are incompatible with the stability axiom of a Grothendieck topology.

Take \(G=C_2\) acting on \(X=\mathbb C\) by \(z\mapsto-z\), so \(X^G=\{0\}\). The allowed generalized orbits \[P=\mathbb C^*\times(\{e\}\backslash G),\qquad
 E=\varnothing\times(G\backslash G)\] satisfy \(P\ne\varnothing\) and \(P|_{s(G)}=P\times_X X^G=\varnothing\). The unique map \(P|_{s(G)}\to E\) is continuous, equivariant and over \(X\). Since \(\{e\}\subset G\), Definition A.4(c) makes it a morphism \(P\to E\).

Definition A.6 explicitly makes the empty family cover \(E\). Pulling its empty covering sieve back along \(P\to E\) gives the empty sieve on \(P\). Stability requires that sieve to cover \(P\), contradicting the stated covering criterion, since its union of images is empty. The example is a finite-dimensional, locally compact Hausdorff complex analytic space with nonempty fixed locus. Empty opens are allowed in A.3; A.6–A.7 explicitly retain the empty object; Example A.5 confirms that the partial-domain convention is intentional.

Interpreting the rule as a generating family for a topology does not supply the asserted theory. For the free action \(X=G=C_2\), each nonempty generalized orbit maps to the empty \(G\)-type orbit in exactly this way. The generated topology forces an empty cover on every object, making the sheaf category terminal. Lemma A.10 instead requires \(\operatorname{Sh}(G;G)\simeq\operatorname{Space}\).

The site needs a compatible replacement, followed by new proofs of the orbit comparison, stalk formulas, functoriality and base change. Changing one exceptional empty-object clause is not a certified repair. This is foundational to the appendix used in Section 5, without disproving the final K-theory equivalence.

Problem 4 (Major in the stated general stack framework).  Definitions A.29(b) and A.31, p. 43, use coarse fixed points as if they supplied coherent fixed objects. The resulting orbit action map need not be defined independently of a coset representative.

Let \(\mathcal X=BC_3\) and let \(G=C_2\) act by inversion on \(C_3\). This is a strict action allowed by A.29(a). Its coarse space is a point, so A.29(b) gives \(\mathcal X^G=\mathcal X\). Take \(H=G\) and \(U=\mathcal X\) in A.31. The unique coset in \(G\backslash G\) can be represented by \(1\) or the nontrivial element \(s\). The formula \((x,Hg)\mapsto x\cdot g\) then gives the identity functor or the inversion functor on \(BC_3\).

These are not naturally isomorphic: a natural isomorphism would be an element \(k\in C_3\) satisfying \(kr=r^{-1}k\) for a generator \(r\). Since \(C_3\) is abelian, that would imply \(r=r^{-1}\). Thus passing to a 2-categorical interpretation does not resolve the failure. Coarse fixed points alone do not provide the required trivialization of the subgroup action.

One must restrict actions or retain coherent fixed-object data and verify the subsequent descent constructions. The actual map \(M'\to[\mathfrak{sl}_n/PGL_n]\) on p. 21 has a target described as carrying trivial \(\Gamma\)-action. The example above is not asserted to occur there. The general framework is overbroad even if that specific application can be constructed in a narrower framework.
# The gerbe quantifier

Problem 5 (Major for the arbitrary-Brauer-class argument).  Theorem 6.11, p. 27, allows an arbitrary Brauer class. Corollary 6.16 and its use in Corollary 6.17, p. 30, identify the corresponding character cover with a fixed geometric cover by using a property specific to the universal-family obstruction gerbe.

For the zero equivariant gerbe, the line bundles \(L_{\gamma'}\) of Sections 2.5 and 6.3 are trivial and their algebra is the ordinary group algebra. Therefore, for \(c=\langle\gamma\rangle\), \[C_c^0=M^\gamma\times c^* .                             \tag{6}\] Take \(n=2,d=1\), a curve of genus at least 2, and nonzero \(\gamma\in J[2]\). The associated connected étale double cover \(\widetilde C_\gamma\) has connected rank-one Higgs moduli \[\widetilde M_\gamma=T^*\operatorname{Pic}^1(\widetilde C_\gamma).\] The deck involution acts freely on \(\operatorname{Pic}^1\): an invariant line bundle can be linearized for the cyclic group over \(\mathbb C\) and descended, but a pullback from the base has even degree. Thus \(M^\gamma=\widetilde M_\gamma/\mu_2\) is connected, using the geometric description also stated in Proposition 6.15. The left side of Corollary 6.16 for \(\alpha=0\) has two connected components by (6), whereas \(\widetilde M_\gamma\) has one. They are not isomorphic.

If that corollary is interpreted as concerning only the canonical obstruction gerbe, this example does not refute the restricted interpretation. It does show that such a corollary cannot justify the arbitrary-\(\alpha\) reduction as written. Its proof invokes the obstruction property without a new restriction after the arbitrary gerbe assertions on pp. 27–29. The repair must state and track the canonical-gerbe hypothesis, and separately prove any claimed extension to arbitrary Brauer classes. This does not establish that Theorem 6.11 itself is false.
# Local corrections with bounded repairs
Problem 6 (Minor).  Lemma 3.3, p. 12, requires the support of every semisimple perverse summand to meet the open set. It must instead control every simple constituent.

On \(B=\mathbb A^1\), with \(B^\heartsuit=\mathbb G_m\), set \(T=\mathbb Q_B[1]\oplus\mathbb Q_{\{0\}}\), \(\mathcal F=T\) and \(\mathcal G=\mathbb Q_B[1]\). Let \(f\) be projection and \(g\) inclusion. The support of \(T\) is \(B\); \(gf\) restricts to the identity on the open set, but on global sections \(\mathbb Q[1]\oplus\mathbb Q\) it is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\). It is not unipotent and \(\Gamma(B,\mathcal F)\) is not a retract of \(\Gamma(B,\mathcal G)\). As usual zero summands are ignored; if desired, periodizing this example gives nonzero \(T_i=T\) in every integer degree with the same failure degree by degree.

Requiring each simple constituent’s support to meet the open set removes this example. Situation 3.8(b), p. 14, already explicitly describes that stronger middle-extension condition. The local lemma defect therefore does not by itself refute that application.
Problem 7 (Minor).  In the proof of Lemma 3.5, p. 13, the quotient \(\widetilde F^{b-2}/\ker(\bar d^{b-1}\widetilde d^{b-2})\) does not extend the original complex term.

On the original open set \(U\), the composite is zero, so its kernel is the whole term and the quotient restricts to zero. Even \(U=W\) and a nonzero three-term complex with all differentials zero exhibits the error. Replace the quotient by \(\ker(\bar d^{b-1}\widetilde d^{b-2})\) itself. Noetherian coherence is preserved; restriction to \(U\) is the original term; the composite vanishes. Repeating the construction gives the intended descending extension. This corrects the construction without refuting extension existence.
Problem 8 (Minor; the space-valued proof).  Claim A.22, p. 40, that internal \(\operatorname{Map}(H\backslash G,-)\) preserves arbitrary colimits is false.

Let \(G=C_2\), \(H=e\), and use the coproduct of two terminal objects in \(\operatorname{Space}_G\). Evaluate the proposed comparison at the free orbit \(G\). The left side has two points. The right side consists of \(G\)-maps \(G\times G\to\{0,1\}\), where the two-point target is trivial. There are two free orbits in \(G\times G\), hence four such maps. The comparison is not an equivalence.

A finite coproduct of representables gives a finite product of mapping values, which does not preserve arbitrary coproducts of spaces. This invalidates the indicated proof of Lemma A.21, not necessarily its target identity. A restriction–coinduction or slice-category proof in a corrected equivariant theory is needed. Finite products and coproducts agree for spectra, so this particular space-valued example is not automatically a counterexample to the stable analogue.
Problem 9 (Minor).  Lemma 6.8, p. 26, gives \(m\) copies after setting \(m=\gcd(k,n)\); the component count is \(m^{2g}\) for a genus-\(g\) Jacobian.

For an elliptic curve, \(l=1\) and \(k=n=2\), the pullback is \(\{(x,L):2L=2\operatorname{AJ}(x)\}=C\times J[2]\). It is four copies of \(C\), not two. In general the components of the isogeny pullback are indexed by \(J[m]\). The single-factor torsion-free reduction survives the corrected finite multiplicity. It does not resolve the two-factor obstruction in Problem 1.

Problem 10 (Minor).  Lemma 4.6, p. 18, gives the rank of \(R^q\pi_*\mathcal O\) for a \(\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)\)-torsor as \(\binom gq\). With the notation fixed on p. 16, the correct rank is \(\binom{g_C}q\).

Here \(g\) is the arithmetic genus of the spectral curve and \(g_C\) the genus of the base curve. For example, a smooth genus-one curve mapping finitely to \(\mathbb P^1\) has \(g=1,g_C=0\). The torsor has zero-dimensional trivial group, so \(\pi\) is an isomorphism and \(R^1\pi_*\mathcal O=0\), not rank one. The subsequent cohomological range already uses \(g_C\); this is a local correction, without a counterexample to the intended Prym equivalence.
# Counterevidence, dependencies and coverage limits

The ordinary unipotent argument in Theorem 3.10, p. 15, has a valid integral mechanism: on a torsion-free group, rational nilpotence implies integral nilpotence, and a finite geometric series in the nilpotent operator gives the inverse. Corollary 3.11 should cite the integral torsion-free-quotient conclusion of Theorem 3.10. Rational isomorphism and absence of torsion alone would be insufficient, as multiplication by 2 on \(\mathbb Z\) shows.

Several additional formulas and scope transitions merit explicit clarification. Equation (4), p. 12, should use twisted K-theory of \(\mathcal X\), rather than untwisted K-theory of \(I\mathcal X\) on its left. For \(\mathcal X=BC_2,\alpha=0\), the literal latter reading has rank 4, while the stated inertia-cohomology right side has rank 2. The expected Proposition 3.1 is not refuted by this notation issue.

Claim 2.26, p. 11, passes from a stabilizer stratum to Lemma 2.24, which assumes trivial action of the whole group. The reduction should handle the free quotient and choose a suitable stabilizer subgroup, rather than an arbitrary cyclic subgroup without explanation. The Heisenberg-twist test does not give a counterexample: the residual quotient acts nontrivially on the character cover, correcting a naive rank count. Construction 3.9 also needs to explain how the proved finite-abelian-quotient comparison covers its more generally stated finite-quotient framework; the Higgs group \(\Gamma\) is abelian. These are recorded as proof-interface limits, not additional confirmed false main theorems.

In the appendix, the source and target variables in A.39–A.40, p. 46, must be made consistent. The main application needs a smooth map to the target with trivial group action. Theorem A.35, p. 44, has explicit topological-space and hypercompleteness hypotheses; Corollary A.41, p. 47, needs a descent argument for any broader stack scope. No separate counterexample to the actual representable quotient-torsor application is established here.

A suspected error from the index \(i\in\mathbb N\) was withdrawn: if \(P_B=\mathbb Q_B[d]\) is perverse, then \(\mathbb Q_B=P_B[-d]\) has perverse cohomology in degree \(+d\), not \(-d\). It supplies no adopted finding. An additional twisted elliptic-surface proposal was not independently completed and is excluded. A periodic direct sum alone is also not an obstruction to the unipotence argument: finite-dimensional support gives uniformly bounded perverse-cohomology amplitude degree by degree.

Positive bounded checks include the Brauer-class torsion argument of Proposition 3.12, the finite-field Betti-number criterion via universal coefficients, the smooth affine-complement mechanism of Lemma 6.7 under its actual hypotheses, and the large-degree projective-bundle case for a single symmetric power. The Prym spectral-sequence strategy and determinant-of-cohomology descent were traced, but all external Cohen–Macaulay, relative duality and motivic inputs have not been independently reconstructed. Full source coverage does not mean complete independent certification of every external theorem.

analysis: The partial-domain morphisms in Definition A.4, p. 34, and the covering rule in Definition A.6, p. 35, are incompatible with the stability axiom of a Grothendieck topology.

Take \(G=C_2\) acting on \(X=\mathbb C\) by \(z\mapsto-z\), so \(X^G=\{0\}\). The allowed generalized orbits \[P=\mathbb C^*\times(\{e\}\backslash G),\qquad
 E=\varnothing\times(G\backslash G)\] satisfy \(P\ne\varnothing\) and \(P|_{s(G)}=P\times_X X^G=\varnothing\). The unique map \(P|_{s(G)}\to E\) is continuous, equivariant and over \(X\). Since \(\{e\}\subset G\), Definition A.4(c) makes it a morphism \(P\to E\).

Definition A.6 explicitly makes the empty family cover \(E\). Pulling its empty covering sieve back along \(P\to E\) gives the empty sieve on \(P\). Stability requires that sieve to cover \(P\), contradicting the stated covering criterion, since its union of images is empty. The example is a finite-dimensional, locally compact Hausdorff complex analytic space with nonempty fixed locus. Empty opens are allowed in A.3; A.6–A.7 explicitly retain the empty object; Example A.5 confirms that the partial-domain convention is intentional.

Interpreting the rule as a generating family for a topology does not supply the asserted theory. For the free action \(X=G=C_2\), each nonempty generalized orbit maps to the empty \(G\)-type orbit in exactly this way. The generated topology forces an empty cover on every object, making the sheaf category terminal. Lemma A.10 instead requires \(\operatorname{Sh}(G;G)\simeq\operatorname{Space}\).

The site needs a compatible replacement, followed by new proofs of the orbit comparison, stalk formulas, functoriality and base change. Changing one exceptional empty-object clause is not a certified repair. This is foundational to the appendix used in Section 5, without disproving the final K-theory equivalence.
result: Result: Foundational site inconsistency affects subsequent stalk, functor and vanishing-cycle formalism.
Impact: Foundational site inconsistency affects subsequent stalk, functor and vanishing-cycle formalism.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Replace with compatible definitions and reprove orbit comparison, stalks, functoriality and base change.

problems.title: Coarse fixed points do not provide well-defined orbit action maps for stacks

analysis: Definitions A.29(b) and A.31, p. 43, use coarse fixed points as if they supplied coherent fixed objects. The resulting orbit action map need not be defined independently of a coset representative.

Let \(\mathcal X=BC_3\) and let \(G=C_2\) act by inversion on \(C_3\). This is a strict action allowed by A.29(a). Its coarse space is a point, so A.29(b) gives \(\mathcal X^G=\mathcal X\). Take \(H=G\) and \(U=\mathcal X\) in A.31. The unique coset in \(G\backslash G\) can be represented by \(1\) or the nontrivial element \(s\). The formula \((x,Hg)\mapsto x\cdot g\) then gives the identity functor or the inversion functor on \(BC_3\).

These are not naturally isomorphic: a natural isomorphism would be an element \(k\in C_3\) satisfying \(kr=r^{-1}k\) for a generator \(r\). Since \(C_3\) is abelian, that would imply \(r=r^{-1}\). Thus passing to a 2-categorical interpretation does not resolve the failure. Coarse fixed points alone do not provide the required trivialization of the subgroup action.

One must restrict actions or retain coherent fixed-object data and verify the subsequent descent constructions. The actual map \(M'\to[\mathfrak{sl}_n/PGL_n]\) on p. 21 has a target described as carrying trivial \(\Gamma\)-action. The example above is not asserted to occur there. The general framework is overbroad even if that specific application can be constructed in a narrower framework.

Impact: General allowed stack construction is not well-defined.

problems.title: Arbitrary Brauer class is replaced by the canonical obstruction gerbe without justification
