analysis: Theorem 6.11, p. 27, allows an arbitrary Brauer class. Corollary 6.16 and its use in Corollary 6.17, p. 30, identify the corresponding character cover with a fixed geometric cover by using a property specific to the universal-family obstruction gerbe.

For the zero equivariant gerbe, the line bundles \(L_{\gamma'}\) of Sections 2.5 and 6.3 are trivial and their algebra is the ordinary group algebra. Therefore, for \(c=\langle\gamma\rangle\), \[C_c^0=M^\gamma\times c^* .                             \tag{6}\] Take \(n=2,d=1\), a curve of genus at least 2, and nonzero \(\gamma\in J[2]\). The associated connected étale double cover \(\widetilde C_\gamma\) has connected rank-one Higgs moduli \[\widetilde M_\gamma=T^*\operatorname{Pic}^1(\widetilde C_\gamma).\] The deck involution acts freely on \(\operatorname{Pic}^1\): an invariant line bundle can be linearized for the cyclic group over \(\mathbb C\) and descended, but a pullback from the base has even degree. Thus \(M^\gamma=\widetilde M_\gamma/\mu_2\) is connected, using the geometric description also stated in Proposition 6.15. The left side of Corollary 6.16 for \(\alpha=0\) has two connected components by (6), whereas \(\widetilde M_\gamma\) has one. They are not isomorphic.

If that corollary is interpreted as concerning only the canonical obstruction gerbe, this example does not refute the restricted interpretation. It does show that such a corollary cannot justify the arbitrary-\(\alpha\) reduction as written. Its proof invokes the obstruction property without a new restriction after the arbitrary gerbe assertions on pp. 27–29. The repair must state and track the canonical-gerbe hypothesis, and separately prove any claimed extension to arbitrary Brauer classes. This does not establish that Theorem 6.11 itself is false.

Impact: Cor6.16 cannot serve the stated arbitrary-Brauer scope without more input.

report: Abstract: The VEM potential reconstruction in the reviewed manuscript is not well defined: its prescribed wedge pairing is degenerate, and legitimate lowest-order data on a triangle make its defining equation inconsistent. An interval already gives nonuniqueness. This Major issue affects the potential and its polynomial-consistency theorem, whereas the separately defined VEM cochain complex and its cohomology argument do not use the defective reconstruction. Five local corrections concern the zero-degree Hodge Laplacian, the boundary scope of adjoint consistency, a polynomial degree, and two signs. The DDR algebraic proof chain receives positive checks. These conclusions are an initial review of an exact author-manuscript version; independent acceptance remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Well-posedness of local potentials
in a polytopal exterior calculus
# Source and scope

The primary source is Francesco Bonaldi, Daniele Antonio Di Pietro, Jérôme Droniou and Kaibo Hu, An exterior calculus framework for polytopal methods, arXiv:2303.11093v3, 18 January 2025, 55 pages [main]. Printed and one-based PDF page numbers agree. All 55 text pages were read and all 55 source page images actually viewed. The publisher identifies DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1602, acceptance on 10 November 2024 and online publication on 17 March 2025 [publisher]. The acquired v3 carries a submitted-manuscript header; equivalence with the journal PDF has not been established.

The review checked the Koszul decompositions and traces, both discrete-space definitions, local and global operators, complex and commutation arguments, polynomial consistency, cohomology reductions, the conditional Hodge-Laplacian application, and the appendix’s conventions. The external analytic estimates cited as [34], [36], [44] and [47] in the paper were not independently re-proved in their entirety. In particular, the paper explicitly leaves a unified general-degree adjoint-consistency proof to future work (p. 21); this acknowledged limitation is not treated as a proved error.
# The VEM potential is not well defined

Problem 1 (Major).  Equation (4.9), p. 37, does not in general define a unique element of \(\mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^k(f)\), and for permitted data it need not have a solution. The inference from moments to equality in the proof of Theorem 31, p. 40, uses the same invalid nondegeneracy assertion.

The test forms \(\mathrm d\mu+\nu\) in (4.9) span \(\mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^{d-k}(f)\) by (2.17). That fact does not imply that \[(P,\rho)\longmapsto\int_f P\wedge\rho,\qquad
 \mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^k(f)\times
 \mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^{d-k}(f)\longrightarrow\mathbb R
                                                        \tag{1}\] is a perfect pairing. The Hodge star does not preserve trimmed spaces in the way this conclusion would require.
## Nonuniqueness on an interval

Take \(f=(-1,1)\), \(d=1\), \(k=r=0\), and \(x_f=0\). Give all endpoint and cell components in (4.1) the value zero. The derivative (4.4), the boundary potentials (4.8), and \(\widetilde D\) in (4.10) are then zero. The trial space in (4.9) is \[\mathcal P^-_1\Lambda^0(f)=\operatorname{span}\{1,x\},\] whereas \(\mathcal K^0_1(f)=\operatorname{span}\{x\}\) and \(\mathcal K^1_1(f)=0\). Thus (4.9) requires only \(\int_{-1}^{1}P(x)\,\mathrm dx=0\). Both \(P=0\) and \(P=x\) satisfy every test. No endpoint matching condition is imposed on this reconstructed potential: the separately reconstructed boundary values merely enter its right-hand side.
## Nonexistence on a regular triangle

A stronger example avoids relying only on a dimension mismatch. Let \[T=\{x>0,\ y>0,\ x+y<1\},\quad
 d=2,\quad k=1,\quad r=0,\quad x_T=(1/3,1/3),\] and set \(X=x-1/3\), \(Y=y-1/3\) and \[\alpha=-Y\,\mathrm dx+X\,\mathrm dy=\kappa_T(\mathrm dx\wedge\mathrm dy)
 \in\mathcal K^1_1(T).\] Set every edge component to zero, the cell component to \(\omega_T=\alpha\), and \(D_{\omega,T}=0\). These are legal independent components of the Cartesian space (4.1): on this \((k+1)\)-cell its factor is \(\mathcal K^1_1(T)\times\mathcal K^0_0(T)\), with the second space zero. Equation (4.4) gives \(\mathrm d_{0,T}^1\underline\omega_T=0\), and the edge potentials are zero.

Here \[\mathcal P^-_1\Lambda^1(T)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathrm dx,\mathrm dy,\alpha\}.\] For every allowed trial \(P\), the centroid identities give \[\int_T P\wedge\alpha=0.\] Indeed, \(\int_T X=\int_T Y=0\) and \(\alpha\wedge\alpha=0\). Testing (4.9) with \((\mu,\nu)=(0,\alpha)\) instead requires \[0=\int_T\star^{-1}\alpha\wedge\alpha
   =\int_T(X^2+Y^2)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy
   =\frac1{18}.                                         \tag{2}\] The sign here follows from the paper’s own Hodge convention: \(\star^{-1}\alpha=X\,\mathrm dx+Y\,\mathrm dy\). Each centered second moment is \(1/36\), obtained from \(\int_Tx=1/6\), \(\int_Tx^2=1/12\), and \(|T|=1/2\). Thus the defining linear system is inconsistent even on a convex shape-regular cell.
## A three-dimensional check and the repair boundary

The same obstruction occurs for \(f=(-1,1)^3\), \(d=3\), \(k=2\), \(r=0\). Take all face components zero, \(\omega_f=x\,\mathrm dy-y\,\mathrm dx\) and \(D_{\omega,f}=0\). The proxy of any trial in \(\mathcal P^-_1\Lambda^2(f)\) has the form \(a+b(x,y,z)\). Its integral pairing with the proxy \((-y,x,0)\) vanishes, by oddness and pointwise radial orthogonality. Equation (4.9) at \((0,\omega_f)\) demands instead \(0=-16/3\). This is the squared-norm integral with the factor \((-1)^{k+1}=-1\).

Impact. The claimed map on the whole VEM space, the potential identity (4.12), and constructions using this map, including the higher-dimensional derivative (4.11), require substantive redesign. The last step of the proof of Theorem 31 only proves equality of moments in the degenerate pairing (1). For polynomial inputs, satisfying those moments alone cannot select the asserted unique polynomial.

Counterevidence. The global differential (4.6) uses (4.4) and the stored derivative components, not (4.9). Lemma 32, Propositions 33–34, and the cohomology argument in Theorem 30 survive this particular objection. The potentials in its extension (4.20) are DDR(0) potentials. No counterexample to the VEM cohomology theorem or to the DDR complex is asserted here.

Repair. A nondegenerate trial–test pair and a compatible polynomial-reproduction argument are needed. Simply replacing the target by \(\star^{-1}\mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^{d-k}\) would restore a Riesz pairing but does not preserve the theorem: in the interval example the new target is constants, so the interpolant of \(x\) could reconstruct only its mean rather than \(x\). No complete alternative VEM construction is certified in this review.
# The Hodge-Laplacian application’s scope

Problem 2 (Minor).  Section 3.2.1, p. 18, includes \(k=0\) while inferring that all harmonic spaces vanish from topological triviality. Consequently the unrestricted uniqueness claim and the inf-sup inequality (3.21), p. 19, fail at that endpoint.

On a nonempty connected contractible domain the unreduced de Rham complex used in (1.2) has \(H^0\cong\mathbb R\). Let \(c_h=I_r^0 1\). Polynomial consistency and commutation give \[c_h\ne0,\qquad \mathrm d_r^0c_h=0.\] Even with the usual convention \(X_r^{-1}=0\), \[\mathcal A_h((0,c_h),(0,v_h))=0
 \quad\hbox{for every }v_h,\qquad
 \lVert(0,c_h)\rVert_{\mathrm{graph}}>0.\] This contradicts (3.21). For zero forcing there are multiple constant solutions; for \(g=1\), testing with \(c_h\) gives zero on the left and \((c_h,c_h)_{0,h}>0\) on the right.

Restricting the displayed application to \(1\le k\le n\) on a contractible domain repairs this endpoint. Alternatively, impose zero mean and compatible forcing at \(k=0\), or retain the harmonic unknown and the usual orthogonality condition. Remark 21 already describes the relevant kind of harmonic correction. This does not refute (3.20): a constant input has zero differential and admits the chosen preimage zero. Nor does it refute Theorem 14, whose cohomology statement correctly retains constants.
Problem 3 (Minor).  The universal smooth-form scope of the adjoint-consistency estimate (3.24), p. 20, omits the boundary condition needed to remove the continuous boundary pairing.

Take \(\Omega=(0,1)^3\), \(\ell=0\), \(r\ge1\), a regular refining mesh, \(\omega=\mathrm dx_1\), and \(\mu_h=I_r^0x_1\). Then \(\delta\omega=0\) and \(\mathrm d_r^0\mu_h=I_r^1\mathrm dx_1\). Polynomial consistency, (3.16), and vanishing stabilization on polynomial interpolants give exactly \[\widetilde E_{r,h}^0(\mathrm dx_1;I_r^0x_1)=-1,\qquad
 \lVert I_r^0x_1\rVert_{\mathrm{graph}}^2=\frac13+1=\frac43. \tag{3}\] No constant independent of \(h\) can make (3) bounded by \(Ch^{r+1}\sqrt{4/3}\) as \(h\to0\). The forms are smooth, so additional piecewise regularity alone cannot exclude the example.

The statement should specify the Hilbert-adjoint domain, with the corresponding homogeneous normal trace (in smooth notation, \(\operatorname{tr}_{\partial\Omega}(\star\omega)=0\)), or explicitly retain the boundary term. The weak mixed equations can enforce the appropriate natural conditions for the actual solution \(u\) and \(\mathrm du\). Thus this counterexample targets the stated general estimate, not the conditional convergence argument after its boundary assumptions are restored. The paper’s acknowledged dependence on external Poincaré and adjoint estimates is separately retained as a coverage limitation.
# Local formula corrections
Problem 4 (Minor).  The two-dimensional radial proxy in (2.11), p. 7, has \(\mathcal P_{r+1}(F)\) where \(\mathcal P_{r-1}(F)\) is required.

By (2.5), \(\mathcal K_r^1(F)=\kappa_F\mathcal P_{r-1}\Lambda^2(F)\). After the specified rotation its vector proxy is therefore \[\mathcal R_r^c(F)=(x-x_F)\mathcal P_{r-1}(F).\] At \(r=0\), (2.6) makes the left-hand space zero, while the printed \((x-x_F)\mathcal P_1(F)\) is nonzero. Correcting the degree also corrects the explicit proxy interpretation in Example 3, Table 1, Example 13 and Table 2. The formal Koszul and trimmed-space definitions used in the algebraic DDR proofs have the correct degree; those proofs are not invalidated by this local proxy formula.
Problem 5 (Minor).  The second bullet following (A.6), p. 50, reverses the cross-product order for contraction of a two-form.

With the proxy convention on p. 49, take \(\omega=\mathrm dx_1\wedge\mathrm dx_2\), whose proxy is \(w=e_3\), and \(v=e_1\). The first-slot definition (A.6) gives \[\iota_{e_1}(\mathrm dx_1\wedge\mathrm dx_2)=\mathrm dx_2
 \longleftrightarrow e_2,\] whereas the printed \(v\times w=e_1\times e_3=-e_2\). The correct proxy is \(w\times v\). The formal definition of contraction, and hence the formal Koszul spaces, remains usable; changing the sign of a space generator does not change its span. Implementations translating the operator through this bullet need the correction.
Problem 6 (Minor).  The unnumbered integration-by-parts reformulation of (3.4), p. 47, has the wrong sign on its volume derivative.

Write \(a=\star^{-1}\omega_f\) and let \(P_{\partial f}\) denote the boundary potential. Stokes’ formula (2.1) and (3.4) give \[\int_f\mathrm d_r^k\underline\omega_f\wedge\mu
 =\int_f\mathrm da\wedge\mu+
   \int_{\partial f}(P_{\partial f}-\operatorname{tr}a)\wedge\operatorname{tr}\mu.   \tag{4}\] The printed first term is its negative. For a concrete check, take the interval \((0,1)\), \(k=0\), \(r=2\), and DDR data \(I_2^0x\). The cell component has \(a=x\), the endpoint potentials equal its traces, and the reconstructed derivative is \(\mathrm dx\). Testing with \(\mu=1\) makes (4) read \(1=1\); the printed formula reads \(1=-1\). Replacing the volume minus sign by a plus sign is a complete local repair. The original (2.1), (3.4) and the proved complex property use the correct sign and are not refuted by this explanatory rewrite.
# Proof coverage, counterevidence and remaining limits

The following positive checks delimit the adverse conclusions. For DDR, the full polynomial wedge pairing in (3.4) is nondegenerate; the Koszul decomposition (2.9) supplies the full test space in (3.5). The trace lemma accounts for the translation between cell centers. Boundary-of-boundary cancellation, with the orientation factors of (3.6), proves Lemma 22. Theorem 23 then establishes the complex property and the potential–derivative relation by induction on \(d-k\). Lemma 24 preserves the trimmed moments, Theorem 25 establishes commutation, and Theorem 15 uses these already proved relations in its polynomial-consistency induction. The \(r=0\) and \(d=k\) base cases were checked separately. These arguments do not invoke the defective VEM pairing.

For DDR cohomology, reduction \(R\) takes the lowest-dimensional component means. Constant tests in (3.56)–(3.58) show that it is a surjective cochain map. Its kernel is exactly the zero-mean complex, which Lemma 27 proves acyclic by constructing moments dimension by dimension. Consequently \[0\longrightarrow\ker R\longrightarrow\operatorname{DDR}(r)
   \longrightarrow\operatorname{DDR}(0)\longrightarrow0\] induces a cohomology isomorphism. The lowest-order complex is the cellular cochain complex after volume scaling. This independently checks the central reduction without erasing \(H^0\).

For VEM, Lemma 35 explicitly constructs a primitive in the kernel of the analogous mean reduction. Its lowest-dimensional compatibility uses zero integral, not a false identification of Koszul vanishing at a point with zero mean. Equations (4.19)–(4.23) give the reduction and extension through DDR(0), independently of (4.9). Theorem 30 therefore has a proof chain not contradicted by Problem 1.

Several smaller scope and notation points are retained without inflating the problem count. Equation (4.11), p. 37, defines the higher-dimensional derivative only for \(d\le n-1\), whereas (4.13) includes \(d=n\); the intended upper bound should be \(n\), subject to repairing the potential. The Hodge-space statement in Remark 5, p. 11, should distinguish \(\star^{-1}\mathcal P_r^-\Lambda^{d-k}\) from \(\mathcal P_r^-\Lambda^k\). For instance, in dimension three at \(r=1\) the latter has dimension six when \(k=1\), while \(\mathcal P_1^-\Lambda^2\) has dimension four. The malformed space membership following (3.39), p. 25, can be read correctly using the Hodge-transformed trimmed space; the moment argument then remains valid. Index slips in the reduction–extension prose were not promoted into false cohomology counterexamples.

The approximation arguments on pp. 27–28 were checked as reductions to the cited projector and stability estimates, rather than as new independent proofs of every mesh-uniform constant. No numerical convergence experiment or author implementation was run. No article-specific executable supplement was established by the bounded title/DOI, publisher, arXiv and repository searches. The Oxford repository lists an accepted manuscript; it was not silently substituted for the acquired v3. Absence of code is not a scientific defect. The current arXiv history still lists v3 as its latest version [main]; no journal-version correction is inferred from that fact.
# Supporting checks

The initial assessment is Major, because the stated VEM potential map fails to exist for valid input. This does not require the entire paper, either cohomology theorem, or every numerical application to be false. The other five numbered issues admit local corrections with the scope indicated above. A complete replacement reconstruction has not been proved here.

Three existing native helpers supplied bounded text-based checks. problems.title: VEM potential wedge pairing is degenerate and can be inconsistent
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 6 Pdf pages: 8 Pdf pages: 9 Pdf pages: 35 Pdf pages: 36 Pdf pages: 37 Pdf pages: 38 Pdf pages: 40 Pdf pages: 41 Pdf pages: 42 Pdf pages: 43 Labels: (2.5), (2.12), (2.17) Labels: (4.1), (4.4), (4.9), (4.10) Labels: Theorem 31 / (4.12)-(4.13) Source location: Eq4.9 PDF37; definitions2.5/2.12/2.17,4.1/4.4; Theorem31 PDF40
claim: Equation (4.9) defines a unique map from all VEM data to P^-_{r+1} Lambda^k; its moments imply polynomial reproduction.
Legal r=0, convex regular interval/triangle/cube, centers specified, Cartesian DOFs exactly from (4.1).
analysis: Equation (4.9), p. 37, does not in general define a unique element of \(\mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^k(f)\), and for permitted data it need not have a solution. The inference from moments to equality in the proof of Theorem 31, p. 40, uses the same invalid nondegeneracy assertion.

The test forms \(\mathrm d\mu+\nu\) in (4.9) span \(\mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^{d-k}(f)\) by (2.17). That fact does not imply that \[(P,\rho)\longmapsto\int_f P\wedge\rho,\qquad
 \mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^k(f)\times
 \mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^{d-k}(f)\longrightarrow\mathbb R
                                                        \tag{1}\] is a perfect pairing. The Hodge star does not preserve trimmed spaces in the way this conclusion would require.

Take \(f=(-1,1)\), \(d=1\), \(k=r=0\), and \(x_f=0\). Give all endpoint and cell components in (4.1) the value zero. The derivative (4.4), the boundary potentials (4.8), and \(\widetilde D\) in (4.10) are then zero. The trial space in (4.9) is \[\mathcal P^-_1\Lambda^0(f)=\operatorname{span}\{1,x\},\] whereas \(\mathcal K^0_1(f)=\operatorname{span}\{x\}\) and \(\mathcal K^1_1(f)=0\). Thus (4.9) requires only \(\int_{-1}^{1}P(x)\,\mathrm dx=0\). Both \(P=0\) and \(P=x\) satisfy every test. No endpoint matching condition is imposed on this reconstructed potential: the separately reconstructed boundary values merely enter its right-hand side.

A stronger example avoids relying only on a dimension mismatch. Let \[T=\{x>0,\ y>0,\ x+y<1\},\quad
 d=2,\quad k=1,\quad r=0,\quad x_T=(1/3,1/3),\] and set \(X=x-1/3\), \(Y=y-1/3\) and \[\alpha=-Y\,\mathrm dx+X\,\mathrm dy=\kappa_T(\mathrm dx\wedge\mathrm dy)
 \in\mathcal K^1_1(T).\] Set every edge component to zero, the cell component to \(\omega_T=\alpha\), and \(D_{\omega,T}=0\). These are legal independent components of the Cartesian space (4.1): on this \((k+1)\)-cell its factor is \(\mathcal K^1_1(T)\times\mathcal K^0_0(T)\), with the second space zero. Equation (4.4) gives \(\mathrm d_{0,T}^1\underline\omega_T=0\), and the edge potentials are zero.

Here \[\mathcal P^-_1\Lambda^1(T)=\operatorname{span}\{\mathrm dx,\mathrm dy,\alpha\}.\] For every allowed trial \(P\), the centroid identities give \[\int_T P\wedge\alpha=0.\] Indeed, \(\int_T X=\int_T Y=0\) and \(\alpha\wedge\alpha=0\). Testing (4.9) with \((\mu,\nu)=(0,\alpha)\) instead requires \[0=\int_T\star^{-1}\alpha\wedge\alpha
   =\int_T(X^2+Y^2)\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy
   =\frac1{18}.                                         \tag{2}\] The sign here follows from the paper’s own Hodge convention: \(\star^{-1}\alpha=X\,\mathrm dx+Y\,\mathrm dy\). Each centered second moment is \(1/36\), obtained from \(\int_Tx=1/6\), \(\int_Tx^2=1/12\), and \(|T|=1/2\). Thus the defining linear system is inconsistent even on a convex shape-regular cell.

The same obstruction occurs for \(f=(-1,1)^3\), \(d=3\), \(k=2\), \(r=0\). Take all face components zero, \(\omega_f=x\,\mathrm dy-y\,\mathrm dx\) and \(D_{\omega,f}=0\). The proxy of any trial in \(\mathcal P^-_1\Lambda^2(f)\) has the form \(a+b(x,y,z)\). Its integral pairing with the proxy \((-y,x,0)\) vanishes, by oddness and pointwise radial orthogonality. Equation (4.9) at \((0,\omega_f)\) demands instead \(0=-16/3\). This is the squared-norm integral with the factor \((-1)^{k+1}=-1\).

Impact. The claimed map on the whole VEM space, the potential identity (4.12), and constructions using this map, including the higher-dimensional derivative (4.11), require substantive redesign. The last step of the proof of Theorem 31 only proves equality of moments in the degenerate pairing (1). For polynomial inputs, satisfying those moments alone cannot select the asserted unique polynomial.

Counterevidence. The global differential (4.6) uses (4.4) and the stored derivative components, not (4.9). Lemma 32, Propositions 33–34, and the cohomology argument in Theorem 30 survive this particular objection. The potentials in its extension (4.20) are DDR(0) potentials. No counterexample to the VEM cohomology theorem or to the DDR complex is asserted here.

Repair. A nondegenerate trial–test pair and a compatible polynomial-reproduction argument are needed. Simply replacing the target by \(\star^{-1}\mathcal P^-_{r+1}\Lambda^{d-k}\) would restore a Riesz pairing but does not preserve the theorem: in the interval example the new target is constants, so the interpolant of \(x\) could reconstruct only its mean rather than \(x\). No complete alternative VEM construction is certified in this review.
result: Result: Confirmed nonuniqueness and nonexistence for permitted inputs; not a numerical approximation.
Impact: VEM potential as a map, Theorem 31's moment-to-polynomial inference and dependent higher-dimensional reconstruction (4.11) need substantial repair.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Redesign a nondegenerate trial/test pairing compatible with desired reproduction and DOFs.

problems.title: The k=0 harmonic mode invalidates the unrestricted inf-sup claim
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 2 Pdf pages: 15 Pdf pages: 18 Pdf pages: 19 Pdf pages: 21 Pdf pages: 25 Pdf pages: 29 Pdf pages: 31 Labels: Section 3.2.1 Labels: (3.18)-(3.21) Labels: Remark 21 Labels: Theorem 14 Source location: Section3.2.1 PDF18; inf-sup3.21 PDF19
claim: Topologically trivial Omega has trivial harmonic spaces, for k>=0, giving uniqueness and (3.21).
Nonempty connected contractible domain, unreduced de Rham complex, natural boundary weak formulation, standard zero negative-degree space.
analysis: Section 3.2.1, p. 18, includes \(k=0\) while inferring that all harmonic spaces vanish from topological triviality. Consequently the unrestricted uniqueness claim and the inf-sup inequality (3.21), p. 19, fail at that endpoint.

On a nonempty connected contractible domain the unreduced de Rham complex used in (1.2) has \(H^0\cong\mathbb R\). Let \(c_h=I_r^0 1\). Polynomial consistency and commutation give \[c_h\ne0,\qquad \mathrm d_r^0c_h=0.\] Even with the usual convention \(X_r^{-1}=0\), \[\mathcal A_h((0,c_h),(0,v_h))=0
 \quad\hbox{for every }v_h,\qquad
 \lVert(0,c_h)\rVert_{\mathrm{graph}}>0.\] This contradicts (3.21). For zero forcing there are multiple constant solutions; for \(g=1\), testing with \(c_h\) gives zero on the left and \((c_h,c_h)_{0,h}>0\) on the right.

Restricting the displayed application to \(1\le k\le n\) on a contractible domain repairs this endpoint. Alternatively, impose zero mean and compatible forcing at \(k=0\), or retain the harmonic unknown and the usual orthogonality condition. Remark 21 already describes the relevant kind of harmonic correction. This does not refute (3.20): a constant input has zero differential and admits the chosen preimage zero. Nor does it refute Theorem 14, whose cohomology statement correctly retains constants.
result: Result: Confirmed endpoint counterexample.
Impact: Application's unqualified endpoint solvability and inf-sup range are false.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Restrict application to 1<=k<=n on contractible domain, or impose zero mean, compatible forcing and/or harmonic unknown at k=0.

analysis: The universal smooth-form scope of the adjoint-consistency estimate (3.24), p. 20, omits the boundary condition needed to remove the continuous boundary pairing.

Take \(\Omega=(0,1)^3\), \(\ell=0\), \(r\ge1\), a regular refining mesh, \(\omega=\mathrm dx_1\), and \(\mu_h=I_r^0x_1\). Then \(\delta\omega=0\) and \(\mathrm d_r^0\mu_h=I_r^1\mathrm dx_1\).  \lVert I_r^0x_1\rVert_{\mathrm{graph}}^2=\frac13+1=\frac43. \tag{3}\] No constant independent of \(h\) can make (3) bounded by \(Ch^{r+1}\sqrt{4/3}\) as \(h\to0\). The forms are smooth, so additional piecewise regularity alone cannot exclude the example.

The statement should specify the Hilbert-adjoint domain, with the corresponding homogeneous normal trace (in smooth notation, \(\operatorname{tr}_{\partial\Omega}(\star\omega)=0\)), or explicitly retain the boundary term. The weak mixed equations can enforce the appropriate natural conditions for the actual solution \(u\) and \(\mathrm du\). Thus this counterexample targets the stated general estimate, not the conditional convergence argument after its boundary assumptions are restored. The paper’s acknowledged dependence on external Poincaré and adjoint estimates is separately retained as a coverage limitation.

report: Abstract: The full automorphism range asserted in the reviewed author manuscript does not ensure the ribbon structure needed to define the twisted invariant. A sixteen-dimensional Hopf algebra already used in the paper gives an explicit obstruction: a degree-preserving, cointegral-fixing involution exchanges every possible square root of the distinguished grouplike. This Major finding concerns existence and scope, rather than a numerical counterexample to a defined genus invariant. Three local corrections concern a right cup, the sign of a crossing tensor, and the variable and writhe factors in the ADO comparison. The Seifert-surface and filtration argument receives positive checks under the required ribbon hypotheses. This is a version-limited initial review; independent acceptance remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Ribbon data and degree bounds
for twisted quantum invariants
# Source and scope

The primary source is Daniel López Neumann and Roland van der Veen, Genus bounds for twisted quantum invariants, arXiv:2211.15010v1, 28 November 2022, 31 pages [main]. Printed and one-based PDF page numbers agree. All 31 text pages were read, and all 31 primary-source page images were actually viewed. The publisher lists DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1603, submission on 24 March 2023, acceptance on 12 October 2023, and online publication on 24 February 2025 [publisher]. The journal PDF was not collated with the acquired v1; the conclusions below attach to that exact author version.

The review followed the definitions of the twisted double, the ribbon hypotheses, the tangle operations, the Seifert-surface formula, the filtration proof, and the ADO comparison. Two exact versions of the paper’s reference [23] were checked at the ribbon propositions [dep1, dep2]; these sources support, rather than remove, the restriction in Problem 1. They were not reviewed in their entirety. The general Reshetikhin–Turaev invariance theorem, every tangle move in the cited literature, and every tabulated knot coefficient were not independently re-proved.
# The representation range needs a ribbon restriction

Problem 1 (Major; M25-0230-P1).  The claim on p. 3 that the degree-twisted invariant is defined for every \(\rho\) with values in \(\operatorname{Aut}^0_{\mathbb N^m}(H)\), and the inference to \(G'\)-ribbon in §3.4, p. 13, are too broad. Fixing the cointegral does not guarantee the requisite invariant ribbon data.

Section 2.4, p. 8, correctly requires a subgroup \(G\) fixing a chosen Kauffman–Radford pair \((b,\beta)\), together with a square-root homomorphism for \(r_H|_G\). Section 3, p. 9, likewise assumes a \(G\)-ribbon structure. Section 3.4 then takes \(G=\operatorname{Aut}^0_{\mathbb N^m}(H)\) and obtains \(G'\)-ribbon solely from the displayed square root of \(r_{H'}\). The latter condition does not supply the former one. The same full \(G\) is used at the start of §4, p. 20.
## A counterexample within the paper’s own family

Take \(p=2\) in §5, pp. 24–25. Thus \[H_2=\mathbb C\langle k,E\rangle/(k^8-1,E^2,kE-iEk),\qquad
 \Delta(E)=E\otimes k^2+1\otimes E,\quad \Delta(k)=k\otimes k.
 \tag{1}\] The basis is \(k^jE^e\), \(0\le j<8\), \(e=0,1\), and \(|E|=1\), \(|k|=0\). Define \[\tau(k)=k^5,\qquad \tau(E)=E.                 \tag{2}\] Since \(i^5=i\), \((k^5)^2=k^2\), and \(25\equiv1\pmod8\), this is a degree-preserving Hopf involution. The left cointegral \[\Lambda=\sum_{j=0}^7 k^j E\] is fixed by \(\tau\), which merely permutes its eight summands. Consequently \(\tau\in\operatorname{Aut}^0_\mathbb N(H_2)\).

For completeness, the distinguished grouplike can be obtained without guessing it from the proposed pivot. Define the right integral by \[\lambda(k^6E)=1,\qquad
 \lambda(k^jE^e)=0\quad\hbox{on the other basis vectors}.\] The identity \[\Delta(k^jE)=k^jE\otimes k^{j+2}+k^j\otimes k^jE\] gives \[(\lambda\otimes\operatorname{id})\Delta(x)=\lambda(x)1,\qquad
 (\operatorname{id}\otimes\lambda)\Delta(x)=\lambda(x)k^6.\] Thus the distinguished grouplike is \(a=k^6\).

All grouplikes of \(H_2\) are powers of \(k\). Indeed, if a grouplike had a nonzero highest homogeneous component of positive degree \(d\), its tensor square would have a nonzero component of bidegree \((d,d)\), whereas its coproduct has total degree at most \(d\). Hence it lies in the degree-zero group algebra, whose grouplikes are exactly the \(k^j\). The only possibilities for \(b^2=a\) are therefore \[b=k^3\quad\hbox{or}\quad b=k^7.\] They satisfy \[\tau(k^3)=k^7,\qquad \tau(k^7)=k^3,      \tag{3}\] so neither is fixed.

This example does satisfy the earlier assumption that \(D(H_2)\) is ribbon. The paper’s pair is \[b=k^3,\qquad \beta(k)=e^{3\pi i/4},\qquad\beta(E)=0.\] Here \(b^2=k^6\), \(\beta^2(k)=-i\) is the distinguished character, and both \(\operatorname{ad}_b\) and \(\operatorname{ad}_{\beta^{-1}}\) multiply \(E\) by \(-i\), giving \(S^2(E)=-E\).
## Why another ribbon choice does not remove the obstruction

The neutral ribbon element must be fixed by \(\varphi_\tau\), by condition (4) on p. 7. The canonical Drinfeld element \(u\) of \(D(H_2)\) is invariant under this action, since the canonical \(R\)-tensor and the antipode are natural under Hopf automorphisms. Thus its pivot must be invariant as well. Any ribbon pivot has the form \(\beta'\otimes b'\), with \((b')^2=a\). Equivalently, the full correspondence in [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition 2.3, p.~9]{dep2}] requires \(G\)-invariant grouplikes \(b',\beta'\). Equation (3) rules out every possible \(b'\). There can be no compensating scalar in the other tensor factor: \(\beta'(1)=1\), so equality of the two simple tensors forces equality of their \(H_2\) factors.

This is consistent with the earlier cited version: [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition 2.3, p.~9]{dep1}] already explicitly requires \(G\) to fix \(b,\beta\). The reference number Proposition 2.4 used in the reviewed manuscript does not match the ribbon proposition in either acquired version of [23]; the mathematical hypothesis, rather than the numbering, is the substantive point.

For any knot, abelianization followed by reduction modulo two gives a representation sending a meridian to \(\tau\). It lies in the stated \(\operatorname{Aut}^0_\mathbb N(H_2)\) range. Adding the degree twist does not repair the obstruction: \(\theta\) fixes \(k\), so \(\tau\theta\) still exchanges both roots in (3), even if one restricts to the image generated by \(\tau\theta\).
## Impact and checked repair

This disproves the asserted availability of the needed structure for the full advertised representation range. It does not produce a numerical violation of the genus inequality for an already defined invariant. Reading the opening \(G\)-ribbon assumption of §3 as an additional implicit restriction saves a conditional result, but then the quantifiers of the introduction and Theorem 1 must retain that restriction.

A concrete repair is to specify \[G\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}^0_{\mathbb N^m}(H),\qquad
 G\text{ fixes a valid }(b,\beta),\qquad \operatorname{im}\rho\subseteq G,
 \tag{4}\] with the required square-root character. The graded extension is compatible with these data: grouplikes have degree zero, and a character vanishes on the positive-degree nilpotent ideal, so \(\theta\) fixes \(b,\beta\). The displayed square root in §3.4 then has the required multiplicativity.

The obstruction does not affect the standard degree-scaling subgroup used for ADO, which fixes \(k\) and its selected pair. Nor does it invalidate the exterior-algebra specialization with its canonical pair. These are material counterchecks on the scope of the finding.
# Two local tangle formulas
Problem 2 (Minor; M25-0230-P2).  The right cup on p. 29, §5.6, is not inverse to the displayed right cap. Its exponent of the basis index has the wrong sign.

Write \(q=\zeta_p=e^{\pi i/p}\). The printed coefficients are \[a_i=q^{\alpha(1-p)-2i},\qquad
 b_i=q^{-\alpha(1-p)-2i}.\] With the stated ordinary dual basis, the snake composite on \(v_i\) is multiplication by \[a_i b_i=q^{-4i}.                \tag{5}\] At \(p=3\), \(i=1\), this is \(q^2\ne1\), independently of \(\alpha\); a generic \(\alpha\) may therefore be used. At \(p=2\) the same check is identically one, which explains why that endpoint alone cannot detect the error. Since (5) depends on \(i\), an overall normalization cannot fix it.

The cap agrees with the pivot. In the paper’s notation \(\mathbf k=q^{\alpha/2}\bar k\) and \(\mathbf k v_i=q^{\alpha/2-i}v_i\), so \[g_\alpha v_i
 =q^{-\alpha(p-1)}\bar k^{\,2p+2}v_i
 =q^{\alpha(1-p)-2i}v_i.\] The corrected cup is consequently \[1\longmapsto
              \sum_{i=0}^{p-1}q^{-\alpha(1-p)+2i}
                            v_i^*\otimes v_i.             \tag{6}\] Its snake composite is the identity on every basis vector. The proof of Proposition 5.4 says that the cap and cup use \(g_\alpha^{\pm1}\), which is the correct conceptual prescription. The finding is a local correction to the printed construction; it is not a counterexample to the corrected ADO invariant.
Problem 3 (Minor; M25-0230-P3).  The formal tensor \(R_D\) on p. 12 omits the inverse for negative crossings, despite the correct rule on p. 11.

The displayed tensor uses \(\bigotimes_j R_{\alpha_j,\beta_j}\) for all crossings, even though the paragraph distinguishes the label conventions at positive and negative crossings. It must use \(R_{\alpha_j,\beta_j}^{\operatorname{sign}(c_j)}\) with the conventions already given on p. 11.

This discrepancy is visible in an ordinary example without super signs. Let \(H=\mathbb C[C_3]\), \(G=1\), and give \(H\) degree zero. For a generator \(g\) and the dual functions \(\delta_j\), the double has \[\begin{split}
 R&=\sum_{j=0}^2(\varepsilon\otimes g^j)\otimes(\delta_j\otimes1),\\
 R^{-1}&=\sum_{j=0}^2(\varepsilon\otimes g^{-j})\otimes(\delta_j\otimes1).
 \end{split}                                             \tag{7}\] The terms with \(\delta_1\) distinguish the tensors. In a single negative open crossing, each strand has one bead, the crossing action is trivial, and the subsequent permutation is invertible; hence it cannot erase the difference. The correct inverse in (7) multiplies \(R\) to the unit. Since p. 11 already supplies the correct rule, this is a local repair of the total formula, not a demonstrated failure of the invariant defined by those rules.
# The ADO comparison and its scalar factors
Problem 4 (Minor; M25-0230-P4).  The proof of Proposition 5.4, pp. 29–30, changes the declared variable in one line and omits a writhe factor in its final comparison.
The definition immediately above the proposition uses \(t=q^{2\alpha}\). Thus the proof’s \(ADO_p(K,q^\alpha)\) should read \(ADO_p(K,q^{2\alpha})\) under the convention chosen in this paper.

More substantively, let \(w=w(D)\). The last display on p. 29 gives \[Z_\alpha v_0
   =q^{w\alpha^2}
        \sum_{i,j}\lambda_{ij0}q^{\alpha(i-j)/2}v_0.\] The sum is the counit evaluation used in the next paragraph. The correct comparison is therefore \[\left.\varepsilon(Z^\theta_{D(H_p)})\right|_{t=q^{2\alpha}}v_0
                  =q^{-w\alpha^2}Z_\alpha v_0,            \tag{8}\] rather than the printed equality without that factor. For example, \(p=3\), \(\alpha=1/2\), \(w=1\) gives the nontrivial phase \(q^{w\alpha^2}=e^{\pi i/12}\). At zero writhe this issue disappears.

There is a positive repair check: combine the preceding ADO normalization \(q^{w(-\alpha^2+\alpha(p-1))}\) with the factor \(q^{w\alpha^2}\) relating \(Z_\alpha\) to the counit. The result is \[q^{w\alpha(p-1)}
                    =t^{w(p-1)/2},\] exactly the factor in equation (2), p. 14, and in the definition of \(P_{H_p}^{\theta}\) on p. 29. Thus the corrected calculation supports the intended final equality; these two formula corrections do not disprove it.
# Positive checks on the proof chain
## Seifert surfaces and the filtration

Under (4) and the correct tangle rules, the essential degree mechanism in §4 can be reconstructed. A genus-\(g\) Seifert surface is presented as a disk with \(2g\) bands. The two boundary strands of a band have opposite meridian homology classes, so \[\theta(\mu_i'\mu_i'')=1.\] Thus the invariant of the underlying \(2g\)-component tangle \(T\) has no \(t\)-powers. The partial longitudes in the stated surface-framing construction have zero knot homology. The coproduct, the modified antipode, the crossing maps and the permutation in Proposition 4.1 then give the boundary invariant. The source diagrams for these operations, including Figures 4–8, were actually inspected.

Put \(N=d(H)\). For a homogeneous term \((p\otimes a)t^{-J}\), use the budget \[d(a)+d(J).\] In multiplication, the extra exponent is \(-|a_{(3)}|\), while the remaining \(H\) factor is \(a_{(2)}b\). Nonnegative grading gives \[d(a_{(2)})+d(a_{(3)})\le d(a),\] so Lemma 4.2 preserves the sum of the two input budgets. In Lemma 4.3 the two factors \[t^{-|a_{(2)}|}
                  t^{|\alpha^{-1}(a_{(2)})|}\] cancel because \(\alpha\) preserves degree. The residual multiplication is controlled by Lemma 4.2. These are inequalities for every homogeneous summand; no absence of cancellation is assumed.

Each of the \(2g\) modified antipodes contributes \(t^{|\Lambda|/2}\) through the inverse pivot. Removing the common \(t^{g|\Lambda|}\) leaves a term of filtration degree at most \(2gN\). Consequently the total exponents of surviving monomials lie in \[[\,g\,d(\Lambda)-2gN,\;g\,d(\Lambda)\,],
                                                               \tag{9}\] whose width is \(2gN\). Evaluation and cancellation can only shrink this interval, and the framing normalization is one common monomial. The argument does not need the additional assertion \(d(\Lambda)=N\) to obtain this width.

For \(g=0\), the straight unknot gives \(Z=1\) and \(P=1\) directly; one need not interpret the iterated-multiplication symbol with exponent \(4g-1=-1\). The zero-polynomial case needs a conventional assignment of degree, or a statement for nonzero invariants, because the max/min definition on p. 3 otherwise has empty support.

The displayed filtration is not exhaustive on the whole Laurent coefficient module, since it contains only nonpositive integral powers. This does not invalidate the argument: after removing the explicit pivot monomial, all terms used in the proof lie in the specified part. Similarly, p. 19’s language about exact extrema must allow coefficient cancellation; the required upper bound survives.
## The quantum-group comparison

Several delicate components of §5 also pass direct checks. The group indexing the degree-scaled family is the additive group \(\mathbb C\). The character \(q^{\alpha(p-1)}\) is a square root there; at even \(p\) its possible failure to descend to the image in \(\operatorname{Aut}(H_p)\) is not an error in this explicitly \(\mathbb C\)-indexed construction.

For \(J_{\alpha,\beta}=1\otimes\mathbf k^\alpha\), both sides of the cocycle identity reduce to \(1\otimes\mathbf k^\alpha\otimes\mathbf k^{\alpha+\beta}\). Conjugation by \(J\) removes the extra scalar factors in the coproducts of \(E\) and \(F\). The diagonal conjugations in the braid argument cancel under the stated partial closures, with the unchanged pivot.

problems.title: The full cointegral-fixing automorphism group need not admit the required ribbon structure
problems.source_location: PDF/printed p.3, 'defined for any rho' and Theorem 1; p.13, Section 3.4, inference to G'-ribbon for G=Aut^0_{N^m}(H); p.20, Section 4. Correct restricted assumptions occur on pp.8-9; counterexample algebra is defined on pp.24-25. Source locations: Primary pp.3,7-9,13,20 Source locations: Reference [23] v1 and v2 pp.8-9; v2 Proposition 2.3
claim: Degree preservation and fixing the left cointegral, together with D(H) ribbon, suffice for the stated full automorphism range of the twisted invariant.
Ordinary Hopf algebra over C; H=H_2 from Section 5, dimension 16, k^8=1, E^2=0, kE=iEk, Delta(E)=E tensor k^2+1 tensor E, deg E=1, deg k=0. D(H_2) is ribbon with the paper's valid KR pair.
analysis: The claim on p. 3 that the degree-twisted invariant is defined for every \(\rho\) with values in \(\operatorname{Aut}^0_{\mathbb N^m}(H)\), and the inference to \(G'\)-ribbon in §3.4, p. 13, are too broad. Fixing the cointegral does not guarantee the requisite invariant ribbon data.

Section 2.4, p. 8, correctly requires a subgroup \(G\) fixing a chosen Kauffman–Radford pair \((b,\beta)\), together with a square-root homomorphism for \(r_H|_G\). Section 3, p. 9, likewise assumes a \(G\)-ribbon structure. Section 3.4 then takes \(G=\operatorname{Aut}^0_{\mathbb N^m}(H)\) and obtains \(G'\)-ribbon solely from the displayed square root of \(r_{H'}\). The latter condition does not supply the former one. The same full \(G\) is used at the start of §4, p. 20.

Take \(p=2\) in §5, pp. 24–25. Thus \[H_2=\mathbb C\langle k,E\rangle/(k^8-1,E^2,kE-iEk),\qquad
 \Delta(E)=E\otimes k^2+1\otimes E,\quad \Delta(k)=k\otimes k.
 \tag{1}\] The basis is \(k^jE^e\), \(0\le j<8\), \(e=0,1\), and \(|E|=1\), \(|k|=0\). Define \[\tau(k)=k^5,\qquad \tau(E)=E.                 \tag{2}\] Since \(i^5=i\), \((k^5)^2=k^2\), and \(25\equiv1\pmod8\), this is a degree-preserving Hopf involution. The left cointegral \[\Lambda=\sum_{j=0}^7 k^j E\] is fixed by \(\tau\), which merely permutes its eight summands. Consequently \(\tau\in\operatorname{Aut}^0_\mathbb N(H_2)\).

For completeness, the distinguished grouplike can be obtained without guessing it from the proposed pivot. Define the right integral by \[\lambda(k^6E)=1,\qquad
 \lambda(k^jE^e)=0\quad\hbox{on the other basis vectors}.\] The identity \[\Delta(k^jE)=k^jE\otimes k^{j+2}+k^j\otimes k^jE\] gives \[(\lambda\otimes\operatorname{id})\Delta(x)=\lambda(x)1,\qquad
 (\operatorname{id}\otimes\lambda)\Delta(x)=\lambda(x)k^6.\] Thus the distinguished grouplike is \(a=k^6\).

All grouplikes of \(H_2\) are powers of \(k\). Indeed, if a grouplike had a nonzero highest homogeneous component of positive degree \(d\), its tensor square would have a nonzero component of bidegree \((d,d)\), whereas its coproduct has total degree at most \(d\). Hence it lies in the degree-zero group algebra, whose grouplikes are exactly the \(k^j\). The only possibilities for \(b^2=a\) are therefore \[b=k^3\quad\hbox{or}\quad b=k^7.\] They satisfy \[\tau(k^3)=k^7,\qquad \tau(k^7)=k^3,      \tag{3}\] so neither is fixed.

This example does satisfy the earlier assumption that \(D(H_2)\) is ribbon. The paper’s pair is \[b=k^3,\qquad \beta(k)=e^{3\pi i/4},\qquad\beta(E)=0.\] Here \(b^2=k^6\), \(\beta^2(k)=-i\) is the distinguished character, and both \(\operatorname{ad}_b\) and \(\operatorname{ad}_{\beta^{-1}}\) multiply \(E\) by \(-i\), giving \(S^2(E)=-E\).

The neutral ribbon element must be fixed by \(\varphi_\tau\), by condition (4) on p. 7. The canonical Drinfeld element \(u\) of \(D(H_2)\) is invariant under this action, since the canonical \(R\)-tensor and the antipode are natural under Hopf automorphisms. Thus its pivot must be invariant as well. Any ribbon pivot has the form \(\beta'\otimes b'\), with \((b')^2=a\). Equivalently, the full correspondence in [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition 2.3, p.~9]{dep2}] requires \(G\)-invariant grouplikes \(b',\beta'\). Equation (3) rules out every possible \(b'\). There can be no compensating scalar in the other tensor factor: \(\beta'(1)=1\), so equality of the two simple tensors forces equality of their \(H_2\) factors.

This is consistent with the earlier cited version: [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition 2.3, p.~9]{dep1}] already explicitly requires \(G\) to fix \(b,\beta\). The reference number Proposition 2.4 used in the reviewed manuscript does not match the ribbon proposition in either acquired version of [23]; the mathematical hypothesis, rather than the numbering, is the substantive point.

For any knot, abelianization followed by reduction modulo two gives a representation sending a meridian to \(\tau\). It lies in the stated \(\operatorname{Aut}^0_\mathbb N(H_2)\) range. Adding the degree twist does not repair the obstruction: \(\theta\) fixes \(k\), so \(\tau\theta\) still exchanges both roots in (3), even if one restricts to the image generated by \(\tau\theta\).

This disproves the asserted availability of the needed structure for the full advertised representation range. It does not produce a numerical violation of the genus inequality for an already defined invariant. Reading the opening \(G\)-ribbon assumption of §3 as an additional implicit restriction saves a conditional result, but then the quantifiers of the introduction and Theorem 1 must retain that restriction.

A concrete repair is to specify \[G\subseteq\operatorname{Aut}^0_{\mathbb N^m}(H),\qquad
 G\text{ fixes a valid }(b,\beta),\qquad \operatorname{im}\rho\subseteq G,
 \tag{4}\] with the required square-root character. The graded extension is compatible with these data: grouplikes have degree zero, and a character vanishes on the positive-degree nilpotent ideal, so \(\theta\) fixes \(b,\beta\). The displayed square root in §3.4 then has the required multiplicativity.

The obstruction does not affect the standard degree-scaling subgroup used for ADO, which fixes \(k\) and its selected pair. Nor does it invalidate the exterior-algebra specialization with its canonical pair. These are material counterchecks on the scope of the finding.
result: Result: Confirmed obstruction to the asserted construction and advertised representation range, including a failure of the p.13 inference. Not a numerical counterexample to an already defined genus invariant.
Impact: Theorem 1's applicability and the existence of the invariant for all stated rho must be restricted; no claim that the whole paper or its conditional degree bound is false.

paragraphs: Take an explicitly specified G subset Aut^0_{N^m}(H) fixing a chosen valid KR pair (b,beta), with the required square-root character, and require im rho subset G; alternatively explicitly assume the corresponding G-ribbon structure and its graded extension.

problems.title: The right cup coefficient fails the snake identity
problems.source_location: PDF/printed p.29, Section 5.6, first displayed cap/cup formulas; compare the pivot on p.25 and module action on p.28. Source locations: Primary p.29 right caps and cups; preceding pivot definition
claim: The displayed right caps and cups implement the pivotal evaluation/coevaluation and can be pasted to define the ADO tangle invariant.
p>=2; zeta_p=exp(pi i/p); basis v_i and its ordinary dual; generic alpha may be used.
analysis: The right cup on p. 29, §5.6, is not inverse to the displayed right cap. Its exponent of the basis index has the wrong sign.

Write \(q=\zeta_p=e^{\pi i/p}\). The printed coefficients are \[a_i=q^{\alpha(1-p)-2i},\qquad
 b_i=q^{-\alpha(1-p)-2i}.\] With the stated ordinary dual basis, the snake composite on \(v_i\) is multiplication by \[a_i b_i=q^{-4i}.                \tag{5}\] At \(p=3\), \(i=1\), this is \(q^2\ne1\), independently of \(\alpha\); a generic \(\alpha\) may therefore be used. At \(p=2\) the same check is identically one, which explains why that endpoint alone cannot detect the error. Since (5) depends on \(i\), an overall normalization cannot fix it.

The cap agrees with the pivot. In the paper’s notation \(\mathbf k=q^{\alpha/2}\bar k\) and \(\mathbf k v_i=q^{\alpha/2-i}v_i\), so \[g_\alpha v_i
 =q^{-\alpha(p-1)}\bar k^{\,2p+2}v_i
 =q^{\alpha(1-p)-2i}v_i.\] The corrected cup is consequently \[1\longmapsto
              \sum_{i=0}^{p-1}q^{-\alpha(1-p)+2i}
                            v_i^*\otimes v_i.             \tag{6}\] Its snake composite is the identity on every basis vector. The proof of Proposition 5.4 says that the cap and cup use \(g_\alpha^{\pm1}\), which is the correct conceptual prescription. The finding is a local correction to the printed construction; it is not a counterexample to the corrected ADO invariant.
result: Result: Confirmed failure of the local duality identity for the displayed cup.
Impact: Literal reproduction from the displayed cup fails tangle duality. The problem is a local exponent sign and does not establish failure of the corrected ADO invariant or its genus bound.

problems.title: The formal tensor R_D omits the sign of negative crossings
problems.source_location: PDF/printed p.12, displayed definition of R_D; compare the explicit negative-crossing rule on p.11. Source locations: Primary pp.11-12 universal crossing tensor formula

analysis: The formal tensor \(R_D\) on p. 12 omits the inverse for negative crossings, despite the correct rule on p. 11.

The displayed tensor uses \(\bigotimes_j R_{\alpha_j,\beta_j}\) for all crossings, even though the paragraph distinguishes the label conventions at positive and negative crossings. It must use \(R_{\alpha_j,\beta_j}^{\operatorname{sign}(c_j)}\) with the conventions already given on p. 11.

This discrepancy is visible in an ordinary example without super signs. Let \(H=\mathbb C[C_3]\), \(G=1\), and give \(H\) degree zero. For a generator \(g\) and the dual functions \(\delta_j\), the double has \[\begin{split}
 R&=\sum_{j=0}^2(\varepsilon\otimes g^j)\otimes(\delta_j\otimes1),\\
 R^{-1}&=\sum_{j=0}^2(\varepsilon\otimes g^{-j})\otimes(\delta_j\otimes1).
 \end{split}                                             \tag{7}\] The terms with \(\delta_1\) distinguish the tensors. In a single negative open crossing, each strand has one bead, the crossing action is trivial, and the subsequent permutation is invertible; hence it cannot erase the difference. The correct inverse in (7) multiplies \(R\) to the unit. Since p. 11 already supplies the correct rule, this is a local repair of the total formula, not a demonstrated failure of the invariant defined by those rules.

report: Abstract: This review checks the principal theorem’s quantifiers and edge balance, then examines the random perfect-matching tool used by its embedding algorithm. The additive cut-count estimate in Lemma 2.7 is false under the stated super-regularity assumptions: an explicit dense bipartite graph family makes it fail for every perfect matching. The estimate is used in the proofs of Lemmas 2.10 and 3.10. The supported assessment is Major for a substantive defect in a core proof tool. This does not disprove the tree-decomposition theorem. A corrected matching statement and verification of downstream error bounds remain necessary. Scientific adjudication is pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: A verification of a matching estimate in
Ringel’s tree packing conjecture in quasirandom graphs
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed work is Peter Keevash and Katherine Staden, Ringel’s tree packing conjecture in quasirandom graphs, Journal of the European Mathematical Society 27 (2025), 1769–1826, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1604 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1604). The primary input is the exact publisher PDF acquired on 26 October 2026, whose SHA-256 begins `5dd8b480ab983bdf`. It has 58 PDF pages. Here page references use printed pagination: PDF page \(j\) is printed page \(1768+j\).

Close inspection covers Theorem 1.1 (p. 1770), regularity and super-regularity (p. 1788), Lemma 2.7 and its proof (pp. 1789–1790), the definition of Match (p. 1781), and the specific cut-count uses in Lemmas 2.10 (pp. 1792–1793) and 3.10 (pp. 1807–1808). The proof overview and selected surrounding passages were read for context. The other hypergraph-matching and exact-decomposition arguments were not re-proved. An acquired arXiv manuscript is a separate version, not a verified substitute for the publisher text. No separate supplement or dedicated author code was identified in the bounded searches; no author code was executed.
# Quantifiers and definitions

Theorem 1.1 first fixes a typicality order \(s\), then chooses a tolerance and size threshold for each fixed density \(p>0\). Subject to \(p(n-1)/2\in\mathbb Z\), a tree with \(p(n-1)/2\) edges is to decompose a sufficiently typical \(n\)-vertex graph into \(n\) copies. Its edge balance is consistent: \[n\,p(n-1)/2=p\binom n2.\] For \(p=1\), admissible odd \(n\) gives the stated large-order Ringel result. The theorem is not being interpreted as a uniform statement for arbitrary sparse densities depending on \(n\).

Equation reference: eq:regular, eq:false. The finding concerns the assumptions of Lemma 2.7. For \(B\subseteq X\times Y\), \(|X|=|Y|=n\), write \(\rho=d(B)=|B|/n^2\). The paper defines \(\alpha\)-regularity by the absolute cut condition \[
 \bigl||B[S,T]|-\rho|S||T|\bigr|\leq\alpha n^2
 \quad(S\subseteq X,\ T\subseteq Y).\] Super-regularity additionally requires each degree to lie in \((1\pm\alpha)\rho n\). Lemma 2.7 assumes \(n^{-1}\ll\alpha\ll d\), \(\rho\geq d\), and an auxiliary bipartite graph \(Z\) of maximum degree less than \(n^{0.4}\). It asserts a distribution on perfect matchings avoiding alternating \(MZMZ\) cycles, with approximately uniform edge marginals and, for every fixed \(X'\subseteq X\), \(Y'\subseteq Y\), the high-probability estimate \[
 |M[X',Y']|=\frac{|B[X',Y']|}{\rho n}\pm n^{0.8}.\] The following counterexample refutes this cut estimate, not the separate approximate-marginal assertion.
# A deterministic counterexample

Problem 1 (Degree imbalance invalidates the cut-count center).  The final estimate of Lemma 2.7, p. 1789 (PDF p. 21), is false even for \(Z=\varnothing\). The argument on p. 1790 does not control the bias between the actual expectation and the center in [eq:false] (#eq:false).
## Construction and every hypothesis

Equation reference: eq:parameters. Choose an integer \(q\geq2\), arbitrarily large, and set \(\alpha=1/q\), \(d=1/2\). Choose an arbitrarily large multiple \(n\) of \(2q\) satisfying \[
 n>(4q-2)^5,\qquad m=n/2,\qquad k=n/(2q).\] Let \(X=X_+\sqcup X_-\), where \(X_+=\{a_0,\ldots,a_{m-1}\}\) and \(X_-=\{b_0,\ldots,b_{m-1}\}\), and let \(Y=\{y_0,\ldots,y_{n-1}\}\). From \(K_{n,n}\) delete precisely the edges \(b_i y_j\) for which \[(j-i)\bmod m\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}.\] Set \(Z=\varnothing\).

Each \(a_i\) has degree \(n\), each \(b_i\) has degree \(n-2k\), and each \(y_j\) has degree \(n-k\). Thus \[|B|=n(n-k),\qquad \rho=1-\frac1{2q}\geq\frac12.\] The largest relative degree deviation from \(\rho n\) is \[\frac{k}{n-k}=\frac1{2q-1}\leq\frac1q=\alpha.\] All degree conditions are satisfied.

For the cut condition let \(H=K_{n,n}\setminus B\); then \(|H|=nk\). For arbitrary \(S,T\), \[|B[S,T]|-\rho|S||T|=\frac{k}{n}|S||T|-|H[S,T]|.\] Each term before subtraction lies in \([0,nk]\). Hence the absolute difference is at most \(nk=\alpha n^2/2\), proving [eq:regular] (#eq:regular) for every cut. This verifies the paper’s precise definition, including its absolute normalization.

The graph \(Z\) has maximum degree zero and introduces no alternating cycle. A perfect matching exists explicitly: match \(b_i\) to \(y_{(i+k)\bmod m}\) and \(a_i\) to \(y_{m+i}\). Choose \(q\) first, sufficiently large for \(\alpha\ll d\), and then make \(n\) arbitrarily large. The quantified hierarchy \(n^{-1}\ll\alpha\ll d\) is respected; no small-size exception is being used.
## Claimed value versus the exact value

Equation reference: eq:gap. Fix \(X'=X_+\) and \(Y'=Y\) before choosing any matching. Every perfect matching satisfies \[|M[X_+,Y]|=n/2.\] Since \(|B[X_+,Y]|=n^2/2\), the center in [eq:false] (#eq:false) is \(n/(2\rho)\). The deterministic error is \[
 \frac{n}{2\rho}-\frac n2
 =\frac{nk}{2(n-k)}
 =\frac{n}{4q-2}>n^{0.8}.\] The inequality follows directly from [eq:parameters] (#eq:parameters). The claimed event has probability zero for every distribution on perfect matchings. No simultaneous-over-all-cuts reading or adaptive choice of \(X',Y'\) is needed.
## Proof diagnosis and counterevidence

Any replacement with the same deterministic center must accommodate the degree-imbalance contribution or impose conditions excluding it. report: Abstract: The publisher version of Martino Lupini’s paper contains a false equivalence between potential \(\Sigma^0_2\) complexity of a coset relation and \(D(\Pi^0_2)\) membership of its subgroup. Title: A version-specific review of a corrected
potential-complexity criterion
# Version and scope

The primary source is M. Lupini, Complexity classes of Polishable subgroups, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 28 (2026), 2197–2232, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1605 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1605). The acquired 36-page publisher PDF has SHA-256 beginning `cafc0b5fb2d8c752`; PDF page \(j\) is printed page \(2196+j\). Its first page carries copyright 2025. The frozen project identifier M25-0232 and year mapping are retained.

The separately acquired Corrigendum to Complexity Classes of Polishable Subgroups, dated 10 September 2026, is Zenodo version 3, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22686173 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22686173). Its 35-page PDF has SHA-256 beginning `c64a640eef9ba856`. The public record confirms that date and version. The original and corrigendum are different scientific objects; no replacement of the frozen source is implied.

Close reading covers the introductory statements and definitions, original Theorem 3.3 and its proof, the first Solecki-stage description, and Lemmas 6.2–6.8 with their immediate dependencies. Corrigendum pp. 1–12 were read, concentrating on Proposition 2, Example 3, the diagnosis on pp. 8–9 and the restricted replacement on pp. 9–11. The later transfinite operator-range constructions were not independently re-proved. This scope does not certify all original or corrected classifications.
# The false assertion and its hypotheses

Here \(D(\Pi^0_2)\) means differences of two \(G_\delta\) sets, equivalently an intersection of a \(G_\delta\) set with an \(F_\sigma\) set. A Polishable subgroup has its unique compatible Polish group topology, which may be finer than the ambient subspace topology. Potential complexity refers to membership after a Borel-preserving Polish refinement, not an assertion of an exact minimal class.

Problem 1.  Original Theorem 3.3(2), p. 2201 (PDF p. 5), asserts that \(E_H^G\) is potentially \(\Sigma^0_2\) if and only if \(H\in D(\Pi^0_2)(G)\). Its converse is false. The potential-\(\Sigma^0_2\) assertion of Lemma 6.5, p. 2208 (PDF p. 12), is also false.

We reproduce and verify the author’s Example 3 rather than infer an error solely from the existence of a corrigendum. Put \(G=\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\) with its product topology and \[H=bv_0(\mathbb R)=
 \left\{x:x_n\longrightarrow0,\quad
              \sum_{n\ge1}|x_n-x_{n+1}|<\infty\right\}.\] This is an additive subgroup. With norm \(\|x\|_{\rm var}=\sum_{n\ge1}|x_n-x_{n+1}|\), it is isometrically isomorphic to \(\ell^1\) via \[(a_n)\longmapsto\left(\sum_{k\ge n}a_k\right)_n,
 \qquad a_n=x_n-x_{n+1}.\] The inverse formula follows by telescoping and the limit-zero condition. Also \(|x_n|\leq\|x\|_{\rm var}\), so inclusion into \(G\) is continuous. Thus \(H\) is a Polishable subgroup of the Polish group \(G\).
## Why this subgroup is not \(F_\sigma\)

Suppose \(H=\bigcup_j C_j\) with \(C_j\) product-closed in \(G\). Their inverse images in the Banach topology of \(H\) are closed. Baire category gives \(z\in H\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(z+B_{\rm var}(0,\varepsilon)\subseteq C_j\) for some \(j\). Then \(C_j-z\) is product-closed, is contained in \(H\), and contains this norm ball. Choose \(0<c<\varepsilon\) and define \[x^{(m)}_n=
 \begin{cases}c,&n\leq m,\\0,&n>m.\end{cases}\] Each \(x^{(m)}\) has variation norm \(c\) and belongs to that ball. Coordinatewise it converges to the nonzero constant sequence \((c,c,\ldots)\), which is not in \(H\). This contradicts product-closedness. Thus \(H\notin\Sigma^0_2(G)\).
## Why the coset relation is not potentially \(\Sigma^0_2\)

The necessary criterion can be proved without assuming the disputed theorem. For a Borel subgroup \(K\) of a Polish group \(P\), suppose \(E_K^P\) Borel-reduces to an \(F_\sigma\) equivalence relation via \(f:P\to Y\). There is a comeager \(G_\delta\) set \(C\) on which \(f\) is continuous. Hence for closed sets \(D_j\subseteq P^2\), \[E_K^P\cap C^2=\bigcup_j(D_j\cap C^2).\] Use the convention \(xE_K^Py\iff x^{-1}y\in K\); inversion interchanges this with the original paper’s convention. For \(h\in P\) put \(A_j(h)=\{x:(x,xh)\in D_j\}\). These sets are closed. On the comeager set \(C\cap Ch^{-1}\), their union contains every point if \(h\in K\) and no point otherwise. If \((V_i)\) is a countable basis of nonempty open sets of \(P\), Baire category gives \[K=\bigcup_{j,i}\{h:\ \forall x\in V_i,\ (x,xh)\in D_j\}.\] Each set in this union is closed, as an intersection of closed inverse images. Therefore potential \(\Sigma^0_2\) implies \(K\in\Sigma^0_2(P)\). Conversely, the map \((x,y)\mapsto x^{-1}y\) immediately gives the reverse implication. This verifies the corrected criterion in the author’s Proposition 2.

Applied to \(H=bv_0(\mathbb R)\), the necessary direction and the preceding non-\(F_\sigma\) proof show that \(E_H^G\) is not potentially \(\Sigma^0_2\). All hypotheses of both disputed assertions are satisfied. No finite simulation or conjectural complexity lower bound is being substituted for proof.
# Proof diagnosis, impact, and repair boundary

In the original proof of Lemma 6.5, p. 2209 (PDF p. 13), a refined Polish topology \(t\) makes the left \(H\)-action continuous and certain sets \(U_n\) closed. The map \(x\mapsto(U_nx)_n\) is then treated as taking values in the hyperspace of \(t\)-closed sets. The stated properties do not establish that the right translates \(U_nx\) are \(t\)-closed for arbitrary \(x\in G\). The subsequent calculation of inverse images of hit sets addresses measurability and does not supply this missing closed-valuedness. The author’s diagnosis on corrigendum pp. 8–9 agrees with this reading. Requiring joint continuity of the right action of the original group would force the refinement to be the original topology by the orbit map at the identity; that condition cannot simply be inserted.

The supported severity is Major: an asserted equivalence between two complexity invariants is false, and its central proof lemma is invalid. Theorem 3.3 explicitly invokes Lemma 6.5. Lemmas 6.7 and 6.8 on p. 2210 also invoke it in the classification argument. This dependency does not mean that every dependent conclusion is false.

For this criterion, the verified repair is to replace \(D(\Pi^0_2)\) by \(\Sigma^0_2\) in Theorem 3.3(2). The example does not refute the separate subgroup conclusion \(H\in D(\Pi^0_2)\) of Lemma 6.5: our example satisfies it. The author refutes that separate unrestricted conclusion using a different operator construction, and gives the valid \(\Delta^0_3\) restriction. The restricted proof and the distinction between Lemmas 6.7 and 6.8 were read; the later operator constructions were not completely audited here.

The corrigendum also reports changes to Theorems 1.1, 1.3, 1.4, 6.1 and 10.2, while retaining the non-Archimedean list of Theorem 1.2. These are recorded as author-documented broader corrections, not additional independently established findings of this report. No blanket certification of the 35-page correction is intended.
# Conclusion

Confirmed issue | False potential-\(\Sigma^0_2\) criterion in the exact publisher version
Impact | Major; theorem-level assertion and core proof lemma
Decisive evidence | Polishable \(bv_0(\mathbb R)\in D(\Pi^0_2)\setminus\Sigma^0_2\) and a proved necessary criterion
Repair status | Criterion corrected and verified above; wider classification not fully re-proved
Author status | Existing dated corrigendum v3; no new author communication
Scientific decision | Pending; human reviews empty
# Supporting checks

The proof above is analytic; no author code or artificial finite test was run. Exact source, TeX, compiler, dependency, PDF and actual page-view bindings are retained under `verification/0232`. The acquired arXiv manuscript remains a separate source version. The bounded supplement search located the author’s corrigendum and its TeX; no dedicated computational package was identified. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect.

All new review reasoning and actual compilation/inspection were performed by this assigned web executor. The visible UI/model observation is attributed to Main; backend equivalence was not independently verified. This is an initial review, not independent acceptance.

Title: Checks on the nonround classification
in Hopf–Berger spheres
# Identity and inspected scope

The bound source is C. E. Olmos and A. Rodríguez-Vázquez, Hopf fibrations and totally geodesic submanifolds, arXiv:2302.11711v3, dated 8 December 2023, 48 pages. Its SHA-256 begins `4ed333d0d46c755a`. PDF and printed page numbers coincide. The associated journal record is DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1606 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1606), published online on 6 February 2025. The present findings concern the acquired v3 manuscript; equivalence with the journal text is not assumed.

Actual reading covers pp. 1–25, except that the classification tables on p. 12 and surrounding background were used contextually, then pp. 30–32 and pp. 44–45. Detailed checking concentrates on the metric scaling, Table 5, Lemma 4.1, the dimension implication in Corollary 4.5, and the dependency chain into Theorem 4.4. The proof of Theorem 5.7 and the final homogeneity argument were read but not fully independently re-established. Sections 5.1, 5.3, 6 and the full octonionic orbit classification were not completely audited. A programmatic full-text scope search is retained; search hits do not count as reading the corresponding full pages.
# Checks that support the nonround argument

The metric is obtained by multiplying the vertical part of the round metric tensor by \(\tau>0\) (p. 2). Thus \(\tau\) is a squared-length factor. From the radial Jacobi fields in a compact rank-one symmetric space, the vertical and horizontal squared-length factors are \(\frac14\sin^2(2t)\) and \(\sin^2t\). Their ratio is \[\frac{\sin^2(2t)}{4\sin^2t}=\cos^2t=\tau.\] The hyperbolic calculation gives \(\cosh^2t=\tau\). This agrees with (7), p. 14, and the derivation on pp. 22–23. The common length homothety is \(\sin t=\sqrt{1-\tau}\) in the compact case, and \(\sinh t=\sqrt{\tau-1}\) in the noncompact case. The round point is a limiting normalization, not a nonzero-radius member of these two formulas.

Write \(f=\dim_{\mathbb R}\mathbb F\), and let the tangent decomposition be \(\mathfrak p=\mathfrak p_1\oplus\mathfrak p_2\), with vertical dimension \(f-1\). For a unit vertical \(X\), Table 5 (p. 18) gives spectra \(\{0,1/\tau\}\) on \(\mathfrak p_1\) and \(\{\tau\}\) on \(\mathfrak p_2\), omitting zero-multiplicity entries. For a unit horizontal \(Y\), it gives \(\{\tau\}\) on \(\mathfrak p_1\) and \(\{0,1,4-3\tau\}\) on \(\mathfrak p_2\), again with the stated multiplicities. For \(\tau>0\), overlap occurs only at \(\tau=1\). In particular, \(\tau=4-3\tau\) and \(\tau=1/\tau\) have no other positive solutions.

If a totally geodesic tangent subspace contains such an \(X\) or \(Y\), it is invariant under the corresponding self-adjoint Jacobi operator. With disjoint spectra, the projections onto \(\mathfrak p_1\) and \(\mathfrak p_2\) are polynomials in that operator. They therefore preserve the subspace, proving the splitting used in Lemma 4.1 (p. 21). This is a full linear-algebra justification of that step, rather than a check on sample vectors. Also, if its dimension is at least \(f\), its intersection with \(\mathfrak p_2\) has dimension at least \(d-(f-1)>0\). This validates the dimension argument on p. 24 within the nonround domain.

The outer-normal shape eigenvalues on p. 13 are \(-2\cot(2t)\) and \(-\cot t\) in the compact case. They are distinct for \(0<t<\pi/2\); the first vanishes at \(t=\pi/4\), corresponding to \(\tau=1/2\). Hence the half-parameter boundary cannot be folded into a nondegenerate argument without a separate step. Theorem 5.7 explicitly treats that boundary on pp. 30–32. Its polynomial covariant-derivative eliminations and its converse integration step have not all been independently verified here. Curvature invariance alone is not silently substituted for the complete analytic criterion in Theorem 2.1.
# Scope clarification at the round metric

Theorem A on p. 3 explicitly assumes \(\tau\ne1\), as do Lemmas 4.1–4.2, Theorem 4.4 and Theorem 5.7. Remark 1.1 (p. 4) and the discussion on p. 14 separately identify \(\tau=1\) as round. By contrast, Theorems B and C on pp. 5–6 do not repeat this exclusion; the paragraph before them on p. 4 discusses each \(\tau>0\). A literal reading that applies their tables at \(\tau=1\) fails.

For Theorem B, take \(n=1\), \(\tau=1\), and \[S^4=S^7\cap(\mathbb R^5\times\{0\}^3)
       \ \subset\ S^7_{\mathbb H,1}.\] This is a connected, complete, embedded proper submanifold of dimension \(4\ge2\). It is totally geodesic: for \(x\) in this intersection and a unit tangent vector \(v\), the ambient geodesic \(\gamma(s)=\cos(s)x+\sin(s)v\) stays in the same linear subspace. Table 1 for \(n=1\) has only dimensions \(2\) and \(3\) among its nonempty entries; Table 2 is restricted to \(\tau<1/2\). The great \(S^4\) is absent, and no ambient congruence can change dimension.

Similarly, \[S^8=S^{15}\cap(\mathbb R^9\times\{0\}^7)
       \ \subset\ S^{15}_{\mathbb O,1}\] satisfies every explicitly written completeness and dimension hypothesis of Theorem C. It is totally geodesic by the same formula. Table 1 lists no octonionic case of dimension \(8\) (its largest listed dimension is \(7\)), and Table 3 has \(\tau<1/2\). This example is absent from that literal classification as well.

The neighboring explicit exclusions, the separately discussed round case, and the spectral collision at \(\tau=1\) support the intended nonround reading. Accordingly the recorded outcome is `scope_clarification`. These examples establish the need to state that boundary accurately; they do not demonstrate an error in the nonround classification or in the exceptional projective and nonhomogeneous examples. A precise presentation is to state Theorems B and C for \(\tau>0\), \(\tau\ne1\), and give the usual round-sphere classification separately: complete connected totally geodesic images are great spheres, one congruence class per dimension. The geodesic formula proves this boundary assertion; it does not prove the remaining nonround tables.
