report: Abstract: The regularization argument controls incidence without establishing the directed extension property required of split paths. An explicit configuration for the multiplicative function \(g\equiv1\) satisfies all the properties listed in Lemma 3.4, including strong separation and a positive density of admissible prime pairs, but admits no split path of the length required in Lemma 5.4. This exposes a Major gap in the central proof chain. It is not a counterexample to Theorem 1.1. A separate exact calculation disproves the pointwise inequality (2.1); the uniform pyramid estimate can instead be obtained by propagating allocated error bounds. The review also records successful conditional checks and its version and external-dependency limits. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Directed paths and error propagation in Phase relations and pyramids
# Source and scope

The exact reviewed source is Miguel N. Walsh, Phase relations and pyramids, arXiv:2304.09792v1, submitted 19 April 2023, 14 pages, SHA-256 prefix `c30425cac6dbb2fb`. The associated journal DOI is 10.4171/jems/1613; the publisher records online publication on 6 February 2025. The frozen M25-0240/2025 identity is retained. The subscription version of record has not been compared with this preprint. All locations below refer to the printed/PDF pages of the bound preprint.

All 14 pages, including the references, were read and their page images were actually viewed. The review follows the pre-path interpolation, pyramid errors, configuration reduction, prime-product counting, regularization, long-path construction, and recovery of a global frequency. Original exact computations were executed; no author code was run. This is an initial scientific review, not an independent acceptance.
# Major: incidence regularity does not provide long split paths
## Exact location and logical distinction

Equation reference: step. On p. 6, Definition 3.6 specifies the oriented physical relation \[
 x_{i+1}=\frac{q_i}{p_i}x_i+O(H/K).\] A path is split only when every \(p_i\) belongs to \(\mathcal P_1\) and every \(q_i\) belongs to \(\mathcal P_2\). These sets are disjoint and are fixed in Notation 3.5 on p. 5. Reversing a path, as in Notation 3.7, interchanges the two prime roles. A reversed split path is generally not split.

Definition 3.8 and the deletion argument in Lemma 3.9, pp. 6–7, use connection to other vertices. The deletion estimate subtracting twice the small degree is an incidence-degree argument. In the first paragraph of the proof of Lemma 5.4, p. 10, this is used to infer many split paths of length \(k_0+2\) with a prescribed initial vertex. Incidence degree alone does not imply this directed extension property.
The following construction verifies the obstruction within the paper’s actual numerical and multiplicative-function assumptions. It is not merely an abstract directed-graph example.
## An admissible configuration

Equation reference: scales. Fix \(\eta=1/2\) and \(0<\rho<1\). Choose \(0<\delta<1/10\) and then a fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) as small as required in Lemmas 3.4 and 5.4, also with \(\varepsilon<1/100\). For arbitrarily large \(X\), set \[
 H=X^{1/2},\qquad P=H^{\varepsilon/3},\qquad
 P'=H^{\varepsilon/4},\qquad K=PP'=H^{7\varepsilon/12},
 \qquad R=H/K.\] Thus \(K\in[H^{\varepsilon^2},H^\varepsilon]\) and \(P,P'\ge H^{\varepsilon^2}\). The intervals \([P',2P']\) and \([P,2P]\) are disjoint for sufficiently large \(X\). The lower bound on \(H\) in Theorem 1.1 and Lemma 5.4 holds for every fixed required \(C\) once \(X\) is large enough.

Let \(g(n)=1\) for every positive integer \(n\). This is a 1-bounded multiplicative function, and (1.1) holds by taking \(\alpha=0\). Put \(S=500\) and define \[\mathcal J=\left\{(SRj,0):
    j\in\mathbb Z,\quad \frac{X}{10K}\le SRj\le\frac{2X}{K}\right\}.\] The first coordinates are \(500R\)-separated, with \(|\mathcal J|\asymp X/H\). For any sufficiently small fixed \(c_0\), this is a \((c_0,R)\)-configuration in the interval required in Lemma 3.4. Every associated length-\(R\) sum of \(g(n)e(0n)\) has size \(R+O(1)\), so the local correlation requirement holds.

Equation reference: classes. Take the prime classes \[
 \mathcal P_1=\{p\text{ prime}:P\le p\le 11P/10\},\qquad
 \mathcal P_2=\{q\text{ prime}:19P/10\le q\le2P\}.\] The prime number theorem gives \(|\mathcal P_1|,|\mathcal P_2|\asymp P/\log P\). They are disjoint, as required.

For each \(p\in\mathcal P_1\), \(q\in\mathcal P_2\), consider integers \[\frac{X}{10SH}\le j\le\frac{X}{2SH}.\] There are \(\asymp X/H\) such \(j\), and their number divided by \(p\) tends to infinity. In a complete block of \(p\) consecutive integers, the residues \(qj\bmod p\) run through all residues because \(p\ne q\). A fixed positive proportion therefore satisfy \[\operatorname{dist}(qj/p,\mathbb Z)\le 1/100.\] Consequently, \(\gg X/H\) of the indicated \(j\) have this property, uniformly in \(p,q\). Choose the nearest integer \(\ell\) to \(qj/p\), and set \(x=SRj\), \(y=SR\ell\). Both vertices lie in the displayed interval defining \(\mathcal J\) for large \(X\), and \[|y-(q/p)x|\le5R,\qquad
 |x/p-y/q|\le\frac{5R}{q}\le\frac{5H}{PK}.\] All phases are zero, so \(\|p\alpha_x-q\alpha_y\|_{p'}=0\) for every prime \(p'\in[P',2P']\). Hence this construction supplies \[\gg \frac XH\left(\frac P{\log P}\right)^2\] admissible ordered quadruples, each valid for \(\gg P'/\log P'\) auxiliary primes. It satisfies every property stated in Lemma 3.4, including its final restriction to \(\mathcal P_1\times\mathcal P_2\). It even retains the stronger separation used in the cited construction. For each edge the zero phases and zero intermediate phase give a pre-path with any positive permitted error bounds. Auxiliary prime products do not share primes with the path parameters.
## No required split path exists

Let \(M\) be any fixed constant implicit in the error in [step] (#step). Every split step for these data obeys \[x_{i+1}\ge \frac{19}{11}x_i-MR.\] Since \(x_i\ge X/(10K)\), \[\frac{MR}{x_i}\le 10M\frac HX\longrightarrow0.\] For large \(X\), every split step therefore satisfies \(x_{i+1}\ge(3/2)x_i\). Yet the ratio of the largest allowed first coordinate to the smallest is at most \(20\), whereas \[(3/2)^8=\frac{6561}{256}>20.\] Thus there is no split path of length \(8\) or greater, for any modulus. The requirement that all path primes be distinct can only reduce this set of paths.

On the other hand, for the paper’s fixed constant \(B\), \[\frac{\log(X/(HB\log X))}{2\log(2P)}
       \longrightarrow \frac{3}{2\varepsilon}.\] Our fixed small \(\varepsilon\) makes \(k_0+2>7\) for all sufficiently large \(X\). No vertex pair can have even one of the split paths demanded by Lemma 5.4, much less two with disjoint prime sets. Its lower bound \(|\mathcal J_0|\ge X/H^{1+\delta}=H^{1-\delta}\) is positive and tends to infinity. The long-path conclusion is therefore false for data allowed by all the stated configuration properties.

If connected in Definition 3.8 is read as an outgoing connection, then Lemma 3.9 already fails for these data: the largest-coordinate vertex of any nonempty finite subset has no outgoing split edge. If connection means incidence in either direction, the deletion argument can produce an undirected regular core, but that core supplies no such directed paths. Neither reading justifies the inference on p. 10.
## Impact and repair boundary

Lemma 5.4 is the input to Proposition 6.1, pp. 11–12, and to the global-frequency selection on p. 13. The missing directed extension property affects the central proof of Theorems 3.2 and 1.1; the assessment is Major. The construction does not contradict Theorem 1.1: \(g\equiv1\) is itself pretentious. Nor does it disprove the existence assertion of Lemma 3.4, or rule out a better choice of prime classes. It shows that the properties explicitly retained in Notation 3.5 are insufficient for the subsequent long-path assertion and its proof.

A repair must establish an appropriate directed minimum-degree condition for a suitable choice of data, or change the path scheme and redo the counting argument. Merely reversing edges is insufficient: the fixed prime roles are used in Corollary 5.3, p. 10, to place a shared prime in both products and factor it out. Allowing arbitrary changes of orientation requires a corresponding replacement for that counting step. No complete replacement is claimed in this review.
# Minor: the pointwise inequality (2.1) is false

Equation reference: printed. On p. 4, the proof of Lemma 2.4 asserts \[
 \|q_k\alpha_1^{(k+1)}-\alpha_1^{(k)}\|_Q
 \le \frac{\|p_1\alpha_1^{(k)}-\alpha_2^{(k-1)}\|_Q}{p_1}.\] Lemma 2.2 controls an allocated upper bound for a preceding residual. It does not give this inequality in terms of the actual preceding residual.
## A direct correction

Let \(E^p_{i,j}\) and \(E^q_{i,j}\) denote allocated bounds for the edges from \(\alpha_i^{(j+1)}\) to \(\alpha_{i+1}^{(j)}\) with multiplier \(p_i\), and to \(\alpha_i^{(j)}\) with multiplier \(q_{i+j-1}\), respectively. Propagating the bounds in Lemma 2.2 gives \[E^p_{i,1}=\epsilon/q_i,\quad E^q_{i,1}=\epsilon/p_i,\qquad
 E^p_{i,j}=\frac{E^q_{i+1,j-1}}{q_{i+j-1}},\quad
 E^q_{i,j}=\frac{E^p_{i,j-1}}{p_i}.\] Alternating these recurrences down to the first row gives \[E^q_{1,j}=
 \epsilon\left(\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor(j-1)/2\rfloor+1}p_i\right)^{-1}
 \left(\prod_{i=1}^{\lceil(j-1)/2\rceil}q_{j-i}\right)^{-1},\] which is precisely the asserted uniform bound. Thus one can replace [printed] (#printed) by a proof using the allocated bounds without changing Lemma 2.4 or the estimates in Section 4. This established preservation of the result, rather than the brevity of the correction alone, supports the Minor assessment of this separate issue.
# Other checks, evidence, and limitations
The following parts of the argument were checked without an additional confirmed core defect.

- The closest-root interpolation in Lemma 2.1 and the strict hypotheses in the preceding counterexample were checked exactly. The allocated-bound recurrence was derived algebraically and verified with rational arithmetic for lengths \(1\) through \(12\).

- The physical product estimates in Lemma 4.1 and Corollary 4.2 give bounded products along an existing path and displacement \(O(kH/K)\). Together with the corrected uniform pyramid bound, the telescoping estimates in Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4 have the stated scale. They do not create paths.

- The separation of unequal rational prime products in Lemma 5.1 and the factorial multiplicity in Lemma 5.2 were checked. The cited construction supplies stronger interval separation than the abbreviated configuration definition alone; no separate uniqueness defect is charged on that basis.

- Conditional on the required paths, the losses in Lemma 5.4 have logarithmic size \(O((L/h)\log L)\), with \(L=\log X\) and \(h=\log H\), apart from small powers of \(H\). The condition \(h^2\ge C^2L\log L\), after the stipulated choices of constants, has the appropriate scale to absorb them. This check does not resolve the directional obstruction.

- In Proposition 6.1, the two disjoint prime sets make the integer difference of products nonzero. The estimates for its small denominator, for \(T_y\), and for the rational comparison modulo a large common divisor were followed. The final interval shortening and Taylor approximation were checked subject to the missing path input. On p. 13 the final two correlation displays should retain the absolute values used in their hypotheses; they are otherwise comparisons of possibly complex sums.

The original calculation script uses exact fractions and independently generated primes. It checked the full-period residue count for \(208\) pairs from the separated prime intervals \([1000,1100]\) and \([1900,2000]\), as well as every hypothesis and residual in the counterexample to (2.1). Its exit code was zero. These finite computations support the exact identities and modular argument; the proof for all sufficiently large \(X\) is the analytic construction above, not an unverified extrapolation from a finite graph.

For external dependencies, the acquired versions were Matomäki–Radziwiłł–Tao, arXiv:1812.01224v1 (4 December 2018, 52 pages), and Matomäki–Radziwiłł–Tao–Teräväinen–Ziegler, arXiv:2007.15644v3 (9 June 2022, 107 pages). Pages 23–29 of the former and 85–93 of the latter were read for the configuration, separation, uniform counting, and final reduction. Pages 95–96 of the latter were also read incidentally; this does not constitute a review of that separate paper. Actual images of the former’s pp. 26, 29 and the latter’s pp. 85, 91 were inspected. The complete supporting Matomäki–Radziwiłł short-interval theorem was not independently re-proved. These external preprints are not asserted to be identical to their published versions.

Bounded searches of arXiv, the publisher, and the author’s institutional publication page found no separate supplement, matched author code, or dedicated correction for the reviewed preprint. The arXiv record still lists only v1. The publisher’s subscription PDF was not accessed. The correction to the cited Fourier-uniformity paper, DOI 10.1007/s00222-019-00931-z, was opened and concerns an acknowledgement, not the path-direction issue. Absence of code is not treated as a mathematical defect. No claim of an exhaustive search or of equivalence with the journal version is made.
# Assessment

Major, because the directed long-path step in the main proof is not established by the stated assumptions and fails for an explicitly admissible configuration. The separate error in (2.1) has a verified local repair preserving the uniform estimate. Theorem 1.1 itself has not been disproved.

report: Abstract: This claim-focused review of Horbez and Huang’s arXiv:2206.00884v3 identifies a false adjacency criterion in Lemma 3.9. The unrestricted auxiliary vertices permit a degenerate witness for every eligible adjacent pair. An explicit example in \(\operatorname{BS}(1,2)\) verifies all hypotheses. Requiring four distinct vertices restores the lemma; a general proof of this local correction is given. The supported assessment is Major for the affected core proof step. Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: A Quantifier Defect in the Adjacency Criterion
for Higman Group Rigidity
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed work is Camille Horbez and Jingyin Huang, Measure equivalence rigidity among the Higman groups, associated with Journal of the European Mathematical Society, DOI `10.4171/jems/1614`. The actual source is the 58-page author manuscript arXiv:2206.00884v3, submitted on 30 January 2025; its title page is dated 31 January 2025 [HH, arxiv]. PDF page numbers are one-based and agree with the printed page numbers. The journal record gives publication on 8 April 2025 [EMS]. The author manuscript is described as the final accepted version, but textual equivalence to the publisher’s version has not been established. The finding below concerns only the acquired manuscript.

The examination traced the statements in Section 1, relevant Baumslag–Solitar geometry in Sections 2–3, the combinatorial rigidity argument in Section 4, and the application of Theorem 5.1 on pp. 30–31. The detailed check concerns Lemma 3.9, its prerequisites in Lemmas 3.3–3.6 and Corollary 3.7, and its use in Proposition 3.1. The non-isolation hypothesis in the Higman-group application was also checked, with a separately attributed bounded auxiliary check. The full measured-groupoid proof of Theorem 5.1, the external coupling rigidity results, and the \(W^*\) consequences were not independently reproved. This is not a certificate of whole-paper correctness.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

For nonzero integers \(m,n\), write \[\operatorname{BS}(m,n)=\langle a,t\mid ta^mt^{-1}=a^n\rangle.\] The source assumes \(|m|<|n|\) in Section 3. A standard \(a\)-line or \(t\)-line is a left coset of \(\langle a\rangle\) or \(\langle t\rangle\), respectively. The bipartite intersection graph \(\Lambda\) has these lines as vertices, with an edge when two lines intersect. Its \(a\)-type vertices correspond to vertices of the Bass–Serre tree \(T\). Positive \(t\)-edges define the orientation and partial order used below [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~16--17]{HH}]. Set \[\Lambda_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}_\Lambda(u_i)\cap\operatorname{lk}_\Lambda(u_j).\] Lemma 3.9 further requires \(m\mid n\), and \(u_1,u_2\) must be strictly comparable \(a\)-type vertices.

Equation reference: eq:nesting. Corollary 3.7 states that if \(v_a<v_b<v_c\) and \(\Lambda_{ac}\ne\varnothing\), then, in this divisible case, \[
 \Lambda_{ac}\subsetneq\Lambda_{ab},\qquad
 \Lambda_{ac}=\Lambda_{bc}.\] The distinction between strict containment and equality is essential. Lemma 3.6 uses \(h=\gcd(|m|,|n|)\), \(p=|m|/h\), and \(q=|n|/h\). For separation by \(d\) tree edges the relevant spacings are \(hp^d\) and \(hq^d\). When \(m\mid n\), \(p=1\) and \(q>1\), giving [eq:nesting] (#eq:nesting). The arithmetic argument on p. 19 was checked: the endpoint divisibility conditions imply \(h\mid s q^{d-1}\) and \(h\mid s p^{d-1}\); coprimality of \(p,q\) therefore implies \(h\mid s\). Negative parameter signs do not change these spacings.
# Substantive finding
## Exact counterexample and evaluation

Take \(m=1,n=2\). These parameters are nonzero, \(|m|<|n|\), and \(m\mid n\). Let \(u_2\) correspond to \(\langle a\rangle\) and \(u_1\) to \(t\langle a\rangle\). The lines are distinct: the height homomorphism sending \(a\) to \(0\) and \(t\) to \(1\) separates them. The \(t\)-edge from \(1\) to \(t\) projects to an oriented edge of \(T\), so \[\bar u_2<\bar u_1,\qquad d_T(\bar u_2,\bar u_1)=1.\] They satisfy the type and comparability hypotheses and are genuinely adjacent. The \(t\)-line \(\langle t\rangle\) meets both \(a\)-lines, so \(A:=\Lambda_{12}\ne\varnothing\).

Now choose \[u_3=u_1,\qquad u_4=u_2,\qquad i=2.\] These choices belong to the stated quantifier domains and give \[\Lambda_{34}=A=\Lambda_{32},\qquad A\subseteq A.\] Both [eq:w1] (#eq:w1) and [eq:w2] (#eq:w2) hold. The claimed right-hand condition, that no such witnesses exist, is false, whereas actual adjacency is true. This is an exact counterexample, not a finite sampling diagnostic.

An explicit set realization is also available. In \(\operatorname{BS}(1,2)=\mathbb Z[1/2]\rtimes\mathbb Z\) use \((r,k)(s,\ell)=(r+2^k s,k+\ell)\), \(a=(1,0)\), and \(t=(0,1)\). The \(t\)-lines are \(V_r=\{(r,j):j\in\mathbb Z\}\). The two \(a\)-lines are \(\{(z,0):z\in\mathbb Z\}\) and \(\{(2z,1):z\in\mathbb Z\}\), giving \(A=\{V_{2z}:z\in\mathbb Z\}\). The counterexample already follows from the coset definitions and does not depend on this additional realization.
## Alternative readings and source checks

The rendered source p. 21 was inspected: the first relation is \(\subseteq\), and the domain of \(u_3,u_4\) contains no exclusion of \(\{u_1,u_2\}\). This is not an OCR substitution for strict inclusion. No convention making all indexed vertices automatically distinct was found in the checked discussion or the targeted full-text search. In contrast, Lemma 3.8 on p. 20 explicitly excludes \(u_1,u_2\) from its auxiliary vertex domain.

The proof of Lemma 3.9 assumes, for adjacent \(u_2<u_1\), that the remaining positions for \(u_3\) are \(u_2<u_1<u_3\) or \(u_3<u_2<u_1\). It omits the endpoint coincidences allowed by its statement. This indicates the intended distinct-vertex interpretation, but does not make the literal quantifiers valid. The failure is systematic: the degenerate witness works for every pair with nonempty \(\Lambda_{12}\).
# A verified local correction

Proposition 1.  Retain all assumptions and both relations of Lemma 3.9. Replace the witness domain by \[u_3,u_4\in\Lambda^{(0)}\setminus\{u_1,u_2\},
 \qquad u_3\ne u_4.\] With this restriction the asserted adjacency equivalence is valid.

Proof. Assume \(u_2<u_1\). First let the corresponding tree vertices be adjacent, and suppose distinct witnesses satisfy \(\varnothing\ne A=\Lambda_{12}\subseteq\Lambda_{34}\). An element of \(A\) supplies a single \(t\)-line meeting all four \(a\)-lines, so their projections lie in a single oriented chain.

If \(u_j>u_1\), for \(j=3\) or \(4\), then [eq:nesting] (#eq:nesting) applied to \(u_2<u_1<u_j\) gives \(\Lambda_{2j}\subsetneq A\), whereas the witness inclusion gives \(A\subseteq\Lambda_{2j}\), a contradiction. No tree vertex lies strictly between adjacent endpoints, and endpoint coincidences have been excluded. Thus both \(u_3,u_4\) lie below \(u_2\).

If \(u_4<u_3<u_2<u_1\), apply [eq:nesting] (#eq:nesting) to \(u_4<u_3<u_i\), for \(i=1,2\), obtaining \(\Lambda_{3i}=\Lambda_{4i}\subsetneq\Lambda_{43}\). If \(u_3<u_4<u_2<u_1\), apply it to \(u_3<u_4<u_i\), obtaining \(\Lambda_{3i}\subsetneq\Lambda_{34}\) directly. Both orders contradict [eq:w2] (#eq:w2).

Conversely, suppose the endpoints are not adjacent. If \(A=\varnothing\), the proposed adjacency condition already fails. Otherwise choose a common \(t\)-line and vertices along it with \(u_4<u_2<u_3<u_1\). An intermediate \(u_3\) exists by non-adjacency; a lower \(u_4\) exists because the \(t\)-line extends in both directions. The four vertices are distinct. Formula [eq:nesting] (#eq:nesting) gives \[A\subsetneq\Lambda_{23}=\Lambda_{34}=\Lambda_{32}.\] These are permitted witnesses with \(i=2\), so the nonexistence condition fails as required. ◻

This is a sufficient correction throughout the original parameter domain of Lemma 3.9. It is not asserted to be minimal and does not constitute a reproof of every step in Proposition 3.1 or the main theorem.
# Dependency, impact, and conclusion

The first paragraph of the proof of Proposition 3.1 on p. 22 explicitly uses Lemma 3.9 to obtain preservation of tree adjacency when \(m\mid n\). Proposition 4.3 uses Proposition 3.1 to propagate order preservation across the interlocking Baumslag–Solitar subgroups [HH, p. 25]. Theorem 4.2 identifies the automorphism group of the intersection graph; the proof of Theorem 1.5 on p. 31 uses that identification on the route to Theorem 1.1. The affected branch includes the classical parameters \((1,2)\) and is not an unused peripheral lemma.

The supported impact is Major for the invalid core-dependent criterion as stated. The short repair does not change that dependency. The counterexample does not refute the line-preserving rigidity theorem or the main measure equivalence conclusion, and Proposition Proposition 1 (#prop:repair) restores the identified lemma. No empirical rerun is implicated. The remaining groupoid and operator-algebra arguments require their own checks before whole-proof validation could be asserted.

The consulted arXiv record still lists v3 as its latest version. A bounded search of that record and the publisher record did not locate a correction to this lemma. This is neither a first-discovery claim nor proof that no correction exists elsewhere. The finding is not attributed to the uninspected publisher full text.

# Evidence and review limits

The counterexample and repair are analytic arguments. No author code was executed and no numerical experiment substitutes for proof. Source images, actual viewing records, extracted passages, coverage, findings, compiler output, dependency inventories, and current hashes are retained in the matching verification directory. The PDF is bound to this exact TeX by separate build and page-inspection records.

Primary reasoning, report, compilation, and final image checks belong to the assigned current-conversation executor. Their actual read ranges and attribution are retained separately. This initial review is not independent acceptance.

Title: Initial scientific assessment of
A universal formula for the \(x-y\) swap in topological recursion
Authors. Alexander Alexandrov, Boris Bychkov, Petr Dunin-Barkowski, Maxim Kazarian and Sergey Shadrin.
Journal identifier. DOI `10.4171/JEMS/1615`; 2025 membership retained from the frozen assignment.

Reviewed source. arXiv:2212.00320v3, 30 July 2024, 51 pages. Page references below are both PDF and printed page numbers. The publisher’s version was not obtained for comparison; the findings are restricted to this author manuscript.
# Assessment and scope

Assessment: Minor. Two explicit formula errors occur in the Airy two-point specialization on p. 49. Both admit exact tests within the stated spectral-curve assumptions. They concern a subsidiary application; the inspected dependency chain for the universal swap theorem does not use these formulas. The classification follows this restricted mathematical impact, rather than the ease of a correction. No counterexample to Theorems 1.8 or 1.14 has been established.

The review checked the spectral-curve hypotheses, the unstable terms, the finite differential-operator formulation, and the closing pole and period argument. It also independently calculated low-order Airy correlators and tested the suspect two-point identities. The primary executor read pp. 2–4, 6–12, 38–39, 42–43 and 47–49 (the bibliography continuation on p. 49 was not a scientific target). Thirteen source pages were actually viewed as images: 2, 3, 6, 8, 10–12, 39, 42–43 and 47–49. The full Fock-space and graph-combinatorial derivations in Sections 2–4, the entire higher-loop induction, and the other enumerative examples have not been independently certified. Auxiliary checks of specified passages are recorded separately in the provenance.
# Hypotheses and positive checks

The input in Section 1.1 requires simple zeros of \(dx\), regular \(y\) there, and nonvanishing \(dy\) there. In Theorems 1.8 and 1.14, \(x\) is also regular at the simple zeros of \(dy\). Consequently \(dx\) cannot vanish at such a point: that would contradict the original input condition. Thus the disjointness used in Section 5.3 is implied by the stated setting.

The initial forms \(\omega_{1,0}^{(0)}=-y\,dx\) and \(\omega_{2,0}^{(0)}=B\) are specified separately. The extra term in (1.13) supplies \(\omega_{0,1}^{(0)}=-x\,dy\), and the two-point initial form remains \(B\) (pp. 8, 42). Stable pole statements must not be applied to this diagonal double pole. The closing argument invokes Proposition 5.3 (p. 39), the cancellation results, and the vanishing of periods via the exact differential in Lemma 5.10 (p. 43). The local exponent \(1+2(s-1)\sum r_i\) in (5.18) is nonnegative, including \(s=1\).

For \(S=\mathbb P^1\), \(x=z^2/2\), \(y=z\) and \(B=dz_1dz_2/(z_1-z_2)^2\), the only zero of \(dx\) is the simple zero \(0\); \(dy=dz\) has none. Direct use of (1.1), with involution \(z\mapsto-z\), gives \[\omega_{3,0}^{(0)}=\frac{dz_1dz_2dz_3}{z_1^2z_2^2z_3^2},
 \qquad
 \omega_{1,0}^{(1)}=\frac{dz}{8z^4}.\] These agree with the checked terms of (7.6), (7.10), (7.12) and (7.17). On the swapped side all stable correlators vanish because there are no recursion points. These tests are consistency checks, not a proof of the universal formula.
# Finding F1: incorrect differentials in (7.20)
# Finding F2: repeated operator index in (7.19) and (7.21)

Location and status. The second line of (7.19), and (7.21), p. 49, print \((D_1^3+D_1^3)^i\). The exponential in the preceding line depends on \(w_1^3+w_2^3\), so coefficient extraction instead gives \((D_1^3+D_2^3)^i\).

Here is a test at genus one. Write \(F=(z_1-z_2)^{-2}\) and \(G=(z_1-z_2)^{-4}\), suppressing \(dz_1dz_2\) while letting the operators act on its coefficient as above. The corrected expression is \[C=\frac{D_1^3+D_2^3}{24}F+\frac{(D_1+D_2)^2}{4}G
 =\frac{5}{8z_1^6z_2^2}+
   \frac{3}{8z_1^4z_2^4}+\frac{5}{8z_1^2z_2^6}.\] It agrees with a direct residue evaluation of (1.1) using the low-order forms above. At \((1,2)\) it equals \(97/512\). The printed second line, with \(2D_1^3\) in its first term, instead gives \(-13/64\), differing by \(-201/512\). This computation also exposes the loss of symmetry in the two variables.

Counter-evidence considered. The preceding exponential and the symmetric polynomial \((u_1^3+u_2^3)^i\) in (7.22) indicate the intended index. They support an index correction, but cannot make the printed line true. Correcting the repeated index in both occurrences removes this particular discrepancy. The \(k=0\) term in the later rewriting with \((D_1+D_2)^{k-1}\) requires its intended cancellation or primitive interpretation; this review does not elevate that presentation issue to a further confirmed defect.
# Impact, limitations and disposition

The dependence proceeds from the universal formula (1.13) to the unramified-\(y\) graph formula (7.9), then to the Airy examples. The two incorrect displayed identities occur at the last stage. They invalidate those literal computational lines and should be corrected before relying on them as written. The initial forms, the low-order residue tests, and the symmetric expression (7.22) provide positive counter-evidence against extending this finding to the main swap theorem.

The source manifest’s bounded supplementary-material and code search was retained; no paper-specific code was obtained or executed. Code absence is not a mathematical defect. The arXiv version history and the official publisher page were checked; no equivalence with the journal PDF is asserted. A bounded correction search found no relevant notice, which does not establish that no correction exists.

This is an initial scientific assessment. The scientific decision and adjudication remain pending; no human reviews or independent acceptance are claimed. The actual computations, source-page receipts, current compilation inputs, dependencies, logs and report-page checks are bound in the accompanying evidence.

Title: Initial scientific assessment of
Local transfer for quasi-split classical groups and congruences mod \(\ell\)
Authors. Alberto Mínguez and Vincent Sécherre, with an appendix by Guy Henniart.
Primary source. Journal of the European Mathematical Society 27 (2025), 5173–5234; DOI `10.4171/JEMS/1616`, acquired journal PDF, 62 pages.
Associated correction. Guy Henniart, Alberto Mínguez and Vincent Sécherre, JEMS 27 (2025), 5235–5238; DOI `10.4171/JEMS/1690`, acquired complete four-page PDF.
A separate 58-page arXiv:2302.04532v2 manuscript is retained; it is not substituted for either published source.
# Assessment

Assessment: Major. The known error in Proposition B.1 has a published repair for the relevant orthogonal construction. A separate obstruction remains in the printed Lemma 9.1 for symplectic groups at the allowed coefficient prime \(\ell=2\): no auxiliary place satisfying its conditions can exist. This invalidates the stated auxiliary lemma and its use in that part of the main proof. No counterexample to the conclusion of Theorem 1.1 is claimed.
Finding | Mathematical impact | Acquired correction
F1: split even orthogonal, level zero | Core auxiliary construction | Repair checked
F2: symplectic, \(\ell=2\) | Core auxiliary existence | Not addressed

Both findings are Major because their assertions are used to produce the cuspidal global transfer on which the main proof relies. Repairability alone is not the basis for a lower classification. F1 is expressly recorded as a known, reproduced issue; F2 is a bounded finding in the acquired sources, without a claim of priority.

Theorem 1.1 assumes odd residual characteristic \(p\), a prime \(\ell\ne p\), and integral irreducible cuspidal representations with \(r_\ell(\pi_1)\le r_\ell(\pi_2)\). It concludes integrality of the transfers, agreement of supercuspidal supports, and a unique common generic component except for split \(\operatorname{SO}_2\) (journal p. 5174, PDF p. 2). The distinction between these conclusions and equality of the entire reductions is maintained throughout this assessment.
# F2: an impossible auxiliary place at \(\ell=2\)
## Exact location and counterexample

Lemma 9.1, journal p. 5217 (PDF p. 45), requires a finite place \(u
e w\) with \(u
mid\ell\) and a unitary cuspidal representation of \(\mathbf G(k_u)\) whose standard transfer is cuspidal. Its symplectic proof chooses \(k_u\simeq\mathbb Q_2\) and invokes Theorem C.1. The condition \(u
mid\ell\) is also imposed in Section 3.4, p. 5188 (PDF p. 16), and at the start of Section 4, p. 5193 (PDF p. 21). Thus it is not merely an isolated phrase in Lemma 9.1.

Take the allowed data \[F=\mathbb Q_3,\qquad G=\operatorname{Sp}_2(F),\qquad \ell=2.\] For any globalization of the prescribed kind, every permitted \(u\nmid2\) has odd residue characteristic and \(\mathbf G(k_u)\) is a split symplectic group. A cuspidal standard transfer would require an irreducible orthogonal three-dimensional Weil representation. None exists. Consequently the existential assertion of Lemma 9.1 is false for these data, regardless of which permitted \(u\) is tried. The same argument applies to \(\operatorname{Sp}_{2n}\) for every \(n\ge1\), whose standard representation has dimension \(2n+1\).
This is a counterexample to the auxiliary existence statement. It does not purport to exhibit two original representations violating the congruence conclusion of Theorem 1.1.
## Proof of the local obstruction

Let \(E\) have odd residue characteristic \(r\), and suppose \(V\) is an irreducible self-dual smooth complex representation of \(W_E\) of odd dimension \(d>1\). The image \(H\) of wild inertia is a finite \(r\)-group. Clifford theory decomposes \(V|_H\) into equally repeated irreducible constituents forming one orbit. Since \(d\) is odd, this orbit has odd size. Duality permutes it by an involution, so one constituent is self-dual.

A finite group of odd order has no nontrivial self-dual irreducible complex representation. Indeed, for a nontrivial irreducible character \(\chi\), the Frobenius–Schur indicator is \[\frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{h\in H}\chi(h^2)
 =\frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{h\in H}\chi(h)=0,\] because squaring permutes \(H\); a self-dual irreducible constituent would have indicator \(1\) or \(-1\). Hence that constituent is trivial, and orbit transitivity makes wild inertia trivial on all of \(V\).

The remaining inertia characters are tame and form one Frobenius orbit of odd size. Inversion preserves the orbit and has a fixed character, of order at most two. The residue cardinality is odd, so Frobenius fixes this character. Its orbit therefore has size one. Inertia acts by scalars; a Frobenius eigenline is then stable under the entire Weil group. Irreducibility forces \(d=1\), a contradiction.

For a cuspidal \(\operatorname{GL}_{2n+1}\) transfer the Weil parameter is irreducible, with trivial \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) factor; the dual group \(\operatorname{SO}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)\) supplies self-duality. This is exactly the impossible case above. The paper itself states the corresponding local obstruction in Section 1.6, p. 5178 (PDF p. 6). The independent proof makes the limiting example explicit.
## Counter-evidence and repair boundary

Theorem C.1 does supply the needed representation over \(\mathbb Q_2\) (journal p. 5225, PDF p. 53). This is useful counter-evidence against a claim that the auxiliary representation never exists. However, at \(\ell=2\) that place divides \(\ell\), so it is outside the setup of Theorems 3.1 and 4.4. The official corrigendum repairs the orthogonal branch and does not alter this symplectic condition.

The use is direct: p. 5218 (PDF p. 46) chooses \((u,\rho)\) from Lemma 9.1, applies Theorem 4.4, obtains cuspidal global transfers, and invokes Theorem 8.2 at \(w\). Theorem 4.4 on pp. 5195–5196 (PDF pp. 23–24) inherits the setup at p. 5193, and applies the Section 3 lifting argument. In particular, Section 3.6, p. 5190 (PDF p. 18), requires integral type lattices and a reduction isomorphism of the form \[\operatorname{Hom}_K(L_\Lambda,\operatorname{Alg}_{\overline{\mathbb Z}_\ell})
 \otimes\overline{\mathbb F}_\ell
 \simeq
 \operatorname{Hom}_K(\overline\Lambda,\operatorname{Alg}_{\overline{\mathbb F}_\ell}).\] Its cited hypotheses must be revalidated if the auxiliary place is allowed to divide \(\ell\).

One repair is to restrict the symplectic coefficient-prime range to odd \(\ell\); this narrows the published statement. To retain \(\ell=2\), a suitable simultaneous globalization at an auxiliary \(u\mid\ell\), or another argument, must be proved. Merely deleting \(u\nmid\ell\) and enlarging the exceptional set \(S\) does not establish that extension. The later Galois step applies at the target \(w\nmid\ell\), which remains true here; the outstanding obligation is the prescribed-type lifting step, not an automatic failure of every later argument. This review has not proved or disproved such an extension.
# F1: the known split even orthogonal error and its correction
## Original assertion and an explicit obstruction

Proposition B.1, journal p. 5224 (PDF p. 52), asserts the existence of a level-zero cuspidal representation with cuspidal transfer for the split orthogonal groups specified on p. 5223. The corrigendum expressly rejects this assertion for split \(\operatorname{SO}_{2n}\), \(n\ge2\), and identifies the error in the Lemma B.2 construction.

Here is a concrete instance. Let \(F=\mathbb Q_3\) and \(G=\operatorname{SO}_4\) split. In the level-zero setting, a cuspidal transfer would give a tame irreducible orthogonal Weil parameter of dimension four with determinant one. More generally, consider a self-dual tame irreducible parameter of dimension \(2n\). In a Frobenius-cycle basis \(e_0,\ldots,e_{2n-1}\), write \(\Phi^{2n}=cI\). The distinct inertia characters pair with their inverses at opposite positions. For an invariant \(\varepsilon\)-symmetric nondegenerate form, \[B(e_0,e_n)
 =B(\Phi^ne_0,\Phi^ne_n)
 =B(e_n,ce_0)
 =c\varepsilon B(e_0,e_n).\] Thus \(c=\varepsilon\) and \(\det\Phi=(-1)^{2n-1}c=-\varepsilon\). In the orthogonal case \(\varepsilon=1\), so \(\det\Phi=-1\); inertia has determinant one by reciprocal pairing. The determinant is the nontrivial unramified quadratic character, incompatible with the split even orthogonal parameter. This reproduces the obstruction described in the corrigendum.

The primary executor also checked a finite parameter illustrating the invalid placement in Section B.3: \[P(T)=\Phi_{10}(T)=T^4-T^3+T^2-T+1
 \quad\text{over }\mathbb F_3.\] The powers of \(3\) modulo \(10\) are \(1,3,9,7\), a full orbit, and \(3^2\equiv-1\). Hence \(P\) is irreducible and reciprocal and its roots have order ten. But \(|\operatorname{SO}_4^+(3)|=3^2(3^2-1)^2=576\), which is not divisible by five. Such a parameter cannot lie in that split finite orthogonal group. Exact polynomial, matrix, pairing and determinant checks are retained in the evidence. This is a failure of the claimed parameter placement; it is not misrepresented as a counterexample to a Lusztig-series assertion after assuming an unavailable membership hypothesis.
## What the acquired corrigendum actually repairs

Corrigendum Proposition 1.1, p. 5236 (PDF p. 2), replaces the false range by split odd orthogonal groups and unramified, non-split, quasi-split even orthogonal groups. Its parity and determinant calculation matches the obstruction above.

The character-existence step can be checked explicitly. For the unramified extension \(L/F\) of degree \(2n\), choose a residue character of order \(q^n+1\). Its Frobenius orbit has length \(2n\): for \(0<j<n\), \(q^j-1<q^n+1\); for \(j=n+r<2n\), \(q^j\equiv-q^r\) and \(q^r+1<q^n+1\). Also \(\chi^{q^n}=\chi^{-1}\) and the character is trivial on the residue units of the degree-\(n\) subfield. Choosing its uniformizer value to be \(1\) or \(-1\), with the corrigendum’s unramified quadratic twist before induction, produces the two required parities. The orthogonal choice has the nontrivial unramified quadratic determinant required by the non-split form.

The original Lemma 9.1 chooses a split auxiliary orthogonal completion and calls B.1. Corrigendum Section 1.4 and Lemma 1.2, pp. 5237–5238 (PDF pp. 3–4), instead choose the global discriminant so that an auxiliary \(u\nmid2\ell\) has a non-split unramified even orthogonal completion. Proposition 2.4 and Theorem 2.8 (journal pp. 5181, 5183; PDF pp. 9, 11) allow the discriminant and, where needed, Hasse invariant to retain the prescribed local form at \(w\) while keeping real compactness and finite quasi-splitness.

This verifies the relevant repair of the orthogonal dependency. It changes the choice of global data; it does not assert that every previously fixed global model in the wording of Proposition 1.2 is left intact. The main construction needs an appropriately chosen globalization. The corrected orthogonal branch does not dispose of F2, which concerns a different family and coefficient prime.
# Coverage and disposition

All three actual input PDFs were parsed and bound to their current sizes and hashes. The primary scientific text reading covered journal PDF pp. 1–9, 11, 16–19, 21–26, 43–46, 48–49 and 51–53, and all four corrigendum pages. Twenty-one journal pages and all four corrigendum pages were actually inspected as images; the exact lists and image hashes are in the page-inspection receipt. Their roles, model self-reports and limits are separately recorded.

The split \(\operatorname{SO}_2\) exception was checked against Section 9.3: its transfer can be nongeneric, so it cannot be silently folded into conclusion (3). The reduction-support conclusion is not replaced by an assertion of equality of complete reductions. The lengthy local and global Langlands results, all modular representation arguments, and the complete Appendix C proof have not been independently re-proved. Nor has the equal-residue-characteristic extension of the type-lifting argument been certified.

The report is an initial scientific assessment. The scientific decision and adjudication remain pending, with `human_reviews=[]`; no independent acceptance is asserted. The source manifest, English TeX, actual compiled PDF, proof and calculation records, current dependency and log hashes, and actual page checks accompany this report.

Title: Initial scientific review of
Compressed sensing for inverse problems and the sample complexity of the sparse Radon transform
Article. Giovanni S. Alberti, Alessandro Felisi, Matteo Santacesaria, and S. Ivan Trapasso. Journal identifier: 10.4171/JEMS/1617.

Version actually examined. The 57-page author manuscript `arXiv:2302.03577v2`, submitted 3 May 2024, with PDF date 6 May 2024. Page references below are its PDF and printed page numbers, which coincide. The journal record belongs to the frozen 2025 batch; this does not change the date of the acquired manuscript. Equality with the journal version has not been established.
# Scope and evidence

The review checked the definitions, quantifiers, operator normalizations, weighted sparsity, restricted isometry to null-space reduction, truncation estimates, quasi-diagonalization, and the Radon specialization. Root read manuscript text on pp. 1–7 and 12–45, and inspected the actual images of all pages used as evidence. The exact image list and hashes are recorded separately. The complete PDF was parsed, but Appendix A’s concentration and entropy proof has not been independently audited in full. External wavelet and Sobolev results remain dependencies.
Their roles and self-reported model labels are retained in the provenance, separately from the controller’s UI observation. This is an initial review, not an independent acceptance.
# F1. Truncation constants and feasibility: Major
## A counterexample to Proposition 5.8, second branch

On p. 34, condition (30) is \[m\ge \left\lVert G_1^{-1}\right\rVert^2\left\lVert G_2^{-1}\right\rVert^2\left\lVert G_2\right\rVert^2
       \log(1/\gamma).\] For the second branch, only \(\left\lVert G_1^{-1}\right\rVert\ge c\) is required. The conclusion claims a constant \(C_1\) depending only on \(C_F,c\): \[\left\lVert G_2^{-1}\right\rVert\left\lVert QAP_\Lambda^\perp x^\dagger\right\rVert
 \le C_1c_\nu^{-1/2}
 \bigl(\left\lVert F\Phi^*\iota_{\Gamma\setminus\Lambda}\right\rVert\left\lVert G_2^{-1}\right\rVert+1\bigr)r.
\tag{F1.1}\] Let \(H_1=\mathbb C^2\), \(H_2=\mathbb C\), \(\Phi=I\), \(\Lambda=\{1\}\), and \(D=\{0,1\}\). Give \(\mu=\nu\) mass \(\eta\) at \(1\), where \(0<\eta<1\), and define \[F_t(x_1,x_2)=x_1+t x_2.\] All relevant assumptions hold: \(f_\nu=c_\nu=1\), \(Q=I\), \(B=\omega_i=1\), \(\sup_t\left\lVert F_t\right\rVert\le\sqrt2\), \(\left\lVert F\right\rVert\le\sqrt2\), and the actual retained matrix is \(G=1\). Set \(x^\dagger=e_2\), \(r=1\), \(\beta=0\), and \[G_1=1,\qquad G_2=\sqrt\eta,\qquad c=1,\qquad
\gamma=\eta/2.\] The tail operator norm is \(\sqrt\eta\). Take \(m=\lceil L\log(2/\eta)\rceil\) for any fixed sufficiently large \(L\ge1\). This satisfies (30), and can also satisfy the sample condition of Theorem 3.5 if that condition is included in the phrase setting of Theorem 3.5.

For \(N=\sum_{k=1}^m t_k\), one has \(N\sim\operatorname{Bin}(m,\eta)\) and \(\left\lVert QAP_\Lambda^\perp x^\dagger\right\rVert=\sqrt{N/m}\). Thus (F1.1) is equivalent to \[\sqrt{N/m}\le 2C_1\sqrt\eta.
\tag{F1.2}\] For any fixed candidate \(C_1=C_1(\sqrt2,1)\), choose \(\eta\) so small that \(4C_1^2m\eta<1\). This is possible since \(m\eta\to0\). Every event \(N\ge1\) violates (F1.2), yet \[\Pr(N\ge1)=1-(1-\eta)^m\ge\eta>\gamma.\] Consequently no constant with the stated dependence exists.

For numerical corroboration, \(\eta=2^{-20}\) and \(m=21\) give \(\gamma=4.76837158203125\cdot10^{-7}\) and \(\Pr(N\ge1)=2.002696965179746\cdot10^{-5}\). This instance defeats \(C_1<111.72756\); the family above, rather than that one numerical threshold, rules out every finite uniform constant.
## Exact failure and repair boundary

Theorem 3.11 invokes the second branch with \(G_1=GD\) and \(G_2=GW^\zeta\) on p. 40. There are further, independently checkable issues in that application. Page 39 extends \(W\) by \(1\) outside \(\Lambda_{j_0}\), while p. 40 asserts \[\left\lVert P_{\Lambda_{j_0}}^\perp W^{-\zeta}x^\dagger\right\rVert
 \le 2^{-\zeta bj_0}r.\] A unit tail vector has left side \(1\) under that extension, so this inequality fails when \(r=1\), \(\zeta bj_0>0\). Also, bounding \(\left\lVert F\widetilde W^\zeta\right\rVert\) does not bound \(\sup_t\left\lVert F_t\widetilde W^\zeta\right\rVert\), which is required by the truncation argument.

This disproves the high-probability feasibility step, not an error inequality conditional on an existing minimizer. It does not by itself disprove the particular Radon instance. Repair requires suitable pointwise tail control or altered sample/tolerance hypotheses, in addition to a corrected Proposition 5.8. The issue is Major because it breaks an actual proof dependency and the proposed reconstruction program.
# F2. The numerical truncation tolerance in the rate theorems: Major

Theorem 3.11 (p. 20) allows a supplied \(r\) with \(\left\lVert P_{\Lambda_{j_0}}^\perp x^\dagger\right\rVert\le r\). Program (12), p. 22, uses the numerical radius \(\beta+C_3 2^{-bj_0}r\). Theorem 3.17 (pp. 23–24) adds the existence of a sharper tail bound \(C2^{-aj}\) but does not prescribe replacing \(r\) in that program. A smaller available bound does not change an estimator already defined using a larger one.

Here is a deterministic counterexample to the literal inherited quantifiers. Let \(D\) be a singleton of probability one and \(H_1=H_2=\ell^2(\Gamma)\), with \(\Gamma=\{(j,n):j\ge0,\ 1\le n\le2^j\}\). Set \(\Phi=I\) and \[F_t=A,\qquad Ae_{j,n}=2^{-j}e_{j,n}.\] Choose \(b=d=1\), \(d_{j,n}=2^j\), \(B=\omega_{j,n}=f_\nu=c_\nu=1\). Quasi-diagonalization is exact, \(C_F=1\), and \(|\Lambda_j|=2^{j+1}-1\le2\,2^j\). The signal \(x^\dagger=e_{0,1}\) satisfies the added assumptions with \(a=2\), \(p=1\), \(c=1\), \(C=2\). All its tails and best \(s\)-term errors for \(s\ge1\) are zero. Nevertheless \(r=1\) is permitted. Use exact data; it satisfies the noise bound for every \(\beta>0\).

At scale \(J\), (12) reduces to \[\min\left\lVert x\right\rVert_1\quad\hbox{subject to}\quad
\left\lVert Ax-e_{0,1}\right\rVert_2\le\eta_J,\qquad
\eta_J=\beta+C_3 2^{-J}.\] For \(0<\eta_J<1\) the unique minimizer is \((1-\eta_J)e_{0,1}\). The first coordinate of the constraint forces \(|x_{0,1}|\ge1-\eta_J\); equality in the objective forces every other coordinate to vanish. Hence the error is exactly \(\eta_J\), independently of \(m\).

With dyadic logarithms, take \(\beta_J=2^{-3J}\), so \(j_0=J\). The prescribed sample scale is \(m\asymp\beta_J^{-4/3}\log^4(1/\beta_J)\), or one may take larger \(m\). The asserted rate is \(O(2^{-2J})\), whereas the actual error is at least \(C_3 2^{-J}\). No fixed constant reconciles them. For natural logarithms, take \(\beta_J=e^{-3J}\) instead: the asserted rate is \(O(e^{-2J})\), and the same lower bound still contradicts it. The objection therefore does not depend on choosing between these conventional logarithm bases.

The same problem occurs in Theorem 4.6 (p. 28), which inherits (16) from pp. 26–27. For a correctly constructed orthonormal wavelet basis, choose a normalized atom \(\phi_i\) supported strictly inside \(B_1\), and set \(u^\dagger=\phi_i\), \(a=p=1\), \(r=1\). A fixed \(C\) gives the required tail bounds at all scales. Let \(B_0=\sup_\theta\left\lVert F_\theta\phi_i\right\rVert>0\) and \[\delta=\frac{\beta+C_3 2^{-J/2}}{2B_0}<1.\] The competitor \((1-\delta)\phi_i\) is feasible for every angle sample set. Every minimizer has \(\ell^1\) coefficient norm at most \(1-\delta\), so its \(i\)th coefficient differs from \(1\) by at least \(\delta\). Its error is therefore at least \(\delta\). For dyadic \(\beta_J=2^{-3J/2}\), the claimed large-\(m\) rate is \(O(2^{-J})\), while this lower bound is of order \(2^{-J/2}\).
#### Counterevidence and repair.

The proof on p. 41 clearly uses \(r\) of order \(2^{-aj_0}\). Explicitly prescribing that numerical value in the program, or requiring the supplied \(r\) to satisfy that bound, removes these counterexamples. The earlier estimates retaining \(+r\) are not contradicted. The defect is Major because the stated rates fail for an admissible estimator under the inherited quantifier, even with exact data and arbitrarily many samples.

There is a separate algebraic discrepancy in the same rate statements. Page 41 gives \(\widetilde m\gtrsim m/\log^4(1/\beta)\) and an error term proportional to \(\widetilde m^{-p}\). Substitution yields \(\log^{4p}(1/\beta)\), whereas pp. 24 and 28 print \(\log^{4/p}(1/\beta)\). For \(p\le1\) the printed factor is no smaller; for \(p>1\) the stronger printed factor is not obtained by this proof. No estimator lower bound disproving that stronger logarithmic rate has been established here. The consistent correction is \(4p\), or a new proof is needed. The counterexamples above use \(p=1\) and are independent of this discrepancy.
# Further confirmed local issues
## F3. Wavelet scale indices: Minor

Page 12 defines \(\mathbb N\) as the positive integers. Page 25 defines \(\psi_{j,n}=D^1_{j-1}\tau_n\psi\) only for \(j\ge1\). The tensor prototypes on p. 26 use the undefined \(\psi_{0,n}\) and then apply \(D_j^2\).

Extending the preceding formula to zero does not repair the construction. For the regular compact orthonormal multiresolution system intended there, write \(\psi(t)=\sqrt2\sum_k g_k\chi(2t-k)\). That extension gives \[\psi_{0,m}(t)=\sum_k g_k\chi(t-2m-k).\] Some \(g_k\ne0\), hence \(\langle \chi_k,\psi_{0,0}\rangle\ne0\). The printed type-1 and type-3 tensors \(D_j^2(\psi_{0,0}\otimes\chi_k)\) and \(D_j^2(\psi_{0,0}\otimes\psi_{0,0})\) have nonzero inner product, despite both having norm one. For large \(j\), their compact supports lie in \(B_1\). This uses the regular refinement identity, not an inadmissible Haar substitution.

Use prototypes \(\tau_n\psi=\psi_{1,n}\) and dilations \(D_{j-1}^2\) for \(j\ge1\), keeping scaling atoms at level zero. The Minor classification reflects that the abstract hypothesis remains orthonormality, supplied by the standard corrected construction; it does not treat every locally repairable core defect as Minor.
## F4. Support area in Lemma 4.2: Minor

On p. 25, the uniform fixed-angle operator bound is said to depend only on \(|K|\). Under the usual area meaning this is false. Take \[K_L=[0,L]\times[0,L^{-1}],\qquad u_L=\mathbf1_{K_L}.\] Then \(|K_L|=\left\lVert u_L\right\rVert_2=1\), but \(R_{\pi/2}u_L=L\mathbf1_{[0,L^{-1}]}\) and \(\left\lVert R_{\pi/2}u_L\right\rVert_2=\sqrt L\). A maximal chord length, or \(\operatorname{diam}(K)\), supplies the bound by Cauchy–Schwarz. If diameter was intended by \(|K|\), that notation needs a definition. The application fixes its compact support through the wavelet basis, so this example does not refute its boundedness.
## F5. Fan-beam Jacobian: Minor

The calculation on p. 43 inserts \(t\) and \(1/t\) into an integral over \(t\in\mathbb R\). For \(x=\rho e_\theta+t e_{\theta+\alpha}\in B_d\), \(\rho>d\), and \(|\alpha|<\pi/2\), one has \(t=(x\cdot e_\theta-\rho)/\cos\alpha<0\). The Jacobian is \(|t|\); for a normalized atom the displayed integral with weight \(t\) equals \(-1\), not \(1\). The corrected proof is \[\left\lVert D_\theta\phi_{j,n}\right\rVert_2^2
\le C2^{-j}\int|\phi_{j,n}|^2\,dt\,d\alpha
\le \frac{C2^{-j}}{\rho-d}
       \int|\phi_{j,n}|^2|t|\,dt\,d\alpha
=\frac{C2^{-j}}{\rho-d}.\] Thus the stated coherence scale is unchanged. The defect is the displayed sign step, not the resulting bound.
## F6. One parameter display in Theorem 3.5’s proof: Minor

Page 36 prints \(\lambda=C_0\left\lVert G^{-1}\right\rVert^2\left\lVert G\right\rVert\,s\). Theorem 5.6 on p. 32, at \(\delta=1/2\), \(\rho'=1/3\), requires \(\lambda\ge135\left\lVert G^{-1}\right\rVert^2\left\lVert G\right\rVert^2s\). For \(G=aI\) this threshold is \(135s\), whereas the former with \(C_0=135\) is \(135s/a\). The omitted square must be restored. The final \(\tau=B^2\left\lVert G^{-1}\right\rVert^4\left\lVert G\right\rVert^2s\) in Theorem 3.5 is already consistent with the corrected choice, so this display mismatch does not disprove that theorem.
# Positive checks and remaining limits

The normalization of \(A\) includes \(m^{-1/2}\), and \(Q\) removes the sampling density: \(\mathbb E[(QA)^*(QA)]=G^2\). The checked restricted-isometry to null-space parameters produce the stated norm powers in Theorem 3.5. Its fixed-signal, nonuniform nature and uniform \(r=0\) exception are acknowledged on p. 17.

For Radon data, one angle returns an entire detector function, not a scalar. Page 11 identifies the semi-discrete model and leaves detector-coordinate sampling open. The exact-recovery assertion on p. 28 requires \(r=\beta=0\) and a sparse finite expansion. For a corrected orthonormal basis, substituting \(b=1/2\) and \(d_{j,n}=2^{j/2}\) gives \(\tau\asymp2^{j_0}s\) for the unweighted program and \(\tau\asymp s\) for the weighted program. These checks constrain the adverse findings.

Title: Initial scientific review of
Finite index rigidity of hyperbolic groups
Article. Nir Lazarovich. Journal identifier: 10.4171/JEMS/1618.

Version examined. The 29-page author manuscript `arXiv:2302.04484v3`, submitted 13 October 2024. PDF and printed page numbers coincide. The frozen journal record belongs to 2025; equivalence of this manuscript with the journal version has not been established.
# Scope and principal dependencies

The reviewer read all 29 pages of the acquired source text and inspected the actual images of all 26 body pages. The review traced the definitions and quantifiers, the bicombing coefficient estimates, the weighted-pattern construction, the shortening argument, the compactly supported cohomology obstruction, and the passage from complexity to index rigidity. Roles and self-reported model labels are recorded separately from the controller’s UI observation.

Theorem B is the central estimate: for a fixed locally finite one-ended hyperbolic graph \(X\) and a free cocompact action, \[\operatorname{Vol}(X/G)\asymp_X C_{2,m}(G),\qquad m=\dim(\partial X)+1.\] The upper bound constructs a bounded-diameter subcomplex of an iterated join. For the lower bound, Proposition 6.1 controls total track weight by complexity; Proposition 7.1 and Corollary 3.7 force a positive weight near each member of a packing in the quotient. Theorem C then compares complexity to subgroup index, and the normalized limit inferior gives exact multiplicativity.

The construction of Mineyev’s bicombing, the full Bestvina–Mess/Walsh boundary-cohomology inputs, the cited controlled-filling results, and Sykiotis’s reduction for groups with more than one end have not been independently reproved. The full source was parsed, but that is not a certification of every external dependency. An official publisher and manuscript-record search yielded no additional source used for this review; missing code or supplementary material is not classified as a mathematical defect.
# Confirmed issues and their limits
## F1. The definition at \(m=1\) does not support the stated general rank comparison (Minor)
Location. The definition on p. 2, the comparison with rank on p. 3, and the action-based restatement and finiteness assertion on p. 25.

The definition on p. 2 minimizes over simplicial complexes \(\overline L\) satisfying \(\pi_1(\overline L)=G\) and having \((m-1)\)-connected universal cover. If \(m=1\), such a complex is a graph, whose fundamental group is free. Take \[G=\pi_1(\Sigma_2).\] Then \(\operatorname{rank}(G)=4\), but \(H_2(G;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\), whereas a free group has zero second homology. Thus there is no admissible graph and the printed definition gives \[C_{1,1}(G)=\infty.\] This is a one-ended hyperbolic example, so the unrestricted rank comparison cannot follow merely from hyperbolicity.

For a nontrivial free group \(F_d\), the intended comparison does hold. A graph formed from \(d\) triangles sharing one vertex has \(1+2d\) vertices and \(3d\) edges, and hence \[d\le C_{1,1}(F_d)\le 1+5d\le 6d .\] At the trivial group, comparison with \(1+\operatorname{rank}(G)\) is the appropriate formulation. The action-based definition on p. 25 differs at \(m=1\): a connected complex with a free \(G\)-action need not be simply connected, and therefore need not be the universal cover of its quotient.

Impact and repair. Restrict the introductory comparison to nontrivial free groups, or define a separate action-based invariant for \(m=1\). For \(m\ge2\), the connectivity condition makes the two definitions agree. The principal estimate uses \(C_{2,m}\) with \(m\ge2\); this counterexample does not contradict that estimate.
## F2. The simplicial quotient and Cayley-action conventions need a precise model (Minor)
Location. The proof that Theorem B implies Theorem C on p. 4; the definition of a free action on p. 6 and the subdivision assertion continuing on p. 7.

There are two distinct points. First, one barycentric subdivision need not make the quotient an abstract simplicial complex. Let \(\mathbb Z\) act by translation on the integer line. The action is free on the realization. After one subdivision, the quotient has two vertices joined by two distinct edges. A simplicial complex cannot have two different edges on the same pair of vertices. A second subdivision gives a four-cycle. The same generator-loop phenomenon can occur in a one-ended torsion-free surface-group Cayley graph.

Second, vertex-freeness of an ordinary undirected Cayley action is insufficient for the geometric freeness stipulated on p. 6. Let \[G=\pi_1(\Sigma_2)\times C_2\] and include the nontrivial involution \(s\) in the generating set. The group is one-ended and hyperbolic. Left multiplication by \(s\) reverses the edge \(\{1,s\}\) and fixes its midpoint. Subdivision preserves that fixed point.

Counterevidence and repair. Neither observation is a counterexample to index rigidity. A uniform replacement gives the exact hypothesis needed on p. 4. Choose a finite genuine simplicial presentation complex \(P\) with \(\pi_1(P)=G\), and take \(X'\) to be the one-skeleton of its universal cover. The deck action is free and cocompact, \(X'/G=P^{(1)}\) is simplicial, and \(X'\) is quasi-isometric to \(G\), hence one-ended and hyperbolic. For every finite-index subgroup \(H\), \[\operatorname{Vol}(X'/H)=[G:H]\operatorname{Vol}(X'/G).\] Theorem B therefore gives precisely Theorem C, with constants depending on the fixed model. This also avoids claiming that subdivision can remove torsion fixed points. The later Rips target is expressly allowed to have a proper action; the finite-stabilizer extension of the pattern argument is discussed below.
## F3. The proof of Corollary 1.1 omits the zero-power case (Minor)
Location. Page 2, the assertion that the subgroup has index \(|k|\) for every \(k\).

Under the literal cyclic-subgroup notation, \(\langle\phi^0\rangle\) is trivial. Consequently \(F_d\rtimes\langle\phi^0\rangle=F_d\) is the kernel of the homomorphism from the mapping torus to \(\mathbb Z\), and has infinite index, not index zero. The finite-index proof applies to \(k\ne0\).

This does not supply a counterexample to the corollary in its usual nontrivial atoroidal setting. For \(d\ge2\), a nonzero-power mapping torus has Euler characteristic zero, while \(\chi(F_d)=1-d\ne0\). Thus one zero exponent and one nonzero exponent cannot give isomorphic groups; two zero exponents cause no difficulty. For nonzero opposite exponents, inverting the stable letter gives the expected isomorphism.

Repair boundary. Either specify nonzero integer exponents, or add this zero-case argument. If instead an abstract infinite cyclic factor is intended even for the identity automorphism, the notation and proof must say so; it is then the identity mapping torus \(F_d\times\mathbb Z\), not the stated index-zero subgroup.
## F4. An omitted \(m\)-skeleton reduction for the Rips target (Minor)

Location. Proposition 7.1 on p. 23 assumes that \(Y\) is \(m\)-dimensional, where \(m=\dim\partial Y+1\). Section 8 takes the full contractible Rips complex on p. 25 and applies the proposition on p. 26 to obtain (8.3).

The dimension need not agree. For a closed surface group, \(m=2\). In a Rips complex of sufficiently large radius \(d\ge3\), four consecutive vertices of a geodesic have pairwise distances at most three and span a \(3\)-simplex. The full Rips complex can therefore have dimension greater than \(m\). This is a counterexample to the required dimensional inference, not to quasi-surjectivity.

Standard target interpretation. Put \(Z=Y^{(m)}\), where \(Y\) is the full Rips complex and \(m\ge2\). The complex \(Z\) has the same one-skeleton and boundary as \(Y\), and inherits its proper cocompact action. Since \(Y\) is contractible, its \(m\)-skeleton is \((m-1)\)-connected. It has dimension \(m\). The extension from the free \(m\)-dimensional source \(L\) may be chosen cellular and equivariant, relative to the already selected geodesic edges. Its image then lies in \(Z\). Controlled relative equivariant cellular approximation in uniformly bounded simplicial stars preserves the controlled-filling inclusion (8.2), up to a constant depending only on the fixed, locally finite, finite-dimensional Rips complex. Any auxiliary subdivision is used only to construct the map and does not alter the original complexity or pattern count. Proposition 7.1 now applies with its printed hypotheses to \(Z\), and its conclusion on the common one-skeleton gives the estimate needed in (8.3). The upper-bound argument on p. 25 already uses an explicit \(m\)-skeleton. Thus the finding is the omitted skeletal reduction and literal target specification, not an established new obstruction in the core cohomology argument.

Additional counterevidence for the full target. The proof of Proposition 7.1 only needs the target vanishing \[\widetilde{\check H}^{\,m-1}(Y\cup\partial Y;\mathbb Z)=0.\] For the actual full Rips target, its compactification is contractible by the same input invoked on p. 24, so this vanishing holds without the target-dimension assumption. Retain the \(m\)-dimensional, \((m-1)\)-connected source \(L\). Its connecting map remains injective by Lemma 7.2. Choose \[0\ne a\in\widetilde{\check H}^{\,m-1}(\partial Y;\mathbb Z).\] Exactness and naturality give \[\Phi^*D_Y(a)=D_L((\partial\Phi)^*a)\ne0,\] because \(\partial\Phi\) is a homeomorphism and both relevant connecting maps are injective. The compactly supported class \(D_Y(a)\) is represented in \(H^m(Y,Y\setminus K;\mathbb Z)\) for a fixed compact \(K\). If \(\Phi(L)\) avoided \(K\), its pullback would be zero, a contradiction. Finally, cocompactness of \(\operatorname{Aut}(Y)\) moves this fixed compact obstruction to uniformly bounded distance from every target point. One applies the same argument after conjugating the target action and composing \(\Phi\) with an automorphism. The resulting neighborhood radius depends only on \(Y\).

Thus the displayed vanishing also suffices if one retains the full target. The source hypothesis and the quantitative conclusion needed for (8.3) remain unchanged. The Minor classification is based on the available standard skeletal interpretation of the actual construction; it does not reclassify a demonstrated unclosed core gap merely because a replacement proof can be supplied.
# Substantive checks supporting the main argument
## The normalized limit inferior

On pp. 4–5, order finite-index subgroups by reverse inclusion. For fixed finite-index \(H\le G\), the subgroups \(K\le H\) form the final segment starting at \(H\), so restricting to them does not change the net limit inferior. Since \[[G:K]=[G:H][H:K],\] the normalization gives \[\overline C_{2,m}(H)=[G:H]\overline C_{2,m}(G).\] The two-sided bounds in Theorem C imply \(0<\overline C_{2,m}(G)<\infty\). An isomorphism preserves both the complexity and the finite-index subgroup lattice. Equal complexities of isomorphic subgroups therefore force equal indices. Residual finiteness is not needed.
## Bicombing coefficients and weighted patterns

The checks of Lemmas 3.5–3.6 and Corollary 3.7 use the stated rational chains, without assuming a common denominator. In Lemma 3.6, the decomposition \(a=a_x+a_z+a_y\) yields boundary chains \(b_x,b_y\) with disjoint supports and augmentation one. Therefore \[\|a_z\|_1\ge\tfrac12\|\partial a_z\|_1
 =\tfrac12(\|b_x\|_1+\|b_y\|_1)\ge1.\] The fixed finite number of edges in a ball supplies the uniform coefficient bound, including endpoint choices of the point on the geodesic.

For the perfection step, subtracting total track defect from its maximal connector weight gives a nonnegative weight no greater than every surviving connector weight. Singular tracks then have zero surviving weight. In the resolution, a track has a single unoriented target-edge label; a domain edge has at most one connector with that label. This controls embeddedness and the crossing estimates. The triangle defect is bounded by the bicombing defect, together with a bounded central region for labels occurring on all three sides.

In Proposition 6.1, total edge displacement takes nonnegative integer values, so a minimizing equivariant vertex map exists. Compact regular tracks, one-endedness, and the finite number of track orbits give the bounded-side and outermost choices. Summing the shortening inequality and using minimality bounds the perfected total weight. Additive endpoint constants are absorbed by the stated \(X\)-dependent constants; they do not furnish a counterexample to the final estimate.
## Proper targets and the volume lower bound

Although Section 5 initially uses a free target, Proposition 6.1 states a proper target action. For a fixed target edge \(f\), its stabilizer is finite. The connector set has finitely many \(G\)-orbits; each such orbit contributes at most \(|\operatorname{Stab}(f)|\) connectors to the fiber of the equivariant label map over \(f\). Thus tracks remain compact, with finite stabilizer. The equivariant choices use freeness of the source \(K\), which is retained. No additional stabilizer factor is needed in the local coefficient and edge-count bounds.

On p. 26, the packing argument counts tracks rather than merely connectors: disjoint selected quotient balls have different target-edge orbits, and a track has only one such label. Hence their positive weights belong to distinct quotient tracks. A collapsed image edge causes no obstruction: follow a domain path to the first noncollapsed edge; a globally constant equivariant map is impossible for this proper action of an infinite group. These checks support the deduction from local bicombing mass to the lower bound in Theorem B, subject to the explicitly stated external inputs and the correction in F4.
# Disposition

Revise the four specified points, retaining the full group range of Theorems A–C through the precise graph conventions and the standard skeletal target specification. The initial review has not established a false main theorem. This report is a scoped scientific assessment of the acquired manuscript, not an assertion about an unexamined journal version or an independent acceptance.

## F2. Lemma 67 is false for signed measures (Major)
Location. Pages 46–47, Lemma 67; applications include Proposition 73 on p. 50 and Proposition 81 and its proof, including Lemma 84, on pp. 54–59.

Take \[X=[-1,1],\quad Y=\{0\},\quad f=\mathbf1_{(0,1]},\qquad
 \mu_n=\delta_{1/n}-\delta_{-1/n},\quad 
u=0.\] The function is bounded and continuous outside \(Y\). For every continuous \(g\), \[\int g\,d\mu_n=g(1/n)-g(-1/n)\longrightarrow0,\] so \(\mu_n\) converges weakly to \(
u\), with \(\|\mu_n\|_{m TV}=2\). Nevertheless, \[\int f\,d\mu_n=1,\qquad
 2|
u|(Y)\|f\|_\infty=0.\] Thus the stated bound fails even with uniformly bounded variation. The proof on p. 46 uses monotonicity of integration against a signed measure: \(f\le h_t^+\) does not imply the corresponding inequality of integrals.

Given a weakly convergent sequence of signed invariant measures, uniform boundedness gives bounded variation. Pass to a common subsequence of their Jordan parts: \[\mu_n^+\Rightarrow a,\qquad \mu_n^-\Rightarrow b.\] The limits are invariant positive measures, \(a-b=\nu\), and both give zero mass to \(E_R^\pm\). Positive-measure Portmanteau applies separately; subtraction proves the desired sequential convergence. Applying this to a further subsequence of every subsequence removes dependence on the chosen Jordan limits.

For the two-input kernel, first prove the positive-input version of the cutoff argument in Lemma 84. Take common Jordan limits in both variables, choose exceptional atom neighborhoods for those positive limits, and combine the four pairs by bilinearity. Choosing neighborhoods only from \(|\nu_\infty|\) is insufficient: positive and negative limiting atoms may cancel in the signed limit. The existing total-variation tail estimates can then be used.
