# Further proof defects and scope corrections
## F3. The density statement does not justify the positive approximation used in Lemma 31 (Major)
Location. Page 11, Lemma 14, compared with Lemmas 77–78 on pp. 52–53.

Consider the unit-roof suspension of \[A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.\] For the period-one orbit \(\gamma\) over a fixed point, let \(\mu=\sqrt2\,\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma\). The closed base-circle form \(dt\) gives \[[\mu]_\phi\cdot[dt]=\sqrt2.\] Every periodic orbit has integer winding around that circle. Every rational-coefficient multi-orbit therefore pairs rationally with \(dt\) and cannot have exactly this homology class.

The probability enhancement fails independently. With constant roof \(\sqrt2\), all orbit periods are \(n\sqrt2\). Every rational multi-orbit has mass in \(\sqrt2\mathbb Q\), never equal to one, whereas normalized periodic probability measures exist.

Lemmas 77–78 naturally produce real coefficients and do not establish the extra rational assertion. Use real coefficients for arbitrary homology. For a finite null-homologous combination, the weights satisfy \(Ac=0\) for an integer homology matrix \(A\); rational vectors in \(\ker A\) are dense. On a fixed positive support, sufficiently close rational weights preserve positivity. Exact mass normalization may then require real coefficients.

Core dependency. Lemma 31 on p. 22 obtains its positive intersection lower bound for positive multi-orbits whose support avoids \(\partial S\), then invokes Lemma 14 to pass to an arbitrary null-homologous invariant probability. Lemma 14 supplies avoidance without the required positivity, and supplies its probability conclusion only for an empty excluded set. Lemma 77 supplies positivity, whereas Lemma 78 obtains avoidance by a signed subtraction. These statements do not justify the asserted limiting inequality. The resulting Reeb-like condition is used in Theorem 34 on p. 31, from which the proof of Theorem A starts on p. 37. This missing justification is a Major defect in the derivation. The suspension examples separately refute the rationality clauses; they do not refute the skewed main theorem.

Repair boundary. A repair must prove suitable positive approximation avoiding the prescribed finite orbit set, or justify another passage of the intersection estimate to the limit. A homological-fullness route requires proving the existence of positive avoiding periodic measures whose homology convex hull contains zero in its interior. Once that construction and positive avoiding approximations of homology \(h_n\to0\) are established, a positive correction of mass \(O(\|h_n\|)\) can cancel \(h_n\), followed by normalization. This report does not certify those missing inputs merely by naming homological fullness and shadowing. The real-coefficient and rational-kernel observations alone do not complete this step.
## F4. The local time-change formula is inverted (Major)
Location. The convention on p. 33 and the construction before Proposition 48 on p. 34.

The convention \(f\,\partial_t\psi^f=\partial_t\phi\) implies \[T^f(x)=\int_0^{T^1(x)} f(\phi_t x)\,dt.\] The printed constant-on-segment choice \(f=T^1g\) gives \((T^1)^2g\), not \(g\). Taking \(T^1=1/2\) and \(g=1\) yields \(f=1/2\) and \(T^f=1/4\), and also violates the intended range \(f\in[1,2]\).

Use \(f=g/T^1\) instead. This gives \(f=2\) and \(T^f=1\) in the same test. To retain \(f\in[1,2]\), the chosen target time must satisfy \(T^1\le g\le2T^1\), with room for compatible regularization. This verifies the corrected local identity.

Dependency and scope. On p. 34 the claimed equality \(T^f=g\) is the stated idea for the inductive construction of regular short return times. The printed choice gives \((T^1)^2g\), whose regularity does not follow from that of \(g\) when \(T^1\) is only continuous. Lemma 49 and Proposition 48 use regular return times to construct the required \(C^{1+H}\) atlas on p. 35. Theorem A on p. 37 uses that atlas and its regular invariant volume. The failed calculation is therefore a Major construction defect. The quotient repairs the local identity, but all global inductive compatibility and range choices have not been independently completed. No counterexample to atlas existence is asserted.
## F5. The pressure competitor requires probability normalization (Major)
Location. Page 29, proof of Lemma 38; the orbit-measure convention is on p. 9.

The paper defines \(\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma\) to have mass \(T_\gamma\). Hence \(p|_\gamma=D\) gives \[\int p\,d\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma=DT_\gamma,\] not \(D\). For \(T_\gamma=2\) and \(D=1\), the two values are two and one. The pressure variational principle also takes probability measures.

Replace the competitor by \(\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma/T_\gamma\), whose entropy is zero. The proof then reads \[D\le\int p\,d\mu_p+h_{\mu_p}
 \le C\mu_p(M\setminus U)+D\mu_p(U)+h_{\rm top},\] and yields exactly the stated concentration bound. This verifies the concentration bound with an admissible probability competitor.

Dependency and scope. The printed comparison uses a measure outside the probability class and drops its period factor. Lemma 39 on p. 30 invokes Lemma 38 to force concentration; Proposition 37 and Lemma 41 use Lemma 39. Theorem 34 on p. 31 uses these concentration and degree arguments to obtain the required Reeb-like Gibbs measure, from which Theorem A starts on p. 37. This invalid probability comparison is part of the core derivation and is assessed Major. The normalized calculation restores the same bound; neither the concentration conclusion nor the corrected main theorem is disproved.
## F6. The spanning chain has the opposite orientation (Major)
Location. Page 61, the definition of \(S\), Claim 1 and the intersection calculation; \(\Gamma\) is defined on p. 60.

The displayed boundaries give \[\partial e_i=a_i+b_i+\gamma_{s_i}-\operatorname{segment}_i(r),
 \qquad \partial C=\sum_i(a_i+b_i).\] Therefore \[\partial\Bigl(\sum_i e_i-C\Bigr)
   =\sum_i\gamma_{s_i}-\gamma_r=-\Gamma,\] not \(\Gamma\). Moreover, since the \(e_i\) avoid \(\Gamma'\), the printed chain intersects \(\Gamma'\) as \(-C\cdot\Gamma'\), while the proof uses the positive sign. Define \(S=C-\sum_i e_i\) instead: both \(\partial S=\Gamma\) and \(S\cdot\Gamma'=C\cdot\Gamma'\) are restored. The corrected orientation supports the intended local kernel sign used in F1.

Dependency and scope. The chain in Lemma 87 has the opposite boundary and intersection sign from those asserted. On p. 63, Theorem 80 explicitly invokes Lemmas 87–88 to identify the local kernel integral with finite-orbit linking, an identification required by the cumulative construction on p. 64. This invalid spanning-chain derivation is therefore Major. Reversing the chain restores both required identities; no opposite-sign counterexample to the corrected linking theorem is claimed.
## F7. The Reeb-like minimum needs an empty-set convention (Minor)
Location. Page 13, Definition 20; suspension cases are discussed on pp. 5 and 68.

For a unit-roof suspension, \(dt(X)=1\), so every invariant probability \(\rho\) satisfies \([\rho]_\phi\cdot[dt]=1\). Thus \(\mathcal M_p^0(\phi)\) is empty, and its ordinary real minimum is undefined. Specify an extended infimum with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\), or an explicitly quantified convention. This does not create a false Reeb volume in the suspension: a positive invariant volume has nonzero homology and already fails the other defining condition.
# Positive checks and remaining qualifications

The ambient orientation is explicitly preserved by orbit equivalence on p. 6; an orientation-reversing-map objection would not meet the hypotheses. The contact criterion has the consistent sign \[\alpha\wedge\iota_XV=\alpha(X)V.\] The separation and time-averaging argument makes \(\alpha(X)\) uniformly positive while preserving \(d\alpha=\iota_XV\). The final smoothing construction subtracts the cohomology correction with the correct sign. In the orientation double cover on pp. 65–66, transfer doubles both projected measure and intersection count, so the factor \(1/2\) is consistent.

After F5 is corrected, the Gibbs concentration estimate supports the orthant degree argument. A fixed-orthant subsequence uses the appropriate signed homology basis; the zero-dimensional homology case should be handled directly rather than via a negative-dimensional sphere. The positive Birkhoff-section construction was traced, while its external geometric inputs remain outside an independent proof certification.

Two regularity/topology qualifications remain separate from confirmed theorem counterexamples. First, smooth functions are not dense in the full endpoint Hölder norm: for \(0<\alpha<1\), the seminorm distance from \(|r|^\alpha\) to any smooth function near zero is at least one. The smoothing step on p. 40 therefore needs an exponent strictly below available regularity. Since the exponent is chosen in the construction, this can be accommodated by retaining such slack; no failure of the main theorem follows from this observation. Second, transverse transfer under orbit equivalence does not generally preserve probability mass. Positive normalization is needed where probability compactness is used in Lemma 56; it preserves the relevant positivity and can be controlled for converging time changes.

The source image on p. 58 resolves an extraction ambiguity: the definition of the cutoff set uses intersection. No set-difference error is reported. The report also makes no unsupported claim that absence of an acquired supplement or executable code is a mathematical flaw.
# Disposition

The assessment remains Major. F1–F6 identify invalid definitions or proof steps with demonstrated roles in the linking construction, the Reeb-like Gibbs-measure argument, or the regular atlas needed by the main proof. Correct the cumulative indices and chain orientation, replace the signed-measure argument with justified positive-measure and Jordan-limit reasoning, supply the missing passage of the positive intersection estimate, and correct the time-change and probability normalization. F7 additionally needs its empty-set convention. The local repairs do not certify the positive-avoidance construction, all atlas compatibility choices, or full joint weak-topology continuity. No counterexample to the corrected orbit-equivalence theorem has been established, and that theorem has not been independently certified in its entirety. Scientific decision and adjudication remain pending; author adoption is unknown.

claim: The printed multiplicative time-change formula does not yield the asserted return time.
analysis: Location. The convention on p. 33 and the construction before Proposition 48 on p. 34.

The convention \(f\,\partial_t\psi^f=\partial_t\phi\) implies \[T^f(x)=\int_0^{T^1(x)} f(\phi_t x)\,dt.\] The printed constant-on-segment choice \(f=T^1g\) gives \((T^1)^2g\), not \(g\). Taking \(T^1=1/2\) and \(g=1\) yields \(f=1/2\) and \(T^f=1/4\), and also violates the intended range \(f\in[1,2]\).

Use \(f=g/T^1\) instead. This gives \(f=2\) and \(T^f=1\) in the same test. To retain \(f\in[1,2]\), the chosen target time must satisfy \(T^1\le g\le2T^1\), with room for compatible regularization. This verifies the corrected local identity.

Dependency and scope. On p. 34 the claimed equality \(T^f=g\) is the stated idea for the inductive construction of regular short return times. The printed choice gives \((T^1)^2g\), whose regularity does not follow from that of \(g\) when \(T^1\) is only continuous. Lemma 49 and Proposition 48 use regular return times to construct the required \(C^{1+H}\) atlas on p. 35. Theorem A on p. 37 uses that atlas and its regular invariant volume. The failed calculation is therefore a Major construction defect. The quotient repairs the local identity, but all global inductive compatibility and range choices have not been independently completed. No counterexample to atlas existence is asserted.

claim: An unnormalized orbit measure is used as a probability competitor.
analysis: Location. Page 29, proof of Lemma 38; the orbit-measure convention is on p. 9.

The paper defines \(\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma\) to have mass \(T_\gamma\). Hence \(p|_\gamma=D\) gives \[\int p\,d\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma=DT_\gamma,\] not \(D\). For \(T_\gamma=2\) and \(D=1\), the two values are two and one. The pressure variational principle also takes probability measures.

Replace the competitor by \(\operatorname{Leb}_\gamma/T_\gamma\), whose entropy is zero. The proof then reads \[D\le\int p\,d\mu_p+h_{\mu_p}
 \le C\mu_p(M\setminus U)+D\mu_p(U)+h_{\rm top},\] and yields exactly the stated concentration bound. This verifies the concentration bound with an admissible probability competitor.

claim: The orientation of the printed spanning chain is reversed.
analysis: Location. Page 61, the definition of \(S\), Claim 1 and the intersection calculation; \(\Gamma\) is defined on p. 60.

The displayed boundaries give \[\partial e_i=a_i+b_i+\gamma_{s_i}-\operatorname{segment}_i(r),

   =\sum_i\gamma_{s_i}-\gamma_r=-\Gamma,\] not \(\Gamma\). report: Abstract: The assessment is Major. Equation (4.20) supplies a false identity to the gauge monotonicity proof used in the main image-cover estimate. Title: Initial scientific review of
Distortion of Hausdorff measures under
Orlicz–Sobolev maps
Article. Andrea Cianchi, Mikhail V. Korobkov and Jan Kristensen. Journal identifier: 10.4171/JEMS/1620.

Version examined. The 37-page manuscript `arXiv:2208.08152v2`, 26 May 2023. PDF and printed page numbers coincide. The publisher records online publication on 19 March 2025. The frozen 2025 record is retained; equivalence between this manuscript and the journal version has not been established.
# Scope and central mechanism

The primary reviewer read all 37 source-text pages and actually inspected all 35 rendered body/support pages. Page 28 was recovered through a complete UTF-8 read with ASCII-escaped JSON after the text reader rejected it; the actual PDF page was also checked. They did not perform source-image inspection. Roles and model self-reports are recorded separately from the controller’s UI observation; this report is an initial review, not an independent acceptance.

The main construction uses \[J(s)=sB^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\varphi(s)}{s^n}\right),
 \qquad \psi(r)=\varphi(J^{-1}(r)).\] The Young function \(B\) is obtained from \(A\) by (2.27), with \(B=A\) when \(n=1\). The restrictions (2.26), (2.29), (2.30) give finite positive functions, suitable endpoint behavior, and classical inverses. The standing condition \(\varphi(s)/s^n\) nonincreasing must remain part of every gauge statement. The crossing inequality in Lemma 4.4 combines with the Orlicz–Morrey estimate (2.28) and disjoint dyadic covers. The stronger finite-measure-to-zero conclusion additionally uses \(\varphi(s)/s^n\to\infty\) and the two small-scale conditions (3.10).

The proof was checked at the algebraic, covering, modular-integral and limiting stages. The random-series sharpness argument was checked through the cutoff norm, branching, overlap, coefficient summability and energy calculation. The external Orlicz–Morrey theorem with its precise constant, and the full general theorem on continuity from below of Hausdorff content, were not independently reproved. No additional supplement or code artifact was acquired in the bounded search. The publisher’s PDF required a subscription, and an Oxford repository request returned HTTP 403; neither limitation was bypassed or classified as a mathematical defect.
# Confirmed issues
## F1. The introductory positive-measure assertion is too strong (Minor)
Location. Page 3, the final sentence of the first paragraph.

For every \(0<\alpha\le n\), \[\mathcal H^\alpha(E)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal L^n(E)=0.\] For \(\alpha<n\), apply \(\operatorname{diam}(U)^n\le\delta^{n-\alpha}\operatorname{diam}(U)^\alpha\) to sufficiently fine covers of bounded pieces; the endpoint \(\alpha=n\) follows from proportionality with Lebesgue measure. The Lusin \(N\) property stated in the same paragraph therefore forces \(\mathcal H^n(u(E))=0\) for the indicated target \(\mathbb R^n\).

Already \(n=m=1\) supplies a direct obstruction independent of the higher-dimensional cited result: the relevant space is locally absolutely continuous, and such maps send length-zero sets to length-zero sets. Thus the printed assertion about a positive \(n\)-dimensional image measure cannot hold. An image can have Hausdorff dimension \(n\) while having zero \(\mathcal H^n\) measure. Retain the supported full-dimension assertion and remove the positive-measure inference. This concerns the introduction, not a counterexample to the main distortion results.
## F2. Exact normalization must be separated from multiplicative equivalence (Minor)
Location. Page 5, the assertion preceding (2.6); p. 10, Remark 3.2; related power normalization in (3.24) on p. 13.

In dimension one, \(\varphi(r)=2r\) gives \[\mathcal H^\varphi=2\mathcal L^1\ne\mathcal L^1,\qquad
 \frac{\varphi(r)}r=2.\] Thus literal inequality of the measures is not equivalent to the divergent limit in (2.6). The statement should concern failure of equivalence up to multiplicative constants. The actual divergent-limit hypothesis used in Theorem 3.4 is unaffected.

Likewise, if \(\varphi(s)=s^n\), the definitions give exactly \[J(s)=sB^{-1}(1),\qquad
 \psi(r)=\frac{r^n}{[B^{-1}(1)]^n}.\] For \(n=1\) and \(A(t)=4t^2\), this is \(\psi(r)=2r\), not \(r\). One may retain the constant, use multiplicative equivalence, or explicitly normalize \(B(1)=1\). For \(n\ge2\) and \(A=t^p\), direct conjugation gives \[B(t)=c_Bt^p,\quad c_B=(n'-p')^{p-1},\qquad
 \psi(r)=c_B^{\alpha/(p+\alpha-n)}
 r^{\alpha p/(p+\alpha-n)}.\] Thus the exact equality in (3.24) also needs its normalization. Positive scalar factors preserve zero sets, finiteness and the distortion exponent, which explains the limited impact.
## F3. The explicit constant in Example 3.6 fails when \(n=1\) (Minor)
Location. Page 12, equation (3.16).

Take \[n=m=1,\quad p=2,\quad\alpha=1,\qquad
 u(x)=\min\{\max\{x,0\},1\},\quad E=[0,1].\] The homogeneous Sobolev assumption is satisfied, and \[\|u'\|_{L^2(\mathbb R)}=1,\qquad
 \mathcal H_\infty^1(E)=\mathcal H_\infty^1(u(E))=1.\] Under the usual convention \(n'=\infty\), the factor \[\left(\frac{p-1}{n'-p'}\right)^{
       \alpha(p-1)/(\alpha+p-n)}\] vanishes. Equation (3.16) would therefore give \(1\le0\). Without that convention, the formula is undefined for an admitted dimension.

Complete one-dimensional replacement. Restrict the printed \(n'-p'\) formula to \(n\ge2\). When \(n=1\), put \[\tau=\frac{\alpha p}{p+\alpha-1},\qquad 0<\alpha\le1,\quad p>1.\] On an interval \(I\), \[\operatorname{diam}u(I)\le |I|^{1-1/p}
 \left(\int_I|u'|^p\right)^{1/p}.\] Replace covering sets by their convex intervals and merge overlapping intervals. Since \(\alpha\le1\), this does not increase the sum of their \(\alpha\)-powers. The remaining intervals have disjoint interiors. Hölder’s inequality for the resulting sum gives \[\sum_I\operatorname{diam}u(I)^\tau
 \le \|u'\|_p^\tau
       \left(\sum_I |I|^\alpha\right)^{(p-1)/(p+\alpha-1)}.\] Infimizing proves \[\mathcal H_\infty^\tau(u(E))
 \le \|u'\|_p^\tau
       [\mathcal H_\infty^\alpha(E)]^{(p-1)/(p+\alpha-1)}.\] The clamp example attains equality for \(\alpha=1\). Theorem 3.5 itself uses \(B=A\) in dimension one and is not refuted by the bad specialized constant.
## F4. Equation (4.20) omits the \(n\)-th power (Major)
Location. Page 19, Lemma 4.3 and its following monotonicity argument.

The proof also needs the corresponding stronger monotonicity. Namely, \[\frac{v}{[B^{-1}(v)]^n}=\frac{B(z)}{z^n},
 \qquad z=B^{-1}(v),\] is nondecreasing by the already established (4.6). Since \(v(s)\) is nonincreasing, the composition is nonincreasing, exactly proving (4.17). In dimension one the same assertion follows from convexity of \(A=B\). This corrected argument establishes the gauge lemma; its conclusion is not contradicted.

Dependency and scope. The source proves (4.6), but the actual Lemma 4.3 proof uses the false (4.20) and the different monotonicity of \(v/B^{-1}(v)\). The available premise supplies a replacement justification, not a second printed proof of (4.17). On p. 23, Theorem 3.1 invokes Lemma 4.3 in (5.6) to convert normalized image-cover costs to unscaled costs; this gives (5.9) and the measure conclusion and is retained in (5.13) for the content conclusion. Lemma 4.10 on pp. 22–23 also invokes (4.17) for the monotonicity of \(\Xi_{\psi,B}\). The invalid derivation therefore has a demonstrated core dependency, warranting Major classification. The corrected calculation preserves those uses; no false main theorem is claimed.
## F5. The critical exponential inverse comparison is false (Minor)
Location. Page 14, the \(\alpha=0\) branch of (3.28). Here and below, \(\asymp\) denotes comparison by positive multiplicative constants.

Take \(n=1\), \(q=1\), \(\beta=-1\), and \[A(t)=t\log(1+t).\] This is a finite positive Young function with \[A''(t)=\frac{t+2}{(t+1)^2}>0,\qquad
 \lim_{t\to0}\frac{A(t)}t=0,\quad
 \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{A(t)}t=\infty.\] For \(L=\log(1/s)\ge16\), define \[\varphi(s)=sA\!\left(\frac4{sL^2}\right)
 =\frac4{L^2}\log\!\left(1+\frac{4e^L}{L^2}\right).\] Extend it beyond \(s=e^{-16}\) linearly, with \(\varphi(s)/s\) constant. This is an admissible increasing continuous gauge with \(\varphi(s)/s\) nonincreasing and \(\varphi(s)\asymp1/\log(1/s)\). For completeness, if \(z=4e^L/L^2\), its derivative with respect to \(L\) has sign \[-2\log(1+z)+(L-2)\frac{z}{1+z}
 <-L+4\log L-2\log4-2<0
 \quad(L\ge16).\] The ratio \(\varphi(s)/s=A(4e^L/L^2)\) decreases with \(s\), including across the linear extension.

Since \(B=A\), the definitions give exactly \[J(s)=\frac4{[\log(1/s)]^2},\qquad
 J^{-1}(r)=e^{-2/\sqrt r}.\] The printed comparison in (3.28) is \(e^{-1/\sqrt r}\). Their ratio is \(e^{-1/\sqrt r}\to0\), so they are not comparable in the stated sense.
## F6. The zero-volume limit and image labels in Theorem 3.7 need correction (Minor)
Location. Pages 27–28, especially (5.28) and the following paragraph.

When \(\mathcal L^n(E)=0\), the bound involves \[\frac{[B^{-1}(r)]^n}{r}=\Phi_B(1/r).\] It tends to zero as \(r\to\infty\), not as \(r\to0\). For \(n=1\), \(A(t)=4t^2\), it equals \(1/(2\sqrt r)\) and diverges at zero. Reverse the printed limiting direction.

The cube cover directly controls \[\mathcal H_\infty^n(u(E))\le\sum_i\operatorname{diam}(u(Q_i))^n\] in \(\mathbb R^m\). The printed \(\mathcal L^n(u(E))\) on pp. 27–28 should retain this content label, especially since \(m>n\) is allowed. With \(V=\mathcal L^n(E)>0\), the choice \[r=\frac{\kappa}{n^{n/2}V}\] in the corrected cover estimate gives exactly \[2\kappa^{n+1}\|\nabla u\|_{L^A}^n
 \Phi_B\!\left(\frac{n^{n/2}V}{\kappa}\right).\] For \(V=0\), use \(r\to\infty\). Exhaustion and content continuity from below give the general-set conclusion. These corrections complete the intended step. The zero-content case of Theorem 3.5 can similarly cite Theorem 3.1(ii), which also covers \(\varphi(r)=r^n\), instead of relying on the more restricted Theorem 3.4.
## F7. The Cantor construction data are inconsistent as printed (Major)
Location. Page 32, (6.12)–(6.15), and their use on pp. 33–34.

The source specifies \(\#\mathcal A_j=\lfloor2^{j
u}floor\) and \(0<\mathcal H^\varphi(M)<\infty\), but (6.14) gives cylinder mass at most \(c2^{-j}\). The allowed value \(
u=1/2\) yields \[0<\mathcal H^\varphi(M)
 \le c\lfloor2^{j/2}floor2^{-j}
 \le c2^{-j/2}\longrightarrow0,\] a contradiction. The required and subsequently used bound on p. 34 is \(c2^{-j
u}\).

There is a separate finite-level obstruction. For \(n=1,\nu=3,j=1\), the construction asks for eight different dyadic intervals of length \(1/4\) in \([0,1]\), where only four exist. The theorem permits these parameters.

A construction closing both defects. Start at sufficiently large \(j_0\) and set \[\delta_j=2^{-2^j},\qquad N_j=2^{\lfloor j
ufloor}\asymp2^{j
u}.\] Use \(N_j\) separated cubes of side \(\delta_j\), with \[b_j=N_{j+1}/N_j\le2^{\lceil
uceil}\] children per parent. There are enough dyadic locations for all \(j\ge j_0\); choose the initial cubes and expanded cutoff supports inside a fixed compact subset of \((0,1)^n\). Give each level-\(j\) cylinder natural mass \(1/N_j\).

For \(\delta_{j+1}\le r\le\delta_j\), a radius-\(r\) ball intersects only a dimensional bounded number of level-\(j\) dyadic cubes. Since adjacent gauge values have bounded ratio, \[\mu(B(x,r))\le C/N_j\le C2^{-j\nu}\le C'\varphi(r).\] The mass-distribution argument gives positive \(\mathcal H^\varphi(M)\), and level covers give finite measure. Covering a fixed cylinder by its descendants gives \[\mathcal H^\varphi(Q\cap M)\le C/N_j\le C2^{-j\nu}.\] The later proof needs these comparisons and bounded branching, not the exact integer-part count in (6.12).

The norm cancellation remains \[-\frac{\nu}{\sigma}+\frac{\nu}{n}
       +\frac{q-n+1}{n}=0.\] Bounded overlap also supplies the \(\ell^1\) condition required in Lemma 6.4, although p. 34 states only \(\ell^\infty\): \[\sum_Q|a_Q(x,y)|
 \le C\sum_jj^{-\delta}2^{-j\nu/\sigma}<\infty.\] Retaining the fixed comparison constant in the level-\(j+2\) separation estimate yields a kernel bound \(Cj^{\delta\sigma-\mu}2^{j\nu}\). The cylinder mass cancels its exponential factor, leaving \[C\sum_jj^{\delta\sigma-\mu}<\infty
 \quad\text{for}\quad
 1<\delta<\frac{\mu-1}{\sigma}.\] This interval is nonempty by \(\mu>1+\sigma\). The replacement construction supplies the same sharpness conclusion within the checked scope.

Dependency and scope. Theorem 6.2’s finite-energy estimate on p. 34 explicitly uses the cylinder-mass assertion (6.14). The required \(2^{-j\nu}\) factor cancels the kernel’s \(2^{j\nu}\), leaving the summable polynomial series. The incompatible p. 32 data do not supply a set and measure with these properties. Thus the printed proof lacks the admissible witness needed for its central sharpness conclusion, warranting Major classification. The replacement construction verifies the required estimates without validating the original one or refuting the corrected theorem.
# Further substantive checks and limits

For Theorem 3.1, fix \(\lambda>\|\nabla u\|_{L^A}\). The function \(A(|\nabla u|/\lambda)\) is integrable, and absolute continuity of its integral on small-volume cube unions supplies the required uniform threshold. This does not require a \(\Delta_2\) condition or order continuity of the Orlicz norm. In the content proof, choose the threshold below the cost of a fixed-size cube; then every cube in a sufficiently inexpensive cover has bounded diameter, supplying the scale restriction used in (5.14).

For Theorem 3.4, the decisive estimate is \[\left|\bigcup_iQ_i\right|
 \le C(\mathcal H^\varphi(E)+\varepsilon)
       \frac{\delta^n}{\varphi(\delta)}
 \longrightarrow0.\] The proof fixes its auxiliary parameter first, shrinks \(\delta\), and only afterwards sends that parameter to zero. This is consistent with the quantifiers and correctly excludes the Lebesgue endpoint from the finite-measure-to-zero assertion. The bars over \(E\) and \(E_j\) on pp. 25–26 were checked on the actual images: the argument concerns compact closures. No compactness error based on text extraction is reported.

The \(\Xi_{\psi,B}\) estimate in Theorem 3.5 follows by choosing \(r=\kappa/(c_n\mathcal H_\infty^\varphi(E))\) after the cover sum. The infinite-content case is treated by exhaustion; the relevant continuity-from-below theorem remains an explicit external dependency.

A bounded reconstruction of the omitted proof of Theorem 6.1 uses separated cubes of side \(2^{-Lj}\), number comparable to \(2^{Lj\alpha}\), and coefficients \[j^{-\delta}2^{-Lj(\alpha+p-n)/p}.\] Their gradient norms sum for \(\delta>1\). With \(\sigma=\alpha p/(\alpha+p-n)\), the same random-energy argument leaves \(\sum_jj^{\delta\sigma-\gamma}\), convergent when \(1<\delta<(\gamma-1)/\sigma\). This verifies the exponent mechanism stated in the paper. It does not resolve the smaller logarithmic exponents or the general-gauge optimality questions that the authors explicitly leave open.
# Disposition

The assessment is Major because F4 invalidates a derivation used in the main distortion estimates and F7 invalidates the construction supplying the finite-energy witness for Theorem 6.2. The explicit replacements restore these steps; no counterexample to the principal distortion or sharpness conclusions is established. F1–F3, F5 and F6 retain their stated local scope and Minor classification. The external-dependency limits and the distinction between the examined manuscript and the unexamined journal version remain. Scientific decision and adjudication are pending; author adoption is unknown.

For every \(0<\alpha\le n\), \[\mathcal H^\alpha(E)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal L^n(E)=0.\] For \(\alpha<n\), apply \(\operatorname{diam}(U)^n\le\delta^{n-\alpha}\operatorname{diam}(U)^\alpha\) to sufficiently fine covers of bounded pieces; the endpoint \(\alpha=n\) follows from proportionality with Lebesgue measure. Already \(n=m=1\) supplies a direct obstruction independent of the higher-dimensional cited result: the relevant space is locally absolutely continuous, and such maps send length-zero sets to length-zero sets. Thus the printed assertion about a positive \(n\)-dimensional image measure cannot hold. An image can have Hausdorff dimension \(n\) while having zero \(\mathcal H^n\) measure. Retain the supported full-dimension assertion and remove the positive-measure inference. This concerns the introduction, not a counterexample to the main distortion results.
result: Impact: Introductory overstatement; no counterexample to a main Orlicz-Sobolev distortion theorem.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Retain only the supported full-dimension statement, with zero n-dimensional measure allowed; remove the positive-measure inference.

problems.title: Two exact equalities/inequalities omit multiplicative normalization.
problems.source_location: p.5 equation(2.6), p.10 Remark3.2; related exact power normalization p.13 equation(3.24)
claim: Two exact equalities/inequalities omit multiplicative normalization.
analysis: Location. Page 5, the assertion preceding (2.6); p. 10, Remark 3.2; related power normalization in (3.24) on p. 13.

In dimension one, \(\varphi(r)=2r\) gives \[\mathcal H^\varphi=2\mathcal L^1\ne\mathcal L^1,\qquad
 \frac{\varphi(r)}r=2.\] Thus literal inequality of the measures is not equivalent to the divergent limit in (2.6). The statement should concern failure of equivalence up to multiplicative constants. The actual divergent-limit hypothesis used in Theorem 3.4 is unaffected.

Likewise, if \(\varphi(s)=s^n\), the definitions give exactly \[J(s)=sB^{-1}(1),\qquad
 \psi(r)=\frac{r^n}{[B^{-1}(1)]^n}.\] For \(n=1\) and \(A(t)=4t^2\), this is \(\psi(r)=2r\), not \(r\). One may retain the constant, use multiplicative equivalence, or explicitly normalize \(B(1)=1\). For \(n\ge2\) and \(A=t^p\), direct conjugation gives \[B(t)=c_Bt^p,\quad c_B=(n'-p')^{p-1},\qquad
 \psi(r)=c_B^{\alpha/(p+\alpha-n)}
 r^{\alpha p/(p+\alpha-n)}.\] Thus the exact equality in (3.24) also needs its normalization. Positive scalar factors preserve zero sets, finiteness and the distortion exponent, which explains the limited impact.
result: Impact: Normalization of displayed examples; the measure-equivalence, distortion exponent and Lusin N deductions remain valid.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use the displayed exact constants or explicitly state multiplicative equivalence. Theorem3.4's actual limit condition(2.6) remains the correct substantive hypothesis.

problems.title: The explicit constant does not cover the allowed one-dimensional case.
problems.source_location: p.12 Example3.6, equation(3.16)
claim: The explicit constant does not cover the allowed one-dimensional case.
analysis: Location. Page 12, equation (3.16).

Take \[n=m=1,\quad p=2,\quad\alpha=1,\qquad
 u(x)=\min\{\max\{x,0\},1\},\quad E=[0,1].\] The homogeneous Sobolev assumption is satisfied, and \[\|u'\|_{L^2(\mathbb R)}=1,\qquad
 \mathcal H_\infty^1(E)=\mathcal H_\infty^1(u(E))=1.\] Under the usual convention \(n'=\infty\), the factor \[\left(\frac{p-1}{n'-p'}\right)^{
       \alpha(p-1)/(\alpha+p-n)}\] vanishes. Equation (3.16) would therefore give \(1\le0\). Without that convention, the formula is undefined for an admitted dimension.

Complete one-dimensional replacement. Restrict the printed \(n'-p'\) formula to \(n\ge2\). When \(n=1\), put \[\tau=\frac{\alpha p}{p+\alpha-1},\qquad 0<\alpha\le1,\quad p>1.\] On an interval \(I\), \[\operatorname{diam}u(I)\le |I|^{1-1/p}
 \left(\int_I|u'|^p\right)^{1/p}.\] Replace covering sets by their convex intervals and merge overlapping intervals. Since \(\alpha\le1\), this does not increase the sum of their \(\alpha\)-powers. The remaining intervals have disjoint interiors. Hölder’s inequality for the resulting sum gives \[\sum_I\operatorname{diam}u(I)^\tau
 \le \|u'\|_p^\tau
       \left(\sum_I |I|^\alpha\right)^{(p-1)/(p+\alpha-1)}.\] Infimizing proves \[\mathcal H_\infty^\tau(u(E))
 \le \|u'\|_p^\tau
       [\mathcal H_\infty^\alpha(E)]^{(p-1)/(p+\alpha-1)}.\] The clamp example attains equality for \(\alpha=1\). Theorem 3.5 itself uses \(B=A\) in dimension one and is not refuted by the bad specialized constant.
result: Impact: False quantitative example at n=1; the general theorem uses B=A there and is not refuted.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Restrict the n'-p' formula to n>=2 and state the one-dimensional Holder estimate separately.

problems.title: The denominator lacks its n-th power; the cited monotonicity is correspondingly insufficient as written.
problems.source_location: p.19 Lemma4.3, equation(4.20) and the following monotonicity argument; correct input p.17 equation(4.6)
claim: The denominator lacks its n-th power; the cited monotonicity is correspondingly insufficient as written.
analysis: Location. Page 19, Lemma 4.3 and its following monotonicity argument.

The proof also needs the corresponding stronger monotonicity. Namely, \[\frac{v}{[B^{-1}(v)]^n}=\frac{B(z)}{z^n},
 \qquad z=B^{-1}(v),\] is nondecreasing by the already established (4.6). Since \(v(s)\) is nonincreasing, the composition is nonincreasing, exactly proving (4.17). In dimension one the same assertion follows from convexity of \(A=B\). This corrected argument establishes the gauge lemma; its conclusion is not contradicted.

Dependency and scope. The source proves (4.6), but the actual Lemma 4.3 proof uses the false (4.20) and the different monotonicity of \(v/B^{-1}(v)\). The available premise supplies a replacement justification, not a second printed proof of (4.17). On p. 23, Theorem 3.1 invokes Lemma 4.3 in (5.6) to convert normalized image-cover costs to unscaled costs; this gives (5.9) and the measure conclusion and is retained in (5.13) for the content conclusion. Lemma 4.10 on pp. 22–23 also invokes (4.17) for the monotonicity of \(\Xi_{\psi,B}\). The invalid derivation therefore has a demonstrated core dependency, warranting Major classification. The corrected calculation preserves those uses; no false main theorem is claimed.
result: Impact: The false equality and insufficient monotonicity proof establish Lemma4.3, explicitly used in Theorem3.1 p23(5.6), (5.9) and (5.13), and in Lemma4.10. Major for an invalid derivation in the main distortion machinery. Correcting it preserves the conclusions.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Restore the exponent n and use B(z)/z^n monotonicity, not merely the Young-function property B(z)/z.

problems.title: The exponential inverse is not determined up to multiplicative constants by the stated slowly varying comparability.
problems.source_location: p.14 Example3.9, first branch of equation(3.28), alpha=0
claim: The exponential inverse is not determined up to multiplicative constants by the stated slowly varying comparability.
analysis: Location. Page 14, the \(\alpha=0\) branch of (3.28). Here and below, \(\asymp\) denotes comparison by positive multiplicative constants.

Take \(n=1\), \(q=1\), \(\beta=-1\), and \[A(t)=t\log(1+t).\] This is a finite positive Young function with \[A''(t)=\frac{t+2}{(t+1)^2}>0,\qquad
 \lim_{t\to0}\frac{A(t)}t=0,\quad
 \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{A(t)}t=\infty.\] For \(L=\log(1/s)\ge16\), define \[\varphi(s)=sA\!\left(\frac4{sL^2}\right)
 =\frac4{L^2}\log\!\left(1+\frac{4e^L}{L^2}\right).\] Extend it beyond \(s=e^{-16}\) linearly, with \(\varphi(s)/s\) constant. This is an admissible increasing continuous gauge with \(\varphi(s)/s\) nonincreasing and \(\varphi(s)\asymp1/\log(1/s)\). For completeness, if \(z=4e^L/L^2\), its derivative with respect to \(L\) has sign \[-2\log(1+z)+(L-2)\frac{z}{1+z}
 <-L+4\log L-2\log4-2<0
 \quad(L\ge16).\] The ratio \(\varphi(s)/s=A(4e^L/L^2)\) decreases with \(s\), including across the linear extension.

Since \(B=A\), the definitions give exactly \[J(s)=\frac4{[\log(1/s)]^2},\qquad
 J^{-1}(r)=e^{-2/\sqrt r}.\] The printed comparison in (3.28) is \(e^{-1/\sqrt r}\). Their ratio is \(e^{-1/\sqrt r}\to0\), so they are not comparable in the stated sense.
result: Impact: False intermediate inverse comparison; the final critical gauge exponent survives the explicit calculation and corrected logarithmic argument.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use logarithmic comparability/two exponential bounds. Also read the displayed J(s) asymptotics on pp.14-15 near zero, not the printed near-infinity label.

problems.title: The zero-measure branch takes the auxiliary parameter in the wrong direction; image-content labels are inconsistent with m>=n.
problems.source_location: pp.27-28, proof of Theorem3.7 and equation(5.28)
claim: The zero-measure branch takes the auxiliary parameter in the wrong direction; image-content labels are inconsistent with m>=n.
analysis: Location. Pages 27–28, especially (5.28) and the following paragraph.

When \(\mathcal L^n(E)=0\), the bound involves \[\frac{[B^{-1}(r)]^n}{r}=\Phi_B(1/r).\] It tends to zero as \(r\to\infty\), not as \(r\to0\). For \(n=1\), \(A(t)=4t^2\), it equals \(1/(2\sqrt r)\) and diverges at zero. Reverse the printed limiting direction.

The cube cover directly controls \[\mathcal H_\infty^n(u(E))\le\sum_i\operatorname{diam}(u(Q_i))^n\] in \(\mathbb R^m\). The printed \(\mathcal L^n(u(E))\) on pp. 27–28 should retain this content label, especially since \(m>n\) is allowed. With \(V=\mathcal L^n(E)>0\), the choice \[r=\frac{\kappa}{n^{n/2}V}\] in the corrected cover estimate gives exactly \[2\kappa^{n+1}\|\nabla u\|_{L^A}^n
 \Phi_B\!\left(\frac{n^{n/2}V}{\kappa}\right).\] For \(V=0\), use \(r\to\infty\). Exhaustion and content continuity from below give the general-set conclusion. These corrections complete the intended step. The zero-content case of Theorem 3.5 can similarly cite Theorem 3.1(ii), which also covers \(\varphi(r)=r^n\), instead of relying on the more restricted Theorem 3.4.
result: Impact: Incorrect limiting direction and labels in a proof; the corrected cover argument proves the intended step without changing Theorem3.7.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use r->infinity for zero volume and H^n_infinity for all target images in the proof. Zero-content cases of Theorem3.5 may invoke3.1(ii), covering phi=r^n as well.

problems.title: The printed Cantor cylinder mass exponent is inconsistent, and exact counts cannot start at j=1 for every permitted parameter.
problems.source_location: p.32 equations(6.12)-(6.15), with the use on pp.33-34
claim: The printed Cantor cylinder mass exponent is inconsistent, and exact counts cannot start at j=1 for every permitted parameter.
analysis: Location. Page 32, (6.12)–(6.15), and their use on pp. 33–34.

The source specifies \(\#\mathcal A_j=\lfloor2^{j
u}floor\) and \(0<\mathcal H^\varphi(M)<\infty\), but (6.14) gives cylinder mass at most \(c2^{-j}\). The allowed value \(
u=1/2\) yields \[0<\mathcal H^\varphi(M)
 \le c\lfloor2^{j/2}floor2^{-j}
 \le c2^{-j/2}\longrightarrow0,\] a contradiction. The required and subsequently used bound on p. 34 is \(c2^{-j
u}\).

There is a separate finite-level obstruction. For \(n=1,\nu=3,j=1\), the construction asks for eight different dyadic intervals of length \(1/4\) in \([0,1]\), where only four exist. The theorem permits these parameters.

A construction closing both defects. Start at sufficiently large \(j_0\) and set \[\delta_j=2^{-2^j},\qquad N_j=2^{\lfloor j
ufloor}\asymp2^{j
u}.\] Use \(N_j\) separated cubes of side \(\delta_j\), with \[b_j=N_{j+1}/N_j\le2^{\lceil
uceil}\] children per parent. There are enough dyadic locations for all \(j\ge j_0\); choose the initial cubes and expanded cutoff supports inside a fixed compact subset of \((0,1)^n\). Give each level-\(j\) cylinder natural mass \(1/N_j\).

For \(\delta_{j+1}\le r\le\delta_j\), a radius-\(r\) ball intersects only a dimensional bounded number of level-\(j\) dyadic cubes. Since adjacent gauge values have bounded ratio, \[\mu(B(x,r))\le C/N_j\le C2^{-j\nu}\le C'\varphi(r).\] The mass-distribution argument gives positive \(\mathcal H^\varphi(M)\), and level covers give finite measure. Covering a fixed cylinder by its descendants gives \[\mathcal H^\varphi(Q\cap M)\le C/N_j\le C2^{-j\nu}.\] The later proof needs these comparisons and bounded branching, not the exact integer-part count in (6.12).

The norm cancellation remains \[-\frac{\nu}{\sigma}+\frac{\nu}{n}
       +\frac{q-n+1}{n}=0.\] Bounded overlap also supplies the \(\ell^1\) condition required in Lemma 6.4, although p. 34 states only \(\ell^\infty\): \[\sum_Q|a_Q(x,y)|
 \le C\sum_jj^{-\delta}2^{-j\nu/\sigma}<\infty.\] Retaining the fixed comparison constant in the level-\(j+2\) separation estimate yields a kernel bound \(Cj^{\delta\sigma-\mu}2^{j\nu}\). The cylinder mass cancels its exponential factor, leaving \[C\sum_jj^{\delta\sigma-\mu}<\infty
 \quad\text{for}\quad
 1<\delta<\frac{\mu-1}{\sigma}.\] This interval is nonempty by \(\mu>1+\sigma\). The replacement construction supplies the same sharpness conclusion within the checked scope.

Dependency and scope. Theorem 6.2’s finite-energy estimate on p. 34 explicitly uses the cylinder-mass assertion (6.14). The required \(2^{-j\nu}\) factor cancels the kernel’s \(2^{j\nu}\), leaving the summable polynomial series. The incompatible p. 32 data do not supply a set and measure with these properties. Thus the printed proof lacks the admissible witness needed for its central sharpness conclusion, warranting Major classification. The replacement construction verifies the required estimates without validating the original one or refuting the corrected theorem.
result: Impact: The incompatible p32 data cannot supply the admissible set and measure used in Theorem6.2. The p34 finite-energy proof needs cylinder factor2^(-jnu) to cancel kernel2^(jnu). This absent witness is a Major core construction failure. The explicit replacement verifies the required estimates; the corrected sharpness conclusion is not refuted.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use2^{-jnu}, begin at sufficiently fine levels, and use asymptotic counts with bounded integer branching. State the l1 justification and retain fixed comparison constants.

report: Abstract: The initial assessment is Major. The admitted two-dimensional zero-parameter case invalidates the proposed nonlocal inner products and coercivity theorem. The zero-frequency compatibility conditions are vacuous as printed and admit elementary unsolvable data. Independently, the mixed Hodge–Laplace representation has reversed boundary signs, with an explicit counterexample at a positive parameter and with smooth data on each side. Further confirmed issues concern an overstated Newton-potential range, insufficient hypotheses for the graph traces used in representation formulas, and degree-inconsistent displayed operators. Concrete counterexamples, counterevidence and bounded repairs are supplied. The positive-parameter structural idea is not refuted as a whole. Scientific decision and adjudication remain pending.
Date: Frozen batch M25-0248; initial review, decision pending

Title: Initial scientific review of
Boundary integral exterior calculus
Article. Erick Schulz, Ralf Hiptmair and Stefan Kurz. Journal identifier: 10.4171/JEMS/1621.

Version examined. ETH SAM Research Report 2022-36, July 2022, whose cover specifies latest revision August 2022; 39 PDF pages. Below, p. means the printed page, and its PDF page is one greater. PDF page 1 is the cover. The publisher records online publication on 26 March 2025. The SAM directory also lists a December 2022 revision. Neither that later revision nor the journal version was acquired or compared in this review. The frozen 2025 identifier is retained, but every mathematical finding below is restricted to the actual August 2022 file.
# Scope and mathematical mechanism

The primary reviewer read all 39 source-text pages and actually inspected all 39 rendered source pages. Their roles, actual text and image ranges, and developer-provided model self-reports are recorded separately from the controller’s UI observation. This is an initial review, not independent acceptance.

The paper starts with \(D=d+\delta\) and \(-\Delta_\ell=d_{\ell-1}\delta_\ell+\delta_{\ell+1}d_\ell\). Tangential and normal traces generate two boundary de Rham complexes. Atomic potentials \(S_\lambda^\ell\) and \(D_\lambda^\ell\) are formed from the Newton potential and dual trace maps. Their commutation and jump identities lead to representations and first-kind boundary integral operators. The intended structural identification is made through bilinear forms and the nonlocal boundary inner products, rather than an unqualified equality of maps between different pivot spaces.

Valid potential spaces and positive boundary products are required to define the Hilbert adjoints used in the boundary Hodge structure. The distinction between \(\lambda>0\) and \(\lambda=0\), and between a maximal distributional domain and the separate \(d,\delta\) graph domains, is essential. The review checked these distinctions, endpoint degrees, signs, compatibility, and the mixed Schur complements. The full general Lipschitz trace theory, compact-manifold kernel theory and external Gaffney theorems were not independently reproved. No paper-specific supplement or code artifact was acquired in the bounded searches; this is an access/coverage limitation, not a mathematical defect.
# Confirmed issues
## F1. Zero-parameter coercivity fails in the allowed dimension two (Major)
Location. Assumption A, p. 17 (PDF 18); (3.15a) and Lemma 3.5, p. 19; Theorem 3.6, p. 20; (3.17)–(3.22), p. 21. Dependent structural conclusions occur on pp. 25–26, 30 and 34.

Take \(M=\mathbb R^2\), \(\Omega=B_R\), \(\ell=0\), \(\lambda=0\) and the nonzero smooth density \(h=1\) on \(\partial B_R\). These are permitted by Assumption A. For the logarithmic fundamental solution \[\Phi_0(r)=c-\frac{1}{2\pi}\log r\] with any fixed real constant \(c\), the circular logarithmic average gives \[tS_0^0h=R(2\pi c-\log R),\qquad
 (h,h)_{-1/2,0,t}=2\pi R^2(2\pi c-\log R).\] For completeness, the average of \(\log|e^{it}-e^{is}|\) is zero: it is the boundary limit of the zero mean of \(\log|1-\rho e^{i(s-t)}|\) for \(0<\rho<1\), with the integrable logarithmic singularity allowing the limit. Thus at \(R=e^{2\pi c}\) the proposed norm vanishes on a nonzero density; at larger radii it is negative. For the standard normalization \(c=0\), the unit disk already contradicts the coercive lower bound in Theorem 3.6.

The exterior energy explains the failure of the proof. With \(c=0\), \[S_0^0h(x)=-R\log|x| \quad (|x|>R),\qquad
 \int_{R<|x|<T}|\nabla S_0^0h|^2\,dx
   =2\pi R^2\log(T/R)\longrightarrow\infty.\] Consequently, the finite whole-space energy identity used in Lemma 3.5 is unavailable here. Boundedness of \(\Omega\) does not remove the exterior contribution at infinity. Adding a constant to the kernel does not change this energy obstruction, and a fixed constant cannot make the asserted product positive for every bounded domain.

There are also two distinguishable errors in the displayed coercivity proof. At \(\lambda=0\), the whole-space inhomogeneous \(H^1\) equivalence (3.21) fails: for \(V_R(x)=\chi(x/R)\), \[\|V_R\|_2^2=R^N\|\chi\|_2^2,\qquad
 \|\nabla V_R\|_2^2=R^{N-2}\|\nabla\chi\|_2^2.\] Further, the dual suprema in (3.17) and (3.22) are homogeneous of degree one in the density, whereas the displayed squared norms are homogeneous of degree two. Formula (3.18) should use a global variational identity on \(M\), not just \(\Omega\).

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The introduction emphasizes positive shifts, and compact manifolds are explicitly restricted to positive parameters. Neither fact cancels the Euclidean zero case admitted later. The counterexample does not refute the Yukawa case \(\lambda>0\), or establish failure of standard zero-parameter single-layer coercivity in \(N\ge3\). For \(\lambda>0\), a corrected proof starts from the unsquared dual norm, uses a bounded global trace lifting and \[a_\lambda(S_\lambda h,V)=\langle h,tV\rangle_\Gamma,\] applies Cauchy–Schwarz and the positive-parameter energy equivalence, and squares at the end. A low-dimensional zero-parameter theory instead needs explicit charge/capacity restrictions or a changed normalization and space, with corresponding new proofs. Since the boundary Hilbert products underlie the main adjoint and Fredholm arguments, this is a substantive scope defect.
## F2. The zero-frequency compatibility kernels are interchanged (Major)
Location. (2.4a,b) and (2.5a,b), p. 8 (PDF 9); the compatibility discussion and (2.9b), p. 9.

By definition, \(nV=0\) on \(\ker D_n\) and \(tV=0\) on \(\ker D_t\). Hence the printed conditions \[\langle g,nV\rangle_\Gamma=0\quad(V\in\ker D_n),\qquad
 \langle h,tV\rangle_\Gamma=0\quad(V\in\ker D_t)\] are both automatic.

Let \(\Omega\) be the unit disk in \(\mathbb R^2\) and \(\kappa=0\). Prescribe only the tangential degree-one component \(g_1=d\theta\), with all other components zero. Any \(DU=0\) in the declared graph domain must satisfy \(dU_1=0\). Weak Stokes gives \[0=\int_\Omega dU_1=\int_{\partial\Omega}tU_1,
 \qquad
 \int_{\partial\Omega}g_1=2\pi,\] so no solution exists, although (2.5a) is satisfied. Likewise, prescribing only the normal scalar component \(h_0=1\) is incompatible with \(\delta U_1=0\), because its total outward flux is \(2\pi\) instead of zero.

The correct tangential compatibility tests against \(\ker D_t\), and the correct normal compatibility tests against \(\ker D_n\). The constant volume form in \(\ker D_t\) detects the first obstruction; the constant scalar in \(\ker D_n\) detects the second. The right-hand side of (2.9b) should also involve \(tV\), as in (2.8b), rather than the printed \(nV\).

Impact and limits. These examples disprove the asserted solvability of the original zero-frequency problems, including on an orthogonal complement. A solvable augmented system with a nonzero harmonic multiplier does not solve the original homogeneous equation. The kernel-label correction is short, but it changes the actual compatibility criterion and is central to the stated BVP scope. The nonzero-\(\kappa\) problems are not counterexamples.
## F3. The mixed representation has reversed boundary signs (Major)
Location. Proposition 4.6 and its proof, p. 31 (PDF 32); potential definitions, p. 32. Compare the general scheme on p. 22 and the jump convention on p. 18.

This is an explicit pointwise discrepancy away from the boundary. The radial Yukawa potential is \[q(r)=
 \begin{cases}
 1-\dfrac2e\,\dfrac{\sinh r}{r},&0<r<1,\\[4pt]
 \dfrac{e^{-(r+1)}}r,&r>1.
 \end{cases}\] With \(q(0)=1-2/e\), it is regular at zero, is \(C^1\) at \(r=1\), solves \((-\Delta+1)q=1\) inside and \(0\) outside, and decays at infinity. At \(r=2\), the printed first component is \(e^{-3}>0\), while \(U_0=0\). These identities were also checked symbolically from the displayed radial functions.

Correct form and dependency. With the potential definitions retained on p. 32, the representation must read \[U=N[M]F-\operatorname{SL}[M]\,[T_M^nU]+\operatorname{DL}[M]\,[T_M^tU].\] In the example, the corrected formula applies \(A\) to \((-q,-P)\) and recovers \(\mathbf1_{B_1}\). In general, distributional differentiation gives the normal source vector \(-(t'_{\ell-1}[n_\ell U_\ell],t'_\ell[n_{\ell+1}d_\ell U_\ell])\) and the tangential source vector \((0,n'_\ell[t_{\ell-1}U_{\ell-1}]+\delta_{\ell+1}n'_{\ell+1}[t_\ell U_\ell])\). Applying the stated inverse gives exactly these corrected signs.

A related display on p. 28 (PDF 29) gives the normal jump of \(\operatorname{SL}[\Delta]\) as the positive input vector. It must be its negative, consistent with (3.14b). For the scalar Laplace single layer of constant density on the unit sphere, the potential is \(1\) inside and \(1/r\) outside, so the normal-derivative jump is \(-1\).

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The outer differential factor in Proposition 4.6 is present: actual image inspection shows that the large parenthesis encloses every term. An earlier missing-factor candidate was rejected. The confirmed sign error is different and survives positive parameters and regular graph traces. Reverse the two boundary signs in the proposition and its proof and recheck the Calderón equations with the fixed convention. The structural weak forms of the separately defined BIOs are not thereby disproved. Nevertheless, a central representation theorem used to connect the BVP and BIE is false as printed, which warrants Major classification.
## F4. The Newton-potential range is too strong across its source (Minor)
Location. The graph-space definitions on p. 3 (PDF 4), (3.3) on p. 17, and Lemma 3.3 on p. 18.

The asserted mapping from \(H^{-1}_{\mathrm{comp}}\) includes \(H_{\mathrm{loc}}\Lambda(\Delta,M)\), whose definition requires the relevant second derivatives to be locally square-integrable. In \(M=\mathbb R\), with \(\lambda=1\), \[f=\delta_0\in H^{-1}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbb R),\qquad
 N_1^0f(x)=\tfrac12e^{-|x|}.\] Membership of \(\delta_0\) in \(H^{-1}\) follows from the finite integral \(\int_\mathbb R(1+\xi^2)^{-1}\,d\xi\). The potential is in \(H^1\), but its first derivative has jump \(-1\), and \[(N_1^0f)''=N_1^0f-\delta_0\notin L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}.\] In higher dimensions a nonzero smooth hypersurface density \(t'h\in H^{-1}\setminus L^2\) gives the same contradiction by applying \(-\Delta+\lambda\) to the proposed graph-regular potential.

Impact and repair. Keep the global \(H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\) conclusion and restrict second-order regularity to the complement of the source support, or strengthen the source class. For the intended boundary graph densities, \(\delta S h=S\delta h\) gives sidewise \(d\delta S h\in L^2\); the homogeneous side equation then gives \(\delta dS h\in L^2\). Thus the surplus across-source regularity can be removed without changing the intended sidewise potential calculus. This explicit closure, rather than mere presumed repairability, supports the Minor classification.
## F5. The representation hypotheses do not provide the declared traces (Minor)
Location. Proposition 4.3 and its proof, pp. 23–24 (PDF 24–25); Proposition 4.5, p. 27; graph domains on pp. 3–4.

In the unit disk take the holomorphic series \[f(z)=\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-1/2}z^k=u+iw\] and extend its real and imaginary parts by zero outside. Orthogonality gives \[\int_{B_1}|u|^2=\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{k(k+1)}
 =\frac{\pi}{2},
 \qquad
 \int_{B_1}|\nabla u|^2=\pi\sum_{k\ge1}1=\infty.\] The scalar function is piecewise harmonic and satisfies the printed assumptions of Proposition 4.5 with \(F=\lambda u\), even for \(\lambda>0\). But its boundary Fourier series is not in \(H^{1/2}(S^1)=H^{-1/2}\Lambda^0(d,S^1)\), the declared tangential graph-trace space.

For Proposition 4.3 set \(U=u-w\,dx\wedge dy\). The Cauchy–Riemann equations give \[\delta(-w\,dx\wedge dy)=-du,\qquad DU=0\] on each side. For any \(\kappa\ne0\), take \(F=i\kappa U\). The compactly supported \(L^2\) and piecewise equation assumptions hold, but \(dU\) and \(\delta U\) are not separately \(L^2\). Hence \[U\notin H\Lambda(D)
 =H\Lambda(d)\cap H\Lambda(\delta),\] contrary to the regularity implication used to justify the independent traces.

Impact and repair boundary. Require the appropriate piecewise componentwise graph domains in these propositions. Those are precisely the domains of the intended BVPs and of the Green identities used in the proofs. Alternatively, explicitly develop maximal-domain weak traces and their larger distribution spaces. This finding does not deny the existence of such weak traces or disprove a suitably extended representation theorem. Restricting to the already-declared BVP domains closes this domain issue, while the regular example in F3 remains a counterexample to its printed signs.
## F6. Degree labels in several operator displays are inconsistent (Minor)
All corrections follow from the stated maps \(d_j:\Lambda^j\to\Lambda^{j+1}\), \(\delta_j:\Lambda^j\to\Lambda^{j-1}\), \(\star_j:\Lambda^j\to\Lambda^{N-j}\).

- The full-star matrix must satisfy \((\star U)_i=\star_{N-i}U_{N-i}\). Its top-right block is \(\star_N\), and its bottom-left block is \(\star_0\), the reverse of (1.5). Already \(N=1\) detects the domain mismatch.
- In (3.7), \(D_\lambda^\ell=N_\lambda^\ell n_\ell'\), not \(N_\lambda^\ell n_{\ell-1}'\). In (3.15b), the normal pairing uses \(n_{\ell+1}D_\lambda^{\ell+1}\), not \(n_{\ell+1}D_\lambda^\ell\).
- The upper-right block of (4.16b), (4.19b) and Fig. 4 is \(-d_{\ell-1}^*\); the analogous bulk block in (2.28a) is \(d_{\ell-1}^*\). The printed \(d_\ell^*\) has the wrong input and output degrees.

- In (2.21), \(d_{\ell+1}\delta_\ell\) must be \(d_{\ell-1}\delta_\ell\). In (2.25) and Fig. 4, \(d_\ell V_{\ell-1}\) must be \(d_{\ell-1}V_{\ell-1}\). The tangential product below (2.16) must be ordered \((\ell-1,\ell)\), consistently with (1.16).

The adjoint error can be tested against the preceding weak form. On \(S^1\), choose \(\ell=1\), \(\lambda>0\), \(g_1=d_0(\sin\theta)\), \(v_0=\sin\theta\), and \(g_0=v_1=0\). Formula (4.15) gives \(-\|g_1\|_{-1/2,\lambda,n}^2<0\). The printed block \(d_1^*\) is not defined on a one-form; extending that zero top-degree operator by zero cannot produce this response. The corrected matrix is \[W=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 I&-d_{\ell-1}^*\\
 -d_{\ell-1}&-d_\ell^*d_\ell-\lambda I
 \end{pmatrix},\] whose Schur complement is \(-(d_{\ell-1}d_{\ell-1}^*+d_\ell^*d_\ell+\lambda I)\). The intended positive-parameter Hodge–Laplace structure is thereby restored. The correctly typed weak forms are counterevidence against interpreting these display errors as a failure of every underlying structural argument.
# Positive checks, limitations and recommendation

Actual source images show the necessary outer grouping in both (4.8) and Proposition 4.6, and the relevant conjugations and absolute values in the complex coercivity argument. These text-extraction candidates were explicitly excluded. In a valid nonlocal Hilbert complex, self-adjointness gives \[\|(T-i\kappa)x\|^2=\|Tx\|^2+\kappa^2\|x\|^2,\] supporting the nonzero imaginary-shift argument. The corrected mixed matrix has the expected positive Laplace Schur complement. In a legitimate zero-parameter complex, the kernels of the two mixed operators correspond to harmonic degrees \(\ell-1\) and \(\ell\), respectively; the review does not reject the abstract Hilbert-complex theory.

The required substantive revisions to this frozen version are an explicit valid parameter/domain range for the nonlocal products, the correct zero-mode compatibility conditions, and a consistent representation/jump-sign derivation. The graph-domain and degree corrections should then be propagated through the displayed statements and summary figures. A corrected positive-parameter theory is plausible and is supported by several checked identities, but that observation cannot certify the printed statements or the unexamined journal version.

The evidence package contains per-finding hypotheses, exact source pages, proofs, counterevidence and repair limits; a reviewer-authored symbolic check; actual image-inspection records; the current TeX/PDF/compiler/dependency hashes; and retained earlier candidates and tool failures. No author code was executed. Final scientific decision and human review remain pending.

problems.title: The nonlocal inner products and coercivity fail in the admitted two-dimensional zero-parameter case
problems.source_location: PDF18/printed17, Assumption A PDF20/printed19, (3.15a), Lemma3.5 PDF21/printed20, Theorem3.6 PDF22/printed21, (3.17)–(3.22) PDF26–27,31,35: dependent boundary Hilbert-complex conclusions
claim: Recorded check: The nonlocal inner products and coercivity fail in the admitted two-dimensional zero-parameter case
analysis: Location. Assumption A, p. 17 (PDF 18); (3.15a) and Lemma 3.5, p. 19; Theorem 3.6, p. 20; (3.17)–(3.22), p. 21. Dependent structural conclusions occur on pp. 25–26, 30 and 34.

Take \(M=\mathbb R^2\), \(\Omega=B_R\), \(\ell=0\), \(\lambda=0\) and the nonzero smooth density \(h=1\) on \(\partial B_R\). These are permitted by Assumption A. For the logarithmic fundamental solution \[\Phi_0(r)=c-\frac{1}{2\pi}\log r\] with any fixed real constant \(c\), the circular logarithmic average gives \[tS_0^0h=R(2\pi c-\log R),\qquad
 (h,h)_{-1/2,0,t}=2\pi R^2(2\pi c-\log R).\] For completeness, the average of \(\log|e^{it}-e^{is}|\) is zero: it is the boundary limit of the zero mean of \(\log|1-\rho e^{i(s-t)}|\) for \(0<\rho<1\), with the integrable logarithmic singularity allowing the limit. Thus at \(R=e^{2\pi c}\) the proposed norm vanishes on a nonzero density; at larger radii it is negative. For the standard normalization \(c=0\), the unit disk already contradicts the coercive lower bound in Theorem 3.6.

The exterior energy explains the failure of the proof. With \(c=0\), \[S_0^0h(x)=-R\log|x| \quad (|x|>R),\qquad
 \int_{R<|x|<T}|\nabla S_0^0h|^2\,dx
   =2\pi R^2\log(T/R)\longrightarrow\infty.\] Consequently, the finite whole-space energy identity used in Lemma 3.5 is unavailable here. Boundedness of \(\Omega\) does not remove the exterior contribution at infinity. Adding a constant to the kernel does not change this energy obstruction, and a fixed constant cannot make the asserted product positive for every bounded domain.

There are also two distinguishable errors in the displayed coercivity proof. At \(\lambda=0\), the whole-space inhomogeneous \(H^1\) equivalence (3.21) fails: for \(V_R(x)=\chi(x/R)\), \[\|V_R\|_2^2=R^N\|\chi\|_2^2,\qquad
 \|\nabla V_R\|_2^2=R^{N-2}\|\nabla\chi\|_2^2.\] Further, the dual suprema in (3.17) and (3.22) are homogeneous of degree one in the density, whereas the displayed squared norms are homogeneous of degree two. Formula (3.18) should use a global variational identity on \(M\), not just \(\Omega\).

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The introduction emphasizes positive shifts, and compact manifolds are explicitly restricted to positive parameters. Neither fact cancels the Euclidean zero case admitted later. The counterexample does not refute the Yukawa case \(\lambda>0\), or establish failure of standard zero-parameter single-layer coercivity in \(N\ge3\). For \(\lambda>0\), a corrected proof starts from the unsquared dual norm, uses a bounded global trace lifting and \[a_\lambda(S_\lambda h,V)=\langle h,tV\rangle_\Gamma,\] applies Cauchy–Schwarz and the positive-parameter energy equivalence, and squares at the end. A low-dimensional zero-parameter theory instead needs explicit charge/capacity restrictions or a changed normalization and space, with corresponding new proofs. Since the boundary Hilbert products underlie the main adjoint and Fredholm arguments, this is a substantive scope defect.

problems.title: The zero-frequency compatibility conditions are vacuous because the two kernels are interchanged
problems.source_location: PDF9/printed8, (2.4a,b), (2.5a,b) PDF10/printed9, (2.9b) and compatibility discussion
claim: Recorded check: The zero-frequency compatibility conditions are vacuous because the two kernels are interchanged
analysis: Location. (2.4a,b) and (2.5a,b), p. 8 (PDF 9); the compatibility discussion and (2.9b), p. 9.

By definition, \(nV=0\) on \(\ker D_n\) and \(tV=0\) on \(\ker D_t\). Hence the printed conditions \[\langle g,nV\rangle_\Gamma=0\quad(V\in\ker D_n),\qquad
 \langle h,tV\rangle_\Gamma=0\quad(V\in\ker D_t)\] are both automatic.

Let \(\Omega\) be the unit disk in \(\mathbb R^2\) and \(\kappa=0\). Prescribe only the tangential degree-one component \(g_1=d\theta\), with all other components zero. Any \(DU=0\) in the declared graph domain must satisfy \(dU_1=0\). Weak Stokes gives \[0=\int_\Omega dU_1=\int_{\partial\Omega}tU_1,
 \qquad
 \int_{\partial\Omega}g_1=2\pi,\] so no solution exists, although (2.5a) is satisfied. Likewise, prescribing only the normal scalar component \(h_0=1\) is incompatible with \(\delta U_1=0\), because its total outward flux is \(2\pi\) instead of zero.

The correct tangential compatibility tests against \(\ker D_t\), and the correct normal compatibility tests against \(\ker D_n\). The constant volume form in \(\ker D_t\) detects the first obstruction; the constant scalar in \(\ker D_n\) detects the second. The right-hand side of (2.9b) should also involve \(tV\), as in (2.8b), rather than the printed \(nV\).

Impact and limits. These examples disprove the asserted solvability of the original zero-frequency problems, including on an orthogonal complement. A solvable augmented system with a nonzero harmonic multiplier does not solve the original homogeneous equation. The kernel-label correction is short, but it changes the actual compatibility criterion and is central to the stated BVP scope. The nonzero-\(\kappa\) problems are not counterexamples.

problems.title: The mixed Hodge–Laplace representation has reversed boundary signs
problems.source_location: PDF32/printed31, Proposition4.6 and proof PDF33/printed32, definitions of SL[M], DL[M] PDF19/printed18, jump convention and (3.14b) PDF23/printed22, general representation and Calderon scheme PDF29/printed28, displayed normal jump of SL[Delta]
claim: Recorded check: The mixed Hodge–Laplace representation has reversed boundary signs
analysis: Location. Proposition 4.6 and its proof, p. 31 (PDF 32); potential definitions, p. 32. Compare the general scheme on p. 22 and the jump convention on p. 18.

This is an explicit pointwise discrepancy away from the boundary. The radial Yukawa potential is \[q(r)=
 \begin{cases}
 1-\dfrac2e\,\dfrac{\sinh r}{r},&0<r<1,\\[4pt]
 \dfrac{e^{-(r+1)}}r,&r>1.
 \end{cases}\] With \(q(0)=1-2/e\), it is regular at zero, is \(C^1\) at \(r=1\), solves \((-\Delta+1)q=1\) inside and \(0\) outside, and decays at infinity. At \(r=2\), the printed first component is \(e^{-3}>0\), while \(U_0=0\). These identities were also checked symbolically from the displayed radial functions.

Correct form and dependency. With the potential definitions retained on p. 32, the representation must read \[U=N[M]F-\operatorname{SL}[M]\,[T_M^nU]+\operatorname{DL}[M]\,[T_M^tU].\] In the example, the corrected formula applies \(A\) to \((-q,-P)\) and recovers \(\mathbf1_{B_1}\). In general, distributional differentiation gives the normal source vector \(-(t'_{\ell-1}[n_\ell U_\ell],t'_\ell[n_{\ell+1}d_\ell U_\ell])\) and the tangential source vector \((0,n'_\ell[t_{\ell-1}U_{\ell-1}]+\delta_{\ell+1}n'_{\ell+1}[t_\ell U_\ell])\). Applying the stated inverse gives exactly these corrected signs.

A related display on p. 28 (PDF 29) gives the normal jump of \(\operatorname{SL}[\Delta]\) as the positive input vector. It must be its negative, consistent with (3.14b). For the scalar Laplace single layer of constant density on the unit sphere, the potential is \(1\) inside and \(1/r\) outside, so the normal-derivative jump is \(-1\).

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The outer differential factor in Proposition 4.6 is present: actual image inspection shows that the large parenthesis encloses every term. An earlier missing-factor candidate was rejected. The confirmed sign error is different and survives positive parameters and regular graph traces. Reverse the two boundary signs in the proposition and its proof and recheck the Calderón equations with the fixed convention. The structural weak forms of the separately defined BIOs are not thereby disproved. Nevertheless, a central representation theorem used to connect the BVP and BIE is false as printed, which warrants Major classification.

problems.title: The Newton-potential target in (3.3) incorrectly includes second-order graph regularity across its source
problems.source_location: PDF4/printed3, definitions of H Lambda(Delta) PDF18/printed17, (3.3) PDF19/printed18, Lemma3.3
claim: Recorded check: The Newton-potential target in (3.3) incorrectly includes second-order graph regularity across its source
analysis: Location. The graph-space definitions on p. 3 (PDF 4), (3.3) on p. 17, and Lemma 3.3 on p. 18.

The asserted mapping from \(H^{-1}_{\mathrm{comp}}\) includes \(H_{\mathrm{loc}}\Lambda(\Delta,M)\), whose definition requires the relevant second derivatives to be locally square-integrable. In \(M=\mathbb R\), with \(\lambda=1\), \[f=\delta_0\in H^{-1}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbb R),\qquad
 N_1^0f(x)=\tfrac12e^{-|x|}.\] Membership of \(\delta_0\) in \(H^{-1}\) follows from the finite integral \(\int_\mathbb R(1+\xi^2)^{-1}\,d\xi\). The potential is in \(H^1\), but its first derivative has jump \(-1\), and \[(N_1^0f)''=N_1^0f-\delta_0\notin L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}.\] In higher dimensions a nonzero smooth hypersurface density \(t'h\in H^{-1}\setminus L^2\) gives the same contradiction by applying \(-\Delta+\lambda\) to the proposed graph-regular potential.

Impact and repair. Keep the global \(H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\) conclusion and restrict second-order regularity to the complement of the source support, or strengthen the source class. For the intended boundary graph densities, \(\delta S h=S\delta h\) gives sidewise \(d\delta S h\in L^2\); the homogeneous side equation then gives \(\delta dS h\in L^2\). Thus the surplus across-source regularity can be removed without changing the intended sidewise potential calculus. This explicit closure, rather than mere presumed repairability, supports the Minor classification.

problems.title: The representation hypotheses do not imply the componentwise graph traces used in their proofs
problems.source_location: PDF4–5/printed3–4, graph domains PDF24–25/printed23–24, Proposition4.3 and trace assertion PDF28/printed27, Proposition4.5
claim: Recorded check: The representation hypotheses do not imply the componentwise graph traces used in their proofs
analysis: Location. Proposition 4.3 and its proof, pp. 23–24 (PDF 24–25); Proposition 4.5, p. 27; graph domains on pp. 3–4.

In the unit disk take the holomorphic series \[f(z)=\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-1/2}z^k=u+iw\] and extend its real and imaginary parts by zero outside. Orthogonality gives \[\int_{B_1}|u|^2=\frac{\pi}{2}\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{k(k+1)}
 =\frac{\pi}{2},
 \qquad
 \int_{B_1}|\nabla u|^2=\pi\sum_{k\ge1}1=\infty.\] The scalar function is piecewise harmonic and satisfies the printed assumptions of Proposition 4.5 with \(F=\lambda u\), even for \(\lambda>0\). But its boundary Fourier series is not in \(H^{1/2}(S^1)=H^{-1/2}\Lambda^0(d,S^1)\), the declared tangential graph-trace space.

For Proposition 4.3 set \(U=u-w\,dx\wedge dy\). The Cauchy–Riemann equations give \[\delta(-w\,dx\wedge dy)=-du,\qquad DU=0\] on each side. For any \(\kappa\ne0\), take \(F=i\kappa U\). The compactly supported \(L^2\) and piecewise equation assumptions hold, but \(dU\) and \(\delta U\) are not separately \(L^2\). Hence \[U\notin H\Lambda(D)
 =H\Lambda(d)\cap H\Lambda(\delta),\] contrary to the regularity implication used to justify the independent traces.

Impact and repair boundary. Require the appropriate piecewise componentwise graph domains in these propositions. Those are precisely the domains of the intended BVPs and of the Green identities used in the proofs. Alternatively, explicitly develop maximal-domain weak traces and their larger distribution spaces. This finding does not deny the existence of such weak traces or disprove a suitably extended representation theorem. Restricting to the already-declared BVP domains closes this domain issue, while the regular example in F3 remains a counterexample to its printed signs.

report: Abstract: The initial assessment is Major. The coefficient \(O_3\) in the sonic-coordinate equation is algebraically inconsistent with the original potential-flow equation. An exact, strictly elliptic local solution gives residual \(1/192\) in the printed transformed equation. The same coefficient prevents the cancellation of lower-order terms claimed in constructing the iteration operator. This affects a core proof dependency, even though a concrete correction is available and the leading sonic degeneracy appears unchanged. Two further Major derivation errors affect the radial comparison used in the subsonic-corner hodograph argument and the twice-differentiated identity used for shock joining in Theorem 2.2(i). Their corrected arguments restore the specified local steps. Four other groups of bounded errors concern mapping estimates, vacuum, the normal endpoint and Bernoulli algebra. The global existence, regularity and convexity theorems themselves have not been disproved. Scientific decision and adjudication remain pending.
