Title: Initial scientific review of
Global solutions of the two-dimensional Riemann problem with four-shock interactions for the Euler equations for potential flow
Article and binding. Gui-Qiang G. Chen, Alex Cliffe, Feimin Huang, Song Liu and Qin Wang. Frozen journal identifier: 10.4171/JEMS/1622.

Version examined. The acquired file is arXiv:2305.15224v1, submitted 24 May 2023, with PDF date 25 May 2023 and 75 pages. Page numbers below are both printed and 1-based PDF page numbers. The frozen title uses of potential flow and the frozen author field is Alexander J. Cliffe; the actual PDF uses for potential flow and Alex Cliffe. These fields are retained separately. The publisher records online publication on 14 April 2025 and requires a subscription. No equivalence to the journal version has been established. All findings below concern the acquired v1.
# Scope, hypotheses and dependency chain

The primary reviewer fully read all 75 source-text pages and actually inspected 55 rendered source pages, including every page used below as evidence. Their text ranges, absence of independent image inspection, and developer-provided model self-reports are recorded in the supporting files. The primary reviewer independently evaluated the calculations and arguments reported here. This is initial scientific review, not independent acceptance or human review.

The model is compressible, irrotational, isentropic potential flow. It is not the full Euler system with arbitrary vorticity. In self-similar coordinates, the pseudo-potential \(\varphi\) satisfies \[\operatorname{div}(\rho\mathrm D\varphi)+2\rho=0,\qquad
 \rho=\left(1+(\gamma-1)
       \left(B-\frac{|\mathrm D\varphi|^2}{2}-\varphi\right)\right)^{1/(\gamma-1)},\] with the exponential interpretation for \(\gamma=1\). The physical self-similar potential is \(\phi=\varphi+|\boldsymbol\xi|^2/2\). The normalization is \(\rho_2=\rho_4=1\), \(u_2=v_1=0\), \(B=v_2^2/2\) and \(v_{\min}<v_2<0\). The two incident angle pairs are related by reflection symmetry, leaving two independent angles, not four arbitrary independent incoming shocks.

Compatibility fixes the incident densities using \[\ell(\rho,1)=\sqrt{\frac{2(\rho-1)h(\rho)}{\rho+1}},
 \qquad
 \ell(\rho_1,1)\cos\theta_1
 =\ell(\rho_3,1)\cos\theta_2=-v_2.\] The vacuum critical angle, sonic angle and detachment angle have distinct roles. The theorem’s parameter region \(\Theta=[0,\theta^d)^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}\) includes unilateral zero angles and mixed reflection types. Normal reflection is an explicitly supplied limiting configuration and a base point for the degree argument. Sonic arcs collapse in the appropriate subsonic cases. These boundary cases were retained in the review.

Theorem 2.1 claims existence and convergence to normal reflection, not unrestricted uniqueness. Theorem 2.2 separates \(C^{1,1}\) regularity near noncollapsed sonic arcs from \(C^{1,\alpha}\) corner regularity and specifies the second-derivative jump and endpoint failure of a Hessian limit. Theorem 2.3 concerns strict convexity and uniform convexity on compact subarcs of the relative interior; the flat normal shock is outside \(\Theta\).

The proof proceeds through directional monotonicity and a priori estimates, moving-domain flattening, an iteration map on weighted spaces, a fixed-point index at normal reflection, and a continuation argument. At a fixed point, the shock graphs must agree and the modified equation must reduce to the original one. F1 concerns precisely this latter identification. The review also checked the normal-reflection formulas, the positivity range of the incident densities, the logic of the directional-derivative contradiction in Lemma 3.1, and the scaling in the four sonic/corner regimes. General Schauder estimates and the full external existence and convexity results cited as [1], [2], [10], [12] and [48] were not independently reproduced.
# Confirmed issues
## F1. An incorrect sonic coefficient changes the iteration equation (Major)

Location. Equations (3.24)–(3.26), pp. 25–26, especially \(O_3\) on p. 26; the modified coefficients and assertion that Cartesian lower-order terms vanish, p. 46; the fixed-point identification in Proposition 4.23, Step 3, p. 57.

For an exact rational check, set \[\gamma=2,\quad c=2,\quad x=\tfrac12,\quad
 z=\tfrac1{16},\quad p=\tfrac14,\quad q=0,\qquad
 \psi_{xx}=\psi_{xy}=0,\quad\psi_{yy}=\tfrac38.\] Then \[a=\tfrac{113}{32},\quad |\mathrm D\varphi|^2=\tfrac{49}{16},
 \quad a-|\mathrm D\varphi|^2=\tfrac{15}{32}>0,
 \quad O_3^{\rm corr}=\tfrac{41}{144},\quad
 O_3^{\rm print}=\tfrac{43}{144}.\] The original transformed equation has residual zero, while (3.25) with the printed \(O_3\) has residual \(1/192\).

This jet can be realized by an actual local constant-state solution, not merely an arbitrary Hessian. At \(r_0=c-x\) and angle \(y_0\), take \[\psi(r,y)=-p\,r\cos(y-y_0)+z+pr_0.\] This is affine in Cartesian coordinates; \(\varphi=\varphi_5+\psi\) is a constant-state pseudo-potential. At the selected point its polar derivatives are exactly those above, including \(\psi_{yy}=r_0p\). Continuity gives a strictly elliptic neighborhood. This is a local equation counterexample, not a global free-boundary counterexample.

The defect persists arbitrarily near a sonic point and for any \(c>0\). For \(\gamma=2\), \(0<x<c\), take \(p=x/2\), \(z=x^2/4\), \(q=0\) and the same affine construction. Then \[a-|\mathrm D\varphi|^2=\frac{cx}{2}-\frac{x^2}{8}>0,
 \qquad \text{printed residual}=\frac{p^3}{cr}>0.\] Thus the discrepancy cannot be dismissed as a jet far outside a small sonic neighborhood.

Core impact. After cancelling removable factors in the formula for \(O_4\), the correct coefficient satisfies \[r(1/c+O_3^{\rm corr})=1+O_4,\qquad O_5=O_2/r.\] These identities cancel the first-order terms when converting the polar equation back to Cartesian coordinates. The printed coefficient leaves an extra multiple of \(\psi_x\): \[\left(\frac{(\gamma-1)p^2}{cr}
       +\frac{\gamma q^2}{cr^3}\right)\psi_x.\] The claim on p. 46 that these terms vanish is therefore false for the stated coefficients. A cutoff construction does not create the missing algebraic identity in the region where the cutoffs leave the original quantities unchanged.

Counterevidence and repair boundary. Replacing \(O_3\) by the derived expression restores the cancellation. For gradients of order \(x\), the difference is of quadratic order, so it does not change the leading coefficient responsible for sonic degeneracy. This supports the possibility of repairing the construction. However, the actual modified operator, its estimates, and the fixed-point recovery of the Euler equation must then be rechecked with the corrected coefficient. A repair formula alone does not validate those dependencies. The \(\gamma=1\) endpoint also requires cancelling the removable \((\gamma-1)\) factors in \(O_4\) before evaluation. The classification is Major because the as-printed core operator identification fails, not because a main theorem has been shown false.
## F2. The moving-domain estimates omit essential dependence (Minor)
Location. Definition 4.7, p. 41; Lemma 4.8(iv), p. 42, and the second estimate in Lemma 4.8(vi), p. 43.

The local \(C^{2,\alpha}(K)\) estimate for the differences of \(\varphi\circ F\) and \(\psi\circ F\) is bounded only by a local norm of \(u-\widetilde u\) on \(K\) and the parameter difference. However, \(F\) depends on the top boundary trace \(u(s,1)\), which is not determined by that interior norm.

Use the permitted normal-reflection extension at \(\theta=(0,0)\), \(\gamma=2\), \(v_2=-1\). Then \[\rho_0=\frac{5+\sqrt{17}}4,\qquad
 \eta_0=\frac{\sqrt{17}-1}4>0,\qquad
 \varphi_0=-\frac{|\boldsymbol\xi|^2}{2}-\eta_0.\] Let \(\widetilde u=0\) and \(u_\varepsilon(s,t)=\varepsilon a(s)b(t)\), with \(a\) smooth, compactly supported in the middle of \((-1,1)\) and \(a(0)=1\). Choose \(b=0\) near a compact interior set \(K\) containing \((0,t_0)\) and \(b(1)=1\). For sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), the smallness requirement is satisfied; for each such smooth perturbation the required finite higher norm bound can be chosen. All side traces vanish.

The central fiber of the first flattening has \(G_1(0,\eta)=(0,\eta)\). Since \(\varphi_2-\varphi_0=\eta_0-\eta\), the perturbed shock height is \(g_\varepsilon(0)=\eta_0-\varepsilon\), and \[F_\varepsilon(0,t)=(0,t(\eta_0-\varepsilon)).\] Although \(u_\varepsilon-\widetilde u\) is identically zero near \(K\) and the parameter difference is zero, the potential difference at \((0,t_0)\) is \[(\varphi\circ F_\varepsilon-\widetilde\varphi\circ F_0)(0,t_0)
 =t_0^2\left(\eta_0\varepsilon-\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}\right)>0
 \quad (0<\varepsilon<2\eta_0).\] The asserted right-hand side vanishes, contradicting the estimate.

There is also an omitted dependence in the \(C^{2,\alpha}\) bound for \(F\) in (iv): its constant is stated to depend only on \(\gamma,v_2,\theta_*\), although the hypothesis admits an arbitrary higher norm bound \(M\) in (4.19). With fixed small \(\varepsilon\) and a central cutoff \(\chi\), choose the top trace \[a_N(s)=\varepsilon N^{-1-\alpha}\chi(s)\cos Ns.\] The \(C^{1,\alpha}\) norms remain uniformly small, while \(|a_N''(0)|=\varepsilon N^{1-\alpha}\to\infty\). Near the central fiber the height is \(\eta_0-a_N(s)\), so the second derivative of the vertical component of \(F(s,t)\) equals \(-t a_N''(s)\). Every member has a finite admissible \(M_N\), but no common bound independent of \(M_N\) is possible.

Counterevidence and repair. Add control of the top trace, or a norm of \(F-\widetilde F\), to the local composition estimate; permit dependence on the relevant higher norm bound in (iv). The later argument uses globally controlled sequences, for which the missing trace information is available. This calculation refutes the stated estimates, not compactness of the corrected iteration map.
## F3. The strict normal-sign statement needs positive density (Minor)
Location. Definition 2.1 and the discussion following (2.3), p. 5; the admitted vacuum configuration, p. 7.

The weak-solution class permits vacuum, but the subsequent strict same-sign conclusion for the two normal derivatives does not. Let \(\gamma=2\), \(B=0\), with interface \(\xi=0\), and set \[\varphi_L=-\tfrac12(\xi^2+\eta^2)+\sqrt2\,\xi
 \quad(\xi<0),\qquad
 \varphi_R=-\tfrac12(\xi^2+\eta^2)
 \quad(\xi>0).\] The continuous piecewise smooth potential is locally Lipschitz. Bernoulli’s law gives \(\rho_L=0\) and \(\rho_R=1\). The mass equation holds in each half-plane and distributionally: the normal mass flux on either side of the interface is zero. The energy inequality allows equality at vacuum. Yet the normal derivatives are \(\sqrt2\) and \(0\), not two strictly same-sign nonzero numbers, and the gradient magnitude jumps.

Counterevidence and repair. If both traces of density are strictly positive, the Rankine–Hugoniot condition gives equal-sign normal derivatives. A zero common flux would force both to vanish; continuity of the tangential derivative would then rule out a shock with a gradient-magnitude jump. Thus adding positive densities supplies the claimed strict conclusion. The main nonvacuum parameter range excludes this example. The defect is in the general statement accompanying the weak formulation.
## F4. The radial comparison uses the wrong gradient (Major)
Location. Radial coordinates about the upstream sonic center, p. 24; identity (3.44), p. 32.

Let \(w=\varphi_2-\varphi\) and \(e=\mathrm D\varphi_2(P_0^1)/|\mathrm D\varphi_2(P_0^1)|\). Since the radial unit vector about the upstream center is \(-\mathrm D\varphi_2/|\mathrm D\varphi_2|\), the correct identity is \[\partial_e w=-\partial_r w+
 \left(e-\frac{\mathrm D\varphi_2}{|\mathrm D\varphi_2|}\right)\cdot\mathrm Dw.\] The last normalized vector in (3.44) is instead \(\mathrm D\varphi/|\mathrm D\varphi|\).

At a subsonic reference corner, write \(R=\xi_{P_0^1}\), \(u=u_5\), \(v=v_2\) and \(M=\sqrt{R^2+v^2}\), with \(0<u<R\) and \(v<0\). The reference gradients are \[\mathrm D\varphi_2=(-R,v),\quad \mathrm D\varphi=(-(R-u),0),\quad
 \mathrm Dw=(-u,v).\] The printed right-hand side minus the correct left-hand side is \[\frac{v^2}{M}\left(1-\frac{u}{M+R}\right)>0.\] The mismatch at the continuous endpoint also prevents the identity from holding on an adjacent open shock segment.

Counterevidence and repair. The nonzero discrepancy at the reference corner prevents the printed correction from being treated as a quantity tending to zero. Equation (3.44) is used immediately on p. 32 to obtain the positive directional derivative for hodograph coordinates. The resulting subsonic-corner estimates enter Theorem 2.2(i) on p. 60. Thus F4 is Major for an invalid derivation on the central regularity proof path.

Restoring the subscript \(2\) makes the error vector tend to zero; the available gradient and radial bounds then give the intended directional bound after shrinking the neighborhood. This supported repair does not validate the printed identity. No counterexample to hodograph monotonicity or the regularity theorem is asserted.
## F5. Normal reflection exposes a strict inequality and a pullback sign error (Minor)
Location. Lemma 4.17, Step 2, p. 52; the pullback introduced in the compactness proof on p. 58; normal-reflection calculation on p. 59.

At \((u,\theta)=(u^\sharp,\theta^\sharp)=(0,0)\), condition (4.40) holds with zero distance. The normal solution gives \[\widehat\phi=v_2\eta_0,\qquad
 \varphi_0^*=-|\boldsymbol\xi|^2/2+v_2\eta_0.\] Thus \(\widehat\phi-(\varphi_\theta^*+|\boldsymbol\xi|^2/2)=0\), contradicting the strict positive inequality asserted in Step 2 for every nearby member. Normal reflection belongs to the extended iteration set used in that statement.

On p. 58 the displayed definition of \(\widehat w\) uses \[(\widehat\phi+|\boldsymbol\xi|^2/2-\varphi_\theta^*)\circ G_1^{-1}.\] The sign before \(|\boldsymbol\xi|^2/2\) must be minus, consistently with (4.24) and (4.41). At normal reflection the printed expression is \(|\boldsymbol\xi|^2\) before composition, whereas the intended perturbation is identically zero.

Counterevidence and repair. Separate the exact normal solution from the nonzero-angle positivity argument, and use nonnegativity where the extended parameter range includes zero. Correct the pullback sign. The normal solution already satisfies (4.39) with zero perturbation norm, so this example does not refute that estimate or compactness.
## F6. The endpoint differentiation and mean-value step are incorrect as written (Major)
Location. Equation (5.3), p. 60; (5.5)–(5.6) and the intervening mean-value assertion, p. 61.

Put \(f=f_{5,\mathrm{sh}}\), \(g=f_{5,0}\) and \(Q=\overline\psi_{25}\). Differentiating \(Q(x,f(x))-Q(x,g(x))=\psi(x,f(x))\) twice gives \[\begin{aligned}
 Q_y(x,f)(f-g)''={}&
 \sum_{k=0}^2\binom2k
 \bigl[(g')^k\partial_x^{2-k}\partial_y^kQ(x,g)
       -(f')^k\partial_x^{2-k}\partial_y^kQ(x,f)\bigr]\\
 &+[Q_y(x,g)-Q_y(x,f)]g''
   +f''\psi_y(x,f)\\
 &+\sum_{k=0}^2\binom2k
     (f')^k\partial_x^{2-k}\partial_y^k\psi(x,f).\end{aligned}\] The printed terms use powers of \(f,g\) instead of their derivatives in the relevant chain-rule factors, show incorrect derivative indices in \(A_1\), and give the wrong sign to \(A_3\). A simple identity test is \[Q(x,y)=y,\qquad \psi(x,y)=x^2,\qquad f(x)=x^2,\qquad g(x)=0.\] It satisfies the starting identity and the matching conditions at zero. The left-hand side is \(2\), while the printed right-hand side is \(-2\); the corrected expression is \(2\). This is a test of the claimed differentiation identity, not an assertion that these functions solve the fluid problem.

The later implication from \(F(0)=0\) and \(F(x)/x\to0\) to positive points with \(F'(x_m)=0\) is also false: \(F(x)=x^2\) has \(F'(x)>0\) for every \(x>0\). The mean value theorem instead gives, for \(h_m\downarrow0\), some \(x_m\in(0,h_m)\) with \[F'(x_m)=F(h_m)/h_m\longrightarrow0.\] This weaker, correct conclusion suffices for the subsequent limiting argument. In (5.6), differentiation along the curve likewise requires the factor \(f'(x_m)-\omega/10\), not \(f(x_m)-\omega/10\).

Counterevidence and repair. On p. 60, the twice-differentiated identity (5.3) is used to deduce the matching second derivative and \(C^{2,\alpha}\) shock joining in Theorem 2.2(i). Its failure is Major for that core derivation. The identity test is not an Euler solution counterexample.

The separate exact-zero assertion on p. 61 has a narrower effect: the subsequent limit needs only \(F'(x_m)\to0\), already supplied by the mean value theorem under the given hypotheses. In (5.6), both printed and corrected factors are bounded and multiply \(\psi_{xy}\to0\). These overstatements do not supply another failure of the limiting conclusion.

The corrected twice-differentiated formula and the existing derivative, corner and vanishing bounds restore the specified endpoint argument. That repair does not lower the severity of the original derivation. The claimed optimal regularity has not been disproved.
## F7. Two Bernoulli displays have incorrect algebra (Minor)
Location. Lemma 3.3, Step 2, p. 19; the Bernoulli difference displayed on p. 24.

Set \(C=1+(\gamma-1)(B-\varphi)\). Then \[c^2=C-\frac{\gamma-1}{2}|\mathrm D\varphi|^2.\] Strict subsonicity implies \(|\mathrm D\varphi|^2<2C/(\gamma+1)\), but it does not imply the displayed equality \(c^2=2C/(\gamma+1)\) for \(\gamma>1\). For instance, \(\gamma=2\), \(C=1\), \(\mathrm D\varphi=0\) gives \(c^2=1\), not \(2/3\). The correct strict inequality follows by rearranging \(|\mathrm D\varphi|^2<c^2\) directly.

Since \(h(\rho_2)=h(1)=0\), subtraction of the two Bernoulli equations also gives \[|\mathrm D\varphi_2|^2-|\mathrm D\varphi|^2
 =2h(\rho)+2(\varphi-\varphi_2).\] The second term on the right of the p. 24 display is missing the factor \(2\).

Counterevidence and repair. The first correction gives the same upper bound needed for the Lipschitz estimate. For the second, the available Lipschitz control and equality \(\varphi=\varphi_2\) on the shock allow the neighborhood to be made small enough even with the corrected factor. Neither algebraic correction contradicts the intended positive-gap estimate.
# Unresolved dependencies and rejected candidates

Definition 4.11 of the extended iteration set on p. 45 retains (i)–(v) of the preceding definition and omits its ellipticity condition. Yet away from the sonic collars the matrix on p. 46 is \(c^2I-\mathrm D\varphi\otimes\mathrm D\varphi\), and later assertions require ellipticity for the full extended set. It is not immediate from the printed geometric, density and norm conditions that the omitted inequality follows. This is recorded as an unresolved proof dependency, not a confirmed error: no global member satisfying every retained condition and violating ellipticity was constructed. A proof of that implication or an explicit additional restriction would settle it.

Several apparent extraction-based problems were rejected after inspection of the actual page images. On pp. 21–22 the limiting parameter lies in the closed parameter region. In the weak formulation, test functions have support in the closed upper half-plane. The weighted spaces change their weight together with the Hölder exponent; an alleged compactness obstruction based on a fixed weight was therefore inapplicable. Endpoint traces that follow automatically from the weighted norm do not create the suggested nonopenness problem. None of these rejected candidates contributes to the assessment.

The proof uses external results for mixed boundary problems, degenerate Schauder estimates and shock convexity. The full original proofs of those cited results were not reacquired and reproduced in this review. This limitation must not be replaced by a declaration that every dependency is verified.
# Supporting checks

F1 invalidates the core equation identification, including its stated Cartesian cancellation. F4 invalidates the radial-comparison step used for subsonic-corner hodograph estimates. F6 invalidates the differentiated identity used for shock joining in Theorem 2.2(i); its separate exact-zero assertion is stronger than the limiting argument needs. These are the three supported Major findings. F2, F3, F5 and F7 remain Minor within their stated application and parameter boundaries.

The corrected radial and differentiation arguments restore the specified local steps. A corrected \(O_3\) is necessary, but closure of every subsequent estimate and the fixed-point construction still requires checking. Repairability does not reduce a core derivation error. No counterexample to Theorems 2.1–2.3 as existence, regularity or convexity assertions has been established.

The primary reviewer’s own SymPy calculation checks the coefficient difference, elliptic jet, normal mapping example, vacuum example and radial discrepancy; no author code was executed. Source rendering and actual image inspection are recorded separately. All superseded bounded-check drafts and corrected extraction candidates are retained.

A bounded publisher/arXiv and supplement/code search found no acquired paper-specific supplement or code artifact. Generic arXiv code widgets are not evidence of an associated program. Absence of an acquired code artifact is not a mathematical deficiency. The Oxford repository surfaced as an alternative source but its file was not acquired or compared. This review remains restricted to the frozen v1 file.

 \quad(\xi>0).\] The continuous piecewise smooth potential is locally Lipschitz. Bernoulli’s law gives \(\rho_L=0\) and \(\rho_R=1\). claim: Chain-rule factors/signs and exact-zero conclusion of mean value theorem are wrong.
analysis: Location. Equation (5.3), p. 60; (5.5)–(5.6) and the intervening mean-value assertion, p. 61.

Put \(f=f_{5,\mathrm{sh}}\), \(g=f_{5,0}\) and \(Q=\overline\psi_{25}\). Differentiating \(Q(x,f(x))-Q(x,g(x))=\psi(x,f(x))\) twice gives \[\begin{aligned}
 Q_y(x,f)(f-g)''={}&
 \sum_{k=0}^2\binom2k
 \bigl[(g')^k\partial_x^{2-k}\partial_y^kQ(x,g)
       -(f')^k\partial_x^{2-k}\partial_y^kQ(x,f)\bigr]\\
 &+[Q_y(x,g)-Q_y(x,f)]g''
   +f''\psi_y(x,f)\\
 &+\sum_{k=0}^2\binom2k
     (f')^k\partial_x^{2-k}\partial_y^k\psi(x,f).\end{aligned}\] The printed terms use powers of \(f,g\) instead of their derivatives in the relevant chain-rule factors, show incorrect derivative indices in \(A_1\), and give the wrong sign to \(A_3\). A simple identity test is \[Q(x,y)=y,\qquad \psi(x,y)=x^2,\qquad f(x)=x^2,\qquad g(x)=0.\] It satisfies the starting identity and the matching conditions at zero. The left-hand side is \(2\), while the printed right-hand side is \(-2\); the corrected expression is \(2\). This is a test of the claimed differentiation identity, not an assertion that these functions solve the fluid problem.

The later implication from \(F(0)=0\) and \(F(x)/x\to0\) to positive points with \(F'(x_m)=0\) is also false: \(F(x)=x^2\) has \(F'(x)>0\) for every \(x>0\). The mean value theorem instead gives, for \(h_m\downarrow0\), some \(x_m\in(0,h_m)\) with \[F'(x_m)=F(h_m)/h_m\longrightarrow0.\] This weaker, correct conclusion suffices for the subsequent limiting argument. In (5.6), differentiation along the curve likewise requires the factor \(f'(x_m)-\omega/10\), not \(f(x_m)-\omega/10\).

Counterevidence and repair. On p. 60, the twice-differentiated identity (5.3) is used to deduce the matching second derivative and \(C^{2,\alpha}\) shock joining in Theorem 2.2(i). Its failure is Major for that core derivation. The identity test is not an Euler solution counterexample.

The separate exact-zero assertion on p. 61 has a narrower effect: the subsequent limit needs only \(F'(x_m)\to0\), already supplied by the mean value theorem under the given hypotheses. In (5.6), both printed and corrected factors are bounded and multiply \(\psi_{xy}\to0\). These overstatements do not supply another failure of the limiting conclusion.

The corrected twice-differentiated formula and the existing derivative, corner and vanishing bounds restore the specified endpoint argument. That repair does not lower the severity of the original derivation. The claimed optimal regularity has not been disproved.

report: Abstract: The assessment is Major for the unsupported quantitative derivation in Corollary 1.6, with explicit coverage limits. An arbitrary marked geodesic length does not descend to the pants-twist quotient used in the coordinate discussion; a once-punctured torus gives an exact matrix counterexample. Two all-genus corollaries require a graded-versus-completed Lie algebra convention, and the critical-base growth estimate is stronger than the cited free-Lie lower-bound argument supports. An introductory short exact sequence also needs its low-complexity exceptions. Each issue is confined below, with counterevidence and a concrete repair. No counterexample to the principal classifying-space theorem or the degreewise weight-zero factorization has been established. Scientific decision and adjudication remain pending.

Title: Initial scientific review of
Top weight cohomology of moduli spaces of Riemann surfaces and handlebodies
Article. Louis Hainaut and Dan Petersen. Frozen journal identifier: 10.4171/JEMS/1623.

Actual version. arXiv:2305.03046v1, submitted 4 May 2023 at 17:59:07 UTC; 24 PDF pages. Printed and 1-based PDF page numbers agree. The publisher records online publication on 10 March 2025; its mathematical journal text was not acquired. The frozen 2025 assignment is retained separately from the manuscript date. No equivalence to the journal version is assumed.
# Scope and main mathematical claims

The primary reviewer fully read all 24 source-text pages and actually inspected all 24 source-page images. The primary reviewer independently evaluated the arguments used in this report. Three supporting primary references were acquired, hashed and parsed in full; six selected evidence pages were actually inspected, not the entire proofs of those references. This is initial scientific review, not independent acceptance or human review.

The principal hypothesis is \(2g-2+n+m>0\). The space \(\mathcal{HM}^m_{g,n}\) consists of hyperbolic surfaces with \(n\) cusps and \(m\) parametrized geodesic boundaries of a fixed small length \(\varepsilon\), whose \(\varepsilon\)-short geodesics cut the surface into genus-zero pieces. Theorem 1.4 identifies this space with a classifying space of \(\operatorname{HMod}^m_{g,n}\). For \(m=0\) this is explicitly an orbifold statement; for \(m>0\) the parametrized boundary removes finite stabilizers. The exceptional unmarked genus-one component of the modular-envelope theorem is outside the stated stable range.

The proof uses the thick hyperbolic surface operad, Giansiracusa’s derived modular-envelope theorem, a stable-graph homotopy-colimit model, and Reedy cofibrancy to identify a thick cutting locus \(X^m_g\). A deformation retraction and a boundary-to-marking comparison then give the claimed handlebody model. The tropicalization map records all short geodesics with lengths \(-\log(\ell/\varepsilon)\) and is used on coarse spaces for rational compactly supported cohomology. It yields the factorization \[H_c^k(\mathcal{CV}_{g,n};\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow
 H_c^k(\mathcal{HM}_{g,n};\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H_c^k(\mathcal M_{g,n};\mathbb Q).\] Away from the stated \((g,n)=(1,1)\) exception, the composite identifies the graph contribution with \(W_0H_c^k(\mathcal M_{g,n};\mathbb Q)\), so the first arrow is injective. Poincaré duality places this contribution in handlebody homology of degree \(6g-6+2n-k\).

Section 5 distinguishes the representation multiplicity theorem from two conjectural spectral-sequence/local-system comparisons. In particular, an assertion made only after semisimplification was not treated as an assertion about all extensions. The full imported Giansiracusa and Ji–Wolpert proofs and the complete sheaf-theoretic spectral-sequence machinery were not independently reconstructed.
# Confirmed issues and their precise limits
## F1. A marked length function does not descend to the pants-twist quotient (Minor)
Location. Section 2.1, p. 9, the asserted extension of \(\ell_\gamma\) for any simple closed curve to \(\mathbb C^{3g-3+n}\); its use in Proposition 4.1, p. 17.

The chart construction starts from \[T(S)/\mathbb Z^{3g-3+n}\simeq
 (\mathbb R_{>0})^{3g-3+n}\times(S^1)^{3g-3+n}.\] A length function attached to a fixed marked curve can descend to this quotient only if it is invariant under the pants Dehn twists. A curve crossing a pants curve fails this requirement.

Here is a finite exact example. Let \(X\) be the complete once-punctured Markoff torus with holonomy generators \[A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}.\] Their realization by gluing two ideal triangles is described in [Retained latex: \cite[p.~27, PDF p.~2]{abe}]. The corresponding simple curves \(a,b\) intersect once, and \(a\) alone is a pants decomposition. Exact multiplication gives \[\operatorname{tr}A=\operatorname{tr}B=\operatorname{tr}(AB)=3,\qquad
 A^2B=\begin{pmatrix}-1&4\\-2&7\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \operatorname{tr}(A^2B)=6.\] Both determinants are one and \(\operatorname{tr}[A,B]=-2\), as expected for the cusp. Since a hyperbolic element of trace \(t>2\) has translation length \(2\operatorname{arcosh}(t/2)\), \[\ell_b(X)=2\operatorname{arcosh}(3/2),\qquad
 \ell_b(T_a^{-2}X)=2\operatorname{arcosh}(3).\] The sign of the twist can be reversed if the opposite marking convention is used; the two lengths remain different. Yet the two marked metrics have exactly the same image in \(T(S)/\langle T_a\rangle\). The proposed function is therefore not even defined on that quotient, before considering its extension across the origin.

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The pants-curve lengths themselves descend, as do lengths of curves whose isotopy classes are unchanged by the twisting subgroup. Arbitrary individual curve lengths are valid on Teichmüller space or on a locally chosen marked lift. The global assertion should be restricted accordingly.

There is additional counterevidence in Proposition 4.1. Its set \(C\) contains all curves crossing a node, and pants twists permute \(C\). The collective predicate \[\ell_\gamma(Y)>M\quad\hbox{for every }\gamma\in C\] is therefore independent of the marked lift, although individual crossing-curve functions do not descend. The collar lemma already invoked on p. 17 gives a uniform bound exceeding \(M\) for all such curves once the finitely many nodal pants curves are sufficiently short. The source’s argument on normalized components controls the remaining short curves.

Thus the global individual-function assertion is false, but the collective condition actually needed for continuity is meaningful and has the required local control from an existing lemma. F1 establishes neither a missing central continuity premise nor a counterexample to tropicalization continuity. This actual dependency boundary supports Minor.
## F2. The all-genus statements mix direct sums with the completed Lie algebra (Minor)
Location. Corollary 1.2, p. 4, and Corollary 1.5, p. 6.

The printed statements use \[\bigoplus_{g\ge2}W_0H_c^{2g}(\mathcal M_g;\mathbb Q)\simeq\mathfrak{grt}_1,
 \qquad
 \mathfrak{grt}_1\xhookrightarrow{}
       \bigoplus_{g\ge2}H_{4g-6}(\operatorname{HMod}_g;\mathbb Q).\] For the standard completed \(\mathfrak{grt}_1\) used in the cited theorem, these cannot hold literally. Willwacher distinguishes complete product gradings from direct-sum gradings and defines \(\mathfrak{grt}_1\) by Lie series in the completed free Lie algebra [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~3, 21]{will}]. The comparison in [Retained latex: \cite[p.~11, (2.4.2)]{cgp}] likewise uses the algebraic dual of a direct sum.

Choose a nonzero homogeneous element \(\sigma_{2j+1}\) in each odd degree \(2j+1\ge3\), as supplied by the free-Lie injection used by the paper itself. The defining relations of \(\mathfrak{grt}_1\) are homogeneous linear relations on completed Lie series. Hence every formal sum \[\sum_{j\ge1}a_j\sigma_{2j+1},\qquad (a_j)_{j\ge1}\in\mathbb Q^{\mathbb N},\] belongs to \(\mathfrak{grt}_1\), and distinct sequences give distinct elements. Thus the standard completed algebra contains an uncountable set.

Each compact-support cohomology group of \(\mathcal M_g\) is finite-dimensional, so the first direct sum is countable as a set. For the second target, no finiteness theorem about handlebody Betti numbers is even needed: \(\operatorname{HMod}_g\) is a countable subgroup of the countable mapping class group. Its rational bar chain complex is countable-dimensional in every degree, as are its homology groups. A countable direct sum of such vector spaces is still countable-dimensional and, over \(\mathbb Q\), countable as a set. An uncountable set cannot inject into either target. Concretely, the formal series \(\sum_{j\ge1}\sigma_{2j+1}\) cannot be represented by the intended degreewise map in a finite-support direct sum.

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The surrounding discussion plainly seeks a genus-graded statement and finite-genus classes. If the authors intend \[\mathfrak{grt}_1^{\mathrm{gr}}=\bigoplus_d(\mathfrak{grt}_1)_d,\] they should say so and use that algebra in the two corollaries. Alternatively, replace the targets by products and take the completed degreewise map. Each fixed-genus statement survives either consistent choice. Thus this is a literal all-genus convention defect with an explicit obstruction, not a counterexample to the geometric theorem or the individual detected classes.
## F3. The critical-base growth bound does not follow from the stated lower-bound mechanism (Major)
Location. Corollary 1.6, p. 6; the free-Lie discussion on p. 4.

Let \(\beta_0>1\) satisfy \(\beta_0^3-\beta_0-1=0\). The source states \[\liminf_{g\to\infty}\beta_0^{-g}
       \dim H_{4g-6}(\operatorname{HMod}_g;\mathbb Q)\ge1.\] The cited free-Lie argument gives a weaker normalization. This is a confirmed gap in that inference; the actual endpoint inequality for the full handlebody group is not proved false here.

Put \[L=\operatorname{Lie}(\sigma_3,\sigma_5,\sigma_7,\ldots),\qquad
 a_g=\dim L_g.\] The generator series is \(f(t)=t^3/(1-t^2)\). PBW and the tensor-algebra description of the universal enveloping algebra give the exact identity \[\prod_{g\ge1}(1-t^g)^{-a_g}
       =\frac1{1-f(t)}
       =\frac{1-t^2}{1-t^2-t^3}.\] Let \(r_1=\beta_0,r_2,r_3\) be the roots of \(r^3-r-1=0\), and put \(P_n=\sum_i r_i^n\). Taking logarithms and comparing coefficients yields \[\sum_{d\mid n}d\,a_d=P_n-2\,\mathbf1_{2\mid n},
 \qquad
 n a_n=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)
    \bigl(P_{n/d}-2\,\mathbf1_{2\mid n/d}\bigr).\] The two nonreal roots have modulus \(\beta_0^{-1/2}<1\). The term \(d=1\) is \(\beta_0^n+O(1)\), and all proper-divisor contributions together are \(O(\tau(n)\beta_0^{n/2}+\tau(n))\). Therefore \[a_n\sim\frac{\beta_0^n}{n},\qquad
 \beta_0^{-n}a_n\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 n\beta_0^{-n}a_n\longrightarrow1.\] The following independently computed values illustrate the proved asymptotic; the proof is the coefficient argument, not a numerical fit: \[\begin{array}{r|r|c|c}
 n&a_n&\beta_0^{-n}a_n&n\beta_0^{-n}a_n\\ \hline
 20&13&0.04693263&0.93865258\\
 40&1911&0.02490713&0.99628534\\
 80&73583124&0.01249984&0.99998695
 \end{array}\] The primary calculation used exact integers through degree 200 and independently checked the truncated PBW product through degree 60. The auxiliary’s separate integer calculation through degree 1000 is also retained.

Why this is a bounded countercalculation. The integer sequence \(B_g=a_g\) satisfies the given free-Lie lower-bound mechanism, including its claimed nonvanishing genera, but fails the printed critical normalization. Thus that mechanism alone cannot imply the endpoint estimate. This sequence is not being identified with the actual handlebody Betti numbers: additional classes could make those numbers larger.

Corollary 1.6 on p. 6 presents this quantitative conclusion as an immediate consequence of the central genus-graded injection following Theorem 1.4 and Corollary 1.5. The calculation invalidates that deduction at the stated critical normalization. F3 is therefore Major for the quantitative derivation. Surviving nonvanishing genera and qualitative exponential growth do not establish the stronger guarantee. The actual handlebody Betti sequence is not claimed to violate it.
## F4. The introductory boundary-twist exact sequence needs low-complexity exceptions (Minor)
Location. Section 1.1, p. 1; compare the stability condition before Theorem 1.4 on p. 6 and the actual use in Corollary 3.7 on p. 16.

The introductory sequence is stated without a complexity restriction: \[0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\longrightarrow\operatorname{HMod}^{m+1}_{g,n}
       \longrightarrow\operatorname{HMod}^m_{g,n+1}\longrightarrow1.\] Take \((g,m,n)=(0,0,0)\). The mapping class group of a three-ball fixing a boundary disk is trivial, as is that of a three-ball fixing one boundary point. One can equally use the paper’s genus-zero identification with the surface groups: the disk-relative mapping class group and the orientation-preserving one-pointed sphere mapping class group are trivial. The displayed sequence would therefore begin \(0\to\mathbb Z\to1\), which is not exact.

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The subsequent application in Corollary 3.7 has \(2g-2+n+m>0\) and excludes this case. State the appropriate stable range or low-complexity exceptions at the introductory assertion. This is a range qualification, not a failure of the boundary-twist argument in its actual stable application.
# Checks supporting the main mechanism
## Hyperbolic and operadic construction

The thick-locus construction is compatible with gluing along parametrized boundaries of length \(\varepsilon\): a newly short geodesic crossing a glued seam would contradict the collar lemma, and a short curve disjoint from the seams lies in an original thick piece. The genus-zero subcategory has the correct closure property for the restriction of the latching diagrams. A subgraph contracting to a genus-zero vertex can contain neither a cycle nor a positive-genus vertex; thus an incoming contraction to a graph with all genus-zero vertices stays in that subcategory. This supports the Reedy-cofibrancy restriction used on p. 15.

For an actual surface with parametrized boundary, an isometry fixing that boundary pointwise is the identity. The corresponding finite graph stabilizers therefore act freely in the indicated model. The no-boundary case is treated separately by the source with finite-level covers and orbifold information. Distinct genus-zero cutting systems at a common metric have a common refinement by the full collection of length-\(\varepsilon\) curves, which are disjoint. The relevant contractions back to the cutting systems are forests. These checks support the colimit-to-cutting-locus identification.

A potential objection to adjoining the two unstable monoidal-unit components on p. 11 was rejected. The quantity \[2g-2+n=\sum_v\bigl(2g(v)-2+n(v)\bigr)\] is preserved by graph contraction. Every semistable vertex contributes a nonnegative integer, and a stable vertex contributes a positive integer. A graph mapping to an unstable component of total value zero cannot contain any stable vertex. Consequently, maps into the new unit components only involve tensors of units, while inserting bivalent unit vertices in a stable graph uses the unit constraint. No additional augmentation from an arbitrary stable component is required.

There is also a direct response to an apparent local corner obstruction in Proposition 3.5. Near a point of the closed handlebody locus, cut along all threshold curves and put \(x_e=\log(\ell_e/\varepsilon)\) on the remaining critical edges. The condition is that the positive-edge subgraph be a forest. When there are cycles, set \[F(x)=\max_{\text{cycles }C}\min_{e\in C}x_e.\] The closed and open loci are locally \(F\le0\) and \(F<0\), respectively, and \(F(x+t\mathbf1)=F(x)+t\). Decomposing along \(\mathbf1\) makes the boundary a continuous graph and supplies a local topological collar. If there are no cycles, the condition is locally vacuous. Thus the union-of-orthants observation does not furnish a counterexample to the interior-inclusion homotopy equivalence. It should not be confused with a proof of a preferred smooth embedded corner structure.
## Tropicalization, compact supports and degrees

An extension to compactifications alone would not establish properness. Here the preceding definition supplies the necessary extra fact: a nodal source curve produces an edge of infinite length, and a smooth curve produces only finite lengths. Hence the inverse image of the finite-length tropical locus is precisely the smooth moduli locus. The preimage of a compact subset of that locus is closed in the compact Deligne–Mumford coarse space and lies entirely in its interior, proving properness once continuity is established.

The square defining \(\mathcal{HM}\) is Cartesian. The map \(\mathcal{HM}\to\mathcal{CV}\) is proper by base change, and \(\mathcal{HM}\to\mathcal M\) is open. Proper pullback followed by extension by zero on compactly supported cohomology gives exactly the original tropical pullback after the open inclusion \(\mathcal{CV}\to\mathcal M^{\mathrm{trop}}\). This checks the direction of both arrows and the injection into the intermediate compact-support group.

If a genus-\(g\) graph has \(E\) edges, its compact-support degree is \(E\). The \(GC_2\) degree is \(E-2g\), so a class of degree \(k\) gives \[H_c^{2g+k}(\mathcal{HM}_g;\mathbb Q)
       \simeq H_{4g-6-k}(\operatorname{HMod}_g;\mathbb Q).\] In particular, \(k=0\) gives \(4g-6\), as in the main corollaries. This also agrees with the listed higher-degree examples on p. 7. No shift error was found in these displayed homology consequences.

The augmented edge-free graph accounts for reduced cohomology of the tropical link. The exceptional pair \((g,n)=(1,1)\) is meaningful: the unweighted locus is a positive ray, with \(H_c^1=\mathbb Q\), whereas the full tropical space is a closed ray with vanishing compactly supported cohomology. The pair is explicitly excluded in Theorem 1.1. For \((0,3)\) both relevant spaces are a point and the degree-zero corolla contributes \(\mathbb Q\).

Automorphism signs are essential: a genus-two rose with two loop edges has a loop-swap automorphism acting by \(-1\) on the orientation line of the two-dimensional edge-length cell, so that rational generator vanishes. The source signals the sign issue and uses the determinant-twisted graph construction; it was not interpreted as a sign-free count of graph isomorphism classes.

Remark 4.4, p. 18, explicitly repairs the preceding informal description of stratum closures by using normalized boundary branches. The weight-zero row is then the \(H^0\) row of the proper smooth normalized algebraic pieces, compared with contractible tropical pieces. The initial simplified wording was not counted again as an unaddressed defect.
## Configurations and the status of conjectures

The handlebody-to-spine comparison concerns compactly supported configuration cohomology. For compact \(X\), this is modeled by the relative cohomology of \((X^n,\Delta_{\mathrm{fat}})\). A homotopy equivalence \(X\to Y\) gives a homotopy equivalence of these pairs: applying the same homotopy to all coordinates preserves every diagonal equality. Thus the noninvariance of ordinary configuration-space homotopy types does not refute this compact-support comparison.

At \(n=1\), the degree-one Lagrangian inclusion matches one copy of the standard \(GL(g)\) representation with one untwisted standard \(Sp(2g)\) representation. The surface’s degree-two orientation class is Tate-twisted and is excluded from the untwisted comparison. At \(n=2\), the diagonal relative-cohomology sequence yields the two tensor components on the graph side, matched by the symmetric and primitive alternating symplectic components; additional scalar terms on the surface side carry a Tate twist. These are useful low-arity checks of Theorem 5.2, not a replacement for the general representation-theoretic argument.

Conjectures 5.1 and 5.3 remain conjectures in the reviewed source. The later discussion of extensions and Torelli actions is explicitly beyond semisimplification. No claim of a proof of those conjectures is made here.
# Unresolved or unverified points

The normalization of the Teichmüller metric in Theorem 2.4 is not explicit. Its displayed coefficient is one; the usual normalization \(d_T=\tfrac12\inf\log K\) prompts a factor-two question. The original Wolpert lemma was not fully reacquired, and no independent finite-distance counterexample under a source-specified convention was completed. This remains a convention check, not a confirmed error.

Corollary 3.7 identifies a quotient of fixed-length boundary moduli with a cusped model and restricts that identification to the short-curve locus. Quotienting rotations directly removes boundary parametrizations; a further compatible geometric identification with cusps is needed. An adapted construction may supply it, but preservation of this locus was not independently established or disproved. It remains a stated coverage limit.

The abstract and Remark 1.9 use ordinary-cohomology language. The explicit factorization reviewed here naturally gives compactly supported cohomology and then homology; dualization reverses arrows. A claim of a specified ordinary-cohomology injection would require the relevant splitting or additional graded model to be stated. This formulation note is not a counterexample to the degreewise factorization, and is not counted as a confirmed fifth finding.

More generally, the complete disk-complex proof behind Giansiracusa’s theorem, the Ji–Wolpert vector field and its locus-preservation details, finite-level descent in the homotopy-colimit construction, and the full normalized-strata spectral sequence were not independently reproduced. The review does not replace these limits with a blanket proof certificate.
# Supporting checks

F3 is a Major quantitative inference gap: the free-Lie injection gives order \(\beta_0^g/g\) and does not imply the printed critical-base normalization. The actual stronger Betti inequality remains unresolved. Retaining qualitative exponential growth does not reduce the severity of that unsupported consequence.

F1, F2 and F4 remain Minor for their demonstrated dependency boundaries. In F1 the collective all-crossing-curves condition is twist invariant, and the existing collar lemma supplies local control. F2 needs a consistent graded or completed formulation while preserving each genus. F4 lies outside the stable range of the actual application. No counterexample to the principal classifying-space theorem or degreewise weight-zero factorization is established.

The frozen PDF and manifest, added reference PDFs, current report source, compiler, dependencies, cache changes, logs, compiled PDF and actual inspected images are covered by the accompanying provenance and inventory. Rendering-only records remain separate from actual image-inspection receipts. No author code was executed.

Bounded searches of the publisher, arXiv and the author’s publication page did not yield a paper-specific supplement or code artifact. The author’s GH-ConfSpace repository is explicitly associated with a different paper and was excluded. Missing code is not a mathematical defect. All failed reference-fetch attempts and auxiliary checkpoints are retained. The delivery is an initial review with scientific decision pending and no human reviews.

problems.title: Marked crossing-curve length is not invariant on the pants-twist quotient.
problems.source_location: Section2.1 arbitrary curve length extension; Proposition4.1 proof
claim: Marked crossing-curve length is not invariant on the pants-twist quotient.
analysis: Location. Section 2.1, p. 9, the asserted extension of \(\ell_\gamma\) for any simple closed curve to \(\mathbb C^{3g-3+n}\); its use in Proposition 4.1, p. 17.

The chart construction starts from \[T(S)/\mathbb Z^{3g-3+n}\simeq
 (\mathbb R_{>0})^{3g-3+n}\times(S^1)^{3g-3+n}.\] A length function attached to a fixed marked curve can descend to this quotient only if it is invariant under the pants Dehn twists. A curve crossing a pants curve fails this requirement.

Here is a finite exact example. Let \(X\) be the complete once-punctured Markoff torus with holonomy generators \[A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}.\] Their realization by gluing two ideal triangles is described in [Retained latex: \cite[p.~27, PDF p.~2]{abe}]. The corresponding simple curves \(a,b\) intersect once, and \(a\) alone is a pants decomposition. Exact multiplication gives \[\operatorname{tr}A=\operatorname{tr}B=\operatorname{tr}(AB)=3,\qquad
 A^2B=\begin{pmatrix}-1&4\\-2&7\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \operatorname{tr}(A^2B)=6.\] Both determinants are one and \(\operatorname{tr}[A,B]=-2\), as expected for the cusp. Since a hyperbolic element of trace \(t>2\) has translation length \(2\operatorname{arcosh}(t/2)\), \[\ell_b(X)=2\operatorname{arcosh}(3/2),\qquad
 \ell_b(T_a^{-2}X)=2\operatorname{arcosh}(3).\] The sign of the twist can be reversed if the opposite marking convention is used; the two lengths remain different. Yet the two marked metrics have exactly the same image in \(T(S)/\langle T_a\rangle\). The proposed function is therefore not even defined on that quotient, before considering its extension across the origin.

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The pants-curve lengths themselves descend, as do lengths of curves whose isotopy classes are unchanged by the twisting subgroup. Arbitrary individual curve lengths are valid on Teichmüller space or on a locally chosen marked lift. The global assertion should be restricted accordingly.

There is additional counterevidence in Proposition 4.1. Its set \(C\) contains all curves crossing a node, and pants twists permute \(C\). The collective predicate \[\ell_\gamma(Y)>M\quad\hbox{for every }\gamma\in C\] is therefore independent of the marked lift, although individual crossing-curve functions do not descend. The collar lemma already invoked on p. 17 gives a uniform bound exceeding \(M\) for all such curves once the finitely many nodal pants curves are sufficiently short. The source’s argument on normalized components controls the remaining short curves.

Thus the global individual-function assertion is false, but the collective condition actually needed for continuity is meaningful and has the required local control from an existing lemma. F1 establishes neither a missing central continuity premise nor a counterexample to tropicalization continuity. This actual dependency boundary supports Minor.

problems.title: Completed standard grt1 cannot be identified with or injected into the printed all-genus direct sums.
problems.source_location: Corollaries1.2,1.5
claim: Completed standard grt1 cannot be identified with or injected into the printed all-genus direct sums.
analysis: Location. Corollary 1.2, p. 4, and Corollary 1.5, p. 6.

The printed statements use \[\bigoplus_{g\ge2}W_0H_c^{2g}(\mathcal M_g;\mathbb Q)\simeq\mathfrak{grt}_1,
 \qquad
 \mathfrak{grt}_1\xhookrightarrow{}
       \bigoplus_{g\ge2}H_{4g-6}(\operatorname{HMod}_g;\mathbb Q).\] For the standard completed \(\mathfrak{grt}_1\) used in the cited theorem, these cannot hold literally. Willwacher distinguishes complete product gradings from direct-sum gradings and defines \(\mathfrak{grt}_1\) by Lie series in the completed free Lie algebra [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~3, 21]{will}]. The comparison in [Retained latex: \cite[p.~11, (2.4.2)]{cgp}] likewise uses the algebraic dual of a direct sum.

Choose a nonzero homogeneous element \(\sigma_{2j+1}\) in each odd degree \(2j+1\ge3\), as supplied by the free-Lie injection used by the paper itself. The defining relations of \(\mathfrak{grt}_1\) are homogeneous linear relations on completed Lie series. Hence every formal sum \[\sum_{j\ge1}a_j\sigma_{2j+1},\qquad (a_j)_{j\ge1}\in\mathbb Q^{\mathbb N},\] belongs to \(\mathfrak{grt}_1\), and distinct sequences give distinct elements. Thus the standard completed algebra contains an uncountable set.

Each compact-support cohomology group of \(\mathcal M_g\) is finite-dimensional, so the first direct sum is countable as a set. For the second target, no finiteness theorem about handlebody Betti numbers is even needed: \(\operatorname{HMod}_g\) is a countable subgroup of the countable mapping class group. Its rational bar chain complex is countable-dimensional in every degree, as are its homology groups. A countable direct sum of such vector spaces is still countable-dimensional and, over \(\mathbb Q\), countable as a set. An uncountable set cannot inject into either target. Concretely, the formal series \(\sum_{j\ge1}\sigma_{2j+1}\) cannot be represented by the intended degreewise map in a finite-support direct sum.

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The surrounding discussion plainly seeks a genus-graded statement and finite-genus classes. If the authors intend \[\mathfrak{grt}_1^{\mathrm{gr}}=\bigoplus_d(\mathfrak{grt}_1)_d,\] they should say so and use that algebra in the two corollaries. Alternatively, replace the targets by products and take the completed degreewise map. Each fixed-genus statement survives either consistent choice. Thus this is a literal all-genus convention defect with an explicit obstruction, not a counterexample to the geometric theorem or the individual detected classes.

problems.title: The displayed free-Lie lower bound does not imply the printed endpoint normalization.
problems.source_location: Corollary1.6 critical-base estimate and its free-Lie derivation
claim: The displayed free-Lie lower bound does not imply the printed endpoint normalization.
analysis: Location. Corollary 1.6, p. 6; the free-Lie discussion on p. 4.

Let \(\beta_0>1\) satisfy \(\beta_0^3-\beta_0-1=0\). The source states \[\liminf_{g\to\infty}\beta_0^{-g}
       \dim H_{4g-6}(\operatorname{HMod}_g;\mathbb Q)\ge1.\] The cited free-Lie argument gives a weaker normalization. This is a confirmed gap in that inference; the actual endpoint inequality for the full handlebody group is not proved false here.

Put \[L=\operatorname{Lie}(\sigma_3,\sigma_5,\sigma_7,\ldots),\qquad
 a_g=\dim L_g.\] The generator series is \(f(t)=t^3/(1-t^2)\). PBW and the tensor-algebra description of the universal enveloping algebra give the exact identity \[\prod_{g\ge1}(1-t^g)^{-a_g}
       =\frac1{1-f(t)}
       =\frac{1-t^2}{1-t^2-t^3}.\] Let \(r_1=\beta_0,r_2,r_3\) be the roots of \(r^3-r-1=0\), and put \(P_n=\sum_i r_i^n\). Taking logarithms and comparing coefficients yields \[\sum_{d\mid n}d\,a_d=P_n-2\,\mathbf1_{2\mid n},
 \qquad
 n a_n=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)
    \bigl(P_{n/d}-2\,\mathbf1_{2\mid n/d}\bigr).\] The two nonreal roots have modulus \(\beta_0^{-1/2}<1\). The term \(d=1\) is \(\beta_0^n+O(1)\), and all proper-divisor contributions together are \(O(\tau(n)\beta_0^{n/2}+\tau(n))\). Therefore \[a_n\sim\frac{\beta_0^n}{n},\qquad
 \beta_0^{-n}a_n\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 n\beta_0^{-n}a_n\longrightarrow1.\] The following independently computed values illustrate the proved asymptotic; the proof is the coefficient argument, not a numerical fit: \[\begin{array}{r|r|c|c}
 n&a_n&\beta_0^{-n}a_n&n\beta_0^{-n}a_n\\ \hline
 20&13&0.04693263&0.93865258\\
 40&1911&0.02490713&0.99628534\\
 80&73583124&0.01249984&0.99998695
 \end{array}\] The primary calculation used exact integers through degree 200 and independently checked the truncated PBW product through degree 60. The auxiliary’s separate integer calculation through degree 1000 is also retained.

Why this is a bounded countercalculation. The integer sequence \(B_g=a_g\) satisfies the given free-Lie lower-bound mechanism, including its claimed nonvanishing genera, but fails the printed critical normalization. Thus that mechanism alone cannot imply the endpoint estimate. This sequence is not being identified with the actual handlebody Betti numbers: additional classes could make those numbers larger.

Corollary 1.6 on p. 6 presents this quantitative conclusion as an immediate consequence of the central genus-graded injection following Theorem 1.4 and Corollary 1.5. The calculation invalidates that deduction at the stated critical normalization. F3 is therefore Major for the quantitative derivation. Surviving nonvanishing genera and qualitative exponential growth do not establish the stronger guarantee. The actual handlebody Betti sequence is not claimed to violate it.

report: Abstract: This report examines the exact 2025 published version of Balister, Bollobás and Janson’s Consistent random vertex-orderings of graphs. The second sentence of Theorem 4.14 overstates the classification of an arbitrary, unreduced finite template. A three-vertex example disproves that intermediate assertion. The reduced-template classification and the infinite-blow-up consequence used in Theorem 1.3 are unaffected. This is a local scope defect, assessed as Minor. The moment, exchangeability and Bernoulli-polynomial arguments examined below yielded no further substantive issue. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: A Scope Correction in the Classification
of Non-uniform Graph Templates
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The primary source is Paul N. Balister, Béla Bollobás and Svante Janson, Consistent random vertex-orderings of graphs, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 27 (2025), 2623–2652, doi: 10.4171/JEMS/1624 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1624) [published]. The acquired publisher Version of Record is a 30-page PDF; its first page states a revision date of 7 November 2024. The publisher records publication on 27 March 2025. Here PDF page \(p\) corresponds to printed page \(2622+p\). The separately preserved arXiv:1506.03343v1, submitted 10 June 2015, is used only for the specific version comparison in Section 5 (#sec:version).

All 30 pages of the published paper were read as extracted text. The claim-focused checks cover consistency and induced subgraphs; the constructions in Section 2; the rank representation in Section 3; the moment and template arguments leading to Theorems 1.3 and 1.5; the gluing and forest arguments in Section 5; and the Bernoulli calculations in Appendix A. Actual source-page checks are separately recorded with image hashes and performing roles. Standard external results such as de Finetti’s theorem, Ramsey’s theorem and the cited graph-limit equivalence were not independently reproved. No claim of a formal or exhaustive correctness certificate is made.
# Definitions and the precise scope distinction

A template \(T\) is a finite graph whose vertices are labelled full or empty. In \(T_\infty\), a vertex \(v\) is replaced by a countable blob \(W_v\), a clique if \(v\) is full and an independent set if \(v\) is empty. Edges between two blobs are complete or absent according to the corresponding edge of \(T\) [Retained latex: \cite[Section 3, PDF p.~9]{published}].

A random ordering is consistent when the induced order distributions are preserved by every isomorphism between finite induced subgraphs. A template is uniform when its blow-up admits only the uniform consistent ordering. A template is reduced when it has neither adjacent full twins nor nonadjacent empty twins. Merging those twins preserves the isomorphism type of the countable blow-up, but need not preserve the finite underlying graph [Retained latex: \cite[PDF p.~19]{published}].
# A local scope defect in Theorem 4.14

Problem 1 (The complete-or-empty assertion requires reduction).  The second sentence of Theorem 4.14, printed p. 2641 / PDF p. 19, asserts, for any non-uniform template \(G\), that \(G\) itself is complete or empty before deriving the classification of \(G_\infty\). The first sentence explicitly assumes reduction; the second does not. The unrestricted finite-template assertion is false.
## A counterexample satisfying the literal hypotheses

Let \[V(T)=\{a,b,c\},\qquad E(T)=\{\{a,b\}\},
 \qquad a,b,c\text{ all full}.\] This is a permitted finite template. It has one edge out of three possible edges, so its underlying graph is neither complete nor empty. By definition, \[T_\infty=C\sqcup D,\qquad C=W_a\cup W_b,\quad D=W_c,\] where \(C\) and \(D\) are countably infinite cliques.

Equation reference: eq:block. Use a fair coin to put all of \(C\) before all of \(D\), or vice versa, and use independent uniform random orders inside the two cliques. This is a measurable random total order. Its consistency can be verified for every finite induced subgraph, not merely for the three vertices used below. If that subgraph meets both cliques in \(r,s>0\) vertices, each of its allowed block orders has probability \[\frac{1}{2r!s!}.
 \] This depends only on the induced graph. It is invariant under internal permutations and, when applicable, interchange of the two components. If restriction removes a component, the remaining clique retains its uniform internal order. Thus every induced-subgraph isomorphism preserves the law.

Choose distinct \(a_1,a_2\in C\) and \(c_1\in D\). The block ordering gives \[\Pr(a_1<c_1<a_2)=0,\] whereas the uniform order on these three labelled vertices gives \(1/6\). Therefore \(T\) is non-uniform and satisfies every literal assumption of the second sentence. The claimed finite-graph conclusion fails. An exact enumeration of the six orders, retained in the evidence files, gives four probabilities \(1/4\) and two probabilities \(0\), summing to one. The enumeration checks this finite calculation; the preceding argument proves consistency for all finite induced subgraphs.
## Counterevidence and supported correction

The preceding paragraph of the paper says that it suffices to consider reduced templates. This makes the intended reduced-representative interpretation clear. It does not make the independently re-quantified unrestricted assertion true. In the example, \(a,b\) are adjacent full twins: the counterexample is deliberately not reduced and does not challenge the theorem’s first sentence.

Merging \(a,b\) produces a reduced template \(R\) consisting of two full vertices with no edge. Then \(R_\infty\cong T_\infty\), exactly as the reduction argument requires. A supported replacement for the second sentence is:
> For any non-uniform template \(T\), its blow-up \(T_\infty\) is a disjoint union of cliques or a complete multipartite graph.

Indeed, reduce \(T\) to \(R\) without changing the blow-up, apply the first sentence and its full/empty label restrictions to \(R\), and pass the resulting classification through \(R_\infty\cong T_\infty\). Alternatively, explicitly attribute the complete-or-empty assertion to the reduced representative.
## Dependency and severity

The proof of Theorem 1.3 on PDF p. 20 uses only the valid blow-up conclusion. Its witness graph is neither a disjoint union of cliques nor a complete multipartite graph and is an induced subgraph of the constructed blow-up. Both classes are hereditary, so the valid blow-up classification already gives the necessary contradiction. The subsequent use of Lemma 4.15 also does not require the false assertion about the unreduced finite template.

The assessment is Minor: a mathematical statement has an explicit counterexample, but the inspected central implication and classification of infinite blow-ups survive. The grading rests on that dependency analysis, not on the shortness of the correction. The counterexample is not evidence against Theorem 1.3, the reduced classification, or the paper’s general programme.
# Other inspected reasoning
## Moment and exchangeability arguments

The rank variables in Section 3 require more than marginal uniformity. Finite permutations within blobs give independent uniform internal orders; the tail-invariance argument then makes their rank labels independent of the random distribution functions. This supports the random-argument evaluations used in Section 4. Atoms are explicitly accommodated by comparing the relevant ranks; they are not silently discarded.

In Lemma 4.10, with the right-continuous inverse interpreted as in (3.8), \[\mathbb E X^2+\mathbb E Y^2
 =\frac23+\int_0^1(F(x)-x)^2\,dx.\] The equality case, monotonicity and right continuity identify the uniform distribution. This identity supports the equality arguments in Lemmas 4.11 and 4.15. The conditional expectations and Cauchy–Schwarz step in Lemma 4.12 were checked against the source equations (4.2)–(4.11); no additional substantive defect was established.

For Theorem 5.1, two independent uniform blocks supplied by the induction hypothesis force the de Finetti mixing measure to be deterministic: \(\mathbb E\mu(S)^2=(\mathbb E\mu(S))^2\) on a countable determining family. Conditioning on a positive-probability event in the fixed base ordering preserves exchangeability; the already deterministic empirical limit again forces the same mixing law. This justifies independence from the base ordering. The constructions for Theorem 1.6 require only vertex gluing and heredity. In Theorem 1.8, the finite pigeonhole step is supplemented by heredity to descend from an unbounded sequence of leaf counts to every required finite count. The edgeless and single-edge boundary cases were checked.
## Non-uniform constructions and low-dimensional checks

For Lemma 2.3, fixing an edge and imposing the signed sum modulo one gives Haar measure on an affine subtorus. Deleting any coordinate yields product uniform measure because every coefficient is \(1\) or \(-1\). Averaging over edges makes the law invariant under graph automorphisms. Proper subsets remain uniformly ordered.

The two Fourier calculations in Lemma A.2 reproduce its Bernoulli-polynomial coefficients. In the nonregular case, \[|E(G)|(P_{1,2}-P_{2,1})
 =(d_1-d_2)\frac{(-1)^n}{(n-1)!}\binom n2 B_{n-1}(\alpha).\] For \(n=3,\alpha=0\), the edge-conditioned difference is \(-1/4\), also obtained by an elementary area integral. In the regular case \(n=4\), the \(B_3\) coefficient cancels and \[|E(G)|(P_{1,2,3}-P_{2,1,3})=-B_2(\alpha).\] Thus \(\alpha=0\) gives \(-1/24\) for \(C_4\) and \(-1/12\) for \(2K_2\) after dividing by the respective numbers of edges. These are analytic checks, not simulation. The general argument uses linear independence of different-degree Bernoulli polynomials. Appendix A’s actual \(\omega=-2\pi it\) convention and inclusive \(n\ge3,n\ge4\) bounds were checked visually; extraction artefacts do not constitute findings.
# Version comparison and remaining limits

The preserved arXiv v1, Theorem 4.14 on its PDF p. 19, gives the reduced classification followed directly by the weaker, correct blow-up consequence [arxiv]. The extra unrestricted finite-template clause occurs in the reviewed publisher PDF. This identifies a difference between two acquired versions; it does not identify who introduced it or whether intermediate versions contain it.

A bounded title-plus-erratum search and inspection of the publisher and arXiv records did not identify a separate correction. This is not an assertion that none exists. Claim: Every non-uniform template G has a complete or empty underlying finite graph.
A finite full/empty-labelled template. Non-uniformity of its infinite blow-up under induced-isomorphism consistency. No reduced hypothesis in the second sentence.
analysis: The second sentence of Theorem 4.14, printed p. 2641 / PDF p. 19, asserts, for any non-uniform template \(G\), that \(G\) itself is complete or empty before deriving the classification of \(G_\infty\). The first sentence explicitly assumes reduction; the second does not. The unrestricted finite-template assertion is false.

Let \[V(T)=\{a,b,c\},\qquad E(T)=\{\{a,b\}\},
 \qquad a,b,c\text{ all full}.\] This is a permitted finite template. It has one edge out of three possible edges, so its underlying graph is neither complete nor empty. By definition, \[T_\infty=C\sqcup D,\qquad C=W_a\cup W_b,\quad D=W_c,\] where \(C\) and \(D\) are countably infinite cliques.

Equation reference: eq:block. Use a fair coin to put all of \(C\) before all of \(D\), or vice versa, and use independent uniform random orders inside the two cliques. This is a measurable random total order. Its consistency can be verified for every finite induced subgraph, not merely for the three vertices used below. If that subgraph meets both cliques in \(r,s>0\) vertices, each of its allowed block orders has probability \[\frac{1}{2r!s!}.
 \] This depends only on the induced graph. It is invariant under internal permutations and, when applicable, interchange of the two components. If restriction removes a component, the remaining clique retains its uniform internal order. Thus every induced-subgraph isomorphism preserves the law.

Choose distinct \(a_1,a_2\in C\) and \(c_1\in D\). The block ordering gives \[\Pr(a_1<c_1<a_2)=0,\] whereas the uniform order on these three labelled vertices gives \(1/6\). Therefore \(T\) is non-uniform and satisfies every literal assumption of the second sentence. The claimed finite-graph conclusion fails. An exact enumeration of the six orders, retained in the evidence files, gives four probabilities \(1/4\) and two probabilities \(0\), summing to one. The enumeration checks this finite calculation; the preceding argument proves consistency for all finite induced subgraphs.
result: The preceding paragraph of the paper says that it suffices to consider reduced templates. This makes the intended reduced-representative interpretation clear. It does not make the independently re-quantified unrestricted assertion true. In the example, \(a,b\) are adjacent full twins: the counterexample is deliberately not reduced and does not challenge the theorem’s first sentence.

Merging \(a,b\) produces a reduced template \(R\) consisting of two full vertices with no edge. Then \(R_\infty\cong T_\infty\), exactly as the reduction argument requires. A supported replacement for the second sentence is:
> For any non-uniform template \(T\), its blow-up \(T_\infty\) is a disjoint union of cliques or a complete multipartite graph.

Indeed, reduce \(T\) to \(R\) without changing the blow-up, apply the first sentence and its full/empty label restrictions to \(R\), and pass the resulting classification through \(R_\infty\cong T_\infty\). Alternatively, explicitly attribute the complete-or-empty assertion to the reduced representative.

The proof of Theorem 1.3 on PDF p. 20 uses only the valid blow-up conclusion. Both classes are hereditary, so the valid blow-up classification already gives the necessary contradiction. The subsequent use of Lemma 4.15 also does not require the false assertion about the unreduced finite template.
