report: Abstract: This report examines arXiv:2211.06096v2 of Chataur, Saralegi-Aranguren and Tanré. Two explicit examples disprove the stated generality of the Van Kampen theorem and of fundamental-group invariance under coarsening. The failures concern ordinary versus perverse connectivity and unrestricted codimensional perversities, respectively. Each is assessed as Major for the named theorem. Neither example refutes the GM-perversity main theorem or the normal Thom–Mather application. The coefficient-domain defect on a cone is Minor because its inspected application already uses a system on the larger space. Two further Major proof defects concern the horn construction establishing the Kan property and the local-to-global step of the main Hurewicz argument. Explicit repairs support the corrected conclusions; they do not validate the original derivations. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Hypothesis Gaps and Core Proof Dependencies
in Intersection Homotopy Theory
# Identity, version and scope

The paper is David Chataur, Martintxo Saralegi-Aranguren and Daniel Tanré, Relation between intersection homology and homotopy groups, doi: 10.4171/JEMS/1625 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1625). The exact reviewed source is the 28-page author manuscript arXiv:2211.06096v2, submitted on 20 February 2025 at 15:16:18 UTC [source]. Its first page separately says 21 February 2025. The publisher records online publication on 11 April 2025 [record]. The acquired author manuscript is not silently identified with the inaccessible publisher Version of Record. All locations below use this manuscript’s PDF page numbers, which agree with its printed numbers.

All source text, including references, was read. The checks cover the allowability definitions, simplicial construction, cone formula, local coefficients, Sections 4–5 and the comparison-map proof of the Hurewicz theorem in Section 6. Source-image inspection is individually attributed in the evidence records. External general-position, local-to-global, fibration and classical homotopy theorems were not all independently reproved. The small-resolution statement on page 4 is explicitly a conjecture, not a proved result being rejected here.

Equation reference: allow. Write \(Dp(S)=\operatorname{codim}S-2-p(S)\). The basic condition is \[
 \dim\sigma^{-1}(S)\leq \dim\Delta-2-Dp(S).\] A simplex belongs to \(\mathcal G_pX\) only when it and every face are allowable [1, Definitions 1.12 and 2.1, pp. 7–8]. In particular, if \(Dp=1\) on every singular stratum, the entire two-skeleton is that of \(\operatorname{Sing}(X\setminus\Sigma)\). Consequently \(\pi_1^p(X)=\pi_1(X\setminus\Sigma)\), with compatible basepoints. This elementary observation supplies the first two counterexamples.
# Van Kampen requires connectivity of allowable paths

Problem 1.  Theorem 4.1, p. 14, assumes that the two open sets and their intersection are ordinarily path-connected. These assumptions do not imply its surjectivity assertion for perverse fundamental groups.
## A counterexample satisfying the stated assumptions

Take the underlying space \(X=\mathbb R^2\) and \[S=\{(0,y):-1\leq y\leq1\},\qquad
 X_0=\{(0,-1),(0,1)\},\quad X_1=S,\quad X_2=X.\] The open segment is a one-dimensional stratum, the endpoints are zero-dimensional strata, and \(X\setminus S\) is regular. This is even a CS set: the middle of the segment has link \(S^0\), and each endpoint has link a circle with one marked singular point. Normality is not required by Theorem 4.1 and does not hold here.

Set \(p=-2\) on the open segment and \(p=-1\) at both endpoints, and \(p=0\) on the regular stratum. Then \(p\leq t\) and \(Dp=1\) on all singular strata. No infinite perversity value is needed. Use the open cover \[U_0=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,y):y\geq\tfrac12\},\qquad
 U_1=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,y):y\leq-\tfrac12\}\] and basepoint \(x_0=(1,0)\). The removed rays are disjoint, so the sets cover \(X\). Both sets are path-connected. Their intersection is path-connected as well: its two sides are joined through the gap \(\{(0,y):-\tfrac12<y<\tfrac12\}\). These are exactly the ordinary connectivity hypotheses on p. 14.

The regular parts are different: \[U_0\setminus S=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,y):y\geq-1\},\qquad
 U_1\setminus S=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,y):y\leq1\}.\] Each is a slit plane and is simply connected. In contrast, \(\mathbb R^2\setminus S\) deformation retracts onto the circle of radius \(2\). An explicit homotopy is \[H_t(z)=\left(1-t+\frac{2t}{\lVert z\rVert}\right)z .\] For points on the vertical axis in the domain, the radius is strictly greater than \(1\) throughout this homotopy; off that axis the homotopy cannot meet \(S\). Thus it is well-defined and fixes the target circle.

Using [allow] (#allow) through dimension two gives \[\pi_1^p(U_0,x_0)=\pi_1^p(U_1,x_0)=1,\qquad
 \pi_1^p(X,x_0)=\mathbb Z .\] The asserted map is therefore \(1*1\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\), which is not surjective. The missing feature is visible directly: \((U_0\cap U_1)\setminus S\) has two components.
## Impact, counterevidence and repair

The proof on p. 14 joins subdivision vertices to the basepoint and says these paths can be chosen in the regular part. Ordinary path-connectivity does not supply those paths. The failure affects the actual conclusion of the stated Van Kampen theorem, a substantive basic result advertised in the paper, so the assessment is Major for that generality.

A supported sufficient correction is to require that the regular parts of \(U_0,U_1,U_0\cap U_1\) are path-connected, together with the finiteness needed for the stated subdivision argument (satisfied for CS sets). Then the connecting paths can be chosen allowable, and the usual subdivision proof applies. A groupoid formulation may admit weaker hypotheses but is not proved in this report. As counterevidence to a broader negative inference, Corollary 4.2 assumes normal Thom–Mather structure; its connected open sets have connected regular parts by the paper’s Remark 1.6. This example does not refute that application.
# Codimensional perversities need compatibility with coarsening

Problem 2.  Theorem 4.6, p. 17, asserts fundamental-group invariance for any codimensional perversity \(p\leq t\) when there is no exceptional stratum. This range is false; the displayed induced map need not even be defined by the stated coarsening.
## An explicit refinement of an axis

Let \(A=\{(0,0,z):z\in\mathbb R\}\) in \(\mathbb R^3\). Give \(Y\) the singular stratum \(A\) of codimension two. Give \(X\) the finer stratification whose singular strata are \(A\setminus\{0\}\) (two rays) of codimension two and \(\{0\}\) of codimension three. Explicitly, \(Y_0=\varnothing\), \(Y_1=Y_2=A\), whereas \(X_0=\{0\}\), \(X_1=X_2=A\); both top skeleta are \(\mathbb R^3\). These are CS sets without codimension-one strata. At the refined origin, the compact link is \(S^2\) with its two poles as singular points. The identity \(\nu:X\to Y\) is a coarsening, the regular parts agree, and no singular stratum becomes regular.

Choose the same codimensional function on both: \[p(2)=-1,\qquad p(3)=1.\] It is zero on regular strata and can be extended, for example, by \(p(1)=-1\) and \(p(c)=c-2\) for \(c\geq4\). It satisfies \(p\leq t\). Its complementary values are \[Dp(2)=1,\qquad Dp(3)=0.\] For \(Y\), all one- and two-simplices avoid \(A\), whence \[\pi_1^p(Y)=\pi_1(\mathbb R^3\setminus A)=\mathbb Z.\] For \(X\), all one-simplices still avoid \(A\), so the regular-part group surjects onto \(\pi_1^p(X)\). Its meridian generator bounds a transverse disk in the plane \(z=0\). Triangulate that disk so that the origin is in the interior of one triangle and on no edge. The resulting two-simplices avoid the open rays. The unique nonempty inverse image of the origin is a point in a two-simplex, which satisfies \(0\leq2-2-Dp(3)=0\); every face avoids the singular set. The disk is an allowable null-homotopy. Therefore \[\pi_1^p(X)=1\ne\mathbb Z=\pi_1^p(Y).\]

The same disk simplex also shows that \(
u\) does not send every \(p\)-full simplex of \(X\) to a \(p\)-full simplex of \(Y\). In the latter stratification the upper bound at the axis is \(2-2-Dp(2)=-1\). Equivalently, Proposition 2.5’s condition \(
u^*Dp\leq Dp\) fails at the origin: \(1
leq0\). Thus the problem is not merely a noncanonical identification of two isomorphic groups.
## Impact and supported restriction

This is a false invariance assertion under all the printed hypotheses, not a missing explanation of a true isomorphism. It is assessed as Major for Theorem 4.6’s general codimensional range. The counterexample is not a GM perversity: \(p(2)\) is negative and \(Dp\) decreases. In particular, it does not refute Theorem A or Theorem 5.1, both of which explicitly impose the GM condition.

A supported repair is to restrict Theorem 4.6 to GM perversities (and the accompanying absence of codimension-one strata). Their complementary perversity is nondecreasing; since coarsening decreases codimension, \(\nu^*Dp\leq Dp\) follows. The source-stratum argument can then establish injectivity, while common regular paths give surjectivity. More general compatible perversities may be possible, but the strongest such range is not established here. The reference to GM perversities immediately after the theorem is counterevidence against treating its intended GM application as disproved; it does not impose a GM hypothesis on the preceding broader statement.
# Coefficient domain and core proof dependencies

Problem 3 (Coefficient system on the wrong member of a pair).  Proposition 2.10, p. 10, quantifies over every local system \(E\) on \(\mathcal G_pL\) while forming \(H_j(\mathcal G_p\mathring cL,\mathcal G_pL;E)\). An arbitrary such system need not extend to the first space.

Take \(L=S^1\) with trivial filtration and \(p(v)=0\) on the apex of its two-dimensional cone, so \(Dp(v)=0\). On \(\mathcal G_pL=\operatorname{Sing}S^1\) choose the rank-one integral local system with monodromy \(-1\). The meridian is null-homotopic in the Gajer cone by the same interior-point disk argument used in the cone formula. Its fundamental group is trivial. Every local system on this connected simply connected simplicial set has trivial monodromy when restricted to \(S^1\). The chosen sign system cannot extend, and the displayed relative group is not defined with those data.

The supported correction is to take \(E\) on \(\mathcal G_p\mathring cL\) and use its restriction on \(\mathcal G_pL\). The common low-dimensional skeleta then give the stated vanishing range. The application in Proposition 5.2, pp. 19–20, already starts with a coefficient system on the larger space, so this defect does not invalidate that use. The assessment is Minor, a real coefficient-domain restriction with the inspected application preserved.

Problem 4 (The specified horn projection).  In the proof of Proposition 2.3, p. 8, radial projection from the barycentre of the missing face is asserted to be an affine map from the whole simplex to the horn. That specified projection is undefined at its centre and has no continuous extension there in dimension two.

For a triangle, approach the midpoint of the missing edge along rays aimed at two distinct points of the other two edges. The projection has two different constant limits. This uses a trivially stratified target, so no perversity condition removes the difficulty.

There is a direct repair. In barycentric coordinates \((t_0,\ldots,t_\ell)\), with face \(k\) missing, put \(m=\min_{i
e k}t_i\) and \[ho_i(t)=t_i-m\ (i
e k),\qquad
 ho_k(t)=t_k+\ell m .\] This is a continuous piecewise linear retraction onto the horn, fixing it pointwise. On the missing face it is a piecewise linear homeomorphism onto the horn: if \(y\) is in the horn, the inverse has \(t_k=0\), \(t_i=y_i+y_k/\ell\) for \(i
e k\). On each linear piece the ambient fibres have dimension at most one; on the missing face they have dimension zero. These facts give precisely the allowability bounds for the whole simplex and each face. The Kan conclusion survives with this replacement. The original construction is nevertheless assessed as Major for its foundational proof dependency. Page 8 calls Proposition 2.3 crucial for the definition of the intersection homotopy groups. Page 12 uses the Kan property to represent homotopy classes and their homotopies by individual full simplices; Proposition 3.5 and the subsequent homotopy arguments use this representation. Page 2 explains why the paper supplies proofs of these basic properties in its general topological setting. The specified discontinuous map cannot supply the required horn fillings.

This finding invalidates that derivation, not the Kan conclusion: the explicit PL construction above restores the necessary allowability bounds. Repair success is distinct from severity. No counterexample to the existence of intersection homotopy groups is asserted.

Problem 5 (The purported local basis omits angular neighborhoods).  The first step in the proof of Theorem 6.4, p. 26, calls the sets \(C\times\mathring c_tL\) and \(C\times L\times(a,b)\) a basis for a conical chart. They are not a basis in general.

Take \(k=2\), \(L=S^2\) with trivial filtration, and the chart \(\mathring cS^2\) with its apex as singular stratum and \(p(v)=0\). The link is simply connected, so the theorem’s link hypotheses hold. An open set \(O\times(a,b)\) away from the apex, with \(\varnothing\ne O\subsetneq S^2\), contains no member of the stated family: each of those sets contains every angular direction at its radii. Thus the assertion that their unions give the full topology, and the subsequent appeal to arbitrary \(W\cap V\), are not justified as written.

The existing depth induction supplies a repair. In a chart with central stratum \(S\), use all open subsets of \(V\setminus S\), whose depth is smaller, together with product tip neighborhoods \(C\times\mathring c_tL\). Compactness of \(L\) makes these a basis at the tip, and the former sets cover the off-tip topology. Finite intersections either remain tip neighborhoods or lie off the tip, so the inductive hypothesis and Proposition 6.6 supply \(P_k\) on each. Proposition 6.7 gives finite unions; compactness of finite chains gives the directed-union passage. The Zorn argument can then be used. Before this repair, however, the first step establishes \(P_k\) only for the indicated angularly saturated sets. The second step requires \(P_k(W\cap V)\) for an arbitrary maximal open set \(W\) and a chart \(V\), and this intersection need not belong to that class. The false basis claim therefore leaves Theorem 6.4 unproved by the printed argument. On p. 26, Theorem 6.4 is then used explicitly to deduce Theorem 6.1(2), stated as the main Theorem B(ii) on p. 3.

The assessment is Major for this invalid derivation on the main Hurewicz proof path. The depth-induction repair supports the corrected result without changing that assessment. The example refutes the basis claim; it does not refute the Hurewicz conclusion.
# Other checked dependencies and limits

The cone formula preserves homotopy groups through \(Dp(v)\) and kills higher groups; it is not an assertion that the Gajer-space homology always equals intersection homology. The examples involving a torus and \(\mathring c(S^2\times S^3)\) correctly distinguish those theories. For Proposition 6.6, when the cutoff \(q=Dp(v)\) is below \(k\), the assumed connectivity of the link makes the Gajer cone weakly contractible. When the required degree is below the cutoff, the comparison is inherited from the link. This accounts for both the isomorphism and epimorphism ranges, rather than silently extending an isomorphism one degree too far.

In Example 6.8, pp. 26–27, the links \(\mathbb{RP}^3,\mathbb{RP}^7\) have fundamental group \(\mathbb Z/2\), so the missing link hypothesis is genuinely absent. The map \(H_3(\mathbb{RP}^7)\to H_3(\mathbb{RP}^{\infty})\) is an isomorphism. The displayed Mayer–Vietoris diagram gives \(J_3\) an isomorphism and \(\operatorname{coker}J_4\cong\mathbb Z/2\). This supports the claimed necessity of the link condition. The double-suspension example concerns a change of regular part and does not contradict the restricted topological-invariance theorem.

The generality of ancillary subdivision statements beyond locally finite CS settings has not been exhaustively certified. No additional false theorem is inferred from that limit. A bounded search of the title, publisher record and arXiv record identified no separate correction; a related later coarsening paper was located but is not treated as a correction or as proof of author adoption. The acquisition manifest’s supplement/code searches and the current record checks found no separate paper-specific package. Absence of code is not a defect in this paper.
# Conclusion and evidence
Item | Assessment | Exact effect
Problem 1 | Major | Van Kampen surjectivity fails under the printed connectivity assumptions.
Problem 2 | Major | Broad codimensional invariance fails; the claimed simplicial map may not exist.
Problem 3 | Minor | Arbitrary link coefficients need not extend to the cone.
Problem 4 | Major | Invalid horn construction in the Kan proof; an explicit PL replacement restores it.
Problem 5 | Major | False basis claim leaves the main Hurewicz local-to-global derivation incomplete.

The report-level assessment is Major for the two false general theorem assertions and the two invalid derivations on the Kan and main Hurewicz proof paths. The coefficient-domain defect in Problem 3 remains Minor because the inspected application already uses the correct ambient coefficient system. Problems 1 and 2 do not refute the GM main theorem or the normal Thom–Mather application; Problems 4 and 5 establish proof defects, not counterexamples to the Kan or Hurewicz conclusions. The specified repairs are analytically supported; their availability does not lower the severity of the affected core derivations. Author adoption is unknown. Normality is not required by Theorem 4.1 and does not hold here.

Set \(p=-2\) on the open segment and \(p=-1\) at both endpoints, and \(p=0\) on the regular stratum. Then \(p\leq t\) and \(Dp=1\) on all singular strata. No infinite perversity value is needed. Use the open cover \[U_0=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,y):y\geq\tfrac12\},\qquad
 U_1=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,y):y\leq-\tfrac12\}\] and basepoint \(x_0=(1,0)\). The removed rays are disjoint, so the sets cover \(X\). Both sets are path-connected. Their intersection is path-connected as well: its two sides are joined through the gap \(\{(0,y):-\tfrac12<y<\tfrac12\}\). These are exactly the ordinary connectivity hypotheses on p. 14.

The regular parts are different: \[U_0\setminus S=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,y):y\geq-1\},\qquad
 U_1\setminus S=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,y):y\leq1\}.\] Each is a slit plane and is simply connected. In contrast, \(\mathbb R^2\setminus S\) deformation retracts onto the circle of radius \(2\). An explicit homotopy is \[H_t(z)=\left(1-t+\frac{2t}{\lVert z\rVert}\right)z .\] For points on the vertical axis in the domain, the radius is strictly greater than \(1\) throughout this homotopy; off that axis the homotopy cannot meet \(S\). Thus it is well-defined and fixes the target circle.

Using [allow] (#allow) through dimension two gives \[\pi_1^p(U_0,x_0)=\pi_1^p(U_1,x_0)=1,\qquad
 \pi_1^p(X,x_0)=\mathbb Z .\] The asserted map is therefore \(1*1\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\), which is not surjective. The missing feature is visible directly: \((U_0\cap U_1)\setminus S\) has two components.

The proof on p. 14 joins subdivision vertices to the basepoint and says these paths can be chosen in the regular part. Ordinary path-connectivity does not supply those paths. The failure affects the actual conclusion of the stated Van Kampen theorem, a substantive basic result advertised in the paper, so the assessment is Major for that generality.

A supported sufficient correction is to require that the regular parts of \(U_0,U_1,U_0\cap U_1\) are path-connected, together with the finiteness needed for the stated subdivision argument (satisfied for CS sets). Then the connecting paths can be chosen allowable, and the usual subdivision proof applies. A groupoid formulation may admit weaker hypotheses but is not proved in this report. As counterevidence to a broader negative inference, Corollary 4.2 assumes normal Thom–Mather structure; its connected open sets have connected regular parts by the paper’s Remark 1.6. This example does not refute that application.
result: Impact: Actual conclusion of a substantive named Van Kampen theorem fails under printed assumptions.

problems.title: Unrestricted codimensional perversities are incompatible with coarsening
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2. Theorem 4.6, p. 17, asserts fundamental-group invariance for any codimensional perversity \(p\leq t\) when there is no exceptional stratum.
claim: Kind: paraphrase
Location. Theorem: 4.6
Location. Pdf page: 17
Claim: For codimensional p<=t a coarsening with no exceptional strata induces isomorphisms of pi0p and pi1p.
X,Y CS sets. Same underlying R³; identity coarsening. No exceptional strata. Same codimensional p<=t.
analysis: Let \(A=\{(0,0,z):z\in\mathbb R\}\) in \(\mathbb R^3\). Give \(Y\) the singular stratum \(A\) of codimension two. Give \(X\) the finer stratification whose singular strata are \(A\setminus\{0\}\) (two rays) of codimension two and \(\{0\}\) of codimension three. Explicitly, \(Y_0=\varnothing\), \(Y_1=Y_2=A\), whereas \(X_0=\{0\}\), \(X_1=X_2=A\); both top skeleta are \(\mathbb R^3\). These are CS sets without codimension-one strata. At the refined origin, the compact link is \(S^2\) with its two poles as singular points. The identity \(\nu:X\to Y\) is a coarsening, the regular parts agree, and no singular stratum becomes regular.

Choose the same codimensional function on both: \[p(2)=-1,\qquad p(3)=1.\] It is zero on regular strata and can be extended, for example, by \(p(1)=-1\) and \(p(c)=c-2\) for \(c\geq4\). It satisfies \(p\leq t\). Its complementary values are \[Dp(2)=1,\qquad Dp(3)=0.\] For \(Y\), all one- and two-simplices avoid \(A\), whence \[\pi_1^p(Y)=\pi_1(\mathbb R^3\setminus A)=\mathbb Z.\] For \(X\), all one-simplices still avoid \(A\), so the regular-part group surjects onto \(\pi_1^p(X)\). Its meridian generator bounds a transverse disk in the plane \(z=0\). Triangulate that disk so that the origin is in the interior of one triangle and on no edge. The resulting two-simplices avoid the open rays. The unique nonempty inverse image of the origin is a point in a two-simplex, which satisfies \(0\leq2-2-Dp(3)=0\); every face avoids the singular set. The disk is an allowable null-homotopy. Therefore \[\pi_1^p(X)=1\ne\mathbb Z=\pi_1^p(Y).\]

The same disk simplex also shows that \(
u\) does not send every \(p\)-full simplex of \(X\) to a \(p\)-full simplex of \(Y\). In the latter stratification the upper bound at the axis is \(2-2-Dp(2)=-1\). Equivalently, Proposition 2.5’s condition \(
u^*Dp\leq Dp\) fails at the origin: \(1
leq0\). Thus the problem is not merely a noncanonical identification of two isomorphic groups.

This is a false invariance assertion under all the printed hypotheses, not a missing explanation of a true isomorphism. It is assessed as Major for Theorem 4.6’s general codimensional range. The counterexample is not a GM perversity: \(p(2)\) is negative and \(Dp\) decreases. In particular, it does not refute Theorem A or Theorem 5.1, both of which explicitly impose the GM condition.

A supported repair is to restrict Theorem 4.6 to GM perversities (and the accompanying absence of codimension-one strata). Their complementary perversity is nondecreasing; since coarsening decreases codimension, \(\nu^*Dp\leq Dp\) follows. The source-stratum argument can then establish injectivity, while common regular paths give surjectivity. More general compatible perversities may be possible, but the strongest such range is not established here. The reference to GM perversities immediately after the theorem is counterevidence against treating its intended GM application as disproved; it does not impose a GM hypothesis on the preceding broader statement.
result: Impact: False central fundamental-group invariance assertion in the claimed broader range; GM main theorem not refuted.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Restrict to GM perversities (and no codim1 strata); then complementary perversity monotonicity gives nu*Dp<=Dp.

problems.title: Local coefficients must be defined on the larger member of the cone pair
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: Problem 3 (Coefficient system on the wrong member of a pair).
claim: Kind: paraphrase
Location. Proposition: 2.10
Location. Pdf page: 10
Claim: Relative cone homology is defined and vanishes for every local system E on GpL.
Compact trivially filtered L=S1. Cone apex p=0, Dp=0. Rank-one integral local system on GpL with monodromy-1.
analysis: Proposition 2.10, p. 10, quantifies over every local system \(E\) on \(\mathcal G_pL\) while forming \(H_j(\mathcal G_p\mathring cL,\mathcal G_pL;E)\). An arbitrary such system need not extend to the first space.

Take \(L=S^1\) with trivial filtration and \(p(v)=0\) on the apex of its two-dimensional cone, so \(Dp(v)=0\). On \(\mathcal G_pL=\operatorname{Sing}S^1\) choose the rank-one integral local system with monodromy \(-1\). The meridian is null-homotopic in the Gajer cone by the same interior-point disk argument used in the cone formula. Its fundamental group is trivial. Every local system on this connected simply connected simplicial set has trivial monodromy when restricted to \(S^1\). The chosen sign system cannot extend, and the displayed relative group is not defined with those data.

The supported correction is to take \(E\) on \(\mathcal G_p\mathring cL\) and use its restriction on \(\mathcal G_pL\). The common low-dimensional skeleta then give the stated vanishing range. The application in Proposition 5.2, pp. 19–20, already starts with a coefficient system on the larger space, so this defect does not invalidate that use. The assessment is Minor, a real coefficient-domain restriction with the inspected application preserved.
result: Impact: Invalid coefficient-domain quantifier, inspected downstream use preserved.

paragraphs: Take E on GpconeL and restrict it to GpL; common low skeleta give vanishing.

problems.title: The specified radial horn projection is not continuous
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: Problem 4 (The specified horn projection).
claim: Kind: paraphrase
Location. Proposition: 2.3 proof
Location. Pdf page: 8
Claim: Radial projection from missing face barycentre defines an affine whole-simplex horn retraction.
Dimension2 triangle. Trivially stratified target horn; all continuous simplices allowable.
analysis: In the proof of Proposition 2.3, p. 8, radial projection from the barycentre of the missing face is asserted to be an affine map from the whole simplex to the horn. That specified projection is undefined at its centre and has no continuous extension there in dimension two.

For a triangle, approach the midpoint of the missing edge along rays aimed at two distinct points of the other two edges. The projection has two different constant limits. This uses a trivially stratified target, so no perversity condition removes the difficulty.

There is a direct repair. In barycentric coordinates \((t_0,\ldots,t_\ell)\), with face \(k\) missing, put \(m=\min_{i
e k}t_i\) and \[ho_i(t)=t_i-m\ (i
e k),\qquad
 ho_k(t)=t_k+\ell m .\] This is a continuous piecewise linear retraction onto the horn, fixing it pointwise. On the missing face it is a piecewise linear homeomorphism onto the horn: if \(y\) is in the horn, the inverse has \(t_k=0\), \(t_i=y_i+y_k/\ell\) for \(i
e k\). On each linear piece the ambient fibres have dimension at most one; on the missing face they have dimension zero. These facts give precisely the allowability bounds for the whole simplex and each face. The Kan conclusion survives with this replacement. The original construction is nevertheless assessed as Major for its foundational proof dependency. Page 8 calls Proposition 2.3 crucial for the definition of the intersection homotopy groups. Page 12 uses the Kan property to represent homotopy classes and their homotopies by individual full simplices; Proposition 3.5 and the subsequent homotopy arguments use this representation. Page 2 explains why the paper supplies proofs of these basic properties in its general topological setting. The specified discontinuous map cannot supply the required horn fillings.

This finding invalidates that derivation, not the Kan conclusion: the explicit PL construction above restores the necessary allowability bounds. Repair success is distinct from severity. No counterexample to the existence of intersection homotopy groups is asserted.
result: Impact: The discontinuous specified map invalidates the Kan proof in Proposition2.3 (p8). Page12 uses Kan to represent homotopy classes and homotopies by individual p-full simplices, including in Proposition3.5. This is a Major invalid derivation on a foundational proof path. The explicit PL repair restores the conclusion without validating the original construction.

paragraphs: m=min_{i!=k}t_i; rho_i=t_i-m(i!=k),rho_k=t_k+ell*m. Missing-face inverse t_i=y_i+y_k/ell,t_k=0; other faces fixed.

problems.title: The conical product family is not a basis
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 5: Problem 5 (The purported local basis omits angular neighborhoods).
claim: Kind: paraphrase
Location. Theorem: 6.4 proof First Step
Location. Pdf page: 26
Claim: C×ctL and C×L×(a,b) form a basis of all open subsets of the chart.
k=2. X=opencone S2 with apex singular. p(apex)=0, Dp=1. LinkS2 is simplyconnected, satisfying theorem link hypothesis.
analysis: The first step in the proof of Theorem 6.4, p. 26, calls the sets \(C\times\mathring c_tL\) and \(C\times L\times(a,b)\) a basis for a conical chart. They are not a basis in general.

Take \(k=2\), \(L=S^2\) with trivial filtration, and the chart \(\mathring cS^2\) with its apex as singular stratum and \(p(v)=0\). The link is simply connected, so the theorem’s link hypotheses hold. An open set \(O\times(a,b)\) away from the apex, with \(\varnothing\ne O\subsetneq S^2\), contains no member of the stated family: each of those sets contains every angular direction at its radii. Thus the assertion that their unions give the full topology, and the subsequent appeal to arbitrary \(W\cap V\), are not justified as written.

The existing depth induction supplies a repair. In a chart with central stratum \(S\), use all open subsets of \(V\setminus S\), whose depth is smaller, together with product tip neighborhoods \(C\times\mathring c_tL\). Compactness of \(L\) makes these a basis at the tip, and the former sets cover the off-tip topology. Finite intersections either remain tip neighborhoods or lie off the tip, so the inductive hypothesis and Proposition 6.6 supply \(P_k\) on each. Proposition 6.7 gives finite unions; compactness of finite chains gives the directed-union passage. The Zorn argument can then be used. Before this repair, however, the first step establishes \(P_k\) only for the indicated angularly saturated sets. The second step requires \(P_k(W\cap V)\) for an arbitrary maximal open set \(W\) and a chart \(V\), and this intersection need not belong to that class. The false basis claim therefore leaves Theorem 6.4 unproved by the printed argument. On p. 26, Theorem 6.4 is then used explicitly to deduce Theorem 6.1(2), stated as the main Theorem B(ii) on p. 3.

The assessment is Major for this invalid derivation on the main Hurewicz proof path. The depth-induction repair supports the corrected result without changing that assessment. The example refutes the basis claim; it does not refute the Hurewicz conclusion.
result: Impact: The false basis claim fails to establish Pk for arbitrary chart opens, particularly W intersection V in the maximal-open step on p26. Theorem6.4 is then used on that page to prove main Theorem6.1(2), equivalently TheoremB(ii). This is a Major core proof gap; depth induction supplies a supported repair, not a counterexample to the Hurewicz conclusion.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Add all opens off centralstratum to tipproduct neighborhoods; intersections have Pk by smaller depth or conelemma; finite unions and directedcompact-chain limits complete proof.

report: Abstract: This report examines the 65-page author manuscript arXiv:2210.00878v2 of Beliakova, Putyra, Robert and Wagner. Three substantive failures in intermediate assertions are established. The total Koszul homology in Proposition 3.13 lacks the asserted natural identification with the gl\(_0\) state-space functor; Proposition 4.21 fails at the permitted specialization \(t=1\); and Theorem A.2 loses filtered extension data while its comparison principle is invoked in the completed Kauffman-state argument. Their actual proof dependencies support Major assessment. They do not establish a counterexample to the completed conclusion of Theorem 5.11 or the final DGR dimension inequality. Six further corrections concern an exact couple, a Schur basis and normalization formulas. Supported Bockstein arguments and the limits of this review are recorded separately. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Functoriality, Coefficient Specialization and
Spectral-Sequence Comparisons
# Identity, source and scope

The frozen record M25-0253 is Anna Beliakova, Krzysztof K. Putyra, Louis-Hadrien Robert and Emmanuel Wagner, A proof of Dunfield–Gukov–Rasmussen conjecture, doi: 10.4171/JEMS/1626 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1626). The actual first-page title of the reviewed PDF is On the Dunfield–Gukov–Rasmussen conjecture. The running title and arXiv metadata retain the former wording. These fields are preserved as a mapping, not silently harmonized. The exact source is arXiv:2210.00878v2, submitted on 17 January 2025 at 10:26:58 UTC; the PDF separately gives 20 January 2025 as its internal date [source]. The publisher records acceptance on 27 December 2024 and publication on 30 May 2025 [record]. This author manuscript is not assumed identical to the subscription-only publisher PDF. All page references below are to the manuscript and agree with its printed numbers.

The initial review records reading all 65 pages, including references. Its scope covers coefficient conventions, elementary webs and quantum Hochschild homology, the cube construction, the two spectral-sequence arguments, the singular Floer comparison and explicit examples. Coherent orientations and holomorphic-disk compactification remain external analytic dependencies, considered in bounded checks and not independently reconstructed in full.

The main claim is the suitably updated DGR statement: two spectral sequences through gl\(_0\) homology give a bigraded dimension inequality after forgetting the \(a\)-grading. It does not assert equality of gl\(_0\) and knot Floer homology in general, nor prove the separate arbitrary-parameter invariance conjecture. The deformation parameter \(q\) is distinguished from \(\mathbf q\), the formal grading shift.
# The total Koszul functor does not have the claimed naturality

Problem 1.  Proposition 3.13 and the last paragraph of its proof (pp. 30–31, equations (26)–(29)) assert a natural isomorphism \(H^{d_0}\cong S_0\), induced by the identity on the reduced ordinary closed-web Soergel space. The assertion is false for the total complex defined in (26). Assessment: Major.

Work over \(\mathbb Q\), within the characteristic-zero hypothesis of Section 3.5. Let \(D_2\) be the annular closure of one dumbbell, with the outer output \(y_1\) marked. This is an elementary pointed web of index two; the proof’s convention sets \(y_1=0\). Its reduced open Soergel algebra is \[B=\mathbb Q[x_1,x_2,y_2]/(x_1+x_2-y_2,\;x_1x_2).\] There is one Koszul factor in (26), with differential \(x_2-y_2+1=1-x_1\). Thus the complex is, up to shifts, \(B\xrightarrow{1-x_1}B\). This multiplication is injective: in \(\mathbb Q[x_1,x_2]\), the polynomial \(1-x_1\) is relatively prime to \(x_1x_2\), so divisibility of \((1-x_1)h\) by \(x_1x_2\) implies divisibility of \(h\). Its cokernel is \[H^{d_0}(D_2)=
 \mathbb Q[x_1,x_2]/(x_1x_2,1-x_1)\cong\mathbb Q,
 \qquad x_1=y_2=1,\quad x_2=0.                   \tag{2.1}\] The source correctly obtains dimension one. The decoration actions are the obstruction.

The state space \(S_0(D_2;\mathbb Q)\) is one-dimensional and graded [1, Theorem 3.11(4), p. 29], so every thin dot of quantum degree two acts as zero. Directly, the two omnichrome colorings give \(S_1(D_2;\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Q[a]/(a^2)\), with the thin variables \(a,-a\). The marked multiplication has image \(\mathbb Qa\), annihilated by either dot. In (2.1), however, the inner output dot \(y_2\) acts as the identity. A natural isomorphism would intertwine identity and zero. To respect the degree-zero morphism convention, view the dotted cylinder as a morphism to the appropriate formal grading shift. The naturality square still has an invertible map composed with \(1\) on one side and a map composed with \(0\) on the other.
Ordinary annular closure also imposes \(x_2=y_2\), whereas (2.1) has \(x_2-y_2=-1\). Thus the total homology cannot be the asserted identity-induced quotient of the ordinary closed-web space.
#### Counterevidence and repair boundary.

The numerical dimension one is correct. Iterated homology is different: putting \(u=x_2\), \(v=y_2\) gives \(B=\mathbb Q[u,v]/(u(v-u))\). For the ordinary differential \(u-v\), \(\operatorname{HH}_0=\mathbb Q[u]\) and the kernel is the ideal \((u)\) in \(B\). The additional identity differential has image \((u)\) in \(\mathbb Q[u]\), so its iterated homology is \(\mathbb Q\) with \(u=v=0\). An associated-graded or iterated-homology identification may support a corrected argument, but requires a compatible filtration and naturality proof. Regrading (2.1) cannot turn identity into zero.

Page 31 uses the false functorial identification to pass from web calculations to a knot spectral sequence. This is a substantive proof defect even though the separately cited Robert–Wagner result may provide another route to the first spectral sequence. The example does not disprove that cited result, Theorem B, or the ultimate dimension inequality.
# Specialization invalidates the coefficient range of Proposition 4.21

Problem 2.  Proposition 4.21 (p. 42) asserts a finite Kauffman-state basis after quotienting by \(\Bbbk\)-torsion for a planar singular knot. Definition 4.8 (p. 35) permits any commutative \(\Bbbk\) and invertible \(t\). The assertion fails for \(\Bbbk=\mathbb Q\), \(t=1\). Assessment: Major.

Take the connected planar single-dumbbell closure \(D_2\), with the marking on the outer thin edge and a trace vertex on the inner edge. It has no real crossings and is a planar singular knot in the source’s sense. At the singular crossing label outgoing outer/inner variables \(a,b\) and incoming variables \(c,d\). Choose \(a=U_0\), matching the marked outgoing outer edge. Exchanging \(a,c\) leads to the same conclusion.

At \(t=1\) the twisting is trivial. The planar model has a unique degree-zero empty-multicycle generator \(x_0\). All boundaries into its degree are given by \[\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{generator or factor}&\text{coefficient of }x_0\\ \hline
\text{singular-crossing deviation}&\pm(ab-cd)\\
\text{inner trace deviation}&\pm(b-d)\\
\text{inner coherent cycle}&\pm(a-c)\\
\mathcal L_S\text{ factor}&a+b-c-d .
\end{array}\] This list is complete: a degree-minus-one planar generator has one deviation and no cycle, or one coherent cycle and no deviation. The inner cycle is the only coherent cycle avoiding the marked edge. The paired local disks have opposite signs by Lemma 4.6. The coherent-cycle disks have counts of magnitude one and opposite signs, as in the degree-zero calculation on pp. 50–51. This uses the low-degree planar calculation, not the asserted higher-homology vanishing of Proposition 4.21.

Hence \[\begin{aligned}
 H_0(\widehat{\operatorname{CFK}}(D_2,t=1)\otimes_R\mathcal L_S)
 &\cong \mathbb Q[a,b,c,d]/
 (a,\;b-d,\;ab-cd,\;a-c,\;a+b-c-d)\\
 &\cong\mathbb Q[b].\end{aligned}\] The last isomorphism sends \(a,c\) to zero and \(d\) to \(b\). Every nonlocal relation can also be checked independently. Assign value zero to the outer circular strand, value \(b\) to the inner strand, and multiset \(\{0,b\}\) to the thick edge. A transverse closed curve has equal incoming and outgoing counts for each closed colored strand. Its products coincide, including the case where both contain a zero factor. Since \(q=t=1\), the coefficient \(q^{2i}\) is one. No additional nonlocal relation can impose a polynomial equation on \(b\).

Over \(\mathbb Q\) the torsion submodule is zero with the intended definition using a nonzero annihilator. The computed space is infinite-dimensional, while a finite diagram has finitely many Kauffman states. The source’s omission of the word nonzero in its torsion definition is not used to manufacture the contradiction.
#### Impact and correction.

The unrestricted coefficient claim and the asserted reduction to \(\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]\) fail at this specialization. A torsion quotient and concentration of homology cannot be passed through arbitrary nonflat specializations. Since the proposition is used for concentration at vertices of the Floer cube, its valid coefficient range matters to the proof.

The example does not refute the generic completed calculation. A repair must specify a completion or localization where the relevant \(1-t^m\) are units and prove concentration there. Page 43 uses a completion with positive powers of \(t^{1/2}\), whereas Theorem 5.11 uses \(\mathbb Z((q))\) with \(t=q^{-2}\). An infinite formal series cannot simply be substituted across these opposite directions. A symmetry or a separate contraction/completion argument is needed. That direction issue is a remaining proof obligation, not an additional counterexample to Theorem 5.11 over its stated ring.
# Filtered modules and the exact couple

Problem 3.  Theorem A.2 (p. 56) omits a compatible map of abutments: an abstract spectral-sequence isomorphism does not determine an isomorphism of completed filtered modules. Proposition 4.21 invokes this comparison principle on p. 43 for its completed Kauffman-state conclusion. Assessment: Major.

Let \(M=\mathbb Z/4\), with \(F^0M=M\), \(F^1M=2M\), \(F^2M=0\), and \(N=(\mathbb Z/2)^2\), with \(F^0N=N\), \(F^1N\) one direct summand, \(F^2N=0\). Extend both filtrations by the whole module in negative degrees and zero in higher degrees. Regard these as degree-zero complexes with zero differential. They are exhaustive, Hausdorff and complete, and have identical constant spectral sequences with two associated-graded copies of \(\mathbb Z/2\). The pagewise identity satisfies the printed hypothesis. Yet only \(M\) has an element of order four; completion changes neither.

The preceding source paragraph correctly assumes an actual filtered map inducing the associated-graded isomorphism. That premise cannot be discarded: the completed modules in this example are not even isomorphic as groups.

The failure enters the principal argument directly. On p. 43, after the associated-graded computation for Proposition 4.21, the source invokes uniqueness of the spectral-sequence limit, referring to Appendix A.1, to conclude that completed homology is free on Kauffman states and concentrated in degree zero. Neither pp. 42–43 nor A.2 supplies a compatible filtered comparison map or constructs the required lifts. Proposition 4.21 is then used in Section 5, including Theorem 5.11. This is an invoked core proof step, not an unused appendix assertion.

A repair must retain an appropriate filtered chain or abutment map and verify its graded comparison and convergence, or construct a separate lifting argument for the particular completed modules. Their free graded pieces may permit this, but the possible repair does not validate the printed inference or reduce its severity. The finite-extension example refutes the general comparison theorem; it does not refute the particular completed conclusion of Theorem 5.11 or the DGR inequality. The finite PID Bockstein argument does not require this invalid uniqueness principle.

Problem 4.  The proof of Proposition A.7 (p. 58) incorrectly says the \((k+1)\)st exact couple is zero when \(p(q)\) is not a unit. Its terminal spectral-sequence page can still be zero. Assessment: Minor.

Take \(L=\mathbb Q[q,q^{-1}]\) and \(C=(L\xrightarrow{(q-1)(q+1)}L)\). These are finite free modules, \(k=1\), and \(p(q)=q+1\) is coprime to \(q-1\). The homology is \(L/((q-1)(q+1))\). The first Bockstein differential between the two copies of \(\mathbb Q\) is multiplication by \(p(1)=2\), so \(E_2=0\). But the next \(D\) term is \[(q-1)L/((q-1)(q+1))\cong L/(q+1)\ne0,\] and multiplication by \(q-1\) on it is multiplication by \(-2\). In general, the coprime torsion remains in \(D\). Replace the zero-couple assertion by vanishing of its \(E\) term, or split off the coprime torsion first. Smith normal form then proves the stated finite stabilization and terminal free-rank formula. Proposition A.7 itself is not refuted. The formula on p. 57 must also use \(g^{(n)}\circ h^{(n)}\) as the differential on \(B^{(n)}\): \(h\) has domain \(B\), whereas the printed \(g^{(n)}\circ f^{(n)}\) has domain \(A\) and is not an endomorphism of \(B\).
# Local algebraic and normalization corrections
Problem 5.  Example 2.5 (p. 10) puts the Schur polynomial in the wrong block. Assessment: Minor.

Take \((3)\prec(2,1)\), \(i=r=1\), over \(\mathbb Q\). The printed formula places \(s_\lambda\) in block two. By the definition of \(T(a,b)\) on p. 8, \(\lambda=(1,1)\) is the maximal rectangle in \(T(1,2)\). The alleged basis element is \(1\otimes e_2(x_3)=0\), yet its stated trace is one. This is impossible for a linear map. Place the Schur polynomial in block \(i\), adjusting the counts of unit tensor factors, or transpose the rectangle and adjust the trace convention when choosing the other block. The standard freeness and Frobenius-extension result survives; this displayed basis error does not refute the later categorical existence statement.
Problem 6.  Example 5.4 (p. 46) loses a factor of two in its exponent and annihilator. Assessment: Minor.

Equation (39), p. 44, uses \(q^{2i}\). Take two nested thin circles, mark the outer circle, work over \(\mathbb Q\), and set \(q=-1\). The inner component has index one. Set every edge variable to zero. All local relations vanish. For a curve meeting the web both nonlocal products vanish; for a curve meeting no edges the relation is \(1-q^{2i}=0\). Thus the algebra has a nonzero augmentation to \(\mathbb Q\), which its printed annihilator \(1-q=2\) cannot annihilate. The corrected exponent is \(2(w_i+\cdots+w_r)\) and a supported annihilator is \(1-q^{2\gcd(w_1,\ldots,w_r)}\). The text after Lemma 5.8 (p. 49) already has \(2w\). Vanishing under the hypothesis that all \(1-q^d\) are units is unchanged, so the generic disconnected-web argument survives.
Problem 7.  The trace-relation sentence in Proposition 5.12’s proof (p. 52) reverses the exponent; the proposition’s map is consistent. Assessment: Minor.

At a nontrace crossing, the incoming edges have level \(r\) and outgoing edges level \(r+1\). The stated map \(x_\alpha\mapsto t^{-n(\alpha)}x_\alpha\) sends \(t(x_a+x_b)-x_c-x_d\) to a unit multiple of \(x_a+x_b-x_c-x_d\). At the trace the incoming level is \(n\) and outgoing level zero. Thus \(x_a=x_c\) becomes \[\widetilde x_a=t^{-n}\widetilde x_c
              =q^2\widetilde x_c,\qquad q=t^{-n/2}.\] The proof prints \(t^n=q^{-2}\) instead. For \(n=1\) the factors \(t,t^{-1}\) are already different in the Laurent polynomial ring. Correcting this sentence to \(t^{-n}\) and \(q^2\) agrees with Example 5.2. Reversing the proposition’s map would spoil the nontrace check.
Problem 8.  Appendix B has an exponent sign error in the cyclic operator’s description and an endpoint-index error in (53), pp. 59–60. Assessment: Minor.

Its definition is \[t_n(a_0\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n)
   =q^{-|a_n|}a_n\otimes a_0\otimes\cdots\otimes a_{n-1}.\] Applying this \(n+1\) times gives \(q^{-d}\) on internal degree \(d\), not the printed \(q^d\). For \(A=\mathbb Q[x]\), \(|x|=2\), \(q=2\), the zero-chain \(x\) is sent by \(T_0\) to \(x/4\), not \(4x\). Also \(\sigma_n=t_{n+1}s_n\) inserts \(1\) at the front, so \(d_i\sigma_n=\sigma_{n-1}d_{i-1}\) for \(1\le i\le n\), and \(d_{n+1}\sigma_n=t_n\). These are the corrected endpoint and range in (53).

The homotopy still satisfies \(\partial h+h\partial=1-T\) with \(T=q^{-d}\). On each positive-degree summand, \((1-q^{-d})^{-1}h\) is a contraction under the source’s unit hypotheses. Nonnegative grading identifies the degree-zero summand with the Hochschild complex of \(A_0\). Thus Proposition B.2 and the generic vanishing mechanism survive. The scalar sign in Proposition 2.11 was also examined, but the scalar-subscript twisting notation leaves a convention issue. It is not counted as another confirmed failure.
Problem 9.  The normalization sentence following the cap formula on p. 18 has the wrong sign in its claimed preimage of one. Assessment: Minor.

Take \(a=b=1\) over \(\mathbb Q\), with \(P(x)=x=e_1\) and \(Q=1\). The denominator in the displayed definition is \(x_j-x_i\). It gives \[e_1\star1=\frac{x_1}{x_2-x_1}+
           \frac{x_2}{x_1-x_2}=-1,\] whereas the sentence claims \(e_a^b\star1=1\). All size and coefficient hypotheses hold. In this case \(-e_1\) is the required preimage of one, so surjectivity is unchanged. More generally the rectangular normalization must account for the sign introduced by the denominator orientation. Changing a global foam convention would require checking its other relations; the supported correction here is to the stated normalization, not a claim that the entire foam functor is invalid.
# Supported arguments, computations and limitations

The quantum Hochschild contraction is chain-level and needs no additional base-ring flatness assumption. Reduction from Bott–Samelson objects through annular web decompositions supports the vanishing strategy of Theorem 2.36, under its invertibility hypotheses.

For pseudo-completion, write \(R=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\), \(S=\mathbb Z((q))\), \(M=\mathcal A_R\) and \(K=\ker(M\to M\otimes_RS)\). Right exactness gives \((M/K)\otimes_RS\cong M\otimes_RS\), since the image of \(K\otimes_RS\) is zero. This justifies the elementary base-change step of Proposition 5.14 without calling \(S\) a field. For a field \(\mathbb K\), however, \(\mathbb K((q))\) contains the fraction field of the PID \(\mathbb K[q,q^{-1}]\). Finite freeness of the web modules and the finite cube then support the rank and finite-stabilization mechanism of Theorem B. The completed Floer comparison and compatible coefficient changes must be supplied within their valid range; this sound algebraic step does not remove Problems 1 and 2.

The signs in Lemma 4.6 were checked against its two boundary-degeneration identities. Initial-diagram admissibility was checked through the periodic-domain inequalities, including connecting necks. The skein maps and planar local/nonlocal relations were checked against actual diagrams. This is not a new analytic proof of the cited orientation and gluing theorems.

The two trefoil matrix pairs on pp. 60–61 were transcribed from actual page images and multiplied exactly. Both products are zero. Their ranks are \((3,2)\) and \((2,3)\) respectively over both \(\mathbb Q\) and \(\mathbb F_2\), giving homology dimensions \((1,1,1)\) in the three occupied degrees, as reported. The figure-eight and cinquefoil grading and Euler-characteristic arguments on pp. 62–63 were inspected; not all figure-eight foam maps were independently recomputed. The \(T(3,4)\) discussion and knot-detection consequences retain their stated external dependencies and characteristic assumptions. No author code was executed.

A bounded search of the arXiv and EMS records, indexed author material, and correction/supplement queries located no separate correction or required supplementary code for this exact source. One direct author-page fetch timed out. This is a search limitation, not proof that no unindexed correction exists. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect.
# Supporting checks

The overall assessment is Major, based on Problems 1–3: the total-homology naturality assertion, unrestricted coefficient claim, and filtered comparison principle actually invoked in the completed Kauffman-state proof. Problems 4–9 remain Minor within their stated scopes. The completed conclusion of Theorem 5.11 and the final DGR inequality are not disproved. Remaining completion, analytic and convention limits are retained explicitly.

The initial analysis and original report were produced in the preceding ChatGPT review conversation. Those historical contributions are distinct from the present focused acceptance and are not human reviews. Detailed coverage, actual page-image inspections, exact calculations and current build records accompany this report. The scientific decision is pending and the human-review list is empty.

problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: Problem 1. Proposition 3.13 and the last paragraph of its proof (pp. 30–31, equations (26)–(29)) assert a natural isomorphism \(H^{d_0}\cong S_0\), induced by the identity on the…

Claim: The total H(dHH+d0) functor is naturally isomorphic to S0 by the identity on the ordinary closed-web Soergel quotient.
Coefficient field Q of characteristic zero. Elementary pointed annular one-dumbbell web D2. Outer output y1=0; permitted formal grading shifts for dotted cylinder.
analysis:
Work over \(\mathbb Q\), within the characteristic-zero hypothesis of Section 3.5. Let \(D_2\) be the annular closure of one dumbbell, with the outer output \(y_1\) marked. This is an elementary pointed web of index two; the proof’s convention sets \(y_1=0\). Its reduced open Soergel algebra is \[B=\mathbb Q[x_1,x_2,y_2]/(x_1+x_2-y_2,\;x_1x_2).\] There is one Koszul factor in (26), with differential \(x_2-y_2+1=1-x_1\). Thus the complex is, up to shifts, \(B\xrightarrow{1-x_1}B\). This multiplication is injective: in \(\mathbb Q[x_1,x_2]\), the polynomial \(1-x_1\) is relatively prime to \(x_1x_2\), so divisibility of \((1-x_1)h\) by \(x_1x_2\) implies divisibility of \(h\). Its cokernel is \[H^{d_0}(D_2)=
 \mathbb Q[x_1,x_2]/(x_1x_2,1-x_1)\cong\mathbb Q,
 \qquad x_1=y_2=1,\quad x_2=0.                   \tag{2.1}\] The source correctly obtains dimension one. The decoration actions are the obstruction.

The state space \(S_0(D_2;\mathbb Q)\) is one-dimensional and graded [1, Theorem 3.11(4), p. 29], so every thin dot of quantum degree two acts as zero. Directly, the two omnichrome colorings give \(S_1(D_2;\mathbb Q)\cong\mathbb Q[a]/(a^2)\), with the thin variables \(a,-a\). The marked multiplication has image \(\mathbb Qa\), annihilated by either dot. In (2.1), however, the inner output dot \(y_2\) acts as the identity. A natural isomorphism would intertwine identity and zero. To respect the degree-zero morphism convention, view the dotted cylinder as a morphism to the appropriate formal grading shift. The naturality square still has an invertible map composed with \(1\) on one side and a map composed with \(0\) on the other.
Ordinary annular closure also imposes \(x_2=y_2\), whereas (2.1) has \(x_2-y_2=-1\). Thus the total homology cannot be the asserted identity-induced quotient of the ordinary closed-web space.
result: The numerical dimension one is correct. Iterated homology is different: putting \(u=x_2\), \(v=y_2\) gives \(B=\mathbb Q[u,v]/(u(v-u))\). For the ordinary differential \(u-v\), \(\operatorname{HH}_0=\mathbb Q[u]\) and the kernel is the ideal \((u)\) in \(B\). The additional identity differential has image \((u)\) in \(\mathbb Q[u]\), so its iterated homology is \(\mathbb Q\) with \(u=v=0\). An associated-graded or iterated-homology identification may support a corrected argument, but requires a compatible filtration and naturality proof. Regrading (2.1) cannot turn identity into zero.

Page 31 uses the false functorial identification to pass from web calculations to a knot spectral sequence. This is a substantive proof defect even though the separately cited Robert–Wagner result may provide another route to the first spectral sequence. The example does not disprove that cited result, Theorem B, or the ultimate dimension inequality.
Impact: False core functor identification used in the supplied first spectral-sequence argument; not a disproof of every possible DGR proof.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Replace unfiltered total homology by a precisely specified filtered/associated-graded or iterated construction and prove naturality and target. Regrading alone cannot fix identity versus zero.

claim: Kind: paraphrase

Claim: For arbitrary coefficient ring with invertible t, quotienting planar singular-knot homology by coefficient torsion gives a finite Kauffman-state basis.
k=Q,t=1, invertible as required. Connected planar singular D2, no real crossings, outer thin marking. Torsion read charitably with NONZERO annihilator, not exploiting printed omission.
analysis: Take the connected planar single-dumbbell closure \(D_2\), with the marking on the outer thin edge and a trace vertex on the inner edge. It has no real crossings and is a planar singular knot in the source’s sense. At the singular crossing label outgoing outer/inner variables \(a,b\) and incoming variables \(c,d\). Choose \(a=U_0\), matching the marked outgoing outer edge. Exchanging \(a,c\) leads to the same conclusion.

At \(t=1\) the twisting is trivial. The planar model has a unique degree-zero empty-multicycle generator \(x_0\). All boundaries into its degree are given by \[\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{generator or factor}&\text{coefficient of }x_0\\ \hline
\text{singular-crossing deviation}&\pm(ab-cd)\\
\text{inner trace deviation}&\pm(b-d)\\
\text{inner coherent cycle}&\pm(a-c)\\
\mathcal L_S\text{ factor}&a+b-c-d .
\end{array}\] This list is complete: a degree-minus-one planar generator has one deviation and no cycle, or one coherent cycle and no deviation. The inner cycle is the only coherent cycle avoiding the marked edge. The paired local disks have opposite signs by Lemma 4.6. The coherent-cycle disks have counts of magnitude one and opposite signs, as in the degree-zero calculation on pp. 50–51. This uses the low-degree planar calculation, not the asserted higher-homology vanishing of Proposition 4.21.

Hence \[\begin{aligned}
 H_0(\widehat{\operatorname{CFK}}(D_2,t=1)\otimes_R\mathcal L_S)
 &\cong \mathbb Q[a,b,c,d]/
 (a,\;b-d,\;ab-cd,\;a-c,\;a+b-c-d)\\
 &\cong\mathbb Q[b].\end{aligned}\] The last isomorphism sends \(a,c\) to zero and \(d\) to \(b\). Every nonlocal relation can also be checked independently. Assign value zero to the outer circular strand, value \(b\) to the inner strand, and multiset \(\{0,b\}\) to the thick edge. A transverse closed curve has equal incoming and outgoing counts for each closed colored strand. Its products coincide, including the case where both contain a zero factor. Since \(q=t=1\), the coefficient \(q^{2i}\) is one. No additional nonlocal relation can impose a polynomial equation on \(b\).

Over \(\mathbb Q\) the torsion submodule is zero with the intended definition using a nonzero annihilator. The computed space is infinite-dimensional, while a finite diagram has finitely many Kauffman states. The source’s omission of the word nonzero in its torsion definition is not used to manufacture the contradiction.

The unrestricted coefficient claim and the asserted reduction to \(\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]\) fail at this specialization. A torsion quotient and concentration of homology cannot be passed through arbitrary nonflat specializations. Since the proposition is used for concentration at vertices of the Floer cube, its valid coefficient range matters to the proof.

The example does not refute the generic completed calculation. A repair must specify a completion or localization where the relevant \(1-t^m\) are units and prove concentration there. Page 43 uses a completion with positive powers of \(t^{1/2}\), whereas Theorem 5.11 uses \(\mathbb Z((q))\) with \(t=q^{-2}\). An infinite formal series cannot simply be substituted across these opposite directions. A symmetry or a separate contraction/completion argument is needed. That direction issue is a remaining proof obligation, not an additional counterexample to Theorem 5.11 over its stated ring.
result: Impact: Substantive coefficient-range error in a planar computation used for cube concentration.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Restrict to appropriate completed/localized coefficients and prove concentration there; justify t-small versus q-small completion direction. Arbitrary nonflat specialization is unavailable.

problems.title: Abstract spectral-sequence isomorphism loses extension data

claim: Kind: paraphrase
Location. Theorem: A.2
Location. Pdf page: 56
Claim: An isomorphism on one page induces an isomorphism of completed filtered abutments without a compatible filtered map.
Z modules. Zero-differential degree0 complexes. Finite exhaustive Hausdorff complete filtrations. Actual pagewise identity of constant spectral sequences.
analysis: Let \(M=\mathbb Z/4\), with \(F^0M=M\), \(F^1M=2M\), \(F^2M=0\), and \(N=(\mathbb Z/2)^2\), with \(F^0N=N\), \(F^1N\) one direct summand, \(F^2N=0\). Extend both filtrations by the whole module in negative degrees and zero in higher degrees. Regard these as degree-zero complexes with zero differential. They are exhaustive, Hausdorff and complete, and have identical constant spectral sequences with two associated-graded copies of \(\mathbb Z/2\). The pagewise identity satisfies the printed hypothesis. Yet only \(M\) has an element of order four; completion changes neither.

The preceding source paragraph correctly assumes an actual filtered map inducing the associated-graded isomorphism. That premise cannot be discarded: the completed modules in this example are not even isomorphic as groups.

Neither pp. 42–43 nor A.2 supplies a compatible filtered comparison map or constructs the required lifts. Proposition 4.21 is then used in Section 5, including Theorem 5.11. This is an invoked core proof step, not an unused appendix assertion.

A repair must retain an appropriate filtered chain or abutment map and verify its graded comparison and convergence, or construct a separate lifting argument for the particular completed modules. Their free graded pieces may permit this, but the possible repair does not validate the printed inference or reduce its severity. The finite-extension example refutes the general comparison theorem; it does not refute the particular completed conclusion of Theorem 5.11 or the DGR inequality. The finite PID Bockstein argument does not require this invalid uniqueness principle.

report: Abstract: The exact 51-page author manuscript arXiv:2303.09069v3 is examined. Ten mathematical discrepancies are established by finite calculations, coefficient comparisons or direct parameter substitutions. One finding is assessed as Major: the printed proof of the central Bailey kernel identity passes through a false double-sum expansion, and the identity is subsequently used in the Bailey-tree argument. A corrected finite expansion repairs that derivation, without establishing that the printed step was valid. Nine further findings are Minor within their demonstrated scopes. The kernel identity and principal results are not disproved. Prior-theorem citations remain counterevidence, but their precise equivalence has not been verified from a retained complete source. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Bailey Transformations, Character Formulas

# Source, identity and review boundary

The frozen record M25-0254 is S. Ole Warnaar, An \(\mathrm A_2\) Bailey tree and \(\mathrm A_2^{(1)}\) Rogers–Ramanujan-type identities, doi: 10.4171/JEMS/1627 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1627). The author manuscript is not assumed identical to the publisher’s version. The frozen DOI and 2025 batch membership remain unchanged. The present independent acceptance re-examined the reported Problems and their dependencies; it does not claim a second complete review of every page. The scope includes the conventions for negative factorial indices, the root-lattice support, the finite inverse matrices, the two- and four-parameter transformations, the Kanade–Russell iteration, the character formulas and the limiting arguments. Throughout, \((a;q)_n\) and \(\theta(z;q)=(z,q/z;q)_\infty\) have the manuscript’s meaning. The arguments are primarily in formal series; analytic arguments below use \(0<|q|<1\) away from poles and then identify the corresponding formal coefficients.
# Confirmed mathematical findings
Problem 1 (Minor; p. 4, first unnumbered identity).  The prefactor for the \(\tau=-1\) specialization has the wrong modulus.

The printed prefactor is \((q^{2k+2};q^{2k+2})_\infty^2\), although the theta factors have modulus \(q^{3k+2}\). Take \(k=1\), \(a=1\), \(b=0\). These integers satisfy every restriction in that display, including \(b\ne k\) and the stated convention \(\mu_0=\infty\). Its left side reduces to \[L(q)=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{q^{n^2}}{(q;q)_n(q;q)_\infty}.\] Indeed, \((1-q)(q^2;q)_\infty=(q;q)_\infty\). Up to degree four the inner series is \(1+q+q^2+q^3+2q^4\), since only \(n=0,1,2\) contribute. Multiplication by \((q;q)_\infty^{-1}=1+q+2q^2+3q^3+5q^4+O(q^5)\) gives \[L(q)=1+2q+4q^2+7q^3+13q^4+O(q^5).\] The printed right side, to the same order, is \[\frac1{(1-q)^2(1-q^2)(1-q^3)}+O(q^5)
 =1+2q+4q^2+7q^3+11q^4+O(q^5).\] Thus it fails by \(2q^4\). Replace \(2k+2\) by \(3k+2\) in the prefactor. Equation (1.5) and the correct product evaluation from (5.16) already use that modulus. The separate main identity and Theorem 1.2 are not refuted by this display error.
Problem 2 (Minor; p. 5, paragraph following Theorem 1.3).  The highest-weight label omits the level shift by three.
Problem 3 (Major; p. 17, proof of Theorem 4.2).  The double sum immediately below the transformed \({}_2\phi_1\) loses a factor and has an incorrect exponent.

Both errors can be separated without approaching a pole. Put \(q=1/2\), \(z=2/3\), \(w=3/5\). At \(n=0,m=1\) the printed sum is \(2\), whereas the preceding expression and \(\Phi_{0,1}\) are \(20/7\). At \(n=2,m=0\) the missing prefactor is one, yet the printed sum is \(71/15\), whereas the preceding expression and \(\Phi_{2,0}\) are \(24/5\).

For a direct derivation of (2.1), use \[(q^{-r};q)_s=(-1)^s q^{-rs+\binom s2}
              \frac{(q;q)_r}{(q;q)_{r-s}}\] and the corresponding formula with \(m\). Multiplication by \((wq^{m+1})^s\) leaves the exponent \(r^2-rs+s^2\), and cancellation of \((q;q)_m\) leaves the displayed prefactor. After \(r\mapsto r+s\), this corrected expression gives the next \({}_1\phi_1\) line of the manuscript. This supplies a finite algebraic repair and supports the kernel identity, but the printed transition performs this shift on a false double sum. The supplied proof therefore contains a substantive failure in a central step. Equation (4.5) is then used on p. 19 for the constant, \(u\) and \(uv\) coefficients in the proof of Theorem 4.4, and for the shifted iteration underlying the Bailey tree. This actual dependency makes the finding Major; it does not make the kernel identity or the principal identities false.

The manuscript cites [8, Theorem 4.3], [89, Theorem 5.1] and [31, Corollary 7.9] as prior formulations on p. 16. These citations and the correct neighboring expressions are counterevidence to a false-theorem interpretation. No retained complete copy of those prior sources was available for this acceptance, so their precise equivalence has not been independently verified and is not counted as an established alternative proof. The corrected finite expansion above is the demonstrated repair.

Problem 5 (Minor; p. 31, last display of the proof of Theorem 1.2).  The final product sign repeats an already expanded three-factor theta product.

The line contains \(\prod_{1\le i<j\le3}\theta(q^{a+1},q^{b+1},q^{a+b+2};q^K)\). The expression following the product sign is independent of \(i,j\); under the manuscript’s multiple-argument convention this cubes the required three-theta product. For \(k=1\), \(\tau=-1\), \(a=1\), \(b=0\) and \(K=5\), that three-theta product is \(1-q+O(q^2)\). The prefactor \((q^5;q^5)_\infty^2/(q;q)_\infty^3\) is \(1+3q+O(q^2)\). The intended result has coefficient \(2\) at \(q\); the printed result has coefficient \(0\). Delete the outer product sign. Alternatively retain the product with its unexpanded factor \(\theta(q^{\nu_i-\nu_j};q^K)\). The preceding general-rank formula and (1.5) both give the correct expression, so the endpoint of the proof is recovered directly.
Problem 6 (Minor; p. 32, parameter bounds preceding Theorem 6.1).  Two primed-parameter bounds are misstated.

Assume exactly the stated range \(2\le k<a\le\lfloor3k/2\rfloor\) and \(0\le b\le3k-2a\). For \[(a',b')=(2k-a,a+b-k),\qquad
 (a'',b'')=(2k-a-b-1,a-k-1),\] the text claims \(a'\le\lceil k/2\rceil\) and subsequently uses \(a'\) where \(a''\) is needed. The admissible choice \((k,a,b)=(4,5,0)\) gives \((a',b')=(3,1)\) and \((a'',b'')=(2,0)\). It contradicts both \(a'\le2\) and the second printed \(a'\le k-2=2\).

The bounds actually implied by the hypotheses are \[0<b'\le a'\le k-1,\qquad
 \lceil k/2\rceil\le a',\qquad
 0\le b''\le a''\le k-2.\] For example \(b'\le a'\) is just \(b\le3k-2a\), and \(a''-b''=3k-2a-b\ge0\). These correct bounds place both parameter pairs in the domain of Theorem 1.2. Consequently the application of the theta three-term relation and the statement of Theorem 6.1 survive.
Problem 7 (Minor; p. 32, first modulus-seven identity).  The factor \((q^7;q^7)_\infty\) needs exponent two.

The unnumbered identity for the below-the-line case \((a,b,k,\tau)=(2,0,1,1)\) has only one such factor. Writing its two summation indices as \(r,s\), separate the numerator into the two exponents \[E_1=r^2-rs+s^2-r+s,\qquad E_2=r^2-rs+s^2+r .\] The common reciprocal denominator is \((1-q)^{-1}(q;q)_r^{-1}(q;q)_s^{-1}(q^2;q)_{r+s}^{-1}\). Exact coefficient multiplication gives coefficient \(126\) at \(q^7\) on the left and \(127\) for the printed product. This calculation is finite: for coefficients through degree \(N\), \[E_1\ge\tfrac12((r-1)^2+(s+1)^2)-1,\qquad
 E_2\ge\tfrac12(r^2+s^2)+r.\] If \(r\) or \(s\) is at least \(N+3\), both exceed \(N\). The denominator introduces no negative powers. Thus the saved enumeration through \(N=10\), with \(0\le r,s\le12\), includes every contribution, including the cases \(2r-s<0\).

Squaring the prefactor gives coefficient \(126\) and agrees through degree ten in the exact computation. Its necessity also follows from the rank-two product normalization displayed on p. 31. The formula is a separately cited example; this correction does not alter the proof or domain of Theorem 6.1.
Problem 8 (Minor; p. 37, equation (7.6)).  The last index in the quadratic exponent must be \(j\).
Problem 9 (Minor; p. 42, equation (8.10b)).  The first argument of the subtracted character is \(z\), not \(q\).
Problem 10 (Minor; p. 46, opening factorial identity).  The base of each factor on the left must be \(q^r\).

The printed equality is \(\prod_{i=1}^r(aq^{r-i};q)_k=(a;q)_{rk}\). Take \(r=k=2\), \(a=1/3\), \(q=1/2\), which are allowed nonzero parameters with no pole. The two sides are respectively \[\frac{275}{648}\quad\hbox{and}\quad\frac{1265}{2592},
 \qquad\hbox{with difference }-\frac{55}{864}.\] The correct identity is \[\prod_{i=1}^r(aq^{r-i};q^r)_k=(a;q)_{rk}.\] Its exponents \(r-i+rj\), for \(1\le i\le r\) and \(0\le j<k\), are exactly \(0,1,\ldots,rk-1\). The preceding instruction \(q\mapsto q^r\) supplies this base, and the following transformed summand uses the resulting contiguous products. The interpolation, rotation and coefficient extraction leading to (A.4) remain available with this correction; (A.4) itself was not refuted.
# Supported proof structure and boundary checks
The following observations distinguish the local errors from the central statements they accompany.
## Finite kernels and the tree

The proof of Lemma 3.3 is polynomial in \(u\). Its constant coefficient is the reproducing identity with \(z/q\); the linear coefficient follows by \(K_{n;r+1}(z/q)=zK_{n-1;r}(zq)\) and \(\Phi_{-1}=0\). The infinite-partition limit in Corollary 3.2 is coefficientwise: a nonzero terminal part after \(h\) iterations carries degree at least \(h\).

For the \(\mathrm A_2\) kernel, the shifted lower bounds in Corollaries 4.5, 4.10 and 4.11 were retained. The apparent ratios in (4.19) cancel into a six-term polynomial, so boundary values such as \(u=d=0\) are interpreted in that polynomial, not by dividing by zero. The two finite inverse-matrix products, the coefficient identities and the conversion of the specialized Gustafson summand were checked. The analytic bilateral identity is used first in its convergence region; its terminating specialization then gives a rational identity. These finite checks supplement the algebraic derivations and do not replace them.
## Iteration to the main product

Equation (5.7) uses \(t\ge2\); the manuscript explicitly identifies the exceptional support at \(t=1\), \(y=(-1,0,1)\). The proof uses \(t=3\), so that exception does not invalidate it. The stages use \(k-a\), \(a-b\) and \(b\) iterations in the range \(0\le b\le a\le k\). At \(a=b\) the central step is justified by (5.9), rather than by an unavailable instance with \(a-1\). Interchanging \(a,b\) is accompanied by \((n,m)\mapsto(m,n)\) and \(y\mapsto(-y_3,-y_2,-y_1)\).

Separate exact checks tested all 39 choices with \(k=1,2\), all allowed \(a,b,\tau\), through \(q^{12}\), and 147 finite root identities at \(q=1/2\), without a mismatch in (1.5) or (5.2). No inference of universal correctness is drawn solely from those tests.
## Characters and principal subspaces

The \(\sigma_i\) in the p. 33 definition of \(v_i\) is unbound. Removing it gives \(v_i=\chi(i\ge b)-\lambda_i\) for \(i<k\), as follows directly from (1.5). These sequences satisfy the monotonicity hypotheses of Lemma 7.1 used in the character conversion. The endpoint \(\tau=-1,b=k\) is handled by the stated symmetry or the separate \(a=b=k\) expression, not by extending Theorem 7.3 beyond its displayed first range. Twenty-five instances of Theorems 7.2 and 7.3 at \(k=1,2\) were checked through \(q^{10}\). The quadratic-form substitution preceding (7.6) provides the specific counterevidence recorded in Problem 8.

For Theorem 8.1, the unit-pair identity (8.5) has finite support \(y_1\le n\), \(y_1+y_2\le m\) with \(y\in Q_+\). The proof follows the same three finite transformations and the endpoint \(a=b\) is explicitly supplied by (8.6). The manuscript itself defines the right side of (8.2) for \(a+b>k\) as an extension of notation; it does not silently assert that those weights are dominant.

For fixed \(a,b\), the nonzero-\(y\) terms in the bosonic formula have valuation at least \[(k-a-b+1)\sum_{y_i>0}y_i .\] For sufficiently large \(k\) this tends to infinity uniformly over nonzero \(y\in Q_+\), leaving the \(y=0\) determinant and proving the indicated coefficientwise passage to Corollary 1.5. On the partition side the positive quadratic tails likewise give finite support at each fixed degree. This addresses the limiting issue without imposing an unwritten analytic ordering on \(x_1,x_2,x_3\).
## Appendix and general-rank discussion

After the base correction in Problem 10, the specialized summand of (A.1) has support independent of \(N\). Clearing the indicated denominator gives polynomials in \(d\) of degree at most \(n\); their equality for \(d=q^{-rN}\) therefore proves the rational continuation used in the argument. The rotation sends a fixed total to the root lattice, and the finite \(q\)-binomial theorem gives (A.4). The root’s independently written calculation tested (A.4) at \(q=1/3\), \(r=2,3,4\), \(0\le m\le n\le4\), a total of 45 exact instances, all equal. Seven additional \(\mathrm A_1\) chain/tree checks at generic rational parameters also agree.

The reversal symmetry and chain (9.2)–(9.3) follow from the Cartan symmetry and splitting the first partition parts in (9.1). The general-rank tree and manifest positivity of the general root identity are presented as open problems. The review does not reinterpret them as proved assertions. The external Whittaker-vector and representation-theoretic results are dependencies whose entire original proofs were not independently reconstructed here.
# Supporting checks

Several remaining notational matters merit correction without turning them into manufactured theorem counterexamples. Conjecture 1.1 and Theorem 1.3 should specify \(k\ge1\) for their displayed terminal-index multisums, or supply a separate \(k=0\) definition. Merely assigning an arbitrary value to an undefined \(g_{\lambda_0,\mu_0}\) is not a valid disproof. On p. 38 the pairing uses the undefined printed symbol \(a_i^\vee\); if the intended symbol is \(\alpha_i^\vee\), the correct convention is \(\langle\Lambda_0,\alpha_i^\vee\rangle=\delta_{0i}\), as the next sentence and the level-one assertion require. The proof text on p. 19 also contains a common-factor label and an \(m\) for \(s\) index slip. The p. 26 inversion sentence should start from \(\tau=+1\) to derive \(\tau=-1\); the independently checked inversion exponents support that correction. The unbound \(\sigma_i\) on p. 33 is a notation issue, as explained above. These do not contradict the independently checked shifted identities.

Each of Problems 1–10 has a concrete mathematical discrepancy. Problem 3 is Major because the supplied proof of the central kernel identity contains a false expansion that is actually used by the subsequent transformations. Its explicit repair does not validate the printed proof. Problems 1–2 and 4–10 are Minor within the demonstrated scopes. In particular, for Problem 4 the explicit constant-term evaluation and multilinearity already yield the next correct line after deleting the erroneous intermediate display. For Problem 5 the correct general product and the stated \(r=3\), \(\nu=(a+b+2,b+1,0)\) substitution already give the required three-theta product. These are identifiable surviving arguments, rather than unproved assumptions supplied to conceal a core gap. The kernel identity and main results are not disproved.
