report: Abstract: The exact author manuscript arXiv:2303.00245v2 is examined. One Major proof defect and six Minor corrections are established. The Major issue concerns the passage from a compatible product of flag spaces to a join in the proof of Lemma 4.22: the stated filtration and hemisphere cover do not have the asserted properties. An explicit finite example disproves the intermediate assertions, while supporting the lemma’s conclusion. A separate counterexample distinguishes ordinary bar homology from absolute Tor in the generality of Proposition 4.9. The remaining corrections concern rank zero, two inclusion–exclusion displays, the definition of splittings and local Morse-filtration claims. The field-connectivity and Koszul-dual conclusions are not disproved by these examples. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Higher Buildings, Rank Filtrations
and the Steinberg Monoid
# Exact source and scope

The frozen record M25-0255 is Jeremy Miller, Peter Patzt and Jennifer C. H. Wilson, On rank filtrations of algebraic \(K\)-theory and Steinberg modules, doi: 10.4171/JEMS/1628 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1628). The reviewed PDF is the 35-page author manuscript arXiv:2303.00245v2, submitted on 25 February 2025 at 04:08:38 UTC; its first page prints the same revision day [source, arxiv]. The publisher records acceptance on 20 February 2025 and online publication on 14 April 2025 [record]. The manuscript is not presumed identical to the journal version. All page and statement references below refer to this exact PDF; its printed and PDF page numbers agree.

All sections and references were read. The review covers the PID splitting hypotheses, the common-basis criterion, the comparison of higher buildings, the categorical bar construction, the connectivity argument and the Tor calculation. The source pages used for the findings were actually inspected as images. The exact field and module examples below are accompanied by reviewer-generated calculations; no author code was executed.

A bounded search checked the arXiv record, the publisher article and ordinary PDF route, the Wilson and Patzt publication pages, and queries for corrections, supplementary material and code. No separate relevant correction or supplement was located. The publisher PDF route led to a subscription page. These results do not establish that no such material exists, and the absence of code is not a mathematical deficiency. The frozen 2025 membership, DOI and original field mapping are retained.
# An essential model-comparison proof

Problem 1 (Major; Lemma 4.22, pp. 29–30).  The filtration used to identify \(D^{a,b}(M)\) with an iterated suspension of \(T^{a,b}(M)\) has a product as its final term, and the proposed two hemispheres do not cover the preceding term.

The lemma asserts \[D^{a,b}(M)\simeq \Sigma^{a+b+1}T^{a,b}(M).\] After establishing \(D^{a,b}\simeq\Sigma\mathring L^{a,b}\), the proof defines \(F_k\subset\mathring L^{a,b}\) by requiring the first \(k\) factors to lie in \(T(M)\) or \(ST(M)\). It then identifies \(F_{a+b}\) with the compatible join \(T^{a,b}(M)\) and claims \(N_k\cup S_k=F_{k-1}\), with both pieces contractible.

Take the field \(\mathbb F_2\), \(M=\mathbb F_2^2\), \(a=2\), \(b=0\). There are exactly three nonzero proper subspaces, \[L_1=\langle e_1\rangle,\qquad L_2=\langle e_2\rangle,
 \qquad L_3=\langle e_1+e_2\rangle.\] Any pair of flags has a common basis. Definition 4.15 therefore gives \(L^{2,0}=L(M)\times L(M)\), and the defined final term is \[F_2=T(M)\times T(M),\] a discrete space with nine points. On the other hand, \[T^{2,0}(M)=T(M)*T(M)=K_{3,3}.\] The graph has six vertices, nine edges and a rank-five incidence matrix. Consequently, \[\widetilde H_0(F_2)=\mathbb Z^8,\qquad
 \widetilde H_0(K_{3,3})=0,\qquad H_1(K_{3,3})=\mathbb Z^4.\] The two spaces are not even homotopy equivalent. This example satisfies the PID and common-basis hypotheses without any degenerate rank convention.

The covering assertion fails independently. In the diagonal simplicial set take the 1-simplex with first flag \(0\subset M\) and second flag \(L_1\subseteq L_1\). It lies in \(\mathring L^{2,0}=F_0\), because the second flag is not full. An interior point has positive weights on both \(0\) and \(M\) in its first factor. It lies in neither \(N_1\) nor \(S_1\). Moreover, with the same example, \[F_1=T(M)\times L(M),\qquad
 N_2=T(M)\times L_{\text{missing }M}(M).\] The second factor is contractible, but the first has three components. Thus \(N_2\) is not contractible either. These are structural failures of the proposed induction, not an indexing change in the suspension exponent.

Counterevidence and impact. The conclusion survives this test. Since \(D^{1,0}(M)\simeq\bigvee^2S^2\), the actual quotient is \[D^{2,0}(M)=D^{1,0}(M)\wedge D^{1,0}(M)
 \simeq\bigvee^4S^4
 \simeq\Sigma^3K_{3,3}.\] No counterexample to the lemma’s conclusion is asserted. The defective proof nevertheless lies on the central chain: Lemma 4.22 is used in Corollary 4.23, the iterated-bar Lemma 1.3, Proposition 5.8 and the comparison in Lemma 6.2. A valid natural comparison is needed before those deductions follow from the written argument. This substantive effect on the core proof warrants Major assessment even though a replacement argument is available.

Repair boundary. For positive rank, the augmented flag spaces have the form \(\Delta^1*T(M)\) and \(\Delta^1*ST(M)\), with nonfull boundary \(\partial\Delta^1*T(M)\) or \(\partial\Delta^1*ST(M)\). Compatibility restricts the interior supports. A correct quotient argument should keep these boundary conditions in all factors. Writing the endpoint and interior weights in factor \(i\) as \((u_i,v_i,s_i)\), put \[t_i=\frac{u_i}{u_i+v_i},\qquad
 y_i=\frac{s_i}{1-s_i},\qquad
 r=\sum_i y_i,\qquad w_i=y_i/r.\] Off the collapsed boundary, \(t_i\in(0,1)\), and the compatible weighted supports \((w_i,x_i)\) describe the join. The radial compactification and the collapsed cube boundary yield \(\Sigma^{a+b+1}T^{a,b}\). At \(r=0\) the support coordinates disappear; at \(r=\infty\) or a cube endpoint one reaches the collapsed boundary. This gives a replacement through finite subcomplexes, extended in the CW topology. Naturality under isomorphisms and forgetting complements must be included. The detailed auxiliary notes record this construction; it does not validate the printed \(F_k\) proof. The cited single-factor comparison in [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 6.1, p.~25]{gkrw}] uses two genuine cone subspaces. Its actual source page was checked; it does not establish the false multifactor filtration assertions. Rank zero must be treated separately, as in Problem 3.
# Additional confirmed corrections

Problem 2 (Minor; Proposition 4.9, p. 27).  Freeness of one module over \(\mathbb Z\) alone does not make the ordinary bar construction compute absolute Tor for an arbitrary \(\operatorname{VB}\)-ring.

Concentrate all objects in \(\operatorname{VB}\)-degree zero, where the monoidal product is the ordinary tensor product over \(\mathbb Z\), and set \[A=\mathbb Z[\epsilon]/(2\epsilon,\epsilon^2),\qquad M=N=\mathbb Z,\] with the augmentation action \(\epsilon\mapsto0\). Both modules are free abelian in every \(\operatorname{VB}\)-degree, including the zero groups in positive degrees. Thus the printed freeness hypothesis holds on both sides.

The augmentation ideal \(I=(\epsilon)\) is \(\mathbb Z/2\). The normalized bar construction has \(I^{\otimes p}\cong\mathbb Z/2\) in every positive degree, and all differentials vanish because \(I^2=0\). In particular \(H_3(B(M,A,N))=\mathbb Z/2\). A free \(A\)-resolution through the degrees needed for \(\operatorname{Tor}_3\) has differentials \[d_1=(\epsilon),\qquad d_2=(2\ \epsilon),\qquad
 d_3=\begin{pmatrix}\epsilon&0&0\\0&2&\epsilon\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 d_4=\begin{pmatrix}
 2&\epsilon&0&0&0\\0&0&\epsilon&0&0\\0&0&0&2&\epsilon
 \end{pmatrix}.\] Exactness follows directly by writing every element of \(A\) uniquely as \(x+\bar y\epsilon\), with \(x\in\mathbb Z\) and \(\bar y\in\mathbb Z/2\): \(\ker d_1=(2,\epsilon)\); \(\ker d_2\) is generated by \((\epsilon,0),(0,2),(0,\epsilon)\); and \(\ker d_3\) is generated by the five displayed columns of \(d_4\). These free modules can be continued to a resolution.

After tensoring with \(\mathbb Z\), the kernel of \(d_3\) is \(\mathbb Ze_1\oplus\mathbb Ze_3\), while the image of \(d_4\) is \(2\mathbb Ze_1\oplus2\mathbb Ze_3\). Hence \[\operatorname{Tor}^A_3(\mathbb Z,\mathbb Z)=(\mathbb Z/2)^2
 \not\cong H_3(B(\mathbb Z,A,\mathbb Z)).\] This is an exact integral calculation, not a numerical test.

Counterevidence, impact and repair. The general statement needs a flatness hypothesis on the underlying algebra, or a derived bar construction with suitable flat replacements. The Steinberg groups actually used later are free abelian, and the simplicial chain groups used in Lemma 6.2 are free. The above torsion algebra is not their algebra. Thus this defect limits the general proposition; it does not by itself invalidate the paper’s specific Koszul calculation. The repair must preserve the distinction between absolute derived functors and a relative bar resolution. The cited [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition 2.33(ii), pp.~18--19]{mpp}] was also checked in its exact source: it requires both its algebra \(R_n\) and its left module \(B_n\) to be free abelian. The algebra hypothesis is therefore present in the original reference and absent from the statement under review.
Problem 3 (Minor; Lemmas 4.12 and 4.22, Proposition 5.8, and Theorem 6.3, pp. 27–34).  Rank zero is included in several formulas that require positive rank.

The paper explicitly sets \(D^{a,b}(0)=S^0\) on p. 29. For Lemma 4.12 take \(A=\mathbf1\), the unit in \(\operatorname{VB}\)-based spaces, and \(\alpha=0\), \(\beta=-1\). Then \(A(0)=S^0\) and \(A(R^n)=*\) for \(n>0\). Every value is nonempty, so the required \((-1)\)-connectivity holds for every \(n\). The bar simplicial spaces are constant and proper. Nevertheless \(BA(0)=S^0\) is not connected, contrary to the conclusion at \(n=0\). The proof’s assertion about degree-zero bar simplices being contractible also only applies at positive rank.

Similarly, for \((a,b)=(1,0)\) the right side of Lemma 4.22 at \(M=0\) is \(\Sigma^2T(0)\). The building is empty. With the usual augmented convention \(\Sigma\varnothing=S^0\), this is \(S^1\), whereas the left side is \(S^0\). With an ordinary unaugmented convention it still cannot give the stated unit. Proposition 5.8 at \(n=0,k=3\) would likewise make \(D^{3,0}_0=S^0\) connected.

Theorem 6.3 explicitly says \(n,i\ge0\). At \(n=i=0\), \[\operatorname{Tor}^{\operatorname{St}(R)}_0(\mathbb Z,\mathbb Z)_0=\mathbb Z,\qquad
 \widetilde H_{-3}(T^2_0(R))=0,\] because \(T^2_0\) is empty and its augmented simplicial chains have no degree \(-3\) term. The first isomorphism is false at that endpoint. The later field formula \(\operatorname{St}_0\otimes\operatorname{St}_0=\mathbb Z\) is itself consistent with the unit.

Counterevidence, impact and repair. The introduction already restricts Theorem 1.5 to \(n\ge1\), and Theorem 5.9 treats the small ranks separately. State the suspension and connectivity bounds for positive rank, retain \(D_0=S^0\), and record the rank-zero Tor value separately. The positive-rank theorems are not contradicted by these unit examples. In applying the bar connectivity argument, zero-rank factors contribute units and should not be treated as extra highly connected factors.
Problem 4 (Minor; last display of the proof of Theorem 2.25, p. 11).  The summation order is reversed in the displayed Möbius-inversion formula.

Take \(R=\mathbb Q\), \(n=2\), \(k=1\), \(U_1=\mathbb Qe_1\) and \(S=\varnothing\). The module is split and has the common-basis property. By Definition 2.15, \(F_{\mathcal U}(\varnothing)=2-1=1\). The printed sum over \(S\supseteq T\) includes only \(T=\varnothing\) and gives \(2\). The correct inversion of the preceding display is \[F_{\mathcal U}(S)=\sum_{T\supseteq S}
 (-1)^{|S|-|T|}\operatorname{rank}(U_T).\] For the example this is \(2-1=1\). Definition 2.24 already has the correct direction, and the corrected formula proves the stated criterion. Thus the counterexample concerns the displayed inversion, not Theorem 2.25.
Problem 5 (Minor; Lemma 2.27, case (i), p. 13).  Two successive terms replace the running intersection \(U_T\) by \(U_A\).

Use \(R=\mathbb Z\), \(n=4\), \(\ell=1\), \(k=3\) and \[U_1=\langle e_1\rangle,\quad
 V_1=\langle e_1,e_2\rangle,\quad
 V_2=\langle e_1,e_2,e_3\rangle,\quad A=\varnothing.\] The flag condition and both required common-basis hypotheses hold using the standard basis. Set \(S=\{2,3\}\). The rank on the left is \(\operatorname{rank}(V_1\cap U_1)=1\). In the offending sum the only running subset is \(T=\{1\}\); replacing \(U_T\) by \(U_A=\mathbb Z^4\) makes its term \(\operatorname{rank}(U_A\cap V_1\cap V_2)=2\). Restoring \(U_T\) in both lines gives the correct value \(1\).

The surrounding cancellation and modular-law argument works with this correction. The compatibility citations on p. 15 should also refer to \(U_1,\ldots,U_{k-2},V_i\), the collections assumed compatible, rather than using \(U_k\) in those lists. These are local substitutions; an independent construction of a compatible basis verifies the lemma itself. They do not supply a counterexample to its conclusion.
Problem 6 (Minor; Definition 3.2 and Proposition 3.3, p. 16).  The simplicial-complex definition of a splitting omits the requirement that its components be nonzero.

The displayed definition only requires \(M=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_k\). Literally it permits \((0,M)\) and \((M,0)\) as vertices of \(ST(M)\). For \(M=\mathbb F\), these form an edge, whereas \(T(M)\) is empty. The proposed map forgetting the complement would take its vertices to \(0\) and \(M\), neither of which belongs to \(T(M)\). At rank two, the allowed size-three tuple \((\mathbb Fe_1,0,\mathbb Fe_2)\) maps in Proposition 3.3 to a repeated vertex, not a 1-simplex.

Counterevidence, impact and repair. Definition 3.5 on the same page explicitly uses proper nonzero components, and the comparison arguments use that interpretation. Add the nonzero requirement in Definitions 3.2 and the statement of Proposition 3.3. Keep the different convention of Definition 4.14: its simplicial set intentionally permits zero components and uses them for degeneracies. The example exposes a definition mismatch; it does not refute the comparison theorem with the intended nonzero splittings.
Problem 7 (Minor; Proposition 3.12 proof, pp. 20–21).  Two descriptions of the Morse filtration are stronger than the properties that hold and are needed.

Let \(M=\mathbb Q^4\), \(V_0=\langle e_1,e_2\rangle\), \(\tau=\sigma=\{V_0\}\), and choose two distinct preimages with complements \[C_1=\langle e_3,e_4\rangle,\qquad
 C_2=\langle e_3,e_4+e_2\rangle.\] These meet all hypotheses of Proposition 3.12: \(r=2\), \(\tau\) is a nonempty flag, and each \(\{V_0,C_i\}\) has a common basis. The bases \((e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4)\) and \((e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4+e_2)\) also show that \(W=\langle e_1,e_3\rangle\) is a vertex of the intersection \(X\). It is not comparable to \(V_0\), and \(W+V_0\ne M\). Yet the printed bound is \[\operatorname{rank}W\le n-\operatorname{rank}V_0-1=1,\] whereas \(\operatorname{rank}W=2\). The valid bound is \(\operatorname{rank}W\le n-2\): the proper split module \(W+V_0\) strictly contains \(W\). This is exactly what the \(A_1,\ldots,A_{n-2}\) filtration requires.

For the assertion about \(G_{k-1}\) on p. 21, retain the same data and put \[W_B=\langle e_2,e_3,e_4\rangle,\quad U=\langle e_3\rangle,
 \quad d=2,\quad k=1.\] Then \(W_B\in B_1\), \(k<d\), and \(U\in\operatorname{Link}^{<}_X(W_B)\cap G_0\). The vertex \(W_B\) has rank at least \(\operatorname{rank}U\) but is not in \(G_0\). Thus \(G_{k-1}\) does not contain every vertex of rank at least \(\operatorname{rank}U\) as claimed.

The actual image \(f(U)=U+(W_B\cap V_0)=\langle e_2,e_3\rangle\) does lie in \(G_0\). In general the required argument is \(f(U)+V_0=U+V_0\ne M\). Also, the homotopy assertion about the order-preserving map uses \(\mathrm{id}\le f\) and \(f^2=f\); order preservation alone would not suffice. These repairs preserve the inductive contractibility argument. The examples do not refute Proposition 3.12.
# Coverage and proof dependencies

The algebraic preliminaries were checked using saturation over a PID. Intersections of summands are saturated, while their sums need not be; the index-two example over \(\mathbb Z\) correctly separates these facts. For the common-basis criterion, proceeding upward through the intersection poset produces complements of the sums of strict lower intersections. Their ranks are the corank function values. When these sums split, the construction gives a minimal common spanning set. Its size is \(n\) exactly when it is a basis. Möbius inversion then yields Theorem 2.25 with the corrected summation direction. The two-step flag lemma was checked through the four membership cases and an independent basis construction.

The comparison in Section 3 was examined at the level of its actual hypotheses. Fullness follows from the flag lemma. In Proposition 3.12 the successive links have the stated cone or retraction after the local corrections above; the case of complements to \(V_0\) reduces the rank and preserves the required distinctness of lifted flags. The higher-building induction removes one join factor. Theorem 3.15 uses a cover obtained by compatible choices of complements; intersections of at least two distinct lifts are contractible and contain the original flag. No additional counterexample to this homology comparison was established.

The direct-sum multiplication and bar identification in Section 4 were checked by restricting compatible flags to the summands of an ordered decomposition. Zero summands encode degeneracies; augmentation faces agree with the nonfull-lattice quotient. The conversion between the product and join models requires the replacement argument in Problem 1. The comparison in Corollary 4.23 must use the suspensions of the natural forgetful maps, not merely unrelated equivalences of the source and target models. The suspended CW comparisons and the small-rank conventions then justify the passage from homology to homotopy.

For Section 5, the fiber of the map to \(\operatorname{CB}_n\) becomes contractible by coning a finite image to a vertex in a fresh join factor. The equality \(T_n^2(F)=T_n(F)*T_n(F)\) uses the field hypothesis; it is not asserted for general PIDs. The bad-edge and bad-vertex modifications prove simple connectivity in rank at least three. After the valid suspended-model comparison and a positive-rank bar-connectivity statement, homology vanishing and Hurewicz give the claimed range. For the conditional PID statements, the hypotheses needed at all ranks occurring in the bar factors should be stated explicitly; no counterexample to the intended uniform reading was established.

Finally, the building has dimension \(n-2\) and is \((n-3)\)-connected, so its top reduced homology is free abelian and there is no other reduced homology. This supplies the concentration used in Lemma 6.2. In the hypertor spectral sequence, for fixed \(\operatorname{VB}\)-degree \(n\), the internal homological degree is \(n\); nonzero higher differentials therefore have no target on that row. The bar length is bounded by \(n\) after normalization in positive rank, supplying convergence. For a field, the join formula and the torsion-free Künneth calculation produce \(\operatorname{St}_n(F)\otimes\operatorname{St}_n(F)\) in the stated degree. Question 1.6 asks for additional algebra and coalgebra structure and is not a proved claim. No-code availability was not used as an adverse criterion.
# Supporting checks

There is one Major proof issue and six Minor corrections. The Major classification concerns the failed core comparison argument, not a claim that every conclusion is false. The Minor classifications reflect the demonstrated limits of their effects on the actual application; local reparability alone did not determine severity. A revised proof should explicitly separate positive rank from the unit, supply the natural quotient/join comparison, and add the flatness conditions needed by the general Tor statement.

R=F2 is a PID, M=F2^2, a=2,b=0. Every pair of flags has a common basis; all constructions are positive rank.
analysis: The filtration used to identify \(D^{a,b}(M)\) with an iterated suspension of \(T^{a,b}(M)\) has a product as its final term, and the proposed two hemispheres do not cover the preceding term.

The lemma asserts \[D^{a,b}(M)\simeq \Sigma^{a+b+1}T^{a,b}(M).\] After establishing \(D^{a,b}\simeq\Sigma\mathring L^{a,b}\), the proof defines \(F_k\subset\mathring L^{a,b}\) by requiring the first \(k\) factors to lie in \(T(M)\) or \(ST(M)\). It then identifies \(F_{a+b}\) with the compatible join \(T^{a,b}(M)\) and claims \(N_k\cup S_k=F_{k-1}\), with both pieces contractible.

Take the field \(\mathbb F_2\), \(M=\mathbb F_2^2\), \(a=2\), \(b=0\). There are exactly three nonzero proper subspaces, \[L_1=\langle e_1\rangle,\qquad L_2=\langle e_2\rangle,
 \qquad L_3=\langle e_1+e_2\rangle.\] Any pair of flags has a common basis. Definition 4.15 therefore gives \(L^{2,0}=L(M)\times L(M)\), and the defined final term is \[F_2=T(M)\times T(M),\] a discrete space with nine points. On the other hand, \[T^{2,0}(M)=T(M)*T(M)=K_{3,3}.\] The graph has six vertices, nine edges and a rank-five incidence matrix. Consequently, \[\widetilde H_0(F_2)=\mathbb Z^8,\qquad
 \widetilde H_0(K_{3,3})=0,\qquad H_1(K_{3,3})=\mathbb Z^4.\] The two spaces are not even homotopy equivalent. This example satisfies the PID and common-basis hypotheses without any degenerate rank convention.

The covering assertion fails independently. In the diagonal simplicial set take the 1-simplex with first flag \(0\subset M\) and second flag \(L_1\subseteq L_1\). It lies in \(\mathring L^{2,0}=F_0\), because the second flag is not full. An interior point has positive weights on both \(0\) and \(M\) in its first factor. It lies in neither \(N_1\) nor \(S_1\). Moreover, with the same example, \[F_1=T(M)\times L(M),\qquad
 N_2=T(M)\times L_{\text{missing }M}(M).\] The second factor is contractible, but the first has three components. Thus \(N_2\) is not contractible either. These are structural failures of the proposed induction, not an indexing change in the suspension exponent.

Counterevidence and impact. The conclusion survives this test. Since \(D^{1,0}(M)\simeq\bigvee^2S^2\), the actual quotient is \[D^{2,0}(M)=D^{1,0}(M)\wedge D^{1,0}(M)
 \simeq\bigvee^4S^4
 \simeq\Sigma^3K_{3,3}.\] No counterexample to the lemma’s conclusion is asserted. The defective proof nevertheless lies on the central chain: Lemma 4.22 is used in Corollary 4.23, the iterated-bar Lemma 1.3, Proposition 5.8 and the comparison in Lemma 6.2. A valid natural comparison is needed before those deductions follow from the written argument. This substantive effect on the core proof warrants Major assessment even though a replacement argument is available.

Repair boundary. For positive rank, the augmented flag spaces have the form \(\Delta^1*T(M)\) and \(\Delta^1*ST(M)\), with nonfull boundary \(\partial\Delta^1*T(M)\) or \(\partial\Delta^1*ST(M)\). Compatibility restricts the interior supports. A correct quotient argument should keep these boundary conditions in all factors. Writing the endpoint and interior weights in factor \(i\) as \((u_i,v_i,s_i)\), put \[t_i=\frac{u_i}{u_i+v_i},\qquad
 y_i=\frac{s_i}{1-s_i},\qquad
 r=\sum_i y_i,\qquad w_i=y_i/r.\] Off the collapsed boundary, \(t_i\in(0,1)\), and the compatible weighted supports \((w_i,x_i)\) describe the join. The radial compactification and the collapsed cube boundary yield \(\Sigma^{a+b+1}T^{a,b}\). At \(r=0\) the support coordinates disappear; at \(r=\infty\) or a cube endpoint one reaches the collapsed boundary. This gives a replacement through finite subcomplexes, extended in the CW topology. Naturality under isomorphisms and forgetting complements must be included. The detailed auxiliary notes record this construction; it does not validate the printed \(F_k\) proof. The cited single-factor comparison in [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 6.1, p.~25]{gkrw}] uses two genuine cone subspaces. Its actual source page was checked; it does not establish the false multifactor filtration assertions. Rank zero must be treated separately, as in Problem 3.
result: Impact: The main model comparison is not established by the written proof, affecting Cor4.23, Lemma1.3, Prop5.8 and Lemma6.2. Major is based on that core dependency, not on an assertion that the final main theorems are false.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Replace the filtration with a compatible product-pair quotient proof. Factor pairs are (Delta1*T_i, boundaryDelta1*T_i); use all boundary factors and cube/radial coordinates, verify CW continuity and naturality. Restrict positive rank and retain separate unit convention.

problems.title: Missing algebra flatness in ordinary-bar/absolute-Tor comparison
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (Minor; Proposition 4.9, p. 27).
claim: Kind: false stated assertion or formula
Location: Proposition4.9, p27
Claim: H_i(B(M,A,N))=Tor_i^A(M,N) when either M_n or N_n is free abelian, with no flatness assumption on A.
Objects concentrated inVB degree0; A=Z[e]/(2e,e²), M=N=Z viaaugmentation. Both modules are free in every degree.
analysis: Freeness of one module over \(\mathbb Z\) alone does not make the ordinary bar construction compute absolute Tor for an arbitrary \(\operatorname{VB}\)-ring.

Concentrate all objects in \(\operatorname{VB}\)-degree zero, where the monoidal product is the ordinary tensor product over \(\mathbb Z\), and set \[A=\mathbb Z[\epsilon]/(2\epsilon,\epsilon^2),\qquad M=N=\mathbb Z,\] with the augmentation action \(\epsilon\mapsto0\). Both modules are free abelian in every \(\operatorname{VB}\)-degree, including the zero groups in positive degrees. Thus the printed freeness hypothesis holds on both sides.

The augmentation ideal \(I=(\epsilon)\) is \(\mathbb Z/2\). The normalized bar construction has \(I^{\otimes p}\cong\mathbb Z/2\) in every positive degree, and all differentials vanish because \(I^2=0\). In particular \(H_3(B(M,A,N))=\mathbb Z/2\). A free \(A\)-resolution through the degrees needed for \(\operatorname{Tor}_3\) has differentials \[d_1=(\epsilon),\qquad d_2=(2\ \epsilon),\qquad
 d_3=\begin{pmatrix}\epsilon&0&0\\0&2&\epsilon\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 d_4=\begin{pmatrix}
 2&\epsilon&0&0&0\\0&0&\epsilon&0&0\\0&0&0&2&\epsilon
 \end{pmatrix}.\] Exactness follows directly by writing every element of \(A\) uniquely as \(x+\bar y\epsilon\), with \(x\in\mathbb Z\) and \(\bar y\in\mathbb Z/2\): \(\ker d_1=(2,\epsilon)\); \(\ker d_2\) is generated by \((\epsilon,0),(0,2),(0,\epsilon)\); and \(\ker d_3\) is generated by the five displayed columns of \(d_4\). These free modules can be continued to a resolution.

After tensoring with \(\mathbb Z\), the kernel of \(d_3\) is \(\mathbb Ze_1\oplus\mathbb Ze_3\), while the image of \(d_4\) is \(2\mathbb Ze_1\oplus2\mathbb Ze_3\). Hence \[\operatorname{Tor}^A_3(\mathbb Z,\mathbb Z)=(\mathbb Z/2)^2
 \not\cong H_3(B(\mathbb Z,A,\mathbb Z)).\] This is an exact integral calculation, not a numerical test.

Counterevidence, impact and repair. The general statement needs a flatness hypothesis on the underlying algebra, or a derived bar construction with suitable flat replacements. The Steinberg groups actually used later are free abelian, and the simplicial chain groups used in Lemma 6.2 are free. The above torsion algebra is not their algebra. Thus this defect limits the general proposition; it does not by itself invalidate the paper’s specific Koszul calculation. The repair must preserve the distinction between absolute derived functors and a relative bar resolution. The cited [Retained latex: \cite[Proposition 2.33(ii), pp.~18--19]{mpp}] was also checked in its exact source: it requires both its algebra \(R_n\) and its left module \(B_n\) to be free abelian. The algebra hypothesis is therefore present in the original reference and absent from the statement under review.
result: Impact: The universal categorical proposition is false, but the torsion counterexample does not refute the specific Koszul application under its actual freeness hypotheses.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Require degreewise algebra flatness plus sufficient module flatness, or use a derived bar. Retain absolute/relative distinction.

problems.title: Rank-zero formulas conflict with the explicitly retained unit
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: Problem 3 (Minor; Lemmas 4.12 and 4.22, Proposition 5.8, and Theorem 6.3, pp. 27–34). Rank zero is included in several formulas that require positive rank.
claim: Kind: false stated assertion or formula
Location: Lemma4.12 p27; Lemma4.22 pp29–30; Prop5.8 p32; Theorem6.3 pp33–34

analysis: Rank zero is included in several formulas that require positive rank.

The paper explicitly sets \(D^{a,b}(0)=S^0\) on p. 29. For Lemma 4.12 take \(A=\mathbf1\), the unit in \(\operatorname{VB}\)-based spaces, and \(\alpha=0\), \(\beta=-1\). Then \(A(0)=S^0\) and \(A(R^n)=*\) for \(n>0\). Every value is nonempty, so the required \((-1)\)-connectivity holds for every \(n\). The bar simplicial spaces are constant and proper. Nevertheless \(BA(0)=S^0\) is not connected, contrary to the conclusion at \(n=0\). The proof’s assertion about degree-zero bar simplices being contractible also only applies at positive rank.

Similarly, for \((a,b)=(1,0)\) the right side of Lemma 4.22 at \(M=0\) is \(\Sigma^2T(0)\). The building is empty. With the usual augmented convention \(\Sigma\varnothing=S^0\), this is \(S^1\), whereas the left side is \(S^0\). With an ordinary unaugmented convention it still cannot give the stated unit. Proposition 5.8 at \(n=0,k=3\) would likewise make \(D^{3,0}_0=S^0\) connected.

Theorem 6.3 explicitly says \(n,i\ge0\). At \(n=i=0\), \[\operatorname{Tor}^{\operatorname{St}(R)}_0(\mathbb Z,\mathbb Z)_0=\mathbb Z,\qquad
 \widetilde H_{-3}(T^2_0(R))=0,\] because \(T^2_0\) is empty and its augmented simplicial chains have no degree \(-3\) term. The first isomorphism is false at that endpoint. The later field formula \(\operatorname{St}_0\otimes\operatorname{St}_0=\mathbb Z\) is itself consistent with the unit.

Counterevidence, impact and repair. The introduction already restricts Theorem 1.5 to \(n\ge1\), and Theorem 5.9 treats the small ranks separately. State the suspension and connectivity bounds for positive rank, retain \(D_0=S^0\), and record the rank-zero Tor value separately. The positive-rank theorems are not contradicted by these unit examples. In applying the bar connectivity argument, zero-rank factors contribute units and should not be treated as extra highly connected factors.
result: Impact: These are endpoint and unit exceptions. The positive-rank induction needs correct treatment of zero-rank unit factors.

paragraphs: State positive-rank bounds and separate rank0 values; do not change the existing unitD0S0.

problems.title: Reversed Boolean-poset order in the last Möbius inversion sum
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: Problem 4 (Minor; last display of the proof of Theorem 2.25, p. 11). The summation order is reversed in the displayed Möbius-inversion formula.
claim: Kind: false stated assertion or formula
Location: Theorem2.25 proof, final display p11
Claim: F(S)=sum_{S superset T}(-1)^{|S|-|T|}rankU_T.
Q,n2,k1,U1=Qe1,Sempty; all common-basis/splitting hypotheseshold.
analysis: The summation order is reversed in the displayed Möbius-inversion formula.

Take \(R=\mathbb Q\), \(n=2\), \(k=1\), \(U_1=\mathbb Qe_1\) and \(S=\varnothing\). The module is split and has the common-basis property. By Definition 2.15, \(F_{\mathcal U}(\varnothing)=2-1=1\). The printed sum over \(S\supseteq T\) includes only \(T=\varnothing\) and gives \(2\). The correct inversion of the preceding display is \[F_{\mathcal U}(S)=\sum_{T\supseteq S}
 (-1)^{|S|-|T|}\operatorname{rank}(U_T).\] For the example this is \(2-1=1\). Definition 2.24 already has the correct direction, and the corrected formula proves the stated criterion. Thus the counterexample concerns the displayed inversion, not Theorem 2.25.
result: Impact: Local false proof display; main common-basis criterion remains valid.

problems.title: Fixed U_A substituted for running U_T in the flag calculation
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 5: Problem 5 (Minor; Lemma 2.27, case (i), p. 13). Two successive terms replace the running intersection \(U_T\) by \(U_A\).
claim: Kind: false stated assertion or formula
Location: Lemma2.27 proof case(i), two consecutive sums p13; accompanying premise citations p15
Claim: Two running-T sums use rank(U_A intersectV1intersectV2).
Z,n4,ell1,k3,U1=<e1>,V1=<e1,e2>,V2=<e1,e2,e3>,Aempty,S{2,3}; genuinecoordinate summands; bothrequiredcompatiblefamilieshold.
analysis: Two successive terms replace the running intersection \(U_T\) by \(U_A\).

Use \(R=\mathbb Z\), \(n=4\), \(\ell=1\), \(k=3\) and \[U_1=\langle e_1\rangle,\quad

problems.title: Nonzero splitting components omitted in the complex model
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: Problem 6 (Minor; Definition 3.2 and Proposition 3.3, p. 16). The simplicial-complex definition of a splitting omits the requirement that its components be nonzero.
claim: Kind: false stated assertion or formula
Location: Definition3.2 and Proposition3.3 p16; forgetfulmap p19
Claim: A splitting is defined only by M=directsumV_i, then all size2splittings are vertices and allsizep+2splittings correspondtop-simplices.
AnyfieldF, rank1M=F forfirstexample; rank2M=F²,p1forsecond. Zero summands satisfy literal definition.
analysis: The simplicial-complex definition of a splitting omits the requirement that its components be nonzero.

The displayed definition only requires \(M=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_k\). Literally it permits \((0,M)\) and \((M,0)\) as vertices of \(ST(M)\). For \(M=\mathbb F\), these form an edge, whereas \(T(M)\) is empty. The proposed map forgetting the complement would take its vertices to \(0\) and \(M\), neither of which belongs to \(T(M)\). At rank two, the allowed size-three tuple \((\mathbb Fe_1,0,\mathbb Fe_2)\) maps in Proposition 3.3 to a repeated vertex, not a 1-simplex.

Add the nonzero requirement in Definitions 3.2 and the statement of Proposition 3.3. Keep the different convention of Definition 4.14: its simplicial set intentionally permits zero components and uses them for degeneracies. problems.title: Overstrong rank descriptions in the Morse filtration
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 7: Problem 7 (Minor; Proposition 3.12 proof, pp. 20–21). Two descriptions of the Morse filtration are stronger than the properties that hold and are needed.
claim: Kind: false stated assertion or formula
Location: Proposition3.12 proof pp20–21
Claim: rankW≤n-rankV0-1 forAvertices; Gk-1containsallXverticesofrankatleastrankU.
Q4,V0=<e1,e2>,tau=sigma{V0},r2distinctcomplementsC1=<e3,e4>,C2=<e3,e4+e2>. Standard and(e1,e2,e3,e4+e2)baseswitnessallcompatibility.
analysis: Two descriptions of the Morse filtration are stronger than the properties that hold and are needed.

Let \(M=\mathbb Q^4\), \(V_0=\langle e_1,e_2\rangle\), \(\tau=\sigma=\{V_0\}\), and choose two distinct preimages with complements \[C_1=\langle e_3,e_4\rangle,\qquad
 C_2=\langle e_3,e_4+e_2\rangle.\] These meet all hypotheses of Proposition 3.12: \(r=2\), \(\tau\) is a nonempty flag, and each \(\{V_0,C_i\}\) has a common basis. The bases \((e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4)\) and \((e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4+e_2)\) also show that \(W=\langle e_1,e_3\rangle\) is a vertex of the intersection \(X\). It is not comparable to \(V_0\), and \(W+V_0\ne M\). Yet the printed bound is \[\operatorname{rank}W\le n-\operatorname{rank}V_0-1=1,\] whereas \(\operatorname{rank}W=2\). The valid bound is \(\operatorname{rank}W\le n-2\): the proper split module \(W+V_0\) strictly contains \(W\). This is exactly what the \(A_1,\ldots,A_{n-2}\) filtration requires.

For the assertion about \(G_{k-1}\) on p. 21, retain the same data and put \[W_B=\langle e_2,e_3,e_4\rangle,\quad U=\langle e_3\rangle,
 \quad d=2,\quad k=1.\] Then \(W_B\in B_1\), \(k<d\), and \(U\in\operatorname{Link}^{<}_X(W_B)\cap G_0\). The vertex \(W_B\) has rank at least \(\operatorname{rank}U\) but is not in \(G_0\). Thus \(G_{k-1}\) does not contain every vertex of rank at least \(\operatorname{rank}U\) as claimed.

The actual image \(f(U)=U+(W_B\cap V_0)=\langle e_2,e_3\rangle\) does lie in \(G_0\). In general the required argument is \(f(U)+V_0=U+V_0\ne M\). report: Abstract: The exact author manuscript arXiv:2305.08668v2 is examined. Four Major findings and eight Minor corrections are established. The printed index definition changes the central bounded-index hypothesis; a double cover of the Clifford torus has ordinary Morse index four but infinite printed index. Independent target normalization invalidates the unqualified Willmore-energy conversion in Appendix A, with an exact \(4\pi\) discrepancy. The global avoidance assertion in the mean-curvature gauge lemma also fails under its expressly local Willmore hypotheses. An uncentered Poincare estimate also fails in the core interior C2 convergence argument. The remaining corrections concern explicit models, formulas and local statements. The principal conformally invariant energy quantization theorem is not disproved by these examples. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Willmore Energy, Conformal Gauss Maps
and the Bounded-Index Hypothesis
# Exact source and review scope

The frozen record M25-0256 is Dorian Martino, Energy quantization for Willmore surfaces with bounded index, doi: 10.4171/JEMS/1629 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1629). The reviewed source is the 50-page author manuscript arXiv:2305.08668v2, submitted on 12 June 2023 at 21:10:04 UTC. The cover prints 12 June 2023. The publisher records acceptance on 2 September 2024 and online publication on 16 April 2025 [source, arxiv, record]. The frozen 2025 membership and DOI are retained; the author manuscript is not presumed to be the journal version. All source pages below are both printed and PDF page numbers.

The full source text, including references, was read. The review examined the definitions and quantifiers, the collar and neck hypotheses, Lorentz gauges, angular estimates, constrained variations, the index count, and Appendices A–C. The source pages supporting the findings were actually inspected as images. Exact symbolic checks and the proofs below were produced by the reviewers; no author code was executed.
# Substantive findings
## P1. Major: the definition does not measure Morse index
Location. Page 5, (1), and page 8, (6); the bounded-index hypothesis of Theorem III, p. 4, and Theorem 4.3, p. 12.

The definitions use \[\dim\operatorname{Span}\{v:Q(v)<0\},\] where \(Q\) is the second variation, rather than the maximum dimension of a subspace on which \(Q\) is negative definite. If \(Q(v)<0\), then for every smooth admissible \(w\) and sufficiently small nonzero \(t\), \(Q(v+tw)<0\). Thus \(w=((v+tw)-v)/t\) belongs to that span. The printed quantity is zero in the absence of negative directions and infinite dimensional whenever a negative direction exists.

A complete geometric example is \[\Sigma=(\mathbb R/4\pi\mathbb Z)\times(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z),\qquad
 \Psi(u,v)=\frac{(\cos u,\sin u,\cos v,\sin v)}{\sqrt2}.\] This unbranched double cover of the Clifford torus is a closed, genus-one Willmore immersion without umbilics. With \(N=2^{-1/2}(\cos u,\sin u,-\cos v,-\sin v)\), its metric is \(g=(du^2+dv^2)/2\), principal curvatures are \(-1,1\), and \(H=0\). Its area is \(4\pi^2\) and \(\mathcal E=8\pi^2\). For a normal velocity \(fN\), direct differentiation gives \[\operatorname{Area}''=\int_\Sigma(|\nabla f|^2-4f^2)\,dA,\qquad
 H'=\tfrac12(\Delta+4)f.\] Since \(\mathcal E=2\int(1+H^2)\,dA-4\pi\chi(\Sigma)\), \[Q_\mathcal E(f)=\int_\Sigma f(\Delta+2)(\Delta+4)f\,dA.
 \tag{P1.1}\] The eigenvalues of \(-\Delta\) are \(2(m^2/4+n^2)\). Only \((m,n)=(\pm1,\pm1)\) lie strictly between two and four. Their Fourier modes give four real negative directions, while all other modes are nonnegative. The ordinary index is exactly four. For example, \[f=\cos(u/2)\cos v,\qquad
 \int_\Sigma f^2\,dA=\pi^2,\qquad Q_\mathcal E(f)=-3\pi^2/4.\] The printed index is infinite.

All these velocities are realized by immersion variations: \(\cos(sf)\Psi+\sin(sf)N\) is immersed for sufficiently small \(s\). The time change \(s=\varepsilon\tanh(t/\varepsilon)\), with derivative one at zero, realizes the same velocity on \((-1,1)\). Stereographic projection from a point outside the image gives \[\Phi(u,v)=\frac{(\cos u,\sin u,\cos v)}{\sqrt2-\sin v},\] a closed immersion in the paper’s Euclidean setting with the same normal index, by conformal invariance of \(\mathcal E\).

Impact and counterevidence. Its constant sequence has bounded energy and ordinary index four, but is excluded by the literal printed hypothesis. The central theorem’s formal coverage is reduced to stable sequences. This scope change warrants Major. The example does not refute quantization: a constant sequence trivially quantizes.

Repair boundary. Both definitions must use \[\operatorname{ind}(Q)=\sup\{\dim L:L\text{ is linear and }Q(v)<0
                           \text{ for every }0\ne v\in L\}.\] Section 7.3 supplies relevant counterevidence: its fields have disjoint compact supports, so their local Hessian has no mixed terms and their span is negative definite. The corrected definition is compatible with that intended mechanism.
## P2. Major: Appendix A loses an inversion contribution
Location. Page 47, the final display converting the \(\mathcal E\) identity into a \(W\) identity; Definition 3.1, pp. 8–9; the equivalence claim on p. 4.

Use the singly covered Clifford torus, with both periods \(2\pi\), and project stereographically from a point outside its image. The resulting embedded closed \(\Phi\) has \[\mathcal E(\Phi)=4\pi^2,\qquad W(\Phi)=2\pi^2,\qquad \int_\Sigma K\,dA=0.\] Take \(\Phi_k=\Phi\), with a fixed normalized flat domain metric. The conformal limit has one component and no nodes. Its index is zero even under the printed definition: the single-cover eigenvalues \(2(m^2+n^2)\) avoid \((2,4)\) in (P1.1). All bounded-energy and bounded-index assumptions hold.

Choose a regular point \(p=\Phi(x_0)\), and set \[I_p(x)=\frac{x-p}{|x-p|^2},\qquad \Phi_\infty=I_p\circ\Phi .\] This is an allowed fixed smooth conformal normalization in \(S^3\) under Definition 3.1. In the Euclidean representative, the limit is a Willmore immersion of the punctured torus with one complete planar end of multiplicity one. Appendix A explicitly allows finitely many ends. There are no bubbles, and convergence is smooth away from \(x_0\). Density invariance gives exactly \[\lim_k\mathcal E(\Phi_k)=\mathcal E(\Phi_\infty)=4\pi^2.\] If a connected orientation-preserving convention is imposed on the conformal group, compose inversion with a reflection; the energies are unchanged.

Set \(r=|\Phi-p|\), \(g=\Phi^*\xi\). The curvature transformation is \[g'=r^{-4}g,\qquad
 K_{g'}\,dA_{g'}=(K_g+2\Delta_g\log r)\,dA_g.\] Excise a small intrinsic disk about \(x_0\). Here \(r=\rho(1+O(\rho))\), and the outward conormal of the punctured domain points into the disk. Hence \[\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}
 \int_{\partial(\Sigma\setminus B_\epsilon)}
       \partial_n\log r\,ds=-2\pi,\qquad
 \int_{\Sigma\setminus\{x_0\}}K_{g'}\,dA_{g'}=-4\pi.\] The pointwise Gauss identity \(W=\mathcal E/2+\int K\,dA\) gives \[W(\Phi_\infty)=2\pi^2-4\pi,\qquad
 \lim_kW(\Phi_k)-W(\Phi_\infty)=4\pi .
 \tag{P2.1}\] Thus the displayed \(W\) identity for these permitted representatives is false, although their \(\mathcal E\) identity holds exactly.

Impact and counterevidence. This affects the asserted energy conversion, not the main \(\mathcal E\) quantization theorem. There is no neck in this constant sequence, so the preceding neck-curvature estimate cannot control an end introduced by target normalization. The topology warning on p. 1 agrees with (P2.1).

Repair boundary. Require compatible normalizations avoiding inversion through the surfaces, or retain the signed \(4\pi\) multiplicity contributions. Here the correction is \(W(\Phi_k)=W(\Phi_\infty)+4\pi\). Existence of differently normalized representatives satisfying a \(W\) identity is not contradicted. Major concerns the printed unconditional conversion for the specified pieces.
## P3. Major: the global avoidance in Lemma 5.2 is unavailable
Location. Section 5.1, pp. 13–15, especially Lemma 5.2, (16), and the last paragraph of its proof.

Page 13 explicitly permits the closed immersion to be non-Willmore outside the annulus. Nevertheless, p. 15 uses a global umbilic-set argument to choose a zero-mean-curvature inversion centre outside the entire surface. The following construction satisfies the stated local hypotheses on a fixed closed genus-one surface and makes every such centre belong to its image.

Start with the ring torus \[F(u,v)=((R+\cos u)\cos v,(R+\cos u)\sin v,\sin u),\qquad R=\sqrt2.\] Its metric is \(du^2+(R+\cos u)^2dv^2\), and, up to orientation, \[H=1-\frac{R}{2(R+\cos u)},\quad
 K=\frac{\cos u}{R+\cos u},\quad
 \Delta H+2H(H^2-K)=\frac{R(R^2-2)}{4(R+\cos u)^3}=0.\] It is a nonumbilic Willmore torus. Retain a fixed isothermal disk \(\phi(z)\) about \(u=v=0\), where \(H\ne0\). For small \(\rho\), let \(\bar Y_\rho\) be the unweighted annular average of its conformal Gauss map on \(\rho<|z|<2\rho\), and \(\bar H_\rho=(\bar Y_\rho)_5-(\bar Y_\rho)_4\). The averages extend smoothly to \(\rho=0\), with \(\bar H_0\ne0\) and \(\langle \bar Y_0,\bar Y_0\rangle_\eta=1\).

The inversion formula on p. 14 shows that zero mean curvature after inversion holds precisely for poles on the round sphere \[S_\rho=\partial B(c_\rho,r_\rho),\qquad
 c_\rho=\frac{(\bar Y_\rho)_{123}}{\bar H_\rho},\qquad
 r_\rho=\frac{\sqrt{\langle \bar Y_\rho,\bar Y_\rho\rangle_\eta}}
               {|\bar H_\rho|}.
 \tag{P3.1}\] Its centres and radii form a smooth compact family, with radii bounded away from zero. A similarity alone has nonzero mean. Every other Mobius map is a similarity after an inversion at its finite pole; therefore its zero-mean condition still forces that pole onto \(S_\rho\).

Extend the retained torus patch as follows. Take two labelled copies of \(S_\rho\), join the torus to the first by a tube, and the first sphere to the second by another tube. All torus surgery is outside the retained disk. On the first sphere modify only two small outer caps \(C_1,C_2\); on the second modify a cap \(C_3\), chosen with closure disjoint from both. Include smoothing collars inside these caps. The unchanged pieces cover the whole sphere exactly: \[(S_\rho\setminus(C_1\cup C_2))
       \cup(S_\rho\setminus C_3)=S_\rho .\] Target self-intersections and coincident sheets are allowed for an immersion. The abstract connected sum \(T^2\#S^2\#S^2\) has genus one.

For completeness, the surgeries have uniform geometric bounds. Choose fixed angular cap sizes, regular connecting arcs with prescribed end tangencies, and tubes of a fixed positive radius less than half the reciprocal of their maximum curvature. Flatten small graph disks inside the surgery neighborhoods and attach regular surface-of-revolution collars. The nonzero meridian velocity and tube curvature margin ensure immersion. Move these choices smoothly with \(c_\rho,r_\rho\), including \(\rho=0\). After decreasing the parameter interval, this is a smooth compact family of immersions on a fixed source, with uniformly nondegenerate metrics and bounded second derivatives. Consequently \[\sup_\rho\int_\Sigma |A_{\Phi_\rho}|^2\,dA<\infty,\qquad
 S_\rho\subseteq\Phi_\rho(\Sigma).\]

Now set \(T_k=k+k_0\), \(\rho_k=e^{-2T_k}\), and \(\Phi_k=\Phi_{\rho_k}\). Embed the flat cylinder \([-T_k,T_k]\times S^1\) in the retained disk by \(z=\rho_ke^{t+i\theta}\). Its image is \(e^{-3T_k}\le|z|\le e^{-T_k}\). The immersion there is exactly the nonumbilic conformal Willmore patch. Since its Gauss map is smooth at the centre, \[\int_{C_k}|\nabla n_k|^2\le Ce^{-2T_k}\longrightarrow0.\] Every unit subcylinder and dyadic subannulus has no more energy. Taking \(k_0\) large meets the prescribed smallness threshold. The global curvature bound and fixed genus were already established. The middle dyadic annulus is precisely the one defining \(S_{\rho_k}\).

Any transformation satisfying (16) must now have a pole in \(S_{\rho_k}\subseteq\Phi_k(\Sigma)\); it cannot give a smooth closed \(\mathbb R^3\)-valued immersion of the same topology. This contradicts the existence assertion independently of estimate (15).

Impact and counterevidence. This invalidates the specific gauge lemma used to establish the core Section 5.1 estimates under their stated hypotheses, and warrants Major. It does not refute the weaker direct conclusion of Theorem 4.1, nor the main theorem for globally Willmore immersions.

Repair boundary. A global Willmore assumption rules out the inserted open spherical pieces on a connected nonumbilic surface, but strengthens the printed hypotheses. An approximate gauge with a new estimate is another possible route; that replacement has not been established here. The distinction between local and global Willmore assumptions must be propagated through the proof.
# Further findings and their limits
## P4. Minor: the \(S^3\) energy identity on p. 5

Write \(B=\int_\Sigma|dN|^2\,dA=\int_\Sigma|A|^2\,dA\). The Gauss equation in the unit three-sphere gives \[\mathcal E=\tfrac12B+\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)-2\pi\chi(\Sigma).
 \tag{P4.1}\] The display following the reference to Gauss–Bonnet instead gives \(\mathcal E=B/2-\chi(\Sigma)\). For the singly covered Clifford torus, \(B=\mathcal E=4\pi^2\), whereas that right side is \(2\pi^2\). This is a closed genus-one example satisfying the stated setup. The subsequent boundedness equivalence remains correct: \[\mathcal E\le B,\qquad B=2\mathcal E-2\operatorname{Area}+4\pi\chi
                    \le2\mathcal E+4\pi\chi .\] The numerical identity requires correction, while the fixed-topology compactness input survives.
## P5. Minor: the collar models omit a twist and use \(\sinh\)
Location. Page 10, the torus paragraph and the hyperbolic metric display.

A general flat torus requires a rotated identification of the ends of its cut cylinder. For a degenerating example, use the lattice \(\Lambda_L=\mathbb Z+(\tfrac12+iL)\mathbb Z\), \(L>1\), and normalize its area. Before normalization the unique shortest vectors are \(\pm1\). Every perpendicular lattice vector is an integral multiple of \(2iL\); the pair \(1,2iL\) generates a sublattice of index two. No rectangular lattice basis can therefore represent this torus isometrically. The printed untwisted gluing misses this family, including \(L\to\infty\). A rotation in the endpoint gluing repairs the model and leaves the local cylinder analysis intact.

For the hyperbolic collar put \(z=re^{i\alpha}\), \(\log r=\ell\theta/(2\pi)\), and \(\alpha=\ell t/(2\pi)\). The half-plane metric pulls back to \[ds^2=\left(\frac{\ell}{2\pi\sin(\ell t/(2\pi))}\right)^2
                  (dt^2+d\theta^2).
 \tag{P5.1}\] The printed denominator has \(\sinh\). For that printed metric, the claimed central circle \(t=\pi^2/\ell\) has length \(\ell/\sinh(\pi/2)\), and the derivative of the logarithmic conformal factor there is \(-\ell\coth(\pi/2)/(2\pi)\ne0\). Thus it is not the claimed geodesic of length \(\ell\). Replacing \(\sinh\) by \(\sin\) repairs the explicit isometry. The underlying local conformal-cylinder description remains available.
## P6. Minor: the limiting straight line is null
Location. Theorem 4.1, p. 11, and Propositions 5.13, 5.15, and 5.19, pp. 26, 27, and 31.

These statements call the nonconstant affine limit time-like. If \(a+tv\) lies in the de Sitter quadric, coefficient comparison in \(\langle a+tv,a+tv\rangle_\eta=1\) gives \(\langle v,v\rangle_\eta=0\), \(\langle a,v\rangle_\eta=0\), and \(\langle a,a\rangle_\eta=1\). Its nonzero velocity is null. This is also the classification proved in Remark 5.14, p. 27, and used in the introduction and later argument.

The actual catenoid Gauss maps in P8 satisfy (26)–(28) and have a nonconstant affine null limit after reparametrization. Thus the causal-type discrepancy in the propositions is not based on an unrelated map. Replace time-like by light-like/null. This correction agrees with the actual convergence argument; it does not refute null-line convergence.
## P7. Minor: the inversion conformal factor has the wrong sign
Location. Page 15, the conformal-factor display in the proof of Lemma 5.2.

For \(I_a(x)=(x-a)/|x-a|^2\), \[(DI_a)^TDI_a=|x-a|^{-4}\operatorname{Id}.\] Consequently, wherever the immersion avoids \(a\), \[\lambda_{I_a\circ\phi}=\lambda_\phi-\log|\phi-a|^2,
 \tag{P7.1}\] not the printed plus sign. This calculation applies to every inversion considered there, without a further surface hypothesis. For example \(\phi(x,y)=(x,y,0)\), inverted about \(a=(0,0,1)\), has conformal factor \(-\log(1+x^2+y^2)\). The following two-sided distance requirement remains appropriate: a positive quantity and its reciprocal are both bounded under the same two-sided bound. This sign correction alone does not invalidate that estimate; the separate global avoidance failure is P3.
## P8. Major: a Poincare step loses the angular mean
Location. Page 29, proof of Lemma 5.17, the first Poincare step following the Cauchy–Schwarz estimate.

The replacement of the integral involving \(|\nabla Y|_\xi^2+|\nabla^2Y|_\xi^2\) by angularly differentiated quantities requires zero angular means that are not available. An actual conformal Gauss map detects the failure. Take \[\Phi(x,\theta)=\epsilon
           (\cosh x\cos\theta,\cosh x\sin\theta,x).\] This is a conformal minimal, hence Willmore, immersion, with \[Y=\left(\operatorname{sech}x\cos\theta,
          \operatorname{sech}x\sin\theta,-\tanh x,
          \epsilon h(x),\epsilon h(x)\right),\qquad
 h(x)=1-x\tanh x .
 \tag{P8.1}\] Restrict \(x=2L+t\), \(|t|\le L/2\), and choose \(\epsilon_L\asymp L^{-1}\) to give a fixed positive Euclidean oscillation \(\delta\). An exact choice exists by continuity: the angular oscillation tends to zero, and the change in \(h\) across the interval is asymptotic to \(L\). Then \(Y\) is uniformly bounded, \(\|\nabla Y\|_\infty=O(L^{-1})\), and \(\int|\nabla Y|_\xi^2=O(L^{-1})\). These are the boundedness, small-gradient and fixed-oscillation assumptions (26)–(28) used in the stated local lemma.

At the middle circle, \[\int_{S^1}|

 =4\pi igl(\operatorname{sech}^2(2L)
                +\epsilon_L^2h'(2L)^2 igr)\asymp L^{-2},\] whereas the integrals of \(|\partial_	heta

Page 30 explicitly combines (55) with (35) to obtain (57); that estimate controls (60)–(61) in Lemma 5.18. ## P9. Minor: the displayed normal family is only locally immersed
Location. Page 35, final construction in Proposition 6.4.

The family \[\widetilde\Psi_t=\frac{\Psi+t fN}{\sqrt{1+t^2f^2}},
 \qquad f=-\langle Z,\nu \rangle_\eta,\] is asserted to remain an immersion throughout \((-1,1)\). For the ordinary Clifford torus and \(f=2\), its second circle factor vanishes at \(t=1/2\). The corresponding \(Z\) is the derivative of a genuine local normal variation and satisfies both constraints; the base surface has no umbilics. Compactness supplies a uniform small-time interval, and the compression \(t\mapsto\varepsilon\tanh(t/\varepsilon)\) preserves the initial derivative while keeping the family inside it. This repairs the construction without changing the proposition’s existence conclusion.
## P10. Minor: the Hessian mixes ambient and covariant derivatives
Location. Page 38, (82)–(83), and the ambient expansion on pp. 40–41.

For a harmonic map into the de Sitter quadric and a tangent field \(V\), the intrinsic integrand is \[|\nabla^{S^{3,1}}V|_\eta^2-|dY|_\eta^2|V|_\eta^2
                                  +|\langle V,dY\rangle_\eta|^2.\] As \(|dV|_\eta^2=|\nabla^{S^{3,1}}V|_\eta^2+|\langle V,dY\rangle_\eta|^2\), the ambient expression is \[Q_\mathcal D(V)=\int (|dV|_\eta^2-|dY|_\eta^2|V|_\eta^2).
 \tag{P10.1}\] Equation (83) retains the extra positive term, while the later expansion differentiates ambient vectors and a constant ambient \(E\).

For a compact-support check, take the Clifford conformal Gauss map \[Y(u,v)=\frac{(\cos u,\sin u,-\cos v,-\sin v,0)}{\sqrt2}.\] Let \(f\) be any nonzero smooth function supported in a coordinate cylinder. The variation \(Y_\tau(u,v)=Y(u+\tau f(u,v),v)\) has \(V=fY_u\), and direct differentiation gives \(\mathcal D''(0)=\tfrac12\int|df|^2\). The printed ambient expression adds \(\tfrac14\int f^2>0\). This tests the arbitrary compactly supported map variations specified before (82), not the normal-immersion constraint in (6).
Deleting the spurious nonnegative term improves a negative upper bound. This local derivative-convention correction does not by itself invalidate the instability argument.
## P11. Minor: the area conversion in Lemma 7.7 misses two
Location. Page 46, first line, and definition (78), p. 37.

By \(\alpha(t)^2=\int_{S^1}|\nabla Y|_\eta^2\,d\theta\) and \(ds=\alpha\,dt\), \[\int\alpha(t(s))\,ds
     =\int|\nabla Y|_\eta^2\,dt\,d\theta=2\mathcal A(Y).\] The source writes \(\mathcal A(Y)\). Its area hypothesis is at least \(\mu>0\), so the identity cannot agree accidentally at zero. Consistently restoring the factor two changes the constants, while preserving the negative sign and its required order.
## P12. Minor: the arclength chain rule has one missing factor
Location. Page 31, the last display in Proposition 5.19; compare the correctly normalized mean-curve formula on p. 26.

Put \(v=|\partial_tY^*|_\xi>0\), \(ds=v\,dt\), and \(W=Y-Y^*\). Direct application of \(\partial_s=v^{-1}\partial_t\) gives \[W_{ss}=\frac{W_{tt}}{v^2}
       -\frac{\langle Y_t^*,Y_{tt}^*\rangle_\xi}{v^4}\,W_t .
 \tag{P12.1}\] The source has \(v^3\) in the second denominator, although \(v_t=\langle Y_t^*,Y_{tt}^*\rangle_\xi/v\). This is not an identity that can hold for the actual local family in P8: there \(W_t\ne0\), \(v\ne1\), and \(\langle Y_t^*,Y_{tt}^*\rangle_\xi\ne0\) for large \(x\). Indeed \(Y_t^*=(0,0,-\operatorname{sech}^2x,
\epsilon h',\epsilon h')\); its scalar product with its derivative is negative for large \(x\), since \(h'<0<h''\). Thus that family also gives a nonvacuous check within (26)–(28).

The relative estimates \(W_t=o(v)\), \(W_{tt}=o(v^2)\), and \(Y_{tt}^*=o(v^2)\) still make the corrected second term \(o(1)\). The missing factor must be restored, but it does not defeat the intended interior \(C^2\) conclusion.
# Positive checks and unresolved proof dependencies
## The constrained variation problem

The signs in (10), (66), and (70)–(71) are consistent. A direct global argument verifies Proposition 4.2. Let \(

For \(W=Z-T(f)\), one obtains \(\langle W,Yangle_\eta=\langle W,

Along genuine conformal-Gauss-map variations, \(\mathcal A(Y_t)=\mathcal E(\Psi_t)/2\). This defines the constrained Hessian at umbilics without asserting differentiability of unrestricted area at every degenerate ambient map. The linear map \(T\) is bijective onto the two-constraint space and preserves negative definite subspaces up to the positive factor two. The intended ordinary-index equality is therefore supported.
## Negative fields, supports, and the final sign

Substitution in (79)–(81) verifies both linear constraints. The reconstructed velocity \(-\langle Z,\nu \rangle_\eta N\) retains compact support. Cutoffs vanish on full endpoint neighborhoods, permitting smooth extension by zero. Disjoint supports give zero mixed Hessian terms, as needed for the corrected index count.

The little-\(o\) error in Lemma 7.5 is not by itself a sign obstruction. Set \[A_k=\int|\nabla f_k|^2,\qquad
 B_k=\int f_k^2|\nabla Y_k|_\eta^2 .\] The area upper bound implies \(A_k=O(\ell_k^{-2})\), and the scalar estimate gives \(B_k-2A_k\ge c\ell_k^{-2}\), after cutoff errors. Hence \(\ell_k^{-2}+A_k+B_k\le C(B_k-2A_k)\), and the stated remainder can be absorbed by the negative main part. No contrary sign result is inferred merely from the presence of \(o(B_k)\).

The final subdivision is justified eventually in a selected subcylinder of area \(\lambda/2\), partitioned into \(J\) equal-area pieces. A liminf lower bound does not warrant, for every \(k\), the printed subdivision of the entire collar into pieces whose total area is at most \(\lambda\). The continuous cumulative-area construction supplies the required disjoint supports. This is a proof-selection clarification, not a separate geometric counterexample.
## Limits of the verification

This review has not supplied a complete replacement for the uniform long-collar estimates of Lemma 7.5. Equation (77) is derived using Euclidean arclength, while (78) introduces Lorentz-average arclength. Their rates need an explicit comparison. The estimates for a fixed global \(E\) under local choices of constant Lorentz gauges also require uniform control. The full corrected field can transform covariantly; failure of one normalized-lift summand to be invariant does not disprove covariance of the full field.

The Appendix C perturbation is generally nonconformal. Subsequent flat-coordinate calculations must track a pulled-back metric or estimate the perturbation errors. Arbitrarily small smooth perturbations are available, which is relevant counterevidence. No all-hypothesis Willmore sequence violating the instability conclusion has been established for these concerns. They remain proof-completeness limitations and are not additional confirmed adverse findings.

The review followed the harmonic-map and angular-energy equations, the comparison of \(\alpha_k,\beta_k,\gamma_k\), the differentiated estimates for \(C^2\) convergence, and the construction and support of constrained fields. The external regularity, compactness and umbilic-set theorems remain identified dependencies; an independent reproof of all cited literature is not claimed.

problems.title: Negative-cone span is not Morse index
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Negative-cone span is not Morse index
claim: Kind: mathematical statement or proof step
Location: p5 equation(1);p8 equation(6);TheoremIII p4 andTheorem4.3 p12
Claim: Index is dimension of the span of individually strictly negative velocities.
Closed smooth genus1 Willmore immersion, normal smooth variations, fixed energy, no umbilics; immersion rather than embedding is allowed.
analysis: Location. Page 5, (1), and page 8, (6); the bounded-index hypothesis of Theorem III, p. 4, and Theorem 4.3, p. 12.

The definitions use \[\dim\operatorname{Span}\{v:Q(v)<0\},\] where \(Q\) is the second variation, rather than the maximum dimension of a subspace on which \(Q\) is negative definite. If \(Q(v)<0\), then for every smooth admissible \(w\) and sufficiently small nonzero \(t\), \(Q(v+tw)<0\). Thus \(w=((v+tw)-v)/t\) belongs to that span. The printed quantity is zero in the absence of negative directions and infinite dimensional whenever a negative direction exists.

A complete geometric example is \[\Sigma=(\mathbb R/4\pi\mathbb Z)\times(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z),\qquad
 \Psi(u,v)=\frac{(\cos u,\sin u,\cos v,\sin v)}{\sqrt2}.\] This unbranched double cover of the Clifford torus is a closed, genus-one Willmore immersion without umbilics. With \(N=2^{-1/2}(\cos u,\sin u,-\cos v,-\sin v)\), its metric is \(g=(du^2+dv^2)/2\), principal curvatures are \(-1,1\), and \(H=0\). Its area is \(4\pi^2\) and \(\mathcal E=8\pi^2\). For a normal velocity \(fN\), direct differentiation gives \[\operatorname{Area}''=\int_\Sigma(|\nabla f|^2-4f^2)\,dA,\qquad
 H'=\tfrac12(\Delta+4)f.\] Since \(\mathcal E=2\int(1+H^2)\,dA-4\pi\chi(\Sigma)\), \[Q_\mathcal E(f)=\int_\Sigma f(\Delta+2)(\Delta+4)f\,dA.
 \tag{P1.1}\] The eigenvalues of \(-\Delta\) are \(2(m^2/4+n^2)\). Only \((m,n)=(\pm1,\pm1)\) lie strictly between two and four. Their Fourier modes give four real negative directions, while all other modes are nonnegative. The ordinary index is exactly four. For example, \[f=\cos(u/2)\cos v,\qquad
 \int_\Sigma f^2\,dA=\pi^2,\qquad Q_\mathcal E(f)=-3\pi^2/4.\] The printed index is infinite.

All these velocities are realized by immersion variations: \(\cos(sf)\Psi+\sin(sf)N\) is immersed for sufficiently small \(s\). The time change \(s=\varepsilon\tanh(t/\varepsilon)\), with derivative one at zero, realizes the same velocity on \((-1,1)\). Stereographic projection from a point outside the image gives \[\Phi(u,v)=\frac{(\cos u,\sin u,\cos v)}{\sqrt2-\sin v},\] a closed immersion in the paper’s Euclidean setting with the same normal index, by conformal invariance of \(\mathcal E\).

Impact and counterevidence. Its constant sequence has bounded energy and ordinary index four, but is excluded by the literal printed hypothesis. The central theorem’s formal coverage is reduced to stable sequences. This scope change warrants Major. The example does not refute quantization: a constant sequence trivially quantizes.

Repair boundary. Both definitions must use \[\operatorname{ind}(Q)=\sup\{\dim L:L\text{ is linear and }Q(v)<0
                           \text{ for every }0\ne v\in L\}.\] Section 7.3 supplies relevant counterevidence: its fields have disjoint compact supports, so their local Hessian has no mixed terms and their span is negative definite. The corrected definition is compatible with that intended mechanism.
result: Impact: The central bounded-index hypothesis formally excludes finite nonzero Morse-index surfaces and reduces to stable sequences; this is a scope change, not a demonstrated false E energy identity.

claim: Kind: mathematical statement or proof step

Claim: For the displayed independently normalized limits, E quantization implies the same uncorrected W sum.

Constant embedded stereographic singly-covered Clifford torus;closed genus1;fixed flat normalized domain;Willmore;E4pi²;ordinary and printed index0;one main component,no bubbles. Independent target Mobius normalizations are allowed, and AppendixA allows finite ends.
analysis: Location. Page 47, the final display converting the \(\mathcal E\) identity into a \(W\) identity; Definition 3.1, pp. 8–9; the equivalence claim on p. 4.

Use the singly covered Clifford torus, with both periods \(2\pi\), and project stereographically from a point outside its image. The resulting embedded closed \(\Phi\) has \[\mathcal E(\Phi)=4\pi^2,\qquad W(\Phi)=2\pi^2,\qquad \int_\Sigma K\,dA=0.\] Take \(\Phi_k=\Phi\), with a fixed normalized flat domain metric. The conformal limit has one component and no nodes. Its index is zero even under the printed definition: the single-cover eigenvalues \(2(m^2+n^2)\) avoid \((2,4)\) in (P1.1). All bounded-energy and bounded-index assumptions hold.

Choose a regular point \(p=\Phi(x_0)\), and set \[I_p(x)=\frac{x-p}{|x-p|^2},\qquad \Phi_\infty=I_p\circ\Phi .\] This is an allowed fixed smooth conformal normalization in \(S^3\) under Definition 3.1. In the Euclidean representative, the limit is a Willmore immersion of the punctured torus with one complete planar end of multiplicity one. Appendix A explicitly allows finitely many ends. There are no bubbles, and convergence is smooth away from \(x_0\). Density invariance gives exactly \[\lim_k\mathcal E(\Phi_k)=\mathcal E(\Phi_\infty)=4\pi^2.\] If a connected orientation-preserving convention is imposed on the conformal group, compose inversion with a reflection; the energies are unchanged.

Set \(r=|\Phi-p|\), \(g=\Phi^*\xi\). The curvature transformation is \[g'=r^{-4}g,\qquad
 K_{g'}\,dA_{g'}=(K_g+2\Delta_g\log r)\,dA_g.\] Excise a small intrinsic disk about \(x_0\). Here \(r=\rho(1+O(\rho))\), and the outward conormal of the punctured domain points into the disk. Hence \[\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}
 \int_{\partial(\Sigma\setminus B_\epsilon)}
       \partial_n\log r\,ds=-2\pi,\qquad
 \int_{\Sigma\setminus\{x_0\}}K_{g'}\,dA_{g'}=-4\pi.\] The pointwise Gauss identity \(W=\mathcal E/2+\int K\,dA\) gives \[W(\Phi_\infty)=2\pi^2-4\pi,\qquad
 \lim_kW(\Phi_k)-W(\Phi_\infty)=4\pi .
 \tag{P2.1}\] Thus the displayed \(W\) identity for these permitted representatives is false, although their \(\mathcal E\) identity holds exactly.

Impact and counterevidence. This affects the asserted energy conversion, not the main \(\mathcal E\) quantization theorem. There is no neck in this constant sequence, so the preceding neck-curvature estimate cannot control an end introduced by target normalization. The topology warning on p. 1 agrees with (P2.1).

Repair boundary. Require compatible normalizations avoiding inversion through the surfaces, or retain the signed \(4\pi\) multiplicity contributions. Here the correction is \(W(\Phi_k)=W(\Phi_\infty)+4\pi\). Existence of differently normalized representatives satisfying a \(W\) identity is not contradicted. result: Impact: The unqualified final W identity for the allowed pieces, and the asserted conversion for those pieces, is false. No counterexample to the main E existence theorem or to a suitably normalized W quantization theorem is claimed.

problems.title: Mean-curvature gauge cannot avoid every global image under local Willmore assumptions
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Mean-curvature gauge cannot avoid every global image under local Willmore assumptions
claim: Kind: mathematical statement or proof step
Location: Section5.1 p13;Lemma5.2 p14 equations(15)–(16);global avoidance proof p15
Claim: A topology-preserving Mobius transformation always makes the unweighted annular mean curvature zero, although the closed immersion need only be Willmore on the cylinder.

Fixed closed genus1 surface;smooth globally immersed family;uniform whole-surface integral|A|²;nonumbilic conformal Willmore neck;total cylinder curvature arbitrarily small;uniform local strip/dyadic energy tends0.
analysis: Location. Section 5.1, pp. 13–15, especially Lemma 5.2, (16), and the last paragraph of its proof.

Page 13 explicitly permits the closed immersion to be non-Willmore outside the annulus. Nevertheless, p. 15 uses a global umbilic-set argument to choose a zero-mean-curvature inversion centre outside the entire surface. The following construction satisfies the stated local hypotheses on a fixed closed genus-one surface and makes every such centre belong to its image.

Start with the ring torus \[F(u,v)=((R+\cos u)\cos v,(R+\cos u)\sin v,\sin u),\qquad R=\sqrt2.\] Its metric is \(du^2+(R+\cos u)^2dv^2\), and, up to orientation, \[H=1-\frac{R}{2(R+\cos u)},\quad
 K=\frac{\cos u}{R+\cos u},\quad
 \Delta H+2H(H^2-K)=\frac{R(R^2-2)}{4(R+\cos u)^3}=0.\] It is a nonumbilic Willmore torus. Retain a fixed isothermal disk \(\phi(z)\) about \(u=v=0\), where \(H\ne0\). For small \(\rho\), let \(\bar Y_\rho\) be the unweighted annular average of its conformal Gauss map on \(\rho<|z|<2\rho\), and \(\bar H_\rho=(\bar Y_\rho)_5-(\bar Y_\rho)_4\). The averages extend smoothly to \(\rho=0\), with \(\bar H_0\ne0\) and \(\langle \bar Y_0,\bar Y_0\rangle_\eta=1\).

The inversion formula on p. 14 shows that zero mean curvature after inversion holds precisely for poles on the round sphere \[S_\rho=\partial B(c_\rho,r_\rho),\qquad
 c_\rho=\frac{(\bar Y_\rho)_{123}}{\bar H_\rho},\qquad
 r_\rho=\frac{\sqrt{\langle \bar Y_\rho,\bar Y_\rho\rangle_\eta}}
               {|\bar H_\rho|}.
 \tag{P3.1}\] Its centres and radii form a smooth compact family, with radii bounded away from zero. A similarity alone has nonzero mean. Every other Mobius map is a similarity after an inversion at its finite pole; therefore its zero-mean condition still forces that pole onto \(S_\rho\).

Extend the retained torus patch as follows. Take two labelled copies of \(S_\rho\), join the torus to the first by a tube, and the first sphere to the second by another tube. All torus surgery is outside the retained disk. On the first sphere modify only two small outer caps \(C_1,C_2\); on the second modify a cap \(C_3\), chosen with closure disjoint from both. Include smoothing collars inside these caps. The unchanged pieces cover the whole sphere exactly: \[(S_\rho\setminus(C_1\cup C_2))
       \cup(S_\rho\setminus C_3)=S_\rho .\] Target self-intersections and coincident sheets are allowed for an immersion. The abstract connected sum \(T^2\#S^2\#S^2\) has genus one.

For completeness, the surgeries have uniform geometric bounds. Choose fixed angular cap sizes, regular connecting arcs with prescribed end tangencies, and tubes of a fixed positive radius less than half the reciprocal of their maximum curvature. Flatten small graph disks inside the surgery neighborhoods and attach regular surface-of-revolution collars. The nonzero meridian velocity and tube curvature margin ensure immersion. Move these choices smoothly with \(c_\rho,r_\rho\), including \(\rho=0\). After decreasing the parameter interval, this is a smooth compact family of immersions on a fixed source, with uniformly nondegenerate metrics and bounded second derivatives. Consequently \[\sup_\rho\int_\Sigma |A_{\Phi_\rho}|^2\,dA<\infty,\qquad
 S_\rho\subseteq\Phi_\rho(\Sigma).\]

Now set \(T_k=k+k_0\), \(\rho_k=e^{-2T_k}\), and \(\Phi_k=\Phi_{\rho_k}\). Embed the flat cylinder \([-T_k,T_k]\times S^1\) in the retained disk by \(z=\rho_ke^{t+i\theta}\). Its image is \(e^{-3T_k}\le|z|\le e^{-T_k}\). The immersion there is exactly the nonumbilic conformal Willmore patch. Since its Gauss map is smooth at the centre, \[\int_{C_k}|\nabla n_k|^2\le Ce^{-2T_k}\longrightarrow0.\] Every unit subcylinder and dyadic subannulus has no more energy. Taking \(k_0\) large meets the prescribed smallness threshold. The global curvature bound and fixed genus were already established. The middle dyadic annulus is precisely the one defining \(S_{\rho_k}\).

Any transformation satisfying (16) must now have a pole in \(S_{\rho_k}\subseteq\Phi_k(\Sigma)\); it cannot give a smooth closed \(\mathbb R^3\)-valued immersion of the same topology. This contradicts the existence assertion independently of estimate (15).

Impact and counterevidence. This invalidates the specific gauge lemma used to establish the core Section 5.1 estimates under their stated hypotheses, and warrants Major. It does not refute the weaker direct conclusion of Theorem 4.1, nor the main theorem for globally Willmore immersions.

Repair boundary. A global Willmore assumption rules out the inserted open spherical pieces on a connected nonumbilic surface, but strengthens the printed hypotheses. An approximate gauge with a new estimate is another possible route; that replacement has not been established here. The distinction between local and global Willmore assumptions must be propagated through the proof.
result: Impact: The asserted intermediate existence lemma feeding the core gauge/epsilon-regularity derivation fails under its expressly permitted local hypotheses. This is a concrete assumption mismatch, not merely a missing citation.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Strengthen to the appropriate global Willmore assumption and propagate scope, or replace exact zero mean by an approximate gauge and prove the necessary estimates; no such complete replacement is claimed.
