Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Curve Exclusion, Effective Axioms
and Regular Amalgamation
# Exact source and scope

The frozen paper M25-0257 is Will Johnson and Jinhe Ye, Curve-excluding fields. The DOI is 10.4171/JEMS/1630 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1630). The source actually reviewed is the 33-page author manuscript arXiv:2303.06063v2, revised on 13 December 2024 at 01:05:52 UTC; its cover also prints 13 December 2024. The publisher records submission on 30 May 2023, acceptance on 10 December 2024 and online publication on 27 March 2025 [source, arxiv, record]. The frozen 2025 membership is retained. Equivalence of this author version to the publisher’s Version of Record has not been established.

All source text, including the references and proposed generalizations, was read. The review checks definitions, the role of characteristic zero, geometric integrality, genus and properness, effective-language assumptions, field-extension quantifiers, relative algebraic closure, and the independence and cyclic-amalgamation steps. Source locations below are both printed and PDF page numbers. The evidence pages were actually viewed as images. The mathematical examples and reconstructions are reviewer work; no author code was executed.
# Confirmed corrections
## P1. Minor: the avoidance definition uses the base field

Location. Page 5, the opening paragraph of Section 2. The displayed definition says that a \(K_0\)-field \(K\) avoids \(C\) when \(C(K_0)=\varnothing\). With the standing hypothesis this is independent of \(K\).

For a concrete check, let \(K_0=\mathbb Q\) and let \(C\) be \[x^4+y^4+1=0.\] Its smooth projective closure is the plane quartic \(X^4+Y^4+Z^4=0\), which is geometrically integral of genus three. Smoothness follows because its three partial derivatives cannot vanish at a projective point in characteristic zero. It has no rational point, since a sum of fourth powers is positive unless all coordinates vanish. On the other hand, with \(K=\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)\), the point \((\zeta_8,0)\) lies on \(C(K)\). The printed condition therefore calls this field avoiding although it contains a point of the excluded curve.

Impact, counterevidence and repair. Replace \(C(K_0)\) by \(C(K)\) in this definition. The abstract, the definition of \(T_{C,K_0}\) on p. 2, condition \((\mathrm{III}_C)\) on p. 10, and the opening of Section 4 already use the latter condition. The subsequent proof of Proposition 2.5 also uses it. Thus the isolated incorrect definition must be repaired, but it does not expose a missing step in the construction under the consistently stated intended avoidance condition.
## P2. Minor: the effective claim needs an effective base

Location. Theorem 1.6, p. 2, and Remark 2.16, p. 10. Theorem 1.6 allows an arbitrary characteristic-zero \(K_0\) and asserts a computably axiomatized theory in the language containing a constant for every element of \(K_0\).

Take \(K_0=\mathbb R\) and the same smooth plane quartic, which has no real point and satisfies the geometric assumptions. The full language \(L(\mathbb R)\) is uncountable. More concretely, suppose an ordinary Turing procedure enumerates axioms for the claimed class. Only countably many real constant names occur among its finite output strings. In any model of the claimed companion, select a nonzero \(r\in\mathbb R\) whose name does not occur, and reinterpret \(c_r\) as zero while leaving the field and all mentioned names unchanged. All enumerated sentences retain their truth values, but the required base-field sentence \(c_r\ne0\) is false. This is a direct obstruction to an absolute computable axiomatization of this full class.

Impact, counterevidence and repair. The existence of the model companion over arbitrary \(K_0\) is not contradicted. The effective arguments are valid over \(\mathbb Q\), or over a base with a specified effective presentation and an effectively available field diagram. Over a general base one should state an axiom scheme relative to that diagram. The actual decidable completion in Theorem 4.19 and the number-field oracle equivalence in Theorem 4.21 use effective bases and are unaffected by this boundary correction. A relative scheme must not be called an absolute Turing enumeration without the additional data.
## P3. Minor: bounded top-dimensional degree is insufficient

Location. Fact 2.10, p. 7; the conventions on pp. 4–5. Varieties are expressly allowed to be reduced and nonintegral, and \(\operatorname{pdeg}(X)\) is defined by intersecting with a generic linear subspace of codimension \(\dim X\). This degree ignores lower-dimensional components. Fact 2.10 nevertheless claims a single definable family containing every projective variety of bounded such degree.

Work over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field. Fix a line \(\ell\subset\mathbb P^2\) and distinct points \(p_1,\ldots,p_N\) outside it, and give \[X_N=\ell\cup\{p_1,\ldots,p_N\}\] the reduced structure. This is a projective variety permitted by the conventions, and a generic line meets it in precisely one point. Hence \(\operatorname{pdeg}(X_N)=1\) for every \(N\). If the asserted single definable family \(\{V_a\}_{a\in Y}\) existed for \(n=2,m=1\), the definable family \(V_a\setminus\ell\) would have finite fibers of every size \(N\). This contradicts the uniform bound on finite fibers in an algebraically closed field. One may see that bound directly from quantifier elimination: a fixed formula has a fixed finite algebraic complexity, so the number of points in its zero-dimensional fibers is uniformly bounded.

Impact, counterevidence and repair. Restrict Fact 2.10 to pure-dimensional varieties, or bound the sum of the degrees of all irreducible components. Chow varieties then provide the required finite union of parameter families. The graph \(\Gamma\) in Fact 2.11 and in the axiom scheme on p. 9 is irreducible, so this corrected version covers the actual use. The counterexample does not refute the degree bound for graphs or the first-order axiomatization.
## P4. Minor: Weil restriction is indexed by embeddings

Location. Lemma 4.13, p. 17, the displayed decomposition of \(W_F\), where \(F\) is a splitting field and \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(F/K)\). The product is indexed by every \(g\in G\). For a non-Galois extension \(L/K\), that repeats the conjugate factors.

Let \(K_0=K=\mathbb Q\), retain the negative Fermat quartic from P1, let \(L=\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})\), and let \(V=\mathbb A^1_L\). Thus \(K\models C\mathrm{XF}_\forall\), \(L/K\) is a proper finite extension, and \(V\) is geometrically integral and affine, as required. The irreducible polynomial \(T^3-2\) has discriminant \(-108\), so its splitting field has group \(S_3\) of order six. But \[\operatorname{Res}_{L/K}\mathbb A^1_L\simeq\mathbb A^3_K.\] Consequently \(W_F\) has dimension three, whereas the printed product of six conjugate affine lines has dimension six.

Impact, counterevidence and repair. The correct decomposition is \[W_F\simeq\prod_{\sigma\in\operatorname{Hom}_K(L,F)} V^\sigma_F,\] equivalently a product indexed by \(G/\operatorname{Gal}(F/L)\) after fixing an embedding. This correction preserves Lemma 4.13: a nonconstant map from the product to the hyperbolic curve depends on one factor by Lemma 4.3; that factor is unique, since a map factoring through two independent factors is constant. A map defined over \(K\) would make this factor \(G\)-invariant, but \(G\) acts transitively on more than one embedding. This is impossible. Hence the PAC conclusion in Theorem 4.14 retains its intended proof.
## P5. Minor: elementary extensions preserve avoidance
Location. Corollary 4.15(1), p. 18. For \(K\models C\mathrm{XF}'\) it asserts that a proper elementary extension \(L/K\) has \(C(L)\ne\varnothing\).

Choose any \(K\models C\mathrm{XF}\) for the curve in P1. Such a model exists by the construction, and it also satisfies \(C\mathrm{XF}'\). There is a proper elementary extension: compactness applied to the elementary diagram and a new constant distinct from every element of \(K\) supplies one, since \(K\) is infinite. But \(C(K)=\varnothing\) is a first-order statement over \(K_0\), so elementarity gives \(C(L)=\varnothing\). This satisfies every printed hypothesis and contradicts the stated conclusion.

Impact, counterevidence and repair. The intended word is algebraic. The preceding Theorem 4.14 proves that every proper algebraic extension is PAC, and hence has a point on the geometrically integral curve \(C\). That implication yields \((\mathrm I_C)\) and Corollary 4.15(2). Thus the incorrect displayed corollary needs correction; the intended redundancy of \((\mathrm I_C)\) does not depend on the false elementary-extension assertion.
## P6. Minor: a rational function field is not already a model
Location. The proof of Theorem 4.24, p. 20, states \(K(t)\models C\mathrm{XF}\). The stated argument only proves avoidance.

For any \(K\models C\mathrm{XF}\), let \(s\) be transcendental and set \(t=s^2\). The extension \(K(s)/K(t)\) is proper of degree two. There is no nonconstant rational map from \(\mathbb P^1_K\) to the smooth projective completion of \(C\): after algebraic closure, Riemann–Hurwitz contradicts genus at least two. Properness extends a rational map across the missing points, and a constant \(K\)-rational map into \(C\) would give a point in \(C(K)\). Thus \[C(K(s))=C(K)=\varnothing .\] This proper finite extension of \(K(t)\) violates \((\mathrm I_C)\), so \(K(t)\not\models C\mathrm{XF}\).

Impact, counterevidence and repair. The correct assertion is \(K(t)\models C\mathrm{XF}_\forall\). That is exactly the hypothesis needed for Theorem 4.16 to produce a regular extension \(K'/K(t)\) with \(K'\models C\mathrm{XF}\). Model completeness then gives \(K\preccurlyeq K'\), and regularity retains the desired relative algebraic closure of \(K(t)\). The Hilbertianity conclusion and its subsequent unboundedness application survive.
## P7. Minor: the recalled TP\(_2\) criterion omits inconsistency

Location. Page 21, the paragraph immediately before Corollary 4.29. It defines TP\(_2\) using only \[\varphi(a_\eta,b_{i,j})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
          \eta(i)=j\qquad(\eta:\omega\longrightarrow\omega).
          \tag{P7.1}\] This does not require the rows to be \(k\)-inconsistent.

In fact (P7.1) is exactly the independence property, IP. Given (P7.1), restrict \(\eta(i)\) to \(0\) or \(1\); the instances with \(b_{i,0}\) realize all subsets of \(\omega\). Conversely, an IP array indexed by the countable set \(\omega\times\omega\) realizes every subset of that set in a sufficiently saturated model. In particular it realizes the graph of every function \(\eta\), giving (P7.1).

A concrete example is the ordinary random graph with \(\varphi(x,y)=R(x,y)\). Its extension property and compactness produce all these path patterns. Yet every finite set of positive adjacency instances in a row has a common neighbor. Thus no row of this array is \(k\)-inconsistent for any finite \(k\). The random graph is a simple, hence NTP\(_2\), theory: quantifier elimination and free graph amalgamation show that forking is algebraic dependence, giving local character. This is the ordinary random graph, not the triangle-free Henson graph mentioned elsewhere in the paper.

Impact, counterevidence and repair. Require a fixed finite \(k\ge2\) such that \(\{\varphi(x,b_{i,j}):j<\omega\}\) is \(k\)-inconsistent for each \(i\), together with consistency of every path. Corollary 4.29 actually invokes the stronger PAC-field theorem, rather than deriving TP\(_2\) merely from (P7.1). The definition is wrong, but this example does not disprove TP\(_2\) for the fields constructed in the paper. The cited PAC result is retained as an external dependency.
# Positive checks and proof dependencies
## Axioms and the geometric complexity bound

With avoidance correctly formulated, Proposition 2.5 reduces existential closedness to finite extensions and regular function-field extensions. In characteristic zero, relative algebraic closure makes the function-field presentation geometrically integral. A rational point over that function field is a rational map to \(C\); absence of such a map gives the required Zariski density by existential closedness. Conversely, the finite-extension condition removes the algebraic part of a finitely generated extension.

For Fact 2.11, put \(d=\dim X\), \(e=\operatorname{pdeg}(X)\) and \(c=\operatorname{pdeg}(C)\). A general complete-intersection curve \(D=X\cap H_1\cap\cdots\cap H_{d-1}\) is smooth and avoids the codimension-at-least-two indeterminacy locus. It maps dominantly to \(C\): the hyperplane sections meet a general fiber properly in a nonempty zero-dimensional intersection, by ampleness. Thus its map to \(C\) is finite and separable. The calculation in Section 3 gives \[\operatorname{pdeg}(\Gamma)=e+d\,\deg(D/C)c,\qquad
       \deg(D/C)\le\frac{g(D)-1}{g(C)-1}\le g(D)-1.\] Here \(\beta^2=0\) on the curve factor accounts for the absence of higher mixed terms in the Segre degree. Together with the cited genus bound \(g(D)\le(e-1)^2\), this yields the displayed computable bound \(e+d(e^2-2e)c\). The apparently problematic small degrees do not provide examples: a curve of genus zero or one cannot dominate \(C\). In dimension zero no such dominant map exists at all. No counterexample to this core graph bound was found.

Resolution and the generic-graph criterion reduce the axiom scheme to smooth projective irreducible sources. These are the cases covered by the repair in P3. The characteristic-zero qualifications in the use of generic rational functions and separability are essential.
## Regular amalgamation and the field-theoretic applications

For a map from \(V_1\times V_2\) to a genus-at-least-two curve, finiteness of nonconstant maps from a fixed smooth projective source forces the map to depend on one factor. The factor descends to \(K\) when the original map does: regularity makes \[\overline K(V_i)\cap K(V_1\times V_2)=K(V_i)\] inside the common scalar extension. This supplies the descent implicit in the transition from Lemma 4.3 to 4.4. It justifies the regular tensor-product amalgam avoiding \(C\).

That amalgam gives elementary agreement over relatively algebraically closed subfields. It supports the classification by \(\operatorname{Abs}(M)\), the solvability-predicate quantifier elimination, and equality of model-theoretic and field-theoretic algebraic closure over \(K_0\). In Lemma 4.8 the perfectness hypothesis supplies a primitive element; the compactness embedding lies in the original relative algebraic closure because algebraic elements do not appear in an elementary extension. The two embeddings of algebraic extensions are isomorphisms by the finite root-set argument given there.

The corrected Weil product yields PAC proper algebraic extensions. The regular-extension construction realizes every allowable algebraic part. Over \(\mathbb Q\), excluding roots of irreducible polynomials of degree greater than one computably states \(\operatorname{Abs}(M)=\mathbb Q\). Completeness then makes the resulting consistent recursively axiomatized theory decidable. For number fields, the two searches in Theorem 4.21 halt on complementary alternatives; root tests are effective for the finitely many solvability predicates. No claim to have implemented a Mordell oracle is made.

The finite-group construction of Lemma 5.3 uses the action through \(\alpha:H\to G\), the regular permutation action on the transcendental variables, and the fixed field. The printed reference to \(\beta:H\to G\) is a symbol slip; the specified domains determine \(\alpha\). Taking invariants of \(C(L(\bar t))=C(L)\) proves avoidance. The compatible algebraic closures in Lemma 5.2 remove the inner-automorphism ambiguity in Theorem 5.4. The extensions used there are small enough for the stated monster saturation; no unrestricted cardinal-size embedding claim is needed.

For Example 4.30, Riemann–Hurwitz forces a dominant map between the two genus-two curves to have degree one. The six branch points give at most \(6!=720\) normalized parameter triples. Uniform finiteness gives a parameter-free definition of the finite-point locus: the numerical bound may be used in a pure ring formula. Thus naming the transcendental base does not invalidate the claimed pure-field algebraicity of its parameter triple.
## NSOP\(_4\), SOP\(_3\), and the limits of this check

The NSOP\(_4\) argument constructs the three initial edges in a regular \(\omega\)-free PAC extension, then reflects the middle vertex to obtain a fourth. Strong independence makes \(\operatorname{acl}(Ac_1)\operatorname{acl}(Ac_3)\) relatively algebraically closed. Consequently both two-edge composita are regular over that field and ACF-independent there. Lemma 4.4 applies to their compositum, which therefore avoids \(C\). Each adjacent pair retains its relative algebraic closure, so its \(\operatorname{Sol}_n\) predicates, and hence its quantifier-free type, are retained. A regular extension to a model of \(C\mathrm{XF}\) then realizes the forbidden cycle. The occurrence of \(\operatorname{acl}(Ac_3c_3)\) on p. 29 and the missing prime on \(L'\models C\mathrm{XF}\) in Claim 6.8 are local notation slips; the correct fields are present in the surrounding displays.

The stronger independence relation in Fact 6.6 can be reconstructed by taking a regular tensor-product amalgam over the relatively algebraically closed base and then a regular PAC extension; quantifier elimination supplies stationarity. The weaker-independence theorem in Fact 6.5 is a substantive cited input. Its original full proof was not independently reproduced or fully obtained in this review. The public publisher route provided access information, and attempted author-hosted routes failed. This access limitation is recorded in the auxiliary notes; a citation has not been substituted for an inspected external proof.

For the SOP\(_3\) instance, the real algebraic numbers avoid \(x^4+y^4+1=0\) and are an allowed algebraic part. Positive integers differ by a fourth power in that field. A directed triangle would yield three nonzero fourth powers with sum zero, and division by the third fourth power would produce a point on the excluded curve. The nonzero qualification prevents division by zero. This verifies the given obstruction and its pure-field formulation. Conjecture 7.3 and the proposals in Section 8 are kept as conjectures and questions.

result: Impact: Overstates algorithmic scope; does not refute model companion or decidable nonlarge example.

report: Abstract: The exact author manuscript arXiv:2109.09301v3 is examined. Four Major proof defects and five Minor corrections are established. The Major defects concern ramified-stalk equivariance, full K3 cohomology, the missing principal-polarization reduction, and the tensor-power step supplying the Artin base case. These defects do not refute the final universality theorem. Explicit replacements are supplied, including a noncircular construction of Artin representations. The remaining checks address proalgebraic completions, tensor powers, equal-characteristic cohomology, polarization, semisimplification, and tangential base points. The main result concerns the semisimplification of cohomology over a number field and functions on the proalgebraic completion. Full extensions and proreductive coefficients require separate arguments. The findings below distinguish false statements and proof steps from conclusions that remain valid after repair.
# Confirmed problems
## P1. Ramified stalks lack the asserted simultaneous equivariance (Major)
Location. Proposition 3.3, pp. 8–9, especially the stalk inclusion and its claimed \(H\)-stability on p. 9. This bridge is used in Corollary 3.4 and the main induction on p. 15.

Example under the actual hypotheses. Take \(F=\mathbb Q\) and \[X=\mathbb P^1\setminus\{1/3,\infty\},\quad x=1,\quad
 f(z)=\frac{27}{4}z(z-1)^2 .\] This is a smooth normal quasi-projective curve with rational point \(x\). The map is quasi-finite on \(X\), finite étale above \(\mathbb P^1\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\), and sends \(x\) to zero. Let \(\mathcal L\) be the rank-one sign local system of the étale cover \(u^2=z-1/3\) of \(X\), and use the unit tangent at zero downstairs. For the quadratic character \(\chi_d\) of \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt d)/\mathbb Q\), the stalk \(\mathcal L_x\) is \(\chi_6\).

There are two ramified branches at \(z=1\) and one unramified branch at \(z=0\). Since \[f(1+h)=\frac{27}{4}h^2+\frac{27}{4}h^3,\] the ramified branches require \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)\). Their Galois module is \(\chi_6\otimes(1\oplus\chi_3)=\chi_6\oplus\chi_2\). The third branch contributes \(\chi_{-3}\). Thus \[(f_*\mathcal L)_{0_v}
     =\chi_6\oplus\chi_2\oplus\chi_{-3}.\] The characters are distinct, so the \(G_\mathbb Q\)-equivariant image of \(\mathcal L_x\) is unique. In branch coordinates it is the line spanned by \(e_1+e_2\), supported on both ramified branches.

The cubic has geometric permutation monodromy \(S_3\): it is connected of degree three and its discriminant \(-19683\,t(t-1)/16\) is not a square in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}(t)\). The subgroup \(H\) for the first branch maps onto its point stabilizer and hence contains an element inducing \((23)\). This sends the support \(\{1,2\}\) to \(\{1,3\}\). Possible Kummer signs do not change the support. The unique Galois-equivariant line is therefore not \(H\)-stable.

Counterevidence, impact, and boundary. A single branch gives an \(H\)-stable stalk that is not Galois-stable; the diagonal over the ramified branches is Galois-stable but not \(H\)-stable. The printed endomorphism-space argument needs both. This false intermediate assertion invalidates a central derivation, warranting Major severity. It does not disprove Proposition 3.3 or Theorem 1.2.

A replacement is available after the independent Artin argument in Section 3. Fix the target tangent \(v\) and use the two tangents \(v_1,v_2\) of Proposition 4.1. After a finite extension \(K/F\) a tangent above \(v_1\) exists. The valid finite-index argument gives \(W\twoheadrightarrow V|_{G_K}\) with \(W\) a finite-dimensional \(G_K\)-stable subspace of the function ring at \(v_1\). Its \(G_F\)-span \(W'\) is finite-dimensional, and \[\operatorname{Ind}_{G_K}^{G_F}W
       \subset W'\otimes\mathbb Q_p[G_F/G_K]
       \quad\hbox{has a quotient }V .\] The Artin factor occurs at \(v_2\); Proposition 4.1 then realizes \(V\) at \(v\). This uses neither a simultaneous stalk inclusion nor membership at every \(K\)-rational tangent. Finite-index induction of geometrically semisimple representations gives the same repair for the proreductive version.
## P2. Full K3 cohomology is reducible (Major)
Location. Corollary 9.7, p. 19, final paragraph; compare Proposition 9.6 and the cited Huybrechts Corollary 6.4.7.

In polarized K3 moduli the polarization class is a nonzero invariant line in the rank-22 system \(R^2\pi_*\mathbb Q_p(1)\). Its primitive orthogonal complement has rank 21. A smooth polarized quartic, for example, has the nonzero hyperplane class of square four. The full representation is therefore reducible. The cited monodromy result fixes this class and concerns the primitive part, as the public Huybrechts draft, PDF p. 118, explicitly states.

Proposition 9.6 cannot be applied to the full \(H^2\) as printed. Knowing the endomorphisms of the primitive part alone does not supply the off-diagonal terms in \(\operatorname{End}(H^2)\). This invalidates the stated proof of a substantive K3 application and is Major, although the conclusion has the following repair.

After the repaired proreductive bridge in P1, write \[H^2(X_{\overline F},\mathbb Q_p)(1)=\mathbb Q_p\oplus M,\qquad \dim M=21 .\] The primitive variation is geometrically absolutely irreducible, so \(\operatorname{End}(M)\in\mathcal C_F^{\mathrm{red}}\). The polarization identifies \(M^\vee\simeq M\). Pass to a finite extension killing the orthogonal determinant character. Then \[\Lambda^2M\ \text{is a subquotient of }\operatorname{End}(M),\qquad
 (\Lambda^2M)^{\otimes10}\twoheadrightarrow
 \Lambda^{20}M\simeq M^\vee\otimes\det M\simeq M .\] Tensor and subquotient closure give \(M\in\mathcal C_F^{\mathrm{red}}\). Hence \[\operatorname{End}(\mathbb Q_p\oplus M)=\mathbb Q_p\oplus M\oplus M\oplus\operatorname{End}(M)\] is in that class, and finite-extension descent finishes. This supplies the missing terms without presuming arbitrary dual or Tate closure of \(\mathcal C_F^{\mathrm{red}}\). The conclusion is not refuted.
## P3. A level structure does not give a principal polarization (Major)
Location. The abelian-variety paragraph of Corollary 9.7, p. 19. Choosing a basis of \(A[3]\) is said to give a point corresponding to \(A\) in the principally polarized moduli space.

An explicit obstruction is obtained from \(J=\operatorname{Jac}(y^2=x^5-x-1)\). The polynomial is irreducible modulo 3 and modulo 2 factors as \[(x^2+x+1)(x^3+x^2+1).\] Its Galois group is a transitive degree-five group containing an element of cycle type \((2)(3)\), hence a transposition. A primitive group containing a transposition is \(S_5\). Zarhin’s theorem for this characteristic-zero hyperelliptic Jacobian gives \(\operatorname{End}(J_{\overline{\mathbb Q}})=\mathbb Z\), and thus \(\operatorname{NS}(J_{\overline{\mathbb Q}})=\mathbb Z[\Theta]\).

Choose a subgroup \(H\) generated by a nonzero point of \(J[2]\), let \(q:J\to A=J/H\), and extend the number field so that \(H\) and a full level-three structure of \(A\) are defined. If \(A\) had a principal polarization \(\lambda\), its pullback would be \(n\Theta\) for a positive integer \(n\). On the surface \(J\) its Euler characteristic would be both \[\chi(q^*\lambda)=\deg(q)\chi(\lambda)=2
       \quad\hbox{and}\quad \chi(n\Theta)=n^2,\] a contradiction. No further extension changes this geometric obstruction. A level-three basis does not make this \(A\) principally polarized.

This missing reduction occurs at the realization step of the abelian-variety assertion in Corollary 9.7. The stated arbitrary abelian variety need not define a point of the principally polarized moduli space, even after a finite extension. Consequently, the displayed application of Proposition 9.6 does not establish that assertion as written. The defect is Major for this derivation.

Passing over a finite extension to a principally polarized abelian variety isogenous to \(A\), and choosing a symplectic level structure there, repairs the argument because rational \(H^1\) is invariant under isogeny. The corollary itself is not refuted.
## P4. Nonnormal finite-index subgroups have no quotient group (Minor)

Location. Remark 2.3, p. 5. Lemma 2.2 assumes only that \(\Gamma_1\) is open of finite index, but the remark calls \(\Gamma/\Gamma_1\) a constant finite group scheme. For the discrete finite group \(S_3\) and \(\Gamma_1=\langle(12)\rangle\), all hypotheses hold and the index is three, while \(\Gamma_1\) is not normal. It cannot be the kernel of a quotient group homomorphism. The homogeneous quotient is a constant finite scheme. Use scheme, or add normality for the group statement. The coordinate restriction lemma and its applications survive.
## P5. Incorrect descent of the cyclic proalgebraic completion (Minor)
Location. Example 2.4, pp. 5–6, the \(\mathbb Q_p\)-product \(\mathbb G_a\times H_0\times T_0\) and the module \(\widehat{\mathbb Z}(1)\) assigned to \(H_0\).

Every finite quotient of the completion of the discrete group \(\mathbb Z\) is generated by the rational image of \(1\); its points are therefore rational. The maximal profinite quotient is constant \(\widehat{\mathbb Z}\), not its cyclotomic twist. A quotient \(\mathbb Z/n\) with nontrivial local cyclotomic action modulo \(n\) distinguishes these group schemes.

Even after correcting the twist, the asserted rational product does not follow. The character sequence \[0\longrightarrow\mu_\infty\longrightarrow
 \overline{\mathbb Q}_p^\times\longrightarrow
 \overline{\mathbb Q}_p^\times/\mu_\infty\longrightarrow0\] has no \(G_{\mathbb Q_p}\)-equivariant splitting. The class \([p^{1/n}]\) is Galois-fixed for every \(n>1\), because its conjugates differ by roots of unity. An equivariant section would send it to an element of \(\mathbb Q_p^\times\) with normalized valuation \(1/n\), impossible. An abstract splitting over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_p\) need not descend.

The safe rational description uses the additive factor and the multiplicative-type group with character module \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_p^\times\) and its actual Galois action. This illustrative description is not needed by the subsequent matrix-coefficient proof, which explains the limited severity.
## P6. Finitely many roots of unity do not force the claimed local-finiteness criterion (Minor)

Location. Example 2.6, p. 7. Take the allowed characteristic-zero field \(K=\mathbb R\), which has only two roots of unity, and \(X=\mathbb G_m\), \(x=1\). Its absolute Galois group has order two, so every function in the geometric proalgebraic coordinate ring has a finite-dimensional Galois orbit.

The continuous character \[\widehat{\mathbb Z}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb Z_p
 \longrightarrow\mathbb Q_p^\times,\qquad
 t\longmapsto(1+p)^t\] has infinite image; for \(p=2\) use \(5^t\). It is a regular matrix coefficient. Complex conjugation interchanges this function with its inverse. It cannot factor through \(\mathbb G_a\times\widehat{\mathbb Z}\): a group-like function factoring there is an algebraic character, trivial on \(\mathbb G_a\) and of finite image on the profinite factor. This contradicts the infinite image.

The printed equivalence is therefore false under its stated field hypothesis. An infinite \(p\)-adic cyclotomic image is the relevant additional condition. Number fields satisfy it, so this example does not contradict the universality theorem.
## P7. Faithfulness is insufficient for one high tensor power (Major)

Location. Lemma 5.1, p. 12. The one-dimensional sign representation of \(C_2\) is faithful, but every tensor power is one-dimensional and cannot contain the two-dimensional regular representation. This meets the printed finite-group and characteristic-zero hypotheses.

The failure occurs in the actual proof: the representations \(W_i\) are only required to be faithful and of bounded dimension, and the printed construction does not require a trivial summand to be retained. The sign representation meets these conditions and can occur as a subrepresentation of the faithful permutation module. The invalid tensor-power assertion supplies the regular representation used to conclude Lemma 5.1. That lemma is used for finite-extension descent in Corollary 5.2 and explicitly as the dimension-zero base case of Theorem 1.2 on p. 15. This is a Major defect in the core derivation.

Retaining a trivial summand allows tensor degrees to be padded. The explicit permutation construction in Section 3 below gives a bounded power containing the regular image representation. These repairs do not refute the Artin conclusion. The earlier p. 12 inference from an action kernel contained in \(G_K\) to a quotient with kernel exactly \(G_K\) is not justified by containment alone; Section 3 bypasses that proof obligation. No counterexample to the geometric Artin conclusion is claimed.
## P8. Arbitrary-field scope fails in characteristic \(p\) (Minor)
Location. Proposition 7.1, p. 14, including the finite-dimensionality claim for continuous cocycles. The preceding setup on p. 6 allows any base field.

Take \(K=\mathbb F_p\), \(X=\mathbb A^1_K\) with base point zero, and \(\mathcal L=\mathbb Q_p\). Let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_p\), \(A=W(k)\), and \(E=A[1/p]\), with Witt Frobenius \(\sigma\). Artin–Schreier–Witt theory gives an additive, Frobenius-equivariant map \[A\longrightarrow H^1_{\mathrm{cont}}(\pi_1(X_k,0),\mathbb Z_p),
           \qquad a\longmapsto[a[x]].\] Indeed the compatible finite-level classes lie in \(W_n(k[x])/(F-1)\) and define continuous characters. For a unit \(a\), the reduction is \(a_0x\), which is not \(b^p-b\): a nonconstant polynomial \(b\) gives degree divisible by \(p\), whereas \(a_0x\) has degree one. For any nonzero \(a\), divide by its finite power of \(p\) and use torsion-freeness of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(\pi_1,\mathbb Z_p)\). The map is therefore injective, and rationalization embeds \(E\) into \(H^1(X_k,\mathbb Q_p)\).

This subspace is not locally finite for Frobenius. For \(n\ge1\) set \[D_n(a)=\det\bigl(\sigma^{i+j}a\bigr)_{0\le i,j<n}.\] An integral normal-basis element \(b\) of the degree-\(n\) unramified extension of \(\mathbb Q_p\) has \(D_n(b)\ne0\). Thus \(D_n(a+tb)\), as a polynomial in \(t\in\mathbb Q_p\), has nonzero leading coefficient. The set \(D_n\ne0\) is open and dense in the complete metric ring \(A\). Baire’s theorem supplies an \(a\) for which every \(D_n(a)\) is nonzero. Any finite \(\mathbb Q_p\)-linear relation among its Frobenius iterates would force one of these determinants to vanish. Its orbit therefore spans an infinite-dimensional space. The inverse-Frobenius convention gives the same conclusion.

The right-hand side of Proposition 7.1, with this trivial stalk, is locally finite by definition, and all its subquotients are locally finite. It cannot have the displayed \(H^1\) as a subquotient. This is a counterexample to the proposition under all its written hypotheses, not merely to finite-dimensionality in the proof. Require the needed finiteness and local-finiteness assumptions, in particular the characteristic-zero setting of Section 8, or an appropriate invertible-coefficient setting. The actual number-field uses avoid the counterexample; the defect is in the added arbitrary-field generality.
## P9. Removing one fibre need not remove ramification (Minor)

Location. Lemma 10.1(ii), p. 20. Over \(\mathbb Q\) take \(D=C=\mathbb P^1\), \(f(t)=t^2\), \(x=1\), and a nonzero tangent at \(x\). The map is finite surjective and even unramified at \(x\). Nevertheless \[D\setminus f^{-1}(f(x))=\mathbb P^1\setminus\{-1,1\}\simeq\mathbb G_m,
 \qquad C\setminus\{f(x)\}\simeq\mathbb A^1.\] The asserted map on geometric fundamental groups is \(\widehat{\mathbb Z}\to1\), which is not injective; the arithmetic map cannot be injective either. Require the restricted map to be finite étale, or delete all branch values and their preimages. The Belyi applications already delete \(\{0,1,\infty\}\), so their finite-index step is unaffected. Existence of a compatible tangent is a local fact and does not establish the claimed global open-subgroup property.
# A noncircular Artin replacement
This argument supplies the independent input needed in P1, without invoking Proposition 3.3 or Corollary 3.4.

Fix a finite Galois extension \(K/F\) with group \(G\). Choose an elliptic curve over \(K\) whose \(j\)-invariant generates \(K\) over \(\mathbb Q\), and a Belyi cover over \(K\). Let \(H\) be its open subgroup in the geometric free profinite group \(\Gamma\) of rank two. Preserving the conjugacy class of \(H\) gives an isomorphism of the proper curves and fixes that \(j\)-invariant; hence its stabilizer in \(G_F\) is \(G_K\).

There are finitely many open subgroups of each bounded index in \(\Gamma\). Intersect those of index at most \([\Gamma:H]\) to obtain a characteristic open subgroup \(N\subset H\). At each tangent \(0_w\) put \(S_w=\Gamma_w/N_w\). These have the same abstract finite group \(S\), with different possible Galois actions. The image \(A_w\subset\operatorname{Aut}(S_w)\) maps onto \(G\): an element in the action kernel fixes \(H\) and hence belongs to \(G_K\). The permutation module \(W_w=\mathbb Q[S_w]\) is a subspace of locally constant functions at \(0_w\) and has a trivial line.

The explicit construction in Lemma 4.2 permits child tangents \[w_1=\frac4{27}w,\qquad w_2=\frac13w .\] Here \(f'(0)=27/4\) and \(h(z)=-3z/(z-4/3)\) maps \((0,1/3,4/3)\) to \((0,1,\infty)\) with \(h'(0)=9/4\). At depth \(n\) in the iterated binary construction, the tangent \((4/27)^i(1/3)^{n-i}w\) occurs \(\binom ni\) times.

The tensor construction can be made an actual injection on locally constant rational functions. Pullback along the surjective product map is injective, and extension by zero from the \(G_F\)-stable open subgroup is an equivariant splitting of restriction. Thus the tensor of all leaf modules embeds in the locally constant functions at the root.

Choose a repeated leaf with multiplicity \(m\ge |S|\). In \(W_w^{\otimes m}=\mathbb Q[S_w^m]\), a tuple whose first \(|S|\) entries enumerate \(S_w\) has trivial \(A_w\)-stabilizer. Its orbit spans the regular representation of \(A_w\), which contains the inflated regular representation of \(G\). Arbitrary tails give \(|S|^{m-|S|}\) distinct free orbits. Taking invariant constant lines in all other leaf factors therefore produces arbitrarily many regular copies at the root as \(m\) increases. Every finite-image rational representation embeds in a finite sum of regular copies. This proves the stronger locally constant embedding claimed in Proposition 1.1, as well as Lemma 5.1 after extending coefficients. Locally constant functions lie in the proreductive ring too. Only Belyi’s theorem, finite generation, and the tensor part of Lemma 4.2/Proposition 4.1 enter; there is no circular use of P1.
# Further proof audit
## Finite translates, finite index, and direct sums

Lemmas 2.1–2.2 and 2.7–2.9 were checked using representative functions, finite-dimensional translation orbits, and finite-index induction. The span \(\mathcal F(\mathcal L)\) of monodromy operators must be distinguished from its dual space of functions.

For direct sums in Proposition 4.1, the quotients \(\Gamma_w\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb Z/2^m(1)\) have \(m+1\) distinct additive orders. Their order indicators are independent Galois-fixed locally constant functions. Hence there are arbitrarily large trivial subrepresentations at a fixed tangent. Given a finite subrepresentation \(A\) yielding \(V\), choose a fixed line disjoint from \(A\); \(A\oplus\mathbb Q_p\) yields \(V\oplus\mathbb Q_p\). This supplies the step without relying merely on large trivial subquotients.
## The Tate character and semisimple induction

In the version-3 proof of Lemma 6.2, nonzero unipotent Legendre monodromy gives an invariant line \(\chi_1\) and quotient \(\chi_1(-1)\). The operators from quotient to invariant line form \(\mathbb Q_p(1)\subset\operatorname{End}(\mathcal L_{0_v})\). Geometric absolute irreducibility embeds these coefficients in the function ring. The remaining CM/abelian-character classification is the cited Fontaine–Mazur input, not an independently reproved theorem here.

On p. 15 the induction supplies \(B^{\mathrm{ss}}\) for \(B=(R^j\pi_*\mathbb Q_p)_x\), but the last paragraph uses \(B\) itself and concludes membership of the full \(H^1\). No counterexample to this stronger membership is claimed. The stated semisimple goal follows by choosing a finite-dimensional coefficient submodule \(A_0\) supporting the finite-dimensional quotient in Proposition 7.1, and filtering \(A_0\), \(B\), and \(A_0\otimes B\) by composition series. Their constituents occur in tensor products of constituents. Subquotient, tensor, and direct-sum closure give the semisimplification of \(H^1\), precisely what Leray needs.

With this formulation, the reductions through cohomological descent, smooth schemes, Gysin/purity, finite étale trace splittings, and an alteration to a proper smooth fibration over an open of \(\mathbb P^1\) were checked. Artin vanishing on the affine base leaves \(H^0\) and \(H^1\). The underlying descent, alteration, and purity theorems remain identified foundational dependencies; their complete source literature has not been independently reproved.
## Weights and proreductive coefficients

The apparent sign discrepancy in Proposition 9.1 is not an error: nonpositive weights on \(\mathcal F(\mathcal L)\) become nonnegative weights on its dual function space. The \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_p\) coefficient field in Lemma 9.5 and absolute irreducibility in the \(\mathbb Q_p\) clause of Proposition 9.6 were checked on actual images. Text extraction must not erase them. Corollary 9.7 itself is stated with \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_p\) coefficients. The polarization arguments in P2–P3 were written over \(\mathbb Q_p\) and remain valid after that coefficient extension.

The companion Petrov manuscript arXiv:2012.13372v3, PDF pp. 17–18, includes tangential base points in the de Rham and almost-everywhere-unramified input. Its exact retrieved version is recorded separately, without equating it to the later Duke version. Lemma 9.3 is a conditional Fontaine–Mazur equivalence, not a proof of that conjecture. The full Deligne, Lafforgue, and Fontaine–Mazur source proofs were not independently reconstructed in this review.

In Lemma 10.1(i), an étale cover extending over \(F[[t]]\) is constant, not necessarily a trivial disjoint union over \(F\): \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)[[t]]\) illustrates this. The geometric-fibre comparison used there is correct, so this wording is not counted as another scientific defect.

analysis: Location. Corollary 9.7, p. 19, final paragraph; compare Proposition 9.6 and the cited Huybrechts Corollary 6.4.7.

In polarized K3 moduli the polarization class is a nonzero invariant line in the rank-22 system \(R^2\pi_*\mathbb Q_p(1)\). Its primitive orthogonal complement has rank 21. A smooth polarized quartic, for example, has the nonzero hyperplane class of square four. The full representation is therefore reducible. The cited monodromy result fixes this class and concerns the primitive part, as the public Huybrechts draft, PDF p. 118, explicitly states.

Proposition 9.6 cannot be applied to the full \(H^2\) as printed. Knowing the endomorphisms of the primitive part alone does not supply the off-diagonal terms in \(\operatorname{End}(H^2)\). This invalidates the stated proof of a substantive K3 application and is Major, although the conclusion has the following repair.

After the repaired proreductive bridge in P1, write \[H^2(X_{\overline F},\mathbb Q_p)(1)=\mathbb Q_p\oplus M,\qquad \dim M=21 .\] The primitive variation is geometrically absolutely irreducible, so \(\operatorname{End}(M)\in\mathcal C_F^{\mathrm{red}}\). The polarization identifies \(M^\vee\simeq M\). Pass to a finite extension killing the orthogonal determinant character. Then \[\Lambda^2M\ \text{is a subquotient of }\operatorname{End}(M),\qquad
 (\Lambda^2M)^{\otimes10}\twoheadrightarrow
 \Lambda^{20}M\simeq M^\vee\otimes\det M\simeq M .\] Tensor and subquotient closure give \(M\in\mathcal C_F^{\mathrm{red}}\). Hence \[\operatorname{End}(\mathbb Q_p\oplus M)=\mathbb Q_p\oplus M\oplus M\oplus\operatorname{End}(M)\] is in that class, and finite-extension descent finishes. This supplies the missing terms without presuming arbitrary dual or Tate closure of \(\mathcal C_F^{\mathrm{red}}\). The conclusion is not refuted.

claim: Kind: statement or proof step

J=Jac(y²=x⁵−x−1), genus2 overQ. Mod3irreducible;mod2irreddegrees2+3⇒GalS5. ZarhinThm2.1/Ex2.2⇒EndJbar=Z, NSJbar=ZTheta. H generatedbynonzero2torsion, A=J/H; finiteFdefinesH andA[3]basis.
analysis: Location. The abelian-variety paragraph of Corollary 9.7, p. 19. Choosing a basis of \(A[3]\) is said to give a point corresponding to \(A\) in the principally polarized moduli space.

An explicit obstruction is obtained from \(J=\operatorname{Jac}(y^2=x^5-x-1)\). The polynomial is irreducible modulo 3 and modulo 2 factors as \[(x^2+x+1)(x^3+x^2+1).\] Its Galois group is a transitive degree-five group containing an element of cycle type \((2)(3)\), hence a transposition. A primitive group containing a transposition is \(S_5\). Zarhin’s theorem for this characteristic-zero hyperelliptic Jacobian gives \(\operatorname{End}(J_{\overline{\mathbb Q}})=\mathbb Z\), and thus \(\operatorname{NS}(J_{\overline{\mathbb Q}})=\mathbb Z[\Theta]\).

Choose a subgroup \(H\) generated by a nonzero point of \(J[2]\), let \(q:J\to A=J/H\), and extend the number field so that \(H\) and a full level-three structure of \(A\) are defined. If \(A\) had a principal polarization \(\lambda\), its pullback would be \(n\Theta\) for a positive integer \(n\). On the surface \(J\) its Euler characteristic would be both \[\chi(q^*\lambda)=\deg(q)\chi(\lambda)=2
       \quad\hbox{and}\quad \chi(n\Theta)=n^2,\] a contradiction. No further extension changes this geometric obstruction. A level-three basis does not make this \(A\) principally polarized.

This missing reduction occurs at the realization step of the abelian-variety assertion in Corollary 9.7. The stated arbitrary abelian variety need not define a point of the principally polarized moduli space, even after a finite extension. Consequently, the displayed application of Proposition 9.6 does not establish that assertion as written. The defect is Major for this derivation.

Passing over a finite extension to a principally polarized abelian variety isogenous to \(A\), and choosing a symplectic level structure there, repairs the argument because rational \(H^1\) is invariant under isogeny. The corollary itself is not refuted.
result: Impact: The nonexistent principally polarized moduli point is the actual realization step of Corollary 9.7 for arbitrary abelian varieties, needed to apply Proposition 9.6. A geometric non-principal-polarizability obstruction survives every finite extension. This is an invalid derivation of a substantive application; the available isogeny reduction does not lower its severity or refute the final cohomological conclusion.

analysis: Location. Example 2.4, pp. 5–6, the \(\mathbb Q_p\)-product \(\mathbb G_a\times H_0\times T_0\) and the module \(\widehat{\mathbb Z}(1)\) assigned to \(H_0\).

Every finite quotient of the completion of the discrete group \(\mathbb Z\) is generated by the rational image of \(1\); its points are therefore rational. The maximal profinite quotient is constant \(\widehat{\mathbb Z}\), not its cyclotomic twist. A quotient \(\mathbb Z/n\) with nontrivial local cyclotomic action modulo \(n\) distinguishes these group schemes.

Even after correcting the twist, the asserted rational product does not follow. The character sequence \[0\longrightarrow\mu_\infty\longrightarrow
 \overline{\mathbb Q}_p^\times\longrightarrow
 \overline{\mathbb Q}_p^\times/\mu_\infty\longrightarrow0\] has no \(G_{\mathbb Q_p}\)-equivariant splitting. The class \([p^{1/n}]\) is Galois-fixed for every \(n>1\), because its conjugates differ by roots of unity. An equivariant section would send it to an element of \(\mathbb Q_p^\times\) with normalized valuation \(1/n\), impossible. An abstract splitting over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_p\) need not descend.

The safe rational description uses the additive factor and the multiplicative-type group with character module \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_p^\times\) and its actual Galois action. This illustrative description is not needed by the subsequent matrix-coefficient proof, which explains the limited severity.

analysis: Location. Example 2.6, p. 7. Take the allowed characteristic-zero field \(K=\mathbb R\), which has only two roots of unity, and \(X=\mathbb G_m\), \(x=1\). Its absolute Galois group has order two, so every function in the geometric proalgebraic coordinate ring has a finite-dimensional Galois orbit.

The continuous character \[\widehat{\mathbb Z}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb Z_p
 \longrightarrow\mathbb Q_p^\times,\qquad
 t\longmapsto(1+p)^t\] has infinite image; for \(p=2\) use \(5^t\). It is a regular matrix coefficient. Complex conjugation interchanges this function with its inverse. It cannot factor through \(\mathbb G_a\times\widehat{\mathbb Z}\): a group-like function factoring there is an algebraic character, trivial on \(\mathbb G_a\) and of finite image on the profinite factor. problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Proposition7.1 arbitrary-field scope fails in characteristic p
claim: Kind: statement or proof step
Location: Proposition7.1 p14; arbitraryfieldsetup p6

analysis: Location. Proposition 7.1, p. 14, including the finite-dimensionality claim for continuous cocycles. The preceding setup on p. 6 allows any base field.

Take \(K=\mathbb F_p\), \(X=\mathbb A^1_K\) with base point zero, and \(\mathcal L=\mathbb Q_p\). Let \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_p\), \(A=W(k)\), and \(E=A[1/p]\), with Witt Frobenius \(\sigma\). Artin–Schreier–Witt theory gives an additive, Frobenius-equivariant map \[A\longrightarrow H^1_{\mathrm{cont}}(\pi_1(X_k,0),\mathbb Z_p),
           \qquad a\longmapsto[a[x]].\] Indeed the compatible finite-level classes lie in \(W_n(k[x])/(F-1)\) and define continuous characters. For a unit \(a\), the reduction is \(a_0x\), which is not \(b^p-b\): a nonconstant polynomial \(b\) gives degree divisible by \(p\), whereas \(a_0x\) has degree one. For any nonzero \(a\), divide by its finite power of \(p\) and use torsion-freeness of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(\pi_1,\mathbb Z_p)\). The map is therefore injective, and rationalization embeds \(E\) into \(H^1(X_k,\mathbb Q_p)\).

This subspace is not locally finite for Frobenius. For \(n\ge1\) set \[D_n(a)=\det\bigl(\sigma^{i+j}a\bigr)_{0\le i,j<n}.\] An integral normal-basis element \(b\) of the degree-\(n\) unramified extension of \(\mathbb Q_p\) has \(D_n(b)\ne0\). Thus \(D_n(a+tb)\), as a polynomial in \(t\in\mathbb Q_p\), has nonzero leading coefficient. The set \(D_n\ne0\) is open and dense in the complete metric ring \(A\). Baire’s theorem supplies an \(a\) for which every \(D_n(a)\) is nonzero. Any finite \(\mathbb Q_p\)-linear relation among its Frobenius iterates would force one of these determinants to vanish. Its orbit therefore spans an infinite-dimensional space. The inverse-Frobenius convention gives the same conclusion.

The right-hand side of Proposition 7.1, with this trivial stalk, is locally finite by definition, and all its subquotients are locally finite. It cannot have the displayed \(H^1\) as a subquotient. This is a counterexample to the proposition under all its written hypotheses, not merely to finite-dimensionality in the proof. Require the needed finiteness and local-finiteness assumptions, in particular the characteristic-zero setting of Section 8, or an appropriate invertible-coefficient setting. The actual number-field uses avoid the counterexample; the defect is in the added arbitrary-field generality.

report: Abstract: The frozen author manuscript arXiv:2306.05008v2 is examined. One Major defect and seven Minor corrections are established. The Major defect is an empty affine minimization class at the polynomial comparison step used for the explicit two-pole coefficients. A cutoff repairs the missing variational definition; the actual Fourier coefficients and principal eigenvalue expansion are not refuted. The remaining corrections concern scalar branches, a zero-order profile, boundary estimates, minimization, rescaled tests, Fourier normalization, and complex phase. This assessment concerns only the frozen author version. The scientific decision remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Variational Domains and Magnetic Spectral Asymptotics
# Source identity and scope

Frozen identifier: M25-0259. Authors: Veronica Felli, Benedetta Noris, Roberto Ognibene, and Giovanni Siclari. Article: Quantitative spectral stability for Aharonov–Bohm operators with many coalescing poles. The frozen DOI is
https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1632.

Its arXiv version is v2, submitted on 9 December 2023 at 22:04:09 UTC. The first-page stamp says 9 December 2023, while the internal revision date is 7 December 2023; these different date fields are retained. The publisher records submission on 3 June 2023, acceptance on 18 April 2024, and online publication on 21 March 2025. Its subscription PDF was not acquired. All locations below refer to the frozen author PDF, not to an assumed pagination or correction status of the journal article. The frozen 2025 membership, identifier, and DOI are unchanged.

The setting includes a bounded simply connected planar domain containing the collision point, half-integer magnetic circulations, fixed distinct ray directions, and a simple limiting eigenvalue for the principal asymptotic theorems. The reduction uses real functions with opposite traces across the cracks. In particular, the two-pole closed formulas require the equal-distance, opposite-pole configuration (2.36). These hypotheses are retained throughout this review.
# Confirmed corrections
## P1. The explicit real scalar branch is not smooth on the asserted domain (Minor)
Location. Equation (2.8), p. 7; the angle choices and equation (3.5), p. 14.

Witness. Take \(\Omega=D_1\), \(k_1=0\), \(k_2=2\), equal radii \(r=1/8\), and \[(\alpha^1,\alpha^2,\alpha^3,\alpha^4)
       =(0,-\pi/2,\pi,\pi/2).\] This satisfies the stated indexing and opposite-direction requirements. The two horizontal angles, with indices \(1,3\), have the same positive sign in (3.5). At \(x=(-2r\varepsilon,0)\), which lies outside the finite horizontal segment and outside the vertical segment, both angle functions jump by \(2\pi\) in the same direction. The vertical angles are smooth there. Consequently \(\Theta_\varepsilon\) has a jump of magnitude \(2\pi\) at a point of \(\mathbb R^2\setminus\Gamma_\varepsilon\) and does not satisfy the first assertion of (2.8).

Counterevidence and effect. The jump disappears in \(e^{i\Theta_\varepsilon}\). On the actual crack segments the exponential has the required sign change, and its local logarithmic derivative gives the prescribed magnetic potential. Thus this example does not invalidate the circle-valued gauge or the spectral equivalence. There is also no separate-pair period obstruction: the segments form a connected cross, so a loop avoiding the cross cannot isolate one entire pair while excluding the other.

Repair boundary. Formulate the gauge directly as a circle-valued function with the appropriate local derivatives, or correct the scalar branch by multiples of \(2\pi\). The literal formula should not simultaneously be retained as a globally smooth real function on the larger claimed domain.
## P2. The even-case profile omits the nonvanishing case (Minor)
Location. Proposition 3.7 and (3.18), p. 17.

Witness. Set \(k_1=0\), \(k_2=1\), \(\Omega=D_1\), and take any allowed small opposite pair of poles. The limiting problem is the ordinary Dirichlet Laplacian. Its positive normalized first eigenfunction is \[v(x)=cJ_0(j_{0,1}|x|),\qquad c>0,\] and the first eigenvalue is simple. Since \(v(0)=c\ne0\), its vanishing order is \(m=0\). Formula (3.18) then gives the zero function on the right, whereas the left converges to \(c\). The interval containing \(\alpha_0\) also contains division by zero. Choosing \(m\ge1\) cannot rescue the assertion, since \(\varepsilon^{-m}v(\varepsilon\,\cdot)\) diverges.

Counterevidence, effect, and repair. The manuscript explicitly treats \(m=0\) separately in (3.19), Propositions 4.1 and 4.3, and the discussion preceding (2.38). Thus the nonvanishing case was intended and is not excluded by a hidden assumption. State its leading profile as a nonzero constant times the gauge sign function; reserve the sine profile and \(\alpha_0\) for \(m\ge1\). The later logarithmic energy bound does not require the erroneous zero sine profile. No claimed nonzero-order two-pole coefficient is refuted by this example.

## P4. Minimization on a half-line is replaced by minimization on the whole line (Minor)
Location. The last displayed identity in the proof of Proposition 6.5, p. 26, after (6.12).

For fixed nonzero \(w\), write the displayed quadratic as \(At^2/2+Bt+C\), with \(A=\int|\nabla w|^2>0\). The asserted value \(C-B^2/(2A)\) is the minimum over \(t\in\mathbb R\), but the stated domain is \(t\ge0\). For \(B>0\) the actual infimum is \(C\).

Witness in the stated spaces. Choose a smooth bump \(w\) supported in a ball inside \(D_\varepsilon\) and away from all cracks, where \(v_0\) has a fixed nonzero sign, and give \(w\) the same sign. Then \(w\in\widetilde{\mathcal H}_\varepsilon\), \(\eta_\varepsilon=1\) on its support, and \(L_\varepsilon(w)=0\). The interior eigenvalue equation gives \[B=\int\nabla w\cdot\nabla v_0
       =\lambda_0\int wv_0>0 .\] This is a counterexample with an admissible direction, not just an unrelated scalar quadratic.

Counterevidence, effect, and repair. The outer optimization includes both \(w\) and \(-w\). Consequently the statement (6.11) remains correct: let \(t\) range over \(\mathbb R\) in the proof, or retain the one-sided minimum and then optimize over both signs. ## P5. Zero extension does not preserve the variational equation for every whole-plane test (Minor)
Location. Equation (6.20), p. 27, and its use in the proof of Proposition 6.7, p. 28.

The rescaled potential is supported in \(\Omega/\varepsilon\). The original weak equation (4.5) permits tests with the corresponding zero outer trace. It does not imply (6.20) for every \(w\in\widetilde{\mathcal H}\) on the plane.

Witness. Use the explicit simple half-flux rectangular model constructed under P8, with \(k_1=1\), \(k_2=0\), and the pole moving on the positive axis. Its real \(v_0\) is positive on a short positive-axis interval. The affine trace condition \(T(V_\varepsilon)=2v_0\) there forces \(V_\varepsilon\ne0\). If (6.20) held for all the stated tests, then in particular the zero extension of \(\widetilde V_\varepsilon\) would be weakly harmonic against every \(C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2\setminus\Gamma_1)\) test: the right side vanishes for these tests. The slit plane is connected. A compactly supported harmonic function there vanishes identically, by interior regularity and unique continuation from its exterior zero set. This contradicts the nonzero affine trace. Thus at least one permitted whole-plane test fails the asserted equality.

Counterevidence and effect. For each fixed compactly supported test, its support is inside \(\Omega/\varepsilon\) once \(\varepsilon\) is sufficiently small. Use those tests first, pass to the limit, and only then use the density from Proposition 6.3. The energy test \(\widetilde V_\varepsilon-\eta\widetilde V_{0,\varepsilon}\) also has valid outer trace for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\). These observations provide the limiting variational equation and strong energy convergence actually needed for Theorem 2.2.

Repair boundary. Restrict the finite-\(\varepsilon\) test space before taking the limit. Also replace the complement of \(\Omega\) immediately after (6.18) by the complement of \(\Omega/\varepsilon\). A zero extension generally introduces an outer boundary flux; it is not a solution on the whole plane at fixed \(\varepsilon\).
## P6. The polynomial comparison functions are outside the defined affine domain (Major)
Location. The assumption \(h\in H_0^1(\Lambda)\) and (7.1), pp. 34–35; the uses \(h=P_m\) and \(h=T_m\) in Propositions 7.2, 7.5, and 7.6, pp. 35–40.

Witness. Take \(P_1(x)=x_1\) and a disk or one of the ellipses \(E_\varepsilon(L)\) containing the segment. If \(V\in\mathcal H_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}\) and \(V-P_1\in\widetilde{\mathcal H}_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}\) as literally required, both have zero outer trace. Subtraction forces the outer trace of \(P_1\) to vanish, which it does not. The admissible set is empty. The same issue occurs for a nonzero homogeneous Taylor polynomial. In addition, an arbitrary \(L>0\) ellipse need not contain the fixed disk \(D_R\) required in the initial generic definition.

Counterevidence and effect. The differential problem (7.2) uses \(h\) only through its value and normal derivative on the crack, and its outer boundary condition concerns \(V\). This is the well-posed local problem used in the subsequent Fourier calculation, including (7.11) on p. 36. It does not retroactively make the earlier affine class for the unmodified polynomial nonempty or redefine its minimum. Propositions 7.2, 7.5 and 7.6 use that undefined variational object in the derivation of the explicit two-pole asymptotics. The failed identification is therefore a Major defect in this substantive proof chain. No error in the actual Fourier coefficients is inferred from the empty-class observation.

Repair boundary. Choose a smooth compactly supported \(\chi\) equal to one in a neighbourhood of the segment and use \(\chi P_m\) or \(\chi T_m\) in the affine constraint. The line functional and the solution of (7.2) are unchanged. A common cutoff in the smaller comparison domain preserves the zero-extension inclusions used in the domain sandwich. For a fixed \(L>0\), containing the segment in the interior, rather than containing the originally fixed \(D_R\), suffices. These repairs give the same computed leading constants; the literal empty minimization problem must nevertheless be corrected.
## P7. The named Fourier basis has a different normalization (Minor)
Location. The final paragraph of p. 36, after the definitions of \(a_{j,\varepsilon}\) and \(b_{j,\varepsilon}\).

The manuscript calls \(a_{j,\varepsilon}(0)\) coefficients relative to the orthonormal basis containing \(\cos(j\eta)/\sqrt\pi\). Its integral definition instead uses the ordinary cosine coefficients \((1/\pi)\int f(\eta)\cos(j\eta)\,d\eta\). For \(m=1\), \(\ell_0=1\), the boundary function is \(\cos\eta\): the defined coefficient is \(a_{1,\varepsilon}(0)=1\), whereas its orthonormal coefficient is \(\sqrt\pi\).

Counterevidence, effect, and repair. Equations (7.14) and (7.15) consistently use the ordinary coefficients and the correct factors \(\pi\) and \(\pi/2\) in Parseval’s identity. There is no propagated error in (7.6). Correct the description of the basis, or rescale all coefficients consistently; the first option leaves the subsequent calculation unchanged.
## P8. The arbitrary complex phase is not tied to the earlier real profile (Minor)
Location. The fixed real \(v_0\) in (2.15), p. 8; the real profile (2.26), p. 9; Theorem 2.4 and (2.32)–(2.33), pp. 10–11; its proof, p. 34.

For a compatible choice \(u_0^*=e^{i\Theta_0}v_0\), let \(u_\varepsilon^*=e^{i\Theta_\varepsilon}v_\varepsilon\) have the required relative normalization. Replacing both by \(iu_0^*,iu_\varepsilon^*\) preserves their norms and the positive real inner product in (2.32). It multiplies the blow-up limit by \(i\), whereas the earlier fixed real \(\Psi_0\) and its real minimizer \(\widetilde V\) leave the right side of (2.33) unchanged. The profile \(\Psi_0-\widetilde V\) is nonzero: \(\Psi_0\) is homogeneous of positive degree and has infinite Dirichlet energy at infinity, while \(\widetilde V\) has finite Dirichlet energy. Therefore these two limits cannot agree.

A model satisfying simplicity. Let \(\Omega=(-1/4,1)\times(-1,1)\), with a half-flux pole at \(0\). In the negative-axis cut formulation, reflection in the horizontal axis splits the spectrum into two problems on \(Q=(-1/4,1)\times(0,1)\), with Dirichlet conditions on the outer sides and top. The even sector has Dirichlet bottom for \(x_1<0\) and Neumann bottom for \(x_1>0\) (DN); the odd sector has the reversed bottom conditions (ND). A DN test equal to \(\sin(\pi x_1)\cos(\pi x_2/2)\) on \(x_1>0\), and zero on \(x_1<0\), gives \(\lambda_{\rm DN}\le5\pi^2/4\). A Neumann cut at \(x_1=0\) in the ND problem gives separate rectangular first eigenvalues \(17\pi^2/4\) and \(5\pi^2/4\). Thus \(\lambda_{\rm ND}\ge5\pi^2/4\), with strict inequality: equality would make the left piece zero and the right proportional to \(\cos(\pi x_1/2)\sin(\pi x_2)\), contradicting matching \(H^1\) traces at the interface. The DN ground state is positive and simple, so the full half-flux ground eigenvalue is simple. Choose \(R=1/8\) and \(a^1=(1/16,0)\). Its even extension is positive along the short positive-axis segment, also supplying the model used in P5.

This example supplies a simple branch for every stated \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\), not just a small subsequence. For a moving pole at \(\delta=\varepsilon/16\), the DN bottom Dirichlet interval has length \(1/4+\delta\). Reflection of the ND problem in the vertical midline gives a DN problem with Dirichlet length \(1-\delta>1/4+\delta\). Strict ground-state monotonicity under enlarging the Dirichlet interval gives \(\lambda_{\rm DN}(\delta)<\lambda_{\rm ND}(\delta)\). Strictness follows from uniqueness and the impossibility of simultaneous zero value and normal derivative on an open boundary interval for a nonzero eigenfunction. The positive DN ground states have positive mutual inner product. Thus the family satisfies the normalization and simplicity hypotheses without numerical assumptions.

Counterevidence, effect, and repair. Remark 3.5 permits a real eigenbasis, and Section 4 explicitly chooses compatible real phases. The proof on p. 34 also redefines \(v_0\) from \(u_0\); these are strong evidence of the intended convention, but a relative inner product alone does not make that \(v_0\) real. Specify \(u_0=e^{i\Theta_0}v_0\) with the previously fixed real \(v_0\), or complexify and transform both profiles with the same phase. The eigenvalue formula and the energy norm in (2.34) are invariant under this change. The correction concerns the phase of the stated vector limit, not a new eigenvalue exponent or a different physical eigenspace.
# Checks of the principal arguments
## General spectral expansion

The real variational problem has a strictly coercive quadratic part on its affine trace class. Compactness can be checked by zero extension into a fixed disk cut into finitely many sectors; this also avoids assuming an unstated smooth outer boundary. The logarithmic cutoff at the collision point preserves opposite traces, and the weak-domain convergence and density argument give \[\|V_\varepsilon\|_{L^2}=o(\|V_\varepsilon\|_{\mathcal H_\varepsilon}).\] The latter argument only tests against functions vanishing near the shrinking segments before using density.
## Odd number of poles

The annular Hardy inequality relies on an odd number of sign changes: a zero-gradient function would be constant on each sector and the cyclic trace equations would force every constant to be zero. Summing annuli, and a local trace estimate, control both the weighted tail and the interior \(L^2\) norm. This establishes a genuine Hilbert norm and the cutoff density used for the limiting problem. With the restricted testing explained under P5, weak convergence identifies the unique limit; admissible energy tests then give strong convergence. The scaling is \(\varepsilon^{-m/2}\) for eigenfunctions and \(\varepsilon^{-m}\) for energy. Here \(m\) counts nodal half-lines and the actual vanishing order is \(m/2\); the phrase vanishing order \(m\) in Theorem 2.2 should be read in light of (2.21).

For poles on nodal rays the trace datum is zero and the nonzero linear functional makes the minimum negative. For bisector directions the linear functional vanishes and the nonzero affine trace makes the minimum positive. The rotation argument changes the data on a fixed space; dominated convergence and coercivity give the required continuity. It gives a zero leading coefficient between these configurations, but supplies no next nonzero exponent in that case. The manuscript itself acknowledges this limit.
## Two opposite poles: exact constants

The comparison problem is understood with the corrected admissibility in P6. Put \(a=\varepsilon r_1\) and \(T=\operatorname{arsinh}(L/a)\). Separation in elliptic coordinates gives the exact energy \[\int |\nabla V|^2
 =\pi a^{2m}\left\{
 \frac{\ell_0^2c_0^2}{2T}
 +\ell_0^2\sum_{j=1}^m j c_j^2\coth(jT)
 +\ell_1^2\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{d_j^2}{j}\tanh(jT)
 \right\}.\] The line functional on the solution equals \[L(V)=-\pi a^{2m}\ell_1^2
                 \sum_{j=1}^m\frac{d_j^2}{j}\tanh(jT).\] The cosine modes have prescribed value at \(\xi=0\) and zero value at \(\xi=T\); the sine modes have prescribed derivative at \(\xi=0\) and zero value at \(\xi=T\). These facts verify the signs independently of an asymptotic transcription. The zero mode contributes only the displayed \(1/T\) term.

For \(j>0\) of the same parity as \(m\), \[c_j=2^{1-m}\binom m{(m-j)/2},\qquad d_j=\frac jm c_j,\] and the other coefficients vanish. The identity \[\frac{m-2h}{m}\binom mh^2
   =\binom{m-1}h^2-\binom{m-1}{h-1}^2\] telescopes for \(0\le h\le\lfloor(m-1)/2\rfloor\) and proves (7.16); the formula for \(d_j\) proves (7.17). Own exact rational computations for \(1\le m\le32\) also checked the transcription. Those finite computations supplement, rather than replace, this proof for every \(m\).

The ellipse sandwich uses no reflection symmetry of \(\Omega\). Taylor’s remainder gives \(\|V_\varepsilon-V_{\varepsilon,T_m,\Omega}\|^2=O(\varepsilon^{2m+1})\). In (7.27), \(p>2\) implies \(1/p'>1/2\), so the remaining exponent \(2m-1/2+1/p'\) is strictly larger than \(2m\). The nodal case has \(\ell_0=0\), \(\ell_1=\pm m\beta\); the bisector case has \(\ell_1=0\), \(\ell_0=\pm\beta\). Combining the exact energy with the factor \(2\) in Theorem 2.1 recovers both coefficients \[\mp\frac{m\pi\beta^2 r_1^{2m}}{4^{m-1}}
       \binom{m-1}{\lfloor(m-1)/2\rfloor}^{\!2}.\] No error in these leading coefficients was found.

In the negative-axis cut formulation, reflection in the horizontal axis splits the spectrum into two problems on \(Q=(-1/4,1)\times(0,1)\), with Dirichlet conditions on the outer sides and top. The even sector has Dirichlet bottom for \(x_1<0\) and Neumann bottom for \(x_1>0\) (DN); the odd sector has the reversed bottom conditions (ND). A DN test equal to \(\sin(\pi x_1)\cos(\pi x_2/2)\) on \(x_1>0\), and zero on \(x_1<0\), gives \(\lambda_{\rm DN}\le5\pi^2/4\). A Neumann cut at \(x_1=0\) in the ND problem gives separate rectangular first eigenvalues \(17\pi^2/4\) and \(5\pi^2/4\). Thus \(\lambda_{\rm ND}\ge5\pi^2/4\), with strict inequality: equality would make the left piece zero and the right proportional to \(\cos(\pi x_1/2)\sin(\pi x_2)\), contradicting matching \(H^1\) traces at the interface. The DN ground state is positive and simple, so the full half-flux ground eigenvalue is simple. Choose \(R=1/8\) and \(a^1=(1/16,0)\). Its even extension is positive along the short positive-axis segment, also supplying the model used in P5.

This example supplies a simple branch for every stated \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\), not just a small subsequence. For a moving pole at \(\delta=\varepsilon/16\), the DN bottom Dirichlet interval has length \(1/4+\delta\). Reflection of the ND problem in the vertical midline gives a DN problem with Dirichlet length \(1-\delta>1/4+\delta\). Strict ground-state monotonicity under enlarging the Dirichlet interval gives \(\lambda_{\rm DN}(\delta)<\lambda_{\rm ND}(\delta)\). Strictness follows from uniqueness and the impossibility of simultaneous zero value and normal derivative on an open boundary interval for a nonzero eigenfunction. The positive DN ground states have positive mutual inner product. Thus the family satisfies the normalization and simplicity hypotheses without numerical assumptions.

Counterevidence, effect, and repair. Remark 3.5 permits a real eigenbasis, and Section 4 explicitly chooses compatible real phases. The proof on p. 34 also redefines \(v_0\) from \(u_0\); these are strong evidence of the intended convention, but a relative inner product alone does not make that \(v_0\) real. Specify \(u_0=e^{i\Theta_0}v_0\) with the previously fixed real \(v_0\), or complexify and transform both profiles with the same phase. The eigenvalue formula and the energy norm in (2.34) are invariant under this change. The correction concerns the phase of the stated vector limit, not a new eigenvalue exponent or a different physical eigenspace.

Title: Canonical Metrics, Orbifold Bundles, and Deformation Arguments
