The version, dates, DOI spelling, and frozen 2025 membership are retained; this report does not identify v1 with the journal final version. Every page location below refers to v1.

The intended setting is a compact complex manifold of dimension \(n>1\) with a nonzero parallel Lee form. The introductory dimension restriction is explicit. The distinction between \(c_1(X)=0\) in real de Rham cohomology and the sign of \(c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(X)\) is essential. Quasi-regularity concerns the compactness of the one-dimensional complex Lee group, and orbifold canonical classes include the branch divisor. These distinctions are retained in the tests below.
# Confirmed findings
## P1. The constructive direction of Theorem 2.4 does not produce the asserted metric (Major)
Location. The last two paragraphs of the proof, p. 9: the positive line bundle, the norm-square potential, and the equality defining \(\Omega_F\).

First witness: positivity. Take \(\mathcal Y=\mathbb P^1\), \(\mathcal L=\mathcal O(1)\) with its positive Fubini–Study Hermitian metric, and \(P=(\mathcal L\setminus0)/\langle\lambda\rangle\), \(0<|\lambda|<1\). This is a smooth compact principal elliptic bundle and is definite as required. In a standard local frame, its squared norm is \[f(z,w)=\frac{|w|^2}{1+|z|^2}.\] At \((z,w)=(0,1)\), the Hermitian matrix of \(f^{-1}i\partial\bar\partial f\) is \[\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Thus the displayed form is indefinite. Interchanging the order of the two Dolbeault operators reverses both eigenvalues and does not restore positivity. The exact Hessian calculation was also executed with the existing symbolic runtime.

Second witness: descent, even after repairing positivity. Let \(E'=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)\), let \(\tau\) be translation by \(1/2\), and let \(q:E'\to E'/\langle\tau\rangle\). Pull back an ample line bundle with a constant-curvature metric to \(\mathcal L\) on \(E'\). The pullback bundle and its elliptic quotient carry the order-two deck action. Start with its invariant normalized Vaisman form \[\Omega_0=\omega_0+\theta_0\wedge J\theta_0,\qquad
 \omega_0=-dJ\theta_0.\] For \(u(x+iy)=\cos(2\pi x)\) and sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\ne0\), perturb the positive line metric by \(e^{\varepsilon u}\) and use the reciprocal potential. Equivalently, the resulting normalized Vaisman forms have Lee forms \(\theta_\pm=\theta_0\pm\varepsilon\,du\) and positive transverse forms \(-dJ\theta_\pm\). The Lee vector is unchanged and remains Killing; \(\tau\) interchanges the two forms. Their arithmetic average is \[\frac{\Omega_++\Omega_-}{2}
   =\Omega_0+\varepsilon^2du\wedge Jdu ,
 \qquad
 -dJ\!\left(\frac{\theta_++\theta_-}{2}\right)
 +\frac{\theta_++\theta_-}{2}
       \wedge J\!\left(\frac{\theta_++\theta_-}{2}\right)
   =\Omega_0.\] The claimed equality therefore fails on a genuine allowed finite pullback cover. There is a stronger obstruction. Write \(\eta=\varepsilon^2du\wedge Jdu\) on the elliptic base. Since \(d\eta=0\), the unique Lee form of this average, if it is to satisfy \(d\Omega=\vartheta\wedge\Omega\), is \[\vartheta=\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_0+\eta}\,\theta_0.\] The coefficient is nonconstant, so \(d\vartheta\ne0\). The average is not even LCK.

Impact and counterevidence. These are failures of the actual metric construction and descent in a central equivalence used for the orbifold models and examples. This justifies Major severity for that proof component; it does not require the headline classification theorems to be false. Both witnesses satisfy the relevant positivity, compactness, and finite-action conditions. Conversely, they do not disprove the existence assertion of Theorem 2.4.

Repair boundary. For a positive line bundle use \(f=\|s\|_h^{-2}\), or use the norm-square potential on the negative dual line bundle, with consistent Lee normalization. For descent define a new form \[\widehat\Omega_F=-dJ\theta_F+\theta_F\wedge J\theta_F,
 \qquad \theta_F=|F|^{-1}\sum_{g\in F}g^*\theta.\] Its transverse part is the average of positive transverse forms. Its restriction in the Lee directions is unchanged, so it is positive, invariant, and has Killing Lee vector. It is therefore Vaisman. It must not be identified with the arithmetic average of the original metrics.
## P2. The printed definition needs the nonzero-Lee restriction (Major)
Location. The introductory definition, pp. 1–2; Definition 2.1, pp. 4–5; Theorems B and C, p. 2.

The strongest counterevidence is the paper’s explicit non-Kähler motivation and its repeated use of a one-dimensional Lee group. Those facts identify the intended strict setting. However, Definition 2.1 introduces normalization \(\|\theta\|=1\) as an additional condition; it does not remove zero-Lee metrics from the preceding definition. Under that explicit printed definition, the examples satisfy the actual hypotheses and contradict the stated conclusions of B(1) and C. The formal theorem-domain defect is therefore Major.
State \(\theta\ne0\) throughout, or explicitly adopt the strict non-Kähler convention. These examples do not refute the theorems with that intended additional restriction.
## P3. The quotient theorem requires effective isotropy (Minor)
Location. Effective chart convention, p. 5; Theorem 2.2, p. 7.

Let \(H=E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)\) and \(K=\langle1/2\rangle\). The action of \(H\) on \(X=(E/K)\times\mathbb P^1\) through its translation action on \(E/K\) is holomorphic, proper, and locally free, with stabilizer \(K\) at every point. Its quotient is \(\mathbb P^1\). An effective orbifold has trivial generic stabilizer; a principal \(H\)-orbibundle above its regular locus must have fiber \(H\). Here the fibers are \(E/K\), not \(H\). Indeed \(E/K\) has modulus \(2i\) after rescaling its lattice, whereas an \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\) transform of \(i\) has imaginary part \(1/(c^2+d^2)\) and cannot equal \(2\). The asserted principal structure over this quotient is therefore impossible.

Require the appropriate faithful slice action, or explicitly permit ineffective orbifolds and retain their generic isotropy. The effective Lee action used in the main applications does not have this counterexample: it is an actual subgroup of \(\operatorname{Aut}(X)\). The correction concerns the broader stated quotient theorem.
## P4. Coarse and orbifold cohomology need a coefficient restriction (Minor)
Location. The assertion following the definition of \(H^\bullet_{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal Y,R)\), p. 7.

Let \(\mathcal Y=[\mathbb P^1/\mu_2]\), where the nontrivial element acts by \(z\mapsto-z\), and use \(R=\mathbf F_2\). This is an effective compact complex orbifold with coarse space \(\mathbb P^1\). The classifying space is the Borel construction. A fixed point gives a section of its projection to \(B\mu_2\), so \(H^\bullet(B\mu_2,\mathbf F_2)\) injects into its cohomology. The periodic resolution has both differentials zero over \(\mathbf F_2\), hence this cohomology is nonzero in every nonnegative degree. The coarse sphere has no cohomology in degree three. Thus the displayed map cannot be an isomorphism for every field.

Characteristic zero suffices; more generally, invert all isotropy orders. The paper’s real and complex cohomological applications satisfy that condition. No counterexample to those applications is claimed.
## P5. The anti-Lee vector is not automatically a lattice element (Minor)
Location. The paragraph beginning with the integrality assertion for \(-JB\), p. 8.

For any strict quasi-regular Vaisman metric \(g\), the metric \(ag\), \(a>0\), has the same Lee form and Lee group but Lee vector \(B/a\). The lattice \(\Lambda\) of this group is fixed and discrete. The nonzero vectors \(-JB/a\) therefore cannot all lie in \(\Lambda\), although all these metrics meet the proof’s hypotheses. Concretely, on a scalar Hopf surface with \(g=g_{\rm Euclidean}/|z|^2\), one has \(B=-2r\partial_r\); the time-one flow of \(-JB\) is multiplication by \(e^{2i}\), not a real scalar deck power.

What is needed is a positive real multiple of a primitive lattice element, or an explicit period normalization. This retains the rational direction of the Chern class, the primitive generator, and the elliptic-group description. It corrects the unjustified metric-dependent integrality, not the existence of that direction.
## P6. Flat principal monodromy has the wrong target group (Major)
Location. The proof of the image criterion for \(\psi_*\), p. 9.

Principal \(G\)-bundle transition maps are translations in \(G\). They are not, in general, holomorphic group automorphisms of \(G\), which fix its identity. For an explicit topologically trivial but holomorphically nontrivial example, take the complex torus obtained from \(\mathbb C^2\) by the lattice generated by \[(1,0),\quad(i,\sqrt2),\quad(0,1),\quad(0,i)\] and project to \(E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)\). Its fiber is the same square elliptic curve \(G\), with translation monodromy \(1\mapsto0\), \(i\mapsto\sqrt2\pmod{\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z}\). A holomorphic section would lift to \(w=az+b\), since its derivative is doubly periodic. Its period conditions require \(a\in\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z\) and \(ia-\sqrt2\in\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z\), which is impossible. Thus the bundle is not the trivial principal bundle. A transition that is both a group automorphism and commutes with every principal translation is the identity. The stated automorphism-valued construction cannot represent this example. Tensoring it with a positive line-induced elliptic bundle places it in the image-criterion argument with the same positive Chern class.

This is the inverse direction of the \(\psi_*\) image criterion used on the same page to construct the line-bundle quotient for \(q^*P\) in Theorem 2.4. The phrase as in the above discussion therefore depends on the invalid representation and lift. The defect is Major in that core construction, even though the image criterion itself has a direct repair: \(c^{\mathbb Z}(P_0)=0\) implies that \(P_0\) is the image of \(u\in H^1(\mathcal Y,\mathcal O_\mathcal Y)\) in the exponential exact sequence. The image of this same \(u\) in \(H^1(\mathcal Y,\mathcal O_\mathcal Y^*)\) maps to \(P_0\) under \(\psi_*\). This avoids both the wrong target and an unsupported lift of an arbitrary representation.
## P7. The deformation tensor is not in the declared fixed bundle (Minor)
Location. The opening projection formula in the proof of Theorem 3.1, p. 10; the graph identity on p. 11.

Use a constant real Beltrami parameter \(0<\mu<1\) on one factor of a complex two-torus. The deformed subspaces are \[T_t^{0,1}=\mathbb C(\bar\partial+\mu\partial),\qquad
 T_t^{1,0}=\mathbb C(\partial+\mu\bar\partial).\] The printed definition gives \[-\pi_t^{1,0}(\bar\partial)
   =\frac{\mu}{1-\mu^2}
                    (\partial+\mu\bar\partial).\] This vector has a nonzero old \((0,1)\) component. Consequently the declared tensor does not belong to \(A^{0,1}\otimes T^{1,0}\) for the fixed original structure, as required by the subsequent Maurer–Cartan and Hodge constructions. The example is an actual integrable deformation of a compact complex manifold.

Use instead the graph tensor obtained by inverting the old \((0,1)\) projection on \(T_t^{0,1}\) and then taking the old \((1,0)\) projection. In the example it is \(\bar\partial\mapsto\mu\partial\), and \(T_t^{0,1}=(1+\phi_t)T_0^{0,1}\). The invariant Kuranishi argument works with this standard tensor. This is a local coordinate/type correction; it does not refute the automorphism dimension theorem.
## P8. Triviality of the entire compact subgroup action requires connectedness (Minor)
Location. The trivial representation argument and equation (7), p. 10; Claim 1, p. 11.

The theorem allows an arbitrary compact complex subgroup \(H\subset\operatorname{Aut}_0(X)\). Take \(X=\mathbb P^1\times E\) and \(H=C_2\times E\), where \(C_2\) acts by \(z\mapsto-z\) and \(E\) acts by translations. This is a compact complex subgroup of positive dimension. The summand \[H^0(\mathbb P^1,T\mathbb P^1)\otimes H^1(E,\mathcal O_E)
       \ \subset\ H^1(X,TX)\] contains \(\partial_z\otimes\eta\), which changes sign under \(C_2\). It is not an invariant class. With an \(H\)-invariant metric, its harmonic representative also contradicts (7). A holomorphic character on a disconnected compact complex group need only be constant on each component.

Apply the argument to \(H^0\). Its dimension is the same as that of \(H\), so the desired dimension bound is retained. The final assertion with \(H=\operatorname{Aut}_0(X)\) already concerns a connected group. This is a false intermediate claim for the broader subgroup, not a counterexample to Theorem F.
## P9. The negative-curvature proof has inconsistent signs and normalization (Minor)
Location. The first paragraph of the proof of Theorem 6.2, p. 20; equation (22) and the contraction following (25), p. 21.

The proof chooses a positive form \(\eta\) representing \(-c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(X)\) and then prescribes \(\rho_0=\eta\). But a Ricci form represents \(2\pi c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(X)\), which has the opposite sign. This is not a permissible prescribed-Ricci target. For a concrete negative-type example, take a definite elliptic bundle over a curve \(C\) of genus two. Every transverse Ricci form has \[\int_C\rho=2\pi\deg TC=-4\pi<0,\] whereas a positive \(\eta\) has positive integral. All strict Vaisman and negative-class hypotheses are met.

Choose \(\eta\) in \(-2\pi c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}(X)\) and prescribe \(\rho_0=-\eta\). Equation (22) already uses this negative sign, which is strong counterevidence against treating the subsequent vanishing mechanism as false. A second displayed sign is also inconsistent: from the stated formula for \(\nabla^{\rm Ch}\theta^{1,0}\) and \(\theta^{1,0}(\xi_0)=0\), one obtains \[\theta^{1,0}(\nabla^{\rm Ch}\xi_0)
    =+\tfrac12 g(\xi_0,\cdot),\] rather than its negative. Only its squared norm is used.

With these corrections the independent computation gives \[\|D\xi_0\|_2^2=\|\xi_0\|_2^2-\|\xi_0\|_{h,2}^2,\qquad
 \|(\nabla^{\rm Ch}\xi_0)_0\|_2^2
                       =-\|\xi_0\|_{h,2}^2.\] Thus \(\xi_0=0\) and the intended one-dimensional automorphism conclusion is retained. Severity reflects the localized transcription and normalization defects, with the corrected core calculation actually checked.
## P10. Continuity does not fix the Chern class of a chosen family of forms (Major)
Location. The last cohomological inference in Corollary 6.6, p. 22.

On the constant family of curves \(C\times\Delta\) with \(g(C)>1\), choose a positive form \([\omega_0]=-c_1(C)\) and put \(\omega_t=(1+|t|^2)\omega_0\). This is a smooth family of fiberwise Kähler forms, obtained by restricting a smooth two-form on the total space, and has the prescribed central class. Nevertheless \([\omega_t]\ne-c_1(C)\) for \(t\ne0\). It satisfies exactly the properties of the chosen form stated before the claimed continuity inference.

This inference is the written step establishing negative type for the deformed fibers in Corollary 6.6, and thus the negative branch of Theorem E on p. 3. Fiberwise Kählerness and continuity do not supply the missing equality of cohomology classes; the source does not assume that the total form is closed or has constant Gauss–Manin class. This is a Major defect in the actual deformation-stability derivation.

The negative-type conclusion is recoverable: extend a positive Hermitian metric on the relative orbifold canonical bundle and use its fiberwise curvature. Its cohomology class is the required Chern class, and positivity persists after shrinking the parameter space. No counterexample to openness of negative Vaisman type is claimed.
## P11. A properly elliptic Vaisman surface can have coarse base genus zero (Minor)
Location. Example 7.1(1), p. 23.

Let \(\mathcal Y=\mathbb P^1(2,3,7)\). Its orbifold canonical degree is \[\deg K_\mathcal Y^{\mathrm{orb}}
   =-2+\left(1-\tfrac12\right)+\left(1-\tfrac13\right)
                               +\left(1-\tfrac17\right)
   =\frac1{42}>0.\] The local character of \(K_\mathcal Y^{\mathrm{orb}}\) is faithful at each orbifold point. Hence the nonzero total space of its negative dual is smooth. A negative-curvature Hermitian metric gives a positive norm-square cone metric, and quotienting by a real fiber contraction \(0<q<1\) gives a compact strict Vaisman surface \(X\). The circle connection makes \(\pi^*c_1(K_\mathcal Y^{\mathrm{orb}})\) exact, so \(c_1(X)=0\) in real cohomology. Since \(K_X=\pi^*K_\mathcal Y^{\mathrm{orb}}\) and the fibers are compact connected elliptic curves, pluricanonical sections descend; their growth gives \(\kappa(X)=1\). Thus \(X\) is properly elliptic but its coarse base is \(\mathbb P^1\), of genus zero.

The correct condition is positive orbifold canonical degree. Genus greater than one is available after a suitable finite orbifold uniformizing cover, not necessarily on the original coarse base. The negative Bott–Chern classification survives this correction.
## P12. The punctured cone is the tautological bundle, not the degree-\(d\) bundle (Minor)
Location. Example 7.4, p. 24, immediately before the adjunction argument.

Take weights \((1,1,1)\) and the smooth Fermat plane cubic \(f=z_0^3+z_1^3+z_2^3\), so \(d=3\). Its affine cone is smooth away from the origin, as required. The punctured cone is \(\mathcal O(-1)|_{Y_f}\) with its zero section removed. This line bundle has degree \(-3\). The printed \(\mathcal O(-d)|_{Y_f}=\mathcal O(-3)|_{Y_f}\) instead has degree \(-9\). Their circle bundles have abelianized fundamental groups \[\mathbb Z^2\oplus\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z
       \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \mathbb Z^2\oplus\mathbb Z/9\mathbb Z,\] respectively, so the claimed identification is genuinely false.

Replace \(\mathcal O(-d)\) by \(\mathcal O(-1)\) in the cone description. The corrected line bundle remains negative, and the adjunction condition \(d=\sum_iw_i\) is unaffected. The construction still yields the asserted Calabi–Yau examples. The problem is the specified bundle and its topology, not the existence of those examples.
# Proof coverage and retained conclusions
## Orbifold correspondence and automorphisms

The integral Chern class, branch divisor, and distinction between effective orbifolds and their coarse spaces were checked. The finite-cover part of Theorem 2.4 can be repaired without asserting that some finite cover has entirely torsion-free \(H_1\). For each \(m\)-torsion Chern component \(\alpha\), the Bockstein \[H^1_{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal Y,\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow
                       H^2_{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal Y,\mathbb Z)[m]\] is onto. The cover defined by the kernel of the corresponding finite character kills \(\alpha\). Intersect the finitely many kernels for the lattice components. The exponential cohomology argument in P6 then gives the line-bundle model. The stronger torsion-free-\(H_1\) assertion was not declared false without a counterexample.

For connected compact \(H\), the holomorphic representations on \(H^q(X,TX)\) are trivial. Averaging the metric makes the harmonic projection and the Kuranishi construction equivariant. The invariant smooth auxiliary germ has the same tangent space as the full auxiliary germ, so the germs agree. The real \(H\) action persists under the corrected graph deformation, and the complex span of its Lie algebra has dimension at least \(\dim_\mathbb CH\). Upper semicontinuity gives equality when \(H=\operatorname{Aut}_0(X)\). P7–P8 isolate the necessary corrections; no counterexample to this argument with \(H^0\) was found.
## Canonical metrics, signs, and deformation

The Bott–Chern kernel description and the Lee cone explain the three signs; this use retains the strict Vaisman hypothesis. In Lemma 4.4, wedging the local transverse canonical form with \(\theta^{1,0}\) gives a holomorphic top form: the potentially nonzero \(\bar\partial\theta^{1,0}\) is horizontal and its wedge with the transverse top form vanishes. Its norm yields \(\rho_\Omega=\rho_0\). The positive-type Kodaira-dimension argument follows from Gauduchon integration of the divisor class against the Vaisman metric; the divisor integral need only be nonnegative.

The actual v2 of Ornea–Verbitsky [OV] was read and its Theorem 4.1 and proof pages were inspected. Its total-volume compatibility does not invalidate Theorem 5.1 here: first rescale the initial metric by a constant to match the target total volume. This changes neither the Lee class nor invariance under the Lee group. For \(c_1^{\mathrm{BC}}=0\), the Ricci potential is basic: its difference under an automorphism is pluriharmonic, hence constant, and boundedness under iteration makes that constant zero. The prescribed volume then produces the claimed Ricci-flat metric, and a pluriharmonic log ratio of two volumes proves uniqueness up to scale.

In the negative case, equations (12)–(18), the conformal adjoints, the \(nD_B\) cancellation, and the Chern orthogonal projection were checked directly. P9 records the two inconsistencies. The hypotheses of the transverse prescribed-Ricci theorem were checked on the retrieved pages of [E90]. In particular, the top basic class is nonzero: if \(\omega_0^{n-1}=d\beta\) were basic exact, integration against \(\theta\wedge J\theta\) and Stokes’ theorem would give zero, since \(\beta\wedge\omega_0\) exceeds the transverse dimension. This contradicts positivity of the total volume. The cited passage assumes transverse complex dimension at least two. In transverse dimension one, the required Ricci prescription follows directly by multiplying the transverse metric by the exponential of a basic potential and then normalizing its basic area. This boundary case was not silently attributed to the higher-dimensional statement.

Faulk’s actual Theorem 1.3 [Faulk] supplies the negative orbifold Kähler–Einstein metric for an effective compact Kähler orbifold. Uniqueness follows from the usual potential and maximum-principle argument. For Theorem 6.3, a closed \(G\)-invariant Lee candidate with the specified positive transverse curvature has positive coefficient in the old Lee direction; closedness eliminates the anti-Lee component, and pairing with a positive transverse power determines its positive sign. Thus the proposed form is positive and its Lee vector is Killing. The missing negative sign in P9, rather than a positive-type reading of this section, is the relevant correction. Theorem B explicitly imposes negativity.
## Decomposition, topology, and examples

The compactness of \(\operatorname{Aut}_0\) in the null case follows by pulling back the unique fixed-volume canonical metric. In the splitting argument, the parallel complex structure preserves the flat factor: a mixed component would give a nonzero parallel one-form on the simply connected compact factor. The primitive integral Chern class on that factor yields the cyclic root cover of the \(\mathbb C^*\)-bundle and the vanishing of its first homology. The retrieved Kollár preprint [Kollar], Proposition 88 on PDF p. 28, has the smooth-total-space, vanishing-\(H_1\), and numerical Calabi–Yau hypotheses needed to eliminate the branch divisor. Its numbering was not identified with the journal’s Proposition 10.2. The remaining pure-orbifold decomposition and unobstructedness inputs remain cited external theorems, not independently reproved results.

The finite canonical cover, the invariant part of a smooth Kuranishi germ, constancy of the holomorphic vector-field dimension, and the extension of a nonvanishing canonical form were checked as the dependency chain for Theorem 5.7. The small fibers are first kept Vaisman by the earlier deformation result. Their Frölicher degeneration and upper semicontinuity then give the required constancy of \(h^{n,0}\). The torsion canonical bundle gives Kodaira dimension zero; the elliptic fibration over a projective base and failure of the \(\partial\bar\partial\) lemma give algebraic dimension \(n-1\).

For a nontrivial simply connected factor, the fundamental group extension has central kernel \(\mathbb Z\oplus T\), \(T\) finite. Odd first Betti number forces the commutator to have rank zero, hence to lie in \(T\). If \(qT=0\), a subgroup generated by suitable \(q\)th powers of base lifts and a free central generator is abelian of finite index; passing to its normal core preserves abelianity. This supplies the needed finite-cover step without invoking an unsupported general virtual torsion-freeness claim. The first-Betti bound can also be obtained directly from the Chern-class sequence. Equality forces the finite base action on the abelian variety to be by translations, recovering a Kodaira manifold.

The weighted hypersurface examples were checked for quasi-smoothness, adjunction degree, and the displayed local stabilizer. Their gradients vanish only at the cone vertex. In the second threefold example the residual \(\mu_2\) acts by \((-1,-1)\) on the two local surface coordinates. P11 and P12 give the actual corrections to the base-genus and cone-bundle descriptions.
# A conditional group-theoretic limitation

Corollary 5.10, p. 18, requires special care if \(H_{\mathbb Z}\) means the usual unimodular integer Heisenberg group. On an abelian surface with polarization type \((1,2)\), the associated Kodaira threefold has group \(\Gamma=\mathbb Z_b\times\Gamma_B\), where \[B=\operatorname{diag}(J,2J),\qquad
 J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\] and the nontrivial basic commutators are \([x_1,y_1]=a\), \([x_2,y_2]=a^2\). This is a strict Vaisman Calabi–Yau example. Suppose a finite-index normal subgroup \(N\) were \(\mathbb Z\) times the standard unimodular Heisenberg group. Let \(V\subset\mathbb Z^4\) be its projected lattice. Then \(Z(N)=N\cap\langle a,b\rangle\). Its derived generator \(a^C\) is primitive in that full rank-two center, so \(N\cap\langle a\rangle=\langle a^C\rangle\). The form \(B/C\) must be unimodular on \(V\). Normality implies \[B(V,\mathbb Z^4)\subset C\mathbb Z,\qquad
 \mathbb Z^4\subset V^\#=V.\] Hence \(V=\mathbb Z^4\), but \(\det(B/C)=4/C^4\ne1\) for every positive integer \(C\). The extra central \(\mathbb Z\) therefore does not remove the obstruction. Dropping normality does: the subgroup generated by \(b,a^2,x_1^2,y_1,x_2,y_2\) is standard and of finite index, but is not normal.

This is a proved obstruction under the specified standard interpretation. It is not entered as an unqualified counterexample to the manuscript’s intended theorem. Example 7.2 itself calls a lattice integral Heisenberg when its commutator equals its center; the type-\((1,2)\) Heisenberg factor already satisfies that broader condition. No formal definition in v1 resolves this terminology. An exact integral classification must specify the lattice, allow the appropriate Heisenberg lattice in the normal subgroup, or assert standard commensurability without normality. The Betti conclusions do not require unimodularity. This interpretive boundary remains part of the pending scientific assessment.

problems.title: The positive-line metric and its finite arithmetic descent fail
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: The positive-line metric and its finite arithmetic descent fail
claim: Kind: definition, statement, construction or proof step
Location: Theorem2.4 converse, p9, norm-square potential and last displayed Omega_F identity
Claim: A positive-line norm-square gives a Vaisman metric and arithmetic averaging over the finite deck group equals the metric formed from the average Lee form.

Y=P1,L=O(1) positive FS,lambda in(0,1),P=Lx/<lambda> smooth compact definite elliptic bundle. For descent use free double cover E'=C/(Z+iZ)->E'/<z+1/2>, pullback of positive constant-curvature ample line, canonical order2 deck lift commuting with fiber G.
analysis: Location. The last two paragraphs of the proof, p. 9: the positive line bundle, the norm-square potential, and the equality defining \(\Omega_F\).

First witness: positivity. Take \(\mathcal Y=\mathbb P^1\), \(\mathcal L=\mathcal O(1)\) with its positive Fubini–Study Hermitian metric, and \(P=(\mathcal L\setminus0)/\langle\lambda\rangle\), \(0<|\lambda|<1\). This is a smooth compact principal elliptic bundle and is definite as required. In a standard local frame, its squared norm is \[f(z,w)=\frac{|w|^2}{1+|z|^2}.\] At \((z,w)=(0,1)\), the Hermitian matrix of \(f^{-1}i\partial\bar\partial f\) is \[\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Thus the displayed form is indefinite. Interchanging the order of the two Dolbeault operators reverses both eigenvalues and does not restore positivity. The exact Hessian calculation was also executed with the existing symbolic runtime.

Second witness: descent, even after repairing positivity. Let \(E'=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)\), let \(\tau\) be translation by \(1/2\), and let \(q:E'\to E'/\langle\tau\rangle\). Pull back an ample line bundle with a constant-curvature metric to \(\mathcal L\) on \(E'\). The pullback bundle and its elliptic quotient carry the order-two deck action. Start with its invariant normalized Vaisman form \[\Omega_0=\omega_0+\theta_0\wedge J\theta_0,\qquad
 \omega_0=-dJ\theta_0.\] For \(u(x+iy)=\cos(2\pi x)\) and sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\ne0\), perturb the positive line metric by \(e^{\varepsilon u}\) and use the reciprocal potential. Equivalently, the resulting normalized Vaisman forms have Lee forms \(\theta_\pm=\theta_0\pm\varepsilon\,du\) and positive transverse forms \(-dJ\theta_\pm\). The Lee vector is unchanged and remains Killing; \(\tau\) interchanges the two forms. Their arithmetic average is \[\frac{\Omega_++\Omega_-}{2}
   =\Omega_0+\varepsilon^2du\wedge Jdu ,
 \qquad
 -dJ\!\left(\frac{\theta_++\theta_-}{2}\right)
 +\frac{\theta_++\theta_-}{2}
       \wedge J\!\left(\frac{\theta_++\theta_-}{2}\right)
   =\Omega_0.\] The claimed equality therefore fails on a genuine allowed finite pullback cover. There is a stronger obstruction. Write \(\eta=\varepsilon^2du\wedge Jdu\) on the elliptic base. Since \(d\eta=0\), the unique Lee form of this average, if it is to satisfy \(d\Omega=\vartheta\wedge\Omega\), is \[\vartheta=\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_0+\eta}\,\theta_0.\] The coefficient is nonconstant, so \(d\vartheta\ne0\). The average is not even LCK.

Impact and counterevidence. These are failures of the actual metric construction and descent in a central equivalence used for the orbifold models and examples. This justifies Major severity for that proof component; it does not require the headline classification theorems to be false. Both witnesses satisfy the relevant positivity, compactness, and finite-action conditions. Conversely, they do not disprove the existence assertion of Theorem 2.4.

Repair boundary. For a positive line bundle use \(f=\|s\|_h^{-2}\), or use the norm-square potential on the negative dual line bundle, with consistent Lee normalization. For descent define a new form \[\widehat\Omega_F=-dJ\theta_F+\theta_F\wedge J\theta_F,
 \qquad \theta_F=|F|^{-1}\sum_{g\in F}g^*\theta.\] Its transverse part is the average of positive transverse forms. Its restriction in the Lee directions is unchanged, so it is positive, invariant, and has Killing Lee vector. It is therefore Vaisman. It must not be identified with the arithmetic average of the original metrics.
result: Impact: Major for actual central constructive direction and descent, which produce an indefinite form and a non-LCK average. Severity follows this core proof impact, not repair length or a requirement that the whole paper fail.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use reciprocal positive-line potential with consistent normalization. Define new -dJtheta_F+theta_F wedge Jtheta_F, prove positivity from averaged transverse curvature/common vertical Lee field, and do not equate it with arithmetic metric mean.

problems.title: Proper locally free actions need compatible effective slice isotropy
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Proper locally free actions need compatible effective slice isotropy
claim: Kind: definition, statement, construction or proof step
Location: Orbifold chart convention p5; Theorem2.2 p7
Claim: Every holomorphic proper locally free H-action has an effective orbifold quotient making its projection a principal H-orbibundle.
H=E=C/Z[i],K=<1/2>,X=(E/K)xP1, action induced by H->E/K. Compact complex dimension2, holomorphic proper action with finite stabilizerK.
analysis: Location. Effective chart convention, p. 5; Theorem 2.2, p. 7.

Let \(H=E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)\) and \(K=\langle1/2\rangle\). The action of \(H\) on \(X=(E/K)\times\mathbb P^1\) through its translation action on \(E/K\) is holomorphic, proper, and locally free, with stabilizer \(K\) at every point. Its quotient is \(\mathbb P^1\). An effective orbifold has trivial generic stabilizer; a principal \(H\)-orbibundle above its regular locus must have fiber \(H\). Here the fibers are \(E/K\), not \(H\). Indeed \(E/K\) has modulus \(2i\) after rescaling its lattice, whereas an \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\) transform of \(i\) has imaginary part \(1/(c^2+d^2)\) and cannot equal \(2\). The asserted principal structure over this quotient is therefore impossible.

Require the appropriate faithful slice action, or explicitly permit ineffective orbifolds and retain their generic isotropy. The effective Lee action used in the main applications does not have this counterexample: it is an actual subgroup of \(\operatorname{Aut}(X)\). The correction concerns the broader stated quotient theorem.
result: Impact: Broader quotient theorem false in stated generality; main Lee quotient remains available.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Require faithful local slice isotropy or explicitly allow ineffective orbifolds retaining generic isotropy. Do not confuse global effectiveness with slice effectiveness for a general H.

problems.title: Coarse-to-orbifold cohomology comparison fails over arbitrary fields
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Coarse-to-orbifold cohomology comparison fails over arbitrary fields
claim: Kind: definition, statement, construction or proof step
Location: p7, after definition of H_orb*(Y,R)
Claim: cl*:H*(Y,R)->H_orb*(Y,R) is an isomorphism for every field R.
Effective compact orbifold[P1/mu2] with involutionz->-z; R=F2; coarseP1.
analysis: Location. The assertion following the definition of \(H^\bullet_{\mathrm{orb}}(\mathcal Y,R)\), p. 7.

Let \(\mathcal Y=[\mathbb P^1/\mu_2]\), where the nontrivial element acts by \(z\mapsto-z\), and use \(R=\mathbf F_2\). This is an effective compact complex orbifold with coarse space \(\mathbb P^1\). The classifying space is the Borel construction. A fixed point gives a section of its projection to \(B\mu_2\), so \(H^\bullet(B\mu_2,\mathbf F_2)\) injects into its cohomology. The periodic resolution has both differentials zero over \(\mathbf F_2\), hence this cohomology is nonzero in every nonnegative degree. The coarse sphere has no cohomology in degree three. Thus the displayed map cannot be an isomorphism for every field.

Characteristic zero suffices; more generally, invert all isotropy orders. The paper’s real and complex cohomological applications satisfy that condition. No counterexample to those applications is claimed.
result: Impact: Coefficient scope correction; no change to actual characteristic0 classification argument.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Assume characteristic0 or invert every isotropy order.

problems.title: The anti-Lee vector need not itself be an integral lattice vector
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: The anti-Lee vector need not itself be an integral lattice vector
claim: Kind: definition, statement, construction or proof step
Location: p8, paragraph after c(P) curvature expression
Claim: -JB is an integral element of the elliptic latticeLambda without specifying period normalization.
Any strict quasiregular Vaisman g and its homotheties ag; same theta,G,Lambda,dualB/a. Explicit scalarHopf normalizedg=4r^-2gEuclidean.
analysis: Location. The paragraph beginning with the integrality assertion for \(-JB\), p. 8.

For any strict quasi-regular Vaisman metric \(g\), the metric \(ag\), \(a>0\), has the same Lee form and Lee group but Lee vector \(B/a\). The lattice \(\Lambda\) of this group is fixed and discrete. The nonzero vectors \(-JB/a\) therefore cannot all lie in \(\Lambda\), although all these metrics meet the proof’s hypotheses. Concretely, on a scalar Hopf surface with \(g=g_{\rm Euclidean}/|z|^2\), one has \(B=-2r\partial_r\); the time-one flow of \(-JB\) is multiplication by \(e^{2i}\), not a real scalar deck power.

What is needed is a positive real multiple of a primitive lattice element, or an explicit period normalization. This retains the rational direction of the Chern class, the primitive generator, and the elliptic-group description. It corrects the unjustified metric-dependent integrality, not the existence of that direction.
result: Impact: Metric normalization error, not loss of rational Chern direction or quasiregularity.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Replace integral by positive real multiple of primitive lattice vector, or impose an explicit period normalization.

problems.title: Flat principal elliptic monodromy is incorrectly typed as group automorphisms
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Flat principal elliptic monodromy is incorrectly typed as group automorphisms
claim: Kind: definition, statement, construction or proof step
Location: p9, flat P0 and rho:pi1orb->Aut_hol,gp(G)
Claim: The general zero-Chern principal difference bundle is associated to holomorphic group-automorphism monodromy, with a lifted C* representation.
Base and fiber E=G=C/Z[i]; total torus C²/lattice<(1,0),(i,sqrt2),(0,1),(0,i)>; Chern0, translation monodromy.
analysis: Location. The proof of the image criterion for \(\psi_*\), p. 9.

Principal \(G\)-bundle transition maps are translations in \(G\). They are not, in general, holomorphic group automorphisms of \(G\), which fix its identity. For an explicit topologically trivial but holomorphically nontrivial example, take the complex torus obtained from \(\mathbb C^2\) by the lattice generated by \[(1,0),\quad(i,\sqrt2),\quad(0,1),\quad(0,i)\] and project to \(E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)\). Its fiber is the same square elliptic curve \(G\), with translation monodromy \(1\mapsto0\), \(i\mapsto\sqrt2\pmod{\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z}\). A holomorphic section would lift to \(w=az+b\), since its derivative is doubly periodic. Its period conditions require \(a\in\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z\) and \(ia-\sqrt2\in\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z\), which is impossible. Thus the bundle is not the trivial principal bundle. A transition that is both a group automorphism and commutes with every principal translation is the identity. The stated automorphism-valued construction cannot represent this example. Tensoring it with a positive line-induced elliptic bundle places it in the image-criterion argument with the same positive Chern class.

This is the inverse direction of the \(\psi_*\) image criterion used on the same page to construct the line-bundle quotient for \(q^*P\) in Theorem 2.4. The phrase as in the above discussion therefore depends on the invalid representation and lift. The defect is Major in that core construction, even though the image criterion itself has a direct repair: \(c^{\mathbb Z}(P_0)=0\) implies that \(P_0\) is the image of \(u\in H^1(\mathcal Y,\mathcal O_\mathcal Y)\) in the exponential exact sequence. The image of this same \(u\) in \(H^1(\mathcal Y,\mathcal O_\mathcal Y^*)\) maps to \(P_0\) under \(\psi_*\). This avoids both the wrong target and an unsupported lift of an arbitrary representation.
result: Impact: The false group-automorphism suspension and unsupported lift prove the inverse psi_* image criterion on p9. The same page invokes that discussion to construct q*P in Theorem2.4. The nonsplit translation bundle can be combined with a positive line-induced bundle in the actual definite case. This invalid core construction warrants Major; the common H1(O) class provides a valid new sheaf-theoretic repair, not a counterexample to the image criterion itself.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use the common H1(O) element in the commuting exponential sequences; if discussing monodromy, use translationsG and justify any lift.

problems.title: Beltrami projection formula has the wrong fixed-bundle type
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Beltrami projection formula has the wrong fixed-bundle type
claim: Kind: definition, statement, construction or proof step
Location: Theorem3.1 proof p10 opening formula; p11 graph identity
Claim: -new(1,0)projection restricted to old(0,1) is a tensor valued in old(1,0).
A constant real Beltrami parameter0<mu<1 on one factor of a compact complex2torus defines an actual integrable small deformation.
analysis: Location. The opening projection formula in the proof of Theorem 3.1, p. 10; the graph identity on p. 11.

Use a constant real Beltrami parameter \(0<\mu<1\) on one factor of a complex two-torus. The deformed subspaces are \[T_t^{0,1}=\mathbb C(\bar\partial+\mu\partial),\qquad
 T_t^{1,0}=\mathbb C(\partial+\mu\bar\partial).\] The printed definition gives \[-\pi_t^{1,0}(\bar\partial)
   =\frac{\mu}{1-\mu^2}
                    (\partial+\mu\bar\partial).\] This vector has a nonzero old \((0,1)\) component. Consequently the declared tensor does not belong to \(A^{0,1}\otimes T^{1,0}\) for the fixed original structure, as required by the subsequent Maurer–Cartan and Hodge constructions. The example is an actual integrable deformation of a compact complex manifold.

Use instead the graph tensor obtained by inverting the old \((0,1)\) projection on \(T_t^{0,1}\) and then taking the old \((1,0)\) projection. In the example it is \(\bar\partial\mapsto\mu\partial\), and \(T_t^{0,1}=(1+\phi_t)T_0^{0,1}\). The invariant Kuranishi argument works with this standard tensor. This is a local coordinate/type correction; it does not refute the automorphism dimension theorem.
result: Impact: Coordinate/type error in proof, not a false automorphism-dimension theorem.

paragraphs: Invert the old(0,1)projection on new(0,1), then take old(1,0). Correct graph is newT0,1=(1+phi)oldT0,1; examplephi=mu partial.

On the constant family of curves \(C\times\Delta\) with \(g(C)>1\), choose a positive form \([\omega_0]=-c_1(C)\) and put \(\omega_t=(1+|t|^2)\omega_0\). problems.title: Properly elliptic Vaisman surfaces need not have coarse base genus greater than one
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Properly elliptic Vaisman surfaces need not have coarse base genus greater than one
claim: Kind: definition, statement, construction or proof step
Location: Example7.1(1), p23
Claim: Properly elliptic Vaisman surfaces are elliptic orbibundles over curvesofgenusg>1.
Y=P1(2,3,7),degreeKorb=1/42; negative dualcanonical line has faithful localcharacters; smooth punctured totalspacequotientedbyfibercontractionq in(0,1).
analysis: Location. Example 7.1(1), p. 23.

Let \(\mathcal Y=\mathbb P^1(2,3,7)\). Its orbifold canonical degree is \[\deg K_\mathcal Y^{\mathrm{orb}}
   =-2+\left(1-\tfrac12\right)+\left(1-\tfrac13\right)
                               +\left(1-\tfrac17\right)
   =\frac1{42}>0.\] The local character of \(K_\mathcal Y^{\mathrm{orb}}\) is faithful at each orbifold point. Hence the nonzero total space of its negative dual is smooth. A negative-curvature Hermitian metric gives a positive norm-square cone metric, and quotienting by a real fiber contraction \(0<q<1\) gives a compact strict Vaisman surface \(X\). The circle connection makes \(\pi^*c_1(K_\mathcal Y^{\mathrm{orb}})\) exact, so \(c_1(X)=0\) in real cohomology. Since \(K_X=\pi^*K_\mathcal Y^{\mathrm{orb}}\) and the fibers are compact connected elliptic curves, pluricanonical sections descend; their growth gives \(\kappa(X)=1\). Thus \(X\) is properly elliptic but its coarse base is \(\mathbb P^1\), of genus zero.

report: Abstract: The reviewed artifact is the Warwick accepted manuscript by Federico Binda, Martin Gallauer and Alberto Vezzani. Its main text was read, with focused checks of the categorical equivalences, weight criterion, comparison argument and Clemens–Schmid construction. One confirmed issue affects a premise explicitly used in the central comparison proof: the stated integrality condition on pure Frobenius modules excludes positive Tate twists allowed by the proposition. This is assessed Major at the level of that derivation, without asserting that the comparison theorem is false. Two further, local issues concern an infinite-product coalgebra and the Hodge exposition. Explicit counterexamples and bounded repairs are given. External foundational theorems and all higher coherence data were not independently reconstructed. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI technical verification

Title: Technical review of
Motivic monodromy and \(p\)-adic cohomology theories
# Identity, source and coverage

The assigned identifier is M25-0261, in the frozen 2025 batch. The original title is Motivic monodromy and \(p\)-adic cohomology theories; the authors are Federico Binda, Martin Gallauer and Alberto Vezzani. The journal identifier is DOI `10.4171/jems/1634`. The actual 51-page PDF is the Warwick WRAP record 188439 accepted manuscript (accepted 20 October 2024; deposited 7 November 2024). Its repository cover expressly distinguishes it from the version of record. The associated arXiv v2 date, 31 October 2024, is not a byte-equivalence claim. The publisher’s online date is 4 April 2025. These dates do not change the frozen membership.

Here PDF page counts the repository cover: printed page \(r\) is PDF page \(r+1\). All main-text pages 2–48 and the bibliography on pages 48–51 were read. The review checks the distinction between ind-nilpotent and arbitrary operators; square-zero and monodromy conventions; the weight-orthogonality criterion; the finite-residue-field comparison and Kummer normalization; and the chain property, degrees and twists of the Clemens–Schmid construction. The accompanying coverage ledger distinguishes reading from independent proof reconstruction. Selected decisive pages were also inspected as rendered source images.

No supplementary mathematical file or author code was identified in the bounded searches recorded with the source manifest. This is an availability limitation, not evidence of absence and not a defect. No author code was executed. The search for corrections did not establish a paper-specific correction to the exact accepted manuscript. A later publisher PDF was located but not compared; no conclusion here is transferred to that version without verification.
# Framework and checked dependencies

Section 2 works in a \(\mathbb Q\)-linear, compactly generated stable symmetric monoidal category \(\mathcal C\), with an object \(t\) satisfying \(\operatorname{Alt}^2(t)=0\). The ind-nilpotent condition is the vanishing of the telescope of \(X\to X\otimes t\to X\otimes t^{\otimes2}\to\cdots\). Theorem 2.1 and Propositions 2.32 and 2.38 use the square-zero algebra \(\mathbf 1\oplus t[-1]\) and the direct sum \(\bigoplus_{n\ge0}t^{\otimes n}\). They must not be conflated with the arbitrary-operator extension in Remark 2.40.

The shift in Lemma 2.31 changes the symmetry sign, so that \(\operatorname{Sym}^n(t[-1])=0\) for \(n\ge2\). In the direct-sum right-adjoint calculation, mapping a compact zero-section generator into the cofree object identifies the fiber of the shift with the degree-zero summand. This checks the relevant adjunction without commuting an arbitrary infinite product through tensor product.

The application to rigid motives is restricted to the stated good-reduction subcategory unless the source supplies the additional hypotheses giving the whole category. Corollary 3.18 requires both underlying-realization compatibility and Kummer normalization. The geometric and arithmetic Frobenius directions are inverses as explained in Remark 2.52; Lemma 4.30 and Remark 4.41 must be read together. The mixed-characteristic construction uses \(\varphi^\sharp\), not the unsuitable naive lift discussed in Remark 4.47.

Example 3.31 needs cohomological dimension at most one, different-weight Hom vanishing and a specified direction of Ext vanishing. It does not assume that an entire mixed category is semisimple. Theorem 4.53 uses finite-field purity for every object of the full Chow heart, and then descends to \(k\subset\overline{\mathbb F}_p\). Corollaries 4.54 and 4.58 retain that residue-field restriction; Corollary 4.58 also fixes the stated uniformizer normalization in characteristic zero.
# Confirmed findings

Problem 1 (Tate twists contradict the purity premise used in the comparison).  Definition 2.42(3), PDF page 18 (printed 17), imposes algebraic integrality on every Frobenius eigenvalue of a pure module. Proposition 4.44(2), PDF page 39 (printed 38), asserts purity for \(R^i\Gamma_{\mathrm{rig}}(M)\) for every \(M\in\mathcal H_k\) when \(k\) is finite. With the stated definition and the full heart, this assertion is false.
## Hypotheses and exact computation

Take \(k=\mathbb F_2\), \(K=K_0=\mathbb Q_2\) and \[M=\mathbf 1(1)[2]=M(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_2)\{1\}.\] The residue field is finite and perfect, the field \(K\) is complete with rational-rank-one value group, and the point is smooth and proper. Example 3.29(1), PDF page 29 (printed 28), includes all integer twists \(\{r\}=(r)[2r]\), so \(M\in\mathcal H_k\).

Example 2.43(2) specifies \(K_0(r)=(K_0,2^{-r}\varphi)\). Remark 4.41 specifies the realization of \(\mathbf 1(-1)\) as \(K_0(-1)\), with Frobenius \(2\varphi\). Exact monoidality and tensor inversion therefore give \[R\Gamma_{\mathrm{rig}}(\mathbf 1(1)[2])\simeq \mathbb Q_2(1)[2].\] Witt Frobenius on \(\mathbb Q_2\) is the identity. The unique nonzero graded piece has eigenvalue \(\lambda=1/2\). Under cohomological indexing it occurs in degree \(-2\); the integrality contradiction is independent of indexing.

If \(1/2\) satisfied a monic integral polynomial of degree \(m\), multiplication of that equation by \(2^m\) would yield \[1+2a_{m-1}+4a_{m-2}+\cdots+2^m a_0=0,\qquad a_j\in\mathbb Z,\] which is impossible modulo \(2\). Thus this nonzero piece is not pure of any weight under the printed integrality definition. Its correct spectral weight is nevertheless \(-2\), since \(|1/2|=2^{-2/2}\).
## Alternative readings, impact and repair

This is not an OCR artifact: the integrality word, the integer-twist quantifier and the universal purity claim were checked on source images. Reversing Frobenius conventions cannot help after Remark 4.41 has fixed the arithmetic realization of \(\mathbf 1(-1)\). Restricting to effective motives would change the stated heart and would not justify the application to all of \(\mathcal H_k\).

The proof of Theorem 4.53, PDF page 41 (printed 40), explicitly invokes Proposition 4.44 for arbitrary \(M\in\mathcal H_k\) before applying Example 3.31 and Corollary 4.38. Thus a demonstrably false universal input occurs in a core comparison derivation, subsequently used in Corollaries 4.54 and 4.58. The assessment is Major for this derivation. It does not assert a counterexample to the resulting Hyodo–Kato comparison or the preceding motivic equivalence. The classification follows the demonstrated dependency, not the length of the repair.

The appropriate local repair is to require nonzero algebraic numbers whose complex absolute values are \(q^{w/2}\), without the extra integrality requirement. Tate twisting then sends an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) to \(q^{-r}\lambda\) and weight \(w\) to \(w-2r\). The orthogonality needed in the proof survives: distinct weights have disjoint spectra for the linear operator \(\varphi^a\), so the corresponding Hom group vanishes. The two terms computing \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ext}}^1\) in Remark 2.48 have equal finite \(\mathbb Q_p\)-dimension; injectivity of their differential therefore gives surjectivity as well. Neither step uses integrality. This verifies the local spectral repair and the relevant Hom/Ext calculation, not a fresh proof of the external Weil theorem or every coherence in the complete comparison argument.

Problem 2 (The product object is not the asserted ordinary internal coalgebra).  Remark 2.40, PDF page 17 (printed 16), identifies all lax fixed points with comodules over \(\widehat H(t)=\prod_{n\ge0}t^{\otimes n}\). The internal-coalgebra and ordinary tensor interpretation established in §2.5 does not support that identification.
## A counterexample in the exact categorical setting

Let \(\mathcal C=D(\mathbb Q)\) and \(t=\mathbb Q[0]\). This is a presentable, compactly generated, \(\mathbb Q\)-linear stable symmetric monoidal category; \(t\) is compact, \(\operatorname{Alt}^2(t)=0\), and \(-\otimes t\) is the identity, which also preserves products. These satisfy the relevant assumptions, including the extra product-preservation condition.

For arbitrary endomorphisms the genuine forgetful right adjoint sends \(X\) to \((\prod_{n\ge0}X,\text{left shift})\); its comonad is \(G(X)=\prod_{n\ge0}X\). For ordinary internal comodules the corresponding functor would be \(\widehat H\otimes X\) with \(\widehat H=\prod_{n\ge0}\mathbb Q\). Put \(X=\bigoplus_{j\ge0}\mathbb Qe_j\). Every element of \[(\prod_{n\ge0}\mathbb Q)\otimes X\longrightarrow\prod_{n\ge0}X\] is a sequence lying in one common finite-dimensional subspace: write the input as a finite sum \(\sum_{\ell=1}^r a^{(\ell)}\otimes x_\ell\). Its coordinates all lie in \(\operatorname{span}(x_1,\ldots,x_r)\). The sequence \((e_n)_{n\ge0}\) does not. It occurs as the orbit of \(e_0\) for the admissible lax fixed point \(S(e_j)=e_{j+1}\). Remark 2.40 expressly permits nonnilpotent operators, so this is in its scope.

There is also a direct obstruction to the proposed canonical comultiplication. At \(\mathbb Q\), the comonad sends \(a=(a_n)\) to \((a_{i+j})_{i,j\ge0}\). Choose \(a_n=1/(n+1)\). Its matrix has infinite rank: for every nonzero \(c\in\mathbb R^m\), \[\sum_{i,j=0}^{m-1}\frac{c_i c_j}{i+j+1}
 =\int_0^1\left(\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}c_i x^i\right)^2\,dx>0.\] Every finite leading block is nonsingular, whereas every image of \(\widehat H\otimes\widehat H\) is a finite sum of rank-one matrices. The canonical map therefore cannot factor through that ordinary tensor product. This does not rule out unrelated coalgebra structures on the underlying vector space.
## Scope and supported correction

Comonadicity of the forgetful functor does not identify a comonad with tensoring by its value on the unit. Keeping coalgebras for the actual comonad \(G\) is a valid replacement in this example. A completed tensor product or a pro-category would require an explicit different statement and its own proof. No such replacement is silently assumed here. The consulted primary discussions [Retained latex: \cite[\S3.5.2]{FG}] and [Retained latex: \cite[Chapter 6, \S2.7.3--2.7.6]{GR}] themselves distinguish product/right-lax constructions from the corresponding comonad; they do not supply the missing internal-tensor identification.

This is Minor: §2.5 explicitly says it is not used later, and the main ind-nilpotent theorem uses a direct sum instead of this product. No central dependency on the false arbitrary-operator extension was established. Its peripheral role, rather than ease of deletion, determines the assessment.

Problem 3 (Two incorrect descriptions in the Hodge realization paragraph).  Remark 4.62, PDF page 44 (printed 43), calls the category of rational polarizable mixed Hodge structures semisimple and gives an off-diagonal vanishing criterion for intersections of Hodge filtrations. Both assertions fail as written.
## A nonsplit object with polarizable weight-graded pieces

The subobject \(\mathbb Qe_1\) and quotient \(\mathbb Q\bar e_0\) give an exact sequence \[0\longrightarrow\mathbb Q(1)\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow\mathbb Q(0)
 \longrightarrow0.\] A rational section must send \(1\) to \(e_0+a e_1\) for \(a\in\mathbb Q\). Preservation of \(F^0\) forces \(a=i\), which is impossible. Hence the sequence does not split and the mixed category is not semisimple. This objection does not misapply the familiar semisimplicity of pure polarizable Hodge structures of a fixed weight.
## The adjacent intersection formula

The same paragraph sets \(V_\mathbb C^{p,q}=F^pV_\mathbb C\cap\overline{F^qV_\mathbb C}\) and requires its vanishing for \(p+q
e n\) to express weight \(n\). The source image confirms the conjugation and the quantifier. Its own next example \(\mathbb Q(1)\) has \(F^{-1}=V_\mathbb C\), hence \(F^{-2}=V_\mathbb C\); therefore \[F^{-2}V_\mathbb C\cap\overline{F^{-2}V_\mathbb C}=V_\mathbb C
e0,\qquad
 (-2)+(-2)=-4
e-2.\] Indeed sufficiently negative indices obstruct this condition for any nonzero finite-dimensional filtered vector space. On a pure weight-\(n\) structure, the intersection formula defines Hodge summands on \(p+q=n\); it must not impose the stated off-diagonal condition on all filtration intersections. An equivalent correct purity criterion is \[V_\mathbb C=F^pV_\mathbb C\oplus\overline{F^{\,n-p+1}V_\mathbb C}
 \quad\hbox{for every }p .\]
## Dependency and repair boundary

The two local errors are assessed Minor. Example 3.31 does not require mixed-category semisimplicity. The correct homological dimension-one statement, different-weight Hom vanishing and higher-weight Ext vanishing suffice for its application. For the last assertion, an extension of pure \(X_i\) by pure \(X_j\) with \(j>i\) splits: strictness of \(W\) identifies \(W_iE\to X_i\) as an isomorphism, providing a section. Together with the correct pure-Hodge criterion, these properties repair the stated local reasoning without discarding mixed extension data. The entire realization theorem is not independently reconstructed here, and these examples do not demonstrate failure of a central motivic or \(p\)-adic conclusion.
# Other checks and remaining limits

The two triangles in Proposition 4.64 produce the chain in Remark 4.68 by composing their connecting maps. With \(A=\iota^!M\), \(B=\iota^*M\), \(C=\chi_{\rm alg}j^*M\), \(D=\Psi\operatorname{An}^*j^*M\) and \(E=D(-1)\), the two triangles are \(C\to D\to E\) and \(A\to B\to C\). Each adjacent composition in \[\cdots\longrightarrow B_n\longrightarrow D_n\longrightarrow E_n
 \longrightarrow A_{n-2}\longrightarrow B_{n-2}\longrightarrow\cdots\] vanishes by one of the original long exact sequences. Remark 4.69 gives \(A=M_k(X_k)\{-d-1\}\); setting \(n=-r\) turns \(A_{n-2}\) into \(H_{2d-r}(X_k)(-d-1)\). This verifies the two-step degree change and twist in Corollary 4.70. The dimension-zero good-reduction case gives the expected segment \(\mathbb Q\xrightarrow{\rm id}\mathbb Q\xrightarrow0\mathbb Q(-1)
\xrightarrow{\rm id}\mathbb Q(-1)\).

Corollary 4.70 has discrete valuation, flatness, properness, regularity, generic smoothness and polystable reduction among its hypotheses. Remark 4.71 conditions exactness on weight–monodromy. Construction of a chain complex was not misread as unconditional exactness. The more general introductory \(\mathcal O_C\) formulation was read, but its full descent bridge from the displayed body hypotheses was not independently established. This is retained as a scope limitation, without a manufactured counterexample. The generalization suggested in Example 4.73 remains explicitly an expectation.

No independent reconstruction of every cited foundational theorem, six-functor formalism, higher coherence, descent argument or weight–monodromy result is claimed. Reading all text and mechanically extracting all pages are recorded separately from the bounded proofs actually checked.
# Conclusion and state

The highest supported assessment is Major, for Problem Problem 1 (#prob:purity)’s false premise in the central comparison derivation. Problems Problem 2 (#prob:product) and Problem 3 (#prob:hodge) have local impact on the evidence checked. The final comparison is not disproved; explicit local corrections have been described with their verification boundaries.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the 19-page arXiv version 2304.01868v4 by Przemysław Berk and Frank Trujillo. All source pages were read, with focused checks of essential values, reflection identities, Rauzy towers, the centre-projection input and the final rigidity construction. A central-tower branch doubles the same return tower, invalidating the local Birkhoff-sum calculation used to produce the essential value minus one. A positive twelve-step Rauzy example, checked by exact arithmetic, makes the error explicit. This is a Major defect in the presented proof; it does not establish that the main ergodicity theorem is false. Two local statement corrections concern positive return times and the order of quantifiers. Infinite subsequence selection and a complete repair of the main proof remain outside the certified result. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI technical verification

Title: Technical review of
On the ergodicity of infinite antisymmetric extensions of symmetric IETs
# Source identity and scope

The assigned identifier is M25-0262. The frozen title is On the ergodicity of infinite antisymmetric extensions of symmetric IETs; its authors are Przemysław Berk and Frank Trujillo, and the journal DOI is `10.4171/jems/1635`. The actual artifact is arXiv `2304.01868v4`, dated 4 April 2024 (submission time 14:39:39 UTC), with 19 pages. The 2025 batch membership is retained. No equivalence to a later publisher version is assumed. All page references below are physical PDF pages, which agree with the printed pagination in this manuscript.

The complete source, including its bibliography, was read. The independent checks concern the hypotheses of Theorem 2.1, the definitions and criterion in Section 4, the cancellation identities in Section 5, the quantifiers and centre locations in Lemma 6.1, and the length, height, measure and Birkhoff-sum steps of Section 7. Selected source pages were inspected as images. The consulted part of the cited centre-location paper [BTU] is pages 19–21, including Lemma 3.12 and its proof; this is not a claim to have independently reviewed that entire paper.

The manifest’s bounded searches identified no supplementary mathematical file or author code. No author code was executed. A separate correction search did not establish an applicable correction to this exact version; the inconclusive search is not evidence that none exists.
# Framework and checks that survive

For a symmetric interval exchange \(T\) on \(I=[0,1)\), the cocycle is \[f=\chi_{(0,1/2)}-\chi_{(1/2,1)},\qquad
 T_f(x,m)=(Tx,m+f(x)).\] Theorem 2.1 asserts ergodicity of \(T_f\) for Lebesgue almost every length parameter, with product Lebesgue and counting measure. Its quantifier does not assert the conclusion for every minimal IET. The special coboundary example and the parity obstruction to ergodicity of \(T_f\times T_f\) therefore do not contradict the theorem.

Away from the exceptional discontinuity orbits, reflection gives \(\iota T=T^{-1}\iota\), and the negative cocycle convention is \(S_{-n}f=-S_nf\circ T^{-n}\). These give the identities in Lemma 5.2 and Corollary 5.3. In particular, \[S_{2n}f(T^{-n}(1/2))=-f(T^n(1/2)).\] This sign was independently checked; it is not the cause of Problem 1.

The partial-rigidity criterion of Proposition 4.2 has a direct verification. If \(\mu(\Xi_j)\to\delta>0\) and \(\mu(T\Xi_j\mathbin{\triangle}\Xi_j)\to0\), every weak-star limit of \(\chi_{\Xi_j}\) is invariant and hence equals \(\delta\) by ergodicity. Approximation of \(\chi_A\) by continuous functions on the compact metric space, together with uniform closeness of \(T^{h_j}x\) to \(x\) on \(\Xi_j\), then gives positive measure to \(A\cap T^{-h_j}A\cap\Xi_j\). If \(S_{h_j}f=a\) there, this supplies the required positive-time essential-value witness. Thus the outstanding core difficulty is the claimed fixed value on the constructed sets.

The measure estimate in the odd case uses \[\mathop{\mathrm{Leb}}(\Xi_k)=q_k\lambda_\alpha^{n_k}/5.\] The preceding sentence on page 14 omits the factor \(1/5\), but the subsequent constant \(10d\rho(\gamma)\) uses the correct factor. Likewise the length comparisons must be read homogeneously after normalizing by \(|I^{n_k}|\). These local presentation slips do not by themselves invalidate the positive lower bound. The near-invariance estimate is \(\mu(T\Xi_k\triangle\Xi_k)\leq2\mu(B_k)\to0\). Neither fact establishes the Birkhoff-sum identity.
# Confirmed findings

Problem 1 (The central branch counts the same tower twice).  In Case A, the time \(h_k=h_\alpha^{n_k}+h_{\bar\alpha}^{n_k}\) is defined on page 12. Figure 1(ii), page 15, explicitly includes \(\alpha=\bar\alpha\), the central label. Claim A4, page 14, asserts \[S_{h_k}f(x)-S_{h_k}f(1/2)=f(T^ix),\qquad 0\leq i<q_k. \tag{A4}\] Its proof counts each level of the two towers once. When the two labels coincide, these are the same tower, traversed twice. The asserted calculation is false in this permitted local branch.
## A genuine positive Rauzy configuration

Use labels \(a,b,c\) and the symmetric permutation \[\pi=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\c&b&a\end{pmatrix}.\] Let \(t\) and \(b\) denote top and bottom wins, respectively. The word \(\eta=(tbtbtb)^2\) returns to \(\pi\) and has length matrix \[B=\begin{pmatrix}5&8&4\\12&21&8\\12&20&9\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det B=1.\] All entries are positive. Define \[\mu_a=1+\frac{\sqrt2}{10^5},\quad
 \mu_b=1,\quad
 \mu_c=1-\frac{\sqrt3}{10^5},\qquad
 L=\mathbf1^{\top}B\mu,\quad \lambda=B\mu/L.\] Every winner inequality in the twelve-step path is strict. The induced lengths at time 12 are \(\mu/L\), the induced permutation is \(\pi\), and the tower heights are the column sums \[(h_a^{12},h_b^{12},h_c^{12})=(29,49,21).\] The normalized vector \(\mu/|\mu|\) belongs to the open set in equation (6) on page 10: each coordinate differs from \(1/3\) by less than \(1/2700\).

The three coordinates of \(\mu\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\). The invertible integer matrix \(B\) preserves this property. Thus this is not a zero-length or terminating rational example. A connection between an interior discontinuity and another would impose a nonzero integer relation on the lengths. The same affine calculation, with half-integer centre coefficients, excludes the midpoint’s landing on a discontinuity in the checked orbit.

Let \(p_{12}\) be the first backwards projection to \(I^{12}\). Direct iteration gives \[\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
 z&c_a&c_b&c_c&1/2\\ \hline
 \text{projection time}&17&27&13&3\\
 p_{12}(z)&c_a^{12}&c_b^{12}&c_c^{12}&|I^{12}|/2 .
\end{array}\] Consequently the centre-set identity used from Lemma 6.1 holds at this time, \(\ell=3\), \(\alpha=\bar\alpha=b\), and \(q=21\). The paper’s time is \(h=98\).
## Exact violation

Equation reference: eq:sums. Set \[y=c_b^{12}+\frac{3\mu_b}{10L},\qquad x=T^3y.\] Since \(1/5<3/10<2/5\), this is a point of the specified base \(B_k\); take \(i=0\) in (A4). In particular, \[x-\frac12=\frac{(\mu_a-\mu_c)/2+3\mu_b/10}{L}>0,\qquad f(x)=-1.\] Exact iteration of the original IET gives \[\begin{aligned}
 S_{49}f(1/2)&=0,& S_{98}f(1/2)&=1,\\
 S_{49}f(x)&=-1,& S_{98}f(x)&=-2.
 \end{aligned}\] Thus the two sides of (A4) are \(-3\) and \(-1\). Equation (15), page 15, asserting \(S_hf(1/2)=0\), also fails here.

For transparency, the midpoint’s first 49 terms contain 24 positive values, 24 negative values and its initial zero. The next 49 contain 25 positive and 24 negative values. The 98 terms at \(x\) contain 48 positive and 50 negative values. The independent calculation stores each Rauzy step, each centre projection, the sign lists, and 2,039 certified comparisons. Coordinates are represented as \(a+b\sqrt2+c\sqrt3\) with rational coefficients. Radical signs are certified by rational lower and upper bounds obtained with integer square roots; no floating-point branch decision or author code is used.

There is also a short obstruction independent of these particular sums. In the central branch \(h=2h_\alpha\) is even. Off the null set of orbits meeting \(0\) or \(1/2\), every term of \(S_hf\) is \(\pm1\), and hence \(S_hf\in2\mathbb Z\). Equation (13), which requires the odd value \(-1\) on \(\Xi_k\), cannot hold almost everywhere in this branch.
## Scope, counterevidence and impact

The finite example checks the positive path, symmetric return, balanced induced lengths, centre projections, tower heights and the admissible point used by the local argument. Its branch calculations persist for nearby lengths; they are not caused by a boundary convention. A bounded affine check gives strict partition margins at \(\mu=(1,1,1)\) of at least \(0.5\) for the midpoint and \(0.2\) for \(x\). The relevant coefficient norms are at most \(40.5\) and \(40.8\). Consequently the inequalities persist in \(|\mu_j-1|<10^{-4}\), \(\mu_a>\mu_c\); the sign at time 49 is set by \(T^{49}(1/2)-1/2=(\mu_c-\mu_a)/L<0\).

This review has not constructed a whole infinite sequence with the specified fixed suffix and time 12 among its members. Nor has it proved that every selectable good subsequence has infinitely many central times. The counterexample refutes the local calculation from the local hypotheses actually used, and the parity argument applies whenever the explicitly admitted central branch occurs. Lemma 6.1 and the consulted centre-location lemma do not state an exclusion of that branch. Avoiding it would require an additional selection argument.

The dependency is Claim A4 \(\Rightarrow\) equations (14)–(15) \(\Rightarrow\) equation (13) \(\Rightarrow\) the use of Proposition 4.2 to obtain \(-1\in\mathop{\mathrm{Ess}}(T_f)\) in the odd case. This is a central derivation, so the assessment is Major. The assessment neither requires nor asserts a counterexample to Theorem 2.1 itself.
## Repair boundary

A concrete repair direction is to use \(h_\alpha\) once when \(\alpha=\bar\alpha\), retaining \(h_\alpha+h_{\bar\alpha}\) otherwise. The displacement estimate (9) is then stronger than the needed central-interval margin, and a single passage restores the once-per-level count. The two values at time 49 in [eq:sums] (#eq:sums) verify this local repair on the explicit example. Combining the corrected single-passage identity with Corollary 5.3 gives the intended zero at the midpoint under the stated local geometry. A complete revision must still check the global choice of times, the partial-rigidity estimates and all branch dependencies; this report does not certify that revision as completed or adopted by the authors.

Problem 2 (Positive-time essential values do not satisfy the stated general theorem).  The definition on page 7 requires \(n\in\mathbb N\), but Theorem 4.1 then asserts a subgroup property and the full ergodicity criterion for arbitrary measurable cocycles.

Take a one-point probability space, \(T=\mathrm{id}\), \(G=\mathbb Z\) with counting Haar measure and \(\varphi=1\). This meets every displayed hypothesis of Theorem 4.1. For a sufficiently small ball around an integer \(a\), the definition holds precisely when \(a=n\) for an allowed \(n\in\mathbb N\). Hence \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ess}}(T_\varphi)\) is the positive integers (or the nonnegative integers if \(0\in\mathbb N\)), not a subgroup. Meanwhile \(T_\varphi\) is the translation \(m\mapsto m+1\) on \(\mathbb Z\); every invariant set is empty or all of \(\mathbb Z\), so it is ergodic. It therefore also contradicts the asserted equivalence.

A consistent invertible formulation uses integer times, including the identity time in the usual convention, or states appropriate recurrence hypotheses and proves the positive-time version. The main cocycle is zero-mean, and Proposition 4.2 supplies the specific positive-time witness needed there, so this example alone establishes no additional failure of the main conclusion. The assessment is Minor, a local definition–theorem mismatch. The recurrence assumption must not be silently added to the theorem when assessing its present text.

Problem 3 (The literal order of quantifiers in Lemma 6.1 is too strong).  Page 9 says that for almost every symmetric IET \(T\), and for every positive-measure subset \(A\) of the length simplex, certain normalized Rauzy iterates belong to \(A\).

Fix any \(T\) for which induction is indefinitely defined, and write \[D_T=\{\lambda^n/|\lambda^n|:n\geq0\},\qquad A_T=\Lambda_{\mathcal A}
 \setminus D_T .\] For \(d\geq2\), \(D_T\) is countable and Borel, while \(A_T\) has full Lebesgue measure in the simplex. No normalized iterate belongs to \(A_T\). Thus no single \(T\) can satisfy the literal universal assertion over all positive-measure measurable sets.

The needed correction is: for each fixed measurable \(A\) of positive measure, the assertion holds for almost every \(T\), allowing the null exceptional set to depend on \(A\). Alternatively, a separately proved uniform statement for open sets may suffice. Section 7 fixes its open set \(A\) in advance for each \(d\), so this correction preserves the intended use; it does not itself repair Problem 1. The consulted recurrence proof in [BTU], pages 19–21, chooses a fixed open neighbourhood before applying recurrence, consistent with this distinction. Assessment: Minor, at the level of the literal statement.
# Coverage limits and disposition

The even case was read, including its special three-tower time and Claims B1–B4. Its measure and invariance estimates were checked, but its entire multi-visit cancellation argument was not independently reconstructed. A possible analogous counting difficulty was not promoted to a finding without a complete admissible counterexample. Boundary identities outside the generic discontinuity-free orbit were likewise not used to claim a main-theorem defect.

The foundational Rauzy–Veech ergodicity results, all external cocycle criteria and a full infinite central-return construction were not independently reproved. These are explicit limits on the coverage, not a substitute for a counterexample. The assessment is one confirmed Major proof-step issue and two local Minor statement issues. The current report concerns only the exact v4 source. Author adoption is unknown; no human review or independent acceptance is asserted.
