Title: Technical review of
The \(2D\) nonlinear shallow water equations
with a partially immersed obstacle
# Source identity and review scope

The assigned identifier is M25-0263. The frozen title is The \(2D\) nonlinear shallow water equations with a partially immersed obstacle, by Tatsuo Iguchi and David Lannes; the journal DOI is `10.4171/jems/1636`. The actual source is `arXiv:2306.15285v1`, submitted 27 June 2023 at 08:18:03 UTC, with 63 pages. The frozen 2025 batch assignment is retained. No equivalence with the publisher’s version is assumed. All page references below refer to this exact PDF; its physical and printed page numbers agree.

The review covers the modeling and potential reduction, definitions of the boundary and time norms, weak dissipativity, generalized vorticity, nonlinear energy estimates, regularization, compatible-data approximation, linear existence, and the final nonlinear closure. Reading every page is distinct from reconstructing every cited external result. The independent derivations below are the decisive checks. Three native AI auxiliaries supplied bounded text and proof checks; the primary reviewer integrated them, independently verified the polar compatibility identities, and performed the recorded source and report image inspections. No human review or independent acceptance is represented.
# Assessment and proof dependencies

The overall assessment is Major. Problem 1 disproves a quantitative conclusion of Theorem 5 under all of its assumptions. Problem 2 invalidates the displayed compatible-approximation construction used in Theorem 4. Problem 3 disproves the basic weak-dissipation estimate from which the higher estimates are derived. Their severity reflects those actual roles; the availability of repairs does not remove the failures as printed.

The dependence is particularly concrete. Proposition 6 enters Propositions 7 and 8 and Theorems 1 and 2, then the transformed shallow-water estimates. Proposition 16 supplies Theorem 4, Step 2, and its compatible approximation is invoked again in Section 7.4. Theorem 5 is the final nonlinear statement. The examples do not disprove its intended existence, uniqueness, or the membership in equation (136). Problems 4 and 5 are Minor: the main-body normalization and the actual nonzero-eigenvalue reconstruction already indicate their local corrections.
# Confirmed substantive findings

Problem 1 (Major: an extra boundary derivative in Theorem 5).  On p. 57, after (136), Theorem 5 asserts \[\|u\|_{\mathbb W_T^m}+|\mathfrak d_{\rm tan}\psi_i|_{\mathbb W_{b,T}^{m+1/2}}
 \le C(c_0^{-1},M_0).\] The hypotheses bound the initial tangential derivative only in \(H^{m-1/2}(\Gamma)\). By the definition on p. 15, the displayed conclusion would bound its \(H^{m+1/2}\) norm at time zero. The following construction verifies that compatibility does not supply this missing derivative.
## A smooth family satisfying every compatibility condition

Take \(\mathcal I\) to be the unit disk, \(\mathcal E=\{r>1\}\), and \(H_0=h_i=g=1\), so \(\zeta_w=0\) and \(\Lambda=|D_\theta|\). These satisfy Assumption 1. Set \(m=3\) and \(c_0=1/4\). For a fixed sufficiently small \(\delta>0\) and integers \(n\ge2\), let \[\psi_n=\delta n^{-7/2}\cos(n\theta),\qquad
 p=\Lambda\psi_n,\qquad q=\partial_\theta\psi_n.\] Thus \(p'=nq\), \(q'=-np\), and \(p^2+q^2\) is constant. Here primes mean tangential derivatives. Prescribe the initial normal jets at \(r=1\) by \[\phi=\psi_n,\quad \phi_r=p,\quad \phi_{rr}=0,\quad \phi_{rrr}=d,
 \qquad \zeta=0,\quad \zeta_r=a,\quad \zeta_{rr}=0,
 \qquad a=\frac{(n-1)(p^2-q^2)}{1+p^2}.\] Set \(v=\nabla\phi\). The irrotationality and potential matching required for Proposition 9 hold, including tangential matching.

Equation reference: R. The initial time jets are generated directly from \[\zeta_t=-\mathop{\mathrm{div}}((1+\zeta)\nabla\phi),\qquad
 \phi_t=-\zeta-\tfrac12|\nabla\phi|^2.\] Write \(G=(1+\zeta)\phi_r-\Lambda(\phi|_\Gamma)\). These recursions are the potential form of (134), and the required conditions (135) are \(G=G_t=G_{tt}=0\). The first two are \[G=p-\Lambda\psi_n=0,\qquad
 G_t=(n-1)(p^2-q^2)-(1+p^2)a=0.\] For completeness, define \[\begin{aligned}
 D&=p+q',& Z&=-D-ap,& U&=-a-qp'+q^2,\\
 Z_{r,0}&=-aD-(-p+p''-2q')-a'q,&
 W&=-3q^2+4qp'-(p')^2,& V&=-Z-pU,\end{aligned}\] and \[
\begin{split}
 R={}&-(1+p^2)Z_{r,0}-2pW-pZD-pqZ'\\
    &+[2Z-p(1+a)]U-qU'-\Lambda V.
\end{split}\] Direct polar differentiation gives \[G_{tt}=(1+3p^2)d+R.\] Choose \(d=-R/(1+3p^2)\). This is a smooth real function and makes the second-order compatibility condition exact.

To make this calculation reproducible, the intermediate identities are \[\zeta_{tr}=Z_{r,0}-d,\qquad \phi_{trr}=W-pd,\] \[\phi_{ttr}=(1+p^2)d-Z_{r,0}-pW-qU',\qquad
 \zeta_{tt}=2pd-ZD-pZ_{r,0}-qZ'-W-(1+a)U.\] The trace \(\phi_t=-(p^2+q^2)/2\) is constant in \(\theta\), and \(\phi_{tt}|_\Gamma=V\). Substitution into \(G_{tt}=\zeta_{tt}p+2ZU+\phi_{ttr}-\Lambda V\) gives [R] (#R). A self-written symbolic differentiation of the polar PDE independently verified these identities with exact zero residuals; it did not execute author code.
## Uniform norms and the contradiction

The jets have the uniform bounds \[\|p\|_{H^{5/2}}+\|q\|_{H^{5/2}}\le C\delta,\qquad
 \|a\|_{H^{3/2}}\le C\delta^2,\qquad
 \|d\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\delta.\] Indeed \(D,Z,U,V\) have the needed \(H^{3/2}\) bounds; \(Z_{r,0}\) and \(R\) have \(H^{1/2}\) bounds. The largest linear second derivative, \(p''\), has amplitude \(\delta n^{-1/2}\) and bounded \(H^{1/2}\) norm. Multiplication by \(H^{3/2}\) functions, the map \(\Lambda:H^{3/2}\to H^{1/2}\), and composition with the positive denominators above preserve these bounds.
## Impact and repair boundary

The excessive uniform estimate is part of the main theorem, rather than a consequence of choosing incompatible data. The proof on pp. 60–61 controls a lower boundary order. A suitable correction uses that order, or explicitly the energy seminorm \[\sup_{0\le t\le T}\sum_{j=0}^{m}
 |\mathfrak d_{\rm tan}\partial_t^j\psi_i(t)|_{H^{m-j-1/2}}.\] The existence and uniqueness conclusion and \(\psi_i\in\mathbb W_{b,T}^{m+1/2}\) are not contradicted. Simply deleting \(\mathfrak d_{\rm tan}\) from the printed bound would introduce another issue: \(M_0\) does not bound the additive constant of \(\psi_i\). Such a full-potential bound needs a gauge or an initial constant-mode bound.

Problem 2 (Major: the approximation in Proposition 16 loses \(g_1\)).  Equation (110), p. 48, requires \(N\cdot u_j^{II}=\Lambda\psi_{i,j}
+(\partial_t^j g_1)|_{t=0}\). The correction displayed in the proof of Proposition 16, p. 52, omits this last term. Its following assertion that the uncorrected residual tends to zero is likewise false for general \(g_1\). Theorem 4, Step 2, p. 54, still treats arbitrary \(g_1^{(n)}\); there is no prior homogeneous reduction.

Use the unit disk with \(h_i=1\) and the constant matrix \(S=I_3\). Choose a smooth radial \(\chi\) equal to one near \(r=1\) and zero for \(r\ge2\). The time-independent fields and data \[u=(0,\chi(r)e_r),\qquad \psi_i=0,\qquad
 f=(\chi'(r)+\chi(r)/r,0,0),\qquad g_1=1,\quad g_2=0\] solve (103)–(105) exactly: \(G_j\partial_j u=f\), \(N\cdot u^{II}=1=\Lambda\psi_i+g_1\), and \(\partial_t\psi_i+u^I=0\). They have all the stipulated regularity and positivity, and all positive time jets vanish. Thus compatibility holds to every order.

This disproves the displayed construction, not the existential statement of Proposition 16. Its role in constructing compatible smooth data for Theorem 4 makes the gap substantive. Nonzero commutator boundary data also occur in the final tangential application on p. 61. A complete corrected approximation proof has not been certified by this review.

Problem 3 (Major: a final signed flux does not bound the past peak).  Equation (45), p. 21, and Proposition 6, p. 22, use the final cumulative signed boundary flux to control the norm \(I_{\lambda,t}\), which includes a supremum over earlier times. Outflow can cancel earlier inflow without erasing that supremum. The following smooth example satisfies Assumption 2 and Definition 2.

Let \(\mathcal E=\{r>1\}\), use a scalar unknown, and set \(S=1\), \(B=f=0\). Put \[T_*=\frac1{100},\qquad b=\frac{T_*}{8\pi},\qquad
 s(t)=-2b\cos(2\pi t/T_*).\] Then \[a(t)=s'(t)=\tfrac12\sin(2\pi t/T_*),
 \qquad A_j=a(t)\frac{x_j}{r}.\] All coefficients are smooth. Since \(|a|\le1/2\) and \(\mathop{\mathrm{div}}A=a/r\le1/2\), Assumption 2 holds with \(\alpha_0=\beta_0=\beta_0^{\rm in}=\beta_1=1\). That assumption does not bound \(\partial_t A\). For nonzero \(\eta\in C_c^\infty(-b,b)\), let \[u(t,x)=\eta(r-1-s(t)).\] Then \(u_t+A_j\partial_j u=0\), \(u(0)=u(T_*)=0\), and \(u\) is nonzero at intermediate times. Its support is in a fixed boundary collar. Prescribe its smooth boundary trace \(g_b=u|_\Gamma\).

Take \(\lambda=1\), and write \(E(t)=\|u(t)\|_2^2\) and \(M=\max_{[0,T_*]}e^{-2t}E(t)>0\). The exterior outward normal is \(-e_r\), so integration by parts gives \[E'(t)=\int_\Gamma a u^2+\int_\mathcal E\frac{a(t)}r u^2.\] Since both endpoint energies vanish, \[F:=\int_0^{T_*}e^{-2t}\int_\Gamma a u^2
 =\int_0^{T_*}e^{-2t}\int_\mathcal E(2-a/r)u^2
 \le\tfrac52 T_*M.\] Definition (28) yields \(I_{1,T_*}(\|u\|_2)^2\ge M\). Equation (45), with zero initial and body-source data, would give \(I^2\le4F\le M/10\). Proposition 6 would give \(I^2\le8(S_{\rm data}-E_{\rm bdry})=8F\le M/5\). Both are contradictions. No choice of the unspecified constant on the vanishing initial and body-source terms can fix them.
## A proved replacement estimate

Equation reference: repair. One must insert weak dissipativity into the endpoint energy identity before taking a supremum. Here is a sufficient repair with explicit, nonoptimal constants. Write \[v(t)=(S(t)u(t),u(t))^{1/2},\quad J=I_{\lambda,t}(v),\quad
 A=(S(0)u(0),u(0)),\quad
 B=\sqrt{\beta_0}\,S^*_{\lambda,t}(\|f\|_2).\] For \(\lambda\ge\beta_1/\alpha_0\), the endpoint inequality and Definition 2 bound, separately, \[X=\sup_{\tau\le t}e^{-2\lambda\tau}v(\tau)^2,\qquad
 Y+E_{\rm bdry}(t)
       =\lambda\int_0^t e^{-2\lambda\tau}v(\tau)^2\,d\tau
          +E_{\rm bdry}(t)\] by \(Q=A+2BJ+S_{\rm data}(t)+J^2/8\). This uses nonnegativity of the boundary energy and monotonicity of the data and source norms; it does not require monotonicity of \(E_{\rm bdry}\). Since \(J^2\le2(X+Y)\), it follows that \[\tfrac12J^2+2E_{\rm bdry}\le4A+8BJ+4S_{\rm data}.\] Young’s inequality \(8BJ\le J^2/4+64B^2\) then gives \[
\begin{split}
 I_{\lambda,t}(\|u\|_2)^2+\frac8{\alpha_0}E_{\rm bdry}
 \le{}&16\frac{\beta_0^{\rm in}}{\alpha_0}\|u(0)\|_2^2\\
 &+256\frac{\beta_0}{\alpha_0}
             \bigl(S^*_{\lambda,t}(\|f\|_2)\bigr)^2
 +\frac{16}{\alpha_0}S_{\rm data}.
\end{split}\] There is no added derivative or coefficient regularity requirement. The foundational estimate and its proof need correction, but [repair] (#repair) preserves the qualitative energy control. Later estimates with an unspecified data constant can accommodate such a change. This is not a counterexample to nonlinear local well-posedness; full propagation through every later constant is not asserted.
# Confirmed local corrections

Problem 4 (Minor: pressure and fixed-energy normalization).  The Bernoulli row in introductory (3), p. 4, omits the density factor present in the physical momentum equations on p. 3 and the consistent main-body formulation on p. 8. Take the unit disk, \(H_0=2\), \(h_i=1\), \(\zeta_w=-1\), \(g=1\), \(\rho=2\), \(P_{\rm atm}=0\), \(\zeta=v=v_i=\phi=\psi_i=0\), and \(\underline P_i=2\). These smooth stationary data satisfy the equations, positive depths, irrotationality, all matching and compatibility conditions, and strict subcriticality. The body uses \(\underline P_i+\rho g\zeta_w=0\), which holds. Equation (3) instead requires \(0=\underline P_i+g\zeta_w=1\). Divide its pressure terms by \(\rho\), or multiply its gravitational and kinetic terms by \(\rho\). The main-body argument already uses the consistent convention.

On p. 31, the equality of reduced energy with \(\mathfrak E_{\rm fluid}/\rho\) also misses the fixed term \((g/2)\int_\mathcal I\zeta_w^2\). For the same equilibrium the reduced energy is zero whereas \(\mathfrak E_{\rm fluid}/\rho=\pi/2\). State equality up to this constant, or specify a relative-energy normalization. Its time derivative is zero, so the conservation argument is unaffected.

Problem 5 (Minor: the first inverse-eigenvalue index).  Assumption 6(i), p. 27, starts its inverse-eigenvalue list at \(\lambda_{n_1}^{-1}\). The intended nonzero block starts at \(n_1+1\), as in Lemma 3. Corollary 2 on p. 39 uses \(n_1=1\), \(n_2=2\), and eigenvalues \(0,1,-1\); these occur already for the constant positive matrix \(S=I_3\). The literal list would therefore require the reciprocal of zero in the very application it is meant to cover. Change its first index to \(n_1+1\). This is a mismatch between a written assumption and its application, not a counterexample to a theorem conditional on a stronger assumption. The actual reconstruction only divides by nonzero eigenvalues.
# Checks without an established defect

The following checks delimit the findings. The interface vorticity flux cancellation follows from mass-flux matching and does not divide by a potentially vanishing normal velocity. The single Jordan boundary, zero interior vorticity, and tangential matching give zero exterior circulation, so the potential reduction includes the needed topological condition. Green’s identity gives positivity and self-adjointness of \(\Lambda\); its constant kernel is correctly handled by a tangential derivative seminorm.

The transformation by \(\Sigma(u)\), the constant matrices \(G_j\), and \(S=\Sigma^{-1}\) was checked algebraically. The generalized vorticity identities cancel the second spatial derivatives; the normal reconstruction needs the invertibility of \(L\), not an extra assumption that \(\widetilde A_0\) is invertible. Applying Lemma 3 to differentiated unknowns retains the original \(Q,W\), so this step does not itself demand an unlisted high derivative of \(Q\). The two-dimensional product estimates and the use of order \(m-1\) in the nonlinear application give the stated derivative count in the checked terms.

For \(m=3\), a uniform \(\mathbb W_T^3\) bound and strong \(\mathbb W_T^2\) continuity yield \(\mathbb W_T^{2,p}\) continuity for every finite \(p\) by interpolation. This supplies the weaker coefficient regularity used in Theorem 4. The two-dimensional acoustic normal block has determinant \((N\cdot v)^2-gh<0\) under subcriticality; conserved curl controls the remaining component. In Proposition 17, differentiated bulk and boundary residuals vanish, and (139) sets their initial values to zero. No separate failure of this recovery step was found.
# Coverage, limitations and disposition

All 63 source pages, including the bibliography, were read and viewed. The checks above reconstruct selected decisive arguments; they are not a new proof of all the external hyperbolic existence, elliptic regularity and Sobolev results cited by the authors. The high-frequency example proves a false uniform estimate, the stationary example proves a failed construction, and the pulse example proves a false energy inequality. None is being enlarged into an unproved assertion about every formulation or version of the main theorem.

Bounded searches for supplements, code and corrections produced no applicable separate item. This is a search limitation, not proof of absence and not a mathematical defect. The publisher text was not obtained for a version comparison. An exploratory concern about Proposition 5’s parameter dependence and a possible Proposition 15 sign discrepancy were not established under all hypotheses and are excluded from the findings.
Prior false or incomplete checkpoints remain historical records. Author adoption is unknown. The initial scientific decision remains pending; the human-review list is empty.

report: Abstract: This report reviews the exact 87-page, author-hosted, publisher-typeset online-first article by Maria Aguareles, Inmaculada Baldomá and Tere M-Seara. The assessment is Major. An analytic energy bound for the degree-two vortex proves that the paper’s prescribed interval contains no root of its exact dominant phase-matching equation. The sign responsible for that failure propagates to the main prefactor derivation. Independent checks identify an incorrect parameter-universality claim for the physical wavenumber, non-equivalent inner fixed-point equations, an overly broad uniform outer estimate, and a reversed matching inverse used in the final Brouwer construction. There are five Major and two Minor findings; the earlier zero-twist candidate is retained only as a scope clarification because its counterexample leaves the printed real-valued class. A fully admissible boundary example disproves a dominant-profile monotonicity assertion. The evidence distinguishes false statements and failed proof constructions from claims about a fully repaired global theorem. All source text pages were read; decisive source pages were also inspected as images. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

# Source identity, scope and assessment

The assigned paper is M25-0264, with frozen title A rigorous derivation of the asymptotic wavenumber in spiral wave solutions of the complex Ginzburg–Landau equation, by Maria Aguareles, Inmaculada Baldomá and Tere M-Seara. The DOI is `10.4171/jems/1637`. The reviewed source is the author-hosted EMS publisher-typeset online-first PDF: 87 pages, 1,470,083 bytes, copyright 2025, received 11 July 2023 and revised 12 January 2024. The EMS record gives publication on 14 May 2025. The author’s filename ending in `online2026.pdf` does not change the frozen year or establish a later scientific version. No byte equivalence with a separately obtained publisher file or the June 2023 arXiv version is assumed. Physical and printed page numbers agree in this source. Its SHA256 is

The review covers definitions, the physical-to-normalized reduction, the selected branch, both singular boundary regimes, all matching steps, the inner and outer fixed-point constructions, the Bessel appendix and the vortex appendix. Reading all pages is distinct from independently reconstructing every external theorem. Three native AI auxiliaries supplied bounded initial checks; the initial reviewer read their records, checked the decisive algebra and asymptotics independently, and performed the recorded source and report image inspections. Those initial checks did not constitute independent acceptance. The current focused acceptance and its read-only auxiliary are separately attributed in verification records. No human review is claimed.

The Major assessment rests on Problems 1–4 and P6 below. Proposition 4.6 is a core matching assertion, Theorem 1.5 states the physical selection, Section 6 supplies the inner family, and Theorems 4.3 and 5.3 supply the outer family and their uniform bounds. P6 breaks the claimed equivalence of the actual nonlinear matching equations and the map used for Brouwer’s theorem. Local repairability does not make these substantial failures immaterial. Problem 5 concerns a narrower domain assertion whose counterexample is outside the actual matching regime; it is Minor. The report does not claim that no spiral exists, that all global branches have been classified independently, or that a complete corrected main theorem has been established.
# Confirmed substantive findings

Problem 1 (Major: the prescribed dominant matching interval has no root).  Theorem 2.5, p. 15, defines \[C_n=\lim_{r\to\infty}
 \left(\int_0^r t f_0(t)^2(1-f_0(t)^2)\,dt-n^2\log r\right).\] Equations (3.21) and (4.11), pp. 21 and 26, reverse both the constant and the quadratic-wavenumber signs in the exact inner integral. The constant sign enters (4.26), p. 30, and the interval of Proposition 4.6, p. 29. For the allowed degree \(n=2\), that proposition is false with every matching hypothesis satisfied.
## The exact expansion and a nonzero constant

Equation reference: groundstate, cnnegative. To exclude the possibility that the constant vanishes, define \[E_R(u)=\int_0^R
 \left(ru'^2+\frac{n^2u^2}{r}+\frac r2(1-u^2)^2\right)\,dr.\] The vortex ODE gives the exact Pohozaev identity \[\left(\frac{r^2f'^2}{2}-\frac{n^2f^2}{2}
                -\frac{r^2(1-f^2)^2}{4}\right)'
       =-\frac r2(1-f^2)^2.\] All origin terms vanish since \(f\sim c r^n\), and the terms at infinity give \[\int_0^\infty r(1-f^2)^2\,dr=n^2.\] Multiplication of the ODE by \(rf\) also gives \[A(R)=\int_0^R\left(rf'^2+\frac{n^2f^2}{r}\right)\,dr-Rf(R)f'(R).\] Since \(Rf(R)f'(R)\to0\), \[C_n=E_{\rm ren}(f)-\frac{n^2}{2},\qquad
 E_{\rm ren}(u)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\bigl(E_R(u)-n^2\log R\bigr).\] No unproved global minimizing property is needed. Writing \(g=fh\) and integrating the ODE yields the identity \[\begin{aligned}
 E_R(g)-E_R(f)
 &=\int_0^R r f^2 h'^2\,dr
   +\frac12\int_0^R r(g^2-f^2)^2\,dr \notag\\
 &\quad+[rff'(h^2-1)]_0^R. \end{aligned}\] Use the admissible comparison \(g(r)=\min\{(r/L)^n,1\}\). It is continuous and locally \(H^1\). The identity applies on either side of \(L\), with cancelling intermediate boundary terms, or by smooth approximation. The endpoint terms vanish: at zero they are \(O(r^{2n})\), and at infinity they are \(O(r^{-4})\). Thus \(E_{\rm ren}(f)\le E_{\rm ren}(g)\), while direct integration gives \[E_{\rm ren}(g)=n-n^2\log L+
                \frac{n^2L^2}{2(n+1)(2n+1)}.\] Taking \(L^2=(n+1)(2n+1)\) proves \[
 C_n\le n-\frac{n^2}{2}\log((n+1)(2n+1)),\qquad
 C_2\le2-2\log15<0.\] The primary exact symbolic check independently verifies the two differential identities and the trial integral. The inequalities and endpoint limits above are analytic, not numerical shooting.
## A contradiction satisfying the complete matching assumptions

Moreover \(kr_0\to0\), \(1/(qr_0)\to0\), \(q|\log q|/\rho\to0\) and \(\rho\to0\). Thus all overlap and smallness conditions (4.4), (4.5), (4.12), (4.13), and (4.19)–(4.22) hold after reducing \(q\). The intermediate Bessel range and the inner restriction \(r_0\le n/(\sqrt2 k)\) also hold. No excluded zero endpoint is used.

The full-family error bounds asserted on pp. 25 and 27 cannot compensate for this gap. After multiplication by \(r_0/q\), they are \[O(q^2\log^3r_0)=O(|\log q|^{-1}),\qquad

#### Impact and repair.

The core construction selects the wrong interval and prefactor. With the present definition of \(C_n\), equation [gap] (#gap) instead requires \[\mu=2e^{\,C_n/n^2-\gamma}
                \bigl(1+O(|\log q|^{-1})\bigr).\] Both signs in [innercorrect] (#innercorrect), the interval, the phase fixed point and the main coefficient statements must be reconciled. The unconditional result here is the false exact dominant matching assertion and the invalid main prefactor derivation. It is not an independent proof of a corrected global existence theorem or a classification of all possible spiral branches.

Problem 2 (Major: the physical wavenumber is not a function of the twist alone).  Theorem 1.5 and Remark 1.6, p. 6, assert a universal physical selection depending only on \(q\). The exact change of variables in Lemma 2.3, pp. 12–13, contradicts that statement and its physical oddness claim.

Use \(A\) for the physical dispersion parameter, to distinguish it from the outer cutoff exponent. For any normalized branch \((F,v)\) with \(0<k<1\), put \[D=1-Aq(1-k^2),\qquad
 \beta=\frac{A+q}{1-Aq},\qquad a=\sqrt D,\] \[\delta^2=\frac D{1-Aq},\qquad
 \Omega=-\frac{A+q(1-k^2)}D.\] If \(\chi'=v\), then \[\mathcal{A}(t,r,\varphi)=
 \delta^{-1}F(r/a)
       e^{i\Omega t+in\varphi+i\chi(r/a)}\] solves the original CGL equation by direct substitution. The primary symbolic calculation verifies both real and imaginary equations. Its physical wavenumber and far-field amplitude satisfy \[K(A,q)=\frac{k}{\sqrt{1-Aq(1-k^2)}},\qquad
 \frac{1-k^2}{\delta^2}=1-K(A,q)^2.\] For \(0<q<1/3\), the parameter pairs \[(A,\beta)=(0,q),\qquad
 (A,\beta)=\left(1,\frac{1+q}{1-q}\right)\] have the same twist and both satisfy \(|A-\beta|<1\). Both frequencies are nonzero, both scalings are positive, and \(0<K<1\) because \(D-k^2=(1-q)(1-k^2)>0\) for the second pair. The regular core, integer winding, unique zero and far-field conditions survive this positive rescaling. Nevertheless, \[K(0,q)=k,\qquad
 K(1,q)=\frac{k}{\sqrt{1-q+qk^2}}>k.\] The universal theorem’s own asserted existence at the first pair therefore constructs a genuine solution at the second with a different physical wavenumber. This is an exact contradiction to existence plus universal \(q\)-only selection, without assuming a numerical approximation or an unrelated branch.

Likewise, normalized oddness \(\kappa(-q)=-\kappa(q)\) gives \[K(A,-q)=
 \frac{-\kappa(q)}{\sqrt{1+Aq(1-\kappa(q)^2)}}\ne-K(A,q)\] for fixed \(A\ne0\). The conjugation symmetry changes \(A\) as well. The correct physical statement must retain \(K(A,q)\) and the spatial, amplitude and frequency rescalings. For each bounded fixed \(A\), \(K/\kappa=1+O(q)\), so this defect alone does not change the leading relative accuracy \(O(|\log q|^{-1})\). Problem 1 concerns that leading coefficient independently.

Problem 3 (Major: the inner fixed-point equations do not solve the stated ODE).  Equation (6.7), p. 60, and Lemma 6.1, p. 61, use opposite inverse signs. The phase rewrite (6.6), p. 59, and its source (6.16), p. 64, also have incorrect coefficients. These affect the construction supplying Theorem 4.5, not an unused auxiliary formula.

Equation reference: greensign. Let \[L_n=\partial_s^2+s^{-1}\partial_s-(1+n^2/s^2).\] The positive kernel printed on p. 60 is \[\mathcal{K}\psi(s)=

The issue persists in the actual nonlinear branch, rather than only for an arbitrary test forcing. Choose allowed \(b=0\), small positive \(q\), \(k<1\), and the actual matching \(\rho\). If the claimed fixed-point representation and (6.7) both held, [greensign] (#greensign) would give \(N_1=0\) and \(\delta g=0\). Near zero, the actual base functions satisfy \[\widetilde f_0=A_0s^n+O(s^{n+2}),\quad
 \widetilde v_0=-d s+O(s^3),\quad
 \widetilde h_0=H s^{n+2}+O(s^{n+4}),\] with \(A_0,d>0\) and \(H\ne0\) for either of the inconsistent signs in the p. 59 definition of \(h_0\). The norm in Theorem 6.6 gives \(\delta v=O(s)\). At \(\delta g=0\) the nonlinear difference in (6.8) is \(O(s^{n+2})\), whereas \[\mathcal{E}[\widetilde h_0]
     =8(n+1)H s^n+O(s^{n+2}).\] Thus \(N_1[0,\delta v]=-4(n+1)Hs^n+O(s^{n+2})\ne0\). No such branch can simultaneously satisfy the displayed fixed-point formula and the differential equation it is claimed to solve.

Equation reference: phasecorrect. Independently, put \(f=f_0+g\) and \(\widehat v=v_0+w\) in the original phase equation (6.4b), and subtract the base equation. Exact algebra gives \[
 w'+\frac wr+2\frac{f_0'}{f_0}w
 =g(g+2f_0)

#### Impact and repair.

The inner fixed-point-to-ODE bridge fails. Correct the shift \(h_0\), the Green sign and linear resolvent, the phase coefficients and the coordinate factors, then re-establish the contraction, endpoint parameterization and estimates. Absolute-value estimates may survive some sign changes, but this review does not certify the complete corrected construction. The overlapping defects are grouped as one core construction problem.

Problem 4 (Major: the outer uniform cutoff range is too broad).  Theorems 4.3 and 5.3, pp. 24–25 and 43–44, quantify uniformly over \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) subject only to \(q^{-1}\epsilon^{1-\alpha}<e_0\), with constants independent of \(\alpha\). Their refined estimate at \(a=0\) is false in that range.

The uniform outer theorem and its refined bound are false. Lemma A.3, p. 79, actually allows \(q_0\) to depend on \(\alpha\); its proof uses \(\epsilon^\alpha\ll q\) and \(\sin(\pi\alpha/2+O(q))\) in a denominator. These are not uniform as \(\alpha\to0\). Restricting to \(\alpha\ge\alpha_*>0\) is a possible repair, provided all bounds are proved uniformly there. The actual matching choice satisfies \(\alpha\to1\), so this counterexample does not itself refute the final matching asymptotic. That distinction does not rescue the stated uniform theorem.
# A confirmed local range defect

Problem 5 (Minor: the dominant outer monotonicity starts too early).  Proposition 4.2(iii), p. 24, asserts \(\partial_rv_0^{\rm out}>0\) when \(kqr\ge2e^{-\pi/(2nq)}\). The endpoint admits a real, regular counterexample.

The cotangent comparison on p. 78 has its inequality reversed. The stronger threshold \(2e^2e^{-\pi/(2nq)}\) used for the Green estimates avoids this example, as does the actual matching point. A corrected monotonicity domain requires a corrected proof.

There is also a literal amplitude-domain obstruction in Proposition 4.2(iv) and Lemma A.3. Take \(n=1\), \(\mu=100\) in a fixed interval \([99,101]\), \(\alpha=1/2\), and \(R_{\min}=2e^2e^{-\pi/(2q)}\). For small \(q\) the stated domain inequalities hold, but \[F_0(R_{\min})^2
 \le1-\left(\frac{100}{2e^2}\right)^2<0.\] An explicit physical-radius or reality restriction is needed. The narrower domain of Theorem 4.3 avoids this case.
# Matching inverse and other checks
The following checks distinguish a core construction failure, a bounded substitution correction and an unconfirmed scope issue.
#### P6 (Major): matching inverse.

For the matching system on pp. 30 and 34, \[Ka-Ib=\Delta,\qquad K'a-I'b=\Delta'/\sqrt2,\qquad
 d=KI'-K'I\ne0,\] direct elimination gives \[a=\frac{I'\Delta-I\Delta'/\sqrt2}{d},\qquad

If the correct second component is \(b_*\), substitution of \((a,-b_*)\) into the displayed linear system leaves residuals \((2Ib_*,2I'b_*)\). Thus the asserted algebraic equivalence does not hold in general.

This sign is used in the comparison with \(b_0\) in (4.39), the Brouwer map in (4.40)–(4.42), and the global matching in (4.43) on p. 36. The actual core map and its consistency estimates therefore require correction. This is Major even though suitable absolute-value bounds may survive the corrected sign. No additional actual nonlinear matched solution or false global existence conclusion is manufactured from an arbitrary \(\Delta\).
#### Local correction P7 (Minor): displayed remainder substitutions.

On p. 33, \(q^3\log^3r_0/r_0=O(\rho^3/r_0)\), not \(O(\rho^3/r_0^2)\). The valid bound still gives \(O(|\log q|^{-1})\) after multiplication by \(r_0/q\). Likewise the normalization of the \(O(\rho^4)\) correction on pp. 34–35 gives \(O(\rho^2)\), which is still \(o(|\log q|^{-1})\). These corrections do not establish a failure of the needed final remainder order.
#### Scope clarification P8: the zero-twist evolution.

The exact transformation at \(q=0\) is \[\mathcal{A}=e^{-iA t}U
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 U_t=(1+iA)(\Delta U+U-|U|^2U).\] However, the equation on p. 5 explicitly restricts the rotated unknown to be real-valued. If \(A\ne0\) and \(U\) remains real, the imaginary part forces \(\Delta U+U-U^3=0\) and hence \(U_t=0\); these restricted solutions also satisfy the displayed real GL equation. For \(A=0\) the transformed equation already is real GL.

The earlier spatially constant solution with \(A=1\), \(U(0)=1/2\) has \(U'(0)=3(1+i)/8\) and immediately leaves that real-valued class. It is therefore not an all-hypothesis counterexample to the restricted statement. Its previous confirmed-Minor status is withdrawn. The rotation does not conjugate the general complex dynamics to real GL, but the intended scope of the prose needs clarification; no additional confirmed error is counted here.
#### Unresolved candidates.

Lemma 2.1, pp. 10–11, does not justify its nonlinear Fourier diagonalization: the cubic coefficient is \(\sum_{j-m+p=\ell}a_j\overline{a_m}a_p\), not \(|A_*|^2a_\ell\) before constant modulus is proved. No genuine CGL wave satisfying every hypothesis of Definition 1.1 was constructed to disprove the classification itself. Generic two-mode profiles and standing waves with a separate global temporal phase do not supply such a counterexample.

The comparison on pp. 38–39 substitutes \(v(r_*)^2\) where the defined operator retains \(v(r)^2\). Additional phase-gradient control is needed for that displayed inference. This review does not prove a nonmonotone global spiral. Questions about differentiation through the inner resolvent and independent smallness of \(q,\rho\) remain proof-scope limitations; they are not promoted to further confirmed false theorems.
# Coverage, counterchecks and limits

The radial reduction, positive rescaling identities, regular core orders, existence of the defining \(C_n\) limit, and the exact Bessel-to-Riccati identity were checked directly. The constants in the phase matching were traced through every normalization, including the factor two in the Bessel argument, Euler’s constant, and the distinction between physical and normalized wavenumbers. The degree-two energy certificate avoids both an assumed numerical value and an unproved variational minimizer assertion.

For the outer analysis, the weighted spaces, the real-order Green bounds, the first-order integral from infinity, boundary-layer decay, derivative control and the actual matching subrange were checked. For the inner analysis, the origin orders, weighted norms, shift, resolvent, phase integrating factor, fixed-point substitution and parameter dependence were read and checked to the extent specified above. A contraction for an incorrectly rewritten system does not prove the required ODE statement.

During the initial review, all 87 source pages, including both appendices and the bibliography, were read. The actual source-image record identifies each visually inspected page; it does not count rendering as viewing. The initial primary reviewer’s self-written Sympy check exited successfully and verified ten exact algebraic residuals. Analytic inequalities, existence implications, remainders and impact were assessed separately. No author code was executed.

Bounded searches of the title, DOI, author source, EMS record and arXiv metadata did not locate a separate applicable supplement, code release or correction. This is not proof of their absence, and lack of code is not treated as a defect. The arXiv metadata was not a full alternate-version comparison. NIST formula pages were consulted as text crosschecks; requests for four equation PNGs returned HTTP 403 and are preserved as failures, without an image-viewing claim. The decisive Bessel formulas used here are also present on the inspected source pages.

The earlier vortex existence and asymptotic results, and the external global uniqueness/classification inputs, were not all independently reproved. The report establishes the stated counterexamples and derivational failures, not a complete audit of every cited work or a fully repaired existence theorem. Runtime self-description and controller-reported UI observations are recorded separately; backend equivalence is not independently verified. The current findings are five Major and two Minor, with P8 withdrawn as a confirmed counterexample and retained as a scope clarification. Proof: ## P1: C_n sign, exact core matching counterexample

The source prints the opposite signs for C_n and k^2 r/2 in (3.21)/(4.11), and propagates +C_n into (4.26).

Writing g=f h and differentiating gives exactly
E_R(g)-E_R(f)=int r f^2 h'^2+(1/2)int r(g^2-f^2)^2+[r f f'(h^2-1)]_0^R.
Choose g=min((r/L)^n,1); it is continuous, piecewise C1 and locally H1, and the intermediate boundary terms cancel. Both endpoint terms vanish by the stated asymptotics. No unsupported global minimizer theorem is needed.
Direct integration gives E_ren(g)=n-n^2 log L+n^2 L^2/[2(n+1)(2n+1)].

Take the actual n=2 vortex, J_mu=[exp(-C_2/4-gamma),3exp(-C_2/4-gamma)], rho=(q/|log q|)^(1/3), r0=exp(rho/q)/sqrt2, epsilon=mu exp(-pi/(4q)), k=epsilon/q. report: Abstract: The assessment of this accepted author manuscript is Major. An exact rank-two example satisfies every hypothesis of the central lagrangian-complement lemma but disproves the basis construction used in its proof. The failure affects the stated route from the plus and minus surgery obstructions to the main classification results. A complete replacement proof of the algebraic lemma is provided, so the finding does not assert that the lemma or the main classification theorems are false. The Euler-characteristic inference used to establish simple connectedness in Corollary D is a second Major proof defect, with a meridian-monodromy repair. Six separate Minor statements require restriction or correction. All 64 physical source pages were read, and the recorded evidence pages were inspected as images. The source version, finite computations, external dependencies and limits of verification are distinguished throughout. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI technical verification

Title: Technical review of
Unknotting nonorientable surfaces
# Source identity and review scope

The assigned paper is M25-0265, Unknotting nonorientable surfaces, by Anthony Conway, Patrick Orson and Mark Powell, DOI `10.4171/jems/1638`. The reviewed file is the University of Glasgow repository’s accepted author version, item 340906: 63 article pages followed by a repository notice, 918,302 bytes. Physical and printed article page numbers agree. Its SHA256 is

The notice records deposit on 6 November 2024. The repository labels the file Accepted Version. The EMS record gives submission on 13 July 2023, acceptance on 20 October 2024 and online publication on 20 May 2025. The associated arXiv record has version 2 dated 23 November 2024. That metadata does not establish that the repository PDF, the arXiv PDF and the publisher PDF are textually identical. The file’s 2026 container timestamps are not used as a scientific revision date. The frozen title, authors, DOI and year are retained.

The principal statements concern locally flat nonorientable \(\mathbb Z_2\)-surfaces: unknottedness in the specified genus and normal Euler-number range, classification relative to a determinant-one boundary knot, stabilization by one orientable tube, branched covers, and realization of a prescribed Guillou–Marin isometry. The review checked the precise range and boundary hypotheses, the homology and intersection forms, the spin gluing, the modified surgery obstruction, the plus/minus algebra, the cancellation step, and the finite discriminant computations.

The assessment comprises two Major and six Minor findings. It includes the essential construction in Lemma 9.12 and the simple-connectedness inference used in Corollary D. Their repairability does not remove their importance to the submitted derivations. The other numbered findings have the specific local scope and counterevidence given below. No counterexample to Theorems A–E is claimed. Full reading is not a claim to have reproved the entire external surgery and four-manifold literature.
# The central algebraic construction

Problem 1 (Major: the dual vectors in Lemma 9.12 need not complete a basis).  On p. 50, after completing a basis of \(V\) to one of \(P\), the proof chooses \(u_i\) by \(\widehat\lambda(u_i)=x_i^*\) and asserts that the \(x_i,u_i\) generate \(P\). This assertion is false under all the stated hypotheses. The error occurs when an integral specialization of a matrix identity is treated as an identity over \(\mathbb Z[\mathbb Z_2]\).
## An exact example satisfying every hypothesis

Put \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z[T]/(T^2-1)\) with the involution used in the paper, and \(P=\Lambda x\oplus\Lambda v\). Define the quadratic representative and its symmetrization by \[Q=\begin{pmatrix}2(1-T)&4-3T\\0&3\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 A=Q+Q^t=
 \begin{pmatrix}4(1-T)&4-3T\\4-3T&6\end{pmatrix}.\] In \(\Lambda\), \[\det A=24(1-T)-(4-3T)^2=-1.\] Thus the hermitian form is nonsingular and even. The module \(V=\Lambda x\) is a free half-rank direct summand. In the natural bases of the eigenspaces, Construction 9.3 gives precisely the specialized matrices \[A_+=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&6\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 A_-=\begin{pmatrix}8&7\\7&6\end{pmatrix}.\] The plus submodule \(\mathbb Zx\) is a lagrangian. In the minus form, \(\mathbb Z(v-x)\) is a direct complement to \(\mathbb Zx\) and is isotropic because \(8-14+6=0\). Its pairing with \(x\) is \(-1\), so it is a lagrangian. These verify every hypothesis of Lemma 9.12, including the integral direct-summand conditions.

Use the allowed basis completion \(x,v\). The uniquely prescribed dual vector is \[u=A^{-1}x^*=-6x+(4-3T)v.\] It satisfies \(\lambda(x,u)=1\) and \(\lambda(v,u)=0\), as required. But \[\det[x,u]=4-3T,\qquad (4-3T)|_{T=-1}=7,\] so \([x,u]\) is not invertible over \(\Lambda\). More concretely, \[P/(V+\Lambda u)\cong \Lambda/(4-3T).\] On the additive basis \(1,T\), multiplication by \(4-3T\) has matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}4&-3\\-3&4\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), whose Smith invariants are \(1,7\). The quotient is therefore \(\mathbb Z/7\), and the asserted generation fails.

This example also has the relevant restricted quadratic form: \(Q|_V=2(1-T)=(1-T)X_1\) in the paper’s notation. Moreover, \[\ell=v-(2+T)x,\qquad Q(\ell)=0,\qquad
 \lambda(x,\ell)=T,\qquad \det[x,\ell]=1.\] Thus \(\Lambda\ell\) is an actual lagrangian complement, and the example can occur as the algebra of an elementary quasi-formation. It disproves the proposed construction, not the conclusion of the lemma.

The exact calculation was independently reproduced using self-written polynomial arithmetic modulo \(T^2-1\) and integer Smith normal form. A simpler companion example with diagonal \(2(1-T),2\) and cross entry \(2-T\) gives quotient \(\mathbb Z/3\). The first check script contained an incorrect expected cross-pairing for that companion; the actual value is \(T\). Its failed exit and original script are preserved. The corrected script exited successfully and checked both examples. No author code was run.
## The invalid identity and its effect

With the notation \(u=Ax+Bv\) of p. 50, the valid specialized identity is \[B(+1)L=I.\] The proof writes \(BL=I\) over \(\Lambda\). Specialization replaces \(b_{ij}\) by \(b_{ij}(+1)\); it cannot justify invertibility of \(B\) over the group ring. The example above has \(B=4-3T\) and \(B(+1)=1\).

There is a further manifestation of the same construction problem. On p. 51 the proof changes \(U_+\) by adding vectors from \(\mathcal E_+(V)\) and expressly notes that \(U_+=\mathcal E_+(U_1)\) may no longer hold. On p. 52 it invokes that identity again to place \(c_i\) in \(U_1\) and infer a new basis. Neither the containment nor invertibility of a general modification follows from the preceding text. These observations are grouped with Problem 1 rather than counted as independent failures of the classification theorem.

Lemma 9.12 is used by Proposition 9.14, then Proposition 9.15 and the obstruction-vanishing argument in Theorem 10.1. The failure is therefore in the core proof chain, not an unused generality. The existence of the repair below limits the conclusion: the printed route is invalid, while this algebraic obstruction to the route can be removed.
## A complete replacement proof of Lemma 9.12

Choose any free complement \(U_0\) to \(V\). Freeness is available from Lemma 3.9. Relative to \(\mathcal E_-(V)\oplus\mathcal E_-(U_0)\), the given complementary minus lagrangian is the graph of an integral matrix. Lift that matrix through \(\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\Lambda\) and replace \(U_0\) by the corresponding graph \(U\). Then \(P=V\oplus U\) and \(\mathcal E_-(U)\) is the given lagrangian.

In bases of \(V,U\), write \[\lambda=\begin{pmatrix}A&Y\\Y^t&D\end{pmatrix}.\] We have \(A(+1)=0\) and \(D(-1)=0\). Nonsingularity of the specialized forms and the block determinant formula give \(\det Y(+1),\det Y(-1)\in\{1,-1\}\). Identify \[\Lambda\cong\{(a_+,a_-)\in\mathbb Z^2:a_+\equiv a_-\pmod2\}.\] The integral matrices \(Y(+1),Y(-1)\) agree modulo 2. Their inverses therefore agree modulo 2 as well and lift to an inverse over \(\Lambda\). Change the basis of \(U\) using \(Y^{-1}\), so the mixed block is \(I\). The vanishing specializations imply \[A=(1-T)A_0,\qquad D=(1+T)D_0\] for integral symmetric matrices \(A_0,D_0\). Evenness of the ambient form makes every diagonal entry of \(D_0\) even. Hence there is an integral matrix \(C\) with \(C+C^t=-D_0\): take \(C_{ii}=-(D_0)_{ii}/2\), the required negative entries above the diagonal, and zero below.

Use the graph map \(u_j\mapsto u_j+\sum_i v_i(1+T)C_{ij}\). This remains a free complement. Its Gram block is \[D+(1+T)(C+C^t)+(1+T)^2C^tAC=0\] because \((1-T)(1+T)=0\). The mixed block remains \(I\) for the same reason. The new complement is therefore its own annihilator. It is a quadratic lagrangian as well, since symmetrization is injective over this particular torsion-free ring with trivial involution. This proves the stated lemma without the invalid dual-basis construction or the inconsistent plus-basis changes.
# Further statements and proof steps requiring correction

Problem 2 (Minor: symmetrization is not injective over every stated ring).  Lemma 3.7 and Corollary 3.8, p. 11, are stated for a general ring with involution. Take \(R=\mathbb F_2\) with trivial involution, \(\varepsilon=1\) and the free module \(P=R\). Then \(Q_+(P)=\mathbb F_2\), while symmetrization is multiplication by 2 and is zero. The nonzero class represented by \([1]\) lies in its kernel.

The zero bilinear form has the two different refinements \(\mu_0(x)=0\) and \(\mu_1(x)=x^2\). They satisfy all three conditions of Definition 3.3. With \(L=P\), the bilinear form vanishes on \(L\) but the nonzero quadratic form does not. Thus both the uniqueness and the claimed isotropic-to-sublagrangian implication fail in this generality. In the proof, a skew-hermitian matrix need not have zero diagonal under the stated hypotheses.

The actual applications here use \(\mathbb Z\) and \(\mathbb Z[\mathbb Z_2]\) with trivial involution and no additive 2-torsion. For these rings the diagonal obstruction vanishes, the triangular argument works, and the projective reduction works. Restrict the lemma and corollary to that valid setting, or give the appropriate general hypothesis on symmetrization. This is a local overstatement; it does not invalidate the intended applications.

Problem 3 (Minor: stable freeness alone does not imply the surjectivity in Remark 3.6).  On p. 11, let \(R=\mathbb Z\), \(P=L=\mathbb Z\), \(\psi=0\), and let \(j\) be the identity. All modules are free, \(L\) is a direct summand and \(L=L^\perp\) under Definition 3.5. Nevertheless \(j^*(1+\mathord\top)\psi:P\to L^*\) is the zero map and is not surjective.

The needed extra condition is ambient nonsingularity, not stable freeness. With that condition the map to \(P^*\) is an isomorphism and restriction \(P^*\to L^*\) is onto for a direct summand. The counterexample is excluded from the nonsingular quasi-formations used later. Correct the remark and the scope of the lagrangian convention; no additional failure of the main surgery argument is inferred.

Problem 4 (Minor: the excision assertion in the proof of Proposition 4.2 has excessive degree range).  On p. 13 the proof identifies the relative homology of the full disc/sphere bundle pair with that over the punctured surface for all degrees. Let \(F=\mathbb{RP}^2\) and \(\xi=TF\). This is a rank-two bundle with \(w_1(\xi)=w_1(F)\), so its total disc bundle is oriented, as required. For its disc/sphere pair \((N,Y)\), the Thom isomorphism with the orientation local system gives \[H_4(N,Y;\mathbb Z)=H_2(F;\mathbb Z_{w_1})=\mathbb Z.\] For the punctured surface \(\dot F\), \[H_4(\dot N,\dot Y;\mathbb Z)
   =H_2(\dot F;\mathbb Z_{w_1})=0.\] The stated all-degree isomorphism is false.

Only degrees 1 and 2 are used at this point. They are respectively zero and \(\mathbb Z/2\) in both cases. Applying the Thom isomorphism in those degrees proves exactly what the subsequent homology argument needs. The counterexample refutes the intermediate universal excision assertion, not Proposition 4.2’s required conclusion.

Problem 5 (Minor: global degree is misstated in Lemma 4.5).  On p. 15, the proof calls the branched double-cover maps degree one. A regular value off the branch locus has two orientation-preserving preimages. The global topological degree is therefore two. Each unbranched sheet has local degree one, and these two notions must be distinguished.

The correct fibre relation gives the stated normal Euler-number identity \(e=2e'\). The global degree-one explanation should be replaced by the local sheet calculation and the squaring map on the normal fibre. This correction preserves the lemma and the later signature formula.

Problem 6 (Major: the mod-2 Euler-characteristic argument for Corollary D).  In the proof on pp. 3–4, if the hypothetical residual fundamental group were \(\mathbb Z_2\), then \(b_1(X;\mathbb F_2)=b_3(X;\mathbb F_2)=1\) by abelianization and Poincare duality. Consequently \[\chi(X)=1-1+b_2(X;\mathbb F_2)-1+1=b_2(X;\mathbb F_2),\] not \(2+b_2(X;\mathbb F_2)\). The claimed contradiction from the lower bound on the mod-2 second Betti number does not follow.

For a concrete counterexample to that auxiliary Euler inference, the free diagonal antipodal quotient \[M=(S^2\times S^2)/((x,y)\sim(-x,-y))\] is closed and oriented, has fundamental group \(\mathbb Z_2\), and satisfies \(\chi(M)=2\) and \(b_2(M;\mathbb F_2)=2\). It is not asserted to be the branched cover of a surface meeting every hypothesis of Corollary D.

The invalid inequality is the printed justification for simple connectedness of the orbit space. This conclusion is then needed to identify that space with \(S^4\) by Freedman’s theorem and apply Theorem A. The defect is therefore Major for the derivation of this stated involution application. The auxiliary quotient above does not refute the corollary under all of its branched-cover hypotheses.

A valid repair uses local monodromy: a meridian has nontrivial image in the deck group of the branched double cover, hence generates the exterior group \(\mathbb Z_2\). The van Kampen quotient kills that generator and establishes simple connectedness without the erroneous Betti-number inequality.

Problem 7 (Minor: the exterior quadratic function cannot be extended linearly).  Definition 6.14 on p. 30 says to extend the half-twist prescription linearly from a basis of \(H_1(F;\mathbb F_2)\) to \(\mathbb Z_4\). Any additive map \(\mathbb F_2\to\mathbb Z_4\) sends its generator to 0 or 2. A one-sided generator has self-intersection 1 and its Guillou–Marin value is odd. For example the standard punctured projective plane in \(D^4\) has such a generator. Thus no additive extension can have the required value.

Use the quadratic extension \(q(x+y)=q(x)+q(y)+2Q_F(x,y)\), with the coefficient conventions of Section 6. Proposition 6.15 supplies the correct geometric identification with the Guillou–Marin form and hence repairs the definition. The disc framing used later is expressly required to extend over the disc on p. 31; this review does not claim that requirement is absent.

Problem 8 (Minor: the genus-three appendix changes its scale).  On pp. 57 and 60 the statement of Proposition A.6 displays \[\theta=2X_3=
 \begin{pmatrix}4&4&4\\0&2&2\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}\] but asks about \(\operatorname{bAut}(V,2\theta)\) and sets \(\psi=2\theta\). These expressions refer to \(4X_3\). The proof instead uses the discriminant form of \(2X_3\) from Lemmas A.4–A.5.

The distinction is detected without numerical approximation: \(\det(2X_3+2X_3^t)=32\), whereas \(\det(4X_3+4X_3^t)=256\). Their discriminant groups have orders 32 and 256 respectively; in Smith form they are \(\mathbb Z_8\oplus\mathbb Z_2^2\) and \(\mathbb Z_{16}\oplus\mathbb Z_4^2\). Thus the displayed group and quadratic values used in the proof cannot be those of its literally defined \(\psi\). A further exact check shows that the literally doubled assertion is false, not merely unsupported. In the coordinates of Lemma A.4 the boundary of \(4X_3\) is \(\mathbb Z_{16}\oplus\mathbb Z_4^2\) with \[q(a,b,c)=\frac{11a^2-16ab+8b^2+8bc+8c^2}{32}\pmod{\mathbb Z}.\] Consider the well-defined automorphism \[U(a,b,c)=(a+8c,\ b+c,\ 3c).\] It has square the identity on this finite group, and \[q(U(a,b,c))-q(a,b,c)=5ac-3bc+21c^2\in\mathbb Z.\] It is therefore a quadratic boundary isometry.

Here is a direct proof that it does not lift. Realize the original integral lattice as the even-coordinate-sum sublattice \(L\subset\mathbb Z^3\), with basis \(2e_1,e_1+e_2,e_1+e_3\) and the Euclidean pairing multiplied by 4. The vectors of Euclidean squared length 4 in \(L\) are precisely \(\{\pm2e_i\}\), so every integral isometry is a signed coordinate permutation. With the unimodular coordinate change \(D=BC\) printed in Lemma A.4, the first two boundary generators have dual representatives \[w_1=(-1,-1,-3)/8,\qquad w_2=(1,0,1)/4.\] A signed permutation fixing the class of \(w_1\) must fix \(w_1\) itself: each coordinate of its difference from \(w_1\) has absolute value less than 1, while a vector of \(L\) has integral coordinates. The only possibilities are the identity and interchange of the first two coordinates. The latter does not fix \(w_2\) modulo \(L\). Thus only the identity fixes both boundary generators. But \(U\) fixes both and is nonidentity. It cannot be induced by an integral isometry. Its double coset is consequently different from the identity double coset in the stated boundary-automorphism set.

A separate exact enumeration finds 384 boundary isometries and 48 distinct integral images; it checks all 256 group elements for the displayed \(U\). The analytic argument above supplies the decisive non-lift proof without relying on the counts. For the intended genus-three application in Proposition 7.44, one needs \(\theta=X_3\) and the boundary of \(2\theta\). Correcting the displayed scale restores the object treated by Lemmas A.4–A.5. This remains a Minor finding because the explicit counterexample addresses the incorrectly doubled auxiliary statement, not the form required by the main classification.
# Further checks and limits of the assessment
## Ranges, topology and geometric compatibility

The ranges of A and B are the low-genus or nonextremal normal-Euler-number cases; the determinant-one condition belongs to B, while the one-tube stabilization in C has its separately stated hypotheses. Theorem E retains the prescribed Guillou–Marin isometry, and its gluing proof must preserve that choice. These distinctions were checked through Sections 10–11.

The displayed Massey range in Theorem 2.4 on p. 9 is malformed. The intended set, consistent with pp. 1 and 10, is \(\{-2h+4j:0\le j\le h\}\). Connected sums of \(a\) positive and \(b\) negative standard projective planes realize the corresponding endpoints and steps with the paper’s sign convention. Example 2.3’s mention of a single 0-handle and a single 1-handle does not explicitly say these are the only handles. To deduce \(\pi_1=\mathbb Z_2\) from a handle description, the square-meridian 2-handle relation should also be supplied. This is recorded as a clarification, not as a false claim that no 2-handles occur.

The boundary and branched-cover homology calculations in Sections 4–5 were checked with the twisted coefficients and Euler characteristic retained. The index-two even lattice calculation and the special \(\sigma=0\) hyperbolic case are consistent. In the definition of \(X_n\) for negative \(n\), the rank is \(|n|\), as the actual matrices and applications require.

The Section 6 construction of nice sections, the use of immersed discs in the simply connected cover, the odd-framing comparison, and the spin structures extending over the exteriors were followed. The line-preserving derivative in Lemma 6.20(2) need not already be the identity: a diagonal linear map is an immediate local example. A positive normalization after fixing the sign provides the required adjustment. No all-hypothesis counterexample to the extension lemma was established.
## Surgery algebra and finite computations

The plus/minus normalization of Construction 9.3 was checked directly: evaluating a matrix at \(T=\pm1\) is consistent with division by \(2(1\pm T)\) on the eigenspace pairings. The nondegenerate Wall form and its minus specialization produce the factor \(2\theta\) used in the integral obstruction. Zero-stable equivalence, formations, quasi-formations and the boundary automorphism double-coset set were kept distinct.

For Proposition 7.44, the discriminant is 2-primary, so the odd-prime generator counts are zero. The rank inequalities in the indefinite case and after stabilization by \(2H_+(\mathbb Z)\) were checked. The small definite cases require the separate appendix; one cannot use the indefinite theorem there. Independent exact calculations for ranks \(1\) through \(16\) recover the Smith pattern \[\mathop{\mathrm{coker}}(2X_n+2X_n^t)\cong
 \begin{cases}
  \mathbb Z_2^{\,n-1}\oplus\mathbb Z_8,&n\text{ odd},\\
  \mathbb Z_2^{\,n-2}\oplus\mathbb Z_4\oplus\mathbb Z_4,&n\text{ even}.
 \end{cases}\] Those finite checks support the algebra and were not presented as a proof for every rank. The index-two parity-lattice description gives the general structural explanation. Enumeration of the rank-two quadratic boundary form gives eight isometries, while the \(4H_+\) boundary form has four. These calculations were made with exact integers and rational values, not floating point.

Remark 7.45 on p. 44 says that no nontrivial extremal examples are known, whereas the introduction cites the newer Pen24 examples in genera six and seven. This is a stale cross-reference in the reviewed version, not a further refutation of a theorem.
## External dependencies and unavailable material

The proof uses deep external results: realization of quadratic enhancements, topological spin bordism, Kreck’s modified surgery, the good-group topological \(s\)-cobordism theorem, integral lattice classification, Nikulin’s boundary-isometry criterion, and the stated cancellation theorem. Their precise uses and hypotheses were traced in the paper; a complete independent reconstruction of those libraries was not performed. In particular, reading the bordism group identification and the cancellation citation is not equivalent to redoing all spectral-sequence differentials or the general cancellation proof.

Bounded searches of the title, DOI, correction and supplementary terms, together with the EMS, Glasgow and arXiv primary records, did not identify an applicable separate correction or public code package. This is not a proof of absence. The appendix names Sage computations and says matrices are available on request. No request was sent and no author code was executed. Lack of public code is not treated as a mathematical defect.
# Verification record and recommendation

The initial primary reviewer read all 64 physical text pages and actually viewed the source images listed in the saved coverage record. Three native AI auxiliaries provided bounded checks within this original review workflow; their individual scope, runtime self-description, inspected pages and limitations are retained. Their initial work did not constitute independent acceptance. The current focused independent acceptance and its read-only auxiliary contribution are separately attributed in the verification records. No human review is claimed. The reported UI verification belongs to the external controller; the runtime’s own identity statement is separately recorded and is not an independent backend attestation.
Rendering alone is not counted as viewing. Every current report page is subject to actual visual inspection before delivery is marked complete.

The recommended mathematical action is to replace the proof of Lemma 9.12, including its downstream citations to the repaired argument, to replace the Corollary D Euler inference by the meridian argument, and to correct the local generality, degree, coefficient and scale statements identified above. The replacement proof here settles that lemma under its actual hypotheses; it does not constitute a new independent verification of every geometric dependency of A–E. The assessment is two Major and six Minor findings, with `scientific_decision=pending` and no human reviews recorded.

claim: Recorded check: Lemma9.12 dual-vector construction does not generate the ambient module

Lambda=Z[T]/(T²-1), trivial involution. Even nonsingular form det-1 on free rank2 module. Free half-rank direct V, pluslagrangian, minuslagrangian complement. Allowed initial completion x,v. Vrestricted quadratic form actualgenus1(1-T)X1.
analysis: On p. 50, after completing a basis of \(V\) to one of \(P\), the proof chooses \(u_i\) by \(\widehat\lambda(u_i)=x_i^*\) and asserts that the \(x_i,u_i\) generate \(P\). This assertion is false under all the stated hypotheses. The error occurs when an integral specialization of a matrix identity is treated as an identity over \(\mathbb Z[\mathbb Z_2]\).

Put \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z[T]/(T^2-1)\) with the involution used in the paper, and \(P=\Lambda x\oplus\Lambda v\). Define the quadratic representative and its symmetrization by \[Q=\begin{pmatrix}2(1-T)&4-3T\\0&3\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 A=Q+Q^t=
 \begin{pmatrix}4(1-T)&4-3T\\4-3T&6\end{pmatrix}.\] In \(\Lambda\), \[\det A=24(1-T)-(4-3T)^2=-1.\] Thus the hermitian form is nonsingular and even. The module \(V=\Lambda x\) is a free half-rank direct summand. In the natural bases of the eigenspaces, Construction 9.3 gives precisely the specialized matrices \[A_+=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&6\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 A_-=\begin{pmatrix}8&7\\7&6\end{pmatrix}.\] The plus submodule \(\mathbb Zx\) is a lagrangian. In the minus form, \(\mathbb Z(v-x)\) is a direct complement to \(\mathbb Zx\) and is isotropic because \(8-14+6=0\). Its pairing with \(x\) is \(-1\), so it is a lagrangian. These verify every hypothesis of Lemma 9.12, including the integral direct-summand conditions.

Use the allowed basis completion \(x,v\). The uniquely prescribed dual vector is \[u=A^{-1}x^*=-6x+(4-3T)v.\] It satisfies \(\lambda(x,u)=1\) and \(\lambda(v,u)=0\), as required. But \[\det[x,u]=4-3T,\qquad (4-3T)|_{T=-1}=7,\] so \([x,u]\) is not invertible over \(\Lambda\). More concretely, \[P/(V+\Lambda u)\cong \Lambda/(4-3T).\] On the additive basis \(1,T\), multiplication by \(4-3T\) has matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}4&-3\\-3&4\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), whose Smith invariants are \(1,7\). The quotient is therefore \(\mathbb Z/7\), and the asserted generation fails.

This example also has the relevant restricted quadratic form: \(Q|_V=2(1-T)=(1-T)X_1\) in the paper’s notation. Moreover, \[\ell=v-(2+T)x,\qquad Q(\ell)=0,\qquad
 \lambda(x,\ell)=T,\qquad \det[x,\ell]=1.\] Thus \(\Lambda\ell\) is an actual lagrangian complement, and the example can occur as the algebra of an elementary quasi-formation. It disproves the proposed construction, not the conclusion of the lemma.

The exact calculation was independently reproduced using self-written polynomial arithmetic modulo \(T^2-1\) and integer Smith normal form. A simpler companion example with diagonal \(2(1-T),2\) and cross entry \(2-T\) gives quotient \(\mathbb Z/3\). The first check script contained an incorrect expected cross-pairing for that companion; the actual value is \(T\). Its failed exit and original script are preserved. The corrected script exited successfully and checked both examples. No author code was run.

With the notation \(u=Ax+Bv\) of p. 50, the valid specialized identity is \[B(+1)L=I.\] The proof writes \(BL=I\) over \(\Lambda\). Specialization replaces \(b_{ij}\) by \(b_{ij}(+1)\); it cannot justify invertibility of \(B\) over the group ring. The example above has \(B=4-3T\) and \(B(+1)=1\).

There is a further manifestation of the same construction problem. On p. 51 the proof changes \(U_+\) by adding vectors from \(\mathcal E_+(V)\) and expressly notes that \(U_+=\mathcal E_+(U_1)\) may no longer hold. On p. 52 it invokes that identity again to place \(c_i\) in \(U_1\) and infer a new basis. Neither the containment nor invertibility of a general modification follows from the preceding text. These observations are grouped with Problem 1 rather than counted as independent failures of the classification theorem.

Lemma 9.12 is used by Proposition 9.14, then Proposition 9.15 and the obstruction-vanishing argument in Theorem 10.1. The failure is therefore in the core proof chain, not an unused generality. The existence of the repair below limits the conclusion: the printed route is invalid, while this algebraic obstruction to the route can be removed.

Choose any free complement \(U_0\) to \(V\). Freeness is available from Lemma 3.9. Relative to \(\mathcal E_-(V)\oplus\mathcal E_-(U_0)\), the given complementary minus lagrangian is the graph of an integral matrix. Lift that matrix through \(\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\Lambda\) and replace \(U_0\) by the corresponding graph \(U\). Then \(P=V\oplus U\) and \(\mathcal E_-(U)\) is the given lagrangian.

In bases of \(V,U\), write \[\lambda=\begin{pmatrix}A&Y\\Y^t&D\end{pmatrix}.\] We have \(A(+1)=0\) and \(D(-1)=0\). Nonsingularity of the specialized forms and the block determinant formula give \(\det Y(+1),\det Y(-1)\in\{1,-1\}\). Identify \[\Lambda\cong\{(a_+,a_-)\in\mathbb Z^2:a_+\equiv a_-\pmod2\}.\] The integral matrices \(Y(+1),Y(-1)\) agree modulo 2. Their inverses therefore agree modulo 2 as well and lift to an inverse over \(\Lambda\). Change the basis of \(U\) using \(Y^{-1}\), so the mixed block is \(I\). The vanishing specializations imply \[A=(1-T)A_0,\qquad D=(1+T)D_0\] for integral symmetric matrices \(A_0,D_0\). Evenness of the ambient form makes every diagonal entry of \(D_0\) even. Hence there is an integral matrix \(C\) with \(C+C^t=-D_0\): take \(C_{ii}=-(D_0)_{ii}/2\), the required negative entries above the diagonal, and zero below.

Use the graph map \(u_j\mapsto u_j+\sum_i v_i(1+T)C_{ij}\). This remains a free complement. Its Gram block is \[D+(1+T)(C+C^t)+(1+T)^2C^tAC=0\] because \((1-T)(1+T)=0\). The mixed block remains \(I\) for the same reason. The new complement is therefore its own annihilator. It is a quadratic lagrangian as well, since symmetrization is injective over this particular torsion-free ring with trivial involution. This proves the stated lemma without the invalid dual-basis construction or the inconsistent plus-basis changes.
result: Impact: P50 claimed basis has cokernelZ7; essential obstruction-vanishing construction invalid. Lemma conclusion and A–E not disproved.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Replace proof by integralgraph lift, simultaneous inverse ofcrossblock, and (1+T) triangular correction; complete proof supplied.

problems.title: Unrestricted symmetrization injectivity and quadratic uniqueness false
problems.source_location: PDF11 Lemma3.7/Cor3.8
claim: Recorded check: Unrestricted symmetrization injectivity and quadratic uniqueness false
R=F2 trivialinvolution. epsilon1,P=F2free.
analysis: Lemma 3.7 and Corollary 3.8, p. 11, are stated for a general ring with involution. Take \(R=\mathbb F_2\) with trivial involution, \(\varepsilon=1\) and the free module \(P=R\). Then \(Q_+(P)=\mathbb F_2\), while symmetrization is multiplication by 2 and is zero. The nonzero class represented by \([1]\) lies in its kernel.

The zero bilinear form has the two different refinements \(\mu_0(x)=0\) and \(\mu_1(x)=x^2\). They satisfy all three conditions of Definition 3.3. With \(L=P\), the bilinear form vanishes on \(L\) but the nonzero quadratic form does not. Thus both the uniqueness and the claimed isotropic-to-sublagrangian implication fail in this generality. In the proof, a skew-hermitian matrix need not have zero diagonal under the stated hypotheses.

The actual applications here use \(\mathbb Z\) and \(\mathbb Z[\mathbb Z_2]\) with trivial involution and no additive 2-torsion. For these rings the diagonal obstruction vanishes, the triangular argument works, and the projective reduction works. Restrict the lemma and corollary to that valid setting, or give the appropriate general hypothesis on symmetrization. This is a local overstatement; it does not invalidate the intended applications.
result: Impact: Auxiliary general-ring claim false; actual torsionfreeZ/Z[Z2] applications valid.

paragraphs: Restrict to actual torsionfree rings withtrivialinvolution; triangularproof thenworks.

problems.title: Stable freeness does not ensure lagrangian surjectivity
problems.source_location: PDF11 Remark3.6/Definition3.5
claim: Recorded check: Stable freeness does not ensure lagrangian surjectivity
RZ. P=L=Z free. psi0,jidentity. LdirectandL=Lperp.
analysis: On p. 11, let \(R=\mathbb Z\), \(P=L=\mathbb Z\), \(\psi=0\), and let \(j\) be the identity. All modules are free, \(L\) is a direct summand and \(L=L^\perp\) under Definition 3.5. Nevertheless \(j^*(1+\mathord\top)\psi:P\to L^*\) is the zero map and is not surjective.

The needed extra condition is ambient nonsingularity, not stable freeness. With that condition the map to \(P^*\) is an isomorphism and restriction \(P^*\to L^*\) is onto for a direct summand. The counterexample is excluded from the nonsingular quasi-formations used later. Correct the remark and the scope of the lagrangian convention; no additional failure of the main surgery argument is inferred.

problems.title: All-degree excision identification false
problems.source_location: PDF13 Proposition4.2 proof
claim: Recorded check: All-degree excision identification false
F=RP2. xi=TF rank2,w1xi=w1F. Totaldisc-bundleoriented. FdotpuncturedF.
analysis:
On p. 13 the proof identifies the relative homology of the full disc/sphere bundle pair with that over the punctured surface for all degrees. Let \(F=\mathbb{RP}^2\) and \(\xi=TF\). This is a rank-two bundle with \(w_1(\xi)=w_1(F)\), so its total disc bundle is oriented, as required. For its disc/sphere pair \((N,Y)\), the Thom isomorphism with the orientation local system gives \[H_4(N,Y;\mathbb Z)=H_2(F;\mathbb Z_{w_1})=\mathbb Z.\] For the punctured surface \(\dot F\), \[H_4(\dot N,\dot Y;\mathbb Z)
   =H_2(\dot F;\mathbb Z_{w_1})=0.\] The stated all-degree isomorphism is false.

Only degrees 1 and 2 are used at this point. They are respectively zero and \(\mathbb Z/2\) in both cases. Applying the Thom isomorphism in those degrees proves exactly what the subsequent homology argument needs. The counterexample refutes the intermediate universal excision assertion, not Proposition 4.2’s required conclusion.

problems.title: CorollaryD mod2 Euler contradiction incorrect
problems.source_location: PDF3-4 CorollaryD proof
claim: Recorded check: CorollaryD mod2 Euler contradiction incorrect
HypotheticalclosedorientedXwithpi1Z2underpaperreductio. PoincaredualityoverF2.
analysis: In the proof on pp. 3–4, if the hypothetical residual fundamental group were \(\mathbb Z_2\), then \(b_1(X;\mathbb F_2)=b_3(X;\mathbb F_2)=1\) by abelianization and Poincare duality. Consequently \[\chi(X)=1-1+b_2(X;\mathbb F_2)-1+1=b_2(X;\mathbb F_2),\] not \(2+b_2(X;\mathbb F_2)\). The claimed contradiction from the lower bound on the mod-2 second Betti number does not follow.

For a concrete counterexample to that auxiliary Euler inference, the free diagonal antipodal quotient \[M=(S^2\times S^2)/((x,y)\sim(-x,-y))\] is closed and oriented, has fundamental group \(\mathbb Z_2\), and satisfies \(\chi(M)=2\) and \(b_2(M;\mathbb F_2)=2\). It is not asserted to be the branched cover of a surface meeting every hypothesis of Corollary D.

The invalid inequality is the printed justification for simple connectedness of the orbit space. This conclusion is then needed to identify that space with \(S^4\) by Freedman’s theorem and apply Theorem A. The defect is therefore Major for the derivation of this stated involution application. The auxiliary quotient above does not refute the corollary under all of its branched-cover hypotheses.

A valid repair uses local monodromy: a meridian has nontrivial image in the deck group of the branched double cover, hence generates the exterior group \(\mathbb Z_2\). The van Kampen quotient kills that generator and establishes simple connectedness without the erroneous Betti-number inequality.
result: Impact: The invalid mod2 Euler inequality is the actual route to simple connectedness in the stated main involution application Corollary D. This is required for the Freedman identification of the orbit space with S4 and the application of Theorem A. The short local-monodromy replacement does not lower the severity of this core application proof failure. The diagonal antipodal quotient refutes only the auxiliary Euler inference, not all Corollary D branched-cover hypotheses.

problems.title: Genus-three appendix doubles the form inconsistently
problems.source_location: PDF57 appendixintro;PDF59-61LemmasA4/A5/PropA6
claim: Recorded check: Genus-three appendix doubles the form inconsistently
Displayedtheta2X3. Statement/proofsetspsi2theta. ActualLemmaA4boundarycomputedfor2X3.
analysis:
On pp. 57 and 60 the statement of Proposition A.6 displays \[\theta=2X_3=
 \begin{pmatrix}4&4&4\\0&2&2\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}\] but asks about \(\operatorname{bAut}(V,2\theta)\) and sets \(\psi=2\theta\). These expressions refer to \(4X_3\). The proof instead uses the discriminant form of \(2X_3\) from Lemmas A.4–A.5.

The distinction is detected without numerical approximation: \(\det(2X_3+2X_3^t)=32\), whereas \(\det(4X_3+4X_3^t)=256\). Their discriminant groups have orders 32 and 256 respectively; in Smith form they are \(\mathbb Z_8\oplus\mathbb Z_2^2\) and \(\mathbb Z_{16}\oplus\mathbb Z_4^2\). Thus the displayed group and quadratic values used in the proof cannot be those of its literally defined \(\psi\). A further exact check shows that the literally doubled assertion is false, not merely unsupported. In the coordinates of Lemma A.4 the boundary of \(4X_3\) is \(\mathbb Z_{16}\oplus\mathbb Z_4^2\) with \[q(a,b,c)=\frac{11a^2-16ab+8b^2+8bc+8c^2}{32}\pmod{\mathbb Z}.\] Consider the well-defined automorphism \[U(a,b,c)=(a+8c,\ b+c,\ 3c).\] It has square the identity on this finite group, and \[q(U(a,b,c))-q(a,b,c)=5ac-3bc+21c^2\in\mathbb Z.\] It is therefore a quadratic boundary isometry.

Here is a direct proof that it does not lift. Realize the original integral lattice as the even-coordinate-sum sublattice \(L\subset\mathbb Z^3\), with basis \(2e_1,e_1+e_2,e_1+e_3\) and the Euclidean pairing multiplied by 4. The vectors of Euclidean squared length 4 in \(L\) are precisely \(\{\pm2e_i\}\), so every integral isometry is a signed coordinate permutation. With the unimodular coordinate change \(D=BC\) printed in Lemma A.4, the first two boundary generators have dual representatives \[w_1=(-1,-1,-3)/8,\qquad w_2=(1,0,1)/4.\] A signed permutation fixing the class of \(w_1\) must fix \(w_1\) itself: each coordinate of its difference from \(w_1\) has absolute value less than 1, while a vector of \(L\) has integral coordinates. The only possibilities are the identity and interchange of the first two coordinates. The latter does not fix \(w_2\) modulo \(L\). Thus only the identity fixes both boundary generators. But \(U\) fixes both and is nonidentity. It cannot be induced by an integral isometry. Its double coset is consequently different from the identity double coset in the stated boundary-automorphism set.

A separate exact enumeration finds 384 boundary isometries and 48 distinct integral images; it checks all 256 group elements for the displayed \(U\). The analytic argument above supplies the decisive non-lift proof without relying on the counts. For the intended genus-three application in Proposition 7.44, one needs \(\theta=X_3\) and the boundary of \(2\theta\). Correcting the displayed scale restores the object treated by Lemmas A.4–A.5. This remains a Minor finding because the explicit counterexample addresses the incorrectly doubled auxiliary statement, not the form required by the main classification.
