report: Abstract: The assessment of the exact acquired author version is Major. A missing factor of eight makes a central comparison lemma false on an effective primitive half-fiber. A general weak Jacobi transformation lemma used in the geometric modularity argument has an explicit counterexample. The exponential rewriting in the Vafa–Witten proof also has the wrong sign, contradicted by an actual primitive pair moduli space. These findings concern essential derivations; none is presented as a counterexample to the intended main enumerative formulas. Explicit repairs are given for the normalization and sign errors, while the weak Jacobi issue requires a stronger input theorem. Two further substantive local corrections, two notation clarifications, and a conditional degeneration-normalization check are separated from these core findings. All 58 physical source pages were read. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI technical verification

Title: Technical review of
Curve counting on the Enriques surface and the Klemm–Mariño formula
# Exact source and scope

This review concerns M25-0266, Curve counting on the Enriques surface and the Klemm–Mariño formula, by Georg Oberdieck, DOI `10.4171/jems/1639`. The acquired PDF is arXiv:2305.11115v3, uploaded on 2 December 2024 at 14:33:06 UTC. Its title page has the internal date 3 December 2024; the margin has the arXiv date 2 December 2024. It has 58 physical pages, with matching printed page numbers, and 694,114 bytes. Its SHA256 is
The manifest has 22,686 bytes and SHA256
> 853eba632820c1aec860b7b7c7e0cb0323bc8ce1b7879a4ec36db7d21c50de26.

The arXiv metadata describes 57 pages; the actual PDF has 58, and both facts are retained. The EMS record gives submission on 15 July 2023, acceptance on 4 December 2023 and online publication on 20 May 2025. Publisher full-text equivalence was not established. The frozen title, DOI and 2025 batch membership have not been changed.

The paper determines the indicated Enriques Gromov–Witten invariants, fiber Donaldson–Thomas invariants on the Enriques Calabi–Yau threefold, and local Vafa–Witten invariants. The review followed the weak Jacobi conventions, lattice-orbit reduction, relative degeneration and anomaly equations, primitive DT calculation, Toda formula, divisibility induction, and local-pair comparison. The v3 metadata explicitly mentions a corrected sign in Theorem 5.14. The current sign in that theorem was checked; the different sign error below is in Section 7.
# The normalization in the central comparison

Problem 1 (Major: equation (6.2) makes Lemma 6.5 false).  Equation (6.2), p. 41, omits the factor \(8\) present in the large \(F^{\mathrm{KM}}\) series and in Proposition 5.16. With the definitions actually printed, Lemma 6.5 on p. 43 has left side \(7\) and right side \(0\) for an effective primitive half-fiber.

Let \(f\) be the effective primitive isotropic half-fiber of Section 4.1, and put \(\beta=f\). Thus \(\beta^2=0\) and \(\operatorname{div}(\beta)=1\). Write \[R(z,\tau)=
 \frac{\Theta(z,2\tau)^2\eta(2\tau)^8}
      {\Theta(z,\tau)^2\eta(\tau)^{16}}.\] The two theta functions have the same leading term at \(q=0\), and the eta quotient has valuation \((2\cdot8-16)/24=0\) and leading coefficient \(1\). Hence \[[R]_{q^0}=1,\qquad f_f^{\mathrm{KM}}=1
 \quad\hbox{under the printed definition (6.2).}\] This also agrees with the calculation of \(\omega_g(0)\) on p. 43.

For every \(v=(r,f,n)\) the relevant divisibility is \(m(v)=\gcd(r,1,2n)=1\). The odd-cover transformation is therefore trivial, and Proposition 5.10 gives \[\mathop{\mathrm{dt}}(r,f,n)=\mathop{\mathrm{DT}}(r,f,n)
 =8[\eta^{-12}]_{q^{(-r^2-2rn)/2}}.\] Consequently every \(\widehat{\mathop{\mathrm{dt}}}(r,f,n)\) defined on p. 42 is zero. In equation (5.5), p. 38, the \(r=0\) terms vanish. Among \(r\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), the inequality \(-r^2-2rn\ge-1\) holds only for \((r,n)=(1,0)\), since \(\eta^{-12}\) begins with \(q^{-1/2}\). The only contribution is thus \(8\), giving \[f_f^{\mathrm{PT}}=f_f^{\mathrm{GW}}=8,\qquad
 \widehat f_f=8-1=7.\] The GW value can also be checked from the two elliptic half-fibers and the fourfold comparison with the threefold. The right side of Lemma 6.5 is a linear combination of the identically zero \(\widehat{\mathop{\mathrm{dt}}}\), so the printed lemma asserts \(7=0\) on this actual allowed class. No zero class or hypothetical DT data are involved.

This discrepancy matters to the proof. Lemma 6.5 transfers the low-genus vanishing of the large difference series to the DT recurrence in the divisibility-two case. The coefficient identification on p. 44 likewise uses the incorrectly normalized small difference. The proof as printed cannot make that transfer. The Major classification reflects this essential dependence, although the normalization has a short repair.
## Repair and a separate coefficient check

Define \(f_\beta^{\mathrm{KM}}=8[R]_{q^{\beta^2/2}}\). Insert the same \(8\) in the expansion of \(f^{\mathrm{KM}}\) in the proof of Lemma 6.5; retain the already correct \(8\) in \(F^{\mathrm{KM}}\) and \(\widehat{\mathop{\mathrm{dt}}}\). Then subtraction of (5.5) gives the intended lemma, and the primitive example has \(\widehat f_f=0\). The closing sentence of the proof of Proposition 5.16, p. 41, also needs its omitted \(8\) restored.

A second exact algebra check is needed on p. 45. The constant term in Lemma 6.5 contains \(r\widehat{\mathop{\mathrm{dt}}}(r,\beta_d,0)\). Substitution \(r=2u\) gives \[-\sum_{u>0}2u(-1)^{u-1}a(d-u^2/2),\] where the displayed formula on p. 45 omits \(2u\). After lower terms vanish by induction, the two correct equations are \[0=-\frac14a(d)-2a(d-\tfrac12),
 \qquad 0=\frac18a(d).\] Their coefficient matrix has determinant \(1/4\), so the intended elimination still works. This is a coefficient correction, not an assertion that an arbitrary nonzero sequence \(a\) is an actual DT sequence. Similarly, the odd-\(n\) sum in the proof of Lemma 5.11, p. 36, should use \[\sum_{\substack{n>0\\n\ {\rm odd}}}np^n
   =\frac{p(1+p^2)}{(1-p^2)^2}.\] Restoring the square makes the subsequent pole-cancellation argument and the stated final rational function consistent.
# Weak Jacobi forms and the geometric modularity step

Problem 2 (Major: Lemma 2.6 does not preserve the stated cusp condition).  Definition 2.3(ii), p. 8, requires nonnegative Fourier exponents at every cusp. Footnote 8 explicitly uses the weak Jacobi convention. Under exactly those definitions, Lemma 2.6, p. 9, is false. The proof through Lemma A.7, pp. 50–52, overlooks the effect of elliptic translation on this condition.

Let \(\Theta_E=\Theta_{E_8}(x,\tau)\), of weight \(4\) and index \(Q_{E_8}/2\), and let \(E_4=240G_4\), with constant term \(1\). Consider the ordinary full-level Jacobi Hecke transform \[B(x,\tau)=8\Theta_E(2x,2\tau)
 +\frac12\bigl(\Theta_E(x,\tau/2)
                  +\Theta_E(x,(\tau+1)/2)\bigr).\] Its finite-coset slash construction gives weight \(4\) and index \(Q_{E_8}\). This uses a regular Jacobi input and does not depend on the defective Laurent truncation discussed below. The only \(q^0\) coefficient of \(B\) is \(9\). Therefore \[F(x,\tau)=\frac{E_4(\tau)B(x,\tau)-9\Theta_E(x,\tau)^2}
                  {\Delta(\tau)}\] is an actual weak Jacobi form for \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\ltimes(\mathbb Z^8\oplus\mathbb Z^8)\), of weight \(-4\) and index \(Q_{E_8}\). The numerator’s entire \(q^0\) coefficient vanishes, \(\Delta\) has no zeros in the upper half-plane, and the level-one group has one cusp. These verify holomorphy in \(x,\tau\) and every weak cusp hypothesis of the lemma with \(m=1\).

Choose \(\alpha_0\in E_8\) of norm \(4\); for example, in the standard Euclidean realization one can take \(\alpha_0=(2,0,\ldots,0)\). Then \[[q^1\zeta^{-\alpha_0}]B=1,\qquad
 [q^1\zeta^{-\alpha_0}]\Theta_E^2=0.\] Indeed, the averaged two summands in \(B\) contribute the norm-four lattice vector once; the first summand would require \(\alpha_0/2\) of norm one in the even lattice. At degree one, \(\Theta_E^2\) has only zero or norm-two charges. Thus \([q^0\zeta^{-\alpha_0}]F=1\).

Since \(F\) is a Jacobi form, its elliptic anomaly derivatives vanish. The actual operator of Lemma 2.6 is therefore \[M_{\alpha_0,1}(F)
   =q^2\zeta^{\alpha_0}F(x+\alpha_0\tau,2\tau),
 \qquad
 [q^{-2}\zeta^0]M_{\alpha_0,1}(F)=1.\] Output charge zero forces input charge \(-\alpha_0\), and the specified output exponent then forces input exponent zero. There can be no cancellation. This violates the claimed weak cusp condition at infinity and is a full-hypothesis counterexample to the stated lemma.

The same failure occurs already in Lemma A.7: take the usual weak form \(\phi_{-2,1}(x/2,\tau)\), index \(1/4\), with lattice \(2\mathbb Z\oplus2\mathbb Z\), and translate by \((1,0)\). Its transformed \(q^{-1/4}\) coefficient is nonzero. The formal transformation law is not the disputed step; cusp growth is.
## Actual dependence and limits of a repair

Page 24 explicitly applies this lemma to \(\Delta^{-m}\mathop{\mathrm{QJac}}_{mQ_{E_8}}\) and deduces Corollary 4.7. That corollary supplies the modularity and pole bound in Theorem 4.3, used again in Proposition 6.3 and the main divisibility induction. A false general preservation assertion does not justify that step. This is the basis for the Major assessment. The example above is not claimed to be a relative GW series, and no counterexample to the intended geometric formula has been established.

A precise sufficient repair can be stated. Let \(\Phi\) be the almost-holomorphic completion of the numerator \(H\), weight \(w\), index \(mQ_{E_8}\), \(m>0\). Require each of its coefficient functions in the nonholomorphic variables to have support \[n\ge\frac{\|\alpha\|^2}{4m}.\] At infinity the translated exponent then satisfies \[2n+\alpha\cdot\alpha_0+2m
       \ge\frac{\|\alpha+m\alpha_0\|^2}{2m}\ge0.\] At the other cusp, direct substitution in the slash operator, with \(S=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), gives for the transformed completion \(G\) \[G|_{w,mQ_{E_8}/2}S
     =2^{-w}\Phi\left(\frac{x+\alpha_0}{2},\frac{\tau}{2}\right).\] Thus cusp zero has no new negative powers. Under this stronger hypothesis the denominator \(\Delta(2\tau)^m\) remains sufficient.

There is a plausible geometric route, but it requires proof for the actual inputs. On a generic rational elliptic surface, for a horizontal irreducible curve \(C\) with \(d=F_{\rm fib}\cdot C>0\) and \(E_8\) charge \(\alpha\), adjunction gives \(C^2\ge d-2\). With \(W=B+F_{\rm fib}/2\), \[W\cdot C\ge\frac{\|\alpha\|^2}{2d}+\frac12-\frac1d
           \ge\frac{\|\alpha\|^2}{2d}-\frac d2.\] Adding effective components and using Cauchy–Schwarz gives, at total degree \(2m\), \(W\cdot\beta\ge\|\alpha\|^2/(4m)-m\). This supplies the desired bound for the holomorphic numerator \(\Delta^m F_R\). It does not by itself establish it for all iterated \(G_2\) and elliptic anomaly coefficients, including the relative and rubber terms. That additional step remains unverified here. Merely enlarging the allowed pole order also requires rechecking later modular arguments.
# The pair-invariant exponential

Problem 3 (Major: the proof of Theorem 7.2 reverses a nonzero pair count).  Equation (7.1), p. 47, contains \((-1)^\ell/\ell!\). The exponential at the bottom of that page and the one at the top of p. 48 both have a positive sign in the exponent. They must both have a negative sign. This error is distinct from the v3 correction to Theorem 5.14.

Put \(A_\delta=(-1)^{\chi(\delta v(n))}
\chi(\delta v(n))\mathop{\mathrm{DT}}(\delta v)\). Expanding the ordered products in (7.1) gives \[f^Q_{v,n}(t)=
 \exp\left(-\sum_{\delta>0} A_\delta t^\delta\right)
      +O(t^{1+}),\] rather than the printed positive exponential. There is no corresponding sign change in the definition of \(t\) or of \(f^Q\).

An actual geometric example removes any dependence on a purely formal test sequence. Let \(v=(1,0,0)=\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal O_Y)\) and use the generic polarization \(H\) of Section 7. Choose a sufficiently large even twist \(n\) and set \[N=\chi(H^n)=1+\frac{n^2H^2}{2}.\] Then \(N\) is positive and odd, and Serre vanishing gives \(h^0(H^n)=h^0(\omega_Y\otimes H^n)=N\). On each of the four Enriques sections of \(Q\) there are the two torsion line bundles \(\mathcal O_Y,\omega_Y\). They give exactly eight stable sheaves in this class, as also computed on p. 36. A K3 fiber has twice the primitive fiber class and cannot contribute. Each sheaf is rigid: \(H^1(\mathcal O_Y)=H^0(\omega_Y)=0\) makes its \(\operatorname{Ext}^1\) on \(Q\) zero. The pair space is therefore eight copies of \(\mathbb P^{N-1}\), with no strictly semistable rank-one decomposition.

The symmetric obstruction theory gives virtual degree \((-1)^{N-1}N\) for each smooth projective space. Hence \[P_v^Q(n)=8(-1)^{N-1}N=8N.\] Equation (7.1) gives this value. The printed positive exponential instead gives \(8(-1)^N N=-8N\) for the coefficient of \(t\). No fractional rank class with \(0<\delta<1\) can obscure this coefficient.

This false rewriting is the bridge to the asserted Vafa–Witten formula. Comparing its positive exponent with the negative expansion in Conjecture B would reverse the sign of \(\mathop{\mathrm{VW}}\). It therefore damages the proof of Theorem 7.2, even though a consistent local correction preserves that theorem.

Indeed, retain Lemma 7.5, \(f^Q=(f^{K_Y})^4\), and take the unique fourth root with constant term one: \[f^{K_Y}_{v,n}(t)=
 \exp\left(-\frac14\sum_{\delta>0} A_\delta t^\delta\right)
       +O(t^{1+}).\] This matches Conjecture B and gives \(\mathop{\mathrm{VW}}(v)=\mathop{\mathrm{DT}}(v)/4\). For the primitive example, the local pair space has two copies of \(\mathbb P^{N-1}\), so \(\mathop{\mathrm{VW}}(1,0,0)=2=8/4\). The general degeneration theorem underlying Lemma 7.5 was not independently reproved in full; the sign contradiction and this primitive check do not require such a reconstruction.
# Local corrections and notation clarifications
## Notation clarification (original Problem 4): Laurent Hecke exponents

Equation (2.7), p. 10, sums only \(v\ge0\) despite starting with a Laurent series. For \(\ell=s=1\), index zero, and \(h=\Delta^{-1}\in\Delta^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{QJac}}_{0,0}\), it gives \[h|V_1=h-q^{-1},\qquad
 \Delta(h|V_1)=1-\Delta/q=24q+O(q^2).\] The latter is nonconstant, whereas the asserted weight-zero, index-zero holomorphic quasi-modular target consists of constants.

The finite-coset definition in Appendix A.3 is the identity for \(\ell=1\), and its formula (A.3) has unrestricted exponents. Include every supported integral \(v\) in (2.7). The actual \(F^{\mathrm{KM}}_{g,1}\) in Section 6 has no negative powers at infinity, so the truncation does not change that input. Corollary 7.3 refers to Appendix A.3’s full operator. The complete definition already appears in Appendix A.3, and no necessary calculation has been shown to use the truncated operator. This inconsistency is retained as a notation clarification and is not counted as a substantive Minor finding.

Problem 4 (Minor: a congruence subgroup in Lemma 2.11 is too large).  The proof on p. 11 uses \(\Gamma_0(2m^2)\subset\gamma^{-1}\Gamma_0(2)\gamma\) for \(\gamma=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1/m\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). For \(m=5\), let \[A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\50&17\end{pmatrix}\in\Gamma_0(50),
 \qquad
 \gamma A\gamma^{-1}
   =\begin{pmatrix}13&9/5\\50&7\end{pmatrix}.\] The conjugate is not integral, although \(\det A=1\).

Use the principal congruence subgroup \(\Gamma(2m^2)\) instead. For a matrix in it, the entries \(a+c/m\), \(b+(d-a)/m-c/m^2\), \(c\), and \(d-c/m\) are integral, and the lower-left entry remains even. This gives the needed common finite-index subgroup. The completion comparison, density argument for \(m>2\), and weight-zero constant alternative then survive. The lemma’s conclusion has not been refuted.

Problem 5 (Minor: genus-zero vanishing needs nonzero curve class).  Remark 4.1(c), p. 19, asserts genus-zero vanishing without excluding \(\beta=0\). Take the same Enriques surface, \(g=0,n=3,\beta=0\), with insertions \((1,1,p)\), where \(\int_Yp=1\). These satisfy Definition 4.2. Then \(\overline M_{0,3}(Y,0)=Y\), its obstruction group is zero, its virtual class is \([Y]\), and the invariant is \(1\).

Page 21 itself retains this constant-map contribution. Restrict the vanishing assertion to \(\beta\ne0\). A rational tail that becomes unstable after forgetting the map must have positive map degree; thus this example does not invalidate the ancestor–descendant comparison or the anomaly equation.
## Normalization clarification (original Problem 7)

Equation (2.1), p. 6, defines \(F_2=G_2-2G_2(2\tau)\). On p. 21 the equality \(2G_2(q)-2G_2(q^2)=G_2(q)+F_2(q)/24\) is false with that definition. The first expression has constant term zero and \(q\) coefficient \(2\); the second has constant term \(-23/576\) and \(q\) coefficient \(25/24\).

Replace the last expression by \(G_2+F_2\). The first expression and the subsequently used \(G_2\) derivative are already correct. No necessary computation is shown to fail because of the redundant rewriting. It is therefore a normalization clarification, not a substantive Minor finding.
# Further checks and remaining limits
## Ordered degeneration: a convention that must be explicit

The relative invariants on p. 22 use ordered contact points and plain virtual integrals. Equation (4.7), p. 29, does not display the usual contact-order and ordering factors or define \(\eta^\vee\) separately. Under an ordinary, unweighted dual interpretation there is a concrete discrepancy.

Take \(g=1,k=1\), no insertions, and the coefficient \(q^0\zeta^0\), the primitive half-fiber \(s\) of the other pencil. The smooth invariant is \(2\). In the degeneration, the relevant rational ruling fibers on \(X_1\) and \(R\) have contact profile \((1,1)\). Their ordered evaluation families in \(E\times E\) are \[\{(e,e+t)\},\qquad \{(e,a-e)\},\] where \(t\) is nonzero two-torsion. Their ordinary intersection has four transverse points, since \(2e=a-t\) has four solutions. The generic ruling can be chosen smooth at these points. The etale double cover on \(X_1\) excludes profile \((2)\); singular ruling components and coincident-contact boundary terms do not contribute at these transverse intersections. Thus the raw ordered contraction is \(4\), while \((1\cdot1)/2!=1/2\) restores \(2\).

The supporting record gives the class selection and genericity conditions. Because the text leaves the dual/sum convention implicit, this is not counted as an unqualified additional confirmed error: a weighted \(\eta^\vee\) or weighted sum resolves it. The convention should be stated and matched to the cited anomaly compatibility. Constant gluing factors do not change the immediate modular-space containment, so this calculation alone does not refute Theorem 4.3.
## Checks that did not produce a further counterexample

The Mukai pullback \((r,\beta,n)\mapsto(r,\pi^*\beta,2n+r)\) has square \(2(\beta^2-r^2-2rn)\) and divisibility \(\gcd(r,\operatorname{div}\beta,2n)\). The odd/even type conditions and the representatives used in Corollary 5.9 were checked with these factors. The orientation-reversing isometries fixing the normal-form vectors account for the passage from full to orientation-preserving lattice orbits. The external orbit and Torelli theorems remain dependencies, rather than new theorems proved by this review.

In the current Toda formula, the weighted pairing contributes \((-1)^{n+r-1}(n+r)\); the change to \((-p)^n\) absorbs \((-1)^n\). The surviving \((-1)^{r-1}\) is consistent. Dividing by an odd cover preserves this parity and leaves the factor \(1/k\). The eight equivariant line-bundle choices and the compensating division by eight were traced separately.

The elliptic anomaly commutator in Appendix B was checked including the two mixed relative-marking terms with ratios \(\eta_i/\eta_j\): they cancel with opposite signs. Its general statement is conditional as written. In the divisibility-two argument the scalar factor has weight \(2g-6\); the extra half-translation reduces it to a level-one cusp form. The stated low-genus vanishing follows, conditional on the earlier modularity input and the repairs above. For divisibility greater than two, the sparse-series argument retains the substantive \(m>2\) condition.

Appendix C was read with the distinction between integral homology and its torsion-free quotient preserved. Its odd-degree equality uses the cited deformation classification; for even multiples of a half-fiber, the maps lie in fibers and only the even integral lift is represented. This is not an identification of the two refined torsion invariants in every class. Statements with any curve class should explicitly retain the effective nonzero scope where needed; the zero-class multiple-cover sum is not defined by the same formula.
## Supporting checks

Three native same-conversation auxiliaries supplied bounded modular, lattice/DT, and GW checks; their precise page coverage, actual image views, historical failed calls, and limitations are retained. They are not human reviewers or independent acceptance authorities. The external controller’s UI observation and the runtime’s own identity statement are recorded separately.

Independent exact integer and rational checks verify the explicit \(E_8\) coefficient, subgroup matrix, Laurent coefficient, normalization values, and corrected recurrence. They do not replace proofs of the external GW/PT correspondence, Hall algebra identities, virtual degeneration, derived Torelli theorem, or all relative anomaly relations. Those cited dependencies were traced but not all independently reconstructed.

Bounded primary-record and title/DOI searches for corrections, supplements and code did not identify an additional applicable item. This does not establish absence. The arXiv source link was not executed; no author code was run, and code availability is not treated as a mathematical requirement. Only the exact acquired v3 is the scientific subject of this report.

The report recommends correction of the central normalization and Section 7 signs, replacement of the weak Jacobi preservation claim by a theorem valid for the actual geometric inputs, and the two substantive local amendments and two notation clarifications above. The intended main enumerative formulas have not been disproved. The remaining geometric support condition is a substantive proof obligation, not an unverified repair represented as completed. The assessment is Major; `scientific_decision=pending` and `human_reviews=[]`. Actual compilation, retained dependency and log files, and inspection of every current report page are recorded separately before delivery completion.

The construction supplying the uniform quantitative input for Theorem B necessarily contains too many elements: a base-expansion argument disproves its asserted size bound for every proposed universal constant. This is a failure of an essential proof input, not a counterexample to the existential small-set lemma or to Theorem B itself. Author: AI technical verification

Title: Technical review of
The Alon–Jaeger–Tarsi conjecture via group ring identities
# Exact source and scope

This review concerns M25-0267, The Alon–Jaeger–Tarsi conjecture via group ring identities, by János Nagy and Péter Pál Pach, DOI `10.4171/jems/1640`. The actual source is arXiv:2107.03956v1, uploaded on 8 July 2021 at 16:31:31 UTC, with 41 physical pages and matching printed numbering. The PDF has 349,710 bytes and SHA256
The source manifest has 21,469 bytes and SHA256
> eb54fffa53fd1e44d1b13e6a9118cb5fdcf3c64e67f6826bb0df640fb1e5f581.

The EMS record reports submission on 2 August 2023, acceptance on 20 November 2024, and online publication on 11 April 2025. The scientific conclusions below apply to the acquired 2021 author version. Equivalence with the later publisher text has not been established. The frozen title, DOI and 2025 batch membership are retained.

Theorem A treats primes \(p>61\), \(p\ne79\), and one forbidden value in each coordinate of \(x\) and \(Mx\). Theorem B asserts a uniform threshold \(p>k^{Kk}\) for \(k\) forbidden values. Theorem C is conditional: the integer-lifting Conjecture 2, for a fixed prime \(p>3\) and all dimensions, implies the Alon–Jaeger–Tarsi conjecture at that prime. These scopes have not been conflated.
# The quantitative construction for Theorem B

Problem 1 (Major: the constructed set in Lemma 2 exceeds its asserted bound).  The last sentence of the proof of Lemma 2, pp. 7–8, asserts that its explicitly constructed union \(A\) has \(|A|\le p^{1/(2k+2)}\) whenever \(p>k^{Kk}\) for a suitable universal \(K\ge32\). A compulsory branch of the printed construction disproves this assertion for every such constant.

This is an analytic counterexample family, with the prime specified by a well-defined minimum and its existence and range proved. No enormous set or uncertified numerical prime is being substituted for the proof.
## Actual impact and repair boundary

Lemma 2 supplies the \(S_k(p)\) estimate used in Corollary 3(ii), p. 10, and then in Theorem 1(iii), pp. 26–30, which is the quantitative Theorem B. The displayed construction does not provide that essential input. The Major assessment reflects this direct loss in the stated proof of the uniform threshold.

The counterexample concerns the cardinality of the constructed union. It does not show that every \(S_k\)-type set is large, nor that Lemma 2’s existence statement or Theorem B is false. A different construction, or a separately proved changed threshold, is needed. A threshold on the scale \(k^{O(k^2)}\) might absorb this particular branch count, but neither the full \(S_k\) property nor such a repaired theorem is established in this review.

There are also literal inconsistencies to correct before any revised construction can be checked: \(A_1\) is printed as \(\{kx,kx\}\), and the separate \(C_2\) formula on p. 7 uses the negative predecessor map \(g\), whereas the general \(C_i\) formula on p. 8 uses \(f\) and interchanges the relevant \(B\) and \(C\) endpoint terms. The cardinality obstruction above survives every interpretation that retains the printed negative \(B_i\) blocks. It is not merely an objection to these typographical inconsistencies.
# Small-set bounds for Theorem A

Problem 2 (Minor: Lemma 1 is false at small primes).  Lemma 1, pp. 5–6, asserts \(S_1(p)\le2\lfloor\log_2p\rfloor\) for every prime \(p\ge3\). With the paper’s intended nonempty-set convention, \(S_1(3)=3>2\) and \(S_1(7)=5>4\).

For \(p=3\), a point and the two distinct endpoints of its nontrivial three-term progression already exhaust the field. For \(p=7\), suppose a set of at most four elements had the required midpoint property. After translation and scaling it contains \(-1,0,1\). With only one additional element \(t\), the midpoint condition for \(1\) requires \(t\in\{2,3\}\), whereas that for \(-1\) requires \(t\in\{4,5\}\). This is impossible. The set \(\{0,1,2,3,4\}\) does satisfy the condition, proving the stated minimum.

The last logarithmic equality on p. 6 fails when \(p+1\) is a power of two. The halving construction does, however, prove the uniform bound \[S_1(p)\le2\lfloor\log_2p\rfloor+2;\] away from that power-of-two boundary its original sharper bound is valid. This suffices to repair Corollary 1. For \(p\ge512\), writing \(h=\lfloor\log_2p\rfloor\ge9\) gives \[(2h+2)^2<2^h-1\le p-1.\] The first inequality holds at \(h=9\) and persists by induction. For \(199\le p<512\), the possible boundary values \(255\) and \(511\) are composite; the original bound works except at \(257\), which is explicitly covered by the table. All remaining required primes are covered by the Appendix, including \(127\).

Every one of the Appendix’s 27 listed sets, containing 251 listed elements in total, was checked with exact modular arithmetic. For each element, a nonzero common difference and both endpoints were verified; all size inequalities \(|A|^2<p-1\) passed. The required prime list has no omissions. The auxiliary witnesses were independently rechecked by the primary reviewer. The claimed optimality through \(p=151\) and the necessity of the excluded-prime range were not exhaustively reproduced; they are not needed for this sufficient-condition repair. This issue therefore does not invalidate the checked route to Theorem A.
# The auxiliary orthogonality characterizations

Problem 3 (Minor: Propositions 2 and 3 use the wrong summation sets).  Proposition 2 on p. 16 and Proposition 3 on p. 17 impose zero sums on hyperplanes obtained by fixing one coordinate. Their proofs require zero sums along coordinate lines. The printed equivalences are false.

Take \(p=5\), \(n=1\) and the nonsingular matrix \(M=[1]\). Each set \(\{v:v_1=x\}\) is a singleton, so the printed hypotheses force \(f=g=0\). The universal pairing condition is consequently true over both \(\mathbb C\) and \(\mathbb F_5\). But \(x=1\) is a nowhere-zero vector with \(Mx=1\), so property \((\mathrm{P}'1)\) is false, and \[(1-g)^2=1-2g+g^2\] is nonzero in both \(\mathbb Z[\mathbb F_5]\) and \(\mathbb F_5[\mathbb F_5]\). Thus the relevant group-ring properties are also false. All matrix, dimension and prime hypotheses are satisfied.
The mismatch also occurs in dimension three: \(f(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_1^4\) on \(\mathbb F_5^3\) has all the printed hyperplane sums zero, but its sum on the first coordinate line through zero is \(-1\).
## Correct statements and verification

Replace the conditions by \[\sum_{t\in\mathbb F_p}f(v+te_j)=0,\qquad
 \sum_{t\in\mathbb F_p}g(v+ta_j)=0
 \quad\hbox{for every }v,j.\] For the unnormalized Fourier transform, these conditions make the respective transforms vanish on the frequency hyperplanes \(u_j=0\) and \(\langle a_j,u\rangle=0\). The correct bilinear Parseval identity is \[\sum_vf(v)g(v)=p^{-n}\sum_u\widehat f(u)\widehat g(-u).\] The frequency hyperplanes are stable under negation. Hence the covering property implies orthogonality. Conversely, a nowhere-zero admissible frequency gives opposite characters with pairing \(p^n\ne0\). This proves the corrected complex version.

Over \(\mathbb F_p\), let \(T_bf(v)=f(v+b)\), \(D=\prod_j(I-T_{e_j})\) and \(D'=\prod_j(I-T_{a_j})\). The regular translation representation is faithful, so the group-ring identity is equivalent to \(DD'=0\). Triangular reduction of monomials shows that \(\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}D\) is spanned by the monomials with every exponent at most \(p-2\); its dimension is \((p-1)^n\). Since \(\sum_{t\in\mathbb F_p}t^{p-1}=-1\), this is precisely the corrected line-sum space. The analogous assertion holds for \(D'\) after a basis change. Finally, \[D^*=(-1)^nT_{-\sum_j e_j}D,\qquad
 (\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}D)^\perp=\mathop{\mathrm{Ker}}D.\] Thus the corrected orthogonality condition is equivalent to \(\mathop{\mathrm{Im}}D'\subset\mathop{\mathrm{Ker}}D\), or \(DD'=0\).

The source’s Lemma 6 already states the correct line-sum condition. The main proof in Section 6 actually invokes Lemma 7’s explicit finite-support binomial functions, whose independent coefficient proof is valid. It does not use the false hyperplane hypotheses of Propositions 2–3. The local classification follows that checked dependence, not merely the availability of a repair.
# Normalization and characteristic-p qualifications
## Normalization clarification (original Problem 4)

Several equalities in Section 5 have missing nonzero normalization or sign factors. The zero criteria used in the checked arguments survive these corrections. No necessary zero or nonzero test is invalidated by these unit factors; this item is not counted as a substantive Minor finding.

With \(\widehat f(u)=\sum_vf(v)\omega^{\langle u,v\rangle}\) and the source’s normalized convolution \(f*g=p^{-n}\sum_wf(w)g(v-w)\), the p. 13 formula should be \[\widehat{f*g}=p^{-n}\widehat f\,\widehat g.\] For \(p=5,n=1,f=g=\mathbf1_{\{0\}}\), its left side is the constant \(1/5\), whereas the printed right side is \(1\). The separate formula for the transform of a pointwise product is consistent with the normalized convolution.

For \(\delta_j=I-T_{e_j}\) on p. 18, the leading coefficient of a product of differences is \((-1)^n\prod_jb_j\), not \(\prod_jb_j\); already \(\delta x=-1\). The p. 20 line sum of \(x^{p-1}\) equals \(-1\), not \(1\). The point-indicator polynomial used on p. 23 takes value \((-1)^n\) at its support, and the top-degree coefficient/pairing identity on p. 24 has the same sign. These statements follow directly from \((X^p-X)'=-1\) and the finite-field power sums. None of the required nonvanishing tests changes. The phrase \((p-1)^n\) functions on p. 18 should refer to the dimension, not the cardinality of the function space.

Problem 4 (Minor: the proof of Lemma 9 divides by a possibly zero factorial).  On pp. 24–25 the proof divides by \(Q!\), although \(Q=\sum r_i=\sum s_j\) need not be less than \(p\). The final coefficient-duality conclusion is nevertheless true.

For \(p=5\), \(M=I_2\), \(r=s=(4,1)\) and \(Q=5\), the target coefficient is \(1\). The intermediate coefficient in \((x_1y_1+x_2y_2)^5\) is \(5=0\) in \(\mathbb F_5\), and \(Q!=0\). The displayed division is therefore undefined in the stated field, under fully permitted exponents.
# Positive proof checks and remaining editorial corrections

Lemma 3’s probabilistic partition estimate was checked, including the ceiling in the number of colors and the integer greedy choice of disjoint progressions. With \(u=p^{1/(2k+1)}\) and \(p>k^{32k}\), the estimates \(\lceil u\rceil^{2k}<2u^{2k}\) and \(u/(8k^2)>2\log p\) suffice for the displayed union bound. Lemma 4’s random dilation argument and Corollary 2 then supply the separation sets whenever \(N_k(p)S_k(p)<p-1\). This valid conditional route is distinct from the failed uniform construction in Problem 1.

Lemma 7’s pairing is exactly a coefficient of the rescaled group-ring product. The tested shifts cover its support. Nonzero rescaling multiplies each factor by a unit whose augmentation is nonzero; the endpoints \(t_i=0,p-1\) cause no exception. Independent exact one-dimensional checks covered 1,600 parameter choices and 14,400 coefficient comparisons, alongside the general argument.

In Lemma 10, an inclusion-maximal support set \(I_u\) and a coordinate \(j\notin I_u\) force every remaining pairing term with \(\ell'_j<k\) to vanish. The surviving \(\ell'_j=k\) term removes the corresponding row factor. The subsequent truncated group-algebra coefficient extracts the lower-dimensional identity. On p. 26 the relevant general reference is Corollary 2. On pp. 29–30 the minor must delete row \(j\) and column \(\ell\), namely \(M_{j,\ell}\); the transposed and later inconsistent subscripts should be corrected. The associated products and quantifiers must omit \(j\) only in the row family, retaining every coordinate index in the other family. These changes restore the checked conditional Theorem 1(i) argument.

Theorem C’s larger-vector-space construction in Lemma 11 was reconstructed. Its two displayed systems are bases; projection supplies the extra row factor, the enlarged product vanishes modulo \(p\), and a Fourier witness with independently scaled blocks makes the integer product nonzero. The equality of the kernels of multiplication by \((1-g^{e_i})^2\) and \((1-g^{e_i})\) holds over the integer group ring by its embedding into the complex semisimple group algebra. In the final derivative calculation, the apparently omitted group elements are eliminated using the original product identity; this is not an additional error. Invertibility then permits the required row-factor removal and dimension reduction.

In Proposition 4’s converse, pp. 36–37, the repeated upper bound \(n+1\) should be \(n\), and the ambient ring should be that of the declared extended space. After scaling to a common affine hyperplane, the map \(v\mapsto v+L(v)w\) is injective and gives the stated lifting argument. The final coefficient basis is triangular in \(1-g^w\). Use \(\sigma_j=0\) for negative \(j\) to cover the small-dimension endpoint. Theorem B’s introductory statement should explicitly quantify a nonsingular \(M\) and put \(X_i,Y_i\subset\mathbb F_p\), as its intended coordinate formulation requires.
# Supporting checks

Native bounded helpers in the same conversation checked additive constructions, group-ring algebra and the main reduction arguments. Their exact roles, inherited runtime descriptions, page coverage, computations and limitations are retained separately. They are AI auxiliaries, not human or independent acceptance reviewers. The runtime self-description is GPT-6 Astra Pro; the controller-reported account and GPT-6/Pro UI observations are separate and the backend was not independently verified.

The new construction obstruction was proposed by the primary reviewer and independently challenged by the additive-combinatorics helper. Earlier checkpoints that had not yet established it remain unchanged. One helper’s initial exact check failed because its own minor-sign assertion was wrong; the failed script and exit status are preserved alongside its corrected successful run. A helper’s accented identity fields were degraded by encoding; the intact frozen manifest and actual title page govern the identity here.

Mechanical extraction and rendering are not counted as scientific reading or visual inspection. No author code was executed. The search of arXiv and EMS metadata and bounded queries for corrections, supplements and code identified no applicable additional item; this does not prove absence, and code availability is not a mathematical defect. External references were not all independently reproved. This report is an initial technical review: `scientific_decision=pending`, with no human review.

report: Abstract: The assessment of the exact acquired author version is Major. The central conservativity proof uses a false interchange between effective slices and the cofiber of rho. An explicit cellular example with finite slice tower proves that the purported formal identity fails. It does not contradict the conservativity theorem: the additional algebraic-closure vanishing premise is not satisfied by that example. A replacement proof, using module conservativity followed by the orthogonality of a pure slice, restores the required step under the stated hypotheses. A separate extension needed in the topological comparison has not been fully verified and is recorded as a limitation, not as a false equivalence. All twelve physical source pages were read. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI technical verification

Title: Technical review of
A motivic analogue of the \(K(1)\)-local sphere spectrum
# Exact source and theorem scope

This review concerns M25-0268, A motivic analogue of the \(K(1)\)-local sphere spectrum, by William Balderrama, Kyle Ormsby, and James D. Quigley (the PDF uses J.D. Quigley), DOI `10.4171/jems/1641`. The acquired source is arXiv:2307.13512v3, uploaded on 6 November 2023 at 18:55:39 UTC, with twelve physical pages and matching printed numbering. Its 210,773 bytes have SHA256
The source manifest has 22,748 bytes and SHA256

The arXiv record calls v3 the pre-proofs version accepted to JEMS. The EMS landing page reports submission on 10 August 2023, acceptance on 30 October 2023, and online publication on 4 April 2025. The acquired PDF has not been shown to coincide with the publisher text. The frozen title, DOI, and 2025 batch membership remain unchanged.

Theorem A treats every base scheme \(S\) on which \(2\) is invertible and every \(X\in\mathrm{SH}(S)\). With \[JQ=\mathop{\mathrm{fib}}\bigl(\psi^3-1:KQ^\wedge_{(2,\eta)}
                  \longrightarrow KQ^\wedge_{(2,\eta)}\bigr),\] it identifies \(L_{KGL/2}X\) with \((X\otimes JQ)^\wedge_{(2,\eta)}\) and the corresponding fiber on completed \(X\otimes KQ\). Here \(KQ\) and \(KGL\) are the absolute motivic spectra specified by the authors; their representability interpretation on regular bases must not be substituted for the definition on all bases. The completion in the result is essential. No uncompleted smashing-localization assertion is inferred.
# A false formal step in the conservativity proof

Equation reference: wrong. Problem 1 (Major: slices do not commute with the rho cofiber as asserted).  In the proof of Theorem 3.1, p. 8, exactness is invoked to identify \[
 s_*(C(\rho)\otimes X/2)\simeq C(\rho)\otimes s_*(X/2).\] A Tate suspension changes the slice index. Consequently this is not a valid consequence of exactness, and the claimed ordinary module identity is false.

Equation reference: correct. For any motivic spectrum \(Y\), the correct slice triangle is \[
 \Sigma^{-1,-1}s_{q+1}Y\longrightarrow s_qY
       \longrightarrow s_q(C(\rho)\otimes Y).\] Indeed, \(s_q(\Sigma^{-1,-1}Y)
=\Sigma^{-1,-1}s_{q+1}Y\). Replacing \(s_{q+1}Y\) by \(s_qY\) would incorrectly remove the weight shift. Keeping the slice grading does not solve this problem: the first term requires reindexing, and forgetting that grading does not turn the induced map into ordinary multiplication by \(\rho\) on each slice.
## A concrete counterexample at the precise formal scope

Work over \(k=\mathbb Q\), and put \(H={H\mathbb F_2}_{\mathbb Q}\). This is a cellular pure zero-slice. For the cellularity assertion, the acquired Röndigs–Spitzweck–Østvær reference [RSO], arXiv v2, Proposition 3.31 and Lemma 3.32 (physical p. 29), supplies a cell presentation of \(H\mathbb Z_{\mathbb Q}\); taking the cofiber of \(2\) gives \(H\). Its zero-slice property follows from the same reference, Definition 2.1 and Theorem 2.7, physical pp. 5–6.

First the triangle \[\Sigma^{-1,-1}H\xrightarrow{\rho}H\longrightarrow C(\rho)H\] gives \[s_0(C(\rho)H)=H,\qquad
 s_{-1}(C(\rho)H)=\Sigma^{0,-1}H,\qquad
 s_q(C(\rho)H)=0\quad(q\ne-1,0).\] Thus even the simple example \(Y=H\) distinguishes the two sides of the asserted interchange after inverting \(\rho\). For an example satisfying more of the structural hypotheses in the surrounding argument, take \[X=C(\rho)H,\qquad Y=X/2.\] Then \(X\) is cellular and \(2\)-torsion, and its slice tower has only the two nonzero slices just computed. It is therefore convergent. Its real-points Betti realization vanishes, since \(\rho\) realizes to an equivalence. These are the relevant structural hypotheses.

Equation reference: nonzero. Because \(X\) is an \(H\)-module, \(2\) acts trivially, and hence \[Y\simeq X\oplus\Sigma^{1,0}X,\qquad
 s_1Y=0,\qquad s_0Y=H\oplus\Sigma^{1,0}H.\] Equation [correct] (#correct) at \(q=0\) now yields \[
 s_0(C(\rho)\otimes Y)=H\oplus\Sigma^{1,0}H.\] The total slice object on the left of [wrong] (#wrong) therefore has nonzero \(\rho\)-localization.

Here is an explicit check of that nonvanishing. In mod-\(2\) Milnor \(K\)-theory, the sign rule \[\{a\}\longmapsto \epsilon(a)t,\qquad
 \epsilon(a)=
 \begin{cases}1,&a<0,\\0,&a>0,\end{cases}\] defines a homomorphism \(k_*^M(\mathbb Q)\to\mathbb F_2[t]\). Multiplicativity of the sign verifies the bilinear relations, and \(\epsilon(a)\epsilon(1-a)=0\) verifies the Steinberg relation. In particular, \(\{-1\}^n\) maps to \(t^n\ne0\) for every \(n\). Using \(\pi_{*,*}H=k_*^M(\mathbb Q)[\tau]\), this proves \(H[\rho^{-1}]\ne0\), as required in [nonzero] (#nonzero). On the other hand, \[\bigl(C(\rho)\otimes s_*Y\bigr)[\rho^{-1}]=0\] by the definition of \(C(\rho)\). The two ordinary module objects in [wrong] (#wrong) cannot be equivalent.

The scope of this counterexample is crucial. The chosen \(X\) is not killed by pullback to an algebraic closure. It is a counterexample to the purported general formal interchange, including the structural conditions listed above, but it is not a counterexample to the vanishing implication used in Theorem 3.1, to Theorem 3.1 itself, or to Theorem A.
## Why this affects a core argument

Theorem 3.1 is the principal conservativity result of Section 3. Its proof uses [wrong] (#wrong) to treat the slices as \(\rho\)-torsion and apply Proposition 3.8. Equation [nonzero] (#nonzero) shows directly why this inference is unavailable: slices of a \(\rho\)-torsion object need not themselves be \(\rho\)-torsion. The resulting gap lies in the central reduction to \(\mathbb C\), used by Proposition 3.12 and then Theorem A. The Major assessment concerns this essential proof step; it does not assert a false final theorem or require that the defect be irreparable.
# Replacement argument and its boundary

A pure slice supplies exactly the additional fact needed to repair the argument. If \(M\) is a cellular \({H\mathbb F_2}_k\)-module, is a pure \(q\)-slice, and becomes zero over an algebraic closure of a prime field \(k\ne\mathbb F_2\), then \(C(\rho)\otimes M\) is cellular, \(\rho\)-torsion, and also becomes zero there. Proposition 3.8 gives \(C(\rho)\otimes M=0\). Therefore \[\rho:\Sigma^{-1,-1}M\xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }M.\] A \(q\)-slice lies in \(\mathrm{SH}(k)^{\mathrm{eff}}(q)\) and is right orthogonal to \(\mathrm{SH}(k)^{\mathrm{eff}}(q+1)\). But the equivalence implies \[M\simeq\Sigma^{1,1}M
      \in\mathrm{SH}(k)^{\mathrm{eff}}(q+1).\] Thus its identity morphism is zero, and \(M=0\).

The global order of the argument also matters. It avoids assuming that arbitrary base change preserves an infinite slice-completion limit. Let \(S_0=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z[1/2]\) and let \(X\) satisfy the original hypotheses of Theorem 3.1, with \(X_{\mathbb C}=0\). Put \[Y=C(\rho)\otimes X/2,\qquad N_q=s_qY
 \quad\text{over }S_0.\] By Lemma 3.3, \(X_K=0\) for every algebraic closure \(K\) of a prime field \(k\ne\mathbb F_2\). Cellular slice base change identifies \((N_q)_k\) with \(s_q(Y_k)\) and identifies its pullback to \(K\) with zero. The applicable reference is [RSO], Corollary 2.17, arXiv v2 physical p. 12. Its connected compatible-pair assumptions hold for \(S_0\) with coefficients \(\mathbb Z_{(2)}\), for these prime fields, and for their algebraic closures; see Definition 2.1 and Remark 2.2, physical p. 5.

Lemma 3.5 makes \((N_q)_k\) a cellular \({H\mathbb F_2}_k\)-module, since \(Y_k=(C(\rho)\otimes X_k)/2\). Apply the preceding pure-slice argument to obtain \((N_q)_k=0\) for every such \(k\). Lemma 3.2 then gives \(N_q=0\) over \(S_0\). This holds for every \(q\). The original convergence hypothesis on \(X\) passes to \(Y\) through finite cofibers and Tate shifts, so \(Y=0\) over \(S_0\).

Finally, for each prime field \(k\ne\mathbb F_2\), \(C(\rho)\otimes(X_k/2)=0\). Lemma 3.4 applies: over finite fields \(\rho\) is nilpotent, and over \(\mathbb Q\) the original real Betti hypothesis supplies the required vanishing. Hence \(X_k/2=0\). Lemma 3.2 gives \(X/2=0\) globally. Since \(X\) is \(2\)-torsion, invertibility of \(2\) on \(X\) forces \(X=0\).

This is a complete replacement of the faulty step relative to the named module-conservativity, field comparison, and slice-base-change results. It preserves the original theorem’s hypotheses. It neither treats [wrong] (#wrong) as correct nor assumes convergence after pullback. No stronger conservativity statement is claimed, and no author adoption of this repair is known.
# Other proof checks and an unresolved comparison qualification

The argument in Section 2 was checked using \(KGL\simeq KQ/\eta\) and the finite \((2,\eta)\) quotient. Completed \(KQ\)-modules supply the stated local objects; testing the unit map after smashing with \(KGL/2\) reduces the arbitrary-\(X\) assertion to the sphere. The use of completion was retained throughout.

The base-change claim in Lemma 3.9 concerns the appropriate finite-quotient object: \[KGL/2\otimes JQ\simeq
 KGL/2\otimes\mathop{\mathrm{fib}}\bigl(\psi^3-1:
 KQ[1/3]\longrightarrow KQ[1/3]\bigr).\] It does not require a general assertion that raw completed \(JQ\) commutes with every base change. Real-points Betti realization in Lemma 3.11 was distinguished from the equivariant Betti realization discussed in the introduction. The needed slice-convergence reduction is over \(S_0\); this review does not independently certify the broadest arbitrary-base wording of Lemma 3.10.

In Lemma 3.6, \(\tau\)-free is explicitly defined to mean free over \(\mathbb F_2[\tau]\), not merely torsion-free. The iterative construction kills the maps on low homotopy groups, and its colimit supplies the connective approximation. Lemma 3.7 can also be checked directly: construct the stem-zero approximation to \({H\mathbb F_2}_k\) by successively killing negative-stem free cells. A map representing an element of a module concentrated in stem zero extends through each step because the obstruction groups in negative stems vanish. This identifies the approximation with \(E\) and produces the required maps from weight shifts of \(E\). The resulting basis map is an equivalence by cellularity. This check avoids relying on an unstated convergence claim for the displayed universal coefficient spectral sequence. Proposition 3.8 then uses the finite stem range of \(C(\rho)\otimes{H\mathbb F_2}_k\) for the specified prime fields; its prime-field restriction was not omitted.

For Section 4, the acquired published GIKR reference [GIKR], physical p. 14 (printed p. 3610), Proposition 3.18, preserves the relevant cofiber sequence when the map on odd \(MU\)-homology is injective. This corresponds to Proposition 3.17 in the cited preprint numbering. The evenness argument was checked: the Wood cofiber sequence and triviality of \(\eta\) on \(MU\) make \(MU\otimes KO\) a retract of \(MU\otimes KU\). The latter has even, torsion-free homotopy, so the mod-\(2\) objects needed here also have even \(MU\)-homology. Thus the stated fiber-sequence use of that result has the required input.

There remains a precise limit to the tensor comparison check. GIKR’s Proposition 3.26, physical pp. 16–17 (printed pp. 3612–3613), requires its first variable to be a bounded-below, finite-type even-cell complex. This is Proposition 3.25 in the earlier numbering. The source paper instead applies it to periodic \(KU\), which is not bounded below, after describing \(KU\) as a filtered colimit of finite even-cell complexes. The adjacent GIKR colimit lemma has a uniform bounded-below and increasing-connectivity hypothesis. Consequently the cited statement alone does not literally cover the passage used on source p. 10.

No counterexample to \[\Gamma_*(KU)\otimes_{\Gamma_*(\mathbb S)}\Gamma_*(KO)
       \simeq\Gamma_*(KU\otimes KO)\] has been established here. Results for synthetic spectra give a plausible extension route for filtered colimits of finite \(MU\)-projectives, but the full compatibility with this \(\Gamma_*\) construction has not been independently completed. This is recorded as an unverified dependency qualification, not as a second confirmed false statement. A revised proof should give the appropriate extension or a compatible alternative comparison.
# Coverage, evidence, and limitations

All twelve source pages, including the introduction, every lemma and proof, bibliography, and affiliations, were read as text and actually viewed as page images. The review separately checked the exactness argument, the explicit Milnor-\(K\) sign computation, the counterexample’s hypotheses and exclusions, and the replacement pure-slice proof. These are analytic checks; no author’s code was executed and no numerical test is presented as a proof.

The primary reviewer read their saved checks, reconciled the counterexample scope, and performed the report assessment. These are AI assistance records, not human reviews or independent acceptance. The runtime self-description and the externally reported UI selection are recorded separately; backend equivalence is not independently verified.

The acquired RSO reference pages used above and the three GIKR evidence pages were inspected at their actual formulas. This is not a claim to have independently reproved those entire references. The additional reference checks and their restricted coverage are preserved in the supporting records. Bounded searches of the arXiv and publisher records and for corrections, supplements, and code found no applicable separate correction or computational supplement. This does not establish nonexistence; absence of code is not a defect of this mathematical paper.

One intermediate checkpoint prematurely listed source images whose tool response had been truncated. That record was retained, and a later correction records the separate successful viewing of those images. Rendering-time records likewise retain their original false inspection values; actual later viewing is recorded separately.

The assessment is therefore Major, at the core-proof-step scope specified in Problem 1, with a complete local replacement argument and the separate comparison limitation above. The acquired version’s main localization theorem has not been disproved. `scientific_decision` remains `pending`; `human_reviews` is empty.

analysis:
In the proof of Theorem 3.1, p. 8, exactness is invoked to identify \[
 s_*(C(\rho)\otimes X/2)\simeq C(\rho)\otimes s_*(X/2).\] A Tate suspension changes the slice index. Consequently this is not a valid consequence of exactness, and the claimed ordinary module identity is false.

Equation reference: correct. For any motivic spectrum \(Y\), the correct slice triangle is \[
 \Sigma^{-1,-1}s_{q+1}Y\longrightarrow s_qY
       \longrightarrow s_q(C(\rho)\otimes Y).\] Indeed, \(s_q(\Sigma^{-1,-1}Y)
=\Sigma^{-1,-1}s_{q+1}Y\). Replacing \(s_{q+1}Y\) by \(s_qY\) would incorrectly remove the weight shift. Keeping the slice grading does not solve this problem: the first term requires reindexing, and forgetting that grading does not turn the induced map into ordinary multiplication by \(\rho\) on each slice.

Work over \(k=\mathbb Q\), and put \(H={H\mathbb F_2}_{\mathbb Q}\). This is a cellular pure zero-slice. For the cellularity assertion, the acquired Röndigs–Spitzweck–Østvær reference [RSO], arXiv v2, Proposition 3.31 and Lemma 3.32 (physical p. 29), supplies a cell presentation of \(H\mathbb Z_{\mathbb Q}\); taking the cofiber of \(2\) gives \(H\). Its zero-slice property follows from the same reference, Definition 2.1 and Theorem 2.7, physical pp. 5–6.

First the triangle \[\Sigma^{-1,-1}H\xrightarrow{\rho}H\longrightarrow C(\rho)H\] gives \[s_0(C(\rho)H)=H,\qquad
 s_{-1}(C(\rho)H)=\Sigma^{0,-1}H,\qquad
 s_q(C(\rho)H)=0\quad(q\ne-1,0).\] Thus even the simple example \(Y=H\) distinguishes the two sides of the asserted interchange after inverting \(\rho\). For an example satisfying more of the structural hypotheses in the surrounding argument, take \[X=C(\rho)H,\qquad Y=X/2.\] Then \(X\) is cellular and \(2\)-torsion, and its slice tower has only the two nonzero slices just computed. It is therefore convergent. Its real-points Betti realization vanishes, since \(\rho\) realizes to an equivalence. These are the relevant structural hypotheses.

Equation reference: nonzero. Because \(X\) is an \(H\)-module, \(2\) acts trivially, and hence \[Y\simeq X\oplus\Sigma^{1,0}X,\qquad
 s_1Y=0,\qquad s_0Y=H\oplus\Sigma^{1,0}H.\] Equation [correct] (#correct) at \(q=0\) now yields \[
 s_0(C(\rho)\otimes Y)=H\oplus\Sigma^{1,0}H.\] The total slice object on the left of [wrong] (#wrong) therefore has nonzero \(\rho\)-localization.

Here is an explicit check of that nonvanishing. In mod-\(2\) Milnor \(K\)-theory, the sign rule \[\{a\}\longmapsto \epsilon(a)t,\qquad
 \epsilon(a)=
 \begin{cases}1,&a<0,\\0,&a>0,\end{cases}\] defines a homomorphism \(k_*^M(\mathbb Q)\to\mathbb F_2[t]\). Multiplicativity of the sign verifies the bilinear relations, and \(\epsilon(a)\epsilon(1-a)=0\) verifies the Steinberg relation. In particular, \(\{-1\}^n\) maps to \(t^n\ne0\) for every \(n\). Using \(\pi_{*,*}H=k_*^M(\mathbb Q)[\tau]\), this proves \(H[\rho^{-1}]\ne0\), as required in [nonzero] (#nonzero). On the other hand, \[\bigl(C(\rho)\otimes s_*Y\bigr)[\rho^{-1}]=0\] by the definition of \(C(\rho)\). The two ordinary module objects in [wrong] (#wrong) cannot be equivalent.

The scope of this counterexample is crucial. The chosen \(X\) is not killed by pullback to an algebraic closure. It is a counterexample to the purported general formal interchange, including the structural conditions listed above, but it is not a counterexample to the vanishing implication used in Theorem 3.1, to Theorem 3.1 itself, or to Theorem A.

Theorem 3.1 is the principal conservativity result of Section 3. Its proof uses [wrong] (#wrong) to treat the slices as \(\rho\)-torsion and apply Proposition 3.8. Equation [nonzero] (#nonzero) shows directly why this inference is unavailable: slices of a \(\rho\)-torsion object need not themselves be \(\rho\)-torsion. The resulting gap lies in the central reduction to \(\mathbb C\), used by Proposition 3.12 and then Theorem A. The Major assessment concerns this essential proof step; it does not assert a false final theorem or require that the defect be irreparable.
