report: Abstract: The assessment of the exact acquired author version is Major. Three core proof defects are confirmed. Two essential identities are incorrect: the moving coordinate system loses a phase connection, and the negative distorted spectral branch is assigned an incorrect local cubic dynamics. Direct differentiation and a realizable mixed-scattering profile give decisive evidence. A uniform oscillatory-integral remainder used in the stationary-phase argument is also false. These are errors in the proof, not counterexamples to the main stability theorem. Consistent phase coordinates and a reduction to the positive branch give specific repair routes, whose remaining analytic obligations are identified. Several local statements also require correction, including projection hypotheses and normalization. All 106 physical source pages were read; the report distinguishes this coverage from a complete independent reconstruction of every cited theorem. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI technical verification

Title: Technical review of
Asymptotic stability of solitary waves for one-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equations
# Source identity and precise scope

This review concerns M25-0269, by Charles Collot and Pierre Germain, with the title above and DOI `10.4171/jems/1642`. The acquired PDF is arXiv:2306.03668v1, submitted on 6 June 2023 at 13:31:38 UTC, with 106 physical pages and matching printed numbering. Its 936,176 bytes have SHA256
The 22,116-byte manifest has SHA256
> 061add4808e5f55f2166fd4f4fd7e4a83c3caa0fb3da1fa41008df1a5879541b.

The publisher landing page records submission on 22 August 2023, acceptance on 10 November 2024, and online publication on 22 April 2025. The publisher full text has not been established to equal this earlier author version. The frozen title, identifier, DOI, and 2025 batch membership are retained.

The equation and standing wave convention are \[iv_t-v_{xx}-F'(|v|^2)v=0,\qquad
 v=e^{-i\omega t}\Phi_\omega,\qquad
 \Phi_\omega''-\omega\Phi_\omega+F'(\Phi_\omega^2)\Phi_\omega=0.\] Theorem 1.1 assumes a smooth branch of positive even localized profiles, the positive slope \(c_\omega=\partial_\omega\int\Phi_\omega^2>0\), no discrete spectrum other than zero, and no resonance at either spectral edge. The nonlinearity has a nondegenerate minimum at zero, with \(L=F''(0)>0\). Small perturbations belong to \(H^1\cap L^{2,1}\). The conclusion includes a limiting soliton, decaying radiation, a modified scattering profile, convergence of the modulation parameters, and continuity of the scattering data. These quantifiers and the distinction between the physical radiation and its two distorted spectral components matter below.
# Core defects

Problem 1 (Major: omitted connection in the moving frame).  Equations (8.1)–(8.2), p. 47, and (8.9), p. 48, omit \(-y\dot p\) in the coefficient of the phase direction. This coefficient propagates to (8.26), p. 54, (9.18), p. 60, and the modulation estimates used in (12.13), Section 12.6, p. 87.
## Exact differentiation and an admissible witness

Put \(z=x+y(t)\) and \(w(t,z)=\Phi_{\omega(t)}(z)+u(t,z)\). The actual ansatz in (8.1) is \(v(t,x)=e^{i(p(t)x-\gamma(t))}w(t,x+y(t))\). Directly, \[e^{-i(px-\gamma)}(iv_t-v_{xx})
 =iw_t-w_{zz}+i(\dot y-2p)w_z+
   \bigl(\dot\gamma+p^2-\dot p(z-y)\bigr)w .\] Consequently the right-hand modulation coefficient is \[a=\omega-p^2-\dot\gamma-y\dot p,\] rather than the printed \(\omega-p^2-\dot\gamma\). The omitted vector term is \(-y\dot p(\Xi_0+\sigma_3U)\).

This failure occurs under the stated hypotheses of Section 8.1.1, which at this point allow arbitrary \(C^1\) frame parameters. Fix any actual soliton in the assumed branch and the exact solution \(v=e^{-i\omega t}\Phi_\omega(x)\). Near \(t_0\), choose \(p=A(t-t_0)\), \(y=b\ne0\), and \(\gamma=\omega t\), and set \[u(t,z)=e^{-ip(t)(z-b)}\Phi_\omega(z-b)-\Phi_\omega(z).\] These choices satisfy the ansatz identically. The residual of the printed scalar equation at \(t_0\) is \(-Ab(\Phi_\omega+u)\), which is nonzero for \(A\ne0\). The perturbation at \(t_0\) can be made small by taking \(b\) small. This is an exact coordinate-identity counterexample; it is not claimed to satisfy the later orthogonality choice or to furnish a counterexample to Theorem 1.1.
## Impact and repair boundary

The omitted coefficient is not automatically an integrable error. The estimates \(y=O(t)\) and \(\dot p=O(t^{-2+2\alpha})\) give only \(y\dot p=O(t^{-1+2\alpha})\). Thus the equation from which the phase estimates are derived is materially different. This affects a central derivation even though a change of phase coordinates can repair it.

One can consistently replace the printed phase defect by \(a\) throughout the modulation system, and then reconstruct the physical \(\gamma\). Alternatively one can change the ansatz to include the primitive of \(y\dot p\) in its phase. The geometric phase in (8.22), p. 52, can also be used, provided the conversion is explicit: if \(\gamma=-\gamma_{\rm geom}-py\), then \(a=\omega-p^2+\dot\gamma_{\rm geom}+p\dot y\). That alternative chart does not make the literal identity (8.1)–(8.2) correct.

There is enough conditional decay to reconstruct the desired physical phase. If the corrected equations establish \(p-p_\infty=O(t^{-1-\nu})\), \(y=O(t)\), and \(\dot y=O(1)\), then \[\int_t^\infty y(s)\dot p(s)\,\mathrm ds
 =-y(t)(p(t)-p_\infty)
   -\int_t^\infty\dot y(s)(p(s)-p_\infty)\,\mathrm ds
 =O(t^{-\nu}).\] This verifies the needed tail estimate. A fully consistent rewrite of every subsequent phase variable and of the final continuity argument is still required.

Problem 2 (Major: incorrect negative-branch cubic identity).  The identity (13.10), p. 92, its use in Lemma 13.5, p. 98, and the common local phase evolution for both signs in Proposition 13.1 and pp. 99–100 are false for the negative spectral branch. The reality relation (8.16), p. 50, mixes the two frequency signs through scattering.
## A profile satisfying the spectral reality constraints

For \(\xi>0\), write \[F_+=\binom{A}{B}=\binom{\widetilde f_+(\xi)}{\widetilde f_+(-\xi)},
 \quad F_-=\binom{C}{D},\quad
 R=\begin{pmatrix}r&s\\s&r\end{pmatrix},\quad
 J=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(1,-1).\] Here \(r=r(\xi)\), \(s=s(\xi)\), and the conventions of (5.31) and (8.16) give \[R^*R=I,\qquad F_-=-R^*\overline{F_+}.\] Expanding the actual coefficient table in (13.10) gives \[\Theta_-(\xi)=\bar r\,|A|^2\bar A+
                      \bar s\,|B|^2\bar B .
 \tag{1}\] It is not in general \(-|C|^2C\).

The paper’s own scattering properties imply the existence of an actual frequency \(\xi_*>0\) with \(|s(\xi_*)|^2=|r(\xi_*)|^2=1/2\): use continuity, \(s(0)=0\), \(s(\xi)\to1\), and unitarity. Thus the example does not rely on assuming that an arbitrary unitary matrix is realized by a potential. Choose a smooth compactly supported positive-branch profile near \(-\xi_*\), with value \(a\ne0\) there and zero near \(+\xi_*\). Define the negative branch by the exact reality relation. These profiles have zero trace at the origin, all required weighted and \(H^1\) regularity, and arbitrarily small norms after scaling. The inverse distorted transform is a legitimate continuous spectral physical-real vector.

At \(\xi_*\), \(A=0\), \(B=a\), \(C=-\bar s\bar a\). Equation (1) gives \(\bar s|a|^2\bar a\), whereas the printed expression gives \(|s|^2\bar s|a|^2\bar a\). Their difference has modulus \(|a|^3/(2\sqrt2)\). This disproves the algebraic identity on its admissible profile class. It does not assert that this chosen profile extends to an entire trapped nonlinear solution.

An independent exact check summed every sign term in the coefficient table. At the auxiliary algebraic fixture \(s=3/5\), \(r=4i/5\), \(A=0\), \(B=1\), the positive branches agree with the printed reduction. The two negative differences are \(48/125\) and \(-36i/125\). This rational fixture checks the algebra; the preceding intermediate-value argument supplies the actual-potential witness.
## Correct dynamics and implications

Let \(N(z_1,z_2)=(|z_1|^2z_1,|z_2|^2z_2)\) and \(k=L/(2t)\). If the verified positive equation is \[i\partial_tF_+=kN(F_+)+\tau\xi JF_++E,\] then conjugation and the reality relation force \[i\partial_tF_-=
 -kR^*N(RF_-)-\tau\xi R^*JR\,F_-+R^*\bar E .
 \tag{2}\] The leading cubic term is of order \(t^{-1}\) and cannot be discarded into an integrable remainder. Even in the reflectionless limit its sign differs from the common printed sign. For mixed scattering, two positive-branch phases are combined; there is no single local negative phase of the asserted form.

The linear \(\tau\) discrepancy need not invalidate the separate modulation estimate. Indeed \[R^*JR+J=
 \begin{pmatrix}2|r|^2&2\bar r s\\2\bar s r&-2|r|^2\end{pmatrix}.\] The decay and derivative bounds for \(r\) make \(\xi(R^*JR+J)\) an order-zero bounded multiplier with the needed derivative control. It can be assigned to the integrable remainder. The cubic discrepancy cannot.

A viable repair is to prove the pointwise bound and modified scattering only for \(F_+\), then reconstruct \(F_-\) using reality. In particular \(\|F_-\|_\infty\le\sqrt2\|F_+\|_\infty\), paired \(L^2\) norms are preserved, and derivatives of \(R\) are controlled. The first physical component in Section 14 has a propagating positive-branch contribution; the opposite branch occurs through localized eigenfunction remainders. This explains why the final physical \(L^2\) conclusion may survive. The single-phase assertion for both signs must be withdrawn, and the plus signs in the positive-branch formulas (14.1)–(14.2) must agree with the negative phase in Theorem 1.1. A complete proof of uniform profile regularity and continuity after these changes is not certified here.
# Additional defects and independently checked boundaries

Problem 3 (Minor: missing continuous-spectral hypotheses).  Lemma 5.15, p. 38, and Proposition 6.3, pp. 40–41, state identities in terms of the distorted transforms of unrestricted inputs. They need \(P_{\mathrm e}f=f\) and, for the cubic identity, the corresponding conditions on \(g,h\).

Here is an explicit operator satisfying (H1)–(H3). For \(a=1/2\), put \[L_a=-\partial_x^2-a(a+1)\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x,\quad
 H=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(L_a+1,-L_a-1),\quad \phi=\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^a x.\] Its potentials are even, smooth and exponentially decaying. With \(A_a=\partial_x+a\tanh x\), \[L_a=A_a^*A_a-a^2,\qquad
 A_aA_a^*-a^2=-\partial_x^2+a(1-a)\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x\ge0.\] Intertwining shows that the only negative eigenvalue of \(L_a\) is \(-a^2\), with eigenfunction \(\phi\). There is no bounded zero-energy solution: for such a solution \(u\), \(A_au\) solves the positive-partner zero-energy equation. Integration by parts, with vanishing boundary derivative terms, makes both its kinetic and positive potential energies zero. Hence \(A_au=0\), which is incompatible with \(L_au=0\) unless \(u=0\). Positive-energy square-integrable solutions are excluded by the short-range scalar Jost asymptotics. It follows that \(H\) has only the two discrete eigenvalues \(\pm3/4\), no embedded eigenvalues, and no threshold resonance.

Take \(f=\phi e_1\), a Schwartz discrete eigenvector, and \(W(x)=xe^{-x^2}\). Then \(\widetilde f=0\), but \(Wf\) is nonzero and odd, hence entirely continuous spectral. Its distorted transform is nonzero. The two sides of Lemma 5.15 are therefore different. For Proposition 6.3 use \(f=g=h=\phi e_1\), \(j=k=\ell=m=1\), and the same \(W\), with \(L=0\). The left side is the transform of the nonzero odd vector \(W\phi^3e_1\); the right side is zero.

These are literal failures of the stated input scope, not failures of the transform on \(P_{\mathrm e}L^2\). The main application already separates discrete and continuous terms, notably on pp. 63 and 88. Add the projection assumptions and keep all discrete contributions in physical space. In particular, one should not apply a continuous spectral norm to a discrete basis vector as in the shorthand estimate around (9.23), p. 62. Direct localized \(H^1\) estimates of \(W\Xi_jU_{\mathrm e}\) give the required bound. No counterexample to the resulting nonlinear estimate is asserted.

Problem 4 (Minor: local linearization and illustrative examples).  The sign of \(F''(\Phi^2)\Phi^2\) in \(V_1\) on p. 11 is inconsistent with the actual linearization. The illustrative embedded-eigenvalue argument on p. 10 also has the wrong scalar operator. The cubic–quintic example on p. 5 uses the wrong primitive \(F\).

For \(F(z)=z^2\), \(\omega=1\), \(\Phi=\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}x\), the soliton equation holds and \(c_\omega=1/\sqrt\omega>0\). The printed p. 11 choice gives \(V_1=0\) and \(V_2=-2\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x\), and consequently \[H(\Phi,-\Phi)^\top=4\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^3x(1,1)^\top\ne0.\] This contradicts the claimed zero mode under the local linearization hypotheses. The correct formula is \(V_1=-F'(\Phi^2)-F''(\Phi^2)\Phi^2\). It is already used on p. 4 and in (8.7), pp. 47–48. The pure cubic profile is used here only for that local identity, not as an example satisfying the main theorem’s absence-of-resonance assumption.

For the p. 10 example, take \(V_1=2\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x\), \(V_2=0\). The asserted scalar operator \(-\partial_x^2-V_1\) has eigenpair \((\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}x,-1)\), but \[H(0,\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}x)^\top=(0,-4\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^3x)^\top,\] which is not an eigenvector relation. A correct embedded example is \(V_1=-6\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x\), \(V_2=0\): \((-\partial_x^2+V_1)\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x=-4\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x\) and \(H(0,\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x)^\top=3(0,\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x)^\top\). Thus the existence claim remains true after replacing its example.

Finally \(F(z)=z^3-z^5\) produces \(3|v|^4v-5|v|^8v\) and has \(F''(0)=0\). It is not the stated cubic–quintic case. The expression \(F(z)=z^2-z^3\) used on p. 12 supplies that case. These inconsistencies are local; the later principal linearization has the correct sign.

Problem 5 (Minor: three defective steps in the linear estimates).  A derivative bound in (4.19), p. 18, the translation argument in Lemma 4.8, pp. 24–25, and an integration by parts in Lemma 7.3, p. 45, require correction.

Write \(b(\xi)=\sqrt{\xi^2+2}\), as in the paper. The asserted bound for derivatives of \(e^{-zb(\xi)+iz\xi}\) with exponential factor \(e^{-z(b(\xi)-1)}\) is false. For \(z=1\) and one derivative, the ratio of the left side to the proposed bound without its constant is \[e^{-1}b(\xi)|i-\xi/b(\xi)|\longrightarrow\infty.\] A valid bound, sufficient for every stipulated \(0<\beta<1\), is \[|\partial_\xi^k e^{-zb(\xi)+iz\xi}|
 \le C_k b(\xi)^{-k}e^{-(3/4)zb(\xi)},\qquad z\ge0.\] It follows by scaling \(zb(\xi)\) and absorbing its polynomial factors into the remaining exponential. The inequality \(3\sqrt2/4>1\) preserves the required decay margin.

The translation \(f_1(x,\xi)=\check f_1(x+100,\xi)\) on p. 25 does not preserve the prescribed outgoing coefficient. Already for \(V=0\) it has leading term \(e^{100i\xi}e^{ix\xi}\) instead of \(e^{ix\xi}\), contrary to (4.43). This example meets the hypotheses of that Jost construction, which does not require the later threshold assumption. Multiply by \(e^{-100i\xi}\). The translated exponentially decaying component then has the factor \(e^{-100(b(\xi)+i\xi)}\), with the derivative bounds needed there.

Finally the integration by parts on p. 45 must include \[-\frac1{2it}\int e^{it\xi^2}
 \left(\frac{g'F+gF'}{\xi}-\frac{gF}{\xi^2}\right)\,\mathrm d\xi .\] The last summand is omitted in the displayed expansion. After division by \(\langle x\rangle\), the eigenfunction estimate \(|F(x,\xi)|\lesssim\min(\langle x\rangle|\xi|,1)\) bounds the omitted term by \(C t^{-1}\int |g(\xi)|/|\xi|\,\mathrm d\xi\). For \(g(0)=0\), the integral on \(|\xi|<1\) is bounded by \(C\|g'\|_2\) using \(|g(\xi)|\le\sqrt{|\xi|}\|g'\|_2\), and the complementary integral by \(C\|g\|_2\). The stated local decay rate therefore survives.

Problem 6 (Minor: spectral normalization is inconsistent).  The kernel in Lemma 5.15, p. 38, and the scalar bilinear kernel (6.6), p. 40, have incorrect normalization. The cubic notation changes normalization between (6.10)–(6.12), (8.20), (12.4), and Section 13.1.

The cubic distribution in (6.10) already contains \(1/(4\pi^2)\). Reusing that symbol with an additional \(1/(4\pi^2)\) in (8.20) and (12.4) counts the factor twice. On pp. 85 and 91–93 the calculation effectively uses the unnormalized symbol instead. A consistent correction is to reserve \(m\) for (6.10) and set \(\mu=4\pi^2m\) wherever an external factor is retained. The delta and principal-value stationary phase calculations then do yield the positive-branch coefficient \(L/(2t)\). This review does not claim that that final coefficient is wrong. The separate negative-branch defect in Problem Problem 2 (#pr:branch) remains.

Problem 7 (Minor: local modulation coordinates and energy).  The stated reality of all discrete coefficients on p. 49, the scalar extraction in Section 10.1, p. 64, derived from (8.24)–(8.26), pp. 53–54, and the boost-energy identity on p. 56 need correction.

For the stated generalized null basis, physical reality makes \(a_0,a_3\) purely imaginary and \(a_1,a_2\) real. For example \(U=i\Xi_0=(i\Phi,-i\Phi)^\top\) satisfies \(\sigma_1\bar U=U\) and has \(a_0=i\), not a real coefficient. The estimates use their absolute values and are unchanged.

With the paper’s leading matrix entries \((M_0)_{01}=c_\omega\) and \((M_0)_{23}=-\int\Phi_\omega^2\), vector of defects \((a,-i\dot\omega,i(2p-\dot y),\dot p)\), and right side \(-b_j=-\langle B,\sigma_3\Xi_j\rangle\), solving the two rows gives \[\dot\omega=-i c_\omega^{-1}b_0,\qquad
 \dot p=\left(\int\Phi_\omega^2\right)^{-1}b_2 .\] The displayed extraction loses the first factor \(i\) and changes the second sign. This is distinct from the omitted phase connection in Problem Problem 1 (#pr:frame); it does not alter the absolute-value decay bounds.

For the Hamiltonian convention in the paper, direct expansion of the kinetic energy gives \[H(e^{ipx}w)=H(w)+p^2M(w)+2pP(w),\qquad
 P(w)=\operatorname{Im}\int w_x\bar w\,\mathrm dx.\] The last two terms are absent from the p. 56 identity. The orthogonality to the translation mode removes the linear \(\Phi/u\) cross term in \(P(\Phi+u)\). Since \(p=O(\epsilon_1)\), the remaining boost contributions are bounded by \(C\epsilon_1^2+
C\epsilon_1\|u\|_{H^1}^2\) and can be absorbed in the coercive estimate. This verifies a local repair, without claiming that the uncorrected conservation identity is true.

Problem 8 (Minor: cutoffs at subunit scales and phase size).  The inhomogeneous decomposition of Section 2.2, p. 9, does not define the subunit high-frequency cutoffs used on pp. 65 and 69–70. A product of dyadic scales is also mistakenly used for a maximum on p. 79.

The explicit sum \(\varphi_{<\ell}=\sum_{0\le k<\ell}\varphi_k\) is zero for \(\ell<0\), and therefore \(\varphi_{>-m\kappa}=1\) for \(m>0\) under the stated partition. It cannot exclude frequencies near zero. Furthermore the precise smooth support requirements \(\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\varphi_0=[-1,1]\) and \(\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\varphi_1\subset[1,4]\) leave every summand zero at \(x=1\), so they cannot form a smooth partition of unity. This is an inconsistency in the definitions, not an attempt to supply a counterexample satisfying an impossible partition assumption.

A concrete repair uses an overlapping inhomogeneous partition for time and macroscopic frequency, and an independent rescaled cutoff for actual small frequency. Let \(\chi=1\) near \([-1,1]\), \(\chi=0\) outside \([-2,2]\), \(\delta=t^{-1/2}\), and \[f_L(\xi)=\chi(\xi/\delta)f(\xi),\qquad f_H=f-f_L.\] For \(f(0)=0\) and \(D=\|f'\|_2\), elementary integration gives \[\|f_L\|_1\lesssim\delta^{3/2}D,\quad
 \|f_L\|_2\lesssim\delta D,\quad
 \|f_H'\|_2\lesssim D,\] \[\|\xi^{-1}f_H'\|_1\lesssim\delta^{-1/2}D,\qquad
 \|\langle \xi\rangle\xi^{-1}f_H'\|_2\lesssim\delta^{-1}D .\] These prove the five intended powers in (10.7), including the derivative of the cutoff. An identical construction at scale \(t^{-\kappa}\) fixes the earlier high-frequency split. Merely changing every index to range over all integers would require new summation checks; that shortcut is not justified here.

On p. 79 the relevant scale is \(2^{\max(j,k_1,k_2)}t^{-\kappa}\), not \(2^{j+k_1+k_2}t^{-\kappa}\). For \(\xi=\eta=\sigma=R\) in the positive quadratic channel, the phase is \(-\omega-R^2\); a lower bound proportional to \(R^3\) is impossible as \(R\to\infty\). Writing \(M=\max(|\xi|,|\eta|,|\sigma|,1)\), the correct nonresonant bound \(|\Phi|\gtrsim Mt^{-\kappa}\) and \(|\eta\sigma|\lesssim M^2\) yield \[|\partial_\eta\partial_\sigma(\Phi^{-1})|
 \lesssim t^{3\kappa}/M .\] The analogous differentiated cutoffs have the same usable scale. These repairs address the identified local steps; they are not a claim to have rederived every omitted term in Sections 10–13.

Problem 9 (Major: false uniform oscillatory-integral remainder).  Lemma 13.4, pp. 96–98, has both an incorrect leading constant in its statement and a false uniform remainder. The optimization concluding Lemma 13.3, p. 96, also does not produce the exponent stated in that lemma.
## The leading constant has a direct fixed-function test

The convention is \(\widehat\phi(0)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}\). Set \(\rho=\xi=1\) and \(F=a\psi\), where \(\psi\in C_c^\infty((-1/4,1/4))\), \(\psi(0)=1\), and \(a\ne0\) is sufficiently small. Then \(F(1)=0\) and \(\|F\|_\infty+t^{-\alpha}\|F\|_{H^1}\lesssim1\) for all \(t\ge1\). On this support the substitution \(u=2p-p^2\) is monotone. It turns the principal-value integral into \(\int e^{-itu}b(u)/u\,\mathrm du\) with \(b(0)=a/\sqrt{2\pi}\). Splitting \(b\) into \(b(0)\) times a cutoff and a function divisible by \(u\) proves the limit \[-i\pi b(0)=-i\sqrt{\pi/2}\,a .\] For \(0<\alpha<1/2\) and \(0<\kappa<1\), all printed errors tend to zero, but the printed leading term is \(-ia/2\). The correct constant is already obtained in the proof on p. 97 and used on pp. 91 and 93. Thus this statement error does not change the verified positive-branch cubic coefficient.
## A counterexample to the remainder even after fixing the constant

Fix \(0<\alpha<1/4\), \(\kappa=\alpha/2\), \(\rho=1\), and a nonzero nonnegative \(\eta\in C_c^\infty((1,11/10))\). For large \(t\) put \[\xi_t=t^{-\alpha},\quad w_t=t^{-1+\alpha},\quad
 a_t=t^\alpha\sqrt{w_t}=t^{-1/2+3\alpha/2},
 \qquad F_t(p)=c\,a_t\,\eta(p/w_t).\] Here \(c>0\) is fixed and small. Both \(F_t(0)\) and \(F_t(\xi_t)\) vanish for all sufficiently large \(t\). Moreover \[\|F_t'\|_2=c\,t^\alpha\|\eta'\|_2,\qquad
 \|F_t\|_2=c\,t^{-1+2\alpha}\|\eta\|_2,
 \qquad \|F_t\|_\infty\lesssim c.\] One may set \(F_t=0\) on an initial finite time interval, with a transition after the supports are separated. Every printed hypothesis then holds for all \(t\ge1\).

Substitution \(p=w_tq\) and dominated convergence give \[\frac{K(t,\xi_t)}{c\,a_t}\longrightarrow
 \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int e^{-2iq}\frac{\eta(q)}q\,\mathrm dq
 \ne0.\] The real part is strictly negative because \(\cos(2q)<0\) on the support. The three printed errors have respectively the powers \[-\tfrac12+\tfrac54\alpha-\tfrac12\alpha^2,\qquad
 -\tfrac12+\alpha,\qquad
 -\tfrac34+\tfrac52\alpha .\] The actual power \(-1/2+3\alpha/2\) exceeds them by \(\alpha/4+\alpha^2/2\), \(\alpha/2\), and \(1/4-\alpha\), all strictly positive. This is a uniform-estimate counterexample satisfying all of the lemma’s hypotheses, not a numerical asymptotic guess.

The defective local step on p. 97 uses \(t^{-1/2}\) where \(H^1\) gives only \[|F(t^{-1/2}P)-F(0)|
 \le t^{-1/4}|P|^{1/2}\|F'\|_2 .\] Its corrected contribution is \(O(t^{\alpha-1/4})\). After the external \(t^{-1}\) in the application, this is \(O(t^{-5/4+\alpha})\), which is smaller than \(t^{-15/14}\) for \(\alpha<5/28\). For the paper’s small choice of \(\alpha\), this particular corrected contribution also fits the high-frequency error budget in Lemma 13.5. This checks only one term, however; it does not supply a complete replacement for the false uniform remainder. Proposition 13.2 explicitly invokes Lemma 13.4 on p. 94, and Lemma 13.5 invokes Proposition 13.2 on p. 98 to justify the pointwise cubic dynamics. Thus a core uniform estimate is false on its full stated hypothesis class and the required replacement has not been established here. The assessment of this component is Major, even though the leading-constant correction and the local Hölder correction are explicit. No counterexample to Proposition 13.2 on its more structured inputs, to an entire nonlinear trajectory, or to Theorem 1.1 is asserted.
## A complete replacement for the insufficient optimization

The last line of the proof of Lemma 13.3 bounds the error by \(t^{-1-\delta}+t^{-5/4+\alpha+5\delta/2}\). Balancing gives \(\delta=(2/7)(1/4-\alpha)\), not the stated \((1/3)(1/4-\alpha)\) gain. This arithmetic failure does not by itself refute the lemma. The following independent Fourier argument supplies the needed estimate.

Replace the second exponential in (3) by \(1\). The result is \((\pi/t)g_1(P)g_2(-P)g_3(P)\). For \(0<\delta<1/4\), use \(|e^{iz}-1|\le C_\delta|z|^\delta\) and \[|(x_2-x_3)(x_1-x_2)|^\delta
 \lesssim\prod_{j=1}^3\langle x_j\rangle^{2\delta},
 \qquad
 \|\langle x\rangle^{2\delta}h_j\|_1
 \le
 \left(\int\langle x\rangle^{4\delta-2}\,\mathrm dx\right)^{1/2}
 \|\langle x\rangle h_j\|_2 .\] The error is \(O_\delta(t^{-1-\delta+3\alpha})\), uniformly in \(P\). Taking \(\delta=1/8\) and \(\alpha<1/64\) gives a gain strictly larger than \((1/3)(1/4-\alpha)\), with difference \((1-64\alpha)/24>0\). Schwartz approximation extends the identity to the stated \(H^1\) and weighted \(L^2\) class: the latter gives \(g_1\in L^1\), and the original integral is controlled by \(\|g_1\|_1\|g_2\|_2\|g_3\|_2\). Thus this replacement is a verified repair of the identified Lemma 13.3 proof gap.

Every physical text page 1–106 was read by the primary reviewer. The review covered the following dependencies.
Source pages | Actual scope and limits

In particular, the inference near (14.7), p. 101, from an \(o(L^2)\) statement and Plancherel alone does not supply an \(o(H^1)\) conclusion. The physical scattering claim there uses \(L^2\), but the stronger profile regularity and continuity in Theorem 1.1 require their own uniform high-frequency argument. problems.title: Missing phase connection in the literal moving coordinate system
claim: Recorded check: Missing phase connection in the literal moving coordinate system

Section8.1.1 permits arbitrary C1 frame parameters before orthogonality is imposed. Use any actual admitted soliton Phi_omega and exact solution exp(-i omega t)Phi_omega. Choose p=A(t-t0), y=b!=0, gamma=omega t, and u(t,z)=exp(-ip(t)(z-b))Phi(z-b)-Phi(z). This witness is a coordinate identity test, not a claim to satisfy later orthogonality or an entire trapped nonlinear orbit.
analysis: Equations (8.1)–(8.2), p. 47, and (8.9), p. 48, omit \(-y\dot p\) in the coefficient of the phase direction. This coefficient propagates to (8.26), p. 54, (9.18), p. 60, and the modulation estimates used in (12.13), Section 12.6, p. 87.

Put \(z=x+y(t)\) and \(w(t,z)=\Phi_{\omega(t)}(z)+u(t,z)\). The actual ansatz in (8.1) is \(v(t,x)=e^{i(p(t)x-\gamma(t))}w(t,x+y(t))\). Directly, \[e^{-i(px-\gamma)}(iv_t-v_{xx})
 =iw_t-w_{zz}+i(\dot y-2p)w_z+
   \bigl(\dot\gamma+p^2-\dot p(z-y)\bigr)w .\] Consequently the right-hand modulation coefficient is \[a=\omega-p^2-\dot\gamma-y\dot p,\] rather than the printed \(\omega-p^2-\dot\gamma\). The omitted vector term is \(-y\dot p(\Xi_0+\sigma_3U)\).

This failure occurs under the stated hypotheses of Section 8.1.1, which at this point allow arbitrary \(C^1\) frame parameters. Fix any actual soliton in the assumed branch and the exact solution \(v=e^{-i\omega t}\Phi_\omega(x)\). Near \(t_0\), choose \(p=A(t-t_0)\), \(y=b\ne0\), and \(\gamma=\omega t\), and set \[u(t,z)=e^{-ip(t)(z-b)}\Phi_\omega(z-b)-\Phi_\omega(z).\] These choices satisfy the ansatz identically. The residual of the printed scalar equation at \(t_0\) is \(-Ab(\Phi_\omega+u)\), which is nonzero for \(A\ne0\). The perturbation at \(t_0\) can be made small by taking \(b\) small. This is an exact coordinate-identity counterexample; it is not claimed to satisfy the later orthogonality choice or to furnish a counterexample to Theorem 1.1.

The omitted coefficient is not automatically an integrable error. The estimates \(y=O(t)\) and \(\dot p=O(t^{-2+2\alpha})\) give only \(y\dot p=O(t^{-1+2\alpha})\). Thus the equation from which the phase estimates are derived is materially different. This affects a central derivation even though a change of phase coordinates can repair it.

One can consistently replace the printed phase defect by \(a\) throughout the modulation system, and then reconstruct the physical \(\gamma\). Alternatively one can change the ansatz to include the primitive of \(y\dot p\) in its phase. The geometric phase in (8.22), p. 52, can also be used, provided the conversion is explicit: if \(\gamma=-\gamma_{\rm geom}-py\), then \(a=\omega-p^2+\dot\gamma_{\rm geom}+p\dot y\). That alternative chart does not make the literal identity (8.1)–(8.2) correct.

There is enough conditional decay to reconstruct the desired physical phase. If the corrected equations establish \(p-p_\infty=O(t^{-1-\nu})\), \(y=O(t)\), and \(\dot y=O(1)\), then \[\int_t^\infty y(s)\dot p(s)\,\mathrm ds
 =-y(t)(p(t)-p_\infty)
   -\int_t^\infty\dot y(s)(p(s)-p_\infty)\,\mathrm ds
 =O(t^{-\nu}).\] This verifies the needed tail estimate. A fully consistent rewrite of every subsequent phase variable and of the final continuity argument is still required.
result: Impact: The missing term y*p_dot is only O(t^-1+2alpha) from the preliminary bounds and cannot simply be discarded as integrable. The phase evolution and subsequent reconstruction rest on an incorrect exact equation. Major is based on this actual core derivation damage, not irreparability or a false main theorem.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use the corrected connection a throughout, or consistently reparameterize the phase, and reconstruct physical gamma. For the geometric chart gamma=-gamma_geom-p*y, a=omega-p^2+gamma_geom_dot+p*y_dot.

problems.title: Negative distorted spectral branch has mixed cubic dynamics
problems.source_location: PDF36 (5.31), PDF50 (8.16), PDF92 (13.10), PDF98 Lemma13.5, PDF89 Proposition13.1, PDF99-100 phase ODE
claim: Recorded check: Negative distorted spectral branch has mixed cubic dynamics

xi>0, R=[[r,s],[s,r]] unitary with s(0)=0, s(infinity)=1; spectral reality F_-=-R*conjugate(F_+). Intermediate value supplies an actual xi* with |s|^2=|r|^2=1/2. Positive profile smooth compactly supported near -xi*, value a!=0, zero near +xi*; negative profile set by exact reality. Profiles have zero trace at zero, weighted L2 and H1 regularity, arbitrarily small norms, and a physical-real inverse in the continuous spectral subspace. No entire trapped NLS trajectory claimed.
analysis: The identity (13.10), p. 92, its use in Lemma 13.5, p. 98, and the common local phase evolution for both signs in Proposition 13.1 and pp. 99–100 are false for the negative spectral branch. The reality relation (8.16), p. 50, mixes the two frequency signs through scattering.

For \(\xi>0\), write \[F_+=\binom{A}{B}=\binom{\widetilde f_+(\xi)}{\widetilde f_+(-\xi)},
 \quad F_-=\binom{C}{D},\quad
 R=\begin{pmatrix}r&s\\s&r\end{pmatrix},\quad
 J=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(1,-1).\] Here \(r=r(\xi)\), \(s=s(\xi)\), and the conventions of (5.31) and (8.16) give \[R^*R=I,\qquad F_-=-R^*\overline{F_+}.\] Expanding the actual coefficient table in (13.10) gives \[\Theta_-(\xi)=\bar r\,|A|^2\bar A+
                      \bar s\,|B|^2\bar B .
 \tag{1}\] It is not in general \(-|C|^2C\).

The paper’s own scattering properties imply the existence of an actual frequency \(\xi_*>0\) with \(|s(\xi_*)|^2=|r(\xi_*)|^2=1/2\): use continuity, \(s(0)=0\), \(s(\xi)\to1\), and unitarity. Thus the example does not rely on assuming that an arbitrary unitary matrix is realized by a potential. Choose a smooth compactly supported positive-branch profile near \(-\xi_*\), with value \(a\ne0\) there and zero near \(+\xi_*\). Define the negative branch by the exact reality relation. These profiles have zero trace at the origin, all required weighted and \(H^1\) regularity, and arbitrarily small norms after scaling. The inverse distorted transform is a legitimate continuous spectral physical-real vector.

At \(\xi_*\), \(A=0\), \(B=a\), \(C=-\bar s\bar a\). Equation (1) gives \(\bar s|a|^2\bar a\), whereas the printed expression gives \(|s|^2\bar s|a|^2\bar a\). Their difference has modulus \(|a|^3/(2\sqrt2)\). This disproves the algebraic identity on its admissible profile class. It does not assert that this chosen profile extends to an entire trapped nonlinear solution.

An independent exact check summed every sign term in the coefficient table. At the auxiliary algebraic fixture \(s=3/5\), \(r=4i/5\), \(A=0\), \(B=1\), the positive branches agree with the printed reduction. The two negative differences are \(48/125\) and \(-36i/125\). This rational fixture checks the algebra; the preceding intermediate-value argument supplies the actual-potential witness.

Let \(N(z_1,z_2)=(|z_1|^2z_1,|z_2|^2z_2)\) and \(k=L/(2t)\). If the verified positive equation is \[i\partial_tF_+=kN(F_+)+\tau\xi JF_++E,\] then conjugation and the reality relation force \[i\partial_tF_-=
 -kR^*N(RF_-)-\tau\xi R^*JR\,F_-+R^*\bar E .
 \tag{2}\] The leading cubic term is of order \(t^{-1}\) and cannot be discarded into an integrable remainder. Even in the reflectionless limit its sign differs from the common printed sign. For mixed scattering, two positive-branch phases are combined; there is no single local negative phase of the asserted form.

The linear \(\tau\) discrepancy need not invalidate the separate modulation estimate. Indeed \[R^*JR+J=
 \begin{pmatrix}2|r|^2&2\bar r s\\2\bar s r&-2|r|^2\end{pmatrix}.\] The decay and derivative bounds for \(r\) make \(\xi(R^*JR+J)\) an order-zero bounded multiplier with the needed derivative control. It can be assigned to the integrable remainder. The cubic discrepancy cannot.

A viable repair is to prove the pointwise bound and modified scattering only for \(F_+\), then reconstruct \(F_-\) using reality. In particular \(\|F_-\|_\infty\le\sqrt2\|F_+\|_\infty\), paired \(L^2\) norms are preserved, and derivatives of \(R\) are controlled. The first physical component in Section 14 has a propagating positive-branch contribution; the opposite branch occurs through localized eigenfunction remainders. This explains why the final physical \(L^2\) conclusion may survive. The single-phase assertion for both signs must be withdrawn, and the plus signs in the positive-branch formulas (14.1)–(14.2) must agree with the negative phase in Theorem 1.1. A complete proof of uniform profile regularity and continuity after these changes is not certified here.
result: Impact: The asserted negative-branch local t^-1 cubic phase and its pointwise argument are false; this nonintegrable term cannot be hidden in the error. Main physical theorem not disproved.

a=1/2, L_a=-d_x^2-a(a+1)sech^2, H=diag(L_a+1,-L_a-1), phi=sech^a. Smooth even exponential potentials; factorization proves only discrete eigenvalues±3/4, no embedded spectrum or threshold resonance, meeting H1-H3. f=phi e1 is Schwartz; W=x exp(-x^2), cubic f=g=h and indices1 with L=0 satisfy the literal stated assumptions.
analysis: Lemma 5.15, p. 38, and Proposition 6.3, pp. 40–41, state identities in terms of the distorted transforms of unrestricted inputs. They need \(P_{\mathrm e}f=f\) and, for the cubic identity, the corresponding conditions on \(g,h\).

Here is an explicit operator satisfying (H1)–(H3). For \(a=1/2\), put \[L_a=-\partial_x^2-a(a+1)\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x,\quad
 H=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(L_a+1,-L_a-1),\quad \phi=\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^a x.\] Its potentials are even, smooth and exponentially decaying. With \(A_a=\partial_x+a\tanh x\), \[L_a=A_a^*A_a-a^2,\qquad
 A_aA_a^*-a^2=-\partial_x^2+a(1-a)\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x\ge0.\] Intertwining shows that the only negative eigenvalue of \(L_a\) is \(-a^2\), with eigenfunction \(\phi\). There is no bounded zero-energy solution: for such a solution \(u\), \(A_au\) solves the positive-partner zero-energy equation. Integration by parts, with vanishing boundary derivative terms, makes both its kinetic and positive potential energies zero. Hence \(A_au=0\), which is incompatible with \(L_au=0\) unless \(u=0\). Positive-energy square-integrable solutions are excluded by the short-range scalar Jost asymptotics. It follows that \(H\) has only the two discrete eigenvalues \(\pm3/4\), no embedded eigenvalues, and no threshold resonance.

Take \(f=\phi e_1\), a Schwartz discrete eigenvector, and \(W(x)=xe^{-x^2}\). Then \(\widetilde f=0\), but \(Wf\) is nonzero and odd, hence entirely continuous spectral. Its distorted transform is nonzero. The two sides of Lemma 5.15 are therefore different. For Proposition 6.3 use \(f=g=h=\phi e_1\), \(j=k=\ell=m=1\), and the same \(W\), with \(L=0\). The left side is the transform of the nonzero odd vector \(W\phi^3e_1\); the right side is zero.

These are literal failures of the stated input scope, not failures of the transform on \(P_{\mathrm e}L^2\). The main application already separates discrete and continuous terms, notably on pp. 63 and 88. Add the projection assumptions and keep all discrete contributions in physical space. In particular, one should not apply a continuous spectral norm to a discrete basis vector as in the shorthand estimate around (9.23), p. 62. Direct localized \(H^1\) estimates of \(W\Xi_jU_{\mathrm e}\) give the required bound. No counterexample to the resulting nonlinear estimate is asserted.
result: Impact: The literal lemmas are overbroad. Applications already separate Ud/Ue, so projection restrictions and localized physical estimates preserve the required use; no counterexample to the repaired nonlinear estimate.

problems.title: Jost derivative, translation and integration-by-parts steps
problems.source_location: PDF18 (4.19); PDF24-25 Lemma4.8; PDF45 Lemma7.3
claim: Recorded check: Jost derivative, translation and integration-by-parts steps
z>=0, b=sqrt(xi^2+2); test z1,k1,xi→infinity. The Jost translation lemma needs H1-H2 only; zero potential is an admissible exact witness. Local decay input g in H1 with g(0)=0.
analysis: A derivative bound in (4.19), p. 18, the translation argument in Lemma 4.8, pp. 24–25, and an integration by parts in Lemma 7.3, p. 45, require correction.

Write \(b(\xi)=\sqrt{\xi^2+2}\), as in the paper. The asserted bound for derivatives of \(e^{-zb(\xi)+iz\xi}\) with exponential factor \(e^{-z(b(\xi)-1)}\) is false. For \(z=1\) and one derivative, the ratio of the left side to the proposed bound without its constant is \[e^{-1}b(\xi)|i-\xi/b(\xi)|\longrightarrow\infty.\] A valid bound, sufficient for every stipulated \(0<\beta<1\), is \[|\partial_\xi^k e^{-zb(\xi)+iz\xi}|
 \le C_k b(\xi)^{-k}e^{-(3/4)zb(\xi)},\qquad z\ge0.\] It follows by scaling \(zb(\xi)\) and absorbing its polynomial factors into the remaining exponential. The inequality \(3\sqrt2/4>1\) preserves the required decay margin.

The translation \(f_1(x,\xi)=\check f_1(x+100,\xi)\) on p. 25 does not preserve the prescribed outgoing coefficient. Already for \(V=0\) it has leading term \(e^{100i\xi}e^{ix\xi}\) instead of \(e^{ix\xi}\), contrary to (4.43). This example meets the hypotheses of that Jost construction, which does not require the later threshold assumption. Multiply by \(e^{-100i\xi}\). The translated exponentially decaying component then has the factor \(e^{-100(b(\xi)+i\xi)}\), with the derivative bounds needed there.

Finally the integration by parts on p. 45 must include \[-\frac1{2it}\int e^{it\xi^2}
 \left(\frac{g'F+gF'}{\xi}-\frac{gF}{\xi^2}\right)\,\mathrm d\xi .\] The last summand is omitted in the displayed expansion. After division by \(\langle x\rangle\), the eigenfunction estimate \(|F(x,\xi)|\lesssim\min(\langle x\rangle|\xi|,1)\) bounds the omitted term by \(C t^{-1}\int |g(\xi)|/|\xi|\,\mathrm d\xi\). For \(g(0)=0\), the integral on \(|\xi|<1\) is bounded by \(C\|g'\|_2\) using \(|g(\xi)|\le\sqrt{|\xi|}\|g'\|_2\), and the complementary integral by \(C\|g\|_2\). The stated local decay rate therefore survives.
result: Impact: Three explicit local proof steps are wrong but the intended linear estimates retain their rates after the displayed repairs.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use derivative bound C_k b^-k exp(-3zb/4); normalize translation exp(-100i xi); retain the IBP term and bound integral|g|/|xi| by H1 using trace0.

problems.title: Local modulation reality, extracted coefficients and boost energy
problems.source_location: PDF49 discrete reality; PDF64 Section10.1 last display before10.2 (scalar extraction), using PDF53-54 (8.24)-(8.26); PDF56 Hamiltonian identity
claim: Recorded check: Local modulation reality, extracted coefficients and boost energy

Physical reality sigma1 conjugate(U)=U and the stated generalized null basis. Use printed leading matrix entries M01=c_omega,M23=-mass and RHS-b_j. Hamiltonian is the paper's kinetic-minus-potential convention; p=O(epsilon1), later orthogonality imposed for repair.

For the stated generalized null basis, physical reality makes \(a_0,a_3\) purely imaginary and \(a_1,a_2\) real. For example \(U=i\Xi_0=(i\Phi,-i\Phi)^\top\) satisfies \(\sigma_1\bar U=U\) and has \(a_0=i\), not a real coefficient. The estimates use their absolute values and are unchanged.

problems.title: Undefined subunit cutoffs and an incorrect phase-size product
problems.source_location: PDF9 Section2.2; PDF65 high cutoffs; PDF69-70 (10.7); PDF79 phase lower bound
claim: Recorded check: Undefined subunit cutoffs and an incorrect phase-size product

Indices explicitly k>=0; phi_<ell=sum0<=k<ell; exact smooth supports printed. The support inconsistency means no such exact partition exists; no false claim of a witness meeting an impossible premise. For corrected estimates f in H1, f(0)=0 and delta=t^-1/2.
analysis: The inhomogeneous decomposition of Section 2.2, p. 9, does not define the subunit high-frequency cutoffs used on pp. 65 and 69–70. A product of dyadic scales is also mistakenly used for a maximum on p. 79.

The explicit sum \(\varphi_{<\ell}=\sum_{0\le k<\ell}\varphi_k\) is zero for \(\ell<0\), and therefore \(\varphi_{>-m\kappa}=1\) for \(m>0\) under the stated partition. It cannot exclude frequencies near zero. Furthermore the precise smooth support requirements \(\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\varphi_0=[-1,1]\) and \(\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\varphi_1\subset[1,4]\) leave every summand zero at \(x=1\), so they cannot form a smooth partition of unity. This is an inconsistency in the definitions, not an attempt to supply a counterexample satisfying an impossible partition assumption.

A concrete repair uses an overlapping inhomogeneous partition for time and macroscopic frequency, and an independent rescaled cutoff for actual small frequency. Let \(\chi=1\) near \([-1,1]\), \(\chi=0\) outside \([-2,2]\), \(\delta=t^{-1/2}\), and \[f_L(\xi)=\chi(\xi/\delta)f(\xi),\qquad f_H=f-f_L.\] For \(f(0)=0\) and \(D=\|f'\|_2\), elementary integration gives \[\|f_L\|_1\lesssim\delta^{3/2}D,\quad
 \|f_L\|_2\lesssim\delta D,\quad
 \|f_H'\|_2\lesssim D,\] \[\|\xi^{-1}f_H'\|_1\lesssim\delta^{-1/2}D,\qquad
 \|\langle \xi\rangle\xi^{-1}f_H'\|_2\lesssim\delta^{-1}D .\] These prove the five intended powers in (10.7), including the derivative of the cutoff. An identical construction at scale \(t^{-\kappa}\) fixes the earlier high-frequency split. Merely changing every index to range over all integers would require new summation checks; that shortcut is not justified here.

On p. 79 the relevant scale is \(2^{\max(j,k_1,k_2)}t^{-\kappa}\), not \(2^{j+k_1+k_2}t^{-\kappa}\). For \(\xi=\eta=\sigma=R\) in the positive quadratic channel, the phase is \(-\omega-R^2\); a lower bound proportional to \(R^3\) is impossible as \(R\to\infty\). Writing \(M=\max(|\xi|,|\eta|,|\sigma|,1)\), the correct nonresonant bound \(|\Phi|\gtrsim Mt^{-\kappa}\) and \(|\eta\sigma|\lesssim M^2\) yield \[|\partial_\eta\partial_\sigma(\Phi^{-1})|
 \lesssim t^{3\kappa}/M .\] The analogous differentiated cutoffs have the same usable scale. These repairs address the identified local steps; they are not a claim to have rederived every omitted term in Sections 10–13.
result: Impact: Definitions and one phase scale do not support the literal operations. Independent scaled cutoffs and max-frequency estimates retain the needed local exponents; no wholesale homogeneous-index rewrite claimed.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use overlapping inhomogeneous macroscopic partition plus chi(xi/delta) for small scales. Replace j+k1+k2 bymax(j,k1,k2); use |Phi|>=M t^-kappa and |eta sigma|<=M².

problems.title: Oscillatory-integral constant, uniform remainder, and proof exponent
problems.source_location: PDF94-96 Lemma13.3; PDF96-98 Lemma13.4; applicationsPDF91,93,98
claim: Recorded check: Oscillatory-integral constant, uniform remainder, and proof exponent

Constant witness rho=xi1,F=a psi supported(-1/4,1/4),psi0=1,0<alpha<1/2,0<kappa<1; all norm/cancellation hypotheses. Remainder witness0<alpha<1/4,kappa=alpha/2,eta>=0 smoothcompact(1,11/10),xi=t^-alpha,w=t^-1+alpha,a=t^-.5+1.5alpha,F=c a eta(p/w), optional finite-time cutoff. F(xi)=F0=0,uniform L∞+t^-alpha H1<=1 for smallc, t>=1; uniform-norm estimate, not nonlinear orbit.
analysis: Lemma 13.4, pp. 96–98, has both an incorrect leading constant in its statement and a false uniform remainder. The optimization concluding Lemma 13.3, p. 96, also does not produce the exponent stated in that lemma.

The convention is \(\widehat\phi(0)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}\). Set \(\rho=\xi=1\) and \(F=a\psi\), where \(\psi\in C_c^\infty((-1/4,1/4))\), \(\psi(0)=1\), and \(a\ne0\) is sufficiently small. Then \(F(1)=0\) and \(\|F\|_\infty+t^{-\alpha}\|F\|_{H^1}\lesssim1\) for all \(t\ge1\). On this support the substitution \(u=2p-p^2\) is monotone. It turns the principal-value integral into \(\int e^{-itu}b(u)/u\,\mathrm du\) with \(b(0)=a/\sqrt{2\pi}\). Splitting \(b\) into \(b(0)\) times a cutoff and a function divisible by \(u\) proves the limit \[-i\pi b(0)=-i\sqrt{\pi/2}\,a .\] For \(0<\alpha<1/2\) and \(0<\kappa<1\), all printed errors tend to zero, but the printed leading term is \(-ia/2\). The correct constant is already obtained in the proof on p. 97 and used on pp. 91 and 93. Thus this statement error does not change the verified positive-branch cubic coefficient.

Fix \(0<\alpha<1/4\), \(\kappa=\alpha/2\), \(\rho=1\), and a nonzero nonnegative \(\eta\in C_c^\infty((1,11/10))\). For large \(t\) put \[\xi_t=t^{-\alpha},\quad w_t=t^{-1+\alpha},\quad
 a_t=t^\alpha\sqrt{w_t}=t^{-1/2+3\alpha/2},
 \qquad F_t(p)=c\,a_t\,\eta(p/w_t).\] Here \(c>0\) is fixed and small. Both \(F_t(0)\) and \(F_t(\xi_t)\) vanish for all sufficiently large \(t\). Moreover \[\|F_t'\|_2=c\,t^\alpha\|\eta'\|_2,\qquad
 \|F_t\|_2=c\,t^{-1+2\alpha}\|\eta\|_2,
 \qquad \|F_t\|_\infty\lesssim c.\] One may set \(F_t=0\) on an initial finite time interval, with a transition after the supports are separated. Every printed hypothesis then holds for all \(t\ge1\).

Substitution \(p=w_tq\) and dominated convergence give \[\frac{K(t,\xi_t)}{c\,a_t}\longrightarrow
 \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int e^{-2iq}\frac{\eta(q)}q\,\mathrm dq
 \ne0.\] The real part is strictly negative because \(\cos(2q)<0\) on the support. The three printed errors have respectively the powers \[-\tfrac12+\tfrac54\alpha-\tfrac12\alpha^2,\qquad
 -\tfrac12+\alpha,\qquad
 -\tfrac34+\tfrac52\alpha .\] The actual power \(-1/2+3\alpha/2\) exceeds them by \(\alpha/4+\alpha^2/2\), \(\alpha/2\), and \(1/4-\alpha\), all strictly positive. This is a uniform-estimate counterexample satisfying all of the lemma’s hypotheses, not a numerical asymptotic guess.

The defective local step on p. 97 uses \(t^{-1/2}\) where \(H^1\) gives only \[|F(t^{-1/2}P)-F(0)|
 \le t^{-1/4}|P|^{1/2}\|F'\|_2 .\] Its corrected contribution is \(O(t^{\alpha-1/4})\). After the external \(t^{-1}\) in the application, this is \(O(t^{-5/4+\alpha})\), which is smaller than \(t^{-15/14}\) for \(\alpha<5/28\). For the paper’s small choice of \(\alpha\), this particular corrected contribution also fits the high-frequency error budget in Lemma 13.5. This checks only one term, however; it does not supply a complete replacement for the false uniform remainder. Proposition 13.2 explicitly invokes Lemma 13.4 on p. 94, and Lemma 13.5 invokes Proposition 13.2 on p. 98 to justify the pointwise cubic dynamics. Thus a core uniform estimate is false on its full stated hypothesis class and the required replacement has not been established here. The assessment of this component is Major, even though the leading-constant correction and the local Hölder correction are explicit. No counterexample to Proposition 13.2 on its more structured inputs, to an entire nonlinear trajectory, or to Theorem 1.1 is asserted.

The last line of the proof of Lemma 13.3 bounds the error by \(t^{-1-\delta}+t^{-5/4+\alpha+5\delta/2}\). Balancing gives \(\delta=(2/7)(1/4-\alpha)\), not the stated \((1/3)(1/4-\alpha)\) gain. This arithmetic failure does not by itself refute the lemma. The following independent Fourier argument supplies the needed estimate.

Replace the second exponential in (3) by \(1\). The result is \((\pi/t)g_1(P)g_2(-P)g_3(P)\). For \(0<\delta<1/4\), use \(|e^{iz}-1|\le C_\delta|z|^\delta\) and \[|(x_2-x_3)(x_1-x_2)|^\delta
 \lesssim\prod_{j=1}^3\langle x_j\rangle^{2\delta},
 \qquad
 \|\langle x\rangle^{2\delta}h_j\|_1
 \le
 \left(\int\langle x\rangle^{4\delta-2}\,\mathrm dx\right)^{1/2}
 \|\langle x\rangle h_j\|_2 .\] The error is \(O_\delta(t^{-1-\delta+3\alpha})\), uniformly in \(P\). Taking \(\delta=1/8\) and \(\alpha<1/64\) gives a gain strictly larger than \((1/3)(1/4-\alpha)\), with difference \((1-64\alpha)/24>0\). Schwartz approximation extends the identity to the stated \(H^1\) and weighted \(L^2\) class: the latter gives \(g_1\in L^1\), and the original integral is controlled by \(\|g_1\|_1\|g_2\|_2\|g_3\|_2\). Thus this replacement is a verified repair of the identified Lemma 13.3 proof gap.
result: Impact: The uniform remainder in Lemma13.4 is false under every printed hypothesis. Proposition13.2 explicitly invokes it at PDF94 and Lemma13.5 invokes that proposition at PDF98 for pointwise cubic evolution. The correctly used leading constant and the integrability of one corrected Holder contribution do not establish the full required replacement. Major reflects this actual essential proof-input failure, not an asserted counterexample to Proposition13.2 on its structured inputs or to Theorem1.1.

paragraphs: Use-i sqrt(pi/2), correct H1 incrementt^-1/4|P|^.5||F'||2, and replace Lemma13.3 optimization with reportEq3 Fourier proof.

report: Abstract: The assessment of the exact acquired author version is Major. A random-operator domination step cancels coefficients before applying distinct temporal translations; an explicit two-phase construction disproves that step. The transported-density formula also has an incorrect sign and normalization under the Gaussian law explicitly fixed in the paper. These defects affect the local probabilistic estimates and the central density bootstrap. They are not counterexamples to the main quasi-invariance theorem. The density identification admits a consistent scalar repair; a replacement proof of the random-operator estimate remains necessary. Local normalization, time-localization, moment, and flow-identity corrections are proved separately. All 64 physical source pages were read, and the numerical threshold was independently rederived. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical review of
Quasi-invariance of Gaussian measures of negative regularity for fractional nonlinear Schrödinger equations
# Source identity and scope

This review concerns M25-0270, by Justin Forlano and Leonardo Tolomeo, DOI `10.4171/jems/1643`, with the title above. The acquired source is arXiv:2205.11453v1, submitted on 23 May 2022 at 16:44:20 UTC, with 64 physical pages. The PDF has 702,808 bytes and SHA256
> cfb449714ab5e1f71c2615fef4cde0aa0b796aab1f7faaa166e9f227cebb4a73.
The 22,389-byte source manifest has SHA256

The publisher landing page records submission on 1 September 2023, acceptance on 10 November 2024, and online publication on 3 June 2025. The publisher full text and a separately indexed accepted manuscript were not established to coincide with this v1. The frozen identifier, title field, DOI, and 2025 batch membership are retained. Page references below are to the acquired PDF; its printed numbering agrees with its physical numbering.

The positive-sign equation used in the calculations is \[iu_t+(-\partial_x^2)^\alpha u+
 \left(|u|^2-2\int_\mathbb T|u|^2\,\mathrm dx\right)u=0,
 \qquad S(t)=e^{it(-\partial_x^2)^\alpha},\] on the torus with normalized Lebesgue measure. It is one of the signs explicitly allowed in (1.1). The data are \[u_0=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\frac{g_n}{\langle n\rangle^s}e^{inx},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Re}g_n,\operatorname{Im}g_n
 \ \hbox{independent }N(0,\tfrac12).\] Theorem 1.1 assumes \(\alpha>1\) and \(s_*(\alpha)<s\le1/2\). It asserts almost-sure global well-posedness, quasi-invariance of \(\mu_s=\operatorname{Law}(u_0)\), and polynomial growth in every \(H^\sigma\), \(\sigma<s-1/2\). The auxiliary finite measure is \[\,\mathrm d\rho_{s,\gamma}=
 e^{-|M_{\rm Wick}(u)|^\gamma}\,\mathrm d\mu_s,\qquad
 M_{\rm Wick}=\sum_n\frac{|g_n|^2-1}{\langle n\rangle^{2s}}.\] For \(s>1/4\) this Wick mass is finite almost surely and the weight is positive, so \(\rho_{s,\gamma}\) and \(\mu_s\) are equivalent. The high modes of the truncated flow remain linear. Smooth test data below are used only for identities that claim to hold for such data; positive-measure extensions are given where a probabilistic assertion is involved.
# Core proof defects

Problem 1 (Major: temporal translations lost in the random kernel).  In the proof of Proposition 3.6, p. 25, the first inequality after the dyadic definition of \(K_{\tilde\tau_1}^{N_1,N_2}\) is false. It replaces a sum of differently translated test functions by a norm of the scalar sum of their coefficients. The same reduction is invoked in Lemma 5.6, pp. 45–46.
## An all-hypotheses counterexample to the displayed step

Write \(\tau=\tilde\tau_1\) and \(\Phi=n_1^{2\alpha}-n_2^{2\alpha}+n_3^{2\alpha}-n_4^{2\alpha}\) with absolute values in the general definition. Choose \[\alpha=2,\quad s=\tfrac25,\quad \sigma=0,\quad q=2,
 \quad b=\tfrac38,\quad b'=\tfrac13,\quad r=48.\] These satisfy \(b_J=1/(2\alpha)=1/4<b'<b<1/2\) and \(r>1/(b-b')=24\). Choose the small increase in \(q'+\) consistent with this Hölder exponent. Both \(\langle 10\rangle\) and \(\langle 12\rangle\) lie in the same dyadic block. In this finite block set \[g_{10}=g_{12}=g_{-12}=1,\qquad g_{-10}=-1,\] and set its other coordinates to zero. Fix \((n_3,n_4)=(-1,1)\). The piecewise threshold in Theorem 1.1 was checked independently from (5.20)–(5.21) and (5.30), rather than accepted from Remark 5.12. Write \(a=\alpha\) and, for \(s<1/2\), \(U=(1-2s)^{-1}\). ## What the terminal argument does establish conditionally

Assuming a valid local convergence theorem and uniform bounds for the actual densities, the weak-limit argument on p. 59 is coherent. Since \(\rho\) is finite, a uniform \(L^2(\rho)\) bound supplies a weakly convergent subsequence for each fixed \(t\). Bounded continuous functions on \(H^{-1}\) are valid \(L^2(\rho)\) tests. Pathwise truncated convergence identifies the weak limit with the transported measure, and preserves positivity and total mass. A common weak subsequence for uncountably many times is not required for this identity.

For integer-step continuation, absolute continuity pulls the local good set back to a full-measure set. Countable iteration and local uniqueness permit patching. Complex conjugation preserves the measures and conjugates positive to negative time, giving the backward construction. For a fixed \(t\), the inverse identities from uniqueness and backward absolute continuity imply the reverse absolute continuity as well. The paper defines quasi-invariance using the forward relation; the stronger equivalence follows with this additional step.

The one-unit threshold in the first event inclusion on p. 59 should also be kept consistent: use \(\|\mathcal V_N\|\le C=e^M\), with \(N\ge N_0(u_0,C)\), to deduce \(\|\mathcal V\|\le C+1\). The printed occurrence of \(e^M+1\) for the truncated norm can be repaired by this choice or by enlarging \(C\) consistently. It is not a demonstrated failure of the limiting global solution.

A fully specified invariant measurable flow domain, and the passage in footnote 9 from the finite-dimensional variational bound to the infimum defining \(r\), were not completely reconstructed here. In particular, the assertion that \(r(P_Nu)\) has the requisite limiting property is not proved by merely writing that approximation. These are recorded reconstruction limits, not promoted into counterexamples. The full-time \(J\) norms are invariant under free time shifts by translating both test functions. Together with the corrected cubic-iterate identity, this provides the needed local time-shift mechanism.

problems.title: Distinct temporal translations are lost in the scalar random-kernel domination
problems.source_location: PDF24 Proposition3.6 (3.32)/(3.36); PDF25 first displayed inequality after dyadic K definition, between(3.38) and(3.39); PDF26-27 propagation; PDF45-46 Lemma5.6
claim: Recorded check: Distinct temporal translations are lost in the scalar random-kernel domination

alpha=2,s=2/5,sigma=0,q=2,b=3/8,bprime=1/3,r=48; bJ=1/4<bprime<b<1/2 andr>24. Chooseqprimeplus=48/23 so1/2+23/48+1/48=1. One finite dyadic high block contains+/-10,+/-12; n3=-1,n4=1. analysis: In the proof of Proposition 3.6, p. 25, the first inequality after the dyadic definition of \(K_{\tilde\tau_1}^{N_1,N_2}\) is false. It replaces a sum of differently translated test functions by a norm of the scalar sum of their coefficients. The same reduction is invoked in Lemma 5.6, pp. 45–46.

Write \(\tau=\tilde\tau_1\) and \(\Phi=n_1^{2\alpha}-n_2^{2\alpha}+n_3^{2\alpha}-n_4^{2\alpha}\) with absolute values in the general definition. Choose \[\alpha=2,\quad s=\tfrac25,\quad \sigma=0,\quad q=2,
 \quad b=\tfrac38,\quad b'=\tfrac13,\quad r=48.\] These satisfy \(b_J=1/(2\alpha)=1/4<b'<b<1/2\) and \(r>1/(b-b')=24\). Choose the small increase in \(q'+\) consistent with this Hölder exponent. Both \(\langle 10\rangle\) and \(\langle 12\rangle\) lie in the same dyadic block. In this finite block set \[g_{10}=g_{12}=g_{-12}=1,\qquad g_{-10}=-1,\] and set its other coordinates to zero. Fix \((n_3,n_4)=(-1,1)\). The only nonzero summands satisfying \(n_1-n_2+n_3-n_4=0\) and the nonresonance exclusions are \[(n_1,n_2)=(12,10),\quad(-10,-12).\] Their phases are \(\Delta\) and \(-\Delta\), where \(\Delta=12^4-10^4=10736\), and their coefficients are \(c,-c\), where \(c=(\langle 10\rangle\langle 12\rangle)^{-s}>0\). The indicators involving \(\langle \Phi\rangle\) are identical. Consequently \[K_\tau^{N_1,N_2}(-1,1)=0,\qquad
 G^{N_1,N_2}(-1,1)=0\] for all \(\tau\), with exactly the definitions on p. 25.

Let \(\eta\ge0\) be a nonzero smooth function supported in \((-1,1)\), choose \(L\gg\Delta\) inside the permitted modulation region, and set \[f(-1,\tau)=\eta(\tau-L),\qquad
 g(1,\lambda)=\eta(\lambda-L-\Delta),\] with all other spatial components zero. The original dyadic pairing in that display equals \[c\int_\mathbb R\frac{\eta(\tau-L)^2}{\langle \tau\rangle^b}\,\mathrm d\tau>0.\] The contribution with phase \(-\Delta\) vanishes by disjoint support. The proposed first upper bound, \[\sum_{n_3,n_4}G^{N_1,N_2}(n_3,n_4)
       \|f(n_3,\cdot)\|_{L^q}
       \|g(n_4,\cdot)\|_{L^{q'+}},\] is zero. All test norms are finite; inverse temporal Fourier transforms are Schwartz functions. This is a failure of the specific domination inequality, not merely a complaint about an omitted estimate.

The exact Gaussian coordinate assignment has probability zero, but that does not limit the evidence to an exceptional input. For this fixed finite block the original pairing and the \(L^r_\tau\) scalar-kernel norm depend continuously on its finitely many Gaussian coordinates. The latter vanishes at the displayed point while the former is positive. For every fixed proposed implicit constant there is therefore an open neighborhood where the inequality fails. Such a neighborhood has positive Gaussian probability. Coordinates outside the block are irrelevant to this dyadic inequality.

The Hilbert–Schmidt estimates on pp. 25–26 estimate the collapsed kernel, whose norm need not dominate the actual operator. The same issue affects the truncation estimate (3.36) on p. 27. These bounds enter the enhanced-data norm (3.16), the contraction time (3.50), regularity persistence, and Lemma 4.1 on p. 38. They are essential inputs to the global construction.

For the energy version on pp. 45–46, take instead all four displayed Gaussian coordinates equal to \(1\). The factors \(\Psi_s\) are \(\langle 12\rangle^{2s}-\langle 10\rangle^{2s}\) and its negative. Thus the scalar energy kernel again cancels at \((-1,1)\), whereas the temporal translations remain different. The same tests isolate one term; a unit complex rotation of a test makes its \(\operatorname{Re}(i\,\cdot)\) pairing nonzero. The parameters \(b=2/5\), \(\alpha=2\), \(s=2/5\), \(\sigma=0\), \(q=2\) satisfy the energy condition \(4b\alpha+4\sigma>3\). Lemma 5.6 explicitly invokes the preceding reduction, so its proof inherits the defect.

A repair must estimate a random operator on joint spatial and temporal frequencies, retaining the translations \(\tau\mapsto\tau+\Phi\) until after the appropriate operator norm is taken. Summing absolute values discards the cancellation that supplies the intended random gain, and is not a verified substitute at the stated exponents. No complete replacement estimate, including its truncation convergence, was established in this review. Neither Proposition 3.6’s final moment statement nor Theorem 1.1 is asserted to be false. The Major assessment concerns a disproved essential proof step and its demonstrated dependencies.

 \sigma_3=0,\quad p=1,\quad

They are orthogonal third-order Gaussian chaos terms; interchanging \(a,b\) reinforces the coefficient, and no different triple cancels that same monomial. It follows that \[\|L(F)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\ge cTM^{1-s}.\] Third-chaos hypercontractivity gives \(\|L(F)\|_4\le C\|L(F)\|_2\). Interpolation between \(L^1\), \(L^2\), and \(L^4\) then gives \(\mathbb E|L(F)|\ge c\|L(F)\|_2\). Therefore \[\frac{\mathbb E\|F\|_{X_2^{0,-1/2-\varepsilon}}}{T}

The continuation formula on p. 60 must read \[\mathcal V(u_0)(t)=\mathcal V(\Phi_1u_0)(t-1)+S(t-1)\mathcal V(u_0)(1).\] The printed last term instead applies \(S(t-1)\) to the function \(\mathcal V(\Phi_1u_0)\) without the required evaluation or initial state. For the cubic iterate defined by (3.24), direct splitting of its time integral gives \[X^{(3)}[S(t_0)u_0](t)

The next estimate on p. 60 bounds \(\|\mathcal V(S(t_0)u_0+v)(t)\|_2\) by a constant times \(\|v\|_2\). The definition of the control quantity \(r\) already has a positive term \((1-t_0)^{-1}\ge1\), so this additive constant is absorbed in the ensuing local-growth estimate.

On p. 61 the upper-bound argument must start with \(+\log\int e^{r(u)}\,\mathrm d\rho\), not its negative. An upper bound on \(-\log I\) cannot establish that \(I\) is finite: the numerical values \(I=e^L\), \(L\to\infty\), satisfy such a bound for arbitrarily large \(I\). Likewise the good event in Corollary 6.2, p. 58, must use all \(t\ge0\) to be the complement of the bad event in (6.2). report: Abstract: This report checks the testing conditions and the passage from one-sided tail estimates to the full \(L^p\) bound in Theorem 3.6 of the acquired author manuscript. A finite commutative martingale satisfies every stated hypothesis at every positive scale but violates the asserted bound at \(p=4\). The unsupported step is the extension of a one-sided test to the opposite sign. The finding concerns arXiv:1805.07057v2 only; correspondence with the later publisher text has not been established. Author: AI technical review
Title: A missing two-sided hypothesis in a good-\(\lambda\) moment estimate
# Identity, version, and coverage

The assigned paper is Noncommutative good-\(\lambda\) inequalities, by Yong Jiao, Adam Osękowski, and Lian Wu, frozen identifier M25-0271 and journal DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1644. The actual reviewed document is arXiv:1805.07057v2, dated 19 November 2018, 52 pages [source]. All page references below are one-based PDF pages; these coincide with the printed page numbers in this source.

The publisher record gives publication on 7 May 2025, submission on 7 September 2023, and acceptance on 5 August 2024 [publisher]. The arXiv landing page separately lists a 2024 journal-reference year. These facts do not establish textual equivalence. The publisher full text was not available in the supplied source set; no current-journal defect is asserted.

The review read the introduction and preliminaries, followed Definitions 3.2–3.3 and Theorems 3.4–3.6 through their displayed proofs, and checked the sign dependence of the application in Theorem 4.1 (pp. 1–20). Theorem 4.2 was read only through its opening construction on p. 20. The remaining applications in Sections 4–6 and their external proof dependencies were not independently verified. Every supplied PDF page was parsed, which is distinct from this narrower scientific coverage. Source images for pp. 1, 5, and 9–20 were actually viewed.
# The tested assertion

Equation reference: test1, test2, asserted. Throughout Section 3 the martingale \(y=(y_n)_{n=0}^N\) is self-adjoint; it is not assumed positive. The differences include \(dy_0=y_0\) (p. 5). For a positive threshold \(\mu\), write the source’s stopping projections as \[R_{-1}^{\mu}=I,\qquad
 R_n^\mu=R_{n-1}^\mu
 \mathbf 1_{(-\infty,\mu)}(R_{n-1}^\mu y_nR_{n-1}^\mu).\] At threshold one, Definition 3.2 (p. 10) requires \[\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{n=0}^N\sum_{k=n+1}^N
 \tau((R_{n-1}-R_n)dy_kR_{n-1}dy_k(R_{n-1}-R_n))
 &\le \tau((I-R_N)x_N^2), \\
 \tau(Pdy_k^2P)&\le \tau(Pz_N^2P)
 \quad(0\le k\le N,\ P\in\mathcal M_k\text{ a projection}).\end{aligned}\] Theorem 3.6 (p. 17, (3.25)) assumes these conditions for \((x_N/\mu,y/\mu,z_N/\mu)\) for every \(\mu>0\), with \(x_N,z_N\in L^p\), and asserts, for \(2<p<\infty\), \[
 \|y_N\|_p\le
 \frac{12p}{\sqrt{1-(1+1/p)^{2-p}}}
 \bigl(\|x_N\|_p^2+\|z_N\|_p^2\bigr)^{1/2}.\] Testing the upper crossings of \(y\) is intrinsically one-sided. The stronger conditions in Definition 3.3 are different assumptions; they involve squared differences and are sign invariant.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (The full moment bound does not follow from the stated one-sided tests).  Theorem 3.6 is false under its printed hypotheses. In its proof, the negative-side estimate (3.29) on p. 18 does not follow from the positive-side estimate (3.28).
## A finite counterexample and all assumptions

Equation reference: choice. The walk is nonnegative and absorbed at zero. Its increments have zero conditional mean, since \(\mathbf 1_{\{X_{k-1}>0\}}\) is measurable at time \(k-1\). Thus \(X\) is a finite martingale. Set \[
 y_k=-X_k,\qquad x_N=0,\qquad z_N=1,\qquad p=4.\] All variables are real, self-adjoint, and bounded by \(N+1\) in absolute value; in particular every required \(L^p\) membership holds.

For any \(\mu>0\), \(y_k/\mu\le0<1\). The projections generated by this scaled martingale are therefore all \(I\). Both sides of [test1] (#test1) are zero. Moreover, \[(dy_0)^2=1,\qquad
 (dy_k)^2=\mathbf 1_{\{X_{k-1}>0\}}\le1\quad(k\ge1).\] For every allowed projection \(P\), \[\tau\bigl(P(dy_k/\mu)^2P\bigr)
 \le\mu^{-2}\tau(P)
 =\tau\bigl(P(z_N/\mu)^2P\bigr).\] This proves [test2] (#test2), including \(k=0\), for every positive scale. The large but finite value of \(N\) is admissible: the asserted constant has no dependence on the number of martingale steps or on the algebra dimension.
## Exact evaluation and contradiction

In contrast, the right-hand side of [asserted] (#asserted) is exactly \[\frac{48}{\sqrt{1-(5/4)^{-2}}}
 (0^2+1^2)^{1/2}=80.\] Hence [lower] (#lower) contradicts the stated conclusion. This is an analytic finite counterexample, not a simulation or an extrapolation. The independently written calculation file checks the constant and integer comparison exactly and verifies [reflection] (#reflection) against direct finite path counting for small lengths; those finite checks support, but do not replace, the argument above.
## The precise failed inference and counterevidence

The missing sign condition fails explicitly in this same construction. For \(-y=X\) at \(\mu=1\), the strict cutoff gives \(R_0(X)=0\) because \(X_0=1\). The \(n=0\) contribution to the left side of [test1] (#test1) is then \[\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathbb E(dX_k)^2\ge \mathbb E(dX_1)^2=1,\] whereas its right side is zero. Thus testing for \(-y\) is not an automatic consequence of testing at every positive scale for \(y\).

There is no zero-initial-value assumption to exclude the construction. Self-adjointness does not impose nonnegativity. The quantifier \(\mu>0\) does not include a change of sign. Definition 3.3 would provide stronger information, but cannot silently replace Definition 3.2 in the statement being tested. The actual page images confirm these formulas, excluding a text-extraction error as the explanation.

The one-sided Theorems 3.4 and 3.5 are not contradicted: their tail projections are trivial for the chosen nonpositive martingale. The assertion of \(L^p\) membership in Theorem 3.6 is not separately refuted; all counterexample variables are bounded.
# Impact and a bounded repair

The supported assessment is Major for the acquired author version. Theorem 3.6 is explicitly presented as a main result and supplies the abstract passage from testing conditions to moment estimates. Its norm conclusion fails, with every stated assumption satisfied. A short possible repair does not reduce the mathematical impact of that false core implication.

A precise necessary change to the proof strategy is to require the Definition 3.2 tests for both \[(x_N/\mu,y/\mu,z_N/\mu)
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 (x_N/\mu,-y/\mu,z_N/\mu)
 \qquad\text{for every }\mu>0.\] These assumptions supply the missing input for (3.29). In the finite-dimensional tracial setting the inspected one-sided arguments, followed separately for the two signs and combined as on p. 19, give [asserted] (#asserted) with the same constant. This verifies a restricted repair on that domain. A new, independent proof of every unbounded semifinite technical passage is not claimed. The sign-invariant strong conditions in Definition 3.3 also remove the demonstrated obstruction.

Theorem 4.1 provides concrete counterevidence against treating all applications as false. Its choice \(x_N=z_N=(\sum_kdy_k^2)^{1/2}\) and its verification on p. 20 work for either sign of \(y\). This application survives the demonstrated sign correction. The other downstream applications require their own sign checks and are outside the present verified scope. No experiments or author-code execution are required to establish the counterexample.

A bounded search for an erratum or corrigendum and inspection of the arXiv and publisher landing pages identified no correction to this exact statement. This does not establish priority or the absence of a correction. The later publisher abstract differs from the author manuscript, reinforcing the need for a separate publisher-text comparison before any journal-version attribution.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Issue judgment | Confirmed false norm bound; Major in arXiv v2.
Repair verification | Both-sign input closes the identified step; same bound checked in the finite-dimensional tracial setting.
Scientific decision | Pending; initial review is not independent acceptance.
Author adoption | Unknown; no author contact or adoption claim.
Remaining work | Publisher-text comparison; unexamined applications and general semifinite repair details.

No human review is recorded and no author code was executed. The earlier candidate checkpoint and rendering-time false inspection records remain preserved alongside the later completed checks.
