report: Abstract: This review examines the necessity argument in Theorem 1.49, concentrating on the critical structure-coefficient condition, the reference-volume change and the limiting momentum constraint. The equality case of the structural condition is supported by a positive uniform decay margin. The apparent logarithmic divergences in the momentum constraint cancel under the stated Hamiltonian identity. No substantive issue was confirmed in this scope. This is a limited initial review, not a verification of all asymptotic estimates or of the proposed global parametrisation of solutions.
Author: AI technical review
Title: Constraint and boundary checks for singular initial data
# Identity and inspected scope

The paper is Hans Ringström, Initial data on big bang singularities, M25-0272, DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1645. The reviewed file is the EMS Press version of record, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 28 (2026), no. 7, 3049–3130, 82 PDF pages [paper]. Its first page records receipt on 22 August 2022 and revision on 26 September 2024. The publisher separately records acceptance on 26 March 2025 and publication on 9 June 2025 [publisher]. The frozen 2025 membership is preserved; it is distinct from the 2026 issue year. One-based PDF page \(j\) is printed page \(3048+j\).

Actual text coverage comprised PDF pp. 1–6, 13–14, 23–29, 59–61, 64–66 and 70–77. The review followed the necessity proof and its momentum constraint calculation, inspected the convergence hypotheses and selected derivative estimates, and performed the independent checks below. All 82 pages were programmatically parsed; that fact does not enlarge the scientific coverage. Sections 2–4, most of Sections 5–6, the full anisotropic bootstrap and the external results cited as [67] and [69] in the paper were not independently proved here. In particular, the curvature identity used before (7.43) remains an explicitly identified dependency.
# Hypotheses and logical direction

Definition 1.10 (PDF p. 13) asks for a Riemannian metric \(\bar h\), a symmetric endomorphism \(\mathfrak K\) with distinct eigenvalues \(p_A\), and scalar data \(\Phi_1,\Phi_0\), satisfying \[\operatorname{tr}\mathfrak K=1,\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}\mathfrak K^2+\Phi_1^2=1,\qquad
 \operatorname{div}_{\bar h}\mathfrak K=\Phi_1\,d\Phi_0.\] For distinct indices it also requires the corresponding eigenframe structure coefficient to vanish on a neighbourhood whenever \(q_{ABC}=1+p_A-p_B-p_C\leq0\) at the point in question.

Theorem 1.49 is conditional. Its first part assumes the 2-standard assumptions, the scalar-field estimate (1.32) with \(k=1\), and the limiting Hamiltonian identity \(\bar\Phi_a^2+\operatorname{tr}\mathfrak K^2=1\). The full conclusion adds \(k\)-standard assumptions for \(k\geq2\) and the scalar estimate at that order. The Hamiltonian identity is therefore an input to this necessity theorem, not a conclusion derived from convergence alone.

Definitions 1.39–1.45 (PDF pp. 23–25) include a closed spatial manifold, zero shift, positive lapse, a positive lower mean-curvature bound (with the extra stated bound when \(\Lambda>0\)), uniform \(\varrho\to-\infty\), a uniform spectral gap, and spatially differentiated exponential decay with \(\epsilon(x)\geq\epsilon_0>0\). The higher-order lapse assumption controls spatial derivatives of \(\log\widehat N\) polynomially in \(\varrho\). These qualifications cannot be dropped in reading the result.

The integration step in Lemma 7.1 is consistent with these quantifiers: \(\widehat U\varrho=1\), and zero shift keeps \(x\) fixed along each integral curve. Thus a bound \(C\langle s\rangle^a e^{2\epsilon(x)s}\) is integrable at \(s=-\infty\), uniformly using \(\epsilon_0\). The claimed limit is not obtained by integrating an arbitrary pointwise convergence statement.
# The critical structural condition

The potentially delicate part of Theorem 1.49 is the neighbourhood conclusion at \(q_{ABC}=0\). The following check reproduces the decisive implication on PDF p. 76, including the direction of the inequality when \(\varrho<0\).

This also disposes of the suggested boundary objection: the proof does not merely infer a neighbourhood statement from pointwise vanishing. The uniform positive \(\eta\) covers nearby small positive values of \(q\). Without a positive rate margin this particular argument would not work. The derivation of [eq:positive] (#eq:positive) uses the scalar-curvature identity cited in the source and the preceding asymptotic estimates; the present check verifies the implication once those estimates hold and does not replace their full verification.
# Reference volume and momentum constraint

The reference-volume change on PDF p. 28 has the correct sign: \[\bar\varrho=\varrho-r_\theta,\qquad
 \bar\Phi_a=\Phi_1,\qquad
 \bar\Phi_b=\Phi_0+r_\theta\Phi_1.\] Indeed \(\bar\Phi_a\bar\varrho+\bar\Phi_b
=\Phi_1\varrho+\Phi_0\) exactly. Ignoring this change would give the wrong constant term for the scalar field.

The cancellation in Lemma 5.21 (PDF pp. 59–61), reused on pp. 76–77, can be checked without interchanging separate divergent limits. For a limiting frame derivative \(D\), the potentially singular combination is \[\sum_A p_A D(-p_A\log\theta)
 +\Phi_1D(-\Phi_1\log\theta+\Phi_0)+D\log\theta .\] Its coefficient of \(\log\theta\) is \(-\sum_Ap_A Dp_A-\Phi_1D\Phi_1\); its coefficient of \(D\log\theta\) is \(1-\sum_Ap_A^2-\Phi_1^2\). Both vanish by the Hamiltonian identity and its differential. The remaining term is \(\Phi_1D\Phi_0\). The exponentially decaying remainders multiplied by polynomial factors still tend to zero.

For an orthonormal eigenframe \(E_A\) and \([E_A,E_C]=\gamma^D_{AC}E_D\), the connection terms give \[(\operatorname{div}_{\bar h}\mathfrak K)(E_C)
 =E_Cp_C+\sum_A(p_C-p_A)\gamma^A_{AC}.\] This follows directly by expanding \(\sum_A\bar h((\nabla_{E_A}\mathfrak K)E_C,E_A)\) and using metric compatibility. It agrees with the source’s limiting expression. The rescaling in the proof of Theorem 1.49 places the calculation in the orthonormal frame for the extracted \(\bar h\).
# Independent exact examples and limits

On \(\mathbb T^3\times(0,t_+)\), take \(\Lambda=0\) and \[g=-dt^2+\sum_{i=1}^3t^{2p_i}(dx^i)^2,\qquad
 \phi=a\log t+b,\qquad \sum_i p_i=1,\quad \sum_i p_i^2+a^2=1.\] The nonzero Ricci coefficients are \(R_{00}=(\sum p_i-\sum p_i^2)t^{-2}\) and \(R_{ii}=p_i(\sum p_j-1)t^{2p_i-2}\). Thus \(R_{\alpha\beta}=\partial_\alpha\phi\,\partial_\beta\phi\); the wave equation has coefficient \(a(\sum p_i-1)=0\). Here \(\theta=t^{-1}\), \(\varrho=\log t\), \(\mathcal K=\operatorname{diag}(p_i)\) and \(\widehat U\phi=a\). All rate residuals vanish. The normalized lapse is spatially constant, \(\widehat N=t^{-1}\), so every spatial derivative of \(\log\widehat N\) vanishes. The structure coefficients and both sides of the momentum constraint are zero. The lower bound on \(\theta\) holds on any sufficiently short interval.

Exact rational substitution was run for \((p_1,p_2,p_3;a)=(-2/7,3/7,6/7;0)\) and \((0,1/3,2/3;2/3)\). Each has distinct eigenvalues; the corresponding \(q_{123}\) is \(-4/7\) and \(0\), respectively. Every computed Einstein and wave coefficient residual was exactly zero. These are admissible consistency checks, including a critical-wall example; they do not prove the general theorem.

No confirmed Major or Minor issue follows from these checks. A bounded title-plus-erratum search and the publisher page did not identify a correction; this is not proof that no correction exists. The supplied manifest records bounded supplement/code searches with no associated material identified. No author code was executed, and absence of optional code is not a mathematical defect.

Author: AI technical review
Title: A support-selector boundary issue and checks of the LIS argument
# Identity, version and scope

The paper is Jacopo Borga, Ewain Gwynne and Xin Sun, Permutons, meanders, and SLE-decorated Liouville quantum gravity, M25-0273, DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1646. The exact acquired file is the 57-page EMS Press version of record, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 28 (2026), no. 11, 4893–4949 [paper]. PDF page \(j\) corresponds to printed page \(4892+j\). The PDF records receipt on 10 November 2022 and revision on 28 October 2024. The publisher separately records acceptance on 23 March 2025 and publication on 12 June 2025 [publisher]. Frozen 2025 membership is unchanged.

Actual text inspection covered PDF pp. 1–4, 9–15, 21–31, 37 and 40–41. The main audit concerns the construction and support lemmas, Proposition 3.2, the measure-theoretic deductions in Section 3, and the use of Lemma 2.10 in re-rooting. All pages were parsed, which is distinct from scientific inspection. The full SLE flow-line and LQG absolute-continuity results, the support-dimension upper bound, the pattern-density formula and the physical/meander conjectures were not independently verified.
# The confirmed endpoint concern

Equation reference: eq:def. Section 1.2 allows \(\gamma\in(0,2)\), \(\kappa_1,\kappa_2>4\) and an arbitrary coupling of two whole-plane space-filling SLE curves \(\eta_1,\eta_2\), sampled independently of a unit-area LQG sphere field \(h\). They are then parametrized by \(\mu_h\)-mass on \([0,1]\). A Lebesgue-measurable selector satisfies \[\eta_1(t)=\eta_2(\psi(t))\quad(t\in[0,1]),\qquad
 \pi(B)=\int_0^1\mathbf 1_B(t,\psi(t))\,dt. \] These are (1.1)–(1.2), PDF p. 4. No endpoint normalization of \(\psi\) is imposed.

Problem 1 (Minor: a fixed-endpoint assertion is false).  The last assertion of Lemma 2.10, PDF p. 24 (printed 4916), says that for every admissible selector and each fixed \(t\in[0,1]\), almost surely \(\psi(t)\) is the unique \(s\) with \((t,s)\in\operatorname{supp}\pi\). It fails at \(t=0\) under the permitted identical-curve coupling.

Complete admissible counterexample. Take \(\gamma=1\), \(\kappa_1=\kappa_2=8\). Sample \(h\) and a whole-plane space-filling \(\mathrm{SLE}_8\) curve \(\eta\) independently and put \(\eta_1=\eta_2=\eta\). Both curve marginals have the required law, the pair is independent of \(h\), and identical coupling is expressly allowed. Their common area parametrization gives \(\eta(0)=\eta(1)=\infty\); the closed-loop endpoint convention also appears in Definition 5.1, p. 37.

Define the Borel function \[\psi(t)=\begin{cases}1,&t=0,\\t,&0<t\leq1.\end{cases}\] At zero, [eq:def] (#eq:def) holds because both endpoints map to infinity; elsewhere it holds because the curves coincide. Thus the parameter ranges, curve laws, independence from \(h\), allowed coupling, parametrization and selector requirements all hold.

For every Borel \(B\), \[\pi(B)=\int_0^1\mathbf 1_B(t,t)\,dt,\qquad
 \operatorname{supp}\pi=\{(u,u):0\leq u\leq1\}.\] The integral is unchanged by a singleton modification. Every relative neighbourhood of a diagonal point has positive diagonal Lebesgue mass, whereas every off-diagonal point has a disjoint neighbourhood. Hence the support fibre at \(t=0\) is \(\{0\}\). The lemma identifies it with \(\psi(0)=1\), but \((0,1)\) is not in the support. This contradiction holds on every realization where the specified objects are defined. ◻
## Source step, counterevidence and impact

The final proof paragraph of Lemma 2.10 invokes property (vi) of Section 2.4 (PDF p. 21). That hitting property concerns each fixed \(z\in\mathbb C\), and does not include infinity, attained at both interval endpoints. The example needs no claim about independence at deterministic interior times.

The first conditional assertion of Lemma 2.10 survives: it assumes that \(\eta_2\) hits \(\eta_1(t)\) only once, a premise that fails at the chosen endpoint. Lemma 2.8’s selector independence is preserved exactly. The discussion above Lemma 2.10 already notes diagonal support for identical curves and selector-dependent extra graph points.

Theorem 1.13 has stricter coupling alternatives (p. 9); the example does not refute its LIS conclusion. Theorem 1.22 requires independent SLE curves and uses a support coordinate for its shift. The example does not meet that independence hypothesis. Its footnote 3 (p. 14) and proof (p. 40) nevertheless need care when invoking unique hitting at endpoints. Shifts by \(0\) and \(1\) agree modulo one; no failure of the re-rooting distributional identity is established. Minor reflects this demonstrated local damage, not merely the ease of repair.
## Verified repair boundary

Keep the conditional unique-hit assertion. A supported further statement is: almost surely there is a Lebesgue-null set \(N\) such that for every admissible selector and every \(t\notin N\), \(\psi(t)\) is the unique support coordinate over \(t\). The proof of Lemma 2.8 (p. 23) supplies the null set of times at which \(\eta_1(t)\) is a multiple point of \(\eta_2\). Outside it, the first assertion of Lemma 2.10 applies to all selectors. An independently sampled uniform time avoids \(N\) almost surely.

This verifies only the almost-everywhere/uniform-time replacement. Deleting the endpoints alone does not prove a replacement at every deterministic interior time under arbitrary coupling. No such stronger repair or author adoption is claimed.
# Checks of the core LIS route
Proposition 3.2 (pp. 25–26) asserts that \(\pi^{\sigma_n}\Rightarrow\pi\), \(|\sigma_n|\to\infty\), and zero \(\pi\)-mass for every monotone set imply \(\operatorname{LIS}(\sigma_n)/|\sigma_n|\to0\).

An independent compactness check is as follows. If increasing subsequences occupy a fixed fraction \(c>0\), let \(A_n\) be the union of their closed permutation cells. They are nonempty compact sets with \(\pi^{\sigma_n}(A_n)\geq c\). Pass to a Hausdorff limit \(A\) and a weak limit \(
u\) of \(
u_n=\pi^{\sigma_n}|_{A_n}\). For each nonnegative continuous \(f\), \(\int f\,d
u\leq\int f\,d\pi\), so \(
u\leq\pi\). Testing \(1\) gives \(
u([0,1]^2)\geq c\); Hausdorff convergence gives \(\operatorname{supp}
u\subseteq A\). Thus \(\pi(A)\geq c\).

The two-dimensional cells need not themselves be monotone. Their diameters vanish, however. Relative to a selected cell’s upper-right corner, earlier selected cells lie southwest and later cells lie northeast. The order relation is closed under limits, so \(A\) is monotone, contradicting the premise. Only a closed monotone limit is needed. Actual image inspection confirms closure bars on both neighbourhoods in (3.3): the displayed Portmanteau inequality is valid.

The scale-invariant positive mass ratio in Lemma 3.4 yields a positive limsup without independence between scales. If every event \(\{R_{r_n}\geq c\}\) has probability at least \(p\), its limsup event has probability at least \(p\); letting \(p\uparrow1\) gives the assertion. The SLE geometric input giving positive interior and the LQG absolute-continuity input remain external dependencies of this check.

For Proposition 3.5 (p. 30), positive limsup density of the disjoint set \(Q_z\) gives a strict deficit in the density of \(X\) along a sequence: \[\liminf_{r\downarrow0}
 \frac{\mu_h(B_r(z)\cap X)}{\mu_h(B_r(z))}<1.\] This contradicts the full density limit \(1\). The displayed (3.15) uses a stronger limsup formulation. The sufficient liminf calculation validates the intended contradiction; this is a proof-reading clarification, not another confirmed defect in the main conclusion.

The simultaneous statement for every monotone set in Proposition 3.6 is needed, including sets depending on the realized permuton. A subsequence/Skorokhod argument then transfers Proposition 3.2 to the convergence-in-law setting and yields convergence in probability of normalized LIS. It does not give almost-sure convergence under an arbitrary original coupling. The theorem’s coupling restriction remains essential.

claim: Recorded check: Endpoint selector need not equal unique support coordinate
analysis: The last assertion of Lemma 2.10, PDF p. 24 (printed 4916), says that for every admissible selector and each fixed \(t\in[0,1]\), almost surely \(\psi(t)\) is the unique \(s\) with \((t,s)\in\operatorname{supp}\pi\). It fails at \(t=0\) under the permitted identical-curve coupling.

Complete admissible counterexample. Take \(\gamma=1\), \(\kappa_1=\kappa_2=8\). Sample \(h\) and a whole-plane space-filling \(\mathrm{SLE}_8\) curve \(\eta\) independently and put \(\eta_1=\eta_2=\eta\). Both curve marginals have the required law, the pair is independent of \(h\), and identical coupling is expressly allowed. Their common area parametrization gives \(\eta(0)=\eta(1)=\infty\); the closed-loop endpoint convention also appears in Definition 5.1, p. 37.

Define the Borel function \[\psi(t)=\begin{cases}1,&t=0,\\t,&0<t\leq1.\end{cases}\] At zero, [eq:def] (#eq:def) holds because both endpoints map to infinity; elsewhere it holds because the curves coincide. Thus the parameter ranges, curve laws, independence from \(h\), allowed coupling, parametrization and selector requirements all hold.

For every Borel \(B\), \[\pi(B)=\int_0^1\mathbf 1_B(t,t)\,dt,\qquad
 \operatorname{supp}\pi=\{(u,u):0\leq u\leq1\}.\] The integral is unchanged by a singleton modification. Every relative neighbourhood of a diagonal point has positive diagonal Lebesgue mass, whereas every off-diagonal point has a disjoint neighbourhood. Hence the support fibre at \(t=0\) is \(\{0\}\). The lemma identifies it with \(\psi(0)=1\), but \((0,1)\) is not in the support. This contradiction holds on every realization where the specified objects are defined. ◻

The final proof paragraph of Lemma 2.10 invokes property (vi) of Section 2.4 (PDF p. 21). That hitting property concerns each fixed \(z\in\mathbb C\), and does not include infinity, attained at both interval endpoints. The example needs no claim about independence at deterministic interior times.

The first conditional assertion of Lemma 2.10 survives: it assumes that \(\eta_2\) hits \(\eta_1(t)\) only once, a premise that fails at the chosen endpoint. Lemma 2.8’s selector independence is preserved exactly. The discussion above Lemma 2.10 already notes diagonal support for identical curves and selector-dependent extra graph points.

Theorem 1.13 has stricter coupling alternatives (p. 9); the example does not refute its LIS conclusion. Theorem 1.22 requires independent SLE curves and uses a support coordinate for its shift. The example does not meet that independence hypothesis. Its footnote 3 (p. 14) and proof (p. 40) nevertheless need care when invoking unique hitting at endpoints. Shifts by \(0\) and \(1\) agree modulo one; no failure of the re-rooting distributional identity is established. Minor reflects this demonstrated local damage, not merely the ease of repair.

Title: Initial scientific report on
Random tangled currents for \(\varphi^4\)

Source. Trishen S. Gunaratnam, Christoforos Panagiotis, Romain Panis and Franco Severo, Random tangled currents for \(\varphi^4\): Translation invariant Gibbs measures and continuity of the phase transition, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 28 (2026), no. 12, 5343–5426, DOI `10.4171/JEMS/1647`. The inspected publisher PDF records receipt on 23 November 2022 and revision on 12 December 2024. The publisher record gives acceptance on 23 March 2025 and online publication on 28 May 2025. The frozen annual membership remains 2025. No equivalence to another manuscript version is assumed.

Assessment: No Issue Found in the inspected scope. No confirmed Major or Minor mathematical defect was established. This is a claim-focused initial review, not certification of the entire 84-page article. The positive conclusions below distinguish independently checked deductions from substantial inputs whose complete proofs were not reconstructed. Scientific decision remains pending; no human or independent acceptance is recorded.
# Claims, assumptions and scope

Theorem 1.2 (PDF p. 5, printed p. 5347) concerns invariant tempered Gibbs measures on an infinite vertex-transitive graph of polynomial growth, with \(g>0\), \(a\in\mathbb R\) and an admissible ferromagnetic interaction satisfying (C1)–(C4) on PDF p. 4. Its first conclusion describes invariant states as mixtures of the plus and minus states. Its second conclusion gives uniqueness among all tempered Gibbs states under the free-state correlation criterion \[\liminf_{d_G(o,x)\to\infty}\langle\varphi_o\varphi_x\rangle_\beta^0=0.\] These conclusions have different scopes.

Theorem 1.3 (PDF p. 8, printed p. 5350) adds translation invariance on \(\mathbb Z^d\), reflection positivity and transience of the associated walk. The critical-temperature deduction checked here uses \(0<\beta_c<\infty\), in particular the nearest-neighbour case \(d\ge3\). The one-dimensional discussion is expressly qualified by the existence of a nontrivial transition in Remark 1.4 (PDF p. 9); this review does not establish that existence in every long-range case.

The actual source-text coverage comprises PDF pp. 2–5, 7–12, 19–24 and 60–72. It includes the finite-volume current expansion, the reduction to equality of even correlations, the architecture and quantifiers of the Section 6 contradiction, the infrared-bound deduction and the relevant uniqueness and continuity arguments. The complete extracted file was parsed separately; parsing is not scientific reading.
# Finite-volume expansion and structural reduction

Proposition 3.1 and its proof (PDF pp. 23–24, printed pp. 5365–5366) expand the interaction exponential and retain precisely the terms with the required parity of sources. This expansion has a direct analytic justification. In finite volume the sum of absolute Taylor terms is dominated by the integral of \[\exp\!\left(\beta\sum_{\{x,y\}}J_{x,y}|\varphi_x\varphi_y|
       +\beta\sum_x|h_x||\varphi_x|\right)
 \prod_x \rho_{g,a}(d\varphi_x).\] For \(g>0\), the quartic tails dominate every finite quadratic and linear term. Thus the integral is finite and the exchange of summation and integration is justified absolutely. Evenness of the single-site law gives the parity restriction. At \(\beta=0\), this reduces to the product single-site moments. A signed expansion for real \(h\) is not a positive current probability representation unless the required nonnegativity conditions are imposed.

Proposition 2.15 (PDF pp. 19–22) reduces invariant-state structure to equality of free and plus even correlations. Its final extremal-measure argument is consistent with spin-flip symmetrization and uniqueness of the extremal decomposition. The intermediate moment and coupling arguments require the stated uniform regularity estimates; those estimates were not re-proved in full.

Section 6 assumes a positive plus/free edge-correlation gap and derives bridges. Lemma 6.5 (PDF p. 62) yields a bound of two disjoint infinite paths and decay of the probability of two disjoint connections to a distant vertex. The two cases on PDF pp. 63–64 contradict these respective properties. In the nonpercolating-free-current case, the localization radius and lower volume threshold may depend on the chosen pair of vertices; the positive constants in the final comparison must remain uniform in the distant vertex. The displayed argument preserves this distinction. The switching construction, positivity of admissible tanglings and all local modification estimates remain substantive dependencies of this structural proof, not results independently certified by the present audit.
# Independent verification of the critical deduction
## Temperature limit

Write \(C_\Lambda(\beta)=\langle\varphi_x\varphi_y\rangle_{\Lambda,\beta}^0\) and \(C(\beta)=\langle\varphi_x\varphi_y\rangle_\beta^0\). Finite-volume continuity, together with monotonicity in volume and \(\beta\), gives \[C(\beta_c)
 =\sup_\Lambda\sup_{\beta<\beta_c}C_\Lambda(\beta)
 =\sup_{\beta<\beta_c}\sup_\Lambda C_\Lambda(\beta)
 =\lim_{\beta\uparrow\beta_c}C(\beta).\] The exchange is of two suprema. For fixed finitely supported \(v\), the quadratic form in (7.2), PDF p. 68, contains only finitely many correlations; it therefore passes to \(\beta_c\) entry by entry. This is done before taking the spatial averaging limit. The factor \((2\beta|J|)^{-1}\) has a finite limit when \(0<\beta_c<\infty\).

The derivation of (7.2) itself invokes an external reflection-positive infrared bound and the regularity estimates needed to pass unbounded moments from torus measures to infinite-volume measures. Weak convergence alone would not suffice. These are explicit dependencies.
## Spatial average and liminf

By transience, the Fourier kernel \((1-\widehat p(k))^{-1}\) is integrable. Its Fourier coefficients \(G(z)\) tend to zero and satisfy \(|G(z)|\le G(0)\). For \(N=|B_n|\) and any fixed radius \(R\), \[\frac1{N^2}\sum_{x,y\in B_n}|G(y-x)|
 \le \frac{|B_R|G(0)}N+\sup_{|z|>R}|G(z)|.\] First letting \(n\to\infty\) and then \(R\to\infty\) gives zero. The critical infrared inequality (7.3), PDF p. 68, implies the same zero limit for the nonnegative correlation average. If instead \(\liminf_{|z|\to\infty}C(z)>0\), some \(c>0\) would satisfy \(C(z)\ge c\) outside a fixed ball, forcing that average to be at least \[c\left(1-\frac{|B_R|}{N}\right).\] This contradiction proves the required liminf criterion. It does not assert pointwise correlation decay along every sequence.
## Uniqueness and the direction of continuity

Theorem 1.2 now gives uniqueness at criticality. Equivalently, the plus and minus states coincide, and spin-flip symmetry forces \(m^*(\beta_c)=0\). The implication to uniqueness of all Gibbs states also agrees with Proposition C.2 (PDF p. 72): stochastic domination provides ordered couplings, while equal coordinate means force coordinate equality almost surely. Countability then yields equality of the laws.

Appendix A (PDF p. 69) proves the needed right continuity of \(m^*\) in \(\beta\). Its argument first uses finite-volume continuity with a tail error uniform over \(\delta\in[0,1]\), and only then sends the volume to infinity. Monotonicity supplies the reverse inequality. This is the correct direction for approaching criticality from the ordered phase. It is distinct from the left continuity of the free two-point function used above.
# Counterchecks, limitations and recommendation

The apparent periodicity concern does not invalidate the transient Green-kernel argument. Neither an absent code deposit nor an unverified external input is treated as a mathematical defect. No admissible counterexample to the inspected claims was obtained, and no repair is proposed as an established correction.

The full construction of the tangled-current switching measure, all admissible-partition positivity results, the complete infinite-volume mixing and uniqueness arguments, the full Appendix D regularity proof, and the external infrared-bound references have not been independently reconstructed. These limitations preclude an unconditional certification of the complete structural theorem. They do not negate the verified deductions above.

The source manifest records bounded searches for supplementary material and code, without identifying a separate associated deposit. A further exact-title correction search and inspection of the publisher record did not identify a correction in the returned material; this does not prove nonexistence. No author code was executed.

The primary session performed the scientific assessment, report preparation, compilation and actual source/report page viewing. A native read-only auxiliary checked PDF pp. 4–5, 7–10, 68–69 and 72 and the critical-limit argument; it did not perform image inspection, compilation or independent acceptance. Its runtime self-description, like that of the primary, is GPT-6 Astra Pro; the backend was not independently verified. The controller’s earlier UI observations are attributed to the controller, separately from this runtime statement.
Disposition. Retain No Issue Found in the inspected scope with the dependency limits above. Scientific decision: pending. Human reviews: none.

Title: Initial scientific report on
Affine Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequalities

Inspected source. Julián Haddad and Monika Ludwig, Affine Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev inequalities, arXiv:2212.12194v3, 15 July 2025, 22 pages. The frozen publisher mapping is Julián Eduardo Haddad; Monika Ludwig, DOI `10.4171/jems/1648`. The publisher record lists submission on 23 February 2023, acceptance on 23 March 2025 and online publication on 28 May 2025. These findings concern the acquired author v3; equality of its content with the subscription publisher PDF has not been established. Page numbers below are both PDF and printed numbers.

Assessment: Major. Two confirmed issues affect sharp equality conclusions or their central proof chain. Two further local analytic proof errors are recorded separately. The inequality bounds themselves are not refuted by the counterexamples. The log-concave reverse branch has substantial positive verification. Scientific decision remains pending; no human review or independent acceptance is recorded.
# F1: false equality family in Theorem 14 (Major)

Location. Theorem 14, p. 11, the necessary and sufficient equality clause; the same power occurs after (15), p. 9. For \(\alpha>n\), the claimed family is \[f(x)=a(1+|\varphi(x-x_0)|^2)^{-(n-\alpha)/2}.\] Every member with \(a>0\) and \(\varphi\in GL(n)\) grows at infinity, so it lies outside \(L^{2n/(n+\alpha)}(\mathbb R^n)\). There is also an admissible nonzero equality example excluded by this classification.

Complete counterexample. Take \(n=2\), \(\alpha=4\), \(p=2/3\) and \[f(x)=(1+|x|^2)^{-3}.\] This is nonnegative, nonzero and in \(L^p\). Direct polar integration gives \[M_0=\int f=\frac{\pi}{2},\qquad
 M_2=\int |x|^2f=\frac{\pi}{2},\qquad \int f^{2/3}=\pi.\] The first moment vanishes by symmetry. All relevant moments are finite, so \[\iint f(x)f(y)|x-y|^2\,dx\,dy=2M_0M_2=\frac{\pi^2}{2}.\] Formula (2), p. 1, gives \(\gamma_{2,4}=1/(2\pi)\), while \(\|f\|_{2/3}^2=\pi^3\). Thus the theorem’s left side is \(\pi^2/2\).

By rotation invariance, \(S_4f\) is a ball. If its radius is \(R\), the defining polar identity (11), p. 6, gives \(2\pi R^4=\pi^2/2\), hence \(R^4=\pi/4\). Its affine expression is \[2\pi^{-1}|S_4f|^2=2\pi R^4=\frac{\pi^2}{2}.\] All three terms of Theorem 14 are equal. The printed growing profile cannot represent this decaying \(f\). The saved independent symbolic calculation verifies the integrals and equalities exactly; no author code was executed.

Counterevidence, impact and repair boundary. The proof on p. 12 uses \(f^\star(x)=a(1+\lambda|x|^2)^{-n/p}\), whose power is \(-(n+\alpha)/2\). That agrees with the example and identifies the apparent intended correction. The Major grade concerns the false sharp optimizer classification in a principal theorem, which excludes every nonzero admissible optimizer; it does not assert that the inequality bound is false. Replacing \(n-\alpha\) by \(n+\alpha\) repairs this example and restores integrability. A complete global equality classification still requires a correct equality argument, including F2; it is not certified merely by changing the sign.
# F2: the shared affine map is lost in equality lemmas (Major)

Locations. Lemma 8, p. 7; Lemmas 9–10, p. 8; Lemma 11, p. 10; Lemmas 12–13, p. 11. They assert that equality requires \(f\) to be a translate of \(f^\star\). Theorem 1’s proof on p. 9 invokes Lemma 10 for its affine equality classification, and Theorem 14’s proof on p. 12 invokes Lemma 13.

Admissible counterexample. In dimension two set \[A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1/2),\quad g(x)=e^{-|x|^2},
 \quad f(x)=g(A^{-1}x),\quad K=AB^2.\] Since \(\det A=1\), one has \(f^\star=g\) and \(K^\star=B^2\). The function belongs to every positive \(L^p\) space, its positive superlevel sets have finite measure, and \(g\) is strictly symmetric decreasing. The singular kernel integral for \(q=1\) in Lemma 8 and the polynomial kernel integral for \(q=2\) in Lemma 11 are finite.

Under \(x=Au\), \(y=Av\), the Jacobian is one and \(\|x-y\|_K=|u-v|\). Consequently, \[\iint\frac{f(x)f(y)}{\|x-y\|_K}\,dx\,dy
 =\iint\frac{g(u)g(v)}{|u-v|}\,du\,dv\] and \[\iint f(x)\|x-y\|_K^2f(y)\,dx\,dy
 =\iint g(u)|u-v|^2g(v)\,du\,dv.\] These are equality cases of the two printed rearrangement inequalities. But \(f\) is not a translate of \(g\): the Hessian of \(\log f\) is \(-2\operatorname{diag}(1/4,4)\), whereas every translate of \(\log g\) has Hessian \(-2I\).

The radial definition similarly gives \[S_\alpha f=A S_\alpha g,\qquad |S_\alpha f|=|S_\alpha g|<\infty
 \quad(\alpha>0).\] Thus Lemma 10 at \(\alpha=1\) and Lemma 13 at \(\alpha=4\) have equality without the claimed translate condition. The printed \(p=2\alpha/(n+\alpha)\) in Lemma 10 does not exclude the Gaussian.

Counterevidence and actual damage. Theorem 1 itself correctly includes \(GL(n)\) in its equality family, the source states affine covariance on p. 2, and its quoted Burchard theorem on p. 4 retains a common volume-preserving linear map. These support the intended theorem but contradict the auxiliary classifications. The damage is to the central proof of the affine sharp equality families, not a demonstrated failure of the volume bounds. The Major grade reflects loss of the essential affine degree of freedom in this proof chain; local editability does not remove that damage.

Verified bounded repair. In the finite positive-volume, strictly decreasing-profile setting of Lemma 8, retain the same \(A\), \(|\det A|=1\), in \[K=AK^\star,\qquad f(x)=f^\star(A^{-1}(x-x_0)).\] Necessity follows from the common map in the quoted Theorem 5; equality of the outer functions makes their translations agree and removes the homogeneous kernel’s translation. Sufficiency is the exact substitution above. The corrected finite-volume equality statement for Lemma 10 then follows from this and covariance.

For the reverse layer-cake argument, the Burchard condition must also be applied over a nonempty interval \(|r_1-r_2|<r_3<r_1+r_2\) of the kernel-level radius, not at an arbitrarily small radius when the outer level radii differ (p. 11). The full generality of that repaired equality proof is not independently certified here. The counterexample does not depend on assuming the repair.
# F3: compact support does not imply the asserted finiteness (Minor)
Location. Lemma 10, pp. 8–9, especially the sentence after (14). Its printed exponent \(p=2\alpha/(n+\alpha)\) differs from Theorem 1’s \(2n/(n+\alpha)\).

Take \(n=2\), \(\alpha=1\), define \(f(0)=0\), and set \[f(x)=|x|^{-2}\mathbf 1_{\{0<|x|<1\}}.\] Then \(\int f^{2/3}=3\pi<\infty\), but \(\int f=\infty\). For every \(k\ge1\), the compact-support truncation \(f_{(k)}=f\mathbf 1_{kB^2}\) is unchanged. For each \(\xi\in S^1\) and \(0<t<1/2\), integration near \(x=0\) gives \[\int f(x)f(x+t\xi)\,dx=\infty:\] the second factor is bounded below by a positive constant there, and the first has a logarithmically divergent integral. Every radial value of \(S_1f_{(k)}\) is therefore infinite, contrary to the asserted finiteness.

This refutes the approximation sentence on its stated domain. It does not refute the volume comparison, which reads \(\infty\le\infty\) for this radial example. The singular \(f\) is also outside Theorem 1’s intended \(L^{4/3}\) domain. This limited demonstrated effect supports Minor.

A verified replacement is \(f_k=\min(f,k)\mathbf 1_{kB^n}\). Boundedness and compact support bound each directional autocorrelation uniformly and restrict its \(t\)-support, giving \(|S_\alpha f_k|<\infty\). Monotone convergence then passes radial volumes and rearrangements to the limit. This also supplies the comparison at Theorem 1’s actual exponent without assuming an unjustified inclusion between the two global \(L^p\) spaces.
# F4: reciprocal error in the Mellin substitution (Minor)

Location. Equation (29) and accompanying monotonicity sentences, p. 16. The substitution gives \[\int_0^\infty t^{\beta-1}\omega(t/\zeta(\alpha))\,dt
 =\zeta(\alpha)^\beta\int_0^\infty u^{\beta-1}\omega(u)\,du,\] where the source prints \(\zeta(\alpha)^{-\beta}\).

Take \(\omega(t)=e^{-t}\), \(\phi(t)=t/2\), \(\alpha=1\), \(\beta=2\). All stipulated positive and regularized negative moments are finite; \(\phi\) increases and \(\phi(t)/t\) is nondecreasing. Then \(\zeta(1)=2\) and the integral is \(4\), whereas the printed expression is \(1/4\). The uses of increasing on that page likewise conflict with the lemma’s decreasing conclusion. This is a confirmed calculation error, not a counterexample to the monotonicity lemma or reverse inequalities.

For the exponential-weight case used in the log-concave branch, an independent proof is available. Normalize \(F(t)=g(t\xi)/g(0)\), where \(g=f*f^-\), and define \[I_p(F)=
 \begin{cases}\int_0^\infty t^{p-1}F(t)\,dt,&p>0,\\
 \int_0^\infty t^{p-1}(F(t)-1)\,dt,&-1<p<0,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad Z(p)=\bigl(I_p(F)/\Gamma(p)\bigr)^{1/p}.\] For \(a=Z(p)\), \(H(t)=F(t)-e^{-t/a}\) changes sign from nonnegative to nonpositive and has zero \(p\)-weighted integral. Multiplication by the increasing factor \(t^{q-p}\) makes its \(q\)-weighted integral nonpositive for \(q>p\). If \(q<0\), division by \(\Gamma(q)<0\) and taking the negative power \(1/q\) reverse direction twice; if \(q>0\) neither reversal occurs. Both give \(Z(q)\le Z(p)\). The regularized expansion supplies continuity at zero. Compact support is permitted with \(-\log0=+\infty\). Thus the needed log-concave conclusion survives; the demonstrated damage is a local proof calculation, supporting Minor.
# Positive checks and coverage limits

For the simplex exponential \[f(x)=e^{-(x_1+\cdots+x_n)}\mathbf 1_{\mathbb R_+^n}(x),\] product integration gives \(\|f\|_1=1\), \(\|f\|_2^2=2^{-n}\) and \(g(y)=2^{-n}e^{-\|y\|_1}\). As \(|B_1^n|=2^n/n!\), the first and middle expressions of Theorem 2 both equal \(2^{\alpha-n}\). An amplitude \(a\) and invertible map \(A\) multiply both by \(a^2|\det A|^{1+\alpha/n}\). These verify its sufficient equality examples without using F2.

The normalization in (30)–(32) yields Theorem 2’s stated constant. The negative Mellin parameter \(p=-2s\) gives the range \(0<s<1/2\) in Theorem 19; the negative volume power reverses inclusion as required. The endpoint \(p=-1\) can diverge even for the exponential example. Normalized bodies are used for nonzero functions; the zero case of the unnormalized inequality is separate.

problems.title: False sharp optimizer family in Theorem14
problems.source_location: Pdf page: 11 Claim: Theorem14 necessary/sufficient equality clause
claim: Recorded check: False sharp optimizer family in Theorem14
analysis: Location. Theorem 14, p. 11, the necessary and sufficient equality clause; the same power occurs after (15), p. 9. For \(\alpha>n\), the claimed family is \[f(x)=a(1+|\varphi(x-x_0)|^2)^{-(n-\alpha)/2}.\] Every member with \(a>0\) and \(\varphi\in GL(n)\) grows at infinity, so it lies outside \(L^{2n/(n+\alpha)}(\mathbb R^n)\). There is also an admissible nonzero equality example excluded by this classification.

Complete counterexample. Take \(n=2\), \(\alpha=4\), \(p=2/3\) and \[f(x)=(1+|x|^2)^{-3}.\] This is nonnegative, nonzero and in \(L^p\). Direct polar integration gives \[M_0=\int f=\frac{\pi}{2},\qquad
 M_2=\int |x|^2f=\frac{\pi}{2},\qquad \int f^{2/3}=\pi.\] The first moment vanishes by symmetry. All relevant moments are finite, so \[\iint f(x)f(y)|x-y|^2\,dx\,dy=2M_0M_2=\frac{\pi^2}{2}.\] Formula (2), p. 1, gives \(\gamma_{2,4}=1/(2\pi)\), while \(\|f\|_{2/3}^2=\pi^3\). Thus the theorem’s left side is \(\pi^2/2\).

By rotation invariance, \(S_4f\) is a ball. If its radius is \(R\), the defining polar identity (11), p. 6, gives \(2\pi R^4=\pi^2/2\), hence \(R^4=\pi/4\). Its affine expression is \[2\pi^{-1}|S_4f|^2=2\pi R^4=\frac{\pi^2}{2}.\] All three terms of Theorem 14 are equal. The printed growing profile cannot represent this decaying \(f\). The saved independent symbolic calculation verifies the integrals and equalities exactly; no author code was executed.

Counterevidence, impact and repair boundary. The proof on p. 12 uses \(f^\star(x)=a(1+\lambda|x|^2)^{-n/p}\), whose power is \(-(n+\alpha)/2\). That agrees with the example and identifies the apparent intended correction. The Major grade concerns the false sharp optimizer classification in a principal theorem, which excludes every nonzero admissible optimizer; it does not assert that the inequality bound is false. Replacing \(n-\alpha\) by \(n+\alpha\) repairs this example and restores integrability. A complete global equality classification still requires a correct equality argument, including F2; it is not certified merely by changing the sign.
result: Impact: Principal theorem's sharp equality classification false; excludes all nonzero admissible optimizers.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Replace n-alpha with n+alpha; correct F2 proof chain.

problems.title: Shared affine map lost in equality lemmas
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 7 Pdf pages: 8 Pdf pages: 10 Pdf pages: 11 Claims: Lemmas8–13 equality clauses
claim: Recorded check: Shared affine map lost in equality lemmas
analysis: Locations. Lemma 8, p. 7; Lemmas 9–10, p. 8; Lemma 11, p. 10; Lemmas 12–13, p. 11. They assert that equality requires \(f\) to be a translate of \(f^\star\). Theorem 1’s proof on p. 9 invokes Lemma 10 for its affine equality classification, and Theorem 14’s proof on p. 12 invokes Lemma 13.

Admissible counterexample. In dimension two set \[A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1/2),\quad g(x)=e^{-|x|^2},
 \quad f(x)=g(A^{-1}x),\quad K=AB^2.\] Since \(\det A=1\), one has \(f^\star=g\) and \(K^\star=B^2\). The function belongs to every positive \(L^p\) space, its positive superlevel sets have finite measure, and \(g\) is strictly symmetric decreasing. The singular kernel integral for \(q=1\) in Lemma 8 and the polynomial kernel integral for \(q=2\) in Lemma 11 are finite.

Under \(x=Au\), \(y=Av\), the Jacobian is one and \(\|x-y\|_K=|u-v|\). Consequently, \[\iint\frac{f(x)f(y)}{\|x-y\|_K}\,dx\,dy
 =\iint\frac{g(u)g(v)}{|u-v|}\,du\,dv\] and \[\iint f(x)\|x-y\|_K^2f(y)\,dx\,dy
 =\iint g(u)|u-v|^2g(v)\,du\,dv.\] These are equality cases of the two printed rearrangement inequalities. But \(f\) is not a translate of \(g\): the Hessian of \(\log f\) is \(-2\operatorname{diag}(1/4,4)\), whereas every translate of \(\log g\) has Hessian \(-2I\).

The radial definition similarly gives \[S_\alpha f=A S_\alpha g,\qquad |S_\alpha f|=|S_\alpha g|<\infty
 \quad(\alpha>0).\] Thus Lemma 10 at \(\alpha=1\) and Lemma 13 at \(\alpha=4\) have equality without the claimed translate condition. The printed \(p=2\alpha/(n+\alpha)\) in Lemma 10 does not exclude the Gaussian.

Counterevidence and actual damage. Theorem 1 itself correctly includes \(GL(n)\) in its equality family, the source states affine covariance on p. 2, and its quoted Burchard theorem on p. 4 retains a common volume-preserving linear map. These support the intended theorem but contradict the auxiliary classifications. The damage is to the central proof of the affine sharp equality families, not a demonstrated failure of the volume bounds. The Major grade reflects loss of the essential affine degree of freedom in this proof chain; local editability does not remove that damage.

Verified bounded repair. In the finite positive-volume, strictly decreasing-profile setting of Lemma 8, retain the same \(A\), \(|\det A|=1\), in \[K=AK^\star,\qquad f(x)=f^\star(A^{-1}(x-x_0)).\] Necessity follows from the common map in the quoted Theorem 5; equality of the outer functions makes their translations agree and removes the homogeneous kernel’s translation. Sufficiency is the exact substitution above. The corrected finite-volume equality statement for Lemma 10 then follows from this and covariance.

For the reverse layer-cake argument, the Burchard condition must also be applied over a nonempty interval \(|r_1-r_2|<r_3<r_1+r_2\) of the kernel-level radius, not at an arbitrarily small radius when the outer level radii differ (p. 11). The full generality of that repaired equality proof is not independently certified here. The counterexample does not depend on assuming the repair.
result: Impact: Auxiliary necessary classifications used to establish core affine sharp equality families are false.

problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 8 Pdf pages: 9 Claim: p=2alpha/(n+alpha) and sentence after14
claim: Recorded check: Compact support alone does not imply finiteSvolume on printed domain
analysis: Location. Lemma 10, pp. 8–9, especially the sentence after (14). Its printed exponent \(p=2\alpha/(n+\alpha)\) differs from Theorem 1’s \(2n/(n+\alpha)\).

Take \(n=2\), \(\alpha=1\), define \(f(0)=0\), and set \[f(x)=|x|^{-2}\mathbf 1_{\{0<|x|<1\}}.\] Then \(\int f^{2/3}=3\pi<\infty\), but \(\int f=\infty\). For every \(k\ge1\), the compact-support truncation \(f_{(k)}=f\mathbf 1_{kB^2}\) is unchanged. For each \(\xi\in S^1\) and \(0<t<1/2\), integration near \(x=0\) gives \[\int f(x)f(x+t\xi)\,dx=\infty:\] the second factor is bounded below by a positive constant there, and the first has a logarithmically divergent integral. Every radial value of \(S_1f_{(k)}\) is therefore infinite, contrary to the asserted finiteness.

This refutes the approximation sentence on its stated domain. It does not refute the volume comparison, which reads \(\infty\le\infty\) for this radial example. The singular \(f\) is also outside Theorem 1’s intended \(L^{4/3}\) domain. This limited demonstrated effect supports Minor.

A verified replacement is \(f_k=\min(f,k)\mathbf 1_{kB^n}\). Boundedness and compact support bound each directional autocorrelation uniformly and restrict its \(t\)-support, giving \(|S_\alpha f_k|<\infty\). Monotone convergence then passes radial volumes and rearrangements to the limit. This also supplies the comparison at Theorem 1’s actual exponent without assuming an unjustified inclusion between the two global \(L^p\) spaces.
result: Impact: Auxiliary approximation assertion fails; limited demonstrated damage.

problems.title: Reciprocal factor in Mellin substitution
problems.source_location: Pdf page: 16 Claim: Eq29 and increasing sentences
claim: Recorded check: Reciprocal factor in Mellin substitution
analysis:
Location. Equation (29) and accompanying monotonicity sentences, p. 16. The substitution gives \[\int_0^\infty t^{\beta-1}\omega(t/\zeta(\alpha))\,dt
 =\zeta(\alpha)^\beta\int_0^\infty u^{\beta-1}\omega(u)\,du,\] where the source prints \(\zeta(\alpha)^{-\beta}\).

Take \(\omega(t)=e^{-t}\), \(\phi(t)=t/2\), \(\alpha=1\), \(\beta=2\). All stipulated positive and regularized negative moments are finite; \(\phi\) increases and \(\phi(t)/t\) is nondecreasing. Then \(\zeta(1)=2\) and the integral is \(4\), whereas the printed expression is \(1/4\). The uses of increasing on that page likewise conflict with the lemma’s decreasing conclusion. This is a confirmed calculation error, not a counterexample to the monotonicity lemma or reverse inequalities.

For the exponential-weight case used in the log-concave branch, an independent proof is available. Normalize \(F(t)=g(t\xi)/g(0)\), where \(g=f*f^-\), and define \[I_p(F)=
 \begin{cases}\int_0^\infty t^{p-1}F(t)\,dt,&p>0,\\
 \int_0^\infty t^{p-1}(F(t)-1)\,dt,&-1<p<0,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad Z(p)=\bigl(I_p(F)/\Gamma(p)\bigr)^{1/p}.\] For \(a=Z(p)\), \(H(t)=F(t)-e^{-t/a}\) changes sign from nonnegative to nonpositive and has zero \(p\)-weighted integral. Multiplication by the increasing factor \(t^{q-p}\) makes its \(q\)-weighted integral nonpositive for \(q>p\). If \(q<0\), division by \(\Gamma(q)<0\) and taking the negative power \(1/q\) reverse direction twice; if \(q>0\) neither reversal occurs. Both give \(Z(q)\le Z(p)\). The regularized expansion supplies continuity at zero. Compact support is permitted with \(-\log0=+\infty\). Thus the needed log-concave conclusion survives; the demonstrated damage is a local proof calculation, supporting Minor.
result: Impact: Local displayed calculation/direction error; no reverseinequalitycounterexample.

report: Author: Initial scientific review: M25-0276
Date: 27 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific report on
Universal coding, intrinsic volumes, and metric complexity

Source and version. Jaouad Mourtada, Universal coding, intrinsic volumes, and metric complexity, arXiv:2303.07279v2, 56 pages, DOI mapping `10.4171/jems/1649`. The acquired PDF watermark and submission history say 7 April 2025; its title page says 8 April 2025. These are separate recorded dates. The publisher record lists submission on 17 March 2023, acceptance on 23 March 2025 and online publication on 23 May 2025. Publisher-PDF equivalence was not established; this report concerns the acquired author v2.

Assessment: Minor in the inspected scope. Two local mathematical statements need correction; a separate notation clarification is not counted as a substantive finding. Complete admissible checks are given below. The main Gaussian/Wills identity and the metric comparison admit the checked proofs presented here. No Major defect was established. This initial review does not certify all quantitative redundancy and chaining results; scientific decision remains pending and human reviews are empty.
# F1: the boundary-area description excludes a permitted case (Minor)

Location. The paragraph after Definition 2.1 on p. 10 identifies \(V_{n-1}(K)\) with one half of the \((n-1)\)-dimensional Hausdorff measure of \(\partial K\). The definition on p. 9 expressly permits compact convex sets with empty interior.

Take the permitted convex body \(K=[-1,1]\times\{0\}\subset\mathbb R^2\). Its parallel set consists of a rectangle and two semicircles, so \[\operatorname{Vol}_2(K+rB^2)=4r+\pi r^2.\] Comparison with the source’s Steiner formula (2.10) gives \(V_1(K)=2\), \(V_2(K)=0\) and \(V_0(K)=1\). Since the ambient topological boundary of \(K\) is \(K\) itself, \[\tfrac12\mathcal H^1(\partial K)=1\ne2=V_1(K).\] All hypotheses of the paper’s convex-body definition are met.

The counterevidence is the correct intrinsic-volume definition and Steiner expansion on the same pages. Theorem 2.1 uses those coefficients, not the unqualified boundary-area description. For this example the regret is correctly \(\log(1+2/\sqrt{2\pi})\). The actual damage is a false geometric interpretation for a permitted boundary case, so the grade is Minor. Restrict the half-boundary-area description to full-dimensional bodies; for codimension-one bodies the intrinsic volume equals the volume within their affine span. The segment calculation verifies this distinction directly.
# F2: the interpolation sign requires \(\beta\ge1\) (Minor)
Locations. The smoothing family is introduced for every \(\beta>0\) on p. 19; after (4.3), p. 20, its interpolation is asserted to decrease under contractions.

For an exact admissible counterexample to that intermediate assertion, take \(A=\{-a,a\}\subset\mathbb R\), \(a>0\), \(B=\{0\}\) and the constant contraction \(\varphi:A\to B\). Retain the two source indices, as in the proof, so that the two target coordinates coincide. At \(\beta=1/2\), with \(s=a^2(1-t)\), the interpolated Gaussian coordinates are \(\pm\sqrt{s}\,Z\), each with variance \(s\), where \(Z\sim N(0,1)\). Consequently, \[F_{1/2}(t,t)
 =\mathbb E\!\left(e^{(\sqrt{s}Z-s/2)/2}
            +e^{(-\sqrt{s}Z-s/2)/2}\right)^2
 =2+2e^{-s/2}.\] This is strictly increasing in \(t\), contrary to the stated direction. The map is surjective and contracts every pairwise distance; all Gaussian expectations are finite.

The correct derivative, independently recomputed and agreeing with (4.3), is \[\frac{d}{dt}F_\beta(t,t)
 =\frac{\beta-1}{4}
 \sum_{i,j}\mathbb E[f(t)p_i(t)p_j(t)]
 \bigl(\Delta_{ii}+\Delta_{jj}-2\Delta_{ij}\bigr),
 \qquad \Delta=\Sigma^B-\Sigma^A.\] The bracket is nonpositive by contraction. Thus decrease follows for \(\beta\ge1\), with equality of this derivative at \(\beta=1\). This restriction is sufficient for the limit \(\beta\to\infty\). It leaves Theorem 4.1 unchanged and supplies its complete finite-set comparison. The issue is graded Minor because the excessive range concerns an intermediate smoothing claim; it does not give a counterexample to the principal comparison theorem. The verified repair is to choose \(\beta>1\) throughout that argument.
# F3: Notation clarification for Lemma 4.1

The definition of \(X(t)\) in Lemma 4.1, p. 20, should read \[X(t)=\sqrt{1-t}\,X^A+\sqrt t\,X^B,\] using the stipulated independent Gaussian vectors, rather than their covariance matrices. The main comparison proof on p. 19 already uses this construction. Gaussian integration by parts then gives (4.4). No invalid step in that proof is attributed to this notation error. This clarification retains the original F3 identifier for traceability and is not counted as a substantive Minor finding.
# Independent checks of the main deductions
## Envelope integral, intrinsic volumes and degenerate bodies

For nonempty \(A\subset\mathbb R^n\), the usual continuous Gaussian densities have the measurable envelope \[h_A(x)=(2\pi)^{-n/2}e^{-\operatorname{dist}(x,A)^2/2}.\] If a predictive density \(q\) has worst-case regret at most \(c\), then \(h_A\le e^c q\), so \(\int h_A\le e^c\). Conversely, if \(Z_A=\int h_A<\infty\), the normalized envelope \(h_A/Z_A\) has constant regret \(\log Z_A\). This checks (2.12), including the infinite-integral alternative, without interchanging a minimax operation.

For a convex compact \(K\), Tonelli and the layer-cake substitution give \[\int e^{-\operatorname{dist}(x,K)^2/2}\,dx
 =\int_0^\infty\operatorname{Vol}_n(K+rB^n)\,r e^{-r^2/2}\,dr.\] Inserting Steiner’s formula and using \[\kappa_m\int_0^\infty r^{m+1}e^{-r^2/2}\,dr=(2\pi)^{m/2}\] yields \(\sum_{j=0}^n V_j(K)(2\pi)^{-j/2}\) after division by \((2\pi)^{n/2}\). This confirms the scale in Theorem 2.1, pp. 11–12, including lower-dimensional bodies. A singleton gives regret zero; a segment of length \(L\) gives \(\log(1+L/\sqrt{2\pi})\), and adding orthogonal zero coordinates changes neither answer.
## Metric comparison and limits

For finite sets, the covariance drift \(-\Sigma_{ii}(t)/2\) is essential: its derivative cancels the extra diagonal term and leaves the factor \(\beta-1\) in F2. The computation above therefore also checks the sign of the variance correction. Degenerate covariance matrices are allowed, including the repeated target coordinates in the counterexample.

For \(\beta\ge1\), \[e^{\max_i z_i}\le\left(\sum_i e^{\beta z_i}\right)^{1/\beta}
 \le N^{1/\beta}e^{\max_i z_i}.\] The exponential maximum is bounded by a finite sum of Gaussian exponentials with finite expectation. Hence this sandwich passes to \(\beta\to\infty\), establishing the required comparison. For arbitrary subsets of \(\ell_2\), lift each finite target subset through the surjective contraction, apply the finite comparison, and take the supremum over finite subsets as in (3.1), p. 14. This avoids any assumption that the whole set lies in a finite-dimensional space. No independent infinite-dimensional Lebesgue density is required.
## Local width and covering estimates

The local width uses centers in \(A\), as do the covering numbers in (4.5)–(4.6), pp. 20–21. The mixture bound on p. 44 follows from \(\sup_i h_{A_i}\le\sum_i h_{A_i}\): \[R^*(A)\le\log\sum_i e^{R^*(A_i)}
 \le\max_iR^*(A_i)+\log N.\] Together with the stated McMullen bound, applying this to \(A_i=A\cap B(\theta_i,r)\) gives the upper bound in (4.10).

For the local lower bound, the Gaussian representation and Jensen give \(R^*(A)\ge w_A(r)-r^2/2\). If \(r<r_*(A)\), the definition as a supremum supplies \(r'\ge r\) with \(w_A(r')\ge r'^2\); it is not necessary to assume that \(r_*\) is an attained continuous fixed point. Thus \(R^*(A)\ge r_*^2/2\). Likewise, for \(r>\max(r_*,\widetilde r)\), both defining complexity functions are below \(r^2\), proving (8.10), p. 45. These implications remain valid for discontinuous nonconvex local widths.

The remaining covering-number lower bound in (4.9) depends on the minimax-redundancy result from Section 8.3. That proof was not independently audited here. Consequently the complete two-sided quantitative theorem is not certified by the checks above.

As an exact boundary check, a two-point set at distance \(d\) has \[R^*(A)=\log\bigl(2\Phi(d/2)\bigr),\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function: integrate the larger of the two densities on each side of their midpoint. The variational expression in (4.10) equals \(\min(\log2,d/\sqrt{2\pi})\) for this set. This matches the linear small-distance behavior and bounded large-distance behavior of the exact regret. It does not by itself establish the general theorem.
# Coverage, dependencies and disposition

The primary actually read extracted PDF pp. 1–4, 8–16, 18–24 and 44–45. The full 56-page PDF was parsed and hashed separately; parsing is not review. The used source evidence images and every final report page were actually viewed. The source renderer’s p. 1 Symbol-font warning is retained; title, author and both dates remained readable in the inspected image.

The independent checks cover the Gaussian envelope/Wills identity, its normalization and degenerate cases, the full finite metric-comparison argument with its limit extension, and the displayed local-width/covering deductions. They do not reconstruct the full redundancy lower bound, generic chaining characterization, all sum/difference-body results, asymptotic expansions, ellipsoid and \(\ell_1\) examples, or all external convex-geometric theorems. These are review limitations, not established errors.

A native read-only auxiliary inspected pp. 13–14 and 18–20 and independently checked the comparison proof. It performed no image viewing, compilation or independent acceptance. The primary made the findings, wrote and compiled the report and performed the page checks. Runtime self-description is GPT-6 Astra Pro; backend identity was not independently verified. Controller UI observations are attributed separately.

The original manifest’s bounded supplement/code searches and an additional exact-title correction search identified no separate associated deposit or correction in the returned material; nonexistence is not proved. No author code was executed. The inaccessible publisher PDF is not claimed to contain these v2 issues.
Disposition. Correct the two substantive local items and the notation; retain the positive verification and explicit limits above. Scientific decision: pending. Human reviews: none.

report: Author: Initial scientific review: M25-0277
Date: 27 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific report on
Local limit theorem for directed polymers beyond the \(L^2\)-phase

Source and version. Stefan Junk, Local limit theorem for directed polymers beyond the \(L^2\)-phase, arXiv:2307.05097v3, 28 pages; DOI mapping `10.4171/jems/1650`. The acquired PDF watermark and arXiv history date this revision to 2 July 2025, whereas its title-page date is 3 July 2025. The arXiv comment says Accepted version; this does not establish equality with the publisher PDF. The publisher records submission on 1 August 2023, acceptance on 23 March 2025 and online publication on 20 May 2025. This report addresses the acquired v3, not an uninspected publisher version.

Assessment: Major in the inspected core proof, with local Minor corrections. The averaging estimate used to derive the local limit theorem needs a substantive correction to its admissible domain and moment exponent. The literal printed domain and its natural intended correction are distinguished below: no spread-out counterexample is falsely claimed to satisfy a singleton domain. Several auxiliary statements are also false as written, with exact admissible tests given here. No counterexample to the qualitative local limit conclusion itself is established. The full text was read, but this is not a certification of every external input. Scientific decision remains pending; human reviews are empty.
# F1: The core averaging estimate and its use (Major)
## Literal domain and actual failed application

Equation (10), p. 5, prints \[\nu\big((a,b)+[M\sqrt n,M\sqrt n]^{2d}\big)=1.\] Both interval endpoints are positive and identical in the actual page image. The displayed set is a singleton. Thus every member of the printed \(\mathcal E_n(\alpha,M)\) is a point mass, if the singleton lies in the lattice; otherwise that choice gives no member. This cannot supply the spread-out endpoint estimate described immediately below (13).

The actual use is on p. 20, in the proof of Corollary 1.6: the law \(\nu_{\omega,r}\) is the distribution of \((X_r,X_{n-r})\) under the bridge weighted only in the initial and terminal strips. For \(x=y=0\), \(r\geq1\), and sufficiently large even \(n\geq r^{4(1+\varepsilon)}\), at least two such pairs are reachable. All finite real environments give every admissible path strictly positive weight. Consequently \(\nu_{\omega,r}\) has at least two atoms and is not a member of the literal \(\mathcal E_{n-2r}(\alpha,M)\) for any centers and any \(M\). This is a direct failure of the hypothesis required in the displayed application of Theorem 1.1(ii). Small positive Gaussian disorder as specified below satisfies all disorder and moment assumptions of Corollary 1.6. The counterexample here is to that claimed applicability, not to (13) on its printed singleton domain.

## Independent test of the intended spread-out statement
Suppose only the evident missing minus sign in (10) is supplied. Then the full-\(p^*\) rate in (12)–(13) is false for the following explicit class of models.

Choose \(p=9/5\). For every \(P\geq10\), this lies in the first branch of (12), and \[\xi(P,p)=\frac{P-1}{P+1}\left(1-\frac{5}{3P}\right)
 \geq\frac{15}{22}.\] Let \(n=2k^2\), let \(B_k\) be the even-parity lattice sites in \([0,k]^3\), and let \(\mu_k\) be uniform on \(B_k\), with \(N_k=|B_k|\asymp k^3\). Set \(\nu_k=\mu_k\otimes\mu_k\). For \(k\) large, every pair is reachable in time \(n\), the center separation is zero, and the support lies in the corrected box with \(M=1\). Both marginal maxima are \(N_k^{-1}\).

Condition the averaged pinned partition function on the first environment layer. Independence and normalization of every other layer give exactly \[\mathbb E[W_{0,n}^{\beta,\nu_k}-1\mid\omega_{1,\cdot}]
   =S_k:=\sum_z a_z\eta_z,\qquad
 \eta_z=e^{\beta\omega_{1,z}-\beta^2/2}-1,\] where \(a_z\geq0\), \(\sum_z a_z=1\), and at most \(Ck^3\) coefficients are nonzero. The centered independent variables \(\eta_z\) have variance \(\sigma^2>0\) and finite fourth moment. Expansion of the fourth moment yields \[\mathbb ES_k^2=\sigma^2\sum_z a_z^2,\qquad
 \mathbb ES_k^4\leq C\left(\sum_z a_z^2\right)^2.\] Paley–Zygmund applied to \(S_k^2\), followed by conditional Jensen, therefore gives \[\|W_{0,n}^{\beta,\nu_k}-1\|_p
 \geq \|S_k\|_p
 \geq c\left(\sum_z a_z^2\right)^{1/2}
 \geq c k^{-3/2}.\] At the admissible value \(\varepsilon=1/22\), (13) would instead give an upper bound \(C k^{-3(\xi-\varepsilon)}\leq Ck^{-21/11}\). Since \(21/11>3/2\), these estimates contradict each other for large \(k\). This proves that fixing the domain typo alone does not restore the intended quantitative estimate. It is explicitly not a counterexample satisfying the uncorrected singleton definition.
## Impact, counterevidence and bounded repair

The damage concerns a central quantitative estimate and its actual invocation in the local limit proof. That is the basis of the Major grade; neither global falsity nor irreparability is asserted. Counterevidence is the correctly restricted exponent range in Lemmas 2.2, 3.1, 3.2 and Theorem 1.1(i). The title’s beyond-\(L^2\) regime has \(p^*\leq2\); the counterexample tests the larger range that the theorem also states.

A bounded repair is to use the two-sided box and, for a requested \(p\), select \[p<q<p^*\wedge2.\] Repeating the optimization on pp. 18–19 with \(q\) in every auxiliary moment bound yields a positive norm exponent \[\xi_q=\min\left\{\frac{q-1}{q+1},\frac{q-p}{q}\right\}
          \left(1-\frac{1+2/d}{q}\right).\] This formula includes the meeting point of the two branches. Indeed the competing powers of the marginal size \(u\) in the \(p\)th moment are \(ap/2\), \(\frac p2(q-1)(1-(1+2/d)/q-a/2)\) and \((q-p)(1-(1+2/d)/q-a/2)\). Equating the increasing power with the smaller decreasing one and then taking the \(p\)th root gives the displayed formula. Using \(q<p^*\wedge2\) respects every cited moment range. # F2: The bridge comparison needs its actual hypotheses (Minor)
Locations. Lemma 2.3, p. 12, defines \(f,g\) as real-valued measurable functions and uses \(|x-y-nm(\lambda)|\leq M\sqrt n\); its proof is on p. 13.
## A signed-function counterexample with positive denominator
## The printed drift sign fails even for positive functions

Take \(\lambda=(\log2,0,0)\), so \(m(\lambda)=(3/13,0,0)\). For an integer \(\ell\geq1\), let \(n=26\ell\), \(x=x'=0\) and \(y=y'=-6\ell e_1\). These endpoints are reachable and satisfy the printed drift condition with equality zero. Put \(s=n/2\), \(t=n\), \(g=1\) and \(f=4^{-X_s^{(1)}}\) on the first walk. Every function is positive and finite. Under \(P^\lambda\) the one-step probabilities in the first coordinate are \(4/13,1/13\), with the other four directions having probability \(2/13\) each. Hence \(E^\lambda4^{-X_s^{(1)}}=1\). Conditioned on \(X_n=y\), increments are exchangeable, so \(E[X_s^{(1)}\mid X_n=y]=-3\ell\). Jensen’s inequality gives a bridge numerator at least \(4^{3\ell}=64^\ell\). No uniform constant in the stated lemma can bound this ratio.

The repair is to require nonnegative functions, with positive finite denominators, and the drift condition \(|y-x-nm(\lambda)|\leq M\sqrt n\) (and likewise for the second walk). With that condition the bridge-kernel ratio in the source proof has a denominator of order \(n^{-d/2}\) and a numerator at most \(C(t-s)^{-d/2}\). The resulting positive-kernel comparison proves the corrected part (i). For part (ii), actual possible positions satisfy \(|z_1-x|\leq s\) and \(|z_2-y|\leq n-t\). Using these bounds, rather than the smaller powers printed on p. 13, gives the required errors \(O(n^{-1/4-3\varepsilon})+O(n^{-2\varepsilon})\) in the Gaussian ratio, conditional on the correctly normalized moderate-deviation local limit input.

The actual Boltzmann functions on pp. 18 and 20 are nonnegative, and p. 16 already chooses \(m(\lambda)=(b-a)/n\), with the corrected direction. This is decisive counterevidence to treating the two examples as a disproof of the intended core polymer comparison. The local lemma’s excessive hypotheses are false; its corrected version supplies the needed use. The grade is Minor on that actual impact.
# F3: The strong-disorder liminf assertion is false (Minor)
Location. Theorem B(ii), p. 3, claims that under strong disorder the quantity \[\liminf_n\max_x\mu^\beta_{\omega,n}(X_{n+1}=x)\] is almost surely bounded below by a strictly positive constant.

Fix \(\epsilon>0\). Choose an integer \(L\) with \(\|P_L\|_\infty<\epsilon/2\) and let \(\delta=(\epsilon/2)e^{-\beta L}\). At an arbitrary block-start time \(m\), let \(\rho\) be the polymer endpoint distribution. There are at most \(1/\delta\) sites with \(\rho(x)>\delta\). Require every future environment value in the \(L\)-step reachable tubes from these heavy sites to equal zero. The number of sites in this event is bounded by a constant depending only on \(L,\delta\), not on \(m\) or \(\rho\). Conditioned on the past its probability is therefore at least a fixed \(q_\epsilon>0\).

On this event, work with the unnormalized weights \(e^{\beta H}\); the common \(\lambda(\beta)\) normalization cancels. The total future normalization is at least one because all weights are at least one. Heavy starting sites contribute at most \(\|P_L\|_\infty\) to the mass at any final site. The remaining sites contribute at most \(e^{\beta L}\|\rho_{\rm light}*P_L\|_\infty\leq e^{\beta L}\delta\). Thus the maximum endpoint probability at time \(m+L\) is at most \(\epsilon\). Its subsequent unweighted step also has maximum at most \(\epsilon\).

For disjoint blocks, iterated conditional probabilities bound the chance of avoiding this event for \(N\) consecutive blocks by \((1-q_\epsilon)^N\). It therefore occurs infinitely often almost surely. Taking the intersection over \(\epsilon=1/j\) proves \[\liminf_{n\to\infty}\max_x\mu^\beta_{\omega,n}(X_{n+1}=x)=0
 \quad\hbox{almost surely}.\] This contradicts precisely the printed assertion.

The core weak-disorder proof uses Theorem B(i), not this strong-disorder liminf. The actual damage is to the stated background localization result, and the grade is Minor. Replacing liminf by the appropriate limsup localization statement requires the correct cited theorem and hypotheses; the argument above proves falsity of liminf, not a new universal localization theorem.
# F4: Strict moment monotonicity omits the constant-environment case (Minor)

Locations. Assumption (2), p. 2; Theorem 1.2(ii), p. 6; its proof, pp. 19–20. The stated iid and exponential-moment assumptions allow \(\omega_{t,x}=0\) deterministically. Then \(\lambda(\beta)=0\), \(W_n^\beta=1\) and \(p^*(\beta)=+\infty\) for every \(\beta\geq0\). Taking \(\beta=1\) and \(\beta'=1/2\) satisfies the finite-support hypothesis and \(p^*(\beta)>1\), but the claimed strict inequality would be \(+\infty>+\infty\). The related assertion \(\beta_{\rm cr}=0\) in dimensions one and two also excludes this permitted case.

Nondegeneracy would exclude this counterexample. For completeness, finite \(p^*(\beta)\) for a nonconstant finite-support law and \(\beta>0\) can be checked directly. Let \(b\) be its largest value, of probability \(q_b\in(0,1)\). Then \(c=\beta b-\lambda(\beta)>0\). Choose a finite box whose killed-walk spectral radius \(\rho_B\) satisfies \(e^c\rho_B>1\). On the event that every environment variable in this box through time \(n\) equals \(b\), whose probability is \(q_b^{|B|n}\), the partition function is at least \(c_0(e^c\rho_B)^n\). For sufficiently large moment order its expectation therefore grows exponentially. This proves the finiteness needed in the hypercontractive argument.

There is also a repairable parameter-selection error on p. 20: \(\epsilon_0=(1+P)/2\) need not lie in \((0,P-1)\), and the stated monotonicity of \(p(P-\epsilon)/(P-\epsilon)\) has the opposite direction to that supplied by Theorem D. Given finite \(P=p^*(\beta)>1\), choose \(1<q_0<P\) and write \(r_0=p(q_0)/q_0>1\). For \(q<P\) sufficiently close to \(P\), with \(q>q_0\) and \(q>P/r_0\), Theorem D yields \(p(q)\geq q r_0>P\). Together with (49), this verifies the required strict moment improvement. The external hypercontractivity theorem itself is retained as an input. The verified repair concerns this boundary and parameter choice; no failure for nonconstant finite-support disorder has been established.
# F5: The introductory exact density omits the terminal weight (Minor)
# F6: Editorial clarification of the upper-bounded condition

Location. The display labelled (u-bd.), p. 3, says \(\exists K>0:\mathbb P(\omega_{0,0}\leq K)=0\). An upper-bounded Bernoulli law on \(\{0,1\}\) fails this condition for every \(K>0\). Conversely \(\omega=2+|Z|\), with \(Z\) standard Gaussian, satisfies the printed condition with \(K=1\) while having no finite upper bound. Both laws satisfy (2). Thus the display is not equivalent to the property it names. It should read \(\mathbb P(\omega_{0,0}>K)=0\), or equivalently \(\mathbb P(\omega_{0,0}\leq K)=1\). The correct boundedness condition used in Theorem E on p. 24 and the later general-environment inputs are counterevidence to a resulting failure of the main theorem. The surrounding prose and that later formulation identify the intended assumption. No invalid derivation is attributed to this display alone. It is retained as an editorial clarification, not counted as a substantive Minor finding.
# F7: The lattice and Gaussian formulas in Appendix A3 (Minor)
Locations. The assertion \(X_{2i}/2\in\mathbb Z^d\) on pp. 13 and 25; equation (63), p. 25; the Gaussian integral on p. 26.

A correct lattice is \(H=\{z\in\mathbb Z^d:\sum_jz_j\text{ is even}\}\) for the two-step walk. Use a lattice basis of \(H\), for example \(e_i-e_d\) for \(i<d\) and \(2e_d\), to identify it with \(\mathbb Z^d\); the two-step walk has a self-loop and is aperiodic on this lattice. Replace the lower side of (63) by \(r^{-1}|t|^2\) and use the inverse covariance in the transform. On the compact tilt cube the corrected covariance eigenvalues remain uniformly bounded above and away from zero. These corrections preserve the coarse upper and central lower orders \(n^{-d/2}\) of Theorem F. The counterevidence is that those orders do not depend on the erroneous linear norm or the interchange of covariance and inverse covariance. The local formulas are false, but no false conclusion of Theorem F is established; grade Minor. This report checks these repairs and the kernel normalization, not every remainder estimate in the cited random-walk monograph.
# Positive checks, dependencies and limits

The main summability threshold was independently recomputed: Young’s inequality and the heat-kernel bound give \[\sum_z(\mu*P_t^\lambda(z))^p
 \leq\min\{\|\mu\|_p^p,Ct^{-d(p-1)/2}\}.\] Splitting at \(T\) of order \((\max_x\mu(x))^{-2/d}\) gives \((\max_x\mu(x))^{p-1-2/d}\); the tail is summable precisely when \(p>1+2/d\). The exponent appearing as \(p-(1-2/d)\) in (27), p. 12, must be replaced by this \(p-(1+2/d)\) in that derivation. Both are positive in the working range, so the smallness/continuity argument still works with the derived exponent.

The separated-collision argument was traced on pp. 14–18: independence occurs across disjoint time slabs, the \(p/2<1\) power permits subadditivity, the small return mass gives geometric decay in the number of separated collisions, and choosing sufficiently large fixed \(K,L\) absorbs the polynomial cost of pinning. At least one macroscopic interval avoids collisions when these counts are controlled; one can take \(L\geq2\) in the covering step. The bridge comparison is used only with positive Boltzmann factors. This tracing supports the mechanism after the explicit local corrections above, rather than validating every printed equality.

For Corollary 1.6, the inner environment is independent of the random endpoint law determined by the outer strips. A positive averaging exponent, and weak-disorder endpoint delocalization from Theorem B(i), then give convergence of the normalized ratio. The unnormalized version uses a slightly higher moment below \(p^*\wedge2\) and Hölder; the two outer strips are independent. For \(n\geq r^{4(1+\varepsilon)}\), choose a smaller bridge parameter \(\varepsilon'<\varepsilon/(4(1+\varepsilon))\) to ensure \(r\leq n^{1/4-\varepsilon'}\). Reachability and parity must remain in each supremum. This argument does not include \(p^*=1+2/d\), which the source itself excludes.

For the overlap estimates on pp. 22–23, the finite reachable cone has only \(O(n^d)\) sites. The exponential far-endpoint bound is therefore summable. The near-endpoint bound reduces to \(\sum_n n^{-d(p-1)/2}<\infty\). One must use \(\sup_n(W_n^\beta)^{-p}<\infty\) in weak disorder rather than pull a varying \(W_n^{-p}\) outside a sum. Likewise finite-cone restrictions must be retained when replacing a zero endpoint weight by an exponential upper bound. These bounded corrections establish the claimed summability mechanism conditional on the corrected pinned moment bound. The rate comparison in (58) correctly uses \(p^*\wedge2\).

Given finite \(P=p^*(\beta)>1\), choose \(1<q_0<P\) and write \(r_0=p(q_0)/q_0>1\). For \(q<P\) sufficiently close to \(P\), with \(q>q_0\) and \(q>P/r_0\), Theorem D yields \(p(q)\geq q r_0>P\). Together with (49), this verifies the required strict moment improvement. The external hypercontractivity theorem itself is retained as an input. The verified repair concerns this boundary and parameter choice; no failure for nonconstant finite-support disorder has been established.
result: Impact: Excluded trivial disorder case is unstated; parameter proof needs correction. No false nondegenerate finite-support conclusion established.
