Title: Technical verification of
Maximal commutative unipotent subgroups and a characterization of affine spherical varieties
# Source, scope, and assessment

The reviewed work is by Andriy Regeta and Immanuel van Santen. The actual source is arXiv:2112.04784v2, 3 August 2023, 30 PDF pages. The frozen DOI is `10.4171/jems/1651`. The EMS landing page records submission on 7 September 2023, acceptance on 17 April 2024, and publication on 8 May 2025. These dates do not turn the earlier author manuscript into the publisher’s version. The arXiv record describes a substantially revised version; it does not label this file an accepted manuscript. Publisher-text equivalence has not been established. All page references below refer to this exact author PDF.

Assessment: Major. Theorem A, the principal classification theorem, is false in its stated scope: the trivial unipotent subgroup of a torus satisfies one of its equivalent conditions and fails another. This is a defect of a central conclusion, even though a nontriviality restriction repairs the scope. Two further Major findings concern the stabilizer argument needed by the centralizer proof and the regular-root construction used to synchronize field automorphisms. Four Minor findings have the narrower effects established below. A previously reported eighth item is withdrawn because it misread the source. No counterexample to the spherical reconstruction theorems or Theorem E is claimed.

The entire 30-page text was read. Source images on pages 1–28 were actually inspected. The audit concentrated on definitions, closedness, trivial groups, stabilizer families, root dimensions and characters, field twists, the passage to weight monoids, and the dimension restriction in the torus theorem. Reading the whole text is not a claim to have reconstructed every cited theorem.
# F1. Major: the central classification includes a false trivial-group case

Location. Theorem A, p. 2; Proposition 4.1, p. 8 and Claim 1 on p. 9; Corollary 5.2, pp. 12–13. Neither the general conventions nor these statements require the relevant unipotent group to be nontrivial.

Work over \(k=\mathbb C\) and take \(X=\mathbb G_m\). Every algebraic \(\mathbb G_a\)-action is trivial. Indeed its pullback sends the unit \(z\) of \(k[z,z^{-1}]\) to a unit of \(k[s,z,z^{-1}]\). Such a unit is \(c z^m\), independent of \(s\). Evaluation at \(s=0\), where the action is the identity, forces \(c=1,m=1\). Thus the action fixes the coordinate ring.

Consequently \(G=\{1\}\) is a closed commutative unipotent subgroup and is maximal among commutative unipotent subgroups: there are no other unipotent elements under the definition on p. 2. Condition (b) of Theorem A holds. Condition (a) fails, since \(G\) is properly contained in the commutative group of scalings \(\mathbb G_m\subset\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb G_m)\). This counterexample satisfies all the global hypotheses, even the stronger normality and uncountability conditions used later. It does not depend on a convention for replicas of the identity.

The same omission also affects Proposition 4.1. For \(X=\mathbb A^1,U=\{1\}\), the natural replica construction gives \(R_X(U)=\{1\}\), whereas the centralizer of the identity replicas is all of \(\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb A^1)\). The exact failure in the proof is visible in Claim 1: it chooses \(u\in U\setminus\{1\}\), a nonzero locally nilpotent derivation \(D_u\), and \(h\) with \(D_u h\ne0\).

Counterevidence and repair boundary. For \(U\ne\{1\}\), the cancellation in Claim 1 is valid in the integral coordinate ring, and the rest of the translation argument can be recovered after F2. State Proposition 4.1 for nontrivial \(U\), and Theorem A/Corollary 5.2 for nontrivial \(G\), with nontrivial \(U\) in condition (c). Treat the identity separately: it is maximal unipotent exactly when no nonidentity unipotents exist, and maximal commutative exactly when the whole automorphism group is trivial. The latter follows because the closure of any cyclic subgroup is commutative.

This restriction does not by itself refute Corollary 5.3. For a nonidentity unipotent \(u\), its cyclic closure is \(\mathbb G_a\); its replica group is uncountable. Its image has at most countably many connected components, so its identity component is nontrivial. The corrected nontrivial classification is therefore available in that proof; the identity element is handled separately. The Major rating concerns the actual false universal classification, not a claim that every application fails.
# F2. Major: a maximal-dimensional stabilizer component need not dominate
Location. Proposition 4.1, p. 9, the paragraph beginning with the stabilizer family \(E\), after the choice of \(U'\).

Consider the faithful action of \(U=\mathbb G_a^4\) on \(X=\mathbb A_x^2\times\mathbb A_t^1\): \[(a,b)\cdot(x,t)=(x+t a+b,t),\qquad a,b,x\in k^2.\] The quotient is \(t\), every fibre is a transitive \(U\)-orbit, and the stated product trivialization is already global over the smooth affine base \(B=\mathbb A^1\). At \(b_0=1,x_0=(0,1)\), the subgroup \(U'=\{(a,0)\}\) complements the stabilizer \(\{(a,-a)\}\). Nevertheless \[E=\{(a,t):t a=0\}
   =(\{0\}\times\mathbb A^1)\ \cup\ (\mathbb A^2\times\{0\}).\] Every fibre is an irreducible linear subspace, and \(E_1=\{0\}\). The component of maximal dimension is the vertical component of dimension two. It does not dominate \(B\), contrary to the assertion used in the proof.

Repair and impact. Apply rank openness instead. The infinitesimal action of \(\operatorname{Lie}U'\) along the zero section is injective at \(b_0\), hence on an open neighborhood. In characteristic zero, a zero-dimensional subgroup of a vector group is trivial. On each remaining fibre, commutativity makes stabilizers constant along the transitive \(U\)-orbit; the dimension calculation \(U'+U_x=U\) gives transitivity of \(U'\). The resulting map \(U'\times B\to\pi^{-1}(B)\) is bijective, birational and quasi-finite between smooth varieties, hence an isomorphism by Zariski’s main theorem. The manuscript’s translation argument then continues. The example disproves the intermediate dominance assertion, not the nontrivial centralizer result. The invalid step supplies the free translation model needed to finish Proposition 4.1, on which Theorem A explicitly depends (p. 2). This is a failure in the core derivation, assessed Major even though the rank-openness replacement recovers that step.
# Further findings
## F3. Minor: ordinary and generalized root subgroups

On p. 6 an ordinary root subgroup has dimension one. Proposition 8.1 on p. 18 permits a generalized root subgroup \(V\) of arbitrary positive dimension, but calls its image an ordinary root subgroup of the same dimension. Take \(X=Y=\mathbb A^2\), \(\theta=\mathrm{id}\), \(H=\mathbb G_m\) acting by scalar dilation, and \(V=\mathbb G_a^2\) acting by translations. All hypotheses, including the algebraicity of \(\theta(H)\) and the nontrivial weight, hold. The image has dimension two.

The conclusion must say generalized. The proof’s last paragraph on p. 19 establishes the algebraic group and dimension; it supports this reading. To make the scalar-character conclusion explicit, take two coordinate lines in \(V\) and their diagonal. The one-dimensional argument applies to all three. The image of the diagonal is an algebraic \(\mathbb G_a\) subgroup in the product of the two image lines, and both projections are bijective homomorphisms. In characteristic zero they are algebraic isomorphisms. Equivariance forces the two conjugation characters to coincide. Applying this to every pair gives a common nontrivial scalar character on the whole image. This supplies the generalized statement needed later; the example does not disprove it.
## F4. Major: regular replicas require a nonnegative choice

In Proposition 6.1(2), pp. 14–15, an integer vector outside finitely many forbidden affine sublattices is chosen and \(f=\prod_j f_j^{a_j}\) is declared regular. Let \(X=\mathbb A^2_{x,y}\), \(H={\mathbb G_a}_x\times{\mathbb G_m}_y\), with translation in \(x\) and dilation in \(y\). This is a connected solvable algebraic group with nontrivial unipotent radical, satisfying the proposition with finite central factor \(\{1\}\). Take \(U={\mathbb G_a}_x,T_1={\mathbb G_m}_y,f_1=y\). The forbidden exponent is zero; \(a_1=-1\) satisfies the printed selection, but \(y^{-1}\notin k[X]\). Its rational replica \((x,y)\mapsto(x+s/y,y)\) does not extend to an automorphism for \(s\ne0\).

Also, for higher-dimensional \(T_i\), the forbidden sublattice need only have rank at most \(m-1\). On \(\mathbb A^3_{x,y,z}\) with \(H={\mathbb G_a}_x\times{\mathbb G_m}_y^{}\times{\mathbb G_m}_z^{}\), take \(T_1=T_2=\mathbb G_m^2\), \(f_1=y,f_2=z\), and \(U={\mathbb G_a}_x\). Both forbidden sets are \(\{(0,0)\}\), of rank zero, whereas \(m-1=1\). The statement does not require the \(T_i\) to be distinct.

Choose instead a vector in \(\mathbb N^m\) outside the forbidden sets. Each proper affine sublattice is contained in the zero set of a nonzero affine linear polynomial over \(\mathbb Q\). Their product cannot vanish on all of \(\mathbb N^m\), by induction on the number of variables. This simultaneously proves existence, regularity and the required nonzero weights. The proposition’s conclusion survives; the defect is in the stated selection argument. Its use is substantive: on p. 23, Proposition 6.1(2) provides a single root subgroup noncommuting with all the selected tori. Lemma 7.5 then synchronizes the field automorphisms in Theorem 8.5(a), which feeds Theorem 9.1 and Theorem C. Without a regular replica the printed construction does not supply that subgroup. This core construction error is Major; the separate overstatement of the lattice rank is Minor.
## F5. Minor: exceptional primes for a disconnected diagonalizable group

The proof of Lemma 8.2, p. 20, identifies the \(p\)-torsion of \(D\) with \((\mathbb Z/p)^{\dim D}\) for every prime \(p\). For \(X=Y=\mathbb A^2,\theta=\mathrm{id}\), the closed diagonalizable subgroup \[D=\{(x,y)\mapsto(t x,\epsilon y):t\in k^*,\ \epsilon\in\{1,-1\}\}
       \simeq\mathbb G_m\times\mu_2\] satisfies every hypothesis. Its dimension is one and its 2-torsion has rank two. Choose a prime not dividing the order of \(D/D^\circ\). The needed torsion-rank bound then holds and still yields \(\dim\theta(D)^\circ\le\dim D\). The conclusion of Lemma 8.2 is not refuted.
## F6. Minor: two uses of Theorem 8.5 exceed its hypotheses

In the toric case of Proposition 8.6, p. 25, Theorem 8.5(c) is applied to \(H=DU\). That theorem, p. 22, requires \(H\subseteq G\); here \(G\) is a torus and \(U\simeq\mathbb G_a\) is nontrivial. Already \(X=\mathbb A^1,G=\mathbb G_m,U=\mathbb G_a,D=\{1\}\) realizes all the construction’s hypotheses with \(H\not\subset G\).

The same paragraph has already established that \(H\) and \(\theta(H)\) are connected algebraic groups. Proposition 8.1(a), corrected as in F3, therefore applies to \(\theta\) and \(\theta^{-1}\), giving the required dimension-preserving correspondence of generalized roots with nontrivial weight. Roots of trivial weight lie in the respective self-centralizing groups \(D\times\mathbb G_a\); projection to the torus is trivial, so their dimension is at most one. Proposition 8.7 now gives the desired open orbit.

In the first case of Theorem E, p. 27, Theorem 8.5(c),(d) is invoked with source \(X=T\) a torus, which 8.5 explicitly excludes. Here \(Y\) is already known to be toric. Instead apply Corollary 5.3 to \(\theta^{-1}\): because \(T\) has no nonidentity unipotents, neither can \(Y\). Lemma 3.4 then forces \(Y\) to be a torus. Both conclusions are retained by these explicit replacements; merely changing a citation without the generalized-root argument would be insufficient.
## F7. Minor: the dimension statement omits the \(n=1\) boundary

Theorem 10.1, p. 27, states that a finite-index subgroup \(\Gamma\le\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb Z)\) embedding into \(\operatorname{Aut}(Z)\), for irreducible quasi-affine \(Z\), forces \(\dim Z\ge n\). Set \(n=1,\Gamma=\{1\}=\mathrm{SL}_1(\mathbb Z)\), and \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}k\). The index is one, the embedding exists, and \(\dim Z=0<1\).

The actual finite-kernel application in Theorem E can only have \(n\ge3\). For \(n=1\) the intermediate integer dimension \(0<r<n\) is impossible. For \(n=2\), \(r=1\) and the target \(\mathrm{GL}_1(\mathbb Z)\) is finite, so the homomorphism from the infinite source cannot have finite kernel. Restricting the auxiliary statement to the used range removes this counterexample. The full external Cantat–Xie theorem, including any \(n=2\) treatment, was not independently reconstructed. No failure of the actual \(n\ge3\) application is asserted.
## Withdrawn item F8: the postcomposition map was not asserted closed

The earlier report attributed a closed-immersion assertion to \(\operatorname{End}(W)\to\operatorname{Mor}(W,X)\). The actual text on p. 11 calls this postcomposition map only a morphism. Its closed-immersion assertion concerns instead precomposition \(\operatorname{End}(X)\to\operatorname{Mor}(W,X)\). The proof then obtains a locally closed orbit image and uses that a locally closed subgroup of an algebraic group is closed. The family \(z\mapsto az\) tests the stronger statement that the source did not make. It therefore establishes no defect in Proposition 4.6(2), and F8 is withdrawn.
# Positive checks, dependencies, and limits

For the nontrivial case of Proposition 4.1, fixing all invariant functions forces an automorphism onto the fibres of the generic quotient. After the corrected free \(U'\)-bundle argument, commuting with fibre translations makes it translation by invariant rational coefficients, exactly the prescribed replica product. Such globally regular rational translations are unipotent: on a finite set of coordinate generators, their integer iterates are polynomial in the iterate parameter with rational coefficients. A Vandermonde inversion at distinct integers shows that every coefficient is actually regular. The same polynomial formulas therefore define an algebraic \(\mathbb G_a\)-action. This checks the unipotence assertion used in Remark 4.4.

The invariant-field argument of Lemma 5.1 terminates after at most \(\dim X\) strict transcendence-degree drops. The countable-index density step in Corollary 5.3 retains uncountability. The toric lattice calculations retain finite kernel components and use the primitiveness of a root to obtain a connected kernel in Lemma 3.5. The product generation of simple factors and the common nonfinite subgroup in Lemma 7.4 account for compatibility of the field automorphisms in Theorem 8.5; separate factors cannot silently receive unrelated twists.

Theorem 9.1 retains the twist \(X^\tau\). Identifying it equivariantly with \(X\) requires the stated \(\mathbb Q\)-defined variety, group and action. Normality is required for the weight-monoid conclusion, and smoothness for the quoted uniqueness result. In Theorem E the hypothesis \(\dim Y\le\dim X\), the finite-index elementary-matrix argument and uncountability all remain essential in the inspected proof.

The full Cantat–Regeta–Xie result, the generic-quotient theorem, Borel–Tits, the root-weight/weight-monoid reconstruction and Losev uniqueness, and the Cantat–Xie/Margulis inputs were not independently reproved. A bounded attempt to inspect the external Cantat–Xie PDF returned a publisher 403 and an author-site timeout; these are recorded as failures, not as reading. The projective examples were read but not independently classified in full. No associated separate supplement or computational repository was identified in the recorded searches; this does not establish nonexistence and is not a mathematical defect. No author code was executed.

Proposition6.1(2) is actually used on p23 for a single root subgroup noncommuting with Di,Tj, then Lemma7.5 synchronizes field automorphisms in Theorem8.5(a), Theorem9.1/TheoremC. problems.title: p-torsion rank of diagonalizable D equals dimD for every prime
problems.source_location: Lemma8.2 proof p20 final sentence
claim: p-torsion rank of diagonalizable D equals dimD for every prime
analysis:
The proof of Lemma 8.2, p. 20, identifies the \(p\)-torsion of \(D\) with \((\mathbb Z/p)^{\dim D}\) for every prime \(p\). For \(X=Y=\mathbb A^2,\theta=\mathrm{id}\), the closed diagonalizable subgroup \[D=\{(x,y)\mapsto(t x,\epsilon y):t\in k^*,\ \epsilon\in\{1,-1\}\}
       \simeq\mathbb G_m\times\mu_2\] satisfies every hypothesis. Its dimension is one and its 2-torsion has rank two. Choose a prime not dividing the order of \(D/D^\circ\). The needed torsion-rank bound then holds and still yields \(\dim\theta(D)^\circ\le\dim D\). The conclusion of Lemma 8.2 is not refuted.
result: Impact: Auxiliary torsion calculation false at exceptional primes; dimension inequality still follows.

problems.title: Theorem8.5 applies to H=DU and to a torus source
problems.source_location: Prop8.6 proof p25; Thm8.5 hypotheses p22; ThmE first case p27
claim: Theorem8.5 applies to H=DU and to a torus source
analysis: In the toric case of Proposition 8.6, p. 25, Theorem 8.5(c) is applied to \(H=DU\). That theorem, p. 22, requires \(H\subseteq G\); here \(G\) is a torus and \(U\simeq\mathbb G_a\) is nontrivial. Already \(X=\mathbb A^1,G=\mathbb G_m,U=\mathbb G_a,D=\{1\}\) realizes all the construction’s hypotheses with \(H\not\subset G\).

The same paragraph has already established that \(H\) and \(\theta(H)\) are connected algebraic groups. Proposition 8.1(a), corrected as in F3, therefore applies to \(\theta\) and \(\theta^{-1}\), giving the required dimension-preserving correspondence of generalized roots with nontrivial weight. Roots of trivial weight lie in the respective self-centralizing groups \(D\times\mathbb G_a\); projection to the torus is trivial, so their dimension is at most one. Proposition 8.7 now gives the desired open orbit.

In the first case of Theorem E, p. 27, Theorem 8.5(c),(d) is invoked with source \(X=T\) a torus, which 8.5 explicitly excludes. Here \(Y\) is already known to be toric. Instead apply Corollary 5.3 to \(\theta^{-1}\): because \(T\) has no nonidentity unipotents, neither can \(Y\). Lemma 3.4 then forces \(Y\) to be a torus. Both conclusions are retained by these explicit replacements; merely changing a citation without the generalized-root argument would be insufficient.
result: Impact: Two invalid dependency invocations, with complete local replacements; no counterexample to either conclusion.

problems.title: All n satisfy dimZ>=n for finite-index SLn(Z) embeddings
problems.source_location: Theorem10.1 p27; actual finite-kernel invocation same page
claim: All n satisfy dimZ>=n for finite-index SLn(Z) embeddings
analysis: Theorem 10.1, p. 27, states that a finite-index subgroup \(\Gamma\le\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb Z)\) embedding into \(\operatorname{Aut}(Z)\), for irreducible quasi-affine \(Z\), forces \(\dim Z\ge n\). Set \(n=1,\Gamma=\{1\}=\mathrm{SL}_1(\mathbb Z)\), and \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}k\). The index is one, the embedding exists, and \(\dim Z=0<1\).

The actual finite-kernel application in Theorem E can only have \(n\ge3\). For \(n=1\) the intermediate integer dimension \(0<r<n\) is impossible. For \(n=2\), \(r=1\) and the target \(\mathrm{GL}_1(\mathbb Z)\) is finite, so the homomorphism from the infinite source cannot have finite kernel. Restricting the auxiliary statement to the used range removes this counterexample. The full external Cantat–Xie theorem, including any \(n=2\) treatment, was not independently reconstructed. No failure of the actual \(n\ge3\) application is asserted.
result: Impact: Low-dimensional boundary false; actual TheoremE application n>=3 not refuted.

report: Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: M25-0279 / focused independent acceptance

Title: Technical verification of
Ergodic optimization theory for a class of typical maps
# Source and assessment

The source is by Wen Huang, Zeng Lian, Xiao Ma, Leiye Xu and Yiwei Zhang. The actual reviewed file is arXiv:1904.01915v3, 22 August 2019, 28 PDF pages. The frozen DOI is `10.4171/jems/1652`. The EMS article record gives submission on 9 September 2023, acceptance on 20 February 2025, and publication on 17 June 2025. The acquired author manuscript is not labelled accepted, and equivalence to the substantially later publisher text has not been established. Every source page cited below refers to this exact 2019 file.

Assessment: Major. Two core proof defects concern the radius estimate in the locking argument and the full-norm estimates and perturbation quantifier in the smooth approximation. These steps support the two parts of Theorem 2.1 through Propositions 3.2 and 3.9, respectively. A third group consists of local formulas in the higher-regularity proof. The admissible examples disprove the specified estimates, not the main generic-periodic optimization conclusions. The independently checked replacements below preserve the quantified conclusions of Propositions 3.2, 3.9 and 4.1. Their repairability does not lower the severity of the failed core derivations.

All 28 text pages were read. Source images on p. 1 and pp. 3–26 were actually viewed. The review followed the periodic-orbit approximation, calibrated weighted potential, escape-block argument, strict uniqueness, \(C^1\) approximation and higher-regularity locking. Deep external inputs remain identified dependencies rather than independently reconstructed results.
# F1. Major: the radius estimate and its stated sufficient bounds fail

Location. Lemma 3.8, p. 13, the displayed estimate below the bound for \(|a_O|\), its following sufficient conditions, and (3.10) on p. 14. The constants on p. 17 and the uniqueness completion on p. 18 were also checked.

Take \(X=\{0,1\}\), \(d(0,1)=1\), and \(T=\mathrm{id}\). ASP holds with \(\delta=1/2,C=L=1,\lambda=\log2\): every pair of \(\delta\)-close points is equal, and every allowed periodic pseudo-orbit is constant. MCGBP holds with \(K=1,v=0\), since \(u-\min_Xu\ge0\). Set \[\alpha=\varepsilon=1,\quad \psi=1,\quad O=\{0\},\quad
 u(0)=\frac3{50},\quad u(1)=0,\quad h=\frac1{10}.\] Then \(\bar u=u\), \(Z_{u,\psi}=\{1\}\), \(\|\bar u\|_1=3/25\), \(D(O)=1/2\), \(L_O=1/2\), and \(a_O=4/25\). The negative-region radius used in the paper is \[R=\frac{|a_O|\|\psi\|_0+\|h\|_0}{\varepsilon}=\frac{13}{50}.\] The printed intermediate requirements hold: \[L_O=\frac12>\frac{12}{25}
 =2(2\operatorname{Lip}_T)\|\bar u\|_1,\qquad
 \|h\|_0=\frac1{10}<\frac18.\] Nevertheless \(R=13/50>1/4=D(O)/(2\operatorname{Lip}_T)\). The displayed radius inequality itself gives the false comparison \(26/25\le22/25\).

This example tests the explicit intermediate conditions, not the final stronger choice on p. 17. A separate exact-rational check with \(u(0)=10^{-6},u(1)=0,h=-10^{-4}\), on the same system, satisfies even those final printed parameter restrictions while still falsifying the intermediate displayed inequality: \[\frac{R}{D/2}=\frac{199}{250000}>
 \frac{51}{125000}=\text{its printed right-hand side}.\] Here the radius conclusion itself does hold. In both examples the resulting \(G\) is zero on \(O\) and strictly positive at the other point. Thus neither example is misrepresented as a counterexample to Proposition 3.2. The initial review’s rational-arithmetic script and its actual successful execution are retained. The radius condition controls the escape construction in Lemma 3.8 and Proposition 3.2, the second main step in the proof of Theorem 2.1(I) on p. 7. Its false quantitative derivation therefore concerns a core proof step. The smaller example does not refute the final radius conclusion, and neither example is a counterexample to the theorem.
## A complete replacement retaining the original quantifiers

Write \(N=\#O\), \(D=D(O)\), \(r=d_{\alpha,Z_{u,\psi}}(O)\), and \[m=\psi_{\min},\quad M=\|\psi\|_0,\quad P=\|\psi_K\|_\alpha,\quad
 B=\|\bar u\|_\alpha,\quad b=\|\bar u\|_0.\] For the prescribed coefficient \(\varepsilon>0\), set \(t=\varepsilon/2\) and \(H=10\varepsilon\). Define \[A=\frac{4C^\alpha}{t(1-e^{-\lambda\alpha})}
       \left(B+H+\frac{b+\delta^\alpha}{m}P\right),
 \qquad L_1=\frac{t}{(2\operatorname{Lip}_T)^\alpha},\] \[L_2=(A+2)\frac{MB}{m},\qquad
 L_3=(A+2)\left(1+\frac{M}{m}\right),\qquad
 \widehat L=1+\frac{3L_2}{L_1},\qquad
 \widehat\delta=\min\left\{1,\frac{L_1}{3L_3}\right\}.\] These constants are independent of \(O\). Assume \(D^\alpha>\widehat Lr\), \(\|h\|_\alpha\le10\varepsilon\), and \(\|h\|_0<D^\alpha\widehat\delta/N\), the correct elementary bound is \[Q:=|a_O|M+\|h\|_0
 \le \frac{MB}{mN}r+\left(1+\frac{M}{m}\right)\|h\|_0.\] In particular \(Q<L_1D^\alpha/3\), so the radius for coefficient \(t\) is less than \(D/(2\operatorname{Lip}_T)\).

For \(G_t=\bar u+t\,d^\alpha(\cdot,O)+h-a_O\psi_K\), the same escape construction as on pp. 14–17 gives a comparison-distance sum at most \(4C^\alpha Q/[t(1-e^{-\lambda\alpha})]\). The periodic remainder is at least \(-NQ\), and the escape contribution is at least \(L_1D^\alpha-Q\). Hence the block sum is at least \[L_1D^\alpha-(A+N+1)Q
 \ge L_1D^\alpha-L_2r-L_3N\|h\|_0
 >\frac13L_1D^\alpha.\] Here \(A+N+1\le N(A+2)\) uses \(N\ge1\). Orbits staying close to a fixed periodic phase forever are generic for \(\mu_O\), by ASP. For other generic points, concatenation of positive blocks gives \(\int G_t\,d\mu\ge0\).

Positive finite blocks alone do not establish a strictly positive asymptotic mean. The reserved coefficient does: \(a_O\) is independent of \(t\), since the distance term vanishes on \(O\), so \[G_\varepsilon=G_t+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}d^\alpha(\cdot,O).\] Every invariant probability other than \(\mu_O\) has positive integral of \(d^\alpha(\cdot,O)\). This proves strict uniqueness at the originally prescribed \(\varepsilon\), retaining the entire \(10\varepsilon\) perturbation budget. It also makes precise the informal modification on p. 18, where \(d\), rather than \(d^\alpha\), is printed in the added term. The source’s calibration and escape mechanism are valid counterevidence against an interpretation that the main locking conclusion has been disproved.
# F2. Major: the smoothing proof mixes a norm and a seminorm

Location. Norm definition on p. 5; Proposition 3.9 and Theorem 3.10, pp. 18–19; (3.19)–(3.20) and the subsequent perturbation condition, p. 20. The defined norm is \(\|v\|_1=\|v\|_0+[v]_1\). A bound on the gradient controls the second term, not both terms.

For a complete admissible model take the Riemannian circle \(M=\mathbb R/(2\mathbb Z)\), \(f=\mathrm{id}\), \(X=\{0\}\), \(u=0,\psi=1,O=\{0\}\). The subsystem has ASP and MCGBP automatically, and the multiplicative condition (3.18) holds. Put \(q=\varepsilon d(\cdot,O)\). Then \(\|q\|_0=[q]_1=\varepsilon\), so \(\|q\|_1=2\varepsilon\). If \(\|w-q\|_0<\eta\), evaluation at \(0\) and its antipode gives \[\|w\|_0\ge\varepsilon-\eta,\qquad [w]_1\ge\varepsilon-2\eta.\] Consequently \(\|w\|_1+\|q\|_1\ge4\varepsilon-3\eta>2\varepsilon+\eta\) when \(0<\eta\le\varepsilon/8\), contradicting the middle estimate in (3.20), with \(h=0\). Positive smooth periodic mollification supplies such a \(w\) with \(\|w\|_1\le\|q\|_1\), so the example respects the approximation theorem.

Moreover, the proposition allows \(\|Dh\|_0<5\varepsilon\), whereas the end of its proof imposes \(\|h\|_1<5\varepsilon\). These are different even at an arbitrarily small allowed uniform radius. On the same circle take \[h(x)=a\sin(\pi kx),\qquad
 a=\frac{5\varepsilon}{\pi k+1/2}.\] Then \(\|Dh\|_0=5\varepsilon-a/2<5\varepsilon\), but \(\|h\|_1=5\varepsilon+a/2>5\varepsilon\). Its uniform norm meets any positive prescribed radius when \(k\) is large. Thus the proof does not cover every perturbation allowed by Proposition 3.9. The source explicitly uses that proposition together with Proposition 3.1 to obtain Theorem 2.1(II) (p. 18). The false norm estimates and altered quantifier affect that core passage from Lipschitz locking to the claimed \(C^1\) neighborhood; they are assessed Major. This does not assert that the repaired \(C^1\) genericity conclusion is false.

Counterevidence. Theorem 3.10 explicitly defines its Lip-dense property as uniform approximation with an almost preserved norm bound. It does not assert convergence of the difference in Lipschitz norm. A cusp example against that stronger density would not refute the stated result.

Repair. The two actual approximation inequalities imply \[[w]_1=\|w\|_1-\|w\|_0
 <\|q\|_1+\eta-(\|q\|_0-\eta)
 =[q]_1+2\eta.\] Let \(c_O=D(O)/N\le\delta\) and \(a_0=c_O\widehat\delta\), using corrected Proposition 3.2 constants from F1 with \(\alpha=1\). Choose \[\eta=\min\{\varepsilon/4,a_0/4\},\qquad
 \widehat\delta_1=\min\{\widehat\delta/2,\varepsilon\sigma_*/(\delta+1)\},
 \qquad \widehat\delta'_1=\operatorname{diam}(M)+1.\] Here \(\sigma_*=1\) on a connected manifold. For a disconnected manifold with a fixed compatible distance agreeing with geodesic distance on components, put \(\sigma_*=\min\{1,\sigma\}\), where \(\sigma>0\) is the minimum intercomponent distance. Compactness gives finitely many components. Then \([w]_1<1.5\varepsilon<2\varepsilon\) and \(\|w\|_0<(\operatorname{diam}M+1)\varepsilon\). For every perturbation allowed by Proposition 3.9 with the new \(\widehat\delta_1\), set \(g=w-q+h\). On each component \([h]_1\le\|Dh\|_0<5\varepsilon\). For different components the quotient is at most \(2\|h\|_0/\sigma<2\varepsilon\), by the strengthened uniform radius. Consequently the global seminorm is less than \(5\varepsilon\), and \[[g]_1<7.5\varepsilon,\qquad
 \|g\|_0<1.25\varepsilon,\qquad
 \|g\|_0<3a_0/4.\] Thus \(\|g\|_1<8.75\varepsilon<10\varepsilon\), while the required uniform locking radius also holds. The orbit-dependent accuracy \(\eta\) is permitted by the quantifiers; all constants required to be independent of \(O\) remain so. The perturbation is \(C^1\)-small as \(\varepsilon\to0\), and the main \(C^1\) conclusion is retained. The additional factor \(\sigma_*\) depends only on the ambient metric, not on \(O\), and is unnecessary when \(M\) is connected.
# F3. Minor: local formulas in the higher-regularity argument
Locations. Proposition 4.1 on p. 21, (4.7) and the following block calculation on p. 24, and the final sentence of its proof on p. 25. The correctly stated proposition includes \(u+w+h\).

A common nondegenerate test system is \(M=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\), \(f(x)=3x\bmod1\), with geodesic distance, \(\psi=1\) and \(u=0\). It has ASP with \(C=L=1,\lambda=\log3,\delta=1/8\). Indeed, signed differences of successive \(\delta\)-close iterates satisfy \(q_{i+1}=3q_i\), because the possible integer discrepancy has modulus less than one. The endpoint exponential bound follows. A periodic pseudo-orbit is corrected by the geometric inverse-branch series with error at most half its pseudo-orbit error.

For completeness, MCGBP with \(K=1\) also has a direct verification. The operator \[\mathcal Lv(x)=\min_{fy=x}\{u(y)+v(y)\}\] satisfies \([\mathcal Lv]_\alpha\le3^{-\alpha}([u]_\alpha+[v]_\alpha)\). After normalization at a base point, it preserves the compact convex Hölder ball with seminorm bound \([u]_\alpha/(3^\alpha-1)\). A fixed point modulo constants gives \(\mathcal Lv=v+c\). Integration gives \(\beta(u)\ge c\), and empirical limits of calibrated backward orbits give \(\beta(u)\le c\). Thus the examples below satisfy the full system assumptions.
## The perturbation \(w\) cannot be dropped

Take \(O=\{0\}\), \(w(x)=\kappa(1-\cos2\pi x)\), with \(\kappa>0\) small enough for the prescribed \(C^{s,\alpha}\) bound, and \(h(x)=-\tau(1-\cos2\pi x)\), where \[0<\tau<\min\{\kappa/2,\varrho/[4(1+\pi)]\}.\] All required perturbation bounds hold. The function \(u+w+h\) is nonnegative and vanishes on \(O\), as required by the proposition. But the other fixed point \(1/2\) has \((u+h)(1/2)=-2\tau<0=(u+h)(0)\). Hence the final p. 25 sentence asserting minimization of \(u+h\) is false. Restore \(w\); the proposition on p. 21 already gives the correct conclusion.
## The escape threshold uses \(\operatorname{Lip}_f\), not \(C\)

The lower bound in (4.3), p. 23, uses \(\theta(D/(2\operatorname{Lip}_f))\), correctly. It is changed on p. 24 to \(\theta(D/(2C))\). In the preceding system, keep \(O=\{0\}\), \(w\) as above and \(h=0\). Choose \(\rho=1/100\) and \(z=1/300\). Then \(D=1/8\), \(\operatorname{Lip}_f=3\), and the first escape time is \(m_2=2\): the distances are \(1/300,1/100,3/100\); the last return to \(\mathrm{Area}_1\) is \(m_3=1\). The printed block bound would imply \[w(1/300)+w(1/100)+w(3/100)\ \ge\ \theta(1/16).\] Its left side is at most \(182\pi^2\kappa/90000<\kappa/32\), whereas \(1-\cos x\ge2x^2/\pi^2\) on \([0,\pi]\) gives \(\theta(1/16)\ge\kappa/32\). Thus the displayed bound is false. Restore \(2\operatorname{Lip}_f\) throughout; the initial choice of \(\varrho\) on p. 22 already uses that correct threshold.
## The sign and the periodic remainder

Below (4.7), the claimed pointwise bound must be \(G\ge-\|h\|_0-|a_O|\|\psi\|_0\), not the printed plus sign. In the same system take \(h(x)=c-rd(x,O)\), with \(c=r=\varrho/4\). It is Lipschitz, \(\|h\|_1=\varrho/2<\varrho\), and \(a_O=c\). For sufficiently small positive \(x\), \[G(x)=\kappa(1-\cos2\pi x)-rx<0,\] while the printed lower bound equals \(-c+c=0\). The corrected bound is precisely the one required for the periodic remainder.

If \(m_3=pN+q\), \(0\le q<N\), that remainder starts at \(pN=m_3-q\), not \(m_3-q-1\) as printed in (4.7). For a concrete period-two orbit use \(O=\{1/8,3/8\}\), with \(h(x)=a\cos(4\pi(x-1/8))\), \(a>0\) arbitrarily small, and a positive smooth \(w\) vanishing exactly on \(O\). Then \(G\) has successive orbit values \(a,-a\). For \(m_3=1\), the true sum is zero, whereas the printed range, interpreted by periodic continuation, gives \(-a\). This value of \(m_3\) is realized by \(z=1/8+3/1000,\rho=1/100,m_2=2\) in the same escape construction. The corrected remainder has at most \(N\) terms, so its stated lower bound with factor \(N\) is retained.

These defects are local formula errors, not counterexamples to Proposition 4.1. The correct conclusion is already in the proposition on p. 21, the correct escape threshold is in (4.3) and the original choice of \(\varrho\), and the needed negative remainder bound is already printed in (4.7). These internal checks delimit the effect of F3 independently of the length of its repair. With the correct threshold, sign and remainder, the exponential comparison bounds the total negative contribution by a constant times \(\varrho\). The prescribed positive escape cost dominates for sufficiently small \(\varrho\); concatenation gives the required nonnegative integral. Adding \(u\ge0\), zero on \(O\), preserves the weighted minimum. Robust minimization for every sufficiently small perturbation also forces uniqueness in the interior of the perturbation ball: otherwise a smooth test function separating two minimizing measures contradicts that robustness. This verifies the local-locking implication needed in Theorem 4.2.
# Positive coverage and external dependencies

The symbolic coding on p. 9 explicitly uses the closure of the coded set; the overline is visible in the source image. Its finite words are unchanged. With the stated Bressaud–Quas combinatorial bound, candidate block periods grow subexponentially and shadowing errors decay exponentially. Taking the running maximum of candidate periods justifies the passage from the constructed subsequence to all large period bounds.

The short-gap splitting in Proposition 3.1 halves the period at each step. Applying ASP to the available indices \(0,\ldots,n_1-1\) and summing the two geometric tails gives a period-independent error multiplier. At most \(\log_2 n\) splittings occur; the initial approximation exponent can be chosen larger than the logarithm of that multiplier. If the closure of \(Z\) already contains a periodic orbit, its deviation is zero and the multiplicative inequality \(D^\alpha>\widehat Ld_{\alpha,Z}\) handles the case without division by zero. Otherwise compactness forces approximation periods to tend to infinity.

Strict positivity of \(\psi\) is preserved in every ratio and calibration. The normalized potential is nonnegative and zero on the closed union of minimizing supports; integral identities use invariance under \(T\). For Appendix A, the useful identity is also \[\beta(u_K;f^K)=\beta(u;f).\] Given an \(f^K\)-invariant measure \(\nu\), averaging its first \(K\) pushforwards gives an \(f\)-invariant measure \(\mu\) with \(\int u_K\,d\nu=\int u\,d\mu\). Conversely an \(f\)-invariant minimizing measure is \(f^K\)-invariant. This independently checks the change of iterate needed before applying the cited calibrated-subaction result.

The full external Bressaud–Quas combinatorial theorem, Greene–Wu global smoothing theorem, and Bousch’s theorem with the general Anosov adapted-iterate construction were not independently reproved. The explicit tripling-map verification above is not presented as a proof of that general Anosov theorem. The higher-regularity result is relative density in the periodic-minimizer class, not a claim of density in all \(C^{s,\alpha}\) observables. No separate supplement or computational repository was identified in the recorded bounded searches; this does not establish nonexistence and is not a mathematical defect. No author code was executed.
# Supporting checks

The complete-paper coverage and original computation receipts above describe the frozen initial review. Its report, attempts, original false render records and subsequent actual page inspections remain preserved.

The present focused independent acceptance rechecked all three reported groups, their assumptions, exact source statements, admissible examples, counterevidence, repair quantifiers and downstream use. F1 and F2 are revised to Major; F3 remains Minor for the specific internal reasons given above. The assigned acceptance assistant made the final scientific decisions, revised this report, and performed its actual compilation, PDF parsing and required current-page inspection. The native bounded read-only assistant `/root/check_0278_0279` cross-checked the three groups and the rational examples.

The controller’s account, Chat selection and Pro observations remain attributed to that controller. Runtime instructions identify GPT-6 Astra Pro; backend correspondence was not independently verified. Scientific adjudication remains `pending`; `human_reviews=[]`. No author code was run.

 >\frac13L_1D^\alpha.\] Here \(A+N+1\le N(A+2)\) uses \(N\ge1\). Orbits staying close to a fixed periodic phase forever are generic for \(\mu_O\), by ASP. For other generic points, concatenation of positive blocks gives \(\int G_t\,d\mu\ge0\).

Positive finite blocks alone do not establish a strictly positive asymptotic mean. The reserved coefficient does: \(a_O\) is independent of \(t\), since the distance term vanishes on \(O\), so \[G_\varepsilon=G_t+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}d^\alpha(\cdot,O).\] Every invariant probability other than \(\mu_O\) has positive integral of \(d^\alpha(\cdot,O)\). This proves strict uniqueness at the originally prescribed \(\varepsilon\), retaining the entire \(10\varepsilon\) perturbation budget. It also makes precise the informal modification on p. 18, where \(d\), rather than \(d^\alpha\), is printed in the added term. The source’s calibration and escape mechanism are valid counterevidence against an interpretation that the main locking conclusion has been disproved.
result: Impact: False quantitative derivation controls Lemma3.8 escape construction and Proposition3.2, which p7 uses as the main second step for Theorem2.1(I). Major core proof correction. The two-point witnesses refute specified inequalities; neither is a counterexample to Proposition3.2 or the final genericity theorem. A complete replacement preserves original coefficient and perturbation budget.

problems.title: Proof uses full Lipschitz norms as if seminorms and replaces derivative-only h bound by full norm bound
problems.source_location: Norm p5; Proposition3.9/Theorem3.10 pp18-19;(3.19)-(3.20) and final perturbation condition p20
claim: Proof uses full Lipschitz norms as if seminorms and replaces derivative-only h bound by full norm bound
analysis: Location. Norm definition on p. 5; Proposition 3.9 and Theorem 3.10, pp. 18–19; (3.19)–(3.20) and the subsequent perturbation condition, p. 20. The defined norm is \(\|v\|_1=\|v\|_0+[v]_1\). A bound on the gradient controls the second term, not both terms.

For a complete admissible model take the Riemannian circle \(M=\mathbb R/(2\mathbb Z)\), \(f=\mathrm{id}\), \(X=\{0\}\), \(u=0,\psi=1,O=\{0\}\). The subsystem has ASP and MCGBP automatically, and the multiplicative condition (3.18) holds. Put \(q=\varepsilon d(\cdot,O)\). Then \(\|q\|_0=[q]_1=\varepsilon\), so \(\|q\|_1=2\varepsilon\). If \(\|w-q\|_0<\eta\), evaluation at \(0\) and its antipode gives \[\|w\|_0\ge\varepsilon-\eta,\qquad [w]_1\ge\varepsilon-2\eta.\] Consequently \(\|w\|_1+\|q\|_1\ge4\varepsilon-3\eta>2\varepsilon+\eta\) when \(0<\eta\le\varepsilon/8\), contradicting the middle estimate in (3.20), with \(h=0\). Positive smooth periodic mollification supplies such a \(w\) with \(\|w\|_1\le\|q\|_1\), so the example respects the approximation theorem.

Moreover, the proposition allows \(\|Dh\|_0<5\varepsilon\), whereas the end of its proof imposes \(\|h\|_1<5\varepsilon\). These are different even at an arbitrarily small allowed uniform radius. On the same circle take \[h(x)=a\sin(\pi kx),\qquad
 a=\frac{5\varepsilon}{\pi k+1/2}.\] Then \(\|Dh\|_0=5\varepsilon-a/2<5\varepsilon\), but \(\|h\|_1=5\varepsilon+a/2>5\varepsilon\). Its uniform norm meets any positive prescribed radius when \(k\) is large. Thus the proof does not cover every perturbation allowed by Proposition 3.9. The source explicitly uses that proposition together with Proposition 3.1 to obtain Theorem 2.1(II) (p. 18). The false norm estimates and altered quantifier affect that core passage from Lipschitz locking to the claimed \(C^1\) neighborhood; they are assessed Major. This does not assert that the repaired \(C^1\) genericity conclusion is false.

Counterevidence. Theorem 3.10 explicitly defines its Lip-dense property as uniform approximation with an almost preserved norm bound. It does not assert convergence of the difference in Lipschitz norm. A cusp example against that stronger density would not refute the stated result.

Repair. The two actual approximation inequalities imply \[[w]_1=\|w\|_1-\|w\|_0
 <\|q\|_1+\eta-(\|q\|_0-\eta)
 =[q]_1+2\eta.\] Let \(c_O=D(O)/N\le\delta\) and \(a_0=c_O\widehat\delta\), using corrected Proposition 3.2 constants from F1 with \(\alpha=1\). Choose \[\eta=\min\{\varepsilon/4,a_0/4\},\qquad
 \widehat\delta_1=\min\{\widehat\delta/2,\varepsilon\sigma_*/(\delta+1)\},
 \qquad \widehat\delta'_1=\operatorname{diam}(M)+1.\] Here \(\sigma_*=1\) on a connected manifold. For a disconnected manifold with a fixed compatible distance agreeing with geodesic distance on components, put \(\sigma_*=\min\{1,\sigma\}\), where \(\sigma>0\) is the minimum intercomponent distance. Compactness gives finitely many components. Then \([w]_1<1.5\varepsilon<2\varepsilon\) and \(\|w\|_0<(\operatorname{diam}M+1)\varepsilon\). For every perturbation allowed by Proposition 3.9 with the new \(\widehat\delta_1\), set \(g=w-q+h\). On each component \([h]_1\le\|Dh\|_0<5\varepsilon\). For different components the quotient is at most \(2\|h\|_0/\sigma<2\varepsilon\), by the strengthened uniform radius. Consequently the global seminorm is less than \(5\varepsilon\), and \[[g]_1<7.5\varepsilon,\qquad
 \|g\|_0<1.25\varepsilon,\qquad
 \|g\|_0<3a_0/4.\] Thus \(\|g\|_1<8.75\varepsilon<10\varepsilon\), while the required uniform locking radius also holds. The orbit-dependent accuracy \(\eta\) is permitted by the quantifiers; all constants required to be independent of \(O\) remain so. The perturbation is \(C^1\)-small as \(\varepsilon\to0\), and the main \(C^1\) conclusion is retained. The additional factor \(\sigma_*\) depends only on the ambient metric, not on \(O\), and is unnecessary when \(M\) is connected.
result: Impact: False full-norm bounds and changing every derivative-small perturbation to the smaller full-norm ball leave the core Proposition3.9 transfer unsupported as printed. Source p18 uses3.9 plus3.1 for Theorem2.1(II). Major core proof correction; no claim of a false corrected C1 genericity conclusion.

problems.title: Section4 omits w in conclusion and prints incorrect escape denominator, sign and remainder index
problems.source_location: Proposition4.1 p21; (4.3) p23; (4.7) and block bound p24; final proof sentence p25
claim: Section4 omits w in conclusion and prints incorrect escape denominator, sign and remainder index
analysis: Locations. Proposition 4.1 on p. 21, (4.7) and the following block calculation on p. 24, and the final sentence of its proof on p. 25. The correctly stated proposition includes \(u+w+h\).

A common nondegenerate test system is \(M=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\), \(f(x)=3x\bmod1\), with geodesic distance, \(\psi=1\) and \(u=0\). It has ASP with \(C=L=1,\lambda=\log3,\delta=1/8\). Indeed, signed differences of successive \(\delta\)-close iterates satisfy \(q_{i+1}=3q_i\), because the possible integer discrepancy has modulus less than one. The endpoint exponential bound follows. A periodic pseudo-orbit is corrected by the geometric inverse-branch series with error at most half its pseudo-orbit error.

For completeness, MCGBP with \(K=1\) also has a direct verification. The operator \[\mathcal Lv(x)=\min_{fy=x}\{u(y)+v(y)\}\] satisfies \([\mathcal Lv]_\alpha\le3^{-\alpha}([u]_\alpha+[v]_\alpha)\). After normalization at a base point, it preserves the compact convex Hölder ball with seminorm bound \([u]_\alpha/(3^\alpha-1)\). A fixed point modulo constants gives \(\mathcal Lv=v+c\). Integration gives \(\beta(u)\ge c\), and empirical limits of calibrated backward orbits give \(\beta(u)\le c\). Thus the examples below satisfy the full system assumptions.

Take \(O=\{0\}\), \(w(x)=\kappa(1-\cos2\pi x)\), with \(\kappa>0\) small enough for the prescribed \(C^{s,\alpha}\) bound, and \(h(x)=-\tau(1-\cos2\pi x)\), where \[0<\tau<\min\{\kappa/2,\varrho/[4(1+\pi)]\}.\] All required perturbation bounds hold. The function \(u+w+h\) is nonnegative and vanishes on \(O\), as required by the proposition. But the other fixed point \(1/2\) has \((u+h)(1/2)=-2\tau<0=(u+h)(0)\). Hence the final p. 25 sentence asserting minimization of \(u+h\) is false. Restore \(w\); the proposition on p. 21 already gives the correct conclusion.

The lower bound in (4.3), p. 23, uses \(\theta(D/(2\operatorname{Lip}_f))\), correctly. It is changed on p. 24 to \(\theta(D/(2C))\). In the preceding system, keep \(O=\{0\}\), \(w\) as above and \(h=0\). Choose \(\rho=1/100\) and \(z=1/300\). Then \(D=1/8\), \(\operatorname{Lip}_f=3\), and the first escape time is \(m_2=2\): the distances are \(1/300,1/100,3/100\); the last return to \(\mathrm{Area}_1\) is \(m_3=1\). The printed block bound would imply \[w(1/300)+w(1/100)+w(3/100)\ \ge\ \theta(1/16).\] Its left side is at most \(182\pi^2\kappa/90000<\kappa/32\), whereas \(1-\cos x\ge2x^2/\pi^2\) on \([0,\pi]\) gives \(\theta(1/16)\ge\kappa/32\). Thus the displayed bound is false. Restore \(2\operatorname{Lip}_f\) throughout; the initial choice of \(\varrho\) on p. 22 already uses that correct threshold.

Below (4.7), the claimed pointwise bound must be \(G\ge-\|h\|_0-|a_O|\|\psi\|_0\), not the printed plus sign. In the same system take \(h(x)=c-rd(x,O)\), with \(c=r=\varrho/4\). It is Lipschitz, \(\|h\|_1=\varrho/2<\varrho\), and \(a_O=c\). For sufficiently small positive \(x\), \[G(x)=\kappa(1-\cos2\pi x)-rx<0,\] while the printed lower bound equals \(-c+c=0\). The corrected bound is precisely the one required for the periodic remainder.

If \(m_3=pN+q\), \(0\le q<N\), that remainder starts at \(pN=m_3-q\), not \(m_3-q-1\) as printed in (4.7). For a concrete period-two orbit use \(O=\{1/8,3/8\}\), with \(h(x)=a\cos(4\pi(x-1/8))\), \(a>0\) arbitrarily small, and a positive smooth \(w\) vanishing exactly on \(O\). Then \(G\) has successive orbit values \(a,-a\). For \(m_3=1\), the true sum is zero, whereas the printed range, interpreted by periodic continuation, gives \(-a\). This value of \(m_3\) is realized by \(z=1/8+3/1000,\rho=1/100,m_2=2\) in the same escape construction. The corrected remainder has at most \(N\) terms, so its stated lower bound with factor \(N\) is retained.

These defects are local formula errors, not counterexamples to Proposition 4.1. The correct conclusion is already in the proposition on p. 21, the correct escape threshold is in (4.3) and the original choice of \(\varrho\), and the needed negative remainder bound is already printed in (4.7). These internal checks delimit the effect of F3 independently of the length of its repair. With the correct threshold, sign and remainder, the exponential comparison bounds the total negative contribution by a constant times \(\varrho\). The prescribed positive escape cost dominates for sufficiently small \(\varrho\); concatenation gives the required nonnegative integral. Adding \(u\ge0\), zero on \(O\), preserves the weighted minimum. Robust minimization for every sufficiently small perturbation also forces uniqueness in the interior of the perturbation ball: otherwise a smooth test function separating two minimizing measures contradicts that robustness. This verifies the local-locking implication needed in Theorem 4.2.
result: Impact: Minor local inconsistencies: p21 already states u+w+h; p22 parameter choice and p23(4.3) have Lipf; p24(4.7) contains the required negative remainder bound. Correct remainder has <=N terms. These existing ingredients support the needed estimate, without a new main hypothesis.

report: Author: Assigned initial scientific reviewer

Title: Initial scientific report on
Prime geodesic theorem and closed geodesics for large genus
# Source and assessment

The source is by Yunhui Wu and Yuhao Xue. The reviewed file is arXiv:2209.10415v3, 2 July 2024, 63 PDF pages. The frozen DOI is `10.4171/jems/1653`. The EMS record gives submission on 11 September 2023, acceptance on 27 June 2024, and publication on 21 May 2025. The arXiv metadata labels the manuscript Journal of the European Mathematical Society, to appear. Although this revision postdates the recorded acceptance, its equality to the publisher text has not been established. All page references below refer to the acquired author manuscript.

Assessment: Minor. Four groups of local errors are confirmed: a missing length-range restriction in Theorem 4(1), an exponent sign, two intersection-recursion formulas, and normalization factors in a second-moment proof. Each has a fully admissible counterexample or an independent calculation. Their actual effects and repairs are described separately below. No Major defect was established in the large-genus prime-geodesic bounds, the intersection-number estimate, or the asserted transition for diverging lengths around \(\sqrt g\).

All 63 text pages were read. Source images on pp. 1–6 and 8–60 were actually viewed: 59 pages, including every source evidence page used in this report. The complete proofs of the external geometric and spectral inputs were not independently reconstructed. A further verification limit concerning the arbitrary-\(A\) formulation of Theorem 33 is stated explicitly in Section 7; it is not labelled a confirmed error.
# F1. Minor: the short-length statement needs a restriction
Location. Theorem 4(1), p. 4; its denominator remark, p. 5; the actual short-length result, Theorem 49, p. 47.

Theorem 4(1) allows some fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\), whereas Theorem 49 explicitly requires \(\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)\). The difference matters. Take the exact sequence \[\varepsilon_0=1,\qquad L(g)=g^{-1}.\] It satisfies both printed hypotheses: \(L(g)\ge(1-\varepsilon_0)\log g=0\) and \(L(g)^2/g=g^{-3}\to0\).

Counterevidence and effect. The p. 5 argument expressly invokes \(L(g)\to\infty\); Theorem 49 has the missing restriction. Thus the defect is a boundary quantifier and well-posedness error in the introductory formulation. It does not refute the growing-length transition proved by the subsequent estimates.

Repair boundary. Replace \(\varepsilon_0>0\) in Theorem 4(1) by \(0<\varepsilon_0<1\), as in Theorem 49. This implies divergence of \(L(g)\) and makes the discarded \(N=0\) event negligible. A formulation for all diverging \(L=o(\sqrt g)\) can also combine the shorter-than-logarithmic equality of counts on p. 4 with the p. 5 nonemptiness result. A claim covering bounded or vanishing lengths requires an explicit empty-count convention or a different statement.
# F2. Minor: the spectral-mean calculation changes the sign of an exponent
Location. Proof of Theorem 30, p. 24, the line containing \(g^{3-\varepsilon}\), immediately after the sum of integrals.

The preceding expression contains \[\sum_{j=1}^{2g-3}\int_{1/2}^1
       \frac{t^s}{s}\frac{c(\varepsilon)}j\,g^{3-4s+\varepsilon}\,ds.\] Factoring the powers of \(g\) produces \(g^{3+\varepsilon}\), not \(g^{3-\varepsilon}\). This is a false asymptotic comparison, not merely a choice of a differently named constant.

Here is an admissible sequence testing the comparison directly. Fix \(\varepsilon=1/10\), set \(t=3g^4>2g^4\), and write \[H_g=\sum_{j=1}^{2g-3}j^{-1},\quad
 I=\int_{1/2}^1 3^s\,ds>0,\quad
 J=\int_{1/2}^1 \frac{3^s}{s}\,ds>0.\] The actual integral term is \(c(\varepsilon)g^{3+\varepsilon}H_gJ\); the printed replacement is \(c(\varepsilon)g^{3-\varepsilon}H_gI\). The accompanying term \(g\operatorname{Li}(\sqrt t)\) has size \(g^3/\log g\). Since \(H_g\asymp\log g\), the ratio of the actual full upper expression to the printed comparison expression has order \(g^\varepsilon(\log g)^2\to\infty\). A multiplicative constant independent of \(g\) cannot repair the printed sign.

Counterevidence and repair. The following line on p. 24 already uses \(g^{-1+\varepsilon}\), which is the result of the correct plus sign. With that sign, the remaining estimate is valid uniformly for \(t>2g^4\): \[\frac{\log t}{\log t-4\log g}
 \le 1+\frac{4\log g}{\log2}.\] The harmonic sum and this logarithmic loss can be absorbed in the stated small powers of \(g\). Also \(g\operatorname{Li}(\sqrt t)=O(g^{-1}\operatorname{Li}(t))\) in this range. This recovers Theorem 30 and, after the stated choice of a smaller \(\varepsilon\), Theorem 3. In the latter application \(gt^{-1/6}\le g^{-1}\) for \(t>g^{12}\). The error therefore has no demonstrated effect on those theorem conclusions.
# F3. Minor: two recursion formulas have excluded-index cases
## The general \(j\) reindexing

Location. Equation (46), p. 35, and the first display on p. 37. The old and new indices satisfy \[L_{\rm new}=d_1+d_j+L_{\rm old}-1.\] Thus the coefficient must be \(a_{L-d_1-d_j+1}\). The manuscript prints \(d_2\) in place of \(d_j\).

Take the stable, top-dimensional input \[(g,n)=(0,4),\qquad d=(0,0,1,0),\qquad j=3.\] Here \(|d|=1=3g-3+n\), and both sums have only the new index \(L=0\). The target volume is \(V_{0,3}=1\), since the moduli space of a sphere with three labelled points is a point. As \(a_0=1/2\) and \(a_1=\pi^2/12\), the original sum equals \[8(2d_3+1)a_0V_{0,3}=12,\] whereas the printed reindexed sum equals \(24a_1=2\pi^2\ne12\). This verifies the discrepancy within every degree and stability constraint.
## The zero-index step

Location. The last inequality in (51), p. 37. For \[g=1,\qquad n+1=2,\qquad d'=(2,0),\qquad j=2,\] one has \(|d'|=2=3g-3+(n+1)\), so the input is allowed. Using the source’s explicit convention that negative-index intersection numbers are zero, the sum in the penultimate line of (51) is \[4\bigl([\tau_{-1}]_{1,1}+[\tau_0]_{1,1}\bigr)=4V_{1,1}.\] Its alleged lower bound in the last line is \(8V_{1,1}\). The inequality is false because \(V_{1,1}>0\). A negative-index zero cannot be compared using monotonicity among nonnegative indices.
This counterexample concerns that particular step. It does not prove the entire inequality (52) false: positive terms discarded earlier may compensate for it.
## Counterevidence and the complete repair needed by the main proof

The actual use in (53) chooses \(j=2\) and \[a=\left\lfloor\frac{d_1+2}{2}\right\rfloor,\qquad
 b=\left\lceil\frac{d_1+2}{2}\right\rceil\ge1,\qquad a+b=d_1+2.\] Thus the wrong general-\(j\) subscript and the \(d'_j=0\) comparison are both avoided. Correct the general subscript, and restrict that monotonicity step to \(d'_j\ge1\). Weak inequalities suffice for zero or empty recursion summands; the individual strict inequalities on p. 36 are not needed.
# F4. Minor: the second-moment proof loses factors two and four
Location. Lemma 61, p. 55, the expansions following So and Similarly. Compare the correct first-moment calculation on pp. 45–46.

Define \[I(L)=\int_0^L\frac{\sinh^2(x/2)}x\,dx.\] The exact integration formulas and the volume estimates printed on p. 55 give \[\mathbb E_g N_{\rm nsep}^{s}(X,L)
 =2I(L)\bigl(1+O(L^2/g)\bigr),
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_gY_1(X,L)=4I(L)^2\bigl(1+O(L^2/g)\bigr)\] when \(L\to\infty\) and \(L^2/g\to0\). Indeed, each repeated boundary variable contributes \[\left(\frac{\sinh(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2
       =\frac{4\sinh^2(x/2)}{x^2}.\] The single-curve prefactor \(1/2\) therefore leaves a factor two. The two-curve prefactor \(1/4\), multiplied by the two factors four, leaves a factor four. The printed proof instead gives \(I(L)\) and \(I(L)^2\).

The sequence \(L(g)=\log g\) meets all hypotheses and has \(L^2/g\to0\). Along it, the ratios of the actual leading expressions to the printed ones tend to two and four. Neither difference is absorbed by the vanishing relative error.
# Core arguments independently checked
## Prime-geodesic estimates

The orientation convention is consistent: \(\pi_X(e^L)\) counts oriented primitive geodesics and \(N(X,L)=\pi_X(e^L)/2\). The real Fourier transforms of the two smoothing functions in Section 3 have the required opposite signs. Their imaginary-axis terms use a uniform \(\cosh\) estimate for \(s_j\in[1/2,1]\). The short-iterate contribution is harmonic, \(\sum_{k\le\epsilon/\ell}1/k\), yielding \(\log(\epsilon/\ell)\). It is not replaced by an unjustified uniform bound near a pinched geodesic.

With \(T=\log t\), the choice \(\epsilon=e^{-T/6}\) balances \[g\epsilon e^T
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 g\epsilon^{-2}e^{T/2}\] at \(ge^{5T/6}\); the remaining short-geodesic logarithmic term has scale \(e^{2T/3}\). The extra \(\epsilon T\) is bounded. The source images confirm absolute-value bars in (15), (21), (35) and (36); their omission from extracted text is not a mathematical defect.

The expectation argument keeps the \(j\)-factor in the spectral counting event: \(\lambda_j\le1/4-r^2\) forces at least \(j\) contributing eigenvalues. Uniformity over \(0\le r<1/2\) permits a common small-exponent choice. The layer-cake identity has derivative \(d\operatorname{Li}(t^s)/ds=t^s/s\). Together with the harmonic sum and the correction in F2 it gives the required mean bound. The integrability of \(1/\operatorname{sys}(X)\), the small-eigenvalue estimate and the trace formula remain cited external inputs.
## Uniformity of the intersection and volume bounds

Put \(q=2g-2+n\ge1\), \(m=3g-3+n\le3q/2\) and \(B=120/(10-\pi^2)\). The proof uses the uniform volume increment \(V_{g,n+1}/V_{g,n}\le Bq\) from Theorem 10(1), rather than a fixed-\(n\) asymptotic outside its scope.

For \(h_i=2d_i^2/(3Bq)>1\), select \(p_i=1+\lfloor\log_4h_i\rfloor\). Writing \(s=\#\{i:h_i>1\}\), the concavity calculation yields \[|p|\le s+\frac{m}{Bs}<2q.\] Here \(s\le q\): for \(g\ge1\), use \(s\le n\le q\); for \(g=0\), use \(s\le|d|\le n-3=q-1\). The product estimate in (57) is equivalent, for \(x=\log_4h>0\) and \(p=1+\lfloor x\rfloor\), to \((p-x)^2\le p\). This follows from \(0<p-x\le1\). Moreover \(\sup_{h\ge1}h^{1-\frac12\log_4h}=2\), giving a fully uniform constant in Theorem 5.
## The two length regimes and the tuple argument

For \(L^2/g\to\infty\), the volume estimate gives \(\mathbb E_gN^s\ll_k\operatorname{Li}(e^L)(g/L^2)^{k+1}\). Markov’s inequality loses one power, as stated. On the PGT good set, \(N\ge\operatorname{Li}(e^L)/4\), since \(ge^{-L/4}\to0\). For \(12\log g<L=o(\sqrt g)\), the mean of the nonseparating count and the expected PGT bound control the nonnegative difference \(N-N_{\rm nsep}^s\); the same denominator bound completes the argument.

For \(L=O(\log g)\) and \(L\to\infty\), the large-complexity cutoff can be fixed in terms of the constant in \(L\le C\log g\). The factors \(T^4e^{5T}/g^m\) are then negligible for the chosen large \(m\), and the fixed-complexity polynomial is absorbed into a small exponential loss. After F4, the decomposition into the diagonal, \(Y_1\), separating pairs and intersecting pairs gives relative variance \[O_C\!\left(Le^{-L}+(\log g)^2g^{-1/2}\right).\] Chebyshev and Markov inequalities have the stated limiting effects. The distinct-pair convention is supplied on p. 48 and explicitly retained in Definition 60; diagonal pairs are counted separately.

The appendix’s integer length-bin induction gives \(m^k(1+L)^{k-1}e^L\). For \(n=0\), Corollary 15 supplies the initial bound directly, without a boundary-doubling construction. In the boundary-shortening application, a negative reduced length yields zero tuples; otherwise its polynomial factor is bounded by \((1+L)^{k-1}\). The full geometric shortening argument cited from [WX22] remains an external dependency, not an independently reconstructed theorem in this review.
# Verification limits and attribution

Arbitrary-\(A\) scope. Theorem 33 is stated with a constant independent of \(A\). The optimization on p. 30 uses \(\epsilon=\sqrt A e^{-T/4}<1\), directly covering \(T>2\log A\). This review did not complete a proof, from the supplied estimates alone, uniform in a growing \(A\) throughout the remaining transition range. It also did not find a surface contradicting Theorem 33. For example, setting \(R=\sqrt A e^{-T/4}\), the fixed-smoothing and crude-counting bounds leave an unclosed comparison when \(1\ll R\ll T\). This is recorded as a verification limit, not a confirmed finding.

The main random-surface application uses one fixed universal \(A=A_0\) from Theorem 32. Its remaining bounded \(T\)-interval can be handled uniformly in \(X,g\) by Corollary 15 and the finite small-spectrum bound. The endpoint terms in partial integration are also bounded with this fixed \(A_0\). Thus no arbitrary-\(A\) interpolation is required for that application.

The full external results of Selberg, Wolpert, Mirzakhani, Otal–Rosas, Monk, [WX22], [LW24] and the cited Weil–Petersson volume asymptotics were not reproved. In particular, the orbital-subsurface estimates on pp. 51–53 and the geometric construction in Theorem 65 are retained as explicit dependencies. The present assessment is not an independent verification of all those references.

The primary reviewer made all scientific and severity decisions, independently checked the counterexamples and repairs, wrote the report, compiled the actual TeX and viewed all used source and final report images. The existing native bounded assistant `/root/bounded_identity_pages` directly read only pp. 35–40, with definitions and earlier theorem statements explicitly supplied by the primary. Its additional arbitrary-\(A\) check used supplied formulas only, with no further direct source-page coverage. It performed no image inspection, file writing, compilation, author-code execution, UI operation or independent acceptance.

Runtime instructions identify ChatGPT / GPT-6 Astra Pro; backend correspondence was not independently verified. Account, Chat selection and Pro observations remain attributed to the external controller. No separate supplement or computational repository was identified in the recorded bounded searches; that is not a proof of nonexistence and is not a mathematical defect. No author code was run.

The supporting inventory binds the actual source, manifest, report pair, evidence, coverage, build inputs, compiler, dependency cache and page checks. Historical false records and drafts remain preserved. Initial review is not independent acceptance: `scientific_decision=pending`, `human_reviews=[]`.
