A formulation for all diverging \(L=o(\sqrt g)\) can also combine the shorter-than-logarithmic equality of counts on p. 4 with the p. 5 nonemptiness result. A claim covering bounded or vanishing lengths requires an explicit empty-count convention or a different statement.
result: Impact: Introductory boundary-quantifier/well-posedness defect; the subsequent growing-length results have the necessary range. No core asymptotic transition failure established.

problems.title: Factoring g^(3-4s+epsilon) incorrectly changes the exponent to 3-epsilon.
problems.source_location: Proof of Theorem30, PDF p24, g^(3-epsilon) line following the sum of integrals
claim: Factoring g^(3-4s+epsilon) incorrectly changes the exponent to 3-epsilon.
analysis: Location. Proof of Theorem 30, p. 24, the line containing \(g^{3-\varepsilon}\), immediately after the sum of integrals.

The preceding expression contains \[\sum_{j=1}^{2g-3}\int_{1/2}^1
       \frac{t^s}{s}\frac{c(\varepsilon)}j\,g^{3-4s+\varepsilon}\,ds.\] Factoring the powers of \(g\) produces \(g^{3+\varepsilon}\), not \(g^{3-\varepsilon}\). This is a false asymptotic comparison, not merely a choice of a differently named constant.

Here is an admissible sequence testing the comparison directly. Fix \(\varepsilon=1/10\), set \(t=3g^4>2g^4\), and write \[H_g=\sum_{j=1}^{2g-3}j^{-1},\quad
 I=\int_{1/2}^1 3^s\,ds>0,\quad
 J=\int_{1/2}^1 \frac{3^s}{s}\,ds>0.\] The actual integral term is \(c(\varepsilon)g^{3+\varepsilon}H_gJ\); the printed replacement is \(c(\varepsilon)g^{3-\varepsilon}H_gI\). The accompanying term \(g\operatorname{Li}(\sqrt t)\) has size \(g^3/\log g\). Since \(H_g\asymp\log g\), the ratio of the actual full upper expression to the printed comparison expression has order \(g^\varepsilon(\log g)^2\to\infty\). A multiplicative constant independent of \(g\) cannot repair the printed sign.

Counterevidence and repair. The following line on p. 24 already uses \(g^{-1+\varepsilon}\), which is the result of the correct plus sign. With that sign, the remaining estimate is valid uniformly for \(t>2g^4\): \[\frac{\log t}{\log t-4\log g}
 \le 1+\frac{4\log g}{\log2}.\] The harmonic sum and this logarithmic loss can be absorbed in the stated small powers of \(g\). Also \(g\operatorname{Li}(\sqrt t)=O(g^{-1}\operatorname{Li}(t))\) in this range. This recovers Theorem 30 and, after the stated choice of a smaller \(\varepsilon\), Theorem 3. In the latter application \(gt^{-1/6}\le g^{-1}\) for \(t>g^{12}\). The error therefore has no demonstrated effect on those theorem conclusions.
result: Impact: False intermediate upper comparison; corrected local factor recovers Theorem30 and the actual Theorem3 application.

problems.title: The general-j recursion uses d2 instead of dj, and the zero-index monotonicity step compares a negative-index zero to a positive volume.
problems.source_location: Equation(46) p35; first display and final inequality of (51) p37; actual split and iteration (53) pp37-38
claim: The general-j recursion uses d2 instead of dj, and the zero-index monotonicity step compares a negative-index zero to a positive volume.
analysis: Location. Equation (46), p. 35, and the first display on p. 37. The old and new indices satisfy \[L_{\rm new}=d_1+d_j+L_{\rm old}-1.\] Thus the coefficient must be \(a_{L-d_1-d_j+1}\). The manuscript prints \(d_2\) in place of \(d_j\).

Take the stable, top-dimensional input \[(g,n)=(0,4),\qquad d=(0,0,1,0),\qquad j=3.\] Here \(|d|=1=3g-3+n\), and both sums have only the new index \(L=0\). The target volume is \(V_{0,3}=1\), since the moduli space of a sphere with three labelled points is a point. As \(a_0=1/2\) and \(a_1=\pi^2/12\), the original sum equals \[8(2d_3+1)a_0V_{0,3}=12,\] whereas the printed reindexed sum equals \(24a_1=2\pi^2\ne12\). This verifies the discrepancy within every degree and stability constraint.

Location. The last inequality in (51), p. 37. For \[g=1,\qquad n+1=2,\qquad d'=(2,0),\qquad j=2,\] one has \(|d'|=2=3g-3+(n+1)\), so the input is allowed. Using the source’s explicit convention that negative-index intersection numbers are zero, the sum in the penultimate line of (51) is \[4\bigl([\tau_{-1}]_{1,1}+[\tau_0]_{1,1}\bigr)=4V_{1,1}.\] Its alleged lower bound in the last line is \(8V_{1,1}\). The inequality is false because \(V_{1,1}>0\). A negative-index zero cannot be compared using monotonicity among nonnegative indices.
This counterexample concerns that particular step. It does not prove the entire inequality (52) false: positive terms discarded earlier may compensate for it.
result:
The actual use in (53) chooses \(j=2\) and \[a=\left\lfloor\frac{d_1+2}{2}\right\rfloor,\qquad
 b=\left\lceil\frac{d_1+2}{2}\right\rceil\ge1,\qquad a+b=d_1+2.\] Thus the wrong general-\(j\) subscript and the \(d'_j=0\) comparison are both avoided. Correct the general subscript, and restrict that monotonicity step to \(d'_j\ge1\). Weak inequalities suffice for zero or empty recursion summands; the individual strict inequalities on p. 36 are not needed.
Impact: Two false local recursion formulas. Their actual use in the large-index estimate survives after a fully legal top-degree telescoping argument; no failure of Theorems41 or5 established.

problems.title: The first and ordered two-curve moments omit factors two and four.
problems.source_location: Lemma61 PDF p55, expansions following 'So' and 'Similarly'; compare Lemma48 pp45-46
claim: The first and ordered two-curve moments omit factors two and four.
analysis: Location. Lemma 61, p. 55, the expansions following So and Similarly. Compare the correct first-moment calculation on pp. 45–46.

Define \[I(L)=\int_0^L\frac{\sinh^2(x/2)}x\,dx.\] The exact integration formulas and the volume estimates printed on p. 55 give \[\mathbb E_g N_{\rm nsep}^{s}(X,L)
 =2I(L)\bigl(1+O(L^2/g)\bigr),
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_gY_1(X,L)=4I(L)^2\bigl(1+O(L^2/g)\bigr)\] when \(L\to\infty\) and \(L^2/g\to0\). Indeed, each repeated boundary variable contributes \[\left(\frac{\sinh(x/2)}{x/2}\right)^2
       =\frac{4\sinh^2(x/2)}{x^2}.\] The single-curve prefactor \(1/2\) therefore leaves a factor two. The two-curve prefactor \(1/4\), multiplied by the two factors four, leaves a factor four. The printed proof instead gives \(I(L)\) and \(I(L)^2\).

The sequence \(L(g)=\log g\) meets all hypotheses and has \(L^2/g\to0\). Along it, the ratios of the actual leading expressions to the printed ones tend to two and four. Neither difference is absorbed by the vanishing relative error.
result: Impact: Incorrect normalization in intermediate moment expansions. The variance order and concentration theorem remain supported.

report: Abstract: The reviewed source is arXiv:2307.13235v1. Reading covers its 26 pages, with detailed checks of weighted densities, the semisimplicity-to-splitting dependency, and the Ricci-flat appendix argument. The last inference in the proof of Proposition 7.1 confuses a zero induced Killing field with a zero element of a quotient Lie algebra. An effective hyperbolic-space action disproves that inference under the stated geometric assumptions. This is assessed as Major because it occurs in the central orbit-symmetry argument; a precise replacement of this inference is supplied. Three further local defects concern the explicit Gram–Schmidt calculation, the sign in an automorphism transformation law, and a global group-lifting assertion. These findings do not constitute counterexamples to the geometric splitting conclusions. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted initial technical review

Title: Technical verification of
Non-compact Einstein manifolds
with unimodular isometry group
# Identity, version and inspection scope

The paper is by Christoph Böhm and Ramiro A. Lafuente, Non-compact Einstein manifolds with unimodular isometry group, associated with JEMS DOI 10.4171/jems/1654 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1654). The actual source inspected is the 26-page author manuscript arXiv:2307.13235v1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13235v1), dated 25 July 2023. All locations below use one-based PDF pages, equal to the printed page numbers. The source hash is retained in Appendix 6 (#app:record) and the accompanying provenance.

The frozen publisher and arXiv metadata identify the same title and authors. The normal publisher PDF route did not supply the version of record, and textual equivalence to that version has not been established. Thus every finding below concerns this exact v1, not an assumed unchanged journal article. The recorded source search and a bounded additional title/erratum search did not locate a separate correction or supplement. This does not establish absence of an erratum. No author implementation was located or executed; its absence is not a mathematical criticism.

Sections 1–9 and Appendices A–C were read. The detailed checks below are independent of the uninspected proofs in external references, notably the results imported from the authors’ earlier paper [BL23]. A whole-paper correctness certificate is not claimed.
# Assumptions and the main dependency

The negative Einstein setting uses a complete Riemannian manifold, a connected unimodular Lie group acting properly and cocompactly, and the normalization \(\operatorname{ric}=-g\). Section 2 and Appendix A explicitly pass to effective actions; Section 5 again discusses quotienting the ineffective kernel. These conventions matter: adjoining a trivially acting compact circle is not a counterexample to the effectively interpreted argument. The report treats this as a scope clarification, rather than presenting an ineffective action as a new defect.

The principal route is weighted-density control and Theorem 4.1, followed by polarity (Proposition 5.4), transitivity of a minimal parabolic on each orbit (Proposition 6.1), symmetry of the orbits (Proposition 7.1), trivial polar group (Corollary 7.4), and the final splitting argument in Section 8. Problem 1 concerns the step from Proposition 6.1 to Proposition 7.1. The defects in Problems 2–4 have the more limited dependencies stated individually.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (A zero induced field need not be a zero quotient-algebra element).  Assessment: Major; invalid inference in a central proof.
## Source claim and suspect step

On pp. 17–18, the proof of Proposition 7.1 sets \(\Phi:\mathfrak q\to\mathfrak q/\mathfrak n\) and \(\check Z=\Phi(Z)\) for \(Z\in\mathfrak m\). Its Bochner calculation gives \(\check Z^{*}=0\) as a Killing field on \(N\backslash M\). It then concludes \(\check Z=0\) and \(Z=0\), invoking injectivity of \(\Phi|_{\mathfrak m\oplus\mathfrak a}\). The action of \(Q/N\) on \(N\backslash M\) has not been shown effective. Injectivity of \(\Phi\) on the indicated subspace does not make the map from \(\mathfrak q/\mathfrak n\) to Killing fields injective.
## An example satisfying the geometric hypotheses

Take the upper half-space \[M=\{(x,y,z):z>0\},\qquad
 g=\frac{2}{z^2}(dx^2+dy^2+dz^2),\qquad L=\mathrm{SO}_0(3,1).\] This metric is complete hyperbolic three-space of sectional curvature \(-1/2\), so \(\operatorname{ric}=-g\). The group \(L\) is connected, semisimple without compact simple factors, and has finite center. Its usual action is effective, isometric, proper (the stabilizer is the compact group \(\mathrm{SO}(3)\)), and transitive, hence cocompact. These are Assumption 5.2, not weakened substitutes for it.

Choose \(N\) to be horizontal translations, \(A\) positive dilations, and the connected compact centralizer \(M_0=\mathrm{SO}(2)\) to be rotations in the \((x,y)\) plane. Then \(N\backslash M\) is parameterized by the height \(z\). The nonzero generator \[Z^{*}=-y\partial_x+x\partial_y\] belongs to \(\mathfrak m\). It induces the zero field on \(N\backslash M\), since \(Z^{*}z=0\), but it is not a zero Killing field on \(M\): at \((1,0,1)\) it equals \(\partial_y\). Moreover, \(\Phi(Z)\ne0\) because \(\mathfrak m\cap\mathfrak n=0\). Consequently the implication \[\check Z^{*}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \Phi(Z)=0\] is false even in an effective action satisfying all the geometric assumptions. The independent symbolic check verifies the displayed field identities and \([Z^{*},x\partial_x+y\partial_y+z\partial_z]=0\); the geometric hypothesis checks above are analytic.
## Counterevidence, impact and a supported replacement

The example has symmetric orbits, so it is not a counterexample to Proposition 7.1 itself. Writing \(\check Z=0\) informally for a zero field cannot justify the subsequent appeal to injectivity of the algebra map. Likewise, the assertion on p. 17 that \(M\leq H\) is equivalent to \(Q/N=G/N\) cannot be read as equality of the abstract groups in this example; the former concerns isotropy and the latter would eliminate the nontrivial compact centralizer.

There is a direct replacement for the final inference. Retain the established conclusion \(\check Z^{*}=0\). At a point \(p\) satisfying (11), Corollary 6.6 makes \(Z_p^{*}\) \(N\)-horizontal, while Lemma 7.2 makes it \(N\)-vertical because its projection vanishes. Hence \(Z_p^{*}=0\) and \(Z\in\mathfrak h\). This yields \(\mathfrak m\subseteq\mathfrak h\) and therefore \(M_0\subseteq H\). With the preceding relation \(K=M_0H\) in (14), it follows that \(K=H\), as required. This checks the replacement of this inference, conditional on the preceding lemmas; it is not a fresh verification of all imported curvature results.

The invalid inference sits in the proof establishing orbit symmetry, which is used by Corollary 7.4 and the proof of Theorem A. That core dependency supports Major under the assigned calibration. The short replacement and the survival of the geometric conclusion do not reduce the grading of the false derivation.
Problem 2 (The explicit non-diagonal density in Example 3.10 is incorrect).  Assessment: Minor; an erroneous illustrative calculation.

On p. 8, for the three-dimensional Heisenberg algebra \([e_1,e_2]=e_3\), the example states for an arbitrary positive-definite inner product \(h\) that backwards Gram–Schmidt uses \[u_2=e_2-\frac{h_{23}}{h_{33}}e_3,\qquad
 u_1=e_1-\frac{h_{12}}{h_{22}}e_2-\frac{h_{13}}{h_{33}}e_3,\] and then gives \[v_{\beta^+}(h)^3=h(u_1,u_1)\,h(u_2,u_2)\,h_{33}^{\,2}.\] Set \[H=(h_{ij})=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\1&2&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}.\] Its leading principal minors are \(2,3,4\), so it satisfies the stipulated positive-definiteness assumption. The stated vector \(u_1=e_1-\tfrac12e_2-\tfrac12e_3\) has inner product \(-1/2\) with each of \(e_2,e_3\) and is not the required orthogonal residual. The published expression gives \(v_{\beta^+}^3=9\).

The diagonal specialization in the paper is correct. No orthogonality of \(e_2,e_3\) is assumed for the general formula, so that specialization does not rescue it. Definitions 3.7 and Proposition 3.8 define the functional without this explicit example; no downstream use of the incorrect non-diagonal formula was identified. The demonstrated impact is therefore local.
Problem 3 (The transformation law needs an absolute determinant).  Assessment: Minor; a sign error outside the determinant-one application.
Lemma 3.11 (p. 8) permits any automorphism \(\phi\) that is an isometry from \((\mathfrak n,h_1)\) to \((\mathfrak n,h_2)\), but states \(v_{\beta^+}(h_2)=\det(\phi)^{-1}v_{\beta^+}(h_1)\).

Use the nonabelian nilpotent algebra \(\mathfrak n=\mathfrak h_3\oplus\mathbb R\), with only \([e_1,e_2]=e_3\) nonzero, and the standard correctly gauged orthonormal metric \(h_1=h_2\). The map \(\phi=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,-1)\) preserves every bracket and this metric but has determinant \(-1\). The weighted density of the background metric is \(1\) by its definition. The stated equality thus gives \(1=-1\). All 16 basis-pair bracket checks, orthogonality and determinant were verified exactly.

The consistent factor is \(|\det\phi|^{-1}\), in agreement with the absolute determinants used in Proposition 3.4. An orientation-preserving restriction would also remove this counterexample, but it is not present in Lemma 3.11. The main use in Lemma 4.2 is for determinant-one transformations; this sign defect does not invalidate that use. The report does not infer a failure of the semisimplicity argument from this local extension error.
Problem 4 (An effective group action need not lift as the same group).  Assessment: Minor; the additional global group assertion in Theorem 9.2.

Theorem 9.2 (p. 19; also the statement after Theorem B on p. 2) adds, for an effective action, \(G^0\subseteq\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb R^k)\). Its proof says that the action of \(G\) lifts to the universal cover as a proper isometric action.

Let \(M=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)\) with its flat metric and let \(G=S^1\) act by translations. The manifold is complete and Ricci-flat; the action is effective, proper and transitive, and its orbit space is compact. Its universal cover is \(\mathbb R\), so \(k=1\). But \(S^1\) cannot be a subgroup of \(\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb R)\): its connected image must lie in the additive translation group \(\mathbb R\), which has no nontrivial compact subgroup. The infinitesimal action does lift, and its connected covering group acts by translations, but the lifted translation by \(2\pi\) is nontrivial on \(\mathbb R\) although its projection is the identity on \(M\).

Theorem 9.2 does not impose noncompactness on \(M\). Even if such a restriction were intended, the flat cylinder with the transitive action \(S^1\times\mathbb R\) exhibits the same descent obstruction: a circle subgroup of the Euclidean plane is conjugate to rotations, and its continuous centralizer has no independent commuting translation subgroup.

The safe conclusion concerns lifted Killing fields or a covering group of \(G^0\), with the kernel specified; it is not an embedding of \(G^0\) itself. No assertion of a faithful lifted universal covering group is needed here. The geometric splitting of the universal cover remains true in these examples, and the cocompactness argument can use the group of all lifts together with deck transformations. This defect is assessed as local to the additional group-level assertion, rather than as a counterexample to the splitting theorem.
# Other checks and boundaries

The positivity of the weights in Proposition 3.8 is essential to vanishing at degenerate limits. Its determinant argument is compatible with bounded metric coefficients and divergent inverse triangular scale; the faulty explicit example is not needed there. The maximum-principle contradiction in Theorem 4.1 has the expected sign: at a maximum, \(\Delta\log v\leq0\), while strict negative Ricci curvature paired with positive \(\beta^+\) is negative, contradicting Lemma 4.3.

The section-wise scaling factors in (16)–(18) should be understood pointwise; the maximum-principle use can be read through the homothetic irreducible-factor metrics. No separate counterexample to that step was established. External GIT, curvature and polar-action results were traced as dependencies but not reproved. The mathematical errors listed above were checked against source images, excluding a PDF extraction explanation.
# Conclusion and states
Item | Impact | Repair verification | Adoption / remaining work
Proposition 7.1 inference | Major | Local replacement established | Not requested; external lemmas not reverified
Example 3.10 | Minor | Correct formula and exact example checked | Unknown
Lemma 3.11 sign | Minor | Absolute determinant supported | Unknown
Theorem 9.2 group claim | Minor | Obstruction proved; replacement scope delimited | Covering kernel must be stated

The highest supported assessment is Major for the specific proof inference in Problem Problem 1 (#p:kernel). This is an initial AI review of the pinned author manuscript. Scientific adjudication is pending, author adoption has not been requested, and no human review or independent acceptance is asserted.

Theorem 9.2 (p. 19; also the statement after Theorem B on p. 2) adds, for an effective action, \(G^0\subseteq\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb R^k)\). Its proof says that the action of \(G\) lifts to the universal cover as a proper isometric action.

Let \(M=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)\) with its flat metric and let \(G=S^1\) act by translations. The manifold is complete and Ricci-flat; the action is effective, proper and transitive, and its orbit space is compact. Its universal cover is \(\mathbb R\), so \(k=1\). But \(S^1\) cannot be a subgroup of \(\operatorname{Isom}(\mathbb R)\): its connected image must lie in the additive translation group \(\mathbb R\), which has no nontrivial compact subgroup. The infinitesimal action does lift, and its connected covering group acts by translations, but the lifted translation by \(2\pi\) is nontrivial on \(\mathbb R\) although its projection is the identity on \(M\).

Theorem 9.2 does not impose noncompactness on \(M\). Even if such a restriction were intended, the flat cylinder with the transitive action \(S^1\times\mathbb R\) exhibits the same descent obstruction: a circle subgroup of the Euclidean plane is conjugate to rotations, and its continuous centralizer has no independent commuting translation subgroup.

The safe conclusion concerns lifted Killing fields or a covering group of \(G^0\), with the kernel specified; it is not an embedding of \(G^0\) itself. No assertion of a faithful lifted universal covering group is needed here. The geometric splitting of the universal cover remains true in these examples, and the cocompactness argument can use the group of all lifts together with deck transformations. This defect is assessed as local to the additional group-level assertion, rather than as a counterexample to the splitting theorem.
result: Result: The global group-level assertion fails, while the universal-cover geometric splitting holds.
Impact: Additional group assertion and wording of lifting step; not the negative Einstein splitting result.

report: Abstract: The exact source reviewed is arXiv:2211.07961v1, read in full over 51 PDF pages. Author: AI-assisted initial technical review

Title: Technical verification of
An effective classification of
Borel Wadge classes
# Identity and scope

The authors are Adam Day, Noam Greenberg, Matthew Harrison-Trainor and Dan Turetsky. The frozen identity is associated with JEMS DOI 10.4171/jems/1655 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1655). The actual source is the author manuscript arXiv:2211.07961v1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.07961v1), submitted 15 November 2022, 51 pages. References to pages below mean one-based PDF pages, which agree with printed page numbers. Equivalence to the publisher’s version of record has not been established: the ordinary publisher download route returned a subscription landing page. All findings are confined to this v1.

The full source text, including Sections 1–7 and the reference list, was read. Detailed verification concentrated on definitions of forests and names, uniformity, ordinal convergence witnesses, the universal function construction, and the dependency of the separation/classification theorems on these constructions. The true-stage construction and the later game arguments were read and traced, but the proofs imported from [DGHTT], [GTa], [LSR88b], and Simpson’s book were not independently reconstructed. This is a bounded technical review, not a certificate of every transfinite or reverse-mathematical argument.

The acquisition record and a bounded additional search of the title with correction, code and supplement terms on the publisher and arXiv sites did not locate separate supplementary code or a correction. No claim of exhaustive absence is made. No author code was executed; lack of code is not a defect in this mathematical paper.
# Claim, assumptions and dependencies

The paper studies subsets of Baire space and their characteristic functions. Class descriptions are well-founded labelled trees, with an oracle computing the ordinal data; names use computable forests and ordinal-bounded approximations. The ordinal codes and their initial-segment convention in Section 2.2 matter: claims of uniformity are stronger than statements merely about ordinal order types. The report does not replace effective containment by ordinary set inclusion.

The main chain is: true stages and forest representations; effective operations on names; universal functions and non-self-duality (Proposition 3.14); classification of acceptable descriptions (Theorem 4.4); the separation theorem (Theorem 5.1); and classification of all Borel Wadge classes and determinacy (Theorems 6.8–6.10). Section 6 explicitly adds \(\Pi^1_1\) induction at the minimal-description step. Its distinction between no infinite descending sequence and existence of minimal elements on real-coded objects is appropriate and was retained in the review.

For \(\alpha=0\), the true-stage order is ordinary prefix order. Definition 2.4 permits any convex set of finite strings as a forest, including finite components with no infinite path. In particular, disjointness of the represented sets of infinite paths does not imply that the finite representing forests are disjoint. This is the relevant boundary case for Problem 1.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (Simultaneous entry is not excluded by Lemma 2.11).  Major: a failed effective construction used in the core proof chain.
## Source and witness

Lemma 2.11, p. 8, starts with uniformly computable sets \(U_i\) that are \(\alpha\)-open in \(S\), representing pairwise disjoint sets \(Z_i\). After arranging \(|\sigma|_\alpha>i\) on \(U_i\), it recursively places \(\sigma\) in \(W_i\) if \(\sigma\in U_i\) and no proper \(\alpha\)-predecessor of \(\sigma\) belongs to a competing \(W_j\), for \(j<|\sigma|_\alpha\). There is no rule for two sets claiming the same string at the same height.

Here is a witness with a nonempty represented domain. Set \(\alpha=0\) and write \(1^n\) for the length-\(n\) string of ones. Let \[S=\{\langle0,0\rangle\}\cup\{1^n:n\geq1\},\qquad
 U_0=S,\quad U_1=\{\langle0,0\rangle\},\quad U_i=\varnothing\ (i\geq2).\] The set \(S\) is a computable prefix-convex forest. Both \(U_0\) and \(U_1\) are computable and open in \(S\) in the precise sense of Definition 2.2. The height conditions hold: every element of \(U_0\) has positive length, and the sole element of \(U_1\) has length two. Their represented sets are \[[S]_0=Z_0=\{1^\omega\},\qquad Z_1=Z_2=\cdots=\varnothing.\] These are uniformly effectively open relative to \([S]_0\), pairwise disjoint, and even form a partition of that nonempty space. Thus no extra nonemptiness convention on the domain rescues the printed recursion.

The string \(\sigma=\langle0,0\rangle\) has no proper predecessor in \(S\). Every \(W_j\) is a subset of \(S\), so the exclusion test is false for both \(i=0\) and \(i=1\). Consequently \[\sigma\in W_0\cap W_1.\] Definition 2.10 requires every cross-pair to be incomparable, and a string is comparable to itself. The constructed forests are therefore not orthogonal. The independently written finite check retains the first eight strings on the infinite component and verifies both memberships at \(\langle0,0\rangle\); the analytic argument above establishes the infinite-domain hypotheses without relying on truncation.
## Impact and counterevidence

This is a counterexample to the displayed construction, not to the existence assertion of Lemma 2.11. For this particular input, taking \(W_0=S\) and \(W_i=\varnothing\) for \(i>0\) already proves the existence assertion. Nevertheless, the printed uniform construction supplies an essential guarantee: orthogonality makes a later rule assigning the unique index at a node well-defined. It is used in gluing (Proposition 3.17), the limit case of Proposition 4.9 (p. 28), construction of the separator name (p. 34), and the proof of Proposition 2.14 (p. 49). The gap is thus on the main effective proof route, even though a local repair is available.
## A repair with its invariant

For each \(\sigma\in S\), inspect its finitely many \(\alpha\)-predecessors in \(S\), including itself. Find the earliest such \(\rho\) belonging to at least one \(U_i\), and at that \(\rho\) assign the least eligible index \(i\). Keep that owner at all extensions in \(S\). If there is no hit, give no owner. The height bound makes each search over indices finite and uniformly computable.

The resulting \(W_i\) are open in \(S\): comparable strings that have an owner have the same first hit and owner. They are pairwise orthogonal and lie in \(U_i\), since each \(U_i\) is upward closed in \(S\). Their union is computable. On a path \(x\in Z_i\), some true prefix lies in \(U_i\); its owner cannot be \(j\ne i\), since that would give \(x\in Z_j\) as well. Hence \([W_i]_\alpha=Z_i\). These invariants should replace the missing simultaneous-entry argument. They use the computability of the representing forest implicit in the effective applications; the exhibited witness already satisfies that stronger assumption.
Problem 2 (The totalization reads the wrong argument).  Major: failure of totality in the universal-name construction.
## Exact statement and failed step

Lemma 3.11, p. 13, permits partial \(z\)-computable input functions \(f\) and \(\beta\). It promises total output functions \(g\) and \(\gamma\) regardless of whether the inputs satisfy the additional validity assumptions in clause (iv). At a nonempty string \(\sigma\), the proof searches for a longest \(\rho\leq_\xi^z\sigma\) such that both \(f(\rho)\) and \(\beta(\rho)\) converge within \(k=|\sigma|_\xi^z\) steps and \(\beta(\rho)<\gamma(\tau)\), where \(\tau\) is the immediate predecessor. When such a \(\rho\) is found, the printed assignment is \[g(\sigma)=f(\sigma),\qquad \gamma(\sigma)=\beta(\sigma).\] The search has certified convergence at \(\rho\), not at \(\sigma\).

Even after generously correcting the preceding initialization from \(f(\varnothing)=n^*\) to \(g(\varnothing)=n^*\), this assignment is invalid. Choose \(z\) computable, \(\xi=0\), \(\eta=1\), and \(n^*=0\). Let both input programs return \(0\) on the empty string and diverge on every nonempty string. They are legitimate partial computable functions of the required types. Let \(T\) be a finite positive bound by which both empty-input computations halt. Along any prefix chain, before the first stage admitting this convergence the output is still the default with \(\gamma=1\). At that first eligible stage the only possible selected ancestor is \(\rho=\varnothing\), with \(\beta(\rho)=0<1\). The displayed rule then asks for \(f(\sigma)\) and \(\beta(\sigma)\) at a nonempty \(\sigma\), so fails to return. This contradicts the promised unconditional totality.

The saved independent check uses an explicit partial-value table and an illustrative finite convergence bound \(T=3\). It evaluates the printed selection and records the undefined requested lookup, rather than pretending to decide general halting. The mathematical nontermination assertion follows from the explicit input program specification; the number three is a chosen demonstration bound, not a measured step count for the paper’s universal machine.
## Dependency and repair

The text immediately uses Lemma 3.11 to enumerate total names; Lemmas 3.12–3.13 then construct a universal function, and Proposition 3.14 obtains non-self-duality by diagonalization. Later separation and minimal-class arguments repeatedly use that universal function. Thus totality is a necessary core guarantee, not a harmless output-format issue. There is no demonstrated counterexample to those existence theorems or to Borel Wadge determinacy.

Initialize \(g(\varnothing)=n^*\) and retain the supplied \(f\) unchanged. In the successful branch use \[g(\sigma)=f(\rho),\qquad
                  \gamma(\sigma)=\beta(\rho).\] The values are now certified by the bounded search. The finite predecessor search is computable; each change strictly lowers the ordinal witness, and the default persists at the top value. Along a true path the output therefore stabilizes. For valid total input, if the eventual output disagreed with the input limit, either it would still be the default at height \(\eta\) or it would have last sampled a true ancestor with a different value. The input default condition in clause (iv) in the first case and the input convergence-witness condition in the second give a later true prefix with \(\beta\) strictly below the current \(\gamma\). Eventually its computation is seen by the bounded search, forcing another update, a contradiction. This supplies the missing justification for clause (iv). It should be written explicitly and then propagated through the universal-name construction.
# Other checks, limits and recommended response

The zero-type convention, default branch, successor/limit distinction in Proposition 4.9, and the different notions of effective and ordinary containment were checked while reading. The game proof tracks two different oracles for the original name and the separator; footnote 4 on p. 34 explicitly addresses this, so it was not treated as an oracle inconsistency. The later induction on descriptions and the passage through hyperarithmetic codes were traced without claiming a separate formalization in second-order arithmetic.

Several other symbol/index slips were encountered, but were not promoted to additional findings without a distinct verified mathematical effect. Nor is the finite computation in Problem 1 a substitute for proving the effective transfinite constructions. The two defects above suffice to request correction of the relevant proof steps and an author check of their dependents in this version. Both are classified by their role in the proof, not downgraded solely because the replacements are short. The appropriate overall initial technical assessment is major proof corrections required for the inspected v1; human scientific adjudication remains pending.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the 56-page arXiv:2212.08152v2 source. The frozen initial review read the full text; the present independent acceptance rechecks its three reported Problems. The generalized small-cycle proof contains a false connectivity assertion, disproved by an admissible three-connected cubic graph. The actual later applications inspected use at most three deleted cycle edges, for which connectivity holds; a replacement also proves the full stated estimate. Two further issues concern normalized equality witnesses and fixed versus optimized representation weights. All three are assessed Minor within these precise limits. Initial exact positive calculations are retained with their original attribution. No counterexample to Theorems A–C is established. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical verification of
Positive curvature, torus symmetry,
and matroids
# Source identity and coverage

The paper is by Lee Kennard, Michael Wiemeler and Burkhard Wilking, associated with JEMS DOI 10.4171/jems/1656 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1656). The inspected file is arXiv:2212.08152v2 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08152v2). Its side label says 10 June 2025 and its internal date says 12 June 2025. The actual PDF has 56 pages; the metadata comment’s 55-page description is not used to override that count. These are preserved version details, not evidence of a scientific defect. All locations below use one-based PDF pages, agreeing with printed numbers.

The source manifest binds this exact author manuscript. Its equivalence to the journal version of record has not been established; the normal publisher PDF route returned a subscription page. The report therefore makes no claim about an uninspected publisher revision. Acquisition searches and an additional bounded publisher/arXiv search did not locate separate code, supplements or an erratum. That is not an exhaustive absence claim. No author software was executed, and lack of code is not counted against the paper.

The frozen initial review read Sections 1–5 and the references. Its coverage is retained as historical; the present acceptance focuses on the reported Problems and their actual dependencies. Detailed checks are identified below. The graph-embedding case analysis on pp. 23–26, the external obstruction lists, Seymour’s theorem, and the imported connectedness, splitting and periodicity theorems were not independently reproved. The geometrical proof was traced through its stated dependencies, not formally certified.
# Scope of the principal conclusions

Theorem A assumes a closed, oriented, positively curved manifold, an effective isometric torus action with a fixed point, and odd numbers of isotropy components near that point. Its conclusions concern rational cohomology, globally for rank nine and through degree \(n/3\) for rank six. It does not assert diffeomorphism classification or remove the isotropy hypothesis.

Theorems B and C provide graph systole and regular-matroid cogirth bounds through rank nine. Their tables differ at rank five: \(s(5)=3/8\) whereas \(c(5)=2/5\), because the sporadic matroid contributes. Confusing these two optimizations would lose an essential distinction. The route to Theorem A passes through the codimension bounds, the six-involution refinement, and the periodicity arguments. Section 5.4 supplies a separate shorter route for rank nine; it still uses the matroid bounds and geometric input theorems.
# Findings
Problem 1 (Deletion of cycle edges need not preserve connectivity).  Minor: false general-range proof assertion, with the inspected downstream range unaffected.

Lemma 2.3 on p. 14 asserts \[\operatorname{sys}(G)^{-1}\geq \frac hg+s(b-h)^{-1},
 \qquad 1\leq h\leq\min(g,b-1),\] for a three-connected graph of Betti number \(b\) containing a \(g\)-cycle. Its proof handles one deleted edge, then deletes the \(h\) heaviest edges of the cycle. The last paragraph asserts that the graph remains connected, even after deleting the whole cycle, on the basis of three-connectivity. This inference is false.
## A witness satisfying the actual range

Take the ordinary cube graph with vertices the three-bit strings, encoded by integers \(0,\ldots,7\), and edges joining strings that differ in one bit. It is cubic, three-edge-connected and three-vertex-connected; the independent finite check verifies both connectivity conventions after every deletion of at most two edges or vertices. It has \(12\) edges, \(8\) vertices and \(b=5\). Choose \[C=(0,1,3,2,6,7,5,4,0),\qquad g=8,\qquad h=4.\] Thus \(h\leq\min(8,5-1)\), exactly as required. Let \[A=\{01,23,45,67\}\subset E(C).\] Give edges in \(A\) weight \(2/16\) and the remaining eight edges weight \(1/16\). The total is one and the four edges in \(A\) are the strictly heaviest edges of \(C\), eliminating any tie-breaking concern.

Deleting \(A\) leaves the two four-cycles on the even and odd vertices. The graph is disconnected, and \[b_1(G\setminus A)=8-8+2=2,\qquad b-h=1.\] The precise connectivity and Betti-number premise used to generalize the proof therefore fails on an admissible input. The witness does not dispute the numerical inequality.
## Replacement derivation and impact

Let \(t\) be the shortest cycle length for a normalized nonnegative weighting, let \(A\) be the \(h\) heaviest edges of the chosen cycle, and set \(a=\lambda(A)\). Then \[a\geq (h/g)\lambda(C)\geq (h/g)t.\] Even if \(H=G\setminus A\) disconnects, its Betti number is at least \(b-h\geq1\). Delete further non-bridge edges as needed to obtain a subgraph \(H'\) of Betti number exactly \(b-h\). Its total weight \(L\) is at most \(1-a\), and all its cycles remain cycles of \(G\). If \(H'\) is disconnected, join its components by zero-weight bridge edges. This operation preserves the Betti number, total weight and cycles, exactly as in the first step of Lemma 2.2 on p. 13. Thus the connected-graph convention in the systole definition causes no difficulty. The inductive bound at Betti number \(b-h\) gives \[t\leq Ls(b-h)\leq(1-a)s(b-h)
       \leq \bigl(1-(h/g)t\bigr)s(b-h).\] If \(L=0\), a zero-weight cycle already gives the desired conclusion; otherwise the normalization is legitimate. Rearrangement proves the stated estimate without the false connectivity claim.

The affected range must be separated from the actual uses. Page 16 applies the estimate with \(h=1\) and with \(h=2\) when \(b=10,g=3\); strict monotonicity also follows from \(h=1\). Page 21 uses \(h=g=3\) for \(b=9\). The two cases of Lemma 2.8 on p. 22 delete pairs of edges from a four-cycle, rather than deleting that whole cycle.

For any three-edge-connected graph and any \(A\subseteq E(C)\) with \(|A|\leq3\), disconnection would give a nonempty cut \(\delta(S)\subseteq A\). Three-edge-connectivity forces \(|\delta(S)|=3\), whereas a cycle meets a cut in an even number of edges. This contradiction proves connectivity in precisely the inspected downstream cases. The cube example with \(h=4\) therefore exposes the overextended proof assertion, but does not invalidate those applications or the table and geometric conclusions. The Minor assessment rests on this actual dependency boundary, not on the shortness of a repair. The replacement is still required for the lemma’s full advertised range.
Problem 2 (The displayed equality weights are not normalized).  Minor: local equality-witness corrections, with independently verified replacements.

On p. 19, the \(F_{12}\) calculation uses orbit sizes \(8,8,2\) and the normalization \[8\lambda+8\mu+2\nu=1.\] Its displayed equality choice is \[(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=(1,2,3)/28.\] This has total weight \(30/28=15/14\), so is not admissible for the optimization as defined on p. 12. The printed three cycle lengths are \(8/28\), \(9/28\) and \(8/28\). After normalizing the total weight, the shortest cycle has length \(4/15\), strictly less than \(2/7\). Thus the stated triple does not certify the asserted equality.

Replacing the last numerator by two gives \[(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=(1,2,2)/28.\] It has total weight one and makes the three displayed cycle constraints equal to \(2/7\). More strongly, an independent exhaustive enumeration of all \(104\) simple cycles of the graph reconstructed from Figure 2.2 verifies that every cycle has length at least \(2/7\). Together with the paper’s averaging upper bound, this proves \(\operatorname{sys}(F_{12})=2/7\) with the corrected weights.

The reconstruction uses the printed vertices \(1,\ldots,9\); label the unnumbered upper-left vertex \(10\) and the upper/lower inner-right vertices \(11,12\). The four edges in the left square and four in the right square have weight \(\mu\); the eight connecting diagonal edges have weight \(\lambda\); the top and bottom horizontal edges have weight \(\nu\). The exact adjacency and all cycle records are saved with the calculation, so the finite model can be audited against the source figure.

Similarly, p. 16 assigns weight \(1/4\) to all six edges of \(K_4\) while working with total weight one. The normalized value is \(1/6\). Enumerating its seven simple cycles gives minimum \(1/2\) with the corrected weighting. Unlike \(F_{12}\), merely rescaling the erroneous uniform \(K_4\) weighting already preserves the desired ratio. These are local witness defects: the \(F_{12}\) upper bound does not use the erroneous equality triple, and the corrected attainments support the stated constants.
Problem 3 (A fixed representation is confused with a maximum over weights).  Minor: false displayed equality in the explanatory reduction.

On p. 12 the correct identity for fixed multiplicities is followed by \[c(\rho)=\max_\lambda\min_C\lambda(C).\] The left side depends on the given representation; the right side is the optimized invariant of the underlying graph. The equality does not hold for arbitrary multiplicities.

For a concrete admissible example, take the cographic theta representation of \(T^2\), with weights \((1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\) and multiplicities \(1,1,10\). problems.title: Deletion of cycle edges need not preserve connectivity
problems.source_location: Lemma2.3 p.14
claim: Removing the h heaviest cycle edges preserves connectivity for all allowed h
Cubic; both 3-edge and 3-vertex connected verified; h<=min(g,b-1); normalized positive weights.
analysis: Minor: false general-range proof assertion, with the inspected downstream range unaffected.

Lemma 2.3 on p. 14 asserts \[\operatorname{sys}(G)^{-1}\geq \frac hg+s(b-h)^{-1},
 \qquad 1\leq h\leq\min(g,b-1),\] for a three-connected graph of Betti number \(b\) containing a \(g\)-cycle. Its proof handles one deleted edge, then deletes the \(h\) heaviest edges of the cycle. The last paragraph asserts that the graph remains connected, even after deleting the whole cycle, on the basis of three-connectivity. This inference is false.

Take the ordinary cube graph with vertices the three-bit strings, encoded by integers \(0,\ldots,7\), and edges joining strings that differ in one bit. It is cubic, three-edge-connected and three-vertex-connected; the independent finite check verifies both connectivity conventions after every deletion of at most two edges or vertices. It has \(12\) edges, \(8\) vertices and \(b=5\). Choose \[C=(0,1,3,2,6,7,5,4,0),\qquad g=8,\qquad h=4.\] Thus \(h\leq\min(8,5-1)\), exactly as required. Let \[A=\{01,23,45,67\}\subset E(C).\] Give edges in \(A\) weight \(2/16\) and the remaining eight edges weight \(1/16\). The total is one and the four edges in \(A\) are the strictly heaviest edges of \(C\), eliminating any tie-breaking concern.

Deleting \(A\) leaves the two four-cycles on the even and odd vertices. The graph is disconnected, and \[b_1(G\setminus A)=8-8+2=2,\qquad b-h=1.\] The precise connectivity and Betti-number premise used to generalize the proof therefore fails on an admissible input. The witness does not dispute the numerical inequality.

Let \(t\) be the shortest cycle length for a normalized nonnegative weighting, let \(A\) be the \(h\) heaviest edges of the chosen cycle, and set \(a=\lambda(A)\). Then \[a\geq (h/g)\lambda(C)\geq (h/g)t.\] Even if \(H=G\setminus A\) disconnects, its Betti number is at least \(b-h\geq1\). Delete further non-bridge edges as needed to obtain a subgraph \(H'\) of Betti number exactly \(b-h\). Its total weight \(L\) is at most \(1-a\), and all its cycles remain cycles of \(G\). If \(H'\) is disconnected, join its components by zero-weight bridge edges. This operation preserves the Betti number, total weight and cycles, exactly as in the first step of Lemma 2.2 on p. 13. Thus the connected-graph convention in the systole definition causes no difficulty. The inductive bound at Betti number \(b-h\) gives \[t\leq Ls(b-h)\leq(1-a)s(b-h)
       \leq \bigl(1-(h/g)t\bigr)s(b-h).\] If \(L=0\), a zero-weight cycle already gives the desired conclusion; otherwise the normalization is legitimate. Rearrangement proves the stated estimate without the false connectivity claim.

The affected range must be separated from the actual uses. Page 16 applies the estimate with \(h=1\) and with \(h=2\) when \(b=10,g=3\); strict monotonicity also follows from \(h=1\). Page 21 uses \(h=g=3\) for \(b=9\). The two cases of Lemma 2.8 on p. 22 delete pairs of edges from a four-cycle, rather than deleting that whole cycle.

For any three-edge-connected graph and any \(A\subseteq E(C)\) with \(|A|\leq3\), disconnection would give a nonempty cut \(\delta(S)\subseteq A\). Three-edge-connectivity forces \(|\delta(S)|=3\), whereas a cycle meets a cut in an even number of edges. This contradiction proves connectivity in precisely the inspected downstream cases. The cube example with \(h=4\) therefore exposes the overextended proof assertion, but does not invalidate those applications or the table and geometric conclusions. The Minor assessment rests on this actual dependency boundary, not on the shortness of a repair. The replacement is still required for the lemma’s full advertised range.
result: Impact: False general-range connectivity step, but actual applications checked on pp16,21,22 remove at most three cycle edges and remain connected by cut parity and three-edge-connectivity. The h4 cube witness does not invalidate these core applications or TheoremsA-C. Severity follows this dependency boundary, not mere repairability.

problems.title: The displayed equality weights are not normalized
problems.source_location: F12 p.19 and K4 p.16
claim: Recorded check: The displayed equality weights are not normalized
analysis: Minor: local equality-witness corrections, with independently verified replacements.

On p. 19, the \(F_{12}\) calculation uses orbit sizes \(8,8,2\) and the normalization \[8\lambda+8\mu+2\nu=1.\] Its displayed equality choice is \[(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=(1,2,3)/28.\] This has total weight \(30/28=15/14\), so is not admissible for the optimization as defined on p. 12. The four edges in the left square and four in the right square have weight \(\mu\); the eight connecting diagonal edges have weight \(\lambda\); the top and bottom horizontal edges have weight \(\nu\). The exact adjacency and all cycle records are saved with the calculation, so the finite model can be audited against the source figure.

report: Abstract: This report reviews the complete 53-page arXiv:2202.06833v2 manuscript, including its categorical appendices. The formal representability and ambidexterity arguments were traced through their stated dependencies. Two substantive qualifications concern the unrestricted coefficient convention in the geometric realization and the printed definition of convolution. Explicit admissible examples exhibit the failure of the relevant identifications and unit law, respectively. Three local corrections concern compactness, the quantifier in the description of spherical cubes, and pullback variance. These findings do not constitute a disproof of the intended complex-coefficient mirror equivalence with standard convolution. Higher categorical foundations and imported theorems were not independently certified. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted initial technical review

Title: Technical verification of
Perverse schobers and 3d mirror symmetry
# Identity, material and scope

The paper is by Benjamin Gammage, Justin Hilburn and Aaron Mazel-Gee, associated with JEMS DOI 10.4171/jems/1657 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1657). The exact reviewed source is arXiv:2202.06833v2 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.06833v2), revised 29 May 2023, with 53 actual PDF pages. Locations below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with the printed numbering. The journal version of record was not compared byte-for-byte or scientifically with this manuscript; conclusions are restricted to the manifest-bound source.

All pages were read, including the introduction, Sections 1–3, Appendices A–C, footnotes and bibliography. The review emphasized the distinction between formal stable-category statements and geometric interpretations, the direction of adjunctions, coefficients, compact objects, and the quantifiers defining the objects under study. Detailed checks are recorded below. Reading the appendices is not an independent reconstruction of the entire enriched infinity-category framework.

The bound source inventory and additional public arXiv/EMS/author-page searches did not identify a separate erratum, supplement or article-specific code repository. This is a bounded search result, not a proof of nonexistence. The v2 metadata records revisions throughout and the addition of the Kleisli and monoidal-localization appendices; those are part of the inspected version. No author code was executed. Mathematical work without code is not treated as deficient.
# Argument and its actual range

Proposition 1.5 identifies algebra objects with suitably coherent ideals in a stably monoidal category. The coherence is substantive: the argument does not replace a monad by just its underlying coaugmented endofunctor. Lemma 1.3 uses the equivalence between the pushout-product and pointwise arrow-category structures, while Lemma 1.6 supplies the augmented Lurie–Dold–Kan comparison.

Theorem 2.6 identifies the associated-graded adjunction as a corepresentative for evaluation at the vanishing-cycle category. Its chain uses the Kleisli property, Proposition 1.5, inversion of the twist, and the localization in Appendix C. Corollary 2.10 gives the other evaluation functor. Theorem 2.15 is the resulting formal module-category description; Proposition 2.17 then identifies its algebra with a geometric convolution category.

Theorem 3.2 is ambidexterity in the category of presentable enriched categories over a groupoid. It is not an assertion that arbitrary limits and colimits coincide inside every coefficient category. Cartesian and cocartesian sections coincide over the groupoid, and the enrichment is carried along through the module-category description. Theorem 3.11 uses the torus character/cocharacter lattice, rather than a nonabelian Langlands assertion. Section 3 explicitly specializes to complex coefficients on p. 30.

Theorem 3.23 concerns the exact torus sequence and Gale-dual toric cotangent stacks. The hypertoric extension and parameter-dependent microlocal constructions in the introduction remain proposals for subsequent work. Theorem 3.24 identifies a regraded cotangent function algebra through the center and formal-loop calculation; the degree-two regrading must be retained. No claim of unshifted equality, a general hypertoric equivalence, or a classification of all three-dimensional theories follows here.
# Findings
Problem 1 (Unrestricted coefficients do not justify the geometric identifications).  Major scope gap in the spectral realization over general coefficients.

Section 0.3 (p. 11) and Appendix A.2 (p. 43) allow an arbitrary commutative ring or ring spectrum \(k\). They define \(V_k=\operatorname{Perf}(k)\), and \(gV_k\) to consist of finitely supported graded perfect \(k\)-modules. On p. 21, however, \(gV_k\) is identified with \(\operatorname{Coh}(B\mathbb G_m)\); on p. 29 the proof of Lemma 2.18 uses these coherent/perfect identifications and the assertion that smoothness permits replacing \(\operatorname{Perf}(Y)\) by \(\operatorname{Coh}(Y)\). These statements require qualifications absent from the general coefficient convention.

Here is an example within that convention. Set \[R=\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2),\qquad K=R/(\epsilon),\] and give \(K\) weight zero. It is a coherent sheaf on \(B\mathbb G_{m,R}\), but is not perfect over \(R\). Indeed, \[\cdots \xrightarrow{\epsilon}R\xrightarrow{\epsilon}R
          \xrightarrow{\epsilon}R\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow0\] is exact: the image and kernel of multiplication by \(\epsilon\) are both \((\epsilon)\). Applying \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,K)\) makes all differentials zero, so \[\operatorname{Ext}^j_R(K,K)\simeq\mathbb C
                  \quad\hbox{for every }j\geq0.\] Consequently \(K\) cannot be a perfect complex. The usual coherent category contains this object, whereas the stated \(gV_R\) does not. In fact every object of \(gV_R\) has bounded self-Ext, so the discrepancy is more than a missing choice of a representative. Smoothness relative to a singular base does not eliminate this obstruction.

This invalidates a premise in the general-coefficient proof of Lemma 2.18 and its use in Proposition 2.17; it is not merely a terminology issue about a peripheral example. The report does not claim a counterexample to the formal Theorem 2.15, nor to Section 3 after its explicit specialization \(k=\mathbb C\). The coefficient issue is graded major because a central geometric realization is presented under a broader convention than the argument supports. Restrict the geometric statements to a base for which the stated coherent/perfect and kernel theorems apply, or formulate and prove an appropriate relative-perfect replacement. Merely calling the stacks smooth over an arbitrary \(k\) does not suffice.
Problem 2 (The printed convolution does not have the stated unit).  Major correction to the operation used in the spectral statement.

On p. 28 the convolution diagram has projections \(p_{12},p_{13},p_{23}\), but the formula below it is \[M\star N=(p_{13})_*(p_{12}^*M\otimes p_{13}^*N).\] The second pullback must be \(p_{23}^*N\). Proposition 2.17 explicitly refers to the convolution structure defined above, so the literal formula cannot be silently substituted into that proposition.

For a concrete test, take \(X=\{a,b\}\), \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C\), and \(X\to Y\) the finite proper surjection. Both are smooth perfect stacks. Kernels on \(X\times X\) are matrices of finite complexes, with ordinary convolution given by matrix multiplication. Restricting to vector spaces in degree zero, the printed formula instead gives \[(M\star_{\rm printed}N)_{ik}
                   =\bigoplus_j M_{ij}\otimes N_{ik}.\] For the one-dimensional kernel \(M=E_{12}\) and diagonal kernel \(I\), \[M\star_{\rm printed}I=E_{11}\ne E_{12}.\] More generally, \(E_{11}\star_{\rm printed}U=E_{12}\star_{\rm printed}U\) for every \(U\); hence no common right unit could restore both kernels. This is an actual failure of the claimed monoidal operation on an admissible geometric model, not an untested candidate example.

The diagram, the subsequent matrix-algebra description and the appeal to integral kernels all indicate the intended standard formula \[(p_{13})_*(p_{12}^*M\otimes p_{23}^*N).\] With this correction the finite test gives \(MI=M\). The reason for the major classification is the role of the erroneous formula as the defining operation in a central monoidal equivalence; a one-subscript repair does not make the literal unit failure harmless. No later independent calculation using the wrong formula was identified, and this finding does not refute the intended equivalence with standard convolution.
Problem 3 (The polynomial algebra lies in an enlargement of the graded category).  Minor: an explicit ambient-category correction is needed.

The finite-support requirement on \(gV_k\) is stated on p. 11, but p. 21 writes \(k[x]\in\operatorname{CAlg}(gV_k)\), with \(x\) of weight \(-1\). For nonzero \(k\), the summands \(kx^m\) are nonzero in every weight \(-m\), \(m\geq0\). Thus \(k[x]\) is not an object of the category just defined, even for \(k=\mathbb C\).

Put the algebra in the presentable category \[\operatorname{Ind}(gV_k)
       \simeq \operatorname{Fun}((\mathbb Z^\delta)^{\rm op},
                                 \operatorname{Mod}_k)\] and then take the appropriate compact/perfect graded modules over it. The analogous notation for \(k[\beta]\) should use the same convention. This is assessed separately from Problem 1: allowing infinite weight support for the algebra corrects its type but does not make all coherent \(R\)-modules perfect. The intended compact module category is recognizable and is used consistently in the generators \(k[x]\langle n\rangle\); the missing ambient enlargement is a local definitional imprecision, with no separately verified failure of the formal representability theorem.
Problem 4 (The concrete spherical-cube condition includes impossible identities).  Minor correction to the alternative description in Definition 3.20.

On p. 39 the definition first sets \(\operatorname{Sph}_n=\operatorname{Sph}^{\otimes n}\), then describes it as functors \(\operatorname{Adj}^{\times n}\to\mathrm{St}_k\) carrying all 1-morphisms to spherical functors. The latter condition is false literally, since it includes identity 1-morphisms.

Specify the coordinate generating adjunctions that must be spherical, together with the necessary coherences, rather than imposing this on every 1-morphism. The primary tensor-product definition and the tensor-product proof of Proposition 3.22 do not use the impossible identity condition. That traced independence, rather than the ease of editing the sentence, limits the finding to the secondary description. The corrected presentation still deserves a precise justification.
Problem 5 (Pullback has the opposite variance to the displayed signature).  Minor: repeated source/target error.

Definition 3.5 (p. 33) and Lemma A.4 (p. 46) write \[(Bf)^*:\operatorname{Loc}^{(3)}(BG)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Loc}^{(3)}(BH),
       \qquad f:G\longrightarrow H.\] Precomposition by \(Bf:BG\to BH\) instead gives \[(Bf)^*:\operatorname{Fun}(BH,\mathcal P)
            \longrightarrow\operatorname{Fun}(BG,\mathcal P).\] Thus the displayed \(BG,BH\) must be exchanged. Theorem 3.11’s diagram (38), on p. 35, already uses the correct direction; the left/right Kan-extension discussion in Appendix A is also the one for this correct restriction functor. Consequently no separate failure of the gauging theorem is established. The repeated signature should nevertheless be corrected so that the adjacent adjunction notation has a well-typed interpretation.
# Checks, dependencies and assessment

The fiber/cofiber conventions were checked against Observation 2.5: \(T_\Phi=\langle-1\rangle\) and \(T_\Psi=\Sigma^2\langle-1\rangle\) make \(S T_\Phi\simeq\Sigma^{-2}T_\Psi S\), as required. The shearing in Observation 2.9 and the choice in Observation 2.11 give the intended left-category twist used in the spectral matrix. The representability chain (13)–(19) was read with its Kleisli, ideal and localization dependencies, rather than treating it as a bare Yoneda assertion.

For ambidexterity, the empty indexing groupoid gives the zero presentable category as both limit and colimit in the relevant categorical setting; a discrete indexing set is governed by product/coproduct ambidexterity of presentable categories, not by a false equality of sums and products of vector spaces. The essential groupoid hypothesis was retained. In Theorem 3.23, the endpoint cases \(G=\{1\}\) and \(G=D\) respectively retain the \(D^\vee\)-quotient and remove it, in agreement with the exact dual torus sequence. These are consistency checks, not full proofs of all higher coherences.

The independent script verifies the dual-number linear maps and the finite-kernel unit calculation using the actual inputs above. Its command, versions, stdout, stderr and exit code zero are retained. The infinite periodic resolution is justified analytically by the repeating kernel/image calculation; a finite computation is not claimed to establish a general infinity-categorical theorem.

The imported kernel/center equivalences of BZNP17, enriched categorical foundations, the full Lurie–Dold–Kan equivalence, and the formal-loop/Koszul-duality calculation were not independently reproved. In particular, this review is not a certification of the \(E_3\) refinement in Theorem 3.24. No further defect is asserted merely because these external dependencies remain.

The initial technical recommendation is to qualify the general-coefficient geometric statements, correct the convolution definition, and make the three local categorical corrections explicit. The intended complex-coefficient core remains plausible under the stated dependencies, but this review issues no independent acceptance decision.
# Supporting checks

The packet, complete scientific prompt and exact source manifest are bound in the accompanying provenance. Evidence pages 11, 21, 28, 29, 33, 35, 39, 43 and 46 were actually viewed. Coverage distinguishes complete text reading from detailed mathematical checking and image inspection.
Controller UI observations and session runtime self-description remain distinct; backend equivalence and independent scientific acceptance are not claimed.

The diagram, the subsequent matrix-algebra description and the appeal to integral kernels all indicate the intended standard formula \[(p_{13})_*(p_{12}^*M\otimes p_{23}^*N).\] With this correction the finite test gives \(MI=M\). The reason for the major classification is the role of the erroneous formula as the defining operation in a central monoidal equivalence; a one-subscript repair does not make the literal unit failure harmless. No later independent calculation using the wrong formula was identified, and this finding does not refute the intended equivalence with standard convolution.
result: Impact: Literal operation used to specify central monoidal equivalence fails unit law; diagram and kernel proof identify intended standard operation.

problems.source_location: p11 finite support; p21 polynomial algebra
claim: Recorded check: The polynomial algebra lies in an enlargement of the graded category
analysis: Minor: an explicit ambient-category correction is needed.

The finite-support requirement on \(gV_k\) is stated on p. 11, but p. 21 writes \(k[x]\in\operatorname{CAlg}(gV_k)\), with \(x\) of weight \(-1\). For nonzero \(k\), the summands \(kx^m\) are nonzero in every weight \(-m\), \(m\geq0\). Thus \(k[x]\) is not an object of the category just defined, even for \(k=\mathbb C\).

Put the algebra in the presentable category \[\operatorname{Ind}(gV_k)
       \simeq \operatorname{Fun}((\mathbb Z^\delta)^{\rm op},
                                 \operatorname{Mod}_k)\] and then take the appropriate compact/perfect graded modules over it. The analogous notation for \(k[\beta]\) should use the same convention. This is assessed separately from Problem 1: allowing infinite weight support for the algebra corrects its type but does not make all coherent \(R\)-modules perfect. The intended compact module category is recognizable and is used consistently in the generators \(k[x]\langle n\rangle\); the missing ambient enlargement is a local definitional imprecision, with no separately verified failure of the formal representability theorem.
