report: Abstract: The frozen initial review read the complete 53-page arXiv:2301.13172v2 manuscript. The present independent acceptance rechecks its seven reported findings and supports six Major issues and one Minor correction. The printed path-pair composition fails an identity law; an exceptional matrix is not Hermitian; two admissible even-level boundary blocks fail the Hecke relation. Further core proof issues concern Galois lifting, the level-one antisymmetrizer, and the gauge formula explicitly used in the main equivalence theorem. The braid-eigenvalue statement requires a local correction. These findings concern the exact supplied preprint and do not establish nonexistence of the intended module categories. Historical reviewer calculations are retained with their original attribution. Author notebooks were not executed or equated with the v2 manuscript. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: Focused independent acceptance

Title: Technical verification of
Cell systems for \(\overline{\operatorname{Rep}(U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_N))}\) module categories
# Identity, source and review scope

The paper is by Daniel Copeland and Cain Edie-Michell, associated with JEMS DOI 10.4171/jems/1658 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1658). The reviewed mathematical source is exactly arXiv:2301.13172v2 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.13172v2), dated 15 February 2023, with 53 actual PDF pages. Its SHA256 is
`3bc67372527898f0a9fe55f69bf17aee4992d506b7a4a3029ccf4d279dafeaef`

All locations below refer to one-based pages in this PDF, which agree with its printed numbering. The publisher page identifies a later journal article; equality with the journal version of record was neither assumed nor established.

The frozen initial review read every page. Its historical coverage includes the oriented planar-algebra framework, the Kazhdan–Wenzl presentation and reduction, embedding and gauge arguments, all exceptional examples, all three infinite families, subfactor applications, footnotes and bibliography. The initial reviewer actually viewed thirty-eight selected source pages to resolve diagrams, signs, bars and matrix entries. These are historical views. The present acceptance separately records its focused source reading and actual image checks in the provenance. Full text extraction and archive/notebook parsing remain distinct from scientific reading.

The manifest also binds a historical v1 PDF, two source archives, and 65 distinct notebook files. The archives were read and inventoried without extraction or author-code execution. The v1 archive contains notebook material, including duplicated directory trees; the v2 archive contains no `.nb` files. Consequently the existing notebook files are historical v1 evidence, not automatically the computational witness for the inspected v2 formulas. The inventory verifies actual bytes and hashes; it is not a claim that every notebook computation was scientifically reproduced. Public arXiv and EMS metadata searches did not identify a separately linked erratum or new version-specific supplement in the inspected records. That bounded result is not a proof of absence. No author code was run.
# What the paper establishes and what it imports

Theorem 1.1 aims to identify module categories with solutions of a KW cell system at the unitary root \(q=\exp(\pi i/(N+k))\), modulo gauge and graph relabelling. The chain is substantive: the oriented embedding theorem in Section 4, the simplified skein presentation in Section 3, and the coordinate system in Section 5 must all be compatible. The positivity assumption is used to deduce relations from zero norms and cannot be dropped for arbitrary Galois conjugates.

Theorem 3.4 derives a presentation from (R1), (R2), (R3), (Hecke), braid absorption, rotational invariance and normalization. Section 4 realizes the graph planar algebra in matrix-valued vector spaces, with the Frobenius–Perron vector controlling duality. Section 5 translates the diagrams into scalar equations and identifies unitary changes of edge bases as gauge transformations. The trace identities in Section 5.1 are useful consequences, not substitutes for all the defining relations.

Sections 6.1–6.6 give six exceptional constructions at levels 4, 6 and 8 and additional associator twists; the rank-eight example is asserted for \(\omega=\pm i\). The statement that there appears to be no solution at \(\omega=-1\) is not a proved nonexistence theorem. Sections 6.7–6.8 treat charge conjugation, unfolding, and an even-level orbifold family. The orbifold procedures are described partly as ways to find candidate cells; the paper then claims direct verification. The use of a heuristic to discover a candidate is therefore not itself a defect. The findings below test the claimed final formulas.

The completeness count in Theorem 1.3 is imported from [EMG23], listed as In Preparation on p. 52. Constructing the displayed families does not by itself reprove that external classification or its count. The subfactor consequences in Section 7 likewise depend on the module-category construction and the cited categorical/subfactor correspondence. Neither external proof was independently reconstructed here.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The printed graph planar-algebra composition fails the identity law).  Major error in a foundational operation, pp. 8 and 20.

Definition 2.9 associates \((p,q)\) to a source path \(p\) and target path \(q\), but equation (1) gives \[(p',q')\circ(p,q)=\delta_{q',p}(p',q).\] This contracts the wrong paths for the stated source/target convention. In the graph with one vertex \(v\) and one directed loop \(e\), let \(f=(v,e):\varnothing\to+\) and \(\operatorname{id}_+=(e,e)\). The displayed formula gives \[\operatorname{id}_+\circ f=0\ne f,\] because the empty path \(v\) differs from \(e\). The graph is finite and connected, and has norm \(1\); it is also compatible with \([N]_q=1\) at level one. Thus this is not an objection obtained by leaving the class of graphs being defined.

The functor in Theorem 4.1, p. 20, sends the basis vector \(\psi_p\) to \(\psi_q\). Its composition requires \[(p',q')\circ(p,q)=\delta_{q,p'}(p,q').\] The discrepancy is therefore not resolved by silently choosing the opposite convention. As printed, the operation does not define the category used in the embedding theorem, so the subsequent formal chain cannot be applied literally. Correcting the matrix-unit convention repairs this specific failure; the intended abstract embedding theorem is not disproved.
Problem 2 (A displayed level-eight exceptional matrix is not Hermitian).  Major error in an explicit constructive witness, p. 42.

For the graph \(\Gamma_{\Lambda_1}^{4,8,\mathrm{Twist}}\), the paper displays the largest block \(U^7_{15}\) with ordered intermediate vertices \((22,23,26,29,30)\). At \(q=e^{\pi i/12}\), put \([n]=\sin(n\pi/12)/\sin(\pi/12)\). The actual PDF gives \[(U^7_{15})_{2,4}=\frac{\sqrt{[3][5]^2}}{[4][6]},
 \qquad
 (U^7_{15})_{4,2}=-\frac{\sqrt{[5]}}{\sqrt{[2]^2[3][4]^2}}.\] Every quantum integer occurring here is positive. The first entry is positive and the second is negative, so they cannot be complex conjugates. Numerically they are approximately \(0.4771487196\) and \(-0.1808094866\), respectively. These numerical values supplement an exact sign argument.

Relation (R2) explicitly requires Hermiticity; the opening paragraph of p. 42 also says the chosen cells are real and hence symmetric. The display therefore contradicts both that requirement and the nearby assertion of a computer verification of (R2). This concerns the only large block publicly printed for this construction and affects the explicit witness used for Theorem 6.15. It is not a cosmetic disagreement about notation.

A corrected complete matrix, with its basis order and version-bound verification of the coupled relations, is needed. Merely changing one sign is not proved sufficient: the magnitudes differ as well. The calculation does not show that no valid cell system exists, that every historical notebook is wrong, or that the abstract existence result and all twists in Theorem 6.16 are false. Those stronger conclusions would require evidence not supplied by this local contradiction.
Problem 3 (Even-level boundary blocks fail the Hecke relation).  Major errors in the formulas supporting the infinite family, pp. 47–51.

The relation is \(U^2=[2]U\), with ordinary matrix multiplication on the indicated path basis. Two admissible low-level instances of p. 48 fail it. Throughout, \(a=(i,j)\) and \(\bar a=(i+j,j)\), as on p. 43.

First boundary block. When \(\bar a_1=(k+2)/2\), the printed block for target \(a+\epsilon_1\pm\epsilon_2\) has denominator \([\bar a_1-\bar a_2]\) for both signs, although its numerator uses \(\bar a_1\mp\bar a_2\). Choose \(k=4\), \(a=(1,2)\), and the minus sign. Then \(\bar a=(3,2)\), and the target is \((3,1)\), which is split. Take source \(((1,2),+)\) and target \(((3,1),-,\chi_+)\). The two intermediate vertices are \[((2,2),+,\chi_+),\qquad ((2,1),+).\] They satisfy both the directed-edge sign rule on p. 45 and the split-edge character rule on p. 47. Exhaustive enumeration of the small defined graph confirmed exactly these two paths.

The printed matrix, in that order, is \[M=\frac1{[1]}
 \begin{pmatrix}[6]&\sqrt{[6][4]}\\
 \sqrt{[6][4]}&[4]\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad q=e^{\pi i/8}.\] It has rank one and \[M^2=([6]+[4])M=[2][5]M\ne[2]M,
 \qquad [5]=1+\sqrt2.\] Replacing the denominator by \([\bar a_1+\bar a_2]=[5]\) repairs this block’s Hecke equation. It does not on its own verify the rest of the cell system.

Split-to-split return block. For \(\bar a_1=(k+4)/2\) and \(\chi_\ell\chi_{\ell'}=\delta\), the last matrix on p. 48 is printed without the \(1/\lambda_a\) normalization present in the related formulas. Choose \(k=2\), \(a=(2,1)\), so \(\bar a=(3,1)\), and source/target \[((2,1),+,\chi_+),\qquad ((2,1),-,\chi_+).\] The valid intermediates are \(((1,1),-)\) and \(((1,2),-,\chi_+)\). The formal intermediate \(a+\epsilon_{-2}=(3,0)\) is not a vertex and is removed; it is not used in the counterexample.

The paper’s unsplit weights give \(\lambda_a=6\) and \(w_{a,-1}=w_{a,2}=4\sqrt3\). Here the signed-index convention is \(\bar a_{-1}=-\bar a_1=-3\), so \([\bar a_{-1}+\bar a_2+1]=[-1]=-1\); this cancels the leading minus sign in the off-diagonal entry. The mother-graph weight \(\lambda_{(3,1)}=2\sqrt3\) occurs in the printed diagonal formula, but \((3,1)\) is not being used as an orbifold intermediate path vertex. Substitution therefore reduces the displayed matrix to \[M=\begin{pmatrix}2\sqrt3&2\sqrt6\\2\sqrt6&4\sqrt3\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad [2]=\sqrt3,\] and exact calculation gives \[M^2-[2]M
 =\begin{pmatrix}30&30\sqrt2\\30\sqrt2&60\end{pmatrix}\ne0.\] Dividing this local block by \(6\) makes its Hecke residual zero. The expansion in the proof of Lemma 6.22 on p. 49 already contains a \(w_{a,2}/\lambda_a\) term, consistent with a missing factor in the display.

These are failures of explicit formulas claimed to satisfy (R2), (R3) and (Hecke) and then used in Lemmas 6.22–6.23 and Theorem 6.24. They require corrections and renewed checks of all coupled boundary relations. The easy description of plausible local factors does not reduce their effect on the advertised constructive witness. Conversely, neither example proves nonexistence of the even-level module categories.
Problem 4 (The antisymmetrizer argument does not cover level one as written).  Major boundary proof gap in the presentation reduction, pp. 12–13, 19 and 26.

The recursive formula for \(p_{\Lambda_i}\) divides by \[D_i=\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}q^{-2j}.\] Lemma 2.16 uses \(p_{\Lambda_{N+1}}\), its trace and positivity to deduce the additional antisymmetry relation. At the permitted level \(k=1\), \(q=e^{\pi i/(N+1)}\), one has \[D_{N+1}=0,\qquad q^2\ne1.\] For example \(N=2,k=1,q=(1+i\sqrt3)/2\) gives \(1+q^{-2}+q^{-4}=0\) exactly. Thus the stated exclusion \(q^2\ne1\) does not make the recursively normalized idempotent available.

Theorem 3.4 invokes Lemma 2.16, and the proof of Theorem 1.1 includes positive \(k\), hence this endpoint. A separate level-one argument, or a carefully formulated unnormalized antisymmetrizer argument with its positivity justification, is required. A formal \(0/0\) specialization is not a proof. This finding concerns the validity of the presented reduction at an included boundary parameter; it is not a counterexample to the expected pointed-category result.
Problem 5 (The Galois-lifting proof uses a false cyclic decomposition).  Major proof correction for the general-root reduction, pp. 12–13.

Lemma 2.14 sets \(L=\operatorname{lcm}(2(N+k),N)\) and uses a decomposition \[\mathbb Z_L\cong
 \mathbb Z_{2(N+k)}\times\mathbb Z_{L/(2(N+k))}\] to construct the required Galois automorphism. Such a decomposition requires coprime factors. With \(N=4,k=3\), they are \(14\) and \(2\), and \(L=28\). The left side has an element of order \(28\); the right side has exponent \(14\).

The needed conclusion can instead be proved by surjectivity of the reduction map \[(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^\times\longrightarrow
 (\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^\times,\qquad m=2(N+k).\] For a unit \(\ell\bmod m\), keep that residue and choose a nonzero residue at every prime divisor of \(L\) not dividing \(m\); the Chinese remainder theorem produces a lift coprime to \(L\). At primes already dividing \(m\), any lift is automatically a unit. This supplies the automorphism used by the lemma without the false product isomorphism.

Remark 1.2 on p. 2 explicitly invokes Lemma 2.14 to extend the classification obtained from Theorem 1.1 to non-unitary roots. This is the actual core use of the failed proof step. The unit-lifting argument repairs the stated general-root reduction under the same hypotheses; its availability does not turn the printed false group decomposition into a valid proof. No counterexample to the corrected lemma is asserted. The unitary-root constructions do not acquire a counterexample from this observation. The actual image of p. 12 reads \(q^\ell=e^{2\pi i/m}\); a different exponent objection suggested by text extraction was rejected after viewing the page and is not a finding.
Problem 6 (The printed gauge formula does not preserve cell systems).  Major proof correction in the equivalence-class correspondence, pp. 2 and 25–26.

The displayed formula in Definition 5.5 multiplies the \(B\)-cell by only the matrices for its first and last edges. There is no intervening product in the actual display. The proof diagram on the same page has a \(V\)-coupon on every one of the \(N\) strands. A change of edge bases acts tensorially on all \(N\) edge factors.

For a concrete check take \(N=4,k=1,q=e^{\pi i/5},\omega=1\), the oriented four-cycle, constant positive Frobenius–Perron weights, scalar \(U=c=[2]\), and loop cells \(B_v=(-1)^v\). The graph norm is \([4]=1\), and \(c=[2]=[3]=(1+\sqrt5)/2\). Every allowed boundary has a unique internal path. Thus all relations of Definition 5.2 on pp. 23–24 can be checked explicitly: (R1) is \(c=[3]\), (R2) is \(c=\overline c\), (R3) has \(c^3-c\) on both sides, and (Hecke) is \(c^2=[2]c\). Rotational invariance is \(B_{v-1}=-B_v\), braid absorption is \(cB_v=[2]B_v\), and normalization is \(|B_v|^2=1\). The starting cell system therefore satisfies the complete defining relations.

The edge phases \((i,1,1,1)\) satisfy the unitary condition in Definition 5.5. They leave \(U\) unchanged, since the two path factors cancel their conjugates. The printed two-factor formula gives \[(B'_0,B'_1,B'_2,B'_3)=(i,-i,1,-1),\] which violates \(B'_{v+1}=-B'_v\), since \(B'_2=1\ne i=-B'_1\). Including all four factors gives \(iB\), which preserves the complete relations. Thus the printed expression is not the coordinate action of general unitary changes of edge bases and does not preserve the solution set.

Theorem 1.1 on p. 2 expressly uses Definition 5.5 for its equivalence relation on cell systems. The last paragraph of its proof on p. 26 asserts that expansion of the all-strand diagram gives exactly that definition. The displayed two-factor formula contradicts this central identification. The Major assessment concerns that actual proof dependency. The diagram provides the intended repair, but the example does not prove that the existential equivalence classes have different cardinality after correcting the definition, or that any intended module category fails to exist.
# Local formula correction
## Braid eigenvalue, p. 12

Minor. Remark 2.13 gives eigenvalues \(-1,q^2\) for \(Y=U/q-\operatorname{id}\). Since \(U\) has eigenvalues \(0,[2]=q+q^{-1}\), the two values are actually \[-1,\qquad [2]/q-1=q^{-2}.\] The later calculations on pp. 15 and 18 use \(q^{-2}\), which is consistent with the corrected convention. This is a local statement correction, not a separate disproof of the later skein calculations.
# Supporting checks

The initial review checked the diagrammatic proofs in Section 3 against actual images rather than flattened text. Conjugate \(\omega\)-factors and strand orientations matter. The positivity step was distinguished from the algebraic relations, and the Galois exponent concern described above was explicitly withdrawn after image verification.

The initial review performed two independent numerical controls at 80 decimal digits on the displayed \(U^3_4\) block at level four (p. 30) and the five-by-five \(U^{d_i}_{d_{i+1}}\) block at level six (p. 33). Both are Hermitian; the maximum entrywise Hecke residual in each check was about \(4.22\times10^{-81}\). These are bounded numerical checks of those two matrices, not proofs of all relations or all exceptional cases.

The retained initial SymPy calculations checked the two even-level counterexamples, their actual graph paths, the stated local normalizations, and the level-one denominator. The graph enumerator enforces \(i,j\ge1\), \(i+2j\le k+3\), the split threshold, the directed sign rule and the split-character rule. This makes the admissibility of the examples independently reproducible. The composition and gauge witnesses and the finite Galois-group obstruction are also included. No assertion that all \(B\)-coefficients or every exceptional notebook has been verified is made.

It imports no author code. The command, timestamps, exit code \(0\), input hash, stdout/stderr hashes and structured output hash are retained in `computation_receipt.json`. Exact identities are identified as such; floating-point residuals are not presented as exact proofs.

The remaining limits are material. The external classification count was not reproved. The full coupled exceptional systems, especially the unprinted \(B\)-cells, were not independently regenerated. The heuristic orbifold origin is not a defect once a valid direct verification exists, but the printed failing blocks cannot themselves constitute that verification. The source archives and retained historical outputs cannot establish equality with a later source version without an explicit binding.
# Supporting checks
Its complete-reading ledger, actual source views, initial report, computation receipts and physical history remain preserved. The historical notebook material retains its exact v1 attribution.

The assigned acceptance assistant independently checked all seven findings: the source definitions and quantifiers, all counterexample assumptions, diagram and matrix entries, proof dependencies, internal counterevidence, severity, repairs and their limits. It inspected the current report, findings and coverage, and rechecked the retained reviewer calculation inputs and outputs. F6 is revised from Minor to Major for the direct equivalence-theorem dependency above; the other six severities are retained. The transient signed-index concern about the second boundary block was resolved by the source’s negative-index convention, and is not an additional finding.

The native bounded read-only assistant `/root/check_0284_0285` cross-checked source statements, the two admissible boundary path sets, signed indices and the full four-cycle gauge example. Its exact coverage and contribution are recorded in the provenance. The acceptance assistant performed this revision, the actual offline compilation, PDF parsing and every required current report-page view.

The controller’s account, Chat and Pro observations remain attributed to that controller. Runtime instructions identify GPT-6 Astra Pro; backend correspondence was not independently verified. Current source, TeX, PDF, compiler, dependencies, logs, retained payloads and actual page views are bound in the accompanying provenance and delivery inventory. Original failed attempts and false render records remain historical; subsequent actual checks document recovery without overwriting them.
No author code, shell escape, installation or paid alternative was used. Scientific adjudication remains `pending`; `human_reviews=[]`.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the pinned author manuscript arXiv:2008.13656v7. A nonadditive proposed filtration obstructs the stated Rees construction. A separate example contradicts the identification of the constructed open set with the inverse image of the smooth locus of its moment polytope. Three local defects concern an illustrative toric equation, a completeness hypothesis, and a zero-weight exception. These conclusions do not disprove the existence of collective integrable systems asserted in the paper. The scientific disposition remains pending.
Date: 27 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review of
Stratified gradient Hamiltonian vector fields
and collective integrable systems
# Identity, scope, and conventions

The authors are Benjamin Hoffman and Jeremy Lane. The associated journal identifier is DOI `10.4171/jems/1659`. The reviewed object is the 50-page PDF of arXiv:2008.13656v7, submitted 21 April 2025 and described there as the final accepted version; its first page is dated 22 April 2025. Page numbers below are the numbered PDF pages. Equivalence to the publisher’s version of record has not been established. The PDF SHA256 is

The full text was read, with particular attention to Definitions 4.1 and 4.7, the construction in Section 4.1.2, Theorems 3.7, 4.16, 5.5 and 6.2, Propositions 6.8–6.11, and Appendix A. Source images were actually viewed for the claims and dependency steps used below. The pinned TeX source was also acquired and inspected at the disputed Rees formulas and toric example.

The review distinguishes checking the logic of a stated construction from proving a main theorem false. External theorems cited by the authors were not independently re-proved. In particular, the uniform limiting assertion of Lemma A.6, whose proof is omitted on p. 47, has not been completely reconstructed here. No defect is inferred merely from that omission. No author code was run. Missing separately released computational code is not a mathematical criticism.
# The construction and its dependencies

Theorem 1.1 constructs a collective map for a compact connected Lie group, with a torus action on a dense connected open subset of each connected Hamiltonian manifold. Its compact-case assertions include connected fibers, a convex polytope, and a description of that open subset using the smooth locus of the polytope. Section 3 supplies a stratified gradient-flow construction under (GH1)–(GH6). Section 4 uses a good valuation to produce the required degeneration, and Section 5 applies it to the base affine space. Section 6 transfers the construction to Hamiltonian manifolds.

The valuation convention is the maximum convention: \(v(f+g)\leq\max\{v(f),v(g)\}\), together with multiplicativity and invariance under nonzero scalar multiplication. Conditions (v1)–(v5) control an ordered lattice \(L\), a grading map \(w\), finite grading fibers, and finite refinements by integral linear functionals. A refinement for finitely many specified comparisons is not automatically an order-preserving function on all of \(L\). This distinction is essential to Problem 1.
# Problem 1: the proposed filtration need not be additive
## Claim and location

Equation reference: eq:filtration. On p. 20, following (15), the paper defines \[
 A_{\leq k}=\{f\in A:e(v(f))\leq k\text{ or }f=0\}\] and calls these sets subspaces forming a filtration. The Rees algebra (16) and Proposition 4.5 then use that assertion. The choice of \(e\) is constrained by nonnegativity on the value semigroup and the finitely many comparisons associated with the chosen relation generators.
## A complete counterexample to additivity

Take \(A=\mathbb C[x,y]\), \(L=\mathbb Z^2\), and the lexicographic order on pairs \((a,b)\), with \(a\) compared first. For a nonzero polynomial define \(v(f)\) to be its largest monomial exponent in this order. The value semigroup is \(S=\mathbb N^2\), which is finitely generated and saturated. Leading coefficients show that the valuation has one-dimensional leaves: two polynomials with the same leading exponent have a unique scalar multiple canceling that leading term. Multiplication adds leading exponents, and addition satisfies the required maximum inequality.

Let \(H=(\mathbb C^*)^2\), with the standard multigrading, and set \(w=\mathrm{id}_L\). Then (v1) holds for the induced lexicographic grading order; \(0\) is the least element of \(w(S)\), as required by (v2); every fiber in (v3) is a singleton; and each homogeneous polynomial is a scalar monomial, so (v4) holds. For (v5), there are no unequal elements with the same \(w\)-value. Every requested finite set of strict comparisons is therefore empty, and a nonnegative integral functional suffices.

Use the identity embedding \(\mathbb C^2\hookrightarrow E=\mathbb C^2\) and the homogeneous Khovanskii basis \(\{x,y\}\). The associated graded ring is \(\mathbb C[x,y]\), so its presentation has no ideal generators: \(J=0\). Consequently (15) imposes no strict inequalities. The choice \(e(a,b)=a+b\) satisfies all the stated restrictions. But, for \[f=x,\qquad g=-x+y^2,\] one has \[v(f)=v(g)=(1,0),\quad e(v(f))=e(v(g))=1,
 \qquad v(f+g)=(0,2),\quad e(v(f+g))=2.\] Thus \(f,g\in A_{\leq1}\), while \(f+g\notin A_{\leq1}\). The set in [eq:filtration] (#eq:filtration) is not a vector subspace. In particular, the displayed direct sum in (16) is not even closed under addition with these allowed data.
## An additional obstruction in the preceding displayed formulas

Lemma 4.4 and (14)–(15), p. 20, use the evaluated quantities \(v(\bar g_j(f_1,\ldots,f_n))\) and \(v(p_j(f_1,\ldots,f_n))\). If \(g_j=\bar g_j+p_j\) lies in the kernel of evaluation and both evaluated terms are nonzero, these values are equal. If both terms vanish, the displayed valuation is undefined. The intended formal degree \(s_j\) of \(\bar g_j\) is different from that evaluated value.

For a nonzero concrete case, keep \(A=\mathbb C[x,y]\) but order exponents lexicographically by \((a+2b,a)\), and let \(w(a,b)=a+2b\). Use the homogeneous Khovanskii basis \[f_1=x,\qquad f_2=y,\qquad f_3=x^2+y .\] It gives a closed equivariant embedding in \(\mathbb C^3\). Here \(S=\mathbb N^2\), the leaves are one-dimensional, \(w(S)=\mathbb N\) has least element zero, and each \(w\)-fiber is finite. The grading condition holds. Moreover, for a fixed value \(\lambda=a+2b\), the functional \(e(a,b)=2a+2b=\lambda+a\) strictly respects every comparison in that fiber and is nonnegative. Thus (v1)–(v5) hold.

The graded relation is \(\bar g=z_3-z_1^2\), of formal degree \(s=(2,0)\). Its lift is \(g=z_3-z_1^2-z_2\), with \(p=-z_2\). However, \[\bar g(f_1,f_2,f_3)=y,\qquad p(f_1,f_2,f_3)=-y,\] so both evaluated values are \((0,1)\). No \(e\) can satisfy the strict inequality in (15) for this single correction monomial. The acquired TeX source contains the same expressions; this is not a PDF extraction error.
## Alternative interpretation, impact, and repair status

Replacing the evaluated degree by \(s_j\) addresses the latter local notation error. In this particular example it gives the valid equation \(z_3-z_1^2-t^2z_2=0\), since substitution of \((z_1,z_2,z_3)=(t^2x,t^2y,t^4(x^2+y))\) makes it vanish. That local repair does not address the preceding nonadditivity counterexample. A construction using an appropriate homogeneous basis or weight filtration needs a new argument; none is asserted here as a complete repair of the paper.

This is a Major defect in the stated construction, rather than a classification based on a typographical error alone. Section 4.3.1 explicitly applies Section 4.1.2 in Proposition 4.13 (p. 24), which supplies Theorem 4.16 (p. 27); Theorem 5.5 (p. 33) and the Section 6 construction depend on it. The example disproves the claimed general filtration step. It does not prove that no valid degeneration or collective system can be constructed by another argument. Evidence: source pp. 19–24, 27, 33; calculation record `recovery_checks_output.json`.
# Problem 2: the constructed open set need not map to the smooth locus
## Claim and assumptions

Proposition 6.10(iii), p. 39, identifies the image of the constructed open piece with the smooth locus of the corresponding moment image. The proof on p. 40 treats \(\Delta_Y\cap\sigma\) as smooth. No multiplicity-free hypothesis is imposed on \(Y\). The proof of Theorem 1.1 on p. 41 invokes Proposition 6.10 for its first and third assertions.
## Counterexample and the construction in the abelian case

Let \(K=\mathbb T^3\) and \(Y=\mathbb {CP}^6\), with its standard invariant Fubini–Study form. Act diagonally with weights \[w_0=0,\quad w_1=e_1,\quad w_2=-e_1,\quad
 w_3=e_2,\quad w_4=-e_2,\quad w_5=e_3,\quad w_6=-e_3 .\] This is a compact connected smooth Hamiltonian \(K\)-manifold. The action is effective because the coordinate of weight zero and the three positive coordinate weights force a projectively trivial torus element to be the identity. With a harmless choice of moment-map normalization, \[\mu([z_0:\cdots:z_6])
   =\frac{\sum_{j=0}^6 |z_j|^2w_j}{\sum_{j=0}^6|z_j|^2},
 \qquad
 \Delta_Y=\mathop{\mathrm{conv}}\{\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_3\}
          =\{p:|p_1|+|p_2|+|p_3|\leq1\}.\] Every convex combination is realized by choosing squared coordinate moduli, so this is an equality of images, not merely an inclusion.

For a torus the semisimple factor in Section 6.2 is trivial. There is only one Weyl-chamber stratum, \(\sigma=\mathfrak t^*\); the universal space is \(T^*\mathbb T^3\), with \(c=F=\mathrm{id}\) on moment coordinates. Symplectic implosion leaves \(Y\) unchanged. The reduction \((Y\times T^*\mathbb T^3)//\mathbb T^3\) is canonically \(Y\): the moment equation determines the cotangent coordinate, and the free translation factor supplies a unique representative with torus coordinate one. This also identifies the reduced symplectic form with that of \(Y\). All the universal space is smooth. Consequently the constructed open piece \(U\), and its inverse image \(D\), are the whole of \(Y\).

At \(p=e_1\), four distinct facets of the octahedron are active: their outward primitive normals are \((1,\pm1,\pm1)\). Each supporting hyperplane is indeed a facet, since it contains three affinely independent signed coordinate vertices. A three-dimensional smooth rational polytope is simple at a smooth vertex; here four facets meet. Equivalently the tangent cone is not a simplicial unimodular cone. Thus \(e_1\) is not in the smooth locus in the toric, lattice sense used by the paper. Yet \(\mu(U)=\mu(Y)=\Delta_Y\) contains \(e_1\). This contradicts the asserted identification for the constructed \(U\).
## Scope and alternatives

The example has positive complexity: the complex dimension is six and the effective torus dimension is three. Smoothness of a Hamiltonian manifold does not force its moment polytope to be smooth in this setting. Results about smooth toric manifolds therefore do not remove the example.

The defect is Major because the main proof explicitly uses this identification. It does not refute convexity, connected fibers, or the existential form of Theorem 1.1 by itself. In the example one can restrict the existing torus action to the inverse image of the polytope’s smooth locus; this demonstrates why a false claim about the specific constructed set is different from a proof of nonexistence. A general corrected construction and its connectedness assertions have not been verified here. Evidence: source pp. 3, 36–37, 39–41; exact facet calculation in the independent-check output.
# Problem 3: the displayed equations for an illustrative toric variety

Example 4.17, (21), p. 28, describes the toric variety using only \[y_3y_6=y_4y_5,\qquad y_1y_5=y_2y_3 .\] Its six displayed semigroup generators are \[\begin{aligned}
 v_1&=(0,1,0,0),&v_2&=(0,1,0,1),&v_3&=(1,0,0,0),\\
 v_4&=(1,0,1,0),&v_5&=(1,0,0,1),&v_6&=(1,0,1,1).
\end{aligned}\] The equality \(v_1+v_6=v_2+v_4\) requires the toric relation \(y_1y_6-y_2y_4=0\): under the semigroup-algebra map both monomials map to the same basis element. The point \(q=(1,0,0,0,0,1)\) satisfies both printed equations, but the required binomial has value one. Hence the printed zero set strictly contains the toric variety. Saturating on a torus chart could remove extra points, but the displayed equality is an affine zero-set description, not such a saturation.

This is Minor. The text on p. 27 explicitly states that the example is not used in subsequent results. No claim is made that appending this one missing equation suffices scheme-theoretically. As counterevidence against a broader criticism of the example, its rectangle/trapezoid lattice counts agree: \[\sum_{j=0}^{a}(2a+b-2j+1)=(a+1)(a+b+1)
 \quad(a,b\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}),\] and the corresponding areas are both \(a(a+b)\). The symbolic identity and 49 finite parameter checks were reproduced; they do not independently prove the claimed symplectic statement. Evidence: source pp. 27–29 and the exact binomial residual calculation.
# Problem 4: properness onto the image does not imply complete flow

Lemma A.1, p. 44, assumes that \((\pi,\psi)\) is proper as a map onto its image, and concludes existence of the gradient Hamiltonian flow starting in \(U_0\) for every real time. Take the smooth affine variety \[X=\mathbb C\setminus\{-1\},\qquad \pi(z)=z ,\] with the restricted Euclidean Kähler form. Let the connected group \(K=S^1\) act trivially and set \(\psi=0\). The action is Hamiltonian, preserves the metric and every fiber, and its moment map is continuous. There are no critical or singular points, so \(Z=\varnothing\subset X_0\), and \(U_0=\{0\}\) is nonempty. The map \(z\mapsto(z,0)\) is a homeomorphism onto its image, hence proper onto that image.

The normalized negative gradient field of \(\operatorname{Re}\pi\) is \(-\partial_{\operatorname{Re}z}\). Its unique trajectory from zero is \(\varphi_t(0)=-t\), which leaves \(X\) at time \(t=1\). The all-real-time conclusion is false with every listed assumption satisfied. A compactness argument over a segment in the full target fails because its intersection with the image need not be compact in that image.

This is Minor with the present dependency evidence. Condition (GH4)II on p. 12 instead requires properness to the full target. The example fails that stronger assumption, and therefore does not contradict Theorem 3.7. Full-target properness excludes this escape mechanism; a replacement proof of the entire lemma under modified hypotheses is not claimed. Evidence: source pp. 12, 44–45 and the explicit trajectory.
# Problem 5: the pointed-cone criterion needs a zero-weight exclusion

Lemma 2.2(ii), p. 7, ends with an equivalence between properness of a linear unitary torus moment map and strong convexity of its image. Take the \(S^1\)-representation \(E=\mathbb C_0\oplus\mathbb C_1\). Its standard moment map is \[\mu(z_0,z_1)=\tfrac12|z_1|^2 .\] The image \([0,\infty)\) contains no line and is strongly convex, but the fiber of zero contains \((n,0)\) for every positive integer \(n\); it is not compact. Thus the moment map is not proper.

The earlier criterion in the same lemma, excluding a nontrivial nonnegative combination of the weights equal to zero, correctly detects this example. The final equivalence loses the possibility of zero weights. For a finite set of weights the corrected criterion is: its cone is pointed and every weight is nonzero. Indeed, a pointed finitely generated cone admits a linear functional strictly positive on all of its nonzero generators. If its values on the weights are at least \(c>0\), then \(\ell(\mu(z))\geq c\|z\|^2/2\); inverse images of compact sets are closed and bounded, hence compact. Conversely, a zero weight gives the unbounded fiber above; a nontrivial nonnegative zero relation similarly gives a ray of preimages of zero by taking squared moduli proportional to that relation.
This is Minor: Lemma 4.10, p. 23, explicitly excludes zero weights in the relevant later application. Its properness use is therefore not refuted by this example. Evidence: source pp. 7, 23.
# Overall assessment and remaining work

There are two supported core derivation concerns and three local concerns, with no severity quota applied. A full repair of the Rees construction and of the smooth-locus argument remains open in this review. The main existence theorem has not been disproved. No author adoption or human decision is recorded.

The omitted details of Lemma A.6 remain a coverage limit, not a demonstrated defect. No later arXiv version was listed on the consulted v7 page. Take the smooth affine variety \[X=\mathbb C\setminus\{-1\},\qquad \pi(z)=z ,\] with the restricted Euclidean Kähler form. Let the connected group \(K=S^1\) act trivially and set \(\psi=0\). The action is Hamiltonian, preserves the metric and every fiber, and its moment map is continuous. There are no critical or singular points, so \(Z=\varnothing\subset X_0\), and \(U_0=\{0\}\) is nonempty. The map \(z\mapsto(z,0)\) is a homeomorphism onto its image, hence proper onto that image.

The normalized negative gradient field of \(\operatorname{Re}\pi\) is \(-\partial_{\operatorname{Re}z}\). Its unique trajectory from zero is \(\varphi_t(0)=-t\), which leaves \(X\) at time \(t=1\). The all-real-time conclusion is false with every listed assumption satisfied. A compactness argument over a segment in the full target fails because its intersection with the image need not be compact in that image.

This is Minor with the present dependency evidence. Condition (GH4)II on p. 12 instead requires properness to the full target. The example fails that stronger assumption, and therefore does not contradict Theorem 3.7. Full-target properness excludes this escape mechanism; a replacement proof of the entire lemma under modified hypotheses is not claimed. Evidence: source pp. 12, 44–45 and the explicit trajectory.
result: Impact: Standalone completeness lemma overstated; core theorem not refuted by this example

problems.title: Strong convexity criterion loses zero-weight exception
problems.source_location: p.7 Lemma 2.2(ii) p.23 Lemma 4.10
claim: Recorded check: Strong convexity criterion loses zero-weight exception
analysis: Lemma 2.2(ii), p. 7, ends with an equivalence between properness of a linear unitary torus moment map and strong convexity of its image. Take the \(S^1\)-representation \(E=\mathbb C_0\oplus\mathbb C_1\). Its standard moment map is \[\mu(z_0,z_1)=\tfrac12|z_1|^2 .\] The image \([0,\infty)\) contains no line and is strongly convex, but the fiber of zero contains \((n,0)\) for every positive integer \(n\); it is not compact. Thus the moment map is not proper.

The earlier criterion in the same lemma, excluding a nontrivial nonnegative combination of the weights equal to zero, correctly detects this example. The final equivalence loses the possibility of zero weights. For a finite set of weights the corrected criterion is: its cone is pointed and every weight is nonzero. Indeed, a pointed finitely generated cone admits a linear functional strictly positive on all of its nonzero generators. If its values on the weights are at least \(c>0\), then \(\ell(\mu(z))\geq c\|z\|^2/2\); inverse images of compact sets are closed and bounded, hence compact. Conversely, a zero weight gives the unbounded fiber above; a nontrivial nonnegative zero relation similarly gives a ray of preimages of zero by taking squared moduli proportional to that relation.
This is Minor: Lemma 4.10, p. 23, explicitly excludes zero weights in the relevant later application. Its properness use is therefore not refuted by this example. Evidence: source pp. 7, 23.
result: Impact: Local equivalence false; cited downstream properness not refuted

report: Abstract: The reviewed object is arXiv:2207.10554v3. Three auxiliary statements require correction: a Lorentz bound uses the boundary dimension in place of the ambient dimension, an averaging map cannot preserve norms of arbitrary signed sequences, and a Harnack lower estimate lacks a sign hypothesis. Explicit counterexamples are given below. Their identified uses in the main arguments admit more restricted formulations, so these are classified as Minor. A separate ambiguity concerning the admissibility of corona roots remains a request for evidence, not a verified counterexample to the main regularity theorem. The scientific disposition remains pending.

Title: Initial scientific review of
Solvability of the Poisson–Dirichlet problem
with interior data in \(L^{p'}\)-Carleson spaces
and its applications to the \(L^p\)-regularity problem
# Identity and review scope

The authors are Mihalis Mourgoglou, Bruno Poggi, and Xavier Tolsa. The associated journal identifier is DOI `10.4171/jems/1660`. The acquired object is the 69-page author manuscript arXiv:2207.10554v3, submitted on 21 November 2024; its first page is dated 22 November 2024. Its equivalence to the publisher’s version of record has not been established. All locations below refer to this pinned PDF, whose SHA256 is

The initial reviewer read the whole extracted text, including the appendix and references. Source images were actually viewed for the statements, counterexamples, and dependency steps cited below. The matching arXiv source archive was also obtained through its normal public link. Its TeX was inspected statically at Lemma 2.10, Definition 2.12, and the sequence averaging argument; no author code or author TeX build was executed.

The initial review’s scope is retained; the stated Problems have subsequently undergone focused independent acceptance. The complete geometric proofs imported from the cited corona and regularity literature have not been reconstructed. In particular, the root issue in Section 6 (#sec:root) prevents this report from certifying every step of the regularity argument. Absence of a separately released implementation or supplement is not treated as a mathematical defect.
# Main statements, quantifiers, and dependency checks

Write \(d=n+1\geq3\), \(L=-\mathop{\mathrm{div}}A\nabla\), and \[2^*=\frac{2d}{d-2},\qquad 2_*=\frac{2d}{d+2}.\] The coefficient matrix is real, bounded, strongly elliptic, and need not be symmetric. The distinction between \(L\) and \(L^*\) is essential. Theorem 1.11 assumes a corkscrew domain with \(n\)-Ahlfors regular boundary, and also assumes either that \(\Omega\) is bounded or that \(\partial\Omega\) is unbounded. For \(p>1\), with \(p'\) its Hölder conjugate, solvability of \((D^L_{p'})\) yields the Poisson–Dirichlet estimate with \(\widetilde N_{2^*}w\), \(\mathcal C_{2_*}(\delta H)\), and \(\mathcal C_2(F)\). The initial construction uses bounded compactly supported interior data; the appendix supplies the density passage. The restriction on the domain is retained throughout this review.

Theorem 1.22 relates this Dirichlet problem to Poisson–Regularity estimates for the adjoint operator and to local landscape and Green function estimates. The open exponent ranges in those assertions are not replaced by endpoint claims. In particular, Remark 1.13 uses the conjugates \(q'\) and \(r'\) in the Carleson functionals; treating these as \(q\) and \(r\) would produce a spurious criticism.
The following checks support the main Poisson argument.

1. The near-pole estimate on pp. 24–25 uses Definition 2.12(vii), the energy mappings \(L^{-1}:L^{2_*}\to L^{2^*}\) and \(L^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{div}}:L^2\to L^{2^*}\). Their exponents have \(1/2_*+1/2^*=1\) and \(d/2-d/2^*=1\), giving the required factor \(\delta\) for the divergence data. It does not require the erroneous quantitative Lorentz assertion identified in Problem 1.

2. The choice \(p_1>p\) in the reverse Hölder argument gives \(p_1'<p'\). Consequently \(p'/p_1'>1\), which is the range needed for the subsequent maximal-operator estimate. Far-field contributions carry a positive Hölder exponent and a summable geometric factor.

3. In the duality step on p. 31, \(L^*v=H\) and \(Lw=-\mathop{\mathrm{div}}F\) give \[\int_\Omega Hw=\int_\Omega A^T
abla v\cdot
abla w
            =\int_\Omega F\cdot
abla v.\] The adjoint orientation is consistent. The analogous identity with vector test data and the Caccioppoli estimate account for the \(\delta^{-1}F\) term in Poisson–Regularity.

Theorem 1.33 concerns a bounded corkscrew domain with uniformly rectifiable boundary and a DKP matrix with an arbitrary finite global DKP constant. In the orientation of its statement, \((D^{L^*}_{p'})\) implies \((R^L_p)\). The reduction on pp. 33–34 passes through the conormal functional of Proposition 4.4. Section 5 constructs Lipschitz pieces with small local coefficient control; Theorem 6.3 then invokes a local regularity theorem. Section 7 estimates the almost elliptic extension and completes the conormal estimate. Retaining \(\mathcal C_2(F)\), including in the term \(T_{222}\), is substantive: a bound only with \(\mathcal C_{p'}(F)\) would not supply the same conclusion when \(p\leq2\).

The reading checked the stated hypotheses, the direction of these reductions, the scaling, signs, conjugate exponents, and the near/far decompositions. It is not a claim to have independently re-proved every external geometric or elliptic theorem used in Sections 5–7.
# Problem 1: the Lorentz estimate has the wrong dimension
## Statement and exact location

Definition 2.12(v), p. 21, asserts an \(L^\infty\) estimate for the Green representation with \[H\in L^{n/2,1}(\Omega),\qquad F\in L^{n,1}(\Omega),
 \qquad
 \|w\|_\infty\lesssim
 \|H\|_{L^{n/2,1}}+\|F\|_{L^{n,1}}.\] Here the ambient space is \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\). The same exponents occur in the acquired TeX, so this is not a text-extraction error.
## Counterexample within the geometric and elliptic assumptions
## Correction and impact

For the scalar data, the critical Lorentz exponent indicated by the Green kernel is \(d/2=(n+1)/2\). Indeed the upper bound \(G(x,y)\lesssim |x-y|^{2-d}\) and rearrangement give \[|L^{-1}H(x)|
 \lesssim \int_0^\infty s^{2/d-1}H^*(s)\,ds
 \lesssim \|H\|_{L^{d/2,1}}.\] This verifies the scalar \(L^\infty\) repair; it does not by itself prove every assertion about the vector data or the energy-space membership on unbounded domains. Those assertions should be stated with their own hypotheses.

The confirmed impact is Minor. The erroneous uniform bound is a preliminary assertion, while the main quantitative near-pole estimate uses the correctly scaled energy mappings in part (vii). Bounded compactly supported data still have a valid Green representation. The counterexample does not contradict Theorem 1.11.
# Problem 2: signed sequences invalidate Lemma A.9
## Statement and mechanism

On pp. 58–59 the passage from sequences to functions is \[F(u)(x)=\frac{\sum_Q u_Q(x)\mathbf1_{w^*(Q)}(x)}
                   {\sum_Q\mathbf1_{w^*(Q)}(x)}.\] Lemma A.9, (A.10)–(A.11), claims two-sided norm equivalences for every sequence. Its proof assumes \(u_Q\geq0\) without loss of generality. Such a reduction is valid for an upper estimate, but fails for a lower estimate of a signed averaging map.
## An admissible overlap and a nonzero kernel vector

Use \(\Omega=\mathbb R^3_+\). To respect the dyadic normalization on p. 17, at generation \(j\) partition its boundary into half-open squares of geometric side \(2^{-j-1}\) and assign them the manuscript’s scale \(\ell(Q)=2^{-j}\). Their diameter is \(2^{-j}/\sqrt2\leq\ell(Q)\), their area is \(\ell(Q)^2/4\), and the nested partitions satisfy the thin-boundary condition. These boundary scales differ from the ordinary geometric side lengths of the interior Whitney cubes. Use the following \(1/2\)-Whitney decomposition. For every \(a=2^m\), \(m\in\mathbb Z\), tile the slab \([64a,128a]\) by cubes of side \(a\) with vertical intervals \([ja,(j+1)a]\), \(j=64,\ldots,127\), and the standard horizontal grid. Interiors are disjoint and the slabs cover all positive heights. In the notation of p. 19, \(\widehat c=1/2\) gives \(k=3\), and each such cube satisfies \[32\,\operatorname{diam}I
 \leq\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}(I,\partial\Omega)
 \leq256\,\operatorname{diam}I,\] because \(32\sqrt3<64\) and \(127<256\sqrt3\).

Let \[I=[0,1]^2\times[64,65],\quad
 Q=[0,\tfrac12)\times[0,\tfrac12),\quad
R=[\tfrac12,1)\times[0,\tfrac12).\] The boundary cubes are disjoint and have assigned scale \(\ell(Q)=\ell(R)=1=\ell(I)\), although their geometric sides are \(1/2\). Both have distance \(64\) from \(I\), hence satisfy (2.7), whose bound is \(512\operatorname{diam}I\). Thus \(I\subset w(Q)\cap w(R)\) and also \(I\subset w^*(Q)\cap w^*(R)\).

Set \(u_Q=\mathbf1_I\), \(u_R=-\mathbf1_I\), and all other coordinates equal to zero. Then \(F(u)=0\) everywhere, whereas the discrete non-tangential sequence functional is strictly positive on \(Q\cup R\). For \(p=q=2\), write \(V_Q=m(w^*(Q))\) and \(V_R=m(w^*(R))\). Both are finite and positive, and the squared non-tangential sequence norm is \(\tfrac14(V_Q^{-1}+V_R^{-1})>0\). The discrete Carleson sequence norm is also finite and nonzero. It is positive on \(Q\) and locally bounded by \(4(\sqrt{V_Q}+\sqrt{V_R})\). A dyadic ancestor containing \(Q\) or \(R\) and a distant point \(\xi\) has area bounded below by a constant times \(|\xi|^2\). The functional therefore decays as \(O(|\xi|^{-2})\), whose square is integrable on the two-dimensional boundary. Both claimed equivalences therefore fail for these signed data.
## Repair and actual downstream use

For arbitrary signed sequences, retain the bounds from the sequence norm to the norm of \(F(u)\). They follow from \(|F(u)|\leq F(|u|)\) and the positive estimates. The reverse inequalities can be stated for coordinatewise nonnegative sequences: bounded overlap then gives \(u_Q\leq C F(u)\) on \(w^*(Q)\), which is precisely the pointwise argument in the manuscript.

This correction has bounded impact. In Lemma A.18 on p. 61, the duality argument may first replace the function by its absolute value and choose nonnegative dual sequence coordinates. Replacing those coordinates by their absolute values preserves their sequence norm and improves their pairing with a nonnegative function. The corrected positive version of Lemma A.9 therefore suffices there.

In Appendix A.3 on p. 63, the difference \(S(H)-h^k\) need not be nonnegative. However, the needed convergence follows from the upper inequality \[\|\mathcal C_q^d F(S(H)-h^k)\|_{L^p}
 \lesssim\|\mathcal C_q^s(S(H)-h^k)\|_{L^p}\longrightarrow0.\] The displayed two-sided comparison is unnecessary for that conclusion. This is a Minor correction to an overbroad lemma, not a counterexample to Proposition 2.4 or the main PDE results.
# Problem 3: a sign condition is missing from the Harnack estimate

A fixed-sign hypothesis is necessary for the Harnack part. The local boundedness and Hölder estimates do not require that extra sign restriction in the same way. On pp. 24–25, the Harnack comparison is applied to the positive Green function; the boundary arguments also explicitly use nonnegative solutions or elliptic measure. The counterexample therefore does not invalidate those applications. The identified impact is Minor. The review does not claim a new proof of the full rough-coefficient Harnack theorem.
# An unresolved root condition in the corona argument

On p. 36 the family \(\mathcal B(\varepsilon,\theta)\) contains cubes with either excessive bilateral flatness error or \(\lambda_\Omega(Q)>\theta\). The local construction begins with \(R\notin\mathcal B\). In contrast, the explicit inductive definition of \(\mathrm{Top}\) on p. 41 imposes only \(b\beta_\sigma(k_1R)\leq\varepsilon\) on the roots it selects.

The proof of Lemma 5.28 on p. 43 uses the assertion that a cube in the tree has either \(\lambda_\Omega(S')\leq\theta\) or a parent with that bound. At the root this requires particular care if the root itself were allowed to be coefficient-bad. The earlier condition \(R\notin\mathcal B\) may be intended to remain implicit when defining \(\mathrm{Top}\); that reading should be made explicit and checked against the packing and buffer estimates.

The requested evidence is a precise root admissibility rule and its propagation through Lemmas 5.22, 5.28, and Theorem 6.3. This review has not completed a counterexample satisfying all the geometric choices, nor a full repair of the corona construction. Accordingly this is recorded as Needs Evidence, with no confirmed Major or Critical finding attributed to it. Its position on the dependency chain to Theorem 1.33 warrants resolution even though the main theorem has not been disproved.
# Supporting checks

The supported classification is Minor: three false auxiliary statements have explicit counterexamples and delimited consequences. The unresolved corona issue is kept separate from those confirmed findings. No numerical quota was used in determining severity. There is no claim that all theorems are proved correct by this review.

Independent symbolic checks verify the piecewise Poisson equation, interface values and derivatives, boundary value, Green integral, diverging norm ratio, the ball moment in Problem 3, the Whitney inequalities and cancellation in Problem 2, and the elementary exponent identities used above. They are exact checks supporting the analytic arguments, not numerical evidence about general elliptic operators. The authored script, its actual command and exit status, standard output and error, and JSON results are retained with the report.

The source pages actually viewed are 5, 7, 10, 19–21, 24–25, 31, 33–36, 41, 43, 46, 58–59, 61, and 63–64. The full text was read on all 69 pages. A truncated final text response was closed by a targeted reread before this report was completed. No visual-inspection claim is made for other source pages. The final report is separately compiled, parsed, rendered, and actually viewed on every page; its exact hashes and execution evidence are recorded in the accompanying provenance.

The publisher PDF was not obtainable through the checked normal public link. The pinned manuscript is therefore the sole object of the findings. No separately released code or supplement was located in the documented bounded searches. Neither limitation is itself a scientific finding. The root question, the full imported corona geometry, and the external local regularity theorem remain outside a completed independent proof reconstruction.

Title: Scientific review of
Neck pinch singularities and Joyce conjectures in Lagrangian mean curvature flow with circle symmetry

Jason D. Lotay and Gonçalo Oliveira
Journal of the European Mathematical Society; DOI: 10.4171/jems/1661
Reviewed source: arXiv:2305.05744v2, 20 December 2024, 27 pages.
# Scope and assessment
This report concerns the exact author manuscript identified above. The frozen main PDF has SHA256

The ordinary publisher download returned a subscription page rather than a PDF. Equivalence with the publisher’s version of record has not been established. The manuscript describes itself as accepted in JEMS, with changes to the proofs of Propositions 3.4 and 4.2. Those changes are part of the version reviewed here.

Outcome: Major for P3; P1, P2 and P4 remain Minor. Other proof questions remain Needs Evidence. Four defects are established below: inconsistent preliminary normalizations, a false gradient evolution identity, an invalid first-contact argument in the convexity proof, and a missing stationary exception in Proposition 3.5. P3 concerns a proof step explicitly used to obtain compact finite-time singularities and the phase-order conclusion of a main theorem. A corrected convexity proof is supplied, with its assumptions verified separately; no counterexample to Theorems 1.1 or 1.4 is asserted. The ALE exterior argument and the passage from rescaled curves to the hypotheses of the imported singularity theorems require more precise justification; the present review neither certifies those steps nor asserts an unproved counterexample. The severity assessment concerns the affected derivations and their demonstrated dependencies. The scientific decision remains pending, and the human-review list is empty.
# Coverage and mathematical structure

All 27 PDF pages were read as extracted text. Actual page images were inspected for pages 2–4 and 8–27, including all six figures. The source TeX was additionally checked at the disputed normalization, evolution, convexity and area formulas. The archive returned by arXiv is a single gzip-compressed TeX file: the initial tar-extraction failure is preserved, and its subsequent correct decoding has a separate receipt.

The essential hypotheses are retained throughout: a complete ALE or ALF Gibbons–Hawking space, a finite set of centres, the potential \[\phi=m+\sum_{i=1}^k\frac1{2|x-p_i|},\qquad m\geq0,\] circle invariance, embeddedness and almost calibration where stipulated. A compact connected invariant Lagrangian is represented by an arc with centre endpoints; the noncompact examples have a different existence-at-infinity requirement. With Euclidean arclength \(s\), the reduction is \[\gamma_t=a\kappa N,\qquad a=\phi^{-1},\qquad \kappa=\theta_s,\qquad
 \kappa_t=(a\kappa)_{ss}+a\kappa^3.\] The direct moving-frame derivation on pp. 8–9 is consistent with this curvature equation. Also \[|\nabla\phi|\leq\sum_i(2r_i^2)^{-1}\leq2\phi^2,\qquad |\nabla a|\leq2;\] the signs and powers in the stated lower bound for \((a\kappa)_t\) follow.

The proof chain read was: preliminary convexity and disk variation (Section 3); localisation at centres, blow-up classification and Lawlor-neck identification (Section 4.1–4.2); finite-time barriers (Section 4.3–4.4); restart and the finite-centre argument (Section 5.1); convex-hull and stability alternatives (Section 5.2); long-time and current convergence (Section 5.3); and the distinction between chain order and phase order (Section 6). The perfect-Morse hypothesis in Theorem 1.4(d) and the allowance of equal limiting phases were not dropped. Figures 6.1–6.2 illustrate a nonconvex case and do not contradict the phase-order conclusion restricted by that hypothesis.
# P1: preliminary Gibbons–Hawking normalizations
Severity: Minor. Locations: p. 4, definition of \(\alpha_i\), (2.1), and Proposition 2.1(a),(c).

The manuscript defines \(|\xi|^2=\phi^{-1}\), \(\eta(\xi)=1\), with \(\ker\eta=\xi^\perp\), and \(\alpha_i=I_i(\phi^{-1}\eta)\), but writes \(g=\phi^{-1}\eta^2+\sum_i\alpha_i^2\). Choose a \(g\)-orthonormal coframe \(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3\) adapted to \(\xi\). Then \(\eta=\sqrt{\phi}\,e^0\) and, up to irrelevant signs, \(\alpha_i=\phi^{-1/2}e^i\). Consequently the printed right-hand side is \[(e^0)^2+\phi^{-1}\bigl((e^1)^2+(e^2)^2+(e^3)^2\bigr),\] which differs from \(g\) whenever \(\phi\ne1\).

A consistent orthonormal convention is \[\alpha_i=I_i(\phi^{-1/2}\eta),\qquad
 g_E=\phi^{-1}\sum_i\alpha_i^2,\qquad
 \mathrm{vol}_g=\phi^{-1/2}\eta\wedge\alpha_1\wedge\alpha_2\wedge\alpha_3.\] It yields the usual metric (2.4) and forms (2.5) already printed in the manuscript. Thus this is a repairable normalization defect in the preliminaries, not a counterexample to the later analysis formulated using (2.4). The positive factor in the printed volume form does not by itself change orientation; the issue is metric normalization. The source TeX confirms the powers, excluding an extraction artefact.
# P2: the gradient evolution identity omits moving-metric terms
Severity: Minor. Location: p. 8, the unnumbered identity following (3.2).

The asserted identity is \[(\partial_t+\Delta)|d\theta|^2=-2|\nabla d\theta|^2,
 \qquad \Delta=d^*d.\] A counterexample can be made within the graded, circle-invariant setting; a whole product torus, which is not graded, is unnecessary. In flat \(\mathbb C^2\), put \[R(t)^2=R_0^2-2t,\qquad
 L_t=\{(R(t)e^{iu},R(t)e^{iv}):u+v\pmod{2\pi}\in(-\delta,\delta)\},
 \quad 0<\delta<\pi/2 .\] This is a smooth open annulus, invariant under the tri-Hamiltonian action \((z_1,z_2)\mapsto(e^{i\alpha}z_1,e^{-i\alpha}z_2)\). It is a restriction of the normal mean curvature flow of the product of two shrinking circles. It has a global grading \(\theta=u+v+\pi\) on the chosen branch and angle oscillation \(2\delta<\pi\). Intrinsically, \[g_t=R(t)^2(du^2+dv^2),\quad
 |d\theta|^2=\frac2{R(t)^2},\quad
 \nabla d\theta=0,\quad
 \Delta|d\theta|^2=0,\quad
 \partial_t|d\theta|^2=\frac4{R(t)^4}>0.\] The displayed identity is therefore false even in flat ambient geometry and for a global grading. This is a local identity test on an open annulus, not a compact-flow counterexample to Theorem 1.4.

In Euclidean ambient space the missing contribution can be written \(2|A(\nabla\theta,\cdot)|^2\) in the standard moving-metric Bochner formula; curved ambient space also requires its curvature terms. The identity should be removed or replaced with a correctly stated formula. The subsequent curvature equation has a separate direct proof and is not invalidated by this example. No essential later use of the false equality was established in this review.
# P3: the first-contact argument crosses its sign domain
Severity: Major. Location: Proposition 3.4, pp. 10–11, (3.8)–(3.9).

Set \(f=a\kappa\). The manuscript obtains \(f_t\geq a f_{ss}-cf\) only on the set \(f\geq0\), then applies it at a first zero of \(f^\varepsilon=f+\varepsilon t\), with \(t_0>0\). At that point \[f(t_0,x_0)=-\varepsilon t_0<0,\] so the preceding sign-restricted inequality is unavailable. The text also replaces this value by zero. This invalidates the written contradiction, independently of the separate assertion about short-time positivity of the mean-curvature norm.

The statement has a direct repair under the smoothness and bounded-curvature assumptions invoked in this proof. Since \(a_t=(\partial_Na)f\), the exact curvature equation gives \[f_t=a f_{ss}+b f,\qquad b=\kappa\,\partial_Na+a\kappa^2.\] On the stipulated compact smooth time interval, \(|\nabla a|\leq2\), bounded \(\kappa\), and bounded \(a\) give \(|b|\leq B\). Take \(K>B\) and \(w=e^{-Kt}f\). Then \[w_t=a w_{ss}+(b-K)w.\] Initially \(w\geq0\), and its endpoint values are zero. If it had a negative value, a negative minimum over a compact preceding spacetime interval would lie at positive time and at an interior spatial point. There \(w_t\leq0\), \(w_{ss}\geq0\), and \((b-K)w>0\), a contradiction. Hence \(f\geq0\). The strong maximum principle on interior regions, where \(a>0\), gives strict interior positivity from the strictly positive initial curvature. Endpoint degeneracy does not interfere with the negative-minimum argument, since the endpoint values are zero.

This repairs the relevant convexity conclusion without assuming a maximum principle for \(|H|\). It applies on the smooth compact time intervals, with bounded curvature and zero endpoint values, stipulated in the source proof. It does not certify weaker endpoint regularity or the separate passage through singular times.

Dependency and impact. Proposition 3.4 is explicitly invoked in Theorem 4.13 (p. 19), which supplies Theorem 4.14 and the compact examples in Theorem 1.1(b). It is also explicitly invoked in Corollary 5.5 (p. 22); that convex-hull result is then used for the phase-order conclusion of Theorem 5.9(b) (p. 24), and hence Theorem 1.4(d) (p. 3). The written first-contact contradiction is therefore a demonstrated invalid derivation tied directly to central contributions. This supports Major for P3. The replacement proof above restores this convexity step under its stated assumptions; repair verification is separate from the severity of the original argument, and does not certify the remaining global proof.
# P4: Proposition 3.5 includes stationary straight lines
Severity: Minor. Location: p. 11, Proposition 3.5.

The proposition assumes only \(\kappa_0\geq0\), yet concludes \(\kappa_t>0\) for every \(t\in[0,T]\). Take a single centre at the origin and \[\phi(x)=\frac1{2|x|},\qquad \gamma_t(s)=(s,1,0),\quad s\in\mathbb R.\] This embedded planar curve avoids the centre, has \(\kappa_t=0\), and satisfies \(\partial_t\gamma=a\kappa N=0\) for all time. It meets every hypothesis of this auxiliary proposition and violates its conclusion even for \(t>0\). Inclusion of \(t=0\) is an additional immediate problem for initially nonnegative curvature with zeros.

A strict-positivity statement must exclude the identically straight solution and start at \(t>0\); in a noncompact formulation it must also specify the conditions allowing the relevant global maximum principle. These are necessary corrections, not a certification of every possible noncompact extension. The manuscript introduces this proposition for possible future study, and no dependence of the principal compact theorem on its overbroad form was identified.
# Area convention and the finite-time barrier

Definition 4.9 calls the pacman disk a planar region, whereas Proposition 4.10 uses an area derivative derived from the Kähler area of a lift. These agree only after specifying the weight. For a planar region \(D_t\), put \[E(t)=\int_{D_t}dA_E,\qquad B(t)=\int_{D_t}\phi\,dA_E .\] With consistent orientation and only \(\gamma_t\) moving, \[E'(t)=\int_{\gamma_t}a\kappa\,ds,\qquad
 B'(t)=\int_{\gamma_t}\kappa\,ds
       =\theta_t(p_+)-\theta_t(p_-).\] The latter is also the Kähler area density supplied by (2.5) on the plane \(\mu_1=\mathrm{constant}\). The centre singularities \(1/r\) are locally integrable in two dimensions.

The natural weighted-area interpretation repairs this specific issue. It is recorded as a clarification with a conditional counterexample, not as a fifth unconditional theorem defect. For general triads made of broken straight segments, the proof’s assertion that the chord lines \(\ell_\pm\) are parts of the barrier also needs explanation; the convex-polygon application has extra angle-order information. No verified counterexample to that full application is asserted.
# Unresolved dependencies and rejected overstatements
## ALE exterior control

On p. 15, the proof of Proposition 4.3 infers uniform equivalence with ordinary curve shortening outside a compact set from finiteness of the centre set. For ALE spaces, \[\phi(x)\sim\frac{k}{2|x|},\qquad a(x)\sim\frac{2|x|}{k}\longrightarrow\infty .\] An upper uniform comparison of coefficients is false. For ALF with \(m>0\), \(a\to1/m\), so the two cases differ. A weighted parabolic existence and asymptotic-preservation argument, or a precise match to the hypotheses of the cited work of Su, is needed for the noncompact branch. The full hypotheses of that external existence theorem were not accessible through the checked normal links. This is Needs Evidence concerning a core proof step, not a proven failure of existence.
## Blow-up and imported theorems

Theorem 1.1 of Lambert–Lotay–Schulze, arXiv:1901.05383v2, requires an ancient exact almost calibrated solution with uniformly bounded area ratios and angle, and a blow-down consisting of two transverse multiplicity-one planes. Its conclusion classifies that ancient solution. Its statement and the adjoining discussion of exactness of Type II blow-ups were checked on pp. 1–2. A graphical projected curve alone should not be substituted for this entire list; the transversality, multiplicity and actual blow-down must be supplied.

The Hopf model has \(\pi_H(\rho z)=\rho^2\pi_H(z)\). A base dilation \(\lambda\) therefore corresponds to ambient dilation \(\sqrt\lambda\) and the usual MCF time scale \(\lambda^{-1}\), not \(\lambda^{-2}\). In the one-centre equation \(a=2r\), the base-space/time rescaling used in (4.8) has an extra factor \(\lambda^{-1}\) in its velocity equation. It can be useful for a stationary spatial limit, but is not itself a standard parabolic tangent-flow scaling. The record-minimum condition (4.7), imposed after an arbitrary sequence of times is specified, also needs a selection or interpolation argument. These observations identify what the bridge to a tangent flow must prove; they do not show that the Lawlor-neck conclusion is false.

Theorems 1.1–1.2 of Lotay–Schulze–Székelyhidi, arXiv:2208.11054v1, were checked on pp. 1–2. They give tangent-flow uniqueness and a restart from a \(C^1\) immersed limit when the stipulated zero-Maslov/rational and two-plane tangent hypotheses hold at the first singular time. Hence an objection that the citation contains no restart theorem is rejected. The current manuscript’s localisation from a compact Calabi–Yau ambient space to the bounded Gibbons–Hawking region still needs its analytic justification. Neither external paper was independently reproved in full.

Title: Scientific review of
Long time energy averages and a lower resolvent estimate for damped waves

Matthieu Léautaud
Journal of the European Mathematical Society; DOI: 10.4171/jems/1662
Reviewed source: arXiv:2309.12709v1, submitted 22 September 2023, 53 pages.
The document itself is dated 25 September 2023.
# Scope and assessment
This review concerns the exact author manuscript identified above, not an assumed equivalent publisher text. The frozen PDF has SHA256
The normal publisher download did not supply the version of record. The pinned arXiv source was subsequently acquired and the disputed formulas were checked in its TeX as well as in the PDF.

Outcome after focused independent verification: Major. Lemma B.5 has an incorrect variational constant, and the resulting abstract pointwise estimate (3.6) is false under its stated hypotheses. Section 3 below gives both the correct variational argument and a full analytic counterexample to (3.6). The defect propagates to quantitative coefficients in several principal statements. Six further findings are described in Section 4. P4 and P5 also invalidate steps explicitly used in the central logarithmic-resolvent proof and are classified as Major. P2, P3, P6 and P7 remain Minor for the bounded reasons given with each finding.

The counterexample is an abstract finite-dimensional contraction semigroup. It is not a counterexample to the geometric PDE statement of Theorem 5.1. The qualitative logarithmic lower bound remains accessible by the paper’s method after changing the optimization constant and making the local corrections below. Nor is the vector-valued averaged estimate in Section 6 refuted. This revised report incorporates focused independent AI verification of the reported Problems and their proof dependencies. Scientific adjudication remains pending; no human review or author adoption is claimed.
# Coverage, hypotheses and proof structure

In the preserved initial review, all 53 pages were read as extracted text, including the appendices and bibliography. The source-page images recorded as inspected in that review were 1, 3–5, 9–14, 18–20, 23, 27, 31–36, 38–39, 41, 45–46 and 48–50. The review distinguishes text reading, actual image viewing, independent calculation, and imported results. The initial review also checked the source TeX at the variational lemma, Theorem 3.1, the smoothing construction, the diagonal damping and the transformed initial condition. The focused independent verification revisited P1–P7 and their relevant source passages, including the principal-symbol convention on p. 43; it does not claim a second exhaustive review.

The geometric setting is a smooth compact connected manifold without boundary, with nonpositive Laplacian, damping \(b\geq0\), and the mass parameter treated separately for \(m>0\) and \(m=0\). For \(m>0\), the energy is a norm; for \(m=0\), the displacement must be taken modulo constants while the velocity remains unrestricted. The first-order formulation uses \(\Lambda_m=\sqrt{-\Delta+m}\) and \[\mathsf P_m=\Lambda_m\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)
       +\frac{ib}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.\] The conjugations, damping sign, energy factors, and the distinct roles of generators, resolvents and semigroups were checked. The zero-mode formulas require the repairs in P2.

Section 3 starts with a selfadjoint \(P_h\) on an \(h\)-independent domain, a bounded accretive \(Q_h\), and \[\mathsf P_h=P_h+ihQ_h,\quad
 \Pi_\varepsilon=\chi((P_h-1)/\varepsilon),\quad
 \left\|(\mathsf P_h-\tau)^{-1}\right\|\leq G(h)/h.\] The normalization of the semiclassical Fourier transform, contraction estimate, division by \(T_h\), and the off-window remainder were traced. The unoptimized time-average estimate (3.4) and the ratio in (3.5) are consistent with this argument. The subsequent optimization is not. The higher-order off-window parametrix in Section 3.2 explicitly assumes a smooth time cutoff; its use for the stated \(H^1\) weights needs the clarification in Section 5.

The logarithmic propagation argument has the strict loss condition \[d=\mu\Upsilon_1+\max(ho,
u)<	frac12.\] Its Egorov remainder is \(O(th^{1-2d})\), and coherent-state evaluation costs \(O(h^{1/2-d})\). Smoothing contributes \(O(t\omega(\kappa h^
u))\), which tends to zero at \(t=\mu\log(1/h)\) under the stated modulus condition. In the resolvent comparison, choosing \(\widetilde\delta=h^{(1-2ho)/4}\) makes \[\widetilde\delta^{-2}h^{1-2ho}\log(1/h)
 =h^{(1-2ho)/2}\log(1/h)\longrightarrow0.\] Thus the strict restrictions on \(ho,
u,\mu\), rather than endpoint equality, are essential. The symbolic calculus and imported functional-calculus results were read as dependencies; they were not all independently reproved.

Section 6 is logically separate from the erroneous optimization. Its weighted resolvent hypotheses, accretivity, vector-valued Plancherel argument, dyadic summability conditions and damping regularity assumptions were traced. The incorrect operator-norm restatement P6 is distinct from the valid vector inequality used in Theorem 1.5.
# P1 — Major: the optimization constant and an abstract counterexample
## The exact variational value

Lemma B.5, pp. 49–50, claims the infimum \(2\) for \[I=\inf\left\{\int_\mathbb R|\psi'(t)|^2\,\mathrm dt:
 \psi\in H^1_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbb R),\
 \operatorname{supp}\psi\subset[0,\infty),\
 \int_0^1|\psi(t)|^2\,\mathrm dt=1\right\}.\] In fact, \[I=\frac{\pi^2}{4}.\] For the lower bound, \(\psi(0)=0\). Reflect its restriction to \([0,1]\) about \(1\) to obtain \(v\in H^1_0(0,2)\). The sine-series Dirichlet inequality on \((0,2)\) gives \[2\int_0^1|\psi'|^2
 =\int_0^2|v'|^2
 \geq\frac{\pi^2}{4}\int_0^2|v|^2
 =\frac{\pi^2}{2}.\] The energy outside \([0,1]\) is nonnegative. For the upper bound, take \(L>1\) and \[\psi_L(t)=
 \begin{cases}
  \sqrt2\sin(\pi t/2),&0\leq t\leq1,\\
  \sqrt2(L-t)/(L-1),&1<t\leq L,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}\] Then \(\int_0^1\psi_L^2=1\) and \(\int_\mathbb R|\psi_L'|^2=\pi^2/4+2/(L-1)\). These admissible \(H^1\) functions establish the infimum; smoothing and a small translation, followed by normalization, give the same limiting ratio if smooth cutoffs away from zero are needed. The infimum is not attained by a compactly supported function: equality on \([0,1]\) forces a nonzero value at \(1\), while equality in the total energy would require zero tail energy.

The paper’s proposed first segment \(\sqrt2\,t\) has squared \(L^2(0,1)\) norm \(2/3\), not \(1\). Its linear tail also gives energy \(2/(L-1)\), not the printed tail contribution. The problem is therefore not a harmless choice of normalization in an otherwise sharp variational proof.
## A counterexample to Theorem 3.1, equation (3.6)

The following construction verifies every hypothesis of the abstract theorem. It uses a finite-dimensional space of fixed, large dimension; no matrix of that dimension was allocated or numerically simulated.

Let \(n=100000000\), \(\mathcal H=\mathbb C^n\), and let \(J\) be the right shift: \(Je_j=e_{j+1}\) for \(j<n\), \(Je_n=0\). Put \[A=J-I,\qquad D=\frac{A-A^*}{2i},\qquad
 Q=-\frac{A+A^*}{2}.\] Since \(\left\|J\right\|\leq1\), \(Q\geq0\) and \(\left\|Q\right\|\leq2\). Also \(D=D^*\) and \(iD-Q=A\). Set \[P_h=I+hD,\qquad \mathsf P_h=P_h+ihQ=I-ihA.\] The domain is the entire fixed space \(\mathcal H\). All real numbers belong to \(\rho(\mathsf P_h)\), since its only eigenvalue is \(1+ih\), and \[e^{it\mathsf P_h/h}=e^{it/h}e^{tA}\] is a contraction. Choose \(\varepsilon=1/2\) and an allowed \(\chi\) which equals \(1\) near \(0\). For all sufficiently small \(h\), the functional-calculus cutoff \(\Pi_\varepsilon\) is exactly \(I\).

The exact uniform resolvent constant for \(A\) is \[G:=\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}\left\|(is-A)^{-1}\right\|
 =\left\|(I-J)^{-1}\right\|
 =\frac1{2\sin(\pi/(4n+2))}.\] Here the finite expansion \((is-A)^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1+is)^{-k-1}J^k\) has entrywise absolute value bounded by the nonnegative matrix \((I-J)^{-1}\). This implies the operator-norm upper bound, with equality at \(s=0\). For completeness, \(B=I-J\) has \(B^*B\) tridiagonal, with diagonal \(2\) except for the final entry \(1\), and off-diagonal \(-1\). The eigenvector recurrence has \(v_j=\sin(j\theta)\), \(v_0=0\), \(v_{n+1}=v_n\); its smallest eigenvalue corresponds to \(\theta=\pi/(2n+1)\) and is \(4\sin^2(\pi/(4n+2))\). This proves the displayed formula for every \(n\). Scaling gives \(\left\|(\mathsf P_h-\tau)^{-1}\right\|\leq G/h\) for every real \(\tau\). Thus \(G(h)=G\) satisfies (3.3).

Take \[T=95000000,\qquad a=100000,\qquad m=4000000,\qquad
 u=m^{-1/2}\sum_{j=1}^{m}e_j.\] The exponential series can be written \[e^{TA}u=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}e^{-T}\frac{T^k}{k!}J^ku.\] If \(K\) is a Poisson variable of mean and variance \(T\), then \(\Pr(|K-T|\leq a)\geq1-T/a^2=1981/2000\), by the elementary second-moment bound. For each integer \[T+a+1\leq j\leq T-a+m,\] the \(j\)-th coordinate contains every term with \(|k-T|\leq a\). These \(m-2a\) coordinates all lie within \(\{1,\dots,n\}\). Consequently \[\left\|e^{TA}u\right\|^2
 \geq \frac{m-2a}{m}\left(\frac{1981}{2000}\right)^2
 =\frac{74562859}{80000000}
 =0.9320357375.\]
## Propagation and repair

The error enters the optimization on p. 23, the final assertion of Theorem 3.3, Theorem 1.6 (1.10), Theorem 3.7 (3.34), and the use of (5.6) in deriving (5.15)–(5.16). The ratio in (3.5) supports a coefficient arbitrarily close to \(\pi^2/4\), with the same kind of cutoff-dependent remainder. The long tail of \(\psi_L\), with \(L-1\) of order \(\delta^{-1}\), has \(L^1\) norm of order \(\delta^{-1}\), so the \(\delta^{-2}\) remainder order can be retained after changing its constant.

With this repair, the method yields a logarithmic resolvent coefficient approaching \(2\mu/\pi\), rather than \(\mu/\sqrt2\). For positive \(\Upsilon_{\max}\), the corresponding leading coefficient in the first part of Corollary 5.2 becomes \(1/(\pi\Upsilon_{\max})\), rather than \(1/(2\sqrt2\,\Upsilon_{\max})\).
