# Further findings and repairs
## P2 — Minor: zero-mode reconstruction and generators

Corollary 2.5(6), p. 13, identifies the reduced state with \((u,u_t)\) while requiring \(u\) to remain mean-free. Take \(b=1\), a normalized constant function \(e_0\), and reduced initial data \((0,e_0)\). The reduced semigroup gives \((0,e^{-t}e_0)\), but the actual wave displacement is \((1-e^{-t})e_0\), which is not mean-free. The correct reduced state is \((\Pi_+u,u_t)\). The displacement is reconstructed by integrating its constant-mode velocity, as in Lemma 2.8, p. 14.

The additive kernel projectors in the generator identities (2.20) are also incorrect. Apply the first identity to \((e_0,0)\): the actual generator gives zero, while the printed right-hand side gives \((e_0,0)\). The analogous test uses the kernel vector \((e_0,-e_0)\) for \(\mathsf P\). Remove these additive projectors from the generator identities. They do belong, with the appropriate scalar factors, to the resolvent and semigroup identities. A displayed undamped upper-right identity on a mean-free first component must likewise be read as the projection \(\Pi_+\). The reconstructed solution and energy equivalence in Lemma 2.8 explain why these corrections do not invalidate the intended massless high-frequency argument.
## P3 — Minor: the transformed initial condition

In the proof of Proposition 2.11, pp. 18–19, \(W=(I-K)V\), with \(K=O(h)\), is followed by the unsupported assumption \(W(0)=V(0)=V_0\). In fact, \[W(0)=(I-K)V_0.\] The Duhamel formula must therefore contain \[W(t)=e^{it\mathsf P_{\rm diag}}V_0
       -e^{it\mathsf P_{\rm diag}}KV_0
       +i\int_0^t e^{i(t-s)\mathsf P_{\rm diag}}R e^{is\mathsf P_{\rm cut}}V_0\,\mathrm ds .\] The omitted term is bounded by \(Ch\,e^{Cth^{1-2\nu}}\left\|V_0\right\|\), which is already allowed by the proposition’s final estimate. This is a repairable proof defect, not a counterexample to that estimate.
## P4 — Major: loss of the half-damping factor

In Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 5.1, \(\mathsf P^
u\) contains \(ib_{h^
u}/2\) in every damping-matrix entry. In Step 2, (5.9) and the definition of \(\mathsf P_{m hw}\), p. 34, its diagonal damping has become \(ib_{h^
u}\). The resulting comparison is false. The following argument first identifies the discrepancy and then realizes it under the theorem’s geometric assumptions.

The contractive Duhamel estimate applied to these residuals therefore yields, for each fixed \(t>0\), \[e^{it\mathsf P^\nu}U_k
   =v_k\otimes(e^{itP_{\lambda_k}}e_1)+O_{L^2}(k^{-1}),\qquad
 e^{it\mathsf P_{\rm diag}^{\rm printed}}U_k
   =e^{it\lambda_k-t}U_k+O_{L^2}(k^{-1}),\] where the constant matrix in the first expression has \(b=1\). Consequently the norm of the difference, also after the displayed \(\chi_0\) cutoff, is bounded below by \(e^{-t/2}-e^{-t}+o(1)>0\). The asserted bound \(C(th_k^{1-2\nu}+h_k)\) tends to zero. Fixed \(t\) lies in \(0\leq t\leq\mu\log(1/h_k)\) for large \(k\). Thus the discrepancy occurs with all the geometric, regularity, time and localization requirements retained.

This comparison is the link from the actual wave evolution to (5.10), the scalar Egorov formula (5.11), and the coherent-state estimate (5.14). Its demonstrated failure is a central proof error and supports Major. Restore \(b_{h^\nu}/2\) in the diagonal and scalar operators. The squared-norm transport factor then becomes \(\exp(-\int_0^t b_{h^\nu}\circ\varphi^{-s}\,\mathrm ds)\). It equals \(1\) on an undamped trajectory for a zero-preserving regularization, so the corrected comparison preserves the intended lower-bound strategy. No failure of the qualitative logarithmic conclusion is inferred from this comparison error, and this repair does not repair P1.
## P5 — Major: the stated regularization does not preserve zeros

Proposition A.5(2), p. 45, asserts a property of the specific function defined by (A.10): it vanishes throughout the metric \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood of \(\{b=0\}\). The proof checks that the pre-convolution function vanishes at the evaluation point and then treats this as vanishing of its convolution. This inference is false, even at a point of the original zero set.

Take a circle with arclength coordinate \(x\) near \(0\), set \(b(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,0)\), and choose the valid modulus \(\omega(r)=r\). Use an admissible chart \(y=x/4\), with partition weight \(1\) near \(0\) and auxiliary cutoff \(1\) on a larger neighborhood. Choose an even, nonnegative, normalized smooth mollifier \(N\) supported where \(1/2<|z|<3/4\). For sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), every point in the convolution at \(0\) satisfies \[b(4\varepsilon z)=4\varepsilon|z|>2\varepsilon,\qquad
 \chi\bigl(b(4\varepsilon z)/\omega(\varepsilon)\bigr)=0.\] All coordinate and partition cutoffs are \(1\) on this support. Hence (A.10) gives the exact expression \[b_\varepsilon(0)=4\varepsilon\int |z|N(z)\,\mathrm dz,\qquad
              2\varepsilon<b_\varepsilon(0)<3\varepsilon ,\] although \(b(0)=0\). The atlas in Appendix A.1 has no metric-normalization restriction that excludes this chart. This refutes Proposition A.5(2) for its specified construction. It does not refute the existence of a different regularization satisfying Corollary A.6.

The asserted zero preservation is used explicitly through Corollary A.6 in (5.12), and then to replace the transport weight by \(1\) in the core coherent-state calculation (5.13). The provided construction fails to supply that stated premise. This invalid derivation in the main proof supports Major, independently of the availability of a repair.

For an explicit repair, choose a uniform constant \(L\) controlling distances under the inverse charts on the relevant compact neighborhoods, enlarge it for the finitely many remaining scales if needed, and take \(C\geq1+L\). Replace the cutoff denominator in (A.10) by \(\omega(C\varepsilon)\). If \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\{b=0\})\leq\varepsilon\), each sampled point is at distance at most \(C\varepsilon\) from that zero set. Its \(b\)-value is at most \(\omega(C\varepsilon)\), so the whole convolution integrand vanishes. Derivatives still fall on the mollifier, giving the same \(O(\varepsilon^{-|\alpha|})\) bounds; the cutoff and convolution errors are bounded by a constant times \(\omega(\kappa'\varepsilon)\). If the denominator vanishes at a relevant positive scale, connectedness and the modulus inequality force \(b\) to be constant, in which case take \(b_\varepsilon=b\). These choices preserve the logarithmic smallness assumption.

There is also useful counterevidence against claiming that the logarithmic conclusion itself fails: the approximation estimate alone gives \(0\leq b_{h^
u}\leq C\omega(\kappa h^
u)\) along an undamped trajectory. Therefore its transport factor is \(1+O(t\omega(\kappa h^
u))\), which tends to \(1\) at the allowed logarithmic times. This supplies an alternative bounded repair of the final asymptotic; it does not make the exact zero assertion or its original proof valid.
## P6 — Minor: supremum and time integration

The line introduced as another formulation of Lemma 6.3, p. 38, uses \(L^2(\mathbb R;\mathcal L(\mathcal H))\). The lemma instead controls the norm of a map \(\mathcal H\to L^2(\mathbb R;\mathcal H)\). These norms cannot be interchanged.

Here is a counterexample satisfying the lemma’s hypotheses. Let \[\mathcal H=\bigoplus_{n\geq1}\mathbb C^{N_n},\qquad
 N_n=2^n,\qquad q_n=2^{-n}.\] In block \(n\), with \(0\leq j<N_n\), define \[P_0e_{n,j}=(10n+jq_n)e_{n,j},\quad
 B_n=q_n I,\quad P=P_0+iB,\quad
 C_nu=q_n\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{N_n-1}u_j\Big)e_{n,0}.\] The real diagonal operator \(P_0\) is selfadjoint on its natural domain, \(B\) is bounded nonnegative, and \(e^{itP}\) is a contraction. All real \(\tau\) belong to \(\rho(P)\): each finite block has positive imaginary part, and the real parts of the blocks escape to infinity. Also \(\left\|C_n\right\|=\sqrt{q_n}\to0\), so \(C\) is bounded and compact.

On the other hand, \[\left\|C_ne^{itP_n}\right\|^2=q_n e^{-2q_nt}.\] For \(2^n\leq t\leq2^{n+1}\), this is at least \(2^{-n}e^{-4}\). Each of the disjoint intervals contributes at least \(e^{-4}\) to \(\int\left\|Ce^{itP}\right\|^2\,\mathrm dt\), so that integral diverges. Take \(\psi(t)=\min(t,1)\) for \(t\geq0\), and \(0\) for \(t<0\). It satisfies the stated \(H^1_{\rm loc}\) and support conditions, with \(\left\|\psi'\right\|_2=1\). The printed operator-valued left-hand side is infinite and its right-hand side is finite. Compactness of \(C\) also ensures norm continuity here; the issue is not measurability.

The valid formulation places the norm in \(\mathcal L(\mathcal H,L^2(\mathbb R;\mathcal H))\). Equation (6.6) and its vector-valued Plancherel proof use that correct order, as does the application to Theorem 1.5. Accordingly this isolated false reformulation is classified as Minor.
## P7 — Minor: the time scale in Lemma B.1

Lemma B.1, p. 48, defines \(P_Q=P+iQ\) but prints an estimate for \(e^{itP_Q/h}\) with exponent \(C_0th^{1-2
u}\). The principal-symbol convention matters here: Appendix A.4 takes the order-zero symbol modulo \(h^{1-2
u}S_
u^{-1}\).

An admissible counterexample is obtained on \(M=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z\), with \(N=1\), \(\nu=0\), \(P=0\) on all of \(L^2(M)\), and \[Q_h=-h\chi(hD_x),\qquad D_x=-i\partial_x,\qquad
 \chi\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb R;[0,1]),\quad \chi(0)=1 .\] The Fourier multiplier \(\chi(hD_x)\) is semiclassically smoothing, so \(Q_h\in h\Psi^{-\infty}\subset h\Psi^{-1}\). Its order-zero principal symbol is therefore exactly the zero class under the paper’s definition and admits the nonnegative representative \(0\). The optional stronger assumption \(\operatorname{Re}Q_h\geq0\) is not imposed in the first assertion of the lemma and is not claimed here. For the normalized constant function \(e_0\), \[P_Qe_0=-ih e_0,\qquad
 \left\|e^{itP_Q/h}e_0\right\|=e^t,\] which exceeds \(e^{C_0ht}\) for every fixed \(t>0\) and all sufficiently small \(h\), regardless of the proposed finite \(C_0\). The unscaled evolution on the same mode is \(e^{ht}\), as required by the intended estimate.

The corrected general statement is \(\left\|e^{itP_Q}ight\|\leq e^{C_0th^{1-2
u}}\); for the scaled evolution its exponent is \(C_0th^{-2
u}\). With the paper’s sign convention, \(iP_Q-C_0h^{1-2
u}I\) is dissipative and generates a contraction. In Section 4.2, p. 30, the scaled operator is explicitly \(P_Q=h\widetilde P_Q\), where \(\widetilde P_Q=\Lambda\widetilde\chi_0(h\Lambda)+iQ\). Applying the corrected unscaled statement to \(\widetilde P_Q\) gives precisely the growth estimate used on p. 32; Section 2.3 likewise uses an unscaled evolution. Thus the literal displayed lemma is false, while this defect has not been shown to invalidate the actual semigroup bound required by the main proof. This is the reason for the Minor classification.
# Unresolved questions and limits of the conclusions

Theorem 3.3 assumes \(\psi\in C^\infty_c((0,\infty))\), and its improved remainder depends on \(\|\psi^{(N)}\|_1\). Theorems 1.6 and 3.7 state arbitrary \(H^1_{\mathrm{comp}}\) weights. Approximation in \(H^1\) alone does not uniformly control the higher-derivative remainder. An explicit extension argument or a restriction of the stated weight class is needed. This review has neither a counterexample nor a complete repair of that extension; it remains Needs Evidence, rather than a confirmed additional failure.

Remark 5.3 uses a small positive upper threshold for \(\omega(\varepsilon)\log\varepsilon\), a nonpositive quantity for small \(\varepsilon\). The proof’s error budget involves \(\omega(\varepsilon)\log(1/\varepsilon)\). The sign and the precise intended quantitative condition should be clarified; this is not used here to assert failure of Theorem 1.1.

The hypotheses of all imported pseudodifferential, spectral and semigroup results were traced where used, but a complete independent reconstruction of every cited theorem is not claimed. No numerical PDE solution or empirical experiment was performed. Missing released code or a publisher PDF is not counted as a mathematical defect.
# Verification evidence

The preserved initial calculation record and the independently written `acceptance_checks.py` both have actual successful execution records. The latter ran with Python 3.13.5 and SymPy 1.13.3, with exit code \(0\). It independently verified the cutoff integrals, exact rational gap in P1, the sine recurrence, the constant-mode ODE, the \(2\times2\) damping identity, the positive block integral in P6, and the scalar action in the revised P7 example. The torus construction in P4 is an analytic residual and Duhamel argument; no PDE solver was run. The large-dimensional example in P1 is also analytic, with bounded exact arithmetic support.

The exact acquired PDF and source manifest remain unchanged. The affected predecessor report and verification files are preserved in this paper’s revisions. The current findings and coverage distinguish the initial review from the focused independent check. In particular, the initial P7 example \(Q=-hI\) was not admissible under the source’s principal-symbol quotient and has been replaced by the localized multiplier above. P4 now includes the non-GCC geometry, and P4/P5 are graded by their documented core-proof dependencies. Source identities, calculations, actual source-page inspection, final compilation, dependency bindings and final report-page inspection are recorded in the existing verification structure.

The scientific analysis and newly performed computations, compilation, PDF parsing and page viewing belong to the primary executor of the respective initial or independent-verification conversation, as separately attributed in provenance. No scientific operation in the present independent check was delegated. Controller-reported UI observations and runtime self-description remain distinct. Scientific adjudication is pending, human reviews are empty, and no author adoption is asserted.

problems.title: Incorrect variational constant and false optimized abstract pointwise estimate
problems.source_location: Lemma B.5, pp.49-50 Theorem3.1 (3.6), p.20, optimization p.23 Theorem1.6 (1.10), p.5 Theorems3.3/3.7, pp.23/27 Theorem5.1, Corollary5.2 and (5.6),(5.15)-(5.16), pp.32-35
claim: Recorded check: Incorrect variational constant and false optimized abstract pointwise estimate
analysis:
Lemma B.5, pp. 49–50, claims the infimum \(2\) for \[I=\inf\left\{\int_\mathbb R|\psi'(t)|^2\,\mathrm dt:
 \psi\in H^1_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbb R),\
 \operatorname{supp}\psi\subset[0,\infty),\
 \int_0^1|\psi(t)|^2\,\mathrm dt=1\right\}.\] In fact, \[I=\frac{\pi^2}{4}.\] For the lower bound, \(\psi(0)=0\). Reflect its restriction to \([0,1]\) about \(1\) to obtain \(v\in H^1_0(0,2)\). The sine-series Dirichlet inequality on \((0,2)\) gives \[2\int_0^1|\psi'|^2
 =\int_0^2|v'|^2
 \geq\frac{\pi^2}{4}\int_0^2|v|^2
 =\frac{\pi^2}{2}.\] The energy outside \([0,1]\) is nonnegative. For the upper bound, take \(L>1\) and \[\psi_L(t)=
 \begin{cases}
  \sqrt2\sin(\pi t/2),&0\leq t\leq1,\\
  \sqrt2(L-t)/(L-1),&1<t\leq L,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}\] Then \(\int_0^1\psi_L^2=1\) and \(\int_\mathbb R|\psi_L'|^2=\pi^2/4+2/(L-1)\). These admissible \(H^1\) functions establish the infimum; smoothing and a small translation, followed by normalization, give the same limiting ratio if smooth cutoffs away from zero are needed. The infimum is not attained by a compactly supported function: equality on \([0,1]\) forces a nonzero value at \(1\), while equality in the total energy would require zero tail energy.

The paper’s proposed first segment \(\sqrt2\,t\) has squared \(L^2(0,1)\) norm \(2/3\), not \(1\). Its linear tail also gives energy \(2/(L-1)\), not the printed tail contribution. The problem is therefore not a harmless choice of normalization in an otherwise sharp variational proof.

The following construction verifies every hypothesis of the abstract theorem. It uses a finite-dimensional space of fixed, large dimension; no matrix of that dimension was allocated or numerically simulated.

Let \(n=100000000\), \(\mathcal H=\mathbb C^n\), and let \(J\) be the right shift: \(Je_j=e_{j+1}\) for \(j<n\), \(Je_n=0\). Put \[A=J-I,\qquad D=\frac{A-A^*}{2i},\qquad
 Q=-\frac{A+A^*}{2}.\] Since \(\left\|J\right\|\leq1\), \(Q\geq0\) and \(\left\|Q\right\|\leq2\). Also \(D=D^*\) and \(iD-Q=A\). Set \[P_h=I+hD,\qquad \mathsf P_h=P_h+ihQ=I-ihA.\] The domain is the entire fixed space \(\mathcal H\). All real numbers belong to \(\rho(\mathsf P_h)\), since its only eigenvalue is \(1+ih\), and \[e^{it\mathsf P_h/h}=e^{it/h}e^{tA}\] is a contraction. Choose \(\varepsilon=1/2\) and an allowed \(\chi\) which equals \(1\) near \(0\). For all sufficiently small \(h\), the functional-calculus cutoff \(\Pi_\varepsilon\) is exactly \(I\).

The exact uniform resolvent constant for \(A\) is \[G:=\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}\left\|(is-A)^{-1}\right\|
 =\left\|(I-J)^{-1}\right\|
 =\frac1{2\sin(\pi/(4n+2))}.\] Here the finite expansion \((is-A)^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1+is)^{-k-1}J^k\) has entrywise absolute value bounded by the nonnegative matrix \((I-J)^{-1}\). This implies the operator-norm upper bound, with equality at \(s=0\). For completeness, \(B=I-J\) has \(B^*B\) tridiagonal, with diagonal \(2\) except for the final entry \(1\), and off-diagonal \(-1\). The eigenvector recurrence has \(v_j=\sin(j\theta)\), \(v_0=0\), \(v_{n+1}=v_n\); its smallest eigenvalue corresponds to \(\theta=\pi/(2n+1)\) and is \(4\sin^2(\pi/(4n+2))\). This proves the displayed formula for every \(n\). Scaling gives \(\left\|(\mathsf P_h-\tau)^{-1}\right\|\leq G/h\) for every real \(\tau\). Thus \(G(h)=G\) satisfies (3.3).

Take \[T=95000000,\qquad a=100000,\qquad m=4000000,\qquad
 u=m^{-1/2}\sum_{j=1}^{m}e_j.\] The exponential series can be written \[e^{TA}u=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}e^{-T}\frac{T^k}{k!}J^ku.\] If \(K\) is a Poisson variable of mean and variance \(T\), then \(\Pr(|K-T|\leq a)\geq1-T/a^2=1981/2000\), by the elementary second-moment bound. For each integer \[T+a+1\leq j\leq T-a+m,\] the \(j\)-th coordinate contains every term with \(|k-T|\leq a\). These \(m-2a\) coordinates all lie within \(\{1,\dots,n\}\). Consequently \[\left\|e^{TA}u\right\|^2
 \geq \frac{m-2a}{m}\left(\frac{1981}{2000}\right)^2
 =\frac{74562859}{80000000}
 =0.9320357375.\]

The error enters the optimization on p. 23, the final assertion of Theorem 3.3, Theorem 1.6 (1.10), Theorem 3.7 (3.34), and the use of (5.6) in deriving (5.15)–(5.16). The ratio in (3.5) supports a coefficient arbitrarily close to \(\pi^2/4\), with the same kind of cutoff-dependent remainder. For an explicit repair, choose a uniform constant \(L\) controlling distances under the inverse charts on the relevant compact neighborhoods, enlarge it for the finitely many remaining scales if needed, and take \(C\geq1+L\). Replace the cutoff denominator in (A.10) by \(\omega(C\varepsilon)\). If \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\{b=0\})\leq\varepsilon\), each sampled point is at distance at most \(C\varepsilon\) from that zero set. Its \(b\)-value is at most \(\omega(C\varepsilon)\), so the whole convolution integrand vanishes. Derivatives still fall on the mollifier, giving the same \(O(\varepsilon^{-|\alpha|})\) bounds; the cutoff and convolution errors are bounded by a constant times \(\omega(\kappa'\varepsilon)\). If the denominator vanishes at a relevant positive scale, connectedness and the modulus inequality force \(b\) to be constant, in which case take \(b_\varepsilon=b\). These choices preserve the logarithmic smallness assumption.

There is also useful counterevidence against claiming that the logarithmic conclusion itself fails: the approximation estimate alone gives \(0\leq b_{h^
u}\leq C\omega(\kappa h^
u)\) along an undamped trajectory. Therefore its transport factor is \(1+O(t\omega(\kappa h^
u))\), which tends to \(1\) at the allowed logarithmic times. This supplies an alternative bounded repair of the final asymptotic; it does not make the exact zero assertion or its original proof valid.
result: Impact: The invalid construction is used viaA.6 to assert(5.12), then the exact unit transport weight in core(5.13). Major concerns that demonstrated proof failure, not theorem-wide collapse.

problems.title: An operator-valued restatement exchanges supremum and time integration
problems.source_location: After Lemma6.3, p.38
claim: Recorded check: An operator-valued restatement exchanges supremum and time integration
analysis: The line introduced as another formulation of Lemma 6.3, p. 38, uses \(L^2(\mathbb R;\mathcal L(\mathcal H))\). The lemma instead controls the norm of a map \(\mathcal H\to L^2(\mathbb R;\mathcal H)\). These norms cannot be interchanged.

Here is a counterexample satisfying the lemma’s hypotheses. Let \[\mathcal H=\bigoplus_{n\geq1}\mathbb C^{N_n},\qquad
 N_n=2^n,\qquad q_n=2^{-n}.\] In block \(n\), with \(0\leq j<N_n\), define \[P_0e_{n,j}=(10n+jq_n)e_{n,j},\quad
 B_n=q_n I,\quad P=P_0+iB,\quad
 C_nu=q_n\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{N_n-1}u_j\Big)e_{n,0}.\] The real diagonal operator \(P_0\) is selfadjoint on its natural domain, \(B\) is bounded nonnegative, and \(e^{itP}\) is a contraction. All real \(\tau\) belong to \(\rho(P)\): each finite block has positive imaginary part, and the real parts of the blocks escape to infinity. Also \(\left\|C_n\right\|=\sqrt{q_n}\to0\), so \(C\) is bounded and compact.

On the other hand, \[\left\|C_ne^{itP_n}\right\|^2=q_n e^{-2q_nt}.\] For \(2^n\leq t\leq2^{n+1}\), this is at least \(2^{-n}e^{-4}\). Each of the disjoint intervals contributes at least \(e^{-4}\) to \(\int\left\|Ce^{itP}\right\|^2\,\mathrm dt\), so that integral diverges. Take \(\psi(t)=\min(t,1)\) for \(t\geq0\), and \(0\) for \(t<0\). It satisfies the stated \(H^1_{\rm loc}\) and support conditions, with \(\left\|\psi'\right\|_2=1\). The printed operator-valued left-hand side is infinite and its right-hand side is finite. Compactness of \(C\) also ensures norm continuity here; the issue is not measurability.

The valid formulation places the norm in \(\mathcal L(\mathcal H,L^2(\mathbb R;\mathcal H))\). Equation (6.6) and its vector-valued Plancherel proof use that correct order, as does the application to Theorem 1.5. Accordingly this isolated false reformulation is classified as Minor.
result: Impact: False isolated reformulation; no contradiction to Lemma6.3 vector statement or Theorem1.5.

claim: Recorded check: Appendix semigroup estimate mixes scaled and unscaled time
analysis:
Lemma B.1, p. 48, defines \(P_Q=P+iQ\) but prints an estimate for \(e^{itP_Q/h}\) with exponent \(C_0th^{1-2
u}\). The principal-symbol convention matters here: Appendix A.4 takes the order-zero symbol modulo \(h^{1-2
u}S_
u^{-1}\).

An admissible counterexample is obtained on \(M=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z\), with \(N=1\), \(\nu=0\), \(P=0\) on all of \(L^2(M)\), and \[Q_h=-h\chi(hD_x),\qquad D_x=-i\partial_x,\qquad
 \chi\in C^\infty_c(\mathbb R;[0,1]),\quad \chi(0)=1 .\] The Fourier multiplier \(\chi(hD_x)\) is semiclassically smoothing, so \(Q_h\in h\Psi^{-\infty}\subset h\Psi^{-1}\). Its order-zero principal symbol is therefore exactly the zero class under the paper’s definition and admits the nonnegative representative \(0\). The optional stronger assumption \(\operatorname{Re}Q_h\geq0\) is not imposed in the first assertion of the lemma and is not claimed here. For the normalized constant function \(e_0\), \[P_Qe_0=-ih e_0,\qquad
 \left\|e^{itP_Q/h}e_0\right\|=e^t,\] which exceeds \(e^{C_0ht}\) for every fixed \(t>0\) and all sufficiently small \(h\), regardless of the proposed finite \(C_0\). The unscaled evolution on the same mode is \(e^{ht}\), as required by the intended estimate.

The corrected general statement is \(\left\|e^{itP_Q}ight\|\leq e^{C_0th^{1-2
u}}\); for the scaled evolution its exponent is \(C_0th^{-2
u}\). With the paper’s sign convention, \(iP_Q-C_0h^{1-2
u}I\) is dissipative and generates a contraction. In Section 4.2, p. 30, the scaled operator is explicitly \(P_Q=h\widetilde P_Q\), where \(\widetilde P_Q=\Lambda\widetilde\chi_0(h\Lambda)+iQ\). Applying the corrected unscaled statement to \(\widetilde P_Q\) gives precisely the growth estimate used on p. 32; Section 2.3 likewise uses an unscaled evolution. Thus the literal displayed lemma is false, while this defect has not been shown to invalidate the actual semigroup bound required by the main proof. This is the reason for the Minor classification.
result: Impact: False literal time-scale statement; no failure of the actual growth bound required atpp17/30-32 is established.

report: Date: Recovery-0024 M25-0290

Title: Initial scientific review of
The global stability of the Kaluza–Klein spacetime

Cécile Huneau, Annalaura Stingo, and Zoe Wyatt
Journal of the European Mathematical Society; DOI: 10.4171/jems/1663
Reviewed source: arXiv:2307.15267v1, 28 July 2023, 80 pages.
# Scope and initial assessment
This report concerns the exact author manuscript identified above. Its frozen PDF has SHA256

A publisher version was not available for comparison; equivalence with a version of record is not assumed. The pinned arXiv source was acquired, and the disputed formulas were checked in the TeX and in actual images of the corresponding PDF pages.

Initial outcome: Major. Two substantive issues affect the written proof. First, hyperboloidal paths used for sharp estimates leave the regions on which their input bounds have been established. This occurs in the exterior argument and again in the scaling-ray treatment of the nonzero modes. Second, the characteristic estimate in Lemma 4.13 is false as stated; an explicit smooth flat-metric example is given below, together with distinct boundary and mass-hypothesis problems in its application. Six local corrections concern definitions, algebra, time-flux bookkeeping and a source cutoff. A separate question about uniform flux positivity as the mass tends to zero is retained as NeedsEvidence, with its precise limitations.

None of the examples below is asserted to disprove the global stability theorem for vacuum Einstein data. The conclusions concern the argument in this particular manuscript. The proposed repairs identify work that would be needed; they do not certify a completed replacement proof. Severity reflects the role of each issue in the core argument. This is an initial scientific review, not independent acceptance. The scientific decision remains pending, and the human-review list is empty.
# Coverage, hypotheses and proof structure

All 80 pages were read as extracted text, including both appendices and the bibliography. Actual source-page images were inspected on pages 1, 3, 7–9, 14–16, 19–20, 22–23, 26–27, 36–40, 46–51, 59–63 and 65–77: 43 pages in total. The TeX was examined at the definitions, characteristic lemma, hyperboloidal operator formulas, oscillator argument and relevant cutoff constructions. The cited Huneau–Stingo manuscript [HS] was read in the relevant part of Section 5, and its pages 28–32 were actually viewed. A complete review of that separate paper is not claimed.

The reduced equation for \(h^1\) has weak-null, classical null, and higher-order terms, together with the differentiated mass-tail source. The exterior argument uses weighted energies for \(Z^{\leq N}h^1\) and for one additional ordinary derivative. Wave gauge improves the \(LT\) components; the improved bounds feed the commutator and weak-null estimates. The exterior energy inequality then supplies the flux through \[\widetilde{\mathcal H}=\{(t-1)^2-r^2=1,\ t\geq2\}.\] The actual exterior slice is \(r\geq\sqrt{t^2-2t}\), while the intended interior hyperboloids are \[\mathcal H_s=\{t^2-r^2=s^2\}\cap\mathcal D^i,
 \qquad
 \mathcal D^i=\{t\geq1+\sqrt{1+r^2}\}.\] Consequently \(t\leq s^2/2\) on \(\mathcal H_s\).

The interior proof fixes \(N\geq14\) and \(N_1=N-5\). The full energy allows a half-power loss, the zero-mode energy has a smaller loss, and a restricted number of Lorentz-vector-field derivatives admits the intermediate energy hierarchy. The zero-average component has a circle Poincaré inequality; the zero mode does not. Averaging eliminates pure zero-mode interactions from the zero-average equation, but mixed commutators remain. These distinctions were checked in the energy and derivative allocations, rather than treating all modes as a finite Klein–Gordon system.

The argument proceeds through hyperboloidal Sobolev and Hardy bounds, second-derivative estimates for the zero modes, improved \(TU\)-component decay, weak-null estimates and high-order commutators. The ray oscillator estimate yields improved nonzero-mode pointwise bounds. Enhanced zero-mode energies and scalar wave estimates then improve the zero-mode pointwise bound, followed by the mutual refinement in Proposition 4.32 and the energy closure in Section 4.10.

The ordering \(\zeta_i\ll\gamma_j\ll\delta_k\) is not, by itself, evidence of circularity. The final closure expressly replaces relevant \(\gamma\)-losses by \(c\sigma\) using Proposition 4.32. For finitely many indices, \(\sigma\) can be selected after the constants in that refinement so that \(c\sigma\) is smaller than the necessary gaps between \(\zeta\)’s. The review does not count the preliminary exponent ordering as a defect. The outstanding problems instead concern the domains and hypotheses needed to obtain those improved estimates.
# P1: sharp estimates use paths outside their established domains (Major)
## The exterior hyperboloidal path

In Proposition 3.3, Step 1 on page 22, the proof selects a time \(\tau_k\in[2^k,2^{k+1})\cap[2,T_0)\), then integrates the hyperboloidal derivative through a point \((t,x)\) until the path meets either \(\tau=\tau_k\) or \(r=2\tau\). The bounds being integrated have been established in \(\mathcal D^e\).

Let \(s_*^2=t^2-r^2\) denote the constant along this path. The exterior condition on that same hyperbola is \[r(\tau)^2=\tau^2-s_*^2\geq\tau^2-2\tau
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s_*^2\leq2\tau.\] Thus a backwards portion of a hyperbola through a point on \(\widetilde{\mathcal H}\) immediately enters \(\mathcal D^i\). For example, take \[t=15,\qquad r^2=195,\qquad s_*^2=30,\qquad \tau_k=9.\] Both times lie in the dyadic interval \([8,16)\). At time \(9\), the path has \(r^2=51\), while the exterior slice requires \(r^2\geq63\). The path has not met \(r=2\tau\), since \(r(\tau)<\tau\). The intermediate interval \(9\leq\tau<15\) is outside the domain of the exterior bounds used in (3.19).

This is not a peculiarity of choosing \(9\). Any selected \(\tau_k<16\) precedes some \(t\in[8,16)\); the separator point at that later \(t\) gives the same obstruction. Strictly exterior points sufficiently close to the separator also leave the exterior region before reaching the selected time. Consequently the stated endpoint alternatives do not justify the integration for all points being estimated.

A repair must use a path contained in the available region, control an additional boundary contribution, or establish estimates in an enlarged region. Selecting a later averaging window may help in part of a slab, but requires a separate argument near a finite bootstrap endpoint. The current review does not supply such a uniform replacement. The improved \(LT\) decay is used in subsequent commutator and flux estimates, so this is more than a notation correction.
## The scaling-ray initial term

For Proposition 4.22, pages 61–62, write \[p_\lambda=\left(\frac{\lambda t}{s},\frac{\lambda x}{s}\right),
 \qquad s^2=t^2-r^2.\] The proof of (4.100) treats \(p_{s_0}\) as lying on the truncated \(\mathcal H_{s_0}\), and uses its boundedness in \(t+r\) and the energy \(E^i(s_0,Z^{\leq2}\mathbf W)\). Direct substitution gives \[(t_\lambda-1)^2-r_\lambda^2-1
 =\lambda\left(\lambda-\frac{2t}{s}\right).\] For positive \(\lambda\), the ray lies in \(\mathcal D^i\) precisely when \(\lambda\geq2t/s\). Its natural entry parameter is therefore \[\lambda_0=\max\{s_0,2t/s\},\] not always \(s_0\).

A strictly interior example is \[t=49,\quad s=10,\quad r^2=2301,\quad s_0=\frac{21}{10}.\] Here \(49<s^2/2=50\), but \[t_{s_0}=\frac{1029}{100},
 \qquad
 \max_{\mathcal H_{s_0}}t=\frac{s_0^2}{2}=\frac{441}{200},
 \qquad
 \lambda_0=\frac{49}{5}>s_0.\] The starting point lies well outside \(\mathcal H_{s_0}\). For targets approaching the separator at large \(s\), its time is unbounded; the claim that \(1+t+r=O(1)\) at that starting point is therefore unavailable.

There is also a direct functional obstruction to the displayed use of the truncated initial energy. Choose a smooth spacetime bump supported near \(p_{s_0}\), outside a neighbourhood of the compact \(\mathcal H_{s_0}\), and multiply it by \(\cos y\). It has zero circle average. All its derivatives vanish on \(\mathcal H_{s_0}\), so \(E^i(s_0,Z^{\leq2}\mathbf W)=0\), but \(Y_{tx}(s_0)>0\) if the bump is nonzero at the ray point. This disproves a trace estimate of the form (4.100) from that truncated energy alone. It is a test of the claimed functional implication, not an Einstein counterexample.

The estimates for \(A_{tx}\) and \(B_{tx}\) likewise require justification on the part of the ray before it enters \(\mathcal D^i\). Merely changing the lower integration limit leaves a boundary term \(Y_{tx}(\lambda_0)\) to estimate with the required directional weight. The directly stated exterior bound for a generic zero-average component is of size \(\epsilon t^{-1+\sigma}\) near the separator. At an entry point with \(k=t/s\), one has \(\lambda_0=2k\), \(t_{\lambda_0}=2k^2\); its contribution to \(\lambda_0^{3/2}\left\|\mathbf W\right\|\) is only \(O(\epsilon k^{-1/2+2\sigma})\). This observation does not exclude a sharper estimate, but it does show why the required \(k^{-3/2}\) factor cannot simply be inserted from that bound.

The analogous argument in Huneau–Stingo [Retained latex: \cite[Section~5, pp.~28--32]{HS}] explicitly extends the relevant estimates to whole hyperboloids before applying the ray argument. In particular, its initial term in (5.19) is used in that enlarged setting. Those estimates concern a different quasilinear system and are not a proof of the missing extension for the present Einstein problem.
#### Effect and required evidence.

The nonzero-mode pointwise estimate (4.12) and the later refinement in Proposition 4.32 depend on this step. A whole-hyperboloid extension, or a boundary-start ray argument with all required traces and coefficient estimates, is needed. Together with the exterior path problem, this leaves two concrete links in the core bootstrap chain unproved as written. No conclusion that the main theorem itself is false follows.
# P2: the characteristic lemma and its application (Major)
## A smooth counterexample to the printed inequality

Lemma 4.13, equation (4.72), has a left-hand side \(t|(\partial_t-\partial_r)u|\), while its boundary term controls \((\partial_t-\partial_r)(ru)\). These quantities differ by a zeroth-order term: \[r(\partial_t-\partial_r)u
 =(\partial_t-\partial_r)(ru)+u.\] The omitted \(u\) cannot be discarded in the stated general lemma.

Take \(g=m\), so \(\pi=0\). Choose a smooth radial function \(\rho\) that vanishes for \(r\leq1/2\) and equals \(1\) for \(r\geq1\), and put \[u(t,x)=\frac{\rho(|x|)}{|x|},\] extended by zero near the origin. This is a globally smooth, time-independent function. Its smooth forcing \(F=\Box u=\Delta u\) is supported in \(r<1\); in particular, no singular source at the origin is being used.

Set \(s=5\), \(t=10\), and \(x=11e_1\). This point lies in the printed exterior part of \(\mathcal D_s\), since \[t/2<r<2t-3,\qquad t\leq s^2/2.\] The flat characteristic is \(x(\tau)=(\tau+1)e_1\). For \(2\leq\tau\leq10\), its radius is at least \(3\), so \(F=0\) along the whole integration segment. All angular terms vanish because \(u\) is radial, and all \(\pi\)-terms vanish. On the listed lateral boundary, with its inherited condition \(t\geq2\), one has \(r\geq1\), hence \(ru=1\) and \[(\partial_t-\partial_r)(ru)=0.\] Thus the entire right-hand side of (4.72) is zero. The left-hand side is \[t|(\partial_t-\partial_r)u|(10,11e_1)
 =\frac{10}{121}>0.\] All metric smallness hypotheses are satisfied exactly by \(\pi=0\). This is a counterexample to the literal auxiliary lemma, not to Einstein evolution.
## Boundary geometry and the mass tail
There are two further problems independent of that missing term.

First, the listed inner boundary retains \(r=t/2\) only for \(t\leq8/3\). With \(\pi=0\), the backwards ray from \((t,r)=(10,6)\), taking \(s=6\) in the printed \(\mathcal D_s\), is \(r(\tau)=\tau-4\). It first reaches \(r=\tau/2\) at \((8,4)\), which is excluded by the stated time restriction. The outer boundary \(r=2\tau-3\) would be reached at \(\tau=-1\), outside the domain. The assertion that every such curve meets the listed boundary is false. Also, the printed condition \(r\leq\sqrt{t^2-s^2}\) selects the region above the terminal hyperboloid, whereas a backward propagation argument using estimates already known up to \(s\) needs a carefully specified region below it.

Second, the hypothesis \[|\pi_{LL}|\leq \epsilon\frac{|t-r|}{t+r}\] forces \(\pi_{LL}=0\) on \(r=t\). In the proposed application \(\pi=(H^{\boldsymbol\mu\boldsymbol\nu})^\flat\), the asymptotic tail instead gives \[\pi_{LL}(t,t)=-\frac{2M}{t}
       +O(\epsilon t^{-3/2+2\sigma}).\] For fixed \(M>0\) and sufficiently small \(\sigma<1/4\), the second term cannot cancel the first for all large \(t\). The cited improved \(H^1_{LL}\) estimate does not establish the printed hypothesis for the full \(H\).
#### Effect and repair status.

The exact transport identity suggests retaining a \(u\)-term and correcting the lateral boundary. A characteristic formulation compatible with the mass tail is also required. Simply adding \(1\) to \(|t-r|\) does not by itself verify all of the new characteristic geometry. Proposition 4.12 and the ensuing good-component weak-null estimates use this lemma. Because a replacement and its application are not proved here, this is classified as a substantive proof defect, despite some locally apparent corrections.
# P3: flux positivity and the mass parameter (NeedsEvidence)

Appendix A uses decay of \(H\) and of \(H_{LL}+2\chi(r/t)\chi(r)M/r\) to compare the curved flux on \(\widetilde{\mathcal H}\) with a positive form involving \[\left(\frac{1}{2(1+r^2)}+\frac{M}{2r}\right)|\partial_tW|^2
       +|\widetilde\nabla W|^2\] where the cutoffs are one. The distinction between smallness relative to a fixed \(M\) and smallness uniform in \(M\) must be made explicit.

Here is a test of the auxiliary metric assumptions. Near a large point on the separator, let the inverse metric be diagonal, with \[g^{00}=-1-m+a,\quad g^{ij}=(1-m)\delta^{ij},\quad g^{44}=1,
 \qquad m=M/r,\quad a=\epsilon(1+t+r)^{-3/2}.\] The perturbation \(a\) can be smoothly localized near the chosen point. The mass part is the prescribed \(H^0\), and the only added component is \(H^{00}=a\). Thus \[H_{LL}+2M/r=a,\] which has the required residual decay with \(\delta=1/2\). The general smallness bound for \(H\) is also satisfied with small parameters. The metric remains Lorentzian.

This example shows that the decay assumptions alone do not yield a positivity assertion uniform over independently vanishing \(M\). For \(0<\delta<1\), comparison of a residual \(\epsilon r^{-1-\delta}\) with \(r^{-2}+Mr^{-1}\) involves the size of \[\sup_{r\geq1}\frac{\epsilon r^{1-\delta}}{1+Mr},\] which is of order \(\epsilon M^{\delta-1}\) for small \(M\), up to constants depending on \(\delta\). For each fixed positive \(M\), choosing \(\epsilon\) sufficiently small depending on \(M\) may restore the comparison.

The constructed metric is not asserted to satisfy the Einstein equations, wave gauge or the initial constraints. Such structure, or an explicitly allowed dependence of the smallness threshold on \(M\), might resolve the application. The requested evidence is the relevant dependence or an additional argument deriving positivity for the actual data class. This is why the nonlinear consequence is NeedsEvidence, rather than a confirmed counterexample to Theorem 1.2.
# Local corrections
## P4: consistent energy domains (Minor)

On pages 9 and 19 the exterior energy integrates over \(r\geq t-1\), whereas \(\Sigma_t^e\) on page 16 is \(r\geq\sqrt{t^2-2t}\). The assertion (3.5) uses the larger slice. This is not a literal consequence of the narrower energy: at \(t=4\), a smooth spacetime bump supported near \(r=2.9\), inside \[\sqrt{t^2-2t}<r<t-1,\] has zero energy on all the stated narrow slices, but a nonzero gradient norm on \(\Sigma_4^e\). The bump is a functional test, not a nonlinear solution.

Define the exterior energy over the actual slices of \(\mathcal D^e\), with its corresponding spacetime region. Likewise, the page 16 truncation \(t\geq r+1\) on \(\mathcal H_s\) gives \(t\leq(s^2+1)/2\), while the separator truncation used on page 9 and in (4.18) gives \(t\leq s^2/2\). These definitions should be made consistent. The correction is local; it does not automatically supply the missing path estimates in P1.
## P5: the mixed coefficient in (1.18) (Minor)
This correction changes numerical constants in subsequent estimates such as (4.65); it does not force a different decay rate.
## P6: the wave-operator drift and equation signs (Minor)

For \(\underline\partial_a=\partial_a+(x_a/t)\partial_t\), the exact identity is \[-\Box_{tx}
 =(s/t)^2\partial_t^2
 +2(x^a/t)\underline\partial_a\partial_t-\underline\partial^a\underline\partial_a
 +\left(\frac3t-\frac{r^2}{t^3}\right)\partial_t.\] The sign in front of \(r^2/t^3\) is positive in (4.62). Applying that printed expression to \(u=t\) gives \(2r^2/t^3\), whereas \(-\Box t=0\). Symbolic differentiation including derivatives of the frame coefficients confirms the corrected identity for a general function.

The same sign must be corrected in the definition of \(Q\) in Proposition 4.21 and in the expansion following (4.104). With \[P=\mathcal S^2+2\mathcal S+\frac34,\qquad \mathcal S=t\partial_t+x^a\partial_a,\] the printed \(Q\) differs from \(P-s^2(s/t)^2\partial_t^2\) by \(2s^2r^2t^{-3}\partial_t\).

There are associated signs to track when isolating the second time derivative. If \[\Box u+A\,u_{tt}+R[u]=G,\qquad -\Box u=(s/t)^2u_{tt}+L[u],\] then \[((s/t)^2-A)u_{tt}=-L[u]+R[u]-G.\] This is the identity to use in place of the inconsistent signs in (4.63)–(4.64). Also, the mass-tail source has a minus sign in (1.8), but is defined with a plus sign in (3.9) and (4.14).

Within \(r<t\), the corrected drift has the same \(O(t^{-1})\) size, and the small-coefficient argument still uses \(|A|\leq(s/t)^2/2\). The estimates mainly take absolute values, so these are local algebraic corrections. They should be carried out before claiming the exact PDE identities; they do not resolve P1.
## P7: oscillator energy and the mass cutoff (Minor)

Write the ray equation schematically as \[b\omega''-c\omega_{yy}-d\omega'_y=\mathcal R,
 \qquad c=1+(H^{1,44})^\flat.\] The coefficients are independent of \(y\). For \(E=\int_{\mathbb S^1}(b|\omega'|^2+c|\omega_y|^2)\,\mathrm dy\), integration by parts gives \[E'=b'\left\|\omega'\right\|_2^2+c'\left\|\omega_y\right\|_2^2
       +2\langle\mathcal R,\omega'\rangle.\] The mixed \(d\)-term integrates to zero. The displayed equality on page 61 omits the \(c'\)-term. For the explicit test \(\omega=\lambda\cos y\), \(b=1\), \(c=1+\alpha\lambda\), the omitted quantity is \(\pi\alpha\lambda^2\), which is nonzero for \(\alpha>0\).

The definition of \(A_{tx}\) already includes the scaling derivative of \((H^{1,44})^\flat\), so the missing term can be included in the existing Gronwall budget. In the same argument, several occurrences of \(\chi(t/r)\) should be \(\chi(r/t)\), consistently with (1.7) and the definition of \(a(t,x)\) in the proof. These cutoffs are not interchangeable: their supports differ even inside the cone. Restoring the original cutoff and the missing derivative repairs these local identities, subject to the separate domain issue in P1.
## P8: uniform time-flux bookkeeping (Minor)

The existence of \(l\in L^1([2,T_0))\) on each finite bootstrap interval does not alone give a bound independent of \(T_0\). To see the distinction, let a cumulative flux be \[F(t)=t^{2\sigma}-2^{2\sigma},\qquad
 l(t)=t^{-2\sigma}F'(t)=\frac{2\sigma}{t}.\] Its total integral is \(2\sigma\log(T_0/2)\). The function is integrable on every finite interval; the issue is uniformity, not finite-interval integrability.

What the polynomial cumulative bound does provide is uniform dyadic control. If \(F(t)\leq C\epsilon^2t^{2\sigma}\), with nonnegative flux density \(f=F'\), then for \(l=f/(C\epsilon^2t^{2\sigma})\), \[\int_R^{2R}l(t)\,\mathrm dt\leq2^{2\sigma}.\] Consequently Cauchy–Schwarz yields \[\int_R^{2R}t^{-a}\sqrt{l(t)}\,\mathrm dt
 \leq C_a R^{1/2-a}.\] The dyadic sum converges for \(a>1/2\). This supplies the appropriate mechanism for the weighted integrals in the exterior proof. Parameter margins must be stated accordingly; one may take \(\sigma<1/6\) for a weight \(a=1-3\sigma\), and arrange \(2\sigma<\rho<\kappa/2\) where the \(\rho\)-dependent estimates require it.

A final partial dyadic interval can have arbitrarily short length, so its average cannot automatically be bounded by the inverse of the full dyadic scale. A full-window argument or a separate endpoint treatment is needed. These scalar estimates clarify the bookkeeping; they do not certify the path used in Proposition 3.3, whose domain problem was proved in P1.
## P9: support of the zero-mode source split (Minor)

Pages 68–70 split the forcing using \(\chi((r+1/2)/t)\), where this cutoff is one on \(B_{1/2}\) and supported in \(B_1\). Its complement is then treated as supported in \(t\leq r+1/2\). This support claim is false. For example, choose an admissible smooth decreasing cutoff with \(\chi(3/4)=1/2\). At \((t,r)=(10,7)\), \[1-\chi((r+1/2)/t)=\frac12,\qquad t-r=3>\frac12.\] Thus the complementary forcing can be nonzero well inside the claimed separating cone.

A suitable replacement is a smooth \(\eta(t-r)\) that is zero for \(t-r\leq1/2\) and one for \(t-r\geq1\). The first forcing is then supported where the interior source estimate in Lemma 4.29 applies, and the complementary forcing lies in \(\mathcal D^e\). The transition strip lies in the overlap where the exterior bounds can be used. The Cauchy data should consistently be imposed at \(t=2\), as in the actual proof of Proposition 4.31; the introductory display on page 68 instead uses \(t=0\). This is a local correction of the decomposition.
# Independent checks, evidence and limitations

The calculations were written and executed by the current primary executor. They use Python 3.13.5 and SymPy 1.13.3, with no execution of author code. The script `verification/0290/independent_checks.py` completed with exit code \(0\); its SHA256 was identical before and after execution:
`513e72def5b732ce3fd0819a2a98b84a7b28ea6a01ece05d785dca4f8217dc0f`.

The results include exact rational ray geometry, the smooth flat-metric example, the null-frame conversion for a general radial tensor, exact differential-operator residuals, the oscillator energy defect, and an analytic sign bound for the flux witness. Numerical values only illustrate a sign already established by inequalities. No nonlinear PDE simulation or unbounded matrix computation was used.

The complete derivations are given in the report; the machine-readable checks and their actual command, exit code, stdout, stderr and script bindings are in `independent_checks.json` and `independent_checks_execution.json`. The additional exterior path calculation is recorded in `exterior_path_check.json`. The pinned source archive, extracted TeX and bibliography, source PDF parsing, rendered pages and separate actual-inspection records are included in the support inventory. The source archive was treated as text, not executed.

The final report build is recorded separately in `build_final.json`: it uses the existing approved Tectonic, an isolated dependency cache, untrusted mode and a cached final pass. Compiler, TeX, dependencies and output bindings, real commands and logs are retained there. PDF parsing and actual viewing of every report page have separate records. Rendering alone is not recorded as viewing. Earlier false render flags and the failed direct read of the cited reference’s first text block are preserved; the latter block was subsequently read through the recorded Python process.

No defect is inferred from unavailable author executable code or publisher text. The bibliography was read, but every cited result was not independently reconstructed. In particular, the external whole-hyperboloid argument was checked only for its relevance to P1 and is not imported as a proof for the Einstein system. The tentative concern that Lemma 4.28 needs an ordering between \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) is not retained: the null-coordinate majorant uses integrability of the two weights for \(\mu>1,\nu>1\), and no counterexample or missing ordering was established.

The elementary witnesses have deliberately limited roles. The bump tests a trace implication; the smooth radial example refutes the printed auxiliary characteristic inequality; and the Lorentzian metric tests uniform positivity under decay assumptions. None is claimed to satisfy the vacuum Einstein constraints and evolution in Theorem 1.2. A repaired exterior/interior sharp-estimate chain, a mass-compatible characteristic lemma, and the precise mass dependence in the flux argument remain necessary before treating the proof as complete.

The mechanical inventory and a non-scientific contract-field checklist were the only auxiliary contributions. Controller-supplied UI observations and the runtime self-description are recorded separately in provenance; no independent backend verification is claimed.

problems.title: Hyperboloidal integration and the scaling-ray initial term leave the available bootstrap domains
problems.source_location: p22 Proposition3.3 Step1 and(3.19) pp59–65 Propositions4.21–4.22, especially(4.99)–(4.103) pp9,16,37–40 domain and energy definitions
claim: Recorded check: Hyperboloidal integration and the scaling-ray initial term leave the available bootstrap domains
analysis: In Proposition 3.3, Step 1 on page 22, the proof selects a time \(\tau_k\in[2^k,2^{k+1})\cap[2,T_0)\), then integrates the hyperboloidal derivative through a point \((t,x)\) until the path meets either \(\tau=\tau_k\) or \(r=2\tau\). The bounds being integrated have been established in \(\mathcal D^e\).

Let \(s_*^2=t^2-r^2\) denote the constant along this path. The exterior condition on that same hyperbola is \[r(\tau)^2=\tau^2-s_*^2\geq\tau^2-2\tau
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad s_*^2\leq2\tau.\] Thus a backwards portion of a hyperbola through a point on \(\widetilde{\mathcal H}\) immediately enters \(\mathcal D^i\). For example, take \[t=15,\qquad r^2=195,\qquad s_*^2=30,\qquad \tau_k=9.\] Both times lie in the dyadic interval \([8,16)\). At time \(9\), the path has \(r^2=51\), while the exterior slice requires \(r^2\geq63\). The path has not met \(r=2\tau\), since \(r(\tau)<\tau\). The intermediate interval \(9\leq\tau<15\) is outside the domain of the exterior bounds used in (3.19).

This is not a peculiarity of choosing \(9\). Any selected \(\tau_k<16\) precedes some \(t\in[8,16)\); the separator point at that later \(t\) gives the same obstruction. Strictly exterior points sufficiently close to the separator also leave the exterior region before reaching the selected time. Consequently the stated endpoint alternatives do not justify the integration for all points being estimated.

A repair must use a path contained in the available region, control an additional boundary contribution, or establish estimates in an enlarged region. Selecting a later averaging window may help in part of a slab, but requires a separate argument near a finite bootstrap endpoint. The current review does not supply such a uniform replacement. The improved \(LT\) decay is used in subsequent commutator and flux estimates, so this is more than a notation correction.

For Proposition 4.22, pages 61–62, write \[p_\lambda=\left(\frac{\lambda t}{s},\frac{\lambda x}{s}\right),
 \qquad s^2=t^2-r^2.\] The proof of (4.100) treats \(p_{s_0}\) as lying on the truncated \(\mathcal H_{s_0}\), and uses its boundedness in \(t+r\) and the energy \(E^i(s_0,Z^{\leq2}\mathbf W)\). Direct substitution gives \[(t_\lambda-1)^2-r_\lambda^2-1
 =\lambda\left(\lambda-\frac{2t}{s}\right).\] For positive \(\lambda\), the ray lies in \(\mathcal D^i\) precisely when \(\lambda\geq2t/s\). Its natural entry parameter is therefore \[\lambda_0=\max\{s_0,2t/s\},\] not always \(s_0\).

A strictly interior example is \[t=49,\quad s=10,\quad r^2=2301,\quad s_0=\frac{21}{10}.\] Here \(49<s^2/2=50\), but \[t_{s_0}=\frac{1029}{100},
 \qquad
 \max_{\mathcal H_{s_0}}t=\frac{s_0^2}{2}=\frac{441}{200},
 \qquad
 \lambda_0=\frac{49}{5}>s_0.\] The starting point lies well outside \(\mathcal H_{s_0}\). For targets approaching the separator at large \(s\), its time is unbounded; the claim that \(1+t+r=O(1)\) at that starting point is therefore unavailable.

There is also a direct functional obstruction to the displayed use of the truncated initial energy. Choose a smooth spacetime bump supported near \(p_{s_0}\), outside a neighbourhood of the compact \(\mathcal H_{s_0}\), and multiply it by \(\cos y\). It has zero circle average. All its derivatives vanish on \(\mathcal H_{s_0}\), so \(E^i(s_0,Z^{\leq2}\mathbf W)=0\), but \(Y_{tx}(s_0)>0\) if the bump is nonzero at the ray point. This disproves a trace estimate of the form (4.100) from that truncated energy alone. It is a test of the claimed functional implication, not an Einstein counterexample.

The estimates for \(A_{tx}\) and \(B_{tx}\) likewise require justification on the part of the ray before it enters \(\mathcal D^i\). Merely changing the lower integration limit leaves a boundary term \(Y_{tx}(\lambda_0)\) to estimate with the required directional weight. The directly stated exterior bound for a generic zero-average component is of size \(\epsilon t^{-1+\sigma}\) near the separator. At an entry point with \(k=t/s\), one has \(\lambda_0=2k\), \(t_{\lambda_0}=2k^2\); its contribution to \(\lambda_0^{3/2}\left\|\mathbf W\right\|\) is only \(O(\epsilon k^{-1/2+2\sigma})\). This observation does not exclude a sharper estimate, but it does show why the required \(k^{-3/2}\) factor cannot simply be inserted from that bound.

The analogous argument in Huneau–Stingo [Retained latex: \cite[Section~5, pp.~28--32]{HS}] explicitly extends the relevant estimates to whole hyperboloids before applying the ray argument. In particular, its initial term in (5.19) is used in that enlarged setting. Those estimates concern a different quasilinear system and are not a proof of the missing extension for the present Einstein problem.

The nonzero-mode pointwise estimate (4.12) and the later refinement in Proposition 4.32 depend on this step. A whole-hyperboloid extension, or a boundary-start ray argument with all required traces and coefficient estimates, is needed. Together with the exterior path problem, this leaves two concrete links in the core bootstrap chain unproved as written. No conclusion that the main theorem itself is false follows.
result: Impact: The sharpened exterior LT estimate and nonzero-mode pointwise bootstrap enter the main energy closure; this is a proof-domain gap, not a counterexample to Theorem1.2.

problems.title: The characteristic estimate in Lemma4.13 is false as printed and its boundary and mass hypotheses need revision
problems.source_location: pp49–50 Lemma4.13,(4.72)–(4.74) pp48,51 Proposition4.12 p21(3.17), proof continuing p22
claim: Recorded check: The characteristic estimate in Lemma4.13 is false as printed and its boundary and mass hypotheses need revision
analysis:
Lemma 4.13, equation (4.72), has a left-hand side \(t|(\partial_t-\partial_r)u|\), while its boundary term controls \((\partial_t-\partial_r)(ru)\). These quantities differ by a zeroth-order term: \[r(\partial_t-\partial_r)u
 =(\partial_t-\partial_r)(ru)+u.\] The omitted \(u\) cannot be discarded in the stated general lemma.

Take \(g=m\), so \(\pi=0\). Choose a smooth radial function \(\rho\) that vanishes for \(r\leq1/2\) and equals \(1\) for \(r\geq1\), and put \[u(t,x)=\frac{\rho(|x|)}{|x|},\] extended by zero near the origin. This is a globally smooth, time-independent function. Its smooth forcing \(F=\Box u=\Delta u\) is supported in \(r<1\); in particular, no singular source at the origin is being used.

Set \(s=5\), \(t=10\), and \(x=11e_1\). This point lies in the printed exterior part of \(\mathcal D_s\), since \[t/2<r<2t-3,\qquad t\leq s^2/2.\] The flat characteristic is \(x(\tau)=(\tau+1)e_1\). For \(2\leq\tau\leq10\), its radius is at least \(3\), so \(F=0\) along the whole integration segment. All angular terms vanish because \(u\) is radial, and all \(\pi\)-terms vanish. On the listed lateral boundary, with its inherited condition \(t\geq2\), one has \(r\geq1\), hence \(ru=1\) and \[(\partial_t-\partial_r)(ru)=0.\] Thus the entire right-hand side of (4.72) is zero. The left-hand side is \[t|(\partial_t-\partial_r)u|(10,11e_1)
 =\frac{10}{121}>0.\] All metric smallness hypotheses are satisfied exactly by \(\pi=0\). This is a counterexample to the literal auxiliary lemma, not to Einstein evolution.
There are two further problems independent of that missing term.

First, the listed inner boundary retains \(r=t/2\) only for \(t\leq8/3\). With \(\pi=0\), the backwards ray from \((t,r)=(10,6)\), taking \(s=6\) in the printed \(\mathcal D_s\), is \(r(\tau)=\tau-4\). It first reaches \(r=\tau/2\) at \((8,4)\), which is excluded by the stated time restriction. The outer boundary \(r=2\tau-3\) would be reached at \(\tau=-1\), outside the domain. The assertion that every such curve meets the listed boundary is false. Also, the printed condition \(r\leq\sqrt{t^2-s^2}\) selects the region above the terminal hyperboloid, whereas a backward propagation argument using estimates already known up to \(s\) needs a carefully specified region below it.

Second, the hypothesis \[|\pi_{LL}|\leq \epsilon\frac{|t-r|}{t+r}\] forces \(\pi_{LL}=0\) on \(r=t\). In the proposed application \(\pi=(H^{\boldsymbol\mu\boldsymbol\nu})^\flat\), the asymptotic tail instead gives \[\pi_{LL}(t,t)=-\frac{2M}{t}
       +O(\epsilon t^{-3/2+2\sigma}).\] For fixed \(M>0\) and sufficiently small \(\sigma<1/4\), the second term cannot cancel the first for all large \(t\). The cited improved \(H^1_{LL}\) estimate does not establish the printed hypothesis for the full \(H\).

The exact transport identity suggests retaining a \(u\)-term and correcting the lateral boundary. A characteristic formulation compatible with the mass tail is also required. Simply adding \(1\) to \(|t-r|\) does not by itself verify all of the new characteristic geometry. Proposition 4.12 and the ensuing good-component weak-null estimates use this lemma. Because a replacement and its application are not proved here, this is classified as a substantive proof defect, despite some locally apparent corrections.
result: Impact: Invalidates a stated auxiliary lemma used for good-component decay and the ensuing weak-null estimates. It does not disprove the nonlinear Einstein stability theorem.

problems.title: Separate fixed-mass smallness from uniform positivity of the separating-surface flux
problems.source_location: pp72–75 PropositionA.1,(A.1),(A.6) and flux comparison pp36–40(3.49)–(3.50),(4.16)–(4.18) p8 Theorem1.2
claim: Recorded check: Separate fixed-mass smallness from uniform positivity of the separating-surface flux
analysis:
Appendix A uses decay of \(H\) and of \(H_{LL}+2\chi(r/t)\chi(r)M/r\) to compare the curved flux on \(\widetilde{\mathcal H}\) with a positive form involving \[\left(\frac{1}{2(1+r^2)}+\frac{M}{2r}\right)|\partial_tW|^2
       +|\widetilde\nabla W|^2\] where the cutoffs are one. The distinction between smallness relative to a fixed \(M\) and smallness uniform in \(M\) must be made explicit.

Here is a test of the auxiliary metric assumptions. Near a large point on the separator, let the inverse metric be diagonal, with \[g^{00}=-1-m+a,\quad g^{ij}=(1-m)\delta^{ij},\quad g^{44}=1,
 \qquad m=M/r,\quad a=\epsilon(1+t+r)^{-3/2}.\] The perturbation \(a\) can be smoothly localized near the chosen point. The mass part is the prescribed \(H^0\), and the only added component is \(H^{00}=a\). Thus \[H_{LL}+2M/r=a,\] which has the required residual decay with \(\delta=1/2\). The general smallness bound for \(H\) is also satisfied with small parameters. The metric remains Lorentzian.

This example shows that the decay assumptions alone do not yield a positivity assertion uniform over independently vanishing \(M\). For \(0<\delta<1\), comparison of a residual \(\epsilon r^{-1-\delta}\) with \(r^{-2}+Mr^{-1}\) involves the size of \[\sup_{r\geq1}\frac{\epsilon r^{1-\delta}}{1+Mr},\] which is of order \(\epsilon M^{\delta-1}\) for small \(M\), up to constants depending on \(\delta\). For each fixed positive \(M\), choosing \(\epsilon\) sufficiently small depending on \(M\) may restore the comparison.

The constructed metric is not asserted to satisfy the Einstein equations, wave gauge or the initial constraints. Such structure, or an explicitly allowed dependence of the smallness threshold on \(M\), might resolve the application. The requested evidence is the relevant dependence or an additional argument deriving positivity for the actual data class. This is why the nonlinear consequence is NeedsEvidence, rather than a confirmed counterexample to Theorem 1.2.
result: Impact: A quantitative parameter-dependence and application check is needed before treating the boundary flux bound as uniform over M tending to0.

problems.title: Use consistent exterior slices and truncated hyperboloids
claim: Recorded check: Use consistent exterior slices and truncated hyperboloids
analysis: On pages 9 and 19 the exterior energy integrates over \(r\geq t-1\), whereas \(\Sigma_t^e\) on page 16 is \(r\geq\sqrt{t^2-2t}\). The assertion (3.5) uses the larger slice. The bump is a functional test, not a nonlinear solution.

Define the exterior energy over the actual slices of \(\mathcal D^e\), with its corresponding spacetime region. problems.title: Correct the semi-hyperboloidal drift and associated equation signs
problems.source_location: pp46–48(4.62)–(4.64) pp59–60 Q and oscillator expansion p63 following(4.104) p7(1.8),p20(3.9),p39(4.14)
claim: Recorded check: Correct the semi-hyperboloidal drift and associated equation signs
analysis:
For \(\underline\partial_a=\partial_a+(x_a/t)\partial_t\), the exact identity is \[-\Box_{tx}
 =(s/t)^2\partial_t^2
 +2(x^a/t)\underline\partial_a\partial_t-\underline\partial^a\underline\partial_a
 +\left(\frac3t-\frac{r^2}{t^3}\right)\partial_t.\] The sign in front of \(r^2/t^3\) is positive in (4.62). Applying that printed expression to \(u=t\) gives \(2r^2/t^3\), whereas \(-\Box t=0\). Symbolic differentiation including derivatives of the frame coefficients confirms the corrected identity for a general function.

The same sign must be corrected in the definition of \(Q\) in Proposition 4.21 and in the expansion following (4.104). With \[P=\mathcal S^2+2\mathcal S+\frac34,\qquad \mathcal S=t\partial_t+x^a\partial_a,\] the printed \(Q\) differs from \(P-s^2(s/t)^2\partial_t^2\) by \(2s^2r^2t^{-3}\partial_t\).

There are associated signs to track when isolating the second time derivative. If \[\Box u+A\,u_{tt}+R[u]=G,\qquad -\Box u=(s/t)^2u_{tt}+L[u],\] then \[((s/t)^2-A)u_{tt}=-L[u]+R[u]-G.\] This is the identity to use in place of the inconsistent signs in (4.63)–(4.64). problems.title: Restore the variable-mass derivative in the oscillator energy and the original cutoff argument
problems.source_location: pp59–62 Proposition4.21 energy calculation and b,R,A definitions p7(1.7)
claim: Recorded check: Restore the variable-mass derivative in the oscillator energy and the original cutoff argument
analysis:
Write the ray equation schematically as \[b\omega''-c\omega_{yy}-d\omega'_y=\mathcal R,
 \qquad c=1+(H^{1,44})^\flat.\] The coefficients are independent of \(y\). For \(E=\int_{\mathbb S^1}(b|\omega'|^2+c|\omega_y|^2)\,\mathrm dy\), integration by parts gives \[E'=b'\left\|\omega'\right\|_2^2+c'\left\|\omega_y\right\|_2^2
       +2\langle\mathcal R,\omega'\rangle.\] The mixed \(d\)-term integrates to zero. The displayed equality on page 61 omits the \(c'\)-term. For the explicit test \(\omega=\lambda\cos y\), \(b=1\), \(c=1+\alpha\lambda\), the omitted quantity is \(\pi\alpha\lambda^2\), which is nonzero for \(\alpha>0\).

The definition of \(A_{tx}\) already includes the scaling derivative of \((H^{1,44})^\flat\), so the missing term can be included in the existing Gronwall budget. In the same argument, several occurrences of \(\chi(t/r)\) should be \(\chi(r/t)\), consistently with (1.7) and the definition of \(a(t,x)\) in the proof. These cutoffs are not interchangeable: their supports differ even inside the cone. Restoring the original cutoff and the missing derivative repairs these local identities, subject to the separate domain issue in P1.
result: Impact: Local repairs preserve the available Gronwall structure within its valid domain; the unresolved domain issue remains P1.

problems.title: State the uniform time-flux estimate actually needed in the exterior bootstrap
problems.source_location: p20 definition of l(t) p22 dyadic choice pp27–37 time integrals
claim: Recorded check: State the uniform time-flux estimate actually needed in the exterior bootstrap
analysis:
The existence of \(l\in L^1([2,T_0))\) on each finite bootstrap interval does not alone give a bound independent of \(T_0\). To see the distinction, let a cumulative flux be \[F(t)=t^{2\sigma}-2^{2\sigma},\qquad
 l(t)=t^{-2\sigma}F'(t)=\frac{2\sigma}{t}.\] Its total integral is \(2\sigma\log(T_0/2)\). The function is integrable on every finite interval; the issue is uniformity, not finite-interval integrability.

What the polynomial cumulative bound does provide is uniform dyadic control. If \(F(t)\leq C\epsilon^2t^{2\sigma}\), with nonnegative flux density \(f=F'\), then for \(l=f/(C\epsilon^2t^{2\sigma})\), \[\int_R^{2R}l(t)\,\mathrm dt\leq2^{2\sigma}.\] Consequently Cauchy–Schwarz yields \[\int_R^{2R}t^{-a}\sqrt{l(t)}\,\mathrm dt
 \leq C_a R^{1/2-a}.\] The dyadic sum converges for \(a>1/2\). This supplies the appropriate mechanism for the weighted integrals in the exterior proof. Parameter margins must be stated accordingly; one may take \(\sigma<1/6\) for a weight \(a=1-3\sigma\), and arrange \(2\sigma<\rho<\kappa/2\) where the \(\rho\)-dependent estimates require it.

A final partial dyadic interval can have arbitrarily short length, so its average cannot automatically be bounded by the inverse of the full dyadic scale. A full-window argument or a separate endpoint treatment is needed. These scalar estimates clarify the bookkeeping; they do not certify the path used in Proposition 3.3, whose domain problem was proved in P1.
result: Impact: A uniform-in-lifespan justification is missing in the written inference. Weighted dyadic control provides the required analytic mechanism; path-domain issues are still P1.

report: Abstract: This review examines the exact author manuscript arXiv:2309.13910v1. Two local assertions require correction: the unconditional uniform \(L^p\) statement in Theorem 2.3(iii), and global \(L^1\) convergence in the appendix. Explicit analytic examples establish both discrepancies. Their required corrections preserve the uses checked in the main energy argument; neither example refutes Theorem 2.4. The report assessment is Minor. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical review of distributional vorticity uniqueness
# Identity and inspected scope

The paper is Viorel Barbu, Michael Röckner and Deng Zhang, Uniqueness of distributional solutions to the 2D vorticity Navier–Stokes equation and its associated nonlinear Markov process [paper]. The reviewed file is arXiv:2309.13910v1, submitted 25 September 2023, 29 physical PDF pages. Printed and physical page numbers agree. The journal identifier is DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1664 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1664); publisher metadata records publication on 10 June 2025. The journal-final PDF was not obtained and equivalence to it is not established.

All 29 pages were read in extracted text. Detailed checks concentrated on Theorem 2.3, the hypotheses and resolvent argument of Theorem 2.4, Corollary 3.1, the linearized uniqueness calculation, and the appendix. The probabilistic conclusions and their dependence on external results were traced, but the cited superposition, martingale-problem and nonlinear Markov results were not independently re-proved. In particular, the full claimed pathwise-uniqueness class in Theorem 4.5 is not certified by this review. An attempted access to the cited Grube thesis was blocked by the institutional site’s access challenge.
# Necessary assumptions and checks

Write \(Kf=k*f\), where \[k(x)=\frac{x^\perp}{2\pi |x|^2},\quad
 x^\perp=(-x_2,x_1),\quad \Phi_\varepsilon=(\varepsilon I-\Delta)^{-1}.\] Theorem 2.4 (p. 11) assumes, for every finite \(T>0\), \[u_1,u_2\in L^4(0,T;L^4\cap L^{4/3}),\quad
 u_1-u_2\in L^\infty(0,T;H^{-1}),\quad
 u_1(t)-u_2(t)\in L^1\ \text{a.e.},\] together with the weak zero-initial-difference condition (2.22). These conditions must accompany the uniqueness statement. They do not follow for arbitrary measure data merely from the smoothing bound (2.4).

The regularized energy \(h_\varepsilon=\langle\Phi_\varepsilon z,z\rangle
=\|\nabla\Phi_\varepsilon z\|_2^2+\varepsilon\|\Phi_\varepsilon z\|_2^2\) has the correct nonnegative sign. The density argument at (3.16) uses both the \(H^{-1}\) bound and the stated initial trace. The interpolation at (3.19) produces a fourth power of \(\|u_2\|_{4/3}\), which is integrable under the actual hypotheses. The coefficient in the final Gronwall argument likewise has the required integrability. These checks are conditional on the stated function spaces.
# Established local findings

Problem 1 (Uniform propagation requires the corresponding initial norm).  Theorem 2.3(iii), p. 9, asserts \(u\in L^\infty(0,T;L^p)\) for every \(p\in[1,\infty]\), assuming only \(u_0\in L^q\) for some \(q\in(1,2)\), in addition to the hypotheses of Theorem 2.1. The membership assertion is false as written.
## Complete analytic check

Fix \(\nu=1\) and set \[u_0(x)=\frac{\mathbf 1_{\{0<|x|<1\}}}{2\pi |x|}.\] This is a nonnegative finite Radon density of total mass one. For every \(1\le q<2\), \[\|u_0\|_q^q=(2\pi)^{1-q}\int_0^1 r^{1-q}\,dr
 =\frac{(2\pi)^{1-q}}{2-q}<\infty.\] In particular \(q=4/3\) is admissible. Its Biot–Savart velocity is tangential with magnitude \(1/(2\pi)\) inside the unit disk and \(1/(2\pi r)\) outside. Consequently \(y_0=K(u_0)\in L^{2,\infty}\), \(\operatorname{div}y_0=0\), and \(\operatorname{curl}y_0=u_0\) distributionally. There is no point mass at the origin: circulation tends to zero with the radius. Thus the initial hypotheses of Theorem 2.1 are met.

Equation reference: eq:heat. The heat evolution \(u(t)=G_t*u_0\) remains radial. Its velocity is tangential, so \(K(u)\cdot\nabla u=0\), and it solves the full vorticity equation. It is smooth for \(t>0\), converges to \(u_0\) as a measure, and is obtained by radial smooth approximation. At the origin, \[
 u(t,0)=\frac{1}{4\pi t}\int_0^1 e^{-r^2/(4t)}\,dr
       =\frac{\operatorname{erf}(1/(2\sqrt t))}{4\sqrt{\pi t}}
       \sim\frac{1}{4\sqrt{\pi t}}\quad(t\downarrow0).\] Hence the essential supremum over \(t\in(0,T)\) of \(\|u(t)\|_\infty\) is infinite. The claimed membership for \(p=\infty\) fails despite all the stated initial assumptions being satisfied. This is an analytic counterexample; finite numerical values only illustrate [eq:heat] (#eq:heat).
## Counterevidence, impact and precise correction

The proof on p. 10 explicitly inserts the condition \(u_0\in L^p\) before applying Young’s inequality. Reading that condition back into the theorem gives the defensible statement \[u_0\in L^q\cap L^p,\ q\in(1,2)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \|u\|_{L^\infty(0,T;L^p)}\le C_p\|u_0\|_p.\] For \(1\le p<\infty\), positivity and the two mass-one kernel identities stated on p. 10 give this propagation by Jensen’s inequality followed by integration; \(p=\infty\) follows directly. This verifies the conditional repair within the paper’s kernel representation.

An estimate with an infinite right-hand side would be vacuous and does not justify the separately asserted membership. The downstream applications checked on pp. 23 and 25 assume probability densities in \(L^4\); interpolation supplies \(L^{4/3}\), and the corrected propagation suffices there. The supported impact is Minor: an overstatement of the auxiliary theorem’s range, without demonstrated damage to these uses or a counterexample to the central uniqueness theorem.

Problem 2 (The appendix’s convergence cannot be global in \(L^1\)).  In the proof of Lemma .1, p. 26, the display after (0.19) claims \(\nabla^\perp\Phi_{\varepsilon'}\varphi\to-K\varphi\) in \(L^1\), and consequently in distributions, for \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)\). The global \(L^1\) claim is false.
## Complete analytic check

Choose the radial nonnegative bump \[\varphi(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 C\exp[-1/(1-|x|^2)],&|x|<1,\\
 0,&|x|\ge1,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad C^{-1}=\int_{|x|<1}\exp[-1/(1-|x|^2)]\,dx.\] It belongs to the stipulated test-function class and has integral one. For \(r>1\), radial symmetry and circulation give \(K\varphi(x)=x^\perp/(2\pi r^2)\). Therefore \[\int_{|x|>1}|K\varphi(x)|\,dx=\int_1^\infty dr=\infty.\] For each fixed \(\varepsilon'>0\), the heat-resolvent representation (0.15) gives \[\|\nabla g_{\varepsilon'}\|_1
 \le C_0\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon't}t^{-1/2}\,dt<\infty.\] Thus \(\nabla^\perp\Phi_{\varepsilon'}\varphi\in L^1\), whereas its proposed limit is not in \(L^1\). In fact their difference is not in \(L^1\) for any \(\varepsilon'>0\), ruling out the printed norm convergence.
## Repair and dependence

The kernels converge in \(L^1_{\rm loc}\): on every bounded set, (0.17)–(0.18) provide the integrable dominating function \(1/(2\pi|x|)\). Convolution with a compactly supported smooth function preserves this local convergence and yields exactly the distributional convergence required next. Replace the global \(L^1\) assertion by \(L^1_{\rm loc}\), or state distributional convergence directly.
# Overall assessment and remaining scope

The examples disprove precisely the local assertions identified above. Neither purports to be a pair-of-solutions counterexample satisfying all hypotheses of Theorem 2.4. The sign of \(zK(u_2)\) printed in (3.1) differs from direct subtraction; the subsequent estimates take its absolute value, so this sign does not invalidate the inspected energy bound. It is not treated as a separate substantive finding.

The distributional uniqueness proof was inspected in detail; external elliptic identification and probabilistic transfer theorems remain dependencies. The full scope of Corollary 3.1’s mass-conservation justification and the passage from a fixed drift to the pathwise uniqueness class in Theorem 4.5 remain outside a completed external-dependency check. No stronger defect is inferred from these limits.

A bounded search of publisher/arXiv pages and author-related sources did not locate a separate erratum, supplement or code release. The source-search auxiliary’s work is distinguished from this primary review. No author code was run. Absence of located code is not a mathematical defect, and no first-discovery claim is made.
