report: Abstract: The exact journal version is examined. A two-torsion example disproves the stated pole classification and characteristic-function limit for the \(c\)-cost. A constant positive weight also disproves two uniform estimates used in the spectral argument. These are substantive defects in stated core ingredients, although they do not by themselves refute the near-zero Gaussian laws. Two additional local corrections concern the unweighted counting constant and a missing centering hypothesis. The overall assessment is Major; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical review of dynamics of continued fractions and modular symbols
# Identity, scope and necessary assumptions

The reviewed paper is Jungwon Lee and Hae-Sang Sun, Dynamics of continued fractions and distribution of modular symbols, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 27 (2025), 3527–3582, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1665 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1665) [paper]. This is the 56-page publisher PDF, received 8 April 2020 and revised 3 February 2025, published 19 June 2025. Physical page \(k\) has printed page \(3526+k\). The distinct arXiv:1902.06277v3, dated 7 May 2025, was found in the metadata search; no textual equivalence to that manuscript is asserted.

All 56 pages were read as extracted text. Detailed checks addressed Definitions 1.1 and the costs \(b_\psi,c_\psi\), the hypotheses of Theorems A–E, the finite-coset coboundary arguments, the passage from operators to Dirichlet series, the real-weight estimates, the residue, and the centering used in the Hessian calculation. Selected source pages were actually viewed to verify every decisive formula below. Reading the entire text does not constitute an independent reconstruction of every cited theorem.

Throughout the paper, \(\Gamma\) has finite index in \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\) and is normalized by \(j=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\). Rational numbers have their canonical continued fraction, with final digit greater than one. The sample space is \[\Omega_M=\bigcup_{2\le n\le M}
 \{a/n:1\le a<n,\ (a,n)=1\},\] with interval restriction and, where specified, a nonnegative nonzero endpoint weight. The Gaussian conclusions require nondegenerate covariance, expressed through real coboundaries. Residual conclusions require the stated conditions modulo the actual modulus; a real coboundary condition cannot silently substitute for them. The averaging is over denominators up to \(M\), not a resolution of the fixed-denominator conjecture.
# Confirmed problems

Problem 1 (Two-torsion produces cancellation, not the asserted pole).  Definition 1.1(2), p. 3530 (physical 4), permits a nonzero constant \(c\)-coboundary in a group with two-torsion. Proposition 2.6 and Corollary 2.7, p. 3542 (physical 16), omit this possibility. It propagates to Proposition 3.2(1), p. 3544 (physical 18), and Theorem 3.8, p. 3547 (physical 21).

Complete analytic counterexample. Take \[\Gamma=\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z),\quad d=1,\quad
 g=c,\quad \psi\equiv1,\quad J=(0,1),\quad \Psi\equiv1,\quad v=\pi.\] There is one coset, the index is finite, and \(j\) normalizes \(\Gamma\). All test functions are admissible and nonzero. The real-valued function \(v\psi\), reduced in \(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z\), is a \(c\)-coboundary associated with \(\beta=0\): the left side of Definition 1.1(2) is \(\pi+\pi=0\) in that group, for every pair of digits. Thus the hypothesis of Proposition 3.2(1) holds.

Dependency and impact. In the same example over \(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\), the constant function \(1\) is a nonzero \(c\)-coboundary with constant \(\beta=0\). This directly contradicts Proposition 2.6 and the asserted description in Corollary 2.7(1). The passage in Section 10.1, p. 3579 (physical 53), conjugates the final operator as if it had the same coboundary transformation as the even-step operator. For this example the even-step weight is \(e^{2i\pi}=1\), while the odd terminal part carries a minus sign; the leading contributions cancel. An eigenvalue of the even-step operator alone does not establish a pole of the evaluated series.

The impact is Major: an explicit admissible example disproves two principal analytic and distributional statements used in Section 3, not merely a line of exposition. The example does not disprove Theorem A near zero, nor does it establish failure of every modular-symbol specialization or of every sufficient condition in Theorem B.

Repair boundary. The torsion hypothesis and the final even/odd contributions must be handled explicitly. Restricting a finite coefficient group to odd order removes this particular two-torsion example, but is not a verified complete repair of the published general statements. The condition for a pole must include nonvanishing of the actual residue after the final operator is applied. A full replacement classification, especially for even moduli, is outside the completed repair here.

Problem 2 (Missing exponential weights in uniform spectral estimates).  Proposition 7.4(1), p. 3568 (physical 42), and Lemma 8.4(1), p. 3573 (physical 47), state bounds uniform in the iterate \(n\) without necessary weight factors.

Dependency and impact. Proposition 7.4 is used in the spectral-radius argument of Proposition 7.5. More seriously, Lemma 8.4(1) is explicitly used in the estimate for the close-pair contribution \(I^{(1)}\), immediately below (8.4), which feeds Proposition 8.3 and Theorem 8.5. The weight omission therefore invalidates a quantitative step of the central vertical-strip proof as printed. This problem is Major on that proof impact. It is not an assertion that the Dolgopyat-type conclusion is false.

Verified local repair and remaining work. Direct differentiation and bounded distortion yield the defensible bound \[\|\partial\mathcal H_{\sigma,\eta}^{\,n}\Psi\|_\infty
 \le C\,\|\mathcal H_{\sigma,\eta}^{\,n}1\|_\infty
 \bigl(|\sigma|\|\Psi\|_\infty+
              \rho^n\|\partial\Psi\|_\infty\bigr),
 \tag{2.3}\] because all real branch weights are positive. In the constant-cost example it retains exactly the missing \(e^{n\varepsilon}\). Likewise (2.2) is repaired in that example by inserting the cylinder weight \(e^{n\varepsilon}\) in the numerator. For nonconstant costs the corresponding weight depends on the branch and coset. Replacing the stated comparisons and propagating these weights through the full close-pair estimate has not been completed here. The normalized operator of (8.1), p. 3571, is relevant counterevidence to a claim that all later estimates must be false, but it does not make the two displayed unnormalized statements true.

Problem 3 (The unweighted counting constant contains an extra factor).  Equation (3.3), p. 3546 (physical 20), states the leading constant \(3|J|/(\pi^2\log2)\) for \(|\Omega_{M,J}|\). For \(J=(0,1)\) the constant is \(3/\pi^2\).

Independent derivation. The definition of the sample space gives exactly \(|\Omega_M|=\sum_{n=2}^M\varphi(n)\). Counting coprime ordered pairs by Möbius inversion gives \[\sum_{n=1}^M\varphi(n)
 =\frac12\left(1+\sum_{d=1}^M
               \mu(d)\lfloor M/d\rfloor^2\right)
 =\frac{3}{\pi^2}M^2+O(M\log M).\] Here \(\sum_{d\ge1}\mu(d)/d^2=1/\zeta(2)=6/\pi^2\); the replacement of floors costs \(O(M\sum_{d\le M}d^{-1})\), and the tail costs \(O(M)\). Removing \(n=1\) affects only a constant. Thus the error in (3.3) has nonzero order \(M^2\), while the preceding Proposition 3.4 requires an error \(O(M^\delta)\) with \(\delta<2\). The paper itself uses the correct totient constant on p. 3555 (physical 29).

Impact and repair. This is Minor on the demonstrated scope: the raw counting and residue normalization must be corrected, including the calculation on p. 3579. A common multiplicative normalization cancels from the ratios forming a moment generating function, so this discrepancy alone does not disprove the normalized Gaussian or residual laws. An independent sieve calculation is retained as a finite diagnostic; the asymptotic derivation above is the decisive evidence.

Problem 4 (The variance identity needs a centered parameter direction).  Section 9 introduces an arbitrary fixed real \(h\), p. 3574 (physical 48). Proposition 9.2, p. 3575 (physical 49), then states an uncentered second-moment limit and its proof assumes \(\kappa'(0)=0\) without imposing it.

Exact counterexample and correction. Use the one-coset \(b\)-system, \(\psi=1\), and \(h=0\). Then \(\kappa(w)=\lambda_{1,w}=e^w\), so \(\kappa'(0)=\kappa''(0)=1\), and the cost \(\Upsilon=2h\log x+\psi\) is identically one. The right-hand side of Proposition 9.2 is \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n
   \int\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}1\right)^2\Phi\,dx
 =\lim_{n\to\infty}n=+\infty,\] whereas its left-hand side equals one. The hypothesis needed by the proof is \(\kappa'(0)=0\), equivalently zero mean for the cost in this normalized setting. One must restrict \(h\) to the corresponding centered direction, or use a correctly centered variance and logarithmic eigenvalue derivative.

The downstream use in (10.1)–(10.2), p. 3578 (physical 52), does select \(h=s'(0)\) from \(\lambda(s(w),w)=1\); differentiation then gives precisely \(\kappa'(0)=0\). This verified compatibility limits the demonstrated impact to Minor: the overbroad proposition is false, but this example does not invalidate its intended centered use in the Hessian argument.
# Assessment, coverage and limits

The overall assessment is Major, based on Problems 1 and 2. Problem 1 disproves an actual characteristic-function limit and pole assertion under all their stated assumptions. Problem 2 disproves uniform estimates at arbitrarily small admissible real weights and identifies the core estimate that uses them. Neither assessment requires the entire paper to be false, and possible repair is not used as a reason to lower the grade.

The continued-fraction conventions, finite-index and normalization assumptions, interval weighting, nondegeneracy requirements, and the distinction between \(b\)- and \(c\)-costs were tracked. The operator-series representation and terminal parity were checked in the explicit one-coset example. The totient asymptotic, scalar operator identities, and centering counterexample are independently derived above. The complex perturbation, full UNI/Dolgopyat argument, and modular-form cohomology/period results depend on cited work and were not independently reconstructed in full.

In particular, the modular-symbol specializations, all even-prime arithmetic cases, and the optimal-period identifications are not certified by this review. No elliptic-curve counterexample is claimed. The report does not infer that the unrestricted arXiv version contains the same issues. A bounded official-page and author-page search did not locate a separate target erratum, supplementary file or released implementation; this is a search limitation. No author code was run.

claim: Recorded check: Missing centering assumption in Proposition 9.2
analysis: Section 9 introduces an arbitrary fixed real \(h\), p. 3574 (physical 48). Proposition 9.2, p. 3575 (physical 49), then states an uncentered second-moment limit and its proof assumes \(\kappa'(0)=0\) without imposing it.

Exact counterexample and correction. Use the one-coset \(b\)-system, \(\psi=1\), and \(h=0\). Then \(\kappa(w)=\lambda_{1,w}=e^w\), so \(\kappa'(0)=\kappa''(0)=1\), and the cost \(\Upsilon=2h\log x+\psi\) is identically one. The right-hand side of Proposition 9.2 is \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n
   \int\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}1\right)^2\Phi\,dx
 =\lim_{n\to\infty}n=+\infty,\] whereas its left-hand side equals one. The hypothesis needed by the proof is \(\kappa'(0)=0\), equivalently zero mean for the cost in this normalized setting. One must restrict \(h\) to the corresponding centered direction, or use a correctly centered variance and logarithmic eigenvalue derivative.

The downstream use in (10.1)–(10.2), p. 3578 (physical 52), does select \(h=s'(0)\) from \(\lambda(s(w),w)=1\); differentiation then gives precisely \(\kappa'(0)=0\). This verified compatibility limits the demonstrated impact to Minor: the overbroad proposition is false, but this example does not invalidate its intended centered use in the Hessian argument.

report: Abstract: The exact 72-page journal version is examined. Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical review of universality for monotone cellular automata
# Identity and scope

The reviewed article is Paul Balister, Béla Bollobás, Robert Morris and Paul Smith, Universality for monotone cellular automata, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 28 (2026), 4725–4796, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1666 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1666) [paper]. The publisher PDF records receipt on 6 November 2022 and revision on 10 September 2024; the publisher landing page labels 3 June 2025 as Published. These dates and the 2026 issue year are distinct. The frozen Math2025 membership is unchanged. The arXiv metadata identifies 2203.13806v3, dated 7 November 2022; this report does not presume equality with that manuscript. Physical page \(k\) has printed page \(4724+k\).

All 72 pages were read as extracted text, including Appendix A and the references. Detailed checks followed the recursive resistance definition, the bounding-tree construction, closure on shifted lattices, iceberg containers, weighted diameter, subadditivity and the one-step probability induction. Decisive source formulas were also checked in actual page images. This coverage is not a claim to have independently reproved every lemma and every external reference.

For a fixed critical finite update family \(\mathcal U\) in \(d\) dimensions, Theorem 3.1, p. 4736, proves the lower bound \[p_c(\mathbb Z_n^d,\mathcal U)\ge
 \left(\frac1{\log_{(r-1)}n}\right)^{d-1+o(1)},
 \qquad r=r(\mathcal U),\quad n\longrightarrow\infty.\] Updates are finite nonempty subsets of \(\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}\); the initial infections are Bernoulli with parameter \(p\). The constants may depend on the fixed update family and tree. The resistance lies in \(2,\ldots,d\) for critical families. Upper bounds and the subcritical part of the broader universality classification use companion papers; they are not all established within this article.
# A confirmed local defect

Problem 1 (Absolute support coordinates are not bounded by diameter).  In the proof of Lemma 6.12, p. 4767 (physical 43), equation (48) bounds each \(d_v(\mathcal X)\) by \(C\operatorname{wd}_{u_i}(G_{u_i}([K]_{u_j}))+O(1)\). The middle inequality of (49) similarly bounds \(d_v(\mathcal Y)\) by \(C\operatorname{wd}_{u_i}(\mathcal Y)\). Here Definition 6.2, p. 4761, defines \(d_v(B)=\sup_{x\in B}\langle x,v\rangle\), without centering. No origin is selected in this proof. Lemma 6.3 makes the weighted diameter translation invariant, but an individual support coordinate has no such invariance.
## A complete admissible counterexample

Take \(d=r=3\), \(\Lambda=\mathbb Z^3\), and the three-neighbour family \(\mathcal U=\mathcal N_3^3\): every three-element subset of \(\{\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_3\}\) is an update. Its stable set is the union of the three coordinate great circles. Choose the root children of the bounding tree to be \(\{\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_3\}\). For each such axis \(u\), choose the four children \[au+be_j,\quad au-be_j\qquad(e_j\perp u),\qquad
 a^2+b^2=1,\quad 0<b\ll a.\] This is an admissible two-level good bounding tree: the four local directions surround \(u\) on its small sphere, the axis has induced resistance two, each selected child is stable with the required induced resistance one, and every nonroot path is linearly independent. The radii can be made as small as required. For each path \(0\to u\to v\), the union of the two negative half-spaces contains at most two of the six nearest-neighbour vectors. It therefore contains no update, verifying the extra closure condition of Proposition 4.10, not merely individual stability. Choose the permitted root weights to be \(1/6\).

Let \(u_1=e_1\), \(k=1\), \(i=j=0\), and for integers \(N\ge1\) put \[K_N=\{(0,N,0),(0,N+1,1)\}.\] This finite nonempty set lies outside \(H_T(e_1)=\{x_1<0\}\); \(e_1\) is not a leaf. With only two seeds its ordinary closure is \([K_N]_0=K_N\). With the ocean \(x_1<0\) infected, both missing corners of the square receive one ocean neighbour and two planar neighbours. Consequently \[[K_N]_{e_1}=\{0\}\times\{N,N+1\}\times\{0,1\}\ne[K_N]_0.\] The displayed square is closed with the ocean: a site of the plane outside the square has at most one infected planar neighbour, and a site with \(x_1\ge1\) has at most one neighbour in the square. Thus the changed-closure case used in the proof really occurs.

Using precisely Definition 6.6, let \[A=G_0([K_N]_0)=\{0\}\times[N,N+1]\times[0,1].\] Then \(\operatorname{wd}_0(A)=1/3\). The set \(\mathcal Y=G_{e_1}(A)\) is given by \[\begin{gathered}
 x_1\ge0,\qquad ax_1+bx_2\le b(N+1),\qquad
 ax_1-bx_2\le-bN,\\
 ax_1+bx_3\le b,\qquad ax_1-bx_3\le0.
 \end{gathered}\] Its coordinate extrema give \[\mathcal X=G_0(\mathcal Y)
 =[0,b/(2a)]\times[N,N+1]\times[0,1].\] In particular, for \(v=e_2\in N_T^\to(0)\), \[d_{e_2}(\mathcal X)=d_{e_2}(\mathcal Y)=N+1.\] Equation (48) would give \(N+1\le C/3+O(1)\) for all \(N\), although its constants depend only on \(T\) and the update range. This is impossible. Likewise the middle inequality of (49) fails: \(\mathcal Y\) is simply translated by \(Ne_2\), so its weighted diameter stays fixed. All tree, closure, finiteness, lattice and nonleaf conditions are retained.
## The required weighted estimate can be recovered
The preceding counterexample concerns an unnecessarily strong intermediate statement. The actual conclusion (46), and hence Lemma 6.12, admits the following replacement proof.

Keep the notation of that proof and set \[S=[K]_{u_j},\qquad A=G_{u_i}(S),\qquad
 Y=G_{u_{j+1}}(A),\qquad X=G_{u_i}(Y).\] If the two closures agree, (46) is immediate. Otherwise \(A\) is strongly connected to the new half-space. If \(S\) already intersects it this is immediate; if not, the first new infection must use both the old closure and the new ocean, as in the paper’s closure argument. Also \(S\subset A\), since it stays outside the earlier oceans. Lemmas 6.10, 6.5 and 6.4 now yield \[\operatorname{diam}Y\le C\operatorname{wd}_{u_i}(A)+O(1),\qquad
 \operatorname{diam}A\le C\operatorname{wd}_{u_i}(A).                         \tag{1}\] There is no support-coordinate claim in (1).
## Impact and repair boundary

Lemma 6.12 feeds Lemma 6.14, which supplies the size estimates used in the Aizenman–Lebowitz and extremal lemmas and the one-step hierarchies. This is a central dependency, so a false line in its proof warrants explicit attention. However, (1)–(2) verify the exact weighted conclusion needed by those downstream uses. The counterexample refutes neither Lemma 6.12 nor the lower bound of Theorem 3.1. On this established scope the assessment is Minor: replace (48)–(49) with a centered argument. This grading rests on the demonstrated preservation of the needed conclusion, not simply on the apparent ease of editing the text.
# Other checks, boundary cases and limitations

The construction of a good tree was checked against the union-of-oceans closure condition; stability of each half-space alone would not suffice. Shifted lattices are explicitly allowed, and the geometric constants must not depend on their translation. The choice of iceberg type uses a permissible sequence and the deepest eligible vertex; replacing it by an arbitrary smallest droplet would change the proof. The root case \(u=0\), nonleaf restrictions, and the extra depth factor in \(\operatorname{diam}^{**}\) were retained in the probability induction.

Section 8 fixes \[(d-1)^{-1}>\varepsilon(2)>\cdots>\varepsilon(r)>0,\qquad
 x(s)=\exp_{(s-2)}(p^{-\varepsilon(s)}).\] It explicitly assumes \(p\) sufficiently small after the geometric constants have been fixed. The base estimate uses \(x^{d-1}p\to0\); the restrictions on \(\varepsilon(2)\) are essential. The disjoint-witness cases use the BK inequality; the crossing case uses events depending on disjoint subsets after the inner iceberg is fixed. Remark 7.7 makes the translated ocean a deterministic function of the selected droplets and vertex, which is needed in counting choices. These are not arbitrary independent events.

The final torus argument was checked for the scale condition \(n\gg x(r)\). For a lower bound it suffices, by monotonicity in \(p\), to work at \(p=(\log_{(r-1)}n)^{-1/\varepsilon}\), where \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon(r)\) is fixed. At that density, \[x(r)=\exp_{(r-2)}
 \bigl((\log_{(r-1)}n)^{\varepsilon(r)/\varepsilon}\bigr)\ll n,\] while \(x(r)\gg\log n\), so the final exponential bound defeats the polynomial number of droplets. The scale condition need not hold for every smaller \(p\); monotonicity transfers the conclusion from the displayed density. The iterated-exponential comparison and the polynomial count of faces in the final union bound were read.

The full chain of deterministic lemmas and all three probabilistic cases were read; the local geometric estimate above was independently reproved. Not every combinatorial subcase or external result has been independently reconstructed. The companion papers and all cited sharp-threshold results were not independently verified. A bounded search of publisher, arXiv and author sources did not locate a separate target erratum, supplement or implementation. Oxford ORA returned 403 and the Morris homepage returned empty redirect content. Absence from this search is not a defect, and no author code was run.

report: Abstract: The reviewed paper is by Keshav Aggarwal, Wing Hong Leung and Ritabrata Munshi, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1667. An elementary infinite family contradicts the generic square-free-modulus bound in Lemma B.1, even with both coefficient parameters invertible modulo the modulus. Its local degeneracy at one prime is not detected by the stated congruences modulo the entire modulus. This estimate enters the main Cauchy–Schwarz iteration. Title: Verification of the character-sum input to
a short second moment bound for GL(3) \(L\)-functions
# Identity, versions and scope

This report concerns M25-0294, Short second moment bound and subconvexity for \(\mathrm{GL}(3)\) \(L\)-functions [vor]. The principal source is the 75-page publisher PDF: J. Eur. Math. Soc. 28 (2026), 4797–4871, revised 15 February 2025, copyright 2025. The publisher labels its publication date 12 June 2025 [publisher]. The collection’s frozen 2025 membership is unchanged. Here a publisher PDF page \(k\) has printed page \(4796+k\).

The separately retained 58-page author manuscript arXiv:2206.06517v3 is dated 21 September 2025 [v3]. Its page numbers are its PDF page numbers. The arXiv record says Fixed errors and grammatical mistakes [arxiv]. That statement is not a list of corrections and does not establish equivalence to the publisher text. Both full texts, including Appendices A and B, were read in this conversation. The current continuation reuses the unchanged publisher text and the earlier reading of v3 pages 1–21; it completes the reading of v3 pages 22–58 and performs the decisive checks below. Selected original pages, including every passage used for the finding and its principal dependency, were also actually viewed as images.

The review followed the fixed-form quantifiers in Theorems 1.1–1.2, the approximate-functional-equation and short-moment reduction, the delta/Voronoi transformations, the four ranges of the Poisson frequency, and the character-sum and stationary-phase iteration. This is not a formal verification of every oscillatory-integral estimate or of all externally cited theorems. No author code was run. No separately released supplement or implementation was located in the bounded publisher, arXiv and author-page searches; their absence from those searches is not a mathematical defect.
# Supporting checks

Equation reference: eq:moment. The main theorem fixes a Hecke–Maass cusp form \(\pi\) for \(\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(t^{1/2}<M<t^{1-\varepsilon}\), Theorem 1.1, printed p. 4800, claims \[
 \int_{t-M}^{t+M}|L(1/2+iv,\pi)|^2\,dv
 \ll_{\pi,\varepsilon}t^\varepsilon
 \left(\frac{t^{9/4}}{M^{3/2}}+
 \frac{M^3}{t^{21/20}}+M^{7/4}t^{3/40}
 +M^{15/14}t^{15/28}\right).\] Together with the short-interval pointwise reduction, \(M=t^{2/3}\) gives the claimed \(5/8+\varepsilon\) pointwise exponent in Theorem 1.2, printed p. 4801. Direct exponent checking gives \(5/4,19/20,149/120,5/4\) for the four second-moment terms. This final substitution is consistent; the concern is an earlier uniform arithmetic estimate.

Equation reference: eq:C. Put \(e_c(u)=\exp(2\pi i u/c)\) and use the unnormalized Kloosterman sum \[S(A,B;c)=\sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/c\mathbb Z)^\times}
             e_c(Ax+B\bar x),\] where a bar denotes a multiplicative inverse modulo the current modulus. Appendix B.1, printed pp. 4861–4862 (PDF pp. 65–66), defines \[\begin{aligned}

 \mathcal C(a,b_1,b_2,b_3,c,q_1,q_2)
 ={}&\sum_{\gamma\bmod c}^{*} e_c(a\gamma)\nonumber\\
 &{}\times S(b_1-\bar q_1b_2+\bar\gamma b_2,\,
                  b_3(\gamma-q_1);c)\nonumber\\
 &{}\times S(b_1-\bar q_2b_2+\bar\gamma b_2,\,
                  b_3(\gamma-q_2);c).\end{aligned}\] The inverses on \(q_j\), as well as on \(\gamma\), are part of the original formula and were checked on the actual PDF.

Equation reference: eq:exception. Problem 1 (Partial prime-factor degeneracy is omitted).  Lemma B.1 assumes integer parameters, square-free \(c\), \((q_1q_2,c)=1\), and \(c\nmid b_2,b_3\). It claims \(\mathcal C\ll c^{2+\varepsilon}\) if at least one of \[
 q_1=q_2,\quad
 b_1\pm b_2(\bar q_1-\bar q_2)=0,\quad
 b_1-\bar q_1b_2=0,\quad b_1-\bar q_2b_2=0
 \pmod c\] holds, and otherwise claims \(\mathcal C\ll c^{3/2+\varepsilon}\). The latter estimate is false uniformly in the stated parameters.
## A complete family satisfying the hypotheses

For any prime \(p>7\), write \[S_p(z)=S(1,z;p),\qquad
 z_p=\min\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{1\le z<p} S_p(z)^2.\] This specifies \(z_p\) exactly: the least residue attaining the minimum of a finite collection of real algebraic numbers. Indeed, \(S(A,B;p)\) is real, since complex conjugation followed by \(x\mapsto-x\) leaves the sum unchanged. Let \(d_p=49z_p\pmod p\); this is nonzero.

Equation reference: eq:parameters. Set \(c=7p\), \(a=0\), and choose the unique residues modulo \(c\) specified by the Chinese remainder theorem: \[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 & \bmod 7 & \bmod p\\ \hline
 q_1 &1&1\\
 q_2 &2&1\\
 b_1 &2p&1\\
 b_2 &p&1\\
 b_3 &p&d_p
\end{array}\] All entries are interpreted in the indicated residue field. The modulus is square-free; \(q_1,q_2,b_2,b_3\) are units modulo \(7p\). Thus the example satisfies even the stronger condition \((b_2b_3,c)=1\), not merely \(c\nmid b_2,b_3\).

Equation reference: eq:nonexceptions. None of the exceptions [eq:exception] (#eq:exception) holds. It suffices to examine them modulo 7. There \(\bar q_1=1\), \(\bar q_2=4\), and their respective left sides are \[
 -1,\qquad -p,\quad 5p,\qquad p,\qquad -2p .\] All five residues are nonzero because \(p>7\) is prime. There are no restrictions on \(a\) excluding zero. In particular, every original hypothesis and the claimed otherwise branch have been verified.
## Exact independent evaluation

Equation reference: eq:factor, eq:D. For coprime moduli \(m,n\), the elementary factorization \[S(A,B;mn)=
 S(A\bar n,B\bar n;m)\,S(A\bar m,B\bar m;n)\] follows by applying CRT to the summation variable and to the additive character. Applying it to [eq:C] (#eq:C), the coefficient choices [eq:parameters] (#eq:parameters) give \[
 \mathcal C(0,b_1,b_2,b_3,7p,q_1,q_2)=K D_p,
 \qquad K=\mathcal C(0,2,1,1,7,1,2),\] where, with \(k=7^{-1}\pmod p\), \[D_p=\sum_{\gamma\in\mathbb F_p^\times}
         S(k\bar\gamma,kd_p(\gamma-1);p)^2.\] Because the first Kloosterman argument is nonzero, a change of variable gives \[S(k\bar\gamma,kd_p(\gamma-1);p)
       =S_p\bigl(k^2d_p(1-\bar\gamma)\bigr)
       =S_p\bigl(z_p(1-\bar\gamma)\bigr).\] As \(\gamma\) runs through \(\mathbb F_p^\times\), its last argument runs bijectively through \(\mathbb F_p\setminus\{z_p\}\). Consequently \[
 D_p=\sum_{z\in\mathbb F_p}S_p(z)^2-S_p(z_p)^2
     =p(p-1)-S_p(z_p)^2 .\] For completeness, the orthogonality identity used here has the following direct proof: \[\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{z\in\mathbb F_p} S_p(z)^2
 &=\sum_{x,y\in\mathbb F_p^\times}e_p(x+y)
                 \sum_{z\in\mathbb F_p}e_p\bigl(z(x^{-1}+y^{-1})\bigr)\\
 &=p\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_p^\times}e_p(x-x)=p(p-1).\end{aligned}\] Also \(S_p(0)=-1\). By the definition of \(z_p\), \[S_p(z_p)^2\le
 \frac{p(p-1)-1}{p-1}
 =p-\frac1{p-1}<p,
 \qquad D_p>p^2-2p.\] Thus the lower bound does not require a numerical approximation or an appeal to a deep bound for Kloosterman sums.

Equation reference: eq:hist. It remains to check that the fixed factor \(K\) is nonzero. Expanding its two sums expresses it as a sum of \(6^3=216\) seventh roots of unity, each with integer multiplicity. report: Abstract: This report reviews Jan Nienhaus and Matthias Wink’s exact author manuscript arXiv:2303.04832v3, associated with DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1668. The proof’s coordinate changes, cone linearization, angle barrier and intersection mechanism were examined. Two local defects are confirmed: a missing compactness restriction in the preliminary geometric discussion, and an unjustified assertion about repeated entry into a disk in the rotation lemma. Explicit examples establish both defects. A first-arrival truncation repairs the latter argument without changing the intersection bound used in the main theorem. The supported assessment is Minor; no counterexample to the three-metric existence theorem was found. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: A technical review of
Einstein metrics on the ten-sphere
# Exact source and review scope

M25-0295 is Einstein metrics on the ten-sphere, by Jan Nienhaus and Matthias Wink [paper]. The reviewed source is the 28-page arXiv:2303.04832v3 PDF, dated 11 September 2024; the version-history timestamp is 02:42:07 UTC. Its SHA256 is `4981f7e92e1a221f3b468adb539406b7d4321c69fe582621f6dfa0b334e11b13`. All page numbers below refer to this PDF, whose printed and physical pagination agree. The frozen collection title and identifier are retained; the manuscript capitalizes Ten-Sphere differently.

EMS lists publication on 30 May 2025, online first, and requires a subscription for its PDF [publisher]. This review does not establish identity with that unavailable journal text. The arXiv comment says that references were updated [metadata]; it does not establish cross-version equivalence.

All 28 pages were read, including references and the discussion of numerical observations. Fourteen source pages were actually viewed as images, including both finding locations and the key estimates and figures. The review traced the existence proof and independently checked selected algebraic identities. The cited singular initial-value and homogeneous classification theorems were not reproved. The numerical plots were viewed as illustrations, not used as certified computations or as uniqueness proofs. No author code was run. Bounded searches of the publisher, arXiv and author pages located no separate correction, supplement or code release; this is not a proof of absence and is not itself a defect.
# Main argument and independent checks

Theorem A on p. 1 asserts at least three pairwise non-isometric, non-round positive-scalar-curvature Einstein metrics on \(S^{10}\). The construction uses \[g=dt^2+f_1(t)^2g_{S^{d_1}}+f_2(t)^2g_{S^{d_2}},
 \qquad (d_1,d_2)\in\{(2,7),(3,6),(4,5)\}.\] The smooth endpoint conditions (5)–(6), p. 7, collapse different sphere factors at the two ends. The cited singular initial-value result supplies the one-parameter family with \(f_1(0)=0\), \(\dot f_1(0)=1\), \(f_2(0)>0\), \(\dot f_2(0)=0\). Endpoint smoothness is substantive, not merely positivity of the interior warping functions.

Independent symbolic calculations reproduced the change from the \(Y_i\) equations to \(Z'\), the weighted-square constraint, and \[\frac{d}{ds}\log\mathcal F=2d_1d_2\Delta^2H\] in the interior. At \(p_1^+\) the computed eigenvalues are \(2/d_1\) twice and \(-(d_1-1)/d_1\), for each of the three pairs. At the positive cone base point with \(n=9\), the transverse matrix is \[\begin{pmatrix}0&-16/81\\1&-8/9\end{pmatrix},\] with double eigenvalue \(-4/9\) and eigenvector \((4,9)\). This agrees with the direction used in Corollary 2.17.

The angle equation is \[\varphi'=\cos^2\varphi+\frac{16}{81}\sin^2\varphi
              -\frac89 h\sin\varphi\cos\varphi,\qquad
 h(s)=-\tanh(s/9).\] Its completed-square form in (12) was independently verified. The four comparisons in Proposition 4.2 and the uniform perturbation in Lemma 4.3 were read with attention to reversing \(s\) versus \(h\). The comparison point is \[h_*=\tanh\bigl(\operatorname{artanh}(1/2)+\pi/8\bigr).\] Its decimal evaluation, and that of \(h_*+1/4\), are retained as diagnostics; the proof uses the explicit inequalities, not plot resolution.

For the helicoidal barrier in Proposition 5.1, direct symbolic linearization of the normal component gives \[\langle N,E\rangle
       =\frac{1-h^2}{9}\bigl(\delta r+O(r^2)\bigr).\] The positive leading coefficient was checked for all three pairs. The invariant \(\mathcal F\)-tube then keeps nearby trajectories on the required side. The resulting strict angle bounds exceed \(2\pi\) on each unreflected curve; after reflection the difference exceeds \(4\pi\). The rotation argument yields at least two intersections, one round and at least one non-round. Remark 5.2 distinguishes the three non-round metrics by the topology of their principal orbits and the cited classification of homogeneous Einstein metrics. No claim of exactly three such metrics is proved; the stronger numerical uniqueness discussion on pp. 25–27 remains conjectural.
# Confirmed local findings

Problem 1 (Missing restriction in the preliminary discussion).  Section 1.1, p. 6, introduces an arbitrary Riemannian manifold with an isometric cohomogeneity-one action, then asserts that an Einstein metric is flat or has positive scalar curvature. Compactness is not included in those stated hypotheses. The assertion is false at that level of generality.
## Decisive example and all hypotheses

For any \(n\ge2\), take hyperbolic space \[M=\mathbb H^{n+1},\qquad
 g=dr^2+\sinh^2(r)\,g_{S^n}.\] The polar expression extends smoothly across \(r=0\), since \(\sinh r=r+O(r^3)\), and gives a complete manifold. The group \(\mathrm{SO}(n+1)\) acts isometrically by rotations, with principal orbits \(S^n\), one singular center and one-dimensional orbit space \([0,\infty)\). For \(r>0\), the radial and tangential sectional curvatures are \[-\frac{(\sinh r)''}{\sinh r}=-1,\qquad
 \frac{1-((\sinh r)')^2}{\sinh^2r}=-1.\] They extend across the center. Hence \(\operatorname{Ric}=-ng\), so this is neither flat nor of positive scalar curvature. The curvature identities were also checked exactly by the independent script.
## Impact and correction boundary

The counterexample satisfies the written preliminary hypotheses, even completeness and compactness of the acting group. It is noncompact, and therefore does not satisfy the later sphere setting explicitly imposed in Section 1.2, p. 7. The narrow correction is to state the compact setting at the start of Section 1.1, or to restrict its curvature conclusion to the closed spheres under consideration. Completeness must accompany any general invocation of Myers’ theorem.

For the actual \(S^{10}\) setting, the positivity restriction does not rely on the erroneous noncompact generalization. A nonzero Killing field on a closed Einstein manifold satisfies the integrated Bochner identity \(\int|\nabla X|^2=\int\operatorname{Ric}(X,X)\), excluding negative Einstein constant. If the constant were zero, every Killing field would be parallel; a nonzero parallel field cannot exist on \(S^{10}\), whose Euler characteristic is 2. The group action supplies nonzero Killing fields. The issue is therefore Minor: its demonstrated effect is on the scope of the preliminary statement, not on the positive-curvature construction on the compact sphere. No adoption of this correction by the authors has been established.

Problem 2 (The disk-entry assertion in Lemma 3.4’s proof).  In the first paragraph of the proof of Lemma 3.4, p. 16, continuity is used to conclude that both simple curves enter each sufficiently small disk just once and remain there. Continuity and injectivity do not imply that assertion.
## An example within the lemma’s curve hypotheses

Identify \(\mathbb R^2\) with \(\mathbb C\). For \(0\le t<1\), put \(u=1-t\), \(R=2+\sin1\), and define \[\alpha(t)=u\bigl(2+\sin(1/u)\bigr)e^{iu},
 \qquad
 \beta(t)=Ru\,e^{i(2-u)}.\] Both curves are nonzero and continuous, have the same initial point \(Re^{i}\), and extend to zero at \(t=1\). Each is injective because its angle is strictly monotone through an interval of length less than \(2\pi\). Their interiors are disjoint: their respective angular ranges are \((0,1)\) and \((1,2)\). Taking \(\gamma_1=\beta\), \(\gamma_2=\alpha\), their truncated angles are \(1-u\) and \(u-1\). For all sufficiently small \(u>0\) these are at least \(1/2\) and at most \(-1/2\), respectively. Thus the eventual inequalities in Definition 3.3 hold with \(\theta_0=1\). Their limits \(1\) and \(-1\) alone would not justify the endpoint choice \(\theta_0=2\). The example does not contradict the lemma’s intersection bound; it contradicts the asserted truncation property.

Indeed, let \(0<\rho<1/(2\pi)\). Choose an integer \(k\) such that \[x=2\pi k+\pi/2\in[2/\rho,\,2/\rho+2\pi).\] At phases \(1/u=x-\pi,x,x+\pi\), the radii of \(\alpha\) are \[\frac1{x-\pi}<\rho,\qquad
 \frac3x>\rho,\qquad
 \frac1{x+\pi}<\rho.\] The inequalities follow from \(x-\pi>1/\rho\) and \(x<3/\rho\). The initial radius is larger than \(\rho\). As \(t\) increases, the curve therefore enters, exits, and enters this disk again. This holds for every such \(\rho\), not merely for isolated radii. All of the curve assumptions, including finite mutual intersection, have been retained.
## Verified replacement of the truncation step

The proof can instead use the first arrival at the radius. For each curve and sufficiently small \(r>0\), set \[t_i(r)=\min\{t\in[a_i,b_i):|\gamma_i(t)|=r\}.\] This time exists by continuity and convergence to zero, and \(|\gamma_i(t)|>r\) for \(a_i\le t<t_i(r)\). Moreover \(t_i(r)\to b_i\) as \(r\downarrow0\): for every \(\eta>0\), the compact initial segment \(\gamma_i([a_i,b_i-\eta])\) has a strictly positive minimum distance from the origin. Choosing \(r\) below that minimum forces the first arrival to occur after \(b_i-\eta\).

Retain only these initial segments, irrespective of later exits. Consequently the eventual angle bounds of Definition 3.3 still hold at the truncation times. In particular this applies to the two separate strict bounds used on pp. 22–24. The retained prefixes are strictly outside the circle except at their endpoints. A positively oriented circular arc joining those endpoints adds a nonnegative angle and introduces no intersection with the prefixes. For small \(r\), the endpoints are distinct since the mutual intersections are finite and away from zero. Thus the closed-curve argument has exactly the same allowed source of self-intersections and the same winding lower bound as required in the original proof.

This replacement removes the false assertion without adding radial monotonicity, endpoint differentiability, or a stronger hypothesis on the Einstein trajectories. In the main application, the strict difference remains greater than \(4\pi\), hence the integer winding number is at least 3 and the required intersection count remains at least 2. This is why the issue is assessed as Minor: a locally verified correction preserves the actual core count. No false rotation-lemma conclusion or false metric-existence conclusion is asserted. Author adoption is unknown.
# Assessment and limitations
Dimension | Result
Issue judgment | Two confirmed Minor findings in the exact v3.
Repair verification | Geometric scope restriction justified for \(S^{10}\); first-arrival truncation preserves the angle and intersection bounds used in Theorem A.
Core theorem | No counterexample found; selected central algebra and the dependency chain checked, not a formal certification of every cited theorem.
Numerical claims | Viewed as illustrative and conjectural; no author code or certified numerical uniqueness proof executed.
Version/adoption | Journal-text equivalence unestablished; author adoption unknown.
Scientific decision | Pending; human reviews empty. Current independent acceptance is recorded in the associated provenance.
# Supporting checks

The symbolic tests verify identities and selected linear terms; their success is not a substitute for the analytic arguments above. The radial decimal samples and \(h_*\) evaluations are labeled floating diagnostics.

The exact report is compiled with the approved existing Tectonic 0.17.0 route and `–untrusted`, using only this paper’s cache and temporary directory. Actual TeX, source, compiler, dependency and PDF hashes, commands, exit codes and retained logs are bound in the build record. Rendering and actual page viewing have separate records.

Native helpers supplied only bounded metadata searches and mechanical file-binding checks. The controller’s UI observation of Personal Chat/GPT-6/Pro is recorded as its observation, separately from runtime self-description; no independent backend identity verification is claimed.

analysis: In the first paragraph of the proof of Lemma 3.4, p. 16, continuity is used to conclude that both simple curves enter each sufficiently small disk just once and remain there. Continuity and injectivity do not imply that assertion.

Identify \(\mathbb R^2\) with \(\mathbb C\). For \(0\le t<1\), put \(u=1-t\), \(R=2+\sin1\), and define \[\alpha(t)=u\bigl(2+\sin(1/u)\bigr)e^{iu},
 \qquad
 \beta(t)=Ru\,e^{i(2-u)}.\] Both curves are nonzero and continuous, have the same initial point \(Re^{i}\), and extend to zero at \(t=1\). Each is injective because its angle is strictly monotone through an interval of length less than \(2\pi\). Their interiors are disjoint: their respective angular ranges are \((0,1)\) and \((1,2)\). Taking \(\gamma_1=\beta\), \(\gamma_2=\alpha\), their truncated angles are \(1-u\) and \(u-1\). For all sufficiently small \(u>0\) these are at least \(1/2\) and at most \(-1/2\), respectively. Thus the eventual inequalities in Definition 3.3 hold with \(\theta_0=1\). Their limits \(1\) and \(-1\) alone would not justify the endpoint choice \(\theta_0=2\). The example does not contradict the lemma’s intersection bound; it contradicts the asserted truncation property.

Indeed, let \(0<\rho<1/(2\pi)\). Choose an integer \(k\) such that \[x=2\pi k+\pi/2\in[2/\rho,\,2/\rho+2\pi).\] At phases \(1/u=x-\pi,x,x+\pi\), the radii of \(\alpha\) are \[\frac1{x-\pi}<\rho,\qquad
 \frac3x>\rho,\qquad
 \frac1{x+\pi}<\rho.\] The inequalities follow from \(x-\pi>1/\rho\) and \(x<3/\rho\). The initial radius is larger than \(\rho\). As \(t\) increases, the curve therefore enters, exits, and enters this disk again. This holds for every such \(\rho\), not merely for isolated radii. All of the curve assumptions, including finite mutual intersection, have been retained.

The proof can instead use the first arrival at the radius. For each curve and sufficiently small \(r>0\), set \[t_i(r)=\min\{t\in[a_i,b_i):|\gamma_i(t)|=r\}.\] This time exists by continuity and convergence to zero, and \(|\gamma_i(t)|>r\) for \(a_i\le t<t_i(r)\). Moreover \(t_i(r)\to b_i\) as \(r\downarrow0\): for every \(\eta>0\), the compact initial segment \(\gamma_i([a_i,b_i-\eta])\) has a strictly positive minimum distance from the origin. Choosing \(r\) below that minimum forces the first arrival to occur after \(b_i-\eta\).

Retain only these initial segments, irrespective of later exits. Consequently the eventual angle bounds of Definition 3.3 still hold at the truncation times. In particular this applies to the two separate strict bounds used on pp. 22–24. The retained prefixes are strictly outside the circle except at their endpoints. A positively oriented circular arc joining those endpoints adds a nonnegative angle and introduces no intersection with the prefixes. For small \(r\), the endpoints are distinct since the mutual intersections are finite and away from zero. Thus the closed-curve argument has exactly the same allowed source of self-intersections and the same winding lower bound as required in the original proof.

This replacement removes the false assertion without adding radial monotonicity, endpoint differentiability, or a stronger hypothesis on the Einstein trajectories. In the main application, the strict difference remains greater than \(4\pi\), hence the integer winding number is at least 3 and the required intersection count remains at least 2. This is why the issue is assessed as Minor: a locally verified correction preserves the actual core count. No false rotation-lemma conclusion or false metric-existence conclusion is asserted. Author adoption is unknown.
result: Impact: The asserted truncation property is false; the lemma conclusion is not disproved.

report: Abstract: This report examines Piotr Pstrągowski’s exact manuscript arXiv:2304.04685v2, associated with DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1669. Two substantive assertions are false as stated. The base-change surjectivity theorem fails for a connective rational square-zero extension, including with a connective even flat input module. The asserted strong monoidal structure on the module filtration fails for two suspensions of the rational Eilenberg–Mac Lane spectrum. Explicit computations establish both failures and isolate the affected conclusions. A narrower connective base-change statement is proved, and the distinction between lax and strong monoidality is essential. The supported assessment is Major for this exact manuscript; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: A technical review of
Perfect even modules and the even filtration
# Source, scope and method

M25-0296 is Perfect even modules and the even filtration, by Piotr Pstrągowski [paper]. The source is arXiv:2304.04685v2, submitted on 24 October 2024 at 09:13:03 UTC, with 57 PDF pages. Its SHA256 is `37cd80d462acf94fca5c6ffb30e4b0bc2728ba245927e30fb68d0217e4786210`. Printed and physical page numbers agree. EMS records publication on 11 July 2025 and acceptance on 20 October 2024 [publisher]. The journal PDF was not available in the acquired source set; identity between that version and this author manuscript is unestablished. The frozen 2025 identifier and original title mapping are preserved.

All 57 pages were read, including the references. Fourteen source pages were actually viewed as images to check the statements, notation, hypotheses, formulas and decisive proof passages. The review followed the perfect-even site, sheaf construction, even cohomology, module structure, even flatness, envelopes, resolutions, descent, comparison and connective estimates. Reading all pages does not certify every external infinity-categorical result or every descent proof. No author code was run. Bounded searches of arXiv, EMS and the author’s publication page located no separate correction, supplement or code release; this is a search limitation, not a claim of nonexistence.

The independent program retained with the evidence checks the rational square-zero multiplication, all eight basis associativity triples, the unit, and the exact degree tables below. It uses rational arithmetic and no author routines. The ring-spectrum realization and categorical identifications are justified analytically here, rather than attributed to that finite computation.
# The construction and the dependencies used

Perfect even \(R\)-modules are generated by \(\Sigma^{2k}R\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\), under finite extensions and retracts (Definition 2.2, p. 7). Thus negative even suspensions are allowed. An even flat module is a filtered colimit of perfect even modules (Proposition 4.3 and Definition 4.4, pp. 30–31); it is homologically even by Remark 4.17. Homotopy-even modules are also homologically even, but the several notions must not be interchanged without their hypotheses.

Theorem 8.1, p. 51, assumes both a connective ring and a connective, homologically even module. It identifies \(H_{\mathrm{ev}}^{0,0}(R,M)\) with \(\pi_0M\) and gives vanishing for \(p>q\). Proposition 4.11, p. 32, makes the connective-envelope assertion only when both \(R\) and \(M\) are connective. These restrictions matter in Problem 1.
# Confirmed findings

Equation reference: eq:base. Problem 1 (Major: the base-change surjectivity region is false).  Theorem 1.10 on p. 6 and Theorem 8.8 on p. 55 assert that, for a right homologically even map \(f:R\to S\) of connective \(E_1\)-rings and an even flat \(R\)-module \(M\), the comparison \[\pi_0S\otimes_{\pi_0R}H_{\mathrm{ev}}^{p,q}(R,M)
 \longrightarrow H_{\mathrm{ev}}^{p,q}(S,S\otimes_R M)             \] is surjective for \(p\ge q-1\).
## A connective counterexample satisfying every hypothesis

Let \(R=H\mathbb Q\) and let \[S=R\oplus\Sigma^2R\] be the split square-zero \(R\)-algebra. Equivalently, realize the differential graded rational algebra \(\mathbb Q[e]/(e^2)\), with \(|e|=2\) in homological grading and zero differential. The multiplication is unital and associative; the resulting ring spectrum is connective. The inclusion \(f:R\to S\) is a map of connective \(E_1\)-rings. As a right \(R\)-module, \(S\) is a finite direct sum of even suspensions of \(R\). Hence it is perfect even, even flat, and homologically even, as required. Also \(\pi_0R=\pi_0S=\mathbb Q\), with the identity map on these rings.

Take \(M=R\). This module is both connective and perfect even. At \((p,q)=(0,1)\), equation [eq:even] (#eq:even) identifies [eq:base] (#eq:base) with \[\mathbb Q\otimes_\mathbb Q\pi_2R=0
 \ \longrightarrow\ \pi_2S=\mathbb Q.\] The map is not surjective, although \(0\ge1-1\). The target class is the square-zero generator \(e\). Thus adding connectivity of \(M\) alone does not repair the stated range. This example also has an even flat cofiber \(\Sigma^2R\); a stronger faithful-even-flat assumption would not remove this particular obstruction.
## Why changing only the inequality is insufficient

Keep \(R,S,f\), but set \(M=\Sigma^{-2}R\). Definition 2.2 permits this perfect even, hence even flat, module. At \((p,q)=(0,0)\), the same comparison becomes \[\mathbb Q\otimes_\mathbb Q\pi_0(\Sigma^{-2}R)=0
 \ \longrightarrow\
 \pi_0(\Sigma^{-2}S)=\pi_2S=\mathbb Q.\] This fails even on the Milnor line \(p=q\). It satisfies every printed hypothesis but \(M\) is not connective, a condition absent from Theorems 1.10 and 8.8. Consequently, replacing \(p\ge q-1\) by \(p\ge q\) alone is also insufficient.
## Proof location and dependency

The first sentence of the proof on p. 55 invokes Theorem 8.1 for the \(q=0\) case without its connectivity hypothesis on \(M\). The subsequent choice of an envelope \(M\to E\) with \(C=\operatorname{cofib}(M\to E)\) 2-connective likewise invokes the connective part of Proposition 4.11 without assuming connectivity of \(M\).

There is a separate index issue. The displayed diagram on p. 55 has right column in cohomological degree \(p+1\), while the text assumes \(p\ge q-1\). Even when its other steps apply, this reaches degree \(r=p+1\ge q\), not the advertised degree \(q-1\). It does not reach the first counterexample at \(p=0,q=1\). Both issues are witnessed by actual non-surjective maps, so the finding does not depend merely on a missing explanatory sentence.
## A verified narrower statement and its boundary
A valid consequence of the earlier lemmas is obtained by imposing that \(M\) is connective and claiming surjectivity only for \(p\ge q\), with integer weights. Here is the corrected induction.

For \(q=0\), Theorem 8.1 identifies the only possible group on or above that line with \(\pi_0M\). Connectivity gives \(\pi_0(S\otimes_R M)\cong\pi_0S\otimes_{\pi_0R}\pi_0M\). For \(q>0\), choose the connective envelope \(M\to E\to C\) with \(C\) 2-connective. Both \(C\) and \(E\) are even flat, and \(E\) has even homotopy. The right-module form of Theorem 4.16 implies that \(S\otimes_R E\) also has even homotopy. For \(r\ge q>0\), the two long exact sequences therefore give surjections \[H_{\mathrm{ev}}^{r-1,q}(R,C)\twoheadrightarrow H_{\mathrm{ev}}^{r,q}(R,M),
 \qquad
 H_{\mathrm{ev}}^{r-1,q}(S,S\otimes_R C)
 \twoheadrightarrow H_{\mathrm{ev}}^{r,q}(S,S\otimes_R M).\] The same is true of the first row after tensoring by \(\pi_0S\), by right exactness. Put \(C'=\Sigma^{-2}C\). It is connective and even flat, and \(H_{\mathrm{ev}}^{r-1,q}(R,C)=H_{\mathrm{ev}}^{r-1,q-1}(R,C')\). The induction hypothesis applies because \(r-1\ge q-1\). Naturality and the two surjective rows prove the assertion in degree \(r\). Negative weights vanish for connective homologically even modules by Theorem 8.1 and vanishing in negative cohomological degrees.

This argument verifies a narrower statement, not an optimal replacement and not the originally claimed off-diagonal range. The advertised base-change theorem is itself a main result; its genuine loss of scope supports Major severity. The examples do not disprove the construction of the filtration, the descent theorem, or the connective convergence results.

Problem 2 (Major: the module filtration is not strongly monoidal).  Corollary 3.38, p. 29, claims that for an \(E_n\)-ring \(R\) the module filtration functor \[\mathrm{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^{*}:\operatorname{Mod}_R(\operatorname{Sp})
 \longrightarrow
 \operatorname{Mod}_{\mathrm{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^{*}(R)}(\mathrm{Fil}\operatorname{Sp})\] is canonically \(E_{n-1}\)-monoidal. The assertion is also advertised in item (2) after Theorem 1.3 on p. 3. Section 1.1, p. 7, explicitly distinguishes monoidal (strongly monoidal) from lax monoidal functors.
## An explicit failure of the tensor comparison

Use \(R=H\mathbb Q\), which is an \(E_\infty\)-ring, and let \(M=N=\Sigma R\). These are legitimate modules in the claimed domain; the statement imposes no evenness restriction on them. Write \(f_j(X)\) for the filtered object equal to \(X\) in weights \(k\le j\) and zero in weights \(k>j\), as in Notation 3.14, p. 21. Its tensor product is Day convolution. By [eq:post] (#eq:post), \[A:=\mathrm{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^{*}(R)=f_0(R),\qquad
 \mathrm{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^{*}(\Sigma R)=f_0(\Sigma R)=\Sigma A .\] These last objects are free suspensions of the unit \(A\)-module. Their relative tensor product is therefore \[\mathrm{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^{*}(M)\otimes_A\mathrm{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^{*}(N)
 \simeq \Sigma^2 A=f_0(\Sigma^2R).\] In contrast, \[\mathrm{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^{*}(M\otimes_R N)
 =\mathrm{Fil}_{\mathrm{ev}/R}^{*}(\Sigma^2R)=f_1(\Sigma^2R).\] At weight \(1\), the comparison has source zero and target \(\Sigma^2H\mathbb Q\), whose \(\pi_2\) is \(\mathbb Q\). It cannot be an equivalence. In fact the two filtered objects are inequivalent, so choosing a different comparison morphism cannot supply the asserted strong structure. The filtrations in this example are complete; completion does not eliminate the nonzero weight-\(1\) discrepancy.
## Impact and repair boundary

Theorem 3.37 on p. 28 asserts a lax symmetric monoidal functor on algebra–module pairs. The counterexample is consistent with that weaker assertion: a map \(0\to\Sigma^2H\mathbb Q\) exists, but is not invertible. The passage to the fixed-\(R\) fiber in the proof of Corollary 3.38 does not turn a lax comparison into an equivalence. The construction therefore does not justify the strong conclusion printed in the corollary.

A revision to lax \(E_{n-1}\)-monoidality, together with the corresponding correction in the introduction, is compatible with Theorem 3.37 and the example. A strong theorem would need additional restrictions or a different filtration; no maximal subcategory on which it holds is certified here. This is Major because an advertised structural conclusion fails on elementary objects in its stated domain, independently of the practical length of a textual correction. No failure of the lax multiplicative construction is claimed.
# Coverage and residual limitations

The review distinguished the even-epimorphism topology and sheafification from objectwise truncation (pp. 7–16), and followed the compact-generator and filtered-module constructions (pp. 17–29). In this part, Problems 1–2 use especially Corollary 2.37, Proposition 2.40, the filtered generators, and the strong/lax distinction.

The calculus of evenness and the envelope construction (pp. 29–37) were read with particular attention to right versus left modules, negative suspensions and connectivity. The resolution and totalization arguments (pp. 37–40) retain the distinction between an actual equivalence and an equivalence after completion. The change-of-rings and descent sections (pp. 40–47) were examined for their faithful-even-flat and commutativity requirements. The HRW comparison and nonagreement examples (pp. 48–51) do not justify universal cross-construction equivalence; the manuscript itself gives counterexamples. The connective vanishing, convergence and low-weight calculations (pp. 51–55) were traced into Theorem 8.8. References on pp. 56–57 were read, but the full contents of all cited works were not independently rederived.

No additional confirmed defect is inferred from a proof that was not fully reconstructed, from unavailable supplements, or from the absence of code. The report establishes two precise false assertions in this exact v2 source. It does not certify that every remaining theorem is correct, nor establish whether the unavailable journal text contains corrections.
# Assessment and evidence record

The supported initial assessment is Major. Each finding has an explicit example, a check of all printed hypotheses, a nonzero obstruction, a dependency trace and a limited repair analysis. The saved evidence contains the exact source and image bindings, the independent calculation input, output and exit status, the page coverage ledger, and the current compiler, dependency, TeX, PDF and report-page receipts. Primary scientific review and actual visual inspection are recorded separately from bounded auxiliary metadata and file-binding work. This is an initial review, not independent acceptance. The scientific decision remains pending and the human-review list is empty.

report: Abstract: The exact manuscript arXiv:2310.08765v2 is reviewed. Three substantive problems concern the sign of the group velocity in a defining hypothesis, cancellation in the critical resolvent decomposition, and the explicit high-frequency resolvent expansion. The last problem admits a direct counterexample to the stated remainder estimate using compactly supported smooth test functions. An additional regularity estimate is false even on a uniformly bounded sequence of smooth odd inputs. These findings require corrections to hypotheses and core linear arguments. They do not constitute a counterexample to the intended nonlinear stability theorem after correction. The supported assessment is Major for this exact version; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: A technical review of
Stability of coherent pattern formation through invasion in the FitzHugh–Nagumo system
# Exact source and review scope

M25-0297 is by Montie Avery, Paul Carter, Björn de Rijk and Arnd Scheel [paper]. The examined file is arXiv:2310.08765v2, submitted on 24 March 2026 at 19:29:38 UTC, with 83 pages and seven figures. Its SHA256 is `0f68ecc6295f2931c2916281ea410c684ddb33d91ba83a2d61b9df25783900f6`. Physical and printed page numbers agree. EMS associates the title with DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1670, acceptance on 23 March 2025 and online publication on 27 July 2025 [publisher]. Thus this author version postdates the publication date. The journal PDF was unavailable in the acquired set; no equivalence with the journal version is asserted. The frozen 2025 identifier and original title mapping are retained.

All 83 pages, including appendices and references, were read. Twenty-nine source pages were actually viewed as images, including all seven figures and the decisive formulas below. Coverage includes the hypotheses, weighted spaces, spectral branches, Fredholm bordering, contour estimates, resolvent decomposition, phase modulation, nonlinear damping, bootstrap and appendices A–E. This is not a formal verification of all external spectral theory or of the companion works.

Independent symbolic calculations checked the signs, algebraic decompositions, kernel jumps, polynomial remainders and exact norm formulas used here. Analytical arguments below supply the functional and operator implications. No author code, numerical front solver or Evans-function computation was run. Bounded searches of arXiv, EMS and author publication pages located no separate correction or code release. The related 2026 preprint Diffusive synchronization of phase waves in the FitzHugh–Nagumo system is publicly listed [related, author]; it is not silently identified with the differently titled in preparation reference [4] of the reviewed manuscript, nor was its 103-page proof independently certified. An unlocated supplement or code release is not itself a mathematical defect.
# Main statement and dependencies

The system is \[u_t=u_{xx}+u(u+a)(1-u-a)-w,\qquad
 w_t=\varepsilon(u-\gamma w),\] with \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\), \(0<a<1/2\), \(0<\gamma<4\), and sufficiently small positive \(\varepsilon\). Theorem 1.1 supplies the pulled front in its specified parameter range. The precise nonlinear result, Theorem 2.2 (pp. 14–15), additionally assumes diffusive spectral stability of the wave train, outgoing group velocity, and absence of unstable point spectrum and a bounded zero resonance (Hypotheses 1–3, pp. 13–14).

Its perturbation is small in \(\|\omega w_0\|_{L^1_{0,1}}+\|\omega w_0\|_{H^3\times H^2}\). The conclusions distinguish the unmodulated decay, the faster decay after a spatially varying phase correction, and the improved \(t^{-3/2}\) leading-edge estimate. In particular, stability near an already constructed front is not a proof of selection from all steep or compactly supported initial data. The discussion on p. 56 leaves that selection question for further work.

The proof passes from spectral information in Section 3 to the resolvent in Section 6, the linear estimates of Theorem 7.1, and the nonlinear estimates and bootstrap in Sections 8–9. Appendix A supplies the high-frequency contour control used in Proposition 4.3. The issues below are evaluated on these dependencies, rather than by requiring a counterexample to the whole nonlinear conclusion.
# Confirmed substantive problems

Problem 1 (Major: the group-velocity hypothesis has the opposite sign).  Equation (2.14), as invoked explicitly in Hypothesis 2, is incompatible with the Bloch operator and dispersion expansion printed on p. 13.

u)

u)^2+c_\mathrm{lin}(\partial_\xi+
u)+F'(u_\mathrm{wt}).\] Under Hypothesis 1, its zero eigenvalue is algebraically simple with right eigenvector \(u_\mathrm{wt}'\). The adjoint vector is normalized by \(\langle u_{m ad},u_\mathrm{wt}'angle=1\). Equation (2.13) defines \(\lambda_\mathrm{wt}(
u)=-c_g
u+D_{m eff}^{\mathrm{wt}}
u^2+O(
u^3)\); (2.14) instead sets \[c_g=2\langle u_{m ad},Du_\mathrm{wt}''angle+c_\mathrm{lin}.\] Hypothesis 2 (p. 14) requires the quantity given by (2.14) to be negative.

Decisive calculation. Differentiate the simple eigenvalue equation and pair with the adjoint kernel. The differentiated eigenvector term vanishes, yielding \[\lambda_\mathrm{wt}'(0)
 =\langle u_{\rm ad},(2D\partial_\xi+c_\mathrm{lin})u_\mathrm{wt}'\rangle
 =:K=2\langle u_{\rm ad},Du_\mathrm{wt}''\rangle+c_\mathrm{lin}.\] Consequently (2.13) requires \(c_g=-K\), whereas (2.14) gives \(c_g=K\). Together these equalities would force \(K=c_g=0\), excluded by Hypothesis 2. If the hypothesis is read literally as \(K<0\), the spatial root has \(\nu_\mathrm{wt}'(0)=1/K<0\), opposite to the positive coefficient required in Proposition 3.1 (p. 17) and Section 6.1. The direction also follows from the Fourier factor \(e^{ik\xi+\lambda_\mathrm{wt}(ik)t}\): the packet velocity is \(-K\).

Impact and repair boundary. This reverses the admissibility condition selecting an outgoing mode; it is not an inconsequential label within the proof. Keeping (2.13) requires replacing (2.14) by \(c_g=-K\), so the intended condition is \(K>0\). Then inversion gives \[\nu_\mathrm{wt}(\lambda)=-\lambda/c_g
                  +D_{\rm eff}^{\mathrm{wt}}\lambda^2/c_g^3+O(\lambda^3),\] consistent with the signs in Proposition 3.1 when \(c_g<0\). The differentiation and inversion have been checked independently. Whether a particular front satisfies the corrected spectral hypotheses must still be established; no front satisfying all the inconsistent printed conventions is claimed as a counterexample.

Problem 2 (Major: the critical resolvent residual does not cancel).  The displayed residual in (6.7) fails the identity from which it is defined and therefore lacks the small spectral factor required in Lemma 7.4. The final decomposition (6.28) has a further sign error.

Exact algebra and location. On p. 31, let \(K_\lambda g\) denote the integral in (6.5) without its leading minus sign. Let \(K_0(\lambda)g\) denote the same integral with \(Q,Q^{-1},P_\mathrm{wt}^{cu}\) frozen at zero, retaining the exponential \(e^{\nu_\mathrm{wt}(\lambda)(\xi-\zeta)}\). Equation (6.5) gives \[(L_\mathrm{wt}-\lambda)^{-1}g=-K_\lambda g+\bar s_e^\mathrm{wt}(\lambda)g.\] The next display extracts \(-K_0(\lambda)\), so the necessary residual is \(K_0(\lambda)-K_\lambda\). But (6.7) prints \(-K_0(\lambda)-K_\lambda\): the first integrand has a minus sign and the second integral is also subtracted. Reconstruction therefore has error \(-2K_0(\lambda)g\), rather than zero.

This is a nonzero operator, not merely a formal possibility. The rank-one neutral spectral projection represents the simple translation mode. Its adjoint pairing with suitable compactly supported forcing is nonzero. Equivalently, the injection \(\Lambda_1 g\) cannot have zero neutral projection for all \(g\): a nonzero adjoint first-order Floquet solution cannot have both its second and third components identically zero, since its adjoint equations would then force its first component to vanish. After output projection, the associated mode is \(u_\mathrm{wt}'\ne0\). Thus the error survives on permitted smooth test data. It does not acquire a factor \(\lambda\).

The second integral in Lemma 7.4, p. 45, is estimated by explicitly asserting such an extra factor in (6.7), to gain \(t^{-1/2}\). This assertion fails for the displayed residual. The faster residual decay in Theorem 7.1, p. 41, is then used in (9.9)–(9.13), p. 54.

There is a separate exact mismatch in (6.28), p. 39. Write \(r=u_\mathrm{fr}'\), \(w=u_\mathrm{wt}'\), and \(q=q(\cdot,\sigma^2)\). The contribution being split is \(\alpha_-\chi_-e^
u q\). The principal part is \(\alpha_-\chi_-e^
u r\); the printed residual uses \((r-w)+(w-q)\). Their sum is \(\alpha_-\chi_-e^
u(2r-q)\), with error \(2\alpha_-\chi_-e^
u(r-q)\). The residual must instead use \((w-r)+(q-w)\).

Neutral vector and forcing normalization. Lemma 6.10 (p. 37) also prints \(q(\cdot,0)=u_\mathrm{wt}\). The zero mode required by Hypothesis 1 is \(u_\mathrm{wt}'\), as used later on p. 39 and in (7.14), p. 45. For this nonconstant wave, \[L_\mathrm{wt}u_\mathrm{wt}=F'(u_\mathrm{wt})u_\mathrm{wt}-F(u_\mathrm{wt})
       =\big((1-2a)u_{\mathrm{wt},1}^2-2u_{\mathrm{wt},1}^3,\,0\big)^T\ne0.\] Nonvanishing follows because a nonconstant continuous first component cannot take values only in the finite zero set of this polynomial. A constant first component would also force the second component constant through the traveling-wave equations.

In the first-order reduction (6.2), p. 30, the stated variables \(U=(u,u_\xi,v)^T\) additionally require \(G=(0,g_1,g_2/c_\mathrm{lin})^T\), because the original second equation has coefficient \(c_\mathrm{lin}\partial_\xi v\). The displayed \(\Lambda_1 g=(0,g_1,g_2)^T\) misses this factor. That local normalization error alone need not change decay exponents, but must be corrected in an exact resolvent identity.

Repair and limits. Replacing the residual by \(K_0-K_\lambda\) produces an analytic coefficient difference of order \(\lambda\); reversing both differences in (6.28), using \(q(\cdot,0)=u_\mathrm{wt}'\), and correcting \(\Lambda_1\) restore the corresponding local identities. These algebraic repairs have been checked. A fully propagated proof of all subsequent estimates is not supplied here. Major severity reflects failure of an essential cancellation supporting the main linear and nonlinear estimates, not a demonstrated nonlinear instability.

Problem 3 (Major: the explicit high-frequency approximation has the wrong sign).  The kernels in (A.3) and (A.9) represent the negatives of the inverses claimed there. The remainder estimate of Lemma A.4 is false for the explicit terms (A.10)–(A.16) as printed.

Kernel identities. Appendix A sets \[\begin{gathered}
 L_0^{11}=\partial_X^2-i\kappa,\qquad
 L_0^{22}=c\partial_X-\widetilde b\mu-i\kappa/\mu+\mu B_0,\\
 c=c_\mathrm{lin}>0,\qquad B_0\le0,\qquad\widetilde b=b+\varepsilon\gamma>0.
 \end{gathered}\] For \(k=\sqrt{i\kappa}\) with positive real part, (A.9), p. 60, uses \(G^p(X)=e^{-k|X|}/(2k)\). Its derivative jump at zero is \(-1\). It solves \((\partial_X^2-i\kappa)G^p=-\delta_0\), not \(+\delta_0\). Likewise the kernel (A.3), p. 58, including its oscillatory factor, equals \(1/c\) at \(X=Y\) from the left and zero from the right. The coefficient of the delta distribution after applying \(c\partial_X\) is \(-1\). Away from the diagonal the homogeneous equation holds, including the actual \(B_0\) term. Thus it too is the negative inverse. These are identities for the printed operators and allowed coefficients, not counterexamples using a different model.

Counterexample to Lemma A.4. The following uses the actual smooth bounded front coefficients. Fix \(b>0\) within the permitted strip and \(0\ne\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R,\mathbb R)\). Let \(\lambda=b+i\Omega\), \(\Omega\to+\infty\), and define \[U=(0,\phi)^T,\qquad
 g_\Omega=(L_\mathrm{fr}-\lambda)U
   =\bigl(-\phi,\,
       c\phi'+(b_0-\varepsilon\gamma-b-i\Omega)\phi\bigr)^T.\] These data are compactly supported and smooth, and \(\|g_\Omega\|_{L^p}=O(\Omega)\), for example with \(p=2\). For sufficiently large \(\Omega\) the resolvent exists: the diagonal inversion and small block-coupling argument of Appendix A applies with the corrected inverse signs; those signs do not affect the norm bounds. Hence \((L_\mathrm{fr}-\lambda)^{-1}g_\Omega=U\).

Let \(T_\Omega\) be the positive transport kernel printed in (A.11)–(A.12), and \(H_\Omega\) the positive heat kernel in (A.10). The jump calculation gives exactly \[T_\Omega\bigl(c\partial_\xi+b_0-\varepsilon\gamma-\lambda\bigr)\phi
 =-\phi.\] The exponential bound \(b_0\le0\) implies \(\|T_\Omega\|_{L^p\to L^p}\le(b+\varepsilon\gamma)^{-1}\); the heat-kernel \(L^1\) bound implies \(\|H_\Omega\|_{L^p\to L^p}\le C/\Omega\). Consequently the printed formulas give \[\begin{aligned}
 v_0&=T_\Omega g_{\Omega,2}=-\phi,\\
 v_1&=-\varepsilon T_\Omega H_\Omega g_{\Omega,1}=O_{L^p}(\Omega^{-1}),\\
 v_2&=-\varepsilon T_\Omega H_\Omega T_\Omega g_{\Omega,2}
       =O_{L^p}(\Omega^{-1}).
 \end{aligned}\] The second component of the remainder in Lemma A.4 therefore tends to \(2\phi\) in \(L^p\), while its asserted upper bound is \(C\Omega^{-3/2}\|g_\Omega\|_{L^p}=O(\Omega^{-1/2})\to0\). This is a contradiction. If the lemma’s real-valued test-space notation is enforced, its claimed bound on all real data implies the complex-data bound by splitting real and imaginary parts, with at most a fixed factor in the constant. The same contradiction applies.

Dependence and repair boundary. Lemma A.4 is used for the contour shift and Proposition A.5, hence Proposition 4.3 and the high-frequency part of Theorem 7.1. Each diagonal Green kernel needs a leading minus sign. Terms with two such inverses, such as \(u_1,v_1\), keep their sign; terms with an odd number, including \(u_0,v_0,v_2\), reverse sign. A global negation of every displayed term is not the repair. The corrected Neumann-series normalization is explicit, but the complete contour proof has not been recertified here. The actual false remainder estimate, rather than the ease of changing a symbol, determines Major severity.
# Additional confirmed regularity issue
Problem 4 (Minor: the \(L^1\)-to-\(W^{2,\infty}\times W^{1,\infty}\) estimate is false).  Lemma 6.7, (6.17), p. 34, cannot hold for every odd \(g\in L^1_{0,1}\) as stated.

Fix any sufficiently small positive real \(\sigma\) in its stated sector. The constant-coefficient differential operator \(L_+-\sigma^2\) maps \(W^{2,\infty}\times W^{1,\infty}\) boundedly into \(L^\infty\). Take \(g=(h,0)^T\), where \[h(\xi)=\operatorname{sgn}(\xi)|\xi|^{-1/2}
                 {\bf1}_{0<|\xi|<1}.\] This is odd, lies in the required weighted \(L^1\) space, and does not belong to \(L^\infty\). A solution in the claimed target space would make \(g=(L_+-\sigma^2)u\) bounded, a contradiction in distributions. For reference, \(\int|h|=4\) and \(\int|\xi h|=4/3\).

Restricting to smooth inputs does not restore a uniform estimate. Set \(h_n(\xi)=n^2\xi e^{-n^2\xi^2}\). These are odd Schwartz functions, with \[\|h_n\|_1=1,\qquad
 \int|\xi h_n(\xi)|\,d\xi=\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2n},\qquad
 \|h_n\|_\infty=\frac{n}{\sqrt{2e}}.\] Thus their \(L^1_{0,1}\) norms remain bounded, while composition of the claimed resolvent bound with \(L_+-\sigma^2\) would give a uniform \(L^\infty\) bound on \(h_n\). The contradiction uses all the printed input hypotheses, including oddness.

In the first-order Green representation, differentiating once introduces the delta term in \(\partial_\xi T=MT+\delta_0 I\). The highest derivatives therefore retain the unsmoothed forcing. The discussion around (B.3), pp. 69–70, cannot justify the stated extra derivatives by ignoring that jump.

The natural weaker target is \(W^{1,\infty}\times L^\infty\); highest derivatives require an additional \(L^\infty\) norm of the input. The commutator in Lemma 6.9 needs only the first derivative of the first component, and Lemma 6.16 needs only the \(L^\infty\) bound; the separate \(L^2\) statement is Lemma 6.8. Accordingly this overstatement does not, by itself, establish failure of the main decay conclusion. Minor severity is based on that restricted downstream use. The local kernel argument supports the weaker target in the prescribed sector; no estimate in a larger spectral region is claimed.
# Other checked points and limits

Problem 5 (Minor: local weight sign and exponential norm power).  Lemma 3.2 (p. 18) has the wrong sign for the leading-edge weight, and the heuristic following (5.1), p. 23, gives the wrong power for the half-line \(L^2\) norm.

Lemma 3.2 (p. 18) prints \(\eta_\mathrm{lin}<0\), whereas the growing weight and the tail \(e^{-\eta_\mathrm{lin}\xi}\) require the positive branch. At \(\varepsilon=0\) the double root gives \(\eta_\mathrm{lin}=\sqrt{a(1-a)}>0\); the branch remains positive for sufficiently small positive \(\varepsilon\). Also the heuristic \(L^2\) blowup following (5.1), p. 23, uses \(|\sigma|^{-1}\) for the norm. Directly, \(\int_0^\infty e^{-2\sigma\xi}\,d\xi=(2\sigma)^{-1}\), so the norm scales as \(|\sigma|^{-1/2}=|\lambda|^{-1/4}\) in a fixed sector. The later Lemmas 6.8 and 6.15 use the correct half-power. These local corrections are recorded as Minor; no extra core failure is inferred from them.

The inverse modulation algebra, the quadratic/cubic FitzHugh–Nagumo remainder, and the role of the dissipative second component were checked against the displayed equations. In particular, \[f(u+z)-f(u)-f'(u)z=(1-2a-3u)z^2-z^3.\] The phase-coordinate construction and nonlinear damping are read with their small-derivative and regularity assumptions; they are not declared valid merely because their formal exponents close. The convolution powers in (9.9)–(9.13) rely on the corrected faster linear residual bounds, precisely where the above issues matter.

The review establishes the local identities, the explicit failure of the printed Appendix A remainder, and the regularity counterexamples. It has not computed an unstable front, proved failure of the intended nonlinear stability theorem, independently proved Hypotheses 1–3 for the full parameter range, or propagated every proposed correction through all 83 pages. No numerical evidence is substituted for these missing tasks. The exact manuscript requires substantive revision; scientific adjudication remains pending and human reviews are empty. Current independent acceptance is recorded in the associated provenance.
