report: Abstract: This report examines the exact author manuscript arXiv:2205.00935v1. The advertised toric formula omits the factor \(n!\) required by the paper’s stated measure convention. A round ellipsoid gives an exact counterexample. A universal bound under bundle automorphisms is also false, although a bound depending on the fixed automorphism repairs the asymptotic invariance argument. Additional local errors concern trace conversion, homothetic tensor formulas and a minimum on an open face. Their effects and repair boundaries are separated. The main qualitative convexity distinction is not disproved; indeed the normalization correction preserves the growth used in that construction. The supported assessment is Major for the false central quantitative formula, with scientific adjudication pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: A technical review of
The Ruelle invariant and convexity in higher dimensions
# Source and method

M25-0298 is The Ruelle invariant and convexity in higher dimensions, by Julian Chaidez and Oliver Edtmair [paper]. The examined source is arXiv:2205.00935v1, submitted on 2 May 2022 at 14:33:57 UTC, with 29 pages and two figures. The original arXiv capitalization is retained in the source mapping. The PDF SHA256 is `8d75e6701cf816340d465b8b99f437052e6659744a3479d5cc8876eaefba7398`. EMS records DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1671, acceptance on 18 April 2024 and publication on 25 July 2025 [publisher]. The journal PDF was unavailable in the acquired set. This 2022 manuscript is not identified with that later version, and the frozen 2025 identifier is unchanged.

All 29 pages, including references, were read. Nineteen source pages were actually viewed as images, including both figures and every decisive statement below. The review covers the cocycle construction, quasimorphisms and index conventions, ergodic limit, choice invariance, homothetic geometry, Laplacian variation, sandwich estimate, ellipsoid comparison, toric density, dynamical convexity and the concave-domain construction.

Independent exact computations checked the ellipsoid normalization, a scalar gauge family, complex and real traces, homothetic identities, open-face optimization and the flat-ellipsoid growth. No author code was run. The symbolic program supports those specific calculations, not the general ergodic, capacity or smoothing theorems. Bounded searches of arXiv, EMS and an author’s publication page [author] found no separate correction, supplement or code release. This is not a proof of absence. The review does not certify all cited literature or the inaccessible journal version.
# Framework and scope of the conclusions

The basic data are a compact base \(Y\), a flow \(\phi\), a symplectic cocycle on a bundle \(E\) with \(c_1(E)=0\), and a homotopy class of determinant trivializations. The rotation function is obtained by lifting the determinant of the unitary polar factor; its asymptotic slope is the Ruelle density. The invariant integrates that density against the chosen invariant measure. The finite invariant measures used in the geometric applications supply the integrability needed by the ergodic argument.

For a Liouville domain the canonical Hamiltonian is defined away from the skeleton. The manuscript uses invariant annuli and a limit towards the skeleton. For a star-shaped toric domain, \(\mu_j(z)=\pi|z_j|^2\), \(\theta_j\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\), and \(H=f_\Omega\circ\mu\). The flow factors as a diagonal rotation times \(I+tM\), with \(M^2=0\). The latter factor has zero asymptotic rotation, so the density \(\sum_j\partial_jf_\Omega\) is consistent with the explicit flow. The integration measure is the problematic step.

Theorem 1.12 asserts an upper bound for \(\operatorname{Ru}(X)c(X)/\operatorname{vol}(X)\) on convex domains. It uses the trace bound, a comparison of Laplacian integrals, and John’s ellipsoid theorem. The toric construction then produces unbounded Ruelle invariant with bounded volume and a systole bounded below, while strict monotonicity supplies dynamical convexity. The intended contact application is in dimensions \(2n-1\ge3\). No claim about one-dimensional contact index conventions is inferred.
# Confirmed findings
Problem 1 (Major: the toric invariant formula has a missing factorial).  Propositions 1.9 (p. 4) and 5.6 (p. 24) are false under the measure convention explicitly used elsewhere in the manuscript.

Conventions and exact calculation. Example 1.3 (p. 2) uses the invariant measure \(\omega^m\); Example 1.5 (p. 3) uses \(\alpha\wedge(d\alpha)^{n-1}\); Lemma 1.7 (p. 4) equates the domain and boundary invariants. The proof of Theorem 1.12, p. 22, explicitly writes \(\int_X\operatorname{tr}(\nabla^2H)\omega^n=n!\int_X\Delta H\,dV_g\). Thus the distinction between \(\omega^n\) and \(\omega^n/n!\) is not a matter of interpreting an unspecified notation.

On the free torus-action locus, \[\omega=\sum_{j=1}^n d\mu_j\wedge d\theta_j,\qquad
 \omega^n=n!\,d\mu_1\,d\theta_1\cdots d\mu_n\,d\theta_n.\] Each angular coordinate has period one. Coordinate hyperplanes have zero volume. Integrating the asserted, independently checked density therefore gives \[\boxed{\ \operatorname{Ru}_\omega(X_\Omega)
       =n!\int_\Omega\sum_{j=1}^n\partial_jf_\Omega\,d\mu\ }.\] Both printed propositions omit \(n!\).

Take the round ellipsoid \[X=E(a,\ldots,a)=\{\pi\textstyle\sum_j|z_j|^2\le a\},\qquad a>0,\ n\ge2.\] It is smooth, strictly convex, star-shaped and toric, with trivial tangent bundle and the standard determinant trivialization. Its canonical Hamiltonian is \(H=\pi\sum_j|z_j|^2/a\), so \(T\Phi_t=e^{2\pi it/a}I_n\). The lifted determinant has slope \(n/a\). Its moment simplex has Euclidean volume \(a^n/n!\), whereas \(\int_X\omega^n=a^n\). Consequently \[\operatorname{Ru}_\omega(X)=n a^{n-1},
 \qquad
 \text{printed toric expression}=\frac{n a^{n-1}}{n!}.\] Already \(n=2,a=1\) gives \(2\) versus \(1\). All assumptions of the toric proposition hold, and there is no degenerate-orbit exclusion in that proposition.

Dependence, impact and repairs. This is an explicit central quantitative result, advertised in the introduction and reused in Proposition 5.16, not only a typesetting error in an auxiliary proof. Major severity is based on the incorrect value of the defined invariant. It does not assert that the final existence of nonconvex dynamically convex domains is false.

Keeping the stated measures requires the factorial above. Alternatively, normalizing the domain measure by \(n!\) would require corresponding changes to the boundary measure, Lemma 1.7 and trace formulas; one cannot change only the toric formula’s interpretation. For the flat ellipsoid in Proposition 5.16, the corrected lower bound is \[n!\left(\frac{1}{n!A}-\frac{B^{n-1}}{A^n}\right)
       \left(A^n+\frac{n-1}{A}\right)
       \sim A^{n-1}\longrightarrow\infty
 \quad(n\ge2).\] Thus the normalization correction preserves the divergence used there. The replacement of an estimated volume by an equality on p. 28 should also be an inequality; the same lower bound remains valid.

The volume convention in the last inequality on p. 23 needs explicit attention: with \(V_g=\int\omega^n/n!\), the displayed chain retains a factorial; with \(V_\omega=\int\omega^n\), it cancels. This observation alone does not disprove the stated constant. In fact, the same numerical constant can be recovered even for \(V_g\) by a small, independently justified improvement of the sandwich argument, as shown in Section 4 below.
Problem 2 (Minor: the automorphism bound is not uniform over automorphisms).  Lemma 3.10 and equations (3.3)–(3.4), p. 15, replace an endpoint gauge transformation by pointwise conjugation.

For definiteness write a gauge transform as \[\Phi^\Psi(t,x)=\Psi(\phi_t x)\Phi(t,x)\Psi(x)^{-1}.\] The inverse convention gives the same issue after replacing \(\Psi\) by \(\Psi^{-1}\). In a trajectory trivialization the two endpoint factors occur at \(t\) and \(0\), respectively. Equation (3.3) instead uses \(\Psi_\Xi(t)\) on both sides of \(\Phi_\Xi(t)\), and the proof consequently claims the universal bound \(3c\), independent of \(\Psi\).

Let \(Y=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\), \(\phi_t(x)=x+t\), with normalized Lebesgue measure. Take the trivial symplectic line bundle, its standard determinant trivialization, and the identity cocycle. For any \(N>0\), let \[h_N(x)=N\sin(2\pi x),\qquad \Psi_N(x)=e^{2\pi i h_N(x)}.\] This is a smooth unitary, hence symplectic, bundle automorphism homotopic to the identity through \(e^{2\pi i s h_N}\). The transformed cocycle has rotation lift \(h_N(x+t)-h_N(x)\), with zero initial lift. At \(x=1/4,t=1/2\) its value is \(-2N\), whereas the original rotation lift is zero. No universal \(C\), and in particular no fixed \(3c\), bounds all these differences. The statement concerns lifts, so an integer endpoint winding is not discarded.

For a fixed automorphism, however, a bounded lift exists over compact \(Y\) under the stated homotopy assumption. Let \(B_\Psi\) bound its rotation value in unitary trivializations, and \(D\) be a quasimorphism defect bound. Applying the quasimorphism inequality to the correct endpoint product gives, for example, \[|\widetilde u_T(\Phi^\Psi)-\widetilde u_T(\Phi)|
       \le 2B_\Psi+3D .\] Unitary changes of frame preserve the determinant polar rotation; the bound is finite and independent of \(T,x\), though it depends on \(\Psi\). Dividing by \(T\), and integrating against a finite measure when required, gives zero. This weaker bound is sufficient for the fixed change of complex structure in Proposition 3.11, pp. 15–16. The asymptotic density is zero for every cocycle in the explicit counterexample as well. Minor severity reflects this verified repair of the actual downstream use, despite the false universal statement.
Problem 3 (Minor: the complex-to-real trace conversion has a factor error).  Equation (2.2), p. 8, has coefficient \(2i\) where \(i/2\) is required.

Let \(A=I_{2n}\), \(S=I_{2n}\), and let \(J=\Omega\) be the displayed standard complex structure. All hypotheses of Lemma 2.2 hold, including positive definiteness of \(S\). The polar derivative in direction \(J\) is \(TU_I(J)=J\). The left side of (2.2) is \(\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb CJ=ni\), while its right side is \[2i\,\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb R(J^{-1}J)=4ni.\] For any skew-Hermitian \(K\), diagonalization with eigenvalues \(i\theta_j\) gives the correct identity \(\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb CK=(i/2)\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb R(J^{-1}K)\).

The subsequent real-trace estimate on p. 9 is \(8n^2\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb RS\). With the correct conversion it yields the stronger complex-trace bound \(4n^2\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb RS\), so the stated weaker \(16n^2\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb RS\) bound in Lemma 2.2 still follows. Proposition 2.9 and Lemma 3.14 therefore do not lose their stated upper constants through this error. This is a false identity with a verified harmless direction for the bound, hence Minor.
Problem 4 (Minor: two homothetic identities have incorrect factors or slopes).  The second identity in Lemma 4.4 (p. 18) and the divergence assertion in Corollary 4.6 (p. 19) are false as printed.

Use \(M=\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}\), \(d\ge2\), the Euclidean metric and \(V=x/2\). This is cylindrical with spherical section, \(\mathcal L_Vg=g\), and \(
abla V=	frac12I\). For \(U=W=\partial_{x_1}\), the left side of the printed identity is \[\langle
abla_UV,Wangle+\langle U,
abla_WVangle=1,\] while the stated right side is \(1/2\). The correct right side is \(\langle U,Wangle\). The proof immediately below already obtains that correct identity; the symmetric part of \(
abla V\) is consequently \(	frac12I\), as used in Lemma 4.7.

If \(\mathcal L_VU=aU\), then \(\mathcal L_V(\operatorname{div}U)=a\operatorname{div}U\). Divergence is the natural contraction of \(
abla U\); unlike the gradient or Laplacian of a function, it introduces no inverse-metric factor. For the concrete \(U=V\), one has \(a=0\) and \(\operatorname{div}V=d/2
e0\), which has slope zero, not \(-1\). The function statements in Corollary 4.6, \(
abla F\) and \(\Delta F\) of slope \(a-1\), are consistent.

The variation proof on p. 20 uses the correct slope one for \(\operatorname{div}(h\nabla H)\). Correcting these local statements therefore agrees with the calculation actually needed for Propositions 4.8 and 4.10. No failure of the sandwich estimate is established by this issue.
Problem 5 (Minor: the bracket minimum need not exist on the stated open face).  Definition 5.13, p. 27, is not well-defined for every permitted \(v\), even for the round ball.

Take the moment region \(\Omega=\{(x_1,x_2)\ge0:x_1+x_2\le1\}\). Its toric domain is a smooth star-shaped ball and its complement in the orthant is convex. For \(v=(1,2)\), the support is \(S=\{1,2\}\). The definition restricts to \[\partial_+\Omega_S=\{(1-s,s):0<s<1\}.\] The objective is \(1+s\), with infimum \(1\) and no minimum. Thus the displayed minimum fails to assign a value to this admissible integer vector.

Replacing the minimum by an infimum, or taking the closure of the relative face before minimizing, repairs this defect. For smooth compact star-shaped regions the closure is compact and the linear functional is continuous; the infimum on the face equals the minimum on its closure. Radial comparison also preserves the monotonicity of these infima under inclusion. The claimed systole formula of Lemma 5.14 is cited from external capacity theory; this review does not independently reprove it. The example identifies a local domain error, not a counterexample to systole monotonicity or Proposition 5.16 after the definition is corrected.
# Verified repairs of the quantitative argument

For clarity, the following refinement handles the factorial in the convex-domain bound without claiming optimal constants. In Proposition 4.10 assume its stated convexity and self-adjointness conditions and \(G\le H\le LG\). Put \(F_t=(1-t)H+tG\). On \(X_1=\{G\le1\}\), \[-(L-1)\le G-H\le0.\] The proof of the proposition uses the weaker lower bound \(-L\). Keeping \(-(L-1)\), the variation formula and \(|\nabla F_t|^2\le2\Delta F_t\) on \(\{F_t=1\}\) give \[\frac{d}{dt}S(F_t)\ge
       -\frac{(L-1)d^2}{2}\,S(F_t),\qquad
 S(H)\le e^{(L-1)d^2/2}S(G).\] Indeed the bracket \((d+2)|\nabla F_t|^2/2-2\Delta F_t\) is at most \(d\Delta F_t\); multiplication by the nonpositive \(G-H\) yields the required lower bound, also when that bracket is negative. The homogeneity identity then converts the boundary integral of \(\Delta F_t\) to \((d/2)S(F_t)\).

Using \(L=(2n)^2\), \(d=2n\), and the source’s trace constant gives \[\operatorname{Ru}_\omega(X)c(X)
 \le 32n^3(2n)^{2n}n!\,e^{8n^4-2n^2}V_g(X).\] Since \(\log(n!)\le n\log n\le n^2\) for \(n\ge1\), this is bounded by \[C(n)V_g(X),\qquad C(n)=2^{2n+5}n^{2n+3}e^{8n^4}.\] Thus a factorial omitted in the printed chain does not by itself falsify the numerical upper constant: the repaired calculation above recovers it. This distinguishes the false exact toric formula from the much less sharp upper convexity bound.

Problem 6 (Minor: lower-index formulas exceed the declared domain of \(CZ\)).  Definition 2.11 and Lemma 2.12(b), pp. 10–11, use \(CZ\) without the nondegeneracy restriction required by its definition. The direct-sum statement for arbitrary endpoints requires \(LCZ\).

The dynamical-convexity argument was also traced through its dependencies. For a closed orbit with \(m\) nonzero coordinates, the diagonal loop contributes at least \(2m\), the unipotent block at least \(-m\), and the remaining positive rotations at least \(n-m\), giving the required Hamiltonian lower index \(n\). The conversion to the contact lower index uses the constant two-plane contribution \(-1\) in Lemma 2.16. This verification uses the lower semicontinuous index, including degenerate orbits, rather than silently imposing nondegeneracy. The printed \(CZ\) in the general direct-sum line of Lemma 2.12(b) must be read as \(LCZ\); \(CZ\) itself is not defined at an identity endpoint. Likewise the approximating sequence in Definition 2.11 must have nondegenerate endpoints. These are domain/notation corrections to the stated index convention, not a newly demonstrated failure of the \(2m-m+(n-m)\) bound.
# Assessment and limitations

The normalization counterexample changes a central explicit conclusion of the exact manuscript. Its repair is dimension-dependent and must be propagated consistently across measures, domain and boundary invariants, and toric calculations. The other confirmed issues are narrower: their corrections were checked against the specific downstream arguments.

No counterexample to the qualitative existence of dynamically convex, nonsymplectically convex domains has been established. The finite-measure ergodic framework, capacity input, contact index foundations and concave smoothing are not fully rederived here. The reviewed construction uses gauges and canonical Hamiltonians away from the origin or skeleton; no unjustified global smoothness at that singular set is used in the checks. The scientific decision remains pending and human reviews are empty. Current independent acceptance is recorded in the associated provenance.

Let \(A=I_{2n}\), \(S=I_{2n}\), and let \(J=\Omega\) be the displayed standard complex structure. All hypotheses of Lemma 2.2 hold, including positive definiteness of \(S\). The polar derivative in direction \(J\) is \(TU_I(J)=J\). The left side of (2.2) is \(\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb CJ=ni\), while its right side is \[2i\,\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb R(J^{-1}J)=4ni.\] For any skew-Hermitian \(K\), diagonalization with eigenvalues \(i\theta_j\) gives the correct identity \(\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb CK=(i/2)\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb R(J^{-1}K)\).

The subsequent real-trace estimate on p. 9 is \(8n^2\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb RS\). With the correct conversion it yields the stronger complex-trace bound \(4n^2\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb RS\), so the stated weaker \(16n^2\operatorname{tr}_\mathbb RS\) bound in Lemma 2.2 still follows. Proposition 2.9 and Lemma 3.14 therefore do not lose their stated upper constants through this error. This is a false identity with a verified harmless direction for the bound, hence Minor.

claim: Recorded check: Unattained bracket minimum on an open face
analysis: Definition 5.13, p. 27, is not well-defined for every permitted \(v\), even for the round ball.

Take the moment region \(\Omega=\{(x_1,x_2)\ge0:x_1+x_2\le1\}\). Its toric domain is a smooth star-shaped ball and its complement in the orthant is convex. For \(v=(1,2)\), the support is \(S=\{1,2\}\). The definition restricts to \[\partial_+\Omega_S=\{(1-s,s):0<s<1\}.\] The objective is \(1+s\), with infimum \(1\) and no minimum. Thus the displayed minimum fails to assign a value to this admissible integer vector.

For smooth compact star-shaped regions the closure is compact and the linear functional is continuous; the infimum on the face equals the minimum on its closure. Radial comparison also preserves the monotonicity of these infima under inclusion. The claimed systole formula of Lemma 5.14 is cited from external capacity theory; this review does not independently reprove it. The example identifies a local domain error, not a counterexample to systole monotonicity or Proposition 5.16 after the definition is corrected.
result: Impact: Local domain defect; no counterexample to corrected capacity statement or systole monotonicity claimed.

Title: A technical review of
Embeddings of matrix algebras into uniform Roe algebras and quasi-local algebras
# Source, scope and method

M25-0299 is Embeddings of matrix algebras into uniform Roe algebras and quasi-local algebras, by Narutaka Ozawa [paper]. The reviewed PDF is arXiv:2310.03677v3, submitted on 22 April 2024 at 14:07:29 UTC, eight pages; its internal date line reads 23 April 2024. These two date fields are preserved separately. The PDF SHA256 is `d4ac1e9626750e5116584bd4168dad859c4763ede2f1dc23ed06d2c67410a4c8`. EMS records DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1672, acceptance on 21 April 2024 and publication on 12 June 2025 [publisher]. The journal PDF was unavailable in the acquired source set. No equivalence with that version is assumed, and the frozen 2025 identifier and original title mapping are unchanged.

All eight pages, including references, were read and actually viewed as source images. The review covers the definitions, Theorems A and B, Corollary C, Lemmas 1–4, the property A definition, Theorem 5 and Lemma 6. Independent exact calculations checked the initial-index obstruction, admissible radii on \(\mathbb Z\), a two-dimensional irreducible representation of \(S_3\), the Rademacher fourth moment and the final approximation constant. The general arguments below are analytic checks; finite symbolic examples are not represented as a machine proof of the theorems. No author code was run.

Bounded searches of the exact title, arXiv version history, the EMS record and the author’s publication list [author] located no separate correction, supplement or associated code release for this paper. Corrections attached to other papers on that list are not attributed to this one. Absence from these searches is not proof of exhaustive absence. The external concentration theorem and all bibliographic literature were not independently reconstructed.
# Definitions, quantifiers and principal dependencies

Throughout, \(X\) is a uniformly locally finite metric space: \(N_X(R)=\sup_x|\operatorname{Ball}(x,R)|<\infty\) for each finite \(R>0\). The algebra \(C_{\rm u}^*[X]\) is the norm closure of the finite-propagation operators on \(\ell_2X\). Quasi-locality requires finite \(\varepsilon\)-propagation for every \(\varepsilon>0\), with the radius allowed to depend on \(\varepsilon\).

Theorem A excludes even nonunital embeddings of \(\prod_{n\ge1}\mathbb M_n\) into \(C_{\rm u}^*[X]\) for every such \(X\). Theorem B assumes an expander sequence in \(X\), and embeds that product into \(C_{\rm ql}^*[X]\). These imply proper inclusion in Corollary C for spaces containing expanders. The discussion of all spaces without property A is an expectation, not another theorem proved here. Theorem 5 gives equality under property A, together with \(\operatorname{dist}(u,C_{\rm u}^*[X])<18\varepsilon^{1/4}\) for contractions with finite positive \(\varepsilon\)-propagation.
## The nonembedding mechanism

For Lemma 1 the approximation \(\pi(g)+b_g\) has norm at most one, since its two terms occupy orthogonal corners. Averaging with \(\overline{\pi(g)}\) and compressing to the first corner gives an invariant vector, and hence the lower bound \(1-\varepsilon\). The graph partition and the coefficient estimate then give \[\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2N_X(R)}
 < \frac{1+\varepsilon}{\sqrt n}.\] If \(\varepsilon<1\), the hypothesis \(N_X(R)<\sqrt n/8\) implies \(4(1-\varepsilon)<1+\varepsilon\), or \(\varepsilon>3/5\). The case \(\varepsilon\ge1\) already satisfies that conclusion. Subtracting the added \(1/10\) yields the required distance bound. This checks the constants and the role of the nonunital complementary corner.

Once valid radii tending to infinity have been selected as below, the product argument needs no normality of the alleged embedding. For the product element \(a=(a_n)_n\), the element obtained by setting its \(n\)-th coordinate to zero has norm at most one and maps into the complementary corner of the \(n\)-th matrix unit. Lemma 1 applies directly to this algebraic difference. No identification of the image with a strongly convergent diagonal sum is necessary.
# Confirmed findings and repairs

Problem 1 (Major: the first random-subspace requirement is impossible).  In the proof of Theorem B, p. 5, the choices \[\delta_k=\frac1k,\qquad
 \varepsilon_k=100\sqrt{\delta_k\log(1/\delta_k)}\] are followed by the requirement \[\max_{\substack{E\subset[d(n)]\\ |E|/d(n)\le\delta_k}}
       \|P_{V(n)}|_{\ell_2E}\|<\varepsilon_k
 \quad\hbox{for every }k=1,\ldots,n.\] At \(k=1\), one has \(\delta_1=1\) and \(\varepsilon_1=0\). The permitted set \(E=[d(n)]\) gives the norm of the orthogonal projection onto the nonzero \(n\)-dimensional space \(V(n)\), namely one. The requirement is therefore \(1<0\), for every possible choice of \(V(n)\). This is an exact contradiction under all the stated dimension and coordinate-set conditions, not a numerical failure of a particular random sample. In addition, Lemma 4 assumes \(0<\delta<1/10\), which excludes the first ten listed parameters.

A complete parameter repair is \[\widehat\delta_k=\frac1{k+10},\qquad
 \widehat\varepsilon_k
 =100\sqrt{\widehat\delta_k\log(1/\widehat\delta_k)}.\] Every \(\widehat\delta_k\) lies in the lemma’s domain, and \(\widehat\varepsilon_k\to0\). For each fixed \(n\), Lemma 4 applies to the finitely many parameters \(k\le n\). A union bound, followed by an increase of the ambient dimension, gives a positive probability of satisfying all these requirements simultaneously. Thus there is such a subspace. The ambient dimensions can be chosen from a sufficiently large subsequence of the expander sizes.

The downstream argument requires only this vanishing sequence and a finite family of requirements at each stage. The uniform estimate, including the early blocks, is checked in Section 4. Nevertheless, the printed requirement is impossible for every stage, so the subspace selection feeding Theorem B and Corollary C fails as stated. This is a Major core construction error. The explicit repair retains the theorem range and supplies counterevidence to theorem falsity; it does not reduce the severity of the invalid printed construction.

Problem 2 (Minor: the displayed radii are not defined at the initial indices).  The proof of Theorem A, p. 3, states that Lemma 1 supplies an element for each \(n\), with \[R_n=\sup\{R>0:N_X(R)<\sqrt n/8\}-1.\] For every nonempty \(X\), \(N_X(R)\ge1\). When \(1\le n\le64\), the set in this expression is empty. Consequently \(R_n\) is not a positive admissible radius for Lemma 1. For instance \(X=\mathbb Z\) with its usual metric satisfies all the metric hypotheses and has \(N_X(R)=2\lfloor R\rfloor+1\); the same defect is immediate there. This is a defect in the chosen auxiliary sequence, not a counterexample to the nonembedding theorem.

One may instead form the finite set \[J_n=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:64N_X(j)^2<n\}.\] When \(J_n\ne\varnothing\), take \(r_n=\max J_n\) and use Lemma 1. When it is empty, take \(a_n=0\) and impose no radius requirement. For every fixed integer \(j\), uniform local finiteness implies that \(j\in J_n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). Hence only finitely many sets are empty, and \(r_n\to\infty\) along the remaining indices. All chosen radii are finite and satisfy exactly the strict hypothesis of Lemma 1. This also avoids an infinite supremum for a finite space. Finite \(X\) in any case cannot admit arbitrarily large matrix corners.

For any prescribed propagation radius, a sufficiently late coordinate now gives distance at least \(1/2\), as required in the proof of Theorem A. No finite initial coordinate affects that argument. The scope and constant of Theorem A are preserved.
# Checks of the random-subspace and block construction

The central concentration estimate was checked beyond the parameter error. Write \(e=25\sqrt{\delta\log(1/\delta)}\). If \(e>1/4\), the claimed strict bound \(4e\) exceeds one and is automatic. For \(e\le1/4\), the single-sphere concentration estimate and entropy bound in the manuscript give, for all sufficiently large \(d\), \[{\mathbb P}\left\{\max_{|E|\le\delta d}\|1_E x\|>2e\right\}
 <2\exp(-e^2d/4).\] The median bound becomes less than \(e\) after increasing \(d\). For nonintegral \(\delta d\), use \(\lfloor\delta d\rfloor\) and extend smaller coordinate sets to that size. The entropy inequality is valid because \(H(\delta)<2\delta\log(1/\delta)<e^2/4\) for \(0<\delta<1/10\).

Here is a direct uniformization of the final net step on pp. 5–6. The span of the independent uniform sphere vectors has the invariant Grassmann distribution. Choose a Haar orthonormal frame \(Q:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^d\) for that subspace. For every fixed unit \(\alpha\), \(Q\alpha\) is uniform on the sphere. An \(e\)-net of the unit sphere of \(\mathbb R^n\) has at most \((1+2/e)^n\) elements. The union bound therefore makes all its coordinate restrictions at most \(2e\), except on a set of probability at most \[2(1+2/e)^n\exp(-e^2d/4).\] Since \(\|1_EQ\|\le1\), net approximation raises the bound only to \(3e<4e\). For fixed \(n,\delta\), increasing \(d\) absorbs the prefactor into \(\exp(-e^2d/8)\). Finally \(\|P_V|_{\ell_2E}\|=\|1_E|_V\|\). Thus the stated conclusion follows with positive constants of the required quantifier dependence. This argument supplies the quantitative uniformity implicit in the manuscript’s almost-orthonormal discussion. It relies on the cited sphere concentration input; it is not a new numerical validation of that external theorem.
# Property A estimate and assessment

For Theorem 5 the chosen property A families have successive variation bounds at \(\delta=\sqrt\varepsilon\). With \(f_z(x)=\sqrt{\nu_x(z)}\), the map \(\Phi_\nu(u)=\sum_z f_zuf_z\) is unital completely positive and has propagation at most \(2T\). Uniform local finiteness bounds the random function \(f_\omega=\sum_z\omega_zf_z\), and its moments are \[\mathbb E f_\omega(x)^2=1,\qquad
 \mathbb E f_\omega(x)^4
 =3-2\sum_z f_z(x)^4\le3.\] The exact fourth-moment expansion was independently checked. Clipping at \(C=\delta^{-1/2}\) and averaging with the first property A family give \(g,h\) with \[\mathbb E|f-g|^2\le3C^{-2},\quad
 \mathbb E|g-h|^2<\delta,\quad
 |h(x)-h(y)|\le C\delta\quad(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\le R).\] Apply Lemma 6 to \((h+C)/(2C)\), whose variation parameter is \(\delta/2\). Its commutator estimate is \[\|[h,u]\|
 \le 2C(2\delta+4\varepsilon/\delta)=12\sqrt\delta.\] The operator Cauchy–Schwarz estimate for replacing \(f\) by \(h\) costs at most \(2(\sqrt3+1)\sqrt\delta\). Consequently the actual constant is bounded by \(14+2\sqrt3<18\), which supplies the stated strict inequality. The band decomposition in Lemma 6 uses at most two neighboring diagonals for its \(2\delta\|u\|\) contribution, and the \(\varepsilon\)-propagation bound for the separated diagonals. No zero-\(\varepsilon\) extension of the strict estimate is assumed.

The supported assessment for this exact manuscript is Major, on account of the impossible core construction in Problem 1. The two literal finite-index defects and their dependencies are documented with explicit repairs. No counterexample to Theorems A, B or 5, or Corollary C, is established. The review does not certify the unavailable journal text, every external concentration result, or the full additional remark on arbitrary maximal completions. This revision incorporates focused independent acceptance of the reported findings and their severity. The original review coverage is retained without claiming a second full review. Scientific decision remains pending, and human reviews are empty.

report: Abstract: The exact manuscript arXiv:2309.09504v2 is reviewed. The reduction from domino constraints through decorated \(p\)-adic Sudoku to translational monotiling is traced, with attention to exceptional rows, precision, finite group encodings and periodic targets. Title: A technical review of
Undecidability of translational monotilings
# Exact source and review scope

M25-0300 is Undecidability of translational monotilings, by Rachel Greenfeld and Terence Tao [paper]. The reviewed source is arXiv:2309.09504v2, submitted on 24 October 2023 at 19:41:53 UTC, with 44 pages and ten figures. Its 3,684,687-byte PDF has SHA256 `1c4aea6c36efb1f269f3df2e1bd7aec3a8b3bc6ad9cb72c1b7d0310bbad100ca`. The EMS record gives DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1673, submission on 24 October 2023, acceptance on 27 June 2024 and publication on 21 June 2025 [publisher]. The journal PDF was unavailable in the acquired material. No equivalence with that text is asserted. The frozen 2025 identifier and original title mapping are retained.

All 44 pages, including references, were read. Thirty-five source pages were actually viewed as images, including every figure and every page containing a substantive finding below. The small-prime illustrations are illustrative examples, not instances of the large-prime classification theorem. Exact integer calculations were executed independently, without running author code. The infinite Sudoku counterexamples are proved below for every required line; finite tests supplement those proofs and do not replace them.

The author publication entry, author discussion, exact arXiv history and EMS record were checked [author, discussion]. Bounded searches located no separate correction, supplement or associated code release. This is not an exhaustive absence assertion, and lack of code is not a mathematical defect. Two cited reduction papers were acquired at precisely identified versions [GT21, MSS22]. Their relevant statements and proof portions were read; neither entire reference was independently certified.
# Quantifiers and dependency structure

Theorem 1.3 concerns inputs consisting of a finite Abelian group \(G_0\), a subset \(E\subseteq G_0\), and a finite set \(F\subset\mathbb Z^2\times G_0\), and the existence of translations tiling \(\mathbb Z^2\times E\). The finite group varies with the input. Corollary 1.5 concerns a periodic target in \(\mathbb Z^d\), with \(d\) also part of the input. It does not establish undecidability for one fixed \(d\), or require the target to be the whole group. Remark 6.2 and Section 7 explicitly distinguish these stronger questions. The author discussion gives the same qualification.

The dependency chain is \[\begin{aligned}
 \text{domino constraints on }\mathbb N^2
 &\ \longrightarrow\ \text{decorated Sudoku}\\
 &\ \longrightarrow\ \text{weak functional constraints}\\
 &\ \longrightarrow\ \text{one translational prototile}.
\end{aligned}\] Section 2 uses the classical domino undecidability input and compactness. The finite-box argument in Lemma 2.5 is valid: compatible infinite configurations follow by a diagonal subsequence in a finite alphabet. This does not claim a computable bound on the box size witnessing failure. The conversion from Wang colors to neighbor relations is effective. The external undecidability theorem itself was not reproved.

Write \(B=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}\times\mathbb Z\). Definition 4.5 requires, for each nonvertical line \(m=jn+i\), a nondegenerate integer affine form \(an+b\) whose last nonzero base-\(p\) digit agrees with the line whenever \(\nu_p(an+b)\le1\). The function \(f_p\) has \(f_p(0)=1\). Its multiplicativity must not be used across a zero factor. Theorem 4.6 assumes \(p>48\), \(p^2\mid N\), and, in its converse, nonconstant columns. Its conclusion deliberately excludes the points where the limiting affine form is zero.

Theorem 4.7 supplies an initial affine description outside one exceptional residue set. Theorem 4.9 iterates that description to arbitrary finite precision, using the Tetris map \(m\mapsto pm\). Compactness then gives Theorem 4.6(ii). In Section 5 the fixed choices are \[p_1=53,\quad p_2=59,\quad N=p_1^2p_2^2=9,778,129.\] The symbols decorating the two digit sequences encode neighboring domino values at adjacent valuation levels. Thus the precision and coefficient comparisons in that section are essential to the reduction, even though the coefficients themselves are auxiliary objects.
# Confirmed findings

Problem 1 (Major: Corollary 4.10 does not preserve nonconstant columns).  On p. 25, Corollary 4.10 asserts that every \(S_{p,N}\)-Sudoku solution with nonconstant columns retains that property after \(F(n,m)\mapsto F(n,pm)\). Take \(p=53\), \(N=p^2\), and \[F(n,m)=f_p(m+1).\] All stated prime and width hypotheses hold. Every column is nonconstant, since its values at \(m=0,1\) are \(1,2\).

Here is a direct verification of every line constraint. For a line with \(j=i+1=0\), take the constant affine form \(1\). Otherwise put \[d=\min\{
u_p(j),
u_p(i+1)\},\qquad
 a=j/p^d,\quad b=(i+1)/p^d.\] The pair \((a,b)\) is nondegenerate modulo \(p\). If \(an+b
e0\), removal of the power \(p^d\) preserves its last nonzero digit. If \(an+b=0\), both original and normalized arguments are zero and both have the assigned value \(1\). Consequently \(F(n,jn+i)=f_p(an+b)\) everywhere on the line, in particular at every point required by Definition 4.5. Thus this is a genuine admissible Sudoku solution, not merely a sampled array.

Its Tetris image is \[F(n,pm)=f_p(pm+1)=1
                         \qquad(m\in\mathbb Z).\] Every column becomes constant. This disproves the preservation claim under all its printed hypotheses. The independent calculation checked 151,650 regulated line digits on selected lines and 6,001 Tetris values; the proof above establishes the unrestricted statement.

The error is in the corollary’s inference from the \(r=1\) affine description. A coefficient \(B^{(1)}\) that is a unit does not suffice: the constant \(A^{(1)}n+C^{(1)}\) can keep the entire sampled column away from the singular residue class. In this example it is \(1\). Proposition 3.4(iii) preserves being a Sudoku solution; it does not supply the additional column condition.

A sufficient corrected hypothesis is the normalization already used in (4.11): \[F(n,m)=\pi_p(bm)\quad\text{when }p\nmid m,\qquad p\nmid b.\] For such \(F\), apply Theorem 4.7 to its Tetris image, obtaining coefficients \(A_1,B_1,C_1\). The comparison of affine forms on pp. 23–24, culminating in (4.22), gives \(B_1\equiv b\pmod p\). This comparison precedes and does not invoke Corollary 4.10. Since \(B_1\) is a unit, Theorem 4.7 implies that the Tetris image has nonconstant columns. Hence the restricted claim is proved.

The general induction on p. 25 first imposes (4.23), which includes this normalization, before invoking the corollary. With the precision repair in Problem 3, that particular invocation is justified. The false unrestricted corollary remains false and must be replaced. Major severity concerns a named preservation guarantee in the core structural recursion; the fact that its actual later use admits a verified restriction is recorded separately, and is not a counterexample to Theorem 4.6 or Theorem 1.3.

Problem 2 (Minor: the claimed bijection loses the exceptional row).  Remark 4.11, pp. 26–27, upgrades the description \[F(n,m)=c f_p(m-Dn-E)\quad(m\ne Dn+E)\] to a one-to-one correspondence with triples \((c,D,E)\). For the same \(p=53\) and \(N=p^2\), define, for \(k=1,2\), \[F_k(n,m)=
 \begin{cases}f_p(m),&m\ne0,\\k,&m=0.\end{cases}\] Both have nonconstant columns. On the zero row use the constant nondegenerate form \(k\). On every other line, divide \(jn+i\) by the common power of \(p\) in \(j,i\). Any zero of the resulting nondegenerate form has infinite valuation and is excluded from the constraints in Definition 4.5. All regulated points therefore agree. Both \(F_k\) are admissible, but they are distinct and both satisfy the displayed description with \((c,D,E)=(1,0,0)\). This refutes the asserted bijection. It does not refute the root-excluding conclusion of Theorem 4.6(ii).

Two printed identities in the accompanying uniqueness argument also fail. With \(F=f_p(m)\), \(m=p-1=52\), both \(m\) and \(m+1\) are nonzero, but in \(\mathbb F_p\) \[F(n,53)-F(n,52)=1-52=2\ne1=c.\] The increment identity is valid if both affine arguments are units, not merely nonzero. In the next display on p. 27, the definition \(h_{n,m}=(m-Dn-E)/p^{r-1}\) gives \(c\pi_p(h+h_{n,m})\), valid when \(h\not\equiv-h_{n,m}\pmod p\), rather than the printed difference. For \(r=1,D=E=0,m=1,h=2,c=1\), the actual value is \(3\); the printed value is \(1\), although its exclusion condition is met.

Uniqueness of the parameters can be retained independently. Comparing two descriptions away from their exceptional residues gives equality of their nonzero affine forms modulo \(p\), which first determines \(c\) and \(Dn+E\bmod p\). Using columns \(n=0,1\) determines \(D,E\bmod p\). At each successive precision, restrict \(m\) to the already determined root residue and compare the two affine functions of the next digit, away from at most two excluded residues. This determines the next digits of \(D,E\). This argument proves uniqueness of the parameters from \(F\); it does not determine \(F\) on an actual zero locus from the parameters.

The last display on p. 17 has a related zero-domain issue: with \(A=C=0,B=2,m=0\), its left side is \(f_p(0)=1\) and its right side is \(f_p(2)f_p(0)=2\). Restricting that factorization to nonzero arguments is sufficient for the nonconstant-column conclusion, since the unit residues already give varying values. Section 5 uses existence of the root-excluding representation, not the false bijection. These local extra assertions therefore do not remove a needed core input.

Problem 3 (Major: the precision used for last-digit normalization is insufficient).  On p. 25, immediately before (4.23), the affine forms are matched modulo \(p^r\), after which equality of \(f_p\) is asserted through valuation \(r\). On p. 30, the CRT choices of \(D,E\) likewise use \(p_l^{r_l}\), followed by (5.1) through valuation \(r_l\). The required modulus is one power higher.

An exact test of the inference is \(F(n,m)=f_p(m+p^r)\), with affine coefficients \(A=0,B=1,C=p^r\), and \(D=E=0\). The printed congruence modulo \(p^r\) is satisfied. At \(m=p^r\), whose valuation is \(r\), the original value is \(2\), whereas the claimed normalized value is \(1\). This is an admissible nonconstant-column Sudoku solution by the line argument in Problem 1 with a different shift. The independent script verifies this discrepancy for \(r=1,2,3,4\); the displayed calculation proves it for every \(r\ge1\).

This test disproves the asserted consequence of the stated congruence. It does not disprove the existence of better choices of \(D,E\), or the existence conclusions of the theorems. For a unit \(B\), choose \[D\equiv-A/B,\qquad E\equiv-C/B\pmod {p^{r+1}}.\] After shearing, the two affine arguments differ by a multiple of \(p^{r+1}\). Whenever one has valuation \(k\le r\), division by \(p^k\) shows that their unit residues modulo \(p\), and therefore their \(f_p\) values, agree. For the two-prime argument choose \(D,E\) simultaneously modulo \(p_1^{r_1+1}\) and \(p_2^{r_2+1}\). CRT provides these choices because the primes are distinct. No enlargement of the board or new hypothesis is needed.

This is an invalid precision inference at every recursive scale and at the normalization feeding domino recovery. Its placement in the core derivations warrants Major severity at that level, even though the stronger congruence supplies an explicit repair. The repair, rather than the insufficient printed modulus, is used in the subsequent checks in this report.

Problem 4 (Major: the domino-recovery calculation omits cross-prime units).  At the bottom of p. 31, after setting \(j=p_1^{s_1}p_2^{s_2}\), the proof asserts \(F_l(n,jn)=\pi_{p_l}(cn)\) for \(p_l\nmid n\). The correct coefficient is \[\lambda_1=\pi_{p_1}(c p_2^{s_2}),\qquad
 \lambda_2=\pi_{p_2}(c p_1^{s_1}).\] Removing the power of one prime leaves the other prime as a unit.

For a complete admissible instance, take \(W=\{w\}\), both domino relations equal to \(\{(w,w)\}\), and the constant decoration \(w\). The forward construction of Proposition 5.2 gives \[F(n,m)=(f_{53}(m),f_{59}(m),w).\] All line witnesses follow by division at each prime and CRT modulo \(53^2,59^2\), as in the forward proof. Both digit components have nonconstant columns. Use \(r=(1,1)\), \(s=(0,1)\), \(j=59\), \(c=1\), and \(n=1\). These lie in the prescribed ranges, but \[F_1(1,59)=6\ne1.\] The same missing factor occurs in the level-one comparison: \(F_1(53,59\cdot53)=6\), rather than \(1\). The exact script checks both valuation levels for several \(s,n\). Thus the coefficient identity is false for a genuine decorated Sudoku solution satisfying the operative hypotheses.

Here is the repaired domino extraction. For each \(l\), compare \(\lambda_l n\) with the line witness \(a_{j,0}n+b_{j,0}\) away from the excluded residue classes. Affine extrapolation gives \[a_{j,0}\equiv\lambda_l\pmod {p_l},\qquad
 b_{j,0}\equiv0\pmod {p_l}.\] Both \(\lambda_l\) are units. Consequently (5.6) still holds when \(n\) is a unit at both primes. Multiplication by these unit factors permutes the pairs of nonzero digit residues, so CRT still eliminates the final-digit dependence in (5.5).

For a horizontal domino with \(s_1+1\le r_1\), compare the first component at the column \(p_1n\), using \(0\le n<N/p_1\) and \(p_1\nmid n\). The two expressions are \[\lambda_1 n,\qquad
 \pi_{p_1}\!\left(a_{j,0}n+b_{j,0}/p_1\right).\] Extrapolation now yields \(b_{j,0}\equiv0\pmod {p_1^2}\). At an \(n\) coprime to both primes, the witness therefore has valuation pair \((1,0)\) at \(p_1n\) and \((0,0)\) at \(n\). Equation (5.3) reads the two entries of \(T_{j,0}\), giving the required horizontal relation. The vertical argument is symmetric. There are more than enough residue representatives in the stated width. Using \(0\le n<N/p_1\) also removes the printed upper endpoint that would put column \(p_1n=N\) outside the board.

The preceding sentence on p. 31 asserting an equivalence between \(\nu_{p_l}(j)>\nu_{p_l}(i)\) and equality of last digits also needs the equality of the two finite valuations. That equality is explicit in the actual application immediately below it, so the application remains valid.

The missing factors invalidate the printed coefficient comparison on which the reverse domino reduction depends. Major severity concerns that core calculation. The corrected unit factors recover the valuation transitions checked above; the example does not disprove the equivalence of domino and decorated-Sudoku solvability.

Problem 5 (Minor: the sets in Remark 2.4 do not form a topology).  On p. 8, the proposed open sets \(U_\Omega\) contain the vertices of \(\Omega\) and all domino edges whose endpoints lie in \(\Omega\). For adjacent vertices \(s,t\), the sets \(U_{\{s\}}=\{s\}\) and \(U_{\{t\}}=\{t\}\) belong to the specified family. Their union \(\{s,t\}\) does not: its vertex set forces \(\Omega=\{s,t\}\), for which \(U_\Omega\) also contains the edge \([s,t]\). Closure under unions fails.

A corrected incidence topology permits a vertex set \(S\) together with any edge set \(D\) whose endpoints belong to \(S\). Sections assign labels to \(S\) and impose the relations for the edges in \(D\). Compatible sections glue, because each included edge and its endpoints occur together in a member of an open cover. On the original \(U_\Omega\) this gives the intended domino sections. Vertex stalks have alphabet \(W\); edge stalks instead have the allowed pairs in the appropriate relation, so the assertion on p. 9 that all stalks are \(W\) also needs correction. The manuscript explicitly does not use this sheaf interpretation later. This is a substantive local mathematical error, with no core reduction depending on it.

Problem 6 (Minor: zero board width contradicts the uniqueness assertion).  Section 1.5, p. 6, explicitly includes zero in \(\mathbb N\). Definition 4.5 allows a natural width, and Theorem 4.7, p. 18, only requires \(p^2\mid N\). At \(N=0\), the board is empty. The unique empty function satisfies all line conditions, and the affine identity (4.5) is vacuous. Both constant forms \(1\) and \(2\) are nondegenerate modulo \(p=53\) and satisfy it, but their coefficients are different modulo \(p\), contradicting the stated uniqueness. Lemma 4.8 also cannot locate a square on that board. State \(N>0\), equivalently \(N\ge p^2\) here. Every main application already uses the positive width \(53^2 59^2\); the empty-board defect has no effect on that reduction.
# Further checks and interpretive boundaries
## The structural recursion after the stated repairs

The good-square counting argument uses the coefficient \(48/p<1\), with the remaining finite-width term harmless for \(N\ge p^2\). The row, diagonal and antidiagonal propagation on a \(4\)-by-\(4\) square was checked against the figure and its affine identities. Affine extrapolation removes at most two exceptional residue classes, leaving distinct usable residues since \(p>48\). In the \(r=1\) comparison, the relevant arithmetic progression has step coprime to \(p\) and contains at least \(p\) terms. It therefore provides every residue needed to derive \(B_1\equiv B^{(0)}\pmod p\).

For the general induction use the stronger precision in Problem 3 and the normalized Tetris claim in Problem 1. At the level \(p^r m\), factor the new affine form by its common power \(p^j\), with \(j\le r-1\). Comparing its unit residues with \(B^{(r)}m\) outside at most two exceptional affine zero sets forces \(j=r-1\), \(A_{r+1},C_{r+1}\) divisible by \(p^r\), and \(B_{r+1}\equiv B^{(r)}\pmod p\). The coefficients \((pA_{r+1},B_{r+1},pC_{r+1})\) then cover the next valuation level. The first display on p. 25 should use \(m'\), rather than \(m\), inside \(A_1n+B_1m'+C_1\) when \(m=pm'\).

Compactness in \(\mathbb Z_p^3\) gives a convergent subsequence, with the middle coefficient still a unit because the units form a closed set. At any nonzero limiting affine argument, its valuation and last digit eventually stabilize. This proves precisely the root-excluding limit assertion. It imposes no value at an actual zero and therefore cannot justify the bijection refuted above.
## Effective finite rules and the encoding

The decorated rule is finite and effectively enumerable despite the large board. For a line witness, its relevant valuation and digit tests depend only on the coefficients modulo \(p_1^2p_2^2\); the possible small domino decorations are finite. The forward construction divides the two line coefficients by their common \(p_l\)-power separately, uses CRT, and translates the domino configuration by the two removed valuations. The identically zero line is handled separately. No running-time bound or explicit enumeration of all \(9,778,129\) columns was claimed or attempted in this review.

The choice \(q=p_1p_2\) in the initial condition requires genuine permutations of \(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z\). On the converse side, a CRT linear permutation with unit slope supplies the needed labels. In Section 6, finite conjunctions and existentially quantified auxiliary functions have finite constructive descriptions. The Boolean constraint uses an order-two direction; the non-wraparound bound on \(L\) is essential. The auxiliary-sum construction of Lemma 6.12 works for odd numbers of coordinates by excluding the two constant sign vectors; an extension can be chosen on each order-two orbit and negated on its partner. Exact checks for \(3,5,7,9\) coordinates covered 680 sign vectors. These are checks of the elementary arithmetic, not exhaustive tests of all encodings. In Lemma 6.13, consecutive windows each contain every antipodal label once. Comparing adjacent windows makes the antipodal label \(q\)-periodic and hence a permutation. The signs themselves need not be periodic.

There are several typing and indexing omissions that should be corrected before treating Section 6 as a literal specification. Use columns \(0,\ldots,N-1\) consistently, scalar sign coordinates \(\omega_{a,b,n}\in\{-1,1\}\), and codomain \(\Sigma\) for \(F\). Proposition 6.3 should say that \(F\) tiles \(G\times E'\); its proof has that target. Most significantly, add the word permutation to clause (4) on p. 41. The proof on p. 42 and Lemma 6.13 explicitly use that intended meaning.

For clarity, dropping bijectivity really would change the constraint. After consistent reindexing, take \(N=1,q=2\), \(\Sigma=\{a\}\), the single constant Sudoku word, and \(C=\{(0,a)\}\). No permutation can satisfy the initial condition. With \(s_0=2,L=13\), \[\iota_0(0)=(1,1),\quad \iota_0(1)=(1,-1),\quad
 \iota_1(a)=(1,1),\] all four scalar functions \(\alpha_{a,b,0}((i,j),t)=(-1)^t\) satisfy (1)–(3) and the weakened (4) with the constant map \(\sigma\equiv0\). The dimension and \(L>4s_0N+4\) conditions hold. This is a test of the weakened reading after reindexing; it is not a counterexample to the intended bijective Theorem 6.4, whose surrounding text states the missing requirement. It is recorded as a clarification, not an additional Major finding.

With that meaning explicit, invariance along \((-n,1)\) makes the decoded functions depend only on \(jn+i\). The disjoint antipodal images make the decoded symbols unique, and the permutation condition gives the original initial condition. The simultaneous global sign in \(\Omega\cup-\Omega\) is necessary; independent signs would not encode the same word.
# External reduction checks

For the merger into one tiling equation, Theorem 1.15 of the exact GT21 version [GT21] applies with one translation unknown. Its hypotheses include nonempty tiles and an extra cyclic group of order greater than the number of equations. The proof on pp. 15–16 uses the fact that a proper consecutive interval in that cyclic group has trivial translation stabilizer. Thus all centers have the distinguished extra coordinate, and slicing recovers the original equations. This keeps one prototile. The independent script checked that stabilizer fact in 300 small cases; the interval argument proves the general fact.

The functional graph equation in the manuscript has the correct shift sign: a tile at \(-h\) meets a fiber at \(x\) through \(\alpha(x+h)\). Empty or contradictory constraints must be preprocessed when invoking the nonempty-tile merger. An empty tile with empty target is discarded; an empty tile with nonempty target, or a nonempty tile with empty target under the graph condition, is an immediate impossibility. One can output a fixed impossible periodic-target instance in those cases. Overlapping components at the same shift likewise signal a violated disjoint-sum condition and can be detected before the merger.

Theorem 1.1 of MSS22 [MSS22] is stated for tiling the entire quotient group. Its printed statement alone should not be treated as a proved periodic-subset variant. For the actual constraints here, the GT21 periodic-target construction provides a route. The following explanation is an applicability check using its rigid-tile lemma, rather than a claim to have reproved that lemma.

Lift the function domain \(\mathbb Z^2\times\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\) to \(\mathbb Z^3\) and impose period two in its last coordinate. The encoded codomain is \(H=(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^K\), with \(L\ge5\). Let \(\pi:\mathbb Z^K\to H\), \(\Lambda=\ker\pi\), and take the finite rigid fundamental tile \(R\) from GT21 Lemma 9.3. For a center set \(A\subset\mathbb Z^3\times\mathbb Z^K\), the equation \[A\oplus(\{0\}\times R)=\mathbb Z^{3+K}\] forces each fiber \(A_x\) to be a coset \(\pi^{-1}(\alpha(x))\). For each finite functional rule, replace a subset \(E_{ij}\subset H\) by its representatives \(\widetilde E_{ij}=R\cap\pi^{-1}(E_{ij})\), and form the finite tile \[F_i=\bigsqcup_j \{-h_{ij}\}\times\widetilde E_{ij}.\] Then \[A\oplus F_i=\mathbb Z^3\times\pi^{-1}(E_i')\] is exactly the corresponding disjoint functional partition. The target is periodic. Theorem 9.1 of GT21 combines this finite system, still with one center unknown, into a single tile in one additional integer dimension and a periodic target. The dimension varies with the finite encoding, as required.

GT21 Lemma 9.3 and its geometric argument were inspected on pp. 27–28, including the bump-and-hole figure. Its asserted exhaustive geometric case analysis was not independently enumerated in every dimension; this remains an external proof dependency. The full MSS22 proof, the source’s suggested connected Euclidean analogue, and all later variants were not independently certified. Logical independence statements also retain the set-theoretic assumptions identified in GT21, rather than asserting consistency of ZFC from within ZFC.
# Assessment

Problems 1, 3 and 4 identify failed core guarantees or calculations, with exact counterexamples to the particular assertions and explicit dependencies. They warrant an overall Major assessment under a claim-level standard. The repaired normalization, restricted Tetris step and cross-prime calculations recover the portions of the main reduction checked here. No contradiction to the main undecidability conclusion is established. Problems 2, 5 and 6 are local defects with their narrower impact stated.

This distinction is material: a repairable core derivation is still a failed derivation as printed, while a counterexample to an auxiliary assertion must not be represented as a counterexample to the entire paper. The report does not certify the unavailable journal version or every external theorem. It is an initial technical review; scientific decision remains pending, human reviews are empty, and no independent acceptance is claimed.

analysis: On p. 25, immediately before (4.23), the affine forms are matched modulo \(p^r\), after which equality of \(f_p\) is asserted through valuation \(r\). On p. 30, the CRT choices of \(D,E\) likewise use \(p_l^{r_l}\), followed by (5.1) through valuation \(r_l\). The required modulus is one power higher.

An exact test of the inference is \(F(n,m)=f_p(m+p^r)\), with affine coefficients \(A=0,B=1,C=p^r\), and \(D=E=0\). The printed congruence modulo \(p^r\) is satisfied. At \(m=p^r\), whose valuation is \(r\), the original value is \(2\), whereas the claimed normalized value is \(1\). This is an admissible nonconstant-column Sudoku solution by the line argument in Problem 1 with a different shift. The independent script verifies this discrepancy for \(r=1,2,3,4\); the displayed calculation proves it for every \(r\ge1\).

This test disproves the asserted consequence of the stated congruence. It does not disprove the existence of better choices of \(D,E\), or the existence conclusions of the theorems. For a unit \(B\), choose \[D\equiv-A/B,\qquad E\equiv-C/B\pmod {p^{r+1}}.\] After shearing, the two affine arguments differ by a multiple of \(p^{r+1}\). Whenever one has valuation \(k\le r\), division by \(p^k\) shows that their unit residues modulo \(p\), and therefore their \(f_p\) values, agree. For the two-prime argument choose \(D,E\) simultaneously modulo \(p_1^{r_1+1}\) and \(p_2^{r_2+1}\). CRT provides these choices because the primes are distinct. No enlargement of the board or new hypothesis is needed.

This is an invalid precision inference at every recursive scale and at the normalization feeding domino recovery. Its placement in the core derivations warrants Major severity at that level, even though the stronger congruence supplies an explicit repair. The repair, rather than the insufficient printed modulus, is used in the subsequent checks in this report.
result: Impact: The stated congruence does not justify the core normalization at its boundary. Existence conclusions are not disproved.

problems.title: Cross-prime unit factors missing from reverse domino reduction
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 30 Pdf pages: 31 Pdf pages: 32 Items: p31 last display F_l(n,jn)=pi_p_l(cn) Items: p32 affine extrapolation and level-one comparison Items: j=p1^s1 p2^s2
claim: Recorded check: Cross-prime unit factors missing from reverse domino reduction
analysis:
At the bottom of p. 31, after setting \(j=p_1^{s_1}p_2^{s_2}\), the proof asserts \(F_l(n,jn)=\pi_{p_l}(cn)\) for \(p_l\nmid n\). The correct coefficient is \[\lambda_1=\pi_{p_1}(c p_2^{s_2}),\qquad
 \lambda_2=\pi_{p_2}(c p_1^{s_1}).\] Removing the power of one prime leaves the other prime as a unit.

For a complete admissible instance, take \(W=\{w\}\), both domino relations equal to \(\{(w,w)\}\), and the constant decoration \(w\). The forward construction of Proposition 5.2 gives \[F(n,m)=(f_{53}(m),f_{59}(m),w).\] All line witnesses follow by division at each prime and CRT modulo \(53^2,59^2\), as in the forward proof. Both digit components have nonconstant columns. Use \(r=(1,1)\), \(s=(0,1)\), \(j=59\), \(c=1\), and \(n=1\). These lie in the prescribed ranges, but \[F_1(1,59)=6\ne1.\] The same missing factor occurs in the level-one comparison: \(F_1(53,59\cdot53)=6\), rather than \(1\). The exact script checks both valuation levels for several \(s,n\). Thus the coefficient identity is false for a genuine decorated Sudoku solution satisfying the operative hypotheses.

Here is the repaired domino extraction. For each \(l\), compare \(\lambda_l n\) with the line witness \(a_{j,0}n+b_{j,0}\) away from the excluded residue classes. Affine extrapolation gives \[a_{j,0}\equiv\lambda_l\pmod {p_l},\qquad
 b_{j,0}\equiv0\pmod {p_l}.\] Both \(\lambda_l\) are units. Consequently (5.6) still holds when \(n\) is a unit at both primes. Multiplication by these unit factors permutes the pairs of nonzero digit residues, so CRT still eliminates the final-digit dependence in (5.5).

For a horizontal domino with \(s_1+1\le r_1\), compare the first component at the column \(p_1n\), using \(0\le n<N/p_1\) and \(p_1\nmid n\). The two expressions are \[\lambda_1 n,\qquad
 \pi_{p_1}\!\left(a_{j,0}n+b_{j,0}/p_1\right).\] Extrapolation now yields \(b_{j,0}\equiv0\pmod {p_1^2}\). At an \(n\) coprime to both primes, the witness therefore has valuation pair \((1,0)\) at \(p_1n\) and \((0,0)\) at \(n\). Equation (5.3) reads the two entries of \(T_{j,0}\), giving the required horizontal relation. The vertical argument is symmetric. There are more than enough residue representatives in the stated width. Using \(0\le n<N/p_1\) also removes the printed upper endpoint that would put column \(p_1n=N\) outside the board.

The preceding sentence on p. 31 asserting an equivalence between \(\nu_{p_l}(j)>\nu_{p_l}(i)\) and equality of last digits also needs the equality of the two finite valuations. That equality is explicit in the actual application immediately below it, so the application remains valid.

The missing factors invalidate the printed coefficient comparison on which the reverse domino reduction depends. Major severity concerns that core calculation. The corrected unit factors recover the valuation transitions checked above; the example does not disprove the equivalence of domino and decorated-Sudoku solvability.
result: Impact: Printed core calculation false on a valid decorated solution. Corrected calculation restores both needed valuation transitions; main undecidability not refuted.

problems.title: Proposed sheaf topology is not closed under unions
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 8 Pdf pages: 9 Items: Remark2.4 open sets U_Omega Items: Claim about stalks
claim: Recorded check: Proposed sheaf topology is not closed under unions
analysis: On p. 8, the proposed open sets \(U_\Omega\) contain the vertices of \(\Omega\) and all domino edges whose endpoints lie in \(\Omega\). For adjacent vertices \(s,t\), the sets \(U_{\{s\}}=\{s\}\) and \(U_{\{t\}}=\{t\}\) belong to the specified family. Their union \(\{s,t\}\) does not: its vertex set forces \(\Omega=\{s,t\}\), for which \(U_\Omega\) also contains the edge \([s,t]\). Closure under unions fails.

A corrected incidence topology permits a vertex set \(S\) together with any edge set \(D\) whose endpoints belong to \(S\). Sections assign labels to \(S\) and impose the relations for the edges in \(D\). Compatible sections glue, because each included edge and its endpoints occur together in a member of an open cover. On the original \(U_\Omega\) this gives the intended domino sections. Vertex stalks have alphabet \(W\); edge stalks instead have the allowed pairs in the appropriate relation, so the assertion on p. 9 that all stalks are \(W\) also needs correction. The manuscript explicitly does not use this sheaf interpretation later. This is a substantive local mathematical error, with no core reduction depending on it.
result: Impact: The proposed topology and universal stalk identification are false locally; no central reduction depends on them.

problems.title: Zero-width boundary contradicts affine uniqueness
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 6 Pdf pages: 15 Pdf pages: 18 Items: Section1.5 N includes0 Items: Definition4.5 natural width Items: Theorem4.7 uniqueness and Lemma4.8 square
claim: Recorded check: Zero-width boundary contradicts affine uniqueness
analysis: Section 1.5, p. 6, explicitly includes zero in \(\mathbb N\). Definition 4.5 allows a natural width, and Theorem 4.7, p. 18, only requires \(p^2\mid N\). At \(N=0\), the board is empty. The unique empty function satisfies all line conditions, and the affine identity (4.5) is vacuous. Both constant forms \(1\) and \(2\) are nondegenerate modulo \(p=53\) and satisfy it, but their coefficients are different modulo \(p\), contradicting the stated uniqueness. Every main application already uses the positive width \(53^2 59^2\); the empty-board defect has no effect on that reduction.
result: Impact: False zero-width extension without effect on the actual reduction.

report: Abstract: The exact 23-page arXiv version is examined through its internal proof structure. An admissible convex entropy function gives both a coherent and a noncoherent normalized pure state generalized entropy equal to negative infinity. This identifies a finiteness qualification needed for the literal uniqueness assertion in Remark 4(e), without refuting Theorem 3’s extended-real inequality. Independent checks also identify local formula corrections in the two proofs and a distance-normalization correction in the explicit pure-state constant. Their repairs are verified without asserting a counterexample to the main stability inequalities. The evidence is bound to the precise preprint version.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Verification of
The Generalized Wehrl Entropy Bound in Quantitative Form
# Identity and scope

Rupert L. Frank, Fabio Nicola and Paolo Tilli, The generalized Wehrl entropy bound in quantitative form, arXiv:2307.14089v3, 1 November 2023 [source]. The associated journal DOI is 10.4171/JEMS/1674; online publication is recorded as 8 July 2025 [publisher]. Equality of this preprint and the journal version has not been established. Page references are physical PDF pages, which agree with printed pages 1–23.

All 23 pages of extracted text were read. Internal checks covered Proposition 6, Proposition 8, Theorem 9, the mixed-state estimates in Lemma 10, the distribution-function proof of Theorem 3, the pure-state argument in Section 3, and the Fock-space application in Section 4. Independent verification additionally read pp. 1–2 and 6–18 of the exact 46-page arXiv:2307.09304v1 of Gómez, Guerra, Ramos and Tilli [ggrt]: all five steps of Lemma 2.1, Corollary 2.2, Lemmas 2.3–2.5 and the assembly of the function-stability estimate were checked against their use here. This is not certification of that entire reference. Remark 12’s higher-dimensional extension was read but not fully verified. Source pages 1–3, 5–6, 9–14 and 18–21, and reference pages 1–2, 11–14 and 16–17, were actually inspected as bound page images.
# Assumptions and proof structure

Equation reference: ineq. For a positive trace-class operator \(\rho\) of trace one, the source defines \[u_\rho(z)=\sum_jp_j|F_j(z)|^2e^{-\pi|z|^2},\qquad
 D[\rho]=\inf_w\|\rho-|\varphi_w\rangle\langle\varphi_w|\|_{\mathcal S^1},\] where the Bargmann transforms have unit norm in the Fock space. Theorem 3 assumes \(\Phi:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) continuous, convex, non-linear, and \(\Phi(0)=0\), and asserts \[
 I_\Phi(\rho)\leq I_\Phi(\rho_{\rm coh})-c_\Phi D[\rho]^2,\qquad
 I_\Phi(\rho)=\int_{\mathbb C}\Phi(u_\rho)\,dA.\] The proof on p. 12 explicitly allows negative-infinite integrals.

The estimate \(D[\rho]\leq2\sqrt{1-T}\), \(T=\max u_\rho\), follows from the two-dimensional pure-state trace-norm calculation, the triangle inequality and concavity of the square root. The numerator in Proposition 8 is nonnegative by Cauchy–Schwarz. Coarea and planar isoperimetry then give \(\mu'(t)\leq-1/t\) on \((0,T)\). The single crossing of \(\mu-\mu_0\) supplies the sign required in (37)–(39). The three threshold cases in the final comparison with \(H(t_*)\) were checked, including \(t_1>T\) and a non-smooth convex \(\Phi\).

For the imported part of Lemma 10, set \(\delta^2=(1-T)/T\) and use the conjugated harmonic term in source (25). Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[|h|\leq\sqrt2\pi\delta r^2e^{\pi r^2/2},\quad
 |h_r|\leq2\sqrt2\pi\delta r e^{\pi r^2/2},\quad
 |h_{rr}|\leq C\delta(1+r^2)e^{\pi r^2/2}.\] The last estimate follows by retaining the same coefficient factor in the second-derivative calculation; source (31) prints a valid weaker bound without \(\delta\). For fixed \(t_0>0\) and sufficiently small \(\delta\), the defining function \(g_\theta\) in (32) satisfies \(g_r\geq\pi t_0 r e^{\pi r^2}\). Its level radius \(r_\sigma\) is unique, \(\pi r_\sigma^2\leq\log(2/t_0)\), and implicit differentiation gives \(|r_\sigma'|\leq C\delta r_\sigma/t_0\) and \(|r_\sigma''|\leq C\delta^2r_\sigma/t_0^3\). For \(A(\sigma)=\tfrac12\int r_\sigma^2\,d\theta\), the harmonic mean-value identity gives \(A'(0)=0\), while \(|A''|\leq C\delta^2A(0)/t_0^3\). This includes Step V of the reference, in addition to its Steps III–IV.

Writing \(q=T/t\) and using \(\delta^2\leq t_0/2\), the initial radius obeys \[\pi r_0^2=\log q+\log(1-\delta^2)-\log(1-\delta^2q)
 \leq(1+2\delta^2/t_0)\log q .\] Indeed the extra logarithm is at most \(2\delta^2(q-1)\leq2\delta^2t_0^{-1}\log q\). This verifies the stated mixed-state distribution estimate. It bounds the crossing point away from one. On a fixed interval \([a,T]\) sufficiently close to one, it then gives \(\mu_0(t)-\mu(t)\geq(1-T)/2\) when \(T\) is close to one. Integration gives \(H(t_*)\geq c(1-T)\); when \(T\) stays away from one, \(H(t_*)\geq(1-T)^2/2\) supplies the same linear conclusion. Thus the relevant reference argument for Lemma 11 transfers without an additional pure-state assumption.

For Section 4, the monomial expansion directly verifies \[\pi^{-1}\|F'\|^2=\sum n|a_n|^2,\qquad
 \pi\int|z|^2|F|^2\,d\mu=\sum(n+1)|a_n|^2 .\] These identities justify the integration-by-parts limit when the energy is finite. Scaling and the unitary Bargmann correspondence give the asserted Fock-space implication; no sharper constant is inferred.
# A finiteness qualification for uniqueness

Problem 1 (Degenerate extended-real maximizers).  Remark 4(e), p. 3, says that the generalized entropy functional is maximized only by coherent states when \(\Phi\) is non-linear. The literal stated class includes a function for which this functional is negative infinite at a noncoherent state as well.
## Admissibility of the entropy function

Equation reference: phi. Set \(a=e^{-1}\) and \[
 \Phi(0)=0,\qquad
 \Phi(t)=\begin{cases}
 -(1-\log t)^{-1},&0<t\leq a,\\
 -(1+et)/4,&a\leq t\leq1 .
 \end{cases}\] For \(0<t<a\), let \(L=1-\log t>2\). Direct differentiation gives \[\Phi'(t)=-\frac1{tL^2},\qquad
 \Phi''(t)=\frac{L-2}{t^2L^3}>0.\] At \(a\), both branches have value \(-1/2\) and derivative \(-e/4\). The limit at zero is zero. Thus \(\Phi\) is continuous, convex and non-linear on \([0,1]\), with \(\Phi(0)=0\). The linear branch is essential: the first branch is not being used outside its convexity interval.
## Normalized states and divergent integrals

For the coherent state at zero, \(u_0=e^{-\pi|z|^2}\). In radial integrals put \(s=\pi|z|^2\), so that \(dA=ds\). For \(s\geq1\), \[\Phi(e^{-s})=-\frac1{1+s},\qquad I_\Phi(\rho_0)=-\infty.\] Take the Fock function \(F_1(z)=\sqrt{\pi}\,z\). Its normalization is exact: \[\int_{\mathbb C}\pi|z|^2e^{-\pi|z|^2}\,dA
 =\int_0^\infty se^{-s}\,ds=1.\] The source’s unitary Bargmann correspondence therefore supplies an admissible rank-one density matrix \(\rho_1\). Its Husimi function is \(u_1=se^{-s}\), with maximum \(e^{-1}<1\). It is noncoherent and, by Remark 7, \[D[\rho_1]=2\sqrt{1-e^{-1}}>0.\] Since \(se^{-s}\leq e^{-1}\), the first branch of [phi] (#phi) applies. For \(s\geq1\), \[\Phi(se^{-s})=-\frac1{1+s-\log s}\leq-\frac1{1+s}.\] The integrand is nonpositive, hence this comparison proves \(I_\Phi(\rho_1)=-\infty\). No numerical truncation is being used to infer divergence.
## Counterevidence, impact and exact repair

The source’s opening paragraph on p. 12 expressly discusses \(I_\Phi(\rho_{\rm coh})=-\infty\) and says the other integral is then negative infinite as well. This is evidence that the proof does not mistake an infinite quantity for a finite one. If the uniqueness sentence is read as restricted to finite optima, its intended conclusion is consistent; that restriction is absent from the literal statement.

Equation [ineq] (#ineq) remains valid as \(-\infty\leq-\infty\). The example does not refute Theorems 1 or 3 or establish a defect in the Fock-space application. Its supported impact is local, corresponding to a supported Minor qualification. The relevant source wording has now been visually confirmed. It is not a demonstrated failure of the core stability inequalities.

Restrict the uniqueness assertion to \[\int_0^1\frac{\Phi(t)}t\,dt>-\infty .\] The positive part is already bounded by convexity and \(\Phi(0)=0\). With a finite coherent-state optimum, equality in [ineq] (#ineq) forces \(D[\rho]=0\) and the closed coherent-projector family gives a coherent state. This verifies the repair to the corollary conditional on Theorem 3; it is not an independent proof of that theorem.
# Local formula corrections with complete repairs

Problem 2 (Conjugation, ratio and negative-part notation).  Three local formulas require consistent notation. In source (22), p. 9, the coefficient \(a_0^{(j)}\) should be conjugated, as it already is in (20) and (25). On p. 18, the variable following (48) must be \(s=e^{-|E|}/\tau\), and the integrand in (49) must be \((u_0-\tau)_-\), as in (47)–(48).

The conjugation correction is fixed by the expansion of \(|F_j|^2\). Multiplying \(F_j\) by \(i\) preserves the density matrix but reverses the unconjugated product in (22); the conjugated expression is phase invariant. Formula (25) already supplies the correct expression used in the subsequent estimates. This local correction does not invalidate the estimates verified above.

The sign error in (49) has a counterexample under the actual hypotheses. Use the normalized \(F_1\) above, \(u_1=se^{-s}\), and \(\tau=e^{-3}\). For \(E=\{u_1>\tau\}\), the radial annulus \(e^{-2}\leq s\leq4\) is contained in \(E\): the values at both ends exceed \(e^{-3}\) and the function is unimodal. Thus \[|E|\geq4-e^{-2}>3+\log2=|F_\tau|+\log2,
 \qquad e^{-|E|}<\tau/2 .\] The strict inequality follows from \(e^{-2}<1/4\) and \(\log2<3/4\). The centered disk \(E^*\) therefore strictly contains \(F_\tau=\{u_0>\tau\}\). The printed integral of \((u_0-\tau)_+\) over \(E^*\setminus F_\tau\) is zero, whereas the printed lower bound is strictly positive.

With the negative part, \(s=e^{-|E|}/\tau\in(0,1)\) and \(\Omega=E^*\setminus F_\tau\), the exact integral is \[\int_{\Omega}(u_0-\tau)_-\,dA
 =e^{-|E|}-\tau+\tau|E|-\tau|F_\tau|
 =\tau(s-\log s-1)
 \geq\frac{\tau}{2}(1-s)^2 .\] The last inequality follows by differentiating \(s-\log s-1-(1-s)^2/2\), whose derivative is \(-(1-s)^2/s\leq0\) and whose value at one is zero. For \(s<1/2\) the remainder is at least \(\tau/8\). Since \(D[f]^2\leq2\) and the coherent hinge integral is at most one, the continuation on p. 19 follows with the claimed universal form. These are Minor local formula errors with verified repairs, not a counterexample to Theorem 13.
# Distance normalization in the explicit constant

Problem 3 (A missing conversion in the deduction on p. 19).  Theorem 13 measures the unit-phase \(L^2\) distance \(D[f]\). Theorem 3, equation (4), measures the trace distance \(D[\rho]\). The displayed explicit coefficient on p. 19 identifies the same constant across these two distances without the conversion.

For a normalized pure state \(\rho=|f\rangle\langle f|\), the identities on pp. 5–6 give \[D[f]^2=2(1-\sqrt T),\qquad
 D[\rho]^2=4(1-T)=2(1+\sqrt T)D[f]^2 .\] Let \(c\) be the actual constant in Theorem 13, and put \[A_\Phi=\int_0^1
 \tau\bigl(1-\tau-\tau\log(1/\tau)\bigr)\,\Phi''(d\tau).\] The superposition argument establishes an entropy gap at least \(cA_\Phi D[f]^2\). It therefore guarantees the coefficient \(cA_\Phi/4\) in front of \(D[\rho]^2\), rather than directly giving \(cA_\Phi\) as printed for (4). For \(\Phi(t)=t\log t\), \(A_\Phi=1/4\), so this route guarantees \(c/16\) in (2); the stated \(c/4\) is the coefficient for \(D[f]^2\).

This is a Minor constant-accounting defect in the explicit deduction. No counterexample to the larger numerical constant is claimed: an independently stronger estimate might exist. The existence assertions of Theorems 1 and 3 are unchanged. One can either include the factor \(1/4\) or explicitly rename the universal constant after reducing it. Theorem 14 can still use the constant from Theorem 1, because \(D[f]^2\leq D[\rho]^2\); its deduction requires an implication, not an equality of those distances.
# Conclusion

The independent checks support a finite-optimum qualification for Remark 4(e), local formula repairs, and an explicit distance-constant conversion. Each has a complete local repair and a supported Minor impact. The p. 12 extended-real discussion, the corrected conjugation already present in (25), and the separate first proof of Theorem 3 limit broader interpretations. No counterexample to the main stability inequalities has been established.

On p. 18, the variable following (48) must be \(s=e^{-|E|}/\tau\), and the integrand in (49) must be \((u_0-\tau)_-\), as in (47)–(48).

The conjugation correction is fixed by the expansion of \(|F_j|^2\). Multiplying \(F_j\) by \(i\) preserves the density matrix but reverses the unconjugated product in (22); the conjugated expression is phase invariant. Formula (25) already supplies the correct expression used in the subsequent estimates. This local correction does not invalidate the estimates verified above.

The sign error in (49) has a counterexample under the actual hypotheses. Use the normalized \(F_1\) above, \(u_1=se^{-s}\), and \(\tau=e^{-3}\). For \(E=\{u_1>\tau\}\), the radial annulus \(e^{-2}\leq s\leq4\) is contained in \(E\): the values at both ends exceed \(e^{-3}\) and the function is unimodal. Thus \[|E|\geq4-e^{-2}>3+\log2=|F_\tau|+\log2,
 \qquad e^{-|E|}<\tau/2 .\] The strict inequality follows from \(e^{-2}<1/4\) and \(\log2<3/4\). The centered disk \(E^*\) therefore strictly contains \(F_\tau=\{u_0>\tau\}\).  =e^{-|E|}-\tau+\tau|E|-\tau|F_\tau|
 =\tau(s-\log s-1)
 \geq\frac{\tau}{2}(1-s)^2 .\] The last inequality follows by differentiating \(s-\log s-1-(1-s)^2/2\), whose derivative is \(-(1-s)^2/s\leq0\) and whose value at one is zero.
