Title: Initial scientific review
A strict maximum principle for nonlocal minimal surfaces

Paper. Serena Dipierro, Ovidiu Savin and Enrico Valdinoci, arXiv:2308.01697v2, 28 November 2024, 42 pages. Frozen identifier: M25-0302. Journal mapping: DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1675. All locations below refer to the acquired preprint, not to the publisher’s version.
# Assessment and scope

The main result asserts that nested \(s\)-minimal sets, \(0<s<1\), which share a boundary point in a ball of minimality coincide. The argument uses a normal separation function, a geometric integral equation, compactness away from the singular set, and a Harnack inequality.

One Major proof defect is supported by the inspected text: the measurable-set translation estimate (3.24) is false, and it is used to obtain an error estimate in the principal geometric equation. The counterexample below refutes precisely that auxiliary assertion; it does not refute Theorem 1.1. A known perimeter estimate provides a credible, mathematically specific repair for the minimal-set application. The severity reflects the role of the invalid derivation, not a claim that the main result is false.

All 42 pages were read as extracted text. The normal-coordinate calculations, the cut-off and capacity argument, the barrier estimates, the blow-up selection and the final dependency chain were examined. This is not a complete independent proof of the imported regularity and Harnack theorems. The cited arXiv version of the BV estimate was also checked visually at its title, Theorem 1.1 and Definitions 1.5–1.6; its full proof is not independently certified. Exact image hashes and observations accompany the provenance. The scientific decision and adjudication remain pending.
# P1. The translation bound for arbitrary measurable sets
## Location and assertion

Equation reference: bad. On printed/PDF page 15, equation (3.24) asserts, for all \(r>0\), \(\tau\in\mathbb R^n\) and measurable \(L\), a bound of the form \[
 |B_r\cap((L+\tau)\setminus L)|\leq C r^{n-1}|\tau|.\] It is substituted into (3.23), together with (3.17), in the last paragraph of the proof of Lemma 3.2. The resulting \(O(w(x_0)\eta)\) term enters Theorem 3.4, equation (3.26), and subsequently equations (8.12), (8.15) and (8.17), on pages 36–38.

The first equality in the proposed proof identifies the one-sided gain with the absolute value of \(|B_r\cap(L+\tau)|-|B_r\cap L|\). The signed difference is the gain minus the loss; taking its absolute value does not generally recover the gain. For example, with \(L=(0,1)\), \(r=2\), and \(0<\tau<1\), the gain has length \(\tau\), whereas the difference of the two intersection lengths is zero.
## A fixed-set counterexample satisfying every stated condition

A single fixed measurable set already contradicts [bad] (#bad), even if \(C\) were allowed to depend on that set. Work in \(\mathbb R^2\) with \(r=1\). Put \[a_j=2^{-2j},\qquad b_j=2^{-(2j-1)}=2a_j,\qquad
 A=\bigcup_{j\geq1}(a_j,b_j),\qquad L=A\times\mathbb R.\] This is an open, hence measurable, set. For any positive integer \(N\), let \(h_N=2^{-(2N+2)}\) and \(\tau_N=(h_N,0)\). For \(1\leq j\leq N\), consider \[Q_{j,N}=(b_j,b_j+h_N)\times(-1/2,1/2).\] These rectangles are pairwise disjoint and satisfy \[Q_{j,N}\subset B_1\cap((L+\tau_N)\setminus L).\] Indeed, \(a_j\geq a_N=4h_N\), so \(x_1-h_N\in(a_j,b_j)\) for \(x_1\in(b_j,b_j+h_N)\). On the other hand, the interval to the right of \(b_j\) is a gap of \(A\) (the next interval, if present, starts at \(a_{j-1}=2b_j\)), so \(x_1\notin A\). Finally, \[x_1\leq \frac12+h_N\leq\frac9{16},\qquad |x_2|<\frac12,\qquad
 \left(\frac9{16}\right)^2+\left(\frac12\right)^2
 =\frac{145}{256}<1 .\] Each rectangle has area \(h_N\). Consequently \[\frac{|B_1\cap((L+\tau_N)\setminus L)|}{|\tau_N|}
 \geq N .\] There is no finite \(C\) for all \(N\). This is an analytic, infinite-family counterexample, not an extrapolation from a numerical experiment. An independent exact-rational program checks the interval, gap, disjointness and ball-containment inequalities for representative \(N\); the argument above proves them for every \(N\).
## Impact and counterevidence

The invalid bound is used for the symmetric difference between \(E_1\) and a translate of \(E_1\) in the balls covering the bad set. The intended bound is proportional to \(w(x_0)\sum_j r_j^{n-1}=w(x_0)\eta\). After normalization of the separation function, this becomes the error that must vanish when the singular-set covering is removed. Thus it occurs in the derivation of the core limiting inequality, rather than only in incidental exposition.

The counterexample is not \(s\)-minimal and is not offered as a counterexample to Theorem 1.1 or to Lemma 3.2 with additional perimeter assumptions. Minimality is important counterevidence: Cinti–Serra–Valdinoci prove a universal classical-perimeter bound for stable fractional-minimal sets [CSV]. The reviewed paper itself cites their work on page 38 for a perimeter estimate. Lemma 3.3 concerns a signed weighted tail integral and uses a change of variables; the present counterexample does not invalidate that separate argument.
## Repair and its limits

A correction should therefore replace (3.24) by this qualified estimate, state the additional hypothesis wherever Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 3.4 require it, and explain the uniformity of constants over the bad-set covering and the blow-up index. Alternatively, a valid signed-integral argument with controlled covering boundaries could be supplied. The unrestricted measurable-set assertion cannot be retained. The BV route is a checked repair mechanism; this review does not claim that a fully revised proof has been adopted by the authors or that every imported result has been independently proved.
# Other checks and limitations

The range \(0<s<1\) makes the local quadratic remainder integrable against the hypersurface kernel of order \(1+s\). The positive-part barrier estimates in Sections 6 and 7 and the normalization in Section 8 were traced to their stated local hypotheses. The final argument requires common tangent cones along the relevant subsequences, a regular normalization point separated from the singular set, and a nonzero normalized limit. Appendix A was read with those requirements in view.

A potentially misleading odd-difference expression in the normal-coordinate discussion was not promoted to a separate finding: the auxiliary averaging function is even, and its evenness can supply the required cancellation. No counterexample to the main strict maximum principle was established. The weak Harnack theorem, capacity approximation, and external smooth-convergence inputs were identified but not fully reproved. No author code was run. Targeted title/erratum and arXiv searches did not locate a correction or separate supplement in the inspected results; this is a bounded search result, not proof of absence. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect.
# Supporting checks
The precise acquired PDF has SHA256
and source-manifest SHA256
The source preparation token is preserved separately in the original manifest.

This is an initial review, not independent acceptance. Actual compiler commands, exit codes, dependency payloads, before/after hashes and PDF-page records are retained outside this scientific narrative. Initial `EMFILE` failures and the earlier incomplete report are preserved. Rendering and viewing remain separately recorded; the prior mathematical analysis and exact-rational check were reused.

Valdinoci, Quantitative flatness results and BV-estimates for stable nonlocal minimal surfaces, J. Differential Geom. 112 (2019), 447–504, DOI 10.4310/jdg/1563242471. Theorem 1.1 was consulted in arXiv:1602.00540v2; no version equivalence beyond that consulted statement is asserted.

Title: Initial scientific review
Uniqueness of the 2D Euler equation on rough domains

Paper. Siddhant Agrawal and Andrea R. Nahmod, arXiv:2308.12926v1, 24 August 2023, 33 pages. Frozen identifier M25-0303; journal DOI mapping 10.4171/JEMS/1676. This report concerns the acquired preprint only.
# Assessment

No substantiated mathematical defect was established in the inspected argument. This is a bounded initial-review conclusion, not a certification of every imported theorem. All 33 pages were read as extracted text, including the appendix. Particular attention was given to the three conditions of Assumption 1.1, the construction of the angular change of variables, and the closure of the uniqueness estimate. The necessary bound source images and every report page were actually inspected in the same-chat continuation. The earlier image-return failure and incomplete delivery state are preserved in the verification history. The scientific decision, human review and independent adjudication remain pending.
# Definitions, hypotheses and scope

Theorem 1.2 concerns a bounded, simply connected Jordan domain and bounded initial vorticity. In conformal coordinates it requires a positive lower and upper bound for \(|\Psi_z|\), a uniform \(\dot H^{1/2}\) bound on the circular traces of \(\Psi_z\), and a uniform \(L^\infty\) bound for the Hilbert transform of \(|\Psi_z|^2\). None of these conditions was discarded in reviewing the proof.

The solution class is the Yudovich class of Definition 3.1, with the weak vorticity equation and orthogonality to gradient fields expressing incompressibility and the boundary condition. Simple connectivity is used in recovering the velocity from vorticity. The flow argument also uses conservation of the physical area measure, which becomes \(|\Psi_z(y)|^2\,dy\) on the disc. No uniqueness claim for arbitrary \(L^p\) vorticity or arbitrary \(C^{1,\alpha}\) domains with \(\alpha\leq1/2\) is inferred. The remarks about unbounded or multiply connected domains are extensions discussed by the authors, not separately verified theorems in this review.
# Checks of the main proof
## Flow and boundary avoidance

The Biot–Savart representation and its conformal transformation were followed in equations (12)–(20). Lemma 3.2 provides the bounded log-Lipschitz field \(\widetilde b\) and its vanishing normal component on the circle. Its boundary estimate is \(|\widetilde b\cdot\widehat r|\lesssim\phi(1-r)\), where \(\phi(q)=q\max\{-\log q,1\}\). Combined with the lower bound on \(|\Psi_z|\), this gives the Osgood control preventing trajectories from reaching the boundary in finite time. The local smoothing argument for measure preservation and the transport identity in Lemma 3.4 were read, with the external transport theorem treated as an imported dependency.
## The change of variables

The positive function \(G\), its circular average \(c(r)\) and \(L_\theta=G/c(r)\) give \(F(re^{i\theta})=re^{iL(r,\theta)}\), with \(F\) equal to the identity near the origin. Periodicity and strict monotonicity in the angular coordinate give a disc homeomorphism. Direct calculation gives \[\det DF=L_\theta=\frac{G}{c(r)}>0 .\] Together with the derivative bounds of Lemma 4.2 this controls both \(DF\) and \(DF^{-1}\) on the disc, as required by Lemma 4.3.

The nontrivial primitive estimate in Lemma 4.1 uses the real and imaginary parts of the holomorphic function \(\Psi_z\), the identity \(|\partial_\theta|a=b_\theta\), the quadratic identity (74), and the Hilbert-transform hypothesis. Thus the required bounded radial derivative is not being inferred merely from a bounded \(G\). The second-derivative bounds and Lemma 4.7 were traced to the \(\dot H^{1/2}\) and Poisson estimates.

Near the boundary, where \(G=|\Psi_z|^2\), the tangential coefficient has the exact cancellation \[\frac{|\Psi_z|^{-2}}{r}F_\theta
 =\frac{i e^{iL}}{c(r)} .\] The remaining radial coefficient has a difference bound involving the reciprocal distance to the boundary. On page 25 the proof splits according as the separation \(\delta\) is smaller or larger than that distance \(d\). In the first case \(\phi(d)\delta/d\lesssim\phi(\delta)\); in the second case the bounded coefficient and \(\phi(d)\leq\phi(\delta)\) suffice. These are the estimates that recover a log-Lipschitz bound despite the rough conformal derivative.
## Energy closure and domain examples

The three terms of the derivative of energy (63) were followed: an interior term, the transformed near-boundary term, and the difference between the two transported vorticities. The last uses the common initial vorticity, preservation of \(|\Psi_z|^2dy\), the reflected Biot–Savart kernel, and Fubini. The kernel comparison follows from \[|1-y\overline z|^2-|y-z|^2
 =(1-|y|^2)(1-|z|^2)\geq0 .\] The normalization to a probability measure before applying Jensen’s inequality is explicit on page 27. Small time ensures that the argument lies in the concavity interval of \(\phi\). The resulting inequality \(E'\lesssim\phi(E)\) and \(\int_{0+}dq/\phi(q)=+\infty\) yield uniqueness from \(E(0)=0\). The time step depends on the conserved vorticity bound and the domain, so iteration gives the global result.

For Proposition 1.3 the trace-composition argument, the strict threshold \(\alpha>1/2\), and the convex-domain tangent-angle variation bound were checked. Continuity of the logarithmic lift is used in Lemma 6.4; it is not an unrestricted lifting assertion for arbitrary measurable functions. Lemma 6.5 was read with its nonnegative, nonzero vorticity hypothesis; its lack-of-regularity claim is not being used as a general nonuniqueness result.
# Independent checks and remaining limits

An independently written SymPy program verifies the polar Jacobian identity, the reflected-kernel identity, a test-mode normalization of (74), and the divergent Osgood integral. These calculations check specific algebraic and limiting steps; they do not replace the analytic proof.

Two possible extraction-based concerns were rejected after consulting the version-matched arXiv mathematical HTML: Lemma 6.1 assumes \(|y'|\leq c\phi(y)\), and the coefficient in Lemma 4.5 is \(4g'/r-2g/r^2\). Neither is recorded as a paper defect. These two readings were also checked against the exact bound PDF images on pages 20 and 29 during the same-chat continuation.

The external weak-solution existence theorem, the full transport theorem and the conformal boundary regularity theorems were not independently reproved. A bounded title/erratum search and the author’s publication page did not reveal a separate correction, supplement or relevant code in the inspected results. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect, and no author code was run.

Title: Initial scientific review
Three-point correlation functions in the \(\mathfrak{sl}_3\) Toda theory II: the Fateev–Litvinov formula

Binding. Baptiste Cerclé, arXiv:2208.12085v3, 17 December 2024, 73 pages; frozen identifier M25-0304; journal DOI mapping 10.4171/JEMS/1677. Only this acquired preprint is assessed; equality with the publisher version is not assumed.
# Assessment and scope

Major corrections are required in the argument as written. The principal concerns are the passage from real to complex uniform bounds, the reciprocal normalization of the hypergeometric coefficients, and a divergent integral used to bound an OPE remainder. The first and third identify failures of specific proof steps; they do not disprove the Fateev–Litvinov formula. The second concerns an explicit intermediate formula and its monodromy.

All 73 pages were read as extracted text. The root normalization \(\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=2\), the domain \(\mathcal A_N\), reflection counterterms, exceptional pole loci and restrictions on degenerate insertions were retained. Theorem 1.2 concerns a semi-degenerate insertion \(\alpha_1=\kappa\omega_2\) and \(\gamma\in[1,\sqrt2)\); no formula for arbitrary three weights, other Lie algebras or all \(0<\gamma<1\) is inferred.

The findings have analytic evidence and independently written calculation checks. Selected equations were corroborated against the version-matched mathematical HTML. The necessary bound source images and every report page were actually inspected in the same-chat continuation. The original image-return failure and incomplete delivery state remain preserved. Scientific decision and independent adjudication remain pending.
# Major comment P1: complex domination is not implied

Location. Page 34, Section 2.4.7, first paragraph; the closing proof of Lemma 2.3 and Theorem 2.2. For fixed \(c\), the manuscript establishes holomorphy in the weights; for real weights in \(\mathcal O\) it establishes uniform exponential decay in \(c\). It then infers a uniform bound in a complex neighborhood from these facts and continuity in \(c\).

It is a counterexample to the stated inference, not a claim that the actual Toda integrand equals this family. Complex domination is needed for interchanging contour and \(c\) integration and applying Morera’s theorem. Theorem 2.2 is then used in the BPZ continuation on pages 36–38 and the OPE/shift continuations on pages 55, 59 and 65–70. The fixed-\(c\) regularization argument in Section 2.4.2 and the real-weight estimates of Lemma 2.4 do not, as stated, supply the missing uniform complex estimate.

Repair boundary. Prove a locally uniform integrable complex-weight majorant for the actual subtracted integrand, including reflection terms, away from the specified poles. Decay remaining positive under small imaginary perturbations would suffice. This review has not supplied that estimate; it does not assert that such an estimate is impossible.
# Major comment P2: reciprocal hypergeometric coefficients

Location. Equations (3.4)–(3.7), page 35; Proposition 3.2 and (3.12), page 38; pages 40–41. Write the coefficient printed in (3.7) as \[D_i=
 \frac{\prod_{j=1}^3l(A_j)l(B_i-A_j)}{l(B_1)l(B_2)}
 \frac{l(1+B_1+B_2-2B_i)}{l(B_i-1)},\qquad
 l(x)=\frac{\Gamma(x)}{\Gamma(1-x)}.\] For precisely the unscaled functions \(H_i\) in (3.2), (3.4) and (3.5), single-valuedness requires \(D_i^{-1}\), whereas (3.6), (3.7) and (3.12) use \(D_i\).

Use the infinity basis with leading term \((-z)^{-A_i}\). The real connection coefficients of \(H_0\) are \[K_{0i}=
 \frac{\Gamma(B_1)\Gamma(B_2)\prod_{j\ne i}\Gamma(A_j-A_i)}
 {\prod_{j\ne i}\Gamma(A_j)\Gamma(B_1-A_i)\Gamma(B_2-A_i)}.\] For row \(k=1,2\), substitute \(A_j\mapsto1-B_k+A_j\) and \((B_1,B_2)\mapsto(2-B_k,1-B_k+B_{3-k})\). The branch phase is common to each row and cancels in \(|H_k|^2\). The cross coefficients of \(\sum_{k=0}^2\lambda_k|H_k|^2\) at infinity are \(\sum_k\lambda_kK_{ki}K_{kj}\), \(i\ne j\). Euler’s reflection formula reduces their cancellation to \[\sin x\sin(b_1-b_2)-\sin(b_1-x)\sin b_2
 +\sin(b_2-x)\sin b_1=0,
 \qquad \lambda_iD_i=\lambda_0.\] This agrees with the manuscript’s own definition \(\widetilde\lambda_i=\lambda_iD_i\) and conclusion \(\lambda_0=\widetilde\lambda_1=\widetilde\lambda_2\) at the end of the proof.

For a concrete nonresonant check take \[(A_1,A_2,A_3)=(1/100,1/4,1/3),\qquad
 (B_1,B_2)=(1/2,3/4).\] All six numbers in Proposition 3.2 are distinct modulo integers; \(B_i<1\), so the corrected expression has value \(1\) at zero. The retained 60-digit computation evaluates the connection matrix: printed weights leave nonzero cross coefficients, while reciprocal weights cancel them to the working precision. These floating-point results are corroboration, not certified interval enclosures. Analytically, keep the other four parameters fixed and let \(A_1=\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Then \(D_1\sim C/\varepsilon\) with \(C>0\), whereas the required coefficient tends to zero. For all sufficiently small positive \(\varepsilon\), these are different expressions under every hypothesis of the proposition. The reciprocal expression is real, solves (3.3), and is invariant around zero and infinity, hence also around one. It provides a counterfamily to (3.12).

The defect changes the explicit BPZ solution and the coefficient identification underlying (5.7). Every ensuing \(A/B\) ratio must be reconciled with the independent \(\Upsilon\) calculation; correcting one inverse is not a full amended proof. The final Fateev–Litvinov expression has not been disproved.

There is also a local sign error in (3.13), page 40: \(G_i\) has prefactor \((-z)^{A_i}\). Substitution of \(z^\lambda\) in (3.3) gives the infinity indicial condition \(\prod_j(\lambda+A_j)=0\), requiring \((-z)^{-A_i}\). The corrected basis is the one used in the independent connection calculation above.
# Major comment P3: the OPE diagonal integral diverges

The actual weight restrictions do not exclude this obstruction. Take \(\gamma=6/5\), \(q=43/15\), and arbitrarily small generic \(\delta>0\), with \[\alpha_0=(2/\gamma-\delta)\omega_1+(q-\delta)\omega_2,\quad
 \alpha=-\gamma\omega_1,\quad\alpha_1=(q-\delta)\omega_2,\] \[\alpha_\infty=(q-\delta)\omega_1+(2/\gamma-\delta)\omega_2.\] Every weight is strictly below \(Q\) in both root coordinates and has at least one root deficit exceeding \(\gamma\). For \(s=\alpha_0+\alpha+\alpha_1+\alpha_\infty-2Q\), \[\langle s,\omega_1\rangle=-\frac{47}{45}-\frac73\delta>-\gamma,
 \qquad
 \langle s,\omega_2\rangle=\frac{14}{45}-\frac83\delta>0\] for \(0<\delta<1/100\). Thus the tuple lies in \(\mathcal A_4\), \(\kappa<q\), and \(\gamma<\langle\alpha_0,e_1\rangle<2/\gamma\). Shrinking \(\delta\) meets the two proximity restrictions; generic choices avoid the pole hyperplanes.

The divergent integral cannot justify the asserted \(O(z^2)\) remainder bound used before identifying coefficients in Lemma 4.2 and Theorem 4.1. This does not establish divergence of the original damped expectation. A repair must retain sufficient exponential damping or prove a suitable fusion estimate at \(x=y\), with the required uniformity in \(z\) and integrability in \(c\).
# Localized corrections
## P4: positive-moment thresholds (Minor)

Page 18, (2.33)–(2.34), uses a maximum in a moment condition. For (2.34), let \(\gamma=1\), \(\alpha=Q-\frac12\omega_1-\frac74\omega_2\) and \(p_1=1,p_2=0\). Both root deficits are positive and both printed strict inequalities hold, including \(1<\max(2,1/2)\). However \(\langle\alpha,e_1\rangle=5/2\). Normalized subcritical GMC has mean Lebesgue measure on the unit disc centered at zero, so Tonelli gives \[\mathbb E\int_{\mathbb D}|x|^{-5/2}M^{e_1}(d^2x)
 =2\pi\int_0^1r^{-3/2}\,dr=\infty.\] The same local obstruction refutes (2.33). A scalar moment range must enforce both the bulk threshold and every insertion threshold, rather than their maximum.

The impact is limited by counterevidence: the next sentence states the correct sufficient first-moment condition, and the explicit use on page 27 has insertion deficit greater than \(\gamma\). No additional core failure is established from this misstatement alone. The external moment lemma was not fully audited; its publisher PDF fetch was blocked.
## P5: subtraction sign in Lemma 4.3 (Minor)

On page 55, \(r_{a,b}\) has a plus sign before \(\frac b2(1/x+1/\bar x)\) when \(0<a-b<1\). For \(a=3/2,b=1\), all hypotheses hold, but at \(x=re^{i\theta}\) the numerator of (4.13) has leading term \(-2\cos\theta\). On a sector with \(\cos\theta>1/2\) its absolute integral diverges as \(\int^\infty r^{-1/2}\,dr\). The ordinary Lebesgue integral is therefore not defined. A circular principal value is a different, unstated convention.

The correction is a minus sign inside \(r_{a,b}\), since \[|x-1|^b=|x|^b
 \left(1-\frac b2(1/x+1/\bar x)+O(|x|^{-2})\right).\] For \(0<a-b<1\) the corrected subtraction is integrable at zero and infinity. This correction, and the corresponding Taylor subtraction on page 49, must be propagated into the coefficient calculation. It is a localized sign error with an explicit integrability repair, distinct from P3.
# Coverage and remaining limits

Sections 1–2 were read for the definitions, Seiberg domains, Weyl cocycle, pole exclusions, subtractions, Brownian decompositions and real decay estimates. Section 3 was checked for the BPZ dependency, basis normalization and nonresonance assumptions. Sections 4–5 were followed through the three OPE regimes, reflection cancellations, nonempty parameter sets, two shift lengths, dense-period argument and DOZZ residue normalization. The dual-shift restriction \(\gamma>1\) and continuity argument at \(\gamma=1\) were retained.

Imported reflection asymptotics, Ward identities, full fusion theorems and the DOZZ theorem were not independently reproved. The probabilistic error estimates were read and their dependencies traced; a new proof of every uniform estimate is not claimed. The gamma reflection identity on page 40 was corroborated as correct, so extraction order there is not a finding. Explicit pole discussions in Section 2 prevent interpreting every use of analyticity as a claim that all poles are removable.

An independently written SymPy/mpmath program checks the divergent integrals, exact weight inequalities, sine identity, subtraction expansion and connection matrix. No author code was run. Bounded title, correction, supplement and code searches did not locate a separate relevant supplement, code package or correction in the inspected results. This is a search limitation, not proof of absence.

Title: Initial scientific review
A symplectic dynamics approach to the spatial isosceles three-body problem

Paper. Xijun Hu, Lei Liu, Yuwei Ou, Pedro A. S. Salomão and Guowei Yu, arXiv:2308.00338v1, 1 August 2023, 66 pages. Frozen identifier M25-0305; journal DOI mapping 10.4171/JEMS/1678. Only the acquired preprint is evaluated here.
# Assessment and scope

One substantive incorrect conclusion is established in Remark 6.5: the specified action–angle transformation does not convexify the limiting zero-energy surface. This is a Major finding because it invalidates the asserted geometric conclusion, with an explicit family of boundary points witnessing nonconvexity. Its location in a remark does not reduce that mathematical impact. The finding does not refute the periodic-orbit theorems or the separate finite-parameter convexity classification in Theorem 2.11. A localized energy-rescaling error on page 12 is also documented.

All 66 pages, including both appendices, were read as extracted text. The necessary source images, including Figures 6.1, 8.2 and 8.3, and every report page were actually inspected in the same-chat continuation. The original image-return failure and incomplete state remain preserved. Scientific decision and human adjudication remain pending.
# Hypotheses and proof coverage

The normalized Hamiltonian has \(\alpha,\varpi>0\), negative energy, and compact regular levels in \[1<2\varpi^2|h|<(1+4/\alpha)^2.\] After setting \(h=-1\), the parameters \(\beta=(1+4/\alpha)^{-1}\) and \(e=(1-2\varpi^2\beta^2)^{1/2}\) lie in \(D=\{(\beta,e):\beta,e>0,\ \beta^2+e^2<1\}\). The extended square used to study the Euler orbit is distinguished from this physical parameter domain.

The reduction, unique critical point of the effective potential, compactness thresholds, contact-type argument, and winding-based intersection estimates were followed. The positive rotation of \((p_z,z)\) on a compact level ensures repeated crossings of the disc bounded by the Euler orbit. The construction of a simple symmetric brake orbit and the disc and annular section arguments use imported tight-contact and global-section results; those external theorems were not independently reproved.

The large-\(\alpha\) scaling separates the limiting Hamiltonian into \[K_\infty=\frac{p_v^2}{2}+4v^2+K_2(p_u,u),\qquad
 K_2=\frac{p_u^2}{2}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{1/4+4u^2}}.\] The monotone quarter-period, the finite collection of transverse shooting intersections and their persistence were traced in Section 6. The reversible half-return map, its square, the symmetry/parity classification and the boundary/interior rotation comparison were read in Section 7.

The Euler variational equation reduces to \(x''+(1+7\beta/(1+e\cos\theta))x=0\). The periodic coexistence argument, antiperiodic recurrence, monotonicity in \(\beta\), negative hyperbolic bands, and the alternative Maslov-index treatment were examined. The exclusion of positive hyperbolicity uses coexistence and phase monotonicity; the two bands inside \(D\) are distinguished from the bands on the extended parameter square. Imported index and reversible-map theorems remain dependencies.

The curvature criterion and the critical-parameter classification in Section 8 and Appendix B were followed, including the boundary test, exclusion of competing stationary branches, and the monotonicity/concavity argument for \(e_{\rm conv}(\beta)\). An independent symbolic differentiation verifies the polynomial for the scaled curvature quantity in (8.7)–(8.9). This is a check of that identity, not exhaustive certification of every lengthy auxiliary polynomial inequality.
# Major finding P1: the claimed convexification fails
## Location and sign error
## A counterexample to convexity of the actual image

A negative \(h_u''\) alone would not establish nonconvexity of the energy surface, so the following argument concerns the surface itself. Under the claimed transformation \(I=\pi(x^2+y^2)\), let \[\widetilde K(p_v,v,x,y)=p_v^2/2+4v^2+h_u(\pi(x^2+y^2)).\] For every \(0<\varepsilon<4\), take two exact points on \(\widetilde K^{-1}(0)\) with \(v=y=0\): \[P_\varepsilon=\left(\sqrt{2\varepsilon},
              \sqrt{I(-\varepsilon)/\pi}\right),\qquad
 Q_\varepsilon=\left(\sqrt{2\varepsilon/16},
              \sqrt{I(-\varepsilon/16)/\pi}\right),\] where the displayed coordinates are \((p_v,x)\). Both corresponding one-dimensional energies lie in \((-4,0)\); there is no use of an unbound orbit or an excluded endpoint.

An independent 60-digit quadrature at \(\varepsilon=1/100\) gives \[I_m=196.1055521845\ldots,\qquad
 I(-25\varepsilon/64)=138.7821948443\ldots .\] Their difference is \(57.3233573402\ldots>0\). These floating-point values corroborate the analytic counterfamily; they are not represented as interval-certified estimates. The program and its actual output are retained.
## Impact and repair boundary

Changing the sign of the displayed derivative cannot rescue the convexification claim: the specified image is nonconvex. The claim should be withdrawn, or replaced by a different transformation with a new proof. This review does not exclude the existence of some other convex embedding. The argument does not invalidate the preceding dynamical-convexity estimate, nor the finite-\(\alpha\) classification in Section 8, which does not rely on this convexification. As a further normalization check, the small oscillation period is \(\pi/4\), so the Hessian in these action coordinates tends to \(8I_2\), rather than the printed \(32I_2\).
# Minor finding P2: the energy rescaling is inverted

On page 12, after (3.9), put \(c=m^{5/2}/\sqrt2>0\) and write the old Hamiltonian as \[H_{\rm old}=\frac{p_r^2+p_z^2}{2}
   +\frac{\varpi_{\rm old}^2}{2r^2}-cU_0(r,z).\] The stated normalization of angular momentum is \(\varpi_{\rm new}^2=\varpi_{\rm old}^2/c\). With the corresponding momentum/time rescaling, \(H_{\rm new}=H_{\rm old}/c\), so \(h_{\rm new}=h_{\rm old}/c\). The text instead states \(h_{\rm new}=c h_{\rm old}\).

For an exact example, set \(c=2\), \(\alpha=4\), \(\varpi_{\rm old}^2=2\), and \((p_r,p_z,r,z)=(0,0,1,0)\). Positive physical masses realizing \(c\) are obtained by taking \(m=(2\sqrt2)^{2/5}\) and \(m_3=m/4\). Then \(U_0=2\), \(H_{\rm old}=-3\), and \(H_{\rm new}=-3/2\). The printed rule assigns energy \(-6\) to the same normalized configuration. In fact, the normalized minimum is \(-2\), so that assigned level is empty. The old energy is strictly between its minimum \(-4\) and escape threshold \(-1\). The repair is the reciprocal energy factor, with the momentum and time rescaling stated explicitly. The theorems formulated directly for the normalized Hamiltonian are unaffected by this localized error.
# Supporting checks

Version-matched arXiv HTML independently confirms both disputed formulas. The publisher record and an author’s institutional page were consulted; no equality with a publisher PDF was assumed. A bounded title search for an erratum, code and supplementary material located no separate correction or computational supplement. Mathematica is cited in Appendix B, but no author program was obtained or run. Absence of such code is not a mathematical defect.

The checks were performed by the assigned primary executor, using an independently written SymPy/mpmath program. They include the turning-point derivative, the action-limit integral, the midpoint action comparison, the local series, the curvature polynomial and the exact energy example. External contact, index, and reversible-map results were not fully reproved; the necessary source diagrams and every page of this final report were actually inspected in the same-chat continuation. The prior mathematical review and computations were reused. No independent acceptance or backend-model equivalence is claimed.

Title: Initial scientific review
On \(\mathrm{NSOP}_2\) theories

Paper. Scott Mutchnik, Journal of the European Mathematical Society 28 (2026), no. 8, 3475–3498, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1679. The acquired version of record was published online on 25 September 2025; its first page records revision on 3 December 2024. Frozen identifier M25-0306 remains in the assigned 2025 collection.
# Assessment

No substantive defect invalidating the main implication \(\mathrm{NSOP}_2\Rightarrow\mathrm{NSOP}_1\) was established in the inspected proof. A Minor terminal indexing mismatch is identified below, together with an exact correction and a direct verification of the resulting three-cycle contradiction. This assessment is an initial review, not independent acceptance.

All 24 pages, including references, were read as extracted text. The proof’s actual quantifiers and its nonstandard coheir-based definition of Kim-dividing were tracked. The necessary bound source and reference images and every report page were actually inspected in the same-chat continuation. The original image-return failure and incomplete state remain preserved; the scientific decision remains pending.
# Definitions and scope

The argument is for an arbitrary complete first-order theory with a sufficiently saturated and homogeneous monster, and independence over small elementary submodels. No simplicity, countability, base-monotonicity or existence assumption over arbitrary sets is silently added. In this article Kim-dividing is witnessed by coheir Morley sequences, not by all invariant types. Fact 2.2 explicitly supplies the symmetry criterion in this coheir formulation.

The distinction between one witnessing Morley sequence and every coheir Morley sequence is essential: the latter is Conant-dividing. A canonical coheir is defined using the canonical relation \(\mathrel{\perp}^{CK}\); it need not be a unique extension. Strong canonical coheirs carry the additional lifting property of Lemma 5.6. The weak independence theorem requires this stronger hypothesis and is not asserted for arbitrary coheirs.

The secondary application, Theorem 4.9 and Corollary 4.10, is stated under \(\mathrm{NDCTP}_2\). The possible extension to all \(\mathrm{NATP}\) theories is explicitly conditional. No such unproved extension is included in this review’s positive assessment.
# Proof-chain checks
## Descending combs and the replacement of an older dependency

Pages 3480–3482 distinguish weak \(k\)-\(\mathrm{TP}_1\) from \(k\)-\(\mathrm{DCTP}_1\). The current proof does not use the defective strong-indiscernibility assertion from the older weak-tree argument. Lemma 2.8 instead works with the descending sequence of forks \(\eta_i=0^i1\), fixes the previously chosen paths as parameters, and takes the subtree rooted at \(0^{n-1}\). Its position relative to those parameter paths preserves their quantifier-free tree configuration. The maximal consistent number of paths then gives the two inconsistent path-types needed for path collapse.

The path-collapse statement and proof in Chernikov–Ramsey’s arXiv:1505.00454v2, Lemma 4.6 (differently numbered in the journal reference), were consulted. They use strong indiscernibility over the parameter set, indiscernibility of the chosen path over the realizer, compactness and finite elongation. The corrected subtree placement in the reviewed article supplies precisely the sensitive parameter-set condition. This does not amount to a complete reproof of the general tree-modeling theorem.
## Canonical coheirs without an NSOP assumption

Section 3 first uses finite satisfiability and left extension to lift a coheir sequence to a sequence of larger tuples. The ideal-valued broom argument then turns relative Kim-forking into relative quasi-dividing. Right extension is used in proving that relative inconsistency defines an ideal; quasi-strong finite character is used when passing from an inconsistent infinite family to a finite subfamily. These are distinct uses and cannot be omitted.

The derived relation preserves existence, monotonicity, right extension and quasi-strong finite character. Lemma 3.12 makes successive relations stronger and provides the finite-stage chain condition. Their decreasing intersection has the desired chain condition by compactness. The proof that this is the weakest relation with the stated properties was also followed. The passage to a larger monster in Lemma 4.1, with the orientation \(b\mathrel{\perp}^{CK}_M c\), produces a global coheir; the converse orientation is not assumed.
## Finite trees, a uniform bound and symmetry

Lemma 4.4 extends the chain condition to finite-height coheir trees. Lemma 4.5 adds copies of a tree before adding its new root: paths are read towards the root, whereas descending combs are read in lexicographic order. A descending comb crossing different immediate subtrees consists of a comb in the earliest subtree and one final node in a later subtree. Any second later node would repeat the common meet instead of strictly lowering it. This explains why the induction preserves the required canonical sequence property.

Theorem 4.6 uses a fixed inconsistency degree \(k\): arbitrarily long consistent coheir sequences would give trees of every finite height with \(k\)-inconsistent combs, hence \(k\)-\(\mathrm{DCTP}_1\) by compactness. This yields the required finite bound, which is stronger than merely comparing two infinite Morley sequences.

Proposition 5.2’s removal of unused parameters uses the coheir lifting lemma. Finite disjunctions are handled along a single coheir sequence by an infinite subsequence and the pigeonhole principle. The canonical chain condition then supplies the trees in Theorem 5.5; the uniform bound from Theorem 4.6 makes their descending combs inconsistent, proving symmetry by contradiction.
## Strong extension and the final configuration

The larger-model construction in Lemma 5.6 supplies the strong canonical extension used in Proposition 5.8. Its role is to lift a prescribed tuple while preserving the chosen coheir marginal; ordinary right extension alone would not provide that step. The joint independence in Claim 5.9 is obtained using symmetry and a canonical sequence indiscernible over the other parameter.

In Section 6, failure of equality between Kim-dividing independence and Conant-independence is converted to pairwise inconsistency by Claim 6.1. The maximal independent block has positive length and is strictly shorter than the original inconsistency degree. Grouping consecutive blocks and then using a canonical sequence in the other variable supplies the claimed reduction to two-inconsistency. Claim 6.2 follows by extending an invariant type over the indiscernible sequence. The construction of the switching sequences \(J_n\) then uses the weak independence theorem with its strong canonical hypothesis intact.
# Minor finding P1: the last witness needs a one-step shift
## Exact location and evidence

On page 3496 (PDF page 22), condition (1) defines \(J_n\) to use \(b_i^2\) for \(i<n\) and \(b_i^1\) for \(i\geq n\). On page 3497 (PDF page 23), \(a_n\) is chosen to realize the instances of \(r\) along \(J_n\), and the text asserts that the resulting array satisfies Fact 6.3(1). With \(\varphi(x,d_j)=\rho(x,b_j^1)\) and \(\psi(x,d_j)=\rho(x,b_j^2)\), the construction gives \[\varphi(a_i,d_j)\quad(j\geq i),\qquad
 \psi(a_i,d_j)\quad(j<i).\] Fact 6.3(1), however, requires \(\psi(a_i,d_i)\) as well.

This is not merely a failure to infer a diagonal value. Condition (2) on page 3496 holds for \(i\leq j\), so \(\rho(x,b_i^1)\land\rho(x,b_i^2)\) is inconsistent. Since \(\rho(a_i,b_i^1)\) holds, \(\psi(a_i,d_i)\) is false. Thus the stated choice cannot satisfy the printed nonstrict condition at the diagonal. The bound publisher PDF images confirm both inequalities.
## Repair and actual impact

Choose \(a_n\) along \(J_{n+1}\) instead. Then \(\varphi(a_i,d_j)\) holds for \(i<j\), and \(\psi(a_i,d_j)\) for \(i\geq j\), exactly as required. In Fact 6.3(2), the undeclared \(b_i,b_j\) should also read \(d_i,d_j\). The correction is local; no new independence or compactness assumption is needed.

For completeness, the actual strict off-diagonal pattern already suffices for the terminal contradiction. Define \[\chi(y,z):=\neg\exists x\,(\varphi(x,y)\land\psi(x,z))\] and \[R((x,y),(x',y')):=
 \varphi(x,y')\land\psi(x',y)\land\chi(y,y').\] The constructed sequence \((a_i,d_i)\) satisfies \(R\) for \(i<j\). A three-cycle with vertices \((x_\ell,y_\ell)\), \(\ell=1,2,3\), would imply \(\varphi(x_1,y_2)\) from its first edge, \(\psi(x_1,y_3)\) from its third edge, and \(\chi(y_2,y_3)\) from its second edge, an immediate contradiction. All formulas involve finitely many coordinates, even when an earlier intermediate tuple was infinite. This gives the defining \(\mathrm{SOP}_3\) configuration and confirms that the indexing correction does not impair Theorem 1.6.
# Independent checks, searches and limitations

An independently written finite combinatorial program enumerated binary-tree descending combs of sizes two through five at height four (367, 1231, 1287 and 315 respectively), confirming the subtree decomposition used above. It also checked the switching convention at all pairs of indices below 20: the unshifted condition fails exactly on the diagonal, and the shifted condition has no failures. The three-cycle witness clause has no satisfying Boolean assignment. These finite checks support specific combinatorial steps; they are not a decision procedure for arbitrary first-order theories or a substitute for the compactness arguments.

The publisher record and the arXiv version history were consulted. The latter explicitly records replacement of the earlier faulty dependency; the arXiv preprint was not silently substituted for the acquired journal text. Bounded searches located no separate post-publication erratum, supplement or author program for this article. No author code was run. Attempts to retrieve Conant’s corrected v5 text returned a disabled-fetch error; its full proof was not inspected. The direct three-cycle argument above removes reliance on that inaccessible proof for this local check. General Ramsey/modeling and saturation results remain imported dependencies. The necessary source symbols, the cited path-collapse lemma pages, and every page of this final report were actually inspected in the same-chat continuation. The prior mathematical review and computations were reused.

Title: Initial scientific review
Columnar order in random packings of \(2\times2\) squares on the square lattice

Paper. Daniel Hadas and Ron Peled, Journal of the European Mathematical Society 28 (2026), no. 11, 5023–5106, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1680. The acquired version of record records revision on 14 November 2024 and online publication on 30 July 2025. The frozen 2025 identifier M25-0307 is retained.
# Assessment and exact scope

The inspected argument establishes a detailed route from reflection positivity to four columnar phases. One Major proof defect is identified in the conditioning argument for the quantitative offset-tile estimate, and one Minor parity defect in a sharpness construction. The first is a false intermediate assertion, not a counterexample to the main theorem; the report supplies a rigorous counterexample to that assertion and describes the necessary repair. The earlier classification of periodic Gibbs measures does not use the defective quantitative step.

All 84 pages, including references, were read as extracted text. The earlier EMFILE failure and incomplete state remain preserved. Scientific decision remains pending; this is an initial review, not independent acceptance.

The model is the hard-core model for square tiles with centers in \(\mathbb Z^2\), excluding both nearest and diagonal simultaneous centers. Parity refers to the bottom-left corner of a tile. The distinction between nearest-neighbor and diagonal connectivity is maintained throughout. The four-phase classification concerns periodic Gibbs measures at sufficiently large fugacity. It neither classifies all nonperiodic Gibbs measures nor asserts convergence for a particular boundary condition. The slow vertical correlation scale is of order \(\sqrt\lambda\) in the upper bound; matching infinite-distance lower bounds are not proved. The simulations and broader predictions in Section 10 are not treated as theorems.
# Proof-chain coverage
## Boundary comparison and chessboard estimates

Sections 2–3 were checked with the vacancy weight \(\lambda^{-v/4}\) and the exact boundary conventions intact. The boundary replacement changes only a strip, and its multiplicity and weight cost are exponential in perimeter. Reflection positivity uses conditioning on lines of vertices. The finite-torus chessboard estimate requires the stated even divisibility conditions. The infinite-volume seminorm is a limsup along factorial-sized tori, not an assumed thermodynamic limit.

Proposition 3.8 applies to periodic Gibbs measures. In its proof, a common full-rank translation sublattice exists; boundary comparison is applied to a box containing the tested blocks, so that its perimeter cost disappears relative to their number. The perturbation \(g=1+\epsilon f\) and the concavity of the geometric-mean power then recover the single-event inequality. No ergodicity assumption is inserted into this step.
## Weighted counting and mesoscopic rectangles

Section 4’s one-dimensional transfer matrix is \(T=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\lambda^{-1/2}&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). The even-length trace bound and the free-boundary count with one missing tile were independently checked. For a nontrivial marked component, the inequalities \(v_H\geq4\) and \(v_H\geq2(k_H-1)\) combine with the compressed planar-graph count and at most \(M^{k_H-2}\) length assignments. The resulting series is bounded by a constant times \(M/\lambda\).

The shared-vacancy assertion in Lemma 4.11 uses planar boundary crossings. Its textual proof was followed, and the exact bound drawing in Figure 4.2 has now been visually checked for correspondence. The later multivalued retilling map has disjoint images, and its gain of order \(M^2/\lambda\) offsets at most order \(\operatorname{len}(A)/M\) marked intervals. Choosing \(M\) proportional to \(\sqrt\lambda\) then supplies the negative area exponent in Lemma 4.1. The constants can be chosen in the stated order.
## Percolation, four phases and uniqueness

Sections 5–7 keep rarity separate from independence: the finite-set bound for a rare set is the input to the Peierls argument, without an independent-site assumption. Nearest-neighbor separation and diagonal boundary connectivity give the infinite component and its finite complement components. Block changes and intersections incur the displayed roots and finite constants. Ergodicity is used when selecting one of separated orientations or parities.

The fine-width phase is obtained by decreasing the even width from the mesoscopic square scale. A change of orientation at successive widths would force crossing sticks. Opposite vertical parities in a narrow rectangle force a row of vacancies, enabling the second phase split. Translation and reflection symmetries then relate the four measures.

In Section 8, a sealed rectangle forces a disagreement component through it to stay in a single column and within a bounded vertical interval. A vacancy pair in one configuration provides a common zero with the other configuration, breaking that column’s disagreement path. Coarse nonsealed paths yield the anisotropic tail bound. Swapping finite disagreement clusters is an involution preserving the product Gibbs law, by the common external boundary and the domain Markov property. This proves uniqueness within each phase and tail triviality. Averaging over a finite quotient of translation lattices, followed by ergodic decomposition, gives the stated classification for all periodic Gibbs measures.
## Quantitative columnar order

Section 9 first seeks an exponentially weighted four-vacancy estimate to obtain an \(O(\lambda^{-1})\) offset probability. Finding P1 concerns this step. Given that estimate, the horizontal-disagreement bound follows by balancing a strip union bound against the vertical tail at \(d\asymp\sqrt\lambda\log\lambda\). The two correlation estimates are combined by partitioning the target set according to which estimate is smaller; one cannot simply interchange a minimum and a sum. Where the same-column cap is one, the trivial covariance bound by one handles the capped case. The final lower offset bound is obtained by removing one tile and sliding another, while the dominant-column deficit follows from the vacancy and occupied-face seminorm bounds.
# Major finding P1: rarity does not survive the stated conditioning
## Location and false assertion

On page 5091 (PDF page 69), the proof of Theorem 9.1 chooses an arbitrary measurable \(\widetilde\Omega\supset J\) with \[\mu(\widetilde\Omega)=q:=\lambda^{-1}\epsilon_1^{-4},
 \qquad \widetilde\mu=\mu(\,\cdot\mid\widetilde\Omega).\] In the paragraph immediately after (9.3), it claims that \(X_{K\times L}\overline{E^c}\) is \(\epsilon\)-rare under \(\eta\widetilde\mu\), where \(\epsilon=\max\{\lambda^{-1/4},\|E^c\|_R\}\). Its supporting chessboard bound has an intersection with \(J\); the asserted conditional conclusion drops that intersection. Both the arbitrary conditioning and the dropped event matter.
## Counterexample within the stated Gibbs setting

Use the paper’s measure \(\mu=\mu_{(\mathrm{ver},0)}\), whose existence was already proved. Let \(f=[0,1]^2\) and let \(V_f\) be the event that \(f\) is vacant. Set \(R=f\), \(k=K=l=L=1\), \(\eta\) equal to the identity, and \(E=V_f^c\). This is an \(R\)-local event invariant under the two central reflections, as required by Lemma 6.7(4). Corollary 4.5 and Proposition 3.8 give, for some fixed \(c>0\) and sufficiently large \(\lambda\), \[\|V_f\|_f\leq\lambda^{-1/4},
 \qquad \mu(V_f)\geq c\lambda^{-1/2}.\] Take the allowed \(J\) corresponding to a tile at \((0,0)\) and the four nearest side vacancies at horizontal positions \(-1\) and \(1\), in the notation of Section 9.1. This is a feasible local event of positive Gibbs probability; \(J\cap V_f=\varnothing\) and the paper’s four-vacancy estimate gives \(j:=\mu(J)\leq\lambda^{-1}\).
## Impact and repair boundary

The false assertion is used to justify (9.3), then (9.4), (9.2) and (9.1), and hence the sharp offset estimate in Theorem 9.1 and the later quantitative parts of Theorem 1.1. It is therefore a Major quantitative proof gap. This does not disprove those conclusions, and it does not affect the earlier four-phase classification.

The relevant rare set should include the condition \(J\): outside \(J\), the auxiliary set \(\Theta\) is already all of \(\mathbb Z^2\). Moreover the conditioning parameter must remain in the bound. Writing \(s=\|E^c\|_R\), the preceding chessboard estimate and \(\mu(J)\leq\lambda^{-1}\) yield \[\widetilde\mu\bigl(J\cap\{A\subset
 X_{K\times L}\overline{E^c}\}\bigr)
 \leq \epsilon_1^4 s^{\max\{|A|-4,0\}}
 \leq \max\{\epsilon_1,s\}^{|A|}.\] They do not yield a parameter tending to zero as \(\lambda^{-1/4}\) for fixed \(\epsilon_1\). A viable repair is to choose a separate, smaller parameter \(\delta\) in \(\mu(\widetilde\Omega)=\lambda^{-1}\delta^{-4}\), retain \(J\) in every bad-set event, and use \(\max\{\delta,s\}^{1/r}\) after the block change. Choose \(\delta\) to absorb all fixed roots and intersection constants, then choose the rectangle width and \(\lambda\). The resulting prefactor \(\delta^{-4}\) is still a universal constant. The corrected quantitative chain, with this hierarchy written explicitly, is required; the original inference cannot be retained unchanged.
# Minor finding P2: odd block lengths in Remark 4.7

On page 5055 (PDF page 33), Remark 4.7 defines a global event \(\widetilde E_M\) by requiring \(\sigma(x,y)=0\) whenever \(2\mid x\) or \(M\mid y\). It then equates its fully packed and free-boundary partition functions and applies Proposition 4.4, which requires even length.

Take the even rectangle \(\Lambda=R_{2\times2}\) and \(M=1\). Then \(M\mid L\), \(M\leq\max(K,L)\), and the hypothesis \(M<\sqrt\lambda/C\) holds for any sufficiently large \(\lambda\). The event \(\widetilde E_1\) forces global emptiness. It is incompatible with the prescribed fully packed exterior, whereas with free boundary it has exactly one configuration and four vacant faces. Thus \[Z^1_\Lambda(\widetilde E_1)=0,\qquad
 Z^0_\Lambda(\widetilde E_1)=\lambda^{-1}.\] The asserted equality and lower bound greater than one fail. Restricting this particular construction to even integer \(M\) removes the parity conflict. To cover general \(M\), use a comparable even block size and handle the bounded small sizes separately. This affects the explanatory sharpness construction; it does not refute the upper bound in Lemma 4.6.
# Independent checks and limitations

An independently written program enumerated all 6,427 allowed center configurations in \(R_{6\times6}\) with a fully packed odd–odd exterior. It reconstructed 6,893 nontrivial marked components. Each satisfied \(v_H\geq4\) and \(v_H\geq2(k_H-1)\); the latter had minimum slack zero. This is finite support for the combinatorial check, not a proof of the infinite-volume statement.

Exact symbolic checks verified the periodic transfer-matrix identity and the free-boundary coefficient for even lengths 2 through 10. Rational arithmetic also checked the conditional normalization and the repaired finite-set inequality above. The arithmetic illustration is not a sampled Gibbs measure; the counterexample is the analytic construction in P1. No author program was executed.

General reflection-positivity and ergodic-decomposition theorems, the external planar-graph enumeration bound, and the external ground-state classifications in Section 10 were not independently reproved. Simulation figures and highlighted tables have now been visually checked against their captions; simulations were not rerun or independently validated. Bounded searches of the publisher, arXiv record and author page did not locate a separate code archive, supplement or erratum. The later arXiv v3 record reports minor corrections; it is an auxiliary comparison and is not assumed identical to the acquired version of record.

Title: Initial scientific review
The master equation for mean field game systems with fractional and nonlocal diffusions

Paper. Espen R. Jakobsen and Artur Rutkowski, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1681. Exact inspected source: arXiv:2305.18867v2, 24 January 2025, 61 pages. The publisher records online publication on 30 July 2025; equivalence with its subscription version has not been established.
# Assessment and scope

The paper develops a substantial analytical route from whole-space nonlocal MFG systems to a classical master equation without moment assumptions. Three Major issues concern a tightness estimate, the value-dependent uniqueness argument, and the literal quantifiers in the diffusion assumption. Further corrections are required in several auxiliary results. No pair of distinct solutions to the master equation is exhibited. The main theorem is therefore not declared false on the evidence below.

All 61 pages, including Appendices A–D and references, were read as extracted text. The earlier EMFILE failure and incomplete state are preserved. Scientific decision remains pending; this is an initial review, not independent acceptance. No author code was executed.
# Coverage of the scientific argument

The analysis concerns constant-coefficient Lévy generators with a positive semidefinite local part and the stated Lévy integrability condition. The metric on probability measures is the bounded Lipschitz metric \(d_0\), not a Wasserstein metric imposing moments. The subadditive smooth tightness function replaces polynomial moments. All quantifiers in (H1)–(H3), (F1), (F2), (G1), (G2) and (M1)–(M4) were checked. In particular, Sections 5–6 require a Hamiltonian independent of the value variable, uniform convexity in momentum, and the stronger dual-space positivity (M2). Lasry–Lions monotonicity alone is not silently substituted for (M2). The measure derivative has a gauge freedom; the authors’ discussion of normalization and the odd-kernel example was checked.

Section 2 distinguishes the full dual \(C_b^{-\gamma}\) from the measure-representable subspace \(\mathfrak C_b^{-n}\). A functional at infinity need not mollify to an \(L^1\) function. The initial datum in Theorem 5.5 is explicitly measure-representable; a proposed objection using a Banach limit was rejected for violating this hypothesis. Iterated spatial Hölder norms, weak convergence, and differentiation along convex combinations of measures were followed with their specified domains.

Section 3 uses integrability of \(t^{-1/\alpha}\), hence \(\alpha>1\), for fixed points and Duhamel estimates. The positive, source-free probability equation supports the moment-free Schauder construction in Theorem 4.3. This must be distinguished from the signed equation with an additive divergence source in Lemma 3.5, where P1 applies. Uniform spatial regularity of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation and its time continuity in a slightly weaker norm were traced separately from the overstrong time-derivative modulus in P6.

In Section 4 the existence map has uniform drift, tightness and \(d_0\) equicontinuity bounds. For uniqueness, the last inference of Lemma 4.2 is unsupported as detailed in P2. For a Hamiltonian independent of the value variable, the usual monotonicity identity does give the energy estimate used later; that case does not need the defective extension.

Theorem 5.3 combines the backward estimate with a forward duality estimate containing the square root of an energy term, and absorbs the resulting product. Theorem 5.5 uses a regular-data fixed point, dual backward test functions, (M2), and ellipticity of \(\Gamma\). The energy/absorption calculation (5.15)–(5.21) was checked. Its compactness step on page 37 expressly invokes Lemma 3.5(e), so P1 is a core dependency. Approximation of initial functionals and sources uses the representable subspace and weaker dual norms; Appendix A needs the correction in P4.

Lemma 5.7’s weighted smoothing requires \(\gamma<\alpha\); the beta-integral at the initial time and the divergence-source term were checked. The passage removing an arbitrarily small loss on page 41 needs uniform constants or a direct estimate; no counterexample to the intended smoothing result is asserted. The time origin in Corollary 5.8 must be shifted as in P7. Dirac difference quotients in Proposition 5.10 give the first and second \(y\) derivatives, and the integrable smoothing exponent \(1+\sigma<\alpha\) controls its coefficient differences. Proposition 5.11 needs a correct composition estimate, P5, to obtain its superlinear measure Taylor remainder.

Section 6 differentiates the MFG solution along its measure flow. The weak Fokker–Planck formulation and the bounded, uniformly continuous derivatives of the candidate justify the limiting integrals. The uniqueness construction solves the induced Fokker–Planck equation for a competing classical solution and returns to the value-independent MFG uniqueness. Appendices B–D were read: the weaker spatial-norm time modulus is valid in the displayed Duhamel argument; mild-to-weak conversion requires the stated test-function regularity and integrable kernel singularities. The initial-time stability argument uses the spatial modulus, not the false forcing-independent modulus for \(\partial_tu\).
# Findings with decisive evidence
## P1. Major: a divergence source has uncontrolled weighted absolute mass
Location. Lemma 3.5(e), page 24; its proof, page 26; Theorem 5.5, compactness step 2, page 37.

The proposed bound controls \(\int\psi|\rho(t)|\) using only the initial weighted mass, unweighted \(L^1\) bounds for \(V_2,\rho\), and fixed coefficients. Translating a source disproves that bound in the Gaussian example expressly included in the paper. Here and in P6, Gaussian tests use the necessary per-order interpretation of (K) explained in P3; they are not claimed to satisfy the impossible literal all-order hypothesis.

Set \(d=1\), \(T=1\), \(\mathcal L=\Delta\), \(V_1=0\), \(\rho_0=0\), and \(V_2(t,x)=G_1(x-R)\), where \(G_s(x)=(4\pi s)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(4s)}\). These data are smooth and \(\left\|V_2(t)\right\|_1=1\). The solution of (3.10) is \[\rho_R(t,x)=\int_0^t\partial_xG_{1+s}(x-R)\,ds.\] Put \(h(y)=\int_0^1\partial_yG_{1+s}(y)\,ds
=\tfrac12[\operatorname{erf}(y/(2\sqrt2))
-\operatorname{erf}(y/2)]\). Its sign is opposite to \(y\), and direct integration gives \[M:=\int_\mathbb R|h(y)|\,dy=\frac{2(\sqrt2-1)}{\sqrt\pi}>0,
 \qquad \int_\mathbb R|y|\,|h(y)|\,dy=1 .\] For \(\psi(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}\), which is smooth, nonnegative, subadditive and has bounded first two derivatives, \[\int_\mathbb R\psi(x)|\rho_R(1,x)|\,dx\ge RM-1\longrightarrow\infty .\] Every quantity permitted on the right of Lemma 3.5(e) remains bounded independently of \(R\), including \(\sup_{t\le1}\left\|\rho_R(t)\right\|_1\le M\). The initial weighted mass is zero and the jump measure is zero. If a probability initial datum is preferred, add \(G_1\) initially; the solution acquires \(G_{t+1}\) and the same lower bound loses only a fixed finite weighted mass.

Testing a signed equation with \(\psi\) estimates a signed moment, not its absolute moment. The cited positive, source-free argument does not establish the asserted estimate. The compactness input therefore requires replacement. For the actual fixed-point family, the special source \(m\Gamma Dz+c\) has more structure: uniform tails of the fixed \(m,c\) and bounded \(Dz\) can support a Duhamel tail argument. Such an argument must be supplied; the counterexample does not rule it out or refute Theorem 6.2.
## P2. Major: the last Gronwall inference does not follow
Location. Last display of page 31 and first display of page 32, Lemma 4.2; Theorem 4.3(b).

Writing \(A(s)=\int u^+m^++\int u^-m^-\ge0\), the proof obtains \[A(s)+c_2\int_s^T A(t)\,dt\ge J(s)\] and concludes \(J(t_0)\le C A(t_0)\). This inference is false even with \(J\) nonnegative, decreasing, absolutely continuous and \(J(T)=0\), as in the proof. Take \(t_0=0\), \(T=c_2=1\), \[A(s)=s^2,\qquad J(s)=\int_s^1t^2\,dt=(1-s^3)/3 .\] The premise holds for every \(s\), while \(A(0)=0<J(0)=1/3\). Thus Gronwall cannot justify the conclusion. This is a counterexample to the actual scalar inference, not a constructed nonunique MFG solution.

The general value-dependent uniqueness conclusion under (M4) needs an additional estimate or a different argument. For \(H_2(x,u)=\beta u\) with constant \(\beta\), an integrating factor can handle the corresponding energy identity; this does not prove the stated general \(x,u\)-dependent case. The value-independent uniqueness used in Sections 5–6 has a separate valid monotonicity argument.
## P3. Major as written: the diffusion hypothesis has an empty literal scope
Location. Assumption (K), Section 2.5.2, page 14, and the examples on page 16.

The stated quantifier is one finite \(\mathcal K\) for every multi-index \(\beta\). A Lévy characteristic function has the form \(\widehat K_t(\xi)=e^{-t\Psi(\xi)}\), which is nonzero at each finite \(\xi\). The proposed \(L^1\) estimate implies, for all \(n\), \[(|\xi_1|t^{1/\alpha})^n|\widehat K_t(\xi)|\le\mathcal K .\] Choosing \(|\xi_1|>t^{-1/\alpha}\) gives a contradiction as \(n\to\infty\). In particular even the Gaussian example fails the literal hypothesis. This is an exact Fourier argument, not a numerical failure to find an operator.

The intended formulation is presumably a constant \(\mathcal K_\beta\) for each derivative order, or a common constant for a specified finite range of orders. That change must be explicit wherever theorem hypotheses refer to (K). For mixed anisotropic orders, estimates using the smallest order also need a finite time horizon or appropriate large-time bounds. The Major classification concerns the actual scope of the stated main theorem; it does not claim the intended finite-order semigroup theory is impossible.
## P4. Minor norm correction, with a replacement for the closure argument
Location. Lemma 2.6, page 8; Appendix A, pages 50–51, especially the inference after (A.6).

With the paper’s norm \(\left\|\phi\right\|_{C_b^1}=\left\|\phi\right\|_\infty+\left\|\phi'\right\|_\infty\), the functional \(\rho(\phi)=\phi(0)+\phi'(0)\) has norm one. Every representation \(\rho(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu_0+\int\phi'\,d\mu_1\) has \(\left\|\mu_0\right\|_{TV}\ge1\) by testing the constant one. Taking \(\phi_\epsilon(x)=\epsilon q(x/\epsilon)\) with \(q\in C_c^\infty\), \(q(0)=0\), \(q'(0)=1\), and letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\), gives \(\mu_1(\{0\})=1\). Hence \(\left\|\mu_1\right\|_{TV}\ge1\); the least sum is two, attained by \(\mu_0=\mu_1=\delta_0\). The claimed exact identity with the sum of total variations is false. The dual of the sum norm on the jet product uses a maximum norm.

In addition, equality of each chosen lift’s norm with its functional’s norm does not imply the lifts are Cauchy. The closure conclusion itself remains correct: restriction identifies the representable subspace isometrically with \((C_0^n)^*\). Hahn–Banach on the finite jet product and Riesz representation show surjectivity. For a representable functional, cutoffs \(\chi(x/R)\phi\) and dominated convergence give equality of its \(C_b^n\) and restricted \(C_0^n\) norms, since the cutoff derivative error tends to zero. Thus this subspace is complete and closed without choosing Cauchy representatives. This replacement preserves the closure used downstream, while the exact norm formula needs correction.
## P5. Minor: the composition estimate omits individual Lipschitz bounds
Location. Lemma 5.9, page 42; applications on pages 44 and 46.

Choose \(\sigma=1/2\), \(\epsilon=1/4\), \(f(x,y)=\sin y\), \(y_1(x)=\sin(Nx)\) and \(y_2(x)=y_1(x)+\pi\). All functions have the stated bounded smooth regularity. The norm of \(y_1-y_2\) is the constant \(\pi\), and \(\left\|f\right\|_{C_b^{3/4}}\le1+2^{1/4}\). The left side of the proposed estimate is at least \[4\sin(1)(N/\pi)^{1/2},\] by testing \(x=\pi/(2N)\) and \(3\pi/(2N)\), whereas its right side is at most \(2(1+2^{1/4})(2+\sqrt\pi)\pi^{1/4}\), independently of \(N\). Already \(N=10^6\) contradicts the displayed inequality.

A correct composition/interpolation estimate includes the individual Lipschitz norms of \(y_1,y_2\). In the actual applications these are gradients of solutions with a uniform \(C_b^{3+\sigma}\) bound, so that dependence can be absorbed in the existing generic data constant. The counterexample refutes the standalone lemma; it does not by itself refute the superlinear remainder claimed in Proposition 5.11. Its proof and constants should be rewritten.
## P6. Minor corrections to temporal and endpoint estimates
Locations. Lemma 3.3(b), page 21; Theorem 3.10, (3.27), page 29; Lemma 3.5(c), page 25.

For \(\mathcal L=\Delta\), zero initial data and zero drift, \(f_n(t,x)=\sin(nt)\) gives \(z_n(t,x)=(1-\cos nt)/n\). The forcing’s spatial norms are one, but \(|\partial_tz_n(\pi/(2n))-\partial_tz_n(0)|=1\). There is no common vanishing time modulus for these derivatives depending only on the displayed spatial bounds. The same spatially constant example works with \(H(p)=|p|^2\). Each derivative is continuous; the error is the asserted uniformity. The forcing’s own time modulus must enter. The weaker spatial-norm modulus proved in Appendix B is not contradicted, and is the part used in Appendix D.

At \(\alpha=2\), the page-25 integral is \(\int_\epsilon^t r^{-1}\,dr=\log(t/\epsilon)\), not a constant times \(\epsilon^{\,0}\). The displayed argument establishes at best a logarithmic endpoint modulus, or any smaller positive Hölder exponent, which still suffices for translation compactness. No counterexample to the entire compactness conclusion is claimed.
## P7. Minor: time origin and additional formula corrections
Locations. Corollary 5.8, page 42; mild HJB formulas on pages 20 and 29; Lemma 2.3, page 7.

Corollary 5.8 needs \((t-t_0)^{\gamma/\alpha}\) in place of \(t^{\gamma/\alpha}\). For \(\mathcal L=\Delta\), \(F=G=0\), \(H(p)=|p|^2/2\) and the zero backward solution, the forward datum \(\rho_0=\partial_{xx}\delta_0\) is measure-representable of order two. At \(t_0>0\), set \(\tau=t-t_0\) and test \(\rho(t)=\partial_{xx}G_\tau\) with \(\phi_\tau(x)=\tau^{1/4}\cos(x/\sqrt\tau)\). Its \(C_b^{1/2}\) norm is uniformly bounded for \(0<\tau\le1\), whereas the pairing is \(-e^{-1}\tau^{-3/4}\). Thus the printed weight cannot stay bounded at \(t_0\). The intended integrability used later survives the shift.

For the forward-time equation \(\partial_tu-\mathcal Lu+H=f\), the Duhamel source is \(f-H\); the printed \(H-f\) has the opposite sign. With \(H(u)=u\), \(f=0\), \(u(0)=1\), it gives \(e^t\) instead of \(e^{-t}\). This corrects the displayed fixed-point map, not the norm-based contraction argument.

Finally the arbitrary rate \(\epsilon^\delta\) in Lemma 2.3 needs the standard restriction on the smoothing exponent. For an even nontrivial mollifier, \(\rho=\delta_0\), \(\gamma=0\) and the test \(\cos x\), the error is \(\frac12\epsilon^2\int y^2\eta(y)\,dy+o(\epsilon^2)\); it is not \(O(\epsilon^3)\). Convergence in the weaker dual norm still follows using a smaller positive exponent.
# Evidence, limitations and disposition

The independent program checks the Gaussian mass identities and translated weighted integrals, the scalar polynomial inference, the high-frequency composition bound, the temporal forcing example, and the Fourier growth. It is reviewer-written code; numerical quadrature supports exact analytical arguments and is not presented as a rigorous numerical enclosure or a simulation of an MFG solution.

The arXiv version record, exact-v2 HTML, publisher metadata and the author’s publication page were searched for supplements, code and corrections. No separate relevant supplement, code archive or erratum was located in that bounded search. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect. Reference [34]’s full proof and all external functional-analytic or semigroup results were not independently reproved; the report does not certify them. The prospective \(N\)-player convergence work is outside this paper’s established results.

The required revisions must separate the value-dependent uniqueness claim from the value-independent master equation, repair the signed-source compactness argument, and state a nonempty heat-kernel hypothesis. The remaining corrections have the narrower effects described above. Scientific decision remains pending; human reviews are empty. Exact source, TeX, compiler, dependencies, PDF, actual-view records and preserved unsuccessful visual-check records are bound in the per-paper provenance and inventory.

problems.title: Weighted absolute moment controlled without source tail information
problems.source_location: Lemma3.5(e)p24;proofp26;Theorem5.5step2p37
claim: Weighted absolute moment controlled without source tail information

Smooth signed L1 equation, unit source norm, bounded drift, admissible psi. Gaussian is intended advertised operator after necessary per-order correction P3; no claim it satisfies impossible literal(K).
analysis: Location. Lemma 3.5(e), page 24; its proof, page 26; Theorem 5.5, compactness step 2, page 37.

The proposed bound controls \(\int\psi|\rho(t)|\) using only the initial weighted mass, unweighted \(L^1\) bounds for \(V_2,\rho\), and fixed coefficients. Translating a source disproves that bound in the Gaussian example expressly included in the paper. Here and in P6, Gaussian tests use the necessary per-order interpretation of (K) explained in P3; they are not claimed to satisfy the impossible literal all-order hypothesis.

Set \(d=1\), \(T=1\), \(\mathcal L=\Delta\), \(V_1=0\), \(\rho_0=0\), and \(V_2(t,x)=G_1(x-R)\), where \(G_s(x)=(4\pi s)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(4s)}\). These data are smooth and \(\left\|V_2(t)\right\|_1=1\). The solution of (3.10) is \[\rho_R(t,x)=\int_0^t\partial_xG_{1+s}(x-R)\,ds.\] Put \(h(y)=\int_0^1\partial_yG_{1+s}(y)\,ds
=\tfrac12[\operatorname{erf}(y/(2\sqrt2))
-\operatorname{erf}(y/2)]\). Its sign is opposite to \(y\), and direct integration gives \[M:=\int_\mathbb R|h(y)|\,dy=\frac{2(\sqrt2-1)}{\sqrt\pi}>0,
 \qquad \int_\mathbb R|y|\,|h(y)|\,dy=1 .\] For \(\psi(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}\), which is smooth, nonnegative, subadditive and has bounded first two derivatives, \[\int_\mathbb R\psi(x)|\rho_R(1,x)|\,dx\ge RM-1\longrightarrow\infty .\] Every quantity permitted on the right of Lemma 3.5(e) remains bounded independently of \(R\), including \(\sup_{t\le1}\left\|\rho_R(t)\right\|_1\le M\). The initial weighted mass is zero and the jump measure is zero. If a probability initial datum is preferred, add \(G_1\) initially; the solution acquires \(G_{t+1}\) and the same lower bound loses only a fixed finite weighted mass.

Testing a signed equation with \(\psi\) estimates a signed moment, not its absolute moment. The cited positive, source-free argument does not establish the asserted estimate. The compactness input therefore requires replacement. For the actual fixed-point family, the special source \(m\Gamma Dz+c\) has more structure: uniform tails of the fixed \(m,c\) and bounded \(Dz\) can support a Duhamel tail argument. Such an argument must be supplied; the counterexample does not rule it out or refute Theorem 6.2.
result: Impact: Invalid compactness dependency in linearized-system proof; main theorem not refuted.

problems.title: False scalar Gronwall inference
problems.source_location: Lemma4.2pp31-32;Theorem4.3(b)
claim: False scalar Gronwall inference
A>=0,J>=0 decreasing absolutely continuous J1=0; these are the displayed scalar premises. Not an MFG nonuniqueness example.
analysis: Location. Last display of page 31 and first display of page 32, Lemma 4.2; Theorem 4.3(b).

Writing \(A(s)=\int u^+m^++\int u^-m^-\ge0\), the proof obtains \[A(s)+c_2\int_s^T A(t)\,dt\ge J(s)\] and concludes \(J(t_0)\le C A(t_0)\). Take \(t_0=0\), \(T=c_2=1\), \[A(s)=s^2,\qquad J(s)=\int_s^1t^2\,dt=(1-s^3)/3 .\] The premise holds for every \(s\), while \(A(0)=0<J(0)=1/3\). Thus Gronwall cannot justify the conclusion. The general value-dependent uniqueness conclusion under (M4) needs an additional estimate or a different argument. For \(H_2(x,u)=\beta u\) with constant \(\beta\), an integrating factor can handle the corresponding energy identity; this does not prove the stated general \(x,u\)-dependent case.
