problems.title: One finite constant for all derivative orders makes literal operator class empty
problems.source_location: Section2.5.2(K)p14;examplesp16
claim: One finite constant for all derivative orders makes literal operator class empty
Any Levy semigroup with probability density and stated L1 derivative estimate; finite xi exponential never zero.
analysis: Location. Assumption (K), Section 2.5.2, page 14, and the examples on page 16.

The stated quantifier is one finite \(\mathcal K\) for every multi-index \(\beta\). A Lévy characteristic function has the form \(\widehat K_t(\xi)=e^{-t\Psi(\xi)}\), which is nonzero at each finite \(\xi\). The proposed \(L^1\) estimate implies, for all \(n\), \[(|\xi_1|t^{1/\alpha})^n|\widehat K_t(\xi)|\le\mathcal K .\] Choosing \(|\xi_1|>t^{-1/\alpha}\) gives a contradiction as \(n\to\infty\). In particular even the Gaussian example fails the literal hypothesis. This is an exact Fourier argument, not a numerical failure to find an operator.

The intended formulation is presumably a constant \(\mathcal K_\beta\) for each derivative order, or a common constant for a specified finite range of orders. That change must be explicit wherever theorem hypotheses refer to (K). For mixed anisotropic orders, estimates using the smallest order also need a finite time horizon or appropriate large-time bounds. The Major classification concerns the actual scope of the stated main theorem; it does not claim the intended finite-order semigroup theory is impossible.
result: Impact: Literal main-theorem scope empty, not a disproof of intended finite-order theory.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: K_beta or specified finite maximum derivative order; finite time horizon for anisotropic-minimum order.

problems.title: Exact representation norm false and chosen-lift Cauchy inference invalid
problems.source_location: Lemma2.6p8;AppendixApp50-51afterA.6
claim: Exact representation norm false and chosen-lift Cauchy inference invalid
analysis: Location. Lemma 2.6, page 8; Appendix A, pages 50–51, especially the inference after (A.6).

With the paper’s norm \(\left\|\phi\right\|_{C_b^1}=\left\|\phi\right\|_\infty+\left\|\phi'\right\|_\infty\), the functional \(\rho(\phi)=\phi(0)+\phi'(0)\) has norm one. Every representation \(\rho(\phi)=\int\phi\,d\mu_0+\int\phi'\,d\mu_1\) has \(\left\|\mu_0\right\|_{TV}\ge1\) by testing the constant one. Taking \(\phi_\epsilon(x)=\epsilon q(x/\epsilon)\) with \(q\in C_c^\infty\), \(q(0)=0\), \(q'(0)=1\), and letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\), gives \(\mu_1(\{0\})=1\). Hence \(\left\|\mu_1\right\|_{TV}\ge1\); the least sum is two, attained by \(\mu_0=\mu_1=\delta_0\). The claimed exact identity with the sum of total variations is false. The dual of the sum norm on the jet product uses a maximum norm.

In addition, equality of each chosen lift’s norm with its functional’s norm does not imply the lifts are Cauchy. The closure conclusion itself remains correct: restriction identifies the representable subspace isometrically with \((C_0^n)^*\). Hahn–Banach on the finite jet product and Riesz representation show surjectivity. For a representable functional, cutoffs \(\chi(x/R)\phi\) and dominated convergence give equality of its \(C_b^n\) and restricted \(C_0^n\) norms, since the cutoff derivative error tends to zero. Thus this subspace is complete and closed without choosing Cauchy representatives. This replacement preserves the closure used downstream, while the exact norm formula needs correction.
result: Impact: Norm equality wrong; closure result preserved by full alternative proof.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use dual maximum product norm; restrict representable functionals to(C0^n)*, HahnBanach/Riesz and scaled cutoffs give isometric onto map, hence completeness.

problems.title: Composition inequality omits individual map Lipschitz norms
problems.source_location: Lemma5.9p42;usespp44,46
claim: Composition inequality omits individual map Lipschitz norms
analysis: Location. Lemma 5.9, page 42; applications on pages 44 and 46.

Choose \(\sigma=1/2\), \(\epsilon=1/4\), \(f(x,y)=\sin y\), \(y_1(x)=\sin(Nx)\) and \(y_2(x)=y_1(x)+\pi\). All functions have the stated bounded smooth regularity. The norm of \(y_1-y_2\) is the constant \(\pi\), and \(\left\|f\right\|_{C_b^{3/4}}\le1+2^{1/4}\). The left side of the proposed estimate is at least \[4\sin(1)(N/\pi)^{1/2},\] by testing \(x=\pi/(2N)\) and \(3\pi/(2N)\), whereas its right side is at most \(2(1+2^{1/4})(2+\sqrt\pi)\pi^{1/4}\), independently of \(N\). Already \(N=10^6\) contradicts the displayed inequality.

A correct composition/interpolation estimate includes the individual Lipschitz norms of \(y_1,y_2\). In the actual applications these are gradients of solutions with a uniform \(C_b^{3+\sigma}\) bound, so that dependence can be absorbed in the existing generic data constant. The counterexample refutes the standalone lemma; it does not by itself refute the superlinear remainder claimed in Proposition 5.11. Its proof and constants should be rewritten.
result: Impact: Standalone lemma false; actual application has uniform individual gradient C1 bounds, so generic-data constant can absorb corrected dependence.

paragraphs: Correct composition/interpolation estimate with individual map bounds.

report: Author: Assigned initial-review executor

Title: Initial scientific review
Constraint maps with free boundaries: the Bernoulli case
Paper. Alessio Figalli, André Guerra, Sunghan Kim and Henrik Shahgholian.

DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1683. The binding source is the 43-page accepted author manuscript from CVGMT record 6723. That record was created on 8 August 2024 and updated on 19 August 2024; these are record dates, not verified PDF revision dates. Publisher metadata gives online publication on 8 August 2025. No equivalence to the publisher’s subscription version or to arXiv:2311.03006v3 is assumed.
# Assessment and scope

The paper combines harmonic-map compactness, Bernoulli nondegeneracy and scalar free-boundary regularity in a substantial argument. Three Major issues require attention: the uniform geometry used in the half-space approximation, admissibility in the scalar reduction for a general target, and the dimension endpoint in the full-regularity corollary. The first two findings identify invalid proof steps, with explicit counterexamples to the assertions actually used. They do not exhibit a discontinuous small-energy minimizer or disprove the main free-boundary separation theorem. The dimension finding concerns an unsupported extension of the cited classification; no conjectural five-dimensional cone is asserted to exist.

All 43 pages, including Appendices A–C and references, were read as extracted text. The earlier EMFILE failure and incomplete state are preserved. This remains an initial review, with scientific decision pending and no human reviews. No author code was run.

The maps take values in \(\overline M\), while the volume penalty uses the open set \(M\). The distinction is essential in the examples below. The parameter is \(q\ge0\) for small-energy regularity, but \(q>0\) for the quantitative separation of singularities from the noncoincidence set. Uniform convexity of the complement is used only in the second part of the paper. A singular point of the map is not the same as a singular point of its free boundary.
# Proof-chain coverage

The signed distance is positive in \(M\), and the chosen normal points into \(M\). The projection/distance decomposition and the identities for tangential derivatives in Section 2 were checked. Uniform principal-curvature bounds alone do not give the uniform tubular radius claimed in the varying-target argument; P1 isolates this issue. The almost monotonicity formula in Appendix A follows from domain variations of both energy terms. Its nonnegative \(q^2\) contribution gives the stated error of order \(q^2r^2\). Zero-homogeneous tangent maps minimize the Dirichlet energy, since the rescaled weight is \(rq\to0\). Appendix B yields strong convergence on compact subdomains, rather than the global convergence stated in Lemma 2.3; see P4.

Section 3’s distance inequality uses an inward variation supported where the distance is positive. Tangential flows preserve the phase indicator and give the projection equation. The \(W^{2,p}\) estimate then follows from its quadratic right-hand side. The next scalar-minimization argument permits arbitrarily long normal rays; P2 is precisely where the general target geometry does not justify that permission.

Section 4 rescales a small-energy sequence by its energy size. For a genuinely uniform tubular neighborhood, flattening errors, truncation, Luckhaus interpolation on a thin annulus and the vanishing annular penalty give the intended local strong limit. The finite-distance case is supposed to decouple into harmonic tangential components and a scalar one-phase minimizer. The infinite-distance case instead has a harmonic limit. P1 explains why the stated curvature-only class also admits a different, two-boundary limit and needs an additional argument. Minor corrections to the auxiliary flattening choices are recorded in P7.

Section 5 applies weak maximal-function estimates, a Vitali covering argument and a geometric distribution-tail bound to obtain finite \(W^{1,p}\) norms. The printed strong maximal inequality has the wrong target norm, P6, but the finite-\(p\) conclusion also follows directly from pointwise domination by the maximal function. The ensuing bootstrap gives a Hölder map, then a Lipschitz projected component, and finally invokes the scalar reduction for the Lipschitz distance component. Thus P2 is a core dependency of Theorem 1.1, not an unused remark. The phase-boundary assertion in Corollary 5.7 needs the restriction in P5.

Sections 6–9 were followed separately under convexity. A nonnegative zero-homogeneous subharmonic distance is constant; a positive constant gives a harmonic tangent map, while a zero constant and the subharmonic local supremum estimate force continuity of the original distance. At singular points, tangents lie in \(\partial M\). In Proposition 7.1, strong \(W^{1,2}\) convergence, strict tangential curvature and unique continuation for a nonconstant limiting harmonic map force the phase density to vanish. The product passage is valid against bounded tests using strong \(L^1\) convergence of the quadratic coefficient and weak-star convergence of indicators; it is not an \(L^\infty\) bound on that product.

Proposition 8.1 uses a truncated harmonic radial barrier, projection to the convex obstacle and Young’s inequality. Its absorption requires \(q>0\). The contradiction in Lemma 9.2 then compares linear nondegeneracy with higher-order vanishing. The passage involving suprema needs the subharmonic estimate spelled out in P7; almost-everywhere convergence by itself is insufficient. The compactness application also needs control of translations of the image, since its displayed energy bound controls derivatives, not the full \(W^{1,2}\) norm.

Sections 10–11 use the scalar Bernoulli equation with a tangentially regular lower-order term, flatness improvement, hodograph regularity and transmission estimates. Piecewise higher regularity of \(\Pi\circ u\) yields \(C^{1,1}\) across a regular free boundary, not global \(C^2\) across it. The dependence on target smoothness and the distinction between BMO and bounded second derivatives were retained. Appendix C uses the one-sided target condition to exclude nonconstant tangent maps through the cited removable-singularity theorem. Its proof explicitly involves the bound on \(q\).
# Findings and decisive evidence
## P1. Major: curvature control does not justify the half-space limit
Location. (2.4)–(2.5), pages 8–9; Proposition 4.1 and the uniform tubular-neighborhood assertion on page 17; Lemma 4.3, pages 18–22.

Two parallel boundary components can approach each other while all their principal curvatures remain zero. Take \[M_k=\mathbb R\times(-\epsilon_k/2,\epsilon_k/2),\qquad
 \epsilon_k\downarrow0 .\] These are connected smooth domains with a common curvature bound. The nearest boundary point is not unique on their midline, and a two-sided tubular neighborhood with unique nearest projection has width at most \(\epsilon_k/2\). There is no lower width bound depending only on curvature. Moreover \(\epsilon_k^{-1}M_k=\mathbb R\times(-1/2,1/2)\) is a strip, not a half-space.

This is also compatible with the variational, mean and energy data used in the limit argument. On \(B_4=(-4,4)\) let \[v(x)=\max\{-1/2,\min\{x,1/2\}\},\quad
 u_k(x)=(0,\epsilon_k v(x)),\quad q_k=\epsilon_k .\] The mean of \(u_k\) is zero, \(\int_{-4}^4|u_k'|^2=\epsilon_k^2\), and \(q_k/\epsilon_k=1\). Each \(u_k\) is a global minimizer with its endpoint values. For any absolutely continuous competitor, its second component must traverse the strip’s full height; on the interior phase, \[|p'|^2+\epsilon_k^2\ge2\epsilon_k|p'|,
 \qquad
 \int_{\{|p|<\epsilon_k/2\}}|p'|\ge\epsilon_k .\] The resulting lower bound \(2\epsilon_k^2\) is attained by \(u_k\); tangential motion only adds energy.

Choosing the lower nearest boundary point gives the proposed half-space \(H=\{a_2>-1/2\}\). The limit \((0,v)\) does not minimize the one-phase energy in \(H\): shifting its transition to the right by \(d\in(0,1)\) preserves the endpoint data and Dirichlet energy but reduces the positive-phase length by \(d\). For \(d=1/2\), its half-space energy drops from \(11/2\) to \(5\). The strip energy stays equal to \(2\).

This example verifies the curvature, weight, mean, energy and minimality premises used for the geometric/variational inference. It is not asserted to satisfy the hypothetical failure-of-approximation condition (4.3); the example itself is Lipschitz. It therefore does not disprove Proposition 4.1. It shows that the proof cannot exclude two-boundary limits from curvature control alone. A uniform reach or chart radius, included in the constants and preserved under the contradiction sequence, would remove this obstruction. Alternatively, the additional possible flat-target limits need their own approximation argument. The fixed-target main theorem may survive such a repair; the claimed curvature-only uniformity has not been established.
## P2. Major: unrestricted normal competitors can leave the target
Location. Lemma 3.9, first paragraph of its proof, page 16; use in (5.19), page 28.

The proof takes any \(w\ge0\) with the distance’s boundary trace and declares \(V=\Pi\circ u+w
u\circ u\) admissible. This implication is false for a general smooth target. Let \(M=B_1(0)\subset\mathbb R^2\), choose \(p\in\partial M\), and let \(u\equiv p\) on a source ball. This is a minimizing constraint map for every \(q\ge0\): its energy is zero. Its image is in the tubular neighborhood and \(\Pi\circ u\) is Lipschitz. Here \(ho\circ u=0\) and \(
u(p)=-p\). Choose a nonnegative smooth compactly supported \(w\) equal to \(3\) on a smaller ball. It has exactly the required zero trace, but \(V=(1-w)p=-2p\) there, so \(V
otin\overline M\).

All assumptions of Lemma 3.9 and of this competitor construction are satisfied before the invalid admissibility conclusion. The calculation refutes that step, not the claimed scalar minimality for this constant example. The general-target Lipschitz bootstrap relies on the reduction, so a local-height comparison argument with justified scalar regularity is needed. Restricting heights to an admissible normal segment is not by itself a proof of minimality against all scalar competitors. When the complement is convex, the outward normal rays remain outside it and this particular obstruction disappears.
## P3. Major: the low-dimensional corollary includes an unsupported endpoint
Location. Corollary 1.10 and the paragraph after Theorem 1.11, page 5.

The source states \(n_*\in\{5,6,7\}\) and regularity for \(n\le n_*\). The cited scalar classification instead gives regularity below the first singular dimension \(d_*\). Jerison–Savin, Theorem 1.1, proves flatness in dimensions \(n\le4\); its introduction distinguishes the conjectural higher dimensions and the De Silva–Jerison singular minimizer in dimension seven. De Silva–Jerison, Theorem 1.1, explicitly constructs that seven-dimensional global minimizer. Together these give \(d_*\in\{5,6,7\}\) and the condition \(n<d_*\), not \(n\le d_*\).

The target’s uniform convexity does not remove the scalar obstruction: if \(w\) is a scalar nonnegative global minimizer, then \(u=(1+w)e_1\) is a constraint minimizer for \(M=\mathbb R^m\setminus\overline B_1\). For every admissible competitor \(V\), the scalar map \(|V|-1\) has the same scalar trace, the same phase indicator, and no larger Dirichlet energy. Thus scalar minimality proves vectorial minimality, with the same free boundary and a smooth uniformly convex obstacle.

In particular the known seven-dimensional example lifts within the target class. This does not refute the corollary’s bare existential wording by itself: its parameter might be five or six. The decisive problem is that the cited argument does not establish the asserted dimension-five conclusion or the included critical endpoint. No unknown five-dimensional counterexample is asserted. State \(n<d_*\), or use a largest regular dimension in \(\{4,5,6\}\), unless an additional classification theorem is proved. The unconditional low-dimensional consequence for the image map needs the same correction.
## P4. Minor: compactness is local, not global
Location. Lemma 2.3, page 10; Appendix B, pages 39–41.

On the unit disk in \(\mathbb R^2\), take the fixed target \(M=\{y_2>0\}\) and \(q_k=0\), and set \[u_k(z)=(k^{-1/2}\operatorname{Re}z^k,1).\] These are unconstrained harmonic Dirichlet minimizers and therefore constraint minimizers with their own traces. Their \(W^{1,2}\) norms are bounded and \(u_k\to(0,1)\) in \(L^2\), but \[\int_{B_1}|Du_k|^2=\pi,\qquad
 \int_{B_r}|Du_k|^2=\pi r^{2k}\quad(0<r<1).\] No subsequence converges strongly in \(W^{1,2}(B_1)\). The proof actually establishes strong \(W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}\) convergence, which suffices for the tangent-map applications that restrict to a smaller ball. The global conclusion needs additional boundary control or replacement by the local one.
## P5. Minor scope correction: the negligible nonreduced boundary needs positive weight
Location. Corollary 5.7, page 29, stated for \(q\ge0\).

Let \(q=0\), \(M=\mathbb R^2\setminus\overline B_1\), and \(u(x)=(1,x_1)\) on a source ball in \(\mathbb R^n\). This affine harmonic map lies in \(\overline M\) and is an unconstrained Dirichlet minimizer, hence a constraint minimizer. Its positive phase is \(\{x_1\ne0\}\), whose characteristic function is one almost everywhere. Its reduced boundary is empty, but its topological free boundary is \(\{x_1=0\}\), of positive \(\mathcal H^{n-1}\) measure in the ball. Thus the final measure-zero assertion in Corollary 5.7 fails.

The distributional identity with the factor \(q=0\) is not contradicted by this example. Nor is the main \(q>0\) separation theorem. Separate the zero-weight obstacle geometry from the positive-weight Bernoulli perimeter assertion.
## P6. Minor: maximal-function target norm and weak-form sign
Locations. Theorem 2.9(i), page 12; footnote 5, page 16.

The strong \((p,p)\) maximal inequality must have an \(L^p\) norm on its left, not \(L^\infty\). In one dimension with \(p=2\), \(f_N=\sqrt N\,\mathbf1_{(-1/N,1/N)}\) has \(\|f_N\|_2=\sqrt2\), whereas the source’s normalization gives \(Mf_N(0)=2\sqrt N\). The later weak estimate is correctly available, and \(|Du|^2\le cM(|Du|^2)\) gives the needed finite-\(p\) conclusion.

The strong equation in Lemma 3.9 is \(\Delta(\rho\circ u)-H=q\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\), where \[H=\operatorname{Hess}\rho_u(Du,Du)\chi_{\{u\in M\}} .\] Its weak form has \(-\int H\phi\), not the printed plus sign. Locations. Pages 18–20, 25–27, 31–32 and 35.

In (4.12), \(|\rho_k(0)|/\epsilon_k\to|\gamma|\) does not give \(|a_k|\le2|\gamma|\epsilon_k\) when \(\gamma=0\); use \((|\gamma|+1)\epsilon_k\). For (4.17), additionally choose \(\widetilde R_k\le\widetilde\epsilon_k^{-1/2}\) (with the obvious convention at zero) so that \(\widetilde\epsilon_k\widetilde R_k\to0\). The missing factor \(\epsilon^2\) in the threshold in (5.5) must also be restored when applying the weak bound. These changes preserve the intended limiting estimates.

In (7.3) the factor \(\overline\chi_k\) is needed on the right, as the subsequent argument itself uses. The product \(H_k\overline\chi_k\) has the required weak pairing limit from strong \(L^1\) convergence of \(H_k\); it need not converge weak-star in \(L^\infty\). For Corollary 7.3, a modulus-dependent radius does not by itself give the claimed uniform constants. Instead apply Proposition 7.1 at each rescaled radius, using the common small upper bound on the distance and the almost-monotonicity energy bound, and then iterate (7.5). This gives a uniform density factor without an unspecified individual modulus.

Finally, the passage from (9.2) to a supremum bound for the limit cannot rely only on almost-everywhere convergence. For each fixed small \(r\), subharmonicity gives \[\sup_{B_{2r}(x_k)}\rho\circ u_k
 \le \frac{C}{|B_{3r}|}\int_{B_{3r}(x_0)}\rho\circ u_k\] for large \(k\), after a harmless enlargement of the outer radius. Local \(L^1\) convergence passes the right side to the limit, and the higher-order bound makes it \(O(r^2)\), contradicting (9.2). This supplies the missing passage. A separate justification is still needed for the full-norm compactness hypothesis in Lemma 9.2: derivative-energy boundedness alone does not control target translations. No sequence satisfying its bad-energy premise is claimed here to disprove that lemma.
# Verification limits and requested revision

The reviewer-written independent program checks the strip energies and mean exactly, the inadmissible normal competitor, the disk harmonic-mode energy, the scalar-distance Hessian identity and the maximal-function scaling. These calculations support the analytical constructions; they do not replace the proof of the main regularity theorems.

The CVGMT record, publisher metadata, arXiv version history and an author publication page were checked for code, supplementary material and corrections. No separate relevant code archive, supplement or erratum was located. The manuscript’s data-availability statement says its necessary data are included. Absence of code is not a defect. The related arXiv HTML was used to check selected notation, without replacing or identifying it with the frozen PDF. The critical-dimension references were checked at their theorem statements; their full proofs, Luckhaus’s extension lemma, the scalar flatness theorem, unique continuation, and the cited transmission/hodograph results were not independently reproved.

The revision should first make the target geometry in the approximation argument uniform and justify the scalar comparison class for general targets. The dimension statement and the auxiliary scope/formula corrections should then be made consistently. The central strategy may remain viable; the findings establish the defects specified above, not failure of every principal conclusion. Exact source, TeX, compiler, dependencies, PDF, actual-view records, retained logs and preserved failed image attempts are listed in the per-paper provenance and inventory.

problems.title: Bounded principal curvature supplies a uniform tubular radius and excludes strip limits
problems.source_location: (2.4)-(2.5)pp8-9;Proposition4.1p17;Lemma4.3pp18-22
claim: Bounded principal curvature supplies a uniform tubular radius and excludes strip limits
analysis: Location. (2.4)–(2.5), pages 8–9; Proposition 4.1 and the uniform tubular-neighborhood assertion on page 17; Lemma 4.3, pages 18–22.

Two parallel boundary components can approach each other while all their principal curvatures remain zero. Take \[M_k=\mathbb R\times(-\epsilon_k/2,\epsilon_k/2),\qquad
 \epsilon_k\downarrow0 .\] These are connected smooth domains with a common curvature bound. The nearest boundary point is not unique on their midline, and a two-sided tubular neighborhood with unique nearest projection has width at most \(\epsilon_k/2\). There is no lower width bound depending only on curvature. Moreover \(\epsilon_k^{-1}M_k=\mathbb R\times(-1/2,1/2)\) is a strip, not a half-space.

This is also compatible with the variational, mean and energy data used in the limit argument. On \(B_4=(-4,4)\) let \[v(x)=\max\{-1/2,\min\{x,1/2\}\},\quad
 u_k(x)=(0,\epsilon_k v(x)),\quad q_k=\epsilon_k .\] The mean of \(u_k\) is zero, \(\int_{-4}^4|u_k'|^2=\epsilon_k^2\), and \(q_k/\epsilon_k=1\). Each \(u_k\) is a global minimizer with its endpoint values. For any absolutely continuous competitor, its second component must traverse the strip’s full height; on the interior phase, \[|p'|^2+\epsilon_k^2\ge2\epsilon_k|p'|,
 \qquad
 \int_{\{|p|<\epsilon_k/2\}}|p'|\ge\epsilon_k .\] The resulting lower bound \(2\epsilon_k^2\) is attained by \(u_k\); tangential motion only adds energy.

Choosing the lower nearest boundary point gives the proposed half-space \(H=\{a_2>-1/2\}\). The limit \((0,v)\) does not minimize the one-phase energy in \(H\): shifting its transition to the right by \(d\in(0,1)\) preserves the endpoint data and Dirichlet energy but reduces the positive-phase length by \(d\). For \(d=1/2\), its half-space energy drops from \(11/2\) to \(5\). The strip energy stays equal to \(2\).

This example verifies the curvature, weight, mean, energy and minimality premises used for the geometric/variational inference. It is not asserted to satisfy the hypothetical failure-of-approximation condition (4.3); the example itself is Lipschitz. It therefore does not disprove Proposition 4.1. It shows that the proof cannot exclude two-boundary limits from curvature control alone. A uniform reach or chart radius, included in the constants and preserved under the contradiction sequence, would remove this obstruction. Alternatively, the additional possible flat-target limits need their own approximation argument. The fixed-target main theorem may survive such a repair; the claimed curvature-only uniformity has not been established.
result: Impact: Central varying-target halfspace approximation argument lacks justified geometry; main fixed-target theorem not disproved.

problems.title: Fullregularity for n<=n_star withn_star in{5,6,7} deduced from cited scalar classification

claim: Fullregularity for n<=n_star withn_star in{5,6,7} deduced from cited scalar classification
analysis: Location. Corollary 1.10 and the paragraph after Theorem 1.11, page 5.

The source states \(n_*\in\{5,6,7\}\) and regularity for \(n\le n_*\). The cited scalar classification instead gives regularity below the first singular dimension \(d_*\). Jerison–Savin, Theorem 1.1, proves flatness in dimensions \(n\le4\); its introduction distinguishes the conjectural higher dimensions and the De Silva–Jerison singular minimizer in dimension seven. De Silva–Jerison, Theorem 1.1, explicitly constructs that seven-dimensional global minimizer. Together these give \(d_*\in\{5,6,7\}\) and the condition \(n<d_*\), not \(n\le d_*\).

The target’s uniform convexity does not remove the scalar obstruction: if \(w\) is a scalar nonnegative global minimizer, then \(u=(1+w)e_1\) is a constraint minimizer for \(M=\mathbb R^m\setminus\overline B_1\). For every admissible competitor \(V\), the scalar map \(|V|-1\) has the same scalar trace, the same phase indicator, and no larger Dirichlet energy. Thus scalar minimality proves vectorial minimality, with the same free boundary and a smooth uniformly convex obstacle.

In particular the known seven-dimensional example lifts within the target class. This does not refute the corollary’s bare existential wording by itself: its parameter might be five or six. The decisive problem is that the cited argument does not establish the asserted dimension-five conclusion or the included critical endpoint. No unknown five-dimensional counterexample is asserted. State \(n<d_*\), or use a largest regular dimension in \(\{4,5,6\}\), unless an additional classification theorem is proved. The unconditional low-dimensional consequence for the image map needs the same correction.

report: Abstract: We examine marginal preservation, the conditional logarithmic Sobolev argument, and Gaussian specializations in the specified preprint. A local quantitative discrepancy is established: the rate defined by the displayed formulas equals \(2\varepsilon(\alpha_U+\alpha_V)\) in the isotropic Gaussian case, whereas the subsequent first-order description gives one quarter of this coefficient. Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: A verification note on projected Langevin dynamics
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed work is Giovanni Conforti, Daniel Lacker, and Soumik Pal, Projected Langevin dynamics and a gradient flow for entropic optimal transport [paper], frozen identifier M25-0311. The actual 51-page file is arXiv:2309.08598v1, dated 15 September 2023. Its institutional repository labels it a publisher version, but the first-page version stamp establishes the preprint identity. The associated journal article has DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1684 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1684); the publisher records online publication on 25 August 2025 [journal]. Equivalence to that later article has not been established. Page numbers below are both physical PDF pages and printed manuscript pages.

The principal statements on pp. 3, 6–8 were read with their quantifiers. Detailed checks concern Lemma 3.2 (p. 20), the conditional-score identity of Lemma 4.6 (p. 32), the argument of Theorem 1.2 (pp. 38–39), the algebra in Corollary 1.3 (pp. 6–7 and 40), and the Gaussian Riccati calculation (p. 9). The reduction of long-time convergence to Lemmas 4.1–4.2 and Proposition 4.3 was checked on pp. 29–30, conditional on those ingredients. The full existence/compactness arguments, the asymptotically log-concave transport estimates in Section 5.3, and Appendix A were not independently reconstructed. Section 2’s geometric discussion was checked for its explicitly formal status and dimension restriction, not proved as a general manifold theory.
# Assumptions and checks that survive

Theorem 1.1 assumes \(c,U,V\in C^2\), normalized densities \(e^{-U},e^{-V}\), subgaussian marginals, nonnegative \(c\) with bounded Hessian, Hessians of \(U,V\) bounded below, gradient moments of order \(p>2(d+1)\), and integrable \(U,V\). It quantifies over every initial coupling \(P_0\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\). The initialization condition is essential; the authors separately identify nonstationary marginals as an open problem.

For a test function depending only on \(X\), the centered conditional force has zero expectation by the tower property. The resulting generator is \(\varepsilon(\Delta-\nabla U\cdot\nabla)\), preserving \(e^{-U}\); the same argument holds for \(Y\). This verifies the cancellation in (1.7) and Lemma 3.2, while the invoked Fokker–Planck uniqueness theorem remains an external dependency.

In the notation of Theorem 1.2, write \(A=\kappa^{X|Y}>0\), \(B=\kappa^{Y|X}>0\), and let \(\bar I\) denote the projected information. The conditional LSIs give \(I\ge(A+B)H\). The transport estimates used in (5.4) bound the squared conditional-mean discrepancies by \(4H/B\) and \(4H/A\), respectively. Consequently, \[\bar I\ge
\left(A+B-\frac4{\varepsilon^2}\left(\frac1A+\frac1B\right)\right)H
=\frac r\varepsilon H,
\quad
r=\varepsilon(A+B)\left(1-\frac4{\varepsilon^2AB}\right).\] Thus the coefficient in (1.19) agrees with the proof when \(\varepsilon\sqrt{AB}>2\). Combining this bound with the dissipation inequality (4.2) yields the stated exponential estimate. Sign reversals in conditional-mean expressions disappear under the squares and do not invalidate this argument. This check does not independently prove the external transport inequality or every weak-regularity passage.

For centered one-dimensional Gaussian marginals with variances \(u,v>0\), Itô’s formula gives \[\dot s=(u^{-1}+v^{-1})[uv-s(s+\varepsilon)].\] This agrees with the scalar specialization on p. 9. The negative root \(-\varepsilon/2-\sqrt{\varepsilon^2/4+uv}\) is outside the admissible covariance interval \([-\sqrt{uv},\sqrt{uv}]\) for \(\varepsilon>0\). The limiting case \(\varepsilon=0\) cannot be substituted into the positive-noise uniqueness assertion.
# A local quantitative finding

Problem 1 (Gaussian rate coefficient; Minor).  The paragraph following (1.24), p. 7, describes the first-order rate defined by (1.19) and (1.23) as \(\varepsilon(\alpha_U+\alpha_V)/2\). For the admissible isotropic Gaussian family this coefficient is incorrect.
## Hypotheses and decisive calculation
## Counterevidence, dependency, and correction boundary

The inspected source image confirms the factor \(1/2\); this is not a text-extraction artifact. If the sentence merely intended the order \(r=\Theta(\varepsilon)\), that order is correct. A rate four times smaller is also a valid conservative rate when the stronger estimate is valid. Neither interpretation makes it the first-order coefficient of the specifically defined \(r\).

The discrepancy lies in the explanatory specialization following the corollary. It is not used in the proof of the projected LSI, in the proof of the corollary, or in the qualitative convergence reduction inspected here. No core conclusion is shown to fail; hence Major is unsupported. The precise local repair is to replace that first-order coefficient by \(2\varepsilon(\alpha_U+\alpha_V)\) under the stated isotropic Gaussian equalities, where it is exact. No change to (1.19), (1.23), or their positivity condition is justified by this calculation. No claim of author adoption or first discovery is made.
# Conclusion and remaining scope

One bounded quantitative discrepancy is established in the acquired v1 preprint. The checked marginal-preservation and LSI algebra survives. A search of the exact title with correction/code terms and the publisher and arXiv records did not locate an erratum or separate code/supplement; this bounded search does not establish their absence. No author code was run. The journal-final version and the unexamined technical proofs remain outside this report’s validity claims.

Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical review of
The non-Hermitian skin effect with three-dimensional long-range coupling
# Scope and principal dependencies

The paper relates subwavelength resonances to a gauge capacitance matrix, then establishes localized pseudo-eigenvectors using a banded approximation. The checks covered the physical model and conventions, Theorem 4.4, the Toeplitz approximation and off-diagonal estimate in Section 5, the statements and proofs of Theorems 6.1–6.2, and Appendix A. The full layer-potential expansion, every estimate in Section 5, and the numerical multipole implementation were not independently reconstructed. No claim of complete proof certification or independent acceptance is made.

The distinction between small residual and proximity to an exact eigenvector is material. Theorem 6.1 supplies vectors with an exponentially localized profile and an explicit residual bound. Theorem 6.2 transfers a residual bound to the dense matrix under the decay hypothesis \(0<\rho<1-\varepsilon _1\). Its proof uses the action of the omitted tails on a localized vector, rather than asserting that the entire discarded matrix has small norm. The \(1/|i-j|\) entry bound alone would not justify the latter assertion. The geometric-series denominators in (6.7) are positive under the stated hypothesis, and its two tail contributions match the proof on pp. 23–25.
# Confirmed local finding

Problem 1 (Minor: infinite-operator spectrum in Theorem A.3).  On p. 33, Theorem A.3 includes \[\Lambda(A)+\Delta_\varepsilon
 \ \subset\ \Lambda_\varepsilon(A_{N,l}),
 \qquad \varepsilon=C\rho^N,\] as one term of its asserted union, for every \(r<1\), \(\rho>r\), with \(C\) independent of \(N\). Here \(A\) is the semi-infinite Toeplitz operator, \(A_{N,l}\) its finite section, and \(\Delta_\varepsilon\) the open disk about zero. Pages 31–32 distinguish this operator from a Laurent operator and define \(\Lambda(A)\) as its spectrum. The inclusion above is false.

Assumptions and decisive counterexample. On \(\ell^2(\mathbb N)\), take \[(Au)_j=u_{j+1},\qquad
 a_1=1,\quad a_k=0\ (k\ne1),\qquad l=1,\quad f(z)=z.\] This is a bounded Toeplitz operator satisfying the exact bandwidth condition \(a_k=0\) for \(|k|>l\). Set \(r=1/4\), \(\rho=1/2\), and \(\lambda=3/4\). All radius hypotheses hold, including \(\rho<1\) if that additional restriction were imposed. The nonzero square-summable vector \((1,\lambda,\lambda^2,\ldots)\) is an eigenvector of \(A\). Consequently \(\lambda\in\Lambda(A)+\Delta_\varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\), since \(0\in\Delta_\varepsilon\).

Equation reference: eq:resolvent. Let \(J_N=A_{N,1}\). It has ones on the first superdiagonal and \(J_N^N=0\). Since \(\lambda\ne0\), \[(\lambda I-J_N)^{-1}
   =\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\lambda^{-k-1}J_N^k,\qquad
 \|(\lambda I-J_N)^{-1}\|_2
   \le 4\big((4/3)^N-1\big).
 \] For every fixed finite \(C>0\), therefore, \[C2^{-N}\|(\lambda I-J_N)^{-1}\|_2
 <4C(2/3)^N\longrightarrow0.\] For sufficiently large \(N\), the resolvent norm is strictly less than \((C2^{-N})^{-1}\). Also \(\lambda\notin\Lambda(J_N)=\{0\}\). Thus \(\lambda\notin\Lambda_{C2^{-N}}(J_N)\), contradicting Theorem A.3 by Definition A.2(iii). Equivalently, every unit vector has residual strictly greater than \(C2^{-N}\). The strict inequality makes the convention at the pseudospectral boundary immaterial. Allowing \(C\) to depend on this fixed \(\lambda\) does not repair the contradiction.

Counterevidence and impact. The truncated geometric vector has residual of order \(\lambda^N\); the example does not dispute exponential localization at an appropriate spectral-point-dependent rate. It disputes inclusion of the entire semi-infinite spectrum at the prescribed, faster scale. It is an example within the general hypotheses of A.3, not a proposed physical gauge capacitance matrix.

Theorem A.4 on p. 34 omits the offending spectral-thickening term. Its proof constructs vectors from roots inside the smaller circle, cancels the boundary rows, and estimates the remaining residual. Theorem 6.1 explicitly invokes A.4 on p. 19, and Theorem 6.2 uses the entry-decay estimate from Proposition 5.9. This inspected dependency path does not use the disproved term. The Minor classification rests on that limited impact, not on the ease of a possible typographical repair.

Repair boundary. Replacing this particular term by \(\Lambda(A_{N,l})+\Delta_\varepsilon\) makes that term’s inclusion valid for every finite matrix: for a unit eigenvector \(w\) with eigenvalue \(\mu\), \(\|(A_{N,l}-\lambda I)w\|=|\mu-\lambda|<\varepsilon\). This verifies the replacement term only. The rest of the theorem and all uniformity claims require their own proof. The cited Reichel–Trefethen paper, Theorem 3.2, printed p. 173, was also inspected and displays the same notation; it does not remove the contradiction above. No correction adopted by the authors has been established.
# Interpretation, computation and limitations

The discussion following Theorem 6.2 (p. 25), the abstract, and the conclusion use language about exact eigenmodes more broadly than the residual estimates alone establish. Section 6 also acknowledges the difficulty of proving exact-eigenvector decay for dense Toeplitz matrices and uses numerical evidence. The present review does not turn this difference in scope into a second confirmed defect: it supplies no counterexample within the physical family and no proof that the claimed physical localization is false. The rigorous result verified here should be read as a pseudo-eigenvector result unless additional eigenvector stability estimates are supplied.

The complete 63-file repository snapshot `jinghaocao/skin_effect`, commit `1bc8d74162f8d647b4448ea5190cd5ef71168037`, was inventoried. Static reading covered `Run_SKIN.m`, `symbol.m`, and `produce_condensation.m`. The code uses an inclusive diagonal cutoff whereas (6.1) uses \(|i-j|<k\); this is a parameter-convention distinction, with no demonstrated numerical error here. The scripts use real parts of computed eigenvectors in some plots; this review did not establish that this changes any displayed conclusion. Author code was not executed, and computed figures were not reproduced.

The recorded scientific text coverage is pp. 1–5, 9, 13–14, 16–25, 31–37 and 39; selected evidence pages were also viewed as images. Uninspected technical passages and numerical data remain limitations. Source reading, impact judgment, report composition, compilation, and page inspection were performed in the present review conversation. The administrative scientific decision remains pending, with no human review or independent acceptance recorded.

Title: Technical review of
Trigonometric K-matrices for finite-dimensional representations of quantum affine algebras
# Version, hypotheses and proof coverage

The exact source is the supplied arXiv v5, not an assumed copy of the journal article published online on 11 August 2025. The arXiv record identifies Remark 7.8.2 as an addition in v5. Its extension beyond Kirillov–Reshetikhin modules is therefore retained as a version-specific statement. All 37 PDF pages were read as extracted text; the selected evidence and main-argument pages were also inspected as images.

The algebraic setting is untwisted affine type over \(\mathbb F=\overline{\mathbb C(q)}\), with the alternative non-root-of-unity complex specialization noted by the authors. The finite-dimensional category \(\mathcal C\) is the type-1, level-zero category from Section 2.3. The QSP construction retains the generalized Satake conditions, the parameter restrictions \((\gamma,\sigma)\in\Gamma\times\Sigma\), and the admissible gauge requirements of Section 4.2. Theorem 4.2.1 is not read as allowing arbitrary twisting automorphisms.

The following central steps were checked. For Proposition 4.3.1(d), a fixed nonzero grading bounds the number of occurrences of a selected \(E_i\); between these occurrences, the other generators belong to a finite-type positive subalgebra and act nilpotently on the finite module. This supplies finiteness of each spectral coefficient without requiring the erroneous cone formula below. The identity \(\psi\Sigma_z=\Sigma_{1/z}\psi\) explains the target of the intertwiner in (4.1); its admissible-gauge hypothesis is essential.

For Lemma 5.1.1, rank of the finite linear intertwining system is unchanged on extending \(\mathbb F(z)\) to a Laurent-series field. Thus a nonzero formal solution yields a nonzero rational solution. Once the intertwiner space is one-dimensional, clearing denominators and removing the common polynomial factor gives the primitive polynomial representative in Theorem 5.1.2(b). The term non-vanishing here includes removal of common zeros, not merely exclusion of the identically zero matrix.

The support/depth induction in Theorem 6.2.4 was reconstructed: a monomial carrying a lower weight component to the top weight kills the top component, reducing support; otherwise an \(E_i\) decreases the chosen minimal depth. Distinct weight components remain distinct under a common weight shift, so cancellation does not invalidate this step. This uses Proposition 6.2.1 as an external input. For the specialization argument in Section 6.3, polynomial lifts of a basis of the fiber have determinant nonzero at zero and hence form a basis over \(\mathbb F(z)\). Under the principal grading, \(z\Sigma_z(\widetilde F_i)\) specializes to \(F_i\), since every correction lies in the nonnegative Borel. This verifies the deformation mechanism used for generic restricted irreducibility.
# Confirmed local findings

Problem 1 (Minor: incomplete affine positive-root descriptions).  On p. 6, Section 2.1 states \[\widehat\Delta^{\rm re}_+=\Delta_++\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\delta.\] On p. 12, Remark 3.2.1(c) also states \[\widehat Q_+=Q_+\oplus\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\delta.\] With the positive-root and nonnegative-cone conventions introduced on pp. 5–6, both right-hand sides omit the affine simple root.

Decisive example and assumptions. Take untwisted type \(A_1^{(1)}\), so \(\Delta_+=\{\alpha_1\}\), \(\vartheta=\alpha_1\), and \(\delta=\alpha_0+\alpha_1\). The affine simple root \(\alpha_0=\delta-\alpha_1\) is a positive real root and an element of \(\widehat Q_+\). Its coefficient of \(\alpha_1\), in the independent basis \((\alpha_1,\delta)\), is \(-1\). Every element of the two displayed right-hand sides has nonnegative finite-root coefficient (and the first has coefficient exactly \(1\)). Thus \(\alpha_0\) belongs to neither. For the setting of Remark 3.2.1, one may take the allowed generalized Satake diagram \(X=\varnothing,\tau=\mathrm{id}\); the root-cone contradiction is unchanged. There is no restriction on \(q\) or QSP parameters needed for this root-lattice calculation.

Equation reference: eq:cone. Correction and repair boundary. For the untwisted affine positive real roots, the missing branch is \[\widehat\Delta^{\rm re}_+
 =(\Delta_++\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\delta)
   \cup(-\Delta_++\mathbb Z_{>0}\delta).\] For the cone, the exact formula is \[\widehat Q_+
 =\{\,\beta+n\delta:\ \beta\in Q,\ n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\
       \beta+n\vartheta\in Q_+\,\}.
 \] Indeed \(n\alpha_0+\gamma=(\gamma-n\vartheta)+n\delta\) for \(n\ge0,\gamma\in Q_+\), and this identity proves both directions of [eq:cone] (#eq:cone). The group decomposition \(\widehat Q=Q\oplus\mathbb Z\delta\) does not yield a product decomposition of the positive cone.

Impact and counterevidence. These are false preliminary descriptions, but the checked descent proof uses monomials in all affine simple generators, and Section 6 explicitly uses the projection \(\overline{\alpha_0}=-\vartheta\) (p. 26). In particular, that proof does not assume that every positive affine root has positive finite projection. The rank-one implication \(\widehat Q^{-\theta}=\mathbb Z\delta\) can be obtained from the rank and the primitive element \(\delta\), without the false cone decomposition. No failure of Theorems 4.2.1, 5.1.2 or 6.1.1 has been established from these descriptions.

Problem 2 (Minor: invariant integer gradings need not be indicator functions).  On p. 16, Section 4.1 first allows any group homomorphism \(s:\widehat Q\to\mathbb Z\), then asserts that \(\tau\)-invariance is equivalent to \(s\), on affine simple roots, being the characteristic function of a union of \(\tau\)-orbits. The necessity assertion requires an additional \(0/1\)-valued restriction.

Decisive example. Again use \(A_1^{(1)}\), \(X=\varnothing,\tau=\mathrm{id}\), and define \(s(\alpha_0)=s(\alpha_1)=2\). Since the simple roots freely generate \(\widehat Q\), this is a group homomorphism satisfying all hypotheses of the general sentence. It commutes with the identity diagram automorphism and has \(s(\delta)=4>0\), but it is not an indicator function. Directly on generators, invariance is equivalent to \[s(\alpha_{\tau(i)})=s(\alpha_i)\quad\text{for every }i.\] Thus the correct general description is an arbitrary integer constant on each orbit. Equivalently, \(s=\sum_O m_O{\bf1}_O\) on simple roots, \(m_O\in\mathbb Z\).

Impact and repair boundary. Replace the indicator-function claim by orbitwise constancy, or explicitly restrict that sentence to \(0/1\)-valued gradings. The subsequently defined \(\tau\)-minimal grading is indeed \(0/1\)-valued and invariant; the principal grading used in Section 6 also satisfies the required invariance. The counterexample does not invalidate those selected gradings or the resulting spectral operators. The finding is local for this reason, not because the textual correction is short.
# Boundary checks and limitations

Propositions 5.4.1–5.5.1 retain the stated \(\psi\)-involutivity or \(\psi\)-fixedness assumptions and the irreducibility condition at a special value. The pole argument uses an invertible leading intertwiner and the non-vanishing normalization of its partner; it does not assert that reducibility must always produce a pole. The explicit constant representative in Section 7.9(c) has \[J_
u= egin{pmatrix}0&-
u^{-1}\ 
u&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad J_
u^2=-I.\] Accordingly \(iJ_
u\) supplies a unitary scalar normalization. This computation is consistent with a pole-free representative and with the preceding qualification that the solution is determined up to a scalar; it is not used to refute the existence theorem.

The shifts, amenability assumptions and the exceptional affine \(D_{2n}\) case in Section 7 were retained. The full universal K-matrix construction from the cited earlier work, the classification of generalized Satake diagrams, all R-matrix normalization identities, and every representation-theoretic identification in Section 7 were not independently reproved. Reading the whole body does not remove these dependencies.

The source manifest and bounded searches of the arXiv, publisher and author pages did not identify separate computational supplements or an author repository. No author code was executed; absence of code is not a mathematical defect. All source inspection, dependency assessment, reporting, compilation and page review were performed in the present initial review conversation. The scientific decision remains pending; no human review or independent acceptance is recorded.

Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical review of
Nondegeneracy of the spectrum of the twisted cocycle for interval exchange transformations
# Source, hypotheses and coverage

The supplied source is the arXiv v1, not an assumed copy of the journal article published online on 15 August 2025. All 29 pages were read as extracted text, including the bibliography; fifteen selected source pages were also inspected as images. The main result retains \(g>1\), an irreducible Rauzy class, and the two specified invariant measures. The full-torus average exponent and the exponent for the ergodic homological subtorus measure are distinguished.

The review followed the chain from the twisted matrices (3.3), rational-fiber measures and Proposition 3.9, through the stopping-time construction, untwisting lemma, geometric realization, genus/singularity bounds, Proposition 5.2 and the limiting argument. The root-of-unity cancellation in (4.12)–(4.17) and the Vandermonde spanning argument were checked. For Proposition 3.9, balanced tower heights relate the induction time to \(\log N\); subexponential return blocks control the sum of tower contributions. The case of zero growth rate can be handled with the same positive-\(\epsilon\) bounds before letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\).

The EKZ sum estimate, Chaika–Eskin directional regularity, affine orbit-closure theorem, and Rauzy–Veech group classification are external inputs, not independently reproved here. The discussion below does not certify every large-deviation or correlation estimate in Proposition 3.4, nor every application in Section 6.
# Confirmed findings

Problem 1 (Major: the prescribed geometric realization is not a side pairing).  The location is p. 18, Section 4.1, from the choice of \(\lambda^*\) through the top–bottom identification of the square. Equation (4.2), p. 15, gives \[F_p(\widehat\lambda,s)
 =\left(\frac{s}{p}\widehat\lambda,1-\frac{s}{p}\right).\] Equation (4.20), p. 19, correspondingly gives \(|\widetilde I|=1-s\). Nevertheless, Section 4.1 chooses \[s_*=\frac{p+1}{2p}
 \quad\hbox{and asserts}\quad |\widetilde I|=\frac12.\] The actual length is \((p-1)/(2p)\). Moreover, for \(P=[0,\sqrt2/2]^2\), the printed top–bottom map is \[(x,\sqrt2/2)\longmapsto
 \left(\sqrt2\,S_{\vec n,p}(x/\sqrt2)-\sqrt2,0\right).
 \tag{2.1}\] Since \(S_{\vec n,p}\) takes values in \([0,1)\), its first coordinate is negative. Taken literally, (2.1) does not map the top side into the bottom side.

Counterexample satisfying the geometric hypotheses. Take \[\pi=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3&4\\4&3&2&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \widehat\lambda=(1/3,1/3,1/3),\qquad
 \vec n=(1,1,1,1).\] This permutation is irreducible and satisfies \(\pi_b\pi_t^{-1}(4)=1\). Its intersection matrix has entries \(-1\) above the diagonal and \(1\) below it, and determinant \(1\); thus its rank is \(4\) and \(g=2\). For every prime \(p\ge3\), put \[a=\frac{p+1}{6p^2},\quad
 s=\frac{p+1}{2p},\quad
 \lambda^*=(a,a,a,1-3a).\] All coordinates are positive, sum to one, and \(\lambda^*_4>(p-1)/p\); indeed they also satisfy the stronger bound \(\lambda^*_4>p/(p+1)\) used at the start of the proof on p. 16. The condition \(p\nmid n_{\alpha_t}\) holds. Since the integer observable \(\vec n\) is constantly one, its first zero sum modulo \(p\) occurs exactly at time \(p\), so \(S_{\vec n,p}=T_{\lambda^*,\pi}^{p}\).

A modulo interpretation still fails. The left–right identification might suggest reading the bottom coordinate modulo the square width. In the normalized coordinate \(u=x/\sqrt2\), that would make the bottom map \(S(u)\bmod(1/2)\). Define \[e=\frac{1}{2p^2},\qquad
 u_1=2a-\frac e2,\qquad
 u_2=\frac12-\frac e2 .\] These are distinct interior points of \((0,1/2)\). The point \(u_1\) lies in the second small interval. The first iterate moves it into the long interval, where the remaining \(p-1\) iterates subtract \(3a\) each. Consequently \[S(u_1)=u_1+1-s.\] The point \(u_2\) lies in \(T^{-(p-1)}(I_1)\); its first \(p-1\) iterates stay in the long interval before the last step uses \(I_1\). Thus \[S(u_2)=u_2+1-s+2a,\qquad S(u_2)-S(u_1)=\frac12.\] Their bottom images modulo \(1/2\) coincide. The points are inside continuity intervals, and the two image intervals overlap in positive length. This is not a harmless identification of polygon vertices.

For \(p=3\), the data are \[\lambda^*=(2/27,2/27,2/27,7/9),\quad
 (u_1,u_2)=(13/108,17/36),\quad
 (S(u_1),S(u_2))=(49/108,103/108).\] An independently written exact-fraction computation reproduced these values and the corresponding collisions for \(p=5,7,101\); no author code was executed. The general calculation above establishes failure for arbitrarily large primes, and the positive-length overlap persists under small parameter perturbations preserving the branch itineraries.

Dependency, impact and repair boundary. The surface \(X\), its \(p\)-fold covering of \(Y\), Lemmas 4.4–4.6, and the orbit closure used at the beginning of Section 5 all depend on this realization. Thus the stated construction does not currently supply the geometric object to which the external exponent formula is applied. This is the reason for the Major assessment. No claim is made that the positivity theorem itself is false.

A plausible correction is to take \(s_*=1/2\) and replace the translation in (2.1) by \(-\sqrt2/2\). The first change gives the required half-length interval; the second has the appropriate range when the relevant image is \([1/2,1)\). A complete repair must verify the corrected edge pairing, covering/deck transformation, singularity orders, and directional return-map identity for the allowed parameters. Those geometric verifications are not replaced here by the assertion that the two textual changes look small.

Problem 2 (Major: the positive-proportion count in (5.5)).  On p. 21, writing \(D=\dim V_c\) and \(m=\#\{1\le k\le p-1:O_k(\mathbb C^d)\not\subset V_c\}\), the middle expression of (5.5) is \[\frac1{p-1}\left(1-\frac D{d-1}\right).\] It is then bounded below by \(c(g-1)/d>0\) for all sufficiently large \(p\). This is impossible: \(D\ge0\) makes the expression at most \(1/(p-1)\), which tends to zero.
# Further checks and limits

The lower bound in (5.2) uses \(m(m+2)/(m+1)=m+1-(m+1)^{-1}\ge m+1/2\) for \(m\ge1\). Together with \(\sum m_i=2g-2\) and at least one genuine singularity when \(g>1\), it yields the displayed \(p(4g-3)/24\) bound. The subsequent estimate on the average exponent and its positive-proportion consequence were checked arithmetically.

For (5.11), upper semicontinuity has the correct direction. Its use with the unbounded Zorich cocycle requires the integrable base domination and null discontinuity boundaries: finite-time twisted products are dominated entrywise in modulus by ordinary products, and all approximating measures have the same base projection. This explains the relevant truncation mechanism; it is not a blanket continuity claim for arbitrary cocycles or arbitrary varying base measures.

Section 6 was read with its quantified hypotheses. The discrepancy proof contains additional steps concerning the selected nonzero character and logarithmic growth that would merit a separate detailed reconstruction. They are not promoted here to further confirmed theorem failures. The spectral-dimension application retains its external spectral-cocycle theorem and almost-everywhere roof/frequency qualifications.

Bounded searches of the arXiv and publisher records and exact-title searches did not locate a separate computational supplement or author repository. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect. The journal PDF was subscription-restricted and its equivalence with the reviewed v1 was not established. The present revision incorporates focused independent acceptance of the reported findings, including the severity correction for Problem 2. It retains the original review’s scope and limitations. The scientific decision remains pending, and human reviews are empty.

report: Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Initial scientific review of
Sparse equidistribution of geometric invariants of real quadratic fields

Paper: M25-0315. Authors: Peter Humphries and Asbjørn Christian Nordentoft. DOI: https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1691. Reviewed object: publisher Version of Record, JEMS 28 (2026), 5113–5192, 80 PDF pages; publisher publication date 25 August 2025. The frozen 2025 assignment is retained. This is not a review of an assumed equivalent arXiv revision.
# Assessment and scope

Assessment: Major, confined to a demonstrated failure of the stated regularisation and its continuous-spectrum proof dependency. The main equidistribution conclusions have not been disproved. One confirmed problem is established below by an admissible geodesic and the paper’s own Fourier expansion. The proposed local repair is natural, but its ease does not make the literal undefined integral a valid proof.

All 80 pages of extracted text were read; the extraction has defective mathematical glyphs, so 28 selected source pages were also visually inspected, including every page used for the confirmed problem and its immediate dependency. This is a substantive initial review, not a formal verification of every cited analytic theorem. Decision and adjudication remain pending; there are no human reviews or independent-acceptance claims.
# Quantifiers and positive checks

The distinctions among the four main theorems matter. Theorem 1.1 assumes a positive squarefree fundamental discriminant and a split odd prime level, with \(q\le D^\delta\), \(\delta<1/36\); its conditional range is \(\delta<1/12\). Theorem 1.2 fixes the level and allows a coset of a subgroup of relative size \(\gg D^{-\delta}\), with \(\delta<1/2826\) (conditionally \(1/4\)). Its fundamental discriminant need not be squarefree. Theorems 1.3–1.4 return to squarefree fundamental discriminants and level one; the discrepancy supremum is explicitly over injective balls.

The geometric volume lower bound in Proposition 3.9 is used together with the narrow class number formula. The trace estimate after the parabolic-block decomposition on p. 5138 yields \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal F_A(q))\gg\log\epsilon_D/\log(qD)\), rather than an unjustified bound from ordinary word length alone. The homological boundary contributions in Section 5 and Proposition 6.1 cannot generally be omitted when the modular curve has positive genus.

The stated level error \(q^{3+\varepsilon}D^{-1/12+\varepsilon}\) indeed gives the strict range \(\delta<1/36\). The fixed-level subgroup argument is also arithmetically consistent: the three squared Weyl-sum bounds give savings \(1/2826\), \(1/2114\), and \(1/1889\) after taking square roots. Character orthogonality supplies \((|H|/h_D^+)|H^\perp|=1\); it introduces no additional class-number factor. The slowest saving gives the printed \(1/2826\). These calculations do not extend the fixed-level theorem to growing levels.

For small scales, the three relative errors in (9.11) match at \(R=D^{-1/12}\) and \(D^{-5/12}\). At \(R=D^{-\delta}\) the final branch tends to zero for \(\delta<1/2\). Multiplication by the ball area, of order \(R^2\), is consistent with the discrepancy exponent. These exponent checks are conditional on the analytic identities and moment inputs, including the regularisation discussed next.
# Confirmed problem

Problem 1 (Major: the cusp cutoffs do not define the claimed regularised integral).  Location. Section 5.3, p. 5154 (physical PDF p. 42), (5.8)–(5.11), especially Lemma 5.4. The dependency is explicit in Lemma 6.10 and its proof, pp. 5165–5166 (physical pp. 53–54).

The definition is \[\mathfrak F_b(Y)=
 \{z\in\mathbb H:0<\Re(\sigma_b^{-1}z)<1,\
                         \Im(\sigma_b^{-1}z)\ge Y\},
 \qquad \sigma_b\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z),\quad\sigma_b\infty=b.\] It is asserted to be independent of \(\sigma_b\), and equivariant under the modular group. Both assertions fail for these subsets of \(\mathbb H\). For \(b=\infty\), the allowed matrices \(I\) and \(T=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) give strips \(0<x<1\) and \(1<x<2\), respectively. The point \(1/2+2iY\) belongs only to the first. With the first choice fixed, \(T\mathfrak F_\infty(Y)\ne\mathfrak F_{T\infty}(Y)\).

There is a direct failure of Lemma 5.4, not merely a set-theoretic ambiguity. Take the permitted geodesic \[\mathcal C=\{iy:y>0\},\qquad b_1=\infty,\quad b_2=0,\qquad
 \sigma_\infty=I,\quad
 \sigma_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] For \(z=iy\), both \(\sigma_\infty^{-1}z=iy\) and \(\sigma_0^{-1}z=i/y\) have real part zero. Consequently \[\mathcal C\setminus
       (\mathfrak F_\infty(Y)\cup\mathfrak F_0(Y))=\mathcal C
 \quad\hbox{for every }Y.\] The displayed limit (5.11) has not truncated either endpoint. Boundary sets of area zero cannot be discarded here: the whole integration curve lies on the excluded boundaries.

To verify divergence independently, put \(s=1/2+i\). The Fourier expansion (4.10), p. 5142, gives \[E(iy,s)=y^s+\varphi(s)y^{1-s}+O(e^{-c y}\,\mathrm{poly}(y)),
 \qquad
 \varphi(s)=\frac{\xi(1-2i)}{\xi(1+2i)}.\] On this axis, the \(x\) derivative vanishes by the symmetry of the Fourier coefficients, and \(R_0=iy\partial_x+y\partial_y\). Thus the upper-end integral from \(iA\) to \(iB\) equals \[i\bigl(B^s+\varphi(s)B^{1-s}\bigr)+C_A+o(1).\] Choose \(\theta\) with \(e^{i\theta}+\varphi(s)e^{-i\theta}\ne0\) and set \(B_n=e^{\theta+2\pi n}\). The displayed leading term is a fixed nonzero complex number times \(B_n^{1/2}\), so the ordinary improper integral does not converge. The endpoints, scaling matrices and spectral parameter satisfy the lemma’s stated hypotheses.
## Impact, contrary evidence, and repair boundary

Lemma 6.10 uses exactly these cusp zones in its Stokes truncation and invokes Lemma 5.4 for the Eisenstein boundary periods. Hence the literal definitions do not supply the claimed continuous-spectrum identities used subsequently in the level and subgroup arguments. This is a failure in a core proof dependency, which warrants Major at the proof level; it is not evidence that the equidistribution assertions themselves are false. The cuspidal decay argument and the elementary exponent checks above are not refuted by this example.

A precise candidate correction is to use full horoballs \[\mathcal H_b(Y)=
       \{z:\Im(\sigma_b^{-1}z)\ge Y\}.\] Two allowed scaling matrices differ by right multiplication by \(\pm T^n\), which preserves imaginary part. This restores scaling independence and modular equivariance. In the example it leaves the finite segment \(z=iy\), \(1/Y<y<Y\). Indeed modular invariance gives \(E(iY,s)=E(i/Y,s)\), so the corrected symmetrically truncated integral is exactly zero. This supplies genuine counterevidence against claiming that the intended regularised value is impossible.

A quotient-space reading can likewise be made meaningful only by taking the complete preimage of the cusp neighbourhood when truncating an arbitrary lifted geodesic. Changing the strict strip boundaries alone does not restore scaling independence. The author should replace the cutoff definition and check the general two-endpoint cancellation, the scaling law (5.10), and the Stokes boundary terms with that same convention. This review verifies the correction for the exhibited case, not every subsequent regularised identity.
# Unresolved checks and limitations

The topological terms in (6.19)–(6.20), p. 5168, appear without the inverse Laplace eigenvalue present in Lemma 6.10. The original page was checked, but this review has not supplied a permitted instance with a provably nonzero total topological term. It is therefore recorded as an unresolved normalisation check, not a second confirmed error.

Similarly, the equality between a periodised ball kernel and an indicator in Section 9 has an injectivity qualification. Extending the proof uniformly through larger balls or elliptic centres requires care with multiplicities. This review has not established a counterexample to Theorem 1.3 from that issue.

The adèlic normalisation chain, raising operators, parity factor, and fixed-level character counting were traced. The external toric-period theorem with its modified archimedean test vector, the general fractional-moment extension in (9.6), and all uniform analytic estimates were not independently reproved. No claim of exhaustive mathematical certification is made.
# Supporting checks
The acquired PDF has SHA256
00000TOKEN

and its manifest, title encoding, author names, issue year and publisher date are retained. A bounded exact-title search and the author’s research page located an official author-maintained Errata.pdf. Its four pages were read and viewed; the retrieved copy contains no entry for this paper. Its absence of an entry is not a claim that no correction exists elsewhere. No separate supplementary dataset or author code was located, and none was executed.

The current web initial-review executor performed the source reading, analysis, report preparation and actual source/report image inspections. An existing native auxiliary independently checked only the supplied exponent algebra, coset involution and cusp-counterexample calculation; it did not inspect the paper, run author code, or perform acceptance. Its role is recorded separately. The controller’s GPT-6/Pro UI observations are attributed to the controller; backend identity is not independently asserted.

Actual Tectonic 0.17.0 compilation, exit status, complete logs, dependency snapshots and retained payloads, exact input/output hashes, PDF parsing, and separate visual-inspection receipts accompany this report. Render-time false inspection records remain unchanged. This report is an initial-review deliverable with scientific decision pending.

report: Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Initial scientific review
The exact rank of sparse random graphs

Assignment. Authors. Margalit Glasgow, Matthew Kwan, Ashwin Sah and Mehtaab Sawhney. Exact source. arXiv:2303.05435v1, 9 March 2023, 17:27:44 UTC, 46 PDF pages. DOI: 10.4171/jems/1692 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1692). The journal record was published on 2 September 2025; no equivalence of that record and this preprint is assumed.
# Assessment and scope

Major revision of the stated technical results. The robust random-walk theorem, a central tool introduced for the rank argument and for possible wider use, is false over its stated initial-condition range. A deterministic counterexample satisfies every hypothesis. Three further auxiliary statements omit necessary hypotheses. The principal sparse-graph rank conclusions have not been disproved: in particular, their random walk starts with a stronger negative margin that excludes the counterexample. This distinction determines the scope of the assessment.

All 46 pages were read as extracted text, including the appendix and references. Thirty-one source pages were also inspected as images. The review checked the theorem ranges, Karp–Sipser reductions, special-cycle kernel vectors, degree conditioning, rank-boosting hypotheses, random-walk application, stalk dependency chain and asymptotic distributions. Exact arithmetic and elementary linear algebra were independently computed in reviewer-written Python; no author code was run.
# Confirmed problems

Problem 1 (Major: Theorem 7.2 permits an insufficient initial margin).  Theorem 7.2, pp. 21–22, assumes \(X_N\le(1-\varepsilon)\delta N\), upward jumps at most \(C\), downward drift at good positive steps, and the prefix bound \[|R\cap\{0,\ldots,t\}|\le \delta t/(32C)\] with probability at least \(1-p\). It concludes \(\Pr(X_0>0)=O_{C,\delta,\varepsilon}(p)\).

Set \(C=\delta=1\), \(\varepsilon=1/100\), \(N=3200\), \(R=\{3101,\ldots,3199\}\), and \(X_N=3168\). Define the entire process deterministically, backwards, by \[X_t=X_{t+1}+1\quad(t\in R),\qquad
 X_t=X_{t+1}-1\quad(t\notin R).\] Take \(G_t\) deterministic and encoding \(X_t\) and membership in \(R\). Then W0 and W2 hold, W1 is equality, and W3 holds with probability one: every good positive step decreases by \(\delta\), and every other step belongs to \(R\). All \(X_t\) are positive. For \(t\le3100\) the prefix count is zero; for \(3101\le t\le3199\) it is \(t-3100\le t/32\); at \(t=3200\) it is \(99\le100\). Thus W4 also holds surely. Nevertheless \[X_0=3168-3200+2(99)=166>0.\] The same process satisfies the assumptions for every \(p>0\), so its probability one cannot be bounded by a fixed constant times \(p\) as \(p\downarrow0\). The family \(N=3200k\), \(|R|=100k-1\) gives \(X_0=168k-2\), excluding a large-\(N\) escape.

The proof on p. 22 reduces the effective downward drift to \(1/2\) when adding the debt process, but retains an initial bound sized for drift \(1\). This invalidates the appeal to Lemma 7.1. Theorem 7.2 is explicitly used in the proofs of Theorem 1.12(A1) and (B1), pp. 28–29 and 39–40. However, in (A1) the actual initial value is \(X_N\le N/8-N/4=-N/8\), and the bipartite application has a comparable negative margin. These facts are substantial counterevidence to any claim that the main rank formula fails.

A corrected theorem must either strengthen the initial bound to match the reduced drift or make the bad-step budget depend on \(\varepsilon\). Restricting the initial value to be nonpositive would cover the displayed applications. The deterministic budget and location of the failed parameter transfer are established here; a complete revised stochastic theorem and its rounding details still require proof.

Problem 2 (Minor: independence is absent from Lemma 3.3).  On p. 12, the bounded-difference hypothesis for \(Z=f(X_0,\ldots,X_n)\) is stated without independence or an appropriate martingale increment condition. Take sixteen variables all equal to a fair Bernoulli variable \(U\), and define \(f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{15}x_j\) on the whole Boolean cube. Changing one coordinate changes \(f\) by at most \(1\). Yet \(Z=16U\), \(\mathbb{E}Z=8\), and, at \(t=8\), \[\Pr(|Z-\mathbb{E}Z|\ge8)=1>2e^{-2}.\] This directly contradicts the printed bound. Add independence, or state a sufficient conditional martingale hypothesis. The application on pp. 18–19 uses independent truncated Poisson variables, so this omission does not establish a failure of that application.

Problem 4 (Minor: the rank-boosting lemmas include a deterministic slice).  Lemmas 8.2 and 8.4(a), pp. 22–23, assume only \(d\ge1\), although their input Lemma 8.5 explicitly requires \(d\le n/2\). For even \(n\), put \(\eta=1/4\), \(E=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(d=n\), and \(B=A=J_n\), the all-ones matrix. The vector with half its entries \(1\) and half \(-1\) is an \(\eta\)-balanced kernel vector, as required; arbitrary real matrices and symmetric real matrices are allowed. The random slice vector is deterministically \(x=\mathbf1\). Thus \[\operatorname{rank}[J_n\mid\mathbf1]=1,\qquad
 \operatorname{rank}\begin{pmatrix}J_n&\mathbf1\\
 \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}=2.\] The claimed rank increments, respectively one and two, fail with probability one for every even \(n\), contradicting an \(O_\eta(d^{-1/2})\) failure bound. Add \(1\le d\le |E|/2\), or formulate a symmetric slice bound that degenerates appropriately at both endpoints. In the actual graph applications, \(d=O(\log n)\) while \(|E|\) is linear in \(n\), so this range is available. No independent counterexample to part 8.4(b) is asserted.
# Positive checks and remaining limits

A leaf and its neighbour contribute an invertible \(2\)-by-\(2\) block; its Schur complement on the remaining graph is unchanged, proving the exact adjacency-rank drop of two. Alternating signs on the degree-two half of a special \(4k\)-cycle give the claimed kernel vector. An isolated such cycle gives two independent vectors. Their addition across cycles requires disjointness, supplied later in Claims 10.4 and Lemma 11.6, rather than assumed solely from the definition.

The restrictions \(c\ne e\), \(c>1\) for the giant 2-core, and \(n_1-n_2\to\infty\) in the degree-constrained bipartite theorem were retained. The critical-window assertion is existence of a sequence \(np_n\to e\); it is not a theorem for \(p=e/n\). The v1 CLT range is \(c<1\) or \(c>e\). Section 13 explicitly supplies sub-Gaussian concentration to control moments; the potential objection that an \(O_p(1)\) comparison alone is insufficient is therefore not a finding.

The Poisson factors for isolated and nonisolated special cycles and the positivity of the giant-core mean were checked. The extraction log-concavity calculation and the main conditioning dependencies were traced. The full combinatorial stalk enumeration, every external spectral and core-process theorem, and the complete bipartite proof sketch were not independently reconstructed. Consequently this report is not an exhaustive correctness certificate.

The publisher record, arXiv history and an author publication page were searched for supplementary material and corrections. No separate author code or supplement was located in that bounded search; absence of code is not a defect. All source reading, evidence inspection, scientific classification and report production belong to the present initial-review execution. No independent acceptance or human review is claimed.

The exact source, TeX, compiler, dependencies, PDF and inspected images are bound by SHA256 in the accompanying provenance and inventories. The calculation script and its actual output preserve the deterministic walks, configuration probabilities and rational matrix ranks. The source version above is retained without substitution by the journal version. Scientific adjudication remains pending, and the human-review list is empty.

claim: Recorded check: Theorem 7.2 permits an insufficient initial margin
C=delta=1,epsilon=.01,N=3200; deterministic Gt; R=3101..3199; XN3168.
analysis: Theorem 7.2, pp. 21–22, assumes \(X_N\le(1-\varepsilon)\delta N\), upward jumps at most \(C\), downward drift at good positive steps, and the prefix bound \[|R\cap\{0,\ldots,t\}|\le \delta t/(32C)\] with probability at least \(1-p\). It concludes \(\Pr(X_0>0)=O_{C,\delta,\varepsilon}(p)\).

Set \(C=\delta=1\), \(\varepsilon=1/100\), \(N=3200\), \(R=\{3101,\ldots,3199\}\), and \(X_N=3168\). Define the entire process deterministically, backwards, by \[X_t=X_{t+1}+1\quad(t\in R),\qquad
 X_t=X_{t+1}-1\quad(t\notin R).\] Take \(G_t\) deterministic and encoding \(X_t\) and membership in \(R\). Then W0 and W2 hold, W1 is equality, and W3 holds with probability one: every good positive step decreases by \(\delta\), and every other step belongs to \(R\). All \(X_t\) are positive. For \(t\le3100\) the prefix count is zero; for \(3101\le t\le3199\) it is \(t-3100\le t/32\); at \(t=3200\) it is \(99\le100\). Thus W4 also holds surely. Nevertheless \[X_0=3168-3200+2(99)=166>0.\] The same process satisfies the assumptions for every \(p>0\), so its probability one cannot be bounded by a fixed constant times \(p\) as \(p\downarrow0\). The family \(N=3200k\), \(|R|=100k-1\) gives \(X_0=168k-2\), excluding a large-\(N\) escape.

The proof on p. 22 reduces the effective downward drift to \(1/2\) when adding the debt process, but retains an initial bound sized for drift \(1\). This invalidates the appeal to Lemma 7.1. Theorem 7.2 is explicitly used in the proofs of Theorem 1.12(A1) and (B1), pp. 28–29 and 39–40. However, in (A1) the actual initial value is \(X_N\le N/8-N/4=-N/8\), and the bipartite application has a comparable negative margin. These facts are substantial counterevidence to any claim that the main rank formula fails.

A corrected theorem must either strengthen the initial bound to match the reduced drift or make the bad-step budget depend on \(\varepsilon\). Restricting the initial value to be nonpositive would cover the displayed applications.
