Indeed \(|f|\notin I\): the quotient \(|f|/f\) has one-sided values 1 and \(i\), respectively. Nor can self-adjointness be inserted as an unstated hypothesis, since the theorem explicitly concerns arbitrary ideals and is used to prove automatic self-adjointness later.

The example does not refute the squeezing theorem itself. The defect is the claimed identification used in its proof.

report: Abstract: The principal identification of the circular Gaussian multiplicative chaos with a randomly weighted spectral measure was checked through its normalization, change of measure, diffusion limit, entrance law, and conditional limiting argument. No substantive defect in that identification was established in the inspected scope. Corollary 2.4 needs a precise distinction between the Hausdorff dimension of a measure and that of its topological support. The latter is the full circle for the stated Verblunsky law, including the critical case. This is a Minor correction to the formulation of the dimensional consequence, not a refutation of the measure correspondence. Actual page inspection also confirms a reversed probability-event sign in the entrance-law proof; the preceding correct tail split supplies its local repair.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Chaos, spectral measures and the meaning of dimension
# Bound source and scope

This report concerns Reda Chhaibi and Joseph Najnudel, On the circle, Gaussian multiplicative chaos and Beta ensembles match exactly, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1700 [paper]. The bound source is the 77-page publisher PDF, serial-article file 52155, with SHA256

The hash is recorded without abbreviation in the accompanying provenance and inventory. Its first page gives J. Eur. Math. Soc. 28, 1–77 (2026) and copyright 2025; the publisher records publication on 7 November 2025 and acceptance on 14 February 2025. The first page records receipt on 1 September 2019 and revision on 18 January 2024. These facts do not change the frozen identifier M25-0324 or its assigned 2025 collection. No substitution of an arXiv revision or an online-first PDF has been made.

All 77 source pages, including Appendix A and the references, were read as extracted text. In the same-chat continuation, all 25 required source evidence images were actually displayed and inspected. This confirms the support notation and resolves the previously unconfirmed probability-event sign on page 68. Earlier `EMFILE` failures and false viewing records are retained. The public publisher text remains secondary corroboration; the exact bound PDF supplies the actual visual evidence.
# Objects, parameters, and dependencies

Write \(q=2/\beta=\gamma^2\). The independent Verblunsky coefficients have rotation-invariant laws with \[|\alpha_j|^2\sim{\rm Beta}(1,(j+1)/q).\] The limiting probability measure \(\mu^\beta\) uses this infinite coefficient sequence. The finite approximation involves random spectral weights after reversing the finite coefficient order; it is not the unweighted empirical eigenvalue measure. Equality of the finite spectral point law does not identify those weights with the usual independent Dirichlet weights.

The real Gaussian field has covariance \(-2\log|1-w\bar z|\). Thus the radial subcritical regularization has factor \((1-r^2)^{\gamma^2}\), with normalized angular measure. For \(\beta>2\), the total-mass factor is \[C_0=\prod_{j\ge0}(1-|\alpha_j|^2)^{-1}
                       \left(1-\frac{q}{j+1}\right).\] It is a functional of the same coefficients as \(\mu^\beta\); independence of mass and normalized measure is not asserted. At \(\beta=2\) the first deterministic factor vanishes, and the theorem uses the separately renormalized expression with leading factor \(2\). The critical chaos is defined through the subcritical limiting normalization. Applying the subcritical product without that change would be incorrect. The supercritical comparison in Section 2.5 is explicitly prospective; the main identification does not prove equivalence with either freezing or KPZ-dual constructions.

The proof’s substantial bridge is not merely convergence of the analytic polynomial inside the disk. It is the weighted \(L^1\) estimate of Lemma 4.1 and the conditional expectation limit of Lemma 4.2. These are supplied only in Section 7 after the estimates of Section 5 and the diffusion analysis of Section 6. The distinction is essential because radial and polynomial-degree limits cannot be exchanged on the basis of compact interior convergence alone.
# A dimensional formulation requiring correction

Problem 1 (Minor: Corollary 2.4, page 11).  With the conventional meaning of topological support, the displayed equalities \(\dim_H\operatorname{supp}(\mu^\beta)=1-2/\beta\) for \(\beta>2\), and \(\dim_H\operatorname{supp}(\mu^2)=0\), are false. The intended measure dimension must be defined and used explicitly. The analogous GMC displays require the same distinction.
## A counterexample within the stated law

Take \(\beta=4\), so all of the subcritical assumptions hold. For any \(0<\varepsilon<1\), the exact beta tail is \[\mathbb P(|\alpha_j|>\varepsilon)
   =(1-\varepsilon^2)^{2(j+1)}.\] The sum over \(j\) is finite. Borel–Cantelli and a countable sequence of \(\varepsilon\)’s give \(\alpha_j\to0\) almost surely. This argument works for every \(\beta>0\), not only for the illustrative value \(4\).

Here is a direct spectral reason why that implies full topological support. In the CMV representation used on pages 19–21, each \(2\)-by-\(2\) block differs from its zero-coefficient block by entries tending to zero: the diagonal entries are \(\alpha_j\) and its conjugate, up to signs, and the off-diagonal difference is \(\sqrt{1-|\alpha_j|^2}-1\). Consequently the difference between the corresponding infinite CMV unitary and the free CMV unitary is compact; indeed the block-diagonal differences are norm limits of their finite truncations.
## Impact and repair boundary

A singular measure can have a dense carrier of small Hausdorff dimension and nevertheless have full closed support. An appropriate quantity to state here is, for example, \[\dim_H\mu=\inf\{\dim_H E:E\text{ Borel},\ \mu(E)=1\}.\] The intended assertions about this quantity, and any stronger exact-dimensional interpretation, should be tied explicitly to the spectral theorem cited by the authors. This report does not independently reprove Simon’s Theorem 12.7.7 or the extension of its antecedent hypotheses mentioned in the paragraph following the corollary.

The finding is classified as Minor because it concerns specification of the dimensional object in a consequence. It neither invalidates the main random-measure identity nor establishes a false value of the intended measure dimension. The phrase and notation should nevertheless be changed: no nonstandard definition of \(\operatorname{supp}\) resolving the distinction was located in the full text.
# Checks of the main proof
## Analytic martingales and change of measure

The logarithm of the reversed polynomial is based at zero; its nonvanishing inside the disk permits that branch. Rotational independence gives the martingale increments mean zero. Proposition 3.6 uses the exponential cubic-sum hypothesis and a conditional bounded-differences estimate after conditioning on moduli. The trace expansion in Lemma 3.5 provides a cubic remainder with an absolute bound. The conditional quadratic dependence in the phase variables is summable under the stated fourth-power bound, which is itself covered by the hypothesis. The Hilbert-space argument uses moment bounds and holomorphy to pass from Fourier-coefficient convergence to convergence on compact disks. Identification of the Gaussian coefficients uses finite-dimensional trace limits, with the cited result or Appendix A as an external symmetric-function input.

For fixed \(r<1\), the density in (4.7) is a genuine positive martingale, bounded in \(L^p\) by the already established polynomial moment bounds. The conditional angular average of the Poisson kernel is one. This verifies the change-of-measure step and explains why the moduli retain their independent beta laws under \(\mathbb Q_{r,\theta}\). The subsequent limit concerns this \(r\)-dependent law; it is not an unjustified application of a theorem under a single fixed probability measure.
## Moment and tail estimates

The angular series in Lemma 5.2 was checked against the constant and quadratic terms. Under the tilted law, the conditional drift and variance of the modulus recursion give the coefficients in (5.6)–(5.8). The fourth-moment cancellation uses the alternating binomial coefficients \(1,-4,6,-4,1\). The early finitely many beta variables, whose inverse moments may diverge, are treated by truncation rather than by extending a large-index moment bound to every index.

In Proposition 5.5, the logarithmic error splits into a centered martingale and a nonpositive remainder. The concavity inequality for \(\log(1-aq)\) supplies that sign. The uniform exponential bound uses positive moments of that error, not nonexistent negative moments. The tail proof in Proposition 5.4 is naturally an \(A\ge1\) argument. For \(0<A<1\), the additional initial sum is bounded deterministically by a harmonic sum of size \(O(1+\log(1/A))\), which is \(O(1/A)\); this supplies the harmless small-\(A\) extension. No core failure is inferred from the compressed treatment of that range.
## Diffusion, entrance, and uniqueness

The mesh is \(\log(1/r^2)\), with \(1-r^2\) asymptotically equal to it. On intervals \([\varepsilon,A]\), the coefficients have the required uniform convergence and the fourth-moment estimates imply tightness. The coefficients only need bounded extensions outside the invariant state interval \([0,1]\); the displayed quadratic drift should not be mistaken for a bounded function on all of \(\mathbb R\) without such an extension. The earlier tightness estimate near zero supplies the additional entrance restriction \(1-X_t=O(t^{1-\varepsilon_0})\). The SDE on positive times alone does not select that entrance.

Problem 2 (Minor: the first probability display on page 68).  Actual inspection confirms that the first probability on the right uses the lower-tail event \(I_t\leq\alpha\), where \[I_t=\int_0^t\frac{4(1-X_u)}{\beta u}\,du.\] The last display on page 67 instead has the required upper-tail event \(I_t\geq\alpha\).

Under precisely the stated near-zero assumption, choose \(\varepsilon_0=1/2\). Then \(0\leq1-X_u\leq C(\omega)\sqrt u\) for small \(u\), with \(C(\omega)<\infty\) almost surely. Direct integration gives \[0\leq I_t\leq\frac{8C(\omega)}{\beta}\sqrt t\longrightarrow0.\] For every fixed \(\alpha>0\), bounded convergence therefore yields \(\mathbb P(I_t\leq\alpha)\to1\), whereas \(\mathbb P(I_t\geq\alpha)\to0\). Thus the lower-tail term printed on page 68 cannot be dropped in the subsequent limit. Replacing its sign by the upper-tail sign already present on page 67 restores the inference; the remaining Brownian supremum tail tends to zero as \(\alpha\downarrow0\). This is a confirmed local transcription correction, not a counterexample to the entrance law. The exact integral was independently checked symbolically, and the analytic probability limits above require no simulation or author code.
## Conditional limit and mass

The last section first removes the logarithmic error using uniform exponential integrability, then truncates the exponential of the remaining variable. The sign-event decomposition on page 72 permits conditioning events to depend on \(r\), which is explicitly allowed in Proposition 6.1. Thus weak convergence for those conditioned processes, with small- and large-time tails controlled separately, proves the needed \(L^1\) conditional convergence. Ordinary unconditioned weak convergence would not suffice.

For a finite product with \(U_n=1-|\alpha_{n-1}|^2\), \(U_n\sim{\rm Beta}(n/q,1)\), an independent beta integral gives \[\mathbb E[C_N^z]
   =\prod_{n=1}^N\frac{(1-q/n)^z}{1-qz/n}.\] Its gamma-product limit is \[\frac{\Gamma(1-qz)}{\Gamma(1-q)^z},\] in the stated safe range of Mellin parameters. This agrees with the claimed inverse-exponential total mass and does not assume independence between the mass and normalized measure. The critical prefactor follows from \(\Gamma(1-\gamma^2)^{-1}/(1-\gamma)\to2\). An exact symbolic check was executed for the Itô drift and its derivative; a rational finite-chain check confirmed the two-endpoint Weyl-sequence norm. These are reviewer-created checks, not author code, and the analytic support argument is not inferred from numerical samples.
# Coverage and limitations

The introduction and corollaries (pages 1–15), analytic and trace arguments (16–27), conditional proof framework (27–33), estimates (34–47), diffusion and entrance proofs (47–70), final limiting argument (70–74), and Appendix A and references (74–77) were read. No independent reproof of the full OPUC correspondence, all cited critical-chaos results, Dufresne’s identity, or the Macdonald scalar-product theorem is claimed. The detailed ledger identifies these dependencies.

A bounded title/author search and the publisher record did not locate a verified paper-specific supplementary file, code repository, or erratum. Absence of retrieved code is not a mathematical defect, and no author code was executed. No supplementary material is declared absent merely because it was not located.

The present scientific assessment is Minor, with no confirmed Major finding in the inspected scope. It remains an initial technical review, not independent acceptance. The machine-readable `scientific_decision` remains `pending`, human review fields remain empty. The 25 source evidence pages have now been actually inspected. The prior report and all failed or false records are preserved. This revised TeX must be freshly compiled and every resulting PDF page actually inspected before completion; the continuation provenance binds the current source, TeX, compiler, dependencies, PDF and observed images.

report: Abstract: Lemma 4.5 is false under its stated hypotheses. A product over the blow-up of the projective plane, with the identity map on total spaces and the blow-down on bases, satisfies every hypothesis but has a dimension jump in the descended fibers. The proof also makes an invalid assertion about curves lying over a contracted base curve. The lemma is invoked directly in Theorem 4.9 and in the final proof of Theorem 1.1, so this is a Major defect in the written proof chain. A second Major proof-inference issue is the canonical-bundle-free vanishing used in Lemma 4.4: a smooth plane quartic gives a nonzero cohomology group under the stated choices. A corrected choice of the auxiliary ample divisor repairs that vanishing step. A missing constant in Lemma 2.8 is Minor. No counterexample to the principal structure theorem is claimed.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Birational descent, local triviality, and two auxiliary estimates
# Exact source and review scope

The bound source is Shin-ichi Matsumura and Juanyong Wang, Structure theorem for projective klt pairs with nef anti-canonical divisor, arXiv:2105.14308v3 [paper]. The upload timestamp is 30 August 2023, 03:32:48 UTC; the supplied 42-page PDF internally prints Date: August 31, 2023, version 0.01. Its SHA256 is recorded in full in provenance and inventory. The associated journal DOI is 10.4171/JEMS/1702. The publisher records submission on 25 January 2024, acceptance on 6 July 2025, and online publication on 30 September 2025 [journal]. The arXiv record does not identify v3 as the accepted journal text. The findings below apply to the exact supplied preprint; equivalence with the later journal article was not established.

All 42 pages were read as extracted text, including the references. The official version-specific HTML was also consulted and retained for the three disputed passages. Its generated date in 2026 is not treated as a new author revision. The source PDF remains governing. All 30 required source evidence pages were actually displayed and inspected in the same-chat continuation, including the birational and universal-cover diagrams, the exact assumptions of Lemma 4.5, the vanishing formula, and their uses in the main proof. The earlier `EMFILE` failures and false viewing records are preserved. This visual check does not alter the three mathematical findings.
# The main logical route

The theorem concerns complex projective klt pairs with effective rational boundary and nef \(- (K_X+\Delta)\). It allows a finite quasi-etale cover before obtaining a holomorphic, locally constant MRC fibration. Locally constant is defined through a monodromy representation on a fixed fiber over the universal cover, and is stronger than merely locally trivial. The theorem does not claim that the original variety already has this structure without a cover. The fundamental-group statements in Section 1.3 are explicitly conjectures and are not used as proved inputs.

The initial reduction takes a maximally quasi-etale cover and a crepant terminal model. Terminality supplies smoothness in codimension two, which is used in Theorem 3.8. For each normalized direct image, Proposition 3.9 converts a further quasi-etale cover into an etale one by maximality and descends local freeness. This handles the different sheaves without an unproved simultaneous infinite tower construction.

Theorem 3.2 descends the selected flat connection along rationally connected general fibers, then extends it across a general point of each relevant divisor using a reduced component and a local section. The normalization of the graph, rather than the whole resolution exceptional set, is important: only the former exceptional set is known not to dominate the base. Proposition 3.3(d) supplies compatibility of multiplication maps, which is required by Proposition 2.5 and cannot be dropped on a noncompact base. The subsequent foliation argument gives the birational structure. The obstruction identified below occurs in the later passage from that structure to a locally trivial fibration.
# A false birational descent lemma

Problem 1 (Major: Lemma 4.5, pages 29–30).  The assertion that \(f\) must be locally trivial does not follow from the hypotheses stated in Lemma 4.5. There is an explicit smooth projective counterexample.
## Construction and complete hypothesis check

Let \[W=\mathbb P^2,\qquad b:W'=\operatorname{Bl}_p\mathbb P^2\longrightarrow W,\qquad
 V'=V=W'\times\mathbb P^1.\] Put \[\beta_W=b,\quad \beta_V=\operatorname{id}_{V'},\quad
 f'=\operatorname{pr}_{W'},\quad f=b\circ f',\quad \Delta'=0 .\] The square commutes. All four varieties are smooth, normal, and projective. Both horizontal maps are projective birational morphisms; the identity is a birational morphism. Both vertical maps are proper surjective morphisms with connected fibers, exactly the meaning of fiber space used in the paper. No equidimensionality requirement is included in that definition or in Lemma 4.5.

The map \(f'\) is a product fibration with fiber \(\mathbb P^1\), hence is locally constant and has simply connected fiber. The base \(W\) and the pair \((V',0)\) are smooth and therefore klt. Finally, \[K_{V'/W'}=\operatorname{pr}_{\mathbb P^1}^{*}K_{\mathbb P^1},\qquad
 - (K_{V'/W'}+\Delta')=2\operatorname{pr}_{\mathbb P^1}^{*}\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)\] is nef. This verifies the precise relative, rather than absolute, positivity hypothesis in the lemma.

If \(q\ne p\), then \(f^{-1}(q)\simeq\mathbb P^1\), of dimension one. At the blown-up point, \[f^{-1}(p)=b^{-1}(p)\times\mathbb P^1\simeq\mathbb P^1\times\mathbb P^1,\] of dimension two. A locally trivial analytic fibration cannot have that dimension jump. This is a counterexample to the lemma’s conclusion, not merely a concern about an omitted justification.

## The precise failed inference

On page 30, in the paragraph beginning with an ample divisor on \(V\), the proof chooses a curve \(C_1\) above a curve \(C_0\) contracted by \(\beta_W\), and asserts that \(C_1\) must be contracted by \(\beta_V\). In the example, let \(E=b^{-1}(p)\) and \(C_1=E\times\{z_0\}\). Then \(f'(C_1)=E\), while \(\beta_V\) is the identity and does not contract \(C_1\). The claimed zero intersection can also be contradicted with an ample divisor. \operatorname{pr}_{\mathbb P^1}^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)\) is ample on \(V\), yet \(\beta_V^*A\cdot C_1=1\), not zero.
## Dependence and repair limits

Lemma 4.5 is invoked on page 36 in Step 3 of Theorem 4.9 and on page 37 in Step 2 of Theorem 1.1. Its failure therefore affects a core descent step. The counterexample does not disprove Theorem 1.1: the theorem asserts existence after a cover, and the counterexample is directed at an auxiliary statement about a specified diagram.

The applications have additional geometric information, including equidimensionality established earlier. It may permit a narrower replacement lemma. This report does not claim that adding equidimensionality alone proves the desired descent, nor that the original curve argument becomes correct after adding it. A repaired argument must justify the necessary contraction or descent property in the actual diagrams, check the pair and boundary, and then revisit both uses of Lemma 4.5. The invalid general lemma cannot simply be cited.
# Vanishing without the canonical twist

Problem 2 (Major proof inference: Lemma 4.4, pages 28–29).  The final part of the proof asserts \[H^i\bigl(W,E_m\otimes\mathcal O_W((d+1-i)A)\bigr)=0\quad(i>0)\] for a very ample \(A\), by Nakano vanishing. Here \(d\) must mean the dimension of \(W\); the source writes \(Y\). The asserted vanishing without a canonical twist or a stronger choice of \(A\) is false, even for trivial \(E_m\).

Let \(C\subset\mathbb P^2\) be a smooth plane quartic, for example the Fermat quartic over \(\mathbb C\). By adjunction, \[g(C)=3,\qquad K_C\simeq\mathcal O_C(1).\] Take \[W=C,\quad V=C\times\mathbb P^1,\quad h=\operatorname{pr}_C,\quad D=0,\quad
 B=h^*\mathcal O_C(1)+\operatorname{pr}_{\mathbb P^1}^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1).\] This is a locally constant product with irregularity-zero fiber; \((V,D)\) is klt, the relative anti-canonical divisor is nef, and \(B\) is ample, hence nef and big. The normalized decomposition in Lemma 2.4 may be taken as \(B_0=\operatorname{pr}_{\mathbb P^1}^*\mathcal O(1)\), \(B_W=\mathcal O_C(1)\). Consequently \[E_m=h_*\mathcal O_V(mB_0)\simeq\mathcal O_C^{\oplus(m+1)}.\] Choose the very ample divisor \(A=\mathcal O_C(1)=K_C\), which satisfies the choice made in the source. For \(d=i=1\), Serre duality gives \[h^1(C,E_m\otimes A)=(m+1)h^1(C,K_C)=m+1>0 .\] Thus all of the lemma’s geometric hypotheses and the displayed positivity of the twisted trivial bundle hold, but the cited vanishing does not.

This inference supplies Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity, uniform global generation, and ultimately nefness of \(B_0\). Lemma 4.4 is then used in Lemma 4.5 and explicitly in Theorem 4.12 on page 36. The Major classification concerns that written core inference; it does not assert that Lemma 4.4’s conclusion is false.

A local repair of this particular step is available. Choose a single very ample \(A\) with \(A-K_W\) ample, after the reduction to smooth \(W\). For \(1\le i\le d\), \((d+1-i)A-K_W\) is ample. Use the already established numerical flatness of \(E_m\), not an unqualified assertion about arbitrary flat bundles: its filtration by unitary flat quotients permits Kodaira–Nakano vanishing for each quotient twisted by this ample line bundle, and the resulting long exact sequences give the required vanishing for \(E_m\). This uses the same fixed \(A\) for every \(m\).

The relative basepoint-free step on page 29 should also use the klt pair \((V,D)\), the nefness of \(- (K_{V/W}+D)\), and sufficiently divisible multiples of the relatively nef and big \(B_0\). The hypothesis does not assert that \(-K_{V/W}\) itself is nef. This supplies the intended type of closing argument under the earlier numerical-flatness conclusions; it does not repair the false Lemma 4.5.
# A boundedness estimate with a missing factor
Problem 3 (Minor: Lemma 2.8, page 14).  The displayed estimate for \(e=\sum_{i=1}^m s_i\otimes f_i\) omits a factor \(m\).

For the identity morphism of a smooth disk, the trivial line bundle with its trivial metric, and \(s_1=s_2=f_1=f_2=1\), every hypothesis of Lemma 2.8 holds. The written inequality becomes \(4\le2\). The valid estimate is \[\left|\sum_i f_i s_i\right|^2
       \le m\sum_i |f_i|^2|s_i|^2.\] Alternatively one can use the product of the two sums of squared norms. This fixed local factor does not change local upper boundedness or the plurisubharmonic extension argument. It is therefore Minor and does not invalidate Lemma 2.8’s conclusion. Local generation of the pullback can be implemented after shrinking the neighborhoods; no global section-tensor identity on arbitrary large analytic open sets is needed.
# Further checks and limits

The quasi-etale reductions were checked at the stated level: normality and codimension-two complements enter the fundamental-group diagram in Theorem 2.12; the selected terminal model remains maximal. The example in Section 3.3 correctly warns that a quasi-etale cover can change the MRC fiber dimension. It is therefore essential to recompute the fibration after taking the cover, as the construction does.

The singular-metric discussion distinguishes locally free pullback from torsion-free pullback and supplies reflexivity and codimension hypotheses in Lemma 2.8. The metric comparison in Lemma 2.10 requires its exceptional potential adjustment; a curvature lower bound with a resolution metric cannot be pushed down unchanged as a bound by a fixed metric on the base. The direct-image normalization uses \(m/r\in\mathbb Z\) and a fixed large exceptional coefficient. Those restrictions were retained in checking Theorem 3.2.

The connection descent uses smooth rationally connected general fibers, so the needed vanishing of one-forms is applied there. No defect is asserted from a possible convention concerning torsion in differential sheaves on singular varieties in the introductory Theorem 2.2. Likewise, the selected connection associated with the numerical-flatness construction is not identified with every possible flat connection on the same holomorphic bundle.

In the local-constancy criterion, compatibility of the graded multiplication maps and the boundary ideal is substantive. Remark 2.6(c) reduces the needed data to finitely many degrees; the proof does not need removal of an uncontrolled countable union of codimension-two sets. The relative anti-canonical theorem and the later foliation results depend on several external positivity, semistable reduction, and integrability theorems. Their use and advertised hypotheses were traced, but those external proofs and the modifications described as carrying over are not independently certified here. The Calabi–Yau product consequence on page 4 likewise depends on the cited Ambro and Druel inputs.

Title: Seifert surfaces in the four-ball: diagrammatic and algebraic checks, a genus correction, and review limits
# Exact text and equivalence relations

The bound paper is Kyle Hayden, Seungwon Kim, Maggie Miller, JungHwan Park, and Isaac Sundberg, Seifert surfaces in the 4-ball, arXiv:2205.15283v3, uploaded on 2 May 2023 at 02:41:43 UTC [paper]. The supplied main PDF has 33 pages; the associated Additional documentation has five pages [supp]. Both complete texts, including references and the displayed software transcripts, were read. The arXiv record describes the v3 change as a correction to the floating of Figure 27. The journal association is DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1703; the publisher lists acceptance on 18 April 2025 and online publication on 29 September 2025 [journal]. Identity with that later published text was not established.

Three distinctions are essential throughout. A boundary-fixed isotopy is stronger than an ambient isotopy allowing motion on the boundary. A topological obstruction is stronger than a smooth obstruction. Minimal Seifert genus is asserted for some examples, whereas the Whitehead-double surfaces used for the simplest cobordism-map distinction need not be minimal. The report does not transfer a claim from one of these settings to another.

Theorem 1.3 and the intersection forms provide topological nonisotopy for the basic pair. For the Whitehead doubles, Alexander polynomial one and the cited topological classification supply topological isotopy relative to the boundary. The Khovanov maps then give a smooth distinction. Upgrading a boundary-fixed distinction to an unrestricted ambient distinction requires the separate symmetry argument or the asymmetric-knot construction; it does not follow solely from different maps for a chosen diagram.
# Independent algebraic checks
## The orientable branched covers

On page 21, the printed matrices are \[V_0=\begin{pmatrix}-6&-2\\-3&-2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 V_1=\begin{pmatrix}-6&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] Exact symbolic calculation gives \[\det(V_i-tV_i^T)=6t^2-11t+6,\qquad
 Q_0=V_0+V_0^T=\begin{pmatrix}-12&-5\\-5&-4\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 Q_1=\begin{pmatrix}-12&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}.\] Both forms have determinant 23 and are negative definite. The Alexander polynomial has span two, consistent with minimal genus one for the displayed genus-one surfaces. Figure 18 was subsequently inspected at enlarged resolution. Its framed links have diagonal framings \((-12,-4)\) and \((-12,-2)\); the signed mixed-crossing sums are \(-10\) and \(2\), giving off-diagonal linking numbers \(-5\) and \(1\). The shown basis curves intersect once. The doubled-band construction, together with this skew intersection, recovers the printed matrices, up to compatible basis orientations.

Equation reference: eq:square. The vector \((0,1)\) has square \(-2\) under \(Q_1\). Write \(q(m,n)=6m^2+5mn+2n^2\). Then \[
 8q(m,n)=(4n+5m)^2+23m^2.\] If \(q=1\), this identity forces \(m=0\), and then \(2n^2=1\) is impossible. The equation \(q=-1\) is impossible by nonnegativity. Thus \(Q_0\) represents neither \(2\) nor \(-2\). This includes the orientation-reversing possibility for a proposed homeomorphism of the branched covers. It verifies the integer obstruction in Theorem 4.1. The separate actual comparison of the coloured basis curves, doubled bands, and framed links supplies the previously unchecked diagrammatic input. The general branched-cover algorithm is used as the cited standard result; it is not reproved here.
## The nonorientable variant and the rank-one case

The forms printed in Remark 4.5 are \[R_0=\begin{pmatrix}-12&-5\\-5&-3\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 R_1=\begin{pmatrix}-12&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.\] They have determinant 11. The second represents \(-1\); the first does not, because \[12(12m^2+10mn+3n^2)=(6n+10m)^2+44m^2.\] For a value \(1\), this forces \(m=0\), followed by \(3n^2=1\); a negative value is again excluded.

For Corollary 4.6, a one-minimum ribbon Möbius band gives the stated single-two-handle branched-cover description. Figure 21 was actually inspected: the disk and nonorientable band lift to the displayed single trefoil handle, with framing \(9\) in that example. In the general one-minimum case the form is \([\pm\det J]\). When \(\det J>1\), no integer vector has square \(1\) or \(-1\), excluding a projective-plane summand by the indicated branched-cover argument. The pretzel determinant computation also checks: \[\left|(2n)(-2n-1)+(-2n-1)(2n+1)+(2n)(2n+1)\right|
 =(2n+1)^2\quad(n\geq1).\]
## What the Frobenius algebra does and does not verify

Over \(\mathbb F_2\), take \(A=\mathbb F_2[x]/(x^2)\) with \[\Delta(1)=1\otimes x+x\otimes1,\quad
 \Delta(x)=x\otimes x,\quad
 \epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(x)=1.\] Then \(\mu(x\otimes x)=0\) and \(\mu\Delta=0\) on both basis vectors. These exact identities support the algebraic mechanisms in Propositions 3.1 and 3.5: merging two \(x\)-labeled components kills the generator, and an added handle kills the cobordism map. The calculation was performed independently as matrices over \(\mathbb F_2\).

The geometric input was checked separately in the continuation. All five rows of Figure 11 and the three local models in Figure 12 were actually inspected at enlarged resolution. A further 400-dpi crop makes the gray \(0\)-resolution bands of the initial state legible: each joins distinct resolved components. Thus every outgoing differential on the all-\(x\) state vanishes. Following the pictured saddles and Reidemeister moves keeps the all-\(x\) term with coefficient one and ends in disk boundaries; each final counit is \(\epsilon(x)=1\). The complementary surface admits a saddle merging distinct \(x\)-components and hence gives zero. This checks the specific state and movie using the standard cited Reidemeister chain maps; no Khovanov program was run.

For the Whitehead double, the three Figure 12 models have compatible paired-sheet resolutions, and the clasp removes an \(x\)-labelled circle with coefficient one. Figure 13 supplies the complementary zero-producing saddle. The doubled quasipositive models in Figure 15 and the trefoil extension in Figure 17 were also traced. In particular, the nonzero movie value is not inferred solely from the abstract identity \(\mu\Delta=0\). That identity separately shows why a stabilized surface has zero map over \(\mathbb F_2\).
# Confirmed finding

Problem 1 (Minor: genus after stabilization).  Page 22, Remark 4.4, first sentence, describes adding a tube to each of the genus-one, one-boundary-component surfaces \(\Sigma_0,\Sigma_1\) and calls the resulting surfaces genus one. The genus must be two.

For either original surface, \(\chi(\Sigma_i)=2-2(1)-1=-1\). An interior tube removes two disks and inserts an annulus. Consequently the new Euler characteristic is \(-3\), and the boundary still has one component: \[-3=2-2g-1,\qquad g=2.\] This calculation uses exactly the operation stated in the remark. It is not a conjectural objection about the drawing. The same wording is present in the official version-specific HTML.

The correction is to replace genus-1 by genus-2 in this sentence. The statement about stabilization distance one is consistent with genus two and need not be changed on this account. Figure 19 has now been inspected. Its intermediate band movie allows the endpoints to slide on the surgered link, after which the other three bands are restored. This is consistent with the stated relative-boundary isotopy in the four-ball. The correction remains a local genus misstatement, not evidence against the main nonisotopy theorems.
# Proof dependencies and coverage limits
## Satellites, symmetry, and minimal genus

The genus comparison in Proposition 2.5 has the required strict inequality: removing two copies of a single-boundary-component subsurface of genus \(f\geq1\) and reconnecting by an annulus changes the genus by \(-2f+1<0\). The single boundary component matters for the connectivity and Euler-characteristic calculation.

Proposition 2.6 supplies the special meridional-torus-twist isotopy for the satellites in question. It is not a statement that all torus twists of arbitrary Seifert surfaces become boundary-fixed isotopies. Proposition 2.9 analyzes the relevant knot symmetries and is used to extend boundary motion over the surface pair. Figures 8–10 were actually inspected: the outer parallel sheets can be untwisted through the product region in the four-ball, and the pictured half-turn representatives preserve the two surface pieces. The exhaustion of all boundary symmetries still uses the cited JSJ classification. The extension across a collar in Proposition 2.10 is compatible with a time reparametrization constant near the inner end of the collar.

The strongly quasipositive construction in Theorem 1.6 distinguishes a non-destabilizable surface from a stabilized one. This is an intrinsic distinction and avoids identifying maps after an arbitrary boundary symmetry. The specified genus is \(2g(J)\); minimal genus is not asserted for that pair.
## The ancillary computations

The five-page supplement contains substantial supporting information: Dowker–Thistlethwaite input, a genus computation, a hyperbolic symmetry argument, and a finite-slope loop. It is therefore incorrect to describe the paper as having no computational support. All five supplementary pages, including Figures A–C and every displayed command, were actually inspected. The crossing circle in Figure C surrounds the connecting band; its \((1,-n)\) filling has the stated full-twist interpretation. None of the author’s commands was executed during this review.

Proposition A.1 uses the computed genus-three base case together with the band-sum genus inequality and its equality case. The argument for the family depends on that base case, not merely on the existence of a genus-three Seifert surface.

In Section B, the systole bound, the normalized-length threshold, and the finite list of exceptional slopes play different roles. Using the printed cusp area \(18.8600\ldots\), the numerical ratio \(46/\sqrt{18.86}\) is about \(10.59\), still larger than \(10.1\). The text’s rounded use of \(18.6\) therefore does not defeat the required numerical separation. This arithmetic is conditional on the actual cusp-area and slope computations.

The supplement explicitly uses `verified=True` for the short-slope and canonical-retriangulation computations, while displaying ordinary length-spectrum and cusp-area calls for the preliminary bounds. Current official documentation distinguishes floating-point output from verified output, and notes that `verify_hyperbolicity` returns a success Boolean [snappy]. report: Abstract: Five Major proof issues are established in the bound first preprint: the Thue-inequality lemma omits a necessary finite-type restriction; the cubic-surface upper argument loses logarithmic factors; its lower argument can select only excluded zero points; the partial-two-torsion argument uses a field that need not be Galois; and the moment proof does not respect the stated range of its exponential-moment input. Each issue is supported by an explicit example or a quantified calculation. Three additional local errors are recorded. These findings do not constitute counterexamples to the principal density theorems. Some repairs can be carried through algebraically, while others require a replacement estimate or a new argument.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Quadratic twists and integral points: auxiliary counting statements and hypothesis checks
# Bound source and theorem scope

The reviewed source is Tim Browning and Stephanie Chan, Almost all quadratic twists of an elliptic curve have no integral points, arXiv:2401.04375v1, uploaded on 9 January 2024 at 06:29:39 UTC [paper]. The supplied 38-page PDF internally prints 10 January 2024. All 38 pages, including references, were read as extracted text. Version-specific official HTML was used to corroborate the disputed formulas; its generated date in 2026 is not an author revision.

The associated DOI is 10.4171/JEMS/1704. The publisher records acceptance on 20 June 2025 and online publication on 17 September 2025 [journal]. The later journal text was not compared with the supplied first preprint; no finding below is automatically attributed to that later text. The author’s publication pages and the arXiv record were searched for supplementary material and code. No separate exact-version supplement, repository, or erratum was located in that bounded search. No author code was executed.

The family is the fixed integral short Weierstrass model \[E_D:\quad y^2=x^3+AD^2x+BD^3,\qquad D\text{ square-free},\] with fixed integers \(A,B\) and \(4A^3+27B^2\neq0\). The counting statements exclude the affine two-torsion points; their presence is not a counterexample. The model \(Dy^2=x^3+Ax+B\) has a different set of integral points. The irreducible cubic case is unconditional. Full rational two-torsion is also treated unconditionally. The partial case is unconditional in the two subcases specified in Theorem 2.3, and otherwise uses a weak Hall–Lang hypothesis uniform in the changing coefficients. The report preserves these distinctions.
# The core Thue bound

Problem 1 (Major: Lemma 5.5 is false, including on the constructed image).  Page 15, Lemma 5.5 and its proof, assert a uniform finite bound for all integral pairs satisfying \(|F(X,Y)|\leq m\) when \(F\) is an integral binary form with nonzero discriminant. These assumptions allow infinitely many such pairs.

Take the nonsingular curve \(E:y^2=x^3+2x+1\) and its nontorsion-or-torsion unrestricted integral point \(P=(1,2)\); in particular \(y(P)\neq0\), so this point is not two-torsion. In Lemma 5.1 take \(D=M=1\) and \(k=0\), which satisfies the congruence modulo one. Equations (5.3)–(5.4) give \[F_P(X,Y)=X^4-6X^2Y^2+16XY^3-11Y^4
 =(X-Y)(X^3+X^2Y-5XY^2+11Y^3).\] Its invariants are \(I=-8\), \(J=-4\), and \(I^3-27J^2=-944\neq0\); its ordinary polynomial discriminant is \(-241664\). Nevertheless \(F_P(t,t)=0\) for every \(t\in\mathbb Z\). For every \(m\geq1\), the set counted in Lemma 5.5 is infinite. All assumptions hold, and the example occurs in the precise quartic construction used subsequently.

Thunder’s Theorem 2 requires finite type, which includes finiteness on nontrivial rational subspaces, not only finiteness of the two-dimensional area [thunder]. Here the line \(X=Y\) has infinite restricted measure. Thus the citation does not justify the assertion that checking the area alone suffices.

Equation (5.17), Lemma 5.6, and the final small-gcd estimates invoke this lemma. This is a Major defect in that proof chain. The points actually needed there have \(F(\alpha,\beta)=M\neq0\), and the transformed vector is primitive. These facts suggest a narrower replacement statement, but neither fact makes Lemma 5.5 true as printed. In particular, restricting to forms without rational linear factors would discard the example above from the image. A repair must prove or cite a suitable uniform bound for the required nonzero values, with all reducible quartics that arise included. Such a replacement was not established by this review; the density theorem itself has not been disproved.
# The cubic-surface count

Problem 2 (Major: logarithmic factors are lost in Lemma 3.5).  Page 9, the first displayed estimate in the proof of Lemma 3.5, claims \(\sum_{U\leq|u|<2U}f(|u|)\ll U\) from Lemma 3.2. For the allowed reducible cubics this is false.

Choose \[C(x_1,x_2)=x_1(x_1-x_2)(x_1+x_2).\] It is separable, \(C(1,0)=1\), and \(\Delta(C)=4\). For every odd prime \(p\) and \(v\geq1\), the function in (3.12) has \(f(p^v)=3\). Thus for odd \(n\), \(f(n)=3^{\omega(n)}\). The three-factor case of (3.6), equivalently its Euler-product mean-value calculation, gives \(\sum_{n\leq T}f(n)\asymp T(\log T)^2\). If the printed dyadic bound held for all \(U\), summing dyadically would instead give \(O(T)\), a contradiction. This is an asymptotic contradiction for one fixed allowed cubic, not a numerical estimate of an unknown constant.

The appropriate general bound at this step is \(U(\log(2U))^{\lambda-1}\). There is a second bookkeeping point: the next displayed estimate contains \(f(h_2)B/(h_1h_2)\), so its subsequent sum over \(h_1\) also contributes a harmonic logarithm. Retaining these factors in the written argument yields the conservative upper bound \[N^\circ(B)\ll B(\log(2B))^{2\lambda},\qquad \lambda=1,2,3.\] Indeed the first term has exponent \((\lambda-1)+1+\lambda=2\lambda\), while the second has exponent \((\lambda-1)+2=\lambda+1\leq2\lambda\). This does not prove the sharper stated exponent \(\max\{\lambda,2\}\) in Theorem 1.4.

The effect on the main density strategy can be bounded. Using this weaker cubic estimate in the remainder of Lemma 5.6 would give logarithmic exponents \(3,6,7\) for \(\lambda=1,2,3\), respectively, after including the stated \(r=0\) exceptions. For full two-torsion one could then choose the large-gcd cutoff parameter \(15\) in place of \(13\), giving \(7-15/2=-1/2\). This shows a possible route to preserve the main logarithmic density saving, conditional on repairing the other inputs. It does not repair Theorem 1.4 as stated or certify the exact exponent \(6\) in the full-torsion version of Lemma 5.6.

Problem 3 (Major: the lower-bound construction can lie entirely on the deleted lines).  Page 9, Lemma 3.6, passes from a nonzero short lattice vector obtained by Minkowski’s theorem to a contribution to \(N^\circ(B)\). Nonzero vectors need not have \(C(x_1,x_2)\neq0\), and the required coprimality is not supplied either.

Use the same separable cubic and an odd integer \(q=x_3\). The allowed root \(\alpha=0\bmod q^2\) produces the lattice \[\Lambda_q=\mathbb Z(q^2,0)+\mathbb Z(0,1).\] For any fixed constant \(c>0\) and \(q>c\), a vector in \(\Lambda_q\) with \(\max(|x_1|,|x_2|)\leq cq\) must have \(x_1=0\). Hence \(C(x_1,x_2)=0\) and the resulting \(x_4=0\), which is excluded by Theorem 1.4. For prime \(q>2c\), the other two roots \(1,-1\) similarly force \(x_1=x_2\) or \(x_1=-x_2\) throughout that box. Thus none of the three root lattices at such a prime supplies the admissible point claimed by the construction.

The exact finite check \(q=101\), \(c=10\) illustrates the first case; the argument above proves the obstruction for arbitrarily large \(q\). Minkowski’s theorem is not being contradicted: the short nonzero vectors exist, but lie on excluded lines. The lower estimate in Theorem 1.4 requires a new admissible construction, including coprimality and multiplicity control. The lower estimate for the elliptic-twist density has a separate proof in Lemma 5.8 using square-free values, and is not disproved by this issue.
# The partial-two-torsion field

Problem 4 (Major: the fields in Section 8 do not meet the Galois hypothesis).  Page 33 defines \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{A^2-4B})\), \(\alpha=(-A+\sqrt{A^2-4B})/2\), and \(L=K(\sqrt\alpha)\). The Artin-symbol description uses \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)\) and \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K(\sqrt B))\). Page 35 then applies Theorem 6.1 with \(K_{21}=K\) and \(\alpha_{21}=\alpha R_{21}\). The claimed Galois setup need not exist.

In the model (8.1), take \(A=0\), \(B=-2\). The curve is \(y^2=x(x^2-2)\), and \(A^2-4B=8\) is not a rational square, as required. Then \[K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2),\qquad \alpha=\sqrt2,\qquad
 L=\mathbb Q(\sqrt[4]2).\] The polynomial \(T^4-2\) is Eisenstein at \(2\). Its real root generates a real field that omits the conjugates \(\pm i\sqrt[4]2\); hence \(L/\mathbb Q\) is not Galois. Moreover \(\sqrt B=\sqrt{-2}\notin L\), so \(K(\sqrt B)\) is not even a subfield of \(L\). The displayed relative Galois group is consequently undefined.

The failure also reaches the actual theorem invocation. The admissible fixed parameter choice \(\delta=\gamma_1=\gamma_2=\widetilde D=1\) has \(R_{21}=1\). Then \(K_{21}(\sqrt{\alpha_{21}})=L\) violates the explicit Galois assumption of Theorem 6.1. This concerns an allowed partial-two-torsion curve, including a subcase intended to be unconditional.

A natural repair starts from \(K'=K(\sqrt B)\) and \(L'=K'(\sqrt\alpha)\), which contains both conjugate square roots and is a splitting field over \(\mathbb Q\). The character must be defined on the primes splitting in \(K'\), with its support, discriminant bound, and parameters in Theorem 6.1 checked again. The non-square-root cases need not be declared false; rather, the written Galois/character argument does not apply as specified. This repair was identified, but the full revised character-sum proof was not independently completed.
# Moment quantifiers

Problem 5 (Major: the range of Theorem 2.5 is not respected).  Page 5, the proof of Theorem 2.4 sets \(m=qk\sigma\log c\) and then \(q=1/\varepsilon\). It uses \(m\ll\log\log\log N\) as if this implied \(m<C'\log\log\log N\), the actual hypothesis on page 4. These are different quantified bounds.

This is a Major gap in the stated uniform moment conclusion, not a counterexample to its truth. The same calculation allows the argument on a smaller range such as \[k\leq \frac{C'\varepsilon}{2a}\log\log\log N,\] subject also to a valid normalization of the moment input. A stronger input or a separate argument is required to recover coefficient one for every prescribed loss. The density theorems do not depend on this later moment-upgrading argument.

Problem 6 (Minor: the asserted small-\(m\) normalization is impossible).  Page 4, Theorem 2.5 asserts the exponential-moment bound with right side \(\exp(Cm^2)\) for every \(m>0\) in its range. For a family with any positive-rank member, this fails as \(m\downarrow0\).

Take \(E:y^2=x^3-2\). Its point \((3,5)\) is not torsion: doubling gives \(x(2P)=129/100\), whereas rational torsion points on an integral short Weierstrass equation have integral coordinates by the Nagell–Lutz theorem. For fixed sufficiently large \(N\), let \(M=\#\mathcal D(N)\). Since \(D=1\) is present, the mean in Theorem 2.5 is at least \[1+\frac{e^m-1}{M}.\] The derivative of this expression at zero is \(1/M>0\); the derivative of \(e^{Cm^2}\) is zero. The inequality therefore fails for all sufficiently small positive \(m\), which are within the required upper range. The same small-\(m\) wording occurs in the consulted cited theorem; it is not used here to invalidate all large-\(m\) moment information.

An input with a fixed prefactor, an exponent \(C(m+m^2)\), or an explicit lower restriction on \(m\) avoids this particular obstruction. The application’s \(m\) is bounded away from zero, so this local normalization error is separate from the Major endpoint-range issue above.
# Two further local corrections

Problem 7 (Minor: the numerical choice of \(\varepsilon\) in Lemma 8.4).  Page 35 chooses \(\varepsilon=5/8\) to change an error exponent \(-1/2+\varepsilon\) to \(-1/8\). The actual value is \(+1/8\).

The exact correction \(\varepsilon=3/8\) gives \(-1/8\). Since the preceding estimate allows any positive \(\varepsilon\), this correction restores the intended numerical step, conditional on the corrected field setup. No separate deterioration of the intended final exponent is forced by this arithmetic error.

Problem 8 (Minor: the displayed short Weierstrass model in Section 8.2).  Page 37, the proof of Theorem 8.1, omits twist powers and uses the old variable in the equation following \((X,Y)=(9x+3AD,27y)\).

Direct expansion gives the correct identity \[Y^2=X^3+27(3B-A^2)D^2X+
             27A(2A^2-9B)D^3.\] For the allowed example \(A=-4\), \(B=2\), \(D=2\) and \((x,y)=(1,1)\), one has \(A^2-4B=8\) and \((X,Y)=(-15,27)\). The corrected right side is \(729=Y^2\). The printed right side is \(-5157\) if its \(x\) is taken literally, or \(-837\) if read as \(X\). This is an actual integral point satisfying the original hypotheses.

The corrected expression has fixed integral coefficients multiplying \(D^2\) and \(D^3\), and \(\gcd(X,D)\mid9\gcd(x,D)\) still holds. Thus the intended reduction to the same fixed twist-family setting is recovered by the explicit algebraic correction; this local display error is not an additional obstruction to that reduction.
# Other checks and limits

The independent script verifies the full quartic seminvariant identity \[4H^3-Ia^2H-Ja^3-R^2=0\] using the definitions on page 11. The Hensel argument in Lemma 5.1 correctly needs odd \(M\) and invertible \(x_0\); these follow from \(\gcd(M,2x_0)=1\). In the large-gcd irreducible case, square-freeness gives \(g^2\mid y\) from \(g^3\mid y^2\), and \(\gcd(g,\widetilde D)=1\) makes the root congruence valid. The fixed-point proportions \(2/3\) for \(S_3\) and \(1/3\) for \(C_3\) give the asserted prime-density upper bound.

The linked-index analysis distinguishes double-oscillation estimates from the small-conductor Hecke-character step. An independent exact graph enumeration verifies maximum unlinked size four for the twelve indices in Section 7.1, and size eight for the thirty-two indices in Section 7.3. All size-eight sets in the latter computation use at most two first-index rows, as required for containment in one of the specified excluded sets. This checks the combinatorics, not the full analytic estimates.

The Pell reductions keep the square-free product and positivity restrictions; \(cd>ab\) excludes the simultaneous square case in the cited step. In Section 8 the exceptional positive, nonsquare-\(B\) points are controlled only under the displayed height restriction. Applying a uniform weak Hall–Lang bound makes that restriction automatic eventually, since \(N^{1-\eta}=o(N/(\log N)^c)\) for fixed \(\eta,c>0\). No unproved Hall–Lang assertion is treated as an unconditional theorem.

The manuscript’s remaining analytic and arithmetic foundations, including the full Cremona reduction, square-free-value theorem, simultaneous-Pell estimate, and Hecke-character estimates, were not re-proved from first principles. The exact source has been read; that is not a claim of exhaustive independent certification of every cited result. The identified gaps are sufficient to require substantial proof revision of this version, without asserting that the main density results are false.

The exact check script, source excerpts, external primary passages, compiler invocation, dependency cache, PDF text parse, and rendered pages are retained with hashes. The finite dyadic counts illustrate the logarithmic growth; the asymptotic contradiction uses the proved mean-value relation, not those finite samples. The original `EMFILE` failures and false visual flags are preserved. In the same-conversation continuation, all 33 selected source evidence pages were actually displayed through the documented native image output and checked against the report. This includes the exact moment quantifiers, both cubic-count arguments, the quartic construction and Thue bound, the Galois hypotheses and their later instantiation, and the two local formula errors. No scientific finding changed as a result of these page checks.

The previous report is retained, and this updated TeX is genuinely recompiled using the approved runtime and the paper’s own retained dependencies. The command, exit status, source/TeX/compiler and dependency hashes, resulting PDF, and actual inspection of every current report page are bound in the continuation records. Scientific decision remains pending and human reviews are empty. Delivery completion records an initial-review package within the stated scientific limits; it is not independent acceptance.

Hence \(C(x_1,x_2)=0\) and the resulting \(x_4=0\), which is excluded by Theorem 1.4. For prime \(q>2c\), the other two roots \(1,-1\) similarly force \(x_1=x_2\) or \(x_1=-x_2\) throughout that box. Thus none of the three root lattices at such a prime supplies the admissible point claimed by the construction.

The exact finite check \(q=101\), \(c=10\) illustrates the first case; the argument above proves the obstruction for arbitrarily large \(q\). Minkowski’s theorem is not being contradicted: the short nonzero vectors exist, but lie on excluded lines. The lower estimate in Theorem 1.4 requires a new admissible construction, including coprimality and multiplicity control. The lower estimate for the elliptic-twist density has a separate proof in Lemma 5.8 using square-free values, and is not disproved by this issue.
result: Impact: The claimed lower-bound proof for Theorem 1.4 counts inadmissible vectors. The main elliptic-family lower bound has a separate Lemma 5.8 argument and is not refuted.

problems.title: the fields in Section 8 do not meet the Galois hypothesis
problems.source_location: PDF pp.33-35, definition L=K(sqrt(alpha)), Artin symbols, Lemma 8.4 application of Theorem 6.1
claim: Specified L/Q and K21(sqrt(alpha21))/Q are Galois and contain K(sqrt(B)).
analysis: Page 33 defines \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{A^2-4B})\), \(\alpha=(-A+\sqrt{A^2-4B})/2\), and \(L=K(\sqrt\alpha)\). The Artin-symbol description uses \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/\mathbb Q)\) and \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K(\sqrt B))\). Page 35 then applies Theorem 6.1 with \(K_{21}=K\) and \(\alpha_{21}=\alpha R_{21}\). The claimed Galois setup need not exist.

In the model (8.1), take \(A=0\), \(B=-2\). The curve is \(y^2=x(x^2-2)\), and \(A^2-4B=8\) is not a rational square, as required. Then \[K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2),\qquad \alpha=\sqrt2,\qquad
 L=\mathbb Q(\sqrt[4]2).\] The polynomial \(T^4-2\) is Eisenstein at \(2\). Its real root generates a real field that omits the conjugates \(\pm i\sqrt[4]2\); hence \(L/\mathbb Q\) is not Galois. Moreover \(\sqrt B=\sqrt{-2}\notin L\), so \(K(\sqrt B)\) is not even a subfield of \(L\). The displayed relative Galois group is consequently undefined.

The failure also reaches the actual theorem invocation. The admissible fixed parameter choice \(\delta=\gamma_1=\gamma_2=\widetilde D=1\) has \(R_{21}=1\). Then \(K_{21}(\sqrt{\alpha_{21}})=L\) violates the explicit Galois assumption of Theorem 6.1. This concerns an allowed partial-two-torsion curve, including a subcase intended to be unconditional.

A natural repair starts from \(K'=K(\sqrt B)\) and \(L'=K'(\sqrt\alpha)\), which contains both conjugate square roots and is a splitting field over \(\mathbb Q\). The character must be defined on the primes splitting in \(K'\), with its support, discriminant bound, and parameters in Theorem 6.1 checked again. The non-square-root cases need not be declared false; rather, the written Galois/character argument does not apply as specified. This repair was identified, but the full revised character-sum proof was not independently completed.
result: Impact: Undefined relative Galois group and invalid stated character-sum instantiation in the partial-torsion density argument.

problems.title: the range of Theorem 2.5 is not respected
problems.source_location: PDF pp.4-6, Theorem 2.5 range and proof of Theorem 2.4
claim: m=O(logloglog N) suffices for the strict fixed-multiplier range m<Cprime logloglog N when k<=logloglog N and q=1/epsilon.
analysis: Page 5, the proof of Theorem 2.4 sets \(m=qk\sigma\log c\) and then \(q=1/\varepsilon\). It uses \(m\ll\log\log\log N\) as if this implied \(m<C'\log\log\log N\), the actual hypothesis on page 4. These are different quantified bounds.

This is a Major gap in the stated uniform moment conclusion, not a counterexample to its truth. The same calculation allows the argument on a smaller range such as \[k\leq \frac{C'\varepsilon}{2a}\log\log\log N,\] subject also to a valid normalization of the moment input. A stronger input or a separate argument is required to recover coefficient one for every prescribed loss. The density theorems do not depend on this later moment-upgrading argument.
result: Impact: Uniform endpoint moments in Theorem 2.4 and their stated application are not justified by this invocation. No counterexample to the conclusion is asserted.

problems.title: the asserted small-\(m\) normalization is impossible
problems.source_location: PDF p.4, Theorem 2.5 universal m>0 normalization
claim: The moment is <=exp(C m^2) for every sufficiently small positive m.
analysis: Page 4, Theorem 2.5 asserts the exponential-moment bound with right side \(\exp(Cm^2)\) for every \(m>0\) in its range. For a family with any positive-rank member, this fails as \(m\downarrow0\).

Take \(E:y^2=x^3-2\). Its point \((3,5)\) is not torsion: doubling gives \(x(2P)=129/100\), whereas rational torsion points on an integral short Weierstrass equation have integral coordinates by the Nagell–Lutz theorem. For fixed sufficiently large \(N\), let \(M=\#\mathcal D(N)\). Since \(D=1\) is present, the mean in Theorem 2.5 is at least \[1+\frac{e^m-1}{M}.\] The derivative of this expression at zero is \(1/M>0\); the derivative of \(e^{Cm^2}\) is zero. The inequality therefore fails for all sufficiently small positive \(m\), which are within the required upper range. The same small-\(m\) wording occurs in the consulted cited theorem; it is not used here to invalidate all large-\(m\) moment information.

An input with a fixed prefactor, an exponent \(C(m+m^2)\), or an explicit lower restriction on \(m\) avoids this particular obstruction. The application’s \(m\) is bounded away from zero, so this local normalization error is separate from the Major endpoint-range issue above.
result: Impact: Small-m formulation is false; the later intended m is bounded away from zero. Separate from P5.

problems.title: the numerical choice of \(\varepsilon\) in Lemma 8.4

No separate deterioration of the intended final exponent is forced by this arithmetic error.

problems.title: the displayed short Weierstrass model in Section 8.2

Direct expansion gives the correct identity \[Y^2=X^3+27(3B-A^2)D^2X+

report: Abstract: Two Major issues affect the proof of the higher-dimensional classification in the bound author manuscript. Its stated Bochner inequality fails on an explicit positive entire solution with the prescribed normalization. The subsequent annular integration by parts omits an inner-boundary flux; a translated solution makes the omitted contribution strictly positive in the upper estimate. Two local normalization errors are also recorded. These findings do not disprove either classification conclusion. The weighted argument in homogeneous dimension four was checked separately, with the stated limitations concerning its external rigidity input.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: A Liouville theorem in the Heisenberg group: normalization and boundary terms
# Source, assumptions, and scope

This report concerns the 23-page CVGMT-hosted manuscript by Giovanni Catino, Yanyan Li, Dario D. Monticelli, and Alberto Roncoroni, A Liouville theorem in the Heisenberg group [paper]. The exact source has 438267 bytes and SHA256 \[\text{\textnormal{
7d4636e5a79dcc6e4d8a0f4a57b547417de162a7b1ca73d4f772cc8bffb2cb05}}.\] All 23 pages, including references, were read as extracted text. CVGMT labels its record an accepted paper and gives 27 November 2024 as the record’s update date. That date is not an authenticated revision date for this PDF. Exact alignment with the accepted version, with arXiv:2310.10469, or with the journal version was not established. The associated journal DOI is 10.4171/JEMS/1705; the publisher records online publication on 15 September 2025 [journal]. Findings below are attributed only to the bound CVGMT file.

The equation is \[-\Delta_{\mathbb H^n}u=2n^2u^{1+2/n},\qquad u>0\quad\hbox{on }\mathbb H^n.\] Theorem 1.1 treats \(n=1\) without a finite-energy or symmetry assumption. Theorem 1.2 treats \(n\geq2\) under \(u(\xi)\leq C/(1+|\xi|^n)\). This borderline decay alone need not give finite critical energy. No unconditional classification in every dimension is attributed to Theorem 1.2.

In the manuscript’s convention, \[X_j=\partial_{x_j}+2y_j\partial_t,\quad
 Y_j=\partial_{y_j}-2x_j\partial_t,\quad
 \Delta_{\mathbb H^n}=\tfrac12\sum_j(X_j^2+Y_j^2),\quad
 |\nabla f|^2=\tfrac12\sum_j((X_jf)^2+(Y_jf)^2).\] Thus \(|\nabla f|^2=2|\partial f|^2\). Writing \(f=n^{-1}\log u\) gives \[\Delta_{\mathbb H^n}f=-n|\nabla f|^2-2ne^{2f},\qquad
 g=|\partial f|^2+e^{2f}-if_0,\quad f_0=\partial_tf.\] The factors of two matter in both findings below.
# A false Bochner input

u\), is \[
 \Delta_{\mathbb H^n}|

  rac{(\Delta_{\mathbb H^n}f)^2}{n}+nf_0^2+
 2\langle
abla f,
abla\Delta_{\mathbb H^n}fangle

abla f_0|^2.\] It is false even when \(f\) is obtained from a positive solution satisfying the assumptions of Proposition 4.1.

Take \(n=2\), put \(\rho=|z|^2\) and \(S=(1+\rho)^2+t^2\), and set \[u=S^{-1},\qquad f=-\tfrac12\log S.\] Direct differentiation gives \(-\Delta_{\mathbb H^2}u=8u^2\) identically. The function is smooth and positive on the entire group and satisfies \(u\leq1\) everywhere. In particular, the local upper bound in Proposition 4.1 holds with center zero, \(R=1\), and \(a=1\).

At \(z=(1/2,0)\), \(t=0\), and \(\nu=5/4\), the relevant exact quantities are \[\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{quantity}&\text{value}\\ \hline
|\nabla f|^2&8/25\\
|\nabla f_0|^2&128/625\\

These computations were independently executed symbolically with rational arithmetic. One implementation used, for a radial function \(h(\rho,t)\), \[\Delta_{\mathbb H^n}h=2\rho(h_{\rho\rho}+h_{tt})+2nh_\rho,\quad
 \langle\nabla f,\nabla h\rangle
 =2\rho(f_\rho h_\rho+f_th_t).\] A second implementation differentiated the real fields \(X_j,Y_j\) directly in all four horizontal variables. Both gave the displayed values, and the equation for \(u\) was checked as an identity, not just at the selected point. Thus this is not a test function that fails the governing differential equation.

Equation (4.4) is used to obtain the differential inequality for the maximum-principle quantity in Proposition 4.1. That proposition supplies the gradient decay required in Theorem 1.2. The defect therefore affects a core proof dependency. A repaired proof must derive a Bochner inequality with constants consistent with these vector fields and then redo the torsion absorption and barrier estimates. No complete replacement argument is claimed here. The example is itself a classified bubble, so it does not contradict the proposed classification.
# The inner boundary of the annulus

Problem 2 (Major: equation (4.9) through (4.10), page 18).  The proof of Theorem 1.2 integrates by parts over \(A_R=B_R\setminus B_{R/2}\) using a cutoff \(\eta\) equal to one on \(B_{R/2}\). The multiplier \(\eta^{s-2}\) therefore does not vanish on the inner boundary. The displayed integration-by-parts equality omits that boundary contribution.

Equation reference: divfield. The missing term need not be zero or have a sign that permits its removal in an upper bound. For the \(n=2\) bubble of the preceding section, direct calculation gives \[
 \operatorname{Re}\sum_\alpha Z_{\bar\alpha}V_\alpha
   =\frac{2(\rho^2-1-t^2)}{((1+\rho)^2+t^2)^3}.\] This identity was checked with the actual complex vector fields. Translate this bubble by the group element \((z_0,0)\) with \(z_0=(10,0)\), and take \(R=2\). It remains a positive entire solution and satisfies the decay hypothesis of Theorem 1.2 for some finite constant. On the inner Koranyi ball \(B_1\) about zero, its coordinates relative to its center satisfy \[|z'|\geq9,\qquad |t'|\leq1+20=21.\] The numerator factor in [divfield] (#divfield) is consequently bounded below by \[|z'|^4-1-(t')^2\geq9^4-1-21^2=6119>0.\] The integral of the divergence over \(B_1\) is strictly positive. The inner boundary has the opposite orientation as a boundary component of \(A_2\), so the annular inner flux is strictly negative. Its subtraction in the integration-by-parts formula adds a strictly positive term. The displayed equality on page 18 omits exactly this contribution.

This refutes the integration identity used to reach (4.10). It does not, by itself, prove that every possible inequality with an unspecified constant in (4.10) is false. The current proof supplies neither the omitted flux nor a bound for it. A possible repair is to introduce a cutoff vanishing at both boundaries of a larger annulus and keep every resulting derivative term; the required estimates and absorptions would then have to be proved. The compactly supported integration over the whole ball in Section 3 does not incur this particular boundary error. The present finding is independent of the Bochner coefficient problem.
# Two local normalization corrections

Problem 3 (Minor: the amplitude in equation (1.3), page 2).  For \[U_{\lambda,\mu}(z,t)=
 \frac{C}{|t+i|z|^2+z\cdot\mu+\lambda|^n},\qquad
 \operatorname{Im}\lambda>|\mu|^2/4,\] the amplitude is written as \(C=C(n,\lambda)\). It also depends on \(\mu\).

In the stated normalization the required amplitude is \[C=(\operatorname{Im}\lambda-|\mu|^2/4)^{n/2}.\] Indeed, complete the square with \(z'=z+i\overline\mu/2\) and \(t'=t+\operatorname{Re}(z\cdot\mu)+\operatorname{Re}\lambda\). The remaining scale is \(a=\operatorname{Im}\lambda-|\mu|^2/4>0\). For an explicit check, take \(n=1\), \(\lambda=i\), and evaluate at the origin. With \(\mu=0\), the equation requires \(C^2=1\); with \(\mu=1\), it requires \(C^2=3/4\). Both choices satisfy the positivity constraint, and the corresponding values of \(-\Delta_{\mathbb H^1}U(0)\) are respectively \(2C\) and \(3C/2\), while \(2U(0)^3=2C^3\) in each case. This corrects the parametrization without producing an extra solution outside the intended bubble family.
Problem 4 (Minor: equations (1.4)–(1.5), page 2).  The Euclidean background equation has coefficient \(n(n-2)/4\), whereas its displayed bubble has the normalization for coefficient \(n(n-2)\).

For \(n\geq3\) and \[V(x)=\left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda^2+|x-x_0|^2}\right)^{(n-2)/2},\] one has \(-\Delta V=n(n-2)V^{(n+2)/(n-2)}\). Already \(n=3\), \(\lambda=1\), and \(x=x_0=0\) give \(-\Delta V(0)=3\), against the printed right side \(3/4\). Either multiply \(V\) by \(2^{(n-2)/2}\) or replace the coefficient in (1.4) by \(n(n-2)\). This is a local background normalization error; the Heisenberg proof does not rely on that displayed Euclidean parametrization.
# Coverage of the remaining proof

The definitions and contractions in Section 2 were followed with the manuscript’s derivative order and with repeated indices summed. The equation for \(f\), the relation \(f_{\alpha\bar\alpha}=-ng\), and the positivity \(|g|\geq e^{2f}\) were checked. The Jerison–Lee identity in Proposition 2.1 is used as an external differential identity; its long expansion and the rigidity conclusion from its vanishing were not independently reconstructed in full.

For \(n=1\), the weighted integral argument was checked separately from Section 4. Its weight \(\Psi=|g|^2e^{-2f}\) is positive. The vector-field and weight-derivative bounds in Lemma 2.2 give the stated absorption condition \(12\beta<1\). The unweighted Lemma 2.3 follows by the corresponding Cauchy–Schwarz absorption. The superharmonic lower bound in Proposition 2.4 is combined with positivity on compact sets, so negative powers of \(u\) have the polynomial bounds used on \(B_R\).

In Section 3 the restrictions on small positive \(\beta\) can be met simultaneously. For example, \(\beta=1/100\) and \(s=8\) give \[12\beta<1,\quad 2-36\beta>0,\quad 2-40\beta>0,\quad
 s-\frac{6-8\beta}{1-4\beta}=\frac{11}{6}>0.\] The estimates for \(I_3'\), the Young inequality in the estimate for \(I_4'\), and the absorption of \(I_2\) lead to the stated uniform weighted bound for \(I_1\) and the bound \(I_2\leq CR^2\). In particular the intermediate factor \(R^{36\beta-16\beta^2}\) is bounded by \(R^{36\beta}\) for \(R\geq1\). The final annular tail tends to zero because the weighted nonnegative density is integrable. No limit \(\beta\downarrow0\) and no unproved finite-energy assumption is needed at that step. These checks did not identify a further defect in that argument.

For the higher-dimensional proof, the parameter \(t\in[0,1]\) in Proposition 4.1 is a homotopy parameter, distinct from the group’s vertical coordinate. Conditional on its earlier differential inequality, the continuity of the maximum and threshold-crossing argument is coherent. Applying a local gradient estimate to the decay assumption requires balls away from the origin, which can be selected on the annulus; an origin-centered large ball does not satisfy a uniformly small upper bound merely from decay at infinity. The final scaling uses \(e^{2(n-1)f}\lesssim R^{-(Q-4)}\), \(|\partial f|^2\lesssim R^{-2}\), and volume of order \(R^Q\). Those exponents are compatible with the claimed annular estimates, but they do not repair the two Major issues established above.
# Verification limits and disposition

An independent Python/SymPy program executed the differential identities, the rational point evaluations, the positive flux lower bound, the two amplitude checks, and the parameter inequalities. It did not execute author code. Its first run completed the mathematical assertions but failed while serializing a SymPy Boolean value to JSON. That failed run is retained. A second run converted the output flags to native Boolean values and re-executed the checks successfully; both scripts, commands, exit codes, and outputs are retained.

The CVGMT and publisher records, the available preprint listing, and title-specific searches were checked for associated supplementary material, code, or corrections. No separate exact-version supplement or paper-specific code repository was located in this bounded search. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect. The official AMS route to the cited Jerison–Lee article returned HTTP 403, and its Section 3 rigidity proof was not read in full in this review. The classification conclusions are therefore not independently certified by this report.

The original image-read failure and its EMFILE records are preserved. In this same-chat continuation, all 23 pages of the exact bound source were actually displayed through the authorized file connection and inspected in the scientific session. The displayed conventions, quantifiers, coefficients in (4.4), and annular domains in (4.9)–(4.10) agree with the evidence above. This inspection did not change the scientific findings or remove the external-foundation limitations.

This revision is genuinely recompiled with the existing official Tectonic 0.17.0 and retained per-paper dependencies. Its delivery record binds the source, revised TeX, compiler, dependency payloads, resulting PDF, and actual observations of every resulting report page. The earlier false visual states and unsuccessful executions remain in the paper’s verification history.

The supported overall severity is Major, based on the two independent proof defects in Section 4. The two normalization corrections are Minor. These are initial-review findings for the exact bound source, not an independent acceptance decision. The scientific decision remains pending and the human-review list remains empty. Delivery completion is recorded only after the current source and report views, compilation, and required artifact bindings have actually passed their checks; it denotes completed initial-review delivery and is not independent scientific acceptance.
