report: Abstract: One Major issue is established in the bound second preprint: the parameter selection initiating the optimal higher-differentiability argument is impossible in part of the stated range. An explicit admissible parameter tuple and a feasible replacement recurrence are given. Six Minor comments identify normalization, scaling, uniformity, and difference-quotient errors, with their actual downstream uses distinguished from the false general displays. These findings do not give counterexamples to the principal regularity theorems. The full 58-page text and selected passages of two direct dependencies were read; the limits of the mathematical and visual verification are recorded explicitly.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Nonlinear nonlocal potential theory: exponent feasibility and scale checks
# Exact source and theorem scope

The source reviewed is Lars Diening, Kyeongbae Kim, Ho-Sik Lee, and Simon Nowak, Nonlinear nonlocal potential theory at the gradient level, arXiv:2402.04809v2, submitted on 8 August 2024 at 09:34:45 UTC [paper]. The bound PDF has 58 pages and 923837 bytes, with SHA256
`f48abfb9404846ddb2f2ec7cfded2ce87a9fa64ff1517a09a7533d5b3833f8eb`.

The arXiv record says that the paper is to appear in the Journal of the European Mathematical Society. The publisher records acceptance on 5 August 2024 and publication on 22 September 2025, under DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1706 [journal]. Neither this chronology nor the arXiv comment proves exact identity with the accepted or final journal text. All findings below concern the bound v2 file.

The assumptions are \(n\geq2\), \(0<s<1\), and an odd scalar function \(\Phi\) that is globally Lipschitz and strongly monotone with constants controlled by \(\Lambda\). No derivative of \(\Phi\) is assumed. Theorem 1.5 concerns homogeneous equations throughout \(0<s<1\). The measure-data results require \(s>1/2\), finite signed Radon data, and either global energy solutions or the specified SOLA approximation class. In particular, the allowed higher-differentiability range is \[0<\sigma<2s-1,\qquad
 1\leq q<\frac{n}{n-2s+1+\sigma}.\] The excluded endpoint \(\sigma=2s-1\), \(q=1\) is not asserted. The results are not claims for general fractional \(p\)-growth nonlinearities, which need not satisfy Assumption 1.1.

All 58 pages, including the references, were read as extracted text. Version-specific official HTML was used to check selected formulas and the closed-ball notation in the SOLA definition. The original PDF remains the source binding; generated HTML is corroborating evidence.
# The higher-differentiability parameter obstruction

Equation reference: impossible. Problem 1 (Major: Lemma 4.6, page 42, equation (4.21)).  For every \(\sigma\in(0,2s_0-1)\), the proof asks for \(\beta\in(0,1)\) such that \[
 2s_0\beta-1>\frac{\sigma+1}{2}>\sigma.\] This selection is not possible throughout the stated range.

Take \[s=s_0=\frac35,\qquad \sigma=\frac1{10}.\] Then \(0<\sigma<2s_0-1=1/5\), exactly as required. Nevertheless, every \(\beta<1\) satisfies \[2s_0\beta-1<\frac15<\frac{11}{20}
       =\frac{\sigma+1}{2}.\] Indeed, [impossible] (#impossible) would require \(\beta>31/24\). These are realizable PDE parameters: \(n=2\), \(\Phi(t)=t\), \(\Lambda=1\), \(u=0\), \(\mu=0\), and \(R=1\) satisfy all assumptions of Lemma 4.6. The contradiction concerns the claimed parameter existence, not a failure of that particular solution to be regular.

In general, the first strict inequality in [impossible] (#impossible) can hold with \(\beta<1\) only if \[\sigma<4s_0-3.\] For \(s_0\leq3/4\) it cannot hold for any positive \(\sigma\). For every \(3/4<s_0<1\), it still excludes a nonempty part of the advertised interval \((0,2s_0-1)\).

The condition is used again on pages 44–45 to select the \(\sigma_j\) and remove the minimum in the recurrence. Lemma 4.6 is then used in the proof of Theorem 1.9 on page 47 and in the gradient comparison of Corollary 5.2 on page 48. It is therefore a core proof obstruction for the claimed optimal differentiability and subsequent potential-estimate chain. The homogeneous Theorem 1.5 does not depend on Lemma 4.6. No counterexample to the main regularity conclusions is claimed.
## A concrete repair of the parameter arithmetic

The obstruction can be removed at the level of exponent selection. For fixed \(1/2<s_0<1\) and \(0<\sigma<2s_0-1\), set \[a=\frac{\sigma+2s_0-1}{2},\qquad
 \beta=\frac12\left(1+\frac{a+1}{2s_0}\right),\qquad
 K=2s_0\beta-1,\qquad T=\frac{s_0(1+\sigma)}2.\] Then \(0<\beta<1\), \(\sigma<a<K\), and \[T-\sigma=(1-s_0)^2+
       \frac{(2-s_0)(2s_0-1-\sigma)}2>0.\] Starting from \(b_0=0\), the capped recurrence \[b_{j+1}=\min\{a,\ \beta b_j+T(1-\beta)\}\] increases to \(\min\{a,T\}>\sigma\) and crosses \(\sigma\) after finitely many steps. It retains strict margins below the data exponent \(K\) and below the available gain \(\beta b_j+s(1-\beta)\), since \(T<s_0\leq s\). For the explicit example above, \(a=3/20\), \(\beta=47/48\), \(K=7/40\), and \(T=33/100\); exact rational iteration first crosses \(\sigma=1/10\) at step 18.

This gives a viable replacement for the impossible arithmetic, rather than an unproved conjectural repair. It does not constitute a complete revised proof of all the covering, tail, localization, and constant estimates. Those estimates must be written with the new exponents and strict margins. Also, the standing lower bound \(s_0\) in Sections 4–5 must be taken above \(1/2\) whenever \(2s_0\beta-1>0\) is required. Merely correcting that standing interval does not fix [impossible] (#impossible), since the counterexample already has \(s_0>1/2\).
# Normalization and scale corrections

The following three changes of variables use smooth admissible functions and exact powers. The counterexamples to scale-dependent displays are families, so an unspecified constant depending only on the listed fixed parameters cannot absorb the discrepancy.

Problem 2 (Minor: formal operator versus weak form, pages 1, 2, and 5).  The formal operator (1.2) has prefactor \(1-s\), whereas the double integral in (1.15) also has prefactor \(1-s\). With the stated oddness, the latter represents twice the formal operator.

Let \(\mathcal L_{\rm pv}\) denote exactly (1.2). For smooth compactly supported functions, symmetrization gives \[(1-s)\iint
 \Phi\left(\frac{u(x)-u(y)}{|x-y|^s}\right)
 \frac{\psi(x)-\psi(y)}{|x-y|^{n+s}}\,dx\,dy
 =2\int(\mathcal L_{\rm pv}u)\psi\,dx.\] The identity follows first with a symmetric exclusion \(|x-y|>\varepsilon\) and then by passage to the limit. For a decisive nonzero example take \(\Phi(t)=t\) and \(\psi=u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)\) nonconstant. The Dirichlet integral is positive, so the factor cannot disappear. The measure \((\mathcal L_{\rm pv}u)\,dx\) has finite total variation, since the density is bounded locally and decays as \(|x|^{-n-2s}\) outside a compact set.

The variation of energy (1.4) agrees with the printed weak form, hence with \(2\mathcal L_{\rm pv}u=\mu\). One may change the formal prefactor to \(2(1-s)\) while preserving the weak form and energy, or halve both their integral prefactors while preserving (1.2). The estimates have unspecified constants and the later localization calculation consistently uses the weak form, so this is a normalization correction rather than a refutation of those qualitative results.
Problem 3 (Minor: Lemma 2.3, page 14).  The left side is an averaged Sobolev norm, but the right side is the unnormalized seminorm without its required scale factor.

Problem 4 (Minor: equation (4.5), page 35).  With the chosen differentiability index \(h=2s-1\), the power \(R^{-s/2+2s-n}\) is inconsistent with scaling. The corresponding power before the measure mass is \(R^{1-n}\).

Take \(n=2\), \(s=3/4\), \(\Phi(t)=t\), and a nonzero smooth bump \(\phi\) supported in \(B_{1/2}\). Put \(u_R(x)=R^{2s}\phi(x/R)\). Its homogeneous replacement on \(B_R\) with the same exterior data is \(v_R=0\). Define \(\mu_R\) by the printed weak formulation, so that its density is a fixed smooth bounded function evaluated at \(x/R\) and \(|\mu_R|(B_R)=R^nM\) with a fixed \(M>0\). All assumptions of the comparison step hold.

The normalized double integral on the left of (4.5) is \(R A\) for a fixed \(A>0\). The printed right side is \(cR^{3s/2}M=cR^{9/8}M\). Their ratio diverges as \(R\downarrow0\). In the cited comparison lemma [kms], the generic factor is \(r^{-h}r^{2s-n}\), which indeed becomes \(r^{1-n}\) here. The displayed stability prefactor itself is consistent: \[\frac{(1-h)^2}{(1-s)(s-h)}=4,\qquad h=2s-1.\] The normalized \(R=1\) estimate used later is not refuted by this scale test. Correcting the power and restoring the corresponding Poincare factor yields the stated \(R^{2s-n}\) degree in the zero-order comparison. Uniform constants still require the normalization and dependency estimates to be retained.
Problem 5 (Minor: Lemma 3.6, page 31).  The nonhomogeneous term lacks the factor \(R^{2s}\) present in Lemma 2.13. Its printed radius-uniform estimate is false.

For an explicit admissible family choose \(\Phi(t)=t\), \(n=2\), \(s=3/4\), and \(\phi\in C_c^\infty(B_1)\) with \(\phi(x)=x_1\) on \(B_{1/2}\). Such a function is obtained by multiplying \(x_1\) by a smooth cutoff equal to one on \(B_{1/2}\). For \(L>3\), set \[w_L(x)=L\phi(x/L),\qquad R=L^2,\qquad h=e_1,\qquad\beta=1.\] Use the weak-form forcing \(f_L\) for \(w_L\). If \(F\) is that forcing for \(\phi\), homogeneity in this linear test case gives \(f_L(x)=L^{1-2s}F(x/L)\). Smoothness of \(\phi\) implies \(\|\nabla F\|_\infty<\infty\).

At the origin \(\delta_hw_L(0)=1\), so the left side of the claimed estimate is at least one. Yet \[\frac{1}{|B_R|}\int_{B_R}|\delta_hw_L|\,dx\leq CL^{-n},\qquad
 \operatorname{Tail}(\delta_hw_L;B_R)=0,\qquad
 \|\delta_hf_L\|_\infty\leq CL^{-2s}.\] The tail vanishes because the difference is supported in \(B_{L+1}\subset B_R\). Thus the entire printed right side tends to zero. The functions are smooth energy functions with finite tails, \(f_L\) is bounded on \(B_{2R}\), and \(|h|<R/8\). Restoring \(R^{2s}\|\delta_hf/|h|^\beta\|_\infty\) gives the scaling supplied by Lemma 2.13. The later nonhomogeneous bootstrap uses Lemma 3.6 after unit-ball rescaling; Lemma 3.10 uses \(f=0\). These actual uses do not depend on the missing factor.
# Two further local corrections
Problem 6 (Minor: equation (1.19), page 8).  For arbitrary \(\beta\in(0,n)\), the comparison of truncated and classical Riesz potentials cannot have a constant depending only on \(n\).

Take \(n=2\), \(\mu=\delta_{e_1}\), \(x_0=0\), \(\beta=2-\varepsilon\), and \(R=\exp(1/\varepsilon)\). The classical potential equals one, whereas \[I_\beta^{|\mu|}(0,R)=
 \int_1^{\exp(1/\varepsilon)}t^{-1-\varepsilon}\,dt
 =\frac{1-e^{-1}}{\varepsilon}.\] This is unbounded as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Tonelli’s theorem gives the correct factor \(1/(n-\beta)\). In the actual gradient applications \(\beta=2s-1<1\) and \(n\geq2\), so \(n-\beta>1\) and a dimension-only upper constant is available. The correction concerns the overly general uniformity assertion, not those applications.

Problem 7 (Minor: difference-quotient displays in Lemmas 2.9–2.10).  Two local displays have the wrong power or difference order. The preceding product calculation and the intended conclusions identify the corresponding corrections.

On page 19, in the displayed application of Lemma 2.8 after (2.15), the left side is a \(q\)th-power integral, while the right side still has a \(1/q\) power. For \(q=2\), take a nonzero smooth cutoff product \(H=G\xi\) obtained, for example, from \(g(x)=x_1^2\). Both seminorms are finite and positive. Scaling \(g\) by an amplitude \(A\) scales the left side by \(A^2\) but the printed right side by \(A\). No amplitude-independent constant makes that display valid. Remove the \(1/q\) power after raising Lemma 2.8 to the \(q\)th power; the following bound already has \(M^q\).
# Coverage of the proof chain

The tail space, excess functionals, weak form, and all seven SOLA conditions were checked. In particular, Definition 1.7(6) uses \(\limsup_j|\mu_j|(B)\leq|\mu|(\overline B)\), with a closed ball on the right. The fractional embedding condition \(\gamma-n/q\leq\widetilde\gamma-n\) in Lemma 2.4 has the correct direction. The proof of Lemma 2.6 uses the fundamental theorem of calculus and tail integration, accounting for its \(s^{-1}\) factor. The covering arguments require overlap bounds for enlarged balls; those factors must be combined with the volume factors before summing fractional seminorms.

In Section 3, the localization forcing is supported by interactions outside the inner ball. Lipschitz continuity of \(\Phi\) controls its size by the tail and transfers the local Holder exponent without differentiating \(\Phi\). Difference quotients have a uniformly elliptic secant coefficient, so the De Giorgi argument does not require \(\Phi\) to be \(C^1\). The nonlinear rescaling in Lemma 3.8, \[w_R(x)=R^{-s}w(Rx+x_0),\qquad f_R(x)=R^sf(Rx+x_0),\] preserves the argument of \(\Phi\) exactly. It is not arbitrary amplitude homogeneity. The bootstrap exponents may be decreased slightly to avoid the excluded equality \(\beta+\gamma=1\) in Lemma 3.7. The final use of subtracting a constant to replace \(\widetilde E\) by \(E\) is legitimate. The unrestricted homogeneous regularity conclusion was not refuted by the checks above.

For the comparison input, rewriting \(u\) with its own kernel does not by itself make its nonlinear replacement \(v\) solve the equation with that same frozen kernel. The appropriate direct verification uses the secant between the two differences: \[A(x,y)=
 \frac{\Phi(a_u)-\Phi(a_v)}{a_u-a_v},\qquad
 a_w=\frac{w(x)-w(y)}{|x-y|^s}.\] For \(a_u\ne a_v\), Assumption 1.1 gives \(\Lambda^{-1}\leq A\leq\Lambda\). On the zero-difference set one may choose any value in this interval. Oddness gives symmetry. Consequently \(u-v\), which vanishes outside the comparison ball, satisfies a linear uniformly elliptic weak equation with that secant kernel. This verifies the structural route to the comparison estimate, without assuming that the two individual frozen kernels coincide.

The applications of the \(q\)-independent differentiability exponent in Lemma 4.3 and the embedding bootstrap in Lemma 4.4 were followed. One may decrease the free exponent to avoid landing exactly on an infinite Sobolev conjugate. The obstruction in Lemma 4.6 is different: its impossible choice occurs for fixed admissible \(s_0,\sigma\), and requires the replacement recurrence described above. The initial gradient-integrability step in Lemma 4.7 refers to the iterative argument of [kns]. The relevant source passages were read, but a full independent reconstruction of every localization constant in that adaptation is not claimed.

Theorem 1.9 uses a strict intermediate exponent \(\widetilde\sigma\) with \(\widetilde\sigma-n\geq\sigma-n/q\), possible precisely because the target \(q\) lies below its displayed endpoint. Compactness of gradients gives local \(L^1\) convergence along a subsequence; the lower semicontinuity needed for the final nonnegative seminorm bound is supplied by Fatou’s lemma. No pointwise dominating function for that seminorm is furnished merely by a uniform Sobolev bound.

In Section 5, the interpolation exponent \(\theta=1/(1+\kappa)\), the Young-inequality absorption, and the convergence of the geometric tail sum with \(\alpha_1<1<2s\) were checked. For the discrete potential iteration, the outermost radius needs care: a measure concentrated in a thin shell near \(R\) shows that \(|\mu|(B_R)/R^{n-\beta}\) is not bounded by a fixed multiple of \(I_\beta^{|\mu|}(x_0,R)\) alone. One can start the summation one scale inward, controlling the first excess by the initial excess, or use a larger potential radius and subsequently shrink the working ball. This is a required bookkeeping clarification, not a counterexample here to Proposition 5.4.

For passage from the approximating data to the SOLA, a safe order is to retain finite sums of ball masses, pass to the limit using the closed-ball limsup condition at continuity radii, and then increase the number of scales. Weak convergence of measures alone does not justify pointwise dominated convergence of their full potentials. Finally, for the global energy solution, the computed decay \[E(u/R;B_R(x_0))\leq C R^{-n/2-1}\|u\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^n)}
       \longrightarrow0\] has the correct power. The gradient-potential order \(2s-1\) and the Lorentz exponents in Corollary 1.14 agree with the classical potential scaling.

No separate exact-version supplement, paper-specific repository, or correction was located in that bounded search. The generic arXiv HTML issue-reporting link is not author code. claim: At h=2s-1 the normalized comparison seminorm has RHS R^(-s/2+2s-n) times measure mass.
n=2,s=3/4,Phi identity,u_R=R^(2s) phi(x/R) with nonzero C_c^infty(B_1/2) bump; v_R=0 since exterior values vanish; mu_R is its weak-form forcing, bounded in B_R.
analysis: With the chosen differentiability index \(h=2s-1\), the power \(R^{-s/2+2s-n}\) is inconsistent with scaling. The corresponding power before the measure mass is \(R^{1-n}\).

Take \(n=2\), \(s=3/4\), \(\Phi(t)=t\), and a nonzero smooth bump \(\phi\) supported in \(B_{1/2}\). Put \(u_R(x)=R^{2s}\phi(x/R)\). Its homogeneous replacement on \(B_R\) with the same exterior data is \(v_R=0\). Define \(\mu_R\) by the printed weak formulation, so that its density is a fixed smooth bounded function evaluated at \(x/R\) and \(|\mu_R|(B_R)=R^nM\) with a fixed \(M>0\). All assumptions of the comparison step hold.

The normalized double integral on the left of (4.5) is \(R A\) for a fixed \(A>0\). The printed right side is \(cR^{3s/2}M=cR^{9/8}M\). Their ratio diverges as \(R\downarrow0\). In the cited comparison lemma [kms], the generic factor is \(r^{-h}r^{2s-n}\), which indeed becomes \(r^{1-n}\) here. The displayed stability prefactor itself is consistent: \[\frac{(1-h)^2}{(1-s)(s-h)}=4,\qquad h=2s-1.\] The normalized \(R=1\) estimate used later is not refuted by this scale test. Correcting the power and restoring the corresponding Poincare factor yields the stated \(R^{2s-n}\) degree in the zero-order comparison. problems.title: Lemma 3.6, page 31
problems.source_location: p.31 Lemma3.6, compare p.22 Lemma2.13
claim: The inhomogeneous difference-quotient Holder estimate has no R^(2s) multiplying its data term.
n=2,s=3/4,Phi identity,beta=1,h=e1; phi smooth supported B1 and equal x1 on B1/2; w_L=L phi(x/L),R=L^2,L>3; f_L is the weak-form forcing. All energy/tail/bounded-forcing hypotheses and h<R/8 hold.
analysis: The nonhomogeneous term lacks the factor \(R^{2s}\) present in Lemma 2.13. Its printed radius-uniform estimate is false.

For an explicit admissible family choose \(\Phi(t)=t\), \(n=2\), \(s=3/4\), and \(\phi\in C_c^\infty(B_1)\) with \(\phi(x)=x_1\) on \(B_{1/2}\). Such a function is obtained by multiplying \(x_1\) by a smooth cutoff equal to one on \(B_{1/2}\). For \(L>3\), set \[w_L(x)=L\phi(x/L),\qquad R=L^2,\qquad h=e_1,\qquad\beta=1.\] Use the weak-form forcing \(f_L\) for \(w_L\). If \(F\) is that forcing for \(\phi\), homogeneity in this linear test case gives \(f_L(x)=L^{1-2s}F(x/L)\). Smoothness of \(\phi\) implies \(\|\nabla F\|_\infty<\infty\).

At the origin \(\delta_hw_L(0)=1\), so the left side of the claimed estimate is at least one. Yet \[\frac{1}{|B_R|}\int_{B_R}|\delta_hw_L|\,dx\leq CL^{-n},\qquad

report: Abstract: The reviewed source is arXiv:2307.01140v2, dated 10 November 2023. A bounded union of balls with logarithmically modified capacities disproves the exact exponent estimate in Theorem 3.1 under the source’s definition of volume-decay order. An independent pullback calculation also shows that the displayed displacement map in Proposition 6.1 is not symplectic. These are assessed as Major at the level of the affected quantitative theorem and core construction. A separate incorrect parallel-body identity is a local Minor finding: its required convex-domain lemma is proved here under the original hypotheses. The dimension inequality and the principal packing obstructions are not refuted. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Review of
Boundaries of Open Symplectic Manifolds
and the Failure of Packing Stability
# Identity, version, and review scope

The source is D. Cristofaro-Gardiner and R. Hind, Boundaries of open symplectic manifolds and the failure of packing stability, arXiv:2307.01140v2 [CGH]. The associated journal identifier is DOI `10.4171/JEMS/1707`; the publisher lists online publication on 17 September 2025 [EMS]. The acquired 32-page PDF is the November 2023 arXiv revision, not a verified copy of the accepted manuscript or the journal version of record. No finding below is asserted to persist in the unacquired journal text.

Page numbers are one-based PDF pages, coinciding with printed pages. All 32 pages were read as text. Detailed checks concern Section 2.1, Lemma 2.3, Theorem 3.1 and its proof, the capacity optimization in Proposition 4.6, Section 5’s dependencies, and the explicit maps in Proposition 6.1. The construction of ECH and the external theorems quoted by the authors were not reproved. All regularity and injectivity claims in the folding construction have not been independently certified.

The existing acquisition searches and a new bounded search of the arXiv record, publisher page, and author research page did not identify a separate supplement, paper-specific implementation, or correction notice. This is not proof of nonexistence. No author code was executed. Delivery remains incomplete until the outstanding source-image and final report-image checks in the execution appendix are actually completed.
# Definitions and dependencies

For an open set \(Z\subset\mathbb R^4\), the source defines \[V_d(Z)=\operatorname{vol}\{z\in Z:\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial Z)<d\},\qquad
 q=\liminf_{d\downarrow0}\frac{\log V_d(Z)}{\log d}.\] Equation (2.2), p. 7, calls this number the order of volume decay. It is a logarithmic exponent and does not assert \(V_d=O(d^q)\). The inner upper Minkowski dimension is \(4-q\). The subleading capacity term is \(e_k(Z)=c_k(Z)-2\sqrt{k\operatorname{vol}Z}\). A four-dimensional ball of capacity \(a\) has radius \(\sqrt{a/\pi}\) and volume \(a^2/2\). The ball and disjoint-union capacity formulas used below are stated in Section 2.2 and used in (4.4)–(4.6), pp. 16–17.

Theorem 3.1 is presented as the quantified form of the fractal Weyl law. Its estimate enters (5.4), p. 22, in the proof of Theorem 5.2, from which Theorems 1.2 and 1.4 follow. Proposition 6.1 constructs the bounded symplectic realization underlying Proposition 1.3. A defect in one statement does not automatically invalidate all these separate conclusions.
# The exact exponent in Theorem 3.1

Equation reference: eq:claimed. Problem 1 (A logarithmic correction violates the stated bound).  Theorem 3.1, p. 11, assumes that \(Z\) is relatively compact and open and has volume-decay order \(q\), and concludes that a constant \(C>0\) satisfies \[
 e_k(Z)>-Ck^{(2-q)/4}\qquad\hbox{for all }k.\] The proof on p. 13 treats the boundary tube as \(O(d^q)\). Under the definition in (2.2), [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed) is false.
## One fixed admissible open set

Equation reference: eq:S. Use natural logarithms and fix \[A=10^{-3},\quad m=10,\quad
 a_i=A\frac{\log(i+m)}{(i+m)^{3/5}},\quad
 r_i=\sqrt{a_i/\pi},\qquad i\ge1.\] The \(a_i\) are strictly decreasing, positive, and square summable. The derivative of \(x^{-3/5}\log x\) is negative for \(x\ge11\), and \[\begin{aligned}
 S:=\sum_i a_i^2
 &\le A^2\int_{10}^{\infty}x^{-6/5}(\log x)^2\,dx\\
 &=5A^2\,10^{-1/5}\bigl((\log10)^2+10\log10+50\bigr)
 <445A^2.\end{aligned}\] The integrand is decreasing on \([10,\infty)\), justifying the comparison; the last bound follows from \(\log10<3\).

Choose a dyadic length \(\ell_i\) with \(2r_i\le\ell_i<4r_i\). Then \(\sum_i\ell_i^4<256S/\pi^2<1\). Place these dyadic cubes, in nonincreasing side length, in \([0,1]^4\), each time choosing the lexicographically first unoccupied cube of the required grid. Such a cube always exists: earlier larger cubes occupy integer numbers of grid cells, and exhausting the grid would contradict the total volume bound. Put disjoint open balls of radii \(r_i\) at their centers \(c_i\) and define \[Z=\bigcup_{i\ge1}B(c_i,r_i).\] This is open in standard symplectic \(\mathbb R^4\), with compact closure in \([0,1]^4\) and volume \(S/2\). Theorem 3.1 has no connectedness hypothesis, and Example 5.3, p. 23, explicitly considers infinitely disconnected sets. Thus every domain assumption holds for this one fixed \(Z\), independent of \(k\).
## The volume-decay hypothesis holds with \(q=2/3\)

Equation reference: eq:tube, eq:N. Each constituent sphere belongs to \(\partial Z\), even when two closed balls touch. Therefore \[
 V_d(Z)=\frac{\pi^2}{2}\sum_i
 \left(r_i^4-(r_i-d)_+^4\right).\] Let \(N(d)=\max\{i:r_i\ge d\}\). Inverting the radius formula gives \[
 N(d)\asymp d^{-10/3}\bigl(\log(1/d)\bigr)^{5/3}.\] Indeed, substituting \(C d^{-10/3}(\log(1/d))^{5/3}\) in \(\log(n+m)/(n+m)^{3/5}\) yields a constant multiple of \(d^2\). Small and large fixed \(C\), together with monotonicity, give the two bounds.

Equation reference: eq:volume. For \(0<d\le r\), \(dr^3\le r^4-(r-d)^4\le4dr^3\). Thus integral comparison gives \[\begin{aligned}
 V_d(Z)&\asymp \sum_{i>N(d)}r_i^4+
                 d\sum_{i\le N(d)}r_i^3,\\
 \sum_{i>N}r_i^4&\asymp N^{-1/5}(\log N)^2,\qquad
 \sum_{i\le N}r_i^3\asymp N^{1/10}(\log N)^{3/2}.\end{aligned}\] Substitution of [eq:N] (#eq:N) now yields \[
 V_d(Z)\asymp d^{2/3}\bigl(\log(1/d)\bigr)^{5/3}.\] The limit defining \(q\) therefore exists and equals \(2/3\), while \(V_d(Z)/d^{2/3}\to\infty\).
## The actual capacity deficit exceeds every proposed constant

Equation reference: eq:optimization. The capacity axioms give \[
 c_k(Z)=\max\left\{\sum_i a_i d_i:
 d_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\
 \sum_i d_i(d_i+1)/2\le k\right\}.\] Every compact Liouville subdomain meets only finitely many component balls, and finite ball unions can be exhausted from inside; hence the infinite union causes no extra hypothesis. Every feasible vector has at most \(k\) positive entries. Rearranging these onto the first \(k\) balls leaves a finite optimization problem, so a maximum exists. Its cost equals \(k\): integer slack could otherwise be spent by setting an unused positive-capacity ball’s \(d_i\) to \(1\).

Equation reference: eq:deficit, eq:contradiction. Take a decreasing optimizer, positive on the first \(n\) entries, and set \(D=\lceil\sqrt{2k}\rceil\), \(N=n+D\). Cauchy–Schwarz and saturation imply \[\begin{aligned}
 -e_k(Z)
 &=\sqrt{2Sk}-\sum_{i\le n}a_i d_i\\
 &\ge\sum_{i\le n}a_i(\sqrt{d_i^2+d_i}-d_i)
 \ge(\sqrt2-1)\sum_{i\le n}a_i.\end{aligned}\] For each active \(j\), reducing \(d_j\) by one frees exactly \(d_j\) units of cost. Spending them on \(n+1,\ldots,n+d_j\) gives, by optimality, \[a_j\ge\sum_{\ell=n+1}^{n+d_j}a_\ell\ge d_j a_N.\] Since \(d_j\le D\), we obtain \[k\le\sum_{j\le n}d_j^2\le S/a_N^2,\qquad
 \frac{(N+m)^{6/5}}{\log^2(N+m)}\ge \frac{A^2}{S}k.\] First using \(\log(N+m)>1\), and then substituting the resulting polynomial bound into the logarithm, proves \(N+m\gtrsim k^{5/6}(\log k)^{5/3}\). Subtracting \(D=O(k^{1/2})\) preserves this bound for \(n\). Summing over \(\lceil n/2\rceil\le i\le n\) gives \(\sum_{i\le n}a_i\gtrsim n^{2/5}\log n\). Consequently \[
 -e_k(Z)\ge c\,k^{1/3}(\log k)^{5/3}
 \quad\hbox{for every sufficiently large }k.\] For \(q=2/3\), [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed) requires \(-e_k(Z)<Ck^{1/3}\), contradicting [eq:contradiction] (#eq:contradiction) for every finite \(C\). This is an analytic counterexample, not an asymptotic inference from finite numerical samples.
## Alternative readings, impact, and repair boundary

Interpreting volume-decay order as a uniform power upper bound would exclude this counterexample. That stronger premise is explicitly stated in Proposition 3.2, but is not the definition in (2.2). Alternatively, retaining the logarithmic definition gives, for each \(0<\varepsilon<q\), a bound \(V_d\le C_\varepsilon d^{q-\varepsilon}\). The uniform-bound argument gives \[e_k(Z)\ge-C_\varepsilon k^{(2-q+\varepsilon)/4}.\] Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) retains \(d_{\rm ECH}\le4-q\) in Theorem 1.9. The strict exponent separation in Theorem 5.2’s proof likewise allows a sufficiently small loss. The finding is Major for the false quantitative theorem and its asserted equivalence. It does not refute the dimension inequality or principal packing-obstruction conclusions. No claim is made about the unacquired journal text.
# The displacement map in the bounded realization

Problem 2 (The displayed shear is not symplectic).  In Proposition 6.1, Steps 2a–2b, pp. 25–26, the source sets \(G=v+\tfrac12\), \(H=\chi(x)G\), and \(X_G=\partial_u\). Equations (6.1)–(6.2) describe \[\Psi(x,y,u,v)=
 (x,\ y+(v+\tfrac12)\chi'(x),\ u+\chi(x),\ v).\] With \(\omega=dx\wedge dy+du\wedge dv\), this is not symplectic wherever \(\chi'\ne0\).

Equation reference: eq:pullback. Differentiation gives \[\begin{aligned}
 \Psi^*(dx\wedge dy)&=dx\wedge dy+\chi'(x)\,dx\wedge dv,\\
 \Psi^*(du\wedge dv)&=du\wedge dv+\chi'(x)\,dx\wedge dv,\end{aligned}\] and hence \[
 \Psi^*\omega-\omega=2\chi'(x)\,dx\wedge dv.\] The \(\chi''\) term vanishes because it multiplies \(dx\wedge dx\).

The defect occurs where the source prescribes \(\chi(x)=x\) for \(x\le1\). Choose the admissible smooth function \(f(r)=(1+r)^{-3/2}\): it is decreasing, \(f(0)=1\), and its integral is finite. On any interior fiber patch with \(0<x<1\), the defect is \(2dx\wedge dv\). The original pairing \(\omega(\partial_x,\partial_v)\) is \(0\); the pulled-back pairing is \(2\). The retained independent rational-matrix calculation reproduces this discrepancy exactly.

The convention \(X_G=\partial_u\) requires \(X_H=\chi\partial_u-G\chi'\partial_y\). Changing the global Hamiltonian convention changes both signs and cannot justify the displayed two positive shears. Negating the \(y\) displacement cancels [eq:pullback] (#eq:pullback); this local repair is verified. The corresponding image-strip, wrapping, global injectivity, and boundary-dimension arguments have not all been rechecked, so the whole construction is not declared repaired.

This is Major for the explicit construction in Proposition 6.1 and its use in Proposition 1.3. The existence of a bounded symplectic realization has not been disproved. The defect concerns an essential map; a short local correction does not by itself supply the global verification.
# The convex-domain parallel-body identity

Problem 3 (Erosion followed by dilation need not recover a convex domain).  Lemma 2.3, p. 9, describes \(Z\) as the radius-\(d\) tube around \(Z(d)=\{z\in Z:\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial Z)\ge d\}\) and identifies the inner boundary-layer volume with \(N_d(Z(d))-N_0(Z(d))\). That equality is false.

Let \(Z=(0,1)^4\) and \(0<d<1/2\). Then \(Z(d)=[d,1-d]^4\). For \(x=(d/4,d/4,d/4,d/4)\), \[\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial Z)=d/4<d,\qquad
 \operatorname{dist}(x,Z(d))=3d/2>d.\] Both inequalities persist on a neighborhood, so the discrepancy has positive volume and is unaffected by open versus closed tubes. Writing \(a=1-2d\), the actual volume is \(1-a^4\), while the stated tube difference is \[8a^3d+6\pi a^2d^2+\frac{16\pi}{3}ad^3+\frac{\pi^2}{2}d^4.\] At \(d=1/4\) the values are \(15/16\) and \(1/4+13\pi/96+\pi^2/512\), respectively.

The lemma’s conclusion holds under its original assumptions. Translate an interior point to the origin and choose \(r\overline B\subset K=\overline Z\subset R\overline B\). For \(K_d=K\ominus d\overline B\) and \(0<d<r\), \[(1-d/r)K\subset K_d\subset(1-d/R)K.\] The first inclusion follows from convexity. For the second, in each unit direction \(u\), \(x\in K_d\) satisfies \(\langle x,u\rangle\le h_K(u)-d
\le(1-d/R)h_K(u)\), since \(h_K(u)\le R\). Taking volumes yields \[\frac{\operatorname{vol}K}{R}d\le V_d(Z)\le\frac{4\operatorname{vol}K}{r}d.\] This verifies the linear decay premise used for the convex case of Theorem 1.4, p. 22. The finding is Minor: it concerns a background identity, and the downstream geometric premise is established here without changing its assumptions or conclusion.
# Conclusion
The overall assessment is Major for Problems 1 and 2, with the separate Minor finding in Problem 3.
Item | Assessment | Repair verification | Adoption
1 | Major | Small exponent loss; dimension implication retained | Not established
2 | Major | Local sign repair; full construction unchecked | Not established
3 | Minor | Convex tube bounds under original assumptions | Not established

Scientific decision is pending and no human review is recorded. The analytic discrepancies need no experiments or author-code execution. Checking whether they persist in the journal text requires that exact version and is outside the present acquired-source claim.

 d_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\
 \sum_i d_i(d_i+1)/2\le k\right\}.\] Every compact Liouville subdomain meets only finitely many component balls, and finite ball unions can be exhausted from inside; hence the infinite union causes no extra hypothesis. Every feasible vector has at most \(k\) positive entries. Rearranging these onto the first \(k\) balls leaves a finite optimization problem, so a maximum exists. Its cost equals \(k\): integer slack could otherwise be spent by setting an unused positive-capacity ball’s \(d_i\) to \(1\).

Equation reference: eq:deficit, eq:contradiction. Take a decreasing optimizer, positive on the first \(n\) entries, and set \(D=\lceil\sqrt{2k}\rceil\), \(N=n+D\). Cauchy–Schwarz and saturation imply \[\begin{aligned}
 -e_k(Z)
 &=\sqrt{2Sk}-\sum_{i\le n}a_i d_i\\
 &\ge\sum_{i\le n}a_i(\sqrt{d_i^2+d_i}-d_i)
 \ge(\sqrt2-1)\sum_{i\le n}a_i.\end{aligned}\] For each active \(j\), reducing \(d_j\) by one frees exactly \(d_j\) units of cost. Spending them on \(n+1,\ldots,n+d_j\) gives, by optimality, \[a_j\ge\sum_{\ell=n+1}^{n+d_j}a_\ell\ge d_j a_N.\] Since \(d_j\le D\), we obtain \[k\le\sum_{j\le n}d_j^2\le S/a_N^2,\qquad
 \frac{(N+m)^{6/5}}{\log^2(N+m)}\ge \frac{A^2}{S}k.\] First using \(\log(N+m)>1\), and then substituting the resulting polynomial bound into the logarithm, proves \(N+m\gtrsim k^{5/6}(\log k)^{5/3}\). Subtracting \(D=O(k^{1/2})\) preserves this bound for \(n\). Summing over \(\lceil n/2\rceil\le i\le n\) gives \(\sum_{i\le n}a_i\gtrsim n^{2/5}\log n\). Consequently \[
 -e_k(Z)\ge c\,k^{1/3}(\log k)^{5/3}
 \quad\hbox{for every sufficiently large }k.\] For \(q=2/3\), [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed) requires \(-e_k(Z)<Ck^{1/3}\), contradicting [eq:contradiction] (#eq:contradiction) for every finite \(C\). This is an analytic counterexample, not an asymptotic inference from finite numerical samples.
result: Interpreting volume-decay order as a uniform power upper bound would exclude this counterexample. That stronger premise is explicitly stated in Proposition 3.2, but is not the definition in (2.2). Alternatively, retaining the logarithmic definition gives, for each \(0<\varepsilon<q\), a bound \(V_d\le C_\varepsilon d^{q-\varepsilon}\). The uniform-bound argument gives \[e_k(Z)\ge-C_\varepsilon k^{(2-q+\varepsilon)/4}.\] Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) retains \(d_{\rm ECH}\le4-q\) in Theorem 1.9. The strict exponent separation in Theorem 5.2’s proof likewise allows a sufficiently small loss. The finding is Major for the false quantitative theorem and its asserted equivalence. It does not refute the dimension inequality or principal packing-obstruction conclusions. No claim is made about the unacquired journal text.

Decisive result: V_d asymptotic up to constants to d^(2/3)(log(1/d))^(5/3), while -e_k >= c k^(1/3)(log k)^(5/3) for all sufficiently large k. Every finite C in the displayed theorem fails for this one fixed Z.

Impact: The exact endpoint estimate and its asserted equivalence are false. This quantitative theorem is a central input, hence Major. The dimension inequality and principal packing obstructions are not refuted.

problems.title: The double-positive shear in Proposition 6.1 is not symplectic
problems.source_location: Page: 24 Label: Proposition 6.1 and coordinates Page: 25 Label: Steps 2a-2b, G and Hamiltonian vector field Page: 26 Label: Equations (6.1)-(6.2), displayed displacement maps
claim:
For an open set \(Z\subset\mathbb R^4\), the source defines \[V_d(Z)=\operatorname{vol}\{z\in Z:\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial Z)<d\},\qquad
 q=\liminf_{d\downarrow0}\frac{\log V_d(Z)}{\log d}.\] Equation (2.2), p. 7, calls this number the order of volume decay. It is a logarithmic exponent and does not assert \(V_d=O(d^q)\). The inner upper Minkowski dimension is \(4-q\). The subleading capacity term is \(e_k(Z)=c_k(Z)-2\sqrt{k\operatorname{vol}Z}\). A four-dimensional ball of capacity \(a\) has radius \(\sqrt{a/\pi}\) and volume \(a^2/2\). The ball and disjoint-union capacity formulas used below are stated in Section 2.2 and used in (4.4)–(4.6), pp. 16–17.
The displayed composition is a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism used in the bounded symplectic realization.
analysis:
In Proposition 6.1, Steps 2a–2b, pp. 25–26, the source sets \(G=v+\tfrac12\), \(H=\chi(x)G\), and \(X_G=\partial_u\). Equations (6.1)–(6.2) describe \[\Psi(x,y,u,v)=
 (x,\ y+(v+\tfrac12)\chi'(x),\ u+\chi(x),\ v).\] With \(\omega=dx\wedge dy+du\wedge dv\), this is not symplectic wherever \(\chi'\ne0\).

Equation reference: eq:pullback. Differentiation gives \[\begin{aligned}
 \Psi^*(dx\wedge dy)&=dx\wedge dy+\chi'(x)\,dx\wedge dv,\\
 \Psi^*(du\wedge dv)&=du\wedge dv+\chi'(x)\,dx\wedge dv,\end{aligned}\] and hence \[
 \Psi^*\omega-\omega=2\chi'(x)\,dx\wedge dv.\] The \(\chi''\) term vanishes because it multiplies \(dx\wedge dx\).

The defect occurs where the source prescribes \(\chi(x)=x\) for \(x\le1\). Choose the admissible smooth function \(f(r)=(1+r)^{-3/2}\): it is decreasing, \(f(0)=1\), and its integral is finite. On any interior fiber patch with \(0<x<1\), the defect is \(2dx\wedge dv\). The original pairing \(\omega(\partial_x,\partial_v)\) is \(0\); the pulled-back pairing is \(2\). The retained independent rational-matrix calculation reproduces this discrepancy exactly.

The convention \(X_G=\partial_u\) requires \(X_H=\chi\partial_u-G\chi'\partial_y\). Changing the global Hamiltonian convention changes both signs and cannot justify the displayed two positive shears. Negating the \(y\) displacement cancels [eq:pullback] (#eq:pullback); this local repair is verified. The corresponding image-strip, wrapping, global injectivity, and boundary-dimension arguments have not all been rechecked, so the whole construction is not declared repaired.

This is Major for the explicit construction in Proposition 6.1 and its use in Proposition 1.3. The existence of a bounded symplectic realization has not been disproved. The defect concerns an essential map; a short local correction does not by itself supply the global verification.
result: Decisive result: For Psi=(x,y+(v+1/2)chi'(x),u+chi(x),v), Psi^*omega-omega=2chi'(x) dx wedge dv. On the selected patch the pairing on (partial_x,partial_v) is 2 instead of 0.
Impact: The explicit core construction in Proposition 6.1 and its use in Proposition 1.3 lack a valid displayed symplectic map. Existence of a bounded realization is not disproved.

problems.title: Convex erosion followed by dilation does not recover the domain
problems.source_location: Page: 9 Label: Lemma 2.3, proof and parallel-body identity Page: 22 Label: Use of linear volume decay for the convex case of Theorem 1.4
claim:
For an open set \(Z\subset\mathbb R^4\), the source defines \[V_d(Z)=\operatorname{vol}\{z\in Z:\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial Z)<d\},\qquad
 q=\liminf_{d\downarrow0}\frac{\log V_d(Z)}{\log d}.\] Equation (2.2), p. 7, calls this number the order of volume decay. It is a logarithmic exponent and does not assert \(V_d=O(d^q)\). The inner upper Minkowski dimension is \(4-q\). The subleading capacity term is \(e_k(Z)=c_k(Z)-2\sqrt{k\operatorname{vol}Z}\). A four-dimensional ball of capacity \(a\) has radius \(\sqrt{a/\pi}\) and volume \(a^2/2\). The ball and disjoint-union capacity formulas used below are stated in Section 2.2 and used in (4.4)–(4.6), pp. 16–17.
The convex domain is the radius-d tube around its inner erosion, giving V_d=N_d(Z(d))-N_0(Z(d)).
analysis: Lemma 2.3, p. 9, describes \(Z\) as the radius-\(d\) tube around \(Z(d)=\{z\in Z:\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial Z)\ge d\}\) and identifies the inner boundary-layer volume with \(N_d(Z(d))-N_0(Z(d))\). That equality is false.

Let \(Z=(0,1)^4\) and \(0<d<1/2\). Then \(Z(d)=[d,1-d]^4\). For \(x=(d/4,d/4,d/4,d/4)\), \[\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial Z)=d/4<d,\qquad
 \operatorname{dist}(x,Z(d))=3d/2>d.\] Both inequalities persist on a neighborhood, so the discrepancy has positive volume and is unaffected by open versus closed tubes. Writing \(a=1-2d\), the actual volume is \(1-a^4\), while the stated tube difference is \[8a^3d+6\pi a^2d^2+\frac{16\pi}{3}ad^3+\frac{\pi^2}{2}d^4.\] At \(d=1/4\) the values are \(15/16\) and \(1/4+13\pi/96+\pi^2/512\), respectively.

The lemma’s conclusion holds under its original assumptions. Translate an interior point to the origin and choose \(r\overline B\subset K=\overline Z\subset R\overline B\). For \(K_d=K\ominus d\overline B\) and \(0<d<r\), \[(1-d/r)K\subset K_d\subset(1-d/R)K.\] The first inclusion follows from convexity. For the second, in each unit direction \(u\), \(x\in K_d\) satisfies \(\langle x,u\rangle\le h_K(u)-d
\le(1-d/R)h_K(u)\), since \(h_K(u)\le R\). Taking volumes yields \[\frac{\operatorname{vol}K}{R}d\le V_d(Z)\le\frac{4\operatorname{vol}K}{r}d.\] This verifies the linear decay premise used for the convex case of Theorem 1.4, p. 22. The finding is Minor: it concerns a background identity, and the downstream geometric premise is established here without changing its assumptions or conclusion.
result: Decisive result: dist(x,boundary Z)=d/4<d but dist(x,Z(d))=3d/2>d. At d=1/4 actual layer volume is 15/16, whereas the claimed tube difference is 1/4+13pi/96+pi^2/512 (about 0.6947005763).

Impact: The identity is false, but the lemma's order-one conclusion and its downstream convex-domain premise hold with unchanged assumptions. This is a local Minor finding, not a refutation of Theorem 1.4.

Title: Technical Review of
Uniqueness and Minimality of Euler’s Elastica
with Monotone Curvature
# Identity, scope, and conventions

The source is T. Miura and G. Wheeler, Uniqueness and minimality of Euler’s elastica with monotone curvature, arXiv:2402.12771v2 [MW], associated with DOI `10.4171/JEMS/1708`. The arXiv record calls this the accepted version; equivalence to the unacquired publisher PDF is not established. Its arXiv revision date is 28 March 2025, while its first page separately prints March 31, 2025. Both labels are retained. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, equal to printed pages. The initial review read all 21 pages as text; the present continuation visually inspected source pages 1–19.

Detailed checks covered the first variation and no-flux condition, the reductions in Sections 3–4, the explicit elliptic maps, the half-line normalization, the pinned classification in Remark 4.3, and the strict length-monotonicity argument in Section 5. The cited bootstrap and compactness theorems and the external singular-limit results used in Section 5 were not completely reproved. The abstract record for the cited phase-transition paper was located, but attempts to obtain its full text through the web reader failed; its theorem-level verification is a remaining limit. No author code was executed. Bounded acquisition and follow-up searches did not locate a separate supplement, paper-specific implementation, or correction; this is not proof of their nonexistence. Absence of code is not a mathematical defect.
# Checked assumptions and central proof chain

The energy is \(B[\gamma]=\int k^2\,ds\) on arc-length \(W^{2,2}\) immersed planar curves. Clamped competitors fix both endpoints and both unit tangents; fixed-length and variable-length classes are distinct. The multiplier equation is \[2k''+k^3-\lambda k=0,\qquad E^\lambda=B+\lambda L.\] Theorem 1.1 assumes nonconstant monotone signed curvature. Theorem 1.2 additionally excludes subcritical wavelike curves. Theorem 1.4 fixes nonzero angles strictly between \(-\pi\) and \(\pi\) and only asserts uniqueness sufficiently close to the straightening limit.

For the free-boundary classes, endpoint tangents are horizontal while endpoint vertical positions are free. In the boundary first variation, a test \(\eta=\varphi N\) with \(\varphi(0)=1\), \(\varphi'(0)=0\) isolates \(2k'(0)\), giving the no-flux condition; the other endpoint is similar. Classification then confines nonconstant minimisers to complete curvature-monotonicity intervals. The fixed-length scaling rule is \(B[\Lambda\gamma(\cdot/\Lambda)]=\Lambda^{-1}B[\gamma]\). The repeated-half-period reduction strictly reduces energy when the number of repetitions exceeds one, while preserving horizontal extent and endpoint tangents. Fixing both endpoint positions removes the residual vertical translation/reflection freedom. Replacement of a clamped subarc preserves \(W^{2,2}\) admissibility; equality competitors would contradict uniqueness of the full arc.

The orbitlike parameter map \[f_o(m)=\frac{2E(m)}{mK(m)}+1-\frac2m\] is strictly decreasing: with \(g=(1-m)K^2-E^2\), one has \(g(0)=0\), \(g'=-(K-E)^2/m<0\), and \(f_o'=g/[m^2(1-m)K^2]<0\). For its length-penalised counterpart the source’s numerator comparison is supported by the exact identity \[(m^2-8m+8)^2(1-m)-(4m^2-12m+8)^2=m^4(1-m)>0.\] These computations use \(0<m<1\). The wavelike penalised map is decreasing on \([m_0,1)\) because \(2E-K\leq0\) is decreasing while \(\sqrt{4m-2}>0\) is increasing. Thus the restriction excluding subcritical waves is material.

For Lemma 5.3, the two minimality inequalities first imply monotonicity of length with \(\varepsilon\). Equality of lengths forces equality of bending energies and makes one nonstraight curve critical for two distinct multipliers. Subtraction of the multiplier equations gives \((\lambda_1-\lambda_0)k=0\), a contradiction. This verifies the strictness needed for the inverse length map. The boundary-layer convergence and generic-angle assertions remain conditional on the cited singular-limit results, whose full proofs were not independently checked.
# A local pinned-classification defect

Equation reference: bad. Problem 1 (Remark 4.3 omits an actual pinned critical curve).  On pp. 16–17 the source asserts that every nonstraight pinned critical point of \(E^\lambda\) is an isometric image of \[
 \gamma(s)=N\sqrt{\frac{4m-2}{\lambda}}\,
 \gamma_w\!\left(
 N^{-1}\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{4m-2}}\,(s-K(m)),m\right),
 \quad 0\leq s\leq2NK(m),\] where \(m\in(1/2,1)\), \(N\in\mathbb N\), and \(|2(2E-K)\sqrt{4m-2}|=\ell\sqrt\lambda/N\). The family as displayed does not classify the stated critical points.
## A fully admissible counterexample

Equation reference: true. Set \[m=\frac{51}{100},\quad \lambda=1,\quad N=2,\quad a=\frac15,\quad
 K=K(m),\quad E=E(m),\] and use the source’s exact wavelike parametrisation from Theorem 2.4: \[
 \Gamma(s)=a\bigl(\gamma_w(s/a-K,m)-\gamma_w(-K,m)\bigr),
 \qquad 0\leq s\leq 4aK.\] It is smooth and has unit speed. Since \(\operatorname{cn}(-K,m)
=\operatorname{cn}(3K,m)=0\), its endpoints are \((0,0)\) and \((\ell,0)\), where \[\ell=4a(2E-K)>0.\] Positivity needs no floating-point elliptic evaluation. From \(\sqrt{1-t}\geq1-t\) for \(0\leq t\leq1\) and the integral definitions, \[E\geq\frac\pi2(1-m/2),\qquad
 K\leq\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{1-m}}=\frac{5\pi}{7}.\] Consequently \[2E-K\geq \left(\frac{149}{200}-\frac57\right)\pi
 =\frac{43\pi}{1400}>0.\] The curvature is \(k(s)=2\sqrt m\,a^{-1}\operatorname{cn}(s/a-K,m)\). It vanishes at both endpoints and satisfies the multiplier equation with \((4m-2)/a^2=1\). For pinned variations the endpoint displacement is zero; the remaining boundary term is \([2kN\cdot\eta']_0^L=0\). Thus [true] (#true) is an actual critical point for all admissible pinned variations, with exactly the positive multiplier and nonnegative endpoint distance required in the remark.
## Why the displayed family cannot contain it

Every member of [bad] (#bad) has unit speed, so its geometric length is \(2NK(m)>\pi\), independently of isometry. In contrast, \[L[\Gamma]=\frac45K(51/100)\leq\frac{4\pi}{7}<\pi.\] This proves omission even if arbitrary reparametrisation is allowed. There is also an independent multiplier mismatch: the scale \(N\sqrt{(4m-2)/\lambda}\) in [bad] (#bad) gives multiplier \(\lambda/N^2\), rather than \(\lambda\) when \(N>1\). The executed rational check records \(1\) for the multiplier of [true] (#true) and \(1/4\) for the displayed \(N=2\) scale.
## Repair boundary and impact

The natural repeated-wave construction instead uses \[a=\sqrt{\frac{4m-2}{\lambda}},\qquad
 a\bigl(\gamma_w(s/a-K,m)-\gamma_w(-K,m)\bigr),
 \quad 0\leq s\leq2NaK.\] Here \(N\) changes the number of half-periods, not the multiplier. Allowing a horizontal reflection, its endpoint-distance relation agrees with the relation already printed in the source: \[\left|2(2E-K)\sqrt{4m-2}\right|=\frac{\ell\sqrt\lambda}{N}.\] The absolute-value bars are present in the original page image. The earlier text-extraction-based report incorrectly described them as missing; that allegation is withdrawn. The correction established here concerns the curve’s scaling, phase and parameter interval, while retaining the published endpoint-distance equation. This does not establish every root-count or zero-distance case in the remark.

The discrepancy is Minor: the false assertion is an additional classification of pinned critical points. The proofs of Theorems 1.1, 1.2, and 1.4 do not use this remark, and the fixed-multiplier formulas actually used in Theorems 4.1 and 4.4 have the correct scaling. The issue is not downgraded because a correction is short; its demonstrated dependency is local. No journal-version persistence or author adoption is asserted.
# Normalization clarifications already resolved in the proofs

These are not counted as additional substantive findings. On p. 9, Theorem 3.1 describes the inverse of \(f_w(m)=2E(m)/K(m)-1\) as increasing and reverses the signs of \(\ell\) relative to \(m-m_0\). In fact \(E'(m)<0<K'(m)\), so \(f_w'<0\); equation (3.3), p. 11, and the actual supercritical argument on p. 16 use the correct relation. The resulting unique-parameter argument requires injectivity, which remains valid.

The display in Theorem 3.7, pp. 13–14, omits the \(\lambda\)-dependent scale, whereas its proof on p. 15 explicitly supplies \(a=\sqrt{2/\lambda}\) and \(aM\gamma_b(s/a)\). A direct global check confirms that proof. For a finite-energy curve, \(T+e_1\in H^1(0,\infty)\), hence \(T\to-e_1\). A continuous angle lift starts at \(0\) and tends to an odd multiple of \(\pi\). Therefore \[\widetilde E^\lambda
 =\int_0^\infty\bigl(\theta'^2+\lambda(1+\cos\theta)\bigr)\,ds
 \geq 2\sqrt\lambda\int_0^\infty
       |\theta'|\sqrt{1+\cos\theta}\,ds
 \geq4\sqrt{2\lambda}.\] Equality requires the nearest half-turn, monotonicity, and \(\theta'=\pm\sqrt{\lambda(1+\cos\theta)}\). Its solutions give precisely \(aM\gamma_b(s/a)\). For \(\lambda=8\), the unscaled curve has energy \(20\), while \(a=1/2\) gives \(16\). Thus the omitted normalization cannot be used literally, but the source’s own proof already establishes the correct result needed by Corollary 3.8. No damage to that corrected central argument has been demonstrated.
# Conclusion
Item | Judgment | Verified scope and remainder
Remark 4.3 | Minor | An actual pinned critical curve is omitted; scaling and interval repaired; published endpoint relation retained.
Central minimisation chain | No issue found in checked steps | External singular-limit and regularity proofs remain dependencies.
Displays in Theorems 3.1 and 3.7 | Clarification | Correct relations are already present in their proofs.
Independent acceptance | Pending | This is an initial-review continuation; no human review is recorded.
Scientific decision is pending; no human review or author adoption is recorded.

Title: Technical Review of
Reflexive Calkin Algebras
# Identity, scope, and terminology

The source is P. Motakis and A. Pelczar-Barwacz, Reflexive Calkin algebras, arXiv:2401.18037v1 [MP]. The exact revision was submitted on 31 January 2024 at 18:01:20 UTC. The associated journal identifier is `10.4171/JEMS/1709`; the publisher records online publication on 24 September 2025 [EMS]. The acquired 85-page preprint has no verified equivalence to the accepted manuscript or journal version. Every statement below concerns this precise acquired version. Page numbers are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with printed pages. All 85 pages were read as extracted text.

Here \(\mathcal L(X)\) denotes bounded operators, \(\mathcal K(X)\) compact operators, and \(\mathcal{SS}(X)\) strictly singular operators. These ideals must not be interchanged. The main algebra is \(\mathcal L(X)/\mathcal K(X)\). The auxiliary Proposition 4.4 instead concerns the quotient by \(\mathcal{SS}(X)\). A projection may be nonzero and still belong to both ideals when its range is finite-dimensional.

The main result assumes a normalized unconditional basis of \(U\) with no \(c_0\) asymptotic version, in the alternating block-choice sense of Definition 1.1. It constructs a Banach space \(\mathfrak X_U\) and mutually annihilating infinite-rank projections \(I_s\) such that \[\mathcal L(\mathfrak X_U)
 =\mathcal K(\mathfrak X_U)\oplus[I_s:s\geq1]\oplus\mathbb CI,\] with \((I_s)\) equivalent to the basis of \(U\). The conclusion is a Banach-algebra realization of the unitization of \(U\) with coordinate multiplication. It does not assert a Hilbert-space \(C^*\)-algebra realization.
# Checked proof chain and limits

The review followed the following substantive dependencies. In Proposition 4.1, pp. 16–17, the lower estimate for the quotient by compact operators uses successive vectors annihilating earlier members of a norming set. The compact images admit close pairs; their difference gives the factor \(2C\) in the lower bound. No unjustified weak-null conclusion from a merely norming set is needed. The finite-dimensional cancellation in the bonding construction, particularly Proposition 6.12 and the estimates in 6.15–6.17, supplies the hypotheses of this proposition.

The Bourgain–Delbaen construction uses triangular extension functionals and self-determined subsets. The coordinate projections in Section 6 depend on the bounds for the extension operators, and the ground-coordinate cancellation controls the maximum of component norms. The lower and upper estimates then give the equivalence constant used in Theorem 10.1. Section 7 and Appendix A pass from absence of a \(c_0\) asymptotic version to a lower block \(\ell_q\) estimate and a dual upper \(\ell_p\) estimate. The quantifier order in the block choices is essential; an arbitrary lower estimate on single fixed blocks would not suffice.

The operator argument in Section 10 uses scalar-plus-compact behavior on each component, compactness between distinct components, and horizontal scalar-plus-compact behavior on the whole space. These are proved later by rapidly increasing sequences and dependent sequences in Sections 12–13. The final step, Theorem 10.8, is a norm-distance-to-compact argument for the tails of \(\sum_s\lambda_s I_s\); it does not assume bounded completeness of the basis of \(U\). The cancellation vector has norm at most \(8\), while the ground correction has norm at most \(4N_0+12\). The chosen tail bound \(\varepsilon/(8N_0+24)\) makes its image smaller than \(\varepsilon/2\), producing the required contradiction to horizontal compactness.

The local antichain defect below was traced to its actual use in Proposition 11.8. This review does not certify every constant in every rapidly increasing or dependent-sequence induction. The external Bourgain–Delbaen and asymptotic-structure theorems, and all omitted componentwise translations in Section 13, have not been independently reproved in full. # A vacuous hypothesis in the strictly singular quotient proposition

Problem 1 (Finite-rank projections satisfy the printed hypotheses).  Proposition 4.4, p. 18, asserts an equivalence in \(\mathcal L(X)/\mathcal{SS}(X)\) for mutually annihilating projections \(I_s\), writing \(X_s=I_sX\). Its condition \((\gamma)\) quantifies over subspaces \(Y\) such that \(Y\cap X_s\) is infinite-dimensional for every \(s\). No infinite-rank hypothesis on the \(I_s\) is stated.
## An exact counterexample

Take \[U=X=\ell_1,\qquad u_s=e_s,\qquad I_sx=x_se_s,
 \qquad B=\beta=C=1.\] The basis of \(U\) is normalized and \(1\)-unconditional. The nonzero norm-one projections are mutually annihilating. For \(x_s=c_se_s\) and \(x_0\in\bigcap_{s=1}^N\ker I_s\), disjoint supports give \[\left\|\sum_{s=1}^Nx_s+x_0\right\|_1
 =\sum_{s=1}^N|c_s|+\|x_0\|_1
 \geq
 \left\|\sum_{s=1}^N\|x_s\|_1u_s\right\|_1.\] Thus condition \((\beta)\) holds with \(B=1\). Every \(X_s\) is one-dimensional. There is no subspace \(Y\) meeting the premise of \((\gamma)\), so its universal assertion is true, with the displayed positive \(\beta,C\).

Each \(I_s\) has finite rank and belongs to \(\mathcal{SS}(X)\). Consequently its quotient class is zero. A zero sequence cannot be equivalent to \((u_s^*)\), whose individual norms are one. Also \(0\neq I_1\in[I_s]\cap\mathcal{SS}(X)\), contradicting the claimed direct-sum conclusion. This checks every printed hypothesis; no numerical approximation or unverified structural example is involved.

The unquotiented sequence \((I_s)\) in \(\mathcal L(\ell_1)\) is indeed isometric to the unit-vector sequence spanning \(c_0\) in \(\ell_\infty\). The counterexample does not refute that separate part of the proposition.
## A sufficient repair
Add the requirement that every \(X_s\) be infinite-dimensional. Here is a direct verification of the quotient estimate under that additional premise and the original \((\beta),(\gamma)\).

For \(T\in\mathcal{SS}(X)\) and \(\delta>0\), choose a normalized basic sequence \((z_n)\) with basis constant at most \(2\), cycling through the spaces \(X_s\) so that each is visited infinitely often, and \[\|Tz_n\|\leq \delta\,2^{-n}/4.\] At each step the finitely many norming constraints used to continue a basic sequence leave an infinite-dimensional subspace of the chosen \(X_s\). Strict singularity guarantees a unit vector there with arbitrarily small image. The coefficient functionals have norms at most \(4\). Hence the closed span \(Y=[z_n]\) satisfies \(\|T|_Y\|\leq\delta\), and \(Y\cap X_s\) is infinite-dimensional for every \(s\).

Set \[P=\sum_{s=1}^N\lambda_sI_s,\qquad
 \Lambda=\left\|\sum_{s=1}^N\lambda_su_s^*\right\|_{U^*}.\] Condition \((\beta)\), applied to \(x_s=I_sx\) and \(x_0=x-\sum_{s=1}^NI_sx\), gives \[\|Px\|\leq\sum_s|\lambda_s|\|I_sx\|\leq B\Lambda\|x\|.\] Choose \(a_s\geq0\) with \(\|\sum_s a_su_s\|=1\) and \(\sum_s|\lambda_s|a_s=\Lambda\); finite-dimensional duality and unconditionality justify this choice. Apply \((\gamma)\) in \(Y\) to these \(a_s\) and \(b_s=\lambda_sa_s\). It supplies \(x=\sum_s a_sx_s-x_0\in Y\) with \[\|x\|\leq C,\qquad \|Px\|\geq\beta\Lambda.\] Since \(\|Tx\|\leq\delta\|x\|\), \[\beta\Lambda\leq C\bigl(\|P+T\|+\delta\bigr).\] Letting \(\delta\downarrow0\) and taking the infimum over \(T\) proves \[\frac{\beta}{C}\Lambda
 \leq \|P+\mathcal{SS}(X)\|
 \leq \|P\|\leq B\Lambda.\] These are the stated equivalence bounds. They extend to the closed spans. The identity is independent modulo \(\mathcal{SS}(X)\): outside the support of any finite sum of projections, its restriction to \(X_s\) is the identity on an infinite-dimensional space. Approximation by finite sums rules out membership in the closed span modulo \(\mathcal{SS}(X)\). Thus the added infinite-dimensionality premise also gives the directness asserted for the identity extension.
## Impact

The source explicitly says that Proposition 4.4 is not used. The actual construction proceeds through Proposition 4.1, which has different hypotheses and the compact-operator quotient. This defect is therefore Minor at the demonstrated scope. The strengthened proposition above is verified, but neither author adoption nor persistence in the journal text is asserted.

## Correct support-sensitive estimates

Write \[S_{\mathcal B}=\bigcup_{t\in\mathcal B}\operatorname{supp}f_t.\] The claimed estimate is valid if \(\operatorname{supp}f\cap\operatorname{supp}x\subseteq S_{\mathcal B}\). Equivalently, every root-to-terminal path whose leaf acts nontrivially on \(x\) must meet \(\mathcal B\).

 \leq\theta n^{-1/p}\sum_r|f_r(x)|

      \left(\sum_r|f_r(x)|^q\right)^{1/q}

The proof on pp. 56–57 separates precisely the missing set \(K\). Its blocks have \(\operatorname{supp}y_i\subseteq I_i\), with the \(I_i\) successive and disjoint. The antichain is partitioned into \(\mathcal B_i\), and the source explicitly defines \[J=\bigcup_i\bigcup_{t\in\mathcal B_i}(\operatorname{supp}f_t\cap I_i),

 \qquad z_i=y_i|_{D_i},\] disjointness of the antichain supports gives the exact identity \[(f-f')(y_i)=(f|_K)(y_i)+f(z_i).\] Applying [restricted] (#restricted) to the cross antichain yields \[|f(z_i)|\leq
 \left(\sum_{t\in\bigcup_{\ell\ne i}\mathcal B_\ell}
                    |f_t(y_i)|^q\right)^{1/q}.\] Thus the local separation estimate used there is valid with constant one and no changed assumptions on Proposition 11.8. Title: Technical Review of
Scalar Curvature and Volume Entropy
of Hyperbolic 3-Manifolds
# Identity and review scope

The source is D. Kazaras, A. Song and K. Xu, Scalar curvature and volume entropy of hyperbolic 3-manifolds, arXiv:2312.00138v3 [KSX]. The revision timestamp is 4 June 2025, 23:34:28 UTC; the arXiv record describes it as the final version accepted by JEMS. The associated DOI is `10.4171/JEMS/1710`; the publisher records online publication on 10 September 2025 [EMS]. Equivalence to the unacquired publisher PDF has not been verified. The frozen 2025 identity is retained. All 15 source pages, including references, were read as extracted text. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages.

Theorem 0.2 fixes a closed hyperbolic three-manifold \((M,g_0)\). It asserts the existence of metrics with \(R_g\geq-6\) and \(h(g)>2\), with either arbitrarily large entropy or arbitrarily small \(C^0\) distance from \(g_0\). These are different families; the two limiting requirements are not asserted simultaneously. Indeed a uniform comparison \(e^{-2\delta}g_0\leq g\leq e^{2\delta}g_0\) bounds entropy between \(2e^{-\delta}\) and \(2e^\delta\).

The actual scientific checks cover the complete local construction in Theorem 1.1, the scalar-curvature calculation, smoothness at the core, the short-loop argument, the limiting distance comparison, and the rescaling to the exact scalar-curvature bound. The stated comparison results were checked against the original references: the author-hosted Balacheff–Merlin text and Song’s arXiv:2302.07422v3, Theorem 3.5. The full external proofs of graph entropy, sphere equidistribution and the general comparison theorem were not independently reproved. The introductory claims about failure of volume stability in several metric-measure topologies were read but were not separately established by a complete intrinsic-flat convergence argument.
# The drawstring metric and its estimates

In a tube about a simple closed geodesic, the source uses \[g=e^{-2u}dr^2+e^{-2u}h^2\sinh^2r\,d\theta^2
                    +e^{2u}\cosh^2r\,dt^2.\] The radial functions are constant or even to the required orders near the core: \(u\) is constant and \(h=1-c_1r^2/(2r_2)\) there. With radial arclength \(\rho=e^{-u(0)}r\), the angular warping function is \(\rho+O(\rho^3)\) and the axial coefficient is even. This supplies the smooth extension at the core. Radial invariance also makes the local formula compatible with the normal holonomy around the geodesic.

For an independent curvature calculation, set \[X=h'/h,\quad Y=u',\quad H_2=h''/h,\quad U_2=u'',\quad
 C=\coth r,\quad T=\tanh r.\] If \(A=e^{-u}h\sinh r\) and \(B=e^u\cosh r\), their logarithmic \(r\)-derivatives are \(\alpha=-Y+X+C\) and \(\beta=Y+T\). The doubly warped scalar-curvature formula, using \(d/d\rho=e^u d/dr\), gives \[R_g=-2e^{2u}
  \bigl(\alpha'+\beta'+\alpha^2+\beta^2+\alpha\beta
                                      +Y(\alpha+\beta)\bigr).\] The bracket is \[H_2+2CX+Y^2+TX+2YT+3,\] because \(CT=1\). An independently executed symbolic expansion gave residual \(CT-1\) before that identity and exactly zero afterwards. Thus equation (13), pp. 6–9, has the correct signs and normalization. For \(h=1,u=0\) it returns \(R_{g_0}=-6\).

The order of parameter choices is material: \(r_1\) is chosen below the normal radius and \(e^{-100}\); \(c_1\) is small relative to \(r_1\) and the curvature tolerance; then \(r_2\) is made small enough that \(u(0)=a<0\) can be achieved with \(0<c_2<c_1\). The divergence of \(\int ds/(s\log(1/s))\) at zero permits any fixed negative \(a\). On the inner region, the positive terms from \(h\) dominate \((u')^2\) because \(c_2^2\leq c_1\) and \(\zeta(r/(4r_2))\leq\zeta(r/r_2)\). The remaining terms are bounded by the small tolerance using \(\log(1/r)>100\).

For the outer annulus \(r\in[r_1/4,r_1]\), \(u=0\) and \(\zeta(r/r_2)=1\). Although \(\psi(r)\) itself retains an additive dependence on \(r_2\), the uniform bound \(\psi\leq1/2\) suffices: \[|h'|+|h''|\leq C(r_1)c_1\] uniformly for \(0<r_2<r_1/64\), for any fixed smooth cutoff with bounded first and second derivatives. This is the uniform estimate needed before choosing \(r_2\).

The radial crossing bound follows from \(e^{-u(r)}\leq(\log(1/r))^{r_1}\). Integration by parts yields an endpoint term at most \(2r_1\) and a remaining integral at most \(r_1^2\), hence \(\int_0^{r_1}e^{-u}\,dr\leq3r_1\). This estimate is independent of the large contraction along the core and is essential to keeping the second based loop short.
# The impossible smooth cutoff constant

Problem 1 (The bounds in equation (7) cannot all hold).  On p. 5 the source requires a smooth function \(\zeta\) with \(\zeta=0\) on \([0,1/2]\), \(\zeta=1\) on \([1,\infty)\), \(0\leq\zeta'\leq4\), and \(|\zeta''|\leq16\). The same bounds, with reversed monotonicity, are imposed on \(\eta\). There is no such \(C^2\) function.
## A decisive nonexistence proof

Let \(v(t)=\zeta'(1/2+t)\) for \(0\leq t\leq1/2\). Smooth matching to the constant pieces gives \(v(0)=v(1/2)=0\), while the total increment requires \(\int_0^{1/2}v(t)\,dt=1\). The derivative bound implies \[v(t)\leq16\min(t,1/2-t)=:\mathcal T(t).\] The triangular upper envelope has area \[\int_0^{1/2}\mathcal T(t)\,dt
 =\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot4=1.\] Since \(\mathcal T-v\) is continuous and nonnegative and its integral is zero, \(v=\mathcal T\) everywhere. But \(\mathcal T\) is not differentiable at \(t=1/4\). This contradicts \(v\in C^1\). The contradiction concerns all functions satisfying the stated bounds, not just one failed candidate cutoff. Replacing \(\eta\) by \(1-\eta\) gives the same obstruction for \(\eta\).
## An explicit admissible repair

Define a nonnegative continuous trapezoid \(v_0\) supported in \([13/24,23/24]\). It rises with slope \(36\) from zero to \(3\) on \([13/24,15/24]\), stays equal to \(3\) on \([15/24,21/24]\), and falls with slope \(-36\) to zero on \([21/24,23/24]\). Then \[\int v_0
 =2\left(\frac12\cdot\frac1{12}\cdot3\right)
       +\frac14\cdot3=1,\qquad
 0\leq v_0\leq3,\qquad \|v_0'\|_\infty\leq36.\] Convolve with a nonnegative smooth unit-mass mollifier of support radius \(1/48\). The resulting \(v\) is smooth, supported strictly inside \((1/2,1)\), has integral one, and satisfies \(0\leq v\leq3\), \(|v'|\leq36\). Set \[\zeta(x)=\int_0^x v(t)\,dt,\qquad \eta=1-\zeta.\] All endpoint, support, range and monotonicity conditions in (7) now hold, including the original first-derivative bound \(4\). Only the second-derivative bound changes from \(16\) to \(36\). The trapezoid area, slope and strict support margins were also checked by exact rational arithmetic.
## Repair boundary and actual impact

In the inner-region estimate (15), the argument uses \(\zeta'\geq0\), the cutoff values between zero and one, and the parameter inequalities; the constant \(16\) is not used. The second derivative enters the outer-annulus estimate through a fixed finite bound on \(\eta''\). The uniform estimate established above remains valid with \(36\), and choosing \(c_1\) smaller gives the same prescribed curvature tolerance. All subsequent choices of \(r_2,c_2\) and the radial crossing estimate remain available. The original conclusions (i)–(iv) of Theorem 1.1 are thus preserved by this repair, with their original hypotheses.

The literal preliminary cutoff selection is false. Its demonstrated impact is Minor, because the needed construction and bounds are established here after replacing a numerical auxiliary bound, without weakening the geometric theorem. This assessment is based on the verified downstream estimates, not merely on the brevity of the correction. No author adoption or journal-version persistence is asserted.
# Entropy arguments and boundary cases
## Arbitrarily large entropy

A shortest nontrivial closed geodesic can be chosen simple. In the hyperbolic fundamental group, powers of suitable noncommuting elements generate a free subgroup of rank two. The core loop length tends to zero under the drawstring construction, while a transverse based representative of the second generator has uniformly bounded length by the radial crossing estimate.

The precise inequality needed from Balacheff–Merlin [BM], Corollary 2, is \[\frac1{1+\exp(h\ell_1)}+\frac1{1+\exp(h\ell_2)}\leq\frac12.\] If \(h\) had a bounded subsequence while \(\ell_1\to0\) and \(\ell_2\leq L\), the first summand would tend to \(1/2\) and the second would remain bounded away from zero. Therefore \(h\to\infty\). The loop-independence condition, rather than arbitrary nontriviality of the loops, is essential. From \(R_{g_i}\geq-7\), the rescaling \(\widehat g_i=(7/6)g_i\) gives \(R_{\widehat g_i}\geq-6\) and \(h(\widehat g_i)=\sqrt{6/7}\,h(g_i)\to\infty\).
## Metrics close to the hyperbolic metric

Fix \(\delta>0\), choose \(a=-\delta\) and curvature tolerance and tube radius tending to zero. The uniform comparison \(e^{-2\delta}g_0\leq g_i\leq e^{2\delta}g_0\) gives equicontinuity and a subsequential uniform limit of the distance functions. The limit is bi-Lipschitz to \(d_{g_0}\). For sufficiently close distinct points on the core geodesic, the shortened core segment is strictly shorter than their original minimizing segment, so the limiting identity is not an isometry.

For a minimizing \(g_0\)-geodesic, each passage through the thin tube can be replaced by radial legs and a core path. The added error is at most \(6/i\) per passage. Every intervening exterior segment has length at least \(s_I/2\) for sufficiently large \(i\). If there are \(n\) passages and \(D=\operatorname{diam}(M,g_0)\), the immediately justified count is \[(n-1)s_I/2\leq D,\qquad n\leq1+2D/s_I.\] Consequently the argument gives the sufficient bound \[d_{g_i}(x,y)\leq d_{g_0}(x,y)
             +(6+12D/s_I)i^{-1}.\] This verifies the limiting \(1\)-Lipschitz property. The omitted \(+1\) in the printed count and the repeated \(d_{g_i}\) in equation (31), p. 13, are local corrections; they do not change the \(O(i^{-1})\) conclusion. No independent geometric counterexample to the claimed main distance bound is asserted.

In Song’s Theorem 3.5 [Song], take the open set \(A_i=M\), the homotopy equivalence \(f_i=\mathrm{Id}\), and the limiting bi-Lipschitz map \(\Psi=\mathrm{Id}\). Uniform distance convergence supplies the required approximate isometry. The theorem therefore gives a strict limiting entropy gap above \(2\). Its orientation hypothesis can be handled for a nonorientable \(M\) by the oriented double cover: the lifted radial construction has the same distance comparisons and a strictly shortened local core segment, and volume entropy is unchanged by a finite cover. Finally \(\widehat g_i=(1+1/(6i))g_i\) imposes \(R_{\widehat g_i}\geq-6\); the factor tends to one, preserving the strict limiting gap. Taking \(\delta\) small and then \(i\) large proves the stated \(C^0\) approximation regime.
# Assessment

There is one confirmed local Minor finding, equation (7). Its sufficient repair and downstream scope are proved above. The checked main proof chain is not refuted. External entropy-comparison results remain explicit dependencies, and the informal introductory stability consequences have not received a separate complete verification here. Scientific decision is pending, with no human review or adoption recorded.

claim: Smooth cutoff rises from 0 on [0,1/2] to 1 on [1,infinity), with 0<=zeta'<=4 and |zeta''|<=16; eta has reversed endpoints and the same absolute derivative bounds.
v(t)=zeta'(1/2+t) is C1 on [0,1/2]. v vanishes at both endpoints by smooth matching. Integral v is exactly1 by the prescribed total increment. |v'|<=16.
analysis: On p. 5 the source requires a smooth function \(\zeta\) with \(\zeta=0\) on \([0,1/2]\), \(\zeta=1\) on \([1,\infty)\), \(0\leq\zeta'\leq4\), and \(|\zeta''|\leq16\). The same bounds, with reversed monotonicity, are imposed on \(\eta\). There is no such \(C^2\) function.

Let \(v(t)=\zeta'(1/2+t)\) for \(0\leq t\leq1/2\). Smooth matching to the constant pieces gives \(v(0)=v(1/2)=0\), while the total increment requires \(\int_0^{1/2}v(t)\,dt=1\). The derivative bound implies \[v(t)\leq16\min(t,1/2-t)=:\mathcal T(t).\] The triangular upper envelope has area \[\int_0^{1/2}\mathcal T(t)\,dt
 =\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot4=1.\] Since \(\mathcal T-v\) is continuous and nonnegative and its integral is zero, \(v=\mathcal T\) everywhere. But \(\mathcal T\) is not differentiable at \(t=1/4\). This contradicts \(v\in C^1\). The contradiction concerns all functions satisfying the stated bounds, not just one failed candidate cutoff. Replacing \(\eta\) by \(1-\eta\) gives the same obstruction for \(\eta\).

Define a nonnegative continuous trapezoid \(v_0\) supported in \([13/24,23/24]\). It rises with slope \(36\) from zero to \(3\) on \([13/24,15/24]\), stays equal to \(3\) on \([15/24,21/24]\), and falls with slope \(-36\) to zero on \([21/24,23/24]\). Then \[\int v_0
 =2\left(\frac12\cdot\frac1{12}\cdot3\right)
       +\frac14\cdot3=1,\qquad
 0\leq v_0\leq3,\qquad \|v_0'\|_\infty\leq36.\] Convolve with a nonnegative smooth unit-mass mollifier of support radius \(1/48\). The resulting \(v\) is smooth, supported strictly inside \((1/2,1)\), has integral one, and satisfies \(0\leq v\leq3\), \(|v'|\leq36\). Set \[\zeta(x)=\int_0^x v(t)\,dt,\qquad \eta=1-\zeta.\] All endpoint, support, range and monotonicity conditions in (7) now hold, including the original first-derivative bound \(4\). Only the second-derivative bound changes from \(16\) to \(36\). The trapezoid area, slope and strict support margins were also checked by exact rational arithmetic.
