report: Abstract: This review concerns the acquired 67-page arXiv:2401.03053v1 manuscript. One substantive Minor finding is established: the last equality of Lemma 8.7 confuses graded rank with graded dimension. An admissible rank-one example gives different degree-two coefficients. The interchanged left and right redundancy labels in Definition 4.15 are retained as a scope clarification, without a demonstrated affected calculation. The corrected forms preserve the subsequent bimodule construction and counting argument. Independent finite-group and Frobenius-algebra calculations support selected interfaces of the proof. No Major defect has been established in the basis theorems. This is a bounded initial review. The retained source evidence images have now been inspected; several external results remain dependencies, and scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical review of
Singular light leaves
# Source identity and precise scope

The source is B. Elias, H. Ko, N. Libedinsky and L. Patimo, Singular light leaves, arXiv:2401.03053v1 [source]. The arXiv submission is 5 January 2024 at 20:09:40 UTC; the acquired PDF’s first page separately says 9 January 2024. Both dates are retained. The associated journal DOI is 10.4171/JEMS/1715, with online publication on 24 October 2025 according to EMS Press [ems]. The acquired preprint has not been verified as the accepted manuscript or journal version. All findings here apply only to its exact bytes. The frozen identifier M25-0338 and assigned year 2025 are unchanged.

All 67 PDF pages were read through the retained Poppler text extraction. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with printed pages. The review followed the double-coset reduction, Hecke coefficients, grading conventions, Frobenius maps, construction of sprinkles, dual sequences, and the independence–spanning argument. Many formulas in Sections 5–8 are diagrams. The bounded continuation visually inspected all 53 retained source evidence pages, including the relevant oriented crossings and proof diagrams. This confirms the displayed notation and cited interfaces; it does not independently reprove the full Frobenius cube calculus.

Theorem 7.49, p. 47, asserts a basis after applying the evaluation functor to singular Bott–Samelson bimodules. It is not a complete generators-and-relations presentation of the diagrammatic category. The coefficient rings \(R_p\) vary with the double coset; the displayed global basis is a \(\Bbbk\)-basis after choosing homogeneous bases of these rings. These restrictions are essential to a faithful assessment.
# Hypotheses, normalization, and proof structure

Section 4.1, p. 17, fixes a field and a faithful, balanced, reflection-faithful realization with generalized Demazure surjectivity. All parabolics in the expressions are finitary. The manuscript explicitly warns that the required realization need not exist in positive characteristic for an infinite Coxeter group. Nothing in this review extends its theorem to those excluded realizations.

Write \(\underline p,\overline p\) for minimal and maximal representatives, and \(\ell(I)=\ell(w_I)\). These decorations must be kept distinct: text extraction sometimes collapses them. The source’s conventions are \[R=\operatorname{Sym}(V),\qquad \deg V=2,\qquad
 M(n)_j=M_{j+n}.\] For a multistep expression with intermediate maxima \(K_j\) and minima \(I_j\), its Bott–Samelson shift is \[\sigma=\sum_j\ell(K_j)-\sum_{j\geq1}\ell(I_j).\] Thus an increasing step \(I\subset K\) gives \(R^I\) without a shift, whereas the reverse step gives \(R^I(\ell(K)-\ell(I))\). The duality is \(\operatorname{Hom}_{R^I}(-,R^I)\). This agrees with the comprehensive normalization in Williamson’s appended erratum, arXiv:1010.1283v3, Section 8.4 [williamson]. The erratum does not by itself invalidate this manuscript’s normalization.

For \(p\subset q\), where the right parabolic changes from \(J\) to \(Js\), the upward defect is \[d_\uparrow=\ell(\underline q)-\ell(\underline p)
             -\ell(\operatorname{LR}(q))+\ell(\operatorname{LR}(p)),
 \qquad
 d_\downarrow=d_\uparrow+\ell(Js)-\ell(J).\] The upward polynomial is \(\pi^+(\operatorname{LR}(q))/\pi^+(\operatorname{LR}(p))\), and the downward polynomial is \(1\). Grassmannian reduction isolates the nontrivial local pair and preserves these data. Summing over subordinate paths gives the standard-basis coefficient \(c_p(v)\). With the target self-dual, the Hom formula uses \[\operatorname{gd}\operatorname{Hom}(B,B')=\sum_p c_p(v)c'_p(v)\,\operatorname{gd}R_p .\] In particular, the polynomial factors must not be dropped.

The local Frobenius pairing evaluates a light leaf with a dual sprinkle to a Kronecker delta modulo positive-degree elements. With homogeneous choices \(P_L\) of degree \(2\ell(w_L)\), degree comparison removes the possible remainder in the diagonal and triangular cases. Such choices exist: take that homogeneous component of any preimage of \(1\) under the degree \(-2\ell(w_L)\) Demazure operator. This is the graded choice used in the audit, not a verification for arbitrary inhomogeneous replacements.

The dual sequence is injective on coterminal sprinkled paths. At the last place where their underlying cosets differ, that step must be increasing; equality of the dual elements would put the two Grassmannian minima in the same double coset, a contradiction. Lexicographic comparison then yields Proposition 8.26. Evaluating a nonzero combination on the maximal dual test tensor detects its coefficient. Lower-term separation, followed by the corrected graded count, gives the basis modulo lower terms. Finally, induction on the finite Bruhat support gives spanning of double leaves; the full Hom dimension gives independence. The two-sided triangular order, rather than either individual total order alone, controls Theorem 7.51.
# Scope clarification: the redundancy inclusions

Definition 4.15, p. 21, writes \(K=\operatorname{LR}(p)\subset J\) and \(L=\operatorname{RR}(p)\subset I\). These containing labels are interchanged. The following example confirms the textual correction; it is not counted as a substantive Problem. Take type \(A_2\) over \(\mathbb Q\) with its usual reflection realization, \(s=(12)\), \(t=(23)\), \(I=\{s\}\), \(J=\{t\}\), and \(w=ts\). This realization satisfies the stated hypotheses, and all the parabolics are finite. With composition acting rightmost first, \[W_IwW_J=\{ts,sts\},\qquad \ell(ts)=2,\quad\ell(sts)=3.\] Hence \(w=\underline p\). Direct conjugation gives \[wtw^{-1}=s,\qquad w^{-1}sw=t,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{LR}(p)=I,\quad \operatorname{RR}(p)=J.\] Since \(s\ne t\), neither printed cross-inclusion holds. The retained permutation calculation reproduces the coset and its two lengths exactly.

The correct statements are \[K=\operatorname{LR}(p)\subset I,\qquad L=\operatorname{RR}(p)\subset J.\] They follow directly from Section 2.2, p. 10. They also give exactly the ring inclusions needed by the existing construction: \[R^I\subset R^K,\qquad
 R^J\subset R^L,\qquad
 \underline p R^L=R^K.\] Thus left multiplication by \(R^I\) and the right action \(m\cdot f=(\underline p f)m\) preserve \(R^K\) and commute. In the displayed example \(R_p=R^I\), and every left-linear endomorphism is multiplication by its value at \(1\); it automatically commutes with the twisted right action. Consequently \(\operatorname{End}(R_p)=R_p\) here.

Impact and repair boundary. This is a scope clarification of the containing labels. The named redundancy subgroups are correctly defined on p. 10 and are the subgroups actually used in the subsequent construction. No changed action, calculation, realization assumption, basis element, or conclusion has been demonstrated. The annotation error alone is therefore excluded from the substantive finding count. The corrected labels agree with the existing actions; no failure of the standard-bimodule theory is inferred.
# Graded rank versus graded dimension

Problem 1 (A missing polynomial-ring factor in (179)).  The last equality of Lemma 8.7, p. 52, equates the finite light-leaf degree polynomial with \(\operatorname{gd}\operatorname{Hom}_{\not<p}(\operatorname{BS}(I_\bullet),\operatorname{BS}(Y_p))\). With the full graded-dimension convention used in Theorem 4.16, this equality is false.

Use type \(A_1\) over \(\mathbb Q\), \(R=\mathbb Q[x]\), \(\deg x=2\), and the identity expression \(I_\bullet=Y_p=[\varnothing]\), \(p=e\). There is one subordinate path, no sprinkles, and one leaf, the identity of degree zero. There is no lower Bruhat layer. Therefore \[\sum_{\mathrm{LL}}v^{\deg\mathrm{LL}}=1,\qquad
 \operatorname{Hom}_{\not<e}(R,R)=R,\qquad
 \operatorname{gd}R=\frac{1}{1-v^2}.\] The degree-two coefficients are respectively \(0\) and \(1\). This is an exact counterexample under all the paper’s hypotheses; it is not a finite numerical extrapolation or a grading-shift ambiguity.

Actual downstream effect. Lemma 8.8, p. 53, explicitly restores the factor \(\sum_{b\in B_p}v^{\deg b}=\operatorname{gd}R_p\). Proposition 8.32, p. 63, expressly compares graded ranks. Thus the main counting argument uses the corrected quantity. This is assessed as Minor because the proof’s needed count is recovered under the same hypotheses and its later use is consistent with that count. It is not evidence that the full polynomial multiples of leaves are absent from the proposed basis.
# Independent checks and a proof interface
## Finite Coxeter calculations

The retained independent Python program enumerates all 555 pairs relevant to Grassmannian reduction in \(S_4\), over every pair of standard parabolics and every allowed added simple reflection. It verifies the minimal-element factorization \(\underline p=\underline q\,\underline m\), length additivity, redundancy conjugacy, reduced coset lengths, and both defect identities. A separate Hecke multiplication implementation in \(S_3\), using \[h_s^2=1+(v^{-1}-v)h_s,\] checks 42 upward and 24 downward instances of Proposition 3.4. It also reproduces the six distinct dual sequences in Example 8.21 and the order in Example 8.24: \[sts\prec ts\prec s\prec st\prec t\prec e .\] All assertions passed. These finite checks support the stated interfaces; they do not prove the arbitrary-Coxeter theorem.
## Rank-one Frobenius and Hom calculations

Let \(s(x)=-x\), \(A=\mathbb Q[x^2]\), and \(\partial f=(f-sf)/(2x)\), so \(\partial x=1\). For \(B=R\otimes_A R(1)\), use the left \(R\)-basis \(e=1\otimes1,\ f=1\otimes x\). Right multiplication by \(x\) has matrix \[X=\begin{pmatrix}0&x^2\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] A left-linear matrix commutes with \(X\) precisely when it is \[M=\begin{pmatrix}a&x^2c\\c&a\end{pmatrix}.\] Writing \(\epsilon\) for multiplication and \(\eta(1)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x\), we have \[T=\eta\epsilon=x\,\mathrm{id}+X,\qquad
 T^2=2xT,\qquad
 \operatorname{End}_{R-R}(B)=R\,\mathrm{id}\oplus R\,T.\] The basis degrees are \(0,2\), and the graded rank is \(1+v^2\).

For the singular object \(R(1)\) over \((A,A)\), the correct answer has a negative-degree term: \[\operatorname{End}_{A-A}(R(1))
 =R\,\mathrm{id}\oplus R\,\partial,\qquad
 \operatorname{gd}\operatorname{End}_{A-A}(R(1))
 =(1+v^{-2})\operatorname{gd}R=(v+v^{-1})^2\operatorname{gd}A.\] Indeed, a map taking \(1\) to \(u\) and \(x\) to \(z\) is \(u\,\mathrm{id}+(z-xu)\partial\). The four \(A\)-matrix units have degrees \(0,0,2,-2\). A common shift of source and target does not change them. These formulas agree with the manuscript’s shifts and Hom formula. An initial analytical test expectation for this singular case was corrected during the bounded auxiliary discussion before code execution; it was not treated as a paper defect.
## The lower-term separation used in Theorem 8.31

Proposition 4.20 is stated with a reduced source as well as a reduced target, whereas Theorem 8.31 applies the separation property to arbitrary source expressions. The needed extension can be checked without assuming the light-leaves theorem. The cited companion paper’s Theorem 3.30 identifies lower maps with maps into \(\Gamma_{<p}\) of the target. Its Proposition 3.34 proof constructs the target quotient \[q_p:\operatorname{BS}(Y_p)\longrightarrow R_p(\text{grading shift}),
 \qquad q_p(h1^\otimes)=h.\] Thus, for any source \(M\) and lower map \(F:M\to\operatorname{BS}(Y_p)\), \(q_pF=0\). If \(F(z)=h1^\otimes\), then \(h=0\). The source need not be reduced. The companion’s exact sequences and this implication were checked in arXiv:2307.15726v2 [lower]. This supplies the required interface; no counterexample to the independence argument follows from the abbreviated citation.
# Coverage, dependencies, and assessment

The textual chain through Sections 2–8 has been followed, including the well-founded Bruhat induction, the distinction between a reduced target and an arbitrary expression, and the final cellular packaging. The local dual-basis hypotheses in Theorem 8.15 were compared with Lemma 4.13 and Theorem 4.14 of arXiv:2307.15021v2 [demazure]. The relevant lower-term quotient statements and the normalization in Williamson’s erratum were checked at their cited primary sources. Their complete foundational proofs, the full Frobenius cube calculus, and every diagram in this 67-page manuscript have not been independently reproved. The cited source evidence diagrams have now been visually inspected; external primary-source consultations are retained facts of the original execution and are not credited as new image inspections.

For a homogeneous free-module map with the stated independent generators and the same graded ranks, equality of the finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces supplies spanning. In the last Bruhat induction one may use a finite downward-closed support, as Remark 8.36 explicitly allows; no single maximal element of an arbitrary infinite Coxeter group is needed. The cellular statement concerns the category of Bott–Samelson objects in the theorem’s setting and uses the chosen identity leaf for a reduced object. It is not asserted here for an unspecified enlarged category.

The bounded source search checked the arXiv record, publisher metadata, an author publication page, and correction/dependency records. No separate paper-specific code release or supplement was located. The publicly linked companion papers are mathematical dependencies. The publisher page requires a subscription for the article, so the journal text was not acquired through this review. Initial direct versioned dependency requests returned tool errors; their public author links led to the accessible v2 HTML records used above. The initial publisher-erratum fetch failed; the author’s link to the appended arXiv erratum supplied the normalization check. These limitations are retained, not interpreted as absence of a correction. No author code was run.

The overall finding is Minor, for the graded-count discrepancy in Lemma 8.7. The redundancy-label interchange is a separate scope clarification, not a substantive finding. No Major issue has been established within the actual coverage. That statement is not an independent acceptance or an unconditional certification of the basis theorem. The source evidence images have been inspected in the bounded continuation; the exact final report build and page inspections are recorded separately in the recovery evidence.

Title: Technical review of
Bitangents of real algebraic curves:
signed count and constructions
# Identity, version, and scope

The source is T. Blomme, E. Brugallé and C. Garay, Bitangents of real algebraic curves: signed count and constructions, arXiv:2402.03993v1, submitted 6 February 2024 at 13:45:19 UTC [source]. The associated journal DOI is `10.4171/JEMS/1716`. The publisher lists acceptance on 11 April 2025 and online publication on 7 November 2025 [publisher]. The acquired 38-page PDF is the arXiv version, not a verified copy of the accepted or journal text. The frozen identifier and year remain M25-0339 and 2025. Every page was read as extracted text, including the references. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with the printed pagination.

The audit follows the hypotheses of genericity, the sign convention, the Hilbert-square stratification, the real deformation count, the stated construction counts, and the arithmetic assertion in Section 5. It includes independent exact symbolic calculations and analytic proofs. The bounded continuation visually inspected all 35 retained source evidence pages, including Figures 1–22. The displayed schemes, labels and cited proof interfaces were checked; this does not independently reprove every Brusotti/Harnack realization. The external existence and regularity theorems used by the authors have not all been reproved.

A bounded search of the arXiv record, publisher record, author-related publication records, and title-based correction/code/supplement queries did not locate a separate paper-specific implementation, supplement, or correction notice. This is not proof of absence. No author code was run, and absence of code is not a defect. The publisher requires a subscription for its article text; no equivalence to that unacquired text is asserted.
# Definitions, proof chain, and checks without a finding

A generic plane curve here is smooth and has dual singularities consisting only of ordinary nodes and cusps (pp. 1–2). For degree \(d=2k\), write \(p,n\) for the numbers of even and odd real ovals. The bitangent sign is unchanged if the two complementary sign regions are exchanged. Real bitangents with conjugate contact points contribute positively; for two real contacts the sign is the product of the two local side signs. These distinctions matter in passing from an unsigned count to \(t_s\).
## Euler-characteristic bookkeeping

For the double plane \(S\) branched along the curve, put \(a=p-n\). The identities used on pp. 9–14 are \[\chi(\mathbb CS)=6+d(d-3),\qquad
 \chi(\mathbb RS)=2a,\qquad
 \chi(\mathbb RP^+)=a,\quad \chi(\mathbb RP^-)=1-a.\] Compactly supported Euler characteristic is used on strata. The real sign regions are two-dimensional manifolds, so their ordinary and compactly supported Euler characteristics agree. There is no sign discrepancy from that passage.

For a nodal curve of arithmetic genus \(g\), with \(k_+\) hyperbolic real nodes, \(k_-\) elliptic real nodes, and \(k_{\mathbb C}\) conjugate pairs of non-real nodes, set \(r=k_--k_+\). The normalization and local Hilbert-square contributions give \[\chi(\mathbb RC^{[2]})
 =\frac{r^2+(2-2g+k_++k_-+2k_{\mathbb C})}{2}-k_+-k_-
 =1-g+k_{\mathbb C}-k_++\binom{k_--k_+}{2}.\] The cusp term is \(1-g\). These formulas reproduce the two integrations in the paper. For the projection from pairs on \(S\), the distinct-real-pair part contributes \[\frac{\chi(\mathbb RS)^2-\chi(\mathbb RS)}2-\chi(\mathbb RP^+)

## Degeneration and counting

The \(k\)-section has Newton triangle with vertices \((0,0)\), \((0,k)\) and \((4k,0)\), is smooth in the affine chart, and has nonrepeated factors on the upper edge (Definition 3.3, pp. 17–18). The projection general-position condition on p. 22 requires distinct simple critical values, exactly \[N=4k(k-1)=d(d-2)\] in number. It does not prohibit concurrency among unrelated limiting chords.

Proposition 3.6 constructs the degree-\(2k\) family by replacing the normal coordinate with \((y^2-xz)/t\). The local dual-curve argument in Theorem 3.9 gives one nearby bitangent for each chord joining distinct critical values, and \(2(k-2)\) near each tangent to the conic. The algebraic total is \[\binom{N}{2}+2(k-2)N
 =\frac{d(d-2)(d-3)(d+3)}2,\] the full complex bitangent count. The distinct-chord branches are simple intersections in the dual degeneration.

For the coalescing case, the local model can be checked by writing a ramified branch as \(x=u^4+t\alpha(u)\), \(y=u^2+\cdots\) with \(\alpha'(0)\ne0\), and an unramified branch with a different value \(\widehat\alpha(0)\). After \(t=s^2\), \(u=s\xi\), \(v=s\eta\), the leading tangent equations are \[\eta=\frac{\alpha'(0)}{4\xi},\qquad
 \eta^2=\widehat\alpha(0)-\alpha(0).\] The roots are simple when the two heights differ. The arithmetic of the sextic count on p. 30 gives \[276+2\{12-(p+n-1)\}+4(p-1)=298+2(p-n).\] The Harnack-family sum on p. 31 is \[\sum_{i=1}^{k-2}4i(k-1-i)=\frac{2k(k-1)(k-2)}3;\] doubling gives the number of non-real bitangents. # Arithmetic specialization does not preserve the ground field

Problem 1 (A rational limiting chord can have no nearby rational bitangent).  Section 5(7), p. 34, asserts that Theorem 3.9 has a weak version over every field \(K\) of characteristic different from two: a limiting chord defined over \(K\) deforms to a bitangent defined over \(K\) of \(C_t\) for \(t\in K\). The following example over \(K=\mathbb Q\) violates that specialization assertion, including arbitrarily small rational parameters.
## An admissible two-section and the prescribed family

Take \[\mathcal A=\left\{\frac12,2,\frac13,3\right\},\qquad
 P(u)=\prod_{a\in\mathcal A}(u^2-a^2),\qquad C:\ w^2=P(u).\] All eight roots \(\pm a\) are distinct rational numbers. At a root \(r\), the projection has the expansion \(u=r+w^2/P'(r)+O(w^4)\), so its eight critical points are nondegenerate with distinct critical values. The affine curve is smooth. The constant term is nonzero and the upper-edge equation is \(w^2-u^8\), with distinct factors. In the chart at infinity, \(s=1/u\), \(W=w/u^4\), the equation is \[W^2=\prod_{a\in\mathcal A}(1-a^2s^2).\] At \(s=0\) the two points \(W=\pm1\) are smooth and unramified. Thus the compactified two-section also meets the required boundary conditions.

Equation reference: quartic. Proposition 3.6 gives exactly the rational quartic family \[F_t(x,y,z)=(y^2-xz)^2-t^2\prod_{a\in\mathcal A}(x-a^2z)=0.
 \] On the limiting conic, use \((x,y,z)=(u^2,u,1)\). Two of its specified rational chords are \[L_1:\ y=\frac25(x+z),\quad (u=\tfrac12,2),
 \qquad
 L_2:\ y=\frac3{10}(x+z),\quad (u=\tfrac13,3).\] The reciprocal symmetry does not violate any stated projection assumption.
## Exact bitangent equations

Equation reference: restriction, mbranches. Set \(x=U+V\), \(z=U-V\), and \(c=625/9\). Direct multiplication gives \[\prod_{a\in\mathcal A}(x-a^2z)
 =16U^4-cU^2V^2+cV^4.\] Restrict [quartic] (#quartic) to \(y=2mU\), and put \(A=4m^2-1\). The restriction is \[(1-ct^2)V^4+(2A+ct^2)U^2V^2+(A^2-16t^2)U^4.
 \] For \(0<|t|<3/25\) this is a quadratic square exactly when \[cA^2+cA+16+\frac{c^2-64c}{4}t^2=0.\] Its discriminant in \(A\) is \((175/9)^2(1-ct^2)\). Consequently the two positive-slope branches satisfy \[m_\pm(t)^2=\frac18\pm\frac7{200}
                 \sqrt{1-\frac{625}{9}t^2},
 \qquad
 m_+(0)=\frac25,\quad m_-(0)=\frac3{10}.
 \] These are exact algebraic equations, independently reproduced in the retained calculation.

For every integer \(N\ge105\), \[(3N-1)^2<9N^2-625<(3N)^2.\] Hence \(\sqrt{1-625/(9N^2)}\) is irrational. Formula [mbranches] (#mbranches) shows that \(m_\pm(1/N)^2\), and therefore \(m_\pm(1/N)\), are irrational. A line \(y=m(x+z)\) is defined over \(\mathbb Q\) exactly when its normalized coefficient \(m\) is rational. Both displayed bitangents fail that condition.
## No second, nonsymmetric rational branch is available

This uniqueness point is essential. A general nearby line has the form \(y=hU+\ell V\). Set \[A=h^2-1,\qquad B=2h\ell,\qquad D=1+\ell^2.\] Its restriction is \[(AU^2+BUV+DV^2)^2-t^2(16U^4-cU^2V^2+cV^4).\] If it is a bitangent, this binary quartic is a square \((aU^2+bUV+eV^2)^2\) over the algebraic closure. Comparison of coefficients gives \[ab=AB,\quad be=BD,\quad
 a^2=A^2-16t^2,\quad e^2=D^2-ct^2.\] In neighborhoods of \(L_1,L_2\), the numbers \(h,A,D\) are nonzero. If \(\ell\ne0\), division gives \(a/e=A/D\), hence, for \(t\ne0\), \[cA^2=16D^2.\] At the two limiting chords, respectively, \(cA^2-16D^2\) equals \(-7\) and \(112/9\). It remains nonzero on fixed neighborhoods. Thus every nearby bitangent has \(\ell=0\). The quadratic equation above has one separated root near each corresponding value \(A=-9/25,-16/25\), and the positive limiting \(h\) fixes its square root. Each specified chord has exactly the one nearby branch already computed. This argument also holds in complex neighborhoods.
## Smoothness and two ordinary real contacts

The quartic is a quadratic form in \((U^2,V^2,y^2)\), with matrix \[Q_t=\begin{pmatrix}
 1-16t^2&-1+ct^2/2&-1\\
 -1+ct^2/2&1-ct^2&1\\
 -1&1&1
 \end{pmatrix}.\] For \(0<t<3/25\), its first-order principal minors are nonzero. Its second-order principal minors are \[-16t^2-\frac{30625}{324}t^4,\qquad -16t^2,\qquad -ct^2,\] and its determinant is \(-30625t^4/324\). If a projective singular point existed, its nonzero-coordinate support would give a nonzero vector in the kernel of a principal submatrix of \(Q_t\). The listed minors exclude this. The quartic is therefore smooth over \(\mathbb C\) throughout this interval.

For \(t=1/N\), \(N\ge105\), both roots satisfy \[-\frac{16}{25}<A<-\frac9{25},\quad
 1-ct^2>0,\quad 2A+ct^2<0.\] Equation [restriction] (#restriction) becomes \[(1-ct^2)\left(V^2+
       \frac{2A+ct^2}{2(1-ct^2)}\,U^2\right)^2.\] The quadratic has two distinct real roots. Since the curve is smooth, these give two distinct contacts of intersection multiplicity exactly two. The lines are actual ordinary real bitangents, not formal candidates or hyperflexes.
## An independently certified generic specialization

Take \(t=1/1000\). The non-square integer above is \(8999375\), between \(2999^2=8994001\) and \(3000^2=9000000\). The seven principal minors at this parameter are \[\frac{62499}{62500},\quad \frac{14399}{14400},\quad 1,\quad
 -\frac{8294449}{518400000000},\quad
 -\frac1{62500},\quad-\frac1{14400},\quad
 -\frac{49}{518400000000}.\] To verify the stronger generic-dual hypothesis, denominators in \(F_{1/1000}\) were cleared and its homogeneous Hessian determinant \(H\) computed independently.  \partial_U\overline F\,\partial_V\overline H-
 \partial_V\overline F\,\partial_U\overline H\right)\] is \((1)\). On \(y=0,U=1\), the ideal consisting of \(\overline F,\overline H\) and all three projective gradient minors also has basis \((1)\). At the only omitted projective point \([0:1:0]\), \(\overline F=8\ne0\). These exact finite-field computations certify transverse intersection of the quartic and its Hessian. The projective bad-intersection locus is closed over the integers localized away from the denominators; properness implies that a characteristic-zero bad point would specialize to a bad point here. There is none.

Thus the characteristic-zero quartic has no hyperflex. A smooth plane quartic without hyperflex has dual with ordinary nodes and cusps: a line cannot be tangent at three distinct points by Bézout, nor be both a flex tangent and an additional tangent, and distinct contact points give distinct tangent directions on the dual. The specialization meets the source’s genericity requirement. This is a deterministic certificate, not a floating-point discriminant test.

The same one-parameter algebraic family has a proper closed set of nongeneric parameters, since a generic member has just been certified. That set is finite. Infinitely many of the rational parameters \(1/N\) therefore remain generic and approach zero, while the irrationality and uniqueness arguments apply to all \(N\ge105\). Restricting to sufficiently small generic parameters cannot repair the assertion.
## Impact and repair boundary

The conclusion fails for the precise rational family [quartic] (#quartic) and rational limiting chords satisfying the stated assumptions. No claim is made that this curve has no other rational bitangents. The counterexample concerns the asserted lifting of each specified chord.

There is a meaningful weaker statement: the two branches [mbranches] (#mbranches) belong to \(\mathbb Q[[t]]\), since the inner square root has constant term \(1\) and the outer roots have nonzero rational constants \(2/5,3/10\). Formal or appropriate Henselian lifting does not imply rationality at a rational specialization. An analytic real branch also gives no such implication. Replacing the assertion by a formal/Henselian statement, with its hypotheses, or restricting it to suitable analytic fields changes its arithmetic content.

This is Major for the claimed arbitrary-field extension and its proposed use to bound \(K\)-bitangents. The real deformation and counting theorems are not refuted by it. The location in Perspectives does not make the false arithmetic conclusion a notation error. No correction in the unacquired journal text, or author adoption of this repair boundary, is asserted.
# The non-real root prescription

Problem 2 (The stated root count can be odd).  In the proof of Lemma 4.7, p. 33, the real degree-\(k\) perturbing polynomials \(R_1,R_2\) are required to have simple roots and \(\lfloor k/2\rfloor\) non-real roots. For \(k=2\) or \(3\), this requires exactly one non-real root. A real polynomial has conjugate non-real roots with equal multiplicities, so the requirement is impossible. The same obstruction occurs for \(k\equiv2,3\pmod4\).

The natural correction is \(\lfloor k/2\rfloor\) pairs of non-real roots. More is needed than that wording to justify the subsequent assertion of zero or two real critical points of \(R_1/R_2\). The following explicit choices supply that property.

Choose distinct small positive numbers \(a_j,b_j\) with \(a_jb_j<1\), avoiding common roots, and write \[H(z)=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\frac{z+a_j}{1+b_jz}.\] Every factor is positive for \(z\ge0\) and has derivative \((1-a_jb_j)/(1+b_jz)^2>0\). Thus \(H'(z)>0\) for \(m>0\).

For \(k=2m+1\), take \(R_1(\theta)=\theta\prod_j(\theta^2+a_j)\) and \(R_2(\theta)=\prod_j(1+b_j\theta^2)\) as homogeneous binary forms of degree \(k\). The second form has its single real root at infinity. Then \[\frac{d}{d\theta}\left(\theta H(\theta^2)\right)
 =H(\theta^2)+2\theta^2H'(\theta^2)>0.\] At infinity the map is asymptotic to a nonzero constant times \(\theta\), so it is unramified there as well. A sufficiently small real Möbius change of the domain moves the pole at infinity to a finite point and gives affine polynomials of exact degree \(k\), still arbitrarily close to \(\theta^k\) and \(1\). It preserves simple roots, their real/non-real status, and absence of real critical points. Each polynomial has \(2m\) non-real roots and one real root. The case \(k=1\) is the identity map with the same conclusion.

This verifies a local algebraic replacement for the root prescription and the asserted real critical-point counts. Persistence and chosen smoothing of all the rational curve’s nodes additionally use the source’s geometric construction and Brusotti input; the displayed diagrams have now been inspected, while the external existence and smoothing results remain dependencies. The finding is Minor: the impossible prescription can be replaced under the original degree and reality conditions, and no counterexample to Lemma 4.7 or Proposition 1.6 is established.
# Further clarifications and limits

The unnumbered proposition on pp. 31–32 states \(r_k=k^2+O(k)\), whereas its proof specifies \(r_k=4k(k-1)\) for odd \(k\), and at least \(4(k-1)(k-2)\) for even \(k\). Together with the total ramification bound \(4k(k-1)\), these displayed proof counts give \(r_k=4k^2+O(k)\). This stronger estimate yields \(\binom{r_k}{2}=8k^4+O(k^3)\), matching the leading complex bitangent count in degree \(2k\). The printed weaker leading coefficient alone would give only \(k^4/2+O(k^3)\) and would not imply Theorem 1.12. The normalization should be made consistent. This is recorded as a text-level clarification, not as a proven counterexample to an existential proposition or to the complete connectedness construction.

For Proposition 5.1, the leading conic count is compatible with Gathmann’s primary formula: the enumerative polynomial has leading term \(d^{10}/5!\) [gathmann]. The source’s \(9k(k-1)\) branch values for degree \(d=3k\) give \(\binom{9k(k-1)}5=d^{10}/5!+O(d^9)\). This checks the leading arithmetic only. The full real cubic-normal-bundle construction and all conic transversality claims in the Perspectives section have not been independently certified. The unrelated questions posed there are not treated as established theorems or as defects.

The \(k\)-section and local analytic conditions have been kept distinct from the stronger claim that every arithmetic specialization preserves a ground field. No arbitrary positive-characteristic theorem, no full independent graphical-realization proof, and no journal-version result is certified by this report.
# Conclusion

The overall assessment is Major, confined to the false arithmetic specialization assertion in Section 5(7), with the separate Minor issue in Lemma 4.7. The signed-count identity and checked real local-deformation algebra are not contradicted. The real graphical construction claims retain the explicit verification limits above. Scientific adjudication remains `pending`; no human review or independent acceptance is recorded.

This is Major for the claimed arbitrary-field extension and its proposed use to bound \(K\)-bitangents. The real deformation and counting theorems are not refuted by it. The location in Perspectives does not make the false arithmetic conclusion a notation error. No correction in the unacquired journal text, or author adoption of this repair boundary, is asserted.
result: Impact: Invalidates the asserted arithmetic extension and proposed per-chord K-bitangent bound. Does not refute the real signed-count and deformation theorems; does not claim the whole quartic has no other Q-bitangents.

problems.title: The prescribed number of non-real roots can be odd
problems.source_location: Lemma4.7 proof,p33
claim: A generic plane curve here is smooth and has dual singularities consisting only of ordinary nodes and cusps (pp. 1–2). For degree \(d=2k\), write \(p,n\) for the numbers of even and odd real ovals. The bitangent sign is unchanged if the two complementary sign regions are exchanged. Real bitangents with conjugate contact points contribute positively; for two real contacts the sign is the product of the two local side signs. These distinctions matter in passing from an unsigned count to \(t_s\).
Real degree-k small perturbations R1,R2 with simple roots and floor(k/2) non-real roots.
k=2 or3 allowed in Lemma4.7. R1,R2 real polynomials with only simple roots.
analysis: In the proof of Lemma 4.7, p. 33, the real degree-\(k\) perturbing polynomials \(R_1,R_2\) are required to have simple roots and \(\lfloor k/2\rfloor\) non-real roots. For \(k=2\) or \(3\), this requires exactly one non-real root. A real polynomial has conjugate non-real roots with equal multiplicities, so the requirement is impossible. The same obstruction occurs for \(k\equiv2,3\pmod4\).

The natural correction is \(\lfloor k/2\rfloor\) pairs of non-real roots. More is needed than that wording to justify the subsequent assertion of zero or two real critical points of \(R_1/R_2\). The following explicit choices supply that property.

Choose distinct small positive numbers \(a_j,b_j\) with \(a_jb_j<1\), avoiding common roots, and write \[H(z)=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\frac{z+a_j}{1+b_jz}.\] Every factor is positive for \(z\ge0\) and has derivative \((1-a_jb_j)/(1+b_jz)^2>0\). Thus \(H'(z)>0\) for \(m>0\).

For \(k=2m+1\), take \(R_1(\theta)=\theta\prod_j(\theta^2+a_j)\) and \(R_2(\theta)=\prod_j(1+b_j\theta^2)\) as homogeneous binary forms of degree \(k\). The second form has its single real root at infinity. Then \[\frac{d}{d\theta}\left(\theta H(\theta^2)\right)
 =H(\theta^2)+2\theta^2H'(\theta^2)>0.\] At infinity the map is asymptotic to a nonzero constant times \(\theta\), so it is unramified there as well. A sufficiently small real Möbius change of the domain moves the pole at infinity to a finite point and gives affine polynomials of exact degree \(k\), still arbitrarily close to \(\theta^k\) and \(1\). It preserves simple roots, their real/non-real status, and absence of real critical points. Each polynomial has \(2m\) non-real roots and one real root. The case \(k=1\) is the identity map with the same conclusion.

This verifies a local algebraic replacement for the root prescription and the asserted real critical-point counts. Persistence and chosen smoothing of all the rational curve’s nodes additionally use the source’s geometric construction and Brusotti input; the displayed diagrams have now been inspected, while the external existence and smoothing results remain dependencies. The finding is Minor: the impossible prescription can be replaced under the original degree and reality conditions, and no counterexample to Lemma 4.7 or Proposition 1.6 is established.
result: Impact: Impossible local prescription in the proof. Corrected real polynomials exist with original degrees and arbitrary closeness; no counterexample to Lemma4.7 or Proposition1.6.

report: Abstract: The reviewed source is arXiv:2212.03124v2, submitted on 12 February 2023. Two quantitative statements are false under their printed hypotheses. A sequence of radial harmonic maps into the circle contradicts the finite-stage collar estimate when the limiting image length is zero. A compactly supported Jacobian concentrated near the outer boundary contradicts the weighted Wente inequality. Both affect analytic ingredients of the main proof and are assessed as Major. A corrected weighted inequality is proved here; the collar argument requires a finite-stage error which its printed estimate omits. Two further Minor findings concern nearest-point projection derivatives and the inhomogeneous function space in the annular extension lemma. The main index inequalities are not disproved. The source formulas have been checked against actual page images; the original exact computations are retained. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical review of
Morse index stability for critical points
to conformally invariant Lagrangians
# Identity, version, and scope

The source is F. Da Lio, M. Gianocca, and T. Rivière, Morse Index Stability for Critical Points to Conformally Invariant Lagrangians, arXiv:2212.03124v2 [source]. The associated journal identifier is DOI `10.4171/jems/1718`. EMS Press lists acceptance on 27 May 2025 and online publication on 25 September 2025 [ems]. The acquired 60-page PDF carries the February 2023 arXiv revision. Its equivalence to either the accepted manuscript or the journal version of record is not established. None of the findings below is asserted to persist in an unacquired version.

The original executor read all 60 source pages as text; this continuation reuses that recorded review and its unchanged calculations. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed numbering. The review follows the definitions of criticality, index and nullity, both main theorems, the second-variation formulas, the neck estimates, the weighted spectral argument, the collar extension, and Appendices A–G. Detailed independent checks concern the four problems below, the annular Hardy scale, the dyadic recurrence, and the distinction between a tangent operator and its ambient expression.

This is not a complete independent reconstruction of every cited compactness, gauge, Lorentz-space, or regularity theorem. In particular, the general-target regularity passages and all iterations of the bubble tree have not been independently rebuilt from first principles. In recovery, the 43 retained source evidence pages were inspected as actual images: pp. 1–6, 10–11, 13, 15–20, 22–27, 29, 31, 33, 35–43, 45–49, and 54–58. The cited formulas and their surrounding hypotheses agree with the retained analysis. The verification records distinguish historical text reading and calculations from these new inspections and from final report-page checks.

The acquisition record and an additional bounded search of the arXiv record, EMS page, and author publication page [authorpage] did not locate a separate paper-specific supplement, code repository, or correction notice. This is not proof of nonexistence. The journal text requires subscription through the checked route. No author code was run. Absence of code is not a defect in this analytic work.
# The claims and their dependencies

The functional is the Dirichlet energy with a pulled-back two-form on a closed oriented surface. The admissible variations are sections of the pullback tangent bundle. In the harmonic-map case, the quadratic form displayed on p. 11 is \[Q_u(w)=\int_\Sigma |dw|_h^2
 -\int_\Sigma\langle I_u(du,du)_h,I_u(w,w)\rangle,
 \qquad w(x)\in T_{u(x)}N.\] For the general functional, the additional first-order and zeroth-order terms involving the three-form tensor are retained. They cannot be discarded when discussing the full theorem. The counterexamples in Problems 1 and 3 use the allowed special case in which that tensor vanishes.

Theorem I.1, p. 4, asserts an upper bound for \(\operatorname{Ind}+\operatorname{Null}\) along a bubble-convergent sequence on a fixed closed surface, by the corresponding sum for the base limit and the bubbles. Theorem I.2, p. 6, addresses degenerating conformal structures under the specified finite collar decomposition, absence of collar bubbles, and a strict smallness condition on the limiting collar image lengths. Neither statement is an unrestricted assertion for arbitrary maps on arbitrary annuli.

The principal proof chain is as follows. Angular Lorentz control and the holomorphic Hopf differential give full \(L^{2,1}\) neck control on a fixed surface. The antisymmetric-potential gauge, a Hodge decomposition, and harmonic Fourier modes separate a logarithmic neck mode from the other modes. Weighted Wente and dyadic estimates then produce pointwise control. A weighted Poincaré inequality makes the Hessian positive on the neck. Finally, weighted nonpositive eigensections are transferred to the base and bubble limits; a linear combination vanishing in both limits would contradict neck positivity.

The small-potential hypotheses and gauge conclusion were checked against Theorem I.4 of the accessible primary preprint of Rivière [riviere]. The angular estimate was compared with Theorem 0.2, the Lorentz argument in its proof, and the annular weak-\(L^2\) estimate in the accessible Laurain–Rivière preprint [laurain]. These are interface checks. Equation numbering in that preprint differs from the journal reference used by the source; the source’s citation of an estimate numbered (56) is not equated with the preprint’s weak-\(L^2\) equation solely because the numbers match.

For \(T=\log(\eta^2/\delta)\), the radial change of variable \(s=\log(r\eta/\delta)\) gives the exact one-dimensional Dirichlet scale \(\pi^2/T^2\). This explains why an error multiplied by \(T^2\), and not just an unweighted error tending to zero, matters to the neck argument. The printed weights add boundary-decay terms to this logarithmic scale. The limiting singular weights belong to \(L^p\) for suitable \(p>1\), so the compact embedding used in Appendix B follows from Rellich compactness and Hölder’s inequality. A piecewise-defined weight need not be smooth across its matching circles for this quadratic-form argument.

The unprojected ambient eigen-equation on p. 31 should be read with care: pp. 33 and 35, equations (IV.48), (IV.67), and (IV.68), and Appendix B explicitly use the tangent projection. Those later formulas prevent treating the earlier omission as a demonstrated failure of the spectral proof. The argument with any fixed finite family of eigensections and their linear combinations supplies the required dimension comparison without assuming a uniform dimension bound in advance.
# The collar estimate and a vanishing limiting length

Equation reference: eq:printed-collar. Problem 1 (A limit is substituted for a nonzero finite-stage error).  Lemma V.1, p. 36, equations (V.1)–(V.3), assumes vanishing energy on individual doubling annuli and a finite limiting averaged radial length \(\Lambda\). It asserts constants \(C>0\), \(0<\beta<2\), independent of \(k\), such that \[
 r^2|\nabla u_k|^2
 \le C\left[\left(\frac r\eta\right)^\beta
       +\left(\frac{\delta_k}{\eta r}\right)^\beta\right]
       \int_{A(2\eta,\delta_k)}|du_k|^2
       +\frac{C\Lambda^2}{\log^2(\eta^2/\delta_k)}.\] This pointwise finite-stage estimate is false under the stated local hypotheses.
## An admissible sequence

Take the closed target \(N=S^1\subset\mathbb R^2\), zero two-form, and \[\delta_k=e^{-k},\qquad
 u_k(r,\theta)=
 \left(\cos\frac{\log r}{k^2},\,
       \sin\frac{\log r}{k^2}\right).\] The map is defined on the entire punctured plane, so its restrictions to both annuli occurring in [eq:printed-collar] (#eq:printed-collar) exist. The phase is harmonic. Direct differentiation gives the sphere harmonic-map equation \[\Delta u_k+|\nabla u_k|^2u_k=0,
 \qquad |\nabla u_k|^2=\frac{1}{k^4r^2}.\] Thus these are smooth critical points on the required annuli, with the flat metric in conformal coordinates. On every doubling annulus, \[\int_{B_{2\rho}\setminus B_\rho}|\nabla u_k|^2
 =\frac{2\pi\log2}{k^4}\longrightarrow0.\] The map is independent of \(\theta\), so either averaging the radial derivative first and then taking its norm, or averaging its norm, gives the same radial length. For fixed \(\eta\) and sufficiently large \(k\), \[\ell_{\eta,k}
 =\int_{\delta_k/\eta}^{\eta}|\partial_r u_k|\,dr
 =\frac{k+2\log\eta}{k^2}
 \longrightarrow0.\] Consequently the iterated limiting length in (V.2) is \(\Lambda=0\). The annular energies are bounded and in fact tend to zero. The construction satisfies every local hypothesis of Lemma V.1.
## Failure at the middle circle

Set \(r_k=\sqrt{\delta_k}=e^{-k/2}\), which lies in \(A(\eta,\delta_k)\) for every fixed \(\eta>0\) and sufficiently large \(k\). Then \[r_k^2|\nabla u_k(r_k)|^2=k^{-4},
 \qquad
 \int_{A(2\eta,\delta_k)}|\nabla u_k|^2
 =\frac{2\pi}{k^4}\bigl(k+2\log(2\eta)\bigr).\] Since the \(\Lambda\)-term is exactly zero, division of the proposed right side by the left side gives \[4\pi C\eta^{-\beta}e^{-\beta k/2}
       \bigl(k+2\log(2\eta)\bigr)\longrightarrow0.\] This contradicts [eq:printed-collar] (#eq:printed-collar) for any fixed \(C\) and any positive \(\beta\), even if \(C\) were allowed to depend on the fixed \(\eta\). The symbolic calculation verifies the harmonic-map residual, the energy expressions, and this limit exactly; no extrapolation from finite numerical samples is used.
## Impact and necessary repair

This is Major for the quantitative lemma used in Section V’s proof of Theorem I.2. The defect is the replacement of a finite-stage logarithmic mode by its limiting length with no residual error. A statement compatible with the example must retain an error \(R_{\eta,k}\) for which an appropriate assertion has the form \[\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\limsup_{k\to\infty}
 \log^2(\eta^2/\delta_k)\,R_{\eta,k}\le C\Lambda^2,\] or an eventual bound with \(\Lambda+\varepsilon\), with thresholds depending on \(\varepsilon\). When \(\Lambda=0\), this permits a nonzero error of smaller order than \(T^{-2}\); it does not set that error identically to zero. In the example, \(R_{\eta,k}=k^{-4}\) has precisely this permitted behavior.

A strict margin below the critical collar length could absorb a sufficiently controlled residual of this kind. The full general collar estimate with that residual is not proved here. This report therefore does not certify the complete repair of Theorem I.2’s argument. It also does not disprove Theorem I.2: no extension of the example to critical maps on the degenerating closed surfaces of that theorem is claimed. The fixed-surface global conservation and Hopf-differential information used in Section III are additional restrictions, absent from the local lemma.
# The weighted Wente inequality at the outer boundary

Equation reference: eq:printed-wente. Problem 2 (The displayed weight vanishes at an uncontrolled boundary).  Lemma E.1, p. 45, equations (E.1)–(E.3), states that a Dirichlet solution of \[-\Delta\varphi=J(a,b):=\partial_1a\,\partial_2b
                         -\partial_2a\,\partial_1b
 \quad\hbox{in }B_1,\qquad \varphi|_{\partial B_1}=0\] satisfies \[
 \int_{B_1}|x|^2|\nabla\varphi|^2
 \le C\left(\int_{B_1}|\nabla a|^2\right)
       \left(\int_{B_1}f(|x|)|\nabla b|^2\right),
 \quad
 f(r)=r^2\log^2(1+1/r)\log(1+\log(1/r)).\] The constant is asserted to be universal. The weight tends to zero as \(r\uparrow1\), and this makes the assertion false even for compactly supported data.
## An explicit Jacobian and its exact solution

Equation reference: eq:energies. Write \(s=|\xi|^2\). Define the following functions inside \(B_1\), extending them by zero outside: \[\begin{aligned}
 \psi(\xi)&=(1-s)^4,\\
 \varphi_0(\xi)&=\partial_2\psi=-8\xi_2(1-s)^3,\\
 b_0(\xi)&=-\Delta\psi=16(1-s)^2(1-4s).\end{aligned}\] Their zero extensions have respectively \(C^3\), \(C^2\), and \(C^1\) regularity. In particular, no boundary distribution is introduced in the identity below. Put \[a_0(\xi)=\xi_1\chi(s),\qquad
 \chi(s)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&s\le1,\\
 (s-4)^2(2s+1)/27,&1<s<4,\\
 0,&s\ge4.
 \end{cases}\] This is a compactly supported \(C^1\) function on \(B_2\), and \(\nabla a_0=e_1\) on the support of \(\nabla b_0\). It follows, including across the support boundary, that \[J(a_0,b_0)=\partial_2b_0=-\Delta\varphi_0.\] All three functions belong to \(W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^2)\). Their Dirichlet energies are positive and finite. Exact polynomial integration gives \[
 E_\varphi=\frac{384\pi}{35},\qquad
 E_b=\frac{3072\pi}{5},\qquad
 E_a=\frac{184\pi}{35}.\] For example, with \(g(s)=-8(1-s)^3\), \[E_\varphi=2\pi\int_0^1s^2g'(s)^2\,ds,
 \qquad
 E_b=4\pi\int_0^1s
       \left[\frac{d}{ds}\{16(1-s)^2(1-4s)\}\right]^2ds.\] The retained independent computation checks these integrals and the Jacobian identity exactly.
## Concentration near the outer boundary

For \(0<\varepsilon<1/10\), let \[c_\varepsilon=(1-3\varepsilon,0),\qquad
 (a_\varepsilon,b_\varepsilon,\varphi_\varepsilon)(x)
 =(a_0,b_0,\varphi_0)\left(\frac{x-c_\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right).\] The support of \(a_\varepsilon\) is inside \(B_{2\varepsilon}(c_\varepsilon)\Subset B_1\), and the other two supports are inside \(B_\varepsilon(c_\varepsilon)\). Thus these are admissible Dirichlet data and an exact Dirichlet solution. The equation scales by \(\varepsilon^{-2}\) on both sides, and the three Dirichlet energies are unchanged in dimension two.

On the support of \(\varphi_\varepsilon\) and \(b_\varepsilon\), \[1-4\varepsilon\le |x|\le1-2\varepsilon.\] Consequently, \[\begin{aligned}
 \int_{B_1}|x|^2|\nabla\varphi_\varepsilon|^2
   &\ge(1-4\varepsilon)^2E_\varphi,\\
 \int_{B_1} f(|x|)|\nabla b_\varepsilon|^2
   &\le E_b\sup_{1-4\varepsilon\le r\le1-2\varepsilon}f(r).\end{aligned}\] The exact boundary limit is \[\lim_{r\uparrow1}\frac{f(r)}{1-r}=(\log2)^2.\] The first quantity stays bounded away from zero, whereas the proposed right side in [eq:printed-wente] (#eq:printed-wente) is \(O(\varepsilon)E_aE_b\). This disproves every possible universal constant.

For a fully elementary bound, on the relevant interval \(r>1/2\), \[\log(1+1/r)<2,\qquad
 \log(1+\log(1/r))\le\log(1/r)\le2(1-r)\le8\varepsilon.\] Hence \(f(r)\le32\varepsilon\). For any proposed \(C>0\), taking \[0<\varepsilon<
 \min\left\{\frac1{10},\,\frac{9E_\varphi}{800CE_aE_b}\right\}\] already gives a strict contradiction. The example satisfies more support and regularity conditions than the lemma requires.
## A verified replacement

Equation reference: eq:repair-wente. The following replacement retains the analytic property needed later: \[
 \int_{B_1}|x|^2|\nabla\varphi|^2
 \le C\left(\int_{B_1}|\nabla a|^2\right)
       \int_{B_1}|x|^2
       \left(1+\log\frac1{|x|}\right)^2|\nabla b|^2.\] Here is a proof, including the endpoint summation.

Use the decomposition of gradients in Lemma E.2, pp. 45–47, with \(\operatorname{supp}
abla b_j\subset A_j\cup A_{j+1}\), \(A_j=B_{2^{-j}}\setminus B_{2^{-j-1}}\), and \[x_j=\|
abla b_j\|_2,\qquad
 x_j^2\le C\int_{A_j\cup A_{j+1}}|
abla b|^2,\qquad
 A=\|
abla a\|_2.\] Let \(\varphi_j\) be the zero-boundary solution for \(J(a,b_j)\). The classical Wente estimate, together with the harmonic annular estimates underlying Lemma E.3, gives \[\|
abla\varphi_j\|_{L^2(A_k)}
 \le CA\,2^{-|j-k|}x_j .\] A bounded shift of an index changes only \(C\). For completeness, outside the support one subtracts the outer constant of \(b_j\), so the total Jacobian integral is zero and there is no logarithmic harmonic mode. Inside the support’s inner circle the solution is harmonic, and the interior energy scales quadratically with radius. The neighboring annuli use the unweighted Wente bound. The first outer annulus is included in this last bound; no vanishing of \(b\) at the outer boundary is assumed.

The repaired weight is positive at \(r=1\), and it is \(o(r^\alpha)\) as \(r\downarrow0\) for every \(0<\alpha<2\). On the annuli bounded away from zero used in (F.7), p. 55, [eq:repair-wente] (#eq:repair-wente) bounds the unweighted solution energy. The harmonic splitting in Lemma F.1 and the rescaling and geometric summation in Lemma F.2 therefore retain their stated type of estimates with this replacement and changed constants.
## Impact

This is Major for the claimed weighted inequality and its explicit use in (F.7), which feeds the pointwise neck argument. Case 1 of the printed proof, p. 49, gives a weight \(r^2\); that bound cannot be absorbed uniformly into the displayed \(f\) near \(r=1\). The fact that a replacement is available does not make the printed core analytic assertion true. The replacement above repairs this specific interface. It is not a full independent certification of all remaining steps of either main theorem, and no counterexample to those main theorems is asserted.
# Projection derivatives in the second variation

Problem 3 (Nearest-point differentiation away from the target).  On p. 10, the text before (II.1) identifies the derivative of the nearest-point projection at \(u+t\phi\) with the tangent projection at its footpoint. Equations (II.1)–(II.2) then give an incorrect acceleration for general ambient \(\phi\). On p. 11, the first formula in (II.14) also has an incorrect sign.

Take the allowed harmonic constant map \(u=e_1\in S^1\), and an ambient constant variation \(\phi=ae_1+be_2\). The nearest-point projection is \[\pi(z)=\frac z{|z|},\qquad
 D\pi_z=|z|^{-1}P_{\pi(z)}.\] The missing scalar factor already refutes the asserted off-target identity. More decisively, \[\left.\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\pi(e_1+t(ae_1+be_2))\right|_{t=0}
 =-b^2e_1-2ab e_2,
 \qquad
 D_{be_2}P_{e_1}(ae_1+be_2)=-b^2e_1-ab e_2.\] For \(a=b=1\), the actual acceleration is \((-1,-2)\), whereas the printed formula gives \((-1,-1)\). The independent symbolic derivative verifies the discrepancy exactly.

For a sphere, \[P_u=I-u\otimes u
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 dP_u=-du\otimes u-u\otimes du.\] The printed difference of tensors in (II.14) is skew-symmetric, whereas a derivative of a symmetric projection must be symmetric. Its contraction with \(du\) also has the wrong sign. The subsequent formula (II.15) nevertheless displays the correct value \(-u|du|^2\).

The necessary second-variation calculation is repaired without altering the final harmonic Hessian. Any curve in \(N\) with initial velocity \(w\) has normal acceleration \(I_u(w,w)\). The error in the explicit circle example is tangential. At a harmonic map, the first-variation vector is normal, so the pairing relevant to (II.8) is unchanged. Alternatively, choosing the ambient variation \(\phi=w\) tangent along \(u\) from the outset gives the correct normal acceleration directly. At a critical point of the full functional, the Hessian likewise depends only on the initial tangent velocity, because the term containing a change of acceleration is the first variation. Thus the corrected projection calculus supplies the needed path-independent Hessian.

The assessment is Minor. The pointwise identities are genuinely false, but their correct replacements recover the indicated second-variation interface. The final sphere quadratic form and the correctly projected spectral operator are not refuted.
# The annular extension space

Problem 4 (An inhomogeneous whole-plane extension cannot obey the stated bound).  Lemma C.1, p. 42, asserts an extension \(\widetilde a\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb C)\) with compactly supported gradient and a gradient estimate depending only on \(\nabla a\) in the original annulus. With the usual inhomogeneous meaning of \(W^{1,2}\), this is false.

Take \(r=1\), \(R=3\), and \(a\equiv1\) on \(B_R\setminus B_r\). The hypotheses \(0<2r<R\) and \(a\in W^{1,2}\) hold. Equation (C.1) forces \(\nabla\widetilde a=0\) almost everywhere. A function with zero weak gradient on the connected plane is constant; equality to \(a\) on the annulus forces that constant to be \(1\). It is not in \(L^2(\mathbb C)\), hence not in inhomogeneous \(W^{1,2}(\mathbb C)\). This is an exact counterexample, not a question of the unspecified universal constant.
## The correct extension and boundary matching

The appropriate assertion is \[\widetilde a\in W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb C),\qquad
 \nabla\widetilde a\in L^2(\mathbb C),
 \qquad
 \widetilde a-a_R\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb C),\] where \(a_R\) is the mean on \(B_R\setminus B_{R/2}\). Its homogeneous class is sufficient for the gradient and Jacobian operations in the proof.

The inner cutoff and inversion in the source provide the inner extension. For the outer extension, the displayed formula on p. 43 needs \(\chi_{R/2}\), not \(\chi_R\), where \(\chi_t(x)=\chi(|x|/t)\), \(\chi=1\) on \([0,1]\), and \(\chi=0\) on \([2,\infty)\). Define inside \(B_R\) \[\breve a=(1-\chi_{R/2})a+\chi_{R/2}a_R,\] interpreting it as the constant \(a_R\) on \(B_{R/2}\). This only uses values of \(a\) on its domain because \(R/2>r\). It agrees with \(a\) at radius \(R\), is constant at radius at most \(R/2\), and obeys \[\int_{B_R}|\nabla\breve a|^2
 \le C\int_{B_R\setminus B_{R/2}}|\nabla a|^2\] by the scaled Poincaré inequality. Invert it outside \(B_R\): \[\widetilde a(x)=\breve a\left(R^2x/|x|^2\right),\qquad |x|>R.\] The traces match, the extension is constant for \(|x|\ge2R\), and conformal invariance of the planar Dirichlet integral gives (C.2). The analogous inner construction gives (C.3); adding the original annulus gives (C.1). After subtracting \(a_R\), the extension has compact support and finite \(W^{1,2}\) norm.

By contrast, the printed \(\chi_R\) is identically one throughout \(B_R\), so that formula cannot generally match the original boundary trace. The inversion must also use the outer function \(\breve a\); the printed use of the inner-function symbol there is inconsistent with its following energy identity.

The assessment is Minor. The homogeneous formulation and corrected outer cutoff establish the extension required for the gradients in Sections III and V. If the original notation was intended to denote a homogeneous Sobolev class, the function-space issue becomes a necessary clarification; the explicit cutoff correction is still required. No main index conclusion is disproved by this issue.
# Assessment and limits
Item | Assessment | Verified scope of repair
1 | Major | Finite-stage residual is necessary; the full general collar estimate with that residual is not proved here.
2 | Major | A replacement weighted inequality is proved, with the decay property needed by the following Morrey estimates.
3 | Minor | Correct projection derivatives and normal acceleration recover the second-variation interface.
4 | Minor | Homogeneous extension and corrected outer cutoff recover the required gradient estimates.

The overall initial assessment is Major for the two analytic statements whose exact quantified bounds fail. None of the four counterexamples relies on executing author code, on a conjectural asymptotic, or on dropping a hypothesis of the statement it refutes. The local collar example is deliberately distinguished from the closed-surface theorems.

The fixed-domain logarithmic-mode argument, the strict collar-length threshold, the projected weighted spectral decomposition, and the full general-target regularity requirements remain separate obligations. The proof interfaces described above were examined, but no claim of complete independent certification of all external results is made. A missing projection in an earlier ambient display is not counted as an additional core failure because the later proof writes the correct tangent operator explicitly. Typographical constants in Lorentz quasi-norm displays are not used to infer a false asymptotic conclusion.

Scientific decision is pending, and no human review or independent acceptance is recorded. Whether the identified discrepancies remain in the accepted or published text requires acquiring that exact version.

problems.title: Lemma V.1 substitutes a limiting length for a nonzero finite-stage logarithmic error
problems.source_location: PDF/printed p.36, Lemma V.1, (V.1)-(V.3); proof pp.37-38; Theorem I.2 p.6 is a separate global claim.
claim: Recorded check: Lemma V.1 substitutes a limiting length for a nonzero finite-stage logarithmic error
analysis:
Lemma V.1, p. 36, equations (V.1)–(V.3), assumes vanishing energy on individual doubling annuli and a finite limiting averaged radial length \(\Lambda\). It asserts constants \(C>0\), \(0<\beta<2\), independent of \(k\), such that \[
 r^2|\nabla u_k|^2
 \le C\left[\left(\frac r\eta\right)^\beta
       +\left(\frac{\delta_k}{\eta r}\right)^\beta\right]
       \int_{A(2\eta,\delta_k)}|du_k|^2
       +\frac{C\Lambda^2}{\log^2(\eta^2/\delta_k)}.\] This pointwise finite-stage estimate is false under the stated local hypotheses.

Take the closed target \(N=S^1\subset\mathbb R^2\), zero two-form, and \[\delta_k=e^{-k},\qquad
 u_k(r,\theta)=
 \left(\cos\frac{\log r}{k^2},\,
       \sin\frac{\log r}{k^2}\right).\] The map is defined on the entire punctured plane, so its restrictions to both annuli occurring in [eq:printed-collar] (#eq:printed-collar) exist. The phase is harmonic. Direct differentiation gives the sphere harmonic-map equation \[\Delta u_k+|\nabla u_k|^2u_k=0,
 \qquad |\nabla u_k|^2=\frac{1}{k^4r^2}.\] Thus these are smooth critical points on the required annuli, with the flat metric in conformal coordinates. On every doubling annulus, \[\int_{B_{2\rho}\setminus B_\rho}|\nabla u_k|^2
 =\frac{2\pi\log2}{k^4}\longrightarrow0.\] The map is independent of \(\theta\), so either averaging the radial derivative first and then taking its norm, or averaging its norm, gives the same radial length. For fixed \(\eta\) and sufficiently large \(k\), \[\ell_{\eta,k}
 =\int_{\delta_k/\eta}^{\eta}|\partial_r u_k|\,dr
 =\frac{k+2\log\eta}{k^2}
 \longrightarrow0.\] Consequently the iterated limiting length in (V.2) is \(\Lambda=0\). The annular energies are bounded and in fact tend to zero. The construction satisfies every local hypothesis of Lemma V.1.

Set \(r_k=\sqrt{\delta_k}=e^{-k/2}\), which lies in \(A(\eta,\delta_k)\) for every fixed \(\eta>0\) and sufficiently large \(k\). Then \[r_k^2|\nabla u_k(r_k)|^2=k^{-4},
 \qquad
 \int_{A(2\eta,\delta_k)}|\nabla u_k|^2
 =\frac{2\pi}{k^4}\bigl(k+2\log(2\eta)\bigr).\] Since the \(\Lambda\)-term is exactly zero, division of the proposed right side by the left side gives \[4\pi C\eta^{-\beta}e^{-\beta k/2}
       \bigl(k+2\log(2\eta)\bigr)\longrightarrow0.\] This contradicts [eq:printed-collar] (#eq:printed-collar) for any fixed \(C\) and any positive \(\beta\), even if \(C\) were allowed to depend on the fixed \(\eta\). The symbolic calculation verifies the harmonic-map residual, the energy expressions, and this limit exactly; no extrapolation from finite numerical samples is used.

This is Major for the quantitative lemma used in Section V’s proof of Theorem I.2. The defect is the replacement of a finite-stage logarithmic mode by its limiting length with no residual error. A statement compatible with the example must retain an error \(R_{\eta,k}\) for which an appropriate assertion has the form \[\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}\limsup_{k\to\infty}
 \log^2(\eta^2/\delta_k)\,R_{\eta,k}\le C\Lambda^2,\] or an eventual bound with \(\Lambda+\varepsilon\), with thresholds depending on \(\varepsilon\). When \(\Lambda=0\), this permits a nonzero error of smaller order than \(T^{-2}\); it does not set that error identically to zero. In the example, \(R_{\eta,k}=k^{-4}\) has precisely this permitted behavior.

A strict margin below the critical collar length could absorb a sufficiently controlled residual of this kind. The full general collar estimate with that residual is not proved here. This report therefore does not certify the complete repair of Theorem I.2’s argument. It also does not disprove Theorem I.2: no extension of the example to critical maps on the degenerating closed surfaces of that theorem is claimed. The fixed-surface global conservation and Hopf-differential information used in Section III are additional restrictions, absent from the local lemma.
result: Impact: A false quantitative lemma in the collar proof of Theorem I.2; this is not a counterexample to the global closed-surface theorem.

problems.title: The weighted Wente estimate fails for boundary concentration because the weight tends to zero at r=1
problems.source_location: p.45, Lemma E.1, (E.1)-(E.3); p.49 Case 1; p.55 (F.7), with downstream Morrey estimates pp.54-56.
claim: Recorded check: The weighted Wente estimate fails for boundary concentration because the weight tends to zero at r=1
analysis:
Lemma E.1, p. 45, equations (E.1)–(E.3), states that a Dirichlet solution of \[-\Delta\varphi=J(a,b):=\partial_1a\,\partial_2b
                         -\partial_2a\,\partial_1b
 \quad\hbox{in }B_1,\qquad \varphi|_{\partial B_1}=0\] satisfies \[
 \int_{B_1}|x|^2|\nabla\varphi|^2
 \le C\left(\int_{B_1}|\nabla a|^2\right)
       \left(\int_{B_1}f(|x|)|\nabla b|^2\right),
 \quad
 f(r)=r^2\log^2(1+1/r)\log(1+\log(1/r)).\] The constant is asserted to be universal. The weight tends to zero as \(r\uparrow1\), and this makes the assertion false even for compactly supported data.

Equation reference: eq:energies. Write \(s=|\xi|^2\). Define the following functions inside \(B_1\), extending them by zero outside: \[\begin{aligned}
 \psi(\xi)&=(1-s)^4,\\
 \varphi_0(\xi)&=\partial_2\psi=-8\xi_2(1-s)^3,\\
 b_0(\xi)&=-\Delta\psi=16(1-s)^2(1-4s).\end{aligned}\] Their zero extensions have respectively \(C^3\), \(C^2\), and \(C^1\) regularity. In particular, no boundary distribution is introduced in the identity below. Put \[a_0(\xi)=\xi_1\chi(s),\qquad
 \chi(s)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&s\le1,\\
 (s-4)^2(2s+1)/27,&1<s<4,\\
 0,&s\ge4.
 \end{cases}\] This is a compactly supported \(C^1\) function on \(B_2\), and \(\nabla a_0=e_1\) on the support of \(\nabla b_0\). It follows, including across the support boundary, that \[J(a_0,b_0)=\partial_2b_0=-\Delta\varphi_0.\] All three functions belong to \(W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^2)\). Their Dirichlet energies are positive and finite. Exact polynomial integration gives \[
 E_\varphi=\frac{384\pi}{35},\qquad
 E_b=\frac{3072\pi}{5},\qquad
 E_a=\frac{184\pi}{35}.\] For example, with \(g(s)=-8(1-s)^3\), \[E_\varphi=2\pi\int_0^1s^2g'(s)^2\,ds,
 \qquad
 E_b=4\pi\int_0^1s
       \left[\frac{d}{ds}\{16(1-s)^2(1-4s)\}\right]^2ds.\] The retained independent computation checks these integrals and the Jacobian identity exactly.

For \(0<\varepsilon<1/10\), let \[c_\varepsilon=(1-3\varepsilon,0),\qquad
 (a_\varepsilon,b_\varepsilon,\varphi_\varepsilon)(x)
 =(a_0,b_0,\varphi_0)\left(\frac{x-c_\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\right).\] The support of \(a_\varepsilon\) is inside \(B_{2\varepsilon}(c_\varepsilon)\Subset B_1\), and the other two supports are inside \(B_\varepsilon(c_\varepsilon)\). Thus these are admissible Dirichlet data and an exact Dirichlet solution. The equation scales by \(\varepsilon^{-2}\) on both sides, and the three Dirichlet energies are unchanged in dimension two.

On the support of \(\varphi_\varepsilon\) and \(b_\varepsilon\), \[1-4\varepsilon\le |x|\le1-2\varepsilon.\] Consequently, \[\begin{aligned}
 \int_{B_1}|x|^2|\nabla\varphi_\varepsilon|^2
   &\ge(1-4\varepsilon)^2E_\varphi,\\
 \int_{B_1} f(|x|)|\nabla b_\varepsilon|^2
   &\le E_b\sup_{1-4\varepsilon\le r\le1-2\varepsilon}f(r).\end{aligned}\] The exact boundary limit is \[\lim_{r\uparrow1}\frac{f(r)}{1-r}=(\log2)^2.\] The first quantity stays bounded away from zero, whereas the proposed right side in [eq:printed-wente] (#eq:printed-wente) is \(O(\varepsilon)E_aE_b\). This disproves every possible universal constant.

For a fully elementary bound, on the relevant interval \(r>1/2\), \[\log(1+1/r)<2,\qquad
 \log(1+\log(1/r))\le\log(1/r)\le2(1-r)\le8\varepsilon.\] Hence \(f(r)\le32\varepsilon\). For any proposed \(C>0\), taking \[0<\varepsilon<
 \min\left\{\frac1{10},\,\frac{9E_\varphi}{800CE_aE_b}\right\}\] already gives a strict contradiction. The example satisfies more support and regularity conditions than the lemma requires.

Equation reference: eq:repair-wente. The following replacement retains the analytic property needed later: \[
 \int_{B_1}|x|^2|\nabla\varphi|^2
 \le C\left(\int_{B_1}|\nabla a|^2\right)
       \int_{B_1}|x|^2
       \left(1+\log\frac1{|x|}\right)^2|\nabla b|^2.\] Here is a proof, including the endpoint summation.

Use the decomposition of gradients in Lemma E.2, pp. 45–47, with \(\operatorname{supp}
abla b_j\subset A_j\cup A_{j+1}\), \(A_j=B_{2^{-j}}\setminus B_{2^{-j-1}}\), and \[x_j=\|
abla b_j\|_2,\qquad
 x_j^2\le C\int_{A_j\cup A_{j+1}}|
abla b|^2,\qquad
 A=\|
abla a\|_2.\] Let \(\varphi_j\) be the zero-boundary solution for \(J(a,b_j)\). The classical Wente estimate, together with the harmonic annular estimates underlying Lemma E.3, gives \[\|
abla\varphi_j\|_{L^2(A_k)}
 \le CA\,2^{-|j-k|}x_j .\] A bounded shift of an index changes only \(C\). For completeness, outside the support one subtracts the outer constant of \(b_j\), so the total Jacobian integral is zero and there is no logarithmic harmonic mode. Inside the support’s inner circle the solution is harmonic, and the interior energy scales quadratically with radius. The neighboring annuli use the unweighted Wente bound. The first outer annulus is included in this last bound; no vanishing of \(b\) at the outer boundary is assumed.

The repaired weight is positive at \(r=1\), and it is \(o(r^\alpha)\) as \(r\downarrow0\) for every \(0<\alpha<2\). On the annuli bounded away from zero used in (F.7), p. 55, [eq:repair-wente] (#eq:repair-wente) bounds the unweighted solution energy. The harmonic splitting in Lemma F.1 and the rescaling and geometric summation in Lemma F.2 therefore retain their stated type of estimates with this replacement and changed constants.

This is Major for the claimed weighted inequality and its explicit use in (F.7), which feeds the pointwise neck argument. Case 1 of the printed proof, p. 49, gives a weight \(r^2\); that bound cannot be absorbed uniformly into the displayed \(f\) near \(r=1\). The fact that a replacement is available does not make the printed core analytic assertion true. The replacement above repairs this specific interface. It is not a full independent certification of all remaining steps of either main theorem, and no counterexample to those main theorems is asserted.
result: Impact: False core weighted analytic inequality and its explicit application at (F.7); the main index theorems themselves are not disproved.

problems.title: Nearest-point projection acceleration and a sphere projection-derivative sign are incorrect
problems.source_location: p.10, paragraph before (II.1) and (II.1)-(II.2); p.11, first formula in (II.14), compared with the correct subsequent (II.15).
claim: Recorded check: Nearest-point projection acceleration and a sphere projection-derivative sign are incorrect
analysis: On p. 10, the text before (II.1) identifies the derivative of the nearest-point projection at \(u+t\phi\) with the tangent projection at its footpoint. Equations (II.1)–(II.2) then give an incorrect acceleration for general ambient \(\phi\). On p. 11, the first formula in (II.14) also has an incorrect sign.

Take the allowed harmonic constant map \(u=e_1\in S^1\), and an ambient constant variation \(\phi=ae_1+be_2\). The nearest-point projection is \[\pi(z)=\frac z{|z|},\qquad
 D\pi_z=|z|^{-1}P_{\pi(z)}.\] The missing scalar factor already refutes the asserted off-target identity. More decisively, \[\left.\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\pi(e_1+t(ae_1+be_2))\right|_{t=0}
 =-b^2e_1-2ab e_2,
 \qquad
 D_{be_2}P_{e_1}(ae_1+be_2)=-b^2e_1-ab e_2.\] For \(a=b=1\), the actual acceleration is \((-1,-2)\), whereas the printed formula gives \((-1,-1)\). The independent symbolic derivative verifies the discrepancy exactly.

For a sphere, \[P_u=I-u\otimes u
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 dP_u=-du\otimes u-u\otimes du.\] The printed difference of tensors in (II.14) is skew-symmetric, whereas a derivative of a symmetric projection must be symmetric. Its contraction with \(du\) also has the wrong sign. The subsequent formula (II.15) nevertheless displays the correct value \(-u|du|^2\).

The necessary second-variation calculation is repaired without altering the final harmonic Hessian. Any curve in \(N\) with initial velocity \(w\) has normal acceleration \(I_u(w,w)\). The error in the explicit circle example is tangential. At a harmonic map, the first-variation vector is normal, so the pairing relevant to (II.8) is unchanged. Alternatively, choosing the ambient variation \(\phi=w\) tangent along \(u\) from the outset gives the correct normal acceleration directly. At a critical point of the full functional, the Hessian likewise depends only on the initial tangent velocity, because the term containing a change of acceleration is the first variation. Thus the corrected projection calculus supplies the needed path-independent Hessian.

The assessment is Minor. The pointwise identities are genuinely false, but their correct replacements recover the indicated second-variation interface. The final sphere quadratic form and the correctly projected spectral operator are not refuted.
result: Impact: Local second-variation derivation identities; the final sphere Hessian and the later explicitly projected spectral operator are not refuted.

problems.title: Annular extension requires a homogeneous whole-plane class and a corrected outer cutoff
problems.source_location: pp.42-43, Lemma C.1, (C.1)-(C.7), especially the outer cutoff displayed on p.43.
claim: Recorded check: Annular extension requires a homogeneous whole-plane class and a corrected outer cutoff
analysis: Lemma C.1, p. 42, asserts an extension \(\widetilde a\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb C)\) with compactly supported gradient and a gradient estimate depending only on \(\nabla a\) in the original annulus. With the usual inhomogeneous meaning of \(W^{1,2}\), this is false.

Take \(r=1\), \(R=3\), and \(a\equiv1\) on \(B_R\setminus B_r\). The hypotheses \(0<2r<R\) and \(a\in W^{1,2}\) hold. Equation (C.1) forces \(\nabla\widetilde a=0\) almost everywhere. A function with zero weak gradient on the connected plane is constant; equality to \(a\) on the annulus forces that constant to be \(1\). It is not in \(L^2(\mathbb C)\), hence not in inhomogeneous \(W^{1,2}(\mathbb C)\). This is an exact counterexample, not a question of the unspecified universal constant.

The appropriate assertion is \[\widetilde a\in W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb C),\qquad
 \nabla\widetilde a\in L^2(\mathbb C),
 \qquad
 \widetilde a-a_R\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb C),\] where \(a_R\) is the mean on \(B_R\setminus B_{R/2}\). Its homogeneous class is sufficient for the gradient and Jacobian operations in the proof.

The inner cutoff and inversion in the source provide the inner extension. For the outer extension, the displayed formula on p. 43 needs \(\chi_{R/2}\), not \(\chi_R\), where \(\chi_t(x)=\chi(|x|/t)\), \(\chi=1\) on \([0,1]\), and \(\chi=0\) on \([2,\infty)\). Define inside \(B_R\) \[\breve a=(1-\chi_{R/2})a+\chi_{R/2}a_R,\] interpreting it as the constant \(a_R\) on \(B_{R/2}\). This only uses values of \(a\) on its domain because \(R/2>r\). It agrees with \(a\) at radius \(R\), is constant at radius at most \(R/2\), and obeys \[\int_{B_R}|\nabla\breve a|^2
 \le C\int_{B_R\setminus B_{R/2}}|\nabla a|^2\] by the scaled Poincaré inequality. Invert it outside \(B_R\): \[\widetilde a(x)=\breve a\left(R^2x/|x|^2\right),\qquad |x|>R.\] The traces match, the extension is constant for \(|x|\ge2R\), and conformal invariance of the planar Dirichlet integral gives (C.2). The analogous inner construction gives (C.3); adding the original annulus gives (C.1). After subtracting \(a_R\), the extension has compact support and finite \(W^{1,2}\) norm.

By contrast, the printed \(\chi_R\) is identically one throughout \(B_R\), so that formula cannot generally match the original boundary trace. The inversion must also use the outer function \(\breve a\); the printed use of the inner-function symbol there is inconsistent with its following energy identity.

The assessment is Minor. The homogeneous formulation and corrected outer cutoff establish the extension required for the gradients in Sections III and V. If the original notation was intended to denote a homogeneous Sobolev class, the function-space issue becomes a necessary clarification; the explicit cutoff correction is still required. No main index conclusion is disproved by this issue.
result: Impact: Function-space and construction errors in the extension lemma; gradient operations in the subsequent proof admit the corrected formulation.
