Title: Sutured Floer Isomorphisms: Initial Technical Review
# Identity and reviewed version

The reviewed work is Vincent Colin, Paolo Ghiggini and Ko Honda, Sutured Heegaard Floer and embedded contact homologies are isomorphic, DOI 10.4171/jems/1719 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1719). The bound source is the 35-page PDF retrieved from NSF PAR record 10674738. It carries EMS online-first typesetting, copyright 2025, and the dates received 25 March 2024 and revised 15 April 2025. The publisher metadata records publication on 24 September 2025. NSF labels the deposit Accepted Manuscript; this report preserves that label and does not assert byte identity with the subscription PDF. All locators below are one-based PDF pages, which agree with printed pages. The source SHA256 begins `bdab696774a331ed`; its full value is retained in the accompanying source manifest and verification files.
# Scope and operative assumptions

The preserved initial review read the entire extracted text, including references. Its unchanged scientific checks are reused here. The deeper checks concern Theorems 1.3 and 3.2, Lemmas 3.4, 4.16, 4.19 and 4.22, the scope of Theorem 5.1 and Corollaries 5.4 and 5.6, and the counting argument of Theorem 6.3. Geometric construction details and the cited analytic foundations were traced as dependencies rather than independently reproved.

The coefficient field is \(\mathbb F_2\) (p. 4). The balanced sutured three-manifolds of Definition 2.1 are compact, have no closed components, and have surfaces \(R_\pm\) without closed components and with matching Euler characteristic. Definition 2.2 imposes the adapted-contact-form conditions at the boundary. Nondegeneracy and the hyperbolic multiplicity-one condition enter the ECH chain complex on pp. 6–7.

Theorem 1.3 is an ungraded, summed isomorphism \[\operatorname{ECH}(M,\Gamma,\xi)\cong\operatorname{SFH}(-M,-\Gamma).\] It is explicitly weaker than Conjecture 1.1 on p. 2. In particular, this paper does not prove the asserted correspondence of contact invariants in that conjecture or an unrestricted relative Spin\(^c\) splitting. Remark 1.2 also explains why the integer-coefficient extension has not been supplied. These are scope boundaries, not contradicted claims.
# Checks of the closure argument
## Euler-class matching and the doubled summand

The closure uses an auxiliary surface of genus at least three. On p. 10, the contact Euler-class pairing is \(\chi(\Sigma)-2\). Since \(c_1(\mathfrak s_\xi+\operatorname{PD}(A))
=c_1(\mathfrak s_\xi)+2\operatorname{PD}(A)\), the condition \(A\cdot[\Sigma]=1\) gives the required pairing \(\chi(\Sigma)\) in Lemma 3.4. The factor of two and the selected summand agree.

Theorem 3.2 gives two copies of the sutured ECH group, one shifted. Lemma 3.6 supplies the analogous two copies of SFH. Cancellation is valid for the ungraded vector-space conclusion of Theorem 1.3; it is not an argument for the stronger graded or contact-invariant conjecture. The genus-minimizing and non-genus-minimizing cases are separated in Lemmas 3.5–3.6. The underlying adjunction and broken-fibration inputs are external dependencies, not independently reproduced here.
## The index bound and the acyclic summand

In the second case of Lemma 4.16 (pp. 22–23), the displayed final upper bound is \[-2ng+2n+3=-2n(g-1)+3\leq -4n+3\leq-1
 \quad(g\geq3,\ n\geq1).\] Thus the numerical conclusion is strict even at the boundary \(g=3,n=1\). This verifies the final arithmetic, conditional on the geometric Euler-characteristic, relative-Chern-class and asymptotic-index computations that precede it.

For Lemma 4.19, write \(a\otimes1\) and \(a\otimes h_0\) for the two types of generators. Its differential has the form \[d(a\otimes1)=d'a\otimes1,\qquad
 d(a\otimes h_0)=d'a\otimes h_0+a\otimes1.\] Define \(K(a\otimes1)=a\otimes h_0\) and \(K(a\otimes h_0)=0\). Direct substitution gives \(dK+Kd=1\) over \(\mathbb F_2\). The claimed acyclicity of \(C_1\) therefore follows from the stated differential; this calculation does not infer that differential from holomorphic geometry.
## The two surviving telescope classes

The seven rules on p. 25 give two families of relations \[d(e_nh_0)=e_{n+1}+e_n,\qquad
 d(h_nh_0)=h_{n+1}+h_n\qquad(n\geq1).\] For either family the direct-sum complex has one surviving class: every finite sum of even coefficient parity is a sum of adjacent differences, whereas a single generator has odd parity and is not a boundary. No infinite sum or boundary at infinity is allowed. The remaining quotient is the mapping cone of the identity on the relative Morse complex. It is acyclic. Consequently the auxiliary homology has precisely the two classes asserted in Lemma 4.22.

An independently written exact GF(2) calculation checks finite invariant subcomplexes for \(g\in\{3,4,7\}\) and \(N\in\{1,2,5,20\}\). At cutoff \(N\), the terminal generators \(e_Nh_0,h_Nh_0\) are omitted so that the differential stays within the subcomplex. In all twelve cases, \(d^2=0\) and \(\dim H=2\). This is a finite consistency check of the transcribed differential; the preceding direct-sum argument supplies the infinite algebraic step. The script and full outputs are retained.
# Refinements, applications and remaining dependencies

Theorem 5.1 (pp. 27–28) is stated for cosets of the subgroup \[K_\psi=\operatorname{Im}(i_{-*}\psi_*-i_{+*}).\] Corollary 5.4 additionally requires the two free-quotient hypotheses of Lemma 5.2 and \(\dim K_\pm\ne1\). It cannot be used as an unrestricted solution of Conjecture 1.1. The integral-lattice construction in Lemma 5.3 was read and its role identified; it was not independently certified in every rank. For the knot case the argument instead uses annular \(R_\pm\) and \(K_\psi=0\) (Corollary 5.6). The zero-flux hypothesis is retained for the periodic-Floer formulation.

For Theorem 6.3 (p. 32), if there are only \(r\) simple hyperbolic orbits and no elliptic ones, the admissible orbit sets are subsets of these orbits, including the empty set. Hence the chain rank is \(2^r\). The lower bound \(2^{k+1}\) on homology therefore forces \(r\geq k+1\). The tautness, irreducibility, depth, \(H_2(M)=0\) and nondegeneracy hypotheses remain part of that argument. The planar assumption in the no-trapping conclusion of Theorem 6.1 is also essential to the stated scope; the nonplanar extension is posed as Question 6.2.

The blocking/trapping arguments, Morse–Bott correspondence, curve enumeration of Lemma 4.20, cobordism maps and contact-topological classification inputs remain substantial analytic/geometric dependencies. Reading their use and checking downstream algebra does not constitute an independent proof of those inputs. Figures 1–4 and the cited source pages were visually inspected in the recovery continuation. Their labels and displayed formulas agree with the bounded reading above. This inspection does not independently establish the geometric curve counts.
# Outcome

No substantive defect is established in the declared inspected scope. There is no proposed correction and no author-adoption claim. The bounded publisher, arXiv and author-publication-page search did not locate a separate correction, supplement or computational repository for this work. This is a search outcome, not proof of nonexistence. The earlier arXiv version was not substituted for the bound NSF PDF.

Title: The Functional Volume Product under Heat Flow: Initial Technical Review
# Identity and scope

The reviewed work is Shohei Nakamura and Hiroshi Tsuji, The functional volume product under heat flow, DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1720 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1720). The exact bound source is the University of Birmingham accepted author manuscript, SHA256 prefix `d0896dde54adc8cd`. It comprises a repository cover and 19 manuscript pages. Below, manuscript page \(j\) means PDF page \(j+1\).

The preserved initial review read all extracted pages, including references. Its unchanged checks are reused here. The detailed checks cover Theorems 1.2, 1.5 and 2.1, Lemma 2.2, Corollary 1.6, the limiting argument (2.6)–(2.8), and the differentiation leading to (2.12). # Main proof and assumptions

Theorem 1.2 assumes a nonzero, nonnegative, even \(f_0\in L^1(dx)\); it does not assume log-concavity or Gaussian tails. The evolution is \(\partial_t f_t=\Delta f_t+\operatorname{div}(xf_t)\). Theorem 1.5 has \(p=1-e^{-2s}\in(0,1)\) and \(q=1-e^{2s}=p'=p/(p-1)<0\), with even nonnegative inputs. Evenness is essential, and is precisely what centers the measure \(F_t^q\,dx\) in the variance argument. General nonsymmetric inputs are not covered.

Writing \[F_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{\langle x,z\rangle/p}f_t(z)^{1/p}\,dz,
 \qquad Q_p(t)=\log\int F_t^q,\] the corrected differentiation gives \[-\frac pq Q_p'(t)
 =-\mathbb E_\mu|x|^2
   -(1-p)\mathbb E_\mu\mathbb E_{h_{t,x}}\Delta\log f_t,
 \qquad \mu=\frac{F_t^q}{\int F_t^q}\,dx .\] Here \(-p/q=1-p>0\). Moreover \(\nabla^2(-\log F_t^q)=-q\,\operatorname{Cov}(h_{t,x})/p^2\). Brascamp–Lieb bounds the first expectation by \((-p^2/q)\mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Tr}\operatorname{Cov}(h_{t,x})^{-1}\). The matrix Cramér–Rao inequality then gives \[\mathbb E_\mu|x|^2
 \leq -\frac pq\,\mathbb E_\mu\mathbb E_{h_{t,x}}
                    \Delta(-\log f_t).\] Consequently the displayed derivative is nonnegative. The signs, normalization of \(h_{t,x}\), and \(p/q=p-1\) agree. The cancellation of the two dimension terms uses \(p/q=-(1-p)\).

For completeness, the Cramér–Rao step does not require \(h_{t,x}\) to be log-concave: integration by parts gives \(\mathbb E[(Z-\mathbb EZ)(-
abla\log h)^T]=I\), and the covariance matrix inequality yields \(\operatorname{Cov}(h)^{-1}\preceq
\mathbb E[(
abla\log h)(
abla\log h)^T]
=\mathbb E[-
abla^2\log h]\) under the decay conditions of the bounded-support approximation. The strict log-concavity used in Brascamp–Lieb belongs instead to \(F_t^q\).
# Problem 1: the asserted everywhere limit is false (Minor)
## Claim, location and admissible example

On manuscript p. 10, equation (2.6) is stated for every \(x\) and footnote 7 justifies finiteness of \(F_t^{(p)}(x)\) by claiming Gaussian decay of \(f_t\). Neither statement holds for all the \(L^1\) initial data in Theorem 1.2.

Take \(n=1\), \(f_0(y)=\tfrac12e^{-|y|}\), and any \(t>0\). This input is nonnegative, nonzero, even, and has mass one. Put \(a=e^t\) and \(\sigma^2=1-e^{-2t}\). The actual solution is \[f_t(z)=\frac a2\,\mathbb E e^{-a|z-\sigma Z|},\qquad Z\sim N(0,1).\] With \(C=\tfrac a2e^{a^2\sigma^2/2}\), \[e^{az}f_t(z)\leq C,\qquad
 \lim_{z\to+\infty}e^{az}f_t(z)=C>0 .\] The inequality follows from \(z-|z-\sigma Z|\leq\sigma Z\); dominated convergence gives the limit. Thus \(f_t^\circ(a)=C^{-1}>0\). On the other hand, \[F_t^{(p)}(a)=\int_{\mathbb R}
                  \big(e^{az}f_t(z)\big)^{1/p}\,dz=\infty
       \quad\text{for every }0<p<1.\] Since \(q=p/(p-1)<0\), its \(q\)th power is zero. This contradicts (2.6) at \(x=a\). At \(t=\log2\) the right side is \(e^{-3/2}\). The same example has exponential, rather than Gaussian, tails. The counterexample is exact; numerical tail evaluations are only supporting checks.
## Impact and a verified correction
This is a failure of the everywhere assertion, not a counterexample to the integrated limit (2.7) or to Theorem 1.2. The distinction can be proved without assuming Gaussian decay.

For fixed \(t>0\), let \[D=\{x:\sup_z e^{\langle x,z\rangle}f_t(z)<\infty\}.\] This set is convex. If \(x\) is in its interior, bounds at \(x\pm\delta e_i\) imply \(e^{\langle x,z\rangle}f_t(z)\leq M e^{-\delta\|z\|_\infty}\). The usual large-\(r\) norm limit, with \(r=1/p\), proves (2.6) there. Outside \(D\) the supremum is infinite. Continuity provides a positive-volume set above every finite level, which forces the large-\(r\) norm to diverge, so the limit is again correct and equals zero. The boundary of a full-dimensional convex set has Lebesgue measure zero; if \(D\) has empty interior, \(D\) itself is null. Therefore (2.6) holds almost everywhere.

For \(t>0\), positivity on a cube supplies the exponential majorant used in (2.8), independently of upper Gaussian tails. Dominated convergence now proves (2.7) with the almost-everywhere statement. Thus the integral needed in the main implication survives. The Minor assessment is based on this verified impact boundary, not on the mere ease of editing the text. Replace the universal pointwise claim and footnote 7 by this almost-everywhere argument. No author adoption of this correction has been verified.
# Problem 2: impossible lower derivative bounds (Minor)

Equation (2.11), manuscript p. 12, places \(c_1(1+|x|+|x|^2)\gamma_\beta\) below the list \(f_t,|\nabla f_t|,|\Delta f_t|\), with \(c_1,\beta>0\). The gradient lower bound is false even after the proof’s bounded, compactly supported approximation.

Indeed, choose \(n=1\) and \(f_0=\tfrac12\mathbf1_{[-1,1]}\). All the operative assumptions, including evenness, boundedness and compact support, hold. The convolution formula makes \(f_t\) smooth and even, hence \(f_t'(0)=0\) for every \(t>0\). The proposed lower bound at zero is strictly positive for every \(c_1,\beta>0\). This is a direct contradiction.

The subsequent integration by parts requires a lower bound on \(f_t\) and upper bounds on its derivatives, not positive lower bounds on those derivatives. A valid replacement is \[c_1\gamma_\beta\leq f_t,\qquad
 f_t+|\nabla f_t|+|\Delta f_t|
       \leq c_2(1+|x|+|x|^2)\gamma .\] For bounded compact support and fixed \(t>0\), the Gaussian convolution provides the lower bound by integrating over a positive-mass bounded set. For the upper bound, the kernel variance is \(1-e^{-2t}<1\), so its quadratic decay absorbs the bounded-center linear term, including the polynomials from differentiating the kernel. Constants can be chosen locally uniformly for \(t\) in a compact subinterval of \((0,\infty)\). The false extra lower bounds are not used in the monotonicity inequality; this limits the defect to the displayed estimate.
# Problem 3: one exponent in the generator expansion (Minor)

On manuscript p. 12, in the expansion of \(L_z[e^{\langle x,z\rangle/p}f_t^{1/p-1}]\) immediately after (2.11), the term multiplying \(\Delta\log f_t\) contains \(f_t^{1/p-2}\). It must instead contain \(f_t^{1/p-1}\).

Put \(\alpha=1/p-1\), \(\ell=\log f_t\), and \(w=e^{\langle x,z\rangle/p+\alpha\ell}\). Direct differentiation gives \[L_zw=w\left[
 \frac{|x|^2}{p^2}+\frac{2\alpha}{p}\langle x,\nabla\ell\rangle
 +\alpha^2|\nabla\ell|^2+\alpha\Delta\ell
 -\frac{\langle x,z\rangle}{p}
 -\alpha\langle z,\nabla\ell\rangle\right].\] Every bracketed term has the same prefactor \(w\). An independent symbolic calculation gives zero residual for this formula.

The discrepancy is nonzero for admissible bounded-support data as well. Use the input of Problem 2, \(t=\log2\), \(p=1/2\), and \(x=z=0\). Here \(0<f_t(0)<1\) and \(f_t''(0)<0\), since the convolution centers lie in \([-1/2,1/2]\) while the kernel variance is \(3/4\). Thus \(\ell''(0)<0\), and replacing \(f_t\ell''\) by \(\ell''\) changes the value. This verifies that the exponent is not an alternative identity.

The very next displayed integrated expression already uses \(f_t^{1/p}\Delta\log f_t\), as the corrected expansion requires after multiplication by \(f_t\). Equation (2.12) also agrees with independent differentiation. The local exponent error therefore does not propagate to the final sign argument. It should be corrected in the displayed expansion; no corresponding revision by the authors is established here.
# Other checks and conclusion

The \(t=0\) step uses truncation \(f_0^{(N)}=f_0\mathbf1_{[-N,N]^n\cap\{f_0\leq N\}}\), monotone convergence for its Laplace transform, and Fatou in the direction appropriate to \(q<0\). For fixed positive time, a fixed nonzero truncation supplies the uniform cube lower bound needed for the inverse-power majorant. The upper end \(t\to\infty\) uses the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equilibrium and the same domination mechanism.

For Corollary 1.6, direct Gaussian integration for \(f(z)=e^{-\langle z,Az\rangle/2}\) verifies both the determinant cancellation and the constant \((2\pi)^{n/p'}(p^{1/p}/|p'|^{1/p'})^{n/2}\). The extension from the endpoint exponents in Theorem 1.5 uses monotonicity of generalized Gaussian-measure norms; the Gaussian tests establishing sharpness are cited from the authors’ prior paper and were not independently reproduced for every outside-range regime. Section 3 keeps its conjectural general-data discussion separate from the proved result and includes a note on later positive-coefficient work.

The three recorded defects are Minor for the specific reasons established above. No Major defect or counterexample to the principal monotonicity theorems has been established. This is not certification of every cited result. A bounded search of the publisher, repository and arXiv record located no separate erratum, supplement or released computational repository; absence from that search is not proof of nonexistence. The arXiv record currently identifies a 20 March 2024 revision, which is not substituted for this dated accepted manuscript. No author code was run. Title: Hölder Regularity and Smoothness of Complex Analytic Sets: Initial Technical Review
# Bound source and coverage

The work is José Edson Sampaio, Log-Lipschitz and Hölder regularity imply smoothness for complex analytic sets, arXiv:2404.06943v2, 29 October 2024. The corresponding publisher title adds the word regularity after log-Lipschitz; DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1721. The bound 23-page PDF has SHA256 prefix `6434ffcfac02e237`. Page numbers below refer to this PDF. The publisher’s 25 September 2025 publication date is not the preprint date.

All extracted pages and references were read. A distinct 26-page author-hosted PDF was consulted only at its introductory definition and section structure. It has different numbering and no established internal revision date; it is not substituted for v2. The arXiv record says v2 corrected a mistake in Proposition 3.2. That earlier correction is not itself a new finding.

The deeper checks concern Definitions 2.1–2.3, Theorems 2.14–2.15, Claims 3.1.1–3.1.8, Proposition 3.2, the diameter-distance proof, Theorem 5.1 and the scopes of Corollaries 5.2 and 5.5. External topology is traced at the steps below rather than represented as independently reproved in full.
# Problem 1: the log-Lipschitz modulus has the wrong sign (Minor)
## Location and decisive contradiction

On pp. 3 and 7 the displayed definition bounds \(\|h(x)-h(y)\|\) by \[C\|x-y\|\log\|x-y\|,\qquad C>0,\quad0<\|x-y\|<1/2.\] For every allowed distance \(\delta\) the right side is negative, whereas the left side is nonnegative, even for a constant map. For example, \(\delta=1/4\) gives \((C/4)\log(1/4)<0\). No map on a set having such a pair can satisfy this literal definition. A smooth complex line therefore fails condition (3) of Theorem 3.1 under that definition, despite satisfying (4) and (5). The separate author-hosted PDF retains the expression in its introductory passage; no corrected version was established.
## Correction and impact

Replace the modulus by \(C\delta|\log\delta|=C\delta\log(1/\delta)\). It is positive, and \(|\log\delta|\geq\log2\) on the specified interval, so every Lipschitz map satisfies the corrected bound after increasing the constant. For each fixed \(\alpha<1\), \[\sup_{0<\delta<1/2}\delta^{1-\alpha}|\log\delta|<\infty ,\] which proves the needed Hölder comparison.

The uncorrected definition and the literal equivalence component are false. The substantive proof of \((1)\Rightarrow(5)\) uses only Hölder charts and never uses the negative expression. The Minor assessment concerns a miswritten modulus for the identified regularity class; it is supported by this separation of dependencies, rather than merely by ease of editing. The evidence does not contradict the intended positive-modulus log-Lipschitz theorem or the all-exponent Hölder conclusion. No author adoption of the proposed correction is claimed.
# Quantifiers and the tangent cone

Definition 2.2 correctly distinguishes a possibly different chart for each \(\alpha<1\) from one chart valid for all \(\alpha<1\). The proof starts with the weaker hypothesis. The extension-and-shear construction on pp. 11–12 loses \(\alpha\) to \(\alpha^2\). Availability of exponents arbitrarily close to one absorbs this loss; neither a common chart nor a uniform Hölder constant is assumed.

In Claim 3.1.2, passage through a chart and back changes the horn exponent from \(b''\) to \(\alpha^4b''\). Fix \(b''>1\) in the stability interval, then take \(\alpha\) sufficiently close to one that \(1<\alpha^4b''<b''\). Changes in fixed horn amplitudes can be absorbed after restricting the germ. The step from bounding in a thicker horn to vanishing in the original horn uses the stabilized maps on homology, not just equality of group ranks.

This dependency was checked in the original research source Moderately discontinuous homology, arXiv:1910.12552v3, 22 January 2020, pp. 47–50: Theorem 112, the proof of Theorem 107, Remark 117 and Corollary 118. The direct limit is built from neighborhood maps, its stabilization uses homologically trivial cobordisms, and Remark 117 treats amplitudes. These passages support the naturality needed here. Their numbering differs from the published citation; editions are not conflated. The broader MD-homology theory and tangent-cone theorem remain external foundations.

For Claim 3.1.3, stabilization to \(N\geq k+4\) makes \(H^2(P,\widetilde V)\) and \(H^3(P,\widetilde V)\) vanish through the complement-homology bound. Thus the hyperplane class generates \(H^2(\widetilde V)\cong\mathbb Z\). The Gysin sequence propagates this generator to the top degree using the link cohomology vanishing. The fundamental-class pairing then forces degree one. Integral coefficients matter: rational rank alone would not suffice. Alexander duality, the affine-complement theorem and the Gysin sequence for the relevant singular base were traced, not fully reproved here.
# Covering sheets and the sharpness example

With a linear tangent cone, a proper projection is a finite covering away from its branch set. Two distinct lifts of a generic radial arc would have outer separation of order \(b>1\). Every connecting path must leave a branch-free conical sector, giving inner distance at least a positive multiple of \(t\). Connecting the two subanalytic lifts through zero gives the matching upper order \(t\).

A bi-\(\alpha\)-Hölder chart transfers a straight segment to a path of diameter at most a constant times \(\|u-v\|^{\alpha^2}\). The finite pancake argument gives \(d_{\rm inn}\leq mC\,d_{\rm diam}\). Hence two sheets would imply \(t\lesssim t^{\alpha^2b}\), impossible for \(\alpha^2b>1\). This checks the direction of the decisive inequality. Near-minimizing paths suffice in the noncompact version of the last-exit construction; exact geodesic attainment is unnecessary.

For Proposition 3.2 choose \(n>1\) and \(\alpha<b=n/(n+1)<1\) on \(x^n=y^{n+1}\). The link is a smooth embedded circle with two positive constant coordinate moduli, say \(a,c\). The weighted radial map \(F(tv)=(t f_1(v),t^b f_2(v))\) is \(b\)-Hölder by \(|s^b-t^b|\leq|s-t|^b\) and the Lipschitz link parametrization. For an independent inverse estimate, when \(0<t\leq s\leq1\) the first coordinate controls \(s-t\) by \(a^{-1}\) times the output distance, while \[t^{1-b}(s^b-t^b)\leq b(s-t)\leq s-t .\] Together these bound \(t\) times the difference of link points. The Lipschitz inverse link map then bounds the inverse radial map. Products with \(\mathbb C^{d-1}\) give the stated dimensions. No defect in this corrected v2 construction was established.

The statement of Proposition 4.1 displays the automatic direction \(d_{\rm diam}\leq mC\,d_{\rm inn}\), whereas its proof concludes the useful converse on p. 19. The statement should match that proved converse; the argument actually supplies the input to Theorem 4.2. The historical Theorem 1.1 should explicitly retain the complex-surface dimension from its preceding paragraph. These editorial observations are separated from the proved sign error.
# Infinity, outcome and limitations

Theorem 5.1 assumes algebraicity. Inversion takes asymptotic outer separation order \(b<1\) to \(2-b>1\), recovering the two-sheet contradiction. The pure-dimensional reduction and possible finite exceptional set are retained. Corollary 5.2 extends the result to entire analytic sets only for Lipschitz regularity, through a cited algebraicity theorem; it does not assert the all-Hölder statement for arbitrary entire analytic sets. Corollary 5.5 assumes a biholomorphism and uses holomorphic growth control for its affine conclusion.

One Minor definition error is recorded with exact repair and impact. No Major defect was established in the substantive inspected proof. This is not certification of every external theorem or every source page. A bounded publisher, arXiv and author-page search located no separate code or supplementary file. Known version corrections and the distinct author manuscript are retained as version information. No author code was run. The recovery inspected 18 source pages, the five identified MD-homology evidence pages and three introductory pages of the distinct author manuscript. Historical image-access failure is retained in the prior evidence. Final report-page viewing and compilation facts are recorded separately. Scientific decision is pending and human reviews are empty.

For example, \(\delta=1/4\) gives \((C/4)\log(1/4)<0\). No map on a set having such a pair can satisfy this literal definition. A smooth complex line therefore fails condition (3) of Theorem 3.1 under that definition, despite satisfying (4) and (5). The separate author-hosted PDF retains the expression in its introductory passage; no corrected version was established.

Replace the modulus by \(C\delta|\log\delta|=C\delta\log(1/\delta)\). It is positive, and \(|\log\delta|\geq\log2\) on the specified interval, so every Lipschitz map satisfies the corrected bound after increasing the constant. For each fixed \(\alpha<1\), \[\sup_{0<\delta<1/2}\delta^{1-\alpha}|\log\delta|<\infty ,\] which proves the needed Hölder comparison.

The uncorrected definition and the literal equivalence component are false. The substantive proof of \((1)\Rightarrow(5)\) uses only Hölder charts and never uses the negative expression. The Minor assessment concerns a miswritten modulus for the identified regularity class; it is supported by this separation of dependencies, rather than merely by ease of editing. The evidence does not contradict the intended positive-modulus log-Lipschitz theorem or the all-exponent Hölder conclusion. No author adoption of the proposed correction is claimed.

report: Abstract: Three defects are established in the proof as written in arXiv:2404.07138v1: the local nodal-stability corollary is false on its specified half-tube; the purported smoothed metric remains discontinuous; and the stated variational decomposition is not a direct sum and does not have its claimed orthogonality. Findings are restricted to the exact preprint, with no claim about the uninspected publisher version. The recovery visually checked all 17 pages of this source.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Steklov Nodal Constructions: Initial Technical Review
# Identity, version and scope

The reviewed work is Alberto Enciso, Angela Pistoia and Luigi Provenzano, Nonexistence of Courant-type nodal domain bounds for eigenfunctions of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator, arXiv:2404.07138v1, 10 April 2024; corresponding journal DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1722. The bound 17-page PDF has SHA256 prefix `11db23b7960a94fdd`. The publisher records acceptance on 27 May 2025 and publication on 9 October 2025. The v1 preprint is not asserted to be equivalent to that later version.

All extracted pages, both appendices and references were read. The primary checks cover the product sloshing spectrum, the spectral ordering as \(\beta\to0\), Corollary 2.2, the two min–max bounds, the smoothing step, and the transition from nodal hypersurfaces to boundary nodal counts. Formula locations were additionally retained through raw extraction of pp. 7–13. The recovery inspected all source page images, including Figure 1 and both appendices.

The counterexamples below use \(n=3\), a connected smooth rounded cylinder containing \([-2,2]\times\overline D^2\) with a cylindrical side near this product, and \(\Sigma=\{0\}\times\overline D^2\). The ends are rounded outside this product. This is a smooth compact manifold with boundary; \(\Sigma\) is connected, separating, has nonempty boundary, and meets the manifold boundary transversally. Use the smooth product metric \(dt^2+\beta^2|dy|^2\) on the cylindrical part, extended smoothly over the ends. These examples do not rely on disconnected manifolds or an empty-boundary convention.
# Problem 1: nodal stability fails on the specified half-tube (Major)
## Source claim and a counterexample satisfying its hypotheses

Corollary 2.2 on p. 7 claims that every sufficiently small \(C^1\) perturbation of any of the first \(K\) sloshing eigenfunctions, restricted to \(\Omega_{1/2}\), has a nodal component isotopic to \(\Sigma\). Its proof asserts \(w_k(0,y)=0\) for all these modes.

Use the separation label \(\ell\) from (2.7), avoiding the inconsistent \(k\) versus \(k-1\) indexing. The \(\ell=2\) ground mode is \[w(t,y)=c\,I_0(\pi\beta|y|)\cos(\pi(t+1))
       =-c\,I_0(\pi\beta|y|)\cos(\pi t),\qquad c>0.\] Here \(I_0\) is the modified Bessel function; its power series has positive coefficients, and the radial equation is \(\Delta_y I_0(\pi\beta r)=\pi^2\beta^2 I_0(\pi\beta r)\). Thus this is precisely a positive transverse ground state times the second Neumann cosine. Choose \(c\) to impose the paper’s boundary normalization.

This mode belongs to the first three relevant modes for \(\beta=1/100\). Indeed, the disk’s first nonconstant transverse Steklov eigenvalue is \(1/\beta=100\), and adding a nonnegative potential can only increase it. The constant test function bounds the first three ground branches by \[\mu_0^\ell(\beta)\leq\frac{\pi^2\ell^2\beta}{8}
 \leq\frac{9\pi^2}{800}<100,\qquad1\leq\ell\leq3 .\] The ground branches strictly increase with the potential, by applying the smaller-potential Rayleigh quotient to a normalized minimizer of the larger-potential problem. Hence the asserted simplicity and low-mode ordering hold. Taking \(K=3\) includes \(\ell=2\) under either zero-mode indexing convention appearing in the manuscript.

On the whole closed half-tube \(|t|\leq1/2\), \(w\leq0\). For any proposed stability radius \(\delta>0\), put \(u=w-\eta\) with \(0<\eta<\delta\). Then \(\|u-w\|_{C^1}=\eta\), but \(u<0\) throughout \(\Omega_{1/2}\). Its nodal set is empty. This directly refutes the quantified corollary. The cosine is nonzero at \(t=0\) for every positive even \(\ell\), and its derivative there vanishes; the proof’s displayed central-slice calculation is also false.
## Dependency, repair and limits

This is the nodal-persistence input used in Step 5 to conclude Theorem 1.2 for the first \(K\) modes. Its failure is therefore Major under a core-dependency criterion, without claiming the existence theorem is false.

A precise repair is to work on \(\Omega_\tau\) with, for example, \(\tau=3/4\). For every \(\ell\geq1\), choose a zero \(t_\ell=(2m+1)/\ell-1\) closest to zero. Then \(|t_\ell|\leq1/2<\tau\), and \(|\partial_t w_0^\ell(t_\ell,y)|
=(\pi\ell/2)v_0^\ell(y)\) is uniformly positive on the compact slice. For finitely many modes choose disjoint local collars as needed and a common positive stability tolerance. Boundary-preserving isotopy applies to these transverse slices, each isotopic to \(\Sigma\). The paper already states convergence in \(C^r(\Omega_\tau)\) for every fixed \(\tau<1\) on p. 13, so this repair has the needed convergence input. It changes the false corollary and its application; it is not a verification of the corollary as printed.
# Problem 2: the proposed smoothing does not produce a smooth metric (Major)

Step 4 on p. 8 defines a smooth factor \(\rho_{\varepsilon,h}\) tending to \(1\) on \(\Omega\) and \(\varepsilon\) on \(\Omega^c\), but then sets \[g_{\varepsilon,h}=\rho_{\varepsilon,h}^2g_\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 g_\varepsilon=\begin{cases}g&\text{on }\Omega,\\
                         \varepsilon^2g&\text{on }\Omega^c.
             \end{cases}\] For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), at an interior interface point the two traces are \(\rho^2g\) and \(\rho^2\varepsilon^2g\). Smoothness and the stated positive lower bound on \(\rho\) make these unequal. Multiplication by a smooth positive scalar cannot remove this jump. For example, \(\varepsilon=1/2\) and an interface value \(\rho=3/4\) give coefficients \(9/16\) and \(9/64\).

Away from the transition strip on \(\Omega^c\), the displayed family equals \(\varepsilon^4g\), and tends to that value, rather than the target \(\varepsilon^2g\). Thus both asserted properties of this family—smoothness and convergence to the stated discontinuous metric—fail. Proposition 2.4 cannot be invoked for the written family, and Step 5 has not produced the smooth metric required by the main theorem. This is a Major construction defect, even though its likely correction is short.

Replace the definition by \(\widetilde g_{\varepsilon,h}=\rho_{\varepsilon,h}^2g\), using the original smooth metric, and choose \(\varepsilon\leq\rho_{\varepsilon,h}\leq1\) globally. The resulting metrics are smooth, agree with \(g\) on an interior tube, and converge to \(g_\varepsilon\) for fixed \(\varepsilon\). Uniform ellipticity at fixed \(\varepsilon\), convergence of the volume and boundary weights, compact trace embedding, and elliptic estimates on the unchanged interior tube give the appropriate setting for the cited spectral-approximation argument. This verifies the corrected geometric construction; it does not establish that the authors adopted this correction in the later journal version.
# Problem 3: the lower-bound decomposition and auxiliary estimate are invalid (Major)
## Failure of the stated direct sum and orthogonality

On p. 11, \(H_1\) is defined by harmonicity on \(\Omega^c\) alone. The claimed direct sum (4.6) and orthogonality (4.8) then fail. On the rounded cylinder described in Section 1, take \[h(t,y)=(t-1)_+ .\] Use the flat product metric on the whole rounded domain. This function lies in \(H^1(M)\), is zero on \(\Omega\), and is harmonic separately on the two components of \(\Omega^c\). It has zero trace on \(\partial_L\Omega\) and is approximable in \(H^1(\Omega^c)\) by functions vanishing near that interface. Consequently \(h\in H_1\cap H_2\) under the printed definitions, although \(h\ne0\).

Taking \(\psi=\psi'=h\) in (4.8) gives \(\int_M|\nabla h|^2>0\), not zero. Already the subcylinder \((1,2)\times D^2\) contributes \(\pi\beta^2>0\). The missing condition is the homogeneous Neumann condition on \(\partial_V\Omega^c\), which is imposed in the construction (4.7) but omitted from the definition of \(H_1\).
## The unweighted norm bound cannot hold uniformly

Equation (4.11), p. 12, also bounds the full \(\|\psi\|_{H^1(\Omega^c)}^2\) by a constant times the inside boundary norm of \(\psi_1\). The low-Rayleigh restriction does not supply such an \(\varepsilon\)-uniform bound.

Let \(z\in C_c^\infty(\Omega^c)\) be nonzero and set \(\psi=1+c\varepsilon^{-(n-2)/2}z\). Its mixed harmonic extension part is \(\psi_1=1\). All boundary traces of \(\psi\) equal one, while its weighted energy is \(c^2\int|\nabla z|^2\), independent of \(\varepsilon\). Choosing \(c\) sufficiently small gives a uniformly bounded Rayleigh quotient below the stated threshold. It can also be included in the low-energy trial subspaces: adjoin the finitely many extended sloshing modes, use their positive spectral margin, and note that the compactly supported bump is energy-orthogonal to their harmonic exterior extensions. Nevertheless the unweighted exterior gradient norm diverges as \(\varepsilon^{-(n-2)}\), whereas the right side of (4.11) is fixed. Thus the displayed estimate cannot serve as the asserted uniform input.
## A replacement lower-bound argument

Define \(H_1\) instead by the weak mixed problem: harmonicity on \(\Omega^c\) together with zero exterior normal flux on \(\partial_V\Omega^c\). Write \(\psi=a+b\), where \(a\) is the mixed harmonic extension of \(\psi|_\Omega\) and \(b\in H_2\). Then energy orthogonality is valid.

This supplies a replacement for the broken estimates and uses the actual boundary condition. The printed decomposition, orthogonality and uniform estimate are not thereby made true. Their central role in Proposition 2.3 and then Theorem 1.2 supports Major severity; whole-paper falsity is not required.
# Other checks, counterevidence and outcome

The conformal factors in the Rayleigh quotient (2.3) are correct: energy scales by \(\varepsilon^{n-2}\) and boundary mass by \(\varepsilon^{n-1}\). This explains the \(n\geq3\) restriction. For the upper bound, use the span including the zero mode, \(\{w_0,\ldots,w_k\}\), with mixed exterior extensions. The exterior energy is \(O(\varepsilon^{n-2})\) and the boundary Gram matrix tends to the identity. The source alternates between zero-based and one-based labels; this needs consistent correction but is not counted as a separate Major finding.

Appendix A’s completeness argument is valid after normalizing the zero cosine: for each \(\ell\) the transverse traces are complete, and Fubini followed by the countability of the \(\ell\) set gives a common full-measure set on which all cosine coefficients vanish. Appendix B’s extension estimates use nonempty boundary pieces and connected components meeting the Dirichlet part. The construction requires \(\partial\Sigma\ne\varnothing\). The phrase with boundary is read in that intended sense here; no additional finding is based on allowing a closed separating hypersurface.

The distinction between nodal-set components and nodal domains is retained; in particular the exact-\(N\) wording in Theorem 1.1 is not treated as an assertion of a single sign domain for a nonconstant boundary eigenfunction. The finite-\(K\) construction also does not refute an asymptotic bound on one fixed metric, as the authors explicitly explain.

The three Major findings concern invalid core steps in the exact v1. Counterexamples and repair limits have been checked; no counterexample to the main existence theorem is asserted. An independent symbolic calculation verifies the cosine values, the Bessel-series recurrence, the metric jump and exterior-energy scaling. Its actual script and successful output are retained. The publisher, arXiv and Sapienza repository search located no separate erratum or released code; the arXiv record lists only v1 and the repository reports no attached file. This does not establish absence of a correction in the inaccessible journal PDF. No author code was executed, no author adoption was verified, and no independent acceptance was performed. Scientific decision remains pending and human reviews are empty. The original image-access failure remains historical evidence.

Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Holomorphic Partial Hyperbolicity: Initial Technical Review
# Identity and review scope

The reviewed manuscript is Disheng Xu and Jiesong Zhang, On holomorphic partially hyperbolic systems, arXiv:2401.04310v3, 24 May 2025, 29 pages, corresponding to DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1723. The bound PDF has SHA256 prefix `577a686a7a62c8d9`. The publisher records acceptance on 20 June 2025 and publication on 21 October 2025; equivalence to that later journal version is not assumed.

All extracted pages, Sections 1–10, both appendices and references were read. Particular attention was paid to the quantifiers in Definitions 3.1–3.2, the use of Proposition 3.3 in Lemma 8.3, the heat-semigroup and holonomy arguments, the higher-dimensional construction, and the Lie algebra calculation underlying Theorem 1.5. The formulas in Example 10.2 were additionally checked in raw PDF extraction. Independent SymPy calculations were actually executed; their script, output and exit status are retained. No author code was run.
# Problem 1: the stated dichotomy has neither alternative in a basic product example (Major)
## Exact claim and admissible example

Definition 3.2, p. 10, requires a set \(B\subset\operatorname{supp}\mu\) which has full leafwise volume in the entire center-unstable plaque \(L^{cu}_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\), as well as the fiberwise contraction property. Proposition 3.3, p. 11, claims that every ergodic Gibbs \(u\)-state satisfies this definition or Definition 3.1.

Let \(E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)\) and set \[M=E^2\times\mathbb P^1,\qquad
 A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 f(b,z)=(Ab,z/2).\] This is a holomorphic diffeomorphism of a compact complex threefold. The center fibration is the genuine product fibration with fibers \(\mathbb P^1\). In the flat metric on \(E^2\), the stable and unstable multipliers are \[\lambda_-=(3-\sqrt5)/2<1/2,\qquad
 \lambda_+=(3+\sqrt5)/2>2.\] For the spherical metric, the derivative norm of \(z\mapsto z/2\) is \[q(r)=\frac{2(1+r^2)}{4+r^2},\qquad 1/2\le q(r)\le2.\] Consequently all the strict partial-hyperbolicity and domination inequalities hold already for one iterate.

Let \(\mu=m_{E^2}\times\delta_0\). Haar measure is ergodic for \(A\): on the underlying real torus the eigenvalues are \(\lambda_\pm\), each repeated twice, and none is a root of unity. Thus \(\mu\) is ergodic. Its conditional measures on strong unstable plaques are Lebesgue measures, so it is a Gibbs \(u\)-state in Section 2.4. Its support is \(E^2\times\{0\}\).
## Failure of both branches

Every subset of this support has zero four-dimensional volume inside each center-unstable plaque: its intersection is contained in a two-dimensional unstable plaque. Hence no set allowed by Definition 3.2 can have the required full volume.

The system is not a \(\mu\)-center isometry either. Suppose the uniformly bounded fiber metrics of Definition 3.1 existed. Let \(a(b)>0\) be the norm, in the fiber metric at \((b,0)\), of the same fixed nonzero tangent vector to \(\mathbb P^1\) at \(0\). The isometry identity gives \[a(Ab)=2a(b),\qquad a(A^n b)=2^n a(b)\] on an invariant full-measure set. The uniform upper bound on the fiber distances implies a uniform upper bound on these tangent norms, contradicting the last equality. This argument permits the metrics to depend measurably on \(b\); it does not assume a common fixed spherical metric.

Thus Proposition 3.3 is false with its printed definition. The counterexample meets compactness, holomorphicity, fiberedness, complex dimension, domination, ergodicity and Gibbs-state hypotheses. It does not use a non-fibered quotient or an exceptional center leaf.
## Impact and repair boundary

Lemma 3.7 on p. 12 constructs a full-fiber set outside a countable exceptional set; it never proves that this set lies in \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\). The defect propagates to the dichotomy invoked in Lemma 8.3, p. 20, a key step in the proof of Theorem 1.3. This is a Major failure of a core statement and its application, even though the necessary wording correction is short.

Remove the requirement \(B\subset\operatorname{supp}\mu\), or replace it by \(B\subset\pi^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\widehat\mu)\). For the explicit example, \(B=E^2\times(\mathbb P^1\setminus\{\infty\})\) then works: all pairs in a center fiber converge to \(0\), and the omitted section has zero center volume. More generally, the construction in Lemma 3.7 and the full-volume/quasiconformal argument in Section 4 use exactly this larger set, rather than the prohibited support restriction. This identifies a coherent repair to the dependency. It neither verifies the statement as printed nor constitutes a counterexample to the final rigidity theorem, which is plainly satisfied by this product example.
# Problem 2: the construction proving Theorem 1.5 does not preserve its Lie bracket (Major)
## Decisive calculation

Example 10.2, p. 25, specifies the only nonzero brackets as \[[e_1,e_2]=[e_3,e_4]=e_5\] and defines \[Fe_1=2e_1+e_3,\quad Fe_2=2e_2+e_4,\quad
 Fe_3=e_1+e_3,\quad Fe_4=e_2+e_4,\quad
 Fe_5=e_5,\quad Fe_6=e_6.\] A Lie algebra homomorphism must satisfy \([FX,FY]=F[X,Y]\). Here \[[Fe_1,Fe_2]=5e_5\ne e_5=F[e_1,e_2],
 \qquad
 [Fe_1,Fe_4]=3e_5\ne0=F[e_1,e_4].\] Thus the first assertion of the construction is false. Commuting with the almost complex structure does not repair failure to preserve the Lie bracket. A group automorphism cannot have this linear map as its derivative; the asserted lift and quotient diffeomorphism do not follow.

The independent calculation checked every basis pair and found four nonzero bracket residuals (for pairs \(12,14,23,34\)), while also confirming that \(FJ=JF\). This separates the false algebra claim from the true commutation calculation.
## Actual impact

The example is explicitly the proof of Theorem 1.5, which claims a compact holomorphic partially hyperbolic threefold with five-dimensional accessibility classes. The supplied construction does not establish that theorem. This is Major regardless of the location in the examples section. It does not establish nonexistence of such systems.
## A verified alternative construction

A repair requires changing the bracket or the map and checking the lattice; one cannot retain the displayed structure unchanged. For example keep \(F\) and \(Je_1=e_2\), \(Je_3=e_4\), \(Je_5=e_6\), but replace the bracket by \[[e_1,e_2]=-2e_5,\quad [e_1,e_4]=e_5,\quad
 [e_3,e_2]=e_5,\quad [e_3,e_4]=2e_5.\] Its alternating form is nondegenerate on the horizontal four-space. In complex notation its real symmetric coefficient matrix is \[Q=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \det Q=-5,\qquad A^TQA=Q.\] These identities make \(F\) a Lie algebra automorphism. The Nijenhuis tensor vanishes on every basis pair; this was checked independently and also follows from the type \((1,1)\) bracket.

Take the simply connected group with this Lie algebra and the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff lattice \[\gamma'=\mathbb Z e_1+\cdots+\mathbb Z e_4
             +\tfrac12\mathbb Z e_5+\mathbb Z e_6,\qquad
 \Gamma'=\exp(\gamma').\] The group law \(X*Y=X+Y+\tfrac12[X,Y]\) preserves \(\gamma'\). Both \(F\) and \(F^{-1}\) preserve it. Use a left quotient \(\Gamma'\backslash G\) for the left-invariant complex structure (or consistently use the right-invariant convention). It is compact and its center leaves are two-tori. The stable and unstable horizontal spaces have multipliers \(\lambda_\pm\); the center has multiplier one. Their mixed brackets generate \(\mathbb R e_5\), because the nondegenerate \(Q\) pairs the two distinct null eigenspaces nontrivially. The resulting accessibility classes have tangent space \(E^s\oplus E^u\oplus\mathbb R e_5\), of real dimension five.

This is a concrete replacement establishing feasibility of the claimed phenomenon; it changes the construction in the submitted proof. It is not evidence of author adoption or journal correction. On this compact quotient the classes are compact Heisenberg quotients, not copies of the simply connected group \(H_5(\mathbb R)\).
# Problem 3: the exponential of the stated integer lattice need not be a subgroup (Minor)

In Example 10.1, p. 24, the paper sets \(\Gamma=\exp(\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Z}\{e_1,\ldots,e_6\})\) in the complex Heisenberg group. With the stipulated \([e_1,e_2]=e_3\), \[\log(\exp e_1\exp e_2)=e_1+e_2+\tfrac12e_3\] in exponential coordinates of the first kind. This does not belong to the indicated integer lattice. Therefore the displayed \(\Gamma\) is not a subgroup, and its quotient is not defined as written. The same issue must be addressed in Example 10.2, in addition to its bracket failure.

For Example 10.1, enlarge the central Gaussian-integer lattice to half Gaussian integers, keeping the horizontal lattice. The step-two BCH law then closes, and the displayed integral determinant-one horizontal map preserves the enlarged lattice in both directions. The accessible Iwasawa example is thereby recovered with the same map and Lie algebra. This isolated lattice specification does not change the rigidity or higher-dimensional construction and is classified Minor. It is not dismissed merely because it is easy to fix.
# Problem 4: the determinant degree is missing a factor of two (Minor)

In Proposition 9.3, p. 23, \(W=L^{\oplus 2n}\) is correctly specified, but the next display gives \(\deg(\det W)=n\deg L\). In fact \[\det W=L^{\otimes 2n},\qquad \deg(\det W)=2n\deg L.\] For example \(n=2\) gives \(4\deg L\), not \(2\deg L\). The argument uses only strict positivity, which is unchanged. This is a local numerical error with no damage to the nontriviality or non-Kähler conclusion.
# Other proof checks and counterevidence

The one-complex-dimensional hypotheses are essential wherever a complex derivative is called conformal. The threefold argument uses one-dimensional stable, center and unstable distributions; it must not be generalized by the unqualified sentence on p. 7 to higher-dimensional complex bundles. The separately stated higher-dimensional examples do not use that false generalization.

The KAK argument in Appendix A has the correct conclusion: after normalization, an unbounded sequence in \(\operatorname{PSL}(2,\mathbb C)\) has a subsequential rank-one limit, so all points except its kernel direction coalesce. This supports the repaired contraction argument.

For the isometric case, the heat-semigroup intertwining identity has the correct pullback/pushforward direction. Its limiting measure can be justified without assuming that arbitrary weak convergence commutes with disintegration: for each bounded continuous \(\varphi\), apply fiberwise heat convergence and dominated convergence to the fixed base measure \(\widehat\mu\). The limit is the integral of normalized fiber volumes. These are the volumes of the invariant fiber metrics, which are equivalent to the smooth leafwise volumes.

The actual Corollary 4.3 of Avila–Viana was checked in the author-hosted primary paper, together with the preceding holonomy-invariance setup. Its inverse version gives \(u\)-invariance when the largest fiber exponent is nonpositive. A full-measure disintegration may be extended over its holonomy-saturated set. Thus the absence of a stated local product assumption in this particular one-sided invocation is not counted as an error. The entire external proof was not re-proved.

Appendix B uses Gibbs \(cu\) equivalence, not just a Gibbs \(u\) measure, when applying Fubini to pairs of center points. Lusin sets and common recurrent times yield equivariance of the almost-everywhere derivative. Conjugation by a conformal map does not amplify the operator-norm error, even though a general real-linear derivative need not commute with complex rotations. Absolute continuity then gives affine linearity, and the zero normalization removes the translation. The common-time requirement comes from Lemma B.3; the two different sequence labels in the next paragraph should not be read as permission to use unrelated times.

The compact elliptic-fibration argument in Section 7 correctly uses constancy of the one-dimensional moduli parameter and continuity of the real-linear holonomy: the relevant lattice automorphism ambiguity is discrete modulo the finite isotropy. The higher-dimensional moduli space is not substituted here. Section 8’s open, invariant, center-saturated set and the Cesàro construction from a positive unstable-volume complement were traced through to holomorphicity almost everywhere and then everywhere.

For Section 9, the four proposed holomorphic sections do form a real frame. Writing \((s_1,s_2)=(a+ib,c+id)\), their real determinant is \[(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)^2>0.\] The independently executed symbolic expansion confirms this; no spurious dependence issue is reported. Integer hyperbolic matrices acting among the copies preserve the translation lattice. The real-analytic continuation argument distinguishes local holomorphicity from the real-analytic product trivialization. Taking an elliptic product supplies the even dimensions, without settling the separate dimension-four problem.

Example 10.3’s involution is free on the total threefold because of its nontrivial half-period shift. Its sixteen exceptional center fibers arise from the \(4\cdot4\) two-torsion points in the first two elliptic factors. The quotient of the base has the stated orbifold singularities, so this example is not a counterexample under the genuine fibered hypothesis.
# Outcome, evidence and limitations

The exact preprint has two confirmed Major findings and two Minor findings above. The Major findings damage core proof steps; neither is claimed to refute the respective main theorem. Explicit repairs and their scope are stated separately from the authors’ arguments.

The arXiv history confirms v3 and describes additional Section 8 arguments. The author homepage links the arXiv and publisher records. Bounded searches of these primary sources located no separate correction, supplement or released code; this is not proof that none exists. No source-version equivalence or author adoption has been verified.

All source text was read in the original review. The recovery reused its hash-bound substantive report and calculations and supplied actual inspection of 22 source pages, including both appendices. The historical image-access failure remains in the preserved evidence. The identified Avila–Viana dependency was checked from retained text; no external PDF page image is claimed viewed. Scientific decision is pending, human reviews are empty, and this is initial review rather than independent acceptance.

problems.title: the stated dichotomy has neither alternative in a basic product example (Major)
problems.source_location: Definition 3.2 p.10; Proposition 3.3 p.11; Lemma 3.7 p.12; Lemma 8.3 p.20
claim: Every ergodic Gibbs u-state is either a center isometry or has a contracting full-cu-volume set contained in supp(mu).

Compact complex threefold; genuine product center fibration; stable multiplier (3-sqrt(5))/2<1/2 and unstable multiplier (3+sqrt(5))/2>2; spherical center derivative between 1/2 and 2; Haar base mixing and Gibbs u condition verified.
analysis: Definition 3.2, p. 10, requires a set \(B\subset\operatorname{supp}\mu\) which has full leafwise volume in the entire center-unstable plaque \(L^{cu}_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x\), as well as the fiberwise contraction property. Proposition 3.3, p. 11, claims that every ergodic Gibbs \(u\)-state satisfies this definition or Definition 3.1.

Let \(E=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)\) and set \[M=E^2\times\mathbb P^1,\qquad
 A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 f(b,z)=(Ab,z/2).\] This is a holomorphic diffeomorphism of a compact complex threefold. The center fibration is the genuine product fibration with fibers \(\mathbb P^1\). In the flat metric on \(E^2\), the stable and unstable multipliers are \[\lambda_-=(3-\sqrt5)/2<1/2,\qquad
 \lambda_+=(3+\sqrt5)/2>2.\] For the spherical metric, the derivative norm of \(z\mapsto z/2\) is \[q(r)=\frac{2(1+r^2)}{4+r^2},\qquad 1/2\le q(r)\le2.\] Consequently all the strict partial-hyperbolicity and domination inequalities hold already for one iterate.

Let \(\mu=m_{E^2}\times\delta_0\). Haar measure is ergodic for \(A\): on the underlying real torus the eigenvalues are \(\lambda_\pm\), each repeated twice, and none is a root of unity. Thus \(\mu\) is ergodic. Its conditional measures on strong unstable plaques are Lebesgue measures, so it is a Gibbs \(u\)-state in Section 2.4. Its support is \(E^2\times\{0\}\).

Every subset of this support has zero four-dimensional volume inside each center-unstable plaque: its intersection is contained in a two-dimensional unstable plaque. Hence no set allowed by Definition 3.2 can have the required full volume.

The system is not a \(\mu\)-center isometry either. Suppose the uniformly bounded fiber metrics of Definition 3.1 existed. Let \(a(b)>0\) be the norm, in the fiber metric at \((b,0)\), of the same fixed nonzero tangent vector to \(\mathbb P^1\) at \(0\). The isometry identity gives \[a(Ab)=2a(b),\qquad a(A^n b)=2^n a(b)\] on an invariant full-measure set. The uniform upper bound on the fiber distances implies a uniform upper bound on these tangent norms, contradicting the last equality. This argument permits the metrics to depend measurably on \(b\); it does not assume a common fixed spherical metric.

Thus Proposition 3.3 is false with its printed definition. The counterexample meets compactness, holomorphicity, fiberedness, complex dimension, domination, ergodicity and Gibbs-state hypotheses. It does not use a non-fibered quotient or an exceptional center leaf.

Lemma 3.7 on p. 12 constructs a full-fiber set outside a countable exceptional set; it never proves that this set lies in \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\). The defect propagates to the dichotomy invoked in Lemma 8.3, p. 20, a key step in the proof of Theorem 1.3. This is a Major failure of a core statement and its application, even though the necessary wording correction is short.

Remove the requirement \(B\subset\operatorname{supp}\mu\), or replace it by \(B\subset\pi^{-1}(\operatorname{supp}\widehat\mu)\). For the explicit example, \(B=E^2\times(\mathbb P^1\setminus\{\infty\})\) then works: all pairs in a center fiber converge to \(0\), and the omitted section has zero center volume. More generally, the construction in Lemma 3.7 and the full-volume/quasiconformal argument in Section 4 use exactly this larger set, rather than the prohibited support restriction. This identifies a coherent repair to the dependency. It neither verifies the statement as printed nor constitutes a counterexample to the final rigidity theorem, which is plainly satisfied by this product example.
result: Impact: The central dichotomy and its invocation in Lemma 8.3 fail as stated. No counterexample to Theorem 1.3: the product has holomorphic center.
Limits: Verified counterexample and compatible repair; author adoption and journal correction not verified.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Remove B subset supp(mu), or allow B in the center saturation of supp(mu). Lemma 3.7 constructs such a larger set; Section 4 uses its full-volume property, not the invalid support restriction.

Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Verification of
Improvement of Flatness for Nonlocal Free Boundary Problems
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The source is Xavier Ros-Oton and Marvin Weidner, Improvement of flatness for nonlocal free boundary problems, arXiv:2404.15975v2, 23 March 2025, associated in the acquired identity record with Journal of the European Mathematical Society, DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1724 [RW]. The reviewed file is the 57-page author manuscript, not a verified byte-equivalent publisher version. Page references below are PDF pages; the displayed page numbers agree with them.

All 57 source pages were read, including the definitions, hypotheses, proofs, and references. Detailed analytic checks addressed the problems below, the tail scaling and thin-strip limit in the compactness argument, and the logarithmic energy scaling in dimension two. Actual images of the decisive cited pages were inspected. Full reading is distinct from independent verification of every proof: the external regularity and energy perturbation theorems were not consulted, and the uniform boundary-test remainder passage in the compactness proof was not independently closed.
# Definitions and assumptions

Equation reference: eq:L. For \(s\in(0,1)\), the source assumes a symmetric homogeneous kernel satisfying \[\lambda |h|^{-n-2s}\le K(h)\le\Lambda |h|^{-n-2s},
 \qquad K(-h)=K(h),\qquad
 K(h)=|h|^{-n-2s}K(h/|h|),\] with \(0<\lambda\le\Lambda\). Its operator convention is \[
 Lu(x)=2\mathop{\mathrm{PV}}\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u(x)-u(y))K(x-y)\,dy\] [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~2--3, (1.2)--(1.3)]{RW}]. The main regularity statements additionally assume \(K\in C^{1-2s+\beta}(S^{n-1})\) for \(\beta>\max\{0,2s-1\}\). Theorem 1.1 concerns minimizers of the one-phase functional whose zero set near a free-boundary point lies between two sufficiently close parallel hyperplanes. Theorem 1.5 concerns viscosity solutions trapped between translated half-space profiles, with the stated small tail bound. Both claim \(C^{1,\alpha}\) free-boundary regularity for every \(\alpha\in(0,s/2)\) [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~3, 6]{RW}].

The first two findings concern steps in these proofs. They do not assert a solution violating the regularity conclusion. The third finding concerns the independently stated exterior expansion for an \(L\)-harmonic function and uses all its required geometric hypotheses.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (The transformed kernel and domain in Lemma 4.12).  The shear displayed in the proof of Lemma 4.12 does not produce the displayed kernel or the asserted fixed half-ball domain.
## Claim and calculation

Equation reference: eq:shear. Lemma 4.12 assumes \(\gamma\in(0,s)\), \(f\in L^\infty(B_1)\), and \(\omega\in S^{n-1}\) with \(\omega_n\ge\delta>0\). For a viscosity solution of \[L((x_n)_+^{s-1}v)=f \quad\text{in }B_1\cap\{x_n>0\},
 \qquad
 \partial_\omega v=0 \quad\text{on }B_1\cap\{x_n=0\},\] it claims a \(C^{1,\gamma}\) boundary expansion with constants controlled by \(n,s,\lambda,\Lambda,\delta,\gamma\) [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~35--36]{RW}]. The proof defines \[a=\frac{\omega'}{\omega_n},\qquad
 S=\begin{pmatrix}I&a\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 w(x)=v(Sx).\] Here \(\det S=1\), and \(S\) preserves the last coordinate. With \(F(y)=(y_n)_+^{s-1}v(y)\) and \(W=F\circ S=(x_n)_+^{s-1}w(x)\), substitution \(y=Sz\) gives \[
 (LF)(Sx)=2\mathop{\mathrm{PV}}\int_{\mathbb R^n}
       (W(x)-W(z))K(S(x-z))\,dz.\] Consequently, the correct kernel is \[K_{\rm new}(h)=K(Sh)=K(h'+a h_n,h_n).\] The oblique derivative transforms as intended: \(\partial_nw=\omega_n^{-1}(\omega\cdot\nabla v)\circ S\).

The original equation supplies the transformed equation on \(S^{-1}B_1\cap\{x_n>0\}\), rather than necessarily on the printed \(B_{3/4}\cap\{x_n>0\}\). Indeed, if \(\omega=(\sqrt3/2,1/2)\) and \(x=(0,7/10)\), then \[|x|=7/10<3/4,\qquad |Sx|=7/5>1.\] The assumed equation and \(f\in L^\infty(B_1)\) give no equation at \(Sx\). Moreover, the printed prefactor becomes unbounded as \(\omega'\to0\) while \(\omega_n\ge1/2\), so it does not supply the asserted ellipticity constants uniformly in \(\delta\).
## Impact and bounded correction

The proof of Theorem 4.1 explicitly invokes Lemma 4.12 for its affine expansion on page 38. That improvement-of-flatness theorem feeds Theorem 1.5, and the proof on page 51 deduces Theorem 1.1 from Theorem 1.5. The invalid reduction is therefore a Major proof issue in the stated dependency chain. The evident local repair does not establish that the regularity theorem is false, nor does it verify every remaining step.
Problem 2 (The final argument reverses the exponent dependence).  Shrinking the iteration radius does not increase the exponent supplied by the displayed error decay.
## Claim and calculation

Equation reference: eq:gamma. At scales \(r_k=\rho_0^k/2\), Lemma 4.14 obtains error \(C2^{-ks}\). Pages 42–43 correctly relate the resulting exponent to the radius by \[
 \rho_0^\gamma=2^{-s},
 \qquad
 2=\rho_0^{-\gamma/s},
 \qquad
 \gamma=\frac{s\log2}{\log(1/\rho_0)}.\] These relations follow directly by comparing \(2^{-ks}\) with \(\rho_0^{k\gamma}\).

The last paragraph of the proof of Theorem 1.5 on page 45 instead prints \(2=\rho_0^{-s/\gamma}\), and argues that decreasing \(\rho_0\) allows \(\gamma\) to approach \(s\). It then claims every exponent \[\alpha=\frac{s\gamma}{s+\gamma}<\frac{s}{2}.\] Both the reciprocal discrepancy and the direction of the radius argument were checked on actual page images. With the relation [eq:gamma] (#eq:gamma) required by the iteration, smaller \(\rho_0\) gives smaller \(\gamma\), and hence smaller \(\alpha\). For \(s=1/2\), for example, \[\begin{array}{c|cc}
 \rho_0&\gamma&\alpha\\ \hline
 1/4&1/4&1/6\\
 1/16&1/8&1/10
\end{array}\] is an exact comparison. Approaching \(\gamma=s\) in [eq:gamma] (#eq:gamma) requires \(\rho_0\) to approach \(1/2\), rather than to decrease from the small radius supplied by the improvement theorem.
## Impact, counterevidence, and a complete parameter correction

The erroneous final argument is a Major proof issue: it does not establish the full exponent range in the principal regularity theorem. The existence of a short repair does not make this central invalid derivation merely a presentation defect. The earlier estimates supply a repair of the advertised geometric range, conditional on the other lemmas of the paper. Fix any target \(0<\alpha<s/2\), and choose \[\alpha<q<\gamma_{\rm lin}<s .\] Use \(\gamma_{\rm lin}\) in the affine estimate on pages 38–39. Equations (4.40) and the total tail estimate on pages 40–41 give, at a fixed sufficiently small radius \(\rho\), \[\text{rescaled flatness}\le (c_0/2)\varepsilon\rho^{\gamma_{\rm lin}},
 \qquad
 T_{\rm new}\le C\varepsilon
       (\rho^{\gamma_{\rm lin}}+\rho^s).\] The sum of the two tails outside the translated barriers is bounded by the tail of the absolute difference from the central profile. Set \(\theta=\rho^q\), and choose \(\rho\), once and for all, so that \[(c_0/2)\rho^{\gamma_{\rm lin}-q}\le1,\qquad
 C(\rho^{\gamma_{\rm lin}-q}+\rho^{s-q})\le\delta_0 .\] Both inequalities are possible because their powers are positive. Also require \(c_0\rho^{\gamma_{\rm lin}}<1\). Fix this radius before choosing the small flatness threshold \(\varepsilon_0\), as required by the compactness passage and Lemma 4.13. The improved flatness \(\theta\varepsilon\) then satisfies the same tail hypothesis \(T_{\rm new}\le\delta_0\theta\varepsilon\). The constants can be uniform under the rotations of the iteration, since rotation preserves the kernel bounds and its indicated regularity norm.

Thus one common finite entry scale suffices for each target exponent; after rotation, switch to the strengthened iteration. u_{k+1}-
u_kvert\le C\varepsilon_k\). The convergent sum yields, at every free-boundary center in a fixed smaller neighborhood, a limiting normal and a uniform strip estimate \[ igl|(x-x_0)\cdot
u_{x_0} igr|
       \le C|x-x_0|^{1+q}
 \quad	ext{for nearby free-boundary points }x .\] Here the constants and the allowed radius are independent of the center; the initial translation and scaling are those on page 42. Problem 3 (The exterior expansion in Lemma 3.3 has the wrong sign).  Under the positive operator convention [eq:L] (#eq:L), the half-space profile has a negative exterior operator, contrary to the displayed positive leading term.
## Claim and admissible example

Lemma 3.3 assumes (1.2), a \(C^{1,\alpha}\) domain \(\Omega\) with \(0\in\partial\Omega\), and \(Lu=0\) in \(B_1\cap\Omega\), \(u=0\) in \(B_1\setminus\Omega\). It asserts \[u(x)=U_0d(x)^s+O(|x|^{s+\alpha}),\qquad
 Lu(x)=B(\nu)U_0d(x)^{-s}+O(|x|^\alpha)d(x)^{-s}\] on the respective sides, with \(B(\nu)>0\). Equation (3.4) repeats this positive exterior sign for a half-space profile [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~11--12]{RW}].

Take \(n=2\), \(s=1/2\), \(K(h)=|h|^{-3}\), \(\Omega=\{x_2>0\}\), and \(u(x)=\sqrt{(x_2)_+}\). The kernel satisfies all conditions with \(\lambda=\Lambda=1\); the boundary is smooth; \(U_0=u/d^s=1\); and the weighted tail is finite, since its radial growth at infinity gives an integrable \(r^{-1-s}\) bound. Tangential integration yields \[\int_{\mathbb R}(z^2+b^2)^{-3/2}\,dz=2b^{-2}.\] For positive height, the resulting one-dimensional principal value is zero, as explicitly verified in Appendix 5 (#app:halfspace). Thus \(u\) satisfies the required interior equation.

Equation reference: eq:outside. At \(x=(0,-a)\), \(a>0\), direct integration instead gives \[
 Lu(0,-a)=-4\int_0^\infty\frac{\sqrt t}{(a+t)^2}\,dt
        =-2\pi a^{-1/2}<0.\] A positive \(B(e_2)a^{-1/2}\) cannot agree with [eq:outside] (#eq:outside) up to an \(O(a^\alpha)a^{-1/2}\) remainder. This is a counterexample to the exterior expansion as printed.
## Impact and correction

The missing minus persists in (3.6), page 13. The subsequent expression \(-\int uLv_\varepsilon\) is then treated as positive, which is consistent with a negative exterior operator. Replacing the exterior signs by minus repairs this immediate conflict. This is a Minor local sign defect: no damage to the positive Bernoulli normalization in Proposition 3.1 has been demonstrated. A full independent reconstruction of that variational argument and its constants has not been performed.
Problem 4 (A missing symmetric term in the min–max identity).  The pointwise identity (5.8) on page 54 omits one of the two possible orientations of a crossing pair.

Write \(a=w_1-\varphi_1\) and \(b=w_2-\varphi_2\). The correct identity is \[\begin{split}
 &[(w_1\wedge\varphi_1)-(w_2\wedge\varphi_2)]^2
 +[(w_1\vee\varphi_1)-(w_2\vee\varphi_2)]^2\\
 &\qquad=(w_1-w_2)^2+(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)^2
              -2(a_+b_-+a_-b_+).
\end{split}\] For \(w_1=0,\varphi_1=1,w_2=1,\varphi_2=0\), the left side is zero and the printed right side is two. The corrected formula follows by separating the cases \(ab\ge0\) and the two signs of \(ab<0\). After integration over the symmetric pair domain, the two cross terms have equal integrals. The displayed integrated coefficient should accordingly be four rather than two. This is a Minor local algebraic defect: the factor is absorbed by the unspecified constant in Lemma 5.8 and does not invalidate its estimate or demonstrate a counterexample to the classification theorem.

The logarithmic-cutoff argument on pages 52–55 was also checked at its scaling steps. Its annular sum is of order \(\log R\), which with \((\log R)^{-2}\) gives the stated \((\log R)^{-1}\) bound; the inverse logarithm printed for the sum on page 53 is a local typographical error. In dimension two, the three terms defining \(S_R\) are uniformly bounded by the stated growth estimates, so the subsequent \(R\to\infty\) step is consistent with that decay. These checks do not independently reprove the external energy perturbation and half-space Liouville results.
# Conclusion

The incorrect shear reduction and the invalid derivation of the full exponent range are both Major proof issues in the principal regularity chain. The geometric exponent range has a verified parameter and geometric repair using the manuscript’s preceding estimates, with a coarse-iteration entry step preserving the original flatness threshold. This does not establish exponent-uniform constants for the external boundary regularity estimate. The exterior sign and min–max algebra are local correctable defects. No counterexample to the main regularity or classification theorem, and no author adoption of these corrections, is established.

# Half-space harmonicity and exterior integral

At height one, the one-dimensional integral from \(t<0\) equals \(\int_{-\infty}^0(1-t)^{-2}\,dt=1\). For \(t>0\), the substitution \(t=q^2\) gives \[\mathop{\mathrm{PV}}\int_0^\infty\frac{1-\sqrt t}{(1-t)^2}\,dt
 =\mathop{\mathrm{PV}}\int_0^\infty\frac{2q}{(1-q)(1+q)^2}\,dq=-1,\] using \[\frac{2q}{(1-q)(1+q)^2}
 =\frac1{2(1-q)}+\frac1{2(1+q)}-\frac1{(1+q)^2}.\] An antiderivative is \(-\frac12\log|1-q|+\frac12\log(1+q)+(1+q)^{-1}\); the principal value singularities cancel. Scaling proves interior harmonicity at every positive height. For the exterior integral, \(t=az\) gives \[\int_0^\infty\frac{\sqrt t}{(a+t)^2}\,dt
 =a^{-1/2}\int_0^\infty\frac{\sqrt z}{(1+z)^2}\,dz
 =\frac{\pi}{2}a^{-1/2}.\] These are analytic calculations; no symbolic or numerical software execution is asserted.

report: Abstract: The finite-field reembedding criterion is examined together with its uses in the proof of unramified Grothendieck–Serre. Under the standard meaning of rational points, Definition 2.5 does not give a sufficient condition for Lemma 2.6. An explicit connected scheme over \(\mathbb F_2\) satisfies every stated finite-extension point-count inequality but cannot embed in the prescribed open affine line. The corrected finite-field criterion counts closed points of each exact residue degree. Two special applications in the manuscript satisfy this stronger condition; the external cover used in the main proof has not been independently checked here.
