Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Verification of
Unramified Grothendieck–Serre for Isotropic Groups
# Paper identity and scope

The reviewed source is Kęstutis Česnavičius and Roman Fedorov, Unramified Grothendieck–Serre for isotropic groups, arXiv:2311.08660v3, 21 November 2025 [CF]. The PDF carries an internal date of 24 November 2025. The acquired identity record associates it with Journal of the European Mathematical Society, DOI https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1725, and describes it as the final author manuscript with journal numbering updated. No publisher byte equivalence is asserted.

All 24 pages of the inherited text extraction were read, including the bibliography. This does not constitute verification of all proofs or cited works. The substantive checks concern the finite-field criterion, its concrete applications, and selected reductions in Theorem 3.5 and the concluding proofs. Actual images of pages 1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 11, 15, 16, 18, 19, and 20 were inspected. PDF and printed page numbers agree.
# Hypotheses and distinctions between the main claims

Theorem 1.2, restated as Theorem 4.3, assumes a Noetherian semilocal ring \(R\), flat and geometrically regular over a Dedekind ring \(\mathcal O\), and a reductive \(R\)-group \(G\) whose adjoint quotient is totally isotropic. It asserts \[\ker\bigl(H^1(R,G)\longrightarrow H^1(\mathop{\mathrm{Frac}}(R),G)\bigr)=\{*\}\] [CF, p. 2]. Section 1.3 defines total isotropy factorwise through the finite étale and Weil restriction decomposition of the adjoint group: the simple factors admit proper parabolic subgroups Zariski locally, containing no whole fiber [CF, p. 4]. No assertion for arbitrary ramified \(R\) or arbitrary anisotropic factors is substituted for this statement.

Theorem 3.5 has a different scope: a torsor under any reductive group over a semilocal \(A\) is sectionwise constant on \(\mathbb P_A^d\). The stronger affine-line triviality in Theorem 4.2 retains total isotropy, although it allows arbitrary \(A\). Proposition 5.1 lifts generically trivial torsors to the simply connected derived group under the unramified ring hypotheses. The issue below is confined to an auxiliary reembedding criterion used in these arguments.
# A finite-field counterexample to the printed criterion

Problem 1 (Rational-point inequalities do not ensure closed embeddings).  With \(k'\)-points understood as \(\operatorname{Hom}_k(\mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}k',-)\), the condition in Definition 2.5 is insufficient for the sufficiency direction of Lemma 2.6.
## Original claim

Definition 2.5 calls the finite-field obstruction absent if, over every finite residue field \(k\) of the base and every finite extension \(k'/k\), the number of \(k'\)-points of the source does not exceed that of the target. Lemma 2.6 states that a finite \(k\)-scheme \(Y\) embeds as a closed subscheme of a nonempty open \(V\subset\mathbb A_k^1\) if and only if this condition holds and \(Y\) is a closed subscheme of some smooth \(k\)-curve [CF, p. 8]. The first sentence of its proof on page 9 uses this condition to choose an embedding of the closed point of a connected \(Y\). The actual page images confirm this wording.
## Parameters and verification of all hypotheses

Set \[k=\mathbb F_2,\qquad P(t)=t^2+t+1,\qquad
 Y=\mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}\mathbb F_4,\qquad
 V=\mathop{\mathrm{Spec}}\mathbb F_2[t,1/P(t)].\] The polynomial \(P\) has no root in \(\mathbb F_2\), so it is irreducible of degree two. Thus \(Y\) is the closed subscheme of the smooth connected curve \(C=\mathbb A_{\mathbb F_2}^1\) cut out by \(P\). It is finite and connected. The target \(V=D(P)\) is a nonempty open of the affine line; both 0 and 1 belong to it. The field \(k\) is itself a semilocal base with its sole residue field equal to \(k\).
## Failure of the asserted embedding

Equation reference: eq:map. A closed embedding \(Y\hookrightarrow V\) would induce a surjective map \[
 \mathbb F_2[t,1/P(t)]\longrightarrow\mathbb F_4.\] Write \(a\) for the image of \(t\). If \(a\in\mathbb F_2\), the image of [eq:map] (#eq:map) lies in \(\mathbb F_2\), so the map is not surjective. If \(a\notin\mathbb F_2\), then \(P(a)=0\), contradicting the fact that \(P(t)\) is inverted in the source ring. These cases exhaust \(\mathbb F_4\). Thus no closed embedding exists. Equivalently, the unique degree-two closed point of \(\mathbb A_{\mathbb F_2}^1\) has been deleted from \(V\).
This is an admissible counterexample to the printed sufficiency criterion. It does not construct a nontrivial generically trivial torsor under the hypotheses of the principal theorem.
## Correct finite-field condition

Equation reference: eq:degrees. Let \(c_d(T)\) denote the number of closed points of \(T\) with residue degree exactly \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_q\). A necessary condition for a closed embedding is \[
 c_d(Y)\le c_d(V)\qquad(d\ge1).\] The rational-point counts satisfy \[\#T(\mathbb F_{q^m})=\sum_{d\mid m}d\,c_d(T).\] Inequalities between these sums do not imply inequalities between their individual terms. In the example, \(c_2(Y)=1\) and \(c_2(V)=0\); the degree-one points of \(V\) mask that shortage in [eq:Vcounts] (#eq:Vcounts).

For finite \(k\), condition [eq:degrees] (#eq:degrees), together with the assumed smooth-curve embedding of \(Y\), is also sufficient. Each local component of \(Y\) has the form \(k_d[u]/(u^e)\), because a finite field is perfect and the curve is smooth. Choose distinct target points of \(V\) of the corresponding degrees. Their length-\(e\) infinitesimal neighborhoods have the same local form, so the components embed. A prescribed embedding on a closed subscheme \(Y_0\) can be retained: keep its target points and extend each truncated coordinate isomorphism. The nonzero linear coefficient of a uniformizer change remains nonzero at every larger truncation order.

This verifies the finite-field correction, including the extension aspect in that case. It is not a new proof of the infinite-field inseparable argument or of every subsequent application. If the intended meaning of \(k'\)-points was closed points having residue field \(k'\), the intended condition is [eq:degrees] (#eq:degrees); that interpretation requires an explicit change from the usual rational-point meaning analyzed above.
# Dependency, surviving applications, and limits

The criterion is a substantive reembedding input. The proof of Theorem 4.3 first invokes a finite étale cover from the externally cited Lemma 6.1 of the paper’s reference [Čes22a], states the absence of a finite-field obstruction, and then applies Lemmas 2.6 and 2.7 to pass to an affine-line excision square [CF, p. 18]. The general criterion used in that inference is false as written. The affected reembedding justification is closely tied to the core proof, so the issue is assessed as Major under the claim-level severity convention.

This assessment has two qualifications. First, the external cover on page 18 has not been independently inspected here. It may satisfy the stronger exact-degree condition. The present finding does not assert that it fails, and does not refute Theorem 4.3. Second, two concrete uses in the manuscript already satisfy the stronger condition.

In Proposition 2.8 the fibers have been reduced to support on one rational point, and an additional disjoint rational point is introduced [CF, p. 11]. The affine line has at least two rational points over every field, including \(\mathbb F_2\). The required degree-one slots therefore exist, and no higher-degree slots are needed. This special application survives.

In the proof of Theorem 3.5, the construction \(Y=Y_N\sqcup Y_{N+1}\) on page 16 also meets [eq:degrees] (#eq:degrees) for sufficiently large \(N\). Over a finite residue field \(\mathbb F_q\), write the finitely many components of \(Y_0\) as residue fields of degrees \(d_i\). The constructed covers have degrees \(d_iN\) and \(d_i(N+1)\), and a bounded number of components. If \(I_q(m)\) is the number of degree-\(m\) closed points of \(\mathbb G_m\), then for \(m>1\) \[mI_q(m)\ge q^m-\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}q^j,\] since every element of \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) of degree less than \(m\) lies in a proper subfield of degree at most \(m/2\). Hence \(I_q(m)\to\infty\). The available exact-degree points eventually exceed the fixed component count. Semilocality gives only finitely many residue fields, so a single large \(N\) works for all of them. This verifies the relevant correction for the page-16 finite-field construction.

What remains for a complete correction of the affected main proof is to state [eq:degrees] (#eq:degrees) and verify it for the particular cover and shrinking used on page 18. No author correction or adoption is established by the material consulted.
# Other reductions checked

The projective-line reduction in Theorem 3.5 respects the semilocal hypothesis [CF, p. 15]. Given two sections, choose in each closed fiber a third point different from both. Even \(\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_2)\) has three points. Chinese remainders lift the finitely many choices to a unimodular vector over \(A\), hence an \(A\)-section. Two disjoint sections span a rank-two direct summand: their rank-two minors generate the unit ideal. Their span therefore gives a projective line. This checks the geometric reduction, without certifying the subsequent loop-group surjectivity theorem.

The split-torus boundary case is consistent with the same hypothesis: \(\mathop{\mathrm{Pic}}(A)=0\) for semilocal \(A\), so every pullback of \(\mathcal O(1)\) by an \(A\)-section is trivial. The map \([x:y]\mapsto[x^d:y^d]\) fixes zero and infinity and pulls \(\mathcal O(1)\) back to \(\mathcal O(d)\). It therefore preserves the endpoint comparison in the reduction, even when \(d\) is not invertible.

At the end of the main proof, an open \(C\subset\mathbb A_R^1\) containing an \(R\)-section has finite complement in \(\mathbb P_R^1\) [CF, p. 19]. Each fiber of \(C\) is nonempty, so its closed complement in the corresponding projective line is zero-dimensional. The complement is proper and quasi-finite over \(R\), hence finite. This validates that premise, conditional on the earlier successful reembedding.

In Proposition 5.1, the restriction \(H^1(V,Z)\to H^1(R,Z)\) at infinity is surjective: pullback from \(R\) is a right inverse because \(V\) contains the infinity section [CF, p. 20]. The argument from generic vanishing to the clopen neutral-gerbe locus is consistent after decomposition into domains. The cited purity and gerbe equivalence results themselves were not independently proved here.
# Conclusion

One substantive issue is established: the stated rational-point-count condition does not imply the finite-field reembedding assertion. The finite-field replacement using exact residue degrees is verified locally, and two special applications are checked to satisfy it. The property of the external cover in the main proof remains outside the verified scope. No counterexample to the principal Grothendieck–Serre theorem, sectionwise constancy, or simply connected reduction is asserted.

Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical verification of
Serrin’s overdetermined problem in rough domains
# Identity and inspected scope

The paper is by Alessio Figalli and Yi Ru-Ya Zhang, with journal identifier 10.4171/jems/1726 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1726). The primary text inspected is arXiv:2407.02293v2, whose watermark gives 29 March 2025 and whose internal date is 1 April 2025 [primary]. Its 18 PDF pages are the page convention used below. The separately retained author manuscript dated 9 March 2026 [revision] and the author’s preserved erratum page [erratum] were compared at the affected passages. They are distinct sources; equivalence with the publisher edition is not asserted.

All primary-source pages were read. Detailed checks concern Theorem 1.3, Lemma 2.2, the boundary limit on page 8, the final \(P\)-function argument on page 12, and the slit-domain hypotheses and cancellations on pages 13–16. The regularity and harmonic-measure results used in Lemmas 2.1 and 3.2 were traced as dependencies, not independently re-proved. Bibliographic references were read as references; their full texts were not independently reviewed. These limits do not constitute defects.
# Definitions and hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:density, eq:source. Theorem 1.3 assumes a bounded indecomposable set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) of finite perimeter with \[
 \mathcal H^{n-1}(B_r(x)\cap\partial^*\Omega)\leq A r^{n-1}
 \quad\text{for $\mathcal H^{n-1}$-a.e. $x\in\partial^*\Omega$, $0<r<1$,}\] and a function \(u\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^n)\) satisfying, distributionally, \[
 u=0\text{ a.e. outside }\Omega,\qquad
 \Delta u=c\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}\partial^*\Omega-\mathbf1_\Omega\,dx .\] Here \(c>0\), and \(\nu_x\) is the inward measure-theoretic normal. The conclusion is that \(\Omega\) is a ball, up to translation, with the corresponding quadratic torsion function.

The slit extension also includes a rectifiable set \(\Sigma\), an additional measure \(2c\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}\Sigma\), and the specified two-sided blow-up \[r^{-1}u(x+rz)\longrightarrow c\,|\nu_x\cdot z|
 \quad\text{for $\mathcal H^{n-1}$-a.e. $x\in\Sigma$.}\] This equal-slope condition is stronger than a statement about the total measure density \(2c\). It is needed for the slit contribution to the centered boundary limit to vanish; it must not be omitted when interpreting Theorem 4.1.
# A surface-measure scaling error

Problem 1 (The finite-difference Laplacian in Lemma 2.2).  The displayed formula immediately before (2.6), on page 7 of [primary], assigns coefficients \((1+\epsilon)^2c\) and \((1-\epsilon)^2c\) to the Hausdorff measures on the dilated reduced boundaries. For the stated distributional equation, the coefficients are instead \((1+\epsilon)c\) and \((1-\epsilon)c\). The same issue occurs in the slit calculation on page 14.
## Original calculation

Equation reference: eq:phi. The proof uses \[
 \phi_\epsilon(x)=
 \frac{u((1+\epsilon)x)-u((1-\epsilon)x)}{2\epsilon}-2u(x).\] Writing \(a=1+\epsilon\) and \(b=1-\epsilon\), the printed singular part of \(\Delta\phi_\epsilon\) is \[\frac{c}{2\epsilon}
 \bigl(a^2\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}a^{-1}\partial^*\Omega
       -b^2\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}b^{-1}\partial^*\Omega\bigr)
 -2c\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}\partial^*\Omega .\] The remaining term is explicitly absolutely continuous, of the form \(O(\epsilon^{-1})\,dx\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}N_\epsilon\). The actual page image confirms the squares; the issue is not an extraction error.
## Distributional calculation and admissible example

Equation reference: eq:correctscale. For \(v_a(x)=u(ax)\), \(a>0\), and a smooth compactly supported test function \(\eta\), \[\langle\Delta v_a,\eta\rangle
 =a^{2-n}\langle\Delta u,\eta(\,\cdot\,/a)\rangle.\] Applying this to [eq:source] (#eq:source), and changing variables in the surface integral, gives \[
 \Delta[u(a\,\cdot)]
 =ac\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}a^{-1}\partial^*\Omega
   -a^2\mathbf1_{a^{-1}\Omega}\,dx.\] Indeed, the factor \(a^{2-n}\) is multiplied by the surface Jacobian \(a^{n-1}\). The volume and surface terms therefore scale differently.

For a complete test under the original hypotheses, take \[n=2,\quad \Omega=B_1(0),\quad
 c=\frac12,\quad u(x)=\frac{(1-|x|^2)_+}{4}.\] The disk is bounded and indecomposable, has finite perimeter, and satisfies [eq:density] (#eq:density), for example with \(A=2\pi\). The compactly supported Lipschitz function \(u\) is in \(W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^2)\), vanishes outside \(\Omega\), and satisfies \[\Delta u=\tfrac12\mathcal H^1\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}S^1-\mathbf1_{B_1}\,dx.\] Thus all hypotheses relevant to Lemma 2.2 are met.

Equation reference: eq:numbers. Set \(\epsilon=1/10\), so \(a=11/10\). At the circle \(r=10/11\), only \(u(ar)\) in [eq:phi] (#eq:phi) has a derivative jump. Its interior radial derivative is \(-a/2\), and its exterior derivative is zero. Consequently the actual singular coefficient of \(\Delta\phi_\epsilon\) there is \[
 \frac{ca}{2\epsilon}=\frac{11}{4},
 \qquad\text{whereas the printed coefficient is}\qquad
 \frac{ca^2}{2\epsilon}=\frac{121}{40}.\] Their difference is \(11/40\). An absolutely continuous remainder cannot absorb a nonzero measure supported on this circle. An independently written exact-rational calculation, retained in the verification evidence, confirms [eq:numbers] (#eq:numbers); the distributional argument itself is exact.
## What the correction restores

Equation reference: eq:quotient. Changing variables after [eq:correctscale] (#eq:correctscale) replaces the exponent \(3-n\) in (2.6)–(2.7) by \(2-n\). This does not change the relevant limit. To see this explicitly, define \[Q_s(x)=
 \frac{a^s u(x/a)-b^s u(x/b)}{2\epsilon}.\] Then \[
 Q_{3-n}(x)-Q_{2-n}(x)
 =\frac{a^{2-n}u(x/a)+b^{2-n}u(x/b)}2.\] On \(\partial^*\Omega\), the boundary representative has \(u(x)=0\). The Lipschitz regularity obtained in the paper and boundedness of \(\Omega\) imply that the right side of [eq:quotient] (#eq:quotient) is uniformly \(O(\epsilon)\). Its integral tends to zero because the perimeter is finite. The same calculation applies to the slit term with its prescribed vanishing representative and finite surface measure.

Thus the printed finite-\(\epsilon\) distributional identity is false, while the corrected identity has the same limiting boundary contribution. The volume identity \[(n+2)\int_\Omega u\,dx=c^2n|\Omega|\] and the ensuing rigidity argument are not refuted by this example. This is an invalid derivation in the new proof of a central lemma, so its assessment is Major at the derivation level. That assessment does not assert that the main theorem is false. The correction and the vanishing of its limiting effect have been checked.

The author revision retains the squared coefficients in the slit calculation on its page 14 and the exponent \(3-n\) on its page 8. The retained erratum does not list this surface-scaling correction. Author adoption of this correction is therefore unknown; no claim of first discovery is made.
# Documented sign correction and surviving reasoning

The author erratum [erratum] separately corrects the sign of the boundary limit for \(\psi_\epsilon\), the corresponding integrated sign, the analogous slit calculation, the boundary-integral label, and a lemma reference. Its own page locators refer to a different layout. The corresponding primary-source passages are on pages 8, 14 and 16.

This sign can be checked directly. At a reduced-boundary point, put \(t=\nu_x\cdot x\). The half-space blow-up gives \[\phi_\epsilon(x)\longrightarrow \frac{ct}{2},
 \qquad
 Q_{2-n}(x)\longrightarrow-\frac{ct}{2}.\] Hence \(\psi_\epsilon=\phi_\epsilon-Q_{2-n}\) tends to \(ct\), rather than \(-ct\). With the inward normal, \[\int_{\partial^*\Omega}\nu_x\cdot x\,d\mathcal H^{n-1}=-n|\Omega|,\] and the corrected sign yields the positive volume identity above. Actual views of the separate 2026 manuscript confirm the sign and boundary-label corrections on pages 8 and 14 and the corrected Lemma 4.4 reference on page 16. These are known-issue reproductions, not new allegations against the revised text.

The final rigidity calculation also gives useful counterevidence against overstating the scaling defect. Conditional on the gradient bound and volume identity, let \(P=|\nabla u|^2+2u/n\). Since \(\Delta u=-1\) in the interior, \[\Delta P
 =2|D^2u|^2+\frac2n\Delta u
 =2|D^2u+I/n|^2.\] The intermediate sign printed before \((2/n)\Delta u\) on page 12 needs an algebraic correction, but the displayed final square has the correct value. The integral equality and \(P\leq c^2\) force \(P=c^2\); the Hessian is \(-I/n\), and indecomposability supplies the single-ball conclusion. The slit estimate likewise uses \(|a_+-a_-|\leq a_++a_-\) for the two Green-function slopes. These checks do not independently establish the regularity and harmonic-measure inputs on which that argument depends.
# Conclusion

The verified substantive concern is the surface-measure scaling in a central finite-difference proof. Its repair preserves the limiting identity. The historical sign errors have documented author corrections, separately checked in the retained revision.

problems.title: Surface-measure coefficient in the finite-difference Laplacian
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: Problem 1 (The finite-difference Laplacian in Lemma 2.2).
claim:
Equation reference: eq:density, eq:source. Theorem 1.3 assumes a bounded indecomposable set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) of finite perimeter with \[
 \mathcal H^{n-1}(B_r(x)\cap\partial^*\Omega)\leq A r^{n-1}
 \quad\text{for $\mathcal H^{n-1}$-a.e. $x\in\partial^*\Omega$, $0<r<1$,}\] and a function \(u\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^n)\) satisfying, distributionally, \[
 u=0\text{ a.e. outside }\Omega,\qquad
 \Delta u=c\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}\partial^*\Omega-\mathbf1_\Omega\,dx .\] Here \(c>0\), and \(\nu_x\) is the inward measure-theoretic normal. The conclusion is that \(\Omega\) is a ball, up to translation, with the corresponding quadratic torsion function.

The slit extension also includes a rectifiable set \(\Sigma\), an additional measure \(2c\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}\Sigma\), and the specified two-sided blow-up \[r^{-1}u(x+rz)\longrightarrow c\,|\nu_x\cdot z|
 \quad\text{for $\mathcal H^{n-1}$-a.e. $x\in\Sigma$.}\] This equal-slope condition is stronger than a statement about the total measure density \(2c\). It is needed for the slit contribution to the centered boundary limit to vanish; it must not be omitted when interpreting Theorem 4.1.
Representation: paraphrase
Location: Primary PDF p7, unnumbered Delta phi_epsilon formula before(2.6); exponent3-n in(2.6)-(2.7),pp7-8; slit analoguep14
Text: For u(ax), the singular coefficient on a^-1 reduced boundary is printed a^2 c.

Bounded finite-perimeter domain with upper surface-density bound(1.4). u in W1,2(Rn),zero outside,Delta u=c H^(n-1)|boundary-1_Omega dx. Counterexample uses n2,unitdisk,c1/2,u=(1-r²)_+/4,epsilon1/10; all stated assumptions met.
analysis: The displayed formula immediately before (2.6), on page 7 of [primary], assigns coefficients \((1+\epsilon)^2c\) and \((1-\epsilon)^2c\) to the Hausdorff measures on the dilated reduced boundaries. For the stated distributional equation, the coefficients are instead \((1+\epsilon)c\) and \((1-\epsilon)c\). The same issue occurs in the slit calculation on page 14.

Equation reference: eq:phi. The proof uses \[
 \phi_\epsilon(x)=
 \frac{u((1+\epsilon)x)-u((1-\epsilon)x)}{2\epsilon}-2u(x).\] Writing \(a=1+\epsilon\) and \(b=1-\epsilon\), the printed singular part of \(\Delta\phi_\epsilon\) is \[\frac{c}{2\epsilon}
 \bigl(a^2\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}a^{-1}\partial^*\Omega
       -b^2\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}b^{-1}\partial^*\Omega\bigr)
 -2c\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}\partial^*\Omega .\] The remaining term is explicitly absolutely continuous, of the form \(O(\epsilon^{-1})\,dx\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}N_\epsilon\). The actual page image confirms the squares; the issue is not an extraction error.

Equation reference: eq:correctscale. For \(v_a(x)=u(ax)\), \(a>0\), and a smooth compactly supported test function \(\eta\), \[\langle\Delta v_a,\eta\rangle
 =a^{2-n}\langle\Delta u,\eta(\,\cdot\,/a)\rangle.\] Applying this to [eq:source] (#eq:source), and changing variables in the surface integral, gives \[
 \Delta[u(a\,\cdot)]
 =ac\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}a^{-1}\partial^*\Omega
   -a^2\mathbf1_{a^{-1}\Omega}\,dx.\] Indeed, the factor \(a^{2-n}\) is multiplied by the surface Jacobian \(a^{n-1}\). The volume and surface terms therefore scale differently.

For a complete test under the original hypotheses, take \[n=2,\quad \Omega=B_1(0),\quad
 c=\frac12,\quad u(x)=\frac{(1-|x|^2)_+}{4}.\] The disk is bounded and indecomposable, has finite perimeter, and satisfies [eq:density] (#eq:density), for example with \(A=2\pi\). The compactly supported Lipschitz function \(u\) is in \(W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^2)\), vanishes outside \(\Omega\), and satisfies \[\Delta u=\tfrac12\mathcal H^1\!\mathbin{\rule{0.4pt}{1.1ex}\rule{0.7ex}{0.4pt}}S^1-\mathbf1_{B_1}\,dx.\] Thus all hypotheses relevant to Lemma 2.2 are met.

Equation reference: eq:numbers. Set \(\epsilon=1/10\), so \(a=11/10\). At the circle \(r=10/11\), only \(u(ar)\) in [eq:phi] (#eq:phi) has a derivative jump. Its interior radial derivative is \(-a/2\), and its exterior derivative is zero. Consequently the actual singular coefficient of \(\Delta\phi_\epsilon\) there is \[
 \frac{ca}{2\epsilon}=\frac{11}{4},
 \qquad\text{whereas the printed coefficient is}\qquad
 \frac{ca^2}{2\epsilon}=\frac{121}{40}.\] Their difference is \(11/40\). An absolutely continuous remainder cannot absorb a nonzero measure supported on this circle. An independently written exact-rational calculation, retained in the verification evidence, confirms [eq:numbers] (#eq:numbers); the distributional argument itself is exact.

Equation reference: eq:quotient. Changing variables after [eq:correctscale] (#eq:correctscale) replaces the exponent \(3-n\) in (2.6)–(2.7) by \(2-n\). This does not change the relevant limit. To see this explicitly, define \[Q_s(x)=
 \frac{a^s u(x/a)-b^s u(x/b)}{2\epsilon}.\] Then \[
 Q_{3-n}(x)-Q_{2-n}(x)
 =\frac{a^{2-n}u(x/a)+b^{2-n}u(x/b)}2.\] On \(\partial^*\Omega\), the boundary representative has \(u(x)=0\). The Lipschitz regularity obtained in the paper and boundedness of \(\Omega\) imply that the right side of [eq:quotient] (#eq:quotient) is uniformly \(O(\epsilon)\). Its integral tends to zero because the perimeter is finite. The same calculation applies to the slit term with its prescribed vanishing representative and finite surface measure.

Thus the printed finite-\(\epsilon\) distributional identity is false, while the corrected identity has the same limiting boundary contribution. The volume identity \[(n+2)\int_\Omega u\,dx=c^2n|\Omega|\] and the ensuing rigidity argument are not refuted by this example. This is an invalid derivation in the new proof of a central lemma, so its assessment is Major at the derivation level. That assessment does not assert that the main theorem is false. The correction and the vanishing of its limiting effect have been checked.

The author revision retains the squared coefficients in the slit calculation on its page 14 and the exponent \(3-n\) on its page 8. The retained erratum does not list this surface-scaling correction. Author adoption of this correction is therefore unknown; no claim of first discovery is made.
result: Result: False finite-epsilon distributional identity; discrepancy11/40 cannot be absorbed by an absolutely continuous remainder.
Impact: Invalid derivation closely tied to the new proof of central volume identity Lemma2.2; Major at derivation level. Explicit repaired limiting calculation survives.

report: Abstract: The change of measure stated in Theorem 1.12 has an incorrect constant: for one particle it gives a deterministic density below one, although the two chains have identical unit jump rates. The proof supplies the corrected constant. The unrestricted parameter range of the stronger asymptotic statement, Theorem 4.1, also fails: the finite-n sine prefactor cannot be replaced uniformly when p = k/n is unbounded. This does not refute the fixed-p limit of Theorem 1.4. A further factor one half is missing from an intermediate mixed determinantal identity; it cancels in the normalized correlation ratio. Exact algebra and finite diagnostics support the stated boundaries of these findings. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical verification of
Continuous Kasteleyn theory for the bead model
# Identity, definitions and scope

The inspected source is Samuel G. G. Johnston, Continuous Kasteleyn theory for the bead model, arXiv:2207.13538v6, 18 September 2025, 49 PDF pages [source]. The journal identifier is 10.4171/jems/1728 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1728). All locations below refer to the retained preprint. Byte or textual equivalence with the journal edition is not assumed.

Equation reference: eq:delta. A bead configuration on \(\mathbb T_n=[0,1)\times\mathbb Z_n\) has \(k\) beads on each string, neighboring strings interlace, and its occupation number is \(\ell\). The volume \(\operatorname{Vol}^{(n)}_{k,\ell}\) measures the corresponding ordered configurations. The empty case has separately defined weights \(\operatorname{Vol}^{(n)}_{0,\ell}=\binom n\ell\). The infinite-horizontal process has \(1\leq\ell\leq n-1\) particles, state \(E\subset\mathbb Z_n\), and \[
 \Delta(E)=\prod_{1\leq j<r\leq\ell}
 \left|e^{2\pi i h_r/n}-e^{2\pi i h_j/n}\right|,
 \qquad E=\{h_1,\ldots,h_\ell\}.\] An allowed jump replaces \(h\in E\) by \(h+1\notin E\), with addition modulo \(n\).

All 49 source pages were read. Detailed checks address the determinant parity and coefficient extraction in Sections 3–4, the scope of Theorem 4.1, the mixed normalization in Section 5, and the generators and change of measure in Section 6. The free-probability discussion in Section 2 and its external references were not independently re-proved. Process tightness, Gibbs uniqueness and the complete analytic justification of all Fredholm operations were not independently certified. No absence of author code is treated as a defect.
# The probability density in Theorem 1.12
## A complete admissible counterexample

Take any \(n\geq2\), \(\ell=1\), and the same fixed initial state for both chains. This is permitted by Definition 1.9. Every state is a singleton, so the empty product in [eq:delta] (#eq:delta) is \(1\), and \(\operatorname{Traffic}(E)=\#\{h\in E:h+1\in E\}=0\). Theorem 1.11, page 8, gives the rate \(\Delta(E')/\Delta(E)=1\). The TASEP rate is explicitly \(1\) in (1.24), page 9, and in the generator (6.22), page 45. Both chains therefore have generator \[Gf(h)=f(h+1)-f(h)\] and identical laws. Their Radon–Nikodym derivative is identically \(1\).

In contrast, \(\mu_{n,1}=1\), so the right side of [eq:printedRN] (#eq:printedRN) is the deterministic quantity \[\exp\{-(1-1/n)t\}<1\qquad(t>0).\] It has total mass below one and cannot be the claimed probability density or unit-mean martingale. For \(n=2\) it is \(e^{-t/2}\); at \(t=1\) the retained calculation gives approximately \(0.60653066\). The contradiction is exact and does not depend on that numerical approximation. Starting both chains from their common uniform one-particle distribution gives the same contradiction.
## Correction and counterevidence

The factor \(1/n\) does occur legitimately in the per-string bead density in Theorem 1.10, page 8. It does not occur in either global generator. Actual source images confirm the distinction, so neither an extraction error nor a justified common time rescaling removes the counterexample.

This is Major: a stated principal theorem gives an invalid probability-density normalization. The proof supports a short, fully checked correction. The other determinant formulas and the construction of the process are not refuted by this example. Author adoption of the correction is unknown.
# The unrestricted range in Theorem 4.1
## An admissible family and the exact dominant contribution

For \(\ell=n/2\), the \(n\) consecutive blocks of roots maximize the modulus of the inner sum, with value \(M_n\). This can also be seen by projecting any root sum onto its own direction: the \(\ell\) largest projections select consecutive roots. Equality at the maximum gives a consecutive block. Formula (4.14), page 23, shows that the \(N\)-th powers of all these blocks have the same sign, which is canceled by the prefactor in [eq:volume] (#eq:volume). Every other block has strictly smaller modulus.

Equation reference: eq:dominance. Thus, for each such \(n\), there are \(0\leq\rho_n<1\) and finite \[B_n=\frac{\binom n{n/2}-n}{n}\] such that the exact formula implies \[
 \operatorname{Vol}^{(n)}_{k,n/2}
 =\frac{nM_n^N}{N!}(1+\varepsilon_{n,k}),
 \qquad
 |\varepsilon_{n,k}|\leq B_n\rho_n^N.\] This bound controls possible complex cancellations in the nonmaximal terms; it does not assume that each term is positive.
## Contradiction with the claimed uniform estimate

Equation reference: eq:ratio. Write the Stirling remainder as \[N!=\sqrt{2\pi N}(N/e)^N e^{r_N},
 \qquad 0<r_N<\frac1{12N}.\] Using [eq:dominance] (#eq:dominance), the ratio of the left side of [eq:uniform] (#eq:uniform) to \(e^{p\pi^2/6}/\sqrt{2\pi p}\) is \[
 (1+\varepsilon_{n,k})\exp\{pA_n-r_N\},
 \qquad
 A_n=n^2\log\frac{\pi/n}{\sin(\pi/n)}-\frac{\pi^2}{6}.\] For \(n\geq16\), the convergent expansion of \(-\log(\sin x/x)\) gives \[A_n=\frac{\pi^4}{180n^2}+O(n^{-4})>0.\] For every even \(n\), choose an integer \(k=k_n\) sufficiently large that \[B_n\rho_n^{nk_n}\leq\frac1n,\qquad
 \frac{k_n}{n}A_n\geq n,\qquad k_n\geq n^3.\] Such integers exist, and the resulting family satisfies every printed parameter condition. By [eq:ratio] (#eq:ratio), its actual ratio tends to infinity.

However, at \(\tau=1/2\) the bracket asserted on the right of [eq:uniform] (#eq:uniform) is \[\mathcal P(e^{-2\pi^2p})^2
 +O(e^{-cp\log n/2})\longrightarrow1.\] This contradicts the unrestricted estimate for every universal \(c>0\). The counterexample concerns the parameter range of the theorem, not a floating-point instability. Retained high-precision calculations of the sine prefactor are corroborating diagnostics only.
## Scope of the failure

The last step of the proof, page 29, uses \[\left(\frac{\sin(\pi/n)}{\pi/n}\right)^{pn^2}
 =(1+o(1))e^{-p\pi^2/6}.\] Its logarithmic error begins at order \(p/n^2\), so this replacement is not uniform over all lower-bounded \(p\). Retaining the exact finite-\(n\) sine and factorial prefactor avoids this particular loss; it does not by itself prove a corrected uniform bound for the remaining terms.

In contrast, Theorem 1.4, page 5, fixes \(p>0\) and \(\tau\in(0,1)\) before sending \(n\) to infinity. The present obstruction then vanishes. Neither that fixed-parameter conclusion nor its free-energy corollary is disproved by this argument, and this report does not certify their other analytic steps. The stronger uniform guarantee in Theorem 4.1 is Major within the advertised fine-volume asymptotics. A complete repaired parameter range and remainder have not been verified.
# A local factor in the mixed determinant

Problem 3 (Theorem 5.2 omits \(1/2\)).  The mixed determinant formula in Theorem 5.2, page 31, and Lemma 5.4, page 34, omit the factor \(1/2\) present in the defining density (5.11), page 30, and in the unmixed formula (3.12), page 17.

Take \(n=2\), \(\theta=(1,1)\), \(\lambda=\log2\), and one occupied observation \(w=(o,t,0)\), with no beads. Thus \(N=1\), \(k=0\), \(\ell_o=1\), \(\ell_u=0\). A single time satisfies the distinct-times condition, and all kernel denominators are nonzero. Let \(\beta=\lambda+\pi i\); since \([0]_o=1\), (5.13) gives \[C^{\beta,1}(w,w)
 =-\frac{e^{-\beta}}{1-e^{-\beta}}
 =\frac13.\] The left side printed in Theorem 5.2 equals \[(1+\tfrac12)^2\cdot\tfrac13=\frac34,\] while the density in (5.11) equals \[g_1^{\lambda,\theta}(w)
 =\frac12\cdot\frac12(1+\tfrac12)=\frac38.\] This is a nonempty determinant, so the mismatch cannot be explained by a convention for \(0\times0\) determinants. Exact rational arithmetic confirms the discrepancy.

The left sides of Theorem 5.2 and Lemma 5.4 need the prefactor \(1/2\); the associated prefactors in (5.29)–(5.30), page 38, require the same correction. The constant then cancels between numerator and denominator in the normalized ratio (5.31). Consequently this check does not show that Theorem 1.7’s normalized correlation kernel is false. Its bounded assessment is Minor: a local intermediate normalization error with the cancellation explicitly verified.
# Supporting checks and overall impact

The elementary interlacing determinant in Lemma 3.3 was checked by row operations, including the cyclic alternative. Independent exact arithmetic also checked 580 small cases with weak coincidences and \(\zeta\in\{0,1,2/3,2\}\). The three-versus-one sign identity and (3.23) agree algebraically; 840 finite parity cases and seven empty-configuration partition identities passed.

For \(k=1\), every strict ordering of the \(n\) bead times gives a simplex of volume \(1/n!\). Counting its cyclic descents independently determines \(\ell\). For \(n=2,\ldots,7\), these exact counts agree with numerical evaluations of [eq:volume] (#eq:volume) for every \(\ell\), including the zero-volume endpoints, to absolute error below \(6\cdot10^{-16}\). For \(n=2,\ldots,8\), all 494 nontrivial occupancy states give [eq:totalrate] (#eq:totalrate) within \(1.8\cdot10^{-15}\); the stationary weights \(\Delta(E)^2/n^\ell\) sum to one within \(9\cdot10^{-16}\). These finite diagnostics corroborate the specific calculations. They do not prove a universal theorem.

The first finding concerns a false normalization in a principal probability theorem, with a correction supplied by its own proof. The second concerns the stronger asymptotic range, while preserving the distinction from a fixed-\(p\) limit. The third is local and cancels in the normalized kernel formula. The highest supported assessment is Major; it is not a claim that every result of the paper fails.
# Conclusion
Dimension | Recorded state
Theorem 1.12 | Major; remove the factor \(1/n\) from the constant
Theorem 4.1 | Major; unrestricted \(p\)-range disproved
Theorem 5.2 | Minor; restore the canceled factor \(1/2\)
Repair verification | Generator correction and determinant factor checked; no complete uniform asymptotic repair
Author adoption | Unknown for these corrections
Scientific adjudication | Pending; no human review or independent acceptance
# Supporting checks

The script was independently written and run once with the existing Python runtime; no author code was executed. It uses exact fractions for the elementary determinant and factor checks, ordinary floating arithmetic for finite root sums and generators, and 90-digit decimal arithmetic for the sine-prefactor diagnostic. The analytic counterexamples do not rely on numerical tolerances.

Actual inspected source images are PDF pages 5, 8, 9, 17, 19, 22, 23, 29, 30, 31, 34, 38, 45 and 46. Full text reading has the broader 49-page extent, while proof checking has the narrower scope stated in Section 1. External reference texts, a publisher-version reconciliation, and complete independent verification of the process-limit arguments are outside that scope.
No separate human review, independent acceptance, or fictional historical execution is claimed.

# Paper identity and review scope

The paper is Classification results, rigidity theorems and semilinear PDEs on Riemannian manifolds: A P-function approach, by Giulio Ciraolo, Alberto Farina and Camilla Chiara Polvara, associated with the Journal of the European Mathematical Society, DOI 10.4171/jems/1729 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1729) [CFP]. The full source text was read. Detailed checks concern the transformation and P-function identities, the curvature absorption and cutoff argument in Theorem 1.5, and the parameter ranges and decisive reductions in Theorems 1.1–1.4. # Substantive finding

Problem 1 (The curvature coefficient in the proof of Theorem 1.5).  The parameter choice in source (3.12) does not imply the nonnegative coefficient asserted immediately before (3.13). The subsequent nonexistence proof therefore does not establish Theorem 1.5 with its stated non-strict curvature threshold.
## Original claim and precise assumptions
## Coefficient calculation

Equation reference: eq:factor. The prescribed values in (3.12) are \[t=n-2,\qquad
 \varepsilon=n-2-\frac12-\frac{n-d}{4},\qquad
 \delta=\frac{n-d}{4}.\] Substitution gives \[

   =\frac{n-d}{6(n-2)^2}S^2=\frac K2,\] whereas the unnumbered equality before (3.13) prints \(K\). Consequently [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed) does not imply \(c_1\ge0\). The actual displayed source images of pp. 12–14 confirm both the coefficients and the parameter choice; this is not an extraction ambiguity.

An exact local diagnostic is \(d=3\), \(n=4\), \(p=3\), \(p_S=5\), \(S=1\) and \(\rho=1/16\). These parameters satisfy the displayed algebraic domains and \(\rho\le K=1/12\). Nevertheless, \(\varepsilon=5/4\), \(\delta=1/4\), \(c_1=-1/24\) and \(c_2=1/8\). The independent rational-arithmetic calculation retained with this report reproduces these values. This diagnostic refutes the coefficient implication. It does not construct a manifold or a solution satisfying the theorem’s geometric hypotheses, and is not a PDE counterexample.
## Counterevidence and supported repairs

The original choice does give \(c_1\ge0\) and \(c_2=(n-d)/(2n)>0\) if [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed) is strengthened to \(\rho\le K/2\), equivalently if \(1/48\) is replaced by \(1/96\). The subsequent cutoff argument then closes under the original volume assumption.

A less restrictive repair is to replace \(\rho\le K\) by \(\rho<K\). Keep \(t=n-2\) and choose \[\delta=\frac{n-d}{4}+\frac{3t^2\rho}{4S^2},
 \qquad \varepsilon=t-\frac12-\delta.\] For \(0\le\rho<K\), this gives \(0<\delta<(n-d)/2\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), since \(t-\tfrac12-(n-d)/2=(n+d-5)/2>0\). Equations [eq:c1] (#eq:c1)–[eq:c2] (#eq:c2) become \[c_1=K-\rho>0,\qquad
 c_2=\frac{3t^2}{2nS^2}(K-\rho)>0.\] Thus the strict version has a verified repair using the same remaining argument, detailed in Appendix 6 (#app:cutoff).

Theorem 4.5 (p. 16) is not a general replacement: it requires \(V_g(B_R)=o(R^{2p/(p-1)})\). For \(d=3\), \(p=3\), this is \(o(R^3)\), whereas Theorem 1.5 allows \(O(R^6)\). The hypotheses therefore do not supply that alternative proof. The evident negative signs in the growth exponents in parts of the prose on p. 14 do not repair [eq:factor] (#eq:factor); the intended positive growth is explicit in (3.6).
## Impact

The finding is assessed as Major: it is a demonstrated invalid derivation in the proof of the advertised small-negative-curvature nonexistence result. This assessment is confined to that derivation. It does not disprove Theorem 1.5, does not invalidate the P-function identities, and does not transfer to the nonnegative-curvature classification results. No author correction or adoption of the repairs above has been verified.
# Other checked reductions and limits

For Theorem 1.1, the statement requires \(\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}\ge0\) and either \(d=3,4,5\), or \(d\ge6\) with the specified decay, or \(d\ge6\) with \(u\in L^{2d/(d-2)}\). The dimension-dependent estimates were checked within this scope (pp. 17–22). In dimension four the displayed \(t=7/10\) and \(\gamma=9/5\) give the admissible moment exponents \(14/5\) and \(37/15\). In dimension five, for example, \(\delta=1/100\), \(t=51/100\), \(s=100/53\), \(\gamma=5/4\) satisfy the relevant parameter inequalities; both final powers of \(R\) are \(-51/100\). For the higher-dimensional decay case, the limiting exponent is \[E_0=-\frac{2\alpha(d-4)}{d-2}+\frac{d-6}{2}.\] The strict threshold in (1.7) is exactly \(E_0<0\), and permits a small positive auxiliary parameter in (5.29). At \(\alpha=(d-2)/2\), the big-\(O\) bound alone need not imply critical integrability, as stated locally on p. 21; the proof can instead use a smaller decay exponent still above (1.7). No failure of the stated classification follows from that local inference.

The finite-energy reduction in (5.17)–(5.23), and the implication from constant \(P\) to \(\nabla^2v=(P/d)g\), were checked. The latter uses the rigidity result reproduced as Theorem A.1. Its original external proof was not reverified. In the subcritical nonnegative-curvature case, \(n>d\) makes the cutoff exponent \(d-2n+2\) negative (pp. 10–11). For the Liouville result, (6.5) bounds \(\int_{B_R}P\) by \(CR^2G(2R)\); the choice \(U=P^t\), \(1/2\le t<1\), and \(\tau=1/t>1\) satisfies the exponents of the Karp theorem reproduced as Theorem A.2 (pp. 22–23). The external surface classification and sharpness examples remain outside the independent verification scope. No additional substantive defect is established by these checks.

# Closure of the repaired cutoff argument

For either repair above, \(c_1\ge0\) and \(c_2>0\). Put \(A=P^{n-1}v^{1-n}>0\), \(q=(n-2)/(n-1)\in(0,1)\), and choose \(\theta\ge2(n-1)\). Source (3.9), with \(t=n-2\), yields \[I_\varphi:=\int_M A\varphi^\theta
 \le \frac{C}{R^2}
   \left(\int_{B_{2R}\setminus B_R}A\varphi^\theta\right)^q
   V_g(B_{2R})^{1/(n-1)}.\] The exponent \(\theta-2-q\theta\) is nonnegative, so the indicated Hölder estimate is valid for \(0\le\varphi\le1\). Using the whole cutoff support on the right gives \(I_\varphi\le CR^{-2(n-1)}V_g(B_{2R})\le C\). It follows that \(A\in L^1(M)\). Applying the annular form again, the volume factor combined with \(R^{-2}\) is bounded, while the annular integral tends to zero. Hence \(\int_{B_R}A\to0\), contradicting \(A>0\). This completes the unchanged end of the proof for the two explicitly repaired hypotheses, but not for the unproved endpoint.

report: Abstract: The analytic reduction from exponential completeness to weak-star approximation is examined in the exact March 2025 author manuscript. Title: Technical review of Complete frequencies for Koenigs domains
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed work is Complete frequencies for Koenigs domains, by Filippo Bracci, Eva A. Gallardo-Gutiérrez, and Dmitry Yakubovich, arXiv:2311.17470v3, dated 25 March 2025, 57 pages [paper]. The frozen journal identity is DOI 10.4171/JEMS/1730 (https://doi.org/10.4171/JEMS/1730). The publisher lists online publication on 21 October 2025 [publisher]. The acquired author PDF is reviewed; equivalence to the publisher PDF is not asserted. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with printed article pages.

Checked material comprises the statements and distinctions in Sections 1–3; Lemma 2.4; the Laplace approximation arguments in Section 4; the analytic and topological reduction in Section 5 through page 25; the assembly of Theorems 1.1–1.3 on page 50; and the statements and argument structure in Section 10. The detailed prime-end, contact-arc, and discontinuity classifications of Sections 6–8 were not independently reconstructed. The external theorems of Sarason and the authors’ cited rational-approximation theorem remain explicit dependencies, not independently certified results.
# Definitions and checks of the central framework

The source uses conformally invariant Hardy spaces: \(f\in H^p(\Omega)\) when \(|f|^p\) admits a harmonic majorant, and \(H^\infty(\Omega)\) consists of bounded holomorphic functions. For a non-elliptic semigroup its univalent Koenigs map satisfies \[h(\varphi_t(z))=h(z)+t,\qquad \Omega+t\subseteq\Omega\quad(t\geq0).\] Thus \(e^{\lambda h}\circ\varphi_t=e^{\lambda t}e^{\lambda h}\). The frequency set is \(\Lambda_p(\Omega)=\{\lambda:e^{\lambda z}\in H^p(\Omega)\}\), including \(\lambda=0\), and \(E_p\) is its linear span. Keeping the constant eigenfunction is essential.

Lemma 2.4 correctly uses weak-star continuity of the inclusion into reflexive \(H^p\), \(1<p<\infty\), followed by equality of weak and norm closures of a linear subspace. Density in \(H^1\) follows by the continuous dense inclusion from any such \(H^p\). Proposition 3.3’s rescaling is consistent: \(\Lambda_q=(p/q)\Lambda_p\), since \(|e^{(p/q)\lambda z}|^q=|e^{\lambda z}|^p\).

For \(S=\{|\operatorname{Im}z|<\pi/2\}\), the key transform in Theorem 4.3 is \[\int_0^\infty e^{itz}e^{-\beta t}\,dt=(\beta-iz)^{-1},
 \qquad \operatorname{Re}\beta>\pi/2.\] Its tail is uniformly bounded by \(e^{-R(\operatorname{Re}\beta-\pi/2)}/(\operatorname{Re}\beta-\pi/2)\). Finite atomic approximations are uniformly bounded on \(S\) and converge pointwise, giving weak-star convergence by the criterion on page 10. The pole is \(-i\beta\); reversing the sign of \(t\) supplies the other side of the strip. This verifies the transform mechanism conditional on the cited rational-density theorem.

Theorems 5.5 and 5.8 distinguish complement connectivity in a half-plane from that in a strip. Their respective hypotheses remain distinct in the proof assembly on page 50. The no-half-plane case of Theorem 1.3 follows from \(|e^{\lambda z}|=e^{\operatorname{Re}(\lambda z)}\): a nonzero bounded frequency supplies a containing half-plane. This is a bounded-frequency argument and does not exclude the finite-\(p\) examples in Section 10.
# A peripheral substantive error

Problem 1 (Elliptic semigroups can have complete eigenvectors).  Section 1, page 3, in the paragraph beginning It is here worth emphasizing, asserts that the analogous completeness questions always have negative answers in the elliptic case because of a common fixed point. This universal assertion is false under the eigenvector-completeness formulation motivating the paper.
## Counterexample and verification of hypotheses

Set \[\varphi_t(z)=e^{-t}z,\qquad z\in\mathbb D,\quad t\geq0.\] Each map is a holomorphic disk self-map; \(\varphi_0\) is the identity; \(\varphi_t\circ\varphi_s=\varphi_{t+s}\); and dependence on \(t\) is uniform on compact subsets. The point \(0\) is an interior fixed point for every \(t\). This is a nontrivial elliptic semigroup under the source’s definition on page 8.

For \(f_n(z)=z^n\), including \(n=0\), \[C_{\varphi_t}f_n=e^{-nt}f_n,\qquad \Gamma f_n=-n f_n.\] The derivative is a limit of scalar multiples of a fixed vector, so exists in each \(H^p\) norm, \(1\leq p<\infty\). All these eigenvectors are bounded and belong to every finite-\(p\) Hardy space. Their span contains all analytic polynomials, which are norm-dense in \(H^p(\mathbb D)\). The source itself uses this polynomial density in Lemma 2.4 on page 11.

The weak-star assertion also has a direct bounded-approximation proof. Given \(f\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)\), choose \(r_j\uparrow1\). The Taylor series of \(f(r_jz)\) converges uniformly on the closed unit disk. A Taylor polynomial \(P_j\) can therefore satisfy \(\|P_j-f(r_j\cdot)\|_\infty\leq1/j\). Then \[\|P_j\|_\infty\leq\|f\|_\infty+1,\qquad P_j(z)\longrightarrow f(z)
 \quad(z\in\mathbb D).\] The criterion on page 10 gives weak-star convergence. No norm-strong continuity on all of \(H^\infty\) is assumed.
## Alternative readings, impact, and repair

The additive Koenigs relation for non-elliptic semigroups must not be imposed on this elliptic example; elliptic linearization is multiplicative. If the disputed sentence refers only to the additive formulation, that formulation does not define an elliptic analogue and cannot justify a universal negative statement. A shared value does not obstruct density of a linear span, since coefficients are free and the constant eigenfunction is included.

The finding is Minor because its scope is peripheral: Theorems 1.1–1.4 explicitly assume non-ellipticity, and the checked proof assembly uses neither the elliptic assertion nor its consequences. This grading does not depend on ease of editing. A justified local replacement is: The additive Koenigs-domain formulation is restricted to non-elliptic semigroups; elliptic eigenvector completeness is a separate question and can hold, as for the dilation semigroup. Only this introductory replacement has been verified.
# Other checks and limitations

The arbitrary-measure approximation in Theorem 4.6, pages 18–19, needs attention to a possible atom at \(R\), since the displayed intervals are half-open. Choosing \(R\) strictly above compact support removes this issue before forming the approximation. The final bound should use finite total variation \(|\mu|([0,R])\), rather than the modulus of complex mass. These available choices do not supply a counterexample to the theorem and are not counted as additional central defects.

For Proposition 10.4, choosing the separating smooth function compactly supported away from \([0,M]\) supplies the required decay. In Proposition 10.6, a subsequence with almost-everywhere convergence suffices for the contradiction. Neither observation refutes the stated conclusion.

No separate supplement, released computational repository, or correction of the elliptic assertion was located in the bounded searches retained with the evidence. This is not proof of absence. Author programs were not executed. The unchecked geometric classification and external proofs prevent a whole-paper correctness claim.

problems.title: Universal failure of elliptic eigenvector completeness
problems.source_location: Pdf page: 3 Printed page: 3 Section: 1 Anchor: paragraph beginning It is here worth emphasizing
claim: The source uses conformally invariant Hardy spaces: \(f\in H^p(\Omega)\) when \(|f|^p\) admits a harmonic majorant, and \(H^\infty(\Omega)\) consists of bounded holomorphic functions. For a non-elliptic semigroup its univalent Koenigs map satisfies \[h(\varphi_t(z))=h(z)+t,\qquad \Omega+t\subseteq\Omega\quad(t\geq0).\] Thus \(e^{\lambda h}\circ\varphi_t=e^{\lambda t}e^{\lambda h}\). The frequency set is \(\Lambda_p(\Omega)=\{\lambda:e^{\lambda z}\in H^p(\Omega)\}\), including \(\lambda=0\), and \(E_p\) is its linear span. Keeping the constant eigenfunction is essential.

Lemma 2.4 correctly uses weak-star continuity of the inclusion into reflexive \(H^p\), \(1<p<\infty\), followed by equality of weak and norm closures of a linear subspace. Density in \(H^1\) follows by the continuous dense inclusion from any such \(H^p\). Proposition 3.3’s rescaling is consistent: \(\Lambda_q=(p/q)\Lambda_p\), since \(|e^{(p/q)\lambda z}|^q=|e^{\lambda z}|^p\).

For \(S=\{|\operatorname{Im}z|<\pi/2\}\), the key transform in Theorem 4.3 is \[\int_0^\infty e^{itz}e^{-\beta t}\,dt=(\beta-iz)^{-1},
 \qquad \operatorname{Re}\beta>\pi/2.\] Its tail is uniformly bounded by \(e^{-R(\operatorname{Re}\beta-\pi/2)}/(\operatorname{Re}\beta-\pi/2)\). Finite atomic approximations are uniformly bounded on \(S\) and converge pointwise, giving weak-star convergence by the criterion on page 10. The pole is \(-i\beta\); reversing the sign of \(t\) supplies the other side of the strip. This verifies the transform mechanism conditional on the cited rational-density theorem.

Theorems 5.5 and 5.8 distinguish complement connectivity in a half-plane from that in a strip. Their respective hypotheses remain distinct in the proof assembly on page 50. The no-half-plane case of Theorem 1.3 follows from \(|e^{\lambda z}|=e^{\operatorname{Re}(\lambda z)}\): a nonzero bounded frequency supplies a containing half-plane. This is a bounded-frequency argument and does not exclude the finite-\(p\) examples in Section 10.
Elliptic analogues of the completeness questions invariably have negative answers because of a common fixed point.
analysis: Section 1, page 3, in the paragraph beginning It is here worth emphasizing, asserts that the analogous completeness questions always have negative answers in the elliptic case because of a common fixed point. This universal assertion is false under the eigenvector-completeness formulation motivating the paper.

Set \[\varphi_t(z)=e^{-t}z,\qquad z\in\mathbb D,\quad t\geq0.\] Each map is a holomorphic disk self-map; \(\varphi_0\) is the identity; \(\varphi_t\circ\varphi_s=\varphi_{t+s}\); and dependence on \(t\) is uniform on compact subsets. The point \(0\) is an interior fixed point for every \(t\). This is a nontrivial elliptic semigroup under the source’s definition on page 8.

For \(f_n(z)=z^n\), including \(n=0\), \[C_{\varphi_t}f_n=e^{-nt}f_n,\qquad \Gamma f_n=-n f_n.\] The derivative is a limit of scalar multiples of a fixed vector, so exists in each \(H^p\) norm, \(1\leq p<\infty\). All these eigenvectors are bounded and belong to every finite-\(p\) Hardy space. Their span contains all analytic polynomials, which are norm-dense in \(H^p(\mathbb D)\). The source itself uses this polynomial density in Lemma 2.4 on page 11.

The weak-star assertion also has a direct bounded-approximation proof. Given \(f\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)\), choose \(r_j\uparrow1\). The Taylor series of \(f(r_jz)\) converges uniformly on the closed unit disk. A Taylor polynomial \(P_j\) can therefore satisfy \(\|P_j-f(r_j\cdot)\|_\infty\leq1/j\). Then \[\|P_j\|_\infty\leq\|f\|_\infty+1,\qquad P_j(z)\longrightarrow f(z)
 \quad(z\in\mathbb D).\] The criterion on page 10 gives weak-star convergence. No norm-strong continuity on all of \(H^\infty\) is assumed.
result: The additive Koenigs relation for non-elliptic semigroups must not be imposed on this elliptic example; elliptic linearization is multiplicative. If the disputed sentence refers only to the additive formulation, that formulation does not define an elliptic analogue and cannot justify a universal negative statement. A shared value does not obstruct density of a linear span, since coefficients are free and the constant eigenfunction is included.

The finding is Minor because its scope is peripheral: Theorems 1.1–1.4 explicitly assume non-ellipticity, and the checked proof assembly uses neither the elliptic assertion nor its consequences. This grading does not depend on ease of editing. A justified local replacement is: The additive Koenigs-domain formulation is restricted to non-elliptic semigroups; elliptic eigenvector completeness is a separate question and can hold, as for the dilation semigroup. Only this introductory replacement has been verified.
Impact: Peripheral scope-setting assertion is false; no core theorem dependency demonstrated.

Title: Technical review of Light bulb smoothing for topological surfaces in 4-manifolds
# Identity and scope

The reviewed paper is by Jae Choon Cha and Byeorhi Kim, Light bulb smoothing for topological surfaces in 4-manifolds, arXiv:2303.12857v2, 8 August 2025, 28 pages [paper]. Its journal identity is DOI 10.4171/jems/1731 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1731). The reviewed file is the author manuscript incorporating referee comments, not a byte-verified publisher edition. Page references mean one-based PDF pages, which agree with the printed article pages.

The actual text inspection covers pages 1–19: the introductory statements and conventions, Sections 2–4, and the beginning of Section 5. The principal targets are Theorems C and D, Lemmas 3.2 and 3.4, Lemma 4.5, and Theorems 4.7 and 4.10. The sphere classifications, Section 7 applications, Appendix A, and the rest of Section 5 were not independently checked. The full PDF was parsed, but parsing is not treated as reading or proof verification.

Surfaces and isotopies are locally flat and proper; isotopies fix the boundary. The paper assumes orientability, connected ambient 4-manifolds, and compact connected surfaces except where multiple components are expressly allowed. A geometric dual is a framed embedded sphere meeting the surface transversely in one point. The smoothness of this dual is essential to Theorem C. Theorem D allows a number of stabilizations depending on the given embedded surface; it does not assert a uniform bound.
# Checked reasoning and dependencies
## Light bulb smoothing

On pages 5–8, the argument first equips a topological normal bundle \(V\) of \(R\) with its intrinsic smooth structure. Quinn’s theorem is applied to the inclusion into the ambient smooth manifold, not as an assertion that the original inclusion is smooth. The relative construction on page 6 keeps the isotopy fixed near the smooth dual \(G\). This is what allows the maps on \(V\) and on \(\nu(G)\) to be glued.

Gabai’s lemma then supplies a surface \(R''\) smoothly isotopic to \(R\) in the plumbed neighborhood \(N=V\cup\nu(G)\) and lying where the terminal embedding is smooth. Composing the isotopy in \(N\) with the topological embedding, followed by the terminal ambient isotopy, gives the claimed topological isotopy in \(M\). Smoothness is asserted only for the final surface. Shrinking \(V\) and \(\nu(G)\) gives the stated support control. There is no inference here that the intermediate Whitney disks were already smooth in \(M\).

Quinn’s theorem, the extension of topological normal bundles, and Gabai’s lemma are substantive external inputs. Their original proofs were not independently reproduced. The manuscript’s explanation of their use was checked; the pictures of the Norman moves were not visually inspected because of the recorded image-interface failure.
## Stable smoothing and the complement fundamental group

Lemma 3.2, pages 9–10, has the necessary compactness and embedding assumptions. If \(g(x)=g(y)\) and \(g\) is \(\epsilon\)-close to the embedding \(f\), then \[d(f(x),f(y))<2\epsilon.\] Uniform continuity of \(f^{-1}\) yields a short path from \(x\) to \(y\) in the domain. The selected constants place its image under \(g\) in a contractible neighborhood in the target. This proves existence of a null-homotopic double point loop; it does not assert that every arbitrary choice of a loop is null-homotopic for a nonsimply connected domain.

That distinction is respected in Lemma 3.4. The controlled regular homotopy selects null-homotopic loops first. The bundle exact sequence and the cited complement isomorphism identify the relevant kernel with a cyclic group generated by a meridian. Twisting the push-off changes its meridional power and makes the chosen parallel null-homotopic in the complement of the immersed surface and the Whitney disks. Null-homotopy merely in the ambient manifold would not suffice; the proof explicitly supplies the stronger complement statement.

Pages 12–13 construct immersed geometric duals, use separate \(S^2\times S^2\) summands to remove their intersections, and then apply Theorem C in disjoint neighborhoods of each Whitney disk and its dual. The resulting smooth Whitney disks remain topologically isotopic to the disks that reverse the original finger moves. Thus the argument retains the original surface’s isotopy class. Simply resolving double points of an arbitrary approximation by the Norman trick would not establish this, as the manuscript itself notes in Remark 3.1. The controlled form of Quinn’s theorem and the complement isomorphism cited from earlier work remain external dependencies.
## Dax invariance and the unstabilized indeterminacy

Lemma 4.5, page 15, uses a sufficiently close generic approximation of an embedded honest track. Lemma 3.2 supplies trivial double point labels. Here the domain \(I^3\) is simply connected, so changing the connecting path does not introduce another label. Definition 4.1 counts only nonidentity labels, and hence the sum is zero. This establishes the needed vanishing for a topological isotopy between smooth disks without claiming a general topological jet-transversality theorem.

Definition 4.6 deliberately takes values modulo \(d(\pi_3(M))\), although the smoothings lie in a stabilization. Theorem 4.7 does not silently enlarge that denominator. For fixed \(H\), changing the smoothing isotopies inserts topological isotopies between smooth disks, whose Dax values vanish by Lemma 4.5. For two choices \(H,K\) in \(M\), the difference is \[\operatorname{dax}(h_0^{-1}HK^{-1}h_0).\] The reparametrization on pages 16–17 cancels the smoothing paths and produces a kernel map in the original \(M\). Its value lies in \(d(\pi_3(M))\), as required. This is the decisive distinction between the original and stabilized indeterminacies.

The point-avoidance argument of Lemma 4.11 uses the nonempty boundary to place a point outside a collared isotopy and move it to the prescribed omitted point while fixing the endpoint surfaces. The passage to an almost smooth manifold then uses Lemma 4.12 to identify the Dax image after puncturing. The almost smooth structure is fixed in Theorem F; independence of an arbitrary choice of such a structure is not claimed by that theorem and has not been inferred here. The smooth Dax theory and its generic-track theorem are accepted as the paper’s cited inputs, not freshly proved in this review.
# Assessment and limits

No admissible counterexample or decisive invalid step was established in these checked chains. This is a scoped No Issue Found outcome, not certification of every theorem or of the publisher version. No numbered Problem or unsupported repair is supplied.

Title: Technical review of Gravitating vortices and symplectic reduction by stages
# Identity, version, and assumptions

The reviewed work is by Luis Álvarez-Cónsul, Mario Garcia-Fernandez, Oscar García-Prada, Vamsi Pritham Pingali, and Chengjian Yao, arXiv:2406.03639v1, 5 June 2024, 48 pages [paper]. The frozen journal identity is DOI 10.4171/jems/1732 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1732). The acquired preprint predates the journal’s acceptance and publication; identity of the work does not establish equality of the mathematical text. The frozen 2025 identifier is retained. All page numbers are one-based PDF pages and agree with printed pages.

The principal checked claims are Theorems 1.1/5.3, 1.3/5.7, and 1.4/5.8. Text inspected comprises pages 1–5, 8–11, 15–16, 31–37, and 39–45. The complete lower-regularity construction of Section 3, the estimates in Sections 4.1–4.4, and the full proof of Theorem 5.5 were not independently reconstructed. Figure/equation image confirmation remains a separate incomplete check.

For the main analysis, the operative assumptions on pages 9 and 33 include \(N=\deg L>0\), a nonzero holomorphic section \(\phi\), \(\tau>0\), \(\alpha>0\), and \(V>4\pi N/\tau\). The introduction initially allows a general real coupling parameter when defining the equations; that broader definition is not substituted for the explicit positive-coupling assumptions of Section 5. The uniqueness claim excludes infinitesimal automorphisms through the genus or zero-divisor conditions. The existence result for genus at least one additionally imposes the two strict numerical inequalities.
# Checks of the proof structure
## Integrated equations and uniqueness

Integration of the vortex equation gives \[\int_\Sigma |\phi|_h^2\omega=\tau V-4\pi N>0.\] Integrating the scalar equation then yields \[c=\frac{2\pi(\chi(\Sigma)-2\alpha\tau N)}{V},\] consistent with (1.2). The strict volume bound and nonzero section are essential; the zero-section boundary case is not an admissible counterexample to the results under review.

The variation formula in Proposition 2.8 contains nonnegative squared norms for \(\alpha>0\). On the graph of the vortex solution the first residual vanishes, and on a smooth geodesic the geodesic residual vanishes. The weak-geodesic argument subsequently needs the uniform estimates and limiting results of Sections 3–4. The inspection checked this dependency and the sign structure, without certifying every intermediate estimate or extracting an error from ambiguous PDF notation.

For uniqueness, Lemma 5.2 uses the absence of infinitesimal automorphisms to obtain local branches of critical points of \(K_\alpha+\lambda J_\xi\). The proof of Theorem 5.3 compares two such branches along a weak geodesic. The endpoint sub-slope inequalities and convexity imply \[0\geq \lambda\bigl(J_\xi'(1)-J_\xi'(0)\bigr)
   \geq \lambda C\,d(\omega_{\varphi_0^\lambda},
                     \omega_{\varphi_1^\lambda})^2\] for small positive \(\lambda\). The two metrics coincide and remain equal as \(\lambda\to0^+\). This does not assert strict convexity of the unperturbed functional without the perturbation argument. The cited elliptic invertibility and weak-geodesic distance inequality remain external inputs.
## Polystability and the historical correction

Theorem 5.7 separates the already treated divisor supported on at most two points from the case with at least three distinct zeroes. In the latter case Theorem 5.6 supplies properness on normalized potentials. Along the specified projective one-parameter subgroup, the proof obtains the limiting slope \[\lim_{t\to+\infty}K_\alpha'(t)
   =2\alpha\tau(N-2n_1)\left(V-\frac{4\pi N}{\tau}\right).\] The normalized geodesic has distance growing linearly in \(t\). Properness therefore forces a strictly positive slope, giving \(2n_1<N\). The chosen point can be any point of the divisor, so this supplies the strict multiplicity inequalities needed for stability in this case. Replacing properness by a bare lower bound would not justify that strict conclusion; the manuscript does use the stronger input.

The authors explicitly state on page 3 that an earlier paper’s proof of the obstruction was flawed and that the present argument rectifies it. That statement is preserved as attributed historical context. This review did not reproduce the original flaw and does not classify it as a current defect in the bound manuscript. The uniform convergence of the normalized vortex solutions along the ray and the cited Futaki calculation are dependencies, not new computations performed here.
## Independent check of the existence condition

Equation reference: eq:coefficient. The main numerical implication of (5.24)–(5.26), pages 43–44, can be checked directly. Put \[B=\frac{4\pi N}{\tau},\qquad
C_0=-c=\frac{2\pi(2g-2+2\alpha\tau N)}{V}>0,\qquad
A=-\frac{1}{V}\int_\Sigma f\,\omega_0,
\quad X=\int_\Sigma i\partial f\wedge\bar\partial f.\] Absorbing bounded constants, (5.24) implies \(X\leq 2\pi N A+C\). Equation (5.25) then implies \[\left[\alpha\tau(V-B)-\frac{2\pi\alpha^2\tau^2N}{C_0}\right]A\leq C.\] The coefficient has the exact form \[\frac{\alpha\tau}{2g-2+2\alpha\tau N}
\left[(2g-2)(V-B)+\alpha\tau N(V-2B)\right].
\] All factors used in multiplying or dividing are positive. Positivity of this coefficient is precisely \[\alpha\tau\left(\frac{8\pi N}{\tau}-V\right)
  <\frac{2g-2}{N}\left(V-\frac{4\pi N}{\tau}\right),\] the manuscript’s condition (5.26). The already available upper bound on the average of \(f\) and this lower bound control that average, and (5.24) then controls the gradient terms.

This algebra was independently executed in a small reviewer-written SymPy script. The difference between the original coefficient and [eq:coefficient] (#eq:coefficient) simplified exactly to zero, with process exit code 0. For the admissible consistency example \(g=N=\tau=m=1\), \(V=12\pi\), and \(\alpha=1/4\), the coefficient is \(\pi/2\) and \(2\alpha\tau m=1/2<1\). This example is a check of the formula, not an existence simulation or counterexample.

The multiplicity threshold also has the expected local integrability role. Near a zero of order \(m_j\leq m\), \(|\phi|\asymp r^{m_j}\); the density used on page 43 is bounded in magnitude by a constant times \[|\log r|\,r^{-(2-\epsilon)m_j/m}.\] With the area factor \(r\,dr\), it is integrable for \(\epsilon>0\). The strict condition \(2\alpha\tau m<1\) permits the required positive \(\epsilon<2(1-2\alpha\tau m)\). No claim at the excluded endpoint is inferred. The subsequent bootstrap relies on the stated Green-function and Moser–Trudinger estimates; it was checked as a dependency chain, not re-proved in all analytic details.
# Outcome and limits

No decisive current defect is established in these checked arguments. The assessment is No Issue Found within the inspected scope. It is not a verification of the whole finite-energy theory or of the journal version, and it does not erase the historical correction acknowledged by the authors.

Title: Technical review of The \(L_p\)-Minkowski problem with super-critical exponents
# Identity and review scope

The paper is by Qiang Guang, Qi-Rui Li, and Xu-Jia Wang, The \(L_p\)-Minkowski problem with super-critical exponents, DOI 10.4171/jems/1733 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1733), J. Eur. Math. Soc. 28 (2026), 735–775 [paper]. The exact reviewed file is the publisher version, first published online on 13 November 2025. The existing 2025 frozen identifier is retained. PDF page \(j\) corresponds to printed page \(734+j\).

Actual text reading covers PDF pages 1–20 and 32–36. Targets are Theorem 1.1, the monotonicity and compactness mechanism, Theorem 3.7 and its role in Lemma 3.8, the subsequence limit, and the architecture of the curvature estimates. Pages 21–31 and most of Appendix A were not individually audited. A separate exact argument below checks the central homology statement without claiming to have checked every step of Section 4.

The range is \(p<-n-1\), \(n\geq1\). The support function must be positive and arise from a convex body containing the origin in its interior. The smooth theorem assumes positive \(f\in C^{1,1}(S^n)\); the weak corollary retains two positive bounds on the density. The review does not replace these with mere nonnegativity, assume evenness, or assert uniqueness. The publisher metadata confirms the negative signs in the super-critical range; the PDF text extraction drops some mathematical glyphs, so ambiguous extraction alone is not used to diagnose errors.
# Checked analytic mechanism

Write \(D=\det(\nabla^2u+uI)=K^{-1}\). Equation (2.4) is \[u_t=u-\frac{fu^p}{D}.\] The support-function variation of volume gives the independent identity \[\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dt}\left(\operatorname{Vol}(\Omega)
      -\frac1p\int_{S^n}fu^p\,d\sigma\right)
 &=\int_{S^n}(D-fu^{p-1})u_t\,d\sigma\\
 &=\int_{S^n}\frac{u}{D}(D-fu^{p-1})^2\,d\sigma\geq0.\end{aligned}\] Under the positive and uniformly convex hypotheses, equality is equivalent to the elliptic equation. This agrees with Lemma 2.1 (PDF page 7, printed page 741).

Lemmas 2.2–2.4 address degeneration toward the origin, extreme volume, and large eccentricity. In Lemma 2.2, the volume and polar-cone estimates combine into a lower bound proportional to \(d^{-(-p-n-1)}\) for \(J^2\). The exponent is positive precisely in the stated super-critical range. No corresponding coercive conclusion at \(p=-n-1\) is inferred. Together with the John ellipsoid inclusions, an upper bound for \(J\) gives both inner and outer radius control.

The stopped flow in Section 3 is part of the topological construction. It is stationary at energy at least \(9A_0/10\), whereas the selected trajectories at the prescribed times have energy at most \(A_0/2\). The monotonicity and the continuous-dependence argument in Remark 3.11 are needed to ensure the limiting selected trajectory never reaches the stopping threshold. Lemma 3.12 gives the stricter \(3A_0/4\) bound. Thus one cannot infer compactness for arbitrary initial data merely from energy monotonicity; the selected initial data supply the missing upper bound.

The curvature-estimate architecture is consistent: an upper bound for the product of the principal curvatures, together with a positive lower bound for each curvature, also bounds each curvature above. Equivalently, the eigenvalues of \(\nabla^2u+uI\) stay between positive constants. Sections 2.2 and 5 then invoke parabolic and elliptic regularity. The auxiliary-function argument and its endpoint cases were read, but every differentiated tensor coefficient and each cited regularity theorem were not independently reconstructed.
# Independent verification of the central ellipsoid homology

Let \(m=n+1\) and let \(\mathcal E\) be the space called \(E\) in (3.4): origin-centred ellipsoids of volume \(\operatorname{Vol}(B_1)\) with eccentricity \(\bar e>1\), carrying the Hausdorff topology. This is the boundary of the corresponding bounded-eccentricity set of symmetric ellipsoids, not the larger space allowing translation.

Every such ellipsoid has a unique representation \[E_A=A B_1,\qquad A=A^{\mathsf T}>0,\quad \det A=1.\] The eigenvalues of \(A\) are its semiaxis lengths. This representation and its inverse are continuous: the support function is \(h_{E_A}(x)=|Ax|\), so \(h_{E_A}^2\) determines the symmetric matrix \(A^2\), and the positive square root is unique and continuous. Repeated semiaxes therefore create no choice of eigenbasis in this parametrization.

Set \(H=\log A\). This identifies determinant-one positive definite matrices with \[\mathcal V=\{H=H^{\mathsf T}:\operatorname{tr}H=0\},
\qquad \dim\mathcal V=\frac{m(m+1)}2-1.\] For nonzero \(H\in\mathcal V\), define \[w(H)=\lambda_{\max}(H)-\lambda_{\min}(H)>0.\] It is continuous and satisfies \(w(rH)=r\,w(H)\) for \(r>0\). Moreover, \(w(H)=0\) in \(\mathcal V\) forces \(H=0\). The eccentricity condition is exactly \[w(H)=\log\bar e.\] Consequently the map from the Frobenius unit sphere in \(\mathcal V\), \[H\longmapsto \frac{\log\bar e}{w(H)}H,\] is a homeomorphism onto this spectral-width level set; its inverse is radial normalization. Composing with the matrix exponential and \(A\mapsto E_A\) proves \[\mathcal E\cong S^q,\qquad
q=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}2-2
  =\frac{n(n+1)}2+n-1.\] In particular, \[H_q(\mathcal E;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z,\qquad
H_k(\mathcal E;\mathbb Z)=0\quad(k>q).\] This verifies Theorem 3.7 and the higher-degree vanishing used in (4.31). It is an analytic/topological proof, not a finite numerical experiment.

In the contradiction on PDF page 17, take \(k=q+n>q\). The Künneth term \(H_{k-n}(\mathcal E)=H_q(\mathcal E)=\mathbb Z\) survives, whereas \(H_k(\mathcal E)\) and \(H_k(S^n)\) vanish. Thus the contradiction does not require cancellation of an unspecified infinite abelian group. The surrounding retraction and Mayer–Vietoris constructions are inspected at the level described in the coverage ledger; the independent sphere model verifies the decisive homology input.
# Limit, outcome, and boundaries

With the selected trajectory uniformly controlled, \(J\) is bounded and nondecreasing. Therefore there exist \(t_i\to\infty\) with \(J'(t_i)\to0\).
