Take the smooth boundary datum \(f\equiv1\) and \[u=\frac{1-r^2}{2},\qquad U=\rho^{s-n}u=e^{-\phi}.\] Then \(-\Delta_{g_+}u-2u=0\), \(U|_{S^3}=1\), and \(U\) is smooth on the compactified closed ball and belongs to the required energy space (\(a=0\)). No Schwartz assumption is involved in Proposition 2.13, which allows arbitrary smooth boundary data. The correct extension satisfies \[-\Delta_{\bar g}U+\frac16 R_{\bar g}U=0.\] In contrast, (2.28) gives \(C_{\mathrm{printed}}=1/96\), and the residual in the printed equation is \[
 -\Delta_{\bar g}U+\frac1{96}R_{\bar g}U
 =\frac{15}{16}(r^2-4)e^{\,3(r^2-1)/2}.\] At \(r=0\) this equals \(-\tfrac{15}{4}e^{-3/2}\), and is nonzero. This is an actual example under the extension-reduction hypotheses, not a formal unconstrained test function. The radial identities and residual were also independently checked with exact SymPy arithmetic; the retained script, output, and exit code are part of the evidence.
## Impact, counterevidence, and repair boundary

Proposition 2.13 incorporates the coefficient from Lemma 2.11 into the equation whose conormal derivative is identified with \(P_{2\gamma}f\). The explicit spectral extension above fails that printed equation. Later curved arguments repeatedly use \(J_{\bar g}=C_{n,\gamma}R_{\bar g}\), and the unique-continuation transfer in (4.86) again invokes the spectral interpretation. This establishes a failure of a central proof connection and warrants Major classification; it need not refute every singular-set theorem.

The flat model has \(R_{\bar g}=0\), so it does not reveal this error. Many estimates in Section 4 use only boundedness of a smooth lower-order potential, which is evidence that parts of the proof may survive the correction. Replacing the coefficient by [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) is necessary. The extension correspondence, uniqueness/coercivity arguments, frequency definitions, and transfer to boundary solutions must then be checked with that corrected equation. The present review does not certify this entire repair or assert that the final dimension bounds are false.
# Problem 2: the displayed Caccioppoli estimate has inconsistent homogeneity
Location and status. Lemma 2.15, p. 14, (2.39), with the local equation (2.38) on p. 13. Confirmed local error; Minor.

For \(\beta>1\) the left side involves \(\nabla(\eta U^{\beta/2})\), whereas the right side contains \(U^2\) with a constant stated to depend only on \(r,a,\bar g\). Fix \(\beta=4\). In the Euclidean compactification of the hyperbolic upper-half-space model already described in the paper, take \(a=0\), \(J=0\), and the local energy solution \(U=A>0\). Fix a nonzero smooth cutoff supported strictly inside the unit ball and set \(I=\int|\nabla\eta|^2>0\). The asserted inequality would say \[A^4 I\leq C A^2 I.\] For any proposed uniform \(C\), choosing \(A^2>C\) contradicts it. All quantities are finite on the local ball. This is a counterexample to the local estimate, not to a global theorem requiring a Schwartz trace. More generally, multiplication of any nonzero admissible local solution by \(A\) produces the same incompatible amplitude powers whenever the cutoff expression is nonzero.

A direct corrected estimate can be obtained without assuming the disputed formula. For positive \(U\), \(\beta\geq2\), and \(w=\rho^a\), define \[A_0=\int w\eta^2 U^{\beta-2}|\nabla U|^2,\quad
 B=\int wU^\beta|\nabla\eta|^2,\quad
 D=\int w|J|\eta^2U^\beta.\] Testing the equation by \(\eta^2U^{\beta-1}\) and applying Young’s inequality gives \[A_0\leq\frac{4B}{(\beta-1)^2}+\frac{2D}{\beta-1},\] and hence \[\int w|\nabla(\eta U^{\beta/2})|^2
 \leq\left(2+\frac{2\beta^2}{(\beta-1)^2}\right)B
       +\frac{\beta^2}{\beta-1}D.\] For signed solutions the corresponding absolute-value regularization must be specified. This calculation supplies the correctly homogeneous input needed for the usual iteration. The displayed version cannot justify iteration as written, but this check has not shown a failure of the later regularity conclusion or the novel geometric estimates. That demonstrated scope, rather than ease of correction alone, is the reason for the Minor classification.
# Problem 3: the sign of the radial weight derivative
Location and status. Lemma 4.1, p. 32, (4.9)–(4.10). Confirmed; Minor.

For the full permitted interval \(a\in(-1,1)\) the paper displays \[\partial_r\rho^a=\frac{a\rho^a}{r}(1+O(r))\] and then asserts nonnegativity. Choose \(a=-\tfrac12\), equivalently \(\gamma=\tfrac34\). Along any inward ray on which \(\rho>0\), and for sufficiently small positive \(r\) such that \(|O(r)|<1/2\), the displayed derivative is strictly negative. In the flat normal-ray model \(\rho=r\) it is exactly \(-1/(2r^{3/2})\). This countercheck concerns the defining function and needs no unverified assumption about a solution \(U\).

The correct sign for small positive \(r\) is the sign of \(a\), with zero derivative for \(a=0\). The subsequent computations inspected on pp. 37–38 use the signed coefficient \(a+O(t)\) or \(a/r+O(rt)\), rather than the erroneous nonnegativity claim. This is counterevidence to a claim that the sign typo itself destroys the almost-monotonicity argument. It should be corrected, but this review does not establish such a downstream failure.
# Problem 4: high-order extension across the doubled boundary
Location and status. Proposition 4.20, pp. 43–45, especially (4.101)–(4.110), and its use in Theorem 4.19. Needs Evidence; not a confirmed theorem counterexample.

The negative-side formula in (4.110) reverses the signs of odd Taylor coefficients. For a nonzero odd coefficient \(c_\ell\) with \(\ell\leq2m^2\), the polynomial contribution to the two one-sided \(\ell\)th normal derivatives is respectively \[\ell!c_\ell\quad\hbox{and}\quad-\ell!c_\ell.\] A Taylor remainder with vanishing jets through that order cannot remove this discrepancy. Thus the statement that the displayed construction is clearly \(C^{2m^2}\) needs a proof that the relevant odd jets vanish, or a different extension construction with matching jets and controlled remainder. Smoothness on the positive side alone does not prove this. The finite regularity of the doubled coefficients, explicitly discussed in Remark 4.21, makes the distinction material.

Lemma 2.19 provides relevant counterevidence: (2.42)–(2.43), p. 14, state \(C^{k,\alpha}\) estimates for every \(k\), and the proof describes the estimates as holding across the doubled boundary. If these estimates apply with the stated two-sided regularity in Proposition 4.20, the evenness of \(U\) forces every odd normal derivative through order \(2m^2\) to vanish at the boundary. The conditional jet calculation would then present no obstruction to matching those derivatives.

The scope and justification of this regularity must therefore be reconciled with Remark 2.20, p. 15, which describes generically finite smoothness, and Remark 4.21, p. 43, which explains why the required high-order approximation cannot be obtained directly from the doubled coefficients. These statements do not by themselves establish that either regularity assertion or Proposition 4.20 is false. No admissible Poincaré–Einstein solution satisfying the frequency and approximation hypotheses with a nonzero offending jet has been constructed here. The assessment remains Needs Evidence, concerning the applicable regularity and the quantitative extension estimate, rather than a confirmed failure of the proposition or the Hausdorff bound.

There is also a quantifier discrepancy to clarify: Proposition 4.20 introduces \(\delta\), but (4.101) displays \(\epsilon\) in the approximation hypothesis, while (4.103) estimates by \(C_k\delta\). A revised proof should state the smallness parameter actually required. This is included in the same evidence request, not counted as an additional confirmed Major issue.
# Coverage, limits, and conclusion

The core path inspected runs from the spectral extension through weighted regularity, frequency control, quantitative rigidity and cone splitting, effective coverings, and the high-order stability step for Hausdorff measure. The source’s horizontal/mixed boundary decomposition was retained; codimension two for the horizontal part was not incorrectly applied to the entire trace singular set. The normalization and decay restrictions were checked before considering polynomial tests. Several tempting tests were rejected because they did not satisfy the global Schwartz/energy hypotheses.

The references on weighted regularity, quantitative stratification, and complex-analytic stability were identified through the paper, but their complete proofs were not independently re-established. In particular, the complex isolated-zero premise used in the stability reduction was not turned into a confirmed defect without the missing admissible evidence. The remark on rectifiability is likewise not independently certified here.

A bounded search of the exact arXiv record, an author research page, and queries for corrections, code, and supplements found no linked correction or separate implementation for this exact source during the check. This is a search limitation, not proof that no additional material exists. Acquisition metadata also records the inability to obtain the publisher PDF. No author code was executed; lack of code is not a mathematical defect.

The decisive result is the explicit failure of the curvature coefficient and of the extension identification using it. The repair boundary is stated above. Two narrower displayed formulas also require correction. The separate high-order extension question remains open in this review.
# Supporting checks

Backend equivalence was not independently verified. The initial review’s calculations, full-text reading, and page inspections retain their original attribution. In the present independent acceptance, the primary scientific conversation rechecked the reported Problems, corrected the discussion of counterevidence in Problem 4, and invoked the revised report’s compilation and actual page inspection. The primary verifier made the final judgments. Exact command and page records distinguish reused historical checks from new operations. Rendering alone is not counted as viewing; the scientific decision remains pending and the human-review list is empty.

report: Author: Scientific review record
Date: 27 October 2026

Title: Initial Scientific Review
M25-0362

Manuscript. Sven Hirsch and Yiyue Zhang, Initial data sets with vanishing mass are contained in pp-wave spacetimes. Exact reviewed source: arXiv:2403.15984v2, 23 September 2025, 33 PDF pages. Associated DOI: https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1741. This assessment does not assert equivalence to the published article.

Assessment: Major revision of the proof. One incorrect interpolation identity is used in the proof of the principal regularity-dependent rigidity theorem. A replacement argument under the stated regularity is supplied below. Two further displayed formulas require local corrections. None of these findings supplies a counterexample to the principal embedding or rigidity theorems. This is an initial scientific review; the recorded scientific decision remains pending and no human or independent acceptance is represented.
# Scope and proof structure

All 33 source pages, including the appendical topology argument and references, were read. The review traced the hypotheses of Theorems 1.1, 1.3 and 1.4 through the spinorial equality case, flat level sets, global coordinates, the construction of the pp-wave metric, the decay-dependent rigidity argument and the borderline examples. Source page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed numbering.

The asymptotic-flatness definition is substantive: the manifold is connected, complete and without boundary, the ends are finite in number, the metric and second fundamental form have the specified weighted Hölder regularity, \(\mu,J\) are integrable, and \(q\in((n-2)/2,n-2]\). The nonzero equality case in Theorem 1.1 also requires spin, the dominant energy condition and \(E=|P|\). Theorem 1.3 uses the strict additional threshold \(q>n-1-s-\alpha\); the \(E=0\) case has its separate threshold. These hypotheses have not been dropped in assessing the main results.

The equality spinors yield the bilinear field \(X\), its norm \(N\), and the spacetime-harmonic equation \(
abla^2u=-k|
abla u|\). The leaf-flatness argument uses the family of parallel spinors obtained from varying the asymptotic spinor, rather than the existence of just one parallel spinor. Codazzi identities and decay eliminate the transverse curl of the shift, giving \(Y=
abla^\Sigma\ell\). The resulting metric has profile \[F=|
abla u|^{-2}+|
abla^\Sigma\ell|^2-2\ell_u,
 \qquad \mu=-	frac12|
abla u|^2\Delta_\Sigma F.\] The latter identity, proved in Lemma 6.6, is the correct general-slice identity and is relevant to the second finding.

The checks below include exact symbolic matrix multiplication, a complete Christoffel/Ricci calculation for the pp-wave ansatz, and an explicit interpolation calculation. The retained script was authored for this review and executed with exit code zero. No author code was executed.
# Major finding: the interpolation remainder has the wrong derivative order
## Location and decisive calculation

This is an independent calculation disproving the interpolation identity used in the proof. It is not an asymptotically flat initial-data counterexample to Theorem 1.3: no assertion is made that this test profile satisfies its strict weighted decay threshold. That distinction is essential.
## Effect and a repair at the available regularity

Replacing the derivative in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) by one of order \(s-1\) would give the usual classical remainder only with an extra derivative. The manuscript has \(F-1\in C^{s-2,\beta}_{-q}\) at this step, so an index correction alone is not an adequate justification.

The manuscript’s lower bound, obtained before invoking (7.7), is \[R(u_0,\rho)>\tfrac14c(u_0)\rho^{3-n}.\] Together with [eq:repair] (#eq:repair), this is impossible when \(q+k+\beta>n-3\), equivalently \(q>n-1-s-\beta\). The strict threshold permits the appropriate choice of \(\beta<\alpha\). This replaces (7.7), (7.10) and (7.11), and also avoids assigning derivative values to unspecified intermediate points.

The repair is conditional on the upstream weighted-coordinate estimate (7.1) and the radial mass asymptotics already established in the paper. It repairs the identified analytic step; it is not an independent reconstruction of all global geometric estimates. The finding is classified as Major because an essential step of a principal theorem’s proof is invalid as written, even though a repair is available under the same regularity.
# Minor finding: the energy density is slice dependent
## Location and admissible example

Theorem 3.3 on p. 6 quantifies over any initial data set in the pp-wave spacetime, while its displayed energy formula uses \(\mu=-\tfrac12F^{-1}\Delta_\Sigma F\). The factor \(F^{-1}\) is appropriate for the \(t=0\) slice, not for an arbitrary spacelike graph.

For the ambient metric \[ ar g=-2\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dt+F\,\mathrm du^2+|\,\mathrm dy|^2\] and graph \(t=-\ell(u,y)\), the induced metric and inverse \(uu\) coefficient are \[ egin{aligned}
 g&=(F+2\ell_u)\,\mathrm du^2+2\ell_a\,\mathrm du\,\mathrm dy_a+|\,\mathrm dy|^2,\
 |
abla u|_g^2&=(F+2\ell_u-|
abla_y\ell|^2)^{-1}.\end{aligned}\] The exact Ricci calculation gives \(\operatorname{Ric}_{uu}=-\Delta_yF/2\) and scalar curvature zero. The normal contraction therefore gives \[\mu=-	frac12|
abla u|_g^2\Delta_yF.\]

For a global example, take \(y\in\mathbb R^3\), \[F(y)=1+(1+|y|^2)^{-1/2},\qquad \ell(u,y)=u/2 .\] Here \(\Delta_yF=-3(1+|y|^2)^{-5/2}<0\) and the graph metric is \((F+1)\,\mathrm du^2+|\,\mathrm dy|^2\), uniformly equivalent to the Euclidean metric and complete on \(\mathbb R^4\). It is a smooth spacelike initial data set in the specified pp-wave spacetime; its null-dust energy satisfies the dominant energy condition. At \(y=0\), \(F=2\) and \(\Delta_yF=-3\). The actual energy density is \(1/2\), whereas the displayed formula gives \(3/4\).

Theorem 3.3 does not impose asymptotic flatness on this arbitrary-slice assertion. The example satisfies that assertion’s hypotheses, but is not claimed to satisfy the asymptotic-flatness assumptions of Theorems 1.1 or 1.3.
## Impact and correction

Replace \(F^{-1}\) by \(|\nabla u|^2\), or explicitly restrict the displayed formula to the \(t=0\) slice. The later Lemma 6.6 (p. 20) and the borderline construction (p. 26) already use the correct factor. This counterevidence limits the demonstrated impact to the earlier general-slice statement; it does not establish a defect in the principal construction. The finding is therefore Minor.
# Minor finding: a factor is missing in the inverse metric

Equation (6.8), p. 18, displays the metric and its inverse. Writing \(f=|\nabla u|^{-1}\) and the shift as a column \(Y\), the metric is \[G=\begin{pmatrix}f^2+|Y|^2&Y^T\\Y&I\end{pmatrix}.\] Its correct inverse is \[G^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}
 f^{-2}&-f^{-2}Y^T\\
 -f^{-2}Y&I+f^{-2}YY^T
 \end{pmatrix}.\] The printed lower-right block is \(I+YY^T\), missing \(f^{-2}\). For the admissible positive-definite test \(f=2\), \(Y=(1,0)^T\), exact multiplication of \(G\) by the printed candidate gives \[\begin{pmatrix}1&3/4&0\\0&7/4&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\] rather than the identity. Multiplication by the corrected matrix gives the identity exactly. The first row of the printed inverse, used to recover \(|\nabla u|\) and the normal/shift relation, is correct. No downstream failure of the embedding has been demonstrated from the erroneous lower block. Correcting this displayed matrix is a Minor revision.
# Coverage, dependencies and limits

The analysis included the dimension and regularity thresholds, the finite-end and integrability hypotheses, the leaf-spinor argument, the closed-shift calculation, the constraint identity, the interpolation contradiction, and the coordinate cancellation in the borderline construction. The topology appendix and both figures were read or visually inspected in their actual source pages. In particular, the borderline example is a \(C^{2,\alpha}\) construction; its dimension restriction includes \(n-3-\alpha>(n-2)/2\), so in dimension five one must have \(\alpha<1/2\). It has not been represented as proving optimality for all higher \(s\) by the same construction.

External positive-mass, weighted elliptic and Reeb-stability results were checked for their roles as cited dependencies, but were not each independently reproved or fully retrieved. The global coordinate estimates and every term of the lengthy asymptotic-coordinate calculation were followed in the supplied manuscript; this review does not certify a separate formal derivation of each estimate.

The arXiv version record and the primary publisher landing page were inspected, together with a targeted search for corrections, supplements and associated code. report: Abstract: The review examines the reduction argument and its simple-group applications in the 52-page preprint arXiv:2507.19618v1. A nonbasic spin character of \(\widetilde A_{10}\), labelled by the strict partition \((9,1)\), is rational valued and does not extend to \(\widetilde S_{10}\). It contradicts the exhaustive alternatives in Theorem 7.15(iv), leaving a missing case in the stated proof of the alternating-group application. This is a Major proof issue with a specific local repair. A separate local error concerns the split-class description and spin-character values in Lemma 7.3 and Theorem 7.5. Exact Clifford-matrix calculations and rational symmetric-function calculations support the findings. Neither finding is a counterexample to the Feit conjecture or to the main reduction theorem. Independent scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 27 October 2026

Title: A technical review of
A reduction theorem for the Feit conjecture
# Identity, scope, and outcome

The reviewed work is A reduction theorem for the Feit conjecture, by Robert Boltje, Alexander Kleshchev, Gabriel Navarro, and Pham Huu Tiep [BCNT]. The exact source is arXiv:2507.19618v1, dated 25 July 2025, with 52 PDF pages. All page references below use the one-based PDF page; these agree with the printed numbers in the cited passages. The associated journal identifier is 10.4171/jems/1742 (https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1742). The journal page records publication on 24 November 2025, but no claim is made that its typeset text equals the reviewed preprint. The frozen annual identity is M25-0363.

All 52 pages were read as extracted text, including proofs and references. The review followed the Galois-character-triple conditions, the central-product and primitive-character reductions, the ordinary and spin alternating-group arguments, the Lie-type cases, and the solvable case of Conjecture E. Reading a cited theorem in this manuscript is distinct from independently proving that external theorem. In particular, the stated GAP computations for sporadic and exceptional covering groups were not rerun. No author code was executed.

The supported assessment is Major, arising from Problem 1. Problem 2 is assessed separately as Minor: its corrected formulas preserve the field information used subsequently, so its additional central damage has not been established. Actual inspection of the source evidence images confirms the typeset statements used in both findings. Appendix 6 (#app:repro) records the inspected pages, the earlier image-tool failure, and the separate records binding visual checks to each PDF revision.
# Definitions, hypotheses, and the dependency chain

The paper uses \(\mathcal G=\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}^{\mathrm{ab}}/\mathbb{Q})\). For a nonabelian finite simple group \(S\) and its universal covering group \(X\), Definition 3.1 requires, for every \(\chi\in\operatorname{Irr}(X)\), a proper subgroup \(U<X\) and \(\eta\in\operatorname{Irr}(U)\) such that \(U\) is self-normalizing and intravariant in \(X\), the stabilizers of \(\chi\) and \(\eta\) in \(\Gamma\times\mathcal G\) agree, where \(\Gamma=\operatorname{Aut}(X)_U\), and the specified central Galois-triple relation holds. Theorem 3.2(a) supplies the latter relation when these conditions hold and \([\chi|_U,\eta]=1\).

Theorem A concerns primitive characters and assumes the inductive Feit condition for nonabelian composition factors. The subsequent passage to the Feit conjecture for all characters uses the stronger hypothesis in Corollary B that all relevant simple groups involved satisfy that condition. This distinction matters when induction passes to subgroups. Theorem C asserts the inductive condition for all alternating simple groups. Its concluding proof, Theorem 7.17 on page 37, explicitly combines Theorems 6.3, 7.15, 7.16, and Lemma 5.2. Thus the nonbasic spin-character case of Theorem 7.15 is part of a principal application.

Equation reference: eq:presentation. Write \(D(n)\) for strict partitions of \(n\), \(O(n)\) for partitions with odd parts, and \(\ell(\lambda)\) for the number of parts. The parity convention is that \(\lambda\in D_{\bar0}(n)\) when \(n-\ell(\lambda)\) is even. For a strict partition, \(z_\lambda=\prod_j\lambda_j\). The double cover used on page 33 has central element \(z\) and generators \(t_1,\ldots,t_{n-1}\) with \[
 z^2=1,\qquad t_j^2=z,\qquad (t_jt_{j+1})^3=z,\qquad
 t_jt_k=zt_kt_j\quad (|j-k|>1).\] A spin character has \(z\) acting as \(-1\). For \(\lambda\in D_{\bar0}(n)\) the self-associate irreducible character \(\varphi^\lambda\) of \(\widetilde S_n\) restricts as \(\psi^\lambda_++\psi^\lambda_-\) to \(\widetilde A_n\), with distinct irreducible constituents interchanged by odd conjugation. Basic spin characters correspond to \(\lambda=(n)\).
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (A rational nonextendible nonbasic spin character is omitted).  Theorem 7.15(iv), page 36, is false as an exhaustive alternative. The last paragraph of its even-partition proof incorrectly concludes that the character field always has degree two.
## Claim and complete input

For every nonbasic \(\chi\in\operatorname{Irr}^-(\widetilde A_n)\), Theorem 7.15 claims a suitable \(m\ne n/2\) and \(\eta\in\operatorname{Irr}^-(\widetilde A_{n-m,m})\) satisfying multiplicity one, equality of fields, and one of two alternatives. In paraphrase, these are: (a) \(\mathbb{Q}(\chi)=\mathbb{Q}\) and both characters extend to the respective symmetric covers; or (b) \([\mathbb{Q}(\chi):\mathbb{Q}]=2\), both characters are nonextendible, and their Galois and outer-conjugation orbits coincide.

Equation reference: eq:input. Take \[
 n=10,\qquad \lambda=(9,1),\qquad
 \chi=\psi^\lambda_+\quad\hbox{or}\quad\psi^\lambda_- .\] This is a strict partition, is nonbasic, and satisfies \(n-\ell(\lambda)=8\). The group \(\widetilde A_{10}=2A_{10}\) is the universal cover in the range used by the alternating-group application; \(n\ne6\). The constituents are genuine irreducible spin characters of degree 64. No hypothesis requires a nonsquare discriminant.
## Exact calculation and contradiction

Equation reference: eq:field. Corollary 7.7(i), page 34, gives the field \[
 \mathbb{Q}(\chi)=\mathbb{Q}\!\left(\sqrt{(-1)^{(10-2)/2}z_{(9,1)}}\right)
        =\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt9)=\mathbb{Q}.\] This conclusion also follows from the corrected classical value formula, rather than depending on the faulty piecewise formula discussed below. The sum of the two constituents is \(\varphi^{(9,1)}|_{\widetilde A_{10}}\); their difference is supported on the exceptional split cycle type and has values \(\pm3\) there. The classification and difference formula are also recorded in [Retained latex: \cite[Theorems 4.0.7--4.0.8]{Livesey}]. The remaining values follow from rational Schur \(Q\)-function coefficients, so both constituents are rational valued.

Equation reference: eq:Q. For an exact finite check, the reviewer expanded \[
 q_r=\sum_{\mu\in O(r)}\frac{2^{\ell(\mu)}}{z_\mu}p_\mu,
 \qquad Q_{(9,1)}=q_9q_1-2q_{10}.\] The resulting constituent degree is 64; on cycle type \((9,1)\) the values are \(1\) and \(-2\), with the labels interchanged on the other alternating class. The complete odd-cycle-type calculation appears in Appendix 5 (#app:values). It gives squared norm one and mutual inner product zero, and all values are rational. These checks corroborate the analytic classification; a norm calculation by itself would not construct an arbitrary irreducible character.

Neither constituent extends to \(\widetilde S_{10}\). Indeed, \(\varphi^{(9,1)}\) restricts to two distinct constituents, which are interchanged by the nontrivial coset of \(\widetilde A_{10}\). A character extending to \(\widetilde S_{10}\) would be invariant under that conjugation. Consequently alternative (a) fails by nonextendibility and alternative (b) fails by [eq:field] (#eq:field). These failures concern \(\chi\) alone; no choice of \(m\) or \(\eta\) can make either alternative true.
## Alternative readings and bounded impact

The example is not a basic spin character, a small exceptional cover, or an excluded \(n=6\) case. Interpreting the quadratic-field notation as allowing \(\mathbb{Q}\) does not repair the explicit degree-two requirement. Nor does fixing the overlap in Theorem 7.5 change the square discriminant. The source itself treats square discriminants separately for basic spin characters in Theorem 7.16(b), page 37, but no corresponding case is provided in Theorem 7.15.

The displayed structural theorem is therefore false, and the printed argument for the nonbasic part of Theorem C does not cover this case. This establishes a Major issue in that core application. It does not prove Theorem C false, does not affect the logical content of the conditional reduction in Theorem A, and supplies no counterexample to the Feit conjecture.
## Precise repair and its checked range

For the usual universal double-cover range \(n\ge8\), add a third alternative to Theorem 7.15(iv): \[\mathbb{Q}(\chi)=\mathbb{Q}(\eta)=\mathbb{Q},\qquad
 \chi\text{ does not extend to }\widetilde S_n,\quad
 \eta\text{ does not extend to }\widetilde S_{n-m,m}.\] It arises when the even-partition discriminant is a square. Choose \(\eta\) as in Corollary 7.13(ii). Multiplicity one remains valid, and Corollary 7.11 identifies the two fields. Odd conjugation interchanges the two constituents on each side, while inner conjugation fixes them; hence the stabilizers in the subgroup-preserving automorphism group agree. Both rational characters are fixed by all of \(\mathcal G\), so \((\Gamma\times\mathcal G)_\chi=(\Gamma\times\mathcal G)_\eta\). With the same proper intravariant parabolic subgroup, self-normalizing inside \(X=\widetilde A_n\), Lemma 3.3(i) and Theorem 3.2(a) complete this case. This repairs the omitted route to the inductive condition; it does not make the original two-case assertion true. Exceptional universal covers must still be handled separately as in Lemma 5.2. No author adoption or corrected journal version has been verified.

Problem 2 (Missing average term and missing split classes).  Lemma 7.3 and Theorem 7.5, page 33, omit the extra splitting and the rational average contribution when a strict even partition also has distinct odd parts.
## Claim and admissible boundary

For \(\lambda\in D_{\bar0}(n)\), Theorem 7.5 gives one branch on \(\mu\in O(n)\) and another on \(\mu=\lambda\). These conditions overlap. Take \(n=5\) and \(\lambda=\mu=(5)\). All hypotheses of that theorem hold; unlike Theorem 7.15, it does not exclude basic spin characters. Here \(Q_{(5)}=q_5\) and \([q_5,p_5]=1\). The first printed branch gives \(1/2\); the second gives \(\pm\sqrt5/2\).
## Independent matrices in the stated presentation

Let \[X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1),\] and let \[\gamma_1=X\otimes I,\quad \gamma_2=Y\otimes I,\quad
 \gamma_3=Z\otimes X,\quad \gamma_4=Z\otimes Y,\quad
 \gamma_5=Z\otimes Z.\] Set \(e_j=i\gamma_j\), \(t_j=(e_j-e_{j+1})/\sqrt2\), and \(z=-I_4\). The identities \(e_je_k+e_ke_j=-2\delta_{jk}I_4\) verify every relation in [eq:presentation] (#eq:presentation). Thus the computation uses the cover and generator normalization actually stated in the manuscript.

Equation reference: eq:matrix. Put \(E=(e_1+\cdots+e_5)/\sqrt5\) and \(P_\pm=(I_4\mp iE)/2\). Then \(E^2=-I_4\), \(E\) anticommutes with each \(t_j\), and \(P_\pm\) are rank-two projections commuting with even products. The full-generator commutant has dimension one, and the commutant of the even generators \(t_jt_{j+1}\) has dimension two, as verified by exact linear algebra. Complete reducibility therefore identifies the rank-two summands as distinct irreducible constituents. The irreducible self-associate four-dimensional representation is labelled by \((5)\), the only strict even partition of five. The retained irreducibility script records this check; its exact path and hash are included in the evidence inventory. For the manuscript’s canonical five-cycle lift \(w=t_1t_2t_3t_4\), exact multiplication yields \[
 \operatorname{tr}(w)=1,\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}(P_\pm w)=\frac{1\mp\sqrt5}{2}.\] The characteristic polynomial of \(w\) is \(x^4-x^3+x^2-x+1\). The script checks all defining relations symbolically and evaluates [eq:matrix] (#eq:matrix) exactly. Neither ordering of the two overlapping printed branches produces these values. In particular, \(1/2\) cannot be the value of a finite-group character, since a rational algebraic integer is an integer.

The class count also changes. The five-cycles of \(A_5\) already form two classes. In \(2A_5\), a lift has centralizer of order ten: it is the preimage of the cyclic centralizer of order five, and that preimage is abelian. Its class has size \(120/10=12\). There are 48 elements above all five-cycles, hence four classes, rather than the two claimed for \(\widetilde C_{(5)}\) in Lemma 7.3(ii).
## Correct formula, interpretation, and impact

Equation reference: eq:correct. Write \(\Delta_\lambda=\psi^\lambda_+-\psi^\lambda_-\). The correct relation on the even cover is \[
 \psi^\lambda_\pm(g)=
 \frac{\varphi^\lambda(g)\pm\Delta_\lambda(g)}{2},\] where \(\Delta_\lambda\) vanishes off the exceptional cycle type \(\lambda\) and, on the chosen exceptional lift, is \(i^{(n-\ell(\lambda))/2}\sqrt{z_\lambda}\) up to the constituent labels. When \(\lambda\in O(n)\), the average term need not vanish. Equation [eq:correct] (#eq:correct), with the extra alternating classes retained, gives [eq:matrix] (#eq:matrix); central multiplication changes the signs and odd conjugation interchanges the constituents. The difference formulation in [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 4.0.8(3)]{Livesey}] is consistent with this correction.

This is a numerical and class-theoretic error, not merely a missing citation. Giving priority to either printed branch does not fix it. The missing rational term does not change the quadratic field generated by the values, so Corollary 7.7’s field description can survive. No additional loss of the principal reduction has been established from this error alone; its severity is therefore Minor. Actual inspection of page 33 confirms that the overlapping branches and the two-class statement are present in the typeset source, rather than artifacts of text extraction.
# Coverage, surviving arguments, and conclusion

The central-product construction in Theorem 4.3 was followed through its eight steps, including the use of perfectness to remove a homomorphism into an abelian kernel. The passage through Galois-triple isomorphisms in Theorem 4.7 and the conductor induction in Corollary 4.8 were checked with their respective hypotheses retained. No additional substantive issue was established in those arguments.

The ordinary alternating-character branching argument was examined analytically; an independent enumeration checked its indicated removable-box criterion for 1,546 non-self-conjugate partitions with \(5\le n\le18\). That enumeration is a finite diagnostic, not a replacement for the general proof. The Lie-type analysis was read with the field-automorphism and odd-exponent restrictions retained. The solvable proof of Conjecture E was read separately from the stronger, unproved all-finite-group conjecture. Sporadic character-table computations and the full cited classification theorems remain external dependencies.

A bounded search of the arXiv record, journal record, and title/code/correction queries did not locate accompanying author code or an applicable erratum. This does not establish absence or priority. The Stembridge publisher page was inaccessible during the search; that source is not represented as independently read. The consulted Livesey preprint was read in the relevant classification and Clifford-representation passages, not in its entirety. No change to a later or journal version is presumed.

# Exact values for the counterexample

The rational arithmetic in [eq:Q] (#eq:Q) gives the following values, with one choice of constituent labels. Here \(1^k\) denotes \(k\) fixed points. For type \((9,1)\), odd conjugation exchanges the last two columns. Multiplication by the central involution negates spin values. The values vanish at remaining even cycle types.

For the exceptional type the two alternating classes contribute \((1^2+(-2)^2)/9\) to either norm and \(2(1)(-2)/9\) to the mutual inner product. Each other row contributes \(2v^2/z_\mu\) and \(2v_+v_-/z_\mu\), respectively. The totals are exactly one and zero. The computation is retained in `verification/0363/independent_checks.py` with its actual standard output, error output, execution timestamps, interpreter path, and exit code zero.

 z^2=1,\qquad t_j^2=z,\qquad (t_jt_{j+1})^3=z,\qquad

For \(\lambda\in D_{\bar0}(n)\) the self-associate irreducible character \(\varphi^\lambda\) of \(\widetilde S_n\) restricts as \(\psi^\lambda_++\psi^\lambda_-\) to \(\widetilde A_n\), with distinct irreducible constituents interchanged by odd conjugation. Let \[X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
 Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1),\] and let \[\gamma_1=X\otimes I,\quad \gamma_2=Y\otimes I,\quad
 \gamma_3=Z\otimes X,\quad \gamma_4=Z\otimes Y,\quad
 \gamma_5=Z\otimes Z.\] Set \(e_j=i\gamma_j\), \(t_j=(e_j-e_{j+1})/\sqrt2\), and \(z=-I_4\).  \operatorname{tr}(w)=1,\qquad

report: Abstract: The review covers the 58-page preprint arXiv:2403.11007v2, including its algebraic foundations, nearby-cycle constructions, geometric arguments, Wakimoto filtration and Hecke-algebra application. The specific augmentation bimodule used in Definition and Lemma 2.9 does not give a faithful derived tensor functor. An explicit nonzero map between finite free differential graded modules is sent to zero. This establishes a Major construction issue in the stated Koszul-duality step and the monodromy enhancement that uses it. It does not disprove the existence of a correctly implemented Koszul duality or the underlying geometric conclusions. A two-term complex identifies the missing action and explains why merely resolving the stated bimodule cannot repair the problem. Independent scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 27 October 2026

Title: A technical review of
Central motives on parahoric flag varieties
# Identity, version and scope

The reviewed work is Central motives on parahoric flag varieties, by Robert Cass, Thibaud van den Hove and Jakob Scholbach [paper]. The exact source is arXiv:2403.11007v2, dated 6 December 2025, with 58 PDF pages. Page references below are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed pagination. The associated journal identifier is DOI 10.4171/jems/1748; its public record dates online publication to 8 December 2025 [journal]. No equivalence between the journal typesetting and this preprint has been established. The frozen annual identity is M25-0364.

All 58 pages, including references, were read as extracted text. Fourteen selected source pages were also inspected as actual images: 1, 6–8, 12, 16–17, 22, 32, 38–40, 43 and 48. In particular, the source image on page 7 confirms the exact augmentation-bimodule construction and equations (2.7)–(2.9); the issue below is not an extraction artifact. The displayed diagrams on the inspected pages were checked against their surrounding arguments.

The assessment is Major, for the concrete foundational construction in Problem 1. This is an initial technical review, not independent acceptance or author adoption. External results on motivic six operations, geometric Satake, hyperbolic localization, local models and classical Hecke algebras were followed as cited dependencies; their complete proofs have not all been independently reconstructed.
# Definitions, hypotheses and principal dependencies

Equation reference: eq:E. Section 2.1.2 works in the category \(\mathrm{Ch}^{\mathbb Z}\) of complexes of internally \(\mathbb Z\)-graded abelian groups. Write \(\mathcal D^\mathbb Z\) for its derived category. The polynomial algebra \[\Sigma=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathbb Z(n)=\mathbb Z[t]\] has \(t\) in cohomological degree zero and internal degree \(-1\), with primitive coproduct \(t\mapsto t\otimes1+1\otimes t\). The square-zero differential graded algebra on page 7 is \[
 I=\mathbb Z(-1)[-1],\qquad E=\mathbb Z\oplus I,\qquad I^2=0.\] In cohomological notation its generator \(\epsilon\) has degree \(1\) and internal degree \(1\); all differentials are zero. The source uses the right-induced projective model structure on \(E\)-modules, and a left-induced model structure on \(\Sigma\)-modules whose weak equivalences are the underlying quasi-isomorphisms. Both present the respective usual derived module categories.

The general motivic base \(S\) is connected and smooth of finite type over a Dedekind ring or a field (Notation 2.11). The geometric construction uses a split reductive group and facets in the closure of a fixed alcove. Assertions involving the mixed Tate heart retain the stated Beilinson–Soulé hypothesis, except where reduced motives remove that requirement. Integral motives and rationally defined monodromy are distinguished throughout the review.

The dependency relevant here is specific. Corollary 2.20, whose proof continues on page 12, invokes Lemma 2.9 to identify the reduced Tate category on \(\mathbb G_m\) with \(\operatorname{Nilp}\), and uses rational coefficients for the corresponding unreduced identification. Definition 2.24 then forms the functor with values in \(\operatorname{Nilp}_{\mathbb Q}\operatorname{DTM}(S)\). In the proof of Theorem 3.2, page 16 explicitly forms extension of scalars through this functor. The same foundational construction is repeated in several variables on page 22, and enters the monodromy-compatible convolution construction in Lemma 4.20, page 32. Thus this is an operative step in the paper’s enhanced nearby-cycle construction.
# Substantive finding

Problem 1 (The specified augmentation functor kills a nonzero morphism).  On page 7, the paragraph before (2.7) gives \(\mathbb Z\) its \(\Sigma\)–\(E\) bimodule structure by the two augmentations, in \(\mathrm{Ch}^{\mathbb Z}\). The derived functor of the displayed left Quillen functor \[\mathbb Z\otimes_E-:\operatorname{Mod}_E(\mathrm{Ch}^{\mathbb Z})^{\mathrm r}
       \longrightarrow\operatorname{Mod}_\Sigma(\mathrm{Ch}^{\mathbb Z})^{\mathrm l}\] is not faithful. Consequently the full-faithfulness assertion of Definition and Lemma 2.9, as constructed in (2.7)–(2.9), is false.
## Complete admissible input

Equation reference: eq:input. Use exactly the algebras in [eq:E] (#eq:E), over \(\mathbb Z\), and the strict bimodule specified in the paper. Consider the left \(E\)-modules \[
 A=E\otimes_{\mathbb Z} I=E(-1)[-1],\qquad B=E.\] They are free \(E\)-modules on internally graded complexes consisting of one copy of \(\mathbb Z\) in a single degree. They are therefore cofibrant in the source model structure specified on page 7. They are also compact objects of the derived category. No boundedness, coefficient, finiteness or nilpotence restriction in Lemma 2.9 excludes these inputs.

Equation reference: eq:f. Let \(a=1\otimes\epsilon\) denote the free generator of \(A\), and let \(b=\epsilon a\). Define \[
 f:A\longrightarrow B,\qquad f(a)=\epsilon,\qquad f(b)=0.\] The map has cohomological degree zero and internal degree zero. Indeed, the bidegrees of \(a,b\) are \((1,1),(2,2)\), and those of \(1,\epsilon\) in \(B\) are \((0,0),(1,1)\). The only nonzero image has matching bidegree. It is \(E\)-linear because \(f(\epsilon a)=0=\epsilon f(a)\), and it is a chain map since both differentials vanish.
## The morphism is nonzero in the derived category

Equation reference: eq:nonzero. Since \(A\) is free on \(I\), the derived mapping complex is obtained from the ordinary graded mapping complex: \[\operatorname{RHom}_E(E\otimes I,E)\simeq \operatorname{RHom}_{\mathrm{Ch}^{\mathbb Z}}(I,E).\] The degree-zero, internal-degree-zero maps form \(\mathbb Z\), generated by the inclusion of \(I\) into \(E\). All differentials in this mapping complex are zero, so the indicated class is not a boundary. Equivalently, a chain homotopy would contribute \(d_Bh+hd_A=0\) and cannot kill \(f\). Thus \[
 0\neq[f]\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Mod}_E(\mathcal D^\mathbb Z)}(A,B).\] This argument uses cofibrant inputs; it does not confuse an arbitrary underived map with a nonzero derived morphism.
## Its image under the stated derived functor is zero

Equation reference: eq:zero. Let \(F\) be the derived functor in (2.8), obtained from (2.7) as in the source proof. On the two cofibrant objects [eq:input] (#eq:input) and their map, its value is computed by the stated ordinary tensor construction: \[F(A)=\mathbb Z\otimes_E(E\otimes I)\cong I,\qquad
 F(B)=\mathbb Z\otimes_E E\cong\mathbb Z.\] The left \(\Sigma\)-action on both is the augmentation action. The right \(E\)-action on the bimodule \(\mathbb Z\) also is the augmentation action, so \[
 F(f)(1\otimes a)=1\otimes\epsilon
       =(1\cdot\epsilon)\otimes1=0.\] It follows that \(F(f)=0\) as an actual chain map, and hence as a derived \(\Sigma\)-module morphism. Equations [eq:nonzero] (#eq:nonzero) and [eq:zero] (#eq:zero) contradict faithfulness. The same calculation works after tensoring all data with \(\mathbb Q\); changing to rational coefficients does not remove this defect.

An independent exact calculation retained with this review verifies the square-zero algebra, all bidegrees, \(E\)-linearity of the matrix for \(f\), the rank-one degree-zero mapping group, and the zero map induced in the augmentation quotient. This is a finite corroboration of the explicit witness. The passage to the derived category is justified by the freeness argument above, not by numerical testing.
## Why the proof’s endomorphism calculation does not settle the matter

The resolution \[0\longrightarrow\Sigma(1)\xrightarrow{\,t\,}\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\longrightarrow0\] does compute the graded groups of \(\operatorname{RHom}_\Sigma(\mathbb Z,\mathbb Z)\) and proves the needed compactness of \(\mathbb Z\). It does not show that the particular adjunction unit supplied by the augmentation bimodule is a quasi-isomorphism. An abstract identification of the derived endomorphism algebra with a square-zero algebra cannot replace verification of that unit map. The morphism [eq:f] (#eq:f) tests its positive-degree information directly and is killed by the displayed functor.

One might instead read the notation \(\mathbb Z\) as a derived Koszul bimodule carrying a nontrivial higher action. Such a construction can have different behavior. However, the source explicitly chooses the two augmentation actions in the ordinary category of complexes, then derives the resulting Quillen functor. That explicit construction fixes the interpretation tested here.
## Repair boundary

Equation reference: eq:Kaction. A two-term complex makes the missing information concrete. Set \[K^{-1}=\Sigma u\cong\Sigma(1),\qquad K^0=\Sigma,\qquad d(u)=t,\] where the notation means that \(u\) has cohomological degree \(-1\) and internal degree \(-1\). Give \(K\) the right \(E\)-action \[
 u\epsilon=1,\qquad 1\epsilon=0,\] extended \(\Sigma\)-linearly. Its bidegrees match, its square is zero, and the differential is compatible with the right action. As a left \(\Sigma\)-complex, \(K\) resolves \(\mathbb Z\). Nevertheless, the usual augmentation \(K\to\mathbb Z\) is not a map to the strict augmentation \(\Sigma\)–\(E\) bimodule: it sends \(u\epsilon\) to \(1\), whereas the augmentation of \(u\) multiplied by \(\epsilon\) is zero.

Thus the missing action cannot be supplied by merely taking a resolution within the derived category of the already specified bimodule. A corrected construction must specify a different derived bimodule or an equivalent Koszul-duality implementation, and identify its endomorphism action. The calculation [eq:Kaction] (#eq:Kaction) isolates that necessary change; this review does not assert a full repair of the symmetric monoidal structure, its coherences, or all of the monodromy and convolution compatibilities.
## Impact and severity

This is a Major issue because an asserted foundational fully faithful functor is not even faithful, and that specific functor supplies the paper’s description of \(\operatorname{Nilp}\) and the subsequent monodromy enhancement. The explicit uses in Corollary 2.20, Definition 2.24, the proof of Theorem 3.2, and Section 3.10 must be revisited with a correct construction. The tensor identifications in the monodromy triangle, Proposition 3.9, also require the correct module actions, rather than only an equality of underlying complexes.

The counterexample does not refute a properly implemented Koszul duality. Nor does it establish that the underlying central-motive, Whitney–Tate, Wakimoto or Hecke-algebra conclusions are false. In particular, the construction before retaining monodromy and the geometric arguments have substantial content independent of the specific failed action. The scope of the finding is the construction and its stated proof chain; a repaired proof could preserve the intended conclusions. No author correction or adoption of this repair has been verified.
# Coverage of the remaining arguments

The higher-algebra preliminaries were read with the compact-generation and rigidity assumptions retained. The distinctions between integral and rational formality of the motive of \(\mathbb G_m\), reduced motives, and the finite-characteristic obstruction discussed in Remark 2.19 were kept in scope. The problem established above concerns the later use of the specified bimodule, rather than the mere existence of the polynomial and square-zero algebras.

The nearby-cycle discussion was followed through its proper and smooth functoriality, projection-formula qualifications for trivial families, hyperbolic localization under the stated monodromicity and local linearizability hypotheses, realization comparisons, and the multivariable diagonal and iterated comparisons. Natural comparison maps were not treated as isomorphisms where the paper does not assert that.

In Section 4 the review followed the global and local convolution diagrams, the distinction between étale and Zariski local sections, finite-jet reductions, fixed-point and attractor descriptions, Demazure induction, and the noetherian induction detecting Tateness and anti-effectivity. The proof of Theorem 4.36 reduces the relevant assertions to the trivial family using hyperbolic localization and conservativity. The centrality and monoidality assertions in Theorems 4.38 and 4.41 were checked with their stated homotopy-category coherence scope. The mixed-Tate tensor-product assumption in Theorem 4.49 was retained; no stronger general centrality theorem is inferred.

Section 5 was read through standard and costandard convolution, the invertibility twist, the group-completion construction of Wakimoto functors, the bounded-support criterion and filtration, constant terms, and the shift and twist in Theorem 5.24. The passage to general parahorics in Theorem 5.30 uses a suitable Borel, smooth conservative pullback, and the two one-sided exactness arguments; it does not assume nearby cycles are generally t-exact at the outset.

Section 6 was checked for the sign in the standard basis, the quadratic relation, specialization to a finite-field Hecke algebra, the extra twist in the Bernstein elements, and the triangular basis argument in Theorem 6.9. The central map is asserted to be an isomorphism at Iwahori level; the review does not silently extend that conclusion to arbitrary parahorics. No additional substantive error is established by these checks. This statement records the actual review outcome and does not certify every imported theorem or every higher categorical coherence independently.

A bounded search of the exact arXiv record, journal record, public author pages, and title/code/correction queries did not locate accompanying author code, supplementary data or an applicable erratum. This does not establish their absence or the priority of the present observation. No author code was executed, and lack of code is not a mathematical defect.
# Conclusion
Item | Recorded result
Problem 1 | Major: explicit nonzero derived morphism killed by the specified functor.
Repair | A different bimodule action is necessary; full monoidal and geometric repair remains unverified.
Other conclusions | No independent counterexample to the geometric conclusions established.
Scientific decision | Pending; this is an initial review.
Human reviews | Empty.
Author adoption | Unverified.
# Supporting checks

The finite matrix witness uses the ordered bases \((a,\epsilon a)\) and \((1,\epsilon)\): \[R_\epsilon=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad f=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad (1\ \ 0)\,f\,\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}=0.\] For the illustrative complex \(K\), in the ordered \(\Sigma\)-basis \((1,u)\), the differential and right action are \[d_K=\begin{pmatrix}0&t\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad r_\epsilon=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Both squares and both mixed products vanish. The augmentation row times \(r_\epsilon\) is \((0\ \ 1)\), proving the failure of bimodule linearity stated above. The successful execution used the existing Python runtime and SymPy 1.13.3. An earlier execution reached the mathematical assertions but failed when serializing SymPy integers to JSON; its unchanged script, exit-one record and error output are preserved. That reporting failure is not attributed to the authors.

The source manifest, metadata, complete extracted text, selected source images, actual visual observations, evidence and complete support inventory are retained in the allocated staging directories. Source image inspection covers the selected fourteen pages; full text reading covers all 58.

Compilation uses the existing approved Tectonic 0.17.0 runtime with shell escape disabled. Exact TeX, compiler and dependency payloads before and after compilation, commands, exit codes, PDF parsing, and actual final-page inspection are recorded separately. Rendering alone is not visual inspection, and delivery is marked complete only after the final PDF and those records are checked.

report: Abstract: This review examines the 41-page preprint arXiv:2310.20674v3. The printed velocity-reconstruction matrix can be singular at a frequency in the upper half-plane and does not follow from the stated Euler equations. A separate defect occurs in the Sobolev semigroup bootstrap: its stated Hölder exponent does not exist, and a subsequent estimate has the wrong target integrability. These are Major issues in the written derivation, with identifiable routes to repair. Exact elimination confirms the underlying radial Rayleigh equation and its Liouville transformation. Further local corrections concern a nonuniform potential bound, the sign of the eigenvalue correction, the complex Hermite scaling, and a strict hypothesis that excludes the advertised constant-pitch example. No counterexample to the two principal instability conclusions is established. Independent scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 27 October 2026

Title: A technical review of
Linear and nonlinear instability of vortex columns
# Identity, scope, and dependency chain

The reviewed work is by Dallas Albritton and Wojciech S. Ożański [paper]. Its exact source is arXiv:2310.20674v3, dated 8 December 2025, comprising 41 PDF pages. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with the printed numbers. The associated journal DOI is https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1749; the publisher records online publication on 11 December 2025. The journal full text was not substituted for the bound preprint, and equality of those versions is not presumed. The frozen annual identifier is M25-0365.

All 41 pages were read as extracted text, including the appendix and bibliography. Seventeen selected source pages, including both figures and every principal evidence display discussed below, were also inspected as actual images. The review follows both the inner–outer construction and the nonlinear argument, retaining their different hypotheses.

In the linear part, the mode convention is \(e^{i(\alpha z-n\theta)}\), \(\lambda=-i\omega\), and \[\beta=\alpha/n,\qquad \gamma=\alpha W-nV/r-\omega=n\Lambda-\omega.\] Assumption A requires smooth even extensions of \(\Omega=V/r\) and \(W\), decay of their derivatives, positive bounded pitch, and a distinguished \(r_0,\beta>0\) with \(b'(r_0)=\Lambda'(r_0)=0\), \(b_0>0\), \(\Lambda''(r_0)>0\), and no other finite point at the same value of \(\Lambda\). Theorem 1.1 constructs localized radial solutions near this point; Section 3.2 must then recover a velocity eigenfunction.

The nonlinear theorem separately assumes a smooth bounded background, decay \(|\bar\omega|+r|\nabla\bar\omega|\lesssim r^{-b}\), \(b>0\), and an unstable vorticity eigenfunction in \(L^Q_\sigma\), \(1<Q<2\). It seeks arbitrarily small \(L^Q\cap H^N\) initial vorticity perturbations whose velocities later separate in \(L^\infty\). Its proof uses modewise spectral theory, the \(H^k\) semigroup estimate of Lemma 3.5, finitely many Picard iterates, a high-order remainder estimate, and a backward-time limiting solution. Neither a uniform estimate over all Fourier modes nor instability in the energy norm is among the proved statements under review.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The stated velocity recovery can fail at an unstable frequency).  Equation (1.13), page 4, and its following determinant assertion are false as printed. The defect affects the recovery used in Section 3.2 and Corollary 3.2, pages 26–27.

Complete counterexample to the recovery assertion. Use the smooth Batchelor profiles with \(q=1/2\), and put \[E=e^{-1},\quad r=n=\alpha=1,\quad
 \omega=-\tfrac12+E+\tfrac i2 E,\quad
 u_r(1)=1,\quad u_r'(1)=-1.\] Here \(V(1)=(1-E)/2\), \(W(1)=E\), and \(\operatorname{Im}\omega=E/2>0\). The right side is \((-E,0)^{\mathsf T}\). The printed matrix is \[\begin{pmatrix}
 i(-1+i)E/2&i(1-i)E/2\\ i&-i
 \end{pmatrix}.\] Its rank is one, whereas its augmentation by the stated right side has rank two. Indeed, the second row requires \(u_z=u_\theta\), making the first left side zero, although its required value is \(-E\). The corrected matrix has determinant \((-1+i)E\) and gives \(u_z=u_\theta=(1-i)/2\).

These are admissible local Cauchy data for the radial equation: its coefficients are analytic near \(r=1\), its leading coefficient is nonzero, and \(\gamma\) cannot vanish because \(\operatorname{Im}\omega>0\). Local ODE existence supplies the corresponding radial solution. This tests the general reconstruction identity preceding Assumption A. It is not presented as a global \(H^1_0\) eigenmode or as a counterexample satisfying the separate, literally strict pitch condition in Assumption A.

Impact and repair. This is a Major defect in the stated passage from a radial solution to an Euler mode, not a merely cosmetic change to a determinant. Its repair is explicit: use [eq:recovery] (#eq:recovery) and [eq:det] (#eq:det). Independent symbolic elimination of pressure then gives exactly (1.9); the residual after comparison is zero. The Liouville substitution (1.17) also gives precisely the potential (1.19)–(1.20). Consequently this calculation does not disprove the radial construction or the possibility of the claimed velocity instability. The endpoint regularity argument must be attached to the corrected recovery formula.
Problem 2 (A missing estimate in the nonlinear semigroup bootstrap).  The derivation of Lemma 3.5 on page 31 does not justify its \(L^Q\cap H^k\) growth estimate as written.

The displayed estimate (3.35) invokes \[\|\bar\omega\cdot\nabla u\|_2
 \lesssim \|\bar\omega\|_p\|\nabla u\|_Q,\qquad
 \frac12=\frac1p+\frac1Q.\] For every allowed \(1<Q<2\), it requires \(1/p<0\). For example, the fully admissible value \(Q=3/2\) requires \(1/p=-1/6\). There is no Hölder exponent \(p\in[1,\infty]\) satisfying this relation.

For \(Q<6/5\), (3.37) estimates another forcing term in \(L^{6/5}\), whereas (3.39) requires an \(L^2\) forcing bound. The transport matrix semigroup in (3.33) is a multiplication operator and supplies no spatial smoothing. Even on one fixed Fourier mode, \(L^{6/5}\) control cannot alone imply \(L^2\) control: for a nonzero smooth function \(\chi\) supported in \((-1/4,1/4)\), \[f_\epsilon(r,\theta,z)
 =\epsilon^{-5/6}\chi((r-1)/\epsilon)e^{2i\theta}e_z\] is smooth, divergence-free, independent of \(z\), and supported away from the axis. Its \(L^{6/5}\) norm is bounded above and below independently of \(\epsilon\), while \(\|f_\epsilon\|_2\asymp\epsilon^{-1/3}\). This demonstrates the missing implication between the forcing norms. It does not assert that every such \(f_\epsilon\) is the particular nonlinear or Biot–Savart forcing of the manuscript.

Repair route and its limits. One must estimate the actual modewise operator \(B_{n,\alpha}\), using the derivative gain of velocity and the mode identities, rather than use the impossible exponent. For \(\alpha\ne0\), the two-dimensional resolvent \((-\Delta_{x'}+\alpha^2)^{-1}\) on this fixed axial mode gives an order-minus-one velocity operator; its kernel is locally of size \(|x'|^{-1}\) and decays at infinity. Young’s inequality with \(1/s=3/2-1/Q\), \(1<s<2\), gives \(\|u\|_2\lesssim_{\alpha,Q}\|\omega\|_Q\). The mode identity for \(\bar\omega\cdot\nabla u\) has bounded coefficients multiplying \(u\), and the other term is treated similarly.

For \(\alpha=0\), Lemma 3.1 supplies \(u\in L^{Q_2^*}\), \(Q_2^*=2Q/(2-Q)>2\). The coefficients in the modewise forcing are bounded near the axis and decay like \(r^{-b-1}\) at infinity. They belong to \(L^{Q/(Q-1)}(\mathbb R^2)\), giving the required \(L^2\) estimate by \[\frac12=\frac1{Q_2^*}+\frac{Q-1}{Q}.\] These observations identify a valid replacement for the base forcing estimate. The corresponding higher-derivative argument, with Cartesian components and coefficient bounds retained, should be written out; it is not supplied merely by changing the sign of the exponent in (3.35).

There is also a loss of the arbitrarily small spectral slack between (3.31) and (3.49), page 32. Lemma 3.5 provides \(e^{(S+\delta)t}\), not automatically \(e^{St}\). Choosing \(0<\delta<2a-S\) preserves the convergence of the backward integral. The estimates on Picard iterates used subsequently need only hold for \(t\le0\), not all \(t\in\mathbb R\) as printed.

The missing Sobolev bootstrap is Major because it is an essential input to the high-order nonlinear construction. This is a supported proof issue, not a claimed counterexample to nonlinear instability. The stated repair route is not an author-adopted correction or a completed replacement proof of all of Lemma 3.5.

Problem 3 (The first real-part bound is not uniform on its stated range).  The assertion \(\operatorname{Re}k=O(n^{3/2})\) in (2.58), page 16, is false on the full interval \(Cn^{-3/4}\le |r-r_0|\le C^{-1}n^{-1/2}\).

Equation reference: eq:scale. Fix any background satisfying the local hypotheses, choose \(\omega=\omega_{\rm app}\), and set \(r_n=r_0+c n^{-1/2}\), where \(0<c<C^{-1}\) is fixed. These points lie in that interval for all sufficiently large \(n\), and \(|\omega-\omega_{\rm app}|=0\) satisfies the frequency hypothesis for every \(B\ge1\). Write \(s=\sqrt{b_0}>0\) and \(t=\Lambda''(r_0)c^2/2>0\). The stated definitions and Taylor hypotheses give \[\frac{k(r_n)}{n^2}\longrightarrow
 p_0\left(1+\frac{s^2}{(t-is)^2}\right),\] and exact algebra yields \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{Re}k(r_n)}{n^2}
 =p_0\frac{t^2(t^2+3s^2)}{(t^2+s^2)^2}>0.
 \] This is incompatible with the claimed uniform \(O(n^{3/2})\) bound. Making \(C\) large does not remove the contradiction for fixed \(C\).

The coercivity argument only needs a lower bound on the negative part. Near this scale, the leading real expression in [eq:scale] (#eq:scale) is nonnegative; perturbing \(b\), \(p\), and the imaginary part of \(\omega\) gives the weaker bound \(\operatorname{Re}k\ge -C_1n^{3/2}\), which can be combined with the positive imaginary part. The incorrect two-sided size estimate should be replaced by that lower bound, and Figure 2 should be interpreted accordingly. No loss of outer coercivity is established by the positive \(n^2\) term. This issue is assessed as Minor, with the scope of the replacement stated explicitly.

Problem 4 (The eigenvalue-correction term has the wrong sign).  Equations (2.7), (2.76), (2.87), and (A.3), on pages 10, 20, 21, and 36, put a positive \(i\) in the leading \(\widehat\omega\) term of the potential error. The definitions give a negative \(i\).

At \(r_0\), \(\gamma=-is-\mu_m-\widehat\omega\), \(s=\sqrt{b_0}\). Direct differentiation gives \[\left.\frac{d}{dh}\left(1+\frac{s^2}{(-is-h)^2}\right)\right|_{h=0}
 =-\frac{2i}{s}.\] Consequently, on the prescribed scale, \[k_{\rm err}(r_0)=-\frac{2ip_0n^2}{s}\widehat\omega+O(n).\] For \(\widehat\omega=d\,n^{-1/2}\) with fixed sufficiently small nonzero \(d\), the difference from the printed sign is of order \(n^{3/2}\), which cannot be hidden in the stated \(O(n)\) remainder at \(r=r_0\). The displayed calculation (A.4) itself has the negative sign.

Both leading terms \(f\) and \(g\) in the reduced equation must receive the corrected sign. Their absolute-value estimates and the nonvanishing leading coefficient in Rouché’s theorem are unchanged. The magnitude bounds and qualitative zero count can therefore survive this correction; this local issue is assessed as Minor. The manuscript’s complex-valued Taylor remainder on page 38 should also be written in integral form, rather than requiring a single real intermediate point for both real and imaginary parts.
Problem 5 (The complex Hermite argument is misstated).  Lemma 2.5, page 14, gives \(G_m(e^{i\zeta}\,\cdot)\) where the eigenspace requires \(G_m(e^{i\zeta/2}\,\cdot)\).

The admissible choice \(m=1\), \(\zeta=\pi/4\) makes the printed function \(G_1(e^{i\pi/4}x)=e^{-ix^2/2}\), whose absolute value is one. It is not in \(L^2(\mathbb R)\), and substitution also fails the stated eigenvalue equation. The corrected function is \(e^{-e^{i\pi/4}x^2/2}\); direct differentiation verifies its eigenvalue \(-e^{i\pi/4}\) for \(d^2/dx^2-ix^2\). The correct half-angle already occurs in (2.34), (2.51), and Corollary 2.7, and is compatible with the standard parabolic-cylinder normalization [dlmf]. Correct the repeated argument in (2.52) and Remark 2.8 as well. Since the actual Weber ansatz and the adjoint range calculation use the half-angle, this is a Minor inconsistency, not evidence against the intended oscillator spectrum.

Problem 6 (The written pitch hypothesis excludes the stated example).  Assumption A, page 4, contains \(0<\inf q<\sup q<+\infty\), but the paragraph immediately following it identifies a constant-pitch Batchelor vortex as an example satisfying the assumption.

For its displayed profiles, \[-\frac{(rV)'}{W'}=q\qquad(r>0).\] Hence \(\inf q=\sup q\), and the middle strict inequality fails. This is an explicit mismatch of hypotheses and application, not an inadmissible counterexample to Theorem 1.1. The appropriate condition for the stated example is \(0<\inf q\le\sup q<+\infty\). The proof uses positive upper and lower bounds, not strict variation of the pitch. The Appendix A.1 parameter argument concerns the other conditions (1.14) and does not change this strict inequality. This local hypothesis correction is assessed as Minor.
# Coverage, surviving checks, and limitations

The inner construction was followed through its scaled Weber operator, closed range, adjoint projection, Gaussian estimate, overlapping cutoffs, and the projected-system contraction. The scalar solvability equation was checked against its nonzero bilinear integral and the Rouché radius. The two cases of reverse gluing were read separately; the corrected half-angle and frequency-error sign are needed consistently. This review does not claim a new proof of every cited theorem of Kato or of the full parabolic-cylinder asymptotic theory.

The outer estimates were checked by separating the \(n^{-3/4}\), \(n^{-1/2}\), and fixed-radius regimes. Besides Problem 3, the first estimate in the proof on page 17, \(|k-pn^2|\lesssim n^{-2}\), is not the order obtained by inserting \(\gamma=O(n)\): the lower-order terms generically contribute \(O(1)\). The needed relative control is weaker. A global lower bound for \(|\Lambda-\Lambda(r_0)|\) outside a finite neighborhood also needs care if \(\Lambda(r_0)=0=\lim_{r\to\infty}\Lambda(r)\); compact separation alone is insufficient. Decay of \(a,b\) provides a separate far-field route. These qualifications are retained rather than treated as counterexamples to coercivity.

For the nonlinear part, the zero and nonzero axial Biot–Savart components, modewise compact perturbation argument, smoothness bootstrap, finite-mode Picard construction, remainder energy estimate, and compactness passage were all read. The derivative-loss strategy and the choice \(2a>S\) are coherent once the required semigroup estimate and spectral slack are supplied. The argument estimates only finitely many modes at each fixed iteration; a uniform bound over all modes was not assumed. The exclusion of \((\pm1,0)\) in the selection on page 32 requires justification if used in full generality. No new unstable mode restricted to those indices was constructed here, so this point is retained as a limitation, not a confirmed counterexample.

The direct calculation also reproduces the parameter values in Figure 1 for \(q=1/4\): \[r_0=0.825200682117\ldots,\qquad
 \beta=0.158943819853\ldots,\qquad
 \sqrt{b_0}=0.193664783541\ldots.\] The sufficient threshold is \(1.251296996204\ldots\). These floating-point checks are diagnostics of the figure and appendix; the substantive contradictions above use exact algebra or asymptotic limits, not numerical guesses. The threshold is not a proof of stability outside the stated interval, and physical vortex breakdown is not a conclusion of the theorem.

A bounded search of the exact arXiv record, publisher page, author publication pages, and title/identifier queries for corrections, supplements, and code located no applicable correction or accompanying author code. One current author-site URL was inaccessible through the search tool, and some search results were irrelevant. This is a search limitation, not evidence of absence or priority. No author code was executed, and lack of code is not a mathematical defect. The full journal text and the paper’s full external reference list were not independently re-proved or presumed equivalent to the reviewed version.

The overall assessment is Major, based on the velocity-recovery failure and the missing nonlinear semigroup justification. Explicit local repairs and surviving calculations are recorded. Neither principal instability theorem has been disproved by this review.

report: Abstract: This review examines the exact preprint arXiv:2309.15382v3. The definition of intertwining permits a union of a horizontal and a vertical invariant line. Consequently the nonempty generic rigidity assertion used in the main proof cannot hold under that definition. A separate problem concerns the all-critical-point PCE and PR assertions in the dynamical André–Oort argument: persistently periodic critical sections violate them identically. These are Major issues in the stated proof chain, with specific, bounded repair routes. A missing cycle-length factor in the elementary counting lemma is a Minor error whose correction preserves its conclusion. None of these findings gives a counterexample to generic injectivity of the multiplier spectrum. Independent scientific adjudication remains pending.
