Title: A technical review of
The multiplier spectrum morphism is generically injective
# Identity, scope, and proof structure

The reviewed work is The multiplier spectrum morphism is generically injective, by Zhuchao Ji and Junyi Xie [target], frozen identity M25-0366. The exact source has 22 PDF pages and is arXiv:2309.15382v3, submitted on 22 September 2025; its first page separately prints 23 September 2025. The associated DOI is https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1750. The journal record dates online publication to 7 November 2025. No equality between the journal full text and the reviewed preprint is presumed. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with the printed numbers.

All 22 pages, including proofs, the alternative approach, and references, were read as extracted text. Twelve source pages and six reference pages were also actually inspected as images. This is an initial scientific review, neither an independent acceptance nor a human review.

For degree \(d\geq2\), \(S_n\) encodes the multipliers of all \(d^n+1\) fixed points of \(f^n\), counted with fixed-point multiplicity. The descending closed equivalence relations defined by the truncated data stabilize by Noetherianity. The resulting \(\tau_d\) must have a singleton full fiber at a generic point (Definition 1.2). The theorem is generic injectivity, not injectivity everywhere.

For \(d\geq4\), the proof combines disjoint-type PCF parameters, curves with \(2d-3\) prescribed superattracting cycles, a non-diagonal finite étale fiber relation for \(\tau_d\), a two-family DAO argument, and generic rigidity of intertwined simple maps. Degrees two and three are treated by external results. The stated conjectures about small periods, length spectra, and the full exceptional locus are kept separate from the proved claims.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The reducible-curve definition makes the rigidity premise universal).  Definition 3.1, page 11, permits a reducible invariant curve whose two projections are surjective. Under this definition every pair of rational maps is intertwined. Thus the nonempty form of Theorem 3.3 used on pages 15 and 17 is false.

Complete counterconstruction. Let \(d\geq4\), and let \(f,g\in\operatorname{Rat}_d(\mathbb C)\) be arbitrary. Each map has a fixed point on \(\mathbb P^1\); choose \(f(p)=p\) and \(g(q)=q\). Set \[Z=(\{p\}\times\mathbb P^1)\ \cup\ (\mathbb P^1\times\{q\}).\] This is a closed, reduced, pure one-dimensional algebraic curve. Both projections of the whole \(Z\) are surjective. Since a nonconstant rational self-map of \(\mathbb P^1\) is surjective, \((f\times g)(Z)=Z\). Thus every requirement of Definition 3.1 holds, including equality invariance.

Suppose the open set \(W_d\) used in Theorem 3.3 were nonempty, and choose \(f\in W_d\). Choose \(g\) in the simple-map locus outside the closure of the conjugacy orbit of \(f\). Such a \(g\) exists: the simple locus is a nonempty open subset of the \(2d+1\)-dimensional variety \(\operatorname{Rat}_d\), whereas a \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\)-orbit and its closure have dimension at most three. Now \(f\in W_d\), \(g\) is simple, and \(f,g\) are intertwined by the displayed \(Z\), but they are not conjugate. This construction works for every possible \(f\) in any proposed nonempty \(W_d\); it does not assume that a chosen numerical map belongs to an unspecified generic set.

Impact and alternative readings. Theorem 3.3 does not explicitly say that \(W_d\) is nonempty, so the empty set would make its isolated existential statement vacuous. That reading cannot supply the explicitly nonempty open \(U\) on page 15. Reading surjectivity component by component adds a condition absent from Definition 3.1. The issue affects the central rigidity implication used to close the main contradiction. It is Major, even though the necessary correction is short.

Bounded repair. Require finite projections, or a periodic irreducible component dominating both factors. A finite product self-map permutes the components of an invariant finite union, so a component is invariant under an iterate. The consulted version of Pakovich’s Theorem 1.4 [pak], page 3, expressly assumes an irreducible curve that is neither horizontal nor vertical. It applies to this corrected situation, followed by the same-entropy rigidity step.

The objects \(\operatorname{Corr}(\mathbb P^1)^{f_t\times g_t}_*\) actually introduced on page 14 have finite projections. Thus the DAO construction aims at a stronger object capable of supporting the repair. The correction changes the definition and the valid theorem interface; it does not prove the original broad assertion. No counterexample to Theorem 1.3 is established.

Problem 2 (The all-critical-point typicality assertions are false).  The PCE and PR definitions on page 12 quantify over every marked critical point. Assertions (4) and (5) on page 14 then claim these properties almost everywhere under Theorem 3.4’s hypotheses. These claims fail for admissible families and for the periodic critical sections in the main construction.

An explicit family satisfying all theorem hypotheses. Take \(V=\mathbb A^1_\mathbb C\) and \(f_t(z)=g_t(z)=z^2+t\). These are algebraic degree-two families, non-isotrivial, and not flexible Lattès families. The product of the two finite fixed-point multipliers is \(4t\), which verifies non-isotriviality. Equality of the two families is allowed.

There are infinitely many simultaneous PCF parameters. Put \[P_1(t)=t,\qquad P_{n+1}(t)=P_n(t)^2+t.\] Then \(P_n(t)=f_t^n(0)\), its degree is \(2^{n-1}\), and its linear coefficient is one. For each prime \(p\), \(P_p\) has a simple zero at zero and at least one other complex zero. At a nonzero zero, \(0\) has exact period \(p\): its period divides \(p\) and cannot be one. Different primes give distinct parameters. Infinity is fixed, so these parameters are PCF.

In the coordinate \(w=1/z\), the family near infinity is \[w\longmapsto \frac{w^2}{1+tw^2}.\] The marked critical section at infinity is constant and fixed. At every iterate its parameter derivative and its distance to the critical set are zero. Neither a positive exponential PCE lower bound nor the PR lower bound can hold at any parameter. The obstruction is not a null exceptional set.

Even restricting to the active section \(c_0(t)=0\) leaves the printed PCE condition at \(n=0\) false: \[\frac{d}{dt}f_t^0(c_0(t))=0.\] A finite-prefix convention is necessary as well as the restriction on critical points.

Direct relevance to the main families. For a persistently periodic critical section \(c\) of period \(r\), \[\xi_{c,kr}(t)=c(t),\qquad
 \left\|d\xi_{c,kr}(t)/dt\right\|=\left\|dc(t)/dt\right\|.\] At a fixed parameter the right-hand side is finite and independent of \(k\); it cannot dominate \(C\lambda^{kr}\) with \(C>0,\lambda>1\). At the same iterates the distance to the critical set is zero. The curves in Lemma 2.5 and (3.1) have persistently periodic critical points after marking. Thus the literal conditions (4),(5) are incompatible with the families used by the main argument.

Dependency check and repair boundary. The consulted DAO preprint [dao] defines conditions for a marked pair. Its proof on page 52, condition (b), restricts them to active critical points; Proposition 7.8, page 50, uses the selected marked points. This supports a repair using only the active \(a_1,b_1\). The cited preprint’s Definition 4.1 also prints \(n\geq0\), so citing that definition alone does not fix the constant-section obstruction. One must allow a finite initial prefix, or pass to iterated marked sections and check measure scaling and renormalization hypotheses. The last paragraph on target page 14 also switches from \(b_1\) to \(b_2\); the active point must be kept consistent.

This is a Major issue in the stated DAO proof: the purported full-measure set supplying its inputs can be empty. The contradictions are established; a complete replacement of the deep two-family argument is not claimed. The diagonal intertwines the explicit example even in the stronger sense, so it is not a counterexample to Theorem 3.4 or generic injectivity. Section 3.4 is an outline, not an independently expanded replacement proof in this review.
Problem 3 (The cycle-count inversion omits cycle length).  The two counting formulas at the end of Lemma 3.5’s proof, page 16, confuse cycles with fixed points.

Write \(u_n\) for the number of zero multipliers among fixed points of \(f^n\), and \(m_\ell\) for the number of critical cycles of exact length \(\ell\). Each such cycle contributes \(\ell\) points when \(\ell\mid n\). These are simple fixed points of \(f^n\), since a zero multiplier makes the derivative of the local fixed-point equation equal to \(-1\). Thus \[u_n=\sum_{\ell\mid n}\ell m_\ell,\qquad
 m_n=\frac1n\sum_{\ell\mid n}\mu(\ell)u_{n/\ell}.\] The printed formulas omit \(\ell\) and \(1/n\).

For \(f(z)=z^2-1\), the critical cycles are fixed infinity and \(0\mapsto-1\mapsto0\). This is a degree-two hyperbolic PCF map of disjoint type \((1,2)\); choosing \(g=f\) also meets the same-spectrum premise. Here \(u_1=1,u_2=3\), while \(m_2=1\). The printed inversion gives two. An independent exact polynomial calculation of the greatest common divisors of \(f^n(z)-z\) and \((f^n)'(z)\), with infinity added, verified \[(u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4)=(1,3,1,3),\qquad
 (m_1,m_2,m_3,m_4)=(1,1,0,0).\] This is Minor: the corrected identities still determine every critical cycle length. Having \(2d-2\) distinct superattracting cycles exhausts the critical-point budget, so Lemma 3.5’s intended conclusion survives.
# Remaining coverage and qualifications

The Noetherian truncation and full-fiber injectivity were checked. In Lemma 2.5, application of the curve lemma to a higher-dimensional critical-relation locus requires a non-isotrivial curve slice. If the remaining critical point were persistently preperiodic, a forbidden non-isotrivial PCF family would already result. These are relevant implicit steps; no counterexample to that lemma was constructed.

The off-diagonal finite étale relation in Section 3.3 was followed through its curve lifts and common base change. Dominant curve maps may be restricted to dense opens. The equality of spectra and inequality of conjugacy classes were distinguished from the faulty final rigidity interface. The reduction to \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\), active bifurcation measures, transcendental-parameter lifting, and CE/TCE implications were read with their external dependencies retained.

The polynomial proof is brief. Reusing the rational-map count of prescribed relations requires adaptation to the number of finite polynomial critical points. Its cited rigidity results and the full Favre–Gauthier monograph were not independently reconstructed. This review also does not independently reprove the full arithmetic equidistribution, every distortion estimate in the DAO paper, the low-degree external results, or Remark 1.6’s Berkovich specialization sketch. These are coverage limits, not asserted counterexamples.

A bounded search of the exact arXiv and journal records and of the title with code, supplement, and correction terms found no applicable supplementary artifact or erratum. Absence and priority are not established. No author code was executed. The two reference PDFs were consulted only in the recorded passages; later published versions are not silently substituted.
The supported overall assessment is Major, arising from Problems 1 and 2. Problem 3 has a complete elementary correction. This review has not disproved the main generic-injectivity theorem.

Title: A technical review of
Trace field degrees in the Torelli group
# Identity, scope, and dependency structure

The reviewed work is Trace field degrees in the Torelli group, by Erwan Lanneau and Livio Liechti [source]. The exact input is arXiv:2405.17194v2, dated 12 December 2025, with 25 PDF pages. The associated journal identifier is DOI 10.4171/jems/1752; its publication page records 8 December 2025. The journal text and the author’s separately linked manuscript have not been assumed identical to this input. The frozen annual identifier is M25-0367. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed numbering.

Theorems 1 and 2 concern existence in the Torelli group for every genus \(g\geq2\), with trace degrees \(1\leq d\leq3g-3\) and stretch degrees \(2d\). Theorem 3 uses filling multicurves; its Torelli construction applies for \(g\geq3\), while the genus-two Torelli case is supplied separately by the words on page 3. For an intersection matrix \(X\), write \(\mu\) for the Perron eigenvalue of \(XX^\top\). The intersection degree is \([\mathbb Q(\mu):\mathbb Q]\), whereas the bipartite degree is \([\mathbb Q(\sqrt\mu):\mathbb Q]\). These are distinct from the stretch factor degree.

Theorem 4 obtains the quadratic extension over the trace field after choosing powers of the multitwists. Its norm argument, the nonzero roots of the reciprocal minimal polynomial, and the eventual-square argument were followed with their quantifiers retained. In the Torelli application the exponent signs are opposite. Separating twists act trivially on homology, and matched bounding pairs give equal actions for the two multitwists; their opposite powers therefore remain in Torelli. Section 6 instead studies same-sign products without the adjustable power supplied by Theorem 4. The paper explicitly makes that section independent of Theorems 1–3.

All 25 pages, including the references, were read as extracted text. Nineteen source pages were also inspected as images, including all eleven numbered figures, the genus-two diagram, and the decisive displays below. The assessment is Major, arising from Problem 1. It is an initial review; independent scientific adjudication remains pending.
# Findings

Problem 1 (The signature argument does not cover all allowed parameters).  Theorem 14, page 22, is stated for an example described in Section 6.1. In Case 2 of its proof, page 23, a one-dimensional block parameter is then set to \(3\) without retaining that restriction in the statement or in the preceding construction.
#### Exact admissible construction.

Equation reference: C. Take \(g=3\), \(d=4\), so that \(f=2g-d=2\) in Section 6.1, Case 2. In Figure 11 take \(k=2\) and remove both handle-separating red components. The remaining one-dimensional block parameters may be any positive distinct integers, as page 22 expressly allows. Choose \[y_1=5,\qquad y_2=6,\qquad y_{\rm inner}=10.\] There are \(10^2-2=98\) copies of the inner connecting blue curve. The matrix before closure is \[A=\begin{pmatrix}400&2&2\\2&5&0\\2&0&6\end{pmatrix}.\] Close the surface by the construction on pages 12–13, using \(y_{\rm close}=20\). Since \(A_{11}/4=100\), the new blue curve has \(20^2-100=300\) copies, a positive integer. The resulting matrix is \[
 C=XX^\top=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 400&200&1&1\\200&400&2&2\\1&2&5&0\\1&2&0&6
 \end{pmatrix}.\] Thus this is the stated filling construction, with its permitted positive multiplicities; it does not rely on a hypothetical matrix unrelated to the curves. More explicitly, an intersection matrix has the following column types and multiplicities: \[\begin{array}{c|rrrrrr}
\text{column}&(1,2,1,0)^\top&(0,0,1,0)^\top&(1,2,0,1)^\top&
(0,0,0,1)^\top&(1,2,0,0)^\top&(1,0,0,0)^\top\\
\text{multiplicity}&1&4&1&5&98&300
\end{array}\] These give a \(4\times409\) matrix \(X\) and reproduce [C] (#C) exactly.
#### Decisive calculation.

Equation reference: failure. The successive leading principal minors of \(C-4I\) are \[396,\qquad116816,\qquad115636,\qquad230092.\] Sylvester’s criterion proves that every eigenvalue of \(C\) exceeds \(4\). For \(\Omega=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&X\\X^\top&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the eigenvalues other than zero are the four pairs \(\pm\sqrt{\mu_j}\). Consequently \(\Omega+2I\) has \(409\) positive and four negative eigenvalues, and no zero eigenvalues. Its dimension is \(413\), so \[
 \sigma(\Omega+2I)+\operatorname{null}(\Omega+2I)=405
 =\dim\Omega-2d.\] The strict lower inequality in equation (1), page 22, fails. This is a counterexample to the assertion that the stated construction automatically satisfies the criterion used to prove Theorem 14.

The issue is substantive for this proof: replacing a freely chosen block parameter by \(3\) changes the example. It cannot prove the asserted conclusion for the original parameters. The shifts in the signature notation on pages 23–24 should also be written consistently as \(\Omega'+2I\); restoring that shift does not change [failure] (#failure).
#### What is and is not disproved.

This calculation does not disprove the stretch degree conclusion. Indeed, the independently calculated polynomial \[\begin{split}
 z^4\chi_C(2+z+z^{-1})={}&z^8-803z^7+123982z^6-838374z^5\\
 &+1660480z^4-838374z^3+123982z^2-803z+1
\end{split}\] is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). Thus this particular example has the claimed degree eight. The confirmed defect is failure of the proof’s decisive criterion over the theorem’s declared parameter range, assessed as Major. No false universal stretch-degree statement is inferred from failure of a sufficient criterion.
#### Bounded repair.

An existentially chosen subfamily can retain one remaining one-dimensional block parameter \(y_i\leq3\), with the other parameters fixed distinctly and the large free parameters selected by the same irreducibility construction. A Rayleigh quotient then gives an eigenvalue below \(4\); sufficiently large free parameters also give an eigenvalue above \(4\). Hence the number of eigenvalues above \(4\) lies strictly between \(0\) and \(d\), which is precisely the signature requirement. This repairs a suitably restricted existence formulation. It does not supply a proof of the unrestricted Theorem 14. The main Torelli existence argument through Theorem 4 is not contradicted, and the maximal-degree construction of Section 6.3 is not the low-degree family in this example.

Problem 2 (Zero is allowed as the simple eigenvalue in Remark 8).  Remark 8, page 7, extends Proposition 7 by replacing the characteristic-polynomial variable \(t\) with \(t^n\) for every \(n>0\). Under the proposition’s stated hypotheses this extension is false.

Take \[M=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1&0\\-5&2&1\\-2&0&2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad N=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.\] These are integer matrices, and \(N\) is exactly the prescribed principal submatrix. Their characteristic polynomials are \(\chi_M=t(t-1)^2\) and \(\chi_N=(t-2)^2\), so they have no common eigenvalue and \(M\) has the simple eigenvalue \(\rho=0\). Choose the allowed values \(c=1\), \(p=2\), and put \(\widetilde M=M+y^2E_{11}\). Direct determinant calculation gives \[\chi_{\widetilde M}(t^2,y)
 =\bigl[t(t^2-1)-y(t^2-2)\bigr]
  \bigl[t(t^2-1)+y(t^2-2)\bigr],\] a nontrivial factorization in \(\mathbb Z[t,y]\).

The proposed Eisenstein element \(\mu_\rho(t^n)\) need not be irreducible; when \(\rho=0\), substitution also multiplies its root multiplicity. A sufficient repair is to require a nonzero simple eigenvalue. Its minimal polynomial has nonzero simple roots, so after substitution each irreducible factor still occurs with multiplicity one and is coprime to the substituted coefficient polynomial. One such factor can be used in Eisenstein’s criterion. The positive simple Perron eigenvalues in Lemmas 10–11 meet this repaired condition. Thus the broad remark is false, but no additional loss of the intended positive-matrix applications is established; the issue is Minor.

Problem 3 (The full characteristic polynomial is not always the Perron factor).  The opening assertion in the proof of Theorem 5, page 20, says the preceding construction gives an irreducible full characteristic polynomial of degree \(d\) for every degree. The preceding low-degree construction explicitly retains a factor \((t-4)^f\).

For example, take \(g=4\), \(d=2\), and \(f=g-1-d=1\) in Section 5.2.3, with the two repeated parameters equal to one. The displayed family is \[R(y)=\begin{pmatrix}64y^2&32&32\\32&4&0\\32&0&4\end{pmatrix},\] and exact calculation gives \[\chi_{R(y)}(t)
 =(t-4)\underbrace{\bigl[t^2-(64y^2+4)t+256y^2-2048\bigr]}_{P(t,y)}.\] Positive copy counts are available, for example at \(y=3\); the parameter \(\rho\) in the source then equals \(y^2-6=3\). The polynomial \(\chi_{R(y)}(t^2)\) always retains \(t^2-4\) and cannot be the minimal polynomial of the Perron square root as claimed. This is an actual factorization, not a possible exceptional Hilbert specialization.

The local correction is to use the factor containing the Perron eigenvalue. For the displayed example, \(P(t^2,y)\) is irreducible, as checked exactly. More generally, if \(s=f+1\) identical leaves have diagonal entry \(4\), the equal-leaf subspace has an integer quotient matrix. Its first-row coupling to that leaf is multiplied by \(s\), while the reverse coupling is unchanged. The other leaf entries are distinct. Removing the first row and column gives a diagonal matrix with distinct entries; evaluation of the quotient characteristic polynomial at any of them is a nonzero coupling product times the remaining differences. Hence there is no common eigenvalue. The zero-parameter quotient is nonnegative and irreducible, with a positive simple Perron eigenvalue. Proposition 7 and the corrected nonzero-eigenvalue version of Remark 8 apply to this quotient. The discarded difference subspaces account for \((t-4)^f\).

This restores the low-degree algebraic step with its multiplicity weights retained. At degree one, duplicating one of a separating filling pair of curves twice gives \(\mu=2m^2\), where \(m\) is the original intersection number, and hence bipartite degree two. The polynomial-identification error is Minor: a concrete surviving Perron-factor argument is available. No counterexample to Theorem 5 is claimed.
# Coverage and surviving calculations

The induction in Sections 4–5 was followed through the boundary-component counts, matrix sizes, positive parallel-copy restrictions, distinct block polynomials, and the separate genus-three construction. The figures were inspected for the separating and bounding-pair descriptions and for the placement of the curves used in the matrix calculations. Visual reading is not represented as a machine-certified combinatorial proof of every surface complement.

The norm proof of Theorem 4 uses \(\mu'=\epsilon\mu\ne0\) and the norm of \((n\mu')^2-\mu'\). Its reciprocal polynomial has nonzero simple roots; an eventual-square contradiction supplies arbitrarily large usable choices, allowing hyperbolicity to be retained. The homological cancellation needed for opposite multitwist powers was checked independently of commutativity of twists across the two multicurves.

Independent exact calculations confirmed the irreducibility of the Figure 4 matrices at \(y=2,3\), the Block 1 matrices at \(y=1,2\), and the genus-three matrices of sizes six, five, and four obtained by the indicated deletions. The three genus-two polynomials printed on page 3 are also irreducible. This last check verifies the polynomials, not their identification with the three mapping-class words, their pseudo-Anosov status, or their singularity patterns. Those flipper-based identifications were not independently reproduced.

The claimed full computation for genera up to 201 was not rerun. Hilbert irreducibility and the cited Thurston–Veech theory remain external mathematical dependencies. The paper’s citations to the earlier abelian-differential work were read in context but that entire work was not independently audited. These are coverage limits, not additional mathematical findings.

A bounded search of the exact arXiv record, the EMS article page, both authors’ publication pages, and title/code/supplement/erratum queries found no accompanying code or applicable correction for this exact version. The GP/Pari and Sage links on Lanneau’s page refer to a different, older Prym-locus paper and were not attributed to this manuscript. No author code was executed. A missing code deposit is not counted as a mathematical defect.

report: Abstract: This review concerns only arXiv:2408.12987v2. Two false proof inferences affect the central relative-barrier iteration and the lower Green-function argument. A separately asserted extension of the source space admits an explicit unbounded energy solution. These are Major issues in their stated scopes; no counterexample to the original weighted-source boundary regularity theorem or its final Green-function estimate is established. Five further issues concern first oscillations, an integer regularity endpoint, a kernel example, a weak-solution sign, and the Poisson normalization. Each is accompanied by an admissible example or an exact calculation. The initial review read all 58 pages as text and inspected its recorded source pages as images. The present independent acceptance focuses on the reported Problems and corrects the average convention used in Problem 4. The scientific decision remains pending.

Title: A technical review of
Optimal boundary regularity and Green function estimates for nonlocal equations in divergence form
# Identity, scope, and dependencies

The reviewed paper is by Minhyun Kim and Marvin Weidner [KW], with frozen annual identity M25-0368. The exact source is the 58-page preprint arXiv:2408.12987v2, dated 17 September 2025. The associated identifier is https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1760; the publisher records online publication on 11 December 2025. Its subscription journal text was not compared with this preprint, and equivalence is not presumed. Page references below are one-based PDF pages, which agree with the printed numbering.

The global assumptions include \(n>2s\), \(0<s<1\), symmetry and ellipticity \[\lambda |x-y|^{-n-2s}\le K(x,y)=K(y,x)\le\Lambda|x-y|^{-n-2s},
 \qquad Lu(x)=2\,\mathrm{p.v.}\!\int_{\mathbb R^n}(u(x)-u(y))K(x,y)\,dy.\] The coefficient condition (1.3) is Hölder continuity under simultaneous translation of \(x,y\), with exponent \(0<\sigma<s\), on the stated set \(A\). It is not angular smoothness or homogeneity. Theorem 1.6 assumes a \(C^{1,\alpha}\) domain, \(0<\alpha<s\), \(d_\Omega^{s-p}f\in L^q\), \(0<p\le s\), and \(q>n/p\). Its Hopf assertion additionally assumes nonnegative global \(u\), nonnegative bounded \(f\). Theorem 1.8 requires every completely frozen kernel to be homogeneous. Corollary 1.2 assumes \(s>1/2\).

The proof passes through weighted source estimates, freezing comparisons, a first Morrey iteration, locally frozen barriers, the relative Campanato estimate in Lemma 6.6, and Lemma 6.7. Theorem 6.8 then yields the normalized boundary quotient used in Theorem 6.1 and hence Theorem 1.6. The Hopf argument and the Green-function construction follow separately, with Section 9 invoking those boundary estimates. These dependencies matter: a defect in Lemma 6.6’s proof is a defect in a central derivation even without disproving its eventual conclusion.
# Major findings

Problem 1 (Subtracting a barrier changes the equation).  The first paragraph of the proof of Lemma 6.6, page 32, applies Proposition 6.2(iii) to \(v-c_0\psi\) as a homogeneous \(L\)-solution. The barrier \(\psi\) was defined for a different operator.

Equation reference: eq:forcing. Exact hypotheses and counterevidence. On pages 25–26, \(L\) is translation invariant, whereas \(\widetilde L\) need only coincide with \(L\) for jumps shorter than \(1/2\). Equation (6.1) gives \(\widetilde L\psi=0\) in \(D\); equation (6.2) explicitly retains \[L\psi=(L-\widetilde L)\psi .\] Proposition 6.2(iii), however, assumes \(Lv=0\). Consequently \[
 L(v-c_0\psi)=-c_0(L-\widetilde L)\psi ,\] which need not vanish.

Equation reference: eq:perturb. Here is a smooth admissible family making it nonzero. Work in dimension two, for example with \(s=1/2\), and a smooth domain with a boundary point at the origin. Choose \(D\) as in (6.1), with \(\Omega_1\subset D\subset\Omega_2\). Put \(k_0(h)=c|h|^{-n-2s}\). Let \(a,b\) be nonnegative smooth compactly supported functions bounded by one, with \(a\) supported inside \(D\), \(b\) supported outside \(B_3\), and the supports more than \(1/2\) apart. For \(0<\delta<1\), set \[
 \widetilde K(x,y)=k_0(x-y)
 \bigl[1+\delta(a(x)b(y)+a(y)b(x))\bigr].\] This kernel is symmetric, uniformly elliptic, satisfies simultaneous-translation Hölder bounds, and equals \(k_0\) for short jumps. Choose the allowed exterior datum \(g\), \(0\le g\le1\), to equal one on \(\operatorname{supp}b\). The variational Dirichlet solutions \(\psi\) for \(\widetilde L\) and \(v\) for \(L_0\), both with exterior datum \(g\), exist, are positive in \(D\), and satisfy \(0<\psi<1\). The strict upper inequality follows from the positive kernel and the exterior region where \(g=0\).

Equation reference: eq:nonzero. For \(x\in D\) with \(a(x)>0\), the exact operator identity is \[
 L_0\psi(x)=2\delta a(x)(1-\psi(x))
             \int_{\mathbb R^n}b(y)k_0(x-y)\,dy>0 .\] Take a small ball allowed in Lemma 6.6 meeting this support. The actual choice \(c_0=\mathop{\mathrlap{\mkern 3mu-}\int}\nolimits_{\Omega_R}(v/\psi)\) is positive, so [eq:forcing] (#eq:forcing) is nonzero even for the coefficient selected in the proof, not merely for an irrelevant arbitrary constant. One can arrange \(a(x_0)=b(x_0)=0\) at the freezing point while \(a\) is positive elsewhere in that ball. Then (1.9) freezes \(\widetilde K\) to \(k_0\) exactly, and (6.12) gives back \(\widetilde K\). Thus this obstruction also occurs in the actual locally frozen setup of Lemma 6.7.

Impact and repair boundary. This is a false application of a homogeneous estimate, not just an omitted citation. Lemma 6.7 invokes Lemma 6.6 on page 33, and Theorem 6.8 invokes the resulting iteration on page 36. The issue is therefore Major for the proof of the main regularity result and its dependent applications. The example does not disprove the full inequality of Lemma 6.6 or the final \(C^s\) conclusion. A repair must prove an inhomogeneous relative-barrier estimate with the term in [eq:forcing] (#eq:forcing), and show that its scale contribution is absorbed in the iteration. Alternatively, barriers and replacements could be made harmonic for the same operator, but the locally frozen closeness argument would then have to be reconsidered. Neither full replacement proof is asserted here.

Problem 2 (The printed source-space extension admits unbounded solutions).  Remark 3.2, pages 14–15, proposes replacing the weighted \(L^q\) source hypothesis in the main theorems by a space \(X\). The displayed support exponent has the wrong sign for that purpose.

Write \(a=1/2+p/n-1/q>0\). The displayed norm multiplies \(\int fw/[w]_{H^s}\) by \(|\{w\ne0\}\cap B_R|^{a}\). On the bounded testing region \(\Omega_1\), every energy-dual datum has finite such norm: \[\left|\int fw\right|\le C_f[w]_{H^s},
 \qquad
 |\{w\ne0\}\cap B_R|^a
       \frac{\left|\int fw\right|}{[w]_{H^s}}
 \le |\Omega_1|^a C_f .\] The supremum over both signs of \(w\) makes the lack of an absolute value in the numerator immaterial.

For a concrete counterexample, take \(n=2\), \(s=p=1/2\), \(q=\infty\), \(\alpha=\sigma=1/4\), and \(\Omega=B_2\). Choose \(0\le\eta\le1\), \(\eta\in C_c^\infty(B_3)\), equal to one on \(B_2\), and set \[u(x)=\eta(x)|x|^{-1/4},\qquad f=(-\Delta)^{1/2}u
       \quad\hbox{in }B_1 .\] Use the constant kernel normalized so that (1.1) equals this fractional Laplacian. All coefficient and domain assumptions hold. The local zero condition in \(B_1\setminus\Omega\) is vacuous, which is allowed by the localized Theorem 1.6. The singularity has finite energy: its dyadic \(H^s\) contributions are bounded by a convergent geometric series with scale exponent \[n-2(1/4)-2s=1/2>0 .\] Away from zero the cutoff is smooth; the same splitting controls the interactions between separated annuli. Thus \(u\in H^{1/2}(\mathbb R^2)\), and the required weighted \(L^1\) tail is finite. The weak datum \(f\) is an energy-dual functional by Cauchy–Schwarz in the Dirichlet form, so it belongs to the printed \(X\).

This is Major for the explicit extension of the main regularity statement. It is not a counterexample to the original weighted-\(L^q\) theorem: this \(f\) is not bounded. To encode (3.1), the support factor must instead have exponent \(-a\). A formulation based solely on (3.2) must specify the corresponding scale-dependent dual bound and justify each subsequent source estimate. The positive-exponent assertion cannot be retained.

Problem 3 (A lower-bound Harnack chain leaves the harmonic domain).  In Case 2 of the lower-bound proof of Theorem 1.1, pages 52–53, the auxiliary function is prescribed to vanish at some points at which the proof claims it is bounded below by a positive constant.

The proof sets \(R=2|x-y|\) and defines \(u\) by \[Lu=0\text{ in }\Omega_{R/4}(x_0),\quad
 u=1\text{ on }B_{\kappa R}(z),\quad
 u=0\text{ outside }\Omega_{R/4}(x_0)\cup B_{\kappa R}(z).\] After (9.5), the branch \(x\notin\Omega_{R/8}(x_0)\) invokes a Harnack chain to claim \(u(x)\ge c_1>0\).

Take a constant fractional kernel, \(n=2\), \(s=1/4\), \(\alpha=\sigma=1/8\), and \[\Omega=B_{10}((0,10)),\quad x_0=(0,0),\quad
 x=(0,3/4),\quad y=(0,7/4),\quad z=(0,4),\quad\kappa=1/8 .\] Then \(|x-y|=1\), \(R=2\), and \[d_\Omega(x)=3/4<1\le d_\Omega(y)=7/4,\quad
 2\le|y-z|=9/4\le4,\quad 2<|x_0-z|=4\le4.\] The ball \(B_{\kappa R}(z)=B_{1/4}(z)\) is inside \(\Omega\setminus B_R(x_0)\). All specified Case 2 geometric requirements hold. But \(x\) is outside \(\Omega_{R/4}(x_0)=\Omega\cap B_{1/2}(0)\) and outside \(B_{1/4}(z)\). Consequently the defining data give \(u(x)=0\) exactly. A Harnack chain for this \(u\) cannot reach \(x\) through a region where it is harmonic.

The issue is Major for the displayed proof of a principal lower Green-function bound; Case 3 reuses the same mechanism. It does not refute that final bound. A plausible repair is to propagate the lower bound for \(G(\cdot,y)\) itself through a chain avoiding its pole, or to change the comparison domain and radii. Such a repair must cover the bounded-domain large-scale geometry as well; it is not supplied merely by asserting a chain for the present \(u\).
# Further bounded findings

Problem 4 (First oscillations cannot have a superlinear decay exponent).  Lemma 5.5, page 23, asserts decay of the mean oscillation after subtracting only a constant with exponent \(\beta=\min\{2s-n/q,1+\sigma-\varepsilon\}\).

Take \(n=2\), \(s=3/4\), \(\sigma=1/4\), \(\varepsilon=1/8\), \(q=\infty\), \(u(x)=x_1\), \(R=1\), \(x_0=0\), and a constant fractional kernel. The affine function is locally in the required energy space and belongs to \(L^1_{2s}\), since its tail integral is proportional to \(\int_1^\infty r^{-2s}\,dr<\infty\). Its principal-value operator is zero by oddness. All hypotheses hold with \(f=0\). The source defines \((u)_{B_\rho}\) as the average of \(|u|\) (page 10). Reflection symmetry and \(|a-m|+|-a-m|\ge 2|a|\) imply, for every \(m\in\mathbb R\), \[\mathop{\mathrlap{\mkern 3mu-}\int}\nolimits_{B_\rho}|x_1-m|\,dx
 \ge \mathop{\mathrlap{\mkern 3mu-}\int}\nolimits_{B_\rho}|x_1|\,dx
 =\frac{4\rho}{3\pi}.\] Taking \(m=(u)_{B_\rho}\), we therefore obtain \[\mathop{\mathrlap{\mkern 3mu-}\int}\nolimits_{B_\rho}|u-(u)_{B_\rho}|\,dx
 \ge \frac{4\rho}{3\pi},
 \qquad \beta=\frac98.\] The right side of the proposed estimate is a fixed finite multiple of \(\rho^{9/8}\), an impossibility as \(\rho\downarrow0\). The proof’s step from a \(C^\beta\) seminorm to a pointwise difference of order \(|x-y|^\beta\) is invalid when \(\beta>1\).

This issue is Minor in its established impact. The subsequent uses for Theorem 1.7 and barrier closeness target exponents below \(s<1\), for which a suitable weaker estimate can suffice. For noninteger regularity exponents above one, cap the first-oscillation exponent at one; higher Campanato exponents require affine approximants. The critical integer endpoint also requires the restriction described in Problem 5. No additional failure of a principal conclusion is inferred from this example.
Problem 5 (The critical interior endpoint is not \(C^1\)).  Proposition 3.5, page 16, includes the integer endpoint \(2s-n/q=1\) without an exception.

To see the failure of Lipschitz continuity, split \(f\) into its radial and odd angular parts. For the odd part, pair \(y\) and \(-y\) on \(y_1>0\). The quotient of \[|te_1-y|^{-1/2}-|te_1+y|^{-1/2}\] by \(t>0\) is nonnegative. Its pointwise limit, multiplied by the odd datum and integrated angularly, is a positive multiple of \[\int_0^{1/4}\frac{dr}{r\sqrt{\log(e/r)}}=\infty .\] Fatou’s lemma makes the odd-part difference quotient tend to \(+\infty\). The radial part contributes a bounded quotient: split at \(r=2t\); the inner contribution is \(O(t)\) by scaling, and angular cancellation of the first derivative in the outer part leaves \(O(t^2\int_{2t}^{1/4}r^{-2}\,dr)=O(t)\). Therefore \((u(te_1)-u(0))/t\to+\infty\). The claimed exponent is exactly one, so both the Lipschitz and the continuously differentiable interpretations of \(C^1\) fail.

This is a Minor auxiliary endpoint issue in the established dependency analysis. The principal boundary targets are below one. The gradient corollary uses a homogeneous equation with \(s>1/2\), avoiding this particular endpoint. Exclude the integer endpoint, weaken the exponent, or supply a correctly stated endpoint space and estimate.
Problem 6 (The advertised kernel class need not freeze homogeneously).  The example immediately after Theorem 1.8, page 9, does not satisfy that theorem’s extra homogeneity assumption in general.

For \(0<\delta<1\), take the even angular density \(a_x(\theta)=2+\delta\cos x_1\), independent of \(\theta\), and the printed kernel \[K(x,y)=|x-y|^{-n-2s}
          \bigl(a_x((x-y)/|x-y|)+a_y((x-y)/|x-y|)\bigr).\] It is symmetric, elliptic, and smooth under simultaneous translations. But (1.9) at the origin gives \[|h|^{n+2s}K_0(h)=4+\delta(1+\cos h_1),\] which varies along the ray \(h=re_1\). Hence \(K_0\) is not homogeneous. This Minor issue invalidates the claimed example, not Theorem 1.8 under its actual hypothesis. An \(x\)-independent even angular density is a valid restricted example.
Problem 7 (The supersolution definition reverses only one sign).  Definition 2.1, page 11, says to replace \(u\) by \(-u\) in (2.2), without also replacing \(f\) by \(-f\).

For \(f=1\) and \(u=0\), both printed inequalities hold for all nonnegative tests, so the resulting literal definition calls \(u\) a solution, although \(Lu=0\ne1\). The correction is \(\mathcal E^K(u,\varphi)\ge\langle f,\varphi\rangle\), equivalently reversing both \(u\) and \(f\). This is Minor: the proofs otherwise use the intended equation. The counterexamples in Problems 2 and 5 have nonnegative \(f\) and satisfy exact weak equality, so they also satisfy both printed inequalities; they do not depend on exploiting this sign error.
Problem 8 (The Poisson formula misses the operator’s factor two).  Equation (9.6), page 53, is inconsistent with (1.1) and the inverse Green-function normalization in Definition 9.1, page 50.

Let \(g\) be a smooth exterior datum supported away from \(\overline\Omega\), and let \(u\) be its \(L\)-harmonic extension. The zero exterior extension \(v=u\mathbf1_\Omega\) satisfies \[Lv(x)=2\int_{\Omega^c}g(z)K(x,z)\,dz .\] Applying the inverse Green operator and interchanging the nonnegative integrals yields \[P(x,z)=2\int_\Omega G(x,y)K(y,z)\,dy .\] The printed formula lacks this factor. Equivalently, exterior data \(g=1\) have harmonic extension \(u=1\); the printed kernel has total mass \(1/2\) instead of one. This follows by approximation with bounded exterior data supported away from the boundary, or directly from \(L\mathbf1_\Omega=2\int_{\Omega^c}K(x,z)\,dz\) in \(\Omega\). The exact representation needs correction, while the two-sided estimates up to unspecified multiplicative constants can absorb the factor. The established impact is Minor.
# Coverage, surviving arguments, and limitations

The initial review read all source pages 1–58, including the references. The distinction between homogeneous frozen operators and locally frozen barriers is essential. Section 8 uses a barrier harmonic for the same frozen operator, so the particular subtraction defect in Problem 1 does not apply to that step itself. Its uses of earlier general regularity remain dependencies. The final displays on page 49 contain an extra factor two in a decay exponent; the weaker exponent stated in Theorem 1.8 is the one targeted by the preceding iteration. No independent counterexample to that theorem under the explicit homogeneity assumption is established.

The proof of the upper Green estimate was checked as a truncation and comparison argument. The gradient proof retains \(s>1/2\), the distance to the pole, and the boundary distance when choosing interior balls. Remark 9.8’s proposed extension to smaller \(s\) is explicitly a sketch in the source and is not promoted here to a proved theorem or a confirmed defect.

The assessment is Major, based on Problems 1–3. It does not assert that all main results are false. The exact repairs of the full Campanato and Green-function chains require further work; local algebraic corrections alone are not represented as a completed replacement proof. No author adoption or journal correction has been verified. problems.source_location: Lemma 6.6 pp31-33, particularly p32 first paragraph; (6.1)-(6.2) p25, (6.12)-(6.13) p29; application Lemma 6.7 p33
claim: v-c0 psi satisfies the homogeneous equation required by Proposition 6.2(iii).
analysis: The first paragraph of the proof of Lemma 6.6, page 32, applies Proposition 6.2(iii) to \(v-c_0\psi\) as a homogeneous \(L\)-solution. The barrier \(\psi\) was defined for a different operator.

Equation reference: eq:forcing. Exact hypotheses and counterevidence. On pages 25–26, \(L\) is translation invariant, whereas \(\widetilde L\) need only coincide with \(L\) for jumps shorter than \(1/2\). Equation (6.1) gives \(\widetilde L\psi=0\) in \(D\); equation (6.2) explicitly retains \[L\psi=(L-\widetilde L)\psi .\] Proposition 6.2(iii), however, assumes \(Lv=0\). Consequently \[
 L(v-c_0\psi)=-c_0(L-\widetilde L)\psi ,\] which need not vanish.

Equation reference: eq:perturb. Here is a smooth admissible family making it nonzero. Work in dimension two, for example with \(s=1/2\), and a smooth domain with a boundary point at the origin. Choose \(D\) as in (6.1), with \(\Omega_1\subset D\subset\Omega_2\). Put \(k_0(h)=c|h|^{-n-2s}\). Let \(a,b\) be nonnegative smooth compactly supported functions bounded by one, with \(a\) supported inside \(D\), \(b\) supported outside \(B_3\), and the supports more than \(1/2\) apart. For \(0<\delta<1\), set \[
 \widetilde K(x,y)=k_0(x-y)
 \bigl[1+\delta(a(x)b(y)+a(y)b(x))\bigr].\] This kernel is symmetric, uniformly elliptic, satisfies simultaneous-translation Hölder bounds, and equals \(k_0\) for short jumps. Choose the allowed exterior datum \(g\), \(0\le g\le1\), to equal one on \(\operatorname{supp}b\). The variational Dirichlet solutions \(\psi\) for \(\widetilde L\) and \(v\) for \(L_0\), both with exterior datum \(g\), exist, are positive in \(D\), and satisfy \(0<\psi<1\). The strict upper inequality follows from the positive kernel and the exterior region where \(g=0\).

Equation reference: eq:nonzero. For \(x\in D\) with \(a(x)>0\), the exact operator identity is \[
 L_0\psi(x)=2\delta a(x)(1-\psi(x))
             \int_{\mathbb R^n}b(y)k_0(x-y)\,dy>0 .\] Take a small ball allowed in Lemma 6.6 meeting this support. One can arrange \(a(x_0)=b(x_0)=0\) at the freezing point while \(a\) is positive elsewhere in that ball. Impact and repair boundary. This is a false application of a homogeneous estimate, not just an omitted citation. Lemma 6.7 invokes Lemma 6.6 on page 33, and Theorem 6.8 invokes the resulting iteration on page 36. The issue is therefore Major for the proof of the main regularity result and its dependent applications. The example does not disprove the full inequality of Lemma 6.6 or the final \(C^s\) conclusion. A repair must prove an inhomogeneous relative-barrier estimate with the term in [eq:forcing] (#eq:forcing), and show that its scale contribution is absorbed in the iteration. Alternatively, barriers and replacements could be made harmonic for the same operator, but the locally frozen closeness argument would then have to be reconsidered. Neither full replacement proof is asserted here.

Scope: Confirmed false proof inference in the core Campanato chain to Theorems 6.8,6.1,1.6 and Green applications. No counterexample to the claimed final regularity or to the complete Lemma 6.6 inequality established.

To see the failure of Lipschitz continuity, split \(f\) into its radial and odd angular parts. For the odd part, pair \(y\) and \(-y\) on \(y_1>0\). The quotient of \[|te_1-y|^{-1/2}-|te_1+y|^{-1/2}\] by \(t>0\) is nonnegative. Its pointwise limit, multiplied by the odd datum and integrated angularly, is a positive multiple of \[\int_0^{1/4}\frac{dr}{r\sqrt{\log(e/r)}}=\infty .\] Fatou’s lemma makes the odd-part difference quotient tend to \(+\infty\). The radial part contributes a bounded quotient: split at \(r=2t\); the inner contribution is \(O(t)\) by scaling, and angular cancellation of the first derivative in the outer part leaves \(O(t^2\int_{2t}^{1/4}r^{-2}\,dr)=O(t)\). Therefore \((u(te_1)-u(0))/t\to+\infty\). The claimed exponent is exactly one, so both the Lipschitz and the continuously differentiable interpretations of \(C^1\) fail.

This is a Minor auxiliary endpoint issue in the established dependency analysis. The principal boundary targets are below one. The gradient corollary uses a homogeneous equation with \(s>1/2\), avoiding this particular endpoint. Exclude the integer endpoint, weaken the exponent, or supply a correctly stated endpoint space and estimate.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: n=2,s=3/4,q=4,sigma=1/4,epsilon=1/8. f=(1+cos theta)r^{-1/2}[log(e/r)]^{-1/2} on r<1/4 is nonnegative L4. Its Riesz potential u=I_{3/2}f has finite local energy and tail but u(te1)-u(0) divided by t tends to infinity: the odd angular component gives integral dr/(r sqrt(log(e/r))), while the radial component contributes O(1) to this quotient.
Scope: Critical interior auxiliary statement false. The main boundary targets are below one; Corollary 1.2 uses homogeneous equations and s>1/2, so this example does not refute those conclusions.

problems.title: The advertised kernel class need not freeze homogeneously
problems.source_location: Example immediately after Theorem 1.8 p9; frozen kernel (1.9) p7
claim: The displayed variable a_x symmetric kernel class satisfies the frozen homogeneity assumption.
analysis: The example immediately after Theorem 1.8, page 9, does not satisfy that theorem’s extra homogeneity assumption in general.

For \(0<\delta<1\), take the even angular density \(a_x(\theta)=2+\delta\cos x_1\), independent of \(\theta\), and the printed kernel \[K(x,y)=|x-y|^{-n-2s}
          \bigl(a_x((x-y)/|x-y|)+a_y((x-y)/|x-y|)\bigr).\] It is symmetric, elliptic, and smooth under simultaneous translations. But (1.9) at the origin gives \[|h|^{n+2s}K_0(h)=4+\delta(1+\cos h_1),\] which varies along the ray \(h=re_1\). Hence \(K_0\) is not homogeneous. problems.title: The supersolution definition reverses only one sign
problems.source_location: Definition 2.1 p11
claim: A supersolution is obtained from (2.2) by replacing u alone by -u.
analysis: Definition 2.1, page 11, says to replace \(u\) by \(-u\) in (2.2), without also replacing \(f\) by \(-f\).

For \(f=1\) and \(u=0\), both printed inequalities hold for all nonnegative tests, so the resulting literal definition calls \(u\) a solution, although \(Lu=0\ne1\). problems.title: The Poisson formula misses the operator’s factor two
problems.source_location: Poisson representation (9.6) p53; normalization (1.1) p1 and Definition 9.1 p50
claim: P(x,z)=integral_Omega G(x,y)K(z,y)dy with the given L=2 p.v. normalization.
analysis: Equation (9.6), page 53, is inconsistent with (1.1) and the inverse Green-function normalization in Definition 9.1, page 50.

Let \(g\) be a smooth exterior datum supported away from \(\overline\Omega\), and let \(u\) be its \(L\)-harmonic extension. The zero exterior extension \(v=u\mathbf1_\Omega\) satisfies \[Lv(x)=2\int_{\Omega^c}g(z)K(x,z)\,dz .\] Applying the inverse Green operator and interchanging the nonnegative integrals yields \[P(x,z)=2\int_\Omega G(x,y)K(y,z)\,dy .\] The printed formula lacks this factor. Equivalently, exterior data \(g=1\) have harmonic extension \(u=1\); the printed kernel has total mass \(1/2\) instead of one. This follows by approximation with bounded exterior data supported away from the boundary, or directly from \(L\mathbf1_\Omega=2\int_{\Omega^c}K(x,z)\,dz\) in \(\Omega\). The exact representation needs correction, while the two-sided estimates up to unspecified multiplicative constants can absorb the factor. The established impact is Minor.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: For smooth exterior data g supported away from Omega, the zero exterior extension of u solves Lv=2 integral g(z)K(x,z)dz. Inverting L gives P=2 integral GK. For g=1 on Omega^c, the printed kernel has total mass 1/2 instead of 1.
Scope: Exact representation normalization is wrong; multiplicative constants in the two-sided Poisson estimates can absorb the factor.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Insert factor 2 in (9.6), consistently with (1.1) and the inverse Green definition.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the exact 74-page preprint arXiv:2112.09044v3. The concentration-plane argument in the proof of the higher-dimensional lower box bound makes a false geometric inference. A fixed pair of separated, uniformly two-dimensional measures in \(\mathbb R^4\), neither charging any hyperplane, violates its required estimate at infinitely many scales. A separate issue in the cylindrical-slicing mechanism identifies an oriented ray slice with a full-plane slice; an elementary rectangle gives a counterexample. These are Major proof issues in the stated scopes. Four further findings concern a generic slicing bound and local normalization, robustness, and entropy bookkeeping. No counterexample to a main distance-set conclusion is established. All source pages were read as text, and 33 source pages, including all four figures, were actually inspected. Independent scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 27 October 2026

Title: A technical review of
On the distance sets spanned by sets
of dimension \(d/2\) in \(\mathbb R^d\)
# Identity, hypotheses, and proof structure

The reviewed work is by Pablo Shmerkin and Hong Wang [SW], with frozen annual identity M25-0369. The exact source is arXiv:2112.09044v3, dated 13 August 2024. Its actual PDF has 74 pages. The arXiv comment says 71 pages, while the associated journal article, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-024-00696-5, has pagination 283–358 and an online date of 9 January 2025. These are distinct records; no equivalence of the preprint and journal text is assumed. All locations below use one-based PDF pages, agreeing with the printed numbering.

Write \(\Delta^y(x)=|x-y|\), \(\pi_x(y)=(y-x)/|y-x|\), and \[\phi(u)=\frac{u+\sqrt{4+u^2}-2}{2}.\] Theorem 1.1 treats planar Borel sets of Hausdorff dimension \(u\le1\). Theorem 1.2 gives a Hausdorff bound in \(\mathbb R^3\), whereas Theorem 1.3, for \(d\ge4\) and \(\dim_{\mathrm H}X\ge d/2\), gives a lower box bound. Theorem 1.4 assumes \(\dim_{\mathrm H}X=\dim_{\mathrm P}X=d/2\); its assertion that the supremum is attained almost everywhere additionally uses positive critical Hausdorff measure. Dimension one and positive Lebesgue measure are not interchangeable here. The radial-projection results retain their restrictions on \(k\), the dimension interval, and containment in a \(k\)-plane.

The proof uses normalized dyadic restrictions \(\mu^Q\), quantitative Frostman bounds, and robust measures. Definition 2.2 says that \(\rho\) is \((\delta,s,r)\)-robust when \[\rho(E)>r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |E|_\delta>\delta^{-s}.\] The multiscale entropy propositions require full-rank \(C^2\) maps and disjoint intervals with \(B_j\le2A_j\). Their nonlinear applications use an adapted family of derivative directions and a combinatorial profile in \(\mathcal L_{d,u}\). This class consists of nondecreasing piecewise-linear \(d\)-Lipschitz functions on \([0,1]\), vanishing at zero and lying above \(ux\). The thin-tube statements allow restrictions of positive mass; their strong versions also require compact incidence sets.

The planar bootstrap combines the improved Kaufman estimate with the profile optimization. Higher-dimensional arguments then use orthogonal and cylindrical slices, the radial mechanism in Theorem 6.7, and the exclusion of line-supported slices. The special argument in Section 7.4 replaces quantitative hyperplane nonconcentration by an asserted single-scale substitute. That substitute is the subject of the first finding.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (A false transversality inference in the proof of Theorem 1.3).  Section 7.4.3, page 69, claims that a hyperplane meeting \(Z\) and \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\setminus V^{(c_\varepsilon)}\) has an intersection with \(V\)’s small neighborhood coverable by a bounded number of \((k-1)\)-plates. This is used in (7.12), then (7.15), and finally (7.20)–(7.23), pages 69–71. The assertion fails when the concentration plane has dimension at most \(d-2\).
## The elementary obstruction

If \(x\notin V\) and \(\dim V=k\le d-2\), a hyperplane can contain \(\operatorname{aff}(V,x)\). It then contains \(V\) as well as \(x\). Its intersection with \(V^{(\delta)}\) contains an entire bounded \(k\)-dimensional patch, requiring an unbounded number of \((k-1)\)-plates as \(\delta\downarrow0\). Separation of \(x\) from \(V\) gives no transversality of this hyperplane to \(V\).

A planar measure by itself illustrates this obstruction, but an exact-plane example could obscure the preliminary nonconcentration assumptions. The following construction avoids that issue and supplies fixed measures, not measures changed independently at each tested scale.
## A fixed admissible pair

Equation reference: eq:mixture. Set \(d=4\), \(Q=[-1/10,1/10]^2\), and let \(\lambda_Q\) be normalized planar Lebesgue measure on \(Q\). Define \[F_*(u,v)=(u,v,1+u^2,v^2),\qquad
 \mu=(F_*)_*\lambda_Q.\] For \(j\ge1\), put \[m_j=2j,\quad a_j= rac1{j+2},\quad e_j=2^{-4j},\quad
 F_j(u,v)=(u,v,a_j+e_j u^2,e_j v^2),
 \quad 
u_j=(F_j)_*\lambda_Q,\] and \[
 
u=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} rac{
u_j}{j(j+1)}.\] The weights sum to one. The patches \(F_j(Q)\) are disjoint: their third-coordinate intervals have length at most \(e_j/100\), much less than the separation of consecutive \(a_j\). Their only additional limiting patch is \(Q	imes\{(0,0)\}\). Thus \(
u\) has compact support. The supports of \(\mu,
u\) are separated by more than \(0.6\). A single fixed similarity puts the construction in any required bounded coordinate cube; it changes only fixed comparison constants.

Every graph map has the first two coordinates \((u,v)\), with a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant. Hence \[\mu(B_r),\ \nu_j(B_r),\ \nu(B_r)\le C r^2.\] In particular they satisfy the \(2-\varepsilon\) Frostman assumptions and have finite \(s\)-energy for every \(s<2\), by integrating \(r^{1-s}\) near zero. The union of the patches and their limiting patch has Hausdorff and packing dimension exactly two.

Neither measure charges any affine hyperplane. Indeed, the restriction of a nonzero affine functional to a graph \(F_j\) is \[Au+Bv+C(a_j+e_j u^2)+D e_jv^2+E.\] Since \(e_j>0\), this polynomial can vanish identically only if all five coefficients of the affine functional vanish. Its zero set otherwise has planar Lebesgue measure zero. The same argument applies to \(F_*\). Countable summation proves the assertion for \(\nu\). It also implies the uniform small-neighborhood condition (7.11) for \(\mu\), by compactness of the relevant family of hyperplanes.
## The actual contradiction

Fix the small positive \(\varepsilon'\) used in Section 7.4, and take \(j\) sufficiently large. Set \[\delta_j=2^{-\varepsilon'm_j},\quad
 Y=F_j(Q),\quad
 V_j=\mathbb R^2\times\{(a_j,0)\}.\] Then \[\nu(Y)=\frac1{j(j+1)}>\frac1{m_j^2},\qquad
 \nu_Y=\nu_j,\qquad
 Y\subset V_j^{(\delta_j)}.\] For a line \(L\), projection to the first two coordinates gives \(\nu_j(L^{(\delta_j)})\le C\delta_j\); for a point the bound is \(C\delta_j^2\). Exponential decay therefore makes these quantities smaller than \(m_j^{-8}\) and \(m_j^{-10}\), respectively. These are precisely the lower-dimensional thresholds in (7.10) for \(d=4\). The smallest concentration dimension is thus \(k=2\), and \(V=V_j\) is an allowed choice. Here \(Z=Y\).

Equation reference: eq:massone. For any \(x\in\operatorname{supp}\mu\), let \[H_{j,x}=\operatorname{aff}(V_j,x).\] This is a three-dimensional hyperplane. It contains \(x\), contains \(V_j\), and meets \(Z\) at \(F_j(0,0)\). Also \(x\) is a fixed positive distance from \(V_j\). A normal vector is \[n_{j,x}=(0,0,-x_4,x_3-a_j).\] Direct substitution, also checked symbolically, gives \[n_{j,x}\cdot\bigl(F_j(u,v)-(0,0,a_j,0)\bigr)
 =e_j\bigl(-x_4u^2+(x_3-a_j)v^2\bigr).\] It follows that the whole patch \(Z\) is within \(\sqrt2 e_j/100\) of \(H_{j,x}\), hence within \(\delta_j\) for all large \(j\). Therefore \[
 \nu_Z\bigl(H_{j,x}^{(\delta_j)}\bigr)=1,\] contrary to (7.12)’s \(O_\varepsilon(m_j^{-2})\). The corresponding angular mass in a \(\delta_j\)-neighborhood of the linear hyperplane \(H_{j,x}-x\) is also one, contradicting (7.15). Every fixed integer \(T\) divides infinitely many \(m_j=2j\), so the restriction to multiples of \(T\) does not avoid the example.

There is a separate arithmetic error in (7.12): \[\frac{m^{-2(d-k)}}{m^{-2(d-k+1)}}=m^2,\] whereas the display gives \(m^{-2}\). Using the threshold for dimension \(k-1\) would put \(d-k+2\) in the numerator exponent. That correction cannot resolve [eq:massone] (#eq:massone); the required geometric covering is false.
## Impact and repair boundary

Equation (7.15) is the precise input used for Lemma 3.11 in (7.20). Its failure leaves the lower-dimensional entropy branch, and thus the printed proof of Theorem 1.3, unsupported. This is a Major issue in a principal result’s proof. The example does not show that Theorem 1.3, Theorem 1.4, or the Falconer conjecture is false; its smooth patches themselves have large distance sets.

A replacement must handle the possibility that the chosen concentration plane and the pin lie in a common hyperplane. Merely changing the exponent ratio, moving the pin farther from \(V\), or adding the assumption that both measures charge no hyperplane does not suffice. A new dimension-reduction or concentration argument is needed. No complete repair of this branch is established here.

Problem 2 (Oriented cylindrical fibers and full-plane slices).  Lemma 6.5, page 51, and the fiber identities immediately preceding it identify the oriented cylindrical slice with a full affine-plane slice. Theorem 6.6, page 52, then uses a false angular density identity. The definitions on pages 31 and 50 explicitly use the sphere-valued oriented projection.

Take \(d=k=2\), \(V=\mathbb R^2\), \(x=0\), and \[d\nu=16\,1_{[1/4,1/2]\times[-1/8,1/8]}\,d\mathcal L^2.\] This is a probability measure supported inside the unit disk, separated from \(x\). Both slices exist. At \(\theta=-e_1\), the cylindrical slice in (6.3) is zero: sufficiently small angular caps around \(-e_1\) see no part of the rectangle. The orthogonal slice on the full line \(\mathbb Re_1\), defined by (6.1), is \(16\,1_{[1/4,1/2]}\,dr\), of mass \(4\). The two measures cannot be mutually absolutely continuous. At \(+e_1\), the cylindrical slice instead has mass \[16\int_{1/4}^{1/2}r\,dr=\frac32.\] Thus this is a support error, not just a missing normalization factor.

For the integrated full-line measure \(\Lambda=\int_{S^1}\nu_{\mathbb R\theta}\,d\theta\), polar coordinates give \(d\Lambda(y)=2|y|^{-1}\,d\nu(y)\). The oriented angular density of \(\pi_0\Lambda\) is \(8\) at \(+e_1\) and \(0\) at \(-e_1\). The final identity in the proof of Theorem 6.6 gives \(4\) at both. The discrepancy holds on angular neighborhoods, not merely at an isolated point. Replacing the pin by a small smooth measure near zero gives the same orientation obstruction on a positive set of pins.

This is a Major issue in the stated disintegration argument: a false equivalence of measures and a false pushforward identity are used in the mechanism underlying Theorem 6.7. A bounded repair of this particular step is available. If \(W=x+V^\perp+\mathbb R	heta\), compare \[
u_W\quad\hbox{with}\quad
 
u^{\mathrm{cyl}}_{V,x,	heta}
 +
u^{\mathrm{cyl}}_{V,x,-	heta},\] rather than either summand alone. On separated bounded supports the radial weights are bounded above and below, so the two-sided comparison follows from the neighborhood definitions. Integration gives the required comparison with \(
u\), up to a fixed factor. The full-slice mass is bounded by a constant times the sum of the two antipodal angular densities; the inequality \((a+b)^p\le2^{p-1}(a^p+b^p)\) then gives the desired \(L^p\) bound using the same external radial-projection input. At the end of Theorem 6.7, use two antipodal caps instead of one. This repair preserves the desired estimates; it does not validate the printed identities or remove Problem 1.

Problem 3 (The wrong extremum in the generic box-slicing bound).  Lemma 6.13, page 61, has \(\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm B}(E\cap W)\le\min(\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm B}E-k,0)\). For \(E=[-1,1]^3\) and \(k=1\), every plane cutting the interior has a two-dimensional section, while the displayed bound is zero. Such planes form a set of positive \(\lambda_{3,2}\)-measure.

The usual corrected bound is \(\max(\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm B}E-k,0)\), with the appropriate empty-section convention. To see the positive-difference case directly, cover \(E\) at scale \(r\) by at most \(C_\epsilon r^{-D-\epsilon}\) cubes, where \(D=\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm B}E\). The measure of affine codimension-\(k\) planes hitting one such cube is \(O(r^k)\). Markov’s inequality and summation over dyadic \(r\) give an almost-everywhere section count bounded by \(r^{-D+k-2\epsilon}\) eventually. Letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) gives the corrected bound. When \(D<k\), almost every section is empty. This is Minor in its demonstrated impact: the subsequent applications use the intended positive dimension difference, and no extra loss of their target exponent follows from this transcription error.

Problem 4 (Two incorrect profile normalizations).  The rescaling before (5.15), page 47, is printed as \(\widetilde f(x)=a f(x/a)\). The dimension profile in Section 7.4.6, page 70, omits its factor \(1/\ell\).

In the first location \(f\) is defined only on \([0,1]\), and the actual \(a\) lies in \((0,1/2]\). The printed expression is undefined for \(x>a\). The required function is \[g(x)=\frac{f(ax)}a,\qquad 0\le x\le1.\] It belongs to the same \(\mathcal L_{2,u}\): it is nondecreasing, vanishes at zero, remains \(2\)-Lipschitz, and satisfies \(g(x)\ge ux\). A \(\sigma\)-superlinear interval \([A,B]\) for \(g\) gives a \(\sigma\)-superlinear interval \([aA,aB]\) for \(f\); its length and allowance threshold are multiplied by \(a\). This is exactly the transport needed at (5.15).

In the second location, taking \(d=4\), \(\ell=8\), and all \(\beta_i=2\) gives the printed profile \(f(1)=16\) and slope \(16\), contrary to its declared range and Lipschitz constant \(4\). The correct formula is \[f(j/\ell)=\ell^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^j\beta_i,\] already printed in Section 4.6.1, page 26. It gives \(f(1)=2\) and slope \(2\) in this example. These are Minor normalization errors with explicit local corrections. Correcting them does not supply the missing geometry of Problem 1.

Problem 5 (A vacuous robustness threshold).  Lemma 3.10, page 18, asserts \((\delta,t/d+\eta,\delta^{-\eta})\)-robustness and then adaptedness. Under Definition 2.2, its robustness clause is vacuous for every \(0<\delta<1\), \(\eta>0\).

A probability measure has no set of mass greater than \(\delta^{-\eta}>1\). For example, \(\delta=2^{-16}\), \(\eta=1/4\) gives threshold \(16\). The preceding clause therefore does not provide the asserted nonvacuous implication. A positive mass exponent is required, in the form supplied by the cited discretized projection theorem. This is a Minor sign error in the recorded formulation. This review does not replace the full proof of that external theorem merely by changing the sign.

Problem 6 (The conditional-entropy covering is reversed).  In Lemma 3.11, page 19, the proof says that each dyadic cube meets \(O_d(a^d)\) atoms of the joint projection partition. The factor tends to zero as \(a\downarrow0\), and the stated direction does not control the conditional entropy actually used.

The needed quantity is the number of dyadic cubes meeting one joint atom. For \(d=2\), rows \((1,0)\) and \((\sqrt{1-a^2},a)\) form a projection matrix of determinant \(a\). A joint atom has area \(2^{-2m}/a\) and crosses on the order of \(a^{-1}\) dyadic squares. More generally the Gram–Schmidt condition gives determinant at least \(a^{d-1}\). If \(A\) is this matrix, the union of dyadic cubes meeting \(A^{-1}(2^{-m}Q)\) lies in its enlargement by a cube of side \(O(2^{-m})\). Applying \(A\) puts that enlargement in a cube of side \(O_d(2^{-m})\), since the rows have unit norm. Volume comparison gives at most \(O_d(a^{-(d-1)})\le O_d(a^{-d})\) dyadic cubes. Hence \[H(\mu,\mathcal D_m\mid\mathcal D'_m)
 \le d\log(1/a)+O_d(1),\] as needed. The lemma survives this correction. The issue is Minor, with no separate reduction of its stated entropy bound.
# Coverage, surviving structure, and limits

All 74 text pages, including the references, were read. The review followed the energy-to-Frostman restrictions, robust entropy, derivative linearization, uniform-measure decompositions, superlinear interval merging, planar bootstrap, higher-dimensional slicing and induction, the three distance-set regimes, and the norm and Assouad extensions. All four schematic figures were inspected; they provide geometric explanations and are not numerical data.

The requirement \(B_j\le2A_j\) has the expected role in quadratic Taylor control. The two-dimensional profile normalization in Section 4.6.1 supplies the local correction above. The distinction between summable bad sets for Hausdorff conclusions and a scale-dependent mass loss for the lower box conclusion is substantive; it is the reason the failed Section 7.4 substitute matters. The exact calculation of \(\phi\) and the separation of Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 were retained throughout.

Several proof-accounting details remain limitations rather than independently established counterexamples. In Proposition 4.2, the positive Frostman factor in (4.3) is restated with a negative exponent, and applying adaptedness requires careful reallocation of the \(\varepsilon\)-losses. Theorem 6.11’s upper support-dimension hypothesis must be accounted for when it is invoked on slices in Corollary 6.12; finite energy alone supplies a lower dimension constraint. The initial reductions from the product-zero hyperplane condition to Proposition 6.8’s separate zero-mass conditions, and the small ambient dimensions in the final corollary invocations, also require explicit attention. This report does not certify every missing quantitative or range detail by an implicit change of constants. These observations are not promoted to further confirmed false conclusions.

The square-root placement in Lemma 5.9 was checked on the actual page and is \(1-\sqrt c\); a misleading text extraction was not treated as an error. External results of Bourgain, Orponen, He, and the cited slicing and distance-set papers remain dependencies. Reading their statements as quoted here is not an independent reproof of all of them. No claim of priority, author adoption, an applicable correction, or equivalence to a later or typeset version is made.

A bounded search covered the exact arXiv and publisher records, title/correction/code queries, and both authors’ public publication pages. No accompanying author code or applicable erratum was identified in those routes. That is a search limit, not a mathematical defect or proof that no supplement exists. No author code was executed.

problems.source_location: Section 7.4.3, p.69, geometric plate assertion and (7.12); (7.15), (7.20)-(7.23), pp.69-71
claim: Moving x outside the minimal concentration plane V is asserted to make every hyperplane through x transverse to V, giving nu_Z(H^(delta))=O(m^-2).
analysis: Section 7.4.3, page 69, claims that a hyperplane meeting \(Z\) and \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\setminus V^{(c_\varepsilon)}\) has an intersection with \(V\)’s small neighborhood coverable by a bounded number of \((k-1)\)-plates. This is used in (7.12), then (7.15), and finally (7.20)–(7.23), pages 69–71. The assertion fails when the concentration plane has dimension at most \(d-2\).
