Separation of \(x\) from \(V\) gives no transversality of this hyperplane to \(V\).

A planar measure by itself illustrates this obstruction, but an exact-plane example could obscure the preliminary nonconcentration assumptions. The following construction avoids that issue and supplies fixed measures, not measures changed independently at each tested scale.

Equation reference: eq:mixture. Set \(d=4\), \(Q=[-1/10,1/10]^2\), and let \(\lambda_Q\) be normalized planar Lebesgue measure on \(Q\). Define \[F_*(u,v)=(u,v,1+u^2,v^2),\qquad
 \mu=(F_*)_*\lambda_Q.\] For \(j\ge1\), put \[m_j=2j,\quad a_j= rac1{j+2},\quad e_j=2^{-4j},\quad
 F_j(u,v)=(u,v,a_j+e_j u^2,e_j v^2),
 \quad 
u_j=(F_j)_*\lambda_Q,\] and \[
 
u=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} rac{
u_j}{j(j+1)}.\] The weights sum to one. The patches \(F_j(Q)\) are disjoint: their third-coordinate intervals have length at most \(e_j/100\), much less than the separation of consecutive \(a_j\). Their only additional limiting patch is \(Q	imes\{(0,0)\}\). Thus \(
u\) has compact support. The supports of \(\mu,
u\) are separated by more than \(0.6\). A single fixed similarity puts the construction in any required bounded coordinate cube; it changes only fixed comparison constants.

Every graph map has the first two coordinates \((u,v)\), with a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant. Hence \[\mu(B_r),\ \nu_j(B_r),\ \nu(B_r)\le C r^2.\] In particular they satisfy the \(2-\varepsilon\) Frostman assumptions and have finite \(s\)-energy for every \(s<2\), by integrating \(r^{1-s}\) near zero. The union of the patches and their limiting patch has Hausdorff and packing dimension exactly two.

Neither measure charges any affine hyperplane. Indeed, the restriction of a nonzero affine functional to a graph \(F_j\) is \[Au+Bv+C(a_j+e_j u^2)+D e_jv^2+E.\] Since \(e_j>0\), this polynomial can vanish identically only if all five coefficients of the affine functional vanish. Its zero set otherwise has planar Lebesgue measure zero. The same argument applies to \(F_*\). Countable summation proves the assertion for \(\nu\). It also implies the uniform small-neighborhood condition (7.11) for \(\mu\), by compactness of the relevant family of hyperplanes.

Fix the small positive \(\varepsilon'\) used in Section 7.4, and take \(j\) sufficiently large. Set \[\delta_j=2^{-\varepsilon'm_j},\quad
 Y=F_j(Q),\quad
 V_j=\mathbb R^2\times\{(a_j,0)\}.\] Then \[\nu(Y)=\frac1{j(j+1)}>\frac1{m_j^2},\qquad
 \nu_Y=\nu_j,\qquad
 Y\subset V_j^{(\delta_j)}.\] For a line \(L\), projection to the first two coordinates gives \(\nu_j(L^{(\delta_j)})\le C\delta_j\); for a point the bound is \(C\delta_j^2\). Exponential decay therefore makes these quantities smaller than \(m_j^{-8}\) and \(m_j^{-10}\), respectively. These are precisely the lower-dimensional thresholds in (7.10) for \(d=4\). The smallest concentration dimension is thus \(k=2\), and \(V=V_j\) is an allowed choice. Here \(Z=Y\).

Equation reference: eq:massone. For any \(x\in\operatorname{supp}\mu\), let \[H_{j,x}=\operatorname{aff}(V_j,x).\] This is a three-dimensional hyperplane. It contains \(x\), contains \(V_j\), and meets \(Z\) at \(F_j(0,0)\). Also \(x\) is a fixed positive distance from \(V_j\). A normal vector is \[n_{j,x}=(0,0,-x_4,x_3-a_j).\] Direct substitution, also checked symbolically, gives \[n_{j,x}\cdot\bigl(F_j(u,v)-(0,0,a_j,0)\bigr)
 =e_j\bigl(-x_4u^2+(x_3-a_j)v^2\bigr).\] It follows that the whole patch \(Z\) is within \(\sqrt2 e_j/100\) of \(H_{j,x}\), hence within \(\delta_j\) for all large \(j\). Therefore \[
 \nu_Z\bigl(H_{j,x}^{(\delta_j)}\bigr)=1,\] contrary to (7.12)’s \(O_\varepsilon(m_j^{-2})\). The corresponding angular mass in a \(\delta_j\)-neighborhood of the linear hyperplane \(H_{j,x}-x\) is also one, contradicting (7.15). Every fixed integer \(T\) divides infinitely many \(m_j=2j\), so the restriction to multiples of \(T\) does not avoid the example.

There is a separate arithmetic error in (7.12): \[\frac{m^{-2(d-k)}}{m^{-2(d-k+1)}}=m^2,\] whereas the display gives \(m^{-2}\). Using the threshold for dimension \(k-1\) would put \(d-k+2\) in the numerator exponent. That correction cannot resolve [eq:massone] (#eq:massone); the required geometric covering is false.

Equation (7.15) is the precise input used for Lemma 3.11 in (7.20). Its failure leaves the lower-dimensional entropy branch, and thus the printed proof of Theorem 1.3, unsupported. This is a Major issue in a principal result’s proof. The example does not show that Theorem 1.3, Theorem 1.4, or the Falconer conjecture is false; its smooth patches themselves have large distance sets.

A replacement must handle the possibility that the chosen concentration plane and the pin lie in a common hyperplane. Merely changing the exponent ratio, moving the pin farther from \(V\), or adding the assumption that both measures charge no hyperplane does not suffice. A new dimension-reduction or concentration argument is needed. No complete repair of this branch is established here.
result: Impact: The entropy branch using Lemma 3.11 in the proof of Theorem 1.3 lacks its required hypothesis. No counterexample to the theorem itself is claimed.

problems.title: Oriented cylindrical fibers and full-plane slices
problems.source_location: Lemma 6.5 and preceding fiber identities, p.51; Theorem 6.6 density identity, p.52; Figures 3-4
claim: An oriented cylindrical slice is identified with a full affine-plane slice and asserted mutually absolutely continuous to it; the full-plane slice mass is then identified with an oriented angular density.
analysis: Lemma 6.5, page 51, and the fiber identities immediately preceding it identify the oriented cylindrical slice with a full affine-plane slice. Theorem 6.6, page 52, then uses a false angular density identity. The definitions on pages 31 and 50 explicitly use the sphere-valued oriented projection.

Take \(d=k=2\), \(V=\mathbb R^2\), \(x=0\), and \[d\nu=16\,1_{[1/4,1/2]\times[-1/8,1/8]}\,d\mathcal L^2.\] This is a probability measure supported inside the unit disk, separated from \(x\). Both slices exist. At \(\theta=-e_1\), the cylindrical slice in (6.3) is zero: sufficiently small angular caps around \(-e_1\) see no part of the rectangle. The orthogonal slice on the full line \(\mathbb Re_1\), defined by (6.1), is \(16\,1_{[1/4,1/2]}\,dr\), of mass \(4\). The two measures cannot be mutually absolutely continuous. At \(+e_1\), the cylindrical slice instead has mass \[16\int_{1/4}^{1/2}r\,dr=\frac32.\] Thus this is a support error, not just a missing normalization factor.

For the integrated full-line measure \(\Lambda=\int_{S^1}\nu_{\mathbb R\theta}\,d\theta\), polar coordinates give \(d\Lambda(y)=2|y|^{-1}\,d\nu(y)\). The oriented angular density of \(\pi_0\Lambda\) is \(8\) at \(+e_1\) and \(0\) at \(-e_1\). The final identity in the proof of Theorem 6.6 gives \(4\) at both. The discrepancy holds on angular neighborhoods, not merely at an isolated point. Replacing the pin by a small smooth measure near zero gives the same orientation obstruction on a positive set of pins.

This is a Major issue in the stated disintegration argument: a false equivalence of measures and a false pushforward identity are used in the mechanism underlying Theorem 6.7. A bounded repair of this particular step is available. If \(W=x+V^\perp+\mathbb R	heta\), compare \[
u_W\quad\hbox{with}\quad
 
u^{\mathrm{cyl}}_{V,x,	heta}
 +
u^{\mathrm{cyl}}_{V,x,-	heta},\] rather than either summand alone. On separated bounded supports the radial weights are bounded above and below, so the two-sided comparison follows from the neighborhood definitions. Integration gives the required comparison with \(
u\), up to a fixed factor. The full-slice mass is bounded by a constant times the sum of the two antipodal angular densities; the inequality \((a+b)^p\le2^{p-1}(a^p+b^p)\) then gives the desired \(L^p\) bound using the same external radial-projection input. At the end of Theorem 6.7, use two antipodal caps instead of one. This repair preserves the desired estimates; it does not validate the printed identities or remove Problem 1.
result: Impact: The printed central disintegration proof contains a false mutual absolute-continuity step and a false density identity. This is a proof issue, not a counterexample to the desired integrated comparison or final distance results.

problems.title: The wrong extremum in the generic box-slicing bound
problems.source_location: Lemma 6.13, p.61
claim: Generic box slice dimension is bounded by min(dim_B E-k,0).
analysis: Lemma 6.13, page 61, has \(\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm B}(E\cap W)\le\min(\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm B}E-k,0)\). For \(E=[-1,1]^3\) and \(k=1\), every plane cutting the interior has a two-dimensional section, while the displayed bound is zero. Such planes form a set of positive \(\lambda_{3,2}\)-measure.

The usual corrected bound is \(\max(\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm B}E-k,0)\), with the appropriate empty-section convention. To see the positive-difference case directly, cover \(E\) at scale \(r\) by at most \(C_\epsilon r^{-D-\epsilon}\) cubes, where \(D=\overline{\dim}_{\mathrm B}E\). The measure of affine codimension-\(k\) planes hitting one such cube is \(O(r^k)\). Markov’s inequality and summation over dyadic \(r\) give an almost-everywhere section count bounded by \(r^{-D+k-2\epsilon}\) eventually. Letting \(\epsilon\downarrow0\) gives the corrected bound. When \(D<k\), almost every section is empty. This is Minor in its demonstrated impact: the subsequent applications use the intended positive dimension difference, and no extra loss of their target exponent follows from this transcription error.
result: Impact: False displayed bound; later applications use the intended positive dimension difference rather than zero.

problems.title: Two incorrect profile normalizations
problems.source_location: Proposition 5.17 proof (5.15), p.47; normalized profile in Section 7.4.6, p.70; compare p.26
claim: The induction uses a f(x/a) on [0,1]; the later dimension profile omits 1/ell.
analysis: The rescaling before (5.15), page 47, is printed as \(\widetilde f(x)=a f(x/a)\). The dimension profile in Section 7.4.6, page 70, omits its factor \(1/\ell\).

In the first location \(f\) is defined only on \([0,1]\), and the actual \(a\) lies in \((0,1/2]\). The printed expression is undefined for \(x>a\). The required function is \[g(x)=\frac{f(ax)}a,\qquad 0\le x\le1.\] It belongs to the same \(\mathcal L_{2,u}\): it is nondecreasing, vanishes at zero, remains \(2\)-Lipschitz, and satisfies \(g(x)\ge ux\). A \(\sigma\)-superlinear interval \([A,B]\) for \(g\) gives a \(\sigma\)-superlinear interval \([aA,aB]\) for \(f\); its length and allowance threshold are multiplied by \(a\). This is exactly the transport needed at (5.15).

In the second location, taking \(d=4\), \(\ell=8\), and all \(\beta_i=2\) gives the printed profile \(f(1)=16\) and slope \(16\), contrary to its declared range and Lipschitz constant \(4\). The correct formula is \[f(j/\ell)=\ell^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^j\beta_i,\] already printed in Section 4.6.1, page 26. It gives \(f(1)=2\) and slope \(2\) in this example. These are Minor normalization errors with explicit local corrections. Correcting them does not supply the missing geometry of Problem 1.
result: Impact: Local normalization errors prevent literal application of the stated combinatorial class; the explicit corrections preserve the intended scale argument.

problems.title: A vacuous robustness threshold
problems.source_location: Lemma 3.10, p.18; Definition 2.2, p.12
claim: The projected probability measure is declared robust with mass threshold delta^(-eta), followed by a nonvacuous adaptedness assertion.
analysis: Lemma 3.10, page 18, asserts \((\delta,t/d+\eta,\delta^{-\eta})\)-robustness and then adaptedness. Under Definition 2.2, its robustness clause is vacuous for every \(0<\delta<1\), \(\eta>0\).

A probability measure has no set of mass greater than \(\delta^{-\eta}>1\). For example, \(\delta=2^{-16}\), \(\eta=1/4\) gives threshold \(16\). The preceding clause therefore does not provide the asserted nonvacuous implication. A positive mass exponent is required, in the form supplied by the cited discretized projection theorem. This is a Minor sign error in the recorded formulation. This review does not replace the full proof of that external theorem merely by changing the sign.
result: Impact: The printed robustness clause is vacuous and does not furnish the advertised implication.

problems.title: The conditional-entropy covering is reversed
problems.source_location: Lemma 3.11 proof, p.19
claim: Each dyadic cube is said to meet O_d(a^d) joint-partition atoms, and this is used for the reverse conditional entropy.
analysis: In Lemma 3.11, page 19, the proof says that each dyadic cube meets \(O_d(a^d)\) atoms of the joint projection partition. The factor tends to zero as \(a\downarrow0\), and the stated direction does not control the conditional entropy actually used.

The needed quantity is the number of dyadic cubes meeting one joint atom. For \(d=2\), rows \((1,0)\) and \((\sqrt{1-a^2},a)\) form a projection matrix of determinant \(a\). A joint atom has area \(2^{-2m}/a\) and crosses on the order of \(a^{-1}\) dyadic squares. More generally the Gram–Schmidt condition gives determinant at least \(a^{d-1}\). If \(A\) is this matrix, the union of dyadic cubes meeting \(A^{-1}(2^{-m}Q)\) lies in its enlargement by a cube of side \(O(2^{-m})\). Applying \(A\) puts that enlargement in a cube of side \(O_d(2^{-m})\), since the rows have unit norm. Volume comparison gives at most \(O_d(a^{-(d-1)})\le O_d(a^{-d})\) dyadic cubes. Hence \[H(\mu,\mathcal D_m\mid\mathcal D'_m)
 \le d\log(1/a)+O_d(1),\] as needed. The lemma survives this correction. The issue is Minor, with no separate reduction of its stated entropy bound.
result: Impact: The displayed justification for the entropy inequality has the wrong direction and exponent; the lemma's conclusion survives a corrected cover argument.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the exact 33-page preprint arXiv:2302.09058v2. Its combinatorial extraction, Baire category exclusion, matroid coloring, and geometric lower-bound constructions were examined with their different quantifiers retained. Three local errors are confirmed: the concluding planar chromatic minimum is misstated, a preliminary collinear dichotomy is false, and an entropy display omits a factor. Explicit arguments repair these points without an identified loss of the main results. The supported assessment is Minor; no Major issue is established. Reviewer-authored exact finite calculations corroborate several counting steps, with their finite scope stated below. All source pages were read as text and 24 source pages were actually inspected as images. Independent scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Date: 27 October 2026

Title: A technical review of
Unit and distinct distances in typical norms
# Identity, scope, and principal claims

The reviewed work is by Noga Alon, Matija Bucić, and Lisa Sauermann [ABS], with frozen annual identity M25-0370. The exact source is arXiv:2302.09058v2, submitted on 7 November 2024; its actual PDF has 33 pages. The associated journal identifier is DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-025-00698-x. The publisher records online publication on 24 January 2025 and pagination 1–42 in volume 35. The journal record and the acquired preprint are distinct bindings. No equality of their texts is assumed, and the frozen annual identity is not changed by the preprint date. Locations below are one-based PDF pages, agreeing with the printed numbers.

For a norm on \(\mathbb R^d\), \(U(n)\) maximizes the number of unordered unit-distance pairs among \(n\) distinct points, whereas \(D(n)\) minimizes the number of distinct distances between different points. The space \(\mathcal B_d\) consists of closed, bounded, centrally symmetric convex bodies with the origin in their interior, with the Hausdorff metric. A typical norm means a norm outside a meagre subset of this space. It is not a probabilistic assertion about a randomly chosen norm.

Theorem 1.1 states, for fixed \(d\ge2\), that a residual collection of norms satisfies \[U(n)\le \frac d2 n\log_2 n\] for every \(n\) and every corresponding configuration. Theorem 1.2 instead applies to every norm and gives, as \(n\to\infty\) with \(d\) fixed, \[U(n)\ge \frac{d-1-o(1)}2 n\log_2 n.\] Theorem 1.3 gives \(D(n)=(1-o(1))n\) for typical norms. Theorem 1.4 gives planar unit-distance chromatic number four for typical norms; Theorem 6.1 proves the stronger upper bound \(2^d\) for the odd-integer-distance graph. These quantifiers are essential: the lower-bound construction does not require a typical norm, while the generic exclusion must hold simultaneously for all finite configurations.

All 33 pages, including the references, were read as extracted text. The image inspection covered the identity pages, the three findings, the combinatorial inequalities, the algebraic exclusion, the coloring argument, and the lower-bound constructions. It did not consist of inspecting only a manifest or an index. No numbered figures were identified in the full text. The absence of a confirmed Major issue is a bounded review conclusion, not a formal verification or an independent acceptance decision.
# Examination of the main proof mechanisms
## Independent directions, forests, and weighted extraction

Lemma 4.3, pages 10–12, assumes linearly independent directions over an arbitrary field and separately requires the edges in each direction to form a forest. The latter hypothesis cannot be dropped: even collinear point sets can otherwise give dense graphs. In the connected case, the proof fixes one direction and partitions the vertices by its coefficient in the independent-coordinate representation. Non-red edges stay within coefficient fibers. Distinct vertices in one fiber cannot belong to the same red-tree component, since that would place their nonzero difference in two disjoint linear spans. Consequently, the red forest has at least as many components as the largest fiber.

Writing the fiber sizes as \(n_1\ge\cdots\ge n_\ell\), this yields \[e(G)\le n-n_1+\frac12\sum_i n_i\log_2 n_i
       \le \frac12 n\log_2 n.\] The last inequality is the correctly stated Lemma 4.4. Problem 3 below concerns a defective intermediate display in its proof; the preceding binary-entropy computation already supplies the missing factor. The forest argument itself retains the correct expression.

Lemma 4.5, page 13, uses the closure bound \[|\{j:u_j\in\operatorname{span}_F(u_i:i\in I)\}|\le d|I|+m\] for every index set \(I\), and weights \(0\le\lambda_j\le M\). Sorting weights and greedily selecting independent vectors gives indices \[j_s\le (s-1)d+m+1,\qquad k\le dr+m.\] Grouping the sorted weights into blocks of size \(d\), after the first \(m\) weights, then gives \[d\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_j\ge\sum_{j=1}^k\lambda_j-mM.\] The proof has two local \(m/r\) index slips noted below, but the greedy definition establishes independence for all \(r\) selected vectors. No new structural hypothesis is needed.

For Lemma 4.1, the field is \(\mathbb Q\), and a fixed unit direction generates disjoint paths in a finite point configuration. Combining the weighted extraction with the forest bound therefore gives the claimed excess-closure alternative. Lemma 4.2 uses a subfield \(F\subset\mathbb R\), non-collinearity over \(\mathbb R\), and sufficiently large \(n\). Its use of the direction theorem is confined to the finite-dimensional real span of the finite configuration; the ambient vector space need not be finite-dimensional.

The collapse procedure in Lemma 4.2 leaves a set of size \(h>\mu n/(3d)\), unless the alternative already contradicts the assumed closure bound. In the remaining case the direction forests have weights \(\lambda_i\le3d/\mu\), and pair coverage gives \[\sum_i\lambda_i\ge \frac{\mu}{24d}h^2.\] For sufficiently large \(n\), weighted extraction produces an independent-direction graph with at least \(\mu h^2/(48d^2)\) edges. This contradicts \(e(G)\le h\log_2 h/2\). The dependence on \(d,\mu\), the exclusion of the collinear case, and the rounding of \((1-\mu)n\) were retained in checking this argument.
## Nowhere density and the universal configuration quantifier

Section 5, pages 17–23, encodes a bad finite configuration by a rational matrix in the unit-distance case, or by rational functions over \(\mathbb Q\) in the distinct-distance case. The latter functions are evaluated only where their denominators are nonzero. The distance field need not be purely transcendental: every element of the field generated by the actual distances has a rational-function representative with a denominator nonzero at those distances.

For fixed matrix and a positive rational angular separation, approximate a unit ball by a centrally symmetric polytope with small facets. A hypothetical separated family of unit directions must use different pairs of opposite facets. For a fixed assignment and signs, the \(d\ell+m+1\) selected support parameters are rational functions of only \(d\ell+m\) variables. Their image therefore satisfies a nonzero polynomial equation. There are only finitely many facet assignments and sign choices. Their union lies in a proper closed algebraic subset of the support-parameter space.

This closed algebraic enclosure is important. It permits choosing a small box of support parameters disjoint from all achievable tuples, even when a possible bad configuration could have unbounded auxiliary coordinates or nearly vanishing denominators. Small Hausdorff changes of the resulting polytope preserve the facet-pair separation, and the nearby unit vectors would create another achievable tuple in the forbidden box. The proof thus excludes a neighborhood, which is the needed nowhere-density conclusion.

The countability step involves integer configuration sizes, matrix sizes, rational angular thresholds, and coefficients in a countable rational-function field. For the asymptotic distinct-distance statement, one also takes a countable sequence \(\mu\downarrow0\). These countable operations preserve the common residual collection needed for all configurations. The two preliminary approximation lemmas and the boundary Hausdorff argument were followed in this use. Local stability of the small-facet bound is sufficient; the proof does not require a global assertion about continuity of every exposed face across all polytope degenerations.
## The coloring argument and its external input

For the finite set of unit directions arising from a finite odd-distance graph, the absence of an excess closure implies the matroid rank criterion. Indeed, for any subset \(A\) of the direction indices, choose a basis \(I\subset A\). Then \[|A|\le|\operatorname{cl}(I)|\le d|I|=d\,\operatorname{rk}(A).\] The finite vector matroid can therefore be partitioned into \(d\) independent sets by Edmonds’ theorem. Its original statement and vector-matroid setting were checked in [Edmonds], PDF pages 1 and 3, printed pages 67 and 69.

Each resulting graph is bipartite: an odd cycle would give a relation among independent directions, and at least one direction would have an odd integer coefficient, hence a nonzero coefficient. Combining the \(d\) two-colorings gives \(2^d\) colors. The finite-subgraph reduction uses the de Bruijn–Erdős theorem. No claim of an explicit or measurable coloring follows from this argument.

Although Section 5 begins with \(d\ge2\), the \(d=1\) endpoint of Theorem 6.1 can also be checked directly. Write the norm as \(c|x|\). Within each coset of \(c^{-1}\mathbb Z\), parity of the integer coordinate gives a two-coloring of odd-distance edges; different cosets have no such edges. The planar equality four additionally uses the cited universal lower bound of Chilakamarri. That external lower-bound proof was not independently reconstructed in this review.
## Lower bounds for every norm

For a strictly convex planar norm, Lemma 7.2 constructs unit triangles successively while avoiding collisions between all their sums. The finite forbidden-choice argument uses that two distinct translates of the strictly convex unit circle have at most two common points. This can also be understood by taking the translation horizontal: intersection endpoints correspond to a fixed horizontal chord length, and the strictly concave chord-width function attains that positive length at at most two heights. The construction only needs the Cartesian power of \(K_3\) as a subgraph; extra unit edges would improve the lower bound.

The resulting \(3^k\) points have at least \(k3^k\) unit edges. The ternary expansion of an arbitrary \(n\), with separately translated blocks, gives at least \[\sum_i a_i i3^i\ge \lfloor\log_3 n\rfloor n-\frac32 n.\] For a norm that is not strictly convex, the existing boundary segment supplies the stronger quadratic construction. Thus this planar lower bound does not impose strict convexity on the final proposition.

For the general-dimensional construction, the compact set \(U'\) of Lemma 7.4 contains, through its product parametrization, a closed set of dimension at least \[d+(d-1)^2=d(d-1)+1.\] The projection target has dimension \(d(d-1)\). Compactness follows from boundedness of the \(x_i\) and \(\|x\|\le\|x_1\|+1\); closedness follows from continuity. The Hurewicz dimension-lowering theorem therefore yields a fiber of positive dimension and hence an infinite set of common unit neighbors. The unit boundary has the needed local dimension because radial projection identifies it with a sphere.

The grid in Lemma 7.5 remains injective after a sufficiently small perturbation of its finitely many generators. The infinite common-neighbor set then allows each further binary generator to avoid the finitely many collisions with earlier sums. This establishes distinctness of all \[n'=k^{d-1}2^m\] points before their edges are counted.

For fixed \(i,j\), the counted edge decreases grid coordinate \(i\) by one and increases binary coordinate \(j\) from zero to one. Its difference is \(z_j-x_i\), a unit vector. The two endpoint labels uniquely identify these changed coordinates, so the counted unordered pairs for different \((i,j)\) are disjoint. The count is therefore \[(d-1)m(k-1)k^{d-2}2^{m-1}.\] This justification uses injectivity of the labels, not an unstated assumption that all geometric difference vectors are distinct. With the manuscript’s choices of \(m\) and \(k\), one has \(m=\log_2 n-O(\log\log n)\), \(k\to\infty\), and \(n'=(1-o(1))n\). Padding by extra points completes the all-\(n\) conclusion without losing edges.
# Confirmed local findings

Problem 1 (The planar chromatic minimum is misstated).  In Section 8, page 29, the paragraph beginning A related problem says that the minimum possible chromatic number of a planar norm’s unit-distance graph is two. This is false for every planar norm.

Fix any planar norm and a point \(x\) on its unit circle. The unit circle is a continuous radial image of the Euclidean circle, so there is a continuous arc from \(x\) to \(-x\). The continuous function \(y\mapsto\|y-x\|\) has endpoint values zero and two on that arc. It therefore takes the value one at some \(y\). The three distinct points \(0,x,y\) have all three mutual distances equal to one. Hence every planar norm’s unit-distance graph contains \(K_3\) and cannot be two-colored.

This universal argument is needed: merely exhibiting a Euclidean unit triangle would not by itself refute a minimum taken over all planar norms. It applies without strict convexity or genericity. The intended value is four, consistently with the universal lower bound cited on pages 3 and 23 and the paper’s typical-norm upper bound. The proof of Theorem 1.4 already uses four correctly. The error is a local concluding misstatement, assessed as Minor; it does not invalidate that theorem.

Problem 2 (The collinear dichotomy omits a boundary/interior pair).  The preliminary strict-convexity discussion on page 7 asserts that distinct collinear points \(a,b\) of the unit ball either have \(\max\{\|a\|,\|b\|\}<1\) or satisfy \(a=-b\).

In the Euclidean unit disk, take \[a=(1,0),\qquad b=(1/2,0).\] They are nonzero, distinct, collinear, and belong to the ball. Their maximum norm is one, and they are not antipodal. Thus all relevant hypotheses hold and the stated alternative fails. At \(\alpha=1/2\), however, the midpoint has norm \(3/4\), consistent with the desired strict-convexity conclusion.

Replacing \(\max\) by \(\min\) repairs the alternative. If one norm is strictly below one, the convex-combination norm is strictly below one. If both norms equal one and the points are distinct and collinear, they are antipodal, giving norm \(|2\alpha-1|<1\) for \(0<\alpha<1\). Equivalently, write \(a=tu,b=su\) with \(\|u\|=1\), \(s,t\in[-1,1]\), and \(s\ne t\). A strict convex combination cannot be an endpoint of that interval. The stated criterion for strict convexity survives. This is a Minor error in its local explanation.

Problem 3 (A missing factor in the entropy induction display).  In the final display of the proof of Lemma 4.4, page 11, the middle expression subtracts \(\sum_{i=2}^{\ell-1}n_i\log_2 n_i\), where a factor \(1/2\) is required.

Take \(\ell=3\) and \(n_1=n_2=n_3=2\), so \(n=6\) and \(n'_1=4\). These satisfy every hypothesis of the lemma. The three displayed quantities, as printed, become \[-1,\qquad -2,\qquad 6-3\log_2 6.\] The asserted second inequality is false, since \[-2<6-3\log_2 6
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 6^3<2^8,\] and \(216<256\). Thus this is not merely an uncertainty about numerical rounding.

The corrected induction chain is \[\begin{split}
 n_1-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}n_i\log_2 n_i
 &\ge n'_1-\frac12n'_1\log_2 n'_1
       -\frac12\sum_{i=2}^{\ell-1}n_i\log_2 n_i\\
 &\ge n-\frac12n\log_2 n.
\end{split}\] The preceding two-variable computation on the same page proves exactly the first corrected inequality using \(H(t)\ge2-2t\) for \(1/2\le t\le1\). The induction hypothesis gives the second. For the example, the corrected middle value is \(-1\).

The conclusion of Lemma 4.4 is unchanged, and its use in the forest proof already has the correct factor. problems.title: The planar chromatic minimum is misstated
problems.source_location: Pdf page: 29 Section: 8 Anchor: Paragraph beginning A related problem
claim: The minimum possible chromatic number of a planar norm's unit-distance graph is two.
Any norm on R^2; no genericity or strict convexity assumption is needed for the refutation.
analysis: In Section 8, page 29, the paragraph beginning A related problem says that the minimum possible chromatic number of a planar norm’s unit-distance graph is two. This is false for every planar norm.

Fix any planar norm and a point \(x\) on its unit circle. The unit circle is a continuous radial image of the Euclidean circle, so there is a continuous arc from \(x\) to \(-x\). The continuous function \(y\mapsto\|y-x\|\) has endpoint values zero and two on that arc. It therefore takes the value one at some \(y\). The three distinct points \(0,x,y\) have all three mutual distances equal to one. Hence every planar norm’s unit-distance graph contains \(K_3\) and cannot be two-colored.

This universal argument is needed: merely exhibiting a Euclidean unit triangle would not by itself refute a minimum taken over all planar norms. It applies without strict convexity or genericity. The intended value is four, consistently with the universal lower bound cited on pages 3 and 23 and the paper’s typical-norm upper bound. The proof of Theorem 1.4 already uses four correctly. The error is a local concluding misstatement, assessed as Minor; it does not invalidate that theorem.
result: Impact: False concluding local statement. Theorem 1.4 and its Section 6 proof use four correctly; no principal theorem damage established.

problems.title: The collinear dichotomy omits a boundary/interior pair
problems.source_location: Pdf page: 7 Section: 3.1 Anchor: Strict-convexity discussion before Fact 3.1
claim: Distinct collinear a,b in the unit ball either have max(||a||,||b||)<1 or a=-b.
Distinct nonzero collinear points in a norm unit ball; choose the Euclidean unit disk.
analysis: The preliminary strict-convexity discussion on page 7 asserts that distinct collinear points \(a,b\) of the unit ball either have \(\max\{\|a\|,\|b\|\}<1\) or satisfy \(a=-b\).

In the Euclidean unit disk, take \[a=(1,0),\qquad b=(1/2,0).\] They are nonzero, distinct, collinear, and belong to the ball. Their maximum norm is one, and they are not antipodal. Thus all relevant hypotheses hold and the stated alternative fails. At \(\alpha=1/2\), however, the midpoint has norm \(3/4\), consistent with the desired strict-convexity conclusion.

Replacing \(\max\) by \(\min\) repairs the alternative. If one norm is strictly below one, the convex-combination norm is strictly below one. If both norms equal one and the points are distinct and collinear, they are antipodal, giving norm \(|2\alpha-1|<1\) for \(0<\alpha<1\). Equivalently, write \(a=tu,b=su\) with \(\|u\|=1\), \(s,t\in[-1,1]\), and \(s\ne t\). A strict convex combination cannot be an endpoint of that interval. The stated criterion for strict convexity survives. This is a Minor error in its local explanation.
result: Impact: False local explanatory dichotomy; no loss of the strict-convexity criterion or later geometric approximation established.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Replace max by min. If either norm is below one the convex-combination bound is strict; if both equal one distinct collinear points are antipodal, giving |2 alpha-1|<1.

report: Abstract: This review checks the finite-energy reparametrization argument in the publisher version of Optimal Transport Between Algebraic Hypersurfaces. A continuous semialgebraic family of binary quadratic forms satisfies every stated hypothesis of Theorem 5.13, but every asserted power reparametrization has infinite quadratic Wasserstein energy. The obstruction is a parameter-speed singularity at a regular terminal hypersurface. This is a Major defect in a lemma used in the core metric construction. It does not refute the final existence theorem. Scientific adjudication and independent acceptance remain pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review: Finite-Energy Reparametrization for Algebraic Hypersurfaces
# Identity, reviewed version, and scope

The reviewed paper is Paolo Antonini, Fabio Cavalletti, and Antonio Lerario, Optimal Transport Between Algebraic Hypersurfaces, Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 43–112, DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00699-w (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-025-00699-w) [ACL]. The assigned identity is M25-0371. The source is the acquired 70-page publisher version of record, bound to the hashes in Appendix 5 (#app:record). Throughout this report, source page references are printed journal pages; the corresponding one-based physical PDF page is the printed page minus 42.

The focused review covers the definitions of admissibility and energy, the quantifiers in Theorem 5.13, its proof, and its explicit use in Corollary 5.14 and Theorem 5.15. The one-dimensional measure construction and the paper’s Fubini–Study normalization are checked where needed for the counterexample. The continuity/injectivity discussion and the lower-semicontinuity argument received a supporting text inspection, not a complete independent reconstruction. The general Hamiltonian isotopy argument, the Kähler calculation, the higher-dimensional root-regularity results, and the condition-number application have not been fully verified. This is a claim-focused initial review, not a certificate of whole-paper correctness or independent acceptance.
# Definitions and the precise claim

Let \(P_{n,d}\) denote the projective space of nonzero degree-\(d\) homogeneous polynomials in \(n+1\) complex variables, and let \(\Delta_{n,d}\) be the discriminant of polynomials whose projective zero equation is singular. In dimension \(n=1\), the measure \(\mu([p])\) is the probability measure assigning to each projective root its multiplicity divided by \(d\); see pp. 45–47 and Theorem 3.8, p. 69.

Definition 5.1, p. 77, requires \[\mu\circ\gamma\in AC^2([0,1];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb{CP}^{n})),
 \qquad
 \mathcal E(\gamma)=\int_0^1|\dot\mu_t|^2\,dt.\] The speed is measured using the ambient \(W_2\) distance. The formal definition of \(AC^2\) in Definition 2.2, p. 57, supplies an \(L^2\) upper gradient for distances between every two times. Thus an almost-everywhere metric speed with divergent square integral rules out admissibility. References below to infinite energy use the extended-energy convention; they do not assert that a nonadmissible curve belongs to the domain of Definition 5.1.

Problem 1 (A terminal speed singularity survives every asserted power reparametrization).  Theorem 5.13, p. 86 (PDF p. 44), asserts that whenever a continuous semialgebraic curve \(\gamma:[0,1]\to P_{n,d}\) satisfies \[\gamma(0)\in\Delta_{n,d},\qquad
 \gamma(t)\notin\Delta_{n,d}\quad(0<t\leq1),\] there is a positive integer \(m\) for which \(\alpha_m(s)=\gamma(s^m)\) has finite energy. This statement is false with its stated regularity hypothesis.
## Every hypothesis is satisfied

Equation reference: eq:example. Take \(n=1\), \(d=2\), and define \[
 r(t)=t\bigl(1+\sqrt{1-t}\bigr),\qquad
 p_t(z_0,z_1)=z_0^2-r(t)^2z_1^2,\qquad
 \gamma(t)=[p_t],\quad 0\leq t\leq1.\] The square root is its nonnegative real branch. The coefficient of \(z_0^2\) is always one, so the projective representative never vanishes. The curve is continuous and semialgebraic: its coefficients are obtained by polynomial operations from the algebraic branch \(u\geq0\), \(u^2=1-t\). In fact, it is smooth on \([0,1)\).
## The actual metric speed

Appendix A.1, p. 106, normalizes the Fubini–Study metric by the Riemannian submersion from the unit sphere. For the real coordinate \(r\), the normalized lift \[b(r)=\frac{(r,1)}{\sqrt{1+r^2}}\] has horizontal derivative of squared norm \((1+r^2)^{-2}\). Hence the projective speed of either root is \(|r'(t)|/(1+r(t)^2)\).

Equation reference: eq:speed. Near any fixed \(t>0\), the two roots are separated by a positive distance. The uncrossed matching between \(\mu_t\) and \(\mu_{t+h}\) has cost tending to zero, whereas the crossed matching has a positive limiting cost. The transport problem between these two equal-weight two-point measures minimizes a linear function over the \(2\times2\) doubly stochastic matrices, whose extreme points are precisely these two matchings. Thus the uncrossed matching is optimal for sufficiently small \(h\). Both matched roots have the same speed, so averaging their squared speeds gives \[
 |\dot\mu_t|^2=g(t):=\frac{r'(t)^2}{(1+r(t)^2)^2},\qquad 0<t<1.\] This derivation uses the measure itself and is unaffected by rescaling a homogeneous representative.
## Failure for every positive integer \(m\)

Equation reference: eq:limit-power. For \(
u_s=\mu_{s^m}\), the local matching argument and the chain rule yield \[|\dot
u_s|^2=m^2s^{2m-2}g(s^m).\] Since \[ rac{1-s^m}{1-s}=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}s^j\longrightarrow m,\] equation [eq:limit-original] (#eq:limit-original) gives, for each integer \(m\geq1\), \[
 \lim_{s\uparrow1}(1-s)|\dot
u_s|^2= rac{m}{16}>0.\] In particular, on a sufficiently small left neighborhood of \(1\), \[|\dot
u_s|^2\geq rac{m}{32(1-s)}.\] Therefore \(\int_0^1|\dot
u_s|^2\,ds=\infty\), and \(\mu\circ\alpha_m
otin AC^2\), for every allowed \(m\). The asserted finite-energy conclusion is contradicted by a universal analytic calculation, not by testing finitely many integers.
## The failing proof step and alternative readings

In the proof on p. 87 (PDF p. 45), immediately after splitting the energy integral at \(r_0\), regularity of the hypersurface equation is used to conclude that the integrand is bounded on \([r_0,1]\). Regularity controls the geometric denominator but does not bound the derivative of a merely continuous semialgebraic coefficient path. In [eq:example] (#eq:example), the roots stay separated near \(1\), while \(r'(t)\) has a square-root singularity and the square speed is nonintegrable.

The assertion and this proof step were checked in the actual publisher-page images; the issue is not inferred from an OCR anomaly. An additional \(C^1\) assumption up to the terminal endpoint would exclude this example. The source does impose \(C^1\) hypotheses in other results, including Theorem 5.3, but it does not impose that hypothesis in Theorem 5.13. A local assertion on a sufficiently short interval adjacent to \(0\) is also not refuted. Neither alternative is the global statement printed in the reviewed version.
# Core dependency and repair boundaries

Corollary 5.14, p. 87, invokes Theorem 5.13 to connect a point on the discriminant to a regular point by a finite-energy curve. The proof of Theorem 5.15, pp. 87–88, then uses Corollary 5.14 in establishing the intrinsic metric and its geodesic construction. The false quantified lemma and its invalid boundedness step therefore occur in an explicit proof chain supporting a core contribution. The supported impact is Major under the assigned core-derivation standard.

This conclusion has a precise boundary. The counterexample does not show that the two endpoints admit no finite-energy connection. It does not refute the continuity/injectivity of the measure map, the ultimate completeness or geodesicity claim, or the separate Kähler and condition-number results. The existence argument may be repairable by choosing better parameterized paths. No difficulty-of-repair claim is needed for the impact assessment.

Equation reference: eq:repair, eq:repair-bound. For this particular example there is an explicit verified repair using a different reparametrization: \[
 \phi(s)=1-(1-s)^2,\qquad
 r(\phi(s))=(2s-s^2)(2-s)=4s-4s^2+s^3 .\] The function \(\phi\) is a continuous, strictly increasing semialgebraic bijection of \([0,1]\) with its endpoints fixed. The repaired roots are smooth. Their \(W_2\) energy satisfies \[
 \mathcal E(\gamma\circ\phi)
 =\int_0^1\frac{(4-8s+3s^2)^2}
 {\{1+(4s-4s^2+s^3)^2\}^{2}}\,ds
 \leq\int_0^1(4-8s+3s^2)^2\,ds
 =\frac{47}{15}<\infty .\] The endpoint collision at \(s=0\) is harmless: pairing the two smooth roots supplies a bounded metric upper gradient on the whole interval. The quantity \(47/15\) is an upper bound, not the claimed exact energy. This verifies a repair of the example; it does not prove a revised global theorem for every continuous semialgebraic path or certify a complete replacement proof of Corollary 5.14.
# Version checks and conclusion

The inspected publisher PDF is the only full article version used for the finding. The public publisher HTML also displays the same unrestricted Theorem 5.13. A bounded exact-title correction/erratum search and a search of that article page identified no correction. The arXiv landing page lists v3, revised 16 July 2023, as its latest version [arxivmeta]; its full PDF was not substituted for the publisher version or compared line by line. These checks do not establish novelty of the finding or absence of an unpublished correction.

The acquisition manifest records bounded searches for supplements and research code without identifying a target-specific release. No author code was executed. No additional experiment is required to establish the analytic counterexample.

Appendix A.1, p. 106, normalizes the Fubini–Study metric by the Riemannian submersion from the unit sphere. For the real coordinate \(r\), the normalized lift \[b(r)=\frac{(r,1)}{\sqrt{1+r^2}}\] has horizontal derivative of squared norm \((1+r^2)^{-2}\). Hence the projective speed of either root is \(|r'(t)|/(1+r(t)^2)\).

Equation reference: eq:speed. Near any fixed \(t>0\), the two roots are separated by a positive distance. The uncrossed matching between \(\mu_t\) and \(\mu_{t+h}\) has cost tending to zero, whereas the crossed matching has a positive limiting cost. The transport problem between these two equal-weight two-point measures minimizes a linear function over the \(2\times2\) doubly stochastic matrices, whose extreme points are precisely these two matchings. Thus the uncrossed matching is optimal for sufficiently small \(h\). Both matched roots have the same speed, so averaging their squared speeds gives \[
 |\dot\mu_t|^2=g(t):=\frac{r'(t)^2}{(1+r(t)^2)^2},\qquad 0<t<1.\] This derivation uses the measure itself and is unaffected by rescaling a homogeneous representative.

Equation reference: eq:limit-power. For \(
u_s=\mu_{s^m}\), the local matching argument and the chain rule yield \[|\dot
u_s|^2=m^2s^{2m-2}g(s^m).\] Since \[ rac{1-s^m}{1-s}=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}s^j\longrightarrow m,\] equation [eq:limit-original] (#eq:limit-original) gives, for each integer \(m\geq1\), \[
 \lim_{s\uparrow1}(1-s)|\dot
u_s|^2= rac{m}{16}>0.\] In particular, on a sufficiently small left neighborhood of \(1\), \[|\dot
u_s|^2\geq rac{m}{32(1-s)}.\] Therefore \(\int_0^1|\dot
u_s|^2\,ds=\infty\), and \(\mu\circ\alpha_m
otin AC^2\), for every allowed \(m\). The asserted finite-energy conclusion is contradicted by a universal analytic calculation, not by testing finitely many integers.

In the proof on p. 87 (PDF p. 45), immediately after splitting the energy integral at \(r_0\), regularity of the hypersurface equation is used to conclude that the integrand is bounded on \([r_0,1]\). Regularity controls the geometric denominator but does not bound the derivative of a merely continuous semialgebraic coefficient path. In [eq:example] (#eq:example), the roots stay separated near \(1\), while \(r'(t)\) has a square-root singularity and the square speed is nonintegrable.

The assertion and this proof step were checked in the actual publisher-page images; the issue is not inferred from an OCR anomaly. An additional \(C^1\) assumption up to the terminal endpoint would exclude this example. The source does impose \(C^1\) hypotheses in other results, including Theorem 5.3, but it does not impose that hypothesis in Theorem 5.13. A local assertion on a sufficiently short interval adjacent to \(0\) is also not refuted. Neither alternative is the global statement printed in the reviewed version.

report: Abstract: This focused initial review checks the linear-algebra argument for the cylinder criterion and the terminal arithmetic in the maximal-zero-exponent proof in arXiv:2103.02133v1. Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of Minimal Homological Dimension and the Lyapunov-Exponent Argument
# Identity, version, and scope

The assigned paper is M25-0372, Paul Apisa, Invariant Subvarieties of Minimal Homological Dimension, Zero Lyapunov Exponents, and Monodromy. The reviewed source is the 47-page arXiv:2103.02133v1, dated 3 March 2021 [source]. Its association with the 2025 journal item, DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00700-6, is an identity mapping; equivalence to the publisher version has not been established. All page numbers below are the source’s printed pages, equal to physical PDF pages.

The inspected targets are Definitions 1.1–1.3, Theorem 1.7 and its proof on pp. 12–13, and the algebraic reduction in Section 9, pp. 41–45, conditional on its stated geometric and dynamical inputs. Definitions of cylinder equivalence and good covers were consulted. The induction proving Theorem 1.5, the full theory of geminal varieties, boundary degeneration results, and the original external references were not independently reconstructed. This is not an exhaustive whole-paper correctness assessment.
# The cylinder criterion

Write \(r=\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal M)\) and let \(h\) be its homological dimension: the maximum dimension of the span of horizontal cylinder core curves over horizontally periodic surfaces. The rank is half the complex dimension of the absolute tangent space \(p(T\mathcal M)\). Minimal homological dimension means \(h=r\), not merely \(h\geq r\). Cylinder equivalence means persistence of parallelism throughout a neighborhood in \(\mathcal M\), not just parallelism on a single surface (Definition 2.1, p. 6).

In the forward implication of Theorem 1.7, the reduction to a cylindrically stable surface uses Lemma 2.7, p. 8, as an input. Let \(W\subset H_1(X;\mathbb R)\) be the span of the horizontal core curves there. Restriction of homology functionals to the absolute tangent space gives a map \(\varphi\). The stated stability property supplies \[\dim\varphi(W)=r,\qquad \dim W\leq h=r.\] Therefore \(\dim W=r\) and \(\varphi|_W\) is injective. Collinearity of the functionals of equivalent cylinders consequently implies collinearity of their homology classes.

The final conversion from collinearity to equality also has a topological justification. A cylinder core is an embedded simple closed curve with nonzero period, so it is nonseparating and its integral homology class is primitive. Collinear primitive integral classes are equal up to sign. Orienting parallel cores in the common positive direction fixes the sign through their positive periods. This checks the homologous-core conclusion; arbitrary proportional integral classes would not suffice.

Conversely, when cores within an equivalence class \(\mathcal C\) are homologous, the absolute image of the standard deformation is \[p(\sigma_{\mathcal C})=
 \left(\sum_{C\in\mathcal C}h_C\right)\operatorname{PD}(\gamma),
 \qquad \sum_{C\in\mathcal C}h_C>0 .\] The cylinder deformation theorem, used here as stated in the source, places these classes in \(p(T\mathcal M)\). Thus the complexification of \(\operatorname{PD}(W)\) lies in that \(2r\)-dimensional complex symplectic space. Disjoint horizontal cores have zero pairwise intersection, so this subspace is isotropic and has dimension at most \(r\). Together with the source’s lower bound \(h\geq r\), this yields \(h=r\). The proof’s use of the word Lagrangian on p. 13 can be weakened to isotropic for this dimension estimate; maximality is not needed. No failure of the claimed implication follows from that wording.
# The final arithmetic in Section 9

Theorem 1.8 asserts a classification under exactly \(2g-2r\) zero exponents, the maximum allowed at rank \(r\). It does not assert that every minimal-homological-dimension locus has this many zero exponents. Section 9 first excludes \(r=1\) by an explicitly cited external classification, then assumes \(r>1\), non-full rank, and maximal vanishing.

For the remaining audit, take as inputs the preceding classification, Lemma 9.1’s non-varying sum, the optimal-cover property, and Corollary 6.13. Let \(d\geq2\) be the cover degree, \(g'\geq2\) the base genus, \(R\) total ramification, and \(P\) the number of regular Weierstrass points on the base. Goodness of the cover (Definition 6.9, p. 27) is essential to the single-preimage-cylinder property: a cylinder has unchanged height and circumference multiplied by \(d\). Consequently the finite-coset average in (9.0.2)–(9.0.3) acquires a factor \(1/d\); it is not a claim for arbitrary covers.

Equation reference: eq:sum, eq:finite. Put \[w(m)=\frac{m(m+2)}{m+1},\qquad
 A=\sum_iw(m_i),\quad A'=\sum_iw(m_i'),\quad
 S=\sum_{d_i\ \mathrm{odd}}\frac{1}{d_i+2}.\] The positive zero orders \(m_i\geq1\) must be distinguished from regular marked points. Equation (9.0.6), multiplied by 12, is \[
 3(1-d^{-1})S=A-d^{-1}A'.\] Since \(1<(m+2)/(m+1)\leq3/2\), the strict inequality in (9.0.7) is justified by at least one positive zero. Riemann–Hurwitz gives \(2g-2=d(2g'-2)+R\). The inputs \(R\geq P-1\) and \(S\leq P+(2g'+2-P)/3\), followed by \(P\leq2g'+2\), yield exactly \[
 18d-24>(2d^2-4d+3)(2g'-2).\] The coefficient of \(P\) at the substitution step is \(2d-4\geq0\), so its direction is correct even at \(d=2\).

This really excludes all larger degrees, not just tested examples. At \(g'=2\), the right side minus the left in [eq:finite] (#eq:finite) is \(2(2d-3)(d-5)\), nonnegative for \(d\geq5\). For \(g'\geq3\), it is at least \(2(4d-9)(d-2)\), nonnegative for every integer \(d\geq2\). Hence only \(g'=2\) and \(d\in\{2,3,4\}\) remain.
## Ramification cases and a bounded clarification

For \(P=6\), the exact strict upper bounds on \(R\), for \(d=2,3,4\), are \(13/2,7,25/4\); since \(R\geq5\) and \(R\) is even, \(R=6\). For \(P=5\) the bounds are \(11/2,17/3,19/4\), and \(R\geq4\) forces \(R=4\). Parity follows directly from Riemann–Hurwitz.

Equation reference: eq:weight. There is a safer direct check of the \(P=6\) contradiction than the count of order-one zeros stated on p. 45. A ramification index \(e\) over a base simple zero produces a zero of order \(2e-1\), and \[
 w(2e-1)-e\,w(1)=\frac{e^2-1}{2e}\geq0.\] The two base simple zeros therefore contribute at least \(3d\) to \(A\). Each branched regular point contributes at least \(w(1)=3/2\). Branching over at least five such points gives \(A\geq3d+15/2\), which is stronger than the lower bound \(3d+6\) used in the printed contradiction.

For precision, the conditional profile with simple branching over one base simple zero and five regular points has \(2d+3\) order-one zeros and one order-three zero, rather than \(2d+4\) order-one zeros. Its weighted contribution is \(3d+33/4\), so it too satisfies the needed lower bound. This is local pullback bookkeeping, not a construction of an invariant variety satisfying all the contradictory hypotheses. No counterexample to Theorem 1.8 is asserted.

Using even the weaker valid bound, [eq:sum] (#eq:sum) would require \[18(1-d^{-1})\geq3d+6-3d^{-1},
 \quad\text{hence}\quad
 6d^2-24d+30\leq0.\] But \(6d^2-24d+30=6(d-2)^2+6>0\). The printed strict sign at this final step is unnecessary; the non-strict inequality already contradicts positivity. For \(P=5\), four simple regular branch points give \(A=4(3/2)+d(8/3)\) and \(A'=8/3\). The resulting equation is \[8d^2-30d+40=8(d-15/8)^2+95/8=0,\] which has no real solution. These checks preserve the terminal contradictions conditional on the stated inputs.
# Assessment and limits

No substantive issue is established in the inspected cylinder implication or terminal Lyapunov-sum calculation. The local wording and counting clarifications above are not promoted to Problems because the required dimension bound and contradiction remain valid by the displayed arguments. The full classification, external theorems, monodromy corollary, and the publisher version still require their own checks before any broader conclusion.

Abstract: This focused initial review identifies one substantive defect in the published proof of the optimal Gaussian rigidity tail. The deterministic event inclusion at the end of Section 6.4 fails for an explicit family of spectra, including open sets of positive probability for a valid real Gaussian Wigner ensemble. The discrepancy is a leading-order coefficient, not a vanishing smoothing error. A local change of threshold suggests a repair, but a complete revised probability argument is not certified here. The theorem itself is not disproved. Scientific adjudication and independent acceptance remain pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of the Final Counting-Function Step in Optimal Rigidity
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

M25-0373 is Paul Bourgade, Patrick Lopatto and Ofer Zeitouni, Optimal Rigidity and Maximum of the Characteristic Polynomial of Wigner Matrices, Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 161–253, DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00701-5 [source]. The reviewed source is the assigned 93-page version-of-record PDF. Printed page \(p\) is physical PDF page \(p-160\).

The main inspected chain is Definition 1.1, the quantile convention (1.6), Theorem 1.8(ii), the centered trace and smoothing definitions, and the final use of (6.19) in Section 6.4. Earlier moment estimates are treated as inputs to this specific check; no assertion that they have all been verified is made. The maximum-characteristic-polynomial theorems, the full Dyson Brownian motion comparison, the moment replacement induction, and the appendices are not independently certified. Statement and selected proof-page readings outside this chain are distinguished in the coverage record.
# Normalization and the claimed implication

Equation reference: eq:tail. Let \[\rho(x)=\frac{\sqrt{(4-x^2)_+}}{2\pi},\qquad
 F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^x\rho(y)\,dy,\qquad
 F(\gamma_k)=\frac{k-\frac12}{N},\qquad
 \delta=\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{N}.\] The eigenvalues are in increasing order. For a fixed compact bulk range, put \(c_k=\sqrt2/(\pi\rho(\gamma_k))\). Theorem 1.8(ii), printed p. 166, seeks a bound of the form \[\mathbb P\{|\lambda_k-\gamma_k|>u c_k\delta\}
 \leq C\exp\bigl(-(1-\varepsilon)u^2\bigr),
 \qquad 0\leq u\leq A\sqrt{\log N}.
 \] Here \(C\) may depend on the fixed parameters. Part (i) is a separate, signed-maximum statement and is not the finding below.

Equation reference: eq:smoothing. The centered trace on p. 197 is \(\overline{\operatorname{Tr}}f(H)=\sum_j f(\lambda_j)-N\int f(x)\rho(x)\,dx\). Equations (5.38)–(5.40), p. 206, use smoothing width \(\eta_1=\delta\). The first step of Section 6.4, p. 214, specifies the increasing transition as \[f_E(y)=\int_0^1 h(s)\mathbf1_{[E+s\delta,\infty)}(y)\,ds,
 \quad h\geq0,\quad \int_0^1h(s)\,ds=1,
 \] with smooth \(h\) supported in \([0,1]\). The prescribed upper cutoff above \(2.5\) has no effect on the spectra or centering integrals used below.
# Problem 1: a false event inclusion in the core tail proof

Equation reference: eq:claim. Classification: Major. Location: printed p. 215 (physical page 55), paragraph immediately after (6.19), and the resulting Markov bound continuing to p. 216. For fixed \(\varepsilon\), sufficiently large \(N\), and any \(u>1\), the paper claims \[\lambda_k-\gamma_k>u c_k\delta
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \overline{\operatorname{Tr}}f_E(H)>(1-\varepsilon)\frac{u\sqrt2}{\pi}\sqrt{\log N},
 \qquad E=\gamma_k+u(c_k-1)\delta.
 \] The factor \(u\) multiplies the entire parenthesis in the actual PDF. This placement is also present in the publisher HTML consulted for version checking.
## A decisive family satisfying the relevant conditions

Equation reference: eq:spectrum, eq:upper. Take arbitrarily large odd \(N\), \(k=(N+1)/2\), \(\kappa=1/4\), \(A=1\), \(u=4\), and \(\varepsilon=1/4\). Then \(\gamma_k=0\), \(\rho(0)=1/\pi\), \(c_k=\sqrt2\), and \(u\leq A\sqrt{\log N}\) for large \(N\). Define the strictly increasing spectrum \[b=(4\sqrt2+1)\delta,\qquad
 \lambda_j=
 \begin{cases}
  \gamma_j,&j<k,\\
  \gamma_j+b,&j\geq k.
 \end{cases}
 \] The antecedent of [eq:claim] (#eq:claim) is strict. At its printed threshold \(E=4(\sqrt2-1)\delta\), all eigenvalues with \(j<k\) lie below \(E\), and \[\lambda_k-(E+\delta)=4\delta>0.\] All eigenvalues are below \(2.5\) for sufficiently large \(N\). Thus, for every smoothing density in [eq:smoothing] (#eq:smoothing), \(\sum_j f_E(\lambda_j)=(N+1)/2\). Fubini’s theorem and \(F(0)=1/2\) give \[\begin{aligned}
 \overline{\operatorname{Tr}}f_E(H)
 &=\frac12+N\int_0^1h(s)\bigl(F(E+s\delta)-\tfrac12\bigr)\,ds \notag\\
 &\leq\frac12+\frac{4\sqrt2-3}{\pi}\sqrt{\log N},
 \end{aligned}\] where only the exact bound \(\rho(x)\leq1/\pi\) was used. The claimed lower bound is \[\frac{3\sqrt2}{\pi}\sqrt{\log N}.\] Its difference from the upper bound in [eq:upper] (#eq:upper) is \[\frac{3-\sqrt2}{\pi}\sqrt{\log N}-\frac12>0\] for all sufficiently large odd \(N\). This contradicts the implication with strict margins. It is a uniform analytic construction, not an extrapolation from a finite numerical search.

To connect this spectrum to the paper’s probabilistic hypotheses, take the real Gaussian Wigner ensemble with independent upper-triangular entries, off-diagonal variance \(1/N\), and diagonal variance \(2/N\). This satisfies Definition 1.1, including the uniform subexponential tail condition. The diagonal matrix with spectrum [eq:spectrum] (#eq:spectrum) is a point in the support of this ensemble; it is not itself claimed to be a random Wigner ensemble. Gaussian density is positive on the entire real symmetric matrix space. Eigenvalues and the smooth trace are continuous, so the strict antecedent and strict failure persist in an open neighborhood of that diagonal matrix. That neighborhood has positive probability for each sufficiently large odd \(N\).

The example also lies inside the ordinary rigidity bound (2.9) on p. 175 for sufficiently large \(N\): its displacement is \(O(\sqrt{\log N}/N)\), whereas the smallest permitted scale is of order \(\varphi/N\), with \(\varphi=\exp(C_0(\log\log N)^2)\) and \(\varphi/\sqrt{\log N}\to\infty\). Invoking that rigidity event alone does not remove the counterexample. No lower bound on the probability of the violating neighborhood is claimed.
## Dependency and repair boundary

Equation [eq:claim] (#eq:claim) converts the centered-trace moment bound (6.19) into the final Markov estimate and the sharp exponent in [eq:tail] (#eq:tail). Its failure therefore invalidates this core step of the displayed proof. The lost coefficient persists as \(N\to\infty\); it cannot be absorbed by choosing a larger \(N\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). This is the reason for the Major classification, even if a short correction ultimately suffices. The construction does not disprove Theorem 1.8(ii), nor does it refute the characteristic-polynomial maximum theorems.

Equation reference: eq:repair, eq:repairbound. A concrete local repair candidate is \[E_*=\gamma_k+(u c_k-1)\delta,
 \] subtracting one smoothing width outside the factor \(u\). On the spectral event that makes the upper cutoff irrelevant, the antecedent then implies \[\overline{\operatorname{Tr}}f_{E_*}(H)
 \geq \frac12+N\bigl(F(E_*)-F(\gamma_k)\bigr)
 =\left(\frac{u\sqrt2}{\pi}-\rho(\gamma_k)+o(1)\right)\sqrt{\log N}.
 \] The Taylor remainder is uniform on a fixed compact bulk range for \(u\leq A\sqrt{\log N}\): before division by \(\sqrt{\log N}\), it is \(O((1+u)^2\log N/N)=o(\sqrt{\log N})\). Consequently the desired relative coefficient follows for \(u\) above a sufficiently large constant depending on \(\varepsilon\). The bounded-\(u\) range may be absorbed into a larger prefactor \(C\) in [eq:tail] (#eq:tail). A complete repair must still supply the range split, the cutoff exceptional-event estimate, and a consistent moment optimization. In particular, the full low-moment and comparison estimates were not verified here. Only the deterministic correction [eq:repair] (#eq:repair)–[eq:repairbound] (#eq:repairbound) is checked; a repaired complete theorem is not certified.
# Verification and limitations

An independently written scalar script checks rational bounds for \(\sqrt2\), the strict margins, and an illustrative odd dimension \(N=100000001\). It returns an upper bound \(4.129700\) and claimed lower bound \(5.796145\), with positive gap \(1.666445\). These floating-point values illustrate the analytic proof; they are not its justification. No author code was executed and no huge matrix was constructed.

A bounded publisher/arXiv correction search did not identify a correction. The arXiv record lists v2 dated 10 August 2024, but that PDF was not compared with the assigned publisher PDF. Absence from this bounded search does not establish that no correction or supplementary material exists. The scientific finding attaches only to the assigned source bytes.

Other main results | Partial contextual reading | No finding asserted | Outside certified scope

Title: Technical Review of the Tate-Period Coalgebra and Functional Equation
# Source and theorem scope

M25-0374 is Tony Feng and Jonathan Wang, Geometric Langlands Duality for Periods, Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 463–541, DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00702-4 [source]. This review uses the assigned 79-page version-of-record PDF. Printed page \(p\) is physical PDF page \(p-462\).

The distinction made in Theorems 1.2.1 and 1.2.3, pp. 466–467, is essential. In the general examples, the result matches the two pieces of exact triangles under the specified Geometric Langlands equivalence; identifying these pieces alone does not identify the middle object without its extension class. The Tate example receives the additional extension comparison. The singular Rankin–Selberg example is explicitly presented as extending beyond the original smooth setting. None of these qualifications is treated as an error.

The calculations below concern Corollary 6.2.4 and Proposition 6.5.1. Sections 6.2–6.4 were also read for context, but their complete ind-coherent base-change and extension-compatibility arguments were not independently reconstructed. In particular, this report does not certify Theorem 6.1.2 as a whole.
# The local coalgebra in the Tate example

Equation reference: eq:local. Take \(k\) of characteristic zero and \(X=\mathbb A^1\), with its standard \(\mathbb G_m\)-action. The coherent dualizing complex is \(\omega_X=k[x]\,dx[1]\). Local cohomology at the origin is computed by the localization complex \[\bigl[k[x]\longrightarrow k[x,x^{-1}]\bigr]\otimes k\,dx[1].
 \] The unshifted complex has its nonzero cohomology in degree \(1\); after the dualizing shift, the quotient lies in degree \(0\). Hence it has a basis \[e_n=x^{-n-1}dx,\qquad n\geq0.\] With the usual induced action on functions, \(x\) and \(dx\) have weight \(-1\), so \(e_n\) has weight \(n\). This gives precisely the positive grading used in Lemma 6.2.2 and Corollary 6.2.4, pp. 499–500.

The residue pairing is \[\langle e_n,x^m\rangle=\operatorname{Res}_{x=0}(x^{m-n-1}dx)
 =\delta_{nm}.\] It is perfect in each graded component. One must retain this graded qualification: the unrestricted linear dual of an infinite direct sum is a product. The paper explicitly formulates perfection degree by degree.

Equation reference: eq:coproduct. Dualizing polynomial multiplication gives \[\Delta(e_n)=\sum_{a+b=n}e_a\otimes e_b,\qquad
 \epsilon(e_n)=\delta_{n0}.
 \] If \(v\) is the standard weight-one generator of the usual symmetric coalgebra, the identification is \(e_n\leftrightarrow v^n/n!\), because \[\Delta\!\left(\frac{v^n}{n!}\right)
 =\sum_{a+b=n}\frac{v^a}{a!}\otimes\frac{v^b}{b!}.\] Thus the occurrence of \(\operatorname{Sym}^{\bullet}(\mathrm{Std})\), rather than the symmetric algebra on the dual representation, is correct. The characteristic-zero hypothesis makes this divided-power normalization legitimate. The degree-zero term is the coaugmentation and must not be discarded when passing between augmented and non-unital notation.

This verifies the classical one-dimensional instance needed for Corollary 6.2.4. It does not independently establish the full statement of Lemma 6.2.2 for every perfect complex and every derived base, nor Proposition 4.5.2 relating local distributions to factorization homology.
# The functional equation and its shifts

Fix the spin line \(S=\Omega_C^{1/2}\) from Section 2.4.1. On a component of \(\operatorname{Bun}_1\) with \(\deg L=d\), the displayed definitions in Section 6.5 use \[E=R\Gamma(C,L\otimes S),\qquad
 E'=R\Gamma(C,L^{-1}\otimes S).\] The spin twist is necessary. The short fiber description in the first paragraph of Section 6.5.1 omits it, but the displayed definition and the proof on p. 508 include it; the calculation here uses those explicit formulas.

Equation reference: eq:rank, eq:serre. Riemann–Roch and \(\deg S=g-1\) imply \[\operatorname{rank}(E)=\chi(C,L\otimes S)=d,\qquad
 \operatorname{rank}(E')=-d.
 \] Serre duality gives \[E^\vee\simeq E'[1],\qquad E'\simeq E^\vee[-1].
 \] Consequently the derived self-intersection of the zero section in \(\operatorname{Tot}(E^\vee)\) is \(\operatorname{Tot}(E')\). The word derived is indispensable: replacing this self-intersection by its classical intersection would lose the cohomological information in [eq:serre] (#eq:serre).

Equation reference: eq:ft. Write \(\pi\) and \(\pi'\) for the corresponding projections. The functoriality in Section 3.1.5 and the constant/delta transform in Example 3.1.3 give, with the paper’s convention \(\langle n\rangle=\Pi^n[n](n/2)\), \[\pi_! k_{\operatorname{Tot}(E)}
 \simeq z_{E^\vee}^{*}\delta_{E^\vee}\langle-2d\rangle
 \simeq \pi'_! k_{\operatorname{Tot}(E')}\langle-2d\rangle.
 \] The first shift is the sum of the two rank contributions \(-d\); its Tate twist is \(-d\), and its parity change is even. The second isomorphism uses the derived Cartesian square and the stated base-change formalism. These Fourier and base-change results are inputs to this focused check, not results independently reproved here.

As a boundary check, take \(C=\mathbb P^1\), \(S=\mathcal O(-1)\), and \(L=\mathcal O(d)\). Then \[h^0(L\otimes S)=\max(d,0),\qquad
 h^1(L\otimes S)=\max(-d,0).\] The classical truncations of the total spaces have these respective affine dimensions. Their compact-support shifts satisfy \[-2\max(d,0)=-2\max(-d,0)-2d,\] including \(d=0\), where both complexes vanish. This checks the sign in [eq:ft] (#eq:ft). Such fiber calculations alone do not prove a canonical global isomorphism; that role is played by the derived Fourier construction.
# Assessment and verification boundary

The local residue computation and the complete shift arithmetic above produce no substantive defect in the inspected claims. The omitted spin twist in one descriptive sentence is resolved by the source’s displayed definition and proof and is recorded as a clarification, not as a failed theorem.

An independently written exact-arithmetic script verifies the divided-power coefficients through degree \(12\), the \(\mathbb P^1\) boundary formulas for \(-8\leq d\leq8\), and the normalization identity for several genera. The universal equalities follow from the displayed algebra, not from these finite checks. No author code was executed.

The source manifest’s bounded supplement and code searches are retained. A fresh publisher/arXiv identity lookup associates the paper with arXiv:2402.00180; that preprint was not compared with the assigned PDF. No absence-of-resources or version-equivalence claim is made.

Abstract: The equivalence in Proposition 2.1.1(1) fails with its stated allowance of an arbitrary locally closed invariant subset of the moment-map image. The standard Hamiltonian action of \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) on a symplectic plane gives a dimension-zero fiber satisfying the numerical condition while its restricted inverse image is not Lagrangian. Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of the Moment-Map Criterion and a Linear Cotangent Case
# Source and scope

M25-0375 is Michael Finkelberg, Victor Ginzburg and Roman Travkin, Lagrangian Subvarieties of Hyperspherical Varieties, Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 254–282, DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00703-3 [source]. The assigned source is the 29-page version-of-record PDF; printed page \(p\) is physical PDF page \(p-253\).

This review checks the hypotheses and equivalences of Proposition 2.1.1, pp. 258–259, and the standard cotangent/rook argument for the linear side in Section 4.1, pp. 264–265. The exceptional and orthosymplectic enumerations, the complete maze bijections, and the equivariant-slice side are not independently certified. The broader statements in Section 1 remain distinguished as conjectures. In particular, the Weyl-group and categorical conjectures are not presented here as proved results.
# Problem 1: restriction to a closed stratum destroys the claimed equivalence
Classification: Major. Location: Proposition 2.1.1(1)(a)–(c), printed p. 258 (physical page 5), and the proof’s coisotropic-component assertion on p. 259 (physical page 6).

The proposition assumes that \(X\) is a smooth affine Hamiltonian \(G\)-variety, that \(Z\subset\mu(X)\) is a locally closed \(G\)-stable subset, and that a character \(\bar\lambda\in\mathfrak b^*\) has \(Z_{\bar\lambda}=Z\cap(\bar\lambda+\mathfrak b^\perp)\ne\varnothing\). It then declares the following equivalent: \[\begin{aligned}
 &\mu^{-1}(Z_{\bar\lambda})\text{ is Lagrangian in }X; \qquad\text{(a)}\\
 &\mu^{-1}(\lambda)\text{ is isotropic for every }\lambda\in Z_{\bar\lambda}; \qquad\text{(b)}\\
 &\dim F\leq \tfrac12\bigl(\dim X-\dim(G\lambda)\bigr)
 \quad\text{for every irreducible fiber component }F. \qquad\text{(c)}\end{aligned}\] There is no openness hypothesis on \(Z\) in part (1).
## An explicit Hamiltonian counterexample

Equation reference: eq:moment. Let \[G=\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb C),\qquad
 X=\mathbb A^2_{\mathbb C},\qquad
 \omega=dx\wedge dy,\] with the standard linear action, and let \(B\) be the upper-triangular Borel. Identify \(\mathfrak{sl}_2^*\) with \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) by the trace pairing. A moment map is \[\mu(x,y)=\frac12
 \begin{pmatrix}xy&-x^2\\y^2&-xy\end{pmatrix}.
 \] For \(A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&-a\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), its component is \[\langle\mu,A\rangle=axy+\tfrac12by^2-\tfrac12cx^2,\qquad
 \iota_{A(x,y)}\omega=d\langle\mu,A\rangle .\] The matrix formula is \(\operatorname{SL}_2\)-equivariant. Equivalently, for the standard basis \(H,E,F\), the polynomial Hamiltonians \[\mu_H=xy,\quad \mu_E=y^2/2,\quad \mu_F=-x^2/2\] satisfy \(\{\mu_H,\mu_E\}=2\mu_E\), \(\{\mu_H,\mu_F\}=-2\mu_F\), and \(\{\mu_E,\mu_F\}=\mu_H\), with \(\{f,g\}=f_xg_y-f_yg_x\). Changing the overall moment-map sign convention would not affect any zero fiber below.

Choose \[Z=\{0\}\subset\mu(X),\qquad \bar\lambda=0.\] All hypotheses are satisfied: \(G\) is complex reductive, \(X\) is smooth affine symplectic, \(Z\) is closed and \(G\)-stable, and \(0\) is a character of \(\mathfrak b\). Moreover \(Z_{\bar\lambda}=\{0\}\). Equation [eq:moment] (#eq:moment) gives \[\mu^{-1}(0)_{\mathrm{red}}=\{(0,0)\},\qquad
 \dim\mu^{-1}(0)=0,\qquad \dim(G\cdot0)=0.\] Consequently condition (c) is the true inequality \[0\leq\tfrac12(2-0)=1,\] whereas condition (a) is false: a point in a symplectic surface has dimension \(0\), not the required Lagrangian dimension \(1\). Thus (a) and (c) are not equivalent. This conclusion is independent of any convention about isotropy of a nonreduced scheme. With the usual reduced-variety interpretation, the point is also isotropic, so (b) holds as well.

The scheme fiber is defined by \((x^2,xy,y^2)\), but its sole irreducible component still has dimension \(0\); nilpotent structure cannot repair the stated dimension equivalence. The action is even coisotropic generically, since \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) is transitive on \(X\setminus\{0\}\). No failure of the general-orbit condition is being exploited.
## The precise proof failure

The proof on p. 259 asserts that the component \(\Lambda\) under consideration is a component of the fiber of the \(B\)-moment map, and invokes coisotropy of that fiber component. That inference is invalid after restriction to an arbitrary locally closed \(Z\). In this example the origin is not coisotropic: its tangent space is zero and its symplectic orthogonal is the entire tangent plane. The preceding isotropy calculation therefore cannot be upgraded to the Lagrangian conclusion.
## Impact and repair boundary

The finding invalidates a central implication in the general moment-map criterion as actually quantified. It requires a restriction of the proposition’s scope or a different statement, rather than an arithmetic correction inside a valid proof; this is the basis for the Major classification.

An openness hypothesis on \(Z\), as already used in part (2), removes this particular obstruction. In the example, choosing \(Z=\mu(X)\setminus\{0\}\) gives \(\mu^{-1}(Z_0)=\{(x,0):x\ne0\}\), which is Lagrangian. More generally, openness makes \(\mu^{-1}(Z)\) open in \(X\), preventing the specific dimension collapse caused by selecting a smaller closed stratum. This is a repair direction, not an independent certification of every equivalence under a revised hypothesis.

The example does not disprove Proposition 2.1.1(2), the zero-\(B\)-level conjecture, or the numerical equalities in the later case studies. Indeed, its full zero-\(B\)-level [eq:borel] (#eq:borel) is Lagrangian. The report does not infer that the paper’s component counts rely indispensably on the false arbitrary-\(Z\) extension.
# Separate check: the ordinary linear cotangent side

For \(V=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb C^N,\mathbb C^M)\) and the standard cotangent action, the defining identity for the moment map says \[\mu_B(v,\xi)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \xi(\mathfrak b\cdot v)=0.\] Thus the zero level is the union of conormal bundles of the \(B_M\times B_N\)-orbits in \(V\). Each conormal bundle is isotropic and has dimension \(\dim O+\operatorname{codim}_V O=MN\). There are finitely many such orbits, indexed by partial permutation matrices, or non-attacking rook placements. Therefore their distinct closures are exactly Lagrangian components. This argument concerns the full Borel level and has no arbitrary closed-\(Z\) restriction.

The rook count is \[R_{M,N}=\sum_{r=0}^{\min(M,N)}
 \binom Mr\binom Nr r!.\] The southwest rectangular ranks are preserved by left and right upper-triangular row/column operations and determine a partial permutation matrix: each occupied entry is recovered by the corresponding second difference of the ranks. The usual elimination constructs those representatives. An independent enumeration for \(1\leq M,N\leq4\) confirms the formula and uniqueness of their rank profiles; examples are \(R_{1,1}=2\), \(R_{2,2}=7\), \(R_{2,3}=13\), \(R_{3,3}=34\), and \(R_{4,4}=209\). These finite checks support, but do not replace, the geometric argument. No assertion about the other side of Proposition 4.1.1 or the full maze correspondence is made.
# Verification and limits

An independently written exact polynomial script verifies the Hamiltonian derivatives, the three Lie–Poisson identities, and the nilpotent identity \(\mu_H^2+4\mu_E\mu_F=0\), as well as the finite rook enumeration. The dimension obstruction is exact and analytic, not a numerical conjecture. No author code was executed.

The actual source statement and its proof page, the linear-case source pages, and every final report page are displayed and inspected, with exact source, TeX, PDF and compilation bindings in the supporting records. A bounded publisher/arXiv correction search did not identify a correction. Publisher HTML retains the locally closed hypothesis. A preprint retrieval exposed differently organized text; no preprint/PDF equivalence is asserted. Acquisition supplement/code search limitations are retained.
