report: Abstract: Theorem 8.1 of the assigned preprint is false: a factorial-gap power series, analytic near the closed unit disk but singular at radius two, admits supergeometric polynomial approximation along a subsequence of degrees. Separately, the proof of Theorem B uses total rational degree where the Green function requires the local pole order. Proposition 7.6 also omits multiplicities from the interpolation conditions needed for uniqueness. The first two issues are Major because they affect an announced sharpness result and a core approximation proof, respectively. The third has a limited, nonessential consequence. This initial review does not refute Theorem A or the existence conclusion of Theorem B; independent acceptance and adjudication remain pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of Rational Approximation, Interpolation, and the Sharpness Claim
# Source, definitions, and scope

M25-0376 is Christopher J. Bishop, Alexandre Eremenko and Kirill Lazebnik, On the Shapes of Rational Lemniscates, associated with Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 359–407, DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00704-2. The assigned 48-page PDF is arXiv:2407.14610v3: the arXiv margin says 8 February 2025 and the title-page date is 11 February 2025. All locations below refer to that PDF, whose printed and physical pages agree. The publisher landing page was consulted for identity, but its subscription preview did not expose the full proof; equivalence with the published version is not asserted.

A rational lemniscate is \(L_r(c)=\{|r|=c\}\), \(c>0\). The paper uses ambient sphere homeomorphisms of uniformly small spherical displacement, not merely setwise proximity, in Theorem A. Theorem B permits a compact \(K\subset\widehat{\mathbb C}\), exactly one prescribed point in every complementary component, and a function holomorphic on a neighborhood of \(K\). It asserts degree-\(\le n\) rational approximants with poles in that prescribed set and error \(A/B^n\), for some \(A,B>1\).

This review targets Sections 7–8, with the unit Green-function normalization from Section 4. The full vertex construction for Theorem A, quasiconformal surgery, and Julia-set assertions of Theorem C are not independently certified. Parsing all 48 pages is distinguished from substantive reading of the targeted pages.
# Problem 1: arbitrary sparse degrees do not force entire extension
Classification: Major. Location: Theorem 8.1, p. 32; the replacement of a subsequence by consecutive degrees in its proof, p. 33; the corresponding announced sharpness claim, p. 4.

Equation reference: lower. The theorem states that if \(K\) has positive logarithmic capacity and \(f\) does not extend holomorphically to \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus P\), there is \(D>1\) such that, for every \(C>0\) and every admissible sequence \(R_n\), \[
 \|f-R_n\|_K>C D^{-n}\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }n.\] The quantifier on \(n\), including arbitrary subsequences, is essential.
## A counterexample satisfying every hypothesis

Equation reference: gap. Take \(K=\{|z|\le1\}\), \(P=\{\infty\}\), \(U=\{|z|<2\}\), and \[
 f(z)=\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}(z/2)^{j!},\qquad
 R_n(z)=\sum_{\substack{j\ge2\\ j!\le n}}(z/2)^{j!}.\] The series converges locally uniformly on \(U\), which contains \(K\). The disk has positive logarithmic capacity (indeed, capacity one). There is exactly one complementary component on the sphere, containing the single prescribed pole \(\infty\). Every \(R_n\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(n\), so its pole set is contained in \(P\).

The radius of convergence of \(f\) is exactly two: its nonzero coefficients at indices \(j!\) have \(j!\)-th root \(1/2\). More directly, along the real radius \(r\uparrow2\), any fixed number of summands tends to that number, so \(f(r)\to+\infty\). Consequently \(f\) cannot have a holomorphic extension to \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus P=\mathbb C\).
## Failed proof step and repair boundary

For consecutive degrees, the pole order of \(R_{n+1}-R_n\) at a fixed allowed pole is at most \(n+1\). The proof combines this with an error bound \(O(D^{-n})\) to obtain a summable geometric majorant on a smaller Green level. After replacing \(n\) by \(n_k\), the relevant order is instead at most \(n_{k+1}\). The resulting factor is of the form \[D_1^{\,n_{k+1}}\bigl(D^{-n_k}+D^{-n_{k+1}}\bigr),
 \qquad 1<D_1<D,\] which need not decay. The factorial gaps exploit precisely this loss.

An estimate holding for every sufficiently large degree is a different hypothesis, under which the consecutive-degree argument can be used where the Green-function setup applies. In the disk/polynomial case it yields a restriction on the limsup rate, not the claimed lower bound at every large degree. No general repair for arbitrary \(P\) or irregular compact sets is certified here. Theorem B’s existence of a geometric upper bound and Theorem A’s approximation statement are not contradicted by this example.
# Problem 2: total degree is not the Green-function pole order

Classification: Major. Location: equation (7.1) and the proof of Lemma 7.2, p. 29; the resulting estimate (7.10) in the proof of Theorem B, p. 31. The controlling definition is (4.1) and Notation 4.2, pp. 15–16, reiterated on p. 28.

Equation reference: local. The source defines each Green function with a unit logarithmic singularity, and sums one such function per prescribed pole. In Section 7 there is one pole \(p\) per grey face \(F\). If \(r\) has local pole order \(m_p\) there and \(L_r=\{|r|=1\}\), uniqueness for the Dirichlet problem gives, inside that face, \[
 \log|r(z)|=m_p G_F(z,p).\] At a finite pole, both sides have principal term \(-m_p\log|z-p|\); at infinity they have principal term \(m_p\log|z|\). Equation (7.1) instead writes \(u_{L_r,P}=d^{-1}\log|r|\), where \(d=\deg r\). When there is more than one pole, \(m_p<d=\sum_{p\in P}m_p\), and the logarithmic coefficients do not match. The discrepancy occurs inside grey faces, so it is independent of the additional need to truncate to zero on white faces.

For a concrete admissible geometry let \[r(z)=\frac{z^2+1}{3z},\qquad d=2,\qquad P=\{0,\infty\}.\] Both poles are simple. On \(|z|=1\), \(|r(z)|\le2/3<1\), separating the grey component at zero from the one at infinity. The only critical points are \(\pm1\), with critical values \(\pm2/3\); hence the level \(L_r(1)\) is regular. Each grey face contains one pole. On the unbounded face, \[G_F(z,\infty)=\log|z|+O(1),\qquad
 d^{-1}\log|r(z)|=\tfrac12\log|z|+O(1),\] which disproves (7.1).

The subsequent separation implication can also fail for this \(r\). Put \(K=\{|r|\le3/4\}\). Its two smooth boundary curves enclose an annular compact set; its complementary components contain exactly \(0\) and \(\infty\). In those components \(u_{\partial K,P}=\log(|r|/(3/4))\). For \(\rho=3/2\) and \(R=4\), one has \(C_\rho=\{|r|=9/8\}\) and \(C_R=\{|r|=3\}\). A neighborhood \(U=\{|r|<4\}\) meets the required containment and separation conditions. Although \(L_r(1)\) separates \(K\) from \(C_\rho\), the asserted higher level is \(L_r(64/9)\), beyond \(C_R\), and does not separate \(K\) from \(C_R\). This example refutes the proof’s claimed implication for the chosen \(r\); it is not by itself a disproof of the existential statement of Lemma 7.2 with unrestricted poles.
## Impact and a local repair calculation

The normalization enters the degree-dependent estimate used to prove Theorem B, so its effect is substantive even though the existence theorem may survive. Using [local] (#local), let \(\ell=\min_{p\in P}m_p>0\). The same facewise comparison instead gives a usable level \((R/\rho)^\ell\), and hence an estimate of the form \[\|f-R_{dn-1}\|_K\le C_0(R/\rho)^{-\ell n}.\] In terms of degree, a possible geometric base is \(B=(R/\rho)^{\ell/d}>1\), with a suitably enlarged prefactor. This calculation repairs the local normalization and retains a geometric rate, conditional on the existing separation and regularization inputs; it is not a certification of every part of the full revised proof. In addition, the elementary contour estimate uses \(\|f\|_{C_R}\), not \(\|f\|_K\), in \(C_0\). Enlarging the constant also handles the finitely many initially unassigned degrees and the requirement \(A>1\). These constant adjustments are not counted as separate substantive Problems.
# Problem 3: uniqueness omits zero multiplicities
Classification: Minor. Location: Proposition 7.6 and its equation-count argument, p. 32.

The proposition prescribes \(R^{(j)}(a)=f^{(j)}(a)\) for \(0\le j<n\) at each zero \(a\) of \(r\), then claims uniqueness among degree-\(\le dn-1\) rational functions with the same poles and pole orders as the constructed approximant. The proof counts \(dn\) conditions without assuming that \(r\) has simple zeros.

If \(a\) has multiplicity \(m_a\), the defining error actually vanishes to order at least \(nm_a\). Replacing the printed conditions by all jets \(0\le j<nm_a\) supplies \(nd\) conditions, since all zeros are finite after the chosen pole at infinity. With the same pole divisor, a nonzero difference has at most \(dn-1\) zeros, so the corrected uniqueness argument works. Alternatively, simplicity of all zeros would suffice, but is not stated. The source expressly says this proposition is not needed for Theorem B; its error therefore has limited impact and is classified Minor.

The analytic arguments above, rather than the finite checks alone, establish the counterexamples. No author code was executed. The numerator cancellation and degree bound of Lemma 7.4 were read: the intended denominator estimate is \(n\deg q\le n(d-1)\le dn-1\). The printed intermediate inequality involving \(n\deg p\) is not used here as a separate defect.

analysis: Classification: Major. Location: Theorem 8.1, p. 32; the replacement of a subsequence by consecutive degrees in its proof, p. 33; the corresponding announced sharpness claim, p. 4.

Equation reference: lower. The theorem states that if \(K\) has positive logarithmic capacity and \(f\) does not extend holomorphically to \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus P\), there is \(D>1\) such that, for every \(C>0\) and every admissible sequence \(R_n\), \[
 \|f-R_n\|_K>C D^{-n}\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }n.\] The quantifier on \(n\), including arbitrary subsequences, is essential.

Equation reference: gap. Take \(K=\{|z|\le1\}\), \(P=\{\infty\}\), \(U=\{|z|<2\}\), and \[
 f(z)=\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}(z/2)^{j!},\qquad
 R_n(z)=\sum_{\substack{j\ge2\\ j!\le n}}(z/2)^{j!}.\] The series converges locally uniformly on \(U\), which contains \(K\). The disk has positive logarithmic capacity (indeed, capacity one). There is exactly one complementary component on the sphere, containing the single prescribed pole \(\infty\). Every \(R_n\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(n\), so its pole set is contained in \(P\).

The radius of convergence of \(f\) is exactly two: its nonzero coefficients at indices \(j!\) have \(j!\)-th root \(1/2\). More directly, along the real radius \(r\uparrow2\), any fixed number of summands tends to that number, so \(f(r)\to+\infty\). Consequently \(f\) cannot have a holomorphic extension to \(\widehat{\mathbb C}\setminus P=\mathbb C\).

For consecutive degrees, the pole order of \(R_{n+1}-R_n\) at a fixed allowed pole is at most \(n+1\). The proof combines this with an error bound \(O(D^{-n})\) to obtain a summable geometric majorant on a smaller Green level. After replacing \(n\) by \(n_k\), the relevant order is instead at most \(n_{k+1}\). The resulting factor is of the form \[D_1^{\,n_{k+1}}\bigl(D^{-n_k}+D^{-n_{k+1}}\bigr),
 \qquad 1<D_1<D,\] which need not decay. The factorial gaps exploit precisely this loss.

An estimate holding for every sufficiently large degree is a different hypothesis, under which the consecutive-degree argument can be used where the Green-function setup applies. In the disk/polynomial case it yields a restriction on the limsup rate, not the claimed lower bound at every large degree. No general repair for arbitrary \(P\) or irregular compact sets is certified here. Theorem B’s existence of a geometric upper bound and Theorem A’s approximation statement are not contradicted by this example.

Title: Technical Review of the Compactness Hypotheses and Final Tangent-Flow Iteration
# Source and scope

M25-0377 is Kyeongsu Choi, Dong-Hwi Seo, Wei-Bo Su and Kai-Wei Zhao, Uniqueness of Tangent Flows at Infinity for Finite-Entropy Shortening Curves, Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 408–462, DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00705-1 [source]. The assigned source is the 55-page version-of-record PDF. Printed page \(p\) is physical page \(p-407\). The current publisher HTML was consulted for identity and the exact scope of Lemma 3.1; no separate preprint comparison is asserted.

The main setting is a smooth ancient embedded planar curve-shortening flow, with rescaling \(\overline M_\tau=(-t)^{-1/2}M_t\), \(\tau=-\log(-t)\), and finite entropy, the supremum of Gaussian length over all centers and positive scales and all times. Section 2.3 explicitly works with complete curves; the weak flows are integral, unit-regular and cyclic. Incomplete curve fragments are therefore not used as counterexamples.

The review checks the nonvanishing boundary of Lemma 3.1, its application to rough convergence, and the algebra and final iteration in Section 8. The detailed low-entropy classification, finger and vertex geometry, full proof of the graphical-radius estimate, and all external regularity theorems remain outside independent certification.
# Problem 1: the general compactness lemma allows an empty limit
Classification: Minor. Location: Lemma 3.1, printed p. 420 (physical page 13), especially the passage from local compactness to a nonempty line or circle. Its application is Theorem 3.3, pp. 421–423.

Equation reference: defect. The lemma assumes only that \(\overline M_j\) are connected smooth embedded curves with \(F(\overline M_j)<\Lambda\), and \[
 \int_{\overline M_j}
 \left|\boldsymbol\kappa+\frac{x^\perp}{2}\right|^2
 e^{-|x|^2/4}\,d\mathcal H^1\longrightarrow0.\] It concludes subsequential local \(C^{1,\alpha}\) convergence to a line through the origin or a radius-\(\sqrt2\) circle, possibly with multiplicity.
## Why the ancient-flow application is different

Equation reference: anchor, tail. This is not a counterexample to Theorem 1.1. In that application, fix a nonempty time slice at \(\tau_*\). Huisken monotonicity gives \[
 F(\overline M_\tau)\ge F(\overline M_{\tau_*})=:c>0
 \qquad(\tau\le\tau_*).\] The full entropy bound \(\operatorname{Ent}(\overline M_\tau)\le\Lambda\) also implies uniform linear length growth. Taking Gaussian scale \(R^2\) yields \[\mathcal H^1(\overline M_\tau\cap B_R)
 \le \sqrt{4\pi}\,e^{1/4}\Lambda R .\] Therefore, for integer \(N\ge1\), the Gaussian mass outside \(B_N\) is at most \[
 \frac1{\sqrt{4\pi}}\int_{\overline M_\tau\setminus B_N}e^{-|x|^2/4}\,d\mathcal H^1
 \le e^{1/4}\Lambda\sum_{k=N}^{\infty}(k+1)e^{-k^2/4}
 \longrightarrow0\] uniformly in \(\tau\). Choose \(N\) making this tail smaller than \(c/2\). Equations [anchor] (#anchor)–[tail] (#tail) then retain positive mass in a fixed ball.

The local repair is to add an explicit nonvanishing condition to the general lemma, or allow an empty limit and exclude it in the application using the bounds above. The necessary nonvanishing is available under the paper’s ancient-flow assumptions. This verifies the repair of the exhibited escape mechanism, not every remaining compactness or shrinker-classification step. Because the main application supplies what is missing, no substantive failure of the main uniqueness conclusion is established; the issue is Minor.
# Checks of the final analytic mechanism
## Gaussian modes and stable energy

On printed p. 450 the graph equation is \[u_\tau=\mathcal Lu-\frac{u_y^2u_{yy}}{1+u_y^2},
 \qquad \mathcal L=\partial_y^2-\frac y2\partial_y+\frac12,
 \qquad d\gamma=\frac{e^{-y^2/4}}{\sqrt{4\pi}}\,dy.\] Direct calculation gives the normalized modes \[\varphi_1=1,\quad \varphi_2=y/\sqrt2,\quad
 \varphi_3=(y^2-2)/\sqrt8,\qquad
 \mathcal L\varphi_1=\tfrac12\varphi_1,\quad
 \mathcal L\varphi_2=0,\quad
 \mathcal L\varphi_3=-\tfrac12\varphi_3.\] The Gaussian moments are \(E[y^2]=2\), \(E[y^4]=12\), so these normalizations agree with the source. The positive number attached to the stable mode is its decay rate, not a positive eigenvalue of \(\mathcal L\).

For a stable projection \(w=P_-\widehat u\), \[\langle w,\mathcal Lw\rangle
 =-\|w_y\|_{\mathcal H}^2+\tfrac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2,
 \qquad
 \langle w,\mathcal Lw\rangle\le-\tfrac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2.\] Splitting twice this inner product into \(3/2\) and \(1/2\) multiples and using Young’s inequality for \(2\langle P_-E,w\rangle\) gives \[\frac d{d\tau}\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2
 \le-\tfrac12\|w_y\|_{\mathcal H}^2
    -\tfrac14\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2+4\|P_-E\|_{\mathcal H}^2.\] This verifies the coercive arithmetic underlying (68), conditional on the error estimates in Lemma 8.4. The entire nonlinear projection estimate is not certified here.
## Rotation preserves the needed \(L^2\) control

Proposition 8.8, printed p. 456, passes from a nearly linear graph to a rotated graph. A direct change of variable supplies the norm control needed for its regularity step. For rotation by \(-\theta\), write \[x=y\cos\theta+u(y)\sin\theta,\qquad
 v(x)=u(y)\cos\theta-y\sin\theta
      =\cos\theta\,[u(y)-(\tan\theta)y].\] When \(|\theta|\) and \(|u_y|\) are small, \(1/2\le dx/dy\le2\); the interior interval \([-6,6]\) maps back into \([-8,8]\). Hence \[\|v\|_{L^2([-6,6])}\le\sqrt2\,
 \|u-(\tan\theta)y\|_{L^2([-8,8])}.\] This closes the norm conversion directly, without inferring an \(L^2\) estimate from an \(L^1\) estimate alone. The cited parabolic local boundedness and Schauder estimates are retained as external inputs.
## Geometric iteration and exponential rate

Choose \(0<5\delta<\log2/L\). The bound \(Ce^{5\delta\tau}\) yields a graphical radius of order \(e^{-5\delta\tau/4}\) through \(\rho^{-4}=\max_i\|u_i\|_{C^2([-1,1])}\) in Theorem 7.3; this eventually exceeds \(e^{-\delta\tau}\). For each fixed \(R\), the remaining prefactor is absorbed by \(Ce^{5\delta\tau}\le e^{4\delta\tau}\) for sufficiently negative \(\tau\), after the stated interior regularity step. These exponent conversions agree with Theorem 1.2. This is a conditional check of the final implication, not a new proof of the upstream flatness improvement.

report: Abstract: The energy sign, boundary cancellations, and final level-crossing argument are consistent within the scope checked. Two limited defects are identified in the assigned preprint: Lemma 3.2 claims an initial-time \(L^\infty\) bound independent of the initial peak, and the Neumann Parseval identity omits the weight of the zero vertical mode. Explicit smooth data and a single Fourier mode establish these failures. A data-dependent iteration restores the qualitative \(L^2\)-to-\(L^\infty\) implication needed by the blowup criterion, while the Fourier correction changes universal constants. Neither check supplies a counterexample to the main global-regularity theorem. Independent acceptance and scientific adjudication remain pending.

# Problem 1: the initial peak cannot be removed from Lemma 3.2
Classification: Minor. Location: Lemma 3.2, p. 9; its use in Corollary 3.3.
The lemma assumes \(\|\rho(t)-\rho_M\|_2\le2M\) on \([0,T]\), with \(M\ge\max(1,\sqrt{\rho_M})\), and concludes \(\|\rho(t)-\rho_M\|_\infty\le CM^2\) with universal \(C\), including \(t=0\).

Choose \(0\le\phi\in C_c^\infty(B_1(0))\), \(\phi(0)=1\), \(\phi\le1\), and an interior point \(x_*=(0,\pi/2)\). For \(A\ge1\), define \[\rho_{0,A}(x)=A\phi(A(x-x_*)).\] Its support stays away from the boundary and the periodic seam, so the smooth nonnegative data obey the boundary conditions. A change of variables in two dimensions gives \[\|\rho_{0,A}\|_2^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\phi^2\le\pi<4,\qquad
 \rho_{M,A}=\frac{1}{2\pi^2A}\int\phi\le\frac1{2\pi A}.\] Subtracting the mean only decreases the \(L^2\) norm. For any fixed nonzero \(g\), local existence and continuity provide a sufficiently short interval \([0,T_A]\) on which \(\|\rho_A(t)-\rho_{M,A}\|_2\le2\). Thus the lemma’s assumptions hold with \(M=1\). Yet \[\|\rho_{0,A}-\rho_{M,A}\|_\infty
 \ge A-\frac1{2\pi A}\longrightarrow\infty.\] No universal \(C\) can give the stated conclusion. This is a short-time estimate failure, not a singular solution of the coupled system.
## A sufficient qualitative repair

The blowup criterion needs a finite \(L^\infty\) bound for a fixed smooth initial datum when the \(L^2\) norm stays bounded. That weaker statement can retain the initial peak. Here is an independent iteration establishing this distinction.

Equation reference: lp. Suppose \(\sup_{t<T}\|\rho(t)\|_2\le K<\infty\). Set \(Y_p=\int_\Omega\rho^p\), \(w=\rho^{p/2}\), \(p\ge2\). Testing [system] (#system), using incompressibility and the boundary conditions, gives \[
 Y_p'+\frac{4(p-1)}p\|\nabla w\|_2^2
 =(p-1)\int\rho^{p+1}-(p-1)\rho_MY_p.\] The compact-domain two-dimensional interpolation inequality gives \[\int\rho w^2\le K\|w\|_4^2
 \le CK\bigl(\|w\|_2\|\nabla w\|_2+\|w\|_2^2\bigr).\] Young’s inequality in [lp] (#lp) yields \[Y_p'+\|\nabla w\|_2^2\le Cp^2(1+K^2)Y_p.\] The compact-domain Nash inequality gives \[\|\nabla w\|_2^2\ge cY_p^2/Y_{p/2}^2-CY_p.\] Set \(A_{p/2}=\sup_{t<T}\|\rho(t)\|_{p/2}\). The resulting differential inequality bounds \[A_p\le
 \max\left\{\|\rho_0\|_p,\,
 [Cp^2(1+K^2)]^{1/p}A_{p/2}\right\}.\] For \(p=2^j\), the products converge because \(\sum_{j\ge2}2^{-j}=1/2\) and \(\sum_{j\ge2}j2^{-j}=3/2\). This proves a finite bound depending on \(K\), \(\|\rho_0\|_\infty\), and the fixed domain, uniformly in \(T\). The zero-density case is immediate; otherwise all denominators can be treated by the positive lower norms or by the usual zero-case separation.

A bound on \(\|\rho-\rho_M\|_2\) bounds \(K\) because the mean is conserved. Thus the qualitative implication used to exclude finite-time blowup with bounded \(L^2\) remains available. The review does not restore the printed universal \(CM^2\) estimate at \(t=0\), or assert its optimal replacement. This verified distinction limits the impact to Minor.

For completeness, the Riccati step in Corollary 3.3 also has the correct direction: from \(Y'\le C(Y^2+Y)\), \(Z=1+Y^{-1}\) satisfies \(Z'\ge-CZ\). Letting \(Y(t_k)\to\infty\), \(t_k\uparrow T\), gives \(Y(t)\ge(e^{C(T-t)}-1)^{-1}\), upgrading the limsup to a limit.
# Problem 2: the Neumann zero mode needs its normalization weight
Classification: Minor. Location: Section 2.2, p. 7, final gradient Parseval identity; repeated in the discussion of (6.9), pp. 19–20.

The source defines \[\widehat f_N(k_1,k_2)=\frac1\pi\int_\Omega
 f(x)e^{-ik_1x_1}\cos(k_2x_2)\,dx,
 \quad
 f=\frac1\pi\sum_{k_1\in\mathbb Z,\ k_2\ge0}
 \frac{\widehat f_N(k)}{1+\delta_{k_2,0}}e^{ik_1x_1}\cos(k_2x_2).\] Under this convention the correct quadratic form is \[\|\nabla f\|_2^2
 =\sum_{k_1\in\mathbb Z,\ k_2\ge0}
 \frac{k_1^2+k_2^2}{1+\delta_{k_2,0}}|\widehat f_N(k)|^2.\] The printed identity omits the denominator. Take \(f(x)=\cos x_1\). This is smooth, mean zero, satisfies the Neumann condition and also equals its horizontal fluctuation \(\widetilde f\). Its only coefficients are \(\widehat f_N(\pm1,0)=\pi\). The true gradient integral is \(\pi^2\); the printed unweighted sum is \(2\pi^2\).

Inserting the same weight into the \(L^2\) Parseval sums repairs the identity. These weights lie between \(1/2\) and \(1\), so all affected norms remain uniformly equivalent. The cone argument can retain its universal-constant estimates after shrinking its auxiliary parameter and adjusting constants. This verifies the normalization repair and its bounded-factor character, not every lattice-counting or basis-transfer step of Proposition 6.1. No main-result counterexample follows from this defect.
# Checks of the buoyancy mechanism and final contradiction
## Boundary conditions and energy sign

For periodic pressure, the Darcy equation gives \(u=g\nabla^\perp(-\Delta_D)^{-1}\partial_{x_1}\rho\), with \(\nabla^\perp=(-\partial_{x_2},\partial_{x_1})\). Multiplying the density equation by \(x_2\), the boundary conditions eliminate flux terms but retain the vertical diffusion contribution. With \(E(t)=\int_\Omega x_2\rho\), \[E'=-g\|\partial_{x_1}\rho\|_{\dot H^{-1}_0}^2
       -\int_\Omega\partial_{x_2}\rho
       +\int_\Omega\rho\,\partial_{x_2}c,
 \qquad 0\le E\le\pi M_0.\] Horizontal integration by parts fixes the sign: \[\int_\Omega\rho u_2
 =-g\int_\Omega\partial_{x_1}\rho\,(-\Delta_D)^{-1}\partial_{x_1}\rho.\] The diffusion term is the difference of boundary densities and is not presumed nonnegative.

Reflection \(x_2\mapsto\pi-x_2\), with \(u_2\mapsto-u_2\), transforms parameter \(g\) to \(-g\) and preserves the density and no-flux conditions. The positive-\(g\) proof therefore transfers to negative \(g\). If \(M_0=0\), nonnegativity forces the trivial solution; divisions by \(\rho_M\) in nontrivial estimates are unnecessary in that case.
## Level crossing and the finite-energy budget

Write \(Y=\|\rho-\rho_M\|_2^2\). A good level-\(N\) interval goes from \(2^N\) to \(2^{N+1}\), and a bad one goes in the reverse direction. The intermediate-time bounds differ, as stated in Definition 5.1; they are not replaced by endpoint monotonicity. The differential estimate \(Y'\le CY^2\) yields a minimum duration \(c2^{-N}\) for an upward crossing.

At the first hit of level \(Q+1\), every edge between \(N\) and \(N+1\), \(N_0\le N\le Q\), has exactly one more upward crossing than downward crossing. This follows by telescoping the indicator of being above that edge. There are only finitely many crossings before that fixed time, by local smoothness or the upward duration bound. Thus the argument does not need to rearrange an uncontrolled infinite series.

Assume the established interval estimates (6.19) and (6.25): \[\Delta E_{\rm good,N}\le-\frac{c_1g}{N},\qquad
 \Delta E_{\rm bad,N}\le C_1(\rho_M)2^{-N/3}.\] For every fixed \(g>0\), \(N2^{-N/3}\to0\), so a sufficiently large \(N_0\) makes a good/bad pair nonpositive at each level. The unmatched upward crossing then contributes \[E(t_K)-E(t_1)\le-c_1g\sum_{N=N_0}^{Q}\frac1N.\] The harmonic sum can exceed \(\pi M_0/(c_1g)\), contradicting \(0\le E(t_K)\) and \(E(t_1)\le\pi M_0\). This verifies the terminal accounting for arbitrary fixed nonzero coupling, conditional on the technical interval estimates. It supplies no claim of a coupling-independent bound as \(g\to0\).

Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of the Geometric Reduction and Gaussian Rescaling in the Spielman–Teng Argument
# Identity, assumptions, and review boundary

M25-0379 is Ashwin Sah, Julian Sahasrabudhe and Mehtaab Sawhney, On the Spielman–Teng Conjecture, associated with Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 633–671, DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00707-z. The assigned source is the 29-page arXiv:2405.20308v2, dated 8 January 2025 [source, arxiv]. Printed and physical PDF page numbers agree. The publisher page supplies identity and a subscription preview; equivalence with the 39-page journal version has not been established [publisher]. The acquisition record’s unsuccessful alternative-manuscript route is retained without claiming access.

The main random matrix has iid real subgaussian entries of mean zero and variance one. Constants can depend on the entry law. Theorem 1.2 compares its least singular-value distribution with the real Gaussian one, with relative error of order \((\log n)^{-1/16}\) and an exponentially small additive error. The small-scale proof works between exponential and polynomial thresholds; the large-scale and extremely small regimes invoke external results. No complex-matrix extension or uniformity over unbounded subgaussian constants is assumed.

Equation reference: eq:chi. For a deterministic \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\), remove its last row \(Y\) to obtain \(A^*\). When \(A^*\) has full row rank, let \[s_i=\sigma_i(A^*)>0,\quad u_0\in\ker A^*,\quad \|u_0\|=1,\quad
y_i=\langle u_i,Y\rangle,\quad y_0=\langle u_0,Y\rangle,\] where the \(u_i\) form an orthonormal singular basis. Put \[t=\varepsilon n^{-1/2},\qquad
 \widetilde\chi^2=1+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{y_i^2}{s_i^2}.
 \] All 29 source pages were read for statements and dependencies. Independent derivation is concentrated on Sections 3–4 and the fixed-matrix part of Section 9. Reading the remaining proofs is not a claim of their full verification.
# Problem 1: Lemma 3.3 needs its small-parameter range
Classification: Minor. Location: Lemma 3.3, p. 7, implication (21), and its proof on p. 8.

Equation reference: eq:claimed. The stated hypothesis is \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(s_{n-1}\geq \varepsilon^{3/4}n^{-1/2}\). The claimed implication is \[\sigma_n(A)\leq \varepsilon n^{-1/2}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 |y_0|\leq (1+\varepsilon^{1/4})\varepsilon n^{-1/2}\widetilde\chi .
 \] There is no upper bound on \(\varepsilon\) in this deterministic statement.

For any \(n\geq2\), take \(\varepsilon=1\), \(t=n^{-1/2}\) and \[A=\operatorname{diag}(t,\ldots,t,3t),\qquad u_0=e_n.\] Then \(A^*\) has full row rank with every positive singular value equal to \(t\). Its last row is \(Y=3te_n\), so \(y_i=0\) for \(i<n\), \(\widetilde\chi=1\), and \(|y_0|=3t\). Both the spectral-gap hypothesis and the antecedent hold with equality: \(s_{n-1}=t=\varepsilon^{3/4}n^{-1/2}\) and \(\sigma_n(A)=t\). The conclusion would require \(3t\leq2t\). Thus the unrestricted statement is false. The example uses a unit kernel vector and works for arbitrarily large \(n\); it does not exploit missing normalization or small dimension.
## Exact repair in the range actually used

Equation reference: eq:schur. For \(0<t<s_{n-1}\), a Schur complement in \(A^{\mathsf T}A-t^2I\) gives the exact criterion \[\sigma_n(A)\leq t
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 y_0^2\leq t^2\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}
                  \frac{y_i^2}{s_i^2-t^2}\right).
 \] Indeed the upper-left block is positive definite and its scalar Schur complement is \[-t^2+\frac{y_0^2}{1+\sum_i y_i^2/(s_i^2-t^2)}.\] This argument includes \(y_0=0\) and equality at the tested threshold.

If \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/16\) and \(s_{n-1}\geq\varepsilon^{3/4}n^{-1/2}\), then \(t<s_{n-1}\) and \[1+\sum_i\frac{y_i^2}{s_i^2-t^2}
 \leq \frac{\widetilde\chi^2}{1-\sqrt\varepsilon}.\] Writing \(q=\varepsilon^{1/4}\leq1/2\), \[(1+q)^2(1-q^2)-1=q(2-2q^2-q^3)>0.\] Taking square roots proves [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed) throughout this corrected range.

The converse implication (22) also has a robust proof. If \(\sigma_n(A)>t\), rank-one interlacing gives \(s_{n-1}>t\); [eq:schur] (#eq:schur) then implies \(|y_0|>t\widetilde\chi\). If \(A^*\) is rank deficient, \(A\) is singular and this antecedent is impossible; the undefined inverse weights should not be evaluated on that stratum.

The counterexample lies outside the small-scale range used to prove the main theorem. Restricting the deterministic lemma as above preserves that use, and Section 4’s range \(\varepsilon\leq(\log n)^{-4}\) eventually lies inside it. This is the reason for a local Minor assessment. It is not a counterexample to a random-matrix theorem and does not establish a failure of the claimed leading probability constant.
# Spectral notation and pole endpoints

Equation reference: eq:det. Lemma 3.2, p. 7, mixes \(s_i^2-x\) in the product with \(s_i^2-x^2\) in the denominator, while calling \(x\) a singular value. The determinant calculation immediately below uses the squared spectral parameter. With \(\lambda\) denoting that parameter, the consistent polynomial identity is \[\det(A^{\mathsf T}A-\lambda I)
 =\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(s_i^2-\lambda)
   \left(1+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{y_i^2}{s_i^2-\lambda}\right),
 \qquad s_0=0.
 \] The right side is interpreted after polynomial cancellation, or by continuity at its apparent poles. To use the singular-value variable \(x\), replace every \(\lambda\) by \(x^2\).

For example, \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,3)\) has singular values \(2,3\). The mixed formula printed in the lemma gives \((-x)(4-x)(1-9/x^2)\), which equals \(5\) at \(x=2\). The corrected determinant is \((4-\lambda)(9-\lambda)\). This check identifies a spectral-parameter inconsistency; the following determinant proof already points to the correction. It is treated as a clarification rather than an additional substantive Problem.

The assertion before (23) that the least singular value is always an interior secular root also needs an endpoint convention. For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\) the true least singular value is \(1\), but the equation on \((0,1)\) becomes \(1=4/x^2\) and has no root there. The first singular direction has zero projection onto \(Y\), so the claimed divergence at that pole is absent. The Schur criterion [eq:schur] (#eq:schur) avoids this issue in the relevant range \(t<s_{n-1}\). No generic nonzero-projection assumption is silently imposed on discrete random entries.
# The truncation estimate on the regularity event

Equation reference: eq:lower. On the event \(R\) defined on p. 9, let \(\ell=\lfloor\sqrt{\log n}\rfloor\), \(k_0=\lfloor(\log\log n)^2\rfloor\) and \[\chi^2=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\frac{y_{n-i}^2}{s_{n-i}^2}.\] Rounding these indices does not change the asymptotic estimates. For sufficiently large \(n\), \(k_0\leq\ell\). The two conditions \(R_3,R_4\) give directly \[\chi^2\geq \frac{n}{(\log\log n)^6}
                  \sum_{i\leq k_0}y_{n-i}^2
       \geq \frac{n}{(\log\log n)^5}.
 \] Thus this lower bound applies to the retained sum itself, not merely to the full sum.
# A direct Gaussian rescaling check

Lemma 9.2, pp. 21–22, starts from the correct two-sided event \(|W_0|\leq\varepsilon f\) for independent standard Gaussians, but its proof subsequently writes \(W_0\leq\varepsilon f\) and uses a bound of order \(\varepsilon f\). Taken literally, the latter event has probability \(1/2\) at \(\varepsilon=0\), whereas the claimed rescaling has zero right-hand side. The initial lemma statement makes the intended absolute value unambiguous.

There is also a cutoff mismatch: Lemma 9.2 assumes \(s_{n-1}\geq(\log n)^{-1}n^{-1/2}\), whereas \(E^*\) on p. 18 only supplies \((\log n)^{-3}n^{-1/2}\). The latter event does not imply the former. The following calculation proves the rescaling under the weaker cutoff actually available, so these local issues do not supply a main-theorem counterexample.

Equation reference: eq:gaussian. Put \(L=\log n\) and \[f=\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\frac{W_i^2}{s_{n-i}^2}\right)^{1/2},
 \qquad h(z)=\mathbb P(|W_0|\leq z)
            =\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\int_0^z e^{-r^2/2}\,dr .\] For all \(z\geq0\), \[0\leq \sqrt{2/\pi}\,z-h(z)\leq \frac{\sqrt{2/\pi}}6z^3,\] and \(h(z)/z\) decreases on \((0,\infty)\). Therefore, for \(0\leq\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_0\), \[0\leq \mathbb E h(\varepsilon f)
       -\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0}\mathbb E h(\varepsilon_0f)
 \leq \frac{\sqrt{2/\pi}}6\,
          \varepsilon\varepsilon_0^2\,\mathbb E f^3.
 \] The independence of \(W_0\) from \(f\) is essential here.

If \(s_{n-1}\geq L^{-3}n^{-1/2}\), then \(f\leq L^3\|W\|_2\). Since \(\mathbb E\|W\|_2^4=\ell^2+2\ell\), Hölder’s inequality gives \(\mathbb Ef^3\leq C L^{39/4}\) for \(\ell\leq\sqrt L\). For \(\varepsilon_0\leq n^{-c/2}\), the error in [eq:gaussian] (#eq:gaussian) is consequently \[O\!\left(\varepsilon n^{-c}L^{39/4}\right)
   =o\!\left(\varepsilon L^{-1/16}\right).\] This proves the fixed-matrix rescaling, including \(\varepsilon=0\), with the correct event and the \(E^*\) cutoff. It avoids the printed one-sided probability and the inconsistent intermediate rescaling display on p. 22.

problems.title: Deterministic Lemma3.3 lacks its small-epsilon restriction
problems.source_location: Statement: Lemma3.3, p7, implication(21) Proof: p8, equations(23)-(24)
claim: For every epsilon>0, rectangular least singular>=epsilon^(3/4)/sqrt(n), sigma_min(A)<=epsilon/sqrt(n) implies |<u,Y>|<=(1+epsilon^(1/4))epsilon/sqrt(n) chi_tilde.
analysis: Classification: Minor. Location: Lemma 3.3, p. 7, implication (21), and its proof on p. 8.

Equation reference: eq:claimed. The stated hypothesis is \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(s_{n-1}\geq \varepsilon^{3/4}n^{-1/2}\). The claimed implication is \[\sigma_n(A)\leq \varepsilon n^{-1/2}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 |y_0|\leq (1+\varepsilon^{1/4})\varepsilon n^{-1/2}\widetilde\chi .
 \] There is no upper bound on \(\varepsilon\) in this deterministic statement.

For any \(n\geq2\), take \(\varepsilon=1\), \(t=n^{-1/2}\) and \[A=\operatorname{diag}(t,\ldots,t,3t),\qquad u_0=e_n.\] Then \(A^*\) has full row rank with every positive singular value equal to \(t\). Its last row is \(Y=3te_n\), so \(y_i=0\) for \(i<n\), \(\widetilde\chi=1\), and \(|y_0|=3t\). Both the spectral-gap hypothesis and the antecedent hold with equality: \(s_{n-1}=t=\varepsilon^{3/4}n^{-1/2}\) and \(\sigma_n(A)=t\). The conclusion would require \(3t\leq2t\). Thus the unrestricted statement is false. The example uses a unit kernel vector and works for arbitrarily large \(n\); it does not exploit missing normalization or small dimension.

Equation reference: eq:schur. For \(0<t<s_{n-1}\), a Schur complement in \(A^{\mathsf T}A-t^2I\) gives the exact criterion \[\sigma_n(A)\leq t
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 y_0^2\leq t^2\left(1+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}
                  \frac{y_i^2}{s_i^2-t^2}\right).
 \] Indeed the upper-left block is positive definite and its scalar Schur complement is \[-t^2+\frac{y_0^2}{1+\sum_i y_i^2/(s_i^2-t^2)}.\] This argument includes \(y_0=0\) and equality at the tested threshold.

If \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/16\) and \(s_{n-1}\geq\varepsilon^{3/4}n^{-1/2}\), then \(t<s_{n-1}\) and \[1+\sum_i\frac{y_i^2}{s_i^2-t^2}
 \leq \frac{\widetilde\chi^2}{1-\sqrt\varepsilon}.\] Writing \(q=\varepsilon^{1/4}\leq1/2\), \[(1+q)^2(1-q^2)-1=q(2-2q^2-q^3)>0.\] Taking square roots proves [eq:claimed] (#eq:claimed) throughout this corrected range.

The converse implication (22) also has a robust proof. If \(\sigma_n(A)>t\), rank-one interlacing gives \(s_{n-1}>t\); [eq:schur] (#eq:schur) then implies \(|y_0|>t\widetilde\chi\). If \(A^*\) is rank deficient, \(A\) is singular and this antecedent is impossible; the undefined inverse weights should not be evaluated on that stratum.

The counterexample lies outside the small-scale range used to prove the main theorem. Restricting the deterministic lemma as above preserves that use, and Section 4’s range \(\varepsilon\leq(\log n)^{-4}\) eventually lies inside it. This is the reason for a local Minor assessment. It is not a counterexample to a random-matrix theorem and does not establish a failure of the claimed leading probability constant.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Section2 outline restricts the main probabilistic analysis to small epsilon; that does not make the explicitly unrestricted deterministic lemma true.

report: Abstract: The cusp endpoint equation forces a logarithmic term in the inhomogeneous solution used to construct the obstruction space. Consequently Lemma 4.8’s pure-power bound is incompatible with its stated forcing, and its barrier proof loses the relevant power of the endpoint variable. This is a Major defect in a central proof dependency, not a disproof of the main degeneration theorem. A second, local Minor defect concerns a missing complex phase in the expanded identification map; the defining composition and its norm estimates admit an explicit repair. Algebraic smoothness and the principal neck scaling are checked separately. Complete nonlinear gluing and independent acceptance remain unverified.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of the Endpoint Obstruction and Complex-Parameter Identifications in a Cusp-Closing Construction
# Source, quantifiers, and scope

M25-0380 is Xin Fu, Hans-Joachim Hein and Xumin Jiang, A Continuous Cusp Closing Process for Negative Kähler–Einstein Metrics, Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 542–632, DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00708-y [source]. The reviewed source is the 91-page publisher version of record, published 4 March 2025 [publisher]. All page references below use printed journal pagination; physical PDF page \(p\) is printed page \(541+p\). An associated preprint is not substituted for this exact source.

Equation reference: eq:family. The family is the projective closure of \[X_\sigma\cap\mathbb C^3
 =\left\{\sum_{j=1}^3(z_j^6+z_j^3)=\sigma\right\},
 \qquad \sigma\in\Delta\subset\mathbb C.
 \] The Main Theorem, p. 544, quantifies over each fixed \(R>0\) and sufficiently small \(0<|\sigma|\) depending on \(R\). After the local analytic coordinate change and scaling by \(\sigma^{-1/3}\), multiplying the metric by \(|\log|\sigma||^{3/2}\) is asserted to give a Tian–Yau limit with \(C^0\) error \(O_{R,\varepsilon}(|\log|\sigma||^{-1+\varepsilon})\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\). The additional claims about the only bubble, curvature loss and topology are distinct assertions. They are not certified by the endpoint calculations here.

In the neck analysis, \(n\) is the complex dimension and the application has \(n=2\). The coordinates are \(s=1-t/T\) and \(\eta=1-s=t/T\). Thus \(\eta\downarrow0\) is the cusp endpoint, while \(s\downarrow0\) is the Tian–Yau endpoint. The limiting radial operator is denoted by \(L_\infty\). The review concentrates on its homogeneous and inhomogeneous equations, the exact complex-parameter maps, and the dependencies that carry these into Sections 4–5. The complete source was parsed; the accompanying coverage record distinguishes pages actually read from arguments independently checked.
# Problem 1: resonance contradicts the decay in Lemma 4.8

Classification: Major. Exact location: Lemma 4.8, p. 610, equation (4.38), and the cusp-end barrier paragraph in its proof. The necessary operator and homogeneous-solution hypotheses are on pp. 603, 605 and 607, equations (4.6), (4.8), (4.24)–(4.25) and Lemma 4.5.
## The actual hypotheses and their leading coefficient

Equation reference: eq:operator, eq:remainder. Set \(m=n+1\) and write functions in the \(\eta\) coordinate. Lemma 4.3 gives \[L_\infty=\frac1m D_n+\mathcal R,\qquad
 D_n=\eta^2\partial_{\eta\eta}-(n-1)\eta\partial_\eta-(n+1).
 \] The operator error is relative to the weighted derivatives, not an unweighted bounded perturbation. Definition 2.27, p. 570, and the explicit estimate (4.25), p. 607, give the bound \[|\mathcal R f|\leq C\eta^m
     \bigl(|f|+\eta|f'|+\eta^2|f''|\bigr)
 \] near the endpoint. Enlarging the right side to include \(|f|\) is harmless.

Equation reference: eq:indicial. Let \(U(\eta)=\widehat u(1-\eta)\), where \(\widehat u\) is exactly the function of Lemma 4.5. It solves \(L_\infty U=0\), is strictly positive on \((0,1)\), tends to \(1\) at the opposite endpoint, and satisfies \(U=O(\eta^m)\) at this endpoint. Uniform interior estimates for the rescaled ordinary differential equation on \([\eta,2\eta]\) also give \[|U|+\eta|U'|+\eta^2|U''|=O(\eta^m).\] Consequently \(D_nU=O(\eta^{2m})\). The indicial polynomial is \[D_n(\eta^r)=(r+1)(r-m)\eta^r,
 \] so the decaying and growing roots are \(m\) and \(-1\).

Equation reference: eq:quotient, eq:u-leading. For completeness, the coefficient of the decaying root cannot vanish here. Put \(U=\eta^m Z\). A direct calculation gives the useful exact identity \[D_n(\eta^m Z)
   =\eta^m\bigl(\eta^2Z''+(m+2)\eta Z'\bigr)
   =(\eta^{m+2}Z')'.
 \] Integrating \(D_nU=O(\eta^{2m})\) and using boundedness of \(Z\) removes the \(\eta^{-1}\) homogeneous branch. A second integration yields \[U(\eta)=A\eta^m+O(\eta^{2m})
 \] with the corresponding weighted first and second derivative estimates.

Here is an explicit uniqueness check for \(A\neq0\). If \(A=0\), write \(F=D_nU=-m\mathcal RU\). The two zero integration constants in [eq:quotient] (#eq:quotient) give \[Z(\eta)=\int_0^\eta t^{-m-2}\int_0^t F(x)\,dx\,dt.\] For \[M(r)=\sup_{0<\eta\leq r}\eta^{-m}
              (|U|+\eta|U'|+\eta^2|U''|)<\infty,\] equation [eq:remainder] (#eq:remainder) bounds \(F(x)\) by \(CM(r)x^{2m}\). The displayed integral and its first two weighted derivatives then imply \(M(r)\leq Cr^mM(r)\). For small \(r\) this forces \(U=0\); ordinary differential equation uniqueness extends this to the whole interval, contradicting \(\widehat u(0)=1\). Thus \(A\neq0\), and positivity gives \(A>0\). This rules out a vanishing leading coefficient as an escape from resonance.
## The contradiction for the stated inhomogeneous solution

Equation reference: eq:false-bound, eq:contradiction. Lemma 4.8 asks for \(V(\eta)=\widehat v(1-\eta)\) satisfying \[L_\infty V=U,\qquad
 |V|+\eta|V'|+\eta^2|V''|=O(\eta^m).
 \] Assume these exact requirements. Then [eq:remainder] (#eq:remainder) gives \(\mathcal RV=O(\eta^{2m})\), and [eq:u-leading] (#eq:u-leading) implies \[D_nV=mA\eta^m+O(\eta^{2m}).\] With \(V=\eta^m W\), identity [eq:quotient] (#eq:quotient) becomes \[(\eta^{m+2}W')'=mA\eta^m+O(\eta^{2m}).\] Integrating gives \[W'=C\eta^{-m-2}+\frac{mA}{m+1}\eta^{-1}+O(\eta^{m-1}).\] Boundedness of \(W\) first forces \(C=0\), but a second integration then gives \[W(\eta)=\frac{mA}{m+1}\log\eta+C_0+O(\eta^m),
 \] which is unbounded because \(A>0\). Therefore no function satisfies [eq:false-bound] (#eq:false-bound). This uses the actual forcing \(\widehat u\) and the paper’s actual operator error; it is not a counterexample obtained by replacing \(L_\infty\) with its model.

Equation reference: eq:log-term. The leading term required for a corrected decaying solution is \[V(\eta)=\frac{n+1}{n+2}A\eta^{n+1}\log\eta+O(\eta^{n+1}).
 \] Indeed \(D_n(\eta^{n+1}\log\eta)=(n+2)\eta^{n+1}\). In the paper’s dimension this is \[V(\eta)=\frac{3A}{4}\eta^3\log\eta+O(\eta^3).\] The logarithmic leading term is negative, so it does not contradict the desired sign \(\widehat v\leq0\). Adding a multiple of \(\widehat u\) changes the pure \(\eta^{n+1}\) term and cannot remove the logarithm. In particular, the adjustment imposing the Neumann condition at the other endpoint does not repair (4.38).
## The failed barrier and the proof dependency

Equation reference: eq:barrier. The barrier on p. 610 is of the form \[v_{\rm sub}=-C_1\eta^m+C_2\eta^{2m}.\] Its model image is exactly \[\frac1mD_nv_{\rm sub}=(2n+3)C_2\eta^{2m},
 \qquad L_\infty v_{\rm sub}=O(\eta^{2m}).
 \] It cannot dominate \(U\sim A\eta^m\) for all sufficiently small \(\eta\), for any fixed choices of the barrier constants. The proof’s asserted strictly positive constant lower bound omits this vanishing power. Making the endpoint interval smaller cannot change the order discrepancy.

The core dependency is explicit. Definition 4.9, p. 611, cuts off \(\widehat v\) and defines \(\widehat u_\sigma=L_\sigma\widehat v_\sigma\). The first sentence of p. 613 invokes (4.38) to prove the uniform bound \(|\widehat u_\sigma|\leq C\eta^3\) in Lemma 4.10. The dominated convergence argument on p. 614 uses that bound in Proposition 4.2. Theorem 4.12, p. 615, gives the uniform inverse modulo obstructions; p. 621 explicitly uses Proposition 4.2 to eliminate the nonzero limiting obstruction. The fixed-point construction then uses that inverse.

There are further direct uses in Section 5: the projected forcing estimate (5.13) and the gradient bound (5.18), p. 623, use (4.38); Claim 5.3’s projection estimate, p. 625, uses the same pure-power decay against the cusp volume density. Theorem 5.4, p. 626, removes the obstruction, and its estimate is used to deduce the Main Theorem on p. 628. Thus the defect affects a central analytic construction and its propagated estimates. It is classified as Major on this impact, irrespective of the eventual length of a repair.

A plausible repair begins by allowing \(\eta^{n+1}(1+|\log\eta|)\), with two weighted derivatives, and then rebuilding the cutoffs, uniform obstruction estimates, weighted pairings, projection bounds and nonlinear iteration. Logarithms are integrable in several of the displayed pairings and can sometimes be absorbed by a small power; these facts are evidence that a repair may be possible. They do not establish all uniform constants or preserve every stated exponent. Only the forced local logarithmic term is established here. The existence and sign properties with the left Neumann condition, the complete corrected gluing argument and the main theorem remain outside the verified repair. No counterexample to the Kähler–Einstein degeneration itself is claimed.
# Problem 2: the expanded map has the wrong complex phase
Classification: Minor. Exact location: Lemma 2.5, p. 550, the definition of \(\nu_\sigma\) and equations (2.18)–(2.20). The conjugates in Lemma 2.3 and (2.16) are essential.

Equation reference: eq:correct-map. Write \(F(z)=z_1^3+z_2^3+z_3^3\) and \(TY_\sigma=\{F=\sigma\}\). The base map is \[\Phi(w)_j=w_j+\nu(w)\overline w_j^{\,2}.\] Definition 2.4 correctly defines the scaled map by a composition. For a chosen cube root \(\lambda=\sigma^{-1/3}\) this gives \[\Phi_\sigma(z)_j
 =\lambda^{-1}\Phi(\lambda z)_j
 =z_j+\lambda^{-1}\overline\lambda^{\,2}
             \nu(\lambda z)\overline z_j^{\,2}.
 \] The lemma instead uses \(\lambda\nu(\lambda z)\) as the coefficient. In general \(\lambda^{-1}\overline\lambda^{\,2}\neq\lambda\). Their absolute values agree, but their phases need not.
## An admissible complex-parameter check

Equation reference: eq:a. Take \(\sigma=i\rho\) with \(\rho>0\) arbitrarily small, and \[\lambda=\rho^{-1/3}e^{-i\pi/6},\qquad
 z=(r,-r,0),\quad r>0.\] Then \(z\in TY_0\) and \(|\lambda z|>R\) for sufficiently small \(\rho\), so this point lies in the exact domain of Lemma 2.5. Choose the small positive root \(a\) of \[6r^2a-2a^3=\rho;
 \] it exists by the implicit function theorem, with \(a\sim\rho/(6r^2)\). Writing \(L=\rho^{-1/3}\) and \(q=a/(Lr^2)\), direct expansion gives \[F\bigl(\lambda z+q\,\overline{\lambda z}^{\,2}\bigr)
   =6qL^4r^4-2q^3L^6r^6=L^3\rho=1.\] Here the square is componentwise. The small root \(q\) is exactly the branch \(\nu(\lambda z)\) selected in Lemma 2.3.

Equation reference: eq:phase-witness. The composition [eq:correct-map] (#eq:correct-map) therefore sends \(z\) to \((r+ia,-r+ia,0)\), whose cubic value is \(i\rho\). The printed formula instead sends it to \[(r+ae^{-i\pi/6},-r+ae^{-i\pi/6},0).\] The real part of this point’s cubic value is \[3\sqrt3\,r^2a>0.
 \] It is consequently not a point of \(TY_{i\rho}\). This countercheck works for arbitrarily small nonzero parameters in the stated complex family, and respects the large-radius domain of the base map. Restricting to positive real \(\sigma\) would hide the discrepancy, but is not the theorem’s parameter range.
## Repair and boundary

Replace the expanded coefficient by \[
u_\sigma^{m corr}(z)
   =\lambda^{-1}\overline\lambda^{\,2}
u(\lambda z).\] For real-coordinate derivatives, the chain rule and Lemma 2.3 give \[|\partial^k
u_\sigma^{m corr}(z)|
 \leq C_k|\lambda|^{k+1}|\lambda z|^{-4-k}
 =C_k|\sigma|\,|z|^{-4-k}.\] Thus the stated decay estimates survive this correction. Changing the cube root by a third root of unity also leaves the corrected map unchanged: uniqueness of the small branch gives \(
u(\zeta w)=
u(w)\) and \(\zeta^{-1}\overline\zeta^{\,2}=1\). The defining composition (2.17) already contains the correct geometry. The error is therefore local and is classified as Minor: the expanded assertion fails to land in its target, while the composition and the norm estimates have an explicit repair. This does not certify every later coordinate computation in the gluing construction.
# Independent consistency checks and their limits

The family [eq:family] (#eq:family) has affine critical points satisfying \(3z_j^2(2z_j^3+1)=0\). Their critical values are \(-k/4\) for \(k=0,1,2,3\). Hence for \(0<|\sigma|<1/4\) there is no affine singularity, and the central affine fiber has only the origin as a singular point. At infinity the leading Fermat sextic has no projective point at which all its coordinate derivatives vanish. The local map \(z_j\mapsto z_j(1+z_j^3)^{1/3}\) has derivative the identity at the origin and converts [eq:family] (#eq:family) exactly to \(F=\sigma\). These elementary checks agree with the algebraic setup; they do not prove any metric convergence.

Equation reference: eq:horn. The radial equation (2.42), p. 555, with \(\psi',\psi''>0\) integrates to \[\frac{(\psi')^{n+1}}{n+1}=e^{\psi+a}+b,\] as in (2.79), p. 563. For \(b=-B<0\), putting \(y=t-T\) and \(u=\psi-\psi(T)\) gives \[\int_0^u(e^x-1)^{-1/(n+1)}\,dx
       =((n+1)B)^{1/(n+1)}y.\] Near \(y=0\) this yields the leading potential \[u\sim \frac{n^{(n+1)/n}}{n+1}B^{1/n}y^{(n+1)/n}.
 \] The total integral is finite and, after \(x\mapsto e^{-x}\), equals \[c(n)=\mathrm B\!\left(\frac1{n+1},\frac n{n+1}\right)
     =\frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi/(n+1))}.\] It gives the principal relation \(T\sim-(n+1)^{-1/(n+1)}c(n)B^{-1/(n+1)}\) in (2.89), p. 565. For \(n=2\), [eq:horn] (#eq:horn) is \((2\sqrt2/3)B^{1/2}y^{3/2}\). Together with \(T=(2/3)\log|\sigma|\), p. 580, this explains the metric scale \(B^{1/2}\asymp|\log|\sigma||^{-3/2}\). This checks the principal scaling, not all normalization constants or remainder estimates in Section 2.

Figure 1, p. 544, and Figure 2, p. 564, are inspected for geometric orientation. Their schematic regions are not numerical evidence for an asymptotic estimate. The endpoint resonance is established from the equations and the weighted error bound, not inferred from those drawings.

 \] which is unbounded because \(A>0\). Therefore no function satisfies [eq:false-bound] (#eq:false-bound). This uses the actual forcing \(\widehat u\) and the paper’s actual operator error; it is not a counterexample obtained by replacing \(L_\infty\) with its model.

Equation reference: eq:log-term. The leading term required for a corrected decaying solution is \[V(\eta)=\frac{n+1}{n+2}A\eta^{n+1}\log\eta+O(\eta^{n+1}).
 \] Indeed \(D_n(\eta^{n+1}\log\eta)=(n+2)\eta^{n+1}\). In the paper’s dimension this is \[V(\eta)=\frac{3A}{4}\eta^3\log\eta+O(\eta^3).\] The logarithmic leading term is negative, so it does not contradict the desired sign \(\widehat v\leq0\). Adding a multiple of \(\widehat u\) changes the pure \(\eta^{n+1}\) term and cannot remove the logarithm. In particular, the adjustment imposing the Neumann condition at the other endpoint does not repair (4.38).

Equation reference: eq:barrier. The barrier on p. 610 is of the form \[v_{\rm sub}=-C_1\eta^m+C_2\eta^{2m}.\] Its model image is exactly \[\frac1mD_nv_{\rm sub}=(2n+3)C_2\eta^{2m},
 \qquad L_\infty v_{\rm sub}=O(\eta^{2m}).
 \] It cannot dominate \(U\sim A\eta^m\) for all sufficiently small \(\eta\), for any fixed choices of the barrier constants. The proof’s asserted strictly positive constant lower bound omits this vanishing power. Making the endpoint interval smaller cannot change the order discrepancy.

The core dependency is explicit. Definition 4.9, p. 611, cuts off \(\widehat v\) and defines \(\widehat u_\sigma=L_\sigma\widehat v_\sigma\). The first sentence of p. 613 invokes (4.38) to prove the uniform bound \(|\widehat u_\sigma|\leq C\eta^3\) in Lemma 4.10. The dominated convergence argument on p. 614 uses that bound in Proposition 4.2. Theorem 4.12, p. 615, gives the uniform inverse modulo obstructions; p. 621 explicitly uses Proposition 4.2 to eliminate the nonzero limiting obstruction. The fixed-point construction then uses that inverse.

There are further direct uses in Section 5: the projected forcing estimate (5.13) and the gradient bound (5.18), p. 623, use (4.38); Claim 5.3’s projection estimate, p. 625, uses the same pure-power decay against the cusp volume density. Theorem 5.4, p. 626, removes the obstruction, and its estimate is used to deduce the Main Theorem on p. 628. Thus the defect affects a central analytic construction and its propagated estimates. It is classified as Major on this impact, irrespective of the eventual length of a repair.

A plausible repair begins by allowing \(\eta^{n+1}(1+|\log\eta|)\), with two weighted derivatives, and then rebuilding the cutoffs, uniform obstruction estimates, weighted pairings, projection bounds and nonlinear iteration. Logarithms are integrable in several of the displayed pairings and can sometimes be absorbed by a small power; these facts are evidence that a repair may be possible. They do not establish all uniform constants or preserve every stated exponent. Only the forced local logarithmic term is established here. The existence and sign properties with the left Neumann condition, the complete corrected gluing argument and the main theorem remain outside the verified repair. No counterexample to the Kähler–Einstein degeneration itself is claimed.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The negative logarithmic leading term is consistent with vhat<=0.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Several weighted logarithmic integrals remain finite; small power losses might absorb logs, so a full repair may be possible.

problems.title: Complex scaling loses a conjugate phase in Lemma2.5
problems.source_location: Statement: Printed p550, physical9, definition of nu_sigma and equations2.18-2.20 Definition: Definition2.4 equation2.17; base map Lemma2.3 p549 and equation2.16 p550
claim: For lambda=sigma^(-1/3), the expanded composition uses coefficient lambda*nu(lambda z) multiplying conjugate(z_j)^2.
analysis: Classification: Minor. Exact location: Lemma 2.5, p. 550, the definition of \(\nu_\sigma\) and equations (2.18)–(2.20). The conjugates in Lemma 2.3 and (2.16) are essential.

Equation reference: eq:correct-map. Write \(F(z)=z_1^3+z_2^3+z_3^3\) and \(TY_\sigma=\{F=\sigma\}\). The base map is \[\Phi(w)_j=w_j+\nu(w)\overline w_j^{\,2}.\] Definition 2.4 correctly defines the scaled map by a composition. For a chosen cube root \(\lambda=\sigma^{-1/3}\) this gives \[\Phi_\sigma(z)_j
 =\lambda^{-1}\Phi(\lambda z)_j
 =z_j+\lambda^{-1}\overline\lambda^{\,2}
             \nu(\lambda z)\overline z_j^{\,2}.
 \] The lemma instead uses \(\lambda\nu(\lambda z)\) as the coefficient. In general \(\lambda^{-1}\overline\lambda^{\,2}\neq\lambda\). Their absolute values agree, but their phases need not.

Equation reference: eq:a. Take \(\sigma=i\rho\) with \(\rho>0\) arbitrarily small, and \[\lambda=\rho^{-1/3}e^{-i\pi/6},\qquad
 z=(r,-r,0),\quad r>0.\] Then \(z\in TY_0\) and \(|\lambda z|>R\) for sufficiently small \(\rho\), so this point lies in the exact domain of Lemma 2.5. Choose the small positive root \(a\) of \[6r^2a-2a^3=\rho;
 \] it exists by the implicit function theorem, with \(a\sim\rho/(6r^2)\). Writing \(L=\rho^{-1/3}\) and \(q=a/(Lr^2)\), direct expansion gives \[F\bigl(\lambda z+q\,\overline{\lambda z}^{\,2}\bigr)
   =6qL^4r^4-2q^3L^6r^6=L^3\rho=1.\] Here the square is componentwise. The small root \(q\) is exactly the branch \(\nu(\lambda z)\) selected in Lemma 2.3.

Equation reference: eq:phase-witness. The composition [eq:correct-map] (#eq:correct-map) therefore sends \(z\) to \((r+ia,-r+ia,0)\), whose cubic value is \(i\rho\). The printed formula instead sends it to \[(r+ae^{-i\pi/6},-r+ae^{-i\pi/6},0).\] The real part of this point’s cubic value is \[3\sqrt3\,r^2a>0.
 \] It is consequently not a point of \(TY_{i\rho}\). This countercheck works for arbitrarily small nonzero parameters in the stated complex family, and respects the large-radius domain of the base map. Restricting to positive real \(\sigma\) would hide the discrepancy, but is not the theorem’s parameter range.
result: Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The printed coefficient agrees for a positive real parameter and a real cube root; that subcase does not cover the complex theorem.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Definition2.4 itself is correct and is retained.

Title: Initial verification of
Rate Distortion Dimension of Random Brody Curves
# Identity, scope, and assumptions

The assigned journal identity is Rate Distortion Dimension of Random Brody Curves, Masaki Tsukamoto, DOI `10.1007/s00039-025-00709-x`. The reviewed PDF is the explicitly bound preprint [paper], not a verified byte-equivalent copy of the journal version. Page references below mean one-based physical PDF pages; the source’s printed Arabic page numbers agree with them. All 60 pages were read, with claim-focused checking of the main proof chains and selected original dependencies. The accompanying coverage ledger records the exact pages visually inspected and the limits of external-reference checking.

Fix the positive integer \(N\). The compact space \(\mathcal B^N\) consists of holomorphic maps \(f:\mathbb C\to\mathbb {CP}^N\) with \(|df|\leq1\), for the Fubini–Study normalization in which a projective line has area one. The action is \(T^af(z)=f(z+a)\), and the compatible metric is \[d(f,g)=\max_{z\in[0,1]^2}d_{\mathrm{FS}}(f(z),g(z)).\] Uniqueness of holomorphic continuation makes this a metric; compactness and Cauchy estimates provide the topology and continuity needed below. Put \(\psi(f)=2(N+1)|df|^2(0)\) and let \(\rho(f)\) be the supremal large-disc energy density defined in the source. Write \(\rho_*=\sup_{f\in\mathcal B^N}\rho(f)\). For invariant Borel probability measures, the source defines lower and upper rate distortion dimensions using bits per unit area and \(\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\).

Equation reference: eq:upper. Theorem 2.4, p. 7, asserts \[
 \overline{\operatorname{rdim}}(\mathcal B^N,T,d,\mu)\leq\int_{\mathcal B^N}\psi\,d\mu
 \qquad\text{for every invariant }\mu .\] Theorem 2.5 asserts existence of a measure with both dimensions equal to \(\int\psi\,d\mu=c\) for each \(0\leq c<2(N+1)\rho_*\). Neither ergodicity nor attainment of the right endpoint is asserted.
# Checked reasoning and decisive checks
## The universal upper bound

The proof in Sections 5–6 uses potential \(-\psi\). Proposition 6.2 (p. 24) supplies a local covering estimate about an \(R\)-nondegenerate curve: its leading exponent is \(2(N+1)\int_S|df|^2\), with a boundary contribution of order \(L\) for a square of side \(L\). The radius and leading constant may depend on \(R\), but are independent of the covering scale. The statement and relevant proof of the cited covering result [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~10--15, 24--26]{cover}] were checked. Changing the square by a fixed-width collar changes the energy by \(O(L)\); it does not change the area-normalized leading coefficient.

Proposition 6.3, p. 25, and its proof on pp. 29–34 replace a possibly degenerate curve by a nondegenerate one with derivative at most \(1+\eta\). The local metric distortion is controlled by universal constants, and the square-energy error is less than \(\eta L^2\). The rational perturbation has order \(|z-p|^{-3}\); this tail is summable on a two-dimensional lattice. The argument separates the sparse near-center discs from the uniformly small far-field perturbation. These facts support the compact convergence, derivative bound, and energy estimate used in the covering argument.

On p. 27 the square grows from \([0,L]^2\) to \([-3,L+3]^2\). Its extra area is exactly \(12L+36\). Since the original curve has \(|df|^2\leq1\), this contributes \(O(L^{-1})\) after division by \(L^2\). For fixed \(\eta\) and \(\varepsilon\), the \(C_2(\varepsilon)L\) contribution also vanishes. The order is \(L\to\infty\), then \(\varepsilon\to0\), followed by the small-neighborhood and \(\eta\to0\) limits. In particular, the proof does not need uniformity of the boundary constant as \(\varepsilon\to0\).

The local formula with continuous potential was checked against [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~48--55]{potential}]. Its proof removes a nonnegativity restriction by subtracting the minimum of the potential; using \(-\psi\) is therefore legitimate. The entropy-versus-covering inequality in [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~27--28]{potential}] gives \[\overline{\operatorname{rdim}}(\mathcal B^N,T,d,\mu)-\int\psi\,d\mu
 \leq\overline{\operatorname{mdim}}_{M}(\mathcal B^N,T,d,-\psi)=0 .\] This proves precisely [eq:upper] (#eq:upper); it does not give equality for arbitrary invariant measures.
## The lower bound and the extremal measures

The passage from small-set volume to information is developed in Section 8. The Kawabata–Dembo estimate was checked in [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~18--19]{potential}], including its small-distortion condition \(2\varepsilon\log_2(1/\varepsilon)\leq\delta\), its exponent, and its error \(K(s+1)\). In Proposition 8.4 the relevant exponent is \(sL_n^k\). After normalization, the error is \(K(s+L_n^{-k})\), so it survives the block limit only as a constant independent of the distortion scale and disappears in the final dimension quotient.

The finite-alphabet approximation, averaged block code, boundary volume estimate, and mutual-information inequalities on pp. 40–48 were checked. Convexity in the conditional law and concavity in the input law are used in their respective correct directions. Proposition 8.7 (pp. 48–50) additionally requires tame covering growth of the averaged metric and a shifted comparison with a discrete supremum metric. Lemma 9.1 and Proposition 9.2 supply these: the comparison has constant \(4\), and the sampling construction gives logarithmic covering growth \(O((\log(1/\varepsilon))^3)\). The former hypothesis cannot simply be omitted for a general action.

Equation reference: eq:inverse. For a fixed nondegenerate \(f\) with \(\left\lVert df\right\rVert_\infty<1\), Propositions 9.6–9.7, pp. 53–54, use the deformation results [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~7, 13--19]{deform}]. The strict derivative margin is present, the deformation radius may depend on \(f\), and the loss in the complex dimension is \(C_fL\), uniformly over translated squares. For \(w=u-v\) in the chosen finite-dimensional space, \[\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{\infty,\mathbb C}\leq2\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{\infty,S_n},
 \qquad
 \left\lVert w\right\rVert_{\infty,S_n}\leq
 d_{L_n}(T^{a_n}F(u),T^{a_n}F(v))
       +\tfrac18\left\lVert w\right\rVert_{\infty,\mathbb C}.\] Thus \[
 \left\lVert w\right\rVert_{\infty,\mathbb C}
 \leq\tfrac83\,d_{L_n}(T^{a_n}F(u),T^{a_n}F(v)).\] Normalized Lebesgue volume in complex dimension \(m_n\) has real scaling exponent \(2m_n\), not \(m_n\). Combining this with [eq:inverse] (#eq:inverse) gives exactly the small-set exponent on p. 55, \[2m_n\geq 2(N+1)\int_{S_n}|df|^2-2C_fL_n .\] The factor two in the leading coefficient is therefore accounted for.

The averaged measures have invariant subsequential limits: for each fixed translation, the symmetric difference of the averaging squares has relative area tending to zero, uniformly in the initial probability measure. Lemma 7.1, p. 35, compares the energies of two uniformly close Brody curves by a homotopy fixed outside the square. The Kähler form is closed, and the remaining collar has area \(O(L_n)\) and uniformly bounded derivatives. Consequently the limit measure has \[\int\psi\,d\mu=2(N+1)\rho(f).\] The lower bound from Proposition 8.7 and [eq:upper] (#eq:upper) identify both dimensions with this value, as claimed in Theorem 9.8.

Finally, for \(0<c<2(N+1)\rho_*\), Corollary 6.9 provides a nondegenerate \(g\) with \(2(N+1)\rho(g)>c\). Taking \[\lambda=\sqrt{\frac{c}{2(N+1)\rho(g)}},\qquad f(z)=g(\lambda z)\] gives \(0<\lambda<1\), the required strict derivative margin, and \(\rho(f)=\lambda^2\rho(g)\) by change of variables in the disc-energy definition. The case \(c=0\) is supplied by a point mass at a constant curve. These checks explain both the range and the excluded endpoint.
# Counterevidence, limits, and outcome

The periodic elliptic-curve example in Section 2 is counterevidence to interpreting [eq:upper] (#eq:upper) as an equality for every invariant measure: a compact finite-dimensional orbit can be encoded with zero information per unit area while carrying positive energy. The final discussion, pp. 57–58, also explicitly leaves ergodicity open. An ergodic decomposition does not identify the lower and upper rate distortion dimensions of each component at a prescribed \(c\).
No substantive Problem section is warranted by the checks performed.

The notation on p. 39 was checked directly. Let \(M(\tau)\) be the number of sets in the cover. For sufficiently small \(\tau\), tameness gives \[\tau^\eta\log_2 M(\tau)<1.\] The counting argument then yields \[4^{L^k}(2C\tau^{1-\eta})^{sL^k},\] which gives exactly the claimed exponent loss. The printed use of \(\log\#\) for that cardinality is a local notation inconsistency with this immediate reading. It supplies no evidence of a damaged main conclusion.

This review checked applications and selected proofs in the three original dependencies, not every foundational theorem cited by them. It is not a formal proof certification. No author code was run and no empirical reproduction was needed for these mathematical claims. The journal text and any later revisions were not compared line by line. A bounded search did not identify a corrective notice to use in this assessment; that does not establish the absence of all errata. Any materially changed version requires a new comparison.
