Abstract: This initial review identifies one supported Major issue. The equality of group classes in Lemma 6.2 is false, including within the countable, torsion-free range of Theorem 1.6. A self-contained counterexample and a precise class-theoretic repair are given below. The defect leaves a missing directed-union step in the stated proof of Theorems 1.6–1.7; it does not refute their Atiyah or localization conclusions. The extension of the complex finite-rank argument to arbitrary conjugation-closed coefficient fields remains a separate Needs Evidence item. Initial review is not independent acceptance, and the scientific decision remains pending.
Date: Math 2025 initial review — M25-0382

Title: Initial verification of
Universal Localizations, Atiyah Conjectures
and Graphs of Groups
# Identity, scope, and claims

The assigned identity is Pablo Sánchez-Peralta, Universal Localizations, Atiyah Conjectures and Graphs of Groups, DOI `10.1007/s00039-025-00710-4`. The reviewed file is [paper], arXiv:2409.12268v2, dated 23 March 2025, with 30 physical PDF pages. The original supplied manifest and the preserved source copy identify these exact bytes. All 30 pages were read. Page numbers in this report refer to that PDF, not to the journal pagination. The accompanying coverage ledger records the proof-level checks, original-reference passages, and actual page-image inspections. No byte-equivalence with the journal PDF is claimed.

Theorems 1.1–1.2 concern a countable fundamental group of a graph of groups, finite edge groups, a field \(K\subseteq\mathbb C\) closed under complex conjugation, strong Atiyah assumptions on every vertex group, and finite \(\operatorname{lcm}(G)\). Besides preservation of the dimension restriction, the paper asserts faithfulness of the induced rank on finitely generated projectives, universal localization at full maps of projectives, and the two indicated \(K_0\)-surjections. Full maps are defined by factorization through arbitrary finitely generated projectives; they are not restricted to square matrices between free modules. Corollaries 1.3–1.4 address the algebraic and center-valued Atiyah conjectures.

Definition 6.1 explicitly defines \(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\) by finite groups, unrestricted directed unions, and the graph-of-groups operation when its output is virtually locally indicable. Theorem 1.6 asserts semisimplicity and the \(\Sigma(K,G)\)-universal localization property of \(\mathcal R_{K[G]}\), together with the algebraic Atiyah conjecture, for every countable \(G\in\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\) with finite \(\operatorname{lcm}(G)\). Here \(\Sigma(K,G)\) consists of matrices over \(K[G]\) invertible in \(\mathcal U(G)\). Theorem 1.7 uses this to compute weak \(K_1\) over a conjugation-closed ring \(\mathbb Z\subseteq R\subseteq\mathbb C\), with its fraction field \(F\). The broader conjectures in Section 7 are not treated as proved results.
# Problem 1: the class equality in Lemma 6.2 is false

Severity: Major. Location: Definition 6.1, the definition of \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\), and Lemma 6.2, p. 26; the first sentence of the proof of Theorem 1.6, p. 27; its subsequent use in Theorem 1.7, p. 28.

Every member of the paper’s class \(\mathcal Y=\bigcup_\alpha\mathcal Y_\alpha\) is virtually locally indicable: finite groups have the trivial subgroup of finite index, successor stages explicitly impose this property, and a limit stage is a union of classes, not a new operation of taking unions of groups. In contrast, the directed-union operation in Definition 6.1 has no such restriction. The claim that \(\mathcal Y\) is closed under directed unions therefore requires proof and is false.

The group \(\bigoplus_{n\geq1}C_2\) already separates the two classes, but has infinite \(\operatorname{lcm}\). The following construction avoids that limitation and meets the group and coefficient hypotheses of Theorem 1.6.
## A torsion-free, virtually abelian group which is not locally indicable

Write an affine map of \(\mathbb R^3\) as \((D,v)\), with product \((D,v)(E,w)=(DE,Dw+v)\). Let \[a=\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1),(1/2,1/2,0)\bigr),\qquad
 b=\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,-1),(0,1/2,1/2)\bigr)\] and put \(H=\langle a,b\rangle\), \(c=ab\). For translation by \(v\) write \(T_v\). Direct exact calculation gives \[\begin{aligned}
 c&=\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,1),(1/2,0,-1/2)\bigr),\\
 x=a^2&=T_{(1,0,0)},&
 y=b^2&=T_{(0,1,0)},&
 z=c^{-2}&=T_{(0,0,1)},\\
 [a,b]&=xy^{-1}z^{-1},&
 bxb^{-1}&=x^{-1},&
 aya^{-1}&=y^{-1}.\end{aligned}\] The subgroup \(L=\langle x,y,z\rangle\cong\mathbb Z^3\) is normal: conjugation of a translation by \(a\) or \(b\) changes only coordinate signs. Modulo \(L\), the generators commute and have order two. Their four distinct linear parts show that \[H/L\cong C_2\times C_2,\qquad H=L\sqcup La\sqcup Lb\sqcup Lc.\] There are no additional translation cosets.

An element of \(L\setminus\{1\}\) has infinite order. For \(\ell=T_{(p,q,r)}\), \(p,q,r\in\mathbb Z\), the squares of \(\ell a,\ell b,\ell c\) have respectively a translation coordinate \(2p+1\), \(2q+1\), or \(2r-1\), so each is nontrivial. Thus \(H\) is torsion-free and virtually \(\mathbb Z^3\), hence virtually locally indicable.

Nevertheless, if \(f:H\to\mathbb Z\) is a homomorphism, conjugation of \(x\) to \(x^{-1}\) gives \(f(x)=0\), and \(x=a^2\) gives \(f(a)=0\). Similarly, \(aya^{-1}=y^{-1}\) and \(y=b^2\) give \(f(b)=0\). Therefore every such \(f\) is zero. The nontrivial, finitely generated group \(H\) is not locally indicable.
## Membership in the class actually defined in the paper

Equation reference: eq:amalgam. Projection to the first affine coordinate maps \(H\) onto the infinite dihedral group. The images of \(b\) and \(c\) are reflections about \(0\) and \(1/4\), and the kernel is \(L_0=\langle y,z\rangle\cong\mathbb Z^2\). The two vertex preimages are \[B=\langle b,z\mid bzb^{-1}=z^{-1}\rangle,\qquad
 C=\langle c,y\mid cyc^{-1}=y^{-1}\rangle.\] Both are Klein-bottle groups. In \(B\), \(y=b^2\); in \(C\), \(z=c^{-2}\). The subgroup \(L_0\) has index two in each, and \[
 H\cong B*_{L_0}C .\] For completeness, this map is surjective since \(a=cb^{-1}\). A reduced word alternating between the two vertex groups outside \(L_0\) maps to a nonempty reduced word in \(C_2*C_2\); a nontrivial word in \(L_0\) remains a nontrivial translation. This proves injectivity.

The group \(\mathbb Z\) is an HNN extension of the trivial group. The identity HNN extension of \(\mathbb Z\) gives \(\mathbb Z^2\), and its inversion HNN extension gives the Klein-bottle group. Each output is virtually free abelian. Equation [eq:amalgam] (#eq:amalgam) therefore proves \(H\in\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\).

The same argument gives \(H^n\in\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\) for every finite \(n\). Inductively put \(P=H^{n-1}\). Identity HNN extensions construct \(P\times\mathbb Z\) and \(P\times\mathbb Z^2\); an HNN extension with the identity on \(P\) and inversion on \(\mathbb Z\) constructs \(P\) times a Klein-bottle group. Finally, \[P\times H\cong
 (P\times B)*_{P\times L_0}(P\times C).\] All outputs in this finite construction are virtually free abelian, so the additional hypothesis on each graph operation is satisfied.
## The finite-\(\operatorname{lcm}\) counterexample

Set \[G=\bigoplus_{n\geq1}H=\bigcup_{n\geq1}H^n .\] Then \(G\) is countable, torsion-free, belongs to \(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\), and has \(\operatorname{lcm}(G)=1\). Take \(K=\mathbb Q\), which is closed under complex conjugation.

We show that no finite-index subgroup \(J\leq G\) is locally indicable. Its normal core \(N\) has finite index, and the quotient \(Q=G/N\) is finite. There are only finitely many homomorphisms \(H\to Q\), because \(H\) has two generators. Infinitely many coordinate copies of \(H\) therefore have the same restriction \(\rho:H\to Q\) of the quotient map. Let \(m\geq1\) be the exponent of the finite group \(\rho(H)\). Choose \(m\) distinct such coordinates. The diagonal copy of \(H\) on these coordinates maps to \(\rho(h)^m=1\) for every \(h\), so it lies in \(N\subseteq J\). It is a nontrivial finitely generated subgroup without an epimorphism onto \(\mathbb Z\). Consequently \(J\) is not locally indicable.

Thus \(G\notin\mathcal Y\), although it satisfies the hypotheses \(G\in\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\), countability, and finite \(\operatorname{lcm}(G)\). This is a counterexample to Lemma 6.2 within the parameter range used by the main application. The affine identities were also checked independently with exact rational arithmetic. The infinite-group argument above is analytic; it is not inferred from a finite enumeration or from author code.
## Impact and limits

The proof of Theorem 1.6 explicitly reduces all \(G\in\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\) to the classes \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\) using Lemma 6.2. That reduction misses the group just constructed and, more generally, groups produced by unrestricted directed unions which cease to be virtually locally indicable. Theorem 1.7 inherits this gap through its use of Theorem 1.6. This is a supported failure in the derivation of a main stated scope, which warrants Major under the frozen review calibration.

The counterexample does not say that the Atiyah or localization conclusions fail for \(G\). It does not affect the finite-edge amalgam/HNN arguments merely by refuting the separate class lemma. A restriction of the statements to \(\mathcal Y\) would avoid this particular counterexample, but would narrow the class stated in Definition 6.1. The repair below can instead retain that definition.
# A precise repair and its verification boundary

Equation reference: eq:repair. Define \(\operatorname{Loc}(\mathcal Y)\) to be the groups whose nontrivial finitely generated subgroups belong to \(\mathcal Y\). The correct class identity is \[
 \mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}=\operatorname{Loc}(\mathcal Y).\] Here is a proof, independent of the incorrect directed-union claim.

First, each \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\) is subgroup-closed. This is immediate at stage zero. At a successor stage, a subgroup acts on the original Bass–Serre tree; its vertex and edge stabilizers are subgroups of conjugates of the original stabilizers, and remain locally in the previous class. A subgroup of a virtually locally indicable group is virtually locally indicable, by intersection with a locally indicable subgroup of finite index. Limit stages follow directly. Moreover, the stages are increasing: a member of \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\) is locally in \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\), and its one-vertex graph puts it in \(\mathcal Y_{\alpha+1}\).

Induction also gives \(\mathcal Y\subseteq\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\), because a group locally in \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\) is the directed union of its finitely generated subgroups. Hence \(\operatorname{Loc}(\mathcal Y)\subseteq\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\). Conversely, \(\operatorname{Loc}(\mathcal Y)\) contains the finite groups and is closed under directed unions: a finite generating set lies in one member of the directed system. Suppose a virtually locally indicable group is the fundamental group of a graph with vertex and edge groups in \(\operatorname{Loc}(\mathcal Y)\). The finitely generated subgroups of all these vertex and edge groups form a set. Choose one ordinal bounding their \(\mathcal Y\)-ranks. Every vertex and edge group is then locally in that single stage, so the fundamental group belongs to the next stage of \(\mathcal Y\). Minimality in Definition 6.1 proves the other inclusion in [eq:repair] (#eq:repair).

Theorem 1.6 must then begin with a directed-union permanence step, before its induction on \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\). The required checks are concrete. If \(G=\bigcup_iG_i\) is directed, then \[K[G]=\bigcup_iK[G_i],\qquad
 \mathcal R_{K[G]}=\bigcup_i\mathcal R_{K[G_i]}.\] The second equality follows by the finite expression defining each element of the star-regular closure and uniqueness of relative inverses under the subgroup embedding. For a square matrix over \(K[G_i]\), von Neumann dimension induction gives invertibility in \(\mathcal U(G_i)\) exactly when it is invertible in \(\mathcal U(G)\). Consequently \(\Sigma(K,G)\) is the directed union of the corresponding finite-stage matrix sets, and their universal properties give the localization assertion at the limit.

Finite \(\operatorname{lcm}(G)\) ensures \(\operatorname{lcm}(G_i)\mid\operatorname{lcm}(G)\); the strong Atiyah dimension restriction therefore passes to the union and gives semisimplicity by the paper’s regular-closure criterion. For the algebraic assertion, a \(K_0\)-class over the union is represented by finite matrix data and descends to one stage. Surjectivity from finite subgroup rings passes to the union. These observations identify the missing argument without assuming that the union remains virtually locally indicable.

Equation [eq:repair] (#eq:repair) and the counterexample have been checked here. The proposed corrected proof still uses the localization, dimension, and subgroup functoriality results employed elsewhere in the paper. This initial report does not certify a revised manuscript or claim author adoption. In particular, the separate coefficient-field question below is not resolved by repairing the class identity.
# Other proof chains and boundary checks
## Finite-edge amalgams

The definition of a full map, the right-exact cokernel argument in Lemma 2.13, and the split kernel/cokernel argument in Lemma 2.14 were checked with the dimension normalizations on pp. 11–12. Epimorphy of the star-regular closure agrees with the original multiplication-isomorphism proof in [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~24--25]{basechange}].

For \(G=A*_CB\), the normal-form deletion operator in Lemma 3.1 commutes with the right \(B\)-action. Its right-\(A\) commutator is the finite-\(C\) projection expression printed on pp. 13–14. The trace calculation in Lemma 3.2 uses cyclicity with finite-rank operators and ultimately averages over \(C\): \[\sum_{c\in C}T\cdot c=0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 T=\frac1{|C|}\sum_{c\ne1}T\cdot(1-c).\] The division by \(|C|\) and the finite projection are substantive uses of the finite-edge hypothesis. If one vertex equals the edge group, the associated intersection identity reduces directly to the obvious equality.

The Mayer–Vietoris result [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~9--10, Theorem 6]{dicks}] requires lifting, for example flatness, over the vertex rings. The regular vertex rings in Proposition 3.3 satisfy this condition. The complex tensor identification with finite-rank operators then gives the stated Tor vanishing over \(\mathbb C\). Bergman’s actual induced-submodule theorem and projective decomposition [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~3--5, 21--23]{bergman}] have a semisimple amalgamating ring, as supplied here by \(\mathbb C[C]\). They support the hereditary and dimension arguments in Theorem 3.4.

One implicit scalar-extension step can be supplied. Write \(S=\mathcal R_{\mathbb C[G]}\) and \(R_\Gamma\) for the graph ring. Since \(R_\Gamma\to S\) is epic, \(S\otimes_{R_\Gamma}S\cong S\). Since \(S\) is regular, the inclusion \(S\subseteq\mathcal U(G)\) is pure as a right \(S\)-module map: its quotient is flat. Thus \(S\otimes_{R_\Gamma}M\) injects into \(\mathcal U(G)\otimes_{R_\Gamma}M\). Let \(\overline M\) be the image of \(M\) in these modules. The map \(S\otimes_{R_\Gamma}M\to S\otimes_{R_\Gamma}\overline M\) is surjective by right exactness. Its composite with the extended inclusion of \(\overline M\) is an isomorphism by epimorphy, so it is itself an isomorphism. Extending further to \(\mathcal U(G)\) justifies the replacement by \(\overline M\) on pp. 17–18. The induced vertex summands then give dimensions in \(\operatorname{lcm}(G)^{-1}\mathbb Z\), using the vertex denominator restrictions.
## HNN extensions, limits, and stable induction

The kernel of the stable-letter map \(G\to\mathbb Z\) is the tree amalgam of conjugates of the vertex group. The increasing finite amalgams, the skew Laurent description, and the Tor transfer on pp. 20–23 were checked. In Lemma 4.1, semisimplicity gives noetherianity, and the star-closed crossed product is semiprime. Goldie’s theorem alone does not prove that its regular elements are invertible in \(\mathcal U(G)\); the additional analytic input is indeed supplied by [Retained latex: \cite[physical pp.~68--71, Corollary 8.16 and
Proposition 8.17]{reich}]. Their constant-term and semisimple hypotheses match the application.

A \(K_0\)-surjection supplies stable induction, not in general an unstabilized decomposition. This suffices for Proposition 2.16. Explicitly, from \([Q]=[S\otimes P_1]-[S\otimes P_2]\), choose a projective complement \(P'_2\) with \(P_2\oplus P'_2\cong R^m\). Equality in \(K_0(S)\) gives a stable isomorphism; adding a complement to its stabilizing projective yields \[Q\oplus S^{m+n}\cong S\otimes_R(P_1\oplus P'_2\oplus R^n).\] Thus the shorthand on p. 22 need not create a separate defect.

Similarly, faithfulness of the rank on projectives is supported by the actual induced-projective decomposition and positivity at vertices, rather than by a \(K_0\)-surjection alone. Countability of the fundamental group need not force countability of an arbitrarily redundant underlying graph. The exhaustion on pp. 23–25 can be taken over the directed set of finite connected subgraphs. All idempotents, maps, and their relations involve finite data. This supplies the same limit argument without a countability assumption on the graph itself.
## The locally indicable and weak-\(K_1\) inputs

The original locally indicable theorem and the Hughes-free coefficient-field consequence are available in [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~2--3, 30--31, 43]{locally}]. The division ring is therefore the appropriate one for the locally indicable subgroup used in Section 6. The graph-of-division-rings result [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~7, 14, 24, Lemma 7.6]{fisher}] covers general graphs, rather than only a two-vertex amalgam. Its proof uses the semifir property, universality, and maximality of the Hughes-free rank.

For Theorem 1.7, the relevant general statement is [Retained latex: \cite[p.~3, Theorem 1.2]{weak}]: the localization map must be injective and the inverted maps must be endomorphisms of finitely generated projectives. Square matrices over \(R[G]\) meet the latter condition, and the claimed realization inside \(\mathcal U(G)\) supplies injectivity once Theorem 1.6 has been established over \(F\). Nonzero coefficients from \(R\) are among the weakly invertible one-by-one matrices, so the passage to \(F\) is compatible with this localization. The regular closure is rationally closed in \(\mathcal U(G)\). After semisimplicity, Morita invariance and the Dieudonné determinant give the stated product of abelianized division-ring unit groups. This check does not remove the dependence on the scope of Theorem 1.6.
# Needs Evidence and limits of verification
## The coefficient-field passage

The assertions preceding Proposition 3.3, p. 15, at the beginning of Section 4, p. 20, and their use in Section 5, p. 23, extend the proof to every conjugation-closed \(K\subseteq\mathbb C\). The displayed operator identification on pp. 16–17 is over \(\mathbb C\). Replacing its tensor symbol by \(\otimes_K\) is not an isomorphism to complex finite-rank operators.

For example, with \(K=\mathbb Q\), the tensor \[i\delta_e\otimes_{\mathbb Q}\delta_e-
 \delta_e\otimes_{\mathbb Q}i\delta_e\] is nonzero. On the rational span of \(\delta_e,i\delta_e\), take coordinate functionals \(f,g\) with \(f(\delta_e)=g(i\delta_e)=1\) and \(f(i\delta_e)=g(\delta_e)=0\), and extend them rationally. Their tensor product evaluates the displayed tensor to \(-1\). Its image under the complex-bilinear rank-one operator map is zero. The original operator argument in [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~9--11]{sylvester}] also uses the complex tensor product.

This proves only that a mechanical coefficient substitution is insufficient. It is not a counterexample to Tor vanishing over \(K\), or to the strong Atiyah conclusion over \(K\). A coefficient-specific argument, or a descent theorem with its hypotheses checked, would settle this item. No soficity assumption may silently be added. This remains Needs Evidence; it is not counted as a second supported Major Problem.
## External-reference and version limits

Selected original dependencies were obtained and their relevant statements and applications checked, rather than every foundational proof recursively cited by them. Direct access to the Henneke thesis was denied by the repository, and the attempted Dicks 1983 publisher access returned a denial. The cited Schofield book statements were not obtained in full original pages. The paper’s restatements and the surrounding arguments were examined, but these remaining original-source checks are explicitly outstanding. They are verification limitations, not evidence that those standard results are false.

Two attempts to obtain a journal comparison PDF returned non-PDF responses. The assigned preprint remains the reviewed source; publication-page text is not substituted for a byte-verified journal PDF or for page inspection. No corrected author version was adopted in this review.

problems.title: the class equality in Lemma 6.2 is false
problems.source_location: Source p.26 Definition 6.1, Y_alpha hierarchy and Lemma 6.2; p.27 first sentence of Theorem 1.6 proof; p.28 Theorem 1.7 dependency
claim: Recorded check: the class equality in Lemma 6.2 is false
analysis: Severity: Major. Location: Definition 6.1, the definition of \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\), and Lemma 6.2, p. 26; the first sentence of the proof of Theorem 1.6, p. 27; its subsequent use in Theorem 1.7, p. 28.

Every member of the paper’s class \(\mathcal Y=\bigcup_\alpha\mathcal Y_\alpha\) is virtually locally indicable: finite groups have the trivial subgroup of finite index, successor stages explicitly impose this property, and a limit stage is a union of classes, not a new operation of taking unions of groups. In contrast, the directed-union operation in Definition 6.1 has no such restriction. The claim that \(\mathcal Y\) is closed under directed unions therefore requires proof and is false.

The group \(\bigoplus_{n\geq1}C_2\) already separates the two classes, but has infinite \(\operatorname{lcm}\). The following construction avoids that limitation and meets the group and coefficient hypotheses of Theorem 1.6.

Write an affine map of \(\mathbb R^3\) as \((D,v)\), with product \((D,v)(E,w)=(DE,Dw+v)\). Let \[a=\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1),(1/2,1/2,0)\bigr),\qquad
 b=\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,-1),(0,1/2,1/2)\bigr)\] and put \(H=\langle a,b\rangle\), \(c=ab\). For translation by \(v\) write \(T_v\). Direct exact calculation gives \[\begin{aligned}
 c&=\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,1),(1/2,0,-1/2)\bigr),\\
 x=a^2&=T_{(1,0,0)},&
 y=b^2&=T_{(0,1,0)},&
 z=c^{-2}&=T_{(0,0,1)},\\
 [a,b]&=xy^{-1}z^{-1},&
 bxb^{-1}&=x^{-1},&
 aya^{-1}&=y^{-1}.\end{aligned}\] The subgroup \(L=\langle x,y,z\rangle\cong\mathbb Z^3\) is normal: conjugation of a translation by \(a\) or \(b\) changes only coordinate signs. Modulo \(L\), the generators commute and have order two. Their four distinct linear parts show that \[H/L\cong C_2\times C_2,\qquad H=L\sqcup La\sqcup Lb\sqcup Lc.\] There are no additional translation cosets.

An element of \(L\setminus\{1\}\) has infinite order. For \(\ell=T_{(p,q,r)}\), \(p,q,r\in\mathbb Z\), the squares of \(\ell a,\ell b,\ell c\) have respectively a translation coordinate \(2p+1\), \(2q+1\), or \(2r-1\), so each is nontrivial. Thus \(H\) is torsion-free and virtually \(\mathbb Z^3\), hence virtually locally indicable.

Nevertheless, if \(f:H\to\mathbb Z\) is a homomorphism, conjugation of \(x\) to \(x^{-1}\) gives \(f(x)=0\), and \(x=a^2\) gives \(f(a)=0\). Similarly, \(aya^{-1}=y^{-1}\) and \(y=b^2\) give \(f(b)=0\). Therefore every such \(f\) is zero. The nontrivial, finitely generated group \(H\) is not locally indicable.

Equation reference: eq:amalgam. Projection to the first affine coordinate maps \(H\) onto the infinite dihedral group. The images of \(b\) and \(c\) are reflections about \(0\) and \(1/4\), and the kernel is \(L_0=\langle y,z\rangle\cong\mathbb Z^2\). The two vertex preimages are \[B=\langle b,z\mid bzb^{-1}=z^{-1}\rangle,\qquad
 C=\langle c,y\mid cyc^{-1}=y^{-1}\rangle.\] Both are Klein-bottle groups. In \(B\), \(y=b^2\); in \(C\), \(z=c^{-2}\). The subgroup \(L_0\) has index two in each, and \[
 H\cong B*_{L_0}C .\] For completeness, this map is surjective since \(a=cb^{-1}\). A reduced word alternating between the two vertex groups outside \(L_0\) maps to a nonempty reduced word in \(C_2*C_2\); a nontrivial word in \(L_0\) remains a nontrivial translation. This proves injectivity.

The group \(\mathbb Z\) is an HNN extension of the trivial group. The identity HNN extension of \(\mathbb Z\) gives \(\mathbb Z^2\), and its inversion HNN extension gives the Klein-bottle group. Each output is virtually free abelian. Equation [eq:amalgam] (#eq:amalgam) therefore proves \(H\in\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\).

The same argument gives \(H^n\in\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\) for every finite \(n\). Inductively put \(P=H^{n-1}\). Identity HNN extensions construct \(P\times\mathbb Z\) and \(P\times\mathbb Z^2\); an HNN extension with the identity on \(P\) and inversion on \(\mathbb Z\) constructs \(P\) times a Klein-bottle group. Finally, \[P\times H\cong
 (P\times B)*_{P\times L_0}(P\times C).\] All outputs in this finite construction are virtually free abelian, so the additional hypothesis on each graph operation is satisfied.

Set \[G=\bigoplus_{n\geq1}H=\bigcup_{n\geq1}H^n .\] Then \(G\) is countable, torsion-free, belongs to \(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\), and has \(\operatorname{lcm}(G)=1\). Take \(K=\mathbb Q\), which is closed under complex conjugation.

We show that no finite-index subgroup \(J\leq G\) is locally indicable. Its normal core \(N\) has finite index, and the quotient \(Q=G/N\) is finite. There are only finitely many homomorphisms \(H\to Q\), because \(H\) has two generators. Infinitely many coordinate copies of \(H\) therefore have the same restriction \(\rho:H\to Q\) of the quotient map. Let \(m\geq1\) be the exponent of the finite group \(\rho(H)\). Choose \(m\) distinct such coordinates. The diagonal copy of \(H\) on these coordinates maps to \(\rho(h)^m=1\) for every \(h\), so it lies in \(N\subseteq J\). It is a nontrivial finitely generated subgroup without an epimorphism onto \(\mathbb Z\). Consequently \(J\) is not locally indicable.

Thus \(G\notin\mathcal Y\), although it satisfies the hypotheses \(G\in\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\), countability, and finite \(\operatorname{lcm}(G)\). This is a counterexample to Lemma 6.2 within the parameter range used by the main application. The affine identities were also checked independently with exact rational arithmetic. The infinite-group argument above is analytic; it is not inferred from a finite enumeration or from author code.

The proof of Theorem 1.6 explicitly reduces all \(G\in\mathcal T_{\mathrm{VLI}}\) to the classes \(\mathcal Y_\alpha\) using Lemma 6.2. That reduction misses the group just constructed and, more generally, groups produced by unrestricted directed unions which cease to be virtually locally indicable. Theorem 1.7 inherits this gap through its use of Theorem 1.6. This is a supported failure in the derivation of a main stated scope, which warrants Major under the frozen review calibration.

The counterexample does not say that the Atiyah or localization conclusions fail for \(G\). It does not affect the finite-edge amalgam/HNN arguments merely by refuting the separate class lemma. A restriction of the statements to \(\mathcal Y\) would avoid this particular counterexample, but would narrow the class stated in Definition 6.1. The repair below can instead retain that definition.

Title: Initial verification of
Entropy and Stability of Hyperbolic Manifolds
# Identity and scope

The assigned paper is Antoine Song, Entropy and Stability of Hyperbolic Manifolds, Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 877–914, DOI `10.1007/s00039-025-00711-3` [paper]. The reviewed file is the supplied version of record, with 38 physical PDF pages. Physical page \(p\) has printed page number \(p+876\). The complete text and all 38 source-page images were actually read or viewed in this scientific conversation. The source has 1,809,922 bytes and SHA256

The associated manifest, dispatch, task and complete prompt are bound in the provenance record. Review scope is this source version and the mathematical claims it makes. The 52 selected original-reference page images were also actually viewed. Their exact versions, paths, bytes, hashes and physical page numbers are recorded separately; journal-byte equivalence is not inferred for an acquired preprint.
# Claims, hypotheses, and proof structure

Theorem 0.1 concerns a connected closed oriented real hyperbolic \(n\)-manifold \((M,g_0)\), \(n\geq3\), and smooth Riemannian metrics \(g_i\) with \(\operatorname{Vol}(M,g_i)=\operatorname{Vol}(M,g_0)\) and \(h(g_i)\to n-1\). It asserts the existence of smooth exceptional regions \(Z_i\) with both volume and boundary area tending to zero, such that the complements converge in the measured Gromov–Hausdorff sense to \((M,g_0)\). The metric on a complement is its intrinsic path metric. The theorem does not assert convergence of the original, unmodified ambient metric spaces.

Theorem 0.2, made precise in Definition 2.7 and Theorem 2.8 (pp. 894–898), identifies every spherical Plateau limit up to intrinsic isomorphism with \[\left(M,g'\right),\qquad
 g'=\frac{(n-1)^2}{4n}g_0 .\] An isometry for the induced length metric, preserving the current, is weaker than an isometry for the original metric on the current space. The paper expressly leaves the stronger uniqueness question open. The admissible homotopy class is the marked class inducing the identity on the fundamental group, as specified on p. 891; it is not an arbitrary automorphism class.

The essential chain is as follows. The regular representation gives the spherical quotient; a degree-one barycenter map gives the sharp spherical-volume lower bound. Near equality yields almost isometry on regions of almost full volume. Proposition 1.4 turns suitable flat limits and maps into a bi-Lipschitz identification, with a one-sided intrinsic length bound. The stronger neighborhood estimate gives intrinsic uniqueness in Theorem 2.8. For the entropy theorem, Theorem 3.2 additionally removes thin regions to obtain genuine Gromov–Hausdorff convergence of the intrinsic complements. Theorem 3.5 excludes every strict distance shortcut in the limit by producing a uniform entropy increase. Finally Theorem 3.7 and Lemma 3.8 give the asserted measured convergence.

Theorem 3.5 itself is stated for \(n\geq2\), with a bi-Lipschitz, 1-Lipschitz bijection from the hyperbolic metric to the limiting metric, and, for every sufficiently small error and all sufficiently large indices, a global homotopy equivalence whose restriction to an open set is an error-isometry for its intrinsic metric. Those quantifiers and the global homotopy condition are needed to make the entropy gap uniform and to preserve distinct loop classes.
# Problem 1: missing multiplicity control in the auxiliary mass claim

Severity: Minor. Location: Assumption 1.3(a)–(e), printed p. 885 (physical p. 9); equation (3) and the displayed chain immediately following it, p. 887 (physical p. 11); the conversion of small geometric volume into small current mass in the subsequent curve-lifting argument, p. 888.

Assumption 1.3 describes the Riemannian geometry of \(N_i=\operatorname{spt}S_i\) and the volume of its good and bad regions. It does not say that \(S_i=[\![N_i]\!]\), or impose convergence of \(\mathbf M(S_i)\) to \(\operatorname{Vol}(N,h)\). For an integer rectifiable current on a Riemannian support, the mass includes the absolute integer multiplicity. This is explicit in the intrinsic representation and mass formulas of Ambrosio–Kirchheim [Retained latex: \cite[Theorems 9.1 and 9.5]{AK}]. Small unweighted volume therefore does not imply small mass.

Equation (3) claims, with \(O_\eta\) the \(\eta\)-neighborhood of \(\operatorname{spt}S_\infty\) in the complete ambient space, \[\lim_i\|S_i\|(E\setminus O_\eta)=0
 \quad\hbox{for every fixed }\eta>0.\] Its displayed justification identifies \(\lim_i\mathbf M(S_i)\) with \(\operatorname{Vol}(N,h)\). Both claims fail under all of the literal hypotheses, as the following example shows.
## A connected example satisfying every stated hypothesis

Fix a connected closed oriented Riemannian three-manifold \(N\); the round three-sphere is a concrete choice. The construction also works with a closed oriented hyperbolic three-manifold. Put \[E=N\times\mathbb R^4,\qquad S_\infty=[\![N\times\{0\}]\!],
 \qquad r_i=i^{-1},\quad \epsilon_i=i^{-5},\quad m_i=i^3
 \quad(i\geq4),\] and use the product Riemannian distance on \(E\). Choose \(p\in N\). In the vertical fiber \(\{p\}\times\mathbb R^4\), place a round three-sphere of radius \(r_i\), centered at a vector of norm one. Join it to \(N\times\{0\}\) by a smooth three-dimensional neck of cross-sectional radius \(\epsilon_i\) and bounded length, removing caps of radius comparable to \(\epsilon_i\) at the two ends. Denote the resulting oriented connected closed embedded three-manifold by \(N_i\).

Here the neck may be constructed as the side boundary of a thin four-dimensional handle along an embedded arc. Its three-dimensional volume is \(O(\epsilon_i^2)\), and its four-dimensional filling volume is \(O(\epsilon_i^3)\). Normal frames can be rotated along the arc to join the horizontal cap to the vertical cap; the product ambient dimension is seven. Smoothing the two junctions changes these estimates only by uniform constants. The modification is identical to \(N\times\{0\}\) outside an \(O(\epsilon_i)\)-ball about \(p\).

Let \(B_i\) be the spherical part of \(N_i\) with the small attaching cap removed. It lies entirely in the vertical fiber. Its orientation agrees with that of \(N_i\), and \[\operatorname{Vol}(B_i)=2\pi^2 r_i^3-O(\epsilon_i^3),\qquad
 \operatorname{Area}(\partial B_i)=O(\epsilon_i^2).\] Set \[S_i=[\![N_i]\!]+(m_i-1)[\![B_i]\!].\] Thus the multiplicity is one on the neck and the main component and \(m_i\) on \(B_i\). These are integral currents, with \[\operatorname{spt}S_i=N_i,\qquad
 \mathbf M(\partial S_i)=O(m_i\epsilon_i^2)=O(i^{-7})\longrightarrow0.\] In particular, even a uniform mass and boundary-mass bound would not exclude the example.

The natural currents \([\![N_i]\!]\) converge flatly to \([\![N\times\{0\}]\!]\). Indeed the difference is filled by the thin handle and the four-ball bounded by the spherical component, with total filling mass \(O(\epsilon_i^3+r_i^4)\). If \(Q_i\) is the deleted spherical cap, then \[[\![B_i]\!]=\partial[\![\mathbb B^4_{r_i}]\!]-[\![Q_i]\!],
 \qquad \mathbf M(Q_i)=O(\epsilon_i^3).\] Consequently \[\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal F_E(S_i-S_\infty)
 &\leq C(\epsilon_i^3+r_i^4)
       +C m_i(r_i^4+\epsilon_i^3)\\
 &\longrightarrow0 ,\end{aligned}\] because \(m_ir_i^4=i^{-1}\) and \(m_i\epsilon_i^3=i^{-12}\).

Let \(\varphi_i\) be the restriction of the product projection \(E\to N\). It is smooth and 1-Lipschitz for the restricted ambient metric, as required in Assumption 1.3(c). The oriented manifold \(N_i\) is homologous in \(E\) to \(N\times\{0\}\), while the projection is constant on \(B_i\). It follows exactly, not merely in the limit, that \[(\varphi_i)_\# S_i=[\![N]\!] .\] Let \(R_i\) be the unchanged part of \(N\times\{0\}\) outside a slightly larger cap neighborhood. The metric is smooth there and \(\varphi_i\) is exactly a Riemannian isometry. Moreover, \[\operatorname{Vol}(R_i)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Vol}(N),\qquad
 \operatorname{Vol}(N_i\setminus R_i)=O(r_i^3+\epsilon_i^2)\longrightarrow0.\] This verifies (d) and (e). The induced intrinsic metric on \(N_i\) is its smooth Riemannian metric, verifying (a), and \(\partial N_i=\varnothing\), verifying (b). The complete ambient space, the flat convergence, the orientation, and the connectedness requirements have all been retained.

For the fixed value \(\eta=1/4\), all of \(B_i\) lies outside \(O_\eta\) for sufficiently large \(i\). Therefore \[\liminf_i\|S_i\|(E\setminus O_{1/4})
 \ \geq\ \lim_i m_i\operatorname{Vol}(B_i)=2\pi^2>0 .\] In fact \[\mathbf M(S_i)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Vol}(N)+2\pi^2 ,\] which also directly contradicts the mass identification used below equation (3). The supporting manifolds still have volumes converging to \(\operatorname{Vol}(N)\).
## Impact and repair boundary

The example disproves the stated auxiliary mass claim and its displayed derivation. It does not disprove the conclusion of Proposition 1.4: its limiting projection is an isometry. Nor is it a counterexample to Theorems 0.1 or 0.2.

A clean repair is to state explicitly the intended unit-multiplicity condition \(S_i=[\![N_i]\!]\), with the compatible orientation, and carry it through the proof. An alternative is to impose appropriate mass convergence and formulate each estimate with multiplicities; that alternative requires auditing the area and curve-lifting arguments, not simply replacing the term volume once.

The principal applications already have the relevant extra control. In Theorem 3.2, \(D_i=[\![N_i]\!]\) is explicitly defined on p. 901, and the volumes converge to the target value. In Theorem 2.8, pp. 896–897, the minimizing sequence has \(\mathbf M(C_i)\to\operatorname{SphereVol}(M)\), and equation (20) gives a discarded part of vanishing mass before restriction to \(D_i\). These application-specific facts should be stated at the point where Proposition 1.4 is invoked. The demonstrated impact is a repairable overstatement in the auxiliary hypotheses and proof; no failure of the main entropy or intrinsic-uniqueness conclusion has been established. This is the reason for the Minor classification.
# Independent checks of the barycenter estimates
## The modified distance and differential inequality

The smooth modified distance on p. 893 can be checked explicitly: for curvature minus one and \(r=\operatorname{dist}(w,\cdot)\), take \(\rho=\log\cosh r\). Away from \(w\), \[\rho'=\tanh r,\qquad \rho''=\operatorname{sech}^2r,\qquad
 \operatorname{Hess}r=\coth r\,(g_0-dr\otimes dr).\] Consequently \[\operatorname{Hess}\rho
   =g_0-d\rho\otimes d\rho .\] The even radial expansion makes \(\rho\) smooth at \(w\), where the same identity extends. Thus the claimed lower bound holds already for this choice of the parameter. Strict convexity and properness of the finite positive weighted sum give its unique barycenter.

With the notation of [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~16--19]{Song}], set \(H=\sum_\gamma f(\gamma)^2\,d\rho_{\gamma o}\otimes
d\rho_{\gamma o}\) and \(K=\sum_\gamma f(\gamma)^2\operatorname{Hess}\rho_{\gamma o}\). Then \(\operatorname{tr}H<1\) and \(K\geq I-H>0\). Differentiating the barycenter equation, followed by Cauchy–Schwarz, gives \[\left|\operatorname{Jac}\operatorname{Bar}\right|
 \leq 2^n\frac{\sqrt{\det H}}{\det K}
 \leq 2^n\frac{\sqrt{\det H}}{\det(I-H)}.\] The finite-dimensional tangent plane is the relevant domain; no determinant on the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is being taken.
## A direct proof of the sharp matrix bound

For \(n\geq3\), let the nonnegative numbers \(\mu_j\) satisfy \(\sum_{j=1}^n\mu_j\leq1\), and set \[F(\mu)=\prod_{j=1}^n\frac{\sqrt{\mu_j}}{1-\mu_j}.\] The sharp bound is \[F(\mu)\leq\frac{n^{n/2}}{(n-1)^n}.
 \tag{*}\] Each positive factor increases in its argument, so an interior maximum must have trace one. At an interior stationary point on that face, every eigenvalue satisfies \[\frac{1+\mu_j}{2\mu_j(1-\mu_j)}=\lambda .\] There can be at most two distinct values \(a<b\). Equality of these derivatives gives \[(1+a)b(1-b)-(1+b)a(1-a)
       =(b-a)(1-a-b-ab)=0 .\] Hence \(b=(1-a)/(1+a)\). Two occurrences of \(b\), together with one \(a\), are impossible because \[2b+a-1=\frac{(1-a)^2}{1+a}>0.\] If \(b\) occurs once, the trace condition is \((n-1)a+b=1\), which reduces to \[(n-1)a^2+(n-3)a=0.\] This has no positive solution for \(n\geq3\). Thus the only interior stationary point has all eigenvalues equal to \(1/n\).

It also proves the qualitative stability needed here: near-maximal \(F\) forces the eigenvalues to approach \(1/n\). Since \[\|d\operatorname{Bar}\|\leq
 \frac{2\sqrt{\mu_{\max}}}{1-\mu_{\max}},
 \qquad B=\frac{2\sqrt n}{n-1},\] near equality in the Jacobian bound gives an upper bound \(B+o(1)\) for every singular value and a product \(B^n-o(1)\). Each singular value is therefore also at least \(B-o(1)\). The variation estimate for \(H\) and a fixed spectral gap propagate the upper bound to short neighboring curves, as checked in [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~17--20]{Song}]. This verifies both parts of Lemma 2.6, with the exponent \(1/2\) in the length estimate. A typographical \(n/2\) in an intermediate line of the acquired reference’s proof is not present in the statement used by the reviewed paper and is not reported as a defect of this paper.
## Exact arithmetic and its limits

Reviewer-written Python using exact fractions and polynomial coefficient arithmetic was actually executed through the authorized native connection. It verified the displayed stationary-point identity, the strict gap \(27/64-1/4=11/64\), the weighted-bubble orders \(m_ir_i^3=1\), \(m_ir_i^4=i^{-1}\), \(m_i\epsilon_i^3=i^{-12}\), and \(m_i\epsilon_i^2=i^{-7}\), and the frequency estimate used below. The script, native interpreter identity, exit code and result hashes are retained. The geometric construction and the all-dimension matrix proof above are analytic arguments; finite computations are checks of their algebra, not replacements for those arguments. No author code was run.
# Proof-level coverage and counterchecks
## Currents, compactness, and the almost-isometry proposition

Sections 1.1–1.2 were checked with particular attention to support versus positive-density set, orientation, integer multiplicity, restricted ambient distance, induced intrinsic distance, and flat versus weak convergence. Sormani’s Theorem 6.1 [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~30--32]{Sormani}] supplies the limiting Lipschitz map for a fixed compact target. The proof of Basso–Creutz–Soultanis, Lemma 7.3 [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~20--21]{BCS}], gives compatibility with pushforwards. The paper explains its extension through an injective \(L^\infty\) ambient space. The fixed-target current and its boundary have finite mass; the linear homotopy between bounded extensions controls the difference by integrals of their pointwise displacement against those two mass measures. This gives the required limiting pushforward without assuming Gromov–Hausdorff convergence.

Wenger’s original compactness statement [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 1.2, p.~2; proof, pp.~17--19]{Wenger}] requires uniform mass, boundary mass, and diameter bounds and allows nonzero boundaries. The boundaryless formulation in the paper’s Theorem 1.1 is a special case; the applications with vanishing boundary mass use this general original statement. The slicing formulas and preservation of integer multiplicities were checked in [Retained latex: \cite[Theorems 5.6--5.7 and 9.7]{AK}].

With the intended multiplicity control, the proof of Proposition 1.4 uses the area formula to select a region of essentially single-sheeted coverage, coarea to lift short curves while avoiding the boundary and the small bad region, and compactness to obtain a bijective limit with a 1-Lipschitz inverse for intrinsic lengths. For a precise choice of endpoints, one may also discard the preimage of the image of the bad region; its image has vanishing volume by the uniform Lipschitz bound. Injectivity merely on the retained region would not by itself rule out another preimage in the discarded region. The stronger local Lipschitz hypothesis in part (2) is essential: the shortcut example in Remark 1.5 rules out silently replacing ambient distance by intrinsic length.
## Spherical volume and intrinsic uniqueness

For the torsion-free fundamental group, the regular action on the unit sphere is free and proper. Matrix coefficients of the regular representation vanish at infinity, and a vector fixed by an infinite-order translation cannot be square summable. The quotient diameter bound and the current boundary condition give the required compactness.

The finite-support and polyhedral approximations were checked against [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 1.6, pp.~13--14]{Song}]. In applying them to admissible maps, one retains the marked homotopy class and makes a generic perturbation in the available high codimension; arbitrary flat approximation alone would not establish those additional properties. The barycenter has degree one, so its Jacobian bound forces the spherical-volume lower bound. The opposite inequality comes from the entropy maps, and the two constants match after rescaling by \((n-1)^2/(4n)\); see [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 4.1, pp.~27--29]{Song}].

In Theorem 2.8, the mass lower bound and minimizing hypothesis force near equality of the barycenter Jacobian on regions of asymptotically full mass. A coarea choice can be made with collar radii tending to zero slowly enough that discarded mass divided by the radius still tends to zero. This supplies vanishing boundary mass and the local almost-1-Lipschitz estimate needed by Proposition 1.4(2). A short-curve estimate only controls such sufficiently small collars; there is no need to use an unjustified uniform assertion for every collar radius below one. The current-preserving limit then proves intrinsic isomorphism, with no promotion to equality of the original metric spaces.
## Entropy maps and construction of the convergent regions

For \(c>h(g)\), the exponential kernel defining \(\mathcal P_c\) is square integrable on the universal cover. Normalization is an orthogonal projection in the differential calculation, giving the Hilbert–Schmidt bound \(\sum_j|d\mathcal P_c(e_j)|^2\leq c^2/4\). The map sending a function to its \(L^2\)-norm on each fundamental domain translate is 1-Lipschitz by the reverse triangle inequality. Equivariance and the a.e. distance-gradient identity therefore give Lemma 3.1. These checks do not assume differentiability of distance at its cut locus.

After rescaling, \(c_i\to2\sqrt n\). The trace bound and arithmetic–geometric mean give the volume upper bound in (28); the spherical-volume lower bound then forces the singular values to approach one on a region of almost full volume. The same argument is applied to the barycenter composition. Coarea selects a small smooth boundary.

The metric \(\widehat d_i=\min\{\operatorname{dist}_{h_i},6\operatorname{diam}(M,g')\}\) is finite and locally unchanged, even when a region has several components. Thus it permits Wenger compactness. The inverse limit map bounds the limit diameter; on sufficiently small neighborhoods of that limit the cutoff is inactive. Slicing and the degree/Jacobian lower bound show that the remaining volume tends to the full target volume. This proves return to the original intrinsic metric in Step 3.

Step 4 is necessary: intrinsic flat convergence alone does not give Hausdorff convergence of all supporting sets. Nets approximating the limit and small neighborhoods of those nets supply a noncollapsing sequence after another coarea choice. For the intrinsic-ball lower bound, paths can be assembled along a finite chain of nearby net points approximating a limit geodesic. Starting from a point within distance \(t\) of the net, use the margin \(s>2t\) and points in a thinner inner neighborhood to keep the connectors inside the chosen region. The mass outside each such fixed inner neighborhood tends to zero. This gives the positive ball-volume lower bound needed for (36), without requiring a uniform inclusion of every ambient ball up to the outer boundary. Reapplying the limit construction can change the limiting metric space, as the paper correctly notes on p. 904. The homotopy equivalences then become error-isometries for the final intrinsic regions.
## Equidistribution, uniform entropy gap, and measured convergence

The original equidistribution hypotheses were checked in [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 1.2, pp.~2--3, and pp.~5--6, 16--17]{EM}]. For a closed real hyperbolic manifold the lattice is cocompact, the relevant maximal compact subgroup has finite volume, and the semisimple group satisfies the required irreducibility condition. Pushing the compact-orbit averages to the unit tangent bundle gives Theorem 3.3. For the open set in Corollary 3.4, a continuous nonnegative bump supported in it justifies the positive lower bound; convergence for continuous functions is not being applied without justification to an arbitrary indicator.

If a random visitation fraction \(X\in[0,1]\) has \(\mathbb E X\geq c>0\), then \[\mathbb P(X\geq c/2)\geq\frac{c}{2-c}.\] This supplies a positive fraction of directions with a positive frequency of visits. Finitely many initial time blocks and the last incomplete block have vanishing relative contribution. The direction sphere is \(S^{n-1}\); the \(S^2\) notation on p. 906 is a harmless dimension-specific notation slip in an otherwise dimension-independent argument.

A strict shortcut for the limiting 1-Lipschitz map has a fixed positive length gap. Small-error isometries of the intrinsic regions lift sufficiently fine geodesic subdivisions, with homotopy controlled below the injectivity radius. The maps need not themselves be Lipschitz: the additive distortion bound controls the images of sufficiently short subpaths. Approximate endpoints and almost-minimizing paths suffice for open regions; the strict shortcut margin absorbs these errors. Bounded hyperbolic length leaves only finitely many relevant relative homotopy classes, so the shortcut constants may be taken uniformly after subselection, or minimized over that finite collection.

Positive-frequency use of the shortcut reduces the length of a positive-area family of long geodesics by a fixed proportion. A bounded fundamental domain converts this family into exponentially many distinct orbit points; the global homotopy equivalence preserves distinct loop classes. With a fixed \(\theta>0\), the resulting comparison has the form \[\#\{\hbox{classes of }g_i\hbox{-length at most }(1-\theta)L+O(1)\}
 \ \geq\ c_0 e^{(n-1)L}.\] It implies \(h(g_i)\geq(n-1)/(1-\theta)>n-1\) uniformly for large \(i\), giving Theorem 3.5.

Every subsequence then has a further subsequence with the same hyperbolic limit. Choosing exceptional regions by an error functional tending to zero upgrades the subsequential statement to Theorem 3.7 for the full sequence. The remaining regions have mass converging to the target mass. Portegies’s mass-measure lemma [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 2.7, p.~6 in the acquired version]{Portegies}], cited as Lemma 2.1 in the paper’s published reference, applies with precisely this extra mass hypothesis. Together with the Hausdorff convergence already established, it gives the measured conclusion.

The complete assigned paper was read. Core invoked results were checked at the original-reference statement and relevant proof passage level, with the matrix inequality additionally proved above. The original Besson–Courtois–Gallot articles were not all acquired and read in full; the particular real-hyperbolic bound needed here was checked through the acquired detailed exposition and the independent argument above. No conclusion is extended to the unproved general uniqueness question or to unrelated rank-one extensions.

analysis: Severity: Minor. Location: Assumption 1.3(a)–(e), printed p. 885 (physical p. 9); equation (3) and the displayed chain immediately following it, p. 887 (physical p. 11); the conversion of small geometric volume into small current mass in the subsequent curve-lifting argument, p. 888.

Assumption 1.3 describes the Riemannian geometry of \(N_i=\operatorname{spt}S_i\) and the volume of its good and bad regions. It does not say that \(S_i=[\![N_i]\!]\), or impose convergence of \(\mathbf M(S_i)\) to \(\operatorname{Vol}(N,h)\). For an integer rectifiable current on a Riemannian support, the mass includes the absolute integer multiplicity. This is explicit in the intrinsic representation and mass formulas of Ambrosio–Kirchheim [Retained latex: \cite[Theorems 9.1 and 9.5]{AK}]. Small unweighted volume therefore does not imply small mass.

Equation (3) claims, with \(O_\eta\) the \(\eta\)-neighborhood of \(\operatorname{spt}S_\infty\) in the complete ambient space, \[\lim_i\|S_i\|(E\setminus O_\eta)=0
 \quad\hbox{for every fixed }\eta>0.\] Its displayed justification identifies \(\lim_i\mathbf M(S_i)\) with \(\operatorname{Vol}(N,h)\). Both claims fail under all of the literal hypotheses, as the following example shows.

Fix a connected closed oriented Riemannian three-manifold \(N\); the round three-sphere is a concrete choice. The construction also works with a closed oriented hyperbolic three-manifold. Put \[E=N\times\mathbb R^4,\qquad S_\infty=[\![N\times\{0\}]\!],
 \qquad r_i=i^{-1},\quad \epsilon_i=i^{-5},\quad m_i=i^3
 \quad(i\geq4),\] and use the product Riemannian distance on \(E\). Choose \(p\in N\). In the vertical fiber \(\{p\}\times\mathbb R^4\), place a round three-sphere of radius \(r_i\), centered at a vector of norm one. Join it to \(N\times\{0\}\) by a smooth three-dimensional neck of cross-sectional radius \(\epsilon_i\) and bounded length, removing caps of radius comparable to \(\epsilon_i\) at the two ends. Denote the resulting oriented connected closed embedded three-manifold by \(N_i\).

Here the neck may be constructed as the side boundary of a thin four-dimensional handle along an embedded arc. Its three-dimensional volume is \(O(\epsilon_i^2)\), and its four-dimensional filling volume is \(O(\epsilon_i^3)\). Normal frames can be rotated along the arc to join the horizontal cap to the vertical cap; the product ambient dimension is seven. Smoothing the two junctions changes these estimates only by uniform constants. The modification is identical to \(N\times\{0\}\) outside an \(O(\epsilon_i)\)-ball about \(p\).

Let \(B_i\) be the spherical part of \(N_i\) with the small attaching cap removed. It lies entirely in the vertical fiber. Its orientation agrees with that of \(N_i\), and \[\operatorname{Vol}(B_i)=2\pi^2 r_i^3-O(\epsilon_i^3),\qquad

If \(Q_i\) is the deleted spherical cap, then \[[\![B_i]\!]=\partial[\![\mathbb B^4_{r_i}]\!]-[\![Q_i]\!],
 \qquad \mathbf M(Q_i)=O(\epsilon_i^3).\] Consequently \[\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal F_E(S_i-S_\infty)
 &\leq C(\epsilon_i^3+r_i^4)
       +C m_i(r_i^4+\epsilon_i^3)\\
 &\longrightarrow0 ,\end{aligned}\] because \(m_ir_i^4=i^{-1}\) and \(m_i\epsilon_i^3=i^{-12}\).

Let \(\varphi_i\) be the restriction of the product projection \(E\to N\). It is smooth and 1-Lipschitz for the restricted ambient metric, as required in Assumption 1.3(c). The oriented manifold \(N_i\) is homologous in \(E\) to \(N\times\{0\}\), while the projection is constant on \(B_i\). For the fixed value \(\eta=1/4\), all of \(B_i\) lies outside \(O_\eta\) for sufficiently large \(i\). Therefore \[\liminf_i\|S_i\|(E\setminus O_{1/4})
 \ \geq\ \lim_i m_i\operatorname{Vol}(B_i)=2\pi^2>0 .\] In fact \[\mathbf M(S_i)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Vol}(N)+2\pi^2 ,\] which also directly contradicts the mass identification used below equation (3). The supporting manifolds still have volumes converging to \(\operatorname{Vol}(N)\).
