# Claims, hypotheses, and dependencies

For a real vector space \(V\) of dimension \(d>1\), the paper uses \[L=\{[v:\alpha]\in\mathbb P(V\oplus V^*):\alpha(v)>0\},\qquad
 \phi^t[v:\alpha]=[e^t v:e^{-t}\alpha].\] The normalization \(\alpha(v)=1\) is a double cover of this projective space. On it, the Liouville form \(\tau=\alpha\,dv\) has Reeb field \((v,-\alpha)\). The primal and dual transverse distributions give the stable and unstable foliations.

Definition 2.14 uses a finitely generated hyperbolic group and a uniform eigenvalue-gap bound \[\lambda_1(\gamma)-\lambda_2(\gamma)
 \geq c|\gamma|_\infty-c',\qquad c,c'>0,\] where \(\lambda_j\) are logarithms of eigenvalue moduli and \(|\gamma|_\infty\) is stable word length. Torsion-freeness is separately needed for the free quotient. This definition does not itself exclude an infinite cyclic group.

Theorems A and B construct a flow-invariant discontinuity domain, identify a compact invariant set with the full ordered-pair refraction flow, and assert a unique transitive basic set with analytic ambient stable and unstable distributions. The proof chain is: transverse limit maps and convergence dynamics; properness of the action; the Hopf parametrization and cocompactness; identification of non-wandering, periodic-closure, and trapped sets; then the Anosov bundle estimates. Compactness of \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\) does not mean that \(\mathcal M_\Gamma\) is compact.

For mixing, Section 4 explicitly adds non-elementarity, and the principal theorem adds irreducibility. The linear pseudo-exponential map, spanning of the infinitesimal limit set, and a finite compact cover give regular distortion. The other two inputs to Stoyanov’s theorem are Lipschitz stable holonomy and local non-integrability. Theorem C/Theorem 4 concerns every Hölder potential and Hölder observable, with constants permitted to depend on the potential and Hölder exponent. The analytic flow supplies the differentiability required in Stoyanov’s stated mixing corollary [stoyanov].

Section 5 returns to the broader non-trivial torsion-free scope. Theorems D–E and 5–8 concern Euler products over primitive conjugacy classes, meromorphic continuation, a leading pole, a zero-free strip, and prime-orbit asymptotics. Theorems F and 9–11 separately discuss the scalar operator \(A=-X+U\), localized resolvents, resonant states, and wavefront-compatible products. The pseudo-hyperbolic and Benoist–Hilbert applications in Theorems H/G and 12/13 must retain the required group range, operator type, and time normalization. These distinctions are material to the findings below.
# Problem 1: positive entropy is not a scalar leading resonance

Severity: Major. Location: Theorem F, p. 7, especially the \(U=0\) assertions; the scalar definition and resolvent on p. 41; Theorem 12(3), p. 47, and Theorem 13(3), p. 51. Section 5.2.2 on p. 43 must be reconciled with these statements.
## An admissible compact example

Choose a closed oriented hyperbolic surface of genus at least two. Lift its torsion-free cocompact holonomy in \(\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\) to a faithful subgroup \(\Gamma<\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\) not containing \(-I\). Such lifts exist: the obstruction is the Euler class modulo two, and the surface Euler number \(2g-2\) is even. Projection to the surface group is injective, so the lifted group is torsion-free and cocompact modulo the finite center. Its standard action on \(V=\mathbb R^2\) is irreducible, since a cocompact non-elementary Fuchsian group has no invariant real line. It is projective Anosov: the eigenvalue gap is the hyperbolic translation length, uniformly comparable to stable word length by the orbit quasi-isometry. Its limit set is all of \(\mathbb P(\mathbb R^2)\). Thus the example satisfies the theorem’s group, dimension, compactness, smoothness, and potential hypotheses. The paper itself explicitly includes uniform \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\) lattices among its compact cases on p. 3.

Here \(L\) is naturally \(\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\). For a normalized pair \(\alpha(v)=1\), there is a unique \(w\in\ker\alpha\) with \(\det(v,w)=1\). The matrix with columns \(v,w\) identifies the normalized double cover with \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\); \((v,\alpha)\sim(-v,-\alpha)\) gives the quotient by \(\{\pm I\}\). The flow becomes right multiplication by \(\operatorname{diag}(e^t,e^{-t})\). Because the limit set is full, every transverse pair belongs to the domain and to the lifted invariant set. Consequently \[\mathcal M_\Gamma=\mathcal K_\Gamma
 =\overline\Gamma\backslash\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\] is compact. This is the geodesic flow with twice the usual curvature-\(-1\) time parameter, so its entropy \(h\) is positive (\(h=2\) with this normalization).
## Direct resolvent exclusion

Equation reference: eq:scalar-resolvent. Take \(U=0\), which satisfies every support requirement, including on a compact ambient manifold. The contact volume \(\mu=\tau\wedge d\tau\) is finite and invariant. Hence \[T_t f=f\circ\phi^{-t}\] is a unitary group on \(L^2(\mu)\), with generator \(A=-X\). For every \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda>0\), \[
 (A-\lambda)^{-1}
 =-\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}T_t\,dt,\qquad
 \|(A-\lambda)^{-1}\|\leq\frac{1}{\operatorname{Re}\lambda}.\] The strong Laplace integral has tails converging in operator norm, locally uniformly on the open right half-plane. Differentiation is controlled by the integrable bounds \(t^k e^{-t\operatorname{Re}\lambda}\), so it defines a holomorphic bounded-operator family there. Composing with the continuous inclusions from smooth functions to \(L^2\) and from \(L^2\) to distributions gives the same conclusion for the distribution-valued resolvent. Its unique meromorphic continuation cannot have a pole at the positive real number \(h\). On the constant function, \[(A-\lambda)^{-1}1=-\lambda^{-1}1.\] Thus zero is the scalar resonance exhibited by constants, whereas the asserted positive-entropy scalar resonance is absent. This is an analytic contradiction, not a numerical failure to detect a pole.

The counterexample also explains the error’s nature. Humbert’s original Theorem 1 distinguishes the scalar critical pressure \(P(U+J^u)\) from the pressure \(P(U)\) for the appropriate degree of differential forms, where \(J^u\) is the negative infinitesimal unstable Jacobian [humbert]. In the compact constant-curvature example, \(J^u=-2\), \(P(0)=2\), and \(P(J^u)=0\). Dyatlov–Guillarmou likewise distinguish the scalar zero resonance from the entropy-related form contribution to the zeta function [dg2016].
## Impact and repair boundary

The failure changes a headline spectral assertion and the claimed entropy-state identification for the specified scalar operator. Changing only the overall sign of a resolvent does not move its poles and therefore cannot repair it.

The paper’s p. 43 does mention lifts to differential forms. That correct observation is acknowledged here; it does not make the expressly scalar Theorem F true. A repair must specify the operator, form degree, orientation twist when needed, pairing, and resulting invariant distribution, then prove the claimed open-basic-set version. Alternatively a change of potential changes the operator and requires its own regularity and pressure analysis. The compact Anosov result alone does not certify every open-set extension.

The same positive-entropy scalar claim fails for a closed hyperbolic geodesic flow in the applications. Moreover, a Hölder conjugacy alone does not define pullback of arbitrary distributions with specified wavefront sets; the low-regularity Hilbert-flow statement needs an explicit functional interpretation. These are repair obligations, not a claim that exponential mixing, zeta continuation, or the geometric construction is refuted by this compact example.
# Problem 2: the cyclic boundary has two periodic components

Severity: Minor; range correction. Location: Theorems A/B, pp. 3–4; Theorem D, p. 6; Proposition 2.9 and Definition 2.14, pp. 13–14; Theorem 2 and Lemma 3.12, pp. 22–23; the elementary-case sentence on p. 25; Theorem 6, p. 39. The same omitted boundary restriction affects the literal one-dimensional applications.

Let \[g=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \Gamma=\langle g\rangle\simeq\mathbb Z,\qquad \ell=\log2.\] This is a non-trivial torsion-free hyperbolic group. With the standard generator, \(|g^n|_\infty=|n|\), and \[\lambda_1(g^n)-\lambda_2(g^n)=2|n|\log2.\] Thus the literal projective Anosov gap condition holds with positive constants; for example \(c=c'=\log2\) works for every integer \(n\). The primal boundary points are \(\xi(+)=\mathbb Re_1,\ \xi(-)=\mathbb Re_2\), and the dual ones are \(\xi^*(+)=\mathbb Re_2^*,\ \xi^*(-)=\mathbb Re_1^*\). They satisfy the required transverse-pair condition.

The ordered boundary-pair space has two points, \((+,-)\) and \((-,+)\), both fixed by \(\Gamma\). Each corresponding real fiber quotients to a circle. The translations are respectively \(+\ell\) and \(-\ell\), so the canonical \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\) and the full refraction flow are two disjoint periodic circles, each of period \(\ell\). No orbit is dense in their union. This contradicts the canonical construction’s transitivity and unique-basic-set assertion, and the joint A/B identification with the full refraction flow. It does not prove that no different domain could be chosen to retain a single periodic component; Theorem A’s existential wording should not be overstated.

Equation reference: eq:cyclic-zeta. The only primitive conjugacy classes in \(\mathbb Z\) are \(g\) and \(g^{-1}\). They are distinct, and both have period \(\ell\). Consequently the exact Euler product is \[
 \zeta_\Gamma(s)=\bigl(1-e^{-s\ell}\bigr)^{-2}.\] The flow entropy is zero, and \(s^2\zeta_\Gamma(s)\to\ell^{-2}\). There is a double pole at zero, contradicting the simple-pole assertion for this allowed case. The independent rational series check gives \[\frac{z^2}{(1-e^{-z})^2}
 =1+z+\frac{5}{12}z^2+\frac1{12}z^3+\frac1{240}z^4+O(z^5),
 \qquad z=s\ell .\]

The interval \(C=\{[x:y]:x,y>0\}\subset\mathbb P(\mathbb R^2)\) is properly strictly convex under Definition 6.10. The action multiplies \(x/y\) by \(4\), and \(C/\Gamma\) is a compact Hilbert circle of length \(\ell\). Its unit sphere bundle again has two oriented periodic circles. Periodic rotation is not mixing; a nonconstant Fourier mode on either circle has correlations that do not decay. Thus Theorem G/13 needs a non-elementary or dimension restriction under the literal stated definition. The analogous \(p=1,q=0\) pseudo-hyperbolic example is also permitted by the stated range; Theorem H omits the irreducibility condition retained in Theorem 12(1).

The repair is to state non-elementarity wherever transitivity, positive entropy, mixing, or a simple leading pole is used, or to give the elementary case separately with its two-orbit product. BCLS explicitly excludes virtually cyclic groups in its standing conventions on p. 9 [bcls]. Section 4 of the reviewed paper already excludes elementary groups, and the diagonal example is reducible, so it does not refute the intended irreducible mixing theorem. The finding is a localized but genuine scope error.
# Problem 3: the pseudo-hyperbolic embedding has the wrong sign
Severity: Minor. Location: the positive-pairing target on p. 44 and the displayed map \(\Phi_\partial^{p,q+1}\) on p. 45.

Write \(B=\langle\,\cdot,\cdot\,\rangle_{p,q+1}\). A unit spacelike tangent lift satisfies \[B(x,x)=-1,\qquad B(v,v)=1,\qquad B(x,v)=0.\] The printed map is \([x:v]\mapsto[x+v:x-v]\), while its target requires \(B(v_1,v_2)>0\). Directly, \[B(x+v,x-v)=B(x,x)-B(v,v)=-2.\] The sign is unchanged by common projective rescaling. Hence the displayed formula does not land in its stated target for any normalized input. For a completely concrete permitted case take \(p=2,q=0\), \(B=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1)\), \(x=(0,0,1)\), and \(v=(1,0,0)\). Every domain condition holds.

One consistent repair is \[[x:v]\longmapsto[x+v:v-x],\qquad
 [v_1:v_2]\longmapsto[v_1-v_2:v_1+v_2].\] The second formula is homogeneous. For null \(v_1,v_2\) with \(B(v_1,v_2)>0\), a common normalization makes the resulting pair unit tangent. The geodesic equations \(x_t=\cosh(t)x+\sinh(t)v,\ 
v_t=\sinh(t)x+\cosh(t)v\) give \(x_t+v_t=e^t(x+v)\) and \(v_t-x_t=e^{-t}(v-x)\), exactly the required flow relation. The independent calculation verifies these identities at the nontrivial rational point \(\cosh t=5/4,\ \sinh t=3/4\), together with the general bilinear identities used above.

This sign error invalidates the map as printed. The corrected relative sign supplies the intended equivariant local construction. All subsequent domain and inverse formulas should be made consistent with that correction and their common normalization. No counterexample to the intended geometric mixing conclusion is claimed from this repairable formula.
# Problem 4: resolvent residue and starting half-plane conventions
Severity: Minor. Location: Section 5.2 and Theorem 9, p. 41. The quoted spectral-parameter convention in Theorem 10, p. 42, also requires attention.

Keep the compact admissible example from Problem 1 and choose the smooth real potential \(U=c>0\). Its support is compact because the ambient manifold is compact. On constants, \[A1=c1,\qquad (A-\lambda)^{-1}1=(c-\lambda)^{-1}1.\] The residue at \(c\) sends \(1\) to \(-1\). Thus, for the printed definition \(\Pi_c=\operatorname{Res}_{\lambda=c}(A-\lambda)^{-1}\), \[(\Pi_c^2-\Pi_c)1=2\,1\ne0.\] It is not a projection. The required convention is \(-\operatorname{Res}(A-\lambda)^{-1}\), or instead the resolvent \((\lambda-A)^{-1}\) with its positive residue. The rank and pole locations survive this sign correction, but the projector and normalization statements must use one convention consistently.

The same example refutes the assertion that the initial \(L^2\)-resolvent exists for every \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda>0\) for arbitrary \(U\): it has a pole at \(c>0\). A sufficient initial half-plane for the transport integral with invariant volume is \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda>\sup\operatorname{Re}U\). The potential-dependent starting region and the resolvent sign are explicit in the original open-system framework [dg2016].

Jin–Tao use \(P=-iX\) and strips \(\operatorname{Im}z>-\beta\) [jintao]. For the present \(A=-X=-iP\), the corresponding variable is \(\lambda=-iz\), so \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda=\operatorname{Im}z\). A direct transfer of their strip must therefore be written \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda>-\beta\). Their open-system statements, rather than an unqualified use of the compact global statement, are the relevant input after localization. This identifies a citation and convention mismatch; it is not offered as a separate counterexample to every counting inequality printed in Theorem 10. None of these local convention repairs resolves Problem 1.
# Problem 5: the local-product claim needs a basic-set restriction
Severity: Minor. Location: Lemma 4.3(3), p. 28; compare Definition 4.4, p. 29, where subsequent uses already take base points in \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\).

The lemma states that for every ambient point \(y\in B(x,2\varepsilon_1)\), the local intersection \(W^s_{\varepsilon_0}(x)\cap W^{cu}_{\varepsilon_0}(y)\) belongs to \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\). Consider a torsion-free classical Schottky group in \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\). It is non-elementary, irreducible in the standard representation, convex cocompact, and projective Anosov. Its projective limit set is a Cantor set. In the paper’s model, \[\mathcal K_\Gamma\cap W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)\] has a Cantor transverse parameter: the stable leaf fixes the primal endpoint and varies the dual endpoint, which must lie in the dual limit set for membership in \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\).

For every sufficiently small neighborhood of \(x\), choose \(y\in W^s_{\varepsilon_0}(x)\setminus\mathcal K_\Gamma\) in that neighborhood. Such points exist because the dual Cantor set contains no interval. Also \(y\in W^{cu}_{\varepsilon_0}(y)\). The local stable/central-unstable intersection, which is unique by the ordinary ambient local-product property, is therefore \(y\notin\mathcal K_\Gamma\). This satisfies the lemma’s stated ambient quantifier and contradicts its conclusion.

The local-product property inside a locally maximal hyperbolic set requires \(y\in\mathcal K_\Gamma\) as well. Replacing the ambient quantifier by \(y\in\mathcal K_\Gamma\cap B(x,2\varepsilon_1)\) repairs this step. The subsequent holonomy arguments use points in the basic set, so this finding does not refute their intended conclusions. Likewise, the parallel transport mentioned in item (5) should be restricted to the leaf along which it was defined.
# NeedsEvidence: a uniform cone angle in non-integrability
Identifier: NE001. Location: Definition 4.19, p. 34; Lemma 4.20 and Lemma 4.21, pp. 35–36; application in Theorem 3, p. 37.

The strong local non-integrability condition has the quantifier order \[\exists d_0>0\quad
 \forall\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_0)\quad
 \forall z\in\mathcal K_\Gamma\quad
 \forall w\in E^u_z,\ \|w\|=1\quad\cdots.\] Lemma 4.20 proves a cone-angle bound after fixing a neighborhood scale \(\delta>0\). Its compactness argument is uniform in the base point and unit vector for that fixed scale. In Lemma 4.21, however, \(\varepsilon\) is chosen first, then \(\delta\) small enough to fit the stable neighborhood of radius \(\varepsilon\), and then \(d_0\) is supplied by Lemma 4.20. The argument as written produces \(d_0=d_0(\delta(\varepsilon))\); it does not establish a positive lower bound independent of \(\varepsilon\).

The logarithmic estimate itself is valid at a fixed scale: the displayed temporal separation is \(-\log(1+\beta(u)/\beta(v'))\), and for a sufficiently small argument its absolute value is bounded below by one half of that argument’s absolute value. The uniform leaf-chart and parallel transport estimates then give the stated positive \(\kappa\). This verifies the local calculation without silently exchanging the order of the quantifiers.

Stoyanov’s original LNIC also fixes its cone parameter before the small-neighborhood quantifier, but tests tangent directions to the basic set and permits a shifted base point and two stable points [stoyanov, p. 7]. It is weaker than the paper’s proposed strong condition. The requested evidence is either a uniform-angle argument for Definition 4.19 or a direct verification of that original weaker hypothesis. Irreducibility and spanning at each fixed scale alone do not supply the missing uniform lower bound in the written proof. No admissible counterexample to the mixing theorem has been established here; this item remains an unresolved proof obligation.
# Proof-level coverage and independent counterchecks
## Convergence dynamics, properness, and the trapped set

The boundary convergence statements, transverse primal/dual maps, stable word-length estimates, and the properness proof in Sections 2–3 were followed with the elementary exception in Problem 2 kept explicit. The eigenvector-growth contradiction in Theorem 1 uses the positive pairing: if the primal vector grows and a projective normalization shrinks to zero, the normalized pairing would tend to zero, contradicting positivity. The dual alternative is symmetric.

In Lemma 3.5 the dual attracting exponent should be \(-\lambda_d(\gamma)=\lambda_1(\gamma^{-1})\), rather than \(\lambda_1(\gamma)\) in general. Positivity of that exponent suffices for the first contradiction. The subsequent primal calculation still gives the claimed period \(T=\lambda_1(\gamma)\). This is a local proof correction.

The written proof of Lemma 3.10 has incompatible inverse and primal/dual labels. Its conclusion admits a direct correction. Use normalized lifts with \[w_k=e^{t_k}\delta_k v_k,\qquad
 \beta_k=e^{-t_k}\delta_k\alpha_k,
 \qquad t_k\longrightarrow+\infty.\] The sequence \(\delta_k\) is unbounded. After the fixed multiplication supplied by Lemma 2.11, put \(\gamma_k=f\delta_k\), with distinct boundary limits \(\eta_+,\eta_-\). Then \(\gamma_kv_k=e^{-t_k}fw_k\to0\), so the growth lemma shows that \([v]\) is not transverse to \(\xi^*(\eta_-)\). Membership of \([v:\alpha]\) in the domain forces \([\alpha]\) transverse to \(\xi(\eta_-)\). Uniform dual convergence gives \(f[\beta]=\xi^*(\eta_+)\). Since \(f\beta(fw)=1\), the line \(f[w]\) is transverse to this dual hyperplane. Applying inverse convergence to \(f[w_k]\) and using \(\gamma_k^{-1}fw_k=e^{t_k}v_k\) gives \([v]=\xi(\eta_-)\). Thus \([v]\in\Lambda_\Gamma\) and \([\beta]\in\Lambda_\Gamma^*\), as required. The original uniform convergence result and its proof are available in the checked DGK passages [dgk]. No failure of the trapped-set conclusion is inferred from the printed labels.

The Hopf coordinate and its logarithmic cocycle were checked directly. Cocompactness and positive time reparametrization are supported by the original Sambarino construction in its stated geometric setting and by the BCLS general-group construction [sambarino, bcls]. The latter’s non-elementary convention must be retained. Hyperbolicity in Lemma 3.13 uses contraction of the pulled-back projective tangent bundles, as in the actual Guichard–Wienhard definition [gw]. The ambient formula \(d\phi^t(w,0)=(e^tw,0)\) alone would not suffice; the paper correctly explains that distinction on pp. 24–25.
## Regular distortion, holonomy, and mixing

Equations (4.3)–(4.9) give the analytic leaf charts and rational holonomy formulas on their transverse domain. Restricting these smooth maps to a compact neighborhood yields the uniform Lipschitz bounds used later. The corrected basic-set quantifier of Problem 5 is enough for the stated applications.

The local spanning argument in Lemma 4.8 can be made precise by first choosing a smaller open subset whose closure avoids a repelling endpoint and then taking a sufficiently large contracting power. Finite-dimensional invariance and minimality of the non-elementary boundary action yield the global span. For Lemma 4.15 choose its basis points in the ball of radius \(\delta/2\), then shrink the neighborhood so their transported images remain in the ball of radius \(\delta\). If \(L_yu_i=e_i\), \(\|L_y\|\leq b\), and \(A\) is the relevant backward linear map, then for \(\|u\|\leq\varepsilon\), \[\|Au\|
 \leq\sqrt m\,b\,\varepsilon\max_i\|Au_i\|
 \leq\sqrt m\,b\,\varepsilon\,
       \operatorname{diam}A(\Lambda^u\cap B_\delta).\] A factor of two passes from radius to diameter. Compactness provides finitely many such charts. This verifies the regular-distortion mechanism without assuming a pinching condition absent from the paper.

The stronger distortion inequality implies both of Stoyanov’s distortion requirements: the comparison for fixed radii and the arbitrarily small diameter ratio obtained by shrinking the smaller radius. Stoyanov’s Corollary 1.5 explicitly allows Hölder potentials when the flow is \(C^5\); the present analytic flow meets that regularity. There is therefore no supported objection based simply on Hölder, rather than Lipschitz, potentials. The outstanding input is precisely the quantified non-integrability obligation NE001, not those already verified hypotheses.
## Zeta functions and microlocal localization

The primitive-class/period correspondence is compatible with \(\lambda_1(\gamma)\), including both orientations in the cyclic calculation. The global continuation input is genuinely local near a compact locally maximal hyperbolic set: the Dyatlov–Guillarmou afterword constructs a suitable strictly convex isolating block by modification away from the trapped set [afterword]. The noncompact ambient manifold is therefore not by itself an obstruction. The original open-system resolvent and localization-independence argument were checked [dg2016].

Borns-Weil–Shen use the orientation line bundle to handle nonorientable invariant bundles [bws]. Their alternating form trace identity accounts for the sign of the Poincaré determinant. Orientability should not be silently added as an assumption to the reviewed theorem. The wavefront restriction for products of resonant and coresonant states is present in the original theorem. The actual source images on pp. 7 and 42 contain the complex conjugations; losses of overbars in extracted text were not treated as mathematical errors.

For the unweighted counting conclusion, Stoyanov’s stated prime-orbit corollary supplies an absolute exponential remainder. Dividing by \(\operatorname{Li}(e^{ht})\) introduces a factor of order \(t\), which is absorbed by choosing a slightly weaker exponent. This is compatible with the existential constant in Theorem 8. The signs in the displayed remainders of Theorems 12(4) and 13(4) should agree with the decaying sign in Theorem 8; as printed their bounds are weak rather than the claimed decay.

The weighted continuation in Theorem 5 has been checked against Pollicott’s Theorem 2 and its proof, including the general Axiom A statement on printed p. 422 (physical p. 11 of the acquired scan) [pollicott]. The result concerns a weakly mixing flow on a non-trivial basic set and a Hölder potential. Exponential mixing supplies the required weak mixing and holomorphy of the correlation transforms. The proof uses a finite-to-one symbolic coding with a nonvanishing analytic correction factor, and spectral projections that detect the non-leading poles through suitable pairs of observables. Centering the correlations removes the leading pressure contribution. Holomorphy for one arbitrarily chosen pair alone would not suffice. The construction is local to the compact basic set; compactness of the ambient quotient is not required by the coding argument. The group-range issue and NE001 remain separate obligations.

The Dolgopyat–Pollicott author version was also read in full [dp1998]. Its pp. 4–6 describe a collapsed base in \(\mathbb R^n\), where \(n\) is the unstable dimension, and specialize to intervals for surfaces. The reviewed p. 40 imports this interval model into the general-dimensional setting and uses the exact point-evaluation formula (5.5). The survey itself prints such an equality without a detailed derivation; that line does not independently verify the claimed exact identity for the present general model. This proof sketch should be replaced by a justified general-dimensional periodic-sum estimate, or more directly by Stoyanov’s Corollary 1.4. The latter, actually checked above, supplies the desired unweighted zero-free continuation and counting conclusion once its Section 4 hypotheses are met. Thus a verified alternative dependency is available; no independent counterexample to Theorem 7 is asserted.

The germ terminology on p. 39 should also be distinguished from restriction to \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\); a smooth function can vanish on that set without vanishing in a neighborhood. The orbit weights only require the restriction.
## Pseudo-hyperbolic and Hilbert applications

The convex-cocompactness, negative-limit-set, and projective-Anosov hypotheses were compared with the actual DGK definitions and statements [dgk]. The repaired embedding in Problem 3 preserves the flow and the intended domain relation. Restriction to the trapped set is needed when the ambient spacelike geodesic flow is incomplete. The irreducibility qualifier in Theorem 12(1) should also appear in the corresponding introductory claim.

The adjoint representation has highest eigenvalue logarithm \(\lambda_1-\lambda_d\). The projective Anosov bounds for \(\gamma\) and \(\gamma^{-1}\) give the required two extreme gaps, consistently with the original representation-theoretic criterion [gw]. The symmetric boundary graph is Lipschitz by the checked convex-gradient argument in Glorieux–Monclair–Tholozan [gmt]: the monotonicity inequality makes its graph spacelike, and projection onto a maximal positive subspace gives a Lipschitz graph. A smooth-boundary claim is not needed.

In Lemma 6.17 the positive cones and trace-one representatives give the intended inverse to the rank-one tensor formula. The explicit calculation gives \[\Psi\circ\phi_{\rm BH}^t=\phi^{2t}\circ\Psi.\] Accordingly, \(T_{\rm Ad}=2T_{\rm BH}\), \(h_{\rm BH}=2h_{\rm Ad}\), and \(\zeta_{\rm BH}(s)=\zeta_{\rm Ad}(s/2)\). The Hilbert length formula in the original reference confirms the factor \(1/2\) [gmt]. Hölder conjugacy and a constant time change preserve the appropriate qualitative mixing conclusion with adjusted constants and exponents. They do not preserve the numerical period without rescaling, nor do they by themselves transport arbitrary microlocal distributional structures. The ellipsoid case is treated by the classical compact hyperbolic flow; the non-ellipsoid argument requires the stated Zariski-density/irreducibility input. The one-dimensional boundary remains Problem 2.

problems.title: The positive-entropy leading resonance is false for the specified scalar operator
problems.source_location: Theorem F p.7; scalar resolvent p.41; Theorem 12(3) p.47; Theorem 13(3) p.51; distinction from form lifts on p.43.
claim: Recorded check: The positive-entropy leading resonance is false for the specified scalar operator

Dimension and group. V=R^2 satisfies d>1. A closed genus at least two oriented hyperbolic surface has faithful holonomy lift avoiding -I because the Euler class is even; projection is injective, hence the subgroup is torsion-free. Projective Anosov and irreducibility. Cocompact Fuchsian translation lengths control stable word length and the two eigenvalue moduli give the gap. No real invariant line exists for this non-elementary lattice. Assigned domain and basic set. The full RP^1 limit set makes every transverse pair admissible, so M=K=Gamma-bar\PSL(2,R), a compact manifold. This compact case is expressly admitted on source p.3. Potential and operator. U=0 is smooth and compactly supported on the compact manifold, and A=-X is exactly the scalar operator specified. Resolvent and entropy. Contact volume is finite and invariant; composition by the flow is unitary. The right-half-plane resolvent integral is analytic. The flow is the positive constant time rescaling of a compact hyperbolic geodesic flow and has h>0.
analysis: Severity: Major. Location: Theorem F, p. 7, especially the \(U=0\) assertions; the scalar definition and resolvent on p. 41; Theorem 12(3), p. 47, and Theorem 13(3), p. 51. Section 5.2.2 on p. 43 must be reconciled with these statements.

Choose a closed oriented hyperbolic surface of genus at least two. Lift its torsion-free cocompact holonomy in \(\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\) to a faithful subgroup \(\Gamma<\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\) not containing \(-I\). Such lifts exist: the obstruction is the Euler class modulo two, and the surface Euler number \(2g-2\) is even. Projection to the surface group is injective, so the lifted group is torsion-free and cocompact modulo the finite center. Its standard action on \(V=\mathbb R^2\) is irreducible, since a cocompact non-elementary Fuchsian group has no invariant real line. It is projective Anosov: the eigenvalue gap is the hyperbolic translation length, uniformly comparable to stable word length by the orbit quasi-isometry. Its limit set is all of \(\mathbb P(\mathbb R^2)\). Thus the example satisfies the theorem’s group, dimension, compactness, smoothness, and potential hypotheses. The paper itself explicitly includes uniform \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\) lattices among its compact cases on p. 3.

Here \(L\) is naturally \(\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\). For a normalized pair \(\alpha(v)=1\), there is a unique \(w\in\ker\alpha\) with \(\det(v,w)=1\). The matrix with columns \(v,w\) identifies the normalized double cover with \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\); \((v,\alpha)\sim(-v,-\alpha)\) gives the quotient by \(\{\pm I\}\). The flow becomes right multiplication by \(\operatorname{diag}(e^t,e^{-t})\). Because the limit set is full, every transverse pair belongs to the domain and to the lifted invariant set. Consequently \[\mathcal M_\Gamma=\mathcal K_\Gamma
 =\overline\Gamma\backslash\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb R)\] is compact. This is the geodesic flow with twice the usual curvature-\(-1\) time parameter, so its entropy \(h\) is positive (\(h=2\) with this normalization).

Equation reference: eq:scalar-resolvent. Take \(U=0\), which satisfies every support requirement, including on a compact ambient manifold. The contact volume \(\mu=\tau\wedge d\tau\) is finite and invariant. Hence \[T_t f=f\circ\phi^{-t}\] is a unitary group on \(L^2(\mu)\), with generator \(A=-X\). For every \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda>0\), \[
 (A-\lambda)^{-1}
 =-\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}T_t\,dt,\qquad
 \|(A-\lambda)^{-1}\|\leq\frac{1}{\operatorname{Re}\lambda}.\] The strong Laplace integral has tails converging in operator norm, locally uniformly on the open right half-plane. Differentiation is controlled by the integrable bounds \(t^k e^{-t\operatorname{Re}\lambda}\), so it defines a holomorphic bounded-operator family there. Composing with the continuous inclusions from smooth functions to \(L^2\) and from \(L^2\) to distributions gives the same conclusion for the distribution-valued resolvent. Its unique meromorphic continuation cannot have a pole at the positive real number \(h\). On the constant function, \[(A-\lambda)^{-1}1=-\lambda^{-1}1.\] Thus zero is the scalar resonance exhibited by constants, whereas the asserted positive-entropy scalar resonance is absent. This is an analytic contradiction, not a numerical failure to detect a pole.

The counterexample also explains the error’s nature. Humbert’s original Theorem 1 distinguishes the scalar critical pressure \(P(U+J^u)\) from the pressure \(P(U)\) for the appropriate degree of differential forms, where \(J^u\) is the negative infinitesimal unstable Jacobian [humbert]. In the compact constant-curvature example, \(J^u=-2\), \(P(0)=2\), and \(P(J^u)=0\). Dyatlov–Guillarmou likewise distinguish the scalar zero resonance from the entropy-related form contribution to the zeta function [dg2016].

The failure changes a headline spectral assertion and the claimed entropy-state identification for the specified scalar operator. Changing only the overall sign of a resolvent does not move its poles and therefore cannot repair it.

The paper’s p. 43 does mention lifts to differential forms. That correct observation is acknowledged here; it does not make the expressly scalar Theorem F true. A repair must specify the operator, form degree, orientation twist when needed, pairing, and resulting invariant distribution, then prove the claimed open-basic-set version. Alternatively a change of potential changes the operator and requires its own regularity and pressure analysis. The compact Anosov result alone does not certify every open-set extension.

The same positive-entropy scalar claim fails for a closed hyperbolic geodesic flow in the applications. Moreover, a Hölder conjugacy alone does not define pullback of arbitrary distributions with specified wavefront sets; the low-regularity Hilbert-flow statement needs an explicit functional interpretation. These are repair obligations, not a claim that exponential mixing, zeta continuation, or the geometric construction is refuted by this compact example.
result: Impact: A headline spectral conclusion and its entropy-state interpretation fail for the operator actually stated.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Specify the appropriate differential-form degree, any orientation twist, pairing and open-system extension; or change the scalar potential and prove the altered pressure/regularity claims. A global resolvent sign change cannot move poles. A merely Holder conjugacy does not automatically transport wavefront-defined distribution products.

problems.title: The allowed cyclic case has two periodic components and a double zeta pole
problems.source_location: Theorems A/B pp.3-4, D p.6; Proposition 2.9 p.13, Definition 2.14 p.14; Theorem 2/Lemma 3.12 pp.22-23; elementary sentence p.25; Theorem 6 p.39; one-dimensional application ranges pp.47,51.
claim: Recorded check: The allowed cyclic case has two periodic components and a double zeta pole

Group range. Infinite cyclic is non-trivial, torsion-free, finitely generated and hyperbolic; non-elementarity is not in these literal statements. Gap and limit maps. Stable word length of g^n is |n| and eigenvalue-log gap is 2|n|log(2), satisfying c=c'=log(2). The primal maps are e1,e2 and the corresponding dual maps are e2*,e1*, giving cross-pair transversality. Periodic identification. Both ordered endpoint pairs remain distinct under this abelian action. Each real fiber quotients by translation of absolute size log(2). Both g and g^(-1) are primitive and nonconjugate. One-dimensional application. The positive projective interval is properly strictly convex under the stated definition, its Hilbert quotient is compact, and its unit sphere bundle consists of the two oriented periodic circles.
analysis: Severity: Minor; range correction. Location: Theorems A/B, pp. 3–4; Theorem D, p. 6; Proposition 2.9 and Definition 2.14, pp. 13–14; Theorem 2 and Lemma 3.12, pp. 22–23; the elementary-case sentence on p. 25; Theorem 6, p. 39. The same omitted boundary restriction affects the literal one-dimensional applications.

Let \[g=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \Gamma=\langle g\rangle\simeq\mathbb Z,\qquad \ell=\log2.\] This is a non-trivial torsion-free hyperbolic group. With the standard generator, \(|g^n|_\infty=|n|\), and \[\lambda_1(g^n)-\lambda_2(g^n)=2|n|\log2.\] Thus the literal projective Anosov gap condition holds with positive constants; for example \(c=c'=\log2\) works for every integer \(n\). The primal boundary points are \(\xi(+)=\mathbb Re_1,\ \xi(-)=\mathbb Re_2\), and the dual ones are \(\xi^*(+)=\mathbb Re_2^*,\ \xi^*(-)=\mathbb Re_1^*\). They satisfy the required transverse-pair condition.

The ordered boundary-pair space has two points, \((+,-)\) and \((-,+)\), both fixed by \(\Gamma\). Each corresponding real fiber quotients to a circle. The translations are respectively \(+\ell\) and \(-\ell\), so the canonical \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\) and the full refraction flow are two disjoint periodic circles, each of period \(\ell\). No orbit is dense in their union. This contradicts the canonical construction’s transitivity and unique-basic-set assertion, and the joint A/B identification with the full refraction flow. It does not prove that no different domain could be chosen to retain a single periodic component; Theorem A’s existential wording should not be overstated.

Equation reference: eq:cyclic-zeta. The only primitive conjugacy classes in \(\mathbb Z\) are \(g\) and \(g^{-1}\). They are distinct, and both have period \(\ell\). Consequently the exact Euler product is \[
 \zeta_\Gamma(s)=\bigl(1-e^{-s\ell}\bigr)^{-2}.\] The flow entropy is zero, and \(s^2\zeta_\Gamma(s)\to\ell^{-2}\). There is a double pole at zero, contradicting the simple-pole assertion for this allowed case. The independent rational series check gives \[\frac{z^2}{(1-e^{-z})^2}
 =1+z+\frac{5}{12}z^2+\frac1{12}z^3+\frac1{240}z^4+O(z^5),
 \qquad z=s\ell .\]

The interval \(C=\{[x:y]:x,y>0\}\subset\mathbb P(\mathbb R^2)\) is properly strictly convex under Definition 6.10. The action multiplies \(x/y\) by \(4\), and \(C/\Gamma\) is a compact Hilbert circle of length \(\ell\). Its unit sphere bundle again has two oriented periodic circles. Periodic rotation is not mixing; a nonconstant Fourier mode on either circle has correlations that do not decay. Thus Theorem G/13 needs a non-elementary or dimension restriction under the literal stated definition. The analogous \(p=1,q=0\) pseudo-hyperbolic example is also permitted by the stated range; Theorem H omits the irreducibility condition retained in Theorem 12(1).

The repair is to state non-elementarity wherever transitivity, positive entropy, mixing, or a simple leading pole is used, or to give the elementary case separately with its two-orbit product. BCLS explicitly excludes virtually cyclic groups in its standing conventions on p. 9 [bcls]. Section 4 of the reviewed paper already excludes elementary groups, and the diagonal example is reducible, so it does not refute the intended irreducible mixing theorem. The finding is a localized but genuine scope error.
result: Impact: Literal elementary-range transitivity and simple-pole assertions fail; one-dimensional mixing assertions also need a range restriction.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Add non-elementarity where used, or state the cyclic two-orbit case separately. Retain needed irreducibility/dimension qualifiers in applications.

problems.title: A relative sign sends the pseudo-hyperbolic map outside its target
problems.source_location: Positive-pairing target p.44 and displayed map Phi_partial^(p,q+1) p.45.
claim: Recorded check: A relative sign sends the pseudo-hyperbolic map outside its target

Permitted signature. p=2,q=0 is within the stated range. Unit spacelike tangent domain. The explicit x,v have B(x,x)=-1, B(v,v)=1 and B(x,v)=0. Target and quotient. The target requires positive B(v1,v2); both entries have one common projective scaling, so the negative pairing cannot be removed by an allowed common rescaling.
analysis: Severity: Minor. Location: the positive-pairing target on p. 44 and the displayed map \(\Phi_\partial^{p,q+1}\) on p. 45.

Write \(B=\langle\,\cdot,\cdot\,\rangle_{p,q+1}\). A unit spacelike tangent lift satisfies \[B(x,x)=-1,\qquad B(v,v)=1,\qquad B(x,v)=0.\] The printed map is \([x:v]\mapsto[x+v:x-v]\), while its target requires \(B(v_1,v_2)>0\). Directly, \[B(x+v,x-v)=B(x,x)-B(v,v)=-2.\] The sign is unchanged by common projective rescaling. Hence the displayed formula does not land in its stated target for any normalized input. For a completely concrete permitted case take \(p=2,q=0\), \(B=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1)\), \(x=(0,0,1)\), and \(v=(1,0,0)\). Every domain condition holds.

One consistent repair is \[[x:v]\longmapsto[x+v:v-x],\qquad
 [v_1:v_2]\longmapsto[v_1-v_2:v_1+v_2].\] The second formula is homogeneous. For null \(v_1,v_2\) with \(B(v_1,v_2)>0\), a common normalization makes the resulting pair unit tangent. The geodesic equations \(x_t=\cosh(t)x+\sinh(t)v,\ 
v_t=\sinh(t)x+\cosh(t)v\) give \(x_t+v_t=e^t(x+v)\) and \(v_t-x_t=e^{-t}(v-x)\), exactly the required flow relation. The independent calculation verifies these identities at the nontrivial rational point \(\cosh t=5/4,\ \sinh t=3/4\), together with the general bilinear identities used above.

This sign error invalidates the map as printed. The corrected relative sign supplies the intended equivariant local construction. All subsequent domain and inverse formulas should be made consistent with that correction and their common normalization. No counterexample to the intended geometric mixing conclusion is claimed from this repairable formula.
result: Impact: The displayed map does not take values in its declared target.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use [x+v:v-x] with the consistent inverse [v1-v2:v1+v2] and common unit normalization. The geodesic equations then give the required e^t/e^(-t) scaling.

problems.title: The printed residue is the negative projector and the initial half-plane ignores the potential
problems.source_location: Section 5.2 and Theorem 9 p.41; spectral-parameter convention in Theorem 10 p.42.
claim: Recorded check: The printed residue is the negative projector and the initial half-plane ignores the potential

Compact admissible example. All geometric and group hypotheses are the same verified ones as P001. Allowed potential. The real constant c>0 is smooth; its support is compact because the ambient manifold is compact. Exact operator convention. The computation uses precisely the stated A=-X+U and (A-lambda)^(-1), on its invariant constants.
analysis: Severity: Minor. Location: Section 5.2 and Theorem 9, p. 41. The quoted spectral-parameter convention in Theorem 10, p. 42, also requires attention.

Keep the compact admissible example from Problem 1 and choose the smooth real potential \(U=c>0\). Its support is compact because the ambient manifold is compact. On constants, \[A1=c1,\qquad (A-\lambda)^{-1}1=(c-\lambda)^{-1}1.\] The residue at \(c\) sends \(1\) to \(-1\). Thus, for the printed definition \(\Pi_c=\operatorname{Res}_{\lambda=c}(A-\lambda)^{-1}\), \[(\Pi_c^2-\Pi_c)1=2\,1\ne0.\] It is not a projection. The required convention is \(-\operatorname{Res}(A-\lambda)^{-1}\), or instead the resolvent \((\lambda-A)^{-1}\) with its positive residue. The rank and pole locations survive this sign correction, but the projector and normalization statements must use one convention consistently.

The same example refutes the assertion that the initial \(L^2\)-resolvent exists for every \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda>0\) for arbitrary \(U\): it has a pole at \(c>0\). A sufficient initial half-plane for the transport integral with invariant volume is \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda>\sup\operatorname{Re}U\). The potential-dependent starting region and the resolvent sign are explicit in the original open-system framework [dg2016].

Jin–Tao use \(P=-iX\) and strips \(\operatorname{Im}z>-\beta\) [jintao]. For the present \(A=-X=-iP\), the corresponding variable is \(\lambda=-iz\), so \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda=\operatorname{Im}z\). A direct transfer of their strip must therefore be written \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda>-\beta\). Their open-system statements, rather than an unqualified use of the compact global statement, are the relevant input after localization. This identifies a citation and convention mismatch; it is not offered as a separate counterexample to every counting inequality printed in Theorem 10. None of these local convention repairs resolves Problem 1.
result: Impact: Projector normalization and the claimed starting domain are incorrect. The quoted -iX counting strip also needs rotation to the -X parameter.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use -Res(A-lambda)^(-1), or (lambda-A)^(-1); start in Re(lambda)>sup Re(U) with invariant volume. For P=-iX use lambda=-iz, so Re(lambda)=Im(z), and invoke the open-system counting statements with their hypotheses.

problems.title: The local-product point need not belong to the basic set for an arbitrary ambient base point
problems.source_location: Lemma 4.3(3) p.28; compare Definition 4.4 p.29.
claim: Recorded check: The local-product point need not belong to the basic set for an arbitrary ambient base point

Section 4 group hypotheses. A classical torsion-free Schottky group is non-elementary, irreducible in the standard representation, convex cocompact and projective Anosov. Base point and neighborhoods. Take x in K and choose y in the local stable leaf inside the prescribed ambient ball and domain; openness and the nowhere dense Cantor endpoint set permit this for every sufficiently small radius. Ambient plaque and uniqueness. The analytic ambient stable and central-unstable plaques are defined at y. It belongs to both Ws(x) and Wcu(y); their local-product intersection is unique.
analysis: Severity: Minor. Location: Lemma 4.3(3), p. 28; compare Definition 4.4, p. 29, where subsequent uses already take base points in \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\).

The lemma states that for every ambient point \(y\in B(x,2\varepsilon_1)\), the local intersection \(W^s_{\varepsilon_0}(x)\cap W^{cu}_{\varepsilon_0}(y)\) belongs to \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\). Consider a torsion-free classical Schottky group in \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\). It is non-elementary, irreducible in the standard representation, convex cocompact, and projective Anosov. Its projective limit set is a Cantor set. In the paper’s model, \[\mathcal K_\Gamma\cap W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)\] has a Cantor transverse parameter: the stable leaf fixes the primal endpoint and varies the dual endpoint, which must lie in the dual limit set for membership in \(\mathcal K_\Gamma\).

For every sufficiently small neighborhood of \(x\), choose \(y\in W^s_{\varepsilon_0}(x)\setminus\mathcal K_\Gamma\) in that neighborhood. Such points exist because the dual Cantor set contains no interval. Also \(y\in W^{cu}_{\varepsilon_0}(y)\). The local stable/central-unstable intersection, which is unique by the ordinary ambient local-product property, is therefore \(y\notin\mathcal K_\Gamma\). This satisfies the lemma’s stated ambient quantifier and contradicts its conclusion.

The local-product property inside a locally maximal hyperbolic set requires \(y\in\mathcal K_\Gamma\) as well. Replacing the ambient quantifier by \(y\in\mathcal K_\Gamma\cap B(x,2\varepsilon_1)\) repairs this step. The subsequent holonomy arguments use points in the basic set, so this finding does not refute their intended conclusions. Likewise, the parallel transport mentioned in item (5) should be restricted to the leaf along which it was defined.
result: Impact: The ambient quantifier in the lemma is false.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Require y in K intersected with the small ball. Clarify that item (5) parallel transport is along the leaf where it was defined.

report: Abstract: The reductions to equational noetherianity, the stabilization argument for epimorphisms, and selected finite-generation and resolution arguments are examined in the supplied author manuscript. One local auxiliary embedding claim is false: a permitted finite cyclic group need not embed in \(\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\). An explicit uniform embedding into \(\mathrm{GL}(3,\mathbb C)\) repairs that use of linearity without changing the subsequent group-theoretic conclusions. No further substantive defect is established within the declared scope. This is an initial technical review; scientific adjudication and independent acceptance remain pending.

Title: A verification of selected arguments in
Homomorphisms to 3–Manifold Groups
# Identity and scope

The reviewed work is Daniel Groves, Michael Hull, and Hao Liang, Homomorphisms to 3–Manifold Groups, arXiv:2103.06095v3, 12 July 2024 (the title-page date is 15 July 2024), 55 physical PDF pages, including Appendices A and B [paper]. The assigned journal identifier is DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00713-1. Page references use one-based physical PDF pages, which agree with the printed numbering. The acquired preprint is not identified with an unexamined version of record.

The review checks the logical reductions on pp. 1–15, especially Theorems 2.4–2.8, Proposition 3.4 and the first part of Theorem 3.23; it also follows selected non-divergence, resolution, and edge-twisted arguments in Sections 6 and 9 and Appendix A. It does not claim an exhaustive reproof of the collapsed-space geometry, the shortening theorem, the relative JSJ theory, or the external results cited by the authors. The detailed ledger distinguishes those dependencies from arguments checked here. No author code was required or executed.
# Definitions and checked reductions

An equationally noetherian family \(\mathcal G\) has the following uniform property: for every finitely generated \(G\), a finitely presented \(G_0\) admits an epimorphism \(\alpha:G_0\to G\) such that \(\alpha^*:\operatorname{Hom}(G,\Gamma)\to
\operatorname{Hom}(G_0,\Gamma)\) is bijective for every \(\Gamma\in\mathcal G\). With the fixed nonprincipal ultrafilter \(\omega\), the stable kernel is \[K_\omega=\{g:\phi_i(g)=1\ \text{for $\omega$-almost every }i\},
 \qquad L=G/K_\omega .\] Theorem 2.4 equates the family property with \(\omega\)-almost-sure factorization through this quotient. Its external proof is a declared input, rather than a result reproduced here.
## The descending-chain consequence

For the surjections in Theorem B, put \(\rho_i=\tau_i\cdots\tau_1\) and \(K_i=\ker\rho_i\). The composition law gives \(K_i\subseteq K_{i+1}\) and \(K_\omega=\bigcup_i K_i\). Factorization of one \(\rho_j\) through the limit gives \(K_\omega\subseteq K_j\), hence equality and stabilization. Subsequent surjections are injective and therefore isomorphisms. This verifies the argument on pp. 5–6. The reversed inclusion printed on p. 5 is resolved by the definitions and the immediately following ascending-kernel argument; it is not counted as a separate substantive finding.
## Uniformity in finite-index passage

In Proposition 3.4 (p. 7), a finitely generated \(G\) has finitely many subgroups of index at most a fixed \(n\). Their intersection \(H\) has finite index and is finitely generated. Each \(\phi_i(H)\) lies in the selected subgroup of the target. Factorization on \(H\), followed by a finite intersection of \(\omega\)-large sets for coset representatives, gives factorization on \(G\). The finite bound on the index is essential: the argument does not assert a uniform result over unbounded indices.

For the central extension in Corollary 3.18 (p. 9), finite presentation of the quotient and finite generation of the total group give finitely many normal generators for the central kernel; centrality turns these into ordinary generators. The resulting finite generation and finite-presentation deductions are consistent with the stated hypotheses. Lemma 3.19 also retains its centrality requirement: the preimage of a cyclic group in this central extension is abelian.
# Problem 1: an integral linear target is too restrictive

Assessment: Minor, auxiliary proof statement. The first paragraph of the proof of Theorem 3.23 on p. 10 reduces five geometries to subgroups of index at most \(240\) that are cyclic, \(\mathbb Z^3\), or \(\mathbb Z^2\rtimes\mathbb Z\), and asserts that each such group embeds in \(\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\). The actual PDF has \(\mathbb Z\), so this is not an extraction error. Lemma 3.1 (p. 6), used in the next step, only needs one fixed \(\mathrm{GL}(n,K)\).
## An admissible counterexample

Let \(\zeta=\exp(2\pi i/241)\) and let \(C_{241}\) act on \(S^3\subset\mathbb C^2\) by \[(z_1,z_2)\longmapsto(\zeta z_1,\zeta z_2).\] Every nonidentity power acts freely, since a point of \(S^3\) has a nonzero coordinate. Thus the spherical lens space \(L(241,1)\) is a closed geometric 3-manifold with fundamental group \(C_{241}\). The integer \(241\) is prime: none of \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), the primes not exceeding \(\sqrt{241}\), divides it. Its only proper subgroup has index \(241\). Consequently passage to a subgroup of index at most \(240\) cannot remove this example.

If \(C_{241}\) embedded even in \(\mathrm{GL}(3,\mathbb Q)\), the image \(A\) of a generator would have order \(241\). Since \(A^{241}=I\) and \(A\ne I\), some eigenvalue would be a primitive \(241\)st root of unity. Its minimal polynomial over \(\mathbb Q\) is \[\Phi_{241}(x)=1+x+\cdots+x^{240},\] which is irreducible: \(\Phi_{241}(x+1)=((x+1)^{241}-1)/x\) satisfies Eisenstein’s criterion at \(241\). Its degree \(240\) exceeds the degree of the characteristic polynomial of a \(3\times3\) rational matrix. This contradiction excludes an embedding into \(\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\) in particular. It verifies every group and geometry condition used in the stated reduction.
## A uniform repair and its precise effect

The required argument works in the single fixed target \(\mathrm{GL}(3,\mathbb C)\). For a finite cyclic group of order \(m\), use \(\operatorname{diag}(\exp(2\pi i/m),1,1)\). For \(\mathbb Z^3\), use \[(a,b,c)\longmapsto
 \operatorname{diag}(2^a3^b5^c,1,1),\] which is injective by unique prime factorization. Infinite cyclic groups are included by the analogous map \(k\mapsto
\operatorname{diag}(2^k,1,1)\).

Equation reference: eq:repair. For any \(A\in\mathrm{GL}(2,\mathbb Z)\), write the multiplication in \(\mathbb Z^2\rtimes_A\mathbb Z\) as \((v,k)(w,l)=(v+A^k w,k+l)\). Then \[
 (v,k)\longmapsto
 2^k
 \begin{pmatrix}
 A^k&v\\
 0&1
 \end{pmatrix}
 \quad\text{in }\mathrm{GL}(3,\mathbb C)\] is a homomorphism by block multiplication. Its lower-right entry recovers \(k\), and with \(k=0\) its upper-right column recovers \(v\), so it is injective. The scalar factor matters: an unweighted affine representation alone can lose the \(\mathbb Z\) factor when \(A\) has finite order.

Apply Lemma 3.1 with this fixed dimension and field, then the already stated bounded-index result, Proposition 3.4. This restores the first paragraph’s equational-noetherian conclusion under its same classification input. No new uniformity in \(m\), \(A\), or the index is required, and the bound \(240\) is unchanged.

The false integral embedding is a genuine local proof assertion. The repair explicitly supplies the linearity actually required, so the finding does not establish failure of Theorem 3.23, Theorem 2.5, or Theorem A. Its role is an auxiliary geometric-family reduction; the new collapsed-space and resolution mechanisms are not invalidated by this example. This limited dependency and the verified replacement, rather than repair length alone, justify the Minor assessment. No assertion is made about whether a later published version already changes the coefficient ring.
# Finite generation and resolution: checked scope

Theorem 2.7 (p. 13) needs finite generation of the abelian edge groups before applying the vertex-group factorization argument; it does not assume the desired conclusion without comment. For Theorem 2.8 (p. 15), the maps in Theorem 4.20 are injective on stably parabolic subgroups. problems.source_location: Theorem 3.23 proof, physical p10 first paragraph; Lemma 3.1 p6; Proposition 3.4 p7
claim:
An equationally noetherian family \(\mathcal G\) has the following uniform property: for every finitely generated \(G\), a finitely presented \(G_0\) admits an epimorphism \(\alpha:G_0\to G\) such that \(\alpha^*:\operatorname{Hom}(G,\Gamma)\to
\operatorname{Hom}(G_0,\Gamma)\) is bijective for every \(\Gamma\in\mathcal G\). With the fixed nonprincipal ultrafilter \(\omega\), the stable kernel is \[K_\omega=\{g:\phi_i(g)=1\ \text{for $\omega$-almost every }i\},
 \qquad L=G/K_\omega .\] Theorem 2.4 equates the family property with \(\omega\)-almost-sure factorization through this quotient. Its external proof is a declared input, rather than a result reproduced here.
The finite-index cyclic/Z^3/Z^2 semidirect Z groups in the five-geometries reduction all embed in SL(3,Z).

Spherical lens space L(241,1)=S3/<(z1,z2)->(zeta*z1,zeta*z2)>, zeta primitive241st root. C241 acts freely; quotient is closed geometric3-manifold with pi1=C241. 241 is prime and exceeds240, so no proper subgroup has index<=240.
analysis: Assessment: Minor, auxiliary proof statement. The first paragraph of the proof of Theorem 3.23 on p. 10 reduces five geometries to subgroups of index at most \(240\) that are cyclic, \(\mathbb Z^3\), or \(\mathbb Z^2\rtimes\mathbb Z\), and asserts that each such group embeds in \(\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\). The actual PDF has \(\mathbb Z\), so this is not an extraction error. Lemma 3.1 (p. 6), used in the next step, only needs one fixed \(\mathrm{GL}(n,K)\).

Let \(\zeta=\exp(2\pi i/241)\) and let \(C_{241}\) act on \(S^3\subset\mathbb C^2\) by \[(z_1,z_2)\longmapsto(\zeta z_1,\zeta z_2).\] Every nonidentity power acts freely, since a point of \(S^3\) has a nonzero coordinate. Thus the spherical lens space \(L(241,1)\) is a closed geometric 3-manifold with fundamental group \(C_{241}\). The integer \(241\) is prime: none of \(2,3,5,7,11,13\), the primes not exceeding \(\sqrt{241}\), divides it. Its only proper subgroup has index \(241\). Consequently passage to a subgroup of index at most \(240\) cannot remove this example.

If \(C_{241}\) embedded even in \(\mathrm{GL}(3,\mathbb Q)\), the image \(A\) of a generator would have order \(241\). Since \(A^{241}=I\) and \(A\ne I\), some eigenvalue would be a primitive \(241\)st root of unity. Its minimal polynomial over \(\mathbb Q\) is \[\Phi_{241}(x)=1+x+\cdots+x^{240},\] which is irreducible: \(\Phi_{241}(x+1)=((x+1)^{241}-1)/x\) satisfies Eisenstein’s criterion at \(241\). Its degree \(240\) exceeds the degree of the characteristic polynomial of a \(3\times3\) rational matrix. This contradiction excludes an embedding into \(\mathrm{SL}(3,\mathbb Z)\) in particular. It verifies every group and geometry condition used in the stated reduction.

The required argument works in the single fixed target \(\mathrm{GL}(3,\mathbb C)\). For a finite cyclic group of order \(m\), use \(\operatorname{diag}(\exp(2\pi i/m),1,1)\). For \(\mathbb Z^3\), use \[(a,b,c)\longmapsto
 \operatorname{diag}(2^a3^b5^c,1,1),\] which is injective by unique prime factorization. Infinite cyclic groups are included by the analogous map \(k\mapsto
\operatorname{diag}(2^k,1,1)\).

Equation reference: eq:repair. For any \(A\in\mathrm{GL}(2,\mathbb Z)\), write the multiplication in \(\mathbb Z^2\rtimes_A\mathbb Z\) as \((v,k)(w,l)=(v+A^k w,k+l)\). Then \[
 (v,k)\longmapsto
 2^k
 \begin{pmatrix}
 A^k&v\\
 0&1
 \end{pmatrix}
 \quad\text{in }\mathrm{GL}(3,\mathbb C)\] is a homomorphism by block multiplication. Its lower-right entry recovers \(k\), and with \(k=0\) its upper-right column recovers \(v\), so it is injective. The scalar factor matters: an unweighted affine representation alone can lose the \(\mathbb Z\) factor when \(A\) has finite order.

Apply Lemma 3.1 with this fixed dimension and field, then the already stated bounded-index result, Proposition 3.4. This restores the first paragraph’s equational-noetherian conclusion under its same classification input. No new uniformity in \(m\), \(A\), or the index is required, and the bound \(240\) is unchanged.

The false integral embedding is a genuine local proof assertion. The repair explicitly supplies the linearity actually required, so the finding does not establish failure of Theorem 3.23, Theorem 2.5, or Theorem A. Its role is an auxiliary geometric-family reduction; the new collapsed-space and resolution mechanisms are not invalidated by this example. This limited dependency and the verified replacement, rather than repair length alone, justify the Minor assessment. No assertion is made about whether a later published version already changes the coefficient ring.
result: Impact: Auxiliary integral linearity assertion false; Theorem3.23 and mainTheoremA not refuted because required uniform complex embedding explicitly supplied.

Title: A verification of selected arguments in
Local Integral Transforms and Global Spectral Decomposition
# Identity and scope

The source is Valentin Blomer, Subhajit Jana and Paul D. Nelson, Local integral transforms and global spectral decomposition, arXiv:2404.10692v2, 22 May 2025, 41 physical pages [BJN]. The assigned journal identifier is DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00714-0. The report concerns these exact acquired preprint bytes; equivalence with the 57-page journal version has not been established. Page references below use the acquired PDF’s physical numbering, which agrees with its printed pages.

The checks concern Theorems 1–5 and selected supporting arguments. This is not a new proof of the full Whittaker–Plancherel theorem, Ichino’s formula, or the cited spectral moment estimates. Those inputs, and the unverified analytic estimates identified in the ledger, remain dependencies.
# Setting and checked distinctions

The local field is of characteristic zero (§2.1), with self-dual additive measure \(dy\) and \(d^\times y=dy/|y|\). The normalized principal series is denoted \(I(\chi)\), and its inducing character satisfies \(f(n(x)a(y)g)=\chi(y)|y|^{1/2}f(g)\). The introduction permits \(\pi_2=I(\chi_2)\) for some inducing character; it imposes no sign condition on \(\Re\chi_2\).

For the forward transform in Theorem 1, the strip is \[\vartheta_1+\vartheta_2<\sigma<\tfrac12-\vartheta.\] Its inverse is stated only for \(y_1\ne y_2\). The paper explicitly distinguishes absolute convergence of the indicated iterated inverse integrals from joint absolute convergence (pp. 4–5). The latter must not be inserted as an unstated Fubini hypothesis. The change from a shifted pair \((z,yz)\) to the Mellin-over-shift transform in §2.7 is useful, but it does not by itself remove poles of an individual gamma factor.
# Problem 1: the strip in Theorem 2(1)

Assessment: Major, stated local transform theorem. Theorem 2(1), p. 5, claims holomorphy and absolute convergence for \(\vartheta_1<\Re\chi<\tfrac12-\vartheta\), omitting \(\vartheta_2\). Its proof on p. 17 integrates Theorem 1(1). The larger stated strip admits the following counterexample.
## Admissible data and noncancellation

Take \(F=\mathbb Q_3\), an unramified additive character, and self-dual measure normalized by \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathbb Z_3)=1\). Set \[\pi_1=\pi=I(1),\qquad
 \pi_2=I(|\cdot|^{-1/4}),\qquad
 \chi_2=|\cdot|^{-1/4},\qquad \chi_0=1.\] These are irreducible generic unitary principal series, with \(\vartheta_1=\vartheta=0\) and \(\vartheta_2=1/4\); the second is complementary series. Thus even the stronger sum condition of Theorem 1 holds. Choose compact smooth Kirillov restrictions \[W_1(a(z))=\mathbf 1_{\,1+3\mathbb Z_3}(z),\qquad
 W_2(a(z))=\mathbf 1_{\,2+3\mathbb Z_3}(z).\] The compact Kirillov model allows these test vectors. Their values are real, so complex conjugation of \(W_2\) changes nothing.

For \(h(z,yz)=W_1(a(z))\overline{W_2(a(yz))}\), definition (1.10) gives \[H(y,1)=\int_{\mathbb Q_3^\times}h(z,yz)\,d^\times z
       =\frac13\,\mathbf 1_{\,2+3\mathbb Z_3}(y).\] Indeed \(z\equiv1\pmod3\), and \(yz\equiv2\pmod3\) is equivalent to \(y\equiv2\pmod3\). On this support both \(|y|\) and \(|1-y|\) equal one. For the unramified character \(\chi=|\cdot|^s\), the inner integral in (1.12) is therefore exactly \(1/9\), independently of \(s\). In particular, neither the test weight nor the factor involving \(1-y\) can cancel a gamma-factor pole.

Equation reference: eq:pole. For the chosen unramified data, definition (1.6) gives \[\gamma(u,I(1))
 =\left(\frac{1-3^{-u}}{1-3^{u-1}}\right)^2.\] The full \(\chi\)-integrand in Theorem 2(1), on its unramified character component, is consequently \[
 \frac19
 \left(\frac{1-3^{-1/2-s}}{1-3^{-1/2+s}}\right)^2
 \left(\frac{1-3^{-5/4+s}}{1-3^{1/4-s}}\right)^2 .\] At \(s=1/4\), the last denominator has a double zero; both numerators and the first denominator are nonzero. This is a genuine double pole. It lies strictly inside the advertised strip \(0<\Re s<1/2\). On the permitted contour \(\Re s=1/4\), the absolute value is comparable to \(|\Im s|^{-2}\) near zero, and the character integral is not absolutely convergent. The left-hand transform with \(\chi_0=1\) is well-defined by the stated Whittaker decay estimate.
## Scope and repair

This disproves the two assertions about the stated strip, not the existence of the local transform or every identity in the paper. It is a defect in a main local theorem, rather than a harmless choice of normalization. The Major assessment concerns that scope; a short hypothesis correction does not turn the false assertion into a peripheral typographical issue.

A conservative correction retains \[\vartheta_1+\vartheta_2<\sigma<\tfrac12-\vartheta,
 \qquad \vartheta_1+\vartheta_2+\vartheta<\tfrac12,\] when deriving (1.12) directly from Theorem 1(1). The example’s pole is then excluded. Any wider strip requires an explicit continuation prescription, residues where necessary, or additional hypotheses on the inducing character. This report does not certify an optimal replacement theorem. In particular, an unstated decision to use the other inducing character cannot repair the theorem as quantified.
# Problem 2: the diagonal in Theorem 2(2)

Assessment: Minor, omitted domain restriction. Theorem 2(2), p. 5, allows \(y\in F^\times\), while its right-hand side contains \(\chi(1-y)\) and division by \(\chi_0(1-y)|1-y|\). At the allowed value \(y=1\), these expressions are undefined. The proof on p. 17 substitutes \(y_1=z,\ y_2=yz\) into Theorem 1(2), whose hypothesis requires \(y_1\ne y_2\), and then changes variables by multiplication by \((1-y)^{-1}\). Thus the proof itself requires \(y\ne1\).

For compact smooth \(h\), the defining integral \(H(y,\chi_0)\) is well-defined and smooth at \(y=1\): the \(z\)-support stays in a fixed compact subset of \(F^\times\), so differentiation, or local constancy in the nonarchimedean case, passes under the integral. A precise formulation states the displayed formula for \(y\ne1\), with the diagonal recovered by this limiting value if desired. This corrects the domain without purporting to resolve Problem 1’s contour issue.
# Global and application checks
## Normalization and the second diagonal

The cuspidal pairing on p. 20 is half the Petersson integral, and the cuspidal spectral measure on p. 21 is half counting measure. These two factors cancel in the spectral projector. In the triple-product calculation on pp. 26–27, writing \(Z=\zeta_F^{(S)}(2)\), the explicit scalar product \((Z/8)(8/Z^3)Z^2\) equals one. The remaining adjoint factor is squared, as in Lemma 3.6. This checks the displayed algebra conditional on the cited triple-product and local integral identities.

For Theorem 3, the nonzero shift \(b\) kills the one-dimensional spectral contribution: its restriction to the unipotent subgroup is constant, and the nontrivial Fourier coefficient is zero (p. 28). The principal-series assumption at the places in \(S\) is explicit and essential to the chosen local trilinear functional; the source does not claim a general three-supercuspidal formula.

For Theorem 4, the two poles in Lemmas 3.11–3.12 contribute with opposite contour signs. Since the corresponding residues are negatives, the \(1/2\) in the Eisenstein measure leaves one full residue, yielding the second diagonal term on p. 34. Omitting that term would be incorrect. The comparison of \(I\) and \(I_0\) is performed by continuation with residues; their identical formal integral expressions alone do not make them equal. The external convergence and continuation estimates are not independently reproved here.
## The short-window calculation

With \(n_1=n+b,\ n_2=n\), the weight printed at the start of §4 (p. 34) equals \(V((n+b-X)/Y)\). Thus that displayed sum represents \(S(X-b,Y,b)\), with the definition on p. 8. The required weight for \(S(X,Y,b)\) is \[\sqrt{|n_1n_2|}\,
 V_1\!\left(\frac{n_1-(X+b)}Y\right)
 V_2\!\left(\frac{n_2-X}Y\right).\] This is a local centering correction. Running the subsequent auxiliary calculation with center \(X+b\) preserves the scale: \(X\le X+b\le3X/2\). In the mean-square case the shifted interval \([X+b,2X+b]\) lies in \([X+b,2(X+b)]\). This correction supplies no counterexample to the asserted estimates.

The integration-by-parts identity on p. 36 was checked directly. Differentiation in \(t\) produces \(b/Y\) and \(b(1+\tau)/Y\); integration by parts in \(x\) combines them into the stated \(b\tau/Y\) term and \(b/X\) derivative of the outer weight. The support bound \(|\tau|\ll Y/X\) then gives \(b|\tau|/Y\ll b/X\). The final displayed mean-square bound implies (1.18) using \(\sqrt{b/Y}\le(1+b/Y)/2\).

A further contour notation needs checking in any revision: (4.11) is printed with initial lines \(\Re s_j=3/4\), whereas the following paragraph discusses residues at \(1/2\) on shifting to \(1+\varepsilon\). The source’s original transform starts to the left of those poles. The complete application estimate, including all residue and spectral moment bounds, is not certified by this report; this observation is retained in coverage and is not counted as an additional proved theorem failure.
# Conclusion

Problem 1 is a supported Major finding about the scope of a main local transform theorem. Problem 2 is a local domain omission. The checked global normalization and residue algebra provide counterevidence to broader claims that the spectral method fails. No statement is made about author adoption or subsequent journal corrections. Scientific decision is pending, there are no human review entries, and independent acceptance is incomplete.
# Evidence and limitations

The pole and test-vector calculations above are analytic; no finite numerical experiment or author code substitutes for the proof. The original source extraction is reused with its historical execution origin. The hypergeometric appendix, all cited external proofs, and every interchange or estimate outside the stated checks are not claimed as independently verified. The absence of optional author code in the bounded acquisition search is not a mathematical defect.
