Title: A verification of selected arguments in
Non-vanishing of Geodesic Periods of Automorphic Forms
# Identity, scope and principal distinctions

The source is Petru Constantinescu and Asbjørn Christian Nordentoft, Non-vanishing of geodesic periods of automorphic forms, arXiv:2404.12982v2, 29 July 2025, 38 physical pages; its title-page date is 30 July 2025 [CN]. The assigned DOI is 10.1007/s00039-025-00715-z. This exact author manuscript is assessed; identity with the journal version is not established. Physical and printed page numbers agree.

Theorem 1.3 concerns zero periods of a fixed nonzero level-one weight-zero Hecke–Maaß cusp form, with geodesics ordered by length. Theorem 1.5 treats the stated cuspidal cases for groups with a cusp. Theorem 1.9 concerns a graph-weighted distribution, whereas unweighted normality is Conjecture 1.10. The arithmetic application orders real quadratic fields by fundamental unit, not by discriminant, and asserts positive proportion rather than Michel’s question for every sufficiently large field. These distinctions are retained throughout.

The checks below cover selected mathematical arguments and actual cited source-page images, not an independent proof of every external input. In particular, the period-comparison proposition, the cited central limit theorems, and sparse equidistribution are used with their stated hypotheses and remain external dependencies.
# Problem 1: a squared small-interval estimate
## The available quantitative bound

Put \(L=\log N\), \(\rho=\min(\delta,1/2)\), and let \(B_N\) be the neighbours of the exceptional geodesics \(A_N\). Proposition 3.1 gives \[|L_f(x)|\le L^{1/2-\delta}+O(1)
           =O(L^{1/2-\rho}),\qquad x\in B_N.\] The constant error must be retained when \(\delta>1/2\). The real Gaussian input yields \(|B_N|\ll N^2L^{-\rho}\).

Only a degree upper bound is needed. The trace progression gives \(\deg(x)\le N/c(x)+2\). Together with \(\#\{x:c(x)\le t\}=O(t^2)\), partial summation gives \[\sum_{x\in B_N}\deg(x)
 \ll Nt+(N/t+1)|B_N|,\qquad 1\le t\le N.\] Choose \(t=N/L^{\rho/2}\). The right side is \(O(N^2L^{-\rho/2})\). If \(|A_N|\) is already below the resulting target, nothing remains; otherwise its total length meets the threshold of Theorem 4.6. Proposition 4.2 and that sparse equidistribution input then give \(\sum_{y\in A_N}\deg(y)\gg |A_N|L\). Consequently the checked argument proves \[|A_N|\ll
 \frac{N^2}{L^{\,1+\min(\delta/2,1/4)}}.\] This is weaker than the printed assertion for \(0<\delta<1/2\). A new argument or a weaker statement is required. This is a demonstrated failure of the given quantitative derivation, not an exhibited Maaß form contradicting the theorem.
## Why the headline exact-zero exponent survives

For \(P_f(y)=0\), the comparison gives \(|L_f(x)|=O(1)\) directly. Thus \(|B_N|\ll N^2L^{-1/2}\), and the cutoff \(t=N/L^{1/4}\) gives \(|A_N^0|\ll N^2/L^{5/4}\). Since \(|\operatorname{tr}\gamma|=2\cosh(\ell(C_\gamma)/2)\), dyadic summation recovers \(O(e^X/X^{5/4})\). This is a verified repair of the exact-zero deduction conditional on the named source inputs. It is counterevidence to a claim that Problem 1 invalidates the headline non-vanishing result.

The qualitative cuspidal edge argument also needs only small/large normalized-period probabilities tending to zero. Weak Gaussian convergence, absence of an atom at zero, and tightness provide that conclusion by comparison with fixed intervals or rectangles. The degree cutoff can then grow slowly enough to make the exceptional edge mass \(o(N^2)\). The geometric lower bound for a positive-proportion exceptional collection contradicts this. Isolated vertices have degree zero and do not affect this particular edge-sum argument.
# Problem 2: the graph transform need not have mass one

This issue occurs in the actual modular graph, not merely in an unrelated abstract graph. Take \[N=21,\qquad
 \gamma=\begin{pmatrix}-6&-5\\17&14\end{pmatrix}.\] Its determinant is one, \(c_\gamma=17\le21\), and its trace is \(8\). All representatives of its double coset have traces \(8+17k\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\). The closest values to zero are \(8\) and \(-9\); all others have absolute value at least \(25\). None belongs to the required absolute-trace band \([21/2,21]\). Hence its vertex in \(X_{21}\) has degree zero and positive uniform mass.

There are also arbitrarily large examples. For every integer \(m\ge12\), take \[\gamma_m=\begin{pmatrix}m+1&1\\2m+1&2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad N_m=\left\lfloor\frac54(2m+1)\right\rfloor .\] The determinant is one and the traces in the double coset are \(m+3+k(2m+1)\). The two closest values, \(m+3\) and \(2-m\), have absolute value below \(N_m/2\); the next values have absolute value exceeding \(N_m\). This again gives an isolated vertex.
## What is established and what remains necessary

These examples refute exact normalization for the graph as defined. They do not determine the asymptotic proportion \(\zeta_N=\mu_N(I_N)\). In particular, they alone are not a counterexample to a Gaussian limiting assertion.

The general lemma can be repaired by requiring \(\mu(I)=0\), but this hypothesis cannot simply be inserted into the actual application. One possible route is to restrict and normalize \(\mu_N\) on the nonisolated vertices, and prove an adequate bound on \(\zeta_N\). The resulting distributional comparison has an additional \(O(\zeta_N)\) term when \(\zeta_N\) is small. At least \(\zeta_N=o(1)\) is necessary for the intended unit-mass limit; the effective claim needs a corresponding rate. No such bound or replacement graph construction is established in this review. The Major assessment concerns the unverified transfer route for a stated main weighted-distribution result, without asserting that its asymptotic conclusion is false.
# Problem 3: continuity does not supply a uniform density bound

Assessment: Minor, general auxiliary lemma. Lemma 6.2 (pp. 29–30) asserts a uniform interval error \(O_F(h(n)+E(n))\) for any continuous probability density \(F\). Its proof uses \(\int_b^{b+E}F=O_F(E)\) uniformly in \(b\). A continuous integrable density can be unbounded.

Here is a counterexample to the lemma itself, with no isolated vertices. Set \(w_j=2^{-j}/j\) and \[F(x)=\sum_{j\ge1}j\left(1-\frac{|x-3j|}{w_j}\right)_+ .\] The disjoint triangular spikes have masses \(jw_j=2^{-j}\), so \(F\) is a continuous probability density. For each \(n\), take a finite, equally weighted quantile approximation to \(F\) whose uniform interval error is at most \(h(n)\le w_n^2\). Such an approximation is obtained from midpoint quantiles with sufficiently many atoms.

Let the graph be the matching between two copies of these atoms, let \(f_n\) equal their quantile values, and put \(g_n=f_n+w_n\). Every edge has error \(E(n)=w_n\), and the graph transform is a probability measure. On the interval \([0,3n]\), the output distribution differs from the target by \[\int_{3n-w_n}^{3n}F(x)\,dx+O(h(n))
 =\frac{nw_n}{2}+O(w_n^2).\] Its ratio to \(h(n)+E(n)\) tends to infinity. All stated hypotheses of the lemma hold, so its uniform rate is false as quantified.

Requiring \(F\) to be bounded gives the claimed endpoint estimate and repairs this step. More generally the error should use the concentration modulus \(\sup_b\int_b^{b+O(E)}F\), which tends to zero but need not be \(O(E)\). The Gaussian densities used in the application are bounded; this is why the density defect is local to the general lemma. It does not resolve the separate isolated-mass issue in Problem 2.
# Remaining checks and verification limits
## Period comparison and an Eisenstein dependency

On an edge, \(c_\gamma\le N\) and \(|\operatorname{tr}\gamma|\ge N/2\). Therefore the cuspidal error in Proposition 3.1 is \(O_f(1)\), and after division by \(\sqrt{\log N}\) it is \(O_f((\log N)^{-1/2})\). The sign \((-1)^{k/2+1}\) is retained in §6.3 and does not change a centred real or complex Gaussian law. The external proof underlying Proposition 3.1 has not been independently reconstructed here.

For Eisenstein periods there is a separate unresolved normalization discrepancy. Theorem 3.5 on p. 17 visibly divides the vertical period by \(c_{E^*}\sqrt{\log N}\), while pp. 26–27 use \(\sqrt{\log N}(\log\log N)^{3/2}\). The latter matches Theorem 1.6’s length scale \(\sqrt X(\log X)^{3/2}\). The quoted external central limit theorem has not been checked to decide which printed normalization is correct. This is recorded as a NeedsEvidence dependency; the Eisenstein deduction is not certified.
## The positive-proportion arithmetic mechanism

In the stated Heegner setup of §7, character orthogonality turns Waldspurger’s identity into a sum of squared geodesic periods. If every relevant central value vanishes, all those periods vanish. Conditional on the source’s cuspidal non-vanishing and class-number inputs, \[\sum_{D\ {\rm good}}h^+(D)\gg \frac{X^2}{\log X},
 \qquad
 \sum_D h^+(D)^2\ll \frac{X^3}{(\log X)^2}.\] Cauchy–Schwarz then gives \(\#\{D\ {\rm good}\}\gg X\). Together with the counting input this yields a positive proportion. This checks the mechanism, not the printed optimal constant or all wide/narrow class-number conventions. The extension from the explicit square-free level setup of §7 to every level in Corollary 1.7 is not independently verified. No pointwise-in-discriminant conclusion follows from this averaged argument.
# Conclusion

There are two supported Major proof/definition gaps and one Minor auxiliary-lemma defect within the inspected scope. The exact-zero exponent and the qualitative cuspidal edge-count deduction have verified repairs or conditional supporting arguments; a blanket rejection of all non-vanishing results would exceed the evidence. The stronger quantitative small-period bound, the normalization needed for weighted transfer, and the Eisenstein scale require the specified additional work. Author adoption and journal-version changes are unknown. Scientific decision remains pending, human reviews are empty, and this initial continuation is not independent acceptance.
# Scope and references

The Gaussian expansion, matrix trace examples, density construction and edge optimization are analytic checks, not numerical experiments. The original source extraction is reused with its historical execution origin. No author code was executed. Unavailable optional code is not a mathematical defect. External theorems are declared inputs, not relabelled as freshly verified proofs.

report: Abstract: The acquired manuscript is examined through its local-density, cone-summation, geometric-approximation and sieve arguments. The stated cutting proposition has an explicit counterexample, and the radial compactness hypothesis used in the passage to boxes is not satisfied by those boxes. Several local normalization formulas also require correction. Corrected fixed-cone computations provide counterevidence to a blanket rejection of the prime-counting strategy. The findings concern this author-manuscript version; they do not establish that the three final matrix asymptotics are false.

Title: A verification of selected arguments in
Prime Number Theorems for Polynomials from Homogeneous Dynamics
# Identity, statements and scope

The source is Giorgos Kotsovolis and Katharine Woo, Prime number theorems for polynomials from homogeneous dynamics, arXiv:2312.11445v1, 18 December 2023, 38 physical pages; the manuscript date is 19 December 2023 [KW]. The assigned DOI is 10.1007/s00039-025-00716-y. Equivalence with the 53-page journal article has not been established. All page references concern the acquired PDF; its physical and printed numbering agree.

Theorems 1.4, 1.6 and 1.8 concern, respectively, determinants on \(\operatorname{Mat}_n(\mathbb Z)\), Pfaffians on alternating \(2n\)-by-\(2n\) matrices (\(n\ge2\)), and determinants on symmetric \(n\)-by-\(n\) matrices (\(n\ge3\)). Their positive-prime constants are \[\prod_{j=2}^n\zeta(j)^{-1},\qquad
 \prod_{\substack{3\le j\le2n-1\\j\ {\rm odd}}}\zeta(j)^{-1},\qquad
 \prod_{\substack{3\le j\le n\\j\ {\rm odd}}}\zeta(j)^{-1}.\] Positive primes and the two signs counted by the prime-ideal formulation are kept distinct. A statement for positive level-one cones does not alone prove its negative-level counterpart.

The primary executor checked the geometric hypotheses and counterexample, the sieve error scales, and the integration of these findings. Full reading is not a complete audit of the cited equidistribution, mass-formula or sieve theorems. Their exact external normalizations remain declared inputs.
# Problem 1: the cutting proposition and its application

Assessment: Major, geometric implication not justified as stated. Section 4 explicitly drops the dynamical assumptions of §2. Theorem 4.1 assumes that a compact set \(R_0\) is star-shaped about zero and that \[[0,\infty)R_0\cap V_1\] is a nice compact subset of \(V_1=\{F=1\}\). Here nice means that the boundary has measure zero on \(V_1\) (Definition 2.2, p. 6). Definition 4.4 requires a finite collection of compact subsets \(\Omega\subset V_1\) such that \[R_0=E\ \cup\!\bigcup_\Omega[0,1/\operatorname{ht}(\Omega)]\Omega,
 \qquad |E|\le\epsilon,\qquad
 \operatorname{ht}(\Omega)=\sup_{\omega\in\Omega}\|\omega\|_\infty .\] Proposition 4.6 asserts that such a cutting exists under the two stated hypotheses (pp. 14–15).

Take \(V=\mathbb R^2\), \(F(x,y)=x\), and \[R_0=\{(x,y):0\le x\le\tfrac12,\ |y|\le x\}.\] This is a compact convex star-shaped set of area \(1/4\); the polynomial is homogeneous and irreducible. Its radial projection is the nice compact segment \(\{(1,s):-1\le s\le1\}\). Every nonempty \(\Omega\) in a purported cutting must lie in this segment, since its cone is required to be contained in \(R_0\). Consequently \(\operatorname{ht}(\Omega)=1\), and the cone contains a point with \(x=1\), outside \(R_0\). No nonempty cutting piece is possible. An empty collection leaves \(|E|=1/4\), contradicting every \(\epsilon<1/4\). This directly refutes Proposition 4.6 with its printed definition; it is not a numerical example or a failure of an antecedent about prime distribution.

There is a separate failure of the cited application. For the centered unit box in \(\operatorname{Mat}_2(\mathbb R)\), the radial projection onto \(\det=1\) is all of \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\), hence is noncompact. Already \[\begin{pmatrix}t&0\\0&t^{-1}\end{pmatrix},
                  \qquad t\ge1,\] is an unbounded sequence in that projection. The same sequence lies in the radial projection of the nonnegative unit box used in Remark 4.2. Thus the assertion in §5.2 (p. 19) that the matrix box satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 4.1 is incorrect.
## Effect and necessary repair

The cutoff \(1/\operatorname{ht}(\Omega)\) encodes a unit norm boundary, not the radial boundary of an arbitrary \(R_0\). A repaired general construction must use the radial length allowed by \(R_0\), approximate it on the angular pieces, and control the exceptional region. For boxes, compact pieces can instead be obtained after removing a neighborhood of \(F=0\); the theorem and its application must be stated to permit this exhaustion. The asserted finite union of convex exceptional pieces in §5.1 is not supplied by the printed construction. A finite convex outer cover with controlled total volume would suffice for the sieve step, but must be proved with the corrected cutting.

These are defects in the bridge from fixed cones to the advertised regions. They do not give a counterexample to a matrix prime asymptotic. Even for the triangular example above, the actual prime count is \[\sum_{p\le T/2}(2p+1)\sim\frac{T^2}{4\log T},\] which agrees with its prime integral by the ordinary prime number theorem. The invalid cutting statement must therefore be distinguished from the truth of a prime-counting conclusion for a particular region. Remark 1.5’s additional boundary-measure-zero condition is also meaningful and should not be silently replaced by niceness of the radial projection. The ledger records the boundary and zero-measure-cone quantifiers separately; no theorem is refuted by assuming an unverified antecedent.
# Problem 2: inconsistent local normalization formulas

Assessment: Minor, explicitly repairable intermediate formulas. The following discrepancies are confirmed on the actual source pages. They are grouped because each concerns the compatibility of the local normalizations with the later displayed constants.
## Radial shells and level shells

For a concrete determinant patch \[\Omega=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&(1+bc)/a\end{pmatrix}:
           1\le a\le2,\ 0\le b,c\le1\right\},\] the coarea element is \(da\,db\,dc/a\). Thus \(\mu_F(\Omega)=\log2\) and \(\mu_{\rm rad}(\Omega)=2\log2\). The true integral coefficient is \((\log2)/4\), whereas the literal Lemma 2.5 gives \((\log2)/2\). Replacing the shell endpoints by \((1-\epsilon)^{1/d},(1+\epsilon)^{1/d}\), or dividing the radial measure by \(d\), resolves the discrepancy. Remark 2.6 already adopts this coarea normalization.
## Finite-place factors and prime powers
## Symmetric-matrix formulas

For \(S=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,p)\), substitution into the stated mass formula (11), p. 21, makes the ratio of \(\alpha_p(S)^{-1}\) to \((2p)^{-1}(\alpha_p^{\rm std}(S))^{-1}\) equal to \[1+\frac{(-1/p)}p .\] Thus Lemma 6.2’s relative \(O(p^{-2})\) needs \(O(p^{-1})\) at rank three. The weaker error is sufficient and is already used later.

Further displayed factors must be reconciled with their own derivations: the last branch in Proposition 7.4 (p. 24) needs \(1+2^{1-n}/(1+2^{-n/2})\), as in (18); the extra \(1/2\) on p. 29 must cancel against Corollary 7.3’s factor \(2\); and the first even-rank level-count display on p. 36 needs \(p^{(n-1)/2}\). The statements of Lemmas 7.5 and 7.7 must retain the odd-zeta product present in their preceding derivations.

There is concrete counterevidence to interpreting these slips as a failure of the corrected density. An exact enumeration of all \(2^{10}=1024\) symmetric binary \(4\)-by-\(4\) matrices found \(448\) invertible ones: \(28\) alternating and \(420\) nonalternating. A separate exact determinant expansion and a lifting argument give \[\begin{array}{c|cccc}
 p\bmod8&1&3&5&7\\ \hline
 \delta_2(p)&245/256&105/128&231/256&105/128 .
\end{array}\] Their mean is \(7/8=(448/1024)/(1-1/2)\), the directly counted Bateman–Horn local factor. These values agree with corrected (16)–(18). The retained script exhausts the finite cases; the passage to stable \(2\)-adic densities is justified separately by the analytical lifting argument, not inferred from a finite experiment.

For even \(n=2r\ge4\), the source’s \(L\)-series convention omits the Euler factor at \(2\). A fixed-cutoff expansion of that absolutely convergent series, followed by PNT in fixed residue classes, leaves only odd squares and gives \((1-2^{-n})\zeta(n)\) as the mean. The corrected four residue-class multipliers cancel \(1-2^{-n}\). The gamma, even-zeta and parity factors in the definite and indefinite formulas likewise cancel to the stated odd-zeta product. These algebraic implications are checked conditionally on the displayed general mass and measure formulas; no uniform growing-modulus remainder or all-rank genus classification is certified.
# Checks that support the corrected strategy
## Determinant local stability and summation

For each fixed \(\Omega\), a finite-head/tail split justifies summing the level-count error \(o_\Omega(1)\) over primes; no uniformity over all possible cones is required at this step. Ordinary PNT and partial summation give \[\sum_{p\le T^n}p^{n-1}\sim\frac{T^{n^2}}{n^2\log T}.\] Together with the corrected coarea measure this verifies the determinant cone implication, conditional on the cited level-set equidistribution theorem. The corresponding Pfaffian exponent is \(T^{n(2n-1)}/[n(2n-1)\log T]\), as correctly printed on p. 13.
## Sieve scales and order of limits

If a corrected construction supplies \(N(\epsilon)\) convex covering pieces of total volume \(O(\epsilon)\), the remainder is \[O_F\!\left(\frac{\epsilon T^D}{\log T}
               +N(\epsilon)T^{D-1/2}\right).\] For fixed \(\epsilon\), the second term is negligible. One first takes \(T\to\infty\), then \(\epsilon\to0\). This checks the error bookkeeping conditional on the missing geometric construction, without certifying that construction.
# Conclusion and verification limits

One Major defect in the geometric implication and one grouped Minor normalization issue are supported in this acquired version. The explicit repairs and conditional fixed-cone checks are retained as counterevidence. The full matrix asymptotics, all signature cases and all external equidistribution and mass-formula conventions have not been independently certified by this report. Scientific decision remains pending, human reviews are empty, and this initial continuation is not independent acceptance.
# Scope and references

All counterexamples and displayed repairs above are analytical checks. Any finite computation in the symmetric-matrix auxiliary record is identified there with its actual input and scope. The original source extraction is reused with its original execution origin. No author code was executed, and unavailable optional code is not treated as a mathematical defect.

Theorem 4.1 assumes that a compact set \(R_0\) is star-shaped about zero and that \[[0,\infty)R_0\cap V_1\] is a nice compact subset of \(V_1=\{F=1\}\). Here nice means that the boundary has measure zero on \(V_1\) (Definition 2.2, p. 6). Definition 4.4 requires a finite collection of compact subsets \(\Omega\subset V_1\) such that \[R_0=E\ \cup\!\bigcup_\Omega[0,1/\operatorname{ht}(\Omega)]\Omega,
 \qquad |E|\le\epsilon,\qquad
 \operatorname{ht}(\Omega)=\sup_{\omega\in\Omega}\|\omega\|_\infty .\] Proposition 4.6 asserts that such a cutting exists under the two stated hypotheses (pp. 14–15).

Take \(V=\mathbb R^2\), \(F(x,y)=x\), and \[R_0=\{(x,y):0\le x\le\tfrac12,\ |y|\le x\}.\] This is a compact convex star-shaped set of area \(1/4\); the polynomial is homogeneous and irreducible. Its radial projection is the nice compact segment \(\{(1,s):-1\le s\le1\}\). Every nonempty \(\Omega\) in a purported cutting must lie in this segment, since its cone is required to be contained in \(R_0\). Consequently \(\operatorname{ht}(\Omega)=1\), and the cone contains a point with \(x=1\), outside \(R_0\). No nonempty cutting piece is possible. An empty collection leaves \(|E|=1/4\), contradicting every \(\epsilon<1/4\). This directly refutes Proposition 4.6 with its printed definition; it is not a numerical example or a failure of an antecedent about prime distribution.

There is a separate failure of the cited application. For the centered unit box in \(\operatorname{Mat}_2(\mathbb R)\), the radial projection onto \(\det=1\) is all of \(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\), hence is noncompact. Already \[\begin{pmatrix}t&0\\0&t^{-1}\end{pmatrix},
                  \qquad t\ge1,\] is an unbounded sequence in that projection. The same sequence lies in the radial projection of the nonnegative unit box used in Remark 4.2. Thus the assertion in §5.2 (p. 19) that the matrix box satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 4.1 is incorrect.

The cutoff \(1/\operatorname{ht}(\Omega)\) encodes a unit norm boundary, not the radial boundary of an arbitrary \(R_0\). A repaired general construction must use the radial length allowed by \(R_0\), approximate it on the angular pieces, and control the exceptional region. For boxes, compact pieces can instead be obtained after removing a neighborhood of \(F=0\); the theorem and its application must be stated to permit this exhaustion. The asserted finite union of convex exceptional pieces in §5.1 is not supplied by the printed construction. A finite convex outer cover with controlled total volume would suffice for the sieve step, but must be proved with the corrected cutting.

These are defects in the bridge from fixed cones to the advertised regions. They do not give a counterexample to a matrix prime asymptotic. Even for the triangular example above, the actual prime count is \[\sum_{p\le T/2}(2p+1)\sim\frac{T^2}{4\log T},\] which agrees with its prime integral by the ordinary prime number theorem. The invalid cutting statement must therefore be distinguished from the truth of a prime-counting conclusion for a particular region. Remark 1.5’s additional boundary-measure-zero condition is also meaningful and should not be silently replaced by niceness of the radial projection. The ledger records the boundary and zero-measure-cone quantifiers separately; no theorem is refuted by assuming an unverified antecedent.

analysis: Assessment: Minor, explicitly repairable intermediate formulas. The following discrepancies are confirmed on the actual source pages. They are grouped because each concerns the compatibility of the local normalizations with the later displayed constants.

For a concrete determinant patch \[\Omega=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&(1+bc)/a\end{pmatrix}:
           1\le a\le2,\ 0\le b,c\le1\right\},\] the coarea element is \(da\,db\,dc/a\). Thus \(\mu_F(\Omega)=\log2\) and \(\mu_{\rm rad}(\Omega)=2\log2\). The true integral coefficient is \((\log2)/4\), whereas the literal Lemma 2.5 gives \((\log2)/2\). Replacing the shell endpoints by \((1-\epsilon)^{1/d},(1+\epsilon)^{1/d}\), or dividing the radial measure by \(d\), resolves the discrepancy. Remark 2.6 already adopts this coarea normalization.

For \(S=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,p)\), substitution into the stated mass formula (11), p. 21, makes the ratio of \(\alpha_p(S)^{-1}\) to \((2p)^{-1}(\alpha_p^{\rm std}(S))^{-1}\) equal to \[1+\frac{(-1/p)}p .\] Thus Lemma 6.2’s relative \(O(p^{-2})\) needs \(O(p^{-1})\) at rank three. The weaker error is sufficient and is already used later.

Further displayed factors must be reconciled with their own derivations: the last branch in Proposition 7.4 (p. 24) needs \(1+2^{1-n}/(1+2^{-n/2})\), as in (18); the extra \(1/2\) on p. 29 must cancel against Corollary 7.3’s factor \(2\); and the first even-rank level-count display on p. 36 needs \(p^{(n-1)/2}\). The statements of Lemmas 7.5 and 7.7 must retain the odd-zeta product present in their preceding derivations.

There is concrete counterevidence to interpreting these slips as a failure of the corrected density. An exact enumeration of all \(2^{10}=1024\) symmetric binary \(4\)-by-\(4\) matrices found \(448\) invertible ones: \(28\) alternating and \(420\) nonalternating. A separate exact determinant expansion and a lifting argument give \[\begin{array}{c|cccc}
 p\bmod8&1&3&5&7\\ \hline
 \delta_2(p)&245/256&105/128&231/256&105/128 .
\end{array}\] Their mean is \(7/8=(448/1024)/(1-1/2)\), the directly counted Bateman–Horn local factor. These values agree with corrected (16)–(18). The retained script exhausts the finite cases; the passage to stable \(2\)-adic densities is justified separately by the analytical lifting argument, not inferred from a finite experiment.

For even \(n=2r\ge4\), the source’s \(L\)-series convention omits the Euler factor at \(2\). A fixed-cutoff expansion of that absolutely convergent series, followed by PNT in fixed residue classes, leaves only odd squares and gives \((1-2^{-n})\zeta(n)\) as the mean. The corrected four residue-class multipliers cancel \(1-2^{-n}\). The gamma, even-zeta and parity factors in the definite and indefinite formulas likewise cancel to the stated odd-zeta product. These algebraic implications are checked conditionally on the displayed general mass and measure formulas; no uniform growing-modulus remainder or all-rank genus classification is certified.

Title: A verification of selected arguments in
Semiclassical Measures for Complex Hyperbolic Quotients
# Identity and scope

The source is Jayadev Athreya, Semyon Dyatlov and Nicholas Miller, Semiclassical Measures for Complex Hyperbolic Quotients, arXiv:2402.06477v2, 25 July 2025, 72 physical pages [ADM]. The assigned journal identifier is DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00717-x. This report concerns the exact acquired author manuscript; equivalence with the journal version has not been established. Page numbers refer to the acquired PDF and agree with its printed pages.

This report records that bounded contribution. Reading the whole text does not certify every proof or external input. The primary executor separately read the statements and control deduction, checked the support and norm-limit argument, and adjudicated this report. Scientific decision and independent acceptance remain pending.
# Statements and hypotheses

Let \(M\) be a compact complex hyperbolic quotient, with real dimension \(2n\), and let \[(-\Delta_g-\lambda_j^2)u_j=0,\qquad
 \lambda_j\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad
 \|u_j\|_{L^2(M)}=1.\] Set \(h_j=\lambda_j^{-1}\). A semiclassical measure \(\mu\) satisfies \[\langle\operatorname{Op}_{h_j}(a)u_j,u_j\rangle
 \longrightarrow\int_{T^*M}a\,d\mu
 \qquad(a\in C_c^\infty(T^*M)).\] It is a geodesic-flow invariant probability measure supported on \(S^*M\), and its spatial projection is the weak limit of \(|u_j|^2\,d\operatorname{vol}_g\) (pp. 1, 4–5).

Theorem 1.3 asserts the existence of a positive-dimensional compact immersed totally geodesic complex submanifold \(\Sigma\) of \(M\) such that \[S^*\Sigma\subset\operatorname{supp}\mu.\] Here the cosphere bundle is understood through its image in \(S^*M\) under the metric identification. The choice \(\Sigma=M\) is allowed. If there is no proper such submanifold, the conclusion is \(\operatorname{supp}\mu=S^*M\). Theorem 1.2 is the corresponding spatial inclusion \(\Sigma\subset\operatorname{supp}\widetilde\mu\) (pp. 3–5).

These conclusions are support inclusions. They do not assert concentration on a proper submanifold, equality of the support with a proper \(S^*\Sigma\), or positive mass assigned to that lower-dimensional set. Universal full support is separately formulated as Conjecture 1.4.
# The geometric control-set alternative

A set is \(V^\pm\)-dense if it meets every complete orbit of the corresponding fast horocyclic flow. This is an orbit-intersection condition; topological density alone does not suffice (p. 15). Theorem 3.3 identifies the closure of each joint geodesic/fast-horocyclic orbit with \(S\Sigma\) for a compact immersed totally geodesic complex submanifold; the metric identifies the tangent and cotangent statements.

The following use of that theorem in Corollary 3.4 is valid. Let \(\mathcal U\subset S^*M\) be open and invariant under the geodesic flow. If \(\mathcal U\) misses a complete \(V^+\)-orbit, its closed complement contains that orbit. Invariance makes the complement contain its geodesic saturation, and closedness makes it contain the closure of that saturation. By Theorem 3.3 this closure is \(S^*\Sigma\). The same argument applies to \(V^-\). Thus either \(\mathcal U\) meets every fast orbit of both signs, or it misses an entire \(S^*\Sigma\) (p. 17). Both openness and geodesic invariance are used; neither is dispensable in this argument.
# From the control estimate to support
## A single cutoff for both signs

Suppose \(F=\operatorname{supp}\mu\) contains no \(S^*\Sigma\) of the stated type. Invariance of \(\mu\) under the geodesic flow implies invariance of its support, since the flow is a measure-preserving homeomorphism. Consequently \(\mathcal U=S^*M\setminus F\) is open and invariant. The geometric alternative just checked shows that \(\mathcal U\) is \(V^+\)-dense and \(V^-\)-dense.

Lemma 3.1(1) applies separately to the two vector fields. It gives compact sets \(K_+,K_-\subset\mathcal U\), each meeting every orbit of its respective flow. Their union \(K=K_+\cup K_-\) is compact, is contained in \(\mathcal U\), and meets every orbit of both flows. This explains the simultaneous compact-set assertion in the proof on p. 37. The lemma’s exhaustion argument uses compactness of \(S^*M\) (pp. 15–16).

Choose a fixed \(a\in C_c^\infty(T^*M)\), equal to one near \(K\), such that \[\operatorname{supp}a\cap S^*M\subset\mathcal U.\] Smooth separation of the compact set \(K\) from the closed set \(F\), followed by extension to an annular neighborhood of \(S^*M\), provides such a symbol. It satisfies the hypotheses of [eq:control] (#eq:control). In particular, \(a\) and the resulting constant \(C\) are fixed along the sequence.
## The norm limit and contradiction

The ordinary product and adjoint rules, (4.1) and (4.4), give \[\operatorname{Op}_h(a)^*\operatorname{Op}_h(a)=\operatorname{Op}_h(|a|^2)+O(h)_{L^2\to L^2}.\] The conjugation in the adjoint rule is essential; it is explicit in the source image on p. 33. Since \(\|u_j\|_{L^2}=1\), \[\begin{aligned}
 \|\operatorname{Op}_{h_j}(a)u_j\|_{L^2}^2
 &=\langle\operatorname{Op}_{h_j}(|a|^2)u_j,u_j\rangle+O(h_j)\\
 &\longrightarrow\int |a|^2\,d\mu=0.\end{aligned}\] The convergence uses the fixed compact smooth symbol \(|a|^2\). The integral vanishes because \(\mu\) is supported on \(S^*M\) and the cutoff is disjoint from \(F\) there (pp. 32–33, 37).

Smooth eigenfunctions belong to \(H^2(M)\), and \[(-h_j^2\Delta_g-I)u_j=0.\] For all sufficiently large \(j\), [eq:control] (#eq:control) therefore gives \[1\le C\|\operatorname{Op}_{h_j}(a)u_j\|_{L^2},\] a contradiction. This establishes the claimed implication without requiring an additional long-time calculus in this final step (pp. 36–37).
# Projection and boundary checks

Let \(\pi:S^*M\to M\) be the base projection. If \(q\in\operatorname{supp}\mu\), every neighborhood \(O\) of \(\pi(q)\) has an open inverse image containing \(q\), so \((\pi_*\mu)(O)>0\). Thus \(\pi(\operatorname{supp}\mu)\subset\operatorname{supp}(\pi_*\mu)\). Since \(\pi(S^*\Sigma)=\Sigma\) as images, Theorem 1.3 implies Theorem 1.2. An immersion need not be injective for this argument.

The already full-support case is consistent with \(\Sigma=M\); the contradiction argument is needed only when the stated containment fails. The absence of a proper admissible \(\Sigma\) gives the stated full-support corollary. No quantitative lower bound on \(\mu(S^*\Sigma)\) follows from the inclusion alone.

There is also a useful dimensional interpretation. For a connected complex curve, a positive-dimensional complex immersion has the same dimension as its target and is locally a diffeomorphism. Its image is open; compactness makes that image closed. Hence it is the whole curve. Accordingly, if the support conclusion is applied in complex dimension one, it has no proper-submanifold alternative. This elementary observation is not a new proof of the surface theorem or a verification of a dimension-one extension of the higher-dimensional analytic argument.

The residual term in [eq:control] (#eq:control) vanishes for the exact eigenfunctions under consideration. A quasimode application would instead require control of that residual after multiplication by \(\log(1/h)/h\); no additional quasimode theorem is certified here. Similarly, an \(h\)-dependent cutoff cannot be substituted without checking new uniformity assumptions.
# Inputs and noncounted correction

The support deduction depends on Theorem 3.3 and Theorem 4.3. The former uses orbit-closure theory. The latter uses the uniform long-word decay in Proposition 4.9 (p. 42), whose proof invokes porosity, anisotropic semiclassical calculus and Fourier-integral localization. The one-dimensional fractal uncertainty principle is stated in Proposition 5.3 with \[0\le\gamma_1<\tfrac12<\gamma_0\le1\] and attributed to the cited Bourgain–Dyatlov and Dyatlov–Jin–Nonnenmacher work (p. 49). These statements were read and their role was traced. Their complete proofs and the external references were not independently audited in this contribution.

One local notation slip is visible on p. 37: the first paragraph places \(\Sigma\) in \(S^*M\), whereas Theorem 1.3 correctly places \(\Sigma\) in \(M\) and \(S^*\Sigma\) in \(S^*M\). The argument unambiguously uses the latter meaning. This can be corrected locally and is not counted as a substantive mathematical problem.
# Conclusion

No substantive problem is established by the checks reported here. The quantified support conclusion and its deduction from the stated control and geometric inputs are consistent. This finding does not certify the full microlocal or orbit-closure arguments, nor prove universal full support. Scientific decision remains pending, human review entries are empty, and independent acceptance is incomplete.
# Evidence and limitations

The exact source PDF, its version manifest, and the historical text extraction are retained with their original origins. Current native source-page inspections cover pp. 1, 3–5, 15–17, 32–33, 36–37, 42 and 49, with byte and hash bindings recorded separately. The checks above are analytic; no numerical experiment or author code substitutes for them. The earlier bounded acquisition search did not establish journal-version equivalence or locate a separate code package or supplement. These source limitations are not mathematical defects.

Title: A verification of selected arguments in
Affirmative Resolution of Bourgain’s Slicing Problem
Using Guan’s Bound
# Identity and normalizations

The source is Boaz Klartag and Joseph Lehec, Affirmative resolution of Bourgain’s slicing problem using Guan’s bound, arXiv:2412.15044v1, 19 December 2024, 20 pages [KL]. The assigned DOI is 10.1007/s00039-025-00718-w. Equivalence with the journal version has not been established. Page references use the acquired PDF’s physical and printed numbering.

An isotropic probability measure is centered with covariance \(\mathrm{Id}\). For a volume-one convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\), \(L_K=(\det\operatorname{Cov}(K))^{1/(2n)}\), and \(L_n\) is the supremum over such bodies. The entropy convention (3), p. 3, gives \(L_\mu=\exp(-\operatorname{Ent}(\mu)/m)\) for an isotropic measure on \(\mathbb R^m\). Theorem 1.1 requires some affine hyperplane section, with ordinary Euclidean \((n-1)\)-dimensional volume.
# Problem 1: the derivative in equation (56)

Deleting the superscript \(2\) inside the derivative repairs (56). The next displayed line already uses \(d(\mathbb EA_t)/dt=-\mathbb EA_t^2\) and obtains the correct Lemma 3.3(iv). Thus this finding does not refute that lemma or the main theorem. The assessment concerns only the acquired version.
# Conditional verification of the entropy argument
## The lower bound for the mean covariance

Let \(C_G\) be the universal constant in Lemma 2.3. The identities \(d(\mathbb E\operatorname{Tr}A_t)/dt=-\mathbb E\operatorname{Tr}A_t^2\) and \(\mathbb EA_t\le\mathrm{Id}\), with \(t_0=\min\{1/(2C_G),1\}\), give \(\mathbb E\operatorname{Tr}A_{t_0}\ge n/2\). The eigenvalue selection on p. 10 and conditional-covariance monotonicity in Lemma 2.2 give the covariance part of Proposition 2.4. Its isotropic-constant transfer uses the separate geometric Lemma 2.5.

Accordingly, for \(n\ge10\), take the proposition’s isotropic measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^m\), where \(n/4\le m\le n\), \(L_\mu\ge c_pL_n\) and \(\mathbb EA_{t_0}\ge\mathrm{Id}/4\). Here \(c_p>0\) is universal. Put \[\xi=\frac{t_0}{1+t_0},\qquad M(r)=\mathbb E\Gamma_r,\qquad
 a=\frac{\xi}{4},\qquad q(r)=\mathbb E|v_r|^2.\] Lemma 3.3 gives \(\Gamma_r^2\le\Gamma_r/r\), hence \(M'(r)\ge-M(r)/r\). Thus \(rM(r)\) is increasing and, for \(r\ge\xi\), \[a\mathrm{Id}\le \frac{\xi}{r}M(\xi)\le M(r)\le\mathrm{Id}.\] Both \(\xi\) and \(a\) are positive universal constants.
## The variance budget and matrix order

Write \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\) for the Hilbert–Schmidt norm. Since \(Q(r):=\mathbb E(v_r\otimes v_r)=(\mathrm{Id}-M(r))/(1-r)\ge0\), positive-semidefinite trace order gives \[\frac{\|\mathrm{Id}-M(r)\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2}{1-r}
 =\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(Q(r)(\mathrm{Id}-M(r))\bigr)\le(1-a)q(r).\] No commutativity of random matrices is used. In Lemma 3.4, the bound \(\Gamma_r\le\xi^{-1}\mathrm{Id}\) makes the matrix denominator at most \(2\xi^{-1}\mathrm{Id}\); independence of its two copies gives the stated variance coefficient. Together with Lemma 3.5, this yields \[V:=\int_\xi^1
 \frac{\mathbb E\|\Gamma_r-M(r)\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2}{1-r}\,dr
 \le \frac{8m}{\xi}.\]
## The endpoint in (64)

The endpoint can be justified before assuming the desired entropy bound. For \(R<1\), let \(I_R=\int_\xi^R q(r)\,dr\). Lemma 3.3(iii) gives \(q'\ge0\), and ordinary integration by parts gives \[\int_\xi^R(1-r)q'(r)\,dr
 =I_R-(1-\xi)q(\xi)+(1-R)q(R).\] Using the variance decomposition (66) and the trace estimate above, \[aI_R\le V+(1-\xi)q(\xi).\] The omitted endpoint term is nonnegative. This bound first proves \(\int_\xi^1q<\infty\); then \(0\le(1-R)q(R)\le\int_R^1q\to0\). It therefore justifies (64) without a circular assumption.
# Constants and the slicing conclusion

For completeness, the required Euclidean section conclusion follows directly. Let \(X\) be uniform on a volume-one body \(K\), and choose a unit eigenvector \(u\) for the least eigenvalue \(\sigma^2\) of its covariance. Then \[\sigma^2\le(\det\operatorname{Cov}(K))^{1/n}=L_K^2.\] By coarea, the density of \(u\cdot X\) at \(s\) equals the section volume of \(K\cap\{u\cdot x=s\}\). Chebyshev’s inequality places at least \(3/4\) of this marginal mass in an interval of length \(4\sigma\). Hence some section has volume at least \(3/(16\sigma)\ge3/(16L_K)\). A uniform bound \(L_n\le C_*\) gives Theorem 1.1 with, for example, \(c=3/(32C_*)\), allowing its strict inequality. The one-dimensional case is immediate. No affine invariance of Euclidean section area is assumed.
# Evidence, limits and conclusion

The full acquired text and manifest were read. The detailed checks above concern the final implication, its constants, matrix inequalities, endpoint and normalization; full reading is not a proof audit of every preliminary result. Guan’s original covariance proof, the geometric inputs behind Lemma 2.5, and the original Eldan–Mikulincer and Ball–Nguyen entropy results were not independently checked from their source papers. They remain named inputs to the conditional verification.

The primary executor separately checked the acquired text and the constant, endpoint and Gaussian calculations. These calculations are analytic; no author code or numerical experiment is used as a substitute for proof. Compilation and report-page inspection are recorded separately.

Problem 1 is local and does not impair the subsequent calculation. No further substantive defect is established within this checked scope. Scientific decision remains pending, human review entries are empty, and independent acceptance is incomplete.

Title: Technical Verification of
\(\mathbb H^{p,q}\)-Convex Cocompactness and
Higher Higher Teichmüller Spaces
# Identity, source and scope

The paper is Jonas Beyrer and Fanny Kassel, \(\mathbb H^{p,q}\)-Convex Cocompactness and Higher Higher Teichmüller Spaces, associated with the frozen 2025 journal record Geometric and Functional Analysis, DOI 10.1007/s00039-025-00719-9 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-025-00719-9). The reviewed source is arXiv:2305.15031v7 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15031v7), submitted 3 October 2025, with internal date 6 October 2025. It has 76 physical PDF pages; the printed page numbers used below agree with physical pages. No equivalence with the journal version of record is assumed.

The earlier checkpoint records full text reading; that historical reading is not represented here as a completed proof audit. Recovery concentrated on its open candidates: the boundary extension in Section 3, the crown orbit argument in Section 5, the representation theory and non-degeneracy argument in Section 6, and the Appendix A boundary case. The source definitions, operative hypotheses, decisive pages and downstream dependencies of these claims were checked. Selected statements and proofs in Benoist’s retained author manuscript [Benoist] were consulted.

This is an initial technical report with a declared scope, not a certification of every theorem, every cited dependency, or the independent acceptance of the paper. The coverage ledger distinguishes historical reading from the present focused checks. No author program was executed. An unavailable separate code release would not by itself constitute a mathematical defect.
# The reducible positivity extension and deletion rule

Problem 1 (An invalid deletion rule used in the non-degeneracy proof).  Lemma 6.7 (p. 52) and Corollary 6.8(2) (p. 53) are false as stated for reducible representations. Their use in Proposition 6.12 and the proof of Proposition 1.13 creates a Major proof-level issue.
## Original hypotheses

In Definition 6.3, a representation \(\tau\) of the real points \(G\) of a connected reductive real algebraic group is positively \(\Gamma\)-semi-proximal when, for every \(\gamma\in\Gamma\) loxodromic in \(G\), the matrix \(\tau(\gamma)\) has a positive real eigenvalue of maximal modulus. Simplicity of that eigenvalue is not required. Loxodromic means that the Jordan projection belongs to the interior of the positive Weyl chamber.

Lemma 6.7 assumes that \(\Gamma\) is a Zariski-dense subgroup, that \(G'\subset G\) is an open subsemigroup meeting \(\Gamma\), and that \(\tau\) is positively \((\Gamma\cap G')\)-semi-proximal. It concludes global positive \(\Gamma\)-semi-proximality. There is no irreducibility hypothesis. Corollary 6.8 assumes irreducible summands \(\tau_i\) with highest weights \(\chi_i\) and a positively \(\Gamma\)-semi-proximal direct sum. Part (2) says that if some \(X\) in the limit cone satisfies \(\chi_1(X)>\chi_2(X)\), one may delete \(\tau_2\) and retain positive \(\Gamma\)-semi-proximality.
## A counterexample satisfying all of these conditions

Equation reference: eq:group, eq:reps. Let \[
 G=\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R)\times\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb R),\qquad
 \Gamma=\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\times\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z),\] and, with the subscript identifying the factor, set \[
 \tau_1=\mathrm{Sym}^2\mathrm{std}_1,\qquad
 \tau_2=\mathrm{Sym}^2\mathrm{std}_2,\qquad \tau_3=\mathrm{std}_2.\] These are irreducible real algebraic representations of the product, of dimensions \(3,3,2\). The proof of Lemma 6.7 fixes the highest eigenspace \(V^+\) of \(\tau(a)\) and then, using [Retained latex: \cite[Corollary 8.5]{Benoist}], replaces \(ta\) by \(t'a'\) with \(t'\) close to \(t\). For a reducible representation, changing \(a\) to \(a'\) can change which constituent supplies the highest eigenspace. The fixed \(V^+\) need not be the highest eigenspace of \(\tau(a')\). The determinant condition on that old space consequently does not imply the asserted spectral conclusion.

This objection does not refute the irreducible sign argument in [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 6.3]{Benoist}], consulted on pp. 27–28, or the exposed single-summand conclusion of Corollary 6.8(1). The source’s part (1) has an independent irreducible justification; it should not be discarded merely because the new general lemma is false. The compact-factor conclusion of Benoist’s Corollary 8.5, consulted on p. 46, does not control a changing dominant constituent.
## Core dependency, alternative readings and repair limits

Proposition 6.12, Step 1 (p. 55), explicitly invokes Corollary 6.8(2) to delete one member of a pair of non-isomorphic dual constituents under a minimality argument. Step 2 invokes it again on p. 56. In the proof of Proposition 1.13 (p. 58), a minimal subrepresentation of \(\kappa\oplus\kappa^*\) is selected, and the text invokes the argument of Step 1 to obtain disjoint index sets, the dimension bound \(\dim\tau\leq k\), and then the contradiction \(p\leq\delta(\tau)+p-k<p\). The introduction identifies Proposition 1.13 as the second main ingredient of Theorem 1.3 (p. 9); p. 10 explicitly uses it in Theorem 1.17 and then in the closedness deduction for Theorem 1.3. The invalid rule is therefore tied to a central derivation, rather than an unused general observation.

There is a significant limit to this conclusion. The counterexample above does not instantiate the special dual-pair and minimality configuration of Step 1. It disproves the rule cited to justify that step, not the specialized step under every additional hypothesis. It is not a counterexample to Proposition 6.12, Proposition 1.13, or a main theorem. A specialized replacement lemma might restore the argument, but none is proved in this report.

One local improvement is available. In Step 2, once the retained exposed constituents have individually been shown positive by Corollary 6.8(1), their direct sum is positive by Remark 6.5(2). The cone-preserving representation \(\upsilon\), when nontrivial, is also positive by Fact 6.11(2). This replaces the positivity sentence on p. 56. It does not by itself justify Step 1, the remaining minimality and kernel arguments, or the full proposition. The supported assessment is Major for the demonstrated invalid core-related derivation, with a complete repair unverified.
# Strict contraction at the ideal boundary

Problem 2 (A strict interior contraction need not remain strict on the boundary).  The proof of Proposition 3.28(2), p. 33, overstates the strictness of a continuous boundary extension. This is a local Minor finding; the proposition has the following restricted repair.

Here strict \(1\)-Lipschitz means a strict distance inequality for every pair of distinct points, as on p. 28; it does not mean a single uniform Lipschitz constant less than \(1\). Use \(p=2,q=1\) and the map from Example 3.23(ii), p. 29, on the open upper unit hemisphere: \[d=y_1^2-y_2^2,\qquad
 f(y_0,y_1,y_2)=
 \left(\sqrt{\frac{1+d}{2}},\sqrt{\frac{1-d}{2}}\right)\in S^1.\] It is equivalently the source’s formula \((\sqrt{y_0^2/2+y_1^2},\sqrt{y_0^2/2+y_2^2})\). The angular coordinate \(\theta=\tfrac12\arccos d\) satisfies \[\|\nabla_{S^2}\theta\|^2
   =\frac{1-y_0^2-d^2}{1-d^2}
   =1-\frac{y_0^2}{1-d^2}<1 .\] For two interior points the minimizing spherical geodesic lies in a compact subset of the open hemisphere, so integration gives strict contraction. This verifies the operative interior assumption. On the boundary arc \(y(t)=(0,\cos t,\sin t)\), \(0<t<\pi/2\), however, \(f(y(t))=(\cos t,\sin t)\). Distances on this arc are preserved. The continuous extension is thus not strictly \(1\)-Lipschitz on all boundary-boundary pairs.

The proof only needs strictness between an interior point \(x\) and a boundary point \(z\). Choose an interior point \(y\) strictly between them on a minimizing geodesic. The extension is nonexpansive, and \[d(f(x),f(z))
 \leq d(f(x),f(y))+d(f(y),f(z))
 <d(x,y)+d(y,z)=d(x,z).\] This proves precisely the needed replacement and preserves the conclusion of Proposition 3.28(2). No failure of that proposition or of a central theorem follows from the overstatement.
# Straightness of crown orbits

Problem 3 (Metric geodesicity does not imply projective straightness).  The proof of Proposition 5.9, p. 45, asserts projective straightness for every nonzero Cartan direction. The assertion is false in that generality, but the directions used in the quadrilateral construction satisfy a valid stronger restriction. The supported impact is Minor.

Use a \(2\)-crown in signature \((2,2)\), corresponding to \(p=2,q=1\), with its isotropic crown basis and positive orthant \(\mathcal O\). Take \(x=[1:1:1:1]\in\mathcal O\) and \(a=(1,0)\). In the diagonal coordinates of (5.1), p. 43, the orbit is \[x(t)=[e^t:1:e^{-t}:1].\] At \(t=0,\log2,\log4\), the first three coordinates of representatives have determinant \[\det\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\2&1&1/2\\4&1&1/4\end{pmatrix}
 =-\frac34\ne0.\] Their vector span has dimension at least three; the three projective points cannot lie in a projective line. All representatives remain in the positive orthant and the action is the stated crown action. The source’s Hilbert-distance formula (5.3) still gives a metric geodesic. It is the additional projective-line assertion that fails.

For the construction actually used on p. 45, the directions have coordinates of equal absolute value. In this case \(\exp(ta)x=e^{ct}u_++e^{-ct}u_-\) for two fixed vectors, and the orbit does lie in their projective span. Restricting the straightness statement to these directions suffices for that construction. This evidence does not refute Proposition 5.9 or its use in Proposition 5.10 on p. 46.
# Real tensor products and a quaternionic case

Problem 4 (The literal factorization in Fact 6.9 omits a real quaternionic case).  Fact 6.9, p. 53, states an \(\mathbb R\)- or \(\mathbb C\)-tensor factorization for every irreducible real representation of a product of connected reductive real algebraic groups. Its generality is false. The present example does not refute the additional semiproximal case used later; this is a Minor general-statement finding.

Let \(G=\mathrm{Sp}(1)\times\mathrm{Sp}(1)\) be the real algebraic product of unit quaternion groups, and let \(V=\mathbb H\) as a four-dimensional real vector space, with action \[(a,b)\cdot x=axb^{-1}.\] The action is real algebraic, and the groups are connected and reductive. The representation remains irreducible when restricted to either factor: the orbit of any nonzero quaternion under left (or right) multiplication spans \(\mathbb H\) over \(\mathbb R\).

Suppose the factorization stated in Fact 6.9 existed: \(V=W_1\otimes_{\mathbb K}W_2\), \(\mathbb K=\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\), with each \(W_s\) irreducible as a real representation of its factor. On restriction to the first factor, this tensor product is a direct sum of copies of the underlying real representation \(W_1\); the same statement holds for \(W_2\) and the second factor. The two irreducible restrictions of \(V\) would force each \(W_s\) to be isomorphic to a four-dimensional real representation. But the proposed tensor product then has real dimension \(16\) over \(\mathbb R\), or \(8\) over \(\mathbb C\), rather than \(4\). This is the missing quaternionic-type case.

The retained version of [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 5.5]{Benoist}], p. 22, contains the corresponding general assertion; citing it does not remove this explicit dimensional obstruction. This report makes no first-discovery claim. A corrected real representation-theoretic statement requires the relevant quaternionic/real-form treatment, or a proved restriction to an adequate special class.

There is also decisive counterevidence against overstating the application. The compact example is not \(G\)-semiproximal: left multiplication by a nonreal unit quaternion, with the second factor the identity, can have no real eigenvalues. Proposition 6.12, Step 3, has additional semiproximal hypotheses. The example therefore disproves the unrestricted Fact 6.9 but establishes no failure of that special case or central conclusion. No complete replacement theorem is claimed.
# Appendix A scope clarification and overall assessment

Lemma A.8(3), pp. 68–69, uses an inclusion \(\mathbb R^{2,1}\subset\mathbb R^{2,q}\). If equality is permitted, the written \(q\geq1\) scope admits \(q=1,c=0\) and, for the form \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1)\), \[v_0=(0,5/4,3/4),\qquad v_2=(0,5/4,-3/4),\qquad v_1=(1,0,0).\] All three vectors have norm \(1\), the two required pairings with \(v_1\) are zero, and the spanning determinant has absolute value \(15/8\). The pointwise stabilizer of \(v_0,v_2\) in \(\mathrm{SO}(2,1)\) is the identity: it fixes their nondegenerate two-dimensional span, and determinant one forces identity on the remaining line. It cannot move \(v_1\) out of \(\mathbb R^{2,0}\) as requested. A proper-inclusion interpretation excludes this example, and the actual application on p. 71 already separates \(q=1\) and works with \(q\geq2\). This is recorded as a scope clarification, not an unconditional defect in that application. A prior \(c=0\) concern about Lemma A.9 failed its premises and is not promoted as a finding.

The highest supported assessment is Major, attached to Problem 1 and its explicit role in the non-degeneracy/closedness proof. Problems 2 and 3 have proved local repairs. Problem 4 requires qualification but supplies no counterexample under its later semiproximal application. No result here establishes that the paper’s principal theorems are false. No author adoption or independent acceptance is asserted.

analysis: Fact 6.9, p. 53, states an \(\mathbb R\)- or \(\mathbb C\)-tensor factorization for every irreducible real representation of a product of connected reductive real algebraic groups. Its generality is false. The present example does not refute the additional semiproximal case used later; this is a Minor general-statement finding.

Let \(G=\mathrm{Sp}(1)\times\mathrm{Sp}(1)\) be the real algebraic product of unit quaternion groups, and let \(V=\mathbb H\) as a four-dimensional real vector space, with action \[(a,b)\cdot x=axb^{-1}.\] The action is real algebraic, and the groups are connected and reductive. The representation remains irreducible when restricted to either factor: the orbit of any nonzero quaternion under left (or right) multiplication spans \(\mathbb H\) over \(\mathbb R\).

Suppose the factorization stated in Fact 6.9 existed: \(V=W_1\otimes_{\mathbb K}W_2\), \(\mathbb K=\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\), with each \(W_s\) irreducible as a real representation of its factor. On restriction to the first factor, this tensor product is a direct sum of copies of the underlying real representation \(W_1\); the same statement holds for \(W_2\) and the second factor. The two irreducible restrictions of \(V\) would force each \(W_s\) to be isomorphic to a four-dimensional real representation. But the proposed tensor product then has real dimension \(16\) over \(\mathbb R\), or \(8\) over \(\mathbb C\), rather than \(4\). This is the missing quaternionic-type case.

The retained version of [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 5.5]{Benoist}], p. 22, contains the corresponding general assertion; citing it does not remove this explicit dimensional obstruction. This report makes no first-discovery claim. A corrected real representation-theoretic statement requires the relevant quaternionic/real-form treatment, or a proved restriction to an adequate special class.

There is also decisive counterevidence against overstating the application. The compact example is not \(G\)-semiproximal: left multiplication by a nonreal unit quaternion, with the second factor the identity, can have no real eigenvalues. Proposition 6.12, Step 3, has additional semiproximal hypotheses. The example therefore disproves the unrestricted Fact 6.9 but establishes no failure of that special case or central conclusion. No complete replacement theorem is claimed.
result: Impact: This is a literal general-statement counterexample, also requiring care in the cited Benoist Lemma5.5. It is not a counterexample under the additional semiproximal hypotheses used in Proposition6.12 Step3; generic compact rotations in this example lack real eigenvalues. No central damage from this finding alone is established.

report: Abstract: The manuscript proves that sufficiently large spherical caps fail to maximize the first nonconstant Neumann eigenvalue at fixed area, using a symmetric four-hole perturbation. This review identifies one confirmed scope defect: the general hole hypotheses in Section 3 do not exclude a bounded complementary component. A translated annulus invalidates Lemma 7, an auxiliary exterior problem, and the fixed-index conclusion of Proposition 3. The actual main construction uses filled ellipses, and Section 6 expressly assumes a simply connected hole. The demonstrated defect is classified as Minor; no failure of Theorem 1 is established. The numerical helmet-domain discussion is assessed within its expressly non-rigorous scope.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Scientific Review of
Spherical Caps do Not Always Maximize
Neumann Eigenvalues on the Sphere

Paper and version. M25-0392: Dorin Bucur, Richard S. Laugesen, Eloi Martinet, and Mickaël Nahon, Spherical Caps do Not Always Maximize Neumann Eigenvalues on the Sphere. Exact object reviewed: arXiv:2503.15385v1, 19 March 2025, 23 pages. Frozen journal identity: Geometric and Functional Analysis (2025), DOI `10.1007/s00039-025-00721-1`. The conclusions apply to this author manuscript; equivalence to the journal version has not been established. Physical and printed page numbers agree.
# Scope and principal argument

All 23 pages of the selected manuscript were read. The review examined the variational indexing, eigenvalue-cluster hypotheses, boundary normal conventions, ansatz and residual estimates in Sections 3 and 7, parameter choices proving Theorem 1, numerical status of Section 5, and fixed-shape restriction in Section 6. Critical formula pages and Figures 1–4 were also inspected as actual rendered source images. Source and evidence byte counts and SHA256 bindings accompany the report.

Theorem 1 asserts the existence of \(\delta>0\) such that for every \(\theta\in(\Theta-\delta,\pi)\) there is an open set of the same area as \(B_\theta\) with strictly larger \(\mu_1\). Here \(\mu_1(B_\Theta)\sin^2\Theta=1\). Proposition 2 supplies the double eigenspace generated by \(g(t)\cos\varphi\) and \(g(t)\sin\varphi\) and the hot-spot structure of \(g\). These are cited results from Langford and Laugesen [LL]. Their publisher-visible appendices were consulted, including the Wronskian comparison and Legendre-function argument. The complete proofs of their principal Propositions 3.1, 4.1 and 4.2 were not accessible in the material obtained. This review checks the deduction from the manuscript’s stated Proposition 2 and does not claim a complete independent reproof of that external input.

Equation reference: ellipse. For the filled ellipses in Section 4, the virtual-mass coefficients are \[
 \frac{(M_{\omega_\lambda})_{11}}{\pi}=\frac{2}{1+\lambda^{-2}},
 \qquad
 \frac{(M_{\omega_\lambda})_{22}}{\pi}=\frac{2}{1-\lambda^{-2}}.\] The fourfold rotational symmetry preserves the double cluster. On the limiting two-dimensional real eigenspace a quarter-turn has no real one-dimensional invariant subspace, and a commuting self-adjoint operator is scalar there. Continuity of the isolated spectral representation gives the same conclusion for sufficiently small holes.
# A missing topological hypothesis

Problem 1 (Minor: bounded components of the hole complement).  Section 3.1, pages 3–4, permits a smoothly bounded closed set \(\omega\subset\mathbb R^2\) whose interior contains the origin, without requiring \(\mathbb R^2\setminus\omega\) to be connected. Under these stated assumptions, the harmonic-extension estimate in Lemma 7 (page 22) and the fixed-index expansion in Proposition 3 (page 5) are false. The asserted matrix-valued exterior corrector on page 4 may not exist.
## Exact admissible geometry

Equation reference: annulus. Let \(c=(2,0)\) and take \[
 \omega=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:1\leq |x-c|\leq3\}.\] This closed annulus is compact and connected, with two smooth boundary circles. Since \(1<|c|=2<3\), its interior strictly contains the origin. The removed set itself is connected; its complement has the bounded component \(D_1(c)\) and the unbounded component \(\mathbb R^2\setminus\overline{D_3(c)}\).
## Failure of Lemma 7

Equation reference: h, energy. For the open set in Lemma 7 use the interior of [annulus] (#annulus), write \(r=|x-c|\), and define \[
 h(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&r\leq1,\\
 \log(3/r)/\log3,&1<r<3,\\
 0,&r\geq3.
 \end{cases}\] The traces match at both circles, so \(h\) is a compactly supported \(H^1(\mathbb R^2)\) function. It is harmonic in the annulus, and \[
 \int_{\omega}|\nabla h|^2\,\mathrm dx
 =\frac{2\pi}{(\log3)^2}\int_1^3\frac{\,\mathrm dr}{r}
 =\frac{2\pi}{\log3}>0,\qquad
 \int_{\mathbb R^2\setminus\omega}|\nabla h|^2\,\mathrm dx=0.\] No finite constant in Lemma 7 satisfies the asserted estimate. The single-mean Poincaré inequality after inversion is the failed step: functions constant at different values on distinct components have zero gradient and need not equal one common mean.
## Failure of the fixed-index spectral assertion

Equation reference: chart, zero. The same geometry satisfies every stated geometric hypothesis preceding Proposition 3. Set \(M=\Omega=\mathbb S^2\), use one marked point at the south pole, and let the boundary vector field be zero. Empty boundary is explicitly allowed. A conformal chart with conformal factor one at the origin is \[
 \psi(x)=\left(\frac{4x_1}{4+|x|^2},
              \frac{4x_2}{4+|x|^2},
              \frac{|x|^2-4}{4+|x|^2}\right).\] For a fixed chart ball \(B_r\) and \(0<\varepsilon<r/5\), the entire set \(\varepsilon\omega\) lies inside \(B_r\). The cluster \(I=\{1,2,3\}\) satisfies the required gap conditions: \[\mu_0(\mathbb S^2)=0<\mu_1(\mathbb S^2)=\mu_2(\mathbb S^2)
 =\mu_3(\mathbb S^2)=2<\mu_4(\mathbb S^2)=6.\] But \(\Omega^\varepsilon=\mathbb S^2\setminus\psi(\varepsilon\omega)\) has two connected components: the image of the small interior disk and the exterior of the outer circle. Constants on these components form a two-dimensional Neumann kernel. With the paper’s multiplicity indexing and its mean-zero variational definition on page 1, \[
 \mu_0(\Omega^\varepsilon)=\mu_1(\Omega^\varepsilon)=0.\] This contradicts the claimed convergence of the index \(i=1\) to \(2\).

The matrix corrector \(L\) on page 4 faces a further direct obstruction. On \(D_1(c)\) its boundary condition would imply, for either diagonal entry and the outward disk normal \(n\), \[\int_{\partial D_1(c)}\partial_n L_{ii}\,\mathrm ds
 =\int_{\partial D_1(c)}x_i n_i\,\mathrm ds=|D_1(c)|=\pi.\] A harmonic function on the disk has zero total outward flux. Thus this component of the proposed exterior problem is incompatible. Summing a flux identity over all boundary components does not remove the compatibility requirement on each bounded component.
## Counterreadings, impact, and repair limits

If hole is intended to mean a filled obstacle with connected exterior, that interpretation adds the missing hypothesis. It does not follow from smoothly bounded closed set, and the annulus itself is connected. The additional zero mode cannot be discarded silently: the manuscript counts multiplicities and fixes indices. The compactness argument on page 7 fails for the same reason: the \(L^2\)-normalized indicator of the shrinking interior component has zero Dirichlet energy and no strongly convergent \(L^2\) subsequence after extension by zero.

A suitable local correction is to require each removed set to have connected complement, for example to be the closure of a smooth bounded simply connected domain, and to add the matching assumption in Lemma 7. After inversion the complement is then a connected bounded domain. Subtracting one mean permits Poincaré’s inequality; a trace/extension estimate and harmonic energy minimization give the needed Dirichlet-energy bound. Two-dimensional conformal invariance supports the scaling. This identifies the failed step and a correction compatible with the actual applications. It is not an amended theorem allowing cavities, which would need componentwise constants and different spectral indexing.

Section 4 uses filled ellipses; Section 6 explicitly assumes a fixed simply connected hole. The counterexample lies outside both families after the stated correction. No demonstrated dependence failure survives in those applications. This local scope failure is therefore classified as Minor, without claiming a refutation of Theorem 1.
# Further checks and evidence limits
## Analytical versus numerical assertions

Section 5 explicitly identifies its helmet-domain arguments as non-rigorous. The curves in Figure 3 and the mode transition in Figure 4 were actually observed; their numerical intervals are not promoted here to certified bounds. The graph-limit expression and its sign mechanism were examined as heuristics. A rigorous theorem for the lower numerical threshold is neither claimed there nor established by this review.

In Section 6 the sphere eigenspace matrix gives \[\mu_1(\Omega^\varepsilon)+\mu_2(\Omega^\varepsilon)
 =4-3\,\operatorname{cap}[\omega]^2\varepsilon^2+o(\varepsilon^2).\] The argument uses fixed smooth simply connected shapes and the area–capacity comparison with the disk. It expressly does not optimize over arbitrary shape-changing sequences of large domains. The difference between fixed planar hole area and the corresponding spherical area changes only higher orders in the comparison. No counterexample was obtained within this scope.
## Independent calculation and static code inspection

The decisive arguments [energy] (#energy)–[kappa] (#kappa) are analytical. A reviewer-authored script checked the rational coefficients, the origin-in-annulus condition, and an independent composite-Simpson evaluation of [energy] (#energy). It returned \(5.7192017347602535\) for the nonzero energy and zero exterior energy. This is an arithmetic and quadrature check, not an eigenvalue solver or a replacement for the topological and PDE proofs.

The preserved author repository is pinned to commit `159ee85f54e966c530ae5de0ceb093b5c6f7d56e`. Its README and two FreeFem++ scripts were read statically. The eigenvalue script assembles surface \(P_1\) stiffness and mass matrices; the mesh-generation script describes punctured caps. Four retained value tables were programmatically indexed, not reproduced as scientific computations. The 471 mesh files in the preserved index were not acquired, and a direct mapping from the retained material to the helmet curves in Figure 3 was not established. No author code was executed. These are reproducibility limits, not confirmed mathematical defects or evidence that the published curves are false.
# Assessment
Item | Status | Demonstrated consequence
Problem 1 | Minor | Lemma 7 and Proposition 3 need a connected-exterior hypothesis; a cavity also obstructs \(L\).
Theorem 1 | No further confirmed defect in the examined deduction | The filled-ellipse argument avoids the example; Proposition 2 remains an explicitly identified external input.
Section 5 | Numerical; heuristic | Figures were inspected; numerical reproduction and certified thresholds are not claimed.

An explicit topological restriction and a matching correction of the extension/exterior-problem discussion are requested. The absence of additional confirmed findings is limited to the work and evidence described above.
## Supporting checks

No substantive prior report for this paper was recovered. Preserved source bytes and the pinned repository snapshot were reused. The reading, mathematical arguments, reviewer calculation, report, compilation and actual image inspection belong to the current scientific conversation.
The scientific runtime self-description is GPT-6 Astra Pro; backend equivalence was not independently established. The controller contributed scheduling and byte collection.

The report uses the existing Tectonic 0.17.0 runtime without shell escape. Exact source, TeX, compiler, per-paper dependency, log, PDF and actually viewed image bindings are recorded alongside it. Delivery completion records initial-review work only. The scientific decision remains pending, human reviews are empty, and independent scientific acceptance is reserved for a later reviewer.

Frozen journal DOI: `10.1007/s00039-025-00721-1`. J. J. Langford and R. S. Laugesen, Maximizers beyond the hemisphere for the second Neumann eigenvalue, Math. Ann. 386 (2023), 2255–2281. DOI: `10.1007/s00208-022-02455-z`. Only accessible publisher material and appendices were consulted; the principal propositions were not fully independently audited.
