report: Abstract: The paper develops a coupling criterion for random dynamical systems with stationary, possibly correlated noise. The selected v3 repairs the earlier coupling marginal error. Two remaining Major problems concern the transfer of noise regularity to the abstract hypotheses and a common continuous-time invariant set asserted under a sliding-window energy bound. Explicit examples invalidate these steps without disproving the conditional abstract mixing theorem. Two further Minor problems concern time-boundedness of the proposed noise and an unjustified strengthening from dual-Lipschitz to total-variation type mixing. Each finding below includes its hypotheses, decisive proof, actual scope and repair limits.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Scientific Review of
Mixing for Dynamical Systems
Driven by Stationary Noises

Identity and object reviewed. M25-0393: Sergei Kuksin and Armen Shirikyan, Mixing for Dynamical Systems Driven by Stationary Noises. Frozen journal identity: Geometric and Functional Analysis (2025), DOI `10.1007/s00039-025-00722-0`. The exact source is arXiv:2502.11699v3, submitted 25 December 2025, with internal date 29 December 2025, 56 pages. The retained v2 was consulted only for the coupling revision. No equality with the journal version is presumed. Page references below are physical PDF pages, agreeing with printed pages.
# Scope, contribution, and assessment

All 56 pages of the selected source were read, including the assumptions, proofs, applications, appendix and references. The principal chain examined was the Markov lift, the local change-of-noise coupling, recurrence and squeezing, the approximate right inverse in Lemma 3.5, and the use of Theorem 3.4 in the noise constructions and ODE/PDE applications. The coupling construction in v3, pp. 22–23, now glues measures with the same middle marginal \[\Psi(U,U',\cdot)_*\mathcal P(U;\cdot).\] Equation (2.38) also includes the required variation distance between \(\mathcal P(U;\cdot)\) and \(\mathcal P(U';\cdot)\). These are material corrections to the corresponding v2 argument (Proposition 1.4 there); they are credited as current repairs, not repeated as findings.

The measurable gluing hypothesis was checked against Bogachev–Malofeev, Corollary 3.7, in the exact retained preprint arXiv:1904.03642v2, pp. 10–12. The spaces here are Polish and the parameterized pair laws are measurable, so its common-marginal construction fits the corrected step. This is a check of that dependency, not a review of the entire reference. Other cited monographs and PDE papers were not all independently audited.

The recurrence/squeezing mechanism was checked directly: once a pair is within distance \(\theta\), the sum of its subsequent failure probabilities is at most \(N\theta/(1-q)\); the probability of a first failure after \(r\) successful contractions is \(O(q^r)\). Uniform positive-probability access to a smaller neighborhood yields geometric returns and, with \(\theta\) small, exponential control of repeated attempts. Thus the intended dual-Lipschitz coupling conclusion is consistent with the stated local and global criteria. The problems below concern additional assertions and hypothesis verification. The overall first-review assessment is Major, with two Major and two Minor findings. No counterexample to Theorem 3.4 with all its written hypotheses is asserted.
# Noise regularity and the infinite-dimensional applications

Problem 1 (Major: unsupported transfers of noise regularity).  The infinite-dimensional part of \((\eta1)\) on p. 5 does not imply the total-variation Lipschitz condition (SF) on p. 16, contrary to p. 29. Moreover, the spatial product construction (4.16) need not preserve even total-variation continuity. The literal support requirement on the density in (DLP\('\)), p. 28, is itself impossible for a nonzero continuous density on an infinite-dimensional ambient space with compact \(K\).
## A. A literal counterexample to the claimed implication

Set \[f(x)=\tfrac34(1-x^2)\mathbf1_{[-1,1]}(x),\qquad
 a_l=2^{-l},\qquad r_l=4^{-l}.\] The function \(f\) is a globally Lipschitz probability density, \(\int xf(x)\,dx=0\), and \(\int|x|f(x)\,dx=3/8\). For every \(l\), let \((X_{k,l})_{k\in\mathbb Z}\) be a stationary Markov chain with invariant density \(f\) and transition density \[p_l(x,y)=f(y)(1+a_lxy),\qquad -1\leq x,y\leq1.\] Invariance follows by integrating in \(x\), and \(p_l(x,y)\geq(1-a_l)f(y)\geq f(y)/2\). Take these chains independently over \(l\) and put \(\eta_k=\sum_l r_lX_{k,l}e_l\) in \(E=\ell^2\). The coordinate box \(K=\prod_l[-r_l,r_l]\) is compact in \(\ell^2\); positive finite-dimensional cylinder probabilities give full support \(K^{\mathbb Z_-}\) for the past. The conditional kernel is thus defined on every past required by \((\eta1)\), not just a specially chosen null set.

The recurrence assumption \((\eta2)\) also holds. Given a neighborhood of zero, choose finitely many coordinates so that the remaining deterministic \(\ell^2\) tail is smaller than half its radius. In the finitely many selected coordinates, the minorization by \(f/2\) gives a strictly positive lower bound for any prescribed finite block to stay near zero, uniformly over the entire past. Taking the product gives the required uniform block probability. Thus recurrence does not repair [eq:badSF] (#eq:badSF). If a dynamics satisfying the introductory smoothing and controllability assumptions is desired, take \(H=V=\mathbb R\) and \(S(u,\eta)=\langle\eta,e_1\rangle\). Its free map is zero and its noise derivative is onto. This dynamics actually mixes; the example refutes the claimed implication used in the proof, not that mixing conclusion.
## B. Infinite independent spatial copies can destroy continuity

The failure of Proposition 4.10, p. 43, is stronger than a missing constant in a product estimate. Choose a bounded trigonometric orthonormal basis \((\varphi_l)\) of \(L^2(0,1)\) with \(\varphi_1=1\), and positive coefficients \(c_l\) so small that \(\sum_lc_l\|\varphi_l\|_\infty\leq1\). Let \(\nu\) be the law of \(\sum_l c_l Z_l\varphi_l\), where \(Z_l\) have density \(f\) independently, and write \(c_1>0\) for its first radius. Set \[\chi(y)=\max(-1,\min(1,\langle y,\varphi_1\rangle/c_1)),\qquad
 g(\xi,y)=1+\alpha\chi(\xi_0)\chi(y),\quad 0<\alpha<1.\] This is globally Lipschitz on the domain of Proposition 4.7, \(g\geq1-\alpha\), and its normalizing factor \(m(\xi)\) is one by symmetry. The resulting scalar block process has a first coefficient following the Markov kernel \(f(y)(1+\alpha xy)\); its other coefficients can be independent between blocks. It is stationary, has full past support, satisfies scalar (SF), has regular finite-dimensional conditional densities, and satisfies the uniform recurrence condition by the same minorization argument. Every time trajectory is bounded by one.

Take independent identical spatial copies of this scalar process and coefficients \(b_j=2^{-j}\) as in (4.16). Change only the first temporal coefficient in spatial coordinate \(j\) of the most recent past block between \(\pm c_1b_j\). The history distance is \(2c_1b_j\to0\). Nevertheless the event that the same coefficient in the next block is positive has probability difference \(3\alpha/8\), independent of \(j\). Both sequences of pasts approach the zero past; their conditional laws cannot both converge to its law in variation. Hence (SF) fails even at the level of continuity.

Rescaling independent coordinates makes them small in the Hilbert norm, but does not make distinguishable scalar probability laws close in variation. Faster spatial decay of \(b_j\) alone cannot fix this example. The scalar construction has bounded paths, so the additional scalar boundedness assumed in the Navier–Stokes application does not exclude it.
## C. The literal compact-support requirement in DLP-prime

There is a separate formal obstruction that must not be concealed in claiming an example satisfies the printed hypotheses. For fixed \(\xi\), the written (DLP\('\)) requires a Lipschitz function \(\rho_n(\xi,\cdot)\) on all of \(E\), supported in compact \(K\). If \(E\) is infinite dimensional, \(K\) has empty interior. A continuous function nonzero at a point is nonzero on a neighborhood of that point, which here would force an open ball into \(K\). Thus \(\rho_n(\xi,\cdot)\equiv0\), incompatible with a normalized conditional density. For \(g\equiv1\), formula (4.14) itself gives a nonzero product of the first \(n\) coordinate densities independent of the tail; it is not supported in compact \(K\) as a function on all of \(E\).

Accordingly, example B is a failure of the stated construction and of its proposed (SF) transfer after the natural finite-fiber interpretation of (DLP\('\)). It is not presented as satisfying the impossible literal infinite-dimensional support clause. Example A independently satisfies all the actual clauses of \((\eta1)\) and \((\eta2)\) and refutes the explicit implication on p. 29.
## Impact and repair limits

These failures occur in the passage from the advertised noise classes to the hypotheses of the central mixing criterion. In particular, Theorem 5.4’s proof, p. 49, invokes Theorem 3.4 and Proposition 4.10 without establishing the required (SF) for general correlated spatial copies. This is a core application gap, hence Major; it is not merely an omitted factor in an estimate. The abstract theorem with (SF) explicitly assumed is not refuted, nor is mixing of every affected PDE asserted false.

Possible repairs include imposing (SF) directly and proving it for a narrower noise class, or adding quantitative summability of the scaled coordinate variation-Lipschitz constants. Mere summed continuity is insufficient. For identical nontrivial spatial memory, a different noise model or a coupling argument using a weaker metric is needed; the existing product assertion cannot be justified by amplitude decay alone. The density support clause should be formulated in finite fibers (for example, bounded support in the \(F_n\) variable on relevant tail fibers) while the conditional measure remains supported in \(K\). That textual repair removes the empty-interior contradiction but leaves both variation-distance failures intact. A full revised application theorem is not supplied here.
# The common invariant set in the ODE application

Problem 2 (Major: Proposition 5.1’s invariant set is false under (5.3)).  The common compact set asserted on pp. 44–45 for all continuous times does not follow from (BAS), even for a globally exponentially stable linear oscillator system. The proof incorrectly treats concatenated controls as retaining the same sliding-window energy bound.

Use two oscillators, \(n=2\), with \[V(q_1,q_2)=\tfrac12(q_1^2+q_2^2),\qquad \gamma_1=\gamma_2=1.\] Both endpoints are damped, and \(q_i'=p_i,\ p_i'=-q_i-p_i+\zeta_i\). This is precisely a smooth coercive potential in (5.1). For each oscillator let \[A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 P=\begin{pmatrix}3/2&1/2\\1/2&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 A^{T}P+PA=-I.\] The eigenvalues of \(A\) have real part \(-1/2\) and \(P>0\). Writing \(L=\sum_{i=1}^2(q_i,p_i)P(q_i,p_i)^T\) and \(c=1/(2\lambda_{\max}(P))>0\), Young’s inequality gives \[L'(t)\leq-cL(t)+\tfrac52\bigl(|\zeta_1(t)|^2+|\zeta_2(t)|^2\bigr).\] If (5.3) holds with any \(M>0\), splitting the convolution into intervals of length one yields \[L(t)\leq e^{-ct}L(0)+\frac{5M}{2(1-e^{-c})}.\] This proves (BAS), with a small additional margin for finite-time absorption, uniformly over every initial bounded ball. The unforced system converges to zero uniformly on every bounded set. It therefore satisfies the global stability property intended by (SE), including its displayed uniform convergence on any proposed compact \(X\).

Now fix \(M=1\) and suppose a nonempty compact \(X\) were invariant for every control satisfying (5.3). Choose a point \((q^*,p^*)\in X\) at which \(p_1\) is maximal, and set \[A_0=1+|p_1^*|+|q_1^*|,\qquad
 \delta=\frac1{2A_0^2},\qquad
 \zeta_1(t)=A_0\mathbf1_{[0,\delta]}(t),\quad \zeta_2(t)=0.\] Every sliding unit window has total energy at most \(A_0^2\delta=1/2<1\). At time zero, however, \[p_1'(0+)=-q_1^*-p_1^*+A_0>0.\] For sufficiently small positive \(t<\delta\) the trajectory has \(p_1(t)>\max_Xp_1\), so it leaves \(X\). Thus no such nonempty compact invariant set exists. The absorption assertion rules out using an empty \(X\). This counterexample does not depend on a numerical time step or an unproved stability criterion.

The stronger pointwise bound (1.12) would exclude arbitrarily high pulses. It is not a hypothesis of Proposition 5.1: p. 44 expressly treats it as a stronger sufficient condition, whereas (5.3) and (BAS) are the hypotheses under discussion. Similarly, invariance only at integer times is different from the displayed assertion for every \(t\geq0\).

The set built on p. 45 contains states reachable under controls of energy budget \(M\). Extending an arbitrary such state by another admissible control may put pieces of two controls into one sliding window, with energy as large as \(2M\). The asserted invariance therefore does not follow from its definition. It is subsequently used in the reduction of Theorem 5.2 to a compact invariant state space and in formulating (LC), so the false lemma is a Major proof dependency.

An integer-time repair is plausible and more appropriate to the stated mixing conclusion: concatenate aligned unit blocks, use the fact that their arbitrary sliding-window energy is at most \(2M\), and construct an invariant set for the block map using (BAS) at budget \(2M\). Compactness and the domain of (LC) must then be rechecked for that set. Alternatively one can impose a suitable uniform pointwise forcing bound and prove a genuine continuous-time invariant set. Neither option is a proof that the present statement of Proposition 5.1 is valid.

There is also a separate proof-level qualification on p. 46: convergence in (SE) on a compact set does not, by itself, give the global norm contraction on all of \(H\) required by (GD). Uniform attraction on the repaired compact set can instead be used directly for the global accessibility condition of Theorem 2.3. The printed argument needs this change; no counterexample to the final integer-time mixing conclusion is asserted.
# Two local excess claims

Problem 3 (Minor: \(L^2\) coefficient bounds do not give bounded paths).  Propositions 4.9 and 4.10, pp. 42–43, claim almost surely bounded time trajectories from the construction on p. 41. An arbitrary orthonormal basis and \(\sum_l c_l^2<\infty\) do not imply this assertion.

Partition \((0,1)\) into \(I_j=(2^{-j},2^{1-j})\), of lengths \(2^{-j}\). Choose an orthonormal basis whose odd members are \(\varphi_{2j-1}=2^{j/2}\mathbf1_{I_j}\); enumerate, at the even indices, orthonormal bases of the zero-mean subspaces of all the \(L^2(I_j)\). These together form a complete orthonormal basis. Give the odd coefficients radii \(c_{2j-1}=2^{-j/4}\) and the even ones radii \(c_{2j}=2^{-j}\), and take independent coefficients \(\zeta_l=c_lZ_l\) with density \(f\) for \(Z_l\). The prescribed square summability holds, each coefficient density is Lipschitz and compactly supported, and the resulting Hilbert box is compact in \(L^2\). Choose \(g\equiv1\) in the construction.

All even basis functions have integral zero over each \(I_j\). Hence the average of the \(L^2\) random function on \(I_j\) equals \(\zeta_{2j-1}2^{j/2}\). Independently for every \(j\), \[\mathbb P\{|\zeta_{2j-1}|\geq c_{2j-1}/2\}
 =2\int_{1/2}^1f(x)\,dx=\frac5{16}.\] The second Borel–Cantelli lemma implies that infinitely many averages have absolute value at least \(\tfrac12\,2^{j/4}\). No essentially bounded representative can have these averages. The failure already occurs within one time block, despite compact support and uniform boundedness in \(L^2\).

This example satisfies the coefficient and basis assumptions of the construction; it does not purport to satisfy the impossible literal support clause discussed in Problem Problem 1 (#p:noise). A sufficient repair is \(\sum_l c_l\|\varphi_l\|_\infty<\infty\). The Navier–Stokes section separately assumes scalar paths bounded by one, which excludes this example. Thus this demonstrated time-regularity overstatement is Minor; it does not independently refute that application.

Problem 4 (Minor: dual-Lipschitz convergence does not imply (4.11)).  The sentence on p. 39 deducing strong feeble mixing of a stationary weak solution from Proposition 3.7 is false in the stated generality. The supremum in (4.11) has no bound on the Lipschitz constants of its continuous test functions.

This time all hypotheses of Theorem 3.4 can be met literally with finite-dimensional noise. Let \(H=\ell^2\), \(E=\mathbb R\), \(a=1/2\), and \(R\) be the right shift. Take iid noise \(\eta_k\) of density \(f\) and \[S(u,\eta)=\eta e_1+aRu,\qquad
 X=\{u: |u_j|\leq a^{j-1}\}.\] The set \(X\) is compact and invariant. The map is smooth and bounded with its derivatives on bounded sets. Condition (GD) holds in one step. For \(G=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}\), \(\|(I-P_G)D_uS\|=a<1\), and \(D_\eta S\) has image \(G\), so (ALC) holds on the whole ambient space. The iid law has (SF) with constant zero. For (DLP\('\)) take \(F_n=E=\mathbb R\), \(F_n^\dagger=\{0\}\) and \(\rho_n=f\); its compact support is now legitimate. Positivity of \(f\) near zero gives (SRZ).

The stationary solution is \[u_k=(\eta_k,a\eta_{k-1},a^2\eta_{k-2},\ldots).\] Given its past through time zero, \((u_k)_{k+1}=a^k(u_0)_1\) is deterministic. Under the stationary unconditional law, this coordinate is continuously distributed. For a fixed past with \((u_0)_1=z\), take the continuous test function \[g_{k,\varepsilon}(x)=
 \max\left(1-\frac{|x_{k+1}-a^kz|}{\varepsilon a^k},\,0\right).\] Its sup norm is at most one. The conditional expectation is one, whereas its stationary expectation is at most \(3\varepsilon/2\), since \(f\leq3/4\). Thus the supremum in (4.11), already for \(m=1\), is at least \(1-3\varepsilon/2\) for every \(k\), and hence at least one after letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). It does not tend to zero.

The solution process also need not satisfy the noise-style (SF) that precedes the definition on p. 39. One cannot transfer that property from the driving noise to this state process. The example still converges exponentially in dual-Lipschitz distance by synchronous coupling, with its unforced tail shrinking as \(a^k\); it therefore does not challenge Proposition 3.7’s actual weak convergence. Retain the weaker feeble-mixing conclusion, or impose and prove additional total-variation regularization of the state process. The isolated strengthening is Minor relative to the main dual-Lipschitz results.
# Other proof checks and limits

The approximate inverse argument of Lemma 3.5 needs a small local justification: distance to \(A(y)F_n\) need not be continuous when its rank drops. It is upper semicontinuous, since it is the infimum of continuous residual norms over fixed coefficients. Pointwise approximation, monotonicity in \(n\), and a finite cover of the compact parameter–target set give the uniform estimate (3.25). The regularized inverse and its spectral estimate then give the intended conclusion. This was not promoted to another confirmed theorem defect.

Likewise, a Lipschitz extension into finite-dimensional \(F\) from a general Banach domain may cost a finite constant, rather than the Hilbert-space constant one of Kirszbraun’s theorem. Coordinatewise scalar extensions suffice for the appendix after reducing the smallness threshold. The finite-dimensional change-of-variables bound retains order \(O(\kappa)\). No independent counterexample to the appendix’s needed perturbative conclusion was found. The final choice of \(l\) in the proof of Proposition 2.5 should keep the earlier contraction waiting time \(k_*\) rather than replace it by one; the earlier estimates supply the required finite \(l\). These local repairs do not resolve Problems 1 or 2.

The Navier–Stokes energy dissipation and full-noise linear control mechanism, and the declared scope of the complex Ginzburg–Landau application, were read and traced. Theorem 5.5 explicitly assumes (SF); its conditional form is not refuted by Problem 1. Its proposed continuous-noise extensions require the same careful hypothesis check. The literature inputs for PDE regularity were not re-proved in full. No simulation or numerical evidence in this review is used as a proof of infinite-dimensional mixing.
Item | Class | Decisive impact
1 | Major | Noise hypotheses do not transfer as claimed; core application of the abstract criterion is unsupported.
2 | Major | Common continuous-time compact invariant set is false under the written energy hypothesis; ODE reduction needs revision.
3 | Minor | Claimed bounded time paths fail for an allowed orthonormal basis and square-summable coefficient bounds.
4 | Minor | Strong feeble mixing of the state process does not follow; the weaker dual-Lipschitz conclusion survives.

The exact v2/v3 comparison and the cited gluing pages are separately bound to their source bytes.

The selected manuscript contains no numerical reproducibility claim requiring author-code execution; no author code was run. The official arXiv version record was consulted. problems.title: Infinite-dimensional noise regularity does not transfer as asserted
problems.source_location: Pages: 5 Pages: 16 Pages: 28 Pages: 29 Objects: eta1 Objects: SF Objects: DLP-prime Objects: explicit eta1 implication Pages: 41 Pages: 42 Pages: 43 Pages: 49 Objects: Propositions 4.7, 4.9, 4.10 Objects: Navier-Stokes application Source locations: eta1 p.5 and history metric p.4; SF p.16; DLP-prime p.28 and claimed implication p.29; Propositions 4.7/4.9/4.10 pp.41-43; application pp.48-49.
claim: Summed L1 continuity of coordinate conditional densities does not give a common TV-Lipschitz bound; identical spatial copies need not preserve TV continuity; the literal compact support of a continuous finite-fiber density on all of infinite-dimensional E is impossible.
analysis: The infinite-dimensional part of \((\eta1)\) on p. 5 does not imply the total-variation Lipschitz condition (SF) on p. 16, contrary to p. 29. Moreover, the spatial product construction (4.16) need not preserve even total-variation continuity. The literal support requirement on the density in (DLP\('\)), p. 28, is itself impossible for a nonzero continuous density on an infinite-dimensional ambient space with compact \(K\).

Set \[f(x)=\tfrac34(1-x^2)\mathbf1_{[-1,1]}(x),\qquad
 a_l=2^{-l},\qquad r_l=4^{-l}.\] The function \(f\) is a globally Lipschitz probability density, \(\int xf(x)\,dx=0\), and \(\int|x|f(x)\,dx=3/8\). For every \(l\), let \((X_{k,l})_{k\in\mathbb Z}\) be a stationary Markov chain with invariant density \(f\) and transition density \[p_l(x,y)=f(y)(1+a_lxy),\qquad -1\leq x,y\leq1.\] Invariance follows by integrating in \(x\), and \(p_l(x,y)\geq(1-a_l)f(y)\geq f(y)/2\). Take these chains independently over \(l\) and put \(\eta_k=\sum_l r_lX_{k,l}e_l\) in \(E=\ell^2\). The coordinate box \(K=\prod_l[-r_l,r_l]\) is compact in \(\ell^2\); positive finite-dimensional cylinder probabilities give full support \(K^{\mathbb Z_-}\) for the past. The conditional kernel is thus defined on every past required by \((\eta1)\), not just a specially chosen null set.

The recurrence assumption \((\eta2)\) also holds. Given a neighborhood of zero, choose finitely many coordinates so that the remaining deterministic \(\ell^2\) tail is smaller than half its radius. In the finitely many selected coordinates, the minorization by \(f/2\) gives a strictly positive lower bound for any prescribed finite block to stay near zero, uniformly over the entire past. Taking the product gives the required uniform block probability. Thus recurrence does not repair [eq:badSF] (#eq:badSF). If a dynamics satisfying the introductory smoothing and controllability assumptions is desired, take \(H=V=\mathbb R\) and \(S(u,\eta)=\langle\eta,e_1\rangle\). Its free map is zero and its noise derivative is onto. This dynamics actually mixes; the example refutes the claimed implication used in the proof, not that mixing conclusion.

The failure of Proposition 4.10, p. 43, is stronger than a missing constant in a product estimate. Choose a bounded trigonometric orthonormal basis \((\varphi_l)\) of \(L^2(0,1)\) with \(\varphi_1=1\), and positive coefficients \(c_l\) so small that \(\sum_lc_l\|\varphi_l\|_\infty\leq1\). Let \(\nu\) be the law of \(\sum_l c_l Z_l\varphi_l\), where \(Z_l\) have density \(f\) independently, and write \(c_1>0\) for its first radius. Set \[\chi(y)=\max(-1,\min(1,\langle y,\varphi_1\rangle/c_1)),\qquad
 g(\xi,y)=1+\alpha\chi(\xi_0)\chi(y),\quad 0<\alpha<1.\] This is globally Lipschitz on the domain of Proposition 4.7, \(g\geq1-\alpha\), and its normalizing factor \(m(\xi)\) is one by symmetry. The resulting scalar block process has a first coefficient following the Markov kernel \(f(y)(1+\alpha xy)\); its other coefficients can be independent between blocks. It is stationary, has full past support, satisfies scalar (SF), has regular finite-dimensional conditional densities, and satisfies the uniform recurrence condition by the same minorization argument. Every time trajectory is bounded by one.

Take independent identical spatial copies of this scalar process and coefficients \(b_j=2^{-j}\) as in (4.16). Change only the first temporal coefficient in spatial coordinate \(j\) of the most recent past block between \(\pm c_1b_j\). The history distance is \(2c_1b_j\to0\). Nevertheless the event that the same coefficient in the next block is positive has probability difference \(3\alpha/8\), independent of \(j\). Both sequences of pasts approach the zero past; their conditional laws cannot both converge to its law in variation. Hence (SF) fails even at the level of continuity.

Rescaling independent coordinates makes them small in the Hilbert norm, but does not make distinguishable scalar probability laws close in variation. Faster spatial decay of \(b_j\) alone cannot fix this example. The scalar construction has bounded paths, so the additional scalar boundedness assumed in the Navier–Stokes application does not exclude it.

There is a separate formal obstruction that must not be concealed in claiming an example satisfies the printed hypotheses. For fixed \(\xi\), the written (DLP\('\)) requires a Lipschitz function \(\rho_n(\xi,\cdot)\) on all of \(E\), supported in compact \(K\). If \(E\) is infinite dimensional, \(K\) has empty interior. A continuous function nonzero at a point is nonzero on a neighborhood of that point, which here would force an open ball into \(K\). Thus \(\rho_n(\xi,\cdot)\equiv0\), incompatible with a normalized conditional density. For \(g\equiv1\), formula (4.14) itself gives a nonzero product of the first \(n\) coordinate densities independent of the tail; it is not supported in compact \(K\) as a function on all of \(E\).

Accordingly, example B is a failure of the stated construction and of its proposed (SF) transfer after the natural finite-fiber interpretation of (DLP\('\)). It is not presented as satisfying the impossible literal infinite-dimensional support clause. Example A independently satisfies all the actual clauses of \((\eta1)\) and \((\eta2)\) and refutes the explicit implication on p. 29.

These failures occur in the passage from the advertised noise classes to the hypotheses of the central mixing criterion. In particular, Theorem 5.4’s proof, p. 49, invokes Theorem 3.4 and Proposition 4.10 without establishing the required (SF) for general correlated spatial copies. This is a core application gap, hence Major; it is not merely an omitted factor in an estimate. The abstract theorem with (SF) explicitly assumed is not refuted, nor is mixing of every affected PDE asserted false.

Possible repairs include imposing (SF) directly and proving it for a narrower noise class, or adding quantitative summability of the scaled coordinate variation-Lipschitz constants. Mere summed continuity is insufficient. For identical nontrivial spatial memory, a different noise model or a coupling argument using a weaker metric is needed; the existing product assertion cannot be justified by amplitude decay alone. The density support clause should be formulated in finite fibers (for example, bounded support in the \(F_n\) variable on relevant tail fibers) while the conditional measure remains supported in \(K\). That textual repair removes the empty-interior contradiction but leaves both variation-distance failures intact. A full revised application theorem is not supplied here.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Infinite-dimensional noise regularity does not transfer as asserted

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Assume/prove SF directly for a narrower class or require a quantitative summed scaled coordinate TV-Lipschitz bound. Reformulate DLP-prime support in finite fibers while maintaining actual conditional measure support K. Identical nontrivial memory spatial products require a different noise class or a weaker-metric coupling.

 \max\left(1-\frac{|x_{k+1}-a^kz|}{\varepsilon a^k},\,0\right).\] Its sup norm is at most one. The conditional expectation is one, whereas its stationary expectation is at most \(3\varepsilon/2\), since \(f\leq3/4\). Thus the supremum in (4.11), already for \(m=1\), is at least \(1-3\varepsilon/2\) for every \(k\), and hence at least one after letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). It does not tend to zero.

The solution process also need not satisfy the noise-style (SF) that precedes the definition on p. 39. One cannot transfer that property from the driving noise to this state process. The example still converges exponentially in dual-Lipschitz distance by synchronous coupling, with its unforced tail shrinking as \(a^k\); it therefore does not challenge Proposition 3.7’s actual weak convergence. Retain the weaker feeble-mixing conclusion, or impose and prove additional total-variation regularization of the state process. The isolated strengthening is Minor relative to the main dual-Lipschitz results.

report: Abstract: The Donaldson-divisor construction gives a compelling mechanism for circle bundles with positive scalar curvature over large bases. Theorem A survives the local corrections established here. One Major problem concerns the four-dimensional skeletal-compression dependency used to finish Theorem B: a decisive homotopy-group identification in the cited proof is false in the required dimension. This is a confirmed gap in the cited argument, not a counterexample to Theorem B. Three Minor findings concern the boundary-to-spine proof, an impossible alternative in Example 10, and a width constant. Explicit witnesses, repairs where available, and the limits of each conclusion are supplied below.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Scientific Review of
Circle Bundles with PSC
over Large Manifolds

Identity and reviewed version. M25-0394: Aditya Kumar and Balarka Sen, Circle Bundles with PSC over Large Manifolds, Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 1400–1423, DOI `10.1007/s00039-025-00723-z`. The packet’s exact scientific source is arXiv:2412.01047v5, 29 October 2025, 24 pages. Unless otherwise stated, page numbers are physical pages of that PDF, agreeing with its printed pagination. A journal PDF retrieved from the German National Library was separately retained and its identity and selected corresponding passages checked. This limited comparison is described below; full equivalence of the two versions is not assumed.
# Scope, contribution, and overall assessment

All 24 pages of the selected v5 were read, including definitions, proof details, examples, and references. The audit traced the symplectic divisor, its normal circle bundle, the complement’s handle indices, the fundamental-group identifications, rational essentiality, spin covers, the low-dimensional obstruction, and the subsequent examples. No substantive previous report or calculation for this paper was recoverable; the preserved sources and intake records were reused.

For Theorem A, a handle of index \(j\le n+1\) in a \((2n+2)\)-dimensional complement induces a surgery on its \((2n+1)\)-dimensional boundary of codimension \(2n+2-j\ge n+1\ge3\). This meets the PSC surgery range, including \(n=2\). The boundary group agrees with that of the complement by the relative handle range. Its lift admits a Lipschitz uniformly cobounded map to the lifted spine; Problem Problem 2 (#p:spine) gives a complete replacement for the deficient diameter argument.

The symplectically aspherical and amenable case uses a rationally essential divisor and the exact amenability hypothesis of Dranishnikov’s Theorem 1.6 [Dra11]. For the product case, the projection has positive degree, and the even value of \(k\) makes \(c_1(\widehat Z)=\widehat j^{\,*}c_1(\widehat M)-k\widehat j^{\,*}[\widehat\omega]\) even on the selected spin cover. Thus the stated finite-cover definition of enlargeability is respected. The Euler characteristic is a polynomial in \(k\) with nonzero leading term, so it supplies infinitely many distinct homeomorphism types along large even \(k\). The parity adjustment in Example 11 agrees with the twistor Chern-class formula and successive adjunction in Fine–Panov [FP]. The positive-degree map in Example 16 has a proper lift, since it induces a fundamental-group isomorphism; the nonzero locally finite fundamental class fits [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 5.4]{Dra13}]. The full-dimension product claim on p. 5 fits [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 5.7]{Dra13}]; no general additivity assertion for arbitrary metric spaces is needed.

The first-review assessment is Major: one core dependency needs a valid four-dimensional replacement. Three local findings are Minor, with explicit corrections that preserve the surrounding conclusions. No independent acceptance decision is made.
# The four-dimensional obstruction

Problem 1 (Major: the final dependency in Theorem B).  The last paragraph on p. 18 invokes [Retained latex: \cite[Main Theorem and Remark 1.7]{Bol09}] to deform the classifying map of the spin four-manifold \(E\) into \(B\pi^{(2)}\). The proof of that compression in the cited paper uses a false relative-to-quotient homotopy identification when \(n=4\). The same invocation appears on journal p. 1417 (physical p. 18 of the separately acquired journal PDF).
## What is needed and what was checked

After finite covers, the manuscript has an oriented base with torsion-free three-manifold group and an oriented circle bundle. The nontrivial-fiber case is covered by the hypotheses of He’s Theorem 1.9 [He]: there is an aspherical prime summand and the total dimension is four. In the remaining case the fiber is null in \(\pi_1(E)\), so \(\pi_1(E)\cong\pi_1(M)\) and \(\operatorname{cd}\pi\le3\). The splitting \(TE\cong p^*TM\oplus\mathbb R\) does make \(E\) spin. The Baum–Connes result for three-manifold groups is the relevant assembly input [MOP]. Its use here requires the integral real assembly conclusion, not merely rational complex injectivity; the full Baum–Connes isomorphism, with the standard real/complex comparison, is the appropriate route.

Lemma 3.2 prevents a classifying map from landing in the two-skeleton. It does not, by itself, turn a nonequivariant uniformly cobounded map \(\widetilde E\to K^2\) into such a classifying map. Thus a bound on \(\dim_{\mathrm{mc}}\widetilde E\) alone cannot replace the compression assertion.
## A decisive calculation inside the stated group range

Take \(n=4\), \(\pi=\mathbb Z^3\), and the standard cubical model \(B\pi=T^3\). This is a torsion-free group of cohomological dimension \(3=n-1\); it satisfies the assembly hypothesis. Let \[X=\widetilde{B\pi}=\mathbb R^3,\qquad A=\widetilde{B\pi^{(2)}}.\] Here \(A\) is the two-skeleton of the unit cubulation. Choose a closed unit cube \(Q\) and its center \(c\). Every point of \(A\) lies outside the interior of \(Q\). Radial projection from \(c\), using the cubical norm, defines \[r:A\longrightarrow\partial Q\cong S^2,\qquad
 r|_{\partial Q}=\operatorname{id}.\] For example, after centering \(Q\) at the origin with side length one, \(r(x)=x/(2\|x\|_\infty)\). Consequently the inclusion \(i:S^2\hookrightarrow A\) has a retraction and \(i_*:\pi_3(S^2)\to\pi_3(A)\) is injective. The Hopf class \(\eta\in\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb Z\) therefore gives an infinite-order element \(i_*\eta\).

As \(X\) is contractible, the exact sequence of the pair yields \[\pi_4(X,A)\cong\pi_3(A).\] On the other hand, collapsing the two-skeleton identifies \[X/A\cong\bigvee_{\gamma\in\mathbb Z^3}S^3,\qquad
 \pi_4(X/A)\cong\bigoplus_{\gamma\in\mathbb Z^3}\mathbb Z/2.\] There are no Whitehead cross-terms in degree four for a wedge of three-spheres. The relative class represented inside \((Q,\partial Q)\) by \(\eta\) maps to the suspended Hopf class in its \(S^3\) summand. In particular, twice that relative class is nonzero, but its image in \(\pi_4(X/A)\) is zero.

This directly disproves the identification \[\pi_n(\widetilde{B\pi},\widetilde{B\pi}^{(n-2)})
 \ \cong\
 \pi_n(\widetilde{B\pi}/\widetilde{B\pi}^{(n-2)})
 \tag{*}\] used on printed p. 24 of [Bol09], together with the assertion there that the left side is a free \(\mathbb Z_2[\pi]\)-module. All hypotheses of that purely topological identification are met. No PSC assumption enters the asserted identification. This calculation is not presented as a PSC four-manifold violating Theorem B.

The issue is exactly an unstable-dimensional one: the map \(\pi_3(S^2)\to\pi_4(S^3)\) loses twice the Hopf class. Detecting the suspended class in \(KO\) cannot recover this lost information without an additional argument. The subsequent bordism calculation on pp. 25–26 of [Bol09] does not establish that missing injectivity.
## Counterreadings, impact, and repair limits

The main theorem of [Bol09] is stated in a range including \(n=4\), and its proof explicitly concludes skeletal compression. Thus the manuscript has not simply misquoted a dimension restriction. The problem is the invalid step in the proof supporting its decisive citation. The calculation above establishes that gap; it does not prove the stated compression theorem false.

Replacing the citation by Bolotov–Dranishnikov [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 4.1]{BD}] is not an established repair. Dranishnikov explicitly records a gap in that lemma in [Retained latex: \cite[Remark 1.2]{Dra21}]; his treatment excludes almost-spin four-manifolds. The later argument in [DH] also gives its relevant strong-inessentiality theorem for \(n>4\). These observations corroborate the need to check the dimension, but the independent calculation above, rather than a general literature inference, is the decisive evidence.

The gap affects the null-fiber branch of Theorem B and therefore the claimed answer in all dimensions. It does not affect the high-dimensional existence construction in Theorem A or He’s nontrivial-fiber branch. A valid proof specialized to these circle bundles, a direct index obstruction, or another verified four-dimensional result could repair the argument. Such a replacement has not been completed here. Increasing a dimension bound to five would exclude the case that is needed. The current finding is a Major proof-dependency gap, with the truth of Theorem B left open by this review.
# The boundary-to-spine argument

Problem 2 (Minor: retraction and intrinsic diameter).  The introductory deformation-retraction claim on p. 5 is too strong. In Lemma 3.1, pp. 12–13, the assertion that a finite family of inverse images of open stars has a finite maximum intrinsic diameter is unjustified and can fail. The lemma’s conclusion has the complete same-hypothesis repair below.
## The boundary need not retract to the spine

Let \(M=\mathbb{CP}^3\) with its integral hyperplane symplectic class and let \(Z\subset\mathbb{CP}^3\) be a smooth complex hypersurface of sufficiently large degree \(k\). This is an allowed Donaldson divisor with \(n=2\). Its canonical circle bundle has Euler class \(kH|_Z\). Lefschetz gives \(\pi_1(Z)=0\) and a surjection \(\pi_2(Z)\to\pi_2(\mathbb{CP}^3)\cong\mathbb Z\), so the bundle sequence gives \[\pi_1(E)\cong\mathbb Z/k.\] Thus \(\widetilde E\) is a closed oriented five-manifold and \(H_5(\widetilde E;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\). A three-dimensional simplicial complex has zero fifth homology. There can be no deformation retraction of \(\widetilde E\) onto the proposed three-dimensional spine. The complement, rather than its boundary, retracts; composing boundary inclusion with that retraction is sufficient. Indeed \(\widetilde E\) is compact in this example, so its macroscopic dimension is zero. The example refutes only the retraction assertion.
## A counterexample to the stated intrinsic-diameter step

Use \[W=S^1\times D^3,\qquad E=S^1\times S^2,\qquad K=S^1\times\{0\}.\] Both hypotheses of Lemma 3.1 hold and \(E\to W\) induces an isomorphism on \(\pi_1\). For \(x\in[0,1]\), let a degree-one lift of a circle map be \[H(x)=
 \begin{cases}
  3x,&0\le x\le1/3,\\
  2-3x,&1/3\le x\le2/3,\\
  3x-2,&2/3\le x\le1,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad H(x+1)=H(x)+1.\] Write \(h_t([x])=[(1-t)x+tH(x)]\). Then \[R_t(s,z)=\bigl(h_{t|z|}(s),(1-t)z\bigr)\] is a strong deformation retraction from \(W\) onto \(K\). Its terminal map, restricted to \(E\), is \(f(s,z)=h_1(s)\). The boundary map is simplicial after finite triangulations.

Choose an open star corresponding to the arc \(B=(1/4,3/8)\) of the circle. Its inverse image is the product of \(S^2\) with three disjoint intervals: \[(1/12,1/8),\qquad(13/24,7/12),\qquad(3/4,19/24).\] There is no path inside \(U=f^{-1}(B)\) joining different components. Its intrinsic path distance between those components is infinite. Finiteness of the index set of stars therefore does not supply the finite constant \(C\) asserted on p. 13. The exact inverse-interval arithmetic was independently executed in the retained reviewer script.
## Complete repair with unchanged hypotheses

Replace \(f\) by its finite simplicial approximation, which is Lipschitz. Because \(f_*\) is an isomorphism, its lift \(\widetilde f:\widetilde E\to\widetilde K\) is equivariant for the same deck group \(\Gamma\). Choose compact sets \(D_E,D_K\) whose translates cover the two universal covers. Both \(\widetilde f(D_E)\) and \(D_K\) are compact. Properness of the deck action implies that \[F=\{\gamma\in\Gamma:
       \gamma\widetilde f(D_E)\cap D_K\ne\varnothing\}\] is finite. It follows that \[\widetilde f^{-1}(D_K)\subseteq\bigcup_{\gamma\in F}\gamma D_E.\] The right side has finite diameter in the lifted Riemannian metric. For every target point, a deck translate moves it into \(D_K\); equivariance and the isometric deck action give the same diameter bound for every fiber. The lift is Lipschitz, so \(\dim_{\mathrm{MC}}\widetilde E\le k\) follows.

This avoids any connectedness or intrinsic-diameter assumption on inverse images of stars. The introductory sentence should describe this map rather than a retraction of the boundary. The correction is Minor because a full proof of the same lemma and the same Theorem A bound is supplied, without new hypotheses or a restricted family of examples. The analogous intrinsic-diameter passage is also present on journal p. 1411.
# Two local quantitative corrections

Problem 3 (Minor: an impossible branch in Example 10).  The final alternative in Example 10, p. 19, proposes that when \(m=2\) the fiber homomorphism can have nonzero kernel, producing a finite cyclic extension and dimensions \(2n\). For the canonical bundle actually constructed here, that alternative cannot occur. It also appears on journal p. 1417.

Let \(j:Z^{2m}\hookrightarrow T^{2n}\) be any of the stated iterated divisors. The restricted symplectic class is \(j^*[\omega]\). For every \(a:S^2\to Z\), \[\langle j^*[\omega],a_*[S^2]\rangle
 =\langle[\omega],(j\circ a)_*[S^2]\rangle=0,\] because \(\pi_2(T^{2n})=0\). The canonical bundle in the final divisor step has Euler class \(e=k\,j^*[\omega]\) (with the relevant final positive integer \(k\)). The connecting homomorphism in its homotopy sequence is Euler evaluation: \[\partial:\pi_2(Z)\longrightarrow\pi_1(S^1)\cong\mathbb Z,\qquad
 \partial[a]=\langle e,a_*[S^2]\rangle=0.\] This is valid also for \(m=2\), even though \(\pi_2(Z)\) may then be nonzero. Hence the actual group is always a central extension \[1\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\longrightarrow\pi_1(E)
   \longrightarrow\mathbb Z^{2n}\longrightarrow1.\] It is torsion-free and polycyclic of Hirsch length \(2n+1\), so the same polycyclic-group formulas invoked by the paper give \(\mathop{\mathrm{asdim}}\pi_1(E)=\mathop{\mathrm{vcd}}\pi_1(E)=2n+1\). The manuscript’s calculation in Example 15, p. 22, supplies a useful internal cross-check: it also makes the pulled-back Euler class vanish.

This finding does not declare a conditional statement with an impossible antecedent logically false. It corrects the claim that this alternative is available in the described family. Remove that alternative and use the infinite-cyclic extension uniformly. The intended contrast between large group dimension and small total-space macroscopic dimension remains, and is stronger in the \(m=2\) case.

Problem 4 (Minor: the round-sphere width constant).  On p. 3 the projection of \(\widetilde M\times S_r^2\) is used to claim \(\mathrm{UW}_{n-2}\le2r\) for the product Riemannian metric. The fiber’s intrinsic diameter is \(\pi r\), not \(2r\).

The unqualified statement on pp. 2–3 includes \(n=2\) and \(M\) a point, a closed zero-dimensional manifold. Every continuous map from the connected sphere to a zero-dimensional simplicial complex is constant. Consequently \[\mathrm{UW}_0(S_r^2)=\mathop{\mathrm{diam}}(S_r^2)=\pi r>2r.\] This gives an exact counterexample to the literal displayed bound. In every dimension, the projection proves the corrected upper bound \(\mathrm{UW}_{n-2}\le\pi r\). The scalar-curvature scaling argument and the macroscopic-dimension conclusion are unchanged. Even if an implicit \(n>2\) restriction were intended, the stated projection argument still supplies \(\pi r\).
# Counterevidence, dependencies, and completion record

The Steenrod-square line preceding (3.4) on p. 17 deserves a clearer justification, but it does not yield an additional theorem-level defect. Degree one by itself does not imply \(\mathrm{Sq}^1z=0\). Here the oriented rank-two bundle has \(\mathrm{Sq}^1u=w_1u=0\), while \(\mathrm{Sq}^2z=0\) by instability, so the unwanted Cartan terms vanish. Moreover the actual \(z\) obtained by Thom inversion of \(F^*\eta\) lifts integrally, because \(\eta\) and the oriented Thom class lift integrally. This also makes \(\mathrm{Sq}^1z=0\) for the specific class. An arbitrary degree-one class with nonzero square would not satisfy these provenance conditions and is not used as a counterexample.

The finite-cover reduction in the proof of Theorem B is consistent with Kurosh’s subgroup theorem: the kernel of the map to the product of the finite prime factors misses their nontrivial torsion. The term abelianization used earlier for the free-product-to-product map should mean the canonical product homomorphism when a factor is nonabelian. This is a terminology correction, not a separate obstruction. Similarly, the dimension label for the punctured complement in the proof of Theorem A should be \(2n+2\).

The primary-reference check was recorded by actual scope: Bolotov [Bol09], all seven pages, with the central four proof pages visually inspected; [BD], pp. 3 and 7–8; [Dra21], pp. 3 and 12–13; [DH], pp. 3, 9 and 12; [He], pp. 4–5 and 18–21; [MOP], physical pp. 5–7; [Dra11], pp. 3 and 16–17 of the retained preprint; [Dra13], pp. 18–19; and [FP], all four pages. The earlier Thom calculation in [Bol06], pp. 4–5, was also checked. These are bounded dependency checks; downloading or parsing the remaining pages is not counted as scientific reading. The attempted publisher access to Donaldson’s original article encountered a security check; no bypass was attempted. Its standard existence and Morse results are used as stated by the manuscript, with their application and the manuscript’s deductions checked, rather than claiming a new full audit of that external proof.

The separate journal PDF was checked at physical pp. 1, 12–13 and 18–19. It confirms the identity and the corresponding passages identified above; it is not labeled a full journal-version review. The frozen source manifest and selected v5 remain the principal input. No missing code is treated as a mathematical defect; no author code was executed, and no unseen supplement is credited.

Let \(M=\mathbb{CP}^3\) with its integral hyperplane symplectic class and let \(Z\subset\mathbb{CP}^3\) be a smooth complex hypersurface of sufficiently large degree \(k\). This is an allowed Donaldson divisor with \(n=2\). Its canonical circle bundle has Euler class \(kH|_Z\). Lefschetz gives \(\pi_1(Z)=0\) and a surjection \(\pi_2(Z)\to\pi_2(\mathbb{CP}^3)\cong\mathbb Z\), so the bundle sequence gives \[\pi_1(E)\cong\mathbb Z/k.\] Thus \(\widetilde E\) is a closed oriented five-manifold and \(H_5(\widetilde E;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z\). A three-dimensional simplicial complex has zero fifth homology. There can be no deformation retraction of \(\widetilde E\) onto the proposed three-dimensional spine. The complement, rather than its boundary, retracts; composing boundary inclusion with that retraction is sufficient. Indeed \(\widetilde E\) is compact in this example, so its macroscopic dimension is zero. The example refutes only the retraction assertion.

Use \[W=S^1\times D^3,\qquad E=S^1\times S^2,\qquad K=S^1\times\{0\}.\] Both hypotheses of Lemma 3.1 hold and \(E\to W\) induces an isomorphism on \(\pi_1\). For \(x\in[0,1]\), let a degree-one lift of a circle map be \[H(x)=
 \begin{cases}
  3x,&0\le x\le1/3,\\
  2-3x,&1/3\le x\le2/3,\\
  3x-2,&2/3\le x\le1,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad H(x+1)=H(x)+1.\] Write \(h_t([x])=[(1-t)x+tH(x)]\). Then \[R_t(s,z)=\bigl(h_{t|z|}(s),(1-t)z\bigr)\] is a strong deformation retraction from \(W\) onto \(K\). Its terminal map, restricted to \(E\), is \(f(s,z)=h_1(s)\). The boundary map is simplicial after finite triangulations.

Choose an open star corresponding to the arc \(B=(1/4,3/8)\) of the circle. Its inverse image is the product of \(S^2\) with three disjoint intervals: \[(1/12,1/8),\qquad(13/24,7/12),\qquad(3/4,19/24).\] There is no path inside \(U=f^{-1}(B)\) joining different components. Its intrinsic path distance between those components is infinite. Finiteness of the index set of stars therefore does not supply the finite constant \(C\) asserted on p. 13. The exact inverse-interval arithmetic was independently executed in the retained reviewer script.

Replace \(f\) by its finite simplicial approximation, which is Lipschitz. Because \(f_*\) is an isomorphism, its lift \(\widetilde f:\widetilde E\to\widetilde K\) is equivariant for the same deck group \(\Gamma\). Choose compact sets \(D_E,D_K\) whose translates cover the two universal covers. Both \(\widetilde f(D_E)\) and \(D_K\) are compact. Properness of the deck action implies that \[F=\{\gamma\in\Gamma:
       \gamma\widetilde f(D_E)\cap D_K\ne\varnothing\}\] is finite. It follows that \[\widetilde f^{-1}(D_K)\subseteq\bigcup_{\gamma\in F}\gamma D_E.\] The right side has finite diameter in the lifted Riemannian metric. For every target point, a deck translate moves it into \(D_K\); equivariance and the isometric deck action give the same diameter bound for every fiber. The lift is Lipschitz, so \(\dim_{\mathrm{MC}}\widetilde E\le k\) follows.

This avoids any connectedness or intrinsic-diameter assumption on inverse images of stars. The introductory sentence should describe this map rather than a retraction of the boundary. The correction is Minor because a full proof of the same lemma and the same Theorem A bound is supplied, without new hypotheses or a restricted family of examples. The analogous intrinsic-diameter passage is also present on journal p. 1411.

problems.title: an impossible branch in Example 10
problems.source_location: v5 Example10p19 final alternative; internal cross-check Example15p22; journalp1417 Source locations: Example 10 p.19; journal p.1417; Euler pullback calculation p.22.
claim: The proposed finite-cyclic fiber-image alternative at m2 cannot occur for the canonical bundles in this torus-divisor construction.
analysis: The final alternative in Example 10, p. 19, proposes that when \(m=2\) the fiber homomorphism can have nonzero kernel, producing a finite cyclic extension and dimensions \(2n\). For the canonical bundle actually constructed here, that alternative cannot occur. It also appears on journal p. 1417.

Let \(j:Z^{2m}\hookrightarrow T^{2n}\) be any of the stated iterated divisors. The restricted symplectic class is \(j^*[\omega]\). For every \(a:S^2\to Z\), \[\langle j^*[\omega],a_*[S^2]\rangle
 =\langle[\omega],(j\circ a)_*[S^2]\rangle=0,\] because \(\pi_2(T^{2n})=0\). The canonical bundle in the final divisor step has Euler class \(e=k\,j^*[\omega]\) (with the relevant final positive integer \(k\)). The connecting homomorphism in its homotopy sequence is Euler evaluation: \[\partial:\pi_2(Z)\longrightarrow\pi_1(S^1)\cong\mathbb Z,\qquad
 \partial[a]=\langle e,a_*[S^2]\rangle=0.\] This is valid also for \(m=2\), even though \(\pi_2(Z)\) may then be nonzero. Hence the actual group is always a central extension \[1\longrightarrow\mathbb Z\longrightarrow\pi_1(E)
   \longrightarrow\mathbb Z^{2n}\longrightarrow1.\] It is torsion-free and polycyclic of Hirsch length \(2n+1\), so the same polycyclic-group formulas invoked by the paper give \(\mathop{\mathrm{asdim}}\pi_1(E)=\mathop{\mathrm{vcd}}\pi_1(E)=2n+1\). The manuscript’s calculation in Example 15, p. 22, supplies a useful internal cross-check: it also makes the pulled-back Euler class vanish.

This finding does not declare a conditional statement with an impossible antecedent logically false. It corrects the claim that this alternative is available in the described family. Remove that alternative and use the infinite-cyclic extension uniformly. The intended contrast between large group dimension and small total-space macroscopic dimension remains, and is stronger in the \(m=2\) case.
