Date: 28 October 2026

Title: Scientific review of
Oscillatory integral operators and variable Schrödinger propagators: beyond the universal estimates

Reviewed work. Mingfeng Chen, Shengwen Gan, Shaoming Guo, Jonathan Hickman, Marina Iliopoulou and James Wright, arXiv:2407.06980v2, 26 October 2025, 84 physical PDF pages. The frozen annual entry is Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 1425–1525, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-025-00724-y. All page references below concern the exact v2 PDF, whose printed and physical page numbers agree. The journal version is not assumed to be identical to this manuscript.
# Assessment and scope

The manuscript develops a substantial route from analytic non-compression conditions to geometric maximal estimates and then to oscillatory integral and variable propagator estimates. The quantitative analytic sublevel arguments are an important part of that route. Nevertheless, the stated higher-dimensional Nikodym hypothesis admits a concrete five-dimensional phase that has precisely the compression the main results purport to exclude. This is a Major defect in Proposition 4.2(II) and Theorems 2.8(II) and 2.9(II), not merely an unverified difficulty in their proofs. Section 2 (#sec:major) checks every hypothesis and supplies both geometric and oscillatory lower bounds.

Seven further findings concern explicitly identified definitions, normalizations, uniformity claims and local proof steps. Their proposed repairs have bounded scope. In particular, correcting these local steps does not repair the main counterexample. The assessment calls for a substantial revision of the high-dimensional Nikodym assertion. It does not assert failure of the three-dimensional Nikodym theorem, of the analytic sublevel propositions as standalone statements, or of every conditional estimate elsewhere in the paper.

All 84 pages were read, including the appendix and bibliography. The precise source and input manifests were checked before this work. No substantive old report was recoverable for this entry; the preserved sources and intake records were reused, while the present scientific analysis and report are new. The two primary references [KR, Guth] were also read in their entirety (eight and seven pages, respectively). This is an initial review and recovery deliverable. Subsequent independent scientific acceptance remains pending.
# P1. A phase satisfying Hypothesis II with universal compression (Major)
## Location and exact claim

Definition 2.7, pp. 10–11, permits arbitrary row and column sets \(\alpha,\beta\) of size \(d_{\rm crit}(n)\), with no requirement \(\alpha=\beta\). Proposition 4.2(II), proved on pp. 35–36, claims that Hypothesis II implies \(\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm N}(\phi;m_{\rm crit}(n);\kappa)\) for some \(\kappa>0\). Theorem 2.9(II), p. 11, then asserts a strict improvement over the universal Nikodym exponent for every \(p>p(n)\), and Theorem 2.8(II) asserts a corresponding strict propagator improvement. The following example satisfies the actual hypotheses in dimension five.
## A real analytic Hörmander phase

For \(x,y\in\mathbb R^4\), put \[B(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1-t^2&t\\t&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 H(t)=\operatorname{diag}(B(t),B(t)),\qquad
 \phi(x,t;y)=x\cdot y+\tfrac12 y^TH(t)y.\] This is a real polynomial on the required domain. We have \(\partial^2_{xy}\phi=I_4\), so H1 holds everywhere. Moreover \[B'(t)=\begin{pmatrix}-2t&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det H'(t)=1.\] The Gauss normal has a nonzero last component: up to orientation it is \((-H'(t)y,1)/(1+|H'(t)y|^2)^{1/2}\). Consequently the Hessian in H2 is a nonzero scalar multiple of \(H'(t)\) and is nonsingular for every point. Thus H2 also holds everywhere. The inverse defining the curves is explicitly \[\Psi(\omega;t;y)=\omega-H(t)y,\] which is valid on the required small patch and extends polynomially beyond it. In particular there is no inverse-branch or domain obstruction to this example. Also \(\partial_y\phi(0,0;0)=0\).

Hypothesis II and the II parts of the main theorems do not impose the translation-invariant normalization \(\psi(0;y)=0\) of Definition 2.1. Our phase has \(\psi(0;y)=(y_1^2+y_3^2)/2\); this is allowed. It is the five-dimensional specialization of the dagger phase displayed in Section 3.4, p. 18, which is attributed there to Minxing Shen. The present review independently checks its compatibility with the new Hypothesis II; it does not claim authorship of that phase.
## Verification of both parts of Hypothesis II

Here \(d_{\rm crit}(5)=3\). Choose \[\alpha=\{1,2,4\},\qquad \beta=\{2,3,4\}.\] The relevant submatrix is \[[H(t)]_{\alpha,\beta}
 =\begin{pmatrix}t&0&0\\0&0&0\\0&t&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Its 19 nonempty square subminors, with row and column subsets as in \(\mathcal I(\alpha,\beta)\), consist only of \(0,t,t^2\). The nonzero span is exactly \(\operatorname{span}\{t,t^2\}\), independently of \(\omega,y\). Every Taylor polynomial of these functions of order at least two is the function itself. We may therefore take \(d=3\) in Definition 2.7(a). For every centre \(s\) and every \((\omega,y)\), the constant polynomial 1 is not in that span: evaluating a putative identity at \(t=0\) proves this immediately. Hence \(Z_{\rm N}\) is empty, as required.

For part (b), the infinite derivative-column matrix has constant rank \(r=2\) at every \(t\). The columns of \(t,t^2\) are independent because their first and second derivative rows have determinant 2. Equivalently, the normalized order-two jets of \(1,t,t^2\) at \(s\) form \[\begin{pmatrix}1&s&s^2\\0&1&2s\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\] whose determinant is 1. Thus both the finite-jet separation and the constant-rank condition hold uniformly over every parameter required by the definition. The calculation is unchanged if the full zero \(3\times3\) minor is omitted.
## The sublevel conclusion is false

In (5.5) take the admissible measurable maps \(\mathfrak D(\omega)=I_4\) and \(\mathfrak d(\omega)=\omega\); the latter maps the prescribed equal small balls to themselves. Then, up to sign, the determinant matrix in that equation is \[M(t)=I_4-H(t)
 =\operatorname{diag}\left(
 \begin{pmatrix}t^2&-t\\-t&1\end{pmatrix},
 \begin{pmatrix}t^2&-t\\-t&1\end{pmatrix}\right).\] Each block has rank one, so \(\operatorname{rank}M(t)=2\) for all \(t\). Every \(3\times3\) minor is identically zero, whereas the minor on rows and columns \(\{2,4\}\) equals 1. The sublevel set in (5.5) is therefore the whole time interval for every \(\sigma>0\). No positive \(\kappa\) can give the asserted bound \(C_\phi\sigma^\kappa\). This disproves Proposition 4.2(II), with no unverified parameter choices.

The decisive error is visible at the top of p. 36. The constant term of \(\det[H(t)\mathfrak D-I]_{\alpha,\beta}\) is written as \((-1)^{d_{\rm crit}}\). For a non-principal submatrix it is instead \((-1)^{d_{\rm crit}}\det[I]_{\alpha,\beta}\), which can vanish. In our example the whole left-hand side is zero; the displayed right-hand side would be \(-1\) plus a linear combination of \(t,t^2\), already impossible at \(t=0\). There is a second obstruction to that expansion for general \(\mathfrak D\): Cauchy–Binet introduces columns of \(H\) outside the chosen \(\beta\). Requiring a principal submatrix alone has therefore not been proved to repair the general argument.
## Actual failure of the claimed maximal estimate

For every small \(\omega\), select \(y=\omega\). The core curve is \(x=M(t)\omega\) and lies in the smooth three-dimensional set \[S=\{(x,t):x_1=-t x_2,\ x_3=-t x_4\}\] restricted to a fixed compact local patch containing these curves. Its \(\delta\)-neighbourhood has five-dimensional volume at most \(C\delta^2\). With \(g_\delta=\mathbf1_{N_\delta S}\), every selected horizontal \(\delta\)-tube is contained in \(N_\delta S\), so \(\mathcal N^\delta g_\delta(\omega)\geq c\) on a fixed positive-measure ball. Therefore \[\|\mathcal N^\delta\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^5)\to L^p(\mathbb R^4)}
 \gtrsim \delta^{-2/p}.\] This construction persists in arbitrarily small fixed source patches. For example \(p=4>p(5)=3\) gives the universal exponent \(1/2\). If the conclusion held with \(\beta<1/2\) for all \(\varepsilon>0\), choosing \(\varepsilon=(1/2-\beta)/2\) would contradict this lower bound as \(\delta\downarrow0\). Thus Theorem 2.9(II) itself fails.
## Actual failure of the propagator improvement

Choose a nonnegative smooth frequency cutoff \(\psi\), supported near zero and positive on a smaller ball. Choose a compact smooth amplitude equal to 1 on a sufficiently small product neighbourhood. Define \[\widehat f_\lambda(y)=e^{-i\lambda |y|^2/2}\psi(y).\] Stationary phase for the nonsingular quadratic form \(-|y|^2/2\) gives \(|f_\lambda(z)|\leq C\lambda^{-2}\) on \(|z|\leq C_0\lambda\); integration by parts outside that ball gives arbitrarily rapid decay. In particular \[\|f_\lambda\|_{L^q(\mathbb R^4)}\lesssim \lambda^{-2+4/q}.\] The output phase, writing \(\tau=t/\lambda\), is \(x\cdot y-\lambda y^TM(\tau)y/2\). For each block use the orthonormal basis \[v(\tau)=\frac{(1,\tau)}{\sqrt{1+\tau^2}},\qquad
 w(\tau)=\frac{(-\tau,1)}{\sqrt{1+\tau^2}} .\] The quadratic form vanishes in the two \(v\) directions and has eigenvalue \(1+\tau^2\) in the two \(w\) directions. Let \(x\) have \(w\) coordinates \(\lambda r_1,\lambda r_2\), with \(r_j,\tau\) in small fixed intervals. The two-dimensional stationary point in the \(w\) variables remains inside the region where the cutoffs are positive. Stationary phase in those variables gives a nonzero leading term of size \(\lambda^{-1}\); integration in the two free \(v\) variables has a positive leading coefficient. This remains bounded away from zero when the two physical \(v\) coordinates of \(x\) vary in sufficiently small fixed intervals: their additional Fourier factors are then uniformly close to 1. The resulting output region has volume comparable to \(\lambda^3\), since its free macroscopic coordinates are \(t,\lambda r_1,\lambda r_2\). All amplitude and stationary-point restrictions hold uniformly on this smaller patch. Consequently \[\|U^\lambda f_\lambda\|_{L^q(\mathbb R^5)}
 \gtrsim \lambda^{-1+3/q},\qquad
 \|U^\lambda\|_{L^q\to L^q}\gtrsim\lambda^{1-1/q}.\] For \(2<q<3=q(5)\) the latter is precisely \(\alpha_{\rm LS}(5;q)\). At \(q=5/2\) the input, output and ratio powers are respectively \(-2/5,1/5,3/5\). Taking a smaller positive \(\varepsilon\) than any claimed strict gain contradicts Definition 1.1 and Theorem 2.8(II). This proof only claims the lower bound on the valid local patch; it does not copy the overbroad assertion on all points of \(S^\lambda\) on p. 20 when a compact amplitude may vanish elsewhere.
## Impact, repair boundary, and independent checks

The counterexample reaches both high-dimensional II conclusions, not just an auxiliary determinant identity. It does not disprove Theorem 2.4(II) in dimension three, where the critical submatrix is the entire \(2\times2\) Hessian. Nor does it disprove Propositions 5.1 or 5.3 as independent analytic statements. Replacing Hypothesis II by a condition that genuinely implies the sublevel property in Definition 4.1 is necessary; assuming that property directly retains only the later conditional geometric argument, subject to the local corrections below. No sufficient weak replacement for Hypothesis II has been established in this review.

The retained script `independent_phase_checks.py` was written in this review and executed with exact rational polynomial arithmetic. It checks all 19 relevant minors, \(\det H'=1\), every one of the 16 \(3\times3\) minors of \(I-H\), its nonzero \(2\times2\) minor, normalized jets, the false constant term, and the rational exponents above. It executes no author code. The volume and stationary-phase arguments are the analytic proofs given here, not outputs claimed for that script.
# P2. Hypothesis I includes the quantity it excludes (Minor)
Location. Definition of \(\mathcal I(\alpha,\beta)\) and Definition 2.6, p. 10; compare the parenthetical explanation in the proof of Proposition 4.2(I), p. 35.

The defined set \(\mathcal I(\alpha,\beta)\) includes \((\alpha,\beta)\) itself. In the equation defining \(Z_{\rm K}\), set the coefficient of this full minor to 1 and all other coefficients to zero. The equation then holds for every \(t\) and every \(y\), for any phase. Thus \(Z_{\rm K}\) is the whole frequency ball and Hypothesis I is impossible. This is a direct logical obstruction, not a test on a special phase. The conditional higher-dimensional I statements are consequently vacuous as written; the issue is not a counterexample satisfying their impossible hypothesis.

The intended local correction is explicit in the proof on p. 35, which requires \(0<|\alpha'|=|\beta'|<d_{\rm crit}(n)\). Define separate index sets \(\mathcal I_{<}\) and \(\mathcal I_{\leq}\), use the proper-minor set for the Kakeya condition and retain the all-minor set where required in the Nikodym condition. Under Definition 2.1, the Hessian at \(t=0\) vanishes; evaluating at zero removes a possible constant term in a putative linear dependence. This verifies the local transition to Proposition 5.1 after the index correction. It does not validate a global change of \(\mathcal I\) in both hypotheses or repair P1. The error is classified as Minor because the specific intended index restriction is present in the proof and the local algebraic repair is exact.
# P3. The inverse curves require a centering assumption (Minor)

Location. Section 1.2, p. 4, immediately preceding (1.3). H1 alone does not ensure an inverse branch near \(\omega=t=y=0\) with \(x\) in the given unit ball. In dimension three consider \[\phi(x,t;y)=x\cdot y+t|y|^2+100y_1.\] This smooth real analytic phase satisfies H1 with mixed Hessian \(I_2\) and H2 with nonsingular Hessian \(2I_2\) up to the nonzero Gauss normal factor. Nevertheless \(\partial_{y_1}\phi=x_1+2ty_1+100>97\) throughout the stated domain. It cannot equal \(\omega_1\) for any \(\omega\) in a ball of radius \(\rho<1\) about zero. No reduction of that radius fixes the problem.

Specify a local base point and centre the \(\omega\) ball at the actual gradient, or first subtract the appropriate linear function of \(y\) so that \(\partial_y\phi(0,0;0)=0\). H1 then supplies the local inverse-function theorem after shrinking the patch. This subtraction does not change the mixed Hessian or curvature: for the oscillatory operator it is an input modulation, and for the propagator its Fourier modulation corresponds to translation of the input, both preserving the relevant norms. The geometric centre is relabelled accordingly. This is a necessary local normalization, not a counterexample to an estimate formulated with a correctly centred branch. The phase in P1 already has the correct centre.
# P4. The Jacobian in Example 3.1 has the wrong middle sign (Minor)

Location. Section 3.1, p. 16, the displayed formula for \(J\Phi\) and the following definitions of \(A,B,C\). Direct differentiation gives the spatial Jacobian \[D\omega(y)-\operatorname{diag}\left(t,\frac{t}{1-ty_2}\right).\] Its determinant is \[\frac{A(y)t^2-B(y)t+C(y)}{1-ty_2},\] with the same \(A,B,C\) printed in the source, rather than the displayed numerator \(At^2+Bt+C\). For the admissible smooth map \(\omega(y)=y\), at \(y=0,t=1/4\), the actual determinant is \(9/16\); the printed expression is \(25/16\). Both exact rational values were also checked by the independent arithmetic script.

The correction is simply the minus sign before \(Bt\). The example’s special choice \(A=B=C=0\) still makes the determinant zero, so the intended compression example is not refuted by this calculation. This finding concerns the general identity and its use for other choices of \(\omega\), not an unsupported claim that the entire example fails.
# P5. Two semialgebraic proof steps need their missing justifications (Minor)
Location. Section 4.1, Step 3, p. 26, and the multiplicity argument following (4.18), p. 29; Corollary A.5 and Lemma A.6, p. 82.
## Compactness does not follow from semialgebraic selection

Corollary A.5, reproduced from [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 2.2]{KR}], supplies a semialgebraic one-point-per-fibre section, not a compact section. The assertion on p. 26 that the selected \(\mathcal L_{\rm dir}\) and \(\mathcal L_{\rm ctr}\) are compact does not follow from it. For a decisive example to that inference, identify \(\mathbb R^4\) with \(\mathbb C^2\) and take the compact semialgebraic set \[A=\{(a,d):d=a^2,\ 1/4\leq |a|\leq1/2\}.\] A compact section over the annulus of \(d\) values would project continuously and bijectively onto that annulus. Compactness would make the inverse continuous, giving a continuous square root on an annulus around zero. On fundamental groups this would require \(2k=1\) for an integer \(k\), which is impossible. Thus even compact semialgebraic input does not in general admit a compact section. This refutes the invoked general inference; it is not presented as a fully realized counterexample to a particular tube family.

There is a local way to supply the needed parametrization: use a closed tube-containment set, taking a harmless slightly larger closed neighbourhood if necessary, and take the closure of the bounded semialgebraic section within that set. Semialgebraic closure preserves its dimension and bounded complexity. The projection still covers the desired base. Apply the compact parametrization lemma to this closure. Among the finitely many charts select one by the measure of its projection onto the relevant parameter base. This supplies the projected-measure lower bound actually needed later. Selecting merely a chart with large measure in the graph is not the same assertion. The later local inverse selection uses a nonsingular parameter projection on a chart; it does not require the closed graph to remain a one-point-per-fibre global section.
## The inverse-composed map is not generally polynomial

The maps \(\widetilde\Psi_{\iota,v}\) on p. 29 contain an inverse of a polynomial parameter map chosen earlier. Polynomiality is not preserved under this operation. Already \(\widetilde D(z)=z^2/2\), \(\widetilde P(z)=z/2\) on \(1/2<z<1\) and \(\widetilde\Psi(\omega,t;y)=\omega-ty\) give the component \[\widetilde P(\widetilde D^{-1}(y))-ty
 =\sqrt{y/2}-ty .\] The parameter Jacobian is nonzero on this patch, but the result is not a polynomial. Extra coordinates can be appended without removing this obstruction.

For the required Bézout bound, keep the original parameter \(z\) rather than substituting its inverse. If \(c\) coordinates of \(\widetilde D(z)\) (or \(\widetilde P(z)\)) are fixed at \(v\), impose those \(c\) polynomial equations together with the \(n-1\) polynomial output equations, with unknowns \(z\in\mathbb R^{n-1}\) and \(\eta\in\mathbb R^c\). This is a square polynomial system of bounded degree. At a point counted in (4.18), its Jacobian is, up to sign, the product of the nonsingular parameter Jacobian and the nonzero \((u,\eta)\) Jacobian already imposed there. The point is therefore an isolated complex zero. Bézout bounds the number of such zeros by a degree-dependent constant, irrespective of other positive-dimensional components. This restores the particular multiplicity estimate without asserting polynomiality of an inverse. These repairs address the two specified steps; they are not a new proof of every approximation and volume argument in Section 4.
# P6. The multilinear estimate is not uniform in the first derivative alone (Minor)

Location. Definition 6.10, p. 54, and the last quantitative sentence of Theorem 6.11, p. 55. The latter asserts dependence only on \(n,\varepsilon,M_1\) for curves transverse on a measurable set \(X\).

Take \(n=k=p=2\), and for an arbitrarily large integer \(N\) use the two-element smooth family \[\gamma_1(t)=0,\qquad \gamma_2(t)=\frac{\sin Nt}{N},
 \qquad -1<t<1.\] For each fixed \(N\) this is a uniform \(C^\infty\) family in the definition: every higher derivative has a finite bound, while \(M_1=1\) works for all \(N\). Choose a fixed \(0<c<10^{-2}\) and \(\delta=c/N\). Each of the two tube families consists of one \(\delta\)-tube. For zeros \(t_j=j\pi/N\) in \((-1/5,1/5)\) let \(X\) be the union of rectangles \[|x|<\delta/8,\qquad |t-t_j|<\delta/8 .\] There are comparable to \(N\) disjoint rectangles, each of area comparable to \(\delta^2\). They lie in both tubes and in \(B_{1/2}\). If a point of either core is within Euclidean distance \(\delta\) of such a rectangle point, its time differs from \(t_j\) by less than \(9\delta/8\). Hence the second curve’s slope has absolute value at least \(\cos(9c/8)>0.99\). Its unit tangent has wedge product greater than \(1/3\) with the vertical first tangent. The full infimum over nearby core points in Definition 6.10 is therefore bounded below by the fixed \(\nu=1/3\). Also \(\delta<\nu\) as required.

The left-hand side of (6.20) is at least \(c_1\delta\sqrt N\). With \(r=1/2\), its asserted right-hand side is \(C\nu^{-A}\delta^{1-\varepsilon}\), since both family cardinalities are one and the \(r\) exponent is zero. The ratio is bounded below by a constant times \(N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\), which diverges for \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\). This disproves the stated \(M_1\)-only uniformity, while respecting all smoothness and local transversality hypotheses. It does not disprove a bound with dependence on the higher derivatives of a fixed family.

The cited curved theorem [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 7, p.~6]{Guth}] assumes small slopes around a fixed coordinate axis for each family. Local transversality on \(X\) does not itself give that hypothesis. One repair is to allow dependence on appropriate higher derivative bounds and partition curves into uniformly controlled pieces with tangents in fixed small cones. For a fixed smooth phase such dependence is compatible with the manuscript’s phase-dependent constants. The example rules out retaining the stronger uniformity; it does not by itself refute the final phase-dependent estimates. A fully uniform first-derivative-only replacement is not supplied.
# P7. Shrinking-cap symbol scales and packet centering (Minor)
Location. Proposition 9.1, p. 73; the definition of \(f_T\), p. 74; Lemmas 9.2–9.3, p. 75.

The source places a smooth symbol on a cap of diameter \(O(R^{-1/2})\) but requires \(|\partial_y^\beta a_\theta|\lesssim R^{-|\beta|/2}\). These are not the bounds of the cap cutoffs already displayed correctly on p. 74. They would force such symbols to be rapidly small. Indeed, Taylor expansion along a coordinate from a point just outside the support, at distance \(O(R^{-1/2})\), gives \[\|a_\theta\|_\infty\leq C_L R^{-L}
 \quad\hbox{for every integer }L\geq1,\] since all jets vanish at the exterior point and the derivative of order \(L\) is \(O(R^{-L/2})\).

This contradicts the existence assertion of Proposition 9.1 for a fixed nonzero amplitude. Use the normalized constant Hörmander phase \(x\cdot y+t|y|^2\), a smooth amplitude equal to 1 near the origin, a fixed nonnegative nonzero \(f\), and \(\lambda=R\). At \(q=2\), the left side of (9.3) is bounded below on a fixed small ball for all large \(R\). On the right, every proposed cap symbol is \(O_L(R^{-L})\). The number of caps, the volume of \(B_{2R}\) and all prefactors grow only polynomially; the number of \(\gamma\) indices is fixed for fixed \(N,\varepsilon\). Taking \(L\) sufficiently large makes that entire term tend to zero. The \(R^{-N}\|f\|_2\) term also tends to zero. Thus the printed assertion cannot hold.

The needed cap scale is \(R^{|\beta|/2}\) (and \(\lambda^{|\beta|/2}\) in Lemma 9.3), as the neighbouring cutoff formula already shows. Separately, for a ball centred at a physical point \(z_B\), a coherent packet construction is to decompose \(h(y)=e^{i\phi^\lambda(z_B;y)}f(y)\) into \(h_{\theta,\omega}\) and define \[f_T(y)=e^{-i\phi^\lambda(z_B;y)}h_{\theta,\omega}(y).\] Then \(\sum_T f_T=f\), and the packet phase at \(z_B+z\) is \[\phi^\lambda(z_B+z;y)-\phi^\lambda(z_B;y)-\omega\cdot y,\] which is the phase compatible with the stated recentered tubes. The positive modulation printed for \(f_T\) on p. 74 has the opposite sign. When a unit-scale phase is used, its base point must also be \(z_B/\lambda\). The displayed reconstruction proves the corrected algebra and preserves packet norms.

These are local scale and modulation corrections. A unit-size symbol does not satisfy the printed negative derivative bounds, so it would be invalid to use one as a purported all-hypothesis counterexample to Lemma 9.2 itself. The contradiction above instead targets the existential Proposition 9.1, where it is valid. This review does not claim a new complete proof of the corrected reverse square function proposition.
# P8. Local-to-global proof: Whitney separation and the summation range (Minor)
Location. Proof of Lemma 9.5, pp. 79–80, particularly (9.21)–(9.24).

On p. 79, the relation \(Q_1\sim Q_2\) is defined by disjoint dyadic cubes with non-disjoint parents. Such siblings need not be separated: \([0,1)\) and \([1,2)\) have the same parent and distance zero. Products with common intervals give the same example in every dimension. Thus the stated inference \(\operatorname{dist}(Q_1,Q_2)\sim2^k\) is false, and the scale-decay factor in (9.21) cannot follow from that definition. Use the usual Whitney pairs of non-neighbouring cubes whose parents are neighbours. Their separation is comparable to their side length, and the complement of the diagonal admits the required bounded-overlap decomposition. This is the exact geometric property needed for the subsequent kernel bound.

In addition, the large-\(k\) series in (9.24) requires \(s\alpha<(n-1)/2\), not merely the lemma’s stated \(s\alpha<(n+1)/2\). For example, \(n=3,s=2,\alpha=1/2\) obeys the stated range and the available local \(L^\infty\to L^2\) estimate for the constant phase. Yet the large-\(k\) term is \(\min\{\sigma^{-2},2^k\}\), so its infinite sum diverges. This is a failure of that summation argument, not a counterexample to the lemma’s global conclusion.

For the application in odd dimensions \(n\geq3\), first separate the range \(\alpha\geq\alpha_{\rm H}(n,s)\): its requested global exponents are already supplied by the universal theorem. In the remaining range, using \[\alpha_{\rm H}(n,s)=\frac{n+1}{2s}-\frac{n-1}{4},
 \qquad 2\leq s\leq q(n),\] gives \(s\alpha<s\alpha_{\rm H}(n,s)\leq1\leq(n-1)/2\). The strict summability inequality then holds, and the geometric series can be evaluated as intended. At the boundary \(n=3,s=2\), the case of equality is assigned to the universal estimate. Together with the corrected Whitney decomposition this supplies the missing local proof organization. No false global theorem is alleged on the basis of the divergent intermediate bound.

These arguments were checked as analytic statements under their own hypotheses. Their application on p. 36 fails for the algebraic reason in P1. The cell statements are used inside the prescribed ball; an unrestricted assertion that every polynomial complement cell is bounded would be false. Several tempting overstatements were explicitly rejected. The extra constant quadratic term in the dagger phase does not exclude it from Hypothesis II; Definition 2.1 is not imposed there. Conversely, the same example does not establish a failure in dimension three. Failure of the \(M_1\)-only bound does not by itself disprove a fixed-phase estimate with higher-derivative constants. An inverse-composed parametrization need not be polynomial, but Bézout can still be applied in the original variables. The local divergence in the proof of Lemma 9.5 does not imply that its global conclusion is false. The source explicitly omits some details of the positive-definite corollary, Theorem 2.5; this report does not replace that omission with a claim of a new complete proof.

The corrected proper-minor definition, centering operation, Jacobian sign, original-variable multiplicity argument, packet reconstruction and summation range split have the specific verification described above. A new high-dimensional non-compression theorem, the complete corrected reverse square function argument, and a first-derivative-only curved theorem have not been proved here. problems.title: Higher-dimensional Hypothesis II admits full universal compression
problems.source_location: Definition 2.7 pp.10-11; Proposition 4.2(II), proof pp.35-36; Theorems 2.8(II),2.9(II) p.11; compare dagger phase pp.18-20
claim: Recorded check: Higher-dimensional Hypothesis II admits full universal compression
analysis: Definition 2.7, pp. 10–11, permits arbitrary row and column sets \(\alpha,\beta\) of size \(d_{\rm crit}(n)\), with no requirement \(\alpha=\beta\). Proposition 4.2(II), proved on pp. 35–36, claims that Hypothesis II implies \(\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm N}(\phi;m_{\rm crit}(n);\kappa)\) for some \(\kappa>0\). Theorem 2.9(II), p. 11, then asserts a strict improvement over the universal Nikodym exponent for every \(p>p(n)\), and Theorem 2.8(II) asserts a corresponding strict propagator improvement. The following example satisfies the actual hypotheses in dimension five.

For \(x,y\in\mathbb R^4\), put \[B(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1-t^2&t\\t&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 H(t)=\operatorname{diag}(B(t),B(t)),\qquad
 \phi(x,t;y)=x\cdot y+\tfrac12 y^TH(t)y.\] This is a real polynomial on the required domain. We have \(\partial^2_{xy}\phi=I_4\), so H1 holds everywhere. Moreover \[B'(t)=\begin{pmatrix}-2t&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det H'(t)=1.\] The Gauss normal has a nonzero last component: up to orientation it is \((-H'(t)y,1)/(1+|H'(t)y|^2)^{1/2}\). Consequently the Hessian in H2 is a nonzero scalar multiple of \(H'(t)\) and is nonsingular for every point. Thus H2 also holds everywhere. The inverse defining the curves is explicitly \[\Psi(\omega;t;y)=\omega-H(t)y,\] which is valid on the required small patch and extends polynomially beyond it. In particular there is no inverse-branch or domain obstruction to this example. Also \(\partial_y\phi(0,0;0)=0\).

Hypothesis II and the II parts of the main theorems do not impose the translation-invariant normalization \(\psi(0;y)=0\) of Definition 2.1. Our phase has \(\psi(0;y)=(y_1^2+y_3^2)/2\); this is allowed. It is the five-dimensional specialization of the dagger phase displayed in Section 3.4, p. 18, which is attributed there to Minxing Shen. The present review independently checks its compatibility with the new Hypothesis II; it does not claim authorship of that phase.

Here \(d_{\rm crit}(5)=3\). Choose \[\alpha=\{1,2,4\},\qquad \beta=\{2,3,4\}.\] The relevant submatrix is \[[H(t)]_{\alpha,\beta}
 =\begin{pmatrix}t&0&0\\0&0&0\\0&t&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Its 19 nonempty square subminors, with row and column subsets as in \(\mathcal I(\alpha,\beta)\), consist only of \(0,t,t^2\). The nonzero span is exactly \(\operatorname{span}\{t,t^2\}\), independently of \(\omega,y\). Every Taylor polynomial of these functions of order at least two is the function itself. We may therefore take \(d=3\) in Definition 2.7(a). For every centre \(s\) and every \((\omega,y)\), the constant polynomial 1 is not in that span: evaluating a putative identity at \(t=0\) proves this immediately. Hence \(Z_{\rm N}\) is empty, as required.

For part (b), the infinite derivative-column matrix has constant rank \(r=2\) at every \(t\). The columns of \(t,t^2\) are independent because their first and second derivative rows have determinant 2. Equivalently, the normalized order-two jets of \(1,t,t^2\) at \(s\) form \[\begin{pmatrix}1&s&s^2\\0&1&2s\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\] whose determinant is 1. Thus both the finite-jet separation and the constant-rank condition hold uniformly over every parameter required by the definition. The calculation is unchanged if the full zero \(3\times3\) minor is omitted.

In (5.5) take the admissible measurable maps \(\mathfrak D(\omega)=I_4\) and \(\mathfrak d(\omega)=\omega\); the latter maps the prescribed equal small balls to themselves. Then, up to sign, the determinant matrix in that equation is \[M(t)=I_4-H(t)
 =\operatorname{diag}\left(
 \begin{pmatrix}t^2&-t\\-t&1\end{pmatrix},
 \begin{pmatrix}t^2&-t\\-t&1\end{pmatrix}\right).\] Each block has rank one, so \(\operatorname{rank}M(t)=2\) for all \(t\). Every \(3\times3\) minor is identically zero, whereas the minor on rows and columns \(\{2,4\}\) equals 1. The sublevel set in (5.5) is therefore the whole time interval for every \(\sigma>0\). No positive \(\kappa\) can give the asserted bound \(C_\phi\sigma^\kappa\). This disproves Proposition 4.2(II), with no unverified parameter choices.

The decisive error is visible at the top of p. 36. The constant term of \(\det[H(t)\mathfrak D-I]_{\alpha,\beta}\) is written as \((-1)^{d_{\rm crit}}\). For a non-principal submatrix it is instead \((-1)^{d_{\rm crit}}\det[I]_{\alpha,\beta}\), which can vanish. In our example the whole left-hand side is zero; the displayed right-hand side would be \(-1\) plus a linear combination of \(t,t^2\), already impossible at \(t=0\). There is a second obstruction to that expansion for general \(\mathfrak D\): Cauchy–Binet introduces columns of \(H\) outside the chosen \(\beta\). Requiring a principal submatrix alone has therefore not been proved to repair the general argument.

For every small \(\omega\), select \(y=\omega\). The core curve is \(x=M(t)\omega\) and lies in the smooth three-dimensional set \[S=\{(x,t):x_1=-t x_2,\ x_3=-t x_4\}\] restricted to a fixed compact local patch containing these curves. Its \(\delta\)-neighbourhood has five-dimensional volume at most \(C\delta^2\). With \(g_\delta=\mathbf1_{N_\delta S}\), every selected horizontal \(\delta\)-tube is contained in \(N_\delta S\), so \(\mathcal N^\delta g_\delta(\omega)\geq c\) on a fixed positive-measure ball. Therefore \[\|\mathcal N^\delta\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^5)\to L^p(\mathbb R^4)}
 \gtrsim \delta^{-2/p}.\] This construction persists in arbitrarily small fixed source patches. For example \(p=4>p(5)=3\) gives the universal exponent \(1/2\). If the conclusion held with \(\beta<1/2\) for all \(\varepsilon>0\), choosing \(\varepsilon=(1/2-\beta)/2\) would contradict this lower bound as \(\delta\downarrow0\). Thus Theorem 2.9(II) itself fails.

Choose a nonnegative smooth frequency cutoff \(\psi\), supported near zero and positive on a smaller ball. Choose a compact smooth amplitude equal to 1 on a sufficiently small product neighbourhood. Define \[\widehat f_\lambda(y)=e^{-i\lambda |y|^2/2}\psi(y).\] Stationary phase for the nonsingular quadratic form \(-|y|^2/2\) gives \(|f_\lambda(z)|\leq C\lambda^{-2}\) on \(|z|\leq C_0\lambda\); integration by parts outside that ball gives arbitrarily rapid decay. In particular \[\|f_\lambda\|_{L^q(\mathbb R^4)}\lesssim \lambda^{-2+4/q}.\] The output phase, writing \(\tau=t/\lambda\), is \(x\cdot y-\lambda y^TM(\tau)y/2\). For each block use the orthonormal basis \[v(\tau)=\frac{(1,\tau)}{\sqrt{1+\tau^2}},\qquad
 w(\tau)=\frac{(-\tau,1)}{\sqrt{1+\tau^2}} .\] The quadratic form vanishes in the two \(v\) directions and has eigenvalue \(1+\tau^2\) in the two \(w\) directions. Let \(x\) have \(w\) coordinates \(\lambda r_1,\lambda r_2\), with \(r_j,\tau\) in small fixed intervals. The two-dimensional stationary point in the \(w\) variables remains inside the region where the cutoffs are positive. Stationary phase in those variables gives a nonzero leading term of size \(\lambda^{-1}\); integration in the two free \(v\) variables has a positive leading coefficient. This remains bounded away from zero when the two physical \(v\) coordinates of \(x\) vary in sufficiently small fixed intervals: their additional Fourier factors are then uniformly close to 1. The resulting output region has volume comparable to \(\lambda^3\), since its free macroscopic coordinates are \(t,\lambda r_1,\lambda r_2\). All amplitude and stationary-point restrictions hold uniformly on this smaller patch. Consequently \[\|U^\lambda f_\lambda\|_{L^q(\mathbb R^5)}
 \gtrsim \lambda^{-1+3/q},\qquad
 \|U^\lambda\|_{L^q\to L^q}\gtrsim\lambda^{1-1/q}.\] For \(2<q<3=q(5)\) the latter is precisely \(\alpha_{\rm LS}(5;q)\). At \(q=5/2\) the input, output and ratio powers are respectively \(-2/5,1/5,3/5\). Taking a smaller positive \(\varepsilon\) than any claimed strict gain contradicts Definition 1.1 and Theorem 2.8(II). This proof only claims the lower bound on the valid local patch; it does not copy the overbroad assertion on all points of \(S^\lambda\) on p. 20 when a compact amplitude may vanish elsewhere.

The counterexample reaches both high-dimensional II conclusions, not just an auxiliary determinant identity. It does not disprove Theorem 2.4(II) in dimension three, where the critical submatrix is the entire \(2\times2\) Hessian. Nor does it disprove Propositions 5.1 or 5.3 as independent analytic statements. Replacing Hypothesis II by a condition that genuinely implies the sublevel property in Definition 4.1 is necessary; assuming that property directly retains only the later conditional geometric argument, subject to the local corrections below. No sufficient weak replacement for Hypothesis II has been established in this review.

The retained script `independent_phase_checks.py` was written in this review and executed with exact rational polynomial arithmetic. It checks all 19 relevant minors, \(\det H'=1\), every one of the 16 \(3\times3\) minors of \(I-H\), its nonzero \(2\times2\) minor, normalized jets, the false constant term, and the rational exponents above. It executes no author code. The volume and stationary-phase arguments are the analytic proofs given here, not outputs claimed for that script.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: False expansion p.36 has constant -1 instead of -det(I_alpha,beta)=0; evaluate t=0. Compressed local 3-manifold S in R5 has delta-neighbourhood O(delta^2), forcing Nikodym norm >=c delta^(-2/p). Rank-2 stationary phase gives propagator norm >=c lambda^(1-1/q). Explicit p=4,q=5/2 contradict strict gains with epsilon smaller than the gap.

Recorded evidence: Witness: H=diag([[1-t^2,t],[t,0]],same); phi=x.y+y^T H y/2. All selected 19 nonempty minors lie in {0,t,t^2}; span(t,t^2) excludes 1, including all Taylor centres. Take D=I4,d(omega)=omega. I-H has rank 2 for every t, all 16 three-minors vanish, one two-minor equals 1.

problems.title: Kakeya non-compression index set includes the target full minor
problems.source_location: Definition of I(alpha,beta) and Definition 2.6 p.10; proper-minor parenthetical p.35
claim: Recorded check: Kakeya non-compression index set includes the target full minor
analysis: Location. Definition of \(\mathcal I(\alpha,\beta)\) and Definition 2.6, p. 10; compare the parenthetical explanation in the proof of Proposition 4.2(I), p. 35.

The defined set \(\mathcal I(\alpha,\beta)\) includes \((\alpha,\beta)\) itself. In the equation defining \(Z_{\rm K}\), set the coefficient of this full minor to 1 and all other coefficients to zero. The equation then holds for every \(t\) and every \(y\), for any phase. Thus \(Z_{\rm K}\) is the whole frequency ball and Hypothesis I is impossible. This is a direct logical obstruction, not a test on a special phase. The conditional higher-dimensional I statements are consequently vacuous as written; the issue is not a counterexample satisfying their impossible hypothesis.

The intended local correction is explicit in the proof on p. 35, which requires \(0<|\alpha'|=|\beta'|<d_{\rm crit}(n)\). Define separate index sets \(\mathcal I_{<}\) and \(\mathcal I_{\leq}\), use the proper-minor set for the Kakeya condition and retain the all-minor set where required in the Nikodym condition. Under Definition 2.1, the Hessian at \(t=0\) vanishes; evaluating at zero removes a possible constant term in a putative linear dependence. This verifies the local transition to Proposition 5.1 after the index correction. It does not validate a global change of \(\mathcal I\) in both hypotheses or repair P1. The error is classified as Minor because the specific intended index restriction is present in the proof and the local algebraic repair is exact.

problems.title: Local inverse centred at omega=0 is not implied by H1
problems.source_location: Section 1.2 p.4 before (1.3)
claim: Recorded check: Local inverse centred at omega=0 is not implied by H1
analysis: Location. Section 1.2, p. 4, immediately preceding (1.3). H1 alone does not ensure an inverse branch near \(\omega=t=y=0\) with \(x\) in the given unit ball. In dimension three consider \[\phi(x,t;y)=x\cdot y+t|y|^2+100y_1.\] This smooth real analytic phase satisfies H1 with mixed Hessian \(I_2\) and H2 with nonsingular Hessian \(2I_2\) up to the nonzero Gauss normal factor. Nevertheless \(\partial_{y_1}\phi=x_1+2ty_1+100>97\) throughout the stated domain. It cannot equal \(\omega_1\) for any \(\omega\) in a ball of radius \(\rho<1\) about zero. No reduction of that radius fixes the problem.

Specify a local base point and centre the \(\omega\) ball at the actual gradient, or first subtract the appropriate linear function of \(y\) so that \(\partial_y\phi(0,0;0)=0\). H1 then supplies the local inverse-function theorem after shrinking the patch. This subtraction does not change the mixed Hessian or curvature: for the oscillatory operator it is an input modulation, and for the propagator its Fourier modulation corresponds to translation of the input, both preserving the relevant norms. The geometric centre is relabelled accordingly. This is a necessary local normalization, not a counterexample to an estimate formulated with a correctly centred branch. The phase in P1 already has the correct centre.

problems.title: Wrong middle sign in Example 3.1 Jacobian
problems.source_location: Section 3.1 p.16 formula for J Phi and A,B,C
claim: Recorded check: Wrong middle sign in Example 3.1 Jacobian
analysis: Location. Section 3.1, p. 16, the displayed formula for \(J\Phi\) and the following definitions of \(A,B,C\). Direct differentiation gives the spatial Jacobian \[D\omega(y)-\operatorname{diag}\left(t,\frac{t}{1-ty_2}\right).\] Its determinant is \[\frac{A(y)t^2-B(y)t+C(y)}{1-ty_2},\] with the same \(A,B,C\) printed in the source, rather than the displayed numerator \(At^2+Bt+C\). For the admissible smooth map \(\omega(y)=y\), at \(y=0,t=1/4\), the actual determinant is \(9/16\); the printed expression is \(25/16\). Both exact rational values were also checked by the independent arithmetic script.

The correction is simply the minus sign before \(Bt\). The example’s special choice \(A=B=C=0\) still makes the determinant zero, so the intended compression example is not refuted by this calculation. This finding concerns the general identity and its use for other choices of \(\omega\), not an unsupported claim that the entire example fails.

problems.title: Compact selection and inverse-polynomial assertions do not follow
problems.source_location: Section 4.1 Step 3 p.26; after (4.18) p.29; Corollary A.5/Lemma A.6 p.82
claim: Recorded check: Compact selection and inverse-polynomial assertions do not follow
analysis: Location. Section 4.1, Step 3, p. 26, and the multiplicity argument following (4.18), p. 29; Corollary A.5 and Lemma A.6, p. 82.

Corollary A.5, reproduced from [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 2.2]{KR}], supplies a semialgebraic one-point-per-fibre section, not a compact section. The assertion on p. 26 that the selected \(\mathcal L_{\rm dir}\) and \(\mathcal L_{\rm ctr}\) are compact does not follow from it. For a decisive example to that inference, identify \(\mathbb R^4\) with \(\mathbb C^2\) and take the compact semialgebraic set \[A=\{(a,d):d=a^2,\ 1/4\leq |a|\leq1/2\}.\] A compact section over the annulus of \(d\) values would project continuously and bijectively onto that annulus. Compactness would make the inverse continuous, giving a continuous square root on an annulus around zero. On fundamental groups this would require \(2k=1\) for an integer \(k\), which is impossible. Thus even compact semialgebraic input does not in general admit a compact section. This refutes the invoked general inference; it is not presented as a fully realized counterexample to a particular tube family.

There is a local way to supply the needed parametrization: use a closed tube-containment set, taking a harmless slightly larger closed neighbourhood if necessary, and take the closure of the bounded semialgebraic section within that set. Semialgebraic closure preserves its dimension and bounded complexity. The projection still covers the desired base. Apply the compact parametrization lemma to this closure. Among the finitely many charts select one by the measure of its projection onto the relevant parameter base. This supplies the projected-measure lower bound actually needed later. Selecting merely a chart with large measure in the graph is not the same assertion. The later local inverse selection uses a nonsingular parameter projection on a chart; it does not require the closed graph to remain a one-point-per-fibre global section.

The maps \(\widetilde\Psi_{\iota,v}\) on p. 29 contain an inverse of a polynomial parameter map chosen earlier. Polynomiality is not preserved under this operation. Already \(\widetilde D(z)=z^2/2\), \(\widetilde P(z)=z/2\) on \(1/2<z<1\) and \(\widetilde\Psi(\omega,t;y)=\omega-ty\) give the component \[\widetilde P(\widetilde D^{-1}(y))-ty
 =\sqrt{y/2}-ty .\] The parameter Jacobian is nonzero on this patch, but the result is not a polynomial. Extra coordinates can be appended without removing this obstruction.

For the required Bézout bound, keep the original parameter \(z\) rather than substituting its inverse. If \(c\) coordinates of \(\widetilde D(z)\) (or \(\widetilde P(z)\)) are fixed at \(v\), impose those \(c\) polynomial equations together with the \(n-1\) polynomial output equations, with unknowns \(z\in\mathbb R^{n-1}\) and \(\eta\in\mathbb R^c\). This is a square polynomial system of bounded degree. At a point counted in (4.18), its Jacobian is, up to sign, the product of the nonsingular parameter Jacobian and the nonzero \((u,\eta)\) Jacobian already imposed there. The point is therefore an isolated complex zero. Bézout bounds the number of such zeros by a degree-dependent constant, irrespective of other positive-dimensional components. This restores the particular multiplicity estimate without asserting polynomiality of an inverse. These repairs address the two specified steps; they are not a new proof of every approximation and volume argument in Section 4.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: Primary Katz-Rogers Lemma 2.2 supplies semialgebraicity without compactness. Fundamental-group obstruction and explicit inverse formula disprove the two invoked general inferences.

Recorded evidence: Witness: Compact double-cover A={(a,d) in C^2:d=a^2,1/4<=|a|<=1/2} cannot have a compact one-point-per-fibre section, since it would be continuous and imply 2k=1 on pi1. Polynomial D(z)=z^2/2,P(z)=z/2 gives inverse-composed sqrt(y/2)-ty.

problems.title: Local transversality does not yield M1-only multilinear uniformity
problems.source_location: Definition 6.10 p.54; quantitative clause of Theorem 6.11 p.55
claim: Recorded check: Local transversality does not yield M1-only multilinear uniformity
analysis: Location. Definition 6.10, p. 54, and the last quantitative sentence of Theorem 6.11, p. 55. The latter asserts dependence only on \(n,\varepsilon,M_1\) for curves transverse on a measurable set \(X\).

Take \(n=k=p=2\), and for an arbitrarily large integer \(N\) use the two-element smooth family \[\gamma_1(t)=0,\qquad \gamma_2(t)=\frac{\sin Nt}{N},
 \qquad -1<t<1.\] For each fixed \(N\) this is a uniform \(C^\infty\) family in the definition: every higher derivative has a finite bound, while \(M_1=1\) works for all \(N\). Choose a fixed \(0<c<10^{-2}\) and \(\delta=c/N\). Each of the two tube families consists of one \(\delta\)-tube. For zeros \(t_j=j\pi/N\) in \((-1/5,1/5)\) let \(X\) be the union of rectangles \[|x|<\delta/8,\qquad |t-t_j|<\delta/8 .\] There are comparable to \(N\) disjoint rectangles, each of area comparable to \(\delta^2\). They lie in both tubes and in \(B_{1/2}\). If a point of either core is within Euclidean distance \(\delta\) of such a rectangle point, its time differs from \(t_j\) by less than \(9\delta/8\). Hence the second curve’s slope has absolute value at least \(\cos(9c/8)>0.99\). Its unit tangent has wedge product greater than \(1/3\) with the vertical first tangent. The full infimum over nearby core points in Definition 6.10 is therefore bounded below by the fixed \(\nu=1/3\). Also \(\delta<\nu\) as required.

The left-hand side of (6.20) is at least \(c_1\delta\sqrt N\). With \(r=1/2\), its asserted right-hand side is \(C\nu^{-A}\delta^{1-\varepsilon}\), since both family cardinalities are one and the \(r\) exponent is zero. The ratio is bounded below by a constant times \(N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\), which diverges for \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\). This disproves the stated \(M_1\)-only uniformity, while respecting all smoothness and local transversality hypotheses. It does not disprove a bound with dependence on the higher derivatives of a fixed family.

The cited curved theorem [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 7, p.~6]{Guth}] assumes small slopes around a fixed coordinate axis for each family. Local transversality on \(X\) does not itself give that hypothesis. One repair is to allow dependence on appropriate higher derivative bounds and partition curves into uniformly controlled pieces with tangents in fixed small cones. For a fixed smooth phase such dependence is compatible with the manuscript’s phase-dependent constants. The example rules out retaining the stronger uniformity; it does not by itself refute the final phase-dependent estimates. A fully uniform first-derivative-only replacement is not supplied.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: LHS>=c delta sqrt(N), proposed RHS=C nu^-A delta^(1-epsilon); ratio grows N^(1/2-epsilon) for epsilon<1/2.
Recorded evidence: Witness: gamma1=0,gamma2=sin(Nt)/N. Around O(N) zeros, choose rectangles |x|,|t-tj|<delta/8. They lie in both tubes and nearby slopes have absolute cos>0.99.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Allow dependence on suitable higher derivative bounds and controlled fixed-cone pieces; cited Guth Theorem 7 requires fixed-axis small slopes.

problems.title: Shrinking-cap symbol derivative sign and packet centering
problems.source_location: Proposition 9.1 p.73; packet definition p.74; Lemmas 9.2-9.3 p.75
claim: Recorded check: Shrinking-cap symbol derivative sign and packet centering
analysis: Location. Proposition 9.1, p. 73; the definition of \(f_T\), p. 74; Lemmas 9.2–9.3, p. 75.

The source places a smooth symbol on a cap of diameter \(O(R^{-1/2})\) but requires \(|\partial_y^\beta a_\theta|\lesssim R^{-|\beta|/2}\). These are not the bounds of the cap cutoffs already displayed correctly on p. 74. They would force such symbols to be rapidly small. Indeed, Taylor expansion along a coordinate from a point just outside the support, at distance \(O(R^{-1/2})\), gives \[\|a_\theta\|_\infty\leq C_L R^{-L}
 \quad\hbox{for every integer }L\geq1,\] since all jets vanish at the exterior point and the derivative of order \(L\) is \(O(R^{-L/2})\).

This contradicts the existence assertion of Proposition 9.1 for a fixed nonzero amplitude. Use the normalized constant Hörmander phase \(x\cdot y+t|y|^2\), a smooth amplitude equal to 1 near the origin, a fixed nonnegative nonzero \(f\), and \(\lambda=R\). At \(q=2\), the left side of (9.3) is bounded below on a fixed small ball for all large \(R\). On the right, every proposed cap symbol is \(O_L(R^{-L})\). The number of caps, the volume of \(B_{2R}\) and all prefactors grow only polynomially; the number of \(\gamma\) indices is fixed for fixed \(N,\varepsilon\). Taking \(L\) sufficiently large makes that entire term tend to zero. The \(R^{-N}\|f\|_2\) term also tends to zero. Thus the printed assertion cannot hold.

The needed cap scale is \(R^{|\beta|/2}\) (and \(\lambda^{|\beta|/2}\) in Lemma 9.3), as the neighbouring cutoff formula already shows. Separately, for a ball centred at a physical point \(z_B\), a coherent packet construction is to decompose \(h(y)=e^{i\phi^\lambda(z_B;y)}f(y)\) into \(h_{\theta,\omega}\) and define \[f_T(y)=e^{-i\phi^\lambda(z_B;y)}h_{\theta,\omega}(y).\] Then \(\sum_T f_T=f\), and the packet phase at \(z_B+z\) is \[\phi^\lambda(z_B+z;y)-\phi^\lambda(z_B;y)-\omega\cdot y,\] which is the phase compatible with the stated recentered tubes. The positive modulation printed for \(f_T\) on p. 74 has the opposite sign. When a unit-scale phase is used, its base point must also be \(z_B/\lambda\). The displayed reconstruction proves the corrected algebra and preserves packet norms.

These are local scale and modulation corrections. A unit-size symbol does not satisfy the printed negative derivative bounds, so it would be invalid to use one as a purported all-hypothesis counterexample to Lemma 9.2 itself. The contradiction above instead targets the existential Proposition 9.1, where it is valid. This review does not claim a new complete proof of the corrected reverse square function proposition.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: Exact scaling contradiction to existence, and explicit corrected algebra h=e^(i phi_lambda(zB))f, f_T=e^(-i phi_lambda(zB))h_theta,omega.

Recorded evidence: Witness: Taylor from outside support forces proposed symbols rapidly small; polynomially many caps and polynomial output volume cannot dominate a nonzero fixed-ball LHS of (9.3). Positive modulation in f_T also fails to produce the recentered phase difference.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use positive derivative powers R^(|beta|/2), lambda^(|beta|/2), correct opposite modulation, and basepoint zB/lambda in unit phase.

problems.title: Whitney separation and summation range missing in local-to-global proof
problems.source_location: Proof of Lemma 9.5 pp.79-80, equations (9.21)-(9.24)
claim: Recorded check: Whitney separation and summation range missing in local-to-global proof
analysis: Location. Proof of Lemma 9.5, pp. 79–80, particularly (9.21)–(9.24).

On p. 79, the relation \(Q_1\sim Q_2\) is defined by disjoint dyadic cubes with non-disjoint parents. Such siblings need not be separated: \([0,1)\) and \([1,2)\) have the same parent and distance zero. Products with common intervals give the same example in every dimension. Thus the stated inference \(\operatorname{dist}(Q_1,Q_2)\sim2^k\) is false, and the scale-decay factor in (9.21) cannot follow from that definition. Use the usual Whitney pairs of non-neighbouring cubes whose parents are neighbours. Their separation is comparable to their side length, and the complement of the diagonal admits the required bounded-overlap decomposition. This is the exact geometric property needed for the subsequent kernel bound.

In addition, the large-\(k\) series in (9.24) requires \(s\alpha<(n-1)/2\), not merely the lemma’s stated \(s\alpha<(n+1)/2\). For example, \(n=3,s=2,\alpha=1/2\) obeys the stated range and the available local \(L^\infty\to L^2\) estimate for the constant phase. Yet the large-\(k\) term is \(\min\{\sigma^{-2},2^k\}\), so its infinite sum diverges. This is a failure of that summation argument, not a counterexample to the lemma’s global conclusion.

For the application in odd dimensions \(n\geq3\), first separate the range \(\alpha\geq\alpha_{\rm H}(n,s)\): its requested global exponents are already supplied by the universal theorem. In the remaining range, using \[\alpha_{\rm H}(n,s)=\frac{n+1}{2s}-\frac{n-1}{4},
 \qquad 2\leq s\leq q(n),\] gives \(s\alpha<s\alpha_{\rm H}(n,s)\leq1\leq(n-1)/2\). The strict summability inequality then holds, and the geometric series can be evaluated as intended. At the boundary \(n=3,s=2\), the case of equality is assigned to the universal estimate. Together with the corrected Whitney decomposition this supplies the missing local proof organization. No false global theorem is alleged on the basis of the divergent intermediate bound.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: Exact interval distance and geometric-series computation.
Recorded evidence: Witness: Q1=[0,1),Q2=[1,2) have same parent and distance zero, with product analogues. At stated n,s,alpha, large-k term min(sigma^-2,2^k) has divergent sum.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use non-neighbour Whitney pairs with neighbouring parents; split alpha>=alpha_H to universal estimate and apply the series only below alpha_H.

report: Author: Targeted recovery 0025: M25-0396
Date: Exact-source initial review; independent scientific acceptance pending

Title: Initial scientific review of
Nonnegative Cross-Curvature in Infinite Dimensions:
Synthetic Definition and Spaces of Measures

Authors. Flavien Léger, Gabriele Todeschi, and François-Xavier Vialard. Frozen identity. Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 1638–1711; DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-025-00725-x. Reviewed object. The exact 52-page arXiv:2409.18112v3 PDF dated 9 November 2025 on its arXiv margin, with internal date 11 November 2025. All page references below concern this PDF. Equivalence to the journal version is not established.
# Assessment and scope

The variational definition gives a useful framework for discussing nonsmooth cross-curvature. The finite-product argument, the algebraic cost-submersion argument, the compact Gromov–Hausdorff limit argument, and several explicit constructions can be checked directly. However, the submitted version requires major revision. Four substantive issues are established below: a counterexample to the random-variable stability proposition; a false graph inclusion in the measurable-selection argument supporting the principal lifting theorem; an invalid base-space hypothesis in the advertised LMP non-lifting example; and an incompatible use of two cone costs in the WFR application. These have different logical strengths. Only the first is presented as an all-hypothesis counterexample to its stated stability proposition. The second is a decisive failure of a central proof step. The third invalidates the stated counterexample to preservation. The fourth invalidates the written WFR formulas and the stated deduction for the sphere, without asserting that the correctly defined WFR space on the sphere is not NNCC.

Nine local Minor items follow, each with an explicit calculation or counterexample and a bounded correction. Severity reflects actual mathematical impact, with no quota. The whole 52-page source, including Appendices A and B and the reference list, was read. One external primary reference was additionally checked in the relevant cone, normalization, gluing, and truncation sections. Absence of author code is not treated as a mathematical defect; no author code was run.
# Major issues
## P1. Proposition 3.17 is false without control of intermediate expected costs
Location. Proposition 3.17, p. 25, and its proof, p. 26, especially the final integration of (3.11).

Claim and hypotheses. Here \(X,Y\) are Polish, \(c\) is lower semicontinuous and bounded below, and \((X\times Y,c)\) is NNCC. The proposition asserts NNCC for all random elements on any fixed probability space, with cost \(\widehat T_c(T,S)=\mathbb Ec(T,S)\). Unlike Theorem 3.7, it does not assume Assumption 3.5. The definition of a variational segment requires finite cost to the base at every intermediate time.

Counterexample. Set \[X=Y=\mathbb R,\qquad a(x)=4^x\sin^2(\pi x),\qquad
 c(x,y)=a(x)+(x-y)^2.\] This cost is finite, smooth, nonnegative, and NNCC. Indeed, \(a(x)\) cancels from every difference \(c(x,\bar y)-c(x,y)\), which is affine in \(x\); the ordinary affine segment therefore satisfies the NNCC inequality as an equality.

Take \(\Omega=\{1,2,\ldots\}\), all subsets measurable, and \(\Pr\{k\}=2^{-k}\). Define \[T_0(k)=k,\qquad T_1(k)=k+1,\qquad \bar S(k)=k.\] The endpoint expected costs are \(0\) and \(1\), respectively. Suppose that \(T_s\) has finite expected cost to \(\bar S\) and satisfies the required NNCC inequality. For an arbitrary atom \(j\) and arbitrary real \(h\), use the test target \[S^{j,h}(k)=k+h\,{\bf1}_{\{k=j\}}.\] Changing one atom preserves finiteness of all the expected costs used in this comparison. Cancellation gives \[2^{-j}\{2(T_s(j)-j)h-h^2\}
 \le 2^{-j}\{2s h-h^2\}.\] Both signs of \(h\) are allowed, so necessarily \(T_s(j)=j+s\). Every atom has positive mass; thus every possible intermediate random element is forced to have this value at every \(j\).

At \(s=1/2\), however, \[a(k+1/2)=2\,4^k,\qquad
 \mathbb Ec(T_{1/2},\bar S)
 =\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-k}\left(2\,4^k+\frac14\right)=+\infty.\] There is no admissible midpoint. For an exact independent arithmetic check, the first \(N\) terms are \[2^{N+2}-4+\frac14(1-2^{-N}),\] which diverge. This is not a numerical approximation to a trigonometric zero: the integer and half-integer identities above are exact.

Impact and repair limit. Proposition 3.17, the asserted infinite-product extension, is false as stated. Pointwise cancellation does not justify subtracting two infinite expected costs. This example fails Assumption 3.5 because \(\inf_y c(x,y)=a(x)\) is unbounded; hence it does not refute Theorem 3.7 or its metric specialization. A sufficient replacement must provide measurable intermediate selections and integrability of their cost to the base. An integrable pointwise upper bound supplies the latter directly. Assumption 3.5 can also supply that bound through a measurable finite-cost comparison partner, once the selection issue in P2 is separately resolved. Adding an assumption does not by itself repair the existing selection proof.
## P2. The measurable-selection graph reconstruction is incorrect
Location. Lemma 3.3, p. 22; its Appendix B.4 proof, pp. 47–48, equations (B.13)–(B.15) and the asserted inclusion immediately after (B.15).

Decisive example under the lemma’s assumptions. Let \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \(c(x,y)=(x-y)^2\), \(\gamma=\delta_{(0,2,0)}\), and \(s=1/2\). This is a continuous nonnegative NNCC cost, and it also satisfies Assumption 3.5. The unique variational midpoint is \(x=1\): expanding the NNCC inequality for arbitrary \(y\) forces \(x=(1-s)0+s2\).

Choose the nondecreasing continuous approximation \(c_n=c\) and, for every \(k\), choose the valid compact sets \[Z_k^1=Z_k^2=Z_k=\{(0,0),(2,0)\}.\] Both endpoint-plan measures give these sets mass one, and convergence is uniform there with error zero. Thus all the stated prerequisites for (B.13) hold. The tuple \((0,2,0,1)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{Graph}(\widetilde\Lambda_{1/2})\cap\widetilde Z_k\). But every \(F_{k,n,m}\) in (B.15) additionally requires \((x,\bar y)\in Z_k\), whereas \((1,0)\notin Z_k\). Consequently the displayed inclusion is false, as is the ensuing claimed graph identity, on the entire \(\gamma\)-mass.

The problem is not fixed by increasing \(n\) or \(m\). The compact sets were controlled using the two endpoint laws, not the law of an as-yet unselected midpoint. Furthermore, the restricted tests with \((x,z)\in Z_k\) do not automatically recover tests at every \(z\in Y\). Intersecting separately large sets for two different measures need not even give a large set for either measure; using a common Lusin set would only fix that additional preliminary defect.

Impact and repair limit. The proof of Lemma 3.3 does not establish the Borel selections it needs. Lemma 3.4 and the stated general Polish-space lifting theorem depend on it. This is a Major proof dependency, even though the quadratic example itself has the obvious measurable affine selection and is not a counterexample to the lemma’s conclusion. A replacement must establish the actual selection relation under the stated lower semicontinuity assumptions and respect the quantifiers in Definition 3.2: a common full-measure set for the complete selected path, not merely unrelated exceptional sets for individual times. No impossibility theorem for such a replacement is asserted here. Continuous explicit selections in standard examples remain available independently.
## P3. The base space in Example 3.21 does not satisfy global LMP
Location. Section 3.3, p. 28, first paragraph and Example 3.21; Figure 1, p. 29; the continuity requirement in (2.35), p. 18.

The claimed base cost is \(c(x,y)=-\log|x-y|\) off the diagonal in \(\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2\). The text claims that the corresponding \(c\)-segments exist for every finite-cost endpoint pair, and that this space satisfies LMP. Both global assertions fail.

Use even the horizontal points already present in the example: \[x_0=(-1,0),\quad x_1=(1,0),\quad  ar y=(-1/2,0).\] All endpoint costs are finite. At a putative continuous LMP path \(x(t)\), first-order variations of the comparison target near \( ar y\), with both signs in every direction, force \[
abla_y c(x(t), ar y)\in
 [\,
abla_y c(x_0, ar y),
abla_y c(x_1, ar y)\,]
 =[-2e_1,	frac23e_1].\] This follows directly by separating a point outside the segment from the two endpoint vectors in the first-order maximum inequality; differentiability of the path is unnecessary. Since \[
abla_y c(x, ar y)= rac{x- ar y}{|x- ar y|^2},\] its value is continuous along any finite-cost continuous path and is never zero. Its scalar coordinate would have to move from \(-2\) to \(2/3\), so the intermediate value theorem gives a contradiction. An affine-gradient \(c\)-segment likewise cannot cross the missing zero vector.

What the figure does establish. For the displayed four specific curved segments, direct rational evaluation at \(s=1/2\) gives the two squared-distance ratios \(17/5\) and \(17/45\). Thus the plotted average is \[\frac14\log\frac{289}{225}>0,\] with zero endpoint values. The plotted failure for those lifts is real. It does not establish failure of preservation from an LMP base, because that prerequisite fails. Restricting to a smooth region of the cost is not the same as verifying global LMP on a specified Cartesian pair of domains. In particular, a restriction retaining the two horizontal endpoints and an open neighborhood of the displayed base point still has the obstruction above.

Impact and repair limit. The advertised non-lifting conclusion in Section 3.3 lacks a valid example under its own global definition. In addition, Lemmas B.9–B.11 are stated with compact domains and a smooth twisted cost, whereas the example is noncompact and singular on the diagonal. A replacement example must verify the base property and the hypotheses needed to infer a lifted path. The claim that some other valid example may prove non-preservation is left open by this audit.
## P4. The WFR application conflates entropy and Euclidean cone costs
Location. Section 4.5, pp. 35–37; (4.19), Example 4.18 and (4.22), Lemma 4.19 and its proof on pp. 48–49; Example 4.21.

For the KL entropy \(F(t)=t\log t-t+1\), direct minimization of (4.19), for \(r,s>0\), gives \[\inf_{z>0}\left[rF(z/r)+sF(z/s)+cz\right]
 =r+s-2\sqrt{rs}\,e^{-c/2}.\] The derivative vanishes at \(z=\sqrt{rs}\,e^{-c/2}\), and the second derivative is \(2/z>0\). Substituting the printed \(c=-\log(\cos^2(\min(d,\pi)))\) yields an absolute value of the cosine, not the signed cosine in (4.22).

For antipodal points on the unit sphere and \(r=s=1\), the printed entropy cost is \(c=0\). Equation (4.19) therefore gives \(0\), while the printed (4.22) gives \(4\). The resulting literal entropy-transport cost between the distinct unit Dirac masses is also zero: take the unit transport plan, for which both entropy terms and the transport term vanish. It cannot be the asserted WFR metric.

For the usual WFR normalization, the entropy cost is \[c_{\rm ET}(x,y)=-2\log\cos d(x,y)\quad(d<\pi/2),
 \qquad c_{\rm ET}=+\infty\quad(d\ge\pi/2).\] Its pointwise perspective cost is \[c_{\rm ET,C}=r+s-2\sqrt{rs}\cos(\min(d,\pi/2)).\] This differs from the Euclidean cone cost with cutoff \(\pi\). The two can induce the same minimized measure distance when both lifts and the cone-tip reservoir are allowed to vary, but they are not the same pointwise cost. The primary reference [LMS], Remark 7.2, Lemma 7.10, Remark 7.12 and Section 7.6, explicitly distinguishes these operations. Its normalization retains a cone-tip atom; its common-lift result is not a theorem for every prescribed lift.

There is a precise obstruction to using the Euclidean cone and the arbitrary prescribed-lift assertion together. Let \(x,y\) be antipodal and \(\mu=\delta_x,\nu=\delta_y\). Fix the target lift \(\widetilde\nu=\delta_{(y,1)}\), in the manuscript’s mass-radius convention. Any probability lift \(\widetilde\mu\) of \(\delta_x\) has positive-radius part at \(x\), satisfies \(\mathbb Er=1\), and is otherwise allowed to charge the tip. Its squared Euclidean-cone transport cost to the fixed target is \[\mathbb E(r+1+2\sqrt r)=2+2\mathbb E\sqrt r>2.\] The inequality is strict because \(\mathbb Er=1\). Yet the correctly defined squared WFR distance is \(2\), realized by annihilation and creation. The infimum \(2\) with this fixed target lift is approached by placing probability \(\varepsilon\) at radius \(1/\varepsilon\) and the rest at the tip, but it is never attained. Thus the cost-submersion attainment condition used in the paper fails for this Euclidean-cone interpretation.

Impact and repair limit. Correcting only the missing absolute value or changing one cutoff does not preserve the argument of Example 4.21. With the entropy perspective cost, the claimed isometry of the full spherical cone to Euclidean space no longer applies. With the Euclidean cone cost, the asserted fixed-lift attainment fails. The WFR sphere deduction therefore needs a new argument, not just a cosmetic edit. This finding does not refute a correctly formulated NNCC theorem for WFR. The unit-trace PSD example has nonnegative cosine and avoids this specific antipodal obstruction, but the hypotheses for its lifting step must still be supplied. Theorem 4.20 also needs a justified application of the probability-space lifting theorem, including its integrability conditions, for whichever cone cost is actually chosen.
# Local Minor issues with explicit corrections
## P5. Differential prerequisites and a one-sided limit
Location. The sentence preceding Definition 2.2 and (2.10), p. 8.

Bi-twist does not imply nondegeneracy. On \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), let \(c(x,y)=x^3y+xy^3\). For every fixed \(x\), \(y\mapsto3x^2y+y^3\) is strictly increasing onto \(\mathbb R\); the analogous statement holds with \(x,y\) exchanged. Thus smoothness, bi-twist, and the convex-image conditions hold, but \(c_{xy}(0,0)=0\). Keep (2.3) as an independent hypothesis. Theorem 2.4 already lists it explicitly, so this does not refute that theorem.

The division by \(t\) in the proof of Lemma 2.5 reverses the inequality for \(t<0\). For an explicit instance of the lemma’s assumptions, take \(c(x,y)=-x^2y^2\), \(x(s)=s\), and \(\bar y=0\). Then (2.9) is \(s^2y^2\le sy^2\), while (2.10) would assert \(s^2t\le st\), false for \(0<s<1,t<0\). The lemma remains valid: take only \(t\downarrow0\) with an arbitrary signed tangent vector, or differentiate the nonnegative comparison gap at its minimum.
## P6. The semi-geostrophic example requires positive gravity
Location. Example 2.11, p. 11.

The claimed parameter range includes negative \(g\). Let \(H=\mathbb R\), \(g=-1\), \(x_0=-4,x_1=4,a_0=a_1=1\), and base \((\bar y,\bar b)=(0,1)\). The finite endpoint costs are both \(7\). Differentiating the NNCC comparison gap in the target variables at its minimum forces \(x_{1/2}=0\) and \(a_{1/2}=-7\), exactly as the displayed segment formula gives. The latter lies outside \(a>0\); no alternative midpoint is possible. This pointwise necessity does not require continuity of the candidate path. With \(g>0\), the displayed \(a(s)\) is positive and the affine-difference verification works. Restricting to that range repairs the example and retains its physical gravity case.
## P7. Two projection remarks need explicit compatibility hypotheses
Location. Remarks 2.21–2.22, p. 14.

For LMP preservation, continuity of the first projection is needed. Take the quadratic cost on the usual real line upstairs, and the same set with the discrete topology as the first space downstairs. Let both projections be the identity as set maps, with the second target retaining its usual topology. All fibers are singletons and the cost-submersion equalities and attainments hold. Upstairs affine paths satisfy LMP; downstairs no continuous path joins \(0\) to \(1\). Requiring the first projection to be continuous repairs this implication.

For the metric conclusion, require the two quotient maps to be the same map. Otherwise take \(P_1(x)=x\), \(P_2(y)=y+1\) and \(c(x,y)=(x-y)^2\). This is a cost submersion with singleton fibers, but the projected square root is \(|u-v+1|\), which equals \(1\) on the diagonal and vanishes at distinct points. With a common quotient map, the usual lift argument does give separation, symmetry and the triangle inequality. Neither example refutes the purely algebraic NNCC part of Proposition 2.20.
## P8. Compact closure does not guarantee an attained interior support
Location. The paragraph following Theorem 2.35 and (2.40), p. 20.

Let \(X=Y=(0,1)\), \(c(x,y)=-xy\), and \(\psi(x)=-x\). All the smoothness, twist, nondegeneracy and convex-image conditions listed there hold, and \(c\) extends continuously to the compact closure. Nevertheless, \[\phi(y)=\psi^c(y)=\inf_{0<x<1}x(1-y)=0,\qquad
 \phi^c(x)=-x.\] For every interior \(x,y\), \(c(x,y)-\phi^c(x)=x(1-y)>0=\phi(y)\). Thus the finite \(c\)-concave function \(\phi\) has empty \(c\)-subdifferential at every \(y\). The infimum is attained only at an excluded boundary point. Actual compact domains with the appropriate properness assumptions, or explicit nonempty-support assumptions, repair the sentence. Proposition 2.36 already uses the appropriate support class and is not refuted by this example.
## P9. Matrix metric normalization, logarithm range, and completeness
Location. The discussion before Example 3.15, p. 25; (4.16) and Remark 4.11, p. 34.

The printed Frobenius norm is \(\operatorname{tr}(S^\top S)\); its square root is missing on both pages. Literally, in the scalar case the log-distance from \(1\) to \(e^2\) is \(4\), while the two distances through \(e\) sum to \(2\). The triangle inequality fails. Use \(\|S\|_F=\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(S^\top S)}\).

The logarithm maps positive definite matrices onto all symmetric matrices, not onto positive definite matrices: \(\log I=0\), and every symmetric \(A\) is the logarithm of \(\exp A\). This corrected Hilbert-space identification proves the intended log-Euclidean NNCC example. The affine-invariant and log-Euclidean metrics should also be distinguished. At \(S=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), for an off-diagonal symmetric perturbation \(H\), the differential of \(\log\) multiplies the off-diagonal entries by \((\log4)/3\). Congruence by \(S^{-1/2}\) sends the base to \(I\) and multiplies those entries by \(1/2\). These differ: \(e^3>16\), already from the first six terms of its positive series, so \(\log4<3/2\). Therefore the log-Euclidean infinitesimal norm is not invariant under this congruence.

Finally, nondegenerate Gaussian measures are geodesically convex but not geodesically complete. In one dimension the unit-speed covariance path \(S(t)=(1-t)^2\), \(0\le t<1\), has Bures distance \(|t-u|\) and reaches zero variance in finite time. Adjoining degenerate covariances gives the completion. These corrections do not invalidate the corrected Hilbert quotient proof of Theorem 4.10.
## P10. Singular polar factors cannot be obtained from a right inverse
Location. Proposition 4.12 and its proof, pp. 34–35.

The matrices are allowed to be positive semidefinite, but the displayed formula asks for a right inverse of a possibly singular square matrix. Take \(S_2=0\), \(S_0=S_1=I\). No right inverse of zero exists. Replacing it silently by a Moore–Penrose inverse gives \(U_i=0\), which is not orthogonal, and gives \(M_i=0\) instead of the required \(M_iM_i^\top=I\).

The precise repair is to choose an orthogonal polar factor \(U_i\) satisfying \[S_2^{1/2}S_i^{1/2}
 =U_i\bigl(S_i^{1/2}S_2S_i^{1/2}\bigr)^{1/2}.\] Use an orthogonal completion on the null spaces in the singular case. Then \(M_i=S_i^{1/2}U_i^\top\) has the required covariance and is an optimal aligned factor; the quotient proof supplies the segment. The inverse formula is valid when the product is invertible. This local defect does not refute existence in Theorem 4.10.
## P11. The Fisher–Rao formula omits the square of Hellinger distance
Location. Equation (4.5), p. 31, compared with (4.4), p. 30.

Under (4.4), unit square-root densities satisfy \(\langle\sqrt\mu,\sqrt\nu\rangle=1-\mathcal H^2(\mu,\nu)/2\). The induced spherical distance is therefore \(\arccos(1-\mathcal H^2/2)\), with the normalization used in the paper. For disjoint unit Dirac measures, \(\mathcal H=\sqrt2\) and the angle is \(\pi/2\); the printed expression instead gives \(\arccos(1-\sqrt2/2)<\pi/2\). Insert the missing square. The subsequent spherical proof applies to the corrected distance.
## P12. The partial-transport cone formula has the wrong minimum
Location. The paragraph following Example 4.18, p. 36.

For \(F(t)=|t-1|\), \(c=d^q\ge0\), and positive \(r,s\), the definition (4.19) reduces to \[\inf_{z\ge0}\{|z-r|+|z-s|+d^qz\}
 =r+s-\min(r,s)\max(0,2-d^q).\] Splitting at \(0,\min(r,s),\max(r,s)\) proves the formula directly. With \(q=1,r=s=1,d=0\), the true value is \(0\), but the printed expression with \(\min(0,2-d^q)\) is \(2\). Replace that minimum by a maximum. The resulting expression is \(c_C\) as defined in (4.19), without an additional outer \(q\)-th power unless a new root-distance notation is explicitly introduced. This is a local example correction.
## P13. The translation bound in the Procrustes proof needs the means
Location. The last sentence of the proof of Theorem 4.28, p. 39.

Take \(\mu=
u=\delta_a\) on \(\mathbb R\), \(a
e0\). The isometry \(x\mapsto-x+2a\) is optimal with cost zero, but its translation is \(2a\), not bounded by \(W_2(\mu,
u)=0\). For a general isometry \(x\mapsto Qx+b\) in the sublevel set of cost at most \(R=W_2(\mu,
u)\), Jensen’s inequality instead gives \[|b|\le R+|\operatorname{mean}\mu|+|\operatorname{mean}
u|.\] Together with compactness of \(O(n)\), this supplies the required compact parameter set and repairs the existence argument. The theorem is not refuted.
