problems.title: Finite-volume saturation invalidates the central cost lemmas
problems.source_location: p20 definition of Delta and Lemma 3.5 p21 Lemma 3.6 p24 finite-limit branch pp42–43 appendix Lemma 3.5
claim: The finite-graph cost becomes arbitrarily small on a suitable orange interval and is at most 1/log log n when L(n) is green.
analysis: Location. Definition of \(\Delta_t(n)\) and Lemma 3.5, p. 20; Lemma 3.6, p. 21; its finite-limit case, p. 24; appendix proof of Lemma 3.5, pp. 42–43. The dependencies run through Lemma 3.2, pp. 21–22, Proposition 3.1, pp. 17–19, and Claim 6.1, pp. 38–39.

Definitions and scope. Section 3.1 fixes an arbitrary finite transitive graph of degree \(d\). It uses \[\phi(t)=1-2^{-e^t},\quad
 \delta(n)=e^{-\sqrt{\log\log n}},\quad
 R(n)=e^{(\log n)^9},\quad L(n)=\sqrt{\log n},\] and \(\mathcal L=\{n\ge3:\operatorname{Gr}(n)\le e^{(\log n)^{100}}\}\). The integer \(U_t(n)\) is the largest \(b\le n^{1/3}/8\) for which \(\mathbb P_{\phi(t)}(\mathrm{Piv}[4b,n^{1/3}])\le1/\log n\), and \[\Delta_t(n)=
 \left(\frac{\log\log n}{(\log n)\wedge\log\operatorname{Gr}(U_t(n))}\right)^{1/4}.\] There is no upper restriction on \(n\) relative to the diameter or volume. Real radii are rounded down as specified in footnote 9, p. 5.

Exact witness. Take \(G=C_3\), \(d=2\), \(t=0\), so \(\phi(t)=1/2\). Distinct vertices are connected if the direct edge is open or the other two edges are both open. Hence \[\min_{u,v}\mathbb P_{1/2}(u\leftrightarrow v)
 =\frac12+\frac12\left(\frac12\right)^2=\frac58.\] Once \(\lfloor n^{1/3}\rfloor>1\), the outer sphere is empty. The pivotal event is therefore impossible, independently of the percolation parameter. For sufficiently large \(n\), \[U_s(n)=\left\lfloor\frac{n^{1/3}}8\right\rfloor,\quad
 \operatorname{Gr}(U_s(n))=3,\quad
 \Delta_s(n)=\left(\frac{\log\log n}{\log3}\right)^{1/4}
 \longrightarrow\infty\] for every real \(s\). Thus the finite-limit argument on p. 24 has the limit in the wrong direction.

Counterexample to all quantifiers in Lemma 3.6. Choose \(\varepsilon=1/2\) and \(n_1=e^{24}\). Every \(n\ge n_1\) belongs to \(\mathcal L\) and is orange at time \(0\), since \[\delta(n)\le e^{-\sqrt{\log24}}<\frac12<\frac58.\] The restriction \(t\le1/\varepsilon\) is satisfied. Yet, for every \(n\ge n_1\), \[\Delta_{t+\varepsilon}(n)
 \ge\left(\frac{\log24}{\log3}\right)^{1/4}>1>\varepsilon.\] Consequently no proposed \(n_2(2,\varepsilon,n_1)\) can supply an interval \([L(m),m]\subset[n_1,n_2]\) satisfying the conclusion. Every point in any such interval lies in \(\mathcal L\) and violates the asserted bound.

Counterexample to Lemma 3.5 at arbitrarily large scales. Set \(n=\exp(\exp k)\), with \(k\ge48\) arbitrarily large. Here \[L(n)=e^{k/2}\ge e^{24}.\] The scale \(L(n)\) is orange and belongs to \(\mathcal L\). Every tube of radius \(L(n)\) contains the whole triangle, so its endpoint connection probability is at least \(5/8\). Since \(\delta(R(L(n)))\le\delta(L(n))<1/2\), this scale is green. All hypotheses of Lemma 3.5 are satisfied, however large its proposed \(n_0(2)\), whereas \[\Delta_0(n)=\left(\frac{k}{\log3}\right)^{1/4}>1>\frac1k
 =\frac1{\log\log n}.\] The appendix’s claim that the case above the diameter is trivial because \(\Delta_t(n)\le(\log n)^{-1/5}\) is false for the same reason.

Impact and verified repair boundary. These are false core auxiliary assertions in the finite-graph argument. The triangle is not a counterexample to the asymptotic Theorem 1.1: a fixed finite graph does not satisfy its infinite-family hypothesis.

A concrete repair to the saturated branch is to replace the definition by \[\Delta_t^*(n)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&\lfloor n^{1/3}\rfloor>\operatorname{diam}G,\\
 \Delta_t(n),&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}\] In the first case \(B_n=G\) and every tube of radius \(n\) is \(G\). Orange already implies green because \(\delta(R(n))\le\delta(n)\). Thus the zero-cost conclusion required in Lemma 3.4 is valid, and the saturated case of Lemma 3.5 becomes automatic. For a fixed finite graph \(\Delta_t^*(n)\) is eventually zero, repairing the finite-limit branch of Lemma 3.6. In a local limit that is finite, connected regular graphs are eventually that same graph once a sufficiently large ball is matched. For an infinite local limit and each fixed scale, the approximating diameters eventually exceed that scale, so this modification does not change the infinite-limit estimates.

This checks the proposed correction exactly where the displayed failure occurs. It does not make the printed definition correct, or by itself constitute acceptance of every imported estimate. The definition, all cost statements, and the induction must be updated together; the domain issue in P7 also remains necessary. An alternative is a carefully proved scale restriction and an early stopping rule, not the unqualified limit on p. 24.
result: Impact: False central auxiliary assertions used by Lemma3.2 and Proposition3.1. Theorem1.1 itself is not refuted by a fixed triangle.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Set cost to0 when floor(n^(1/3))>diamG, retaining the original cost otherwise; orange already implies green there. Finite-limit costs then vanish, while fixed-scale infinite local limits are unchanged. Propagate the altered definition and address P7 explicitly.

problems.title: Closed-ball overlap invalidates a deterministic packing implication
problems.source_location: p13 Lemma2.7 proof
claim: Recorded check: Closed-ball overlap invalidates a deterministic packing implication
analysis: Location. Lemma 2.7 and its proof, p. 13. The centers have distance at least \(2r\), but the proof adds the sizes of closed \(r\)-balls as if disjoint.

All-hypothesis witness to the proof implication. Let \(G=C_L\square K_{10,10}\), where \(L\) is a sufficiently large even integer; take \(p=\delta=9/10\), \(r=1\), and \(n=55\). The graph is connected, finite, vertex-transitive, and \(12\)-regular, with \(|V|=20L\) and \(|B_1|=13\). Every neighbor is connected to the origin with probability at least \(p=\delta\). For any proposed positive constant \(c(\delta)\), choose even \(L\) so large that \(55\le c(\delta)20L/13\).

Use the bipartition consisting of the first side of \(K_{10,10}\) at even layers and the second side at odd layers as \(W\). It is a maximal set with mutual distances at least two. In the auxiliary graph \(H\), choose a spanning tree containing the star through the ten first-side vertices in layer zero, rooted at one of them. Let \(U\) be these ten vertices. It is tree-connected and has precisely the required size: \[|U|=10=\left\lceil\frac{2\cdot55}{(9/10)13}\right\rceil.\] Consider the configuration with all \(100\) edges of that single \(K_{10,10}\) fibre open and every other edge closed. Its probability is \(p^{100}(1-p)^{|E|-100}>0\). Every \(u\in U\) is connected to its tree parent, and \[|K_u\cap B_1(u)|=11\ge\frac{\delta|B_1|}{2}=\frac{117}{20}.\] Thus every event \(A_u\) used in the proof holds. Nevertheless \(|K_o|=20<55\). The claimed deterministic implication is false. This does not disprove the final probability inequality in Lemma 2.7.

Repair. Put \(R=\lfloor r\rfloor\ge1\) and use a maximal net with distances strictly greater than \(2R\). Then the closed \(R\)-balls are disjoint and the \(2R\)-balls cover \(V\). The auxiliary graph using distance at most \(5R\) is connected: neighboring vertices can be assigned centers at distance at most \(4R+1\le5R\). The volume and Harris estimates, including the five-link bound, now work with the same qualitative constants. The support computation constructs the witness explicitly, rather than merely noting that two balls may overlap.
result: Impact: The proof implication fails; the final lemma inequality is not disproved.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use a maximal net with separation>2 floor(r). Closed balls are disjoint; 2R-cover and H-edges<=5R preserve the volume/Harris argument.

problems.title: Variance bound needs an integer threshold or ceiling
problems.source_location: p14 Lemma2.8 p15 application in Proposition2.6
claim: Recorded check: Variance bound needs an integer threshold or ceiling
analysis: Location. Lemma 2.8, p. 14, and its application with \(n=c|B_r|\log|V|\), p. 15.

The stated quantifier is for all \(n\ge0\). Taken literally for real \(n\), the bound \(\operatorname{Var}_p|X|\le n^2\mathbb E_p|X|\) is false. Take \(G=C_3\), \(p=1/100\), and \(n=6/5\). Here \(X\) is the set of nonisolated vertices. Exact enumeration of the eight configurations gives \[\mathbb E|X|=6p-3p^2=\frac{597}{10000},\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}|X|=12p-33p^2+30p^3-9p^4
 =\frac{11672991}{10^8}.\] But \[n^2\mathbb E|X|=\frac{21492}{250000}
 <\frac{11672991}{10^8}.\] The exploration may reveal \(\lceil n\rceil\) vertices, so the last bound \(|A_i|\le n\) is the failing step.

For integer \(n\) the stated proof gives the claimed bound. For real \(n\), replace \(n^2\) by \(\lceil n\rceil^2\). This explicitly resolves the ambiguity even if an integer convention was intended. In Proposition 2.6 use an integer threshold or the ceiling bound and absorb the bounded rounding error into the constant, treating the finitely many small sizes separately. The real threshold in that application is why the convention should not remain implicit.
result: Impact: Literal real-threshold claim false; integer-threshold proof remains available.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: State n integer or replace n^2 by ceil(n)^2 and round the application, absorbing the bounded error.

problems.title: Corollary2.3 is invoked with lambda below1
problems.source_location: pp15–16 Proposition2.9 3 implies2 p11 Corollary2.3
claim: Recorded check: Corollary2.3 is invoked with lambda below1
analysis: Location. Proof of \(3\Rightarrow2\), pp. 15–16, compared with Corollary 2.3, p. 11.

The substitution \(\lambda=n/\log|V|\) is asserted for every \(n\ge1\), although the corollary requires \(\lambda\ge1\). It fails this hypothesis whenever \(n<\log|V|\). The excluded range grows with the graph, so a graph-independent constant cannot be justified just by calling it a finite range of \(n\).

A direct application of Lemma 2.2 repairs the proof. Write \(p_0=(1-\varepsilon/2)p_c(H)\) and use the chosen radius \(r\) with \(\mathbb P_{p_0}(|K_o|\ge r)\le\varepsilon/4\). For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), set \[h=\frac1r\log\frac1{1-\varepsilon/4}.\] The same union bound as in Corollary 2.3 gives \(\mu_{p_0,h}\le\varepsilon/2\). Hence, for every \(n\ge1\), \[\mathbb P_{(1-\varepsilon/2)p_0}(|K_o|\ge n)
 \le(1-\varepsilon/2)^{-1}e^{-hn}.\] Because \((1-\varepsilon/2)^2\ge1-\varepsilon\), monotonicity yields the desired estimate at \((1-\varepsilon)p_c(H)\) with a uniform constant. The quantitative assertion is therefore locally repairable.
result: Impact: The written all-n exponential-tail inference has a domain gap.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Apply Lemma2.2 directly with h=r^-1 log(1/(1-epsilon/4)), yielding mu<=epsilon/2 and a uniform exponential bound for every n>=1.

problems.title: The chosen radius does not control the displayed error
problems.source_location: pp16–17 Proposition2.9 Case2
claim: Recorded check: The chosen radius does not control the displayed error
analysis: Location. Bottom of p. 16 and top of p. 17, Case 2.

The proof has error \(Cr d^{r+1}/\sqrt n\) and chooses \[r=\log_d\left(\frac{\delta^2\sqrt n}{2Cd^2}\right).\] Substitution gives exactly \(r\delta^2/(2d)\), not a quantity bounded by \(\delta^2/2\) for all large \(n\). It exceeds that target once \(r>d\). For example, \(d=4\), \(C=1\), \(\delta=1/2\), and \(n=2^{46}\) give \(r=8\), error \(1/4\), and target \(1/8\).
result: Impact: The claimed lower bound does not follow from that radius choice.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use half the logarithmic radius, rounded down, and r<=d^r; then error<=delta^2/(2d). New radius still diverges.

problems.title: Unrestricted eta makes a probability lower bound exceed1
problems.source_location: p11 Proposition2.1
claim: Recorded check: Unrestricted eta makes a probability lower bound exceed1
analysis: Location. Proposition 2.1, p. 11, and the initial parameter reduction in its proof.

The conclusion is a connection probability at least \(\eta^2/20\) for every \(\eta>0\). For \(\eta=5\) it exceeds one. The premise is not vacuous: for any proposed \(c=c(2,5)>0\), choose \(\lambda=\exp(1/c+1/c^2)\), so the displayed ball radius \(c\log\lambda-1/c\) equals one. Take \(G=C_N\), \(p=1-N^{-2}\), and \(N\) sufficiently large that \[\lambda\log N\le N,\qquad
 (cN^c)^{-1}\le\frac12,\qquad N\ge3.\] All edges are open with probability at least \(1-N(1-p)=1-1/N\ge1/2\) by a union bound, giving the premise. Under the paper’s clamping convention \(p+\eta\) means probability one, while the required lower bound is \(25/20>1\).

Restrict \(\eta\) to the small range actually used, for example \(0<\eta\le1/2\), or cap the asserted lower bound by the value obtained from a fixed small sprinkling. Merely saying that one may assume \(\eta\le1/2\) does not preserve the printed right-hand side for larger \(\eta\).
result: Impact: The printed parameter-unrestricted proposition is false; intended small-sprinkling application is unaffected after correction.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Restrict eta to the proved small range or cap the asserted bound by a fixed small-sprinkling value.

problems.title: The gamma expression is not real on permitted cycles
problems.source_location: pp17–18 Proposition3.1 p18 alpha parameter
claim: Recorded check: The gamma expression is not real on permitted cycles
analysis: Location. Definition of \(\gamma,\gamma^+\) and statement, pp. 17–18; proof’s choice of \(\alpha\), p. 18.

Here \[\gamma=\operatorname{diam}(G)d_{\mathrm{GH}}\bigl((\pi/\operatorname{diam}G)G,S^1\bigr),\qquad
 \gamma^+=\exp((\log\gamma)^9),\] and the conclusion uses \(\exp(-\sqrt{\log\log\gamma^+})\). For \(G=C_{2m}\), embed its diameter-normalized vertices as equally spaced points on the unit circle with its intrinsic metric. This is isometric, with Hausdorff distance at most \(\pi/(2m)\). Since \(\operatorname{diam}G=m\), one has \(0<\gamma\le\pi/2<e\). If \(\gamma\le1\), \(\log\log\gamma^+\) is undefined; if \(1<\gamma<e\), it is negative, so its square root is not real. In addition, the coloring process is defined only at scales at least three.

The proposition and its deduction should explicitly handle small \(\gamma\) separately, or restrict \(\gamma\) to a sufficiently large domain including the relevant starting scale. Simply flooring \(\gamma\) at three does not by itself prove the new quantitative lower bound. The main application in Section 6 has \(\gamma>\exp((\log\operatorname{diam}G)^{1/9})\) and hence eventually lies in the large domain. This explains the bounded effect on that application. Also the asserted positive \(\alpha\) solving \(\phi(1/\alpha)=1-\varepsilon\) exists only when \(\varepsilon<1/2\); state that harmless small-\(\varepsilon\) reduction explicitly.
result: Impact: The proposition requires a small-gamma case or domain restriction. Section6 has gamma diverging and so eventually avoids this defect.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: State an adequate large-gamma domain including the starting scale, or prove a separate small-gamma conclusion. Also reduce epsilon below1/2 before choosing positive alpha.

problems.title: Uniformly bounded individual cycles cannot approximate a bi-infinite geodesic
problems.source_location: p28 Cycles paragraph
claim: Recorded check: Uniformly bounded individual cycles cannot approximate a bi-infinite geodesic
analysis: Location. First paragraph under Cycles, p. 28.

The text describes a sequence of individual cycles, each of extrinsic diameter at most \(\delta(G)\), converging pointwise to a bi-infinite geodesic, and calls this equivalent to one-endedness. On the one-ended graph \(\mathbb Z^2\), unit plaquettes generate the finite cycle space and \(\delta(G)=2\). Choose two edges of the horizontal axis farther apart than two. Pointwise convergence would put both in every sufficiently late cycle, contradicting that diameter bound.

The intended statement concerns finite sums of bounded generators. For example, boundaries of the rectangles \([-N,N]\times[0,N]\) converge pointwise to the horizontal axis. Each is a sum of unit plaquettes, but its own diameter is unbounded. The actual proof of Lemma 3.17, p. 45, uses a finite cycle-space decomposition and remains valid; it does not require the false sentence. Replace that sentence with the correct formulation or omit it.
result: Impact: The stated explanatory equivalence is false; the actual finite cycle-space proof of Lemma3.17 does not rely on it.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use finite sums of bounded generators. Growing rectangle boundaries provide the correct pointwise approximation in Z2.

problems.title: Density quantiles do not exist for certain events
problems.source_location: p33 sharp-density definition
claim: Recorded check: Density quantiles do not exist for certain events
analysis: Location. Definition of \(p_c(\alpha,\delta)\), p. 33.

The text asserts a unique \(p_c(\alpha,\delta)\in(0,1)\) satisfying \(\mathbb P_p(\|K_1\|\ge\alpha)=\delta\) for every \(\alpha,\delta\in(0,1)\). If \(\alpha\le1/|V|\), the event is certain for every configuration. On \(C_3\), take \(\alpha=1/4\), \(\delta=1/2\): no such parameter exists.

Use the generalized infimum over \(p\in[0,1]\), as in the retained reference’s Definition 3.1, and write the sharp-density condition multiplicatively, \[p_c(\alpha,1-\delta)\le e^\delta p_c(\alpha,\delta),\] to avoid an undefined \(0/0\) quotient when both thresholds are zero. Alternatively, restrict the equality definition to the nontrivial range \(\alpha>1/|V|\). The proof of Proposition 4.1 uses densities well above this microscopic range for large \(|V|\), so this is a definition and endpoint correction, not a refutation of its conclusion.
result: Impact: The equality definition and zero-denominator quotient need endpoint conventions; the large-volume usage is away from this range.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use generalized infimum quantiles in[0,1] and multiplicative sharp-density inequality, or restrict alpha>1/|V|.

report: Author: Targeted recovery 0025: M25-0398
Date: Exact-source initial review; independent scientific acceptance pending

Title: Initial scientific review of
Quadratic Forms in 8 Prime Variables

Author. Ben Green. Frozen identity. Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 1587–1637; DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-025-00727-9. Reviewed object. The exact 55-page arXiv:2108.10401v1 PDF, dated 23 August 2021 on its first-page margin. Source-page numbers below refer to this PDF. Equivalence to the journal version is not assumed.
# Assessment and scope

The manuscript develops a striking approach to quadratic forms in eight prime variables. Its main new ingredient is an averaged exponential-sum estimate obtained from the Weil representation, a bounded convolution argument, and the identification of a subgroup conjugate to \(\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb F_p[\Delta])\). The subsequent exclusion of invariant vectors is especially direct.

Major revision is required for the exact version reviewed. Two Major issues are established. First, the printed local density in (1.3) counts the zero level independently of \(N\). An explicit generic form then gives a positive asserted main term although the actual counting function is identically zero. Second, the subgroup conclusion in Appendix C is false even for exact equality in its norm hypothesis. This is a core auxiliary result explicitly invoked in Section 9. Its failure does not itself refute the intended, corrected asymptotic theorem: the actual measure there has additional structure, which a replacement lemma must use.

Eight Minor issues have bounded repairs or concern the scope of local statements. The full source, including all appendices and references, was read; the relevant source images were actually inspected. Independent exact calculations and selected complete proof units in primary references support this report. No author code was executed. This is completion of an initial scientific review, not independent acceptance.
# Major issues
## P1. The local factor in the main theorem counts the wrong level
Location. Theorem 1.1 and (1.3), p. 2; definition of \(\beta_\infty\), p. 3; the incompatible orthogonality calculation on p. 12.

Counterexample satisfying all genericity assumptions. Put \[Q_0(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^4(x_i-y_i)\bigl(i x_i+(i+1)y_i\bigr),
 \qquad Q=2Q_0,\qquad N=1.
 \tag{R2}\] Then \[a=2\operatorname{diag}(1,2,3,4),\quad b=2I,\quad
 c=-2\operatorname{diag}(2,3,4,5),\quad
 \Delta=\operatorname{diag}(-9,-25,-49,-81).\] Here \(\det a=384\), \(\det b=16\); all four eigenvalues are distinct and avoid \(0,-1\). Every integer value of \(Q\) is even. Consequently the left side of Theorem 1.1 is zero for every \(X\), including its von Mangoldt weights and prime powers.

It remains necessary to prove that the printed main term is positive; a finite residue check alone would not establish this. At the all-ones vector, \(Q_0=0\) and \[\nabla Q_0=(3,5,7,9,-3,-5,-7,-9).
 \tag{R3}\] For an odd prime \(p\), at least one of the binary blocks of \(Q_0\) has nonzero discriminant \((2i+1)^2\) modulo \(p\). Its Hessian is invertible. At any unit vector the gradient of that block cannot vanish. Hence every unit solution of \(Q_0=0\) modulo \(p\) is nonsingular, and each lifts to exactly \(p^7\) unit solutions at the next level. There is at least one such solution, by (R3). Multiplication by \(2\) does not change the zero congruence for odd \(p\). If \(C_p\) counts the unit zeros modulo \(p\), then \[\beta_p^{\rm printed}(1)
 =p^{-7}\left(\frac p{p-1}\right)^8 C_p>0
 \qquad(p\ \hbox{odd}).
 \tag{R4}\]

At \(p=2\), there is one unit vector modulo \(2\), and \(Q_0\) has an odd derivative there. The number of unit zeros of \(Q_0\) modulo \(2^k\) is \(2^{7(k-1)}\). For \(n\ge2\), the number of unit zeros of \(2Q_0\) modulo \(2^n\) is therefore \[2^8\,2^{7(n-2)}=2^{7n-6}.\] The weight in (R1) is \(2^8\), so \(\beta_{2,n}^{\rm printed}(1)=4\) for every \(n\ge2\), and \(\beta_2^{\rm printed}(1)=4\).

The infinite product is also positive. For \(p>7\), each binary form \(q_i(u,v)=(u-v)(iu+(i+1)v)\) is a split nondegenerate form. For \(r\ne0\), \[S_i(r):=\sum_{u,v\in\mathbb F_p^\times}e_p(rq_i(u,v))
 =p-\sum_u e_p(ri u^2)-\sum_v e_p(-r(i+1)v^2)+1.\] The two one-dimensional Gauss sums have modulus \(\sqrt p\), so \(|S_i(r)|\le p+2\sqrt p+1\). Orthogonality gives \[C_p=\frac{(p-1)^8}{p}
       +\frac1p\sum_{r\ne0}\prod_{i=1}^4S_i(r)
     =\frac{(p-1)^8}{p}+O(p^4).\] Together with (R4), this yields \(\beta_p^{\rm printed}(1)=1+O(p^{-3})\). All finitely many remaining factors are positive, so their product with the convergent tail is strictly positive.

Finally, the vector \(x_i=y_i=1/2\) is an interior zero of \(Q\) in \([0,1]^8\) with nonzero gradient. The implicit-function theorem on a small interior box gives a uniformly positive contribution to the level density at \(N/X^2=1/X^2\) for all sufficiently large \(X\). The possible critical point at the origin does not prevent existence of the density for this nondegenerate eight-variable quadratic form; its local contribution is integrable by quadratic scaling. Thus \(\beta_\infty\ge c_Q>0\) for large \(X\). The asserted main term is at least \(cX^6\), while the counting function is zero and the error is \(o(X^6)\) for any fixed \(A>0\). This contradicts the theorem with (R1).

Independent corroboration. Exact residue convolution, with no floating-point arithmetic, checked 18 prime-power cases. At \(p=2\), the printed densities for \(n=1,2,3,4,5\) are \(2,4,4,4,4\); the corrected target-one densities are all zero. These computations support, but do not replace, the all-prime argument above.

Impact and repair boundary. Replace the zero congruence in (1.3) by \(Q(x,y)\equiv N\pmod {p^n}\). The p. 12 calculation already uses \(Q-N\) and supports this interpretation. For (R2), the corrected \(2\)-adic factor vanishes, removing the contradiction. The severity is Major because the printed leading constant makes the main theorem false under all its hypotheses, even though the textual repair is short. This finding does not refute the theorem with the corrected local factors, and it is not transferred to the journal version.
## P2. Symmetric near-extremizers need not be close to a subgroup
Location. Lemma C.2, p. 52; the claim following (C.4) and Corollary C.3, p. 53; their use in Section 9, Step 2, p. 34.

Corollary C.3 assumes that \(\mu\) is a symmetric probability measure on a finite group and \[\|\mu*\mu\|_2\ge(1-\varepsilon)\|\mu\|_2.
 \tag{R5}\] It concludes that \(\mu\) is \(O(\varepsilon^c)\)-close in relative \(\ell^2\) norm to the uniform measure on a subgroup, with additional mass and support conclusions.

Exact counterexample. Let \(G=C_2=\{e,s\}\) with \(s^2=e\), and take \(\mu=\delta_s\). It is a symmetric probability measure and \[\mu*\mu=\delta_e,\qquad \|\mu*\mu\|_2=\|\mu\|_2=1.\] Thus (R5) holds for every positive \(\varepsilon\). The only subgroups are \(\{e\}\) and \(G\), and \[\|\delta_s-\delta_e\|_2^2=2,\qquad
 \|\delta_s-\mu_G\|_2^2=\frac12.
 \tag{R6}\] The latter distance divided by \(\|\mu_G\|_2\) equals \(1\). Neither distance can be \(O(\varepsilon^c)\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). The support conclusion also fails for \(H=G\) when \(\varepsilon\) is small. The same example embeds into \(\operatorname{Sp}_8(\mathbb F_p)\), for odd \(p\), by taking \(s=-I\). For any subgroup containing \(s\), its distance squared from \(\delta_s\) is \(1-1/|H|\ge1/2\); for a subgroup not containing \(s\), it is \(1+1/|H|\).

There is a second, independent normalization problem in Lemma C.2: its printed hypothesis is \[\|\mu*\mu\|_2\ge(1-\varepsilon)\|\mu\|_2^2.
 \tag{R7}\] For every symmetric probability measure, \((\mu*\mu)(e)=\|\mu\|_2^2\le\|\mu*\mu\|_2\), so (R7) imposes no near-equality restriction at all. For example, on \(C_3\), take \(\mu=(1/2,1/4,1/4)\). Exact calculation gives \[\|\mu\|_2^2=\frac38,\qquad
 \|\mu*\mu\|_2^2=\frac{43}{128},\qquad
 \|\mu-\mu_{C_3}\|_2^2=\frac1{24}.\] This also illustrates why merely adding positive definiteness cannot repair the squared norm in (R7). Changing (R7) to (R5), however, still leaves the counterexample (R6).

Where the proof fails. High multiplicative energy can identify a coset of a subgroup. Symmetry of a set does not force such a coset to contain the identity: \(\{s\}\) is already a symmetric coset. The transition from (C.4) to closeness of \(S\) to an unshifted subgroup omits precisely this obstruction. Theorem 3 of Fournier’s primary paper characterizes equality up to left and right translations; its proof explicitly obtains a coset. It does not supply the stronger unshifted conclusion quoted here.

Core impact and repair boundary. Section 9 uses Corollary C.3 to obtain (9.6)–(9.8), then identifies \(H=\Gamma_p\) and derives the bounded convolution estimate in Proposition 8.4. That estimate is one of the two central hypotheses of the amplification argument yielding Proposition 6.2. The erroneous auxiliary assertion therefore has a Major role.

The actual measure in Step 2 is an even symmetrized convolution power. Its convolution operator is positive semidefinite; \(\delta_s\) above does not have this property. Consequently the counterexample disproves the stated general lemma, not Proposition 8.4 for the actual measures. A repair must prove a correctly normalized lemma for this additional class, or retain the coset conclusion and rigorously eliminate the nonidentity coset using the extra structure. Positivity alone is not asserted here to have supplied that missing proof. The printed hypotheses and the existing appeal to Fournier do not complete it.
# Minor issues with bounded repairs
## P3. The determinant factor in (1.4) is incorrect

Location. Equation (1.4), p. 3. The displayed block factorization itself gives \[\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b/2\\b^T/2&c\end{pmatrix}
 =\det a\,
   \det\left(\frac14b^Ta^{-1}b\Delta\right)
 =2^{-8}(\det b)^2\det\Delta.
 \tag{R8}\] There are four factors of \(1/4\), not eight. The coefficient printed in (1.4) is \(2^{-16}\). For the generic form (R2), the actual determinant is \(893025\), while the printed expression is \(893025/256\). Exact rational arithmetic confirms both values. Replace \(2^{-16}\) by \(2^{-8}\). The nonvanishing equivalence used subsequently is unchanged, which bounds the impact.
## P4. Distinct eigenvalues define an open condition

Location. Genericity paragraph, p. 3. The condition that \(\Delta\) has distinct eigenvalues is called Zariski-closed. It is the failure of distinctness that is cut out by the discriminant. For instance, with \(a=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,3,t)\) and \(b=c=I\), the repeated-eigenvalue parameters are \(t=1,2,3\). The full genericity condition on this line excludes only \(0,1/4,1,2,3\), hence is a nonempty open subset which is not closed. Replace the relevant condition by the repeated-eigenvalue condition in the list of closed exceptional loci, or say that distinctness is open. The intended density conclusion survives.
## P5. The first bound of Corollary 6.3 omits a modulus restriction

Location. First statement of Corollary 6.3 and its box-counting proof, p. 18. The first statement asserts \(|S_{F_1,F_2}(r/q)|\ll X^8q^{-2}\) without \(q\le KX\). That restriction is printed only in the second statement. The proof of the first uses \((X/q+1)^8\ll X^8q^{-8}\), which requires it.

Fix any \(X\ge2\), take the generic form (R2), \(r=1\), and let both \(F_i\) be the indicator of the all-ones vector. Then \(S_{F_1,F_2}(1/q)=1\) for every \(q\), while \(X^8q^{-2}\to0\) as \(q\to\infty\). No constant depending only on the fixed form can make the assertion true. If simultaneous large \(X\) is preferred, take primes \(q>X^5\) and the same indicators. Add \(q\le KX\) to the first statement. All its uses in the stated minor-arc range satisfy this restriction.
## P6. The integral dimensions and Fourier localization need correction
Location. The definition of \(f_\varepsilon\), p. 13; (6.10)–(6.13), pp. 19–20.

On p. 13, \(f_\varepsilon\) uses \(\mathbb R^4\)-measure of a set of pairs \((u,v)\) and the discrete condition \(u,v\in[X]^4\). For a level-volume argument this must be \(\mathbb R^8\)-measure with \(u,v\in[0,X]^4\). Literally, the discrete set has zero Lebesgue measure, whereas \(I(0)=X^8>0\). The corrected continuous definition, Fourier inversion, and the scaling \(Q(Xx,Xy)=X^2Q(x,y)\) give the intended \(X^6\) factor.

On p. 19, \(w\) is typed as a function on \(\mathbb R^2\), is required to equal one on \([0,1]^{12}\), and is applied to \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4\). The intended domain and cube are \(\mathbb R^8\) and \([0,1]^8\); the Fourier integral is over \(\mathbb R^8\) with dot products. Equation (6.11) also uses a normalized expectation where \(S\) is an unnormalized sum. With \(X=2\), \(F_1=F_2=1\), \(\eta=0\) and an integral phase, its two sides are \(256\) and \(1\). Replace the expectation by a sum.

The claimed Fourier \(L^1\) growth \(O(\max(1,|\lambda|)^4)\) can be retained, but the displayed two derivatives in each four-dimensional block do not justify it. Indeed \(|\xi|^{-2}\) is not integrable at infinity in \(\mathbb R^4\). Here is a complete replacement estimate. Choose fixed \(w\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^8)\) equal to one on the unit cube, set \(W_\lambda=w e(\lambda Q)\) and \(t=\max(1,|\lambda|)\). Then \[\begin{split}
 \|\widehat W_\lambda\|_1
 &\le
 \left(\int_{\mathbb R^8}(1+|\xi|^2/t^2)^{-6}\,d\xi\right)^{1/2}\\
 &\hspace{1cm}\cdot
 \left\|(1+|\xi|^2/t^2)^3\widehat W_\lambda\right\|_2
 \ll t^4.
 \end{split}
 \tag{R9}\] The first factor is \(O(t^4)\). By Plancherel, the second is bounded by normalized derivatives of orders at most six; each satisfies \(\|D^\alpha W_\lambda\|_2\ll t^{|\alpha|}\) on the fixed compact support. Thus it is \(O(1)\). This repairs (6.12) in the correct dimension and preserves the ensuing \(M^5\) estimate. These are bounded local repairs, not a counterexample to Proposition 3.4 after repair.
## P7. The finite Fourier character and a normalization factor are missing
Location. Proposition 7.2, p. 23; displayed endpoints of the proof of Proposition 7.4, p. 25; (B.3), p. 50.

The Fourier kernel is printed as \(e(x^Ty)\) instead of \(e_q(x^Ty)\). Under the manuscript’s convention \(e(t)=e^{2\pi i t}\), integer residue representatives make the printed kernel identically one. For \(q=3\) and \(f(y)=e_3(y_1)\), this operator sends a nonzero vector of normalized norm one to zero. It cannot be unitary. With the correct kernel, \[3^2\mathbb E_{y\in\mathbb F_3^4} e_3(y_1+x^Ty)
 =9\,1_{\{x=(-1,0,0,0)\}},\] which has normalized norm one. Exact character-exponent counts verify this without numerical cancellation.

The four internal operations on p. 25 use the correct \(e_q\), and Appendix B’s actual CRT calculation on p. 51 also produces \(e_q\). These give an unambiguous local correction. Restore \(e_q\) in the defective displays and restore \(q^2\) before the final double average defining \(T_{f_1,f_2}(1)\). For \(f_1=f_2=1_{\{0\}}\), the true \(T\) is \(q^{-6}\) and the printed double average is \(q^{-8}\). The conclusion of Proposition 7.4 then follows with the intended normalized Fourier transform. Neuhauser’s Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 supply the character kernel and an ordinary representation up to unit phases. No failure of the corrected Weil representation is claimed.
## P8. The stabilization proof does not account for resets of \(\alpha\)

Location. Proof of Proposition 9.3, pp. 33–34. When \(\beta\) jumps at \(j=T'_i\), the inequalities of Lemma 9.2 allow \(\alpha(T'_i+1)\) to increase. The next descending run must start there, not at \(\alpha(T'_i)\). The printed recurrence \(T_{i+1}=T_i+\alpha_*(T_i)\) does not bound these resets.

An exact sequence check isolates the failed deduction. Let \(\alpha_*(1)=1\) and \(\alpha_*(j)=10\) for \(j\ge2\). Set \(\alpha(1)=1\), \(\beta(1)=0\). For \(2\le j\le361\), put \[\alpha(j)=10-((j-2)\bmod10),\qquad
 \beta(j)=\min\left(36,1+\left\lfloor\frac{j-2}{10}\right\rfloor\right),\] and thereafter put \(\alpha(j)=1\), \(\beta(j)=36\). These satisfy positivity, \(\alpha(j)\le\alpha_*(j)\), \(0\le\beta(j)\le36\), monotonicity of \(\beta\), and monotonicity of \(\alpha\) whenever \(\beta\) is constant. The printed recurrence gives \(T_{37}=352\), but the first simultaneous adjacent equality occurs at \(j=361\). All inequalities used in this abstract counting step were checked exactly. This is not asserted to be a sequence arising from the manuscript’s actual measures.

A safe repair is \[S_1=\alpha_*(1),\qquad
 S_{i+1}=S_i+1+\alpha_*(S_i+1).\] There are at most 36 jumps. After any jump at \(j\le S_i\), the next run starts at \(j+1\) with height at most \(\alpha_*(S_i+1)\); positivity bounds its length by that height. After the last jump, the same bound forces an adjacent equality. This gives a finite \(S_{37}\) depending only on \(\alpha_*\); in the example it is \(397\). Increasing the large-prime threshold accordingly preserves the qualitative \(t=O(1)\) conclusion. The earlier descending-run display also needs its missing endpoint \(+1\).
## P9. The coset-intersection union bound loses the size of the ambient set

Location. Section 9, Step 3, p. 35. The displayed chain uses \[|R'|\ge 1-m|\mathbb F_p^\times\setminus R|>\frac{p-1}{2}.\] The intermediate quantity must be \((p-1)-m|\mathbb F_p^\times\setminus R|\). For \(p=101\), \(R=\mathbb F_p^\times\) and \(m=1\), the printed second inequality becomes \(1>50\). These choices are compatible with the set argument (take the original coset to be the whole group). The ordinary union bound gives \(100\), as required. With (9.10) and \(m=O(\log p)\), the corrected bound exceeds \((p-1)/2\) for large \(p\), so the generation argument survives.
## P10. All five splitting types need not occur for a fixed generic form

Location. Paragraph after the ring isomorphism on p. 43. The five possible degree partitions are correctly listed, but the suggestion that all occur as \(p\) varies needs a further arithmetic hypothesis. For (R2), the characteristic polynomial is \[(T+9)(T+25)(T+49)(T+81).\] For every \(p>7\), its four roots remain distinct and lie in \(\mathbb F_p\), so \(\mathbb F_p[\Delta]\cong\mathbb F_p^4\) throughout. None of the other four types occurs. This is a form satisfying the manuscript’s definition of genericity. Delete the occurrence claim or qualify it by a suitable Galois-group condition, such as a full symmetric Galois group for the quartic. The proof handles every splitting type separately and does not require all of them to occur.
# Proof audit, dependencies, and boundaries

Definitions and quantifiers. The theorem’s genericity is over the algebraic closure, not over \(\mathbb Q\) or \(\mathbb F_p\) itself. The bars are visible in the inspected source. Thus the diagonalization on p. 48 is legitimate over \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p\); no erroneous assumption that every good prime splits has been inferred. The form is fixed throughout the asymptotic notation, and the large-prime threshold may depend on it. The counterexample to P1 is one fixed form with one fixed target, so it respects these dependencies.

Circle method and major arcs. The arcs in Section 3 cover the circle but need not form a disjoint partition. The argument bounds the complement of the major arcs by the two minor-arc sets, so overlap is not a defect. The local phase must retain \(N\) as in the orthogonality formula. Zhao’s Section 3 was read as a complete relevant proof unit: its major-arc lemma assumes rank at least five, so an eight-variable nondegenerate form is within the rank requirement. The estimates use character orthogonality, summation by parts and Siegel–Walfisz, and permit the enlarged logarithmic ranges after adjusting constants. The half-integral block notation for an integer-valued quadratic form changes notation, not the residue-class summation argument. These observations do not repair P1 automatically; the statement must be corrected.

Minor arcs and amplification. The first minor-arc argument absorbs the pure quadratic terms into bounded weights and applies Cauchy–Schwarz to the invertible mixed block. In Section 6, the squarefree large-prime part of \(q\) receives the averaged gain and the complementary part is controlled through its large square divisor. The successive weakening of exponents is harmless after decreasing the positive saving exponent if necessary. The Fourier-localization repair (R9) preserves the claimed logarithmic budget. Schur orthogonality and repeated Cauchy–Schwarz in Proposition 8.2 were checked, including the normalized Hilbert-space norm versus the counting-measure norm for probability measures. A phase can be chosen as the unit phase of the matrix coefficient, with arbitrary phase at zero, avoiding any convention about arg.

Algebraic counting. Lemma 9.2 needs a brief clarification in addition to P8. The top-dimensional Lang–Weil coefficient in Proposition 9.1 may be zero for a general variety defined over \(\mathbb F_p\). For example, \(x^2-dy^2=0\) with a nonsquare \(d\) has geometric dimension one and only one rational point. Accordingly, positivity of the particular leading coefficient asserted for the collision varieties should be justified, or the proof should use an effective rational-point dimension obtained by decomposing Frobenius-stable strata. No collision variety satisfying this paper’s special construction has been exhibited as a counterexample here. This concern is recorded as a clarification, not a confirmed false application or an additional Major issue.

After a suitable replacement for P2, the remaining subgroup-identification steps have a coherent structure: intersecting dilated cosets, promoting a dense parameter set to all dilates, identifying the generated subgroup, improving \(\ell^2\) control to \(\ell^\infty\) by convolution, and taking Chinese remainders. The CRT generation argument permits words to be padded by identity generators; this deals with differing word lengths across primes.

Identification of \(\Gamma_p\) and invariant vectors. The DUL factorization, \(BC=\Delta\), and the conjugation by \(\tau=\operatorname{diag}(I,B)\) were checked. The scalar matrix in Lemma 10.5 simplifies to \[M_\theta(r,s)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1+\theta-s\theta/r&1/s-1/r\\
 (s-r)\theta(1+\theta)&1+\theta-r\theta/s
 \end{pmatrix}.\] Direct multiplication verifies the lower-left conjugation polynomial used to exclude triangular and subfield cases; exact rational examples independently corroborate it. The proof establishes the sufficiently-large-characteristic version needed by Proposition 10.1. Its stronger isolated \(p\ge5\) phrasing deserves an explicit small-characteristic justification if retained; no false small-prime case is claimed here.

Goursat’s lemma reduces possible couplings to isomorphisms, and the coefficient comparisons rule out identical and signed factor identifications unless the distinct irreducible factors coincide. Ribet’s lemma then uses perfection. The minimal-degree assertion is needed for \(\operatorname{SL}_2\), although Appendix A states the displayed bound for \(\mathrm{PSL}_2\). It can be supplied directly: restricting a nontrivial representation to the upper unipotent subgroup gives a nontrivial character, whose orbit under the diagonal torus has at least \((|k|-1)/2\) distinct characters. If all such characters were trivial, the normal closure of the unipotent subgroup would act trivially. This provides the needed bound without treating an \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) representation as automatically factoring through its quotient.

For Proposition 11.2, \(C\) is invertible and \(\Delta=BC\) is self-adjoint for \(x^TCy\). Distinct eigenvalues give an orthogonal eigenbasis over \(\overline{\mathbb F}_p\) with nonzero self-pairings. The Vandermonde system forces the common zero locus of \(x^TC\Delta^j x\), \(0\le j\le3\), to be \(\{0\}\). The analogous calculation applies to the Fourier support. A function and its finite Fourier transform cannot both be supported only at zero unless the function is zero. This checks the claimed exclusion of invariant vectors once the Fourier formulas are normalized correctly.

problems.title: The main local density counts zero instead of the target N
problems.source_location: Theorem 1.1 and (1.3), p.2; beta_infinity p.3; orthogonality p.12
claim: Recorded check: The main local density counts zero instead of the target N
analysis: Location. Theorem 1.1 and (1.3), p. 2; definition of \(\beta_\infty\), p. 3; the incompatible orthogonality calculation on p. 12.

Counterexample satisfying all genericity assumptions. Put \[Q_0(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^4(x_i-y_i)\bigl(i x_i+(i+1)y_i\bigr),
 \qquad Q=2Q_0,\qquad N=1.
 \tag{R2}\] Then \[a=2\operatorname{diag}(1,2,3,4),\quad b=2I,\quad
 c=-2\operatorname{diag}(2,3,4,5),\quad
 \Delta=\operatorname{diag}(-9,-25,-49,-81).\] Here \(\det a=384\), \(\det b=16\); all four eigenvalues are distinct and avoid \(0,-1\). Every integer value of \(Q\) is even. Consequently the left side of Theorem 1.1 is zero for every \(X\), including its von Mangoldt weights and prime powers.

It remains necessary to prove that the printed main term is positive; a finite residue check alone would not establish this. At the all-ones vector, \(Q_0=0\) and \[\nabla Q_0=(3,5,7,9,-3,-5,-7,-9).
 \tag{R3}\] For an odd prime \(p\), at least one of the binary blocks of \(Q_0\) has nonzero discriminant \((2i+1)^2\) modulo \(p\). Its Hessian is invertible. At any unit vector the gradient of that block cannot vanish. Hence every unit solution of \(Q_0=0\) modulo \(p\) is nonsingular, and each lifts to exactly \(p^7\) unit solutions at the next level. There is at least one such solution, by (R3). Multiplication by \(2\) does not change the zero congruence for odd \(p\). If \(C_p\) counts the unit zeros modulo \(p\), then \[\beta_p^{\rm printed}(1)
 =p^{-7}\left(\frac p{p-1}\right)^8 C_p>0
 \qquad(p\ \hbox{odd}).
 \tag{R4}\]

At \(p=2\), there is one unit vector modulo \(2\), and \(Q_0\) has an odd derivative there. The number of unit zeros of \(Q_0\) modulo \(2^k\) is \(2^{7(k-1)}\). For \(n\ge2\), the number of unit zeros of \(2Q_0\) modulo \(2^n\) is therefore \[2^8\,2^{7(n-2)}=2^{7n-6}.\] The weight in (R1) is \(2^8\), so \(\beta_{2,n}^{\rm printed}(1)=4\) for every \(n\ge2\), and \(\beta_2^{\rm printed}(1)=4\).

The infinite product is also positive. For \(p>7\), each binary form \(q_i(u,v)=(u-v)(iu+(i+1)v)\) is a split nondegenerate form. For \(r\ne0\), \[S_i(r):=\sum_{u,v\in\mathbb F_p^\times}e_p(rq_i(u,v))
 =p-\sum_u e_p(ri u^2)-\sum_v e_p(-r(i+1)v^2)+1.\] The two one-dimensional Gauss sums have modulus \(\sqrt p\), so \(|S_i(r)|\le p+2\sqrt p+1\). Orthogonality gives \[C_p=\frac{(p-1)^8}{p}
       +\frac1p\sum_{r\ne0}\prod_{i=1}^4S_i(r)
     =\frac{(p-1)^8}{p}+O(p^4).\] Together with (R4), this yields \(\beta_p^{\rm printed}(1)=1+O(p^{-3})\). All finitely many remaining factors are positive, so their product with the convergent tail is strictly positive.

Finally, the vector \(x_i=y_i=1/2\) is an interior zero of \(Q\) in \([0,1]^8\) with nonzero gradient. The implicit-function theorem on a small interior box gives a uniformly positive contribution to the level density at \(N/X^2=1/X^2\) for all sufficiently large \(X\). The possible critical point at the origin does not prevent existence of the density for this nondegenerate eight-variable quadratic form; its local contribution is integrable by quadratic scaling. Thus \(\beta_\infty\ge c_Q>0\) for large \(X\). The asserted main term is at least \(cX^6\), while the counting function is zero and the error is \(o(X^6)\) for any fixed \(A>0\). This contradicts the theorem with (R1).

Independent corroboration. Exact residue convolution, with no floating-point arithmetic, checked 18 prime-power cases. At \(p=2\), the printed densities for \(n=1,2,3,4,5\) are \(2,4,4,4,4\); the corrected target-one densities are all zero. These computations support, but do not replace, the all-prime argument above.

Impact and repair boundary. Replace the zero congruence in (1.3) by \(Q(x,y)\equiv N\pmod {p^n}\). The p. 12 calculation already uses \(Q-N\) and supports this interpretation. For (R2), the corrected \(2\)-adic factor vanishes, removing the contradiction. The severity is Major because the printed leading constant makes the main theorem false under all its hypotheses, even though the textual repair is short. This finding does not refute the theorem with the corrected local factors, and it is not transferred to the journal version.
result: Impact: The exact printed main theorem is false under its full hypotheses.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Change congruence Q=0 to Q=N in (1.3); corrected beta_2(1)=0 for this witness.

problems.title: Symmetric Young near-extremizers may lie on a nonidentity coset
problems.source_location: Lemma C.2 p.52; (C.4) and Corollary C.3 p.53; Section9 Step2 p.34
claim: Recorded check: Symmetric Young near-extremizers may lie on a nonidentity coset
analysis: Location. Lemma C.2, p. 52; the claim following (C.4) and Corollary C.3, p. 53; their use in Section 9, Step 2, p. 34.

Corollary C.3 assumes that \(\mu\) is a symmetric probability measure on a finite group and \[\|\mu*\mu\|_2\ge(1-\varepsilon)\|\mu\|_2.
 \tag{R5}\] It concludes that \(\mu\) is \(O(\varepsilon^c)\)-close in relative \(\ell^2\) norm to the uniform measure on a subgroup, with additional mass and support conclusions.

Exact counterexample. Let \(G=C_2=\{e,s\}\) with \(s^2=e\), and take \(\mu=\delta_s\). It is a symmetric probability measure and \[\mu*\mu=\delta_e,\qquad \|\mu*\mu\|_2=\|\mu\|_2=1.\] Thus (R5) holds for every positive \(\varepsilon\). The only subgroups are \(\{e\}\) and \(G\), and \[\|\delta_s-\delta_e\|_2^2=2,\qquad
 \|\delta_s-\mu_G\|_2^2=\frac12.
 \tag{R6}\] The latter distance divided by \(\|\mu_G\|_2\) equals \(1\). Neither distance can be \(O(\varepsilon^c)\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). The support conclusion also fails for \(H=G\) when \(\varepsilon\) is small. The same example embeds into \(\operatorname{Sp}_8(\mathbb F_p)\), for odd \(p\), by taking \(s=-I\). For any subgroup containing \(s\), its distance squared from \(\delta_s\) is \(1-1/|H|\ge1/2\); for a subgroup not containing \(s\), it is \(1+1/|H|\).

There is a second, independent normalization problem in Lemma C.2: its printed hypothesis is \[\|\mu*\mu\|_2\ge(1-\varepsilon)\|\mu\|_2^2.
 \tag{R7}\] For every symmetric probability measure, \((\mu*\mu)(e)=\|\mu\|_2^2\le\|\mu*\mu\|_2\), so (R7) imposes no near-equality restriction at all. For example, on \(C_3\), take \(\mu=(1/2,1/4,1/4)\). Exact calculation gives \[\|\mu\|_2^2=\frac38,\qquad
 \|\mu*\mu\|_2^2=\frac{43}{128},\qquad
 \|\mu-\mu_{C_3}\|_2^2=\frac1{24}.\] This also illustrates why merely adding positive definiteness cannot repair the squared norm in (R7). Changing (R7) to (R5), however, still leaves the counterexample (R6).

Where the proof fails. High multiplicative energy can identify a coset of a subgroup. Symmetry of a set does not force such a coset to contain the identity: \(\{s\}\) is already a symmetric coset. The transition from (C.4) to closeness of \(S\) to an unshifted subgroup omits precisely this obstruction. Theorem 3 of Fournier’s primary paper characterizes equality up to left and right translations; its proof explicitly obtains a coset. It does not supply the stronger unshifted conclusion quoted here.

Core impact and repair boundary. Section 9 uses Corollary C.3 to obtain (9.6)–(9.8), then identifies \(H=\Gamma_p\) and derives the bounded convolution estimate in Proposition 8.4. That estimate is one of the two central hypotheses of the amplification argument yielding Proposition 6.2. The erroneous auxiliary assertion therefore has a Major role.

The actual measure in Step 2 is an even symmetrized convolution power. Its convolution operator is positive semidefinite; \(\delta_s\) above does not have this property. Consequently the counterexample disproves the stated general lemma, not Proposition 8.4 for the actual measures. A repair must prove a correctly normalized lemma for this additional class, or retain the coset conclusion and rigorously eliminate the nonidentity coset using the extra structure. Positivity alone is not asserted here to have supplied that missing proof. The printed hypotheses and the existing appeal to Fournier do not complete it.
result: Impact: False general auxiliary lemma supplies (9.6)-(9.8), Proposition8.4 and amplification Proposition6.2; this is a core dependency.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Prove a correctly normalized positive-definite/even-convolution version sufficient for the actual measure, or prove coset elimination from that additional structure.

claim: Recorded check: Wrong determinant coefficient

problems.title: Distinct-eigenvalue locus called closed

claim: Recorded check: Distinct-eigenvalue locus called closed
analysis: Location. Genericity paragraph, p. 3. The condition that \(\Delta\) has distinct eigenvalues is called Zariski-closed. It is the failure of distinctness that is cut out by the discriminant. problems.title: Missing modulus bound in the first part of Corollary6.3
problems.source_location: Corollary6.3 first bound and proof p.18
claim: Recorded check: Missing modulus bound in the first part of Corollary6.3
analysis: Location. First statement of Corollary 6.3 and its box-counting proof, p. 18. The first statement asserts \(|S_{F_1,F_2}(r/q)|\ll X^8q^{-2}\) without \(q\le KX\). That restriction is printed only in the second statement. The proof of the first uses \((X/q+1)^8\ll X^8q^{-8}\), which requires it.

Fix any \(X\ge2\), take the generic form (R2), \(r=1\), and let both \(F_i\) be the indicator of the all-ones vector. Then \(S_{F_1,F_2}(1/q)=1\) for every \(q\), while \(X^8q^{-2}\to0\) as \(q\to\infty\). No constant depending only on the fixed form can make the assertion true. If simultaneous large \(X\) is preferred, take primes \(q>X^5\) and the same indicators. Add \(q\le KX\) to the first statement. All its uses in the stated minor-arc range satisfy this restriction.

problems.title: Wrong integral dimension and Fourier localization normalization
claim: Recorded check: Wrong integral dimension and Fourier localization normalization
analysis: Location. The definition of \(f_\varepsilon\), p. 13; (6.10)–(6.13), pp. 19–20.

On p. 13, \(f_\varepsilon\) uses \(\mathbb R^4\)-measure of a set of pairs \((u,v)\) and the discrete condition \(u,v\in[X]^4\). For a level-volume argument this must be \(\mathbb R^8\)-measure with \(u,v\in[0,X]^4\). Literally, the discrete set has zero Lebesgue measure, whereas \(I(0)=X^8>0\). The corrected continuous definition, Fourier inversion, and the scaling \(Q(Xx,Xy)=X^2Q(x,y)\) give the intended \(X^6\) factor.

On p. 19, \(w\) is typed as a function on \(\mathbb R^2\), is required to equal one on \([0,1]^{12}\), and is applied to \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4\). The intended domain and cube are \(\mathbb R^8\) and \([0,1]^8\); the Fourier integral is over \(\mathbb R^8\) with dot products. Equation (6.11) also uses a normalized expectation where \(S\) is an unnormalized sum. With \(X=2\), \(F_1=F_2=1\), \(\eta=0\) and an integral phase, its two sides are \(256\) and \(1\). Replace the expectation by a sum.

The claimed Fourier \(L^1\) growth \(O(\max(1,|\lambda|)^4)\) can be retained, but the displayed two derivatives in each four-dimensional block do not justify it. Indeed \(|\xi|^{-2}\) is not integrable at infinity in \(\mathbb R^4\). Here is a complete replacement estimate. Choose fixed \(w\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^8)\) equal to one on the unit cube, set \(W_\lambda=w e(\lambda Q)\) and \(t=\max(1,|\lambda|)\). Then \[\begin{split}
 \|\widehat W_\lambda\|_1
 &\le
 \left(\int_{\mathbb R^8}(1+|\xi|^2/t^2)^{-6}\,d\xi\right)^{1/2}\\
 &\hspace{1cm}\cdot
 \left\|(1+|\xi|^2/t^2)^3\widehat W_\lambda\right\|_2
 \ll t^4.
 \end{split}
 \tag{R9}\] The first factor is \(O(t^4)\). By Plancherel, the second is bounded by normalized derivatives of orders at most six; each satisfies \(\|D^\alpha W_\lambda\|_2\ll t^{|\alpha|}\) on the fixed compact support. Thus it is \(O(1)\). This repairs (6.12) in the correct dimension and preserves the ensuing \(M^5\) estimate. These are bounded local repairs, not a counterexample to Proposition 3.4 after repair.
result: Impact: Displayed definitions and proof estimates need correction.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use R8 measure and continuous[0,X]^4, w onR8 equal1 on[0,1]^8, unnormalized sum, and report estimate(R9).

problems.title: Finite Fourier character and q^2 factor missing
problems.source_location: Proposition7.2 p.23; Proposition7.4 proof p.25; (B.3) p.50
claim: Recorded check: Finite Fourier character and q^2 factor missing
analysis: Location. Proposition 7.2, p. 23; displayed endpoints of the proof of Proposition 7.4, p. 25; (B.3), p. 50.

The Fourier kernel is printed as \(e(x^Ty)\) instead of \(e_q(x^Ty)\). Under the manuscript’s convention \(e(t)=e^{2\pi i t}\), integer residue representatives make the printed kernel identically one. For \(q=3\) and \(f(y)=e_3(y_1)\), this operator sends a nonzero vector of normalized norm one to zero. It cannot be unitary. With the correct kernel, \[3^2\mathbb E_{y\in\mathbb F_3^4} e_3(y_1+x^Ty)
 =9\,1_{\{x=(-1,0,0,0)\}},\] which has normalized norm one. Exact character-exponent counts verify this without numerical cancellation.

The four internal operations on p. 25 use the correct \(e_q\), and Appendix B’s actual CRT calculation on p. 51 also produces \(e_q\). These give an unambiguous local correction. Restore \(e_q\) in the defective displays and restore \(q^2\) before the final double average defining \(T_{f_1,f_2}(1)\). For \(f_1=f_2=1_{\{0\}}\), the true \(T\) is \(q^{-6}\) and the printed double average is \(q^{-8}\). The conclusion of Proposition 7.4 then follows with the intended normalized Fourier transform. Neuhauser’s Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 supply the character kernel and an ordinary representation up to unit phases. No failure of the corrected Weil representation is claimed.
result: Impact: Local operator displays are false but unambiguously repairable.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Restore e_q and the missing q^2 before the final double average.

problems.title: Stabilization recurrence omits resets after dimension jumps
problems.source_location: Proposition9.3 proof pp.33-34
claim: Recorded check: Stabilization recurrence omits resets after dimension jumps
analysis: Location. Proof of Proposition 9.3, pp. 33–34. When \(\beta\) jumps at \(j=T'_i\), the inequalities of Lemma 9.2 allow \(\alpha(T'_i+1)\) to increase. The next descending run must start there, not at \(\alpha(T'_i)\). The printed recurrence \(T_{i+1}=T_i+\alpha_*(T_i)\) does not bound these resets.

An exact sequence check isolates the failed deduction. Let \(\alpha_*(1)=1\) and \(\alpha_*(j)=10\) for \(j\ge2\). Set \(\alpha(1)=1\), \(\beta(1)=0\). For \(2\le j\le361\), put \[\alpha(j)=10-((j-2)\bmod10),\qquad
 \beta(j)=\min\left(36,1+\left\lfloor\frac{j-2}{10}\right\rfloor\right),\] and thereafter put \(\alpha(j)=1\), \(\beta(j)=36\). These satisfy positivity, \(\alpha(j)\le\alpha_*(j)\), \(0\le\beta(j)\le36\), monotonicity of \(\beta\), and monotonicity of \(\alpha\) whenever \(\beta\) is constant. The printed recurrence gives \(T_{37}=352\), but the first simultaneous adjacent equality occurs at \(j=361\). All inequalities used in this abstract counting step were checked exactly. This is not asserted to be a sequence arising from the manuscript’s actual measures.

A safe repair is \[S_1=\alpha_*(1),\qquad
 S_{i+1}=S_i+1+\alpha_*(S_i+1).\] There are at most 36 jumps. After any jump at \(j\le S_i\), the next run starts at \(j+1\) with height at most \(\alpha_*(S_i+1)\); positivity bounds its length by that height. After the last jump, the same bound forces an adjacent equality. This gives a finite \(S_{37}\) depending only on \(\alpha_*\); in the example it is \(397\). Increasing the large-prime threshold accordingly preserves the qualitative \(t=O(1)\) conclusion. The earlier descending-run display also needs its missing endpoint \(+1\).
result: Impact: The printed quantitative deduction from Lemma9.2 inequalities is invalid.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use S1=alpha_star(1), S_{i+1}=S_i+1+alpha_star(S_i+1), and correct the earlier endpoint+1.

problems.title: Every splitting type need not occur for a fixed generic form
