report: Author: Targeted recovery 0025: M25-0399
Date: Exact-source initial review; independent scientific acceptance pending

Title: Initial scientific review of
Sharp Bound for the Erdős–Straus Non-averaging Set Problem

Authors. Huy Tuan Pham and Dmitrii Zakharov. Frozen identity. Geometric and Functional Analysis 35 (2025), 1712–1738; DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-025-00728-8. Reviewed object. The exact 20-page arXiv:2410.14624v2 PDF, dated 10 September 2025. All source-page references below refer to this file. Equivalence to the journal version is not assumed.
# Assessment and scope

The manuscript combines a convex density increment with homogeneous subset-sum structure to obtain the exponent \(1/4+o(1)\) for non-averaging subsets of an interval, and the exponent \((d-1)/(d+1)+o(1)\) in higher-dimensional boxes. The geometric mechanism and the distinction between ambient dimension and subset-sum dimension are central to the argument.

Major revision is required for this exact version. Three Major findings concern the weighted zonotope step in the proof of Theorem 4, the final cardinality bookkeeping in the iteration, and Lemma 6 without an origin condition. Four Minor findings concern affine approximation, the normalizations in the density-increment proof, the range of the lifted translation in Appendix A, and the non-averaging claim after adjoining zero. Each finding below has an explicit calculation or proof, a precise scope, and a repair boundary. None of these findings is asserted to be a counterexample to the main non-averaging bound. In particular, the numerical iteration witness is a counterexample to a claimed implication between estimates, not a non-averaging set.

The complete assigned PDF was read, including definitions, proofs, Appendix A and references. All 20 source pages were also actually inspected as rendered images. The relevant complete proof units of Conlon–Fox–Pham [CFP], in the exact version stated in Section 5 (#sec:evidence), were examined. The imported structural theorem is treated as a cited theorem; a recursive certification of all its literature dependencies is not claimed. No author software was executed.
# Major findings
## P1. The retained coefficient mass and the centre used in Theorem 4 are not justified
Location. Source pp. 13–15: (13), Lemma 14 and its penultimate mass inequality, and the centres immediately after (15).

There are two distinct defects. Lemma 14 assumes only \(|\bar A_1|\ge c|A_1|\), whereas its proof needs a positive amount of coefficient mass on \(\bar A_1\). Moreover, the centre used on p. 15 is twice the centre in Lemma 14. These are genuine failures of displayed steps even under the structural and irreducibility assumptions of Theorem 4.
#### A family satisfying the setup.

Let \(M\to\infty\), \(N=2M+1\), and take \[A=[-M,M]\cap\mathbb Z,\quad P(A)=A,\quad \widehat A=A,
 \quad A_0=B=[0,2M]\cap\mathbb Z,\quad a=M.\] The identification is \(x\mapsto x+M\). The set may be embedded in \(\mathbb Z^2\) if the notation \(\ell>1\) in Corollary 5 is read literally. Fix the structural constant \(c_0\le1/100\), reducing it if necessary. This is legitimate Corollary 5 data for all sufficiently large \(M\): put \(s=N/\log^2N\), \(k=\lfloor s/4\rfloor\), and \[E=\{\pm1,\ldots,\pm k\}\cup
   \{\pm(M-k+1),\ldots,\pm M\}.\] Then \(|E|=4k\le s\). The first block has every subset sum in \([-R,R]\), where \(R=k(k+1)/2\). The positive partial sums of the second block have gaps at most \(M\) and end at \(T=kM-k(k-1)/2\); use their negatives as well. Since \(2R\ge M\) for large \(M\), the translated intervals overlap and give \[[-k(M+1),k(M+1)]\cap\mathbb Z\ \subseteq\ \Sigma(E).\] This contains \(c_0sP(A)\), which is proper. Thus the origin, subset budget and homogeneous-translate requirements are all met.

Here is also a uniform verification of irreducibility, rather than a finite test of selected subsets. Fix \(\delta>0\). If \(T\subseteq A_0\), \(|T|=t\ge\delta N\), and \(x\in B\), then \(T-x\subseteq[-2M,2M]\). In a reduced structural GAP for \(T-x\), delete coordinates of width one. Its size is at least \(t/2\) for large \(N\). If its rank were \(r\ge2\), properness of \(c_0s(T)P(T-x)\) would give \[s(T)^r t\ll |\Sigma(T')|\ll Ns(T),\qquad
 |T'|\le s(T)=t/\log^2t,\] which is impossible uniformly for \(t\ge\delta N\) as \(N\to\infty\). Thus rank one can be chosen for every such \(T,x\), and \(|P(T-x)|\ge t/2\ge\delta N/2\). With these coherent reduced choices, \(A\) is \((\delta,\gamma)\)-irreducible for every fixed \(\gamma\le\delta/2\). Choose \(\delta\le\mu^C\) and \(\gamma\le\min(\delta/2,\delta^C)\); then take \(N\) large enough for the inverse-logarithmic lower bound on \(\gamma\) in Theorem 4. Choose the fixed \(\delta,\gamma\) using, for example, the lower bound \(\mu>1/11\) that holds for large \(M\); these choices are uniform in the limit.

Put \(L=\lfloor M/10\rfloor\), \(\mu=2L/N\), and assign \[c_{M+i}=c_{M-i}=\frac1{2L}\quad(1\le i\le L),\qquad c_x=0
 \quad\hbox{otherwise}.\] Then \(\sum c_x=1\), \(\sum c_x(x-a)=0\), and \(c_x\le1/(\mu N)\), with equality on the support. The median \(a\) lies in no half-space meeting \(A_0\) in at most \(\mu N\) points, so \(A_0\) is not in \(\mu\)-convex position. The limiting value \(\mu\to1/10\) permits the preceding fixed choices of \(\delta,\gamma\).

Equation reference: eq:weightedsets. Order the zero coefficients first, in pairs \((M-j,M+j)\) for \(j>L\), and then the nonzero coefficients in pairs \((M+i,M-i)\) for \(1\le i\le L\). This is a permitted nondecreasing order in (13). The resulting two sets satisfy \[
 A_1-a=a-A_2=\{-M,\ldots,-L-1\}\cup\{1,\ldots,L\}.\] Choose \(\bar A_1=\{M-j:L<j\le M\}\). Its cardinality is \(M-L\ge0.9|A_1|\), but all its coefficients vanish. Hence the centred retained zonotope in the proof of Lemma 14 is \(\{0\}\). It cannot contain \(\xi NB\) for any \(\xi>0\), and the displayed lower bound \[\sum_{x\in(\bar A_1-a)\setminus H}\Delta_x\ge\mu N/4\] has left side zero. This disproves the stronger retained-zonotope assertion in the proof. The printed statement of Lemma 14 has the full \(Z_{A_1-a}\) on its right side; the preceding example is not represented as a disproof of that weaker statement.
#### The doubled centre fails even after the actual small deletion.

Equation reference: eq:badcentre. For the full \(A_1\) in [eq:weightedsets] (#eq:weightedsets), the centre defined on p. 15 is \[
 z_1=\mu N\sum_{x\in A_1}c_x(x-a)=\frac{L(L+1)}2
       =\max Z_{A_1-a}.\] Thus \(z_1+\xi NB\) leaves the full zonotope for every \(\xi>0\). The proof actually deletes \(O(N/\log N)\) points to form its retained set. Under the natural, consistent interpretation of its shifted indices, the resulting centre obeys \[\bar z_1\ge z_1-O(N^2/\log N).\] The right-hand displacement in \(\xi NB=[0,2\xi NM]\) is of order \(\xi N^2\). For these admissible \(\mu\to1/10\) and fixed \(\gamma>0\), \(\xi=c^\prime\mu\gamma\) stays bounded below by a positive constant, so this eventually exceeds the deletion error. Consequently the displayed inclusion \(\operatorname{conv}(\bar z_1+\xi NB)\subseteq Z_{A_1-a}\) on p. 15 is still false for the actual permitted trimming. The mismatch with the retained zonotope needed in (15) is an additional logical problem.

For a reproducible finite coefficient calculation, \(M=1000\), \(L=100\) gives a retained fraction \(9/10\), retained mass zero, the asserted mass lower bound \(50\), and \[Z_{A_1-a}=[-495450,5050],\qquad z_1=5050,
 \qquad z_1/2=2525.\] The large-\(N\) structural verification above, not this one finite calculation, supplies all asymptotic hypotheses.
#### Impact and repair boundary.

This is a Major proof defect in the implication from irreducibility to intersecting nonempty subset sums, a core input to the main argument. It does not refute the conclusion of Theorem 4: the interval in this example certainly has averaging relations.

A plausible restricted repair must use the actual small deletion and prove a coefficient-mass condition. Alternating a nondecreasing sequence gives mass at least \(1/2-O((\mu|A_0|)^{-1})\) on each side; deleting \(O(N/\log N)\) points loses only \(O((\mu\log N)^{-1})\). Thus each actual retained side has mass at least \(1/3\) for large \(N\). This is substantially stronger than the arbitrary cardinality condition in Lemma 14. Use, for example, \(\lambda=\mu|A_0|/4\), so that \(\lambda c_x\le1/4\), and retain the same interior centre \(\lambda\sum c_x(x-a)\) throughout. The factor \(|A_0|\) also avoids the unsupported assertion \(\mu|A|c_x\le1\) when \(\widehat A\ne A\).

A complete repair must establish the interior inclusion in the retained zonotope, use a symmetric displacement body such as \(B-B\) in the slab argument, account for low-rank lattice slices and the additive endpoint term in lattice counting, and quantitatively produce at least two lattice intersection points. The last printed condition that the intersection differs from \(\{z_1\}\) alone does not rule out \(\{0\}\). These remaining geometric and lattice steps are not certified as repaired here.
## P2. The final iteration confuses two different retention ratios
Location. Source pp. 17–18, Case 3 and the paragraph beginning Finally, we verify.

Equation reference: eq:correctstep. Write \(M=|A|\), \(V=|B|\), and distinguish the preprocessing retention \(r\) from the geometric volume ratio \(\eta\). The preceding Case 3 estimates have the form \[
 M_{\mathrm{new}}\ge c\,\eta^p rM,\qquad
 V_{\mathrm{new}}\le C\,\eta r^K V,\qquad
 p=\frac{d-1}{d+1}+\varepsilon.\] The final paragraph instead defines \(\rho_j=M_{j+1}/M_j\) for the whole step and asserts \(V_{j+1}\ll\rho_j^K V_j\). This does not follow from [eq:correctstep] (#eq:correctstep).

Equation reference: eq:ratio. An exact numerical family makes the failure explicit. Set \(d=2\), \(\varepsilon=1/100\), \(p=103/300\), \(K=100\), \(r=1\), and, for \(t\downarrow0\), \[\eta=t^{300},\qquad \rho=t^{103},\qquad
 V_{\mathrm{new}}/V=\eta,\qquad M_{\mathrm{new}}/M=\rho.\] These satisfy both one-step inequalities with constants one, while \[
 \frac{V_{\mathrm{new}}/V}{\rho^K}=t^{-10000}\longrightarrow\infty.\] The finite check \(t=1/2\) gives the exact ratio \(2^{10000}\). Initial \(M,V\) can be taken arbitrarily large to accommodate polynomial size lower bounds; the obstruction is the missing geometric factor, not rounding. This is an independent disproof of the asserted algebraic implication. No actual non-averaging set realizing this numerical sequence is claimed.

There is a second defect in the same final deduction. After inserting \(\max(1,C\rho_j^K)\), the displayed product has factors equal to one whenever \(C\rho_j^K<1\). The inequality with that maximum provides no lower bound on \(\prod\rho_j\). Also, an upper bound \(\rho_j\le\mu^{c(d)}\) is not a consequence of the displayed lower bound on the selected set’s size. Deliberate trimming could enforce a size quota, but would not validate the missing \(\eta\) factor.
#### Impact and a conditional bookkeeping repair.

The intended contradiction requires all intermediate sets to remain large enough for the structural theorem and the common parameters. The printed argument does not establish that requirement, so this is Major. It does not disprove Theorems 1 or 2.

Equation reference: eq:potential. The following replacement verifies the needed size control conditional on a correct geometric Case 3. In a block of fixed dimension \(d\ge2\), choose \[p_*=\alpha_d+2\varepsilon<1,\qquad
 2\varepsilon<\zeta_0,\qquad Kp_*>1,
 \quad \alpha_d=\frac{d-1}{d+1}.\] For \(F=\log M-p_*\log V\), [eq:correctstep] (#eq:correctstep) gives \[
 F_{\mathrm{new}}-F
 \ge\varepsilon\log(1/\eta)+(Kp_*-1)\log(1/r)-O(1).\] Since \(\eta\le\mu^\tau\to0\) with the original input size, this is nonnegative for sufficiently large input, uniformly in \(r\le1\). At entry to the block, \(M\ge V^{\alpha_d+\zeta}\) and \(\zeta\ge\zeta_0\) imply \[F\ge\frac{\zeta-2\varepsilon}{\alpha_d+\zeta}\log M.\] At every later step, \(M\le V\) implies \(F\le(1-p_*)\log M\). Hence every set in this block retains a fixed positive power of its entry size. There are only boundedly many changes of dimension, by the dimension-increment argument and Observation 15; each such step retains at least a \((1-\varepsilon)\) power. Thus \(M_j\ge M_{\mathrm{original}}^{c(\zeta_0,d)}\) for some \(c(\zeta_0,d)>0\). In particular, \(\log\log M_j=\log\log M_{\mathrm{original}}+O_{\zeta_0,d}(1)\), which is sufficient for the common inverse-logarithmic parameters. The one-dimensional branch can be treated directly: for \(\mu<1/2\) a median of a finite set cannot be in \(\mu\)-convex position.

This proves a useful replacement for the size bookkeeping, not the manuscript’s precise near-original exponent with an absolute \(c\). It remains conditional on the preceding geometric/lattice step, including the repair required by P1.
## P3. Lemma 6 is false for an arbitrary containing affine GAP
Location. Source p. 10, Lemma 6 and its proof; uses in Lemma 10 on pp. 11–13; the translation at the start of Appendix A.

The assertion \(\Sigma(A')\subseteq sP\) requires that shorter subset sums can be padded with zeros in \(P\). The hypothesis \(A\subseteq P\) does not supply \(0\in P\). This affects the stated bound, not just its written proof.

Equation reference: eq:Pzero. Let \(m\to\infty\), \(N=m^4\), and \[A=N+[1,m],\qquad P_{\mathrm{aff}}=N+[1,m],\qquad
 s=m/\log^2m.\] The input GAP has dimension one and size \(m\). It is contained in a box of size \(m\), so the polynomial box-size hypothesis is satisfied; again one may embed it in \(\mathbb Z^2\). There is admissible symmetric rank-two structural data \[
 P_0=\{uN+v: |u|\le1,\ |v|\le m\},\qquad \widehat A=A.\] Both \(P_0\) and \(c_0sP_0\) are proper for fixed \(0<c_0\le1/100\) and large \(m\).

For \(|k-t|\le c_0s\) and \(t/3\le h\le2t/3\), the interval length is \(l(t-l)+h(t-h)\ge13t^2/36\) after harmless endpoint rounding. Adjacent lower endpoints differ by \(m+O(t)\); since \(t^2/m\to\infty\), these intervals overlap. Their union contains \([0.4tm,0.6tm]\) for all sufficiently large \(m\). Consequently \[x_0+c_0sP_0\subseteq\Sigma(A'),\qquad
 x_0=tN+\lfloor tm/2\rfloor.\] This is a homogeneous translate. Thus \(d(A)=2\) and \(P(A)=P_0\) are allowed by the manuscript’s definition, with every Corollary 5 conclusion explicitly verified. Lemma 6 would give \[3(2m+1)=|P_0|\ll m/s,\] which is impossible as \(s\to\infty\). The implied constant cannot absorb the unbounded factor \(s\).

The phenomenon is not removed by insisting on a rank-one structural choice. A rank-one GAP containing \(0\) and more than \((m+1)/2\) points of \(N+[1,m]\) must have integer step one and span at least \(N\). Its \(c_0s\) dilate contains an integer interval of length comparable to \(sN\). But every subset sum of at most \(s\) elements of \(A\) lies in one of the separated bands \([k(N+1),k(N+m)]\), each of width at most \(sm\ll N\). No such interval fits. Hence a reduced rank-one choice is impossible for large \(m\).

The independent finite endpoint certificate uses \(m=2^{20}\), \(t=\lfloor m/392\rfloor=2674\), and exact rational bounds \(13<\log m<14\). It verifies 113,157 intervals and the inclusion for all \(|k-t|\le63\), with offset radius 65,059,860. This is a concrete check of the interval construction. It is not used to assert a sufficiently-large-\(m\) hypothesis at this single numerical value; the asymptotic proof above supplies that part.
#### Impact and repair boundary.

This is a false core structural lemma, used to obtain the up-move savings and the subsequent iteration bounds, and is therefore Major. The set \(A\) here need not be non-averaging: Lemma 6 has no such hypothesis. No conclusion about a counterexample to the main theorem follows.

A valid version can assume an origin-containing, appropriately centered input GAP. Then every subset of at most \(s\) elements has its sum in \(sP\) and the counting proof applies, after deleting width-one coordinates. All applications must be checked with the origin fixed at the point at which their subset-sum dimensions are defined. Translating a set preserves the non-averaging property, but not the subset-sum structure with an adjoined origin. In Appendix A, the initial reduction of an arbitrary box to \([n]^\ell\) therefore also needs justification. One must either supply the higher-dimensional structural proof with its actual origin convention or retain cardinality information when transporting subset sums through a translation. A full repair of every such use is not asserted here.
# Minor findings
## P4. Lemma 2 needs affine functions, a nonempty index set, and a corrected derivative bookkeeping
Location. Source pp. 4–6, Lemma 2, Claim 3 and the proof of Lemma 2.

With the strict meaning of linear, Lemma 2 is false. Take \(d=2\), \(m=1000\), \(c=1\), \(I=[m]\) and \(H\equiv1\) on \((-1,2)\). All displayed domain, range and convexity hypotheses hold. On \(Q_v=[v/m,(v+1)/m]\), the minimum uniform error of \(ax\) is \(1/(2v+1)\), obtained by equating the endpoint errors. Therefore every \(v\in I\) has error at least \(1/2001\), whereas the claimed bound is \[\frac{4d^4m^{d-3}}{c|I|}=\frac{64}{10^6}=\frac1{15625}.\] An affine constant approximates \(H\) exactly. Also require \(I\ne\varnothing\), replace the unrestricted function in Claim 3 by an affine function, and evaluate the base gradient at \(v/m\) rather than at \(v\).
## P5. Three geometric normalizations in Lemma 1 require correction
Location. Source p. 7, from the width assertion through the definition of \(H\); p. 9, the final display in the small-\(K\) case.

First, minimum width \(w\) does not imply inradius at least \(w/2\). An equilateral triangle of altitude \(h\) has minimum width \(h\) and inradius \(h/3\). Thus the claimed factor on p. 7 is not a general convex-geometric implication. A dimension-dependent constant suffices: John’s ellipsoid gives an inscribed ball of radius at least \(w/(2d)\), since \(P\) lies in a \(d\)-dilate of that ellipsoid. Adjust the subsequent constant in \(u\) accordingly. This corrects the intermediate geometric assertion; it is not a counterexample to Lemma 1.

Second, from \[H(x)=1-\frac{h(u(2x-\mathbf1))}{2\sqrt d}\] the inverse coordinate is \(x=y/(2u)+\mathbf1/2\). The printed domain uses \(y/(2u)+\mathbf1\). For example, \(u=1/4\), \(y=0\) maps back to \(y=1/4\) under the printed expression, whereas the correct inverse maps back to zero. The grid is consequently the \(2m\) grid with the correct half-unit translation.

Third, the first case on p. 9 drops the factor \(\eta^{-\alpha_d-\varepsilon}\) and ends with a lower bound greater than one for \(|A\cap\Omega''|/|A|\). A fraction of the original finite set cannot exceed one. The preceding chain controls the normalized fraction \[\frac{|A\cap\Omega''|}{|A|}\eta^{-\alpha_d-\varepsilon},\] and retaining that factor proves the intended conclusion. The power gain is consistent: \(m^{\varepsilon(d+1)}u^2\) has order \(\delta^{-0.3\varepsilon}\delta^{0.2\varepsilon}\) up to constants, which tends to infinity.

Two related presentation points should be made explicit in the same local repair. The selected boundary points need not all be distinct; use an indexed multiset or the bounded overlap of the fixed dilates of grid boxes before replacing their number by \(|Y|\). In the large-\(K\) case, \(h(Q_v)\) can have zero length, so the asserted two-sided volume comparison for \(Q_v\times h(Q_v)\) is not automatic. Use an enclosing interval of controlled length and the required upper volume bound, retaining the exponent slack for constants. Intersect the resulting set with the original convex body to maintain \(\Omega'\subseteq\Omega\). These are bounded repairs to the geometric normalization, and no refutation of the corrected density-increment lemma is asserted.
## P6. The lifted translation in Appendix A is missing a factor of n
Location. Source p. 20, the sentence claiming \(x=\phi^{-1}(x_0)\in[-s,s]^\ell\).

The established inclusion is \(x_0\in sQ\) with \(Q=\phi([-n,n]^\ell)\). It gives \(x\in[-sn,sn]^\ell\), not the printed range. This can occur for actual admissible structural output, rather than just an arbitrary point of \(sQ\).

Take \(\ell=2\), \(A=\{(i,1):1\le i\le n\}\), \(H=n^\kappa\) with the appendix’s \(\kappa=80\), and \(\phi(i,j)=i+Hj\). Then \(A_0=H+[1,n]\). Apply the explicit block construction in P3 with \(m=n\), \(N=H\) and \(s=n/\log^2n\). It has all the stated structural conclusions for large \(n\), and its homogeneous translation is \[x_0=tH+\lfloor tn/2\rfloor,\qquad
 \phi^{-1}(x_0)=(\lfloor tn/2\rfloor,t),\qquad t=\lfloor s/2\rfloor.\] The first coordinate is asymptotic to \(sn/4\), so it exceeds \(s\) by an unbounded factor. The polynomial range and the admissible interval for \(s\) hold for sufficiently large \(n\).

Replace the range by \([-sn,sn]^\ell\) and carry it through the no-carry estimate. This does not require changing the chosen exponent \(\kappa\): since \(s\le |A|\le n^\ell\), \[ns^2(sn)^\ell\le n^{\ell^2+3\ell+1}\ll n^{10\ell^3}.\] The fixed dimension constants can be absorbed by sufficiently large \(n\). This repairs the local range error, without resolving the separate initial translation issue identified in P3.
## P7. Adjoining zero can destroy non-averaging even for every large retained subset
Location. Source p. 10, the first sentence of Section 3.1.

The claimed non-averaging property of \(\phi_P(\widehat A\cup\{0\})\) does not follow from that of \(A\). Here is an arbitrarily large example satisfying a polynomial box bound and surviving the deletion allowed in Corollary 5. Let \(m\to\infty\), \(N=m^3\), and \[p_i=(N+i,(N+i)^2),\qquad
 A=\{p_i,2p_i:1\le i\le m\}\subseteq\mathbb Z^2.\] This set has \(2m\) distinct points and lies in an axis-aligned box of size \(O(m^9)\), hence is a \((2,10)\)-set for large \(m\).

To prove it is non-averaging, suppose \(cp_{i_0}\) is the average of \(k\) other points \(c_jp_{i_j}\), where \(c,c_j\in\{1,2\}\) and \(k\le2m-1\). The first coordinates give \[N\left(kc-\sum_jc_j\right)=\sum_jc_ji_j-kci_0.\] The right side has absolute value less than \(4m^2<N\). Thus \(\sum_jc_j=kc\), which forces every \(c_j=c\). Comparing the remaining first-coordinate terms and the second coordinates then gives \[\sum_ji_j=ki_0,\qquad \sum_ji_j^2=ki_0^2,\qquad
 \sum_j(i_j-i_0)^2=0.\] Every selected point would equal the excluded target, a contradiction.

Every subset of \(A\) with more than \(m\) elements contains one of the pairs \(p_i,2p_i\). The retained set in Corollary 5 has more than \(m\) elements for sufficiently large \(m\). Adjoining \(0\) therefore creates \(p_i=(0+2p_i)/2\). Moreover \(csP\) proper with \(cs\ge2\) and the centered representation ensures \(2P\) is proper. Its identification preserves this two-term relation, so the image also fails to be non-averaging. This checks the exact retained-subset and identification issues that the elementary example \(\{1,2\}\) alone would leave open.

The independent finite test at \(m=8\), \(N=512\) checks all 65,535 nonempty subsets of the 16-point set, finds no averaging relation in \(A\), and verifies all eight doubling pairs. The analytic argument above proves the arbitrary-large family and the structural deletion threshold.

The repair is to claim non-averaging only for \(\phi_P(\widehat A)\), as the actual reduction subsequently does, while keeping \(0\) in the bounding progression for subset-sum structure. The inverse identification is affine, so an averaging relation among image points would imply one among original points. Definition 9 should also restrict the domain of \(\phi_P\) to the retained set unless \(A\subseteq P\) has first been arranged. These are local domain corrections, with no new obstruction to the main iteration.
# Proof audit and excluded candidates
## The dimension-change inequality is valid

Observation 15 is not a confirmed issue. Here is an all-parameter check that also covers the displayed range beyond small \(\zeta\). Set \(h=\widehat d-d\ge1\), \(a=\alpha_d\), \(b=\alpha_{d+h}\), and \[f=(b+\zeta)\bigl((a+\zeta)^{-1}-(1-\varepsilon)h\bigr).\] It increases with \(\varepsilon\), so it suffices to take \(\varepsilon=\zeta/100\). Direct expansion gives \[\begin{aligned}
 (a+\zeta)(1-f)
 &=a-b+hab+h(a+b-ab/100)\zeta\\
 &\quad+h(1-(a+b)/100)\zeta^2-h\zeta^3/100.\end{aligned}\] The constant term is nonnegative. For \(d\ge2\) it equals \[\frac{h((d-1)(d+h-1)-2)}{(d+1)(d+h+1)};\] for \(d=1\) it is \((h-1)(h-2)/(4(h+2))\). Also \(a+b\ge7/12\), \(ab\le1\), \(a+b\le2\), and \(0<\zeta<1\). The quadratic and cubic terms together are nonnegative. Hence \[1-f\ge \frac{43}{150}\zeta>\zeta/4,\] using \(a+\zeta\le2\). Thus \(c(\zeta)=\zeta/4\) is admissible. The independent script also checked 8,000 exact rational instances and the polynomial identity; those samples supplement, rather than replace, this proof.
## Lower bounds, rounding and dependency interfaces

The stated one-dimensional lower-bound family has the expected variance mechanism. For \(n_i=iq^3+i(i+1)/2\), \(1\le i\le q-1\), an averaging relation among distinct indices first forces the linear index sum by the \(q^3\) term, since the remaining quadratic error has magnitude less than \(q^3\). It then forces the sum of squared deviations to vanish. Likewise, the higher-dimensional paraboloid construction is non-averaging by strict convexity, with \(O(N^{d+1})\) box volume and \(N^{d-1}\) points. These checks provide no counterexample to the claimed exponents.

Lemma 13’s zonotope rounding is supported by the complete Bernoulli proof of [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 4.2]{CFP}]: each coordinate has variance at most \(|A|w_i^2/4\), and Chebyshev plus the union bound gives a simultaneous rounding within \(\sqrt{d|A|}w_i\). Adding a zero vector if necessary changes no subset sums or zonotope. The widths must be measured in the corresponding progression coordinates.

The discrete John statement, as recorded in [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma 4.5]{CFP}], concerns a symmetric convex body and independent lattice vectors. It is not directly an axis-aligned box statement in the original coordinates. In Case 3, a proof must identify the lattice coordinate change, handle a possible loss of affine rank, and justify the volume/cardinality comparison. A very thin strip containing many collinear lattice points refutes such a comparison for unrestricted convex sets; it is not supplied here as an example satisfying the manuscript’s full irreducibility assumptions. This remains a clarification and a repair obligation, rather than an additional counted Major finding.

The inspected structural reference uses stability and density arguments that should not be described as verified merely from their prose. For example, a lattice of index \(q\) given by \(x\equiv y\pmod q\) has both coordinate projections equal to \(\mathbb Z\); large index alone does not force a large coordinate-projection index. Similarly, subtracting an axis multiple from a basis vector need not preserve a lattice basis: in \(\mathbb Z^2\), replacing \((3,2)\) in the basis \(((3,2),(1,1))\) by \((0,2)\) or \((-1,2)\) changes the determinant to \(-2\) or \(-3\). These observations mark the limits of a literal reading of the projection/basis shortcuts in the selected reference. A suitable lattice-basis argument is required there; the imported structural theorem itself is not disproved. This review does not count a review of a different paper as an assigned-paper finding.

claim: Recorded check: The retained coefficient mass and doubled zonotope centre fail
analysis: Location. Source pp. 13–15: (13), Lemma 14 and its penultimate mass inequality, and the centres immediately after (15).

There are two distinct defects. Lemma 14 assumes only \(|\bar A_1|\ge c|A_1|\), whereas its proof needs a positive amount of coefficient mass on \(\bar A_1\). Moreover, the centre used on p. 15 is twice the centre in Lemma 14. These are genuine failures of displayed steps even under the structural and irreducibility assumptions of Theorem 4.

Let \(M\to\infty\), \(N=2M+1\), and take \[A=[-M,M]\cap\mathbb Z,\quad P(A)=A,\quad \widehat A=A,
 \quad A_0=B=[0,2M]\cap\mathbb Z,\quad a=M.\] The identification is \(x\mapsto x+M\). The set may be embedded in \(\mathbb Z^2\) if the notation \(\ell>1\) in Corollary 5 is read literally. Fix the structural constant \(c_0\le1/100\), reducing it if necessary. This is legitimate Corollary 5 data for all sufficiently large \(M\): put \(s=N/\log^2N\), \(k=\lfloor s/4\rfloor\), and \[E=\{\pm1,\ldots,\pm k\}\cup
   \{\pm(M-k+1),\ldots,\pm M\}.\] Then \(|E|=4k\le s\). The first block has every subset sum in \([-R,R]\), where \(R=k(k+1)/2\). The positive partial sums of the second block have gaps at most \(M\) and end at \(T=kM-k(k-1)/2\); use their negatives as well. Since \(2R\ge M\) for large \(M\), the translated intervals overlap and give \[[-k(M+1),k(M+1)]\cap\mathbb Z\ \subseteq\ \Sigma(E).\] This contains \(c_0sP(A)\), which is proper. Thus the origin, subset budget and homogeneous-translate requirements are all met.

Here is also a uniform verification of irreducibility, rather than a finite test of selected subsets. Fix \(\delta>0\). If \(T\subseteq A_0\), \(|T|=t\ge\delta N\), and \(x\in B\), then \(T-x\subseteq[-2M,2M]\). In a reduced structural GAP for \(T-x\), delete coordinates of width one. Its size is at least \(t/2\) for large \(N\). If its rank were \(r\ge2\), properness of \(c_0s(T)P(T-x)\) would give \[s(T)^r t\ll |\Sigma(T')|\ll Ns(T),\qquad
 |T'|\le s(T)=t/\log^2t,\] which is impossible uniformly for \(t\ge\delta N\) as \(N\to\infty\). Thus rank one can be chosen for every such \(T,x\), and \(|P(T-x)|\ge t/2\ge\delta N/2\). With these coherent reduced choices, \(A\) is \((\delta,\gamma)\)-irreducible for every fixed \(\gamma\le\delta/2\). Choose \(\delta\le\mu^C\) and \(\gamma\le\min(\delta/2,\delta^C)\); then take \(N\) large enough for the inverse-logarithmic lower bound on \(\gamma\) in Theorem 4. Choose the fixed \(\delta,\gamma\) using, for example, the lower bound \(\mu>1/11\) that holds for large \(M\); these choices are uniform in the limit.

Put \(L=\lfloor M/10\rfloor\), \(\mu=2L/N\), and assign \[c_{M+i}=c_{M-i}=\frac1{2L}\quad(1\le i\le L),\qquad c_x=0
 \quad\hbox{otherwise}.\] Then \(\sum c_x=1\), \(\sum c_x(x-a)=0\), and \(c_x\le1/(\mu N)\), with equality on the support. The median \(a\) lies in no half-space meeting \(A_0\) in at most \(\mu N\) points, so \(A_0\) is not in \(\mu\)-convex position. The limiting value \(\mu\to1/10\) permits the preceding fixed choices of \(\delta,\gamma\).

Equation reference: eq:weightedsets. Order the zero coefficients first, in pairs \((M-j,M+j)\) for \(j>L\), and then the nonzero coefficients in pairs \((M+i,M-i)\) for \(1\le i\le L\). This is a permitted nondecreasing order in (13). The resulting two sets satisfy \[
 A_1-a=a-A_2=\{-M,\ldots,-L-1\}\cup\{1,\ldots,L\}.\] Choose \(\bar A_1=\{M-j:L<j\le M\}\). Its cardinality is \(M-L\ge0.9|A_1|\), but all its coefficients vanish. Hence the centred retained zonotope in the proof of Lemma 14 is \(\{0\}\). It cannot contain \(\xi NB\) for any \(\xi>0\), and the displayed lower bound \[\sum_{x\in(\bar A_1-a)\setminus H}\Delta_x\ge\mu N/4\] has left side zero. This disproves the stronger retained-zonotope assertion in the proof. The printed statement of Lemma 14 has the full \(Z_{A_1-a}\) on its right side; the preceding example is not represented as a disproof of that weaker statement.

Equation reference: eq:badcentre. For the full \(A_1\) in [eq:weightedsets] (#eq:weightedsets), the centre defined on p. 15 is \[
 z_1=\mu N\sum_{x\in A_1}c_x(x-a)=\frac{L(L+1)}2
       =\max Z_{A_1-a}.\] Thus \(z_1+\xi NB\) leaves the full zonotope for every \(\xi>0\). The proof actually deletes \(O(N/\log N)\) points to form its retained set. Under the natural, consistent interpretation of its shifted indices, the resulting centre obeys \[\bar z_1\ge z_1-O(N^2/\log N).\] The right-hand displacement in \(\xi NB=[0,2\xi NM]\) is of order \(\xi N^2\). For these admissible \(\mu\to1/10\) and fixed \(\gamma>0\), \(\xi=c^\prime\mu\gamma\) stays bounded below by a positive constant, so this eventually exceeds the deletion error. Consequently the displayed inclusion \(\operatorname{conv}(\bar z_1+\xi NB)\subseteq Z_{A_1-a}\) on p. 15 is still false for the actual permitted trimming. The mismatch with the retained zonotope needed in (15) is an additional logical problem.

For a reproducible finite coefficient calculation, \(M=1000\), \(L=100\) gives a retained fraction \(9/10\), retained mass zero, the asserted mass lower bound \(50\), and \[Z_{A_1-a}=[-495450,5050],\qquad z_1=5050,
 \qquad z_1/2=2525.\] The large-\(N\) structural verification above, not this one finite calculation, supplies all asymptotic hypotheses.

This is a Major proof defect in the implication from irreducibility to intersecting nonempty subset sums, a core input to the main argument. It does not refute the conclusion of Theorem 4: the interval in this example certainly has averaging relations.

A plausible restricted repair must use the actual small deletion and prove a coefficient-mass condition. Alternating a nondecreasing sequence gives mass at least \(1/2-O((\mu|A_0|)^{-1})\) on each side; deleting \(O(N/\log N)\) points loses only \(O((\mu\log N)^{-1})\). Thus each actual retained side has mass at least \(1/3\) for large \(N\). This is substantially stronger than the arbitrary cardinality condition in Lemma 14. Use, for example, \(\lambda=\mu|A_0|/4\), so that \(\lambda c_x\le1/4\), and retain the same interior centre \(\lambda\sum c_x(x-a)\) throughout. The factor \(|A_0|\) also avoids the unsupported assertion \(\mu|A|c_x\le1\) when \(\widehat A\ne A\).

A complete repair must establish the interior inclusion in the retained zonotope, use a symmetric displacement body such as \(B-B\) in the slab argument, account for low-rank lattice slices and the additive endpoint term in lattice counting, and quantitatively produce at least two lattice intersection points. The last printed condition that the intersection differs from \(\{z_1\}\) alone does not rule out \(\{0\}\). These remaining geometric and lattice steps are not certified as repaired here.
result: Impact: A core step establishing Theorem4 and hence the main iteration is false as written.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use actual small deletions and their retained coefficient mass>=1/3, a consistent interior scaling such as mu|A0|/4, and prove the inclusion in the retained zonotope. Track symmetric displacement bodies, rank-deficient slices, counting endpoint terms and at least two lattice points.

problems.title: Whole-step retention is substituted for preprocessing retention in the final product
problems.source_location: pp.17-18, Case3 and final cardinality verification
claim: Recorded check: Whole-step retention is substituted for preprocessing retention in the final product
analysis: Location. Source pp. 17–18, Case 3 and the paragraph beginning Finally, we verify.

Equation reference: eq:correctstep. Write \(M=|A|\), \(V=|B|\), and distinguish the preprocessing retention \(r\) from the geometric volume ratio \(\eta\). The preceding Case 3 estimates have the form \[
 M_{\mathrm{new}}\ge c\,\eta^p rM,\qquad
 V_{\mathrm{new}}\le C\,\eta r^K V,\qquad
 p=\frac{d-1}{d+1}+\varepsilon.\] The final paragraph instead defines \(\rho_j=M_{j+1}/M_j\) for the whole step and asserts \(V_{j+1}\ll\rho_j^K V_j\). This does not follow from [eq:correctstep] (#eq:correctstep).

Equation reference: eq:ratio. An exact numerical family makes the failure explicit. Set \(d=2\), \(\varepsilon=1/100\), \(p=103/300\), \(K=100\), \(r=1\), and, for \(t\downarrow0\), \[\eta=t^{300},\qquad \rho=t^{103},\qquad
 V_{\mathrm{new}}/V=\eta,\qquad M_{\mathrm{new}}/M=\rho.\] These satisfy both one-step inequalities with constants one, while \[
 \frac{V_{\mathrm{new}}/V}{\rho^K}=t^{-10000}\longrightarrow\infty.\] The finite check \(t=1/2\) gives the exact ratio \(2^{10000}\). Initial \(M,V\) can be taken arbitrarily large to accommodate polynomial size lower bounds; the obstruction is the missing geometric factor, not rounding. This is an independent disproof of the asserted algebraic implication. No actual non-averaging set realizing this numerical sequence is claimed.

There is a second defect in the same final deduction. After inserting \(\max(1,C\rho_j^K)\), the displayed product has factors equal to one whenever \(C\rho_j^K<1\). The inequality with that maximum provides no lower bound on \(\prod\rho_j\). Also, an upper bound \(\rho_j\le\mu^{c(d)}\) is not a consequence of the displayed lower bound on the selected set’s size. Deliberate trimming could enforce a size quota, but would not validate the missing \(\eta\) factor.

The intended contradiction requires all intermediate sets to remain large enough for the structural theorem and the common parameters. The printed argument does not establish that requirement, so this is Major. It does not disprove Theorems 1 or 2.

Equation reference: eq:potential. The following replacement verifies the needed size control conditional on a correct geometric Case 3. In a block of fixed dimension \(d\ge2\), choose \[p_*=\alpha_d+2\varepsilon<1,\qquad
 2\varepsilon<\zeta_0,\qquad Kp_*>1,
 \quad \alpha_d=\frac{d-1}{d+1}.\] For \(F=\log M-p_*\log V\), [eq:correctstep] (#eq:correctstep) gives \[
 F_{\mathrm{new}}-F
 \ge\varepsilon\log(1/\eta)+(Kp_*-1)\log(1/r)-O(1).\] Since \(\eta\le\mu^\tau\to0\) with the original input size, this is nonnegative for sufficiently large input, uniformly in \(r\le1\). At entry to the block, \(M\ge V^{\alpha_d+\zeta}\) and \(\zeta\ge\zeta_0\) imply \[F\ge\frac{\zeta-2\varepsilon}{\alpha_d+\zeta}\log M.\] At every later step, \(M\le V\) implies \(F\le(1-p_*)\log M\). Hence every set in this block retains a fixed positive power of its entry size. There are only boundedly many changes of dimension, by the dimension-increment argument and Observation 15; each such step retains at least a \((1-\varepsilon)\) power. Thus \(M_j\ge M_{\mathrm{original}}^{c(\zeta_0,d)}\) for some \(c(\zeta_0,d)>0\). In particular, \(\log\log M_j=\log\log M_{\mathrm{original}}+O_{\zeta_0,d}(1)\), which is sufficient for the common inverse-logarithmic parameters. The one-dimensional branch can be treated directly: for \(\mu<1/2\) a median of a finite set cannot be in \(\mu\)-convex position.

This proves a useful replacement for the size bookkeeping, not the manuscript’s precise near-original exponent with an absolute \(c\). It remains conditional on the preceding geometric/lattice step, including the repair required by P1.
result: Impact: The printed proof does not preserve the large-set hypotheses through its iteration, a core termination/parameter requirement.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Keep eta and r separate. The report proves a conditional positive-power size bound using F=log M-(alpha_d+2epsilon)log V and a nonnegative increment epsilon log(1/eta)+(Kpstar-1)log(1/r)-O(1).

problems.title: Lemma6 lacks an origin condition and is false for affine containing GAPs
problems.source_location: p.10 Lemma6; pp.11-13 uses; AppendixA initial translation p.19
claim: Recorded check: Lemma6 lacks an origin condition and is false for affine containing GAPs
analysis: Location. Source p. 10, Lemma 6 and its proof; uses in Lemma 10 on pp. 11–13; the translation at the start of Appendix A.

The assertion \(\Sigma(A')\subseteq sP\) requires that shorter subset sums can be padded with zeros in \(P\). The hypothesis \(A\subseteq P\) does not supply \(0\in P\). This affects the stated bound, not just its written proof.

Equation reference: eq:Pzero. Let \(m\to\infty\), \(N=m^4\), and \[A=N+[1,m],\qquad P_{\mathrm{aff}}=N+[1,m],\qquad
 s=m/\log^2m.\] The input GAP has dimension one and size \(m\). It is contained in a box of size \(m\), so the polynomial box-size hypothesis is satisfied; again one may embed it in \(\mathbb Z^2\). There is admissible symmetric rank-two structural data \[
 P_0=\{uN+v: |u|\le1,\ |v|\le m\},\qquad \widehat A=A.\] Both \(P_0\) and \(c_0sP_0\) are proper for fixed \(0<c_0\le1/100\) and large \(m\).

For \(|k-t|\le c_0s\) and \(t/3\le h\le2t/3\), the interval length is \(l(t-l)+h(t-h)\ge13t^2/36\) after harmless endpoint rounding. Adjacent lower endpoints differ by \(m+O(t)\); since \(t^2/m\to\infty\), these intervals overlap. Their union contains \([0.4tm,0.6tm]\) for all sufficiently large \(m\). Consequently \[x_0+c_0sP_0\subseteq\Sigma(A'),\qquad
 x_0=tN+\lfloor tm/2\rfloor.\] This is a homogeneous translate. Thus \(d(A)=2\) and \(P(A)=P_0\) are allowed by the manuscript’s definition, with every Corollary 5 conclusion explicitly verified. Lemma 6 would give \[3(2m+1)=|P_0|\ll m/s,\] which is impossible as \(s\to\infty\). The implied constant cannot absorb the unbounded factor \(s\).

The phenomenon is not removed by insisting on a rank-one structural choice. A rank-one GAP containing \(0\) and more than \((m+1)/2\) points of \(N+[1,m]\) must have integer step one and span at least \(N\). Its \(c_0s\) dilate contains an integer interval of length comparable to \(sN\). But every subset sum of at most \(s\) elements of \(A\) lies in one of the separated bands \([k(N+1),k(N+m)]\), each of width at most \(sm\ll N\). No such interval fits. Hence a reduced rank-one choice is impossible for large \(m\).

The independent finite endpoint certificate uses \(m=2^{20}\), \(t=\lfloor m/392\rfloor=2674\), and exact rational bounds \(13<\log m<14\). It verifies 113,157 intervals and the inclusion for all \(|k-t|\le63\), with offset radius 65,059,860. This is a concrete check of the interval construction. It is not used to assert a sufficiently-large-\(m\) hypothesis at this single numerical value; the asymptotic proof above supplies that part.

This is a false core structural lemma, used to obtain the up-move savings and the subsequent iteration bounds, and is therefore Major. The set \(A\) here need not be non-averaging: Lemma 6 has no such hypothesis. No conclusion about a counterexample to the main theorem follows.

A valid version can assume an origin-containing, appropriately centered input GAP. Then every subset of at most \(s\) elements has its sum in \(sP\) and the counting proof applies, after deleting width-one coordinates. All applications must be checked with the origin fixed at the point at which their subset-sum dimensions are defined. Translating a set preserves the non-averaging property, but not the subset-sum structure with an adjoined origin. In Appendix A, the initial reduction of an arbitrary box to \([n]^\ell\) therefore also needs justification. One must either supply the higher-dimensional structural proof with its actual origin convention or retain cardinality information when transporting subset sums through a translation. A full repair of every such use is not asserted here.
result: Impact: False structural lemma supplies the up-move savings used in the main reduction.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Require an origin-containing centered input GAP, delete width-one coordinates, and recheck every use with the origin fixed. A translation of A cannot silently transport variable-cardinality subset sums.

problems.title: Affine approximation and nonempty-index wording in Lemma2
problems.source_location: pp.4-6, Lemma2, Claim3, derivative telescoping
claim: Recorded check: Affine approximation and nonempty-index wording in Lemma2
analysis: Location. Source pp. 4–6, Lemma 2, Claim 3 and the proof of Lemma 2.

With the strict meaning of linear, Lemma 2 is false. Take \(d=2\), \(m=1000\), \(c=1\), \(I=[m]\) and \(H\equiv1\) on \((-1,2)\). All displayed domain, range and convexity hypotheses hold. On \(Q_v=[v/m,(v+1)/m]\), the minimum uniform error of \(ax\) is \(1/(2v+1)\), obtained by equating the endpoint errors. Therefore every \(v\in I\) has error at least \(1/2001\), whereas the claimed bound is \[\frac{4d^4m^{d-3}}{c|I|}=\frac{64}{10^6}=\frac1{15625}.\] An affine constant approximates \(H\) exactly. Also require \(I\ne\varnothing\), replace the unrestricted function in Claim 3 by an affine function, and evaluate the base gradient at \(v/m\) rather than at \(v\).
result: Impact: Literal strict-linear statement and proof wording are false or incomplete; intended local estimate survives.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Say affine, require nonempty I, evaluate at v/m, and use coordinatewise derivative variation with overlap at most d. Smooth with arbitrarily small domain loss.

problems.title: Width, inverse coordinates and density normalization in Lemma1
problems.source_location: p.7 width and H rescaling; p.9 small-K final display
claim: Recorded check: Width, inverse coordinates and density normalization in Lemma1
analysis: Location. Source p. 7, from the width assertion through the definition of \(H\); p. 9, the final display in the small-\(K\) case.

First, minimum width \(w\) does not imply inradius at least \(w/2\). An equilateral triangle of altitude \(h\) has minimum width \(h\) and inradius \(h/3\). Thus the claimed factor on p. 7 is not a general convex-geometric implication. A dimension-dependent constant suffices: John’s ellipsoid gives an inscribed ball of radius at least \(w/(2d)\), since \(P\) lies in a \(d\)-dilate of that ellipsoid. Adjust the subsequent constant in \(u\) accordingly. This corrects the intermediate geometric assertion; it is not a counterexample to Lemma 1.

Second, from \[H(x)=1-\frac{h(u(2x-\mathbf1))}{2\sqrt d}\] the inverse coordinate is \(x=y/(2u)+\mathbf1/2\). The printed domain uses \(y/(2u)+\mathbf1\). For example, \(u=1/4\), \(y=0\) maps back to \(y=1/4\) under the printed expression, whereas the correct inverse maps back to zero. The grid is consequently the \(2m\) grid with the correct half-unit translation.

Third, the first case on p. 9 drops the factor \(\eta^{-\alpha_d-\varepsilon}\) and ends with a lower bound greater than one for \(|A\cap\Omega''|/|A|\). A fraction of the original finite set cannot exceed one. The preceding chain controls the normalized fraction \[\frac{|A\cap\Omega''|}{|A|}\eta^{-\alpha_d-\varepsilon},\] and retaining that factor proves the intended conclusion. The power gain is consistent: \(m^{\varepsilon(d+1)}u^2\) has order \(\delta^{-0.3\varepsilon}\delta^{0.2\varepsilon}\) up to constants, which tends to infinity.

Two related presentation points should be made explicit in the same local repair. The selected boundary points need not all be distinct; use an indexed multiset or the bounded overlap of the fixed dilates of grid boxes before replacing their number by \(|Y|\). In the large-\(K\) case, \(h(Q_v)\) can have zero length, so the asserted two-sided volume comparison for \(Q_v\times h(Q_v)\) is not automatic. Use an enclosing interval of controlled length and the required upper volume bound, retaining the exponent slack for constants. Intersect the resulting set with the original convex body to maintain \(\Omega'\subseteq\Omega\). These are bounded repairs to the geometric normalization, and no refutation of the corrected density-increment lemma is asserted.
result: Impact: Intermediate normalizations are false, but bounded constant/coordinate corrections retain the intended density increment.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use a dimension-dependent inradius constant, the half-unit translation and the normalized density fraction. Account for bounded overlap and use an enclosing vertical interval/upper volume bound in the flat case.

problems.title: The AppendixA lift range is missing a factor n
problems.source_location: p.20 final lift sentence
claim: Recorded check: The AppendixA lift range is missing a factor n
analysis: Location. Source p. 20, the sentence claiming \(x=\phi^{-1}(x_0)\in[-s,s]^\ell\).

The established inclusion is \(x_0\in sQ\) with \(Q=\phi([-n,n]^\ell)\). It gives \(x\in[-sn,sn]^\ell\), not the printed range. This can occur for actual admissible structural output, rather than just an arbitrary point of \(sQ\).

Take \(\ell=2\), \(A=\{(i,1):1\le i\le n\}\), \(H=n^\kappa\) with the appendix’s \(\kappa=80\), and \(\phi(i,j)=i+Hj\). Then \(A_0=H+[1,n]\). Apply the explicit block construction in P3 with \(m=n\), \(N=H\) and \(s=n/\log^2n\). It has all the stated structural conclusions for large \(n\), and its homogeneous translation is \[x_0=tH+\lfloor tn/2\rfloor,\qquad
 \phi^{-1}(x_0)=(\lfloor tn/2\rfloor,t),\qquad t=\lfloor s/2\rfloor.\] The first coordinate is asymptotic to \(sn/4\), so it exceeds \(s\) by an unbounded factor. The polynomial range and the admissible interval for \(s\) hold for sufficiently large \(n\).

Replace the range by \([-sn,sn]^\ell\) and carry it through the no-carry estimate. This does not require changing the chosen exponent \(\kappa\): since \(s\le |A|\le n^\ell\), \[ns^2(sn)^\ell\le n^{\ell^2+3\ell+1}\ll n^{10\ell^3}.\] The fixed dimension constants can be absorbed by sufficiently large \(n\). This repairs the local range error, without resolving the separate initial translation issue identified in P3.
result: Impact: Printed coordinate range is false, although the chosen no-carry exponent has ample slack.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use [-sn,sn]^ell; n s^2(sn)^ell<=n^(ell^2+3ell+1)<<n^(10ell^3) verifies the remaining scale.

problems.title: Adjoining zero destroys non-averaging of the retained image
problems.source_location: p.10 first sentence of Section3.1; p.11 identification-domain wording
claim: Recorded check: Adjoining zero destroys non-averaging of the retained image
analysis: Location. Source p. 10, the first sentence of Section 3.1.

The claimed non-averaging property of \(\phi_P(\widehat A\cup\{0\})\) does not follow from that of \(A\). Here is an arbitrarily large example satisfying a polynomial box bound and surviving the deletion allowed in Corollary 5. Let \(m\to\infty\), \(N=m^3\), and \[p_i=(N+i,(N+i)^2),\qquad
 A=\{p_i,2p_i:1\le i\le m\}\subseteq\mathbb Z^2.\] This set has \(2m\) distinct points and lies in an axis-aligned box of size \(O(m^9)\), hence is a \((2,10)\)-set for large \(m\).

To prove it is non-averaging, suppose \(cp_{i_0}\) is the average of \(k\) other points \(c_jp_{i_j}\), where \(c,c_j\in\{1,2\}\) and \(k\le2m-1\). The first coordinates give \[N\left(kc-\sum_jc_j\right)=\sum_jc_ji_j-kci_0.\] The right side has absolute value less than \(4m^2<N\). Thus \(\sum_jc_j=kc\), which forces every \(c_j=c\). Comparing the remaining first-coordinate terms and the second coordinates then gives \[\sum_ji_j=ki_0,\qquad \sum_ji_j^2=ki_0^2,\qquad
 \sum_j(i_j-i_0)^2=0.\] Every selected point would equal the excluded target, a contradiction.

Every subset of \(A\) with more than \(m\) elements contains one of the pairs \(p_i,2p_i\). The retained set in Corollary 5 has more than \(m\) elements for sufficiently large \(m\). Adjoining \(0\) therefore creates \(p_i=(0+2p_i)/2\). Moreover \(csP\) proper with \(cs\ge2\) and the centered representation ensures \(2P\) is proper. Its identification preserves this two-term relation, so the image also fails to be non-averaging. This checks the exact retained-subset and identification issues that the elementary example \(\{1,2\}\) alone would leave open.

The independent finite test at \(m=8\), \(N=512\) checks all 65,535 nonempty subsets of the 16-point set, finds no averaging relation in \(A\), and verifies all eight doubling pairs. The analytic argument above proves the arbitrary-large family and the structural deletion threshold.

The repair is to claim non-averaging only for \(\phi_P(\widehat A)\), as the actual reduction subsequently does, while keeping \(0\) in the bounding progression for subset-sum structure. The inverse identification is affine, so an averaging relation among image points would imply one among original points. Definition 9 should also restrict the domain of \(\phi_P\) to the retained set unless \(A\subseteq P\) has first been arranged. These are local domain corrections, with no new obstruction to the main iteration.
result: Impact: The introductory reduction claim is false even under the structural deletion and polynomial box conditions; actual later use omits0.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Claim non-averaging only for phiP(Ahat), retaining0 solely in the bounding progression; restrict identification domains to the retained set until containment is arranged.

report: Abstract: The reviewed source is Yuning Liu’s 38-page manuscript `arXiv:2207.12912v3`, dated 10 May 2023, associated with the frozen 2025 journal record, DOI `10.1002/cpa.22242`. Two major proof defects are established. The weighted normal spheres in Section 4 are used with Euclidean tube radii, invalidating the stated connection estimate and its use in the minimal-pair argument. The construction in Section 5 takes a constant normal extension of general \(H^{1/2}\) traces; an explicit admissible pair of \(H^1\) initial maps makes the constructed map fail to belong to \(H^1\). Eight further findings concern statements or calculations with bounded repair paths. Their scope is stated separately; in particular, a Hausdorff-convergence counterexample is at initial time, and a zero-gradient square-completion defect is an algebraic finding, not a claimed positive-time counterexample. No counterexample to the full main theorems is asserted. Substantial correction of the two major arguments is required for the reviewed version. Human adjudication remains pending. The current focused independent acceptance state is recorded in the accompanying provenance.

The equation is \[\partial_tu_\varepsilon=\Delta u_\varepsilon-\varepsilon^{-2}\partial F(u_\varepsilon),
 \qquad F(u)=f(\operatorname{dist}(u,m_+\sqcup m_-)^2),\] with smooth disjoint connected closed wells, \(0\in m_-\), smooth nearest-point projection in \(B_{2\delta_0}(m)\), and \[f(s)=s\quad(0\leq s\leq\delta_0^2),\qquad

 \psi_\varepsilon=d_F(u_\varepsilon).\] The modulated energy is \[E_\varepsilon=\int_\Omega
 \left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}|\nabla u_\varepsilon|^2+

# P1: weighted and Euclidean radii in the connection estimate (Major)
## Location and claim

The relevant definitions are (4.1)–(4.5), pp. 22–23; the affected statements are Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2, pp. 23–25. They feed directly into (4.16)–(4.20) and the contradiction proving (1.19), p. 26. The weighted semidistance and normal spheres are \[d_F^*(v,w)=\inf_\gamma\int\sqrt{2F(\gamma)}|\gamma'|\,\mathrm dt,\qquad
 N(p,r)=\{z:d_F^*(z,p)=r,\ P_{m_\pm}z=p\}.\] In (4.5), both normal spheres have weighted radius \(\delta_0\), and \(\kappa\) contains the additive correction \(2\delta_0-c_F\). Lemma 4.2 instead stops a curve when it exits the Euclidean tube \(B_{\delta_0}(m_\pm)\).
## A counterexample to the stated lemmas

Set \(a=\delta_0=1/100\) and take two unit circles in \(\mathbb R^2\), \[m_-=\{(1+\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\},\qquad
 m_+=\{(4+\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\}.\] They are compact, connected, smooth and disjoint; \(0\in m_-\), \(D=1\), and the \(2a\)-tubes have smooth nearest-point projections. The closest pair is \(p_-=(2,0)\), \(p_+=(3,0)\).

Choose a monotone smooth \(f\) satisfying the prescribed endpoint conditions, with \(a^2\leq f\leq2a^2\) in the intermediate interval. For completeness, such a \(C^\infty\) choice can be made explicitly. For \(0<z<1\), put \[s(z)=\frac{e^{-1/z}}{e^{-1/z}+e^{-1/(1-z)}},\quad
 b(z)=e^{-1/[z(1-z)]},\quad B=\int_0^1b(z)\,\mathrm dz,
 \quad w(z)=1-s(z)+\frac{b(z)}{2B}.\] Extend \(s\) by \(0,1\) and \(b\) by zero at the endpoints. Symmetry gives \(\int_0^1s=1/2\), hence \(\int_0^1w=1\); \(w\geq0\), \(w(0)=1\), \(w(1)=0\), and all derivatives needed for gluing are flat. Define \[f(t)=a^2\left[1+\int_0^{(t-a^2)/a^2}w(z)\,\mathrm dz\right]
       \quad(a^2<t<2a^2)\] and use \(f(t)=t\) below and \(f(t)=2a^2\) above. Thus the example satisfies the potential hypotheses, including smoothness of \(F\) across the parts where the distance function has a cut locus, because \(f\) is already constant there.

Equation reference: eq:cfbounds. Direct bounds on the defining integral give \[2a-4\sqrt2\,a^2\leq c_F
 \leq 2a-(4-\sqrt2)a^2.\] In particular, \[
 0.019434\leq c_F\leq0.0197415,\qquad a<c_F<2a.\] The displayed decimal bounds are certified by the rational enclosure \(1.414<\sqrt2<1.415\), not by floating-point quadrature.

# P2: the collar construction does not preserve general \(H^1\) data (Major)
## Location

On p. 26, (5.1) calls \(\Psi_\delta^\pm\) global \(C^1\) diffeomorphisms, while requiring \(\Psi_\delta^\pm=P_{\Sigma_0}\) on the entire open collar \(B_\delta(\Sigma_0)\). On p. 27, (5.2) asserts that \(u_0^\pm=u_{\pm}^{\rm in}\circ\Psi_\delta^\pm\) belongs to \(H^1\), and (5.10) uses these extensions to define \(u_\varepsilon^{\rm in}\).

Already at the smooth geometric level, \(DP_{\Sigma_0}\) has rank \(d-1\) in the collar. Such a map is not a diffeomorphism between \(d\)-dimensional domains. The more substantial defect remains even if the map is renamed a collapsing extension.
## Admissible trace counterexample

Take \(\Omega=B_3(0)\subset\mathbb R^2\) and \(\Sigma_0=S^1\), with \(\Omega_0^+=B_1(0)\) and \(\Omega_0^-=B_3(0)\setminus\overline B_1(0)\). A short smooth mean curvature evolution exists, and the separation from the outer boundary meets the geometric hypothesis for small \(\delta_0\). In target space \(\mathbb R^3\), take the parallel circles \[m_-=\{(1-\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)\},\qquad
 m_+=m_-+(0,0,D),\quad D>0.\] They satisfy all well hypotheses, including \(0\in m_-\), and pairs at the same angle have exactly the minimal distance \(D\).

Let \[a(\theta)=c\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}2^{-3j/4}\sin(2^j\theta),
 \qquad c=\frac1{100}.\] The series converges absolutely and uniformly and has \(|a|<\pi/8\). Its Sobolev seminorms satisfy \[\sum_j 2^j\,2^{-3j/2}<\infty,\qquad
 \sum_j 2^{2j}\,2^{-3j/2}=\infty.\] Thus \(a\in H^{1/2}(S^1)\cap C(S^1)\) but \(a\notin H^1(S^1)\). This is a divergence proof, not an inference from finitely many sampled Fourier modes.

Let \(a_+\) be the harmonic extension to the disk, and let \(a_-\) be the harmonic extension to the annulus with inner boundary value \(a\) and outer boundary value zero. The Fourier energy formulas, or the \(H^{1/2}\) trace theorem, give \(a_\pm\in H^1\). The maximum principle keeps their values in \((-\pi/8,\pi/8)\). Define \[u_-^{\rm in}=(1-\cos a_-,\sin a_-,0),\qquad
 u_+^{\rm in}=(1-\cos a_+,\sin a_+,D).\] These are bounded \(H^1\) well-valued maps. The outer boundary value is the smooth constant zero, and their interface traces have distance exactly \(D\). In particular, they satisfy the full minimal-pair assumption (1.23), not merely separate phase membership.

On the collar, (5.1)–(5.2) give the first two coordinates \[(1-\cos a(\theta),\sin a(\theta)),\] constant in the normal coordinate. This is not an \(H^1\) map on any positive-width annulus. If it were, its second component would be \(H^1\) there, and composition with the Lipschitz function \(\arcsin\) on its range would give the constant normal extension of \(a\) in \(H^1\). Integration in the normal variable would imply \(a\in H^1(S^1)\), a contradiction.

The failure persists in the actual final construction (5.10). The two extended maps have identical first two coordinates and differ only in the third coordinate. Therefore interpolation by \(S_\varepsilon\) changes only that third coordinate. The non-\(H^1\) first two coordinates remain unchanged for every \(\varepsilon\). The constructed \(u_\varepsilon^{\rm in}\) is consequently not in \(H^1\).
## Impact and repair boundary

This disproves the claimed construction for admissible inputs of Theorem 1.2. It does not prove that no other preparation sequence exists. A valid proof needs a Sobolev-compatible gluing construction that preserves the minimal-pair constraint and the \(O(\varepsilon)\) modulated-energy bound, possibly with smoothing scales depending on \(\varepsilon\). Alternatively, stronger tangential trace regularity would change the theorem’s stated scope. Renaming \(\Psi_\delta^\pm\), or citing a trace theorem that supplies only \(H^{1/2}\) traces, does not repair the argument. The initial construction in the separately checked Laux–Liu preprint [LL] starts with a global \(H^1\) map and does not supply this missing extension for arbitrary pairs of bulk maps.

# Checks that do not support additional confirmed failures
## Infimum versus attainment of a connection

The value \(C_F(p_+,p_-)=c_F\) for arbitrary well endpoints does not imply that a least-energy heteroclinic joins every such pair. One can move along either connected well at zero potential cost, taking arbitrarily long time to make its kinetic cost arbitrarily small, and use a closest-pair transition in between. This proves the common infimum. Attainment at the least energy forces the straight minimal-pair orbit. The distinction in the checked Lin–Pan–Wang equality-case argument is compatible with the target’s preliminary discussion. It does not cure P1’s incorrect radii.
## The corrected dissipation term in the appendix

The target explicitly retains \[\frac1{2\varepsilon}\int_\Omega
       \bigl(\varepsilon^2|\partial_tu_\varepsilon|^2-|H_\varepsilon|^2\bigr)\,\mathrm dx\] in Lemma A.2. In the exact Laux–Liu arXiv v2 checked here, the corresponding displayed Lemma 4.4 omits this term, while its square-completion calculation (4.35) contains it. The target notices this discrepancy. The reference’s statement therefore cannot be used to accuse the target of omitting that same term. The chain-rule convention in P4 and the zero-normal convention in P10 are separate questions.
## Time quantifiers for the limiting traces

A spatial \(H^1\) conclusion initially obtained for almost every time need not prevent a properly chosen representative from having minimal-pair traces at every time. Away from the smooth moving interface, the strong \(C_tL^2_{\rm loc}\) convergence and bounded values give global \(L^2\) continuity after pulling back the moving domains: the contribution of a collar of width \(\delta\) is bounded by its volume, uniformly in time. The uniform \(H^1\) estimate then extends to every time by weak lower semicontinuity.

On a fixed smooth reference domain the trace interpolation estimate \[\|\operatorname{Tr}v\|_{L^2(\partial\Omega)}^2
 \leq C\|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\|v\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\] gives continuity of the traces in \(L^2\). The minimal-pair constraint is closed under that convergence. Consequently an almost-everywhere-time result can be extended once the representative and these steps are supplied. This is a repair of presentation and quantifiers, not a replacement for the missing connection estimate in P1.

The level choices \(b_k^\pm\) in Proposition 3.5 should likewise make their possible time dependence explicit. A selection made by Fubini at each fixed time does not itself prove the existence of one threshold working at all times. No full counterexample to that stronger uniform selection was established in this review, so it is not counted as a confirmed additional defect.
## The level-perimeter rate can be recovered by clipping

The Chebyshev step on p. 19 does not display the dependence on the small level parameter. The desired level-selection bound can be obtained without relying on that omission. Let \(0<2\delta<c_F\) and define \[T_\delta(z)=\min\{\max\{z-c_F+2\delta,0\},\delta\}.\] With \(A_t=\mathcal H^{d-1}(\Sigma_t)\), the calibration and the \(L^1\) phase-error estimate give \[\begin{aligned}
 \int_{\{c_F-2\delta<\psi<c_F-\delta\}}|\nabla\psi|
 &\leq E_\varepsilon+\int_\Omega\xi\cdot\nabla T_\delta(\psi)\\
 &\leq C\varepsilon+\delta A_t+C\|\psi-c_F\mathbf 1_{\Omega_t^+}\|_{L^1}\\
 &\leq \delta A_t+C\sqrt\varepsilon.\end{aligned}\] Here integration by parts uses \(T_\delta(c_F\mathbf 1_{\Omega_t^+})=\delta\mathbf 1_{\Omega_t^+}\) and the Lipschitz constant one of \(T_\delta\). The coarea formula gives the needed averaged upper bound. For an individual regular level \(s\) in the same interval, \[P(\{\psi>s\};\Omega)
 \geq-\int_{\{\psi>s\}}\operatorname{div}\xi
 \geq A_t-C\frac{\sqrt\varepsilon}{\delta}.\] Combining the two bounds selects a level with the claimed order \(\sqrt\varepsilon/\delta\). Setting \(\delta=\varepsilon^{1/6}\) gives order \(\varepsilon^{1/3}\). This bounded derivation supports the perimeter route; it supplies no Hausdorff control, and hence does not repair P5.
## Passage to harmonic heat flow

Weak \(H^1\) convergence alone would not justify passage through the quadratic second fundamental form. The primary Chen–Struwe argument [CS], Sections II–IV, instead uses a penalized Bochner estimate, a localized monotonicity formula, small-energy regularity, normality of the limiting penalization force off a concentration set, and a cutoff removal argument. The target’s local energy and time-dissipation estimates (3.2), together with its bounded values, supply the type of local inputs needed away from the moving interface. Applying the argument requires localization to fixed space-time cylinders separated from that interface; the whole unscaled energy of the target is not uniformly bounded across the transition layer. This dependency was checked at that local level. No counterexample to the harmonic-flow passage was established. A full independent redevelopment of the entire partial-regularity theory is not claimed.
# What a corrected argument would need to establish

For P1, a replacement quantitative connection lemma must use compatible radii, prove a strict gap for nonminimal endpoint pairs, and give the uniform compactness needed on the positive-measure trace set used in (4.19). It must then be carried through the slicing contradiction. For P2, a new preparation construction must work for the full \(H^1\) class in (1.23), retain the prescribed maps outside \(B_{2\delta}(\Sigma_0)\), and control both \(E_\varepsilon\) and \(B\) by \(C\varepsilon\). Neither task is completed by the local corrections listed for the Minor findings.

The smaller corrections are more sharply delimited: use a valid SBV compactness statement with the available jump-area bound; make the gradient convention consistent; remove or separately prove the Hausdorff assertion; use the coordinate-free projection bound; restrict the curvature identity to its valid region; correct the negative-part sign and bulk coefficient; and make the zero-gradient square completion exact, or estimate its explicit remainder. None requires a claim that the authors have already adopted a correction.

problems.title: Weighted and Euclidean radii are interchanged in the connection estimate
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Weighted and Euclidean radii are interchanged in the connection estimate
claim: Recorded check: Weighted and Euclidean radii are interchanged in the connection estimate
analysis:
The relevant definitions are (4.1)–(4.5), pp. 22–23; the affected statements are Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2, pp. 23–25. They feed directly into (4.16)–(4.20) and the contradiction proving (1.19), p. 26. The weighted semidistance and normal spheres are \[d_F^*(v,w)=\inf_\gamma\int\sqrt{2F(\gamma)}|\gamma'|\,\mathrm dt,\qquad
 N(p,r)=\{z:d_F^*(z,p)=r,\ P_{m_\pm}z=p\}.\] In (4.5), both normal spheres have weighted radius \(\delta_0\), and \(\kappa\) contains the additive correction \(2\delta_0-c_F\). Lemma 4.2 instead stops a curve when it exits the Euclidean tube \(B_{\delta_0}(m_\pm)\).

Set \(a=\delta_0=1/100\) and take two unit circles in \(\mathbb R^2\), \[m_-=\{(1+\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\},\qquad
 m_+=\{(4+\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\}.\] They are compact, connected, smooth and disjoint; \(0\in m_-\), \(D=1\), and the \(2a\)-tubes have smooth nearest-point projections. The closest pair is \(p_-=(2,0)\), \(p_+=(3,0)\).

Choose a monotone smooth \(f\) satisfying the prescribed endpoint conditions, with \(a^2\leq f\leq2a^2\) in the intermediate interval. For completeness, such a \(C^\infty\) choice can be made explicitly. For \(0<z<1\), put \[s(z)=\frac{e^{-1/z}}{e^{-1/z}+e^{-1/(1-z)}},\quad
 b(z)=e^{-1/[z(1-z)]},\quad B=\int_0^1b(z)\,\mathrm dz,
 \quad w(z)=1-s(z)+\frac{b(z)}{2B}.\] Extend \(s\) by \(0,1\) and \(b\) by zero at the endpoints. Symmetry gives \(\int_0^1s=1/2\), hence \(\int_0^1w=1\); \(w\geq0\), \(w(0)=1\), \(w(1)=0\), and all derivatives needed for gluing are flat. Define \[f(t)=a^2\left[1+\int_0^{(t-a^2)/a^2}w(z)\,\mathrm dz\right]
       \quad(a^2<t<2a^2)\] and use \(f(t)=t\) below and \(f(t)=2a^2\) above. Thus the example satisfies the potential hypotheses, including smoothness of \(F\) across the parts where the distance function has a cut locus, because \(f\) is already constant there.

Equation reference: eq:cfbounds. Direct bounds on the defining integral give \[2a-4\sqrt2\,a^2\leq c_F
 \leq 2a-(4-\sqrt2)a^2.\] In particular, \[
 0.019434\leq c_F\leq0.0197415,\qquad a<c_F<2a.\] The displayed decimal bounds are certified by the rational enclosure \(1.414<\sqrt2<1.415\), not by floating-point quadrature.

On the closest segment, write \(z(q)=(2+q,0)\), \(0\leq q\leq1\), and \[S(q)=\int_0^q\sqrt{2f(\min\{r,1-r\}^2)}\,\mathrm dr.\] Then \(S(0)=0\), \(S(1)=c_F\), and \(d_F^*(z(q),p_-)=S(q)\), \(d_F^*(z(q),p_+)=c_F-S(q)\). Here is an independent justification of the lower bounds implicit in these equalities. Put \(h(x)=\min\{1,\max\{0,x_1-2\}\}\). For \(2\leq x_1\leq3\), the distance to the two circles is at least \(\min\{h(x),1-h(x)\}\). Monotonicity of the chosen \(f\) therefore gives \(|\nabla(S\circ h)|\leq\sqrt{2F}\) almost everywhere. Integrating this calibration along any path gives the lower bound; the straight segment attains it. This also excludes shortcuts along the zero-cost wells.

Equation reference: eq:kappapos. Because \(a<c_F\), the spheres \(N(p_\pm,a)\) are nonempty, with explicit points on this segment. Their distance is finite and nonnegative. For every sufficiently small \(\rho\geq0\), the definition (4.5) therefore implies \[
 \kappa(p_+,p_-,\rho)\geq2a-c_F
 \geq \frac{517}{2000000}>0.\] At \(\rho=0\) this contradicts the zero-value conclusion of Lemma 4.1 for the minimal pair \((p_+,p_-)\).

It also contradicts Lemma 4.2 itself. Let \(Q:\mathbb R\to(0,1)\) be the increasing optimal profile \[Q'=\sqrt{2f(\min\{Q,1-Q\}^2)},\qquad Q(-\infty)=0,\quad Q(+\infty)=1,\] and set \(\gamma(\tau)=z(Q(\tau/\varepsilon))\) on a fixed interval \([-h,h]\). For small \(\varepsilon\), \(\gamma(\pm h)\in B_a(m_\pm)\), so (4.7) holds. Along this curve \(d_F(\gamma)=S(Q)\), and pointwise \[\frac12|\gamma'|^2+\frac{F(\gamma)}{\varepsilon^2}
       -\frac{(d_F\circ\gamma)'}{\varepsilon}=0.\] For every fixed \(0<\rho<\rho_0\), the claimed lower bound (4.8) is strictly positive by [eq:kappapos] (#eq:kappapos), whereas its left side is zero. This is an exact counterexample, with no numerical solution of the author’s PDE or code.

The estimate used to force minimal-pair traces is not established. This is a Major issue because (1.19) is a principal advertised conclusion. The counterexample concerns the auxiliary connection lemma, not an actual limiting pair violating Theorem 1.1.

A consistent reconstruction must use a geometric tube radius \(r\) and the distinct weighted radius \(r_F=\int_0^r\sqrt{2f(s^2)}\,\mathrm ds\). The normal spheres and additive correction must then use \(r_F\) and \(2r_F\), while the exit times use the Euclidean tube of radius \(r\). The strict gap for nonminimal endpoint pairs, its compactness and continuity properties, and the resulting curve estimate still require a complete proof. Merely replacing one occurrence of \(\delta_0\) does not verify this repair. The precise minimal-connection equality case in Lin–Pan–Wang [LPW], Section 2, is relevant, but does not by itself validate the printed \(\kappa\) argument.
result: The proof of Lemma 3.4 mentions \(\delta_0\ll c_F\) on p. 18. The unit-gap example does not satisfy that extra informal relation. It does satisfy the explicitly stated hypotheses (1.3)–(1.6). Because the same \(\delta_0\) fixes the height of the plateau in \(f\), shrinking \(\delta_0\) in this example does not make \(\delta_0/c_F\) tend to zero. Thus this relation cannot silently be obtained from the written assumptions by making the tube thinner.

There is also a separate defect even under an arbitrarily strong relation \(\delta_0\ll c_F\). Move the second circle’s center to \((L+3,0)\), so that \(D=L\) can be as large as desired. Then \(c_F\sim2aL\), but an actual Euclidean tube exit at distance \(a\) has weighted distance \[r_a=\int_0^a\sqrt2\,r\,\mathrm dr=\frac{a^2}{\sqrt2}\neq a.\] After correcting the exit-time notation, the optimal straight profile has \(P_m\gamma(t_+)=P_m\gamma(h)=p_+\) and \(\gamma(t_+)\notin N(\overline B_\rho(p_+)\cap m_+,a)\). Case (1) on p. 25 would nevertheless force \(|P_m\gamma(t_+)-P_m\gamma(h)|\geq C_1\rho>0\). This is false even when \(a/c_F\) is arbitrarily small.

Two additional local errors are part of this same proof failure. The printed infimum defining \(t_-\) on p. 24 equals \(-h\) rather than the intended first exit; the printed supremum defining \(t_+\) equals \(h\) rather than the last entrance. The infimum and supremum must be interchanged. Also, the upper bound ending \(d_F^*(N_+,N_-)\leq c_F-2\delta_0+\beta\) on p. 24 does not imply the asserted equality \(\kappa=\beta>0\). The first equality for \(I_0\) in case (3), p. 25, is in general a lower bound obtained by Cauchy–Schwarz.

Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: At Euclidean tube exit a the weighted normal radius is a^2/sqrt(2), rather than a. Certified rational bounds give 0.019434 <= c_F <= 0.0197415 and kappa >= 517/2000000 > 0, including for a minimal pair, whereas the exact optimal-profile integrand in (4.8) vanishes. The stated connection inequality therefore fails under the tested written hypotheses.

problems.title: The collar construction does not preserve the full stated H^1 data class
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: The collar construction does not preserve the full stated H^1 data class
claim: Recorded check: The collar construction does not preserve the full stated H^1 data class
analysis: On p. 26, (5.1) calls \(\Psi_\delta^\pm\) global \(C^1\) diffeomorphisms, while requiring \(\Psi_\delta^\pm=P_{\Sigma_0}\) on the entire open collar \(B_\delta(\Sigma_0)\). On p. 27, (5.2) asserts that \(u_0^\pm=u_{\pm}^{\rm in}\circ\Psi_\delta^\pm\) belongs to \(H^1\), and (5.10) uses these extensions to define \(u_\varepsilon^{\rm in}\).

Already at the smooth geometric level, \(DP_{\Sigma_0}\) has rank \(d-1\) in the collar. Such a map is not a diffeomorphism between \(d\)-dimensional domains. The more substantial defect remains even if the map is renamed a collapsing extension.

Take \(\Omega=B_3(0)\subset\mathbb R^2\) and \(\Sigma_0=S^1\), with \(\Omega_0^+=B_1(0)\) and \(\Omega_0^-=B_3(0)\setminus\overline B_1(0)\). A short smooth mean curvature evolution exists, and the separation from the outer boundary meets the geometric hypothesis for small \(\delta_0\). In target space \(\mathbb R^3\), take the parallel circles \[m_-=\{(1-\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)\},\qquad
 m_+=m_-+(0,0,D),\quad D>0.\] They satisfy all well hypotheses, including \(0\in m_-\), and pairs at the same angle have exactly the minimal distance \(D\).

Let \[a(\theta)=c\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}2^{-3j/4}\sin(2^j\theta),
 \qquad c=\frac1{100}.\] The series converges absolutely and uniformly and has \(|a|<\pi/8\). Its Sobolev seminorms satisfy \[\sum_j 2^j\,2^{-3j/2}<\infty,\qquad
 \sum_j 2^{2j}\,2^{-3j/2}=\infty.\] Thus \(a\in H^{1/2}(S^1)\cap C(S^1)\) but \(a\notin H^1(S^1)\). This is a divergence proof, not an inference from finitely many sampled Fourier modes.

Let \(a_+\) be the harmonic extension to the disk, and let \(a_-\) be the harmonic extension to the annulus with inner boundary value \(a\) and outer boundary value zero. The Fourier energy formulas, or the \(H^{1/2}\) trace theorem, give \(a_\pm\in H^1\). The maximum principle keeps their values in \((-\pi/8,\pi/8)\). Define \[u_-^{\rm in}=(1-\cos a_-,\sin a_-,0),\qquad
 u_+^{\rm in}=(1-\cos a_+,\sin a_+,D).\] These are bounded \(H^1\) well-valued maps. The outer boundary value is the smooth constant zero, and their interface traces have distance exactly \(D\). In particular, they satisfy the full minimal-pair assumption (1.23), not merely separate phase membership.

On the collar, (5.1)–(5.2) give the first two coordinates \[(1-\cos a(\theta),\sin a(\theta)),\] constant in the normal coordinate. This is not an \(H^1\) map on any positive-width annulus. If it were, its second component would be \(H^1\) there, and composition with the Lipschitz function \(\arcsin\) on its range would give the constant normal extension of \(a\) in \(H^1\). Integration in the normal variable would imply \(a\in H^1(S^1)\), a contradiction.

The failure persists in the actual final construction (5.10). The two extended maps have identical first two coordinates and differ only in the third coordinate. Therefore interpolation by \(S_\varepsilon\) changes only that third coordinate. The non-\(H^1\) first two coordinates remain unchanged for every \(\varepsilon\). The constructed \(u_\varepsilon^{\rm in}\) is consequently not in \(H^1\).

This disproves the claimed construction for admissible inputs of Theorem 1.2. It does not prove that no other preparation sequence exists. A valid proof needs a Sobolev-compatible gluing construction that preserves the minimal-pair constraint and the \(O(\varepsilon)\) modulated-energy bound, possibly with smoothing scales depending on \(\varepsilon\). Alternatively, stronger tangential trace regularity would change the theorem’s stated scope. Renaming \(\Psi_\delta^\pm\), or citing a trace theorem that supplies only \(H^{1/2}\) traces, does not repair the argument. The initial construction in the separately checked Laux–Liu preprint [LL] starts with a global \(H^1\) map and does not supply this missing extension for arbitrary pairs of bulk maps.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: Constant-normal extension of that trace has infinite tangential H^1 energy in every collar of positive width. The first two coordinates remain unchanged by the interpolation, so the displayed preparation is not H^1. The nearest-point map has rank d-1 and is not the asserted diffeomorphism.

claim: Recorded check: The stated SBV compactness hypothesis controls jump amplitude rather than jump measure
