Counterexample. On \((0,1)\), let \(\mu_j\) put mass \(2^{-j}\) at the midpoint of each of the \(2^j\) surviving intervals in the \(j\)th middle-third Cantor construction, and let \(v_j(x)=\mu_j((0,x])\). Each \(v_j\) is a step function in \(\operatorname{SBV}\), \(0\leq v_j\leq1\), \(
abla^a v_j=0\), and \[\int_{J_{v_j}}|v_j^+-v_j^-|\,\mathrm d\mathcal H^0=1.\] Choose \(\varphi(t)=t^2\), which satisfies all conditions in Proposition 2.2. The distribution functions converge uniformly to the continuous Cantor function \(v\), and their derivative measures converge weakly to Cantor measure. Thus \(v_j	o v\) weakly star in \(BV\), but \(D^cv
eq0\) and \(v
otin\operatorname{SBV}\). Every assumption in both stated propositions is met.

Impact and correction. A linear jump-amplitude cost does not exclude a Cantor part. An unweighted uniform bound on jump-set measure, together with the other displayed bounds, is sufficient in the actual application. More generally, a jump cost \(\vartheta\) with \(\vartheta(s)/s\to\infty\) as \(s\downarrow0\) supplies the missing small-jump control; see the precise primary theorem [AM], Theorem 1.4 and Proposition 2.5. Theorem 3.6 already invokes the area bound (3.28a), the gradient bound (3.29b), and bounded values. Replacing the quoted compactness theorem by its correct form is therefore a bounded repair, which is why this is Minor despite the false preliminary statements.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: Their uniform and weak-* BV limit is the Cantor function, which has a nonzero Cantor derivative and is not SBV. The printed hypotheses therefore do not imply the printed compactness conclusion.

problems.title: Projected and classical spatial gradients are used incompatibly, with a plus-well sign error
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Projected and classical spatial gradients are used incompatibly, with a plus-well sign error
claim: Recorded check: Projected and classical spatial gradients are used incompatibly, with a plus-well sign error
analysis: Location. The plus-well case of (2.21), p. 8; the unconditional definition (2.35) and the classical-coincidence assertion in Lemma 2.7, p. 11; the convention immediately below (2.40), p. 12; and (2.41).

At a differentiability point, (2.35) projects the classical gradient of \(d_F\) onto \[V=\operatorname{span}\{\partial_tu_\varepsilon,\partial_1u_\varepsilon,
                  \ldots,\partial_du_\varepsilon\}.\] Such a projection need not equal the full classical gradient. This is not merely a possible choice of arbitrary jets: the following exact smooth solution of (1.7) demonstrates it.

Use \(\Omega=(0,\pi)\) and two unit circles in the first two coordinates of \(\mathbb R^5\), centered at \((1,0)\) and \((5,0)\); their last three coordinates are zero. Set \(g=0\), \(\delta_0=0.01\), \(\varepsilon=0.1\), \(K=100\), \(t_*=K^{-2}\), and \(A=\delta_0 e^{-10}/100\). For \(i=1,2,3\), put \[A_i=Ae^{(2/\varepsilon^2+(iK)^2)t_*},\qquad
 u_\varepsilon(x,t)=
 \left(0,0,\left(A_i e^{-(2/\varepsilon^2+(iK)^2)t}\sin(iKx)\right)_{i=1}^3\right).\] The initial amplitude norm is less than \(3.754\times10^{-5}\), well inside the \(0.01\) tube, and decreases in time. The nearest point on \(m_-\) is zero, so \(F(u_\varepsilon)=|u_\varepsilon|^2\); hence this formula solves the actual linearized equation \(\partial_tu_\varepsilon=\partial_{xx}u_\varepsilon-2\varepsilon^{-2}u_\varepsilon\), which is exactly (1.7) throughout its range. The boundary value is zero. No author code or numerical PDE solver is used.

At \(x_*=\pi/(4K)\), \(t=t_*\), set \(b=2/(\varepsilon^2K^2)=1/50\) and \[U=(1/\sqrt2,1,1/\sqrt2),\quad
 V_1=(1/\sqrt2,0,-3/\sqrt2),\quad
 W=((b+1)/\sqrt2,b+4,(b+9)/\sqrt2).\] Then \(u=AU\), \(u_x=AKV_1\) and \(u_t=-AK^2W\) in the last three coordinates. Writing \(D_b=9b^2+64b+116\), exact Gram-matrix calculation yields \[|\operatorname{proj}_{\operatorname{span}(V_1,W)}U|^2
       =2-\frac4{D_b}<2.\] Near \(m_-\), \(d_F(u)=|u|^2/\sqrt2\) and \(\nabla d_F=\sqrt2u\). Thus the literal (2.35) gradient \(g_{\rm pr}\) has \[|g_{\rm pr}|^2=4A^2-\frac{8A^2}{D_b}
     =4A^2\frac{288209}{293209},\] whereas \(|\nabla d_F|^2=4A^2\). The radial projection prescribed in the well tube has \(|\Pi_u u_x|^2=A^2K^2/2\), and therefore \[|\psi_x|^2=2A^4K^2,\qquad
 |\Pi_u u_x|^2|g_{\rm pr}|^2
   =A^4K^2\left(2-\frac4{D_b}\right).\] This contradicts (2.41) if the unconditional (2.35) convention is used there. It also directly disproves the asserted classical coincidence of that projected definition.

The scope qualification is decisive: the actual text immediately below (2.40) says to use the generalized differential when \(d_F\) is not classically differentiable. With the classical gradient at differentiability points, this example no longer contradicts (2.41). That explicit later convention was checked in the source image and is a local repair. The example is not advanced as a counterexample to the well-prepared limit theorem or to its integrated energy estimate.

Finally, differentiating (2.17) near the plus well gives \[\nabla d_F(u)=-\sqrt2\,(u-P_{m_+}u),\] while near the minus well the sign is positive. The common positive sign printed in (2.21) needs correction. Projection onto the resulting line is unchanged by this sign. State one consistent piecewise gradient convention, and correct the sign and the classical-coincidence claim.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: For b=1/50, the projected-gradient norm ratio is 288209/293209 and the chain discrepancy is 10000/293209. Literal unconditional projected-gradient notation does not satisfy the asserted classical chain/norm identities. Near the plus well the potential semidistance gradient also has the opposite displayed sign.

problems.title: The preparation assumptions allow remote small droplets and do not force the stated Hausdorff conclusion
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: The preparation assumptions allow remote small droplets and do not force the stated Hausdorff conclusion
claim: Recorded check: The preparation assumptions allow remote small droplets and do not force the stated Hausdorff conclusion
analysis: Location. Proposition 3.5, (3.28c), pp. 19–20, and the appeal to Blaschke’s theorem in its proof.

Admissible initial-time counterexample. Let \(d=3\), \(\Omega=B_5(0)\), and let the prescribed interface start at \(\Sigma_0=\partial B_2(0)\) and follow \(\Sigma_t=\partial B_{\sqrt{4-4t}}(0)\) for a short time. Use the compact two-circle wells from P1 and the closest segment between \(p_-\) and \(p_+\), with a smooth optimal transition profile. The outside boundary value is \(p_-\), which is an admissible smooth map into \(m_-\). A truncated optimal layer across \(\Sigma_0\) gives \(E_\varepsilon(0)=O(\varepsilon^2)\) and \(B(0)=O(\varepsilon^2)\) when the bulk phases are constant.

For every sufficiently small \(b_\varepsilon\in[\varepsilon^{1/6},2\varepsilon^{1/6}]\), the level set \(\{\psi_\varepsilon=c_F-b_\varepsilon\}\) has a component around \(x_0\). Its displacement from the small sphere is \(O(\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|)=o(r_\varepsilon)\). Points on this component remain a fixed positive distance from \(\Sigma_0\). No subsequence can satisfy the asserted Hausdorff convergence at \(t=0\). At the same time, its extra perimeter is \(O(\varepsilon)\) and its enclosed volume is \(O(\varepsilon^{3/2})\), fully consistent with the perimeter and BV conclusions.

Scope and repair. This is an initial-time counterexample under the stated uniform preparation assumptions. It does not show a remote droplet surviving to a fixed positive time: small droplets may disappear rapidly. Blaschke compactness only supplies some Hausdorff-convergent subsequence of compact sets; it does not identify the limit from perimeter and \(L^1\) convergence. Theorem 3.6 uses (3.28a)–(3.28b), and the minimal-pair proof uses slice convergence, traces and Egorov’s theorem, rather than (3.28c). Removing that unused claim, or replacing it by a separately proved positive-time clearing statement, is a bounded repair.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: The remote droplet still contributes points to the specified level set at time zero, at a fixed distance from the main interface, contradicting the claimed Hausdorff convergence in the initial-time scope tested.

claim: Recorded check: A varying higher-codimension normal frame contributes an omitted connection term
analysis: Location. The normal-coordinate calculation (3.34)–(3.37), pp. 20–21, used for (3.29b) and again in (4.10).

Let \(q(s)=(\cos s,\sin s,0)\) and choose the smooth normal frame \[
u_1(s)=\cos s\,q(s)+\sin s\,e_3,\qquad
 
u_2(s)=-\sin s\,q(s)+\cos s\,e_3.\] For fixed small \(r>0\), set \(u(s)=q(s)+r
u_2(s)\). The nearest point is \(q(s)\) and the normal coordinate \(d_1(u(s))=\langle u(s)-q(s),
u_1(s)angle\) vanishes identically. But at \(s=0\), \[ rac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm ds}d_1(u(s))=0,\qquad
 
u_1(0)\cdot u'(0)=-r
eq0.\] Thus the asserted gradient formula for individual normal coordinates, and the claim that all derivatives of a normal frame are tangential, fail in general codimension. Translating the circle makes \(0\in m_-\); a second distant circle supplies the other well. The example is within a smooth tubular neighborhood.

The required estimate can be proved without this false frame identity. If \(\nu_{\rm rad}=(u-P_mu)/|u-P_mu|\), then \(DP_m(u)\nu_{\rm rad}=0\), and smooth tube geometry gives \(\|DP_m(u)\|\leq1+C\delta_0\). Hence \[|\partial_iP_m(u)|
 \leq(1+C\delta_0)
     |\partial_i u-\Pi_{\rm rad}\partial_i u|.\] This supplies the bounded projection estimate used later. Correcting the normal connection, or using this coordinate-free proof, avoids a loss in the essential energy bound.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: At the tested point d_1'=0 but nu_1 dot u'=-r. Differentiating only the scalar normal coefficients omits the normal-frame connection contribution.

problems.title: The curvature extension is not constant along normals in its cutoff annulus
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: The curvature extension is not constant along normals in its cutoff annulus
claim: Recorded check: The curvature extension is not constant along normals in its cutoff annulus
analysis: Location. The first identity in (2.31), p. 10, compared with (2.30).

For a circle or sphere of nonzero mean curvature, the extended curvature field has the form \(H(x)=\kappa(P_{\Sigma_t}x)\eta_0(x)n(x)\). Choose an admissible radial cutoff, equal to one for \(|d_\Sigma|\leq\delta_0\) and zero for \(|d_\Sigma|\geq2\delta_0\). On a normal ray, \[(n\cdot\nabla)H=\kappa\,\eta_0'(d_\Sigma)n.\] The derivative is nonzero somewhere in the cutoff annulus. For the flat switch \(s\) from P1, choose a smooth \(\chi(r)\) equal to one for \(r\leq7a/4\) and zero for \(r\geq15a/8\). Set \(\eta_0(r)=[1-s((r-a)/a)]\chi(r)\) for \(a<r<2a\), extend by one for \(0\leq r\leq a\), then evenly. Its support lies strictly inside \((-2a,2a)\), as required by (2.29), while \(\eta_0'(3a/2)=-2/a\) is unchanged. Thus the unrestricted normal derivative identity cannot hold throughout \(B_{2\delta_0}(\Sigma_t)\).

On the smaller tube where \(\eta_0=1\), the normal derivative does vanish. Since \(\xi\) is supported in that smaller tube, \((\xi\cdot\nabla)H=0\) remains valid everywhere it is needed. The appendix uses this contracted relation. Restrict the first identity’s domain and retain the contracted identity.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: Set eta_0(r)=[1-s((r-a)/a)]chi(r) on a<r<2a, with chi=1 through7a/4 and chi=0 from15a/8, extend by1 on[0,a], then evenly. Since chi=1 near3a/2, eta_0'(3a/2)=-2/a. Thus (n dot grad)H=kappa eta_0' n is nonzero there for nonzero curvature.

problems.title: The derivative of the negative part has the wrong sign
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: The derivative of the negative part has the wrong sign
claim: Recorded check: The derivative of the negative part has the wrong sign
analysis: Location. The displayed calculation (3.13), p. 16, with the definitions immediately preceding it.

The convention is the positive-valued negative part \(z^-=\max\{-z,0\}\). Away from the interface and where \(0<\psi_\varepsilon<c_F\), the function \[w_\varepsilon=c_F\chi-c_F+2(\psi_\varepsilon-c_F)^-
        =c_F\chi+c_F-2\psi_\varepsilon\] satisfies \(\partial_iw_\varepsilon=-2\partial_i\psi_\varepsilon\). The printed plus sign is incorrect. A nonconstant monotone optimal profile at a point strictly inside one phase has \(\partial_i\psi_\varepsilon\neq0\) and \(\eta(d_\Sigma)\neq0\), so the discrepancy is realized by smooth admissible local data, rather than only at the nondifferentiable threshold.

The subsequent estimates use absolute values and Young’s inequality. Correcting this sign leaves those bounds available. Also, the positive-part auxiliary \((\psi_\varepsilon-c_F)^+\) is identically zero for the bounded phase distance used here; introducing it is redundant but is not itself a mathematical defect.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: The stated combination is w=c_F chi+c_F-2psi, hence its time derivative is -2 partial_t psi rather than +2 partial_t psi.

problems.title: The zero-normal convention loses a term in the final square completion
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: The zero-normal convention loses a term in the final square completion
claim: Recorded check: The zero-normal convention loses a term in the final square completion
analysis: Location. The zero convention in (2.39a), p. 11, and the final square-completion step on p. 35 leading to (A.2a), p. 33.

These pointwise data are compatible with smooth prepared initial data. Start with a truncated optimal layer and choose a small fixed open patch \(U\) in the minus side of the calibration collar, away from the actual layer, where \(\operatorname{div}\xi\neq0\). For the parallel circles in P2, take the closest segment to be vertical and add the smooth perturbation \(\varepsilon\zeta e_3\) to the constant minus phase, where \(\zeta=1\) on \(U\) and is supported in that side of the collar. For small \(\varepsilon\), this adds \(O(\varepsilon)\) to the energy and \(O(\varepsilon^2)\) to the bulk error, and changes no outer boundary value. On \(U\) at \(t=0\), \[u_\varepsilon=\varepsilon e_3,\quad \nabla u_\varepsilon=0,\quad
 F=\varepsilon^2,\quad g=\sqrt2\varepsilon e_3,\quad
 \partial_tu_\varepsilon=-2\varepsilon^{-1}e_3.\] The omitted term after division by \(2\varepsilon\) is \(\varepsilon(\operatorname{div}\xi)^2>0\).

Precise scope. This establishes a defect in the unconditional algebraic completion, with an admissible smooth initial plateau. It is not claimed to construct a fixed positive-time plateau or to refute an almost-everywhere interior-time version of Lemma A.2. Such a stronger assertion would require additional analysis.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: The pre-completion term is c^2|g|^2 while the proposed square vanishes. In the plateau example the omitted normalized term is epsilon(div xi)^2. The displayed equality is not exact with that zero-normal convention.

report: Abstract: This report concerns the acquired 26-page arXiv:2405.03460v1, not an assumed equivalent journal text. A demonstrated failure affects the displayed core proof: the conditional independence and conditional quantile reasoning used in Lemma 3.8. Four local defects concern the path-membership decomposition in (3.28), an overbroad monotonicity statement, the introductory cut-edge argument, and an omitted direct-exit event. Exact finite-network computations support the analytic counterexamples. None disproves the main resistance theorem. The initial assessment is Major within this version; the scientific decision and independent acceptance remain pending.
Author: M25-0401

Title: Initial review of polynomial resistance bounds
for critical long-range percolation
# Identity, scope, and conventions

The reviewed work is Jian Ding, Zherui Fan, and Lu-Jing Huang, Polynomial lower bound on the effective resistance for the one-dimensional critical long-range percolation, arXiv:2405.03460v1, submitted 6 May 2024 [DFH]. The acquired PDF has 26 physical pages; its printed numbers coincide with physical page numbers. All page and equation references below use this PDF. The associated journal identifier is DOI 10.1002/cpa.22243; the publisher lists Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 78 (2025), 1251–1284 [Wiley]. The 34-page journal text was not acquired or compared. These findings must not be relabelled as verified defects of that text.

All 26 source pages were read, including the definitions, quantifiers, proofs, and references. The review followed the chain from Proposition 2.2 through Lemma 3.8, Proposition 3.6, Lemma 3.13, Proposition 3.11, Proposition 3.2, Theorem 3.1, and Section 4. The relevant firework reference was read in its 10-page arXiv version [Gallo]. Independent checks use reviewer-authored Python with rational linear algebra, not author code. No empirical simulation is used to establish a finding.
# Model and hypotheses used in every check

Equation reference: eq:model, eq:sum. The vertex set is \(\mathbb Z\). Every nearest-neighbour edge is present, and distinct long edges are independent, with unit conductance and \[
 \mathbb P(\{u,v\}\text{ absent})=e^{-\beta\lambda_{|u-v|}},\qquad
 \lambda_d=\log\frac{d^2}{d^2-1},\quad d\ge2,\quad \beta>0.\] The expression for \(\lambda_d\) follows by integrating (1.1), p. 1. Telescoping gives \[
 \sum_{d=2}^{\infty}\lambda_d=\log2.\] Consequently, specifying finitely many present long edges and excluding all other long edges incident to a fixed finite vertex set has positive probability: the total excluded intensity is finite. No counterexample below removes a nearest-neighbour edge, changes conductance, or substitutes a different percolation law.

Theorem 1.1, p. 2, quantifies over every \(\beta>0\) and \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2]\): there is an exponent depending only on \(\beta\) and a positive prefactor depending on \(\beta,\varepsilon\), uniformly in the integer size \(N\). Its second bound conditions on the absence of direct edges from \([-N,N]\) to \([-2N,2N]^c\). Failure of a particular proof step is distinguished throughout from failure of either conclusion.
# Problem 1: conditional estimates in Lemma 3.8
## Claim, location, and dependency

Page 12, immediately before (3.12), states that, given \(\mathcal E_n=\mathcal E_{(-\infty,0]\times(0,N]}\), the three events in Definition 3.4 are independent. Page 13 uses this assertion, the unconditional quantile bound (3.12), and the number of good scales to produce the exponentially small failure bound in Lemma 3.8. That lemma is explicitly used in (3.21), hence Proposition 3.6 and the quantile recursion of Proposition 3.11. This is a core probabilistic input, not a background observation.
## Exact counterexample to conditional independence

Equation reference: eq:cond1. Take \(\beta=1/20\), \(\alpha=1/4\), \(n=5\), \(N=32\), and condition on \[
 \mathcal E_n=\{\{0,1\},\{0,16\}\}.\] All other optional crossing edges are absent. This event has positive probability \[64^{-\beta}\bigl((256/255)^\beta-1\bigr)>0.\] Here \(Z=\{1,16\}\), so \(z_1=16\) is a legitimate entrance point. Use \(j=2\). The deterministic nearest-neighbour path shows \(\widehat R_2\le5\). By [eq:sum] (#eq:sum), excluding all long edges incident to \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) has probability at least \(2^{-8\beta}=0.757858\ldots>3/4\), and on that event \(\widehat R_2=5\). Thus \(a_{\alpha,2}=5\) exactly.

Write \(A_+\) and \(A_-\) for events (2) and (3) of Definition 3.4 at this point and scale. Their gap vertex sets are respectively \(\{21,22,23,24\}\) and \(\{9,10,11,12\}\). Each resistance is at most 5. Equality holds precisely when every allowed optional edge incident to its gap is absent. Indeed, any such edge joins different potentials on the length-5 nearest-neighbour chain and strictly reduces resistance. The same argument includes optional edges internal to a gap.

Conditioning in [eq:cond1] (#eq:cond1) leaves all positive-to-positive edges independent with their original laws. The two absence sets share the 16 edges \(\{u,v\}\) with \(9\le u\le12\), \(21\le v\le24\). Their total intensity is \(\log(9/8)>0\). Direct telescoping of the allowed edge intensities gives \[\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb P(A_+\mid\mathcal E_n)&=(1664/17)^{-\beta},&
 \mathbb P(A_-\mid\mathcal E_n)&=64^{-\beta},\\
 \mathbb P(A_+\cap A_-\mid\mathcal E_n)&=(851968/153)^{-\beta}.\end{aligned}\] The joint probability divided by the product of marginals is \((9/8)^\beta>1\). Numerically the joint is \(0.6497008088\) and the product is \(0.6458858665\). The claimed conditional independence is false. These are analytic probabilities, with finite rational products checked independently; they are not estimates from sampling.
## Conditioning can also destroy the quantile bound

Positive association of absence events might replace independence in a single lower bound, but does not justify the conditional marginals or the product over scales used on p. 13. The following separate example makes this obstruction explicit.

Equation reference: eq:cond2. Take \(\beta=1/200\), \(\alpha=1/4\), \(n=5\), \(N=32\) and condition on \[
 \mathcal E_n=\{\{0,1\},\{0,2\},\{0,3\},\{-3,4\},
              \{-11,4\},\{-27,4\},\{-59,4\}\}.\] Again all other crossing edges are absent. Its probability is \[64^{-\beta}\prod_{d\in\{2,3,7,15,31,63\}}
       \left[\left(\frac{d^2}{d^2-1}\right)^\beta-1\right]>0.\] Here \(Z=\{1,2,3,4\}\) and \(z_3=4\). For each \(j=2,3,4,5\), put \(q=2^j\). The nearest-neighbour bound and [eq:sum] (#eq:sum) give \[\widehat R_j\le q+1,\qquad
 \mathbb P(\widehat R_j=q+1)\ge2^{-2q\beta}\ge2^{-0.32}>3/4.\] Thus \(a_{\alpha,j}=q+1\).

Event (3) would require resistance from \((4-q,4+2q]\) to \((-\infty,4-2q]\) at least \(q+1\). Under [eq:cond2] (#eq:cond2), the path \[4\longrightarrow 5-2q\longrightarrow4-2q\] is present, has energy 2, and obeys the deletion rule [eq:mask] (#eq:mask). Its first edge enters the gap; it is not a forbidden direct terminal edge. Its second edge is nearest-neighbour. Hence event (3) has conditional probability zero at every one of these four scales.

The example also fits a complete block in the displayed scale construction: set \(M=21/10\) and \(L=(19/10)/\log(21/10)>2\). Then \(b_0=5\), \(b_1=1\), \(K_n=1\), \(\bar\eta_{b_1}=2\), \(\bar\eta_{b_0}=4\), and \(i=3\) is allowed. The four good conditions (1) are compatible with [eq:cond2] (#eq:cond2). Their simultaneous conditional probability is at least \[\exp\left[-\beta\sum_{j=2}^{5}
                 \log(2+5/2^j)\right]=0.9814225\ldots>0.\] The bound follows by excluding the union of the relevant positive-side long edges; conditioning has already excluded some of them. Even given all four good conditions, all four resistance tests (3) fail. An unconditional quantile statement therefore cannot be inserted as the asserted uniform conditional success probability.
## Judgment, alternative readings, and repair boundary

This is Major: a demonstrated false independence premise and an invalid conditional-quantile inference occur in the core derivation of Lemma 3.8. The positive-probability conditioning examples do not disprove the lemma’s unconditional conclusion; averaging could in principle yield a valid estimate by another argument. The second example uses allowed scale parameters, not a claim that these equal the later sufficiently-large choice in Proposition 3.6.

The negative exponents printed in the final display on p. 13 are a separate evident sign problem; correcting them does not cure the conditional dependence. Nor does single-pair positive association supply the needed upper bound on simultaneous failure across scales. A repair must prove an appropriate conditional or averaged multi-scale estimate under the actual exposed edge set. No such replacement is verified here.
# Problem 2: path membership does not give a flow partition
## Claim and exact check

Page 16 defines \(\theta_i=\sum_{P:z_i\in P}\theta_P\), expressly explaining that \(z_i\in P\) means that \(z_i\) lies on the path. Equation (3.28) then asserts \(\sum_i|\theta_i|=1\) and \(\sum_i\theta_i=\theta\). Lemma 3.15 and the energy argument (3.33)–(3.34) use this partition.

Take \(N=4\) and the positive-probability event that \(\{0,2\}\) is present and all other long edges incident to \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) are absent. The entrance set is exactly \(Z=\{1,2\}\). After contracting source and sink, the relevant graph consists of the nearest-neighbour chain \(0,1,2,3,4,5\) and the edge \(\{0,2\}\). The minimizing unit flow has two self-avoiding paths: \[\begin{array}{c|c}
 P_0=(0,1,2,3,4,5)&1/3\\
 P_1=(0,2,3,4,5)&2/3 .
 \end{array}\] The parallel part from 0 to 2 has resistance \(2/3\); adding the three remaining unit edges gives \(\widehat R_2=11/3\). Exact grounded-Laplacian solution confirms these currents.

Both paths contain \(z_1=2\), while only \(P_0\) contains \(z_0=1\). The literal definition therefore gives \[|\theta_0|=1/3,\quad |\theta_1|=1,\quad
 \sum_i|\theta_i|=4/3.\] On edge \(\{2,3\}\) the alleged sum has current \(4/3\), whereas the original current is 1. This is already a minimizing acyclic unit flow; selecting another path-decomposition algorithm cannot avoid the overlap.
## Impact and exact local repair

This is Minor with a verified local correction: the literal objects fail the stated partition identities, but assigning paths by first entry restores those identities without changing the model or theorem. The counterexample concerns the general decomposition assertion on p. 16; it does not refute Lemma 3.13 on its auxiliary event. The prose about entering the interval, and Figure 6, strongly suggest the intended correction: partition paths by their first vertex in \((0,N]\), not by occurrence anywhere on the path. Every source-to-sink path then belongs to exactly one class. For an acyclic electrical flow, these classes inherit the same edge orientation, so both identities in (3.28) and unidirectionality hold. The example’s corrected masses are \(1/3\) and \(2/3\).

This correction of (3.28) is analytically verified. The passage arguments in Lemmas 3.14–3.15 use the first-entry property and the restored mass partition. A full independent proof of every energy charge in (3.29)–(3.34) remains outside the verified repair; this coverage limit is not evidence of another defect or a reason to increase severity. No claim that the local correction repairs Problem 1 is made.
# Problem 3: the terminal monotonicity is too broad

Lemma 3.3(2), p. 11, asserts \(\widehat R(I_1,I_3)\ge\widehat R(I_1,I_2)\) for every interval \(I_3\subset I_2\). Take \[I_1=(-\infty,0],\qquad I_2=[5,\infty),\qquad I_3=[6,\infty).\] Require \(\{0,5\}\) to be present and all other long edges incident to \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\) to be absent. This has positive probability for every \(\beta>0\) by [eq:sum] (#eq:sum); other edges may be arbitrary. For \((I_1,I_2)\), edge \(\{0,5\}\) is forbidden by [eq:mask] (#eq:mask), leaving a chain of resistance 5. For \((I_1,I_3)\) that edge is allowed: \[\widehat R(I_1,I_2)=5,\qquad
       \widehat R(I_1,I_3)=(1^{-1}+5^{-1})^{-1}+1=11/6<5 .\] The rational network solve reproduces both values.

This is Minor because the displayed general lemma is false, while the uses inspected in (3.12), (4.3), (4.4), and Lemma 4.2 can be formulated with a fixed gap-facing boundary or a fixed edge mask. Shrinking only an outer endpoint, with the gap fixed, deletes admissible connections and cannot reduce resistance. Adding allowed edges with terminals and mask fixed cannot increase it. These restricted statements follow directly from inclusion of admissible flow classes. They do not establish the unrestricted terminal assertion, or the conditional probability step of Problem 1.
# Problem 4: the introductory cut-edge event is impossible

The first proof-outline paragraph on p. 3 defines a cut-edge as an edge whose removal disconnects 0 from \([-N,N]^c\). It then assigns each nearest-neighbour indicator \(\xi_i\) the probability \((2N)^{-\beta}\), for \(0<\beta<1\), and obtains an expectation of order \(N^{1-\beta}\).

The deterministic paths \[(0,1,\ldots,N+1),\qquad (0,-1,\ldots,-N-1)\] are edge-disjoint. Removing any single edge leaves at least one of them. Additional long edges cannot destroy connectivity. Thus every displayed \(\xi_i\) is identically zero. For example, \(\beta=1/2\), \(N=1\) gives actual probability 0 rather than \(2^{-1/2}\). The claimed positive expectation of their sum is also false. An independent finite graph check at \(N=8\) confirms the elementary argument for each of the listed nearest-neighbour edges.

This is Minor: the paragraph is motivational and the formal proof later uses different good-interval events. The main lower bound is not disproved. A valid replacement would need appropriately defined two-sided cutsets or a separately proved one-sided statement; changing a constant does not repair the displayed argument. No unproved replacement polynomial bound is offered.
# Problem 5: direct exits are omitted in the final flow split

On p. 24, immediately before (4.7), the proof asserts that the two portions exiting via \((0,N]\) and \([-N,0)\) have maximum at least \(1/2\). An edge directly from 0 to the exterior carries neither portion. Page 4 explicitly acknowledges this possibility, but the event \(B\) in (4.6) does not exclude it.

For a concrete positive-probability configuration, take \(N=8\), retain \(\{0,9\}\), and exclude every other long edge incident to \([-8,8]\). After contraction of the exterior, there are three parallel paths of resistances \(9,9,1\). The minimizing unit flow has \[R(0,[-8,8]^c)=9/11,\qquad
 |\theta_1|=|\theta_2|=1/11,\qquad
 |\theta_{\rm direct}|=9/11.\] The two truncated one-sided resistances in \(B\) both equal 9. The asserted maximum is false, and the corresponding deterministic quarter-of-the-minimum bound would give \(9/4>9/11\).

This is Minor with a verified local probabilistic repair, conditional on the preceding resistance lemma. Let \(G_N\) exclude all direct edges from 0 to \([-N,N]^c\). Telescoping [eq:model] (#eq:model) gives \[\mathbb P(G_N)=\left(\frac{N}{N+1}\right)^{2\beta},\qquad
 \mathbb P(G_N^c)\le 2\beta/N .\] Use Lemma 4.2 with failure allowance \(\varepsilon/2\) in the joint event \(B\); for \(N\ge4\beta/\varepsilon\), the union bound gives \(\mathbb P(B\cap G_N)\ge1-\varepsilon\). The flow split is valid on this intersection. For finitely many smaller \(N\), resistance is strictly positive almost surely, because the source degree is finite, so a positive finite minimum of suitable lower quantiles supplies the remaining prefactor. This repairs this step of (1.3), assuming the earlier lemmas. It does not resolve Problems 1–2.
# Other checked reasoning and limits

The firework tail statement invoked on p. 8 is present as Proposition 1 on p. 3 of [Gallo]. Its hypotheses include an i.i.d. nonnegative radius law with positive mass at zero and an exponentially approaching distribution function. The proposed dominating law \(\widetilde\alpha(s)=(1-3/(2^{s+1}+2))^{2\beta}\) has these properties. Its infinite product is positive since the logarithmic tail is summable. The source’s minimum-index/range notation must be translated consistently when using this result. Evident indexing and sign inconsistencies were not multiplied into separate findings.

The concentration step can be derived directly from Lemma 2.3: for \(Y_i=1-\xi_i\) and \(t\ge0\), \[\mathbb E\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1+tY_i)
 =\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}t^{|S|}\mathbb E\prod_{i\in S}Y_i
 \le(1+t\kappa)^n.\] Chernoff optimization yields the binary-relative-entropy bound. Thus this particular concentration use needs no independence of the \(Y_i\) beyond the stated mixed-moment hypothesis.

The \(d_k\) bounds on p. 14 yield growth of order \(k\log k\) with fixed parameters. Consequently \(\sum 1/d_k\) diverges. Conditional on the recursion, the finite-sum induction on pp. 20–21 gives a positive exponent; using a fixed median first is what removes dependence of the exponent on the requested failure probability in Theorem 3.1. These downstream implications cannot supply the missing inputs in Problems 1–2.

The reflection coupling in (4.2)–(4.4) was checked with terminals fixed, as were the conditional independence from the forbidden inner-to-outer edges in (4.10) and the distinction between the two bounds in Theorem 1.1. The final non-dyadic extension of the box-to-box statement, p. 26, and a complete re-proof of the aggregate energy charging after correcting the definitions have not been independently established. No additional error is inferred solely from these limits. This report is not a proof of whole-paper correctness outside the specified findings.

The arXiv history consulted during review lists v1. A bounded search of the DOI and correction/erratum terms located publisher metadata but no correction text. This is not evidence that no correction exists. Publisher full-text retrieval was unavailable; no statement about whether the journal revision already repairs these points is justified. No author adoption or author response has been requested.

# Independent calculations and evidence

The retained script `independent_checks_v003.py` constructs grounded graph Laplacians and solves them using Python `fractions.Fraction`; Gaussian elimination and all network values are exact. Floating-point values above are illustrative evaluations of analytic positive expressions, not the basis for strict inequalities. The script also multiplies the rational telescoping factors for Problem 1 and checks the deterministic nearest-neighbour paths. It exited with code 0.

For the conditional independence example, the optional-edge absence intensity bases are \(1664/17\), \(64\), and \(9/8\) for the plus set, minus set, and shared set. Their union base is \((1664/17)\cdot64/(9/8)=851968/153\). For the multi-scale example all four unit paths are admissible regardless of every remaining unexposed edge; adding those edges can only lower the corresponding resistance. Positive probability of the conditioning event follows from its displayed exact product, not from its very small numerical approximation.

Earlier calculation files are retained. Version 2 moved all conditional examples to \(j\ge2\), avoiding reliance on the source’s inconsistent \(n=1\) quantile convention. Version 3 added the path-membership test. Their existence does not imply separate human or independent-model verification.

Equation reference: eq:cond1. Take \(\beta=1/20\), \(\alpha=1/4\), \(n=5\), \(N=32\), and condition on \[
 \mathcal E_n=\{\{0,1\},\{0,16\}\}.\] All other optional crossing edges are absent. This event has positive probability \[64^{-\beta}\bigl((256/255)^\beta-1\bigr)>0.\] Here \(Z=\{1,16\}\), so \(z_1=16\) is a legitimate entrance point. Use \(j=2\). The deterministic nearest-neighbour path shows \(\widehat R_2\le5\). By [eq:sum] (#eq:sum), excluding all long edges incident to \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) has probability at least \(2^{-8\beta}=0.757858\ldots>3/4\), and on that event \(\widehat R_2=5\). Thus \(a_{\alpha,2}=5\) exactly.

Write \(A_+\) and \(A_-\) for events (2) and (3) of Definition 3.4 at this point and scale. Their gap vertex sets are respectively \(\{21,22,23,24\}\) and \(\{9,10,11,12\}\). Each resistance is at most 5. Equality holds precisely when every allowed optional edge incident to its gap is absent. Indeed, any such edge joins different potentials on the length-5 nearest-neighbour chain and strictly reduces resistance. The same argument includes optional edges internal to a gap.

Conditioning in [eq:cond1] (#eq:cond1) leaves all positive-to-positive edges independent with their original laws. The two absence sets share the 16 edges \(\{u,v\}\) with \(9\le u\le12\), \(21\le v\le24\). Their total intensity is \(\log(9/8)>0\). Direct telescoping of the allowed edge intensities gives \[\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb P(A_+\mid\mathcal E_n)&=(1664/17)^{-\beta},&
 \mathbb P(A_-\mid\mathcal E_n)&=64^{-\beta},\\
 \mathbb P(A_+\cap A_-\mid\mathcal E_n)&=(851968/153)^{-\beta}.\end{aligned}\] The joint probability divided by the product of marginals is \((9/8)^\beta>1\). Numerically the joint is \(0.6497008088\) and the product is \(0.6458858665\). The claimed conditional independence is false. These are analytic probabilities, with finite rational products checked independently; they are not estimates from sampling.

Positive association of absence events might replace independence in a single lower bound, but does not justify the conditional marginals or the product over scales used on p. 13. The following separate example makes this obstruction explicit.

Equation reference: eq:cond2. Take \(\beta=1/200\), \(\alpha=1/4\), \(n=5\), \(N=32\) and condition on \[
 \mathcal E_n=\{\{0,1\},\{0,2\},\{0,3\},\{-3,4\},
              \{-11,4\},\{-27,4\},\{-59,4\}\}.\] Again all other crossing edges are absent. Its probability is \[64^{-\beta}\prod_{d\in\{2,3,7,15,31,63\}}
       \left[\left(\frac{d^2}{d^2-1}\right)^\beta-1\right]>0.\] Here \(Z=\{1,2,3,4\}\) and \(z_3=4\). For each \(j=2,3,4,5\), put \(q=2^j\). The nearest-neighbour bound and [eq:sum] (#eq:sum) give \[\widehat R_j\le q+1,\qquad
 \mathbb P(\widehat R_j=q+1)\ge2^{-2q\beta}\ge2^{-0.32}>3/4.\] Thus \(a_{\alpha,j}=q+1\).

Event (3) would require resistance from \((4-q,4+2q]\) to \((-\infty,4-2q]\) at least \(q+1\). Under [eq:cond2] (#eq:cond2), the path \[4\longrightarrow 5-2q\longrightarrow4-2q\] is present, has energy 2, and obeys the deletion rule [eq:mask] (#eq:mask). Its first edge enters the gap; it is not a forbidden direct terminal edge. Its second edge is nearest-neighbour. Hence event (3) has conditional probability zero at every one of these four scales.

The example also fits a complete block in the displayed scale construction: set \(M=21/10\) and \(L=(19/10)/\log(21/10)>2\). Then \(b_0=5\), \(b_1=1\), \(K_n=1\), \(\bar\eta_{b_1}=2\), \(\bar\eta_{b_0}=4\), and \(i=3\) is allowed. The four good conditions (1) are compatible with [eq:cond2] (#eq:cond2). Their simultaneous conditional probability is at least \[\exp\left[-\beta\sum_{j=2}^{5}
                 \log(2+5/2^j)\right]=0.9814225\ldots>0.\] The bound follows by excluding the union of the relevant positive-side long edges; conditioning has already excluded some of them. Even given all four good conditions, all four resistance tests (3) fail. An unconditional quantile statement therefore cannot be inserted as the asserted uniform conditional success probability.

This is Major: a demonstrated false independence premise and an invalid conditional-quantile inference occur in the core derivation of Lemma 3.8. The positive-probability conditioning examples do not disprove the lemma’s unconditional conclusion; averaging could in principle yield a valid estimate by another argument. The second example uses allowed scale parameters, not a claim that these equal the later sufficiently-large choice in Proposition 3.6.

The negative exponents printed in the final display on p. 13 are a separate evident sign problem; correcting them does not cure the conditional dependence. Nor does single-pair positive association supply the needed upper bound on simultaneous failure across scales. A repair must prove an appropriate conditional or averaged multi-scale estimate under the actual exposed edge set. No such replacement is verified here.

problems.source_location: p.16 literal path-membership definition and Eq.3.28; pp.18-20 downstream
claim: Page 16 defines \(\theta_i=\sum_{P:z_i\in P}\theta_P\), expressly explaining that \(z_i\in P\) means that \(z_i\) lies on the path. Equation (3.28) then asserts \(\sum_i|\theta_i|=1\) and \(\sum_i\theta_i=\theta\). Lemma 3.15 and the energy argument (3.33)–(3.34) use this partition.

Take \(N=4\) and the positive-probability event that \(\{0,2\}\) is present and all other long edges incident to \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) are absent. The entrance set is exactly \(Z=\{1,2\}\). After contracting source and sink, the relevant graph consists of the nearest-neighbour chain \(0,1,2,3,4,5\) and the edge \(\{0,2\}\). The minimizing unit flow has two self-avoiding paths: \[\begin{array}{c|c}
 P_0=(0,1,2,3,4,5)&1/3\\
 P_1=(0,2,3,4,5)&2/3 .
 \end{array}\] The parallel part from 0 to 2 has resistance \(2/3\); adding the three remaining unit edges gives \(\widehat R_2=11/3\). Exact grounded-Laplacian solution confirms these currents.

Both paths contain \(z_1=2\), while only \(P_0\) contains \(z_0=1\). The literal definition therefore gives \[|\theta_0|=1/3,\quad |\theta_1|=1,\quad
 \sum_i|\theta_i|=4/3.\] On edge \(\{2,3\}\) the alleged sum has current \(4/3\), whereas the original current is 1. This is already a minimizing acyclic unit flow; selecting another path-decomposition algorithm cannot avoid the overlap.
analysis: This is Minor with a verified local correction: the literal objects fail the stated partition identities, but assigning paths by first entry restores those identities without changing the model or theorem. The counterexample concerns the general decomposition assertion on p. 16; it does not refute Lemma 3.13 on its auxiliary event. The prose about entering the interval, and Figure 6, strongly suggest the intended correction: partition paths by their first vertex in \((0,N]\), not by occurrence anywhere on the path. Every source-to-sink path then belongs to exactly one class. For an acyclic electrical flow, these classes inherit the same edge orientation, so both identities in (3.28) and unidirectionality hold. The example’s corrected masses are \(1/3\) and \(2/3\).

This correction of (3.28) is analytically verified. The passage arguments in Lemmas 3.14–3.15 use the first-entry property and the restored mass partition. A full independent proof of every energy charge in (3.29)–(3.34) remains outside the verified repair; this coverage limit is not evidence of another defect or a reason to increase severity. analysis:
Lemma 3.3(2), p. 11, asserts \(\widehat R(I_1,I_3)\ge\widehat R(I_1,I_2)\) for every interval \(I_3\subset I_2\). Take \[I_1=(-\infty,0],\qquad I_2=[5,\infty),\qquad I_3=[6,\infty).\] Require \(\{0,5\}\) to be present and all other long edges incident to \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\) to be absent. problems.title: the introductory cut-edge event is impossible
problems.source_location: p.3 first proof-outline paragraph
claim: A single nearest-neighbour edge can disconnect0 from both exterior sides with probability(2N)^(-beta)
analysis: The first proof-outline paragraph on p. 3 defines a cut-edge as an edge whose removal disconnects 0 from \([-N,N]^c\). It then assigns each nearest-neighbour indicator \(\xi_i\) the probability \((2N)^{-\beta}\), for \(0<\beta<1\), and obtains an expectation of order \(N^{1-\beta}\).

The deterministic paths \[(0,1,\ldots,N+1),\qquad (0,-1,\ldots,-N-1)\] are edge-disjoint. Removing any single edge leaves at least one of them. Additional long edges cannot destroy connectivity. Thus every displayed \(\xi_i\) is identically zero. For example, \(\beta=1/2\), \(N=1\) gives actual probability 0 rather than \(2^{-1/2}\). The claimed positive expectation of their sum is also false. An independent finite graph check at \(N=8\) confirms the elementary argument for each of the listed nearest-neighbour edges.

This is Minor: the paragraph is motivational and the formal proof later uses different good-interval events. The main lower bound is not disproved. A valid replacement would need appropriately defined two-sided cutsets or a separately proved one-sided statement; changing a constant does not repair the displayed argument. No unproved replacement polynomial bound is offered.

report: Abstract: The reviewed source is the 52-page Wiley version of record of Cancès, Faulstich, Kirsch, Letournel, and Levitt, DOI 10.1002/cpa.22244. The review identifies five groups of local defects: an insufficiently specified interaction-tensor convention; a sign and normalization error in the response formula; inconsistent numerical rank diagnostics and dimension conventions; a fixed-point bifurcation criterion written for the wrong derivative; and transcription errors in the high-level and first-order calculations. Exact finite-dimensional examples establish the failed statements. Explicit repairs preserve the principal local existence and first-order arguments. No counterexample to Theorems 4 or 5, or unresolved Major defect in their core argument, was established. The initial assessment is Minor, subject to the corrections and numerical clarifications below. The scientific decision remains pending.
Author: M25-0402

Title: Initial mathematical review of density matrix
embedding theory near the non-interacting limit
# Identity, version, and review scope

The article is Eric Cancès, Fabian M. Faulstich, Alfred Kirsch, Eloïse Letournel, and Antoine Levitt, Analysis of density matrix embedding theory around the non-interacting limit, Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 78 (2025), 1359–1410 [paper]. The acquired INSPIRE-hosted copy carries the target DOI, the five authors, the journal pagination, and the acceptance date 7 January 2025. It has 52 physical pages. Printed page \(q\) is physical page \(q-1358\). All locations below refer to these exact acquired bytes, whose SHA256 is \[\texttt{be41c6565c96f71d1369f191523404d52daba668005467670398b14ca93c5c95}.\] The duplicate candidate PDF in the manifest is byte-identical. The Crossref snapshot is metadata, not another scientific version. An earlier differently titled preprint was not substituted for this text.

All 52 pages were read, including the proofs, references, notation table, and Appendix B. The review checked the variational definitions before using the explicit formulas, followed the full dependency chain of the main theorems, and examined the numerical assertions separately from the analytical conclusions. Reviewer-authored exact rational calculations and complete finite CAR matrices were used; no author code was executed. The numerical molecular calculations were not independently reproduced. Their absence of a separately acquired code release is not a defect.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and main-theorem boundaries

The real one-particle space is \(\mathbb R^L\), with \(1\leq N<L\) and \(\mathcal D=\{D=D^T=D^2:\operatorname{Tr}D=N\}\). Coordinate fragments partition the \(L\) sites, with sizes \(L_x<N\). The block-density space has tangent space \(\mathcal Y\), consisting of symmetric block-diagonal matrices of total trace zero. The low-level map minimizes the Hartree–Fock energy over projectors with prescribed block density; the high-level map solves the interacting impurity problems with frozen occupied cores and a common chemical potential imposing the total particle number. The fixed-point equation is \(P=F^\mathrm{DMET}_\alpha(P)=F^\mathrm{HL}_\alpha(F^\mathrm{LL}_\alpha(P))\).
The actual hypotheses, pp. 1367–1369 (physical 9–11), are:
1. \(\epsilon_N<0<\epsilon_{N+1}\) for the one-body Hamiltonian \(h\), with \(D_0=1_{(-\infty,0]}(h)\).
2. Both \(D_0X_x\) and \((I-D_0)X_x\) have dimension \(L_x\) for every fragment. Equivalently, every fragment block of \(D_0\) has all eigenvalues strictly between 0 and 1.
3. \(B=\operatorname{Bd}|_{T_{D_0}\mathcal D}:T_{D_0}\mathcal D\to\mathcal Y\) is surjective.
4. The true frozen-impurity density response \(R:\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Y\) to a perturbation \(h+Y\) is invertible.

Theorem 4 asserts existence of a sufficiently small two-sided interval in \(\alpha\) and a neighbourhood of \(D_0\) with a unique real-analytic solution branch there. It does not assert global uniqueness of all DMET solutions, a uniform interval over all Hamiltonians, or convergence of the elementary fixed-point iteration. Theorem 5 asserts \(D^\mathrm{DMET}_\alpha=D^\mathrm{exact}_\alpha+O(\alpha^2)
=D^\mathrm{HF}_\alpha+O(\alpha^2)\) in this local regime. Equality of first derivatives does not require the exact interacting density to remain a projector.

A closing spectral gap, a fragment eigenvalue at 0 or 1, or loss of either surjectivity or response invertibility lies outside these conclusions. In particular, numerical branch behaviour where (A4) fails is not a counterexample to Theorem 4. Assumption (A2) also entails \(L_x\leq \min(N,L-N)\); the prescribed fragmentation must satisfy this feasibility restriction. The paper’s additional convention \(L_x<N\) is retained in every example below.
# Problem 1: the stated tensor symmetry does not justify the effective one-body formulas
## Location and exact failure

On p. 1363 (physical 5), the stated interaction symmetry is only \(V_{ab\,cd}=V_{cd\,ab}\). Equations (21), (25), and (30), pp. 1366, 1368, and 1376 (physical 8, 10, 18), use \(J(D)-K(D)\) as the effective one-body term. Proposition 8 assumes that \(D\) is compatible with the fragmentation; it does not assume (A3) or (A4).

Take \(L=4\), \(N=2\), four singleton fragments, and \[D=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0&0\\1&1&0&0\\
 0&0&1&1\\0&0&1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad h=I-2D.\] This is a rank-two real projector, every fragment population is \(1/2\), and \(h\) has eigenvalues \(-1,-1,1,1\). Thus all assumptions used in Proposition 8 hold, as do (A1)–(A2). For fragment 1, the impurity space is \(\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)\) and the frozen core is \(c=(e_3+e_4)/\sqrt2\).

Let \(S_{13}=S_{31}=1\), \(A_{23}=1\), \(A_{32}=-1\), all other entries zero, and set \[V_{ab\,cd}=S_{ab}A_{cd}+A_{ab}S_{cd}.\] This real tensor satisfies exactly the stated pair-Hermitian symmetry. Its entire two-body operator \(\frac12\sum V_{ab\,cd}a_a^\dagger a_b^\dagger a_d a_c\) vanishes: each summand factorizes with a symmetric pair of creation or annihilation indices, which the CAR relations annihilate. The independent calculation checked all entries of the full \(16\times16\) Fock-space matrix, with exact fractions.

Nevertheless, for the core density \(cc^T\), the restriction of the paper’s \(J(cc^T)-K(cc^T)\) to the impurity space is \[\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] It is nonzero and not symmetric. Its expectation in \((e_1+e_2)/\sqrt2\) is \(1/2\), whereas the exact interaction and its frozen-core restriction are zero. Changing to the paper’s orthonormal impurity basis conjugates this discrepancy and does not remove it. This is an operator-formula counterexample satisfying the proposition’s assumptions, not a counterexample to the main theorems.
## Impact, repair, and counterevidence

A precise harmless normalization of the interaction tensor is needed: \[V^c_{ab\,cd}=\tfrac12(V_{ab\,cd}+V_{ba\,dc}).
 \tag{R1}\] Simultaneously swapping the two creation and the two annihilation indices produces two minus signs. Hence replacing \(V\) by \(V^c\) leaves the many-body Hamiltonian, all variational impurity problems, and the HF energy unchanged. It preserves pair-Hermiticity and imposes \(V^c_{ab\,cd}=V^c_{ba\,dc}\). Wick contraction then gives the \(J-K\) expressions with \(J,K\) formed from \(V^c\). In the example, \(V^c=0\) exactly.

Thus this is Minor: it requires an explicit representative convention, or the corresponding symmetrized contractions throughout, but no restriction on the underlying many-body operator or on (A1)–(A4). Physical interaction conventions may already contain the additional symmetry; it was not part of the displayed mathematical hypothesis. Using the raw nonsymmetric effective operator is not a valid repair.
# Problem 2: response sign and chemical-potential normalization
## Location and derivation

Equations (75)–(76), p. 1397 (physical 39), have a positive overall response sign and identify \(\widetilde\ell(Y)\) with \(\operatorname{Tr}(GY)\). The same page’s last Taylor expansion has another incompatible chemical- potential sign. In contrast, (54), p. 1389 (physical 31), correctly defines the positive operator \(\mathcal L_x^+\) through \(\delta 1_{(-\infty,0]}(h_x)=-\mathcal L_x^+(\delta h_x)\).

Equation reference: eq:mu, eq:response. Write \(C_x=C^x(D_0)\) and \(p_x=C_x^T\Pi_x C_x\). Differentiating the particle-number constraint gives the corrected formulas \[\begin{aligned}
 t&=\sum_x\langle p_x,\mathcal L_x^+(p_x)\rangle>0,\\
 \mu'[Y]&=\frac{\sum_x\langle p_x,
             \mathcal L_x^+(C_x^T Y C_x)\rangle}{t}
          =\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(GY)}{t},\\
 R[Y]&=-\sum_x\Pi_x C_x\mathcal L_x^+
       \bigl(C_x^T Y C_x-\mu'[Y]p_x\bigr)C_x^T\Pi_x.
       \end{aligned}\] Here \(t\) is exactly the positive derivative of the total impurity particle number with respect to chemical potential. There is no hypothesis fixing it to 1. These formulas enforce \(\operatorname{Tr}R[Y]=0\).
## Exact example satisfying all four hypotheses

Let \(L=4\), \(N=2\), with singleton fragments, and set \[u=\tfrac12(1,1,1,1)^T,\quad
 v=\tfrac1{\sqrt{18}}(1,3,-2,-2)^T,\quad
 D=uu^T+vv^T,\quad h=I-2uu^T-3vv^T.
 \tag{R2}\] The spectrum of \(h\) is \((-2,-1,1,1)\). The fragment populations are \(p=(11/36,3/4,17/36,17/36)\), all strictly interior. All off-diagonal entries of \(D\) are nonzero, so a diagonal matrix commuting with \(D\) is scalar; this proves (A3). Define \[z_i=p_i(1-p_i),\quad M_{ii}=z_i,\quad M_{ij}=-D_{ij}^2\ (i\ne j),
 \qquad \sigma=(11/24,3/8,17/42,17/42).\] The positive \(\sigma_i\) are the reciprocal impurity occupied–virtual gaps. Direct two-level perturbation theory gives, for \(Y=\operatorname{diag}y\), \[R[Y]_{ii}=-2\sigma_i\big((My)_i-\mu'[Y]z_i\big).
 \tag{R3}\] If this response is zero, \(My=\mu'z\); summing gives \(\mu'=0\), since \(M\) is a graph Laplacian and \(\sum_i z_i>0\). Its graph is connected, so \(y\) is constant. On the trace-zero space this proves (A4). The exact response matrix also has rank 3 in the independent calculation.

For \(y=(1,-1,0,0)\), exact arithmetic gives \[n:=\operatorname{Tr}(GY)=\frac{95}{1512},\qquad
 t=\frac{6701}{9072},\qquad
 \mu'[Y]=\frac{570}{6701}.\] Using the printed (75)–(76) instead gives \[\operatorname{Tr}R_{\rm printed}[Y]=n(1-t)
       =\frac{225245}{13716864}\ne0.\] It therefore fails even to map \(\mathcal Y\) into \(\mathcal Y\). The corrected response has trace zero exactly. Independently, the overall negative sign follows from the spectral-projector derivative; it is not repaired merely by inserting the denominator.
## Effect on the main proof

The preceding factorization can be retained. With \(A Q=-[D_0,[h,Q]]\) and \(B^*Y=D_0Y(I-D_0)+(I-D_0)YD_0\), the actual operator \(L A^{-1}B^*\) defined in (70)–(71) equals the corrected [eq:response] (#eq:response). Substitution gives the minus sign and [eq:mu] (#eq:mu); it does not give the printed (75)–(76). Consequently \[d_P(F^\mathrm{DMET}_0-I)(P_0)=R(BA^{-1}B^*)^{-1}\] still proves invertibility under (A3)–(A4). The IFT argument is repairable at this displayed calculation. The exact example disproves the printed formula, not invertibility of the true response or Theorem 4. Classification: Minor, with both corrections required.
# Problem 3: the numerical surjectivity diagnostic uses the wrong product

Figure 6 and the accompanying paragraph, p. 1373 (physical 15), identify the lowest eigenvalue of \(S=B^*B\) with (A3). Surjectivity of \(B:T_{D_0}\mathcal D\to\mathcal Y\) instead requires \(BB^*\) to be positive definite on \(\mathcal Y\). When \(\dim T_{D_0}\mathcal D>\dim\mathcal Y\), \(B^*B\) has a zero eigenvalue even for surjective \(B\).

There is also a dimension-convention inconsistency to resolve. Page 1372 (physical 14) specifies \(N_f=3\), \(L_x=2\), \(\dim\mathcal Y=8\), and \(N=10\). Under the definitions in Section 2, \(\sum_x L_x=L=6\) would then violate \(N<L\). Appendix B, pp. 1409–1410 (physical 51–52), instead displays five occupied and seven virtual orbitals and a \(7\times5\) excitation block. If those are the real one-particle spaces and the three fragments have equal size, they imply \(L=12\), \(N=5\), \(L_x=4\), \(\dim\mathcal Y=29\), and \(\dim\mathcal D=35\). This is a conditional inference from the displayed orbital counts, not a claim to have inspected the implementation. Spin summation or spin-paired density conventions may explain the differing numbers, but a precise map to the theorem’s conventions is needed.

The theoretical rank test in Lemma 11, p. 1378, and the adjoint calculation (41), p. 1385, are correct counterevidence: the analytical criterion itself is not disproved. Replace the numerical diagnostic by \(BB^*\) on the declared target space, or state explicitly that only the appropriate nonzero singular values are being measured, and reconcile the dimensions before interpreting Figure 6. Classification: Minor. The published implementation and the corrected numerical curve remain unverified.
# Problem 4: zero versus unit eigenvalue in the fixed-point bifurcation claim

On p. 1374 (physical 16), the discussion asserts a simple eigenvalue of \(dF^\mathrm{DMET}_0(P_0)\) crossing zero, with all remaining eigenvalues having negative real parts, and uses this as evidence for a transcritical bifurcation of \(P=F^\mathrm{DMET}_0(P)\). The exact differentiation is \[\Phi(\Theta,P)=F^\mathrm{DMET}_0(\Theta,P)-P,\qquad
 d_P\Phi=d_PF^\mathrm{DMET}_0-I.
 \tag{R4}\] Under the printed spectral condition, the crossing eigenvalue of \(d_P\Phi\) is \(-1\) and every other eigenvalue is also nonzero. The implicit function theorem then gives a unique local branch; that spectral condition cannot establish the claimed local fixed-point bifurcation. The required singularity is an eigenvalue 1 of \(dF^\mathrm{DMET}_0\), or equivalently 0 of \(d\Phi\).

The paper itself uses the correct residual in Section 7.6.3, equation (67), p. 1394 (physical 36), so this may be a notational substitution in the numerical section. State explicitly which Jacobian was calculated and which equation was solved by Newton’s method. A simple zero crossing of the residual derivative alone also does not certify the transcritical type; the reduced nonlinear coefficients or equivalent nondegeneracy information must distinguish it from other bifurcations. The branch plots in Figure 8 and the orbital discussion are numerical evidence, not that missing nondegeneracy argument.

# Problem 5: local Hamiltonian, charge, and normalization transcription errors
## High-level Hamiltonian and charge constraint

On p. 1393 (physical 35), (64) defines \(\widetilde h_x=C_x^{\sim T}hC_x^\sim\), but the displayed impurity Hamiltonian below (66) has neither the core contraction \(\alpha C_x^{\sim T}(J(D^x)-K(D^x))C_x^\sim\) nor the factor \(1/2\) on its two-body term. These are not scalar environment-energy shifts. Equation (30), and the later first-order calculation on pp. 1403–1404, supply the missing terms.

For the compatible \(L=4,N=2,D\) in Problem 1, now use the canonical tensor \(V_{13\,13}=V_{31\,31}=1\), with all other entries zero. Its interaction is \(n_1n_3\). Freezing \(c=(e_3+e_4)/\sqrt2\) gives the nonzero impurity term \(\frac12 n_1\); the displayed Hamiltonian on p. 1393 omits it. The same example checks the relabelling of \(a_7\) on p. 1382 (physical 24): its four-contraction sum must retain the preceding factor \(1/2\). In a basis containing the normalized core orbital, that inner sum is 1 for the occupied \(e_1\) state, so its energy is \(1/2\), not 1. Restoring the factor reconnects the calculation to the final \(J-K\) expression on p. 1383, after the tensor convention in Problem 1 has been imposed. Separately, \(V_{12\,12}=V_{21\,21}=1\) gives \(n_1n_2\), whose energy on the doubly occupied impurity is 1. Omitting the factor \(1/2\) gives 2. These are exact CAR computations with all compatibility and gap assumptions used in Lemma 13 satisfied.

The same page and p. 1394 impose particle number by summing \(\langle c_\kappa^\dagger c_\lambda\rangle\) over both fragment indices. The sum must be over \(\kappa=\lambda\). An assumption-compliant check is available with \(L=6,N=3\). Let \[P=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/4\\1/4&1/2\end{pmatrix},\quad
 D_4=\begin{pmatrix}P&(\sqrt3/4)I_2\\
                    (\sqrt3/4)I_2&I_2-P\end{pmatrix},\quad
 D=D_4\oplus\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Since \(P(I_2-P)=3I_2/16\), \(D\) is a rank-three projector. Use fragments \(\{1,2\},\{3,5\},\{4,6\}\), reordered into consecutive blocks if desired, and \(h=I-2D\). The block eigenvalues are \((1/4,3/4)\), \((1/2,1/2)\), \((1/2,1/2)\), so (A1)–(A2) hold and \(L_x=2<N\). At the noninteracting solution the actual total fragment trace is 3, but the printed sum of all fragment entries is \(7/2\). This is a mathematical difference, not notation for a trace.
## First-order normalization and signs

On p. 1400 (physical 42), the displayed \(\Psi_0=(N!)^{-1/2}c_N^\dagger\cdots c_1^\dagger|0\rangle\) contains an extra factor for the canonical creation operators defined in Section 2. Their product applied to normalized vacuum already has norm 1. For \(N=2\), the displayed vector has squared norm \(1/2\), contradicting the claimed orthonormal excitation basis. Remove the extra factorial factor. The first-order expansion must also retain the negative excitation-energy denominators. On p. 1401 (physical 43), the two positive intermediate formulas for \([d_1]_{ai}\) lose the minus sign from the preceding sum-over-states formula. Equation (77) already restores the correct negative sign.

The direct and exchange contractions actually printed on that page are \[[J_{W_2}(d)]_{mn}=\sum_{p,q}[W_2]_{npmq}d_{pq},\qquad
 [K_{W_2}(d)]_{mn}=\sum_{p,q}[W_2]_{npqm}d_{pq}.\] Under the tensor normalization (R1), these agree with (21). For the first expression, interchange the dummy indices \(p,q\) and use \(d_{pq}=d_{qp}\). For the second, pair-Hermiticity and simultaneous pair exchange give \([W_2]_{npqm}=[W_2]_{qmnp}=[W_2]_{mqpn}\). Thus there is no additional contraction-index defect under that convention. For the canonical interaction \(n_1n_3\) and the block projector of Problem 1, both expressions give \(J-K=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,0,1/2,0)\). With \(h=I-2D\), the negative response in (77) gives \[D_1=\operatorname{diag}(-1/8,1/8,-1/8,1/8),\] in agreement with the retained exact perturbation calculation in the full six-dimensional two-particle sector. The contrary index counterexample was based on a transcription of the formulas that does not match the source and is withdrawn.

The rewritten impurity Hamiltonian on p. 1404 (physical 46) also already keeps \(-\mu(\alpha)\) outside the factor \(\alpha\): the closing parenthesis follows the two-body term and precedes the chemical-potential term. The subsequent \(W_1\) consistently uses \(\mu'(0)\). No chemical-potential factoring defect is supported by this page; that proposed subclaim is withdrawn. A nonzero \(\mu'(0)\) establishes the term’s first-order importance, but does not show an error in the correctly printed formula.
## Repair boundary

Restore the core term and the half factor, replace the charge sums by diagonal sums, and normalize the determinant according to the CAR convention. The corrected finite-dimensional impurity Hamiltonian remains analytic; the noninteracting gap and positive charge derivative persist locally, so Lemma 13’s analytic IFT argument still works. The singles-only contribution to the one-body first derivative also survives the normalization correction. Classification: Minor. These errors should be corrected explicitly; merely invoking analyticity of the incorrectly displayed Hamiltonian would not prove the result for the variationally defined DMET map.
# Core proof and dependency checks after the specified repairs
## Compatibility, representability, and noninteracting consistency

Lemma 7’s rank/interior equivalences follow from \(x^TDx=\|Dx\|^2\) and the corresponding identity for \(I-D\). The occupied and virtual impurity columns in (28) are orthonormal, mutually orthogonal, and span the asserted \(2L_x\)-dimensional space. The core formula (31) subtracts precisely the occupied impurity projector.

For Lemma 9’s singleton-fragment case, Kadison’s Theorem 6 gives the diagonal characterization, and his Theorem 7 supplies a real projection with the prescribed diagonal [kadison]. The latter’s constructive proof was checked, so passage to the real setting is supported. For two fragments, writing a projector in blocks gives \(CC^T=P_1-P_1^2\) and \(C^TC=P_2-P_2^2\); the off-diagonal projection equation forces complementary fractional eigenvalues, as claimed. The commutant test in Lemma 11 follows by identifying the kernel of the adjoint of \(B\); it tests surjectivity, not injectivity of \(B\).

For Proposition 1, \(D_0\) commutes with \(h\). Compression to the occupied and virtual impurity spaces therefore retains strictly negative and strictly positive spectral sectors. The chemical potential 0 yields the required density. The total impurity particle number is globally nondecreasing in chemical potential, and its local derivative at 0 is strictly positive by (A2). This also excludes another chemical-potential root with the same total particle number. The possible impurity level crossings away from 0 do not invalidate this monotonicity argument.
## Analytic maps and local uniqueness

The noninteracting energy obeys the gap estimate \[\operatorname{Tr}(h(D-D_0))\geq \tfrac{\gamma}{2}\|D-D_0\|_F^2,
 \qquad \gamma=\epsilon_{N+1}-\epsilon_N>0.\] Together with the local submersion from (A3), this localizes every global low-level minimizer for small \(|\alpha|\) and \(P-P_0\). In the displayed estimates on pp. 1391–1392, \(\alpha C_{\rm nl}\) must be bounded by \(|\alpha|C_{\rm nl}\) for the advertised two-sided interval, and the submersion bound may require a fixed local constant. These harmless bound corrections do not affect localization.

In a basis diagonalizing \(D_0\) and \(h\), a tangent vector is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&X^T\\X&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). The Hessian acts on its lower-left block by \(X\mapsto h_+X-Xh_-\) and is positive with lower bound \(\gamma\). This independently verifies the cited Grassmann-Hessian identity, without assuming an external theorem with mismatched hypotheses. The saddle matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&B^*\\B&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) is invertible because \(A>0\) and \(B\) is onto. Hence \[dF^\mathrm{LL}_0=A^{-1}B^*(BA^{-1}B^*)^{-1}.\] For the corrected high-level Hamiltonian, finite-dimensional gapped spectral projectors are analytic by the resolvent formula. The scalar charge equation has derivative \(t>0\), so its chemical potential and density are analytic locally. Global monotonicity of the ground-state charge rules out a second admissible root. Combining these derivatives yields the corrected residual factorization in Problem 2, to which (A4) applies. No assertion of contractivity is needed.
## First-order exactness and limits of numerical evidence

In the determinant expansion, a one-body observable couples the reference determinant only to single excitations. Double excitations therefore do not contribute to the first derivative of the one-body density. The corrected Wick contraction produces the same first-order effective one-body perturbation for the exact and HF densities. In the impurity calculation, the core and occupied impurity densities sum to \(D_0\), giving the same first-order interaction term for the interacting and HF high-level maps. Their scalar chemical-potential derivatives agree by the same charge equation. The invertible fixed-point residual then gives equality of the block-density derivatives, and the low-level map gives equality of the full-density derivatives. This verifies the mechanism of Theorem 5 after the stated local corrections.

The H\(_{10}\) and H\(_6^{4-}\) plots illustrate first-order agreement and second-order disagreement; they are not needed to prove the analytical first-order assertion. The admitted noise near poorly conditioned hypotheses does not itself establish a theorem defect. The qualitative DET remark is not a replacement for an independently stated quantitative invertibility hypothesis; no counterexample to that variant was established here, and it is not counted as a Problem.
# Assessment and retained evidence

Five groups of Minor corrections are supported by exact locations and explicit mathematics. No Major quota was used. The false intermediate identities are substantive enough to require correction, but the report supplies local repairs and checks how they reconnect the main proof; their existence does not justify claiming Theorems 4 or 5 false. Numerical convention and bifurcation clarifications remain author-facing requests, not independently verified facts about the implementation.

The companion findings, coverage, provenance, problem evidence, source/render records, native command logs, and support inventory identify the exact paths, byte counts, and SHA256 hashes. The exact calculation script and its exit-code receipt are retained. The build and image-view records distinguish successful compilation and actual viewing from mere parsing or rendering. This report retains the initial review with the two unsupported subclaims in Problem 5 corrected during focused independent acceptance. The scientific decision remains `pending` and `human_reviews=[]`. The per-paper provenance records the operational acceptance status and its exact artifact bindings.

claim: The real one-particle space is \(\mathbb R^L\), with \(1\leq N<L\) and \(\mathcal D=\{D=D^T=D^2:\operatorname{Tr}D=N\}\). Coordinate fragments partition the \(L\) sites, with sizes \(L_x<N\). The block-density space has tangent space \(\mathcal Y\), consisting of symmetric block-diagonal matrices of total trace zero. The low-level map minimizes the Hartree–Fock energy over projectors with prescribed block density; the high-level map solves the interacting impurity problems with frozen occupied cores and a common chemical potential imposing the total particle number. The fixed-point equation is \(P=F^\mathrm{DMET}_\alpha(P)=F^\mathrm{HL}_\alpha(F^\mathrm{LL}_\alpha(P))\).
1. \(\epsilon_N<0<\epsilon_{N+1}\) for the one-body Hamiltonian \(h\), with \(D_0=1_{(-\infty,0]}(h)\).
2. Both \(D_0X_x\) and \((I-D_0)X_x\) have dimension \(L_x\) for every fragment. Equivalently, every fragment block of \(D_0\) has all eigenvalues strictly between 0 and 1.
3. \(B=\operatorname{Bd}|_{T_{D_0}\mathcal D}:T_{D_0}\mathcal D\to\mathcal Y\) is surjective.
4. The true frozen-impurity density response \(R:\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Y\) to a perturbation \(h+Y\) is invertible.

Theorem 4 asserts existence of a sufficiently small two-sided interval in \(\alpha\) and a neighbourhood of \(D_0\) with a unique real-analytic solution branch there. It does not assert global uniqueness of all DMET solutions, a uniform interval over all Hamiltonians, or convergence of the elementary fixed-point iteration. Theorem 5 asserts \(D^\mathrm{DMET}_\alpha=D^\mathrm{exact}_\alpha+O(\alpha^2)
=D^\mathrm{HF}_\alpha+O(\alpha^2)\) in this local regime. Equality of first derivatives does not require the exact interacting density to remain a projector.

A closing spectral gap, a fragment eigenvalue at 0 or 1, or loss of either surjectivity or response invertibility lies outside these conclusions. In particular, numerical branch behaviour where (A4) fails is not a counterexample to Theorem 4. Assumption (A2) also entails \(L_x\leq \min(N,L-N)\); the prescribed fragmentation must satisfy this feasibility restriction. The paper’s additional convention \(L_x<N\) is retained in every example below.
Recorded check: The stated interaction-tensor symmetry does not justify the effective one-body contractions
analysis: On p. 1363 (physical 5), the stated interaction symmetry is only \(V_{ab\,cd}=V_{cd\,ab}\). Equations (21), (25), and (30), pp. 1366, 1368, and 1376 (physical 8, 10, 18), use \(J(D)-K(D)\) as the effective one-body term. Proposition 8 assumes that \(D\) is compatible with the fragmentation; it does not assume (A3) or (A4).

Take \(L=4\), \(N=2\), four singleton fragments, and \[D=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0&0\\1&1&0&0\\
 0&0&1&1\\0&0&1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad h=I-2D.\] This is a rank-two real projector, every fragment population is \(1/2\), and \(h\) has eigenvalues \(-1,-1,1,1\). Thus all assumptions used in Proposition 8 hold, as do (A1)–(A2). For fragment 1, the impurity space is \(\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)\) and the frozen core is \(c=(e_3+e_4)/\sqrt2\).

Let \(S_{13}=S_{31}=1\), \(A_{23}=1\), \(A_{32}=-1\), all other entries zero, and set \[V_{ab\,cd}=S_{ab}A_{cd}+A_{ab}S_{cd}.\] This real tensor satisfies exactly the stated pair-Hermitian symmetry. Its entire two-body operator \(\frac12\sum V_{ab\,cd}a_a^\dagger a_b^\dagger a_d a_c\) vanishes: each summand factorizes with a symmetric pair of creation or annihilation indices, which the CAR relations annihilate. The independent calculation checked all entries of the full \(16\times16\) Fock-space matrix, with exact fractions.

Nevertheless, for the core density \(cc^T\), the restriction of the paper’s \(J(cc^T)-K(cc^T)\) to the impurity space is \[\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] It is nonzero and not symmetric. Its expectation in \((e_1+e_2)/\sqrt2\) is \(1/2\), whereas the exact interaction and its frozen-core restriction are zero. Changing to the paper’s orthonormal impurity basis conjugates this discrepancy and does not remove it. This is an operator-formula counterexample satisfying the proposition’s assumptions, not a counterexample to the main theorems.

A precise harmless normalization of the interaction tensor is needed: \[V^c_{ab\,cd}=\tfrac12(V_{ab\,cd}+V_{ba\,dc}).
 \tag{R1}\] Simultaneously swapping the two creation and the two annihilation indices produces two minus signs. Hence replacing \(V\) by \(V^c\) leaves the many-body Hamiltonian, all variational impurity problems, and the HF energy unchanged. It preserves pair-Hermiticity and imposes \(V^c_{ab\,cd}=V^c_{ba\,dc}\). Wick contraction then gives the \(J-K\) expressions with \(J,K\) formed from \(V^c\). In the example, \(V^c=0\) exactly.

Thus this is Minor: it requires an explicit representative convention, or the corresponding symmetrized contractions throughout, but no restriction on the underlying many-body operator or on (A1)–(A4). Physical interaction conventions may already contain the additional symmetry; it was not part of the displayed mathematical hypothesis. Using the raw nonsymmetric effective operator is not a valid repair.
result: Impact: The printed effective operator can be nonsymmetric and disagree with the variational Hamiltonian under the displayed tensor hypothesis.

 t&=\sum_x\langle p_x,\mathcal L_x^+(p_x)\rangle>0,\\
 \mu'[Y]&=\frac{\sum_x\langle p_x,
             \mathcal L_x^+(C_x^T Y C_x)\rangle}{t}
          =\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(GY)}{t},\\

       \bigl(C_x^T Y C_x-\mu'[Y]p_x\bigr)C_x^T\Pi_x.

Surjectivity of \(B:T_{D_0}\mathcal D\to\mathcal Y\) instead requires \(BB^*\) to be positive definite on \(\mathcal Y\). The fixed-point equation is \(P=F^\mathrm{DMET}_\alpha(P)=F^\mathrm{HL}_\alpha(F^\mathrm{LL}_\alpha(P))\).
1. \(\epsilon_N<0<\epsilon_{N+1}\) for the one-body Hamiltonian \(h\), with \(D_0=1_{(-\infty,0]}(h)\).
2. Both \(D_0X_x\) and \((I-D_0)X_x\) have dimension \(L_x\) for every fragment. Equivalently, every fragment block of \(D_0\) has all eigenvalues strictly between 0 and 1.
3. \(B=\operatorname{Bd}|_{T_{D_0}\mathcal D}:T_{D_0}\mathcal D\to\mathcal Y\) is surjective.
4. The true frozen-impurity density response \(R:\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Y\) to a perturbation \(h+Y\) is invertible.

Theorem 4 asserts existence of a sufficiently small two-sided interval in \(\alpha\) and a neighbourhood of \(D_0\) with a unique real-analytic solution branch there. It does not assert global uniqueness of all DMET solutions, a uniform interval over all Hamiltonians, or convergence of the elementary fixed-point iteration. Theorem 5 asserts \(D^\mathrm{DMET}_\alpha=D^\mathrm{exact}_\alpha+O(\alpha^2)
=D^\mathrm{HF}_\alpha+O(\alpha^2)\) in this local regime. Equality of first derivatives does not require the exact interacting density to remain a projector.

A closing spectral gap, a fragment eigenvalue at 0 or 1, or loss of either surjectivity or response invertibility lies outside these conclusions. In particular, numerical branch behaviour where (A4) fails is not a counterexample to Theorem 4. Assumption (A2) also entails \(L_x\leq \min(N,L-N)\); the prescribed fragmentation must satisfy this feasibility restriction. The paper’s additional convention \(L_x<N\) is retained in every example below.
Recorded check: The stated fixed-point bifurcation criterion confuses eigenvalues zero and one
analysis:
On p. 1374 (physical 16), the discussion asserts a simple eigenvalue of \(dF^\mathrm{DMET}_0(P_0)\) crossing zero, with all remaining eigenvalues having negative real parts, and uses this as evidence for a transcritical bifurcation of \(P=F^\mathrm{DMET}_0(P)\). The exact differentiation is \[\Phi(\Theta,P)=F^\mathrm{DMET}_0(\Theta,P)-P,\qquad
 d_P\Phi=d_PF^\mathrm{DMET}_0-I.
 \tag{R4}\] Under the printed spectral condition, the crossing eigenvalue of \(d_P\Phi\) is \(-1\) and every other eigenvalue is also nonzero. The implicit function theorem then gives a unique local branch; that spectral condition cannot establish the claimed local fixed-point bifurcation. The required singularity is an eigenvalue 1 of \(dF^\mathrm{DMET}_0\), or equivalently 0 of \(d\Phi\).

The paper itself uses the correct residual in Section 7.6.3, equation (67), p. 1394 (physical 36), so this may be a notational substitution in the numerical section. State explicitly which Jacobian was calculated and which equation was solved by Newton’s method. A simple zero crossing of the residual derivative alone also does not certify the transcritical type; the reduced nonlinear coefficients or equivalent nondegeneracy information must distinguish it from other bifurcations. The branch plots in Figure 8 and the orbital discussion are numerical evidence, not that missing nondegeneracy argument.

Classification: Minor, affecting the stated numerical inference. No claim is made that the reported branches cannot occur, that the code used the wrong residual, or that the perturbative theorems fail. The actual computational convention must be clarified.
