analysis: On p. 1393 (physical 35), (64) defines \(\widetilde h_x=C_x^{\sim T}hC_x^\sim\), but the displayed impurity Hamiltonian below (66) has neither the core contraction \(\alpha C_x^{\sim T}(J(D^x)-K(D^x))C_x^\sim\) nor the factor \(1/2\) on its two-body term. These are not scalar environment-energy shifts. Equation (30), and the later first-order calculation on pp. 1403–1404, supply the missing terms.

For the compatible \(L=4,N=2,D\) in Problem 1, now use the canonical tensor \(V_{13\,13}=V_{31\,31}=1\), with all other entries zero. Its interaction is \(n_1n_3\). Freezing \(c=(e_3+e_4)/\sqrt2\) gives the nonzero impurity term \(\frac12 n_1\); the displayed Hamiltonian on p. 1393 omits it. The same example checks the relabelling of \(a_7\) on p. 1382 (physical 24): its four-contraction sum must retain the preceding factor \(1/2\). In a basis containing the normalized core orbital, that inner sum is 1 for the occupied \(e_1\) state, so its energy is \(1/2\), not 1. Restoring the factor reconnects the calculation to the final \(J-K\) expression on p. 1383, after the tensor convention in Problem 1 has been imposed. Separately, \(V_{12\,12}=V_{21\,21}=1\) gives \(n_1n_2\), whose energy on the doubly occupied impurity is 1. Omitting the factor \(1/2\) gives 2. These are exact CAR computations with all compatibility and gap assumptions used in Lemma 13 satisfied.

The same page and p. 1394 impose particle number by summing \(\langle c_\kappa^\dagger c_\lambda\rangle\) over both fragment indices. The sum must be over \(\kappa=\lambda\). An assumption-compliant check is available with \(L=6,N=3\). Let \[P=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/4\\1/4&1/2\end{pmatrix},\quad
 D_4=\begin{pmatrix}P&(\sqrt3/4)I_2\\
                    (\sqrt3/4)I_2&I_2-P\end{pmatrix},\quad
 D=D_4\oplus\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.\] Since \(P(I_2-P)=3I_2/16\), \(D\) is a rank-three projector. report: Abstract: The acquired 2023 preprint of Fortuna, Garroni and Spadaro is examined with emphasis on the interpolation underlying its grain-boundary cell formula. A constant-input example shows that the displayed construction in Lemma 6.3 does not have the asserted lattice-valued tangential jumps. A recursive residual correction restores the local trace, quantization and energy estimates. This is a demonstrated defect in a construction used by the central proof, rather than a counterexample to the main theorem. A separate local energy estimate omits the common shear component. The findings concern the retained preprint; equivalence with the 2025 journal article has not been established.

Title: Quantization in a grain-boundary interpolation:
a technical verification report
# Paper identity, version and inspected scope

The target record is M25-0403, On the Read–Shockley energy for grain boundaries in 2D polycrystals, by Martino Fortuna, Adriana Garroni and Emanuele Spadaro, DOI 10.1002/cpa.22245 (https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.22245). The actual source is the 43-page institutional copy of arXiv:2306.07742v1, dated 13 June 2023, whose title is On the Read-Shockley energy for grain boundaries in poly-crystals [FGS]. Its numbered pages coincide with PDF pages 1–43. References below to a source equation, theorem or page refer to this version.

The source text, including both appendices, was read. Detailed checks concentrated on the circulation constraint, the quadratic-energy compactness argument, the periodic-cell normalization, the compression construction, and the interpolation used to identify the cell energy. The two findings below are supported by complete local calculations. The external logarithmic estimate and the density argument invoked in the source were not independently re-proved. The statement of the incompatible-field rigidity estimate was compared with the retained reference [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 3.3, p.~8]{MSZ}]; its full proof was not independently certified. Available reference PDFs and earlier extraction/rendering records were retained. No author program was executed.
# Definitions and the relevant dependency

The source works with a matrix field \(A\) and a relatively closed defect set \(S\). In addition to \(\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{Curl}A\subset S\), admissibility requires every relevant closed-loop circulation outside \(S\) to lie in \(\tau\varepsilon\mathbb Z^2\), where \(\tau,\varepsilon>0\) [Retained latex: \cite[p.~4, (H2)]{FGS}]. The energy is the sum of a quadratic distance from \(\mathrm{SO}(2)\) outside the core and the core area, divided by \(\varepsilon\).

Equation reference: eq:M. For the interpolation lemma, put \[Q_{\ell,L}^0=(0,\ell)\times(0,L),\qquad
 G=\ell\int_0^L |g(t)|^2\,dt,\qquad
 q=\frac{\tau\varepsilon}{\ell},\] where \(L,\ell>0\), \(\ell\ge\varepsilon\) and \(g\in L^2_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^2)\). The source additionally assumes \(G<\varepsilon L\) for its quantitative estimate and sets \[
 M=\left(\frac{L\varepsilon}{G}\right)^{1/3},\qquad
 N=\left\lfloor\frac{L}{M\ell}\right\rfloor+1.\] The case \(g=0\) is treated separately. Each complete strip \(E_i\) has height \(M\ell\), and the final strip has the remaining height. On a strip with bottom coordinate \(y_i\), the local primitive is \[u_i(x_1,x_2)=
 \left(1-\frac{x_1}{\ell}\right)\int_{y_i}^{x_2}g(t)\,dt,\qquad A_i=\nabla u_i.\] Thus \(A_i e_1=0\) on its bottom and \[A_i e_1=\bar g_i:=-\ell^{-1}
       \int_{y_i}^{y_i+M\ell}g(t)\,dt\] on its top when the strip is complete.
# A failed quantization step and a local correction

Problem 1 (The offsets in Lemma 6.3 do not preserve the lattice jumps).  Equation [eq:printed] (#eq:printed), printed on source p. 33 immediately before (6.13), does not generally have the asserted \(q\mathbb Z^2\)-valued jumps.
## An example satisfying all hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:parameters, eq:failure. Choose \[
 \tau=1,\quad \varepsilon=\ell=\frac1{10},\quad L=1,\quad
 g(t)=\frac18e_1\quad (t\in\mathbb R).\] The function is locally square integrable and nonzero, \(\ell=\varepsilon\), and \[G=\frac1{640}<\frac1{10}=\varepsilon L.\] Equations [eq:M] (#eq:M) give \(M=4\), \(N=3\). The strip heights are \(2/5,2/5,1/5\), and \(q=1\). For the first two strips, \[\bar g_1=\bar g_2=-\frac12e_1,\qquad
 g_1^\varepsilon=g_2^\varepsilon=-e_1.\] Consequently the offsets in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) are \[(c_1,c_2,c_3)=\left(0,-\frac12e_1,-\frac12e_1\right).\] At the second interface, \(x_2=4/5\), the lower trace is \(\bar g_2+c_2=-e_1\), whereas the upper trace is \(c_3=-e_1/2\). Therefore \[
 [Ae_1]=\frac12e_1\notin\mathbb Z^2=q\mathbb Z^2.\] The first interface happens to have zero jump; this does not repair the second one. The calculations are exact rational arithmetic. An independently written symbolic check reproduces them; its source and actual output are retained with the verification files.

The failure persists at arbitrarily small scales: set \(\ell=\varepsilon\), \(L=1\), retain \(g=e_1/8\), and take \(0<\varepsilon<1/8\). Then \(M=4\), the first two complete strips exist, and their second-interface jump is still \(e_1/2\), whereas \(q=1\).
## Alternative readings

Reversing the orientation of the interface changes the sign in [eq:failure] (#eq:failure), without making the jump integral. The source explicitly sets the lower trace of each local primitive to zero, so interpreting \(u_i\) as a single unshifted global primitive contradicts its displayed endpoint conditions. Its projection is expressly componentwise floor projection. Changing a rounding choice by lattice vectors cannot remove the half-integer residue.

There are two connected defects in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed): the residual is inserted with the wrong sign for the first matching operation, and later interfaces require the previous residual to be carried into the next projection. A sign change alone is not a general repair.
## A corrected interpolation

Equation reference: eq:recurrence. Let \(P_q\) be componentwise floor projection onto \(q\mathbb Z^2\). Set \[
 c_1=0,\qquad
 c_{i+1}=c_i+\bar g_i-P_q(c_i+\bar g_i),\qquad
 \widetilde A|_{E_i}=A_i+c_i\otimes e_1.\] For the example [eq:parameters] (#eq:parameters), this gives \((c_1,c_2,c_3)=(0,e_1/2,0)\), and the two jumps are \(e_1\) and \(0\).

Proposition 1.  Under the hypotheses of Lemma 6.3, the replacement [eq:recurrence] (#eq:recurrence) preserves its prescribed second column, bottom and top first-column conditions, lattice-valued jumps, and the energy order in source (6.11). Constants may depend on the fixed parameters \(\lambda,\tau\).

Proof. At interface \(i\), the jump is \[c_{i+1}-(c_i+\bar g_i)
   =-P_q(c_i+\bar g_i)\in q\mathbb Z^2.\] Every \(c_i\) belongs to \([0,q)^2\), so \(|c_i|<\sqrt2q\). Adding the constant matrix \(c_i\otimes e_1\) changes neither the second column nor the interior curl of \(A_i\). The bottom first column remains zero because \(c_1=0\); the top first column is constant because the primitive’s integral and \(c_N\) are constant there. The only possible new curl lies on the finitely many horizontal strip interfaces.
## Dependency and impact

The source invokes Lemma 6.3 in the proof of Proposition 6.2 and uses it to assert admissibility after (6.21), on p. 35. Section 6.3 then explicitly applies Proposition 6.2 to prove Theorem 5.3. That theorem supplies the identification in Corollary 5.4 and the cell formula used in Section 7.

The demonstrated failure therefore lies on a central proof dependency and is assessed as Major under the stated core-contribution criterion. The assessment concerns the invalid displayed construction. Proposition Proposition 1 (#prop:repair) supplies a complete local replacement, which is counterevidence against treating the example as a false-theorem result. The complete downstream proof has not been independently reconstructed after this replacement, and no statement about an author-adopted correction or the journal-final version is made.
# A local energy bound loses the common shear

Problem 2 (The bound in source (5.21)–(5.22) omits a mean component).  For the general compression-to-compression parameters in Section 5.2.1, the right-hand side of source (5.21) can vanish although its left-hand side is strictly positive.

Choose \(\ell=h=1\), \(r=\rho=1/4\), \(\eta=\widetilde\eta=1\) and \(\mu=\widetilde\mu=1/2\). These satisfy the rectangular size restrictions on source p. 20 and keep the denominators in the construction nonzero. Source (5.15) reduces, on both interpolation regions, to \[\widehat D_i=
 \begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad i=3,4.\] All difference terms on the right-hand side of (5.21) vanish, and \(\eta+\widetilde\eta-2=0\). Its claimed upper bound is therefore zero. However, \[|\widehat D_i-I|^2=\frac14,\qquad
 \operatorname{dist}^2(\widehat D_i,\mathrm{SO}(2))=\frac{17}{4}-\sqrt{17}>0.\] For completeness, minimizing the squared Frobenius distance over rotations gives \(\operatorname{dist}^2(B,\mathrm{SO}(2))=|B|^2+2-2\sqrt{(b_{11}+b_{22})^2+(b_{21}-b_{12})^2}\); substitution gives the displayed value. Thus this is a failure of the actual inequality, not a change of norm or orientation. The corresponding integral bound (5.22) also fails because the interpolation regions have positive area. In this example the circulation around the core is zero by source (5.17), so quantization imposes no excluded parameter condition.

Equation reference: eq:mean-bound. A valid replacement follows directly from the printed gradients. Define \[d=(\widetilde\mu-\mu,\widetilde\eta-\eta),\qquad
 a=\left(\frac{\mu+\widetilde\mu}{2},
          \frac{\eta+\widetilde\eta}{2}-1\right).\] For \(\Delta_3\), the first column of \(\widehat D_3-I\) is \(\frac{h}{2\ell}(1-h/x_2)d\), while the second is \(a+\frac{h^2x_1}{2\ell x_2^2}d\). The corresponding sign in the first column changes on \(\Delta_4\). Applying \(|v+w|^2\le2|v|^2+2|w|^2\) gives \[
 \operatorname{dist}^2(\widehat D_i,\mathrm{SO}(2))
 \le C|d|^2\left[
       \frac{h^2}{\ell^2}
       +\frac{h^4}{\ell^2}
         \left(\frac1{x_2^2}+\frac{x_1^2}{x_2^4}\right)\right]
       +2|a|^2.\] This retains the missing mean shear and a nonnegative squared mean compression. Merely squaring the source’s last term would still omit the common shear.

The specific parameters in source (5.37) satisfy \(\widetilde\mu=-\mu\) and \(\eta+\widetilde\eta=2\cos\alpha\). In that specialization, \(|a|^2=(1-\cos\alpha)^2=O(\alpha^4)\). Summing its integrated contribution over the compression cells, using \(L>h_D\) and \(\ell_D=\varepsilon\tau/\sin\alpha\), gives an additional \(O(L\varepsilon\tau\alpha^3)\) for positive small \(\alpha\). This is below the target \(L\varepsilon\tau\alpha(|\log\alpha|+1)\) order. Thus the counterexample establishes a Minor defect in the general local estimate; it does not demonstrate failure of the specialized Read–Shockley upper bound.
# Outcome and remaining scope

The highest supported impact in the acquired source is Major, from Problem 1’s central construction. Problem 2 has a narrower, local impact. The verified repairs concern the particular interpolation and pointwise estimate, respectively. Neither establishes author adoption or substitutes for a check of a later source version.

The literal extension in Remark 2.8 to an energy comparable to \(\operatorname{dist}(A,\mathrm{SO}(2))\), rather than its square, was identified but is not settled by the quadratic-energy analysis here. A difference between the energies along one sequence would not itself refute a \(\Gamma\)-limit. Likewise, the full treatment of periods around holes in the general domain is outside the repaired rectangular interpolation result. These unresolved scope points do not increase the supported severity.

Lemma 6.3 construction | Major | Local traces, lattice jumps and energy order | Unknown
Source (5.21)–(5.22) | Minor | Pointwise bound with mean terms; specialized extra order | Unknown
Scientific decision | Pending | Independent acceptance remains separate | No human review
# Supporting checks

The main source PDF has SHA256 \[\text{\texttt{3dcfcd72fcf62926793181f23f3ca9dd3ac8d}}\] \[\text{\texttt{4efdef11b1ec387e5ccf79f69fc}}.\] The split above is typographical only; the verification record stores the uninterrupted 64-character value. Calculations in the report are analytic arguments; the finite symbolic script checks the displayed example and algebra, not the entire main theorem.

The report was produced in this recovery session. The controller supplied a Personal/Chat/GPT-6/Pro interface observation; backend equivalence was not independently established. No human-review declaration is supplied.

Equation reference: eq:recurrence. Let \(P_q\) be componentwise floor projection onto \(q\mathbb Z^2\). Set \[
 c_1=0,\qquad
 c_{i+1}=c_i+\bar g_i-P_q(c_i+\bar g_i),\qquad
 \widetilde A|_{E_i}=A_i+c_i\otimes e_1.\] For the example [eq:parameters] (#eq:parameters), this gives \((c_1,c_2,c_3)=(0,e_1/2,0)\), and the two jumps are \(e_1\) and \(0\).

Proposition 1.  Under the hypotheses of Lemma 6.3, the replacement [eq:recurrence] (#eq:recurrence) preserves its prescribed second column, bottom and top first-column conditions, lattice-valued jumps, and the energy order in source (6.11). Constants may depend on the fixed parameters \(\lambda,\tau\).

Proof. At interface \(i\), the jump is \[c_{i+1}-(c_i+\bar g_i)
   =-P_q(c_i+\bar g_i)\in q\mathbb Z^2.\] Every \(c_i\) belongs to \([0,q)^2\), so \(|c_i|<\sqrt2q\). Adding the constant matrix \(c_i\otimes e_1\) changes neither the second column nor the interior curl of \(A_i\). The bottom first column remains zero because \(c_1=0\); the top first column is constant because the primitive’s integral and \(c_N\) are constant there. The only possible new curl lies on the finitely many horizontal strip interfaces.

The source invokes Lemma 6.3 in the proof of Proposition 6.2 and uses it to assert admissibility after (6.21), on p. 35. Section 6.3 then explicitly applies Proposition 6.2 to prove Theorem 5.3. That theorem supplies the identification in Corollary 5.4 and the cell formula used in Section 7.

The demonstrated failure therefore lies on a central proof dependency and is assessed as Major under the stated core-contribution criterion. The assessment concerns the invalid displayed construction. Proposition Proposition 1 (#prop:repair) supplies a complete local replacement, which is counterevidence against treating the example as a false-theorem result. The complete downstream proof has not been independently reconstructed after this replacement, and no statement about an author-adopted correction or the journal-final version is made.
result: Reversing the orientation of the interface changes the sign in [eq:failure] (#eq:failure), without making the jump integral. The source explicitly sets the lower trace of each local primitive to zero, so interpreting \(u_i\) as a single unshifted global primitive contradicts its displayed endpoint conditions. Its projection is expressly componentwise floor projection. Changing a rounding choice by lattice vectors cannot remove the half-integer residue.

There are two connected defects in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed): the residual is inserted with the wrong sign for the first matching operation, and later interfaces require the previous residual to be carried into the next projection. A sign change alone is not a general repair.

Equation reference: eq:M. For the interpolation lemma, put \[Q_{\ell,L}^0=(0,\ell)\times(0,L),\qquad

analysis: For the general compression-to-compression parameters in Section 5.2.1, the right-hand side of source (5.21) can vanish although its left-hand side is strictly positive.

Choose \(\ell=h=1\), \(r=\rho=1/4\), \(\eta=\widetilde\eta=1\) and \(\mu=\widetilde\mu=1/2\). These satisfy the rectangular size restrictions on source p. 20 and keep the denominators in the construction nonzero. Source (5.15) reduces, on both interpolation regions, to \[\widehat D_i=
 \begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad i=3,4.\] All difference terms on the right-hand side of (5.21) vanish, and \(\eta+\widetilde\eta-2=0\). Its claimed upper bound is therefore zero. However, \[|\widehat D_i-I|^2=\frac14,\qquad
 \operatorname{dist}^2(\widehat D_i,\mathrm{SO}(2))=\frac{17}{4}-\sqrt{17}>0.\] For completeness, minimizing the squared Frobenius distance over rotations gives \(\operatorname{dist}^2(B,\mathrm{SO}(2))=|B|^2+2-2\sqrt{(b_{11}+b_{22})^2+(b_{21}-b_{12})^2}\); substitution gives the displayed value. Thus this is a failure of the actual inequality, not a change of norm or orientation. The corresponding integral bound (5.22) also fails because the interpolation regions have positive area. In this example the circulation around the core is zero by source (5.17), so quantization imposes no excluded parameter condition.

Equation reference: eq:mean-bound. A valid replacement follows directly from the printed gradients. Define \[d=(\widetilde\mu-\mu,\widetilde\eta-\eta),\qquad
 a=\left(\frac{\mu+\widetilde\mu}{2},
          \frac{\eta+\widetilde\eta}{2}-1\right).\] For \(\Delta_3\), the first column of \(\widehat D_3-I\) is \(\frac{h}{2\ell}(1-h/x_2)d\), while the second is \(a+\frac{h^2x_1}{2\ell x_2^2}d\). The corresponding sign in the first column changes on \(\Delta_4\). Applying \(|v+w|^2\le2|v|^2+2|w|^2\) gives \[
 \operatorname{dist}^2(\widehat D_i,\mathrm{SO}(2))
 \le C|d|^2\left[
       \frac{h^2}{\ell^2}
       +\frac{h^4}{\ell^2}
         \left(\frac1{x_2^2}+\frac{x_1^2}{x_2^4}\right)\right]
       +2|a|^2.\] This retains the missing mean shear and a nonnegative squared mean compression. Merely squaring the source’s last term would still omit the common shear.

The specific parameters in source (5.37) satisfy \(\widetilde\mu=-\mu\) and \(\eta+\widetilde\eta=2\cos\alpha\). In that specialization, \(|a|^2=(1-\cos\alpha)^2=O(\alpha^4)\). report: Abstract: The retained March 2025 preprint of Nersesyan and Rissel is examined at the passage from localized transport controls to Navier–Stokes controls. Three central statements or derivations require correction: the displayed final control coefficients omit the normalization needed for zero mean; the scaling lemma allows forcing regularity and bounded-set uniformity for which exact shear solutions contradict its conclusion; and the small-time theorem places a single fixed control before an exact-limit quantifier that its approximate-control argument cannot supply. A separate sufficient condition for observability admits removable point discontinuities and is false as stated. Complete bounded arguments are given below. These findings do not constitute a counterexample to the main approximate-controllability conclusion. Repairs are stated only to the extent proved here.

Title: Regularity, control quantifiers, and compatibility
in localized Navier–Stokes control
# Identity, version, and scope

The target is M25-0404, Localized and degenerate controls for the incompressible Navier–Stokes system, by Vahagn Nersesyan and Manuel Rissel, DOI `10.1002/cpa.22246`. The reviewed file is arXiv:2212.01221v2, 10 March 2025, 38 pages [NR]; equivalence with a journal-final file has not been established. Printed and PDF page numbers agree. All source locators below refer to this retained version.

The full source text, including Appendix A and the bibliography, was read. Detailed checks concern the transport localization, preservation of the vorticity mean, the short-time scaling, and the control quantifiers. The generating-drift duality proof and the general cut construction were read and their dependencies mapped, but are not presented as completely independently verified proofs. Available acquisition records describe bounded supplement/code searches; no meaningful target-specific repository was identified there. This is a material-availability limit, not a mathematical defect. No author code was executed.

The source works on \(\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2\) with normalized Lebesgue measure. Its \(H^m\) consists of mean-zero scalar Sobolev functions. The operator \(\Upsilon(w,A)\) is the divergence-free velocity with curl \(w\) and spatial mean \(A\) [source (4.1), p. 22]. The return drift \(\bar y(t)\) is spatially constant, smooth, and has identity time-one flow. Write \[a(t)=\int_0^t\bar y(s)\,ds,\qquad a(1)\in(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2.\] The principal result is approximate controllability with finitely many scalar functions of time. It expressly allows the first control profiles to depend on time and does not claim to settle the original time-independent-profile problem [p. 5]. That distinction is preserved here.
# A normalization lost in the final control formula

Problem 1.  Equations (5.4), (5.14), and (5.15), on pp. 27 and 30, do not reproduce the mean-free control (3.9) on p. 18. For admissible coefficient functions, the displayed final formula can have nonzero spatial mean.

Equation reference: eq:c, eq:correctmean. Let \(K\) denote the number of covering squares, distinct from the Fourier index set \(\mathcal K\). Put \[c=\int_{\mathbb T^2}\chi\,dx,\qquad m(t)=\int_{\mathbb T^2}\widehat\eta(x,t)\,dx,\qquad
 A(t)=\int_0^t m(s)\,ds .\] Since the \(K\) translates of \(\chi\) form a partition of unity in (3.3)–(3.5), integration gives \[Kc=1,\qquad c=K^{-1}.                                      \] The earlier control (3.9) is \[\widetilde\eta
 =\widehat\eta-c^{-1}A(t)\bar y(t)\cdot\nabla\chi
                  -c^{-1}m(t)\chi .                        \] Its spatial integral is zero, because \(\int_{\mathbb T^2}\bar y(t)\cdot\nabla\chi\,dx=0\).

Equation reference: eq:badmean. The profiles in (5.4), however, are printed as \(\bar y\cdot\nabla\chi\) and \(\chi\), and the coefficients in (5.15) are \(-A(t)\) and \(-m(t)\), with no factors \(c^{-1}\). In reference time, even granting that displayed time dependence, their combination is therefore \[\eta_{\rm printed}
 =\widehat\eta-A(t)\bar y(t)\cdot\nabla\chi-m(t)\chi,
 \qquad
 \int_{\mathbb T^2}\eta_{\rm printed}\,dx=(1-K^{-1})m(t).                     \] The additional factor \(\sigma\) in (5.14) scales this nonzero mean; it does not remove it.
## An allowed choice with nonzero \(m\)

This discrepancy is not merely conditional on an impossible mean. Take the covering parameter \(K=36\), so its square side is \(l_K=2\pi/5<\pi/2\), and take \(\mathcal K=\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\), as in Example 5.4. Choose an admissible \(\omega\) containing the reference square and an admissible \(\Omega\) containing the prescribed cuts. The cutoff \(\chi\) is nonnegative and has positive integral \(1/36\).

During the first pause interval, \(\bar y=0\) and the return flow moves \(O_1=(0,l_K)^2\) to the reference square. At the end of that interval the replayed time \(\tau_1(t)\) tends to \(1\). By (3.11), \[\Xi(x,t)\longrightarrow Y(x,t,0)=x-p_\omega
 \quad\hbox{on }\operatorname{supp}\chi.\] Consequently \(\cos(\Xi_1(x,t))\) is strictly positive on that support for \(t\) sufficiently close to the pause endpoint: at the endpoint it is at least \(\cos(l_K)>0\), and the flow is continuous. Choose only the \((1,0)\) cosine coefficient nonzero, with a nonnegative, nonzero smooth time cutoff supported sufficiently close to replayed time \(1\). These are permissible \(L^2\) coefficient functions. Equation (3.10) then gives \(m(t)>0\) on a nonempty part of the first pause. On that part, \[\int_{\mathbb T^2}\eta_{\rm printed}\,dx=\frac{35}{36}m(t)>0.\] All drift, localization, and coefficient requirements used in this calculation are those of the actual construction.
## Impact and the bounded correction

The vorticity space is mean-zero, and the integral of the curl of a periodic vector field is zero. A nonzero-mean force cannot be the curl of the periodic velocity control asserted in (5.18). The failure occurs in the explicit construction used by Theorem 5.2 and the proof of Theorem 1.1, and is therefore assessed as Major under the core-derivation criterion.

Multiplying both correction coefficients by \(K\), or dividing both correction profiles by \(c\), restores exactly [eq:correctmean] (#eq:correctmean) and its mean-zero identity. This is an algebraic repair of this discrepancy, not a verification of the entire advertised profile representation. In particular, the source also lists the \(N+1\) profile as spatially fixed while writing it as \(\bar y(t)\cdot\nabla\chi\). The return drift uses horizontal and vertical translations. A treatment of that time dependence is still required to certify the exact claimed list of fixed profiles. No independent additional severity is assigned to that unresolved representation issue.

An implicit normalization \(\int_{\mathbb T^2}\chi\,dx=1\) would remove the numerical difference but conflicts with the actual partition-of-unity construction [eq:c] (#eq:c). Absorbing \(K\) into a profile is a valid correction, rather than an identity of the printed formulas.
# The scaling lemma exceeds its forcing assumptions

Problem 2.  Lemma 4.2, p. 23, assumes \(g,h\in L^2((0,1);H^{m-1})\) but asserts convergence in \(H^m\), uniformly over bounded sets of those forces. Both the regularity scope and the stated uniformity fail.

Its proof first asserts that the transported solution \(v\) stays bounded in \(C([0,1];H^{m+1})\) from precisely those assumptions [p. 24, after (4.7)]. Transport does not supply that gain. The following solutions also show failure of the conclusion, not just a missing justification.
## A common exact shear reduction

Set \(\nu=1\), \(m=1\), \(w_0=0\), and \(\widetilde U=0\). These meet all initial-state, viscosity, and mean-path requirements. For a mean-zero function of \(x_1\) alone, the zero-mean Biot–Savart velocity has only a second component. It is perpendicular to the vorticity gradient. Its nonlinear self-advection is thus identically zero. Translations by \(a(t)\) preserve this property.

Equation reference: eq:heat. For \(g(t,x)=f(x_1-a_1(t))\) and \(h=0\), the inviscid transport solution is \[v(t,x)=t f(x_1-a_1(t)),\qquad v(1,x)=f(x_1).\] At physical time \(\delta\), the Navier–Stokes vorticity in the moving coordinates solves a one-dimensional forced heat equation. If \(f(x_1)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_n\sin(nx_1)\), its exact endpoint is \[w_\delta(\delta,x)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_n F(\delta n^2)\sin(nx_1),
 \qquad F(z)=\frac{1-e^{-z}}{z}.                             \] Indeed, after putting \(s=t/\delta\) and removing the translation, each coefficient satisfies \(q_n'(s)+\delta n^2q_n(s)=b_n\), \(q_n(0)=0\). The return property removes the terminal translation. The construction works for the actual return drift; it does not replace that drift by zero.
## Failure even for a single fixed allowed \(g\)

Take \(b_n=1/n\). Then \(f\) is mean-zero and in \(H^0=L^2\), because \(\sum n^{-2}<\infty\), but \(f\notin H^1\), because \(\sum n^2n^{-2}=\infty\). Translations preserve its \(L^2\) norm, so \(g\in L^2((0,1);H^0)\) as required. The linear transport solution has \(v(1)=f\notin H^1\).

For every fixed \(\delta>0\), [eq:heat] (#eq:heat) has coefficients bounded by \(1/(\delta n^3)\), hence \(w_\delta(\delta)\in H^1\). Moreover, \[\|\partial_1(w_\delta(\delta)-f)\|_{L^2}^2
 =\frac12\sum_{n\ge1}\bigl(1-F(\delta n^2)\bigr)^2=\infty ,\] since \(F(\delta n^2)\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\). Thus the claimed \(H^1\) difference is not finite for any \(\delta>0\).

All source assumptions hold: \(w_0=0\in H^2\), \(g\in L^2H^0\), \(h=0\in L^2H^0\), and the mean path is zero apart from the prescribed return drift. The vorticity is a genuine shear solution, so no omitted nonlinear term repairs this example.
## Failure of bounded-set uniformity with smooth spatial data

Even restricting \(g\) to zero does not validate the asserted uniformity in \(h\). On \((0,1)\) define \[h_n(t,x)=
 \begin{cases}
 n\sin\!\bigl(n(x_1-a_1(t/\delta_n))\bigr),&0<t<\delta_n,\\
 0,&\delta_n\le t<1 .
 \end{cases}\] These are mean-free, spatially smooth forces with \(\|h_n\|_{L^2_tH^0}^2=1/2\). With \(g=0\) and \(w_0=0\), the inviscid comparison is \(v=0\), while the exact shear endpoint is \[w_{\delta_n}(\delta_n,x)=\frac{1-e^{-1}}{n}\sin(nx_1),
 \qquad
 \|\partial_1w_{\delta_n}(\delta_n)\|_{L^2}
 =\frac{1-e^{-1}}{\sqrt2}>0.\] Boundedness in \(L^2\) alone does not make integrals over shrinking time intervals uniformly small. This is the distinct obstruction in the estimate following source (4.12).
## What a valid restricted argument needs

The examples leave intact the possibility of a scaling statement for the particular smooth controls constructed earlier. A sufficient restricted hypothesis for the standard remainder argument is a uniform bound for \(v\) in \(C H^{m+1}\) together with \[\sup_{h\in\mathcal B}
 \int_0^\delta\|h(t)\|_{m-1}^2\,dt\longrightarrow0 .\] For example, fixed \(h\) has this absolute-continuity property. A bounded set in \(L^2_tH^{m-1}\) need not have it, as the \(h_n\) example demonstrates. The specific time-translated tails of one fixed prescribed force in Theorem 5.2 warrant their own estimate; (5.10) provides useful information of that kind. A complete corrected uniform theorem is not asserted here.

Lemma 4.2 is explicitly the scaling step used in Theorem 5.1, whose uniformity is then invoked in Theorem 5.2. Its false guarantee and unsupported regularity inference are assessed as Major. This does not show that the main theorem, under its stronger actual data and with appropriately quantified controls, is false.
# Fixed controls cannot have the asserted arbitrary exact limit

Problem 3.  Theorem 5.1, pp. 27–28, asserts that one collection \((\zeta_l)_{l=1}^N\subset L^2(0,1)\) can be fixed so that \(w_\delta(\delta)\to w_1\) in \(H^k\) as \(\delta\to0\) for arbitrary \(w_0,w_1\in H^{k+1}\). This places the control choice before the exact-limit quantifier. The proof instead chooses the controls after fixing an approximation tolerance.
## An admissible nonsmooth target

Equation reference: eq:target. Choose \(k=2\), \(w_0=0\), \(h=0\), \(\nu=1\), and \(U=0\), and let \[w_1(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-4}\sin(nx_1).                        \] This target has zero mean, \(\sum n^6n^{-8}<\infty\), and \(\sum n^8n^{-8}=\infty\). It belongs to \(H^3\) but not \(H^4\), so it meets the theorem’s target hypothesis and is not smooth. Zero velocity means are consistent with the mean-free initial and target vorticities.

For any single fixed collection of the asserted controls, put \(g=\widetilde\eta_{\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_N}\), using the correctly normalized earlier formula (3.9). Every spatial profile in (3.9)–(3.12) is smooth, with bounded derivatives of each order on the compact reference time interval. The generating drift is a finite Fourier sum with continuous time coefficients, so its flow and inverse have those spatial derivative bounds. Time replay, multiplication by \(\chi\), and the time-integrated scalar mean correction preserve this property. Therefore \[g\in L^2((0,1);H^q)\quad\hbox{for every integer }q\ge0.\] The constants may depend on the fixed controls, which is sufficient here. The corresponding transported endpoint \[v(1,x)=\int_0^1g(Y(x,1,s),s)\,ds\] is consequently in every \(H^q\), and is smooth.
## The actual limit for fixed smooth controls

Equation reference: eq:remainder, eq:bootstrap. The conclusion just used does not rely on the overbroad version of Lemma 4.2. For these fixed controls its relevant special case can be proved directly. Set \(W_\delta(s,x)=w_\delta(\delta s,x)\), let \(v\) solve \(\partial_sv+\bar y\cdot\nabla v=g\), \(v(0)=0\), and put \(r=W_\delta-v\), \(R=\Upsilon(r,0)\), \(V=\Upsilon(v,0)\). Then \[\begin{split}
 \partial_s r+\bar y\cdot\nabla r
 +\delta(V+R)\cdot\nabla r+\delta R\cdot\nabla v
 -\delta\Delta r
 &=\delta(\Delta v-V\cdot\nabla v),\\
 r(0)&=0 .
 \end{split}                                               \] The spatially constant translation term makes zero contribution to each differentiated \(L^2\) energy. The div–curl estimate gives \(\|R\|_{H^3}\le C\|r\|_{H^2}\). The differentiated product estimates in two dimensions and Young’s inequality thus give, for \(E=\|r\|_{H^2}^2\), \[E'(s)+\delta\|\nabla r\|_{H^2}^2
 \le C\delta(1+E(s)+E(s)^2),\qquad 0<s<1,                    \] where \(C\) depends on fixed Sobolev bounds of \(v\) and not on \(\delta\). For clarity, the transport commutator is bounded by \(C\delta\|V+R\|_{H^3}\|r\|_{H^2}^2\); the term \(R\cdot\nabla v\) is bounded using \(\|v\|_{H^3}\); and \(\delta\Delta v\) pairs with \(r\) through one integration by parts and half the dissipative term. These bounds imply [eq:bootstrap] (#eq:bootstrap). Smooth approximations justify the same energy inequality for the \(L^2\) time coefficients.

On any interval where \(E\le1\), [eq:bootstrap] (#eq:bootstrap) implies \(E(s)\le3C\delta\). Choosing \(\delta<(6C)^{-1}\) and using continuity closes this bound on \([0,1]\). Hence \[w_\delta(\delta)\longrightarrow v(1)\quad\hbox{in }H^2.\] If Theorem 5.1 held for [eq:target] (#eq:target) with a single fixed control, uniqueness of the \(H^2\) limit would force \(w_1=v(1)\). This is impossible because \(v(1)\) is smooth and \(w_1\notin H^4\).
## Quantifiers and impact

The source proof fixes an arbitrary \(\varepsilon>0\), uses Theorem 3.3 to choose a transport control whose terminal error is below \(\varepsilon\), and then takes \(\delta\) small. It establishes a tolerance-dependent control choice. It does not establish one control valid for every tolerance. Allowing a family \(\zeta^\varepsilon\) or \(\zeta^\delta\) changes the asserted quantifiers and avoids the smooth-endpoint contradiction.

The false exact-limit assertion is a central intermediate guarantee, subsequently used to select the activation time in Theorem 5.2. Its supported severity is Major. The main theorem asks for approximation at a given tolerance, which is weaker; the present counterexample does not contradict that conclusion.
# Point discontinuities do not imply observability

Problem 4.  The sufficient construction in Remark 2.5, p. 9, allows functions that are zero as \(L^2\) elements. Mere discontinuity at a dense countable set, even with left and right limits everywhere, does not imply Definition 2.4.

Take the allowed case \(T=1\), \(n=1\). Enumerate a countable dense subset \(D=\{d_1,d_2,\ldots\}\subset(0,1)\) without repetitions and define \[\phi(t)=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j}{\bf1}_{\{d_j\}}(t).\] This is a bounded measurable function. At any point, its left and right limits are both zero: given an error bound, exclude the finitely many points whose weights exceed it, and bound the remaining weights. It is continuous at every point outside \(D\) and discontinuous at every \(d_j\), since its value there is \(2^{-j}\) but its two one-sided limits are zero. All literal requirements of Remark 2.5 are met; the disjointness requirement is vacuous for one set.

Nevertheless \(\phi=0\) almost everywhere. On any subinterval take \(b=0\) and \(a_1=1\). Then \(b+a_1\phi=0\) in \(L^2\) although \(a_1\) does not vanish. This contradicts Definition 2.4. For any larger finite family, disjoint dense countable sets give the same example component by component.
## A verified stronger sufficient condition

Replace the point spikes by \[\psi_j(t)=\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}{\bf1}_{\{t>d_{j,n}\}},\] where the sets \(D_j=\{d_{j,n}\}_n\) are pairwise disjoint and dense. The series converges uniformly, is bounded, has left and right limits, and has a nonzero jump at each point of \(D_j\); every other \(\psi_i\) is continuous there. If \(b+\sum_j a_j\psi_j=0\) almost everywhere, its one-sided limits are zero. Taking their difference at \(d_{j,n}\) gives \(a_j(d_{j,n})2^{-n}=0\). Density and continuity imply \(a_j=0\) everywhere, and then \(b=0\). This proves observability for the strengthened construction.

The distinction is between a nonzero jump and a removable point discontinuity; it is not a choice of an \(L^2\) representative that can be ignored in a sufficient pointwise hypothesis. The main generating-drift theorem separately assumes observability, and the stronger construction supplies it. This local defect is therefore assessed as Minor; no failure of approximate controllability is inferred from this example.
# Dependency, surviving scope, and outcome

The supported highest impact is Major. Problem 1 affects the explicit mean-free force used in the transition to a velocity control. Problems 2 and 3 affect the scaling and limiting statements used in Theorems 5.1 and 5.2. Problem 4 concerns a local sufficient condition that can be strengthened directly.

The analysis also checks several safeguards against overstatement. The first control profiles are allowed to be time-dependent; the source itself distinguishes its conclusion from time-independent-mode controllability. The nonlinear term vanishes exactly in the shear counterexamples, rather than being neglected. The nonsmooth target in Problem 3 has exactly the required Sobolev regularity. Higher spatial regularity of the actual constructed controls is relevant counterevidence to treating every use of the scaling idea as invalid. A corrected proof of the main result would need to reconcile the explicit normalization and profile representation, the required uniform scaling class, and the tolerance-dependent control choice. That complete reconstruction and any author adoption are unverified.

Appendix A was read, but a complete general topological audit was not performed. In particular, if a periodic curl-free field is changed only inside \(\mathbb T\times I\), with \(I\) a proper horizontal interval, the spatial mean of its first component cannot change: \(\int_{\mathbb T}\Lambda_1(x_1,x_2)\,dx_1\) is independent of \(x_2\) and can be evaluated outside \(I\). This constrains the claimed change of that component by the local cut perturbation on p. 38. It is retained as an unresolved scope point, not an additional graded finding or a counterexample to Theorem A.1.

nu=m=1, w0=0 in H2, zero prescribed mean path apart from the actual return drift y(t); g,h in L2_t H0 with zero spatial means. Set a(t)=integral y, a(1) in (2pi Z)^2.
analysis: Its proof first asserts that the transported solution \(v\) stays bounded in \(C([0,1];H^{m+1})\) from precisely those assumptions [p. 24, after (4.7)]. Transport does not supply that gain. The following solutions also show failure of the conclusion, not just a missing justification.

Set \(\nu=1\), \(m=1\), \(w_0=0\), and \(\widetilde U=0\). These meet all initial-state, viscosity, and mean-path requirements. For a mean-zero function of \(x_1\) alone, the zero-mean Biot–Savart velocity has only a second component. It is perpendicular to the vorticity gradient. Its nonlinear self-advection is thus identically zero. Translations by \(a(t)\) preserve this property.

Equation reference: eq:heat. For \(g(t,x)=f(x_1-a_1(t))\) and \(h=0\), the inviscid transport solution is \[v(t,x)=t f(x_1-a_1(t)),\qquad v(1,x)=f(x_1).\] At physical time \(\delta\), the Navier–Stokes vorticity in the moving coordinates solves a one-dimensional forced heat equation. If \(f(x_1)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_n\sin(nx_1)\), its exact endpoint is \[w_\delta(\delta,x)=\sum_{n\ge1}b_n F(\delta n^2)\sin(nx_1),
 \qquad F(z)=\frac{1-e^{-z}}{z}.                             \] Indeed, after putting \(s=t/\delta\) and removing the translation, each coefficient satisfies \(q_n'(s)+\delta n^2q_n(s)=b_n\), \(q_n(0)=0\). The return property removes the terminal translation. The construction works for the actual return drift; it does not replace that drift by zero.

Take \(b_n=1/n\). Then \(f\) is mean-zero and in \(H^0=L^2\), because \(\sum n^{-2}<\infty\), but \(f\notin H^1\), because \(\sum n^2n^{-2}=\infty\). Translations preserve its \(L^2\) norm, so \(g\in L^2((0,1);H^0)\) as required. The linear transport solution has \(v(1)=f\notin H^1\).

For every fixed \(\delta>0\), [eq:heat] (#eq:heat) has coefficients bounded by \(1/(\delta n^3)\), hence \(w_\delta(\delta)\in H^1\). Moreover, \[\|\partial_1(w_\delta(\delta)-f)\|_{L^2}^2
 =\frac12\sum_{n\ge1}\bigl(1-F(\delta n^2)\bigr)^2=\infty ,\] since \(F(\delta n^2)\to0\) as \(n\to\infty\). Thus the claimed \(H^1\) difference is not finite for any \(\delta>0\).

All source assumptions hold: \(w_0=0\in H^2\), \(g\in L^2H^0\), \(h=0\in L^2H^0\), and the mean path is zero apart from the prescribed return drift. The vorticity is a genuine shear solution, so no omitted nonlinear term repairs this example.

Even restricting \(g\) to zero does not validate the asserted uniformity in \(h\). On \((0,1)\) define \[h_n(t,x)=
 \begin{cases}
 n\sin\!\bigl(n(x_1-a_1(t/\delta_n))\bigr),&0<t<\delta_n,\\
 0,&\delta_n\le t<1 .
 \end{cases}\] These are mean-free, spatially smooth forces with \(\|h_n\|_{L^2_tH^0}^2=1/2\). With \(g=0\) and \(w_0=0\), the inviscid comparison is \(v=0\), while the exact shear endpoint is \[w_{\delta_n}(\delta_n,x)=\frac{1-e^{-1}}{n}\sin(nx_1),
 \qquad
 \|\partial_1w_{\delta_n}(\delta_n)\|_{L^2}
 =\frac{1-e^{-1}}{\sqrt2}>0.\] Boundedness in \(L^2\) alone does not make integrals over shrinking time intervals uniformly small. This is the distinct obstruction in the estimate following source (4.12).

The examples leave intact the possibility of a scaling statement for the particular smooth controls constructed earlier. A sufficient restricted hypothesis for the standard remainder argument is a uniform bound for \(v\) in \(C H^{m+1}\) together with \[\sup_{h\in\mathcal B}
 \int_0^\delta\|h(t)\|_{m-1}^2\,dt\longrightarrow0 .\] For example, fixed \(h\) has this absolute-continuity property. A bounded set in \(L^2_tH^{m-1}\) need not have it, as the \(h_n\) example demonstrates. The specific time-translated tails of one fixed prescribed force in Theorem 5.2 warrant their own estimate; (5.10) provides useful information of that kind. A complete corrected uniform theorem is not asserted here.

Lemma 4.2 is explicitly the scaling step used in Theorem 5.1, whose uniformity is then invoked in Theorem 5.2. Its false guarantee and unsupported regularity inference are assessed as Major. This does not show that the main theorem, under its stronger actual data and with appropriately quantified controls, is false.

analysis: Equation reference: eq:target. Choose \(k=2\), \(w_0=0\), \(h=0\), \(\nu=1\), and \(U=0\), and let \[w_1(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-4}\sin(nx_1).                        \] This target has zero mean, \(\sum n^6n^{-8}<\infty\), and \(\sum n^8n^{-8}=\infty\). It belongs to \(H^3\) but not \(H^4\), so it meets the theorem’s target hypothesis and is not smooth. Zero velocity means are consistent with the mean-free initial and target vorticities.

For any single fixed collection of the asserted controls, put \(g=\widetilde\eta_{\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_N}\), using the correctly normalized earlier formula (3.9). Every spatial profile in (3.9)–(3.12) is smooth, with bounded derivatives of each order on the compact reference time interval. The generating drift is a finite Fourier sum with continuous time coefficients, so its flow and inverse have those spatial derivative bounds. Time replay, multiplication by \(\chi\), and the time-integrated scalar mean correction preserve this property. Therefore \[g\in L^2((0,1);H^q)\quad\hbox{for every integer }q\ge0.\] The constants may depend on the fixed controls, which is sufficient here. The corresponding transported endpoint \[v(1,x)=\int_0^1g(Y(x,1,s),s)\,ds\] is consequently in every \(H^q\), and is smooth.

Equation reference: eq:remainder, eq:bootstrap. The conclusion just used does not rely on the overbroad version of Lemma 4.2. For these fixed controls its relevant special case can be proved directly. Set \(W_\delta(s,x)=w_\delta(\delta s,x)\), let \(v\) solve \(\partial_sv+\bar y\cdot\nabla v=g\), \(v(0)=0\), and put \(r=W_\delta-v\), \(R=\Upsilon(r,0)\), \(V=\Upsilon(v,0)\). Then \[\begin{split}
 \partial_s r+\bar y\cdot\nabla r
 +\delta(V+R)\cdot\nabla r+\delta R\cdot\nabla v
 -\delta\Delta r
 &=\delta(\Delta v-V\cdot\nabla v),\\
 r(0)&=0 .
 \end{split}                                               \] The spatially constant translation term makes zero contribution to each differentiated \(L^2\) energy. The div–curl estimate gives \(\|R\|_{H^3}\le C\|r\|_{H^2}\). The differentiated product estimates in two dimensions and Young’s inequality thus give, for \(E=\|r\|_{H^2}^2\), \[E'(s)+\delta\|\nabla r\|_{H^2}^2
 \le C\delta(1+E(s)+E(s)^2),\qquad 0<s<1,                    \] where \(C\) depends on fixed Sobolev bounds of \(v\) and not on \(\delta\). For clarity, the transport commutator is bounded by \(C\delta\|V+R\|_{H^3}\|r\|_{H^2}^2\); the term \(R\cdot\nabla v\) is bounded using \(\|v\|_{H^3}\); and \(\delta\Delta v\) pairs with \(r\) through one integration by parts and half the dissipative term. These bounds imply [eq:bootstrap] (#eq:bootstrap). Smooth approximations justify the same energy inequality for the \(L^2\) time coefficients.

On any interval where \(E\le1\), [eq:bootstrap] (#eq:bootstrap) implies \(E(s)\le3C\delta\). Choosing \(\delta<(6C)^{-1}\) and using continuity closes this bound on \([0,1]\). Hence \[w_\delta(\delta)\longrightarrow v(1)\quad\hbox{in }H^2.\] If Theorem 5.1 held for [eq:target] (#eq:target) with a single fixed control, uniqueness of the \(H^2\) limit would force \(w_1=v(1)\). This is impossible because \(v(1)\) is smooth and \(w_1\notin H^4\).

The source proof fixes an arbitrary \(\varepsilon>0\), uses Theorem 3.3 to choose a transport control whose terminal error is below \(\varepsilon\), and then takes \(\delta\) small. It establishes a tolerance-dependent control choice. It does not establish one control valid for every tolerance. Allowing a family \(\zeta^\varepsilon\) or \(\zeta^\delta\) changes the asserted quantifiers and avoids the smooth-endpoint contradiction.

The false exact-limit assertion is a central intermediate guarantee, subsequently used to select the activation time in Theorem 5.2. Its supported severity is Major. The main theorem asks for approximation at a given tolerance, which is weaker; the present counterexample does not contradict that conclusion.

claim: Recorded check: The sufficient construction in Remark 2.5, p. 9, allows functions that are zero as \(L^2\) elements.
T=1,n=1 and D={d_j} countable dense without repetitions; phi(t)=sum 2^-j 1_{t=d_j}.
analysis: Take the allowed case \(T=1\), \(n=1\). Enumerate a countable dense subset \(D=\{d_1,d_2,\ldots\}\subset(0,1)\) without repetitions and define \[\phi(t)=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j}{\bf1}_{\{d_j\}}(t).\] This is a bounded measurable function. At any point, its left and right limits are both zero: given an error bound, exclude the finitely many points whose weights exceed it, and bound the remaining weights. It is continuous at every point outside \(D\) and discontinuous at every \(d_j\), since its value there is \(2^{-j}\) but its two one-sided limits are zero. All literal requirements of Remark 2.5 are met; the disjointness requirement is vacuous for one set.

Nevertheless \(\phi=0\) almost everywhere. On any subinterval take \(b=0\) and \(a_1=1\). Then \(b+a_1\phi=0\) in \(L^2\) although \(a_1\) does not vanish. This contradicts Definition 2.4. For any larger finite family, disjoint dense countable sets give the same example component by component.

Replace the point spikes by \[\psi_j(t)=\sum_{n\ge1}2^{-n}{\bf1}_{\{t>d_{j,n}\}},\] where the sets \(D_j=\{d_{j,n}\}_n\) are pairwise disjoint and dense. The series converges uniformly, is bounded, has left and right limits, and has a nonzero jump at each point of \(D_j\); every other \(\psi_i\) is continuous there. If \(b+\sum_j a_j\psi_j=0\) almost everywhere, its one-sided limits are zero. Taking their difference at \(d_{j,n}\) gives \(a_j(d_{j,n})2^{-n}=0\). Density and continuity imply \(a_j=0\) everywhere, and then \(b=0\). This proves observability for the strengthened construction.

The distinction is between a nonzero jump and a removable point discontinuity; it is not a choice of an \(L^2\) representative that can be ignored in a sufficient pointwise hypothesis. The main generating-drift theorem separately assumes observability, and the stronger construction supplies it. This local defect is therefore assessed as Minor; no failure of approximate controllability is inferred from this example.

Yet phi=0 almost everywhere, so b=0,a1=1 gives b+a1 phi=0 in L2 without a1=0. Pairwise disjoint dense sets extend the example to larger finite families.

report: Abstract: The highest supported assessment is Major. Two displayed steps in the construction are invalid: the Harnack proof applies discrete energy to an admissible density instead of its potential, and the uniform capacity proof interchanges the coarse level with the refinement depth. A third problem is a false direction of covariance in the stated energy-measure theorem. Complete counterarguments and local repairs are given. These findings do not establish that the corrected Harnack theorem, the existence of the Sobolev space, or the conditional attainment results are false. A separate vertex-count normalization defect is Minor. The selected 93-page author manuscript was read in full; the later long manuscript was consulted only at specified passages. # Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is by Mathav Murugan and Ryosuke Shimizu. Its target journal identifier is DOI 10.1002/cpa.22247 (https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.22247), associated with Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 78 (2025), no. 9, 1523–1608. # Conventions needed for the checks

For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), the paper uses \[\mathcal E_p^G(u)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\in E}|u(x)-u(y)|^p.\] A path \([x_0,\ldots,x_\ell]\) has length \(\ell\), while its weighted length is the sum of a nonnegative density over its vertices. Thus modulus is a vertex \(\ell^p\) minimization, not the discrete energy of the density [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~14--17]{short}].

For the carpet, \(V_n=\{1,\ldots,8\}^n\), and vertices are adjacent when the corresponding closed carpet cells meet. The word \(1\) denotes the lower-left subsquare and \(5\) the upper-right subsquare. For a word \(w\), \(S^k(w)\) is the family of its descendants \(k\) levels deeper. The probability measure \(m\) gives each level-\(n\) cell mass \(8^{-n}\). Put \[d_f=\frac{\log 8}{\log 3},\qquad
 d_w(p)=\frac{\log(8\rho(p))}{\log3}.\] The pushforward convention is the usual one: \((T_*\nu)(A)=\nu(T^{-1}(A))\). This is explicit in the setwise form of equation (8.16), page 60.
# Problem 1: the Harnack estimate uses the energy of the wrong function
## Claim, location, and impact

Equation reference: bad-harnack. In the proof of Theorem 5.4, page 25, write \[\begin{aligned}
 h_\epsilon&=h+\epsilon,\qquad D=\log M-\log m,\\
 u&=h_\epsilon^*=\operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}\!\left(\frac{\log h_\epsilon-\log m}{D}\right),\\
 v(x)&=\widetilde h_\epsilon^*(x)=\max_{y\sim x}|u(x)-u(y)|.
\end{aligned}\] The density \(v\) is admissible for paths between the low and high level sets. The first inequality in the displayed equation (5.4) nevertheless uses \[
 \operatorname{Mod}_p^G(\theta_{\min},\theta_{\max};\delta B)
 \le C\,\mathcal E^G_{p,\delta B}(v).\] Here \(C\) is the constant of Lemma 2.12 and depends on \(p\) and the degree bound, not on the radius. An admissible density controls modulus through its vertex \(\ell^p\) mass. Its discrete energy, which differentiates it once more, need not control modulus.

The following counterexample satisfies the actual hypotheses of Theorem 5.4. It shows that no fixed constant can make [bad-harnack] (#bad-harnack) valid. The defect is Major as a proof step: the estimate is used to derive Harnack, then Hölder cutoff regularity in Theorem 5.6, the uniform cutoff condition in Proposition 6.12, and the regularity part of the Sobolev construction. A valid local replacement is given below; no false-Harnack conclusion is asserted.
## All structural hypotheses on one fixed graph

Take the nearest-neighbor graph on \(\mathbb Z\), \(p=2\), \(d_f=1\), and \(\beta=2\). It is connected, simple, locally finite, and has degree two. For \(r\ge1\), \[\#B(x,r)=2\lceil r\rceil-1,\qquad
 r\le \#B(x,r)\le3r.\] Thus \(\mathrm{AR}(1)\) holds with fixed constants.

For two radius-\(r\) balls separated by at most \(\kappa r\), a shortest connecting path has at most \((\kappa+3)r\) distinct vertices; if the balls overlap, a nontrivial path through the intersection can be used. Every admissible density has squared mass at least the reciprocal of this vertex count by Cauchy–Schwarz. The same path has diameter at most \((\kappa+2)r\). Hence the graph satisfies \(\mathrm{BCL}_2(-1)\) with fixed constants, and \(-1=1-p=d_f-\beta<1\).

For the capacity condition, take a function equal to one on \(B(x,r)\), zero outside \(B(x,2r)\), and linear in the intervening distance. Each edge difference is at most \(1/r\), and at most \(4r+2\) edges contribute. Its energy is at most \(6/r\), which is at most \(6\#B(x,r)/r^2\). Replacing this function by its complement matches the paper’s orientation of the condenser. Thus \(\operatorname{cap}_{2,\le}(2)\) holds uniformly. These verifications use no external theorem and no assumption peculiar to the carpet.
## The positive harmonic family and its exact modulus

Equation reference: mMq. Let \(L\ge2\) be any fixed integer, as may be chosen after increasing the constant used in the proof, and set \[\delta_H=\frac1{8L},\qquad R=8Ln,\qquad
 \delta=4\delta_HL=\frac12,\qquad n\ge2,\qquad \epsilon=1.\] Define, at every integer \(j\), \[h(j)=2R+\max(-R,\min(j,R)).\] This function is strictly positive everywhere and affine on the ball \(B=B(0,R)\). It is therefore \(2\)-harmonic on every vertex of that ball, including those whose neighbors meet its boundary. The small ball is \(B(0,n)\), so \[
 m=(16L-1)n+2,\qquad M=(16L+1)n,\qquad q=M-m=2n-2>0.\] Choose the low path from \(-n+1\) to \(-R+1\) and the high path from \(n-1\) to \(R-1\). They meet the specified inner and outer boundaries and lie respectively in \(\{h_\epsilon\le m\}\) and \(\{h_\epsilon\ge M\}\), exactly as required on page 25.

Equation reference: mod-exact. Interpret the notation for paths in \(\delta B\) in its natural, most favorable sense: their endpoints belong to the portions of those two paths inside \(\delta B\). Every such connecting path visits all \(q+1=2n-1\) vertices of \[I=\{-n+1,-n+2,\ldots,n-1\}.\] The path consisting of \(I\) itself is allowed. Cauchy–Schwarz gives a lower bound \(1/(q+1)\) for any admissible squared mass, and the density \(1/(q+1)\) on \(I\), zero elsewhere, attains it. Consequently, \[
 \operatorname{Mod}_2^G(\theta_{\min},\theta_{\max};\delta B)=\frac1{q+1}.\]

## Verified local repair and alternative readings

Equation reference: harnack-repair. Use \(u=h_\epsilon^*\) as a capacitary potential. It equals zero on the low set and one on the high set. These sets are disjoint because \(m<M\). The modulus–capacity comparison and the \(1\)-Lipschitz truncation give, on the relevant local graph, \[
 \operatorname{Mod}_p^G(\theta_{\min},\theta_{\max};\delta B)
 \le C\operatorname{cap}_p^G(\theta_{\min},\theta_{\max};\delta B)
 \le C\mathcal E^G_{p,\delta B}(u)
 \le C D^{-p}\mathcal E^G_{p,\delta B}(\log h_\epsilon).\] If the local-energy convention includes the exterior boundary, the same argument on that enlarged induced graph gives the corresponding inequality. This restores the estimate needed before the log-Caccioppoli bound (5.5), with harmless changes to fixed constants. It is a general analytic replacement, not merely a check on \(\mathbb Z\).

The symbol \(v\) cannot consistently be read as \(u\): page 25 defines both separately, and the actual PDF shows the tilde in (5.4). Nor can \(\mathcal E(v)\) be read as \(\sum v^p\), because Definition 2.5 explicitly specifies edge differences. A likely notation slip is a plausible explanation of how the error arose, but the displayed essential inequality is false. The later long manuscript retains the same expression in (5.12), page 48 [long]; it supplies no correction at that location. This review verifies only the local replacement [harnack-repair] (#harnack-repair), not a separately rewritten proof of every downstream result.
# Problem 2: the capacity cutoff is built at the wrong scale
## Claim and an admissible finite example

Proposition 8.8(ii), page 53, is the step that establishes the uniform capacity upper bound used to verify Assumption 6.15 for the carpet. The proof defines \(n(R)\) by \[2\cdot3^{n(R)}<R\le2\cdot3^{n(R)+1},\] then chooses \(w\in V_{n(R)}\) and functions \(\varphi_w\) equal to one on \(S^{n-n(R)}(w)\). It defines \[\mathcal N(x,R)=
 \{w\in V_{n(R)}:B_{d_n}(x,R)\cap S^{n-n(R)}(w)\ne\varnothing\},
 \qquad
 \varphi=\sum_{w\in\mathcal N(x,R)}\varphi_w,\] and asserts \(\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset B_{d_n}(x,2R)\). This support assertion fails independently of the choice of the minimizers.

Take \[n=4,\qquad R=7,\qquad x=1111,\qquad y=1555.\] Then \(n(R)=1\). Encode a level-four cell by the integer coordinates of its lower-left corner in the \(81\) by \(81\) grid. The eight allowed ternary digits are \[(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(2,2),(1,2),(0,2),(0,1),\] in the paper’s word order. Thus \(x\) has coordinates \((0,0)\), \(y\) has coordinates \((26,26)\), and \(5555\) has coordinates \((80,80)\). Adjacent closed cells change each grid coordinate by at most one. It follows that \[d_4(x,y)\ge26>14=2R,\qquad
 \operatorname{diam}G_4\ge d_4(x,5555)\ge80>R.\] Therefore \(R\in[2a_*+1,\operatorname{diam}G_4)\), as required in the proof, and every parameter is in its stated range.

Equation reference: support-failure. Because \(x\in S^3(1)\), the coarse word \(1\) belongs to \(\mathcal N(x,7)\). Also \(y\in S^3(1)\), so every permitted \(\varphi_1\) has \(\varphi_1(y)=1\). All the summands are nonnegative. Hence \[
 \varphi(y)\ge1,\qquad y\notin B_{d_4}(x,14).\] This contradicts the stated support property. Clipping the sum at one would leave \(\varphi(y)=1\) and would not fix the scale mismatch.

A separate reviewer-authored reconstruction of the 4096-vertex graph gives \(d_4(1111,1555)=35\) and \(d_4(1111,5555)=107\). These finite graph calculations corroborate [support-failure] (#support-failure); the coordinate lower bounds already prove it without graph enumeration.
## A complete local replacement for the capacity argument
The refinement depth must correspond to the graph radius. The coarse word length is the remaining depth. The following choice also leaves enough space for neighboring cells.

Equation reference: k-scale. Use the constants \(A_1=3\), \(A_2=4\) verified in Proposition 8.4(iv), page 52. Put \(C_0=2A_1+A_2=10\). For \(R>60\), choose \(k\ge1\) such that \[
 20\cdot3^k<R\le60\cdot3^k.\] Since \(R<\operatorname{diam}G_n\le2\cdot3^n\), we have \(k<n\). Put \(j=n-k\) and define the fibers \(Q_w=S^k(w)\) for \(w\in V_j\).

For each \(w\), take a capacitary cutoff \(\psi_w\) equal to one on \(Q_w\), zero outside \[S^k(B_{d_j}(w,2)),\] and between zero and one. The definition of \(C_p^{(k)}\) in (8.3), and (8.6), give \[\mathcal E_p^{G_n}(\psi_w)\le C_p^{(k)}
 \le C\rho(p)^{-k}.\] This uses a finite condenser, so a minimizer exists also when \(p=1\); uniqueness is not needed. Reversing zero and one does not change its energy.

Let \(\mathcal N\) be the set of \(w\in V_j\) for which \(Q_w\) meets \(B_{d_n}(x,R)\), and set \[\psi=\min\left(1,\sum_{w\in\mathcal N}\psi_w\right).\] Then \(\psi=1\) on \(B_{d_n}(x,R)\). If \(\psi_w(y)>0\), the point \(y\) lies in a fiber indexed by either \(w\) or a neighbor of \(w\). Choose \(z\in Q_w\cap B_{d_n}(x,R)\). The two fiber-radius bounds in (6.3) and the center-distance bound (6.4) imply \[d_n(z,y)\le(2A_1+A_2)3^k=C_0\,3^k<R/2.\] Thus \(\operatorname{supp}\psi\subset B_{d_n}(x,3R/2)\subset B_{d_n}(x,2R)\).

For \(1\le R\le60\), the indicator of \(B_{d_n}(x,R)\) is a cutoff supported in \(B_{d_n}(x,2R)\) and has energy at most \(L_*\#B_{d_n}(x,R)\). Increasing the constant by \(60^{d_w(p)}\) gives the same required estimate. Together these two cases prove the local replacement of Proposition 8.8(ii), using its stated geometric and capacity-scaling inputs.
## Counterevidence, version comparison, and severity

The words and descendants are explicitly defined on page 50, so \(S^{n-n(R)}(w)\) cannot be read as a fiber of depth \(n(R)\) without changing the displayed construction. The failure [support-failure] (#support-failure) also holds if one replaces the sum by a maximum or clips it. The later long version repeats the same construction on page 99. Its subsequent Loewner argument on page 103 correctly uses words in \(V_{n-n(R)}\) and descendants \(S^{n(R)}\), supporting the intended distinction between the two scales [long].

This is Major as a construction/proof defect. The selected cutoff is not admissible for the ball condenser, so its asserted properties cannot prove the uniform capacity bound. That bound is an input to the Harnack/cutoff results and to Theorem 8.3(b), which supplies the assumptions used in the core Sobolev construction. Equation [capacity-repair] (#capacity-repair) restores this particular argument. It does not refute the uniform capacity theorem or certify every subsequent proof. The distinction in the scale indices, and the replacement of \(\rho(p)^{-n}\) by the refinement-scale factor \(\rho(p)^{-k}\), must be made in the proof rather than silently assumed.
# Problem 3: the energy-measure covariance has the inverse in the wrong place
## The stated identity and the actual set transport

Equation reference: bad-covariance, right-covariance. Theorem 1.2(v), page 6, and Proposition 8.15(e), page 61, assert, for all \(f\in\mathcal F_p\) and all \(\Phi\in D_4\), \[
 \Phi_*\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle=\Gamma_p\langle f\circ\Phi\rangle.\] Definition 8.1(3), page 49, includes the quarter-turn rotations, so these maps need not be involutions. Under the pushforward convention explicitly used in (8.16), the correct identity is \[
 \Gamma_p\langle f\circ\Phi\rangle=(\Phi^{-1})_*\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle,
 \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
 \Phi_*\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle=\Gamma_p\langle f\circ\Phi^{-1}\rangle.\]

On page 61, the proof defines \(C_{n,\Phi}\) through cells and their coding cylinders. The cylinders meet \(\chi^{-1}(\Phi(A))\). For closed \(A\), its displayed sums give \[m_p\langle f\circ\Phi\rangle(\Sigma_{C_n})
 =m_p\langle f\rangle(\Sigma_{C_{n,\Phi}}).\] Taking the decreasing-cylinder limits gives \[\Gamma_p\langle f\circ\Phi\rangle(A)=\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle(\Phi(A)),\] which is [right-covariance] (#right-covariance). In the final line the paper instead replaces the limiting set \(\chi^{-1}(\Phi(A))\) by \(\chi^{-1}(\Phi^{-1}(A))\). Regularity extends the correct equality from closed sets to all Borel sets. The scalar symmetry \(\mathcal E_p(f\circ\Phi)=\mathcal E_p(f)\) used earlier does not change this set-transport direction.
## A cutoff counterexample on the actual carpet

Fix any \(p\in(1,\infty)\) and let \(a=(-1,-1)\) be the lower-left corner. Let \(\Phi\) be the rotation through \(\pi/2\). In the normalized Euclidean metric of Definition 8.1, the points \(\Phi a\) and \(\Phi^{-1}a\) are distance one apart.

Take \(r=1/16\), let \(C=\overline{B_d(a,2r)}\), and choose the continuous cutoff \(f=\psi_{a,r}\in\mathcal F_p\cap C(K)\) supplied by Proposition 6.21, pages 38–39. It equals one on \(B_d(a,r)\) and vanishes outside \(C\). The ball is proper and there is a nonempty open region outside \(C\). Since \(m\) has full support, \(f\) is nonconstant even as an \(L^p(m)\) class. Thus \[
u:=\Gamma_p\langle fangle,\qquad 
u(K)=\mathcal E_p(f)>0.\] Weak locality, Lemma 8.16, gives \(
u(K\setminus C)=0\): on that open set \(f\) agrees with zero. No assumption that an ordinary coordinate function lies in \(\mathcal F_p\) is needed.

Equation reference: cov-counter. Now \(g=f\circ\Phi\) is continuous and belongs to \(\mathcal F_p\) by the scalar symmetry, and it vanishes outside \(\Phi^{-1}C\). The closed sets \(\Phi C\) and \(\Phi^{-1}C\) are disjoint: their centers are distance one apart and each has radius \(1/8\). The set \(\Phi C\) has an open neighborhood on which \(g=0\). Weak locality therefore yields \[\Gamma_p\langle gangle(\Phi C)=0.\] On the other hand, \[
 (\Phi_*
u)(\Phi C)=
u(C)=
u(K)=\mathcal E_p(f)>0.\] Equations [bad-covariance] (#bad-covariance) and [cov-counter] (#cov-counter) are incompatible. This uses only the paper’s cutoff, nondegeneracy, invariance of \(\mathcal F_p\), and weak locality properties; it does not assume the disputed covariance formula.
## Repair, valid special cases, and impact

Replacing either occurrence of \(\Phi\) in [bad-covariance] (#bad-covariance) by its inverse gives [right-covariance] (#right-covariance), which follows from the cylinder construction as shown above. The printed formula is valid for reflections and the half-turn, since \(\Phi^{-1}=\Phi\) in those cases. Those special cases do not cover \(D_4\). A different pushforward convention is excluded by the explicit inverse-image formula on page 60.

The actual images confirm the missing inverse in both the introductory theorem and the proof. The later long version retains it on page 8 and in the argument on pages 112–113 [long]. No author adoption of the correction was observed in the acquired versions; the final journal version and unacquired revisions remain outside this claim.

This finding is Major for the stated core covariance guarantee: one of the advertised properties of the constructed energy-measure family is false, with distinct masses on a concrete Borel set. The short inverse correction does not change the evidence for that failure. The existence, total mass, self-similarity, and scalar symmetry of the energy remain separate results, and no downstream collapse is asserted.
# Problem 4: vertex modulus requires \(L+1\), not \(L\)

Lemma 2.4, equation (2.2), page 16, states that the existence of a path of length at most \(L\) implies \(\operatorname{Mod}_p^G(\Theta)\ge L^{1-p}\). Page 14 defines length as the number of edges, while pages 14–15 sum a density over vertices.

Take the graph with two vertices \(a,b\) joined by one edge, let \(\Theta\) contain that path, and put \(p=2\), \(L=1\). All graph and parameter hypotheses hold. Its modulus is \[\inf_{\rho(a),\rho(b)\ge0,\ \rho(a)+\rho(b)\ge1}
      \bigl(\rho(a)^2+\rho(b)^2\bigr)=\frac12,\] attained by \(\rho(a)=\rho(b)=1/2\). The printed lower bound is one.

Equation reference: vertex-repair. The corrected universal bound is \[
 \operatorname{Mod}_p^G(\Theta)\ge(L+1)^{1-p},\qquad p\ge1.\] To prove it, choose the given path, whose number \(s\) of distinct vertices is at most \(L+1\). Hölder’s inequality gives \[1\le\sum_{\theta}\rho
 \le s^{1-1/p}\left(\sum_{\theta}\rho^p\right)^{1/p}.\] Thus \(\sum_V\rho^p\ge s^{1-p}\ge(L+1)^{1-p}\). For \(p=1\) the same result follows directly, and for a simple length-\(L\) path with no other paths the uniform density attains equality.

The actual PDF confirms both conventions, so this is not an extraction ambiguity. Reading \(L\) as a vertex count would give a valid alternate statement but would conflict with the defined length. Exact rational checks for \(p=2\), \(L=1,2,3,10\) are retained. The uses on pages 19–21 require only a fixed multiplicative bound, and \((L+1)^{1-p}\ge2^{1-p}L^{1-p}\) for \(L\ge1\). No change to the scaling exponent or central conclusion has been demonstrated. The assessment is therefore Minor, unlike the directly core steps in Problems 1–3.
# Other checked reasoning and limits

The weak monotonicity argument in Theorem 6.13 has the expected structure: the coarse difference is bounded by a fine-scale ball average, Poincaré supplies the factor \(3^{\ell(\beta-d_f)}\), and separation of fiber centers bounds the overlap when the local energies are summed. The subsequent \(\Gamma\)-limit construction uses recovery sequences and weak monotonicity for two-sided comparison with the discrete supremum; the Clarkson estimates give an equivalent uniformly convex norm. The separability step uses the continuous injection into the separable \(L^p(m)\) space together with reflexivity. These arguments were read and their dependencies traced; the cited abstract compactness theorems were not independently reproved.

For the Korevaar–Schoen comparison, the partition operators \(A_r\) converge in \(L^p\), while their energies are controlled by the small-scale difference quotients. Weak compactness and convex combinations then give the density of continuous functions in \(\mathcal F_p\). In using the global converse for an initially arbitrary \(L^p\) function with finite liminf energy, one first obtains a bounded sequence of \(A_r f\) in \(\mathcal F_p\) and identifies its weak limit with \(f\) through the \(L^p\) convergence. This supplies the finite-energy membership step implicit in the concise proof. The review found no independent counterexample to this argument.

The self-similarization in (8.14) averages the iterates of the energy operator. Uniform comparison and a diagonal subsequence on a dense set give a pointwise limiting seminorm. The difference between its shifted and unshifted Cesàro averages is a bounded endpoint term divided by the number of terms, which tends to zero. This explains why the proposed repairs to the earlier estimates can preserve the self-similar construction.

The cylinder masses in Section 8.2 are consistent by the scalar self-similarity identity. Weak locality follows by considering sufficiently small cells inside an open set. The chain-rule proof was read through its local \(C^1\) truncations and inverse-function argument. Continuity of \(f\) is retained where the paper requires it; the review does not extend these statements to arbitrary representatives of \(L^p(m)\) classes.

An apparent additional concern about Proposition 8.22 was rejected after visual inspection. Equation (8.27), page 66, has \(\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle(\overline U)\), with a closure that was lost in the plain-text extraction. The neighborhood-cover argument on page 67 is consistent with that closure. The review does not claim the stronger bound with \(\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle(U)\) for every Borel \(U\).

The Loewner comparison remains conditional on Assumption 9.16. The two-weight estimates lead to comparison on balls; Lemma 9.23 and its Whitney-cover proof give comparison of measures. The norm comparison is proved on continuous functions before extending to the completions. This matters because the two reference measures need not be comparable and their almost-everywhere equivalence classes are different. Theorem 9.26 explicitly introduces the identification map \(\iota\), rather than silently identifying arbitrary representatives. The final result does not prove that Ahlfors regular conformal dimension is attained. No additional defect in that conditional conclusion was established by the checks performed here.

Purely editorial slips, notational repairs with no demonstrated essential consequence, and unused edge cases are not promoted to additional substantive findings. No empirical claims, numerical convergence rates for a released algorithm, or author implementation provenance are inferred from the reviewer’s diagnostic calculations.
# Overall assessment and state

Problems 1 and 2 identify invalid steps directly used in the construction of the Sobolev space and its regularity. Problem 3 refutes the literal covariance guarantee of the main energy-measure theorem. Each has an explicitly verified local correction. These corrections are mathematical proposals in this report; they do not establish author adoption, and they do not amount to an independent acceptance of an amended paper. Problem 4 changes a local numerical bound and remains Minor because the uses checked require only multiplicative constants.

The defect is Major as a proof step: the estimate is used to derive Harnack, then Hölder cutoff regularity in Theorem 5.6, the uniform cutoff condition in Proposition 6.12, and the regularity part of the Sobolev construction. A valid local replacement is given below; no false-Harnack conclusion is asserted.

Fixed nearest-neighbor graph Z, p=2, d_f=1, beta=2, degree2; AR(1), BCL_2(-1) and cap_{2,<=}(2) established with fixed constants in report§3.2. For any fixed integer L>=2 set delta_H=1/(8L), R=8Ln,n>=2,delta=1/2,epsilon=1; h(j)=2R+clamp(j,-R,R) is positive and harmonic throughout B(0,R).
analysis:
Take the nearest-neighbor graph on \(\mathbb Z\), \(p=2\), \(d_f=1\), and \(\beta=2\). It is connected, simple, locally finite, and has degree two. For \(r\ge1\), \[\#B(x,r)=2\lceil r\rceil-1,\qquad
 r\le \#B(x,r)\le3r.\] Thus \(\mathrm{AR}(1)\) holds with fixed constants.

For two radius-\(r\) balls separated by at most \(\kappa r\), a shortest connecting path has at most \((\kappa+3)r\) distinct vertices; if the balls overlap, a nontrivial path through the intersection can be used. Every admissible density has squared mass at least the reciprocal of this vertex count by Cauchy–Schwarz. The same path has diameter at most \((\kappa+2)r\). Hence the graph satisfies \(\mathrm{BCL}_2(-1)\) with fixed constants, and \(-1=1-p=d_f-\beta<1\).

For the capacity condition, take a function equal to one on \(B(x,r)\), zero outside \(B(x,2r)\), and linear in the intervening distance. Each edge difference is at most \(1/r\), and at most \(4r+2\) edges contribute. Its energy is at most \(6/r\), which is at most \(6\#B(x,r)/r^2\). Replacing this function by its complement matches the paper’s orientation of the condenser. Thus \(\operatorname{cap}_{2,\le}(2)\) holds uniformly. These verifications use no external theorem and no assumption peculiar to the carpet.

Equation reference: mMq. Let \(L\ge2\) be any fixed integer, as may be chosen after increasing the constant used in the proof, and set \[\delta_H=\frac1{8L},\qquad R=8Ln,\qquad
 \delta=4\delta_HL=\frac12,\qquad n\ge2,\qquad \epsilon=1.\] Define, at every integer \(j\), \[h(j)=2R+\max(-R,\min(j,R)).\] This function is strictly positive everywhere and affine on the ball \(B=B(0,R)\). It is therefore \(2\)-harmonic on every vertex of that ball, including those whose neighbors meet its boundary. The small ball is \(B(0,n)\), so \[
 m=(16L-1)n+2,\qquad M=(16L+1)n,\qquad q=M-m=2n-2>0.\] Choose the low path from \(-n+1\) to \(-R+1\) and the high path from \(n-1\) to \(R-1\). They meet the specified inner and outer boundaries and lie respectively in \(\{h_\epsilon\le m\}\) and \(\{h_\epsilon\ge M\}\), exactly as required on page 25.

Equation reference: mod-exact. Interpret the notation for paths in \(\delta B\) in its natural, most favorable sense: their endpoints belong to the portions of those two paths inside \(\delta B\). Every such connecting path visits all \(q+1=2n-1\) vertices of \[I=\{-n+1,-n+2,\ldots,n-1\}.\] The path consisting of \(I\) itself is allowed. Cauchy–Schwarz gives a lower bound \(1/(q+1)\) for any admissible squared mass, and the density \(1/(q+1)\) on \(I\), zero elsewhere, attains it. Consequently, \[
 \operatorname{Mod}_2^G(\theta_{\min},\theta_{\max};\delta B)=\frac1{q+1}.\]
A reviewer-authored 80-digit decimal calculation, with exact rational bounds also retained, gives the following diagnostics for \(L=2\). The proof is [ratio] (#ratio), not numerical extrapolation.
\(n\) | Exact modulus | Modulus / density energy

Equation reference: harnack-repair. Use \(u=h_\epsilon^*\) as a capacitary potential. It equals zero on the low set and one on the high set. These sets are disjoint because \(m<M\). The modulus–capacity comparison and the \(1\)-Lipschitz truncation give, on the relevant local graph, \[
 \operatorname{Mod}_p^G(\theta_{\min},\theta_{\max};\delta B)
 \le C\operatorname{cap}_p^G(\theta_{\min},\theta_{\max};\delta B)
 \le C\mathcal E^G_{p,\delta B}(u)
 \le C D^{-p}\mathcal E^G_{p,\delta B}(\log h_\epsilon).\] If the local-energy convention includes the exterior boundary, the same argument on that enlarged induced graph gives the corresponding inequality. This restores the estimate needed before the log-Caccioppoli bound (5.5), with harmless changes to fixed constants. It is a general analytic replacement, not merely a check on \(\mathbb Z\).

The symbol \(v\) cannot consistently be read as \(u\): page 25 defines both separately, and the actual PDF shows the tilde in (5.4). Nor can \(\mathcal E(v)\) be read as \(\sum v^p\), because Definition 2.5 explicitly specifies edge differences. A likely notation slip is a plausible explanation of how the error arose, but the displayed essential inequality is false. The later long manuscript retains the same expression in (5.12), page 48 [long]; it supplies no correction at that location. This review verifies only the local replacement [harnack-repair] (#harnack-repair), not a separately rewritten proof of every downstream result.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: With m=(16L-1)n+2,M=(16L+1)n,q=2n-2, exact modulus is 1/(q+1). For a_j=log((m+j+1)/(m+j))/log(M/m), v has values a0,a0,a1,...,a(q-1) on the crossing interval and zero outside. E(v)=a0^2+a(q-1)^2+sum(aj-a(j-1))^2<=3(M/(mq))^2. Thus Mod/E >=(31/33)^2 q^2/[3(q+1)] ->infinity with all structural constants fixed.
