problems.title: the capacity cutoff is built at the wrong scale
problems.source_location: Selected source p53 Proposition8.8(ii), definitions pp49–50, geometry and capacity scaling pp51–52; later long v4 pp99,103.
claim:
Proposition 8.8(ii), page 53, is the step that establishes the uniform capacity upper bound used to verify Assumption 6.15 for the carpet. The proof defines \(n(R)\) by \[2\cdot3^{n(R)}<R\le2\cdot3^{n(R)+1},\] then chooses \(w\in V_{n(R)}\) and functions \(\varphi_w\) equal to one on \(S^{n-n(R)}(w)\). It defines \[\mathcal N(x,R)=
 \{w\in V_{n(R)}:B_{d_n}(x,R)\cap S^{n-n(R)}(w)\ne\varnothing\},
 \qquad
 \varphi=\sum_{w\in\mathcal N(x,R)}\varphi_w,\] and asserts \(\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset B_{d_n}(x,2R)\). This support assertion fails independently of the choice of the minimizers.

Take \[n=4,\qquad R=7,\qquad x=1111,\qquad y=1555.\] Then \(n(R)=1\). Encode a level-four cell by the integer coordinates of its lower-left corner in the \(81\) by \(81\) grid. The eight allowed ternary digits are \[(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(2,2),(1,2),(0,2),(0,1),\] in the paper’s word order. Thus \(x\) has coordinates \((0,0)\), \(y\) has coordinates \((26,26)\), and \(5555\) has coordinates \((80,80)\). Adjacent closed cells change each grid coordinate by at most one. It follows that \[d_4(x,y)\ge26>14=2R,\qquad
 \operatorname{diam}G_4\ge d_4(x,5555)\ge80>R.\] Therefore \(R\in[2a_*+1,\operatorname{diam}G_4)\), as required in the proof, and every parameter is in its stated range.

Equation reference: support-failure. Because \(x\in S^3(1)\), the coarse word \(1\) belongs to \(\mathcal N(x,7)\). Also \(y\in S^3(1)\), so every permitted \(\varphi_1\) has \(\varphi_1(y)=1\). All the summands are nonnegative. Hence \[
 \varphi(y)\ge1,\qquad y\notin B_{d_4}(x,14).\] This contradicts the stated support property. Clipping the sum at one would leave \(\varphi(y)=1\) and would not fix the scale mismatch.

A separate reviewer-authored reconstruction of the 4096-vertex graph gives \(d_4(1111,1555)=35\) and \(d_4(1111,5555)=107\). These finite graph calculations corroborate [support-failure] (#support-failure); the coordinate lower bounds already prove it without graph enumeration.
n=4,R=7,n(R)=1, x=1111, y=1555 in the paper's closed-cell adjacency graph. R satisfies [2a_*+1,diamG4), a_*=3. All cutoffs lie in [0,1] and equal1 on the specified descendants.
analysis: The refinement depth must correspond to the graph radius. The coarse word length is the remaining depth. The following choice also leaves enough space for neighboring cells.

Equation reference: k-scale. Use the constants \(A_1=3\), \(A_2=4\) verified in Proposition 8.4(iv), page 52. Put \(C_0=2A_1+A_2=10\). For \(R>60\), choose \(k\ge1\) such that \[
 20\cdot3^k<R\le60\cdot3^k.\] Since \(R<\operatorname{diam}G_n\le2\cdot3^n\), we have \(k<n\). Put \(j=n-k\) and define the fibers \(Q_w=S^k(w)\) for \(w\in V_j\).

For each \(w\), take a capacitary cutoff \(\psi_w\) equal to one on \(Q_w\), zero outside \[S^k(B_{d_j}(w,2)),\] and between zero and one. The definition of \(C_p^{(k)}\) in (8.3), and (8.6), give \[\mathcal E_p^{G_n}(\psi_w)\le C_p^{(k)}
 \le C\rho(p)^{-k}.\] This uses a finite condenser, so a minimizer exists also when \(p=1\); uniqueness is not needed. Reversing zero and one does not change its energy.

Let \(\mathcal N\) be the set of \(w\in V_j\) for which \(Q_w\) meets \(B_{d_n}(x,R)\), and set \[\psi=\min\left(1,\sum_{w\in\mathcal N}\psi_w\right).\] Then \(\psi=1\) on \(B_{d_n}(x,R)\). If \(\psi_w(y)>0\), the point \(y\) lies in a fiber indexed by either \(w\) or a neighbor of \(w\). Choose \(z\in Q_w\cap B_{d_n}(x,R)\). The two fiber-radius bounds in (6.3) and the center-distance bound (6.4) imply \[d_n(z,y)\le(2A_1+A_2)3^k=C_0\,3^k<R/2.\] Thus \(\operatorname{supp}\psi\subset B_{d_n}(x,3R/2)\subset B_{d_n}(x,2R)\).

For \(1\le R\le60\), the indicator of \(B_{d_n}(x,R)\) is a cutoff supported in \(B_{d_n}(x,2R)\) and has energy at most \(L_*\#B_{d_n}(x,R)\). Increasing the constant by \(60^{d_w(p)}\) gives the same required estimate. Together these two cases prove the local replacement of Proposition 8.8(ii), using its stated geometric and capacity-scaling inputs.
result: The words and descendants are explicitly defined on page 50, so \(S^{n-n(R)}(w)\) cannot be read as a fiber of depth \(n(R)\) without changing the displayed construction. The failure [support-failure] (#support-failure) also holds if one replaces the sum by a maximum or clips it. The later long version repeats the same construction on page 99. Its subsequent Loewner argument on page 103 correctly uses words in \(V_{n-n(R)}\) and descendants \(S^{n(R)}\), supporting the intended distinction between the two scales [long].

This is Major as a construction/proof defect. The selected cutoff is not admissible for the ball condenser, so its asserted properties cannot prove the uniform capacity bound. That bound is an input to the Harnack/cutoff results and to Theorem 8.3(b), which supplies the assumptions used in the core Sobolev construction. Equation [capacity-repair] (#capacity-repair) restores this particular argument. It does not refute the uniform capacity theorem or certify every subsequent proof. The distinction in the scale indices, and the replacement of \(\rho(p)^{-n}\) by the refinement-scale factor \(\rho(p)^{-k}\), must be made in the proof rather than silently assumed.

Word1 is in N(x,R), and y in S^3(1), so every allowed phi1(y)=1 and the nonnegative sum phi(y)>=1 outside the asserted support. Reviewer graph BFS additionally gives distances35 and107; enumeration is not needed for the analytic contradiction.

problems.title: the energy-measure covariance has the inverse in the wrong place
problems.source_location: Selected source p6 Theorem1.2(v), p61 Proposition8.15(e) and its proof, pushforward convention p60(8.16), D4 p49; cutoff pp38–39, weak locality pp61–62. Long v4 pp8,112–113.
claim: Recorded check: the energy-measure covariance has the inverse in the wrong place

Any p>1 on the actual carpet. Let a=(-1,-1), Phi the quarter-turn pi/2, r=1/16, C=closedB(a,2r). The valid continuous Fp cutoff f=psi_{a,r} is1 on B(a,r), zero outside C, and nonconstant in Lp(m) by full support. Scalar symmetry gives f composed Phi in Fp; locality applies to open zero regions.
analysis:
Equation reference: bad-covariance, right-covariance. Theorem 1.2(v), page 6, and Proposition 8.15(e), page 61, assert, for all \(f\in\mathcal F_p\) and all \(\Phi\in D_4\), \[
 \Phi_*\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle=\Gamma_p\langle f\circ\Phi\rangle.\] Definition 8.1(3), page 49, includes the quarter-turn rotations, so these maps need not be involutions. Under the pushforward convention explicitly used in (8.16), the correct identity is \[
 \Gamma_p\langle f\circ\Phi\rangle=(\Phi^{-1})_*\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle,
 \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
 \Phi_*\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle=\Gamma_p\langle f\circ\Phi^{-1}\rangle.\]

On page 61, the proof defines \(C_{n,\Phi}\) through cells and their coding cylinders. The cylinders meet \(\chi^{-1}(\Phi(A))\). For closed \(A\), its displayed sums give \[m_p\langle f\circ\Phi\rangle(\Sigma_{C_n})
 =m_p\langle f\rangle(\Sigma_{C_{n,\Phi}}).\] Taking the decreasing-cylinder limits gives \[\Gamma_p\langle f\circ\Phi\rangle(A)=\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle(\Phi(A)),\] which is [right-covariance] (#right-covariance). In the final line the paper instead replaces the limiting set \(\chi^{-1}(\Phi(A))\) by \(\chi^{-1}(\Phi^{-1}(A))\). Regularity extends the correct equality from closed sets to all Borel sets. u)(\Phi C)=

problems.title: vertex modulus requires \(L+1\), not \(L\)
problems.source_location: Selected source pp14–16, Lemma2.4 equation(2.2), uses checked pp19–21.
claim: Recorded check: vertex modulus requires \(L+1\), not \(L\)
The finite connected simple two-vertex one-edge graph, path family containing that path, p=2,L=1. Defined path length counts edges, density length sums over the path's vertex set.
analysis: Lemma 2.4, equation (2.2), page 16, states that the existence of a path of length at most \(L\) implies \(\operatorname{Mod}_p^G(\Theta)\ge L^{1-p}\). Page 14 defines length as the number of edges, while pages 14–15 sum a density over vertices.

Take the graph with two vertices \(a,b\) joined by one edge, let \(\Theta\) contain that path, and put \(p=2\), \(L=1\). All graph and parameter hypotheses hold. Its modulus is \[\inf_{\rho(a),\rho(b)\ge0,\ \rho(a)+\rho(b)\ge1}
      \bigl(\rho(a)^2+\rho(b)^2\bigr)=\frac12,\] attained by \(\rho(a)=\rho(b)=1/2\). The printed lower bound is one.

Equation reference: vertex-repair. The corrected universal bound is \[
 \operatorname{Mod}_p^G(\Theta)\ge(L+1)^{1-p},\qquad p\ge1.\] To prove it, choose the given path, whose number \(s\) of distinct vertices is at most \(L+1\). Hölder’s inequality gives \[1\le\sum_{\theta}\rho
 \le s^{1-1/p}\left(\sum_{\theta}\rho^p\right)^{1/p}.\] Thus \(\sum_V\rho^p\ge s^{1-p}\ge(L+1)^{1-p}\). For \(p=1\) the same result follows directly, and for a simple length-\(L\) path with no other paths the uniform density attains equality.

The actual PDF confirms both conventions, so this is not an extraction ambiguity. Reading \(L\) as a vertex count would give a valid alternate statement but would conflict with the defined length. Exact rational checks for \(p=2\), \(L=1,2,3,10\) are retained. The uses on pages 19–21 require only a fixed multiplicative bound, and \((L+1)^{1-p}\ge2^{1-p}L^{1-p}\) for \(L\ge1\). No change to the scaling exponent or central conclusion has been demonstrated. The assessment is therefore Minor, unlike the directly core steps in Problems 1–3.

report: Abstract: The acquired preprint constructs special Lagrangian pairs of pants by inductive Dirichlet problems and identifies their ends with lower-dimensional cylinders. One substantive compatibility defect is established in the explicit prescription for a general positive definite ambient matrix. The printed face potential uses a principal submatrix, whereas the special Lagrangian phase of the asserted cylinder depends on its Schur complement. An admissible three-dimensional example has a nonzero exact phase residual, so the printed prescription and the claimed smooth cylindrical asymptote cannot both hold. A local replacement restores the cylinder’s phase condition; the full construction after that replacement is not verified here. The supported impact is Major, with scientific adjudication pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Metric compatibility in
Special Lagrangian pair of pants
# Paper identity and checked scope

The reviewed work is Yang Li, Special Lagrangian pair of pants, arXiv:2310.15443v1, submitted 24 October 2023; the PDF title page is dated 25 October 2023 [Li]. The acquired source has 36 pages. All page references below use its printed page numbers, which agree with the PDF page indices counted from one. The associated publication is Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 78(7) (2025), 1320–1356, DOI `10.1002/cpa.22248`. The published layout was not acquired for comparison, so this report does not assert that the finding is present in the journal version.

The complete source text, including the appendix and references, was read. The detailed checks concern the explicit two-dimensional potential, its use as three-dimensional face data, the phase of the comparison cylinder, and the dependence of the asymptotic argument on that cylinder. The barrier, current, tangent-cone and topology arguments were read and their dependencies mapped. Their external PDE and geometric-measure-theory inputs were not independently re-proved. Additional local checks of the concavity argument in Lemma 2.16 and of the iteration exponents in Lemma 3.19 did not establish another substantive defect. The coverage record distinguishes this full reading from complete verification of every proof.
# The prescribed geometry

Equation reference: eq:forms. Write the ambient matrix of source §§1.2 and 2.1 (pp. 3 and 6) as \(G=(g_{ij})\), to distinguish it from its inverse. The ambient forms are \[
 \omega=\sum_{j=1}^n dx_j\wedge dy_j,\qquad
 \Omega_G=\bigwedge_{j=1}^n\left(dx_j+\mathrm i\sum_k g_{jk}dy_k\right),
 \qquad G=G^{T}>0.\] A phase-\(\theta\) special Lagrangian must satisfy \(\omega|_L=0\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(e^{-\mathrm i\theta}\Omega_G)|_L=0\). A positive real normalization of the holomorphic volume form does not affect the latter equation.

Equation reference: eq:block, eq:H. For \(n=3\), partition the allowed matrix as \[
 G=\begin{pmatrix}A&b\\ b^{T}&c\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 A\in\mathbb R^{2\times2},\quad c>0,\quad
 S=A-\frac{bb^{T}}c>0.\] The relative interior of the face \(x_3=0\) is \[\Delta_2^\circ=\{x_1>0,\ x_2>0,\ x_1+x_2<\pi\}.\] With \(L'(t)=\log\sin t\), put \[\Phi(x_1,x_2)=L(x_1)+L(x_2)-L(x_1+x_2).\] The identity \(L(t)+L(\pi-t)=L(\pi)\) makes this the numerator of source equation (6), p. 8. Its Hessian is \[
 H_\Phi=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \cot x_1-\cot(x_1+x_2)&-\cot(x_1+x_2)\\
 -\cot(x_1+x_2)&\cot x_2-\cot(x_1+x_2)
 \end{pmatrix}>0,\qquad \det H_\Phi=1.\] These are source Lemma 2.4, p. 9, and also follow directly by differentiation and the cotangent addition identity.
# Problem 1: the face potential and its claimed cylinder are incompatible

Problem 1 (General ambient matrices and the inductive asymptote).  For the literal face prescription [eq:printed] (#eq:printed), the product \(L_2\times\mathbb R_{y_3}\) in Theorem 1.3(2), p. 4, and Lemma 3.8, p. 29, need not be phase-\(\pi\) special Lagrangian in [eq:forms] (#eq:forms). It therefore cannot be the asserted \(C^{k,\alpha}\), in particular \(C^1\), asymptotic limit of a phase-\(\pi\) special Lagrangian.
## Complete local calculation

Equation reference: eq:cyl. Parameterize the portion of the proposed cylinder over \(\Delta_2^\circ\) by \[
 F(x_1,x_2,t)=
 (x_1,x_2,0;\ \partial_1u_A,\partial_2u_A,t),\qquad t\in\mathbb R.\] The pullback of \(\omega\) is zero: the \(x_1,x_2\) contribution is the antisymmetric part of the Hessian, and \(dx_3=0\). Thus this is indeed a Lagrangian cylinder, and failure below concerns the special phase rather than the Lagrangian condition.

Equation reference: eq:factor, eq:residual, eq:generaldefect. Proposition 1.  For any real symmetric Hessian \(H\) in [eq:cyl] (#eq:cyl), \[\begin{aligned}
 \Omega_G(F_{x_1},F_{x_2},F_t)
 &=\mathrm ic\det(I_2+\mathrm iSH),\\
 \operatorname{Im}\!\left(e^{-\mathrm i\pi}
 \Omega_G(F_{x_1},F_{x_2},F_t)\right)
 &=c\{\det S\det H-1\}.\end{aligned}\] For the printed potential [eq:printed] (#eq:printed), this residual equals \[
 -b^{T}A^{-1}b.\] Consequently it is nonzero whenever \(b\ne0\).

Proof. Evaluating the three complex one-forms in [eq:forms] (#eq:forms) on the tangent basis gives the matrix \[Z=\begin{pmatrix}I_2+\mathrm iAH&\mathrm ib\\
                  \mathrm ib^{T}H&\mathrm ic\end{pmatrix}.\] Taking its Schur complement with respect to the nonzero entry \(\mathrm ic\) gives [eq:factor] (#eq:factor). For any real \(2\times2\) matrix \(SH\), \[\det(I_2+\mathrm iSH)=1-\det(SH)+\mathrm i\operatorname{tr}(SH).\] Since \(e^{-\mathrm i\pi}=-1\), this proves [eq:residual] (#eq:residual). For [eq:printed] (#eq:printed), \(\det H=1/\det A\). The matrix determinant lemma gives \[\det S=\det A\left(1-\frac{b^{T}A^{-1}b}{c}\right),\] so substitution gives [eq:generaldefect] (#eq:generaldefect). Positive definiteness of \(A\) makes \(b^{T}A^{-1}b>0\) for nonzero \(b\). ◻

Equation reference: eq:example, eq:exact. Here is a fully explicit admissible example: \[
 G=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1/2\\0&1&0\\1/2&0&1\end{pmatrix},
 \quad A=I_2,\quad c=1,\quad b=\binom{1/2}{0},
 \quad S=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.\] The eigenvalues of \(G\) are \(1/2,1,3/2\), so it obeys the source’s full ambient positive-definiteness condition. Take \(x_1=x_2=\pi/3\), an interior point of the face, and arbitrary \(t\). The prescribed potential is exactly \(\Phi\), its two first derivatives vanish at this point, and \[H=\frac1{\sqrt3}\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det H=1.\] Direct evaluation on the tangent basis gives \[
 \Omega_G(F_{x_1},F_{x_2},F_t)
   =-\frac{7}{2\sqrt3}+\frac{\mathrm i}{4},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Im}(e^{-\mathrm i\pi}\Omega_G)=-\frac14.\] The cylinder is smooth, embedded locally and Lagrangian; the dimension, domain, potential, ambient matrix and claimed phase all agree with the source prescription. The nonzero residual is independent of \(t\), so moving sufficiently far into the claimed end cannot remove it.
## Why this contradicts the stated asymptotic identification

Assume the phase-\(\pi\) submanifold supplied by the construction has the normal-graph asymptote in Theorem 1.3(2) with this prescribed \(L_2\). Translate its \(y_3\to-\infty\) end to a fixed neighborhood of the point in [eq:example] (#eq:example). The ambient forms [eq:forms] (#eq:forms) are invariant under these translations. The stated exponential \(C^{k,\alpha}\) estimate implies \(C^1\) convergence to the cylinder [eq:cyl] (#eq:cyl). Pullback of a fixed smooth three-form is continuous under \(C^1\) convergence of the local parameterizations. Therefore the limiting cylinder must satisfy \(\operatorname{Im}(e^{-\mathrm i\pi}\Omega_G)=0\), contrary to [eq:exact] (#eq:exact). This argument does not require constructing a hypothetical \(u_3\) numerically or deciding whether the printed Dirichlet problem itself has a solution: it proves that the explicit prescription and the stated special-Lagrangian asymptote cannot hold together.

The same incompatibility occurs in the comparison step before that conclusion. Proposition 2.30, p. 23, treats the lower-dimensional function, extended independently of the new momentum variable, as a solution of the same transformed special Lagrangian equation. Lemma 3.8, p. 29, uses this identification to write a homogeneous elliptic equation for the difference of the two potentials. In the admissible example the proposed background cylinder fails the ambient phase equation, so this justification does not apply to the printed face data.
## Alternative readings and valid cases

This calculation uses the lower-index matrix in the actual printed \(\Omega_G\), not an OCR interpretation of \(G^{-1}\). Source p. 6 separately writes the position-space inner product using \(g^{ij}\). Both the ambient form and the explicit denominator on p. 10 were checked in the page images.

There is a natural intended interpretation under which the construction might be repaired: use the metric induced on the face in the position-space metric. Indeed, block inversion yields \[(G^{-1})_{\{1,2\},\{1,2\}}=S^{-1}.\] Its inverse, which is the matrix appearing in the reduced holomorphic volume form, is \(S\). Under this interpretation the denominator should be \(\sqrt{\det S}\), not the explicit ambient principal minor \(\sqrt{g_{11}g_{22}-g_{12}^{\,2}}\) in [eq:printed] (#eq:printed). Silently changing the meaning of those displayed coefficients does not validate the formula as written. A linear change that makes the ambient metric standard also changes the simplex coordinates and the face data; it cannot be used while retaining the unchanged printed prescription.

For an orthogonal splitting \(b=0\), \(S=A\), and this obstruction disappears. The two-dimensional formula itself remains valid. Reversing orientation, using the phase modulo \(\pi\), multiplying \(\Omega_G\) by a nonzero positive normalizing constant, or adding an affine function to \(u_A\) cannot make a nonzero phase residual vanish. No conclusion about failure of every standard-metric construction is drawn from this example.
# A verified local replacement and its limit

Equation reference: eq:repair. The exact compatible replacement for this cylinder is \[
 u_S(x_1,x_2)=\frac{\Phi(x_1,x_2)}{\sqrt{\det S}}.\] It is smooth and strictly convex on \(\Delta_2^\circ\), with \(\det D^2u_S=1/\det S\). Proposition Proposition 1 (#prop:phase) proves that the resulting cylinder is phase-\(\pi\) special Lagrangian. Its orientation may be chosen positively because \[e^{-\mathrm i\pi}\Omega_G(F_{x_1},F_{x_2},F_t)
     =c\,\operatorname{tr}(SD^2u_S)>0.\] For [eq:example] (#eq:example), this replaces \(u_A\) by \((2/\sqrt3)u_A\). At the displayed point the corrected Hessian is \[D^2u_S=\begin{pmatrix}4/3&2/3\\2/3&4/3\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \Omega_G(F_{x_1},F_{x_2},F_t)=-7/3,\] and the phase residual is exactly zero.

This proves a local statement about the cylinder and identifies the appropriate reduced matrix. It does not supply a complete repaired theorem: the all-face inductive prescription, its compatibility at intersections, barrier estimates, transformed PDEs and subsequent geometric argument must be reconciled with the revised metric choices. No author adoption of this replacement is known from the inspected materials.
# Impact and conclusion
Dimension | State
Issue assessment | Major: explicit face data and claimed cylinder are incompatible for an allowed matrix.
Repair verification | Cylinder phase and Lagrangian condition verified for the Schur-complement replacement.
Global revised theorem | Not verified.
Author adoption | Unknown.
Scientific adjudication | Pending; no human review or independent acceptance performed.
# Supporting checks

The source PDF SHA256 is \[\text{\texttt{1c702ba665ad22ed3015c2ac056ff8da50b8312fd11a85530a5321845cbc30f6}}.\] The source manifest and exact file inventories are retained in the matching verification records. It checks the block determinant identity, the general residual identity, the explicit eigenvalues, the Lagrangian pullback, the residual \(-1/4\), and the corrected residual \(0\). The geometric \(C^1\)-limit argument is the analytic proof in the report, not a theorem certified by the script. No author code was run. Missing optional computational code is not treated as a mathematical defect.

report: Abstract: The retained 72-page author manuscript of Halpern and Rauch is examined through its stretched Maxwell, Helmholtz and split-system arguments. Four substantive failures are demonstrated: the boundary spectral identity has incorrect scaling and signs; a complex stretched Rellich identity fails for a constant field; the asserted \(H^2\) solvability is incompatible with the allowed \(L^2\) currents; and the split reconstruction omits the forcing term. A separate general stretching lemma assumes insufficient spatial regularity for holomorphic continuation. Exact counterexamples and bounded algebraic corrections are supplied where justified. These findings concern the acquired manuscript. They do not refute the principal weighted \(L^2\) well-posedness conclusion or establish equivalence with the journal-final version.
Title: Boundary identities and source regularity in a Maxwell PML manuscript
# Identity, scope and definitions

The target is M25-0407, Laurence Halpern and Jeffrey Rauch, Stability of perfectly matched layers for Maxwell’s equations in rectangular solids, DOI 10.1002/cpa.22249 (https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.22249). The reviewed source is the undated author-hosted file `2025CPAM.pdf`, retrieved on 27 October 2026, with 72 pages [HR]. PDF and printed page numbers agree. The acquired bytes have SHA256 \[\texttt{51c36487e49c348cad99ecaf828b3a55f21}\] \[\texttt{bd9382322ee251d150c83d842cf3e}.\] The line break is typographical. The source manifest retains the uninterrupted hash. No accepted-manuscript or version-of-record label is inferred from the filename. The author listing’s issue number and the deposited journal metadata differ; that bibliographic discrepancy is outside the mathematical assessment.

The complete source text was read. Detailed checks covered the spectral projectors, the principal boundary symbol, stretched Green identities, the two boundary estimates, the source regularity in the Helmholtz inversion, and the split reconstruction. The source’s external elliptic, trace, Fredholm and Paley–Wiener results were not independently re-proved. No author code was executed. The report establishes the particular failures below, not exhaustive correctness or incorrectness of every argument.

Write \(W=(E,B)\) and \[A(\xi)(E,B)=(-\xi\times B,\xi\times E),\qquad
 \widetilde\partial_j=\frac{\tau}{\tau+\sigma_j(x_j)}\partial_j .\] The absorptions are nonnegative smooth functions of one coordinate, vanish on the domain of interest \(Q_I\), and have bounded derivatives of every order [Retained latex: \cite[p.~7, Assumption 1.2]{HR}]. Zero absorption is allowed. For the examples with nonzero absorption, take \[Q=(-3,3)^3,\qquad Q_I=(-1,1)^3,\] and choose a smooth bump \(b:\mathbb R\to[0,1]\), supported in \((3/2,5/2)\), equal to one near \(2\). Set \(\sigma_2=b\), \(\sigma_1=\sigma_3=0\). These coefficients satisfy all the stated absorption hypotheses. Choose the smoothing \(Q^\delta\) sufficiently close to \(Q\) that \((0,2,0)\) is an interior point and a neighborhood of \((3,2,0)\) remains a flat boundary patch. This is permitted by Definition 3.1.

For the stretched normal define, as in source Definition 3.3, \[\Pi=\prod_{j=1}^3\frac{\tau+\sigma_j}{\tau},\qquad
 \mathcal M_{ii}=\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{\tau+\sigma_j}{\tau},
 \qquad m=\mathcal M\nu,\qquad s=(m\cdot m)^{1/2}.\] For positive real \(\tau\), \(s=|m|\). For the sufficiently large complex parameters used by the source, the square root is the branch continued from positive real values. Spectral projectors \(\pi^\pm(m)\) refer to the eigenspaces of \(A(m)\) with eigenvalues \(\pm s\). Set \[P_{\mathrm{tan}}(E,B)=(\pi_{m^\perp}E,\pi_{m^\perp}B),\qquad
 C(W)=(-\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}B,\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}E).\] The bilinear dot product, rather than the Hermitian inner product, is used in these algebraic identities.
# The boundary identity and its cancellation

Problem 1 (The spectral formula for the boundary term is false).  Proposition 5.10 on source p. 38 asserts, for \(|\tau|\) sufficiently large and arbitrary \((E,B)\in H^2(Q^\delta)\), \[\pi^\pm(m)\mathcal D(W)=s\,\pi^\pm(m)\bigl(\tau W+C(W)\bigr).
 \tag{2.1}\] This is inconsistent with the definition of \(\mathcal D\) in (5.12), p. 37.
## Exact calculation and all hypotheses

The defined boundary term is \[\mathcal D(W)=\tau P_{\mathrm{tan}}W+
   \bigl((\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}E)\times m,(\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}B)\times m\bigr)
   +\bigl((\widetilde{\operatorname{div}}E)m,(\widetilde{\operatorname{div}}B)m\bigr).
 \tag{2.2}\] At the flat point \(x_0=(3,2,0)\) use the absorptions specified above, and let \(\tau=T>0\) be arbitrarily large. Then \[\nu=e_1,\qquad m=(1+T^{-1})e_1,\qquad s=1+T^{-1}.\] Take the constant fields \(E=e_2\), \(B=e_3\). They are smooth on the bounded \(Q^\delta\), hence belong to \(H^2(Q^\delta)\). Since \(e_3\times e_1=e_2\), \(W=(e_2,e_3)\) belongs to the positive spectral subspace, so \(\pi^+(m)W=W\). All derivatives vanish. Formula (2.2) therefore gives \[\pi^+(m)\mathcal D(W)=TW,\] whereas the claimed right-hand side of (2.1) is \[s\,\pi^+(m)(TW)=(T+1)W.
 \tag{2.3}\] The discrepancy is the nonzero vector \(W\), for every \(T>0\) and thus beyond any fixed large-parameter threshold. Proposition 5.10 imposes no Maxwell equation or boundary condition on this test field, so no hypothesis has been dropped.
## Correct algebra and limited repair

For homogeneous stretched Maxwell equations near the boundary, \(C(W)=-\tau W\) and the divergences vanish. If the absorbing condition \(\pi^-(m)W=0\) holds, (2.4) yields \[\mathcal D(W)=\tau(1-s)\pi^+(m)W.
 \tag{2.5}\] Thus the zero boundary term asserted in Remark 5.2 is not an algebraic consequence of those local conditions. A compatible local illustration on the same flat patch is \[W(x)=e^{-Tx_1}(e_2,e_3).\] Here \(\widetilde\partial_1=\partial_1\), the other derivatives of the field vanish, the homogeneous stretched Maxwell equations and absorbing condition hold locally, and \(\mathcal D(W)=-W\) where \(b(x_2)=1\). This is a local boundary illustration, not a claimed global solution satisfying every face condition.

A precise local correction is available. Replace only the boundary mass part of (2.2) by \(\tau sP_{\mathrm{tan}}W\), calling the resulting vector \(\mathcal D_s(W)\). Then \[\pi^\pm(m)\mathcal D_s(W)=s\,\pi^\pm(m)\bigl(\tau W\pm C(W)\bigr).\] Together with zero divergences, \(C(W)=-\tau W\) and \(\pi^-(m)W=0\), this gives \(\mathcal D_s(W)=0\). In the bilinear form this corresponds to multiplying the boundary mass integrand by \(s\). This establishes a local cancellation for Maxwell solutions. It does not verify every Helmholtz boundary claim in Remark 5.2, nor all estimates for the modified variational form.
## Impact and counterevidence

The unmodified form is used at the start of Section 7 and explicitly in the proof of Theorem 7.6, p. 55, where Proposition 5.10 is invoked to discard the boundary integral. Theorem 7.6 feeds Theorem 8.1 and then the main results. This invalid derivation therefore has Major impact under the core-dependency criterion. The counterexample does not assert instability of the PML. The unstretched positive-projection special case \(s=1\) does not exhibit the scale error, and the local corrected cancellation is counterevidence against a false-main-theorem conclusion.
# A complex stretched Rellich identity

Use the same admissible absorptions, and evaluate near the interior point \((0,2,0)\). Put \(E=e_2\), a constant smooth real field. Let \[\tau=T+i,\quad T>0,\qquad a=\frac{\tau}{\tau+1},\qquad
 d=1+\frac1{\tau}=a^{-1}.\] The coordinate definition (1.13) gives \(\partial_2X_2=d\) near this point, while \(\widetilde\partial_jX_j=1\) for every \(j\). All stretched derivatives of \(E\) vanish. Thus the two sides of (3.1) are respectively \[L=\frac32-a\operatorname{Re}d,\qquad R=\frac12,\] and their exact difference is \[L-R=1-a\operatorname{Re}d=-\frac{i\,a}{T^2+1}\ne0 .
 \tag{3.2}\] For example, \(T=2\) gives \[L=\frac{13}{25}-\frac{7i}{50},\qquad
 R=\frac12,\qquad L-R=\frac{1-7i}{50}.
 \tag{3.3}\] The example meets the entire lemma: \(E\) is \(C^1\), the absorptions obey Assumption 1.2, the point lies in \(Q^\delta\), and \(\operatorname{Re}\tau>0\). Taking \(T\) arbitrarily large also defeats an implicit large-real-part restriction.

The failure is not explained by a complex choice of \(E\), since \(E\) is real. Applying a real part to the whole left side would still leave \(\operatorname{Re}(L-R)=1/50\) in (3.3). The unstretched and positive-real-\(\tau\) identities do hold in this example. The problem is the continuation of a formula containing \(\operatorname{Re}\) of a \(\tau\)-dependent quantity. The source’s valid holomorphic continuation of algebraic differential identities does not justify this step.

The proof of Proposition 6.3 begins by multiplying (6.6) by \(\Pi\) and integrating to obtain (6.9). Proposition 6.1 is then deduced and is explicitly used at (7.9) to close Proposition 7.3. These estimates lead to Theorem 7.6. The failure is therefore Major as a defect in the central estimate’s derivation. It is not a counterexample to the inequalities of Propositions 6.1 or 6.3. A fully justified complex Rellich estimate, with the extra conjugate-dependent terms controlled, remains to be established. No complete repair of that estimate is claimed here.
# The source class does not permit the asserted regularity

Problem 3 (Theorem 8.1 cannot provide \(H^2\) fields for every allowed \(L^2\) current).  On p. 57, Theorem 8.1 assumes that \(J,R\) are holomorphic with values in compactly supported \(L^2\) fields and that \(-\widetilde{\operatorname{div}}J=\tau R\). It concludes that \(W=(F,G)\) is holomorphic with values in \(H^2(Q^\delta)\) and satisfies \[\tau F-\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}G=-J,\qquad \tau G+\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}F=0 .
 \tag{4.1}\] The asserted \(H^2\) regularity is false for the stated source class.

Set every absorption equal to zero, which is allowed by Assumption 1.2. Choose \(\eta\in C^\infty_c(Q_I)\) equal to one on a neighborhood of the origin, and define \[\psi(x)=\eta(x)|x_1|,\qquad
 J=\operatorname{curl}(0,0,\psi)
       =(\partial_2\psi,-\partial_1\psi,0),\qquad R=0.
 \tag{4.2}\] The function \(\psi\) is compactly supported and Lipschitz, so \(J\in L^2\) and \(\operatorname{supp}J\Subset Q_I\). Mixed distributional derivatives commute, hence \(\operatorname{div}J=0\). Treat \(J\) as constant in \(\tau\). It is then an entire \(L^2\)-valued function, as is \(R\), and \(-\operatorname{div}J=\tau R\) holds throughout every required half-plane.

Near the origin, \[J=(0,-\operatorname{sgn}x_1,0).\] Therefore \(\partial_1J_2=-2\delta_{\{x_1=0\}}\) locally in the distributional sense. This nonzero surface measure is not an \(L^2\) function, so \(J\notin H^1\).

If \(F,G\in H^2(Q^\delta)\) satisfied (4.1), then \[J=-\tau F+\operatorname{curl}G\in H^1(Q^\delta),\] contradicting (4.2). The boundary condition cannot remove this interior contradiction. The counterexample works for every positive real \(\tau\), including arbitrarily large values.

The source itself notes on p. 25 that an \(H^2\) Helmholtz field forces additional regularity of the compact current. In the construction on p. 57, however, the \(L^2\to H^2\) Helmholtz inverse is applied to \[(-\tau J-\widetilde{\operatorname{grad}}R,\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}J),\] whose derivative terms need only be distributions of order one for the allowed inputs. This is the precise regularity mismatch.

This has Major impact: Theorem 8.1 is the smooth-domain existence step used to obtain Theorem 1.15, and its \(H^2\) property is used to invoke the converse in Proposition 3.4. The weaker \(L^2\) conclusion of Theorem 1.15 is not contradicted by this example. Starting with sufficiently smooth compatible sources and then proving an appropriate density passage to a weaker solution space is a possible route; that passage and all its trace and parameter claims have not been completed here. Merely changing the notation \(L^2\) to a smoother class would change the theorem’s stated domain.
# The split reconstruction loses the forcing

Problem 4 (Equation (8.12) does not reconstruct the prescribed source).  In the existence proof for Theorem 1.16, source (8.12), p. 63, defines \[\widehat U^k=-(\tau+\sigma_k)^{-1}A_k\partial_kW,
 \qquad \widehat V=W.
 \tag{5.1}\] The subsequent equation (8.15) attributes a nonzero forcing to this formula and concludes that \(\sum_k\widehat U^k=W\). The displayed definition lacks the forcing term.
## A compatible current with an explicit solution

Let \(\sigma_k=0\), choose a nonconstant real \(\phi\in C^\infty_c(Q_I)\), and choose the allowed source weights \(c_1=1\), \(c_2=c_3=0\). For \(t\ge0\) set \[j(t,x)=e^{-t}\nabla\phi(x),\qquad
 \rho(t,x)=-(1-e^{-t})\Delta\phi(x),\] and set both to zero for \(t<0\). Then \(\partial_t\rho=-\operatorname{div}j\) distributionally, with no delta contribution at \(t=0\) because \(\rho(0)=0\). Both sources have the required spatial support and belong to \(e^{\mu t}L^2\) for every \(\mu>0\).

Their Laplace transforms are \[J=\frac{\nabla\phi}{\tau+1},\qquad
 R=-\frac{\Delta\phi}{\tau(\tau+1)}.\] The stretched equations, now unstretched, have the explicit smooth solution \[W=(F,G)=\left(-\frac{\nabla\phi}{\tau(\tau+1)},0\right).
 \tag{5.2}\] Indeed \(\tau F=-J\), \(\operatorname{curl}F=0\), \(\operatorname{div}F=R\), and \(G=0\). The field vanishes near every face, so the absorbing boundary condition holds.

Because \(A(\partial)W=(0,\operatorname{curl}F)=0\), formula (5.1) gives \[\sum_{k=1}^3\widehat U^k
       =-\tau^{-1}A(\partial)W=0\ne W.
 \tag{5.3}\] Thus the error affects the reconstruction of the output, even with smooth compact sources and no absorption. It is not a missing regularity assumption.
## A complete algebraic correction

The source’s preceding transformed equation (8.11), p. 62, contains the forcing and agrees with (5.4). This is strong evidence for an omission in the displayed construction. Interchanging the electric and magnetic block order in nearby source formulas cannot repair the absence of the forcing. The discrepancy is assessed as Major for the invalid existence reconstruction leading directly to Theorem 1.16; the short correction does not change that dependency. The correction proves the local transformed reconstruction, conditional on a suitable stretched solution. It does not repair the separate boundary-estimate and source-regularity problems above.
# A broader holomorphic stretching claim

Problem 5 (Smooth spatial coefficients need not admit holomorphic stretching).  Lemma 1.11, p. 10, asserts that an operator with coefficients smooth in real space and holomorphic in \(\tau\) acquires a holomorphic stretched extension to \(\operatorname{Re}\tau>0\). Spatial smoothness alone is insufficient.

Use the admissible one-direction absorption already fixed, and write \[S=\int_0^2 b(u)\,du>0,\qquad
 h(z)=
 \begin{cases}
  0,&z\le0,\\
  e^{-1/z^2},&z>0.
 \end{cases}\] The real function \(h\) is smooth, including at zero. Let the operator in \(X\) coordinates be multiplication by \[a(X)=h\bigl(X_2-(2+S)\bigr).\] Its coefficient is smooth in \(X\) and independent of \(\tau\), hence holomorphic in \(\tau\) as required. At the fixed point \(x=(0,2,0)\), real positive stretching gives \[X_2(\tau,2)=2+\frac S\tau,\qquad
 a(X(\tau,x))=h\bigl(S(\tau^{-1}-1)\bigr).
 \tag{6.1}\] This is zero for every real \(\tau\ge1\) and strictly positive for \(0<\tau<1\). If the coefficient had a holomorphic extension to the connected half-plane \(\operatorname{Re}\tau>0\), the identity theorem applied to the interval \((1,\infty)\) would make it identically zero, contradicting (6.1). This disproves the asserted extension under the exact coefficient hypotheses.

The source explicitly says at the bottom of p. 10 and top of p. 11 that its use of the correspondence is for spatially constant coefficients. In that restricted case the substitution \(\partial_{X_j}\mapsto\widetilde\partial_j\) has coefficients holomorphic in \(\operatorname{Re}\tau>0\): they are finite sums and products of smooth spatial derivatives of \(\tau/(\tau+\sigma_j(x_j))\) and the original holomorphic coefficients. That restricted construction is valid. The demonstrated overstatement is therefore assessed as Minor; it does not by itself invalidate those constant-coefficient applications. The real-part error in Problem 2 is a separate issue.
# Assessment and remaining scope

The highest supported impact is Major. Problems 1 and 2 invalidate displayed identities used to close the central estimate; Problem 3 disproves the stated \(H^2\) conclusion of a central intermediate theorem; Problem 4 invalidates the printed source-dependent split construction. None of these arguments provides a counterexample to the principal weighted \(L^2\) well-posedness conclusion after appropriate corrections.

The exact algebra also supported the source’s Maxwell symbol identity \(A(\xi)^3=(\xi\cdot\xi)A(\xi)\), the six-dimensional injectivity test for the reduced Lopatinski problem on p. 28, and the three cyclic Turkel–Yefet factorizations on p. 66. These checks do not compensate for the failures above, but delimit what was and was not challenged. The paper explicitly leaves uniform long-time stability and decay through the layer open; they are not treated as proved claims requiring a new counterexample.

 \widetilde\partial_j=\frac{\tau}{\tau+\sigma_j(x_j)}\partial_j .\] The absorptions are nonnegative smooth functions of one coordinate, vanish on the domain of interest \(Q_I\), and have bounded derivatives of every order [Retained latex: \cite[p.~7, Assumption 1.2]{HR}]. Zero absorption is allowed. For the examples with nonzero absorption, take \[Q=(-3,3)^3,\qquad Q_I=(-1,1)^3,\] and choose a smooth bump \(b:\mathbb R\to[0,1]\), supported in \((3/2,5/2)\), equal to one near \(2\). Set \(\sigma_2=b\), \(\sigma_1=\sigma_3=0\). These coefficients satisfy all the stated absorption hypotheses. Choose the smoothing \(Q^\delta\) sufficiently close to \(Q\) that \((0,2,0)\) is an interior point and a neighborhood of \((3,2,0)\) remains a flat boundary patch. This is permitted by Definition 3.1.

For the stretched normal define, as in source Definition 3.3, \[\Pi=\prod_{j=1}^3\frac{\tau+\sigma_j}{\tau},\qquad
 \mathcal M_{ii}=\prod_{j\ne i}\frac{\tau+\sigma_j}{\tau},
 \qquad m=\mathcal M\nu,\qquad s=(m\cdot m)^{1/2}.\] For positive real \(\tau\), \(s=|m|\). For the sufficiently large complex parameters used by the source, the square root is the branch continued from positive real values. Spectral projectors \(\pi^\pm(m)\) refer to the eigenspaces of \(A(m)\) with eigenvalues \(\pm s\). Set \[P_{\mathrm{tan}}(E,B)=(\pi_{m^\perp}E,\pi_{m^\perp}B),\qquad

Q=(-3,3)^3, QI=(-1,1)^3; smooth b supported(3/2,5/2), equal1 near2, values[0,1]; sigma2=b(x2), sigma1=sigma3=0. Qdelta retains a flat patch near(3,2,0). tau=T>0 arbitrarily large. Constant E=e2,B=e3 are H2. Proposition5.10 assumes arbitrary H2 fields and imposes no PDE or boundary condition on this test.
analysis:
Proposition 5.10 on source p. 38 asserts, for \(|\tau|\) sufficiently large and arbitrary \((E,B)\in H^2(Q^\delta)\), \[\pi^\pm(m)\mathcal D(W)=s\,\pi^\pm(m)\bigl(\tau W+C(W)\bigr).
 \tag{2.1}\] This is inconsistent with the definition of \(\mathcal D\) in (5.12), p. 37.

The defined boundary term is \[\mathcal D(W)=\tau P_{\mathrm{tan}}W+
   \bigl((\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}E)\times m,(\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}B)\times m\bigr)
   +\bigl((\widetilde{\operatorname{div}}E)m,(\widetilde{\operatorname{div}}B)m\bigr).
 \tag{2.2}\] At the flat point \(x_0=(3,2,0)\) use the absorptions specified above, and let \(\tau=T>0\) be arbitrarily large. Then \[\nu=e_1,\qquad m=(1+T^{-1})e_1,\qquad s=1+T^{-1}.\] Take the constant fields \(E=e_2\), \(B=e_3\). They are smooth on the bounded \(Q^\delta\), hence belong to \(H^2(Q^\delta)\). Since \(e_3\times e_1=e_2\), \(W=(e_2,e_3)\) belongs to the positive spectral subspace, so \(\pi^+(m)W=W\). All derivatives vanish. Formula (2.2) therefore gives \[\pi^+(m)\mathcal D(W)=TW,\] whereas the claimed right-hand side of (2.1) is \[s\,\pi^+(m)(TW)=(T+1)W.
 \tag{2.3}\] The discrepancy is the nonzero vector \(W\), for every \(T>0\) and thus beyond any fixed large-parameter threshold. Proposition 5.10 imposes no Maxwell equation or boundary condition on this test field, so no hypothesis has been dropped.

For homogeneous stretched Maxwell equations near the boundary, \(C(W)=-\tau W\) and the divergences vanish. If the absorbing condition \(\pi^-(m)W=0\) holds, (2.4) yields \[\mathcal D(W)=\tau(1-s)\pi^+(m)W.
 \tag{2.5}\] Thus the zero boundary term asserted in Remark 5.2 is not an algebraic consequence of those local conditions. A compatible local illustration on the same flat patch is \[W(x)=e^{-Tx_1}(e_2,e_3).\] Here \(\widetilde\partial_1=\partial_1\), the other derivatives of the field vanish, the homogeneous stretched Maxwell equations and absorbing condition hold locally, and \(\mathcal D(W)=-W\) where \(b(x_2)=1\). This is a local boundary illustration, not a claimed global solution satisfying every face condition.

A precise local correction is available. Replace only the boundary mass part of (2.2) by \(\tau sP_{\mathrm{tan}}W\), calling the resulting vector \(\mathcal D_s(W)\). Then \[\pi^\pm(m)\mathcal D_s(W)=s\,\pi^\pm(m)\bigl(\tau W\pm C(W)\bigr).\] Together with zero divergences, \(C(W)=-\tau W\) and \(\pi^-(m)W=0\), this gives \(\mathcal D_s(W)=0\). In the bilinear form this corresponds to multiplying the boundary mass integrand by \(s\). This establishes a local cancellation for Maxwell solutions. It does not verify every Helmholtz boundary claim in Remark 5.2, nor all estimates for the modified variational form.

The unmodified form is used at the start of Section 7 and explicitly in the proof of Theorem 7.6, p. 55, where Proposition 5.10 is invoked to discard the boundary integral. Theorem 7.6 feeds Theorem 8.1 and then the main results. This invalid derivation therefore has Major impact under the core-dependency criterion. The counterexample does not assert instability of the PML. The unstretched positive-projection special case \(s=1\) does not exhibit the scale error, and the local corrected cancellation is counterevidence against a false-main-theorem conclusion.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: At the flat point m=(1+1/T)e1, s=1+1/T, W=(e2,e3) lies in E+(m). Derivatives vanish, so pi+D=TW while the claimed right side is(T+1)W. The discrepancy remains nonzero for all large T. Exact algebra yields pi^±D=tau*pi^±W±s*pi^±C.
Recorded evidence: Suspect step: Both projected boundary terms are stated as s*pi^±(tau W+C), although D has unweighted tau*Ptan W and its cross part is A(m)C.

Use the same admissible absorptions, and evaluate near the interior point \((0,2,0)\). Put \(E=e_2\), a constant smooth real field. Let \[\tau=T+i,\quad T>0,\qquad a=\frac{\tau}{\tau+1},\qquad

Thus the two sides of (3.1) are respectively \[L=\frac32-a\operatorname{Re}d,\qquad R=\frac12,\] and their exact difference is \[L-R=1-a\operatorname{Re}d=-\frac{i\,a}{T^2+1}\ne0 .
 \tag{3.2}\] For example, \(T=2\) gives \[L=\frac{13}{25}-\frac{7i}{50},\qquad
 R=\frac12,\qquad L-R=\frac{1-7i}{50}.
 \tag{3.3}\] The example meets the entire lemma: \(E\) is \(C^1\), the absorptions obey Assumption 1.2, the point lies in \(Q^\delta\), and \(\operatorname{Re}\tau>0\). Taking \(T\) arbitrarily large also defeats an implicit large-real-part restriction.

The failure is not explained by a complex choice of \(E\), since \(E\) is real. Applying a real part to the whole left side would still leave \(\operatorname{Re}(L-R)=1/50\) in (3.3). The unstretched and positive-real-\(\tau\) identities do hold in this example. The problem is the continuation of a formula containing \(\operatorname{Re}\) of a \(\tau\)-dependent quantity. The source’s valid holomorphic continuation of algebraic differential identities does not justify this step.

The proof of Proposition 6.3 begins by multiplying (6.6) by \(\Pi\) and integrating to obtain (6.9). Proposition 6.1 is then deduced and is explicitly used at (7.9) to close Proposition 7.3. These estimates lead to Theorem 7.6. The failure is therefore Major as a defect in the central estimate’s derivation. It is not a counterexample to the inequalities of Propositions 6.1 or 6.3. All absorptions zero; eta smooth compactly supported in QI and equal1 near0; psi=eta|x1|; J=curl(0,0,psi), R=0, with J constant as an L2-valued function of tau. Compact support and -divJ=tau R hold distributionally; J,R are entire in tau.
analysis:
On p. 57, Theorem 8.1 assumes that \(J,R\) are holomorphic with values in compactly supported \(L^2\) fields and that \(-\widetilde{\operatorname{div}}J=\tau R\). It concludes that \(W=(F,G)\) is holomorphic with values in \(H^2(Q^\delta)\) and satisfies \[\tau F-\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}G=-J,\qquad \tau G+\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}F=0 .
 \tag{4.1}\] The asserted \(H^2\) regularity is false for the stated source class.

Set every absorption equal to zero, which is allowed by Assumption 1.2. Choose \(\eta\in C^\infty_c(Q_I)\) equal to one on a neighborhood of the origin, and define \[\psi(x)=\eta(x)|x_1|,\qquad
 J=\operatorname{curl}(0,0,\psi)
       =(\partial_2\psi,-\partial_1\psi,0),\qquad R=0.
 \tag{4.2}\] The function \(\psi\) is compactly supported and Lipschitz, so \(J\in L^2\) and \(\operatorname{supp}J\Subset Q_I\). Mixed distributional derivatives commute, hence \(\operatorname{div}J=0\). Treat \(J\) as constant in \(\tau\). It is then an entire \(L^2\)-valued function, as is \(R\), and \(-\operatorname{div}J=\tau R\) holds throughout every required half-plane.

Near the origin, \[J=(0,-\operatorname{sgn}x_1,0).\] Therefore \(\partial_1J_2=-2\delta_{\{x_1=0\}}\) locally in the distributional sense. This nonzero surface measure is not an \(L^2\) function, so \(J\notin H^1\).

If \(F,G\in H^2(Q^\delta)\) satisfied (4.1), then \[J=-\tau F+\operatorname{curl}G\in H^1(Q^\delta),\] contradicting (4.2). The boundary condition cannot remove this interior contradiction. The counterexample works for every positive real \(\tau\), including arbitrarily large values.

The source itself notes on p. 25 that an \(H^2\) Helmholtz field forces additional regularity of the compact current. In the construction on p. 57, however, the \(L^2\to H^2\) Helmholtz inverse is applied to \[(-\tau J-\widetilde{\operatorname{grad}}R,\widetilde{\operatorname{curl}}J),\] whose derivative terms need only be distributions of order one for the allowed inputs. This is the precise regularity mismatch.

This has Major impact: Theorem 8.1 is the smooth-domain existence step used to obtain Theorem 1.15, and its \(H^2\) property is used to invoke the converse in Proposition 3.4. The weaker \(L^2\) conclusion of Theorem 1.15 is not contradicted by this example. Starting with sufficiently smooth compatible sources and then proving an appropriate density passage to a weaker solution space is a possible route; that passage and all its trace and parameter claims have not been completed here. Merely changing the notation \(L^2\) to a smoother class would change the theorem’s stated domain.

analysis:
In the existence proof for Theorem 1.16, source (8.12), p. 63, defines \[\widehat U^k=-(\tau+\sigma_k)^{-1}A_k\partial_kW,
 \qquad \widehat V=W.
 \tag{5.1}\] The subsequent equation (8.15) attributes a nonzero forcing to this formula and concludes that \(\sum_k\widehat U^k=W\). The displayed definition lacks the forcing term.

Let \(\sigma_k=0\), choose a nonconstant real \(\phi\in C^\infty_c(Q_I)\), and choose the allowed source weights \(c_1=1\), \(c_2=c_3=0\). For \(t\ge0\) set \[j(t,x)=e^{-t}\nabla\phi(x),\qquad
 \rho(t,x)=-(1-e^{-t})\Delta\phi(x),\] and set both to zero for \(t<0\). Then \(\partial_t\rho=-\operatorname{div}j\) distributionally, with no delta contribution at \(t=0\) because \(\rho(0)=0\). Both sources have the required spatial support and belong to \(e^{\mu t}L^2\) for every \(\mu>0\).

Their Laplace transforms are \[J=\frac{\nabla\phi}{\tau+1},\qquad
 R=-\frac{\Delta\phi}{\tau(\tau+1)}.\] The stretched equations, now unstretched, have the explicit smooth solution \[W=(F,G)=\left(-\frac{\nabla\phi}{\tau(\tau+1)},0\right).
 \tag{5.2}\] Indeed \(\tau F=-J\), \(\operatorname{curl}F=0\), \(\operatorname{div}F=R\), and \(G=0\). The field vanishes near every face, so the absorbing boundary condition holds.

Because \(A(\partial)W=(0,\operatorname{curl}F)=0\), formula (5.1) gives \[\sum_{k=1}^3\widehat U^k
       =-\tau^{-1}A(\partial)W=0\ne W.
 \tag{5.3}\] Thus the error affects the reconstruction of the output, even with smooth compact sources and no absorption. It is not a missing regularity assumption.

The source’s preceding transformed equation (8.11), p. 62, contains the forcing and agrees with (5.4). This is strong evidence for an omission in the displayed construction. Interchanging the electric and magnetic block order in nearby source formulas cannot repair the absence of the forcing. The discrepancy is assessed as Major for the invalid existence reconstruction leading directly to Theorem 1.16; the short correction does not change that dependency. The correction proves the local transformed reconstruction, conditional on a suitable stretched solution. It does not repair the separate boundary-estimate and source-regularity problems above.

Same nonzero smooth absorption; S=int_0^2 b>0. h(z)=0 for z<=0 and exp(-1/z^2) for z>0, smooth on R. Operator P is multiplication by a(X)=h(X2-(2+S)), independent of tau and therefore holomorphic in tau.
analysis: Lemma 1.11, p. 10, asserts that an operator with coefficients smooth in real space and holomorphic in \(\tau\) acquires a holomorphic stretched extension to \(\operatorname{Re}\tau>0\). Spatial smoothness alone is insufficient.

Use the admissible one-direction absorption already fixed, and write \[S=\int_0^2 b(u)\,du>0,\qquad
 h(z)=
 \begin{cases}
  0,&z\le0,\\
  e^{-1/z^2},&z>0.
 \end{cases}\] The real function \(h\) is smooth, including at zero. Let the operator in \(X\) coordinates be multiplication by \[a(X)=h\bigl(X_2-(2+S)\bigr).\] Its coefficient is smooth in \(X\) and independent of \(\tau\), hence holomorphic in \(\tau\) as required. At the fixed point \(x=(0,2,0)\), real positive stretching gives \[X_2(\tau,2)=2+\frac S\tau,\qquad
 a(X(\tau,x))=h\bigl(S(\tau^{-1}-1)\bigr).
 \tag{6.1}\] This is zero for every real \(\tau\ge1\) and strictly positive for \(0<\tau<1\). If the coefficient had a holomorphic extension to the connected half-plane \(\operatorname{Re}\tau>0\), the identity theorem applied to the interval \((1,\infty)\) would make it identically zero, contradicting (6.1). This disproves the asserted extension under the exact coefficient hypotheses.

The source explicitly says at the bottom of p. 10 and top of p. 11 that its use of the correspondence is for spatially constant coefficients. In that restricted case the substitution \(\partial_{X_j}\mapsto\widetilde\partial_j\) has coefficients holomorphic in \(\operatorname{Re}\tau>0\): they are finite sums and products of smooth spatial derivatives of \(\tau/(\tau+\sigma_j(x_j))\) and the original holomorphic coefficients. That restricted construction is valid. The demonstrated overstatement is therefore assessed as Minor; it does not by itself invalidate those constant-coefficient applications. The real-part error in Problem 2 is a separate issue.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: At x=(0,2,0), real positive stretching gives a(X(tau,x))=h(S(tau^-1-1)); it vanishes for all tau>=1 and is positive for0<tau<1. A holomorphic extension on the connected right half-plane is impossible by the identity theorem.

report: Abstract: The retained June 2024 preprint of Cipolloni and Landon is examined. For the real Ginibre ensemble, an exact determinant second moment and a holomorphic submean estimate contradict the mesoscopic-strip conclusion of Theorem 2.3 with its printed centering. The probability of one of its asserted lower-bound events is at most \(C n^{-1/5}\), although the theorem requires it to tend to one. A separate variance formula in Lemma 6.2 has a negative leading term for an allowed characteristic. Both signs remain in the selectively compared retained February 2026 preprint. Internal formulas suggest bounded corrections, but a corrected maximum theorem is not proved here. The findings are restricted to the acquired versions and the specified claims.

Title: Centering and variance signs in the maximum
of an i.i.d. characteristic polynomial
# Identity, version, and scope

The target is M25-0408, Maximum of the Characteristic Polynomial of I.I.D. Matrices, by Giorgio Cipolloni and Benjamin Landon, DOI `10.1002/cpa.22250`. The primary source is the 87-page arXiv:2405.05045v2, submitted 6 June 2024 and bearing the title-page date 7 June 2024 [CL2]. Printed and PDF page numbers agree. All unqualified source locators refer to this file. The retained 88-page arXiv:2405.05045v3 was submitted 17 February 2026 and bears the title-page date 18 February 2026 [CL3]. Only its identity and the two relevant statements were compared; it was not reviewed in full. Neither file is represented as a visually verified journal version of record.

The full primary source, including Appendices A–F and the bibliography, was read. The central chain runs from Hermitization and local laws to Gaussian characteristic increments, branching-random-walk comparisons, and the removal of regularization and Gaussian components. Detailed checks below concern the real-case normalization, an exact moment obstruction, and the deterministic variance input. Reading the other arguments is not represented as an independent reconstruction of every local law, coupling, comparison estimate, or cited theorem. The retained acquisition records describe bounded supplement and code searches; a missing identified repository is neither a proof of global absence nor a mathematical defect. No author code was executed.

Write \(p_n(z)=\det(X-zI)\) and \(P_n(z)=\log|p_n(z)|\). Definition 2.1 [p. 11] permits independent real Gaussian entries \(X_{ij}=n^{-1/2}g_{ij}\), \(g_{ij}\sim N(0,1)\): they are centered, have variance \(1/n\), and their rescaled moments of every fixed order are uniformly finite. This ensemble supplies the concrete witness. In the bulk, source (2.3) gives \[\varphi(z)=\frac{|z|^2-1}{2}.\]
# A main strip-maximum statement fails with the printed center

Equation reference: eq:center, eq:claim. Problem 1.  Major. In source (2.5), p. 12, the center is \[
 E_n(z)=n\varphi(z)-\frac14\log q_n(z),
 \qquad q_n(z)=4(\operatorname{Im}z)^2+n^{-1}.\] Theorem 2.3(2.7) then asserts that, for every \(0<\alpha<1/2\), \(0<r<1\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), \[
 \mathbb P\left\{
 \left(\frac1{\sqrt2}-\varepsilon\right)\log n
 \le \max_{z\in S_n}\bigl(P_n(z)-E_n(z)\bigr)
 \le \left(\frac1{\sqrt2}+\varepsilon\right)\log n
 \right\}\longrightarrow1,\] where \[S_n=\{z\in\mathbb C: |z|\le r,\ n^{-\alpha}\le\operatorname{Im}z
                         \le2n^{-\alpha}\}.\] For real Ginibre matrices, \(\alpha=1/4\), \(r=1/2\), and \(\varepsilon=1/\sqrt2-3/5>0\), the probability in [eq:claim] (#eq:claim) instead tends to zero.
## An exact determinant second moment
## A continuum maximum bound

Put \[F_n(z)=e^{-n(|z|^2-1)}|p_n(z)|^2.\] Equation [eq:moment] (#eq:moment) gives \(\mathbb EF_n(z)\le C\sqrt n\) uniformly in \(z\). A bound at one point would not control the maximum, so the following deterministic step is essential.

Equation reference: eq:submean. Fix \(z\) and let \(\rho=n^{-1/2}\). As a function of \(w\), \[g_z(w)=p_n(w)\exp\{-n\overline z(w-z)\}\] is entire. The submean inequality for \(|g_z|^2\), together with \[e^{-n(|z|^2-1)}|g_z(w)|^2
       =F_n(w)e^{n|w-z|^2},\] gives \[
 F_n(z)\le\frac{e}{\pi\rho^2}
                  \int_{B_\rho(z)}F_n(w)\,dA(w)
       =\frac{en}{\pi}\int_{B_\rho(z)}F_n(w)\,dA(w).\] Here the submean inequality follows directly by expanding the holomorphic function in a power series about \(z\): circle integration annuls distinct powers, and all remaining squared terms are nonnegative.

Equation reference: eq:supmoment. Let \(S_n^\rho\) be the Euclidean \(\rho\)-neighborhood of \(S_n\). Every ball in [eq:submean] (#eq:submean) with \(z\in S_n\) is contained in this one deterministic set, so \[\sup_{S_n}F_n\le\frac{en}{\pi}\int_{S_n^\rho}F_n(w)\,dA(w).\] The neighborhood is contained in the rectangle with horizontal width \(2r+2\rho\) and vertical height \(n^{-\alpha}+2\rho\). Since \(\alpha<1/2\), \(|S_n^\rho|\le C_r n^{-\alpha}\). Tonelli’s theorem now gives \[
 \mathbb E\sup_{S_n}F_n\le C_r n^{3/2-\alpha}.\] No random net, derivative estimate, or unproved continuity modulus is used. The polynomial and \(F_n\) are continuous; zeros of the determinant cause no difficulty because the event below can be expressed using the continuous nonnegative quantity \(F_nq_n^{1/2}\).
## A fully specified contradiction
## Counterevidence, repair scope, and impact

The sign was checked on the actual source image, not inferred from text extraction. It is repeated in the plus logarithmic correction of \(\Psi_n\) in (2.20)–(2.21), p. 14. There is substantial internal evidence of an intended opposite sign: the real-axis expression (2.8), p. 12, uses \(P_n-n\varphi+\frac14\log n\); the mean formula (4.3), p. 22, and Appendix E’s mean computation (E.41)–(E.44), p. 79, have the positive logarithmic correction in the expectation. Moreover, the passage (10.27)–(10.28), p. 53, adds \(\alpha\log n\) to the uncorrected doubled logarithm on this strip. That addition is compatible with the negative correction in \(\Psi_n\), whereas the printed (2.21) has a positive one.

Equation reference: eq:correctcenter. The natural candidate center is \[
 E_n^{\rm corr}(z)=n\varphi(z)+\frac14\log q_n(z).\] The following algebraic consequence is fully verified: \[E_n-E_n^{\rm corr}=-\frac12\log q_n
                   =\alpha\log n+O(1)
       \quad\hbox{uniformly on }S_n,\] because \(q_n/n^{-2\alpha}\) stays between positive fixed constants. Thus \[P_n-E_n^{\rm corr}
       =(P_n-E_n)+\alpha\log n+O(1).\] This is a leading-order change on the strip. If a corrected theorem with center [eq:correctcenter] (#eq:correctcenter) and coefficient \(1/\sqrt2\) were established, it would give coefficient \(1/\sqrt2-\alpha\) with the old center. That statement is a conditional implication, not a theorem proved in this report.

The verified repair is the centering algebra and its agreement with the cited internal mean and real-axis formulas. A full repair requires consistent signs in the definitions and all real-case comparison, increment, and branching-random-walk steps. That reconstruction has not been completed here, and no author adoption is asserted. The same (2.5) and (2.7) remain visible on p. 12 of the retained later preprint [CL3].

The severity is Major because [eq:tail] (#eq:tail) directly falsifies an explicit principal conclusion, source Theorem 2.3(2.7), for an allowed ensemble. The lower-bound argument in §11.1 [pp. 56–57] expressly concludes (2.7), using the chain through Theorems 9.5 and 10.7 [pp. 48, 53]. This finding does not itself refute the complex-case Theorem 2.2, the full-disk real maximum (2.6), or every method in the paper. In particular, a false stated strip result used to prove (2.6) does not logically establish that (2.6) is false. No claim about an uninspected journal-final formula is made.
# The integrated variance has the reversed leading logarithm

Problem 2.  Major. In Lemma 6.2(6.5), p. 28, the first logarithm in the integral of a deterministic Brownian variance is printed as \(\log(\eta_s/\eta_{S_1})\). For a permitted characteristic decreasing from a mesoscopic scale to a microscopic scale away from the real axis, the asserted expression is strictly negative of order \(\log n\). An integrated nonnegative variance cannot have this value.
## The statement and all parameter choices

Section 6 takes the real flow \(X_t=\sqrt{1-T}\,Y+n^{-1/2}B_t\), where \(Y\) is real i.i.d. and \(B_t\) has independent standard real Brownian entries. One can take \(Y\) real Ginibre. The self-consistent variance is \(1-T+t\), and is one at \(t=T\). The characteristic satisfies \[\partial_t\eta_t=-\operatorname{Im}m_t^z(i\eta_t),
 \qquad m_t^z(i\eta_t)\ \hbox{constant along it}\] [source (5.6) and the computation on pp. 29–30]. Fix \(z=i/2\), in any bulk disk of radius greater than \(1/2\). Choose an arbitrarily small fixed \(c\in(0,1/4)\) meeting the lemma’s sufficient-smallness conditions, and set \[\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2=c,\quad T=n^{-c},\quad
 \eta_T=n^{-1+c},\quad S_1=0,\quad s=S_2=T.\] The auxiliary \(\xi>0\) in the lemma can be chosen sufficiently small independently. The required \(\eta_T\ge n^{-1+\varepsilon_2}\) holds with equality, and \(0\le S_1<S_2\le T\).

At the endpoint of variance one, write \(m_T^z(i\eta_T)=iv_n\). The bulk cubic equation, or source (6.15), yields \[v_n=\sqrt{1-|z|^2}+O(\eta_T)
     =\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+O(\eta_T).\] For completeness, the cubic at \(\eta=0\) and \(m=iv\) reduces to \(1/v=v+|z|^2/v\), giving \(v^2=1-|z|^2\). The positive bulk root is simple, so the implicit function theorem gives the displayed \(O(\eta_T)\) expansion. Constancy along the characteristic implies exactly \[\eta_0=\eta_T+Tv_n\asymp n^{-c}.\] This characteristic stays positive and in the small bulk regime throughout \([0,T]\).
## A nonnegative quantity with a negative asserted value

On the left, \(V_u\) is deterministic and nonnegative: it occurs under the real square root in the Brownian representation (6.4). The proof moreover defines it in (6.18), p. 30, and explicitly states \(V_u\asymp1/\eta_u>0\). Thus the contradiction is already deterministic. No choice of coupling, high-probability exceptional event, or hidden constant in the stated remainder can repair a negative leading logarithm of diverging magnitude.
## The bounded correction and its limitations

The first logarithm should have the reversed orientation, \(\log(\eta_{S_1}/\eta_s)\). This is checked directly for the leading variance integral: \[\int_{S_1}^s
      \frac{\operatorname{Im}m_u^z(i\eta_u)}{\eta_u}\,du
   =-\int_{\eta_{S_1}}^{\eta_s}\frac{\,d\eta}{\eta}
   =\log\frac{\eta_{S_1}}{\eta_s}.\] Source (5.25), p. 26, already prints this orientation for the corresponding complex-characteristic variance. The additional real contribution is treated by (6.16), p. 30. Reversing the first logarithm removes the exhibited sign obstruction and agrees with these local integrations; it is not a claim to have re-proved every coupling and remainder in Lemma 6.2.

The same reversed ratio is retained in (6.5) on p. 29 of [CL3]. Conversely, the later use of positive variance scales in (6.33) and (6.45) [pp. 33, 35] is evidence that the intended probabilistic argument does not use a negative variance. This counterevidence limits the conclusion: the printed lemma is false, but the report does not infer failure of every subsequent upper bound. Lemma 6.2 is invoked explicitly for the real-case Gaussian tail estimates and the two increment variances used in §6.4. Its invalid displayed guarantee is therefore a core proof input, supporting Major severity under the claim-level standard, despite the local sign correction being simple.
# Coverage, calculation, and repair boundaries
The review distinguishes a disproved principal statement from an invalid core intermediate formula. The following scope is exact.
Finding | Established result | Verified repair boundary

Problem 1 | Source (2.7) is false with (2.5); a specified allowed event has probability at most \(C n^{-1/5}\). | Opposite-sign centering changes the strip value by \(\alpha\log n+O(1)\). The corrected maximum theorem and all its dependencies are not independently proved.

Problem 2 | Source (6.5) gives a negative integrated variance for an allowed characteristic. | The first logarithm must be reversed by direct characteristic integration. Full coupling and error estimates remain beyond this bounded repair.

Independent exact symbolic diagnostics check the determinant second-moment identity for dimensions \(1\) through \(4\), the weighted holomorphic gauge identity, the exponent \(-1/5\), positivity of the chosen \(\varepsilon\), and the opposite leading variance signs. They are retained with their source and actual execution output under this paper’s verification directory. The general determinant and continuum arguments are proved above; finite checks are supporting diagnostics, not substitutes for those proofs. The variance contradiction is analytic and does not depend on numerical simulation.

The full acquired source has been read to the end, with focused visual checks of the identity, hypotheses, exact signs, proof dependencies, internal counterevidence, and later-version comparison. Appendices A–D and F were read for their role in the comparison chain; their external results have not all been independently re-proved. No issue count was imposed. No assertion of correctness for every unreported displayed formula is implied by the absence of an additional finding.

claim: Recorded check: Major. In Lemma 6.2(6.5), p. 28, the first logarithm in the integral of a deterministic Brownian variance is printed as \(\log(\eta_s/\eta_{S_1})\).

Real flow Xt=sqrt(1−T)Y+B_t/sqrt(n) with admissible real-GinibreY; z=i/2 in a fixed bulk disk. Fix sufficiently small0<c<1/4,eps1=eps2=c,T=n^-c,etaT=n^(-1+c),S1=0,s=S2=T; auxiliaryxi sufficiently small. The final eta condition holds with equality.
analysis:
Section 6 takes the real flow \(X_t=\sqrt{1-T}\,Y+n^{-1/2}B_t\), where \(Y\) is real i.i.d. and \(B_t\) has independent standard real Brownian entries. One can take \(Y\) real Ginibre. The self-consistent variance is \(1-T+t\), and is one at \(t=T\). The characteristic satisfies \[\partial_t\eta_t=-\operatorname{Im}m_t^z(i\eta_t),
 \qquad m_t^z(i\eta_t)\ \hbox{constant along it}\] [source (5.6) and the computation on pp. 29–30]. Fix \(z=i/2\), in any bulk disk of radius greater than \(1/2\). Choose an arbitrarily small fixed \(c\in(0,1/4)\) meeting the lemma’s sufficient-smallness conditions, and set \[\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2=c,\quad T=n^{-c},\quad
 \eta_T=n^{-1+c},\quad S_1=0,\quad s=S_2=T.\] The auxiliary \(\xi>0\) in the lemma can be chosen sufficiently small independently. The required \(\eta_T\ge n^{-1+\varepsilon_2}\) holds with equality, and \(0\le S_1<S_2\le T\).

At the endpoint of variance one, write \(m_T^z(i\eta_T)=iv_n\). The bulk cubic equation, or source (6.15), yields \[v_n=\sqrt{1-|z|^2}+O(\eta_T)
     =\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+O(\eta_T).\] For completeness, the cubic at \(\eta=0\) and \(m=iv\) reduces to \(1/v=v+|z|^2/v\), giving \(v^2=1-|z|^2\). The positive bulk root is simple, so the implicit function theorem gives the displayed \(O(\eta_T)\) expansion. Constancy along the characteristic implies exactly \[\eta_0=\eta_T+Tv_n\asymp n^{-c}.\] This characteristic stays positive and in the small bulk regime throughout \([0,T]\).

On the left, \(V_u\) is deterministic and nonnegative: it occurs under the real square root in the Brownian representation (6.4). The proof moreover defines it in (6.18), p. 30, and explicitly states \(V_u\asymp1/\eta_u>0\). Thus the contradiction is already deterministic. No choice of coupling, high-probability exceptional event, or hidden constant in the stated remainder can repair a negative leading logarithm of diverging magnitude.

The first logarithm should have the reversed orientation, \(\log(\eta_{S_1}/\eta_s)\). This is checked directly for the leading variance integral: \[\int_{S_1}^s
      \frac{\operatorname{Im}m_u^z(i\eta_u)}{\eta_u}\,du
   =-\int_{\eta_{S_1}}^{\eta_s}\frac{\,d\eta}{\eta}
   =\log\frac{\eta_{S_1}}{\eta_s}.\] Source (5.25), p. 26, already prints this orientation for the corresponding complex-characteristic variance. The additional real contribution is treated by (6.16), p. 30. Reversing the first logarithm removes the exhibited sign obstruction and agrees with these local integrations; it is not a claim to have re-proved every coupling and remainder in Lemma 6.2.

The same reversed ratio is retained in (6.5) on p. 29 of [CL3]. Conversely, the later use of positive variance scales in (6.33) and (6.45) [pp. 33, 35] is evidence that the intended probabilistic argument does not use a negative variance. This counterevidence limits the conclusion: the printed lemma is false, but the report does not infer failure of every subsequent upper bound. Lemma 6.2 is invoked explicitly for the real-case Gaussian tail estimates and the two increment variances used in §6.4. Its invalid displayed guarantee is therefore a core proof input, supporting Major severity under the claim-level standard, despite the local sign correction being simple.
