report: Abstract: The acquired preprint derives a porous-medium hydrodynamic limit, a dynamical large-deviation principle, and an entropy–action identity from a rescaled zero-range process. The relative entropy printed in its definition lacks the reference-density weight used by the equilibrium law and subsequent calculations. Exact closed events contradict the resulting large-deviation upper bound, and a smooth positive path contradicts the stated entropy–action identity. A separate check of the central gradient-flow proof finds an infeasible proposed control and inconsistent action coefficients. Local discrepancies in a sharp discrete-to-continuum bound, a critical exponential moment, and a uniform mass estimate are also demonstrated. The highest supported assessment is Major. Explicit corrections are verified at the stated local scope; no complete revised irregular-path theory is certified. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Entropy normalization and variational consistency
in the porous medium equation
# Identity, source and scope

The reviewed paper is Benjamin Gess and Daniel Heydecker, The porous medium equation: Large deviations and gradient flow with degenerate and unbounded diffusion, acquired as arXiv:2303.11289v3, 24 March 2025, 62 pages [GH]. The associated publication is Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 78(9) (2025), 1609–1655, DOI `10.1002/cpa.22251`. References to source pages below mean the printed pages of this preprint; they agree with its PDF page indices counted from one.

The entire acquired source, including Appendices A–B and the bibliography, was read. Detailed checks concern the entropy normalization, equilibrium partition function, elementary large-deviation events, variational control algebra, discrete dissipation, and endpoint moment and mass estimates. The nonlinear PDE approximation and uniqueness results imported from the source’s reference [31], and all external tightness and discrete Sobolev theorems, were not independently reproved. Reading those dependencies is distinguished from certifying every theorem of the paper.

A bounded publisher-HTML comparison was made for version context; the journal PDF was not acquired and full version equivalence is not established. All counterexamples below are anchored to the retained v3 PDF, not to a claim of byte-identical journal text. No author correction or adoption of the corrections below is established by the inspected material.
# Definitions used in the checks

Equation reference: eq:printedH, eq:skeleton, eq:action, eq:continuousD. The torus has unit volume. Write \[h(s)=s\log s-s+1,\qquad h(0)=1.\] Source (3.6), p. 12, explicitly defines \[
\mathcal H_\rho(u)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}h(u/\rho)\,dx.\] The measure in that display is \(dx\), with no factor \(\rho(x)\). The definitions in source (1.6)–(1.8), p. 3, are \[
\partial_tu=\tfrac12\Delta u^\alpha-\nabla\cdot(u^{\alpha/2}g),
\qquad
\mathcal J(u)=\tfrac12\inf_g\|g\|_{L^2_{t,x}}^2,
\qquad
\mathcal I_\rho(u)=\alpha\mathcal H_\rho(u_0)+\mathcal J(u).\] The action in source (1.17)–(1.18), p. 5, is \[
\mathcal A(u)=\tfrac12\inf_\theta\|\theta\|_{L^2_{t,x}}^2,
\qquad
\partial_tu+\nabla\cdot(\tfrac12u^{\alpha/2}\theta)=0.\] The infima are over controls satisfying the displayed equations; these constraints cannot be changed when comparing their values. The dissipation in source (1.11), p. 4, is \[
\mathcal D_\alpha(u)=\frac2\alpha\int_{\mathbb T^d}|\nabla u^{\alpha/2}|^2\,dx.\]
# Problem 1: the relative entropy gives the wrong rate

Problem 1 (Major: reference-density weight).  With the literal definition [eq:printedH] (#eq:printedH), the large-deviation upper bound in source Theorem 2 is false. The same normalization also invalidates the relative-entropy identity (1.19) of Theorem 4 for allowed constant reference densities.
## An exact absorbing event

Set \(d=1\), \(\alpha=2\), \(t_{\mathrm{fin}}=1\), \(\rho\equiv\tfrac12\), and \(\chi_N=N^{-2}\). All parameters are allowed: \(\rho\) is continuous and strictly positive, \(\alpha>1\), and the scaling condition (1.2), p. 2, is exactly \(N^2\chi_N=1\). Use the prescribed product initial law \(\Pi_\rho^N\).

Equation reference: eq:partition. Source §3.2, p. 13, gives \[
\pi_\rho^N(\chi_Nm)=
 \frac{(\rho/\chi_N)^{2m}}{(m!)^2 Z_2(\rho/\chi_N)},
\qquad
Z_2(\phi)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\phi^{2m}}{(m!)^2}.\] The zero configuration is absorbing because every jump rate vanishes. Thus the singleton \(E_0=\{u_t\equiv0\}\), a closed subset of the stated Skorokhod space, has the exact probability \[\mathbb P(\eta^N\in E_0)=Z_2(N^2/2)^{-N}.\] The zero path belongs to the energy class, solves [eq:skeleton] (#eq:skeleton) with \(g=0\), and has \(\mathcal J(0)=0\). Its printed rate is \(\mathcal I_{1/2}(0)=2\mathcal H_{1/2}(0)=2\).

Equation reference: eq:zeroContradiction. For completeness, the partition asymptotic needed here follows without any large-deviation theorem. Since its terms are nonnegative, \(Z_2(\phi)\le(\sum_m\phi^m/m!)^2=e^{2\phi}\). For \(m=\lfloor\phi\rfloor\) and \(\phi\ge2\), monotonicity of \(\log\) gives \[\log(m!)\le m\log m-m+1+\log m.\] The single \(m\)-term of the sum consequently gives \[2\phi-4-2\log\phi\le\log Z_2(\phi)\le2\phi.\] In particular, \(\phi^{-1}\log Z_2(\phi)\to2\), consistently with source Lemma 4.1, p. 17. Hence \[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\chi_N}{N}\log\mathbb P(\eta^N\in E_0)
=-\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log Z_2(N^2/2)}{N^2}
=-1.\] The claimed closed-set upper bound (1.9) instead requires this limit to be at most \(-2\). This is a direct contradiction, not an inference from an unproved replacement lemma.
## A strictly positive initial-profile witness

The contradiction does not require admitting a zero-mass fluctuation. Let \(E_1=\{u\in\mathbb D:u_0\equiv1\}\), which is closed because evaluation at time zero is continuous. The exact configuration \(\eta_0^N\equiv1\) has \(m=N^2\) particles per site and positive total mass. Future dynamics are unrestricted in this event. Formula [eq:partition] (#eq:partition) and the elementary factorial asymptotic \(\log(m!)=m\log m-m+o(m)\) yield \[\lim_N\frac{\chi_N}{N}\log\mathbb P(\eta^N\in E_1)=1-2\log2.\] On the other hand, \(\mathcal J\ge0\), and the constant macroscopic path \(u_t\equiv1\) attains \(\mathcal J=0\). Therefore \[\inf_{E_1}\mathcal I_{1/2}=2h(2)=4\log2-2.\] The printed upper bound would be \(2-4\log2\), strictly less than the actual value \(1-2\log2\), since \(\log2>\tfrac12\). This checks the same failure on a strictly positive, finite-entropy initial profile.
## The mismatch in the dual and change-of-measure calculation
## A smooth positive failure of Theorem 4

For a separate direct check, keep \(d=1,\alpha=2,t_{\mathrm{fin}}=1\) and set \[u(t,x)=2+\tfrac t2\cos(2\pi x),\qquad
\theta(t,x)=-\frac{\sin(2\pi x)}{2\pi u(t,x)},\qquad
g=u_x+\tfrac12\theta.\] The path is smooth, has mass \(2\), and satisfies \(3/2\le u\le5/2\). Direct differentiation verifies both equations [eq:skeleton] (#eq:skeleton) and [eq:action] (#eq:action), so all regularity and finite-cost hypotheses hold. These controls attain the respective infima, independently of the source’s dual-action formula: any other one-dimensional periodic control differs by \(c(t)/u\), and \[\int_{\mathbb T}\theta/u\,dx=0,\qquad
\int_{\mathbb T}g/u\,dx=0.\] The first equality follows from oddness in \(x\); the second also uses \(\int u_x/u=0\). The cross terms in the squared norms therefore vanish, proving minimality.

Equation reference: eq:smoothEDI. Put \(\Delta\mathcal H=\mathcal H(u_1)-\mathcal H(u_0)\) and \(D=\int_0^1\mathcal D_2(u_t)\,dt\). Periodic integration by parts in the continuity equation gives \(2\Delta\mathcal H=\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb T}u_x\theta\). Expanding the norm of \(g=u_x+\theta/2\) yields \[
\mathcal J(u)=\Delta\mathcal H+\tfrac12D+\tfrac14\mathcal A(u).\] Strict convexity of \(h\), and the fact that \(u_1\) is nonconstant of mean \(2\), imply \(\Delta\mathcal H>0\). For constant \(\rho\), mass conservation and [eq:printedH] (#eq:printedH) give \(\mathcal H_\rho(u_1)-\mathcal H_\rho(u_0)=\Delta\mathcal H/\rho\). At the allowed choice \(\rho=2\), the right-hand side of source (1.19) is consequently smaller than [eq:smoothEDI] (#eq:smoothEDI) by \(\Delta\mathcal H/2>0\). This refutes the literal identity on an everywhere positive smooth path.
## Correction, counterevidence and impact

Equation reference: eq:correctH. The compatible entropy is \[
\widehat{\mathcal H}_\rho(u)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho\,h(u/\rho)\,dx
 =\int_{\mathbb T^d}\{u\log(u/\rho)-u+\rho\}\,dx.\] It restores the pointwise dual [eq:legendre] (#eq:legendre), both exact event costs, and the smooth calculation above. For constant \(\rho\) on a fixed-mass path, \(\widehat{\mathcal H}_\rho(u_1)-\widehat{\mathcal H}_\rho(u_0)=\mathcal H(u_1)-\mathcal H(u_0)\), as the gradient-flow argument requires.

The case \(\rho=1\) has no discrepancy. Interpreting the measure in source (3.6) as \(\rho\,dx\) would also repair the definition, but the actual page displays \(dx\). This is strong evidence of an intended local correction, especially because (10.24) already contains the required weight; it does not validate the formula as printed. Neither an alternative definition of the equilibrium parameter nor a rescaling of the LDP speed is justified by the explicit laws and hypotheses used above. The positive witness also rules out a repair consisting only of excluding the vacuum.

The assessment is Major: the affected rate is the central conclusion of Theorem 2 and an input to the time-reversal argument for Theorem 4. The corrected formula is locally verified here; the entire revised LDP and irregular-path identity are not independently reproved. The hydrodynamic equation itself is not refuted.
# Problem 2: control and action inconsistencies in the core proof

Problem 2 (Major for the control derivation; local action discrepancy).  Source (11.9), p. 48, proposes an infeasible optimizing control in the proof of Theorem 4. Related action coefficients in (11.6), (11.17) and (B.33)–(B.34) do not agree with [eq:action] (#eq:action).
## The sign of the proposed control

The beginning of source §11, p. 47, correctly maps a continuity control to a skeleton control by \(g=
abla u^{\alpha/2}+	heta/2\). Equation (11.9) instead uses \[g_-=	heta/2-\Pi[u]
abla u^{\alpha/2},\] where \(\Pi[u]\) projects onto the closure of \(u^{\alpha/2}
abla\varphi\). This is asserted to be feasible and optimal.

Take \(\alpha=2\) and \(u(t,x)=v(x)=2+\cos(2\pi x)\) on \([0,1]\times\mathbb T\). The path is smooth, strictly positive and stationary. The continuity minimizer is \(\theta=0\), since it is feasible with zero cost. Also \(v_x=v(\log v)_x\), so the projection fixes \(v_x\). The printed choice is therefore \(g_-=-v_x\), for which the skeleton right-hand side equals \[\tfrac12(v^2)_{xx}-(vg_-)_x=(v^2)_{xx}.\] At \(x=0\) this is \(-24\pi^2\), whereas \(u_t=0\). The candidate is not feasible. The correct choice \(g_+=v_x\) makes the right-hand side identically zero. This verifies every hypothesis without relying on an irregular PDE existence assertion.
## An exact action test

Equation reference: eq:trig. A different positive path detects the coefficient discrepancies: \[u(t,x)=2+\cos(2\pi(x-t)),\qquad
\theta=2-\frac3u,\qquad 0\le t\le1.\] Here \(u_t=-u_x\) and \((u\theta/2)_x=u_x\), so the continuity equation holds. Elementary integration gives \[
\int_{\mathbb T}\frac{dx}{u}=\frac1{\sqrt3},\qquad
\int_{\mathbb T}\frac{dx}{u^2}=\frac2{3\sqrt3},\qquad
\int_{\mathbb T}\frac{\theta}{u}\,dx=0.\] For example, the substitution \(z=\tan(s/2)\) in \((2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}(a+\cos s)^{-1}ds\) gives \((a^2-1)^{-1/2}\); differentiation in \(a>1\) gives the second integral at \(a=2\). Thus these evaluations need no numerical quadrature.

Equation reference: eq:actionvalue. As above, other feasible controls differ by \(c(t)/u\), and [eq:trig] (#eq:trig) proves that \(\theta\) is the unique minimizer. Hence \[
\mathcal A(u)=\tfrac12\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb T}\theta^2=2-\sqrt3>0.\] The correct skeleton minimizer is \(g=u_x+\theta/2\). Since \(\int u_x\theta=0\) and \(\int u_x^2=2\pi^2\), \[\mathcal J(u)=\pi^2+\tfrac14(2-\sqrt3).\] Entropy is constant along this translating path. The literal (11.6) instead gives \(\pi^2+\tfrac12(2-\sqrt3)\), so it is not an identity. The correct coefficient is already visible in source (11.15), p. 49, and in the statement (1.19); it must be retained in (11.6) and (11.17).

For the separate dual formula, let \[B_u(\varphi)=\langle\varphi_1,u_1\rangle-\langle\varphi_0,u_0\rangle
 -\int_0^1\langle\partial_t\varphi,u\rangle\,dt .\] The continuity equation gives \(B_u(\varphi)=\tfrac12\langle\theta,u\nabla\varphi\rangle\). Source (B.33)–(B.34), pp. 58–59, claims \(\mathcal A(u)=\sup_\varphi\{B_u(\varphi)-\tfrac12\|u\nabla\varphi\|_2^2\}\). Completing the square shows that this supremum is actually \(\|\theta\|_2^2/8=\mathcal A(u)/4\). It is attained for the present example: \(\varphi_x=\theta/(2u)\) is smooth and has zero spatial mean by [eq:trig] (#eq:trig), so a smooth periodic \(\varphi\) exists. Thus the displayed dual is \((2-\sqrt3)/4\), not \(2-\sqrt3\).
## Verified algebraic correction and boundaries

Write \(w=\Pi[u]\nabla u^{\alpha/2}\). The feasible projected control is \(g=\theta/2+w\), agreeing with the earlier source p. 47. Under time reversal, its companion is \(g^r=Tw-T\theta/2\), so \[g^r+Tg=2Tw,\qquad g^r-Tg=-T\theta.\] With a valid time-reversal rate identity, the parallelogram calculation therefore yields \[\mathcal J(u)=\tfrac12\{\alpha\Delta\widehat{\mathcal H}_\rho+\|w\|_2^2+\mathcal A(u)/2\}.\] The dual of the action [eq:action] (#eq:action) is normalized by \[\sup_\varphi\{B_u(\varphi)-\tfrac18
 \|u^{\alpha/2}\nabla\varphi\|_2^2\},\] as follows by completing the square with the continuity constraint. The replacement restores the exact smooth examples.

The control error is Major at the derivation level: feasibility and optimality feed (11.11)–(11.15), the central passage from reversibility to the claimed entropy–action identity. The correct map on p. 47 is explicit counterevidence against interpreting this as a new obstruction to the intended theorem. The factor-four appendix dual discrepancy is local: multiplying by the correct positive constant preserves the lower-semicontinuity argument’s qualitative conclusion. Neither example disproves the correctly normalized identity at \(\rho=1\), or the existence of minimizing controls. A complete proof for all irregular finite-cost paths is not supplied by these local corrections.
# Problem 3: the sharp discrete dissipation bound loses a factor two

Problem 3 (Minor: quantitative \(\Gamma\)-lower bound).  Source (5.4) and the conclusion \(\mathcal F_\alpha(u)\le z\) in Lemma 5.1, p. 23, are incompatible with the discrete normalization (5.2), p. 22, and the continuum normalization [eq:continuousD] (#eq:continuousD).

Equation reference: eq:lattice. In dimension one, \(\alpha=2\), nearest-neighbour probabilities are \(p^N(k,k\pm1)=1/2\), as also used in source (B.2), p. 53. Thus \[\mathcal D_{2,N}(\eta)=\frac N2\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}
 (\eta_{k+1}-\eta_k)^2.\] Take \(\chi_N=N^{-2}\), and define a time-independent lattice path by \[\eta_k^N=2+\frac{k(N-k)}{N^2},\quad 0\le k<N.\] These are allowed particle values: the particle counts are the nonnegative integers \(2N^2+k(N-k)\). The paths belong to \(\mathbb D_N\) and converge uniformly, hence in \(\mathbb D\), to the time-independent periodic function \[f(x)=2+x(1-x),\quad 0\le x\le1.\] This function is positive and periodic Lipschitz; the derivative jump at the period boundary is allowed by the lemma and \(f\in H^1(\mathbb T)\). Its entropy is finite. Direct finite summation gives \[
\mathcal D_{2,N}(\eta^N)
 =\frac1{2N^3}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(N-2k-1)^2
 =\frac{N^2-1}{6N^2}\longrightarrow\frac16,
\qquad
\mathcal D_2(f)=\int_0^1(1-2x)^2dx=\frac13.\] Uniform convergence within a fixed positive compact range also gives \(\mathcal H(\eta^N)\to\mathcal H(f)\). With time horizon one, \[\mathcal F_{2,N}(\eta^N)\to\mathcal H(f)+\tfrac16
 <\mathcal H(f)+\tfrac13=\mathcal F_2(f).\] This is a counterexample to (5.4) with all lattice and energy hypotheses checked. Equivalently, choose \(z=\mathcal H(f)+1/4\); the required bound holds for all sufficiently large \(N\), and finitely many earlier terms may be replaced by the constant configuration \(2\) without changing the limit.

This is a local quantitative defect. Finiteness of the energy and the qualitative weak-to-strong and exclusion arguments are not refuted: a fixed factor does not change whether the dissipation is finite. Changing the lattice transition convention would also alter the generator’s displayed \(\tfrac12\Delta\) limit and is not an available interpretation of the original formulas.
# Problem 4: the critical entropy moment can be finite

Problem 4 (Minor: endpoint \(\gamma=\alpha\)).  Remark 4.5 and (4.23), p. 20, assert infinite entropy exponential moments as soon as \(\gamma\ge\alpha\). The endpoint assertion is false for allowed constant reference densities \(0<\rho<1\).

For fixed positive constant \(\rho\), Stirling’s formula sharpens the endpoint summand to a constant times \(\rho^{\alpha m}m^{-\alpha/2}\). Thus the critical moment is finite for \(\rho<1\), infinite for \(\rho>1\), and at \(\rho=1\) finite exactly when \(\alpha>2\). For \(\gamma>\alpha\) and \(\rho>0\), the positive \((\gamma-\alpha)m\log m\) term does imply divergence. The case \(\rho=0\) is the deterministic vacuum and must be excluded from any universal divergence statement.

Replacing \(h(s)\) by \(s\log s\) changes the critical threshold: the linear term cannot be discarded for this endpoint question. The proof of Lemma 4.4 uses that replacement only for an upper bound at \(\gamma<\alpha\), where the present example does not contradict it. The defect is therefore local to the sharpness remark; the theorem’s strictly subcritical hypothesis is not invalidated.
# Problem 5: the mass-uniform prefactor is too small

Problem 5 (Minor: statement of Lemma 5.3).  Source (5.11), p. 24, claims, for some \(\beta>\alpha>1\) and \(C=C(d,\alpha)\), \[\|\eta^N\|_\beta^\beta
 \le C(1+\langle1,\eta^N\rangle)(1+\mathcal D_{\alpha,N}(\eta^N))\] for all nonnegative lattice functions. No such mass-independent constant exists with this linear mass factor.

For any fixed lattice, take \(\eta^N\equiv K\ge1\). It belongs to every required Lebesgue space, its mass is \(K\), and its discrete dissipation is zero. The claim becomes \(K^\beta\le C(1+K)\). Choosing \(K^{\beta-1}>2C\) contradicts it. This works for every \(\beta>\alpha>1\); no choice of the existential exponent repairs the display.

The proof itself ends at (5.16) with the different factor \(1+\langle1,\eta^N\rangle^\beta\). This is consistent with the interpolation in (5.14)–(5.15): with \(a=\|\eta^N\|_1\) and \(\beta=\alpha+1-2/p\), those lines give \[\|\eta^N\|_\beta^\beta
 \le C a^{1-2/p}(a^\alpha+\mathcal D_{\alpha,N})
 \le C(1+a^\beta)(1+\mathcal D_{\alpha,N}).\] The last inequality also holds at \(a=0\). This verifies the mass scaling correction and identifies it in the existing proof; it is not a new proof of the external discrete Sobolev input to (5.14). Subsequent fixed-mass uses may absorb the corrected power into a constant depending on the mass cap. Accordingly no qualitative compactness or hydrodynamic failure is established by this local counterexample.
# Impact and conclusion

The relative-entropy error gives direct counterexamples to core statements with their literal definitions. The action/control problem invalidates specific essential equalities in the gradient-flow derivation, while the correct control map and final coefficients are partly present elsewhere in the same source. The remaining defects are local; their examples do not disprove the qualitative weak-to-strong principle, the strictly subcritical moment bound, or estimates on a fixed mass class.

Unit-volume one-dimensional torus, alpha=2, t_fin=1, chi_N=N^-2 and the prescribed equilibrium product law. rho=1/2 for the two exact LDP events; rho=2 for the smooth entropy-action example. These are continuous strictly positive reference profiles; N^2*chi_N=1. All tested paths have finite energy; the second LDP witness has strictly positive initial density.
analysis: With the literal definition [eq:printedH] (#eq:printedH), the large-deviation upper bound in source Theorem 2 is false. The same normalization also invalidates the relative-entropy identity (1.19) of Theorem 4 for allowed constant reference densities.

Set \(d=1\), \(\alpha=2\), \(t_{\mathrm{fin}}=1\), \(\rho\equiv\tfrac12\), and \(\chi_N=N^{-2}\). All parameters are allowed: \(\rho\) is continuous and strictly positive, \(\alpha>1\), and the scaling condition (1.2), p. 2, is exactly \(N^2\chi_N=1\). Use the prescribed product initial law \(\Pi_\rho^N\).

Equation reference: eq:partition. Source §3.2, p. 13, gives \[
\pi_\rho^N(\chi_Nm)=
 \frac{(\rho/\chi_N)^{2m}}{(m!)^2 Z_2(\rho/\chi_N)},
\qquad
Z_2(\phi)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{\phi^{2m}}{(m!)^2}.\] The zero configuration is absorbing because every jump rate vanishes. Thus the singleton \(E_0=\{u_t\equiv0\}\), a closed subset of the stated Skorokhod space, has the exact probability \[\mathbb P(\eta^N\in E_0)=Z_2(N^2/2)^{-N}.\] The zero path belongs to the energy class, solves [eq:skeleton] (#eq:skeleton) with \(g=0\), and has \(\mathcal J(0)=0\). Its printed rate is \(\mathcal I_{1/2}(0)=2\mathcal H_{1/2}(0)=2\).

Equation reference: eq:zeroContradiction. For completeness, the partition asymptotic needed here follows without any large-deviation theorem. Since its terms are nonnegative, \(Z_2(\phi)\le(\sum_m\phi^m/m!)^2=e^{2\phi}\). For \(m=\lfloor\phi\rfloor\) and \(\phi\ge2\), monotonicity of \(\log\) gives \[\log(m!)\le m\log m-m+1+\log m.\] The single \(m\)-term of the sum consequently gives \[2\phi-4-2\log\phi\le\log Z_2(\phi)\le2\phi.\] In particular, \(\phi^{-1}\log Z_2(\phi)\to2\), consistently with source Lemma 4.1, p. 17. Hence \[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\chi_N}{N}\log\mathbb P(\eta^N\in E_0)
=-\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\log Z_2(N^2/2)}{N^2}
=-1.\] The claimed closed-set upper bound (1.9) instead requires this limit to be at most \(-2\). This is a direct contradiction, not an inference from an unproved replacement lemma.

The contradiction does not require admitting a zero-mass fluctuation. Let \(E_1=\{u\in\mathbb D:u_0\equiv1\}\), which is closed because evaluation at time zero is continuous. The exact configuration \(\eta_0^N\equiv1\) has \(m=N^2\) particles per site and positive total mass. Future dynamics are unrestricted in this event. Formula [eq:partition] (#eq:partition) and the elementary factorial asymptotic \(\log(m!)=m\log m-m+o(m)\) yield \[\lim_N\frac{\chi_N}{N}\log\mathbb P(\eta^N\in E_1)=1-2\log2.\] On the other hand, \(\mathcal J\ge0\), and the constant macroscopic path \(u_t\equiv1\) attains \(\mathcal J=0\). Therefore \[\inf_{E_1}\mathcal I_{1/2}=2h(2)=4\log2-2.\] The printed upper bound would be \(2-4\log2\), strictly less than the actual value \(1-2\log2\), since \(\log2>\tfrac12\). This checks the same failure on a strictly positive, finite-entropy initial profile.

For a separate direct check, keep \(d=1,\alpha=2,t_{\mathrm{fin}}=1\) and set \[u(t,x)=2+\tfrac t2\cos(2\pi x),\qquad
\theta(t,x)=-\frac{\sin(2\pi x)}{2\pi u(t,x)},\qquad
g=u_x+\tfrac12\theta.\] The path is smooth, has mass \(2\), and satisfies \(3/2\le u\le5/2\). Direct differentiation verifies both equations [eq:skeleton] (#eq:skeleton) and [eq:action] (#eq:action), so all regularity and finite-cost hypotheses hold. These controls attain the respective infima, independently of the source’s dual-action formula: any other one-dimensional periodic control differs by \(c(t)/u\), and \[\int_{\mathbb T}\theta/u\,dx=0,\qquad
\int_{\mathbb T}g/u\,dx=0.\] The first equality follows from oddness in \(x\); the second also uses \(\int u_x/u=0\). The cross terms in the squared norms therefore vanish, proving minimality.

Equation reference: eq:smoothEDI. Put \(\Delta\mathcal H=\mathcal H(u_1)-\mathcal H(u_0)\) and \(D=\int_0^1\mathcal D_2(u_t)\,dt\). Periodic integration by parts in the continuity equation gives \(2\Delta\mathcal H=\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb T}u_x\theta\). Expanding the norm of \(g=u_x+\theta/2\) yields \[
\mathcal J(u)=\Delta\mathcal H+\tfrac12D+\tfrac14\mathcal A(u).\] Strict convexity of \(h\), and the fact that \(u_1\) is nonconstant of mean \(2\), imply \(\Delta\mathcal H>0\). For constant \(\rho\), mass conservation and [eq:printedH] (#eq:printedH) give \(\mathcal H_\rho(u_1)-\mathcal H_\rho(u_0)=\Delta\mathcal H/\rho\). At the allowed choice \(\rho=2\), the right-hand side of source (1.19) is consequently smaller than [eq:smoothEDI] (#eq:smoothEDI) by \(\Delta\mathcal H/2>0\). This refutes the literal identity on an everywhere positive smooth path.

Equation reference: eq:correctH. The compatible entropy is \[
\widehat{\mathcal H}_\rho(u)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho\,h(u/\rho)\,dx
 =\int_{\mathbb T^d}\{u\log(u/\rho)-u+\rho\}\,dx.\] It restores the pointwise dual [eq:legendre] (#eq:legendre), both exact event costs, and the smooth calculation above. For constant \(\rho\) on a fixed-mass path, \(\widehat{\mathcal H}_\rho(u_1)-\widehat{\mathcal H}_\rho(u_0)=\mathcal H(u_1)-\mathcal H(u_0)\), as the gradient-flow argument requires.

The case \(\rho=1\) has no discrepancy. Interpreting the measure in source (3.6) as \(\rho\,dx\) would also repair the definition, but the actual page displays \(dx\). This is strong evidence of an intended local correction, especially because (10.24) already contains the required weight; it does not validate the formula as printed. Neither an alternative definition of the equilibrium parameter nor a rescaling of the LDP speed is justified by the explicit laws and hypotheses used above. The positive witness also rules out a repair consisting only of excluding the vacuum.

The assessment is Major: the affected rate is the central conclusion of Theorem 2 and an input to the time-reversal argument for Theorem 4. The corrected formula is locally verified here; the entire revised LDP and irregular-path identity are not independently reproved. The hydrodynamic equation itself is not refuted.

analysis: Source (11.9), p. 48, proposes an infeasible optimizing control in the proof of Theorem 4. Related action coefficients in (11.6), (11.17) and (B.33)–(B.34) do not agree with [eq:action] (#eq:action).

The beginning of source §11, p. 47, correctly maps a continuity control to a skeleton control by \(g=
abla u^{\alpha/2}+	heta/2\). Equation (11.9) instead uses \[g_-=	heta/2-\Pi[u]
abla u^{\alpha/2},\] where \(\Pi[u]\) projects onto the closure of \(u^{\alpha/2}
abla\varphi\). This is asserted to be feasible and optimal.

Take \(\alpha=2\) and \(u(t,x)=v(x)=2+\cos(2\pi x)\) on \([0,1]\times\mathbb T\). The path is smooth, strictly positive and stationary. The continuity minimizer is \(\theta=0\), since it is feasible with zero cost. Also \(v_x=v(\log v)_x\), so the projection fixes \(v_x\). The printed choice is therefore \(g_-=-v_x\), for which the skeleton right-hand side equals \[\tfrac12(v^2)_{xx}-(vg_-)_x=(v^2)_{xx}.\] At \(x=0\) this is \(-24\pi^2\), whereas \(u_t=0\). The candidate is not feasible. The correct choice \(g_+=v_x\) makes the right-hand side identically zero. This verifies every hypothesis without relying on an irregular PDE existence assertion.

Equation reference: eq:trig. A different positive path detects the coefficient discrepancies: \[u(t,x)=2+\cos(2\pi(x-t)),\qquad
\theta=2-\frac3u,\qquad 0\le t\le1.\] Here \(u_t=-u_x\) and \((u\theta/2)_x=u_x\), so the continuity equation holds. Elementary integration gives \[
\int_{\mathbb T}\frac{dx}{u}=\frac1{\sqrt3},\qquad
\int_{\mathbb T}\frac{dx}{u^2}=\frac2{3\sqrt3},\qquad
\int_{\mathbb T}\frac{\theta}{u}\,dx=0.\] For example, the substitution \(z=\tan(s/2)\) in \((2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}(a+\cos s)^{-1}ds\) gives \((a^2-1)^{-1/2}\); differentiation in \(a>1\) gives the second integral at \(a=2\). Thus these evaluations need no numerical quadrature.

Equation reference: eq:actionvalue. As above, other feasible controls differ by \(c(t)/u\), and [eq:trig] (#eq:trig) proves that \(\theta\) is the unique minimizer. Hence \[
\mathcal A(u)=\tfrac12\int_0^1\int_{\mathbb T}\theta^2=2-\sqrt3>0.\] The correct skeleton minimizer is \(g=u_x+\theta/2\). Since \(\int u_x\theta=0\) and \(\int u_x^2=2\pi^2\), \[\mathcal J(u)=\pi^2+\tfrac14(2-\sqrt3).\] Entropy is constant along this translating path. The literal (11.6) instead gives \(\pi^2+\tfrac12(2-\sqrt3)\), so it is not an identity. The correct coefficient is already visible in source (11.15), p. 49, and in the statement (1.19); it must be retained in (11.6) and (11.17).

For the separate dual formula, let \[B_u(\varphi)=\langle\varphi_1,u_1\rangle-\langle\varphi_0,u_0\rangle
 -\int_0^1\langle\partial_t\varphi,u\rangle\,dt .\] The continuity equation gives \(B_u(\varphi)=\tfrac12\langle\theta,u\nabla\varphi\rangle\). Source (B.33)–(B.34), pp. 58–59, claims \(\mathcal A(u)=\sup_\varphi\{B_u(\varphi)-\tfrac12\|u\nabla\varphi\|_2^2\}\). Completing the square shows that this supremum is actually \(\|\theta\|_2^2/8=\mathcal A(u)/4\). It is attained for the present example: \(\varphi_x=\theta/(2u)\) is smooth and has zero spatial mean by [eq:trig] (#eq:trig), so a smooth periodic \(\varphi\) exists. Thus the displayed dual is \((2-\sqrt3)/4\), not \(2-\sqrt3\).

Write \(w=\Pi[u]\nabla u^{\alpha/2}\). The feasible projected control is \(g=\theta/2+w\), agreeing with the earlier source p. 47. Under time reversal, its companion is \(g^r=Tw-T\theta/2\), so \[g^r+Tg=2Tw,\qquad g^r-Tg=-T\theta.\] With a valid time-reversal rate identity, the parallelogram calculation therefore yields \[\mathcal J(u)=\tfrac12\{\alpha\Delta\widehat{\mathcal H}_\rho+\|w\|_2^2+\mathcal A(u)/2\}.\] The dual of the action [eq:action] (#eq:action) is normalized by \[\sup_\varphi\{B_u(\varphi)-\tfrac18
 \|u^{\alpha/2}\nabla\varphi\|_2^2\},\] as follows by completing the square with the continuity constraint. The replacement restores the exact smooth examples.

The control error is Major at the derivation level: feasibility and optimality feed (11.11)–(11.15), the central passage from reversibility to the claimed entropy–action identity. The correct map on p. 47 is explicit counterevidence against interpreting this as a new obstruction to the intended theorem. The factor-four appendix dual discrepancy is local: multiplying by the correct positive constant preserves the lower-semicontinuity argument’s qualitative conclusion. Neither example disproves the correctly normalized identity at \(\rho=1\), or the existence of minimizing controls. A complete proof for all irregular finite-cost paths is not supplied by these local corrections.

 =\frac{N^2-1}{6N^2}\longrightarrow\frac16,

 <\mathcal H(f)+\tfrac13=\mathcal F_2(f).\] This is a counterexample to (5.4) with all lattice and energy hypotheses checked. report: Abstract: The acquired 47-page publisher-formatted paper by Antonelli, Pozzetta and Semola is reviewed at the level of its hypotheses, proof dependencies and selected central calculations. A translated-unit-disk example gives the opposite sign in the printed inward-normal mean-curvature formula. The same formula is used in the graph-estimate proof underlying uniqueness, so this is a Major defect in that derivation. Two Minor local defects concern a metric estimate on an unrestricted Fermi tube and an assertion of Sobolev compactness for every finite exponent. Explicit local repairs are proved. Positive checks cover the exceptional-volume selection and the warped-surface example. None of these examples refutes the main uniqueness or strict-stability theorem. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Normal-graph estimates in Uniqueness on average of large isoperimetric sets: a technical verification report
# Paper identity, claims and scope

The reviewed paper is Gioacchino Antonelli, Marco Pozzetta and Daniele Semola, Uniqueness on average of large isoperimetric sets in noncompact manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature, Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics (2025), DOI 10.1002/cpa.22252 (https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.22252) [APS]. The exact institutional copy is publisher-formatted, says Accepted: 21 February 2025, and prints pages 1–47. The acquisition metadata identifies volume 78, issue 9, pages 1656–1702. This report uses the acquired early-online pagination: PDF page and printed page coincide. A separately repaginated issue version has not been checked.

For a smooth complete manifold \(M^n\), the principal hypotheses are \[\begin{gathered}
 \operatorname{Ric}\geq0,\qquad
 \operatorname{AVR}(M)=
 \lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{vol}(B_r(p))}{\omega_n r^n}>0,\\
 |\operatorname{Riem}(x)|\leq C\,d(p,x)^{-2},
 \qquad M\text{ not isometric to }\mathbb R^n .
 \end{gathered}\] Theorem 1.1 asserts uniqueness and strict volume-preserving stability of isoperimetric sets for volumes in a measurable set \(\mathcal G\) satisfying \[\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{|\mathcal G\cap(r,2r)|}{r}=1 .\] Theorem 1.2 constructs a surface showing why all sufficiently large volumes cannot replace this density-one statement.

All source text, including both appendices and the bibliography, was read. The detailed checks below concern the normal-graph formula and estimates in Section 4.2, their use in Proposition 4.3 and Theorem 4.1, the compactness step of Theorem 3.1, and selected estimates in Sections 2, 3 and 4.4. The source’s external existence, rigidity, regularity and metric-measure convergence theorems were not independently reproved. The coverage record distinguishes complete textual reading from selected proof reconstruction and actual evidence-page viewing. No author code was executed; missing code or supplements are not treated as mathematical defects.
# Problem 1: the inward-normal graph formula has the opposite sign

Problem 1 (Major: Lemma 4.5 and the derivation of Lemma 4.8).  In Section 4.2, Item 2 explicitly uses the unit inner normal to parametrize the graph. Item 1 gives the two isoperimetric boundaries the same positive mean curvature. With \(g_z\) the metric in these Fermi coordinates and \(\dot g_z=\partial_z g_z\), formula (4.37), on source page 26, has the opposite sign from the mean curvature specified by those conventions. The incompatible sign is then used in (4.47), on page 28.
## Conventions and a fully admissible example

Equation reference: eq:printedH. The convention is fixed independently on source page 20: \(H_{\partial E}=\Delta d^s\), where \(d^s\) is positive outside \(E\). Thus a Euclidean unit circle has \(H=1\), while the Fermi coordinate \(z\) increases inward. Write \[q=|\nabla^w w|_{g_w}^{\,2},\qquad Q=\sqrt{1+q},\qquad
 Y=\frac{\nabla^w w}{Q}.\] The printed formula is, in this notation, \[
 H_{\Sigma'}=-\operatorname{div}_{g_w}Y+
 \frac Q2\operatorname{tr}_{g_w}\dot g_w-
 \frac{\dot g_w(\nabla^w w,\nabla^w w)}{2Q}.\]

Equation reference: eq:diskw. Take \(M=\mathbb R^2\), \(E=B_1(0)\), and \(E'=B_1(d e_1)\), with \(0<d<1\). Both sets are smooth isoperimetric sets of area \(\pi\); their mean curvatures are equal to 1. The auxiliary assumptions of Section 4.2 do not exclude the Euclidean ambient manifold. In particular, this is an example against the auxiliary formula, not against the non-Euclidean main theorem. For \(\Sigma=\partial E\), set \[F(z,\theta)=(1-z)(\cos\theta,\sin\theta),\qquad -1<z<1 .\] This is a diffeomorphism onto the punctured disk \(0<|x|<2\); \(a=1\) is a valid tube parameter and \(g_z=(1-z)^2d\theta^2\). The curvature bounds in Item 4 hold with fixed \(K=2\). The translated circle is the normal graph of \[
 \rho_d(\theta)=d\cos\theta+\sqrt{1-d^2\sin^2\theta},
 \qquad w_d(\theta)=1-\rho_d(\theta).\] It has \(\|w_d\|_\infty=d<1\), and \(w_d\to0\) in \(C^\infty\) as \(d\downarrow0\). Thus any stipulated sufficiently small positive height and gradient bounds in Item 5 can also be met. The boundaries are distinct for every \(d>0\); the example does not rely on allowing the same set twice.

At \(\theta=0\), direct differentiation gives \[w_d=-d,\qquad w_d'=0,\qquad w_d''=d+d^2 .\] Consequently \(Q=1\), the last term of [eq:printedH] (#eq:printedH) vanishes, and \[\operatorname{div}_{g_w}Y=\frac{d+d^2}{(1+d)^2}=\frac d{1+d},
 \qquad
 \frac12\operatorname{tr}_{g_w}\dot g_w=-\frac1{1+d}.\] The printed right-hand side is therefore \(-1\), whereas the actual positive mean curvature of \(\partial B_1(d e_1)\) is \(+1\). This exact discrepancy persists for arbitrarily small \(d\). The accompanying independent symbolic calculation reproduces these identities; the analytic argument supplies the quantifiers and hypothesis verification.
## The corrected formula and its derivation

Equation reference: eq:correctH. Proposition 1.  For the inward Fermi coordinate and positive mean-curvature convention above, the graph formula is \[
 H_{\Sigma'}=\operatorname{div}_{g_w}Y-
 \frac Q2\operatorname{tr}_{g_w}\dot g_w+
 \frac{\dot g_w(\nabla^w w,\nabla^w w)}{2Q}.\]

Proof. The graph metric is \(g_w+dw\otimes dw\), so its area is \(A(w)=\int_\Sigma Q\,d\mu_{g_w}\). Differentiating \(A(w+tv)\) at \(t=0\), including the dependence of \(g_w^{-1}\) on \(w\), gives \[A'(w)[v]=\int_\Sigma
 \left\{ rac{g_w(
abla^w w,
abla^w v)}Q
 - rac{\dot g_w(
abla^w w,
abla^w w)}{2Q}\,v
 + rac Q2\operatorname{tr}_{g_w}\dot g_w\,vight\}d\mu_{g_w}.\] The inward graph unit normal is \(N_w=(\partial_z-
abla^w w)/Q\). The velocity \(v\partial_z\) has normal speed \(v/Q\) and \(d\mu_{\Sigma'}=Q\,d\mu_{g_w}\). The first variation with this positive \(H\) convention is therefore \(A'(w)[v]=-\int_\Sigma H_{\Sigma'}v\,d\mu_{g_w}\). Integration by parts yields [eq:correctH] (#eq:correctH). ◻

The source cites Pacard–Sun, Proposition 4.1. In the actually consulted author preprint [PS], pages 7–9 define \(h=-g(\nabla N,\cdot)\), \(H=\operatorname{tr}h\), and print precisely the signs in [eq:correctH] (#eq:correctH). This comparison is restricted to that formula and its local derivation. The independent proof above does not depend on every normalization in the cited preprint.

An outward-coordinate convention would make [eq:printedH] (#eq:printedH) appropriate, but that would change the explicitly stated inner normal. Changing \(H\) to a negative value would conflict with Item 1 and with \(H=\Delta d^s\). Direct inspection of source pages 20, 25–26 and 28 rules out an extraction ambiguity. In particular, \(\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}_{g_0}\dot g_0=-H_\Sigma\), whereas (4.47) substitutes \(+H_\Sigma\).
## A complete local repair of the differential estimate

Equation reference: eq:divrepair. The intended estimate (4.44) nevertheless follows with the correct signs on a uniformly controlled small tube. Put \[\beta(w)=\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}_{g_w}\dot g_w,\qquad
 \gamma(w)=\frac{\dot g_w(\nabla^w w,\nabla^w w)}{2Q}.\] Suppose \(H_{\Sigma'}=H_\Sigma\), \(|H_\Sigma|\leq\eta\), \(q\leq1\), \[|\beta(w)-\beta(0)|\leq C|w|,\qquad
 |\gamma(w)|\leq Cq .\] The small-tube bounds proved in Section 3 (#sec:tube) provide these estimates under the original curvature hypotheses, after restricting the graph height. Since \(\beta(0)=-H_\Sigma\), formula [eq:correctH] (#eq:correctH) gives exactly \[\operatorname{div}_{g_w}Y
 =Q\bigl(\beta(w)-\beta(0)\bigr)+(1-Q)H_\Sigma-\gamma(w).\] Using \(Q\leq\sqrt2\) and \(0\leq Q-1\leq q/2\) proves \[
 |\operatorname{div}_{g_w}Y|\leq C'(|w|+q).\] No sign assumption on \(\beta(w)\) is needed.
## Central dependency and limits

The affected chain is \[\begin{gathered}
 (4.37),\ (4.47)\ \longrightarrow\
 \text{Lemma 4.8}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{Lemma 4.7}\\
 \longrightarrow\ \text{Proposition 4.3}\ 
 \longrightarrow\ \text{Theorem 4.1}.
 \end{gathered}\] On source page 31, Lemma 4.7 supplies (4.65)–(4.66); on page 24, the \(L^\infty\)–\(L^2\) estimate controls the tubular Ricci remainder in (4.27). Thus the discrepancy changes an identity actually used in the central uniqueness derivation, supporting the Major assessment. The corrected local formula, differential bound and iteration are proved here. This is not a complete independent reconstruction of all global geometric inputs to Proposition 4.3 or Theorem 4.1, and no false-main-theorem claim is made.
# Problem 2: the metric estimate needs a smaller tube

Equation reference: eq:claimedmetric. Problem 2 (Minor: the unrestricted quantifier in Lemma 4.6).  On source page 27, Lemma 4.6 assumes only Items 2, 3 and 4, omitting Item 5’s small-height condition. It claims a constant \(C_1=C_1(K,a)\) such that, in particular, \[
 |\nabla^w w|_{g_w}^2
 \leq |\nabla w|_{g_0}^2(1+C_1|w|).\] That assertion fails over the full allowed tube even for the translated unit disks above.

These examples do not satisfy Item 5 with one fixed sufficiently small height. That is why they disprove Lemma 4.6 as written, but do not disprove its later use after the height is made sufficiently small.

Proposition 2 (Sufficient local replacement).  Assume Items 2–4 and the uniform bounds \(\|\mathrm{II}_\Sigma\|_\infty\leq K\), \(\|\operatorname{Riem}\|_\infty\leq K\) on the given tube. Set \[a_*=\min\{a/2,\,[8(K+1)]^{-1}\}.\] For \(|z|\leq a_*\), the metrics \(g_z\) are uniformly equivalent to \(g_0\), and \[\|g_z-g_0\|_{g_0}+\|\dot g_z-\dot g_0\|_{g_0}\leq C(K)|z|.\] In particular, for \(\|w\|_\infty\leq a_*\), \[\left||
abla^w w|_{g_w}^2-|
abla w|_{g_0}^2ight|
 \leq C(K)|w|\,|
abla w|_{g_0}^2 .\] The volume-density ratio differs from 1 by at most \(C(n,K)|w|\).

Proof. Parallel-transport the differential of the normal exponential map to \(T_xM\). For \(v\in T_x\Sigma\), its Jacobi field \(J\) satisfies \(J''=-R_zJ\), \(J(0)=v\), \(|J'(0)|\leq K|v|\). The first-order system and Gronwall’s inequality give \[|J(z)|+|J'(z)|
 \leq (K+1)e^{(K+1)|z|}|v|
 \leq 2(K+1)|v|
 \quad (|z|\leq a_*).\] Hence \(|J(z)-v|\leq2(K+1)|z||v|\leq|v|/4\). It follows that \(\tfrac9{16}g_0\leq g_z\leq\tfrac{25}{16}g_0\). Since \(g_z(v,v)=|J(z)|^2\), the same estimates and the Jacobi equation bound both \(\dot g_z\) and \(\ddot g_z\). Polarization and integration give the displayed Lipschitz bounds. Uniform invertibility gives the inverse-metric estimate; applying the smooth determinant map on this uniformly positive set of matrices gives the volume-density bound. ◻

Shrinking the height once more makes all comparison factors positive with any required fixed margin. This supplies the estimates actually needed in Section 4.2 and in Section 2 of this report. The supported defect is the lemma’s unrestricted domain. The main application already permits arbitrarily small graph height, so central damage from this domain overstatement has not been demonstrated. The assessment is Minor.
# Problem 3: an unnecessary assertion of unrestricted \(L^p\) compactness

Problem 3 (Minor: Theorem 3.1, Step 3, source page 13).  After obtaining uniform \(H^{1,2}\) bounds on \(\bar f_i\), the text asserts a uniform \((p,2)\)-Sobolev inequality and strong \(L^p\) subsequence convergence for every \(p>1\). In hypersurface dimension \(m=n-1\geq3\), that general compactness assertion is false. The argument needs substantially less.

Here is a complete example against the stated compactness implication. Fix a compact smooth \(m\)-manifold, \(m\geq3\), a coordinate chart and a nonzero smooth bump \(\psi\) supported in its interior. For small \(\delta>0\), let \[b_\delta(x)=\delta^{-(m-2)/2}\psi(x/\delta)\] inside the chart and zero outside. Change of variables and smooth uniform metric bounds show \[\|b_\delta\|_2\asymp\delta,\qquad
 \|\nabla b_\delta\|_2\asymp1,\qquad
 \|b_\delta\|_p\asymp
 \delta^{\,m/p-(m-2)/2}.\] For \(m=3,p=8\), the last exponent is \(-1/8\). Subtract the mean of \(b_\delta\), add a fixed smooth mean-zero function \(u\) with \(\|u\|_2=1\), and divide by the resulting \(L^2\) norm. The denominator tends to 1. This produces smooth mean-zero, \(L^2\)-normalized functions with bounded \(H^1\) norm and unbounded \(L^8\) norm. The construction applies on any such compact link, including a scaled three-sphere.

This example addresses the claimed Sobolev/compactness implication. It is not asserted to satisfy the contradictory Rayleigh inequality (3.12) for the paper’s actual sequence, and is not a counterexample to Theorem 3.1. For \(m\geq3\), finite exponents strictly below \(2m/(m-2)\) give the usual compact embedding; in particular an exponent slightly above 2 would already be enough.

There is an even simpler repair that uses only strong \(L^2\) convergence. Pull the metrics back to the limiting compact manifold using the \(C^{1,\alpha}\) convergence obtained in Step 2. Rellich compactness gives \(f_i\to f\) in \(L^2\); the uniformly convergent volume densities preserve the mean-zero condition and \(\|f\|_2=1\). In the source’s notation, \[h_i=\operatorname{Ric}(\nu_{\Sigma_i},\nu_{\Sigma_i})
       +|\mathrm{II}_{\Sigma_i}|^2+\tfrac32\varepsilon_M,
 \qquad
 h_i\longrightarrow c:=n-1+\tfrac32\varepsilon_M
 \quad\hbox{in }L^1 ,\] and \(\|h_i\|_\infty\leq M\) uniformly, with \(M\geq|c|\). On a common fixed measure space, \[\left|\int h_i(f_i^2-f^2)\right|
 \leq M\|f_i-f\|_2(\|f_i\|_2+\|f\|_2)\longrightarrow0 .\] For \(L>0\), the other difference satisfies \[\left|\int(h_i-c)f^2\right|
 \leq L\|h_i-c\|_1+
      2M\int_{\{f^2>L\}}f^2 .\] First let \(i\to\infty\), then \(L\to\infty\). Uniform convergence of the volume densities contributes only vanishing terms of the same type. Thus \[\int h_i f_i^2\,d\mu_i\longrightarrow
 \left(n-1+\tfrac32\varepsilon_M\right)\int f^2\,d\mu
 =n-1+\tfrac32\varepsilon_M .\] Lower semicontinuity of Dirichlet energy now gives precisely the bound in (3.17), which contradicts the spectral gap \(\lambda_1(N)\geq n-1+2\varepsilon_M\) established in Step 1. The term \(3\varepsilon_M/2\) is missing in the intervening printed (3.16), but is already present in (3.13) and (3.17); it is not counted as an additional substantive problem. The unnecessary all-\(p\) assertion can be removed without changing this contradiction, so the supported impact is local and Minor.
# Other checked arguments and limits
## The warped-surface example

The hypotheses of source Lemma 2.2 are nonempty. For example, \[a_j=2^{3j+10},\qquad b_j=2^j,\qquad j\geq0,
 \qquad
 \sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{b_j}{a_j}=\frac1{768}<\frac1{16}.\] These sequences have \(a_{j+1}>a_j+b_j\), \(a_j\geq b_j\), and \(b_j\to\infty\). Choosing \(J_j\) to be the middle half of \([a_j,a_j+b_j]\) permits the smooth concave warping construction described in the paper. Its stated inequalities imply on \(J_j\) \[\varphi\varphi''-(\varphi')^2+1
 \leq -\frac78-\left(\frac78\right)^2+1
 =-\frac{41}{64}<0 .\] The first angular Fourier mode therefore gives negative constrained second variation for the centered circle. Also, on \([a_j,a_j+b_j]\), \[-\frac{\varphi''}{\varphi}
 \leq\frac{16}{7a_jr}
 \leq\frac{32}{7r^2}\leq\frac{16}{r^2}.\] For the chosen central intervals, the corresponding volume interval has length at least \(7\pi a_jb_j/8\), tending to infinity.

The rotation argument has a useful geometric qualification. A smooth finite-volume rotationally invariant constant-mean-curvature region cannot have an inner boundary circle when \(\varphi'>0\): the inner and outer boundary circles would have opposite signs of the oriented mean curvature. Since \(\varphi(r)\geq7r/8\), a finite-volume such region cannot extend to infinity. Thus a rotationally invariant isoperimetric region must be a centered disk. When that disk is unstable, an isoperimetric region is not rotationally invariant; its nontrivial rotation orbit supplies distinct minimizers and a nonzero volume-preserving Jacobi field. This explains the failure of uniqueness and strict stability for those volumes, conditional on the isoperimetric existence result invoked by the source.
## Supporting checks
## Remaining geometric scope

Both appendices were read, including the almost-minimizer regularity input and Proposition B.1’s distinction between a local Jacobi-field estimate and a global first-collision argument. A separate concern was considered at (4.63): a curvature-decay bound is asserted on a unit tube around a rescaled boundary, whereas curvature decay directly controls annuli away from the rescaled basepoint. A smaller annular tube is the natural domain to check. No complete counterexample satisfying all of the isoperimetric hypotheses was established, and no additional severity is assigned to this point. It remains an explicit limit of the global repair claimed here.
# Overall impact and recorded state

Problem 1 establishes an invalid identity and subsequent sign substitution on the proof path to the principal uniqueness result. The corrected formula and local graph estimates support a repair; they do not establish independent acceptance of the entire paper. claim: Recorded check: the inward-normal graph formula has the opposite sign

analysis: In Section 4.2, Item 2 explicitly uses the unit inner normal to parametrize the graph. Item 1 gives the two isoperimetric boundaries the same positive mean curvature. With \(g_z\) the metric in these Fermi coordinates and \(\dot g_z=\partial_z g_z\), formula (4.37), on source page 26, has the opposite sign from the mean curvature specified by those conventions. The incompatible sign is then used in (4.47), on page 28.

Equation reference: eq:printedH. The convention is fixed independently on source page 20: \(H_{\partial E}=\Delta d^s\), where \(d^s\) is positive outside \(E\). Thus a Euclidean unit circle has \(H=1\), while the Fermi coordinate \(z\) increases inward. Write \[q=|\nabla^w w|_{g_w}^{\,2},\qquad Q=\sqrt{1+q},\qquad
 Y=\frac{\nabla^w w}{Q}.\] The printed formula is, in this notation, \[
 H_{\Sigma'}=-\operatorname{div}_{g_w}Y+
 \frac Q2\operatorname{tr}_{g_w}\dot g_w-
 \frac{\dot g_w(\nabla^w w,\nabla^w w)}{2Q}.\]

Equation reference: eq:diskw. Take \(M=\mathbb R^2\), \(E=B_1(0)\), and \(E'=B_1(d e_1)\), with \(0<d<1\). Both sets are smooth isoperimetric sets of area \(\pi\); their mean curvatures are equal to 1. The auxiliary assumptions of Section 4.2 do not exclude the Euclidean ambient manifold. In particular, this is an example against the auxiliary formula, not against the non-Euclidean main theorem. For \(\Sigma=\partial E\), set \[F(z,\theta)=(1-z)(\cos\theta,\sin\theta),\qquad -1<z<1 .\] This is a diffeomorphism onto the punctured disk \(0<|x|<2\); \(a=1\) is a valid tube parameter and \(g_z=(1-z)^2d\theta^2\). The curvature bounds in Item 4 hold with fixed \(K=2\). The translated circle is the normal graph of \[
 \rho_d(\theta)=d\cos\theta+\sqrt{1-d^2\sin^2\theta},
 \qquad w_d(\theta)=1-\rho_d(\theta).\] It has \(\|w_d\|_\infty=d<1\), and \(w_d\to0\) in \(C^\infty\) as \(d\downarrow0\). Thus any stipulated sufficiently small positive height and gradient bounds in Item 5 can also be met. The boundaries are distinct for every \(d>0\); the example does not rely on allowing the same set twice.

At \(\theta=0\), direct differentiation gives \[w_d=-d,\qquad w_d'=0,\qquad w_d''=d+d^2 .\] Consequently \(Q=1\), the last term of [eq:printedH] (#eq:printedH) vanishes, and \[\operatorname{div}_{g_w}Y=\frac{d+d^2}{(1+d)^2}=\frac d{1+d},
 \qquad
 \frac12\operatorname{tr}_{g_w}\dot g_w=-\frac1{1+d}.\] The printed right-hand side is therefore \(-1\), whereas the actual positive mean curvature of \(\partial B_1(d e_1)\) is \(+1\). This exact discrepancy persists for arbitrarily small \(d\). The accompanying independent symbolic calculation reproduces these identities; the analytic argument supplies the quantifiers and hypothesis verification.

analysis:
On source page 27, Lemma 4.6 assumes only Items 2, 3 and 4, omitting Item 5’s small-height condition. It claims a constant \(C_1=C_1(K,a)\) such that, in particular, \[

These examples do not satisfy Item 5 with one fixed sufficiently small height. That is why they disprove Lemma 4.6 as written, but do not disprove its later use after the height is made sufficiently small.

Proposition 2 (Sufficient local replacement).  Assume Items 2–4 and the uniform bounds \(\|\mathrm{II}_\Sigma\|_\infty\leq K\), \(\|\operatorname{Riem}\|_\infty\leq K\) on the given tube. Set \[a_*=\min\{a/2,\,[8(K+1)]^{-1}\}.\] For \(|z|\leq a_*\), the metrics \(g_z\) are uniformly equivalent to \(g_0\), and \[\|g_z-g_0\|_{g_0}+\|\dot g_z-\dot g_0\|_{g_0}\leq C(K)|z|.\] In particular, for \(\|w\|_\infty\leq a_*\), \[\left||
abla^w w|_{g_w}^2-|

abla w|_{g_0}^2 .\] The volume-density ratio differs from 1 by at most \(C(n,K)|w|\).

 \leq (K+1)e^{(K+1)|z|}|v|

 \quad (|z|\leq a_*).\] Hence \(|J(z)-v|\leq2(K+1)|z||v|\leq|v|/4\). It follows that \(\tfrac9{16}g_0\leq g_z\leq\tfrac{25}{16}g_0\). Since \(g_z(v,v)=|J(z)|^2\), the same estimates and the Jacobi equation bound both \(\dot g_z\) and \(\ddot g_z\). Polarization and integration give the displayed Lipschitz bounds. Uniform invertibility gives the inverse-metric estimate; applying the smooth determinant map on this uniformly positive set of matrices gives the volume-density bound. ◻

problems.title: an unnecessary assertion of unrestricted \(L^p\) compactness
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 11 Pdf pages: 12 Pdf pages: 13 Printed pages: 11 Printed pages: 12 Printed pages: 13 Claim: Theorem3.1 Step3 asserts a uniform(p,2)-Sobolev inequality and strong Lp convergence for every p>1 from uniform H1 bounds. Report sections: 4
claim: Recorded check: an unnecessary assertion of unrestricted \(L^p\) compactness

Compact smooth hypersurface dimension m=n-1>=3; a localized smooth bump. Normalization can preserve mean0 and L2norm1 while retaining bounded H1 norm. This example addresses the Sobolev/compactness inference, not the impossible full contradictory Rayleigh sequence.
analysis: After obtaining uniform \(H^{1,2}\) bounds on \(\bar f_i\), the text asserts a uniform \((p,2)\)-Sobolev inequality and strong \(L^p\) subsequence convergence for every \(p>1\). In hypersurface dimension \(m=n-1\geq3\), that general compactness assertion is false. The argument needs substantially less.

Here is a complete example against the stated compactness implication. Fix a compact smooth \(m\)-manifold, \(m\geq3\), a coordinate chart and a nonzero smooth bump \(\psi\) supported in its interior. For small \(\delta>0\), let \[b_\delta(x)=\delta^{-(m-2)/2}\psi(x/\delta)\] inside the chart and zero outside. Change of variables and smooth uniform metric bounds show \[\|b_\delta\|_2\asymp\delta,\qquad
 \|\nabla b_\delta\|_2\asymp1,\qquad
 \|b_\delta\|_p\asymp
 \delta^{\,m/p-(m-2)/2}.\] For \(m=3,p=8\), the last exponent is \(-1/8\). Subtract the mean of \(b_\delta\), add a fixed smooth mean-zero function \(u\) with \(\|u\|_2=1\), and divide by the resulting \(L^2\) norm. The denominator tends to 1. This produces smooth mean-zero, \(L^2\)-normalized functions with bounded \(H^1\) norm and unbounded \(L^8\) norm. The construction applies on any such compact link, including a scaled three-sphere.

This example addresses the claimed Sobolev/compactness implication. It is not asserted to satisfy the contradictory Rayleigh inequality (3.12) for the paper’s actual sequence, and is not a counterexample to Theorem 3.1. For \(m\geq3\), finite exponents strictly below \(2m/(m-2)\) give the usual compact embedding; in particular an exponent slightly above 2 would already be enough.

There is an even simpler repair that uses only strong \(L^2\) convergence. Pull the metrics back to the limiting compact manifold using the \(C^{1,\alpha}\) convergence obtained in Step 2. Rellich compactness gives \(f_i\to f\) in \(L^2\); the uniformly convergent volume densities preserve the mean-zero condition and \(\|f\|_2=1\). In the source’s notation, \[h_i=\operatorname{Ric}(\nu_{\Sigma_i},\nu_{\Sigma_i})
       +|\mathrm{II}_{\Sigma_i}|^2+\tfrac32\varepsilon_M,
 \qquad
 h_i\longrightarrow c:=n-1+\tfrac32\varepsilon_M
 \quad\hbox{in }L^1 ,\] and \(\|h_i\|_\infty\leq M\) uniformly, with \(M\geq|c|\). On a common fixed measure space, \[\left|\int h_i(f_i^2-f^2)\right|
 \leq M\|f_i-f\|_2(\|f_i\|_2+\|f\|_2)\longrightarrow0 .\] For \(L>0\), the other difference satisfies \[\left|\int(h_i-c)f^2\right|
 \leq L\|h_i-c\|_1+
      2M\int_{\{f^2>L\}}f^2 .\] First let \(i\to\infty\), then \(L\to\infty\). Uniform convergence of the volume densities contributes only vanishing terms of the same type. Thus \[\int h_i f_i^2\,d\mu_i\longrightarrow
 \left(n-1+\tfrac32\varepsilon_M\right)\int f^2\,d\mu
 =n-1+\tfrac32\varepsilon_M .\] Lower semicontinuity of Dirichlet energy now gives precisely the bound in (3.17), which contradicts the spectral gap \(\lambda_1(N)\geq n-1+2\varepsilon_M\) established in Step 1. The term \(3\varepsilon_M/2\) is missing in the intervening printed (3.16), but is already present in (3.13) and (3.17); it is not counted as an additional substantive problem. The unnecessary all-\(p\) assertion can be removed without changing this contradiction, so the supported impact is local and Minor.

report: Abstract: This review examines the classification of equivariant harmonic map heat flows and bounded radial critical heat flows in the specified preprint of Kim and Merle. No substantive issue was established in the inspected scope. The review checks the theorem hypotheses, the dependence on soliton resolution, the modified-profile and dissipation arguments, and the transition from modulation estimates to the stated rates. Independent calculations verify the signs and normalizations of the interaction constants and the rate recurrence. This is an initial technical report; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Initial Technical Review of M25-0411
# Paper identity and reviewed scope

The paper is Kihyun Kim and Frank Merle, On classification of global dynamics for energy-critical equivariant harmonic map heat flows and radial nonlinear heat equation, associated with Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 78 (2025), 1783–1842, DOI https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.22253. The reviewed object is the 46-page PDF of arXiv:2404.04247v3, submitted 1 April 2025 [KM]. All page locators below refer to that PDF, whose printed page numbers agree with the PDF page numbers. The journal version was not compared line by line; this report does not silently transfer its conclusion to an uninspected version.

The complete supplied PDF, including Appendix A and its bibliography, was read. All 46 source pages were also visually inspected through the native image route. The main focus was Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.4; Lemmas 2.6–2.7; Proposition 3.1 and its construction; Proposition 4.1; and Proposition 5.2 and Section 5.2. External theorems were not all independently reproved. In particular, the hypotheses of Aryan’s soliton-resolution theorem were checked in the explicitly identified later version [Aryan], pp. 1–3; the full proof of that external paper was not reviewed.

The frozen manifest and a bounded check of the current arXiv entry, author publication page and publisher metadata did not identify a separate correction to this reviewed version. This is a statement about the search performed, not a proof that no correction exists. No relevant separate executable supplement was located in the acquired manifest. No author code was executed, and absence of code is not treated as a mathematical defect.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

For harmonic map heat flow (HMHF), the unknown is the real radial angle \(v(t,r)\) with equivariance index \(D\in\mathbb Z_{\geq3}\): \[\partial_t v=\partial_{rr}v+r^{-1}\partial_rv
             -\frac{D^2}{2r^2}\sin(2v).\] Theorem 1.1, p. 4, concerns every finite-energy datum in the sector \(\mathcal E_{\ell,m}\), with endpoint limits \(\ell\pi\) and \(m\pi\), where \(\ell,m\in\mathbb Z\). It asserts global existence, \(J=|m-\ell|\) bubbles, a common sign \(\operatorname{sgn}(m-\ell)\) when \(J>0\), and the stated universal scales. The case \(J=0\) is the empty-sum, decaying case; the unused limiting scale then has no uniqueness content.

For the nonlinear heat equation (NLH), the statement is restricted to radial solutions of \[\partial_tu=\Delta u+|u|^{4/(N-2)}u,\qquad N\geq7,
 \qquad \sup_{0\leq t<T}\|u(t)\|_{\dot H^1}<\infty.\] Theorem 1.2, p. 5, expressly assumes the statement formulated as Open Question 2.2, p. 13. It therefore does not assert the corresponding classification for arbitrary unbounded, nonradial, or lower-dimensional solutions. Remark 1.3, p. 5, and the paragraph following (2.4), p. 13, explicitly acknowledge the subsequent soliton-resolution work.

The common notation is \[D=(N-2)/2>2,\qquad p=1+2/D,\qquad
 W(r)=\left(1+\frac{r^2}{N(N-2)}\right)^{-D}\] for NLH. For HMHF, \(u=r^{-D}v\), \(N=2D+2\), \(Q(r)=2\arctan(r^D)\) and \(W=r^{-D}Q\). The respective scaling generators are \(\Lambda W=(r\partial_r+D)W\) and \(\Lambda Q=r\partial_rQ\). The transformed HMHF states belong to affine sectors \(\mathcal H_{0,m}\). The paper requires the remainder after subtracting bubbles and the body map to lie in \(\dot H^1\); it does not require the individual transformed HMHF bubble \(r^{-D}Q\) to lie in that space.

Theorem 1.4, p. 10, fixes a finite integer \(J\geq1\), fixed signs, continuous positive scales satisfying \(\lambda_J\ll\cdots\ll\lambda_1\), and convergence of the remainder in \(\dot H^1\). A finite endpoint requires \(\lambda_1(t)\to0\) and an appropriate body map \(z^*\) in the stated affine sector; the global case has \(z^*=0\). These conditions, including the ordered scale ratios, are used essentially. The proof subsequently chooses differentiable modulation parameters asymptotic to the original continuous scales; it does not assume that the initially supplied scales were differentiable.
# Proof dependencies and checks
## The external resolution hypothesis

The reduction on pp. 9–13 uses Proposition 2.1 for HMHF and the statement of Open Question 2.2 for NLH. In the later reference actually inspected, Aryan’s Theorem 1.1 [Aryan], p. 2, assumes radial finite-energy data and boundedness of the energy-space norm near the maximal endpoint. It gives continuous, separated bubble scales, an energy-small remainder, and a body term only at a finite endpoint.
## Modified profiles and dissipation

The essential chain is \[\text{Lemma 2.7}\ \longrightarrow\ \text{Proposition 3.1}\
 \longrightarrow\ \text{Proposition 4.1}\
 \longrightarrow\ \text{Proposition 5.2 and Section 5.2}.\] Lemma 2.7, pp. 15–16, is a norm coercivity statement for the linearized operator after removing one kernel direction at each scale. It is not a claim that the NLH quadratic form has no negative directions. The compactness argument uses fixed finite \(J\), separated scales, orthogonality to a compactly supported test function with nonzero kernel pairing, and Hardy–Rellich bounds in the stated dimension range.

The modified profiles of Proposition 3.1, pp. 16–17, are constructed in pp. 18–29 and Appendix A, pp. 42–44. Their purpose is to make the leading interaction nearly orthogonal to the linearized remainder. The order of the small parameters in (3.26), the local support of the correction, and the Hölder exponent \(p-1>0\) in the derivative iteration are material. In Lemma 3.6, p. 24, the derivative differences are summable because one can choose \(2^{-(p-1)}<a<1\). This remains possible for every fixed \(D>2\), without asserting a uniform contraction rate as \(D\to\infty\).

Equation reference: eq:diss. The weighted remainder estimates (3.10)–(3.12) have different roles: the small \(L^2\) remainder yields the dissipation estimate, while the weighted \(L^1\) estimates control the modulation pairings. Proposition 4.1, pp. 29–35, proves \[
 \int_{t_0}^{T}\left(\mathcal D+\|g\|_{\dot H^2}^2\right)\,dt<\infty,
 \qquad
 \mathcal D=\sum_{j=2}^J\frac{\mu_j^{2D}}{\lambda_j^2},
 \quad \mu_j=\frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_{j-1}}.\] For finite \(T\), the proof first localizes near the origin to make the body map small, then uses Lemma 4.5 for the exterior. For infinite \(T\), global smallness of \(g\) supplies the simpler argument. Treating a finite-endpoint body map as globally small would omit this distinction.
## Why the dimension threshold is operative

For NLH, \(\Lambda W(r)\) has a nonzero leading term proportional to \(r^{-2D}\) at infinity. Hence the radial integrand for \(\|r\Lambda W\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{2D+2})}^2\) behaves like \(r^{3-2D}\). It is integrable precisely when \(D>2\); at \(D=2\) the tail diverges logarithmically. The origin is harmless. This verifies the dimension restriction invoked on p. 10. The identity used on pp. 39–40, \(\Lambda_{-1}\Lambda W=(2-D)\Lambda W+R\), with faster-decaying \(R\), also needs \(2-D\ne0\). The lower-dimensional regimes discussed on p. 6 therefore do not furnish counterexamples to the stated theorems.
## From modulation estimates to rates

Proposition 5.2, pp. 37–40, contains a derivative of an \(o(1)\) correction as well as errors. It cannot be replaced by an exact unperturbed ODE without justification. Section 5.2, pp. 40–42, removes those errors by using \(0<s_2<\cdots<s_J<2\), sign-definite correction terms, and the integrable quantity in [eq:diss] (#eq:diss). It obtains \(\lambda_k^\pm=e^{o(1)}\lambda_k\) with two-sided differential inequalities.

For \(k=1\), \(\mu_1=0\). The upper and lower logarithmic quantities are monotone in opposite directions and differ by \(o(1)\). Each bounds the other near the endpoint, so their common limit is finite, rather than an extended infinite value. This yields \(0<L_\infty<\infty\) and excludes finite \(T\). For \(k\geq2\), integrating the reciprocal power \((\lambda_k^-)^{-(D-2)}\) forces \(\kappa\,\iota_k\iota_{k-1}<0\), since otherwise its positive left side would eventually be bounded above by a negative divergent term. This is the decisive sign argument, not an assumption about the signs.
# Independent calculations
## Interaction constants
The definitions (1.11)–(1.12), p. 9, give opposite signs in the two equations. These signs control the final alternating NLH pattern and the common HMHF sign.

Claim 1.  For the HMHF normalization of the reviewed paper, \[\kappa_{\rm HMHF}=-\frac{4D^2}{\pi}\sin\frac{\pi}{D}<0
 \qquad(D\geq3).\]

Proof. Using \(\Lambda Q=2Dr^D/(1+r^{2D})\) and the substitution \(s=r^{2D}\), \[\int_0^\infty(\Lambda Q)^3r^{D-1}\,dr
 =4D^2\int_0^\infty\frac{s}{(1+s)^3}\,ds=2D^2.\] The same substitution and the beta integral give \[\int_0^\infty(\Lambda Q)^2r\,dr
 =2D\,B(1+1/D,1-1/D)=\frac{2\pi}{\sin(\pi/D)}.\] Substitution into (1.11) proves the formula. ◻

For NLH put \(c=N(N-2)=4D(D+1)\) and \(s=r^2/c\). Then \(\Lambda W=D(1-s)(1+s)^{-D-1}\). Direct beta integration gives \[\int W^pr^{N-1}\,dr=\frac{c^{D+1}}{2(D+1)},\qquad
 \int(\Lambda W)^2r^{N-1}\,dr
 =c^{D+1}\frac{D(D+2)}{D-1}B(D+1,D+1).\] Consequently, \[\kappa_{\rm NLH}=
 \frac{D-1}{2(D+1)(D+2)B(D+1,D+1)}>0.\] The angular surface factor cancels in each ratio.

Independent standard-library quadrature, performed without author code, corroborated these identities: for HMHF at \(D=3,4,5\), the absolute differences were below \(4\times10^{-15}\); for NLH at \(D=5/2,3,4,5\), they were below \(10^{-11}\). The analytic calculation above establishes the formulas; the finite quadrature is not an interval-certified universal proof.

No substantive Problem is asserted. Several apparent discrepancies were tested against the actual PDF and their downstream use. In particular, (3.25), p. 20, contains \(\mu_{J+1}\) inside the parenthesis, not \(\mu_{J+1}^D\); the image resolves a misleading extraction. It does not establish an invalid core derivation or a false final theorem and is not elevated to an in-scope mathematical finding.

The complete supplied proof was read, but the review does not claim a machine-checked formal proof, a new PDE simulation, or a full independent reproof of every cited theorem. Abstract: This review concerns the acquired 94-page arXiv version of the paper by Vadim Gorin and Karl Liechty, arXiv:2310.12735v1, submitted 19 October 2023 (the PDF is dated 20 October 2023), associated with DOI https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.22254.
