Title: Initial Scientific Review
Boundary statistics for the six-vertex model with DWBC
# Version, scope, and principal claims

All 94 pages of the exact acquired source were read, including Appendix A and the bibliography. Page numbers below are the printed PDF pages. The publisher’s 2025 article was identified but was not acquired and compared line by line. Every finding is restricted to the specified arXiv version.

The model has positive homogeneous weights \(a,b,c\), domain wall boundary conditions on an \(n\)-square, and \[\Delta=\frac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}.\] The coordinates \(\lambda_i^k\) form a strictly increasing row of length \(k\), with weak interlacing between adjacent rows. Theorem 1.3 (p. 6) fixes the weights with \(\Delta<1\) and asserts finite-dimensional convergence, after centering by \(mn\) and scaling by \(s\sqrt n\), to GUE corners. This includes \(\Delta=-1\), but not \(\Delta=1\) or weights varying with \(n\). Theorem 1.4 (p. 7) assumes \(\Delta>1\), \(a>b\), and gives an unscaled stochastic six-vertex limit with \(0<b_1<b_2<1\). Reflection handles the opposite ordering; \(a=b>0,c>0\) cannot satisfy \(\Delta>1\). Theorem 1.8 (p. 8) first takes \(c\downarrow0\) at fixed \(n\), then \(n\to\infty\), for fixed \(a>b>0\). It does not divide zero partition functions at literal \(c=0\). Proposition 1.10 (p. 9) instead assumes \(n\log q_n\to\theta\); its density at \(\theta=0\) has the uniform continuous extension.

The proof uses the Izergin–Korepin determinant and orthogonal polynomials for normalized partition-function asymptotics. Propositions 4.4 and 4.6 are the analytic inputs; Sections 4–5 pass from one inhomogeneity to fixed \(k\), and Section 6 identifies laws using symmetric functions, tightness and conditional interlacing measures. Section 7 treats \(c=0\) by a separate permutation argument. Section 3 explicitly presents a conditional alternative; its named conjectures alone are not defects in the separate Appendix A route.

The review examined positivity and convergence domains, fixed-\(k\) restrictions, lattice exclusions, analytic continuation at zero, coalescing inhomogeneities, tightness versus uniform integrability, and the order of limits. It does not certify every theorem in all cited external works. No author code was executed.
# A false uniform tail bound
Problem 1 (Major: Proposition 6.12).  Equation (6.28), p. 58, is false under its stated quantifiers, including the diffusive scaling used in Proposition 6.14.
## Claim and admissible parameters

Equation reference: eq:printed-tail. With \(\widetilde F_\nu\) defined in (6.19), p. 56, put \[r_j=\frac{b(t+\varepsilon\xi_j,\gamma)a(t,\gamma)}
 {b(t,\gamma)a(t+\varepsilon\xi_j,\gamma)}.\] The claimed bound is \[
 \widetilde F_\nu(\varepsilon\xi_1,\ldots,\varepsilon\xi_k)
 \le C_1\prod_{j=1}^k r_j^M
 \exp\left((k+o(1))\sum_{i=1}^k
       |\sigma\varepsilon(\nu_i-M)\xi_i|\right).\] Here \(k,t,\gamma\) and a compact set of real \(\xi\)’s are fixed, \(C_1\) is independent of \(\nu,M\), and the error is uniform. The absolute values in the actual page image are retained.

Take \(k=2\), \(t=0,\gamma=\pi/4\) in the disordered parametrization: \(a=b=1/\sqrt2,c=1,\Delta=0,\sigma=2\). Let the compact set be \(\{(1,0)\}\), and let \(\nu=(M,M+L)\), where \(M,L\) are positive integers and \(n\ge M+L\). These are admissible strict rows, extendable to a monotone triangle with top row \(1,\ldots,n\).
## Exact finite counterexample

In particular, set \(n=2j^2\), \(M=L=j^2\) and \(\varepsilon=n^{-1/2}\). Then \(M=mn\), since \(m=1/2\), and \(\nu_2=n\). Since \(\log r=2\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^3)\), the logarithm of the lower bound is \[\sqrt2\,j-2\log j+O(1)\longrightarrow+\infty .\] A uniform \(o(1)\) cannot alter the zero exponent. Independent direct summation gives the following illustrations; the analytic divergence proves the defect.
\(n\) | Centered \(\widetilde F\) | Endpoint lower bound
## Core dependency and a sufficient replacement

On p. 60, (6.28) and (6.36) justify passage to the limit in (6.35) to obtain (6.38). This is a core uniform-integrability step for Proposition 6.14 and Theorem 1.3. Neither an omitted absolute value nor compactness rescues the claim. An ordering restriction on \(\xi_i\)’s is not stated and would require a new argument.

At \(\varepsilon=n^{-1/2},M=mn\), (6.36), conditional on its preceding inputs, controls a strictly larger exponential of \(R/\sqrt n\). It therefore makes the contribution from \(R/\sqrt n>K\) uniformly small as \(K\to\infty\). This repairs this particular limit step, not the other analytic inputs below. The classification is Major because an invalid bound is explicitly used in a core derivation, even though a local replacement is available.
# The antiferroelectric model depends on n
Problem 2 (Major: Proposition 4.4 and Appendix A.1).  The antiferroelectric model functions cannot have their asserted independence from \(n\).

Proposition 4.4, p. 29, equations (4.30)–(4.33), uses \(M_{\mathrm{AF}}(z),N_{\mathrm{AF}}(z)\). Equation (A.45) and footnote 20, p. 79, explicitly assert independence from \(n\) for the model quantities; p. 80 identifies \(M_{\mathrm{AF}}(z)=\mathbf M(\gamma z)_{22}\). The saddle prefactor on pp. 40–41 is treated as a fixed analytic function in Lemma 4.7 (p. 31), which requires that property.
## A parity obstruction in the cited source

The paper’s reference [15], here [BL], gives \[\Omega_n=\pi+n\pi(1+\zeta),\qquad \zeta=t/\gamma ,\] in (7.5), p. 28. By (8.1), its model jump on the nonempty saturated interval is \(\operatorname{diag}(e^{-i\Omega_n},e^{i\Omega_n})\). Take \(\gamma=1,t=0\), allowed positive weights \(a=b=\sinh1,c=\sinh2,\Delta=-\cosh2<-1\). Then \(\Omega_n=(n+1)\pi\): the jump is \(+I\) for odd \(n\) and \(-I\) for even \(n\). One normalized model matrix cannot satisfy both.

Independent theta-series and product evaluations both gave \(R(\pi/8)=1.00846270596025\). An Abel-integral calculation at \(z=10+i\) gave a parity difference of magnitude approximately \(0.0014108651\). These ordinary floating-point calculations include quadrature refinement but no interval certification; the product proof is decisive.
## Impact, alternative reading, and repair boundary

This input feeds the saddle analysis, extension through \(\xi=0\), Theorem 2.6, and the antiferroelectric part of Theorem 1.3. Implicitly allowing \(M_n\) would contradict the footnote and require the uniformity arguments to be supplied. Fixed weights and the \(z\mapsto\gamma z\) rescaling do not remove the phase (\(\gamma=1\) in our example).

There is counterevidence against a false GUE limit: the relevant saddle tends to infinity as its argument tends to zero, where the model is normalized. A plausible repair keeps \(M_n,N_n\), proves uniform bounds on the required domains, and uses a prefactor \(\psi_n\) satisfying uniformly \[\psi_n(0)=1,\qquad\psi_n(\xi/\sqrt n)=1+O(n^{-1/2})\] for bounded \(\xi\). The Cauchy argument of Lemma 4.7 extends to analytic nonvanishing \(\psi_n\) under appropriate uniform bounds. For fixed nome, theta denominators with real periodic phase are bounded away from zero, supporting this route. That fact alone does not prove all contour and error estimates. The full uniform Riemann–Hilbert repair remains to be checked. The demonstrated invalid core premise is Major; the limit theorem has not been disproved.
# The ferroelectric local factor is unbounded at zero
Problem 3 (Major: Appendix A.2).  The function \(D(z)\) in (A.88), p. 87, is unbounded at the origin, contrary to its use in (A.95); the global estimate (A.98) fails for the error matrix as defined.
## Local calculation and matrix consequence

Equation reference: eq:D, eq:Dpole. Put \(w=nz/2\). For positive real \(z\), the printed definition is \[
 D_n(z)=\frac{\Gamma(w+3/2)e^w}
              {\sqrt{2\pi}\,w^{w+1}}.\] For every fixed \(n\ge1\), \(w^w\to1\) and \(\Gamma(w+3/2)\to\sqrt\pi/2\), so \[
 D_n(z)\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt2\,nz}\qquad(z\downarrow0).\] This does not refute (A.90), restricted to \(|z|\ge\varepsilon\). It refutes the boundedness used inside the origin disk in (A.95), p. 89.

Take \(t=2,\gamma=1\), so \(t>|\gamma|>0\). The shifted nodes in (A.50), p. 81, are \(-1/n,-3/n,\ldots\), with positive weights. The monic orthogonal polynomial \(q_{n,n}\) has only negative zeros, hence \(q_{n,n}(0)>0\). Equations (A.64) and (A.73), pp. 82–83, show that the first column of \(S_n\) has a finite nonzero limit on the positive axis at zero: its diagonal exponential factors are nonzero and \(g(0)\) is finite. The model \(\mathbf M\) in (A.84) is analytic and invertible there; its cut ends at \(\alpha<0\).

Inside the origin disk, (A.91) defines \(X_n=S_nD_n^{\sigma_3}\mathbf M^{-1}\). Writing the columns of \(S_n\) as \(s_1,s_2\), this equals \[D_n s_1(e_1^T\mathbf M^{-1})
 +D_n^{-1}s_2(e_2^T\mathbf M^{-1}).\] The first term has a nonzero \(z^{-1}\) leading coefficient by [eq:Dpole] (#eq:Dpole); the second tends to zero. Thus \(X_n\) is unbounded, contradicting the stated uniform \(X_n=I+O(1/n)\) on all of \(\mathbb C\) in (A.98), p. 89. The small-norm Cauchy representation invoked immediately before (A.98), via (A.34) on p. 76, likewise requires repaired origin behavior or an additional singular contribution.
## Verified scalar repair and unverified matrix repair

Equation reference: eq:D0. The Gamma recurrence suggests \[
 D_n^{(0)}(z)=\frac{nz}{nz+1}D_n(z).\] Directly, \[D_n^{(0)}(z)=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\frac{\Gamma(w+1/2)e^w}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,w^w},
       &\Re z>0,\\[6pt]
 \displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}e^w}
 {\Gamma(1/2-w)(-w)^w},&\Re z<0 .
 \end{cases}\] The one-sided origin limits are \(1/\sqrt2\) and \(\sqrt2\). The apparent pole at \(nz=-1\) cancels the zero in the original left-half-plane formula. The multiplier has equal boundary values on the imaginary axis, preserving the jump, and is \(1+O(1/n)\) for \(|z|\ge\varepsilon\). These scalar facts are proved; independent Gamma evaluations check the recurrence and \(nzD_n(z)\to1/\sqrt2\).

A complete repair must recheck the local matrix, analyticity, matching, all remaining jumps, and small-norm estimates. It is not established by these scalar facts alone. Proposition 4.6 is stated away from the origin, so its conclusion is not directly contradicted. Its proof nevertheless uses the invalid global estimate and feeds Theorem 2.4 and Theorem 1.4. This is a Major proof defect, not a demonstrated false stochastic limit.
# Normalization of the ferroelectric base measure
Problem 4 (Minor: Lemma 2.9 and Remark 2.10).  The measure in (2.15), p. 14, has the wrong Laplace normalization for (2.14), and its asserted normalization to a probability measure is unavailable.

Moreover \(m(\mathbb R)=\infty\), since the positive atomic masses do not even tend to zero. The formal \(\phi(0;\gamma)=-2\coth\gamma<0\) is outside the Laplace convergence domain; it is not a finite positive mass. The normalization proposed in Remark 2.10 is therefore invalid in this phase.

Replacing \(2\sinh(2\gamma k)\) by \(4\sinh(2\gamma k)\) restores (2.14). A probability measure can be obtained by exponential tilting at \(t_0>\gamma\) and dividing by its finite Laplace integral. Alternatively retain the measure and correct its transform and absolute partition-function formulas.

Constant rescaling cancels in the normalized log-gas law, monic orthogonal polynomials, and Cauchy-transform-to-norm ratios. Footnote 11, p. 28, notes a related constant cancellation. This is counterevidence against an effect on the main normalized laws. No core dependency on this erroneous absolute normalization was demonstrated, so the finding is Minor. The infinite-mass normalization assertion is substantive; this is not a typographical finding alone.
# Additional independent checks and review limits

Put \(S=a^2+b^2-c^2>2ab\) and \(d=\sqrt{S^2-4a^2b^2}\). The stochastic parameters in Theorem 1.4 are \(b_1=(S-d)/(2a^2)\), \(b_2=(S+d)/(2a^2)\). For \(a>b>0,c>0,\Delta>1\), they are positive and distinct. Since \(2a^2-S=a^2-b^2+c^2>0\) and \[(2a^2-S)^2-d^2=4a^2c^2>0,\] we obtain \(b_2<1\), and directly \(b_1b_2=b^2/a^2\). Thus their probability range does not rest on numerical examples.

At \(t=0\), (6.6) and (6.8), p. 51, give \[(m,s^2)=(1/2,1/4)\ (\gamma=\pi/4),\qquad
 (m,s^2)=(1/2,3/8)\ (\gamma=\pi/3),\] and \(s^2=(\pi^2/6-1)/4>0\) in the boundary phase at \(\gamma=1\). These checks do not prove positivity of the full antiferroelectric theta expression throughout its parameter range.

For the permutation limit, choosing the \(r\)-th smallest remaining symbol with probability proportional to \(q^{r-1}\) creates \(r-1\) new inversions. Multiplication gives the Mallows law \[\frac{q^{\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}}{\prod_{m=1}^n(1+\cdots+q^{m-1})}.\] Exact rational enumeration for \(q=1/2\), \(1\le n\le7\), checked all 5,913 permutations and mass one. This uses the ascending-word convention of Definition 1.7. The conflicting word largest in Definition 7.1 is read as an orientation typo, not a separate finding. At fixed \(k\), deleting finitely many symbols changes a rank by at most \(k\); convergence of the truncated geometric laws therefore also explains the macroscopic density in Proposition 1.10.

Other textual discrepancies were not promoted into Problems. The boundary derivative of \(\log(b/a)\) is \(1/(\gamma+t)+1/(\gamma-t)\), consistent with p. 51; the minus sign in (6.21) gives no viable scaling at \(t=0\). The intended derivative was used when tracing the argument. Lattice exclusions and the separate \(\xi=0\) argument were respected. Full reading does not mean that every inherited analytic estimate has been independently reproved: the uniform repairs of Problems 2–3 still need complete verification.
# Disposition and version-sensitive follow-up

The acquired version contains three demonstrated invalid core proof steps and a peripheral normalization defect. No counterexample to Theorems 1.3, 1.4 or 1.8 was established. Problem 1 has a proved replacement bound. Problem 2 requires a uniformity argument retaining the \(n\)-phase. Problem 3 has a verified scalar candidate but needs a complete matrix repair. Problem 4’s correction preserves normalized laws.

The arXiv history, publisher landing page and both authors’ publication pages were checked for newer public versions and relevant corrections. No paper-specific erratum was found in that bounded search. The public four-page errata sheet for the cited 2014 book was read and viewed. It concerns that book, not the reviewed paper, and does not remove the explicit phase in [BL]. The journal text was not scientifically compared, so these findings must not be projected onto an unseen revision.

Before adoption, compare the actual journal text or an author correction at the exact locators above, verify complete repairs for Problems 2–3, and recheck the analytic-to-probabilistic dependency chain. The scientific decision remains pending; no human reviews are recorded.

claim: Recorded check: Ferroelectric origin Gamma factor is unbounded
Phase: ferroelectric. T: 2. Gamma: 1. N: any fixed positive integer. Approach: z ->0 along positive real axis inside origin disk.
analysis: The function \(D(z)\) in (A.88), p. 87, is unbounded at the origin, contrary to its use in (A.95); the global estimate (A.98) fails for the error matrix as defined.

Equation reference: eq:D, eq:Dpole. Put \(w=nz/2\). For positive real \(z\), the printed definition is \[
 D_n(z)=\frac{\Gamma(w+3/2)e^w}
              {\sqrt{2\pi}\,w^{w+1}}.\] For every fixed \(n\ge1\), \(w^w\to1\) and \(\Gamma(w+3/2)\to\sqrt\pi/2\), so \[
 D_n(z)\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt2\,nz}\qquad(z\downarrow0).\] This does not refute (A.90), restricted to \(|z|\ge\varepsilon\). It refutes the boundedness used inside the origin disk in (A.95), p. 89.

Take \(t=2,\gamma=1\), so \(t>|\gamma|>0\). The shifted nodes in (A.50), p. 81, are \(-1/n,-3/n,\ldots\), with positive weights. The monic orthogonal polynomial \(q_{n,n}\) has only negative zeros, hence \(q_{n,n}(0)>0\). Equations (A.64) and (A.73), pp. 82–83, show that the first column of \(S_n\) has a finite nonzero limit on the positive axis at zero: its diagonal exponential factors are nonzero and \(g(0)\) is finite. The model \(\mathbf M\) in (A.84) is analytic and invertible there; its cut ends at \(\alpha<0\).

Inside the origin disk, (A.91) defines \(X_n=S_nD_n^{\sigma_3}\mathbf M^{-1}\). Writing the columns of \(S_n\) as \(s_1,s_2\), this equals \[D_n s_1(e_1^T\mathbf M^{-1})
 +D_n^{-1}s_2(e_2^T\mathbf M^{-1}).\] The first term has a nonzero \(z^{-1}\) leading coefficient by [eq:Dpole] (#eq:Dpole); the second tends to zero. Thus \(X_n\) is unbounded, contradicting the stated uniform \(X_n=I+O(1/n)\) on all of \(\mathbb C\) in (A.98), p. 89. The small-norm Cauchy representation invoked immediately before (A.98), via (A.34) on p. 76, likewise requires repaired origin behavior or an additional singular contribution.

Equation reference: eq:D0. The Gamma recurrence suggests \[
 D_n^{(0)}(z)=\frac{nz}{nz+1}D_n(z).\] Directly, \[D_n^{(0)}(z)=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\frac{\Gamma(w+1/2)e^w}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,w^w},
       &\Re z>0,\\[6pt]
 \displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}e^w}
 {\Gamma(1/2-w)(-w)^w},&\Re z<0 .
 \end{cases}\] The one-sided origin limits are \(1/\sqrt2\) and \(\sqrt2\). The apparent pole at \(nz=-1\) cancels the zero in the original left-half-plane formula. analysis: The measure in (2.15), p. 14, has the wrong Laplace normalization for (2.14), and its asserted normalization to a probability measure is unavailable.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the acquired arXiv version 2112.04820v3 (3 April 2025), by Naomi D. Feldheim, Ohad N. Feldheim and Sumit Mukherjee, associated with DOI 10.1002/cpa.22255. Six major issues concern false auxiliary estimates or invalid derivations used in the principal arguments, including the advertised example of nonexistence. A further minor issue concerns the stated ranges of applications and remarks. Explicit counterexamples and local repair arguments are given below. No counterexample to Theorems 1–5 is established here. The scientific decision remains pending; completion of this initial review does not constitute independent acceptance.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Initial scientific review of
Persistence and ball exponents for Gaussian stationary processes
# Version, scope and mathematical framework

All 51 pages of the acquired source, including its references, were read in this conversation. Page numbers below refer to that PDF, and equation numbers prefixed by source refer to the paper. The journal version of record was identified but was not acquired for a line comparison. The current arXiv record states that v3 corrected earlier inaccuracies in Lemmas 1.1 and 1.3. The issues below were checked in v3 itself. The publisher records a separate correction dated 26 June 2025 replacing the infimum by the supremum in the abstract’s ball-exponent definition. That acknowledged correction is not counted as a new finding.

Equation reference: eq:def. The covariance convention used here is \[r_\rho(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-it\lambda}\,d\rho(\lambda),\qquad
 \theta_\rho^\ell(T)=-T^{-1}\log\mathbb P(\inf_{[0,T]}f_\rho>\ell).
 \] The spectral measure is finite, nonnegative and symmetric. The class \(\mathcal L\) imposes a finite logarithmic moment of order \(1+\beta\). The paper explicitly defines \(\mathcal M\) by \(\rho'(0)=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
\rho([-\varepsilon,\varepsilon])/(2\varepsilon)\in(0,\infty]\). Thus an infinite density, including an atom at zero, is allowed. Uniform assertions use fixed \(\alpha,\beta,B,\ell\) and local lower or upper bounds on these averaged densities. The finite positive density case, the infinite density case, and the zero density case must be kept distinct. Ball probabilities use \(\sup|f_\rho|\) and radius \(\ell>0\).

Theorem 1 asserts existence at every real level when \(\rho\in\mathcal L\cap\mathcal M\), and, with a nonzero absolutely continuous component, positivity precisely when \(\rho'(0)<\infty\). Theorem 2 concerns the vanishing ball exponent of singular measures. Theorems 3–5 concern spectral perturbations, continuity and sampling. The main persistence argument uses the finite-time comparison lemmas, the singular ball result, and smooth approximation in a specific order. This dependency structure determines the severity assignments below; repairability does not make an invalid essential derivation valid.
# Global level bound and the Gaussian change of measure

Problem 1 (P01: Major).  Lemma 1.1, p. 7, claims a bound linear in every \(\delta>0\) with a constant independent of \(\delta\). The change-of-measure calculation on p. 19 omits a necessary quadratic cost and uses the likelihood ratio in the wrong direction.
## Hypotheses and decisive counterexample

Equation reference: eq:quadratic. Take \(d\mu=(2\pi)^{-1}\mathbf 1_{[-\pi,\pi]}d\lambda\), \(\ell=0\), \(T=4\). This compactly supported measure belongs to \(\mathcal L_{\beta,B}\), for example for \(\beta=1\) and sufficiently large fixed \(B\), and to \(\mathcal M_{\alpha,1}\) for \(\alpha=1/(4\pi)\). Its covariance is \(\sin(\pi t)/(\pi t)\), so \(f_\mu(0),\ldots,f_\mu(4)\) are independent standard normal variables. Writing \(Q(x)=\mathbb P(Z>x)\), \[\theta_\mu^\delta(4)\ge-\frac54\log Q(\delta)
       =\frac58\delta^2+O(\log\delta).
 \] By continuity of sample paths on the fixed interval, \(\mathbb P(\inf_{[0,4]}f_\mu>-\delta)\to1\), whence \(\theta_\mu^{-\delta}(4)\to0\). Consequently the difference in Lemma 1.1 cannot be at most \(C\delta+\log(2)/4\) for all \(\delta\).

An independent evaluation of the corresponding discrete five-point probabilities gives differences \(43.76680\), \(164.61925\), and \(645.48206\) at \(\delta=8,16,32\). These are exact Gaussian-tail formula evaluations, not measurements of continuous-path probabilities. The analytic argument [eq:quadratic] (#eq:quadratic) establishes the continuous counterexample without that distinction being blurred.
## Proof defect, alternative reading and repair

Equation reference: eq:rn, eq:locallevel. On pp. 18–19 the coefficient \(\zeta\) is shifted to mean \(-a\), where \(a=c\delta\sqrt T\). If \(p\) and \(q\) are the respective densities of \(N(0,1)\) and \(N(-a,1)\), the required ratio is \[\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}=\exp(-ax-a^2/2).
 \] Restricting the shifted coefficient’s integration variable to \(|x|\le\sqrt{MT}\), and using the paper’s tail truncation, therefore gives \[\theta_\mu^{\ell+\delta}(T)-\theta_\mu^{\ell-\delta}(T)
 \le c\sqrt M\,\delta+\frac{c^2}{2}\delta^2+\frac{\log2}{T}.
 \] Here \(M\) can be fixed from the lower persistence bound at level \(\ell\), because the lower event at level \(\ell-\delta\) contains that event. The printed \(p/q\) estimate cannot remove the term \(a^2/2\).

For \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\), [eq:locallevel] (#eq:locallevel) is linear with a constant depending on \(\delta_0\). This supplies the relevant local form once the lower probability input is justified as discussed in P02. The uses in Lemma 1.3 and Theorem 4 involve small level changes. Thus the example refutes the global auxiliary assertion, but does not refute local Lipschitz continuity of the limiting exponent. The proof of Theorem 4 on p. 34 explicitly depends on Lemma 1.1; the same input recurs in the proofs of Theorems 1, 3 and 5. That essential role, rather than a claim of failure of all final results, is the reason for the Major classification.
# An increment estimate cannot bound the absolute supremum

Problem 2 (P02: Major).  Lemma 2.19, pp. 14–15, bounds \(\mathbb E\sup_{[0,h]}|f_\rho|\) by a positive power of \(\sup_{[0,h]}|r_\rho(0)-r_\rho(t)|\). The proof of Lemma 2.22, pp. 16–17, then makes this absolute supremum arbitrarily small by shortening the interval. Both steps fail.
## Counterexample and dependency

For \(\rho=\delta_0\), which satisfies the logarithmic moment assumption, \(f_\rho(t)=Z\) at every time. The proposed right-hand side is zero, whereas \[\mathbb E\sup_{[0,h]}|f_\rho|=\sqrt{2/\pi}>0.\] The issue is not limited to degenerate processes: for every continuous process of nonzero variance, the left side is at least \(\mathbb E|f_\rho(0)|>0\), while the proposed right side tends to zero as \(h\downarrow0\).

For the constant process and radius \(0.1\) the ball probability on every nonempty interval is \(\mathbb P(|Z|<0.1)=0.07965567\). Thus the intermediate conclusion in Lemma 2.22 that a sufficiently short interval has ball probability at least \(1/2\) is also false. Dudley’s bound stated in Proposition 2.15 controls a centered supremum or anchored increments; adding absolute values requires accounting for the base value. The absolute values are present in the actual source images, including the downstream proof.

Lemma 2.22 supplies Lemma 2.23, the uniform lower persistence bound. That bound enters the likelihood truncation in P01, Proposition 3.1, Lemma 5.7 and the comparison arguments for Theorems 1 and 4. The false estimate therefore invalidates an operative proof chain.
## A local correction preserving the claimed lower bound
# The uniform threshold in the concentration lemma

Problem 3 (P03: Major).  Lemma 2.21, pp. 15–16, asserts that variance at most \(\varepsilon/T\) and increment variance at most \(a^2h^2\) imply \(\mathbb P(\sup_{[0,T]}|W|>\delta)\le2e^{-\delta^2T/(8\varepsilon)}\) whenever \(T>c(a^{-1}+\delta^{-1}+1)\), with a universal \(c\). The stated threshold is false.
## A smooth stationary counterexample

Equation reference: eq:entropycontradiction. Fix \(\varepsilon=1/2\), \(a=1\), and \(K=32\). For each \(\delta>0\), put \[T=16\delta^{-2},\qquad \sigma^2=\varepsilon/T=\delta^2/32,\qquad
 D=\sqrt{96}/\delta .\] Let \(W\) have the compactly supported spectral density \(\sigma^2(2D)^{-1}\mathbf 1_{[-D,D]}\). Then \(\operatorname{Var}W=\sigma^2\) and, using \(2(1-\cos x)\le x^2\), \[\operatorname{Var}(W(t+h)-W(t))\le \frac{\sigma^2D^2}{3}h^2=h^2.\] At the points \(j\pi/D\), the values are independent \(N(0,\sigma^2)\). There are \(N=\lfloor TD/\pi\rfloor+1\) such points in \([0,T]\). Consequently, with \(p=\mathbb P(|Z|>\sqrt{32})>0\), \[\mathbb P(\sup_{[0,T]}|W|>\delta)\ge1-(1-p)^N\longrightarrow1
       \quad(\delta\downarrow0).
 \] The claimed upper bound is the constant \(2e^{-4}=0.03663128\). Also \(T/(a^{-1}+\delta^{-1}+1)=16/(\delta+2\delta^2)\to\infty\), so the hypothesis holds for any proposed universal \(c\) when \(\delta\) is sufficiently small. This addresses the unknown constant, not merely one selected numerical value of it.

The independently evaluated lower bounds are \(0.53667678\) at \(\delta=0.01\) and greater than \(0.999\) at \(\delta=0.001\). The computation uses the exact independent-grid formula; it neither simulates paths nor allocates a vector of \(N\) samples.
## Cause, downstream uses and repair boundary

The inference to source (2.5) loses the necessary metric-entropy scale. A valid sufficient estimate, with universal constants, is \[\mathbb E\sup_{[0,T]}|W|\le
 C\sigma\sqrt{\log(2+aT/\sigma)},\qquad \sigma^2=\varepsilon/T.\] This follows by retaining a base point and integrating the covering bound up to diameter at most \(2\sigma\). To use Borell with a deviation \(\delta/2\), it suffices to require \(\delta\ge2C\sigma\sqrt{\log(2+aT/\sigma)}\).

The incorrect lemma is explicitly used on p. 22 in Proposition 3.1 and on pp. 39–41 in Proposition 5.3. Those results feed spectral continuity and existence in Theorems 1 and 4. Their particular processes have additional structure: on p. 22 the actual bounds are \(\sigma^2\le2/(L^2T)\) and \(a_T^2\le2/T^3\). The corrected entropy estimate then gives \[\mathbb E\sup|g|\le
 C\frac{\sqrt{\log(2+L)}}{L\sqrt T},\] which is compatible with the chosen large \(L\) and \(T\). Proposition 5.3 also states a stronger threshold involving \(\varepsilon^{-2}\). These facts make repair plausible, but all its uniform constants and parameter dependencies must be checked. The general lemma itself cannot be retained as stated, and this review does not certify a completed repair of every downstream estimate.
# The truncation argument removes a non-small amount of mass

Problem 4 (P04: Major).  In Proposition 3.1, pp. 21–23, the passage after source (3.9) uses \((1-h^2)\nu_{L/T}(\mathbb R)\le1/T\), claiming this follows when \(L\ge1/(2\alpha')\). The inequality is false even within the proposition’s full parameter range, and the invocation of Lemma 1.3(I) therefore lacks its small-mass hypothesis.
## All parameter restrictions and a counterexample

The proposition assumes \(\mu\in\mathcal M_{\alpha,A}\cap\mathcal L_{\beta,B}\), \(\nu\in\mathcal M_{(0,\alpha'),D}\cap\mathcal L_{\beta,B}\), \(0<D\le1\), \(0<\alpha'\le B\), \(0<\eta<c_1\alpha'\), \(T\ge\max(c_2/\eta,1/A)\) and \(c_3/\eta\le L\le\alpha'D^2T/B\). Choose \(\mu\) as in P01, \(A=\beta=1\), \(B=10\), \(d\nu=\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}d\lambda\), \(\alpha'=2\), and \(D=1/2\). Set \(L=\eta^{-2}\) and \(T=160L\). For every fixed choice of the proposition’s constants all its assumptions hold when \(\eta\) is sufficiently small. In particular \(\alpha'D^2T/B=8L\).

Equation reference: eq:removedmass. With \(M=L^{1/4}\) and the paper’s normalized \(\operatorname{sinc}u=\sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)\), its actual removed mass is \[\begin{aligned}
 \Delta_L
 &=2\int_0^{L/T}\{1-\operatorname{sinc}^4(T\lambda/M)\}\,d\lambda\\
 &=\frac{2}{160}
       -\frac{2M}{T}\int_0^{L/M}\operatorname{sinc}^4 u\,du
       \longrightarrow\frac1{80}.
 \end{aligned}\] For a completely elementary bound, \(\int_0^\infty\operatorname{sinc}^4u\,du\le1+1/(3\pi^4)\). Thus the limit and a positive lower bound follow without numerical quadrature. In contrast \(1/T\to0\). At \(L=10^4\), evaluation of this rigorous lower-bound expression gives \(0.01248746\), whereas \(1/T=6.25\times10^{-7}\).

The intermediate bound \(\nu([-L/T,L/T])\le2\alpha'L/T\) is valid. It implies \(2\alpha'L/T\le1/T\) only for \(L\le1/(2\alpha')\), the opposite inequality. Merely reversing that condition would conflict with the required large-\(L\) regime. Equation [eq:removedmass] (#eq:removedmass) also rules out interpreting the mistake as an innocuous loose estimate of a genuinely tiny removed mass.
## Dependency and a way to avoid the false step
Proposition 3.1 is the truncation input to Lemma 1.3(II), then Proposition 5.2 and the proofs of Theorems 1, 3 and 4. Its conclusion has not been disproved.

A local modification is to apply Lemma 1.2 with base measure \(\mu+
u_{L/T}\) and smoothed measure \(
u-
u_{L/T}\). This gives directly, with the same shortened interval \(I_T\), \[\mathbb P(f_{\mu+
u}>\ell	ext{ on }[0,T])
 \le
 \mathbb P(f_{\mu+
u_{L/T}+h^2(
u-
u_{L/T})}>\ell
       	ext{ on }I_T).\] The high-frequency remainder is exactly the one estimated on p. 22, while the low-frequency measure already has the desired form. No subsequent removal of \((1-h^2)
u_{L/T}\) is necessary. The base retains the same lower local-density bound and has a logarithmic-moment bound with \(2B\) in place of \(B\). This modification removes the demonstrated obstruction. Completion still requires the corrected concentration and local-level bounds in P03 and P01 with appropriate uniform constants.
# The spectral projection fails for an atom at zero

Problem 5 (P05: Major).  Lemma 4.2, pp. 25–26, allows every spectral measure supported on \([-D,D]\) but assigns zero asymmetrically to the first positive bin. The independent decomposition in source (4.2) is false when that bin contains both a zero atom and nonzero spectral mass.
## Exact covariance contradiction

Take \(D=n=1\) and \[\rho=\tfrac13(\delta_{-1}+\delta_0+\delta_1).\] This is a finite symmetric nonnegative measure, including a legitimate purely singular measure for Proposition 4.1. The source defines \(I_1=[0,1]\), \(I_{-1}=[-1,0)\), hence \[C_1(t)=\frac{1+\cos t}{2},\qquad S_1(t)=\frac{\sin t}{2},
 \qquad \rho(I_1\cup I_{-1})=1.\] Its asserted representation would be \(f_\rho(t)=\zeta C_1(t)+\eta S_1(t)+R(t)\), with \(R\) independent of the standard normal coefficients. At \(t=0\) the first term already has variance one, equal to \(\operatorname{Var}f_\rho(0)\). Therefore \(\operatorname{Var}R(0)=0\). At \(t=\pi\) both \(C_1\) and \(S_1\) vanish. Independence consequently forces \(\operatorname{Cov}(f_\rho(0),f_\rho(\pi))=0\). The true spectral covariance is \[r_\rho(\pi)=\tfrac13(1+2\cos\pi)=-\tfrac13,\] a contradiction.

The proof on p. 26 treats the positive and negative bins as equal-mass partners in its Hilbert-space normalization. Here their masses are \(2/3\) and \(1/3\). This cannot be fixed by assigning a value to a zero-denominator expression: both relevant denominators are nonzero.
## Repair and impact boundary

Separate \(\sqrt{\rho(\{0\})}\,Z_0\) as its own independent constant component. Partition the remaining strictly positive spectrum and its reflections into equal-mass pairs, omitting empty bins. The ordinary orthogonal projection then gives the cosine and sine terms and residual estimates for the remaining measure. The additional constant Gaussian component has rank one. It does not affect the sublinear-rank argument in Proposition 4.1: its contribution to a fixed-radius ball event has a positive \(T\)-independent probability. The error is therefore repairable.

As printed, however, Lemma 4.2 is the explicit input at p. 27 to Proposition 4.1, which supplies Theorem 2. The singular ball theorem also enters the persistence approximation on p. 31 and the invariance statements in Theorem 3. Measures with an atom at zero are not excluded there. This invalid core decomposition is Major; it is not a counterexample to the corrected singular ball theorem. The applications in Proposition 5.3 have additional local mass restrictions, so the counterexample is not asserted to violate that proposition’s hypotheses.
# The nonexistence example has a finite positive origin density

Problem 6 (P06: Major).  Remark 1, p. 2, and Section 5.4, pp. 41–42, advertise nonexistence of the zero-level persistence exponent for \[w_{a,b}(\lambda)=
 \left(\frac{a+b}{2}+\frac{b-a}{2}\cos(1/\lambda)\right)
 \mathbf 1_{\{|\lambda|\le1\}},\qquad 0<a<b.\] Source (5.19) claims that the averaged density has lower and upper limits \(a\) and \(b\). In fact its limit is \((a+b)/2\).
Claim 1.  For every \(0<a<b\), the displayed measure belongs to \(\mathcal L\cap\mathcal M\) and has \(\rho'(0)=(a+b)/2\).

Equation reference: eq:correctdensity. Proof. With \(x>0\), \[I(x):=\int_0^x\cos(1/t)\,dt
      =\int_{1/x}^{\infty}\frac{\cos u}{u^2}\,du.\] Integration by parts gives \[I(x)=-x^2\sin(1/x)
       +2\int_{1/x}^{\infty}\frac{\sin u}{u^3}\,du,
 \qquad |I(x)|\le2x^2.\] It follows that \[\frac{\rho([0,x])}{x}
   =\frac{a+b}{2}+\frac{b-a}{2}\frac{I(x)}x
   =\frac{a+b}{2}+O((b-a)x).
 \] Symmetry gives the same limit in the definition of \(\rho'(0)\). The density is bounded, nonnegative and compactly supported, so the logarithmic moment condition also holds. ◻

For \(a=1,b=3\), independent integration-by-parts evaluations at \(x=0.01\) and \(0.001\) give averaged densities approximately \(2.00523288\) and \(1.99917425\). The saved truncation-error formulas are analytic errors for the finite asymptotic expansion; the floating evaluations are not certified interval-arithmetic enclosures. The proof [eq:correctdensity] (#eq:correctdensity), rather than those decimals, is decisive.
## What fails and what could replace it

The low-density subsequence required in the final argument on p. 42 does not follow. For the selected range \(a<b/3\), the actual limiting average is greater than \(3a/2\), so the required eventual values at most \(3a/2\) are absent. The paper’s own Theorem 1 would give existence for this very measure. Thus the advertised example and that theorem cannot both hold as written. This review establishes the false average and invalid nonexistence derivation; it does not use the contested proof of Theorem 1 as an independent proof of the final exponent.

A possible replacement uses a slowly oscillating density, for example near zero \[\widetilde w(t)=\frac{a+b}{2}
    +\frac{b-a}{2}\cos\!\left(\log\log(e/|t|)\right).\] It has the desired averaged lower and upper limits. Indeed, writing \(L_x=\log(e/x)\) and \(t=xu\), \[\int_0^1
 \left|\log\frac{\log(e/(xu))}{\log(e/x)}\right|du
 \le\frac1{L_x}\int_0^1\log(1/u)\,du=\frac1{L_x}.\] The averaged cosine therefore differs from its value at \(x\) by \(O(1/L_x)\). This proves the required oscillation of the averages for a different density. It is not a correction of \(\cos(1/\lambda)\) by reinterpretation. The probability estimates and constants must then be reapplied to the replacement, using the actual assumptions of [ffn]. The sharpness illustration is a substantive stated contribution, and its supplied proof is invalid; this explains the Major classification.
# Missing range restrictions in applications and remarks

Problem 7 (P07: Minor).  Example 3 on p. 8 extends the zero-density conclusion to every real level. Remark 3 on p. 3 omits the finite-origin-density restriction when discussing positivity. Explicit elementary cases contradict those ranges, while the main theorem statements retain relevant distinctions.
## The moving-average example at a negative level

Set \(U_0=1\), \(U_1=-1\), and all other \(U_k=0\). The sequence is square summable, \(\widehat U\) is continuous near zero, and \(\sum U_k=0\). The process is \(X_j=Z_j-Z_{j-1}\) for independent standard normal \(Z_j\). At level \(\ell=-1\), if all \(N+2\) variables indexed from \(-1\) to \(N\) lie in \((-1/2,1/2)\), then \(X_j>-1\) for \(0\le j\le N\). Hence \[\mathbb P(X_j>-1,\ 0\le j\le N)\ge p^{N+2},\qquad
 p=\mathbb P(|Z|<1/2)=0.38292492.\] Therefore \[\limsup_{N\to\infty}\theta_X^{-1}(N)
       \le-\log p=0.95991634<\infty.\] This disproves the displayed equivalence \(\theta_X^\ell=\infty\Longleftrightarrow\sum U_k=0\) at the stated all-real-level scope. No assumption about the existence of the limit is needed to refute an asserted infinite limit. Remark 2 and Lemma 2.24 correctly restrict the zero-density infinite-exponent conclusion to \(\ell\ge0\). Restoring that restriction in the application removes this contradiction.
## Infinite origin density in Remark 3

The paper’s \(\mathcal M\) includes \(\rho'(0)=\infty\). Already \(\rho=\delta_0\) has \(\theta_\rho^\ell=0\) for every finite \(\ell\), since its persistence probability is the constant \(Q(\ell)\). Thus the positive-level conjecture in that remark cannot include the whole class as literally defined.

The nonpositive-level assertion that positivity is equivalent to a nonzero absolutely continuous part also fails at infinite origin density. Let \(f=Z+g\), with \(Z\) independent standard normal and \(g\) an independent unit-variance bandlimited stationary process with nonzero absolutely continuous spectrum. Put \(A_0=\mathbb E\sup_{[0,1]}|g|<\infty\). A union of unit-interval Borell bounds gives, for \(R_T=A_0+\sqrt{2\log(4\lceil T\rceil)}\), \[\mathbb P(\sup_{[0,T]}|g|\le R_T)\ge\tfrac12.\] Thus \[\mathbb P(\inf_{[0,T]}(Z+g)>\ell)\ge\tfrac12 Q(\ell+R_T),
 \qquad -\log Q(\ell+R_T)=O(\log T).\] It follows directly that \(\theta_f^\ell=0\) at every fixed level. Its spectral measure has both a zero atom and a nonzero absolutely continuous component, satisfies \(\mathcal L\), and has infinite origin density. This agrees with Proposition 2.25 and Theorem 1, rather than refuting either.

These are peripheral range errors, with no demonstrated use of the overstated assertions in the core proofs. Accordingly they are Minor. Restricting Remark 3 to finite positive origin density avoids these counterexamples; its positive-level claim must still be presented as a conjecture, not as a proved theorem.
# Coverage, counterevidence and limits

The complete source was read in order, including all definitions, quantifiers, boundary cases, proofs and the bibliography. The singular-measure argument, the order of smooth approximation away from and near the origin, the change-of-level comparisons, and the compact-support condition in persistence sampling were followed. The seven problems above are the demonstrated issues retained after considering alternative readings. They are not a severity quota.

Several apparent problems do not warrant additional substantive findings. In Proposition 2.6 (p. 11), the final bound \((1-2/x)^x\ge e^{-2}\) is false, but the preceding, sharper Gaussian-tail bound retains \(2e^{-1/2}/x\) and suffices for the stated constant \(0.05\). The supremum direction in the displayed Slepian formulation (p. 13) is inconsistent with its subsequent use, whereas the operative infimum comparison has the correct direction. Claim 4.3 (p. 28) uses nonnested interval partitions as though they formed a filtration; differentiation of singular measures supplies the needed almost-everywhere conclusion. These observations do not supply independent counterexamples to those results.

The convexity argument on p. 33 can use a left secant at \(\ell/2\) to obtain the finite upper bound on the relevant derivative. The block count in Lemma 5.7 (pp. 36–38) must retain the factor \(1+\delta\); the resulting error is of the same order as the intended bound. Neither observation is presented as an additional proved failure of a final theorem. The broader statement of Proposition 5.1 includes smooth densities vanishing at zero, whereas its invocation of Lemma 5.7 uses the positive-origin-density hypothesis. The smooth approximants needed in the principal finite-positive-density argument do have that property, after normalizing the variance. This review does not independently establish all zero-density, negative-level cases of that broader proposition.

For Theorem 5, the distinction between ball sampling for \(\rho\in\mathcal L\) and persistence sampling for compactly supported \(\rho\in\mathcal L\cap\mathcal M\) was retained. The aliasing calculation in Proposition 7.2 (p. 47) was checked: the narrow spectral peaks have summable total mass, while their folded density at zero diverges by a harmonic sum. It is consistent with the importance of the compact-support condition and does not supply a new defect.
## External mathematical inputs

Royen’s primary preprint [royen], all seven pages, was read and visually checked for the symmetric-convex Gaussian correlation input used in the local repair of P02. This is a check of the applicable theorem, its degeneracy extension, and its role here; it is not an independent reproof of every multivariate-gamma identity in that paper.

For the spectral persistence estimates cited as source reference [28], the acquired primary text was [ffn], arXiv version 2 of 4 August 2020. Pages 1–5 and 8–25 were read and visually checked. In particular, its normalization and positive-moment convention, the absolutely continuous independent component, the integrated variance estimates, Theorems 4.1 and 5.1, Remark 2, and the proof of Proposition 3 were checked. This preprint has 31 pages; the 2021 journal article has a different pagination and was not acquired for line comparison. No equality of the two texts is asserted.

The observed Remark 2 in [ffn], p. 19, and its proof on p. 23, require the near-origin upper bound at all scales. This matters for a proposed replacement of the nonexistence example in P06: replacing the oscillation alone does not certify the subsequence persistence bounds, their normalization, or the precise applicability of the cited journal version. Those are explicit remaining repair tasks, not an additional version-independent finding established here. The main counterexamples in P01–P07 use direct analytic arguments, rather than an assumption of equivalence between reference versions.

problems.title: Global level comparison omits the quadratic shift cost
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: Problem 1 (P01: Major). Lemma 1.1, p. 7, claims a bound linear in every \(\delta>0\) with a constant independent of \(\delta\).
claim: Recorded check: Global level comparison omits the quadratic shift cost
Measure: (2pi)^-1 indicator[-pi,pi] dλ. Level: 0. T: 4. Alpha: 1/(4pi). A: 1. Beta: 1. B: 10. Delta: arbitrary positive; let delta tend to infinity.
analysis: Lemma 1.1, p. 7, claims a bound linear in every \(\delta>0\) with a constant independent of \(\delta\). The change-of-measure calculation on p. 19 omits a necessary quadratic cost and uses the likelihood ratio in the wrong direction.

Equation reference: eq:quadratic. Take \(d\mu=(2\pi)^{-1}\mathbf 1_{[-\pi,\pi]}d\lambda\), \(\ell=0\), \(T=4\). This compactly supported measure belongs to \(\mathcal L_{\beta,B}\), for example for \(\beta=1\) and sufficiently large fixed \(B\), and to \(\mathcal M_{\alpha,1}\) for \(\alpha=1/(4\pi)\). Its covariance is \(\sin(\pi t)/(\pi t)\), so \(f_\mu(0),\ldots,f_\mu(4)\) are independent standard normal variables. Writing \(Q(x)=\mathbb P(Z>x)\), \[\theta_\mu^\delta(4)\ge-\frac54\log Q(\delta)
       =\frac58\delta^2+O(\log\delta).
 \] By continuity of sample paths on the fixed interval, \(\mathbb P(\inf_{[0,4]}f_\mu>-\delta)\to1\), whence \(\theta_\mu^{-\delta}(4)\to0\). Consequently the difference in Lemma 1.1 cannot be at most \(C\delta+\log(2)/4\) for all \(\delta\).

An independent evaluation of the corresponding discrete five-point probabilities gives differences \(43.76680\), \(164.61925\), and \(645.48206\) at \(\delta=8,16,32\). These are exact Gaussian-tail formula evaluations, not measurements of continuous-path probabilities. The analytic argument [eq:quadratic] (#eq:quadratic) establishes the continuous counterexample without that distinction being blurred.

Equation reference: eq:rn, eq:locallevel. On pp. 18–19 the coefficient \(\zeta\) is shifted to mean \(-a\), where \(a=c\delta\sqrt T\). If \(p\) and \(q\) are the respective densities of \(N(0,1)\) and \(N(-a,1)\), the required ratio is \[\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}=\exp(-ax-a^2/2).
 \] Restricting the shifted coefficient’s integration variable to \(|x|\le\sqrt{MT}\), and using the paper’s tail truncation, therefore gives \[\theta_\mu^{\ell+\delta}(T)-\theta_\mu^{\ell-\delta}(T)
 \le c\sqrt M\,\delta+\frac{c^2}{2}\delta^2+\frac{\log2}{T}.
 \] Here \(M\) can be fixed from the lower persistence bound at level \(\ell\), because the lower event at level \(\ell-\delta\) contains that event. The printed \(p/q\) estimate cannot remove the term \(a^2/2\).

For \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\), [eq:locallevel] (#eq:locallevel) is linear with a constant depending on \(\delta_0\). This supplies the relevant local form once the lower probability input is justified as discussed in P02. The uses in Lemma 1.3 and Theorem 4 involve small level changes. Thus the example refutes the global auxiliary assertion, but does not refute local Lipschitz continuity of the limiting exponent. The proof of Theorem 4 on p. 34 explicitly depends on Lemma 1.1; the same input recurs in the proofs of Theorems 1, 3 and 5. That essential role, rather than a claim of failure of all final results, is the reason for the Major classification.

problems.title: Increment entropy bound loses the absolute base value
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (P02: Major). Lemma 2.19, pp. 14–15, bounds \(\mathbb E\sup_{[0,h]}|f_\rho|\) by a positive power of \(\sup_{[0,h]}|r_\rho(0)-r_\rho(t)|\).
claim: Recorded check: Increment entropy bound loses the absolute base value
Measure: delta0, finite symmetric measure in logarithmic moment class. H: >0. Radius: 0.1.
analysis: Lemma 2.19, pp. 14–15, bounds \(\mathbb E\sup_{[0,h]}|f_\rho|\) by a positive power of \(\sup_{[0,h]}|r_\rho(0)-r_\rho(t)|\). The proof of Lemma 2.22, pp. 16–17, then makes this absolute supremum arbitrarily small by shortening the interval. Both steps fail.

For \(\rho=\delta_0\), which satisfies the logarithmic moment assumption, \(f_\rho(t)=Z\) at every time. The proposed right-hand side is zero, whereas \[\mathbb E\sup_{[0,h]}|f_\rho|=\sqrt{2/\pi}>0.\] The issue is not limited to degenerate processes: for every continuous process of nonzero variance, the left side is at least \(\mathbb E|f_\rho(0)|>0\), while the proposed right side tends to zero as \(h\downarrow0\).

For the constant process and radius \(0.1\) the ball probability on every nonempty interval is \(\mathbb P(|Z|<0.1)=0.07965567\). Thus the intermediate conclusion in Lemma 2.22 that a sufficiently short interval has ball probability at least \(1/2\) is also false. Dudley’s bound stated in Proposition 2.15 controls a centered supremum or anchored increments; adding absolute values requires accounting for the base value. The absolute values are present in the actual source images, including the downstream proof.

Lemma 2.22 supplies Lemma 2.23, the uniform lower persistence bound. That bound enters the likelihood truncation in P01, Proposition 3.1, Lemma 5.7 and the comparison arguments for Theorems 1 and 4. The false estimate therefore invalidates an operative proof chain.

problems.title: Concentration lemma threshold misses an entropy scale
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: Problem 3 (P03: Major). Lemma 2.21, pp. 15–16, asserts that variance at most \(\varepsilon/T\) and increment variance at most \(a^2h^2\) imply…
claim: Recorded check: Concentration lemma threshold misses an entropy scale
Epsilon: 0.5. A: 1. T: 16delta^-2. Variance: delta²/32. Spectral support d: sqrt96/delta. Process: smooth stationary uniform bandlimited spectrum.
analysis: Lemma 2.21, pp. 15–16, asserts that variance at most \(\varepsilon/T\) and increment variance at most \(a^2h^2\) imply \(\mathbb P(\sup_{[0,T]}|W|>\delta)\le2e^{-\delta^2T/(8\varepsilon)}\) whenever \(T>c(a^{-1}+\delta^{-1}+1)\), with a universal \(c\). The stated threshold is false.

Equation reference: eq:entropycontradiction. Fix \(\varepsilon=1/2\), \(a=1\), and \(K=32\). For each \(\delta>0\), put \[T=16\delta^{-2},\qquad \sigma^2=\varepsilon/T=\delta^2/32,\qquad
 D=\sqrt{96}/\delta .\] Let \(W\) have the compactly supported spectral density \(\sigma^2(2D)^{-1}\mathbf 1_{[-D,D]}\). Then \(\operatorname{Var}W=\sigma^2\) and, using \(2(1-\cos x)\le x^2\), \[\operatorname{Var}(W(t+h)-W(t))\le \frac{\sigma^2D^2}{3}h^2=h^2.\] At the points \(j\pi/D\), the values are independent \(N(0,\sigma^2)\). There are \(N=\lfloor TD/\pi\rfloor+1\) such points in \([0,T]\). Consequently, with \(p=\mathbb P(|Z|>\sqrt{32})>0\), \[\mathbb P(\sup_{[0,T]}|W|>\delta)\ge1-(1-p)^N\longrightarrow1
       \quad(\delta\downarrow0).
 \] The claimed upper bound is the constant \(2e^{-4}=0.03663128\). Also \(T/(a^{-1}+\delta^{-1}+1)=16/(\delta+2\delta^2)\to\infty\), so the hypothesis holds for any proposed universal \(c\) when \(\delta\) is sufficiently small. This addresses the unknown constant, not merely one selected numerical value of it.

The independently evaluated lower bounds are \(0.53667678\) at \(\delta=0.01\) and greater than \(0.999\) at \(\delta=0.001\). The computation uses the exact independent-grid formula; it neither simulates paths nor allocates a vector of \(N\) samples.

The inference to source (2.5) loses the necessary metric-entropy scale. A valid sufficient estimate, with universal constants, is \[\mathbb E\sup_{[0,T]}|W|\le
 C\sigma\sqrt{\log(2+aT/\sigma)},\qquad \sigma^2=\varepsilon/T.\] This follows by retaining a base point and integrating the covering bound up to diameter at most \(2\sigma\). To use Borell with a deviation \(\delta/2\), it suffices to require \(\delta\ge2C\sigma\sqrt{\log(2+aT/\sigma)}\).

The incorrect lemma is explicitly used on p. 22 in Proposition 3.1 and on pp. 39–41 in Proposition 5.3. Those results feed spectral continuity and existence in Theorems 1 and 4. Their particular processes have additional structure: on p. 22 the actual bounds are \(\sigma^2\le2/(L^2T)\) and \(a_T^2\le2/T^3\). The corrected entropy estimate then gives \[\mathbb E\sup|g|\le
 C\frac{\sqrt{\log(2+L)}}{L\sqrt T},\] which is compatible with the chosen large \(L\) and \(T\). Proposition 5.3 also states a stronger threshold involving \(\varepsilon^{-2}\). These facts make repair plausible, but all its uniform constants and parameter dependencies must be checked. The general lemma itself cannot be retained as stated, and this review does not certify a completed repair of every downstream estimate.

problems.title: Spectral projection fails for an origin atom
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 5: Problem 5 (P05: Major). Lemma 4.2, pp. 25–26, allows every spectral measure supported on \([-D,D]\) but assigns zero asymmetrically to the first positive bin.
claim: Recorded check: Spectral projection fails for an origin atom
D: 1. N: 1. Measure: (delta_-1+delta0+delta1)/3, compactly supported purely singular. Bins: I1=[0,1],I-1=[-1,0).
analysis: Lemma 4.2, pp. 25–26, allows every spectral measure supported on \([-D,D]\) but assigns zero asymmetrically to the first positive bin. The independent decomposition in source (4.2) is false when that bin contains both a zero atom and nonzero spectral mass.

Take \(D=n=1\) and \[\rho=\tfrac13(\delta_{-1}+\delta_0+\delta_1).\] This is a finite symmetric nonnegative measure, including a legitimate purely singular measure for Proposition 4.1. The source defines \(I_1=[0,1]\), \(I_{-1}=[-1,0)\), hence \[C_1(t)=\frac{1+\cos t}{2},\qquad S_1(t)=\frac{\sin t}{2},
 \qquad \rho(I_1\cup I_{-1})=1.\] Its asserted representation would be \(f_\rho(t)=\zeta C_1(t)+\eta S_1(t)+R(t)\), with \(R\) independent of the standard normal coefficients. At \(t=0\) the first term already has variance one, equal to \(\operatorname{Var}f_\rho(0)\). Therefore \(\operatorname{Var}R(0)=0\). At \(t=\pi\) both \(C_1\) and \(S_1\) vanish. Independence consequently forces \(\operatorname{Cov}(f_\rho(0),f_\rho(\pi))=0\). The true spectral covariance is \[r_\rho(\pi)=\tfrac13(1+2\cos\pi)=-\tfrac13,\] a contradiction.

The proof on p. 26 treats the positive and negative bins as equal-mass partners in its Hilbert-space normalization. Here their masses are \(2/3\) and \(1/3\). This cannot be fixed by assigning a value to a zero-denominator expression: both relevant denominators are nonzero.

problems.title: Rapidly oscillating density does not have the claimed averaged limits
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: Problem 6 (P06: Major). Remark 1, p. 2, and Section 5.4, pp. 41–42, advertise nonexistence of the zero-level persistence exponent for…
claim: Recorded check: Rapidly oscillating density does not have the claimed averaged limits
A: >0. B: >a. Density: [(a+b)/2+(b-a)/2 cos(1/λ)] indicator|λ|<=1. Final argument range: a<b/3.
analysis:
Remark 1, p. 2, and Section 5.4, pp. 41–42, advertise nonexistence of the zero-level persistence exponent for \[w_{a,b}(\lambda)=
 \left(\frac{a+b}{2}+\frac{b-a}{2}\cos(1/\lambda)\right)
 \mathbf 1_{\{|\lambda|\le1\}},\qquad 0<a<b.\] Source (5.19) claims that the averaged density has lower and upper limits \(a\) and \(b\). In fact its limit is \((a+b)/2\).
Claim 1.  For every \(0<a<b\), the displayed measure belongs to \(\mathcal L\cap\mathcal M\) and has \(\rho'(0)=(a+b)/2\).

Equation reference: eq:correctdensity. Proof. With \(x>0\), \[I(x):=\int_0^x\cos(1/t)\,dt
      =\int_{1/x}^{\infty}\frac{\cos u}{u^2}\,du.\] Integration by parts gives \[I(x)=-x^2\sin(1/x)
       +2\int_{1/x}^{\infty}\frac{\sin u}{u^3}\,du,
 \qquad |I(x)|\le2x^2.\] It follows that \[\frac{\rho([0,x])}{x}
   =\frac{a+b}{2}+\frac{b-a}{2}\frac{I(x)}x
   =\frac{a+b}{2}+O((b-a)x).
 \] Symmetry gives the same limit in the definition of \(\rho'(0)\). The density is bounded, nonnegative and compactly supported, so the logarithmic moment condition also holds. ◻

For \(a=1,b=3\), independent integration-by-parts evaluations at \(x=0.01\) and \(0.001\) give averaged densities approximately \(2.00523288\) and \(1.99917425\). The saved truncation-error formulas are analytic errors for the finite asymptotic expansion; the floating evaluations are not certified interval-arithmetic enclosures. The proof [eq:correctdensity] (#eq:correctdensity), rather than those decimals, is decisive.

The low-density subsequence required in the final argument on p. 42 does not follow. For the selected range \(a<b/3\), the actual limiting average is greater than \(3a/2\), so the required eventual values at most \(3a/2\) are absent. The paper’s own Theorem 1 would give existence for this very measure. Thus the advertised example and that theorem cannot both hold as written. This review establishes the false average and invalid nonexistence derivation; it does not use the contested proof of Theorem 1 as an independent proof of the final exponent.

A possible replacement uses a slowly oscillating density, for example near zero \[\widetilde w(t)=\frac{a+b}{2}
    +\frac{b-a}{2}\cos\!\left(\log\log(e/|t|)\right).\] It has the desired averaged lower and upper limits. Indeed, writing \(L_x=\log(e/x)\) and \(t=xu\), \[\int_0^1
 \left|\log\frac{\log(e/(xu))}{\log(e/x)}\right|du
 \le\frac1{L_x}\int_0^1\log(1/u)\,du=\frac1{L_x}.\] The averaged cosine therefore differs from its value at \(x\) by \(O(1/L_x)\). This proves the required oscillation of the averages for a different density. It is not a correction of \(\cos(1/\lambda)\) by reinterpretation. The probability estimates and constants must then be reapplied to the replacement, using the actual assumptions of [ffn]. The sharpness illustration is a substantive stated contribution, and its supplied proof is invalid; this explains the Major classification.

problems.title: Peripheral level and infinite-density ranges overstate positivity
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 7: Problem 7 (P07: Minor). Example 3 on p. 8 extends the zero-density conclusion to every real level.
claim: Recorded check: Peripheral level and infinite-density ranges overstate positivity

Moving average: U0=1,U1=-1,all others0; square summable, sum0, Fourier transformcontinuous. Level: -1. Atom examples: delta0 and delta0+nonzero bandlimited ac spectrum, in L with infinite origin density.
analysis: Example 3 on p. 8 extends the zero-density conclusion to every real level. Remark 3 on p. 3 omits the finite-origin-density restriction when discussing positivity. Explicit elementary cases contradict those ranges, while the main theorem statements retain relevant distinctions.

Set \(U_0=1\), \(U_1=-1\), and all other \(U_k=0\). The sequence is square summable, \(\widehat U\) is continuous near zero, and \(\sum U_k=0\). The process is \(X_j=Z_j-Z_{j-1}\) for independent standard normal \(Z_j\). At level \(\ell=-1\), if all \(N+2\) variables indexed from \(-1\) to \(N\) lie in \((-1/2,1/2)\), then \(X_j>-1\) for \(0\le j\le N\). Hence \[\mathbb P(X_j>-1,\ 0\le j\le N)\ge p^{N+2},\qquad
 p=\mathbb P(|Z|<1/2)=0.38292492.\] Therefore \[\limsup_{N\to\infty}\theta_X^{-1}(N)
       \le-\log p=0.95991634<\infty.\] This disproves the displayed equivalence \(\theta_X^\ell=\infty\Longleftrightarrow\sum U_k=0\) at the stated all-real-level scope. No assumption about the existence of the limit is needed to refute an asserted infinite limit. Remark 2 and Lemma 2.24 correctly restrict the zero-density infinite-exponent conclusion to \(\ell\ge0\). Restoring that restriction in the application removes this contradiction.

The paper’s \(\mathcal M\) includes \(\rho'(0)=\infty\). Already \(\rho=\delta_0\) has \(\theta_\rho^\ell=0\) for every finite \(\ell\), since its persistence probability is the constant \(Q(\ell)\). Thus the positive-level conjecture in that remark cannot include the whole class as literally defined.

The nonpositive-level assertion that positivity is equivalent to a nonzero absolutely continuous part also fails at infinite origin density. Let \(f=Z+g\), with \(Z\) independent standard normal and \(g\) an independent unit-variance bandlimited stationary process with nonzero absolutely continuous spectrum. Put \(A_0=\mathbb E\sup_{[0,1]}|g|<\infty\). A union of unit-interval Borell bounds gives, for \(R_T=A_0+\sqrt{2\log(4\lceil T\rceil)}\), \[\mathbb P(\sup_{[0,T]}|g|\le R_T)\ge\tfrac12.\] Thus \[\mathbb P(\inf_{[0,T]}(Z+g)>\ell)\ge\tfrac12 Q(\ell+R_T),
 \qquad -\log Q(\ell+R_T)=O(\log T).\] It follows directly that \(\theta_f^\ell=0\) at every fixed level. Its spectral measure has both a zero atom and a nonzero absolutely continuous component, satisfies \(\mathcal L\), and has infinite origin density. This agrees with Proposition 2.25 and Theorem 1, rather than refuting either.

These are peripheral range errors, with no demonstrated use of the overstated assertions in the core proofs. Accordingly they are Minor. Restricting Remark 3 to finite positive origin density avoids these counterexamples; its positive-level claim must still be presented as a conjecture, not as a proved theorem.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the acquired 118-page Wiley version of record by Emmanuel Michta, Jiwoon Park and Gordon Slade, DOI 10.1002/cpa.22256. The complete source was read. Three problems affect displayed core proof steps, and three affect peripheral ranges or constants. The evidence establishes the indicated false inequalities, invalid implications or incorrect prefactors; it does not establish that the principal finite-size scaling theorems are false. Each problem includes its hypotheses, proof, dependency and repair boundary. The disposition remains pending independent human review.
Author: Paper M25-0414 Display 0414
Date: 29 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review
Boundary conditions and universal finite-size scaling
for the hierarchical \(|\varphi|^4\) model
in dimensions \(4\) and higher
# Scope, notation and principal dependencies

Source page numbers below are the internal numbers 1–118 of the acquired version, rather than journal pagination 2001–2118. Its first page records acceptance on 2 April 2025. The separate arXiv record 2306.00896v3 is dated 17 March 2025 and describes a 105-page manuscript with editorial improvements; equality with that file is not asserted.

Theorem 1.1 treats the fixed supercritical Gaussian regime. Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 treat, respectively, the non-Gaussian critical window and the larger Gaussian window. Their centre under free boundary conditions is the exact quantity \[\nu_N^{\mathrm F}=\nu_{0,N}(-qL^{-2N})-qL^{-2N}.\] In dimensions at least six, discarding the displayed error in a simpler asymptotic centre would exceed the critical window. The paper retains the exact centre there; Remark 3.5 explicitly recognizes this issue. It is not a finding against the paper.

For the critical profile, put \[I_k(s)=\int_0^\infty x^k e^{-x^4/4-sx^2/2}\,dx,\qquad
 f_n(s)=\frac{I_{n+1}(s)}{nI_{n-1}(s)}\quad(n>0).\] Integration by parts gives \(nI_{n-1}=I_{n+3}+sI_{n+1}\) and the stated recursion for \(f_n\). The \(n=0\) complete-graph statements are separate from the main integer-spin theorems. The paper’s Euclidean-lattice extrapolations and several broader universality statements are identified as conjectural. They are not promoted to theorems in this review.

The proof proceeds through the finite-volume Gaussian identity, RG estimates and critical-point construction, followed by the last-scale integrals. Problems 1–3 concern this chain. Problems 4–6 concern an introductory asymptotic, an unnecessarily broad auxiliary lemma, and an appendix prefactor. The classification Major identifies an invalid core derivation even where a local repair is available; it does not mean that a final theorem has been disproved.
# Problem 1: false quartic separation in the Gaussian identity

Equation reference: eq:quartic-false. Severity: Major. Source: Lemma 2.1, pp. 29–30, especially the final paragraph following (2.34) on p. 30. The proof of analytic continuation uses, for a zero-sum field, the inequality \[
 \sum_x|\varphi_x+y|^4\geq
 \sum_x\bigl(|\varphi_x|^4+|y|^4\bigr).\] All fields in the following example are real, so the issue precedes any choice of interpretation for complex parameters.
Claim 1.  Inequality [eq:quartic-false] (#eq:quartic-false) fails for a scalar zero-sum field in every volume with at least three sites.

Proof. Take \(n=1\), \(\varphi=(2,-1,-1,0,\ldots,0)\) and \(y=-1/10\). Then \(\sum\varphi_x=0\), \(\sum\varphi_x^2=6\) and \(\sum\varphi_x^3=6\). Expanding the fourth powers, the left side minus the right side of [eq:quartic-false] (#eq:quartic-false) is \[4y\sum_x\varphi_x^3+6y^2\sum_x\varphi_x^2
       =-\frac{12}{5}+\frac9{25}=-\frac{51}{25}<0.\] The zero-sum condition cancels the linear sum, not the cubic sum. ◻

This example fits the allowed hierarchical volumes by adding zero entries. For any fixed sufficiently large \(L\), \(d\geq4\) and \(N\geq1\), the zero-mean Gaussian subspace contains these real configurations in its support. Neither small \(g>0\) nor an admissible mass repairs the asserted deterministic inequality.
#### Dependency and counterevidence.

The bound is used to justify integrability and holomorphy when the mass is continued to the negative finite-volume range. Lemma 2.1 feeds Corollary 2.2 and the last-scale representation used in Section 4. Lemma 8.4, pp. 90–91, uses the valid Jensen inequality \(\sum_x|\varphi_x+y|^4\geq M|y|^4\), where \(M\) is the number of sites. That statement does not imply the additional \(\sum|\varphi_x|^4\) term.
#### Repair and impact.

A weaker coercive bound suffices and can be proved directly. Write \(A=\sum_x|\varphi_x+y|^4\). Jensen gives \(M|y|^4\leq A\). The elementary inequality \(|u-v|^4\leq8(|u|^4+|v|^4)\) then gives \(\sum|\varphi_x|^4\leq16A\). Consequently \[A\geq \frac1{17}\left(\sum_x|\varphi_x|^4+M|y|^4\right).\] Positive quartic coercivity dominates every quadratic and linear term uniformly on compact sets of the complex mass half-plane \(\Re a>-L^{-2(N-1)}\). This supplies the required domination. An analytic continuation argument should first cross-multiply the normalized identity; one need not assume that a complex partition function has no zeros. For real admissible parameters its denominator is positive. Thus the displayed inequality is false, while the Gaussian identity has a concrete repair and is not itself disproved.
# Problem 2: an unjustified high-dimensional decay exponent
Severity: Major. Source: (3.3), (3.12), pp. 31–32; (5.27)–(5.29), p. 57; (5.38), p. 58; and (6.10) with the proof of Theorem 3.1(ii), p. 63.
#### A counterexample to the stated domain implication.
This construction disproves the claimed implication from domain membership. It is not asserted to be the RG trajectory from the paper’s initial condition \(K_0=0\).
#### Quantitative consequence and repair.

For the permissible choice \(\varepsilon=1/(2d-6)\) made on p. 63, the exponential rate supplied by [eq:actual-K] (#eq:actual-K) is \(d(1-\varepsilon)/2\). It equals \(17/3\) at \(d=12\), rather than \(6\), and \(247/40\) at \(d=13\), rather than \(13/2\). The particular \(e_N\) estimate used in (3.12) therefore does not follow from the domain estimate cited in its proof. The strict exponent margins in the contraction argument, pp. 99–102, prevent simply setting \(\varepsilon=0\) without further proof.

Retaining \(\rho^{\mathfrak p}\) still gives a positive exponential decay rate. In the last-scale estimates of pp. 50–51, this decay dominates the factor \(\exp(C\sqrt N)\) allowed by the negative critical-window range. Thus weakening \(e_N\) consistently is a plausible repair of the proof of the main scaling limits. Alternatively, the authors could prove a sharper bound for the actual trajectory. Neither the sharper trajectory estimate nor a counterexample to the final scaling theorems is established here.
# Problem 3: mass decay incorrectly attached to arbitrary directions

Equation reference: eq:S1false. Severity: Major. Source: Proposition 9.4 and (9.14), (9.18), p. 101; (9.35)–(9.44), pp. 104–105. The extended norm is defined in Section 8.1, p. 87, and includes \(\lambda_K\) times the norm of the Fréchet derivative in an arbitrary unit \(K\) direction. Proposition 9.4 places the factor \(\widetilde\vartheta_+^3\) outside both terms: \[
 \|S_1\|_{\mathcal W_+(\vec\lambda)}
 \leq C_L\widetilde\vartheta_+^3
           \bigl(\widetilde g_+^3\rho^{\mathfrak a}+\lambda_K\bigr).\]
#### A mass-limit contradiction under the stated hypotheses.

Fix \(n=1\), \(d\geq4\), a sufficiently large \(L\), sufficiently small \(g>0\), scale \(j=0\), \(V(\varphi)=g\varphi^4/4\), and \(K=0\). Let the mass centre and actual mass coincide, \(\widetilde a=a\to\infty\). Put \(\lambda_V=0\) and fix \(0<\lambda_K\leq g^{9/4}\), for instance \(g^{9/4}/2\). These are within the proposition’s restrictions. With \(M=L^d\), \[C_1(a)=\frac1{1+a}\left(I-\frac1M J\right)\longrightarrow0 .\] Choose an even direction \(H(\varphi)=c_0\varphi^6e^{-c\varphi^4}\) with \(c\) sufficiently large and \(c_0>0\) chosen to give unit \(\mathcal W_0\) norm. It has \(\operatorname{Loc}(e^V H)=0\), because its Taylor terms of degree at most four vanish. Hence the local counterterm has zero derivative in this direction. Differentiating the product defining \(S_1\) at \(K=0\), and then letting \(a\to\infty\), gives at any fixed real \(\varphi>0\) \[D_KS_1(V,0)[H](\varphi)
 \longrightarrow M e^{-(M-1)V(\varphi)}H(\varphi)>0 .\] The perturbative constant tends to zero and \(\widetilde g_+\to g\). Dominated convergence is justified by the quartic decay of \(H\) and \(e^{-V}\) and the Gaussian covariance tending to zero. The evaluation term in the regulated output norm, with its positive weight, therefore gives a positive lower bound for the left side of [eq:S1false] (#eq:S1false). The right side tends to zero, because \(\widetilde\vartheta_+=(2a)^{-1}\) in this mass regime.

The shrinking domain for the base value \(K\) cannot exclude this counterexample: \(K=0\) is interior for each finite \(a\), and arbitrary Fréchet directions are not required to carry the small domain radius. The distinction is also stated in the discussion of derivatives on p. 59.
#### Counterevidence, correction and dependency.

The false estimate occurs in the proof of the derivative bounds needed for RG iteration. Its correction leaves the \(q=0\) bounds with mass decay and the general \(q\geq1\) bounds without it, as in the actual statement of Theorem 9.1. The crucial \(q=1\) contraction is supplied separately by Proposition 9.5. Thus the printed uniform estimate and its use in (9.18) are invalid, but the structure of the desired theorem accommodates the corrected estimate. This is not evidence that the main finite-size theorem fails.
# Problem 4: a logarithmic restriction missing from an asymptotic

Take \(s_N=L^N\). Both stated restrictions hold, but substitution in the infinite-volume formula shows that the ratio to the proposed expression tends to \[\left(\frac{\log(1/(s_Nw_N))}{2N\log L}\right)^{\widehat\gamma}
 \longrightarrow 2^{-\widehat\gamma}\neq1 .\] More generally \(s_N=L^{cN}\), \(0<c<2\), gives \((1-c/2)^{\widehat\gamma}\). This is a direct application of the paper’s own fixed-parameter susceptibility asymptotic along a sequence tending to criticality, not a change in model.

The simplification is valid under \(\log s_N=o(N)\), or the original logarithm can be retained. The actual positive growth range in Theorem 1.2, \(s_N\leq L^{\sqrt N}\) in dimension four, satisfies this additional condition. Section 1.5 is not used to prove the main results. The displayed assertion is therefore false in its printed range, with no demonstrated damage to Corollary 1.4 or the main proof.
# Problem 5: a covariance lemma is too broad in polynomial degree

Severity: Minor. Source: Lemma 8.3 and (8.20), pp. 89–90. The lemma allows even mass-independent polynomials of degree at most \(2p\) for every integer \(p\geq1\), and bounds the covariance by a constant times a field-growth factor \(P_h(\varphi)^{2p}\).

Set \(n=1\), \(j=0\), \(a=0\), \(M=L^d>1\) and \(C=I-J/M\). Take \[V_1(B)=V_2(B)=\sum_{x\in B}\varphi_x^6,\qquad p=3,
 \quad \lambda_V=\lambda_K=0,\] and any fixed permitted \(h\geq\mathfrak c_+\). These polynomials are even and mass-independent. If \(S_r=\sum_x\zeta_x^r\), then \(S_1=0\) almost surely and \[\sum_x(\varphi+\zeta_x)^6
 =M\varphi^6+15\varphi^4 S_2+20\varphi^3 S_3
               +15\varphi^2 S_4+6\varphi S_5+S_6 .\] For the stated Gaussian, \(\operatorname{Var}S_2=2\operatorname{tr}(C^2)=2(M-1)\). The covariance of the polynomial with itself is consequently \[450(M-1)\varphi^8+O(\varphi^6)
       \qquad (|\varphi|\to\infty).\] The possible degree-seven cross term vanishes by Gaussian parity. The left norm contains the zeroth-order evaluation, while the claimed right side grows only as \(|\varphi|^6\). No fixed constant can give (8.20).

The quartic instances actually used on pp. 94, 98 and 103 have \(p=2\); their maximum degree \(4p-4\) is precisely four and this example does not refute them. The cited RG book’s Lemma 7.6.1, physical pp. 122–123, has a quartic scope; it does not supply the printed arbitrary-degree extension. A safe repair is to restrict the lemma to the needed degrees \(p=1,2\) and prove those cases. For general \(p\), growth at least \(4p-4\) is necessary even for equal scalar block polynomials. This necessary power is not asserted sufficient under every more general coefficient convention. The classification is Minor because the demonstrated overstatement is outside the operative quartic uses.

# Coverage, independent checks and limitations

All 118 source pages, including definitions, proofs, appendices and bibliography, were read by the primary executor. Coverage included the boundary Laplacian and zero-mode decomposition; the admissible mass range; the scaling, moment and sequence restrictions; last-scale domination; the definition and composition of the RG map; norm weights and strict contraction margins; critical-point construction and its derivative hypotheses; and the profile identities and endpoint asymptotics.

In particular, positive and negative growing-window restrictions were kept distinct. The negative range is at most \((\log N)^{1/4}\) in dimension four and \(N^{1/4}\) above it; the positive range in Theorem 1.2 and the different mesoscopic range in Theorem 1.3 were not interchanged. Appendix A’s extension to negative values of \(n\) explicitly restricts \(s\) above its pole boundary; that is not a counterexample to an unrestricted claim.

Independent reviewer calculations include the exact rational quartic counterexample, the dimension-dependent exponent comparisons, Gaussian quadratic-form moments, the susceptibility ratio, and the endpoint Gaussian integral. Numerical integrations of the profile recurrence for \(n=1,2,3,8\) and \(s=-4,0,4\) had maximum relative floating-point residual \(3.70\times10^{-14}\). These ordinary floating-point checks corroborate the analytic calculations; they are neither interval enclosures nor simulations of an RG orbit. No author code was executed.

problems.title: False quartic separation in the analytic continuation proof
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: # Problem 1: false quartic separation in the Gaussian identity
claim: Recorded check: False quartic separation in the analytic continuation proof
N: 1. D: >=4. L: sufficiently large. N: >=1. G: any allowed positive g. Field: (2,-1,-1,0,...), zero sum. Constant shift: -1/10. Mass: any admitted real mass.
analysis:
Equation reference: eq:quartic-false. Severity: Major. Source: Lemma 2.1, pp. 29–30, especially the final paragraph following (2.34) on p. 30. The proof of analytic continuation uses, for a zero-sum field, the inequality \[
 \sum_x|\varphi_x+y|^4\geq
 \sum_x\bigl(|\varphi_x|^4+|y|^4\bigr).\] All fields in the following example are real, so the issue precedes any choice of interpretation for complex parameters.
Claim 1.  Inequality [eq:quartic-false] (#eq:quartic-false) fails for a scalar zero-sum field in every volume with at least three sites.

Proof. Take \(n=1\), \(\varphi=(2,-1,-1,0,\ldots,0)\) and \(y=-1/10\). Then \(\sum\varphi_x=0\), \(\sum\varphi_x^2=6\) and \(\sum\varphi_x^3=6\). Expanding the fourth powers, the left side minus the right side of [eq:quartic-false] (#eq:quartic-false) is \[4y\sum_x\varphi_x^3+6y^2\sum_x\varphi_x^2
       =-\frac{12}{5}+\frac9{25}=-\frac{51}{25}<0.\] The zero-sum condition cancels the linear sum, not the cubic sum. ◻

This example fits the allowed hierarchical volumes by adding zero entries. For any fixed sufficiently large \(L\), \(d\geq4\) and \(N\geq1\), the zero-mean Gaussian subspace contains these real configurations in its support. Neither small \(g>0\) nor an admissible mass repairs the asserted deterministic inequality.

The bound is used to justify integrability and holomorphy when the mass is continued to the negative finite-volume range. Lemma 2.1 feeds Corollary 2.2 and the last-scale representation used in Section 4. Lemma 8.4, pp. 90–91, uses the valid Jensen inequality \(\sum_x|\varphi_x+y|^4\geq M|y|^4\), where \(M\) is the number of sites. That statement does not imply the additional \(\sum|\varphi_x|^4\) term.
