problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: # Problem 3: mass decay incorrectly attached to arbitrary directions
claim: Recorded check: Mass factor cannot bound arbitrary K derivative directions

N: 1. D: >=4. J: 0. L: fixed sufficiently large. G: fixed sufficiently small. V: g phi^4/4. K: 0. Lambdav: 0. Lambdak: g^(9/4)/2. A tilde and a: coincident, tendtoinfinity. Direction: W0-normalizedH=c0phi^6exp(-cphi^4),Loc(e^V H)=0.
analysis:
Equation reference: eq:S1false. Severity: Major. Source: Proposition 9.4 and (9.14), (9.18), p. 101; (9.35)–(9.44), pp. 104–105. The extended norm is defined in Section 8.1, p. 87, and includes \(\lambda_K\) times the norm of the Fréchet derivative in an arbitrary unit \(K\) direction. Proposition 9.4 places the factor \(\widetilde\vartheta_+^3\) outside both terms: \[
 \|S_1\|_{\mathcal W_+(\vec\lambda)}
 \leq C_L\widetilde\vartheta_+^3
           \bigl(\widetilde g_+^3\rho^{\mathfrak a}+\lambda_K\bigr).\]

Fix \(n=1\), \(d\geq4\), a sufficiently large \(L\), sufficiently small \(g>0\), scale \(j=0\), \(V(\varphi)=g\varphi^4/4\), and \(K=0\). Let the mass centre and actual mass coincide, \(\widetilde a=a\to\infty\). Put \(\lambda_V=0\) and fix \(0<\lambda_K\leq g^{9/4}\), for instance \(g^{9/4}/2\). These are within the proposition’s restrictions. With \(M=L^d\), \[C_1(a)=\frac1{1+a}\left(I-\frac1M J\right)\longrightarrow0 .\] Choose an even direction \(H(\varphi)=c_0\varphi^6e^{-c\varphi^4}\) with \(c\) sufficiently large and \(c_0>0\) chosen to give unit \(\mathcal W_0\) norm. It has \(\operatorname{Loc}(e^V H)=0\), because its Taylor terms of degree at most four vanish. Hence the local counterterm has zero derivative in this direction. Differentiating the product defining \(S_1\) at \(K=0\), and then letting \(a\to\infty\), gives at any fixed real \(\varphi>0\) \[D_KS_1(V,0)[H](\varphi)
 \longrightarrow M e^{-(M-1)V(\varphi)}H(\varphi)>0 .\] The perturbative constant tends to zero and \(\widetilde g_+\to g\). Dominated convergence is justified by the quartic decay of \(H\) and \(e^{-V}\) and the Gaussian covariance tending to zero. The evaluation term in the regulated output norm, with its positive weight, therefore gives a positive lower bound for the left side of [eq:S1false] (#eq:S1false). The right side tends to zero, because \(\widetilde\vartheta_+=(2a)^{-1}\) in this mass regime.

The shrinking domain for the base value \(K\) cannot exclude this counterexample: \(K=0\) is interior for each finite \(a\), and arbitrary Fréchet directions are not required to carry the small domain radius. The distinction is also stated in the discussion of derivatives on p. 59.
result: The false estimate occurs in the proof of the derivative bounds needed for RG iteration. Its correction leaves the \(q=0\) bounds with mass decay and the general \(q\geq1\) bounds without it, as in the actual statement of Theorem 9.1. The crucial \(q=1\) contraction is supplied separately by Proposition 9.5. Thus the printed uniform estimate and its use in (9.18) are invalid, but the structure of the desired theorem accommodates the corrected estimate. This is not evidence that the main finite-size theorem fails.

problems.title: Introductory susceptibility equivalence lacks a logarithmic growth restriction
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: # Problem 4: a logarithmic restriction missing from an asymptotic
claim: Recorded check: Introductory susceptibility equivalence lacks a logarithmic growth restriction
D: 4. N: >=1. G: fixed sufficiently small. Sn: L^N. Restrictions: sN>=epsilon>0 andsN*wN->0 bothhold.
analysis:
Take \(s_N=L^N\). Both stated restrictions hold, but substitution in the infinite-volume formula shows that the ratio to the proposed expression tends to \[\left(\frac{\log(1/(s_Nw_N))}{2N\log L}\right)^{\widehat\gamma}
 \longrightarrow 2^{-\widehat\gamma}\neq1 .\] More generally \(s_N=L^{cN}\), \(0<c<2\), gives \((1-c/2)^{\widehat\gamma}\). This is a direct application of the paper’s own fixed-parameter susceptibility asymptotic along a sequence tending to criticality, not a change in model.

The simplification is valid under \(\log s_N=o(N)\), or the original logarithm can be retained. The actual positive growth range in Theorem 1.2, \(s_N\leq L^{\sqrt N}\) in dimension four, satisfies this additional condition. Section 1.5 is not used to prove the main results. The displayed assertion is therefore false in its printed range, with no demonstrated damage to Corollary 1.4 or the main proof.

problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 5: # Problem 5: a covariance lemma is too broad in polynomial degree
claim: Recorded check: Covariance lemma overstates the arbitrary-degree field growth
P: 3. N: 1. J: 0. A: 0. M: L^d>1. C: I-J/M. V1 and v2: sum_x phi_x^6,even mass-independent. H: fixedallowedh>=c_+. Lambdav: 0. Lambdak: 0.
analysis: Severity: Minor. Source: Lemma 8.3 and (8.20), pp. 89–90. The lemma allows even mass-independent polynomials of degree at most \(2p\) for every integer \(p\geq1\), and bounds the covariance by a constant times a field-growth factor \(P_h(\varphi)^{2p}\).

Set \(n=1\), \(j=0\), \(a=0\), \(M=L^d>1\) and \(C=I-J/M\). Take \[V_1(B)=V_2(B)=\sum_{x\in B}\varphi_x^6,\qquad p=3,
 \quad \lambda_V=\lambda_K=0,\] and any fixed permitted \(h\geq\mathfrak c_+\). These polynomials are even and mass-independent. If \(S_r=\sum_x\zeta_x^r\), then \(S_1=0\) almost surely and \[\sum_x(\varphi+\zeta_x)^6
 =M\varphi^6+15\varphi^4 S_2+20\varphi^3 S_3
               +15\varphi^2 S_4+6\varphi S_5+S_6 .\] For the stated Gaussian, \(\operatorname{Var}S_2=2\operatorname{tr}(C^2)=2(M-1)\). The covariance of the polynomial with itself is consequently \[450(M-1)\varphi^8+O(\varphi^6)
       \qquad (|\varphi|\to\infty).\] The possible degree-seven cross term vanishes by Gaussian parity. The left norm contains the zeroth-order evaluation, while the claimed right side grows only as \(|\varphi|^6\). No fixed constant can give (8.20).

The quartic instances actually used on pp. 94, 98 and 103 have \(p=2\); their maximum degree \(4p-4\) is precisely four and this example does not refute them. The cited RG book’s Lemma 7.6.1, physical pp. 122–123, has a quartic scope; it does not supply the printed arbitrary-degree extension. A safe repair is to restrict the lemma to the needed degrees \(p=1,2\) and prove those cases. For general \(p\), growth at least \(4p-4\) is necessary even for equal scalar block polynomials. This necessary power is not asserted sufficient under every more general coefficient convention. report: Abstract: The acquired arXiv v4 is reviewed in full, including its appendix. Two Major problems concern a false symmetry used in a central Green-kernel argument and an explicit metric construction which gives comparability without the asserted smooth orbifold extension. A separate Minor problem concerns the total mass of a regularized Monge–Ampère equation. Explicit calculations establish these defects. They do not establish a false Bogomolov–Gieseker theorem. A normalization repair is proved for the Green-kernel argument, and the dependence of the main theorem on a different interpolating metric is distinguished from the defective construction. This is a completed initial review, with scientific decision pending.
Author: Bounded initial review executor
Date: 29 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review of
Bogomolov–Gieseker inequality for log terminal Kähler threefolds
# Source, scope, and principal conclusions

The reviewed paper is by Henri Guenancia and Mihai Păun, with an appendix by Frédéric Campana, Andreas Höring, and Thomas Peternell [GP4]. The assigned identity is M25-0415; the journal DOI is https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70000. The exact acquired source is `arXiv:2405.10003v4`, submitted 2 March 2025, comprising 37 PDF pages. Its last page is dated 4 March 2025. Those two dates describe different source facts. Page numbers below refer to this PDF, whose printed pagination agrees with the physical pagination.

The principal theorem assumes a normal compact Kähler threefold with klt singularities, an ambient Kähler form \(\omega_X\), and a coherent reflexive \(\mathbb Q\)-sheaf \(\mathcal F\) of rank \(r>0\) which is stable with respect to \([\omega_X]\). It asserts \[\bigl(2r\,c_2(\mathcal F)-(r-1)c_1(\mathcal F)^2\bigr)\cdot[\omega_X]\geq0,\] with orbifold Chern numbers. The equality statement concerns local freeness and projective Hermitian flatness on \(X_{\mathrm{reg}}\), and extension of the projectivization after a finite quasi-étale Galois cover. It does not claim that the entire pulled-back reflexive sheaf becomes locally free.

All 37 pages were read. Definitions, parameter choices, hypotheses, theorem ranges, proofs, boundary terms, the appendix, and references were examined. All 37 source pages and 44 selected reference pages were also actually viewed as native rendered images. The three Problems below are proved defects of particular assertions or derivations. Neither a false principal theorem nor failure of every possible proof has been established.
# Problem 1: the normalized Green kernel need not be symmetric

Equation reference: eq:normal. Problem 1 (Major; invalid step in the principal analytic dependency).  On p. 6, the Green function is specified by \[
 \Delta_{\omega_\varepsilon}G_x^\varepsilon
 =\delta_x-V_\varepsilon^{-1},
 \qquad \sup_yG_x^\varepsilon(y)=-1.\] The proof of Proposition 3.3 then uses symmetry in the estimates immediately preceding (3.6) and (3.7), p. 8. The normalization in [eq:normal] (#eq:normal) generally destroys that symmetry.

The operative setting is the regularization of a bounded canonical Monge–Ampère metric on a compact klt Kähler space. Proposition 3.3 also assumes Property (P): cutoffs whose \(L^{2+\epsilon}\) gradient norm and \(L^{1+\epsilon}\) Laplacian norm tend to zero, for a fixed \(\epsilon>0\). Its conclusion applies to nonnegative \(C^2\) functions for which the function and the negative part of its Laplacian belong to a sufficiently large \(L^p\) space. None of these conditions forces the maximum of a mean-zero Green kernel to be independent of its pole.

Equation reference: eq:K. Here is an exact example within the smooth compact Kähler case. Regard the unit round sphere as \(\mathbb P^1\), write \(z\) for its height, and choose \(0<\eta<1\). Put \[Y(z)=\frac{3z^2-1}{2},\qquad
 g_\eta=(1+\eta Y(z))g_0,\qquad H(z)=\frac{\eta Y(z)}{24\pi}.\] The density is positive, its integral is \(4\pi\), and \(\Delta_0Y=-6Y\), with the Laplacian convention \(\Delta G=\delta-(4\pi)^{-1}\). Define \[\begin{aligned}
 G_0(x,y)&=\frac{\log(1-x\cdot y)-\log2+1}{4\pi},\\
 K_\eta(x,y)&=G_0(x,y)+H(z_x)+H(z_y)-\frac{\eta^2}{120\pi}.
 \end{aligned}\] Since \(\Delta_{g_\eta}=(1+\eta Y)^{-1}\Delta_0\) in real dimension two, \(\Delta_yK_\eta=\delta_x^{g_\eta}-(4\pi)^{-1}\). Moreover, \(\int K_\eta(x,y)\,dA_{g_\eta}(y)=0\). For the latter identity, use \(\int G_0(x,y)Y(z_y)\,dA_0(y)=-Y(z_x)/6\) and \(\int Y^2\,dA_0=4\pi/5\). Thus [eq:K] (#eq:K) is the symmetric mean-zero kernel.

Equation reference: eq:asym. Let \(m(x)=\max_y K_\eta(x,y)\), let \(P\) be a pole of the sphere, and let \(E\) be an equatorial point. For \(x=P\), both \(G_0(P,y)\) and \(H(z_y)\) attain their joint maximum at \(y=-P\). For \(x=E\), set \(t=E\cdot y\). The inequalities \[\log\frac{1-t}{2}\leq-\frac{1+t}{2},
 \qquad z_y^2\leq2(1+t)\] give \[K_\eta(E,y)-K_\eta(E,-E)
 \leq-\frac{(1-\eta)(1+t)}{8\pi}\leq0.\] Consequently \[m(P)-m(E)=2\bigl(H(1)-H(0)\bigr)=\frac{\eta}{8\pi}.\] The source normalization is precisely \(G_x(y)=K_\eta(x,y)-m(x)-1\), so that \[
 G_P(E)-G_E(P)=-\frac{\eta}{8\pi}\ne0.\] Take \(\omega_X\) to be the Kähler form of \(g_\eta\) and choose the smooth canonical-bundle metric whose associated measure is \(\omega_X\). The canonical potential is then zero; \(X\) is smooth and klt, and Property (P) holds with constant cutoffs. On the identity resolution one may take \(\widehat\omega=\omega_X\), obtaining the scaling family \((1+\varepsilon)\omega_X\). The same defect survives its limit. Thus the example does not rely on singular-space pathology.
## Counterevidence, repair, and impact

Self-adjointness gives symmetry for the mean-zero kernel. It does not give symmetry after pole-dependent shifts. Changing a fixed convention for the Laplacian changes the constants in the example but does not remove the dependence on the pole.

The false identity occurs in the proof of Proposition 3.3, which supplies Corollary 5.11, Theorem 5.15, and the subsequent current-closure argument for the main theorem. This makes the invalid derivation Major under the review criterion, even though the normalization repair is local and preserves the estimates. Equation [eq:asym] (#eq:asym) is not a counterexample to Proposition 3.3 or to the final Chern-number inequality.
# Problem 2: the explicit local potential is not orbifold smooth

Problem 2 (Major; failure of the construction proving Theorem 4.3).  The definition on p. 9 requires a smooth Kähler metric after pullback to an orbifold chart. Theorem 4.3, pp. 11–12, asserts such a metric for a compact klt Kähler threefold whose orbifold singularities are ordinary double points. Claim 4.4 and (4.5), p. 12, prove comparability with the Euclidean metric. The construction and the three assertions on p. 13 do not supply the required smooth extension, and the claimed independence of a local embedding is false.

Equation reference: eq:levi. Let \[X=\mathbb P(1,1,2)\times\mathbb P^1.\] It is compact, projective, and klt. Every singularity is the product of an \(A_1\) surface quotient with a smooth curve; its non-orbifold locus \(Z\) is empty. Thus it satisfies the stated geometric assumptions. A local uniformization is \[\iota(u,v,z)=(u^2,v^2,uv,z),\qquad
 f(Z)=Z_1Z_2-Z_3^2.\] For \(c>0\) set \[F_c(u,v)=\sqrt{|u|^4+|v|^4+c|u|^2|v|^2}.\] Writing \(s=|u|^2\) and \(t=|v|^2\) and differentiating directly gives, for every real \(r>0\), \[
 \frac{\partial^2 F_c}{\partial u\,\partial\bar u}(r,0)=1,
 \qquad
 \frac{\partial^2 F_c}{\partial u\,\partial\bar u}(0,r)=\frac c2.\] Claim 4.4 uses \(c=1\), giving the distinct limits \(1\) and \(1/2\). The actual pullback of the gradient norm in (4.5) is \[|\nabla f|\circ\iota
 =\sqrt{|u|^4+|v|^4+4|u|^2|v|^2}=F_4,\] giving limits \(1\) and \(2\). Thus neither Hessian has a continuous extension at the origin. Euclidean comparability in Claim 4.4 can be true while smooth orbifold extension fails. The transverse coefficients of the pullback of a smooth ambient Kähler form are \(O(r^2)\) on these axes, so adding the prescribed large multiple of that form cannot remove the jump. A partition of unity with one chart equal to one near the point is an allowed local choice in the displayed construction and retains it.
## Counterevidence, repair, and impact

For a suitable fixed chart, an actual orbifold potential is available: \[\sqrt{|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2+2|Z_3|^2}
 \quad\stackrel{\iota^*}{\longmapsto}\quad |u|^2+|v|^2.\] Adding \(|z|^2\) makes its pullback smooth and positive. This proves that the local existence assertion is not refuted. A replacement proof must nevertheless specify compatible potentials, justify their gluing, and verify the stated \(L^p\), \(p>1\), determinant condition on a resolution near the non-orbifold locus. Those global steps are not certified by the local replacement alone.

Theorem 4.3 is a substantive secondary result, and its explicit construction fails its claimed regularity and embedding invariance. The defect is therefore Major. It is not propagated indiscriminately to the Bogomolov–Gieseker theorem: Section 5 starts with a genuine orbifold metric away from a neighborhood of finitely many points and interpolates it with an ambient metric near those points. That construction is different from the gradient-norm formula in Theorem 4.3. The corresponding existence framework is also explicit in [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem~1.4 and Section~6]{CGN}].
# Problem 3: the smoothing changes the total mass

Problem 3 (Minor; incorrect scalar normalization).  Equation (2.3), p. 5, has right-hand side \(c_\varepsilon\prod_i(|s_i|^2+\varepsilon^2)^{a_i}d\widehat V\), while p. 6 fixes \(c_\varepsilon=V_\varepsilon/V\). The hypotheses only imply \(\int\prod_i|s_i|^{2a_i}d\widehat V=V\). They do not imply the same identity after smoothing.

A compact threefold example makes the incompatibility strict. Let \(X=\mathbb P(1,1,1,2)\). Its unique singularity is \(\mathbb C^3/\{\pm1\}\) of type \(\tfrac12(1,1,1)\). Blowing up its vertex gives a smooth resolution with exceptional divisor \(E\simeq\mathbb P^2\) and normal bundle \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(-2)\). Its discrepancy is \(a=1/2\): adjunction gives \(K_{\widehat X}|_E=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(-1)\), whereas \(\pi^*K_X|_E\) is rationally trivial, so \(-2a=-1\). For the smooth positive volume form prescribed by the source, \[I_\varepsilon=\int_{\widehat X}\sqrt{|s|^2+\varepsilon^2}\,d\widehat V
 >\int_{\widehat X}|s|\,d\widehat V=V
 \qquad(\varepsilon>0).\] The printed right-hand side therefore has mass \(V_\varepsilon I_\varepsilon/V>V_\varepsilon\), while every left-hand side has mass \(V_\varepsilon\) by Stokes’ theorem. No smooth solution can satisfy that exact equation.
## Counterevidence, repair, and impact

Replace the scalar by \[c_\varepsilon=\frac{V_\varepsilon}{I_\varepsilon}.\] Since \(a_i>-1\) and the divisors have simple normal crossings, dominated convergence gives \(I_\varepsilon\to V\). The corrected factors tend to one and remain bounded above and away from zero. The uniform \(L^p\) estimate for a suitable \(p>1\) and smooth convergence away from the exceptional divisor are unaffected. This is an isolated normalization repair; the later approximation on p. 19 already describes its coefficient simply as a normalizing constant. The example refutes the printed regularized equation with the printed coefficient, not existence of the canonical metric or the final theorem.
# Other operative assumptions and boundary checks
The following checks delimit the findings and the scope of the review.
## Conditional boundedness and approximation

Property (P) remains a hypothesis for the canonical metric in Proposition B and Proposition 3.3 of v4. It is not silently supplied by the klt condition. The cutoff exponents in the proof can be met by taking \(p_0\) at least the maximum of the indicated conjugate exponents; in particular \(2p'\geq2p\) when \(p\) is conjugate to \(1+\epsilon\) and \(p'\) to \(1+\epsilon/2\). The finite-volume, nonnegative-function, and negative-Laplacian assumptions are essential to the stated application. The projectivity hypothesis of Theorem 4.1 is retained. Its use of Artin approximation, a finite cover, and an \(L^p\) density on a resolution was checked as a dependency argument, not as a new proof of every cited Monge–Ampère regularity theorem.

The hypotheses of the acquired Green-estimate reference include a cohomological intersection bound, entropy with exponent greater than the complex dimension, and a continuous lower density whose zero set is suitably small with connected complement [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~2--3, 18--24]{GPSS}]. In the canonical resolution construction, the \(L^p\), \(p>1\), densities give the entropy bounds; the exceptional divisor has real codimension two. The bounds are compatible with the corrected mass normalization. The fixed positive volume lower bound was explicitly retained in Problem 1. The target’s references to later extensions of the Green estimates are not treated as new hypotheses absent from the acquired reference.
## The interpolating metric and Hermitian–Einstein input

For Section 5 the interpolation equals a fixed multiple of \(\omega_X\) near the finite set \(\{p_i\}\) and is genuinely orbifold outside a larger neighborhood. Cross terms are absorbed by the large ambient coefficient. The finite-cover/resolution Jacobian calculation in Proposition 5.6 gives integrability by choosing a sufficiently small positive power of the reciprocal Jacobian. The local uniformization cutoffs in Lemma 5.9 use fixed loci of complex codimension at least two; their exponents can be chosen small enough to give both required norms.

The Hermitian–Einstein existence and curvature estimates in Theorem 5.12 were compared with the actual Theorems 1.2 and 1.4 of [CGN]. The reference metric on a reflexive sheaf is a quotient metric, and its pullback is not automatically uniformly equivalent to a smooth bundle metric at the branching set. The power bounds and subsequent boundedness argument in Theorem 5.15 address this distinction. There is no valid general inference from a one-sided comparison of bundle metrics to a two-sided comparison of all endomorphism norms. For curvature, however, an algebraic check prevents a spurious objection: on real tangent vectors it is skew-Hermitian for the Chern metric, so its intrinsic squared norm is the sum of squared moduli of its eigenvalues, bounded by its Hilbert–Schmidt norm for any other metric. Thus the quoted curvature bound is not refuted by arbitrary non-normal endomorphism examples.
## Local products, current closure, and equality

Graf–Kirschner’s Lemma 5.8 gives a surface-quotient product after removal of a codimension-three analytic set [GK, p. 896]; in dimension three this set is finite. It should be included in \(\{p_i\}\). The surface quotient need not be a hypersurface in \(\mathbb C^3\). For example, \(\mathbb C^2/\mu_3\) with scalar action has four independent degree-three generators \(u^3,u^2v,uv^2,v^3\). Accordingly the three displayed transverse coordinate functions on p. 26 must be interpreted with an arbitrary finite number of generators in the general klt case. The subsequent Lemma 5.19 is intrinsically two-dimensional and its logarithmic integral argument does not require three ambient generators. The same derivative bounds follow for a finite sum of their squared norms. This is a clarification of the local model; no failure of the intrinsic integral estimate was proved.

The logarithmic cutoff integrals were independently checked using simultaneous principalization of the finitely many analytic ideals. After resolution, the required radial factors have the form \(dr/(r|\log r|)\) on logarithmic annuli; their integrals are uniformly bounded when the endpoints have fixed ratio in the logarithmic variable. For the final boundary integral at \(p_i\), the metric equals an ambient metric, the potential has gradient of order \(|Z|\), and curvature is \(L^2\). These facts give a bounded cutoff/potential factor and an integral over shrinking sets tending to zero by absolute integrability. The exterior derivative in Theorem 5.17 is \(\bar\partial\), as confirmed visually; treating it as \(\partial\) would create an irrelevant bidegree objection.

The equality argument uses nonnegative trace-free curvature density. Its reflexive extension across smooth isolated points and its projective-bundle conclusion are consistent with that range. The non-Cartier line-sheaf example in Remark 5.5 illustrates why the projectivization statement is weaker than local freeness of the whole pulled-back sheaf. It is not a stable-sheaf counterexample to the main theorem.
## Appendix and Chern-number conventions

The appendix’s abundance theorems retain normality, \(\mathbb Q\)-factoriality, terminal singularities, and nefness of \(K_X\); the positivity step also retains the stated numerical-dimension assumption. Proposition A.5 and Lemma A.6 concern the non-algebraic case. The lemma explicitly excludes projective uniruled klt examples with nonnegative Kodaira dimension, so those examples do not refute it. The resolution argument pairs exceptional divisors with the square of a pulled-back nef class and uses the fact that their images have codimension at least two.

For numerical Chern classes the precise general construction in [Retained latex: \cite[Definition~5.2 and Section~5.2]{GK}] is a functional on \(H^{2n-4}(X,\mathbb R)\), obtained from compactly supported cohomology of the orbifold locus. It is not a general theorem identifying that functional with a unique class in \(H^4(X,\mathbb R)\). The integral definition in the target’s (5.3)–(5.4) agrees with the functional construction. This review uses that definition and does not claim a general \(H^4\)-extension theorem from the abbreviated wording in the appendix. No counterexample satisfying the appendix’s full preceding \(\mathbb Q\)-factorial setup was established.
# Supporting checks

The current arXiv record [record] explicitly says that an earlier result was removed because of a proof gap while the main result was unchanged. The metadata does not name a theorem number. A direct comparison of the acquired v3 introduction [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~1--4]{GP3}] with v4 shows that v3 stated general Kähler orbifold regularity as Theorem B and a local Property (P) assertion in Proposition C.2; v4 keeps the relevant boundedness assertion conditional and identifies the general Kähler analogue of Theorem 4.1 as unknown in Remark 4.2. The withdrawn assertion is not counted as a current defect. This is a comparison of the specified introductions, not a full scientific review of v3 or a line-by-line comparison with the journal version.
The source-manifest SHA256 is

The independent Python check uses exact rational arithmetic for algebraic constants and ordinary floating-point evaluations for corroboration. For \(\eta=1/2\), [eq:asym] (#eq:asym) gives approximately \(-0.01989436788648692\). The grid evaluations do not prove the maximum identity; the inequalities above do. The directional Levi coefficients and the redundant-embedding degeneration are also established analytically. The Monge–Ampère mass discrepancy is an analytic integration argument, not a claimed numerical integration on a weighted projective variety. The saved result SHA256 is

problems.title: The gradient-norm potential is not smooth orbifold metric and depends on embedding
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: # Problem 2: the explicit local potential is not orbifold smooth
claim: Recorded check: The gradient-norm potential is not smooth orbifold metric and depends on embedding
analysis: The definition on p. 9 requires a smooth Kähler metric after pullback to an orbifold chart. Theorem 4.3, pp. 11–12, asserts such a metric for a compact klt Kähler threefold whose orbifold singularities are ordinary double points. Claim 4.4 and (4.5), p. 12, prove comparability with the Euclidean metric. The construction and the three assertions on p. 13 do not supply the required smooth extension, and the claimed independence of a local embedding is false.

Equation reference: eq:levi. Let \[X=\mathbb P(1,1,2)\times\mathbb P^1.\] It is compact, projective, and klt. Every singularity is the product of an \(A_1\) surface quotient with a smooth curve; its non-orbifold locus \(Z\) is empty. Thus it satisfies the stated geometric assumptions. A local uniformization is \[\iota(u,v,z)=(u^2,v^2,uv,z),\qquad
 f(Z)=Z_1Z_2-Z_3^2.\] For \(c>0\) set \[F_c(u,v)=\sqrt{|u|^4+|v|^4+c|u|^2|v|^2}.\] Writing \(s=|u|^2\) and \(t=|v|^2\) and differentiating directly gives, for every real \(r>0\), \[
 \frac{\partial^2 F_c}{\partial u\,\partial\bar u}(r,0)=1,
 \qquad
 \frac{\partial^2 F_c}{\partial u\,\partial\bar u}(0,r)=\frac c2.\] Claim 4.4 uses \(c=1\), giving the distinct limits \(1\) and \(1/2\). The actual pullback of the gradient norm in (4.5) is \[|\nabla f|\circ\iota
 =\sqrt{|u|^4+|v|^4+4|u|^2|v|^2}=F_4,\] giving limits \(1\) and \(2\). Thus neither Hessian has a continuous extension at the origin. Euclidean comparability in Claim 4.4 can be true while smooth orbifold extension fails. The transverse coefficients of the pullback of a smooth ambient Kähler form are \(O(r^2)\) on these axes, so adding the prescribed large multiple of that form cannot remove the jump. A partition of unity with one chart equal to one near the point is an allowed local choice in the displayed construction and retains it.
result:
For a suitable fixed chart, an actual orbifold potential is available: \[\sqrt{|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2+2|Z_3|^2}
 \quad\stackrel{\iota^*}{\longmapsto}\quad |u|^2+|v|^2.\] Adding \(|z|^2\) makes its pullback smooth and positive. This proves that the local existence assertion is not refuted. A replacement proof must nevertheless specify compatible potentials, justify their gluing, and verify the stated \(L^p\), \(p>1\), determinant condition on a resolution near the non-orbifold locus. Those global steps are not certified by the local replacement alone.

Theorem 4.3 is a substantive secondary result, and its explicit construction fails its claimed regularity and embedding invariance. The defect is therefore Major. It is not propagated indiscriminately to the Bogomolov–Gieseker theorem: Section 5 starts with a genuine orbifold metric away from a neighborhood of finitely many points and interpolates it with an ambient metric near those points. That construction is different from the gradient-norm formula in Theorem 4.3. The corresponding existence framework is also explicit in [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem~1.4 and Section~6]{CGN}].

Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: F_c=sqrt(|u|^4+|v|^4+c|u|^2|v|^2) has Levi_uu(r,0)=1 and Levi_uu(0,r)=c/2. Claim 4.4 uses c=1 and the actual gradient formula c=4; neither extends continuously at zero. Adding the redundant equation w gives sqrt(1+F4^2), whose potential ratio is unbounded and whose Levi_uu(r,0)=(2r^2+r^6)/(1+r^4)^(3/2) tends to zero instead of one.

problems.title: Incorrect mass normalization in the regularized Monge-Ampere equation
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: # Problem 3: the smoothing changes the total mass
claim: Recorded check: Incorrect mass normalization in the regularized Monge-Ampere equation
analysis: Equation (2.3), p. 5, has right-hand side \(c_\varepsilon\prod_i(|s_i|^2+\varepsilon^2)^{a_i}d\widehat V\), while p. 6 fixes \(c_\varepsilon=V_\varepsilon/V\). The hypotheses only imply \(\int\prod_i|s_i|^{2a_i}d\widehat V=V\). They do not imply the same identity after smoothing.

A compact threefold example makes the incompatibility strict. Let \(X=\mathbb P(1,1,1,2)\). Its unique singularity is \(\mathbb C^3/\{\pm1\}\) of type \(\tfrac12(1,1,1)\). Blowing up its vertex gives a smooth resolution with exceptional divisor \(E\simeq\mathbb P^2\) and normal bundle \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(-2)\). Its discrepancy is \(a=1/2\): adjunction gives \(K_{\widehat X}|_E=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(-1)\), whereas \(\pi^*K_X|_E\) is rationally trivial, so \(-2a=-1\). For the smooth positive volume form prescribed by the source, \[I_\varepsilon=\int_{\widehat X}\sqrt{|s|^2+\varepsilon^2}\,d\widehat V
 >\int_{\widehat X}|s|\,d\widehat V=V
 \qquad(\varepsilon>0).\] The printed right-hand side therefore has mass \(V_\varepsilon I_\varepsilon/V>V_\varepsilon\), while every left-hand side has mass \(V_\varepsilon\) by Stokes’ theorem. No smooth solution can satisfy that exact equation.
result: Replace the scalar by \[c_\varepsilon=\frac{V_\varepsilon}{I_\varepsilon}.\] Since \(a_i>-1\) and the divisors have simple normal crossings, dominated convergence gives \(I_\varepsilon\to V\). The corrected factors tend to one and remain bounded above and away from zero. The uniform \(L^p\) estimate for a suitable \(p>1\) and smooth convergence away from the exceptional divisor are unaffected. This is an isolated normalization repair; the later approximation on p. 19 already describes its coefficient simply as a normalizing constant. The example refutes the printed regularized equation with the printed coefficient, not existence of the canonical metric or the final theorem.

Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: I_epsilon=integral sqrt(|s|^2+epsilon^2)dVhat is strictly greater than V. The printed right-hand side has mass V_epsilon I_epsilon/V>V_epsilon, while the left-hand side has cohomological mass V_epsilon.

report: Abstract: The inspected source is Sun and Tzvetkov’s arXiv:2308.12758v3. The review checks the measure-transport argument, selected normal-form and pairing estimates, and the approximation appendix. One local defect is established: Proposition A.9 does not follow from Definition A.8 and is false with its unrestricted quantifiers. A smooth three-mode initial condition gives an exact counterexample. A uniform bound on the whole orbit restores the refinement assertion; such bounds are available from mass and energy conservation in the subsequent compact-set argument. No failure of the main quasi-invariance theorem is established. The supported assessment is Minor. Independent scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: Initial scientific review: M25-0416
Date: 29 October 2026

Title: Technical Verification of
Quasi-invariance of Gaussian measures for the 3d energy critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation
# Source and scope

Chenmin Sun and Nikolay Tzvetkov, Quasi-invariance of Gaussian measures for the 3d energy critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation, Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 78 (2025), 2305–2353, DOI https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70001. The reviewed file is the 49-page author preprint arXiv:2308.12758v3, dated 8 May 2025 [ST]. References to pages below use the PDF page number, which agrees with the printed numbering. Equality of this file with the journal version has not been established.

The central statement is equivalence of the Gaussian measure \(\mu_s\) and its image under the defocusing quintic NLS flow on \(\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3\), for every \(s\geq10\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\). The present checks cover the definitions and quantifiers, the finite-dimensional transport and compact-limit argument, selected first- and second-generation estimates, the dangerous cross-generation pairing cancellations, and selected assertions in Appendix A. Text reading and proof verification are distinguished: the review does not independently reconstruct every lattice estimate, every case in Section 8, or the complete external global well-posedness proof. The irrational-torus extension is outside the verified scope.
# Definitions relevant to the finding

Equation reference: eq:nls, eq:energy. Write \(u(t)=\Phi(t)\phi\) for the smooth solution of \[
 i\partial_tu+\Delta u=|u|^4u,\qquad u(0)=\phi.\] Use normalized Haar measure, so that \(\|u\|_{H^1}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+|k|^2)|\widehat u(k)|^2\). The conserved mass and energy are \[
 M[u]=\|u\|_2^2,\qquad
 H[u]=\tfrac12\|\nabla u\|_2^2+\tfrac16\|u\|_6^6.\] Changing to unnormalized Lebesgue measure multiplies all squared norms and the calculations below by \((2\pi)^3\) and does not change the argument.

Equation reference: eq:partition. Definition A.8 on p. 44, paraphrased with its quantifiers retained, calls a finite partition \(-T=\tau_0<\cdots<\tau_m=T\) an \((A,\delta)\)-partition with respect to \(\phi\) if \(A>\delta>0\) and \[
 \|\Phi(\tau_{j-1})\phi\|_{H^1}\leq A,\qquad
 \|\Phi(t)\phi\|_{Z([\tau_{j-1},\tau_j])}<\delta
 \quad(1\leq j\leq m).\] The first bound is imposed at the existing left endpoints, not at every time. The critical \(Z\) norm is defined on p. 38. It decreases upon restriction to a subinterval. On intervals of length less than one it is a sum of two time-\(L^p\) Besov norms, with finite \(p=4.1\) and \(p=100\). Consequently, for a smooth trajectory, \(\|u\|_{Z([-T,T])}\to0\) as \(T\downarrow0\).
# A local defect in the refinement assertion

Problem 1 (An endpoint bound need not survive refinement).  Proposition A.9 (p. 44) asserts that every refinement of an \((A,\delta)\)-partition with respect to \(\phi\) is again an \((A,\delta)\)-partition with the same constants. This statement is false under Definition A.8.
## Exact counterexample

Equation reference: eq:phi, eq:coefficients, eq:derivative. Take the smooth initial condition \[
 \phi(x)=1+e^{ix_1}-i e^{2ix_1},\qquad A=\sqrt8,\qquad
 \delta=A/2.\] Its only nonzero Fourier coefficients are \(a_0=1\), \(a_1=1\) and \(a_2=-i\), where the index denotes \((k,0,0)\). Thus \(\|\phi\|_{H^1}^2=1+2+5=8\). Let \(F_k\) be the coefficients of \(|\phi|^4\phi
=\phi^3\overline{\phi}^{\,2}\). Exact multiplication gives \[
 F_0=31+8i,\qquad F_1=31-16i,\qquad F_2=8-31i.\] The remaining coefficients do not enter the derivative at zero, because \(a_k=0\) there. Equation [eq:nls] (#eq:nls) implies \(a'_k=-i(k^2a_k+F_k)\); hence \[\begin{aligned}
 \left.\frac{d}{dt}\|u(t)\|_{H^1}^2\right|_{t=0}
 &=2\operatorname{Im}\sum_k(1+k^2)\overline{a_k}F_k \notag\\
 &=2\operatorname{Im}\bigl[(31+8i)+2(31-16i)+5i(8-31i)\bigr]
 =32. \end{aligned}\] The calculation has been reproduced by exact Gaussian-integer convolution and a separate SymPy Laurent-polynomial expansion; the retained output gives both methods and every coefficient (Appendix 6 (#app:evidence)). As consistency checks, \(M[\phi]=3\), \(\|\nabla\phi\|_2^2=5\), \(\|\phi\|_6^6=93\) and \(H[\phi]=18\). At zero the mass derivative is zero, while the kinetic and potential energy derivatives are \(16\) and \(-16\).

By smooth local existence, \(f(t)=\|\Phi(t)\phi\|_{H^1}^2\) is continuously differentiable near zero. Equation [eq:derivative] (#eq:derivative) allows \(T>0\) to be chosen so small that \(f'(t)>0\) throughout \([-T,T]\). Shrink it further so that \(T<1/2\) and \(\|u\|_{Z([-T,T])}<\delta\). Then \[\|u(-T)\|_{H^1}<A=\|u(0)\|_{H^1}
       <\|u(T/2)\|_{H^1}.\] The one-interval partition \(\{[-T,T]\}\) satisfies every condition in [eq:partition] (#eq:partition). Its refinement at \(T/2\) fails the endpoint condition on the second interval. This is an analytic existence argument for sufficiently small \(T\), not a numerical trajectory or an estimate of a particular positive time.
## Alternative readings and correction

The displayed source image confirms that Definition A.8 has no orbit-wide \(H^1\) hypothesis. The small-time construction is admissible: the later restriction \(T\geq1\) in Proposition A.12 is not part of Definition A.8 or Proposition A.9. An implicit conserved \(H^1\) norm cannot resolve the discrepancy; [eq:derivative] (#eq:derivative) directly excludes it.

Equation reference: eq:globalbound. A valid corrected statement is the following: if [eq:partition] (#eq:partition) holds and, in addition, \[
 \sup_{|t|\leq T}\|\Phi(t)\phi\|_{H^1}\leq A,\] then every refinement is an \((A,\delta)\)-partition. Every new endpoint satisfies [eq:globalbound] (#eq:globalbound), and restriction monotonicity preserves the strict \(Z\) bound. Equivalently, Definition A.8 can impose the supremum bound on each interval.
## Impact

Equation reference: eq:orbit. The common-refinement construction in Proposition A.12, Step 1 (pp. 45–46), cites A.9. This establishes an actual connection to the approximation argument, but does not by itself refute that argument in its application. Conservation and the defocusing sign give \[
 \|\Phi(t)\phi\|_{H^1}^2\leq M[\phi]+2H[\phi].\] For a compact \(K\subset H^1\), the right-hand side has a finite uniform supremum. Choosing the partition constant above its square root gives exactly the additional premise needed for common refinement. On an \(H^1\) ball of radius \(R\), the same bound is a function of \(R\), since \(H^1(\mathbb T^3)\) embeds into \(L^6\). Thus an arbitrary endpoint constant must be replaced by a uniform orbit constant; it need not equal the initial radius.

The demonstrated failure concerns the unrestricted constant-preserving assertion A.9. The source’s subsequent proof already invokes energy-based orbit control; the refinement mechanism survives with that premise stated accurately. No failure of the uniform approximation conclusions or Theorem 1.1 has been established. This supports Minor: a local defect without demonstrated central damage. The classification does not follow merely from the appendix location or the brevity of the correction. No author adoption or earlier identification of this particular issue is known from the inspected material.
# Checks supporting the main proof structure
These checks bound the conclusion of the report and record counterevidence against additional objections.
## Gaussian support and transport

The series defining \(\mu_s\) has support in \(H^\sigma\) for \(\sigma<s-\tfrac32\), as follows by summing \(\langle k\rangle^{2\sigma}/(1+|k|^{2s})\). The covariance convention using \(\langle k\rangle^{-2s}\) is equivalent: the covariance ratio is \(1+O(|k|^{-2})\), and its squared deviations are summable in three dimensions. For \(F(t)=\rho_{s,N}(\Phi_N(t)A)\), the differential estimate used in Lemma 3.3 (pp. 10–12) has the form \[|F'(t)|\leq C p^\beta F(t)^{1-1/p},\qquad \beta<1.\] It implies \(F(t)^{1/p}\leq F(0)^{1/p}+C|t|p^{\beta-1}\). Sending \(p\) to infinity handles \(F(0)=0\); taking \(p\) comparable to \(\log(1/F(0))\) handles small positive masses and gives \(F(t)\leq C_\varepsilon F(0)^{1-\varepsilon}\). The bounded larger-mass case is absorbed in the constant.

Uniform convergence on compact sets, applied also to the inverse flow, gives the inclusion needed on p. 12: \(\Phi(t)K\subset\Phi_N(t)(K+B_\varepsilon)\). Outer regularity passes the estimate to \(K\); inner regularity and a countable union of bounded balls extend it to Borel sets in the Sobolev support. Repeating at \(-t\) gives equivalence of measures. The point-evaluation corollary uses \(\sigma>3/2\) and a nondegenerate Gaussian marginal, and the \(L^1\) isometry uses invertibility and preservation of total variation. These consequences require no extra assertion of a smooth density.
## Normal forms, pairings and interpolation
The sign in (2.4) and the correction in (2.8)–(2.10) agree with \(\partial_t e^{-it\Omega}=-i\Omega e^{-it\Omega}\). The resonance cutoff removes the apparent singularity at \(\Omega=0\).

For the dangerous opposite-sign cross-generation pair in Section 7, the substitution \[(q_3,q_2,q_5,q_4)=(p_2,p_3,p_4,p_5),\qquad q_1=k_1,\] identifies both constraints and cutoffs. The remaining high-frequency factor is \[\chi_N(k_1)^2|w_{k_2}|^2-
 \chi_N(k_2)^2|w_{k_1}|^2.\] The separated leading term is a real coefficient times a squared modulus, so its imaginary part vanishes. Lemmas 7.4 and 7.5 retain the needed low-frequency gain.

An apparent interpolation objection to (7.11) was checked and rejected. Write \(\sigma=s-\tfrac32-\varepsilon\), \(a=1+2\varepsilon\) and \(d=1-2\theta>0\). Even the coarse endpoints \(K^a\) and \(pK^{-d}\) interpolate to \(p^\beta K^{-d/2}\) for \(\beta=1-d/[2(a+d)]<1\), which is summable. Retaining the low-frequency factor \(L_*^2\) gives the stronger endpoint \(pK^{-1}\), because \(L_*^2\prod_j L_j^{3/2-\sigma}\leq1\) when \(\sigma>7/2\). Interpolation with \(\beta=1-2\theta/(a+1)\) then recovers the printed exponent \(-1+2\theta\). This provides counterevidence to treating the compressed interpolation as a defect.

Selected Section 8 exponents also admit simultaneous choices. For example, \(\sigma=s-1.51\), \(\delta_0=0.65\), \(\theta=0.32\) and \(\alpha=0.98\) satisfy \(\theta<\delta_0/2<1/3\) and make the checked exponents \(2(s-1-\sigma)-\theta(\sigma-\tfrac72)\) and \(2s+\tfrac32-(2+\alpha)\sigma\) negative for every \(s\geq10\). This verifies these inequalities, not the entire case analysis.
# Conclusion

One substantive local issue is established in the reviewed preprint. The strengthened refinement statement is proved above. The review does not claim that every step of a revised approximation proof has been independently reconstructed, nor that the journal version contains the same issue.

 \delta=A/2.\] Its only nonzero Fourier coefficients are \(a_0=1\), \(a_1=1\) and \(a_2=-i\), where the index denotes \((k,0,0)\). Thus \(\|\phi\|_{H^1}^2=1+2+5=8\). Let \(F_k\) be the coefficients of \(|\phi|^4\phi
=\phi^3\overline{\phi}^{\,2}\). Exact multiplication gives \[
 F_0=31+8i,\qquad F_1=31-16i,\qquad F_2=8-31i.\] The remaining coefficients do not enter the derivative at zero, because \(a_k=0\) there. Equation [eq:nls] (#eq:nls) implies \(a'_k=-i(k^2a_k+F_k)\); hence \[\begin{aligned}
 \left.\frac{d}{dt}\|u(t)\|_{H^1}^2\right|_{t=0}
 &=2\operatorname{Im}\sum_k(1+k^2)\overline{a_k}F_k \notag\\
 &=2\operatorname{Im}\bigl[(31+8i)+2(31-16i)+5i(8-31i)\bigr]
 =32. \end{aligned}\] The calculation has been reproduced by exact Gaussian-integer convolution and a separate SymPy Laurent-polynomial expansion; the retained output gives both methods and every coefficient (Appendix 6 (#app:evidence)). As consistency checks, \(M[\phi]=3\), \(\|\nabla\phi\|_2^2=5\), \(\|\phi\|_6^6=93\) and \(H[\phi]=18\). At zero the mass derivative is zero, while the kinetic and potential energy derivatives are \(16\) and \(-16\).

By smooth local existence, \(f(t)=\|\Phi(t)\phi\|_{H^1}^2\) is continuously differentiable near zero. Equation [eq:derivative] (#eq:derivative) allows \(T>0\) to be chosen so small that \(f'(t)>0\) throughout \([-T,T]\). Shrink it further so that \(T<1/2\) and \(\|u\|_{Z([-T,T])}<\delta\). Then \[\|u(-T)\|_{H^1}<A=\|u(0)\|_{H^1}
       <\|u(T/2)\|_{H^1}.\] The one-interval partition \(\{[-T,T]\}\) satisfies every condition in [eq:partition] (#eq:partition). Its refinement at \(T/2\) fails the endpoint condition on the second interval. This is an analytic existence argument for sufficiently small \(T\), not a numerical trajectory or an estimate of a particular positive time.

Equation reference: eq:orbit. The common-refinement construction in Proposition A.12, Step 1 (pp. 45–46), cites A.9. This establishes an actual connection to the approximation argument, but does not by itself refute that argument in its application. Conservation and the defocusing sign give \[
 \|\Phi(t)\phi\|_{H^1}^2\leq M[\phi]+2H[\phi].\] For a compact \(K\subset H^1\), the right-hand side has a finite uniform supremum. Choosing the partition constant above its square root gives exactly the additional premise needed for common refinement. On an \(H^1\) ball of radius \(R\), the same bound is a function of \(R\), since \(H^1(\mathbb T^3)\) embeds into \(L^6\). Thus an arbitrary endpoint constant must be replaced by a uniform orbit constant; it need not equal the initial radius.

The demonstrated failure concerns the unrestricted constant-preserving assertion A.9. The source’s subsequent proof already invokes energy-based orbit control; the refinement mechanism survives with that premise stated accurately. No failure of the uniform approximation conclusions or Theorem 1.1 has been established. This supports Minor: a local defect without demonstrated central damage. The classification does not follow merely from the appendix location or the brevity of the correction. No author adoption or earlier identification of this particular issue is known from the inspected material.
result: The displayed source image confirms that Definition A.8 has no orbit-wide \(H^1\) hypothesis. The small-time construction is admissible: the later restriction \(T\geq1\) in Proposition A.12 is not part of Definition A.8 or Proposition A.9. An implicit conserved \(H^1\) norm cannot resolve the discrepancy; [eq:derivative] (#eq:derivative) directly excludes it.

Equation reference: eq:globalbound. A valid corrected statement is the following: if [eq:partition] (#eq:partition) holds and, in addition, \[
 \sup_{|t|\leq T}\|\Phi(t)\phi\|_{H^1}\leq A,\] then every refinement is an \((A,\delta)\)-partition. Every new endpoint satisfies [eq:globalbound] (#eq:globalbound), and restriction monotonicity preserves the strict \(Z\) bound. Equivalently, Definition A.8 can impose the supremum bound on each interval.
Result: Refutes the unrestricted local refinement statement in the acquired preprint.
Impact. Dependency: A.12 Step1 pp45-46 cites A.9 for common refinement; p47 uses a common partition for higher regularity.

Impact. Bounded conclusion: Local claim false. Since M+2H uniformly bounds the orbit and is bounded on compact H1 families, that application can satisfy the stronger premise independently. No demonstrated central damage.
Impact. Severity reason: Supported local defect without demonstrated failure of a core conclusion; appendix location and repair length are not the basis for severity.

Title: Technical Verification of
The Brownian loop measure on Riemann surfaces and applications to length spectra
# Identity, conventions and scope

Yilin Wang and Yuhao Xue, The Brownian loop measure on Riemann surfaces and applications to length spectra, Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 78 (2025), 2123–2148, DOI https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70003. The acquired 27-page source is arXiv:2406.09108v3, submitted on 2 October 2025 and dated 3 October 2025 in the PDF [WX]. It postdates the recorded journal online publication. The version metadata mentions a correction to Corollary 1.7; neither the earlier text nor the publisher PDF was compared here. No equivalence with the journal version is asserted. Page references below are PDF pages, matching the printed numbering.

The paper retains loop orientation. Its Brownian generator is \(\Delta\), so the plane kernel is \((4\pi t)^{-1}\exp(-|z-w|^2/(4t))\) and the surface quadratic variation is \(4t\). The loop measure integrates rooted bridges against \(dt/t\) and area before forgetting the root and time parametrization. Essential hyperbolic classes exclude trivial and cusp classes; \(m(\gamma)\) is the positive iteration number.

All source text was read, including the bibliography, but this does not mean that every cited theorem was independently proved or that the bibliography’s external works were read. The checks below concern the displayed arguments, their domains and selected consequences. The full external proofs of the prime geodesic theorem, Selberg trace formula, Brownian background and Grunsky inequality remain dependencies. The two source figures are explanatory geometric diagrams, not experimental results.
# Central loop-mass identities
## Hyperbolic classes

In Lemmas 3.1–3.2 (pp. 10–12), write a hyperbolic element as \(h_0=\delta^m\), with \(\delta\) primitive and \(L=\ell(\gamma)>0\). Its centralizer is generated by \(\delta\). The corresponding fundamental strip has logarithmic height \(L/m\), so unfolding over the conjugacy class contributes exactly one factor \(1/m\).

Equation reference: eq:orbital, eq:hyperbolic. An independent evaluation of the orbital integral avoids relying on the paper’s Abel-transform shortcut. With \(\theta=x/y\), \[\cosh d(z,e^Lz)=\cosh L+2\sinh^2(L/2)\theta^2.\] Substitution in the nonnegative heat-kernel integral, Tonelli’s theorem and the elementary angular integral give \[
 O_\gamma(t)=
 \frac{L}{4m\sqrt{\pi t}\sinh(L/2)}
       e^{-t/4-L^2/(4t)}.\] The time integral \[\int_0^\infty t^{-3/2}e^{-t/4-L^2/(4t)}\,dt
     =\frac{2\sqrt\pi}{L}e^{-L/2}\] therefore yields \[
 \mu_X(C_X(\gamma))=\frac{1}{m(e^L-1)}.\] The antiderivative and both signs in (3.6) also passed exact symbolic checks. No additional orientation factor occurs.

Two qualifications explain compressed proof wording without changing this calculation. The fundamental-domain equality on p. 11 needs invariance under the centralizer; the actual integrand \(p_{\mathbb H}(z,h_0z;t)\) has that invariance because the heat kernel is isometry invariant and \(\delta\) commutes with \(h_0\). On p. 10 a local injectivity radius at the fixed point suffices; a globally positive injectivity radius is unnecessary on cusped surfaces. Neither qualification establishes a substantive defect in the stated loop-mass result.
## Flat tori and punctures

Equation reference: eq:torus. For a nonzero lattice displacement \(\tau\) on a flat torus of area \(A\), Lemma 3.3 (p. 13) gives directly \[
 \frac{A}{4\pi}\int_0^\infty t^{-2}e^{-|\tau|^2/(4t)}\,dt
       =\frac{A}{\pi|\tau|^2}.\] Thus the \(m\)-fold class of a primitive geodesic of length \(\ell\) has mass \(A/(\pi m^2\ell^2)\). There is no further \(1/m\): a torus lattice conjugacy class is a single displacement.

For the closed polar removal in Corollary 4.1, loops hitting the removed set have zero measure. The root set also has zero area; this holds for general polar sets, not merely countable ones. A compact loop trace avoiding a closed removed set lies in a positive-distance exhaustion, which supports the monotone-limit argument. The disjoint decomposition into free homotopy classes then gives Theorems 4.2 and 4.3.

The primitive qualification is also consistent. If \(\gamma'=(\delta')^n\) maps to \(\gamma\) upon filling punctures, then \(\gamma\) is an \(n\)th power in the original fundamental group, up to conjugacy. Its cyclic centralizer implies \(n\mid m(\gamma)\). In particular, a class mapping to primitive \(\gamma\) is primitive. Injectivity of the puncture-filling homomorphism is not required.
# Annular consequences and boundary checks
# Length sums and the determinant

For Corollary 4.9 (pp. 17–18), the cited finite-type infinite-area counting asymptotic has exponent \(\delta<1\). Combining this with [eq:hyperbolic] (#eq:hyperbolic) makes the long primitive sum convergent; higher iterations decay faster. Elementary annular and punctured-disc cases are treated separately. This verifies the consequence conditional on the quoted counting and spectral inputs.

For Proposition 4.11 (pp. 19–22), put \[R(L)=N_X(L)-\widetilde{\operatorname{Li}}(e^L),\qquad w(L)=\frac{1}{e^L-1}.\] The quoted prime-geodesic remainder gives \(R(L)=O_X(e^{(1-\varepsilon)L})\) for some \(\varepsilon>0\). Consequently \(wR\to0\) and \(w'R\) is integrable at infinity. Near zero the measures vanish below the fixed surface’s systole and the cutoff \(\log2\). Integration by parts therefore justifies the renormalized Stieltjes integral. This is a cancellation statement, not the subtraction of two separately finite totals. The nonprimitive sum converges directly.

The normalization used on p. 21 reduces to \[\frac{e^{-t/4}}{\sqrt{4\pi t}}
 \int_0^\infty2\cosh(L/2)e^{-L^2/(4t)}\,dL=1.\] Completing the square proves the identity. Above \(\log2\), the difference of the comparison densities is \(e^L/L-2\sinh L/L=e^{-L}/L\); the cutoff creates no atom because \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Li}}(2)=0\). These observations verify the signs of the three constant terms on p. 22.

Retained high-precision numerical integrations of both displayed forms of \(C_2\), using stable complementary-error-function expressions, give \[C_2=0.9380116642341289954\ldots,\qquad
 C=C_2-\gamma=0.3607959993325961348\ldots.\] Calculations at two precision settings support the printed \(0.9380\) and \(0.3608\). They are numerical diagnostics, not a certified interval-error proof or a numerical evaluation of the determinant for a particular surface.
# Conclusion and evidence
No substantive problem was established within the declared checks.

Abstract: The reviewed source is arXiv:2403.12887v2. Two local statements have incorrect orientations: the characteristic velocity in Proposition 3.2 and the coupling order in the first limit of Lemma 2.2. Explicit one-dimensional examples satisfy the stated hypotheses and contradict the printed formulas. The corresponding corrections are checked, and their implications are separated from the main convergence argument. Title: Technical Verification of
Understanding the training of infinitely deep and wide ResNets with Conditional Optimal Transport
# Identity and scope

Raphaël Barboni, Gabriel Peyré and François-Xavier Vialard, Understanding the training of infinitely deep and wide ResNets with conditional optimal transport, Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 78 (2025), 2149–2205, DOI https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70004. The acquired source is the 49-page preprint arXiv:2403.12887v2, dated 21 July 2025 [BPV]. No identity with the publisher’s version of record was established. All page references below refer to the acquired PDF and agree with its printed numbering.

All source text was read, including the bibliography. This does not mean that every proof or cited external work was independently verified. The checks concentrate on the conditional transport conventions, the gradient-flow definition, the two statements below, the assumptions separating existence and uniqueness, and the kernel criterion for local convergence. No author-code execution or numerical training experiment is claimed.

Write \(s\in[0,1]\) for depth and \(t\) for optimization time. Measures \(\mu\in\mathcal P^{\mathrm{Leb}}_2([0,1]	imes\Omega)\) have fixed first marginal \(ds\), and the conditional transport metric is \[d(\mu,
u)^2=\int_0^1 W_2(\mu(\cdot\mid s),
u(\cdot\mid s))^2\,ds.\] The ordered coupling convention on p. 9 assigns the first weight marginal to the first measure. We use the risk normalization in (5), \(L(\mu)=\mathbb E_{x,y}\ell(x_\mu(1),y)\), and denote the positive first variation in (17) by \(G_\mu=
abla L[\mu]\). Definition 3.2 explicitly specifies velocity \(v_t=-G_{\mu_t}\).
# Problem 1: the characteristic field has the wrong sign
## Claim and hypotheses

Proposition 3.2 (p. 20) assumes that \(\phi\) is twice continuously differentiable and satisfies Assumptions 1–3. For a gradient flow \((\mu_t)_{t\geq0}\), it sets \[V_t(s,\omega)=(0,G_{\mu_t}(s,\omega)),\qquad
 \dot X_t=V_t\circ X_t,\quad X_0=\operatorname{Id},\] and asserts \(\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0\). The sign is confirmed by the actual source image; it conflicts with the continuity equation in Definition 3.2.
## Check and result

Take \(d=p=1\), \(\Omega=\mathbb R\), \(\phi(\omega,x)=\omega\), data distribution \(\delta_{(0,0)}\), and loss \(\ell(z,y)=\tfrac12(z-y)^2\). The feature map is smooth, has the required growth, and satisfies all three local Lipschitz and derivative assumptions. The data distribution is compactly supported. Set \[a(t)=e^{-t},\qquad \mu_t=ds\otimes\delta_{a(t)}.\] The forward and adjoint equations give, for every \(s\in[0,1]\), \[x_{\mu_t}(s)=s e^{-t},\qquad
 p_{\mu_t}(s)=e^{-t},\qquad G_{\mu_t}(s,\omega)=e^{-t}.\] This curve is absolutely continuous in \(d\), has finite second moment, and its actual velocity is \(a'(t)=-e^{-t}=-G_{\mu_t}\). It therefore is a gradient flow in the stated sense, for all \(t\geq0\).

The positive field prescribed by Proposition 3.2 instead sends the initial weight \(1\) to \[1+\int_0^t e^{-r}\,dr=2-e^{-t}.\] Thus its pushforward is \(ds\otimes\delta_{2-e^{-t}}\), and \[d\bigl((X_t)_\#\mu_0,\mu_t\bigr)=2(1-e^{-t})>0
 \quad(t>0).\] At \(t=\log2\) the distance is exactly \(1\). This is a counterexample to the printed representation, with no limiting argument or simulation.
## Correction, counterevidence and impact

The required field is \(V_t=(0,-G_{\mu_t})\). In the example its flow is \[X_t(s,\omega)=(s,\omega-1+e^{-t}),\] which has exactly the required pushforward. In general this sign matches the actual continuity equation, so the characteristic representation uses the negative field under the proposition’s regularity assumptions.

The source itself supplies counterevidence to a more serious interpretation. Definition 3.2 uses the minus sign, and Part 2 of Theorem 3.1 (p. 28) explicitly concludes \(v_t=-G_{\mu_t}\) from the energy-dissipation identity. The representation is cited for finite-width consistency and in Appendix A, but the latter’s support and uniqueness estimates use norms and remain compatible with the negative field. The example does not refute the local convergence theorem.

The finding is therefore Minor: an auxiliary identity is false as printed, while failure of a central conclusion has not been established. This classification is based on the demonstrated mathematical impact. The corrected example and sign are verified; no exhaustive reconstruction of the external characteristic-flow theorem or author adoption of this correction is claimed.
# Problem 2: reversed coupling order in Lemma 2.2
## Claim and hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:printed. The first assertion of Lemma 2.2 (p. 15) takes \(\gamma_t^h\in\Pi_o^{\mathrm{Leb}}(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)\) and claims \[
 \left(\pi^1,\pi^2,\frac{\pi^3-\pi^2}{h}\right)_\#\gamma_t^h
 \longrightarrow (\pi^1,\pi^2,v_t)_\#\mu_t
 \quad\hbox{in }W_2 .\] Here \(v_t\) is the minimal tangent field from Proposition 2.4. The stated order of the measures and the displayed signs were checked on the source images.
## Check and result

Let \(I=(0,1)\), \(\Omega=\mathbb R\), and \(\mu_t=ds\otimes\delta_t\). Then \(d(\mu_t,\mu_u)=|t-u|\); the curve satisfies all the lemma’s assumptions and \(v_t=1\). For every interior \(t\) and sufficiently small nonzero \(h\), the unique declared conditional optimal coupling is \[\gamma_t^h=ds\otimes\delta_{(t+h,t)}.\] The left side of [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) is consequently \(ds\otimes\delta_{(t+h,-1)}\), whereas the proposed limit is \(ds\otimes\delta_{(t,1)}\). Their ordinary \(W_2\) distance in the stated product space equals \[\sqrt{h^2+4}\longrightarrow 2.\] The claimed convergence fails at every such \(t\), so the almost-everywhere qualification does not remove the counterexample.
## Correction, counterevidence and impact

With the displayed pushforward unchanged, the coupling must be chosen in \(\Pi_o^{\mathrm{Leb}}(\mu_t,\mu_{t+h})\). For this example the corrected pushforward is exactly \(ds\otimes\delta_{(t,1)}\). Alternatively, keeping the printed coupling order requires the map \((\pi^1,\pi^3,(\pi^2-\pi^3)/h)\).

The proof on p. 16 says that the first marginal is \(\mu_t\) and uses the forward difference \(\varphi(\omega')-\varphi(\omega)\). Those steps agree with the corrected ordering. Moreover, the lemma’s second assertion, \[d\bigl(\mu_{t+h},(\operatorname{Id}+h(0,v_t))_\#\mu_t\bigr)=o(|h|),\] is exact in the translation example. This is the approximation used in the subsequent differentiation arguments. Thus the first display is false, but this example supplies no counterexample to the chain rule or the principal convergence result.

The finding is Minor. The correction is checked exactly in the example and matches the proof’s intended marginal convention. A complete independent proof of the cited general tangent-space theorem is outside this review. Journal correspondence and author adoption remain unverified.
# Checks of the main framework
## Well-posedness and the descent convention

Assumption 1 makes the forward NODE a Carathéodory equation with depth-integrable Lipschitz and growth bounds controlled by the second moment. Assumptions 2–3 support the local Lipschitz flow and adjoint estimates. With the stated risk convention, the chain rule and energy-dissipation identity give \[L'(\mu_t)=-\|G_{\mu_t}\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}^2.\] Conversely the maximal-slope argument on p. 28 gives \[-\langle v_t,G_{\mu_t}\rangle
 \geq \tfrac12\bigl(\|v_t\|^2+\|G_{\mu_t}\|^2\bigr),\] which forces \(v_t=-G_{\mu_t}\). This checks the core sign against Problem 1.

The hypotheses of Theorems 3.2–3.4 are distinct. The existence argument uses Assumption A with \(1\leq\alpha<2\); a uniform second-moment bound then controls the \(\alpha\)-moment tails needed in the narrow-limit argument. Uniqueness uses Assumption B on second derivatives and local Lipschitz continuity of the loss gradient. The finite-time stability estimate adds Assumption C and the quadratic loss. The general SHL architecture does not automatically satisfy all these global assumptions.

Appendix A treats compactly supported SHL initial measures. Its continuation argument can use a bound independent of an assumed global solution: along any local descent curve, \[d(\mu_t,\mu_0)\leq\sqrt{T L(\mu_0)},\qquad
 \mathcal E_2(\mu_t)\leq
 \bigl(\sqrt{\mathcal E_2(\mu_0)}+\sqrt{T L(\mu_0)}\bigr)^2
 \quad(0\leq t\leq T).\] These follow from energy dissipation and Cauchy–Schwarz. Together with the linear-growth characteristic estimate they supply a finite-time support bound for the cutoff construction. The apparent use of a full-orbit bound before existence therefore does not by itself establish an existence counterexample. The external minimizing-movement and transport theorems remain dependencies.
## Local convergence and its scope

For a curve of maximal slope satisfying \(|\nabla L|^2\geq mL\) in a ball of radius \(R\), its length before a first exit is at most \(2\sqrt{L(\mu_0)/m}\). The strict condition \(L(\mu_0)<mR^2/4\) thus prevents exit, gives \(L(\mu_t)\leq e^{-mt}L(\mu_0)\), and makes the tail length finite. This verifies the radius mechanism in Theorem 4.1, conditional on existence for the time interval in question.

For the normalization (5), the feature Gram matrix is positive semidefinite and the calculation on pp. 35–36 gives \[|\nabla L|^2
 =N^{-2}\int_0^1 p_\mu(s)^\top K_\mu(s)p_\mu(s)\,ds,\qquad
 \|p_\mu(s)\|^2\geq 2N e^{-C} L(\mu).\] The kernel lower bound therefore gives (31). The local Lipschitz estimate in Proposition 4.2 preserves half the initial eigenvalue integral \(\lambda_0\) on a ball of radius \(\min\{1,c(\mathcal E_2(\mu_0))\lambda_0/N\}\). Combining this with \(m\) proportional to \(\lambda_0/N\) explains the \(N^{-3}\lambda_0^3\) threshold in Theorem 4.2. The displayed risk on p. 35 has an extra factor \(1/2\) relative to (5), and the initial-loss value on p. 42 omits the half in its defined quadratic loss. The checks here use the explicit definition (5); these local normalization inconsistencies do not provide a further counterexample to the stated qualitative convergence criterion.

The theorem requires a positive initial Gram bound and sufficiently small initial risk, and concerns an existing gradient flow. The smooth SHL assumptions are not a well-posedness theorem for ReLU. Finite-feature conclusions use convergence in \(W_2\) and openness of the initialization conditions; no unconditional guarantee for arbitrary random initialization or discrete training is inferred. In Proposition 4.5, lifting makes the initial output in the target coordinates zero, while the rescaling increases the loss’s PL constant by \(\alpha^2\). This verifies the stated large-scaling mechanism when its Gram and smoothness assumptions hold.

Equation reference: eq:printed. The first assertion of Lemma 2.2 (p. 15) takes \(\gamma_t^h\in\Pi_o^{\mathrm{Leb}}(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)\) and claims \[
 \left(\pi^1,\pi^2,\frac{\pi^3-\pi^2}{h}\right)_\#\gamma_t^h
 \longrightarrow (\pi^1,\pi^2,v_t)_\#\mu_t
 \quad\hbox{in }W_2 .\] Here \(v_t\) is the minimal tangent field from Proposition 2.4. The stated order of the measures and the displayed signs were checked on the source images.
I=(0,1),Omega=R,mu_t=ds tensor delta_t; COT distance|t-u|,locally absolutely continuous, unique minimal tangent v_t=1.
analysis: Let \(I=(0,1)\), \(\Omega=\mathbb R\), and \(\mu_t=ds\otimes\delta_t\). Then \(d(\mu_t,\mu_u)=|t-u|\); the curve satisfies all the lemma’s assumptions and \(v_t=1\). For every interior \(t\) and sufficiently small nonzero \(h\), the unique declared conditional optimal coupling is \[\gamma_t^h=ds\otimes\delta_{(t+h,t)}.\] The left side of [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) is consequently \(ds\otimes\delta_{(t+h,-1)}\), whereas the proposed limit is \(ds\otimes\delta_{(t,1)}\). Their ordinary \(W_2\) distance in the stated product space equals \[\sqrt{h^2+4}\longrightarrow 2.\] The claimed convergence fails at every such \(t\), so the almost-everywhere qualification does not remove the counterexample.

With the displayed pushforward unchanged, the coupling must be chosen in \(\Pi_o^{\mathrm{Leb}}(\mu_t,\mu_{t+h})\). For this example the corrected pushforward is exactly \(ds\otimes\delta_{(t,1)}\). Alternatively, keeping the printed coupling order requires the map \((\pi^1,\pi^3,(\pi^2-\pi^3)/h)\).

The proof on p. 16 says that the first marginal is \(\mu_t\) and uses the forward difference \(\varphi(\omega')-\varphi(\omega)\). Those steps agree with the corrected ordering. Moreover, the lemma’s second assertion, \[d\bigl(\mu_{t+h},(\operatorname{Id}+h(0,v_t))_\#\mu_t\bigr)=o(|h|),\] is exact in the translation example. This is the approximation used in the subsequent differentiation arguments. Thus the first display is false, but this example supplies no counterexample to the chain rule or the principal convergence result.

The finding is Minor. The correction is checked exactly in the example and matches the proof’s intended marginal convention. A complete independent proof of the cited general tangent-space theorem is outside this review. Journal correspondence and author adoption remain unverified.
result: Impact: False local first-order limit as printed; corrected ordering directly resolves the example and matches the proof's convention. Minor; not a central theorem counterexample.

report: Abstract: The acquired source is arXiv:2402.18983v3. Its critical free-energy formula uses an inconsistent matrix-size scaling in the Tracy–Widom argument. Its precritical characteristic-polynomial prefactor also disagrees with the stated free-energy expansion. Both discrepancies are established by exact transformations, with admissible parameter examples. A separate Laurent calculation finds an uncancelled pole in the displayed refined Riemann–Hilbert construction. The diagonal coefficient used for the fixed-phase free energy nevertheless agrees with the claimed expression. The assessment is Major at these stated scopes; no rejection of all results is inferred. Scientific adjudication and independent acceptance remain pending.
