Title: Technical Verification of
Free energy expansions of a conditional GinUE and large deviations of the smallest eigenvalue of the LUE
# Source, conventions and scope

Sung-Soo Byun, Seong-Mi Seo and Meng Yang, Free energy expansions of a conditional GinUE and large deviations of the smallest eigenvalue of the LUE, Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 78 (2025), 2247–2304, DOI https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70005. The reviewed document is the 43-page preprint arXiv:2402.18983v3 [BSY], submitted on 15 May 2025 and internally dated 16 May. Equality with the publisher’s version was not established. All source page and equation references below concern this acquired version; PDF and printed page numbers agree.

All 43 pages of source text were read. Selected formulas, proofs and boundary cases were checked in detail, with actual source-image inspection for the decisive evidence. Reading the bibliography does not constitute reading its external works. No author code or empirical simulation is used as a substitute for a mathematical argument.

The potential is \(Q(z)=|z|^2-2c\log|z-a|\), with \(c>0\), and \(dA=d^2z/\pi\). Rotation permits \(a\geq0\). Write \[b=\sqrt{c+1}-\sqrt c.\] The strict precritical phase is \(a>b\); the postcritical phase is \(a<b\). Critical scaling requires a separate argument. We write \(n\) for the GinUE particle number and \(m\) for the LUE matrix dimension whenever both occur. This distinction is essential.
# Problem 1: the critical Tracy–Widom argument
Location. Equation (1.20), p. 6; Proposition 2.5 and (2.17), p. 9; the duality and soft-edge formulas (6.3)–(6.9), pp. 38–39.

Equation reference: eq:acrit, eq:duality, eq:edge, eq:critical-limit. For the critical scaling in (1.20), write \[
 a_n=b-Ds\,n^{-2/3}+O(n^{-4/3}),\qquad
 D=\frac{b^{1/3}}{2c^{1/6}(c+1)^{1/6}} .\] The exact duality in the source identifies \[
 \mathbb P_{m=cn,\,\alpha=1/c}
 \{\lambda_{\min}>a_n^2/c\}
 =e^{-cn^2a_n^2}\frac{Z_n(a_n,c)}{Z_n(0,c)} .\] In particular, the dimension appearing in the soft-edge scale is \(m=cn\), not \(n\). The lower edge and the parameter in (6.7) become \[\lambda_-=\frac{b^2}{c},\qquad
 \delta=\frac{c^{3/4}(c+1)^{1/4}}{b^2}.\] Direct expansion of [eq:acrit] (#eq:acrit) gives \[\lambda_--a_n^2/c
 =B s\,n^{-2/3}+O(n^{-4/3}),\qquad
 B=\frac{b^{4/3}}{c^{7/6}(c+1)^{1/6}} .\] Although \(B\delta^{2/3}=c^{-2/3}\), the actual normalized variable is \[
 y_n=(\delta m)^{2/3}(\lambda_--a_n^2/c)
     =s+O(n^{-2/3}),
 \qquad B\delta^{2/3}c^{2/3}=1 .\] Thus the edge law quoted in (6.8), together with continuity of its limit, gives \[
 \log Z_n(a_n,c)-\log Z_n(0,c)-cn^2a_n^2
 \longrightarrow \log F_{\mathrm{TW}}(s).\] By contrast, subtracting the radial reference (3.6) from (2.17) gives \(\log F_{\mathrm{TW}}(c^{-2/3}s)+o(1)\). All other terms at order one coincide; an omitted radial term of order \(n^{-1}\) cannot remove the discrepancy.

An admissible integer sequence makes the conflict explicit. Take \[c=\frac9{16},\quad s=1,\quad n=16k,\quad m=9k,\quad
 a_{16k}=\frac12-15^{-1/3}(16k)^{-2/3}.\] Here \(b=1/2\), \(\lambda_-=4/9\), \(\lambda_+=64/9\), and \(\delta=3\sqrt{15}/4\). The rectangular dimensions are \(9k\) and \(25k\), so there is no integrality ambiguity. The actual limiting argument in [eq:edge] (#eq:edge) is \(1\), whereas the printed expression uses \((16/9)^{2/3}\). These produce distinct values: from (2.15), \[\frac{d}{ds}\log F_{\mathrm{TW}}(s)=\int_s^\infty q(x)^2\,dx>0,\] where \(q\) is the real Hastings–McLeod solution specified in (2.16). Its nonzero Airy asymptotic excludes an identically zero tail.

Counterchecks and correction. Equation (6.9) can be read consistently with its \(N\) denoting the LUE dimension; it must then be converted before use with (1.20). Changing that convention silently in Proposition 2.5 does not preserve the stated scaling. The special cases \(c=1\) or \(s=0\) conceal the error and do not settle the general statement. For unchanged (1.20), the consistent limiting term is \(\log F_{\mathrm{TW}}(s)\). This check establishes the order-one correction, conditional on the edge law explicitly invoked by the paper. It does not newly prove that external law or the stated \(O(n^{-2/3})\) remainder rate.

The large-negative-\(s\) comparison (2.22) supplies a related internal check. Substitution into the tail formula (2.19) yields \[\log F_{\mathrm{TW}}(c^{-2/3}s)
 =\frac{\log2}{24}+\zeta'(-1)-\frac18\log|s|
  +\frac{\log c}{12}-\frac{|s|^3}{12c^2}
  +O(|s|^{-3})\] for fixed \(c>0\); the \(c\)-dependent terms cannot simply be omitted. This is part of the same scaling issue, not a separate finding.
Severity: Major. The discrepancy changes the advertised critical order-one term by a nonvanishing amount on an admissible sequence.
# Problem 2: the precritical moment prefactor
Location. Theorem 2.2, (2.9), p. 7; Theorem 2.7, (2.32), p. 10; the exact partition-function ratio (1.8) and radial normalization (3.7), p. 15.

For an exact admissible example, take \[a=1,\quad q=\frac12,\quad c=\frac{27}{8},\quad
 R=\frac54,\quad \kappa=\frac9{16},\quad w=2 .\] These satisfy (1.16)–(1.18), including \[q^6-\frac{a^2+4c+2}{2a^2}q^4+\frac1{2a^4}=0,\] and \(f(2)=1\). The branch is strict precritical and \(\kappa>0\). Equation [eq:prefactor] (#eq:prefactor) equals \(6912/4375\), whereas the twenty-fourth power printed in (2.32) equals \(186624/4375\). Their prefactor ratio is \(3^{1/8}\). One may take \(n\) through multiples of eight if \(cn\) is required to be an integer.

Correction and scope. Replacing \((F(a)-1)^3\) by \((F(a)^2-1)^3\) gives exactly the constant implied by (2.9). This is a verified algebraic correction conditional on that free-energy formula. The computation proves an internal incompatibility of the two stated main asymptotics; it is not an independent derivation of the full nonradial moment limit. No claim that the authors adopted this correction, or that it occurs in the journal version, is made.
Severity: Major. The error concerns the explicitly advertised constant-accurate characteristic-polynomial asymptotic, not only its presentation.
# Problem 3: an uncancelled pole in the refined parametrix
Location. The global parametrix (5.5), p. 29; (5.11)–(5.12), p. 30; the Airy coefficient (5.21), p. 32; Definition 5.8 and (5.30)–(5.35), p. 34; the use of holomorphy on p. 35.

Equation reference: eq:residual. The matrix \(H_1\) in (5.30) thus has \[
 \operatorname{Res}_{z=\lambda}H_1(z)
 =\frac{(1+i)CB}{384\rho n}
 \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] At the admissible parameters used in Problem 2, the off-diagonal entry is exactly \[\frac{(1-i)(3845+304\sqrt5\,i)}{35280n}\ne0 .\] Hence \(H_1\) is not holomorphic at \(\lambda\) as asserted. This pole is of order \(n^{-1}\); on a fixed punctured neighborhood it cannot be absorbed into the claimed \(O(n^{-2})\) matrix error.

Impact, counterevidence and repair limit. Multiplying both printed off-diagonal entries of \(h_{11}\) by \(i\), with the corresponding conjugate change at the upper endpoint, restores the checked local principal part. A complete revised matching construction and global remainder proof were not supplied in this review. The literal holomorphic-parametrix argument for the fine polynomial asymptotic (3.44) is therefore incomplete as written.

Equation reference: eq:diag. There is substantial counterevidence against extending this finding to a false free-energy coefficient. The general identity \[
 n[z^{-1}]R_{11}(z)
 =-\frac{q^2(1-a^4q^4)^2}
 {16a(1-q^2)(1-a^4q^6)^2}\] agrees exactly with Proposition 3.10. The correction in [eq:h11] (#eq:h11) changes only off-diagonals; at infinity, the first diagonal coefficient is \((h_{11}+h_{21})_{11}\), and cross products start at \(z^{-2}\). Thus neither this calculation nor the secondary conjugation issue disproves Theorem 2.2. No counterexample to the actual orthogonal polynomial asymptotic is claimed.

Severity: Major, within the proof-construction scope. The order-\(n^{-1}\) pole invalidates the displayed analytic error problem at the precision used for a stated central refinement. The classification does not assert that the refinement is unrepairable or that every resulting scalar coefficient is wrong.
# Checks supporting the analysis
## Exact references and phase algebra

At \(a=0\), the norms \[h_j=\frac{\Gamma(j+cn+1)}{n^{j+cn+1}},\qquad
 Z_n(0,c)
 =\frac{n!\,G((c+1)n+1)}
        {G(cn+1)n^{(c+1/2)n^2+n/2}}\] give an exact radial reference. Expanding its logarithm reproduces (3.6), including all checked coefficients through \(n^{-6}\). For example, the \(n^{-1}\), \(n^{-2}\), \(n^{-3}\) coefficients are \[\frac1{12},\qquad
 \frac{c^{-2}-(c+1)^{-2}}{240},\qquad -\frac1{360}.\] The corresponding GinUE ratio was also checked. An initial computational display of coefficient extraction was corrected in a separately retained run; the symbolic identity and the final coefficient extraction agree.

The cubic constraint gives \[c=\frac{a^2q^2}{2}+\frac1{4a^2q^4}-\frac{a^2+2}{4},\qquad
 \frac{q'}q
 =\frac{1+a^4q^4-2a^4q^6}{2a(a^4q^6-1)} .\] Using this derivative, the displayed energy and constant derivatives in (3.17)–(3.18) agree exactly. The difference of the phase energies has derivative \[\frac{(1-q^2)^2(1-a^4q^4)}{2aq^4}>0\] on the admissible precritical branch, where \(\kappa>0\) implies \(aq<1\). The alternative phase wording using \(c_{\rm cri}=(1-a^2)^2/(4a^2)\) requires \(0<a<1\); for \(a\geq1\) the inequality \(a>b\) always applies. This domain qualification is kept separate from the three findings.
## Differential identity, energy and local asymptotics

The determinant/tau-function derivation in Lemma 3.8 and Proposition 3.9 was read with its finite-dimensional normalization and rotation factors. Explicit moment determinants for \(n=1,2\), \(c=1\) satisfy the checked differential identity. The initial determinant must be understood as the empty determinant \(D_0=1\), not as a single moment whose derivative is generally nonzero. This check does not establish all contour nonvanishing assumptions.

The Section 4 rational partial fractions, Green residues, the closed-form energy relation, and the expansion of \(g'\) at infinity were verified algebraically. Their potential-theoretic input from the cited external work remains an input. The local-coordinate ratio \(\gamma_{12}/\gamma_{11}\), the leading Airy conjugation, and [eq:diag] (#eq:diag) were also checked exactly.

For the postcritical construction, the nilpotence of the upper triangular correction gives the stated cancellation at leading order. On a fixed endpoint-circle, \(\zeta\) has size \(n^{1/2}\), so the remaining Gaussian Cauchy-transform term has order \(n^{-3/2}\). The first-column invariance is consistent with the displayed polynomial formula. The full all-order iteration, all sectorial estimates, and the global small-norm theorem were not reproved. The differing exponential normalization in (5.51) and (5.53) is retained as a local notation issue, not an additional theorem counterexample.
## LUE large deviations

For the fixed-phase LUE transformation, the substitution is \(n=\alpha m\), \(c=1/\alpha\), \(t=a^2/c\). It reproduces the rate \(\alpha^2(I^{\rm pre}-I^{\rm post})\), the term \(-\log(\alpha m)/12\), and the stated constant difference. The cubic edge-rate coefficient \(\sqrt{\alpha+1}/(12\lambda_-^2)\) was checked exactly. These statements concern fixed \(\alpha>0\); they are not a hard-edge result for \(\alpha=0\). Their compatibility does not remove the separate critical-size error in Problem 1.
# Coverage and disposition

The principal definitions, all advertised main asymptotics, and their dependencies were examined. The checks establish exact algebraic inconsistencies and a defect in the written local construction; they do not certify every theorem in the source. In particular, integrating a derivative remainder from \(a\) to infinity requires an integrable bound uniform in that parameter, or another controlled treatment of the tail. Theorem 3.11 states uniformity in the spatial variable for fixed parameters, whereas Remark 4.9 gives decay of displayed coefficients. This review did not establish the needed remainder bound and does not treat that unverified dependency as a separate proved defect.
Finding | Verified consequence | Assessment
1 | Critical order-one formula conflicts with the stated dimension conversion and edge law. | Major
2 | Two stated main constant-accurate asymptotics are algebraically incompatible. | Major
3 | The refined parametrix has an uncancelled pole; its required holomorphic error argument is incomplete. | Major, proof scope

No substantive predecessor report was recovered in the bounded preserved inventory for this paper. Accordingly, this is an initial review of the available source. Historical acquisition, extraction and render evidence were retained with their original attribution. The source PDF, manifest, calculations, limitations and complete execution evidence accompany the report. Illustrative plots were not independently reproduced. Absence of author code is not a mathematical defect.

The overall assessment is Major for the acquired preprint. The explicit correction scopes above should be resolved before the affected statements and proof are accepted. The mathematical adjudication remains pending, with no human review or independent acceptance recorded.

# Source and scope

The reviewed work is by Michel Alexis, Lin Lin, Gevorg Mnatsakanyan, Christoph Thiele, and Jiasu Wang, associated with DOI 10.1002/cpa.70007 (https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70007). All locators below refer to the 44-page author manuscript arXiv:2407.05634v3, revised 4 March 2026 [reviewed]. The 2025 online journal record and the later author revision are distinct. Equivalence with the publisher’s typeset article is not asserted.

The complete manuscript text and all 44 source-page images were inspected. The checking concentrates on Theorems 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, and 12 and their operative dependencies. The underlying reference [amt] was consulted at selected, explicitly recorded pages, including the actual squared estimate (8.5). Its entire proof corpus was not independently re-proved. The acquired QSPPACK snapshot is related author software; its README was read, but no author code was executed and no claim is made to reproduce the paper’s historical experiments.
# Claims, hypotheses, and dependency structure

In Theorem 1 (page 4), \(f\) is real and measurable, with an even extension to \([-1,1]\), \(|f|\leq1\), and \[\int_0^1\frac{\log(1-f(x)^2)}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx>-\infty.\] The claimed phases satisfy both the weighted \(L^2\) convergence and the nonlinear Plancherel equality. Uniqueness is subject to these simultaneous requirements, rather than to convergence alone. The norm is \[\|f\|_{\mathcal S}^2=\frac2\pi\int_0^1
       \frac{|f(x)|^2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx.\] The Lipschitz assertion concerns \(0<\eta<1/2\) and \(f,f'\in\mathcal S_\eta=\{f:\|f\|_\infty\leq1-\eta\}\), with constant \(1.6\eta^{-3}\) from \(\mathcal S\) to \(\ell^\infty\).

Under \(x=\cos\theta\), \(z=e^{2i\theta}\), the circle datum \(b=if\) is purely imaginary and reflection symmetric. The complementary factor has \(a^*\) outer, \(a^*(0)>0\), and \(|a|^2+|b|^2=1\). Theorem 4 supplies this normalization. Theorem 5 and Lemmas 9–11 use a densely defined, potentially unbounded operator; the bounded polynomial algorithm cannot replace this endpoint argument. The self-adjointness of \(iM\), its resolvent bound, and the weak testing identity are the relevant steps. The proof of Theorem 12 uses the resolvent comparison and the outer normalization.

Theorem 2 concerns even polynomials of degree \(2d\), \(d\geq1\), a strict positive gap \(\eta\), and \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Its numerical claims do not include \(\eta=0\). The error analysis uses the annular extension, Fourier alias estimates, invertibility of the Hankel block system, and a lower bound for the normalization denominator. These dependencies are separate from the defective Lipschitz estimate below.
# Problem and decisive evidence

Equation reference: eq:false, eq:false-delta. Problem 1 (Major: false outer-factor estimate in a core derivation).  On page 32, Section 4.5, the unnumbered display introduced by By [1, (8.5)] asserts \[
 \|a-a'\|_2\leq
 \big\|\sqrt{1-|b|^2}-\sqrt{1-|b'|^2}\big\|_2
 +\frac14\big\|\log(1-|b|^2)-\log(1-|b'|^2)\big\|_2.\] The subsequent display introduced by Thus we obtain asserts \[
 \|a-a'\|_2\leq(\delta^{-1}+\tfrac12\delta^{-2})\|b-b'\|_2,
 \qquad \delta^2=\tfrac32\eta .\] Both statements are false under the hypotheses used in that proof. The cited estimate has the squares of all three norms.

All circle integrals below use normalized measure \(d\phi/(2\pi)\). Set \[p=\frac1{10},\qquad r=\frac1{100},\qquad t=\frac1{100},\qquad
 \alpha=\pi p,\qquad
 q(e^{i\phi})=\mathbf1_{\{|\phi|<\alpha\}}.\] Let \[r'=re^t,\quad c=\sqrt{1-r^2},\quad c'=\sqrt{1-r'^2},\quad
 \eta=1-c,\quad b=icq,\quad b'=ic'q.\] Here \(0<c'<c=1-\eta<1\) and \(0<\eta<1/2\). In the paper’s interval variable these are \[f(x)=c\,\mathbf1_{\{x>\cos(\pi p/2)\}},\qquad
 f'(x)=c'\,\mathbf1_{\{x>\cos(\pi p/2)\}},
 \quad 0\leq x\leq1,\] with even extensions. They are measurable and belong to \(\mathcal S_\eta\); both Szegő logarithms are bounded. Endpoint choices for the indicator have measure zero.

Write \(h=Hq\) for the circle Hilbert transform. Up to the harmless choice of its sign, \[h(\phi)=\frac1\pi\log\left|
       \frac{\sin((\phi+\alpha)/2)}{\sin((\phi-\alpha)/2)}
                         \right|.\] The normalized complementary factors are \[a=\exp\big((\log r)(q-ih)\big),\qquad
 a'=\exp\big((\log r+t)(q-ih)\big).\] Their conjugates are outer, have positive value \(r^p\) and \((r')^p\) at the origin, and satisfy the required modulus identities. Thus the construction uses exactly the normalization of Theorem 4.

Equation reference: eq:lower. Lemma 1.  For this pair, \[
 \|a-a'\|_2^2\geq
 t^2p\left(\frac23-p-\frac{t^2}{2}\right).\] In particular, \(\|a-a'\|_2>(3/4)t\sqrt p\).

The logarithmic singularities of \(h\) give \(h\in L^4\). The function \(g=q-p+ih\) is the boundary value of an analytic function with zero constant coefficient. Hence \(\int g^4=0\) and its real part yields \[\int h^4=6\int(q-p)^2h^2-\int(q-p)^4\leq6p.\] On \(E^c\), both moduli equal one and \(|a-a'|^2=2(1-\cos(th))\). The elementary inequality \(2(1-\cos u)\geq u^2-u^4/12\), valid for every real \(u\), now proves [eq:lower] (#eq:lower). Finally \(2/3-p-t^2/2=17/30-1/20000>9/16\). ◻

The right-hand side of [eq:false] (#eq:false) is exactly \[\left[r(e^t-1)+\frac t2\right]\sqrt p
 <0.005101\sqrt p,\] using \(e^{0.01}-1<0.0101\). The lemma gives a left-hand side larger than \(0.0075\sqrt p\), proving the first failure.

The next coefficient is not rescued by reading the first display as a missing-square typographical error. Indeed, \[\delta^2=\frac{3r^2}{2(1+c)},\qquad
 c-c'=\frac{r^2(e^{2t}-1)}{c+c'}.\] Since \(\delta^{-1}<6/(5r)\), \(1/(2\delta^2)<2/(3r^2)\), \(c+c'>1.99\), and \(e^{0.02}-1<0.0203\), \[\begin{aligned}
 (\delta^{-1}+\tfrac12\delta^{-2})\|b-b'\|_2
 &<\left(\frac65r+\frac23\right)
                  \frac{0.0203}{1.99}\sqrt p\\
 &<0.007\sqrt p<\|a-a'\|_2.\end{aligned}\] The exponential inequalities follow directly from their convergent positive Taylor series with a geometric bound on the remaining tail. Thus neither contradiction depends on a numerical quadrature.
An independent 70-digit computation, retained with its source and actual execution record, gives the following corroboration:
Quantity | Numerical value
Analytic lower bound, [eq:lower] (#eq:lower) | \(0.0023803711195245725\)
Right side of [eq:false] (#eq:false) | \(0.0016129202489354139\)
Right side of [eq:false-delta] (#eq:false-delta) | \(0.0021663463577285112\)
These floating-point evaluations are corroborating checks; the preceding inequalities are the proof of the counterexample.
# Repair, counterevidence, and impact

Equation reference: eq:true. The correct squared estimate is \[
 \|a-a'\|_2^2\leq
 \big\|\sqrt{1-|b|^2}-\sqrt{1-|b'|^2}\big\|_2^2
 +\frac14\big\|\log(1-|b|^2)-\log(1-|b'|^2)\big\|_2^2 .\] It is visible as (8.5) on page 30 of the acquired arXiv version of [amt]. It also follows directly here: the pointwise cosine identity bounds the squared difference by the squared modulus difference plus the squared phase difference; the phase difference is the Hilbert transform of the difference of the logarithmic moduli, and \(H\) is an \(L^2\) contraction. This argument requires no small-signal hypothesis when the logarithms are in \(L^2\), as they are on \(\mathcal S_\eta\).

Equation reference: eq:repair. On \(0\leq x\leq1-\eta\), the derivative bounds used by the manuscript are valid: \(\delta^{-1}\) for \(\sqrt{1-x^2}\) and \(2\delta^{-2}\) for \(\log(1-x^2)\). Applying them to [eq:true] (#eq:true) gives \[\|a-a'\|_2\leq
       \sqrt{\delta^{-2}+\delta^{-4}}\,\|b-b'\|_2.\] Together with the quotient decomposition on page 32 this yields \[\left\|\frac b a-\frac{b'}{a'}\right\|_2
 \leq\left(\delta^{-1}
       +\delta^{-2}\sqrt{\delta^{-2}+\delta^{-4}}\right)\|b-b'\|_2.\] Theorem 12 contributes \(\sqrt2\,\delta^{-2}(1+\delta)\). The arctangent map has Lipschitz constant at most one, and the circle-to-interval substitution preserves the relevant \(L^2\) norm. The same shift argument applies to each phase. Therefore the corrected constant in the theorem is bounded by \[\begin{aligned}
 C_\eta
 &\leq \sqrt2\,\delta^{-6}(1+\delta)
                    \left(\delta^3+\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\right)\notag\\
 &\leq \eta^{-3}\frac{8\sqrt2}{27}
     \left(1+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)
     \left(\frac{3\sqrt3}{8}+\frac{\sqrt7}{2}\right)
 <1.6\eta^{-3}.                                      \end{aligned}\] The last strict inequality is elementary, not a floating-point assumption: replacing \(\sqrt2,\sqrt3,\sqrt7\) by the rational upper bounds \(1.415,1.733,2.646\), respectively, already gives a number below \(1.55\). The sharper evaluated coefficient is approximately \(1.5422422668\).

Severity and boundary. The false estimates are used in the quantitative proof of a main theorem, and both are contradicted within its full hypotheses. This supports a Major classification for the core derivation. The local repair above proves that this particular defect does not invalidate the stated \(1.6\eta^{-3}\) conclusion. No failure of existence, uniqueness, or the separate algorithmic theorem is established. The report recommends replacing the two estimates and the ensuing constant calculation, not withdrawing the final theorem. Author adoption of this repair is unknown.

The most favorable alternate reading is that squares were omitted in copying the reference. It explains the origin of the first display, but cannot justify the second, disproved coefficient. Conversely, simply taking a triangle bound with coefficient \(1/2\) in the unsquared display loses unnecessary sharpness; the squared estimate retains enough margin to prove [eq:repair] (#eq:repair). A bounded exact-title search of the primary author and journal records did not locate a relevant correction. This is not a claim that no correction exists anywhere.
# Independent checks and findings not established

For a separate exact check, let \(f_\rho=\rho T_2\), \(0\leq\rho\leq1\), and put \(s=\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\), \(A=(1+s)/2\), \(B=(1-s)/2\). Then \[a=A-Bz^{-2},\qquad b=\frac{i\rho}{2}(z+z^{-1})\] satisfy \(|a|^2+|b|^2=1\). The symmetric phase sequence \[\psi_0=0,\qquad \psi_1=\tfrac12\arcsin\rho,\qquad
 \psi_j=0\quad(j\geq2)\] gives the required polynomial. With \(u=\rho/(1+s)\), \(1/(1+u^2)=A\), so the nonlinear energy is \(2\log(1+u^2)=-2\log A\), in agreement with the outer-factor identity. At \(\rho=1\), the isolated endpoint zeros still have integrable logarithm and the phase is \(\pi/4\). This checks a genuine Szegő boundary case; it does not extend Theorem 2’s algorithm to zero gap.

A reviewer-written implementation of Algorithms 1–2, using NumPy float64/complex128 and no author imports, tested \(0.1T_2\), \(0.8T_2\), \(0.999T_2\), and \(0.2+0.3T_2-0.1T_4\). Fourier sample counts were 2048, 2048, 524288, and 2048, respectively. The maximum reconstruction discrepancy on 1001 equally spaced points of \([0,1]\) was at most \(3.34\times10^{-16}\); the linear-system residuals were at most \(1.12\times10^{-16}\). The first three phase sequences agreed with the exact family to \(2.23\times10^{-16}\). These are finite checks, not a proof of the asymptotic precision or work bounds.

In the manuscript’s proof of Theorem 8, the required \[N\geq\frac{8d}{\eta}\log\frac{576d^2}{\eta^4\varepsilon}\] provides a positive-gap Fourier error budget. The purely imaginary Hankel coefficients make the corresponding off-diagonal block skew-Hermitian, giving the singular-value lower bound used in Proposition 24. The normalization lower bound prevents division by a vanishing coefficient. These checks did not reveal another substantive defect.

Several isolated sign, logarithm, index, or projection-label inconsistencies were considered against their surrounding definitions and actual uses. They were not counted as additional Problems where the operative argument was unambiguous or the stated final bound retained sufficient margin. In particular, the resolvent-domain reasoning was checked as an unbounded-operator argument, not by assuming a uniformly positive modulus in the full Szegő existence theorem.
# Supporting checks

The coverage record distinguishes full text and image inspection from independent derivation. Sections 1–3, the proofs in Sections 4–5, both algorithms, the numerical figures on pages 17–18, and the references were read. The principal dependency checks included the outer construction, domain density, the self-adjoint resolvent, the factorization normalization, the inner-factor term in the Plancherel comparison, symmetry and uniqueness, analytic continuation and alias bounds, and the linear-system error budget. The manuscript’s bit-complexity model was inspected; arbitrary hardware implementations and the reported empirical timings were not certified.

The support package contains the exact source PDF and manifest, the independent scripts and actual results, source/reference renders with separate inspection receipts, this TeX source, and the compiler/dependency/PDF records. An earlier arithmetic evaluation of the manuscript’s printed coefficient is preserved; it is not treated as a valid proof after Problem Problem 1 (#prob:outer). Only the corrected chain [eq:repair] (#eq:repair) supports the conclusion about the constant.

The reviewed reference PDF is arXiv:2310.12683v2 (3 June 2024), SHA256 4f6e2ad09f2afd41e877f73938dfe185a3d2f9b0445d655ad24b92705cbf17d6. Scientific decision remains pending and no human review is recorded.

report: Abstract: The acquired manuscript is read through its definitions, main results, proofs, appendix and references. Five concrete mathematical corrections are established by elementary examples and direct differentiation: the model-selection implication in Lemma 3.15 admits an omitted wet-region branch; the variable-angle first-variation formula has the wrong derivative; the refined boundary flux uses the wrong trigonometric coefficient; two total-variation estimates omit a negative-mass contribution; and the boundary-normal linearization has an incorrect linear coefficient. The first issue is rated Major because an invalid model-selection step is explicitly used in the main regularity proof. The remaining issues have verified local corrections and are rated Minor. These findings do not establish failure of the principal regularity theorems. Scientific adjudication and independent acceptance remain pending.

Title: Initial Technical Review of
Regularity of Minimal Surfaces
with Capillary Boundary Conditions
# Identity, version and scope

The paper is by Luigi De Masi, Nick Edelen, Carlo Gasparetto and Chao Li, Regularity of minimal surfaces with capillary boundary conditions, DOI https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70008. This review concerns precisely arXiv:2405.20796v1, dated 31 May 2024, with 60 physical pages; physical and printed page numbers agree. The journal landing page identifies a 2025 publication, but the journal full-text request returned HTTP 403. Equivalence with the final journal text is not asserted. The current arXiv record and the author’s publication list did not supply a later arXiv revision or an identified correction in the bounded checks performed.

All 60 source pages were read as text. The displayed source pages supporting the findings were also visually inspected. Independent calculations concern the five examples below; reading the remaining arguments is not a claim to have independently reproved every external regularity or compactness theorem. No author code was executed. The scientific work and image inspection belong to this primary scientific conversation; native assistance was confined to mechanical binding and helper preparation.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

Equation reference: eq:capillary. Write \(W=\{x_1=0\}\), \(S_-=\{x\in W:x_{n+1}<0\}\) and \(S_+=\{x\in W:x_{n+1}>0\}\). The manuscript permits signed varifolds \[V=V_I+\cos\beta[S]_g,\qquad V_I\ \hbox{integral in }\{x_1<0\},\] where \(g,\beta\) are \(C^1\), \(S\) is measurable, and, for compactly supported \(C^1\) vector fields tangent to \(W\), \[
 \delta_{\beta,g}V(X)
 =\int\operatorname{div}_{V,g}X\,d\mu_{V_I}
  +\int_S\operatorname{div}_{W,g}(\cos\beta X)\,d\mathcal H_g^n
 =-\int g(H^{\rm tan},X)\,d\mu_{V_I}.\] This is Definition 1.1, p. 3, and Definition 2.1, pp. 13–14. In particular, negative wall weights are expressly allowed. The model is \[P_\theta^-=\{\cos\theta\,x_1+\sin\theta\,x_{n+1}=0,\ x_1\leq0\},
 \qquad V^{(\theta)}=[P_\theta^-]+\cos\theta[S_-].\] For \(0<\theta<\pi\), \[\Theta_{V^{(\theta)}}(0,1)+(\cos\theta)^-
   =\frac{1+|\cos\theta|}{2}<1.\] Here \(a^-=\max\{-a,0\}\). This shifted signed density must not be confused with normalized total variation.

The first-variation theorem requires a strict density gap \(1-\alpha\) and small \(H^{\rm tan}\), metric error and \(D\beta\). The main graph theorem excludes the right angle and requires the origin in the interior support and closeness to a half-plane. The version based on varifold distance also requires \(C^1\) closeness of the angle, not merely small \(D\beta\). The finite-perimeter conclusion for \(S\) is used only where \(|\cos\beta|\) stays away from zero. The dense regular-set assertion and the stronger almost-everywhere assertion in Theorem 1.19 have different density hypotheses. None of these restrictions is removed in this review.
# Established problems

Problem 1 (M25-0422-P001: The missing wet-region branch).  Severity: Major. Lemma 3.15, pp. 37–38, implication (3.38) and the angular conclusion, are false as stated. The omitted branch enters the first sentence of the proof of Theorem 1.11 on p. 54.
## Claim and admissibility

The lemma quantifies over \(\theta\) separated from \(0,\pi/2,\pi\), a \(C^1\) metric and angle, and a capillary varifold with \[0\in\operatorname{spt}V_I,\quad
 \Theta_V(0,1)+(\cos\beta(0))^-
 \leq\frac34+\frac{|\cos\theta_0|}{4},\] and arbitrarily small \(H^{\rm tan}\), metric error and \(D\beta\). It claims that small \(\operatorname{osc}_{P_\theta}(V_I,B_1)\) forces \(\mathcal D(V,V^{(\theta)})\) small and \(\beta\) close to \(\theta\), allowing addition of an integer multiple of \(\pi\).

Equation reference: eq:branch. Choose \(n=1\), \(g=g_{\rm eucl}\), \(\theta=\pi/3\), \(\theta_0=\pi/12\), \(\beta=2\pi/3\), and \[
 V=[P_{\pi/3}^-]-\tfrac12[S_+].\] Both angles are in their required ranges, \(V_I\) has multiplicity one, \(0\in\operatorname{spt}V_I\), and its oscillation relative to \(P_{\pi/3}\) is zero.

Exact counterexample. The outward conormal of the interior ray at the origin is \(\sin\theta\,e_1-\cos\theta\,e_2\). The conormal of the upper wall ray is \(-e_2\); multiplying by \(-\cos\theta\) cancels the tangential component. Thus [eq:capillary] (#eq:capillary) holds with \(H^{\rm tan}=0\). All differential smallness quantities vanish. The normalized signed density is \(1/4\), so the shifted density is \(3/4\), strictly below \(3/4+\cos(\pi/12)/4\).

Nevertheless \[V-V^{(\pi/3)}=-\tfrac12[W]\ne0.\] Consequently their distance in the manuscript’s varifold metric is a fixed positive number. Taking a constant sequence of [eq:branch] (#eq:branch) disproves (3.38) for any smaller prescribed distance tolerance and every positive smallness threshold. Moreover \[\inf_{k\in\mathbb Z}|2\pi/3+k\pi-\pi/3|=\pi/3,\] so the stated angular normalization does not rescue the conclusion. ◻
## Dependency, counterevidence and repair boundary

At the end of p. 37 the limiting wall coefficients satisfy \(k_\pm\in\{0,\cos\theta'\}\). Stationarity gives \(k_--k_+=\cos\theta\); it does not force the single solution asserted at the top of p. 38. Besides \((\cos\theta,0)\), the solution \((0,-\cos\theta)\) is allowed.

The manuscript itself supplies the relevant counterevidence to any claim of irreparable failure: Example 1.3 explicitly swaps the wet region without changing \(V_I\), and p. 40 announces an acute-angle normalization for Sections 4–6. The example is already a perfectly smooth half-plane, so it contradicts neither the graph conclusion nor capillary regularity. A corrected lemma should allow both signed models, or impose a compatible wet-region/sign normalization. For \(\beta,\theta\in(0,\pi)\), matching the signs of their cosines selects the intended branch; smallness of \(D\beta\) alone does not. The proof of Theorem 1.11 must make that selection before asserting the quoted convergence. This is a demonstrated invalid core reduction, not a demonstrated false final regularity theorem. A complete replacement proof with all parameter choices is not claimed here.

Problem 2 (M25-0422-P002: The derivative of the wall weight).  Severity: Minor. Equation (2.10), the definition of \(H_{\beta,g}\), and (2.12), p. 14, use \(\nabla_W^g\sin\beta\) where the product rule requires \(\nabla_W^g\cos\beta\). The second first-variation identity in Theorem 2.2, p. 15, is consequently false with the printed definition.

The hypotheses here are exactly the capillary definition, \(C^1\) metric and angle, integral interior part, and locally integrable tangential mean curvature. No density smallness is needed for this claim. In the Euclidean two-dimensional unit ball, take \(V_I=[P_{\pi/2}^-]\), \(S=W\), and \(\beta(y)=\pi/4+\kappa y\), where \(y=x_2\) and \(\kappa=1/10\). The wall weight is positive throughout the ball. The horizontal interior ray has zero tangential first variation, and the integral of \((\cos\beta X_2)'\) over the entire wall vanishes. Thus this is an admissible example with \(H^{\rm tan}=0\).

Equation reference: eq:weight. Opposite signs in the asserted identity. Let \(\phi(y)=(1-16y^2)^2\) for \(|y|<1/4\), extended by zero. This is a nonzero, nonnegative \(C^1\) function. Extend \(Y=(0,\phi(y))\) compactly into \(B_1\) with a normal cutoff equal to one near \(W\). The generalized boundary term is normal to \(W\) and hence vanishes on \(Y\). Directly, \[
 \delta V(Y)=\int\cos\beta\,\phi'\,dy
 =\kappa\int\sin\beta\,\phi\,dy>0.\] The printed \(H_\beta=(\nabla_W\sin\beta)/\cos\beta=\kappa e_2\) instead gives \(-\kappa\int\cos\beta\,\phi\,dy<0\). The two numerical values are approximately \(0.0188553390525\) and \(-0.0188553390525\); their signs follow analytically, without quadrature. ◻

The corrected identity is \[\delta_{ eta,g}V(X)=\delta_gV(X)
       +\int_S g(X,
abla_W^g\cos eta)\,d\mathcal H_g^n,\qquad
 H_{ eta,g}= rac{
abla_W^g\cos eta}{\cos eta}.\] Define the quotient to be zero on \(\{\cos eta=0\}\) in the weighted almost-everywhere sense. The derivative vanishes almost everywhere on that level set, and \(|H_{ eta,g}|\,|\cos eta|\leq|
abla_W^g eta|\). The required weighted \(L^1\) control therefore survives. The variable-angle compactness, monotonicity and first-variation estimates must use this corrected field; their small-error bounds are not disproved by the example. The analogous product-rule display in Remark 3.2, p. 25, should be corrected consistently. For constant \( eta\), both derivatives vanish, explaining why constant-angle tests do not expose the error.

Problem 3 (M25-0422-P003: Normal flux in the refined boundary formula).  Severity: Minor. Theorem 3.16, p. 38, the text following (3.41), and the corresponding conclusion on p. 40 identify \(g(\eta_{V_I,g},\nu_g)\) with \(\cos\beta\). The coefficient is \(\sin\beta\) for the paper’s model.

Take \(n=1\), \(g=g_{\rm eucl}\), \(\beta=2\pi/3\), \(S=S_-\), \(V=V^{(\beta)}\), and \(\alpha=1/5\). The metric, curvature and angle-gradient errors are zero. The shifted density is \(3/4<4/5=1-\alpha\), so every smallness hypothesis of Theorem 3.16 holds. Its set \(BS\) contains the origin.

Model computation. For any \(0<\beta<\pi\), \[\eta_{V_I}=\sin\beta\,e_1-\cos\beta\,e_2,\qquad \nu=e_1.\] The lower wall ray contributes \(\cos\beta\,e_2\) at its endpoint. Thus \[\delta V(Y)=\sin\beta\,Y_1(0),\qquad
 \sigma_V=\sin\beta\,\delta_0 .\] At \(\beta=2\pi/3\) the actual positive coefficient is \(\sqrt3/2\), whereas the printed coefficient is \(-1/2\). The latter cannot be a nonnegative boundary measure. ◻

This is a false quantitative conclusion in the refined theorem, not an ambiguity about normal orientation: the outward normal is fixed to point in the positive \(e_1\) direction. For normalized angles in \((0,\pi)\), replace the coefficient on \(BS\) by \(\sin\beta\); the coefficient on its free-boundary complement remains one. This leaves the vector identity (3.41) and its geometric classification compatible with the model. Section 3.4 explicitly is not needed for the maximum principle or the main Allard-type regularity argument; the density classification used later in Theorem 1.19 is distinct from this flux coefficient. No failure of those qualitative conclusions follows from this example.

Problem 4 (M25-0422-P004: Total variation versus shifted signed mass).  Severity: Minor. Remark 3.3, (3.11), p. 25, and (3.33), p. 35, undercount the negative wall contribution when bounding \(|\mu_V|\).

Equation reference: eq:signedmass. Use \(n=1\), the Euclidean metric, the nonzero free-boundary horizontal ray \(V_I=[P_{\pi/2}^-]\), \(S=W\), and constant angle \(\cos\beta=-9/10\). This is capillary with \(H^{\rm tan}=0\); the full wall has no tangential boundary, and \(D\beta=0\). For every radius \(r\), with \(\omega_1=2\), \[
 \frac{\mu_V(B_r)}{\omega_1r}=-\frac25,\qquad
 \frac{|\mu_V|(B_r)}{\omega_1r}=\frac75,\qquad
 \Theta_V(0,r)+(\cos\beta)^-=\frac12.\] Taking \(\alpha=1/4\) verifies the strict density assumption \(1/2\leq3/4\), with zero differential errors. Nevertheless the conclusion (3.11) would bound \(7/5\) by \(7/8\), and (3.33) would bound \(7/5\) by one.

The exact measure identity is \[|\mu_V|=\mu_V+2\mu_V^- .\] For a wall density bounded below by \(-a\), a valid total-variation estimate uses \(\Theta_V+2a\), with the appropriate metric errors. In contrast, \(\mu_{V_I}\leq\mu_V+a\mathcal H_g^n\!\llcorner W\) does use only one copy of \(a\). The strict bound needed for interior boundary rigidity therefore survives. In Lemma 3.8, p. 33, the total mass controls an error of the form \(c\delta|\mu_V|(B_1)\); a uniform dimensional bound, rather than a bound strictly below \(\omega_n\), suffices for that use. Replacing the affected estimates by this valid bound repairs the identified mass accounting. This example does not refute the Ahlfors conclusions: the interior ray and its boundary are regular.

Problem 5 (M25-0422-P005: Incorrect linearization of the boundary normal).  Severity: Minor. The second Taylor expansion in Section 2.1, p. 10, has coefficient \(\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-1\) on \(D_1u\). It is reused in (5.7), p. 45, and in the boundary-viscosity argument of Theorem 6.3, p. 52.

The correct first-order expansion is \(\cos\theta-\sin^3\theta\,D_1u+O_\theta(|Du|^2)\) in the Euclidean metric. Its coefficient remains strictly negative for a fixed angle away from the endpoints. Therefore the homogeneous Neumann condition obtained in the blow-up argument is unchanged; the barrier constants and displayed Taylor bounds must be adjusted. This is a disproved intermediate estimate with an explicit local repair, not a counterexample to the limiting elliptic problem.
# Coverage, alternate readings and limitations

The proof chain was followed from boundary first-variation control and rigidity (Sections 2–3 and Appendix 8), through the maximum principle (Section 4), partial Harnack estimates (Section 5), viscosity blow-up and decay (Section 6), to the main conclusions (Section 7). The role of the strict density gap, integral interior multiplicity, signed wall component, angle normalization, bounded mean curvature, metric regularity and non-right-angle restriction was checked at the corresponding transitions.

For Problem Problem 1 (#prob:branch), merely changing the representative of \(\beta\) by a multiple of \(\pi\) cannot change the actual signed varifold. Swapping \(S\) and its complement can, and is the relevant repair. For Problems Problem 2 (#prob:gradient)–Problem 5 (#prob:normal), the counterexamples identify actual mathematical equalities or estimates that fail; their likely typographical origin does not make the printed formulas true. Their severities are limited because the stated corrections preserve the estimates or geometric conclusions at the specific uses examined.

The interior Allard statement on p. 23 also needs a clear centering convention if its \(C^{1,1/2}\) norm includes the graph height: the oscillation defined on p. 9 is invariant under normal translation. The notation for the zero generalized-boundary assumption there is ambiguous. This observation is not promoted to an additional unqualified counterexample or to a claim that Allard’s theorem fails. Uses at actual support points were read in their usual centered sense.

External results invoked for Allard regularity, rectifiability, compactness and the strong maximum principle were identified but not independently reproved from their original publications. No separate supplement resolving the findings was located in the bounded primary-source checks. The inaccessible journal full text remains a genuine version limit; the present findings must not be silently attributed to that unseen version. No claim of exhaustive absence of corrections is made.

This is capillary with \(H^{\rm tan}=0\); the full wall has no tangential boundary, and \(D\beta=0\). For every radius \(r\), with \(\omega_1=2\), \[

report: Abstract: The acquired 85-page preprint is examined with particular attention to hypotheses, dimension dependence and the vanishing-viscosity limit. Eight substantive corrections are established. The general-drift extension of a weighted Lipschitz estimate is false and its direct use in the gradient argument requires new justification. Separately, the literal displayed semimonotonicity assumption admits an inviscid limit with a shock; the apparent intended correction excludes that example. Six further problems concern label estimates, coupling, empirical measures, matrix arguments, representation formulae and an auxiliary compactness lemma. Their errors and repair boundaries are distinguished from the principal conclusions. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: Initial scientific review: M25-0423
Title: Technical Review of A Priori Estimates and Large Population Limits for Some Nonsymmetric Nash Systems with Semimonotonicity
# Identity, version and scope

The authors are Marco Cirant and Davide Francesco Redaelli; the journal identifier is https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70009. The reviewed object is arXiv:2406.10822v2, dated 18 June 2025 in its arXiv stamp and 19 June 2025 internally [source]. Its 85 physical PDF pages coincide with the printed numbers used below. The source PDF has 1,111,681 bytes; its SHA256 and the manifest binding are recorded in the accompanying provenance. No equivalence with an unseen journal PDF is asserted.

All text, including both appendices and the bibliography, was read by the primary scientific executor. All source pages supporting the findings were also inspected as actual rendered images. Independent analytic examples were derived, and a reviewer-written script checked symbolic identities, a scalar root and Gaussian integrals. Author code was not executed.

The publisher’s indexed text records a correction dated 27 September 2025 concerning the placement or appearance of footnote marker 7 in Lemma 7.15 [journal]. It does not describe an algebraic correction to the estimates below. Selected indexed journal excerpts retain some displayed formulae; full HTML retrieval exceeded the tool’s size limit, and the journal PDF was not examined. The author page and arXiv version history were checked [arxiv, author]; no exhaustive absence of further corrections is claimed.
# Definitions, assumptions and dependencies

Equation reference: eq:nash, eq:weight. For quadratic Hamiltonians, the backward system is \[
-\partial_t u^i-\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\sigma I+\beta J)D^2u^i\bigr)
+\frac12|D_i u^i|^2+\sum_{j\ne i}D_j u^j\cdot D_j u^i=f^i,
\qquad u^i(T,\cdot)=g^i.\] Here \(J=J_N\otimes I_d\), \(\sigma>0,\beta\ge0\). The paper uses Euclidean vector norms and quadratic-form matrix order even for nonsymmetric matrices. Its distinguished weighted norm is \[
\|x\|_i^2=|x^i|^2+\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}|x^j|^2.\] The mean-field conditions (MF) control own-state and off-diagonal derivatives with different powers of \(N\); they do not uniformly bound the full Frobenius norm of a diagonal matrix.

The \(\mathcal D\)-condition controls the one-sided Lipschitz constant of \(x\mapsto(D_i h^i(x))_i\). The \(\mathcal L\)-condition concerns sums of four-point rectangular differences. Neither supplies symmetry of the mixed Jacobian. Theorems 3.8 and A.1 require small semimonotonicity constants and large \(N\), with additional convexity hypotheses for general Hamiltonians. The heterogeneous limit requires bounded smooth data, symmetry in other players’ states, and label regularity (LP). Section 7 sets \(\sigma=1,\beta=0\); Section 8 instead takes \(\sigma=\sigma_N\downarrow0\) with a lower bound on \(\sigma_N\log\log N\).

The principal dependency requiring further work is the application of Lemma 4.3 in Proposition 8.1 to obtain a gradient bound independent of \(N\) and \(\sigma_N\). Problems 1 and 2 concern different aspects of that argument and its statement. The remaining problems have more local repair boundaries.
# A weighted estimate used outside its proved structure

Problem 1 (False arbitrary-drift extension; Major).  Remark 4.4 (p. 30) extends Lemma 4.3 to transport \(\sum_j b^jD_j u^i\) assuming only the Euclidean one-sided condition (4.2). Proposition 8.1 (p. 69), deriving (8.4), directly applies the weighted estimate to \(D_i u^i\), saying that only the forcing condition (4.3) remains to be checked.
## Decisive example and hypotheses

Take \(d=1,i=1,\sigma=1,\beta=0,N\ge2\), and fixed \(a>0\). Set \[b(x)=(a\sin x^2,0,\ldots,0),\qquad f=0,\qquad g(x)=\sin x^1.\] The drift and data are bounded and smooth. The eigenvalues of the nonzero block of \((Db+Db^\top)/2\) are \(\pm a\cos(x^2)/2\), so (4.2) holds with \(M=a/2\), independent of \(N\). The weighted Lipschitz constant of \(g\) is one.

Equation reference: eq:driftex. In forward time \(s=T-t\), consider the two-variable periodic solution \[
v_s-\Delta v+\frac12(v_{x^1})^2+a\sin(x^2)v_{x^1}=0,
\qquad v(0,x)=\sin x^1.\] It exists smoothly on a fixed short interval independently of \(N\): the heat-semigroup integral equation is a contraction in a bounded \(C^1\) ball for small time, because the gradient kernel has integrable \(s^{-1/2}\) norm and the quadratic term is locally Lipschitz there. Smooth data give the needed initial derivatives. Extend the solution constantly in the other coordinates.

Proof. At \(s=0\), \[v_s=-\sin x^1-\tfrac12\cos^2x^1-a\sin x^2\cos x^1,
\qquad \partial_s\partial_{x^2}v(0,0)=-a.\] Thus \(\partial_{x^2}v(s_*,0)\ne0\) for a fixed small \(s_*>0\). The proposed weighted bound, with \(c_1\) depending only on dimension-independent quantities, implies \[|\partial_{x^2}v(s_*,0)|\le c_1N^{-1/2}.\] Its left side is independent of \(N\) and nonzero, a contradiction. Omitting the quadratic term gives the same initial jet and refutes the linear-transport reading as well. ◻

If a separate \(\mathcal D[u]\) lower bound is retained in this reading, take the other components to be zero: the smooth solution has only a fixed two-dimensional nonzero Jacobian block and a uniform lower symmetric-part bound.
## Counterevidence and repair boundary

The original Nash-specific Lemma 4.3 is not refuted. At its doubling maximum, (4.6)–(4.7) give equality of the distinguished derivatives and allow the own-component cancellation in (4.9)–(4.10), pp. 28–29. Arbitrary \(b\) lacks that cancellation.

The counterexample is not asserted to be the actual Nash drift in Proposition 8.1. Its extra structure may support a different argument. Nevertheless, the false general extension does not justify the componentwise invocation, and checking only the forcing term does not establish a weighted drift hypothesis. A new game-specific gradient argument or a verified weighted one-sided estimate is needed for the \(\sigma\)-uniform compactness used on p. 70. No complete replacement proof or counterexample to the intended final theorem is claimed.
# The literal hypothesis of the inviscid-limit theorem

Problem 2 (Repeated own-state argument in (3.9); Major).  Equation (3.9), p. 23, contains \[\sum_i\bigl(D_xF(x^i,m_{x^{-i}})
-D_xF(x^i,m_{y^{-i}})\bigr)\cdot(x^i-y^i)\ge-M|x-y|^2.\] Theorem 3.17 (p. 24) expressly invokes this assumption for \(F\) and \(G\).
## A bounded smooth example

Take \(d=1,T=2,H=p^2/2,\beta=0,F=0\), and \(G(x,m)=\cos x\). All spatial derivatives are bounded and smooth and all measure derivatives vanish, so Remark 3.15’s regularity conditions hold. The printed left side of (3.9) is identically zero. For sufficiently large \(N\), choose \(\sigma_N=(\log\log N)^{-1/2}\). Then \(\sigma_N\to0\) and \(\sigma_N\log\log N\to\infty\), meeting any finite threshold; the finitely many smaller terms may be positive arbitrarily.

Equation reference: eq:cole. The uncoupled exact Cole–Hopf solution is \[
v_\sigma(s,x)=-2\sigma\log\left[
(4\pi\sigma s)^{-1/2}\int_\mathbb R
e^{-[\cos y+(x-y)^2/(2s)]/(2\sigma)}\,dy\right].\] It is bounded and smooth on finite time intervals. As \(\sigma\downarrow0\), \[v_\sigma(s,x)\longrightarrow V(s,x)=\min_y\{\cos y+(x-y)^2/(2s)\}.\] This follows by elementary Laplace upper and lower bounds near minimizers and outside a fixed compact interval; the quadratic term confines the minimizers and controls the tails. No derivative convergence is assumed.

Proof. At \(s=2,x=0\), let \(\phi(y)=\cos y+y^2/4\). Then \(\phi''(0)=-1/2\). Positive critical points satisfy \(y=2\sin y\); strict decrease of \(\sin y/y\) on \((0,\pi)\) gives one positive nonzero solution \(a\). Outside \([-\pi,\pi]\), \(\phi(y)\ge-1+\pi^2/4>1=\phi(0)\), so the global minimizers are precisely \(\pm a\). The tilt \(-xy/2\) selects \(a\) on the right and \(-a\) on the left. Hence \[\partial_x^-V(2,0)=a/2,\qquad \partial_x^+V(2,0)=-a/2.\] Independent computation gives \(a\approx1.895494267033981\) and \(\phi(a)\approx0.5792021049470533\). Thus the value limit is not differentiable, contrary to the bounded Lipschitz derivative required by Theorem 3.17 and (3.11), even along a subsequence. ◻
## Intended reading and impact

The description \(\mathcal D\)-semimonotonicity and Section 8’s invocation of Proposition 5.1 strongly suggest replacing the second \(x^i\) in (3.9) by \(y^i\). Under that correction, \(G''\ge-1\) gives a nonzero constant, and the intended smallness condition at \(T=2\) excludes the example. The literal statement is false; the intended corrected theorem is not disproved. Correcting (3.9) does not fill the separate gap in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:drift).
# Dependence on all player labels

Problem 3 (Normalization and terminal data in Lemma 7.1; Minor).  Lemma 7.1 (p. 51) bounds the value and own-gradient differences by \(C(|\lambda_1-\lambda'_1|+N^{-1}|\widehat\lambda-\widehat\lambda'|)\). The norm is Euclidean by p. 13. Equation (7.3), p. 52, also omits a terminal-gradient contribution.
## Exact Nash solutions satisfying the hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:labelg. Set \(d=1,\sigma=1,\beta=0,H=p^2/2\), and \[
f^i=0,\qquad
g^i(x)=\lambda_i\sin x^i+\frac{\varepsilon}{N-1}\sum_{j\ne i}\sin x^j,
\qquad 0<\varepsilon\le1,\quad\lambda_i\in[0,1].\] These data are bounded and smooth uniformly in \(N\), symmetric in the other states, and satisfy (LP). They satisfy (MF), for example with \(L_g=2\), and their \(\mathcal L\)-rectangular differences vanish. Thus the \(\mathcal L\)-semimonotonicity constant is zero; arbitrarily large \(N\) and any fixed horizon are allowed.

Equation reference: eq:labelsol. Define \[v_\lambda(s,x)=-2\log\mathbb Ee^{-\lambda\sin(x+\sqrt2B_s)/2},
\qquad w_\lambda=\partial_\lambda v_\lambda.\] The identities \(v_s=v_{xx}-v_x^2/2\) and \(w_s=w_{xx}-v_xw_x\) show by direct substitution that \[
u^i(t,x)=v_{\lambda_i}(T-t,x^i)
+\frac{\varepsilon}{N-1}\sum_{j\ne i}w_{\lambda_j}(T-t,x^j)\] is the exact Nash solution with terminal data [eq:labelg] (#eq:labelg). Its own derivative is \(v'_{\lambda_i}\); the remaining terms cancel the other-player transport in [eq:nash] (#eq:nash).

Choose \(\lambda_1=\lambda'_1=0\), all other labels one versus zero, and all states zero. At any fixed \(s>0\), \(w_0(s,0)=0\), whereas \[w_1(s,0)=\frac{\mathbb E[S e^{-S/2}]}{\mathbb E[e^{-S/2}]}<0,
\qquad S=\sin(\sqrt2 B_s).\] The symmetric law gives \(\mathbb E[S e^{-S/2}]=-\mathbb E[S\sinh(S/2)]<0\). The value difference is therefore \(\varepsilon|w_1(s,0)|>0\), independent of \(N\); the asserted right side is \(C\sqrt{N-1}/N\). At \(s=1,\varepsilon=1/4\), independent quadrature gives approximately \(0.05956859624\).
## Repair and limits

The summation on p. 52 is an \(\ell^1\) sum. Its consistent scale is \[C\left(|\lambda_1-\lambda'_1|
+\frac1N\sum_{j>1}|\lambda_j-\lambda'_j|\right)
\le C\left(|\lambda_1-\lambda'_1|
+\frac{|\widehat\lambda-\widehat\lambda'|_2}{\sqrt N}\right).\] At \(\tau=T\), (7.3) would also force \(D_i(g_\lambda^i-g_{\lambda'}^i)=0\), contradicted by [eq:labelg] (#eq:labelg) when the own label changes. The terminal derivative must be retained before short-interval iteration.

The corrected counting scale is compatible with the Wasserstein continuity in Theorem 7.5, and a single-label change still has scale \(N^{-1}\). However, a valid componentwise gradient estimate with its terminal data must be supplied; a full replacement gradient proof is not certified here. The false statement is Lemma 7.1 as written, not the heterogeneous limit theorem.
# Conditional couplings and empirical weights

Problem 4 (Two coupling corrections in Lemma 7.13; Minor).  The all-label estimate (7.25), p. 60, lacks a label-distance term, and the coupling PDE there has the opposite mixed-diffusion sign from a synchronous coupling.

The lemma permits any bounded drift Lipschitz in \((\lambda,x,\mu)\). Take \(d=1\), \(B^\lambda=\lambda\), uniform label law \(\rho\) on \([0,1]\), and \(\mu_0=\widetilde\mu_0=\rho\otimes\delta_0\). All initial conditionals equal \(\delta_0\), while at time \(t\) they are \(\mathcal N(\lambda t,2t)\). Therefore \[W_2(m_t^\lambda,m_t^{\lambda'})=t|\lambda-\lambda'|,\] although the right side of (7.25) is zero. A term \(C|\lambda-\lambda'|\) is necessary.

Problem 5 (Missing label cost in Lemma 7.15; Minor).  After (7.32), p. 64, the squared joint label-state Wasserstein distance caused by changing population weights is bounded by \(2\max_i|X^i|^2\sum_k|a_k-\theta_k|\), where \(a_k=\#I_k^N/N\).

Take labels \(0,1\), target weights \(1/2,1/2\), zero initial states, zero costs and drift, and an alternating partition. At every odd \(N\), each weight differs from the target by \(1/(2N)\). All moment hypotheses hold, including \(q>4\), and the natural densities are correct. At time zero, \[W_2^2\left(a_1\delta_{(0,0)}+a_2\delta_{(1,0)},
\tfrac12\delta_{(0,0)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(1,0)}\right)=\frac1{2N}>0,\] but the asserted upper bound is zero. This works for arbitrarily large \(N\).

Equation reference: eq:massrepair. A local repair also avoids any rate assumption on the counts. Put \(\eta_k=\delta_{\lambda_k}\otimes\nu_k\). Retain common masses \(\min(a_k,\theta_k)\) and couple the excess and deficit: \[
W_2^2\left(\sum_k a_k\eta_k,\sum_k\theta_k\eta_k\right)
\le2\sum_k|a_k-\theta_k|\int(1+|x|^2)\,d\nu_k(x).\] Indeed the moved mass is \(\tfrac12\sum_k|a_k-\theta_k|\). Its label cost is at most one per unit mass; on a product coupling of the remaining equal masses use \(|x-y|^2\le2|x|^2+2|y|^2\). This proves [eq:massrepair] (#eq:massrepair) with room in the constant.

Bounded drift supplies uniform individual and group-average second moments, but not a uniform bound for the maximum over independent Brownian particles. The average-moment bound converges in expectation for finitely many groups whenever \(a_k\to\theta_k\), as assumed. It corrects the error entering (7.34). The periodic partitions actually chosen later have a stronger count rate. Neither the convergence conclusion nor Theorem 7.11 is refuted.
# Matrix order and dimension dependence

Problem 6 (Three auxiliary matrix implications; Minor).  Remark 3.4 (p. 15), the equivalence following (9.8) (p. 75), and the Frobenius estimate below (9.9) (p. 76) require correction under the declared conventions.

For \(N=2,d=1\), take \[h^1(x)=\sin x^1\sin x^2,\qquad h^2(x)=-\sin x^1\sin x^2.\] Their \(\mathcal L\)-rectangular expressions cancel exactly. The zero-diagonal mixed matrix is \[\begin{pmatrix}0&c\\-c&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad c=\cos x^1\cos x^2.\] It has zero quadratic form but is not generally zero. Moreover \(D_{12}h^1(0)=1\), excluding the own-state-plus-other-state separation asserted in Remark 3.4. Only the symmetric part must vanish.

Likewise \(K=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) satisfies \(-0I\le K\le0I\) in that order, but \(\|K\|_{\rm op}=1\). Thus two-sided quadratic-form control is not equivalent to (9.8). The forward implication from the actual operator bound is valid and suffices for the following drift comparison.

Finally \(g^i(x)=\sin x^i\) satisfies (MF) with \(L_g=2\), independently of \(N\), but \[\sum_{i,j}\|D_{ji}g^i\|_\infty^2=N>2L_g^2\quad(N>8).\] Its gradient map still has operator norm at most one. In general, splitting diagonal and off-diagonal parts and using (MF) yields \[\|J_g\|_{\rm op}\le\|\operatorname{diag}J_g\|_{\rm op}
+\|J_g-\operatorname{diag}J_g\|_{\rm F}\le2L_g.\] Thus \(C_g^2\le4L_g^2\) suffices, without the false full-Frobenius estimate. The corrections preserve the needed \(N\) independence; no false general-Hamiltonian theorem is established.
# Representation formulae in the existence appendix

Problem 7 (Signs, Hamiltonian offsets and the heat kernel; Minor).  Theorem A.1, pp. 79–82, uses an incorrect representation (A.2) and a value bound omitting positive Hamiltonian offsets. Its kernel expansion and time integral on p. 80 also require correction.

Take \(d=1,\sigma=1,\beta=0\), \(f^i=g^i=0\), and \(H^i(x,p)=c+p^2/2\), \(c>0\). These satisfy smoothness, bounded-below, (H0), convexity, both zero-semimonotonicity alternatives and (MF), with arbitrarily large \(N\). The exact solution is \[u^i(t,x)=c(t-T),\qquad -\partial_tu^i+H^i(x,0)=0.\] Printed (A.2) gives \(c(T-t)\). The final supremum bound on p. 82 is zero because \(f=g=0\) and \((\inf H)^-=0\), although \(\sup|u^i|=cT\).

Along drift \(-D_pH\), the correct running cost is \[f^i-H^i(x^i,p)+D_pH^i(x^i,p)\cdot p,\] and the forward equation has \(-\sum_j\operatorname{div}_{x^j}(D_pH^j\,\rho)\). Convexity gives lower integrand bound \(f^i-H^i(x^i,0)\), rather than the positive sign on p. 82. The value estimate needs the positive part of \(H^i(\cdot,0)\) as well as its negative lower bound. Such dependence is compatible with fixed-Hamiltonian continuation constants; the example itself is a regular solution and does not refute existence or uniqueness.

The backward Duhamel integral is \(\int_t^T\Phi(s-t)*(f-w(s))\,ds\); the printed \(w(s-t)\) may lie outside its domain \([\tau,T]\). These are local formula corrections. A value bound can be restored with the indicated Hamiltonian dependence, but external Schauder and continuation inputs are not all reproved here.
# Quantifiers in the compactness lemma

Problem 8 (Arbitrary metric parameter spaces; Minor).  Lemma 7.3 (pp. 52–53) assumes an arbitrary metric space \(\Gamma\), yet asserts one subsequence converging on every compact subset of \(\Gamma\times\mathcal P_p(E)\).

Let \(\Gamma=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) carry the discrete metric, \(E=\mathbb R\), and \(h_N(\gamma,v)=\gamma_N\). These functions are symmetric in \(v\), bounded by one, and satisfy (7.4) with concave moduli \(\omega(r)=r\). For any proposed subsequence \(N_k\), choose a single \(\gamma\) with \(\gamma_{N_k}=k\bmod2\). The sets \(H=\{\gamma\}\) and \(K=\{\delta_0\}\) are compact, but \(h_{N_k}(\gamma,0)\) alternates, disproving the conclusion.

Separability of \(\Gamma\) is sufficient: \(\mathcal P_p(E)\) is separable, and a dense-set diagonal subsequence plus equicontinuity gives uniform convergence on every compact set. The actual application on p. 54 has \(\Gamma=[0,T]\times[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\), which satisfies the added condition. This repairs the general statement without refuting the application’s compactness conclusion.
# Assessment and limits

Problems Problem 1 (#prob:drift) and Problem 2 (#prob:hyp) are Major for distinct reasons: an invalid core invocation and a literal theorem hypothesis admitting a counterexample. The intended corrected inviscid theorem is not declared false. Problems Problem 3 (#prob:labels)–Problem 8 (#prob:compact) are Minor within the repair boundaries proved above. The componentwise label-gradient replacement and the sigma-uniform weighted-gradient argument remain revision tasks.

The reading covered the positive-noise derivative estimates, both semimonotonicity bootstraps, heterogeneous limits, general Hamiltonians and both appendices. This is a bounded initial technical review, not a formal certification of all calculations or all cited external theorems. No additional unproved suspicion is promoted to a finding, and no whole-paper failure is inferred from the local errors.

claim:
Equation reference: eq:nash, eq:weight. For quadratic Hamiltonians, the backward system is \[
-\partial_t u^i-\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\sigma I+\beta J)D^2u^i\bigr)
+\frac12|D_i u^i|^2+\sum_{j\ne i}D_j u^j\cdot D_j u^i=f^i,
\qquad u^i(T,\cdot)=g^i.\] Here \(J=J_N\otimes I_d\), \(\sigma>0,\beta\ge0\). The paper uses Euclidean vector norms and quadratic-form matrix order even for nonsymmetric matrices. Its distinguished weighted norm is \[
\|x\|_i^2=|x^i|^2+\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}|x^j|^2.\] The mean-field conditions (MF) control own-state and off-diagonal derivatives with different powers of \(N\); they do not uniformly bound the full Frobenius norm of a diagonal matrix.

The \(\mathcal D\)-condition controls the one-sided Lipschitz constant of \(x\mapsto(D_i h^i(x))_i\). The \(\mathcal L\)-condition concerns sums of four-point rectangular differences. Neither supplies symmetry of the mixed Jacobian. Theorems 3.8 and A.1 require small semimonotonicity constants and large \(N\), with additional convexity hypotheses for general Hamiltonians. The heterogeneous limit requires bounded smooth data, symmetry in other players’ states, and label regularity (LP). Section 7 sets \(\sigma=1,\beta=0\); Section 8 instead takes \(\sigma=\sigma_N\downarrow0\) with a lower bound on \(\sigma_N\log\log N\).

The principal dependency requiring further work is the application of Lemma 4.3 in Proposition 8.1 to obtain a gradient bound independent of \(N\) and \(\sigma_N\). Problems 1 and 2 concern different aspects of that argument and its statement. The remaining problems have more local repair boundaries.

analysis: Remark 4.4 (p. 30) extends Lemma 4.3 to transport \(\sum_j b^jD_j u^i\) assuming only the Euclidean one-sided condition (4.2). Proposition 8.1 (p. 69), deriving (8.4), directly applies the weighted estimate to \(D_i u^i\), saying that only the forcing condition (4.3) remains to be checked.

Take \(d=1,i=1,\sigma=1,\beta=0,N\ge2\), and fixed \(a>0\). Set \[b(x)=(a\sin x^2,0,\ldots,0),\qquad f=0,\qquad g(x)=\sin x^1.\] The drift and data are bounded and smooth. The eigenvalues of the nonzero block of \((Db+Db^\top)/2\) are \(\pm a\cos(x^2)/2\), so (4.2) holds with \(M=a/2\), independent of \(N\). The weighted Lipschitz constant of \(g\) is one.

Equation reference: eq:driftex. In forward time \(s=T-t\), consider the two-variable periodic solution \[
v_s-\Delta v+\frac12(v_{x^1})^2+a\sin(x^2)v_{x^1}=0,
\qquad v(0,x)=\sin x^1.\] It exists smoothly on a fixed short interval independently of \(N\): the heat-semigroup integral equation is a contraction in a bounded \(C^1\) ball for small time, because the gradient kernel has integrable \(s^{-1/2}\) norm and the quadratic term is locally Lipschitz there. Smooth data give the needed initial derivatives. Extend the solution constantly in the other coordinates.

Proof. At \(s=0\), \[v_s=-\sin x^1-\tfrac12\cos^2x^1-a\sin x^2\cos x^1,
\qquad \partial_s\partial_{x^2}v(0,0)=-a.\] Thus \(\partial_{x^2}v(s_*,0)\ne0\) for a fixed small \(s_*>0\). The proposed weighted bound, with \(c_1\) depending only on dimension-independent quantities, implies \[|\partial_{x^2}v(s_*,0)|\le c_1N^{-1/2}.\] Its left side is independent of \(N\) and nonzero, a contradiction. Omitting the quadratic term gives the same initial jet and refutes the linear-transport reading as well. ◻

If a separate \(\mathcal D[u]\) lower bound is retained in this reading, take the other components to be zero: the smooth solution has only a fixed two-dimensional nonzero Jacobian block and a uniform lower symmetric-part bound.
result: The original Nash-specific Lemma 4.3 is not refuted. At its doubling maximum, (4.6)–(4.7) give equality of the distinguished derivatives and allow the own-component cancellation in (4.9)–(4.10), pp. 28–29. Arbitrary \(b\) lacks that cancellation.

The counterexample is not asserted to be the actual Nash drift in Proposition 8.1. Its extra structure may support a different argument. Nevertheless, the false general extension does not justify the componentwise invocation, and checking only the forcing term does not establish a weighted drift hypothesis. A new game-specific gradient argument or a verified weighted one-sided estimate is needed for the \(\sigma\)-uniform compactness used on p. 70. No complete replacement proof or counterexample to the intended final theorem is claimed.

analysis:
Equation (3.9), p. 23, contains \[\sum_i\bigl(D_xF(x^i,m_{x^{-i}})
-D_xF(x^i,m_{y^{-i}})\bigr)\cdot(x^i-y^i)\ge-M|x-y|^2.\] Theorem 3.17 (p. 24) expressly invokes this assumption for \(F\) and \(G\).

Take \(d=1,T=2,H=p^2/2,\beta=0,F=0\), and \(G(x,m)=\cos x\). All spatial derivatives are bounded and smooth and all measure derivatives vanish, so Remark 3.15’s regularity conditions hold. The printed left side of (3.9) is identically zero. For sufficiently large \(N\), choose \(\sigma_N=(\log\log N)^{-1/2}\). Then \(\sigma_N\to0\) and \(\sigma_N\log\log N\to\infty\), meeting any finite threshold; the finitely many smaller terms may be positive arbitrarily.

Equation reference: eq:cole. The uncoupled exact Cole–Hopf solution is \[
v_\sigma(s,x)=-2\sigma\log\left[
(4\pi\sigma s)^{-1/2}\int_\mathbb R
e^{-[\cos y+(x-y)^2/(2s)]/(2\sigma)}\,dy\right].\] It is bounded and smooth on finite time intervals. As \(\sigma\downarrow0\), \[v_\sigma(s,x)\longrightarrow V(s,x)=\min_y\{\cos y+(x-y)^2/(2s)\}.\] This follows by elementary Laplace upper and lower bounds near minimizers and outside a fixed compact interval; the quadratic term confines the minimizers and controls the tails. No derivative convergence is assumed.

Proof. At \(s=2,x=0\), let \(\phi(y)=\cos y+y^2/4\). Then \(\phi''(0)=-1/2\). Positive critical points satisfy \(y=2\sin y\); strict decrease of \(\sin y/y\) on \((0,\pi)\) gives one positive nonzero solution \(a\). Outside \([-\pi,\pi]\), \(\phi(y)\ge-1+\pi^2/4>1=\phi(0)\), so the global minimizers are precisely \(\pm a\). The tilt \(-xy/2\) selects \(a\) on the right and \(-a\) on the left. Hence \[\partial_x^-V(2,0)=a/2,\qquad \partial_x^+V(2,0)=-a/2.\] Independent computation gives \(a\approx1.895494267033981\) and \(\phi(a)\approx0.5792021049470533\). Thus the value limit is not differentiable, contrary to the bounded Lipschitz derivative required by Theorem 3.17 and (3.11), even along a subsequence. ◻

The description \(\mathcal D\)-semimonotonicity and Section 8’s invocation of Proposition 5.1 strongly suggest replacing the second \(x^i\) in (3.9) by \(y^i\). Under that correction, \(G''\ge-1\) gives a nonzero constant, and the intended smallness condition at \(T=2\) excludes the example. Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence. Proof: Choose F=0 and G(x,m)=cos(x), independent of m. All measure derivatives vanish; all spatial derivatives are bounded. Printed (3.9) uses x_i in both terms, so its left side is identically zero. Choose sigma_N=(log log N)^(-1/2) for sufficiently large N. The uncoupled Cole-Hopf solutions converge to V(s,x)=min_y{cos(y)+(x-y)^2/(2s)}, s=T-t. Recorded check: Nonsymmetric matrix order does not imply the claimed vanishing or norm equivalence
analysis: Remark 3.4 (p. 15), the equivalence following (9.8) (p. 75), and the Frobenius estimate below (9.9) (p. 76) require correction under the declared conventions.

For \(N=2,d=1\), take \[h^1(x)=\sin x^1\sin x^2,\qquad h^2(x)=-\sin x^1\sin x^2.\] Their \(\mathcal L\)-rectangular expressions cancel exactly. The zero-diagonal mixed matrix is \[\begin{pmatrix}0&c\\-c&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad c=\cos x^1\cos x^2.\] It has zero quadratic form but is not generally zero. Moreover \(D_{12}h^1(0)=1\), excluding the own-state-plus-other-state separation asserted in Remark 3.4. Only the symmetric part must vanish.

Likewise \(K=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) satisfies \(-0I\le K\le0I\) in that order, but \(\|K\|_{\rm op}=1\). Thus two-sided quadratic-form control is not equivalent to (9.8). The forward implication from the actual operator bound is valid and suffices for the following drift comparison.

Finally \(g^i(x)=\sin x^i\) satisfies (MF) with \(L_g=2\), independently of \(N\), but \[\sum_{i,j}\|D_{ji}g^i\|_\infty^2=N>2L_g^2\quad(N>8).\] Its gradient map still has operator norm at most one. In general, splitting diagonal and off-diagonal parts and using (MF) yields \[\|J_g\|_{\rm op}\le\|\operatorname{diag}J_g\|_{\rm op}
+\|J_g-\operatorname{diag}J_g\|_{\rm F}\le2L_g.\] Thus \(C_g^2\le4L_g^2\) suffices, without the false full-Frobenius estimate. The corrections preserve the needed \(N\) independence; no false general-Hamiltonian theorem is established.

claim:
Equation reference: eq:nash, eq:weight. For quadratic Hamiltonians, the backward system is \[
-\partial_t u^i-\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\sigma I+\beta J)D^2u^i\bigr)
+\frac12|D_i u^i|^2+\sum_{j\ne i}D_j u^j\cdot D_j u^i=f^i,
\qquad u^i(T,\cdot)=g^i.\] Here \(J=J_N\otimes I_d\), \(\sigma>0,\beta\ge0\). The paper uses Euclidean vector norms and quadratic-form matrix order even for nonsymmetric matrices. Its distinguished weighted norm is \[
\|x\|_i^2=|x^i|^2+\frac1N\sum_{j\ne i}|x^j|^2.\] The mean-field conditions (MF) control own-state and off-diagonal derivatives with different powers of \(N\); they do not uniformly bound the full Frobenius norm of a diagonal matrix.

The \(\mathcal D\)-condition controls the one-sided Lipschitz constant of \(x\mapsto(D_i h^i(x))_i\). The \(\mathcal L\)-condition concerns sums of four-point rectangular differences. Neither supplies symmetry of the mixed Jacobian. Theorems 3.8 and A.1 require small semimonotonicity constants and large \(N\), with additional convexity hypotheses for general Hamiltonians. The heterogeneous limit requires bounded smooth data, symmetry in other players’ states, and label regularity (LP). Section 7 sets \(\sigma=1,\beta=0\); Section 8 instead takes \(\sigma=\sigma_N\downarrow0\) with a lower bound on \(\sigma_N\log\log N\).

The principal dependency requiring further work is the application of Lemma 4.3 in Proposition 8.1 to obtain a gradient bound independent of \(N\) and \(\sigma_N\). Problems 1 and 2 concern different aspects of that argument and its statement. The remaining problems have more local repair boundaries.

analysis: Theorem A.1, pp. 79–82, uses an incorrect representation (A.2) and a value bound omitting positive Hamiltonian offsets. Its kernel expansion and time integral on p. 80 also require correction.

Take \(d=1,\sigma=1,\beta=0\), \(f^i=g^i=0\), and \(H^i(x,p)=c+p^2/2\), \(c>0\). These satisfy smoothness, bounded-below, (H0), convexity, both zero-semimonotonicity alternatives and (MF), with arbitrarily large \(N\). The exact solution is \[u^i(t,x)=c(t-T),\qquad -\partial_tu^i+H^i(x,0)=0.\] Printed (A.2) gives \(c(T-t)\). The final supremum bound on p. 82 is zero because \(f=g=0\) and \((\inf H)^-=0\), although \(\sup|u^i|=cT\).

Along drift \(-D_pH\), the correct running cost is \[f^i-H^i(x^i,p)+D_pH^i(x^i,p)\cdot p,\] and the forward equation has \(-\sum_j\operatorname{div}_{x^j}(D_pH^j\,\rho)\). Convexity gives lower integrand bound \(f^i-H^i(x^i,0)\), rather than the positive sign on p. 82. The value estimate needs the positive part of \(H^i(\cdot,0)\) as well as its negative lower bound. Such dependence is compatible with fixed-Hamiltonian continuation constants; the example itself is a regular solution and does not refute existence or uniqueness.

The backward Duhamel integral is \(\int_t^T\Phi(s-t)*(f-w(s))\,ds\); the printed \(w(s-t)\) may lie outside its domain \([\tau,T]\). These are local formula corrections. A value bound can be restored with the indicated Hamiltonian dependence, but external Schauder and continuation inputs are not all reproved here.

Recorded check: Compactness lemma lacks a separability condition on the parameter space
analysis: Lemma 7.3 (pp. 52–53) assumes an arbitrary metric space \(\Gamma\), yet asserts one subsequence converging on every compact subset of \(\Gamma\times\mathcal P_p(E)\).

Let \(\Gamma=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) carry the discrete metric, \(E=\mathbb R\), and \(h_N(\gamma,v)=\gamma_N\). These functions are symmetric in \(v\), bounded by one, and satisfy (7.4) with concave moduli \(\omega(r)=r\). For any proposed subsequence \(N_k\), choose a single \(\gamma\) with \(\gamma_{N_k}=k\bmod2\). The sets \(H=\{\gamma\}\) and \(K=\{\delta_0\}\) are compact, but \(h_{N_k}(\gamma,0)\) alternates, disproving the conclusion.

Separability of \(\Gamma\) is sufficient: \(\mathcal P_p(E)\) is separable, and a dense-set diagonal subsequence plus equicontinuity gives uniform convergence on every compact set. The actual application on p. 54 has \(\Gamma=[0,T]\times[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\), which satisfies the added condition. This repairs the general statement without refuting the application’s compactness conclusion.
