report: Abstract: Eight supported problems are reported for the acquired 72-page manuscript: a counterexample to the literal finite-height localization, an incorrect transport hierarchy, two false auxiliary energy bounds, a nonmonotone truncation argument, a derivative-budget gap, false uniform amplitude dependence in a corollary, and two local algebraic or mollifier defects. The first six problems affect a stated core estimate or its derivation and are classified Major; the last two are Minor. Additional norm-power slips within Problem 6 are local Minor subfindings. These classifications do not assert failure of every principal theorem. The global first-order estimate and intended mean-field limit theorem are not refuted here. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: Bounded scientific review: M25-0424

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Sharp Commutator Estimates of All Order
for Coulomb and Riesz Modulated Energies
# Identity, version, and scope

The reviewed paper is by Matthew Rosenzweig and Sylvia Serfaty [source], Sharp commutator estimates of all order for Coulomb and Riesz modulated energies, DOI https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70010. The acquired source is arXiv:2407.15650v2, dated 28 October 2025, 72 pages. Page numbers below are the printed and physical PDF page numbers, which agree. The preserved original review records a complete reading of every page, including Appendix A and the references. This continuation reuses that documented scope and checks the eight existing problems against the bound source and retained evidence. The examined PDF has SHA256 `0b6f9013592e6d07054c32766cfb89860cbb97553c3a7a4775d2f046dfc9e70b`.

The arXiv record labels this version final and lists v1 and v2. The author’s publication page identifies the eventual journal publication as volume 79, issue 2 (2026), pp. 207–292 [authorrecord]. The publisher’s indexed record gives first publication on 24 September 2025 [publisherrecord]. The annual task’s 2025 identity is retained; the acquired manuscript is not silently replaced by a different journal PDF. A full publisher-page retrieval failed. Indexed publisher text corroborates the fixed-\(v\) definitions and transport identity discussed in Problem 2, but it does not establish whole-document equivalence.

The source itself, p. 29, footnote 4, states that an editing discrepancy in the journal’s (3.46) and subsequent computations is corrected in this version. That correction was read and visually checked. The already corrected journal discrepancy is not counted as a new problem here. Targeted checks of the arXiv, publisher, and author records did not identify a further correction addressing the findings below; this limited search does not prove that none exists.
# Framework and checked hypotheses

Write \[\nu_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{x_i}-\mu,\qquad
 K_n(x,y)=\nabla^{\otimes n}g(x-y):(v(x)-v(y))^{\otimes n}.\] The energy integrals in the statements remove the particle diagonal. The logarithmic examples use \(g=-\log|\cdot|\). The three-dimensional Coulomb example uses \(g=|\cdot|^{-1}\). Thus their normalizations agree with the source. The extension has \(k=1,\gamma=0\) for \(d=1,s=0\), and \(k=0\) for the Coulomb cases \(d=2,s=0\) and \(d=3,s=1\).

Theorem 1.2 assumes \(\mu\in L^1\cap L^\infty\), mass one, and absolute logarithmic interaction integrability when \(s=0\). It does not assume \(\mu\geq0\); the removal of nonnegativity is explicitly discussed on p. 17. It sets \(\lambda=(N\left\lVert \mu\right\rVert_{L^\infty(\Omega)})^{-1/d}<1\). For (1.12), \(\Omega\) contains the \(2\lambda\)-neighborhood of \(\operatorname{supp}\nabla v\), with \(v\) Lipschitz. For (1.13), the additional assumptions include \(v\in C^{2n-1,1}\), a ball \(\Omega'\) of radius \(\ell\) containing a neighborhood of \(\operatorname{supp}v\), and a \(5\ell\)-neighborhood of \(\Omega'\) in \(\Omega\). Section 5 uses a \(2\lambda\)-neighborhood instead of the statement’s \(\lambda\)-neighborhood; the examples below satisfy the stronger condition whenever Section 5 is used. All particle configurations used here are pairwise distinct, and all backgrounds in the discrete examples are bounded and compactly supported. Their absolute logarithmic integrals are therefore finite.
# Substantive problems

Problem 1 (Finite-height localization without compact support: Major).  The literal estimate (1.12), p. 5, is false for the stated signed-background class and a Lipschitz field whose derivative has compact support but whose values do not vanish at infinity.
## Decisive example and complete verification

Take \(d=1,s=0,N=2\), \(\Omega=[-3,3]\), and \(\ell=3\). Fix a smooth bounded field \(v\) which is \(-1\) on \((-\infty,-1]\), zero on \([-1/2,1/2]\), and \(1\) on \([1,\infty)\); its two transitions are confined to the remaining intervals. Set, for \(R>10\) and an integer \(j\geq1\), \[\begin{aligned}
 x_1&=R-\tfrac14,&x_2&=R+\tfrac14,\\
 p_R(y)&=2\,\mathbf1_{[-R-1/4,-R+1/4]}(y),&
 q_j(y)&=8\cos(2\pi j y)\,\mathbf1_{[-1/2,1/2]}(y),&
 \mu_{R,j}&=p_R+q_j .\end{aligned}\] The background has mass one and belongs to \(L^1\cap L^\infty\). Its local and global essential supremum norms are exactly 8, independently of \(R,j\). Thus \(\lambda=1/16\), the required \(2\lambda\)-neighborhood of \(\operatorname{supp}v'\) is contained in \(\Omega\), and \(\ell>\lambda\). Neither particle belongs to \(\Omega\), so \(\#I_\Omega=0\). The source radii (2.17) are both \(r_i=1/64\). On \(Q=[-3,3]\times[-3,3]\), truncation leaves their potentials unchanged.

Equation reference: eq:localcounter, eq:localenergy. Since \(v=0\) on \(\operatorname{supp}q_j\), its self-commutator vanishes exactly. All its interactions with the other two supports tend to zero by oscillatory weak convergence against smooth separated kernels. Taking \(j\to\infty\) at a fixed \(R\), the commutator in (1.12) therefore tends to \[
 I_R=2\sum_{a=R\pm1/4}\int\frac{p_R(y)}{a-y}\,\mathrm dy
     =4\log\frac{2R+1/2}{2R-1/2}\sim\frac2R .\] Let \(h_R=g*(\tfrac12\delta_{x_1}+\tfrac12\delta_{x_2}-p_R)\). Every source point is horizontally at least \(R-13/4\) from \(Q\). The total variation of this source is 2 and \(|\nabla g(X)|=|X|^{-1}\); hence \[
 \int_Q|\nabla h_R|^2\leq\frac{144}{(R-13/4)^2}.\] If (1.12) held with its stated universal constant, the \(j\)-limit would give \(I_R\leq C\left\lVert v'\right\rVert_\infty\,144/(R-13/4)^2\) for every \(R\). The left side is of order \(R^{-1}\) and the right side is of order \(R^{-2}\), an impossibility. This is an analytic counterexample sequence, not an inference from finite numerical samples.
## Origin, alternate readings, and impact

Remark 3.1, p. 23, uses \(\widetilde v(x,z)=\chi(z/\ell)(v(x),0)\). Its vertical derivative contains \(\ell^{-1}\chi'(z/\ell)v(x)\), which remains nonzero on a nonzero plateau where \(v'(x)=0\). Thus the support replacement invoked in the local arguments on pp. 27 and 31 is unavailable for this field. The compact support premise needed for (3.5) is absent from the first part of Theorem 1.2.

A natural repair route is to retain the full vertical domain \(\Omega\times\mathbb R^k\) with the trivial extension. Another is to impose the compact-support and domain hypotheses needed by the cutoff proof and use the actual support of \(\nabla\widetilde v\). A full replacement theorem under either amended set of assumptions is not certified here. A nonnegative-background-only statement would also exclude this particular counterexample, but that is a genuine restriction of the printed class. A fixed finite change to \(\ell\) does not repair the \(R^{-1}\) versus \(R^{-2}\) discrepancy. The example does not refute the compactly supported higher-order estimate, the global estimate (1.7), or the mean-field application of that global estimate.

Problem 2 (The transported commutator hierarchy omits a chain-rule term: Major).  Equations (1.31)–(1.32), p. 8, and Lemma A.3, especially (A.6)–(A.10), p. 63, use an incorrect transport identity for the explicitly fixed field \(v\).
## Exact differentiation

Equation reference: eq:correcttransport. For the source definition \[\kappa_t^m(x)=\int\nabla^{\otimes m}g(x-y-tv(y)):
                        (v(x)-v(y))^{\otimes m}\,\mathrm df(y),\] differentiation gives, for \(m\geq1\), \[\begin{aligned}

 (\partial_t+v\cdot\nabla)\kappa_t^m
  ={}&\kappa_t^{m+1}\\
 &+m\int\nabla^{\otimes m}g(x-y-tv(y)):
 \bigl((v\cdot\nabla v)(x)\otimes
       (v(x)-v(y))^{\otimes(m-1)}\bigr)\,\mathrm df(y).\nonumber\end{aligned}\] The last term differentiates the factors \(v(x)-v(y)\). It is absent from (A.7). For \(m=1\), it is exactly \((v\cdot\nabla v)(x)\cdot\nabla h_t(x)\).

This defect occurs with all the qualitative conventions used in the source. Take \(d=3,s=1\), and a smooth compactly supported \(v\) equal to \(x\) on \(B(0,3)\). Let \(\widehat\psi\) be an even, nonnegative smooth function supported in \(1<|\xi|<2\) with \(\int \xi_1^2\widehat\psi(\xi)\,\mathrm d\xi>0\). Choose \(a>0\) so that \(h(x)=a\,\partial_1\psi(x-e_1)\) satisfies \(\partial_1h(e_1)=-2\), and set \(f=-\Delta h/(4\pi)\). Then \(f\) is Schwartz, has zero mean, has Fourier support away from zero, and \(g*f=h\), since \(-\Delta g=4\pi\delta_0\). At \(x=e_1,t=0\), the omitted term is exactly \(-2\). Thus even the standing Fourier-gap convention after (3.21), p. 25, does not eliminate the counterexample.

For transparent independent arithmetic, one may also take \(f=\phi-\phi(\,\cdot-2e_1)\), with \(\phi\) a radial smooth unit-mass bump in \(B(0,1/4)\). Newton’s identity gives, near \(x=e_1\) on the axis, \[\kappa_t^1(xe_1)=-\frac1x+\frac{2-x}{(2+2t-x)^2}.\] At \(x=1,t=0\), direct differentiation gives \(\partial_t\kappa_t^1=-4\), \(v\cdot\nabla\kappa_t^1=2\), and \(\kappa_0^2=0\). The discrepancy is again \(-2\). This second example illustrates the calculation; the preceding annular Fourier construction meets the additional Fourier-support convention exactly.
## Dependency and repair boundary

Lemma A.5 uses (A.7) in (A.16), p. 64; Lemma A.7 and the proof of Proposition A.1 on pp. 67–69 then use that representation. Therefore the advertised alternative proof is not valid as written. Introducing the transported velocity \(v_t=v\circ(I+tv)^{-1}\), which satisfies a Burgers transport relation, can cancel a corresponding acceleration term in a different hierarchy. It does not validate (A.6) with its fixed \(v\); definitions and the coefficient induction would have to be redone. Section 4 supplies a separate PDE approach, so this finding does not by itself falsify the estimate in Proposition A.1 or the principal estimates.

Problem 3 (Two false auxiliary energy bounds in the local renormalization: Major).  The integral in Lemma 5.1, (5.7), p. 51, can contain an unsmeared particle singularity. Independently, the global neutral-cell bound (5.40), p. 55, fails for the logarithmic kernel even for nonnegative backgrounds.
## An infinite left side in Lemma 5.1

Section 5 sets \(\eta_i=r_i/2\) for \(x_i\in\Omega'\) and \(\eta_i=0\) otherwise, explicitly leaving the other particles as Dirac masses ((5.1), p. 50). Yet (5.7) integrates \(|z|^\gamma|\nabla\bar h_{N,\vec\eta}|^2\) over \((\operatorname{supp}\nabla\widetilde v)\cup(\Omega\times[-\lambda,\lambda]^k)\).

Take \(d=1,s=0,N=2\), \(\mu=\mathbf1_{[-1/2,1/2]}\), particles \(0,4\), a smooth \(v\) supported in \([-1,1]\), \(\Omega'=[-3,3]\), and \(\Omega=[-18,18]\). Here \(\ell=3,\lambda=1/2\); all the stronger Section 5 neighborhood conditions hold. The particle at 4 lies in \(\Omega\setminus\Omega'\) and is not smeared. Near \(X=(4,0)\), \[\bar h_{N,\vec\eta}(X)=-\tfrac12\log|X-(4,0)|+H(X),
 \qquad H\ \hbox{smooth there}.\] The energy on an annulus of radii \(\varepsilon,\varepsilon_0\) is \((\pi/2)\log(\varepsilon_0/\varepsilon)+O(1)\), and diverges. The right side \(\Xi\) in (5.2) is finite: it uses \(h_{N,\vec r}\), which truncates both particles at positive radii. The closing appeal to (2.30) on p. 52 cannot remedy the unsmeared point.
## A separated logarithmic cell with unbounded global energy

Now take \(d=2,s=0,N=2\), particles \(0,e_1\), \(\Omega'=\overline{B(0,3)}\), \(\Omega=\overline{B(0,18)}\), and a fixed smooth \(v\) supported in \(B(0,1)\). Let \(
u_b\) be the uniform probability density on the disk of radius \(1/10\) centered at \(b\), and, for \(R>50\), set \[\mu_R=	frac14
u_0+	frac14
u_{Re_1}
                         +	frac12
u_{3Re_1}.\] This is a nonnegative bounded probability density. In \(\Omega\) its essential supremum is \(25/\pi\), so \(\lambda=\sqrt{\pi/50}<1\), independently of \(R\). The radii \(\eta_i=\lambda/8\) are fixed. Choose a fixed radial smooth unit-mass mollifier at this scale with the required vanishing moments. Such a signed mollifier can be obtained from two radial dilates with coefficients \(4/3,-1/3\), which cancel the second moments. Its support can be made smaller than \(\eta_i/2\).
## Other hypotheses, dependency, and bounded repair

The two examples are independent and use nonnegative \(\mu\). The printed theorem’s larger signed class presents an additional issue: \(\int_{B(x_i,R_i)}\mu=1/N\) does not bound \(\int_{B(x_i,R_i)}|\mu|\), as needed when estimating the integrals in (5.28)–(5.39). Signed moment-cancelling mollifiers likewise require total-variation constants instead of a probability-density argument.

Lemma 5.1 is used in the estimate of the smeared term and in the passage after (5.45), p. 56. The neutral-cell estimate enters the local regularity step for Term 2. One must restrict the energy to regions without unsmeared singularities and retain a genuinely local cell norm, or supply another valid estimate. Merely enlarging a local norm to the global energy loses the logarithmic cancellation illustrated above. These counterexamples invalidate the displayed auxiliary bounds and their current uses; they do not prove that the intended high-order commutator estimate is false. Section 5.4’s global treatment uses a different, cruder Term 2 estimate and is not refuted by [eq:logcell] (#eq:logcell) alone.

Problem 4 (The mesoscale truncation path is not monotone: Major).  The monotonicity used between (2.46) and (2.47), p. 21, does not follow from Lemma 2.2. It is false for the path (2.44), even after correcting the fixed-potential typo in (2.45).
## Exact counterevidence to the proof step

The path chooses \(\eta_i^k=2^k\lambda\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(x_i,\partial\Omega)\geq2^k\lambda\), and otherwise resets it to \(r_i\). A point at distance \(3\lambda\), with \(r_i=\lambda/4\), therefore has the successive radii \[\lambda,\quad2\lambda,\quad\lambda/4 .\] This is not a coordinatewise increasing path.

The issue is not only logical. In \(d=3,s=1\), take the half-space \(\Omega=\{x_3\geq0\}\), particles \(x_1=(0,0,3\lambda)\), \(x_2=(3\lambda,0,3\lambda)\), and \(0<\lambda<1\). Put a bounded probability density of height \(1/(2\lambda^3)\) in a cube of volume \(2\lambda^3\), far from these particles and their balls but inside \(\Omega\). This makes the prescribed local scale exactly \(\lambda\), and \(r_i=\lambda/4\). All balls of radius \(2\lambda\) stay in \(\Omega\).

As printed, (2.45) also retains \(h_{N,\vec r}\) instead of \(h_{N,\vec\eta}\). Its energy term then does not vary with \(\vec\eta\). With the background outside all truncation balls, even increasing the radii makes the negative self-energy term increase. Replacing this potential is necessary but leaves the reset obstruction above. For \(k=1\), the preceding vertical-domain replacement additionally uses coincidence only above height \(2^{k+2}\lambda\), which can exceed \(\ell\); the asserted replacement by a slab of height \(\ell\) requires a separate justification.
## Dependency and repair boundary

Proposition 2.5, pp. 20–23, is invoked in (5.14), (5.57), and the later macroscopic estimates. A proof must use admissible comparisons on a fixed interior set, or separately estimate the reset terms and the vertical tails. No completed replacement argument is supplied here. There is also a local sign error in (2.53): for \(f/g=t^{-a}\), its derivative is \(-at^{-a-1}\), which is at most, not at least, \(-a(2^k\lambda)^{-a-1}\) on the interval. For \(\lambda=1/10,a=1,k=2,t=1/10\), the two values are \(-100\) and \(-25/4\). That particular inequality can be repaired with a factor \(4^{a+1}\); it does not repair the nonmonotone path.

Problem 5 (The stated high-order derivative budget is not obtained: Major).  Theorem 1.2, (1.13), p. 5, has undefined summation indices and a regularity budget not delivered by the estimates concluding its proof.
## Index and derivative calculation

The power of \(\lambda\) printed in (1.13) is \(\lambda^{-(n-p)+\sum_{k=1}^p c_{n-k}}\), while the only bound indices are \(c_1,\ldots,c_{n-p}\). At \(n=3,p=2\), the exponent uses \(c_2\), although only \(c_1\) is bound. At \(p=0\), the exponent loses every derivative order. This is not a defined general formula.

Correcting only that index does not settle the proof. Theorem 4.9, (4.119), p. 47, feeds into (5.34), p. 54, and (5.42), p. 55: \[A_{v,p}=\sum_{\substack{a_1,\ldots,a_{n-p}\geq0\\
                        \sum a_i\leq2n}}
 \lambda^{\sum a_i}\prod_{i=1}^{n-p}\left\lVert D^{1+a_i}v\right\rVert_\infty .\] The exact change \(b_i=1+a_i\) gives \[n-p\leq\sum b_i\leq3n-p,\qquad
 \lambda^{\sum a_i}=\lambda^{\sum b_i-(n-p)},\] whereas (1.13) has the upper bound \(2n\). In particular \(p=n-1,a_1=2n\) uses \(D^{2n+1}v\). The hypothesis \(C^{2n-1,1}\) controls derivatives through order \(2n\), not \(2n+1\).

This is a real loss of control, not an assertion that high derivatives must happen to be large for every field. For a fixed smooth compact cutoff \(\chi\) with a plateau, take \[v_J=v_0+J^{-2n}\chi(x)\sin(Jx)\] in one dimension, where \(v_0''\) is nonzero on that plateau. The \(C^{2n-1,1}\) norms stay bounded and the supports stay fixed, while \(\left\lVert D^{2n+1}v_J\right\rVert_\infty\) grows like \(J\). The multiplier \((\ell\left\lVert D^2v_J\right\rVert_\infty)^{n-1}\) of the relevant term in (5.47)/(5.61) does not tend to zero. For fixed admissible \(\lambda,\ell\), the resulting bound cannot be controlled by the printed derivative data.
## Impact and possible repair

The concluding assertion after (5.61), p. 58, therefore needs a sharper regularity argument or a corrected weaker theorem with the derivative budget actually proved. The convention \(A_{v,0}:=1\) printed after (5.42) also has the wrong endpoint: the empty product is at \(p=n\). These observations do not constitute a counterexample to an appropriately defined optimal high-order estimate. The Major classification concerns the missing derivation of the announced regularity and scale dependence.

Problem 6 (Uniform amplitude dependence in Corollary 1.3: Major).  Corollary 1.3, (1.14), p. 6, has \(CM\ell^{-n}\) with the inherited constant independent of \(M\). Its left side is homogeneous of degree \(n\) in the field, so \(M^n\) is required. Related squared-norm displays also lose a power.
## A nonzero example, rather than homogeneity alone

Take \(d=1,s=0,N=2\), \(\mu=\mathbf1_{[-1/2,1/2]}\), and particles \(-1/4,1/4\). Choose \(v_0\) smooth, equal to \(x\) on \([-2,2]\), and supported in \([-4,4]\), with \(\Omega'=[-6,6]\), \(\Omega=[-36,36]\), and \(\ell=6\). Here \(\lambda=1/2\), and even the stronger Section 5 neighborhood conditions hold. Put \(v_A=A v_0\) for \(A>0\). On all the relevant background and particle supports, \[K_n(x,y)=(-1)^n(n-1)!\,A^n,\qquad x\ne y.\] The total mass of \(\nu_N^{\otimes2}\) off the diagonal is \(-1/N\). In particular the signed \(n=2\) integral equals \(-A^2/2\), and its absolute value is \(A^2/2\). The energy bracket in (1.14) is finite and independent of \(A\). One can choose \(M=A M_0\), where \(M_0=\max_{0\leq k\leq4}\ell^k\left\lVert D^kv_0\right\rVert_\infty\). A bound linear in \(M\) cannot hold as \(A\to\infty\).

The source explicitly presents Corollary 1.3 as the precise scale and homogeneity consequence of (1.13), p. 5. The example therefore contradicts a stated quantitative guarantee tied to the central local estimate. This corollary component is Major under the core-contribution criterion. Replacing \(M\) by \(M^n\) restores the required homogeneity, but does not prove the other estimates needed for the corollary. Allowing the constant to depend on \(M\) would change its stated uniformity. The simplicity of the normalization repair does not remove this dependency.
## Local norm-power subfindings: Minor

The same scaling check shows that (1.26), p. 7, needs \(\left\lVert \nabla v\right\rVert_\infty^2\), because it bounds a squared gradient norm; (3.17), p. 25, has the consistent unsquared norm and is counterevidence against treating this as a failure of the whole first-order argument. Similarly the coefficient in the squared high-order norm (1.33), p. 8, must have degree \(2n\) in \(v\), rather than \(n\). Finally, the duality test stated on p. 27 for (3.19) requires \((-\Delta)^{(d-s)/2}\kappa\): using \((-\Delta)^{d-s}\kappa\) gives \(\int\kappa(-\Delta)^{d-s}\kappa=\left\lVert \kappa\right\rVert_{\dot H^{d-s}}^2\), not the claimed \(\dot H^{(d-s)/2}\) square. These are local power corrections with explicit consistent alternatives.

Problem 7 (The Term 3 decomposition omits the diagonal self correction: Minor).  The reduction to Term 2 plus the off-diagonal Term 4 in (5.48), p. 56, omits the smooth–atomic self interactions which survive removal of the particle diagonal.
## Exact algebra and example

Use the \(n=2,A=1\) example in Problem 6 and unit-mass mollifiers with the source’s small supports. Then \(K_2=1\) on every interacting support. Both the fully smoothed signed measure and each \(\delta_{x_i}-\rho_i\) have mass zero, so \[\mathrm{Term}_1=\mathrm{Term}_2=\mathrm{Term}_4=0,\qquad
 \mathrm{Term}_3=-1/N=-1/2 .\] The missing sum in [eq:diagonal] (#eq:diagonal) is exactly \(-1/2\), even when the moment-cancelling mollifiers are signed.
## Repair and limited impact

For fixed smooth mollifier shapes, \(|K_n(x,y)|\leq
C\left\lVert \nabla v\right\rVert_\infty^n|x-y|^{-s}\), with the corresponding bounded kernel estimate when \(s=0\). Scaling the integrals in [eq:diagonal] (#eq:diagonal), using \(s<d\), bounds each by \(C\left\lVert \nabla v\right\rVert_\infty^n/(N^2\eta_i^s)\). For \(s>0\), the self-energy budget (2.28) is the appropriate place to absorb their sum. For \(s=0\), the density-error term in \(\Xi\) directly controls \(\#I_{\Omega'}/N^2\), since \(\lambda^d\left\lVert \mu\right\rVert_{L^\infty(\widehat\Omega)}\geq1/N\). Total-variation constants of signed mollifiers must be retained. Thus the equality is false as written, but a local error term of the expected size is available. This finding alone does not falsify the claimed final inequality.
Problem 8 (The proposed moment-cancelling mollifier has the wrong jet: Minor).  Formula (5.3), p. 50, does not give the stated vanishing moments for arbitrary smooth unit-mass bumps \(\psi,\zeta\).
## Second-order check and constructive repair

Use the Fourier convention \(\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-i\xi x}f(x)\,\mathrm dx\), in one dimension with \(m=2\). Let \(A,B\) be the first moments of \(\psi,\zeta\), and \(S,T\) their second moments. Their Taylor series are \[\widehat\psi=1-iA\xi-\tfrac12S\xi^2+O(\xi^3),\qquad
 \widehat\zeta=1-iB\xi-\tfrac12T\xi^2+O(\xi^3).\] The formula subtracts \(\widehat\zeta(-iA\xi-S\xi^2/2)\). It therefore gives \[\widehat\rho(\xi)=1+AB\xi^2+O(\xi^3),\qquad
 \int x^2\rho(x)\,\mathrm dx=-2AB .\] Take both bumps to be translates of an even smooth probability bump by the displacement 1; then \(A=B=1\), and the purportedly zero second moment is \(-2\).

For every order \(m\), a valid repair is to set \[P(\xi)=\operatorname{Taylor}_m
           \left(\frac{\widehat\psi(\xi)-1}{\widehat\zeta(\xi)}\right),
 \qquad \widehat\rho=\widehat\psi-\widehat\zeta P .\] The denominator is nonzero near zero, \(P(0)=0\), and \(\widehat\rho=1+O(|\xi|^{m+1})\). In several dimensions use the total-degree Taylor polynomial. Fourier inversion gives a finite combination of derivatives of compactly supported smooth bumps, hence the required compact support and smoothness. For the actually used \(m\leq2\), centered symmetric choices also avoid the specific second-order cross term.

The moments are used in the Taylor estimate (5.51), p. 57, and \(m=2\) is selected in the Coulomb case on p. 58. Their construction is therefore operative, but this repair is local. A smooth unit-mass function with all second moments zero cannot be nonnegative: otherwise its mass would be supported at the origin. Estimates using the repaired mollifier must accordingly allow a signed density and keep its fixed total-variation constants. The finding does not show a loss of the intended rate once a valid mollifier and valid surrounding estimates are supplied.
# Dependency assessment and conclusion

The distinction between a false displayed assertion and an unproved intended conclusion is essential here. Problem 1 disproves (1.12) in its literal signed-background, noncompact-field class. Problem 6 disproves the printed uniform \(M\)-dependence of the corollary but has an elementary normalization repair. Problems 2–5 demonstrate failures in substantial derivations or auxiliary assertions; they do not supply counterexamples to all possible correct formulations of the principal high-order estimates. Problems 7–8 have explicit local algebraic repairs.

The primary reading followed the first-order stress identity and truncation arguments, the Section 4 commutator PDE and regularity inductions, the Section 5 renormalization and global/macroscopic variants, the mean-field application, and Appendix A’s alternative induction. Singularity, signedness, diagonal removal, finite-height localization, low-frequency conventions, and derivative counts were checked where operative. No independent counterexample to the global first-order result or the intended mean-field theorem was established. Nor is this report a certification that every uncriticized argument is correct. The cited prior literature was not all independently re-proved or fully retrieved; the decisive evidence here is self-contained.

problems.title: Finite-height first-order localization without compact support
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: Problem 1 (Finite-height localization without compact support: Major).
claim: Recorded check: Finite-height first-order localization without compact support

d=1,s=0,N=2; fixed smooth bounded v with plateaus -1,0,+1 and compactly supported derivative; Omega=[-3,3], ell=3; particles R+-1/4, R>10; mu=p_R+q_j has mass one, global and local Linfinity norm 8, compact support and finite absolute logarithmic energy; lambda=1/16; #I_Omega=0; r_i=1/64.
analysis: The literal estimate (1.12), p. 5, is false for the stated signed-background class and a Lipschitz field whose derivative has compact support but whose values do not vanish at infinity.

Take \(d=1,s=0,N=2\), \(\Omega=[-3,3]\), and \(\ell=3\). Fix a smooth bounded field \(v\) which is \(-1\) on \((-\infty,-1]\), zero on \([-1/2,1/2]\), and \(1\) on \([1,\infty)\); its two transitions are confined to the remaining intervals. Set, for \(R>10\) and an integer \(j\geq1\), \[\begin{aligned}
 x_1&=R-\tfrac14,&x_2&=R+\tfrac14,\\
 p_R(y)&=2\,\mathbf1_{[-R-1/4,-R+1/4]}(y),&
 q_j(y)&=8\cos(2\pi j y)\,\mathbf1_{[-1/2,1/2]}(y),&
 \mu_{R,j}&=p_R+q_j .\end{aligned}\] The background has mass one and belongs to \(L^1\cap L^\infty\). Its local and global essential supremum norms are exactly 8, independently of \(R,j\). Thus \(\lambda=1/16\), the required \(2\lambda\)-neighborhood of \(\operatorname{supp}v'\) is contained in \(\Omega\), and \(\ell>\lambda\). Neither particle belongs to \(\Omega\), so \(\#I_\Omega=0\). The source radii (2.17) are both \(r_i=1/64\). On \(Q=[-3,3]\times[-3,3]\), truncation leaves their potentials unchanged.

Equation reference: eq:localcounter, eq:localenergy. Since \(v=0\) on \(\operatorname{supp}q_j\), its self-commutator vanishes exactly. All its interactions with the other two supports tend to zero by oscillatory weak convergence against smooth separated kernels. Taking \(j\to\infty\) at a fixed \(R\), the commutator in (1.12) therefore tends to \[
 I_R=2\sum_{a=R\pm1/4}\int\frac{p_R(y)}{a-y}\,\mathrm dy
     =4\log\frac{2R+1/2}{2R-1/2}\sim\frac2R .\] Let \(h_R=g*(\tfrac12\delta_{x_1}+\tfrac12\delta_{x_2}-p_R)\). Every source point is horizontally at least \(R-13/4\) from \(Q\). The total variation of this source is 2 and \(|\nabla g(X)|=|X|^{-1}\); hence \[
 \int_Q|\nabla h_R|^2\leq\frac{144}{(R-13/4)^2}.\] If (1.12) held with its stated universal constant, the \(j\)-limit would give \(I_R\leq C\left\lVert v'\right\rVert_\infty\,144/(R-13/4)^2\) for every \(R\). The left side is of order \(R^{-1}\) and the right side is of order \(R^{-2}\), an impossibility. This is an analytic counterexample sequence, not an inference from finite numerical samples.

Remark 3.1, p. 23, uses \(\widetilde v(x,z)=\chi(z/\ell)(v(x),0)\). Its vertical derivative contains \(\ell^{-1}\chi'(z/\ell)v(x)\), which remains nonzero on a nonzero plateau where \(v'(x)=0\). Thus the support replacement invoked in the local arguments on pp. 27 and 31 is unavailable for this field. The compact support premise needed for (3.5) is absent from the first part of Theorem 1.2.

A natural repair route is to retain the full vertical domain \(\Omega\times\mathbb R^k\) with the trivial extension. Another is to impose the compact-support and domain hypotheses needed by the cutoff proof and use the actual support of \(\nabla\widetilde v\). A full replacement theorem under either amended set of assumptions is not certified here. A nonnegative-background-only statement would also exclude this particular counterexample, but that is a genuine restriction of the printed class. A fixed finite change to \(\ell\) does not repair the \(R^{-1}\) versus \(R^{-2}\) discrepancy. The example does not refute the compactly supported higher-order estimate, the global estimate (1.7), or the mean-field application of that global estimate.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: The q_j single-layer gradient tends to zero in global L2 by a low/high Fourier split. The limiting commutator is 4 log((2R+1/2)/(2R-1/2)) ~ 2/R, but the local slab energy is at most 144/(R-13/4)^2. No universal constant works as j->infinity and then R->infinity.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Compactly supported v or nonnegative-only mu would exclude this example. The theorem explicitly permits signed mu. Full vertical integration avoids this finite-height counterexample.

problems.title: Missing acceleration term in fixed-velocity transport hierarchy

claim: Recorded check: Missing acceleration term in fixed-velocity transport hierarchy

d=3,s=1,k=0; smooth compact v equals x near e1; a real annular-Fourier Schwartz potential h has partial_1 h(e1)=-2; f=-Delta h/(4pi) is zero-mean Schwartz with Fourier support away from zero. A separate radial-bump illustration checks exact scalar derivatives.
analysis: Equations (1.31)–(1.32), p. 8, and Lemma A.3, especially (A.6)–(A.10), p. 63, use an incorrect transport identity for the explicitly fixed field \(v\).

Equation reference: eq:correcttransport. For the source definition \[\kappa_t^m(x)=\int\nabla^{\otimes m}g(x-y-tv(y)):
                        (v(x)-v(y))^{\otimes m}\,\mathrm df(y),\] differentiation gives, for \(m\geq1\), \[\begin{aligned}

 (\partial_t+v\cdot\nabla)\kappa_t^m
  ={}&\kappa_t^{m+1}\\
 &+m\int\nabla^{\otimes m}g(x-y-tv(y)):
 \bigl((v\cdot\nabla v)(x)\otimes
       (v(x)-v(y))^{\otimes(m-1)}\bigr)\,\mathrm df(y).\nonumber\end{aligned}\] The last term differentiates the factors \(v(x)-v(y)\). It is absent from (A.7). For \(m=1\), it is exactly \((v\cdot\nabla v)(x)\cdot\nabla h_t(x)\).

This defect occurs with all the qualitative conventions used in the source. Take \(d=3,s=1\), and a smooth compactly supported \(v\) equal to \(x\) on \(B(0,3)\). Let \(\widehat\psi\) be an even, nonnegative smooth function supported in \(1<|\xi|<2\) with \(\int \xi_1^2\widehat\psi(\xi)\,\mathrm d\xi>0\). Choose \(a>0\) so that \(h(x)=a\,\partial_1\psi(x-e_1)\) satisfies \(\partial_1h(e_1)=-2\), and set \(f=-\Delta h/(4\pi)\). Then \(f\) is Schwartz, has zero mean, has Fourier support away from zero, and \(g*f=h\), since \(-\Delta g=4\pi\delta_0\). At \(x=e_1,t=0\), the omitted term is exactly \(-2\). Thus even the standing Fourier-gap convention after (3.21), p. 25, does not eliminate the counterexample.

For transparent independent arithmetic, one may also take \(f=\phi-\phi(\,\cdot-2e_1)\), with \(\phi\) a radial smooth unit-mass bump in \(B(0,1/4)\). Newton’s identity gives, near \(x=e_1\) on the axis, \[\kappa_t^1(xe_1)=-\frac1x+\frac{2-x}{(2+2t-x)^2}.\] At \(x=1,t=0\), direct differentiation gives \(\partial_t\kappa_t^1=-4\), \(v\cdot\nabla\kappa_t^1=2\), and \(\kappa_0^2=0\). The discrepancy is again \(-2\). This second example illustrates the calculation; the preceding annular Fourier construction meets the additional Fourier-support convention exactly.

Lemma A.5 uses (A.7) in (A.16), p. 64; Lemma A.7 and the proof of Proposition A.1 on pp. 67–69 then use that representation. Therefore the advertised alternative proof is not valid as written. Introducing the transported velocity \(v_t=v\circ(I+tv)^{-1}\), which satisfies a Burgers transport relation, can cancel a corresponding acceleration term in a different hierarchy. It does not validate (A.6) with its fixed \(v\); definitions and the coefficient induction would have to be redone. Section 4 supplies a separate PDE approach, so this finding does not by itself falsify the estimate in Proposition A.1 or the principal estimates.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: The chain rule adds m integral D^m g:[(v dot grad)v tensor (v(x)-v(y))^(m-1)]. For m=1 this equals -2 at e1,t=0. The radial-bump arithmetic gives dt kappa1=-4, v dot grad kappa1=2, kappa2=0.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: A time-dependent Eulerian velocity v_t=v composed with (I+t v)^-1 gives a different possible hierarchy. The source explicitly fixes v in A.6. Section 4 has a separate PDE route.

problems.title: Unsmeared singularities and logarithmic cell energy in local renormalization
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: Problem 3 (Two false auxiliary energy bounds in the local renormalization: Major).
claim: Recorded check: Unsmeared singularities and logarithmic cell energy in local renormalization

Example A: d=1,s=0,N=2, mu=1_{[-1/2,1/2]}, particles 0,4, v supported [-1,1], Omega'=[-3,3], Omega=[-18,18], ell=3, lambda=1/2. Example B: d=2,s=0,N=2, particles 0,e1, mu_R=nu0/4+nu_Re1/4+nu_3Re1/2 with uniform disks radius 1/10, R>50; Omega and Omega' are closed balls; local density and radii fixed; genuine radial moment-cancelling mollifier; cell radius 2R has mass 1/2. Both backgrounds are nonnegative.
analysis: The integral in Lemma 5.1, (5.7), p. 51, can contain an unsmeared particle singularity. Independently, the global neutral-cell bound (5.40), p. 55, fails for the logarithmic kernel even for nonnegative backgrounds.

Section 5 sets \(\eta_i=r_i/2\) for \(x_i\in\Omega'\) and \(\eta_i=0\) otherwise, explicitly leaving the other particles as Dirac masses ((5.1), p. 50). Yet (5.7) integrates \(|z|^\gamma|\nabla\bar h_{N,\vec\eta}|^2\) over \((\operatorname{supp}\nabla\widetilde v)\cup(\Omega\times[-\lambda,\lambda]^k)\).

Take \(d=1,s=0,N=2\), \(\mu=\mathbf1_{[-1/2,1/2]}\), particles \(0,4\), a smooth \(v\) supported in \([-1,1]\), \(\Omega'=[-3,3]\), and \(\Omega=[-18,18]\). Here \(\ell=3,\lambda=1/2\); all the stronger Section 5 neighborhood conditions hold. The particle at 4 lies in \(\Omega\setminus\Omega'\) and is not smeared. Near \(X=(4,0)\), \[\bar h_{N,\vec\eta}(X)=-\tfrac12\log|X-(4,0)|+H(X),
 \qquad H\ \hbox{smooth there}.\] The energy on an annulus of radii \(\varepsilon,\varepsilon_0\) is \((\pi/2)\log(\varepsilon_0/\varepsilon)+O(1)\), and diverges. The right side \(\Xi\) in (5.2) is finite: it uses \(h_{N,\vec r}\), which truncates both particles at positive radii. The closing appeal to (2.30) on p. 52 cannot remedy the unsmeared point.

Now take \(d=2,s=0,N=2\), particles \(0,e_1\), \(\Omega'=\overline{B(0,3)}\), \(\Omega=\overline{B(0,18)}\), and a fixed smooth \(v\) supported in \(B(0,1)\). Let \(
u_b\) be the uniform probability density on the disk of radius \(1/10\) centered at \(b\), and, for \(R>50\), set \[\mu_R=	frac14
u_0+	frac14
u_{Re_1}
                         +	frac12
u_{3Re_1}.\] This is a nonnegative bounded probability density. In \(\Omega\) its essential supremum is \(25/\pi\), so \(\lambda=\sqrt{\pi/50}<1\), independently of \(R\). The radii \(\eta_i=\lambda/8\) are fixed. Choose a fixed radial smooth unit-mass mollifier at this scale with the required vanishing moments. Such a signed mollifier can be obtained from two radial dilates with coefficients \(4/3,-1/3\), which cancel the second moments. Its support can be made smaller than \(\eta_i/2\).

The two examples are independent and use nonnegative \(\mu\). The printed theorem’s larger signed class presents an additional issue: \(\int_{B(x_i,R_i)}\mu=1/N\) does not bound \(\int_{B(x_i,R_i)}|\mu|\), as needed when estimating the integrals in (5.28)–(5.39). Signed moment-cancelling mollifiers likewise require total-variation constants instead of a probability-density argument.

Lemma 5.1 is used in the estimate of the smeared term and in the passage after (5.45), p. 56. The neutral-cell estimate enters the local regularity step for Term 2. One must restrict the energy to regions without unsmeared singularities and retain a genuinely local cell norm, or supply another valid estimate. Merely enlarging a local norm to the global energy loses the logarithmic cancellation illustrated above. These counterexamples invalidate the displayed auxiliary bounds and their current uses; they do not prove that the intended high-order commutator estimate is false. Section 5.4’s global treatment uses a different, cruder Term 2 estimate and is not refuted by [eq:logcell] (#eq:logcell) alone.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: A: the unsmeared particle at 4 lies in the integration slab, giving (pi/2)log(epsilon0/epsilon)+O(1) energy while Xi is finite. B: the neutral cell has exactly E0+(1/8)log R logarithmic interaction energy and 2pi E0+(pi/4)log R Dirichlet energy, contradicting C/N^2 for fixed eta.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The needed local cell norm can remain bounded; the proof replaces it by a global norm. The global Section 5.4 estimate uses a different Term 2 bound. Signed backgrounds create further total-variation issues, but the two counterexamples do not depend on signed backgrounds.

problems.title: Nonmonotone mesoscale truncation path
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: Problem 4 (The mesoscale truncation path is not monotone: Major).
claim: Recorded check: Nonmonotone mesoscale truncation path

d=3,s=1,N=2; Omega upper half-space; particles at (0,0,3lambda) and (3lambda,0,3lambda); 0<lambda<1; bounded probability background far from the particle balls within Omega with height 1/(2lambda^3); radii path lambda,2lambda,lambda/4.
analysis: The monotonicity used between (2.46) and (2.47), p. 21, does not follow from Lemma 2.2. It is false for the path (2.44), even after correcting the fixed-potential typo in (2.45).

The path chooses \(\eta_i^k=2^k\lambda\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(x_i,\partial\Omega)\geq2^k\lambda\), and otherwise resets it to \(r_i\). A point at distance \(3\lambda\), with \(r_i=\lambda/4\), therefore has the successive radii \[\lambda,\quad2\lambda,\quad\lambda/4 .\] This is not a coordinatewise increasing path.

The issue is not only logical. In \(d=3,s=1\), take the half-space \(\Omega=\{x_3\geq0\}\), particles \(x_1=(0,0,3\lambda)\), \(x_2=(3\lambda,0,3\lambda)\), and \(0<\lambda<1\). Put a bounded probability density of height \(1/(2\lambda^3)\) in a cube of volume \(2\lambda^3\), far from these particles and their balls but inside \(\Omega\). This makes the prescribed local scale exactly \(\lambda\), and \(r_i=\lambda/4\). All balls of radius \(2\lambda\) stay in \(\Omega\).

As printed, (2.45) also retains \(h_{N,\vec r}\) instead of \(h_{N,\vec\eta}\). Its energy term then does not vary with \(\vec\eta\). With the background outside all truncation balls, even increasing the radii makes the negative self-energy term increase. Replacing this potential is necessary but leaves the reset obstruction above. For \(k=1\), the preceding vertical-domain replacement additionally uses coincidence only above height \(2^{k+2}\lambda\), which can exceed \(\ell\); the asserted replacement by a slab of height \(\ell\) requires a separate justification.

Proposition 2.5, pp. 20–23, is invoked in (5.14), (5.57), and the later macroscopic estimates. A proof must use admissible comparisons on a fixed interior set, or separately estimate the reset terms and the vertical tails. No completed replacement argument is supplied here. There is also a local sign error in (2.53): for \(f/g=t^{-a}\), its derivative is \(-at^{-a-1}\), which is at most, not at least, \(-a(2^k\lambda)^{-a-1}\) on the interval. For \(\lambda=1/10,a=1,k=2,t=1/10\), the two values are \(-100\) and \(-25/4\). That particular inequality can be repaired with a factor \(4^{a+1}\); it does not repair the nonmonotone path.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: The two radius-2lambda shells at separation 3lambda have mutual energy 5/(16lambda), versus 1/(3lambda) at either nonoverlapping radius. Thus F_eta2-F_eta1=1/(192lambda)>0. Literal (2.45) freezes h_N,r and also fails monotonicity. The separate derivative inequality has -100 >= -25/4, which is false.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The selected pair sum in (2.40) may be empty for this proof-step counterexample, so it does not refute the proposition's final estimate. The derivative sign issue alone is repairable with a constant.

problems.title: Undefined indices and unrecovered high-order derivative budget
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 5: Problem 5 (The stated high-order derivative budget is not obtained: Major).
claim: Recorded check: Undefined indices and unrecovered high-order derivative budget
n>=2; fixed compact support, fixed admissible lambda and ell; smooth approximating fields v_J=v0+J^(-2n) chi sin(Jx), with nonzero v0'' on the cutoff plateau.
analysis: Theorem 1.2, (1.13), p. 5, has undefined summation indices and a regularity budget not delivered by the estimates concluding its proof.

The power of \(\lambda\) printed in (1.13) is \(\lambda^{-(n-p)+\sum_{k=1}^p c_{n-k}}\), while the only bound indices are \(c_1,\ldots,c_{n-p}\). At \(n=3,p=2\), the exponent uses \(c_2\), although only \(c_1\) is bound. At \(p=0\), the exponent loses every derivative order. This is not a defined general formula.

Correcting only that index does not settle the proof. Theorem 4.9, (4.119), p. 47, feeds into (5.34), p. 54, and (5.42), p. 55: \[A_{v,p}=\sum_{\substack{a_1,\ldots,a_{n-p}\geq0\\
                        \sum a_i\leq2n}}
 \lambda^{\sum a_i}\prod_{i=1}^{n-p}\left\lVert D^{1+a_i}v\right\rVert_\infty .\] The exact change \(b_i=1+a_i\) gives \[n-p\leq\sum b_i\leq3n-p,\qquad
 \lambda^{\sum a_i}=\lambda^{\sum b_i-(n-p)},\] whereas (1.13) has the upper bound \(2n\). In particular \(p=n-1,a_1=2n\) uses \(D^{2n+1}v\). The hypothesis \(C^{2n-1,1}\) controls derivatives through order \(2n\), not \(2n+1\).

This is a real loss of control, not an assertion that high derivatives must happen to be large for every field. For a fixed smooth compact cutoff \(\chi\) with a plateau, take \[v_J=v_0+J^{-2n}\chi(x)\sin(Jx)\] in one dimension, where \(v_0''\) is nonzero on that plateau. The \(C^{2n-1,1}\) norms stay bounded and the supports stay fixed, while \(\left\lVert D^{2n+1}v_J\right\rVert_\infty\) grows like \(J\). The multiplier \((\ell\left\lVert D^2v_J\right\rVert_\infty)^{n-1}\) of the relevant term in (5.47)/(5.61) does not tend to zero. For fixed admissible \(\lambda,\ell\), the resulting bound cannot be controlled by the printed derivative data.

The concluding assertion after (5.61), p. 58, therefore needs a sharper regularity argument or a corrected weaker theorem with the derivative budget actually proved. The convention \(A_{v,0}:=1\) printed after (5.42) also has the wrong endpoint: the empty product is at \(p=n\). These observations do not constitute a counterexample to an appropriately defined optimal high-order estimate. The Major classification concerns the missing derivation of the announced regularity and scale dependence.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: At n=3,p=2 the lambda exponent uses c2 while only c1 is bound. Relabelling a_i to b_i=1+a_i in (5.42) gives sum b_i<=3n-p, not 2n, and the term p=n-1,a1=2n requires D^(2n+1)v. Its norm grows like J while C^{2n-1,1} stays bounded.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: A sharper local regularity proof could improve the derivative count; the sequence is not a counterexample to the best possible corrected final estimate. The empty product is at p=n, not the printed p=0.

problems.title: False uniform amplitude dependence in Corollary 1.3, with local norm-power subfindings
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: Problem 6 (Uniform amplitude dependence in Corollary 1.3: Major).
claim: Recorded check: False uniform amplitude dependence in Corollary 1.3, with local norm-power subfindings
d=1,s=0,N=2; mu=1 on [-1/2,1/2]; particles +-1/4; compact v_A=A v0, v0=x on [-2,2] and supported [-4,4]; ell=6, Omega'=B6, Omega=B36, lambda=1/2.
analysis: Corollary 1.3, (1.14), p. 6, has \(CM\ell^{-n}\) with the inherited constant independent of \(M\). Its left side is homogeneous of degree \(n\) in the field, so \(M^n\) is required. Related squared-norm displays also lose a power.

Take \(d=1,s=0,N=2\), \(\mu=\mathbf1_{[-1/2,1/2]}\), and particles \(-1/4,1/4\). Choose \(v_0\) smooth, equal to \(x\) on \([-2,2]\), and supported in \([-4,4]\), with \(\Omega'=[-6,6]\), \(\Omega=[-36,36]\), and \(\ell=6\). Here \(\lambda=1/2\), and even the stronger Section 5 neighborhood conditions hold. Put \(v_A=A v_0\) for \(A>0\). On all the relevant background and particle supports, \[K_n(x,y)=(-1)^n(n-1)!\,A^n,\qquad x\ne y.\] The total mass of \(\nu_N^{\otimes2}\) off the diagonal is \(-1/N\). In particular the signed \(n=2\) integral equals \(-A^2/2\), and its absolute value is \(A^2/2\). The energy bracket in (1.14) is finite and independent of \(A\). One can choose \(M=A M_0\), where \(M_0=\max_{0\leq k\leq4}\ell^k\left\lVert D^kv_0\right\rVert_\infty\). A bound linear in \(M\) cannot hold as \(A\to\infty\).

The source explicitly presents Corollary 1.3 as the precise scale and homogeneity consequence of (1.13), p. 5. The example therefore contradicts a stated quantitative guarantee tied to the central local estimate. This corollary component is Major under the core-contribution criterion. Replacing \(M\) by \(M^n\) restores the required homogeneity, but does not prove the other estimates needed for the corollary. Allowing the constant to depend on \(M\) would change its stated uniformity. The simplicity of the normalization repair does not remove this dependency.

The same scaling check shows that (1.26), p. 7, needs \(\left\lVert \nabla v\right\rVert_\infty^2\), because it bounds a squared gradient norm; (3.17), p. 25, has the consistent unsquared norm and is counterevidence against treating this as a failure of the whole first-order argument. Similarly the coefficient in the squared high-order norm (1.33), p. 8, must have degree \(2n\) in \(v\), rather than \(n\). Finally, the duality test stated on p. 27 for (3.19) requires \((-\Delta)^{(d-s)/2}\kappa\): using \((-\Delta)^{d-s}\kappa\) gives \(\int\kappa(-\Delta)^{d-s}\kappa=\left\lVert \kappa\right\rVert_{\dot H^{d-s}}^2\), not the claimed \(\dot H^{(d-s)/2}\) square. These are local power corrections with explicit consistent alternatives.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: The n=2 integral is -A^2/2 and its absolute value A^2/2, while M=A M0 and the energy bracket is independent of A. Squared commutator norms require degree 2n; the fractional duality exponent must be (d-s)/2.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The consistent unsquared estimate (3.17) supports a local correction. Allowing the constant to depend on M changes the uniform corollary.

problems.title: Moment-cancelling mollifier construction has a nonzero second moment
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 8: Problem 8 (The proposed moment-cancelling mollifier has the wrong jet: Minor).
claim: Recorded check: Moment-cancelling mollifier construction has a nonzero second moment
d=1,m=2; Fourier convention exp(-i xi x); psi,zeta are smooth compact unit-mass bumps with first moments A,B, e.g. translates by 1 of centered even probability bumps.
analysis: Formula (5.3), p. 50, does not give the stated vanishing moments for arbitrary smooth unit-mass bumps \(\psi,\zeta\).

Use the Fourier convention \(\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-i\xi x}f(x)\,\mathrm dx\), in one dimension with \(m=2\). Let \(A,B\) be the first moments of \(\psi,\zeta\), and \(S,T\) their second moments. Their Taylor series are \[\widehat\psi=1-iA\xi-\tfrac12S\xi^2+O(\xi^3),\qquad
 \widehat\zeta=1-iB\xi-\tfrac12T\xi^2+O(\xi^3).\] The formula subtracts \(\widehat\zeta(-iA\xi-S\xi^2/2)\). It therefore gives \[\widehat\rho(\xi)=1+AB\xi^2+O(\xi^3),\qquad
 \int x^2\rho(x)\,\mathrm dx=-2AB .\] Take both bumps to be translates of an even smooth probability bump by the displacement 1; then \(A=B=1\), and the purportedly zero second moment is \(-2\).

For every order \(m\), a valid repair is to set \[P(\xi)=\operatorname{Taylor}_m
           \left(\frac{\widehat\psi(\xi)-1}{\widehat\zeta(\xi)}\right),
 \qquad \widehat\rho=\widehat\psi-\widehat\zeta P .\] The denominator is nonzero near zero, \(P(0)=0\), and \(\widehat\rho=1+O(|\xi|^{m+1})\). In several dimensions use the total-degree Taylor polynomial. Fourier inversion gives a finite combination of derivatives of compactly supported smooth bumps, hence the required compact support and smoothness. For the actually used \(m\leq2\), centered symmetric choices also avoid the specific second-order cross term.

The moments are used in the Taylor estimate (5.51), p. 57, and \(m=2\) is selected in the Coulomb case on p. 58. Their construction is therefore operative, but this repair is local. A smooth unit-mass function with all second moments zero cannot be nonnegative: otherwise its mass would be supported at the origin. Estimates using the repaired mollifier must accordingly allow a signed density and keep its fixed total-variation constants. The finding does not show a loss of the intended rate once a valid mollifier and valid surrounding estimates are supplied.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: The printed formula yields rhohat=1+AB xi^2+O(xi^3), so the second moment is -2AB; A=B=1 gives -2.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Centered symmetric bumps avoid this second-order cross term. A Taylor quotient construction works at every order.

report: Abstract: The acquired 24-page manuscript contains a false boundedness assertion in the analytic transfer-operator factorization. An explicit expanding full-branch interval map satisfies even the stronger expansion condition used in the main theorem, but its transfer operator does not map the asserted \(H^\infty\) spaces into one another. This is a Major problem in the derivation of the quantitative convergence estimate. It does not establish a counterexample to the final spectral-convergence conclusion. An isolated typographical error in the Hardy coefficient norm is retained as an uncounted editorial clarification. The finite-sample conditioning argument, polynomial example, and unperturbed Fourier example were also checked. Additional restrictions needed to interpret certain proof steps and numerical examples are stated without promoting them to unproved counterexamples. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: Bounded scientific review: M25-0425

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Convergence Properties of Dynamic Mode
Decomposition for Analytic Interval Maps
# Identity and scope

The source is E. Akindji, J. Slipantschuk, O. F. Bandtlow, and W. Just, Convergence properties of dynamic mode decomposition for analytic interval maps, DOI https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70011. The acquired PDF is arXiv:2404.08512v1, deposited 12 April 2024, with a manuscript date of 10 April 2024 [source]. It has 24 pages and SHA256 `932f2146b632f41c9734c842116236e242665056b9e8927a6c27957e67e4f851`. Every extracted source page, including the numerical discussion and references, was read. Numbered locators refer to this exact version; physical and printed page numbers agree.

The annual task’s DOI identity is retained. No equivalence between this preprint and a later journal version is asserted. The retained source intake does not supply an author-code implementation or a supplementary proof document; the bounded recovery search found no substantive earlier report for this paper. This is therefore an initial review of the acquired source. Missing code is not treated as a mathematical defect, and the published numerical figures were not independently regenerated.
# Framework and checks

Let \(D_s=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<s\}\). The standing assumptions on p. 5 specify finitely many analytic inverse branches \(\phi_\ell\in H^\infty(D_R)\), with \(\phi_\ell(D_R)\subset D_r\) for \(1<r<R\). The transfer operator is \[(\mathcal Lf)(z)=\sum_{\ell=1}^d
 \sigma_\ell\phi_\ell'(z)f(\phi_\ell(z)),\qquad
 \sigma_\ell=\operatorname{sgn}\phi_\ell'(0).\] The signs encode the real branch orientations, and the change of variables gives the bilinear duality in (5). The auxiliary Hardy space has the radial boundary norm and normalized monomials \(e_n(z)=(z/\rho)^n\). The main theorem imposes \[\gamma=(1+\sqrt2)^2,\qquad \gamma r<R,\qquad
 \rho_*=\sqrt{rR/\gamma}.\] Its matrix estimate, for sufficiently many equidistant nodes, is \[\left\lVert V_N(H_N^{(M)})^\dagger G_N^{(M)}V_N^{-1}-L\right\rVert
 \le C\left\{\frac{(\gamma rR)^{N/2}N^2}{M}
                 +\left(\frac{\gamma r}{R}\right)^{N/2}\right\}.\] Here \(L\) is the matrix representation of \(\mathcal L\) on the chosen Hardy space; \(V_N\) changes between monomials and the normalized basis. The finite-section convention matters because \(V_N^{-1}\) is understood on that section.

The Riemann-sum argument and Schur estimate in Lemmas 2.5–2.6 and Proposition 2.7 give the stated order \(N^2/M\). The Gram matrix is positive definite when \(M\ge N\): a nonzero polynomial of degree at most \(N-1\) cannot vanish at all \(M\) distinct nodes. The perturbation argument of Lemma 2.12 then combines the inverse Hilbert-matrix growth \(C\gamma^N\) with the quadrature error and a Neumann-series bound. No failure was established in this conditioning step. The cited sharp Hilbert-matrix asymptotics were used as an external lemma, not independently re-proved or numerically certified.
# Supported problems

Problem 1 (Major: unbounded derivative weights in Lemma 2.3).  Lemma 2.3, p. 7, asserts that \(\widetilde{\mathcal L}:H^\infty(D_r)\to H^\infty(D_R)\) is bounded. Its proof bounds the operator norm by \[B=\sup_{z\in D_R}\sum_{\ell=1}^d|\phi_\ell'(z)|.\] The standing assumptions do not make \(B\) finite. Boundedness of a holomorphic function on an open disk does not imply boundedness of its derivative on that same disk.

Here is an admissible example, including the real full-branch condition. Take \(R=10\), \(r=3/2\), and partition \([-1,1]\) into 101 equal intervals. For \(\ell=1,\ldots,101\), except \(\ell=51\), put \[c_\ell=\frac{2\ell-102}{101},\qquad
 \phi_\ell(z)=c_\ell+\frac{z}{101}.\] For the central interval define \[s_\pm=\sqrt{1\pm 1/10},\qquad
 k=\frac{2}{101(s_+-s_-)},\qquad
 \phi_*(z)=-\frac1{101}
       +k\left(s_+-\sqrt{1-z/10}\right).
 \tag{3.1}\] The principal square root is analytic on \(D_{10}\), since \(\operatorname{Re}(1-z/10)>0\). Each linear branch maps \([-1,1]\) increasingly onto its prescribed interval. The central branch has \(\phi_*(-1)=-1/101\), \(\phi_*(1)=1/101\), and \[\phi_*'(z)=\frac{k}{20\sqrt{1-z/10}}.
 \tag{3.2}\] It too is strictly increasing on the real interval. Rationalizing \(s_+-s_-\) gives \(k=10(s_++s_-)/101<20/101\). Hence \(0<\phi_*'(x)<10/909<1\) for \(-1\le x\le1\); all the inverse branches are contractions there. Their inverses define an expanding analytic full-branch map, with the usual one-sided endpoint convention.

For \(z\in D_{10}\), the noncentral branches satisfy \[|\phi_\ell(z)|<\frac{110}{101}<\frac32.\] For the central branch, using \(s_+<11/10\) and \(\sqrt2<3/2\), \[|\phi_*(z)|
 <\frac1{101}+\frac{20}{101}\left(\frac{11}{10}+\frac32\right)
 =\frac{53}{101}<\frac32.\] Thus every branch belongs to \(H^\infty(D_{10})\) and maps that disk into \(D_{3/2}\). The stronger main-theorem condition is also satisfied: \(\gamma r=9/2+3\sqrt2<9<10=R\).

All real orientation signs are positive. Applying the claimed operator to the admissible function \(f\equiv1\) gives \[(\widetilde{\mathcal L}1)(z)=\frac{100}{101}
                  +\frac{k}{20\sqrt{1-z/10}}.\] This tends to \(+\infty\) as real \(z\uparrow10\). Consequently \(\widetilde{\mathcal L}1\notin H^\infty(D_{10})\). There is no cancellation that could rescue the claim. This is a direct counterexample to Lemma 2.3, not merely a possibly infinite upper bound.
#### Dependency and scope.

Proposition 2.4, pp. 7–8, uses precisely this bounded map in \(\mathcal L=\mathcal J_2\widetilde{\mathcal L}\mathcal J_1\); its constant is \(\rho B/\sqrt{\rho^2-r^2}\). The finite-rank approximation bounds feed Proposition 2.11 and then Theorem 2.14 and Corollaries 2.15–2.17. The proof therefore lacks a finite constant at an essential step. This substantial dependency makes the problem Major even though there are natural repairs.

The example does not show that \(\mathcal L\) is unbounded on every smaller Hardy space, or that the final spectral conclusion fails. Indeed, choosing \(R'\) with \(\gamma r<R'<R\) bounds all branch derivatives on \(D_{R'}\) by Cauchy’s estimate and recovers the displayed factorization with \(R'\). The corresponding proof has new constants, the radius \(\sqrt{rR'/\gamma}\), and a rate involving \(R'\). Alternatively, adding \(\phi_\ell'\in H^\infty(D_R)\), or extension to a neighborhood of the closed disk, supplies the missing hypothesis. Shrinking the disk alone does not verify the quantitative statement with the original fixed \(R\). A revised proof or explicit strengthening is needed at that level.
## Editorial clarification: the Hardy coefficient exponent

After (6), the source prints \[\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{H^2(D_R)}^2=\sum_{n=0}^\infty |f_n|^2 R^{-2n}.\] For the Taylor coefficients defined immediately above, the radial boundary definition instead gives \[\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{H^2(D_R)}^2=\sum_{n=0}^\infty |f_n|^2 R^{2n}.\] Already \(f(z)=z\) and \(R>1\) distinguish the two values, \(R^2\) and \(R^{-2}\). The accompanying summability characterization needs the same correction.

This is local: the proof of Lemma 2.1 on the same page uses the correct positive exponent, as do Lemma 2.2 and the normalized basis later on. No separate failure of the main argument was derived from this typographical error. Replacing both negative exponents on p. 6 is the appropriate repair. This isolated typographical correction is not counted as a substantive Problem.
# Additional proof and example boundaries
#### The radius in Proposition 2.13.

The statement on p. 15 allows every \(\rho\in(r,R)\). In its proof the uniform bound on \(V_NH_N^\dagger G_NV_N^{-1}\) is obtained by quoting the optimized error \((\gamma r/R)^{N/2}\). Proposition 2.11 gives that optimized rate at \(\rho=\rho_*\); its general estimate includes \((\gamma\rho/R)^N\). The printed proof consequently does not justify the asserted uniform bound for an arbitrary \(\rho\) near \(R\). Restricting to \(\rho_*\), as used by Theorem 2.14, resolves this particular range issue. More generally \(r<\rho<R/\gamma\) is sufficient for the displayed boundedness argument, once Problem 1 is repaired. No counterexample to the broader proposition was established, so this observation is retained as a proof-range clarification.

The same proof has local transcription slips: the difference-of-inverses identity requires \(H_N-H_N^{(M)}\) in the correction term, and the later similarity expression needs \(V_N^{-1}\) on the right. Correcting the sign does not change the ensuing triangle estimate. The equality between a norm and the sum of two norms there should be an inequality. These observations do not constitute an additional independent Major finding.
#### Fixed spectral modes.

The standard perturbation argument behind Lemma 2.16 applies to a fixed isolated nonzero eigenvalue of the compact limit, with its finite algebraic multiplicity. If its largest Jordan block has size \(m\), a norm error \(O(e^{-\alpha N})\) can give an eigenvalue error of order \(O(e^{-\alpha N/m})\), still exponential for that fixed mode. This does not supply a uniform rate for the entire accumulating spectrum, nor does it by itself settle behavior at the non-isolated point zero. The Koopman identification through (5) and bounded functionals in (18) was checked; no counterexample to the paper’s fixed nonzero-mode conclusion was obtained.
#### Polynomial and Fourier checks.

For the skewed doubling map let \(p=(1+a)/2\), \(q=(1-a)/2\). Its inverse branches are \(py-q\) and \(qy+p\), so \[\mathcal Ly^n=p(py-q)^n+q(qy+p)^n.\] The polynomial subspaces are invariant, and the triangular diagonal is \(p^{n+1}+q^{n+1}\). Thus the infinite-node monomial EDMD matrices have exactly these finite-section eigenvalues. This confirms the mechanism explained in Section 3.1; it is not a finite-precision stability guarantee.

The two-branch examples do not instantiate the strong expansion hypothesis of Theorem 2.14. For the Blaschke inverse branches displayed on p. 18, \(\phi_\ell'(0)=1/2\). If \(\phi_\ell(D_R)\subset D_r\), Cauchy’s coefficient estimate implies \(r/R\ge1/2\), incompatible with \(r/R<1/\gamma=3-2\sqrt2\). The skewed linear example has the same obstruction because its largest inverse slope is at least \(1/2\). Their observed convergence is therefore evidence about a wider regime or special structure, not an application of that sufficient theorem. This does not refute the observed convergence. The nonlinear exact spectrum quoted from prior work was not independently re-proved, and the source’s plots were not reproduced.
# Conclusion and evidence limits

The review supports one Major problem and no Minor problems in the acquired preprint. The Hardy coefficient typo is retained as an uncounted editorial clarification. The decisive Major evidence is the fully specified full-branch counterexample to Lemma 2.3 and its explicit dependence in the main proof. The weaker conclusion that suitable smaller disks yield bounded derivatives was also checked, so the report does not overstate the consequence as a disproof of all intended convergence results.

The entire acquired text was read; the central source pages were additionally inspected as images. Native bounded helpers checked the analytic factorization and the example calculations.
