problems.title: Ambient convexity used beyond hypothesis(H)
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (P02: Major—ambient convexity is used beyond (H)).
claim: Recorded check: Ambient convexity used beyond hypothesis(H)
analysis: In Lemma 4.12, p. 28, the set \[A_\delta=\Omega_{\mathrm{pl}}\cap\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)>\delta\}\] is called convex and is used as the domain in Merlet’s lemma. Assumption (H) makes \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pl}}\) convex, but does not make this ambient distance truncation convex. The later invocation of Proposition 3.25 on p. 29 has the same hypothesis problem: that proposition explicitly assumes convexity of \(\Omega\), whereas Theorem 4.10 assumes (H).

A calibrated counterexample to the first geometric claim. Start with the upper half-disc \(|z|<3\), \(\operatorname{Im}z>0\). Write \(r=|z|\), \(\theta=\arg z\), \(R=|z+1|\) and \(\phi=\arg(z+1)\). The following restrictions of the classical crack field are explicit: \[\begin{array}{lll}
r>1:&u=2\sqrt r\,\sin(\theta/2),&
 \sigma=r^{-1/2}(-\sin(\theta/2),\cos(\theta/2)),\\[2pt]
r<1:&u=2\sin\phi,&
 \sigma=(-\sin\phi,\cos\phi).
\end{array}\] In the plastic half-disc, \[\nabla u=q\sigma,\qquad
 q=\frac{2(x+1)}{R^2},\qquad
 q-1=\frac{1-r^2}{R^2}>0,\qquad p=(q-1)\sigma.\] In the elastic part \(p=0\) and \(\nabla u=\sigma\). Both fields have zero stress divergence. On \(r=1\), \(\phi=\theta/2\), so \(u\) and \(\sigma\) match and there is no interface jump. The boundary apex \((-1,0)\) has an integrable displacement gradient; \(u\in BV\) and \(\sigma\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\).

Remove the closed disc with centre \(c=(0,21/20)\) and radius \(\rho=1/20\). It lies outside the plastic half-disc and is tangent to its boundary at \((0,1)\). The resulting \(\Omega\) is a bounded connected Lipschitz domain. Prescribe the actual trace of \(u\) on every boundary component. The displayed equilibrium and flow rule calibrate \(u\) as a minimizer, with no boundary plastic measure. Its \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pl}}\) is the upper unit half-disc. Its saturation set is the corresponding closed cap within \(\Omega\), with the single extreme point \((0,1)\) removed; this set is still convex. Thus (H) holds.

For \(0<\delta<3/5\), put \[P_\pm=(\pm\sqrt{\delta/2},\,1-\delta/2),\qquad
 M=(0,1-\delta/2).\] The points \(P_\pm\) lie in \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pl}}\), and the squared excess of their distance from \(c\) over \((\rho+\delta)^2\) is \[\delta\left(\frac9{20}-\frac{3\delta}{4}\right)>0.\] Their distances from the other boundary components also exceed \(\delta\), whereas the distance from \(M\) to the hole is \(\delta/2\). Hence \(P_\pm\in A_\delta\) but their midpoint \(M\notin A_\delta\). For example, \(\delta=1/50\) gives \(P_\pm=(\pm1/10,99/100)\) and the exact positive squared excess \(87/10000\). This example concerns Lemma 4.12’s hypotheses; it does not satisfy, or purport to refute, Theorem 5.1’s simply connected domain assumption.

Local repair of the null-sweep step. A compact noncharacteristic interface arc can be covered by balls \(B\Subset\Omega\) avoiding the exceptional points. Use \(A=\Omega_{\mathrm{pl}}\cap B\), which is convex. The stress is \(H^1(A)\) and extends continuously to \(\overline A\) after shrinking the ball; this uses Proposition 4.2 and interior regularity. On a shorter arc its characteristics meet the interface transversely. Merlet’s lemma therefore applies locally. For the appendix covering argument, choose disjoint small boundary intervals covering the null set; noncrossing characteristic strips are then disjoint. Arbitrary overlapping disc covers would not justify that disjointness.

The local sweep of an interface set of zero length has zero area. Every point farther along a swept characteristic lies at a rational flow time from an interior point in such a local sweep. On compact subsets of \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pl}}\), the field is locally Lipschitz, so the corresponding flow maps are locally Lipschitz. Countably many compact flow charts and rational times propagate the null-area conclusion. This supplies the step used to identify the continuous characteristic representative with the original \(BV\) function, without assuming convexity of \(\Omega\).

Repair of the Proposition 3.25 invocation. The needed statement can also be proved locally. Let \(K=\Omega_{\mathrm{pl}}\) and suppose a nondegenerate characteristic-boundary segment has a relative-interior point \(a\in\Omega\). Convexity of \(K\) gives an exact plastic half-ball at \(a\), with an elastic half-ball opposite it. Every cluster value of \(\sigma(x)\) as \(x\in K\) tends to \(a\) must be a unit normal to this flat boundary: otherwise a fixed short step along the limiting characteristic enters \(K\), and constancy of \(\sigma\) on chords would put \(a\) on an interior characteristic, contradicting its definition. Connectedness fixes the sign of the normal on a shorter subsegment.

The ambient \(H^1\) stress has matching traces on the two half-balls. Thus the elastic harmonic displacement has constant tangential trace and constant unit normal derivative there. Subtract the matching affine function. The remainder has zero Dirichlet and normal traces on the flat diameter, so its extension by zero is weakly harmonic in a full ball. Analyticity forces it to vanish. This would give \(|\nabla u|=1\) in the elastic half-ball, contradicting \(|\sigma|<1\). Openness excludes endpoints as well. Therefore no nondegenerate characteristic-boundary component meets \(\Omega\).

Only at most two isolated characteristic interface points remain. At such a point \(a\), characteristic chords approaching \(a\) have length tending to zero. Indeed, a nondegenerate limiting chord either contains an interior point, which would put \(a\) on its characteristic, or lies in a supporting boundary segment. In the second case choose a nearby noncharacteristic interface point on that segment. Proposition 4.2 and constancy on the approximating chords force its characteristic to be tangent to the supporting line, which cannot meet the interior of the convex set. Both alternatives are impossible.

The endpoints of the shrinking chords are noncharacteristic interface points and tend to \(a\). The locally repaired Lemma 4.12 identifies displacement along each chord with the continuous elastic trace at its endpoints. These values tend to the elastic trace at \(a\), furnishing the desired continuous extension. Continuous local representatives agree on overlapping open sweeps because they agree almost everywhere. This also covers the case where the fan-free component is all of \(K\); it does not assume an unavailable separating characteristic.

These arguments repair the cited continuity steps using the earlier regularity and characteristic results and the original hypotheses. They do not retroactively validate the printed derivation. Theorem 4.10 is a main new regularity result identified on source p. 6. The invalid convex truncation is needed to identify the continuous characteristic representative with the original \(BV\) solution; the unlicensed use of Proposition 3.25 is needed for the subsequent interface argument. These are essential dependencies of that original proof, so the finding is graded Major. The independently checked replacement restores the continuity conclusion; a false theorem or failure of the entire paper is not asserted or required for this classification.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Ambient convexity used beyond hypothesis(H)

report: Abstract: The characteristic-class framework connects equivariant Riemann–Roch, lattice sums and differential Euler–Maclaurin operators. Four substantive corrections are established. Three affect explicit formulae under their stated hypotheses: primitive quotient-ray normalization in proper-face operators, the unnormalized weighted face prefactor, and repeated vertex translation in local cone formulae. The fourth is a false Cox-group product used as a core descent step in both printed characteristic-class derivations. All four findings are Major. A separate divisor-sign discrepancy is an uncounted editorial clarification because the actual subsequent character calculation already uses the correct direction. Exact examples, counterchecks and repairs delimit the conclusions affected. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: Bounded scientific review: M25-0430

Title: Initial Scientific Review of
Equivariant Toric Geometry and Euler–Maclaurin Formulae
# Identity and scope

The reviewed source is S. E. Cappell, L. Maxim, J. Schürmann and J. L. Shaneson, Equivariant toric geometry and Euler–Maclaurin formulae [source], assigned DOI https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70016. The acquired 95-page file is arXiv:2303.16785v3: its margin dates the version 15 September 2025 and its title page gives 16 September 2025. Its SHA256 is `5744803301cdbd3eff18e6543af389246b96f70d6cfcff0d68a1c9282658ad30`. The DOI association comes from the retained acquisition metadata; equivalence with a journal version has not been established. All page and equation references below concern this acquired file, not the separate overview cited as reference [20] in that file.

No usable substantive predecessor report was recovered in the bounded preserved-reference search. This is an initial review. The primary executor and the core native helper each read the complete source, including references. Two additional native checks addressed the face operators and the Cox proof, respectively. Their actual roles and read scopes are separately retained; they are internal auxiliaries, not independent acceptance. The primary executor read the complete analytical evidence and rechecked the decisive calculations and source images. No author code was executed. Optional code and supplements were not located in the bounded acquisition evidence; their absence is not asserted universally and is not a mathematical defect.
# Framework and positive checks

The orbit decomposition weights the dualizing-sheaf contribution of an orbit closure by \((1+y)^{\dim O}\). Proper pushforward and equivariant Riemann–Roch then express twisted characteristic classes as lattice sums. The source distinguishes localization statements for general toric varieties from the explicit Cox formulae and facet operators requiring simplicial fans, hence simple full-dimensional lattice polytopes. Completeness is used for the relevant global pushforwards. With the paper’s left action, a monomial \(\chi^m\) has character \(\chi^{-m}\) and \(s(m)=-c(m)\); these signs matter in both translation checks.

The abstract operator statements, including Theorems 5.18 and 7.10, require a power series representing the actual equivariant Todd class of the chosen sheaf. An incorrect proposed representative does not disprove that conditional theorem. Polynomial insertions permit finite-degree truncation. Exponential cone integrals additionally require a convergence chamber; the real negative parameter used below satisfies it. External Riemann–Roch, localization, resolution and quotient-form results were examined as stated inputs, not independently reacquired or reproved.

Retained exact checks verify the finite-group Molien projection, the single vertex shift in weighted Brion summation, and the global Todd operator on the singular triangle used below. Its weighted count is \(4+y\), including the relative-interior point on its long edge. The interval tests cover 63 exact classical cases; separate checks address interior and weighted formulae. Lattice-normalized Stokes identities and the multiplicity in the face-integral identity were also checked. In particular, at the triangle’s singular vertex the multiplicity \(2\) cancels the mixed-volume derivative \(1/2\). These checks are finite tests with explicit hypotheses, not an exhaustive verification of every characteristic-class identity.
# Established corrections
## P01 (Major): quotient-ray normalization in face operators

Equations (5.29)–(5.36), pp. 74–75, use the ordinary fan \(\operatorname{Star}(\sigma_E)\) but differentiate in the original ambient facet variables. A projected ray need not remain primitive. The source explicitly uses primitive ray generators, the saturated lattice \(N_\sigma=N\cap\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\sigma\), and the quotient \(N/N_\sigma\) (pp. 16–19). These conventions preclude silently replacing the ordinary quotient fan by a different nonprimitive presentation.

Let \[P=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(2,0),(0,1)\},\qquad
 E=\{(0,t):0\leq t\leq1\},\qquad M=N=\mathbb Z^2.\] The primitive inward normals are \(u_1=(1,0)\), \(u_2=(0,1)\) and \(u_3=(-1,-2)\). This is a simple full-dimensional lattice polytope, as required; no Delzant assumption is present. For \(\sigma_E=\mathbb R_{\geq0}u_1\), one has \(\operatorname{mult}(\sigma_E)=1\). In \(N/N_{\sigma_E}\cong\mathbb Z\), the other normals project to \(1\) and \(-2\), while the primitive rays of \(\operatorname{Star}(\sigma_E)\) are \(1,-1\). Thus its toric variety is \(\mathbb P^1\) and its finite local group contribution is trivial.

In this example the intrinsic upper facet offset is \((h_1+h_3)/2\). Replacing the affected derivative by \(2\partial_3\) repairs both values. An alternative nonprimitive quotient presentation with weights \(1,-2\) has a \(\mu_2\) contribution; the nonidentity term supplies the missing \(+1/4\) and \(-1/4\), respectively. That alternative requires a different, explicitly justified construction. A general repair cannot be obtained merely by renaming the ordinary star fan.

This is a false explicit closed- and open-face guarantee under the stated hypotheses, hence Major. It also affects the weighted face formulae at \(y=0\), including (6.18). It does not refute global Brion summation, the general Riemann–Roch theorem, or the leading fundamental-class factor in the face-integral identity. The proof of Theorem 7.12 cites the erroneous full formula (5.34), but its limit (7.13) only needs the lowest-codimension Todd component, namely \([V_{\sigma_E}]\). That component equals \(\operatorname{mult}(\sigma_E)\prod_{\rho\in\sigma_E(1)}F_\rho\) and supplies the required limit directly. Thus the full-series error should not be propagated to Corollary 7.13.
## P02 (Major): the unnormalized weighted face prefactor

Equations (6.14)–(6.17), p. 80, retain the ambient factor \((1+y)^{n-r}\) in an operator for a proper face. Take \(P=[0,1]\), \(E=\{0\}\) and \(f=1\), with \(n=1\), \(r=2\). The zero-dimensional star fan has no rays or nontrivial group. The ambient dilated volume is \[V(h)=1+h_L+h_R.\] The printed unnormalized operator is consequently \((1+y)^{-1}\partial_L\). At \(y=1\) it gives \(1/2\), whereas the right side of (6.16) is the single point’s weight \(1\). The parameter avoids the excluded value \(y=-1\). This smooth example is independent of P01.

Using the face fan’s own dimension and number of rays gives exponent \(0\) for this point, correcting this test. The issue is Major because the explicitly stated weighted face identity is false under its stated hypotheses, even in the smooth case. It is not evidence against every normalized formula. The normalized expression printed below (6.17) removes this prefactor: its point operator is \(\partial_L\), acting on \(P_y(h)\) of length \(1+y+h_L+h_R\), and gives \(1\) as required in (6.18). P01, rather than this point test, supplies the separate \(y=0\) failure of (6.18).
## P03 (Major): a vertex translation is counted twice

The source defines \(\operatorname{Tan}(P,v)=v+C_v\) on p. 66. Equations (5.22), (5.25), (5.28), (6.6) and (6.13) retain an additional \(e^{\langle v,z\rangle}\) in front of a lattice sum already over this translated cone (pp. 73–74, 78, 80). This is one repeated error.

Take \(P=[1,2]\), \(v=1\), \(C_v=[0,\infty)\) and real \(z<0\) arbitrarily near zero. The dilated tangent cone is \([1-h,\infty)\), and \[I(h)=\int_{1-h}^{\infty}e^{xz}\,dx
      =-\frac{e^{(1-h)z}}{z},\qquad
 \left.Q(\partial_h)I(h)\right|_{h=0}
      =\frac{e^z}{1-e^z}.\] The printed additional factor instead produces \[e^z\sum_{m\geq1}e^{mz}=\frac{e^{2z}}{1-e^z}.\] For \(e^z=99/100\), these are \(99\) and \(9801/100\). The relative-interior operator similarly gives \(e^{2z}/(1-e^z)\), while the additional factor gives \(e^{3z}/(1-e^z)\). The weighted versions have the same duplicated shift. The discrepancy occurs within the stated convergence chamber and can be made arbitrarily close to zero; it is not a boundary-value or divergent-series artifact.

One should either remove the exterior exponential from the already translated sum or sum over the unshifted \(C_v\). The repeated explicit local Euler–Maclaurin identities are false, which supports Major severity despite this short correction. The general Proposition 5.22 uses an untranslated local characteristic class and is not the erroneous equation (5.22). Likewise, the global Brion formula (4.19) contains a single shift multiplying an unshifted cone series. Neither statement is refuted by this example.
## P04 (Major): an algebraic-group product need not exist

The proof of Lemma 3.20, p. 42, and the alternative localization argument on p. 61 assert \(G\cong G_\sigma\times(\mathbb C^*)^{r-n}\). For the same triangle fan the Cox map is \[\beta(t_1,t_2,t_3)=(t_1/t_3,t_2/t_3^2),\qquad
 G=\{(t,t^2,t):t\in\mathbb C^*\}.\] For the maximal cone generated by \(u_1,u_3\), the finite stabilizer is \(G_\sigma=\mu_2\). The group \(G\cong\mathbb C^*\) is connected; \(\mu_2\times\mathbb C^*\) is not. The relevant sequence is \[1\longrightarrow\mu_2\longrightarrow\mathbb C^*
 \xrightarrow{\,t\mapsto t^2\,}\mathbb C^*
 \longrightarrow1.\] An algebraic section would require an integer exponent \(k\) with \(2k=1\). Thus neither occurrence is a valid product argument.

There is a direct invariant-module replacement. Let \(I\) be the maximal cone’s rays, \(J\) their complement, \(T_I=(\mathbb C^*)^I\), and \(H=\ker(T_I\to\mathbb T)\). The isogeny \(T_I\to\mathbb T\) has finite kernel \(H\); it need not split. For a Cox character twist \(\widetilde m\), restriction to the slice \(y_J=1\) identifies \[\bigl(\mathbb C[x_I,y_J^{\pm1}]\otimes\mathbb C_{\widetilde m}\bigr)^G
 \ \cong\
 \bigl(\mathbb C[x_I]\otimes\mathbb C_{\widetilde m_I}\bigr)^H.\] To verify surjectivity without a product assumption, an \(H\)-invariant monomial \(x^a\) satisfies \(\widetilde m_I-a=\beta_I^*u\) for a unique \(u\in M\). Its unique Laurent extension has exponent \(b=\widetilde m_J-\beta_J^*u\). This proves the identification on monomial bases and preserves the residual \(\mathbb T=T_I/H\) action. The same argument applies to the coordinate cotangent wedges; the invariant logarithmic forms \(dy_j/y_j\) contribute \((1+y)^{|J|}=(1+y)^{r-n}\).

This replaces the false product step in Lemma 3.20 and the local character calculation. The quotient-form input invoked in the source remains an explicit external dependency. Source p. 43 obtains the main Theorem 3.21 from Lemma 3.20 via Lefschetz–Riemann–Roch; the alternative localization derivation repeats the false splitting on p. 61. The missing valid descent is therefore a core dependency in both printed derivations, which supports Major severity. The independently checked invariant-module replacement restores that bridge. The witness disproves the product assertion and the original proof step; it does not disprove the characteristic-class identity, and the availability of a repair does not retroactively validate the printed derivations.
# Editorial clarification excluded from findings

The paragraph immediately before Corollary 3.16, p. 40, sets \(P'=P_D-m_0\) but prints \(\mathcal O(D-\operatorname{div}\chi^{m_0})
 \cong f^*\mathcal O(D')\) as an equivariant identity. The sign should be plus. For \(P_D=[1,2]\) and \(m_0=1\), the coefficients of \(D\) for the normals \(1,-1\) are \((-1,2)\), while those of \(\operatorname{div}\chi^{m_0}\) are \((1,-1)\). Thus \[D+\operatorname{div}\chi^{m_0}=(0,1)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P'=[0,1],\] whereas the printed minus gives \((-2,3)\) and \([2,3]\). The source’s formula (2.16), p. 20, already has the correct plus sign. The proof on p. 41 also uses the correct factor \(e^{s(m_0)}=e^{-c(m_0)}\). This is a local equivariant translation error, not a counterexample to the underlying nonequivariant line-bundle class or to Corollary 3.16. The discrepancy is confined to this transitional sentence: the actual character calculation follows the correct direction. No essential calculation or conclusion is shown to use the wrong sign. It is therefore retained as an editorial clarification and excluded from the substantive findings.
# Extent of the conclusion

The four Major findings concern three explicit local or face formulae central to the Euler–Maclaurin applications and an invalid Cox-descent bridge in the main characteristic-class derivations. The verified replacement for that bridge preserves the stated result while correcting its original proof. The isolated divisor-sign discrepancy is excluded from the findings because the subsequent character computation already uses the correct sign. Repeated manifestations of one defect have been grouped, and no issue count was imposed.

Several tempting extensions of these objections are unsupported. The ambient face-integral multiplicity is correct; the failed ordinary star Todd series does not invalidate its leading term. The smooth point test does not refute the separately normalized point operator. The source explicitly invokes polynomial continuation for its \(y=-1\) specialization; literal negative dilation should not be substituted for that continuation. The acquired preprint, rather than an unverified journal text, is the sole version covered by these findings.

The accompanying records retain the source bindings, full read coverage, exact calculations and counterchecks, actual source image observations, and the full compiler, parser and report image facts. No equivalence between that selection and native helper backends is asserted. This report is the initial scientific continuation; human scientific adjudication remains pending.

      =\frac{e^z}{1-e^z}.\] The printed additional factor instead produces \[e^z\sum_{m\geq1}e^{mz}=\frac{e^{2z}}{1-e^z}.\] For \(e^z=99/100\), these are \(99\) and \(9801/100\). claim: Recorded check: False Cox group product in two local proofs
analysis:
The proof of Lemma 3.20, p. 42, and the alternative localization argument on p. 61 assert \(G\cong G_\sigma\times(\mathbb C^*)^{r-n}\). For the same triangle fan the Cox map is \[\beta(t_1,t_2,t_3)=(t_1/t_3,t_2/t_3^2),\qquad
 G=\{(t,t^2,t):t\in\mathbb C^*\}.\] For the maximal cone generated by \(u_1,u_3\), the finite stabilizer is \(G_\sigma=\mu_2\). The group \(G\cong\mathbb C^*\) is connected; \(\mu_2\times\mathbb C^*\) is not. The relevant sequence is \[1\longrightarrow\mu_2\longrightarrow\mathbb C^*
 \xrightarrow{\,t\mapsto t^2\,}\mathbb C^*
 \longrightarrow1.\] An algebraic section would require an integer exponent \(k\) with \(2k=1\). Thus neither occurrence is a valid product argument.

There is a direct invariant-module replacement. Let \(I\) be the maximal cone’s rays, \(J\) their complement, \(T_I=(\mathbb C^*)^I\), and \(H=\ker(T_I\to\mathbb T)\). The isogeny \(T_I\to\mathbb T\) has finite kernel \(H\); it need not split. For a Cox character twist \(\widetilde m\), restriction to the slice \(y_J=1\) identifies \[\bigl(\mathbb C[x_I,y_J^{\pm1}]\otimes\mathbb C_{\widetilde m}\bigr)^G
 \ \cong\
 \bigl(\mathbb C[x_I]\otimes\mathbb C_{\widetilde m_I}\bigr)^H.\] To verify surjectivity without a product assumption, an \(H\)-invariant monomial \(x^a\) satisfies \(\widetilde m_I-a=\beta_I^*u\) for a unique \(u\in M\). Its unique Laurent extension has exponent \(b=\widetilde m_J-\beta_J^*u\). This proves the identification on monomial bases and preserves the residual \(\mathbb T=T_I/H\) action. The same argument applies to the coordinate cotangent wedges; the invariant logarithmic forms \(dy_j/y_j\) contribute \((1+y)^{|J|}=(1+y)^{r-n}\).

This replaces the false product step in Lemma 3.20 and the local character calculation. The quotient-form input invoked in the source remains an explicit external dependency. Source p. 43 obtains the main Theorem 3.21 from Lemma 3.20 via Lefschetz–Riemann–Roch; the alternative localization derivation repeats the false splitting on p. 61. The missing valid descent is therefore a core dependency in both printed derivations, which supports Major severity. The independently checked invariant-module replacement restores that bridge. The witness disproves the product assertion and the original proof step; it does not disprove the characteristic-class identity, and the availability of a repair does not retroactively validate the printed derivations.

report: Abstract: This review checks the stochastic-cycle argument in Lemma 9.5 and its place in the remainder estimates, with additional checks of the formulation and selected energy identities. The union in (9.17) makes the ensuing bound on the number of short flights false, even in a ball. An explicit family of admissible trajectories proves the discrepancy. Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Verification of
Ghost Effect from Boltzmann Theory
# Paper identity and inspected scope

The paper is Ghost effect from Boltzmann theory, by Raffaele Esposito, Yan Guo, Rossana Marra and Lei Wu, associated with Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics, DOI 10.1002/cpa.70017 (https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70017). The acquired and reviewed source is the 76-page arXiv version 2301.09427v3, dated 18 September 2023 [EGMW]. Physical PDF pages and printed pages coincide in this source. The journal article is a separate version; its full text was not compared with this preprint.

The main focus is Definitions 9.2–9.4 and Lemma 9.5, pp. 59–60: the geometric count, diffuse measure and link to Proposition 9.1. Theorem 1.2 and its assumptions, selected energy identities, the Section 10 closure and the Section 12 iteration were inspected to establish the meaning and dependence of this step. The earlier stochastic-cycle argument was checked in arXiv:1111.5843v2, especially pp. 27–28 [EGKM]. Its corresponding lemma is numbered 4.2 in that preprint; numbering need not coincide with the published reference.

This review does not independently establish all boundary-layer, elliptic, BV, coercivity or compactness estimates in Sections 2–8 and 11. The coverage ledger distinguishes inspected statements, partly inspected arguments and uninspected proofs. Extraction of the entire PDF is not scientific reading of every page. No author program was executed, and no missing program is treated as a defect.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

Theorem 1.2, p. 7, assumes a bounded \(C^3\) domain \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3\), the small wall-temperature condition (1.14), and a fixed \(P>0\); it asserts the result for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\). The unit ball and constant wall temperature \(T_w=1\) are admissible. The latter makes the temperature-gradient smallness requirement automatic.

In the stochastic cycles, \(n(x)\) is the outward unit normal and \[V_j=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:v\cdot n(x_j)>0\},\qquad
 d\sigma_j=\mu_M(v_j)|v_j\cdot n(x_j)|\,dv_j,\] where \(\mu_M\) is a fixed positive isotropic Gaussian. Definitions 9.2–9.3, p. 59, use \[t_b(x,v)=\inf\{t>0:x-\varepsilon tv\notin\Omega\},
 \qquad t_{j+1}=t_j+t_b(x_j,v_j).\] The initial point may be interior, velocities are nonzero, and boundary hits under consideration are nongrazing. Lemma 9.5 claims an exponentially small diffuse measure of \(t_k<\mathcal T/\varepsilon\) for large \(\mathcal T\) and \(k\) of order \(\mathcal T^{5/4}\). This is a measure estimate, not the absence of individual short trajectories.
# Substantive finding
Problem 1 (The set in (9.17) does not imply the claimed flight count).  The deterministic counting assertion immediately following (9.17), p. 60, is false with the union printed in that equation.
## Original step and location

Equation reference: eq:union. Equation (9.17) defines \[
 V_j^\eta
 =\{v\in V_j:v\cdot n(x_j)>\eta\}
 \ \cup\ \{v\in V_j:|v|<\eta^{-1}\}.\] For small \(0<\eta<1\), the next sentence asserts that \(t_k<\mathcal T/\varepsilon\) permits at most \[M=\left\lfloor C_\Omega\mathcal T/\eta^3\right\rfloor+1\] indices with \(v_j\in V_j^\eta\). Equation (9.18) uses that count to reduce the integral to configurations with at most \(M\) such velocities. The rendered PDF confirms the union symbol; this is not a text-extraction ambiguity.
## Admissible counterexample

Equation reference: eq:delta, eq:velocity. Take \(\Omega=B(0,1)\), \(T_w=1\), any fixed \(P>0\), and any admissibly small \(\varepsilon>0\). For every proposed \(C_\Omega>0\), every \(\mathcal T>0\) and \(0<\eta<1\), define \(M\) as above, choose an integer \(k\ge M+2\), and set \[
 \delta=\min\{\eta/2,\mathcal T/(16k),1/8\}>0.\] At each boundary point \(x_j\), choose a unit tangent vector \(\tau_j\perp x_j\) and put \[
 v_j=\delta x_j+\sqrt{1/4-\delta^2}\,\tau_j.\] Then \(|v_j|=1/2\) and \(v_j\cdot n(x_j)=\delta>0\). Every velocity is nonzero and nongrazing, and belongs to [eq:union] (#eq:union) through the speed condition despite \(\delta<\eta\).

Equation reference: eq:flight. Proof. Starting at \(x\in\partial B(0,1)\) with such a velocity, the next sphere intersection solves \[|x-sv|^2-1=-2s\delta+s^2/4=0.\] The nonzero root is \(s=8\delta\), the intervening segment is inside the ball, and therefore \[
 t_b(x,v)=8\delta/\varepsilon,\qquad
 x_{\rm next}=x-8\delta v\in\partial\Omega.\] Choose \(x_1\in\partial\Omega\), \(v_1\) as above, and start at \(x_0=x_1-4\delta v_1\), \(v_0=-v_1\). Since \(|x_0|^2=1-4\delta^2<1\), the first backward exit is \(x_1\) at \(t_1=4\delta/\varepsilon\). Continue with [eq:velocity] (#eq:velocity) at every hit. It follows that \[t_k=(8k-4)\delta/\varepsilon<\mathcal T/\varepsilon,\] although all \(k-1\ge M+1\) sampled velocities belong to the printed \(V_j^\eta\). This contradicts the asserted count. The construction works for arbitrarily large \(\mathcal T\) and for the integer choices of \(k\) in the proof whenever \(k-1>M\). ◻

The inequalities have strict margins. For each finite \(k\), nearby velocities preserve the violation: transversal sphere hits depend smoothly on the input, and the Gaussian density is positive. Thus this is not an isolated zero-measure trajectory. This observation does not compare that neighborhood’s measure with the claimed exponential bound; it does not refute Lemma 9.5 itself.

The root-authored symbolic check in `verification/0431/problems/P01/` verifies the speed, intersection equation, interior initial point and exact rational examples. The argument above proves the universal counterexample family; finite diagnostics are supplementary.
## Alternative reading and counterevidence

The natural intended set is the intersection of the two conditions. The acquired earlier paper [EGKM], p. 28, explicitly uses an intersection and derives the required flight-time lower bound. This is substantial counterevidence against a failure of the underlying stochastic-cycle method.

Reading the definition as imposing both conditions repairs it, but changes the displayed union. The contradiction under the printed definition remains. A bounded check of arXiv, publisher metadata and the author publication list did not identify a separate correction of (9.17). This does not establish that no correction exists. The journal text and unpublished corrections remain unverified.
## Verified local repair
## Core dependence, severity and boundaries

Proposition 9.1, p. 59, identifies this stochastic-cycle modification as part of its weighted \(L^\infty\) proof. Its bound enters (10.4) and the combined estimate (10.6), p. 61. The iteration (12.3), p. 68, invokes that a priori estimate for the remainder in Theorem 1.2.

The assessment is Major for the displayed derivation: a demonstrated invalid count lies on this core proof chain. Neither the tail bound, the existence theorem nor the ghost-effect limit is thereby proved false. The corrected intersection and argument above restore this specific geometric-probabilistic step; they do not certify all later analytic estimates. The likely typographical origin and the valid earlier construction are part of this assessment.
# Additional checks and limits

The Gaussian coefficient in (5.15), p. 30, survives an independent exact check. For \(V\sim N(0,TI_3)\), \[\mathbb E[V_i^2(|V|^2-5T)^2]=10T^3.\] Multiplication by \(\rho=P/T\) and \(2/(4T^2)\) gives \(5P\), as required. This validates that coefficient, not the entire energy inequality.

The small-data closure and its \(L^\infty\) dependence were traced. Selected apparent difficulties in the positivity discussion were not promoted to findings: a collision lower bound there must be interpreted on the compact velocity range used by the auxiliary cutoff. No global lower bound outside that range is certified. Unresolved normalization questions elsewhere were not used to claim a false theorem.
# Conclusion

One substantive problem is established in the reviewed preprint. Admissible trajectories invalidate the count based on (9.17); the corresponding tail estimate has a verified local repair supported by the earlier reference.

report: Abstract: The arithmetic step used to exclude two orbit points from a reflected pair in Lemma 6.5 fails for two indices in its first interval. The relevant resonance index can equal zero, even for a phase allowed by Theorem 1.6. A different capacity count repairs this step without changing the asserted localization conclusion. The finite-interval solution formula also has incorrect signs under the paper’s stated determinant convention; its use in absolute-value bounds survives correction. A separate exponent-bookkeeping question is retained with an explicit possible repair, rather than promoted to a false theorem claim. The reviewed source is arXiv:2212.05988v2. Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Verification of Avila’s Acceleration via Zeros of Determinants and Applications to Schrödinger Cocycles
# Identity, version and scope

The paper is by Rui Han and Wilhelm Schlag, associated with DOI 10.1002/cpa.70018 (https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70018). The acquired PDF is the 22-page preprint Avila’s acceleration via zeros of determinants, and applications to Schrödinger cocycles, arXiv:2212.05988v2, revised 4 January 2023 [HS]. Physical and printed page numbers coincide. The journal record lists Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 79 (2026), 729–761, first published online 22 October 2025 [journal]. That later full text was not compared. Findings below apply to the acquired preprint only.

All 22 source pages were read as text. Direct checks concentrated on the annular Green average and the zero-count argument in Sections 3–5, the arithmetic and threshold arguments in Section 6, and the finite-interval determinant identities. This is not an independent reconstruction of every cited large-deviation, avalanche-principle, global-theory, or spectral-theory result. In particular, Section 7’s transfer of the long argument in [GS2] was traced as a dependency but not independently established in full. The coverage ledger records these limits. No author program was executed.
# Definitions and hypotheses
# A core counting step and a replacement proof

Problem 1 (Major: invalid derivation in Lemma 6.5).  On p. 19, the proof asserts \(n/4\le \ell_1+\ell_2+n\le11n\) for the indices under consideration and applies [phase] (#phase) with \(k=\ell_1+\ell_2+n-1\). This fails when both indices belong to \(I_1\).

Equation reference: pairs. The intervals, for an integer \(n<y<10n\), are \[I_1=[-\lfloor7n/8\rfloor,-\lfloor n/8\rfloor]\cap\mathbb Z,
 \qquad I_2=y+I_1 .\] The cover inherited from Lemma 6.2 consists of \(N''\le n+o(n)\) pairs \[
 P_j=U_j\cup\bigl(-(n-1)\alpha-U_j\bigr),\] with exponentially short intervals \(U_j\). We use the negative sign in [pairs] (#pairs), as in Lemma 6.2 and the proof of Lemma 6.5; the isolated positive sign in the statement of Lemma 6.5 is not a separate substantive finding.
Claim 1.  For arbitrarily large \(n\), two distinct permitted indices in \(I_1\) give resonance index zero.

Proof. Take \(n=8m+1\), \(m\ge1\), and \(\ell_1=-4m+1,\ \ell_2=-4m-1\). Then \(I_1=[-7m,-m]\cap\mathbb Z\), so both indices belong to it, whereas \[\ell_1+\ell_2+n=1<n/4,\qquad
 \ell_1+\ell_2+n-1=0 .\] Choose, for example, \(y=2n\), which meets all the interval restrictions. At the allowed phase \(\theta=0\), \[\ell_2\alpha=-(n-1)\alpha-\ell_1\alpha\pmod1.\] Consequently an arbitrarily short interval about \(\ell_1\alpha\), together with its reflected partner, can contain both orbit points. The claimed arithmetic separation of such points does not follow from the two Diophantine hypotheses. ◻

This counterexample disproves the printed index bound, not the conclusion of Lemma 6.5. In particular, an arbitrarily selected interval \(U_j\) is not claimed to be the actual zero-generated cover for a specified \(f,E,n\). The analytic and spectral hypotheses do not change the displayed index calculation; additional information about a particular cover would need its own argument. The root-authored exact calculation checks the indices symbolically and at \(n=9,17,25,81,801,8001\).
## Counterevidence and local repair
The two intervals have enough excess capacity to prove the intended conclusion without the false one-point-per-pair assertion.

Claim 2.  Assume the cover [pairs] (#pairs), \(N''\le n+o(n)\), the two stated arithmetic hypotheses, and \(|U_j|\le e^{-n^\rho}\) for a fixed \(\rho>0\). For all sufficiently large \(n\), the cover cannot contain every orbit point indexed by \(I_1\cup I_2\).

Proof. The Diophantine condition on \(\alpha\) ensures at most one of these orbit points in each individual component of \(P_j\): distinct indices differ by a nonzero integer of size \(O(n)\), whose orbit separation is bounded below by a negative power of \(n\) times a logarithmic factor.

If two indices are both in \(I_2\), their sum index \(\ell_1+\ell_2+n-1\) is between positive constant multiples of \(n\), since \(y>n\). The same is true when one index is in \(I_1\) and the other in \(I_2\): \[\ell_1+\ell_2+n-1
 \ge y-2\lfloor7n/8\rfloor+n-1
 \ge n/4-O(1).\] All such indices also have an \(O(n)\) upper bound. Thus [phase] (#phase) excludes two opposite-component points in either case. A pair contains at most two \(I_1\) points, at most one \(I_2\) point, and cannot contain points from both groups.

Writing \(q=\lfloor7n/8\rfloor-\lfloor n/8\rfloor+1\), a cover of all the points would therefore require at least \[\tfrac12\#I_1+\#I_2=\tfrac32q
 \ge \tfrac98n-O(1)>n+o(n)\] pairs, a contradiction. Possible overlaps between different pairs cannot improve this capacity bound. ◻

The proof of Lemma 6.6 then excludes a good index in \(I_1\); Corollary 6.7 supplies one in \(I_2\), and (6.67) yields the localization estimate. This is precisely why the defective step is tied to a principal contribution, Theorem 1.6. The Major assessment concerns that core derivation. Claim Claim 2 (#repair) is substantial counterevidence against inferring a false final theorem: it replaces the bad step under the intended covering hypotheses. It does not verify all preceding analytic inputs or assert that the authors adopted this correction.
# Finite-interval signs

Problem 2 (Minor: the signed identity (2.8)).  For the determinant convention on p. 1 and the operator (1.1), the two uniform minus signs in (2.8), p. 7, are not valid for all interval lengths and interior indices.

This identity is stated for solutions of \(H_{\alpha,\theta}\phi=E\phi\) and an invertible finite restriction. It does not require a polynomially bounded generalized eigenfunction. Choose \(f\equiv0\), \(E=3\), any allowed \(\alpha\), and the formal solution with \(\phi_{-1}=0,\phi_0=1\). The recurrence gives \(\phi_1=3,\phi_2=8\). On \([0,1]\), \[H-E=\begin{pmatrix}-3&1\\1&-3\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad D_0=1,\quad D_1=-3,\quad D_2=8.\] At \(y=0\), the printed (2.8) gives \(-D_1\phi_{-1}/D_2-D_0\phi_2/D_2=-1\), whereas the exact value is \(1\). The finite restriction is invertible. The potential is real analytic and even; also \(L(3)=\log((3+\sqrt5)/2)>0\). This formal solution is not polynomially bounded, and \(3\) is not in the free spectrum; it is therefore not a counterexample to Theorem 1.6.

The independent calculation solves the two-site system exactly and checks both boundary cofactor columns for a symbolic three-site matrix. The downstream inequality (6.66), p. 20, takes absolute values, as does \(u_n\le v_n\) in (2.6). Both remain valid after the sign correction. This is a local mathematical identity error, with no demonstrated loss of the central magnitude estimates, and is assessed Minor.
# Exponent bookkeeping requiring clarification

Problem 3 (NeedsEvidence: identify the exponent being used).  The fixed exponent in (6.47), p. 16, is not the threshold supplied by Lemma 6.4 and used immediately after its proof on p. 18. An implicit reduction of exponents is plausible, but should be made explicit.

Write \(\delta\) for the exponent from Lemma 2.6. The printed bad set is \(\mathcal B_n=\{u_n<L_n-n^{-\delta}\}\). Lemma 6.4 gives a nearby zero only under \(u_n<L_n-C_1n^{-\delta/2}\). For large \(n\), \[\frac{C_1n^{-\delta/2}}{n^{-\delta}}
 =C_1n^{\delta/2}\longrightarrow\infty .\] The latter condition describes a smaller bad set. Thus that lemma alone does not imply the displayed cover of the defined \(\mathcal B_n\). With \(t=\log r,\ a=\log R,\ s=\log|w|\), the independently recomputed circle average in (3.11), p. 8, is \[I(t,a,s)=
 \begin{cases}
 (t+a)(s-a)/(2a),&t\le s,\\
 (t-a)(s+a)/(2a),&t\ge s.
 \end{cases}\] It vanishes at \(t=\pm a\), is continuous at \(t=s\), and its derivative has jump one. Reciprocal pairing of determinant zeros then gives the factor \(-\pi/n\) in (4.24), p. 12. problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: Problem 1 (Major: invalid derivation in Lemma 6.5).
claim: Recorded check: For all m>=1 the claimed sum is1<n/4, and the two orbit points at theta0 are exact mates under x->-(n-1)alpha-x. Exact symbolic and integer computations are retained.
analysis: On p. 19, the proof asserts \(n/4\le \ell_1+\ell_2+n\le11n\) for the indices under consideration and applies [phase] (#phase) with \(k=\ell_1+\ell_2+n-1\). This fails when both indices belong to \(I_1\).

Equation reference: pairs. The intervals, for an integer \(n<y<10n\), are \[I_1=[-\lfloor7n/8\rfloor,-\lfloor n/8\rfloor]\cap\mathbb Z,
 \qquad I_2=y+I_1 .\] The cover inherited from Lemma 6.2 consists of \(N''\le n+o(n)\) pairs \[
 P_j=U_j\cup\bigl(-(n-1)\alpha-U_j\bigr),\] with exponentially short intervals \(U_j\). We use the negative sign in [pairs] (#pairs), as in Lemma 6.2 and the proof of Lemma 6.5; the isolated positive sign in the statement of Lemma 6.5 is not a separate substantive finding.
Claim 1.  For arbitrarily large \(n\), two distinct permitted indices in \(I_1\) give resonance index zero.

Proof. Take \(n=8m+1\), \(m\ge1\), and \(\ell_1=-4m+1,\ \ell_2=-4m-1\). Then \(I_1=[-7m,-m]\cap\mathbb Z\), so both indices belong to it, whereas \[\ell_1+\ell_2+n=1<n/4,\qquad
 \ell_1+\ell_2+n-1=0 .\] Choose, for example, \(y=2n\), which meets all the interval restrictions. At the allowed phase \(\theta=0\), \[\ell_2\alpha=-(n-1)\alpha-\ell_1\alpha\pmod1.\] Consequently an arbitrarily short interval about \(\ell_1\alpha\), together with its reflected partner, can contain both orbit points. The claimed arithmetic separation of such points does not follow from the two Diophantine hypotheses. ◻

This counterexample disproves the printed index bound, not the conclusion of Lemma 6.5. In particular, an arbitrarily selected interval \(U_j\) is not claimed to be the actual zero-generated cover for a specified \(f,E,n\). The analytic and spectral hypotheses do not change the displayed index calculation; additional information about a particular cover would need its own argument. The root-authored exact calculation checks the indices symbolically and at \(n=9,17,25,81,801,8001\).
result: The two intervals have enough excess capacity to prove the intended conclusion without the false one-point-per-pair assertion.

Claim 2.  Assume the cover [pairs] (#pairs), \(N''\le n+o(n)\), the two stated arithmetic hypotheses, and \(|U_j|\le e^{-n^\rho}\) for a fixed \(\rho>0\). For all sufficiently large \(n\), the cover cannot contain every orbit point indexed by \(I_1\cup I_2\).

Proof. The Diophantine condition on \(\alpha\) ensures at most one of these orbit points in each individual component of \(P_j\): distinct indices differ by a nonzero integer of size \(O(n)\), whose orbit separation is bounded below by a negative power of \(n\) times a logarithmic factor.

If two indices are both in \(I_2\), their sum index \(\ell_1+\ell_2+n-1\) is between positive constant multiples of \(n\), since \(y>n\). The same is true when one index is in \(I_1\) and the other in \(I_2\): \[\ell_1+\ell_2+n-1
 \ge y-2\lfloor7n/8\rfloor+n-1
 \ge n/4-O(1).\] All such indices also have an \(O(n)\) upper bound. Thus [phase] (#phase) excludes two opposite-component points in either case. A pair contains at most two \(I_1\) points, at most one \(I_2\) point, and cannot contain points from both groups.

Writing \(q=\lfloor7n/8\rfloor-\lfloor n/8\rfloor+1\), a cover of all the points would therefore require at least \[\tfrac12\#I_1+\#I_2=\tfrac32q
 \ge \tfrac98n-O(1)>n+o(n)\] pairs, a contradiction. Possible overlaps between different pairs cannot improve this capacity bound. ◻

The proof of Lemma 6.6 then excludes a good index in \(I_1\); Corollary 6.7 supplies one in \(I_2\), and (6.67) yields the localization estimate. This is precisely why the defective step is tied to a principal contribution, Theorem 1.6. The Major assessment concerns that core derivation. Claim Claim 2 (#repair) is substantial counterevidence against inferring a false final theorem: it replaces the bad step under the intended covering hypotheses. It does not verify all preceding analytic inputs or assert that the authors adopted this correction.
Result: The printed deterministic arithmetic assertion and resulting uniform one-point-per-pair justification are invalid.

report: Abstract: Lemma 3.3 has a false quantitative conclusion: its coefficient omits the factor \((\gamma')^{\gamma'}/\gamma^\gamma\). An explicit square, with only its first Dirichlet eigenvalue contributing, satisfies every hypothesis and violates the asserted bound by the exact factor \(2^{1/8}\). The same coefficient occurs in the acquired journal version and arXiv v2. The corrected estimate preserves the local exponent improvement used in the qualitative extrapolation argument. In particular, this finding does not disprove the principal semiclassical inequalities below exponent one, the critical-exponent conclusions, or the shape-optimization theorems.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Verification of Semiclassical Inequalities for Dirichlet and Neumann Laplacians on Convex Domains
# Identity, source and scope

The reviewed paper is by Rupert L. Frank and Simon Larson, Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 79 (2026), 762–822, DOI 10.1002/cpa.70019 (https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70019) [FL]. The acquired 62-page PDF consists of a Chalmers cover followed by the 61-page version of record. Thus physical PDF page \(p\geq2\) corresponds to printed journal page \(p+760\). The cover and journal first page identify the version and authors. Its placement in the assigned annual batch is retained.

Root scientific reading covered physical pages 1–34 and 39–42. The detailed audit concentrated on the definitions and principal statements, the improved inequalities in Section 2, the full extrapolation argument in Section 3, the critical-exponent mechanism in Section 4, the product reduction in Section 5.1, and the Dirichlet dependency in the proof of Theorem 1.5. The remaining optimization and collapsing-domain proofs were not independently reconstructed. This report makes no certification of those unread parts or of every cited external result.

For an author-version comparison, arXiv:2410.04769v2, 15 October 2025, was separately acquired and bound [preprint]. Its physical pages 1 and 19–22 were read, and the title and decisive statement/proof pages were viewed. The public arXiv history checked during this review listed v2 as the latest version [history]. This is a bounded version check, not proof that no other correction exists.
# Definitions and exact hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:hyp, eq:false, eq:printedf. Set \(a=d/2\). Lemma 3.3 assumes \(d\geq2\), \(\gamma>0\), an open set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) of finite volume, \(c>0\), and \(0<\Lambda\leq\infty\), with \[
 R_\gamma^D(\lambda)
 \leq cL^{\mathrm{sc}}_{\gamma,d}|\Omega|\lambda^{\gamma+a}
 \quad(0\leq\lambda\leq\Lambda).\] It claims, for every \(q=\gamma'\in[0,\gamma]\), that \[
 R_q^D(\lambda)
 \leq c f_\gamma^D(q)L^{\mathrm{sc}}_{q,d}|\Omega|\lambda^{q+a},
 \qquad
 0\leq\lambda\leq\frac{q+a}{\gamma+a}\Lambda,\] where the printed coefficient is \[
 f_\gamma^D(q)=
 \frac{(\gamma+a)^{\gamma+a}}{(q+a)^{q+a}}
 \frac{\Gamma(1+q+a)\Gamma(1+\gamma)}
 {\Gamma(1+\gamma+a)\Gamma(1+q)}.\] There is no restriction \(\gamma\geq1\) or \(c\geq1\) in the statement.
# A false extrapolation bound

Problem 1 (P01: Major; Lemma 3.3).  The asserted coefficient in [eq:false] (#eq:false) is too small for some allowed exponents. The exact source locator is printed p. 781, physical p. 21, Lemma 3.3. The omitted factor can be tracked through the minimization on printed p. 782, physical p. 22; the subsequent coefficient analysis continues on pp. 783–784. The acquired arXiv v2 has the same statement and minimization on physical pp. 19–20.

Equation reference: eq:parameters. Claim 1.  The square \(\Omega=(0,\pi)^2\), with \[
 d=2,\qquad \gamma=\frac14,\qquad q=\frac18,\qquad
 \Lambda=\frac52,\qquad c=\frac{2}{\pi\,5^{1/4}},\] satisfies every hypothesis of Lemma 3.3, but violates its conclusion at \(\lambda_*=9/4\).

Proof. The square is open, bounded, nonempty, convex and Lipschitz, with area \(\pi^2\). Separation of variables gives the Dirichlet eigenvalues \(k^2+\ell^2\), \(k,\ell\geq1\). The first eigenvalue is \(2\), simple, and the next is \(5\). Thus \(R_\gamma^D(\lambda)=0\) for \(0\leq\lambda\leq2\); for \(2<\lambda\leq5/2\) it is \((\lambda-2)^{1/4}\). Since \(L^{\mathrm{sc}}_{\gamma,2}|\Omega|=\pi/5\), the normalized ratio is \[F(\lambda)=
 \frac{5(\lambda-2)^{1/4}}{\pi\lambda^{5/4}},
 \qquad
 \frac{F'(\lambda)}{F(\lambda)}
 =\frac{5-2\lambda}{2\lambda(\lambda-2)}\geq0.\] Consequently its maximum over this entire energy interval is \(F(5/2)=2/(\pi5^{1/4})=c\). This proves [eq:hyp] (#eq:hyp) for every required energy, including the endpoints; it is not merely a test at one energy.

The exact identities, the logarithmic derivative, the permitted energy endpoint and the corrected equality were independently checked by a root-authored SymPy calculation. Its actual execution exited zero; the script, output, version information and execution receipt are retained with P01. The proof above is sufficient without a floating-point spectral calculation.
# Repair and alternative readings

Equation reference: eq:tau, eq:repair. The scalar comparison preceding the minimization is valid. For \(0<q<\gamma\), its normalized coefficient is \[
 \frac{q^q(\gamma-q)^{\gamma-q}}{\gamma^\gamma}
 \frac{(1+\tau)^{\gamma+a}}{\tau^{\gamma-q}}
 \frac{L^{\mathrm{sc}}_{\gamma,d}}{L^{\mathrm{sc}}_{q,d}},
 \qquad (1+\tau)\lambda\leq\Lambda.\] Indeed, maximizing \(x^q/(x+\delta)^\gamma\) for \(x\geq0\) gives \(x=q\delta/(\gamma-q)\) and the scalar coefficient used in Lemma 3.2. Minimizing [eq:tau] (#eq:tau) gives \(\tau=(\gamma-q)/(q+a)\), exactly the paper’s value. Substitution, however, yields \[
 \widetilde f_\gamma^D(q)
 =\frac{q^q}{\gamma^\gamma}f_\gamma^D(q),\] with the same energy range as [eq:false] (#eq:false). The factors \((\gamma-q)^{\gamma-q}\) cancel, but \(q^q/\gamma^\gamma\) does not. At the diagonal the original assumption applies; at \(q=0\) the corresponding limiting estimate uses \(0^0=1\). In the square example the extra factor is \(2^{1/8}\), so the repaired estimate is an equality.

This is not an alternative normalization of \(L^{\mathrm{sc}}\): the definition in (1.4) and its elementary \(d=2\) specialization were used explicitly. Nor can the extra factor always be discarded as a harmless improvement. It exceeds one in [eq:parameters] (#eq:parameters). Restricting the lemma to \(\gamma=1\) would avoid this counterexample, but changes its stated range.

The correction does preserve the qualitative Dirichlet step in Proposition 3.1. Its hypotheses include \(\gamma_1>\gamma_0\geq0\), \(c<1\), \(\Lambda_1>\Lambda_0>0\), the semiclassical bound for every energy above \(\Lambda_0\) and every exponent in \([\gamma_0,\gamma_1]\), and a strict factor \(c\) at exponent \(\gamma_1\) below \(\Lambda_1\). By continuity of \(\widetilde f_{\gamma_1}^D(q)\) at \(q=\gamma_1\), where it equals one, choose \(q<\gamma_1\) sufficiently close to \(\gamma_1\) that \[c\widetilde f_{\gamma_1}^D(q)<1,\qquad
 \frac{q+a}{\gamma_1+a}\Lambda_1>\Lambda_0,\qquad q\geq\gamma_0.\] The repaired estimate covers the low energies and overlaps the assumed high-energy range. This proves the local exponent improvement used there, without the printed inverse-coefficient formula or any unproved monotonicity assertion for the new coefficient.

There is also direct counterevidence against a claim of failure of the main below-one inequality: for \(\gamma_1=1\) and \(0\leq q\leq1\), \(q^q\leq1\). Thus the printed coefficient is already a weaker valid bound in that special case. The proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 on printed p. 786 explicitly starts at exponent one. The separate Neumann extrapolation in Lemma 3.4 does not have this omitted factor.
# Dependency and impact boundaries
The false general lemma is part of a core argument, not an isolated numerical illustration. The following dependencies are explicit in the acquired source:
1. Proposition 3.1 applies Lemma 3.3 on p. 784. Proposition 4.1 then invokes Proposition 3.1 on p. 786.
2. The implication (ii)\(\Rightarrow\)(i) in Theorem 4.5 uses Proposition 4.1 on p. 788. Theorem 4.5 characterizes the critical exponent and is an announced main ingredient of Theorem 1.5 on p. 799.
3. Section 5, fact (d), p. 791, cites Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4 for continuity of the optimal excess factors as the Riesz exponent varies.

The classification is Major because an asserted quantitative lemma is demonstrably false and its general-exponent derivation serves the paper’s central extrapolation and critical-exponent analysis. It does not assert whole-paper failure. The explicit repair above restores the local qualitative mechanism checked here; the report has not re-proved every downstream optimization or collapsing-domain theorem. A correction should replace the coefficient, revise the associated coefficient discussion and quantitative exponent choices, and check downstream uses.

Other checks did not yield a further supported substantive finding. The all-energy quantifier and the positive-exponent restriction in the example were checked directly. The product eigenvalue reduction in Lemma 5.3 and its use for Proposition 1.4 were followed, as were the strict exponent gap and the role of Theorem 1.8 in the Dirichlet compactness argument. The external two-term asymptotics and the full proof of Theorem 1.8 remain dependencies, not independently certified results of this review. Apparent local typographical slips were not promoted into additional Problems. No author program was run, and no mathematical defect is inferred from code availability.
# Scope and references
This initial report records one proved quantitative defect and its repair boundary. Scientific adjudication remains pending and no independent acceptance is claimed.

report: Abstract: The general profile formula in Corollary 2.32 is false as printed. In its upper one-sided branch, the volume integral in Lemma 2.31 omits the completely filled slices. Title: Technical Verification of Isoperimetric Inequalities on Slabs with Applications to Cubes and Gaussian Slabs
# Identity, version and scope

The reviewed work is Emanuel Milman’s Isoperimetric inequalities on slabs with applications to cubes and Gaussian slabs, DOI 10.1002/cpa.70020 (https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70020) [paper]. The exact acquired source is arXiv:2403.06602v3, 13 October 2025, 63 pages; physical and printed page numbers agree. The journal metadata identifies the later article in Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 79 (2026), 1012–1072. The acquired preprint, rather than an unexamined journal PDF, is the object of the findings below.

Root scientific reading covered pp. 1–54 and p. 59. The audit followed the model-slab reduction, the classification and profile formula in Section 2, the stability framework, the principal cube and Gaussian deductions, and the numerical appendix’s setup. It independently reconstructed the defect below, the high-dimensional finite comparisons and induction inequality, and a volume-preserving Gaussian variation. The derivative and mesh details on pp. 55–58 and 60 were not fully read or reproduced; the bibliography on pp. 61–63 was not fully read. Cited external regularity, classification and maximum-principle results remain dependencies rather than new proofs supplied by this review.

The current arXiv history listed v3 as its latest public version when checked [history]. Publisher access returned HTTP 403, so no comparison with the journal version or publisher correction text is claimed. Crossref supplied no update relation; this is limited metadata evidence and does not establish global absence of an author correction.
# The missing contribution

Problem 1 (P01: Major; a false general profile formula).  Theorem 2.27(3), p. 25, puts the active interval at \([T-L,T]\) when \(v_1=1\) and \(v_0>0\). Thus \(v(t)=1\) on \([0,T-L]\). Nevertheless Lemma 2.31, equation (2.19), p. 26, identifies [eq:printedV] (#eq:printedV) with the whole volume. The first change of variables in its proof, p. 27, drops the constant-volume part of the interval. Corollary 2.32, p. 28, then uses \(\widetilde V_T=\bar v\) as the volume constraint in its third column, together with \(L\leq T\) and \(1=v_1>v_0>0\). This produces a false value for the asserted isoperimetric profile, not only an incorrect description of an auxiliary quantity.

Equation reference: eq:model. Claim 1.  For the model explicitly defined in (2.7), p. 16, \[
 T=1,\qquad I_0(v)=\min\{\sqrt{\pi v},1,\sqrt{\pi(1-v)}\},\] Corollary 2.32 is false at \(w=1/10-\pi/6000\).

Equation reference: eq:values. Proof. Take \[r=\frac1{10},\qquad v_0=1-\frac{\pi r^2}{4},\qquad
 v_1=1,\qquad \ell(v)=\frac{2(1-v)}r.\] These parameters are in the upper square-root zone of [eq:model] (#eq:model), and \(\ell<I_0\) throughout \((v_0,1)\). With \(v=v_0+\pi x^2/4\), \(0<x<r\), one has \[I_0(v)\sqrt{(I_0(v)/\ell(v))^2-1}=\frac{\pi x}{2}
 =\frac{dv}{dx},\qquad
 \sqrt{1-(\ell(v)/I_0(v))^2}=\frac{x}{r}.\] Consequently all integrals are finite and \[
 L=r\leq1,\qquad
 \widetilde V_1=r-\frac{\pi r^3}{6}=w,\qquad
 A_1=\frac{\pi r^2}{2}=\frac{\pi}{200}.\] Thus this pair satisfies every displayed condition in the third column of Corollary 2.32, which would imply \(I(S_1(I_0))(w)\leq\pi/200\).

Gaussian isoperimetry and Lipschitz transference now yield \[I(S_1(I_0))(v)\geq\sqrt2\,I_\gamma(v).\] This is the same type of transference used in the paper on pp. 8 and 17; it follows also by pulling back metric neighborhoods and then taking the perimeter limit. Concavity of \(I_\gamma\), together with \(I_\gamma(0)=0\) and \(I_\gamma(1/2)=1/\sqrt{2\pi}\), gives \[I(S_1(I_0))(v)\geq\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}v>v,
 \qquad 0<v\leq\frac12.\] But \(\pi<4\) implies \[w>\frac{149}{1500}>\frac1{50}>\frac{\pi}{200}.\] This contradicts the value allowed by the printed formula. ◻

The geometry of the omitted volume is explicit. In the model [eq:model] (#eq:model), put \(R=1/2+1/\pi\). Its upper density is \(\varphi_{I_0}(s)=\pi(R-s)/2\) for \(R-2/\pi\leq s<R\). The corresponding downward set has \[f(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 R,&0\leq t\leq1-r,\\
 R-\sqrt{r^2-(1-t)^2},&1-r\leq t\leq1.
 \end{cases}\] Since \(r<2/\pi\), the entire curved boundary stays in that zone. Its actual volume is \(1-\pi r^3/6=1-\pi/6000\); the printed value is smaller by exactly \(1-r=9/10\). The finite weighted perimeter is the value in [eq:values] (#eq:values). No assertion that this set is itself a minimizer is needed or made: the counterexample uses an admissible parameter entry in the asserted infimum and a lower bound for the actual profile. The integral identities and all exact inequalities were also checked by a root-authored symbolic calculation, with actual exit code zero and retained inputs and outputs.
# Repair, counterevidence and impact

Equation reference: eq:repair. For \(v_1=1>v_0>0\), the correction is \[
 V_T^{\mathrm{correct}}(v_0,1)
 =\widetilde V_T(v_0,1)+\frac{T-T(v_0,1)}T.\] The third-column constraint in Corollary 2.32 must use this volume. There is no analogous added term when \(v_0=0\), because the inactive slices are empty, and none when both endpoints are interior, because \(L=T\). The area formula is not affected by the missing full slices.

A possible alternative formulation is to restrict explicitly to nonnegative mean curvature for volumes at most one half and extend by symmetry. Such a restriction would exclude the negative-curvature example above, whose chord slope is \(-2/r=-20\). It is not present in the printed corollary. Merely appealing to complementary sets does not repair a formula which already admits the wrong candidate at \(w<1/2\).

The dependency is direct: Theorem 2.27’s classification leads to Lemma 2.31’s volume calculation, which supplies the feasibility constraints in the general profile characterization of Corollary 2.32. The severity is Major because this central general characterization has an actual false quantitative conclusion. The available repair is local; the classification does not assert that the paper’s headline applications fail.
# Independent positive checks
## High-dimensional finite comparisons and induction

The remaining induction condition at \(n=11\) was also certified: \[D=\log2+\frac12\psi(13/2)-\frac12\log\pi-1>0.\] The stored rational lower bound exceeds \(0.01454\). It uses the half-integer digamma identity, \(\gamma_{\mathrm E}\leq H_{100}-\log100\), and explicit positive-series bounds for logarithms. Log-convexity of \(\Gamma\) then preserves the needed derivative inequality for \(n\geq11\), as in the paper. This checks the numerical and induction component of the high-dimensional argument; the cited geometric exclusion of a tangentially self-touching ball remains an external dependency.
## The Gaussian instability threshold

Lemma 3.1, p. 31, and the last step of Theorem 1.8, p. 48, can be tested by an explicit admissible variation. At any finite height \(a\), put \[h_\varepsilon(t)=a+\varepsilon\cos(\pi t/T)+b(\varepsilon),\] where the implicit function theorem chooses \(b\) so that \(T^{-1}\int_0^T\Phi_\gamma(h_\varepsilon(t))\,dt=\Phi_\gamma(a)\). Then \(b(0)=b'(0)=0\), \(b''(0)=a/2\). The variation satisfies the Neumann endpoint condition. For its weighted area, \[A''(0)=\frac{\varphi_\gamma(a)}2
 \left(\frac{\pi^2}{T^2}-1\right).\] The cosine integrals and cancellations were independently verified symbolically. Thus every nontrivial horizontal half-plane is unstable for \(T>\pi\), as claimed. At \(T=\pi\) this second variation is zero and proves no instability. Nor does this calculation settle the intermediate range \(\sqrt{2\pi}<T\leq\pi\), which the paper leaves with transition parameters rather than an asserted explicit solution.
# Numerical appendix and review limits

Proposition 4.1 is reduced in Appendix A to positivity of an integral and a mesh estimate. The source reports a FLINT/Arb computation, in addition to Mathematica, and says that SageMath 10.6 source code is available on request (p. 54). Page 59 describes a \(647\times535\) implemented mesh and reports a lower bound \(0.0008450618226248\); its displayed error allowance is \(2\varepsilon=0.0006\). These are author-reported computational facts, not a reproduction performed by this review. The omitted derivative details, mesh coverage and interval evaluations have not all been independently certified here.

The frozen manifest contained no separate SageMath program. The exact arXiv source archive was retrieved and its 17 members were listed and hashed mechanically; no common computational code extension was present. The author publication entry linked the preprint. Neither this limited search nor the publisher access failure proves that the code is unavailable everywhere. No author code was executed and no defect is inferred from missing code. The source archive’s HTTP ETag does not equal either its acquired gzip hash or its decoded tar hash; this metadata/payload distinction is preserved explicitly and does not alter the selected PDF binding.

The model reduction is a lower bound for a general base; equality requires appropriately nested minimizing slices. That distinction was retained when reading the torus and Gaussian applications. The cube statements also retain their restricted volume and width ranges; they are not read as a solution of the entire three-dimensional cube conjecture. The positive checks above do not certify all external inputs or the unread appendix details. Local typographical observations without a substantive consequence were not promoted into additional Problems.
# Disposition
This initial report records one proved failure of the general profile formula, a precise correction and bounded impact. Scientific adjudication remains pending; no independent acceptance is claimed.

Title: Technical Verification of Sharp Quantitative Stability of the Dirichlet Spectrum Near the Ball
# Identity, version and scope

The reviewed work is D. Bucur, J. Lamboley, M. Nahon and R. Prunier’s Sharp quantitative stability of the Dirichlet spectrum near the ball, DOI 10.1002/cpa.70021 (https://doi.org/10.1002/cpa.70021). The exact acquired source is arXiv:2304.10916v2, 29 October 2025, 54 pages [paper]. Physical and printed page numbers agree. Journal metadata places the article in Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics 79 (2026), 827–896, with online publication on 14 November 2025. Findings apply to the acquired preprint.

All 54 source pages were read by the root scientific reviewer. The review followed the torsion comparison, penalized minimization, regularity, simple-eigenvalue and cluster variations, and the applications. Full reading is not a new proof of every cited compactness or free-boundary theorem. The explicit counterexample and the independent algebraic checks below delimit what was directly established.

For \(n\geq2\), the Dirichlet spectrum is defined for open sets of positive finite volume. Let \(B_\Omega\) be the ball of the same volume and \(T\) the torsional rigidity. Theorem 1.1, p. 5, controls each eigenvalue by the square root of \(T(\Omega)^{-1}-T(B_\Omega)^{-1}\). The linear estimate of Theorem 1.2, p. 6, requires that the ball eigenvalue be simple. Theorem 1.3, p. 6, instead controls the absolute value of the sum over a complete isolated ball cluster; it does not control the sum of absolute individual differences. The gap \(g_n(k)\) excludes equal ball eigenvalues and is capped at one. Its positivity for each fixed cluster is used; no uniform lower bound in \(k\) is supplied or assumed here.
# An overbroad invertibility assertion

Equation reference: eq:extension. Definition 4.15 and equation (32), p. 26, choose \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R_+^*,[0,1])\) with \(\varphi=0\) on \([0,1/4]\), \(\varphi=1\) on \([1/2,3/2]\), and \(\varphi\) nondecreasing on \([0,1/2]\). They set \[
 \zeta^t(x)=x+t\varphi(|x|)h(x/|x|)\frac{x}{|x|}.\] The text declares this to be a diffeomorphism from \(B\) to \(B_{th}\) for every \(|t|\leq1\). Lemma 4.17, p. 27, assumes \(h\in C^{2,\gamma}(\partial B,[-1/2,1/2])\) and uses the corresponding vector field; its proof forms \((\zeta^t)^{-1}\), \((D\zeta^t)^{-1}\), and the Jacobian.

Problem 1 (P01: Minor; missing invertibility condition).  The amplitude bound on \(h\) does not make [eq:extension] (#eq:extension) injective. Consequently the stated diffeomorphism assertion is false, and this particular pullback is undefined for some allowed parameters. This does not itself refute the analytic spectral-branch conclusion of Lemma 4.17, which may use a valid extension.

Decisive example. Choose \(h\equiv-1/3\), \(t=9/10\), and any unit vector \(e\). Both \(e/5\) and \(e/2\) are interior points of \(B\). The prescribed values of \(\varphi\) give \[\zeta^{9/10}(e/5)=e/5
 =\left(\frac12-\frac9{10}\frac13\right)e
 =\zeta^{9/10}(e/2).\] The points are distinct. This calculation holds for every cutoff satisfying the written requirements, and \(h\) is smooth with values strictly inside the allowed interval. There is no endpoint ambiguity in \(t\). The geometric domains are nevertheless ordinary balls of radius \(1-t/3\), whose eigenvalues are \(\lambda_i(B)/(1-t/3)^2\). Thus this example specifically invalidates the chosen map, while providing counterevidence to any claim that spectral analyticity itself has failed. ◻

Even an implicit equal-volume and centering interpretation does not suffice to rescue the map. In dimension two take \[\rho(\theta)=\sqrt{17/18}+\frac13\cos(2\theta),
 \qquad h(\theta)=\rho(\theta)-1.\] The radial domain has area \(\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\rho^2\,d\theta=\pi\), is centrally symmetric, and has \(-1/2<h<1/2\). At \(\theta=\pi/2\), write \(h_*=\sqrt{17/18}-4/3\). Then \(r_1=1/2+(9/10)h_*\in(0,1/4)\). The two points \(r_1e\) and \(e/2\) again have the same image under \(\zeta^{9/10}\). This example is not asserted to satisfy any additionally prescribed arbitrarily small \(L^1\) threshold or \(C^{3,\gamma}\) bound.
## Repair and impact

Equation reference: eq:repair. Let \(M=\|\varphi'\|_\infty\). Adding, for example, \[
 M\|h\|_\infty\leq\frac12\] gives a direct repair. Along each ray the new radius is \(R_t(r,\theta)=r+t\varphi(r)h(\theta)\), and \[\partial_rR_t=1+t\varphi'(r)h(\theta)\geq\frac12
 \quad (|t|\leq1).\] It is the identity near the origin, remains positive, preserves the angular direction, and is strictly increasing on every ray. Its Jacobian is \((R_t/r)^{n-1}\partial_rR_t>0\). These facts prove injectivity and the required regular inverse, with the boundary mapped to \(1+th\).

The dependency is equation (32), then the analytic pullback in Lemma 4.17, then the second-variation estimates in Propositions 4.18 and 5.20, and the local minimality arguments in Propositions 4.16 and 5.19. The actual main applications, pp. 29, 31 and 46–48, have both a fixed \(C^{3,\gamma}\) bound and a sufficiently small \(L^1\) norm. Interpolation then makes \(\|h\|_\infty\) small enough for [eq:repair] (#eq:repair) after reducing the dimensional constant. The cutoff is fixed, so this does not introduce a new \(k\)-dependent exponent. The examples above are not counterexamples in that arbitrarily small regime. This local repair and the stronger operative hypotheses justify the Minor classification.
# Independent mathematical checks
## Multiplicity and planar sharpness

The area-preserving ellipse with semiaxes \(a=e^\varepsilon\), \(b=e^{-\varepsilon}\) satisfies \[T(E_\varepsilon)=\frac{\pi}{8\cosh(2\varepsilon)},\qquad
 T(E_\varepsilon)^{-1}-T(B)^{-1}
 =\frac{16}{\pi}\varepsilon^2+O(\varepsilon^4).\] This follows directly by integrating its quadratic torsion function. Its first boundary normal velocity is \(\cos(2\theta)\). For the first double disk eigenvalue \(\lambda=j_{1,1}^2\), normalization and radial dilation give squared normal-derivative factor \(2\lambda/\pi\). The Hadamard matrix is therefore \[-\frac{2\lambda}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\cos(2\theta)
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \cos^2\theta&\cos\theta\sin\theta\\
 \cos\theta\sin\theta&\sin^2\theta
 \end{pmatrix}d\theta
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}-\lambda&0\\0&\lambda\end{pmatrix}.\] The individual branches have a nonzero linear splitting, whereas their full-cluster trace has zero first derivative. The angular integrals, torsion expansion and volume constraint were independently verified symbolically. This supports the need for a square-root estimate on individual multiple eigenvalues and a linear estimate only after complete-cluster cancellation. It is not a proof of all-index sharpness in every dimension. Proposition 6.1, pp. 48–49, makes its explicit sharpness statement in dimension two; that limitation is retained.
## Internal cluster cancellation

For the orthonormal analytic eigenbasis in Proposition 5.20, pp. 47–48, let \(C_{ij}=\langle u_i',u_j\rangle\). Differentiating orthonormality gives \(C_{ij}=-C_{ji}\). Hence, for a complete cluster \(I\), \[\sum_{i,j\in I}(\mu_j-\mu_i)C_{ij}^2=0.\] Writing \(v_i=u_i'\), \(z_i\) for its harmonic boundary extension and \(w_i=v_i-z_i\), the off-diagonal coefficient identity is \((\mu_j-\mu_i)v_{ij}=\mu_jz_{ij}\). It yields \[\mu_jw_{ij}^2-\mu_iv_{ij}^2
 =\mu_jz_{ij}^2-(\mu_j-\mu_i)v_{ij}^2.\] The last term cancels after summation. These identities were independently checked with a symbolic skew matrix, including coincident eigenvalues. No division by an internal cluster gap is required. Separation from the exterior spectrum remains necessary.
## Scaling, infinite sums and a nonlinear corollary

Under dilation by \(r\), eigenvalues scale by \(r^{-2}\) and torsional rigidity by \(r^{n+2}\). The factor \(\lambda_1^{1/2}|\Omega|^{1/2}
(T^{-1}-T(B_\Omega)^{-1})^{1/2}\) thus has exactly eigenvalue scaling. The linear estimates’ factor \(|\Omega|(T^{-1}-T(B_\Omega)^{-1})\) does too.

For the summability condition in Proposition 6.3, pp. 50–52, comparison with \(\sum i^a e^{-cti^{2/n}}\) gives small-\(t\) order \(t^{-(a+1)n/2}\). The first derivative weight for the heat trace has order \(t^{-4n-3}\); the second derivative weight has order \(t^{-7n/2-3}\). The latter is dominated by the former for \(n\geq2\) and \(0<t\leq1\); exponential decay handles large \(t\). These independently derived exponents support the final envelope without endorsing every intermediate printed simplification.

For Corollary 1.6 and its proof on p. 49, minimality of \(T^{-1}-\delta\lambda_1\) gives \(T(B)/T(\Omega)\geq1+\delta T(B)(\lambda_1(\Omega)-\lambda_1(B))\). Bernoulli’s inequality for \(p\geq1\) then gives the stated reverse Kohler–Jobin conclusion once \(p\delta T(B)\lambda_1(B)\geq1\). A sufficiently large dimensional \(p>1\) is consistent with the allowed small \(\delta\). No explicit optimal value of that exponent was established.
# Operative assumptions and remaining limits

The main cluster proof retains the smallness \(|\delta|\ll k^{-6-10/n}g_n(k)\). In particular it implies the stronger-than-coarse spectral-separation condition of Lemma 5.6, p. 34, when that lemma is invoked in the viscosity construction on p. 35. The latter is not read as dispensing with its own prerequisites. The vector regularity argument’s condition \(L^2m^2\sqrt{|\delta|}\leq1/8\) is likewise consistent with \(m\lesssim k\) and the main smallness after a dimensional constant is reduced. These checks trace conditions in the actual application; they do not assert a counterexample to an isolated lemma under weaker assumptions.

The revised regularity proof in Lemma 4.14, pp. 25–26, explicitly introduces a positive harmonic auxiliary denominator. In the acquired arXiv version of its reference [22], De Silva–Savin’s Theorem 2.4 [dss], p. 5, requires a positive homogeneous solution as denominator, a \(C^{1,\alpha}\) boundary (as set up on p. 2), and a numerator with \(C^\alpha\) right-hand side. The numerator need not be positive. The harmonic auxiliary construction matches this requirement; one may use signed ratios and square them in the free-boundary condition. The higher-order version on p. 6 provides the corresponding bootstrap framework. Reference pp. 1–6 were read, with the hypothesis and theorem pages visually checked. The 2015 journal PDF was not acquired: its official download returned an empty body, so the retained nine-page arXiv:1403.2588v1 is identified explicitly rather than certified equivalent to the journal text.

For Theorem 1.5, the equality of first derivatives of \(F\) is required within each complete ball cluster at the ball spectrum; global permutation symmetry is not silently assumed. The last index must end a cluster. For the infinite spectral applications, the weighted derivative summability is an essential hypothesis, not a consequence of arbitrary smoothness of \(f\).

Current arXiv metadata listed v2 as the latest public version when checked [history]. The publisher endpoint returned HTTP 403, and Crossref supplied no update relation. These limited checks do not prove the absence of every correction. No author code was executed. This is an analytic paper; unavailable code does not establish a mathematical defect. External compactness, free-boundary regularity and shape-calculus inputs have not all been independently reproved. Purely typographical observations without an established substantive consequence were not promoted into Problems.
# Disposition

One proved auxiliary defect with an explicit local repair is recorded. No main theorem has been disproved. The exact source, TeX, compiled PDF, calculations, coverage, dependency payloads and actual image-inspection records accompany this initial review. Scientific adjudication remains pending and independent acceptance is not claimed.

analysis: The amplitude bound on \(h\) does not make [eq:extension] (#eq:extension) injective. Consequently the stated diffeomorphism assertion is false, and this particular pullback is undefined for some allowed parameters. This does not itself refute the analytic spectral-branch conclusion of Lemma 4.17, which may use a valid extension.

Decisive example. Choose \(h\equiv-1/3\), \(t=9/10\), and any unit vector \(e\). Both \(e/5\) and \(e/2\) are interior points of \(B\). The prescribed values of \(\varphi\) give \[\zeta^{9/10}(e/5)=e/5
 =\left(\frac12-\frac9{10}\frac13\right)e
 =\zeta^{9/10}(e/2).\] The points are distinct. This calculation holds for every cutoff satisfying the written requirements, and \(h\) is smooth with values strictly inside the allowed interval. There is no endpoint ambiguity in \(t\). The geometric domains are nevertheless ordinary balls of radius \(1-t/3\), whose eigenvalues are \(\lambda_i(B)/(1-t/3)^2\). Thus this example specifically invalidates the chosen map, while providing counterevidence to any claim that spectral analyticity itself has failed. ◻
