Title: Technical Verification of
Sharp Bounds for Max-sliced Wasserstein Distances
# Paper identity and scope

The reviewed paper is March T. Boedihardjo, Sharp Bounds for Max-sliced Wasserstein Distances, arXiv:2403.00666v6, dated 26 November 2024, 27 PDF pages [source]. It is associated with DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09690-1 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09690-1) in Foundations of Computational Mathematics. The publisher landing page lists online publication on 22 January 2025 and volume 26, pages 747–778 (2026) [journal]. That page supplied metadata and a subscription preview; the journal’s complete theorem text was not obtained. This report therefore attributes every mathematical finding to the acquired v6 PDF. Printed page numbers and one-based PDF page numbers coincide.

The complete v6 text was read, and all 27 rendered source pages were visually inspected in this scientific conversation. The review followed Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.4, Corollary 1.3, Proposition 1.5 and the supporting arguments in Sections 2–3. It checked the applicability, rather than supplying new proofs, of the invoked majorizing-measure, Dudley, symmetrization and Khintchine inequalities. The external references were not all retrieved or independently audited. The independent computation below uses newly written rational-arithmetic code; no author code was executed. Missing optional code is not treated as a mathematical defect.

A bounded correction/version check consulted the official arXiv record and the publisher page, together with a title-and-correction search. The arXiv record still listed v6 as its latest version. No relevant author correction was identified in these consulted records. This is not evidence that no correction exists elsewhere, nor that the published text retains the issue.
# Definitions and assumptions retained

For probability measures on Euclidean space, the paper’s max-sliced distance is \[W_{p,1}(\mu,\nu)=
 \sup_{\|v\|_2=1}W_p\bigl((\langle v,\cdot\rangle)_\#\mu,
                         (\langle v,\cdot\rangle)_\#\nu\bigr).\] The more general \(W_{1,s}\) of Section 1.3 uses \(s\) coordinate functionals in the dual unit ball; their mutual orthogonality is not an assumption. In the Banach-space results, separability of the dual and the first-moment assumption are retained. In the Hilbert-space moment bounds, the stated \(2+\delta\) or \(2+2\delta\) moments are required where they occur, with \(0<\delta\leq1\). The centered lower bounds require \(\mathbb E X=0\); centering is not silently imposed on the upper bounds.

Equation reference: eq:original. Theorem 1.4 assumes a symmetric probability measure on \(\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\|x\|_2\leq r\}\), where \(r>0\), and independent samples \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) with that law. Write \[\nu_n=\frac1{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n(\delta_{X_i}+\delta_{-X_i}),
 \qquad
 \Sigma=\mathbb E XX^{T},\qquad \kappa=\|\Sigma\|_{\rm op}.\] For \(\kappa>0\), its asserted upper bound is equivalently \[
 \mathbb E W_{2,1}(\mu,\nu_n)^2
 \leq C\left(\frac{r^2\log n}{n}
       +r\sqrt{\frac{\kappa\log n}{n}}\right).\] Neither copy of the theorem, on pages 6 and 22, explicitly states \(n\geq2\). The counterexample below uses \(\kappa>0\) and does not exploit division by zero or an inadmissible distribution.
# A sample-size boundary defect

Problem 1 (Theorem 1.4 at \(n=1\); minor severity).  The literal all-positive-sample-size reading of [eq:original] (#eq:original) is false. The same boundary is absent from Lemma 3.1, on pages 20–21, which supplies the matrix estimate used in its proof.
## Exact input and decisive calculation

Claim 1.  For every possible value of \(X_1\) in [eq:mu] (#eq:mu), \[W_{2,1}\bigl(\mu,\tfrac12(\delta_{X_1}+\delta_{-X_1})\bigr)^2
 =\tfrac12 .\]

Equation reference: eq:direction. Proof. Let \(v=(a,b)\) with \(a^2+b^2=1\), and put \(A=|a|\), \(B=|b|\). The absolute-value image of the projected law of \(\mu\) is \(\tfrac12\delta_A+\tfrac12\delta_B\). If the sampled axis is the first, the corresponding image of the symmetrized empirical law is \(\delta_A\); if it is the second, it is \(\delta_B\). For symmetric one-dimensional laws, quadratic transport equals quadratic transport of their absolute-value images. This follows from monotone quantiles, or by optimally coupling the nonnegative radii and assigning the same independent sign to both variables. The opposite inequality follows from the fact that absolute value is 1-Lipschitz. Thus in either case the projected squared distance is \[
 \tfrac12(A-B)^2=\tfrac12(1-2|ab|)\leq\tfrac12.\] Equality holds at \(v=e_1\) or \(v=e_2\). Taking the supremum proves the claim, including the zero-coordinate cases. ◻

Consequently the left side of [eq:original] (#eq:original) is \(1/2\), whereas the right side is zero because \(\log1=0\), for every finite choice of the universal constant \(C\). This disproves the displayed endpoint assertion itself, not merely one method of proving it.

An independent exact-rational implementation of one-dimensional monotone transport checked 48 cases: all four sample points at 12 rational unit directions. Every computed value agrees with [eq:direction] (#eq:direction); both coordinate directions attain \(1/2\). The saved script, output and execution receipt are `verification/0441/checks/boundary_n1.py`, `boundary_n1.stdout.json` and `execution.json`. The universal statement is proved above; the finite check is corroboration.
## Proof dependency and alternative interpretation

On page 20, Lemma 3.1 chooses the Schatten moment \(p=\lceil\log n\rceil\). At \(n=1\), this gives \(p=0\), outside the positive-moment argument, and the resulting Gaussian matrix estimate would have a zero right side. For example, \(\mathbb E\|gXX^T\|_{\rm op}=\mathbb E|g|>0\) when \(\|X\|_2=1\). Even the lemma’s first inequality fails literally at \(n=1\): uniform mass on \(\{\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_3\}\) gives \(\mathbb E\|XX^T\|_{\rm op}=1\) and \(2\|\mathbb E XX^T\|_{\rm op}=2/3\).

The dependency is direct: Lemma 3.2 and equation (3.2) lift the symmetric transport problem to the matrix law of \(XX^T\); Corollary 2.9 supplies the empirical-process bound; Lemma 3.1 then yields the logarithmic estimate on page 23. Corollary 2.9 also selects \(\delta=1/\lceil\log n\rceil\) on page 18. Its conclusion, however, need not fail at \(n=1\): \[\mathbb E W_{1,1}(\mu,\delta_X)\leq2\mathbb E\|X\|,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E\|gX\|=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\mathbb E\|X\|,\] so its Gaussian term already controls that endpoint after an absolute adjustment of \(C\). This report does not label Theorem 1.2 or Corollary 2.9 false on that account.

An intended restriction \(n\geq2\) is plausible and is supported by the two ceiling-log choices in the proofs. Under that explicit restriction, the counterexample is outside the theorem’s scope. No global restriction or logarithm-truncation convention resolving the literal wording was identified in the reviewed v6 text. This interpretative boundary is why the finding is classified as minor: it changes a stated finite-sample endpoint, while the nontrivial asymptotic claim and its \(n\geq2\) argument survive.
## Repair and impact

Equation reference: eq:repair. One sufficient repair is to state \(n\geq2\) explicitly in the logarithmic matrix lemma and Theorem 1.4, and handle \(n=1\) separately where Corollary 2.9 is used. Alternatively, let \(L(n)=\log(en)\) and formulate the upper bound as \[
 \mathbb E W_{2,1}(\mu,\nu_n)^2
 \leq C\left(\frac{r^2L(n)}n+
                 r\sqrt{\frac{\kappa L(n)}n}\right),\qquad n\geq1.\] For \(n\geq2\), this follows from the checked argument for [eq:original] (#eq:original), because \(L(n)\geq\log n\). For \(n=1\), both projected laws are supported on \([-r,r]\), so their squared quadratic distance is at most \(4r^2\), uniformly in direction and sample. Since \(L(1)=1\), [eq:repair] (#eq:repair) follows after enlarging \(C\) to at least 4. This is a proved endpoint extension, not a claim that the author adopted it. Writing the bound in the expanded form also avoids undefined ratios when \(\kappa=0\); then \(\mu=\delta_0\) and the distance is zero.
# Other checked arguments and counterevidence
The following checks delimit the finding and record why nearby claims were not rejected.
## Empirical-process upper bounds

The product-metric estimate of Lemma 2.1, the weighted Lipschitz covering argument in Lemmas 2.3–2.4, and the Gaussian comparison in Lemma 2.5 were followed on pages 8–16. In particular the dyadic shell sum is finite for \(\delta>0\); the truncation parameter produces the distinct \(s=1\), \(s=2\), and \(s\geq3\) regimes in (2.12). Rescaling in Lemma 2.6 preserves both sides of (2.13); the all-zero sample is handled directly. Gaussian symmetrization in Theorem 2.7 applies to the centered Lipschitz class with the first-moment envelope. The Hilbert second-moment identity and Jensen’s inequality in Corollary 2.8 give the stated moment dependence. No contradictory example or invalid operative step was established in these arguments.

For Corollary 1.3, bounded support gives \(W_p^p\leq(2r)^{p-1}W_1\) after projection. Taking the supremum and then using concavity of the \(p\)-th root yields the claimed rate from Theorem 1.1. These steps retain \(p\geq1\). They do not require the additional symmetry assumption of Theorem 1.4.
## Centered lower bounds and the covariance construction

For Proposition 2.10, the linear test function supplies the norm of the empirical mean. Symmetrizing with an independent centered copy gives the factor \(1/2\), and conditional Jensen removes that copy. The Hilbert-space Khintchine step in Corollary 2.11 then gives the stated \(1/(2\sqrt{2n})\) coefficient. The zero-mean hypothesis is used essentially.

In Lemma 3.2, symmetry permits passage to absolute values, and \((u-v)^2\leq|u^2-v^2|\) for \(u,v\geq0\) permits the square-map comparison. The trace functional represented by \(ww^T\) has dual norm one when \(\|w\|_2=1\). The argument would not justify dropping symmetry; the reviewed theorem does not drop it.

For Proposition 1.5, normalize \(\operatorname{Tr}\Sigma=1\) in the nonzero case and write its eigenvalues as \(\lambda_j\), with \(\lambda_1\leq1/2\). The symmetric coordinate-axis law has the required covariance. The occupancy-vector computation on page 24 gives \[\mathbb E W_{2,1}(\mu,\nu_n)^2
 \geq \frac{1-\sum_j\lambda_j^2}{4n}\geq\frac1{8n}.\] For the complementary regime \(n\lambda_1\geq1\), projection onto the first axis gives \(\mathbb E|Y/n-\lambda_1|\), where \(Y\) is binomial. As an independent sufficiency check, put \(Z=Y-np\), \(p=\lambda_1\), and \(\sigma^2=np(1-p)\geq1/2\). Direct moment expansion gives \(\mathbb E Z^4=3\sigma^4+\sigma^2(1-6p(1-p))
\leq5\sigma^4\). Hölder’s inequality implies \[\mathbb E|Z|\geq
 \frac{(\mathbb E Z^2)^{3/2}}{(\mathbb E Z^4)^{1/2}}
 \geq\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt5},
 \qquad
 \mathbb E|Y/n-p|\geq\sqrt{\frac{p}{10n}}.\] Together with \(1/(8n)\), this is already sufficient for the paper’s \(1/16\) lower bound, by considering whether \(\sqrt{p/n}\) is greater than \(1/n\). It does not verify the sharper external binomial inequality cited on page 25; it independently confirms that the main constant claimed here does not depend on that sharper value.
# Conclusion

The established defect is confined to the literal \(n=1\) scope of the logarithmic covariance estimate and Theorem 1.4. The counterexample is exact and satisfies every hypothesis listed in those statements. An explicit \(n\geq2\) restriction, or the proved extension [eq:repair] (#eq:repair), resolves it without altering the reported large-sample orders. No major or critical issue is established by this review. This is a bounded initial technical report, not an independent acceptance decision.

report: Abstract: This report examines the acquired 73-page arXiv version 2108.11832v2. Explicit examples disprove a normal-cone estimate in the proof of Theorem 3.11, the \(C^1\) form of Theorem 3.9(1), and a subgradient-selection assertion in the proof of Theorem 3.25. A replacement argument for Theorem 3.11 is supplied. For Theorem 6.2, uniform marginal noise is distinguished from the conditional uniformity used in its proof: a measurable generalized iteration satisfying the displayed marginal assumptions converges almost surely to strict saddles. A separate example identifies the missing regularity premise in its vector-field construction. An invariant-interval example also identifies a localization premise missing from the standalone nonconvergence theorem. These findings do not establish failure of the intended algorithms with fresh independent noise and sufficiently smooth active restrictions. Assessment: Major, with the precise boundaries below. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

Title: Technical Verification of
Active Manifolds, Stratifications, and Convergence to Local Minima in Nonsmooth Optimization
# Identity, version, and review scope

The reviewed paper is by Damek Davis, Dmitriy Drusvyatskiy, and Liwei Jiang, associated with DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09691-0. The actual acquired source is arXiv:2108.11832v2, dated 9 January 2023, not the publisher’s version of record [DDJ]. All source page references below refer to its printed pages, which equal its PDF page indices. All 73 pages, including the appendices and reference list, were read. The acquired source and its manifest were checked by bytes and SHA256; they were not replaced by later material.

The official arXiv record checked during this review lists v2 as its latest version and describes the split of the earlier manuscript into two parts. The publisher record identifies a 2025 online publication and a later volume assignment. Its full main text was not available in the consulted preview; identity of its mathematical wording with v2 is not asserted. The bounded correction search included the official arXiv and publisher records and the authors’ publication pages. No separate correction resolving the findings below was located in those materials. Jiang’s May 2024 dissertation [Jiang] repeats the relevant geometric assertions at printed pp. 26–27, 30–31, and 46 (PDF pp. 39–40, 43–44, and 59). This provides later author text for comparison, not an erratum or a substitute for the reviewed version.

The review followed the regularity definitions, calculus, stratification arguments, generalized algorithm assumptions, both shadow/aiming estimates, the stochastic nonconvergence argument, and the appendix proofs. Independent symbolic calculations supplement the universal arguments given here. No author code was executed. No missing-code allegation is made.
# Conventions and operative hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:strong-a. The source uses limiting normal cones \(N_X(x)\), which need not be linear spaces. Its directed gap is \[\Delta(U,V)=\sup_{\substack{u\in U\\\left\|u\right\|=1}}\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}(u,V).\] Strong \((a)\) regularity requires, uniformly for all nearby \(x\in X\) and \(y\in Y\), \[
 \Delta(N_X(x),N_Y(y))\le C\left\|x-y\right\|.\] The projected condition restricts \(y\) to a specified retraction \(\pi(x)\). A retraction in Definition 3.7 must take values in the target set and satisfy \(\left\|z-\pi(z)\right\|\le K\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}(z,Y)\) locally. Function regularity is regularity of \(\mathop{\mathrm{epi}}f\) along \(\mathop{\mathrm{gph}}(f|_{\mathcal M})\) (Definitions 3.2–3.3, p. 12). For a singleton target its normal space is the whole ambient space, so strong \((a)\) is automatic. This elementary case is permitted by the stated theorems.

For the stochastic results, the standing Assumption E (p. 38) requires a measurable generalized map, \(\alpha_k\asymp k^{-\gamma}\), martingale-difference noise relative to \(\mathcal F_k=\sigma(x_j:j\le k;\nu_j:j<k)\), a conditional fourth-moment bound locally bounded in \(x_k\), and iterates in the domain. Assumption A (p. 33) requires local boundedness, a tangential approximation estimate, and proximal aiming, uniformly over every \(\alpha>0\) and every noise vector. It asks for \(f|_\mathcal M\) to be \(C^2\). Theorem 6.2 (p. 42) raises the smoothness of \(\mathcal M\) to \(C^4\), uses \(\gamma\in(1/2,1)\), and requires a negative eigenvalue of \(\nabla_\mathcal M^2 f\) at each point of the target set.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (One-sided normals invalidate equation (3.29)).  The proof of Theorem 3.11, p. 20, contains a false estimate central to its KL derivation. Severity: Major, confined to the submitted proof.
## Claim and exact hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:false-kl. Theorem 3.11 assumes definable sets \(X,Y\) in a Euclidean space, a point \(\bar x\in Y\), a locally closed \(X\), and a \(C^2\) manifold \(Y\) near \(\bar x\). It claims strong \((a)\Rightarrow(b_=)\). The proof defines \[g(x,v)=|\left\langle v,x-P_Y(x)\right\rangle|+\delta_{\mathop{\mathrm{cl}}X}(x)\] and, for unit \(v\in N_X(x)\), asserts \[
 \mathop{\mathrm{dist}}(0,\partial g(x,v))
 \le \left\|DP_Y(x)v\right\|+\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}(x,Y).\] This is the source’s equation (3.29).
## Counterexample and hypothesis verification

The invalid cancellation would require \(-v_t\in N_X(x_t)\). A convex normal cone is a cone, not generally a subspace. The omission of the absolute-value sign in the preceding derivative formula is a further reason to handle branches carefully, but it is not the basis of this counterexample.
## Counterevidence, dependency, and repair

This example does not disprove Theorem 3.11. Indeed, \[\frac{|\left\langle v_t,x_t\right\rangle|}{\left\|x_t\right\|}
 =\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+4t^2}\sqrt{1+t^2}}\longrightarrow0.\] The zero normals in the interior and the multiples of these boundary normals also satisfy \((b_=)\) at the singleton.

The affected argument is the paper’s stated derivation of the implication in its regularity diagram (3.20). The generic function stratification Theorem 3.29 (p. 31) asserts both strong \((a)\) and \((b_=)\); its displayed proof explicitly establishes the former, with this implication supplying the latter for locally closed epigraphs. This is a substantive proof dependency, not merely a misplaced sign without mathematical consequences. Appendix 6 (#app:kl-repair) gives a checked replacement using the signed function \(-\left\langle v,x-P_Y(x)\right\rangle+\delta_{\mathop{\mathrm{cl}}X}(x)\) and the nonsmooth, two-sided KL inequality. It preserves the theorem’s stated hypotheses. No author adoption of that replacement is established.

Problem 2 (The \(C^1\) form of Theorem 3.9(1) is false).  Theorem 3.9(1), p. 17, and estimate (3.22), p. 18, require more than the stated \(C^1\) smoothness of the target manifold. Severity: Minor, a local theorem-range defect.
## Claim, example, and all hypotheses

The theorem allows arbitrary sets \(X,Y\), a point \(\bar x\in Y\), a \(C^1\) retraction onto \(Y\), and a target \(Y\) that is only a \(C^1\) manifold. It asserts equivalence of strong \((a)\) and strong \((a^\pi)\). Let \[X=Y=\{(u,|u|^{3/2}):u\in\mathbb R\},\quad \bar x=0,\quad
 \pi(u,w)=(u,|u|^{3/2}).\] This is a \(C^1\) embedded manifold and a \(C^1\) retraction. To check the quantitative retraction requirement, let \(L\) bound the Lipschitz constant of \(q(u)=|u|^{3/2}\) on a small interval. A nearest graph point to a sufficiently small \(z=(u,w)\) lies in that interval, since the graph contains the origin. For every such candidate \((a,q(a))\), \[|w-q(u)|\le |w-q(a)|+L|u-a|
 \le\sqrt{1+L^2}\left\|z-(a,q(a))\right\|.\] Taking the infimum proves the required distance bound.
## Alternative interpretation and bounded correction

The proof explicitly invokes linear variation of the normal spaces in (3.22); \(C^1\) only supplies continuity. Replacing the target hypothesis by \(C^2\) is sufficient: in a local \(C^2\) graph chart, the normal projector is \(C^1\) and has bounded derivative on a smaller compact neighborhood, hence is locally Lipschitz. The triangle estimate (3.21)–(3.22) then works. A suitable \(C^{1,1}\) normal-variation assumption would also suffice, but \(C^2\) is the correction directly checked here.

The main cited uses already have higher smoothness: Proposition 3.10 uses \(C^3\) (p. 19), Theorem 3.11 uses \(C^2\), and Proposition 3.21 and Theorem 3.25 use \(C^2\) or higher (pp. 27, 29). Thus this example refutes the displayed \(C^1\) theorem, but does not demonstrate failure of those downstream applications. That limited dependency impact motivates the Minor grade.

Problem 3 (Strong \((a)\) does not imply the asserted subgradient selection).  Theorem 3.25’s proof, at the top of p. 30 following its statement on p. 29, uses a false selection estimate. Severity: Major for this spectral transfer derivation; no false final spectral theorem is established.
## Claim and decisive example

Equation reference: eq:false-selection. The hypotheses are a symmetric function \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}\), a symmetric \(C^2\) manifold \(\mathcal M\) containing \(\bar x\), local Lipschitz continuity of \(f\), and \(C^2\) smoothness of \(f|_\mathcal M\). For \(F=f\circ\lambda\), the strong \((a)\) part of the proof asserts that, for \(Y=P_{\lambda^{-1}(\mathcal M)}(X)\) and each \(Z\in\partial F(X)\), one can find \(W\in\partial F(Y)\) with \[
 \left\|Z-W\right\|_F\le C\left\|X-Y\right\|_F\] uniformly near the base matrix.

The theorem includes \(1\times1\) real symmetric matrices. Set \(f(u)=|u|^{3/2}\), \(\mathcal M=\{0\}\), and \(\bar x=0\). Symmetry under permutations of one coordinate is automatic; the manifold is \(C^\infty\), the restriction is constant, and \(f\) is locally Lipschitz. Its epigraph is strongly \((a)\) regular along the singleton \(\mathop{\mathrm{gph}}(f|_\mathcal M)\) because the latter’s normal space is \(\mathbb R^2\). All stated hypotheses hold. Here \(F=f\) and, for \(X=t>0\), \[Y=0,\qquad Z=\tfrac32\sqrt t,\qquad \partial F(0)=\{0\}.\] The only possible selection is \(W=0\), giving \[\frac{\left\|Z-W\right\|_F}{\left\|X-Y\right\|_F}
 =\frac{3}{2\sqrt t}\longrightarrow+\infty.\] Thus the claim is false even before any higher-dimensional eigenvalue multiplicity issue arises.
## Interpretation, dependency, and repair boundary

Strong \((a)\) controls the distance to the normal space of the restriction graph. That space is generally larger than the normals corresponding to actual subgradients of \(F\) at \(Y\). The set-normal argument in Theorem 3.20, p. 26, therefore does not justify [eq:false-selection] (#eq:false-selection) with the stated membership \(W\in\partial F(Y)\).

The proof uses this estimate to establish projected strong \((a)\) and then appeals to Theorem 3.9. It is its explicit justification of the strong \((a)\) spectral-transfer assertion, a central claim of this calculus subsection. A replacement must lift the appropriate restriction-graph normals and control the resulting tangential component; merely choosing a different element of \(\partial F(0)\) cannot fix the example. A complete general spectral replacement proof is not certified in this report. Conversely, the theorem’s conclusion holds in the example because its target is a singleton. Neither this example nor the reported proof failure establishes that the spectral-transfer theorem, or the later algorithmic conclusions, are false.

Problem 4 (Uniform marginals do not supply conditional excitation).  Assumption F and Theorem 6.2 on p. 42 omit the conditional interpretation used in the proof on p. 58. Severity: Major under the literal marginal-only assumptions, with an explicit interpretation boundary.
## The distinction and the operative range

Assumption F writes \(\nu_k\sim\mathop{\mathrm{Unif}}(B_r(0))\) for each \(k\). Together with the standing martingale-difference and fourth-moment requirements, this does not imply \(\mathcal L(\nu_k\mid\mathcal F_k)=\mathop{\mathrm{Unif}}(B_r(0))\). The latter is sufficient for the conditional lower bound in Theorem 6.1(2c). The proof on p. 58 explicitly invokes independence from the iterate history, which is strong evidence for the intended fresh-noise reading. The counterexample below concerns the displayed weaker assumptions of the generalized iteration, not an assertion that the intended independently perturbed subgradient method fails.

## Almost-sure convergence and impact

Equation reference: eq:noise-contradiction. Equation [eq:circle-map] (#eq:circle-map) keeps every subsequent iterate on \(S\). Writing an unwrapped angle \(\theta_k\), \[\theta_{k+1}-\theta_k=-\arctan(\alpha_k\epsilon_kR_k).\] These are mean-zero independent increments with variance at most \(\alpha_k^2\mathbb ER_k^2=\alpha_k^2/2\). Their total variance is finite, so the angle martingale is bounded in \(L^2\) and converges almost surely. Therefore \[
 \mathbb P(\lim_{k\to\infty}x_k\in S)=1,\] contrary to (6.3) under the marginal-only interpretation. Theorem 6.2 explicitly allows arbitrary, nonisolated target sets \(S\); no isolated-saddle premise excludes this construction.

A precise repair to the noise assumption is to require \(\mathcal L(\nu_k\mid\mathcal F_k)=\mathop{\mathrm{Unif}}(B_r(0))\) almost surely. Then for deterministic unit \(w\), or an \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable direction, \(\mathbb E[|\left\langle \nu_k,w\right\rangle|\mid\mathcal F_k]=rc_d\) with \(c_d>0\) by rotational symmetry, and the projection-continuity argument on p. 58 gives the needed positive lower bound. This repairs the identified noise implication; it is not by itself a certification of every other part of Theorem 6.2. The construction uses an admissible generalized map with an \(O(\alpha)\) correction. It does not establish a counterexample to the special subgradient, projected, or proximal algorithms under the intended independent-noise assumptions. Under that intended reading this finding is a necessary statement clarification, rather than a refutation of the intended result.

Problem 5 (The vector field need not be \(C^2\) under Assumption A).  The opening construction on p. 57 does not follow from the smoothness premises of Theorem 6.2. Severity: Minor, a regularity gap in the abstract application.
## Claim, counterexample, and scope

Theorem 6.1 (p. 41) requires a \(C^2\) vector field. On p. 57 the proof sets \(F_p=-
abla(f\circ P_\mathcal M)\) and asserts \(f\circ P_\mathcal M\) is \(C^3\) because \(\mathcal M\) is \(C^4\). But (A2) requires only \(f|_\mathcal M\in C^2\). Take \(\mathcal M=\mathbb R\), \(p=0\), and \[f(t)=-t^2+|t|^{5/2},\qquad G_\alpha(t,
u)=f'(t)+
u .\] The function is closed and \(C^2\), \(f'(0)=0\), and \(f''(0)=-2\). The manifold is \(C^\infty\). Assumption A holds: \(f'\) is locally bounded, (A2) has zero error, and (A3) is vacuous because the projection is the identity. Fresh independent uniform noise and \(\alpha_k=k^{-3/4}\) satisfy E and the stronger intended reading of F. Yet for \(t>0\), \[F_p(t)=2t-	frac52t^{3/2},
 \qquad F_p''(t)=- rac{15}{8\sqrt t},\] so \(F_p\) is not \(C^2\) near zero. This is an example to the claimed regularity implication, not to stochastic nonconvergence.

Requiring \(f|_\mathcal M\in C^3\) in this application is sufficient for this step: a \(C^4\) embedded manifold has a \(C^3\) local nearest-point projection, and composition in manifold charts makes \(f\circ P_\mathcal M\) \(C^3\). The explicit \(C^4\) active-saddle assumptions in Corollaries 6.3–6.4 already require \(f|_\mathcal M\in C^4\) by Definition 2.1 (p. 9). Thus those applications meet this repair. An alternative would be a separate nonconvergence result with weaker vector-field smoothness, which is not supplied or certified here.

Problem 6 (The auxiliary process is not localized under shrinking neighborhoods).  Theorem 6.1, p. 41, does not impose the localization of \(Y_k\) used in the first proof paragraph on p. 50. Severity: Minor in demonstrated application impact, although the unrestricted abstract statement is false.
## A complete example within the displayed hypotheses

Take \(d=1\), \(S=\{0\}\), \(X_k=0\) for all \(k\), \(\epsilon_0=4\), and \(F_0(y)=y-y^2\). The field is \(C^\infty\), \(F_0(0)=0\), and \(F_0'(0)=1>0\); thus its unstable space is \(\mathbb R\). Let \(\alpha_k=\frac14 k^{-3/4}\), \(Y_1=1\), \(E_k=0\), and let \(\xi_k\) be independent equiprobable signs of magnitude \(1/8\). Define \[Y_{k+1}=Y_k+\alpha_k(Y_k-Y_k^2+\xi_k).\] For \(0<\alpha\le1/4\), both maps \(T_\pm(y)=y+\alpha(y-y^2\pm1/8)\) are increasing on \([1/2,3/2]\): their derivatives are at least \(1-2\alpha\ge1/2\). Their extreme endpoint values satisfy \[T_-(1/2)=1/2+\alpha/8\ge1/2,\qquad
 T_+(3/2)=3/2-5\alpha/8\le3/2.\] Hence the entire interval is invariant for either sign and \(Y_k\in[1/2,3/2]\subset B_{\epsilon_0/2}(0)=B_2(0)\) at every step.

For every \(k_0\) and every positive stopping radius \(\delta<4\), \(\tau_{k_0,\delta}(0)=\infty\), since \(X_k=0\). The same bounded process \(Y_k\) restricted to \(k\ge k_0\) supplies the required local iteration. Relative to the stated filtration generated by the \(X\) and \(Y\) histories, the next sign is independent, \(\mathbb E[\xi_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\), its fourth moment is \(1/4096\), and \(\mathbb E[|\xi_k w|\mid\mathcal F_k]=1/8\) for either unit vector \(w\) in \(\mathbb R\). The two error conditions are identically zero. The steps are square summable and not summable. All constants can be fixed numerically, independently of \(\delta\). Nevertheless, \[\mathbb P(\lim X_k\in S)=1.\]
## Intended interpretation, dependency, and correction

The proof on p. 50 chooses \(\epsilon_p\) small enough for Proposition 8.1 and subsequent Lyapunov estimates. Existence of a suitable auxiliary process in one originally supplied ball does not guarantee one in that smaller ball. In this example the admissible process stays away from the unstable equilibrium; no condition in the displayed statement links its location to the size of the stopping neighborhood for \(X\).

One precise way to remove this obstruction is to require the local-process hypotheses for every sufficiently small outer radius \(\epsilon_p\), with the indicated noise constants uniform under that shrinking. The proof can then select its Lyapunov neighborhood before invoking the process hypotheses. Alternatively, a quantitative bound such as \(Y_k\in B_{C\delta_p}(p)\), with fixed \(C\), supplies the needed localization when the stopping radius shrinks.

This latter structure is actually present in Proposition 5.2 (pp. 39–40) and equation (8.8) (p. 57): the constructed shadows belong to \(B_{4\delta}(p)\). Thus the counterexample concerns the standalone abstract theorem’s range, not the existence of a flaw in that particular shadow localization. The standard interpretation that all neighborhoods may be made sufficiently small is consistent with the intended proof; the missing stability of the process hypothesis under that operation should be stated. The repair checked here removes this localization obstruction only, and is not a separate certification of the entire nonconvergence theorem.
# Coverage, dependency limits, and interpretation

The full source was read, including the definitions of Clarke, limiting, and Fréchet objects; the active-manifold sharpness statement and its Fréchet-critical premise; the four regularity conditions; transverse preimages; spectral sets and functions; generic stratifications; the three generalized algorithm examples; the two stochastic pillars; and Appendices A.1–A.8. The review did not substitute the introduction’s informal shadow equation for Proposition 5.2: the formal recursion retains the projected noise. It also retained the stopping events and conditional fourth moments in the estimates of Sections 7–8.

The aiming recurrence, shadow error estimates, and summability arguments were traced as written. The small-step rates and the distinct \(\gamma=1\) constants in the auxiliary lemmas were not silently imported into Theorem 6.2, whose stated range is \(\gamma<1\). The generic convergence corollaries concern bounded iterates and retain their regularity and criticality qualifications. None of the six findings above proves that their intended fresh-noise conclusions fail. The spectral-function gap is localized to the false selection assertion; it is not evidence against the set-level normal formula itself.

The independent checks are exact symbolic identities and limits, with rational sample substitutions as additional checks. They validate the displayed algebra, not the entirety of the source paper. The probability construction is justified analytically by rotational invariance and martingale convergence, not by simulation. The external KL theorem’s statement, sign, lower-semicontinuity and definability requirements, and applicability to limiting subgradients were checked in the actual reference PDF [BDLS]. Other cited foundational results were followed where invoked in the source; their complete external proofs were not all independently reproduced. This is a bounded initial review, not a formal proof certificate or independent acceptance.
# Conclusion

The report supports a Major assessment because it identifies a failed central geometric derivation, a failed explicit spectral-transfer derivation, and a counterexample to the marginal-only statement of the abstract saddle-avoidance theorem. The \(C^1\) theorem-range defect, the vector-field smoothness gap, and the auxiliary-process localization defect have more limited demonstrated downstream impact. The distinctions between false assertions, invalid derivations, and false final statements are material to this assessment.

# A replacement KL argument for Theorem 3.11

Write \(r(x)=x-P_Y(x)\) and use \[h(x,v)=-\left\langle v,r(x)\right\rangle+\delta_{\mathop{\mathrm{cl}}X}(x).\] Work inside a definable projection neighborhood and, if needed, restrict to a smaller closed neighborhood before extending by \(+\infty\). This makes a lower-semicontinuous definable function to which the local argument applies; all considered \(x\) are in its interior neighborhood. Local closedness ensures \(N_{\mathop{\mathrm{cl}}X}(x)=N_X(x)\) at the considered points \(x\in X\). If \(\bar x\notin\mathop{\mathrm{cl}}X\) the required local assertion is vacuous.

Equation reference: eq:signed-bound. The projection is \(C^1\) for \(C^2\) \(Y\) and its derivative is symmetric: \(P_Y\) is the gradient of \(\frac12\left\|x\right\|^2-\frac12\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}(x,Y)^2\). Its range lies in \(T_Y(P_Y(x))\), so it annihilates \(N_Y(P_Y(x))\). For unit \(v\in N_X(x)\) the smooth-plus-indicator rule gives \[\partial h(x,v)
 =\bigl(-(I-DP_Y(x))^{\mathsf T}v+N_X(x)\bigr)\times\{-r(x)\}.\] Choosing the positive normal \(v\) in the first factor is legitimate. Strong \((a)\) and boundedness of \(DP_Y\) therefore give \[
 \mathop{\mathrm{dist}}(0,\partial h(x,v))
 \le \sqrt{\left\|DP_Y(x)v\right\|^2+\left\|r(x)\right\|^2}
 \le K\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}(x,Y).\] This works for either sign of \(\left\langle v,r(x)\right\rangle\).

Theorem 14 and Remark 8 of [BDLS], printed pp. 568–570, yield a continuous definable desingularizing function \(\varphi\), with \(\varphi(0)=0\), positive derivative on a sufficiently small positive interval, and \[1\le\varphi'(|h(x,v)|)\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}(0,\partial h(x,v))\] when \(h\ne0\) is sufficiently small. The reference’s positive continuous radius function has a positive minimum on the compact range under consideration, so this choice is uniform for nearby \(x\) and unit \(v\).

For completeness, \(s\varphi'(s)\to0\) as \(s\downarrow0\). Definability makes \(\varphi'\) eventually monotone. If it is increasing as a function of \(s\), it is bounded above on a smaller interval. If it is decreasing, then \[\frac{s}{2}\varphi'(s)
 \le\int_{s/2}^{s}\varphi'(u)\,du
 =\varphi(s)-\varphi(s/2)\longrightarrow0 .\] Combining this with [eq:signed-bound] (#eq:signed-bound), for \(d=\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}(x,Y)>0\), \[\frac{|\left\langle v,x-P_Y(x)\right\rangle|}{d}
 \le K\,|h(x,v)|\varphi'(|h(x,v)|)\longrightarrow0\] uniformly, since \(|h(x,v)|\le d\). The zero-value case is immediate. This is projected \((b_=)\). Strong \((a)\) implies \((a)\), and the \((a)\) plus projected-\((b)\) part of Theorem 3.9 uses only \(C^1\) Taylor remainder control, not the false Lipschitz estimate in Problem Problem 2 (#pr:c1). It consequently gives the full \((b_=)\) conclusion. The original theorem therefore admits this replacement proof under its stated hypotheses, despite the invalid estimate in its submitted derivation.

claim:
Equation reference: eq:false-kl. Theorem 3.11 assumes definable sets \(X,Y\) in a Euclidean space, a point \(\bar x\in Y\), a locally closed \(X\), and a \(C^2\) manifold \(Y\) near \(\bar x\). Definable X and Y; X locally closed; Y C2 near base point; strong (a); x near base and unit v in limiting N_X(x).
analysis: The proof of Theorem 3.11, p. 20, contains a false estimate central to its KL derivation. Severity: Major, confined to the submitted proof.

The invalid cancellation would require \(-v_t\in N_X(x_t)\). A convex normal cone is a cone, not generally a subspace. The omission of the absolute-value sign in the preceding derivative formula is a further reason to handle branches carefully, but it is not the basis of this counterexample.
result:
This example does not disprove Theorem 3.11. Indeed, \[\frac{|\left\langle v_t,x_t\right\rangle|}{\left\|x_t\right\|}
 =\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+4t^2}\sqrt{1+t^2}}\longrightarrow0.\] The zero normals in the interior and the multiples of these boundary normals also satisfy \((b_=)\) at the singleton.

The affected argument is the paper’s stated derivation of the implication in its regularity diagram (3.20). The generic function stratification Theorem 3.29 (p. 31) asserts both strong \((a)\) and \((b_=)\); its displayed proof explicitly establishes the former, with this implication supplying the latter for locally closed epigraphs. This is a substantive proof dependency, not merely a misplaced sign without mathematical consequences. Appendix 6 (#app:kl-repair) gives a checked replacement using the signed function \(-\left\langle v,x-P_Y(x)\right\rangle+\delta_{\mathop{\mathrm{cl}}X}(x)\) and the nonsmooth, two-sided KL inequality. problems.title: C1 target manifold does not imply Lipschitz normal variation
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (The \(C^1\) form of Theorem 3.9(1) is false).
claim:
The theorem allows arbitrary sets \(X,Y\), a point \(\bar x\in Y\), a \(C^1\) retraction onto \(Y\), and a target \(Y\) that is only a \(C^1\) manifold. It asserts equivalence of strong \((a)\) and strong \((a^\pi)\). Let \[X=Y=\{(u,|u|^{3/2}):u\in\mathbb R\},\quad \bar x=0,\quad
 \pi(u,w)=(u,|u|^{3/2}).\] This is a \(C^1\) embedded manifold and a \(C^1\) retraction. To check the quantitative retraction requirement, let \(L\) bound the Lipschitz constant of \(q(u)=|u|^{3/2}\) on a small interval. A nearest graph point to a sufficiently small \(z=(u,w)\) lies in that interval, since the graph contains the origin. For every such candidate \((a,q(a))\), \[|w-q(u)|\le |w-q(a)|+L|u-a|
 \le\sqrt{1+L^2}\left\|z-(a,q(a))\right\|.\] Taking the infimum proves the required distance bound.
Arbitrary X,Y, base in Y, C1 retraction with local distance control, Y a C1 embedded manifold.
analysis: Theorem 3.9(1), p. 17, and estimate (3.22), p. 18, require more than the stated \(C^1\) smoothness of the target manifold. Severity: Minor, a local theorem-range defect.
result: The proof explicitly invokes linear variation of the normal spaces in (3.22); \(C^1\) only supplies continuity. Replacing the target hypothesis by \(C^2\) is sufficient: in a local \(C^2\) graph chart, the normal projector is \(C^1\) and has bounded derivative on a smaller compact neighborhood, hence is locally Lipschitz. The triangle estimate (3.21)–(3.22) then works. A suitable \(C^{1,1}\) normal-variation assumption would also suffice, but \(C^2\) is the correction directly checked here.

The main cited uses already have higher smoothness: Proposition 3.10 uses \(C^3\) (p. 19), Theorem 3.11 uses \(C^2\), and Proposition 3.21 and Theorem 3.25 use \(C^2\) or higher (pp. 27, 29). Thus this example refutes the displayed \(C^1\) theorem, but does not demonstrate failure of those downstream applications. That limited dependency impact motivates the Minor grade.

problems.title: Auxiliary-process localization is not stable under shrinking the outer ball
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: Problem 6 (The auxiliary process is not localized under shrinking neighborhoods).
claim: Recorded check: Auxiliary-process localization is not stable under shrinking the outer ball

C2 field with unstable symmetric derivative at p; auxiliary process stays in B_(epsilon_p/2) for one fixed outer radius epsilon_p; deterministic summable-square/nonsummable steps; conditional centered excitation and bounded fourth moments; zero errors permitted; all stopping radii and starting indices.
analysis: Theorem 6.1, p. 41, does not impose the localization of \(Y_k\) used in the first proof paragraph on p. 50. Severity: Minor in demonstrated application impact, although the unrestricted abstract statement is false.

Take \(d=1\), \(S=\{0\}\), \(X_k=0\) for all \(k\), \(\epsilon_0=4\), and \(F_0(y)=y-y^2\). The field is \(C^\infty\), \(F_0(0)=0\), and \(F_0'(0)=1>0\); thus its unstable space is \(\mathbb R\). Let \(\alpha_k=\frac14 k^{-3/4}\), \(Y_1=1\), \(E_k=0\), and let \(\xi_k\) be independent equiprobable signs of magnitude \(1/8\). Define \[Y_{k+1}=Y_k+\alpha_k(Y_k-Y_k^2+\xi_k).\] For \(0<\alpha\le1/4\), both maps \(T_\pm(y)=y+\alpha(y-y^2\pm1/8)\) are increasing on \([1/2,3/2]\): their derivatives are at least \(1-2\alpha\ge1/2\). Their extreme endpoint values satisfy \[T_-(1/2)=1/2+\alpha/8\ge1/2,\qquad
 T_+(3/2)=3/2-5\alpha/8\le3/2.\] Hence the entire interval is invariant for either sign and \(Y_k\in[1/2,3/2]\subset B_{\epsilon_0/2}(0)=B_2(0)\) at every step.

For every \(k_0\) and every positive stopping radius \(\delta<4\), \(\tau_{k_0,\delta}(0)=\infty\), since \(X_k=0\). The same bounded process \(Y_k\) restricted to \(k\ge k_0\) supplies the required local iteration. Relative to the stated filtration generated by the \(X\) and \(Y\) histories, the next sign is independent, \(\mathbb E[\xi_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\), its fourth moment is \(1/4096\), and \(\mathbb E[|\xi_k w|\mid\mathcal F_k]=1/8\) for either unit vector \(w\) in \(\mathbb R\). The two error conditions are identically zero. The steps are square summable and not summable. All constants can be fixed numerically, independently of \(\delta\). Nevertheless, \[\mathbb P(\lim X_k\in S)=1.\]

The proof on p. 50 chooses \(\epsilon_p\) small enough for Proposition 8.1 and subsequent Lyapunov estimates. Existence of a suitable auxiliary process in one originally supplied ball does not guarantee one in that smaller ball. In this example the admissible process stays away from the unstable equilibrium; no condition in the displayed statement links its location to the size of the stopping neighborhood for \(X\).

One precise way to remove this obstruction is to require the local-process hypotheses for every sufficiently small outer radius \(\epsilon_p\), with the indicated noise constants uniform under that shrinking. The proof can then select its Lyapunov neighborhood before invoking the process hypotheses. Alternatively, a quantitative bound such as \(Y_k\in B_{C\delta_p}(p)\), with fixed \(C\), supplies the needed localization when the stopping radius shrinks.

This latter structure is actually present in Proposition 5.2 (pp. 39–40) and equation (8.8) (p. 57): the constructed shadows belong to \(B_{4\delta}(p)\). Thus the counterexample concerns the standalone abstract theorem’s range, not the existence of a flaw in that particular shadow localization. The standard interpretation that all neighborhoods may be made sufficiently small is consistent with the intended proof; the missing stability of the process hypothesis under that operation should be stated. The repair checked here removes this localization obstruction only, and is not a separate certification of the entire nonconvergence theorem.

Title: Technical review of
Multilinear Hyperquiver Representations
# Source and scope

The reviewed paper is by Tommi Muller, Vidit Nanda and Anna Seigal, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09692-z (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09692-z). The source is the author-hosted, publisher-typeset online-first PDF associated with 14 February 2025, comprising 43 PDF pages. All page references below mean one-based PDF pages. The focused review covers Definitions 2.1–2.6, Theorems 1.1 and 3.1, the section map in Proposition 4.5, Definition 5.2 and Theorem 5.3, the relevant genericity argument in Section 6, Examples 3.12–3.13, and the inverse problem in Section 8. Standard special-case coefficient calculations were also compared with retained exact computations. This is not a verification of every example, external reference, Appendix A result, or floating-point implementation. No relevant author implementation or separate supplement was located in the preserved acquisition search; absence of code is not a mathematical defect.

Throughout, tensor contraction uses the bilinear pairing \(u^{\mathsf T}v\), without conjugation (Remark 2.4, p. 8). Thus nonzero isotropic vectors are permitted. Definitions 2.1–2.5 explicitly allow repeated vertices and related tensors on distinct edges. These features are essential to the first problem.
# A counterexample to the main theorem

Problem 1 (Generic representations can violate the asserted expected dimension).  Theorem 3.1 (p. 9) asserts that a generic representation has no singular vector tuple if \[N=\sum_{v\in V}(d_v-1)-\sum_{e\in E}(d_{t(e)}-1)<0,\] and otherwise, when nonempty, has pure dimension \(N\) and the stated Chern-class degree. The following representation satisfies its stated genericity conditions and contradicts both branches.

Equation reference: eq:contractions. Take two vertices with spaces \(\mathbb C^2\) and \(\mathbb C^q\), where \(q\geq2\). There are three edges, each with ordered vertex tuple \((1,1,1,2)\) and target vertex 1. Choose one generic tensor \[T\in\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^q.\] Assign its three permuted copies so that the edge contractions are \[
c_0=T(\,\cdot,x,x,y),\quad
c_1=T(x,\,\cdot,x,y),\quad
c_2=T(x,x,\,\cdot,y).\] All three edges form one block of the partition in Definition 2.5. The reference slot orders are \((0,1,2,3)\), \((1,0,2,3)\) and \((2,1,0,3)\). Their pairwise induced permutations send the output slots to three distinct positions, satisfying condition (i.c); the preserved exact check verifies all 18 ordered comparisons. For a generic \(T\), the only tensor constraint is precisely the prescribed permutation relation. No symmetry of \(T\) is imposed. Repeated occurrences of vertex 1 are allowed by Remark 2.2.

Set \(x=(1,i)^{\mathsf T}\) and define the linear functional \[\ell_T(y)=T(x,x,x,y).\] Because \(x^{\mathsf T}x=0\) in \(\mathbb C^2\), the orthogonal complement \(x^\perp\) equals \(\operatorname{span}(x)\). Each contraction in [eq:contractions] (#eq:contractions) satisfies \[x^{\mathsf T}c_j=\ell_T(y).\] For every \(T\), the kernel of \(\ell_T:\mathbb C^q\to\mathbb C\) contains a nonzero vector. Any such \(y\) therefore gives \(c_j\in\operatorname{span}(x)\) for all three edges. Consequently \(([x],[y])\) is a singular vector tuple in the exact sense of Definition 2.6.

For generic \(T\), \(\ell_T\) is nonzero: failure is a proper linear condition on \(T\), as a tensor with its \((0,0,0,0)\) entry equal to one already shows. Thus these solutions contain a projective fibre \(\mathbb P^{q-2}\), whereas the theorem predicts \[N=(2-1)+(q-1)-3(2-1)=q-3.\] For \(q=2\), \(N=-1\) but the variety is nonempty for every \(T\); this also contradicts the equal-dimension statement in Theorem 1.1 (p. 5). For \(q=3\), \(N=0\) but the variety contains a projective line. The formal coefficient in (3.1) is then \[[h_1h_2^2](3h_1+h_2)^3=9,\] which cannot count the positive-dimensional zero set. The same construction uses \(x=(1,-i)^{\mathsf T}\).

The argument is symbolic and uniform in \(T\), so it does not rely on calling one numerical tensor generic. The retained numerical-algebraic witness is only a corroborating specialization: for lexicographically ordered tensor entries \(2,3,5,\ldots,53\), \(x=(1,i)^{\mathsf T}\) and \[y=(96+4i,-87-8i)^{\mathsf T},\] the three outputs are \[(48-136i,136+48i),\quad
(350-288i,288+350i),\quad
(-64-226i,226-64i),\] all proportional to \(x\). The symbolic evaluation map has rank three at the checked nonisotropic point and rank one at the isotropic point. This is the relevant rank collapse, not an OCR or transpose convention.
## Impact and counterevidence

The failure concerns the paper’s central generalization to permitted tensor networks and supports Major severity. It does not refute the classical generic single-tensor counts or every restricted hyperquiver case. Imposing independence of all edge tensors would change this construction’s hypotheses, but Definition 2.5 expressly permits the shared tensor block. Excluding isotropic tuples would change the defined solution space. No complete corrected general theorem is asserted here.
# The stated Bertini hypotheses are insufficient

Problem 2 (Almost generation as defined does not ensure emptiness or smoothness).  Definition 5.2 and Theorem 5.3 (pp. 22–24) allow exceptional subvarieties with lower-rank generated subbundles, without the rank-versus-dimension condition needed to exclude their zeros. Two examples satisfy the stated definition.

For the emptiness assertion, take \[X=\mathbb P^1,\qquad B=\mathcal O(1)\oplus\mathcal O(1),\qquad
\Lambda=\{(aX_0,bX_0):a,b\in\mathbb C\}.\] Use the exceptional subvariety \(Y=\{[0:1]\}\) and the zero subbundle \(B_Y=0\). Off \(Y\), evaluation of \(\Lambda\) spans the rank-two fibre. Along \(Y\), every section is zero and hence generates exactly the stipulated zero subbundle. The exceptional locus is proper and smooth; there are no unresolved intersection conditions. Nevertheless, every nonzero section vanishes at \(Y\), although \(\operatorname{rank}B=2>\dim X=1\). This contradicts Theorem 5.3(a). The proof’s incidence object has fibre dimension zero off \(Y\) and two over \(Y\), so its asserted vector-bundle structure (p. 23) does not hold.

For smoothness, take \[X=\mathbb P^2,\qquad B=\mathcal O(2),\qquad
\Lambda=\operatorname{span}\{X_0X_1\}.\] Use the lines \(Y_1=\{X_0=0\}\), \(Y_2=\{X_1=0\}\) and their intersection \(Y_3\), with zero subbundles on all three strata. Evaluation is onto away from the two lines and zero on the exceptional loci. Every nonzero, hence generic, section vanishes on their union. At \([0:0:1]\), its local equation is \(uv=0\), whose gradient vanishes and whose tangent space has dimension two rather than the curve’s dimension one. Thus the smoothness assertion in Theorem 5.3(c) fails.
## Counterevidence and bounded correction

The consulted Friedland–Ottaviani version [FO], Definition 5 and Theorem 6 (PDF pp. 10–11), includes a requirement that the generated subbundle over each exceptional locus have rank strictly greater than that locus’s dimension. Neither example meets that stronger requirement. The present counterexamples therefore concern the weaker statement in the reviewed paper, not that cited result. Restoring a suitable inequality explains how these two examples can be excluded; it does not, by itself, verify all hypotheses for the hyperquiver construction. The first problem shows why a blanket repair of the main theorem cannot be inferred. Because Theorem 5.3 is a central proof ingredient and is itself false as stated, the supported impact is Major.
# Additional local errors

Problem 3 (The map in Proposition 4.5 need not be bijective).  Proposition 4.5 (pp. 21–22) identifies the tensor parameter space with all global sections of \(B(R)\). The allowed Jordan quiver already contradicts injectivity.

For one vertex of dimension two and one loop, \(B(R)\simeq\mathcal O(1)\otimes Q\simeq\mathcal O(2)\) on \(\mathbb P^1\). Its global-section space has dimension three, whereas the matrix space has dimension four. For \(A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) the induced section is represented by \[\det[x,Ax]=cx_0^2+(d-a)x_0x_1-bx_1^2.\] Its kernel is the scalar matrices. The proof chooses a target vector independently of the source vectors; for a self-loop these are the same projective variable.

There is also a surjectivity obstruction without a loop. For two two-dimensional vertices and edges labeled by \(A\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}\) in a single tensor block, the parameter space has dimension four, while \[B(R)\simeq \mathcal O(1,1)\oplus\mathcal O(1,1)\] has eight independent global sections. The linked assignments cannot parametrize that entire space.

The construction of \(L\) and the zero-locus equivalence in Proposition 4.3 remain meaningful. Working with \(\operatorname{im}L\) is the natural local correction, and the subsequent almost-generation discussion explicitly uses an image linear system. This report does not attribute a separate failure of the final count solely to bijectivity. The supported local severity is Minor; the demonstrated core failures are already isolated above.

Problem 4 (Connected parameter spaces do not give a unique fixed homology class).  Example 3.12 (p. 17) states that a connected parameter space gives exactly one nonzero homology class fixed up to scaling. Let \(P\) be a point and \(X=S^1\vee S^1\), and let \(f\) map the two circles to themselves with degrees two and three. These are compact triangulable spaces and a continuous map of the prescribed kind. On \(H_1(X;\mathbb C)\), \[T_1=f_*=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}.\] The definition in the example permits an arbitrary scalar eigenvalue. It therefore yields two distinct projective eigenlines, not one. If \(f\) is instead the identity, all of \(\mathbb P^1\) consists of fixed classes, which also contradicts the example’s unconditional dimension \(d-1=0\).

Requiring \(\lambda=1\) would change the stated definition and does not recover the claimed count in the first example. An additional genericity assumption is also insufficient to imply uniqueness: a generic two-dimensional matrix has two distinct eigenlines. This is a substantive local application error, graded Minor; no dependence of the main tensor theorem on it is demonstrated.

Problem 5 (The message-passing update need not converge).  Example 3.13, equation (3.8) and the next sentence (p. 18), assert convergence to a fixed point without a contraction or spectral hypothesis. In the allowed one-vertex, one-loop case, set \[A=\operatorname{diag}(2,-2),\qquad x^{(0)}=(1,1)^{\mathsf T}.\] Then \(x^{(k)}=2^k(1,(-1)^k)^{\mathsf T}\). The vector norms diverge, and the projective directions alternate between \([1:1]\) and \([1:-1]\). Normalizing the norm does not remove this period-two behaviour.

The characterization of invariant directions remains useful; it is not a convergence theorem. A dominant-eigenvalue or contraction hypothesis would be additional and must be specified before a convergence statement is justified. This local dynamical claim is graded Minor.
# Checks that did not establish an issue

For the inverse problem (pp. 32–38), the source images confirm conjugated input vectors in the adjoint contractions of equation (8.2) and Algorithm 1, lines 8 and 19. These conjugates are required by the Hermitian inner product used for the minimum-norm problem and are present in the actual source. A supposed missing-conjugation error is therefore not supported.

The affine solution expression in Theorem 8.1 was checked against the contraction constraint. Algorithm 1 is an exact-arithmetic conjugate-gradient recurrence for the corresponding normal equation; the orthogonality and error-invariant arguments support its stated finite-dimensional alternative in the inspected scope. The retained exact complex-arithmetic examples give a consistent solution after two iterations and detect inconsistency in a second case. Those two finite tests corroborate, but do not constitute, the general argument. No floating-point stability claim or execution of an author implementation is made.

The retained coefficient checks reproduce 15 for Example 1.2, 13 for the intended homogeneous product in Example 3.6, and six for the \(2\times2\times2\) independent singular-vector specialization. Correct special cases do not resolve the repeated-vertex counterexample.
# Conclusion
Checked claim | Supported assessment
General dimension/emptiness theorem | Major: explicit admissible counterexample
Stated Bertini theorem | Major: counterexamples to two assertions
Global-section bijectivity | Minor: local false proposition
Connected-parameter homology claim | Minor: realizable counterexamples
Unconditional update convergence | Minor: divergent period-two example
Inspected inverse-problem arguments | No issue established within scope

The overall assessment is Major because the general theorem and a central proof ingredient fail under their stated assumptions. This does not imply failure of all special cases or of the inverse algorithm. No complete repaired hyperquiver theorem has been verified. Title: Technical review of
Optimal Regularization for a Data Source
# Source, scope and valid main argument

The reviewed work is by Oscar Leong, Eliza O’Reilly, Yong Sheng Soh and Venkat Chandrasekaran, associated with DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09693-y (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09693-y). The acquired source is arXiv:2212.13597v4 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13597v4), revised 10 September 2024. All locators refer to that PDF, whose printed and PDF page numbers agree. These findings are not asserted to occur in an uninspected journal-final version.

The review checks the population reduction and Theorems 3–4, continuity and compactness in Section 4, the consistency and noise arguments in Section 5, the principal statistical bounds in Section 6, and Proposition 7. The parameterized applications in Sections 6.3–6.5 were read and checked for their dependence on the general bound; this is not a line-by-line certification of all imported estimates. No author code or numerical experiment was executed. The work is theoretical, and lack of code is not a defect.

Write \(g_K(x)=\|x\|_K\) for the gauge of a star body and \(\rho_K\) for its radial function. Layer-cake integration gives \[Z_K=\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-g_K(x)}\,dx=\Gamma(d+1)\operatorname{vol}(K).\] For \(A=\mathbb Eg_K(X)\in(0,\infty)\), scaling \(K\) by \(c>0\) gives the criterion \(A/c+d\log c+\log\operatorname{vol}(K)\), minimized at \(c=A/d\). Thus unit-volume shape optimization is justified, with this scale subsequently reconstructed.

For the more general exponent \(\alpha>0\), let \[\rho_L(u)^{d+\alpha}=\int_0^\infty t^{d+\alpha-1}p(tu)\,dt .\] Under the explicit positivity and continuity assumptions of Theorems 3–4 (pp. 9–13), \(L\) is a star body and the relevant moment is finite. Polar coordinates and Hölder’s inequality give \[F_\alpha(K)=\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}\rho_K^{-\alpha}\rho_L^{d+\alpha}
 \ge d\,\operatorname{vol}(L)^{(d+\alpha)/d}\operatorname{vol}(K)^{-\alpha/d}.\] Equality requires proportional radial functions; continuity promotes almost-everywhere equality to equality everywhere. Hence the unique unit-volume optimum is \(\operatorname{vol}(L)^{-1/d}L\). This verifies the principal formula, including its hypotheses and equality case.

The common-kernel assumption \(rB\subset\ker K\) makes each gauge \(1/r\)-Lipschitz. On a uniformly bounded class, the gauges on the sphere are bounded above and away from zero. Arzelà–Ascoli, followed by inversion, gives radial compactness; the segment definition of the kernel and the volume integral pass to the limit. This supports Section 4 on nonempty feasible classes. Neither a missing higher-moment assumption in Theorem 4 nor the paper’s looser cone-radius bound furnishes a counterexample to these conclusions.
# Problems in the principal statistical derivations
## P1. Theorem 11: expectation bounds do not give pointwise brackets (Major)

On p. 20 the proof takes an \(\eta\)-net in radial distance and uses \[\underline g=(g_{K_0}-CM_P\eta)_+,\qquad
\overline g=g_{K_0}+CM_P\eta,\qquad C=r^{-2},\quad M_P=\mathbb E\|X\|_2,\] as pointwise brackets for nearby gauges. Corollary 2 controls their expectations, not their pointwise difference.

An explicit admissible example is \(d=1\), \(r=1/4\), \(P=\mathrm{Exp}(1)\), \[K_0=[-1/2,1/2],\quad K=[-51/100,49/100],\quad
\eta=1/100,\quad \varepsilon=8/25.\] Both intervals have volume one and contain the required kernel ball; \(\delta(K,K_0)=\eta\), \(M_P=1\), and \(\eta=\varepsilon/(2CM_P)\). At \(x=4\), \[g_K(4)=400/49,\qquad \overline g(4)=204/25,\qquad
g_K(4)-\overline g(4)=4/1225>0.\] The inequality fails on the whole set \(x>98/25\), of positive \(P\)-probability. Thus the invocation of the bracketing strong law is not justified by the brackets written in the proof.

There is a verified repair. The radial lower bound gives, for every \(x\), \[|g_K(x)-g_L(x)|\le r^{-2}\delta(K,L)\|x\|_2.\] Use instead \((g_L-C\eta\|x\|_2)_+\) and \(g_L+C\eta\|x\|_2\). These are measurable, integrable pointwise brackets of \(L^1(P)\) width at most \(2C\eta M_P\). Finite nets and \(\eta<\varepsilon/(2CM_P)\) supply the strong law; when \(M_P=0\), every loss vanishes almost surely. A countable sequence of finite nets gives a common probability-one event, and continuity in \(K\) supplies separability and measurable suprema. Uniform convergence, compactness and continuity then restore the minimizer-subsequence conclusion of Theorem 8 on a nonempty feasible class.
The invalid step is central to the stated consistency derivation, hence its Major impact. The counterexample refutes the original brackets, not the uniform law or the repaired consistency theorem.
## P2. Theorem 14: the empirical \(L^1\) radius is insufficient (Major)

The deterministic complexity bound on p. 25 uses \[c_{P,m}=\sup_{K\in\mathcal C}\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m g_K(x_i)\] as the radius multiplying \(\sqrt{2\log N/m}\). This is not a valid finite-class bound in general.

Take \(d=m=16\), the sample \(x_i=e_i\), and \(\tau=10^{-3}\). For \(j=1,\ldots,16\) let \(K_j\) be the ellipsoid with gauge \[g_j(x)=\left(x_j^2+\tau^2\sum_{i\ne j}x_i^2\right)^{1/2}.\] All \(K_j\) contain the Euclidean unit ball; this finite class meets Theorem 14’s inner-radius and finite-cover assumptions. Its gauge map is Lipschitz in, for example, the discrete metric. The sample has norm one and can occur under a distribution supported on the basis vectors. The theorem does not impose a unit-volume restriction on this class.

At the sample points, \(g_j(e_i)=1\) if \(i=j\) and \(\tau\) otherwise. With precisely the paper’s \(1/m\) convention, \[\mathcal R(\{g_j\};X_m)
=\frac{1-\tau}{16}\mathbb E\max_j\sigma_j
=\frac{(1-\tau)(1-2^{-15})}{16}>0.0624.\] Meanwhile \(c_{P,m}=(1+15\tau)/16\) and the covering number is \(16\) for sufficiently small radius. The claimed bound, in the limit \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), is \[\frac{1+15\tau}{16}\sqrt{\frac{2\log16}{16}}<0.0374.\] This contradiction concerns an exact deterministic step, without an asymptotic or simulation assumption.

The usual finite-net argument works with the empirical \(L^2\) radius, or the uniform envelope \(1/r_{\mathcal C}\). Indeed the moment-generating-function argument bounds the maximum of the finite Rademacher sums by that \(L^2\) radius times \(\sqrt{2\log N/m}\); approximation contributes at most \(\varepsilon\). This provides a corrected route with changed constants. The example alone does not disprove the final high-probability inequality, which also has a concentration term. The proof of the advertised data-dependent bound, and applications using that precise constant, require correction.
## P3. Section 6.2: the convex-body entropy estimate has the wrong order (Major)
The proof of Corollary 5 on pp. 26–27 asserts a logarithmic-in-\(1/\varepsilon\) bound for the metric entropy of all convex bodies contained in \(R_rB\). This is already impossible in dimension two.

For \(n\ge6\), let \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\) be equally spaced on the unit circle and define \[K_S=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((1/2)B^2\cup\{u_j:j\in S\}\bigr),
 \qquad S\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}.\] If \(j\in S\setminus T\), the support function of \(K_S\) in direction \(u_j\) is \(1\), whereas that of \(K_T\) is at most \(\cos(2\pi/n)\). Therefore these \(2^n\) bodies are pairwise separated in Hausdorff distance by \[h_n=1-\cos(2\pi/n)\asymp n^{-2}.\] At radius \(h_n/3\), every covering has at least \(2^n\) members. Its logarithm is at least \(n\log2\), while the paper’s displayed upper bound is only \(O(\log n)\). All bodies contain an interior ball and lie inside \(B^2\); choose, for example, \(r=1/4\), for which the outer class in the proof contains this family. Rescaling gives the same contradiction for any fixed positive outer radius.

This refutes the actual ambient entropy assertion used by the proof. The packing is not asserted to consist of unit-volume bodies, and is not presented as a direct counterexample to the final risk statement for the constrained subclass.

The same derivation also needs the correct union identity \(\rho_{\cup_iK_i}=\max_i\rho_{K_i}\), rather than the printed minimum. Reciprocals cannot be dropped in the following displayed equality. Correctly, \[\delta\!\left(\bigcup_iK_i,\bigcup_iL_i\right)
 \le\max_i\delta(K_i,L_i)
 \le (R_r/r)\max_i d_H(K_i,L_i)\] when the component bodies contain \(rB\) and lie in \(R_rB\). Intersecting arbitrary ambient cover centres with a constrained class need not retain a cover; centres can instead be chosen from occupied balls with a radius factor of two. These local corrections do not repair the false entropy order. Consequently the claimed rate does not follow from the supplied proof; a corrected quantitative rate is not certified here.
# Local claims requiring correction
## P4. Proposition 7 needs a likelihood bound or normalization (Minor)

On p. 31, the proposition assumes a real-valued potential and finite normalizers, and claims \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu_{P_1},\mu_{P_2})^2\le2D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_1\Vert P_2)/Z_{P_1}^2\). Take \[P_1=\delta_0,\qquad P_2=(\delta_0+\delta_1)/2,\qquad \Phi\equiv-\log4.\] Then \(P_1\ll P_2\), \(Z_{P_1}=Z_{P_2}=4\), and each posterior equals its prior. The left side is \(1/4\) whereas the right side is \((\log2)/8<1/4\). All stated hypotheses hold.

A sufficient repair is \(0<e^{-\Phi}\le1\). More generally, an upper bound \(e^{-\Phi}\le M\) gives a factor \(2M^2/Z_{P_1}^2\): the normalized-measure estimate is \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu_1,\mu_2)\le(2M/Z_1)d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P_1,P_2)\), followed by Pinsker’s inequality. This is invariant under rescaling the likelihood. The Gaussian potential displayed earlier is nonnegative, so this counterexample does not invalidate that example. The correction concerns the proposition’s general scope and its downstream interpretation.
## P5. The Gaussian example has an infeasible normalization (Minor)

The explicit formula on p. 12 uses \(K_*=\kappa_d^{1/d}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/(2d)}E_\Sigma\), where \(\operatorname{vol}(E_\Sigma)=\kappa_d\sqrt{\det\Sigma}\). Its volume is \(\kappa_d^2\), rather than one. For \(d=2\) and \(\Sigma=I\) it gives \(\sqrt\pi B^2\) of area \(\pi^2\), despite a smooth positive Gaussian satisfying Theorem 3. The correct factor is \(\kappa_d^{-1/d}\). The preceding general formula and the optimal ellipsoidal shape are sound; the error is the displayed candidate’s feasibility.
## P6. Existence requires a nonempty constraint class (Minor)

Theorem 7 (p. 17) asserts existence over \(\mathcal S^d(r,1)\) for arbitrary \(r>0\). Since every candidate contains \(rB\), \[1=\operatorname{vol}(K)\ge\kappa_dr^d .\] Thus the class is empty for \(r>\kappa_d^{-1/d}\). The necessary and sufficient feasible range is \(0<r\le\kappa_d^{-1/d}\), witnessed by the unit-volume ball. The general closed, bounded class must also be nonempty. On this corrected domain the compactness and continuity arguments establish existence; this does not refute the convergence results for feasible minimizer sequences.
## P7. The asserted sufficient radial conditions are too weak (Minor)

The paragraph before Theorem 3 (p. 9) says that a continuous density with finite second moments satisfies the theorem’s radial conditions. A smooth probability density supported in \(B(3e_1,1)\) has every finite moment but satisfies \(p(tu)=0\) for all \(t\ge0\) when \(u_1\le0\). Its radial moment vanishes in those directions. Theorem 3 itself explicitly assumes positivity and continuity of that moment and survives; the preceding sufficient-condition assertion must be restricted.
## P8. Absolute continuity alone does not justify the KL interpretation (Minor)

The equivalences on p. 4 require finiteness beyond \(P\ll p_K\). A fully explicit obstruction can satisfy the main theorem’s radial condition. Choose an even smooth probability density \(\phi\) supported in \((-1/4,1/4)\) and set \[a_n=2^{-n-1},\quad w_n=a_ne^{-4^n},\qquad
p(x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{a_n}{w_n}
 \left[\phi\!\left(\frac{x-n}{w_n}\right)+
       \phi\!\left(\frac{x+n}{w_n}\right)\right].\] The supports are disjoint and locally finite. This is a smooth probability density with finite second moment; each one-sided first moment equals \(\sum n a_n=1\). Its radial moment is positive on \(\mathbb S^0\). However, \[\int p\log p=2\sum_{n\ge1}a_n4^n+\int\phi\log\phi=+\infty ,\] with finite negative part. For every unit-length star interval \([-a,b]\), \(a+b=1\), the gauge objective is finite and equals \(1/a+1/b\), uniquely minimized at \(a=b=1/2\). Every associated Gibbs density is positive, so absolute continuity holds, but all KL divergences are infinite. The KL criterion therefore does not select the unique cross-entropy optimizer. A finite-entropy or suitable finite-KL condition repairs this interpretation; the principal cross-entropy result is unaffected.
# Coverage, impact and limits

The conclusions distinguish three failed central proof steps from five local scope or formula corrections. P1 has a complete pointwise-bracketing repair. P2 has a verified finite-net repair with a different radius; the full published probability bound has not been disproved. P3 requires a substantive rederivation of the entropy-dependent rate. These support an overall Major assessment for the acquired version.

The noise-continuity argument was checked through the common-kernel gauge Lipschitz estimate and finite-moment coupling; no defect was established there. The finite-dimensional examples require the corrected general complexity argument. No universal optimality for downstream reconstruction tasks is claimed: the paper itself identifies such performance as further work.

Title: Technical review of
Accuracy Controlled Schemes for the Eigenvalue Problem of the Radiative Transfer Equation
# Source and scope

The source is the publisher open-access version of record by Wolfgang Dahmen and Olga Mula, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09694-x (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09694-x), published online on 21 January 2025 and paginated in Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 689–746. The acquired PDF has 58 pages. A PDF page \(p\) corresponds to printed page \(688+p\). Its 2026 issue pagination does not alter the assigned online-2025 scope.

The review follows the assumptions (H1)–(H6), the reduction to \(C=B^{-1}F\), the residual and Newton scheme, the approximate-update constructions, and the power initialization. Appendix A and the compressed-resolvent argument were checked. The external compact-embedding theorem used for compactness was not independently rederived, nor were all imported Schatten estimates certified. The review concerns the acquired bytes; no author implementation or new numerical benchmark was run.

The principal spectral equation is \[Ce=\mu e,\qquad \mu>0,\quad \lambda^\circ=\mu^{-1}.\] All counterexamples to the Newton and update formulas below take place on this actual principal eigenspace of an admissible operator, rather than assuming that an arbitrary finite matrix is itself a transport model. Normalize \(e\) to have norm one in the paper’s chosen real Hilbert metric. Multiplying the positive fission kernel by a positive constant multiplies \(C\) and \(\mu\) by that constant while preserving (H1)–(H6), with the finite kernel bound adjusted accordingly. Thus choices such as \(\mu=1\) or \(\mu=3\) are admissible for the stated class.
# P1. The written Newton iteration does not satisfy its convergence theorem (Major)
## Two inconsistent definitions

Equation (3.1), PDF p. 17/printed p. 705, fixes \[\|Cu^\circ\|=2.\] The residual on the next page is \[R(u,\nu)=
\begin{pmatrix}(I-\nu C)u\\ 1-\|Cu\|^2/2\end{pmatrix}.\] Consequently \(R(u^\circ,\lambda^\circ)=(0,-1)\), not zero. The proof of Theorem 3.10 explicitly uses \(R(u^\circ,\lambda^\circ)=0\) on PDF p. 32/printed p. 720.

There is a separate derivative error. Over the real space, the actual derivative is \[DR(u,\nu)[h,\eta]
=\begin{pmatrix}(I-\nu C)h-\eta Cu\\-\langle Cu,Ch\rangle\end{pmatrix}.\] Equation (3.2), repeated in (3.5), uses \(-\langle Cu,h\rangle\) in its lower row. The missing \(C\) cannot be removed by changing the eigenvector normalization. The positive conclusions about invertibility of that displayed block matrix do not make it the derivative of the stated residual.
## Direct contradiction of the quadratic estimate

Set \(u=ae\) and take \(\lambda\) close to \(\lambda^\circ\), with \(1-\lambda\mu\ne0\). The explicit updates (3.7)–(3.8) give \[\langle Cu,(I-\lambda C)^{-1}Cu\rangle=\frac{\mu^2a^2}{1-\lambda\mu},
\qquad
a_{\rm next}
=\left(1-\frac\mu2\right)a+\frac1{\mu a}.\] This identity follows by cancellation and is independent of \(\lambda\). At the paper’s target amplitude \(a^\circ=2/\mu\), \[a_{\rm next}=\frac2\mu-\frac12.\] Choose \(u_0=u^\circ\) and \(\lambda_0=\lambda^\circ+\varepsilon\), with \(\varepsilon\ne0\) arbitrarily small and avoiding the other resolvent poles. The initial error is \(|\varepsilon|\), while the eigenvector error after one update is exactly \(1/2\). This contradicts (3.59), \[\|(u_1,\lambda_1)-(u^\circ,\lambda^\circ)\|
 \le \frac{\bar\beta\gamma}{2}|\varepsilon|^2,\] for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\). It also covers the explicit-resolvent scheme’s requirement \(\lambda_0\ne\lambda^\circ\). For an exact rational corroboration, \(\mu=3\), \(a=2/3\) gives \(a_{\rm next}=1/6\).

Replacing the target norm \(2\) by \(\sqrt2\) alone does not repair the scheme. Its residual root on the eigenline is then \(a_*=\sqrt2/\mu\), but \[\left.\frac{d a_{\rm next}}{da}\right|_{a_*}=1-\mu.\] Except when \(\mu=1\), this is not a quadratic local map; for \(\mu>2\) the root is locally repelling. Such eigenvalues are permitted by the fission scaling above.

For comparison, using the true derivative on the eigenline gives \[a_{\rm next}^{\rm Newton}=\frac a2+\frac1{\mu^2a},
\qquad
(a_{\rm next}^{\rm Newton})'(a_*)=0.\] This verifies the local scalar correction. It does not certify the paper’s original neighborhood, inverse bounds, tolerances or general constants after changing the full Jacobian. Those parts require a consistent rederivation. The effect is central: Theorem 3.10 and subsequent uses of its exact error estimate are invalid for the formulas as written.

u f+g\|^2

\quad f=Cu,\quad g=M_\lambda u,\quad s=1-\|f\|^2/2.\] Its actual negative gradient has first component \[-M_\lambda^*(M_\lambda w-
u f+g)

More substantially, the text asserts that the exact update lies in \(f^\perp=\{w:\langle f,wangle=0\}\), and proposes projected descent in that space. The second block of the update equation requires \[\langle f,wangle=s.\] These requirements conflict whenever \(s

A decisive admissible test uses \(\mu=1\), \(\lambda=1\), \(u=ae\), where \(a>0\) and \(s=1-a^2/2
e0\). The initial value prescribed on PDF p. 41 is \(f-P_{\langle fangle}u=0\), with \(
u=0\). On \(w=be\), \[Q(be,
u)= rac12\left(a^2
u^2+(s-ab)^2ight),\] whose exact update is \((b,
u)=(s/a,0)\). At the prescribed initial point, the printed first direction is \(-as\,e\), which equals the positive gradient there. Its directional derivative is \[DQ(0,0)[D(0,0)]=a^2s^2>0.\] Thus the unprojected direction is strictly ascending.
