# P3. The contour formula encloses a forbidden pole (Major)

The alternative construction in (4.33), PDF p. 42/printed p. 730, claims \[(I-\bar\lambda C)^{-1}C\bar u
=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma
  \frac{\bar\mu\zeta}{\bar\mu-\zeta}
  (\zeta I-C)^{-1}\bar u\,d\zeta,
\qquad \bar\mu=\bar\lambda^{-1}.\] Its contour is the boundary of a disc centered at \(\bar\mu\), chosen to enclose the nearby principal eigenvalue. The scalar factor has a pole at the centre \(\zeta=\bar\mu\). It is therefore not holomorphic on the enclosed spectral region, as the claimed functional-calculus identity would require.

Take \(C\bar u=\mu\bar u\) with \(\bar\mu\ne\mu\). With positive orientation, the scalar integrand on this eigenline is \[\frac{\bar\mu\zeta}{(\bar\mu-\zeta)(\zeta-\mu)}.\] The two enclosed residues are \[\frac{\bar\mu\mu}{\bar\mu-\mu},
\qquad
-\frac{\bar\mu^2}{\bar\mu-\mu},\] so their sum is \(-\bar\mu\). The claimed left side is instead \(\bar\mu\mu/(\bar\mu-\mu)\). The clockwise convention printed in Section 3.2 reverses the integral’s sign, giving \(+\bar\mu\), and still does not recover that left side.

For example, after scaling \(\mu=1\), choose \(\bar\mu>1\) sufficiently close to one to meet the paper’s gap-dependent disc conditions. The desired coefficient becomes arbitrarily large as \(\bar\mu\downarrow1\), whereas the contour returns a coefficient tending to \(-1\) or \(+1\). The rational values \(\bar\mu=101/100\), \(\mu=1\) illustrate the discrepancy \(101\) versus \(-101/100\) whenever the stated disc encloses these two points.

This defect remains even with exact resolvent evaluations and a known gap. Convergent quadrature of the proposed integral would converge to the wrong operator action. A repair must exclude the scalar pole or account for its residue and handle the complementary spectral part; the original formula and subsequent error claim are not justified. No repaired implementation or complexity guarantee is certified here.
# P4. The global initialization guarantee fails for permitted initial data (Major)

The setup (5.1), PDF p. 43/printed p. 731, assumes a unit initial vector with \(\langle a_0^\circ,u_1\rangle\ne0\). For a nonnormal operator, the condition that selects the principal spectral component is \(E_C(\mu_1)a_0^\circ\ne0\), determined by the left eigenvector. Right-eigenvector overlap alone is insufficient.

There is an example inside the transport class. Take \(d=1\), \[D=(0,1),\qquad
V=[-3/2,-1]\cup[1,3/2],\qquad
\sigma=s_0>0,\quad \kappa=0,\quad \varphi=c>0.\] The velocity set has Lebesgue measure one, is compact, excludes zero and contains \(\{-1,1\}\). The remaining positivity, boundedness and continuity hypotheses hold. Let \(P_v\) be velocity averaging, the orthogonal projection onto velocity-independent functions in the constant-\(\sigma\) metric. Then \(F=cP_v\) and \(C=T^{-1}cP_v\).

A nonzero principal eigenfunction \(u_1\) cannot be independent of velocity. Otherwise the transport eigen-equation for two distinct velocities implies its spatial derivative is zero; the inflow conditions then force that constant to vanish. Hence \(h=(I-P_v)u_1\ne0\). The initial state \[a_0^\circ=h/\|h\|\] has norm one and \(\langle a_0^\circ,u_1\rangle=\|h\|>0\), yet \(Fa_0^\circ=0\) and \(Ca_0^\circ=0\). The first normalization in (5.1) is undefined. This is a direct failure under the written initial-data condition.

The later Lemma 5.6 (PDF pp. 49–50) explicitly assumes \(a_0^\circ\ge0\) and uses a positive principal Riesz component. This supplies a restricted result that excludes the counterexample. However, Section 5 makes initialization into the Newton convergence neighborhood an overarching objective and explicitly presents Theorem 5.1 as its main result. Under the theorem’s written condition, an admissible transport input prevents even the first normalization. This materially invalidates the stated global initialization guarantee and supports Major severity. The availability of a short positivity restriction does not make that central failure local. Under a nonzero correctly oriented principal component and a strict spectral gap, the qualitative complementary-spectral-radius argument remains sound; power initialization for nonnegative data is not rejected.
# Valid components, coverage and limitations

Appendix A’s weighted contractivity estimate can be recovered from the two kernel integral bounds and weighted Cauchy–Schwarz, with \(\rho\le1-\alpha/\sup\sigma<1\). The resulting Neumann series justifies positivity of \(B^{-1}\) and \(C\). The compactness reduction \[C=(I-T^{-1}K)^{-1}T^{-1}F\] is valid conditional on the cited compactness result for the latter factor. Algebraic simplicity and Fredholm theory also justify bounded invertibility of the compressed resolvent in Lemma 3.1; no complete eigenbasis is needed for that step.

For an actual Newton map at a genuine zero, bounded inverse derivative and Lipschitz derivative yield the standard bound \(e_{n+1}\le(\bar\beta\gamma/2)e_n^2\). An update error of at most \(\eta_n\) adds at most \(\eta_n\) to this estimate. These conditional perturbation principles are valid, but they cannot be applied to the incompatible definitions in P1 or the unsuccessful realization in P2. Likewise, a complementary spectral component with radius below \(\mu_1\) decays at any larger ratio below one, with a possibly large constant. This supports the correctly restricted qualitative power-method statement without certifying every printed Schatten constant.

The paper expressly says in Sections 5.2 and 6 that it does not provide a directly applicable fully certified eigensolver and that the needed spectral information remains difficult to obtain. This acknowledged limitation is not counted as a defect. The bounded acquisition search located no separate author repository or supplement; that status is not a claim of global absence and has no bearing on the mathematical severity.

The four central failures support an overall Major assessment. Their calculations were checked analytically and corroborated by retained reviewer-authored exact symbolic computations; those computations are not numerical reproduction of an author implementation. No usable substantive predecessor report was recovered for this paper in the accessible preserved inventory. Source acquisition and original substantive checks retain their recorded attribution. The focused independent acceptance corrects the severity of P4; the revised report is bound to an actual new compilation and report-page inspections. Scientific adjudication remains pending and human reviews are empty.

report: Abstract: The central construction of common refinements is supported for positive finite pointwise dimension, subject to a local correction in its exchange argument. Four Minor findings concern an auxiliary distance formula, the zero-module boundary of the stability statements, an unnecessarily restrictive condition in that exchange argument, and two overly strong intermediate assertions in the sharpness proof. The latter assertions admit direct repairs preserving the dimension obstruction. No Major counterexample to the positive-dimensional stability theorem or its order of sharpness was established. The separate conjectures remain conjectures.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical review of
Stabilizing Decomposition of Multiparameter Persistence Modules
# Source, definitions and scope

The reviewed source is Håvard Bakke Bjerkevik’s publisher version of record. Its DOI is 10.1007/s10208-025-09695-w (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09695-w), published online on 27 January 2025 and paginated in Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 939–998. The acquired PDF has 60 pages; PDF page \(p\) is printed page \(938+p\). This is an online-2025 assignment.

The distinction between a subquotient, an erosion neighborhood, and a refinement is essential. With the paper’s shift convention, \[\operatorname{Er}_\varepsilon(M)\cong
 \operatorname{im}\bigl(M(-\varepsilon)\longrightarrow M(\varepsilon)\bigr).\] A representative \(I/K\) belongs to \(\operatorname{EN}_\varepsilon(M)\) when \[\operatorname{im}(M(-\varepsilon)\to M)\subseteq I\subseteq M,
 \qquad K\subseteq I\cap\ker(M\to M(\varepsilon)).\] A refinement imposes this condition on each indecomposable summand separately. Pointwise finite dimension (pfd) permits the decomposition arguments; a finite uniform bound \(r=\operatorname{supdim}M\) is additionally used in the main stability estimate. The report checks these different hypotheses separately.

The source definitions, the distance comparisons, the finite-dimensional pruning mechanism, the exchange step, the sharpness construction, and the constrained-invertibility reformulation were examined. Checks of imported decomposition, matching, and density theorems are limited to their stated use. No author code was executed, and no empirical computation is needed for the counterexamples below.
# P1. The printed auxiliary \(d_E\) is not a distance (Minor)

Definition 4.1 requires the triangle inequality. Definition 4.2 (PDF p. 19/printed p. 957) then defines \[M\leq^*N\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \dim M_p\leq\dim N_p\quad\text{for every }p,\] and \[d_E(M,N)=\inf\{\varepsilon\geq0:
       \operatorname{Er}_\varepsilon(M)\leq^*N,\ 
       \operatorname{Er}_\varepsilon(N)\leq^*M\}.\] This formula fails the stated requirement, already for pfd one-parameter modules.

Let \[M=k_{[0,2)},\qquad
 N=k_{[0,1)}\oplus k_{[1,2)},\qquad Q=0.\] The pointwise dimensions of \(M\) and \(N\) agree, including at the common endpoint \(1\), so \(d_E(M,N)=0\). Indeed, the paper itself uses this pair on PDF p. 20. For a half-open interval, \[\operatorname{Er}_\varepsilon(k_{[a,b)})=
 k_{[a+\varepsilon,b-\varepsilon)},\] with an empty interval denoting zero. Thus \[d_E(M,Q)=1,\qquad d_E(N,Q)=\frac12,\] contradicting \(1\leq 0+\frac12\).

The issue is the particular pointwise-dimension formula in this definition. It does not refute an external erosion distance defined on other invariants. The paper’s principal distance \(d_{EN}\) is defined by a common erosion-neighborhood representative; its triangle proof does not use a triangle inequality for \(d_E\). A local correction should remove the distance designation from the displayed formula, or replace the invariant/order and establish the corresponding metric properties.
# P2. Exclude \(r=0\) from the stated stability factor (Minor)

The source explicitly allows \(\operatorname{supdim}M\in\{0,1,\ldots,\infty\}\) on PDF p. 36. Theorem 5.4(ii) and Corollaries 5.5–5.6 (PDF p. 38/printed p. 976) assume only \(r=\operatorname{supdim}M<\infty\).

Take the two-parameter modules \[M=0,\qquad N=k_{[0,1)^2},\qquad \varepsilon=1,\] with diagonal shifts. Zero maps give an \(\varepsilon\)-interleaving because both \(2\varepsilon\) structure maps vanish. However, \(\operatorname{Pru}_\varepsilon(M)=0\), while \[\operatorname{EN}_0(N)=\{N\}\quad\text{up to isomorphism}.\] Consequently \(0\) is not a \(2r\varepsilon=0\) refinement of the nonzero module \(N\), contrary to Theorem 5.4(ii). The same example gives \[d_I(0,N)=f_R(0,N)=\frac12>0,\] whereas the right side of Corollary 5.6 is zero.

This is a boundary correction, not a failure of the positive-dimensional argument. Require \(r\geq1\), or replace the factor \(r\) by \(\max\{1,r\}\). For \(r=0\), an \(\varepsilon\)-interleaving with zero makes \(N\) \(2\varepsilon\)-trivial, so zero is a \(2\varepsilon\)-refinement of \(N\). The latter formulation therefore supplies the missing case directly. Statements with the same zero factor, including the proposed upper bound in Conjecture 4.20, should carry the corresponding qualification; no claim is made here to prove that conjecture for \(r\geq1\).
# P3. Relax the ambient condition in the exchange argument (Minor)

The proof of Theorem 5.4 replaces indecomposable summands of \(\ker\overline{\psi(\varepsilon)}\) by isomorphic copies which lie inside individual summands of \(\overline N\). The definition of a partial decomposition on PDF p. 40/printed p. 978 additionally requires \[X^S\subseteq\ker\overline{\psi(\varepsilon)}.\] The exchange construction sets \(Y^T=\pi_i(Y)\) and proves \(\pi_i(Y)\subseteq\overline Z_i\) on PDF p. 42. This does not imply the additional kernel inclusion. A projection onto a direct summand need not preserve a kernel: the projection of the diagonal line in \(k^2\) onto the first coordinate is the coordinate line itself.

The proof can be formulated without that surplus restriction. Require the replacement copies to be submodules of \(\overline N\), retain their placement in \(\overline Z_j\), their isomorphism types, and both decomposition identities in conditions (i)–(iii). Original summands \(X\) still lie in the kernel. The chain upper-bound argument uses pfd and these decomposition identities. The exchange calculation uses the original \(Y\) and original \(X\)-components when it invokes kernel membership; it does not need the replacement copies to remain there. At maximality, Krull–Schmidt cancellation and the quotients inside the individual \(\overline N_j\) give the required refinement exactly as intended.

Thus the written induction invariant is stronger than what its construction establishes. Removing this condition is a local proof repair. The elementary projection example diagnoses the unsupported implication; it is not offered as a persistence-module counterexample to Theorem 5.4.
# P4. Two local corrections in the sharpness proof (Minor)

The following intermediate assertions in the proof of Theorem 5.9 are stronger than necessary. The repaired argument still yields the claimed obstruction to replacing the dimension-dependent factor by a universal constant.
## Use an inclusion in Lemma 5.10

On PDF p. 44/printed p. 982, the proof uses \[M_{x_c+(\delta,\delta)}=k^{c+n-2}.\] For \(n=3\), \(c=1\), and \(\delta=0\), the actual generators in the preceding page give \(M_{x_1}=\langle e_1\rangle\), while the displayed right side is \(\langle e_1,e_2\rangle\). The valid statement is \[M_{x_c+(\delta,\delta)}\subseteq k^{c+n-2},
 \qquad 0\leq\delta<n-1.\] Indeed, \(\lfloor\delta\rfloor\leq n-2\), which bounds the indices of generators present at this point. The subsequent flag argument needs only this inclusion.
## Use the rank bound for the second image

On PDF pp. 45–46, write \(T=M_{0\to1}\). The proof asserts that \(e_{2n}\) never belongs to \(\operatorname{im}(T-f)\). Near the terminal boundary some earlier coordinates have already died, so this is false. For \(n=2\), consider the map from \((24,24)\) to \((25,25)\). Its domain contains all four coordinate vectors, but \(I_1\) has disappeared at the target. Consequently \[(T-f)e_1=-e_2,\qquad
 (T-f)e_2=e_2-e_3,\qquad
 (T-f)e_3=e_3-e_4.\] Their span contains \(e_4\).

Nevertheless the required estimate \(\dim\operatorname{im}(T-f)\leq2n-1\) holds. If the domain has dimension below \(2n\), it follows immediately. Otherwise the domain is all of \(k^{2n}\) and \((T-f)e_{2n}=0\), so rank–nullity gives the estimate. The other image bound and the block interleaving of Lemma 5.12 remain valid. These corrections repair the route to Theorem 5.9; they do not provide a counterexample to that theorem.
# Positive checks and limits
## Erosion neighborhoods and distances

Lemma 4.4 follows by taking inverse images of the submodule and kernel defining the second quotient. The resulting numerator contains \(\operatorname{im}(M(-\varepsilon-\delta)\to M)\), and the denominator is killed by the \((\varepsilon+\delta)\) shift.

For Lemma 4.5, write two representatives inside the middle module as \(A_i/B_i\). Their common refinement is obtained from \[A_3=A_1\cap A_2,\qquad B_3=(B_1+B_2)\cap A_3.\] Under \(A_1\to A_1/B_1\), the image of \(A_3\) contains the required shifted image, and the image of \(B_3\) lies in the shifted kernel. This proves the triangle inequality for \(d_{EN}\) independently of P1.

Theorem 4.7 was checked by using the two maps from \(M(-\varepsilon)\oplus N(-\varepsilon)\) associated with an interleaving. Naturality and the interleaving identities identify the inverse images of the two quotient kernels, yielding the same quotient in both erosion neighborhoods. Conversely, interleavings through a common representative compose. Thus \(d_{EN}\leq d_I\leq2d_{EN}\) is supported.

For one-parameter half-open bars, the induced-matching proof of Theorem 4.9 controls both endpoint changes by \(\varepsilon\); unmatched bars have length at most \(2\varepsilon\). Bars of exactly that length need not be matched. The general decorated-endpoint case is delegated by the source to its cited matching theorem. The counterexamples in Lemmas 4.10–4.11, refinement composition, the pruning-distance triangle argument, and the thin-summand argument in Theorem 4.22 were also checked. In that last argument, the union of two pointwise subspaces is a submodule because each ambient space has dimension at most one.
## Pruning, stability and sharpness

For \(1\leq r<\infty\), the descending and ascending pointwise chains in Lemma 5.3 stabilize after at most \(r\) strict changes. Their image/kernel inclusions, the induced quotient maps, and the splitting step support Theorem 5.4, with P3’s repaired exchange invariant. This is a finite-dimensional argument; the general-module countable construction in Lemma 5.2 was not independently certified without a finiteness hypothesis. Existence of a largest admissible numerator and smallest admissible denominator can instead be obtained by sums and intersections of admissible submodules.

The flag constraints in Lemma 5.10 and the block-matrix identities in Lemma 5.12 support the sharpness mechanism after P4’s corrections. No numerical sampling is used as a substitute for those arguments.
## Constrained invertibility and conjectural statements

The upset-module reduction and finite constrained-invertibility construction in Section 6 were checked. Theorem 6.14 moves from pfd upset decompositions to finite matrix instances without spelling out the reduction. A finite-witness argument fills this step: interleavings give mutually inverse column-finite matrices; protect the finitely many vertices reachable within the relevant bounded path length from a finite Hall-test set, and extend the maps on these protected columns to inverse finite matrices. No new short neighbors of the test set appear. The finite assumption then implies Hall’s condition. The matching graph is locally finite by pfd, so the infinite matching step applies. This supplies counterevidence to treating the omitted reduction as a theorem failure.

The paper does not claim to prove Conjectures 4.20, 6.1 or 6.10. The review does not resolve them, establish every imported result, or certify a polynomial-time implementation of pruning. Those limits are separate from the four local findings.
# Supporting checks

The appropriate technical assessment is Minor: the auxiliary distance formula and zero-module scope need correction, and two proof passages need the explicit local repairs above. The positive-dimensional core and the dimension-dependent obstruction retain substantive support. This assessment is an initial scientific review, with independent acceptance still pending.

No usable substantive predecessor report for this paper was found in the accessible preserved inventory. The acquired source PDF, manifest, and historical extraction were reused with their original identities. The present mathematical checks, report, source-page inspections, exact-source offline build, and report-page inspections are current work. Detailed file hashes, original and recovery tokens, source/version bindings, limitations, and build/view records are retained with the per-paper verification files.

report: Abstract: The acquired preprint contains four Major problems in the route to its spectral and pointwise convergence estimates. The uniformly stated point-sampling input estimate is false for smooth concentrated data; the empirical estimates do not justify the variational maxima; repeated eigenvalues are not handled by the scalar eigenvector argument; and random local factors and a corrector term are lost in the pointwise argument. A local negative-norm definition also requires correction. These findings concern the specified arXiv v1. They do not establish that the final journal version or a correctly formulated homogenization result is false.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical review of
Optimal Convergence Rates for the Spectrum of the Graph Laplacian on Poisson Point Clouds
# Exact source and intended mathematical setting

The source is Scott Armstrong and Raghavendra Venkatraman, Optimal convergence rates for the spectrum of the graph Laplacian on Poisson point clouds, arXiv:2312.08149v1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08149v1), submitted 13 December 2023; the PDF author date is 14 December 2023. It has 23 numbered pages. The acquisition manifest connects this work to the assigned journal DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09696-9 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09696-9). Equivalence to the journal text is not asserted.

Several evident transcription errors occur in the kernel branches and boundary inequalities in (1.2), (1.3), and (2.1). The checks below use the intended nonnegative symmetric kernel, interior equation, and zero boundary shell. They persist after those local corrections. The barred sums are read as the normalized averages defined on p. 8; no mismatch is inferred merely from the appearance of the summation glyph.
# P1. The uniform point-sampling input estimate is false (Major)

Theorem 1.1 and (1.3)–(1.4), pp. 2–3, assert one random scale and one finite constant for every \(\bar u\in H^2(U_m)\cap H_0^1(U_m)\): \[-\mathcal Lu(x)=-\nabla\cdot\bar a\nabla\bar u(x),
 \qquad
 \|u-\bar u\|_{\underline L^2(\eta_*(U_m))}
 \leq C\|\bar u\|_{\underline L^2(U_m)}R^{-1}L_m,\] where \(L_m=1\) for \(d\geq3\) and \(L_m=\sqrt m\) for \(d=2\). No averaging of the forcing or frequency restriction is stated.

Fix any nontrivial realization with an interior vertex \(x_0\) and invertible Dirichlet matrix \(A_g=-\mathcal L\). Choose a smooth cutoff \(\chi\) supported in the unit ball and equal to one near its center. For \(\rho\) smaller than the distance from \(x_0\) to the other sampled points and to the boundary, put \[\bar u_\rho(x)=
 -\frac{|x-x_0|^2}{2\,\operatorname{tr}\bar a}\,
 \chi\!\left(\frac{x-x_0}{\rho}\right).\] This function is smooth and compactly supported in \(U_m\). At every sampled point its value is zero. Its sampled forcing is one at \(x_0\) and zero everywhere else. Hence \[u_\rho=A_g^{-1}e_{x_0}\ne0\] is independent of \(\rho\), and the left side of the claimed estimate is a fixed positive number. By contrast, \[\|\bar u_\rho\|_{\underline L^2(U_m)}
 =O(\rho^{2+d/2})\longrightarrow0.\] This contradicts (1.4) for every finite \(C\), even at one fixed allowed scale.

The witness uses smooth data, so the objection is stronger than the lack of a canonical point evaluation for a general Sobolev equivalence class. Choosing it after fixing the graph is legitimate for the stated event that is uniform over every \(\bar u\). The restated input is used in (2.15), p. 12.

The cited companion result [AV23b] was not independently retrieved and is not being refuted here. A repair requires the actual sampling or coarse-graining operator, the correct data norm and regularity, and verification that the corrected estimate applies to the trial functions used below. A change of norm label alone is not a verified repair.
# P2. The empirical estimates do not support the variational maxima (Major)
## The selected cluster is not an independent sample

On p. 20, the proof of Lemma A.2 calls the variables indexed by the selected connected component independent and identically distributed, and applies (A.3). This is not the conditional uniform sample formed by all Poisson points. Connectivity-based selection introduces dependence. For example, a selected two-vertex connected component must have its two vertices within unit distance, whereas two independent uniform points in a domain of diameter greater than one need not.

Moreover, the displayed variance-only exponential bound is not the general Bernstein inequality for bounded variables: a range-dependent term, or a justified restriction to its quadratic regime, is needed. Lemma A.3 on p. 21 refers back to the same argument. Thus the stated proofs do not supply the cluster concentration estimates they use.
## Uniform normalization over the trial class is impossible

There is a separate pathwise obstruction to (2.12)–(2.13), pp. 10–11. Those formulas retain a maximum over continuous, continuum-normalized functions with upper bounds on their supremum and gradient energy. The passage from a fixed-function probability estimate to that maximum requires simultaneous control that is false on the stated class.

Take an allowed dimension \(d\geq3\) and a finite realized point set. Choose smooth cutoffs equal to zero at each point and one outside disjoint balls of radius \(\rho\). Their product \(h_\rho\) satisfies \[h_\rho\to1\ \hbox{in }L^2(U_m),\qquad
 \|h_\rho\|_\infty\leq1,\qquad
 \frac{1}{|U_m|}\int_{U_m}|\nabla h_\rho|^2=O(N\rho^{d-2})\to0.\] Normalize \(f_\rho=h_\rho/\|h_\rho\|_{\underline L^2(U_m)}\). Then its continuum normalized \(L^2\) norm is one, its supremum tends to one, and its energy tends to zero, while its empirical squared norm is zero. These are admissible competitors whenever the stated supremum cap has slack above one, as occurs for allowed domains with sufficiently large \(\lambda_{0,1}\), or in the class \(\mathcal A_T\) for sufficiently large \(T\). The competitors are not required to have zero boundary trace. Taking a small positive value at the sample points instead of zero gives nonzero denominators arbitrarily close to zero.

This refutes the required uniform empirical normalization, including under the energy restriction (2.8). It does not refute every possible fixed-function concentration theorem. Restricting one comparison to a deterministic ground state might avoid one maximum, but does not establish the opposite comparison over graph-dependent trial functions.
## The probability and induction closure also need justification

On p. 13 the proof maximizes over \(T\) although the displayed failure probability depends on \(T^{-2}\) in its exponent. A bound with a \(T\)-independent numerical right side does not itself hold on one uniform event. The subsequent choice of \(T\) uses an eigenvector supremum estimate whose derivation already invokes the conditional eigenvalue bound.

The orthogonality transfer (2.33)–(2.34), p. 18, is explicitly granted and is not subsequently established before the proof ends. In (2.36), the extra \(R^{-2}\) in the supremum bound even makes the continuum-normalized class empty for fixed \(K\) and large \(m\); this factor must at least be corrected. These are further missing closure steps, rather than additional claimed counterexamples to the final eigenvalue rate.

A complete repair needs controlled comparison maps or finite-dimensional trial spaces, valid concentration for the selected cluster, and simultaneous estimates with the advertised dependence on \(m\), \(k\), and \(T\). The review does not supply that replacement proof.
# P3. The eigenvector argument needs spectral-subspace control (Major)

The gap in (1.6), p. 4, is the distance to the nearest distinct eigenvalue. Theorem 1.2 does not impose simplicity, and the allowed domains can have repeated Dirichlet eigenvalues. Nevertheless, the induction declares the optimizer in (2.35) unique (p. 18) and extends the ground-state eigenvector argument by changes of notation (p. 17).

A gap to the rest of the spectrum controls a spectral subspace, not an arbitrarily fixed vector within a repeated eigenspace. The exact finite-dimensional diagnostic \[A_0=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,\lambda,\nu),\qquad
 A_\varepsilon=
 \begin{pmatrix}\lambda&\varepsilon&0\\
 \varepsilon&\lambda&0\\0&0&\nu\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad 0<\varepsilon<\lambda<\nu,\] has perturbation norm \(\varepsilon\) and a fixed external gap. Its split eigenvectors, scaled to have inner product one with \(e_1\), are \(e_1\pm e_2\), both at distance one from \(e_1\). A scalar normalization cannot remove the rotation. This is a diagnostic of the perturbation argument, not a claim that these matrices are themselves Poisson graph Laplacians.

For a simple isolated eigenvalue, an appropriately oriented eigenvector estimate may be recovered from a projected resolvent argument. For repeated eigenvalues, the theorem should state a cluster/subspace estimate and an explicit basis-selection convention. Neither repair, with all the claimed constants and probability quantifiers, is completed in the reviewed text.
# P4. Random local factors and a corrector are lost in the pointwise proof (Major)

The proof on pp. 15–17 starts with a local regularity radius \(\mathcal X(x)\) having stretched-exponential integrability. The estimate requires \[R_x=\tfrac12 R\,\operatorname{dist}(\zeta,\partial U_0)
 \geq\mathcal X(x),\qquad x=R\zeta.\] The global condition \(R>\mathcal X\) alone does not establish this for every vertex, particularly near the boundary.

The edge estimate on p. 16 retains a factor \(\mathcal X(x)^{d/2}\). The next page’s pointwise estimate retains a factor of order \(\mathcal X(x)^2\) after taking square roots. Stretched-exponential integrability of these factors does not turn them into the deterministic constant \(C(d,\alpha)\) stated in Theorem 1.3. Uniform control over all centers and all stated scales requires a separate argument, with its resulting factors or probability qualification retained.

A second omission is exact. The proof defines \(w=\phi_m-\phi_0-c\) but later uses \[\|\phi_m\|_\infty\leq\|w\|_\infty+\|\phi_0\|_\infty\] on p. 17. The term \(\|c\|_\infty\) is missing. Controlling \(w\) does not by itself control \(\phi_m-\phi_0\) or produce the deterministic \(T\) used to close P2.

The regularity scaling on p. 14 also needs correction: the wavelength is \(R/\sqrt{\lambda_{0,k}}\), whereas the displayed substitution omits \(R\) and reverses this scale. Interior Hessian estimates cannot simply be applied globally up to every allowed convex-domain boundary. An obtuse planar sector has Dirichlet eigenfunctions behaving like \(r^
u\sin(
u	heta)\), \(1<
u<2\), with unbounded Hessian at the corner; a boundary treatment is required.

These observations invalidate the written derivation of the deterministic pointwise and every-edge estimates. They do not prove that every appropriately qualified replacement theorem is false. The local random factors, the corrector, the boundary regime, and spectral-gap dependence must all be tracked in such a replacement.
# P5. Correct the negative-norm pairing (Minor)

On p. 8 the displayed definition is \[\sup_{g\ne0}\frac{\langle f,g\rangle_{H^1}}{\|g\|_{H^1}},\] with zero-boundary test functions. For a Dirichlet function \(f\), Cauchy–Schwarz and the choice \(g=f\) make this exactly \(\|f\|_{H^1}\), not its negative Sobolev norm. The numerator should use the intended distributional or \(L^2\) pairing. Later applications, including p. 16, use that corrected pairing implicitly. This is a local definitional repair; it does not resolve P1–P4.
# Verified structure, limitations and assessment

The graph energy identity, positivity of the intended Dirichlet inverse, ordinary minmax principle, and continuum scaling \(\mu_{0,k}=R^2/\lambda_{0,k}\) were checked. Conditional on a valid estimate \[|\mu_{m,k}-\mu_{0,k}|\leq C L_m\sqrt{\mu_{0,k}},
 \qquad |\mu_{m,k}-\mu_{0,k}|\leq\tfrac12\mu_{0,k},\] taking reciprocals indeed gives \[|R^2\lambda_{m,k}-\lambda_{0,k}|
 \leq 2C L_m R^{-1}\lambda_{0,k}^{3/2}.\] Thus the desired exponent is consistent with the inverse-eigenvalue scaling. The missing steps are the analytical and stochastic comparisons needed to obtain that premise.

Appendix A.1’s eigenfunction supremum scaling and the formal product identities were checked within their stated regularity scope. The general homogenization, corrector, and large-scale regularity theorems cited from other works were not independently reproduced. Nor was optimality against every admissible random model established. The discussion of higher-order convergence, manifolds, and Neumann conditions was not treated as a proved extension of the complete Dirichlet argument. No missing implementation is counted as a mathematical defect.

The assessment for the acquired v1 is Major. P1 includes a direct smooth-data counterexample, and P2 includes a direct obstruction to the required uniform trial-class estimate. P3 and P4 identify central statement/proof gaps with exact diagnostics and necessary repair conditions. The intended spectral convergence theorem itself is not declared false for the Poisson model, and no conclusion is transferred to uninspected journal bytes.

The bounded preserved inventory supplied no substantive predecessor report for this paper. Source PDF, manifest, and historical extraction were reused with their original identities; the analytic and symbolic checks, actual source-page inspections, report, exact-source offline build, and report-page inspections are current work. A refined constant-function cutoff argument supersedes the preliminary ground-state formulation in the retained check record. Scientific decision and independent acceptance remain pending; no human review is recorded.

problems.title: Uniform relative-L2 bound for every smooth sampled Dirichlet input is false.
claim: Uniform relative-L2 bound for every smooth sampled Dirichlet input is false.
analysis:
Theorem 1.1 and (1.3)–(1.4), pp. 2–3, assert one random scale and one finite constant for every \(\bar u\in H^2(U_m)\cap H_0^1(U_m)\): \[-\mathcal Lu(x)=-\nabla\cdot\bar a\nabla\bar u(x),
 \qquad
 \|u-\bar u\|_{\underline L^2(\eta_*(U_m))}
 \leq C\|\bar u\|_{\underline L^2(U_m)}R^{-1}L_m,\] where \(L_m=1\) for \(d\geq3\) and \(L_m=\sqrt m\) for \(d=2\). No averaging of the forcing or frequency restriction is stated.

Fix any nontrivial realization with an interior vertex \(x_0\) and invertible Dirichlet matrix \(A_g=-\mathcal L\). Choose a smooth cutoff \(\chi\) supported in the unit ball and equal to one near its center. For \(\rho\) smaller than the distance from \(x_0\) to the other sampled points and to the boundary, put \[\bar u_\rho(x)=
 -\frac{|x-x_0|^2}{2\,\operatorname{tr}\bar a}\,
 \chi\!\left(\frac{x-x_0}{\rho}\right).\] This function is smooth and compactly supported in \(U_m\). At every sampled point its value is zero. Its sampled forcing is one at \(x_0\) and zero everywhere else. Hence \[u_\rho=A_g^{-1}e_{x_0}\ne0\] is independent of \(\rho\), and the left side of the claimed estimate is a fixed positive number. By contrast, \[\|\bar u_\rho\|_{\underline L^2(U_m)}
 =O(\rho^{2+d/2})\longrightarrow0.\] This contradicts (1.4) for every finite \(C\), even at one fixed allowed scale.

The witness uses smooth data, so the objection is stronger than the lack of a canonical point evaluation for a general Sobolev equivalence class. Choosing it after fixing the graph is legitimate for the stated event that is uniform over every \(\bar u\). The restated input is used in (2.15), p. 12.

The cited companion result [AV23b] was not independently retrieved and is not being refuted here. A repair requires the actual sampling or coarse-graining operator, the correct data norm and regularity, and verification that the corrected estimate applies to the trial functions used below. A change of norm label alone is not a verified repair.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: Smooth quadratic cutoff at an isolated interior sample gives zero sampled values, forcing e_x0, fixed nonzero graph solution, while continuum norm tends0 asrho^(2+d/2).
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Uses intended boundary convention and smooth functions; no reliance on Sobolev representative ambiguity; external cited theorem not assessed.

problems.title: Cluster iid premise and fixed-to-uniform variational concentration do not justify spectral comparison.
claim: Cluster iid premise and fixed-to-uniform variational concentration do not justify spectral comparison.
analysis: On p. 20, the proof of Lemma A.2 calls the variables indexed by the selected connected component independent and identically distributed, and applies (A.3). This is not the conditional uniform sample formed by all Poisson points. Connectivity-based selection introduces dependence. For example, a selected two-vertex connected component must have its two vertices within unit distance, whereas two independent uniform points in a domain of diameter greater than one need not.

Moreover, the displayed variance-only exponential bound is not the general Bernstein inequality for bounded variables: a range-dependent term, or a justified restriction to its quadratic regime, is needed. Lemma A.3 on p. 21 refers back to the same argument. Thus the stated proofs do not supply the cluster concentration estimates they use.

There is a separate pathwise obstruction to (2.12)–(2.13), pp. 10–11. Those formulas retain a maximum over continuous, continuum-normalized functions with upper bounds on their supremum and gradient energy. The passage from a fixed-function probability estimate to that maximum requires simultaneous control that is false on the stated class.

Take an allowed dimension \(d\geq3\) and a finite realized point set. Choose smooth cutoffs equal to zero at each point and one outside disjoint balls of radius \(\rho\). Their product \(h_\rho\) satisfies \[h_\rho\to1\ \hbox{in }L^2(U_m),\qquad
 \|h_\rho\|_\infty\leq1,\qquad
 \frac{1}{|U_m|}\int_{U_m}|\nabla h_\rho|^2=O(N\rho^{d-2})\to0.\] Normalize \(f_\rho=h_\rho/\|h_\rho\|_{\underline L^2(U_m)}\). Then its continuum normalized \(L^2\) norm is one, its supremum tends to one, and its energy tends to zero, while its empirical squared norm is zero. These are admissible competitors whenever the stated supremum cap has slack above one, as occurs for allowed domains with sufficiently large \(\lambda_{0,1}\), or in the class \(\mathcal A_T\) for sufficiently large \(T\). The competitors are not required to have zero boundary trace. Taking a small positive value at the sample points instead of zero gives nonzero denominators arbitrarily close to zero.

This refutes the required uniform empirical normalization, including under the energy restriction (2.8). It does not refute every possible fixed-function concentration theorem. Restricting one comparison to a deterministic ground state might avoid one maximum, but does not establish the opposite comparison over graph-dependent trial functions.

On p. 13 the proof maximizes over \(T\) although the displayed failure probability depends on \(T^{-2}\) in its exponent. A bound with a \(T\)-independent numerical right side does not itself hold on one uniform event. The subsequent choice of \(T\) uses an eigenvector supremum estimate whose derivation already invokes the conditional eigenvalue bound.

The orthogonality transfer (2.33)–(2.34), p. 18, is explicitly granted and is not subsequently established before the proof ends. In (2.36), the extra \(R^{-2}\) in the supremum bound even makes the continuum-normalized class empty for fixed \(K\) and large \(m\); this factor must at least be corrected. These are further missing closure steps, rather than additional claimed counterexamples to the final eigenvalue rate.

A complete repair needs controlled comparison maps or finite-dimensional trial spaces, valid concentration for the selected cluster, and simultaneous estimates with the advertised dependence on \(m\), \(k\), and \(T\). The review does not supply that replacement proof.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: Selected connected component is dependent; constant-based smooth cutoffs in d>=3 retain continuum norm1, supcap and arbitrarily small energy while empirical norm is0 or arbitrarily small.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: A valid fixed-function theorem is not refuted; deterministic finite test-space or operator methods may repair. T-dependent event and deferred induction are not supplied.

paragraphs: Actual-cluster concentration, controlled approximation space/maps, simultaneous events and noncircular T/induction closure.

report: Abstract: The joint Young–Jucys–Murphy spectrum identifies irreducible constituents and their multiplicities. However, the reversed Kronecker factors in the printed column-vectorized system invalidate Theorem 2 and the decomposition procedure that directly uses it. An exact canonical repeated-\(S_3\) example establishes this central failure, supporting Major severity. Correcting the ordering restores the intended intertwiner construction without changing its polynomial real-arithmetic costs. The retained implementation already uses the correct ordering, so software failure is not established. The application-complexity discussion and proposed validation sketch also require the two local Minor corrections described below.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical review of
Representations of the Symmetric Group are Decomposable in Polynomial Time
# Source, scope, and mathematical setting

The reviewed source is Sheehan Olver, Representations of the Symmetric Group are Decomposable in Polynomial Time, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 1069–1092, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09697-8 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09697-8). This is the acquired publisher version of record, published online on 10 February 2025, with 24 PDF pages. Page references below are printed journal pages. The retained arXiv copy is not substituted for this source.

The input consists of symmetric orthogonal matrices \(A_i=\rho(\tau_i)\), where \(\tau_i=(i,i+1)\) and \(\rho:S_n\to O(d)\) is a representation. The task is to identify partitions \(\lambda\), compute multiplicities \(a_\lambda\), and find an orthogonal change of basis to repeated copies of the canonical Young orthogonal representations.

The article explicitly assumes real arithmetic on p. 1070. Its proved bounds are \(O(n^2d^3)\) for identifying constituents and multiplicities and a further \(O(nd^4)\) for decoupling repeated copies. The complete stated procedure therefore has bound \[O(n^2d^3+nd^4).\] The practical \(O(nd^3)\) behavior and floating-point accuracy are separately discussed as observations or possible improvements. These claims are not interpreted as bit-complexity bounds or as an already certified floating-point implementation. Nor does polynomial dependence on the supplied matrix dimension establish polynomial complexity in a compact partition encoding of the general Kronecker-coefficient problem.
# P1. The printed intertwiner system invalidates the stated decomposition algorithm (Major)
## A concrete error in Theorem 2

Theorem 2, equation (4), p. 1083, explicitly defines \(\operatorname{vec}\) by concatenating columns, but uses blocks \[K_i=A_i\otimes I_l-I_{al}\otimes B_i,
 \qquad A_i\in\mathbb R^{al\times al},\quad B_i=\rho_\lambda(\tau_i)\in\mathbb R^{l\times l}.\] For an intertwiner \(X\in\mathbb R^{al\times l}\) the correct column-vectorization identity is \[\operatorname{vec}(A_iX-XB_i)
   =\bigl(I_l\otimes A_i-B_i^{\mathsf T}\otimes I_{al}\bigr)\operatorname{vec}X.
 \tag{1}\] Here \(B_i^{\mathsf T}=B_i\), but this does not permit exchanging the Kronecker factors while retaining the same reshape convention. The printed matrix instead corresponds to a row-vectorization ordering.

The discrepancy affects even the canonical repeated-copy setting of Lemma 4 and Corollary 4. Take the two-dimensional \(S_3\) representation \[B_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 B_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1/2&\sqrt3/2\\ \sqrt3/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}.\] Let \(P\) exchange coordinates 1 and 3 in \(\mathbb R^4\) and set \(A_i=P(I_2\otimes B_i)P^{\mathsf T}\). These matrices satisfy the orthogonality and Coxeter relations. Their YJM generators are already diagonal, since the exchanged coordinates have the same joint content. Moreover, \(P\) has diagonal \(2\times2\) blocks, as required by the canonical setting.

For the stacked printed matrix, an orthonormal nullspace basis is \[u_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}(0,0,0,1,1,0,0,0)^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad
 u_2=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,0,0,0,0,0,0,1)^{\mathsf T}.\] The prescribed column reshaping of \(\sqrt2\,u_1,\sqrt2\,u_2\) produces \(X_1=[e_4,e_1]\) and \(X_2=[e_1,e_4]\). Thus \([X_1,X_2]\) has rank two rather than four and cannot be orthogonal. This is not fixed by choosing another nullspace basis: every resulting column remains in \(\operatorname{span}\{e_1,e_4\}\).

The intended diagonal-block restriction retains column-vector positions \(\{1,3,6,8\}\). Applied to the printed system, it leaves nullity one instead of the required two. The corrected system (1) has nullity two before and after this restriction, and recovers a full orthogonal intertwiner. These assertions were checked by reviewer-authored exact arithmetic in \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)\); no floating-point tolerance is involved.
## Repair and counterevidence

Replace every block of (4) by (1), and retain column concatenation throughout Corollary 4 and Algorithm 2. Equivalently, a consistent row-vectorization convention with the corresponding support permutation would work. The correction does not change the dimensions or the complexity of the reduced nullspace problem.

Static inspection of the acquired `NumericalRepresentationTheory.jl` v0.3.0 source at commit `b129d05abb7f44bd06e4e299495bb88a7c838b9b` finds the column-vectorized ordering \(I\otimes A_i-B_i\otimes I\). This is material counterevidence to an implementation-failure interpretation. The package was not executed, and the retained source alone is not a complete runtime verification. Theorem 2 asserts that the printed nullspace system and prescribed reshaping produce an orthogonal intertwiner. Corollary 4 uses that system for its support restriction, Corollary 5 derives the decomposition cost, and Algorithm 2, steps 3–4, explicitly solves (4) and reshapes its vectors. The counterexample therefore invalidates a core theorem-to-algorithm dependency, not merely an unused display. This supports Major severity for the written decomposition procedure. The fixed ordering repair and the correct retained implementation preserve the intended construction and its costs, but do not validate the original formula. The nearby indexing slips remain local Minor defects.

Several nearby notation errors should be repaired with this correction. Definition 6, p. 1081, needs \[(\operatorname{Spec}\rho)_{kj}
   =(\widetilde Q^{\mathsf T}\rho(X_j)\widetilde Q)_{kk},\] rather than an entry of the unconjugated matrix. Proposition 3 must use \(X_j=\sum_{i<j}(i\,j)\); its transposition word and displayed sum have shifted indices. In Algorithm 3, p. 1085, the initialization must be \(a_{j-1,j}=b_{j-1,j}=\rho(\tau_{j-1})\), matching the later recursion and returned \(b_{1,j}\). The printed reversed subscripts do not initialize that quantity even at \(n=2\). Lemma 3’s upper endpoint is \(j-1\), as its subsequent enumeration already makes clear. These are local consistency repairs, not additional independent failures of the representation-theoretic argument.
# P2. Application complexity needs a restricted statement (Minor)

On p. 1086, the article describes the dimension growth of a general hook \(\lambda=(m+1,1^{n-m-1})\) as only quadratic. In fact, \[d_\lambda=\binom{n-1}{m}.\] This follows directly by choosing which \(m\) of the entries \(2,\ldots,n\) occupy the rest of the first row of a standard hook tableau. For fixed \(m\) the degree is \(m\), and for central \(m\) the dimension is exponential up to a polynomial factor. For example, \(m\approx(n-1)/2\) cannot be included in a quadratic-growth claim.

The specific families used for Fig. 3 have the dimensions stated in the paper: \[d_{(n-1,1)}=d_{(2,1^{n-2})}=n-1,\qquad
 d_{(n-2,1,1)}=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}2,\quad
 d_{(2,2,1^{n-4})}=\frac{n(n-3)}2.\] Consequently their tensor-product dimensions are \(D_1=(n-1)^2\) and \(D_2=n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)/4\). These examples do have polynomial dimension in \(n\).

A second distinction concerns the exponents. Substitution in the proved multiplicity bound of Corollary 3 gives \(O(n^8)\) and \(O(n^{14})\). The \(O(n^7)\) and \(O(n^{13})\) rates described as worst-case bounds on p. 1086 instead correspond to the improved or practical \(O(nD^3)\) model discussed after Corollary 3. That model should be identified explicitly, or the conservative proved exponents should be quoted. The figures do not by themselves prove a worst-case operation count. This observation does not exclude a sharper algorithm; it corrects the attribution of the displayed bounds.
# P3. The proposed validation sketch has a matrix-identity error (Minor)

The article explicitly calls the practical implementation nonrigorous and proposes validation as future work. Correcting these identities does not itself certify joint eigenvector matching, multiplicities, or every floating-point result; the separate common-eigenvector argument also needs its hypotheses and bounds. The issue concerns the algebra of the sketch, not a demonstrated failure of an existing certified implementation.
# Checks supporting the principal construction

The Young orthogonal generators have symmetric \(2\times2\) blocks with diagonal entries \(1/r,-1/r\) and off-diagonal entry \(\sqrt{1-1/r^2}\). Their joint YJM eigenvalues are integer contents. A content sequence determines the chain of Young diagrams, hence the standard tableau and its partition. Repeated joint eigenvectors therefore count copies of one tableau, while the total number of rows with a given partition is \(a_\lambda d_\lambda\). This justifies the multiplicity division in Algorithm 1.

The real scalar-commutant property needed in Sections 4 and 6 is valid for these \(S_n\) representations. The simple joint YJM spectrum makes a commuting matrix diagonal in the tableau basis. Allowed adjacent tableau swaps connect that basis, and their nonzero off-diagonal generator entries force all diagonal entries to agree. Thus the commutant is \(\mathbb RI\). A generic real finite-group Schur statement would require additional care, but it does not create an obstruction in this setting.

For a full-column-rank intertwiner \(C\), orthogonality gives \(C^{\mathsf T}C=cI\) with \(c>0\). Normalization and the positive definite Gram matrix on the multiplicity space justify the orthogonal isotypic decomposition in Theorem 1. After correction of (4), orthonormal nullspace vectors give intertwiners \(X_i\) satisfying \[X_i^{\mathsf T}X_j=\delta_{ij}I\] after the factor \(\sqrt{d_\lambda}\) is restored. This follows because the cross Gram matrices are scalar and their traces are the vectorized inner products.

The reduced system has \(O(na_\lambda d_\lambda^2)\) rows and \(a_\lambda d_\lambda\) columns. Dense nullspace computation therefore costs \(O(na_\lambda^3d_\lambda^4)\). Since \(a_\lambda^3d_\lambda^4\leq(a_\lambda d_\lambda)^4\) and \(\sum_\lambda a_\lambda d_\lambda=d\), summation gives \(O(nd^4)\). The preliminary unreduced cost quoted in the proof does not follow from its displayed dense matrix dimensions; the reduced bound, which is the relevant conclusion, does.

Reviewer-authored exact symbolic calculations also verify the published \(6\times6\) example on p. 1071: the displayed \(Q\) is orthogonal, the generators satisfy the Coxeter relations, and the YJM contents recover the sign representation once, shape \((3,1)\) once, and the trivial representation twice. An auxiliary exact \(S_6\) character calculation reproduces the multiplicities in Fig. 1 and the total dimensions \(80\) and \(400\). These finite checks support the formulas and examples; they are not claimed as a proof of all inputs or as a run of the author’s software.

The homogeneous-polynomial example has dimension \(\binom{n+p-1}{p}\) and a permutation action on degree-\(p\) monomials. Conjugating this representation by the decomposition matrix gives the stated symmetry-adapted basis. The plotted timings and entrywise residuals are consistent with the limited empirical interpretation given to them; no new timing or stability experiment was performed.
# Supporting checks

The assessment is Major revision: repair the central vectorization system used by Theorem 2 and Algorithm 2, together with the local indexing, application-complexity and validation statements. The Major finding concerns the original written theorem and algorithm. The corrected real-arithmetic construction and the retained implementation’s ordering are preserved as counterevidence to broader failure claims. The formal full-decomposition bound includes both algorithmic stages; practical cubic behavior and rigorous floating-point validation remain separate questions.

The original review records full-source reading, exact calculations, static implementation inspection and actual source-page inspections. Those facts retain their original attribution in the accompanying verification files. This focused independent acceptance checks the existing Problems, their source assumptions, counterevidence and severity; it does not claim another whole-paper review. Imported external references were not newly retrieved or exhaustively audited. No author code was executed, no timings were reproduced, and no complete numerical certification was inferred from the residual plots.

At the original review, no substantive earlier report was recoverable in the bounded preserved inventory. The acquired source, manifest, repository and extraction bytes were reused with their recorded origins. problems.title: Printed Kronecker factor order is inconsistent with declared column concatenation and fails its prescribed canonical decomposition.
problems.source_location: PDF12-17;printed1080-1085;Definition6,Theorem2(4),Cor4,Algorithms2-3
claim: The input consists of symmetric orthogonal matrices \(A_i=\rho(\tau_i)\), where \(\tau_i=(i,i+1)\) and \(\rho:S_n\to O(d)\) is a representation. The task is to identify partitions \(\lambda\), compute multiplicities \(a_\lambda\), and find an orthogonal change of basis to repeated copies of the canonical Young orthogonal representations.

The article explicitly assumes real arithmetic on p. 1070. Its proved bounds are \(O(n^2d^3)\) for identifying constituents and multiplicities and a further \(O(nd^4)\) for decoupling repeated copies. The complete stated procedure therefore has bound \[O(n^2d^3+nd^4).\] The practical \(O(nd^3)\) behavior and floating-point accuracy are separately discussed as observations or possible improvements. These claims are not interpreted as bit-complexity bounds or as an already certified floating-point implementation. Nor does polynomial dependence on the supplied matrix dimension establish polynomial complexity in a compact partition encoding of the general Kronecker-coefficient problem.
Printed Kronecker factor order is inconsistent with declared column concatenation and fails its prescribed canonical decomposition.
analysis:
Theorem 2, equation (4), p. 1083, explicitly defines \(\operatorname{vec}\) by concatenating columns, but uses blocks \[K_i=A_i\otimes I_l-I_{al}\otimes B_i,
 \qquad A_i\in\mathbb R^{al\times al},\quad B_i=\rho_\lambda(\tau_i)\in\mathbb R^{l\times l}.\] For an intertwiner \(X\in\mathbb R^{al\times l}\) the correct column-vectorization identity is \[\operatorname{vec}(A_iX-XB_i)
   =\bigl(I_l\otimes A_i-B_i^{\mathsf T}\otimes I_{al}\bigr)\operatorname{vec}X.
 \tag{1}\] Here \(B_i^{\mathsf T}=B_i\), but this does not permit exchanging the Kronecker factors while retaining the same reshape convention. The printed matrix instead corresponds to a row-vectorization ordering.

The discrepancy affects even the canonical repeated-copy setting of Lemma 4 and Corollary 4. Take the two-dimensional \(S_3\) representation \[B_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 B_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1/2&\sqrt3/2\\ \sqrt3/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}.\] Let \(P\) exchange coordinates 1 and 3 in \(\mathbb R^4\) and set \(A_i=P(I_2\otimes B_i)P^{\mathsf T}\). These matrices satisfy the orthogonality and Coxeter relations. Their YJM generators are already diagonal, since the exchanged coordinates have the same joint content. Moreover, \(P\) has diagonal \(2\times2\) blocks, as required by the canonical setting.

For the stacked printed matrix, an orthonormal nullspace basis is \[u_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}(0,0,0,1,1,0,0,0)^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad
 u_2=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,0,0,0,0,0,0,1)^{\mathsf T}.\] The prescribed column reshaping of \(\sqrt2\,u_1,\sqrt2\,u_2\) produces \(X_1=[e_4,e_1]\) and \(X_2=[e_1,e_4]\). Thus \([X_1,X_2]\) has rank two rather than four and cannot be orthogonal. This is not fixed by choosing another nullspace basis: every resulting column remains in \(\operatorname{span}\{e_1,e_4\}\).

The intended diagonal-block restriction retains column-vector positions \(\{1,3,6,8\}\). Applied to the printed system, it leaves nullity one instead of the required two. The corrected system (1) has nullity two before and after this restriction, and recovers a full orthogonal intertwiner. These assertions were checked by reviewer-authored exact arithmetic in \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)\); no floating-point tolerance is involved.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: Exact repeated-S3 canonical case has printed fullnullity2 but reshapedrank2 and intendedrestrictednullity1; corrected matrix has bothnullities2 and orthogonalrank4 reconstruction.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Static retainedv0.3.0 source uses corrected order. No software failure asserted. Fixed permutation/order repair preserves main proof and costs.

General hooks need not have quadratic dimension; displayed n7/n13 rates do not follow directly from proved Cor3.
analysis: On p. 1086, the article describes the dimension growth of a general hook \(\lambda=(m+1,1^{n-m-1})\) as only quadratic. In fact, \[d_\lambda=\binom{n-1}{m}.\] This follows directly by choosing which \(m\) of the entries \(2,\ldots,n\) occupy the rest of the first row of a standard hook tableau. For fixed \(m\) the degree is \(m\), and for central \(m\) the dimension is exponential up to a polynomial factor. For example, \(m\approx(n-1)/2\) cannot be included in a quadratic-growth claim.

The specific families used for Fig. 3 have the dimensions stated in the paper: \[d_{(n-1,1)}=d_{(2,1^{n-2})}=n-1,\qquad
 d_{(n-2,1,1)}=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}2,\quad
 d_{(2,2,1^{n-4})}=\frac{n(n-3)}2.\] Consequently their tensor-product dimensions are \(D_1=(n-1)^2\) and \(D_2=n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)/4\). These examples do have polynomial dimension in \(n\).

A second distinction concerns the exponents. Substitution in the proved multiplicity bound of Corollary 3 gives \(O(n^8)\) and \(O(n^{14})\). The \(O(n^7)\) and \(O(n^{13})\) rates described as worst-case bounds on p. 1086 instead correspond to the improved or practical \(O(nD^3)\) model discussed after Corollary 3. That model should be identified explicitly, or the conservative proved exponents should be quoted. The figures do not by themselves prove a worst-case operation count. This observation does not exclude a sharper algorithm; it corrects the attribution of the displayed bounds.

report: Abstract: The acquired article combines an exposition of two Euler-flow constructions with a new obstruction to critical compatible metrics. Its reachability definition permits computational difficulty to be placed in an input-dependent computable open target, and the oracle argument in Remark 4.4 does not remove that difficulty. This is a Major definitional and logical issue, without refuting the stronger step-by-step simulations actually used in the constructions. The critical-metric argument has a local geometric repair. A suspension construction answers the stated Hodge-viscosity version of Open problem 4 when the compact manifold and metric may be chosen freely. Several local formula and coordinate corrections are also identified.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical review of
Towards a Fluid Computer
# Source and review scope

The source is Robert Cardona, Eva Miranda, and Daniel Peralta-Salas, Towards a Fluid Computer, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 25 (2025), 1921–1937, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09699-6 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09699-6). The acquired publisher version of record was published online on 13 March 2025 and has 17 PDF pages. References to pages below use the printed pagination.

Although much of the article is expository, Proposition 4.3 is presented as a new consequence, and the paper remains within the assigned research-review scope. The constructions imported from the article’s references [7] and [8] are distinguished from arguments supplied here. Their complete external proofs, and the classification results cited as [2] and [18], were not independently retrieved. Missing details explicitly assigned to those works are not by themselves treated as defects.
# P1. The computable-target definition does not isolate computation by the dynamics (Major)

Definition 2.2, p. 1924, permits a computable point \(p_c\) and a computable open set \(U_c\) depending on the input \(c\), with halting equivalent to the positive orbit meeting \(U_c\). The surrounding paragraph describes computability of an open set through arbitrary-precision approximation, without restricting its geometric presentation. Under the usual computable-real endpoint or effective-open interpretation, even the identity map meets this definition.

Fix the universal machine in the definition. Number its steps from one, and put \[r_c=
 \begin{cases}
  2^{-t},&\textstyle\text{if the machine first halts on }c\text{ at step }t,\\
  0,&\textstyle\text{if it never halts}.
 \end{cases}\] The real number \(r_c\) is uniformly computable. To approximate it with error at most \(2^{-N}\), simulate \(N\) steps. If halting occurs, return \(2^{-t}\); otherwise return zero. A later halting time produces an error at most \(2^{-(N+1)}\). This approximation procedure does not decide whether \(r_c\) is zero.

In the unit disk take the identity map, the fixed rational point \(p_c=(0,0)\), and the nonempty open rectangle \[U_c=(-r_c,1/4)\times(-1/4,1/4).\] Since \(0\leq r_c\leq1/2\), this rectangle lies in the disk. It has uniformly computable endpoints and is uniformly effectively open; its endpoint description can be approximated to every prescribed accuracy. Nevertheless, \[\{\operatorname{Id}^n(p_c):n>0\}\cap U_c\ne\varnothing
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r_c>0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T_U(c)\text{ halts}.\] The orbit does nothing. All undecidability is carried by a boundary-membership question for the target.

The same problem occurs directly in the contact setting. Let \(R=\partial_{\phi_1}+\partial_{\phi_2}\) be the standard Hopf field on the round \(S^3\), take the rational point \((z_1,z_2)=(3/5,4/5)\), and set \[U_c=\{\,|z_1|^2>9/25-r_c\,\}.\] The quantity \(|z_1|^2\) is constant on the orbit, so reachability is again equivalent to \(r_c>0\). The Hopf field is Killing for the standard compatible metric, and therefore its Chern–Hamilton energy is zero. Thus the weak target-based definition cannot support a general exclusion of these flows.

Remark 4.4, p. 1930, assumes an oracle deciding whether two computable sets intersect, then asserts that the relevant halting problem remains undecidable. Applied to \(\{p_c\}\) and \(U_c\), that oracle already decides ordinary halting in the example above. Undecidability of halting relative to the stronger oracle is a different assertion; no simulation of all oracle machines by the fixed constructed system is supplied. The oracle comparison consequently does not establish the claimed exclusion.

This finding does not refute the actual injective, configuration-by-configuration simulations described in Sections 4 and 5. Those have substantially more structure than Definition 2.2. A repair should specify a uniform effective simulation and a restricted decoding or geometric target representation, and verify that the constructions satisfy it. Merely assuming a set-intersection oracle, or merely making an otherwise unrestricted effective-open target independent of the input, does not resolve the issue. If a stronger finite target representation was intended, it must be stated; the displayed counterexample addresses the finite-precision meaning explicitly suggested in the article.
# P2. Proposition 4.3 needs a section-independent argument (Minor)

The proof on pp. 1929–1930 uses the cited classifications to obtain orbital conjugacy to \[R_{l,k}=l\partial_{\phi_1}+k\partial_{\phi_2},\qquad l,k>0.\] On the standard section \(\{\phi_1=0\}\), its return angle is correctly given by \(2\pi k/l\). The proof then infers that this angle vanishes modulo \(2\pi\) because the constructed return map on a transverse disk is the identity near its boundary. Those need not be the same section.

For example, \(R_{2,1}\) has return rotation by \(\pi\) on \(\{\phi_1=0\}\), whereas its return map on \(\{\phi_2=0\}\) is the identity: a return takes time \(2\pi\) and advances \(\phi_1\) by \(4\pi\). Thus the existence of one identity return map does not determine the rotation number of the other.

The conclusion for the selected universal construction can be repaired as follows. The identity collar of its disk return map suspends to an open region of periodic flow orbits. An irrational weighted Hopf flow has only two exceptional closed circles, so orbital conjugacy forces \(l/k\) to be rational. Every orbit of the weighted Hopf flow is then closed, and the same is true for the orbitally conjugate field.

On the other hand, a universal reversible machine has an initial nonhalting run with no repeated configuration. Otherwise, simulation until either halting or a repeated finite configuration would decide halting on every initial input. The injective Cantor encoding and step-by-step conjugacy therefore give an aperiodic return orbit. A closed flow orbit cannot supply this aperiodic orbit of the constructed transverse return map. This is the required contradiction.

This repair uses the actual simulation and the periodic collar, without the weak reachability definition or Remark 4.4. It is conditional on the two quoted classification results, which remain imported dependencies. Proposition 4.3 should explicitly refer to the selected universal construction of Corollary 4.2; Theorem 4.1 also realizes arbitrary disk maps, including the identity, so its full class of Reeb fields cannot satisfy that exclusion. The claim concerns critical compatible metrics, not every metric for which an arbitrary field happens to be Beltrami.
# P3. The stated Hodge-viscosity open problem has an affirmative suspension construction (Minor)

Open problem 4, p. 1935, asks for a Turing-complete steady Navier–Stokes flow on some compact Riemannian three-manifold. Remark 6.1 specifies the Hodge Laplacian as the viscous operator. With this freedom in the manifold and metric, the area-preserving simulation already used in the article supplies such a flow.

Let \(\varphi\) be the simulated area-preserving disk diffeomorphism from Proposition 4.1, equal to the identity in a boundary collar. Extend it by the identity to a closed oriented surface \(\Sigma=S^2\) with area form \(\omega\) agreeing with the disk area. Form the mapping torus \[M=(\Sigma\times[0,1])/\bigl((x,1)\sim(\varphi(x),0)\bigr).\] The vector field \(X=\partial_t\), the one-form \(\alpha=dt\), and the volume form \(\mu=dt\wedge\omega\) descend smoothly, because \(\varphi\) preserves \(\omega\).

Here is an explicit compatible metric construction. Choose a surface metric \(h_0\) with area form \(\omega\), and choose a smooth function \(\beta:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) that is zero near \(t=0\) and one near \(t=1\). Put \[k_t=(1-\beta(t))h_0+\beta(t)\varphi^*h_0,\qquad
 \operatorname{vol}_{k_t}=f_t\omega,\qquad h_t=f_t^{-1}k_t.\] The convex combination is positive definite. Since the surface has dimension two, \(\operatorname{vol}_{h_t}=\omega\). Also \(h_1=\varphi^*h_0\), and the family is constant near its endpoints. Consequently \[g=dt^2+h_t\] descends to a smooth metric on the closed compact mapping torus.

For this metric, \[X^\flat=\alpha,\quad |X|_g=1,\quad
 \operatorname{vol}_g=\mu,\quad
 \operatorname{div}_g X=0,\quad
 d\alpha=0,\quad \delta_g\alpha=0.\] Thus \(\Delta_H\alpha=0\), and the covariant identity \[(\nabla_X X)^\flat=\iota_Xd\alpha+\tfrac12d|X|^2\] gives \(\nabla_X X=0\). Constant pressure and \(X\) solve the unforced steady Navier–Stokes equations for every viscosity, since the Hodge viscous term vanishes. Its sign convention is immaterial here. The kinetic energy is \(\operatorname{Vol}_g(M)/2\), hence finite.

The section \(t=1/2\) has return map \(\varphi\). A computable initial point on that section and a halting target lifted to a fixed product strip, for example \(3/4<t<7/8\), reproduce the discrete orbit’s target visits. This transfers the actual step-by-step simulation, not merely the weak boundary-encoding device of P1.

The construction answers the precise arbitrary-metric, Hodge-viscosity formulation stated in the paper. It does not produce a solution for a prescribed round or flat metric, prove robustness under perturbations, or apply automatically to a different geometric viscous operator. Those restrictions could lead to a substantive revised question. The observation is classified as a bounded correction to the open-problem formulation, not a failure of the principal Euler constructions.
# P4. Local Euler and encoding formulas need correction (Minor)

On p. 1925 the Bernoulli function is printed as \(B=p+\|X\|/2\). The correct formula is \[B=p+\tfrac12|X|^2.\] Indeed \((\nabla_X X)^\flat=\iota_Xd(X^\flat)+\tfrac12d|X|^2\). An exact symbolic check with \(X=(-y,x,0)\) and \(p=(x^2+y^2)/2\) verifies stationary incompressible Euler. At \((1,0,0)\), the components of \(\iota_Xd(X^\flat)\) are \((-2,0,0)\), whereas \(-d(p+|X|/2)\) gives \((-3/2,0,0)\). The squared expression agrees identically. This is a missing exponent, not an obstruction to the corrected Beltrami correspondence.

In the planar encoding, pp. 1932–1933, the one-dimensional interval should be translated by \(2j\): \(I_{(q,t)}^j=I_{(q,t)}+2j\), rather than by the displayed two-dimensional vector \((2j,2j)\). The initial point should likewise be \[p_{c_i}=(2i+\phi(c_i),0),\] to belong to the designated strip \([2i,2i+1]\times[0,\infty)\). The printed \(i+\phi(c_i)\) fails already for \(i=1\). These corrections make the encoding agree with the subsequent curves and figures.
# Positive checks and limits of the review

The finite-tape encoding in Section 4 gives rational ternary coordinates. The four affine branches in Fig. 1 are consistent with its specified \(F,G\) rules: on the indicated blocks they are \[(3x,y/3),\quad(3x-2,y/3-2/9),\quad
 (x,y+2/3),\quad(x,y+2/3).\] Each has determinant one, and the image strips and corner blocks agree with the actual figure. The bijective generalized-shift premise and reversibility are essential when extending to a disk diffeomorphism.

Cartan’s formula verifies preservation of \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha\wedge d\alpha\) by a Reeb field. A positive rescaling \(hR\) preserves \((\alpha\wedge d\alpha)/h\). Together with an adapted metric, the corrected Bernoulli identity yields stationary Euler. This explains the flexibility of the non-prescribed-metric construction; it does not yield a fixed Euclidean metric result.

Section 5 is explicitly a sketch of a different imported construction. The reciprocal prime-power encoding is injective; its intervals can be separated with radii of order the square of their centers. The stated weak robustness uses an error that decays sufficiently rapidly at infinity, and is not uniform perturbation robustness on a compact phase space. The absence of a uniform lower bound on the decoding intervals is explicitly acknowledged.

For the planar Cauchy datum \((F_x,F_y,0)\), the normal curl equation requires \(\partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x=0\), as stated. Theorem 5.2 requires extension of \(F\) to an entire function on \(\mathbb C^2\), not merely real analyticity. This distinction is retained when using the global extension. Tangency makes the plane invariant, so its simulated trajectories remain trajectories of the Beltrami field. The full entire-approximation and global Cauchy–Kovalevskaya results are cited dependencies, not newly certified external theorems. The Euclidean construction’s infinite-energy limitation is acknowledged by the article and is not reported as a hidden defect.

The assessment is Major revision because the computational definition and its exclusion argument require substantive correction. The specific fluid constructions are not shown false. Proposition 4.3 has the conditional repair above, and the additional findings are local or concern the precise scope of an open question. No claim is made to resolve the paper’s fixed-metric Euler, entropy, or celestial-mechanics questions.
# Scope and references

No substantive earlier report for M25-0449 was recoverable in the bounded preserved inventory; inaccessible conversation-only material is recorded as unavailable. The acquired source PDF, manifest, and historical extraction were reused without relabeling their execution. The current review, actual source-page views, symbolic local identity check, and report build are new. Analytic computability and geometric arguments are recorded as arguments, not as numerical simulations.

The exact source, scripts, outputs, helper roles, build inputs and retained dependencies, and actual current report-page inspections are bound in the accompanying verification files. No author code was executed, and absent optional code is not a mathematical defect. Scientific disposition remains pending; no human review or independent acceptance is recorded.

The injective Cantor encoding and step-by-step conjugacy therefore give an aperiodic return orbit. A closed flow orbit cannot supply this aperiodic orbit of the constructed transverse return map. This is the required contradiction.

This repair uses the actual simulation and the periodic collar, without the weak reachability definition or Remark 4.4. It is conditional on the two quoted classification results, which remain imported dependencies. Proposition 4.3 should explicitly refer to the selected universal construction of Corollary 4.2; Theorem 4.1 also realizes arbitrary disk maps, including the identity, so its full class of Reeb fields cannot satisfy that exclusion. The claim concerns critical compatible metrics, not every metric for which an arbitrary field happens to be Beltrami.

claim: Theprecisestatedarbitrary-metricHodge-viscosityproblemhasanaffirmativeadapted-suspensionexample.
analysis: Open problem 4, p. 1935, asks for a Turing-complete steady Navier–Stokes flow on some compact Riemannian three-manifold. Remark 6.1 specifies the Hodge Laplacian as the viscous operator. With this freedom in the manifold and metric, the area-preserving simulation already used in the article supplies such a flow.

Let \(\varphi\) be the simulated area-preserving disk diffeomorphism from Proposition 4.1, equal to the identity in a boundary collar. Extend it by the identity to a closed oriented surface \(\Sigma=S^2\) with area form \(\omega\) agreeing with the disk area. Form the mapping torus \[M=(\Sigma\times[0,1])/\bigl((x,1)\sim(\varphi(x),0)\bigr).\] The vector field \(X=\partial_t\), the one-form \(\alpha=dt\), and the volume form \(\mu=dt\wedge\omega\) descend smoothly, because \(\varphi\) preserves \(\omega\).

Here is an explicit compatible metric construction. Choose a surface metric \(h_0\) with area form \(\omega\), and choose a smooth function \(\beta:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) that is zero near \(t=0\) and one near \(t=1\). Put \[k_t=(1-\beta(t))h_0+\beta(t)\varphi^*h_0,\qquad
 \operatorname{vol}_{k_t}=f_t\omega,\qquad h_t=f_t^{-1}k_t.\] The convex combination is positive definite. Since the surface has dimension two, \(\operatorname{vol}_{h_t}=\omega\). Also \(h_1=\varphi^*h_0\), and the family is constant near its endpoints. Consequently \[g=dt^2+h_t\] descends to a smooth metric on the closed compact mapping torus.

For this metric, \[X^\flat=\alpha,\quad |X|_g=1,\quad
 \operatorname{vol}_g=\mu,\quad
 \operatorname{div}_g X=0,\quad
 d\alpha=0,\quad \delta_g\alpha=0.\] Thus \(\Delta_H\alpha=0\), and the covariant identity \[(\nabla_X X)^\flat=\iota_Xd\alpha+\tfrac12d|X|^2\] gives \(\nabla_X X=0\). Constant pressure and \(X\) solve the unforced steady Navier–Stokes equations for every viscosity, since the Hodge viscous term vanishes. Its sign convention is immaterial here. The kinetic energy is \(\operatorname{Vol}_g(M)/2\), hence finite.

The section \(t=1/2\) has return map \(\varphi\). A computable initial point on that section and a halting target lifted to a fixed product strip, for example \(3/4<t<7/8\), reproduce the discrete orbit’s target visits. This transfers the actual step-by-step simulation, not merely the weak boundary-encoding device of P1.

The construction answers the precise arbitrary-metric, Hodge-viscosity formulation stated in the paper. It does not produce a solution for a prescribed round or flat metric, prove robustness under perturbations, or apply automatically to a different geometric viscous operator. Those restrictions could lead to a substantive revised question. The observation is classified as a bounded correction to the open-problem formulation, not a failure of the principal Euler constructions.
