report: Abstract: The paper constructs local commuting bubbles that preserve the polynomial differential-form spaces individually. The stated shape-regularity-only stability estimate fails in dimension one for the actual averaging operator: a continuous piecewise quadratic on a two-interval mesh gives an unbounded norm ratio while the shape constant stays equal to one. This is a Major qualification of the uniform-stability claim. A boundary-link gauge requires a local convention correction, and several displayed formulas need minor corrections. The algebraic decomposition and the principal support and commutation mechanisms withstand the checks described below. A highest-degree cancellation also verifies the potentially delicate trimmed-space preservation step, conditional on correctly defined weights.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical review of
Local Space-Preserving Decompositions
for the Bubble Transform
# Source and scope

The source is Richard Falk and Ragnar Winther, Local Space-Preserving Decompositions for the Bubble Transform, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 1219–1267, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09700-2 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09700-2). The acquired publisher version of record was published online on 17 March 2025 and has 49 PDF pages. Printed pages are used below; subtract 1218 to obtain the one-based PDF page.

The review covers the assumptions, local chain and weight constructions, order-reduction operators, decomposition identity, polynomial preservation, and stability argument. Section 2.1 assumes a bounded polyhedral Lipschitz domain in \(\mathbb R^n\) and a conforming simplicial mesh; it does not restrict \(n\) to be at least two. Theorem 2.3 and Section 9 retain the all-dimension scope. The claims about the earlier bubble transform and the external averaging estimate from the paper’s reference [7] are distinguished from calculations independently checked here. The complete external papers were not acquired or reread.
# P1. Uniform stability needs a dimension or local-size hypothesis (Major)

Proposition 8.1, p. 1260, asserts that the norms of \(W^k\) and the squared sum of bubble norms are bounded by a constant depending on the mesh only through \[c_{\mathcal T}=\max_{T\in\Delta_n(\mathcal T)}
\frac{\operatorname{diam}(T)}{\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb B_T)},\] with an additional dependence on the fixed dimension. Lemma 8.2, p. 1261, derives local diameter comparability from this constant. This implication fails in dimension one, and the failure propagates to the operator actually constructed.

Fix \(\Omega=(0,1)\) and the mesh \[T_0=[0,\varepsilon],\qquad T_1=[\varepsilon,1],
\qquad 0<\varepsilon<\tfrac12.\] Every interval is its own largest one-dimensional ball up to endpoints, so \(c_{\mathcal T}=1\). Equations (2.12)–(2.13), pp. 1231–1232, give normalized cell densities \(z_T=|T|^{-1}\mathrm dx\) and their arithmetic average at a vertex. In particular, \[z_0=\varepsilon^{-1}\chi_{T_0}\mathrm dx,\quad
z_\varepsilon=\tfrac12\bigl(\varepsilon^{-1}\chi_{T_0}
 +(1-\varepsilon)^{-1}\chi_{T_1}\bigr)\mathrm dx,\quad
z_1=(1-\varepsilon)^{-1}\chi_{T_1}\mathrm dx .\] These are not volume-weighted averages over the vertex patch. The sign convention \(z_{v,\emptyset}=-z_v\) on p. 1233 and the definition following (2.23), p. 1235, therefore yield \[W^0u=\sum_{v\in\{0,\varepsilon,1\}}\lambda_v\int_\Omega u\,z_v .\]

Take \[u_\varepsilon(x)=
\begin{cases}
6(x/\varepsilon)(1-x/\varepsilon),&0\le x\le\varepsilon,\\
0,&\varepsilon\le x\le1.
\end{cases}\] This is a continuous piecewise quadratic with single-valued traces, and it vanishes at both physical endpoints. It belongs to the stated domain and to \(\mathcal P_2\Lambda^0(\mathcal T)\). Its average on the short interval is one, so the three averaging coefficients are \((1,\tfrac12,0)\). Consequently, \[(W^0u_\varepsilon)(x)=
\begin{cases}
1-x/(2\varepsilon),&0\le x\le\varepsilon,\\
(1-x)/(2(1-\varepsilon)),&\varepsilon\le x\le1.
\end{cases}\] Exact integration gives \[\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2=\frac{6\varepsilon}{5},
\qquad
\|W^0u_\varepsilon\|_2^2=\frac{1+6\varepsilon}{12},
\qquad
\frac{\|W^0u_\varepsilon\|_2^2}{\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2}
=\frac{5(1+6\varepsilon)}{72\varepsilon}\longrightarrow\infty .\] Thus Proposition 8.1 and Lemma 8.4 do not hold for this construction with the stated dependence of the constant. The uniform-stability conclusion attributed to the construction in Theorem 2.3 and Section 9 must be qualified. This is an operator counterexample, not merely a missing justification for Lemma 8.2.

The obstruction already occurs at fixed polynomial degree two and on a fixed domain. It also occurs in nested refinements: retain \([1/2,1]\), repeatedly bisect the adjacent left cell toward \(1/2\), and put the same zero-endpoint quadratic on the shrinking cell. Its average contributes \(1/2\) at the shared vertex and creates a fixed-size output on the retained interval.

The counterexample does not refute the algebraic decomposition, commutation, space preservation, or boundedness on each fixed mesh with a mesh-dependent constant. It also does not disprove the existence of some different stable decomposition. For \(n\ge2\), a shared facet contains an edge, and shape regularity compares adjacent element diameters; bounded star cardinality then gives the local comparability used in the proof. The statement can be restricted to \(n\ge2\), or dimension one can be treated with an explicit adjacent-size comparability assumption. Changing the averaging weights would require a new argument and is not offered here as a verified repair.
# P2. The terminal link gauge needs a boundary exception (Minor)

The complex (2.7), pp. 1229–1230, is completed by the oriented terminal functional (2.9). The text observes that the final arrow can be redundant for a boundary link. Nevertheless, Lemma 2.1 imposes \(\delta_{k+1}\widetilde c=0\), and Section 3 explicitly invokes (2.9) for \(\delta_1\) when the link is one-dimensional, immediately after (3.8), p. 1240. If that terminal functional is retained for boundary links, the asserted primitive with this gauge need not exist.

Let \(\Omega\) be a single triangle and let \(f\) be a boundary vertex. Its link is one oriented edge \(e=[a,b]\). In the ordered bases, \[\partial_1 e=(-1,1),\qquad \partial_0(-1,1)=0 .\] The unique primitive of \(c=(-1,1)\) is \(\widetilde c=e\), but (2.9) gives \(\delta_1e=\pm1\), not zero. The same contradiction occurs for the actual right-hand side in (3.8): \[\beta_a=\frac{\lambda_a-\lambda_b}{2},\quad
\beta_b=-\beta_a,\quad
\mu_e=\frac{\lambda_b-\lambda_a}{2}.\] The incidence equation forces this nonzero \(\mu_e\), whereas the terminal gauge would force it to vanish.

The natural correction is precise: on a boundary link, use the ordinary augmented cochain complex of a ball, ending in \(\mathcal C_q(f^*)\to0\), where \(q=\dim f^*\). Retain the terminal integral functional for a closed sphere link. A ball has no top cycle, so its top primitive is already unique; the terminal condition is unnecessary. Under this convention the displayed witness has a solution, and the subsequent identities in Sections 4–5 use \(\partial\mu=\beta\) without imposing the incompatible integral condition. This correction must be propagated through (3.8) and (4.6)–(4.7).

This is a local convention repair, consistent with the paper’s own remark about the final arrow, rather than evidence against a corrected bubble transform. The distinct terminal integral in the full-zero-trace differential-form complex on \(\Omega_f\) is a relative-cohomology condition and must not be deleted. The repair of the link convention and its immediate algebraic consequences were checked; this is not a claim to have independently certified every statement of a rewritten general theorem.
# P3. Local formula and index corrections (Minor)
The following corrections are directly determined by the surrounding definitions.

1. The displayed formula for the exterior derivative on p. 1224 omits the alternating sign. Its summand should be \((-1)^{j+1}\partial_{v_j}u_x(v_1,\ldots,\widehat v_j,\ldots,v_{k+1})\). For \(\alpha=x\,\mathrm dx\) and \(v_1=v_2=\partial_x\), the printed sum equals two, whereas an alternating two-form must vanish on repeated arguments. Later identities use the usual signed exterior calculus; this local omission is not a counterexample to those identities.
2. On p. 1228, the zero-dimensional link case is \(m=n\), not \(m=n-1\), because the preceding convention is \(f\in\Delta_{m-1}\) and \(\dim f^*=n-m\). Section 4.1 uses the correct case.
3. In the proof of Lemma 4.4, p. 1248, the condition \(0\le j<m-n\) must be \(0\le j<n-m\), as in the preceding induction and Corollary 4.2.

4. In (5.4), p. 1251, the target form degree must be \(k-j-1\), not \(k\): \(Q^k_{e,f}\) uses \(\Pi_{j+1}\) and lowers form degree by \(j+1\). The immediately preceding definition states this degree correctly.
# Positive checks and the preservation mechanism
Several potentially serious objections do not survive closer examination.

The affine averaging map stays in each source simplex containing \(f\). At \(b=0\) it restricts to the identity on \(f\), and \(\int z_f=1\) supplies the asserted trace. Averaged pullbacks commute with \(\mathrm d\). The alternating sums defining \(K_{m,f}\) have the required support: on \(\lambda_i=0\), terms indexed by \(g\) and \(g\cup\{i\}\) have equal restricted pullbacks and opposite signs. The top-cell residual in (2.26) legitimately has the larger dependence domain \(\Omega_f^E\); the paper does not claim dependence only on the top cell.

For the weights in Section 4, full vanishing tangential trace on \(\partial\Omega_f\) is explicitly distinguished from support on \(\Omega_f\). That distinction removes the boundary term in the Stokes calculation in Lemma 5.2. The identities involving \(\delta^+\) and the common-face restriction \(G_f(y,L_gx)=G_g(y,L_gx)\) support the sum rearrangements in Sections 5 and 7, subject to the corrected link convention. In Lemma 7.2, the reversible change \(f'=f\setminus\{i\}\), \(e=e_0\cup\{i\}\) accounts for both the index sets and the leading minus sign. Exact finite checks of this signed bijection on one- and two-simplex complexes in dimensions two through four agree. The two lemmas in Section 7 then reproduce \(C_{m-1}^k\) from (2.20), and the differences telescope.

On p. 1255 the parentheses in the alternative expression for \(K_{m,f,g}^k\) matter: the derivative applies to the entire wedge product. Each summand has the form \[\mathrm d\bigl(\eta\wedge T^ku\bigr)+\eta\wedge T^{k+1}\mathrm du\] up to a common sign. Here \(\eta\) is a Whitney-type \((q-1)\)-form and \(T^k\) is the normalized order-reduction operator with \(q\) physical-variable slots. Thus commutation follows from \(\mathrm d^2=0\).

The same expression also explains the trimmed-space property, which is less immediate than ordinary polynomial-degree preservation. On each simplex let \(X\) be the radial vector field, let \(u_r\) be the homogeneous degree-\(r\) part of a trimmed polynomial \(k\)-form, and let \(\eta_1\) be the degree-one part of \(\eta\). The trimmed-space criterion is \(\iota_Xu_r=0\). Removing \(b^q\) from the mixed pullback cancels its \(q\) physical-slot factors. Its remaining evaluation map is affine in \(x\), say \(A(y)x+c(y)\). Moving the radial argument past those \(q\) slots gives \[\iota_X(T^ku)_r=0,\qquad
\iota_X(T^{k+1}\mathrm du)_{r-1}
=(-1)^q(r+k)(T^ku)_r .\] Since \(\iota_X\eta_1=0\), the highest-degree term \(H_{r+1}=\eta_1\wedge(T^ku)_r\) satisfies \(\iota_XH_{r+1}=0\). Cartan’s identity and the wedge sign therefore give \[\iota_X\mathrm dH_{r+1}=(r+k)H_{r+1},\qquad
\iota_X\bigl(\eta_1\wedge(T^{k+1}\mathrm du)_{r-1}\bigr)
=-(r+k)H_{r+1}.\] The unwanted highest-degree contraction cancels. Ordinary degree is at most \(r\), so the result is in \(\mathcal P_r^-\Lambda^k\). The zero-map cases \(q>k\) are handled by the same identities, with \(T^ku=0\). This supplies a direct explanation of the preservation step without assuming a stronger, unstated degree-lowering property for \(R\) or \(Q\).

As a concrete check, triangulate the unit square by its diagonal from \((0,0)\) to \((1,1)\), take \(f=(0,0)\), and use the corrected boundary convention. For \(u=x\,\mathrm dy-y\,\mathrm dx\in\mathcal P_1^-\Lambda^1\), exact rational integration and the weight equations give, on both triangles, \[K_{1,f}^1u=\frac{(1-y)\mathrm dx+(x-1)\mathrm dy}{6},
\qquad
\mathrm dK_{1,f}^1u=K_{1,f}^2\mathrm du
=\frac13\,\mathrm dx\wedge\mathrm dy .\] The separate terms have nonzero highest-degree contractions, which cancel in their sum. This finite calculation supports, but does not replace, the preceding analytic argument.

For the stability proof under local diameter comparability, the powers of the local scale cancel in every operator type. An \(R\) term has factors \(h^{-j}\), \(h^n\) and \(h^{j-n}\). A \(Q\) term can be rewritten using \[\rho_g^{j+1}\mathrm d\!\left(\frac{\phi_e}{\rho_g^{j+1}}\right)
=\mathrm d\phi_e-(j+1)\mathrm d\rho_g\wedge\frac{\phi_e}{\rho_g},\] whose size is \(O(h^{-j-1})\); the normalized averaging factor has size \(O(h^{j+1})\). The \(W\) coefficient and Whitney norm contribute inverse powers \(h^{k-n/2}\) and \(h^{n/2-k}\). Bounded local incidence counts give uniform finite overlap and uniformly bounded inverses for the finite coefficient systems with entries \(0,\pm1\). No increasing polynomial degree enters these constants. The full kernel estimate imported from [7] in Lemma 8.5 was not independently reconstructed; these are checks of its use, the geometric conditions, and the scaling, not a claim to have reread that external proof.
# Supporting checks

The supported assessment is Major, on account of P1: the published construction does not satisfy its asserted shape-only uniform bound in an allowed dimension. P2 and P3 are local corrections. The checked support, commutation, decomposition, and trimmed-preservation mechanisms give positive counterevidence against a broader claim that the construction is intrinsically invalid. A dimension qualification and a consistent boundary-link convention are the principal requirements for a revision. The conclusions concern the acquired publisher bytes only; no later correction or alternate version is inferred.

The available preserved material contained the source and historical extraction/parse evidence, but no recoverable substantive report or scientific partial for this paper. Conversation-only earlier output was unavailable, rather than proved absent everywhere. Accordingly, this is an initial scientific review within the assigned missing subset. The source acquisition and historical parse are reused under their original attribution. The current exact interval calculation, boundary-chain calculation, polynomial diagnostic, analytic checks, source-page inspections, and report production are separately recorded. Native support roles are distinguished from the assigned executor and from the Main-supplied product route. No author code was executed, and absence of optional code is not a mathematical defect.
This report is not independent acceptance. Scientific adjudication remains pending, and no human review is asserted.

report: Abstract: This report checks the grading and algebraic model construction in Section 3 of Ludwig Rahm’s Planar Regularity Structures. Two explicit admissible trees show that Lemma 3.5, with the definitions actually printed, does not establish the claimed regularity structure: one assigned degree is absent from the stated index set, and an allowed resonant regularity produces a nonconstant degree-zero basis element. The algebraic model identities are examined separately and are not refuted by these examples. Both findings concern a central construction; their supported assessment is Major. The later deformed Hopf-algebra theory is not certified or refuted here. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Review of
Planar Regularity Structures
# Identity, version, and inspected scope

The reviewed work is Ludwig Rahm, Planar Regularity Structures, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 1269–1319, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09701-1 [rahm]. This is the 51-page publisher version of record, published online 8 September 2025 and acquired on 27 October 2026. Its exact bytes, rather than the earlier 37-page arXiv version, define this review. Here PDF page means a one-based physical page; printed page \(1268+j\) corresponds to PDF page \(j\).

The focused checks cover Definitions 2.8–2.9, the definition of \(\mathcal{PB}\) and its degree in Section 3, Lemmas 3.3 and 3.5, Proposition 3.6, and the algebraic identities in Theorem 3.8. The introductory account, the setup of Section 4, its discussion of restricted tree spaces, and its final extended-decoration argument were read to bound the impact. The long proofs of the deformed positive and negative Hopf structures and the complete cointeraction calculation were not independently verified. Source text was parsed on all 51 pages; that operation is not claimed as scientific reading of all pages. The coverage ledger records the actual page ranges and unexamined material.
# Definitions and assumptions relevant to the findings

On PDF pages 16–17 (printed 1284–1285), Definition 2.8 requires \[A\subset\mathbb R,\qquad 0\in A,\qquad
 T=\bigoplus_{\beta\in A}T_\beta,\qquad T_0\simeq\mathbb R,\] with a lower-bounded locally finite index set, Banach homogeneous spaces, and a triangular structure-group action. Definition 2.9 explicitly sets aside the usual analytic model bounds. Consequently, the absence of such bounds is not treated as a defect.

Equation reference: eq:printedA. On PDF page 17, \(\mathcal{PB}\) is the vector space of planar rooted trees with edge labels \(0,1,\ldots,n\). A zero label is represented by an undecorated edge. Each nonzero edge ends at a leaf; a vertex has at most one such decorated edge, and that edge is rightmost. On PDF page 18 (printed 1286), the specified index set is \[
 A=\{0\}\cup_i\alpha_i\mathbb N
       \cup_i(\alpha_i\mathbb N-1),\] and the degree of a tree is the sum of \(1\) for every undecorated edge and \(\alpha_i-1\) for every edge decorated by \(i\). The formula is visible in the original PDF; it is not an extraction substitution for an additive sum of sets. No reciprocal-integer or nonresonance restriction on the positive regularities is imposed in this construction. The preceding rough-path definition permits regularity parameters in \((0,1]\) (PDF pages 10–11).

Lemma 3.5, on PDF page 20, asserts that \((A,\mathcal{PB},G)\) is a regularity structure. Its proof assumes that the indicated degree makes \(\mathcal{PB}\) an \(A\)-graded space, then checks triangularity. The following counterexamples test this algebraic assertion. They require no stochastic sample, numerical solver, or extra assumption about a particular rough-path lift. In particular, the time-augmentation and integration condition (17), introduced for the later model, cannot remove basis trees from the already declared space in Lemma 3.5.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (The printed index set omits an allowed tree degree).  For one nonzero edge label, set \(\alpha_1=3/5\). Let \(\tau\) be the chain with four vertices \(v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3\), root \(v_0\), and successive edge labels \(0,0,1\). Then \(\tau\in\mathcal{PB}\) but the assigned degree of \(\tau\) does not belong to [eq:printedA] (#eq:printedA). Thus the first grading assertion in the proof of Lemma 3.5 is false for this allowed parameter.
## Complete check

Every nonroot vertex of the chain has exactly one parent. The only nonzero edge ends at the leaf \(v_3\); it is the only outgoing edge of \(v_2\), and hence is rightmost. There is at most one decorated edge incident to any vertex. These are exactly the tree restrictions on PDF page 17. The chain has positive degree and no decorated edge at the root, so restricting attention to the positive tree space would not remove this example.

Equation reference: eq:degree1. The displayed degree rule gives \[
 |\tau|=1+1+\left(\frac35-1\right)=\frac85.\] For \(8/5\) to lie in either family supplied by \(\alpha_1\), an integer \(k\in\mathbb N\) would have to satisfy \[\frac35k=\frac85 \quad\hbox{or}\quad
 \frac35k-1=\frac85.\] The two required values are \(k=8/3\) and \(k=13/3\), neither an integer. Including a time parameter \(\alpha_0=1\), the interpretation most favorable to the assertion, adds only integer degrees, which still do not include \(8/5\). The argument is unaffected by whether \(\mathbb N\) includes zero. Since \(\tau\) is a nonzero tree basis element with the degree assigned in [eq:degree1] (#eq:degree1), it cannot be placed in any homogeneous component indexed by [eq:printedA] (#eq:printedA) without changing the printed grading.

The retained independent Python check uses exact rational arithmetic, verifies the rooted-tree, leaf, and planar-order conditions, and solves these membership equations. It supplies a finite verification of this witness, while the preceding calculation is the complete argument.
## Alternative interpretations and impact

If all nonzero regularities are chosen as one reciprocal integer \(1/N\), the particular missing-degree obstruction disappears because adding an integer preserves that lattice. That is a valid special case, not an assumption stated in Lemma 3.5. Reading the unions as the additive semigroup generated by the regularities would also change the printed definition. The source image and publisher HTML both show unions.

This is a failure of the specified regularity-structure construction: the model theorem explicitly uses that triple. The supported assessment is Major, because Lemma 3.5 supplies a central structural prerequisite for Theorem 3.8. The example does not show that the recentering identities are false, that a corrected grading cannot work, or that the later Hopf-algebra identities fail.

Problem 2 (A permitted resonant regularity gives a nontrivial zero sector).  Set \(\alpha_1=1/2\). Consider the planar tree \(\sigma\) with edges \[(v_0,v_1;0),\qquad (v_0,v_2;1),\qquad (v_1,v_3;1),\] where \(v_0\) is the root and the edge to \(v_2\) is to the right of the edge to \(v_1\). Then \(\sigma\) is a nonconstant degree-zero basis element of \(\mathcal{PB}\). Together with the unit tree, it contradicts \(T_0\simeq\mathbb R\) in the paper’s Definition 2.8.
## Complete check

Equation reference: eq:degree2. The vertices \(v_2,v_3\) are leaves and receive the two decorated edges. Each of \(v_0,v_1\) has one decorated outgoing edge. At \(v_0\) it is rightmost by construction, and at \(v_1\) it is the sole outgoing edge. Every other restriction of \(\mathcal{PB}\) is satisfied. The degree rule gives \[
 |\sigma|=1+\left(\frac12-1\right)+
                 \left(\frac12-1\right)=0.\] The one-vertex unit tree also has degree zero. The four-vertex tree \(\sigma\) and the one-vertex unit are distinct basis elements in the vector space defined on PDF page 17. No relation identifying them, or quotient deleting \(\sigma\), is imposed there. Hence \[\dim\bigl(\mathcal{PB}_0\bigr)\ge 2,\] whereas the stated Definition 2.8 requires dimension one. No simulation or claimed analytic model evaluation is needed for this dimension argument.
## Alternative interpretations and impact

A convention in which the zero sector merely contains a distinguished copy of \(\mathbb R\) would avoid this specific contradiction, but it is different from the definition used by this paper. Alternatively, carefully chosen nonresonant degrees might exclude nonunit zero-degree trees. Such a hypothesis is absent from Lemma 3.5. A later equation-specific restriction is not specified for the full Section 3 space. This remains a separate obstruction even after enlarging the index set.

The supported assessment is again Major, with the same bounded dependency: Lemma 3.5 does not provide a regularity structure under its own definition for all allowed parameters. This finding does not establish failure of the model’s algebraic identities or of an appropriately restricted construction.
# Checks that survive and the precise repair boundary
## The model identities

Theorem 3.8 assumes time augmentation and condition (17) (PDF pages 20–22). On an element \(B_+\varphi(\omega)\), the proof reduces the model compatibility equation to \[\langle X_{yx}\otimes X_{xt},\Delta_{\mathrm{MKW}}\omega\rangle
 =\langle X_{yx}*X_{xt},\omega\rangle
 =\langle X_{yt},\omega\rangle,\] which is Chen’s identity with the indicated order of endpoints. For a tree with a decorated root edge, the differentiated constant term vanishes because Lemma 3.7 gives \(\Pi_x(1)=1\). Condition (17) is needed for the derivative identification and is explicitly assumed. These steps were read and checked; the two grading counterexamples do not refute them. They prevent those identities, as written, from completing the claimed model on the uncorrected regularity-structure triple.
## What an index-set change actually restores

There is a precise limited correction to Problem 1: replace [eq:printedA] (#eq:printedA) by the set of degrees of the declared admissible trees, including the unit. For finitely many strictly positive \(\alpha_i\), this degree set is lower bounded and locally finite.

Indeed, write \(k\) for the number of undecorated edges and \(m_i\) for the number of edges labeled \(i\), with \(m=\sum_i m_i\). There are \(k+1\) non-noise vertices. The one-noise-edge-per-vertex condition implies \(m\le k+1\). Therefore \[|\eta|=k-m+\sum_i m_i\alpha_i,\qquad k-m\ge-1.\] For \(|\eta|\le R\), the nonnegative counts obey \(\sum_i m_i\alpha_i\le R+1\), so there are only finitely many choices of the \(m_i\), and then only finitely many choices of \(k-m\). The nonunit degrees are bounded below by \(\min(0,\min_i\alpha_i-1)>-1\). This proves the stated index-set properties.

This change restores degree coverage and these two index-set properties only. It does not cure Problem 2, choose a permissible quotient, establish all model-space axioms, or constitute a verified replacement for the full Lemma 3.5. Repair of the zero-sector condition and its compatibility with the coaction remains open in this review.
## Later construction and versions

Section 4 defines its index set as the actual set of regularities (PDF page 26), and explicitly discusses restriction to suitable tree subspaces (PDF page 36). The extended-decoration argument in Proposition 4.28 preserves the degree used in positive projection (PDF page 49). These are reasons to confine the present findings to the stated Section 3 construction rather than infer a refutation of all subsequent algebra.

A bounded check of the publisher page and the arXiv record on 29 October 2026 found no linked correction addressing these points. The arXiv record listed only the earlier version v1 [arxiv]. Its full mathematical content was not compared with the acquired publisher PDF. This bounded search does not establish first discovery or the absence of unpublished corrections. No author contact or author-code execution occurred.
# Conclusion and distinct states
Item | Issue assessment | Repair and remaining work
Problem 1 | Major; missing allowed degree | Actual degree set repairs degree coverage; full construction not re-proved.
Problem 2 | Major; zero-sector dimension | A compatible restriction or revised definition remains to be supplied.
Model identities | No issue established in the checked algebraic steps | Retain condition (17) and time augmentation; this is not a complete analytic model verification.
Scientific decision: pending. Human reviews: none supplied. Author adoption: unknown and not requested. This is an initial review; independent acceptance has not been performed.
# Supporting checks

The exact-rational checker is `grading_check.py`. It is independently written; no author program was executed. The admissibility and degree calculations are analytical arguments in this report supported by that finite check.

Scientific reading, argument assessment, report preparation, compilation, parsing and actual page inspection were performed in the assigned execution conversation. The main dispatcher’s product-interface observation is attributed to that dispatcher; the execution environment’s self-description is recorded separately in provenance without a claim of backend equivalence. An internal helper supplied only a clerical inventory checklist. There is no human review attestation.

Rahm, Planar Regularity Structures, arXiv:2212.04856, version-history metadata consulted 29 October 2026; v1 submitted 9 December 2022. Only the record was consulted for version history. https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04856.

Title: Technical Review of an Unfiltered
Low-Regularity KdV Integrator
# Identity, version and claim

The paper is Buyang Li and Yifei Wu, An Unfiltered Low-Regularity Integrator for the KdV Equation with Solutions Below \(H^1\), DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09702-0. The reviewed source is the undated, unnumbered 50-page institutional author manuscript retrieved from the PolyU URL in Reference [manuscript]. Its exact hash is recorded in Appendix A. Physical PDF pages agree with printed pages. Neither the 42-page arXiv v1 nor the 60-page publisher article is silently substituted or certified byte-equivalent.

For the periodic equation \[u_t+u_{xxx}=\tfrac12\partial_x(u^2),\qquad x\in[0,2\pi],\] Theorem 1.1 (p. 5) assumes \(0<\gamma\le1\), \(u\in C([0,T];H^\gamma)\), and zero initial mean. It asserts \(\max_n\|u(t_n)-u^n\|_{L^2}\le C\tau^\gamma\log(1/\tau)\) for sufficiently small positive \(\tau=T/L\), with constants allowed to depend on the initial norm, \(\gamma\), and \(T\). This is a time-discretization result; a spatial implementation and its aliasing errors are separate questions.

The zero-mean reduction in Remark 1.1 is consistent with the sign of the equation. Writing \(m=P_0u^0\) and \(\widetilde u(t,x)=u(t,x-mt)-m\), the chain rule gives \(\widetilde u_t+\widetilde u_{xxx}=(u-m)u_x
=\frac12\partial_x(\widetilde u^2)\). The projection \(P=I-P_0\) in scheme (1.4), p. 4, removes the constant mode. It is not the step-dependent high-frequency cutoff used by the comparison methods.
# Checks of the new harmonic-analysis ingredients
## The logarithmic loss in Lemma 3.1
## Averaging and resonance in Lemma 3.2
## The phase factor and comparable frequencies

For \(k=k_1+k_2+k_3\), direct expansion gives \[k^3-k_1^3-k_2^3-k_3^3
 =3(k_1+k_2)(k_1+k_3)(k_2+k_3).\] The set \(\Gamma\) on p. 12 excludes all three zero factors. In Lemma 3.3, p. 13, write \(k_0=-k\), sort the four absolute values, and assume \(k_0>0>k_1\). The sum-zero constraint implies \(|k_0|\le3|k_1|\). If \(|k_0|\ge6|k_3|\), then \[|k_0+k_3|\ge\tfrac12|k_0|,\qquad
 |k_0+k_2|=|k_1+k_3|\ge\tfrac16|k_0|.\] The remaining nonzero integer factor has magnitude at least one. Consequently \(|\phi|\ge |k_0|^2/4\), contradicting the strict definition of \(\Gamma_1\). This verifies the stated comparable-frequency step, including its strict boundary. It does not independently establish all operator estimates of Proposition 3.4.
# Perturbation formulation and the final bootstrap

The interpolation (5.4), p. 25, has the correct endpoint values: at \(t_n\) the integrals and linear correction vanish, and at \(t_{n+1}\) it agrees with (5.3). Subtracting (5.6) from (5.1) gives the sign \(e=e^0+\mathcal F-\mathcal R\) in (5.9), p. 26, because \(v^2-\mathcal V^2=2e(v-e/2)\). These algebraic checks do not establish the bounds on \(\mathcal R\).

The dependence is substantive: Lemmas 3.1–3.3 feed the consistency and trilinear estimates; these feed Propositions 7.1 and 8.1; the bootstrap alone is not a substitute for those propositions. No unverified concern about those remaining steps is classified as a defect.
# Numerical scope, versions and outcome

For the data in (10.2), p. 44, \(|\widehat u_k^0|=|k|^{-0.51-\gamma}/10\) for \(k\ne0\). The squared \(H^\gamma\) tail is comparable to \(\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-1.02}\), which converges. At \(\gamma+0.01\) it is comparable to the divergent harmonic series. Thus the declared regularity boundary is correct for the infinite Fourier series. Title: Technical Review of Polynomial
Moment Inequality Certificates
# Source, framework and review scope

The paper is Igor Klep, Victor Magron and Jurij Volčič, Sums of Squares Certificates for Polynomial Moment Inequalities, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09703-z. The reviewed source is the undated 36-page author PDF at https://igorklep.github.io/files/mompoly.pdf; physical and printed page numbers coincide. The 43-page publisher version and 35-page arXiv v2 were identified by metadata, not substituted or certified equivalent.

The algebra \(\mathcal M=\mathbb R[\mathrm{m}_\alpha:\alpha\ne0]\) has \(\mathrm{m}_0=1\). The map \(\mathrm{m}:\mathcal M[x]\to\mathcal M\) is \(\mathcal M\)-linear and sends \(x^\alpha\) to \(\mathrm{m}_\alpha\). For \(S_1\subseteq\mathbb R[x]\), let \(K=K(S_1)\) be its nonnegative locus. For \(S_2\subseteq\mathcal M\), \(\mathcal K=\mathcal K(S_1,S_2)\) consists of probability measures supported on \(K\), with all marginal moments finite, satisfying \(s(\mu)\ge0\) for \(s\in S_2\). The pointwise evaluation is \(f(\mu,X)\), where \(X\in K\) is independent of \(\mu\). Random-variable evaluation instead produces a function \(f[\pi,F]\), ordered almost everywhere (pp. 6–8).

The cone \(\operatorname{QM}(S_1,S_2)\) consists of finite sums of terms \(h^2s\), \(h^2\mathrm{m}(g^2s)\), and \(h^2t\), with \(s\in\{1\}\cup S_1\), \(t\in S_2\), and moment-polynomial coefficients as in Definition 2.2. Its generators are nonnegative on \(\mathcal K\times K\). No global finiteness assumption on \(S_1\) appears in these definitions; Section 5 explicitly imposes finite constraint sets for computation.

The review concentrates on the evaluation bridge, the compact Positivstellensatz and its bounded-set corollary, both Bell applications, and the final noncompact theorem and classical corollary. The Kadison–Dubois and compact moment-representation inputs to Theorem 4.2 were used conditionally, not independently reproved. The pseudo-moment and Hilbert-17th results and the full analytic machinery of Section 6 were not verified.
# Problem 1: almost-everywhere evaluation does not imply the stated pointwise property

Location and assessment: Proposition 2.4, p. 8; Minor. The reverse implication asserts that nonnegativity of \(f[\pi,F]\) for every admissible random variable implies nonnegativity of \(f(\mu,X)\) for every independent \(X\in K\). Taking the coordinate random variable under \(\mu\) only gives nonnegativity \(\mu\)-almost everywhere.

Set \(n=1\), \(S_1=\{1-x^2\}\), \(S_2=\{-\mathrm{m}_2\}\), and \(f=-x^2\). Then \(K=[-1,1]\). Every admissible measure satisfies \(\int x^2\,d\mu\le0\), hence is \(\delta_0\). Every admissible random variable has \(E F^2=0\), so \(F=0\) almost everywhere and \(f[\pi,F]=0\) almost everywhere. Thus condition (ii) holds. However, \[f(\delta_0,1)=-1<0,\qquad (\delta_0,1)\in\mathcal K\times K,\] so condition (i) fails. All moments exist, both constraint sets are finite, and even the ordinary quadratic module is archimedean.

There is no full-support hypothesis. Adding a null-probability point does not change an almost-everywhere assertion. A precise repair is to replace \(X\in K\) by \(X\in\operatorname{supp}\mu\): for fixed \(\mu\), continuity of \(X\mapsto f(\mu,X)\) makes nonnegativity almost everywhere equivalent to nonnegativity on the support. Pushforward of \(\pi\) proves the corresponding equivalence. The original forward implication also remains valid.

This changes the claimed evaluation bridge and the comparison on p. 11. Theorem 4.2 is proved directly for pointwise evaluation, and the Bell objectives are pure moment polynomials, hence constant in the free variable. No failure of those core applications follows from this example; that limited dependency supports Minor.
# Problem 2: boundedness alone does not control an infinite presentation
Location and assessment: Corollary 4.5, p. 16; Minor. The proof infers that the preordering generated by \(S_1\) is archimedean from boundedness of \(K(S_1)\), without assuming \(S_1\) finite.

Take \(n=1\), \(S_2=\varnothing\), and \[S_1=\{s_j=x^2(x^2-j):j=1,2,\ldots\}.\] The feasible set is \(K(S_1)=\{0\}\): if \(x\ne0\), choosing an integer \(j>x^2\) makes \(s_j(x)<0\). Thus \(\mathcal K=\{\delta_0\}\), and \(f=-\mathrm{m}_2\) is zero on \(\mathcal K\times K\), satisfying condition (i).

Let \(\widetilde S_1\) contain the square-free finite products from \(S_1\). Suppose condition (ii) held with \(\varepsilon=1\), so \(1-\mathrm{m}_2\in\operatorname{QM}(\widetilde S_1,\varnothing)\). Any such identity contains only finitely many indices \(j\), say a finite set \(J\). Choose \(R^2>\max(\{1\}\cup J)\). Evaluate the identity at \((\delta_R,R)\). Every used \(s_j(R)\) is positive; products, squares and their moments are nonnegative. The right side is therefore nonnegative, but the left side is \(1-R^2<0\), a contradiction. The test pair need not satisfy the unused constraints: it tests a claimed finite polynomial identity.

Every finite subsystem has an unbounded feasible set, explaining the failure of the asserted archimedean inference. A finite-\(S_1\) interpretation would exclude this witness, but it is not the printed hypothesis. The later explicit discussion of infinitely many constraints on p. 33 reinforces that this is a real scope boundary. A verified modification is to adjoin a valid ball constraint to \(S_1\); the enlarged ordinary module is archimedean and Theorem 4.2 applies to the enlarged cone. This does not establish membership in the original cone. The main archimedean theorem and the finite SDP examples are not refuted, supporting Minor.
# Problem 3: the empty-feasible-set reduction is not nonnegative

Location and assessment: Theorem 6.9, Case (b), p. 31; Major for an invalid derivation of a stated core guarantee. Theorem 6.9, p. 30, permits arbitrary \(S_1\), finite \(S_2\), and \(f\in\mathcal M[x]\), and equates positivity on \(\mathcal K\times K\) with membership of \(f+\varepsilon(\Phi_r+\Psi_r)\) in the moment quadratic module for some \(r\), for every \(\varepsilon>0\). Here \(\Phi_r\) and \(\Psi_r\) are the ordinary and moment perturbations defined in Section 6.

For empty \(\mathcal K\), the proof introduces \(z=x_{n+1}\), \(S'_1=z(\{1\}\cup S_1)\) and \(S'_2=\mathrm{m}_{1,0,\ldots,0}^{\,2}S_2\), and asserts \(zf\ge0\) on the new feasible set in order to apply Case (a). The printed moment index refers to the first original coordinate.

Take \(n=1\), \(S_1=\varnothing\), \(S_2=\{-1\}\), and \(f=-1\). The original feasible measure set is empty, \(S_2\) is finite, and \(f\) is even an ordinary polynomial, as requested within Case (b). The new sets are \[S'_1=\{z\},\qquad S'_2=\{-\mathrm{m}_{1,0}^{\,2}\}.\] The probability measure \(
u=\delta_{(0,1)}\) has all moments, is supported where \(z\ge0\), and satisfies \(-(\int x_1\,d
u)^2=0\). For the admissible point \(X=(0,1)\), nevertheless, \[(zf)(
u,X)=-1.\] This also fails under random-variable evaluation, so Problem 1 does not explain it away. The necessary premise for invoking the nonempty Case (a) is false.

This is a counterexample to the proof step, not to the theorem’s conclusion. Indeed, in this particular original example \(-1\) is already a cone generator. The dependency is the advertised noncompact Positivstellensatz in its empty-set case, not a peripheral notation statement. No complete repair of this reduction is claimed; changing an index alone would require a new argument for all support and moment constraints.
# Problem 4: zero-moment specialization does not preserve the cone

Location and assessment: Corollary 6.14, p. 32; Major for the invalid derivation of the general classical extension. The corollary asserts, for arbitrary \(S\subseteq\mathbb R[x]\), that \(f\ge0\) on \(K(S)\) is equivalent to \(f+\varepsilon\Phi_r\in\operatorname{QM}(S)\) for a suitable \(r\) at every positive \(\varepsilon\). Its proof fixes the free variables and sends every nonconstant moment to zero, claiming \(\zeta(\operatorname{QM}(S,\varnothing))\subseteq\operatorname{QM}(S)\).

Take \(S=\{x^2-1\}\) in one variable. By the definition of the moment cone, \(\mathrm{m}(x^2-1)=\mathrm{m}_2-1\) belongs to \(\operatorname{QM}(S,\varnothing)\). Its image is \(-1\). But \(-1\notin\operatorname{QM}(S)\): at the feasible point \(x=1\), every ordinary quadratic-module element is nonnegative. Thus the claimed cone inclusion fails for a finite constraint set with nonempty feasible set. Correcting the proof’s reference from Theorem 4.2 to Theorem 6.9 would not correct this generator failure.

For nonempty \(K(S)\), evaluation of moments at a feasible Dirac measure \(\delta_a\), rather than at \(\delta_0\), does preserve the cone: the image of \(\mathrm{m}(g^2s)\) is a nonnegative scalar because \(s(a)\ge0\). Handling the resulting perturbation constants still requires an argument, and the empty-set case requires separate treatment. This report does not certify a full repair. The advertised extension to general classical constrained polynomials is the dependency supporting Major. The conclusion itself has not been disproved.
# Problem 5: the printed covariance certificate is a false identity

Location and assessment: Section 5.1, pp. 19–20; Major for the printed exact proof of the covariance upper bound, with a fully verified algebraic repair. The objective \(f=\operatorname{cov}_{3322}(A,B)\) is the sum of the eight covariance terms on p. 19, with \((x_1,\ldots,x_6)=(A_1,A_2,A_3,B_1,B_2,B_3)\in\{-1,1\}^6\). The displayed \(8\times8\) matrix \(G\) and vector \(v\) on p. 20 are asserted to satisfy \[\mathrm{m}(v^\top Gv)=\tfrac92-f
 \quad\text{modulo }x_j^2=1.\] The first, seventh and eighth entries of \(v\) contain \(\mathrm{m}_{110000}\).

Set every random variable equal to \(1\) on a one-point probability space. This is an admissible binary model; Section 5.1 imposes no zero-mean condition. Every moment is one and every covariance zero. The printed vector becomes \[v=(1,0,5,-10,0,1,38/3,38/3)^\top .\] Exact rational multiplication with the printed \(G\) gives \(v^\top Gv=7/2\), whereas \(9/2-f=9/2\). This is a direct failure of the identity, not a violation of the covariance inequality.

The leading principal minors of \(G\), calculated exactly, are \[\frac43,\ \frac1{24},\ \frac1{128},\ \frac5{6144},\
 \frac1{12288},\ \frac1{131072},\
 \frac{19}{100663296},\ \frac1{1073741824}.\] They are all positive, proving positive definiteness. The repaired identity therefore establishes \(f\le9/2\) for every binary probability model. The claimed attainment at \(9/2\) in the external reference was not independently reconstructed.

This correction is supported by both exact algebra and the archived notebook at the bound commit. No author code was executed, and cached notebook outputs were not treated as new computations. The discrepancy does not establish which code generated the published SDP experiment. It also does not establish author adoption in another manuscript version. The printed derivation is central to settling the stated conjecture, which supports Major even though the exact repair preserves that upper bound.
# Positive checks and overall dependencies

The proof architecture of Theorem 4.2 (pp. 15–16) is consistent within the checked scope: archimedean separation produces a character, and compact moment representation recovers an admissible measure. This uses the paper’s cited external representation theorems conditionally. Problems 1 and 2 do not refute this argument.

For the bilocal problem (5.7)–(5.9), pp. 20–22, let \[\eta_1=(1,1,-1,-1),\quad
 \eta_2=(1,-1,1,-1),\quad
 \eta_3=(1,-1,-1,1).\] On uniform independent \(r,s\in\{1,2,3,4\}\), set \(A_i=\eta_i(s)\), \(C_i=\eta_i(r)\), and \(B_i=(1-2\mathbf1_{r=s})\eta_i(r)\). Exact enumeration of all 16 atoms verifies all 64 bilocal factorizations, nine means, twelve off-diagonal pairs, and 21 repeated-index triples. There are zero failed constraints. Moreover \(E B_iC_i=1/2\), \(E A_iB_i=-1/2\), and all six distinct-index triples equal \(-1/2\); the objective is \(4\).

The upper bound can also be checked directly. For each \(i\), \[1-E B_iC_i+E A_iB_i
   =E[(1-B_iC_i)(1+A_iB_i)]\ge0,\] because \(E A_iC_i=0\). For distinct \(i,j,k\), write \(a=E A_iA_k\), \(c=E C_iC_k\) and \(T=(A_iA_k+C_iC_k)B_j+A_iC_i+A_kC_k\). Binary identities and the stated vanishing and bilocal constraints give \[E T^2=4+4ac+4U,\qquad E(TB_j)=a+c,
 \quad U=E A_iB_jC_k+E A_kB_jC_i.\] Consequently \(E(T/2-aB_j)^2=1+U\ge0\). Summing these three pair bounds and the three preceding bounds divided by three yields the objective at most \(4\). Thus this Bell conclusion survives the identified defects.

Location and assessment: Section 5.1, pp. 19–20; Major for the printed exact proof of the covariance upper bound, with a fully verified algebraic repair.  \quad\text{modulo }x_j^2=1.\] The first, seventh and eighth entries of \(v\) contain \(\mathrm{m}_{110000}\).

Set every random variable equal to \(1\) on a one-point probability space. This is an admissible binary model; Section 5.1 imposes no zero-mean condition.  \frac1{12288},\ \frac1{131072},\
 \frac{19}{100663296},\ \frac1{1073741824}.\] They are all positive, proving positive definiteness. The repaired identity therefore establishes \(f\le9/2\) for every binary probability model. The claimed attainment at \(9/2\) in the external reference was not independently reconstructed.

Title: Technical Review of Plane Quartic
Reduction via Cayley Octads
# Identity, scope and logical dependencies

The reviewed paper is R. van Bommel, J. Docking, V. Dokchitser, R. Lercier and E. Lorenzo García, Reduction of Plane Quartics and Cayley Octads, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 1425–1496, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09704-y. The exact source is the 72-page publisher version of record, published online 2 June 2025. Physical PDF page \(p\) has printed page \(1424+p\). Locations below use physical pages unless specified.

For a plane quartic over a non-archimedean local field with residue characteristic different from two, the paper associates valuation data to a Cayley octad of eight points in projective three-space. After normalizing each point to have minimum coordinate valuation zero, the 70 Plücker coordinates are the four-column determinants. A further twisted-cubic index records additional degeneration. Compatible building blocks give an octad picture.

The distinction between claims is essential. Existence of compatible decompositions is Conjecture 5.4 (p. 42); their geometric interpretation as stable reduction is Conjecture 5.12 (p. 44) and Conjecture 6.27 (p. 52). General symplectic equivariance is Conjecture 6.13 (p. 47). Theorems 5.5 and 5.8 concern uniqueness and coordinate invariance in the compatible-decomposition framework. Theorem 6.29 (p. 53) is a finite combinatorial graph correspondence, not an unconditional proof of the geometric conjecture. The absence of a general geometric proof is not reported as a defect.

The review covers the main scope statements, determinant examples, valuation-normalization argument, selected finite-field combinatorics, static computational-proof scripts, and the stated evidence and family-construction limitations. It does not certify all 42 stable types or all appendix correspondences.
# Problem 1: the subspace classification needs the smaller-side restriction
Location: Definition 6.2 and Proposition 6.3, p. 45 (printed p. 1469), followed by Table 8 and Definition 6.4. Assessment: Minor.

Definition 1.19 realizes \(E_3\) as the even subsets of an eight-letter alphabet, modulo complementation. Addition is symmetric difference and \[\langle I,J\rangle=|I\cap J|\pmod2.\] This is a six-dimensional symplectic space over \(\mathbb F_2\). Definition 6.2 calls a subspace merotropic unless it is isotropic of dimension greater than one. Proposition 6.3 claims that, up to \(S_8\) and orthogonal complementation, all such subspaces have one of the eight listed representatives.

Set \[Y=\langle AB,CD\rangle,\qquad X=Y^\perp.\] The two independent generators of \(Y\) are orthogonal, so \(Y\) is isotropic of dimension two. Nondegeneracy of the ambient pairing gives \[\dim X=4,\qquad X^\perp=Y,\qquad
 X\cap X^\perp=Y,\qquad
 \operatorname{rank}(\langle\, ,\,\rangle|_X)=4-2=2.\] Thus \(X\) is not isotropic and is merotropic under the stated definition.

Neither \(X\) nor its complement can occur in the printed list. Dimensions rule out its zero-, one-, and three-dimensional representatives. The two listed two-dimensional representatives are \(\langle AB,AC\rangle\) and \(\langle AB,ACDE\rangle\). Their generators have pairing one, so both are nondegenerate. Their complements have dimension four and rank four. The unordered dimension/rank signature of our pair is \[\{(2,0),(4,2)\},\] whereas those listed two/four-dimensional pairs have signature \(\{(2,2),(4,4)\}\). Permuting letters preserves the pairing and hence cannot eliminate this distinction. All assumptions on \(X\) have been verified; no geometric realization by a quartic is required for this finite-vector-space proposition.

There is a natural narrower reading. Definition 6.4 orders a pair \((X,X^\perp)\) so that \(\dim X\le\dim X^\perp\), and then requires that this smaller member be merotropic. Our example is excluded by that requirement because its smaller member is \(Y\). A precise correction to Proposition 6.3 is therefore: classify orthogonal pairs whose smaller-dimensional member is merotropic, with either representative allowed when dimensions are equal. This is a genuine restriction on the classified objects, rather than a change to the pairing.

The corrected claim was independently checked by exhaustive finite enumeration from the subset definition. Dimensions zero through three contain \(1,63,651,1395\) subspaces. After removing isotropic subspaces of dimensions two and three, the counts are \(1,63,336,1260\). Quotienting the three-dimensional case by orthogonal complementation and taking \(S_8\)-orbits gives: \[\begin{array}{c|l}
\text{smaller dimension}&\text{orbit sizes}\\\hline
0&1\\
1&28,\ 35\\
2&56,\ 280\\
3&35,\ 280,\ 315
\end{array}\] There are exactly eight orbits. Direct span and pairing calculations also verify every orthogonal-complement and radical entry of Table 8. The defect is local to the unrestricted wording; the actual Definition 6.4 domain is unchanged by this repair. No failure of the compatible-subspace machinery or stable-reduction conjecture follows. That bounded impact supports Minor, not a core-contribution Major.
# Exact checks of valuation data and normalization
## Examples 1.1, 1.9 and 3.8

For Example 1.1 (pp. 4–5), every four-column determinant of the displayed rational octad is nonzero. Reduction modulo 17 confirms that its first four columns lie on \(s=0\) and the last four on \(6u+9v+2r=0\). This verifies the stated incidence data, not the subsequent contraction or stable-model identification.

Example 3.8 (p. 30) yields the stated histogram \(16,48,6\) at valuations \(0,1,2\) for \(p=10007\). Every coordinate equals the sum of the four point-coincidence vectors for \(AE,BF,CG,DH\). The 840 twisted-cubic relations, the generic comparison used in the twisted-cubic index, and the geometry of the corresponding stable fibres were not reproduced.
## The determinant update and the normalization coset

In Proposition 3.13 (pp. 31–32), let \(S\) index precisely the points reducing to \((1:0:0:0)\) and let \(T=S^c\). Multiplication by \(\operatorname{diag}(\pi,1,1,1)\) adds one to every four-column determinant valuation. Renormalizing a point in \(S\) subtracts one from each determinant containing it. For a quadruple \(Q\), the net change is therefore \[1-|Q\cap S|
 =-\max(0,|Q\cap S|-1)+\max(0,|Q\cap T|-3),\] exactly the claimed point/plane update, including the cases \(|Q\cap S|=0\) and \(4\). Twisted-cubic invariance uses the balanced-binomial premise of Proposition 3.12; its external 840-polynomial input was not independently reconstructed.

The normalization uniqueness behind Proposition 3.15 can be seen without relying on the repeated coordinate labels in its displayed proof. A determinant valuation changes by \[w_Q=d+\sum_{i\in Q}c_i=\sum_{i\in Q}a_i,
 \qquad a_i=c_i+d/4.\] The eight incidence vectors \(Q\mapsto\mathbf1_{i\in Q}\) span an eight-dimensional space \(W_8\), as verified by exact rank. Imposing zero on the five quadruples from \(A,\ldots,E\) determines \(a_A,\ldots,a_E\) uniquely: the homogeneous equations force these five numbers equal, and then four times their common value is zero. The remaining three parameters independently shift the four coordinates containing \(F\), \(G\), or \(H\) and three of \(A,B,C,D\). Setting each of these three minima to zero fixes them uniquely. Thus the normalized Plücker valuation representative depends only on the original valuation vector.

The point-coincidence vectors have rational rank 28, the complementary-plane vectors rank 35, and their combined rational span rank 42, consistent with Remark 3.10. Equality of integral lattices, rather than rational spans, was not verified.
# Computational evidence and remaining proof obligations

The acquired repository is the paper-cited commit `961e584b694a217b96e9168f16ba4a9a525c6149`. Its README and the complete scripts `UniqueDecomposition.m` and `CheckMinimaCompatibleSums.m` were inspected statically. The latter compares the sum with its full normalized valuation vector. It therefore tests all normalization requirements, rather than only a weak reading of the three-minima sentence on p. 44. For nonnegative block vectors, an unweighted sum having minimum zero means that a common coordinate is zero in every summand; all positive weighted sums then have the same property. This explains why checking supports is relevant for arbitrary positive block coefficients.

The uniqueness script constructs compatible subsets, reduces by letter permutations, and examines kernel signs in the quotient by \(W_8\). Its comments about 2,626,648 sets and 507 representatives are author assertions, not new runtime results. The complete generator implementation, exhaustiveness of those enumerations, sign-branch sufficiency and the reported absence of printed exceptional pairs remain unverified here. The paper’s 16-CPU-hour computation was not rerun, and no conclusion of Theorem 5.5 is certified by merely locating its code.

For the elementary two-line example on pp. 17–19, \(\langle AF\rangle\) and \(\langle AEFH\rangle\) are orthogonal. The displayed graph construction doubles each edge, assigns the two leaves genus zero, contracts them, and leaves a genus-one vertex with two loops. Its total genus is \(1+2=3\), as in Figure 8 and the corresponding Table 11 row. The more complicated relation-index construction and Theorem 6.29’s complete graph isomorphism were not independently verified.

Section 1.4 reports checks for about 180,000 of 186,502 curve/prime pairs, and explicitly describes limitations of the independent comparison for the remaining cases. Section 7.1 gives generic family constructions, with regularity conditions and special singular cases; Figure 20 distinguishes those cases. The omitted blow-up and base-change details for the three-cusp family on p. 59 were not reconstructed. Appendix A explicitly conditions its geometric use on the conjectures. Selected table pages were visually inspected, without claiming a complete row-by-row mathematical audit. No new empirical results or universal geometric proof are inferred.

A bounded primary-source lookup on 29 October 2026 confirmed the publisher identity and arXiv v2 dated 21 February 2024. No linked correction was located in that lookup; this is not an exhaustive absence claim. The arXiv mathematical text was not compared.

report: Abstract: This focused review establishes two false intermediate theorems in the reviewed version and a further invalid initial-condition step in the density-transfer proof. A Gaussian heat flow contradicts the bandwidth dependence in Theorem 5.3. A positive \(H^3\) initial density contradicts the mixed regularity asserted in Theorem 8.11. Title: Technical Review of Non-parametric
Learning of Stochastic Differential Equations
# Identity and mathematical scope

R. Bonalli and A. Rudi, Non-parametric Learning of Stochastic Differential Equations with Non-asymptotic Fast Rates of Convergence, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 1497–1552, DOI https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09705-x. The source is the 56-page publisher version of record, online 6 March 2025. A physical PDF page \(j\) is printed page \(1496+j\); all locations below use physical pages.

The model is \(dX_t=b(t,X_t)\,dt+\sqrt{a(t,X_t)}\,dW_t\). Assumption (A), pp. 12–13, uses \(m\ge1\), a known ellipticity floor \(\alpha>0\), \(p_0\in H^{2m+1}\), and smooth coefficient perturbations \((a-\alpha I,b)\in\mathcal H_m\), with \(a-\alpha I\succeq0\). Assumption (B), p. 20, adds compact spatial support for those perturbations. Thus \(a=\alpha I,b=0\) is admissible; the constant diffusion itself is not incorrectly required to be in \(L^2(\mathbb R^n)\).

At \(M\) equally spaced times the construction uses \(N\) independent marginal samples. Page 14 specifies a product law across times. The empirical model is \[\widehat p(t,x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^M c_\ell(t)\widehat g_\ell(x),
 \qquad
 \widehat g_\ell(x)=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N\rho_R(x-X_{\ell,j}),
 \quad \mathcal F\rho_R=1_{\{|\xi|\le R\}},\] where the time functions are Sobolev-kernel cardinal interpolants. The error in Theorem 5.3 includes both \(\partial_t\) error in \(L^2\) and spatial \(H^2\) error. Coefficients are then fitted to the Fokker–Planck residual by a regularized convex problem.

The final accuracy metric is the \(L^2\) distance between marginal densities with the same initial law (pp. 22, 30), not an error norm on the coefficients or a comparison of full path laws. Marginal nonidentifiability alone therefore does not refute the stated metric. The relevant dependency is Theorem 8.11 and Corollary 5.2 \(\longrightarrow\) Theorem 5.3 \(\longrightarrow\) Lemma 5.7 and Theorem 5.8 \(\longrightarrow\) Theorems 5.13–5.14.
# Problem 1: the bandwidth dependence in Theorem 5.3 is false

Equation reference: rate. Assessment: Major; false stated theorem. Theorem 5.3 (p. 14), for a constant independent of \(M,N,R\), asserts \[
 L(\widehat p)\le C
 \bigl(\|p\|_{H^{m+1,2}}^2+\|p\|_{H^{1,2(m+1)}}^2\bigr)
 \bigl(M^{-2m}+R^{-4m}+R^n\log(4M/\delta)/N\bigr)\] with probability at least \(1-\delta\), for \(M\ge2T\).
## Complete admissible counterexample

Set \(n=m=T=\alpha=1\), \(a=1,b=0\), and let \(p_0\) be the standard Gaussian density. Then \(p(t,\cdot)\) is Gaussian with variance \(1+t\); every displayed regularity norm in [rate] (#rate) is finite. Both coefficient assumptions hold with zero perturbation, for any \(R_*>0\). Fix \(M=2,N=1,\delta=1/4\), and let \(R\) tend to infinity. Write the sampled positions as \(Y_1,Y_2\). Their difference is nonzero almost surely under the specified product law. Put \[A_{ij}=\int_0^1c_i(t)c_j(t)\,dt,\qquad S=A_{11}+A_{22}>0 .\] Positivity follows because the continuous cardinal functions are nonzero, independently of the precise equivalent Sobolev norm used to define the time kernel.

Using the Fourier convention \(e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\), Plancherel gives \[\int_0^1\|\partial_x^2\widehat p(t)\|_2^2dt
 =(2\pi)^4\int_{-R}^R\xi^4
       \bigl(S+2A_{12}\cos(2\pi\xi(Y_1-Y_2))\bigr)\,d\xi .\] The diagonal integral is \(2SR^5/5\). For each fixed nonzero \(Y_1-Y_2\), integration by parts shows that the cross integral is \(O(R^4)\); its constant may depend on that sample difference. Consequently the last display divided by \(R^5\) tends almost surely to \((2\pi)^4\,2S/5>0\). The true Gaussian density has finite second-derivative norm, so the reverse triangle inequality gives the same leading order for \(\int\|\partial_x^2(\widehat p-p)\|_2^2dt\). This is a lower bound for \(L(\widehat p)\). The right side of [rate] (#rate) is only \(O(R)\). For every candidate finite \(C\), its inequality therefore fails eventually almost surely. Bounded convergence applied along integer \(R\) makes its success probability tend to zero, contradicting the claimed probability \(3/4\).
## Proof location, alternatives and consequence

Step (3), p. 17, correctly displays a factor \(R^\nu\) multiplying the stochastic Fourier error; \(\nu=2\) is needed here. Step (2), p. 16, also retains sums weighted by time-interpolant norms. Neither those estimates nor Step (5)’s growing \(H^1\) bounds justify their disappearance in Step (6), p. 19. The counterexample is independent of this diagnostic: fixed \(M\) already disproves the spatial factor.

Allowing \(C\) to depend on \(R\) contradicts the explicit quantifiers. Replacing \(H^2\) by \(L^2\) changes the theorem and loses the residual control used in Lemma 5.7. Gaussian smoothness rules out a regularity loophole. A correct derivative-variance analysis and parameter selection are required. This review does not assert a replacement optimal rate. The counterexample concerns the universal bound [rate] (#rate); it is not a direct counterexample for the coupled \(\varepsilon\)-schedule or for the final optimized coefficients.
# Problem 2: mixed regularity does not follow from the initial data

Assessment: Major; false stated theorem. Theorem 8.11 (p. 41) explicitly asserts \(p\in H^{m+1}(0,T;H^{2(m+1)}(\mathbb R^n))\). For \(m=1\), this requires two time derivatives with values in spatial \(H^4\). The assertion is stronger than separate time and spatial regularity.

Take \(n=m=T=\alpha=1\), \(a=1,b=0\) again, but choose \[p_0(x)=\frac{1+|x|}{4}e^{-|x|}.\] This is the convolution of two probability densities \(e^{-|x|}/2\). It is nonnegative, integrates to one, and, with angular-frequency Fourier variable \(k\), \[\widehat p_0(k)=(1+k^2)^{-2},\qquad
 \widehat p(t,k)=e^{-tk^2/2}(1+k^2)^{-2}.\] The \(H^3\) integrand is proportional at infinity to \(k^6 k^{-8}=k^{-2}\), hence \(p_0\in H^3\), exactly as required. All coefficient and support hypotheses remain satisfied.
## Why this is not merely ambiguous notation

The explicit Bochner space in Theorem 8.11 removes any ambiguity. Furthermore, (5.2), p. 15, integrates time Sobolev norms of spatial derivatives; it actually uses mixed regularity. In contrast, the last paragraph of the proof (p. 53) only obtains \[\partial_t^\ell p\in
 L^2(0,T;H^{2(m+1-\ell)}),\quad 0\le\ell\le m+1 .\] For \(m=1\), the displayed Fourier example satisfies these parabolic orders: \((0,4),(1,2),(2,0)\) all have integrable \(k^{-2}\) tails. The implication from these decreasing spatial orders to the stronger Bochner space is invalid.

Interpreting the theorem as separate parabolic regularity would remove this counterexample to that weaker statement, but would not supply the mixed norms in (5.2). For constant-coefficient heat flow, stronger \(p_0\in H^7\) suffices for \(H^2_tH^4_x\), by the same Fourier computation. This is a verified special-case repair only; no general variable-coefficient repair or revised learning rate is claimed.
# Problem 3: a nonzero empirical initial discrepancy is set to zero

Assessment: Major; core proof gap with a conditional repair. In Theorem 5.8’s proof (p. 23), the paper defines \(\rho=p^{\widehat a,\widehat b}-\widehat p\) and states \(\rho(0)=0\). However, cardinal interpolation gives \[\widehat p(0)=\widehat g_1,\qquad
 p^{\widehat a,\widehat b}(0)=p_0,\qquad
 \rho(0)=p_0-\widehat g_1 .\] For the Gaussian example of Problem 1, this difference is nonzero for every finite \(N,R\) and every realization: \(\widehat g_1\) has Fourier support in \([-R,R]\), whereas the Gaussian Fourier transform is nonzero outside that interval. The coefficient optimizer need not be computed to verify this mismatch. The residual sign in the displayed equation is correct; the invalid step is the zero initial condition and the resulting omission of the initial term in the energy bound.
## Verified conditional correction

Assume, separately, a valid approximation bound \(L(\widehat p)\le\eta^2\), a fitted residual bound \(\|\partial_t\widehat p-\widehat L^*\widehat
p\|_2\le B\eta\), and a uniform coefficient bound making \(\widehat L^*:H^2_x\to L^2_x\) bounded by \(B\). Use \(q=p^{\widehat a,\widehat b}-p\), whose initial value really is zero. It solves \[\partial_tq=\widehat L^*q+F,\qquad
 F=\widehat L^*(p-\widehat p)
   +(\widehat L^*\widehat p-\partial_t\widehat p)
   +(\partial_t\widehat p-\partial_t p).\] Hence \(\|F\|_2\le(2B+1)\eta\). The paper’s energy estimate then gives \(\|q\|_{L^2_{t,x}}\le C_B\eta\). This repairs the transfer argument under the stated extra bounds; it does not repair Problems 1–2 or establish their proposed \(\eta\). The gap is Major because the written proof of a central theorem uses a false premise, even though this particular step admits a short conditional correction.
# Checks, limits and conclusion

The coefficient shift, support condition, Gaussian and nonnegative \(H^3\) examples, Fourier cutoff, probability quantifiers, and relevant energy identity were checked directly. The \(L^2\) observation estimate in Corollary 3.5 follows by Cauchy–Schwarz, with the observable’s \(L^2\) norm retained. The strict convexity and weak lower semicontinuity mechanism in Proposition 5.6 is consistent when its bounded-operator hypotheses hold.

This is a focused dependency review, not verification of all 56 pages. Pages 1–24, 29–30, 41–43, 46 and 51–53 were read; inspection of the longer PDE proofs was selective. The finite-dimensional positive-semidefinite approximation theorem, boundary-kernel construction, complexity claims, full existence proofs and external Sobolev estimates were not independently established. Possible notation issues in Theorem 2.1 are not counted as findings, because the intended isotropic versus mixed coefficient space was not resolved. claim: Recorded check: Theorem5.3 loses derivative bandwidth variance
n=m=T=alpha=1. a=1,b=0; zero supported coefficient perturbation. p0 standard Gaussian, all relevant mixed norms finite. M=2,N=1,delta=1/4; R tends to infinity. Samples follow actual product law.
analysis:
Equation reference: rate. Assessment: Major; false stated theorem. Theorem 5.3 (p. 14), for a constant independent of \(M,N,R\), asserts \[
 L(\widehat p)\le C
 \bigl(\|p\|_{H^{m+1,2}}^2+\|p\|_{H^{1,2(m+1)}}^2\bigr)
 \bigl(M^{-2m}+R^{-4m}+R^n\log(4M/\delta)/N\bigr)\] with probability at least \(1-\delta\), for \(M\ge2T\).

Set \(n=m=T=\alpha=1\), \(a=1,b=0\), and let \(p_0\) be the standard Gaussian density. Then \(p(t,\cdot)\) is Gaussian with variance \(1+t\); every displayed regularity norm in [rate] (#rate) is finite. Both coefficient assumptions hold with zero perturbation, for any \(R_*>0\). Fix \(M=2,N=1,\delta=1/4\), and let \(R\) tend to infinity. Write the sampled positions as \(Y_1,Y_2\). Their difference is nonzero almost surely under the specified product law. Put \[A_{ij}=\int_0^1c_i(t)c_j(t)\,dt,\qquad S=A_{11}+A_{22}>0 .\] Positivity follows because the continuous cardinal functions are nonzero, independently of the precise equivalent Sobolev norm used to define the time kernel.

Using the Fourier convention \(e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\), Plancherel gives \[\int_0^1\|\partial_x^2\widehat p(t)\|_2^2dt
 =(2\pi)^4\int_{-R}^R\xi^4
       \bigl(S+2A_{12}\cos(2\pi\xi(Y_1-Y_2))\bigr)\,d\xi .\] The diagonal integral is \(2SR^5/5\). For each fixed nonzero \(Y_1-Y_2\), integration by parts shows that the cross integral is \(O(R^4)\); its constant may depend on that sample difference. Consequently the last display divided by \(R^5\) tends almost surely to \((2\pi)^4\,2S/5>0\). The true Gaussian density has finite second-derivative norm, so the reverse triangle inequality gives the same leading order for \(\int\|\partial_x^2(\widehat p-p)\|_2^2dt\). This is a lower bound for \(L(\widehat p)\). The right side of [rate] (#rate) is only \(O(R)\). For every candidate finite \(C\), its inequality therefore fails eventually almost surely. Bounded convergence applied along integer \(R\) makes its success probability tend to zero, contradicting the claimed probability \(3/4\).

Step (3), p. 17, correctly displays a factor \(R^\nu\) multiplying the stochastic Fourier error; \(\nu=2\) is needed here. Step (2), p. 16, also retains sums weighted by time-interpolant norms. Neither those estimates nor Step (5)’s growing \(H^1\) bounds justify their disappearance in Step (6), p. 19. The counterexample is independent of this diagnostic: fixed \(M\) already disproves the spatial factor.

Allowing \(C\) to depend on \(R\) contradicts the explicit quantifiers. Replacing \(H^2\) by \(L^2\) changes the theorem and loses the residual control used in Lemma 5.7. Gaussian smoothness rules out a regularity loophole. A correct derivative-variance analysis and parameter selection are required. This review does not assert a replacement optimal rate. The counterexample concerns the universal bound [rate] (#rate); it is not a direct counterexample for the coupled \(\varepsilon\)-schedule or for the final optimized coefficients.

claim: Recorded check: Theorem8.11 claims mixed regularity beyond available parabolic orders
n=m=T=alpha=1,a=1,b=0. p0=(1+|x|)exp(-|x|)/4 nonnegative unit mass. p0 Fourier transform (1+k^2)^-2, so H3 but not stronger required mixed trace regularity.
analysis: Assessment: Major; false stated theorem. Theorem 8.11 (p. 41) explicitly asserts \(p\in H^{m+1}(0,T;H^{2(m+1)}(\mathbb R^n))\). For \(m=1\), this requires two time derivatives with values in spatial \(H^4\). The assertion is stronger than separate time and spatial regularity.

Take \(n=m=T=\alpha=1\), \(a=1,b=0\) again, but choose \[p_0(x)=\frac{1+|x|}{4}e^{-|x|}.\] This is the convolution of two probability densities \(e^{-|x|}/2\). It is nonnegative, integrates to one, and, with angular-frequency Fourier variable \(k\), \[\widehat p_0(k)=(1+k^2)^{-2},\qquad
 \widehat p(t,k)=e^{-tk^2/2}(1+k^2)^{-2}.\] The \(H^3\) integrand is proportional at infinity to \(k^6 k^{-8}=k^{-2}\), hence \(p_0\in H^3\), exactly as required. All coefficient and support hypotheses remain satisfied.

The explicit Bochner space in Theorem 8.11 removes any ambiguity. Furthermore, (5.2), p. 15, integrates time Sobolev norms of spatial derivatives; it actually uses mixed regularity. In contrast, the last paragraph of the proof (p. 53) only obtains \[\partial_t^\ell p\in
 L^2(0,T;H^{2(m+1-\ell)}),\quad 0\le\ell\le m+1 .\] For \(m=1\), the displayed Fourier example satisfies these parabolic orders: \((0,4),(1,2),(2,0)\) all have integrable \(k^{-2}\) tails. The implication from these decreasing spatial orders to the stronger Bochner space is invalid.

Interpreting the theorem as separate parabolic regularity would remove this counterexample to that weaker statement, but would not supply the mixed norms in (5.2). For constant-coefficient heat flow, stronger \(p_0\in H^7\) suffices for \(H^2_tH^4_x\), by the same Fourier computation. This is a verified special-case repair only; no general variable-coefficient repair or revised learning rate is claimed.
result: Impact: Finite constants used in density approximation do not follow from stated initial-data assumption; core regularity premise false.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: For constant heat flow, p0 in H7 suffices for H2_t H4_x by Fourier integration. No general variable-coefficient or full learning-rate repair claimed.

problems.title: Theorem5.8 sets empirical initial discrepancy to zero
problems.source_location: Pdf pages: 14 Pdf pages: 23 Pdf pages: 24 Pdf pages: 29 Printed pages: 1510 Printed pages: 1519 Printed pages: 1520 Printed pages: 1525 Labels: Theorem5.8 proof Labels: Equation5.6 Labels: Theorem5.13 dependency
claim: Recorded check: Theorem5.8 sets empirical initial discrepancy to zero
analysis:
Assessment: Major; core proof gap with a conditional repair. In Theorem 5.8’s proof (p. 23), the paper defines \(\rho=p^{\widehat a,\widehat b}-\widehat p\) and states \(\rho(0)=0\). However, cardinal interpolation gives \[\widehat p(0)=\widehat g_1,\qquad
 p^{\widehat a,\widehat b}(0)=p_0,\qquad
 \rho(0)=p_0-\widehat g_1 .\] For the Gaussian example of Problem 1, this difference is nonzero for every finite \(N,R\) and every realization: \(\widehat g_1\) has Fourier support in \([-R,R]\), whereas the Gaussian Fourier transform is nonzero outside that interval. The coefficient optimizer need not be computed to verify this mismatch. The residual sign in the displayed equation is correct; the invalid step is the zero initial condition and the resulting omission of the initial term in the energy bound.

Assume, separately, a valid approximation bound \(L(\widehat p)\le\eta^2\), a fitted residual bound \(\|\partial_t\widehat p-\widehat L^*\widehat
p\|_2\le B\eta\), and a uniform coefficient bound making \(\widehat L^*:H^2_x\to L^2_x\) bounded by \(B\). Use \(q=p^{\widehat a,\widehat b}-p\), whose initial value really is zero. It solves \[\partial_tq=\widehat L^*q+F,\qquad
 F=\widehat L^*(p-\widehat p)
   +(\widehat L^*\widehat p-\partial_t\widehat p)
   +(\partial_t\widehat p-\partial_t p).\] Hence \(\|F\|_2\le(2B+1)\eta\). The paper’s energy estimate then gives \(\|q\|_{L^2_{t,x}}\le C_B\eta\). This repairs the transfer argument under the stated extra bounds; it does not repair Problems 1–2 or establish their proposed \(\eta\). The gap is Major because the written proof of a central theorem uses a false premise, even though this particular step admits a short conditional correction.
