The trace-polynomial definition on p. 2043 uses products of traces of powers of individual matrices. It does not encompass arbitrary mixed noncommutative words. The normalized-trace proof on pp. 2048–2049 passes from rational multiplicity weights to all simplex weights by density and continuity, conditional on the stated half-degree principle. A common denominator accommodates several groups of rational weights if a common matrix size is required. This explains the change in quantifiers between fixed-size and all-size tests. No additional defect in that particular reduction was established here.
# Problems

Problem 1 (Major: an invalid matrix inference in Lemma 2.17).  The proof on p. 2019 argues that a totally positive matrix has positive simple eigenvalues and therefore \(v^TAv>0\) for every nonzero \(v\). The implication is false for a nonsymmetric matrix.

Consider \[A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\4&6\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad v=\begin{pmatrix}-5/2\\1\end{pmatrix}.\] All four entries are positive and \(\det A=2>0\), so every minor is positive. Its eigenvalues are \((7\pm\sqrt{41})/2\), both positive and distinct. Nevertheless, \[v^TAv=-\frac14,\qquad
 \frac{v^TAv}{v^Tv}=-\frac1{29}.\] Thus even the orthogonal compression to a one-dimensional subspace can be negative. This is not an unrelated matrix: \(A\) is the Jacobian of \[(x_1,x_2)\longmapsto(x_1+x_2,\;x_1^2+x_2^2)\] at \((2,3)\), with unit positive weights and increasing positive exponents \((1,2)\), within the hypotheses of the displayed lemma.

The example refutes the inference used in the proof, not the lemma itself. Indeed, in this two-variable unit-weight example the ordered coordinates can be recovered from their first two moments. The issue is that the manuscript has not obtained the asserted positive projected determinants for arbitrary subspaces by its stated reasoning. Lemma 2.17 is then used for boundary-preimage uniqueness in Lemma 2.18 (p. 2020) and for the curved-simplex parametrization in Lemma 3.5 (p. 2031). A replacement argument must establish the necessary injectivity and face regularity for the full weighted, general-exponent setting, including boundary faces. This is a Major gap in the supplied central derivation; it is not a counterexample to the main boundary theorem.

Problem 2 (Major: the displayed reduction map loses its scaling).  On p. 2046 the geometric variables are \((2e_2,6e_3)\), but the displayed homogenization map \(\tau\) substitutes \(e_2/e_1^2\) and \(e_3/e_1^3\). The equivalence asserted on p. 2047 then fails.

It suffices to take one group, \(k=1\), and the permitted integer polynomial \(p(Y)=1-2Y\). The prescribed coefficient bound is \(M=100\deg(p)(|1|+|-2|)=300\). With \(g(Y)=2Y^2-Y\), the auxiliary polynomial is \[q(Y,Z)=(1-2Y)(1-Y)^6+300(Z-2Y^2+Y).\] At the vertex corresponding to \(n=4\), \[(Y,Z)=\left(\frac34,\frac38\right),\qquad
 Z=g(Y)=L(Y),\qquad
 q(Y,Z)=-\frac1{8192}<0.\] This point belongs to the set \(R\) defined in the proof, so assertion (a) on p. 2047 is satisfied.

In contrast, on the infinite probability simplex \(\Delta\) of p. 2044, the displayed map gives \(\tau(q)=q(e_2,e_3)\), since \(e_1=1\). Every point of \(\Delta\) satisfies \[0\leq e_2=\frac{1-\sum_i x_i^2}{2}<\frac12,\qquad e_3\geq0.\] Consequently both terms in \[q(e_2,e_3)
   =(1-2e_2)(1-e_2)^6
     +300\bigl(e_3+e_2(1-2e_2)\bigr)\] are nonnegative. Assertion (b), which requires a negative value of \(\tau(q)\) somewhere on \(\Delta\), is false. This is a global argument on the stipulated domain, not merely a failure at one sampled preimage. At the uniform four-coordinate point itself, \((e_2,e_3)=(3/8,1/16)\) and the printed expression is \(49167625/1048576>0\).

The adjacent prose explicitly uses \(2e_{2,(i)}=x_i\) and \(6e_{3,(i)}=y_i\). It strongly identifies the intended correction: \[\tau_{\mathrm{corr}}(f)=
 \left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}e_{1,(i)}^{3\deg f}\right)
 f\left(
 \frac{2e_{2,(1)}}{e_{1,(1)}^2},\ldots,
 \frac{2e_{2,(k)}}{e_{1,(k)}^2},
 \frac{6e_{3,(1)}}{e_{1,(1)}^3},\ldots,
 \frac{6e_{3,(k)}}{e_{1,(k)}^3}\right).\] The same homogenizing exponent still clears all denominators. On \(\Delta^k\) this gives precisely the scaled substitution used in the geometric argument; the example then has value \(-1/8192\). The correction is local and explicit. Its locality does not make the printed equivalence valid: that equivalence supplies the reduction for Theorem 6.6 and hence Theorem 6.2. The Major assessment concerns this broken core derivation, without alleging that undecidability itself is false or that all cited inputs have been independently reproved.

Problem 3 (Minor: the critical-point quantifier in Lemma 2.28 is too broad).  On pp. 2025–2026 the lemma classifies critical points, whereas its intended application concerns extrema. Under the intended constraints stated in the proof, a smooth admissible fiber has a critical saddle outside both listed types.

Choose \(n=d=3\), \(\alpha=(2,3)\), \(\beta=(4,6)\), and \[a=\frac{3}{\sqrt{20}},\qquad
 x=(0,a,a),\qquad
 c=\frac{81}{200}.\] The intended domain is \(p_2\leq1\), \(p_4=c\). Here \(p_2(x)=9/10<1\) and \(p_4(x)=c\). With inactive inequality multiplier \(\lambda_0=0\) and \(\lambda_1=-27/40\), \[\nabla p_6(x)+\lambda_1\nabla p_4(x)=0.\] The hypersurface \(p_4=c>0\) is smooth. The fiber \(p_2=1\), \(p_4=c\) is also smooth: dependence of these two gradients forces all nonzero absolute coordinates to be equal, giving \(p_4=1/r\) for \(r=1,2,3\), and \(81/200\) is none of these values. This fiber is nonempty; its squared coordinates can be \[\left(\frac13-\frac{\sqrt{43}}{60},
       \frac13-\frac{\sqrt{43}}{60},
       \frac13+\frac{\sqrt{43}}{30}\right).\] Thus the smoothness hypotheses are not evaded by an empty boundary fiber.

The multiplicity vector of \(x\) is \((m_0,m_1)=(1,2)\). It is not type (1), since \(m_1\neq1\), and not type (2), since \(m_0\neq0\). It is a saddle. Writing \(b=a^2=9/20\), a curve with first coordinate \(t\) and the other fourth powers equal to \(b^2-t^4/2\) gives \[p_6=\frac{729}{4000}-\frac{27}{40}t^4+t^6+O(t^8),\] which is smaller for sufficiently small nonzero \(t\). Keeping the first coordinate zero and taking the other fourth powers \(b^2+s\) and \(b^2-s\) gives \[p_6=\frac{729}{4000}+\frac53s^2+O(s^4),\] which is larger for sufficiently small nonzero \(s\). Both curves remain within \(p_2<1\) by continuity.

This disproves the all-critical-points formulation, not the claimed classification of boundary extrema. Accordingly its demonstrated impact is Minor. The statement should specify the intended extrema and supply the argument for zero-coordinate directions, where smoothness of the constraint alone does not make the objective Morse. The displayed \(\widetilde V\) index should also be reconciled with the number of constraints; the example above uses the explicit constraints in the proof, not an opportunistic reading of that index mismatch.

Problem 4 (Major: the proof of Lemma 2.29 is circular).  The connectedness argument on pp. 2026–2027 assumes that \(M\) is disconnected and concludes that \(M\) is disconnected, labeling that conclusion a contradiction.

The intervening argument establishes connectedness of the nonempty slices of \(M\) at fixed coordinate sum. This forces each such slice to belong to only one member of a proposed separation \(M=A\cup B\). It does not by itself prove that the set of attainable coordinate sums is an interval. In particular, the final empty intermediate slice does not contradict the initial assumption or any connectedness of \(M\) already established in that proof.

For the logical distinction, the compact set \[\bigl([0,1]\cup[2,3]\bigr)\times\{0\}\] is disconnected although each nonempty first-coordinate slice is a singleton. This elementary illustration is not offered as a counterexample to the specific Vandermonde assertion. It shows why connected slices alone cannot supply the missing conclusion.

An independent argument that the attainable sum range is an interval, together with compactness and connected fibers, would close this route: a separation would give two disjoint nonempty compact images partitioning that interval. Alternatively, a valid direct connectedness proof could be supplied. The argument must cover the stated singular values as well. Lemma 2.31 explicitly needs Lemma 2.29 to turn finitely many possible boundary preimages into a unique preimage; Lemma 2.32 and Theorem 2.27 then use that uniqueness. These dependencies give the missing argument Major significance within the sub-probability and limiting-boundary development. No counterexample to the connectedness statement or its downstream conclusions has been established here.
# Assessment and verification limits

The report assessment is Major: Problems 1, 2 and 4 require valid central derivations before the supplied proof chain can be relied upon. Problem 3 is deliberately classified as Minor because its verified saddle only defeats an overbroad auxiliary quantifier. The calculations do not support a claim that the principal results are false.

The exact matrix, rational substitution, multiplier and local-series calculations were independently implemented by this reviewer using existing native SymPy facilities, and completed successfully. Their script and literal outputs accompany the report. These checks supplement the displayed analytic arguments; neither finite sampling nor software assertions are used to claim the missing global theorems. Missing optional author code is not a mathematical defect.

A revision should replace the univalence argument, use the scaled homogenization consistently, distinguish critical points from extrema, and supply the missing connectedness step. The Section 5 test-set argument and the normalized-trace parameterization were checked within the limits stated above. All-page reading does not certify every external result, every singular-fiber assertion or every limiting-face incidence. This is an initial scientific review only; scientific decision remains pending and no independent acceptance or human review is recorded.

analysis: The connectedness argument on pp. 2026–2027 assumes that \(M\) is disconnected and concludes that \(M\) is disconnected, labeling that conclusion a contradiction.

The intervening argument establishes connectedness of the nonempty slices of \(M\) at fixed coordinate sum. This forces each such slice to belong to only one member of a proposed separation \(M=A\cup B\). It does not by itself prove that the set of attainable coordinate sums is an interval. In particular, the final empty intermediate slice does not contradict the initial assumption or any connectedness of \(M\) already established in that proof.

For the logical distinction, the compact set \[\bigl([0,1]\cup[2,3]\bigr)\times\{0\}\] is disconnected although each nonempty first-coordinate slice is a singleton. This elementary illustration is not offered as a counterexample to the specific Vandermonde assertion. It shows why connected slices alone cannot supply the missing conclusion.

An independent argument that the attainable sum range is an interval, together with compactness and connected fibers, would close this route: a separation would give two disjoint nonempty compact images partitioning that interval. Alternatively, a valid direct connectedness proof could be supplied. The argument must cover the stated singular values as well. Lemma 2.31 explicitly needs Lemma 2.29 to turn finitely many possible boundary preimages into a unique preimage; Lemma 2.32 and Theorem 2.27 then use that uniqueness. These dependencies give the missing argument Major significance within the sub-probability and limiting-boundary development. Author: AI-assisted initial technical review

Title: Technical Review of
Interlacing Polynomial Method for Matrix Approximation via Generalized Column and Row Selection
# Identity and review scope

The reviewed source is Jian-Feng Cai, Zhiqiang Xu and Zili Xu, Interlacing Polynomial Method for Matrix Approximation via Generalized Column and Row Selection, arXiv:2312.01715v2, dated 18 April 2025, 44 pages [paper]. The assigned journal identity is DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09719-5 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09719-5), and the assigned paper identifier is M25-0463. The acquired author version is not assumed equivalent to the 50-page journal version identified in the source metadata. All page references below refer to this 44-page PDF; printed and physical page numbers agree.

All pages, including the appendices and bibliography, were read as extracted text. Source evidence on pp. 1, 4–6, 15–18, 20–21, 23–25, 27–29, 35, 37–38 and 40 was additionally inspected as page images. Detailed checks covered the algebraic definitions, the stability/interlacing proof route, coefficient extraction, candidate-domain conditions and the retained-versus-deleted submatrix indices. Existing native SymPy facilities were used for independently written exact checks. No author code was executed and no empirical software performance was reproduced. The external real-stability and barrier results were used as cited inputs, not independently reproved from all their original sources.
# Main constructions and checks

For \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_B}\) and \(C\in\mathbb R^{n_C\times d}\), define \[Q_S=I_n-B_{:,S}B_{:,S}^{\dagger},\qquad
 P_R=I_d-C_{R,:}^{\dagger}C_{R,:}.\] The residual characteristic polynomial is \(p_{S,R}(x)=\det(xI_d-P_RA^TQ_SAP_R)\). The polynomial \(P_{k,r}\) on p. 4 is the sum of these polynomials weighted by \(\det(B_{:,S}^TB_{:,S})\det(C_{R,:}C_{R,:}^T)\). When \(k\leq\operatorname{rank}B\) and \(r\leq\operatorname{rank}C\), some such weights are positive; rank-deficient subsets have zero weight. Thus a zero-volume subset must not be mistaken for a positive-weight interlacing candidate.

The block determinant in Proposition 3.3 has positive semidefinite variable coefficients. Subject to the stated stability-preserving operations and nonvanishing, its derivative/specialization representation gives real-rootedness. Once real-rootedness is known, nonnegative weights and the common sign of the summands on \(x<0\) rule out negative roots. In Lemma 4.1, replacing a column projection changes the associated block Gram matrix by a rank-one term; the convex combination is represented by \((1+\partial_t)\) applied to a determinant with a positive semidefinite \(t\) coefficient. This supports the common-interlacing argument for nonzero projected directions. The successive largest-root comparisons then terminate in the squared spectral norm of the residual.

The error accumulation argument of Theorem 1.2 also has a direct interpretation: minimizing numbers that are each within \(\eta\) of the true largest roots incurs at most \(2\eta\) relative to the best child at each selection. Summing over \(k+r\) steps gives the stated additive \(2(k+r)\eta\), provided the polynomials and candidate set are correct. Problem 1 concerns a supplied route for computing those polynomials, rather than this elementary accumulation inequality.

Exact direct enumeration was compared with formula (3.5b) and the corrected coefficient extraction for six choices \((k,r)\in\{0,1,2\}\times\{0,1\}\) using \[A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\\2&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
 B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\1&0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
 C=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\2&2\end{pmatrix}.\] All agreed exactly, including dependent source columns and rows. Four additional exact instances checked the mixed derivative identity (3.9), using a nonsymmetric \(3\times3\) integer target and \(B=C=I_3\). These finite checks support the inspected derivations but do not substitute for their general proofs.
# Problems

Problem 1 (Major: the wrong coefficient index in (A.16)).  After differentiating \(\widehat k\) times with respect to \(y\) and setting \(y=0\), equation (A.16) on p. 38 uses \(\mu_{j,c_1,\widehat r}\) in place of \(\mu_{j,c_1,\widehat k}\). This computes a different polynomial when the two indices differ.

For an exact admissible example take \[n=d=d_B=2,\quad n_C=1,\quad
 A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix},\quad B=I_2,\quad C=0_{1\times2},
 \quad k=1,\quad r=0,\quad S=R=\varnothing.\] Here \(\operatorname{rank}B=2\), \(\operatorname{rank}C=0\), so all rank conditions hold. The empty row selection uses the explicitly stated empty-determinant convention. Directly from Definition 1.1, \[P_{1,0}(x)=x(x-4)+x(x-1)=2x^2-5x.\] Both column weights are one. In Appendix A.6 the same instance gives \[V=I_2,\qquad W=\operatorname{diag}(1,4,0),\qquad
 g(x,y,z)=(x+z)(x+y-1)(x+y-4).\] The printed final formula instead selects \(\mu_{2,1,0}=-5\) and \(\mu_{3,1,0}=4\), giving \[P_{\mathrm{printed}}(x)=-5x^2+4x.\] Its largest root is \(4/5\), whereas the correct polynomial has largest root \(5/2\). The two feasible residual squared norms are \(4\) and \(1\). Thus \(4/5\) cannot certify any feasible choice in this example. The leading coefficient also changes from the positive total volume weight \(2\) to \(-5\); multiplying by a nonzero scalar cannot repair the wrong root location.

This is a Major defect in the explicit computation and certificate derivation used for Lemma 4.2 and the polynomial evaluation in Algorithm 1. It is locally repairable by the index correction above, which follows for all coefficient arrays and was additionally checked on the six stated configurations. The abstract Algorithm 1 calls for the correctly defined \(P\); no full trajectory violating its guarantee with correctly computed polynomials is claimed. Theorem 1.1 and determinant formula (3.5b) are not refuted by this example.

Problem 2 (Minor: zero directions must be excluded before normalization).  Algorithm 1, p. 21, normalizes every remaining candidate in lines 3 and 10, but excludes zero projected directions only later in lines 5 and 12.

For example, let \(A=I_2\), \(B=[e_1,0,e_2]\), \(C=0_{1\times2}\), \(k=1\) and \(r=0\). The rank conditions hold, yet line 3 visits the second column and requests \(q_2=0/0\). The Moore–Penrose convention elsewhere does not define this normalization.

Restrict candidate preparation and polynomial evaluation to \(\{i:Q_Sb_i\neq0\}\) and \(\{i:P_Rc_i\neq0\}\) before dividing. This is exactly the admissible-set restriction already present in Lemma 4.1. Until the desired rank is reached, the rank assumptions guarantee that an admissible direction remains. The omission is Minor because the proof supplies the correct domain and this guard restores its intended implementation without changing the interlacing argument. No floating-point tolerance rule is prescribed or verified here.

Take \(M=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,3)\) and \(k=2\). The sum is \(3x-6\), so the printed left side is \(3x/2-3\), whereas the derivative is \(6x-12\). Each deletion set is counted \(k!\) times by repeated differentiation, giving the corrected factor.

The following proof of Proposition 3.5 already uses the correct normalization, as seen in the denominator \((k-|S|)!\) immediately below (A.9). Moreover, an overall positive scalar does not change roots. This is therefore a Minor displayed-identity error, not an established failure of Proposition 3.5 or the submatrix bound.

Problem 4 (Minor: the definition of \(\alpha\) needs a projected-zero case).  Theorem 1.3 on p. 6 and Lemma 5.2 on p. 24 define \(\alpha\) using \(U^TAA^TU/\|U^TAA^TU\|_2\) without separately excluding a zero denominator.

For \(A=e_3\in\mathbb R^3\) and \(B=[e_1,e_2]\), one may take \(U=B\), \(m=2\) and \(k=1\). The target is nonzero but \(U^TAA^TU=0\), so the displayed normalized matrix is undefined. It is consequently inappropriate to evaluate the condition involving \(\alpha\) for this input without a convention.

The case is harmless once stated correctly. If \(BB^\dagger A=0\), then every selected-column projection also annihilates \(A\), and the residual is exactly \(A\). Handle this case first, and define \(\alpha\) only when the normalization denominator is positive. This repairs the domain statement; it does not furnish a counterexample to the nondegenerate reconstruction inequality.

Problem 5 (Minor: Lemma 6.1 needs an upper bound on the differentiation order).  On p. 27 the integer \(k\) is required only to exceed \(\beta d/(1+\beta)\). For \(k\geq d\), the iterated Laguerre derivative is constant or zero, so its largest root is not defined by the paper’s stated conventions.

For \[d=2,\qquad p(x)=(x-\tfrac14)(x-\tfrac34),\qquad \beta=\tfrac12,
 \qquad L=\partial_x\,x\,\partial_x,\] the choice \(k=2\) satisfies \(k>2/3\), but \(L^2p=4\). At \(k=3\), \(L^3p=0\), and the radical in the displayed right side is also outside its real range. The usual nonconstant statement should specify \[\frac{\beta d}{1+\beta}<k<d,\] or explicitly handle the exhausted-degree cases with separate conventions.

The application to Theorem 1.4 on p. 29 uses deletion order \(d-k\) with positive retained size \(k\), so it remains below \(d\). This domain omission does not refute that theorem. At \(\beta=0\), the minimizing \(b\) in the proof is the endpoint \(b=1\), which is outside the open domain \(b>1\); the infimum is obtained by the one-sided limit. That endpoint can be treated directly because all original roots are zero.
# Root bounds and assessment limits

The inspected GCSS argument separates the target into its part in \(\operatorname{range}B\) and its orthogonal complement. The cross terms vanish in the residual Gram matrix, and the operator-norm triangle inequality gives Lemma 5.1. The multiaffine expression in Proposition 5.1 uses complement-indexed coefficients and substitution \(z_i=x/2\); the factor of two from differentiating a squared variable explains this substitution. The barrier result then applies conditional on its cited hypotheses, with the positive normalization addressed in Problem 4.

For the square-submatrix result, the derivative order counts deleted rows and columns, whereas Theorem 1.4 counts retained indices. With roots in \([0,1]\), the paired roots of \(p(x^2)\) have mean zero and second moment \(\beta\). The stated barrier estimate yields \[f(b)=(1-\beta)(1-k/d)
       +(1-k/d)(b+\beta-1)
       +\frac{(k/d)\beta}{b+\beta-1}.\] Minimizing the last two terms gives the displayed root bound in the nonconstant range, with the \(\beta=0\) endpoint treated by a limit. These checks do not independently reprove the cited barrier theorem itself.

The report assessment is Major because (A.16), as printed, fails to compute the polynomial on which a central algorithmic certificate relies. The explicit correction restores that coefficient extraction. Problems 2–5 are separately calibrated Minor: the demonstrated effects are local domain or normalization defects, with the relevant repaired reasoning stated above. No counterexample to the correctly formulated interlacing existence theorem, the nondegenerate GCSS inequality or the retained-submatrix bound has been established.

Exact checks were performed with reviewer-written scripts and their literal results are retained. Two unsuccessful helper executions, caused by structural rather than expanded symbolic comparison and an initially rejected overwrite, are preserved alongside the corrected successful execution. They are not scientific counterexamples. No claim of certified bit complexity, numerical stability, author implementation correctness or experimental reproduction is made. Missing optional code is not a defect. This is initial review only: scientific decision is pending, human reviews are empty, and independent acceptance has not been performed.

report: Abstract: The acquired author manuscript develops a useful trace-based framework for multisymplectic finite element methods. The local Green-identity argument and the passage from local conservation to global conservation under a strong flux condition withstand the checks described below. A Major problem occurs in the general reduced-space result: a one-sided orthogonal projection of a symmetric penalty need not be symmetric. A complete one-triangle example satisfies the stated hypotheses and all variational equations but has nonzero multisymplectic boundary pairing. Author: AI-assisted initial technical review

Title: Technical Review of
Multisymplecticity in Finite Element Exterior Calculus
# Identity and scope

The reviewed source is Ari Stern and Enrico Zampa, Multisymplecticity in Finite Element Exterior Calculus, arXiv:2312.03657v2, 30 May 2025, 35 pages [paper]. The assigned identifier is M25-0464 and the journal DOI is 10.1007/s10208-025-09720-y (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09720-y). The source metadata identifies a 50-page journal version, but that version was not compared with this manuscript. No equivalence or correction status is assumed. All page references below use the acquired PDF, whose physical and printed page numbers agree.

All 35 pages were read as extracted text, including the references. Evidence pages 1, 5, 7, 9, 11–12, 14–16, 18–21, 24–26, 28–29 and 31–32 were also visually inspected. The detailed review followed the continuous conservation law, the hybrid formulation, its local and global criteria, and the assumptions for the AFW-H, LDG-H, XG, IP-H and reduced-space constructions. Native SymPy was used for reviewer-written exact polynomial integrals and identities. No author code was executed. The external weak-trace, finite-element stability and approximation results were used conditionally rather than independently reproved.
# Structure of the argument

Lemma 3.9, p. 14, correctly isolates the discrete issue. Testing the two linearized equations against the opposite interior variation and subtracting gives \[[\widehat w_1-w_1,\widehat w_2-w_2]_{\partial K}
       =[\widehat w_1,\widehat w_2]_{\partial K}.\] The symmetry of \(f'\) is essential here. Lemmas 3.12–3.13 then give sufficient flux conditions, provided the stated trace differences belong to the permitted test space. Strong conservativity is a separate requirement: normal traces must reverse sign across an interior facet while tangential traces agree. Under these conditions, the facet terms cancel as required in Theorem 3.17, p. 16. Merely imposing a weak orthogonality condition does not give this cancellation without the trace-space membership argument.

For AFW-H, the trace equality and the Riesz argument on the quotient by tangential bubbles establish the hybrid/conforming equivalence. The two-equilateral-simplex example of Lemma 4.4, p. 19, explains a family-level failure of strong multisymplecticity for conforming scalar elements in dimension greater than one. It does not assert failure for every particular Hamiltonian or every mesh. The \(k=n\) strong-conservation argument uses independently specifiable facet traces; its degree notation needs the correction in Problem 2.

For ordinary LDG-H with the full normal trace space, symmetric penalties give the local cancellation directly. For IP-H, the inclusions \(\delta W_h^k\subset W_h^{k-1}\) and \(dW_h^k\subset W_h^{k+1}\) justify the residual test functions used in Theorem 4.17, pp. 25–26. The residual inner products are symmetric. The primal-hybrid calculation of Theorem 4.27, pp. 31–32, similarly relies on test orthogonality and symmetric penalties. These arguments should be distinguished from the projection step in the next problem.
# Problems

Problem 1 (Major: the normal-containment branch of Theorem 4.21 needs a compatible penalty).  Section 4.2, p. 21, allows a bounded symmetric facetwise penalty operator. Section 4.4, pp. 28–29, sets both approximate trace spaces equal to a broken space \(M\), and equation (49) gives \[\widehat z^\mathrm{nor}=P\bigl[z^\mathrm{nor}-\alpha(\widehat z^\mathrm{tan}-z^\mathrm{tan})\bigr],\] where \(P\) is orthogonal projection onto \(M\). Theorem 4.21 asserts strong multisymplecticity when either \(W_h^\mathrm{nor}\subset M\) or \(W_h^\mathrm{tan}\subset M\). In the first branch, the proof identifies the method with an LDG-H method having projected penalty \(P\alpha\). Symmetry of \(\alpha\) does not imply symmetry of \(P\alpha\).

Here is a complete admissible counterexample. Let the mesh consist of the single triangle \[K=\{(x,y):x\geq0,\ y\geq0,\ x+y\leq1\}.\] Take \(W_h(K)\) to consist only of degree-zero forms in the one-dimensional space \[W_h^0(K)=\mathop{\mathrm{span}}\{\phi\},\qquad
 \phi(x,y)=x(1-x-y)(2x-1+y),\] with all other form degrees zero. These are smooth polynomial forms and meet the regularity and trace assumptions on p. 11. No subcomplex assumption is imposed on the general LDG-H space. Let both approximate trace spaces be \[M=\prod_{e\subset\partial K}\mathcal P_0\Lambda^0(e).\] The normal trace of every interior zero-form is zero, so \(W_h^\mathrm{nor}=\{0\}\subset M\), precisely the first branch of Theorem 4.21.

On the unit-length edge \(e_0=\{y=0\}\), put \[m=1,\qquad t=x(1-x)(2x-1),\qquad
 \langle t,m\rangle_{e_0}=0,\qquad c=\langle t,t\rangle_{e_0}=\frac1{210}.\] Extend \(m\) by zero to the other edges. The trace of \(\phi\) is \(t\) on \(e_0\) and zero on both other edges. Define the penalty on \(e_0\) by \[\alpha v=v+\langle t,v\rangle_{e_0}m+\langle m,v\rangle_{e_0}t,\] and take the identity on the other edges and on unused form degrees. This is a bounded, symmetric, facetwise operator. It is even strictly positive: its perturbation of the identity has operator norm \(\|t\|\|m\|=1/\sqrt{210}<1\). In particular, \[\alpha m=m+t,\qquad \alpha t=t+cm.\] Nevertheless \(P\alpha m=m\), whereas \(\alpha Pm=m+t\).

Choose \(f=0\), the zero base solution, and the following two variations: \[\begin{array}{c|ccc}
 &w_i&\widehat w_i^\mathrm{tan}&\widehat w_i^\mathrm{nor}\\ \hline
 i=1&\phi&0&cm\\
 i=2&0&m&-m .
\end{array}\] They satisfy every equation in Definition 3.6, p. 14. Indeed, for every interior test \(w_h=a\phi\), the bulk term \((w_i,Dw_h)_K\) vanishes by form degree, the test normal trace is zero, and the remaining normal/tangential pairing is a multiple of \(\langle m,t\rangle=0\). Thus (19a) holds. The two unprojected flux residuals in (19b), restricted to \(e_0\), are \[cm+\alpha(-t)=-t,\qquad -m+\alpha m=t.\] Both are orthogonal to \(M\), and all other edge residuals vanish. Finally, there are no interior facets and the approximate tangential test space vanishing on the entire boundary is \(\{0\}\); hence (19c) holds. The system is homogeneous and linear, so these are also variations along actual solution families, not nonintegrable formal directions.

This is a Major defect in the general theorem, with a bounded repair. For its normal-containment branch one can require \(P\alpha=\alpha P\), or the weaker symmetry of \(P\alpha\) on the actual trace-difference space. Then the skew pairing of the two projected penalty terms vanishes. Alternatively, a genuinely self-adjoint compression \(P\alpha P\) can be used. The \(W_h^\mathrm{tan}\subset M\) branch is supported by Lemma 3.13 and is not refuted. Nor does the example refute the standard scalar or compatible graded penalties, which commute with the relevant projection. If only those penalties were intended in Section 4.4, that restriction needs to be stated explicitly.

Problem 2 (Minor: the BDM trace degree in Proposition 4.6).  The first displayed trace-space identity in the proof on p. 20 assigns the same facet space \(\mathcal P_r\Lambda^{n-1}(e)\) to both \(\mathcal P_{r+1}\Lambda^{n-1}(K)\) and \(\mathcal P_{r+1}^{-}\Lambda^{n-1}(K)\). For the full-polynomial choice the degree is \(r+1\); for the trimmed choice it is \(r\).

For example, with \(n=2\) and \(r=0\), the form \(x\,dx\) belongs to \(\mathcal P_1\Lambda^1(K)\), and its tangential trace on \(y=0\) is \(x\,dx\), which is not constant. This directly contradicts the displayed \(\mathcal P_0\) trace identity for the BDM branch. Replace the degree by \(r+1\) in that branch and make the same change in the subsequent jump inclusion. The proof only needs the correct full product of facet trace spaces, whose traces can still be specified independently. Accordingly this correction does not refute the strong-multisymplectic conclusion of Proposition 4.6.

Problem 3 (Minor: an exterior-boundary term is missing in the XG formula).  On p. 24, the piecewise expression following (43) gives \(\check z_h^\mathrm{nor}=-\alpha\check z_h^\mathrm{tan}\) on \(\partial\Omega\). But Definition 3.2 makes the tangential jump equal to the trace itself on the exterior boundary. Equation (42b), as well as the strong expression immediately above the piecewise formula, therefore gives \[\check z_h^\mathrm{nor}=\alpha(z_h^\mathrm{tan}-\check z_h^\mathrm{tan})
       \qquad\text{on }\partial\Omega.\] For scalar boundary values \(z_h^\mathrm{tan}=1\), \(\check z_h^\mathrm{tan}=0\) and \(\alpha=1\), the correct normal correction is \(1\), whereas the printed branch gives \(0\) and leaves a nonzero residual in (42b). Restore \(+\alpha z_h^\mathrm{tan}\). The proof of Theorem 4.15 uses the preceding correct strong expression, so this local displayed error is not a counterexample to the equivalence theorem.
## Constitutive scope of Example 2.24: no established defect

The Maxwell illustration on p. 9 first introduces linear constitutive relations, then identifies \(\epsilon\) and \(\mu\) with Hodge star operators and invokes the reciprocity principle (16). The Hodge star was defined from a symmetric inner product on p. 3, and the derivation of (16) on p. 9 explicitly assumes a symmetric derivative. These qualifications are part of the source claim.

Linearity alone would not suffice. For example, at frequency \(1\), let \(\mu=I\), \[\epsilon=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\-1&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad E_1=e_1,\quad E_2=e_2,\quad H_i=B_i=0,
 \quad D_i=\epsilon E_i,\quad J_i=-i\epsilon E_i.\] Both curl systems hold, while the two displayed Lorentz expressions equal \(-i\) and \(i\). However, this nonsymmetric \(\epsilon\) does not satisfy the metric Hodge identification used in the example. The calculation therefore demonstrates why the qualification matters; it does not refute the example under its full assumptions.

Making reciprocal transpose symmetry \(\epsilon^T=\epsilon\), \(\mu^T=\mu\), the needed nondegeneracy, and the complex-bilinear convention explicit would improve the application statement. Hermitian symmetry is a different condition. This is an explanatory suggestion, not a counted Minor defect. The initial report’s Minor classification of this item has been withdrawn after checking the source’s qualifying sentences; Proposition 2.12 and the conditional reciprocity argument are not contradicted.
# Assessment and limits

The report assessment is Major because Theorem 4.21, with the general bounded symmetric penalties allowed in the manuscript, contains a false branch. Problem 1 supplies the full spaces, operator, base solution, variations, weak-equation checks and nonzero conservation defect. It also identifies why the ordinary symmetry argument breaks and which additional condition restores it. The conclusion is narrower than a rejection of the framework: the Green identity, the local trace criterion, the strong-conservation cancellation and the compatible-penalty examples are not invalidated by this example.

Problems 2–3 have separate Minor calibration because their demonstrated effects are a local degree identity and a displayed boundary term whose surrounding proof retains the right formula. The Maxwell discussion is a scope clarification and is not counted as a mathematical defect. No unverified conjecture is counted as an established defect. No claim is made that conservation alone proves convergence, coercivity, long-time stability or numerical superiority. No empirical solver experiment was reproduced, and missing optional code is not treated as a mathematical defect.

The findings apply only to the acquired version. This report records the initial technical review as corrected during focused independent acceptance, whose checks are recorded in the accompanying provenance. Scientific decision remains pending and human reviews are empty.

report: Abstract: The manuscript develops a useful fixed-Gram parametrization of compatible transport families and applies it to mean-field variational inference. The geometric reduction, the conditional smoothness calculation and much of the approximation argument are supported by the checks below. Four Major issues affect specific stated results: accelerated extrapolation outside the domain of the hypotheses, insufficient monotonicity constraints for the higher-order dictionary, an invalid Gaussian-tail leverage bound, and a missing metric factor in the mixture-flow equations. Five Minor corrections concern attainment, a repairable stochastic-gradient proof, two printed experimental formulas and a static reproduction-script error. The report distinguishes false statements from proof gaps and historical code limitations. It concerns the acquired 49-page arXiv v4; scientific adjudication remains pending.
Author: AI-assisted initial technical review

Title: Technical Review of
Algorithms for Mean-Field Variational Inference Via Polyhedral Optimization in the Wasserstein Space
# Identity, evidence and scope

The source reviewed is Yiheng Jiang, Sinho Chewi and Aram-Alexandre Pooladian, Algorithms for Mean-Field Variational Inference Via Polyhedral Optimization in the Wasserstein Space, arXiv:2312.02849v4, submitted 29 May 2025, with title-page date 10 June 2025 [paper]. The assigned identifier is M25-0465; the journal DOI is 10.1007/s10208-025-09721-x (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09721-x). The 52-page journal version was not compared with this acquired 49-page manuscript. The shorter conference publication is not the reviewed source. Page numbers below are the coinciding physical and printed PDF numbers.

All 49 pages were read, including proofs and bibliography. Evidence pages 1, 8–10, 13, 16–17, 19, 21–27, 35, 37, 40–45 and 47–49 were visually inspected. The associated repository snapshot is `APooladian/MFVI`, commit `67dca0dde3cac127c2d49228240b5af581ec400c`, dated 29 February 2024. Its README, requirements, six Python files and all source cells of three example notebooks were read statically. This older commit is not certified as the source of the v4 figures. No author code was executed. Reviewer-written SymPy calculations, scalar high-precision Gaussian-tail bounds and a static AST check supply the decisive checks below; none is an experimental reproduction.
# Argument and supported components

Compatibility makes the coupling \((T^\lambda,T^\eta)_\#\rho\) optimal, yielding \[W_2^2(\mu_\lambda,\mu_\eta)
       =(\lambda-\eta)^TQ(\lambda-\eta).\] Section 4 assumes \(Q\) positive definite. With dependent generators, the earlier semidefinite formulation needs the corresponding quotient interpretation. For centered generators and a translation parameter, the metric becomes \(Q\oplus I\). The reduction to finite-dimensional optimization is valuable, but the domain on which the objective is smooth remains part of the hypotheses after that reduction.

Under \(\ell I\preceq\nabla^2V\preceq LI\), the mean-field self-consistency equations give the same curvature bounds for the marginal potentials. The one-dimensional monotone transport has derivative between \(L^{-1/2}\) and \(\ell^{-1/2}\). Differentiation of the Monge–Ampere equation, pp. 36–38, supports the stated second- and third-derivative bounds, conditional on the cited contraction and concentration inputs. The piecewise linear approximation then combines Gaussian truncation, interpolation error and tensorization. The higher-order interpolation can improve the approximation order, but its asserted feasible family is too large; this is distinct from disproving the existence of the specially constructed interpolant.

For feasible maps \(T^\lambda=\alpha\,\mathrm{id}+\sum_T\lambda_TT\) with \(DT^\lambda\succeq\alpha I\), Proposition 5.11 bounds the entropy Hessian by the derivative Gram form: \[\nabla^2 H\preceq\alpha^{-2}Q^{(1)}
       \preceq\alpha^{-2}\Upsilon Q.\] The potential contribution is at most \(LQ\). The centering argument correctly separates translations. Lemma 5.13 bounds \(\Upsilon\) using a conditional cell variance of order \(\delta^2\), when \(R\delta\) is controlled. That argument differs essentially from the uniform leverage estimate examined below.

The stochastic theorem assumes one sample for the potential gradient, exact computation of the entropy gradient, and no translation variables. The conditional variance calculation can use covariance bounded by second moments. The mean-field integration-by-parts identity and curvature estimate give the required gradient second-moment control. The resulting theorem conditional on the actual constant \(\Xi\) should be distinguished from the claimed dictionary-specific rate. The experiments also require separate interpretation: the mixture and improper-prior logistic examples lie outside the principal strong-log-concavity assumptions, as the manuscript acknowledges; an empirical covariance distance alone does not verify full Wasserstein convergence.
# Problems

Problem 1 (Major: accelerated extrapolation leaves the assumed domain).  Theorem 4.2, p. 9, assumes strong convexity and smoothness only on \(K_\#\rho\). Algorithm 1, p. 10, evaluates gradients at extrapolated coefficients \(\eta^{(t)}\), which need not belong to \(K\). The following example satisfies the stated hypotheses and produces a permanent two-cycle.

Take \(\rho=N(0,1)\), the single compatible bijection \(T(x)=x+1\), and coefficient set \(K=[1,2]\). Then \[\mu_\lambda=N(\lambda,\lambda^2),\qquad Q=2,\qquad
 W_2^2(\mu_\lambda,\mu_\eta)=2(\lambda-\eta)^2.\] Define \(F(\mu)=g(\mathbb E_\mu X)\), where \[g(x)=x^2+4x+
 \begin{cases}
 48(1-x)^3,&x<1,\\
 0,&1\leq x\leq2,\\
 6(x-2)^3,&x>2.
 \end{cases}\] The function is \(C^2\), and on \(K\) its Hessian is \(2\). Thus \(F\) is geodesically \(m=1\) strongly convex and \(M=4\) smooth in the \(Q\)-metric; a smoothness bound need not be minimal. The minimizer is \(\lambda_\star=1\), \(\kappa=4\), and the momentum coefficient is \(1/3\).

Starting with \(\lambda^{(0)}=\eta^{(0)}=2\), the projected step is \(\lambda^{(t+1)}=\mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{[1,2]}(\eta^{(t)}-g'(\eta^{(t)})/8)\). The exact successive values are \[\begin{array}{c|ccc}
 \eta^{(t)}&g'(\eta^{(t)})&\lambda^{(t+1)}&\eta^{(t+1)}\\ \hline
 2&8&1&2/3\\
 2/3&-32/3&2&7/3\\
 7/3&32/3&1&2/3 .
\end{array}\] The last two rows repeat. At \(t=2\), the objective gap is \(g(2)-g(1)=7\), whereas Theorem 4.2(b) gives \[(1-1/\sqrt4)^2
 \left(7+\frac12 W_2^2(\mu_2,\mu_1)\right)
 =\frac14(7+1)=2.\] Thus the theorem is false under its stated domain assumptions, not merely missing a citation.

The mean-field KL application has a concrete version of the domain gap, although the preceding counterexample is not a KL counterexample. Let \(\rho=\pi=N(0,1)\), \(T(x)=x\), \(\alpha=1\), and \(\lambda\geq0\). Then \[f(\lambda)=\frac12\bigl[(1+\lambda)^2-1-\log(1+\lambda)^2\bigr],
 \qquad f''(\lambda)=1+(1+\lambda)^{-2}\leq2\] on the cone. With \(m=1,M=2,\lambda^{(0)}=1/10\), the first projected iterate is \(1/220\), and the first extrapolate is \[\eta^{(1)}=\frac{-31+21\sqrt2}{110}<0.\] It is greater than \(-1\), so the Gaussian remains defined, but \(f''(\eta^{(1)})>2\). The smoothness bound proved on the cone therefore does not cover this actual query. This leaves the invocation in Theorem 5.12 without the required argument; it does not establish divergence of KL APGD.

A repair must either supply valid smoothness and convexity bounds on every extrapolation point or analyze an accelerated scheme whose gradient queries stay in an appropriate domain. Projecting the momentum point is a possible algorithmic change, but its original rate does not follow merely by inserting that projection.

Problem 2 (Major: the higher-order constraints do not ensure monotonicity).  Equation (24), p. 40, constrains the total signed sum of quadratic coefficients, whereas monotonicity requires all intermediate slopes to be controlled. Let \(d=1\), \(\alpha=\delta=1\), and use adjacent cells \([-1,0]\) and \([0,1]\). Set the negative quadratic coefficient on the first cell to \(1\), the positive quadratic coefficient on the second to \(1\), and all other coefficients, including the linear and cubic coefficients, to zero. Both constraints in (24) hold: the total signed quadratic sum is zero and the negative cubic cap is satisfied.

Writing \(\psi(u)=0\) for \(u\leq0\), \(u^2\) for \(0\leq u\leq1\), and \(2u-1\) for \(u\geq1\), the resulting map is \[T(x)=x-\psi(x+1)+\psi(x).\] On the first cell \(T(x)=x-(x+1)^2\), and on the second \(T(x)=x-(2x+1)+x^2\). Consequently \(T'(0)=-1\), with negative derivative throughout \((-1/2,1/2)\). The map folds and is not the gradient of a convex potential or a bijection. Scaling both nonzero coefficients to \(\alpha\delta\) gives slope \(-\alpha\) at the shared knot for any mesh size \(\delta>0\). This is not a coarse-mesh artifact.

The specially constructed interpolating approximation may satisfy these stronger conditions. The example does not disprove existence of a higher-order approximant with the claimed accuracy. It disproves the blanket monotonicity claim for the specified feasible set, which is needed for the stated geometry and algorithmic use.

Problem 3 (Major: the uniform leverage bound loses Gaussian tail mass).  Lemma 5.15, p. 22, claims \(\Xi\lesssim J^2\), where the centered ramp vector \(s(x)\) has Gram matrix \(Q=\mathbb E[s(Z)s(Z)^T]\), \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), and \[s(x)^TQ^{-1}s(x)\leq\Xi J\quad\text{for all }x.\] Consider its last ramp on \([R-\delta,R]\), denoted \(\psi\), and write \(p=\Pr\{Z\geq R-\delta\}\). Since \(0\leq\psi\leq1\) and \(\psi\) vanishes to the left of that interval, \[s_j(R)=1-\mathbb E\psi\geq1-p,\qquad
 Q_{jj}=\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}(\psi)\leq\mathbb E\psi^2\leq p.\] The coordinate Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in the \(Q\)-metric gives \[s(R)^TQ^{-1}s(R)\geq\frac{s_j(R)^2}{Q_{jj}}
 \geq\frac{(1-p)^2}{p},\qquad
 \frac{\Xi}{J^2}\geq\frac{(1-p)^2}{pJ^3}.\] Here \(Q\) is positive definite: a linear combination of centered ramps that vanishes almost everywhere has zero derivative on every separate cell, forcing every coefficient to vanish.

Take \(R\to\infty\), \(\varepsilon=e^{-R^2/4}\), and \[J=\left\lceil\frac{2R}{\sqrt{\varepsilon/R}}\right\rceil,
 \qquad \delta=\frac{2R}{J}.\] These have the Gaussian truncation and mesh scaling used in the linear approximation; in particular \(R\delta\to0\). Mills’ bound with \(a=R-\delta\) gives \(p\leq e^{-a^2/2}/(a\sqrt{2\pi})\). Since \(J\sim2R^{3/2}e^{R^2/8}\), the displayed lower bound for \(\Xi/J^2\) grows as a positive constant times \[\frac{e^{R^2/8}}{R^{7/2}}\longrightarrow\infty.\] Thus a uniform \(\Xi\lesssim J^2\), even with additional logarithmic factors in this regime, is impossible.

As scalar checks of this analytic argument, the Mills-based lower bounds for \(\Xi/J^2\) at \(R=12,16,20\) are respectively greater than \(3.4\cdot10^3\), \(1.5\cdot10^9\), and \(4.5\cdot10^{16}\). These calculations allocate no enormous dictionary or Gram matrix; the limiting argument, not the finite numerical examples, proves the contradiction.

The proof on p. 47 retains a factor \(\int_I\rho(dx)\) in the cell lower bound and then drops it when summing to assert \(Q\succeq\gamma I\) with \(\gamma\gtrsim\delta^2\). Tail cells have arbitrarily small mass. This is why Lemma 5.13’s conditional-variance argument cannot be reused in that form.

Theorem 5.17 conditional on the actual \(\Xi\) is not refuted. The specific rate in Corollary 5.18 is not justified by this false dictionary estimate. A repair may retain truncation-dependent constants, use a sharper weighted stochastic variance argument, or change the dictionary. The example is not a lower bound proving that the actual stochastic algorithm must have worse complexity.

Problem 4 (Major: mixture coefficient velocities omit \(Q^{-1}\)).  Section 7 explicitly equips the parameter space with metric \(Q\oplus I\). Therefore, if \[b_T=\int\left\langle
 \nabla\log(\mu_P/\pi)\circ T^{\lambda,v},T
 \right\rangle\,d\rho,\] the coefficient velocity is \(\dot\lambda=-Q^{-1}b\), not \(\dot\lambda_T=-b_T\). The latter is printed in both Theorems 7.1 and 7.2, pp. 26–27, and in the intervening particle formula. Equation (30), p. 49, correctly contains \(Q^{-1}\), but the displayed theorem formulas do not.

For an interior one-component example, let \(\rho=\pi=N(0,1)\), choose \(T(x)=2x\), so \(Q=4\), and take \(\alpha=1,\lambda=1,v=0\). The transported law has standard deviation \(3\), and \[F(\lambda)=\frac12\bigl[(1+2\lambda)^2-1-\log(1+2\lambda)^2\bigr],
 \qquad F'(1)=\frac{16}{3}.\] The printed velocity is \(-16/3\), whereas the specified metric gradient velocity is \(-4/3\). In multiple coordinates a non-scalar Gram matrix also changes direction, not just time parametrization.

Insert the inverse Gram matrix acting on the entire coefficient gradient in both theorems and the particle equations. Boundary behavior on the nonnegative coefficient set needs its own normal-cone interpretation if reached. This is Major because the stated gradient-flow identification is false for the stated metric; the correction is local and already visible in the appendix. It does not invalidate the primary finite-dimensional method, which uses \(Q^{-1}\), and no unproved mixture convergence rate is attributed to the paper.

Problem 5 (Minor: strong convexity does not imply attainment on every convex set).  Lemma 5.1, p. 13, asserts a unique KL minimizer over an arbitrary geodesically convex set. Let \(\pi=N(0,1)\) and \[\mathcal C=\{N(a,1):a>0\}.\] This set is geodesically convex and \(\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}(N(a,1)\Vert\pi)=a^2/2\), whose infimum is zero but is not attained. Strong convexity gives at most one minimizer, not existence. State conditional uniqueness and prove attainment separately under suitable closure and compact-sublevel or other appropriate assumptions for each application. This example does not refute existence for the particular well-conditioned mean-field problem or coercive finite-dimensional families.

Problem 6 (Minor: the SPGD proof drops the constrained optimum gradient).  The smoothness step in Appendix B, p. 35, bounds the gradient norm by \(M\) times the distance to the constrained minimizer. This is false when that minimizer has nonzero gradient. For \(f(x)=x^2/2+x\), \(K=[0,1]\), and \(Q=m=M=1\), the minimizer is \(x_\star=0\), yet \(f'(x_\star)=1\).

The claimed conditional rate admits a direct repair. Use the variational-inequality fixed point \[x_\star=\mathop{\mathrm{Proj}}_{K,Q}(x_\star-hQ^{-1}\nabla f(x_\star))\] when comparing the projected noisy step. Nonexpansiveness, unbiased noise \(\xi\), strong monotonicity and smoothness give, with \(r_t=\mathbb E\|x_t-x_\star\|_Q^2\), \[r_{t+1}\leq
 [1-2mh+(M^2+c_1)h^2]r_t+c_0h^2 .\] Under \(h\leq m/(2M^2)\) and \(h\leq m/(2c_1)\), this is at most \((1-mh)r_t+c_0h^2\). Iteration gives \[r_t\leq e^{-mht}r_0+\frac{c_0h}{m}.\] This restores the same conditional accuracy and iteration orders, with appropriate constants and a separate noiseless treatment when \(c_0=0\). The local proof error therefore has Minor calibration; it is not a counterexample to the corrected SPGD result.

Problem 7 (Minor: the Gaussian KL formula has a log-determinant sign error).  The formula in Appendix D.2, p. 48, uses \(+\log\det(\Sigma^{-1})-\log\det A\). The correct term is \(+\log\det\Sigma-\log\det A\). Taking scalar \(A=\Sigma=2\), the printed expression gives \(-\log2\), although identical Gaussian laws have KL divergence zero. Since the target covariance contributes only a constant when optimizing over \(A\), the subsequent optimal diagonal covariance formula \(a_i^\star=1/(\Sigma^{-1})_{ii}\) remains valid.

Problem 8 (Minor: the printed logistic data-generation probability is invalid).  Appendix D.3, p. 49, writes \(Y_i\mid X_i\sim\operatorname{Bern}(\exp(\theta^TX_i))\). For a positive dot product this parameter exceeds one. Replace it by the sigmoid \(\exp(\theta^TX_i)/(1+\exp(\theta^TX_i))\).

The inspected `BayesianUtils.py` and logistic notebook do use the sigmoid. Thus the printed error is not evidence that the published simulation used invalid probabilities. The historical notebook also divides the design matrix by a square root of an eigenvalue, whereas the paper specifies division by the largest eigenvalue itself, and its translation step is \(10^{-2}\) rather than the printed \(10^{-1}\). Moreover the notebook takes the first returned eigenvalue without explicitly selecting the maximum. The actual normalization, step size and figure-generating snapshot should be specified. Their numerical consequences were not tested here.

Problem 9 (Minor: the supplied alpha-sweep loop passes a constant alpha).  In the pinned `examples/ReproduceFigure3.ipynb`, source cell 8 loops over \(\alpha_\star,\alpha_\star/10,\alpha_\star/50\), but each call to `SPGD` passes `alpha_opt` as its first argument rather than the loop variable `alpha`. Static AST inspection confirms this exact binding. The file’s Gaussian experiment corresponds in content to the manuscript’s alpha-sensitivity figure despite its filename.

This snapshot therefore does not implement the labeled sweep. Pass the loop variable and identify the version used for the published figure. No claim is made that this historical snapshot generated the published result, that the paper’s robustness conclusion is false, or that an experiment was rerun during this review.
# Assessment and limitations

The report assessment is Major. Problems 1–4 have demonstrated effects on stated theorem scope or formulas: an exact APGD cycle, a feasible nonmonotone map, a divergent leverage lower bound, and a metric-gradient mismatch. Their repairs require different changes and should not be conflated. The general compatible-family construction and conditional calculations remain useful. In particular, the specially constructed higher-order interpolant, the true-\(\Xi\) stochastic theorem and the ordinary mean-field method are not disproved beyond the precise scope identified above.

Problems 5–9 have Minor calibration because they admit a bounded assumption, proof or formula correction, or concern a historical reproduction path whose link to the published figures is unverified. No missing code is counted as a mathematical defect. External optimal-transport and concentration theorems were not independently reproved; optimizer accuracy, quadrature error, Monte Carlo performance and the figures were not reproduced. The journal version and possible later corrections were not checked.
This is an initial technical review. The scientific decision is pending, human reviews are empty, and independent acceptance has not been performed.

\end{array}\] The last two rows repeat. At \(t=2\), the objective gap is \(g(2)-g(1)=7\), whereas Theorem 4.2(b) gives \[(1-1/\sqrt4)^2

claim: Recorded check: Centered last ramp s with p=P(Z>=R-delta) has s(R)>=1-p, Qjj<=p, so leverage(R)>=(1-p)^2/p and Xi/J^2>=(1-p)^2/(pJ^3). With epsilon=exp(-R^2/4),delta~sqrt(epsilon/R),J~2R^(3/2)exp(R^2/8), Mills bound makes ratio grow exp(R^2/8)/R^(7/2).

Theorem 5.17 conditional on the actual \(\Xi\) is not refuted. The specific rate in Corollary 5.18 is not justified by this false dictionary estimate. A repair may retain truncation-dependent constants, use a sharper weighted stochastic variance argument, or change the dictionary. The example is not a lower bound proving that the actual stochastic algorithm must have worse complexity.

Title: Technical Review of
Gradient Flows and Riemannian Structure in the Gromov–Wasserstein Geometry
# Source and scope

This report concerns Zhengxin Zhang, Ziv Goldfeld, Kristjan Greenewald, Youssef Mroueh and Bharath K. Sriperumbudur, Gradient Flows and Riemannian Structure in the Gromov–Wasserstein Geometry, arXiv:2407.11800v2, 21 May 2025 [paper]. The assigned identifier is M25-0466 and the journal DOI is 10.1007/s10208-025-09722-w (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09722-w). The acquired manuscript has 74 pages; equivalence with the 93-page journal version has not been established.

All 74 source pages, including the bibliography, were read. The actual evidence-page images inspected are 1, 8–9, 11, 13–16, 19, 24–29, 31, 34–44, 50, 54–56, 58, 60, 64–65, 68 and 70. All nine pages of the linked additional-experiments PDF were read and visually inspected. The supplied repository is `ZhengxinZh/IGW`, commit `4cb4c4fc81c5a5a077fd8bb6aea5e41b57703744`. Its README and every source cell of both notebooks were read statically: seven training cells and ten plotting cells, comprising 211 and 553 extracted lines. No author code, neural training or experiment was executed. Exact rational calculations below are reviewer-written checks.
# Mathematical structure and supported scope

The paper uses the uncentered second moment \(\Sigma_\mu=\int xx^T\,d\mu(x)\), despite calling it covariance. Nonzero means therefore do not invalidate the stated identities. Writing \(C_\pi=\int xy^T\,d\pi\), the quadratic expansion gives \[\mathop{\mathrm{IGW}}(\mu,
u)^2
 =\|\Sigma_\mu\|_F^2+\|\Sigma_
u\|_F^2
       -2\max_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,
u)}\|C_\pi\|_F^2.\] The auxiliary quadratic minimization in \(A\) gives \(A=C_\pi/2\). The optimal-transport reduction and the PSD alignment by an orthogonal matrix are consistent with this normalization. The existence of a Monge map uses the source density and invertibility assumptions; it is not an unrestricted assertion for arbitrary discrete measures.

For Theorem 4.1, the hypotheses include orthogonal invariance, a lower-bounded weakly lower semicontinuous regular functional with absolutely continuous effective domain, the specified convexity along aligned generalized geodesics, and the subdifferential/first-variation assumption. The argument controls discrete energy and the smallest second-moment eigenvalue on a small neighborhood. It obtains velocity bounds, an IGW Cauchy estimate of order \(\sqrt{\tau}\), a subsequence converging uniformly in \(W_2\), and a limiting continuity equation. The passage of the nonlocal moment term uses uniform moment bounds and a Young-inequality argument; these steps were read through the auxiliary proofs. The cited subgradient-closure and optimal-transport results are used conditionally here, not independently reproved.

The mobility operator is \[\mathcal L_{A,\mu}v(x)=2Av(x)+2\int yv(y)^T\,d\mu(y)\,x.\] For \(A=\Sigma_\mu\), its quadratic form equals the action tensor and has a rotational nullspace. In particular, \(\mathcal L_{\Sigma_\mu,\mu}(Sx)=0\) for every skew matrix \(S\). The horizontal space \[\mathcal I_\mu=\{v\in L^2(\mu;\mathbb R^d):
                  \mathbb E[v(X)X^T]\ \hbox{is symmetric}\}\] is consequently substantive, rather than a notational convenience.

Theorem 5.2 concerns the intrinsic length distance \(d_{\mathop{\mathrm{IGW}}}\), not the original ambient discrepancy. It assumes the existence of a minimizing curve with a uniform positive lower bound on \(\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{\rho_t})\). Its endpoint is either \(\mu_1\) or a fixed reflection of \(\mu_1\). The reflection alternative is justified by the two components of the orthogonal group; dropping it would change the theorem. The proof’s smoothing, horizontal alignment, continuous rotation correction, action invariance and time-rescaled concatenation were followed. The full quotient tangent theory is not thereby settled.

The entropy extension explicitly uses modified multiplicative generalized geodesics and a local lower bound. The manuscript does not hide the absence of a global entropy lower bound. Likewise, the neural flow-matching examples minimize a discretized action with an MMD penalty; a small penalty value is not an exact endpoint constraint or a certificate of a global minimizing curve.
# Problems requiring revision

Problem 1 (Major: entropy functional, derivative and inverse-domain consistency).  Section 6.1, p. 39, defines negative differential entropy \(H(\mu)=\int\rho\log\rho\), but prints the surrogate \[\widetilde H_+(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
 =\frac1{2n}\sum_i\log\bigl(\epsilon+\|x_i-x_{N(i)}\|^2\bigr),\] and its positive outgoing nearest-neighbor field. Here \(N(i)\) is the nearest neighbor other than \(i\). At \(\epsilon=0\), scaling every point by \(a\) changes this surrogate by \(+\log a\), whereas \(H(a_\#\mu)-H(\mu)=-d\log a\). Thus the printed sign is inconsistent with the stated entropy.

The plotting snapshot instead uses a negative sum of logarithms and a negative outgoing field. This is counterevidence to any assertion that the displayed numerical trajectories necessarily used the printed positive sign. However, even with the sign repaired, the outgoing field is not the derivative of the stated finite-particle functional. On a region with unique nearest neighbors, set \[q_i=\frac{x_i-x_{N(i)}}{\epsilon+\|x_i-x_{N(i)}\|^2}.\] For the negative mean surrogate, its empirical Wasserstein gradient is \[g_i=n\,\partial_{x_i}\widetilde H_-
       =-q_i+\sum_{k:N(k)=i}q_k.\] The incoming-neighbor terms cannot be omitted when differentiating the same particle functional.

This omission also matters to the inverse mobility formula. Take \[\epsilon=\tfrac15,\qquad x_1=(1,0),\quad x_2=(0,2),\quad x_3=(0,3).\] The nearest-neighbor indices are \(2,3,2\), all strict. For the snapshot field \(g_i^{\rm out}=-q_i\), \[\sum_i g_i^{\rm out}=\binom{-5/26}{5/13},\qquad
 \Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1/3&0\\0&13/3\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \frac13\sum_i g_i^{\rm out}x_i^T
 =\begin{pmatrix}-5/78&0\\5/39&-5/18\end{pmatrix}.\] The nonzero sum contradicts the translation invariance of the proposed particle functional; the nonsymmetric moment shows \(g^{\rm out}\notin\mathcal I_\mu\). Applying the printed principal inverse formula to \(w=-g^{\rm out}\) gives residuals \[(\mathcal L v-w)(x_1)=\binom0{5/182},\quad
 (\mathcal L v-w)(x_2)=\binom{-5/91}0,\quad
 (\mathcal L v-w)(x_3)=\binom{-15/182}0.\] These are exact rational values, despite the nonsingular second moment. For comparison, the correct negative-surrogate gradient is \[g_1=\binom{-5/26}{5/13},\quad
 g_2=\binom{5/26}{50/39},\quad
 g_3=\binom0{-5/3};\] its sum is zero, its moment is symmetric, and the same inverse formula has zero residual.

The entropy experiment therefore needs a coherent functional, normalization, gradient and inverse-domain justification. A different consistent score estimator is possible, but it must be identified and justified as such. The affected experiment should be revisited after that choice. This Major assessment concerns the numerical validation and its derivation; it does not disprove the continuous entropy theory or certify which commit generated a published figure.

Problem 2 (Minor: the inverse proposition needs compatible right-hand sides).  Proposition 10.1, pp. 54–55, quantifies over arbitrary \(w\in L^2(\mu;\mathbb R^d)\) and asserts a unique solution, while its derivation uses \(v\in\mathcal I_\mu\). For \(A=\Sigma_\mu=I_2\) and \(w(x)=Sx\), \(S\ne0\) skew, its formula gives \(v=Sx/4\), but \(\mathcal L v=0\ne w\). Full-space uniqueness also fails because of the rotational kernel.

Merely imposing \(w\in\mathcal I_\mu\) is insufficient for general \(A\). Take a centered Gaussian with \[A=\operatorname{diag}(1,2),\quad\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(1,3),
 \quad w(x)=Wx,\quad W=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/3\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(W\Sigma\) is symmetric, but the proof’s Sylvester equation gives \[AB+B\Sigma=\tfrac12W\Sigma,\qquad
 B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/8\\1/6&0\end{pmatrix}.\] This \(B\) is not symmetric. The proposed solution has \(V=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1/24\\1/6&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), and \[2AV+2\Sigma V^T-W
 =\begin{pmatrix}0&1/12\\-1/12&0\end{pmatrix}\ne0.\] The correct general qualification is \(w\in\mathcal L_{A,\mu}(\mathcal I_\mu)\), with uniqueness within \(\mathcal I_\mu\); equivalently the Sylvester solution must satisfy the required symmetry. In the main case \(A=\Sigma_\mu\), restricting \(w\) to \(\mathcal I_\mu\) gives the intended inverse.

Section 5.3 should also retain orthogonal invariance when introducing a formal gradient for \(F\). A noninvariant functional can vary along \(Sx\), although \(g_\mu(u,Sx)=0\) for every \(u\), so no such gradient represents its differential. Main Assumption 1 already supplies this invariance. The finding is thus a correction of scope, not a refutation of the compatible main flow.

Problem 3 (Minor: a spectral branch may have zero multiplicity).  Proposition 10.2, pp. 55–56, claims \(\mathop{\mathrm{spec}}(\mathcal L_{\Sigma_\mu,\mu}|_{\mathcal I_\mu})
 =2(\Lambda_\mu\cup\Gamma_\mu)\) under nonsingularity of \(\Sigma_\mu\). For \(d=1\), \(\mu=\delta_1\), the uncentered second moment is 1, so the assumption holds. But \(L^2(\delta_1)=\mathbb R\), and direct evaluation gives \(\mathcal L v=4v\). Its spectrum is \(\{4\}\), whereas the displayed set is \(\{2,4\}\).

The \(2\Lambda_\mu\) branch requires nonzero fields orthogonal to the coordinate functions. That complement can be empty for minimally supported atomic measures. The proposition should qualify the branches that occur, or add a sufficient non-atomicity condition. The absolutely continuous setting of the main theorem is unaffected by this example.

Problem 4 (Minor: metric derivative and curve-equivalence conventions).  On p. 31 the metric derivative uses denominator \(h\) in a two-sided limit. The curve \(\rho_t=N(0,1+t)\), with \(1+t\) denoting variance, satisfies \(\mathop{\mathrm{IGW}}(\rho_{t+h},\rho_t)=|h|\). The displayed quotient has limits \(1\) and \(-1\). Use \(|h|\), or explicitly take \(h\downarrow0\).

The definition before Lemma 5.3, p. 35, allows any nondecreasing \(h:[0,1]\to[0,1]\). Let \(\alpha_t=N(0,1)\), \(\beta_t=N(0,1+t)\), and \(h\equiv0\). They meet that definition, but their lengths are 0 and 1. Hence the length equality in part (2) of the lemma is not valid for the printed definition. Require an endpoint-preserving continuous surjective nondecreasing reparametrization, as needed to traverse the whole curve.

There are related local scaling slips in (54), p. 65: from \(\mathop{\mathrm{IGW}}(\gamma_i,\gamma_{i-1})^2=\tau^2g_i+R_i\), the sum is \[\tau\sum_i g_i
   =\tau^{-1}\sum_i\mathop{\mathrm{IGW}}(\gamma_i,\gamma_{i-1})^2
      -\tau^{-1}\sum_i R_i
   \le L^2+O(\tau)\] when \(\mathop{\mathrm{IGW}}(\gamma_i,\gamma_{i-1})\le L\tau\) and \(R_i=O(\tau^3)\). The printed remainder and final unsquared length should be corrected accordingly. These corrections are consistent with the surrounding intended argument; no counterexample to the dynamic formula is inferred.

Problem 5 (Minor: an interpolation weight belongs to the other grid).  In (26), p. 24, interpolation in the \(\eta\)-grid uses \((1-\ell_\eta(s))\) and \(\ell_\tau(s)\). For \(\tau=1/2\), \(\eta=1/4\), \(s=1/8\), these coefficients sum to \(3/4\), rather than 1. The corresponding expansion on p. 25 repeats the mismatch. The proof on p. 26 uses the intended \(\ell_\eta\). Replace the second weight and its occurrences in the expansion by \(\ell_\eta(s)\); this is a local correction to the two-grid estimate.

Problem 6 (Minor: the quoted time bound does not match its derivation).  Put \(c=\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{\rho_0})\) and \(E=F(\rho_0)-F^*>0\). Theorem 4.1, p. 14, permits \[\delta<\frac{(1-1/\sqrt2)c}{2^{5/4}E}.\] Proposition 4.1, p. 16, instead gives \(\delta\le\bar\delta^2/(2E)\), with \(\bar\delta=(1-1/\sqrt2)c/2^{1/4}\), hence \[\delta\le\frac{(1-1/\sqrt2)^2c^2}{2^{3/2}E}.\] At \(c=E=1\), the theorem’s upper endpoint is about 4.06 times the derived one. Use the derived bound or supply an additional argument giving the quantitative estimates on the larger interval. Section 10.3’s concatenated global-existence discussion is distinct from this explicit uniform range. This is a proof-range mismatch, not a demonstrated nonexistence result.

Problem 7 (Minor: the pinned plotting routine mixes trajectory and field data).  In `Plots.ipynb`, the flow-matching plotting function evaluates sample velocities at `source_samples` for every time, although the nonlocal term requires samples from the current distribution. The notebook also computes `global_velocities` for the IGW model, subsequently loads the Wasserstein model, and draws its contours/arrows without recomputing those grid velocities.

Evaluate sample velocities on the current trajectory and pass locally computed model-specific grid fields to the plotting routine. This is established by static reading of the supplied snapshot. It does not prove that the published figures were generated by this exact code, and no author code was run.
# Assessment and limits

The useful contribution is the explicit aligned-flow construction and the link between the nonlocal mobility and an intrinsic action. Its hypotheses and its reflection alternative should remain visible. The established numerical inconsistency in Problem 1 warrants Major revision of that validation. The remaining problems are individually calibrated as Minor because their demonstrated effect is a local scope, convention, quantitative statement or snapshot correction; they do not presently negate the main conditional architecture.

A candidate objection to the Gronwall lemma was rejected after actual image inspection: pp. 27 and 60 contain absolute values on \(b(t)\), which the text extraction omitted. The superseded native calculation is retained in the technical records, and the current check explicitly marks it rejected. No defect is counted on that basis.

The qualitative plots do not establish a universal speed comparison with Wasserstein flow. For example, at an isotropic moment \(\Sigma=cI\), the potential-gradient velocity scales as \(x/(4c)\), so its relative time scale depends on \(c\). The paper’s observed damping and its open convergence-rate question should be interpreted accordingly. External analytical inputs, exact figure-generating provenance and the journal version remain outside the verified scope. Scientific adjudication is pending; this is an initial technical review, not independent acceptance.
