report: Abstract: The involution representation gives useful explicit tangent, normal, second fundamental form and Riemann-curvature formulas. Direct checks nevertheless establish three Major issues: the claimed local product of many geodesic two-spheres fails a curvature-operator rank obstruction; the third fundamental form omits the dimension multiplying averaged mean curvature; and the Weyl convention is incompatible with the stated Riemann sign, producing an incorrect nonzero Bach tensor. Four Minor groups concern scalar/delta normalization, a Jacobi factor, tensor and bundle definitions, and a quotient-model comparison. The report supplies exact examples and distinguishes valid foundational formulas from consequences requiring revision.
Author: AI-assisted initial technical review

Title: Technical Review of
Simple matrix expressions for the curvatures of Grassmannian
# Identity and review scope

The reviewed source is Zehua Lai, Lek-Heng Lim and Ke Ye, Simple matrix expressions for the curvatures of Grassmannian, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 2053–2089, published online 27 August 2025, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09723-9 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09723-9) [paper]. The assigned identifier is M25-0467. The acquired file is the published-format 37-page PDF hosted on the author’s institutional site; the online year and the later volume year are distinct metadata facts.

All 37 pages, including all definitions, proofs, model comparisons and 54 bibliography entries, were read. Actual page images inspected were physical pages 1, 3–4, 8–15, 17–30, 32–35. Physical page \(p\) corresponds to printed page \(2052+p\); locations below use the printed pagination. No separate code or supplement was confirmed in the supplied bounded acquisition record, and their absence is not treated as a mathematical defect. Reviewer-written exact matrix calculations check the examples below; no author code was executed. External cited theorems and priority claims were not all independently verified.
# What the basic matrix calculation establishes

Write \(l=n-k\), \(m=kl\), and work at \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(I_k,-I_l)\). For \(B\in\mathbb R^{k\times l}\), let \[X(B)=\begin{pmatrix}0&B\\B^T&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Differentiating \(Q^2=I\) gives this tangent space. Its Frobenius orthogonal complement consists of block-diagonal symmetric matrices. The metric is \(g(X(B),X(C))=2\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(B^TC)\). The second fundamental form in Theorem 4 is \[\mathrm{II}(X(B),X(C))
 =\tfrac12\operatorname{diag}(-BC^T-CB^T,\ B^TC+C^TB).\] It is consistent with differentiating the defining equation twice. It immediately gives zero relative nullity, since \(\mathrm{II}(X,X)=0\) forces \(B=0\). The shape operator along \(H=\operatorname{diag}(H_1,H_2)\) acts by \[B\longmapsto\tfrac12(BH_2-H_1B),\] so its eigenvalues are \((\lambda_{k+j}-\lambda_i)/2\). The mean vector in Corollary 7 is the average \(m^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathrm{II}\), with the stated block entries. These results support the principal and directional Gaussian curvature formulas.

The Gauss equation, with the manuscript’s Riemann convention, gives \[R(X,Y,Z,W)=\tfrac12\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}([X,Y]ZW),\qquad
 R(X,Y,Y,X)=\tfrac14\|[X,Y]\|_F^2.\] Contraction in the orthonormal basis \(X(E_{ij}/\sqrt2)\) gives \[\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}=\lambda g,\qquad \lambda=\frac{n-2}{8},\qquad
 \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_g\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}=m\lambda.\] These formulas pass the exact checks. They also furnish internal tests of several later expressions, without needing a different metric normalization or a different Grassmannian model.
# Major issues

Problem 1 (Major: the local sphere-product theorem is false in an allowed case).  Theorem 23(b), pp. 2080–2081, permits \(k=2,n=6,r=4\). It therefore claims an isometric totally geodesic embedding of an open subset of a product of four round two-spheres into \(\mathop{\mathrm{Gr}}(2,6)\). Both dimensions are eight. Under the paper’s convention that Riemannian embeddings are isometric, such an embedding would be a local isometry.

This is impossible by the curvature operator. On \(\Lambda^2T_Q\mathop{\mathrm{Gr}}(2,6)\), the curvature bilinear form is, up to the harmless ordering sign convention, the positive Gram form \[(X\wedge Y,Z\wedge W)\longmapsto
          \tfrac14\langle[X,Y],[Z,W]\rangle_F.\] The commutators span \(\mathfrak{so}(2)\oplus\mathfrak{so}(4)\), of dimension \(1+6=7\). Indeed, tangent basis pairs with a common column generate the first block, and pairs with a common row generate each skew elementary matrix in the second block. Consequently the curvature operator has rank seven. Exact evaluation of the \(28\times28\) Gram matrix confirms this rank.

For a product of four round two-spheres, each factor contributes one nonzero curvature-operator direction and every mixed two-plane has zero curvature. Its curvature operator has rank four, independently of the positive radii of the factors. A local isometry cannot change this rank. Thus the issue is a counterexample to the stated Riemannian conclusion, not just an omitted proof of the exponential-chart construction.

The proposed map \(\psi\circ\rho\circ\phi^{-1}\) is locally injective after shrinking a chart, but injectivity and orthogonality of selected tangent planes do not prove that it preserves the product metric. Mixed curvature and the relevant Lie-triple-system conditions are missing. In particular, the discussion contrasting the oriented and unoriented Grassmannians cannot remove a local curvature obstruction: a covering has the same local geometry.

Part (a) also needs a range correction unless an assumption \(k\le n/2\) is imposed. For \(k=3,n=4,r=1\), its printed bound holds, but its construction requires a one-dimensional \(W_0\) in the zero-dimensional complement of a four-dimensional block. Moreover \(\mathop{\mathrm{Gr}}(3,4)\) is real projective three-space with a scaled round metric. A complete totally geodesic surface lifts to a great two-sphere in its round universal cover, whose projected image is a projective plane; it cannot be an embedded two-sphere.

The valid orthogonal-block construction requires \[r\le \left\lfloor\frac{\min(k,n-k)}2\right\rfloor.\] This ensures that the fixed \((k-2r)\)-plane fits in the remaining \(n-4r\) dimensions. It supplies a conservative corrected global construction using a geodesic sphere in each \(\mathop{\mathrm{Gr}}(2,4)\) block. It does not establish the much larger local bound asserted in part (b).

Problem 2 (Major: the third fundamental form uses averaged mean curvature without its dimension).  The definition on p. 2061 is \(\mathrm{III}(X,Y)=\sum_\alpha g(S_{\eta_\alpha}X,S_{\eta_\alpha}Y)\), where the normal basis is orthonormal. In particular, \(\mathrm{III}(X,X)\ge0\). But the proof of Corollary 9, pp. 2071–2072, uses \(\mathrm{III}=\langle\mathrm{II},H\rangle-\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}\), although Corollary 7 defines \(H=m^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathrm{II}\).

Contracting the Gauss equation directly gives \[\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}(X,Y)=\langle\mathrm{II}(X,Y),\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathrm{II}\rangle-\mathrm{III}(X,Y),\] so the required formula is \[\mathrm{III}(X,Y)=m\langle\mathrm{II}(X,Y),H\rangle-\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}(X,Y)
          =\frac{n+2}{8}g(X,Y)
          =\frac{n+2}{4}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(B^TC).\] For \(\mathop{\mathrm{Gr}}(2,4)\) and unit \(X=X(E_{11}/\sqrt2)\), summing the six normal-basis shape-operator squares gives \(3/4\). Corollary 9 and Table 1 give zero. For some larger dimensions their coefficient is even negative. This contradicts the paper’s own definition and changes one of its principal new extrinsic formulas. The second fundamental form, averaged mean vector and Ricci tensor need not be changed to obtain the correction.

Problem 3 (Major: the Weyl sign produces a tensor with nonzero Ricci trace).  Let \[K_g(X,Y,Z,W)=g(X,Z)g(Y,W)-g(X,W)g(Y,Z).\] For an orthonormal basis \(e_a\), \[\sum_aK_g(X,e_a,e_a,Y)=-(m-1)g(X,Y).\] The Riemann convention in the paper gives \(\sum_aR(X,e_a,e_a,Y)=\lambda g(X,Y)\). Thus the tensor in Corollary 17, \[W_{\rm printed}=R-\frac{\lambda}{m-1}K_g,\] has contraction \(2\lambda g\), rather than zero. Its algebra follows the sign-incompatible definition on p. 2064, but that definition does not yield the Weyl tensor for the previously fixed Riemann ordering.

The Einstein-case correction is \[W=R+\frac{\lambda}{m-1}K_g.\] The corresponding Ricci-decomposition signs must be changed consistently in Section 3 and the conclusion. As a concrete four-dimensional test, take \(\mathop{\mathrm{Gr}}(1,5)\). The matrix formula gives constant sectional curvature \(1/8\), \(\lambda=3/8\), and the corrected \(W\) vanishes in every component. The printed \(W\) has contraction \(3g/4\).

This error propagates to Corollary 18 and Table 1. In this example the genuine Bach tensor is zero, whereas the printed formula gives \[B_{\rm printed}=\frac9{64}g.\] More generally, with the genuine trace-free Weyl tensor and the parallel Einstein Ricci tensor, the Cotton/derivative contribution and the Ricci contraction in the Bach formula vanish, in dimensions where that formula is defined. Hence the claimed nonzero Bach expression must be replaced by zero. The Codazzi conclusion remains true for this corrected zero tensor; it does not validate the old value.
# Further corrections

Problem 4 (Minor: scalar and delta conventions, and the maximizing basis).  Page 2063 identifies \(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}\) with the sum of sectional curvatures over unordered pairs. The correct identity is \[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}=2\sum_{a<b}\kappa(e_a,e_b).\] The same page uses the unordered-pair sum to define the scalar curvature of a subspace, then asserts that the whole tangent space has the previously defined full scalar curvature. The two conventions cannot both be retained.

For \(m=k(n-k)\), using the unordered-pair scalar consistently gives the delta values \[\overline\delta_{2,r}=\frac{m(n-2)}{16},\qquad
 \underline\delta_{2,r}=\frac{m(n-2)}{16}-\frac r4\] in the intended range. Using full Ricci traces consistently for the ambient tangent space and its two-planes instead gives \[\overline\delta_{2,r}=\frac{m(n-2)}8,\qquad
 \underline\delta_{2,r}=\frac{m(n-2)}8-\frac r2.\] The printed pair mixes the full ambient trace with half-traces on the selected planes. It can describe a specifically named hybrid quantity, but not both scalar conventions at once. For \(\mathop{\mathrm{Gr}}(2,4)\), the unordered scalar is \(1/2\), the full scalar is 1, and the lower invariant at \(r=2\) is zero under either consistent convention; the printed expression is \(1/2\).

There is also a repairable error in the maximizing basis (16), p. 2076. In block notation its two pairs are \[(E_{11}/\sqrt2,\ J/2),\qquad(E_{22}/\sqrt2,\ K/2),
 \quad
 J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\
 K=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Their sectional curvatures are \(1/8\) each, not \(1/4\). Use instead \[(I_2/2,\ K/2),\qquad(D/2,\ J/2),
 \quad D=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1).\] The four full tangent matrices are orthonormal, and each pair has curvature \(1/4\). These blocks repair the attainment calculation for the sectional sums. The original zero-curvature pairs pass the direct check. This is a normalization and witness correction, not a rejection of the block extremization idea.

Problem 5 (Minor: the Jacobi expression is twice its defining symmetrization).  The definition on p. 2062 is \(J(X,Y,Z,W)=\tfrac12(R(X,Y,Z,W)+R(Z,Y,X,W))\). Substitution of Proposition 10 yields \[J(X,Y,Z,W)
 =\tfrac12\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(XYZW)
       -\tfrac14\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\bigl(Y(XZ+ZX)W\bigr).\] Corollary 11, p. 2073, and Table 1 give twice this expression. On \(\mathop{\mathrm{Gr}}(1,3)\), take the orthonormal tangent matrices corresponding to \(B=(1,0)/\sqrt2\) and \(C=(0,1)/\sqrt2\). Then the definition gives \(J(X,Y,X,Y)=-1/8\), while the displayed formula gives \(-1/4\). Multiply both its full-matrix and block formulas by \(1/2\).

Problem 6 (Minor: tensor divergence, bundle language and dimension restrictions).  The rule on p. 2062 that differentiates only the final factor of a decomposable tensor is not well-defined over \(C^\infty(M)\). On the real line, with \(e=\partial_x\), \[(xe)\otimes e=e\otimes(xe).\] The printed rule assigns zero to the first expression and \(e\) to the second. Tensor divergence should contract the covariant derivative of the complete tensor, including derivatives of all factors.

In Proposition 1, p. 2065, vertical cocurvature vanishes because the vertical distribution is tangent to the fibers and hence integrable. The proof instead calls the horizontal distribution integrable with integral manifold \(M\); for a connection with nonzero curvature this is false. Use horizontal lifts and the pullback tangent bundle, rather than a literal global inclusion \(\mathfrak X(M)\subset\mathfrak X(O(M))\). The stated vanishing of torsion, nonmetricity and vertical cocurvature can be retained after this repair.

Finally, formulas containing \(m-2\) or \(m-3\) must carry dimension restrictions. Use the standard Schouten/Cotton definitions for \(m>2\) and the displayed Bach definition for \(m>3\), or state separate extensions. Cancellation of a denominator in a special Einstein expression does not define the original general tensor in excluded dimensions.

Problem 7 (Minor: the general-linear quotient and common-point lifts).  Equation (17), p. 2082, includes \(\mathrm{GL}(n)/(\mathrm{GL}(k)\times\mathrm{GL}(n-k))\). Its dimension is \(2k(n-k)\), twice the dimension of the Grassmannian. The stabilizer of a \(k\)-plane is the block upper-triangular parabolic subgroup, including the off-diagonal \(k\times(n-k)\) block. Substituting that stabilizer repairs the quotient identification.

The subsequent assertion that horizontal lifts must emerge at different representatives is also not inherent. Once \(Q\) is fixed, the map \((d_Q\pi)^{-1}\) used in the paper sends every tangent vector to the horizontal subspace of that same \(T_QO(n)\). Four vectors can therefore be lifted at one chosen \(Q\). Arbitrarily supplied incompatible representatives may need alignment, but a common representative does not.

These corrections leave room for practical advantages of the involution model. Such advantages should be tied to specified operations or algorithms. The affine relation \(Q=2P-I\) gives \(dQ=2\,dP\) and a factor of four in the induced metric; the singularity of a projector as a square matrix alone is not an analysis of the numerical stability of every projector-based algorithm. No comparative numerical experiment was performed in this review.
# Assessment

Major revision is required by the established sphere-product obstruction and the incorrect geometric tensors, independently of the smaller corrections. The verified tangent, normal, second-form, shape and basic curvature calculations provide a substantial usable core. The report therefore does not suggest that every formula in Table 1 fails. Corrections should be propagated consistently through that table, definitions, proofs and geometric consequences, with the Riemann convention and the full-versus-half scalar convention fixed before contraction.

The exact checks include the complete curvature-operator Gram matrix, shape-square sums, Weyl contractions, Jacobi comparison and both the printed and repaired extremizing pairs. They are targeted checks, not a formal verification of every theorem or a reproduction of a numerical experiment. Scientific adjudication remains pending. This is an initial technical review and has not undergone independent acceptance.

report: Abstract: The two regularization parameters give a useful unified framework for barycenters, with credible convexity, Gibbs optimality, bias cancellation and mean-field convergence arguments. An explicit admissible example nevertheless disproves the dual smoothness estimate in the stated weighted oscillation seminorm. Further corrections concern dual support qualifications, Gaussian scaling, the numerical example and released implementation, and several proof normalizations. The review distinguishes these established issues from results that they do not refute, and separates static inspection of a historical code snapshot from experimental reproduction.

Title: Technical Review of
Doubly Regularized Entropic Wasserstein Barycenter
# Identity, material and scope

The reviewed paper is Lénaïc Chizat, Doubly Regularized Entropic Wasserstein Barycenter, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 2091–2128, published online 12 August 2025, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09724-8 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09724-8) [paper]. The assigned identifier is M25-0468. The source is the exact acquired 38-page publisher version of record; the online year and volume year are different metadata facts. No other version or subsequent correction was compared.

All 38 pages, including Appendices A–B and all 87 bibliography entries, were read. Actual source images inspected were physical pages 1, 3 and 5–34. Physical page \(p\) corresponds to printed page \(2090+p\); the locations below use printed pagination. The complete source of all 16 cells of `2023-entropic-bary.ipynb` and all 75 lines of `sinkhorn-acceleration.jl` were inspected in the pinned author repository [code], commit `593a61e7c822be376f6acf95400cecc8592c178b`, dated 21 March 2023. Its link to the article is established, but its identity with the exact execution that produced the published figures is not. No author code was executed, no trajectories or figures were reproduced, and stored outputs were not treated as fresh computations.
# Mathematical structure and results supported by the checks

On the stated compact convex set \(X\subset\mathbb R^d\), the objective is \[F_{\lambda,\tau}(\mu)=G_\lambda(\mu)+\tau H(\mu),\qquad
 G_\lambda(\mu)=\sum_k w_kT_\lambda(\mu,\nu_k),\] where \(T_\lambda\) uses relative entropy with respect to \(\mu\otimes\nu_k\), and \(H\) is the negative differential entropy. The distinction between ordinary linear convexity in measures and displacement convexity is essential. The dual representation of \(T_\lambda\) makes \(G_\lambda\) convex; entropy makes \(F_{\lambda,\tau}\) strictly convex for \(\tau>0\). The compactness and lower semicontinuity argument yields a unique minimizer. With the stated regularity of canonical Schrödinger potentials, its first-order equation is \[d\mu^*_{\lambda,\tau}/dx\ \propto\
       \exp\bigl(-V[\mu^*_{\lambda,\tau}]/\tau\bigr).\] Full support of this primal density does not impose full support on the prescribed marginals.

For the half-squared Euclidean cost, Proposition 3.1 yields the comparison \[T_0(\mu,
u)\le
 T_\lambda(\mu,
u)+	frac{d\lambda}{2}\log(2\pi\lambda)
       +	frac{\lambda}{2} igl(H(\mu)+H(
u) igr)
 \le T_0(\mu,
u)+	frac{\lambda^2}{8}I(\mu,
u).\] The cancellation at \(	au=\lambda/2\), followed by comparison with an unregularized minimizer, correctly gives the first bound in Theorem 3.2. Finite integrated Fisher information is needed for a nonvacuous \(O(\lambda^2)\) bound. The Sinkhorn-divergence estimate additionally contains \(I(\mu^*_{\lambda,\mathrm{div}})\), so a uniform rate requires control of that varying quantity. Merely writing \(	au\sim\lambda/2\) cancels the first-order coefficient; it does not by itself make every residual \(O(\lambda^2)\).

The Gaussian calculation in Appendix A goes beyond a Gaussian ansatz: the quadratic potential and Gibbs equation verify the candidate among all measures in that separately discussed noncompact setting. Its variance and debiasing formulas pass direct algebraic checks: \[b=\frac{\bigl(a+\sqrt{(a-\lambda)^2+4a\tau}\bigr)^2-\lambda^2}{4a},
 \qquad
 \tau^*(\lambda)=\frac{\lambda}{2}+a-\sqrt{a^2+\lambda^2/4}.\] The \(\tau=0\), \(\lambda=0\), \(\tau=\lambda\) and \(\tau=\lambda/2\) limits are consistent. For Dirac marginals the Gibbs variance is \(\tau\) on \(\mathbb R^d\); on a compact domain the density is the corresponding truncated Gibbs density.

The entropy sandwich in Lemma 4.2 follows directly from convexity and the Gibbs formula: \[\tau\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\mid\mu^*)\le F(\mu)-F(\mu^*)
       \le\tau\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}(\mu\mid\exp(-V[\mu]/\tau)/Z).\] The perturbation proof of Theorem 4.1 uses this inequality and bounds on the marginal dual potentials. Corollary 4.3 deliberately switches to the inhomogeneous Sobolev norm. Its actual stated exponent uses \(d'=2\lceil d/2\rceil\); the introductory shorthand with \(d\) should reflect this rounding for odd dimensions. There is no valid objection here based simply on the low-frequency divergence of high-order homogeneous norms.

Theorem 5.1 concerns the continuous-time mean-field equation with no-flux boundary conditions, with finite initial free energy for its displayed estimate. It is not a finite-particle iteration-complexity theorem. The uniform bounded oscillation of \(V\), the stated log-Sobolev perturbation argument and the entropy sandwich give the intended route to exponential decay. The cited implicit-function, entropic asymptotic, PDE and log-Sobolev results were not all independently re-proved or retrieved; the review checks their stated role and the internal deductions.
# Established issues

Problem 1 (Major: the dual smoothness estimate fails in its stated seminorm).  Proposition 2.6, pp. 2100–2102, asserts \(1/\min(\lambda,\tau)\)-smoothness for \[N_1(h)=\sum_k w_k\operatorname{osc}(h_k).\] The definition immediately before the proposition means \(\lvert D^2E(\psi)[h,h]\rvert\le
N_1(h)^2/\min(\lambda,\tau)\).

Take \(X=[0,1]\), \(c=0\), \(K=2\), \(\lambda=\tau=1\), \(w_1=1/8,w_2=7/8\), and \(\nu_1=(\delta_0+\delta_1)/2\). The second marginal can be arbitrary. Let \(\psi_1(y)=ty,\psi_2=0\). Equation (12) reduces exactly to \[E(t)=\frac18\left(\frac t2-\log\frac{1+e^t}{2}\right).\] Consequently \[E''(0)=-\frac1{32},\qquad
 N_1(y,0)^2=\frac1{64}.\] Every domain, cost, weight and marginal assumption is satisfied, but the asserted bound fails by a factor of two. More generally the ratio is \(1/(4w_1)\), which becomes unbounded as the positive weight decreases.

The first displayed Hessian on p. 2101 is consistent with direct differentiation. With \(a_k(x)=\mathbb E[h_k(Y_k)\mid x]\), it is \[-D^2E[h,h]
 =\tau^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mu_\psi}\!\left(\sum_k w_ka_k\right)
 +\lambda^{-1}\mathbb E_{\mu_\psi}
                       \sum_k w_k\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}(h_k(Y_k)\mid x).\] The ensuing application of total variance replaces the second term by the conditional variance of a weighted sum. Its weights would be squared for conditionally independent coordinates, and it is not the displayed weighted sum of variances. No choice of joint law fixes the one-active-coordinate counterexample.

Problem 2 (Minor: dual uniqueness and the auxiliary coupling need support qualifications).  The same proposition optimizes over \(C(X)^K\) and claims uniqueness modulo constants. For \(K=1,c=0,\nu=\delta_0\) and \(X=[0,1]\), Equation (12) gives \(E(\psi)=0\) for every continuous \(\psi\). The functions \(0\) and \(y\) are distinct maximizers whose difference is not constant. The correct uniqueness statement is on the marginal supports, or \(\nu_k\)-almost everywhere modulo constants for positive weights. Canonical Schrödinger extensions provide a distinguished representative, but arbitrary continuous dual maximizers need not equal that extension off the support. Zero-weight components are completely free.

The measure called \(\gamma_{\psi_k}\in\Pi(\mu_\psi,\nu_k)\) on p. 2101 is normalized in its first marginal, but generally not in its second marginal away from stationarity. For the Bernoulli tilt above, its second-marginal mass at 1 is \(e^t/(1+e^t)\), rather than \(1/2\). Calling it a probability measure with first marginal \(\mu_\psi\) is sufficient for differentiating; the second marginal is enforced by the dual optimality condition.

There is also a technical gap in the minimax justification: the quoted Theorem 2.7 assumes a real-valued Lagrangian, whereas \(\tau H(\mu)=+\infty\) at singular \(\mu\) in the compact domain used in the proof. Supply an applicable extended-valued minimax argument, or establish the saddle point directly from the primal Gibbs optimizer and its Schrödinger potentials. This is a repair of the stated justification, not a demonstrated duality gap.

Figure 1 also labels \(d^{-1}W_2=(\sqrt b-\sqrt a)^2\). The exact relation is \(d^{-1}W_2^2=(\sqrt b-\sqrt a)^2\). The acquired notebook actually colors by \(\lvert\sqrt b-\sqrt a\rvert\) at \(a=d=1\), an unsquared distance. Align the plotted quantity and caption. The zero set and the correct debiasing curve are unaffected.

Problem 4 (Minor: the printed example and the snapshot noise do not specify the stated experiment).  On p. 2117 the second marginal contains \((3,1)\). Figure 3 and the notebook instead use \((3,0)\). For the printed marginals, the average of their means has vertical coordinate \(3/4\), while both the claimed unregularized barycenter and the proposed stationary initial measure have mean coordinate \(1/2\). For a common vertical translation by \(t\), \[G_0(\mu(\cdot-te_2))-G_0(\mu)
       =-\frac t4+\frac{t^2}{2}.\] Thus neither displayed measure is stationary for the printed data. Replacing the point by \((3,0)\) matches the figure and removes this mean obstruction.

A separate discrepancy occurs in notebook cell 14 (zero-based). It uses noise \[\tfrac12\sqrt{\lambda\eta}\,Z,\] whose coordinate variance is \(\lambda\eta/4\). Algorithm (27) requires variance \(2\tau\eta\). Therefore this snapshot implements temperature \(\tau=\lambda/8\), whereas the text and Figure 3 specify \(\tau=\lambda/2\). With \(\lambda=0.1,\eta=0.5\), these variances are \(0.0125\) and \(0.05\). Removing the division by two in the noise amplitude gives the stated temperature.

These are explicit coordinate and parameter inconsistencies. The acquired snapshot is historical, so this review does not assert that the published image was necessarily generated by precisely this run. Supply the matching execution parameters, seed and figure provenance. The finite-particle example on \(\mathbb R^2\), initialized atomically, is an illustration outside the compact, finite-initial-entropy estimate as stated; it is not itself a counterexample to the continuous-time theorem.

Problem 5 (Minor: static numerical helper and notebook corrections).  In `dual_objective`, the terms \(\log p_i+\log q_j\) are placed inside division by \(\lambda\). The intended joint mass is \[p_iq_j\exp((u_i+v_j-C_{ij})/\lambda).\] Either multiply the logarithms by \(\lambda\) inside the numerator or put them outside that division. For uniform two-point marginals, \(C=u=v=0\) and \(\lambda=2\), the helper expression returns \(-2\), whereas the correct dual objective is zero. This helper is not called by the visible notebook, so its error is not evidence that the displayed trajectories use that objective.

The final potential reconstruction in `sinkhorn_RNA` uses a mean where the weighted exponent already contains \(p_i\), and therefore needs a sum. It adds \(\lambda\log n\) to \(v\), multiplying the reconstructed joint mass by \(n\). The notebook’s subsequent row-normalized barycentric projection cancels this uniform factor. Thus the returned object is not a normalized coupling, but that normalization error alone does not change the visible drift formula.

The notebook also depends on undeclared prior session state: `bb` is plotted without an assignment, `tol` is commented out before use, and `bary1D` uses `ones(n)` although its local grid dimension is `m`. The later global `n=2` does not repair a 200-point grid. Moreover `Wbary1D` returns a vector of length \(m-200\), which is empty at the displayed \(m=200\); no finer reference-grid construction and resampling step is supplied. Correct these initializations and dimensions and record a clean execution environment. These are findings from full static source reading, not claims of an attempted Julia execution or evidence against the analytic theorems.

Problem 6 (Minor: Appendix B has repairable domination and sign errors).  On p. 2122, the proposed dominating function contains \((\rho^*+M)(|\rho^*|+\log M)\). Finite entropy and integrability of \(\log\rho^*\) do not imply an \(L^2\) bound on \(\rho^*\). The needed domination has the form \[(\rho^*+M)(|\log\rho^*|+C_M),\] which is integrable using Lemma B.1 and finite entropy. The same page reverses the sign after \(0\le\int g^*\,d(\widetilde\mu-\mu^*)\): the conclusion is \(\int g^*\,d\widetilde\mu\ge\int g^*\,d\mu^*\), and the relevant essential extremum is an infimum. Concentration on sublevel sets, followed by positivity of \(\rho^*\), proves constancy.

For \(f(t)=t\log t-t+1\), p. 2123 should read \(f(0)-f(\epsilon)=-\epsilon\log\epsilon+\epsilon\). The printed smaller lower bound is still sufficient for the positivity argument, so this sign error does not overturn Lemma B.1. Finally Proposition B.1 is written for \(G+\mathop{\mathrm{KL}}\) despite mentioning \(\tau>0\); apply it to \(G/\tau\) to derive Theorem 2.5. With these repairs the Gibbs conclusion and the Pinsker proof of strong convexity remain supported.

Problem 7 (Minor: the mean-field proof loses a temperature and misstates a limit).  On p. 2116 the auxiliary Gibbs measure in the proof is written proportional to \(e^{-V[\mu_t]}\), whereas the entropy sandwich and the intended equation require \(e^{-V[\mu_t]/\tau}\). Restore the denominator. The subsequent rate of the form \(\rho_\tau\asymp\tau e^{-L\operatorname{diam}(X)/\tau}\) approaches zero as \(\tau\downarrow0\), not one as stated. The unit-time contraction factor \(e^{-\rho_\tau}\) approaches one. The algorithm, PDE and theorem statement otherwise use the intended temperature, so this is a proof-normalization and interpretation correction.
# Assessment

Major revision is warranted by the false quantitative dual smoothness statement, with the exact example in Problem 1 providing a decisive check. The other issues have localized repairs or concern the reproducibility and interpretation of one illustrative implementation. They do not establish that the primal existence and uniqueness theorem, the exact \(\tau=\lambda/2\) approximation argument, the entropy sandwich or the continuous-time mean-field convergence mechanism is false.

The reviewer-written checks evaluate the dual Hessian, Gaussian scale, translation obstruction, noise variance and helper normalizations independently of author code. They do not constitute an experimental rerun or a formal verification of every cited input. Scientific adjudication remains pending. This initial technical review has not undergone independent acceptance.

report: Abstract: The proposed product formula for generic complex realization components is natural and its reduction to subgraph fiber squares is useful. The printed proof nevertheless contains a false passage from ordinary generic integrality to irreducibility of general complex fibers. The invariant application also uses an invalid identification of arithmetic and geometric genus for smooth affine curves. Exact examples establish both problems. Further corrections are needed in auxiliary orientation and orbit lemmas, the induction boundary cases and the definition of a calligraph. These findings do not supply a counterexample to the main generic component-count formula. A separate static defect is recorded for a nondefault branch of the acquired, later PyRigi snapshot.
Author: AI-assisted initial technical review

Title: Technical Review of
Irreducible Components of Sets of Points in the Plane that Satisfy Distance Conditions
# Identity and inspected material

The source is Niels Lubbes, Mehdi Makhul, Josef Schicho and Audie Warren, Irreducible Components of Sets of Points in the Plane that Satisfy Distance Conditions, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 2129–2163, online 7 August 2025, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09725-7 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09725-7) [paper]. The assigned identifier is M25-0469. The acquired 35-page publisher version of record was reviewed; the online and volume years are distinct. No later correction or alternate version was compared.

All 35 pages, both appendices and all 30 references were read. Actual source page images inspected were physical pages 1, 5–6 and 8–34. Physical page \(p\) is printed page \(2128+p\); locations below use printed pagination. The supplied PyRigi repository [code] was inspected only in the relevant documented implementation: the README, project metadata, the public `rigid_components` wrapper, the complete `rigid_components` and `is_rigid` bodies, and nearby source context. The full inventory of 293 acquired files was mechanically checked for exact bytes and hashes; that inventory check is not scientific reading of all repository files.

The pinned PyRigi commit is `4dfb435260a7417fb4b2c5ab0bc1d434d2618d41`, dated 30 July 2026. It is a related general library cited for decomposition, not a certified historical execution of the article’s calculations. No author code was executed. Reviewer-written symbolic and combinatorial checks support the examples below. The separate calligraph-class software and all external algebraic-geometric references were not independently reproduced or verified.
# Structure, scope and checks that support the approach

The variables are complex plane realizations, and edge labels are squared distances. The transformation group \(T=\mathbb C^2\rtimes\mathrm{SO}(2,\mathbb C)\) is irreducible of dimension three and excludes reflections. This distinction is necessary: two generic mirror images of a rigid triangle belong to different directed-isometry orbits.

For sparse graphs the edge map is dominant by the rigidity characterization, and its generic complex fiber has dimension \(2|V|-|E|\). Maximal tight blocks are edge-disjoint; in a sparse graph their common-edge union argument gives uniqueness of the decomposition, with isolated singleton vertices treated separately. The main assertion is \[c(G,\lambda)=\prod_i c(G_i)\] for a general edge assignment. It does not concern every special assignment, nor the number of real connected components.

The diagram relating the edge map, the subgraph map \(S_G\), and the product of block edge maps commutes because directed isometries preserve squared distances. The submersion calculation in Lemma 8 has the right basic mechanism: the infinitesimal motions of each tight block fill the kernel of its edge differential. Once dominance and the correct orbit hypotheses are supplied, the component-count factorization in Lemma 6 reduces the main question to the general fiber of \(S_G\). The induction then aims to prove irreducibility of its fiber square, controlling the loci where comparison-map fibers increase in dimension.

Several elementary tests are consistent with this strategy. A tree with nonzero general edge labels is built from a free root and irreducible complex distance conics, so its realization space is irreducible. A triangle has two directed-isometry classes, and two otherwise independent triangles sharing a vertex have four choices. A triangle with a leaf has maximal tight blocks consisting of the triangle and the leaf edge. These checks do not prove the general product formula, but they confirm its conventions and small cases.

For the curve application, pinning an edge of nonzero squared length supplies an explicit orbit section. Under the intended one-degree-of-freedom calligraph hypothesis and the cited thinness result \(m(G)=1\), projection to the distinguished vertex is generically one-to-one. Conditional on the quoted class values, the arithmetic in Examples 24–25 is correct: \[2(272)/16=34,\quad 17(15)+1=256,\qquad
 2(11)=22,\quad 11(9)-3(2)-3(2)+1=88.\] The class values themselves were not recomputed. The discussion of real connected components correctly separates a semialgebraic question from the generic complex count. The proposed higher-dimensional extension is explicitly left open; its illustrative three-dimensional count was not independently certified by a full elimination calculation.
# Major proof issues

Problem 1 (Major: ordinary generic integrality does not imply irreducible general complex fibers).  Lemma 27(b), p. 2158, states that a general fiber of a dominant morphism between irreducible varieties is irreducible if and only if \[R=\mathbb C[X]\otimes_{\mathbb C[Y]}\mathbb C(Y)\] is a domain. This is false, even for an everywhere smooth map. Take \[f:\mathbb C^\times\longrightarrow\mathbb C^\times,\qquad x\longmapsto x^2.\] Its generic ring is \(\mathbb C(t)[x]/(x^2-t)\), a field: a rational square has even valuation at \(t=0\), whereas \(t\) has valuation one. Nevertheless every nonzero complex fiber consists of two distinct points. Thus ordinary generic integrality counts one component over \(\mathbb C(t)\), while the geometric generic fiber and general complex fibers have two.

Lemma 32, p. 2160, in fact proves that ordinary generic integrality is automatic for every dominant morphism between irreducible varieties, by localization. Combining it with Lemma 27(b) would incorrectly make all such general fibers irreducible. Example 34 in the paper itself illustrates the same distinction after adjoining a square root.

This error occurs at the final step of the proof of Lemma 10(b), the bridge needed in Lemma 11 and Proposition 12. The conclusion of Lemma 10 is not disproved by the square-map example, since that example’s fiber square is reducible. The problem is that the supplied proof does not establish its conclusion.

The needed replacement is geometric generic irreducibility, or the corresponding regularity of the function-field extension in characteristic zero, followed by a justified passage to general closed fibers. One way to organize the argument is to descend the finite set of geometric generic components to a finite normal extension of the base field. If there were more than one, the pairs of equal components and the pairs of unequal components would be two nonempty Galois-invariant collections in the generic fiber square. This is the obstruction that irreducibility of the fiber square must exclude. The argument needs the geometric components, not merely that \(R\) is a domain.

Two preceding algebraic steps also need correction. In Lemma 29, localizing \(\mathbb C[X]\otimes_{\mathbb C[Y]}\mathbb C[X]\) at all its nonzero elements produces its fraction field, not in general \(\mathbb C(X)\otimes_{\mathbb C(Y)}\mathbb C(X)\). For \(X=\mathbb A^1,Y=\mathrm{point}\), these are \(\mathbb C(x,y)\) and the localization of \(\mathbb C[x,y]\) by nonzero polynomials in the two separate variables. The element \(x+y\) is not invertible in the latter. Localize only at the multiplicative set generated by nonzero elements from the two factors; the desired domain conclusion then follows.

In Lemma 30 the inner sums in the tensor factorization must start at \(j=0\), not \(j=1\), and the linear-independence argument should include \(1,e,\ldots,e^{d-1}\). For the quadratic \(x^2-t\) used above, the correct factor is \(e\otimes1+1\otimes e\). The printed factor omits its second term, so the asserted zero product is not obtained. Finally, the proof of Lemma 10 should not infer global smoothness merely from smooth source and target; the submersion assumption belongs to part (a), with generic smoothness used where appropriate in part (b).

Problem 2 (Major: the invariant proof confuses smooth affine curves with smooth projective completions).  Proposition 33(b), p. 2161, uses \[g(\rho(C))=p_a(C).\] With the preceding Hilbert-polynomial definition of arithmetic genus, this identity is false for a smooth affine curve: its projective closure can be singular at infinity.

An example satisfying the proposition’s hypotheses is \[X=\{(x,z,y)\in\mathbb C^3:y=x^3\},\qquad f(x,z,y)=z^2,\qquad
 \rho(x,z,y)=(x,z).\] The surface \(X\cong\mathbb A^2\) is smooth and irreducible. For a general nonzero value of \(f\), its two components \(C_\pm\) are smooth affine graphs of \(x^3\), and \(\rho\) is an isomorphism on the whole fiber onto two lines. Each projective closure is the plane cubic \[YW^2-X^3=0,\] singular at \([0:1:0]\). Thus \(p_a(C_\pm)=1\), whereas \(g(\rho(C_\pm))=0\). The two components still have equal respective invariants, so this example refutes the proof identity, not the equality conclusions of Proposition 33.

Part (a) also needs a more precise descent argument. An abstract isomorphism of function fields does not preserve degree or the Hilbert polynomial of a chosen embedding: a line and the affine cubic above both have rational function field. What is relevant is the semilinear Galois action on the embedded ideals, which preserves their graded Hilbert functions after projective closure. Choose a finite normal extension of \(\mathbb C(Y)\) over which the geometric generic components are defined, and use its Galois group over \(\mathbb C(Y)\). The printed extension \(E/\mathbb C(Z)\) is not the specified splitting extension of the base field. The leading coefficient of a Hilbert polynomial is generally \(\deg(C)/(\dim C)!\), a positive rational number, not always an integer.

For geometric genus, use the smooth projective normalizations of the component curves; Galois conjugation and birational projection preserve their genus. Finally justify specialization to general closed fibers after shrinking the base and controlling the relevant projective families. These changes can support the intended equal-degree and equal-genus conclusions, but the present proof does not provide them. The issue matters to Corollary 2 and its geometric-genus assertions, not merely to an unused auxiliary identity.
# Auxiliary and boundary corrections

Problem 3 (Minor: Lemma 15 omits orientation and isotropic exceptions).  In Lemma 15(e), pp. 2144–2146, take the ordered triples \[P=((0,0),(1,0),(0,1)),\qquad
 Q=((0,0),(1,0),(0,-1)).\] They are noncollinear and all corresponding pairwise squared distances agree, so the displayed hypothesis on \(\Lambda\) holds. Writing \(p_0=(x,y)\), \(q_0=(u,v)\), the equations defining \(\Gamma\) reduce to \(u=x,v=-y\), giving a two-dimensional reflection graph.

The unique directed isometry fixing the first two corresponding vertices is the identity. Hence the additional condition defining \(\Gamma'\) requires \(u=x,v=y\), and the third distance equation forces \(y=0\). Consequently \[\dim\Gamma=2,\qquad \dim\Gamma'=1,\] contrary to the stated equality. The proof’s assertion that congruent noncollinear triples admit a directed isometry ignores the reflected orientation.

There is a separate complex exception in part (c). Let \(p_1=q_1=0\), \(p_2=(1,i)\), \(q_2=(1,-i)\). The endpoints are distinct and both squared lengths are zero, but no matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}c&-s\\s&c\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) sends \(p_2\) to \(q_2\): its two linear equations are already inconsistent. Thus \(\Gamma'\) is empty. These two-point configurations have full edge-Jacobian rank and are not excluded by the definition of \(U_V\).

Distinguish direct and reflected congruence and treat isotropic pairs explicitly. Alternatively, shrink the generic open sets to exclude the needed null distances, while proving that this restriction preserves the desired generic component counts and supplying the omitted exceptional-stratum bounds. In Lemmas 17–18, equality of distances alone does not justify every claimed reconstruction of a transformation or the asserted surjectivity onto the exceptional locus.

These examples do not refute the main product formula. For instance, the reflected three-point case still has \(\dim\Gamma=2\), which is the upper-dimensional possibility used in one induction case, and a common rigid block fixes the orientation in another. The local statements and their precise uses must nevertheless be corrected.

Problem 4 (Minor: the orbit lemmas require stronger hypotheses and a generic assignment).  Lemma 5, pp. 2137–2138, is false for arbitrary topological spaces with free actions. Let \(X=Y=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^2\), let \(G=\mathbb R\), and fix irrational \(\alpha\). Define \[f(x,y)=(2x,y),\quad
 t\cdot_Y(x,y)=(x+t,y+\alpha t),\quad
 t\cdot_X(x,y)=(x+t/2,y+\alpha t).\] Both actions are free, \(G\) is connected, and \(f\) is equivariant. The fiber over \((0,0)\) has two points. Its inverse image over the \(G\)-orbit consists of two disjoint dense connected irrational-flow orbits, whose union is connected: either orbit is connected and dense in that union. Thus the two component numbers are two and one. In the proof, connectedness need not imply path-connectedness, and a free orbit map need not have a continuous inverse.

For the actual algebraic application, use locally closed algebraic orbits and an explicit orbit trivialization. Restrict to the relevant generic configurations. The action on the entire target in Lemma 6 is not free at coincident realizations or singleton blocks; isolated vertices can be handled separately, with their connected stabilizers. Dominance of \(S_G\) should be deduced from Lemma 8’s submersion, not solely from dominance of the other maps in a commuting diagram.

Lemma 21, pp. 2151–2152, also needs a general-\(\lambda\) hypothesis. For \(G=K_2\) and \(\lambda=0\), one irreducible component is \[r_2-r_1=a(1,i),\qquad a\in\mathbb C.\] It contains both the collapsed realization \(r_1=r_2=0\) and the distinct realization \(s_1=0,s_2=(1,i)\). They cannot be related by any directed isometry, since a bijection preserves coincidence. For a tight graph the existence of the equal-\(S_G\) data in Lemma 21(ii) would imply exactly such congruence. Thus (i) does not imply (ii) at this assignment.

Even generically, the proof’s claim that \(\pi^{-1}(C)=C\times T\) is a fiber component of \(S_G\) is dimensionally wrong for \(K_2\): it has dimension six, whereas an \(S_G\) fiber has dimension three. Use the equivariant product description instead. Corollary 1 already concerns a general assignment, so its stated scope is not contradicted by the special zero-length example.

Problem 5 (Minor: the induction base and comparison fibers need explicit completion).  For one vertex, Proposition 20 identifies \(P(G)\) with \((U_V\times T)^2\), of dimension ten. The defining equation \(t(r)=u(s)\) remains present. The correct parametrization is \[(r,t,u)\longmapsto(r,t;u^{-1}t(r),u),\qquad
 P(G)\cong\mathbb C^2\times T^2,\] of dimension eight, consistent with Lemma 16. The desired irreducibility follows from this corrected parametrization.

The reduction of \(K_2\) deletes its sole one-edge block, leaving \(I^m=\varnothing\) and \(V^m=\varnothing\). Thus the induction needs the additional base \(P(\varnothing)=\mathrm{point}\); it does not always terminate at one vertex. The notation \(\widetilde r_1\) in the universal setup of Lemma 18 is undefined for this example, so the leaf and disappearing-neighbor cases must be treated separately.

More generally, the comparison proof should establish nonempty general fibers or dominance before applying its lower dimension bound. An injective morphism with dense image in an irreducible variety does not alone make its source irreducible. For example, the disjoint union of \(\mathbb A^1\setminus\{0\}\) and a point maps bijectively to \(\mathbb A^1\). In the intended parametrization, prove that the image is an open subset and that reconstruction gives a regular inverse on the stated open set; then irreducibility follows. Supply this argument for the omitted cases and the corrected exceptional configurations.

Finally, the tangent-space calculation in Lemma 8 should treat a singleton separately: its edge kernel has dimension two, not \(2|V_i|-(2|V_i|-3)=3\). In the last line, the displayed choice \(dg(0,\beta)=dg(\alpha,0)-\gamma\) yields \(\gamma=dg(\alpha,-\beta)\). These are repairable details, but they should not be hidden inside the induction.

Problem 6 (Minor: the calligraph definition does not enforce a curve).  The definition on p. 2152 says that adjoining either \(\{1,0\}\) or \(\{2,0\}\) produces a tight graph. As written it includes an already tight triangle on \(0,1,2\): adjoining an existing edge changes nothing. The triangle also passes the stated thinness conditions on p. 2154, since the edge-deletion condition is imposed only for \(|V|>3\), and deletion of two vertices leaves one connected vertex. Its general pinned realization set has two points, not one-dimensional curves.

Require a genuine one-edge deficiency, for example that \(G\) is not tight, \(|E|=2|V|-4\), and at least one genuinely new indicated edge produces a tight graph. The intended examples \(L,R,C_v\) satisfy this requirement. Also state that projected coupler curves mean Zariski closures unless closedness of the projection image is proved; elimination gives the closure in general. In the higher-dimensional discussion on p. 2156, finite general fiber must likewise mean finite modulo Euclidean motions, since translation already prevents the unquotiented fiber from being finite.

Problem 7 (Minor: a nondefault branch of the related library skips size \(n-1\) components).  In the acquired PyRigi `generic.py`, the subgraph enumeration in `rigid_components` uses `range(2, graph.number_of_nodes()-1)`. Python excludes the upper endpoint, so subsets of size \(n-1\) are never tested.

For a triangle on \(0,1,2\) and a leaf edge \(\{2,3\}\), the graph is not rigid, and its maximal rigid blocks are \(\{0,1,2\}\) and \(\{2,3\}\). At \(n=4\), the enumeration tests only pairs. Even with an exact rigidity oracle, this branch therefore misses the triangle and retains its individual edges. A separate exhaustive combinatorial check confirms the correct blocks.

Include subset size \(n-1\). This concerns the `subgraphs-pebble`, `randomized` and `numerical` branches. The default two-dimensional `pebble` branch uses a different closure-based procedure and is not implicated by this check. This is static analysis of the dated snapshot, not an author-code execution or evidence that the paper’s examples used the affected branch.
# Assessment

Major revision is required to replace the ordinary-versus-geometric generic-fiber argument and the affine-genus justification. The orientation, orbit and induction corrections should be propagated through the comparison-map proof with precise open-set and exceptional-fiber hypotheses. The main product formula and the equal-invariant conclusions remain plausible and are not disproved by the explicit examples in this report; the established objections identify false auxiliary assertions and gaps in their printed derivations.

The checks are targeted algebraic and combinatorial validations, not a complete formal proof audit of all external inputs. In particular, no numerical realization-count or calligraph-class package was run. Scientific adjudication remains pending. Focused independent acceptance of the reported Problems, including the correction to the quadratic example above, is recorded in the accompanying provenance.

Supply this argument for the omitted cases and the corrected exceptional configurations.

Finally, the tangent-space calculation in Lemma 8 should treat a singleton separately: its edge kernel has dimension two, not \(2|V_i|-(2|V_i|-3)=3\). In the last line, the displayed choice \(dg(0,\beta)=dg(\alpha,0)-\gamma\) yields \(\gamma=dg(\alpha,-\beta)\). These are repairable details, but they should not be hidden inside the induction.

report: Abstract: The decrease estimates for general self-concordant path following and the conditional restart comparison are useful. Two claims in the feasibility application require substantial revision. The stated square-root logarithmic feasibility bound drops a diameter factor that is essential even in one dimension; an analytic lower bound for the proposed PFS contradicts the claimed rate. The subsequent zero-gap linear-programming embedding has no strictly interior feasible point, so the positive-depth hypothesis cannot be transferred as asserted. Further, localized corrections are needed for the clipped predictor, signed path lemma, Newton hypotheses, finite indices, work counts and cubic regularization parameter. The explicit examples below are separated from the conditional conclusions that they do not refute.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Technical Review of
Improved global performance guarantees of second-order methods in convex minimization
# Identity, material and scope

The reviewed article is Pavel Dvurechensky and Yurii Nesterov, Improved global performance guarantees of second-order methods in convex minimization, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 2165–2205, published online 13 August 2025, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09726-6 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09726-6) [paper]. The assigned identifier is M25-0470. The exact acquired 41-page publisher version of record was reviewed. The 2025 online date and 2026 volume date are distinct. No alternate version or subsequent correction was compared.

The initial reviewer read all 41 text pages, including all 45 reference entries, and inspected all 41 source page images. Focused independent acceptance rechecked the eight reported Problems, their assumptions, decisive evidence and impact boundaries; it did not repeat the whole-paper initial review. Physical PDF page \(p\) corresponds to printed page \(2164+p\); locations below use printed pagination. The two acquired payload files are the article PDF and publisher metadata. Their exact inventory verification is distinct from scientific reading. No separate author implementation or supplement was available in the bounded acquired record; this absence is not treated as a defect.

The checks used reviewer-written symbolic calculations and 100-decimal-digit arithmetic. No author code was executed. The numerical PFS runs implement the displayed mathematical update independently and corroborate an analytic argument; they are not a substitute for that argument. The external literature, priority claims and all cited algorithmic rate theorems were not independently re-fetched. In particular, the Section 7 comparison below is assessed conditionally on the rate assumed in equation (114).
# Mathematical structure and checks supporting the approach

The basic unconstrained setting is a convex \(C^3\) function with positive definite Hessian and an attained minimum, together with \[|D^3f(x)[h]^3|\leq 2M_f\langle \nabla^2f(x)h,h\rangle^{3/2}.\] The dimensionless quantities \(M_f\lambda_f(x)\) and \(\Delta=M_f^2(f(x_0)-f^\ast)\) are the appropriate scaling variables. On their stated local domains, the Hessian comparison and Taylor bounds provide the main estimates. The proof of the damped Newton bound \(\lambda_f(x_+)\leq 2M_f\lambda_f(x)^2\) was checked: integrating the Hessian sandwich gives the required negative semidefinite normalized residual matrix and its operator-norm bound. The local convergence discussion should be read with the qualifications in Problem 5.

The PFS maintains a small decrement for \(f_t(x)=f(x)-t\langle
abla f(x_0),xangle\). Its proof combines a decrease proportional to \(t_k\|
abla f(x_0)\|_{x_k}^{\ast}\) with a reciprocal-sum inequality. Correctly indexed, this gives the \(N^2/\Delta\) exponent in (37). The passage from the exact path to a small decrement at the approximate point then introduces the logarithm involving the level-set diameter \(D\) in (44). That logarithm is part of the theorem and cannot be discarded in a subsequent application. The exact path itself remains in the starting level set: differentiating its defining equation yields \[ rac{d}{dt} f(x(t))
 =t\,\langle
abla f(x_0),[
abla^2f(x(t))]^{-1}
abla f(x_0)angle\geq0.\]

For the predictor-corrector analysis, the positive-direction form of Lemma 4 gives the intended second-order predictor error. With \(\beta=0.0015\), \(\gamma=0.158\), the corrected constants are \[\kappa=0.0350648269066\ldots,\qquad
 (\gamma\kappa)^{-1/2}=13.4349361516\ldots .\] The corresponding corrected centering estimate is \(0.001475674<0.0015\). For the barrier parameters \(\beta=0.06,\gamma=0.254\), it is \(0.059699172<0.06\). Thus the parameter choices themselves remain admissible after the identified sign and cutoff repairs.

The constrained primal certificate in Lemma 6 follows from the barrier gradient bound and the distance to the path. In the dual construction, the norm identity for the affine correction in (109) also checks out, provided the matrix inverses exist: the primal correction norm equals the dual residual norm, and the Dikin ellipsoid gives feasibility. Problems 4 and 7 specify the needed sign and data qualifications.

Finally, the Section 7 implication \[M_f=\frac{H_f}{2\sigma_f^{3/2}},\qquad
 \frac{\sigma_f^3}{2H_f^2}=\frac{1}{8M_f^2}\] is correct. Conditional on (114), the halving schedule and geometric sum give the stated restart exponents \(1/4,1/6,1/7\) for \(p=2,3,7/2\). This conditional conclusion is distinct from claiming that an arbitrary positive cubic parameter already provides (114).
# Major issues in the feasibility application

Problem 1 (Major: an essential logarithmic factor is lost in Section 4.2).  On p. 2185, item 2 claims ordinary \[O\!\left(\sqrt{\nu\log(1/\varepsilon)}\right)\] complexity for the PFS, citing (44). The following discussion uses this to claim a faster dependence on feasibility depth than the usual logarithmic rate. The source page shows an ordinary \(O\), not notation suppressing additional logarithms.

Use the natural corrected depth convention \(0\leq\delta\leq1\) discussed in Problem 7, and let \[Q=[-1,1],\qquad F(a)=-\log(1-a)-\log(1+a),\qquad
 A=1,\quad b=1-\varepsilon,\quad 0<\varepsilon\leq\tfrac14.\] This is a standard self-concordant barrier; \(\nu=2\) is a valid fixed parameter. Its analytic center is \(0\), \(F(0)=0\), and the feasibility depth is precisely \(\varepsilon\). Consider the dual objective actually used in Section 4.2: \[f(y)=F^\ast(y)-by,\qquad y_0=0,\qquad M_f=1.\] Writing \(s=\sqrt{1+y^2}\), elementary conjugacy gives \[a(y)=(F^\ast)'(y)=\frac{y}{1+s},\qquad
 f''(y)=\frac{1}{s(s+1)},\qquad
 F''(a(y))=s(s+1).\] The minimum occurs at \(a=b\), so \[\Delta=f(0)-f^\ast=F(b)=-\log(1-b^2)
       =\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)).\] Moreover \(y^\ast=2b/(1-b^2)\), and both \(0,y^\ast\) belong to the starting level set. Since \(f''(0)=1/2\), \[D\geq \frac{y^\ast}{\sqrt2}=\Theta(1/\varepsilon).\] The logarithm in (44) therefore grows at least on the order of \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) in this family.

Independent 100-digit evaluations of (32) gave the following results. The analytic lower bound is the decisive check. \[\begin{array}{c|r|r}
 \varepsilon & \text{PFS steps to }\lambda_f\leq1/2
 & \text{ceiling of the displayed lower bound}\\ \hline
 10^{-2}&34&21\\
 10^{-4}&72&55\\
 10^{-8}&148&126\\
 10^{-16}&300&268\\
 10^{-32}&603&553
\end{array}\] All checked iterates maintained the prescribed centering tolerance.

Theorem 6 with its full diameter logarithm is not refuted. What fails is the stronger rate asserted in the feasibility application and the ensuing claimed improvement in the depth dependence. Retain and estimate that logarithm, then revise the corresponding contribution and comparison with long-step methods. A bound on an initial objective residual alone is insufficient for the stated conclusion.

Problem 2 (Major: the proposed LP reduction has zero feasibility depth).  On p. 2186, the paper homogenizes primal feasibility, dual feasibility and an exact zero duality gap, then intersects with a simplex and claims that the preceding positive-depth complexity applies to linear programming. Eliminating the simplex equality does not resolve the relevant obstruction.

With the paper’s block notation \(A=(I,B)\), define the homogenized dual variable \[y=\tau c_1-s_1.\] The displayed equalities imply \[Ax=\tau b,\qquad A^Ty+s=\tau c,\qquad
 c^Tx+b^Ts_1-\tau b^Tc_1=0.\] Therefore \[x^Ts=\tau(c^Tx-b^Ty)
     =\tau(c^Tx+b^Ts_1-\tau b^Tc_1)=0.\] Since \(x,s\geq0\), every feasible point satisfies complementarity. In particular, there is no feasible point with all coordinates of \(x,s,\tau\) positive. After eliminating the simplex equality, the same points remain on the boundary of the resulting full-dimensional simplex. The hypothesis \(\varepsilon>0\) required in (56) is not obtained.

For a concrete bounded-optimum example, take \[\min x\quad\text{subject to }x=1,\quad x\geq0.\] The normalized homogeneous system becomes \[x=\tau,\qquad x+s-\tau=0,\qquad x+s+\tau=1,\] whose unique solution is \((x,s,\tau)=(1/2,0,1/2)\). It lies on the boundary \(s=0\). A translation placing the simplex center at the origin does not change the lack of an interior feasible point.

There is a second extraction issue: a nonzero homogeneous solution need not have \(\tau>0\). For \(A=(1,0)\), \(b=1\), \(c=(0,0)\), the point \[x=(0,1),\qquad s=(0,0),\qquad \tau=0\] satisfies the homogeneous equalities and the unit-simplex normalization, but cannot be dehomogenized by division by \(\tau\). The original LP in this example is feasible; the example shows that an arbitrary normalized homogeneous solution is not automatically an optimal solution of it.

A valid transfer needs a suitable perturbed or strictly feasible embedding, a positive-depth bound for that construction, and extraction rules distinguishing the possible homogeneous cases. Alternatively, remove the asserted direct transfer. This objection concerns the particular construction printed here, not the established homogeneous self-dual methods cited in the bibliography.
# Localized algorithmic and proof corrections

Problem 3 (Minor: the predictor must use the clipped parameter change).  In (75), p. 2189, \(t_+\) is clipped at zero, but the predictor still uses the full amount \[\widehat\tau=\frac{\gamma}{M_f\|\nabla f(x_0)\|_x^\ast}.\] When \(t<\widehat\tau\), Lemma 4 controls the residual for \(t-\widehat\tau\), whereas the corrector uses \(t_+=0\). Thus (76) does not follow as stated.

An exact example falsifies the unconditional assertion of Theorem 8. Let \[f(x)=\tfrac12x^2+\tfrac14x^4,\quad M_f=1,\quad
 x=x_0=\frac{100}{2497},\quad t=1.\] This function is globally self-concordant: the maximum of \(3|x|/(1+3x^2)^{3/2}\) is \(2/3\), so \(M_f=1\) is admissible. Here \[\sqrt{f''(x_0)}=\frac{2503}{2497},\qquad
 \lambda_{f_t}(x)=0,\qquad \widehat\tau>1.\] With \(\gamma=79/500\), equation (75) gives \(t_+=0\) and \[y=\frac{100}{2497}-\frac{79}{500}\frac{2497}{2503},
 \qquad
 x_+=y-\frac{y+y^3}{1+3y^2}=\frac{2y^3}{1+3y^2}.\] All these points are rational. Comparing squared decrements exactly yields \[\lambda_f(x_+)=0.003121087486\ldots>0.0015=\beta.\]

Use \[	au=\min\!\left\{t, rac{\gamma}{M_f\|
abla f(x_0)\|_x^\ast}ight\},
 \qquad t_+=t-	au,\qquad
 y=x-	au[
abla^2f(x)]^{-1}
abla f(x_0).\] Handle an initially zero gradient before dividing, and specify the local phase.

The impact should be calibrated carefully. Under the centering condition, clipping implies \[M_f\lambda_f(x)
 \leq M_f t\|\nabla f(x_0)\|_x^\ast+\beta
 \leq\gamma+\beta=0.1595<1/2.\] Thus the clipping problem occurs after the input has already entered the target region. It falsifies Theorem 8 as written and affects continuation of (75), but it does not refute the first-entry complexity in Theorems 9–10. This is why it is classified as Minor here.

Problem 4 (Minor: signed predictor bounds and the dual path label need correction).  Lemma 4, pp. 2187–2188, states (67) for all \(\tau\) with \(|\tau|M_fr<1\), but its bound and proof use \(\tau\) without absolute values. For negative \(\tau\), the norm identity in (69), the Hessian sandwich and integration direction are not justified in that form.

Use the same quartic, now with \[M_f=\tfrac23,\quad x=1,\quad t=0,\quad c=4,\quad
 h=1,\quad r=2,\quad \tau=-\tfrac1{10}.\] The hypothesis is satisfied and the initial decrement is \(1\). Direct substitution gives \[\lambda_{f_{t-\tau}}(x+\tau h)
 =\frac{2029}{100\sqrt{343}}>1.09,
 \qquad
 \text{printed right side of (67)}=\frac{261}{289}<0.904.\] The squared inequality was checked exactly.

Either restrict the displayed bound to \(\tau\geq0\), or replace the controlling occurrences by \(|\tau|\) and reverse the direction consistently when needed. The intended positive-step predictor estimate survives.

There is a related sign error in Lemma 7, p. 2197. Its convention is \(\Phi_t(u)=\Phi(u)-t\langle b,u\rangle\). A predictor \(v=u+\tau[\nabla^2\Phi(u)]^{-1}b\) transports the residual to parameter \(t(u)+\tau\), not \(t(u)-\tau\). Apply Lemma 4 with its plus-linear convention and initial parameter \(-t(u)\), or rewrite the lemma in the dual convention.

For the legitimate one-dimensional interval conjugate \(\Phi=F^\ast\) from Problem 1, at \(u=0\) with \(b=1,\gamma=0.254\), the printed intermediate residual is approximately \(0.523711\), while the intended bound with zero initial residual is \((\gamma/(1-\gamma))^2\approx0.1159\). The corrected-sign residual is approximately \(0.008065\). The minimized residual \(\lambda(v)\) is zero in this one-dimensional check, so the example exposes the intermediate comparison, not a failure of the corrected centering conclusion.

Problem 5 (Minor: state the local Newton hypothesis and fix the scaled distance expression).  Theorem 1, p. 2172, omits the necessary condition \(M_f\lambda_f(x)<1\) for (19). A squared denominator does not extend the local estimate past that condition.

For the globally standard self-concordant quartic \(f(x)=x^2/2+x^4/4\), take \(M_f=1\), \(x=10\). Its Newton point is \(x_+=2000/301\). Exact squared comparisons give \[\lambda_f(10)>50,\qquad \lambda_f(x_+)>25,\] whereas the displayed right side of (19) is less than \((50/49)^2<1.042\). The intended local uses of this theorem are valid once the condition is restored.

In (11), p. 2170, the first expression is correct, but its last expansion has an extra \(M_f\): \[\frac1{M_f}\omega_\ast'(M_f\lambda)
 =\frac{\lambda}{1-M_f\lambda},
 \quad\text{not}\quad
 \frac{M_f\lambda}{1-M_f\lambda}.\] For \(f(x)=x^2/2\), \(M_f=1/2\), \(x=1/5\), the distance to the minimizer is \(1/5\); the printed last expression is \(1/9\), while the correct bound is \(2/9\).

Also separate \(M_f=0\), which is admitted in Definition 1 but makes several displayed inverses undefined. A positive definite quadratic can be solved directly or assigned any positive admissible self-concordance constant. State the real domain \(0\leq\tau<1\) for \(\omega_\ast\), and terminate at zero residual instead of using a ratio \(0/0\). These qualifications do not invalidate the damped Newton proof in its intended regime.

Problem 6 (Minor: correct finite indices, constants and the unit of work).  The proofs of Theorems 5 and 9 define a sum through \(k=N\) while bounding \(t_N\). There are only \(N\) updates from \(t_0\) to \(t_N\); use \(k=0,\ldots,N-1\), or put \(t_{N+1}\) on the left. With consistent indexing, the \(N^2\) bounds (37) and (78) follow by the same argument.

Equation (43), p. 2178, is false as indexed. For \(f(x)=x^2/2\), \(M_f=1,x_0=1,N=0\), the stated pre-region and decrease conditions hold, but its right side is \(1-\gamma(\gamma-2\beta)=0.99319375<1=t_0\). Replace \(N+1\) by \(N\) when the left side remains \(t_N\). In the preceding concave optimization argument, the equal allocation is a maximum, not a minimum. The source image correctly contains a sum of logarithms; no product-of-logarithms defect is alleged.

The actual parameters in (30) give \[\left(\frac{2}{\gamma(\gamma-2\beta)}\right)^{1/2}
 =17.1419825742\ldots,\] so the literal upper bound \(17.1\) in Remark 3 needs corrected rounding or different explicitly stated parameters. In the \(\rho_k\) expression following (83), p. 2191, the argument of the last \(\omega_\ast\) must be \[\frac{\beta}{1-\gamma}+\frac{\gamma^2}{(1-\gamma)^2},\] as required by (82), rather than the printed difference. After this repair, the dimensionless lower bound for \(\rho_k\) is still \(0.0247046210\ldots>0\); this does not overturn the positive-decrease argument.

For adaptive PFS, testing trial indices \(i=0,\ldots,i_k\) costs \(i_k+1\) Newton trials, including the accepted one. Thus the total through outer iteration \(k\) is \[\sum_{j=0}^{k}(i_j+1)
 =2(k+1)+\log_2\frac{\gamma_{-1}}{\gamma_k},\] not merely \(\sum_{j=0}^{k}i_j\). For example, on a quadratic every first trial may be accepted, giving \(i_j=0\) while still requiring one trial at every iteration.

Finally, the PCPFS constants compare outer iterations. A predictor-corrector iteration evaluates Hessians at both the current point and the predictor point, whereas a PFS iteration uses one current Hessian. State this unit when describing improved constants. The algebraic outer-iteration improvement alone does not establish fewer Hessian evaluations or lower running time.

Problem 7 (Minor: feasibility depth and dual inverses need precise data assumptions).  In (56), p. 2183, the maximization must restrict \(0\leq\delta\leq1\). As written, \(\delta\geq0\) makes the depth unbounded for any nonempty affine feasible set. Indeed, because \(0\in\operatorname{int}Q\), a ball of radius \(r>0\) lies in \(Q\). For \(\delta>1\), the reflected dilation \((1-\delta)Q\) contains a ball of radius \((\delta-1)r\), hence eventually any fixed feasible point.

Section 4.2 explicitly assumes that \(0\) is an analytic center, \(\nabla F(0)=0\), and \(F(0)=0\) (p. 2183). These are operative assumptions. The barrier \(-\log(1+x)\) on \((-1,\infty)\) has no analytic center and is therefore outside that setting, not a counterexample under its assumptions. Existence must remain a restriction of the claimed scope rather than a normalization available for every closed convex \(Q\). This is a scope clarification, not an additional established defect.

The dual Hessian \[\nabla^2\Phi(u)=A[\nabla^2F(x)]^{-1}A^T\] is invertible only when \(A\) has full row rank. This is not guaranteed by the arbitrary equality matrix in Section 4.2 or by \(A=(-c^T;B)\) in Section 6.2. For \(Q=[-1,1]^2\), its separable logarithmic barrier, \(B=(1,0)\) and \(c=(1,0)\), the two rows of \(A\) are dependent and the objective is constant on \(Bx=0\). Remove redundant consistent constraints and handle such constant objectives separately before applying the displayed inverses.

Likewise, treat zero directions and initially solved problems before divisions by their local dual norms; write \(\Phi_t(u)=\Phi(u)-t\langle b,u\rangle\) in place of the vector subtraction on p. 2196; and use \(\sigma>0\) in reciprocal certificates (105)–(108). The Major counterexample in Problem 1 uses a bounded set, a genuine analytic center, full rank and a nonzero direction, so it does not depend on any of these degeneracies.

Problem 8 (Minor: specify the cubic parameter and the observable restart termination).  Equation (113), p. 2200, introduces a cubic parameter \(M>0\), followed by a convergence claim. Positivity alone is insufficient for that claim. A standard sufficient condition for the displayed cubic model to majorize \(f\) is \(M\geq H_f\); the parameter assumptions of the imported rate (114) should be stated.

Here is an exact two-cycle with a positive parameter. Let \[f(x)=\tfrac12x^2+K\log\cosh x,\qquad
 K=\frac{10}{\tanh2-4\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2 2}=14.6751448162\ldots .\] The denominator is positive, \(f''(x)=1+K\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x\geq1\), and \[|f'''(x)|=2K\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x\,|\tanh x|
 \leq H_f=\frac{4K}{3\sqrt3}=11.2969317467\ldots .\] Thus the function satisfies the strong convexity and global Lipschitz-Hessian assumptions.

Take \(M=1\). At \(x=2\), the derivative of the strongly convex cubic model with respect to its step \(h\), evaluated at \(h=-4\), is \[f'(2)-4f''(2)-8
 =K(\tanh2-4\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^22)-10=0.\] Hence its unique minimizer sends \(2\) to \(-2\). Evenness sends \(-2\) back to \(2\). The method does not converge to the minimizer \(0\) for this allowed positive \(M\).

This example does not refute Theorem 13, whose starting assumption is the rate (114). It shows why that assumption cannot be inferred from \(M>0\) alone. With the appropriate rate available, the halving proof and the resulting exponents remain intact.

The restart description should also first handle an initial point already in \(\mathcal Q_f\), rather than applying a negative or undefined logarithmic stage bound. Remark 5 makes the stage lengths computable using a known lower bound \(\widetilde f\), but the stopping test \(f(y_k)-f^\ast\leq1/(8M_f^2)\) still involves \(f^\ast\). Supply a predetermined sufficient number of stages based on \(f(x_0)-\widetilde f\), or an observable certificate. This is a specification repair, not a counterexample to the conditional halving argument.
# Assessment

Major revision is required for the feasibility rate and the claimed direct transfer to linear programming. The interval-barrier construction is an analytic counterexample to the asserted uniform PFS rate, while the complementarity calculation identifies a failed hypothesis in the LP reduction. These objections should be propagated to the introduction and the comparison of methods.

The other findings have more limited effects. The clipped-step counterexample lies inside the target region, the signed lemma has a direct corrected version, the repaired predictor constants remain positive, and the restart comparison remains valid under its assumed rate and proper regularization parameters. No conclusion here asserts that every principal theorem of the paper is false.

The reported Problems have undergone focused independent scientific acceptance against the exact acquired version. The analytic-center discussion in Problem 7 has been narrowed to respect the paper’s explicit assumption; the other supported findings and their impact grades are retained. This is not complete formal verification of the paper or its external references. Scientific adjudication remains pending.
