 F''(a(y))=s(s+1).\] The minimum occurs at \(a=b\), so \[\Delta=f(0)-f^\ast=F(b)=-\log(1-b^2)
       =\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)).\] Moreover \(y^\ast=2b/(1-b^2)\), and both \(0,y^\ast\) belong to the starting level set. Since \(f''(0)=1/2\), \[D\geq \frac{y^\ast}{\sqrt2}=\Theta(1/\varepsilon).\] The logarithm in (44) therefore grows at least on the order of \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) in this family.

Independent 100-digit evaluations of (32) gave the following results. The analytic lower bound is the decisive check. \[\begin{array}{c|r|r}
 \varepsilon & \text{PFS steps to }\lambda_f\leq1/2
 & \text{ceiling of the displayed lower bound}\\ \hline
 10^{-2}&34&21\\
 10^{-4}&72&55\\
 10^{-8}&148&126\\
 10^{-16}&300&268\\
 10^{-32}&603&553
\end{array}\] All checked iterates maintained the prescribed centering tolerance.

Theorem 6 with its full diameter logarithm is not refuted. What fails is the stronger rate asserted in the feasibility application and the ensuing claimed improvement in the depth dependence. Retain and estimate that logarithm, then revise the corresponding contribution and comparison with long-step methods. A bound on an initial objective residual alone is insufficient for the stated conclusion.
result: Result: This analytic Omega(log(1/epsilon)) lower bound contradicts the uniform ordinary O(sqrt(nu log(1/epsilon))) claim for fixed nu. D is at least y_star/sqrt(2)=Theta(1/epsilon).

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Retain and estimate the diameter logarithm before asserting a feasibility rate or superiority over long-step schemes. Revise the associated contribution and convergence discussion.

problems.title: The zero-gap LP embedding does not satisfy positive feasibility depth
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, p. 2186
claim: Recorded check: The homogeneous equalities imply x^T s=tau*(c^T x+b^T s1-tau*b^T c1)=0. Thus no point has all x,s,tau positive. For min x subject to x=1,x>=0, the normalized solution is (x,s,tau)=(1/2,0,1/2). A=[1,0],b=1,c=0 additionally admits the tau=0 ray x=(0,1),s=0.
analysis: On p. 2186, the paper homogenizes primal feasibility, dual feasibility and an exact zero duality gap, then intersects with a simplex and claims that the preceding positive-depth complexity applies to linear programming. Eliminating the simplex equality does not resolve the relevant obstruction.

With the paper’s block notation \(A=(I,B)\), define the homogenized dual variable \[y=\tau c_1-s_1.\] The displayed equalities imply \[Ax=\tau b,\qquad A^Ty+s=\tau c,\qquad
 c^Tx+b^Ts_1-\tau b^Tc_1=0.\] Therefore \[x^Ts=\tau(c^Tx-b^Ty)
     =\tau(c^Tx+b^Ts_1-\tau b^Tc_1)=0.\] Since \(x,s\geq0\), every feasible point satisfies complementarity. In particular, there is no feasible point with all coordinates of \(x,s,\tau\) positive. After eliminating the simplex equality, the same points remain on the boundary of the resulting full-dimensional simplex. The hypothesis \(\varepsilon>0\) required in (56) is not obtained.

For a concrete bounded-optimum example, take \[\min x\quad\text{subject to }x=1,\quad x\geq0.\] The normalized homogeneous system becomes \[x=\tau,\qquad x+s-\tau=0,\qquad x+s+\tau=1,\] whose unique solution is \((x,s,\tau)=(1/2,0,1/2)\). It lies on the boundary \(s=0\). A translation placing the simplex center at the origin does not change the lack of an interior feasible point.

There is a second extraction issue: a nonzero homogeneous solution need not have \(\tau>0\). For \(A=(1,0)\), \(b=1\), \(c=(0,0)\), the point \[x=(0,1),\qquad s=(0,0),\qquad \tau=0\] satisfies the homogeneous equalities and the unit-simplex normalization, but cannot be dehomogenized by division by \(\tau\). The original LP in this example is feasible; the example shows that an arbitrary normalized homogeneous solution is not automatically an optimal solution of it.

A valid transfer needs a suitable perturbed or strictly feasible embedding, a positive-depth bound for that construction, and extraction rules distinguishing the possible homogeneous cases. Alternatively, remove the asserted direct transfer. This objection concerns the particular construction printed here, not the established homogeneous self-dual methods cited in the bibliography.
result: Result: Eliminating the simplex equality does not create an interior feasible point, and nonzero homogeneous solutions need not have tau>0. The claimed direct LP complexity transfer is unsupported.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Provide a strictly feasible perturbation or embedding with an explicit positive-depth bound and correct extraction rules; otherwise remove the claimed direct transfer.

problems.title: The predictor and clipped path parameter in (75) are inconsistent
claim: Recorded check: For f=x^2/2+x^4/4,M_f=1,x=x0=100/2497,t=1, H0=(2503/2497)^2, gamma=.158, the input centering residual is zero and t_plus=0. The full predictor and Newton corrector give lambda_f(x_plus)=0.003121087486...>beta=.0015; the violation was checked with exact rational squares.
analysis: In (75), p. 2189, \(t_+\) is clipped at zero, but the predictor still uses the full amount \[\widehat\tau=\frac{\gamma}{M_f\|\nabla f(x_0)\|_x^\ast}.\] When \(t<\widehat\tau\), Lemma 4 controls the residual for \(t-\widehat\tau\), whereas the corrector uses \(t_+=0\). Thus (76) does not follow as stated.

An exact example falsifies the unconditional assertion of Theorem 8. Let \[f(x)=\tfrac12x^2+\tfrac14x^4,\quad M_f=1,\quad
 x=x_0=\frac{100}{2497},\quad t=1.\] This function is globally self-concordant: the maximum of \(3|x|/(1+3x^2)^{3/2}\) is \(2/3\), so \(M_f=1\) is admissible. Here \[\sqrt{f''(x_0)}=\frac{2503}{2497},\qquad
 \lambda_{f_t}(x)=0,\qquad \widehat\tau>1.\] With \(\gamma=79/500\), equation (75) gives \(t_+=0\) and \[y=\frac{100}{2497}-\frac{79}{500}\frac{2497}{2503},
 \qquad
 x_+=y-\frac{y+y^3}{1+3y^2}=\frac{2y^3}{1+3y^2}.\] All these points are rational. Comparing squared decrements exactly yields \[\lambda_f(x_+)=0.003121087486\ldots>0.0015=\beta.\]

Use \[	au=\min\!\left\{t, rac{\gamma}{M_f\|
abla f(x_0)\|_x^\ast}ight\},
 \qquad t_+=t-	au,\qquad
 y=x-	au[
abla^2f(x)]^{-1}
abla f(x_0).\] Handle an initially zero gradient before dividing, and specify the local phase.

The impact should be calibrated carefully. Under the centering condition, clipping implies \[M_f\lambda_f(x)
 \leq M_f t\|\nabla f(x_0)\|_x^\ast+\beta
 \leq\gamma+\beta=0.1595<1/2.\] Thus the clipping problem occurs after the input has already entered the target region. It falsifies Theorem 8 as written and affects continuation of (75), but it does not refute the first-entry complexity in Theorems 9–10. This is why it is classified as Minor here.
result: Result: The unconditional centering statement of Theorem 8 is false when t is clipped.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Set tau=min(t,gamma/(M_f||grad f(x0)||*_x)), use y=x-tau H_x^-1 grad f(x0), and t_plus=t-tau. Define zero-gradient termination and the local phase.

problems.title: The signed predictor lemma and dual parameter substitution use inconsistent signs
claim: Recorded check: Quartic f=x^2/2+x^4/4, M_f=2/3,x=1,t=0,c=4,h=1,r=2,tau=-1/10 satisfies |tau|M_f r<1 but gives lambda_next=1.09555... while the printed right side is 261/289=0.90311.... In Lemma 7, the residual Phi'-tb transported along +H^-1 b requires t+tau, not t-tau.
analysis: Lemma 4, pp. 2187–2188, states (67) for all \(\tau\) with \(|\tau|M_fr<1\), but its bound and proof use \(\tau\) without absolute values. For negative \(\tau\), the norm identity in (69), the Hessian sandwich and integration direction are not justified in that form.

Use the same quartic, now with \[M_f=\tfrac23,\quad x=1,\quad t=0,\quad c=4,\quad
 h=1,\quad r=2,\quad \tau=-\tfrac1{10}.\] The hypothesis is satisfied and the initial decrement is \(1\). Direct substitution gives \[\lambda_{f_{t-\tau}}(x+\tau h)
 =\frac{2029}{100\sqrt{343}}>1.09,
 \qquad
 \text{printed right side of (67)}=\frac{261}{289}<0.904.\] The squared inequality was checked exactly.

Either restrict the displayed bound to \(\tau\geq0\), or replace the controlling occurrences by \(|\tau|\) and reverse the direction consistently when needed. The intended positive-step predictor estimate survives.

There is a related sign error in Lemma 7, p. 2197. Its convention is \(\Phi_t(u)=\Phi(u)-t\langle b,u\rangle\). A predictor \(v=u+\tau[\nabla^2\Phi(u)]^{-1}b\) transports the residual to parameter \(t(u)+\tau\), not \(t(u)-\tau\). Apply Lemma 4 with its plus-linear convention and initial parameter \(-t(u)\), or rewrite the lemma in the dual convention.

For the legitimate one-dimensional interval conjugate \(\Phi=F^\ast\) from Problem 1, at \(u=0\) with \(b=1,\gamma=0.254\), the printed intermediate residual is approximately \(0.523711\), while the intended bound with zero initial residual is \((\gamma/(1-\gamma))^2\approx0.1159\). The corrected-sign residual is approximately \(0.008065\). The minimized residual \(\lambda(v)\) is zero in this one-dimensional check, so the example exposes the intermediate comparison, not a failure of the corrected centering conclusion.
result: Result: Lemma 4 is false for negative tau as written; Lemma 7's intermediate comparison uses the wrong path label.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use absolute tau in the bound or restrict to nonnegative tau and reverse the direction consistently. Replace the dual comparison label by t(u)+tau.

problems.title: Newton and distance formulas need their local and scaling qualifications
problems.source_location: Equation (11), p. 2170; Theorem 1, p. 2172; surrounding definitions
claim: Recorded check: Theorem 1 lacks M_f lambda<1. For the global standard self-concordant quartic at x=10, lambda>50 and lambda_after_Newton>25, whereas its displayed right side is <(50/49)^2. In (11), the last fraction must have numerator lambda, not M_f lambda; f=x^2/2,M_f=1/2,x=1/5 gives distance 1/5>printed bound 1/9.
analysis: Theorem 1, p. 2172, omits the necessary condition \(M_f\lambda_f(x)<1\) for (19). A squared denominator does not extend the local estimate past that condition.

For the globally standard self-concordant quartic \(f(x)=x^2/2+x^4/4\), take \(M_f=1\), \(x=10\). Its Newton point is \(x_+=2000/301\). Exact squared comparisons give \[\lambda_f(10)>50,\qquad \lambda_f(x_+)>25,\] whereas the displayed right side of (19) is less than \((50/49)^2<1.042\). The intended local uses of this theorem are valid once the condition is restored.

In (11), p. 2170, the first expression is correct, but its last expansion has an extra \(M_f\): \[\frac1{M_f}\omega_\ast'(M_f\lambda)
 =\frac{\lambda}{1-M_f\lambda},
 \quad\text{not}\quad
 \frac{M_f\lambda}{1-M_f\lambda}.\] For \(f(x)=x^2/2\), \(M_f=1/2\), \(x=1/5\), the distance to the minimizer is \(1/5\); the printed last expression is \(1/9\), while the correct bound is \(2/9\).

Also separate \(M_f=0\), which is admitted in Definition 1 but makes several displayed inverses undefined. A positive definite quadratic can be solved directly or assigned any positive admissible self-concordance constant. State the real domain \(0\leq\tau<1\) for \(\omega_\ast\), and terminate at zero residual instead of using a ratio \(0/0\). These qualifications do not invalidate the damped Newton proof in its intended regime.
result: Result: The unqualified Newton inequality and the expanded scaled-distance expression are false.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: State M_f lambda<1; retain lambda/(1-M_f lambda). Treat M_f=0 as the quadratic case or use a positive admissible constant, define omega-star on [0,1), and terminate at zero residual.

problems.title: Finite-iteration indices, constants and work counts need correction
problems.source_location: Theorems 5 and 9; Remark 2 and (43); Remark 3; adaptive PFS; rho after (83)
claim: Recorded check: Products for t_N contain N updates, not N+1. At f=x^2/2,M_f=1,x0=1,N=0, (43) says 1<=0.99319375. The specified PFS constant is 17.14198257, not <=17.1. The rho expression needs plus gamma^2/(1-gamma)^2; its corrected margin stays positive. Each adaptive iteration evaluates i_k+1 trial Newton steps.
analysis: The proofs of Theorems 5 and 9 define a sum through \(k=N\) while bounding \(t_N\). There are only \(N\) updates from \(t_0\) to \(t_N\); use \(k=0,\ldots,N-1\), or put \(t_{N+1}\) on the left. With consistent indexing, the \(N^2\) bounds (37) and (78) follow by the same argument.

Equation (43), p. 2178, is false as indexed. For \(f(x)=x^2/2\), \(M_f=1,x_0=1,N=0\), the stated pre-region and decrease conditions hold, but its right side is \(1-\gamma(\gamma-2\beta)=0.99319375<1=t_0\). Replace \(N+1\) by \(N\) when the left side remains \(t_N\). In the preceding concave optimization argument, the equal allocation is a maximum, not a minimum. The source image correctly contains a sum of logarithms; no product-of-logarithms defect is alleged.

The actual parameters in (30) give \[\left(\frac{2}{\gamma(\gamma-2\beta)}\right)^{1/2}
 =17.1419825742\ldots,\] so the literal upper bound \(17.1\) in Remark 3 needs corrected rounding or different explicitly stated parameters. In the \(\rho_k\) expression following (83), p. 2191, the argument of the last \(\omega_\ast\) must be \[\frac{\beta}{1-\gamma}+\frac{\gamma^2}{(1-\gamma)^2},\] as required by (82), rather than the printed difference. After this repair, the dimensionless lower bound for \(\rho_k\) is still \(0.0247046210\ldots>0\); this does not overturn the positive-decrease argument.

For adaptive PFS, testing trial indices \(i=0,\ldots,i_k\) costs \(i_k+1\) Newton trials, including the accepted one. Thus the total through outer iteration \(k\) is \[\sum_{j=0}^{k}(i_j+1)
 =2(k+1)+\log_2\frac{\gamma_{-1}}{\gamma_k},\] not merely \(\sum_{j=0}^{k}i_j\). For example, on a quadratic every first trial may be accepted, giving \(i_j=0\) while still requiring one trial at every iteration.

Finally, the PCPFS constants compare outer iterations. A predictor-corrector iteration evaluates Hessians at both the current point and the predictor point, whereas a PFS iteration uses one current Hessian. State this unit when describing improved constants. The algebraic outer-iteration improvement alone does not establish fewer Hessian evaluations or lower running time.
result: Result: Several literal finite estimates and counts are incorrect, although the corrected principal nonlocal arguments and orders survive.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use sum k=0..N-1 for t_N, or t_(N+1) with N+1 terms; change 'minimum' to 'maximum' in the concave argument, correct rounding and rho sign, count accepted trials, and distinguish outer iterations from Hessian evaluations.

problems.title: Feasibility depth and dual problem data need explicit nondegeneracy conditions
problems.source_location: Equation (56), p. 2183; Sections 4.2 and 6.2; (100) and (105)–(108)
claim: Recorded check: Since 0 lies in int Q, arbitrarily large delta>1 makes (1-delta)Q contain any fixed feasible point; the unrestricted maximum in (56) is unbounded. Dual Hessian A H^-1 A^T is singular unless A has full row rank; B=(1,0),c=(1,0),Q=[-1,1]^2 gives dependent rows A=(-c^T;B).
analysis: In (56), p. 2183, the maximization must restrict \(0\leq\delta\leq1\). As written, \(\delta\geq0\) makes the depth unbounded for any nonempty affine feasible set. Indeed, because \(0\in\operatorname{int}Q\), a ball of radius \(r>0\) lies in \(Q\). For \(\delta>1\), the reflected dilation \((1-\delta)Q\) contains a ball of radius \((\delta-1)r\), hence eventually any fixed feasible point.

Section 4.2 explicitly assumes that \(0\) is an analytic center, \(\nabla F(0)=0\), and \(F(0)=0\) (p. 2183). These are operative assumptions. The barrier \(-\log(1+x)\) on \((-1,\infty)\) has no analytic center and is therefore outside that setting, not a counterexample under its assumptions. Existence must remain a restriction of the claimed scope rather than a normalization available for every closed convex \(Q\). This is a scope clarification, not an additional established defect.

The dual Hessian \[\nabla^2\Phi(u)=A[\nabla^2F(x)]^{-1}A^T\] is invertible only when \(A\) has full row rank. This is not guaranteed by the arbitrary equality matrix in Section 4.2 or by \(A=(-c^T;B)\) in Section 6.2. For \(Q=[-1,1]^2\), its separable logarithmic barrier, \(B=(1,0)\) and \(c=(1,0)\), the two rows of \(A\) are dependent and the objective is constant on \(Bx=0\). Remove redundant consistent constraints and handle such constant objectives separately before applying the displayed inverses.

Likewise, treat zero directions and initially solved problems before divisions by their local dual norms; write \(\Phi_t(u)=\Phi(u)-t\langle b,u\rangle\) in place of the vector subtraction on p. 2196; and use \(\sigma>0\) in reciprocal certificates (105)–(108). The Major counterexample in Problem 1 uses a bounded set, a genuine analytic center, full rank and a nonzero direction, so it does not depend on any of these degeneracies.
result: Result: Some definitions and inverses are not meaningful for the stated general data.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use delta in [0,1], retain the source's explicit analytic-center assumption as a scope restriction, remove redundant consistent constraints, treat constant objectives/zero directions separately, define Phi_t(u)=Phi(u)-t<b,u>, and use sigma>0 for reciprocal certificates.

problems.title: The cubic method requires a regularization condition and a computable stopping rule
problems.source_location: Equation (113), p. 2200; Theorem 13 and Remark 5, pp. 2201–2202
claim: Recorded check: Let f=x^2/2+K log(cosh x), K=10/(tanh(2)-4 sech^2(2))>0. It is 1-strongly convex with Hessian Lipschitz constant 4K/(3sqrt(3))=11.29693.... With cubic M=1, the unique model minimizers send 2 to -2 and back, exactly.
analysis: Equation (113), p. 2200, introduces a cubic parameter \(M>0\), followed by a convergence claim. Positivity alone is insufficient for that claim. A standard sufficient condition for the displayed cubic model to majorize \(f\) is \(M\geq H_f\); the parameter assumptions of the imported rate (114) should be stated.

Here is an exact two-cycle with a positive parameter. Let \[f(x)=\tfrac12x^2+K\log\cosh x,\qquad
 K=\frac{10}{\tanh2-4\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2 2}=14.6751448162\ldots .\] The denominator is positive, \(f''(x)=1+K\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x\geq1\), and \[|f'''(x)|=2K\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^2x\,|\tanh x|
 \leq H_f=\frac{4K}{3\sqrt3}=11.2969317467\ldots .\] Thus the function satisfies the strong convexity and global Lipschitz-Hessian assumptions.

Take \(M=1\). At \(x=2\), the derivative of the strongly convex cubic model with respect to its step \(h\), evaluated at \(h=-4\), is \[f'(2)-4f''(2)-8
 =K(\tanh2-4\mathop{\mathrm{sech}}^22)-10=0.\] Hence its unique minimizer sends \(2\) to \(-2\). Evenness sends \(-2\) back to \(2\). The method does not converge to the minimizer \(0\) for this allowed positive \(M\).

This example does not refute Theorem 13, whose starting assumption is the rate (114). It shows why that assumption cannot be inferred from \(M>0\) alone. With the appropriate rate available, the halving proof and the resulting exponents remain intact.

The restart description should also first handle an initial point already in \(\mathcal Q_f\), rather than applying a negative or undefined logarithmic stage bound. Remark 5 makes the stage lengths computable using a known lower bound \(\widetilde f\), but the stopping test \(f(y_k)-f^\ast\leq1/(8M_f^2)\) still involves \(f^\ast\). Supply a predetermined sufficient number of stages based on \(f(x_0)-\widetilde f\), or an observable certificate. This is a specification repair, not a counterexample to the conditional halving argument.
result: Result: M>0 alone does not imply the cited convergence. The restart theorem remains conditional on (114); its negative/undefined log at an already solved start and stopping test involving f* need qualification.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: State appropriate M, e.g. M>=H_f for the majorizing cubic model, and the hypotheses of each imported rate. Start with an already-in-Q_f case and, with a known lower bound, give a preset stage count or computable certificate.

report: Abstract: We examine the relation between the filtered Lie–Trotter scheme and the discrete variation-of-constants formula in the acquired manuscript of R. Carles. The smooth spectral cutoff is applied repeatedly by the scheme, whereas formula (5.10) retains only one cutoff in each propagation factor. A two-step calculation with admissible smooth data gives a nonzero residual. This is a substantive defect in the derivation of the main error estimates. It does not constitute a counterexample to those estimates themselves.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Filtered propagation in a time-splitting analysis
# Paper, version, and inspected scope

The paper is Rémi Carles, Time splitting and error estimates for nonlinear Schrödinger equations with a potential, associated with DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09727-5. The reviewed source is the complete 42-page author manuscript arXiv:2408.14816v3, revised 21 July 2025 [carles]. All page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed page numbers in this file. The publisher version has different pagination; its substantive equivalence has not been established.

The review traces the definitions in Section 1, the role of the spectral cutoff in Sections 2–3, and the convergence argument in Section 5. The detailed check concerns the exact propagation identity (5.10), its use in (5.11), and the stated dependence of the principal error bounds. It is not a certification of every pseudodifferential estimate, well-posedness argument, or stability bootstrap. No numerical experiment or author program was executed. The source-acquisition record reports no separate supplement or relevant released code located in its bounded search; the present argument uses the acquired main text.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

Equation reference: eq:scheme. The equation is \[i\partial_tu=Hu+Wu+\varepsilon |u|^{2\sigma}u,\qquad H=-\Delta+V.\] Assumption 1.1 (p. 2) requires real smooth \(V\ge1\), with all derivatives of order at least two bounded, and real \(W\in W^{2,\infty}\). The nonlinear subflow is \(N(t)v=v\exp(-itW-it\varepsilon |v|^{2\sigma})\) (p. 3). On p. 4 the cutoff satisfies \[\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;[0,1]),\qquad
 \chi=1\text{ on }[-1,1],\qquad \chi=0\text{ outside }[-2,2].\] Equations (1.4)–(1.6) define, with \(P=\Pi_\lambda\), \[
 P=\chi^2(H/\lambda),\quad S(t)=e^{-itH},\quad S_\lambda(t)=PS(t),
 \qquad u^0=Pu_0,\quad u^{j+1}=S_\lambda(\tau)N(\tau)u^j.\] The main theorems set \(\lambda=\tau^{-1}\). Theorem 1.4 (p. 5) gives an \(L^2\) error of order \(\tau^{1/2}\) for the specified \(\mathcal H^1\) regime; Theorem 1.5 (p. 6) gives \(L^2\) order \(\tau\) and \(\mathcal H^1\) order \(\tau^{1/2}\) for the stated \(\mathcal H^2\) regime, assuming the exact solution exists on \([0,T]\). Their constants may depend on \(T\) and the problem data.
# A propagation identity that does not follow from the scheme
Problem 1 (Repeated filtering is omitted in (5.10)).  For the smooth cutoff specified in [eq:scheme] (#eq:scheme), the discrete Duhamel formula (5.10), p. 27, is generally false.
## The exact discrepancy

Equation reference: eq:printed, eq:true. Put \(B=PS(\tau)\) and \(F(v)=N(\tau)v-v\). After changing the starting index to \(m\), the claim in (5.10) is \[
 u^{m+n}=PS(n\tau)u^m+
       \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}PS((n-k)\tau)F(u^{m+k}).\] This is a paraphrase of its formula, retaining its actual propagator definition. Iterating \(u^{j+1}=Bu^j+BF(u^j)\), however, gives \[
 u^{m+n}=B^nu^m+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}B^{n-k}F(u^{m+k}),\qquad
 B^\ell=P^\ell S(\ell\tau).\] The last equality uses the valid commutation of \(P\) and \(S(t)\). It does not remove powers of \(P\).

Equation reference: eq:residual. Already at \(n=2\), actual iteration minus the right-hand side of [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) equals \[
 D_2=(P^2-P)S(2\tau)N(\tau)u^m.\] Indeed the actual iteration is \(B^2N(\tau)u^m+BF(u^{m+1})\), while the asserted expression is \(PS(2\tau)N(\tau)u^m+BF(u^{m+1})\). Thus the discrepancy does not rely on the formula’s inclusion of \(n=0\).
## An admissible nonlinear example

Take \[d=1,\qquad V=1,\qquad W=0,\qquad \sigma=1,\qquad \varepsilon=+1,
 \qquad \lambda\ge2,\quad \tau=\lambda^{-1}.\] These potentials satisfy Assumption 1.1. The cubic exponent is both \(L^2\)-subcritical in one dimension and allowed by Theorem 1.5. With the unitary Fourier transform, \(P\) is the multiplier \[p(\xi)=\chi^2((\xi^2+1)/\lambda).\] Continuity between the cutoff plateau and its zero region gives a nonempty open frequency interval where \(1/4<p(\xi)<3/4\). Choose nonzero \(\widehat f\in C_c^\infty\) supported strictly in that interval, and put \(g=Pf\), \(u_0=af\), where \(a>0\) will be chosen below. Both \(f\) and \(g\) are Schwartz functions. Hence every initial \(\mathcal H^1\) and \(\mathcal H^2\) regularity requirement holds. The one-dimensional defocusing cubic problem supplies the requisite smooth solution on a time interval containing the two steps. This example does not set the nonlinear coefficient to zero.

The initial numerical state is \(u^0=ag\), so [eq:residual] (#eq:residual) becomes \[D_2=(P^2-P)S(2\tau)
          [ag\exp(-i\tau a^2|g|^2)].\] Define positive finite constants \[c=\left\lVert(P^2-P)g\right\rVert_2,\qquad
 M=\left\lVert g\right\rVert_\infty^2\left\lVert g\right\rVert_2.\] Plancherel’s identity gives \[c^2=\int p(\xi)^4(1-p(\xi))^2|\widehat f(\xi)|^2\,d\xi,
 \qquad c\ge\frac{3}{64}\left\lVert f\right\rVert_2>0,\] since \(p^2(1-p)\ge3/64\) on \([1/4,3/4]\). Also \(\left\lVert P^2-P\right\rVert_{2\to2}\le1/4\). Using unitarity, commutation, and \(|e^{-iz}-1|\le|z|\) for real \(z\), \[\begin{aligned}
 \left\lVert D_2\right\rVert_2
 &\ge ac-\frac a4\left\lVert g(e^{-i\tau a^2|g|^2}-1)\right\rVert_2 \notag\\
 &\ge ac-\frac{\tau a^3M}{4}.\end{aligned}\] For \(0<a\le\min\{1,\sqrt{2c/(\tau M)}\}\), it follows that \[\left\lVert D_2\right\rVert_2\ge ac/2>0.\] This disproves the asserted exact identity for admissible smooth input. It is not a counterexample to an asymptotic error rate for fixed data: the construction may select a different input when \(\tau\) changes. Nor does this check assert the auxiliary stability estimate (5.1); the failure concerns the algebraic identity used to derive the error decomposition from the scheme.
## Counterevidence and alternative readings

The cutoff does commute with the Hamiltonian. The problem is idempotence, not commutation. In particular, p. 35 correctly uses \(\Pi_{4\lambda}\Pi_\lambda=\Pi_\lambda\) to deduce localization under a wider cutoff. That identity does not give \(P^2=P\).

A complete repair of the proof would additionally need suitable uniform estimates for \(P^\ell S(\ell\tau)\) and the resulting convolution, or another justified treatment of repeated filtering. report: Abstract: The acquired journal article develops a method for recovering compact-group representation orbits from point clouds. We check selected structural identities and the passage from estimated Lie algebras to orbit-distance guarantees. An explicit pair of conjugate skew matrices disproves Lemma 5.19. A regular polygon disproves a pushforward-distance estimate in the proof of Theorem 5.22. Both estimates enter the principal robustness argument. A separate inconsistency in the stated local PCA algorithm is limited by the correct definition used in the theoretical analysis and the inspected source release. These checks do not disprove all conclusions of the main theorem.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Stability estimates and local covariance directions in LieDetect
# Source and scope

The reviewed paper is H. Ennes and R. Tinarrage, LieDetect: Detection of Representation Orbits of Compact Lie Groups From Point Clouds, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09728-4 [paper]. The acquired source is the 136-page publisher version of record, published online on 15 September 2025 and paginated 2259–2394 in the 2026 volume. A PDF page below means its one-based file page; the journal page is larger by 2258. No equivalence to an earlier manuscript is assumed.

The detailed checks concern the ideal LiePCA kernel, local covariance directions, Lemma 5.19, and the final distance estimates in Theorem 5.22. The finite representation search, all geometric constants, the full classification arguments, and the empirical applications are not certified. The paper expressly acknowledges nonuniqueness of representations producing an orbit. Its theorem assumes known group and orbit dimension, suitable spectral cutoff and sampling parameters, sufficiently small Wasserstein error, and exact global minimization (PDF pp. 91–92). A local optimization implementation cannot itself verify that last hypothesis.

A retained source snapshot of `HLovisiEnnes/LieDetect`, commit `07434f3a2409f0aaee197d7e9ee22e8d80015ab5`, was inspected statically. Its recorded date is 30 July 2026; it is not established as the revision used for the published experiments. Twelve dataset or generated payloads were excluded at acquisition. No author code was executed. The acquisition record reports no separate supplement found in its bounded search; the appendix in the main PDF was available.
# A structural identity that survives the checks

For a nontrivial compact orbit \(O\), let \[\Lambda_O(A)=\int_O P_{N_xO} A P_{\langle x\rangle}\,d\mu_O(x).\] The first part of Proposition 5.9 (PDF pp. 71–72) identifies its kernel with the infinitesimal linear symmetries. This part has a direct verification. Put \(S_x=\{A:Ax\in T_xO\}\). The map \(A\mapsto P_{N_xO}AP_{\langle x\rangle}\) is the Frobenius orthogonal projection onto \(S_x^\perp\), so \[\langle\Lambda_O A,A\rangle
   =\int_O\left\lVert P_{S_x^\perp}A\right\rVert_F^2\,d\mu_O(x).\] The integrand is continuous and nonnegative, and the orbit measure has full support. Thus the integral vanishes exactly when \(Ax\) is tangent at every point. The compactness and smoothness of the orbit allow the tangent linear vector field to integrate to its preserving flow. This establishes the stated kernel equality. It is not a verification of the separate equivariance assertion for arbitrary nonorthogonal representations.
# The claimed uniform matrix-exponential estimate
Problem 1 (Lemma 5.19).  The estimate in Lemma 5.19, PDF p. 88 (journal p. 2346), is false under its stated assumptions.

Equation reference: eq:claimedexp. The lemma asserts, in paraphrase, that orthogonally conjugate real skew-symmetric matrices with integer spectral frequencies satisfy \[
 \left\lVert e^{tA}-e^{tB}\right\rVert_F\le \left\lVert A-B\right\rVert_F
 \quad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.\] The Frobenius convention is explicit in the notation table, PDF p. 126. The appendix uses integer frequencies \(\omega_j\) in the real rotation blocks; the condition does not mean real eigenvalues of a skew matrix.

Take \[J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 A=\operatorname{diag}(J,2J),\quad B=\operatorname{diag}(2J,J),\quad
 Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_2\\I_2&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(B=QAQ^\top\), \(Q\in SO(4)\), and both spectra are \(\{i,-i,2i,-2i\}\). At \(t=\pi\), \[e^{\pi A}=\operatorname{diag}(-I_2,I_2),\qquad
 e^{\pi B}=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,-I_2).\] Consequently \[\left\lVert A-B\right\rVert_F^2=4,\qquad
 \left\lVert e^{\pi A}-e^{\pi B}\right\rVert_F^2=16.\] All the lemma’s assumptions hold, and its claimed inequality reads \(4\le2\).

The discrepancy also persists for arbitrarily close conjugates. Set \[Q_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta I_2&-\sin\theta I_2\\
                  \sin\theta I_2&\cos\theta I_2\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad B_\theta=Q_\theta A Q_\theta^\top.\] Direct block multiplication gives \[\left\lVert A-B_\theta\right\rVert_F=2|\sin\theta|,\qquad
 \left\lVert e^{\pi A}-e^{\pi B_\theta}\right\rVert_F=4|\sin\theta|.\] Thus a smallness condition on the difference alone does not restore the coefficient one.

The appendix proof (PDF pp. 126–127) decomposes the exponential into cosine and sine blocks. Conjugation may mix blocks with distinct frequencies; their cosine terms do not cancel. The example above has vanishing sine terms at \(\pi\) and a nonzero exponential difference, directly exposing the missing contribution.
## Dependence and possible repairs

Proposition 5.20 explicitly invokes this lemma for its orbit and transport bounds on PDF p. 89. Theorem 5.22 then invokes that proposition in Step 4, PDF pp. 94–96, to derive (59)–(61). The issue therefore affects a substantive intermediate claim in the central robustness proof.

For normal matrices whose frequencies are integers, a coefficient two is valid in Frobenius norm. To see this, use orthonormal eigenbases \((u_j)\), \((v_k)\), with frequencies \(a_j,b_k\in\mathbb Z\), and the identities \[\begin{aligned}
 \left\lVert e^{tA}-e^{tB}\right\rVert_F^2
  &=\sum_{j,k}|e^{ita_j}-e^{itb_k}|^2|\langle u_j,v_k\rangle|^2,\\
 \left\lVert A-B\right\rVert_F^2
  &=\sum_{j,k}|a_j-b_k|^2|\langle u_j,v_k\rangle|^2.\end{aligned}\] For equal frequencies the first summand is zero; for distinct integer frequencies it is at most four times the second. This proves \[\left\lVert e^{tA}-e^{tB}\right\rVert_F\le2\left\lVert A-B\right\rVert_F,\] with sharp constant in the example. This is a repair of this lemma only. The proof of Proposition 5.20 uses unit-norm generators, which need not retain integer frequencies after normalization. Merely doubling every later constant has not been justified here. No counterexample to the complete conclusion of Theorem 5.22 follows from this calculation alone.
# Whitening does not obey the asserted difference-product bound

Problem 2 (Theorem 5.22, final pushforward step).  The inequalities used to obtain (64) on PDF p. 95 and the Wasserstein estimate on PDF p. 96 omit the effect of transporting the original measures by a common nonzero map.

Equation reference: eq:falsepush. Write \(M_X=\Sigma[\mu_X]^{-1/2}\), \(M_O=\Sigma[\mu_O]^{-1/2}\) in the full-span case, and \(P_X,P_O\) for the preceding PCA projections. The proof on p. 96 asserts an upper bound of the form \[
 W_2((M_XP_X)_\#\mu_X,(M_OP_O)_\#\mu_O)
 \le \left\lVert M_X-M_O\right\rVert_{\rm op}\left\lVert P_X-P_O\right\rVert_{\rm op}
                      W_2(\mu_X,\mu_O).\] The directed Hausdorff argument on p. 95 has the same structure. Both assertions require justification beyond a Lipschitz estimate for one common map.

Let \(G=SO(2)\) act in the usual way on \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(O=S^1\), and let \(X_N\) be the \(N\)th roots of unity, \(N\ge3\). With their uniform probability measures, \[\Sigma[\mu_O]=\Sigma[\mu_{X_N}]=\tfrac12I_2,\qquad
 M_X=M_O=\sqrt2 I_2,\qquad P_X=P_O=I_2.\] Put \(d_N=W_2(\mu_{X_N},\mu_O)\). This number is positive, since an atomic measure differs from the circle measure. Moreover \(d_N\to0\). Assigning each equal circular arc to its central vertex gives the exact distance \[d_N^2=2-\frac{2N}{\pi}\sin\frac{\pi}{N}.\] This coupling is optimal because each point is assigned to a nearest vertex and the equal arcs have the required masses. Thus arbitrary smallness assumptions on the input Wasserstein error can be met. The representation is faithful, the orbit spans \(\mathbb R^2\), its dimension is one, its reach and covariance eigenvalues are positive, and the primitive frequency is one. The transitive case applies. The theorem’s covariance threshold can be chosen below \(1/4\), for all sufficiently large \(N\), so both PCA projections really are \(I_2\).

Scaling both measures by the same factor gives exactly \[W_2((\sqrt2I_2)_\#\mu_{X_N},(\sqrt2I_2)_\#\mu_O)=\sqrt2\,d_N>0.\] The right-hand side of [eq:falsepush] (#eq:falsepush) is zero. Even the subsequent asserted bound \(d_N/(\sqrt2\,\sigma_{\min})=d_N\), since \(\sigma_{\min}=1/\sqrt2\), is smaller than the actual transformed distance. This example tests an intermediate inequality of the proof; it does not identify the algorithm’s final output error with this transformed input error.

Equation reference: eq:truepush. The correct general comparison, for linear maps \(T,S\) and probability measures of finite second moment, is for example \[
 W_2(T_\#\mu,S_\#\nu)
 \le \left\lVert T\right\rVert_{\rm op}W_2(\mu,\nu)
       +\left\lVert T-S\right\rVert_{\rm op}
                    \left(\int\left\lVert x\right\rVert^2\,d\nu(x)\right)^{1/2}.\] It follows by inserting \(T_\#\nu\), using the triangle inequality, and coupling \(Tx\) with \(Sx\). The second-to-last displayed estimate in the proof of Proposition 5.6 (PDF p. 67) correctly keeps both types of terms; its last estimate again replaces the common-map norm by a difference norm. The present example also invalidates that last step. The statement of Proposition 5.6 is not thereby disproved.

This is a core proof defect because the p. 96 substitution explicitly concludes (61). The additional normal-estimation term in (61) could dominate the missing contribution; that is counterevidence against inferring that the final theorem is false. Replacing the invalid comparison by [eq:truepush] (#eq:truepush) and carrying its terms through every constant and parameter restriction remains necessary for a complete repair.
# A limited algorithm-description discrepancy
Problem 3 (Local covariance directions).  Section 3.3.2, PDF p. 27, and Algorithm 2, line 3, PDF p. 28, choose the bottom \(l\) eigenvectors as tangent directions.

This choice can reverse tangent and normal. For the circle points \[x_0=(1,0),\qquad x_\pm=(\cos h,\pm\sin h),\qquad 0<h<\pi/2,\] take a local neighborhood containing these three points. The covariance centered at \(x_0\) is \[\tfrac23\operatorname{diag}((1-\cos h)^2,\sin^2h).\] Its bottom eigenvector is horizontal, the true normal direction; its top eigenvector is vertical, the true tangent direction at \(x_0\). Thus following the stated algorithm literally gives the wrong direction.

There is decisive counterevidence limiting the impact. Equation (45), PDF p. 76, explicitly defines the tangent estimate with the top \(l\) eigenvectors. The retained release `src/liepca.py`, lines 194–201, also selects the largest `orbit_dim` eigenvalues before taking the normal complement. The remedy is to make the earlier description agree with that definition. This is a Minor inconsistency in the reproducible algorithm specification, not evidence that the theoretical normal-estimation argument or the inspected implementation uses bottom tangent directions. It does not establish how the historical experiments were run.
# Assessment and limits

The two invalid stability estimates support an overall Major assessment: each is materially connected to the principal robustness argument. Their exact failures, assumptions and dependencies are given above. The supported conclusion is a gap in that proof, together with one false intermediate lemma. No claim is made that the entire method fails, that no corrected theorem is possible, or that the empirical results are invalid.

The coefficient-two exponential estimate and the two-term transport inequality are verified local corrections. A complete repaired theorem has not been proved. Author adoption is unknown. Scientific adjudication remains pending, with no human review or independent acceptance recorded.

Equation reference: eq:falsepush. Write \(M_X=\Sigma[\mu_X]^{-1/2}\), \(M_O=\Sigma[\mu_O]^{-1/2}\) in the full-span case, and \(P_X,P_O\) for the preceding PCA projections. The proof on p. 96 asserts an upper bound of the form \[
 W_2((M_XP_X)_\#\mu_X,(M_OP_O)_\#\mu_O)
 \le \left\lVert M_X-M_O\right\rVert_{\rm op}\left\lVert P_X-P_O\right\rVert_{\rm op}
                      W_2(\mu_X,\mu_O).\] The directed Hausdorff argument on p. 95 has the same structure. Both assertions require justification beyond a Lipschitz estimate for one common map.

Let \(G=SO(2)\) act in the usual way on \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(O=S^1\), and let \(X_N\) be the \(N\)th roots of unity, \(N\ge3\). With their uniform probability measures, \[\Sigma[\mu_O]=\Sigma[\mu_{X_N}]=\tfrac12I_2,\qquad
 M_X=M_O=\sqrt2 I_2,\qquad P_X=P_O=I_2.\] Put \(d_N=W_2(\mu_{X_N},\mu_O)\). This number is positive, since an atomic measure differs from the circle measure. Moreover \(d_N\to0\). Assigning each equal circular arc to its central vertex gives the exact distance \[d_N^2=2-\frac{2N}{\pi}\sin\frac{\pi}{N}.\] This coupling is optimal because each point is assigned to a nearest vertex and the equal arcs have the required masses. Thus arbitrary smallness assumptions on the input Wasserstein error can be met. The representation is faithful, the orbit spans \(\mathbb R^2\), its dimension is one, its reach and covariance eigenvalues are positive, and the primitive frequency is one. The transitive case applies. The theorem’s covariance threshold can be chosen below \(1/4\), for all sufficiently large \(N\), so both PCA projections really are \(I_2\).

Scaling both measures by the same factor gives exactly \[W_2((\sqrt2I_2)_\#\mu_{X_N},(\sqrt2I_2)_\#\mu_O)=\sqrt2\,d_N>0.\] The right-hand side of [eq:falsepush] (#eq:falsepush) is zero. Even the subsequent asserted bound \(d_N/(\sqrt2\,\sigma_{\min})=d_N\), since \(\sigma_{\min}=1/\sqrt2\), is smaller than the actual transformed distance. This example tests an intermediate inequality of the proof; it does not identify the algorithm’s final output error with this transformed input error.

Equation reference: eq:truepush. The correct general comparison, for linear maps \(T,S\) and probability measures of finite second moment, is for example \[
 W_2(T_\#\mu,S_\#\nu)
 \le \left\lVert T\right\rVert_{\rm op}W_2(\mu,\nu)
       +\left\lVert T-S\right\rVert_{\rm op}
                    \left(\int\left\lVert x\right\rVert^2\,d\nu(x)\right)^{1/2}.\] It follows by inserting \(T_\#\nu\), using the triangle inequality, and coupling \(Tx\) with \(Sx\). The second-to-last displayed estimate in the proof of Proposition 5.6 (PDF p. 67) correctly keeps both types of terms; its last estimate again replaces the common-map norm by a difference norm. The present example also invalidates that last step. The statement of Proposition 5.6 is not thereby disproved.

This is a core proof defect because the p. 96 substitution explicitly concludes (61). The additional normal-estimation term in (61) could dominate the missing contribution; that is counterevidence against inferring that the final theorem is false. Replacing the invalid comparison by [eq:truepush] (#eq:truepush) and carrying its terms through every constant and parameter restriction remains necessary for a complete repair.

analysis: Section 3.3.2, PDF p. 27, and Algorithm 2, line 3, PDF p. 28, choose the bottom \(l\) eigenvectors as tangent directions.

This choice can reverse tangent and normal. For the circle points \[x_0=(1,0),\qquad x_\pm=(\cos h,\pm\sin h),\qquad 0<h<\pi/2,\] take a local neighborhood containing these three points. The covariance centered at \(x_0\) is \[\tfrac23\operatorname{diag}((1-\cos h)^2,\sin^2h).\] Its bottom eigenvector is horizontal, the true normal direction; its top eigenvector is vertical, the true tangent direction at \(x_0\). Thus following the stated algorithm literally gives the wrong direction.

There is decisive counterevidence limiting the impact. Equation (45), PDF p. 76, explicitly defines the tangent estimate with the top \(l\) eigenvectors. The retained release `src/liepca.py`, lines 194–201, also selects the largest `orbit_dim` eigenvalues before taking the normal complement. The remedy is to make the earlier description agree with that definition. This is a Minor inconsistency in the reproducible algorithm specification, not evidence that the theoretical normal-estimation argument or the inspected implementation uses bottom tangent directions. It does not establish how the historical experiments were run.

report: Abstract: We examine the performance-difference and entropy-decay arguments in the acquired journal article on Fisher–Rao policy flows. The central decay identity and its stated value and policy bounds pass the checks described here. An extraneous discount factor makes the estimates of Lemma 4.1 false, including in an elementary two-action example. The preceding derivative estimate supplies a direct correction preserving the local Lipschitz property needed for the existence argument. A separate static inspection finds a lagged-value discrepancy in the linked numerical source. Neither finding establishes failure of the principal continuous-time convergence theorem.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Entropy decay, a Lipschitz constant, and policy evaluation in a Fisher–Rao flow
# Source and precise scope

The paper is B. Kerimkulov, J.-M. Leahy, D. Šiška, L. Szpruch and Y. Zhang, A Fisher–Rao Gradient Flow for Entropy-Regularised Markov Decision Processes in Polish Spaces, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09729-3 [paper]. The reviewed source is the 75-page publisher version of record, published online 11 August 2025 and appearing on journal pages 2395–2469 in the 2026 volume. File pages below are one-based PDF pages; journal pages equal file pages plus 2394.

The detailed review covers the bounded-logit policy class, the performance-difference identity, value dissipation, the entropy argument for Theorem 2.8, and the local Lipschitz estimate used in the existence proof. The full differentiability construction, all measure-theoretic lifting details for arbitrary primal solutions, the complete inexact and parameterized-flow analyses, and the discrete theorem are not independently certified. The acquisition record reports no separate supplement found in its bounded search; Appendices A–D are included in the acquired article.
# Definitions, hypotheses, and a successful core check

The state and action spaces are Polish, the transition kernel is measurable, the cost \(c\) is bounded measurable, \(0\le\gamma<1\), \(\tau>0\), and the action reference \(\mu\) is a probability measure (PDF pp. 15–18). The relevant policies have bounded logits: \[\pi(f)(da\mid s)=\frac{e^{f(s,a)}}{\int e^{f(s,a')}\,d\mu(a')}\,\mu(da),
 \qquad f\in B_b(S\times A).\] Thus each log density is bounded, above and below. The result does not start from an arbitrary singular policy. With \[Q_\tau^\pi=c+\gamma PV_\tau^\pi,\qquad
 a_\pi=Q_\tau^\pi+\tau\log(d\pi/d\mu)-V_\tau^\pi,\] the Bellman relation gives \(\int a_\pi\,d\pi(\cdot\mid s)=0\). The flow is \(\dot\pi=-a_\pi\pi\); the centered identity preserves mass. The dual flow on bounded logits and its gauge freedom are stated on PDF p. 19.

For completeness, subtracting the two Bellman equations gives \[(I-\gamma P_\pi)(V_\tau^\pi-V_\tau^{\pi'})
 =\int\left(Q_\tau^{\pi'}+\tau\log(d\pi'/d\mu)\right)
                  d(\pi-\pi')
   +\tau\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi\mid\pi').\] Since \(\left\lVert\gamma P_\pi\right\rVert\le\gamma<1\), the Neumann resolvent exists. Its normalized kernel is the occupancy kernel \(d^\pi=(1-\gamma)\sum_{n\ge0}\gamma^nP_\pi^n\). This reproduces Lemma 2.3, PDF p. 18, including the orientation of the KL divergence and the factor \(1/(1-\gamma)\).

The dissipation calculation in PDF pp. 40–41 then yields \[\frac{d}{dt}V_\tau^{\pi_t}(s)
 =-\frac1{1-\gamma}\int_S\int_A a_{\pi_t}(s',a)^2
                \,\pi_t(da\mid s')d^{\pi_t}(ds'\mid s)\le0.\] The centering term is essential for the square; it is present in the article. Given the bounded-logit differentiability framework used there, the algebra and sign are correct.

Equation reference: eq:entropy. Let \(\pi^*\) be the entropy-regularized optimal policy and fix an initial distribution \(\rho\). Set \[D(t)=\int_S\mathrm{KL}(\pi^*(\cdot\mid s)\mid\pi_t(\cdot\mid s))
                      \,d_\rho^{\pi^*}(ds),\qquad
 G(t)=V_\tau^{\pi_t}(\rho)-V_\tau^{\pi^*}(\rho).\] The occupancy weight here is fixed at the optimal policy; it is not differentiated with the current flow. The log-partition calculation and performance difference give, as on PDF pp. 44–46, \[
 D'(t)=-(1-\gamma)G(t)-\tau D(t).\] Since \(G\ge0\) is nonincreasing, \[D(t)\le e^{-\tau t}D(0),\qquad
 G(t)\le\frac{\tau D(0)}{(1-\gamma)(e^{\tau t}-1)}.\] Pinsker’s inequality in the full total-variation norm gives \[\int_S\left\lVert\pi_t-\pi^*\right\rVert_{M(A)}^2\,d_\rho^{\pi^*}
 \le2e^{-\tau t}D(0).\] These are the quantitative conclusions of Theorem 2.8 (PDF p. 20). The derivation does not require convexity of the value in the policy.

As a separate exact check, in a one-state model with action costs \(c_i\), the action log-density differences satisfy \[\frac{d}{dt}(Z_i-Z_j)=-(c_i-c_j)-\tau(Z_i-Z_j).\] Their solution is \[Z_i(t)-Z_j(t)=e^{-\tau t}(Z_i(0)-Z_j(0))
              -\frac{1-e^{-\tau t}}{\tau}(c_i-c_j).\] This agrees with convergence to the Gibbs policy. The case \(\gamma=0\) remains a valid member of the stated problem class.
# A false auxiliary bound with a direct correction
Problem 1 (Lemma 4.1, PDF p. 41).  The displayed value-function Lipschitz estimate has an extra factor \(\gamma\); the corresponding \(Q\)-estimate inherits it.

Writing \(K=\left\lVert c\right\rVert_\infty+2\tau(\left\lVert f\right\rVert_\infty+\left\lVert g\right\rVert_\infty)\), the lemma asserts \[\left\lVert V_\tau^{\pi(f)}-V_\tau^{\pi(g)}\right\rVert_\infty
 \le\frac{2\gamma K}{(1-\gamma)^2}\left\lVert f-g\right\rVert_\infty,
 \qquad
 \left\lVert Q_\tau^{\pi(f)}-Q_\tau^{\pi(g)}\right\rVert_\infty
 \le\frac{2\gamma^2 K}{(1-\gamma)^2}\left\lVert f-g\right\rVert_\infty.\] Take one state, two actions, self-transition, \(c=0\), \(\mu=(1/2,1/2)\), \(f=(1,-1)\), \(g=(0,0)\), and any \(\tau>0\). All logits and costs are bounded, and both policies belong to \(\Pi_\mu\). Put \[H=\mathrm{KL}(\pi(f)\mid\mu)=\tanh1-\log\cosh1>0.\] Then exactly \[V_\tau^{\pi(f)}-V_\tau^{\pi(g)}=\frac{\tau H}{1-\gamma},
 \qquad
 Q_\tau^{\pi(f)}-Q_\tau^{\pi(g)}=\frac{\gamma\tau H}{1-\gamma}.\] At \(\gamma=0\), the first printed bound has zero right side and strictly positive left side. The problem is not confined to that endpoint. Indeed \[H=\int_0^1 u\,\operatorname{sech}^2u\,du>\tfrac18,\] because \(\cosh1<2\). For \(\gamma=1/100\), validity of either printed inequality would require \(H\le4/99\), which contradicts \(H>1/8\).

Equation reference: eq:correct. The first mean-value inequality in (4.3) inserts the same unsupported factor \(\gamma\). Proposition 3.8, PDF p. 35, instead gives \[\left\lVert dJ(h)\right\rVert\le
 \frac2{(1-\gamma)^2}(\left\lVert c\right\rVert_\infty+2\tau\left\lVert h\right\rVert_\infty),
 \qquad J(h)=V_\tau^{\pi(h)}.\] Applying this along \(h=g+\theta(f-g)\), \(0\le\theta\le1\), and using \(\left\lVert h\right\rVert_\infty\le\left\lVert f\right\rVert_\infty+\left\lVert g\right\rVert_\infty\) proves the corrected bounds \[
 \left\lVert V_\tau^{\pi(f)}-V_\tau^{\pi(g)}\right\rVert_\infty
 \le\frac{2K}{(1-\gamma)^2}\left\lVert f-g\right\rVert_\infty,\qquad
 \left\lVert Q_\tau^{\pi(f)}-Q_\tau^{\pi(g)}\right\rVert_\infty
 \le\frac{2\gamma K}{(1-\gamma)^2}\left\lVert f-g\right\rVert_\infty.\] The second follows from \(Q=c+\gamma PV\). This establishes the correction without a numerical experiment.

The supported assessment is Minor. The estimates as printed are false, but the same preceding proposition supplies finite local Lipschitz constants. The existence argument uses local Lipschitzness and the independent a priori bound of Proposition 4.2 (PDF pp. 41–42), rather than requiring the erroneous extra factor. This finding therefore does not undermine the local existence mechanism, the continuation bound, or the verified identity [eq:entropy] (#eq:entropy).
# A discrepancy confined to the acquired numerical release

Appendix D (PDF pp. 70–72) compares Euler, midpoint and fourth-order Runge–Kutta updates for \[f(Z)=-Q_\tau^{\pi(Z)}-\tau Z+V_\tau^{\pi(Z)}.\] The linked repository was acquired at commit `5624f106bc249044533dbce79137bb4574c72f3f` (recorded 27 January 2025). It is not established that this exact revision generated the published figures.

In `mirror_descent.py`, function `mirror_f`, lines 84–85, the current policy evaluation is assigned to `V`, but the advantage call receives `V=old_V`. The evaluator in `softmax_PIA.py` begins with `V=np.copy(V_old)`, so mutation of the incoming array does not make these values interchangeable. The returned current value is used as a subsequent starting value, not as the value in that same vector-field calculation.

This is not generally an innocuous state-only gauge change. If \(U\) is the supplied old value and \(V\) the current one, the two directions differ by \[f_U(s,a)-f_V(s,a)
 =(U-V)(s)-\gamma\int(U-V)(s')P(ds'\mid s,a).\] The first term is independent of the action and disappears on applying the mirror map. The second can depend on the action. For example, in an abstract three-state MDP, take two actions from a state \(s\) leading respectively to absorbing states of per-step costs zero and one, with zero immediate cost at \(s\). Under uniform initial actions, the two absorbing values differ by \(1/(1-\gamma)\). With \(U=0\), the stale direction gives zero action contrast at \(s\); the current direction gives contrast \(\gamma/(1-\gamma)\). This is an analytic demonstration of the formula’s possible effect, not an execution of the Gridworld class.

The acquired Euler, midpoint and RK4 routines call this function; the source also contains matching figure drivers. Its parameters \(n=11,\gamma=0.8,\tau=0.1\) agree with Appendix D. Passing the freshly evaluated `V` into the advantage calculation would remove this particular lag, subject to policy-evaluation tolerance. No source was modified or executed here, and no corrected experiment was reproduced.

This is a Minor discrepancy in the available numerical implementation. The current source alone does not establish an error in the historical figures or a failure of the analytic flow theorem. The release’s use of \(\tau\log\pi\) instead of KL against a uniform reference differs by an action-independent cost constant; that convention is not itself a policy-update defect.
# Interpretation and remaining limits

The assessed issues are limited to an auxiliary constant and the current code-to-vector-field correspondence. The principal entropy decay argument passes the bounded checks above. This is not a full certification of every existence, differentiability or approximation claim in the article.

The continuous-time result does not automatically supply an exponential rate for every discretization. Theorem 2.14, PDF p. 24, explicitly adds an occupancy-density condition for its exponential discrete estimate. Likewise the unregularized discussion, PDF p. 25, identifies necessary existence and absolute-continuity restrictions; simply setting \(\tau=0\) does not give the same theorem for arbitrary policies. Inexact and parameterized-flow bounds require the stated error and concentrability controls; those quantities were not measured here.

Overall assessment: Minor. The local analytic correction [eq:correct] (#eq:correct) is verified. The numerical routing correction is identified statically, with its experimental effect unverified. Author adoption is unknown. Scientific adjudication remains pending; no human review or independent acceptance is recorded.

1 B. Kerimkulov, J.-M. Leahy, D. Šiška, L. Szpruch and Y. Zhang, A Fisher–Rao Gradient Flow for Entropy-Regularised Markov Decision Processes in Polish Spaces, Found. Comput. Math. 26 (2026), 2395–2469, published online 11 August 2025, https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-025-09729-3.
# Supporting checks

Native helpers in the same session checked selected proof dependencies and the static source correspondence. They did not run author code or inspect source images. The complete extraction was used for navigation; the coverage record distinguishes selected reading from a full scientific audit.
Exact source, build, parse and actual page-view bindings are retained with the report. Controller-observed account/model information and the native runtime label remain separately attributed.

report: Abstract: The acquired article develops Trotter estimates using Favard regularity and, separately, energy constraints. Its identification of Favard spaces with fractional-power domains is false for the stated supremum-based definition. A diagonal self-adjoint operator gives an explicit counterexample, and finite truncations also disprove the claimed norm equivalence. This identification is used in the derivation of the Hilbert-space and singular-potential applications. The resulting assessment is Major, restricted to that proof dependency. The counterexample does not disprove all stated convergence rates. A separate omitted case in an increment lemma admits a direct repair.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Favard regularity and the derivation of Trotter splitting estimates
# Source, contribution, and scope

We review S. Becker, N. Galke, L. van Luijk and R. Salzmann, Convergence Rates for the Trotter Splitting for Unbounded Operators, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09730-w [paper]. The acquired source is the 54-page publisher version of record, published online 29 September 2025, journal pages 2471–2524 in the 2026 volume. Page numbers below refer to one-based PDF pages; the journal page number is obtained by adding 2470.

The main contributions comprise regularity-dependent estimates for contractive semigroups and an energy-constrained approach to unitary splitting. The detailed checks here concern the definitions and parameter restrictions of Section 2, its key commutator argument, Lemma 2.16 and its application dependencies, and selected hypotheses and examples from Section 3. The full article was extracted for navigation, but not every proof, citation, appendix or numerical experiment was independently verified. The acquisition record reports no separate supplement found in its bounded search. No author code was executed.
# The abstract estimate and its actual hypotheses

Let \(A,L\) generate strongly continuous contraction semigroups on a Banach space. For \(L\) relatively \(A\)-bounded with bound less than one, Lemma 2.1 (PDF pp. 9–10) reduces the splitting error on \(D(A)\) to \[t\sup_{s,\tau\in[0,t]}
 \left\lVert[L,e^{sA/n}]e^{\tau(A+L)}x\right\rVert.\] The telescoping sum and the differentiated interpolation in (2.2) have the required order of factors. In particular, both endpoint products are evaluated on the common generator domain; this is not an unrestricted formal manipulation of unbounded operators.

Equation reference: eq:def. For \(0<\alpha<1\), the article defines (PDF p. 12) \[F_\alpha(A)=
 \left\{x\in X:\sup_{\lambda>0}
 \left\lVert\lambda^\alpha A(\lambda-A)^{-1}x\right\rVert<\infty\right\}.
 \tag{2.1}\] For higher orders it uses graph spaces and writes \(\alpha=k_\alpha+r_\alpha\), \(k_\alpha\in\mathbb N_0\), \(0<r_\alpha\le1\). The semigroup-increment characterization (2.14)–(2.16), PDF p. 14, is also a supremum norm.

Theorem 2.8 (PDF pp. 18–20) assumes \[F_\alpha\subset D(L),\qquad LF_\gamma\subset F_\beta,\qquad
 \alpha<\min\{1,\gamma\},\qquad
 k_\gamma<\beta\le\gamma<2,\] with positive exponents. The resulting rate has \(\delta=\min\{1,\beta,\gamma-\alpha\}\) and is \(O(t^{1+\delta}n^{-\delta})\) from \(F_\gamma\) to \(X\). The two terms in \[[L,T_h]=L(T_h-I)-(T_h-I)L\] explain the appearances of \(\gamma-\alpha\) and \(\beta\). The perturbation and domain-invariance steps are substantive hypotheses in this argument. In particular, the later replacement of \(k_\gamma<\beta\) by \(\gamma-1<\beta\) is not already part of this abstract theorem.
# A false identification used in the applications

Problem 1 (Lemma 2.16, PDF pp. 22–23).  For the definition [eq:def] (#eq:def), the asserted equality \(F_\alpha(A)=D(|A|^\alpha)\), including equivalence of norms, is false even for negative self-adjoint generators on a Hilbert space. The asserted unitary analogue is false as well.

Equation reference: eq:dyadic. Let \(X=\ell^2(\mathbb N)\), with indices beginning at one, and set \[Ke_k=2^ke_k,\qquad
 D(K)=\left\{y:\sum_{k\ge1}4^k|y_k|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad A=-K .\] Then \(K\) is positive self-adjoint, \(A\) generates the strongly continuous contraction semigroup \((T_ty)_k=e^{-t2^k}y_k\), and \(0\in\rho(A)\). These meet, and even strengthen, the stated assumptions. Take \(\alpha=1/2\) and \(x_k=2^{-k/2}\). Then \[\left\lVert x\right\rVert^2=\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}=1,\qquad
 \left\lVert K^{1/2}x\right\rVert^2=\sum_{k\ge1}1=\infty .\] On the other hand, for every \(\lambda>0\), \[\left\lVert\lambda^{1/2}A(\lambda-A)^{-1}x\right\rVert^2
 =\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\lambda2^k}{(\lambda+2^k)^2}\le4.
 \tag{3.1}\] Indeed, on \(2^k\le\lambda\) the summand is at most \(2^k/\lambda\), whose geometric sum is at most two. On \(2^k>\lambda\) it is at most \(\lambda2^{-k}\), again with sum at most two. Empty low-frequency sums cause no difficulty. Thus \(x\in F_{1/2}(A)\setminus D(K^{1/2})\).

The same vector disproves the second assertion. The operator \(iK\) generates a strongly continuous unitary group, and \[\left\lVert\lambda^{1/2}iK(\lambda-iK)^{-1}x\right\rVert^2
 =\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{\lambda2^k}{\lambda^2+4^k}\le4\] by the same split. There is no domain or sign exception that excludes this example.

A finite-dimensional approximation makes the failure of norm equivalence particularly explicit. Let \(x^{(N)}\) agree with \(x\) in its first \(N\) coordinates and vanish elsewhere. Each vector belongs to every power domain, its \(X\)-norm is at most one, and the supremum in [eq:dyadic] (#eq:dyadic) is at most two after taking the square root, uniformly in \(N\). Yet \(\left\lVert K^{1/2}x^{(N)}\right\rVert=\sqrt N\). No uniform graph-norm bound in the claimed reverse direction is possible.
## The invalid step

On PDF p. 23 the proof optimizes a scalar spectral integrand at \(\lambda=r t/(1-r)\). This optimizing value depends on the spectral variable \(t\), which is subsequently integrated. In general \[\sup_{\lambda>0}\int g(\lambda,t)\,d\nu(t)
 \ \le\ \int\sup_{\lambda>0}g(\lambda,t)\,d\nu(t),\] and equality does not follow. In the example above, with \(r=1/2\), the left side is finite whereas the right side is \(\tfrac14\sum_{k\ge1}1=\infty\). The analogous optimization for \(iK\) has the same defect. This is not a missing multiplicative constant.
## Dependency and severity

Remark 2.17, PDF p. 22, uses the identification to assert (2.32) and to relax the exponent restriction in the subsequent corollaries. Corollaries 2.19 and 2.22, PDF pp. 24–25, explicitly invoke Lemma 2.16 and that remark. Examples 2.20 and 2.21 identify the corresponding Favard spaces with Sobolev spaces. The discussion of singular potentials on PDF pp. 25–26 and the derivation of Theorem 2.24 on PDF p. 27 rely on this identification, including its combination with perturbation stability in Lemma 2.7. Proposition 2.18, PDF p. 23, also cannot hold as stated: choosing the normal operator \(N=A\) above already contradicts its equality with \(D(|N|^{1/2})\).

The assessment is Major. A false regularity lemma is used to pass from the abstract hypotheses to important stated applications. The issue therefore concerns a central derivation rather than only an incidental description.
## Counterevidence and limits of correction

The forward inclusion \(D(|A|^\alpha)\subset F_\alpha(A)\), \(0<\alpha<1\), survives: the scalar spectral bound used in the proof does establish that direction. It does not establish the stronger assumption \(F_\alpha(A)\subset D(L)\) from a domain assumption involving only \(D(|A|^\alpha)\). Retaining the actual supremum definition is essential; changing it silently would change the theorem.

Nevertheless, some application estimates can be approached directly. For the \(\gamma=1\) setting of Corollary 2.22, let \(H,K\) be self-adjoint, \(0<\alpha,\beta<1\), with \(D(|K|^\alpha)\subset D(H)\) and \(HD(K)\subset D(|K|^\beta)\). Closed-graph boundedness and spectral calculus give, for \(0<|h|\le1\), \[\left\lVert(e^{ihK}-I)y\right\rVert_{D(|K|^\alpha)}
 \lesssim |h|^{1-\alpha}\left\lVert y\right\rVert_{D(K)},\qquad
 \left\lVert(e^{ihK}-I)Hy\right\rVert
 \lesssim |h|^\beta\left\lVert Hy\right\rVert_{D(|K|^\beta)} .\] The first estimate follows by splitting the spectral variable at \(|k|=|h|^{-1}\). The assumption \(\alpha<1\) also makes \(H\) infinitesimally \(K\)-bounded, so the self-adjoint sum has domain \(D(K)\), with equivalent graph norms and invariant graph evolution. The commutator argument on that domain therefore yields \(\delta=\min\{\beta,1-\alpha\}\) without the false equality.

This is a verified restricted alternative, not a repair of all fractional-\(\gamma\) statements or all singular-potential hypotheses. In particular, no counterexample to the published Coulomb rate has been established here, and no unavoidable loss of an extra power of \(n\) is inferred.
# A repairable omitted regularity case
Problem 2 (Lemma 2.6, PDF pp. 14–15).  The proof asserts that \(\gamma-\alpha<1\) implies \(k_\gamma=k_\alpha\). This implication is false.
For example, \(\alpha=3/4\), \(\gamma=5/4\) gives integer parts zero and one in the article’s convention. The omitted case can occur in the range of Theorem 2.8.

There is a direct correction. Write \(\alpha=k+a\), \(\gamma=k+1+b\), where \(0<b<a\le1\), and put \(Y=D(A^k)\) with its graph norm. For \(x\in F_\gamma\), the increment of \(Ax\) in \(Y\) satisfies \(\left\lVert(T_u-I)Ax\right\rVert_Y\lesssim u^b\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{F_\gamma}\). Commutativity and integration of the semigroup derivative yield \[\left\lVert(T_s-I)(T_t-I)x\right\rVert_Y
 \lesssim
 \begin{cases}
 s\,t^b\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{F_\gamma},&s\le t,\\
 t\,s^b\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{F_\gamma},&s>t.
 \end{cases}\] Multiplication by \(s^{-a}\) and taking the supremum gives \(O(t^{1+b-a})\). The remaining graph-norm term is \(O(t)\), hence also \(O(t^{1+b-a})\) for \(0<t\le1\). This is precisely the required \(t^{\gamma-\alpha}\) estimate.
The assessment of this omission is Minor: the printed case division is incomplete, but the missing case has the stated rate. It does not independently invalidate the abstract result.
# Separate checks and interpretation

The energy-constrained argument in Section 3 has distinct hypotheses. Theorem 3.6, PDF pp. 32–33, requires self-adjoint generators with joint energy-stability constants, a core for \(G^{1/2}\), twice continuously differentiable two-parameter products on that core, and a \(G^{1/2}\)-bounded commutator. Its energy-restricted norm estimate is not a claim of convergence in the unrestricted operator norm. The telescoping estimate in Lemma 3.7 correctly accounts for growth of the energy constraint. This part does not invoke the false Favard identification.

For the Schrödinger application, the hypotheses on PDF pp. 37 and 40 include \(V\in C^4\), bounded second derivative, polynomial growth of the third and fourth derivatives, and initial data in \(D(N)\), where \(N=P^2+Q^2\). Equation (3.45), PDF p. 41, visibly omits \(i\) from the potential exponential. The proof on the same page uses \(e^{itP^2/n}e^{itQ^2/n}\), which is the unitary product to which the displayed bound applies. Likewise the potential exponential in (3.43)–(3.44), PDF p. 40, must carry the unitary phase matching the sign of the joint evolution. These are correctable formula errors; a real growing exponential would not define the stated operation on every vector of \(D(N)\).

Overall assessment: Major, because of Lemma 2.16 and its material use in the application derivations. The corrected omitted case of Lemma 2.6, the surviving one-way domain inclusion, and the restricted direct commutator proof are counterevidence against a claim that all results fail. A full replacement of the fractional regularity argument remains to be supplied. Author adoption is unknown. Scientific adjudication is pending, with no human review or independent acceptance recorded.
