report: Abstract: The general regularized oracle and its derivative formulas pass the bounded checks in this review. The reduction of the approximate polynomial GCD problem to matrix singularity, however, admits common roots at infinity that are not part of the ordinary polynomial GCD defined in the paper. A two-linear-polynomial example makes the matrix problem attain its unique optimum at an inadmissible pair of constants, while the stated GCD problem has only an unattained infimum. This gives a Major finding specific to that application equivalence. Two sparse-specialization formulas also require direct corrections; the acquired implementation uses the correct expressions.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Degree loss in the approximate GCD reduction of Riemann-Oracle
# Source and scope

The reviewed article is M. Gnazzo, V. Noferini, L. Nyman and F. Poloni, Riemann-Oracle: A general-purpose Riemannian optimizer to solve nearness problems in matrix theory, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09731-9 [paper]. The source is the 45-page publisher version of record, published online 16 October 2025, journal pages 2525–2569 in the 2026 volume. All page references below are one-based PDF pages; add 2524 for journal pagination.

The contribution is a variable-elimination framework combining structured perturbation oracles, regularization, and optimization on a real Riemannian manifold. Detailed checks here cover the oracle, regularization, derivatives, convergence qualifications, sparse specialization, and approximate GCD reduction. Selected projection and nullity formulations were also read. The full extracted text is a navigation aid, not a claim of verification of every proof or numerical experiment. The existing acquisition record reports no separate supplement found in its bounded search.
# Core formulas and their surviving guarantees

Let \(A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}\), \(m\ge n\), and let \(P^{(1)},\ldots,P^{(p)}\) be a Frobenius-orthonormal perturbation basis, as in Assumption 2.3, PDF p. 6. For a unit vector \(v\), set \[\Delta=\sum_iP^{(i)}\delta_i,\qquad
 M(v)=[P^{(1)}v,\ldots,P^{(p)}v],\qquad r=-Av .\] Then \(\left\lVert\Delta\right\rVert_F=\left\lVert\delta\right\rVert\), and the null-vector constraint is \(M\delta=r\). Consequently Theorem 2.4, PDF pp. 7–8, correctly distinguishes the feasible case \(r\in\operatorname{Im}M\), where \(\delta_*=M^\dagger r\), from the empty constraint set, where the objective is \(+\infty\). Minimizing the pseudoinverse norm alone would lose that distinction; the paper does not make that substitution.

For \(\varepsilon>0\), completing the square gives \[\min_\delta\left(\left\lVert\delta\right\rVert^2+
             \varepsilon^{-1}\left\lVert M\delta-r\right\rVert^2\right)
 =r^*(MM^*+\varepsilon I)^{-1}r,\qquad
 \delta_*=M^*(MM^*+\varepsilon I)^{-1}r.\] The matrix \(M^*M+\varepsilon I\) is positive definite, so this inner minimizer is unique without a rank assumption on \(M\). These are Theorem 2.9, PDF p. 11. The singular-value decomposition used in Theorem 2.11, PDF pp. 12–13, gives the correct pointwise limit: it is \(\left\lVert M^\dagger r\right\rVert^2\) when feasible and \(+\infty\) otherwise. In the latter case a nonzero orthogonal residual contributes \(\varepsilon^{-1}\left\lVert r_\perp\right\rVert^2\). Pointwise convergence alone is not a theorem that every computed local minimizer converges to a global solution.

For the augmented objective, put \(r=-Av-\varepsilon y\), \(z=(MM^*+\varepsilon I)^{-1}r\). Real directional differentiation, also when \(\mathbb F=\mathbb C\), yields \[Df_{\varepsilon,y}(v)[w]
 =-2\operatorname{Re}\,z^*(A+\Delta_*)w,\qquad
 \nabla f_{\varepsilon,y}(v)=-2(A+\Delta_*)^*z.\] Differentiating the linear system for \(z\) gives \[\dot z=-(MM^*+\varepsilon I)^{-1}
           \bigl(M\dot M^*z+(A+\Delta_*)w\bigr),
 \quad
 \dot\delta_*=\dot M^*z+M^*\dot z,\quad \dot M=M(w).\] The Hessian action follows by differentiating the displayed gradient. These checks agree with Theorem 3.1, PDF p. 16, and Appendix A, PDF pp. 41–42.

Proposition 4.1 and its discussion, PDF pp. 17–18, require vanishing inner gradient tolerances, a feasible limit point, and LICQ there. The conclusion is KKT stationarity. The paper explicitly limits the implementation discussion to stationary points; it does not establish a global optimum from a finite tolerance. These qualifications must be retained in interpreting the numerical results.
# Degree loss changes the approximate GCD problem

Problem 1 (Section 7, PDF pp. 25–26).  The stated equivalence between a prescribed ordinary GCD degree and singularity of the fixed-size matrix \(S_d\) fails when perturbed leading coefficients vanish.

Section 7 defines the GCD by divisibility in \(\mathbb C[x]\), and problem (16) minimizes the coefficient perturbation norm subject to \(\deg\gcd(p+\delta p,q+\delta q)\ge d\). The initial leading coefficients are nonzero. The perturbations are allowed to have the same degree as the inputs; the perturbed leading coefficients are not required to remain nonzero.

Take real polynomials, which are also admissible over \(\mathbb C\), \[p(x)=tx+1,\qquad q(x)=tx-1,\qquad 0<t<1,\qquad m=n=d=1.\] The block scalings in the article’s definition of \(S_1\) are one, and hence \[S_1(p,q)=
 \begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\t&t\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 S_1(p,q)S_1(p,q)^*=
 \begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2t^2\end{pmatrix}.\] Its singular values are \(\sqrt2\) and \(\sqrt2\,t\). The unique nearest matrix of rank at most one is therefore \[S_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \left\lVert S_1(p,q)-S_0\right\rVert_F=\sqrt2\,t .\] Here this elementary best-approximation statement can also be checked directly. For any singular \(B\), take a unit vector \(w\in\ker B\). Then \(\left\lVert S_1-B\right\rVert_F\ge\left\lVert(S_1-B)w\right\rVert
=\left\lVert S_1w\right\rVert\ge\sqrt2\,t\). Equality forces \(w\) to lie in the unique smallest singular direction, and \(S_1-B\) to act only on that direction. This forces \(B=S_0\).

The corresponding polynomial perturbations are \[\delta p=\delta q=-tx,\qquad
 p+\delta p=1,\qquad q+\delta q=-1 .\] Both perturbations have exact degree one, so even the literal same-degree requirement is met. But \(\deg\gcd(1,-1)=0\). The matrix optimizer is not feasible for the stated polynomial problem.

The discrepancy also concerns attainment, not only a formal equivalence at an unused point. For real \(h\) with \(0<|h|<t\), consider \[p_h=1+hx,\qquad q_h=-1-hx .\] They share a degree-one factor. Their perturbations have exact degree one and satisfy \[\left\lVert(p_h-p,q_h-q)\right\rVert^2
 =|h-t|^2+|-h-t|^2=2t^2+2h^2\longrightarrow 2t^2 .\] Every pair satisfying the genuine GCD condition maps to a singular matrix, giving the lower bound \(\sqrt2\,t\). The infimum is therefore \(\sqrt2\,t\), but it is not attained: an attaining pair would have to map to the unique nearest singular matrix \(S_0\), whose two polynomials have GCD degree zero. For example \(t=1/2\) gives the exact infimum \(1/\sqrt2\).
## Dependency, correction, and limits

The reduction on PDF p. 26 is the basis for treating approximate GCD within the general oracle framework and for its implementation. The distinction is thus material to one of the paper’s principal application equivalences. The assessment is Major for this claim. It does not invalidate the general regularized matrix oracle.

A homogeneous fixed-grade interpretation counts the limiting common root at infinity and would explain the matrix solution. It would, however, change the ordinary polynomial problem explicitly stated in Section 7. Alternatively, restrictions on the perturbed leading coefficients require a revised optimization problem. Merely requiring them to be nonzero leaves an open condition and does not restore attainment in the example. Closed bounds away from zero, or a carefully specified factor representation with additional constraints, would require separate analysis. Recomputing \(S_d\) from the perturbed degrees would change its dimensions and destroy the fixed linear perturbation map used in the derivation.

The acquired MATLAB routine `nearest_gcd.m`, lines 14–28, uses input array lengths to fix the degrees and permits all coefficients to vary through the general structured routine. The helper `polytoep.m`, lines 17–24, retains the fixed array sizes. There is no leading-coefficient preservation condition in that route, so the boundary example is not excluded by the available source. This is a static observation, not an executed counterexample to a particular optimizer run.

Substantial counterevidence limits the experimental conclusion. On PDF p. 38 the paper describes explicit factor reconstruction and product residuals, and acknowledges a difficult case where the requested factor could not be extracted. The acquired `example_zeng2.m`, lines 55–83, likewise contains nullity analysis, factor reconstruction and residual reporting. The example above does not show that any reported benchmark distance is wrong. It shows that matrix feasibility alone is not the claimed certificate of ordinary GCD degree.
# Correctable sparse formulas
Problem 2 (Section 5, PDF p. 18).  The displayed sparse objective has an extra square in its denominator, and the displayed gradient uses an inconsistent weight.

An exact example checks both differences. Take \[A=\operatorname{diag}(1,2),\quad
 P^{(1)}=E_{11},\ P^{(2)}=E_{22},\quad
 v=(1,1)^T/\sqrt2,\quad \varepsilon=1,\quad y=0 .\] The basis is orthonormal, \(d_1=d_2=1/2\), \(z=-\tfrac23 Av\), and \(\delta_*=(-1/3,-2/3)^T\). The general oracle gives \(f_\varepsilon=5/3\), whereas the printed sparse expression gives \(2\). The true gradient is \[\frac89\,\frac{(1,4)^T}{\sqrt2};\] using the displayed sparse weights and the same defined \(z\) instead gives \[\left(\frac4{\sqrt5}-\frac49\right)
      \frac{(1,4)^T}{\sqrt2}.\] The difference survives projection onto the sphere’s tangent space.

These are Minor formula errors on the available evidence. The corrections follow directly from the valid general theorems. More strongly, `nearest_singular_sparse.m`, lines 45–67, uses \(D_i=(d_i+\varepsilon)^{-1}\), evaluates \(\sum_i|r_i|^2D_i\), and forms the correct gradient through \(z=D\odot r\). Its Hessian code differentiates those expressions. The Orani driver uses this routine, so the printed errors do not establish an erroneous Orani experiment.

A further minor normalization error appears on PDF p. 9: the squared objective for \(A=\sum_iP^{(i)}\alpha_i\) is bounded by \(\left\lVert\alpha\right\rVert^2\), not the displayed \(\left\lVert\alpha\right\rVert\). The scalar case \(A=2,P^{(1)}=1,v=1\) gives \(f=4>2\). The corrected bound follows at once from \(f(v)=\left\lVert M^\dagger M\alpha\right\rVert^2\le\left\lVert\alpha\right\rVert^2\); boundedness and the need for regularization are unaffected.
# Supporting checks

The instability projection argument on PDF pp. 28–29 correctly completes the square as \[f_\varepsilon(v,\lambda)
 =a|\lambda-\lambda_0|^2+c-a^{-1}|b|^2,\qquad a>0 .\] Thus projection supplies the optimal complex \(\lambda\). Differentiation with a fixed optimal projection is valid where that projection is unique; it is not a universal Hessian formula. Remark 8.3 explicitly separates the case of real perturbation coefficients. Likewise the prescribed-nullity formulation on PDF pp. 29–30 uses rank at most \(n-\ell\), an appropriate closed rank condition.

The linked repository is the acquired commit `6841f77b74ffa84dc6904b3e0200ef89c1372157`, recorded 16 September 2026. Its identity with the historical revision used for the paper’s timings is not established. Static checks confirm several formula and parameter correspondences, including the general derivatives and the Orani route described on PDF p. 32. No MATLAB source, test, or benchmark was executed. Timing superiority, the full statistical comparisons, floating-point robustness, and global optimality were not independently reproduced.

Overall assessment: Major, restricted principally to the GCD feasible-set and attainment claim. The central elimination and regularization formulas survive, and the sparse display corrections are verified. report: Abstract: The acquired manuscript’s free-cokernel characterization of interval decomposability passes the detailed checks described here. Its proof uses the cokernels of composite maps in an essential way; checking only neighboring arrows is insufficient. Exact integer examples verify both the obstruction and the intended compatible-basis construction. The printed matrix algorithm and a kernel-filtration formula contain endpoint indexing errors with small counterexamples. The surrounding high-level construction supports direct repairs. The assessment is Major for the acquired arXiv version: the literal algorithm fails its central output guarantee on a legal input. The free-cokernel criterion is not refuted, and no finding is transferred to the journal-final text.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Compatible bases and endpoint indices in persistence over a PID
# Source and exact mathematical scope

We review J. Luo and G. Henselman-Petrusek, Interval Decomposition of Persistence Modules over a Principal Ideal Domain, arXiv:2310.07971v6, dated 3 October 2025 [paper]. The acquired file has 33 pages. Its associated journal DOI is 10.1007/s10208-025-09732-8, but the reviewed bytes are the arXiv manuscript, not a verified journal-final copy. All locators below refer to its one-based PDF pages. No equivalence of versions or journal-final persistence of a finding is claimed.

The later convention \(f_0=f_m=0\), explicitly imposed on PDF p. 9, is obtained by adjoining zero endpoints and relabeling. This does not change the obstruction: new maps from zero have the already free pointwise modules as cokernels, and maps into zero have zero cokernel. The half-open interval convention is understood with these terminal indices.

The detailed review covers necessity, the main complement argument, the high-level sufficiency proof, selected matrix construction steps, and the topological hypotheses. The full lattice-theoretic appendix, all external dependencies, and bit growth through a complete implementation were not independently certified. No author program was executed; the evidence calculations below are exact algebra. The acquisition record reports no standalone supplement found in its bounded search.
# The main proof chain

Necessity, Lemma 2 on PDF p. 10, follows directly from an interval basis: at a target index the image is spanned by the intervals covering both indices, and the remaining interval basis elements form a free complement.

For sufficiency the key issue is primitivity. A submodule \(U\) of a finite free PID module \(V\) has a complement exactly when \(V/U\) is torsion-free, equivalently when \[rz\in U,\quad r\ne0,\quad z\in V
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z\in U .\] Finite generation and the PID hypothesis justify replacing torsion-free by free. Lemma 3, PDF p. 11, uses these conditions correctly. Intersections of primitive submodules remain primitive by this saturation test, and if \(L\subset H\subset V\) with \(L\) primitive in \(V\), then \(H/L\subset V/L\) is free. These are the needed contents of Lemmas 4–5, PDF pp. 12–13.

For \(x\le a\le y\), set \[K=\ker f(a\le y),\qquad I=\operatorname{im}f(x\le a).\] The natural map induced by \(f(a\le y)\) gives \[f_a/(K+I)
 \cong \operatorname{im}f(a\le y)/\operatorname{im}f(x\le y)
 \ \subset\ f_y/\operatorname{im}f(x\le y).\] The final module is free by the hypothesis on the composite \(f(x\le y)\). Therefore the first quotient is free, and \(K+I\) has a complement. This verifies the substantive step of Theorem 7, PDF p. 12. It avoids the false general assertion that the sum of two primitive submodules is necessarily primitive.

To check the construction in Algorithm 1 and Theorem 8, PDF pp. 13–14, write \(J=\operatorname{im}f(i-1\le i)\) and \(K_j=\ker f(i\le j)\). The propagated nonzero elements of the previous basis form a basis of \(J\), adapted to \(J\cap K_j\): the relevant preimage is \(\ker f(i-1\le j)\). The algorithm adds a basis of a complement of \[(J+K_{j-1})\cap K_j\] inside \(K_j\). The preceding primitivity results guarantee existence. Since \[(J+K_{j-1})\cap K_j=(J\cap K_j)+K_{j-1},\] the added vectors extend a basis of \(J+K_{j-1}\) to one of \(J+K_j\), preserving the filtration adaptation. At \(j=m\), \(K_m=f_i\). Each adjacent map then sends a basis vector either to zero or to a distinct next-node basis vector. Following those vectors yields the interval summands. This verifies the main sufficiency mechanism.

The conditional uniqueness proof on PDF p. 9 also passes the check. Tensoring two interval decompositions with \(\operatorname{Frac}(R)\) preserves their interval multisets. Uniqueness over the fraction field therefore gives uniqueness of that multiset over \(R\). It does not assert that the fraction-field barcode classifies every integral persistence module before decomposability has been shown.
# Exact tests of the hypotheses

Consider the integer module, with zero endpoints, \[0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z
 \xrightarrow{A}\mathbb Z^2
 \xrightarrow{B}\mathbb Z\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 A=\binom10,\quad B=(2\ \ 1).\] The adjacent cokernels are \(\mathbb Z\) and zero, but \(BA=[2]\) has cokernel \(\mathbb Z/2\). Thus the module does not decompose into integral intervals. At the middle node \[\operatorname{im}A=\mathbb Ze_1,\qquad \ker B=\mathbb Z(1,-2),\] and their sum has index two. This is precisely the obstruction excluded by the composite-cokernel assumption. It is a check supporting the theorem, not a counterexample to it.

The obstruction is also visible after changing coefficients. For characteristic different from two the barcode is \([1,4)\) together with \([2,3)\). In characteristic two it is \([1,3)\) together with \([2,4)\). Pointwise free integer modules alone therefore do not imply a field-independent barcode.

For a positive exact test, replace \(B\) by \((1\ \ 1)\). The middle basis \(e_1,e_2-e_1\) is unimodular. The first map sends \(1\) to its first vector, and the second sends those two vectors to \(1,0\), respectively. Hence the decomposition is \(I_{\mathbb Z}^{1,4}\oplus I_{\mathbb Z}^{2,3}\).

A second exact test uses \[0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z^2
 \xrightarrow{(2\ \ 3)}\mathbb Z\longrightarrow0.\] Here \[(2\ \ 3)
 \begin{pmatrix}-1&3\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}
 =(1\ \ 0),\qquad
 \det\begin{pmatrix}-1&3\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}=-1.\] Thus the domain basis \((-1,1),(3,-2)\) gives intervals \([1,3)\) and \([1,2)\). The controlling invariant is the unit Smith divisor \(\gcd(2,3)=1\), not the first unreduced coefficient.
# Corrections to the explicit matrix construction
Problem 1 (Major: Algorithm 2, PDF p. 15).  The printed loop endpoints omit a potentially nonzero final node and the final death block.

Line 3 iterates \(i=1,\ldots,m-2\); line 5 iterates \(j=i+1,\ldots,m-1\). But line 11 concatenates the blocks through \(Y_i^m\), which that inner loop has not constructed. The output also includes the initialized, uncomputed \(\beta_{m-1}\).

Take \(m=2\) and \(f_0=f_2=0,\ f_1=R\). Every required cokernel is free and the module is \(I_R^{1,2}\). The outer loop is empty, so the printed algorithm returns \(\beta_1=\varnothing\), which is not a basis of \(R\). This disproves the literal output guarantee without any numerical or implementation assumptions.

The natural corrected ranges are \[i=1,\ldots,m-1,\qquad j=i+1,\ldots,m .\] They already occur in Algorithm 1, PDF p. 13, and the proof of Lemma 6, PDF pp. 15–16, explicitly uses the terminal blocks. The known zero maps from \(f_0\) and into \(f_m\) supply the endpoint operations. With these ranges the minimal example forms \(Y_1^2=[1]\), giving the required basis. The associated prose, coherence convention and loop counts should be aligned as well; the asymptotic operation count is unchanged.
Problem 2 (Major: Proposition 5, PDF p. 28).  The displayed kernel-block formula has its target index shifted by one and omits the first kernel block.

The notation \(F_a\) represents \(f(a\le a+1)\). The proposition defines \[X^k=T_a^+\cdots T_{k-1}^+T_k^-\] but claims that \([X^{a+1}|\cdots|X^k]\) spans \(\ker f(a\le k)\). The factor \(T_k^-\) instead concerns the product \(F_k\cdots F_a\), whose target is \(k+1\).

For an exact witness set \(F_a=[0]\), \(F_{a+1}=[1]\). Then \(T_a^+\) has no columns, so the printed \(X^{a+1}\) has no columns, whereas \(\ker F_a=R\). This can be embedded in the permitted finite module with \(m=4\), \(a=1\), \(F_1=0,F_2=1,F_3=0\), and zero endpoints. All of its structure-map cokernels are free.

A consistent death-index convention is \[X^{a+1}=T_a^-,\qquad
 X^j=T_a^+\cdots T_{j-2}^+T_{j-1}^-,
 \quad a+2\le j\le m .\] Then \([X^{a+1}|\cdots|X^b]\) gives the kernel through target \(b\). To see the intended induction, at each Smith step \(T_k^-\) spans the kernel of the remaining restricted product, while \(T_k^+\) carries its complementary coordinates to the next step. The nonzero Smith diagonal entries give an injective map on that complement over the domain \(R\). Successive unimodular changes therefore split off exactly the new kernel blocks. The first block is necessarily \(T_a^-\). The block pattern in Figure 3, on the same page, is consistent with retaining that initial block.

The assessment of both construction errors is Major. The abstract advertises an algorithm that decides decomposability and returns an interval decomposition. Algorithm 2’s output promise and Theorem 9 on PDF p. 17 make that guarantee explicit. Problem 1 refutes it on a legal input, while Algorithm 2, line 4, explicitly uses Proposition 5 for the kernel filtration affected by Problem 2. Thus the errors damage a central constructive claim, even though short index repairs are available.

The surviving results bound this assessment. Algorithm 1 supplies the required endpoints, the main complement proof is unaffected by these counterexamples, and the corrected indexing has the stated kernel meaning. Neither the free-cokernel criterion nor every result of the paper has been refuted. No general implementation was executed, and this review does not certify every detail of the lattice-based rejection proof.
# Applications, complexity, and remaining limits

Theorem 4, PDF pp. 6–7, assumes that both \(H_k(K_a;\mathbb Z)\) and \(H_{k-1}(K_a;\mathbb Z)\) are free and finitely generated at every index. The exact sequence \[0\longrightarrow\operatorname{coker}\phi_a^b
 \longrightarrow H_k(K_b,K_a;\mathbb Z)
 \longrightarrow\operatorname{im}\partial\longrightarrow0\] then splits because its last term is a subgroup of a free abelian group. This verifies the stated equivalence between free cokernels and free relative homology under those assumptions. The field-independence equivalence also invokes the cited prior result; that external proof was not independently reaudited here.

The universal-cycle discussion on PDF pp. 8–9 correctly retains torsion checks in both dimensions. The lower-dimensional condition removes the \(\operatorname{Tor}\) contribution in the universal coefficient theorem, permitting the natural identification of integer homology tensored with a field and field homology. It should not be dropped in applications.

Proposition 2, PDF p. 17, counts \(O(m^2)\) matrix multiplications/Smith factorizations and \(O(m)\) inversions, expressed as \[O\!\left(m\max\{mM_d,mS_d,R_d\}\right).\] Theorem 10, PDF p. 18, assumes that all structure-map matrices have already been computed before stating the decision bound \(O(m^2S_d)\). These are the operation-level claims checked here. An independent analysis of integer coefficient bit lengths or polynomial degrees throughout all intermediate basis changes has not been completed; no counterexample to the intended polynomial-time claim is inferred from that limitation.

Overall assessment: Major for the acquired v6 manuscript, confined to the explicit matrix construction and its stated output guarantee. The main free-cokernel criterion retains the support of the bounded initial checks. The construction indices require the specific repairs above; the journal-final status and author adoption are unknown. Scientific adjudication remains pending, with no human review recorded. Focused independent-acceptance revisions and their execution evidence are recorded in provenance.

report: Abstract: The acquired manuscript’s scalarization, Hadamard-space recognition, and maximal-cell interior reduction pass the bounded checks given below. The general boundary construction, however, uses a false assertion that a geodesic between two incident cubes must cross their common face. Four unit squares in the Euclidean plane give an exact counterexample, including an incorrect directional derivative. This invalidates the stated construction of the derivative functions used by the boundary semidefinite programs. A separate distinction between bicombing convexity and convexity along every geodesic requires a qualification in an auxiliary attainment proof. The overall assessment is Major for the acquired arXiv version, with the scope of each conclusion specified below.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Weighted-mean recognition and the geometry of cell boundaries
# Source, hypotheses, and scope

We review A. Goodwin, A. S. Lewis, G. López-Acedo, and A. Nicolae, Recognizing weighted means in geodesic spaces, arXiv:2406.03913v1, submitted 6 June 2024, with title-page date 7 June 2024 [paper]. The acquired PDF has 39 pages. The associated journal DOI is 10.1007/s10208-025-09733-7. The reviewed bytes are the arXiv manuscript; no identity with, or persistence of these findings in, the journal-final version is asserted. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages.

The set \(A\) is nonempty and finite, and \[\Delta_A=\{w\in\mathbb R^A:w_a\ge0,\ \sum_a w_a=1\}.\] Zero weights are permitted. An \(A\)-minimal point has no competitor strictly closer to every \(a\in A\). This differs from the Pareto condition, which forbids a simultaneous nonincrease with at least one strict decrease, and from strong minimality, which forbids every distinct simultaneous nonincrease. Theorem 6.1, PDF pp. 15–16, equates \(p\)-means for all \(p\ge1\) with \(A\)-minimal points in a convex metric space. Corollary 6.5 strengthens this to the Pareto and strong-minimality properties in a Hadamard space.

The detailed checks cover these distinctions, the finite-dimensional duality step, the angle and Euclidean tangent criteria, the relative-interior algorithm, and the general boundary construction. The proof of general primal attainment is also tested at its convexity step. All calculations below are exact symbolic arguments. No author program or semidefinite solver was executed. The external geodesic-complexity theorem, a bit-complexity bound for exact SDP decisions, and the numerical sampling experiments were not independently certified. The acquisition record reports no standalone supplement found in its bounded search; that record does not establish that no additional material exists.
# Checks supporting the principal recognition results

Assumption 3.1 on PDF p. 8 gives strict primal feasibility and dual feasibility with \(c\ne0\). In Theorem 3.4, PDF pp. 10–11, the latter condition bounds the perturbation value function below by a finite affine function. Strict feasibility makes it finite near the perturbation \(b\). Metric convexity and the convexity of \(t\mapsto t^p\), \(p\ge1\), give convexity of the value function. A subgradient therefore exists at \(b\); variations in the slack and in \(y\) imply \[\bar w\ge0,\qquad G^*\bar w=c.\] In particular \(\bar w\ne0\), so normalization is legitimate.

For an \(A\)-minimal point \(\bar x\), the intersecting-balls problem with radii \(d_A(\bar x)\) already has the optimum \((\bar x,0)\). The dual certificate in Example 5.4, PDF p. 14, thus establishes the scalarization in Theorem 6.1 without invoking the separate general primal-attainment theorem. In the Hadamard setting, the variance inequality on PDF p. 16, \[\sum_a w_a\bigl(d(a,x)^2-d(a,\bar x)^2\bigr)
 \ge d(x,\bar x)^2,\] excludes every distinct simultaneous nonincrease. This remains valid when some weights vanish.

The angle criterion, Proposition 6.8 on PDF pp. 17–18, also passes the check. A common strict distance decrease gives a strictly acute angle to each point of \(A\). Conversely, minimality along a sequence on a fixed outgoing geodesic supplies an active point of \(A\); finiteness permits a subsequence with the same active point, and first variation gives an angle at least \(\pi/2\). The finiteness hypothesis is used substantively.

When the tangent cone is Euclidean, Theorem 7.12 on PDF p. 23 identifies the mean deficit with \[\operatorname{dist}\left(0,\operatorname{conv}\{v_a:a\in A\}\right),
 \qquad v_a=([\bar x,a],d(\bar x,a)).\] If \(q\) is the closest point of this convex hull to zero and \(q\ne0\), the projection inequality gives \(\langle q,v_a\rangle\ge |q|^2>0\) for every \(a\). First variation then yields a common decreasing direction. If \(q=0\), the convex-combination weights give the certificate. This uses a Euclidean tangent cone, not an arbitrary CAT(0) cone.

Theorem 9.3, PDF pp. 28–29, and Algorithm 9.5, PDF p. 30, require a point in the relative interior of a maximal cell. Its Euclidean neighborhood justifies contracting the geodesics into that cell and extending their initial vectors in its ambient space. The reciprocal contraction factors used to form intermediate weights cancel the factors used in transferring the certificate back. Later bisections preserve already obtained strict distance decreases by convexity.

For an exact elementary check, let \(X=C=[0,1]^2\) and \[A=\{(1/4,1/2),(3/4,1/2)\}.\] At \(\bar x=(1/2,1/2)\), the projection gives zero deficit and weights \((1/2,1/2)\). At \(\bar x=(1/2,3/4)\), it gives \(z=(1/2,1/2)\), deficit \(1/4\), and \[d(z,a)=1/4<\sqrt2/4=d(\bar x,a)\qquad(a\in A).\] Thus \(z\) is the claimed negative certificate. A positive numerical tolerance in the algorithm gives an approximate declaration, rather than an exact positive certificate.
# The general cell-boundary construction

Problem 1 (Major: the common-face distance formula).  On PDF p. 35, Section 11 chooses a cell \(C\) incident to \(\bar x\) and a cell \(Q_a\) containing the initial segment \([\bar x,x_a]\) of the geodesic toward \(a\). It sets \(F_a=C\cap Q_a\) and asserts that every geodesic from \(x_a\) to \(y\in C\) passes through \(F_a\). The resulting formula is \[d(x_a,y)=\min_{x\in F_a}
       \bigl(|x_a-x|_{Q_a}+|x-y|_C\bigr).                 \tag{1}\] The stated cubical hypotheses do not imply this assertion.

Take \(X=[-1,1]^2\), subdivided into four unit squares and their faces, with its Euclidean intrinsic metric. This is a finite, complete CAT(0) cubical complex satisfying the definition on PDF p. 27. Put \[\bar x=0,\quad Q_a=[-1,0]^2,\quad C=[0,1]^2,\quad
 a=x_a=(-1/2,-1/2),\quad y=(1/2,1/4).\] The points \(a,y\) are in the relative interiors of the two maximal cells; the geodesic \([\bar x,a]\) is a single nontrivial segment in \(Q_a\). Their common face is just \(\{0\}\). The actual straight-line distance is \[d(x_a,y)=\sqrt{1+(3/4)^2}=\frac54,\] whereas the right-hand side of (1) equals \[\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+\frac{\sqrt5}{4}>\frac54.\] The strict inequality also follows from strictness in the Euclidean triangle inequality: the segment does not contain zero. It passes through a third square. This example satisfies the additional restriction to maximal cells used later in Section 11.

The discrepancy persists at the derivative used by the algorithm. For \(u=e_1\in T_C(0)\), \[d_a(tu)=\sqrt{(t+1/2)^2+1/4},\qquad
 d'_{a,C}(0;u)=\frac1{\sqrt2}.\] The expression in (1) instead becomes \(\sqrt2/2+t\), whose right derivative is \(1\). Shortening the initial segment toward \(a\) does not fix the directional mismatch. Scaling the finite-distance example toward zero also preserves its strict inequality, so a merely local interpretation is insufficient.

The dependency is material. Page 35 uses (1) to construct a semidefinite representation of \(d_{x_a,C}\), then its subdifferential and support function, identified with the genuine directional derivative \(f_{a,C}=d'_{a,C}(\bar x;\cdot)\). The recognition programs \[(P_C)\qquad \inf_u\max_{a\in A}f_{a,C}(u)\] and the weight-certificate sets \(V_C\) on PDF pp. 36–37 depend on those functions. The counterexample therefore invalidates the given general construction supporting an algorithm advertised in the abstract. This is the basis for the Major assessment.

Several limits are essential. The example does not establish an incorrect final recognition decision: both derivatives in the displayed direction are positive. It does not show that a different semidefinite representation is impossible. If the genuine derivatives are supplied, the conditional convexity argument for common descent on PDF p. 36 remains meaningful. The interior method has a separate justification and is unaffected.

Formula (1) is valid under the additional hypothesis that the relevant geodesic crosses \(F_a\): the triangle inequality gives one bound, and splitting that geodesic at its crossing gives the other. It also works in a tripod. With three unit arms and \(A\) their endpoints, the derivative along arm \(i\), at speed \(t\), is \(-t\) for its own endpoint and \(t\) for the others. The weighted squared-distance objective along that arm is \[1+2(1-2w_i)t+t^2.\] The common vertex is a barycenter exactly when \(w_i\le1/2\) for all \(i\), and equal weights provide a certificate. Thus the construction succeeds in some branching cases. A repair for arbitrary complexes must account for paths through other cells and prove that the resulting derivative representation has the claimed computational properties. Those properties are not established by the restricted correction above.
# A qualification in the auxiliary attainment proof

Problem 2 (Minor: two notions of geodesic convexity).  PDF p. 11 defines a convex set as one containing every geodesic between its points. Theorem 4.3 on PDF pp. 12–13 assumes reflexivity for closed bounded convex sets and a conical bicombing. Its proof shows only that each set \(F_k\) contains the selected bicombing geodesic between its points, then invokes reflexivity. These convexity notions need not coincide.

Let \(X=(\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)\), \(A=\{0\}\), \(p=1\), \(Y=\mathbb R\), \(Gy=y\), \(c=1\), and \(b=0\). Strict and dual feasibility hold with \(\hat x=0,\hat y=1,\hat w=1\). The space is proper, hence satisfies the stated nested-intersection property, and linear interpolation is a conical bicombing. The primal optimum is \(\nu=0\). For \(r=1/k\), the proof’s set is \[F_k=[-r,r]^2.\] Both \((-r,r)\) and \((r,r)\) lie in \(F_k\), but the curve \[\gamma(s)=\bigl(-r+2rs,\ r+2r\min(s,1-s)\bigr),
 \qquad 0\le s\le1,\] is a geodesic with midpoint \((0,2r)\notin F_k\). Indeed its first-coordinate difference is \(2r|s-t|\), and the second-coordinate difference is no larger, so \(\|\gamma(s)-\gamma(t)\|_\infty=2r|s-t|\). Thus the intermediate assertion of all-geodesics convexity is false even in an admissible finite-dimensional example.

This demonstrates a gap in the stated general argument, not nonattainment: the optimum in this example is attained. In a uniquely geodesic space with the stated bicombing, the two notions coincide and the proof goes through. Alternatively, one can assume the nested-intersection property for sets convex along that chosen bicombing. These are verified sufficient qualifications, not a proof that the original broader hypotheses already imply the needed property. Hadamard spaces present no such ambiguity, and the principal recognition theorem does not depend on general primal attainment.

The overall conclusion is consequently specific: the abstract’s general boundary SDP construction needs a substantive replacement for its geometric step, while the inspected main recognition criteria and maximal-cell interior mechanism retain their support. The auxiliary attainment argument needs a narrower convexity convention or hypothesis. Neither finding is an assertion that every result of the paper fails, and neither has been transferred to an unexamined journal-final version.

report: Abstract: The local and nonlocal components of the proposed trace seminorm have the expected common kernel and scaling. The principal Hardy, counting, and averaging mechanisms support the trace and lifting estimates under the stated regularity and quasi-uniformity hypotheses. An exact one-cell calculation also confirms the Schur-complement and boundary-kernel construction used in the numerical section. The printed cube proof nevertheless selects points outside the cube in dimensions at least three. A fixed reduction of the path height repairs this geometric step without changing the powers in the estimates. The extension to spaces without independent face values needs its trace range specified, and the local-to-global argument needs a clear boundary-connectivity convention. The assessment is Minor, with these qualifications and the limits of the review made explicit.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Discrete trace seminorms, lifting, and the range of the geometric construction
# Source and precise setting

We review S. Badia, J. Droniou, and J. Tushar, A Discrete Trace Theory for Non-Conforming Polytopal Hybrid Discretisation Methods, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 2667–2716, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09734-6 [paper]. The acquired 50-page file is the publisher version of record, showing online publication on 3 December 2025. This review concerns that file. The one-based PDF page \(p\) corresponds to journal page \(2666+p\).

Section 2, PDF pp. 4–6, assumes a polytopal domain in \(\mathbb R^d\), \(d\ge2\), a regular mesh in the sense of its cited reference, and quasi-uniformity \(h\le\Psi h_t\) with \(\Psi\) independent of \(h\). These are substantive hypotheses. The results do not assert uniformity over arbitrarily graded meshes, degenerating mesh regularity, or unbounded polynomial degrees. The hidden constants may depend on the domain, mesh regularity, quasi-uniformity parameter, and polynomial degrees.

All 50 pages were read as extracted text, with detailed mathematical checks concentrated on the definitions, central counting and Hardy steps, lifting weights, localisation, and finite-dimensional spectral construction. This does not certify every external lemma or every geometric case. The source’s external mesh-regularity definition and auxiliary discrete functional-analysis results were not independently re-proved. The recorded bounded acquisition search found no standalone supplement. No author software or numerical experiment was run; the finite-dimensional checks below are exact algebra.
# Kernel, scaling, and the main estimates

Every term in \(T_h\) is nonnegative. Its vanishing forces each \(w_f\) to be constant and every pair of face averages to agree. Thus its kernel is the single global constant mode. On a connected face-adjacency mesh, \(E_h=0\) likewise makes each cell constant and transfers that constant across shared face values. The right-inverse claim is compatible with the kernels.

Under \(x=\mu\widehat x\) with unchanged field values, both squared forms scale by \(\mu^{d-2}\): the gradient term contributes \(\mu^{d-2}\), the penalty contributes \(\mu^{-1}\mu^{d-1}\), and the pair term contributes \(\mu^{2d-2}/\mu^d\). The seminorms themselves scale by \(\mu^{(d-2)/2}\). Remark 2.4 on PDF p. 6 should refer to squared seminorms for its exponent \(d-2\). Its conclusion about unchanged comparison constants under common rescaling is correct.

The nonlocal trace estimate groups face pairs in shells of radius approximately \(\ell h\). Lemma 3.2, PDF p. 14, gives at most \(C\ell^{d-2}\) faces in a shell and bounded overlap of vertical cell columns. The factor in (3.31), PDF p. 15, is \[\frac{h^{d-1}h^{d-1}h^{2-d}}{(\ell h)^d}=\ell^{-d}.\] Shell counting leaves \(\ell^{-2}\), before taking the square root. With \(r_m^2=\sum_{t\in L_m}|v_t|_{1,t}^2\), the vertical estimate becomes \[\zeta_\ell\lesssim\frac1\ell\sum_{m=0}^{\ell}r_m.\] Lemma 3.3, stated on PDF p. 15 and proved on pp. 20–21, controls the squared sum by \(18\sum_mr_m^2\). Its summation by parts and Young inequality are consistent: \[\sum_{\ell=1}^L R_\ell^2
 \le\frac4\alpha\sum_{\ell=1}^L R_\ell^2
       +(\alpha+1)\sum_{m=0}^Lr_m^2.\] Taking \(\alpha=8\) gives \(18\), including the \(m=0\) layer. The horizontal counting in Lemma 3.4, PDF p. 17, cancels the remaining shell powers; bounded layer overlap on PDF p. 18 completes that estimate, subject to the geometric correction below.

The lifting (4.13), PDF p. 26, averages boundary face means using \(\rho_t(f)=|f|/|A_t|\) on \(A_t\), averages neighboring cell values at interior faces, and retains the prescribed boundary polynomials. It is linear, preserves constants, and satisfies \(\gamma L_hw=w\) exactly. Its cell gradients vanish. Normalization \(\sum_f\rho_t(f)=1\) permits subtraction of a reference mean in (4.15)–(4.17), PDF p. 27. This cancellation is essential. Lemmas 4.1–4.3, PDF pp. 28–29, give \[\sum_fD_g\rho(f)\lesssim h/\delta_g.\] For faces separated by \(r\), the interior-overlap contribution in Lemma 4.2, PDF pp. 33–34, has the correct tail \(h\sum_{\delta\gtrsim r}\delta^{-d-1}\lesssim r^{-d}\). The symmetric-difference contribution has bounded multiplicity and the same pair weight. Near-grid-scale terms must be retained separately when using the integral comparison; its lower endpoint cannot be moved past contributing layers.

As a further exact check, if every face mean is zero, all cell and interior-face values produced by the lift vanish. Its energy then consists only of \(\sum_{f\subset\partial\Omega}h_t^{-1}\|w_f\|_{L^2(f)}^2\), controlled by the local trace term under mesh regularity. No boundary polynomial degree is lost.

For the global lifting, PDF pp. 40–44, averaged partition functions preserve the trace because \(\sum_i\pi_f^0\eta_i=1\). The cutoff differences are \(O(h_t)\), generating the bulk \(L^2\) term in (5.19). The local bulk estimate and global zero-mean boundary Poincaré inequality provide the stated control. This argument uses the full boundary seminorm, so the separate local-seminorm connectivity concern below does not itself refute the global lifting.
# Geometric and range corrections

Problem 1 (Minor: the height used in the cube proof).  Section 3.2, PDF pp. 9–10, considers a unit cube and places the horizontal path for a pair \(f,g\) at height \(r=|x_f-x_g|\). Section 3.3.2, PDF p. 12, requires cells containing its raised endpoints for every pair of side faces. For \(d\ge3\), these endpoints need not belong to the cube.

Take \(\Omega=(0,1)^3\) with a uniform \(4\times4\times4\) Cartesian mesh. On the bottom side choose \[x_f=(1/8,1/8,0),\qquad x_g=(7/8,7/8,0).\] This is regular and quasi-uniform, but \(r=3\sqrt2/4>1\). Both raised endpoints lie above the cube. The selected cells do not exist and the path-cell set (3.17) is empty. The decomposition on PDF p. 12 cannot be made as printed. The graph-following description on PDF p. 37 again uses the full horizontal distance as height.

A direct repair uses height \(\kappa r\) with \(\kappa=1/(2\sqrt{d-1})\), keeping every raised path below height \(1/2\). Vertical telescoping reaches layers \(m\le\kappa\ell+O(1)\); the Hardy estimate applies, with the bounded endpoint terms estimated separately. Horizontal shell and cone counts are unchanged because their projections are unchanged. Path cells now lie in layers \(|m-\kappa\ell|\le O(1)\). For fixed \(m\), only \(O(1+\kappa^{-1})\) shell indices contribute. The overlap remains bounded independently of \(h\), and the powers in the estimates are preserved. A revised proof should state the adjusted layer ranges and choose nested boundary charts with adequate vertical clearance.

This is an undefined intermediate construction, not a counterexample to the trace inequality. The repair changes dimension-dependent constants rather than the asserted order, supporting a Minor proof correction.

Problem 2 (Minor qualification: spaces without face values).  Remark 5.7, PDF pp. 44–45, embeds broken cell-polynomial spaces by assigning averaged interior traces and actual boundary traces. An embedding transfers a trace bound, but does not supply a right inverse onto the full product of independent boundary-face polynomials.

For a single square cell with degree-zero DG space, a scalar cell value \(c\) induces \((c,c,c,c)\). The independent face datum \((1,0,0,0)\) has no such lift. The hybrid construction’s independent boundary values cannot simply be interpreted as a DG function. This exact range obstruction occurs on a regular mesh.

A precise adaptation must specify the actual DG trace image as target and justify a lifting into the cell space with the appropriate energy estimate, or enrich the space if independent face data are intended. If the remark intends only that natural image, the example is outside its target. The issue is therefore a qualification of the adaptation, not a failure of the hybrid theorem. The mixed-degree argument on PDF p. 44 does work: the constructed cell and interior-face values are constants and the prescribed boundary polynomials retain their allowed degree.

A further domain convention should be explicit. Proposition 5.2, PDF pp. 38–40, joins any two boundary charts by a chain of nonempty boundary overlaps. This uses connectedness of the boundary-overlap graph. If polytopal domain includes a polygonal annulus, take \(\Omega=(-2,2)^2\setminus[-1,1]^2\), with charts each meeting only one boundary component. Data zero on the outer component and one on the inner component have every local seminorm zero, but \[T_h(w)=2\sum_{\substack{f\ \mathrm{outer}\\g\ \mathrm{inner}}}
              \frac{|f|\,|g|}{|x_f-x_g|^2}>0.\] The local-seminorm equivalence needs component-mean terms in this setting. If the intended convention for polytope excludes holes, the example is outside the intended class. The terminology alternates in the text, so this is a hypothesis clarification, not an adopted counterexample to the main theorems.
# An exact spectral check and the assessment

Section 6, PDF pp. 45–47, compares the boundary seminorm with the Schur complement of the bulk form after a rank-one kernel correction. A one-cell calculation checks its normalization independently of any experiment.

Let the cell be the unit square, \(k=0\), and label face values \(w_1,\ldots,w_4\) cyclically. As \(h_t=\sqrt2\) and each face has length one, \[E(v,w)=\frac1{\sqrt2}\sum_{i=1}^4(w_i-v)^2,\qquad
 v_{\min}=\frac14\sum_iw_i.\] Writing \(J=ee^T\), where \(e=(1,1,1,1)^T\), the Schur matrix is \[A_{\rm SC}=\frac1{\sqrt2}(I-J/4).\] Adjacent face centers have squared distance \(1/2\), opposite centers squared distance \(1\). Let \(L\) be the graph Laplacian with adjacent weights \(2\) and opposite weights \(1\). The ordered-pair trace matrix is \(H=2L\), with eigenvalues \(0,12,12,16\). For example, \(w=(1,-1,1,-1)\) has trace energy \(64\) and minimized bulk energy \(2\sqrt2\). The vector \((1,0,-1,0)\) gives \(24\) and \(\sqrt2\), respectively.

Here \(S=(1,1,1,1)\), so \(S^TS=J\). The generalized eigenvalues of \((A_{\rm SC}+J,H+J)\) are \[1,\qquad \frac1{12\sqrt2},\qquad
 \frac1{12\sqrt2},\qquad \frac1{16\sqrt2}.\] The constant mode gives \(1\), while the other modes have zero boundary mean. This supports the pair ordering, Schur construction, and kernel correction. It is a fixed-mesh check, not proof of an \(h\)-uniform bound.

Problem 3 (Minor: the printed local assembly formula).  On PDF p. 46 the local array is defined through differences \(\Delta_{ij}=\overline\phi_i^{\,f_l}-\overline\phi_j^{\,f_m}\) of scalar basis-function means and a contribution \(K\Delta^T\Delta\). This does not give the face-pair energy in (2.2) under its literal displayed interpretation.

For \(k=0\), choose the constant basis \(1\) on each unit-length face. Every basis mean equals one, hence every entry of \(\Delta\) is zero. The printed nonlocal contribution is zero, as is the local oscillation contribution. In contrast, the pair with coefficients \((c_l,c_m)=(1,0)\) has energy \(K(c_l-c_m)^2=K>0\).

Let \(a_l,a_m\) be the vectors of basis means on the two faces. The correct pair vector is the concatenation \(b=(a_l^T,-a_m^T)^T\), with pair matrix \(Kbb^T\). Its quadratic form is exactly \(K(a_l^Tc_l-a_m^Tc_m)^2\). For constants this gives \(K\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). The assembly must also retain the ordered-pair convention. An explicit embedding into the combined pair-coordinate space could clarify the intended notation. The theory does not depend on this paragraph, and the reported nondegenerate \(k=0\) spectra are counterevidence against assuming the program literally used the zero formula. No actual-code defect or incorrect reported spectrum is inferred.

Figure 8’s finite Cartesian-square spectra provide illustrations; they do not verify all dimensions and regular polytopal meshes. No discrepancy in the plotted values is claimed. The review supports the proposed seminorm and the inspected analytic mechanisms, with the concrete path-height repair and the specified trace-range and domain qualifications, and a correction to the printed pair-matrix formula. It does not establish degree-robust constants, a graded-mesh extension, or an independently reproduced numerical result. No supported Major defect in the main estimates was established.

Horizontal shell and cone counts are unchanged because their projections are unchanged. Path cells now lie in layers \(|m-\kappa\ell|\le O(1)\). For fixed \(m\), only \(O(1+\kappa^{-1})\) shell indices contribute. The overlap remains bounded independently of \(h\), and the powers in the estimates are preserved. analysis: Remark 5.7, PDF pp. 44–45, embeds broken cell-polynomial spaces by assigning averaged interior traces and actual boundary traces. An embedding transfers a trace bound, but does not supply a right inverse onto the full product of independent boundary-face polynomials.

For a single square cell with degree-zero DG space, a scalar cell value \(c\) induces \((c,c,c,c)\). The independent face datum \((1,0,0,0)\) has no such lift. A precise adaptation must specify the actual DG trace image as target and justify a lifting into the cell space with the appropriate energy estimate, or enrich the space if independent face data are intended. If the intended convention for polytope excludes holes, the example is outside the intended class. The terminology alternates in the text, so this is a hypothesis clarification, not an adopted counterexample to the main theorems.

report: Abstract: The slicing argument for bounded regular sets has the expected dimension, radius, and component-count structure. A finite counterexample nevertheless disproves the uniform dependence on the sub-Gaussian parameter in the polynomial-sketching corollary. Independent corrections concern rational-map domains, normalized slices, a zero-inequality endpoint, tubular radii, and several application formulas. The assessment is Major because the distributional counterexample invalidates an advertised dimension-reduction guarantee. It does not refute the deterministic covering theorem or the fixed-Gaussian case.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Covering numbers, regularity hypotheses, and the distributional scope of sketching
# Source, scope, and the deterministic result

This review concerns Y. Zhang and J. Kileel, Covering Number of Real Algebraic Varieties and Beyond: Improved Bounds and Applications, arXiv:2311.05116v4, 6 June 2025 [paper]. The associated journal DOI is 10.1007/s10208-025-09735-5. The acquired source is the 38-page preprint, not a verified copy of the journal-final text. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, which coincide with its printed numbering. All pages were read in text; the proofs, counterexamples, and source passages discussed below received targeted inspection. This is not a verification of every cited external theorem or every generalization claim.

Definition 2.1, p. 5, requires at most \(K\) path components in almost every affine slice of codimension at most \(n\), and empty slices almost everywhere above that codimension. Codimension zero therefore bounds the number of components of \(V\) itself. Theorem 2.6, p. 6, asserts, for a bounded regular set with \([V]_N\le t\) and \(0<\varepsilon\le\operatorname{diam}V\), \[\mathcal N(V,\varepsilon)
 \le 2K\left(\frac{2tnN^{3/2}}{\varepsilon}\right)^n
 \qquad (n\ge1).\] For \(n=0\), Lemma 2.3 gives the direct bound \(\mathcal N\le K\).

The proof on pp. 7–9 was checked at its essential transitions. The closure bar in Definition 2.12 matters: a type-I cut component is already a component of \(V\), since a path leaving it would first meet a slicing plane in its closure and in \(V\). A type-II component lies within one cell diameter of an appropriate slice point. Slice nets can consequently be enlarged by that diameter. The induction product satisfies \[\prod_{j=1}^{n}(N-n+j+1)\le \tfrac32N^n
 \quad(1\le n\le N,\ N\ge2),\] and the auxiliary dilation can be chosen close enough to one. The interval test and the scaling \(t/\varepsilon\) are consistent. These checks supply no counterexample to the principal covering estimate.

Appendix A, p. 31, should use a second Fubini step to obtain almost every translation and almost every slice direction; the printed simultaneous assertion for all good directions is stronger than the preceding step establishes. The almost-everywhere statement is sufficient for Lemma 2.2. No stronger all-direction claim is needed in the covering argument.
# Failure of a uniform sub-Gaussian sketching guarantee
Problem 1 (Major: Corollary 3.13(26)).  The sufficient row count on p. 19 is false uniformly over the sub-Gaussian ensembles permitted by Definition 3.6, p. 15.

The paper defines \(S=G/\sqrt m\), with independent, mean-zero, unit-variance entries of \(G\) having \(\psi_2\)-norm at most \(\alpha\). Its convention on p. 5 makes \(c\) an absolute constant. Set \[n=N=d=2,\qquad p(x)=x,\qquad
 \varepsilon=\delta=\tfrac12.\] The identity satisfies the degree-at-most-two assumption, and \(N'=\min\{N,n^d\}=2\). Equation (26) then claims sufficiency of \(m\ge C\alpha^2\), where \(C=28c\log2\).

For any proposed absolute \(c>0\), choose the finite number \(q=\exp(-8C-8)\). Let every entry of \(G\) be an independent copy of \[Z=\begin{cases}
 q^{-1/2},&\text{with probability }q/2,\\
 -q^{-1/2},&\text{with probability }q/2,\\
 0,&\text{with probability }1-q.
 \end{cases}\] Its mean is zero and its variance is one. For the Orlicz norm specified in footnote 9, \[\alpha^2=\frac{1}{q\log(1+1/q)},\qquad
 \mathbb E\exp(Z^2/\alpha^2)
   =1-q+q(1+1/q)=2.\] Thus this is an allowed ensemble, including the exact norm normalization. Put \(m=\lceil C\alpha^2\rceil\). The printed row-count condition holds.

Uniform norm preservation on \(p(\mathbb R^2)=\mathbb R^2\) requires a nonzero first column: if that column vanishes, \(Se_1=0\) although \(\|e_1\|=1\). The union bound gives \[\begin{split}
 \mathbb P(\text{success})
 &\le \mathbb P(\text{some entry of the first column is nonzero})\\
 &\le mq
 \le \frac{C}{\log(1+1/q)}+q
 <\tfrac18+e^{-8}<\tfrac12.
 \end{split}\] This contradicts the stated success probability \(1-\delta=1/2\). The calculation is exact and finite; it uses no simulation.

The affected dependency is the passage from the geometric covering/width bound to a uniform probabilistic embedding bound with the displayed ensemble dependence. This corollary is a substantive application of the paper, so a failure of its stated distributional scope warrants Major even though the deterministic core survives. For the sparse family above, merely avoiding an empty column at fixed confidence requires order \(q^{-1}\) rows, which has order \(\alpha^2\log\alpha\) as \(q\) decreases. This is a necessary obstruction, not a complete replacement theorem.

A correction must either restrict the ensemble or justify a sufficient dependence on its distributional parameter. The witness does not refute a fixed-Gaussian or uniformly bounded \(\alpha\) formulation, nor does it address the separate SORS claim. The final bound in Theorem 3.12(18), p. 18, retains a logarithmic \(\alpha\)-dependence, so its failure does not follow from this example.
# Regularity lemmas: signs, domains, and an endpoint
Problem 2 (Minor: squared normalized-slice equations).  In Lemma 2.15(c), pp. 10–11, the polynomial equations describe a larger set than the asserted preimage of an affine slice.

Take \(p(t)=(t,1)\) and \(L=\{y:y_1=1/\sqrt2\}\). The squared equation and the nonzero constraint admit \(t=1\) and \(t=-1\), both with \(w=1/2\), whereas \(\pi(p(-1))=(-1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)\notin L\). The same sign loss occurs in Lemma 2.16(c), p. 32.

The component bound is repairable without increasing the stated constant. On each path component of the larger algebraic set, \(\langle p(x),e_i\rangle/\|p(x)\|\) is continuous and takes values in \(\{\langle u,e_i\rangle,-\langle u,e_i\rangle\}\). It is therefore constant in each required sign. The unsquared preimage is a union of entire path components. Its component count is no greater than the POMT bound for the larger set. The false equality needs this replacement; the example does not disprove the normalized-image regularity conclusion.
Problem 3 (Minor: arbitrary open dense rational domains).  Lemma 2.17, p. 11 and p. 32, is false for all domains allowed by Definition 3.15, p. 21.

Let \(n=N=d=1\), \[U=\mathbb R\setminus\{1,\ldots,9\},\qquad f(x)=x/1\quad(x\in U).\] The domain is open dense and even Zariski open. The indicated ratio has degree at most one. But \(\operatorname{Im}f=U\) has ten path components, exceeding the asserted \(K=(2Nd+1)^{n+1}=9\) already in the codimension-zero slice.

The proof’s denominator equation becomes \(w=1\), so its algebraic set includes every real \(x\) and does not encode the extra deleted points. Requiring the full domain on which the displayed denominators are nonzero repairs that identification; alternatively, additional domain restrictions need their own complexity bounds. This counterexample concerns the lemma’s quantifier. It does not establish failure of a neural-network entropy bound: a restricted evaluation image may instead be covered through a suitable larger image. Such a replacement must be stated and justified.
Problem 4 (Minor: zero inequality constraints).  The minimum in Lemma 2.18, pp. 11 and 32–33, contains \((cb^2)^N\), although \(b=0\) is explicitly used for varieties.

For \(U=\{x:x^2=0\}\subset\mathbb R\), the number of inequality constraints is zero and \(U\) has one component. The displayed minimum is zero and hence gives \(K=0\), which is impossible. Use the POMT branch at \(b=0\) and restrict the \((cb^2)^N\) branch to \(b\ge1\), or replace \(b\) by \(\max\{1,b\}\) there with an appropriate constant. This corrects the endpoint and leaves the ordinary variety bound available.
# Radius and distortion corrections
Problem 5 (Minor: radius range in Corollary 2.19).  The tube-volume bound on p. 11 omits the range \(0<\varepsilon\le\operatorname{diam}V\) needed for the invoked covering estimate.

For \(V=[-1,1]\subset\mathbb R\) and \(K=n=N=t=1\), the tube has length \(2+2\varepsilon\), while the final printed right-hand side is the constant \(4c\). It cannot hold for all positive radii. The first inequality, obtained by covering the tube with balls of radius \(2\varepsilon\), remains valid.

One may retain the theorem’s radius range. For a nonempty set and \(n\ge1\), a valid all-radius form is \[\operatorname{Vol}(T(V,\varepsilon))
 \le \operatorname{Vol}(B^N)(2\varepsilon)^N
 \max\!\left\{1,\,
 2K\left(\frac{2tnN^{3/2}}{\varepsilon}\right)^n\right\}.\] For radii larger than the diameter, the one-point net proves the first branch. This repair does not challenge Theorem 2.6; it is also not, by itself, a counterexample to the separate probability statement of Corollary 2.20.
Problem 6 (Minor: a vanishing logarithmic complexity term).  There is a separate low-dimensional endpoint failure in Corollary 3.13(26), p. 19.

Set \(n=d=1\), \(N=2\), and \(p(x)=(x,1)\). Then \(N'=1\), so \(n\log(ndN')=0\). Fix \(\varepsilon=1/2\) and any fixed allowed ensemble parameter \(\alpha\). For any proposed constant \(c>0\), choosing \(\delta=\exp[-1/(8c\alpha^2)]\) makes the stated lower bound on \(m\) equal to \(1/2\), so \(m=1\) is allowed. Every row \(S=(a,b)\) nevertheless fails: if \(a\ne0\), take \(x=-b/a\); if \(a=0\), take \(|x|\) sufficiently large. The success probability is zero, contrary to \(1-\delta>0\).

A positive floor such as \(\log(2ndN')\), together with a rechecked dimension argument, removes this particular endpoint. It does not repair Problem 1. The proof’s assertion \(\binom{n+d}{d}=O(n^d)\) also needs a stated uniformity range: for \(n=1\) it compares \(d+1\) with \(1\). No full corrected SORS theorem is inferred here.
Problem 7 (Minor: reversed factors in Remark 3.9).  The displayed approximate-minimizer chain on p. 17 uses the distortion factors in the wrong direction.

In the branch where the sketched minimum exceeds \(\tau\), the valid chain is \[\|f(x)\|\ge
 \frac{\|Sf(x)\|}{1+\varepsilon}\ge
 \frac{\|Sf(x^*)\|}{1+\varepsilon}\ge
 \frac{1-\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon}\|f(x^*)\|.\] The printed chain instead ends with \((1+\varepsilon)(1-\varepsilon)^{-1}\|f(x^*)\|\); setting \(x=x^*\) contradicts it whenever the residual is positive. For example \(f\equiv1\), \(S=1\), and \(\tau<1\) already suffice. The intended near-optimality conclusion survives the corrected chain.
# Entropy notation and the remaining application checks
Problem 8 (Minor: the left side of Theorem 3.18).  Equations (34)–(35) and the intermediate proof display on p. 22 write \(\mathcal N\) where \(\log\mathcal N\) is required.

A literal covering-number interpretation is false. Take a one-layer fully connected network with \(d_0=d_L=2\), the fixed activation \(\rho(z)=z/(1+z^2)\), \(s=2\), \(t=1/2\), and a single sample \(X=0\). The six weights and biases are trainable. The two biases vary independently, so the evaluation image is exactly \([-1/2,1/2]^2\). Area comparison gives \(\mathcal N(\mathcal F(X),\varepsilon)\ge1/(\pi\varepsilon^2)\), whereas the displayed right side is \(6\log((1/2)/\varepsilon)\) plus a fixed constant. For sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\) the inequality fails. The logarithmic version agrees with Theorem 2.6 and with its explicit use in Corollary 3.19 on p. 23. This is a notation correction, not evidence against the intended entropy scaling.

The tensor construction on pp. 13–14 has degree \(d\) and \(r\sum_i n_i\) scalar parameters. In the improved low-rank case \(r\le\min_i n_i\), orthonormal factorization preserves the core norm; telescoping the Kronecker products gives the error allocation \(\varepsilon/2+d(\varepsilon/(2d))\). Lemma 3.3 should explicitly say orthonormal basis, as its proof on p. 33 and its use on p. 14 do. Without that normalization a basis vector of arbitrarily large length cannot satisfy the absolute bound. For example, for orthogonal lines \(E,F\), a basis vector \(2e_1\) of \(E\) has distance at least \(2>\sqrt2\) from every vector of \(F\), whereas the projection distance is one. This is an additional local hypothesis clarification; the actual tensor construction uses the needed normalized bases.

The degree calculation for rational networks in Appendix E, pp. 34–35, checks under its stated width and degree conditions. A preactivation has numerator degree at most \(d_i\theta+1\) and denominator degree at most \(d_i\theta\). Composition gives \(\Delta_{i+1}\le s(1+d_i\Delta_i)\); trainable activation coefficients add one. The convolutional count replaces \(d_i\) by \(c_i k^2\). The geometric-series factor two uses the explicit lower bounds in Lemma E.2.

For the ReLU application, pp. 24 and 35–38, the bounded input, layer norms, and Lipschitz loss are substantive hypotheses. The local error inequality \(\delta_i\le\varepsilon_i+\omega_i\delta_{i-1}\) follows when both preactivations lie in the prescribed approximation interval. This check is not a proof of every constant or of the external rational-approximation theorem.

The available source set did not establish the journal-final wording or provide an independently verified correction of these passages. External embedding and approximation results were not retrieved anew, and their full hypotheses were not independently certified. No author software was executed. The finite counterexamples above establish the stated local failures; they do not imply that all applications, all versions, or the paper’s principal deterministic contribution fail.

report: Abstract: The incidence-dimension method supports the principal transversality thresholds after the allowed sign or phase ambiguity is handled explicitly. The assertion that second-moment identifiability always makes growth faster than the fourth power of the noise level necessary is false: a nontrivial compact-group model satisfying the stated dimension conditions admits recovery from its first moment. An explicit estimator establishes the contradiction in mean square. This application-level failure supports a Major assessment. Several local proof, orbit, arithmetic, and citation corrections are also identified, without inferring failure of the main transversality conclusions.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Transversality, residual ambiguities, and the order of moments needed for recovery
# Source and the actual transversality statements

We review T. Bendory, N. Dym, D. Edidin, and A. Suresh, A Transversality Theorem for Semi-Algebraic Sets with Application to Signal Recovery from the Second Moment and Cryo-EM, Foundations of Computational Mathematics 26 (2026), 2765–2792, DOI 10.1007/s10208-025-09736-4 [paper]. The acquired 28-page publisher file states online publication on 29 September 2025. The review concerns these exact pages. PDF page \(p\) corresponds to journal page \(2764+p\). The complete text was read; the claims below received targeted proof or calculation checks. This does not certify every external dependency or every assertion in the paper.

Write \(D=\dim_{\mathbb R}V\), \(k(H)=\max_x\dim_{\mathbb R}Hx\), and \(K=D-k(H)\). Definition 2.1, PDF p. 5, makes genericity relative to the chosen transformation group and a fixed semi-algebraic prior. The exceptional transformations must have smaller dimension. Theorem 2.2, p. 6, uses \(K>M\) for generic points and \(K>2M\) for every point. Real linear transformations leave a permitted sign ambiguity; real affine transformations give equality. The orthogonal thresholds on p. 7 are \(K>M+2\) and \(K>2M+2\), improved by one for connected orbits.

The proof’s basic calculation, pp. 18–20, is \[\dim\mathcal B\le 2M+\dim\Gamma-\kappa,\] where \(\kappa\) is a lower bound on the codimension of each relevant collision fiber. If \(\kappa>2M\), projection excludes all bad collisions for generic transformations. If \(\kappa>M\), the generic fiber has dimension less than \(M\), so its projection excludes only a lower-dimensional set of prior points. The finite stratification argument provides the required generic-fiber statement. The relation defining relevant collisions needs the correction in Section 3.

The application caveat on p. 8 is substantive: a theorem about generic transformed priors is not a guarantee for a fixed sparsity basis, a particular learned subspace, or a particular trained network. The review retains this distinction.
# A counterexample to the claimed necessary sample growth

Problem 1 (Major: Corollary 4.3).  The conclusion on PDF pp. 16–17 that the minimal necessary sample growth is \(n/\sigma^4\to\infty\) does not follow from the stated second-moment identifiability conditions.

Use precisely the Gaussian-noise MRA model (4.5). Let \(G=SO(2)\) act on \[V=\mathbb R^2\oplus\mathbb R^2,\qquad
 g\cdot(z,w)=(z,R_\theta w).\] This is a nontrivial orthogonal representation of a compact group, with Haar-uniform rotations. The first block is two copies of the trivial representation, and the second is one standard two-dimensional representation. In the notation of (3.4), the block sizes are \((N_1,R_1)=(1,2)\) and \((N_2,R_2)=(2,1)\). Thus \(k=0+1=1\), \(D=4\), and \(K=3\).

Take a known affine-line prior \(\mathcal M=\{p+tu:t\in\mathbb R\}\). Its dimension is \(M=1\), so \(K>2M\), as required by the all-point affine branch of Corollary 3.1, p. 10. Write \(p_0,u_0\in\mathbb R^2\) for the fixed-coordinate components. The condition \(\det(p_0,u_0)\ne0\) is open and generic among affine lines. It implies \(u_0\ne0\).

Both the second moment and the first moment identify \(t\) on these lines. The fixed block of the noise-free second moment is \[(p_0+tu_0)(p_0+tu_0)^T.\] Equality at \(t_1,t_2\) implies \(p_0+t_1u_0=\pm(p_0+t_2u_0)\). The positive sign gives \(t_1=t_2\); the negative sign would make \(p_0,u_0\) dependent. Thus the example meets the actual identifiability conclusion, in addition to its dimension bound.

But the mean is already \((p_0+tu_0,0)\). With \(\overline y_0\) the sample mean of the first two coordinates, define \[\widehat t=\frac{u_0^T(\overline y_0-p_0)}{\|u_0\|^2},
 \qquad \widehat x=p+\widehat t\,u.\] The group action contributes no randomness in these coordinates. Independence and covariance \(\sigma^2 I\) give exactly \[\mathbb E(\widehat t-t)^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{n\|u_0\|^2},
 \qquad
 \mathbb E\|\widehat x-x\|^2
   =\frac{\|u\|^2\sigma^2}{n\|u_0\|^2}.\] Choose \(n=\lceil\sigma^3\rceil\). Recovery is consistent in mean square, although \(n/\sigma^4\to0\). For the concrete line \(x_t=(t,1,t,1)\), the error is \(2\sigma^2/n\). Genericity does not remove the obstruction, since the same argument holds whenever \(\det(p_0,u_0)\ne0\).

The failed dependency is the inference from a sufficient identifying moment to the lowest identifying moment. It affects an advertised information-theoretic application, hence the Major assessment. A corrected statement should give second-moment sufficiency, or impose and prove appropriate first-moment nonidentifiability and lower-bound hypotheses. This example does not refute deterministic transversality, Corollary 3.1, or the sufficiency wording of the cryo-EM Corollary 4.2. It is not a cryo-EM projection counterexample.
# Two repairs to the general proof framework
Problem 2 (Minor: the equivalence used in the fiber lemma).  The relation defined on PDF p. 18 is not always the sign or phase relation used later in the proof.

The definition is \[x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Gamma(x,y)=\Gamma,\qquad
 \Gamma(x,y)=\{\theta:\theta x\in H(\theta y)\}.\] For \(V=\mathbb R^2\), choose \[H=\{I,\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\},\quad
 \Gamma=GL_2(\mathbb R),\quad x=e_1,\quad y=-e_1.\] Here \(K=2\). A collision occurs exactly when the first column of the invertible matrix lies on \(\mathbb R e_1\). Consequently \(\dim\Gamma(x,y)=3\), whereas \(\dim\Gamma-K=2\). The pair is not equivalent under the given definition, since many first columns have two nonzero coordinates. The assertion on p. 21 that the parallel case is empty unless the pair is equivalent therefore does not establish the fiber-lemma hypothesis.

There is a direct repair appropriate to the theorem’s conclusion: define the bad incidence using \(y\ne\pm x\) for real linear and orthogonal transformations. Repeat the incidence argument with that invariant relation. In the complex linear and unitary cases, exclude \(y=\lambda x\), \(|\lambda|=1\). For affine transformations retain equality as the allowed relation. The counterexample above is precisely a pair the real theorem permits; it is not a counterexample to its conclusion.

The remaining column counts on pp. 21–25 check with these exclusions. Independent real vectors give collision codimension at least \(D-k(H)=K\) for \(GL(V)\); for \(O(D)\), the second-column sphere has dimension \(D-2\), giving \(K-2\). For a complex \(n\)-dimensional space, that sphere has real dimension \(2n-3\), giving \(K-3\). In the real affine opposite-vector case, the translation is unique; in the complex affine phase case, it has at most one real parameter. These yield the stated affine offsets.

The connected-orbit improvement can be seen without a special orthogonal-pair exception. Normalize a nonempty collision to \(\|x\|=\|y\|=1\), write \(y=ae_1+be_2\), and put \(w_1=Ae_1\). For independent vectors, \(|a|<1\). Orthogonality of the second column requires \(\operatorname{Re}\langle w_1,hw_1\rangle=\operatorname{Re}a\). At \(hw_1=w_1\) this fails. It therefore cuts a proper algebraic subset of the connected irreducible orbit, lowering dimension by at least one, as required.
Problem 3 (Minor: joint semi-algebraicity).  The pointwise action definition on p. 5 is insufficient for the joint semi-algebraic incidence asserted on pp. 18–19.

Let \(\Gamma=(\mathbb R,+)\) act by \(\theta\cdot(u,v)=(e^\theta u,v)\), let \(H\) consist of identity and coordinate interchange, and take \(\mathcal M=\{e_1\}\cup\{(0,t):t>0\}\). Each fixed-\(\theta\) action is an invertible linear semi-algebraic map, but its collision branch between \(e_1\) and \((0,t)\) is \(t=e^\theta\), which is not semi-algebraic. Requiring the joint map \(\Gamma\times V\to V\) to be semi-algebraic repairs this issue. The actual linear, affine, orthogonal, and unitary actions already satisfy that requirement.
# Orbit dimensions and the cryo-EM formulas

Problem 4 (Minor: connected orbits require a rank condition).  The sentence after (3.4), PDF p. 10, asserts that the orthogonal-product orbits are connected exactly when all irreducible dimensions exceed one. This ignores multiplicity.

For an \(N\times R\) matrix of rank \(r\), the orbit under left multiplication is \(O(N)/O(N-r)\). When \(r<N\), the stabilizer contains a determinant-negative element and the orbit is connected. When \(r=N\), the stabilizer is trivial and the orbit has the two components of \(O(N)\). In particular, \(N=R=2\), \(X=I_2\) gives the disconnected orbit \(O(2)\), although \(N>1\). All orbits in a nonzero block are connected precisely when \(R<N\). For products, apply the condition to every block.

The correction does not invalidate the displayed bounds of Corollary 3.1: that corollary uses the conservative orthogonal offset \(+2\), not the connected-orbit improvement. Products of unitary groups in the complex application are connected, so the real example does not contradict Corollary 7.3.

The stabilizer dimension in (3.4) itself checks. At maximal rank \(r=\min(N,R)\), \[k=\frac{N(N-1)}2-\frac{(N-r)(N-r-1)}2,\qquad
 K=\begin{cases}
 R(R+1)/2,&R\le N,\\
 NR-N(N-1)/2,&R\ge N.
 \end{cases}\] For real Fourier phase retrieval, p. 12, this gives \(K=\lfloor N/2\rfloor+1\). The integer thresholds \(N\ge2M\), \(N\ge4M\), \(N\ge2M+4\), and \(N\ge4M+4\) imply their respective strict inequalities.
Problem 5 (Minor: two displayed cryo-EM simplifications).  The approximation in Theorem 4.1, PDF p. 14, has the wrong sign, and the numerator of (4.4), p. 15, contains an extra factor \(L+1\).

For \(R\ge2L+1\), the exact dimension formula on p. 14 is \[D=R(L+1)^2,\quad
 k=\sum_{\ell=0}^L\binom{2\ell+1}{2}
   =\frac{L(L+1)(4L+5)}6,\quad K=D-k.\] Thus the leading expression is \(L^2(R-2L/3)\); the printed approximation uses a plus sign. The correct ratio is \[\frac KD=
 \frac{R(L+1)^2-L(L+1)(4L+5)/6}{R(L+1)^2}.\] In (4.4), the subtracted term is instead printed as \((L+1)\bigl((L+1)L(4L+5)/6\bigr)\). For \(L=1,R=3\), the exact values are \(D=12,k=3,K=9\), so \(K/D=3/4\); the printed numerator gives \(1/2\).

The exact formula in Theorem 4.1 is correct. It gives \(K/D\to2/3\) when \(R\sim2L\), agreeing with the stated limiting interpretation on p. 15. The resulting generic-point and all-point prior-dimension fractions are \(2/3\) and \(1/3\), subject to the strict inequalities. These independent checks support a local correction of the two displays, not a failure of the exact cryo-EM threshold.
# Sharpness illustration, references, and limits
Problem 6 (Minor: singular parameters in the parabola example).  The numerical witness on PDF p. 8 does not belong to the claimed group \(GL_2\).
For \(ax+by-(cx+dy)^2=0\), the selected coefficients \((1,2,2,4)\) have \(ad-bc=0\). The equation is \((x+2y)-4(x+2y)^2=0\), the union of two parallel lines.

A nonsingular witness is \((a,b,c,d)=(1,5/2,1,1)\), with determinant \(-3/2\). Its parabola contains both \((1,1/2)\) and \((-1,1/2)\). For nonzero \(c,d\), symmetric intersections satisfy \[y=\frac{a}{2cd},\qquad
 x^2=\frac{by-d^2y^2}{c^2}.\] At the corrected coefficients \(y=1/2\) and \(x^2=1>0\); nonzero determinant and strict positivity persist on an open neighborhood. Thus the intended positive-measure sharpness argument survives.
Problem 7 (Minor: citation-to-reference bindings).  Several central body references do not identify their intended sources in the acquired publication.

The following are literal comparisons with the printed bibliography, PDF pp. 26–28. On p. 4 the named Kleiman paper is cited as source reference [17], but [17] is Kam’s electron-micrograph reconstruction paper; the exact named Kleiman title occurs as [36]. On p. 20, Nash stratification and semi-algebraic Sard are cited as [57, Proposition 2.9.10] and [57, Theorem 9.6.2], whereas [57] is Tu’s Manifolds chapter. The pre-image theorem is cited there as [58, Theorem 9.9], but [58] is a paper on sparse multi-reference alignment. The moment-order assertion on pp. 13 and 16 cites [40], which is Deng et al.’s Learning to synthesize: robust phase retrieval at low photon counts.

The acquired publisher HTML reproduces the latter number-to-title bindings, including the proof anchors [57] and [58]. The bibliography contains Bochnak–Coste–Roy’s Real algebraic geometry as [38], but this observation does not verify any replacement theorem locator. The references and links need a systematic correction. These binding failures impede checking proof dependencies; they alone do not establish that the underlying mathematical results are false. The external works were not retrieved or read here.

Finally, the cryo-EM model uses a finite-dimensional truncation, uniform rotations, the stated radial multiplicities, and Gaussian noise. The footnote on p. 14 expressly excludes nonuniform viewing distributions. The discussion on pp. 15–16 does not prove identification of a distribution of continuously varying conformations. Likewise, moment injectivity by itself provides no uniform conditioning constant or reconstruction algorithm.

The permutation application on pp. 17–18 has finite ambiguity group and the consistent count \(nd>2M\). Its warning that arbitrary affine changes need not preserve permutation structure is necessary and is retained. No author code was executed, and no later correction of the acquired source was established. The reported Major finding is the explicit statistical necessity counterexample in Section 2; the other corrections have the narrower scopes proved above.

result: Impact. Dependency: Advertised information-theoretic application infers lowest identifying moment from a merely sufficient moment.
Impact. Scope: Major applies to unconditional necessity/minimality in Cor4.3, not whole-paper failure.
