Title: Scientific review of
A determinantal point process approach to scaling and local limits of random Young tableaux
# Scope and assessment

The examined source is the author-hosted journal-form PDF of J. Borga, C. Boutillier, V. Féray and P.-L. Méliot, Annals of Probability 53 (2025), 299–354, DOI `10.1214/24-AOP1706`. Page references below use the printed journal pagination. All 56 physical pages were read; this does not constitute independent verification of every contour estimate or of the cited external theorems.

The principal finding concerns the treatment of the time endpoints in the local limit theorem and in the proof of the height formula. An exact square tableau calculation contradicts the empty-process conclusion at these endpoints. It also disproves the uniform kernel convergence used to exchange limit and integral in the proof of Theorem 5. This is a Major issue in a derivation of a central result. The calculation does not disprove the height formula or the bulk local limit. Two separate Minor issues concern Proposition 22 and the parameter boundary in Proposition 11.
# Problem 1: endpoint behavior and the proof of Theorem 5

Theorem 16, p. 312, allows \(t_0\in[0,1]\) and asserts convergence to the empty process whenever \((x_0,t_0)\) is outside the liquid region. Propositions 37 and 40, pp. 345–346, explicitly retain the time endpoints. The omitted cases described there include precisely \(x_0=0,t_0=0\) and \(x_0=\eta b_i,t_0=1\).
## An admissible counterexample

Take \(\lambda^0=(1)\). Its \(n\)-fold dilation is an \(n\times n\) square with \(N=n^2\), \(\eta=1\), and interlacing coordinates \(a_0=-1,b_1=0,a_1=1\). Put \(x_0=0,t_0=1\); the arithmetic condition \(x_0\sqrt{|\lambda^0|}\in\mathbb Z\) is satisfied. Equation (8) becomes \[U(x_0+U)=(1-t_0)((x_0+U)^2-1),\qquad U^2=0.\] Thus this point is frozen according to Definition 4, p. 304.

Equation reference: eq:max, eq:nonempty. Let \(V_N\) be the value in the bottom-right box. This is the largest of all \(N\) entries and its Russian horizontal coordinate is zero. The uniform Poissonized law is normalized Lebesgue measure on the order polytope, by the definition on p. 302. Dilating every coordinate by \(s\) maps this polytope onto its subset with all entries at most \(s\). Consequently, exactly, \[
 \mathbb P(V_N\le s)=s^{N},\qquad 0\le s\le1.\] Its bead in the process (22) is at \((0,n(V_N-1))\). For the bounded set \(B=\{0\}\times[-1,0]\), \[
 \mathbb P\bigl(\widetilde M_{\lambda^N}^{(0,1)}(B)\ge1\bigr)
 \ \ge\ 1-(1-1/n)^{n^2}\ \longrightarrow\ 1 .\] Every bounded Borel set is a continuity set for the zero measure. Hence [eq:nonempty] (#eq:nonempty) contradicts convergence in probability to the empty process in the topology of Section 2.2. Equivalently, a continuous function equal to one near \((0,0)\), with bounded support, detects this bead with probability tending to one. There is no endpoint-of-the-test-set ambiguity.

The minimum entry \(W_N\), in the top-left box on thread zero, satisfies \(\mathbb P(W_N>s)=(1-s)^{n^2}\). Thus \(nW_N\to0\) in probability and gives the same contradiction at \((x_0,t_0)=(0,0)\). These examples use the specified Poissonized law, rather than replacing it with deterministic standard-tableau values.
## Failure of the asserted uniform convergence
## Correction and limits of the finding

Restricting the local-limit statement to \(0<t_0<1\) removes the two counterexamples above; any endpoint theorem needs a separate analysis. For example, [eq:max] (#eq:max) gives \(N(1-V_N)\Rightarrow\operatorname{Exp}(1)\), which differs from the paper’s \(\sqrt N\) local scale. This observation identifies one extreme entry, not an entire endpoint point-process limit.

The height formula requires a justified endpoint and critical-time argument in place of the uniformity assertion. A suitable route is to work first away from exceptional times and then control their contribution through the limiting cumulative height or a uniform integrability estimate. The general version of that replacement is not proved here.

There is substantial counterevidence against interpreting the calculation as failure of the height formula: the maximum bead contributes only \(1/n\) to normalized total height, and the proposed square density is integrable, with \[\int_0^t f(s)\,ds=\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\sqrt t,\qquad
 \int_0^1 f(s)\,ds=1.\] The error is nevertheless more than an isolated boundary value in a statement: the false uniformity premise is used in deriving Theorem 5, one of the paper’s stated main contributions (pp. 301, 304). The assessment Major concerns that verified invalid derivation. It does not assert failure of a corrected theorem, of the liquid-region analysis, or of the continuity criterion.
# Problem 2: a countable-event extension of weak convergence

Proposition 22, p. 320, extends convergence of probabilities from cylinder events based on bounded continuity sets to arbitrary countable unions, intersections and complements of such events. This extension is false even for deterministic finite counting measures.

On \(\mathcal X=\mathbb Z	imes\mathbb R\), let \[
u_n=\delta_{(0,1/n)},\qquad 
u=\delta_{(0,0)},\qquad
 B_k=\{0\}	imes(1/k,2),\quad k\ge1 .\] For every bounded continuous test function, its values at \((0,1/n)\) converge to its value at \((0,0)\); hence \(
u_n	o
u\) in the topology defined immediately above the proposition. Each \(B_k\) is bounded and \(
u(\partial B_k)=0\). However, for \[A= igcup_{k\ge1}\{\mu:\mu(B_k)=1\},\] one has \(\mathbb P(
u_n\in A)=1\) for every \(n\), by choosing \(k>n\), whereas \(\mathbb P(
u\in A)=0\).

The finite-dimensional assertions (36)–(37) do not imply setwise convergence on their generated sigma-algebra. A correct replacement uses finite Boolean combinations of the stated cylinder events, or events whose boundary has probability zero under the limiting law. This is Minor: the claim itself is disproved, but no necessary use of its false countable extension was found in the main argument. In particular, the proof of Corollary 19 on pp. 352–353 uses a Skorohod coupling, a finite random height cutoff, and eventual agreement of finite restrictions. That argument is not refuted by this example.
# Problem 3: degenerate shapes in Proposition 11

Thus either the stated domain includes an object for which its proposed strict-coordinate definition fails, or, with the natural degenerate-shape interpretation, the stated continuity characterization is false there. The local correction is to impose \(q<\min(p+2,2r-p)\) for genuine \(L\)-shapes and handle the rectangular boundary separately. This is Minor; it does not challenge the criterion for strictly interlacing nondegenerate shapes.
# Other checks and remaining scope

The diagonal of the bead kernel (21), p. 311, is \(\alpha/\pi\), consistent with the factor in Theorem 5. The terminology intensity \(\alpha\) does not establish a missing factor of \(\pi\). For a direct check of Proposition 20, write the critical equation as \(1-t=U G(x+U)\). Implicit differentiation gives \[U_t=-\frac1{G+UG'},\qquad U_x=-\frac{UG'}{G+UG'},
 \qquad U_t+\frac{U(U_x+1)}{1-t}=0,\] at the simple liquid root. This agrees with the stated equation and its proof on p. 331.

The later height PDE is expressly presented with an informal ingredient on p. 314; it has not been treated as a fully proved theorem. The review follows the contour argument and its dependence on the critical roots, but does not certify all uniform estimates or reprove the external existence and limit-shape inputs. None of the findings depends on absent code, numerical simulation, or an assumption that the acquired journal PDF is identical to an arXiv revision.
# Scope and references

This is the initial review of M25-0488. Scientific adjudication remains pending; independent acceptance has not been performed. The retained source manifest binds the exact 56-page journal-form PDF. The arXiv record and an author’s publication list were consulted for version and correction context; the bounded search identified no specific correction attached to this item, which is not a claim that none exists.

The accompanying coverage and findings files give the precise reading scope, source locators and limitations. Independent calculations retain the square discriminant, exact order-polytope probabilities, positive finite bounds supporting [eq:gap] (#eq:gap), the counting-measure example, the cancelled corner, and the implicit-differentiation identity. No author code was executed. Compiler, dependency, source, PDF parsing, rendering and actual page-view records are retained separately. Rendering alone is not counted as inspection.

Probab. 53 (2025), 299–354. https://doi.org/10.1214/24-AOP1706. The authors, arXiv record 2307.11885, including version history, https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.11885, consulted 29 October 2026. Title: Initial review of a stochastic differential equation
for local times of super-Brownian motion
# Scope and assessment

The principal source is Le Gall and Perkins [LP], arXiv:2309.06899v1 (13 September 2023), an acquired 32-page preprint. Its complete text was read. The additional 36-page journal PDF [LPj], obtained from the second author’s publication site, was compared at selected locations: the main theorem, the drift-constant computation, the end of the SDE proof, and the diffusion reconstruction. It was not reviewed in its entirety. Page references without a journal designation refer to the preprint.

No substantive mathematical defect was established in the checked arguments. In particular, the factors \(4\) and \(8\) in the SDE, the conditioning on one half of the local-time derivative, the localization at positive local time, and the final diffusion’s invariant density are mutually consistent. Two local display corrections are explained below; neither supplies evidence of a failed core derivation. This assessment does not certify the external excursion-theoretic inputs or every probabilistic detail of the paper.
# The statement and its boundary conditions

The normalization in Section 3, p. 11, is branching mechanism \(2u^2\) with initial measure \(\alpha\delta_0\), \(\alpha>0\). At the origin the derivative means the right derivative; the jump between right and left derivatives is \(-2\alpha\). Theorem 1, p. 2, asserts \[\begin{aligned}
 d\dot L^x&=4\sqrt{L^x}\,dB_x+
       g(L^x,\dot L^x/2)\,dx,& dL^x&=\dot L^x\,dx,\\
 g(t,y)&=8t\,\frac{p_t'(y)}{p_t(y)},&&t>0,\end{aligned}\] with \(g(0,y)=0\). Here \(p_t\) is the density of the spectrally positive \(3/2\)-stable process whose Laplace exponent is \(\sqrt{2/3}\lambda^{3/2}\). Uniqueness is asserted for solutions absorbed at \(R=\inf\{x\geq0:L^x=0\}\), with the given initial pair. It is not a claim of unrestricted uniqueness for every continuation from the degenerate boundary. The possible enlargement of the probability space to supply Brownian motion after \(R\) is explicit.

Theorem 2, p. 3, is stated under the probability measure obtained from the canonical excursion measure by conditioning on \(\ell^0>\delta\). This conditioning must be retained. The statement is not, by itself, an SDE theorem for a tree conditioned to have total volume one.

The Lévy measure coefficient is \(c_1=\sqrt{3/(8\pi)}\); indeed \(c_1\Gamma(-3/2)=\sqrt{2/3}\). The sign-function martingale representation on p. 13 gives quadratic variation \(16\int L^x\,dx\), as stated in Proposition 11 on p. 14. Its square root is the noise coefficient \(4\sqrt L\). The moment argument uses \(q<4/3\), not the endpoint: the occupation estimate requires \(q/2<2/3\). These restrictions agree with the estimates used for stopped increments.
# An explicit verification of the drift constant

Equation reference: eq:constant. The constant calculation left to the reader in Lemma 16, p. 24 (journal p. 382), is a decisive normalization check. Write \[\chi(u)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}(u^{3/2}+u^{1/2})
       -2u(u+3/2)e^u\operatorname{erfc}(\sqrt u),\qquad
 \gamma(u)=-\frac83\sqrt\pi\,u^{3/2}(\chi(u)+u\chi'(u)).\] The required identity is \[
 c_1\int_0^\infty
       \left(2-\gamma(3z/2)\right)\frac{dz}{\sqrt z}=8.\] It can be checked without numerical quadrature. Set \[E(v)=e^{v^2}\operatorname{erfc}(v),\quad
 P(v)=-2v^6+3v^4-6v^2+6,\quad
 Q(v)=2v^5-4v^3+12v .\] Using \(E'(v)=2vE(v)-2/\sqrt\pi\), direct differentiation gives \[\int_0^{v^2}u\chi(u)\,du
       =P(v)E(v)+Q(v)/\sqrt\pi-6.\] The erfc expansion displayed on p. 18 implies \[P(v)E(v)+Q(v)/\sqrt\pi=3v/\sqrt\pi+O(v^{-1}),\qquad
 \chi(R)=\frac{3}{2\sqrt\pi}R^{-3/2}+O(R^{-5/2}).\] Integration by parts therefore yields \[\begin{aligned}
 \int_0^R(2-\gamma(u))\frac{du}{\sqrt u}
 &=4\sqrt R+\frac83\sqrt\pi
       \left(R^2\chi(R)-\int_0^R u\chi(u)\,du\right)\\
 &\longrightarrow16\sqrt\pi .\end{aligned}\] The endpoint bounds on pp. 18–19 justify convergence. Changing variables \(z=2u/3\) in [eq:constant] (#eq:constant) multiplies this limit by \(c_1\sqrt{2/3}=1/(2\sqrt\pi)\), proving the value \(8\). An independently written symbolic check verifies the antiderivative, the cancellations, and the excursion-mean derivative in Proposition 13; it does not execute author code.

The compact-uniform limit in Lemma 16 is also consistent with its stated domain \(1/K\leq t\leq K\), \(|y|\leq K\). On this set \(p_t(y)\) has a positive lower bound and its first two derivatives have uniform bounds. The integrable majorant involving \(|2-\gamma(3z/2)|/\sqrt z\) then applies. No uniform assertion down to \(t=0\) is needed.
# Conditional expectations, stopping, and reconstruction

Proposition 14, pp. 19–20, handles the signed sum of excursion derivatives by truncation. It does not replace integrability of that signed sum by an unproved assertion that the sum of absolute derivatives is integrable. On the events \(H_n\), only the specified finitely many large excursions can contribute at the level in question. Conditional independence, the moment bound of Lemma 12, and the separate integrable bound on \(\sum_j Z_j|\gamma(3Z_j/(2h^2))|\) justify the two limiting expectations. This is relevant counterevidence to a possible objection based solely on exchanging an infinite signed sum.

In Section 6 the first localization keeps \(L\) bounded away from zero and both coordinates bounded. The finite drift limit at the boundary is obtained only afterwards. Lemma 17, p. 25, bounds its negative part by \(8C(L^x)^{1/3}\) on a finite interval; the stopped SDE on p. 28 then forces the positive part to have finite integral as well. The resulting absolute integrability is stronger than merely assigning a formal value to a divergent signed integral. Local Lipschitz coefficients on \(L>0\), followed by the stated absorption condition, give the claimed uniqueness.

For Proposition 18, pp. 29–30, put \(Z=\dot L L^{-2/3}\) before \(R\) and use the inverse clock of \(\int_0^x(L^y)^{-1/3}dy\). Itô’s formula gives noise \(4L^{-1/6}dB\) and drift \(L^{-1/3}b(Z)\,dx\), where \[b(z)=8\frac{p_1'(z/2)}{p_1(z/2)}-\frac23z^2.\] The time-changed noise coefficient is consequently \(4\). The proposed density \[\rho(z)=C\,p_1(z/2)^2 e^{-z^3/36}\] satisfies \((\log\rho)'=b/8\), the stationary zero-current identity for generator \(8\partial_z^2+b\partial_z\). The tail formulas on p. 30 are integrable at both ends, while the scale function has unbounded range in both directions.

There is also a useful check on the reconstruction in Proposition 19. With \(u=z/(2\,6^{1/3})\), the Airy representation on p. 2 reduces the stationary weight, up to a positive constant, to \(w(u)=(u\operatorname{Ai}(u^2)+\operatorname{Ai}'(u^2))^2\). For \(u>0\), \[w(u)-w(-u)=4u\operatorname{Ai}(u^2)\operatorname{Ai}'(u^2)<0 .\] Thus the stationary mean of \(Z\) is negative. Together with the finite moments furnished by the displayed tails, this supports the exponential decay of the reconstructed local time and finiteness of its inverse clock. This check is not a substitute for every boundary-continuity step in Proposition 19; that short final reconstruction argument has not been independently expanded into a complete proof here.
# Local display corrections and their limits

In the introduction on p. 3 the excursion-derivative argument is printed as \(3h/(2z^2)\). Proposition 13, equation (33), p. 17, uses \(3z/(2h^2)\), which is the expression obtained by differentiating equation (32) and is used in Proposition 14. The working proof therefore already contains the correct expression.

In the Brownian construction on p. 28, for \(0<\varepsilon'<\varepsilon\), one has \(S_{\varepsilon'}\geq S_\varepsilon\). The displayed variance should be \(\mathbb E[S_{\varepsilon'}\wedge t-S_\varepsilon\wedge t]\); the printed subtraction has the reverse order. The corrected nonnegative expression still tends to zero by bounded convergence and gives the asserted Cauchy property. These are local formula corrections with identified surviving applications, not demonstrated failures of the main theorem. No claim is made here that their status is identical in every version.
# Conclusion

The inspected argument has coherent normalizations and an appropriate absorbed-solution range. The drift constant and diffusion identities have independent analytic support. No substantive issue is assigned. The excursion disintegration and cited foundational results remain external inputs; reading the preprint is not a certification of those sources. The limited journal comparison confirms the inspected core formulas, but does not establish complete version equivalence.

Title: Initial review of branching random walks
on relatively hyperbolic groups
# Scope and assessment

The source reviewed is Dussaule, Wang and Yang [DWY], arXiv:2211.07213v1 (14 November 2022), comprising 50 pages. Its complete text was read. The journal publication has a different pagination, 391–452, and its full text was not obtained through the checked routes. The assessment below concerns the acquired preprint; it does not establish that the same issue persists in the journal version. All page references below are to physical pages of that preprint, which agree with its printed numbering.

One major proof issue is established. On p. 31, the proof of Proposition 5.1 passes from weak convergence of random finite measures to convergence of their quadratic energy integrals. The topology defined in Appendix A controls expectations of linear integrals, and does not imply the asserted convergence of the self-products. A counterexample below satisfies the bounded-mass, tightness, boundary support and uniform energy properties relevant to that inference. This is a defect in a derivation central to the Hausdorff dimension lower bound. It is not a counterexample to the dimension formula itself.

The theorem’s hypotheses must be retained. The group is non-elementary and relatively hyperbolic; the step distribution is symmetric, admissible and finitely supported. The offspring law is on \(\{1,2,\ldots\}\) and has mean \(r\in[1,R]\), where \(R\) is the Green function’s convergence radius. The Bowditch metric assertion uses the specified shortcut metrics with \(\lambda\) sufficiently close to one. The upper bound for the entire Floyd limit set has the additional qualifications in Remark 1.3; the general upper-bound argument concerns its conical part. Neither extinction conditioning nor a theorem for an arbitrary boundary metric should be added to these statements.
# Problem 1: the energy limit in Proposition 5.1
## The precise inference

Equation reference: eq:linear. On p. 29, equation (19) defines \[\chi_n=\frac{\mathbf1_{B_n}}{\mathbb EM_{n,L}}
              \sum_{x\in\mathcal P_{n,L}}D(x),
 \qquad
 B_n=\{\tfrac12\mathbb EM_{n,L}\leq M_{n,L}\leq C\mathbb EM_{n,L}\}.\] In particular, the random mass is bounded by \(C\). Corollary A.23, p. 47, is invoked to obtain a convergent subnet. Definitions A.7 and A.12, pp. 41–42, mean that this convergence is \[
 \mathbb E\int f(x,\omega)\,d\chi_{\alpha,\omega}(x)
 \longrightarrow
 \mathbb E\int f(x,\omega)\,d\chi_\omega(x)\] for each fixed bounded random continuous function \(f\). The argument on p. 30 places the limiting measure on the random boundary limit set.

Equation reference: eq:invalid. The first display after the uniform energy estimate on p. 31 asserts, for each \(\kappa\geq0\), that \[
 \mathbb E\iint K_\kappa(x,y)\,d\chi_\alpha(x)d\chi_\alpha(y)
 \longrightarrow
 \mathbb E\iint K_\kappa(x,y)\,d\chi(x)d\chi(y),
 \qquad K_\kappa=\kappa\wedge\widehat\delta_e^{-h}.\] Both measures in each double integral belong to the same outcome \(\omega\). Bounded continuity of \(K_\kappa\) on \(X\times X\) does not turn this expression into a fixed linear test in [eq:linear] (#eq:linear). The subsequent passage to finite limiting energy uses [eq:invalid] (#eq:invalid). Appendix A contains no additional convergence statement for these self-products.
## A bounded counterexample in a tree compactification

Let \(X\) be the Floyd compactification of the Cayley tree of the free group on generators \(a,b\), with edge length \(\lambda^j\) at depth \(j\), and take \(\lambda=3/4\). Let \(\eta_n\) be the uniform probability measure on the \(2^n\) positive words in \(a,b\) of length \(n\), and let \(\eta\) be the fair Bernoulli measure on infinite positive words. Prefix coupling gives \(\eta_n\Rightarrow\eta\): the distance from a depth-\(n\) prefix to its infinite continuation is at most \(\lambda^n/(1-\lambda)\).

Equation reference: eq:example. On a product probability space let \(Z_1,Z_2,\ldots\) be independent Bernoulli variables with parameter \(1/2\), and set \[
 \chi_n=2Z_n\eta_n,\qquad \chi=\eta .\] Then \(\chi_n(X)\leq2\), \(\mathbb E\chi_n(X)=1\), and \(\pi_\Omega(\chi_n)\leq2\mathbb P\). Tightness is automatic on compact \(X\). The vertices are isolated, the supports escape each finite set of vertices, and \(\chi\) is a nonzero measure on the boundary. Thus the compactness and limiting-support properties used in the argument are present.

We check convergence in the full topology of Definition A.12, not merely against deterministic tests. For a bounded random continuous \(f\), put \(A_n(\omega)=\int f(x,\omega)d\eta_n(x)\) and \(A(\omega)=\int f(x,\omega)d\eta(x)\). Pointwise continuity and boundedness imply \(A_n\to A\) in \(L^1\). Let \(\mathcal F_m=\sigma(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)\). For \(n>m\), independence gives \[\mathbb E[(2Z_n-1)\mathbb E(A\mid\mathcal F_m)]=0,\] and hence \[\left|\mathbb E\int f\,d\chi_n-\mathbb E\int f\,d\chi\right|
 \leq2\mathbb E|A_n-A|+\mathbb E|A-\mathbb E(A\mid\mathcal F_m)|.\] First let \(n\to\infty\), then \(m\to\infty\). The martingale convergence theorem proves [eq:linear] (#eq:linear).

Equation reference: eq:contradiction. Use precisely the diagonal modification made on p. 30: \(\widehat\delta(x,x)=\lambda^{|x|}\) at a vertex, and zero on the boundary diagonal; elsewhere use the Floyd distance. All distances are at most \(2/(1-\lambda)=8\). With \(h=1\) and \(\kappa=1/8\), the bounded continuous kernel is therefore constant, \(K_\kappa\equiv1/8\), including on the boundary diagonal where the truncated infinite inverse distance is \(\kappa\). Consequently, \[
 \mathbb E\iint K_\kappa\,d\chi_n\,d\chi_n
   =\frac18\mathbb E(2Z_n)^2=\frac14,\qquad
 \mathbb E\iint K_\kappa\,d\chi\,d\chi=\frac18.\] The whole sequence converges in the prescribed topology, so choosing a subnet does not remedy this discrepancy.

The example even has uniformly bounded untruncated energy. For distinct depth-\(n\) positive words with common-prefix length \(k<n\), their distance is \(2\sum_{j=k}^{n-1}\lambda^j\). The common-prefix distribution for two independent words is \(2^{-k-1}\), with equality probability \(2^{-n}\). Thus \[I_1(\eta_n)
 = (2\lambda)^{-n}
   +\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}
       \frac{2^{-k-1}}{2\sum_{j=k}^{n-1}\lambda^j}.\] Writing \(t=(2\lambda)^{-1}=2/3\) gives \[I_1(\eta_n)\leq t^n+\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}t^k\leq\frac74,
 \qquad
 \mathbb EI_1(\chi_n)=2I_1(\eta_n)\leq\frac72.\] On the boundary the distance for common-prefix length \(k\) is \(2\lambda^k/(1-\lambda)\), and \[I_1(\eta)=\frac{1-\lambda}{4}\sum_{k=0}^\infty t^k
          =\frac3{16}.\] The same geometric domination yields \(\mathbb EI_1(\chi_n)\to3/8\), whereas \(I_1(\chi)=3/16\). Uniform integrability cannot repair the asserted equality: even the constant bounded kernel in [eq:contradiction] (#eq:contradiction) already fails.

At the level of the measure construction, one may set \(N_n=2^n Z_n\), with \(\mathbb EN_n=2^{n-1}\). Then \(\{\mathbb EN_n/2\leq N_n\leq2\mathbb EN_n\}=\{Z_n=1\}\), and normalizing the selected counting measure as in equation (19) gives [eq:example] (#eq:example). These selected sets are not claimed to be traces of a branching random walk. Their role is to refute the topological implication used in the proof, even with its stated mass and energy bounds.
## Consequence and limits

The issue is major because the disputed step supplies the finite-energy measure needed for Proposition 5.1, not an auxiliary estimate without a later use. The same measure-limit argument is used for Proposition 5.2 on p. 33. Proposition 5.1 supplies the lower bound in Theorem 1.2 and the subsequent hyperbolic specialization, Corollary 1.5; Proposition 5.2 supplies the lower bound for Theorem 1.4.

The counterexample does not refute the compactness conclusion, the support argument, the prelimit energy bound, or the Hausdorff dimension statements. Its limiting measure actually has finite energy. A suitable one-sided energy estimate, a different limiting construction, or additional structure of the branching measures could repair the argument. Any such repair must prove that it applies to the same-outcome products and preserves nonzero mass and the required support. Replacing equality by an inequality without proving that inequality would not resolve the gap. No complete repair for the paper’s measures, and no correction adopted in the journal version, is certified here.
# A local geometric correction

The last display on p. 30 places \(d(x,y)\) within a constant of \(2n-k\), where \(x,y\) have depth \(n\) and \(k\) is the depth of their approximate common branch point. In a tree the exact identity is \[d(x,y)=2n-2k .\] For example, take \(n=2k\), \(x=a^k b^k\) and \(y=a^{2k}\). The actual distance is \(2k\), whereas the printed center is \(3k\). A fixed additive constant, including the bounded error in choosing the branch point, cannot absorb this discrepancy as \(k\to\infty\). The distance-window restriction at the top of p. 31 must accordingly be corrected.

This does not by itself invalidate the exponent \(2n-k\) in equation (22). A decomposition into one common segment of length \(k\) and two segments of length \(n-k\) has total Green-growth exponent \(k\omega+2(n-k)\omega=(2n-k)\omega\). It yields the same intended geometric ratio \(\lambda^{-h}e^{-\omega}\) in the energy sum. Thus the distance formula and the Green-weight exponent must be distinguished. The tree calculation establishes a local factor-two correction; it does not establish a second substantive failure of the prelimit energy estimate in every relatively hyperbolic group.
# Checks on range, normalization and coverage

The upper trace-growth estimate on p. 23 uses \(\mathbb EM_n\leq H_r(n)\), Markov’s inequality and a summable geometric bound from the definition of the limsup growth rate. It does not assume an unproved exact exponential asymptotic. The continuity argument on pp. 13–14 uses the supremum representation and monotonicity to reach \(r=R\); the \(L^2\) Green estimate is used for \(r<R\), and need not be finite at the endpoint.

There is also a useful independent normalization check. For simple random walk on the four-regular tree, write \[u(r)=\frac{4-\sqrt{16-12r^2}}{6r},\qquad R=\frac2{\sqrt3}.\] The edge-hitting parameter satisfies \(3ru(r)^2-4u(r)+r=0\), and \(G_r(e,x)=G_r(e,e)u(r)^{|x|}\). Since the sphere has \(4\cdot3^{n-1}\) vertices, \(\omega_\Gamma(r)=\log(3u(r))\). This gives \(\omega_\Gamma(1)=0\) and \(\omega_\Gamma(R)=\frac12\log3=\frac12v\), consistently with Theorem 1.1. The quadratic identity and endpoint values were checked symbolically.

The second-moment calculations on pp. 27–28 explicitly assume finite offspring variance and initially \(r<R\). The subsequent stochastic truncation of the offspring law, followed by continuity in its mean, addresses the broader range in the main statement. The lower-bound proof on p. 30 invokes this reduction again. Thus the temporary finite-variance assumption is not, by itself, a missing hypothesis in the theorem.

The transition-point geometry, Green-function comparisons, trace growth and the Appendix A definitions were read as part of the proof chain. The checks above concentrate on the stated theorem ranges, the critical-parameter reduction and the energy construction. The full logarithmic tracking argument in Section 6 and all cited external results were not independently reconstructed. No general correctness certification is inferred from reading every page. The major issue assigned here is the specific invalid inference [eq:invalid] (#eq:invalid).
# Evidence and attribution

The original-source SHA256 is `40bdb3db788302d37d8b53d74fd6cd118c61cfbf2d999c19e60ab3b3b1dc8e5a`. The complete 50-page text was read. Images of source pages 1, 2, 4, 9, 13, 14, 23, 24, 27–31, 33, 38, 39, 41–43 and 47 were inspected. Independent rational calculations check the tree energy formula against all pairs at depths 1–5, its uniform bound through depth 64, and the constants in [eq:contradiction] (#eq:contradiction). The general convergence proof is the analytic argument above, not an inference from a finite numerical test. No author code was executed.

The arXiv record and an author’s publication listing were checked for the target version. The journal article route reached an additional security check; the HAL document route returned access denied; the checked official issue-PDF request timed out. No journal PDF was acquired in this review, and no separate relevant correction or supplement was identified in the bounded search. These are limits of the actual search, not claims of nonexistence.

Per-paper evidence retains the original bytes, calculation records, compiler and dependency checks, PDF parsing, rendering, and subsequent actual page inspections. The assigned initial-review AI session performed the scientific work and image inspection. The native helper was restricted to read-only metadata and byte-binding checks. This initial review leaves the scientific decision pending, records no human review, and is not independent acceptance.

report: Abstract: This review checks the conservative-noise rescaling, the ground-state coercivity argument, and the probabilistic end of the nonconservative-noise regularization argument in arXiv:2301.02089v2. The energy argument and the large-imaginary-amplitude probability limit pass the checks stated below. The unrestricted complex-amplitude reading of the limit in Theorem 1.7 is not supported by its decisive probability estimate. A fixed-imaginary-part family disproves that auxiliary limit, without disproving the final non-blow-up theorem. Because fixed-direction amplification is a plausible intended reading, the report records a parameter-scope clarification with assessment Needs Evidence. Scientific adjudication remains pending.

# Identity, version, and coverage

# Definitions and checks that support the arguments
## Conservative rescaling

In the conservative problem, \(W_1=i\sum_k\phi_k\beta_k\) with real spatial coefficients and \(\mu=\frac12\sum_k\phi_k^2\). Hypothesis (H), equation (1.10), imposes square summability in \(H^3\) for the first noise, the additional directional integral condition on its gradients, and square summability in \(H^1\) for the second noise. These are not the spatially constant, complex noise assumptions used in Theorem 1.7.

For a regularized solution, the quadratic variation in \(d\|X\|_2^2\) contributes \(\sum_k\|\phi_kX\|_2^2\,dt\); the drift \(-\mu X\) contributes its negative. The stochastic mass term vanishes because \(\operatorname{Re}(i\phi_k|X|^2)=0\). Real-valued \(\phi_k\) is essential. This verifies the algebra of (1.2), not an independent construction of the infinite-dimensional solution.

The Itô product calculation gives \(u=e^{-W_1}X\) and \[e^{-W_1}\Delta(e^{W_1}u)
 =\Delta u+2

abla u+

abla W_1 igr)u .\] The last contraction is bilinear, without complex conjugation. The explicit expansion in (2.10), p. 8, resolves the possible ambiguity of the preceding \(|
abla W_1|^2\) notation. The wave convolution in (2.6) satisfies \(dT_t=i|
abla|T_t\,dt-i\,dW_2\), giving the stated additive-noise cancellation.

Equation reference: eq:aggregate. One caution in reconstructing the stochastic interchange on p. 12 is that basis indices driven by the same \(\beta_k\) are not independent. The justified aggregate estimate is \[\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}\left|
  \sum_k\int_0^s\sum_j a_{jk}(r)b_j(r)\,d\beta_k(r)\right|^2
 &\le C\mathbb E\int_0^t
       \sum_k\left|\sum_j a_{jk}(r)b_j(r)\right|^2dr \notag\\
 &\le C\mathbb E\int_0^t
       \sum_k\|a_{\cdot k}(r)\|_{\ell^2}^2
                    \|b(r)\|_{\ell^2}^2dr. \end{aligned}\] With the stopped \(L^2\) bound, \(|e^{W_1}|=1\), and \(\sum_k\|\phi_k\|_\infty^2<\infty\), this recovers the finite bound \(tM\|\varphi\|_2^2\sum_k\|\phi_k\|_\infty^2\) needed there. The displayed intermediate diagonal expression on that page should not be used as a general scalar BDG inequality. This review establishes the intended aggregate bound; it does not claim a PDE counterexample to the rescaling theorem from that intermediate display.
## The ground-state argument

Write \(A=\|\nabla u\|_2^2\), \(B=\|u\|_4^4\), and \(C=\|v+|u|^2\|_2^2\). Equations (1.6) and (1.15) give \[E_Z=\frac12 A-\frac14B+\frac14C,\qquad
 K=A-\frac34B,\qquad
 E_Z+\lambda^2M-\frac13K=\frac16A+\lambda^2M+\frac14C.\] The final positive decomposition is exact. For the ground state, the usual Pohozaev identities give \(\|\nabla Q\|_2^2=3\|Q\|_2^2\) and \(\|Q\|_4^4=4\|Q\|_2^2\), hence \(4E_S(Q)M(Q)=J(Q)^2\).

For \(M(X_0)>0\), fixing \(\lambda_*=J(Q)/(2M(X_0))\) completes the square in the energy–mass inequality, exactly as on p. 31. The variational characterization (7.1) prevents \(K(X(t))\) from crossing zero before the energy threshold. The displayed positive decomposition then bounds \(X\) in \(H^1\) and \(Y+|X|^2\) in \(L^2\); the embedding \(H^1(\mathbb R^3)\subset L^4(\mathbb R^3)\) supplies the remaining \(Y\) bound. For zero initial Schrödinger component, \(X=0\) and the linear stochastic wave is bounded on every finite time interval. A uniform bound over an infinite time interval is unnecessary for the blow-up alternative. Thus the checked argument gives existence up to the threshold stopping time, not stochastic energy conservation or an unconditional global-existence statement.
# Parameter scope in the regularization limit

Problem 1 (Which noise component becomes large?).  Theorem 1.7, equation (1.17), p. 6, assumes a spatially constant complex \(\phi=\phi^{(1)}_1\) with \(\operatorname{Im}\phi\ne0\), all other first-noise coefficients zero, and \(W_2=0\). It states a probability limit as \(\phi\to\infty\). Step 3 of its proof, equations (8.44)–(8.45), p. 37, uses a limit that actually requires \(|\operatorname{Im}\phi|\to\infty\). The following check separates that exact requirement from mere growth of \(|\phi|\).
## The decisive computation and all parameters

Equation reference: eq:law. Put \(\phi=a+ib\), where \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) and \(b\ne0\). Equations (2.13)–(2.16), p. 10, yield \[\widehat\mu=\tfrac12(|\phi|^2-\phi^2)=b^2-iab,\qquad
 W_1=i\phi\beta=(ia-b)\beta,\qquad
 h(t)=e^{-2b\beta(t)-2b^2t}.\] Consequently \[
 \|h\|_{L^4(0,\infty)}^4
 =\int_0^\infty e^{-8b\beta(t)-8b^2t}\,dt
 \ \stackrel{\rm law}{=}\
 b^{-2}I,\qquad I=\int_0^\infty e^{-8B_s-8s}\,ds .\] Here \(B\) is a standard real Brownian motion; the equality is in law, not an asserted pathwise identity between different amplitudes. Brownian scaling and the change of variable \(s=b^2t\) prove [eq:law] (#eq:law). The limit \(B_s/s\to0\) almost surely makes \(I\) finite almost surely. It is also strictly positive.

For the fixed threshold \(q=C_3(T,\|X_0\|_{H^1},\|Y_0\|_2)^{-4}>0\) used in (8.44), this gives \[\mathbb P(\|h\|_4^4\ge q)=\mathbb P(I\ge b^2q)\longrightarrow0
 \quad\hbox{if } |b|\longrightarrow\infty .\] The constants in (8.31), (8.41), and (8.45) depend on fixed time and initial-data norms, not on \(a\) or \(b\).

Now fix \(T=1\), \(X_0(x)=e^{-|x|^2}\in H^1(\mathbb R^3)\), \(Y_0=0\in L^2\), \(b=1\), and let \(\phi_n=n+i\). The data are deterministic; the noise has exactly one spatially constant mode with nonzero imaginary part; the remaining modes and the second noise vanish. These are precisely the special noise conditions of Theorem 1.7; hypothesis (H) for the conservative problem is not being imposed on this different model. Although \(|\phi_n|\to\infty\), the random variable in (8.44) has exactly the same law for every \(n\).

Moreover, \(\mathbb P(I\ge q)>0\) for every finite \(q\). Indeed choose \(K\) so that \(e^{8K-16}>q\). The event that \(B_1\in[-K-2,-K-1]\) and \(\sup_{0\le s\le1}|B_{1+s}-B_1|<1\) has positive probability by the nondegenerate Gaussian law and independent Brownian increments. On this event, \(B_t\le-K\) for \(1\le t\le2\), so \(I\ge\int_1^2e^{8K-16}\,dt>q\). Thus the auxiliary limit (8.44) is false along this admissible family under the unrestricted complex-modulus interpretation.
## Counterevidence and the precise impact

A natural intended convention is \(\phi=\lambda\phi_0\), \(\lambda\to+\infty\), with a fixed \(\operatorname{Im}\phi_0\ne0\). That convention does force \(|\operatorname{Im}\phi|\to\infty\) and makes the displayed argument valid. The geometric Brownian coefficient and the last line of (8.45) make this restricted interpretation particularly plausible. The report therefore does not turn the ambiguity into an unconditional assertion that Theorem 1.7 is false.

The issue is central to the probability step of the regularization result: smallness of \(\|h\|_4\) makes both nonlinear stopping-time conditions hold until the fixed horizon. It does not concern Theorems 1.2 or 1.5. Nor does it prove blow-up at fixed \(b\). In fact \[X^{(a+ib)}(t)
 =e^{-b^2t-bB_t}e^{ia(B_t+bt)}z^{(b)}(t),\] and the reduced equations for \(z^{(b)},v^{(b)}\) depend only on \(b\). The extra factor depending on \(a\) is spatially constant and has unit modulus. Increasing \(a\) cannot change the existence event through this transformation, but that observation alone does not determine whether its probability was already one.
## Supported amendment and assessment

An explicit condition \(|\operatorname{Im}\phi|\to\infty\), or explicit amplification of a fixed nonconservative direction, restores the verified probability limit. This is a verified amendment to Step 3, conditional on the preceding deterministic estimates and local construction; it is not an independent full proof of all those estimates. The unresolved item is the intended domain of the limit in the acquired statement and its correspondence with the journal version. The assessment is Needs Evidence, with inspection outcome scope clarification. No Major finding is claimed from an interpretation that may be narrower than the displayed notation.
# Conclusion and state

The checked coercivity and rescaling algebra support their stated uses, subject to the coverage limits above. The regularization proof establishes a large-nonconservative-component regime. Neither arbitrary large complex modulus nor unconditional failure of the final theorem has been established by that proof check.

report: Abstract: The Esscher-transform criterion for convergence in infinite-order Rényi divergence is checked in the acquired arXiv version. The critical-zone argument, its periodic specialization, and a reduction covering an arbitrary initial smoothing index are supported by the calculations below. Several displayed identities have incorrect signs or normalizing factors. Explicit Gaussian and normalization tests establish these local errors; the intended corrections preserve the checked proof. No false final theorem is demonstrated. The assessment is Minor, with the cited external local-limit estimates remaining dependencies rather than independently certified results.

Title: A Technical Review of
Central Limit Theorem for Rényi Divergence of Infinite Order
# Identity, hypotheses, and coverage

The source is the 29-page arXiv:2402.02259v2 by Sergey G. Bobkov and Friedrich Götze, dated 19 June 2024 [paper]. Its associated journal DOI is 10.1214/24-AOP1711. This report applies to that acquired preprint; equivalence with the journal-final text has not been established. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages and agree with the printed numbers.

All substantive source text, Sections 1–11 on pp. 1–27, was read. The references on pp. 27–29 were read as bibliographic entries, not as their underlying papers. The main proof, Esscher identities, explicit periodic examples, and the weighted-convolution argument were checked. The quantitative Fourier-tail estimate imported in Lemma 6.1 and the refined Richter theorem quoted as Theorem 10.2 were not independently re-proved from their original publications. Bounds that use those results retain that dependency. No author code was executed. Bounded source and public-metadata searches identified no separate computational supplement or correction notice; this does not prove their absence. The official arXiv record describes v2 as correcting typos and updating Section 11 [metadata]; it does not certify every displayed formula in v2.

Write \(Z_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{j=1}^nX_j\), where the \(X_j\) are independent copies of a real random variable with mean zero and variance one. The operative assumptions before Theorem 2.1, p. 4, are \[p_{n_0}\le C\varphi\quad\hbox{a.e. for some finite }n_0,C,
 \qquad L(t)=\mathbb E e^{tX}\le e^{t^2/2}\quad(t\in\mathbb R).\] The first is a Gaussian envelope after finitely many summands, stronger than existence of a density. Put \(K=\log L\), \(A=t^2/2-K\ge0\), and \(T_\infty(p\Vert\varphi)=\mathop{\rm ess\,sup}(p/\varphi)-1\). The claimed criterion is \[\lim_{A(t)\to0}\max(A''(t),0)=0.                         \tag{1.1}\] It includes the values at every zero of \(A\), and sequences approaching infinity with \(A(t)\to0\). It is not only a condition near the origin. The Gaussian case \(A\equiv0\) satisfies it. The smallest-positive-period assumption in Theorem 2.3 excludes a constant periodic factor; a Gaussian should instead be handled directly.
# Checks of the main argument
## Tilt, moments, and the critical zone

These bounds justify sufficiency in Section 8: first fix the critical-zone parameter, let \(n\) tend to infinity, and then enlarge that parameter. For necessity, (2.3) and \((A')^2\le2A\) bound \(v_x^2\) by a constant times \(C^2A(x)\). Applying (2.4) on arbitrarily small critical zones forces \(\sigma_x^{-2}\le1+o(1)\), hence (1.1). In the first display on p. 17 the exponential inherited from (2.3) should be \(e^{2A(x)}\). For \(a\le1\) and \(n\ge3\), \(A(x)\le1/2\) and \(12e/\pi<12\); the following bound \(v_x^2\le12C^2A(x)\) is therefore recovered. This correction does not alter the asymptotic argument.

Strict subgaussianity itself is necessary: \(p_n\le(1+o(1))\varphi\) implies \(L(h)^n\le(1+o(1))e^{nh^2/2}\) for every fixed \(h\), by evaluating the moment-generating function at \(h\sqrt n\). Taking logarithms and dividing by \(n\) gives \(A(h)\ge0\).
## The initial smoothing index and all integers \(n\)

Section 8 assumes \(n_0=1\) for simplicity. The following supplies the reduction for its stated general hypothesis. Let \(m=n_0\). The density of \(S_m=\sum_{j=1}^mX_j\) is bounded by \(C\) times the \(N(0,m)\) density. Its tilt has maximum at most \(C(2\pi m)^{-1/2}e^{mA(h)}\). Convolving with the tilted probability law of \(X\) cannot increase that maximum. Using (2.2) for \(N=m+1\) therefore gives \[\frac{p_N(h\sqrt N)}{\varphi(h\sqrt N)}
 \le C\sqrt{N/m}\,e^{-A(h)}\le C\sqrt{N/m}.                \tag{2.5}\] Thus both \(Z_m\) and \(Z_{m+1}\) have finite \(T_\infty\). Their deficit functions are \(A_r(t)=rA(t/\sqrt r)\), with \(A_r''(t)=A''(t/\sqrt r)\). Condition (1.1) is preserved.

Apply the verified \(n_0=1\) argument to both block laws. Every sufficiently large \(N\) can be written \(N=am+b(m+1)\), where \(b\equiv N\pmod m\) is chosen near \(N/[2(m+1)]\); then both component lengths are of order \(N\). Their normalized densities are bounded by \((1+\epsilon_N)\varphi\) and \((1+\delta_N)\varphi\), with both errors tending to zero. Independence and convolution of the corresponding Gaussian bounds yield \(p_N\le(1+\epsilon_N)(1+\delta_N)\varphi\). This proves convergence along every integer, not only multiples of \(m\). The same balanced decomposition preserves a bound \(O((\log N)^3/N)\) when that bound has been established for both block laws; the separation and periodic hypotheses are also preserved by the block transformation.
## An explicit valid periodic example

For Example 9.5, p. 20, put \(P(t)=(1-4\sin^2t)^2\sin^4t\). Direct expansion gives \[P(t)=\frac94-\frac{15}4\cos2t+\frac{17}8\cos4t
                   -\frac34\cos6t+\frac18\cos8t.\] Let these coefficients be \(a_k\), including \(k=0\), and set \[B=\sum_{k\in\{0,2,4,6,8\}}|a_k|e^{k^2/2},\quad c=(2B)^{-1},
 \qquad q(x)=1-c\sum_k a_ke^{k^2/2}\cos(kx).\] Then \(1/2\le q\le3/2\), and \(p=q\varphi\) is a probability density with \(L(t)=e^{t^2/2}(1-cP(t))\). This follows by integrating each Gaussian cosine term. Because \(P(0)=P'(0)=P''(0)=0\), the mean and variance are zero and one, respectively. Since \(P\ge0\), strict subgaussianity holds, and \(T_\infty(p\Vert\varphi)\) is finite.

Writing \(P=Q^2\), \(Q=\sin^2t-4\sin^4t\), gives \(Q(\pi/6)=0\), \(Q'(\pi/6)=-\sqrt3/2\), and \(\Psi''(\pi/6)=-3c/2\) for \(\Psi=1-cP\). At this contact point, (2.4) yields the limiting density ratio \[(1-3c/2)^{-1/2}>1.\] Thus the source’s failure-of-convergence example is valid after the displayed normalization correction below. The contrasting \(\sin^4t\) example has only the endpoint contacts in a fundamental period and vanishing second derivative there.
# A demonstrated local problem and its repair

Problem 1 (Displayed signs and normalizations).  Several formulas in the acquired v2 are false literally. Their corrections are determined by the definitions and can be tested without any unverified example.
For the Gaussian tests below take \(X\sim N(0,1)\), so all mean, variance, strict-subgaussianity, density and finite-divergence assumptions hold. Set \(h=1\) when a nonzero tilt is required.

1. On p. 6, after Definition 3.1, the identity \(Q_h\varphi(x)=\varphi(x+h)\) must read \(\varphi(x-h)\). Completing the square gives a tilted mean \(h\), whereas the displayed right side has mean \(-h\).

2. On p. 7, the proof of Proposition 3.2 divides \(L(t+h)\) by \(L(t)\); every normalizing denominator in that display must instead be evaluated at \(h\). At \(t=0,h=1\), the printed Gaussian expression is \(e^{1/2}\), whereas a probability moment-generating function at zero equals one. Equation (5.1), p. 10, already has the correct denominator.

3. On p. 10, the displayed variance numerator omits the factor \(L(h)\) multiplying \(L''(h)\). For the Gaussian at \(h=1\), the printed fraction equals \(2e^{-1/2}-1\), instead of the true variance one. Formula (2.1) gives the correction.

4. On p. 3, the periodic Laplace factor must be \(e^{+t^2/2}\), as correctly used in (9.1) and (9.4). On p. 13, in the proof of Lemma 6.1, the normal characteristic-function factor must instead be \(e^{-t^2/2}\) in all three displays. With the printed positive exponent, its difference from a bounded characteristic function is not integrable over the real line.

5. On p. 20, Example 9.5 says \(L(t)=1-c\Psi(t)\). Its value at zero is \(1-c\), violating normalization for the stated \(c>0\). The correct formula is \(L(t)=e^{t^2/2}\Psi(t)\), consistent with p. 19 and the explicit positive-density construction above.

6. On p. 25, the \(c_0=0\) convolution has \(q_2(y/c_1)\) and then \(\varphi(y/c_1)\). Both denominators must be \(c_2\). With independent standard Gaussians, \(c_1=\sqrt3/2,c_2=1/2\), the printed expression has integral \(\sqrt3\); the corrected convolution has integral one and variance \(c_1^2+c_2^2=1\).
#### Counterevidence, dependency, and severity.

Definition (3.1), formula (3.7), the correct tilt formula (5.1), the use of \(K''\) in Section 8, and the consistent periodic definition (9.1) identify the intended expressions. Direct substitution of the corrected formulas restores the checked algebra. These are genuine false displayed identities, but they do not establish failure of the central limit criterion or the periodic examples. The assessment is Minor. The repair is verified locally; author adoption and any changes in the journal version are unknown.

Two additional scope details do not warrant a false-theorem claim. The critical zone in (4.5), p. 10, should range over all real \(h\), as it explicitly does in the actual proof on p. 16. Also, signed coefficients in Corollary 11.2 need not be assumed positive without explanation: absorb each sign into its summand, retaining independence, strict subgaussianity and the same Gaussian density bound. Identical distribution is unnecessary in the application of Lemma 11.3. Its contour shift, uniform Riemann–Lebesgue argument and weighted Plancherel bounds on pp. 25–27 then give the stated envelope.
# Assessment and limits

No Major defect or false final theorem was established. The main criterion and the explicit positive and negative periodic tests pass the checks recorded here, with the local corrections in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:typos). The refined rate statements remain conditional on the externally quoted Richter estimate, whose hypotheses are matched in the source but whose original proof was not audited. One-sided relative error is essential: for any compactly supported density, the absolute relative error equals one outside the support of each normalized sum.

problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: Problem 1 (Displayed signs and normalizations).
claim: Recorded check: Displayed signs and normalizing factors require correction

Gaussian tests use independent standard normal variables: mean zero, variance one, strictly subgaussian, bounded density, T_infinity=0. Tilt parameter h=1, test-transform parameter t=0 where specified. Periodic example uses P=(1-4sin^2 t)^2 sin^4 t, c=1/(2B), B=sum |a_k| exp(k^2/2), yielding density p=q*phi with 1/2<=q<=3/2, mean zero and variance one. Convolution test uses c0=0,c1=sqrt(3)/2,c2=1/2 and independent standard normals; c1^2+c2^2=1.
analysis: Several formulas in the acquired v2 are false literally. Their corrections are determined by the definitions and can be tested without any unverified example.
For the Gaussian tests below take \(X\sim N(0,1)\), so all mean, variance, strict-subgaussianity, density and finite-divergence assumptions hold. Set \(h=1\) when a nonzero tilt is required.

1. On p. 6, after Definition 3.1, the identity \(Q_h\varphi(x)=\varphi(x+h)\) must read \(\varphi(x-h)\). Completing the square gives a tilted mean \(h\), whereas the displayed right side has mean \(-h\).

2. On p. 7, the proof of Proposition 3.2 divides \(L(t+h)\) by \(L(t)\); every normalizing denominator in that display must instead be evaluated at \(h\). At \(t=0,h=1\), the printed Gaussian expression is \(e^{1/2}\), whereas a probability moment-generating function at zero equals one. Equation (5.1), p. 10, already has the correct denominator.

3. On p. 10, the displayed variance numerator omits the factor \(L(h)\) multiplying \(L''(h)\). For the Gaussian at \(h=1\), the printed fraction equals \(2e^{-1/2}-1\), instead of the true variance one. Formula (2.1) gives the correction.

4. On p. 3, the periodic Laplace factor must be \(e^{+t^2/2}\), as correctly used in (9.1) and (9.4). On p. 13, in the proof of Lemma 6.1, the normal characteristic-function factor must instead be \(e^{-t^2/2}\) in all three displays. With the printed positive exponent, its difference from a bounded characteristic function is not integrable over the real line.

5. On p. 20, Example 9.5 says \(L(t)=1-c\Psi(t)\). Its value at zero is \(1-c\), violating normalization for the stated \(c>0\). The correct formula is \(L(t)=e^{t^2/2}\Psi(t)\), consistent with p. 19 and the explicit positive-density construction above.

6. On p. 25, the \(c_0=0\) convolution has \(q_2(y/c_1)\) and then \(\varphi(y/c_1)\). Both denominators must be \(c_2\). With independent standard Gaussians, \(c_1=\sqrt3/2,c_2=1/2\), the printed expression has integral \(\sqrt3\); the corrected convolution has integral one and variance \(c_1^2+c_2^2=1\).
result: Definition (3.1), formula (3.7), the correct tilt formula (5.1), the use of \(K''\) in Section 8, and the consistent periodic definition (9.1) identify the intended expressions. Direct substitution of the corrected formulas restores the checked algebra. These are genuine false displayed identities, but they do not establish failure of the central limit criterion or the periodic examples. The assessment is Minor. The repair is verified locally; author adoption and any changes in the journal version are unknown.

Two additional scope details do not warrant a false-theorem claim. The critical zone in (4.5), p. 10, should range over all real \(h\), as it explicitly does in the actual proof on p. 16. Also, signed coefficients in Corollary 11.2 need not be assumed positive without explanation: absorb each sign into its summand, retaining independence, strict subgaussianity and the same Gaussian density bound. Identical distribution is unnecessary in the application of Lemma 11.3. Its contour shift, uniform Riemann–Lebesgue argument and weighted Plancherel bounds on pp. 25–27 then give the stated envelope.

report: Abstract: The acquired arXiv version 2001.11977v2 was reviewed. Title: A Technical Review of
Macroscopic loops in the loop \(O(n)\) model via the XOR trick
# Reviewed object and theorem ranges

The authors are Nicholas Crawford, Alexander Glazman, Matan Harel, and Ron Peled; the associated DOI is `10.1214/24-AOP1712`. The reviewed object is the 35-page PDF of arXiv:2001.11977v2, posted 13 June 2024, whose title page bears 17 June 2024. These dates are not conflated. Its SHA256 is
ae2b8bf449b72aca63ea277ce332a0fa7cff4c8402edaed3b066496a9e50305e
No equivalence with an unexamined journal-final PDF is asserted.

The body on source pages 1–32 was read; references on pages 32–35 were read as bibliographic entries, not as the cited papers. Theorem 1 (p. 5) concerns translation-invariant Gibbs measures for \(1\le n\le1+\delta\), \(1-\delta\le x\le1\), and gives a bi-infinite-path or infinitely-many-surrounding-loops alternative. Corollary 1.1 additionally needs \(x\le1/\sqrt n\) and an external dichotomy for RSW. Theorem 2 (p. 7) requires \(n=1\), \(1<x\le\sqrt3\), and boundary configurations without bi-infinite paths. Theorem 3 (p. 8) concerns the torus for \(1\le n\le2,x=1\). These restrictions are operative.
# Checks of the main mechanisms

In Lemma 1.5 (p. 9), the loops meeting a finite circuit form a finite configuration when bi-infinite paths are excluded. The parity spin at the origin changes under XOR with the surrounding circuit. Every relevant resulting component meets the circuit, giving the diameter conclusion. The no-bi-infinite-path hypothesis cannot simply be omitted.

For the antiferromagnetic proof, (2.5), p. 13, is wired FK at parameter \(1/x\), conditioned on a decreasing compatibility event. Positive association gives the correct direction for decreasing vacant-circuit events in (2.9), p. 14. The endpoint \(1/\sqrt3\) supplies the uniform parameter range. Conditional XOR preserves the joint weight and yields the factor \(1/2\). External FK crossing estimates were not independently reproved.

For the torus, the blue probability \((n-1)/n\le1/2\) gives domination of the blue marginal by the red marginal; it does not make the two colors independent. An independent check of Lemma 3.3 uses mod-two homology: an essential simple torus curve has primitive integral class and hence nonzero mod-two class; unions of contractible curves have zero class, and XOR adds the classes. The external rerouting argument invoked in Lemma 3.4 remains a dependency. Conditional on that lemma, the \(1/4\) probability calculation is consistent. The \(\rho\) subscript \(1\) in (3.2), p. 17, should be \(n\).

Summing vacant-edge defects in (4.1), p. 18, gives \(x^{-|E|+|\omega|}\), while summing colors gives \(n^{\ell(\omega)}\). The extra factor is constant in \(\omega\). An independently written exact-rational computation checked all eight even configurations on a chain of three hexagons at \(n=3/2,x=4/5\), evaluating 72,008 joint color/defect states through product sums. All marginals equaled \(x^{-|E|}x^{|\omega|}n^{\ell(\omega)}\); XOR closure and involutivity also held. This does not test asymptotic percolation.

The domination proof (pp. 21–24) uses planar five-degeneracy, loop clouds of at most six sites, edge clouds of at most three, and \[p(n,x)=\min\!\left\{3\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^{1/6}+6(1-x)^{1/3},1\right\}.\] Underlying cloud coordinates are independent before taking their coordinatewise maximum. Each face meets at most three distinct loops and six edges. The graph used for the external planar-limit theorem is simple, after deleting multiple edges and self-loops.

Lemma 4.10 (p. 26) derives uniform integrability of degrees from translation invariance, long-loop densities and absence of bi-infinite paths, without assuming bounded maximum degree. In Proposition 4.2, subsequential compactness gives the full-sequence conclusion by application to every potentially bad subsequence. The change of root on p. 28 is valid after averaging with a bounded density ratio, not as a pointwise comparison of independently sampled roots. Proposition 4.11 (pp. 28–30) uses Følner recentering, finite energy, Burton–Keane uniqueness, and removal of wiring ambiguity when at most two crossings remain. Those logical uses were checked; the external uniqueness, compactness and planar percolation results were not independently re-established.
# Problem 1: exterior loops and the area estimate
Classification: Major, localized to the second clause of Corollary 1.2.
## Exact assertion and hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:false. Corollary 1.2 (p. 7) permits arbitrary boundary loop configurations \(\xi_k\). The face \(f_k\) is uniform in the faces \(F_k\) of \(D_k=\Lambda_k(0)\), independently of the configuration. As defined on p. 6, \(L(f)\) is the length of the longest loop bordering \(f\), with value infinity for a bordering bi-infinite path. On p. 31, \(V(f)\) uses the outermost loop of the entire configuration surrounding \(f\). The first display on p. 32, obtained from (4.10), asserts \[
\mathbb P[V(f_k)>s]\le6c\,\mathbb E[
 L(f_k)\mathbf1_{\{L(f_k)>\sqrt{s/c}\}}],\] where \(c>0\) is an absolute isoperimetric constant. The sum in (4.10) includes all outermost loops and all bordering faces. Dividing by \(|F_k|\) does not convert this into an average over interior faces.
## Counterexample with all required hypotheses

Fix \(D_k\), and let \(M=|E(D_k)|\). Set \(n=x=1\), in the allowed rectangle. Let \(\xi_k\) consist of one large finite simple loop \(\Gamma\) strictly outside \(D_k\), with an empty intervening region, surrounding \(D_k\) but bordering none of its faces. There are no bi-infinite paths. Every variable loop lies in \(D_k\) and has at most \(M\) edges. For every allowed interior configuration, \[V(f)=\operatorname{Area}(\Gamma),\qquad L(f)\le M\quad(f\in F_k).\] Given any proposed \(c>0\), take \(s=c(M+1)^2\) and choose \(\Gamma\) with area greater than \(s\). Equation [eq:false] (#eq:false) then says \(1\le0\). No change of its finite multiplicative constant fixes the counterexample.

A separate computation instantiated the geometry: the seven-face \(D=\Lambda_1\) has 24 vertices, 30 edges, and 128 even configurations. All were enumerated at \(n=x=1\). The boundary of \(\Lambda_{20}\) has length 246 and area 1261. With illustrative \(c=1,s=961\), the cutoff is 31, whereas the largest bordering-loop length over all configurations is 22. The computed left probability is one and the right tail expectation is zero. The analytic construction, rather than this illustrative value of \(c\), proves failure for every positive constant. No author code was executed.
## Alternate reading and a localized repair

Restricting the outermost loop to loops contained in \(D_k\) avoids this example, but is not the stated definition. That interpretation also requires boundary control and a lower bound uniform in the tail threshold. The following repair proves the affected implication conditional on the first clause of Corollary 1.2.

Assume uniform integrability of \(\{L(f_k)\}\). For fixed \(r\), a crossing in \(C_{r,R}(f_k)\) forces a nearby face, within distance \(r\), to border a loop of length at least a fixed multiple of \(R-r\), or a bi-infinite path. Summation over those nearby faces gives a constant depending on \(r\) times the tail probability of \(L(f_k)\), plus a width-\(r\) boundary-strip error \(O(r/k)\). Tightness yields \[\lim_{R\to\infty}\limsup_{k\to\infty}\mathbb P[C_{r,R}(f_k)]=0 .\] The first clause of the corollary therefore gives arbitrarily large \(r\), with fixed \(R=R(r)\), such that \(\liminf_k\mathbb P[S_{r,R}(f_k)]\ge1/2\). Discarding a width-\(R\) strip costs \(O(R/k)\); the witnessing loop is then contained in \(D_k\) and has area at least \(|F_{\Lambda_r}|\). Put \(s_r=|F_{\Lambda_r}|/2\), to respect strict inequalities. Then \(\liminf_k\mathbb P[V_{D_k}(f_k)>s_r]\ge1/2\). Averaging [eq:fixed] (#eq:fixed) implies \[\liminf_k\mathbb E[L(f_k)\mathbf1_{\{L(f_k)>\sqrt{s_r/c}\}}]
\ge(72c)^{-1}\] along arbitrarily large \(r\), contradicting uniform integrability. Positivity depending on \(r\) alone would not suffice.
## Dependency and impact boundary

The invalid step converts surrounding area into a local length tail, the decisive step for non-uniform-integrability. Repair requires localization, a boundary argument and uniform tail quantifiers, rather than one typographical change. The counterexample establishes an invalid derivation as printed. It does not disprove the corollary, whose affected implication is repaired above, or Theorems 1–3. No whole-paper failure is claimed.
# Problem 2: the domain of the bijection

Classification: Minor. Lemma 4.5, p. 22, claims a bijection from the full cube \(\{0,1\}^{V}\) to coherent triples for a fixed uncolored configuration. Immediately above, face coordinates are deterministic functions of edge and selected loop coordinates; the projection discards face coordinates.

For a single-hexagon domain and the empty uncolored configuration, there are six edge bits and one face bit. The full cube has \(2^7=128\) states, while the coherent triples are the \(2^6=64\) defect-edge sets. Every triple has two preimages. This enumeration was independently executed. At \(n=1\), \(0<x<1\), all 64 edge patterns have positive probability, and the admissible face bit is the OR of the six edge bits.

Restricting the domain to states satisfying the deterministic face rule gives the correct bijection. The significant counterevidence against a stronger defect is that \(\nu_{G,n,x}\) already has that support: its pushforward law and the use in Proposition 4.6 survive unchanged. The repair affects a statement’s domain, not a demonstrated final theorem.
# Assessment, corrections and limits

The initial assessment is Major, with a localized repaired derivation and a separate Minor statement error. Public version metadata describes presentation improvements, particularly for Benjamini–Schramm limits; this is not evidence of a correction to either specific issue. A bounded correction search produced no separately verified notice addressing them. It does not establish that no correction exists.

The per-paper support tree contains independent code, outputs and execution receipts, source bindings, compiler and retained dependency payloads, and actual page-inspection records. The Peled abstract was consulted for the scope of the universal planar-limit input, not its full proof. Original reference PDFs for FK estimates, rerouting, compactness and uniqueness were not inspected; they remain explicit dependencies. Scientific decision remains pending, human reviews remain empty, and this initial report is not independent acceptance.

9 N. Crawford, A. Glazman, M. Harel, and R. Peled, Macroscopic loops in the loop \(O(n)\) model via the XOR trick, arXiv:2001.11977v2 (2024), acquired 35-page version. DOI `10.1214/24-AOP1712`. arXiv, version record for 2001.11977, https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.11977. R. Peled, On the site percolation threshold of circle packings and planar graphs, arXiv:2001.10855, abstract and version record, https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.10855. Full proof not independently reviewed.

report: Abstract: The acquired journal version was read, including its proof of quenched tightness. Several intermediate displays need correction, and the uniform time in Corollary 3.6 is not justified by its written choice of parameters. Explicit replacements are supplied under the existing assumptions. The overall assessment is Major: the written argument does not establish a uniform temporal shift essential to the central tightness proof. Title: A Technical Review of
On the tightness of the maximum of branching Brownian motion in random environment
# Identity, assumptions and scope

The reviewed paper is by Jiří Černý, Alexander Drewitz and Pascal Oswald, Annals of Probability 53 (2025), 509–543, DOI `10.1214/24-AOP1713`. The frozen, university-hosted journal PDF has 35 pages and SHA256
0d0bb57b14898a454c09a7b4ffb1d781fb2861ed05ffdfc3041b41e629f5e8b7

Below, printed journal page numbers are used; subtract 508 for PDF page numbers. The entire body, pp. 509–540, was read, as were the bibliographic entries on pp. 541–543. The corresponding arXiv record is 2212.12390v2, dated 24 June 2024; it is not substituted for the acquired journal file.

Theorem 2.1, p. 513, assumes spatial stationarity, the summable \(\psi\)-mixing condition (2.2), almost-sure local Hölder continuity, and \(0<\mathrm{ei}<\mathrm{es}<\infty\). Offspring numbers are at least one, their mean \(\mu\) exceeds one, and their second moment is finite. The additional ballistic condition \(v_0>v_c\) is essential for the compact negative tilting-parameter interval. The conclusion is tightness for almost every fixed environment under the quenched law; it does not give an environment-uniform radius or convergence in distribution. Figure 1 is expressly a discrete-space numerical motivation for a nonconvergence conjecture, not its proof. No author simulation was executed.
# Independent checks and proof dependencies

The normalization in Remark 3.2 is legitimate even when \(1<\mu<2\): \(\mu+p_1-2=\sum_{k\ge2}(k-2)p_k\ge0\). The new probabilities sum to one, have mean two, and preserve the rates of every genuine branching event. Equivalently, the transformed reaction multiplied by \((\mu-1)\xi\) equals the original reaction multiplied by \(\xi\). Exact symbolic checks used \((p_1,p_2,p_3)=(2/5,3/10,3/10)\), giving new probabilities \(1/3\) each. The Taylor lower bound (6.7) was also checked algebraically.

The tilted diffusion calculation on pp. 522–525 has \(b=(\log Z)'\), \(b'=-2(\zeta+\eta)-b^2\) and \[\sqrt{2|\eta|}\le b(x)\le\sqrt{2(\mathrm{es}-\mathrm{ei}+|\eta|)}.\] This gives a bounded Lipschitz drift and the stopped density in (4.22). The drift comparison can be proved directly on a common Brownian path: \(x+B_t+\underline v t\le X_t\le x+B_t+\overline v t\). The constant-killing diagnostic \(Z(x)=e^{\sqrt{2a}x}\) satisfies \(Z''/2-aZ=0\); it checks signs, not the nondegenerate-environment theorem.

The mixing assumption enters the imported concentration estimates in Section 5 even though it is not used directly in the local PDE steps. Endpoint uniformity requires the union bounds and compact speed set in Lemma 5.3; the compact set must lie strictly above \(v_c\). For Lemma 6.1, perturbations need first be applied at one fixed sufficiently large displacement; monotonicity in the target then extends the result to every larger displacement. Applying a sublinear perturbation estimate directly to arbitrary unbounded displacements would be unjustified.

A useful independent check of the constants in Lemma 6.4 keeps \(s=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_{\widetilde\eta}H_y}\) separate from \(d=\eta-\widetilde\eta>0\), so that \(\widetilde\sigma=ds\) and the integration cutoff is \(\ell=L/s\). From the stated uniform variance and interval normal-approximation estimates, \(s\le b\sqrt{vt}\) and error at most \(C_{17}/\sqrt{vt}\). Choose \(L\ge20bC_{17}\). For fixed \(L\), sufficiently large \(t\) gives the numerator and denominator bounds \[N\le\frac{2\ell e^{-dL}}{1-e^{-dL}},\qquad
D\ge\frac{\ell}{20}e^{-dL/2}.\] Thus \(N/D\le40e^{-dL/2}/(1-e^{-dL})\). With \(dL\ge12\), the computed bound is \(0.099151<1/4\). This tracks the dependence as \(d\) becomes small, instead of treating the lower bound in (6.34) as uniform in \(L\). It verifies the final comparison conditional on the stated variance and normal-approximation inputs; their external proofs were not reproduced.

Finally, the Sturm comparison on p. 540 transfers a nonnegative difference at a negative spatial point to the origin. The quantile law of large numbers places that point in the range of Lemma 6.1. Bounded time intervals are harmless: bounded branching rates and finite offspring mean give finitely many particles on compact time intervals almost surely, with continuous trajectories and maxima. This supplies the compact-time part omitted from the asymptotic argument.
# Problem 1: factors and signs in Proposition 5.1
Severity: Minor; local repairs preserve both perturbation conclusions.
## The missing potential-shift factor

The counterevidence against a false proposition is decisive: its claimed conclusion already permits \(C_1e^{C_1h}\). Restoring [eq:shift] (#eq:shift) and increasing \(C_1\) absorbs the factor without changing an assumption or the conclusion.
## The negative spatial exponent

Equations (5.30)–(5.31), pp. 531–532, retain only an absolute \(O(h)\) estimate, which alone cannot yield the asserted \(e^{-h/C_2}\) decay. With the same tilting parameter \(\eta_* \in\Delta\Subset(-\infty,0)\) in the first difference of (5.30), its actual signed value is \[\log Z^{\zeta,\eta_*}_{y,y+h}
 \le-\sqrt{2|\eta_*|}\,h\le-a h\] for \(a>0\) uniform on \(\Delta\). This follows from (4.17)–(4.18) and \(\zeta\le0\). Keeping the normal-approximation prefactor also contributes an additive bounded constant in the logarithm. The corrected logarithmic bound is \[O(1)-a h+O(h^2/t).\] Because \(h\le t\delta(t)\) with \(\delta(t)\to0\), it yields the required negative exponent for large \(t\). For \(0\le h<1\), monotonicity of the target event and an enlarged prefactor suffice. These corrections repair the displayed derivation feeding Lemma 6.1; they do not demonstrate a false final theorem.
# Problem 2: continuation after a tilted hitting time

Severity: Minor. In (6.17), p. 535, the change-of-measure density stops at \(H_y\), but the next equality uses \(p_y^{\zeta,\eta}(t-H_y)\), the endpoint probability under the tilted continuation. This continuation was not changed by a density measurable at \(H_y\).

On the event \(A=\{H_y\in[t-K,t],\,T_{y,t}\ge t-K\}\), the barrier condition is determined by the path up to \(H_y\): the first barrier crossing occurs no later than \(H_y\). Conditional on this path, the original Brownian continuation satisfies \[P_y(X_{t-H_y}\ge y)=\tfrac12\] for \(H_y<t\); the endpoint \(H_y=t\) is a null event and would give one. The correct stopped-density identity uses this Brownian probability, so it directly yields the final factor \(1/2\) required in (6.17).

This is a false intermediate equality, rather than evidence against the lower bound. Under the tilted continuation the positive drift gives \(p_y^{\zeta,\eta}(s)\ge\Phi(\sqrt{2|\eta|s})>1/2\) for \(s>0\). For the constant-drift diagnostic with drift two at time one, the computed probability is \(0.977249868\), compared with \(1/2\) for Brownian motion. The repair is to condition before tilting and retain the Brownian continuation. The subsequent proof of Lemma 6.2 uses only the unchanged \(1/2\) bound.
# Problem 3: uniformity of the growth time

Severity: Major; a core proof gap with a verified repair. Corollary 3.6, pp. 520–521, requires one time \(T\) for all sufficiently large \(y\) and any \(t\) with \(w^y(t,0)=\varepsilon\). Its proof puts \(t=\tau_y^\varepsilon+s_0\), chooses \(s_1\) using \(s_0\), and sets \(T=s_1-s_0\). Both \(s_0\) and the compact interval on which convergence is used may vary with \(y,t\). Local uniform convergence on fixed compact intervals does not justify this uniform choice. Restricting to first hitting times would set \(s_0=0\), but the stated corollary and its application allow any such \(t\). Theorem 2.1 uses this uniform shift in (7.4) before the Sturm comparison, so the gap affects a necessary step of the central tightness derivation. The Major grade concerns this invalid passage of quantifiers; the availability of the repair below does not validate the written argument or imply that the final theorem is false.

Here is a direct repair under the existing assumptions, in the normalization \(\mu=2\). Write \(q=1-p_1>0\). Formula (3.1) implies \(F(w)\ge q w(1-w)\) on \([0,1]\). By the heat-kernel Duhamel formula, for \(t\ge1\), \[\|\partial_xw^y(t,\cdot)\|_\infty
\le C:=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,(1+2\mathrm{es}),\] using \(0\le w,F\le1\). At a time with \(w^y(t,0)=\varepsilon\), therefore, \(w^y(t,x)\ge\phi(x):=(\varepsilon-C|x|)_+\). Reaction is nonnegative, so one time unit later the profile dominates \(P_1\phi\), strictly positive on every compact interval.

Set \(c=\mathrm{ei}\,q>0\), choose \(R\) so that \(\kappa:=\pi^2/(8R^2)<c\varepsilon/2\), and let \(\psi(x)=\cos(\pi x/(2R))\) on \([-R,R]\). Take \(0<a_0<\min\{1-\kappa/c,\min_{[-R,R]}P_1\phi\}\) and solve \[a'=a(c-\kappa-ca),\qquad a(0)=a_0.\] Then \(a(s)\psi(x)\) is a subsolution on this interval with zero boundary values. Indeed, the reaction-diffusion right side minus its time derivative, divided by \(\psi\), is \(ca(s)^2(1-\psi)\ge0\). Comparison applies because \(\xi F(w)\ge c w(1-w)\). Moreover \(a(s)\uparrow1-\kappa/c>1-\varepsilon/2\). One deterministic time, depending only on \(\varepsilon,\mathrm{ei},\mathrm{es},p\), makes the value at the origin at least \(1-\varepsilon\) for all subsequent times. The large-\(y\) regime ensures the original \(t\ge1\). This proves the corollary’s uniform claim and its use in (7.4), without strengthening the environment assumptions. The symbolic subsolution residual was checked independently.
# Problem 4: introductory normalization displays

Severity: Minor. Equation (1.5), p. 510, subtracts the survival probabilities in the wrong order. Since \(x\mapsto w(t,x)=P(M(t)\ge x)\) is nonincreasing, \(w(t,m+r)-w(t,m-r)\le0\), whereas \(1-\varepsilon>0\). Reverse the subtraction to express the probability of the central interval.

Remark 2.3, pp. 513–514, first states convergence of \((M(nt)-v_0nt)/\sqrt{\sigma^2n}\) to standard Brownian motion, but later assigns the same standardized marginal an \(N(0,\sigma^2)\) limit. At fixed \(t\) the standard-Brownian marginal is \(N(0,t)\), and at \(t=1\) it is \(N(0,1)\). Scaling by \(\sqrt n\) instead yields variance \(\sigma^2t\). These are direct internal normalization inconsistencies. The main quenched tightness proof uses neither erroneous display.
# Assessment and limits

The corrected arguments preserve the theorem’s range and its dependence on \(v_0>v_c\), summable mixing, local regularity, positive bounded branching rates and finite offspring second moment. The zero-number theorem, quenched law of large numbers, mixing concentration and uniform normal-approximation inputs remain external dependencies; their full original PDFs were not inspected. Closed versus open Heaviside values at one point do not affect positive-time Brownian kernels, though that convention should be stated when applying the lower-semicontinuous-data formulation of Proposition 3.1.

The author publication page and arXiv metadata were checked. No separately verified correction addressing these specific displays was found in the bounded search; this is not a claim of exhaustive absence. Source, independent calculations, compiler and retained dependency payloads, and actual page inspections are bound in the support inventory. Scientific decision remains pending and human reviews are empty.
