report: Abstract: This review concerns the acquired 57-page arXiv version 2210.15047v2, dated 20 June 2024, by Francesco C. De Vecchi, Luca Fresta and Massimiliano Gubinelli. Two major, localized proof issues are established: the printed finite-dimensional stochastic-quantization identity has incompatible fermionic signs, and the local part of the graded flow need not satisfy the decay estimate used in its induction. Three further local defects concern Wick indexing, a cutoff definition and a claimed lower asymptotic. These findings do not establish that the final continuum existence or clustering theorems are false. The initial scientific decision remains pending independent review.
Author: Math2025 scientific review
Date: 29 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review of
A stochastic analysis of subcritical Euclidean fermionic field theories
# Scope, conventions and assessment

The reviewed source is [paper], arXiv v2, not a byte-verified copy of the 61-page published article, Annals of Probability 53(3), 906–966 (2025), DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1714. The official arXiv history says that v2 corrected proof errors and typos in the earlier version. The present findings refer to v2 itself; no independent formal erratum was located in the bounded metadata search, and no assertion of exhaustive absence is made.

All source body and appendix pages 1–54 were read, and bibliography entries on pp. 54–57 were examined. The analysis traced the Grassmann probability space, conditional expectations, stochastic calculus, truncated flow, localization, fixed-point argument, cutoff limits and correlation estimates. The source’s ambient state is positive on a \(C^*\)-algebra; its Grassmann observable algebra need not be closed under adjoints. Thus failure of a classical positive-probability interpretation is not counted as an error.

Throughout this report, source page numbers are PDF page numbers. Independent exact computations use reviewer-written exterior-algebra and CAR matrix calculations; no author code was executed. The two Major findings below concern core derivations. Neither is a counterexample to the final continuum Theorems 1.1 and 1.3.
# Problem 1: incompatible signs in stochastic quantization (Major)
## Source and hypotheses

Relevant locations are Definition 2.5 (p. 11), Definitions 2.15–2.16 (p. 13), Definition 3.1 (pp. 14–15), Lemma 3.7 and (3.11) (pp. 16–17), Proposition 3.8 (p. 18), Proposition 3.10 and Remark 3.11 (p. 18), and Theorem 3.12, (3.18)–(3.19) (pp. 19–20). The latter identity is used in the passage to Gibbs functionals; compare (3.30), p. 23, Remark 4.26, p. 43, Lemma 4.29, p. 45, and the generating-functional calculation on p. 48.

Use \(\mathfrak h=\mathbb C^2\), coordinate conjugation \(\Theta\), and \[J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 G_s=sJ,\quad 0\leq s\leq1,\qquad
 V=q e_1e_2,\quad q=\tfrac14.\] The left derivatives specified in the source give \(D_1V=q e_2,\ D_2V=-q e_1\). Its explicit row action (3.17) therefore gives \(JDV=-q(e_1,e_2)\). Choose a norm-compatible Grassmann Brownian motion with \(\omega(X_s^1X_t^2)=\min(s,t)\), zero initial field, and its usual past filtration.

For completeness these data are realizable in a positive ambient space. On the CAR Fock space over \(L^2([0,1];\mathbb C^2)\), set \(\Xi(h)=a^*(Jh)+a(\overline h)\) and \(X_s(f)=\Xi(\mathbf1_{[0,s]}f)\), with \(J\) acting componentwise. The vacuum covariance is the stated skew covariance, the fields jointly anticommute, and the vacuum conditional expectations onto the past CAR algebras are positive, unital bimodule maps with the tower property. Moreover \(\|\Xi(h)\|\leq2\|h\|\); this supplies norm compatibility and norm continuity. These are the actual hypotheses used here, not an assumption that an arbitrary classical Gaussian process is Grassmann-valued.
## A solution of the printed FBSDE with the wrong Gibbs law

Equation reference: eq:fbsde, eq:gibbs. Write \[a(s)=1-q(1-s),\qquad
 Y_s=\int_0^s a(r)^{-1}\,dX_r,\qquad
 \Psi_s=a(s)Y_s.\] Since \(a\geq3/4\), these are bounded, adapted, norm-continuous fields on the entire interval. \(Y\) is a martingale and \(\Psi_1=Y_1\), whence \(\mathbb E_s\Psi_1=Y_s\). Consequently \[d\Psi_s=qY_s\,ds+dX_s
       =-J\mathbb E_s[DV(\Psi_1)]\,ds+dX_s .\] This is exactly the sign of (3.18). Its terminal covariance is \[\omega(\Psi_1^1\Psi_1^2)
   =\int_0^1\frac{dr}{(1-q+qr)^2}
   =\frac1{1-q}=\frac43.                         \] On the other hand \(V^2=0\), \(\omega(X_1^1X_1^2)=1\), and the Gibbs functional asserted in (3.19), evaluated at \(P=e_1e_2\), is \[\frac{\omega(P(X_1)e^{V(X_1)})}{\omega(e^{V(X_1)})}
       =\frac1{1+q}=\frac45.                     \] The denominator is nonzero. Thus Theorem 3.12, with the printed conventions, fails already for an even quadratic potential in dimension two.

An exact four-dimensional CAR representation independently checks [eq:gibbs] (#eq:gibbs): take \(a_1=a\otimes I,\ a_2=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\otimes a\), where \(a=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), and \(\psi_1=a_1-a_2^*,\ \psi_2=a_2+a_1^*\). Their squares and anticommutator vanish and their vacuum ordered pairing is one. This calculation verifies the terminal algebra; the continuous-time construction above supplies the stochastic hypotheses.
## Location of the sign conflict and a second check

For the same \(P=e_1e_2\), the printed operator is \(D_J^2P=\sum J_{ij}\partial_i\partial_jP=-2\). Lemma 3.7’s plus-\(\tfrac12D_J^2\) drift would give expectation \(-t\), whereas the defining covariance gives \(+t\). Moving the odd first derivative past the odd increment in (3.11) requires a minus sign. The order cannot be repaired by silently changing the meaning of derivative composition: the Berezin calculation on p. 9 fixes it.

There is also a direct check of Proposition 3.10. The conditional exponential is \[U_s(\varphi)=1+q(1-s)+q\varphi_1\varphi_2,
 \qquad D\log U_s=\frac{q}{1+q(1-s)}D(\varphi_1\varphi_2).\] Its printed negative-\(G\) drift yields \[\omega(\Psi_1^1\Psi_1^2)
       =\int_0^1[1+q(1-r)]^2\,dr=\frac{61}{48},\] again different from \(4/5\). All normalizing factors are positive real numbers in this example.
## Counterevidence, repair and impact

Reversing that drift gives the correct \(4/5\) in this example. The source itself uses a plus-\(G\) drift in the generating-functional calculation on p. 48, evidence of a plausible intended convention. One can consistently change covariance or derivative conventions, but that requires changing the affected formulas together; it does not validate the incompatible formulas as printed.

The severity is Major because the finite-dimensional identification underlies the claimed Gibbs interpretation. A repair must synchronize the Itô rule, backward equation, effective potential, FBSDE and subsequent flow identities. Absolute-value analytic estimates might survive such a repair, but that has not been proved by this review. The continuum construction and final clustering assertions are not disproved by [eq:fbsde] (#eq:fbsde)–[eq:gibbs] (#eq:gibbs).
# Problem 2: the local graded estimate need not decay (Major)
## Source, allowed data and decisive calculation

The relevant locations are Definitions 4.2 and 4.5 (pp. 30–31), (4.11)–(4.18) and Theorem 4.13 (pp. 34–35), the last inequality of (4.23) (p. 36), and (4.24) and Corollary 4.15 (p. 37). The norm estimate is subsequently used in Proposition 4.20 (pp. 39–40).

Theorem 4.13 allows a nonzero local linear boundary value \(K^{(1)}\); it does not impose the particular cubic initial condition of Corollary 4.15. Choose \[\begin{gathered}
 d=1,\quad \gamma=\tfrac1{10},\quad \beta=\tfrac3{20},\quad
 \alpha=\tfrac{23}{50},\quad \kappa=\tfrac1{50},\\
 n=24,\quad \varepsilon=0,\quad K^{(1)}=mI,\quad K^{(3)}=0,
 \quad m=\tfrac14 .
 \end{gathered}\] Here \(I\) denotes the local identity kernel on the internal components. It is translation and reflection invariant, satisfies the degree-one antisymmetry condition (which is vacuous), and has the required finite initial norm since \(\alpha-\beta>0\). The five margins in (4.14)–(4.16) are respectively \[\tfrac1{100},\quad\tfrac7{100},\quad\tfrac{23}{50},
 \quad\tfrac{177}{100},\quad\tfrac{54}{25}.\] Thus none of the strict parameter assumptions is being dropped.

At zero spatial Fourier frequency the source covariance has the form \(\widehat G_s(0)=g(s)U\), where \(g(0)=0,\ g(\infty)=1\) and \(U^2=I\). On each charge block, the \(\Theta\)-real orthonormal basis \[u_1=(1,1)/\sqrt2,\qquad u_2=(i,-i)/\sqrt2\] turns the original \(U=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) into \(B=iJ\); in particular \(B^2=I\). This uses the actual model block, rather than substituting a covariance with a different square.

Equation reference: eq:local. All degrees \(k\geq3\) remain zero. The Laplacian of a linear map vanishes. The derivative component \(\mathrm{Ren}\) vanishes on constant spatial fields; the zero-frequency coefficient is therefore exactly the local coefficient. If \(A_\ell(s)\) denotes that coefficient in one block, the printed triangular equation and local boundary conditions give \[\frac{d A_{\ell+1}}{dg}
       =-\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}A_jBA_{\ell-j},\qquad
 A_0=mI,\qquad A_\ell(0)=0\quad(\ell\geq1).\] Induction, or differentiation, gives the exact solution \[A_\ell(s)=(-1)^\ell m^{\ell+1}g(s)^\ell B^\ell.   \] The reviewer checked the recurrence through order 24 with exact rational matrix algebra. For example \[A_{24}(\infty)=4^{-25}I\ne0,\qquad
 \alpha-\beta-24\kappa=-\tfrac{17}{100}.\] Already \(A_{16}(\infty)=4^{-17}I\ne0\) while \(\alpha-\beta-16\kappa=-1/100\).

The claimed (4.23)–(4.24) would bound these local coefficients by constants times \(2^{-17s/100}\) and \(2^{-s/100}\), respectively, tending to zero. The local operator norm dominates its action on constant fields. A derivative component cannot cancel that action. This contradicts [eq:local] (#eq:local) and proves failure of the uniform graded-norm induction for admissible boundary data.
## Counterevidence, repair and impact

The last integration in (4.23) runs from \(0\) to \(t\). When an integrable forcing has nonzero total integral, its primitive approaches a nonzero constant; it cannot be bounded by a purely decaying exponential. Bounds with a constant term, or a different boundary condition for high-order local coefficients, would avoid this particular mistake. Changing the overall contraction sign merely changes signs in [eq:local] (#eq:local), leaving the obstruction.

This example does not show nonexistence of the finite-order flow. Nor does it refute the special cubic initial data \(K^{(1)}=0,\ K^{(3)}=\lambda\psi^3\) in Corollary 4.15. It does refute the general estimate invoked to prove that corollary. A repair must treat the high-order local terms separately or establish the needed estimate for the actual cubic data by an additional argument, then revisit the norm input to the fixed-point proof. The Major rating concerns that central unsupported derivation, without asserting failure of the final continuum theorem.
# Three local defects
## Problem 3: Wick recursion omits the last variable (Minor)

Definition 2.16, p. 13, sums contractions over \(j=1,\ldots,n\) for a product of \(n+1\) variables. For \(n=1\) its only covariance is the self-covariance, which vanishes, so the displayed recursion gives \(:X_t^1X_t^2:=X_t^1X_t^2\). For the legitimate Brownian field above its expectation is \(t\), violating the martingale assertion of Proposition 2.17. The needed term is \(-G_t(e_1,e_2)\); with the printed sign convention the contraction index should range over \(j=2,\ldots,n+1\). This is a local indexing repair and is distinct from the calculus sign conflict in Problem 1. It does not independently refute a final theorem.
## Problem 4: the stated smooth cutoff cannot exist (Minor)

On p. 22 immediately before Definition 3.16, the source asks for a smooth nondecreasing function \(\min_\varepsilon(a)\) equal to \(a\) on \([0,A]\), \(A=\varepsilon^{-1}\), and equal to \(A\) on \([A+1,\infty)\). Monotonicity forces the function to be identically \(A\) on \([A,A+1]\). Its left derivative at \(A\) is one and its right derivative zero. Thus it is not even \(C^1\).

A smooth saturation can instead start before \(A\), or have a higher plateau. For example use derivative one up to \(A-1\), smoothly decrease the derivative to zero on \([A-1,A+1]\), with integral one on that interval, and keep the value \(A\) afterwards. A smooth symmetric transition realizes these conditions for \(A\geq1\). This changes the stated identity interval; the covariance and kernel bounds should be checked for the actual replacement. The defect is in the exact regularizer definition, not a demonstrated impossibility of the ultraviolet limit.
## Problem 5: the lower asymptotic needs a mass condition (Minor)

Theorem 1.3, p. 5, permits any \(\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\) with \(\|\chi\|_{L^1}=1\). Remark 1.4, p. 6, then uses the free two-point comparison \((\varepsilon\vee r)^{-2\gamma}\) to obtain a lower-order comparison for the interacting field. The stated test-function assumption does not imply nonzero integral.

Choose a nonconstant compactly supported smooth \(\varphi\) and \(\chi=\partial_1\varphi/\|\partial_1\varphi\|_{L^1}\). Then \(\int\chi=0\). Take a nonvanishing opposite-charge free covariance component \(K(r)\); this avoids the simpler zero pairing between equal charges. For \(0<2\gamma<d\), the source’s heat-kernel representation gives \(|\nabla^2K(z)|\leq C|z|^{-2\gamma-2}\) near zero. Double mean-zero cancellation and Taylor’s formula give, when \(\varepsilon\ll r\), \[\left|\int\chi(u)\chi(v)K(r+\varepsilon(v-u))\,du\,dv\right|
       \leq C\varepsilon^2 r^{-2\gamma-2}.\] With \(\varepsilon=r^2\) and \(r\downarrow0\), the ratio to \(r^{-2\gamma}\) tends to zero. Hence the free lower comparison used in the remark is false for its stated test-function class.

A nonnegative unit-mass mollifier and an explicit nonzero component pairing are plausible intended restrictions; the lower estimate and small-coupling constants must then be justified for that class. The upper difference bound in Theorem 1.3 is not contradicted by this cancellation example.
# Coverage and limits

Several structural checks support the intended framework. The covariance is \(\Theta\)-skew, the norm-compatible realization exists in a positive ambient CAR algebra, and the subcritical parameter constraints have nonempty interior when \(\gamma<\min(d/4,1)\). The additional \(\gamma<1\) restriction corresponds to the use of a mass counterterm without derivative counterterms. These checks do not repair Problems 1–2.

The review examined the kernel estimates, localization gain, weighted norms, finite-volume coupling, fixed-point bounds and claimed ultraviolet and infinite-volume passages. The external constructive-field-theory, functional-analysis and Besov-space results cited by the authors were not independently reproved, and no claim of exhaustive verification of every auxiliary estimate is made. The source’s restrictions on small coupling, regularity losses, cutoff order and the order of limits are retained. Neither missing code nor the absence of a classical probabilistic interpretation is treated as a defect.

The stored evidence includes exact rational calculations, the full hypothesis checks for the two core examples, source locators, and actual inspection of the evidence pages. The acquired arXiv version and the published version are kept distinct. Initial report completion is not independent scientific acceptance.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the 13-page arXiv version 2307.01162v2, dated 13 October 2023, by Barbara Dembin, Dor Elboim and Ron Peled. The perturbation and translation argument, quantitative influence bound, moment exponents and transversal estimate were checked. Two local errors in the written proof are identified and repaired: a claimed identity for exterior modified weights and an overlapping critical case in a geometric sum. Both are Minor; no false main theorem is demonstrated.
Author: Math2025 scientific review
Date: 29 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review of
On the influence of edges in first-passage percolation on \(\mathbb Z^d\)
# Scope and assumptions

The exact acquired source is [paper]. All 13 pages were read, including the bibliography on pp. 12–13; all source pages were inspected as images. The official arXiv history still lists v2 as the latest version. The later journal article is Annals of Probability 53(2), 544–556 (2025), DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1715. Equal page counts do not establish byte or content equivalence, and the review makes no such assertion. A bounded correction and supplement search located no distinct correction; this is not a proof that none exists.

The operative setting is \(d\geq2\), IID absolutely continuous weights on \([a,b]\), \(0<a<b<\infty\), and a strictly positive uniform density lower bound. The sentence before (1.2) uses \(\beta\) where the display uses \(\alpha\); the intended positive lower-bound parameter is retained here. Write \(n=\|v\|_2\), \(p_e=\mathbb P(e\in\gamma(0,v))\). Positivity, boundedness and atomlessness have distinct roles: they give deterministic length control, bounded connecting-path costs, and almost sure uniqueness, respectively.

The paper proves a bound on the number of influential edges. It does not resolve the location of all exceptional edges or the BKS midpoint problem in \(d\geq3\). Figure 1 and the exponent discussion on pp. 3–5 are explicitly heuristic and were not treated as additional theorems.
# Problem 1: exterior weights are not unchanged as defined (Minor)
## Source and counterexample

The issue occurs in the proof of Lemma 4.3, p. 8, immediately after \(t_e^+=g_{\tau_e}^+(t_e)\). The text asserts that \(t_e^+=t_e\) outside \([-n^2,n^2]^d\), citing localization of the geodesic. However Proposition 4.1, p. 7, permits globally positive, summable smooth weights \(q\), with \(\tau_e=q_e/\|q\|_2\). The exponential envelope subsequently used on p. 10 has exactly that property.

For a concrete admissible example take \(G\) uniform on \([1,2]\) and \[q_e=\exp\{-\|c(e)-c(e_0)\|_2/\log n\},\qquad
 g_\tau^+(w)=1+\Phi\!\left(\Phi^{-1}(w-1)+\tau\right)
 \quad(1<w<2),\] with endpoints fixed. Here \(c(e)\) is the edge center and \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function. The ratio condition (4.1) holds because \(e^{-2}\leq q_e/q_{e'}\leq e^2\) at distances at most \(2\log n\). The vector \(q\) belongs to \(\ell^1\cap\ell^2\), and every \(\tau_e>0\). These maps satisfy Lemma 2.1, including its upper increment bound and lower increment on Gaussian compact sets. For every exterior edge, \(g_{\tau_e}^+(w)>w\) throughout \(1<w<2\). Thus the asserted exterior identity is false almost surely in this example. Localization of a geodesic does not set the perturbation parameters to zero.
## Complete local repair and impact

Let \(W\) be a finite edge window containing every possible geodesic from \(0\) to \(v\) for environments in \([a,b]\), and define \(s_e=\tau_e\mathbf1_W(e)\), \(t_e^+=g_{s_e}^+(t_e)\). Such a window exists because \[a|\gamma(0,v)|\leq T(0,v)\leq b\|v\|_1.\] For large \(n\) one may use the source’s box. The modified weights remain in \([a,b]\), so the same localization applies to \(\gamma_0^+\). Moreover \(\sum s_e^2\leq1\), and the finite-dimensional change-of-measure estimate in Lemma 2.1 applies directly.

On \(\gamma_0^+\), \(s_e=\tau_e\), preserving the lower estimate (4.5) and the logarithmic block argument. For a shifted geodesic it is enough that \[T_h^+\leq T_h+C_0\sum_{e\in\gamma_h}s_e
          \leq T_h+C_0 f(\gamma_h).\] The triangle inequalities (4.7)–(4.8) remain valid since all weights are still at most \(b\). In particular, \(\gamma_h\) need not be contained in \(W\). This proves the required repair of Lemma 4.3 with the same type of constants.

The finite-window interpretation is plausible intended counterevidence: the authors explicitly appeal to geodesic localization, and all later bounds need only the localized perturbation just described. The correction is nevertheless a change to the defined coupling. Its severity is Minor because the complete repair uses existing hypotheses and preserves Proposition 4.1 and its applications. No final theorem is refuted.
# Problem 2: the critical geometric-sum case overlaps (Minor)

The last display on p. 11, following (5.2), bounds \[S_{j_0}(\beta)=\sum_{j=1}^{j_0}2^{j(p-\beta)},
 \qquad p=\frac{2d}{d-1}.\] Its first case includes \(1<\beta\leq p\) and bounds the sum by a constant times \(2^{j_0(p-\beta)}\); its next case separately treats \(\beta=p\) by \(Cj_0\). At \(\beta=p\), \[S_{j_0}(p)=j_0,\qquad 2^{j_0(p-p)}=1,\] so the first claimed bound is false as \(j_0\to\infty\), even allowing the constant to depend on the fixed \(\beta\). Here \(j_0=\lfloor\frac{d-1}{d+1}\log_2n-d\log_2\log n\rfloor\) does tend to infinity.

Replace \(\beta\leq p\) in the first case by \(\beta<p\). The separate critical row already gives the required logarithm, and Corollary 1.3 on p. 3 already states the correct critical result. Thus this is an endpoint error in an intermediate display, with a one-symbol repair and no changed final bound.
# Independent checks of the main argument
## Perturbation lemma

The needed version of Lemma 2.1 can be derived under (1.2) without assuming an unverified strengthening of its cited reference. Let \(F\) be the distribution function of \(G\) and \(H=F^{-1}\circ\Phi\). Then \(H\) is increasing and Lipschitz, with constant at most \(1/(\alpha\sqrt{2\pi})\). Define \(g_\tau^+(H(z))=H(z+\tau)\). At almost every \(z\), \(H'(z)>0\). Consequently \[\inf_{0<t\leq1}\frac{H(z+t)-H(z)}t>0\] there: use the positive derivative near zero and strict monotonicity and continuity on the remaining compact interval. The level sets of this infimum give the sets \(B_\delta\) whose \(G\)-mass tends to one.

For a finite Gaussian shift, let \(\mu\) be standard Gaussian measure, \(
u\) its translate by \(	au\), and \(L=d
u/d\mu=\exp(	au\cdot x-\|	au\|_2^2/2)\). Hölder’s inequality under \(
u\), with conjugate exponent \(p/(p-1)\), gives \[
u(A)\geq
 \exp\!\left\{- rac{p\|	au\|_2^2}{2(p-1)}ight\}\mu(A)^p.\] Transporting coordinatewise by \(H\) proves the stated measure comparison. The positive derivative assertion follows from the absolute continuity and positive finite density of \(F\), together with the Lipschitz inverse; no upper uniform bound on the density is required.
## Translation, rare events and dimension

Theorem 1.1’s proof on pp. 6–7 turns a positive-probability gain of order \(\sqrt{|A_\epsilon|}\) into a lower bound of order \(|A_\epsilon|\) for translated intersections within that radius. A geodesic’s segment between its first and last visits to a ball of radius \(r\) has length at most \(C(r+1)\). Summation over translations therefore yields \[|A_\epsilon|^{1+d/2}\leq C|A_\epsilon|^{3/2},\] which bounds \(|A_\epsilon|\) when \(d\geq2\). Small radii and bounded \(n\) are absorbed into constants; finiteness of \(A_\epsilon\) follows already from deterministic length localization.

For Claim 4.2, it suffices to use simple paths, as all positive-weight geodesics are simple. Directly summing the geometric union bound gives \[(2n^2+1)^d\sum_{k\geq\lceil\log n\rceil}
                 (4d)^k e^{-10dk}\leq n^{-5}\] for sufficiently large \(n\). The displayed binomial law in the source can be read as the stochastic lower comparison supplied by \(G(B_{\delta_0})\geq1-e^{-20d}\).

The level argument (4.9) is also sound: failure at every level would give \(\mu\leq\mu/3+\mu/4<\mu\). The exponent \(3/2\) in Lemma 4.3, the ball volume, and \(r=c3^k\mu\) combine into \[\mu^d\leq C(8/3^d)^k\sum_e\tau_e,\qquad k\geq-1 .\] Since \(8/3^d<1\) for \(d\geq2\), this factor is uniformly bounded. The error \(n^{-5}\) is negligible uniformly over \(k\leq\log n\).
## Quantitative and transversal conclusions

Put \(p=2d/(d-1)\) and \(A=d(d+1)/(d-1)\). The exponential envelope has \(\sum q_e\leq C(\log n)^d|A_\epsilon|\) and \(q_e\leq1\). Proposition 4.1 consequently gives \[(\epsilon|A_\epsilon|)^d
   \leq C\big((\log n)^d|A_\epsilon|\big)^{(d+1)/2},\] recovering Theorem 1.2 exactly. Combining \(N(t)\leq\min(Cn/t,C(\log n)^At^{-p})\) at \(t_0=n^{-(d-1)/(d+1)}(\log n)^d\) recovers all three cases of Corollary 1.3. The case \(\beta=1\) follows directly from expected geodesic length, without a divergent endpoint integral. The reviewer checked these exponent identities with exact symbolic algebra.

For Theorem 1.4, a shell covering of the smoothed finite cylinder gives \(\sum q_e\leq C\ell r^{d-1}\) when \(r,\ell\geq\log n\). The resulting expected tube-edge count is \(Cr^{(d^2-1)/(2d)}\ell^{(d+1)/(2d)}\). Setting \(r=c\ell^{1/(d+1)}\) gives a linear bound in \(\ell\); the assumption \(\ell\geq(\log n)^{d+2}\) ensures \(r\geq\log n\) for sufficiently large \(n\).

One can keep endpoint bookkeeping explicit: choose \(c\) so the expected tube-edge count is at most \(\ell/4\). A path crossing the slab has at least \(\ell-1\) slab vertices, and passing between vertices and incident edges costs at most one further endpoint. Thus the expected number of exterior slab vertices is at least \(3\ell/4-2\geq\ell/2\) once \(\ell\geq8\). Increasing \(n_0\) supplies this condition. This checks the precise vertex formulation rather than identifying edge and vertex counts.
# Limits and disposition

The review checked the main theorems under (1.2). The proposed extensions to \(a=0\), more general Lipschitz images and lighter-tailed distributions in Section 1.2 were not independently established here. Historical comparisons with earlier BKS and transversal-fluctuation results were not re-proved from the cited original papers. No original external-reference PDF inspection is claimed. No missing code was treated as a defect, and no author code was run. The quantitative checks and the explicit repairs support a Minor assessment; initial completion remains distinct from independent acceptance.

report: Abstract: This review concerns Stefan Junk’s 36-page arXiv version 2202.02907v3. The exceptional-site construction, conditional concentration argument, quadratic variation and moment-growth proof were examined. Six groups of locally repairable issues are identified, including an auxiliary lower bound at zero temperature parameter, an incorrect moment exponent calculation, and missing qualifications in background statements. Explicit counterexamples and repairs are supplied. These findings are classified as one Major and five Minor findings. The Major finding concerns an invalid core moment-growth derivation; no false main theorem is demonstrated.
Author: Math2025 scientific review
Date: 29 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review of
Fluctuations of partition functions of directed polymers
in weak disorder beyond the \(L^2\)-phase
# Reviewed version, scope and dependencies

The source is [paper], arXiv v3 dated 10 July 2023, with internal date 11 July. Its entire body and appendix, pp. 1–34, were read; the bibliography on pp. 35–36 was read as entries. All 36 source pages were inspected as images. The later journal article is Annals of Probability 53(2), 557–596 (2025), DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1716. The acquired 36-page preprint is not certified equivalent to that 40-page article. The official arXiv history acknowledges a correction to Theorem 1.4(i) in v2 and additional proof details in v3. This review addresses v3 itself and does not identify its findings with that earlier correction.

The model assumes IID real weights with all absolute exponential moments, nearest-neighbor simple random walk, and \(\beta\geq0\). Write \[\eta_{t,x}=e^{\beta\omega_{t,x}-\lambda(\beta)},\qquad
 W_n=E^{\rm SRW}\prod_{t=1}^n\eta_{t,X_t},\qquad
 a(p)=\lim_n n^{-1}\log\mathbb E W_n^p .\] Weak disorder means \(W_\infty>0\) almost surely. The critical indices are \(p^*=\sup\{p\geq1:\sup_n\mathbb E W_n^p<\infty\}\) and \(q^*=\inf\{p\geq1:a(p)>0\}\). The main theorem additionally requires an upper bounded environment and \(\beta>\beta_{L^2}\). These restrictions have different roles from the broader hypotheses printed for Theorem 1.4.

The review checked the geometry and independence of the backward cones, the signed test function, the moment and stopping-time inequalities, and all parameter regimes used by the proof. The relevant construction in Yoshida’s author-corrected reference [yoshida] was checked on pp. 3–8 and 13–18: its matrix assumptions specialize to the polymer, and \(\gamma=e^{\lambda(2\beta)-2\lambda(\beta)}>1/\pi_d\) supplies the finite convolution kernel used for the drift estimate. This construction does not require strong disorder. Its bounded-process and conditional second-moment estimates justify the particular dependency used here. This is a check of that dependency, not a review of every result in Yoshida’s paper.

A later paper by Junk and Lacoin [tail], pp. 3–6, 8–9, 14 and 25, provides relevant counterevidence: it states \(p^*>1\) and \(p^*=q^*\) throughout weak disorder, uses the normalized overshoot factor, and extends the fluctuation result. Its hypotheses and indicated corollary proofs were checked; its complete proof was not independently reproduced. The findings below therefore distinguish an incomplete or false displayed step from a false fluctuation theorem.
# Problem 1: the parameter range needs two qualifications (Minor)
## Zero effective disorder in Theorem 1.4(i)

The model permits \(\beta=0\) (p. 2), while Theorem 1.4(i), p. 6, (19), assumes only \(d\geq3\), weak disorder and a nonzero \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)\). Its following paragraph expressly removes the main theorem’s \(\beta>\beta_{L^2}\) restriction. Take any nonconstant bounded IID environment and set \(\beta=0\). Then, exactly, \[W_n^{0,x}=1,\qquad \mathcal X_n^f=0,\qquad a(p)=0,\qquad q^*=\infty .\] With \(1/\infty=0\), the probability in (19) is one for every \(n\), whereas the asserted limit is zero. Without this reciprocal convention the displayed bound is undefined. The same obstruction occurs for a constant environment at positive \(\beta\), also not excluded explicitly.

This refutes the literal auxiliary theorem at a permitted boundary. It does not refute Theorem 1.1, whose beyond-\(L^2\) condition excludes this case. The proof on p. 19 itself invokes a nonconstant centered environment factor, showing the intended qualification. One should require nonconstant \(\eta\) for the nontrivial lower bound. Then \(q^*<\infty\) follows directly: choose \(a>0\) with \(\mathbb P(\eta\geq1+a)>0\), and a finite box whose killed-walk spectral radius \(\rho\) satisfies \(\rho(1+a)>1\). The event that every weight in the box is good through time \(n\) has probability \(p_0^{|B|n}\), and on it \(W_n\geq c[\rho(1+a)]^n\). A sufficiently large fixed moment consequently grows exponentially.
## Finite critical points are not automatic

Theorem A(i)–(ii), p. 2, asserts finite positive critical points under the standing assumptions. Nondegeneracy alone does not suffice. Let \(\pi_d<1\) be the positive-time meeting probability of two independent walks in \(d\geq3\), and set \(r=(1+\pi_d)/2\). Choose \(\omega\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\mathbb P(\omega=1)=r\). This law is nonconstant, bounded and has every exponential moment. For \(t=e^{-\beta}\in[0,1]\), \[R_\beta=e^{\lambda(2\beta)-2\lambda(\beta)}
 =\frac{r+(1-r)t^2}{[r+(1-r)t]^2}\leq\frac1r.\] Indeed the cleared numerator of this inequality is \((1-r)t[2r+(1-2r)t]\geq0\). The number \(L\) of positive-time meetings is geometric with \(\mathbb P(L=k)=(1-\pi_d)\pi_d^k\), by transience and the renewal property. Thus \[\sup_n\mathbb E W_n^2
 \leq \mathbb E R_\beta^L
 \leq \frac{1-\pi_d}{1-\pi_d/r}<\infty\] for every finite \(\beta\). The \(L^2\) martingale limit has expectation one; the zero-one law then gives weak disorder at every \(\beta\). Both critical points can be infinite.

The correction is to allow extended critical values and qualify assertions of a finite strict gap. The later formulation in [tail], p. 3, explicitly permits infinite critical values. For this example the beyond-\(L^2\) hypothesis is empty, so it is not a counterexample to the main result. The impact is on the stated model range and background theorem, with a complete boundary diagnosis.
# Problem 2: the Gaussian normalization is inconsistent (Minor)

Theorem A(iii), p. 2, scales the endpoint by \(\sqrt n\) and calls \(\varphi\) the standard normal density. The same convention is used in (27), p. 10, and in Lemma 2.6, pp. 13–15. A nearest-neighbor walk on \(\mathbb Z^d\) has one-step covariance \(I_d/d\). At \(\beta=0\), the bounded continuous test \(f(x)=\cos x_1\), permitted in Theorem A(iii), gives \[E\cos(X_n^{(1)}/\sqrt n)
 =\left[1-\frac{1-\cos(1/\sqrt n)}d\right]^n
 \longrightarrow e^{-1/(2d)},\] instead of the printed standard-Gaussian value \(e^{-1/2}\). This is an exact characteristic-function calculation; the independent numeric check in \(d=3\) converges to \(0.8464817249\), whereas the latter value is \(0.6065306597\).

Use \[\varphi_d(x)=\left(\frac d{2\pi}\right)^{d/2}e^{-d|x|^2/2}\] throughout these displays, or consistently rescale the walk. The nonvanishing Fourier-transform argument used to choose \(z\) still works for \(\varphi_d\). For a signed \(f\), \(z\) must be chosen again with \((f*\varphi_d)(z)\ne0\); the old choice for a different covariance need not work. The existence argument and all polynomial fluctuation exponents survive. An intended informal use of standard would explain the notation but does not make the literal normalization correct.
# Problem 3: Proposition 2.1 overstates the fractional domain (Minor)

Proposition 2.1(i)–(ii), p. 8, gives \(a(p)\in[0,\lambda(p\beta)-p\lambda(\beta)]\) and a nondecreasing function on \(\mathbb R_+\). Its proof explicitly includes \(p\in[0,1]\) and says the section does not require weak disorder. The nonnegative bounds are valid for \(p\geq1\); for \(0<p<1\), Jensen’s inequality gives instead \[\lambda(p\beta)-p\lambda(\beta)\leq a(p)\leq0.\] The printed interval can be empty for a nonconstant environment.

For an actual failure of monotonicity, take \(d=1\), standard Gaussian weights, \(\beta=4\), and \(p=1/2\). All standing exponential moments exist. Expanding over \(2^n\) paths and using \((\sum_i z_i)^p\leq\sum_i z_i^p\) gives \[\mathbb E W_n^p
 \leq \exp\{n[(1-p)\log2+\lambda(p\beta)-p\lambda(\beta)]\},
 \qquad
 -2\leq a(1/2)\leq\tfrac12\log2-2<0.\] Yet \(a(0)=a(1)=0\), so \(a\) is not nondecreasing on \(\mathbb R_+\). The superadditive argument supplies existence of the fractional limit. Restrict the nonnegative and monotonicity claims to \([1,\infty)\) and state the reversed fractional bounds separately. This is also the plausible intended reading: the later \(q^*\) argument uses \(p\geq1\). No failure of that argument or of the main theorem follows.
# Problem 4: repair the general lower-bound proof (Minor)
## The unstated moment assumption and its replacement

Lemma 2.6, p. 13, assumes weak disorder but immediately chooses \(p\in(1,p^*)\). This is not justified by the acquired paper’s stated general hypotheses: pp. 2–3 and 6–7 explicitly distinguish weak disorder from \(p^*>1\). Its use of Hölder on p. 15 also requires the bad event \(A_{t,x}^c\), rather than the printed good event. For the main theorem, the upper-bound assumption and Theorem B already provide \(p^*>1\). The later result [tail] supplies another reason not to regard this gap as a false theorem.

The following replacement proves the needed step under uniform integrability alone. Put \(c=|(f*\varphi_d)(z)|>0\), retain the good CLT event \(A_{t,x}\), and write \[b_n=\sup_{t,x}\mathbb P(A_{t,x}^c)\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 u_n=\sup_{t,x}\mathbb E[W_t\mathbf1_{A_{t,x}^c}].\] The supremum uses the source’s space-time window, enlarged by the \(o(n)\) and \(o(\sqrt n)\) shifts from \(\ell_n\). For every \(R>0\), \[u_n\leq Rb_n+\sup_t\mathbb E[W_t\mathbf1_{\{W_t>R\}}]\longrightarrow0,\] first choosing \(R\) large, then \(n\) large. Let \(h_n=\sqrt{u_n}+n^{-1}\). Conditionally on the last \(\ell_n\) layers, the endpoint probabilities \(\mu_x\) sum to one and are independent of the older variables. Consequently \[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_x\mu_xW_x\mathbf1_{A_x^c}\,\middle|\,
             \text{last layers}\right]\leq u_n .\] Markov’s inequality bounds its probability of exceeding \(h_n\) by \(u_n/h_n\leq\sqrt{u_n}\); the corresponding bad signed-\(f\) sum is bounded with the additional factor \(\|f\|_\infty\). On good sites the normalized \(f\) averages have a common sign and absolute value at least \(c/2\). The argument in (44)–(47) therefore reduces to a lower-tail event for \(\sum_x\mu_xW_x\) at a threshold \(C(h_n+n^{-\varepsilon/8})\to0\). Lemma 2.3 and \(\inf_tW_t>0\) almost surely under weak disorder finish the estimate. Only \(p_n\to0\), without a rate, is needed for the later choice of \(N_n\).
## Signed amplitudes and geometric details

In the proof of (55), pp. 19–20, the concentration scale and the event for \(\widehat Z_k\) omit its absolute value. For a nonzero nonpositive \(f\), the coefficients are nonpositive, so \(\{\widehat Z_k\leq\text{positive threshold}\}\) is automatic. It cannot imply the subsequent small-absolute-amplitude event. Use \(Q_{cY}(u)=Q_Y(u/|c|)\) for \(c\ne0\), and replace the scale and event by \(|\widehat Z_k|\). The already absolute truncation-error estimate then supplies the intended conclusion for either sign.

The following local corrections preserve this proof’s power estimates. In Section 2 use \(\xi_q=d/2-(d+2)/(2q^*)\) until equality \(p^*=q^*\) is established; the printed \(\xi\) was defined through \(p^*\). Before (35), p. 12, choose \(\mathbb P(\inf_mW_m>2a)>3/4\), which weak disorder permits, to obtain the stated \(1/2\) bound. On pp. 15–16 the number of nearby spatial grid points is at most \[C\left(1+\frac{n^{(1-\delta)/2}}{\ell_n}\right)^d,\] rather than the printed bound linear in the radius. Dividing by \(|S_n|\asymp n^{d/2}/\ell_n^d\) gives \(O(n^{-d\delta/2})\); hence the same conditioning geometric sum is eventually at most two. The inclusion on p. 18 is \(E_n\subseteq\widehat E_n\).

In (64), p. 21, enlarging visits to near visits can leave an extra \(\eta\) in the path energy. Increase the integration constant to cover both \(\mathbb E|\eta-1|\) and \(\mathbb E[\eta|\eta-1|]\). These moments are finite. The selection-density formula on p. 22 must retain the chosen site’s good-event indicator and the translated time block. That indicator is fixed on the integrated coordinates; the other factors decrease, preserving the product-measure FKG inequality. The correct heat-kernel factor is \(C(\Delta t)^{-d/2}\exp(-c|\Delta x|^2/\Delta t)\). Since the construction gives \(|\Delta x|^2/\Delta t\geq c n^{5\delta/6}\), polynomial factors are still dominated. These corrections support the conditional-independent singleton decomposition and its negligible multiple-visit error. The complete arguments and exact locators are retained with the evidence.

The dependency is the lower bound in Theorem 1.4(i), and thence the main theorem after \(p^*=q^*\). The explicit repairs and later moment result limit severity: the written proof needs correction, but no nondegenerate positive-\(\beta\) counterexample to its conclusion has been obtained.
# Problem 5: the moment-growth exponent and renewal indices (Major)

Lemma 4.7, p. 32, obtains \(C\alpha^{-\lambda(2+\eta)k}\), then sets \(\lambda=p^*(1-\eta/2)\) to claim \(C\alpha^{-2(p^*+\delta)k}\) with \(\delta=\eta^2p^*/2>0\). But the exact calculation is \[\lambda(2+\eta)=p^*(2-\eta^2/2)<2p^*.\] Thus this bound is weaker than the scale it must beat. For example \(p^*=3/2,\eta=1/2\) gives power \(45/16<3\). The independently executed symbolic check confirms the identity; it is not a numerical approximation.

For every \(p^*>1\) and \(0<\eta<1\), set \[L=\max\left\{1,\frac{2p^*}{2+\eta}\right\},\qquad
 \lambda=\frac{p^*+L}{2},\qquad
 \delta=\frac{\lambda(2+\eta)-2p^*}{2}>0.\] Then \(1<\lambda<p^*\), so Doob’s inequality supplies the finite maximal moment. Apply the two stopping-time estimates to the joint event \(\{\sigma_i<\infty,\tau(\alpha^{2k})<\infty\}\), rather than its incorrectly labeled marginal, and take the union over \(i\). This proves (93) with corrected constants.

In the proof of Theorem 1.5, p. 33, further choose \[\eta=\min\left\{\frac{\varepsilon}{2(p^*+\varepsilon+1)},
                   \frac{p^*-1}{2}\right\}.\] This makes the subsequent \(\lambda=p^*-\eta\) admissible. Since \(\sigma<\tau(\alpha^{l+1})\), the remaining gain used for (95) is \(\alpha^{2k-l-1}\); the omitted factor only changes a constant. The renewal variables must also accumulate their increments: \[\begin{split}
 \sigma_{i+1}&=\sigma_i+\sigma\circ\theta_{\sigma_i,Z_i},\\
 Z_{i+1}&=Z_i+Z\circ\theta_{\sigma_i,Z_i}.
 \end{split}\] The printed definitions omit these additions, although (97) uses absolute times and positions.

With these corrections, successive durations and relative locations use fresh independent time layers. If the first \(\lfloor n/T\rfloor\) durations are at most \(T\), their cumulative time is at most \(n\). Each contributes at least \(c_8\alpha^{l-k\eta}\), and the remaining future infimum contributes a fixed positive factor with probability at least \(1/2\). Equations (95)–(96) then give a moment-growth base \(Ck^{-1}\alpha^{k\varepsilon/2}>1\) for large \(k\), preserving the conclusion of Theorem 1.5 conditional on its localization and tail lemmas. These invalid steps materially interrupt the core derivation: the printed exponent cannot make the bad-event probability smaller than the \(\alpha^{-2kp^*}\) lower-tail scale used on p. 33. Thus the acquired proof of Theorem 1.5, and its use to identify the main fluctuation exponent, requires correction. This is Major under a calibration that includes invalid core derivations; proving the final theorem false is not required. The admissible replacement and cumulative renewal construction above repair this segment. The later \(p^*=q^*\) result in [tail] is counterevidence to a false-conclusion claim, not validation of the printed proof.
# Problem 6: upper-bounded weights require normalized constants (Minor)

On p. 27, Lemma 4.3 uses \(W_{n+1}\leq e^{\beta K}W_n\) and \(\alpha=2e^{\beta K}\). The actual bound under \(\omega\leq K\) is \[W_{n+1}\leq MW_n,\qquad M=e^{\beta K-\lambda(\beta)}.\] No centering or \(\lambda(\beta)\geq0\) assumption appears in pp. 1–3. This is not remedied by the upper-bound hypothesis alone. From any nondegenerate admissible model in the intended weak-disorder, beyond-\(L^2\) range, shift the weights by their finite upper bound. All normalized polymer quantities and disorder regimes remain unchanged, but the weights become nonpositive. Since \(W_1\) is nonconstant with mean one, \(\mathbb P(W_1>1+r)>0\) for some \(r>0\). Any \(0<K<\log(1+r)/\beta\) is now an eligible positive upper bound, and the displayed \(n=0\) inequality fails on that event. An executed two-point-law calculation illustrates the same normalization failure; it is not asserted to be a beyond-\(L^2\) parameter witness.

Set \(\alpha=2M\). The overshoot used in (79) is then correctly \(W_{\tau(\alpha^{i-1})}\leq M\alpha^{i-1}=\alpha^i/2\). Also \(0<H_nW_{n-1}\leq1\) gives the valid lower increment bound \(-1\), rather than the printed \(-\alpha^{-1}\). Bounded increments and the quadratic-variation estimates still hold. The exponential-supermartingale step follows directly from the bounded Taylor remainder and conditional mean-zero increments.

In Appendix (98), p. 34, replace \(e^{\beta K}\) by \(M\) as well. The same contradiction supplies an adequate positive tail constant \(\tfrac12M^{-p^*}\), or \(\tfrac12M^{-2}\) when \(p^*<2\). This diagnoses the proof’s normalization; it does not independently disprove the printed tail constant. The later overshoot formula [tail], (2.11), uses precisely the normalized factor.

A related repair to the finite moment calculation on pp. 31–32 is to retain the walk transition probability and use \[A(x)=\frac1{2d}\sum_{|y|_1=1}\eta_{m,x+y}^2 .\] Jensen gives \(\mathbb EA^4\leq\mathbb E\eta^8\) and \(\mathbb E(\sum_x\mu_x\eta_x)^{-8}\leq\mathbb E\eta^{-8}\). Cauchy–Schwarz consequently yields \[\mathbb E(\mathcal R_m^2\mid\mathcal F_{m-1})
 \leq e^{[\lambda(8\beta)+\lambda(-8\beta)]/2}\mathcal R_{m-1}^2.\] This is finite under (1), and is stronger than the required constant. These repairs preserve the route through Lemmas 4.3–4.5. The issue concerns stated constants and normalization, not a demonstrated failure of Theorem 1.5.
# Positive checks and limits of the conclusion

The quadratic variation (69) was independently recovered by conditioning on the next IID environment layer. For the upper bound, the exact finite support is contained in \([-n-L\sqrt n,n+L\sqrt n]^d\), still of order \(n^d\); a maximal moderate-deviation estimate controls the remote portion. The level sum yields power \((d+2)/p\) for \(p\leq2\) and \(1+d/2\) for \(p>2\), up to an arbitrarily small loss. One must retain the dropped \(d\delta\) in the last \(p^*>2\) display on p. 25 and shrink \(\delta\); for \(p^*=\infty\), choose a finite \(p>2\). Stopping before the next predictable-variation threshold and applying Markov to the square gives both tails in (21).

The appendix’s homogenization argument also checks: with \(N=\lfloor n^{1/3}\rfloor\), uniform integrability controls the truncation and the difference \(W_n-W_N\). The nearby-pair contribution is \(O(M^2N^dn^{-d/2})=O(M^2n^{-d/6})\), which vanishes at fixed \(M\); the distant pairs contribute the squared truncation bias.

The primary reference and later-result checks constrain the findings, but do not certify every historical theorem used by the paper. Publisher full-text access was unsuccessful, and no exhaustive absence of later corrections is claimed. No author code was executed. Problem 5 is Major because its wrong exponent invalidates a core probability comparison used to establish \(p^*=q^*\); its explicit repair does not validate the original derivation. Problems 1–4 and 6 remain Minor in their stated scope: the parameter and fractional-moment qualifications, covariance, signs, geometric counts and normalized constants have the bounded impacts and repairs described above. In Problem 4 the missing moment implication concerns the broader auxiliary range, while the main bounded-environment hypotheses already supply it. The auxiliary boundary assertion is false as printed; the main nondegenerate beyond-\(L^2\) theorem has not been refuted. Independent focused acceptance has checked these existing findings and corrected the severity of Problem 5. Scientific disposition remains pending.

problems.title: The auxiliary lower bound and finite critical points require qualifications
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: # Problem 1: the parameter range needs two qualifications (Minor)
claim: Recorded check: The auxiliary lower bound and finite critical points require qualifications

IID real environment with all absolute exponential moments; nearest-neighbor simple random walk. d >= 3; weak disorder; nonzero continuous compactly supported test f. Theorem 1.4 explicitly drops upper-boundedness and beta > beta_L2; beta=0 remains permitted.
analysis: The model permits \(\beta=0\) (p. 2), while Theorem 1.4(i), p. 6, (19), assumes only \(d\geq3\), weak disorder and a nonzero \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)\). Its following paragraph expressly removes the main theorem’s \(\beta>\beta_{L^2}\) restriction. Take any nonconstant bounded IID environment and set \(\beta=0\). Then, exactly, \[W_n^{0,x}=1,\qquad \mathcal X_n^f=0,\qquad a(p)=0,\qquad q^*=\infty .\] With \(1/\infty=0\), the probability in (19) is one for every \(n\), whereas the asserted limit is zero. Without this reciprocal convention the displayed bound is undefined. The same obstruction occurs for a constant environment at positive \(\beta\), also not excluded explicitly.

This refutes the literal auxiliary theorem at a permitted boundary. It does not refute Theorem 1.1, whose beyond-\(L^2\) condition excludes this case. The proof on p. 19 itself invokes a nonconstant centered environment factor, showing the intended qualification. One should require nonconstant \(\eta\) for the nontrivial lower bound. Then \(q^*<\infty\) follows directly: choose \(a>0\) with \(\mathbb P(\eta\geq1+a)>0\), and a finite box whose killed-walk spectral radius \(\rho\) satisfies \(\rho(1+a)>1\). The event that every weight in the box is good through time \(n\) has probability \(p_0^{|B|n}\), and on it \(W_n\geq c[\rho(1+a)]^n\). A sufficiently large fixed moment consequently grows exponentially.

Theorem A(i)–(ii), p. 2, asserts finite positive critical points under the standing assumptions. Nondegeneracy alone does not suffice. Let \(\pi_d<1\) be the positive-time meeting probability of two independent walks in \(d\geq3\), and set \(r=(1+\pi_d)/2\). Choose \(\omega\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\mathbb P(\omega=1)=r\). This law is nonconstant, bounded and has every exponential moment. For \(t=e^{-\beta}\in[0,1]\), \[R_\beta=e^{\lambda(2\beta)-2\lambda(\beta)}
 =\frac{r+(1-r)t^2}{[r+(1-r)t]^2}\leq\frac1r.\] Indeed the cleared numerator of this inequality is \((1-r)t[2r+(1-2r)t]\geq0\). The number \(L\) of positive-time meetings is geometric with \(\mathbb P(L=k)=(1-\pi_d)\pi_d^k\), by transience and the renewal property. Thus \[\sup_n\mathbb E W_n^2
 \leq \mathbb E R_\beta^L
 \leq \frac{1-\pi_d}{1-\pi_d/r}<\infty\] for every finite \(\beta\). The \(L^2\) martingale limit has expectation one; the zero-one law then gives weak disorder at every \(\beta\). Both critical points can be infinite.

The correction is to allow extended critical values and qualify assertions of a finite strict gap. The later formulation in [tail], p. 3, explicitly permits infinite critical values. For this example the beyond-\(L^2\) hypothesis is empty, so it is not a counterexample to the main result. The impact is on the stated model range and background theorem, with a complete boundary diagnosis.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: At beta=0 with any nonconstant bounded IID environment, W_n=1, X_n^f=0, a(p)=0, q*=infinity. With 1/infinity=0 the probability in (19) is one rather than tending to zero; without that convention the bound is undefined. Independently, choose omega in {0,1}, P(omega=1)=r=(1+pi_d)/2. The exact ratio R_beta=[r+(1-r)e^(-2beta)]/[r+(1-r)e^(-beta)]^2 <= 1/r, and E W_n^2 <= (1-pi_d)/(1-pi_d/r) for all finite beta. Thus beta_L2 and beta_cr can both be infinite even for nonconstant bounded weights.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The main Theorem 1.1 assumes beta>beta_L2 and excludes both counterexamples. The proof invokes a nonconstant factor, indicating an intended qualification. Junk-Lacoin v3 p.3 explicitly permits infinite critical temperatures.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Require nonconstant normalized eta for the nontrivial lower bound. Then q* is finite by a favorable finite-box event and killed-walk spectral radius. Permit extended critical values and qualify finite strict-gap assertions.

problems.title: Gaussian covariance is inconsistent with nearest-neighbor normalization
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: # Problem 2: the Gaussian normalization is inconsistent (Minor)
claim: Recorded check: Gaussian covariance is inconsistent with nearest-neighbor normalization
Nearest-neighbor simple random walk on Z^d, d>=3. Endpoint scaled by sqrt(n); phi explicitly called standard normal. At beta=0 the bounded continuous test f(x)=cos(x_1) is admissible.
analysis:
Theorem A(iii), p. 2, scales the endpoint by \(\sqrt n\) and calls \(\varphi\) the standard normal density. The same convention is used in (27), p. 10, and in Lemma 2.6, pp. 13–15. A nearest-neighbor walk on \(\mathbb Z^d\) has one-step covariance \(I_d/d\). At \(\beta=0\), the bounded continuous test \(f(x)=\cos x_1\), permitted in Theorem A(iii), gives \[E\cos(X_n^{(1)}/\sqrt n)
 =\left[1-\frac{1-\cos(1/\sqrt n)}d\right]^n
 \longrightarrow e^{-1/(2d)},\] instead of the printed standard-Gaussian value \(e^{-1/2}\). This is an exact characteristic-function calculation; the independent numeric check in \(d=3\) converges to \(0.8464817249\), whereas the latter value is \(0.6065306597\).

Use \[\varphi_d(x)=\left(\frac d{2\pi}\right)^{d/2}e^{-d|x|^2/2}\] throughout these displays, or consistently rescale the walk. The nonvanishing Fourier-transform argument used to choose \(z\) still works for \(\varphi_d\). For a signed \(f\), \(z\) must be chosen again with \((f*\varphi_d)(z)\ne0\); the old choice for a different covariance need not work. The existence argument and all polynomial fluctuation exponents survive. An intended informal use of standard would explain the notation but does not make the literal normalization correct.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: The exact expectation is [1-(1-cos(1/sqrt(n)))/d]^n -> exp(-1/(2d)), not exp(-1/2). One-step covariance is I_d/d.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: An informal convention for standard might explain the notation; constant covariance changes do not change polynomial fluctuation exponents.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Use phi_d=(d/(2pi))^(d/2)exp(-d|x|^2/2), or consistently rescale the walk. Reselect z with f*phi_d(z) nonzero; the Gaussian Fourier transform gives existence.

problems.title: The fractional-moment domain in Proposition 2.1 is overstated
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: # Problem 3: Proposition 2.1 overstates the fractional domain (Minor)
claim: Recorded check: The fractional-moment domain in Proposition 2.1 is overstated
p in (0,1) explicitly included in proof. IID weights with all exponential moments; section not restricted to weak disorder. Counterexample d=1, standard Gaussian weights, beta=4, p=1/2.
analysis: Proposition 2.1(i)–(ii), p. 8, gives \(a(p)\in[0,\lambda(p\beta)-p\lambda(\beta)]\) and a nondecreasing function on \(\mathbb R_+\). Its proof explicitly includes \(p\in[0,1]\) and says the section does not require weak disorder. The nonnegative bounds are valid for \(p\geq1\); for \(0<p<1\), Jensen’s inequality gives instead \[\lambda(p\beta)-p\lambda(\beta)\leq a(p)\leq0.\] The printed interval can be empty for a nonconstant environment.

For an actual failure of monotonicity, take \(d=1\), standard Gaussian weights, \(\beta=4\), and \(p=1/2\). All standing exponential moments exist. Expanding over \(2^n\) paths and using \((\sum_i z_i)^p\leq\sum_i z_i^p\) gives \[\mathbb E W_n^p
 \leq \exp\{n[(1-p)\log2+\lambda(p\beta)-p\lambda(\beta)]\},
 \qquad
 -2\leq a(1/2)\leq\tfrac12\log2-2<0.\] Yet \(a(0)=a(1)=0\), so \(a\) is not nondecreasing on \(\mathbb R_+\). The superadditive argument supplies existence of the fractional limit. Restrict the nonnegative and monotonicity claims to \([1,\infty)\) and state the reversed fractional bounds separately. This is also the plausible intended reading: the later \(q^*\) argument uses \(p\geq1\). No failure of that argument or of the main theorem follows.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: For p<1 the correct Jensen bounds are lambda(p beta)-p lambda(beta) <= a(p) <= 0. Expanding over 2^n paths gives a(1/2) <= (log 2)/2-2 < 0, whereas a(0)=a(1)=0, contradicting nondecreasing behavior on R_+.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The later q* argument only needs p>=1, suggesting the intended restriction.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Restrict nonnegative bounds and monotonicity to p>=1; give reversed fractional bounds separately.

problems.title: The general lower-bound proof needs a moment replacement and local sign/geometry corrections
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: # Problem 4: repair the general lower-bound proof (Minor)
claim: Recorded check: The general lower-bound proof needs a moment replacement and local sign/geometry corrections

d>=3; weak disorder; general nonzero signed f in C_c. The general lower-bound theorem does not assume p*>1, whereas the proof chooses p in (1,p*). Independent time layers; ell_n=o(sqrt(n)); uniform CLT good-event probabilities over the required window.
analysis: Lemma 2.6, p. 13, assumes weak disorder but immediately chooses \(p\in(1,p^*)\). This is not justified by the acquired paper’s stated general hypotheses: pp. 2–3 and 6–7 explicitly distinguish weak disorder from \(p^*>1\). Its use of Hölder on p. 15 also requires the bad event \(A_{t,x}^c\), rather than the printed good event. For the main theorem, the upper-bound assumption and Theorem B already provide \(p^*>1\). The later result [tail] supplies another reason not to regard this gap as a false theorem.

The following replacement proves the needed step under uniform integrability alone. Put \(c=|(f*\varphi_d)(z)|>0\), retain the good CLT event \(A_{t,x}\), and write \[b_n=\sup_{t,x}\mathbb P(A_{t,x}^c)\longrightarrow0,\qquad
 u_n=\sup_{t,x}\mathbb E[W_t\mathbf1_{A_{t,x}^c}].\] The supremum uses the source’s space-time window, enlarged by the \(o(n)\) and \(o(\sqrt n)\) shifts from \(\ell_n\). For every \(R>0\), \[u_n\leq Rb_n+\sup_t\mathbb E[W_t\mathbf1_{\{W_t>R\}}]\longrightarrow0,\] first choosing \(R\) large, then \(n\) large. Let \(h_n=\sqrt{u_n}+n^{-1}\). Conditionally on the last \(\ell_n\) layers, the endpoint probabilities \(\mu_x\) sum to one and are independent of the older variables. Consequently \[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_x\mu_xW_x\mathbf1_{A_x^c}\,\middle|\,
             \text{last layers}\right]\leq u_n .\] Markov’s inequality bounds its probability of exceeding \(h_n\) by \(u_n/h_n\leq\sqrt{u_n}\); the corresponding bad signed-\(f\) sum is bounded with the additional factor \(\|f\|_\infty\). On good sites the normalized \(f\) averages have a common sign and absolute value at least \(c/2\). The argument in (44)–(47) therefore reduces to a lower-tail event for \(\sum_x\mu_xW_x\) at a threshold \(C(h_n+n^{-\varepsilon/8})\to0\). Lemma 2.3 and \(\inf_tW_t>0\) almost surely under weak disorder finish the estimate. Only \(p_n\to0\), without a rate, is needed for the later choice of \(N_n\).

In the proof of (55), pp. 19–20, the concentration scale and the event for \(\widehat Z_k\) omit its absolute value. For a nonzero nonpositive \(f\), the coefficients are nonpositive, so \(\{\widehat Z_k\leq\text{positive threshold}\}\) is automatic. It cannot imply the subsequent small-absolute-amplitude event. Use \(Q_{cY}(u)=Q_Y(u/|c|)\) for \(c\ne0\), and replace the scale and event by \(|\widehat Z_k|\). The already absolute truncation-error estimate then supplies the intended conclusion for either sign.

The following local corrections preserve this proof’s power estimates. In Section 2 use \(\xi_q=d/2-(d+2)/(2q^*)\) until equality \(p^*=q^*\) is established; the printed \(\xi\) was defined through \(p^*\). Before (35), p. 12, choose \(\mathbb P(\inf_mW_m>2a)>3/4\), which weak disorder permits, to obtain the stated \(1/2\) bound. On pp. 15–16 the number of nearby spatial grid points is at most \[C\left(1+\frac{n^{(1-\delta)/2}}{\ell_n}\right)^d,\] rather than the printed bound linear in the radius. Dividing by \(|S_n|\asymp n^{d/2}/\ell_n^d\) gives \(O(n^{-d\delta/2})\); hence the same conditioning geometric sum is eventually at most two. The inclusion on p. 18 is \(E_n\subseteq\widehat E_n\).

In (64), p. 21, enlarging visits to near visits can leave an extra \(\eta\) in the path energy. Increase the integration constant to cover both \(\mathbb E|\eta-1|\) and \(\mathbb E[\eta|\eta-1|]\). These moments are finite. The selection-density formula on p. 22 must retain the chosen site’s good-event indicator and the translated time block. That indicator is fixed on the integrated coordinates; the other factors decrease, preserving the product-measure FKG inequality. The correct heat-kernel factor is \(C(\Delta t)^{-d/2}\exp(-c|\Delta x|^2/\Delta t)\). Since the construction gives \(|\Delta x|^2/\Delta t\geq c n^{5\delta/6}\), polynomial factors are still dominated. These corrections support the conditional-independent singleton decomposition and its negligible multiple-visit error. The complete arguments and exact locators are retained with the evidence.

The dependency is the lower bound in Theorem 1.4(i), and thence the main theorem after \(p^*=q^*\). The explicit repairs and later moment result limit severity: the written proof needs correction, but no nondegenerate positive-\(\beta\) counterexample to its conclusion has been obtained.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: The stated general hypotheses do not justify choosing p>1 below p*. A complete replacement uses uniform integrability: u_n=sup E[W_t 1_Ac] <= R b_n+sup E[W_t 1_{W_t>R}] ->0. Conditional Markov with h_n=sqrt(u_n)+n^-1 reduces (44)-(47) to the existing lower-tail lemma. For f<=0 the printed event Zhat<=positive is automatic and cannot imply a small-absolute-amplitude event.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: For the main bounded-environment theorem, Theorem B already supplies p*>1. Later Junk-Lacoin Corollary 2.8 gives p*>1 under more general weak disorder. Absolute truncation errors in the source support the signed repair.

paragraphs: Use UI or explicitly justify p*>1; use bad event A^c in Holder; use |Zhat|. Use xi_q until p*=q*, probability >3/4 before (35), C(1+n^((1-delta)/2)/ell_n)^d grid count, E_n subset Ehat_n, constants covering E|eta-1| and E[eta|eta-1|], full chosen-site indicator/translated block in the density, and heat kernel C(Delta t)^(-d/2)exp(-c|Delta x|^2/Delta t).

problems.title: Upper bounds and overlap moments require normalized constants
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: # Problem 6: upper-bounded weights require normalized constants (Minor)
claim: Recorded check: Upper bounds and overlap moments require normalized constants

omega<=K, K>0; normalized eta=exp(beta omega-lambda(beta)). No centering or lambda(beta)>=0 assumption. For the full-range witness start from any nondegenerate admissible main-theorem model and shift by its upper bound.

Any \(0<K<\log(1+r)/\beta\) is now an eligible positive upper bound, and the displayed \(n=0\) inequality fails on that event. An executed two-point-law calculation illustrates the same normalization failure; it is not asserted to be a beyond-\(L^2\) parameter witness.

Set \(\alpha=2M\). The overshoot used in (79) is then correctly \(W_{\tau(\alpha^{i-1})}\leq M\alpha^{i-1}=\alpha^i/2\). Also \(0<H_nW_{n-1}\leq1\) gives the valid lower increment bound \(-1\), rather than the printed \(-\alpha^{-1}\). Bounded increments and the quadratic-variation estimates still hold. The exponential-supermartingale step follows directly from the bounded Taylor remainder and conditional mean-zero increments.

In Appendix (98), p. 34, replace \(e^{\beta K}\) by \(M\) as well. The same contradiction supplies an adequate positive tail constant \(\tfrac12M^{-p^*}\), or \(\tfrac12M^{-2}\) when \(p^*<2\). This diagnoses the proof’s normalization; it does not independently disprove the printed tail constant. The later overshoot formula [tail], (2.11), uses precisely the normalized factor.

A related repair to the finite moment calculation on pp. 31–32 is to retain the walk transition probability and use \[A(x)=\frac1{2d}\sum_{|y|_1=1}\eta_{m,x+y}^2 .\] Jensen gives \(\mathbb EA^4\leq\mathbb E\eta^8\) and \(\mathbb E(\sum_x\mu_x\eta_x)^{-8}\leq\mathbb E\eta^{-8}\). Cauchy–Schwarz consequently yields \[\mathbb E(\mathcal R_m^2\mid\mathcal F_{m-1})
 \leq e^{[\lambda(8\beta)+\lambda(-8\beta)]/2}\mathcal R_{m-1}^2.\] This is finite under (1), and is stronger than the required constant. These repairs preserve the route through Lemmas 4.3–4.5. The issue concerns stated constants and normalization, not a demonstrated failure of Theorem 1.5.

Shifting an admissible model leaves all normalized quantities/disorder unchanged but makes omega<=0. Since W_1 is nonconstant mean one, P(W_1>1+r)>0; choosing eligible 0<K<log(1+r)/beta contradicts the printed n=0 bound. The two-point numerical law is only an illustration, not a beyond-L2 witness.
