report: Abstract: The frozen 54-page arXiv version 2212.03362v2 by Elchanan Mossel, Allan Sly and Youngtak Sohn is examined. Two major problems are established: the self-averaging lemma fails for an admissible offspring family, and the printed numerical certificate omits a Gaussian normalization factor. Several local corrections concern message conventions, a lower-bound proof, conflicting cubic coefficients, and the precise ranges of auxiliary assertions. Counterevidence and possible repairs are supplied. The principal stochastic-block-model theorem is not disproved. Scientific decision remains pending; this initial report is not independent acceptance.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Initial technical review of
Exact Phase Transitions for Stochastic Block Models and Reconstruction on Trees
# Source and scope

The assigned identity is M25-0503, associated with journal DOI https://doi.org/10.1214/24-AOP1723. The actual scientific source is [paper], submitted as v2 on 22 February 2025 and carrying the title-page date 25 February 2025. All locators below refer to its physical pages, which agree with its printed numbering. Its SHA256 is

All 54 pages of extracted text, including both appendices and references, were read in the current scientific conversation. Thirty-six source pages were also actually viewed. No equivalence to the journal version is asserted.

The paper studies the symmetric broadcast channel \(K_\lambda=\lambda I+(1-\lambda)J\), with \(-1/(q-1)\leq\lambda<1\), on Galton–Watson trees of mean offspring \(d>1\). For the stochastic block model, \(d=(a+(q-1)b)/q\) and \(\lambda=(a-b)/(a+(q-1)b)\). Theorem 1.5 asserts impossibility of weak recovery for \(q=3,4\), large fixed \(d\), and \(d\lambda^2\leq1\). The proof passes through tree nonreconstruction, small-magnetization expansions and a large-degree Gaussian approximation, followed by a tree-to-graph coupling.

Here \[x_n=\mathbb Ex_n(T),\qquad
 x_n(T)=\sum_{i=1}^q\mathbb E_\sigma
       \left(\mathbb P(\sigma_\rho=i\mid \sigma(n),T)-1/q\right)^2.\] Assumption 1.10 bounds \(\mathbb Ee^{\theta X_d/d}\) uniformly in \(d\), for every \(\theta\geq0\). Assumption 1.11 keeps \(X_d/d\) in a positive bounded interval with arbitrarily high probability for large \(d\). The latter does not assert convergence to one.
# A false self-averaging lemma

Problem 1 (Major: Lemma 5.2).  On pp. 37–38, Lemma 5.2 claims, under Assumptions 1.10 and 1.11, that for every \(\varepsilon>0\), sufficiently large \(d\) gives \[\mathbb E\left|\widehat x_n-x_n\right|<\varepsilon,\qquad
 \widehat x_n=\frac1d\sum_{j=1}^{\gamma}x_n(T_j).
 \tag{P1}\] This statement is false even at \(n=1\), for \(q=3\) or \(4\) and \(\lambda=d^{-1/2}\).

Proof. For all real \(d>1\), set \(a_d=\lfloor d/2\rfloor\), \(b_d=\lceil3d/2\rceil\), and put mass \((d-a_d)/(b_d-a_d)\) at \(b_d\), with the remaining mass at \(a_d\). The mean is exactly \(d\). Since \(X_d/d\leq5/2\), Assumption 1.10 holds with \(K(\theta)\leq e^{5\theta/2}\). For \(d\geq4\), \(1/4\leq X_d/d\leq7/4\) surely, so Assumption 1.11 also holds. At every even integer \(d\), this is the equal mixture of \(d/2\) and \(3d/2\).

Equation reference: eq:jensen, eq:nonvanish. Conditionally on \(\gamma\), the subtrees are independent copies of \(T\). Consequently \[\mathbb E(\widehat x_n\mid\gamma)=\frac{\gamma}{d}x_n,\qquad
 \mathbb E|\widehat x_n-x_n|
 \geq x_n\mathbb E|\gamma/d-1|=\frac{x_n}{2}.
 \] To bound \(x_1\) away from zero uniformly, fix root degree \(D\), put \(U=\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_\rho=1\}}-1/q\), \(v=(q-1)/q^2\), and \(S=\sum_{j=1}^D(\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_j=1\}}-1/q)\). Direct conditioning gives \[\operatorname{Cov}(U,S)=D\lambda v,\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(S)=Dv\{1+(D-1)\lambda^2\}.\] Projection onto \(S\) is no better than conditioning on all child spins. By colour symmetry, \[x_1(T)=q\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb E[U\mid\sigma(1)])
 \geq \frac{q-1}{q}\frac{D\lambda^2}{1+(D-1)\lambda^2}.\] For \(\lambda^2=1/d\) and \(D\geq d/2\), the last ratio is at least \(1/3\). Thus \[\mathbb E|\widehat x_1-x_1|\geq\frac{q-1}{6q},
 \] for arbitrarily large even \(d\), contradicting (P1). The channel is admissible and the near-critical condition (16) holds for all sufficiently large such \(d\). ◻

The calculation is not an objection merely at depth zero. For example, independent enumeration at \(q=4,d=16,\lambda=1/4\) gives one-generation magnetizations approximately \(0.292802\) and \(0.572411\) at degrees 8 and 24. Their average is \(0.432606\); the conditional Jensen lower bound is \(0.216303\). These floating checks illustrate the exact proof above.
#### Dependency and repair.

The centering in the proof on p. 38 should be \((\gamma/d)x_n\), not \(x_n\). The valid estimate is \[\mathbb E\left|\widehat x_n-\frac{\gamma}{d}x_n\right|
 \leq \sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(x_n(T))}{d}}.\] This exposes the missing offspring fluctuation term. Lemma 5.2 is used in Proposition 5.5, equation (124), on p. 39, to obtain the deterministic approximation \(x_{n+1}\approx g_q(d\lambda^2x_n)\). That approximation is then used on p. 40 in Theorem 1.12. The failure therefore concerns a core derivation, not an unused estimate.

One repair is to strengthen the offspring hypothesis to \(X_d/d\to1\), with the uniform exponential bound providing uniform integrability. A less restrictive approach retains a mixture such as \(\mathbb Eg_q(\lambda^2\gamma x_n)\) and proves its required gap. Assumption 1.11 can supply a positive-probability compact interval on which a strictly positive gap is retained, but the approximation and its constants must be re-established. This report does not supply that full revised proof. Regular and Poisson offspring concentrate after division by \(d\); hence they are counterevidence to extrapolating this defect into a disproof of the SBM theorem.
# The numerical certificate as printed cannot work

Problem 2 (Major: Appendix B, equation (140)).  Equation (138), p. 52, correctly includes \((2\pi)^{-3/2}\) in both Gaussian integrals. The definitions of \(S_n,T_n\) and their sum in (140), p. 54, omit this factor. The subsequent claim that this sum certifies the inequalities (137) is impossible for the printed formula.
#### Counterevidence and correction.

The normalization is present in (138), so an omitted factor is a plausible explanation. Restore it to the complete sum and supply a new rigorous computation, including rounding control. The exterior integration domain should also be written \([-5,5]^3\setminus[-1,1]^3\): the earlier indicator in (138), read literally as all three absolute coordinates being at least one, omits mixed regions. The subsequent sum uses the correct complementary cube domain.

The dependency is Lemma 5.6 \(\to\) the Gaussian contraction in Theorem 1.12 \(\to\) the \(q=4\) SBM result. An invalid certificate for this crucial input warrants Major severity. Neither Lemma 5.6 nor the final theorem is disproved here.
# Local proof and formulation corrections

Problem 3 (Minor: zero-offspring message convention).  The convention \(Y_{i1}=1/q\) on \(\{\gamma=0\}\), p. 8, conflicts with the unconditional independence in Proposition 2.3(b), p. 9, and the first moment in Lemma 3.4, equation (23), p. 13.

For \(p_0=\mathbb P(\gamma=0)>0\), \(\lambda\ne0\), and \(x_n>0\), conditioning gives, under that convention, \[\mathbb E(Y_{11}-1/q)=(1-p_0)\lambda x_n,\] rather than \(\lambda x_n\). Poisson offspring, one of the paper’s principal cases, have \(p_0=e^{-d}>0\). The factorization in Lemma 3.5, p. 15, uses the same unconditional independence. Define an infinite sequence of potential child subtrees and messages independently of \(\gamma\), and use only its first \(\gamma\) entries. This restores the intended identities without changing the actual broadcast process or its empty-product posterior.

Remark 3.3 on p. 13 also needs a nonempty level \(n\) for its strict inequality \(x_n(T)>0\). A singleton tree has no observations at level \(n\geq1\) and \(x_n(T)=0\). The averaged magnetization can still be positive at finite depth. These are locally repairable construction and boundary errors, not counterexamples to the intended expansion.

Problem 4 (Minor: quadratic bound used as a linear bound).  The last inference in Lemma 3.8, p. 18, obtains \(x_{n+1}\geq c\lambda^4x_n^2\) and then claims \(x_{n+1}\geq c\kappa^4x_n\) from \(|\lambda|\geq\kappa\). The power of \(x_n\) cannot be dropped.

There is a stronger valid argument. For fixed \(T\) with a first child, condition first on the depth-\(n\) observations in that child’s subtree only. If its posterior is \(Q_i\), the root posterior is \(1/q+\lambda(Q_i-1/q)\). Conditional-variance monotonicity when the other branches are added gives \[x_{n+1}(T)\geq\lambda^2x_n(T_1),\qquad
 x_{n+1}\geq\mathbb P(\gamma\geq1)\lambda^2x_n.\] Assumption 1.10 bounds \(\mathbb E\gamma^2/d^2\); Cauchy–Schwarz therefore bounds \(\mathbb P(\gamma\geq1)\) away from zero. Since \(|\lambda|\leq1\), this proves the stated \(c\lambda^4x_n\) lower bound as well. The lower bound is used on p. 19 and in the barrier proof on pp. 35–36. Its printed derivation is invalid, but this complete repair supports Minor severity.

Problem 5 (Minor: inconsistent cubic coefficient).  The bracket multiplying \(\{\mathbb E\binom{\gamma}{2}\}^2\lambda^6x_n^3\) in equation (15), p. 10, is one quarter of the bracket in equation (105), p. 35.

The later expression is \[\frac{4q^2(q+1)}{(q-1)^2d(d-1)}
 -\frac{24q^2(q-2)}{(q-1)^2d(d\lambda-1)}.\] For Poisson offspring with \(d=16,q=4,\lambda=-1/4\), all channel and near-critical constraints are admissible. Exact substitution gives cubic coefficient \(-44/15\) in (15), but \(32/45\) in (105). The discrepancy even changes its sign. Equation (106), the displayed \(d^*\) criterion, and the subsequent proof use the later coefficient. Correcting the overview to agree with that derivation is therefore the indicated local repair; this mismatch alone does not invalidate the threshold ultimately stated.

Problem 6 (Minor: antiferromagnetic threshold interpretation).  Theorem 1.13 and the paragraph following it, p. 6, equate \(\lambda^-(q,d)>-d^{-1/2}\) with reconstruction somewhere below the Kesten–Stigum bound for all the stated \(d>1\). The admissible channel interval must be retained.

When \(d<(q-1)^2\), the point \(-d^{-1/2}\) is outside \([-1/(q-1),0)\). The displayed inequality may then be true solely because of this domain endpoint. For a concrete check, take Poisson mean \(d=2\) and \(q=4\). For any admissible negative \(\lambda\), the one-edge total variation contraction is \(|\lambda|\leq1/3\). A coupled broadcast started from different root colours has expected number of disagreements at depth \(n\) at most \((2|\lambda|)^n\leq(2/3)^n\). Thus reconstruction is impossible throughout the admissible negative interval. Nevertheless \(\lambda^-(4,2)=-1/3>-1/\sqrt2\). Poisson offspring satisfy Assumption 1.10, and \(2<d^*_{\rm Poi}\).

This disproves the blanket reconstruction interpretation, not the formal inequality for \(\lambda^-\). The argument on pp. 35–36 that chooses \(\lambda\) near \(-d^{-1/2}\) needs an admissible neighbourhood. Distinguish the vacuous range and restrict that existence interpretation, for example to \(d\geq(q-1)^2\) when the rest of the hypotheses apply. The large-\(d\) nonreconstruction theorem is unaffected by this boundary correction.

Problem 7 (Minor: Appendix A replacement variables).  On p. 49, the definitions of \(S_k,T_k\) use initial segments of the Gaussian variables instead of tails. The displayed Taylor estimates also omit \(\mathbb E\phi(T_k)\).

With the printed sums, \(T_k\) contains \(Z_k\), so their asserted independence fails whenever \(Z_k\) is nondegenerate. Even for zero increments and \(\phi\equiv1\), the printed Taylor remainder inequality becomes \(1\leq0\). Use instead \[S_k=\sum_{j<k}V_j+\sum_{j\geq k}Z_j,\qquad
 T_k=\sum_{j<k}V_j+\sum_{j>k}Z_j,\] and subtract \(\mathbb E\phi(T_k)\) in both Taylor estimates. The constant terms cancel in their difference, while the matched first and second moments leave the usual cubic remainder. The Frobenius-norm identity above (132) likewise requires the norm, not its square, after taking the square root. These explicit corrections recover the standard Lindeberg argument under bounded increments and bounded third derivatives. They concern the proof of Proposition 5.3, used in Proposition 5.5, and do not provide a counterexample to the intended Gaussian approximation.
Problem 8 (Minor: distinct vertices in Corollary 1.6).  The phrase any fixed vertices \(u,v\) on p. 4 must exclude \(u=v\).

For \(u=v\), \(\mathbb P(\sigma_u=i\mid G,\sigma_v=1)=\mathbf1_{\{i=1\}}\) for every \(n\), not \(1/q\), even with \(q=3,4\), large \(d\) and \(d\lambda^2\leq1\). The intended two-point statement and its relation to weak recovery on pp. 44–45 concern distinct vertices. Adding this qualifier repairs the literal counterexample without changing the main theorem.
# Coverage, counterchecks and remaining limits

The posterior identities and reverse-martingale argument were checked against the channel’s colour symmetry, including extinction and the empty-level posterior. The product expansion was followed through the \(u_n,v_n,w_n\) recursions, the weighted polynomial truncation, the near-critical constraints \(d^5|\lambda|^9>1+c_0\), \(1-c_0\leq d\lambda^2\leq1\), and the nonzero denominators \(d-1,d\lambda-1\). An independent check of the \(q=4\) specialization links (105) to (106); the overview mismatch is separated above. The uniform remainder estimates depend on the exponential moment bound. This is a substantive reading and targeted calculation audit, not a symbolic certification of every high-order expansion.

For the Gaussian step, the covariance is positive semidefinite with a zero direction corresponding to the all-ones vector. The softmax is invariant in that direction. Positivity of its mean bias and the exact Gaussian exponential-moment formula were used in the independent Appendix B checks. The small-\(s\) polynomial check succeeded; the large-\(s\) certificate needs repair. Equation (119)’s increment maximum should range over all \(D\) increments in the intended Lindeberg application, as is required in the proof.

The tree-to-SBM argument was read through the coupling, finite neighbourhood types, conditional exchangeability, permutation maximization, and the two-point reformulation. There are additional local bookkeeping corrections: on p. 41 the exact Bernoulli–Poisson distance is \(p(1-e^{-p})\), not \(p-e^{-p}\); on p. 42 the Markov estimate concerns \(\mathbb P(A_1^c)\); the bound on the remaining colour count requires subtraction of \(n/q\). Summing per-vertex \(O(n^{-2/5})\) errors over at most \(n^{1/4}\) revealed vertices gives \(O(n^{-3/20})=o(1)\), and collision probabilities are \(O(n^{-1/2})\). These checks support the coupling conclusion after correction. The tower-property step on p. 44 should be formulated using an observable good event or unconditional conditional expectations with an \(o(1)\) exceptional-event error, rather than silently assuming measurability of a coupling event.

The latest arXiv record and an author’s publication page were checked, together with targeted correction searches, on 29 October 2026. The arXiv record still lists v2; no applicable erratum was identified in that bounded search. The seven-page STOC publication is a different version and DOI. A publisher issue and journal metadata were located, but the journal article was not compared page by page here. These limits prevent transferring every finding automatically to the version of record.

External reconstruction, weak-recovery and contiguity inputs remain cited inputs, not independently re-proved theorems. No author executable was run. Independent scripts and their actual outputs, source/render bindings and page observations are retained with the report. The eight problems have different logical status: a false auxiliary lemma, an unusable printed certificate, locally repairable derivations, and precise formulation counterexamples. None establishes failure of the principal large-degree SBM theorem. Scientific decision remains pending, with no human acceptance recorded.

problems.title: Lemma 5.2
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: Problem 1 (Major: Lemma 5.2). On pp. 37–38, Lemma 5.2 claims, under Assumptions 1.10 and 1.11, that for every \(\varepsilon>0\), sufficiently large \(d\) gives…
claim: Recorded check: Lemma 5.2
q=3 or4; all real d>1 family with exact mean d; uniform exponential moments and tightness away from zero; lambda=d^(-1/2), n=1, arbitrarily large even d.
analysis:
On pp. 37–38, Lemma 5.2 claims, under Assumptions 1.10 and 1.11, that for every \(\varepsilon>0\), sufficiently large \(d\) gives \[\mathbb E\left|\widehat x_n-x_n\right|<\varepsilon,\qquad
 \widehat x_n=\frac1d\sum_{j=1}^{\gamma}x_n(T_j).
 \tag{P1}\] This statement is false even at \(n=1\), for \(q=3\) or \(4\) and \(\lambda=d^{-1/2}\).

Proof. For all real \(d>1\), set \(a_d=\lfloor d/2\rfloor\), \(b_d=\lceil3d/2\rceil\), and put mass \((d-a_d)/(b_d-a_d)\) at \(b_d\), with the remaining mass at \(a_d\). The mean is exactly \(d\). Since \(X_d/d\leq5/2\), Assumption 1.10 holds with \(K(\theta)\leq e^{5\theta/2}\). For \(d\geq4\), \(1/4\leq X_d/d\leq7/4\) surely, so Assumption 1.11 also holds. At every even integer \(d\), this is the equal mixture of \(d/2\) and \(3d/2\).

Equation reference: eq:jensen, eq:nonvanish. Conditionally on \(\gamma\), the subtrees are independent copies of \(T\). Consequently \[\mathbb E(\widehat x_n\mid\gamma)=\frac{\gamma}{d}x_n,\qquad
 \mathbb E|\widehat x_n-x_n|
 \geq x_n\mathbb E|\gamma/d-1|=\frac{x_n}{2}.
 \] To bound \(x_1\) away from zero uniformly, fix root degree \(D\), put \(U=\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_\rho=1\}}-1/q\), \(v=(q-1)/q^2\), and \(S=\sum_{j=1}^D(\mathbf1_{\{\sigma_j=1\}}-1/q)\). Direct conditioning gives \[\operatorname{Cov}(U,S)=D\lambda v,\qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(S)=Dv\{1+(D-1)\lambda^2\}.\] Projection onto \(S\) is no better than conditioning on all child spins. By colour symmetry, \[x_1(T)=q\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb E[U\mid\sigma(1)])
 \geq \frac{q-1}{q}\frac{D\lambda^2}{1+(D-1)\lambda^2}.\] For \(\lambda^2=1/d\) and \(D\geq d/2\), the last ratio is at least \(1/3\). Thus \[\mathbb E|\widehat x_1-x_1|\geq\frac{q-1}{6q},
 \] for arbitrarily large even \(d\), contradicting (P1). The channel is admissible and the near-critical condition (16) holds for all sufficiently large such \(d\). ◻

The calculation is not an objection merely at depth zero. For example, independent enumeration at \(q=4,d=16,\lambda=1/4\) gives one-generation magnetizations approximately \(0.292802\) and \(0.572411\) at degrees 8 and 24. Their average is \(0.432606\); the conditional Jensen lower bound is \(0.216303\). These floating checks illustrate the exact proof above.

The centering in the proof on p. 38 should be \((\gamma/d)x_n\), not \(x_n\). The valid estimate is \[\mathbb E\left|\widehat x_n-\frac{\gamma}{d}x_n\right|
 \leq \sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(x_n(T))}{d}}.\] This exposes the missing offspring fluctuation term. Lemma 5.2 is used in Proposition 5.5, equation (124), on p. 39, to obtain the deterministic approximation \(x_{n+1}\approx g_q(d\lambda^2x_n)\). That approximation is then used on p. 40 in Theorem 1.12. The failure therefore concerns a core derivation, not an unused estimate.

One repair is to strengthen the offspring hypothesis to \(X_d/d\to1\), with the uniform exponential bound providing uniform integrability. A less restrictive approach retains a mixture such as \(\mathbb Eg_q(\lambda^2\gamma x_n)\) and proves its required gap. Assumption 1.11 can supply a positive-probability compact interval on which a strictly positive gap is retained, but the approximation and its constants must be re-established. This report does not supply that full revised proof. Regular and Poisson offspring concentrate after division by \(d\); hence they are counterevidence to extrapolating this defect into a disproof of the SBM theorem.
result: Recorded evidence: Decisive evidence: a=floor(d/2), b=ceil(3d/2), mass (d-a)/(b-a) at b. At even d equal mixture d/2,3d/2. Conditional Jensen gives E|hat_x1-x1|>=x1/2. Projection onto sum of child indicators gives x1>=(q-1)/(3q); hence discrepancy >=(q-1)/(6q), not tending to zero.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Poisson and regular offspring do concentrate after division by d. A mixture Gaussian contraction may repair the general theorem.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Center at gamma*x_n/d; retain offspring mixture, or strengthen to X_d/d->1 with uniform integrability.

report: Abstract: This initial review of the acquired arXiv version identifies an invalid rounding argument in the proof of Proposition 4.13, a false lattice-normalized Bessel asymptotic in Lemma 3.4, and an inadmissible endpoint in Lemma 3.7. Explicit counterexamples and replacement arguments are supplied. The first two defects occur in derivations supporting the main lower- and upper-tail results; the proposed local repairs preserve the needed intermediate conclusions. Title: Technical Verification of
Large Deviations for the \(q\)-Deformed Polynuclear Growth
# Paper identity and scope

The reviewed paper is by Sayan Das, Yuchen Liao, and Matteo Mucciconi, Large deviations for the \(q\)-deformed polynuclear growth, associated with DOI https://doi.org/10.1214/24-AOP1733. The actual acquired source is arXiv:2307.01179v2, dated 3 September 2025, 65 physical pages [DLM]. Page references below are to this PDF; printed and physical page numbers agree. Publisher equivalence is not assumed.

The review follows the upper-tail trace estimate and the lower-tail midpoint-convexity argument. Pages 1–30, 47–54, and 59–61 were read as text, with the evidentiary pages individually rendered and visually inspected. Reading these pages does not certify every cited input or every line of their proofs. The detailed variational analysis and determinant remainder estimates on pages 31–46, the alternative approaches on pages 55–58, and most external references were not independently verified. Section 6, embedded in the acquired PDF, contains the technical lemmas. A separately hosted journal supplement was not successfully acquired. No author code was executed.

Bounded public searches found no target-specific correction resolving the issues below. The current arXiv metadata identifies v2 as the latest version and describes it as the published version with edits and corrections; that author description is not an independent comparison with the publisher file. Absence of a located correction is not proof that none exists.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

Equation reference: eq:rate. Throughout, \(0<q<1\), \(\eta_q=\log(q^{-1})>0\), time \(t\) is real and positive, and the growth process has droplet initial condition. For the principal theorems the nucleation intensity is \(2(1-q)\). Theorem 1.2, pages 3–4, concerns upper deviations \(\mu\ge2\), with speed \(t\) and rate \[
 \Phi_+(u)=2u\mathop{\mathrm{arccosh}}(u/2)-2\sqrt{u^2-4},\qquad u\ge2.\] Theorem 1.3, page 4, concerns \(0\le\mu\le2\), with speed \(t^2\), a convex lower-tail rate \(\Phi_-\), and \(\Phi_-(0)=1-q\). These are distinct claims from the intermediate assertions tested here.

Equation reference: eq:weight, eq:T. A partition is finite, padded with zeros as needed. For a skew partition \(\lambda/\rho\), \(\rho\subseteq\lambda\), write \(s_{\lambda/\rho}(\gamma)\) for its exponential Schur specialization. Definition 2.4 and (2.11), pages 16–17, give \[
 P_t(\lambda/\rho)=K_t q^{|\rho|}s_{\lambda/\rho}(\gamma)^2,\quad
 \gamma=t(1-q),\quad K_t=e^{-t^2(1-q)}(q;q)_\infty.\] Here \(s_{\lambda/\rho}(\gamma)=\gamma^{|\lambda/\rho|}f^{\lambda/\rho}/|\lambda/\rho|!\), with \(f\) the number of standard tableaux. All these weights are positive. Equation (4.35), page 48, defines \[
 \mathcal T_t(a)=-t^{-2}\log\sup_{\rho\subseteq\lambda,\ \lambda_1\le at}P_t(\lambda/\rho)
 \quad(a\ge0),\qquad \mathcal T_t(a)=+\infty\quad(a<0).\] Keeping \(K_t\) explicitly avoids any change of probability normalization.
# Substantive findings

Problem 1 (Uncontrolled accumulated rounding in a core midpoint argument).  The proof of Proposition 4.13 uses a false bound on the total size change under coordinatewise rounding. Severity: Major, for an invalid core derivation; this is not a finding that Proposition 4.13 or Theorem 1.3 is false.
## Original claim, location, and hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:mid. Proposition 4.13, pages 49–50, claims that for every \(a,a'\in\mathbb R\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), for all sufficiently large \(t\), \[
 \mathcal T_t\left(\frac{a+a'}2+\frac1t\right)
 \le\frac{\mathcal T_t(a)+\mathcal T_t(a')}2+\varepsilon.\] Its proof considers arbitrary admissible \(\lambda/\mu,\nu/\rho\) with \(\lambda_1\le at\), \(\nu_1\le a't\). It chooses the ceiling or floor averaged skew shape with larger unweighted Schur square and uses \[\Delta=|\text{chosen averaged inner partition}|-\frac{|\mu|+|\rho|}{2}\le1.\] The operation is coordinatewise, as expressly stipulated in Proposition 4.12. The displayed logarithmic bound on page 50 additionally has \(+t^{-2}\log q^\Delta\); converting the preceding probability inequality requires the opposite sign.
## Decisive evidence

Take \(q=1/2\), \(t=2\), \(\gamma=1\), \(a=0\), \(a'=1\), and \[\lambda=\mu=\varnothing,\qquad \nu=(2,2,2),\qquad \rho=(1,1,1).\] Every partition inclusion and first-row restriction holds. Both rounded outer partitions equal \((1,1,1)\). The ceiling inner partition is \((1,1,1)\), whereas the floor inner partition is empty. Thus the ceiling skew shape is empty and has Schur value \(1\); the floor shape is a column of length three and has Schur value \(1/6\). The ceiling is the unique maximizer required by the proof, and \[\Delta=3-\frac32=\frac32>1.\] Selecting the floor shape is therefore not a valid reinterpretation of that selection rule.

The problem is not confined to small time. For any sufficiently large \(t\ge2\), retain \(q=1/2,a=0,a'=1\), set \(m=\lceil t^3\rceil\), and take \(\nu=(2^m),\rho=(1^m),\lambda=\mu=\varnothing\). The ceiling value is \(1\); the floor value is \((t/2)^m/m!<1\), since \[(t/2)^m/m!\le \left(\frac{et}{2m}\right)^m<1.\] All first-row constraints still hold, but \(\Delta=m/2\), so \(\Delta/t^2\) is not a uniform vanishing error for the arbitrary inputs used in the proof. These configurations are not asserted to maximize the supremum in [eq:T] (#eq:T); they disprove the intermediate estimate, not [eq:mid] (#eq:mid).

For the finite example, using the actual normalized weights, the chosen configuration’s negative logarithm exceeds the incorrectly signed displayed per-configuration upper bound by \[\frac14\log(4/3)>0.\] This independent exact calculation confirms that the sign is consequential at the stated intermediate inequality.
## A proved replacement and counterevidence

Equation reference: eq:product. The same Schur inequality used by the authors provides a direct repair if both rounded shapes are retained. Denote them by \(A_+\) and \(A_-\). The coordinatewise floor and ceiling preserve partition order and inner containment. Proposition 4.12, or Theorem 11 in the inspected preprint of Lam–Postnikov–Pylyavskyy [LPP], yields \[s_{A_+}(\gamma)s_{A_-}(\gamma)
 \ge s_{\lambda/\mu}(\gamma)s_{\nu/\rho}(\gamma).\] Schur positivity implies this numerical inequality because the exponential specialization is nonnegative. Moreover, the two rounded inner sizes add exactly to \(|\mu|+|\rho|\). Equation [eq:weight] (#eq:weight) therefore gives \[
 P_t(A_+)P_t(A_-)\ge P_t(\lambda/\mu)P_t(\nu/\rho).\] Both averaged outer first rows are at most \((a+a')t/2+1\). If \(S_t(b)\) is the supremum in [eq:T] (#eq:T), then \[S_t\left(\frac{a+a'}2+\frac1t\right)^2
 \ge P_t(A_+)P_t(A_-)
 \ge P_t(\lambda/\mu)P_t(\nu/\rho).\] Taking independent suprema, or positive near-maximizers, proves [eq:mid] (#eq:mid) with \(\varepsilon=0\), for every \(t>0\) and \(a,a'\ge0\). If an input is negative the extended-real right-hand side is infinite and the original claim is automatic. No maximum-attainment assumption or bound on \(\Delta\) is needed.
## Dependency and impact boundary

Theorem 4.15 and Proposition 4.16 on pages 52–53 invoke Proposition 4.13; the proof of Theorem 1.3 on page 54 invokes it again to establish the convexity hypothesis for the deconvolution argument. This is an explicit dependency of a principal result, which supports Major severity for the printed derivation. The proof above repairs this particular input and is strong counterevidence against declaring the final theorem false. It does not validate the uninspected variational analysis or every subsequent step. Author adoption of this repair is unknown.

Problem 2 (A lattice phase omitted from the normalized Bessel limit).  Equation (3.14) in Lemma 3.4, page 24, is false for its real-time limit. Severity: Major for a false assertion used in the core trace derivation, with a verified local repair and no demonstrated failure of the final upper-tail rate.
## Claim and decisive analytic check

Equation reference: eq:correctb. Put \(n=\lfloor ut\rfloor\) and \(r=n/t\). A direct saddle calculation gives, uniformly for \(r\) in compact subsets of \((2,\infty)\), \[
 J_n(2t)^2=
 \frac{e^{-t\Phi_+(r)}}{2\pi t\sqrt{r^2-4}}(1+o(1)).\] For completeness, start from the generating-function coefficient integral \[J_n(2t)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint e^{t(z-z^{-1})}z^{-n-1}\,dz.\] Take \(z=e^{\alpha+i\theta}\), with \(\alpha=\mathop{\mathrm{arccosh}}(r/2)>0\). The exponent becomes \[2t\sinh\alpha\cos\theta-n\alpha
       +in(\sin\theta-\theta).\] Its real part has a unique maximum at \(\theta=0\) on \([-\pi,\pi]\). On \(|\theta|\le t^{-2/5}\), the quadratic term is \(-t\sinh\alpha\,\theta^2\), with uniformly vanishing cubic-phase and quartic-real errors. Outside this interval, the absolute integral is exponentially smaller than the saddle contribution, uniformly when \(\alpha\) stays in a compact positive interval. Gaussian integration gives \[J_n(2t)=
 \frac{\exp(2t\sinh\alpha-n\alpha)}
      {\sqrt{4\pi t\sinh\alpha}}(1+o(1)),\] which proves [eq:correctb] (#eq:correctb). This derivation does not use the disputed lemma.

Equation reference: eq:phase. Since \(\Phi_+'(u)=2\mathop{\mathrm{arccosh}}(u/2)\), Taylor expansion shows that the left-hand side of [eq:falseb] (#eq:falseb) equals \[
 \exp\!\big(\Phi_+'(u)\{ut\}\big)(1+o(1)).\] At \(u=3\), along \(t_n=n/3\) its limit is \(1\); along \(s_n=(n+1/2)/3\) it is \[e^{\Phi_+'(3)/2}=\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2}>1.\] Both sequences satisfy every operative hypothesis. Thus the asserted limit does not exist.
## Independent numerical corroboration
An independently written script used mpmath 1.3.0 with 90 decimal digits; no author implementation was executed. Selected values of the exact printed ratio are
Replacing \(u\) by \(n/t\) in the prefactor and exponent yields ratios approaching one in both columns. The analytic subsequence argument establishes the defect; numerical values only corroborate it.
## Alternative interpretation, repair, and dependency

Restricting the limit to \(ut\in\mathbb Z\) would remove this counterexample, but no such restriction appears and time is continuous in the model. Merely dropping a bounded phase is legitimate at logarithmic speed \(t\), not in a normalized limit equal to one.

The proof of Proposition 3.2 invokes (3.14) in (3.30), pages 29–30, with \(d=\lfloor2t\cosh(p/2)\rfloor/t\) and \(p>0\). Formula [eq:correctb] (#eq:correctb) supplies a valid lower bound of the same required order. Writing \(u_*=2\cosh(p/2)\), one has \[pdt-t\Phi_+(u_*)\ge t\big(pu_*-\Phi_+(u_*)\big)-p
 =4t\sinh(p/2)-p.\] This is the lower estimate needed for the ensuing exponential lower bound. The nearby printed upper inequality does not by itself justify a lower bound. The corrected Bessel formula and this elementary lower estimate restore this local passage. The lattice factor in [eq:phase] (#eq:phase) is bounded between fixed positive constants, so it does not alter the rate \(4\sinh(p/2)\). The remainder of the Fredholm analysis is outside the fully verified scope; the final upper-tail theorem is not refuted.

Problem 3 (The endpoint \(v=0\) makes the double sum infinite).  Lemma 3.7, page 25, includes \(v\ge0\), although its asserted finite bound fails at zero. Severity: Minor; no use of the erroneous endpoint was identified in the inspected principal argument.
## Statement, assumptions, and counterexample
## Counterevidence and bounded repair

The preceding definition of \(U_v\) is for \(v>0\), and the lemma’s proof uses the factor \((1-e^{-v})^{-1}\). These facts support an intended positive-\(v\) interpretation, but cannot make the explicit endpoint correct. Replacing \(v\ge0\) by \(v>0\) removes the demonstrated defect. Inspected applications use \(p>0\), \(M>1\) (hence \(v=\log M>0\)), or positive multiples of \(\eta_q\); see pages 28–30. The present finding does not independently certify the full positive-\(v\) estimate and does not show damage to a final theorem.
# Assessment and limitations

The highest supported severity is Major, grounded in the explicit dependency of the first two defective derivations. This classification is separate from rejection, acceptance, or whole-paper falsity. Problem Problem 1 (#pr:round) has a complete replacement proof of the needed midpoint inequality. Problem Problem 2 (#pr:bessel) has a complete corrected local asymptotic and restores the exponential lower estimate at the inspected use. Problem Problem 3 (#pr:zero) has a precise domain correction. None of these statements amounts to verification of every theorem in the paper.

The upper rate also passes the elementary Legendre check: \(\sup_{p\ge0}\{p\mu-4\sinh(p/2)\}\) has optimizer \(p=2\mathop{\mathrm{arccosh}}(\mu/2)\) for \(\mu\ge2\), giving [eq:rate] (#eq:rate). This is a consistency check, not a proof of the probabilistic limit. The lower-tail endpoint and deconvolution hypotheses were traced through pages 48–54 and 59–61, but the entire variational construction and all external convex-analytic inputs remain unverified.

report: Abstract: This review identifies a missing exclusion of driftless compound Poisson subordinators in the stated scope of Theorem 1.6, and a separate, locally repairable coordinate-maximization error in the appendix. An explicit exponential jump law satisfies the stated density conditions but produces an atom in every resolvent; the Green density required by the paper’s definition then does not exist. Title: Initial technical review of
Boundary Harnack principle for nonlocal operators on metric measure spaces
# Identity, scope, and conclusion

The assigned paper is by Zhen-Qing Chen and Jie-Ming Wang, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1734 (https://doi.org/10.1214/24-AOP1734). The acquired source is the 49-page arXiv version dated 5 December 2023, [CW]; its title page uses the spelling non-local. All page locators below refer to this exact PDF, whose physical and printed page numbers agree. The source SHA256 is
> 00000TOKEN.

Text on pages 1–20, 23–31, and 38–46 was read. Reading these pages does not certify every proof on them. The decisive checks concern the hypotheses and occupation kernel in Problem 1, the coordinate estimate in Problem 2, and the two-dimensional critical-cone calculation in Section 4. Pages 21–22, 32–37, and 47–49 and the full proofs in external references have not received complete scientific review. Images of all source pages used as decisive evidence were inspected; the separate coverage record lists them. No author code was executed.

There are two established problems: one Major problem in the scope and deduction of Theorem 1.6, and one Minor proof error in Lemma 4.1. Neither finding establishes that the paper’s principal positive-Gaussian boundary Harnack theorem is false. This is an initial technical report; scientific acceptance remains pending independent review.
# A missing hypothesis in the subordinate Brownian application

Problem 1 (Major: the stated class includes processes without the required Green density).  On page 8, the paragraph preceding (1.11) asserts transition-density regularity for any subordinate Brownian motion. Theorem 1.6 on the same page assumes a discontinuous subordinator with a Lévy density satisfying (1.12), but does not require positive drift or infinite jump activity. These conditions permit a process violating (A1), which is explicitly required in Corollary 1.5 on page 7. For that process the Green function used in (1.6) cannot satisfy Definition 1.1 on page 5.
## Exact hypotheses and an admissible example

Equation reference: eq:assumptions. The subordinator exponent in (1.11) is \[\phi(\lambda)=b\lambda+\int_0^\infty(1-e^{-\lambda s})\mu(s)\,ds,
 \qquad b\geq0,\] where \(\mu\) is nonzero and \(\int_0^\infty(1\wedge s)\mu(s)\,ds<\infty\). The two displayed assumptions (1.12) are, for a fixed finite constant \(c\), \[
 \mu(s)\leq c\mu(2s)\quad(0<s<8),\qquad
 \mu(s)\leq c\mu(s+1)\quad(s>1).\] Take \(b=0\) and \(\mu(s)=e^{-s}\), \(s>0\). Then \[\int_0^\infty\mu(s)\,ds=1,\qquad
 \int_0^\infty(1\wedge s)\mu(s)\,ds=1-e^{-1},\qquad
 \phi(\lambda)=\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda}.\] Both inequalities in [eq:assumptions] (#eq:assumptions) hold with \(c=e^8\), since their ratios are respectively \(e^s\) and \(e\). This is a discontinuous compound Poisson subordinator with rate one and exponential jumps. Its density is completely monotone, so restricting the example to complete Bernstein exponents does not remove it.

Let \(W\) be the independent Brownian motion used in the paper and set \(X_t=W_{S_t}\) in \(\mathbb R^d\), for any \(d\geq1\). The process is a symmetric compound Poisson process; its jump distribution is a mixture of nondegenerate Gaussian distributions and is absolutely continuous. The holding component is the obstruction.

Equation reference: eq:atom. Claim 1.  For every \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), \(t>0\), and \(\alpha>0\), \[
 \mathbb P_x(X_t=x)=e^{-t},
 \qquad G^\alpha(x,\{x\})=\frac{1}{\alpha+1}.\] For every open set \(U\) containing \(x\), the killed occupation measure has mass one at \(\{x\}\).

Proof. There is no subordinator jump before \(t\) with probability \(e^{-t}\). Conditional on \(S_t>0\), \(W_{S_t}\) has a Gaussian-mixture density and therefore no atom at \(x\). Integrating the first equality in [eq:atom] (#eq:atom) against \(e^{-\alpha t}\,dt\) gives the second.

Let \(T_1\) be the first jump time. It has mean one, and the process stays at \(x\) up to \(T_1\), before exiting any open \(U\) containing \(x\). The locations after each positive number of jumps have continuous distributions; with probability one none of these countably many locations equals \(x\). Consequently \[\mathbb E_x\int_0^{\tau_U}\mathbf1_{\{x\}}(X_s)\,ds
   =\mathbb ET_1=1.\] An occupation density with respect to Lebesgue measure would give zero for this bounded Borel test function. This contradicts the defining identity in Definition 1.1. ◻
## Dependency and impact

Assumption (A1), page 4, requires absolute continuity of every positive resolvent for both dual processes. Equation [eq:atom] (#eq:atom) violates it. Theorem 1.3 explicitly assumes (A1), and Corollary 1.5 carries it into the Euclidean Lévy-process application. Page 8 supplies the density assertion to justify the next application. That assertion is false, and the conditions printed in Theorem 1.6 do not supply its missing hypothesis.

This is more than the failure of an optional regularity remark: Theorem 1.6 states an equivalence with a comparison of Green functions defined by an occupation-density identity. Choose, for example, a bounded open ball \(D\); its complement has nonempty interior, so no boundary-domain restriction removes the example. For the compound Poisson process, the corresponding killed Green density does not exist in the paper’s stated sense. Thus the advertised equivalence is not well defined over its entire stated class, and its deduction from Corollary 1.5 is invalid for that class. This is the reason for the Major classification.
## Alternative readings, counterevidence, and repair limits

The word discontinuous permits compound Poisson subordinators; it does not impose infinite activity. Formula (1.11) expressly permits \(b=0\). The positive-drift convention introduced at the start of Section 3, page 23, belongs to that later section. Moreover, page 29, after (3.18), expressly observes that the jump-kernel comparison does not require positive drift. That observation establishes (A3)’ for a wider class; it does not establish (A1).

One could study an off-diagonal density after removing the holding atom. It would not satisfy Definition 1.1 for all bounded nonnegative Borel functions, as the singleton test above shows. Such a formulation would need a changed definition and a new check of the theorem’s proof.

Adding \(b>0\), or excluding finite-activity driftless subordinators by requiring \(\mu(0,\infty)=\infty\), removes this particular resolvent obstruction: \(S_t>0\) almost surely for \(t>0\), and Gaussian mixing then gives absolute continuity. This observation alone does not verify all remaining assumptions of a revised theorem, and does not assert continuity of an arbitrary resulting density. An explicit (A1) hypothesis is another direct way to state the required framework.

There is no counterexample here to the boundary Harnack inequality itself. The abstract metric-space theorem already assumes (A1), and Theorem 1.10 on page 10 expressly requires \(b>0\); neither is refuted by this example. The symbolic integration and atom calculation were independently reproduced in the saved reviewer script `verification/0512/evidence/independent_checks.py`; the analytic argument above is the decisive evidence.
# An invalid coordinate aggregation in the appendix

Problem 2 (Minor: two coordinate maxima cannot be separated).  In Lemma 4.1, Case (i), page 45, the displayed chain immediately after (4.5) replaces the maximum of a sum of two coordinate-dependent terms by the sum of their separate maxima. This equality is false for admissible Lévy triples. Keeping the joint maximum repairs the estimate with the same stated order.
## Hypotheses, exact step, and counterexample

Equation reference: eq:falsemax. The appendix treats any Lévy process in \(\mathbb R^d\) with covariance matrix \(A\), drift vector, and Lévy measure \(\nu\). For fixed \(r>0\), write \[B_i=\int_{|z|\leq2r}z_i^2\,\nu(dz),\qquad
 M=\max_{1\leq i\leq d}\left(\tfrac12a_{ii}+c_2 B_i\right),\] where \(c_2>0\) is the constant in (4.5). The infimum of the exponential integrands in that display is \(\exp(-t\omega^2 M)\). The next equality instead uses \[
 \tfrac12\max_i a_{ii}+c_2\max_i B_i .\] The maximizing indices need not coincide.

For a numerical instance satisfying all hypotheses of Case (i), take \(d=2\), \(r=1\), zero drift, \[A=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,0),\qquad
 \nu=\tfrac12\delta_{(0,1)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(0,-1)},\qquad c_2=1/4.\] The constant \(1/4\) is valid in the cosine estimate for \(|\omega z_i|\leq1\), since \(1-\cos u\geq u^2/4\) there. The measure is a finite symmetric Lévy measure, \(B_1=0\), \(B_2=1\), and \[K(2r)=3/8,\qquad G(2r)=L(2r)=0.\] Thus \(K(2r)\geq\max\{G(2r),L(2r)\}\), exactly the case under discussion. But \(M=1/4\), whereas [eq:falsemax] (#eq:falsemax) equals \(1/2\). For every \(t\omega^2>0\) the printed equality therefore changes the exponential to a strictly smaller value without justification. More generally, for any chosen \(c_2>0\), taking \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2c_2,0)\) with the same measure gives the same factor-two discrepancy.
## Repair and dependency
# A positive boundary-case check

Equation reference: eq:sector. The critical angle in dimension two is \(\pi/4\), corresponding to a sector of opening \(\pi/2\). Lemma 3.14, pages 39–40, predicts the additional logarithm in the Brownian mean exit time at this angle. There is a direct independent calculation for Brownian generator \(\Delta\) on the unit quarter-disk. Write polar coordinates \(0<\theta<\pi/2\). The solution of \(\Delta u=-1\), with zero boundary values, is \[
 u(r,\theta)=\frac{r^2\log(1/r)}{\pi}\sin(2\theta)
 +\sum_{\substack{k\geq3\\k\ {\rm odd}}}
 \frac{r^2-r^{2k}}{\pi k(k^2-1)}\sin(2k\theta).\] Indeed, the sine expansion of the constant function on this interval has coefficients \(4/(\pi k)\) for odd \(k\). The first radial operator sends \(r^2\log(1/r)\) to \(-4\); the higher modes in [eq:sector] (#eq:sector) give the remaining coefficients of \(-1\). The boundary values vanish, and the remainder on the central ray is \(O(r^2)\) by absolute summability. Consequently \[\frac{u(r,\pi/4)}{r^2\log(1/r)}\longrightarrow\frac1\pi
 \quad(r\downarrow0).\] Independent 80-digit partial-sum calculations for \(r=10^{-1},10^{-2},
10^{-3},10^{-4}\) gave approximately \(0.3134170,0.3158632,0.3166787,
0.3170865\), consistent with \(1/\pi\). The proof is the mode calculation, not a numerical extrapolation. This supports the critical logarithmic mechanism used in the later contradiction argument, but does not certify the full cone proof or its external inputs.
# Version checks and remaining limits

The arXiv record inspected during this review listed v1 as the only version. The author’s publication page linked that preprint. Bounded title/DOI searches did not identify a target-specific author correction; this is not a claim that no correction exists. Access to the publisher page reached an additional security check, and no publisher full-text payload was acquired or compared. The two findings therefore apply only to the exact acquired v1. They must not be attributed automatically to the 2025 journal text.

The report separates a false density assertion and invalid theorem application from a false boundary Harnack conclusion, and separates the appendix’s false intermediate equality from its repairable final estimate. Other proofs, versions, and external results outside the declared coverage remain unverified. The supporting records retain source and manifest bindings, reviewer calculations, actual image inspection facts, and the exact build dependencies for this report.

Used only for version/correction discovery, not as proof evidence.

report: Abstract: The acquired journal version contains a false boundary-uniform moment estimate in the central survival-probability argument. A starting point at fixed distance from the moving upper boundary has reproductive weight of order \(N\); its initial two-spine contribution over time \(L^2\) diverges as \(N/L^2\). An associated lower-bound statement also has an impossible uniformity in the time interval. This is a Major defect in the stated derivation, without establishing that the fixed-starting-point main theorem is false. Three further, bounded findings concern an extension to the semipushed regime, a missing factor of two in the Green kernel, and an incorrect high-frequency compactness argument. Exact repairs are supplied for the kernel normalization and the high-frequency norm estimate. The report does not claim a complete replacement proof of the main results.

Title: Initial technical review of
Spectral analysis and \(k\)-spine decomposition of inhomogeneous branching Brownian motions. Genealogies in fully pushed fronts
# Reviewed object, assumptions, and positive checks

This is the initial technical review of M25-0514, by Emmanuel Schertzer and Julie Tourniaire, The Annals of Probability 53(4) (2025), 1382–1433, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1736 (https://doi.org/10.1214/24-AOP1736) [ST]. The acquired version of record has 52 physical pages, without an additional cover. Printed page \(p\) is physical page \(p-1381\). Its SHA256 is
> 00000TOKEN.
Scientific acceptance remains pending independent review.

Equation reference: eq:weights. The model is dyadic branching Brownian motion with unit Brownian variance, drift \(-\mu\), killing at zero, and rate \(r(x)=(1+W(x))/2\). Assumptions (A1)–(A2), page 1383, require a nonnegative \(C^1\) function \(W\) supported in \([0,1]\). For the process also killed at \(L\), let \(v_L\) be the positive Dirichlet principal eigenfunction of \[\tfrac12 v_L''+\tfrac12 Wv_L=\lambda_1(L)v_L,\qquad v_L(1)=1.\] Write \[\lambda_\infty=\lim_{L\to\infty}\lambda_1(L),\quad
 \beta=\sqrt{2\lambda_\infty},\quad
 \mu=\sqrt{1+2\lambda_\infty},\quad
 \alpha=\frac{\mu+\beta}{\mu-\beta},\quad
 w_L=\lambda_\infty-\lambda_1(L).\] The pushed assumption \(H_p\) is \(\lambda_\infty>0\). The main theorems assume \(H_{fp}\), namely \(\lambda_\infty>1/16\), equivalently \(\mu<3\beta\) or \(\alpha>2\). The cutoff in (19) and the weights in (20), page 1393, are \[
 L=L_N=\frac{\log N}{\mu-\beta},\qquad
 H_L(x):=h(0,x)=\frac{e^{\mu x}v_L(x)}
                    {\widetilde c\|v_L\|_2^2},\qquad
 h(s,x)=e^{w_Ls}H_L(x),\] where \(\widetilde c^{-1}=\int_0^\infty e^{-\mu x}v_\infty(x)\,dx\). Here \(v_\infty(x)=e^{-\beta(x-1)}\) for \(x\geq1\), and \(I:=\|v_\infty\|_2^2\in(0,\infty)\).

Several structural calculations check correctly. For \(A=\frac12\partial_{xx}-\mu\partial_x+r\), direct substitution gives \(AH_L=-w_LH_L\). Consequently \[(\partial_s+A)h=0,\qquad
 H_L^{-1}A(H_L f)+w_Lf
   =\tfrac12f''+\frac{v_L'}{v_L}f'.\] Thus the conservative spine has invariant density \(\Pi_L=v_L^2/\|v_L\|_2^2\); its probability current vanishes since \(\frac12\Pi_L'=(v_L'/v_L)\Pi_L\). Also \(r h_\infty\Pi_\infty\) has tail proportional to \(e^{(\mu-3\beta)x}\). Its integrability holds precisely when \(\mu<3\beta\), giving the stated threshold for the finite variance constant \(\Sigma^2=2\int r h_\infty\Pi_\infty\). Near zero the integrand is of order \(x^3\). These checks support the basic transform and the fully pushed integrability criterion; they do not supply the missing uniform estimate identified next.
# A boundary-uniform estimate fails in the survival proof

Problem 1 (Major: the initial boundary contribution is not uniformly bounded).  Lemma 15, page 1424 (physical 43), claims a positive constant \(C_1=C_1(\lambda_\infty)\), independent of \(0<T_1<T_2\), such that \[u(tN,x)\geq \frac{C_1H_L(x)}{1+tN},
 \qquad x\in[0,L],\quad t\in[T_1,T_2],\] where \(u(s,x)=\mathbb P_x(Z_s^L>0)\). Its proof on page 1425 asserts an interval-independent bound on the two-spine expectation. More decisively, the proof of Corollary 8, page 1427 (physical 46), after (94), claims that \[Q_x^{2,L^2}\big[r(\zeta_v)h(|v|,\zeta_v)\big]\] is uniformly bounded in \(N\) and \(x\). Both uniformity claims fail under the actual fully pushed hypotheses.
## An exact admissible boundary sequence

The assumptions are nonempty. For example \(W(x)=200(1-x)^2\) on \([0,1]\), zero elsewhere, is nonnegative and \(C^1\). Testing the Rayleigh quotient with \(\sin(2\pi x)\) on \([0,1/2]\), extended by zero, gives \(\lambda_\infty\geq25-2\pi^2>1/16\). The argument above works for every admissible fully pushed potential, rather than relying on an approximate eigenvalue for this example.

Contradiction to Lemma 15 as quantified. If the positive \(C_1\) is independent of the time interval, choose a fixed \(t<C_1K_d\) and then choose \(0<T_1<t<T_2\). By [eq:boundary] (#eq:boundary), \(C_1H_L(x_N)/(1+tN)\to C_1K_d/t>1\). The claimed probability lower bound therefore exceeds one for large \(N\), which is impossible. Allowing \(C_1\) to depend on \(T_1\) removes this particular contradiction, but changes the statement and does not by itself justify the subsequent limit as the initial macroscopic time tends to zero in (81). ◻
## Direct contradiction to the short-time two-spine bound

Equation reference: eq:q2. The tree construction on pages 1394–1395 and Corollary 1, page 1404, make the sole branch time of a two-spine tree uniform on \([0,T]\). Conditional on that forward time \(s\), the branching location has the one-spine law at \(s\). Therefore, exactly, \[
 Q_x^{2,T}[r(\zeta_v)h(|v|,\zeta_v)]
 =\frac1T\int_0^T
       \mathbb E_x^Q[r(\zeta_s)h(s,\zeta_s)]\,ds .\] This is the unaccelerated \(Q^{2,T}\) used in (94); the accelerated notation elsewhere does not change this identity.

For \(y>1\), the spine drift is \[\frac{v_L'(y)}{v_L(y)}
   =-\beta_L\coth\big(\beta_L(L-y)\big).\] It is uniformly bounded in absolute value on \([L-2d,L-d/2]\) for all large \(N\). Starting from \(x_N=L-d\), there are \(s_0>0\) and \(p>0\), independent of \(N\), such that the spine stays in that interval throughout \([0,s_0]\) with probability at least \(p\). For completeness, stop the SDE at the interval endpoints, bound its drift by \(B\), choose \(Bs_0<d/8\), and use the Brownian event \(\sup_{s\leq s_0}|B_s|<d/8\), which has strictly positive probability. On this event the stopped path cannot reach an endpoint.

Equation reference: eq:diverge. Uniformly over that interval, the same hyperbolic calculation as [eq:boundary] (#eq:boundary) gives \(H_L(y)\geq cN\) for some \(c>0\). Also \(r(y)=1/2\) there and \(h(s,y)\geq H_L(y)\). Applying [eq:q2] (#eq:q2) with \(T=L^2\) proves \[
 Q_{x_N}^{2,L^2}[r(\zeta_v)h(|v|,\zeta_v)]
 \geq \frac{pcs_0}{2}\frac{N}{L^2}
 \longrightarrow\infty .\] Thus the actual estimate invoked after (94) is false, independently of the interpretation of the constants in Lemma 15. For \(T=tN\), the same initial contribution is at least \(pcs_0/(2t)\); this also prevents a single bound valid for all arbitrarily small positive macroscopic times.
## Dependency, alternative readings, and repair boundary

The disputed estimate bounds the Bonferroni pair term in (94). It is used to obtain (96), the lower half of Corollary 8’s all-\(x\) profile approximation. Corollary 8 then enters Lemma 17 and the survival differential equation; page 1428 uses these results to prove Theorem 1. Theorem 1 in turn normalizes the conditional moments and the genealogy limits in Section 7.

The counterexample uses interior starting points at distance \(d\) from the boundary, not a particle started at the absorbing endpoint. It also concerns a positive expectation; there is no cancellation that can remove the initial contribution. Mixing on a scale much shorter than \(N\) controls later times but does not erase the positive integral over \([0,s_0]\). Lemma 13 itself allows a factor \(t^{-(k-1)}\); substituting \(t=L^2/N\) does not give the claimed constant bound.

This is a demonstrated invalid step in a core derivation and merits Major severity. It is not a counterexample to Theorem 1 for fixed \(x>0\), nor a proof that the final Yaglom or genealogy limits are false. A possible repair must control the initial contribution with its spatial dependence, restrict an intermediate uniformity range, or justify a weighted integration that makes the boundary region negligible. The report does not claim to have completed that replacement argument. It also does not infer the falsity of Corollary 8 solely from the failure of its proof.
# The stated pushed range is too broad for the time normalization

Problem 2 (Minor: equation (46) and the second limit of Corollary 2 fail under \(H_p\)).  Lemma 5, page 1407 (physical 26), assumes only \(H_p\) and claims, for \(0<t\lesssim N\), \[h(t,x)=\bigl(1+O(e^{(\mu-3\beta)L})\bigr)h(0,x).\] Corollary 2, pages 1408–1409 (physical 27–28), likewise assumes only \(H_p\), and asserts convergence for bounded continuous tests of \((x,h(tN,x))\), uniformly over bounded macroscopic time intervals. These statements fail in the semipushed range.

Choose an admissible \(W\) with \(\lambda_\infty=1/32\). Such a potential exists in the family \(W_a=a(1-x)^2\mathbf1_{[0,1]}(x)\): the supremum of the Rayleigh quotient is nonnegative, starts at zero, is Lipschitz in \(a\) with constant at most \(1/2\), and tends to infinity by any fixed nonzero test function in \((0,1)\). Continuity gives the asserted value. Then \[\beta=\tfrac14,\quad \mu=\tfrac{\sqrt{17}}4,\quad
 \alpha=\frac{\sqrt{17}+1}{\sqrt{17}-1}\in(1,2).\] At \(t=N\), [eq:gap] (#eq:gap) gives \[w_LN\sim C N^{2-\alpha}\longrightarrow\infty,\qquad C>0.\] But the exact time factor in [eq:weights] (#eq:weights) is \(e^{w_LN}\). It cannot equal \(1+O(N^{2-\alpha})\), whereas \(e^{(\mu-3\beta)L}=N^{2-\alpha}\). The error is an invalid linearization of an exponential whose argument diverges.

There is also a bounded continuous test contradicting the second limit in Corollary 2. Take \(k=1\), \(t_1=1\), and \(f(x,z)=\chi(x)e^{-z}\), where \(\chi\) is a nonnegative, nonzero continuous function with compact support in \((0,\infty)\). On its support \(H_L\to h_\infty>0\) uniformly, so \[\int \chi(x)e^{-h(N,x)}\Pi_L(dx)\longrightarrow0.\] The asserted limit is instead \(\int\chi(x)e^{-h_\infty(x)}\Pi_\infty(dx)>0\). All tests and parameter restrictions in the claimed corollary are satisfied.

The first, time-independent convergence of \(\Pi_L\) is not refuted. Nor is this an example in the fully pushed main-theorem regime. The introductory sentence of Section 4, page 1405, expressly says the results of Sections 4.1–4.2 do not require \(H_{fp}\), so the stronger assumption cannot silently be inserted as the original statement. Requiring \(H_{fp}\) for the \(N\)-time normalization, or restricting time so that \(w_Lt=o(1)\), is a bounded repair. Keeping \(e^{w_Lt}\) exactly is another option when formulating a different limit. The minor severity reflects this range restriction and the main results’ explicit \(H_{fp}\) hypothesis.
# The Green kernel and Wronskian have a factor-of-two discrepancy

Problem 3 (Minor: incorrect normalization in (63) and Lemma 10).  Section 4.3, page 1413 (physical 32), defines \[\omega_\lambda=
 \psi_\lambda(1)\varphi_\lambda'(1)
   -\psi_\lambda'(1)\varphi_\lambda(1),\] where \(\varphi_\lambda,\psi_\lambda\) solve \(\frac12u''+\frac12Wu=\lambda u\), with \(\varphi_\lambda(0)=0\), \(\psi_\lambda(L)=0\), and the normalizations (62). Proposition 13, page 1414, gives the resolvent kernel as \(\omega_\lambda^{-1}\) times the product of fundamental solutions. For the stated diffusion coefficient \(1/2\), that coefficient must be \(2\omega_\lambda^{-1}\). Lemma 10, pages 1416–1417, inherits the same factor discrepancy.

Equation reference: eq:green. Exact jump and Wronskian checks. Put \(\lambda=\lambda_\infty+\xi\), \(\xi>0\), and remove the drift factor by writing \[R_\lambda(x,y)=e^{\mu(y-x)}G_\xi(x,y).\] It must solve \[\left(\lambda-\tfrac12\partial_{yy}-\tfrac12W(y)\right)
 R_\lambda(x,y)=\delta_x(y).\] Integrating across \(y=x\) shows that its derivative jump must equal \(-2\). The continuous product kernel \(\varphi_\lambda(\min(x,y))\psi_\lambda(\max(x,y))/\omega_\lambda\) has derivative jump \(-1\), by the displayed definition of \(\omega_\lambda\). Therefore the exact correction is \[
 G_\xi(x,y)=\frac{2e^{\mu(x-y)}}{\omega_{\lambda_\infty+\xi}}
 \varphi_{\lambda_\infty+\xi}(\min(x,y))
 \psi_{\lambda_\infty+\xi}(\max(x,y)).\] Multiplying fundamental solutions by arbitrary constants leaves this conclusion unchanged.

The identity defining \(G_\xi\) is the time integral of the Lebesgue-density particle kernel, and the governing PDE has diffusion coefficient \(1/2\). Thus neither a speed-measure convention nor a rescaling of the Wronskian can reconcile (63) with those definitions. As a separate algebraic calibration, for \(W=0\), \(\varphi(y)=\sinh(ky)/k\) and \(\psi(y)=\sinh(k(L-y))\), the printed jump is exactly \(-1\). That calibration alone is not asserted to satisfy \(H_p\); the general jump argument above applies to the actual admissible potentials.

The paper uses this resolvent in Lemmas 11–12 to obtain order bounds on escape and moment integrals. The repaired Wronskian still has \(\omega^{-1}=O(N)\) at \(\xi=(TN)^{-1}\) for fixed \(T>0\), so this normalization error alone does not refute those order estimates or the final \(\Sigma^2\). Equations [eq:green] (#eq:green)–[eq:wronskian] (#eq:wronskian) give a direct local repair. The cited handbook page was not accessible in the bounded reference search; the proof here uses the paper’s own PDE and does not attribute an error to that external source.
# A false positive-minimum argument has a local replacement

Problem 4 (Minor: the compactness argument in Lemma 8 fails at zero).  Lemma 8, pages 1410–1411 (physical 29–30), seeks \(\|u_k\|_2^2\geq c_8(1\wedge|\lambda_k|^{-1})\), where \(u_\lambda(0)=0\), \(u_\lambda'(0)=1\). After (55), it rescales the interval by \(1/|\lambda|\) and asserts that the function \(g_2\) on \([-1,0]\) attains a strictly positive minimum. Its continuous extension at zero is actually zero. The asserted norm estimate can nevertheless be proved by a different argument.

Equation reference: eq:g2. Write \(\lambda=-a\), \(a\to\infty\), and \(z_a(t)=a u_{-a}(t/a)\). Since \(u_{-a}''=(-2a-W)u_{-a}\), \[z_a''(t)=-
 \left(\frac2a+\frac{W(t/a)}{a^2}\right)z_a(t),\qquad
 z_a(0)=0,\quad z_a'(0)=1.\] For bounded \(W\), elementary continuous dependence of this integral equation gives \(z_a\to t\) uniformly on \([0,1]\). The integrand used to define \(g_2(-1/a)\) is exactly \(u_{-a}(t/a)^2\), because \(u_\lambda=\rho_\lambda\sin\theta_\lambda\). Therefore \[
 a^2g_2(-1/a)=\int_0^1z_a(t)^2\,dt\longrightarrow\frac13.\] There is no positive minimum. Moreover the lower integral in (55) is only asymptotic to \(1/(3a^3)\), so that particular lower bound cannot yield the desired \(1/a\) scale.

For an actual admissible potential, the independent calculation uses \(W=200(1-x)^2\) on \([0,1]\) as above. An 80-digit power-series solution of the scaled equation gives the following values; degree 40 and degree 60 evaluations agree to the shown precision. They corroborate [eq:g2] (#eq:g2), rather than replacing its proof. \[\begin{array}{c|cccc}
 a&100&1000&10000&10^6\\ \hline
 a^2g_2(-1/a)&0.3306877972&0.3331867085&
              0.3333198669&0.3333332000
\end{array}\] No certified floating-point interval bound is claimed.

A replacement proof of the norm estimate. For \(\lambda=-s^2/2\), variation of constants gives \[u_\lambda(x)=\frac{\sin(sx)}s
   -\frac1s\int_0^x\sin(s(x-y))W(y)u_\lambda(y)\,dy .\] Let \(M=\|W\|_\infty\). Gronwall’s inequality on \([0,1]\) gives \[\|u_\lambda\|_\infty\leq \frac{e^{M/s}}s,\qquad
 \left\|u_\lambda-\frac{\sin(s\,\cdot)}s\right\|_\infty
       \leq\frac{Me^{M/s}}{s^2}.\] For sufficiently large \(s\), \[\left\|\frac{\sin(s\,\cdot)}s\right\|_{L^2(0,1)}
 =\frac1s\left(\frac12-\frac{\sin(2s)}{4s}\right)^{1/2}
 \geq\frac1{2s},\] and the error norm is at most \(1/(4s)\). Thus \[\|u_\lambda\|_{L^2(0,1)}^2
    \geq\frac1{16s^2}=\frac1{32|\lambda|}.\] On the remaining compact range of \(\lambda\leq\lambda_\infty\), continuity of the ODE solution and the nonzero initial derivative give a positive minimum of \(\int_0^1u_\lambda^2\). Since \(L\geq1\), the full norm over \([0,L]\) is at least this norm. Combining the two ranges proves Lemma 8’s claimed order, with a constant depending on the fixed potential. ◻

Lemma 8 supports the normalized-eigenfunction bounds in Proposition 10 and hence the heat-kernel estimate in Proposition 12. The replacement above restores the needed order without the false compactness assertion. Accordingly this is a proof defect with a complete local repair, not a counterexample to the norm lemma or by itself to the main theorem.
# Coverage, counterevidence, and reviewed-version limits

The primary reviewer read the extracted scientific text of all 52 physical pages. The review followed the model assumptions, main theorem range, the many-to-one and many-to-few weights, spectral normalization, moment estimates, survival argument, and their use in conditional metric-space convergence. The four findings above include all hypotheses used by their counterarguments. Reading and checking these dependency paths does not amount to independent certification of every cited theorem or every statement in the paper.

All source pages bearing the reported evidence were also inspected as native images: physical pages 1–6, 12–15, 17–18, 20–24, 26–30, 32–33, 35–36, 39–41, 43–47, and 49–52. The explicit hyperbolic tail, branch-time convention, time quantifiers, Green-kernel coefficient, and high-frequency minimum assertion were checked against those page images. Other extracted pages were read as text, not claimed as image inspections. Mechanical extraction and rendering are recorded separately from actual viewing.

Bounded searches on 29 October 2026 checked the authors’ publication listings, the arXiv record, and title/DOI-specific correction and supplement queries. The public arXiv record lists version 3 dated 18 October 2024 [arxiv]; the author listing identifies the published article [authorpage]. No target-specific correction was found in those checks. This is not a claim that no correction exists. The publisher landing-page route encountered an access/security limit. The acquired version of record remains the reviewed object; the arXiv file was not silently substituted.

The cited Borodin–Salminen DOI resolves to the first edition, copyright 1996, with a 2012 electronic publication date [BSmetadata]. Its public chapter information did not provide the cited page 19. That source page was neither read nor viewed. No claim about the handbook’s own normalization is made. No author code was executed; no lack of author code is treated as a mathematical defect.

Problem 1 remains a substantive gap in the printed core derivation. Problems 2–4 have explicitly bounded impacts, with local repairs where established. These findings do not constitute a proof of failure of the fully pushed fixed-\(x\) limit theorems, a complete revised proof, or an independent acceptance decision.

 z_a(0)=0,\quad z_a'(0)=1.\] For bounded \(W\), elementary continuous dependence of this integral equation gives \(z_a\to t\) uniformly on \([0,1]\). The integrand used to define \(g_2(-1/a)\) is exactly \(u_{-a}(t/a)^2\), because \(u_\lambda=\rho_\lambda\sin\theta_\lambda\). Therefore \[
 a^2g_2(-1/a)=\int_0^1z_a(t)^2\,dt\longrightarrow\frac13.\] There is no positive minimum. Moreover the lower integral in (55) is only asymptotic to \(1/(3a^3)\), so that particular lower bound cannot yield the desired \(1/a\) scale.

For an actual admissible potential, the independent calculation uses \(W=200(1-x)^2\) on \([0,1]\) as above. An 80-digit power-series solution of the scaled equation gives the following values; degree 40 and degree 60 evaluations agree to the shown precision. They corroborate [eq:g2] (#eq:g2), rather than replacing its proof. \[\begin{array}{c|cccc}
 a&100&1000&10000&10^6\\ \hline
 a^2g_2(-1/a)&0.3306877972&0.3331867085&
              0.3333198669&0.3333332000
\end{array}\] No certified floating-point interval bound is claimed.

A replacement proof of the norm estimate. For \(\lambda=-s^2/2\), variation of constants gives \[u_\lambda(x)=\frac{\sin(sx)}s
   -\frac1s\int_0^x\sin(s(x-y))W(y)u_\lambda(y)\,dy .\] Let \(M=\|W\|_\infty\). Gronwall’s inequality on \([0,1]\) gives \[\|u_\lambda\|_\infty\leq \frac{e^{M/s}}s,\qquad
 \left\|u_\lambda-\frac{\sin(s\,\cdot)}s\right\|_\infty
       \leq\frac{Me^{M/s}}{s^2}.\] For sufficiently large \(s\), \[\left\|\frac{\sin(s\,\cdot)}s\right\|_{L^2(0,1)}
 =\frac1s\left(\frac12-\frac{\sin(2s)}{4s}\right)^{1/2}
 \geq\frac1{2s},\] and the error norm is at most \(1/(4s)\). Thus \[\|u_\lambda\|_{L^2(0,1)}^2
    \geq\frac1{16s^2}=\frac1{32|\lambda|}.\] On the remaining compact range of \(\lambda\leq\lambda_\infty\), continuity of the ODE solution and the nonzero initial derivative give a positive minimum of \(\int_0^1u_\lambda^2\). Since \(L\geq1\), the full norm over \([0,L]\) is at least this norm. Combining the two ranges proves Lemma 8’s claimed order, with a constant depending on the fixed potential. ◻

Lemma 8 supports the normalized-eigenfunction bounds in Proposition 10 and hence the heat-kernel estimate in Proposition 12. The replacement above restores the needed order without the false compactness assertion. Accordingly this is a proof defect with a complete local repair, not a counterexample to the norm lemma or by itself to the main theorem.
