report: Abstract: The acquired arXiv version has an incorrect finite-time flat-current formula: its right-hand side drops the initial offset, although exact small-ring probabilities depend on that offset. This is a Major finding about the stated finite-time proposition, with a local repair suggested by the paper’s own derivation. Four further bounded findings concern inconsistent step-limit kernels, a missing deformation factor in the collision rule, the phase of the product of Bethe roots, and an unsupported extension by particle–hole duality. The appendix already gives the correct collision factor, and the later step-limit proof gives the kernel expected from the cited reference. These observations limit the impact of the findings. No claim is made that the large-system fluctuation theorems are false, or that the acquired preprint is identical to the journal version.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Initial technical review of
Contour Integral Formulas for PushASEP on the Ring
# Reviewed object and mathematical setting

This is the initial review of M25-0515 by Jhih-Huang Li and Axel Saenz. The annual record identifies DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1738 (https://doi.org/10.1214/24-AOP1738), The Annals of Probability 53(4) (2025), 1434–1490. The actual acquired scientific object is arXiv:2308.05372v1, submitted 10 August 2023, with 91 physical pages, including Appendices A–F [LS]. Physical and printed page numbers coincide. Its SHA256 is
> 00000TOKEN.
All locators below refer to this version unless another source is named. Journal-version equivalence has not been established.

The state is an ordered configuration \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\) with \(0\leq x_1<\cdots<x_N<L\). Each particle attempts a right exclusion jump at rate \(p\), and a left push at rate \(q\), where \(p,q\geq0\) and \(p+q=1\). A left push moves the consecutive occupied block to the first hole. The total current \(Q\) counts all individual displacements; the local current \(Q_j\) counts net crossings of the edge \(j\to j+1\). The generator (2.8), page 9, rather than an alternative convention about attempted jumps, is used for every calculation in this report.

Equation reference: eq:conservation, eq:gauge. The deformation is \[g(Y,X;\zeta;t)=\mathbb E_Y[\zeta^{Q(t)}\mathbf1_{\{X(t)=X\}}],
 \qquad |\zeta|=1.\] An independently checked conservation law is \[
 Q(t)=\sum_i(x_i-y_i)+LQ_{L-1}(t).\] It holds at each allowed transition, including a push across the origin, and hence along every path. This verifies (3.25) and the gauge relation (3.30), pages 23–24. In particular, \[
 \zeta^L=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 g(Y,X;\zeta;t)=\zeta^{\sum_i(x_i-y_i)}
 \mathbb P_Y(X(t)=X).\] Exact rational enumeration also checked this transition identity and uniform stationarity on the rings \((L,N)=(6,2),(4,3),(3,1)\), comprising 76 allowed transitions at \(p=q=1/2\). These are finite-system checks, not a proof of all contour or asymptotic estimates.

The contour conditions on page 15 require \[\frac{1}{1-\rho}<\beta_1<\frac1\rho,\qquad
 \frac1\rho<\beta_2<\frac{L}{N-1},\qquad \rho=N/L,\] and thus \(2N<L\). Remark 4.4, page 39, supplies modified conditions at \(2N=L\). The generic spectral expansion explicitly excludes finitely many \(\zeta\)’s. Corollary 3.5, page 20, additionally assumes simple coupling roots at \(\zeta=1\); this review does not silently remove that assumption. Remark 4.7, page 41, distinguishes a fixed small contour from its limit as its radius tends to zero, resolving a possible apparent discontinuity in \(u_0\).
# Problem 1: the finite flat-current formula loses the offset
Problem 1 (Major).  Proposition 5.4, page 59, equation (5.37), with the definitions (5.34)–(5.36) on page 58, cannot hold for every initial offset allowed in (5.30).
#### Assertion and hypotheses.

Fix integers \(d\geq2\), \(L=dN\), and \[Y_\delta=(\delta,d+\delta,\ldots,(N-1)d+\delta),\qquad 0\leq\delta<d.\] For an integer threshold \(a\), Proposition 5.4 represents \(\mathbb P_{Y_\delta}(Q_{L-1}(t)\geq a)\) by a contour integral of \(C_N^{(\mathrm{flat})}(z)\det(I+K_z^{(\mathrm{flat})})\). As printed, neither factor defined in (5.34)–(5.36) contains \(\delta\). The root sets, contour radius condition, energy and the map \(V\) are also independent of \(\delta\).

Proof. From \((1,4)\), the rightmost particle can make the two jumps \(4\to5\to0\). This is the unique two-transition path with a positive crossing of edge 5, so its contribution is \(t^2/2\). From \((0,3)\), that particle needs three jumps \(3\to4\to5\to0\), and the particle at 0 must first vacate 0. At least four transitions are required. In the shortest paths, \(0\to1\) can occur in any of the three positions preceding the final crossing. The three ordered paths each contribute \(t^4/4!\), giving \(t^4/8\). Terms with extra transitions or holding-time corrections have higher order. The finite jump rates justify these Taylor expansions. ◻

An independent exact rational computation of the generator on configuration/current pairs reproduced these coefficients through order six. At strictly positive rates \(p=q=1/2\), it gives \[\mathbb P_{(0,3)}(Q_5(t)\geq1)=\tfrac1{128}t^4+O(t^5),\qquad
 \mathbb P_{(1,4)}(Q_5(t)\geq1)=\tfrac18t^2+O(t^3).\] Thus excluding the one-way boundary of the rate parameter would not remove the discrepancy. The choices satisfy \(2N<L\), so this is not a high-density or contour-endpoint objection. A single expression independent of \(\delta\) cannot equal both probabilities.
#### Counterevidence and repair.

Equation reference: eq:offset-repair. The derivation itself retains \(\delta\): equation (5.38), page 60, contains \(w^{1+\delta}\); equation (5.39) contains \(v_j^{-N+\delta+2}\); and page 61 retains \(v^{L-N-Q+\delta}\). Consequently the necessary offset factors are \[
 C_{N,\delta}^{(\mathrm{flat})}
 =C_{N,0}^{(\mathrm{flat})}\prod_{v\in Q_1(z)}v^\delta,
 \qquad
 f_\delta^{(\mathrm{flat})}(w)=w^\delta f_0^{(\mathrm{flat})}(w).\] These factors follow directly from the displayed derivation; this is not a claim to have reverified every other determinant normalization in the proposition.

Spatial translation does not make the finite-time current at a fixed edge independent of the initial phase. It translates the observed edge as well. Conversely, conservation between two edges at distance \(\delta\) bounds the difference of their currents by \(\delta\), because it is a change in the particle count of the intervening arc. For fixed \(d\), this is bounded uniformly in time. It vanishes after the \(\sqrt L\) fluctuation normalization in Theorem 3.13. Thus the counterexample disproves the stated exact finite-time proposition, but does not disprove the asymptotic offset independence asserted on page 27. The core dependency is Proposition 5.4 \(\to\) the flat asymptotic calculation in Section 5.2; the omitted factors must be restored before that derivation is used.
# Problem 2: two different step-limit kernels
Problem 2 (Minor, with an essential formula correction).  Equation (3.41), page 27, defines a different kernel from the one identified in the proof of Theorem 3.14 on page 70.
#### Exact discrepancy.
#### Decisive comparison.

This is not just a renaming of the summation variable. Take \(z=e^{-1/2}\), \(\tau=1\), \(\gamma=0\), \(\xi_1=-1\), and \(\xi_2=-\sqrt{1+4\pi i}\), using the square root with positive real part. Then \(\Re\xi_2<-1\). In [eq:printed-kernel] (#eq:printed-kernel), all \(x\)-dependence factors out as \(e^{x(\xi_1+\xi_2)}\), and its remaining series converges absolutely, since its summands have order \(|\eta|^{-3}\). Therefore \(e^{2x}K_{\rm def}(-1,\xi_2)\to0\) as \(x\to+\infty\). In [eq:proof-kernel] (#eq:proof-kernel), the unique root with maximal real part is \(\eta=-1\). Its nonzero contribution gives \[e^{2x}K_{\rm proof}(-1,\xi_2)
 \longrightarrow
 \frac{\exp\{2/3+4H(-1)\}}{-2(\xi_2-1)}\ne0.\] The remaining terms vanish: along the other roots, \(\Re\eta\leq\Re\xi_2<-1\), while \(\Re\eta^3\) grows positively of order \(|\eta|^3\). Also \(H(\eta)=O(|\eta|^{-1})\). The latter bound follows by integrating horizontally from the left, where \(|\operatorname{Li}_{1/2}(e^{-w^2/2})|
 \leq C_z e^{-\Re(w^2)/2}\). These bounds supply an absolute summable majorant. The two displayed kernels are consequently unequal as functions of \(x\).
#### Counterevidence, dependency and repair.

The cited Baik–Liu manuscript [BL], Section 4.2, equations (4.11)–(4.12), physical page 12, uses precisely the \(\Phi(\xi_1)+\Phi(\eta)\) form. The acquired paper’s own page 70 therefore supplies strong evidence of the intended correction. Replace (3.41) by [eq:proof-kernel] (#eq:proof-kernel), retaining the doubled integral coefficient in (3.42). The definition of \(F_2\) in (3.40) feeds Theorem 3.14 and the stated distributional properties, so this correction is necessary for that identification. The proof above establishes different kernels; it does not by itself establish different final contour-integrated distribution functions, nor a counterexample to the corrected fluctuation theorem. The local nature of the repair and its presence in the proof support the Minor classification.
# Problem 3: the collision rule omits a deformation factor
Problem 3 (Minor).  The exclusion/push rule (2.21), page 11, is incompatible with the claimed free-generator reduction for general \(\zeta\).
#### Hypotheses and direct check.

The extension is asserted for \(|\zeta|=1\), every admissible ordered configuration, and the generating function of total current. For two adjacent coordinates, it prints \(g(Y,(a,a);\zeta;t)=g(Y,(a,a+1);\zeta;t)\). Take \(L=5,N=2,p=1,q=0,Y=X=(0,1)\), and \(t=0\). There is exactly one allowed right jump from \(Y\), namely \(1\to2\). The actual diagonal forward derivative is therefore \(-1\). Even interpreting the free sum (2.22) as intended, over the two particle coordinates, its value under the printed rule is \[\zeta g(Y,(-1,1);\zeta;0)
 +\zeta g(Y,(0,0);\zeta;0)-2g(Y,(0,1);\zeta;0)
 =\zeta-2.\] The first incoming term is zero after the periodic identification; the collision term is one under (2.21). At \(\zeta=i\) the discrepancy is \(i-1\ne0\). The parameters satisfy the low-density range, and this calculation uses the actual generator and initial condition, not a choice of Bethe roots.

Equation reference: eq:collision. The correct local condition is \[
 g(Y,(a,a);\zeta;t)
 =\zeta^{-1}g(Y,(a,a+1);\zeta;t).\] It cancels the spurious incoming term against the loss for a blocked jump. The amplitudes (2.25) independently confirm the same factor. With \(a_j=1-(\zeta w_j)^{-1}\), the two-particle Bethe function at these two configurations, for \(a=0\), is \[u_{\rm coll}=1-\frac{a_2}{a_1},\qquad
 u_{\rm adj}=\frac1{w_2}-\frac{a_2}{a_1w_1}.\] For nonzero \(w_1,w_2,\zeta\) with \(a_1\ne0\), direct simplification gives \(u_{\rm adj}=\zeta u_{\rm coll}\). The symbolic calculation saved with this review checks this identity; the sample values \(w_1=2,w_2=3,\zeta=i\) are algebraic checks only, not asserted solutions of the periodic Bethe equations.
#### Counterevidence, repair and impact.

Lemma B.1, pages 80–81, explicitly proves the factor \(\zeta^{-1}\) in [eq:collision] (#eq:collision). Thus the appendix supplies the correct condition. At \(\zeta=1\) the discrepancy disappears. The chain (2.21) \(\to\) (2.22)–(2.23) \(\to\) Proposition 2.3 is invalid as printed, but correcting (2.21) consistently with Lemma B.1 removes this demonstrated local obstruction. This is not a counterexample to the final eigenfunction identity. The available internal repair supports a Minor classification.
# Problem 4: the product of Bethe roots has a missing phase
Problem 4 (Minor).  Item 1 of Lemma D.1, page 85, incorrectly asserts that the product of the post-change roots is an \(L\)-th root of unity for every unit-modulus \(\zeta\).

Equation reference: eq:root-product. The hypotheses are positive integers \(L\geq N\geq1\), \(\zeta\in\mathbb U\), and a solution of (dBE1)–(dBE2) with pairwise distinct roots. Multiplying the deformed Bethe equations (2.31), page 13, gives, wherever their ratios are defined, \[
 \left(\prod_{j=1}^N w_jight)^L=\zeta^{LN}.\] Indeed, the ratios telescope in the product over \(j\), and the sign is \((-1)^{N(N-1)}=1\). A counterexample within the stated hypotheses is \[L=3,\qquad N=1,\qquad \zeta=i,\qquad w_1=i,\qquad z^3=1-i.\] Here \(z
e0\), \(w_1
e0,1\), and distinctness is automatic. The decoupled equations reduce to \(z^3=w_1^3(1-w_1^{-1})\) and \(z^3=\zeta^3(1-w_1^{-1})\); both equal \(1-i\). Nevertheless \(w_1^3=-i
e1\).

The correct conclusion is that \(\zeta^{-N}\prod_jw_j\) is an \(L\)-th root of unity. The modulus identity \(\prod_j|w_j|=1\) survives, because \(|\zeta|=1\). This is the part used in the subsequent root-size estimate and small-\(z\) exclusion argument on pages 85–86. Those arguments feed the permissible residue contours; this finding does not disprove their final modulus or isolation conclusions. It also does not apply to the pre-change variables, whose product has the unshifted phase. The paper explicitly states after (2.31) that it drops the \(\zeta\) subscript, so interpreting Lemma D.1 as a statement about the old variables would require changing its specified decoupled equations. Correcting the phase is a local repair.
# Problem 5: the stated particle–hole extension needs a proof

Problem 5 (Minor, confined to the claimed extension of range).  Remark 2.5, page 16, does not establish its extension from the contour range \(2N<L\) to all densities by ordinary particle–hole duality for PushASEP with \(q>0\).

The contour inequalities in Section 1 of this report have a nonempty interval for \(\beta_1\) exactly when \(2N<L\). The modified contour conditions on page 39 and in Appendix A cover equality \(2N=L\). A further argument is required for larger densities. Under ordinary complementation (with or without reflection), left pushes of particle blocks become long jumps of holes, not nearest-neighbour pushes of single holes.

For an explicit generator check, take \(L=4,N=3,p=0,q=1\) with occupied sites \(\{1,2,3\}\) and a hole at 0. The clocks at 1, 2 and 3 move that hole respectively to 1, 2 and 3, each at rate one: they shift blocks of lengths one, two and three into 0. In particular, the hole jumps to the opposite site 2 at positive rate. A one-particle PushASEP on the four-cycle, at any choice of the two nearest-neighbour rates, cannot make that jump. Reflection does not change this obstruction. The opposite jump persists at positive rate for every \(q>0\); it is not a singularity specific to \(p=0\).

For \(q=0\), ordinary TASEP particle–hole symmetry does give a nearest-neighbour process, which is relevant counterevidence to any overly broad assertion that particle–hole reasoning always fails. Nor does this example rule out a different algebraic duality, a transformation to another process with a separate formula, or a direct extension of the contour proof. The point is that the unqualified ordinary particle–hole argument does not supply any of these.

The scope of the contour and delta-basis derivation should remain explicit unless the transformed generator, current observable, and resulting formulas are proved. The fully occupied case also needs separate treatment: the configuration generator (2.8) has no allowed move, whereas expressions involving \(1-\rho\) become singular. This is a gap in the claimed range extension, not a counterexample to the low-density contour formula or its fluctuation limits.
# Coverage, independent checks and version limits

All 91 physical pages of the acquired preprint were read, including the six appendices and the reference list. The definitions, hypotheses, quantifiers and immediate proof dependencies of all five findings were checked directly. Thirty-eight source pages containing the model, statements, decisive formulas, derivations, and counterevidence were also inspected as rendered images. The relevant Baik–Liu reference text on physical pages 11–12 was read; its title page and pages 11–12 were viewed. This does not constitute a complete independent review of that reference.

An independently written exact-arithmetic calculation used configuration/current states, the generator (2.8), and matrix powers through order six. It verified the finite flat examples, the transition-by-transition current conservation law, uniform stationarity in the stated small rings, the collision identity, and the one-hole transition obstruction. The source, actual process output, software versions and result payload are saved under this paper’s verification tree. No author code was run. The analytic kernel comparison in Problem 2 and the product identity in Problem 4 are proved above; neither is presented as a numerical experiment.

The full steepest-descent estimates, all uniform error bounds, all external Fredholm determinant results and every cited theorem were not independently reproved. Generic-\(\zeta\) qualifications, the simple-root hypothesis in Corollary 3.5, and exceptional spectral parameters remain part of the theorem range. In particular, the root-product finding is not used to claim that the generic spectral theorem fails at a parameter it excludes. The zero Bethe functions noted in Remark 2.4 are already disclosed by the authors and are not an additional finding. The limiting contour interpretation in Remark 4.7 was taken into account.

The arXiv record and the author’s publication list were checked, together with searches for corrections to this title. No specific author correction was found in those checks; that bounded negative result is not proof that none exists. A supplement request reached a security-check HTML response, and an ordinary request for the official journal issue likewise returned an anti-bot HTML page rather than a PDF. Both actual responses are preserved. The embedded appendices remain available and were read. Unavailable supplementary or journal material is an access limit, not a mathematical defect, and no preprint finding is attributed to an uninspected journal revision.
This report records initial scientific findings only. The scientific decision remains pending and no independent human acceptance is recorded.

claim: The state is an ordered configuration \(X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\) with \(0\leq x_1<\cdots<x_N<L\). Each particle attempts a right exclusion jump at rate \(p\), and a left push at rate \(q\), where \(p,q\geq0\) and \(p+q=1\). A left push moves the consecutive occupied block to the first hole. The total current \(Q\) counts all individual displacements; the local current \(Q_j\) counts net crossings of the edge \(j\to j+1\). The generator (2.8), page 9, rather than an alternative convention about attempted jumps, is used for every calculation in this report.

Equation reference: eq:conservation, eq:gauge. The deformation is \[g(Y,X;\zeta;t)=\mathbb E_Y[\zeta^{Q(t)}\mathbf1_{\{X(t)=X\}}],
 \qquad |\zeta|=1.\] An independently checked conservation law is \[
 Q(t)=\sum_i(x_i-y_i)+LQ_{L-1}(t).\] It holds at each allowed transition, including a push across the origin, and hence along every path. This verifies (3.25) and the gauge relation (3.30), pages 23–24. In particular, \[
 \zeta^L=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 g(Y,X;\zeta;t)=\zeta^{\sum_i(x_i-y_i)}
 \mathbb P_Y(X(t)=X).\] Exact rational enumeration also checked this transition identity and uniform stationarity on the rings \((L,N)=(6,2),(4,3),(3,1)\), comprising 76 allowed transitions at \(p=q=1/2\). These are finite-system checks, not a proof of all contour or asymptotic estimates.

The contour conditions on page 15 require \[\frac{1}{1-\rho}<\beta_1<\frac1\rho,\qquad
 \frac1\rho<\beta_2<\frac{L}{N-1},\qquad \rho=N/L,\] and thus \(2N<L\). Remark 4.4, page 39, supplies modified conditions at \(2N=L\). The generic spectral expansion explicitly excludes finitely many \(\zeta\)’s. Corollary 3.5, page 20, additionally assumes simple coupling roots at \(\zeta=1\); this review does not silently remove that assumption. Remark 4.7, page 41, distinguishes a fixed small contour from its limit as its radius tends to zero, resolving a possible apparent discontinuity in \(u_0\).
Recorded check: The step-limit kernel definition differs from the proof
analysis: Equation (3.41), page 27, defines a different kernel from the one identified in the proof of Theorem 3.14 on page 70.

This is not just a renaming of the summation variable. Take \(z=e^{-1/2}\), \(\tau=1\), \(\gamma=0\), \(\xi_1=-1\), and \(\xi_2=-\sqrt{1+4\pi i}\), using the square root with positive real part. Then \(\Re\xi_2<-1\). In [eq:printed-kernel] (#eq:printed-kernel), all \(x\)-dependence factors out as \(e^{x(\xi_1+\xi_2)}\), and its remaining series converges absolutely, since its summands have order \(|\eta|^{-3}\). Therefore \(e^{2x}K_{\rm def}(-1,\xi_2)\to0\) as \(x\to+\infty\). In [eq:proof-kernel] (#eq:proof-kernel), the unique root with maximal real part is \(\eta=-1\). Its nonzero contribution gives \[e^{2x}K_{\rm proof}(-1,\xi_2)
 \longrightarrow
 \frac{\exp\{2/3+4H(-1)\}}{-2(\xi_2-1)}\ne0.\] The remaining terms vanish: along the other roots, \(\Re\eta\leq\Re\xi_2<-1\), while \(\Re\eta^3\) grows positively of order \(|\eta|^3\). Also \(H(\eta)=O(|\eta|^{-1})\). The latter bound follows by integrating horizontally from the left, where \(|\operatorname{Li}_{1/2}(e^{-w^2/2})|
 \leq C_z e^{-\Re(w^2)/2}\). These bounds supply an absolute summable majorant. The two displayed kernels are consequently unequal as functions of \(x\).
result: The cited Baik–Liu manuscript [BL], Section 4.2, equations (4.11)–(4.12), physical page 12, uses precisely the \(\Phi(\xi_1)+\Phi(\eta)\) form. The acquired paper’s own page 70 therefore supplies strong evidence of the intended correction. Replace (3.41) by [eq:proof-kernel] (#eq:proof-kernel), retaining the doubled integral coefficient in (3.42). The definition of \(F_2\) in (3.40) feeds Theorem 3.14 and the stated distributional properties, so this correction is necessary for that identification. The proof above establishes different kernels; it does not by itself establish different final contour-integrated distribution functions, nor a counterexample to the corrected fluctuation theorem. The local nature of the repair and its presence in the proof support the Minor classification.
Impact: Local essential formula correction; no counterexample to the corrected fluctuation theorem or final integrated distribution asserted.

analysis: The exclusion/push rule (2.21), page 11, is incompatible with the claimed free-generator reduction for general \(\zeta\).

The extension is asserted for \(|\zeta|=1\), every admissible ordered configuration, and the generating function of total current. For two adjacent coordinates, it prints \(g(Y,(a,a);\zeta;t)=g(Y,(a,a+1);\zeta;t)\). Take \(L=5,N=2,p=1,q=0,Y=X=(0,1)\), and \(t=0\). There is exactly one allowed right jump from \(Y\), namely \(1\to2\). The actual diagonal forward derivative is therefore \(-1\). Even interpreting the free sum (2.22) as intended, over the two particle coordinates, its value under the printed rule is \[\zeta g(Y,(-1,1);\zeta;0)
 +\zeta g(Y,(0,0);\zeta;0)-2g(Y,(0,1);\zeta;0)
 =\zeta-2.\] The first incoming term is zero after the periodic identification; the collision term is one under (2.21). At \(\zeta=i\) the discrepancy is \(i-1\ne0\). The parameters satisfy the low-density range, and this calculation uses the actual generator and initial condition, not a choice of Bethe roots.

Equation reference: eq:collision. The correct local condition is \[
 g(Y,(a,a);\zeta;t)
 =\zeta^{-1}g(Y,(a,a+1);\zeta;t).\] It cancels the spurious incoming term against the loss for a blocked jump. The amplitudes (2.25) independently confirm the same factor. With \(a_j=1-(\zeta w_j)^{-1}\), the two-particle Bethe function at these two configurations, for \(a=0\), is \[u_{\rm coll}=1-\frac{a_2}{a_1},\qquad
 u_{\rm adj}=\frac1{w_2}-\frac{a_2}{a_1w_1}.\] For nonzero \(w_1,w_2,\zeta\) with \(a_1\ne0\), direct simplification gives \(u_{\rm adj}=\zeta u_{\rm coll}\). The symbolic calculation saved with this review checks this identity; the sample values \(w_1=2,w_2=3,\zeta=i\) are algebraic checks only, not asserted solutions of the periodic Bethe equations.
result: Lemma B.1, pages 80–81, explicitly proves the factor \(\zeta^{-1}\) in [eq:collision] (#eq:collision). Thus the appendix supplies the correct condition. At \(\zeta=1\) the discrepancy disappears. The chain (2.21) \(\to\) (2.22)–(2.23) \(\to\) Proposition 2.3 is invalid as printed, but correcting (2.21) consistently with Lemma B.1 removes this demonstrated local obstruction. This is not a counterexample to the final eigenfunction identity. The available internal repair supports a Minor classification.
Impact: Minor local inconsistency supported by the author's own correct appendix.

analysis: Item 1 of Lemma D.1, page 85, incorrectly asserts that the product of the post-change roots is an \(L\)-th root of unity for every unit-modulus \(\zeta\).

Equation reference: eq:root-product. The hypotheses are positive integers \(L\geq N\geq1\), \(\zeta\in\mathbb U\), and a solution of (dBE1)–(dBE2) with pairwise distinct roots. Multiplying the deformed Bethe equations (2.31), page 13, gives, wherever their ratios are defined, \[
 \left(\prod_{j=1}^N w_jight)^L=\zeta^{LN}.\] Indeed, the ratios telescope in the product over \(j\), and the sign is \((-1)^{N(N-1)}=1\). A counterexample within the stated hypotheses is \[L=3,\qquad N=1,\qquad \zeta=i,\qquad w_1=i,\qquad z^3=1-i.\] Here \(z
e0\), \(w_1
e0,1\), and distinctness is automatic. The decoupled equations reduce to \(z^3=w_1^3(1-w_1^{-1})\) and \(z^3=\zeta^3(1-w_1^{-1})\); both equal \(1-i\). Nevertheless \(w_1^3=-i
e1\).

Recorded check: Ordinary particle–hole duality does not justify the high-density extension
analysis: Remark 2.5, page 16, does not establish its extension from the contour range \(2N<L\) to all densities by ordinary particle–hole duality for PushASEP with \(q>0\).

The contour inequalities in Section 1 of this report have a nonempty interval for \(\beta_1\) exactly when \(2N<L\). The modified contour conditions on page 39 and in Appendix A cover equality \(2N=L\). A further argument is required for larger densities. Under ordinary complementation (with or without reflection), left pushes of particle blocks become long jumps of holes, not nearest-neighbour pushes of single holes.

For an explicit generator check, take \(L=4,N=3,p=0,q=1\) with occupied sites \(\{1,2,3\}\) and a hole at 0. The clocks at 1, 2 and 3 move that hole respectively to 1, 2 and 3, each at rate one: they shift blocks of lengths one, two and three into 0. In particular, the hole jumps to the opposite site 2 at positive rate. A one-particle PushASEP on the four-cycle, at any choice of the two nearest-neighbour rates, cannot make that jump. Reflection does not change this obstruction. The opposite jump persists at positive rate for every \(q>0\); it is not a singularity specific to \(p=0\).

For \(q=0\), ordinary TASEP particle–hole symmetry does give a nearest-neighbour process, which is relevant counterevidence to any overly broad assertion that particle–hole reasoning always fails. Nor does this example rule out a different algebraic duality, a transformation to another process with a separate formula, or a direct extension of the contour proof. The point is that the unqualified ordinary particle–hole argument does not supply any of these.

The scope of the contour and delta-basis derivation should remain explicit unless the transformed generator, current observable, and resulting formulas are proved. The fully occupied case also needs separate treatment: the configuration generator (2.8) has no allowed move, whereas expressions involving \(1-\rho\) become singular. This is a gap in the claimed range extension, not a counterexample to the low-density contour formula or its fluctuation limits.

report: Abstract: One Minor correction is established: two index ranges omit the wiring vertex, although the immediately surrounding formulas retain it. Taken literally, one range makes a unit flow impossible and the other makes the matrix singular. The intended grounded objects are explicit in the paper, so this is a local notation correction and does not demonstrate a failure of the transience theorems. The review independently checks the shell-flow estimate, the tree moment bound, the hierarchical comparison constants, the conductance criterion and the determinant inequality. External reduction and fluctuation results remain identified inputs; the boundary-condition extension of the latter is recorded as a verification limit, not an established false assertion.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Initial technical review of
Transience of vertex-reinforced jump processes
with long-range jumps
# Reviewed object, scope and hypotheses

The reviewed paper is M25-0516, by Margherita Disertori, Franz Merkl and Silke W. W. Rolles, The Annals of Probability 53(4) (2025), 1491–1509, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1739 (https://doi.org/10.1214/24-AOP1739) [DMR]. The acquired object is the 19-page publisher PDF hosted by TUM. Physical page \(p\) has printed page \(1490+p\). Its SHA256 is
> 00000TOKEN.
The source manifest, exact PDF, all report artifacts and independent checks are bound in the accompanying records. It is an initial review; scientific acceptance remains pending.

The process at \(i\) jumps to \(j\) at rate \(W_{ij}(1+\ell_j(t))\), with symmetric weights and local occupation times. Model 1.1 requires \(d\geq1\), \(\bar W>0\), \(\alpha>1\), a positive decreasing radial function \(w\), and \[W_{ij}=w(\|i-j\|_\infty),\quad
 w(r)\geq \bar W(\log_2 r)^\alpha r^{-2d},\quad
 \sum_{j\ne0}w(\|j\|_\infty)<\infty .\] Theorem 1.2 asserts finite expected numbers of visits, uniformly over the target vertex. Model 1.5 requires \(d\geq3\), \(W_{ij}\geq\bar W\mathbf1_{\{\|i-j\|_2=1\}}\), and a uniformly finite sum of incident weights. Theorem 1.6 uses sufficiently large \(\bar W\); its stated choice is \(\bar W_1=\max\{\bar W_2,10^8\}\). Theorem 1.7 gives moments for \(1\leq m\leq\tfrac12\bar W^{1/8}\), with \(\bar W_2\geq2^8\). The strict inequality \(\bar W>\bar W_2\) in Lemma 1.8 allows an exponent \(m>1\); the endpoint is not silently enlarged.

Wiring adds a vertex \(\rho\), with \(u_\rho=0\) and \(h_i=W_{i\rho}=\sum_{j\notin\Lambda_N}W_{ij}\). These sums are finite under the stated assumptions. Up to the first exit, no outside vertex has accumulated local time, so the total exit rate is exactly the rate of a jump to this wired vertex. Uniform summability also prevents finite-time explosion: up to time \(T\), the total jump rate is bounded by \((1+T)\sup_i\sum_jW_{ij}\). The nearest-neighbour wording in Theorem 2.1 refers to adjacency in the specified graph, which includes its long Euclidean edges.
# Problem 1: retain the wiring vertex in the index ranges

Problem 1 (Minor; local notation correction).  The flow indexing immediately before (2.7), printed page 1496 (physical page 6), and the diagonal sum in (4.9), printed page 1505 (physical page 15), omit \(\rho\).
#### Flow instance.

The hypotheses are those of Theorem 2.1: a finite wired network \(G_N=(\Lambda_N\cup\{\rho\},E_N)\), positive conductances on its edges, and a source \(x\in\Lambda_N\). The paragraph before (2.7) indexes the antisymmetric flow by \(i,j\in\Lambda_N\), and its node sum also uses \(j\in\Lambda_N\), while declaring a unit flow from \(x\) to \(\rho\). Taken with this restricted range, the node equations on \(\Lambda_N\) would imply \[0=\sum_{i,j\in\Lambda_N}\theta(i,j)
   =\sum_{i\in\Lambda_N}\delta_{ix}=1.\] The first equality follows from antisymmetry on a finite set. Thus no such internally indexed flow exists.
#### Matrix instance.

Section 4.1 assumes a finite vertex set \(\Lambda\), nonnegative weights on the extended complete graph, and connectedness of the positive-weight graph \(G_+\). Every component of the internal graph has some positive pinning. Equation (4.9) specifies off-diagonal entries \(-W_{ij}e^{u_i+u_j}\), but its diagonal sum is over \(k\in\Lambda:\{i,k\}\in E_+\). The resulting internal Laplacian \(D_0\) satisfies \(D_0\mathbf1=0\). It cannot have the positive determinant and inverse used in (4.8) and (4.15). For the admissible one-vertex example \(\Lambda=\{i\}\), \(h_i=2\), \(e^{u_i}=3\), the printed sum is empty and gives \(D_{ii}=0\); the grounded value is \(6\).
#### Repair, counterevidence and dependency.
# Checks of the long-range argument
## Shell flow and the role of \(\alpha>1\)
## Tree increments and hierarchical scaling

For the antichain path, consecutive blocks have sizes \(2^{l-2}\) and \(2^{l-1}\), so their interaction is \(2^{2l-3}w^H(l)\geq\bar W^H l^\alpha/8\). The final pinning edge obeys the same bound at \(l=N+1\). The sum of reciprocal edge weights is therefore uniformly bounded by \(8(\bar W^H)^{-1}\sum_{l\geq2}l^{-\alpha}\), exactly the quantity used in (3.12). Uniform pinning is compatible with every antichain, as required for the cited reduction.

The binary interleaving map in Lemma 3.4 gives \(\|i-j\|_\infty<2^{\lceil d_H/d\rceil}\). Monotonicity of \(w\), which is an operative assumption, is needed when transferring this to an interaction lower bound. With \(\bar W^H=\bar Wd^{-\alpha}2^{-2d}\), (3.21) follows from \(\lceil l/d\rceil\geq l/d\) and \(\lceil l/d\rceil\leq1+l/d\). For (3.22), a displacement of maximum norm at least \(2^N\) from any point of the box must leave it. Reindexing by that displacement justifies the apparently unshifted shell in the pinning sum. The last estimate (3.23) uses \(d(N+1)\geq Nd+1\); its discarded factor is at least \(2^{d+2}\). Thus the quoted uniform moment constant (3.24) has the stated powers of \(d\), \(2\), \(m\) and \(\bar W\).
## From moments to expected visits

For a fixed random environment, the number of visits to \(x\) before reaching \(\rho\), conditional on first reaching \(x\), has mean \(c(x)R_N(c,x\leftrightarrow\rho)\). Using the deterministic minimizing flow in the random network gives the upper bound in (2.9), after averaging the ratios \(c_f/c_e\). Dependence between conductances does not invalidate this argument: the chosen comparison flow is deterministic.

Changing the starting point of the environment from \(\rho\) to 0 introduces the density \(e^{u_0}\). Accordingly the integrand in (2.11) has five exponential factors, not four. Hölder’s inequality with exponent five requires the \(m=5\) positive and negative moment bounds. The choice \(\bar W\geq10^8\) ensures \(\tfrac12\bar W^{1/8}\geq5\) in the high-dimensional case. Monotone convergence of the actual stopped visit counts gives the infinite-volume conclusion; a common environment coupling for different \(N\) is not needed for Theorem 2.1.
# Determinant and high-dimensional checks

With the grounded \(D\), write \(\mathcal W_e=W_e e^{u_{e+}+u_{e-}}\), \(Q_e=e^{u_{e+}+u_{e-}}/B_e\), and \(\mathcal G=\sqrt Q F^tD^{-1}F\sqrt Q\). The two square roots in (4.15) were checked on the source image. Sylvester’s identity gives \[\det(I-M\mathcal G)
 =\frac{\det(F(\mathcal W-MQ)F^t)}{\det D}.\] For \(0\leq m_e<W_e\) on positive edges and \(m_e=0\) otherwise, every modified edge weight is positive and every \(1-m_e/(W_eB_e)\) lies in \((0,1]\). The spanning-tree expansion therefore yields \[\det(I-M\mathcal G)\geq
 \prod_{e\in E_+}\left(1-\frac{m_e}{W_e}\right)>0.\] Multiplying by \(\prod B_e^{m_e}\) and using the Ward identity gives (4.18). Positivity is essential; this argument does not extend the bound to \(m_e=W_e\).

An exact rational check on a triangle with vertices \(a,b,\rho\) used \(W_{ab}=3,W_{a\rho}=2,W_{b\rho}=4\), \(e^{u_a}=2,e^{u_b}=1/3\), \(s_a=1/2,s_b=-1\), and \(m=(1,1/2,3/2)\). It gives \[D=\begin{pmatrix}6&-2\\-2&10/3\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \det D=16,\qquad
 \det(I-M\mathcal G)=\frac{1645}{2277}>\frac5{16}.\] The vertex determinant ratio, edge determinant and tree expansion agree exactly. Further exact checks covered the 27 shell coefficients for \(d=1,2,3\), \(k=0,\ldots,8\), and 18 integer tree moments for \(w=1/8,1,10\), \(m=1,2,5\), both signs. Numerical logarithmic margins for the latter are corroboration, not interval-certified inequalities; the Gaussian proof above establishes the inequality analytically. No author code was used.

For (4.31)–(4.33), the Cauchy–Schwarz exponent is \(2m\). The restriction \(2m\leq\bar W^{1/8}\), together with \(\bar W\geq2^{8/7}\), ensures \(2m/\bar W\leq1/2\). The boundary edge has \(W_{j\rho}\geq\bar W\); hence \((1-2m/W_{j\rho})^{-1}\leq2\). Taking the square root of the product of the two bounds \(2^{2m+1}\) gives the stated \(2^{2m+1}\) bound. This checks the numerical range and local algebra, subject to the external fluctuation input discussed next.
# External inputs and the limits of this review
## Fluctuation and localization input

Theorem 1 of Disertori–Spencer–Zirnbauer [DSZ] (physical page 4 of the acquired 54-page author PDF) gives the difference-field bound for dimension three, with analogous estimates stated for higher dimensions and exponent \(m\leq\beta^{1/8}\). The remark on physical page 6 explicitly uses periodic boundaries. Section 13, physical page 41, explains that hard pinning is allowed without a lower bound on the regularization parameter. The current paper applies the fluctuation input to a wired box with general pinning in (4.32). This review has not reconstructed that entire boundary and pinning extension from the cited proof. It is a material limit of the present positive verification, not an established counterexample or a demonstrated invalid extension. Appendix C, Proposition 2 (physical page 53), states localization for smooth, integrable, invariant functions. The current paper’s Ward calculation and growth assumptions were read, but a complete independent proof of the underlying superintegration theorem is outside this review.
## Convex monotonicity input

Poudevigne-Auboiron’s Theorem 6 [PA], printed pages 794–795 (physical pages 6–7), requires finite symmetric weight matrices, zero diagonal, nonnegative off-diagonal entries, entrywise \(W^-\leq W^+\), and connectedness for \(W^-\). The comparison is for a convex function of a nonnegative Green-function ratio. Including \(\rho\) as a vertex supplies the finite connected graph used here. The comparison networks in the current paper retain connectedness, so deletion of the other positive weights is permitted. For the negative moment test \(x^{-m}\), which is not finite at zero, one may first use \((x+\varepsilon)^{-m}\) and then pass to the limit by monotone convergence. This removes a possible endpoint objection to Fact 2.2. The cited coupling theorem itself has not been independently reproved here.
## Hierarchical reduction input

The cited reduction [HIER] requires a maximal antichain compatible with the pinning, with interactions \(2^{\ell(i)+\ell(j)}w(\ell(i\wedge j))\) and pinning equal to the sum over each block. Uniform pinning satisfies compatibility. Corollary 2.3 identifies the joint law at leaves that remain in the antichain, which is the property used for the distinguished leaf in the present proof.

The official ALEA PDF was accessible to the web reader, but the single native download attempt returned a non-PDF rate-limit response. That response was retained, with no retry. An independently acquired primary preprint, `arXiv:2111.08293v1` [HIERPRE], has 24 pages. Its physical pages 7–9 contain the compatible-antichain hypotheses, Theorem 2.2 and Corollary 2.3 just described. The preprint is identified separately; it is not represented as byte-identical to the 20-page journal article. The full external reduction proof was not independently reproved.
# Coverage, version checks and disposition

All 19 physical pages of the acquired paper were read, including all its proof sections and references. All 19 source-page images were actually inspected. The review traced the long-range and high-dimensional branches separately, and checked the summability, connectivity, pinning, monotonicity, dimension and exponent conditions where they enter. The explicit external-proof limits in Section 5 qualify these checks.

Public primary-source follow-up on 29 October 2026 checked the TUM publication identity and the arXiv version record. The latter lists version 2 dated 14 August 2024 and explains that an earlier manuscript was split into two papers. This does not change the reviewed publisher PDF. The bounded correction and supplement searches identified no explicit correction relevant to this reviewed object; they do not prove that none exists. No author program was executed. The independent computations were written for this review, and their script, interpreter, actual exit status and output are preserved with the exact source binding.

Problem 1 is the only established correction. Its Minor severity reflects the explicit correct formulas already present in the surrounding argument. The report does not establish a false main theorem or an invalid intended core derivation. It also does not certify the external inputs beyond the checks and limits stated above. Scientific acceptance remains pending; this completed initial review is not an independent acceptance decision.

analysis: The flow indexing immediately before (2.7), printed page 1496 (physical page 6), and the diagonal sum in (4.9), printed page 1505 (physical page 15), omit \(\rho\).

The hypotheses are those of Theorem 2.1: a finite wired network \(G_N=(\Lambda_N\cup\{\rho\},E_N)\), positive conductances on its edges, and a source \(x\in\Lambda_N\). The paragraph before (2.7) indexes the antisymmetric flow by \(i,j\in\Lambda_N\), and its node sum also uses \(j\in\Lambda_N\), while declaring a unit flow from \(x\) to \(\rho\). Taken with this restricted range, the node equations on \(\Lambda_N\) would imply \[0=\sum_{i,j\in\Lambda_N}\theta(i,j)
   =\sum_{i\in\Lambda_N}\delta_{ix}=1.\] The first equality follows from antisymmetry on a finite set. Thus no such internally indexed flow exists.

Section 4.1 assumes a finite vertex set \(\Lambda\), nonnegative weights on the extended complete graph, and connectedness of the positive-weight graph \(G_+\). Every component of the internal graph has some positive pinning. Equation (4.9) specifies off-diagonal entries \(-W_{ij}e^{u_i+u_j}\), but its diagonal sum is over \(k\in\Lambda:\{i,k\}\in E_+\). The resulting internal Laplacian \(D_0\) satisfies \(D_0\mathbf1=0\). It cannot have the positive determinant and inverse used in (4.8) and (4.15). For the admissible one-vertex example \(\Lambda=\{i\}\), \(h_i=2\), \(e^{u_i}=3\), the printed sum is empty and gives \(D_{ii}=0\); the grounded value is \(6\).

report: Abstract: The exact energy representation in Lemma 9.1 has an incorrect coefficient on the terminal square. This is a Major defect in a core derivation: it gives a wrong short-time coefficient within the paper’s own Gaussian model. Correcting that coefficient preserves the form of the subsequent small-amplitude estimates, so the defect does not disprove the final asymptotic theorem. Five Minor issues concern signs in the comparison equation, the Fourier phase, the rotational invariance argument, initialization and uniformity of a proxy moment bound, and a motivational statement about finite-range Gaussian fields. The review gives explicit repairs and counterevidence, checks the operative Gaussian and homogenization assumptions, and records the finite-time monotonicity step as an unresolved verification limit.

Title: Initial technical review of
The Gaussian free-field as a stream function:
asymptotics of effective diffusivity in infra-red cut-off
# Reviewed object and mathematical setting

The assigned paper is M25-0517, by Georgiana Chatzigeorgiou, Peter Morfe, Felix Otto and Lihan Wang, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1740 (https://doi.org/10.1214/24-AOP1740) [CMOW]. The exact acquired object is arXiv:2212.14244v3, 30 January 2025, not a byte-verified publisher PDF. It has 28 physical pages: printed pages 1–27 and a final unnumbered page containing an uncaptioned plot. All locators below refer to this acquired version; physical and printed page numbers agree through page 27. The source SHA256 is
> `87acbd48e85b30c893ef1c1ec885a8ec604143e6bfb0b0d8082e3cd46c7ed4cb`.
The arXiv comment’s page count is not substituted for the actual PDF count. This is an initial technical review; independent acceptance is pending.
# A false exact energy representation

Problem 1 (Major: terminal energy coefficient).  On page 21, Lemma 9.1, equations (90) and (93), and the energy-test line preceding (93), the coefficient of \(\mathbb Ev(T)^2\) is incorrect. The same coefficient enters the energy definition on page 22 and its expansion (99) on page 23.

Here \(g=\epsilon b\cdot\xi\) and the stationary parabolic solution is defined by the source’s (89): \[\partial_t v-\Delta v-\epsilon b\cdot\nabla v=g,\qquad v(0)=0.\] These hypotheses include smoothness from the ultraviolet cutoff, Gaussian finite moments, stationarity and \(\nabla\cdot b=0\). They justify the following expectation identities, for instance by localization followed by the corresponding finite-moment bounds.

Equation reference: correct-energy. Claim 1.  Writing \(D(T)=\tfrac12\mathbb E(\xi\cdot X_T)^2\), the energy representation compatible with (89) is \[
 D(T)=T+\frac12\mathbb Ev(T)^2+
             \int_0^T\mathbb E|\nabla v(t)|^2\,\mathrm dt .\] The printed representation has coefficient \(1\) in place of \(1/2\) on the terminal square.

Proof. Testing the parabolic equation against \(v\) gives \[\frac12\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm dt}\mathbb Ev^2+\mathbb E|\nabla v|^2=\mathbb E(gv),\] because stationarity and incompressibility remove the transport term. The source’s preceding Itô and stationary heat-kernel calculation gives \(D(T)-T=\int_0^T\mathbb E(gv(t))\,\mathrm dt\). Integrating the displayed energy test, with \(v(0)=0\), proves [correct-energy] (#correct-energy). ◻

Equation reference: variance, short-time. There is a direct contradiction within the specified ensemble, rather than merely a counterexample using a different drift. By [cov] (#cov), \[
 \mathbb E(b\cdot\xi)^2
 =\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^1r\,\mathrm dr\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,\mathrm d\theta
 =\frac14.\] The small-time expansion is \(v(T)=Tg+O_{L^2}(T^2)\), and the integrated gradient energy is \(O(T^3)\). Hence the printed right-hand side is \(T+\epsilon^2T^2/4+O(T^3)\). Independently, apply the generator \(\mathcal L=\Delta+\epsilon b\cdot\nabla\) twice to \(F(x)=(\xi\cdot x)^2\). At the origin, \[\mathbb E\mathcal LF(0)=2,\qquad
 \mathbb E\mathcal L^2F(0)=2\epsilon^2\mathbb E(b\cdot\xi)^2,\] since the mean spatial derivative of \(b\) vanishes. Consequently \[
 D(T)=T+\frac{\epsilon^2}{8}T^2+O(T^3).\] For every fixed nonzero \(\epsilon\), the two coefficients disagree.

An independent spectral check at \(T=1\) confirms the discrepancy. For \(v_1=\partial_\epsilon v|_{\epsilon=0}\), put \(V=\mathbb Ev_1(1)^2\), \(G=\int_0^1\mathbb E|\nabla v_1(t)|^2\,\mathrm dt\), and let \(D_2\) be the coefficient of \(\epsilon^2\) in \(D(1)-1\). The exact integral formulas are \[\begin{aligned}
 V&=\frac12\int_0^1
      \frac{(1-e^{-r^2})^2}{r^3}\,\mathrm dr,\\
 D_2&=\frac12\int_0^1
      \left(\frac1{r^2}-\frac{1-e^{-r^2}}{r^4}\right)r\,\mathrm dr,
 &G&=D_2-\frac12V.\end{aligned}\] The saved 70-digit numerical integration gives \[V=0.1614377782128111,\quad
 G=0.0264611504249972,\quad
 D_2=0.1071800395314027.\] This is corroborating quadrature, not an interval certificate or a simulation of the stochastic differential equation. The analytic energy calculation and [short-time] (#short-time) are the decisive proofs.
#### Alternative readings and impact.

The term is not hidden in a normalization: (89) fixes \(v\), the Brownian coefficient is \(\sqrt2\), and the source itself uses a correct \(1/2\) in the comparison energy test on page 22. A one-symbol error in a preliminary computation might be Minor; here the false identity is the explicit bridge from the parabolic problem to the displacement observable and is used in the main proof. This establishes a Major invalid core derivation as printed.

The repair is to replace every terminal-square coefficient consistently, including the energy definition and the terminal terms in (99). The comparison estimate (98) still controls the corrected terminal contribution. The leading \(1+\mathbb E|\nabla\widetilde\phi_L|^2\), the integrated cross term, and the \(O(|\epsilon|\widetilde\lambda_L)\) error estimates retain their form. Thus this calculation does not refute the \(T\sqrt{\log T}\) scale, the small-amplitude asymptotics, or Theorem 1.2 on the stationary effective diffusivity.
#### Remaining all-amplitude verification limit.

The last paragraph of the proof on page 23 invokes monotonicity of finite-time energy in \(\epsilon^2\) by the argument of Lemma 8.1. The stationary proof on page 20 is valid in its setting. Its parabolic analogue has an additional time pairing. Indeed, for \(w=\partial_\epsilon v\) and \(\epsilon\ne0\), \[(\partial_t-\Delta-\epsilon b\cdot\nabla)w
       =\epsilon^{-1}(\partial_t-\Delta)v,\qquad w(0)=0.\] Testing with \(w\) introduces \(\int_0^T\mathbb E(w\partial_t v)\,\mathrm dt\); differentiating the corrected terminal energy introduces \(\mathbb E(v(T)w(T))\). Identifying these also involves \(\int_0^T\mathbb E(v\partial_t w)\,\mathrm dt\). The stationary calculation does not remove their difference. This review has not proved that the claimed finite-time monotonicity is false for this Gaussian model, nor established a counterexample to the all-amplitude lower bound. A separate justification is needed before that part of the proof can be regarded as independently verified. It is not counted as another demonstrated defect.

This is not an innocuous simultaneous redefinition of \(f_L\). At the first geometric step \(L=M>1\), \(\widetilde\phi_M=\epsilon\phi'_1\). # Fourier phase in the stream-function coupling
Problem 3 (Minor: equation (20)).  On page 6, (20) omits the factor \(i\) required by \(b_L=-J\nabla\psi_L\) and the stated Fourier convention.

Equation reference: phase. For \(k\ne0\), the real stream function satisfies \(\widehat b_L(k)=-iJk\,\widehat\psi_L(k)\). Hence \[
 \widehat\psi_L(k)=
 i|k|^{-2}\mathbf1_{\{|k|\geq L^{-1}\}}\,Jk\cdot\widehat b(k).\] The printed formula lacks \(i\). An odd real Fourier multiplier applied to a real field does not preserve the Hermitian symmetry required of a real stream function; the missing phase is essential.

For an exact mode check, take \(k=(3/5,4/5)\), \(\psi(x)=\cos(k\cdot x)\), and \(b(x)=Jk\sin(k\cdot x)\). Then \(\widehat b(k)=(2i/5,-3i/10)\). The printed multiplier gives \(-i/2\) at both \(k\) and \(-k\), whereas the correct coefficients of \(\psi\) are \(1/2\). Multiplication by \(i\) restores both coefficients. The mode is an operator check, not a claim that a single deterministic wave has the paper’s Gaussian law; the Hermitian-symmetry argument applies to that law itself.

Equation (11), the real Gaussian covariance (13), and the later real-valued energy arguments identify the intended reading. With [phase] (#phase), disjoint Fourier annuli remain independent and all the displayed covariance normalizations are unchanged. The repair is local, so the severity is Minor.
# Rotational invariance and a scalar effective matrix

Problem 4 (Minor: proof of Lemma 3.2).  On page 6, commutation with every planar rotation is used to conclude that the homogenized matrix is a scalar multiple of \(I\). That linear-algebra implication alone is false.

A real \(2\times2\) matrix commuting with all rotations has the form \(\alpha I+\beta J\). For example, \(I+J\) commutes with every rotation and is not scalar. No symmetry of the homogenized matrix has been established by this argument.

The actual field supplies the missing information. For every orthogonal \(Q\), the centered radial Gaussian stream function \[\psi_L^Q(x)=\det(Q)\psi_L(Qx)\] has the same law as \(\psi_L\), and \[Q^\mathsf T a_L(Qx)Q
     =I+\epsilon\psi_L^Q(x)J.\] Covariance of the corrector construction under this change of coordinates implies that the homogenized matrix also commutes with reflections. Taking \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) changes \(\beta J\) to \(-\beta J\), forcing \(\beta=0\). This proves the intended scalar conclusion using an assumption already satisfied by the model.

Counterevidence to any stronger allegation is present in the source: (40), (44) and (67) explicitly use the determinant factor for orthogonal transformations. The later continuum note [Retained latex: \cite[p.~3, (15)]{MOW24}] also distinguishes the scalar-times-rotation consequence of rotation invariance. Insert the reflection step; the lemma’s conclusion and its use in the effective diffusivity are not disproved.
# Initialization and the range of uniform moment bounds

Problem 5 (Minor: initial scale and the constants in (70)).  Page 17, (77), omits the exceptional initial step. Together with the stated constant convention, page 15, (70), also overstates uniformity as \(M\) ranges over all sufficiently large values. The first iteration display on page 14 separately omits the initial constant \(1\).

Let \(M>1\), \(L=M^n\), \(n\geq0\), and \(a=\epsilon^2\log M\). The source starts with \(\widetilde\lambda_1=1\). The last inequality in (77) is \[\frac{a}{1+\epsilon^2\log L}\leq1.\] At \(L=1\) this asserts \(a\leq1\), which is not an assumption. It is valid for \(L\geq M\), or at the initial scale when \(a\leq1\).

Equation reference: recurrence. For the other initialization error, put \(z_n=\widetilde\lambda_{M^n}^{\,2}\). Recurrence (51) gives \[
 z_{n+1}=z_n+a+\frac{a^2}{4z_n},\qquad
 z_0=1,\qquad
 z_N-(1+Na)=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\frac{a^2}{4z_n}.\] The first display on page 14 bounds \(z_N-Na\) by a sum which is empty for \(N=0\), asserting \(1\leq0\). Subtracting \(1\) repairs it. The correctly stated (59) already includes that \(1\), and is supported by [recurrence] (#recurrence). Exact rational checks for four initial steps at \(a=1/100,1/2,2\) agree with this identity.

For the main proofs, \(M\) is selected in a fixed bounded range of sufficiently large constants. Restrict the moment lemma accordingly, treat the first step separately, and allow the declared \(C_\epsilon\) for large \(\epsilon\); for sufficiently small \(\epsilon\) in that fixed range, \(a\leq1\) handles the initial step directly. These repairs address the defective auxiliary statements without changing the claimed asymptotic scale. The issue is Minor under that explicitly restricted use; a uniform bound in the full printed \(M\)-range is false.
# A motivational finite-range assertion

Problem 6 (Minor: introductory Gaussian assertion).  The paragraph following (1) on page 1 asserts uniqueness of white noise among Gaussian processes with a finite range of dependence. With the usual meaning of finite range, that statement is false.

Let \(W\) be scalar spatial white noise and choose a nonzero, nonconstant radial \(K\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)\), supported in a ball of radius \(R\). The centered stationary Gaussian field \(G=K*W\) has covariance \(K*\widetilde K\), supported in a ball of radius \(2R\). Values on sets separated by more than \(2R\) are independent, because all cross-covariances vanish and the field is Gaussian. Yet \(G\) is smooth and has a nontrivial continuous covariance, so it is not white noise. Even the vector field \(J\nabla G\) is a smooth, isotropic, divergence-free Gaussian example with finite range and nonzero covariance.

This example concerns the introductory universal assertion; it does not satisfy, and is not presented as a counterexample to, the particular spectrum [cov] (#cov). If finite range was intended to mean independence at every positive separation, that is a different, zero-range statement. Clarify that distinction or remove the uniqueness claim. There is no operative proof dependency on it, so its impact is limited to the motivation.
# Positive checks, reference checks and limits
## Gaussian structure and external hypotheses

The spectral cutoff gives finite moments of every spatial derivative. Its absolutely continuous spectral measure supplies ergodicity; for finite \(L\), the annular Gaussian stream function has all finite moments. The elementary identities \[\mathbb E|b|^2=\frac12,\qquad
 \mathbb E|b-b_L|^2=\frac1{2L^2},\qquad
 \mathbb E|\nabla(b\cdot\xi)|^2=\frac18\] agree with independent angular and radial integration. Disjoint annuli are independent, not merely uncorrelated non-Gaussian objects. The real phase repair in Problem Problem 3 (#p3) is required when constructing their coupling.

The nonsymmetric coefficient satisfies \(\eta\cdot a_L\eta=|\eta|^2\). In the notation of Bella–Fehrman–Otto [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~1--2, condition (1) and Lemma 1]{BFO}], the lower ellipticity variable is \(1\) and the upper variable is \(1+\epsilon^2\psi_L^2\). Choosing, for example, their exponents \(p=q=3\) gives \(1/p+1/q=2/3<2/d=1\) and finite required moments. Their corrector has finite energy. The resulting flux belongs to \(L^{3/2}\), by the \(L^2\) corrector gradient and the \(L^6\) stream function. For Fehrman’s [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~1--2, (1.11); pp.~13--14,
Proposition 2.4]{Fehrman}] construction, take bounded \(A=I\) and the skew Gaussian stream matrix; stationarity, ergodicity, its defining divergence/gauge relations, and \(L^{2+\delta}\) integrability hold. The needed potential construction can therefore use a finite exponent strictly above one. These are hypothesis checks against the acquired preprints, not a claim to have reproved all their results or checked journal-version equality.
## The internal proof chain

The review checked the Helmholtz decomposition, independence and orthogonality used in (37)–(43); in particular the exact increment variance is \[\mathbb E(\phi'_L)^2
   =\frac{L_+^2-L^2}{4\widetilde\lambda_L^2}.\] This supports the sharper \(1/4\) in (43), even though a coarser intermediate estimate appears in its proof. The recursive proxy construction, its centeredness and orthogonal transformation rules were read through (47)–(79). The use of fourth moments is necessary because of quadratic products of the cumulative proxies and Gaussian increments.

In the residual calculation, centered increments, independent shells and Gaussian parity remove the mixed terms. Inversion gives (83); the residual recurrence (84), the bounds (85)–(86), and the summable exponent \(3/2\) in the discrete Gronwall step give the stated order once the initial-step and constant conventions are repaired. The exact recurrence [recurrence] (#recurrence) controls the diffusivity proxy. The stationary monotonicity identity in Lemma 8.1 follows from testing the differentiated corrector equation and yields a nonnegative square. It is distinct from the unverified finite-time assertion discussed after Problem Problem 1 (#p1).

Appendix A is explicitly heuristic; its scalar differential equation integrates to the proposed logarithmic correction and is not treated as a proof. Appendix B’s flux-corrector hypotheses were checked above. Its external invariance-principle citation to the Komorowski–Landim–Olla monograph was not independently reconstructed in full. The uncaptioned plot on physical page 28 has no identified connection to a numerical method or asserted theorem in the read text; no numerical conclusion is inferred from it. No author code was executed, and unavailable code is not treated as a mathematical defect.
## Version and correction search

Primary arXiv histories were checked for the assigned v3 and the related continuum note [MOW24] and combined follow-up [MOW25]. The note treats the continuum limit of the proxy construction. The combined work restates the displacement result in a small-amplitude regime on page 3. Its literal monotonicity matches on page 43 concern an eigenvalue evolution, not the finite-time displacement step. These texts provide relevant context; they are not identified as errata for the errors established here. A bounded search found no explicit author correction of those formulas. An attempted publisher issue-page retrieval failed; no publisher-byte comparison is claimed.

All 28 physical source pages were read or, for the last page, inspected as an image, and all were actually viewed. The selected reference reading and image inspection covers pp. 1–3 of [BFO], pp. 1–6 and 12–14 of [Fehrman], pp. 1–3 of [MOW24], and pp. 1–5, 21 and 43 of [MOW25]. Other pages of those references are not claimed to have been scientifically read. Exact source, calculation, compilation, dependency, parsing and image bindings are retained in the paper’s support inventory. A complete initial report is not independent acceptance.

 D(T)=T+\frac12\mathbb Ev(T)^2+
             \int_0^T\mathbb E|\nabla v(t)|^2\,\mathrm dt .\] The printed representation has coefficient \(1\) in place of \(1/2\) on the terminal square.

Proof. Testing the parabolic equation against \(v\) gives \[\frac12\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm dt}\mathbb Ev^2+\mathbb E|\nabla v|^2=\mathbb E(gv),\] because stationarity and incompressibility remove the transport term. The source’s preceding Itô and stationary heat-kernel calculation gives \(D(T)-T=\int_0^T\mathbb E(gv(t))\,\mathrm dt\). Integrating the displayed energy test, with \(v(0)=0\), proves [correct-energy] (#correct-energy). ◻

Equation reference: variance, short-time. There is a direct contradiction within the specified ensemble, rather than merely a counterexample using a different drift. By [cov] (#cov), \[
 \mathbb E(b\cdot\xi)^2
 =\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^1r\,\mathrm dr\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2\theta\,\mathrm d\theta
 =\frac14.\] The small-time expansion is \(v(T)=Tg+O_{L^2}(T^2)\), and the integrated gradient energy is \(O(T^3)\). Hence the printed right-hand side is \(T+\epsilon^2T^2/4+O(T^3)\). Independently, apply the generator \(\mathcal L=\Delta+\epsilon b\cdot\nabla\) twice to \(F(x)=(\xi\cdot x)^2\). At the origin, \[\mathbb E\mathcal LF(0)=2,\qquad
 \mathbb E\mathcal L^2F(0)=2\epsilon^2\mathbb E(b\cdot\xi)^2,\] since the mean spatial derivative of \(b\) vanishes. Consequently \[
 D(T)=T+\frac{\epsilon^2}{8}T^2+O(T^3).\] For every fixed nonzero \(\epsilon\), the two coefficients disagree.

An independent spectral check at \(T=1\) confirms the discrepancy. For \(v_1=\partial_\epsilon v|_{\epsilon=0}\), put \(V=\mathbb Ev_1(1)^2\), \(G=\int_0^1\mathbb E|\nabla v_1(t)|^2\,\mathrm dt\), and let \(D_2\) be the coefficient of \(\epsilon^2\) in \(D(1)-1\). The exact integral formulas are \[\begin{aligned}
 V&=\frac12\int_0^1
      \frac{(1-e^{-r^2})^2}{r^3}\,\mathrm dr,\\
 D_2&=\frac12\int_0^1
      \left(\frac1{r^2}-\frac{1-e^{-r^2}}{r^4}\right)r\,\mathrm dr,
 &G&=D_2-\frac12V.\end{aligned}\] The saved 70-digit numerical integration gives \[V=0.1614377782128111,\quad
 G=0.0264611504249972,\quad
 D_2=0.1071800395314027.\] This is corroborating quadrature, not an interval certificate or a simulation of the stochastic differential equation. The analytic energy calculation and [short-time] (#short-time) are the decisive proofs.

The last paragraph of the proof on page 23 invokes monotonicity of finite-time energy in \(\epsilon^2\) by the argument of Lemma 8.1. The stationary proof on page 20 is valid in its setting. Its parabolic analogue has an additional time pairing. Indeed, for \(w=\partial_\epsilon v\) and \(\epsilon\ne0\), \[(\partial_t-\Delta-\epsilon b\cdot\nabla)w
       =\epsilon^{-1}(\partial_t-\Delta)v,\qquad w(0)=0.\] Testing with \(w\) introduces \(\int_0^T\mathbb E(w\partial_t v)\,\mathrm dt\); differentiating the corrected terminal energy introduces \(\mathbb E(v(T)w(T))\). Identifying these also involves \(\int_0^T\mathbb E(v\partial_t w)\,\mathrm dt\). The stationary calculation does not remove their difference. This review has not proved that the claimed finite-time monotonicity is false for this Gaussian model, nor established a counterexample to the all-amplitude lower bound. A separate justification is needed before that part of the proof can be regarded as independently verified. It is not counted as another demonstrated defect.
result: The term is not hidden in a normalization: (89) fixes \(v\), the Brownian coefficient is \(\sqrt2\), and the source itself uses a correct \(1/2\) in the comparison energy test on page 22. A one-symbol error in a preliminary computation might be Minor; here the false identity is the explicit bridge from the parabolic problem to the displacement observable and is used in the main proof. This establishes a Major invalid core derivation as printed.

The repair is to replace every terminal-square coefficient consistently, including the energy definition and the terminal terms in (99). The comparison estimate (98) still controls the corrected terminal contribution. The leading \(1+\mathbb E|\nabla\widetilde\phi_L|^2\), the integrated cross term, and the \(O(|\epsilon|\widetilde\lambda_L)\) error estimates retain their form. Thus this calculation does not refute the \(T\sqrt{\log T}\) scale, the small-amplitude asymptotics, or Theorem 1.2 on the stationary effective diffusivity.

Impact: Demonstrated false exact core identity and invalid printed derivation; not a demonstrated false final theorem. The finite-time monotonicity claim remains a verification limit, not an additional established defect.

problems.title: Missing imaginary unit in the Fourier stream-function coupling
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: Problem 3 (Minor: equation (20)). On page 6, (20) omits the factor \(i\) required by \(b_L=-J\nabla\psi_L\) and the stated Fourier convention.
claim: Recorded check: Missing imaginary unit in the Fourier stream-function coupling
analysis: On page 6, (20) omits the factor \(i\) required by \(b_L=-J\nabla\psi_L\) and the stated Fourier convention.

Equation reference: phase. For \(k\ne0\), the real stream function satisfies \(\widehat b_L(k)=-iJk\,\widehat\psi_L(k)\). Hence \[
 \widehat\psi_L(k)=
 i|k|^{-2}\mathbf1_{\{|k|\geq L^{-1}\}}\,Jk\cdot\widehat b(k).\] The printed formula lacks \(i\). An odd real Fourier multiplier applied to a real field does not preserve the Hermitian symmetry required of a real stream function; the missing phase is essential.

For an exact mode check, take \(k=(3/5,4/5)\), \(\psi(x)=\cos(k\cdot x)\), and \(b(x)=Jk\sin(k\cdot x)\). Then \(\widehat b(k)=(2i/5,-3i/10)\). The printed multiplier gives \(-i/2\) at both \(k\) and \(-k\), whereas the correct coefficients of \(\psi\) are \(1/2\). Multiplication by \(i\) restores both coefficients. The mode is an operator check, not a claim that a single deterministic wave has the paper’s Gaussian law; the Hermitian-symmetry argument applies to that law itself.

Equation (11), the real Gaussian covariance (13), and the later real-valued energy arguments identify the intended reading. With [phase] (#phase), disjoint Fourier annuli remain independent and all the displayed covariance normalizations are unchanged. The repair is local, so the severity is Minor.

problems.title: Rotations alone do not imply a scalar homogenized matrix
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: Problem 4 (Minor: proof of Lemma 3.2).
claim: Recorded check: Rotations alone do not imply a scalar homogenized matrix
analysis: On page 6, commutation with every planar rotation is used to conclude that the homogenized matrix is a scalar multiple of \(I\). That linear-algebra implication alone is false.

A real \(2\times2\) matrix commuting with all rotations has the form \(\alpha I+\beta J\). For example, \(I+J\) commutes with every rotation and is not scalar. No symmetry of the homogenized matrix has been established by this argument.

The actual field supplies the missing information. For every orthogonal \(Q\), the centered radial Gaussian stream function \[\psi_L^Q(x)=\det(Q)\psi_L(Qx)\] has the same law as \(\psi_L\), and \[Q^\mathsf T a_L(Qx)Q
     =I+\epsilon\psi_L^Q(x)J.\] Covariance of the corrector construction under this change of coordinates implies that the homogenized matrix also commutes with reflections. Taking \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) changes \(\beta J\) to \(-\beta J\), forcing \(\beta=0\). This proves the intended scalar conclusion using an assumption already satisfied by the model.

Counterevidence to any stronger allegation is present in the source: (40), (44) and (67) explicitly use the determinant factor for orthogonal transformations. The later continuum note [Retained latex: \cite[p.~3, (15)]{MOW24}] also distinguishes the scalar-times-rotation consequence of rotation invariance. Insert the reflection step; the lemma’s conclusion and its use in the effective diffusivity are not disproved.
result: Impact: Local missing logical step; no false scalar conclusion or main theorem established.
