problems.title: False uniqueness claim about Gaussian finite-range fields
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: Problem 6 (Minor: introductory Gaussian assertion).
claim: Recorded check: False uniqueness claim about Gaussian finite-range fields
analysis: The paragraph following (1) on page 1 asserts uniqueness of white noise among Gaussian processes with a finite range of dependence. With the usual meaning of finite range, that statement is false.

Let \(W\) be scalar spatial white noise and choose a nonzero, nonconstant radial \(K\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)\), supported in a ball of radius \(R\). The centered stationary Gaussian field \(G=K*W\) has covariance \(K*\widetilde K\), supported in a ball of radius \(2R\). Values on sets separated by more than \(2R\) are independent, because all cross-covariances vanish and the field is Gaussian. Yet \(G\) is smooth and has a nontrivial continuous covariance, so it is not white noise. Even the vector field \(J\nabla G\) is a smooth, isotropic, divergence-free Gaussian example with finite range and nonzero covariance.

This example concerns the introductory universal assertion; it does not satisfy, and is not presented as a counterexample to, the particular spectrum [cov] (#cov). If finite range was intended to mean independence at every positive separation, that is a different, zero-range statement. Clarify that distinction or remove the uniqueness claim. There is no operative proof dependency on it, so its impact is limited to the motivation.
result: Impact: Minor incorrect motivational assertion only.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Distinguish zero-range independence from finite positive range or remove uniqueness assertion.

report: Abstract: Theorem 2.4 is false on part of its stated lattice sum-kernel range: the written parameter restriction permits a deterministic connected nearest-neighbor subgraph, whereas the theorem assigns positive probability to an impossible lower-tail event at arbitrarily large volumes. This is a Major range defect. Eight Minor problems concern an introductory asymptotic sign, finite-volume endpoints, a degenerate boundary exponent, a dropped mark restriction, a Palm comparison, a conditioning field, an auxiliary monotonicity claim, and a missing cover-expansion case. Explicit evidence and repairs are given. The identified proof defects do not establish failure of the Poisson cluster-tail or second-component asymptotics. The review also checks the main exponent algebra, coupling, isolation mechanism and cited hypotheses, with version and verification limits stated separately.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Initial technical review of
Cluster-size decay in supercritical
kernel-based spatial random graphs
# Reviewed object, hypotheses and scope

The assigned object is M25-0518, by Joost Jorritsma, Júlia Komjáthy and Dieter Mitsche, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1742 (https://doi.org/10.1214/24-AOP1742) [JKM]. The exact acquired PDF is arXiv:2303.00724v3, 17 October 2024, with 74 physical pages. Physical and printed page numbers agree. All source locators in this report refer to this version. Its SHA256 is
> `dcf5cdc87d169a282eeeea4b7daa8ab5b8a3aceb5526b2caa1f851920bba44f8`.
The scientific decision remains pending.

Equation reference: model. The vertex locations form either a unit-intensity Poisson process in \(\mathbb R^d\) or the lattice \(\mathbb Z^d\). Marks are independent, with \(\mathbb P(W>w)=w^{-(\tau-1)}\) for \(w\geq1,\ \tau>2\), or \(W\equiv1\) when \(\tau=\infty\). Conditional on locations and marks, distinct edges are independent and have probability \[
 q(u,v)=p\left(1\wedge
 \frac{\beta\kappa(w_u,w_v)}{\|x_u-x_v\|^d}\right)^\alpha,
 \qquad \alpha>1,\quad p\in(0,1],\quad\beta>0.\] For \(\alpha=\infty\), the power profile is replaced by its threshold version. The kernels are \(\kappa_\sigma(w,w')=(w\vee w')(w\wedge w')^\sigma\), \(\sigma\geq0\), and \(\kappa_{\rm sum}(w,w')=(w^{1/d}+{w'}^{1/d})^d\). Assumption 1.3 adds \(p\wedge\beta<1\) on the lattice. The intended box \(\Lambda_n=[-n^{1/d}/2,n^{1/d}/2]^d\) has volume \(n\), which is not the exact number of lattice vertices.

Write \(t=\tau-1\). The four candidate boundary exponents are \[\zeta_{\rm short}=(d-1)/d,\qquad
 \zeta_{\rm ll}=2-\alpha,\qquad
 \zeta_{\rm hl}=t/\alpha-(t-1),\qquad
 \zeta_{\rm hh}=1-t\gamma_{\rm hh}.\] For finite \(\alpha\) and \(\tau\leq\sigma+2\), \(\gamma_{\rm hh}=(1-1/\alpha)/(\sigma+1-t/\alpha)\); the other branch is \(1/(\sigma+1)\). The source defines \(\zeta_\star\) as their maximum and \(m_\star\) as the number of maximizing entries. The main matching cluster-tail and second-component bounds are developed when \(\zeta_{\rm hh}>0\), equivalently \(2<\tau<\sigma+2\). Their upper bounds are for Poisson locations, with a separate exponent when \(\tau<\sigma+1\). The lower-tail Theorem 2.4 and Claim 1.4 have a wider stated range. That distinction is essential to the findings below.

All 74 source pages, including Appendices A–C and the references, were read. Actual source-image inspection covered 58 pages, including every page used as evidence for the numbered problems and the main counterevidence. Twenty pages of three acquired references were also read and viewed. Reading an index or parsing a manifest is not counted as mathematical reading. The review checks the finite-volume statements, the cover construction, high-mark backbone and conditional coupling, the cluster-tail reduction, the isolation lower bound, and the appendix calculations. It is not a formal proof certification of every external theorem or every extension left to the reader.
# A false theorem range and endpoint assertions

Problem 1 (Major: the lattice sum-kernel restriction permits certain edges).  Theorem 2.4, p. 10, (2.8), is false under the literal lattice hypotheses of Assumption 1.3, p. 4. The relevant proof uses the strict edge-probability assertion in the lattice adaptation of Lemma 7.2, p. 49, and then the covering argument on pp. 52–53. The comparison \(\kappa_{\rm sum}\leq2^d\kappa_0\) on p. 12 does not preserve the stated nondegeneracy restriction.

Equation reference: zeroevent. Evidence. Take \(d=2,\ W\equiv1,\ \kappa=\kappa_{\rm sum},\
\alpha=2,\ p=1,\ \beta=3/4\). These choices satisfy the displayed assumptions, including \(p\wedge\beta<1\). But \(\kappa_{\rm sum}(1,1)=4\), so every lattice nearest-neighbor edge has probability \((1\wedge3)^2=1\). For \(n=4m^2\), \(m\geq1\), the box is \([-m,m]^2\). Its \((2m+1)^2\) lattice vertices form a connected deterministic nearest-neighbor graph. Consequently, for \(\rho=1/2\), \[
 \mathbb P(|C_n^{(1)}|<\rho n)=0.\] Here \(\zeta_\star=1/2\) and \(m_\star=1\): the short-edge exponent dominates \(2-\alpha=0\), and the heavy-mark mechanisms disappear for unit marks. The right side of (2.8) is \(\exp[-(A/\rho)n^{1/2}]=\exp(-4Am)>0\) for every finite \(A\). Thus the contradiction holds at arbitrarily large volumes. ◻

The phrase explaining that the graph should not be almost surely connected can plausibly express an intended extra hypothesis. It does not follow from the written restriction for this kernel. Suppressing marks near their minimum cannot remove certain nearest-neighbor edges. Moreover, comparison with \(\kappa_0\) changes the effective parameter to \(2^d\beta=3\), precisely outside the claimed lattice restriction when \(p=1\). A sufficient local correction is to require \(p<1\) or \(\beta\kappa(1,1)<1\), with the close-to-one mark cutoff in the isolation proof chosen accordingly. For \(\kappa_{\rm sum}\), this means \(p<1\) or \(2^d\beta<1\). The correction must be propagated through the lattice statement and proof. This is a false final assertion on a stated subfamily, not merely a missing estimate. It does not refute the Poisson upper bounds or the heavy-heavy kernel results on their nondegenerate range.

Problem 2 (Minor: the introductory lower-tail order has the wrong direction).  Theorem 1.1, p. 2, (1.3), gives \(\log\mathbb P(|C_n^{(1)}|<\rho n)=-\Omega(n^\zeta)\) for every \(\rho>0\). The detailed Theorem 2.4 gives a lower bound on this probability, and the discussion on p. 11 and the proof of Theorem 1.1 on p. 54 identify that lower bound as the intended input.

For an explicit permitted heavy-heavy example, take Poisson locations, \(d=1,\sigma=1,\tau=5/2,\alpha=2\), and any fixed \(p\in(0,1]\), \(\beta>0\). Then \(\zeta_{\rm hh}=2/5>\max(\zeta_{\rm ll},\zeta_{\rm short})=0\), as required in the introductory statement. Let \(\rho=2\). Since the number of vertices \(N_n\) is \({\rm Poi}(n)\), \[\mathbb P(|C_n^{(1)}|<2n)\geq \mathbb P(N_n<2n)
 \geq1-\exp[-(2\log2-1)n].\] The logarithm tends to zero and cannot be bounded above by \(-c n^{2/5}\), \(c>0\). The lower bound actually proved in Theorem 2.4 implies \(\log\mathbb P(\cdot)=-O(n^\zeta)\) for each fixed \(\rho\) in the unique-maximizer setting of Theorem 1.1. Replacing \(\Omega\) by \(O\) is consistent with both the proof and the prose. An upper large-deviation estimate would instead need a restriction such as \(\rho<\theta\) and its own argument. This correction concerns the introductory formulation, not the cluster-tail exponent.

Problem 3 (Minor: the all-size quantifiers fail at logarithmic and lattice endpoints).  Theorem 2.1(i), p. 9, states its lower bound for \(k\geq1\); Theorem 2.4, p. 10, states (2.8) for \(n\geq1\) and \(\rho>0\). These quantifiers admit impossible lower bounds.

Take \(d=1,\sigma=1,\tau=5/2,\alpha=3/2\). Then \(\zeta_{\rm ll}=\zeta_{\rm hl}=\zeta_{\rm hh}=1/2\), \(\zeta_{\rm short}=0\), and \(m_\star=3\). For Poisson locations and \(k=1\), the claimed right side of the cluster lower bound is \(\exp[-A\,1^{1/2}(\log1)^2]=1\). At any finite \(n>\max(A,1)\), however, the Palm origin is the sole vertex in the box with probability \(e^{-n}>0\). On that event \(|C_n(0)|>1\) fails, irrespective of the additional condition that the origin be outside the largest component. Thus the left side is strictly below one.

For Theorem 2.4 with the same parameters, \(n=\rho=1\), the right side is again one, while \(\mathbb P(|C_1^{(1)}|<1)=\mathbb P(N_1=0)=e^{-1}\). Independently of logarithmic ties, the lattice always contains the origin; if \(\rho n\leq1\), its lower-tail event is empty, whereas a finite exponential right side is positive. The concentration arguments on pp. 50 and 53 are naturally large-size arguments. Stating the cluster estimate for sufficiently large \(k\), and the giant estimate for sufficiently large \(n\) depending on \(\rho\), removes these particular endpoint contradictions after the nondegeneracy correction in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:lattice). A replacement such as \(\log(2+k)\) addresses the logarithmic endpoint alone; it cannot make an impossible lattice event have positive probability. No asymptotic cluster-tail conclusion is disproved by this problem.

Problem 4 (Minor: the boundary exponent needs a nonempty-edge qualification).  Claim 1.4, p. 7, and Lemma 7.7, p. 47, (7.27), include the threshold and unit-mark limits without a separate nondegeneracy condition. The short-edge lower-bound sketch on p. 69 assumes that a boundary vertex has a positive chance of an edge across the boundary.

Take \(d=2,\ W\equiv1,\ \kappa=\kappa_0=1,\
\alpha=\infty,\ p=1,\beta=3/4\), on \(\mathbb Z^2\). Every distinct pair has \(\|x-y\|^d\geq1>\beta\); hence there are no edges. Assumption 1.3 still holds. The expected downward vertex-boundary size is zero, so its logarithm is undefined as a real number (or is \(-\infty\) in the extended convention). The displayed maximum predicts \(\zeta_{\rm short}=1/2\). This is a separate degenerate case from the connected example in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:lattice). Restrict the claim to a setting with a positive crossing-edge mechanism, or state the empty case separately. Claim 1.4 is not stated only in the supercritical heavy-heavy range; that narrower context would exclude this example. The main supercritical asymptotic theorem is therefore not refuted by it.
# Proof dependencies requiring local repairs

Problem 5 (Minor: a component-wide mark restriction is dropped).  The definition of \(A_{\rm low\text{-}edge}\) in (6.10), p. 36, bounds the two edge-endpoint marks. The event inclusion in the proof of Claim 6.5, p. 39 immediately before (6.24), implicitly needs all vertices on the connecting path to have low marks. This stronger condition is absent from that event.

Evidence and repair. Fix the finite-\(\alpha\) case, with \(p\in(0,1)\), and take \(k\) sufficiently large. Write \(t_k\) for the length cutoff and \(\bar w\) for the mark cutoff. In dimension one put three vertices near \(0,2t_k,4t_k\), inside the box of half-side \(k t_k\). Give the origin mark greater than \(\bar w\), and give the other two marks less than \(\bar w\). Let the only component edges be \(0a\) and \(ab\). Both have length greater than \(t_k\). The full component has size three, at most \(k\), and the low-low edge \(ab\) makes \(A_{\rm low\text{-}edge}\) hold. After all edges of length at least \(t_k\) are deleted, the origin’s component is just the high-mark origin. It contains no low-mark endpoint of the kind required on the right side of the displayed inclusion.

This is a genuine finite-configuration obstruction: use small open position and mark intervals and the specified finite edge pattern. Under finite \(\alpha\) and \(0<p<1\), that pattern has positive conditional probability. For large \(t_k\) the three points do not violate the annular density bounds; further points may be placed sparsely without changing the component. The counterexample refutes the event implication, not the numerical probability bound (6.22).

There is strong counterevidence to a failure of the needed cluster-tail estimate. In (6.19), p. 37, the intersection with \(A_{\rm mark\text{-}giant}\) and the condition of being outside the giant already ensures that every vertex of the relevant component has mark at most \(\bar w\). Retain this restriction when defining the event to be bounded. Along a path from the origin, the first edge of length at least \(t_k\) then has a low-mark endpoint in the short-edge component; the argument before (6.24) applies. Conditional independence of the unrevealed long-edge variables is unchanged. ◻

The defect lies in a core upper-bound reduction, but the required stronger event is available immediately upstream. The repair changes the intermediate statement and its use, without supplying a counterexample to Theorem 2.1(ii)–(iii).

Problem 6 (Minor: the Palm-to-ordinary comparison needs a degree argument).  On p. 50, between (7.37) and (7.38), the proof replaces the probability of a large ordinary largest component by the Palm probability of a large origin component, losing only one vertex in the threshold. Adding a Palm vertex can merge several ordinary components; deleting it need not leave all but one of its component in a single component.

For a concrete obstruction to that general comparison, take a one-dimensional Poisson KSRG in \([-2,2]\), with \(\alpha=\infty,\beta=2,p=1,\sigma=1,\tau=5/2\), without mark truncation. The Palm origin is connected to every ordinary vertex, since distances to it are at most two and all marks are at least one. Hence \[\mathbb P^0(|C_4(0)|>8)=\mathbb P({\rm Poi}(4)\geq8).\] The ordinary event \(|C_4^{(1)}|>7\) is contained in \(\{N_4\geq8\}\). It misses the positive-probability event with exactly four vertices in each of \([-2,-1.8]\) and \([1.8,2]\), no others, and all eight marks in \([1,1.1]\). The two groups cannot connect: their gap is at least \(3.6\), while \(\beta w w'\leq2(1.1)^2=2.42\). That event has probability \[e^{-4}\frac{(1/5)^8}{(4!)^2}
       \bigl[1-(11/10)^{-3/2}\bigr]^8>0.\] Thus the unqualified one-vertex comparison is false even for a KSRG. This finite-box example does not assert failure of the particular eventual, mark-truncated inequality under the additional hypothesis (7.2). It shows why merely ignoring Palm conditioning is not a proof of that step.

A replacement sufficient for the asymptotic lower bound follows from local finiteness. Let \(D_0\) be the degree of the Palm origin in the infinite graph. Under the present kernel, \(\tau>2\) and \(\alpha>1\) imply \(D_0<\infty\) almost surely, also when its unconditional expectation is infinite. Given the positive constant \(\rho\) in (7.2), choose a fixed \(K\) with \(\mathbb P^0(D_0>K)<\rho/2\). On the event that the truncated Palm component has at least \(\rho n\) vertices and \(D_0\leq K\), deletion of the origin leaves at most \(K\) components. One has size at least \((\rho n-1)/K\). The ordinary marked graph has its original law under this deletion. It therefore has a component of a smaller but positive linear density with probability at least \(\rho/2\). Enlarging the outer box by the corresponding fixed factor recovers the outside component needed in (7.7)–(7.38). All exponential powers remain unchanged. The printed constant \(\rho^2\) and threshold cannot simply be retained without this adjustment. Proposition 7.1’s final asymptotic conclusion is not disproved.

Problem 7 (Minor: the conditional field in (A.7) reveals the wrong mark bands).  Equation (A.7), p. 56, conditions on \(G_n[1,w_{\rm hh})\). The proof of Claim A.2 instead requires the intermediate mark bands below \(w_{\rm hh}\) to remain random.

The relevant hypotheses are Poisson locations, \(\zeta_{\rm hh}>0\), a realized high-mark backbone satisfying \(A_{\rm bb}\), regularity of the lowest band \([m_w,2m_w)\), and the origin mark in that band. For sufficiently large \(n\), choose an intermediate band \(I_j=[2^j m_w,2^{j+1}m_w)\), \(j\geq1\), strictly below \(w_{\rm hh}\). Under the literal conditioning in (A.7), the count in \(Q_j(x)\times I_j\) is already known. A realization with count zero has positive probability and is compatible with the lowest-band regularity and the disjoint high-mark backbone. Its conditional probability of a candidate vertex is zero, whereas the positive-mean Poisson lower domination invoked immediately before (A.17), p. 58, assigns positive probability to at least one candidate. The same conditioning also invalidates the later claim that the revealed low-band positions are still uniform.

The last line of p. 57, the explanation on p. 58, and the proofs on pp. 59–60 explicitly describe conditioning only on \(G_n[w_{\rm hh},2w_{\rm hh})\). Replacing the graph in (A.7) by this high-mark graph, while keeping the separately stated lowest-band regularity and origin-mark conditions, restores the independence of the intermediate Poisson bands. This is a locally repairable discrepancy in the definition of a conditional law, not evidence that the linear-component construction is false. In the same argument, the second line of (A.18), p. 59, also needs a minus sign in the exponent: \(1-(1-q)^s\geq1-e^{-sq}\), not \(1-e^{sq}\). The first line supplies the intended Bernoulli bound directly.
#### Notation clarification: box volume.
Equation (2.10), p. 12, contains a local typographical error in the box notation. It is not counted as a scientific Problem.

For \(s>0\) and integer \(d\geq1\), the displayed box \[x+[-s/2^{1/d},s/2^{1/d}]^d\] has volume \(2^{d-1}s^d\), not \(s\). For example \(d=s=2\) gives volume eight. The correct expression is \(x+[-s^{1/d}/2,s^{1/d}/2]^d\). The correctly normalized \(\Lambda_n\) on p. 4 and the explicit box expression on p. 22 are counterevidence to an intended alternative convention. The later tessellation and cover estimates use volume \(s\), so this correction should be made before interpreting those formulas. No altered exponent or false asymptotic theorem follows from this typographical error, so it is excluded from the substantive issue count.

Problem 8 (Minor: the auxiliary function \(g\) is not always monotone).  After (B.16), p. 66, the proof asserts that \(g\) is nondecreasing in both arguments and uses this in (B.18). The \(\alpha=\tau-1,\ \sigma\alpha>\tau-1\) row defining \(g_2\) on p. 65 need not have that property.

Take \(\alpha=\tau-1=3/2,\sigma=6/5,d=1,\gamma=1/4\) and \(C_\beta=1\), so \(\beta=1/2\). Choose \(r_k\geq100\). In the region \(1\leq u\leq v=100\), the row in question reads \[g(100,u)=\bigl(1+\tfrac14\log(100/u)\bigr)u^{3/40}.\] Its derivative at \(u=100\), from the left, is \[-\frac{7}{40}\,100^{-37/40}
 =-\frac{7\,10^{3/20}}{4000}<0.\] All parameters satisfy the stated assumptions, including \(\gamma\leq1/(\sigma+1)\). The positivity of the power does not make the product with a decreasing logarithmic factor monotone.

Problem 9 (Minor: Lemma 5.9 omits the \(s(w)>n\) cover case).  Proposition 4.2, p. 15, requires \(s(w)\leq n\), where \(s(w)=(2^d\beta w)^{1/(1-1/\alpha)}\). Its invocation on p. 31 in the proof of Lemma 5.9 checks the lower bound on \(w=2w_{\rm hh}(k)\), but not this upper bound on \(s(w)\). The ambient size may be any \(n\geq k\).

For finite \(\alpha=11/10,\tau=5/2,\sigma=1\), \(\gamma_{\rm hh}=1/7\), and therefore \[s(2w_{\rm hh}(k))\asymp k^{11/7}.\] At \(n=k\), the required inequality fails for all sufficiently large \(k\). The failure is a domain-of-application omission, not a counterexample to the merging estimate.

Here is the missing case. If \(s(w)>n\), select exactly \(k\) vertices from the component of size greater than \(k\) (the construction uses integer \(k\)). This subset is \(n\)-expandable: every tested box of volume at least \(n\) contains at most \(k\leq n\) selected vertices, hence satisfies the expansion density bound. Set \[w'=\frac{n^{1-1/\alpha}}{2^d\beta}.\] Then \(s(w')=n\) and \(w'<w\). For all sufficiently large \(k\), \(w'\) exceeds Proposition 4.2’s fixed lower threshold. Apply that proposition to the selected subset at \(w'\). It gives a region of volume at least \(c k\). The actual sure-connectors have marks at least \(w\geq w'\), so monotonicity of the kernel preserves their connection probability lower bound. The same thinning calculation then gives \(\exp[-c'k w_{\rm hh}^{-(\tau-1)}]\), the intended heavy-heavy power. Increase the fixed minimum \(k\) to cover the auxiliary threshold, and treat the remaining finite values separately. The \(s(w)\leq n\) case remains the printed proof. This supplies the omitted case without claiming a false final merging result.
# Independent checks and reference audit
## The coupling and the exponent calculation

The sure/unsure construction in Definition 5.6 and Proposition 5.8, pp. 29–30, survives a direct distributional check. If \(s\) independent uniforms are split according to \(B=\{\min U_i>r\}\), with \(r=1-2^{-1/s}\), then \(\mathbb P(B)=1/2\). For \(0\leq z_i\leq1\), \[\mathbb P(U_i\leq z_i\ \forall i\mid B)
   =2\prod_i(z_i-r)_+,\qquad
 \mathbb P(U_i\leq z_i\ \forall i\mid B^c)
   =2\left(\prod_i z_i-\prod_i(z_i-r)_+\right).\] The equally weighted mixture is exactly \(\prod_i z_i\). Independent labels on the split Poisson process and independent edge vectors across connector vertices therefore give the required original graph law. Seven independently computed joint-distribution examples, evaluated with 70-digit working precision, agree with this identity. The algebraic identity, rather than numerical agreement, is the proof.

The high-mark scale satisfies \(k w_{\rm hh}^{-(\tau-1)}\asymp k^{\zeta_{\rm hh}}\). Balancing the expected removed-vertex count with the crossing-edge count gives \[\gamma_{\rm long}
  =\frac{\alpha-1}{\xi_\star+\tau-1},\qquad
 \xi_\star=\max\{0,\alpha-(\tau-1),
                  (\sigma+1)\alpha-2(\tau-1)\},
 \quad
 \gamma_\star=\min\{\gamma_{\rm long},1/(\sigma+1)\}.\] The identities and multiplicity cases of Lemma 7.6 and Appendix C were checked directly, including ties and the threshold limit. In particular, equality with the short-edge exponent introduces the additional logarithmic factor; it must not be discarded at a phase boundary. An independent exact-rational sweep checked 840 parameter cases and found no disagreement in the tested exponent and multiplicity identities. This finite sweep supplements the case algebra; it is not a universal proof by sampling.

The independent evidence file also contains lattice counts for five square boxes, the zero-edge and endpoint witnesses, the short/long-edge graph example, the Palm merge example, the derivative in Problem Problem 8 (#prob:monotone), the cover-scale exponent \(11/7\), and the kernel expectation calculation below. The script was authored for this review and actually executed with exit code zero. No author code was executed. Exact expressions, parameters and execution evidence are retained under this paper’s verification tree.
## Isolation, geometry and the external Erdős–Rényi input

In the Poisson case, the mark-suppression regions are disjoint from the revealed low-mark rectangles once the size is sufficiently large. Their void probability is the exponential of their intensity. For the retained crossing edges, (7.21) bounds individual edge probabilities away from one; conditional edge independence and \(1-q\geq e^{-c q}\), followed by Jensen’s inequality, give (7.31)–(7.32), p. 48. This supplies the lower bound used in the main isolation argument. The lattice needs the additional nondegeneracy discussed in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:lattice). The FKG step on p. 53 uses decreasing isolation and vertex-count events; the source first conditions on the point set and then applies the Poisson association step. Its sign is consistent with the required product lower bound.

The geometric discussion near (B.22), p. 67, informally describes an intersection of two spheres without spelling out a coarea Jacobian. A direct bound avoids relying on that description. At a fixed interior point and exterior boundary distance \(z_v\), the area of the exterior sphere inside a Euclidean ball of radius \(r\) about that point is at most \(C_d r^{d-1}\). Layer-cake integration of the kernel \(r^{-\alpha d}\), starting at distance \(z_u+z_v\), bounds its surface integral by \[C_{d,\alpha}(z_u+z_v)^{-d(\alpha-1)-1}.\] The integral converges because \(\alpha>1\). Combining this bound with the interior or exterior shell measure yields the radial powers used in (B.22)–(B.25). Thus the informal coordinate explanation is not treated here as evidence of a false isolation exponent. The constant-comparison repair for \(g\) remains necessary.

The proof of the backbone invokes O’Connell’s largest-component large-deviation theorem on p. 26. The acquired author-hosted reference [OConnell], physical pp. 1–5, includes Theorem 3.1 on printed p. 279. It concerns \({\rm ER}(m,c/m)\) at fixed \(c>0\); for \(c>1\), the rate function gives an exponential lower-tail estimate below the positive giant density. This matches the fixed-supercritical-mean use after the source’s domination step, with sufficiently large integer \(m\). Small-size conventions and rounding can be absorbed by increasing the minimum backbone scale. The whole nine-page reference proof was not independently certified.
## Local convergence: finite mean is a separate hypothesis

The law-of-large-numbers argument on pp. 40–41 cites Local limits of spatial inhomogeneous random graphs. The acquired version [LocalLimits] is arXiv:2107.08733v3 dated 6 September 2022, with a title-page date of 7 September; its first eight pages were read and viewed. Assumption 1.8(2), p. 5, and Theorems 1.9 and 1.11, pp. 6–7, require an integrable averaged connection bound. That hypothesis is not automatic for every \(\sigma\) allowed in the reviewed paper.

Equation reference: kernelmean. Indeed, with \(t=\tau-1>1\), integration over the ordered marks gives \[
 \mathbb E[\kappa_\sigma(W_1,W_2)]
  =\frac{2t^2}{t-1}\int_1^\infty u^{\sigma-2t}\,\mathrm du,\] which is finite exactly when \(\sigma<2\tau-3\). For finite \(\alpha>1\), spatial integration in [model] (#model) is a positive constant times \(\beta p\,\alpha/(\alpha-1)\) times the kernel; for the threshold profile the corresponding factor is \(\beta p\). For example \(\tau=5/2,\sigma=3,\alpha=2\) is in the heavy-heavy regime, with \(\zeta_{\rm hh}=10/13>0\), but the integral in [kernelmean] (#kernelmean) diverges. This shows that the checked reference theorem alone does not justify that full parameter range.

It does not show a failure of local convergence. For each fixed finite mark \(w\), \[\mathbb E[\kappa_\sigma(w,W)]
 =w\,\mathbb E[W^\sigma;W\leq w]
  +w^\sigma\,\mathbb E[W;W>w]<\infty.\] Thus the Palm degree is finite almost surely, and each fixed graph-radius neighborhood occupies a finite spatial region almost surely. This supplies a direct argument for the present Poisson restriction model. Fix a graph radius and a bounded rooted-neighborhood indicator. Approximate it by the same indicator in a Euclidean window of radius \(R\). The Palm probability that the full graph ball leaves this window tends to zero as \(R\to\infty\). For fixed \(R\), averages over well-separated spatial windows are independent, so their normalized empirical averages converge to the corresponding Palm expectation. Campbell’s formula bounds the average approximation error by the escape probability plus the vanishing boundary fraction of the large box. First let the ambient volume tend to infinity, then \(R\to\infty\). Finally \(N_n/n\to1\) converts volume normalization to uniform-vertex normalization. This proves the needed local convergence in probability without requiring a finite unconditional mean degree.

The random denominator in the uniform-vertex average on p. 41 should likewise be handled by \(N_n/n\to1\) before a Campbell/Palm comparison; conditioning on a uniformly selected point is not exactly the unweighted Palm law at finite volume. This concentration step supplies the asymptotic comparison needed there.

The acquired almost-local reference [AlmostLocal] is the later v3 of 6 October 2025. Its Theorem 2.2, pp. 4–5, requires local convergence in probability and a vanishing normalized count of pairs in distinct large components. The source’s outside-giant tail is sufficient for the pair condition, because at least one of such a pair is outside the largest component. The criterion also extends to random \(N_n\) with \(N_n/n\to1\): apply the same deterministic component-size inequalities with \(N_n\) in place of \(n\), and define the normalized quantities as zero on \(N_n=0\). The finite-mean/uniform-integrability assumption appearing in that reference’s edge-count result is not required for its largest-component result.

These checks record a reference-hypothesis qualification and supply the relevant argument for this model. They are not an allegation that Corollary 2.3 is false. The publisher PDF of the local-limits reference was not acquired, so no identity between its exact journal wording and the inspected preprint is claimed.
# Version limits and overall assessment

The frozen source manifest binds four files, with 2,883,644 aggregate bytes and no binding errors. Two PDF entries have the same main-source hash; they are not two independent versions. The arXiv HTML is a metadata record. The 1,056-byte response associated with the separate supplement DOI is an HTML security challenge, not a PDF. The embedded Appendices A–C were read in the 74-page source; equivalence with a separate journal supplement has not been established. A single ordinary attempt to retrieve an author-institution copy of the journal PDF failed with a connection timeout and produced no PDF. There was no bypass attempt. The findings therefore apply to the exact acquired preprint, without silently transferring them to an uninspected version of record.

A bounded primary-source correction search was performed. The current arXiv record identifies v3 with the same date. A 2026 publisher correction found for the related paper Large deviations of the giant in supercritical kernel-based spatial random graphs concerns editorial received/accepted dates and a different DOI. It is not a correction of the mathematical statements reviewed here. The later almost-local reference explicitly records a correction to its Corollary 2.6 and an added theorem; the actual acquired v3, rather than an assumed old statement, was used for this audit. No mathematical author correction to this exact assigned PDF was established by the bounded search. This is not a claim that no correction exists anywhere.

The detailed finite-\(n\) hyperbolic and fixed-number-of-vertices transfers mentioned on p. 54 are left partly to the reader in the source. Their complete model-dependent coupling and conditioning estimates were not reconstructed here. All external references beyond the specified acquired pages are treated as cited inputs, not as independently verified complete proofs. Missing supplements, unavailable publisher payloads and the absence of executed author code are verification limits, not mathematical defects.

Problem Problem 1 (#prob:lattice) requires a correction to the stated range of a final theorem and to the associated lattice proof. The other numbered problems have explicit local repairs or restricted conclusions. In particular, the false event implication, incorrect conditioning field and invalid monotonicity explanation must be corrected even though their downstream asymptotic estimates can be recovered by the arguments given above. The checked exponent balances, conditional graph-law construction and Poisson isolation mechanism provide substantial counterevidence to a whole-paper failure claim. The scientific decision remains pending.

problems.title: The lattice sum-kernel assumptions permit deterministic connectivity, falsifying Theorem 2.4
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: Problem 1 (Major: the lattice sum-kernel restriction permits certain edges).
claim: Recorded check: The lattice sum-kernel assumptions permit deterministic connectivity, falsifying Theorem 2.4
analysis: Theorem 2.4, p. 10, (2.8), is false under the literal lattice hypotheses of Assumption 1.3, p. 4. The relevant proof uses the strict edge-probability assertion in the lattice adaptation of Lemma 7.2, p. 49, and then the covering argument on pp. 52–53. The comparison \(\kappa_{\rm sum}\leq2^d\kappa_0\) on p. 12 does not preserve the stated nondegeneracy restriction.

Equation reference: zeroevent. Evidence. Take \(d=2,\ W\equiv1,\ \kappa=\kappa_{\rm sum},\
\alpha=2,\ p=1,\ \beta=3/4\). These choices satisfy the displayed assumptions, including \(p\wedge\beta<1\). But \(\kappa_{\rm sum}(1,1)=4\), so every lattice nearest-neighbor edge has probability \((1\wedge3)^2=1\). For \(n=4m^2\), \(m\geq1\), the box is \([-m,m]^2\). Its \((2m+1)^2\) lattice vertices form a connected deterministic nearest-neighbor graph. Consequently, for \(\rho=1/2\), \[
 \mathbb P(|C_n^{(1)}|<\rho n)=0.\] Here \(\zeta_\star=1/2\) and \(m_\star=1\): the short-edge exponent dominates \(2-\alpha=0\), and the heavy-mark mechanisms disappear for unit marks. The right side of (2.8) is \(\exp[-(A/\rho)n^{1/2}]=\exp(-4Am)>0\) for every finite \(A\). Thus the contradiction holds at arbitrarily large volumes. ◻

The phrase explaining that the graph should not be almost surely connected can plausibly express an intended extra hypothesis. It does not follow from the written restriction for this kernel. Suppressing marks near their minimum cannot remove certain nearest-neighbor edges. Moreover, comparison with \(\kappa_0\) changes the effective parameter to \(2^d\beta=3\), precisely outside the claimed lattice restriction when \(p=1\). A sufficient local correction is to require \(p<1\) or \(\beta\kappa(1,1)<1\), with the close-to-one mark cutoff in the isolation proof chosen accordingly. For \(\kappa_{\rm sum}\), this means \(p<1\) or \(2^d\beta<1\). The correction must be propagated through the lattice statement and proof. This is a false final assertion on a stated subfamily, not merely a missing estimate. It does not refute the Poisson upper bounds or the heavy-heavy kernel results on their nondegenerate range.
result: Impact: A demonstrated false final assertion on a stated lattice subfamily at arbitrarily large volumes; not a claim of whole-paper failure.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Require p<1 or beta*kappa(1,1)<1, with the close-to-one mark cutoff adjusted in the lattice proof; for kappa_sum require p<1 or2^d beta<1. Propagate the restriction to Theorem2.4 and the kernel comparison.

problems.title: The introductory negative-Omega lower-tail statement has the wrong direction
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (Minor: the introductory lower-tail order has the wrong direction).
claim: Recorded check: The introductory negative-Omega lower-tail statement has the wrong direction
analysis: Theorem 1.1, p. 2, (1.3), gives \(\log\mathbb P(|C_n^{(1)}|<\rho n)=-\Omega(n^\zeta)\) for every \(\rho>0\). The detailed Theorem 2.4 gives a lower bound on this probability, and the discussion on p. 11 and the proof of Theorem 1.1 on p. 54 identify that lower bound as the intended input.

For an explicit permitted heavy-heavy example, take Poisson locations, \(d=1,\sigma=1,\tau=5/2,\alpha=2\), and any fixed \(p\in(0,1]\), \(\beta>0\). Then \(\zeta_{\rm hh}=2/5>\max(\zeta_{\rm ll},\zeta_{\rm short})=0\), as required in the introductory statement. Let \(\rho=2\). Since the number of vertices \(N_n\) is \({\rm Poi}(n)\), \[\mathbb P(|C_n^{(1)}|<2n)\geq \mathbb P(N_n<2n)
 \geq1-\exp[-(2\log2-1)n].\] The logarithm tends to zero and cannot be bounded above by \(-c n^{2/5}\), \(c>0\). The lower bound actually proved in Theorem 2.4 implies \(\log\mathbb P(\cdot)=-O(n^\zeta)\) for each fixed \(\rho\) in the unique-maximizer setting of Theorem 1.1. Replacing \(\Omega\) by \(O\) is consistent with both the proof and the prose. An upper large-deviation estimate would instead need a restriction such as \(\rho<\theta\) and its own argument. This correction concerns the introductory formulation, not the cluster-tail exponent.
result: Impact: Literal asymptotic sign/quantifier error; cluster-tail and second-component exponents not disproved.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Replace Omega by O in the introductory lower-bound formulation, or separately state and prove any intended restricted upper bound.

problems.title: All-size lower bounds fail at logarithmic and lattice endpoints
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: Problem 3 (Minor: the all-size quantifiers fail at logarithmic and lattice endpoints).
claim: Recorded check: All-size lower bounds fail at logarithmic and lattice endpoints
analysis: Theorem 2.1(i), p. 9, states its lower bound for \(k\geq1\); Theorem 2.4, p. 10, states (2.8) for \(n\geq1\) and \(\rho>0\). These quantifiers admit impossible lower bounds.

Take \(d=1,\sigma=1,\tau=5/2,\alpha=3/2\). Then \(\zeta_{\rm ll}=\zeta_{\rm hl}=\zeta_{\rm hh}=1/2\), \(\zeta_{\rm short}=0\), and \(m_\star=3\). For Poisson locations and \(k=1\), the claimed right side of the cluster lower bound is \(\exp[-A\,1^{1/2}(\log1)^2]=1\). At any finite \(n>\max(A,1)\), however, the Palm origin is the sole vertex in the box with probability \(e^{-n}>0\). On that event \(|C_n(0)|>1\) fails, irrespective of the additional condition that the origin be outside the largest component. Thus the left side is strictly below one.

For Theorem 2.4 with the same parameters, \(n=\rho=1\), the right side is again one, while \(\mathbb P(|C_1^{(1)}|<1)=\mathbb P(N_1=0)=e^{-1}\). Independently of logarithmic ties, the lattice always contains the origin; if \(\rho n\leq1\), its lower-tail event is empty, whereas a finite exponential right side is positive. The concentration arguments on pp. 50 and 53 are naturally large-size arguments. Stating the cluster estimate for sufficiently large \(k\), and the giant estimate for sufficiently large \(n\) depending on \(\rho\), removes these particular endpoint contradictions after the nondegeneracy correction in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:lattice). A replacement such as \(\log(2+k)\) addresses the logarithmic endpoint alone; it cannot make an impossible lattice event have positive probability. No asymptotic cluster-tail conclusion is disproved by this problem.
result: Impact: False literal endpoint range with local range repair; no asymptotic failure established.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: State sufficiently large k and sufficiently large n depending onrho, with the nondegeneracy correction inP1; separately control any finite values actually claimed.

problems.title: The claimed short-edge boundary exponent includes an edgeless threshold case
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: Problem 4 (Minor: the boundary exponent needs a nonempty-edge qualification).
claim: Recorded check: The claimed short-edge boundary exponent includes an edgeless threshold case
analysis: Claim 1.4, p. 7, and Lemma 7.7, p. 47, (7.27), include the threshold and unit-mark limits without a separate nondegeneracy condition. The short-edge lower-bound sketch on p. 69 assumes that a boundary vertex has a positive chance of an edge across the boundary.

Take \(d=2,\ W\equiv1,\ \kappa=\kappa_0=1,\
\alpha=\infty,\ p=1,\beta=3/4\), on \(\mathbb Z^2\). Every distinct pair has \(\|x-y\|^d\geq1>\beta\); hence there are no edges. Assumption 1.3 still holds. The expected downward vertex-boundary size is zero, so its logarithm is undefined as a real number (or is \(-\infty\) in the extended convention). The displayed maximum predicts \(\zeta_{\rm short}=1/2\). This is a separate degenerate case from the connected example in Problem Problem 1 (#prob:lattice). Restrict the claim to a setting with a positive crossing-edge mechanism, or state the empty case separately. Claim 1.4 is not stated only in the supercritical heavy-heavy range; that narrower context would exclude this example. The main supercritical asymptotic theorem is therefore not refuted by it.
result: Impact: False degenerate endpoint of a broad claim; no counterexample to the main supercritical result.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: Qualify the boundary claim with a positive crossing-edge mechanism or state the edgeless case separately.

problems.title: A low-endpoint edge event is used as if the full component had low marks
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 5: Problem 5 (Minor: a component-wide mark restriction is dropped).
claim: Recorded check: A low-endpoint edge event is used as if the full component had low marks
analysis: The definition of \(A_{\rm low\text{-}edge}\) in (6.10), p. 36, bounds the two edge-endpoint marks. The event inclusion in the proof of Claim 6.5, p. 39 immediately before (6.24), implicitly needs all vertices on the connecting path to have low marks. This stronger condition is absent from that event.

Evidence and repair. Fix the finite-\(\alpha\) case, with \(p\in(0,1)\), and take \(k\) sufficiently large. Write \(t_k\) for the length cutoff and \(\bar w\) for the mark cutoff. In dimension one put three vertices near \(0,2t_k,4t_k\), inside the box of half-side \(k t_k\). Give the origin mark greater than \(\bar w\), and give the other two marks less than \(\bar w\). Let the only component edges be \(0a\) and \(ab\). Both have length greater than \(t_k\). The full component has size three, at most \(k\), and the low-low edge \(ab\) makes \(A_{\rm low\text{-}edge}\) hold. After all edges of length at least \(t_k\) are deleted, the origin’s component is just the high-mark origin. It contains no low-mark endpoint of the kind required on the right side of the displayed inclusion.

This is a genuine finite-configuration obstruction: use small open position and mark intervals and the specified finite edge pattern. Under finite \(\alpha\) and \(0<p<1\), that pattern has positive conditional probability. For large \(t_k\) the three points do not violate the annular density bounds; further points may be placed sparsely without changing the component. The counterexample refutes the event implication, not the numerical probability bound (6.22).

There is strong counterevidence to a failure of the needed cluster-tail estimate. problems.title: Palm deletion is incorrectly treated as losing only one vertex of a component
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: Problem 6 (Minor: the Palm-to-ordinary comparison needs a degree argument).
claim: Recorded check: Palm deletion is incorrectly treated as losing only one vertex of a component
analysis: On p. 50, between (7.37) and (7.38), the proof replaces the probability of a large ordinary largest component by the Palm probability of a large origin component, losing only one vertex in the threshold. Adding a Palm vertex can merge several ordinary components; deleting it need not leave all but one of its component in a single component.

For a concrete obstruction to that general comparison, take a one-dimensional Poisson KSRG in \([-2,2]\), with \(\alpha=\infty,\beta=2,p=1,\sigma=1,\tau=5/2\), without mark truncation. The Palm origin is connected to every ordinary vertex, since distances to it are at most two and all marks are at least one. Hence \[\mathbb P^0(|C_4(0)|>8)=\mathbb P({\rm Poi}(4)\geq8).\] The ordinary event \(|C_4^{(1)}|>7\) is contained in \(\{N_4\geq8\}\). It misses the positive-probability event with exactly four vertices in each of \([-2,-1.8]\) and \([1.8,2]\), no others, and all eight marks in \([1,1.1]\). The two groups cannot connect: their gap is at least \(3.6\), while \(\beta w w'\leq2(1.1)^2=2.42\). That event has probability \[e^{-4}\frac{(1/5)^8}{(4!)^2}
       \bigl[1-(11/10)^{-3/2}\bigr]^8>0.\] Thus the unqualified one-vertex comparison is false even for a KSRG. This finite-box example does not assert failure of the particular eventual, mark-truncated inequality under the additional hypothesis (7.2). It shows why merely ignoring Palm conditioning is not a proof of that step.

A replacement sufficient for the asymptotic lower bound follows from local finiteness. Let \(D_0\) be the degree of the Palm origin in the infinite graph. Under the present kernel, \(\tau>2\) and \(\alpha>1\) imply \(D_0<\infty\) almost surely, also when its unconditional expectation is infinite. Given the positive constant \(\rho\) in (7.2), choose a fixed \(K\) with \(\mathbb P^0(D_0>K)<\rho/2\). On the event that the truncated Palm component has at least \(\rho n\) vertices and \(D_0\leq K\), deletion of the origin leaves at most \(K\) components. One has size at least \((\rho n-1)/K\). The ordinary marked graph has its original law under this deletion. It therefore has a component of a smaller but positive linear density with probability at least \(\rho/2\). Enlarging the outer box by the corresponding fixed factor recovers the outside component needed in (7.7)–(7.38). All exponential powers remain unchanged. The printed constant \(\rho^2\) and threshold cannot simply be retained without this adjustment. Proposition 7.1’s final asymptotic conclusion is not disproved.
result: Impact: Invalid general comparison used in proof; supplied degree-controlled repair preserves asymptotic powers, with constants altered.

repair.heading: Recorded correction and verification scope
paragraphs: ChooseK withP0(D0>K)<rho/2, combine with(7.2), deleteorigin, obtain ordinary largest component>=(rho*n-1)/K with probability>=rho/2; enlarge outer box by a fixed factor and adjust constants.

problems.title: The conditional law in(A.7) reveals the wrong mark bands
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 7: Problem 7 (Minor: the conditional field in (A.7) reveals the wrong mark bands).
claim: Recorded check: The conditional law in(A.7) reveals the wrong mark bands
analysis: Equation (A.7), p. 56, conditions on \(G_n[1,w_{\rm hh})\). The proof of Claim A.2 instead requires the intermediate mark bands below \(w_{\rm hh}\) to remain random.

The relevant hypotheses are Poisson locations, \(\zeta_{\rm hh}>0\), a realized high-mark backbone satisfying \(A_{\rm bb}\), regularity of the lowest band \([m_w,2m_w)\), and the origin mark in that band. For sufficiently large \(n\), choose an intermediate band \(I_j=[2^j m_w,2^{j+1}m_w)\), \(j\geq1\), strictly below \(w_{\rm hh}\). Under the literal conditioning in (A.7), the count in \(Q_j(x)\times I_j\) is already known. A realization with count zero has positive probability and is compatible with the lowest-band regularity and the disjoint high-mark backbone. Its conditional probability of a candidate vertex is zero, whereas the positive-mean Poisson lower domination invoked immediately before (A.17), p. 58, assigns positive probability to at least one candidate. The same conditioning also invalidates the later claim that the revealed low-band positions are still uniform.

The last line of p. 57, the explanation on p. 58, and the proofs on pp. 59–60 explicitly describe conditioning only on \(G_n[w_{\rm hh},2w_{\rm hh})\). Replacing the graph in (A.7) by this high-mark graph, while keeping the separately stated lowest-band regularity and origin-mark conditions, restores the independence of the intermediate Poisson bands. This is a locally repairable discrepancy in the definition of a conditional law, not evidence that the linear-component construction is false. In the same argument, the second line of (A.18), p. 59, also needs a minus sign in the exponent: \(1-(1-q)^s\geq1-e^{-sq}\), not \(1-e^{sq}\). The first line supplies the intended Bernoulli bound directly.
Equation (2.10), p. 12, contains a local typographical error in the box notation. It is not counted as a scientific Problem.

For \(s>0\) and integer \(d\geq1\), the displayed box \[x+[-s/2^{1/d},s/2^{1/d}]^d\] has volume \(2^{d-1}s^d\), not \(s\). For example \(d=s=2\) gives volume eight. The correct expression is \(x+[-s^{1/d}/2,s^{1/d}/2]^d\). The correctly normalized \(\Lambda_n\) on p. 4 and the explicit box expression on p. 22 are counterevidence to an intended alternative convention. The later tessellation and cover estimates use volume \(s\), so this correction should be made before interpreting those formulas. No altered exponent or false asymptotic theorem follows from this typographical error, so it is excluded from the substantive issue count.
result: Impact: False conditional justification as written, but intended construction locally recovered; final linear-component claim not disproved.

problems.title: The auxiliary monotonicity claim for g fails on an allowed logarithmic row
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 8: Problem 8 (Minor: the auxiliary function \(g\) is not always monotone).
claim: Recorded check: The auxiliary monotonicity claim for g fails on an allowed logarithmic row
analysis: After (B.16), p. 66, the proof asserts that \(g\) is nondecreasing in both arguments and uses this in (B.18). The \(\alpha=\tau-1,\ \sigma\alpha>\tau-1\) row defining \(g_2\) on p. 65 need not have that property.

Take \(\alpha=\tau-1=3/2,\sigma=6/5,d=1,\gamma=1/4\) and \(C_\beta=1\), so \(\beta=1/2\). Choose \(r_k\geq100\). In the region \(1\leq u\leq v=100\), the row in question reads \[g(100,u)=\bigl(1+\tfrac14\log(100/u)\bigr)u^{3/40}.\] Its derivative at \(u=100\), from the left, is \[-\frac{7}{40}\,100^{-37/40}
 =-\frac{7\,10^{3/20}}{4000}<0.\] All parameters satisfy the stated assumptions, including \(\gamma\leq1/(\sigma+1)\). The positivity of the power does not make the product with a decreasing logarithmic factor monotone.
result: Impact: False auxiliary assertion; exponent and final isolation bound preserved after repair.

paragraphs: Replace monotonicity justification with the stated fixed-constant comparison and treat the other rows directly.

problems.title: The cover expansion invocation omits s(w)>n
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 9: Problem 9 (Minor: Lemma 5.9 omits the \(s(w)>n\) cover case).
claim: Recorded check: The cover expansion invocation omits s(w)>n
analysis: Proposition 4.2, p. 15, requires \(s(w)\leq n\), where \(s(w)=(2^d\beta w)^{1/(1-1/\alpha)}\). Its invocation on p. 31 in the proof of Lemma 5.9 checks the lower bound on \(w=2w_{\rm hh}(k)\), but not this upper bound on \(s(w)\). The ambient size may be any \(n\geq k\).

For finite \(\alpha=11/10,\tau=5/2,\sigma=1\), \(\gamma_{\rm hh}=1/7\), and therefore \[s(2w_{\rm hh}(k))\asymp k^{11/7}.\] At \(n=k\), the required inequality fails for all sufficiently large \(k\). The failure is a domain-of-application omission, not a counterexample to the merging estimate.

Here is the missing case. If \(s(w)>n\), select exactly \(k\) vertices from the component of size greater than \(k\) (the construction uses integer \(k\)). This subset is \(n\)-expandable: every tested box of volume at least \(n\) contains at most \(k\leq n\) selected vertices, hence satisfies the expansion density bound. Set \[w'=\frac{n^{1-1/\alpha}}{2^d\beta}.\] Then \(s(w')=n\) and \(w'<w\). For all sufficiently large \(k\), \(w'\) exceeds Proposition 4.2’s fixed lower threshold. Apply that proposition to the selected subset at \(w'\). It gives a region of volume at least \(c k\). The actual sure-connectors have marks at least \(w\geq w'\), so monotonicity of the kernel preserves their connection probability lower bound. The same thinning calculation then gives \(\exp[-c'k w_{\rm hh}^{-(\tau-1)}]\), the intended heavy-heavy power. Increase the fixed minimum \(k\) to cover the auxiliary threshold, and treat the remaining finite values separately. The \(s(w)\leq n\) case remains the printed proof. This supplies the omitted case without claiming a false final merging result.
result: Impact: Omitted domain case with explicitcompletion; no false final merging theorem demonstrated.

report: Abstract: This review concerns arXiv:2311.04005v1. The exponential estimate in Lemma 14 uses the larger of two step probabilities as a lower-bound base, and its displayed inequality cannot hold with a fixed positive constant. This step supports the upper Cheeger bound and the separation between diameter and typical distance. A uniform corrected estimate restores the required logarithmic scale, conditional on the preceding encoding and conditioning arguments. A separate domain error in a distance decomposition is confined by the exceptional-event restriction used later in the proof. Neither finding refutes the final theorems.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of Distances and Isoperimetric Inequalities in Random Triangulations of High Genus
# Identity and inspected scope

The paper by Thomas Budzinski, Guillaume Chapuy, and Baptiste Louf is associated with The Annals of Probability 53 (2025), 1645–1667, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1746. The reviewed artifact is the 23-page author preprint [paper], arXiv:2311.04005v1, submitted on 7 November 2023; its title-page body date is 8 November 2023. Page numbers below are one-based PDF pages, equal to the printed pages. Equivalence with the journal text is not asserted.

The full extracted main text and references were read. The detailed audit concentrates on Lemma 14’s probability calculation and its use in Theorem 4 and Proposition 17, and on the domain of equation (16). Definitions and Theorems 1–4 were checked; the enumerative, isoperimetric, and ball-growth arguments were followed for dependency and scope. External enumerative results and the full tree-encoding literature were not independently re-proved. This is a claim-focused initial review.
# Definitions and operative assumptions

The model is a uniform rooted triangulation \(T_{2n,g_n}\) of an oriented surface, with \(2n\) faces, loops and multiple edges allowed, and \(g_n/n\to\theta\in(0,1/2)\) [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~2--4]{paper}]. Tentacles arise by recursive insertions into a digon; the core is obtained by removing maximal tentacles [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~16--17]{paper}]. Write \(T_n=an\) and \(M_n=2bn\) for their number and total number of internal faces. Lemma 13 supplies positive lower bounds for \(a,b\) with high probability. The deterministic bounds \(a\leq3\), \(b\leq1\) suffice below, since the original map has \(3n\) edges and \(2n\) faces.

Equation reference: eq:pq. Conditionally on these counts and the core, Lemma 14 uses a walk of length \(L=(a+3b)n\). The independent comparison walk \(W\) has increments \(+2,-1\) with respective probabilities \[
p=\frac b{a+3b},\qquad q=\frac{a+2b}{a+3b}.\] Every admissible positive \(a,b\) satisfies \(p+q=1\) and \(0<p<q<1\). Count integrality is inherited from the conditioning; the analytic argument does not posit a nonintegral triangulation. The conditioned walk \(V\) is obtained by an event with probability \(\Omega(n^{-1/2})\), according to the endpoint estimate and cycle-lemma calculation on page 18.

Equation reference: eq:u. For odd \(\ell\), the prescribed word \(w_\ell\) contains \(\ell-1\) up-steps and \(2\ell-1\) down-steps. Its length and probability are therefore \[
|w_\ell|=3\ell-2,\qquad u_\ell=p^{\ell-1}q^{2\ell-1}.\] These are the source’s pattern and hypotheses.
# Substantive findings
Problem 1 (Incorrect exponential base in equation (12)).  The second inequality of equation (12), in Lemma 14 on page 18, is false with the printed \(c=q=(a+2b)/(a+3b)\) and a fixed \(c'>0\).
## Original claim and decisive proof

Equation reference: eq:required, eq:ratio. Disjoint blocks give the valid estimate \[\mathbb P(W\hbox{ avoids }w_\ell)\leq(1-u_\ell)^{N_\ell},
\qquad N_\ell=\left\lfloor\frac{(a+3b)n}{3\ell-2}\right\rfloor.\] The source then claims that this last expression is at most \(\exp\{-c'nq^{3\ell}/\ell\}\). Taking negative logarithms would require \[
\frac{N_\ell[-\log(1-u_\ell)]}{(n/\ell)q^{3\ell}}\geq c'.\] For fixed admissible positive \(a,b\) and odd \(\ell\to\infty\) with \(\ell=o(n)\), the left-hand side tends to zero: \[
\frac{u_\ell}{q^{3\ell}}
=\frac1{pq}\left(\frac pq\right)^\ell\longrightarrow0,\quad
\frac{\ell N_\ell}{n}\longrightarrow\frac{a+3b}{3},\quad
\frac{-\log(1-u_\ell)}{u_\ell}\longrightarrow1.\] No fixed positive \(c'\) repairs this inequality with the printed base. Uniformly on the positive lower-count event, \(p/q\leq1/2\) and \(1/(pq)\) is bounded, so the same contradiction holds when \(a,b\) vary with \(n\). The contradiction is algebraic throughout the positive parameter domain, not a finite simulation or a selected unusual triangulation.

The claimed condition on \(s_\theta\) is also insufficient. Because \(pq^2<q^3\), there exist \[\frac1{\log(1/(pq^2))}<s<\frac1{3\log(1/q)}.\] For odd \(\ell=s\log n+O(1)\), a union bound over all starting positions gives \[\mathbb P(W\hbox{ contains }w_\ell)\leq Lu_\ell
=O\!\left(n^{1-s\log(1/(pq^2))}\right)\longrightarrow0.\] Avoidance thus tends to one for this independent walk, whereas the claimed upper bound tends to zero. This refutes the intermediate estimate, not the existence assertion of Lemma 14.
## Independent computation and counterevidence

Exact-rational arithmetic for the illustrative walk parameters \(a=3/2,b=1/2\), hence \(p=1/6,q=5/6\), yields \[u_5/q^{15}=36/15625=0.002304,\qquad
u_{11}/q^{33}=36/244140625=1.47456\times10^{-7}.\] The two thresholds above are approximately \(0.4637353\) and \(1.8282716\). The retained calculation is corroborative; these exact counts are not asserted to have been sampled from a triangulation.

The actual page image confirms that \(c=q\) is printed, excluding an extraction reversal. Permitting \(c'\) to vanish with \(\ell\) removes the constant needed in the proof. Interpreting \(c\) as the smaller probability \(p\) does yield a valid local repair, so a wrong choice of constant is a plausible explanation. It does not validate the displayed inequality.
## Uniform repair

Equation reference: eq:repair. On the high-probability count event, take \(a\geq a_0>0\), \(b\geq b_0>0\). Then \[p\geq p_0:=b_0/6>0,\qquad q\geq p\geq p_0.\] Decrease \(p_0\) below \(1\) if necessary. For \(\ell=o(n)\), uniformly for sufficiently large \(n\), \[N_\ell\geq\kappa n/\ell,\quad \kappa=(a_0+3b_0)/6,\qquad
u_\ell\geq p_0^{3\ell-2}\geq p_0^{3\ell}.\] Consequently \[
\mathbb P(W\hbox{ avoids }w_\ell)
\leq\exp\!\left\{-\kappa(n/\ell)p_0^{3\ell}\right\}.\] Choose \(0<s<1/[3\log(1/p_0)]\) and odd \(\ell=s\log n+O(1)\). The exponent magnitude is at least a positive multiple of \(n^\varepsilon/\log n\) for some \(\varepsilon>0\). Dividing this failure probability by the conditioning probability \(\Omega(n^{-1/2})\) still gives zero in the limit. This supplies the missing estimate for a logarithmic tentacle, assuming the paper’s preceding encoding and conditioning construction. It preserves existence of a positive constant, without establishing the larger printed range or independently proving every combinatorial input.
## Dependency, severity, and surviving results

Lemma 14 supplies the upper bound \(h(T_{2n,g_n})=O(1/\log n)\) in Theorem 4 (page 18) and \(H(\vec e^{\,*})\geq(s_\theta/2)\log n\) in Proposition 17 (page 20). The assessment is Major: invalid core-related derivation. A short repair preserves the qualitative conclusions; this bounds the impact without making the original derivation valid. No counterexample to the final graph theorems is established. The isoperimetric theorem and logarithmic diameter bounds precede this calculation and do not depend on it.
Problem 2 (The distance decomposition needs distinct tentacles).  Equation (16), introduced for arbitrary two oriented edges on page 20, cannot hold for two edges within the same deep tentacle.
## Assumptions and complete local counterexample

The displayed distance is the sum of two heights, the core distance between their bases, and an error in \([-2,2]\). Take an oriented edge \(\vec e\) with \(H(\vec e)>1\) inside a sufficiently long ladder, and put \(\vec e_1=\vec e_2=\vec e\). Both the original distance and core distance are zero. The equation requires error \(-2H(\vec e)<-2\), contrary to its bound. Recursive ladder insertion is allowed and preserves genus. More explicitly, fix a sufficiently deep finite ladder with \(2k\) faces and choose a genus-\(g_n\) core with \(2(n-k)\) faces. The necessary condition \(n-k\geq2g_n-1\) holds eventually because \(g_n/n\to\theta<1/2\); insertion produces the required \(2n\)-face triangulation. If the phrase two edges is interpreted as distinct, use two different outgoing oriented edges at the same sufficiently deep interior ladder vertex. Their starting-point distance is zero, their heights are large, and the core distance is nonnegative, again contradicting the bound.
## Alternative reading, correction, and bounded impact

For different tentacles, paths must leave each through its boundary endpoints, which is the intended setting of the core-plus-heights estimate. Page 21 explicitly discards the event that two selected edges belong to the same tentacle. This is counterevidence against treating the overstatement as a failure of Proposition 17. Restrict equation (16) to distinct tentacles and impose that restriction before its uses. The assessment is Minor: local domain overstatement. No additional central damage is demonstrated; the correction narrows the domain, without refuting the final proposition.
# Version checks and conclusion

A bounded official/author-source search did not identify a separate formal erratum. The current arXiv abstract fetch failed, so the complete current revision history was not independently recovered. An opened author-hosted PDF is also dated 8 November 2023 and has 23 pages. These observations do not prove absence of corrections. Journal-final proof text was not compared; the findings apply to the acquired version.

Problem 1 | Major | Corrected uniform exponential bound proved; final theorem not refuted.
Problem 2 | Minor | Restrict to distinct tentacles; later exceptional-event treatment supports intended use.
Decision | Pending | Initial AI review; independent acceptance not performed.

No counterexample to the final graph theorems is established. The isoperimetric theorem and logarithmic diameter bounds precede this calculation and do not depend on it.

problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (The distance decomposition needs distinct tentacles).
claim: The model is a uniform rooted triangulation \(T_{2n,g_n}\) of an oriented surface, with \(2n\) faces, loops and multiple edges allowed, and \(g_n/n\to\theta\in(0,1/2)\) [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~2--4]{paper}]. Tentacles arise by recursive insertions into a digon; the core is obtained by removing maximal tentacles [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~16--17]{paper}]. Write \(T_n=an\) and \(M_n=2bn\) for their number and total number of internal faces. Lemma 13 supplies positive lower bounds for \(a,b\) with high probability. The deterministic bounds \(a\leq3\), \(b\leq1\) suffice below, since the original map has \(3n\) edges and \(2n\) faces.

Equation reference: eq:pq. Conditionally on these counts and the core, Lemma 14 uses a walk of length \(L=(a+3b)n\). The independent comparison walk \(W\) has increments \(+2,-1\) with respective probabilities \[
p=\frac b{a+3b},\qquad q=\frac{a+2b}{a+3b}.\] Every admissible positive \(a,b\) satisfies \(p+q=1\) and \(0<p<q<1\). Count integrality is inherited from the conditioning; the analytic argument does not posit a nonintegral triangulation. The conditioned walk \(V\) is obtained by an event with probability \(\Omega(n^{-1/2})\), according to the endpoint estimate and cycle-lemma calculation on page 18.

Equation reference: eq:u. For odd \(\ell\), the prescribed word \(w_\ell\) contains \(\ell-1\) up-steps and \(2\ell-1\) down-steps. Its length and probability are therefore \[
|w_\ell|=3\ell-2,\qquad u_\ell=p^{\ell-1}q^{2\ell-1}.\] These are the source’s pattern and hypotheses.
For any two oriented edges, distance=H(e1)+H(e2)+core distance+epsilon with epsilon in [-2,2]

Ladders inserted using the definition on p16. Two oriented edges inside the same deep tentacle are allowed by the printed unrestricted quantifier. For e1=e2, H(e)>1; alternatively two distinct outgoing edges at a deep common starting vertex.
analysis: Equation (16), introduced for arbitrary two oriented edges on page 20, cannot hold for two edges within the same deep tentacle.

The displayed distance is the sum of two heights, the core distance between their bases, and an error in \([-2,2]\). Take an oriented edge \(\vec e\) with \(H(\vec e)>1\) inside a sufficiently long ladder, and put \(\vec e_1=\vec e_2=\vec e\). Both the original distance and core distance are zero. The equation requires error \(-2H(\vec e)<-2\), contrary to its bound. Recursive ladder insertion is allowed and preserves genus. More explicitly, fix a sufficiently deep finite ladder with \(2k\) faces and choose a genus-\(g_n\) core with \(2(n-k)\) faces. The necessary condition \(n-k\geq2g_n-1\) holds eventually because \(g_n/n\to\theta<1/2\); insertion produces the required \(2n\)-face triangulation. If the phrase two edges is interpreted as distinct, use two different outgoing oriented edges at the same sufficiently deep interior ladder vertex. Their starting-point distance is zero, their heights are large, and the core distance is nonnegative, again contradicting the bound.
result: For different tentacles, paths must leave each through its boundary endpoints, which is the intended setting of the core-plus-heights estimate. Page 21 explicitly discards the event that two selected edges belong to the same tentacle. This is counterevidence against treating the overstatement as a failure of Proposition 17. Restrict equation (16) to distinct tentacles and impose that restriction before its uses. The assessment is Minor: local domain overstatement. No additional central damage is demonstrated; the correction narrows the domain, without refuting the final proposition.
Impact: Local domain overstatement

Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of Large Gaps of CUE and GUE
# Identity and scope

This report concerns Renjie Feng and Dongyi Wei, Large gaps of CUE and GUE, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1747, associated with The Annals of Probability 53 (2025), 1668–1702. The exact inspected source is the 34-page arXiv:1807.02149v3 PDF [paper], submitted 3 November 2024; the title-page body date is 5 November 2024. Page locators below are one-based PDF pages, equal to printed pages. Equivalence with the journal-final text is not asserted.

The complete extracted text, including references, was read by the primary scientific executor. The detailed checks below concern Theorems 1–2, Lemma 1, the normalization in Lemmas 2 and 8, the integral in Lemma 10, and the determinant comparison and separation conditions in Lemmas 6, 12–14. The imported uniform Toeplitz and Hermite asymptotics were not independently reconstructed from their original proofs.
# Definitions, quantifiers, and dependencies

For CUE, the model is Haar measure on \(U(n)\); consecutive eigenangle gaps include the wraparound gap. For GUE, the density has Gaussian factor \(\exp(-n\sum_i\lambda_i^2/2)\), and both endpoints of a counted gap must lie in a fixed nondegenerate interval \(I=[a,b]\), with \(-2<a<b<2\) [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~1--3]{paper}]. Write \[S=\min_{y\in I}\sqrt{4-y^2}>0,\qquad L=\log n,\quad h=\log(2L).\] The order \(k\) and the thresholds \(x_j\) are fixed as \(n\to\infty\). The conclusions do not provide uniformity for growing \(k\), shrinking intervals, or intervals approaching the spectral edge. The separate general-\(\beta\) statement on page 3 is a conjecture.

Equation reference: eq:density. The proof first obtains mixed excess-gap moments, then uses the finite-difference squeeze of Lemma 1 to recover factorial moments of tail counts [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~3--5]{paper}]. The finite differences are nonnegative, so their products preserve the required inequalities. For \(f(x)=e^{c-x}\), the limiting tail-count mean is \(-f'(x)=e^{c-x}\). Differentiating the Poisson tail yields \[
g_k(x)=\frac{e^{k(c-x)}}{(k-1)!}\exp(-e^{c-x}).\] The substitution \(t=e^{c-x}\) gives total integral one, since the resulting integral is \(\Gamma(k)/(k-1)!\). This verifies both the sign and normalization of the stated order-statistic law; \(k=1\) gives the ordinary Gumbel density.

The determinant argument requires finite-rank self-adjoint operators, \(I-B>0\), and \(I-A\geq0\). The compressed projection kernels and positive gap determinants supply these conditions. Disjoint interval supports make \(B\) block diagonal. The CUE splitting calculation uses fixed distinct locations; the GUE lower bound instead uses locations separated by at least \(\varepsilon_0/\log n\), including their separation from both endpoints [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~12--15,27,30--32]{paper}]. Since \(\sqrt{\log n}/n=o(1/\log n)\), the short empty intervals are disjoint and contained in \(I\). In the symmetric case, coincident absolute rescaled coordinates are excluded in Lemma 13; they form a Lebesgue-null set and do not invalidate Fatou’s lemma.
# Independent mathematical checks
## The two logarithmic corrections
## Endpoint localization and the symmetry factor

Suppose \(a+b<0\), so the least density occurs at \(a<0\). With \(w(y)=\sqrt{4-y^2}/S\), one has \[w(a)=1,\qquad w'(a)=\frac{|a|}{S^2}.\] Writing \(y=a+t/L\), the stretched-gap limit contributes \(\exp(-2|a|t/S^2)\). Consequently the endpoint factor is \[2\int_0^\infty \exp(-2|a|t/S^2)\,dt=\frac{S^2}{|a|}.\] The change of variables and exponential domination in Lemma 10 make this local calculation rigorous: the midpoint cutoff stays strictly negative, so its Jacobian is bounded; the remainder away from the minimizing endpoint is exponentially suppressed in \(L\) [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~19--20]{paper}].

For \(a+b>0\), reflection gives the corresponding factor \(S^2/|b|\). For \(a=-b\), the two endpoints contribute equally, giving \(2S^2/|a|\) [paper, p. 21]. For example, \(I=[-1,0]\) gives \(M(I)=3\), while \(I=[-1,1]\) gives \(M(I)=6\). Since the excess-gap conversion supplies \(S/4\), the intensity constants are \(e^{c_0}3\sqrt3/4\) and \(e^{c_0}3\sqrt3/2\), respectively. This checks the factor of two and the three branches of \(M_0(I)=\log(M(I)S/4)\).
## Determinant comparison and the cutoff scale

For the self-adjoint conjugate \(C=(I-B)^{-1/2}(A-B)(I-B)^{-1/2}\), positivity of \(I-A\) gives \(\lambda_j(C)\leq1\). The scalar inequality \[1\geq e^\lambda(1-\lambda)\geq(1-\lambda^2)_+,\qquad \lambda\leq1,\] and multiplication of nonnegative factors give the lower error \(1-\sum_j\lambda_j(C)^2\). The Hilbert–Schmidt ideal inequality then gives the error in Lemma 6. This derivation does not require \(A\) and \(B\) to commute [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~12--13]{paper}].

The truncation used in Lemma 12 sets \(D_n(\alpha_n)=(n\log n)^{-1}\) and applies the comparison at \(\delta_n'=\alpha_n/\pi\) [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~24--25]{paper}]. Equation (6), evaluated at fixed multiples of \(\sqrt{L}/n\) and combined with monotonicity, gives \[\delta_n'\sim \frac{\sqrt8}{\pi}\frac{\sqrt L}{n}.\] The cutoff therefore lies on the same admissible scale. A sufficiently small fixed lower constant in the comparison estimate includes it, even when the initially chosen \(c_*\) is larger. This resolves the apparent parameter-range concern in the cutoff step. The GUE lower-bound error estimates also decay as required: powers of \(L\) times \(e^{-\sqrt L/2}\) or \(e^{-\sqrt L}\) dominate the needed \(L^{-2}\) bounds, and the extra-empty-interval error is \(O(n^{-1}\sqrt L)\) for fixed \(k\) [Retained latex: \cite[pp.~30--33]{paper}].
# Assessment and limits

No substantive Problem is reported. The checked normalization, endpoint constant, finite-difference criterion, determinant positivity, and separation scales are internally consistent. This is a bounded initial review, not a certification of every imported estimate or an independent acceptance decision.

The primary executor opened the current official arXiv metadata on 29 October 2026; it lists v3, dated 3 November 2024. A bounded official-source correction search found no separate formal erratum. This does not establish absence of corrections or journal-version equivalence. No author code was executed. Optional code or supplementary material was not identified in the bounded acquisition, and that absence is not a mathematical defect.
