Abstract: The acquired version contains an incompatible composition calculus and an invalid construction in the entropy approximation argument. Explicit examples in the bounded, strictly positive class demonstrate these failures. Four additional local issues concern a missing inverse-clock symbol, the admissible compensator domain, the common-noise premise of pathwise uniqueness, and a filtration enlargement. The evidence distinguishes false intermediate assertions from final conclusions: no counterexample to the principal entropy criterion, variational identity, or corrected fixed-driver uniqueness theorem is established.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of Invertibility of Functionals of the Poisson Process and Applications
# Identity, scope, and notation

This report concerns Laure Coutin and Laurent Decreusefond, Invertibility of functionals of the Poisson process and applications, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1748. The exact source is the 41-page arXiv:2307.02887v2 PDF, submitted 28 November 2024 [paper]. All page locators refer to this PDF and agree with its printed page numbers. Equivalence with the 2025 journal-final text is not asserted.

The complete source text, definitions, proofs, and references were read. The review follows the time-change calculus, the invertibility criterion, the entropy approximation, and the weak/strong generalized Hawkes formulation. The paper’s external change-of-measure and martingale representation results were treated as imported dependencies, not independently re-proved from their cited monographs.

Let \(N\) be the canonical unit Poisson process under \(\pi\), with natural filtration \(\mathcal N\). Write \[y(t)=\int_0^t\dot y(s)\,ds,\qquad y^*=y^{-1},\qquad
Y(t)=N(y^*(t)),\qquad m(x)=(1+x)\log(1+x)-x.\] The strong class \(P_\infty^{++}\) requires a predictable intensity bounded above and away from zero and equal to one after a fixed finite time [paper, p. 8]. The deterministic test intensities below satisfy this condition wherever the relevant theorem assumes it. Their integrated clocks are finite, strictly increasing homeomorphisms; their inverse times are deterministic stopping times. Their finite-horizon likelihoods are strictly positive, uniformly integrable, and have expectation one, and all displayed entropy costs are finite. Thus the decisive examples do not depend on explosion, degeneracy, or a change-of-measure integrability failure.
# Composition calculus

Equation reference: eq:double. Problem 1 (Major: incompatible process composition).  Definition 2.8 on page 11 defines \[
\mathbf Y(U)(N,t)=U(Y,y^*(N,t)).\] Under this definition, the stochastic-integral identity (24) in Theorem 2.7, page 12, is false. Its proof on page 13 uses an inconsistent stopped-process composition. The same calculus is invoked in the inverse-likelihood argument of Theorem 3.7, page 21, and the discussion and proof of Theorem 3.9, pages 23–27.

The failure also survives a compactly supported integrand and a terminal-time reading. For \(r(s)=\mathbf1_{(0,1]}(s)\) and \(t=2\), the left side is \(Y(1)=N(1/2)\), while the right side is \(Y(2)=N(1)\). The discrepancy has mean \(1/2\) and is nonzero with probability \(1-e^{-1/2}\). ◻

Alternative readings and counterevidence. Using ordinary configuration pullback \(U(Y,t)\) instead of [eq:double] (#eq:double) does not validate both printed rules: in the Lebesgue-integral identity (23), \(r=1\) gives \(t\) on the left and \(y^*(t)\) on the right. Pure time substitution \(U(N,y^*(t))\) has its own valid change-of-variable rule, with the integrand evaluated at \((N,y^*(s))\); it is distinct from configuration pullback. Theorem 2.6 supplies the usual time-change rule. These three operations need separate notation and proofs.

The example does not disprove the main entropy criterion. Here \(Y\) is invertible, with inverse \(Z(N,t)=N(y(t))\), and the correct entropy is \[H(Y_\#\pi\mid\pi)=\int_0^\infty m(\dot y^*(s)-1)\,ds
=1-\log2.\] For this deterministic clock, the inverse-likelihood identity can be checked directly by ordinary configuration pullback. Consequently the established defect is an invalid core calculus and a resulting proof dependency requiring repair, not a false final entropy theorem. Repair must distinguish configuration pullback, time substitution, and their combination, then recheck the likelihood and entropy deductions for random predictable clocks.
# Entropy approximation

Problem 2 (Major: the approximants in Theorem 4.3 are not valid).  The construction on pages 30–31 does not establish the approximation claimed in Theorem 4.3. There are three independently checkable failures in the displayed intensity and step approximation. Theorem 4.2 explicitly depends on this approximation to obtain its variational representation [paper, p. 29].

The theorem assumes a density \(L=d\nu/d\pi\) with \(L\log L\in L^1(\pi)\) and \(\log L\in L^r(\pi)\) for some \(r>1\). It seeks \(\dot y_n\in P_{\infty,\mathrm{pc}}^{++}\) and convergence involving the density \(d(Y_n)_\#\pi/d\pi\).

Equation reference: eq:factor. Three decisive tests. First, page 31 prints \[
\dot y(N,s)=\frac{\mathbb E_\pi[D_sL\mid\mathcal N_s]}{\mathbb E_\pi[L\mid\mathcal N_s]},
\qquad D_sF(N)=F(N+\epsilon_s)-F(N).\] The admissible bounded density \(L=1\) has \(D_sL=0\), so [eq:factor] (#eq:factor) gives zero, whereas its likelihood intensity must be one. If this zero factor is used up to time \(T>0\), the likelihood is \(e^T\mathbf1_{\{N(T)=0\}}\), not the identity density. The usual likelihood factor includes the additive one; with predictable versions it is \[1+\frac{\mathbb E[D_sL\mid\mathcal N_{s-}]}{\mathbb E[L\mid\mathcal N_{s-}]}.\] For \(0<m\leq L\leq M\), its inserted-density form gives bounds \(m/M\) and \(M/m\). This explains both the missing constant and the needed strict positivity.

Second, the displayed step construction sets \(\dot y_n=0\) on \([0,T/n)\), then claims \(\dot y_n\in P_{\infty,\mathrm{pc}}^{++}\). Each approximant violates the lower bound on an interval of positive length. Its integrated clock is flat there and is not the required homeomorphism. This is not a value-at-one-point convention.

Equation reference: eq:wronggrid. Third, on \([iT/n,(i+1)T/n)\), the printed average is \[
n\int_{(i-1)/n}^{i/n}\dot y(N,s)\,ds,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n-1.\] The integration interval and factor do not match the time mesh unless \(T=1\). To respect also the bounded-density reduction on page 30, take \(T=2\), \(a=1/2\), and set \[g(N,s)=1+\mathbf1_{(0,a]}(s)\mathbf1_{\{N(s-)=0\}},
\qquad \tau=T_1\wedge a.\] This intensity is predictable, lies between one and two, and equals one after \(a\). Its integrated clock is \(y(t)=t+\min(t,\tau)\). Its terminal likelihood satisfies \[L=\Lambda_g=(1+\mathbf1_{\{T_1\leq a\}})e^{-\tau},
\qquad e^{-a}\leq L\leq2,\] and \[\mathbb E_\pi L=e^{-2a}+\int_0^a2e^{-2u}\,du=1.\] Consequently \(L\log L\) and \(\log L\) have all the required integrability, including the proof’s lower and upper density bounds. The clock is a strictly increasing unbounded homeomorphism, its inverse times are stopping times, and \(g\in P_\infty^{++}\).

Equation reference: eq:l2. On \(A=\{N(a)=0\}\), which has probability \(e^{-a}\), the intensity is exactly two on \((0,1/2]\) and one afterwards. Let \(g_n\) be the printed construction, including its zero first interval. For \(n\geq4\) divisible by four, direct pathwise integration on \(A\) gives \[
\int_0^2|g_n(s)-g(s)|^2\,ds=\frac12+\frac{10}{n}.\] The zero first interval contributes \(8/n\), while the erroneously prolonged value two on \((1/2,1+2/n)\) contributes \(1/2+2/n\). Therefore \[\mathbb E_\pi\int_0^2|g_n(s)-g(s)|^2\,ds
\geq e^{-1/2}\left(\frac12+\frac{10}{n}\right)
\not\longrightarrow0.\] Even replacing the first interval by the correct positive value leaves the limiting grid error \(1/2\) on \(A\). The retained exact rational grid calculations apply to this pathwise template; the stopped intensity ensures that the counterexample also satisfies the bounded-density reduction. ◻

Repair and impact boundaries. A positive initial value and the average \((n/T)\int_{(i-1)T/n}^{iT/n}\dot y(s)\,ds\) correct the immediate mesh defects. They do not by themselves complete the theorem. The proof works with likelihoods \(\Lambda_{y_n}\), whereas the conclusion is stated for densities of \((Y_n)_\#\pi\). Page 23 explicitly warns that these are different objects. For the deterministic clock of Problem Problem 1 (#p:composition), \(\pi_y\) has rate two on \((0,1]\), while \(Y_\#\pi\) has rate \(1/2\) on \((0,2]\). A justified inverse-clock passage and the required entropy convergence must therefore be supplied.

This is a demonstrated failure of the printed construction. It is not a counterexample to the existence statement of Theorem 4.3 or to the final variational identity: for \(L=1\), the identity clock already gives the desired approximation. The severity concerns an essential proof input, not an asserted impossibility of repair.
# Additional local problems

Problem 3 (Minor: the wrong clock in Lemma 3.8).  Equation (41), page 22, bounds \(\mathbb E[-\log\Lambda^*_{y^*}]\) by \(\mathbb E\int_0^\infty m(\dot y(s)-1)\,ds\). Under the stated hypotheses this bound is false; the inverse-clock derivative is needed.

The proof on page 23 and the main entropy criterion already use the inverse-clock cost; equation (30), page 16, gives the correct change of variables. These are substantial counterevidence against a defect in the final criterion arising from this symbol alone. Replacing \(\dot y\) by \(\dot y^*\) repairs the displayed bound in the tested setting. The severity is local and minor, separately from Problem Problem 1 (#p:composition).

Problem 4 (Minor: overbroad compensator existence).  Theorem 2.1(2), page 6, asserts existence of a probability law on the simple configuration space for every predictable, nondecreasing, right-continuous process \(y\), null at zero, with \(N-y\) a local martingale localized by the jump times. That domain is too broad.

Set \(y(t)=t+2\mathbf1_{[1,\infty)}(t)\). It is deterministic and predictable, right-continuous, nondecreasing, finite at finite times, null at zero, and unbounded. On the simple configuration space of Definition 2.1, \(\Delta N(1)\in\{0,1\}\). A compensator must satisfy, at this predictable time, \[\Delta y(1)=\mathbb E[\Delta N(1)\mid\mathcal N_{1-}]\leq1,\] in contradiction with \(\Delta y(1)=2\). Localization gives the same necessary jump identity, so allowing a local martingale does not remove the contradiction.

An admissible compensator domain and appropriate existence/nonexplosion conditions must be specified. A jump bound alone should not be presented as a full general existence theorem. The later principal arguments mostly use absolutely continuous clocks and explicitly assume an existing law with stronger regularity. This example therefore refutes the preliminary universal statement, not those later claims under their full hypotheses; that limits its severity to a local domain error.

Problem 5 (Minor: pathwise uniqueness lacks a common-noise premise).  Definition 5.5, page 33, requires any two solutions \((Z,N)\) and \((Z',N')\) on one filtered probability space to satisfy both \(Z=Z'\) and \(N=N'\), without assuming the equality of the drivers.

For \(\dot y=1\), put two independent unit Poisson processes \(N_1,N_2\) on their product space with the joint right-continuous filtration. The pairs \((N_1,N_1)\) and \((N_2,N_2)\) both satisfy every item of Definition 5.2: they are locally finite simple point processes, \(y(Z,t)=t\) is a stopping time, each compensated driver is a local martingale, and the defining equation holds. Nevertheless \[\mathbb P\{N_1(1)=0,\ N_2(1)=1\}=e^{-2}>0,\] so the conclusion of the definition fails even for the identity clock.

The repair is to assume \(N=N'\) as the common driver and conclude indistinguishability of \(Z,Z'\). The proof of Theorem 5.5 on page 37 already compares solutions driven by one \(N\), and the coupling in Theorem 5.3 uses a common third coordinate. Those passages support the intended interpretation. The result is a defective definition and literal formulation, not a disproof of fixed-driver uniqueness or of a corrected Yamada–Watanabe statement.

Problem 6 (Minor: unjustified enlargement of a martingale filtration).  The proof of Lemma 5.2, page 35, asserts that a square-integrable martingale in the driver’s natural filtration is consequently a martingale in the same-time product filtration \(\mathcal N^{\otimes(2)}\). This implication is false for the allowed solution pairs.

Use the bounded deterministic clock of Problem Problem 1 (#p:composition) and the valid solution \(Z(t)=N(y(t))\), on the original natural filtration of \(N\). Let \(s=1/4\), \(t=1/2\), and \(F=\mathbf1_{\{N(t)=0\}}\). The bounded natural-filtration martingale \[M_r=\mathbb E[F\mid\mathcal N_r]-\mathbb E[F]\] has the square-integrable Poisson representation used in the proof. In the product filtration \(\mathcal G_s=\sigma(Z(u),N(u):u\leq s)\), the value \(Z(s)=N(1/2)=N(t)\) is already known. Hence \(M_t=F-e^{-t}\) is \(\mathcal G_s\)-measurable. On \(\{N(t)=0\}\), an event of probability \(e^{-1/2}\), \[\mathbb E[M_t\mid\mathcal G_s]-M_s=1-e^{-1/4}>0.\] Thus \(M\) is not a martingale in the stated enlarged filtration. All solution assumptions hold because the clock times are deterministic stopping times in the original filtration; Definition 5.2 does not require \(Z(t)\) to be measurable at physical time \(t\) there.

The preceding part of the proof claims that the relevant event \(B\) is measurable in the driver’s \(\mathcal N_t\). Given that assertion, the cancellation in the second step can use the original martingale property directly. The time-changed filtrations in the subsequent coupling also differ from this same-time product filtration. The false enlargement assertion is therefore removable from that cancellation, and no additional failure of the final theorem is inferred from it. Repair should delete it or state and establish a suitable compatibility condition.
# Overall assessment and reviewed-version limits

Problems Problem 1 (#p:composition) and Problem 2 (#p:approx) establish invalid steps in central arguments. Problems Problem 3 (#p:cost)–Problem 6 (#p:filtration) are more limited formulation or local proof errors, with explicit counterevidence bounding their impact. The review does not equate any of these with whole-paper failure. The last section of the paper expressly distinguishes its approach from the preceding entropy construction; no blanket transfer of the entropy proof defects to every Hawkes conclusion is warranted.

The primary executor checked the official arXiv metadata on 29 October 2026; it identifies v2 dated 28 November 2024. A bounded official-source search did not identify a separate formal erratum. Using ordinary configuration pullback \(U(Y,t)\) instead of [eq:double] (#eq:double) does not validate both printed rules: in the Lebesgue-integral identity (23), \(r=1\) gives \(t\) on the left and \(y^*(t)\) on the right. Pure time substitution \(U(N,y^*(t))\) has its own valid change-of-variable rule, with the integrand evaluated at \((N,y^*(s))\); it is distinct from configuration pullback. Theorem 2.6 supplies the usual time-change rule. These three operations need separate notation and proofs.

The example does not disprove the main entropy criterion. Here \(Y\) is invertible, with inverse \(Z(N,t)=N(y(t))\), and the correct entropy is \[H(Y_\#\pi\mid\pi)=\int_0^\infty m(\dot y^*(s)-1)\,ds
=1-\log2.\] For this deterministic clock, the inverse-likelihood identity can be checked directly by ordinary configuration pullback. Consequently the established defect is an invalid core calculus and a resulting proof dependency requiring repair, not a false final entropy theorem. Repair must distinguish configuration pullback, time substitution, and their combination, then recheck the likelihood and entropy deductions for random predictable clocks.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Incompatible process composition invalidates Theorem 2.7 as printed

problems.title: Theorem 4.3 approximation construction fails its own conditions
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (Major: the approximants in Theorem 4.3 are not valid).
claim: Recorded check: Theorem 4.3 approximation construction fails its own conditions
analysis: The construction on pages 30–31 does not establish the approximation claimed in Theorem 4.3. There are three independently checkable failures in the displayed intensity and step approximation. Theorem 4.2 explicitly depends on this approximation to obtain its variational representation [paper, p. 29].

The theorem assumes a density \(L=d\nu/d\pi\) with \(L\log L\in L^1(\pi)\) and \(\log L\in L^r(\pi)\) for some \(r>1\). It seeks \(\dot y_n\in P_{\infty,\mathrm{pc}}^{++}\) and convergence involving the density \(d(Y_n)_\#\pi/d\pi\).

Equation reference: eq:factor. Three decisive tests. First, page 31 prints \[
\dot y(N,s)=\frac{\mathbb E_\pi[D_sL\mid\mathcal N_s]}{\mathbb E_\pi[L\mid\mathcal N_s]},
\qquad D_sF(N)=F(N+\epsilon_s)-F(N).\] The admissible bounded density \(L=1\) has \(D_sL=0\), so [eq:factor] (#eq:factor) gives zero, whereas its likelihood intensity must be one. If this zero factor is used up to time \(T>0\), the likelihood is \(e^T\mathbf1_{\{N(T)=0\}}\), not the identity density. The usual likelihood factor includes the additive one; with predictable versions it is \[1+\frac{\mathbb E[D_sL\mid\mathcal N_{s-}]}{\mathbb E[L\mid\mathcal N_{s-}]}.\] For \(0<m\leq L\leq M\), its inserted-density form gives bounds \(m/M\) and \(M/m\). This explains both the missing constant and the needed strict positivity.

Second, the displayed step construction sets \(\dot y_n=0\) on \([0,T/n)\), then claims \(\dot y_n\in P_{\infty,\mathrm{pc}}^{++}\). Each approximant violates the lower bound on an interval of positive length. Its integrated clock is flat there and is not the required homeomorphism. This is not a value-at-one-point convention.

Equation reference: eq:wronggrid. Third, on \([iT/n,(i+1)T/n)\), the printed average is \[
n\int_{(i-1)/n}^{i/n}\dot y(N,s)\,ds,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n-1.\] The integration interval and factor do not match the time mesh unless \(T=1\). To respect also the bounded-density reduction on page 30, take \(T=2\), \(a=1/2\), and set \[g(N,s)=1+\mathbf1_{(0,a]}(s)\mathbf1_{\{N(s-)=0\}},
\qquad \tau=T_1\wedge a.\] This intensity is predictable, lies between one and two, and equals one after \(a\). Its integrated clock is \(y(t)=t+\min(t,\tau)\). Its terminal likelihood satisfies \[L=\Lambda_g=(1+\mathbf1_{\{T_1\leq a\}})e^{-\tau},
\qquad e^{-a}\leq L\leq2,\] and \[\mathbb E_\pi L=e^{-2a}+\int_0^a2e^{-2u}\,du=1.\] Consequently \(L\log L\) and \(\log L\) have all the required integrability, including the proof’s lower and upper density bounds. The clock is a strictly increasing unbounded homeomorphism, its inverse times are stopping times, and \(g\in P_\infty^{++}\).

Equation reference: eq:l2. On \(A=\{N(a)=0\}\), which has probability \(e^{-a}\), the intensity is exactly two on \((0,1/2]\) and one afterwards. Let \(g_n\) be the printed construction, including its zero first interval. For \(n\geq4\) divisible by four, direct pathwise integration on \(A\) gives \[
\int_0^2|g_n(s)-g(s)|^2\,ds=\frac12+\frac{10}{n}.\] The zero first interval contributes \(8/n\), while the erroneously prolonged value two on \((1/2,1+2/n)\) contributes \(1/2+2/n\). Therefore \[\mathbb E_\pi\int_0^2|g_n(s)-g(s)|^2\,ds
\geq e^{-1/2}\left(\frac12+\frac{10}{n}\right)
\not\longrightarrow0.\] Even replacing the first interval by the correct positive value leaves the limiting grid error \(1/2\) on \(A\). The retained exact rational grid calculations apply to this pathwise template; the stopped intensity ensures that the counterexample also satisfies the bounded-density reduction. ◻

Repair and impact boundaries. A positive initial value and the average \((n/T)\int_{(i-1)T/n}^{iT/n}\dot y(s)\,ds\) correct the immediate mesh defects. They do not by themselves complete the theorem. The proof works with likelihoods \(\Lambda_{y_n}\), whereas the conclusion is stated for densities of \((Y_n)_\#\pi\). Page 23 explicitly warns that these are different objects. For the deterministic clock of Problem Problem 1 (#p:composition), \(\pi_y\) has rate two on \((0,1]\), while \(Y_\#\pi\) has rate \(1/2\) on \((0,2]\). A justified inverse-clock passage and the required entropy convergence must therefore be supplied.

This is a demonstrated failure of the printed construction. It is not a counterexample to the existence statement of Theorem 4.3 or to the final variational identity: for \(L=1\), the identity clock already gives the desired approximation. The severity concerns an essential proof input, not an asserted impossibility of repair.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Theorem 4.3 approximation construction fails its own conditions

problems.title: Universal compensator existence has an inadmissibly broad domain
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: Problem 4 (Minor: overbroad compensator existence).
claim: Recorded check: Universal compensator existence has an inadmissibly broad domain
analysis: Theorem 2.1(2), page 6, asserts existence of a probability law on the simple configuration space for every predictable, nondecreasing, right-continuous process \(y\), null at zero, with \(N-y\) a local martingale localized by the jump times. That domain is too broad.

Set \(y(t)=t+2\mathbf1_{[1,\infty)}(t)\). It is deterministic and predictable, right-continuous, nondecreasing, finite at finite times, null at zero, and unbounded. On the simple configuration space of Definition 2.1, \(\Delta N(1)\in\{0,1\}\). A compensator must satisfy, at this predictable time, \[\Delta y(1)=\mathbb E[\Delta N(1)\mid\mathcal N_{1-}]\leq1,\] in contradiction with \(\Delta y(1)=2\). Localization gives the same necessary jump identity, so allowing a local martingale does not remove the contradiction.

An admissible compensator domain and appropriate existence/nonexplosion conditions must be specified. A jump bound alone should not be presented as a full general existence theorem. The later principal arguments mostly use absolutely continuous clocks and explicitly assume an existing law with stronger regularity. This example therefore refutes the preliminary universal statement, not those later claims under their full hypotheses; that limits its severity to a local domain error.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Universal compensator existence has an inadmissibly broad domain

problems.title: Pathwise uniqueness needs a common driver as a premise
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 5: Problem 5 (Minor: pathwise uniqueness lacks a common-noise premise).
claim: Recorded check: Pathwise uniqueness needs a common driver as a premise
analysis: Definition 5.5, page 33, requires any two solutions \((Z,N)\) and \((Z',N')\) on one filtered probability space to satisfy both \(Z=Z'\) and \(N=N'\), without assuming the equality of the drivers.

For \(\dot y=1\), put two independent unit Poisson processes \(N_1,N_2\) on their product space with the joint right-continuous filtration. The pairs \((N_1,N_1)\) and \((N_2,N_2)\) both satisfy every item of Definition 5.2: they are locally finite simple point processes, \(y(Z,t)=t\) is a stopping time, each compensated driver is a local martingale, and the defining equation holds. Nevertheless \[\mathbb P\{N_1(1)=0,\ N_2(1)=1\}=e^{-2}>0,\] so the conclusion of the definition fails even for the identity clock.

The repair is to assume \(N=N'\) as the common driver and conclude indistinguishability of \(Z,Z'\). The proof of Theorem 5.5 on page 37 already compares solutions driven by one \(N\), and the coupling in Theorem 5.3 uses a common third coordinate. Those passages support the intended interpretation. The result is a defective definition and literal formulation, not a disproof of fixed-driver uniqueness or of a corrected Yamada–Watanabe statement.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Pathwise uniqueness needs a common driver as a premise

problems.title: Natural-filtration martingales need not survive the same-time product enlargement
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: Problem 6 (Minor: unjustified enlargement of a martingale filtration).
claim: Recorded check: Natural-filtration martingales need not survive the same-time product enlargement
analysis: The proof of Lemma 5.2, page 35, asserts that a square-integrable martingale in the driver’s natural filtration is consequently a martingale in the same-time product filtration \(\mathcal N^{\otimes(2)}\). This implication is false for the allowed solution pairs.

Use the bounded deterministic clock of Problem Problem 1 (#p:composition) and the valid solution \(Z(t)=N(y(t))\), on the original natural filtration of \(N\). Let \(s=1/4\), \(t=1/2\), and \(F=\mathbf1_{\{N(t)=0\}}\). The bounded natural-filtration martingale \[M_r=\mathbb E[F\mid\mathcal N_r]-\mathbb E[F]\] has the square-integrable Poisson representation used in the proof. In the product filtration \(\mathcal G_s=\sigma(Z(u),N(u):u\leq s)\), the value \(Z(s)=N(1/2)=N(t)\) is already known. Hence \(M_t=F-e^{-t}\) is \(\mathcal G_s\)-measurable. On \(\{N(t)=0\}\), an event of probability \(e^{-1/2}\), \[\mathbb E[M_t\mid\mathcal G_s]-M_s=1-e^{-1/4}>0.\] Thus \(M\) is not a martingale in the stated enlarged filtration. All solution assumptions hold because the clock times are deterministic stopping times in the original filtration; Definition 5.2 does not require \(Z(t)\) to be measurable at physical time \(t\) there.

The preceding part of the proof claims that the relevant event \(B\) is measurable in the driver’s \(\mathcal N_t\). Given that assertion, the cancellation in the second step can use the original martingale property directly. The time-changed filtrations in the subsequent coupling also differ from this same-time product filtration. The false enlargement assertion is therefore removable from that cancellation, and no additional failure of the final theorem is inferred from it. Repair should delete it or state and establish a suitable compatibility condition.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Natural-filtration martingales need not survive the same-time product enlargement

report: Abstract: The chiral asymptotic formula is contradicted by a family of full-height columns whose weights remain of order one. The exact covering integral is also false: its printed measure gives a divergent integral, and the proposed infinite genus series diverges independently of its normalization. The generalized Frobenius probability family is not normalizable for base genus at least two. The tightness argument for the unrestricted limit has a core proof gap, repaired here by a uniform union bound. Three further local errors admit explicit repairs. These findings do not refute the finite-order expansion of the unrestricted unitary partition function; its main domination mechanism is checked separately.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of Gaussian Measure on the Dual of U(N), Random Partitions, and Topological Expansion
# Identity, definitions, and scope

The reviewed paper is Thibaut Lemoine and Mylène Maïda, Gaussian measure on the dual of \(U(N)\), random partitions, and topological expansion of the partition function, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1749. The exact source is the 26-page arXiv:2405.08393v2 PDF, dated 11 April 2025 [paper]. Source locators below use one-based PDF pages, equal to printed pages. The complete source, including proofs and references, was read. Journal-final textual equivalence is not established.

Equation reference: eq:chiral. For a partition \(\alpha\), let \(A=|\alpha|\), \(\ell(\alpha)\) be its number of rows, and \[K(\alpha)=\frac12\sum_i\alpha_i(\alpha_i+1-2i),\qquad
\varphi(q)=\prod_{j\geq1}(1-q^j),\qquad 0<q=e^{-t/2}<1.\] The \(q\)-uniform law assigns mass \(\varphi(q)q^{|\alpha|}\). The unitary Casimir is \[c_{2,N}(\lambda)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i(\lambda_i+N+1-2i).\] The unrestricted partition function sums over all nonincreasing integer \(N\)-tuples. In contrast, the chiral function is explicitly defined on pages 5 and 21 by \[
Z_N^{\mathrm{chir}}(1,t)=
\sum_{\ell(\alpha)\leq N}q^{|\alpha|+2K(\alpha)/N}.\] No fixed-degree restriction or half-height cutoff is imposed in this definition.

The review keeps \(t>0\) and the expansion order fixed when taking \(N\to\infty\). It does not assume uniformity as \(t\downarrow0\), or interchange the expansion order with that limit. A specifically cited supporting source, Novak’s arXiv:2401.00628v1 [novak], was acquired and its relevant definitions and convergence statements were read and visually checked. Other imported representation-theoretic results were followed as dependencies, not independently re-proved.
# The chiral asymptotic statement

Problem 1 (Major: Theorem 1.4 has the wrong leading term).  Theorem 1.4, equation (8), page 5, implies \(Z_N^{\mathrm{chir}}(1,t)\to\varphi(q)^{-1}\). This conclusion is false for the chiral function [eq:chiral] (#eq:chiral). The proof on page 21 transfers estimates whose essential half-height hypothesis is absent from this summation domain.

Proof. The full-height column \(\alpha^{(N)}=(1^N)\) is an admissible partition with \(\ell(\alpha^{(N)})=N\). Its content and Casimir are \[K(\alpha^{(N)})=-\frac{N(N-1)}2,\qquad
c_{2,N}(\alpha^{(N)})=N-(N-1)=1.\] It therefore contributes exactly \(q>0\), for every \(N\).

Equation reference: eq:liminf. This alone is not compared with the entire limiting partition sum; possible double counting must be excluded. Fix an integer \(M\). For \(N>M\), the column \((1^N)\) is distinct from every partition of size at most \(M\), all of which are admissible. Positivity gives \[Z_N^{\mathrm{chir}}(1,t)\geq
q+\sum_{|\alpha|\leq M}q^{|\alpha|+2K(\alpha)/N}.\] First let \(N\to\infty\) with \(M\) fixed, then let \(M\to\infty\). Euler’s partition identity yields \[
\liminf_{N\to\infty} Z_N^{\mathrm{chir}}(1,t)
\geq q+\varphi(q)^{-1}>\varphi(q)^{-1}.\] All hypotheses of Theorem 1.4 are met for every fixed \(t>0\). ◻

Core dependency and alternatives. Lemma 4.1, pages 13–14, uses \(\ell(\alpha),\ell(\beta)\leq N/2\). For a single column of height \(N\), its prospective bound \(c_{2,N}\geq|\alpha|/2\) fails once \(N>2\). Thus its domination cannot be transferred unchanged to [eq:chiral] (#eq:chiral). The proof on page 21 also drops the factor \(\varphi(q)^{-1}\) in its expectation expansion, but restoring that normalization does not fix [eq:liminf] (#eq:liminf).

Restricting the definition to a half-height sector or to fixed degree would exclude the example; either changes the observable or quantifiers. The paper’s repeated explicit domain \(\ell(\alpha)\leq N\) prevents treating such a restriction as implicit. For the stated domain, the leading term and subsequent expansion require a fresh derivation. This is a false final theorem for the chiral sector, not merely a missing proof detail. It does not contradict Theorems 1.1–1.3 for the unrestricted highest-weight model, which retains the central integer and both partitions.
# Infinite expansions and the covering integral

Problem 2 (Major: Corollary 6.2 is a divergent integral).  Corollary 6.2, equation (43), page 22, claims an exact finite covering integral. Its proof on page 23 begins by letting the order \(p\) tend to infinity in Theorem 1.4. That step is invalid, and the proposed infinite series diverges. Independently, the measure in Definition 6.1 makes the asserted integral infinite.

The same lower bound applies to the full expansion in Theorem 4.5: retain only \(\beta=\varnothing\), the central integer \(n=0\), and \(\alpha=(m)\) in its nonnegative even-moment coefficients. Thus the phrase convergent asymptotic expansion in Remark 4.6 cannot mean a convergent infinite \(1/N\) series. Finite-order asymptotics remain a distinct, viable statement. ◻

Divergence under the printed covering measure. Fix the base torus \(X=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\tau\mathbb Z)\). For every \(m\geq1\), the inclusion of lattices \(m\mathbb Z+\tau\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Z+\tau\mathbb Z\) gives a connected unbranched degree-\(m\) covering. It is compact, has Euler characteristic zero, and has exactly \(m\) deck transformations. All its ramifications are simple vacuously, so it belongs to the space in Definition 6.1.

That definition weights this covering by \(m!/|\operatorname{Aut}(Y)|=(m-1)!\). The even-conditioned Poisson branch process is empty with probability \[\mathbb P\{J=0\mid J\text{ even}\}=\frac1{\cosh t},
\qquad J\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(t).\] Consequently the proposed integral is at least \[\frac1{\cosh t}\sum_{m\geq1}q^m(m-1)!=\infty.\] This direct counterexample uses no interchange of an asymptotic expansion. ◻

Normalization checks. The weights \(m!/|\operatorname{Aut}(Y)|\) also disagree with equation (35). In degree two with no branch points, the four commuting pairs in \(S_2\) give four covering classes, each with automorphism group of order two. Standard weighted count is \(4/2=2=p(2)=H_1(2,0)\); the printed weights give four. An independent enumeration verifies these numbers. In addition, an even-conditioned Poisson process assigns branch-count probability \(t^{2k}/((2k)!\cosh t)\), whereas the proof uses the coefficient without \(\cosh t\). Neither correction alone resolves the divergent all-genus sum.

Counterevidence and repair limits. Novak’s Theorem 4.5 [novak, p. 22] proves absolute convergence for fixed degree \(d\) in the stable range \(1\leq d\leq N\), after interchanging a finite representation sum with an exponential series. His Definition 4.6 labels the degree-summed torus object formal, and page 17 explicitly separates the additional interchange needed for the full chiral partition function. This supports the fixed-degree result, not the stronger attribution on page 21 of the reviewed paper. A valid replacement should retain a formal or finite-order coefficient interpretation, or introduce and justify a distinct regularization. The exact positive-measure formula as printed cannot be repaired by an appeal to nonnegativity.
# The generalized probability family

For the row \(\alpha=(m)\), \(m\geq2\), the symmetric-group representation is trivial, so \(\chi_\alpha(1)=1\). Its weight is \[(m!)^{2g-2}\left(\frac{m(m-1)}2\right)^{2g'-2}q^m.\] The ratio of successive terms tends to infinity for every \(q>0\) and \(g\geq2\). The terms therefore fail to tend to zero, already when \(g=2,g'=1\). The alleged probability law does not exist on that parameter range. Propositions 5.1–5.2, written conditionally on a random partition having this law, have no such instance there; the issue is the asserted existence and normalization, not a counterexample to a conditional-expectation identity for an existing probability.

The restriction matters for the proposed general family. It does not invalidate the torus specialization \(g=1\) used in Theorem 5.3 and Theorem 6.3. In that case polynomial content moments are summable under the exponentially decaying \(q\)-partition weights. For \(g=0\), the dimension-square identity provides factorial suppression. Restricting to a normalizable range, or conditioning on fixed degree with positive finite normalizing mass, gives possible repairs; it does not produce the originally asserted family for \(g\geq2\).
# Tightness and auxiliary identities

Problem 4 (Minor: the exponential rate in Lemma 4.4 is false).  Lemma 4.4, page 16, claims, for each fixed \(k\geq1\), \(\mathbb E[F^k\mathbf1_{\Lambda_N^c}]\leq C_{k,q}q^{N/2}\), where \[F=K(\alpha)+K(\beta)+n(|\alpha|-|\beta|),
\quad
\alpha,\beta\sim U(q),\quad n\sim G_1(q)\] independently. The assertion fails for \(k=2\).

The proof’s Cauchy–Schwarz argument instead yields \(\mathbb E[|F|^k\mathbf1_{\Lambda_N^c}]=O(q^{N/4})\), using finite \(2k\)-th moments and the union bound for the two length tails. This still implies every polynomial rate in equation (30), and suffices for equation (32) in the fixed-order expansion. The false stronger exponent is therefore a local minor issue; it does not refute Theorem 4.5.

Problem 5 (Major proof gap: the tightness argument omits the required tails).  On page 15, the proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 controls the complement of \(X_M=\{|\alpha|,|\beta|,|n|\leq M\}\) by an expression containing \(\mathbf1_{\{|\alpha|>M,\ |\beta|>M\}}\mathbf1_{\{|n|>M\}}\). The displayed left indicator also loses its complement. Neither expression represents \(X_M^c\).

For example, \(\alpha=\beta=\varnothing\), \(n=M+1\) belongs to \(\Lambda_N\cap X_M^c\) for every \(N\), with positive weight \(q^{(M+1)^2}\), but its printed intersection indicator is zero. For \(N=1\), only the empty partitions are admissible: the purported intersection bound is zero while the actual \(n\)-tail is positive. The equality is therefore false under both the literal printed indicator and its intended complemented reading.
Problem 6 (Minor: sign in equation (40)).  The middle expression in equation (40), page 20, is \(D\log\varphi(q)\), with \(D=q\,d/dq\). It has the opposite sign from the mean partition size.

Differentiating the Euler product for \(0<q<1\) gives \[D\log\varphi(q)=-\sum_{j\geq1}\frac{jq^j}{1-q^j}<0,
\qquad
\mathbb E_{U(q)}|\alpha|=-D\log\varphi(q)>0.\] Thus the printed equality is false for every allowed \(q\). The preceding general identity uses the correct normalizing function \(F_{1,1}=\varphi^{-1}\), and the Eisenstein-series expression on the right has the positive sign. Inserting a minus sign in the middle term is the local repair; the later differentiated \(F_{1,g}\) formulas need no change from this error alone.

Problem 7 (Minor: coordinate indexing in Proposition 3.3).  The proof on page 12 defines \(\ell_2\) as the first index below the middle coordinate, then uses it as the number of such coordinates; it also prints \(\beta_j=\lambda_k-\lambda_{N-j-1}\). These formulas do not give the claimed partition.

The paper’s own Figure 1, page 2, has \(\lambda=(4,3,3,2,1,-1,-2,-2)\), \(N=8\), \(k=4\), and \(n=2\). The first index below \(n\) is five, whereas the number of entries below \(n\) is four. Using the printed indexing gives \((3,1,0,-1,-1)\), not a partition; the figure correctly gives \(\beta=(4,4,3,1)\). Define instead \[\ell_2=\#\{i:\lambda_i<n\},\qquad
\beta_j=n-\lambda_{N+1-j},\quad 1\leq j\leq\ell_2.\] Together with the corresponding positive deviations above \(n\), this is the intended bijection. Equation (22) and Figure 1 support that interpretation. The existence of a bijection, the Casimir identity, and the later density formula are not disproved by these local indexing slips.
# Checks on the unrestricted finite-order expansion

The preceding distinctions are material: the unrestricted model does satisfy the half-height restriction. With \(A=|\alpha|\), \(B=|\beta|\), \(d=A-B\), the intended bijection gives \[c_{2,N}=A+B+n^2+\frac2N F.\] For a decreasing partition of length \(\ell\), \(\sum_i i\alpha_i\leq(\ell+1)A/2\), so \(\sum_i(1-2i)\alpha_i\geq-\ell A\). Combining this with \(A^2\leq\ell\sum_i\alpha_i^2\) and \(\ell\leq N/2\) proves the bounds used in the domination and remainder arguments: \[\begin{aligned}
A+B+n^2+\frac2N F
 &\geq \frac12(A+B)+\left(n+\frac dN\right)^2,\\
A+B+n^2+\frac3N F
 &\geq \frac14(A+B)+\left(n+\frac{3d}{2N}\right)^2.\end{aligned}\] The shifted Gaussian sum is uniformly bounded, and the partition factors are summable for fixed \(q<1\). All polynomial moments of \(F\) are finite. These facts justify the fixed-order Hölder remainder estimate on pages 17–18 after the local tail-rate repair.

The law is invariant under \((\alpha,\beta,n)\mapsto(\alpha',\beta',-n)\), which sends \(F\) to \(-F\); odd moments therefore vanish. The second coefficient provides a further check: \[a_2(t)=\frac{t^2\theta(q)}{\varphi(q)^2}
\left(\mathbb E[K(\alpha)^2]+\mathbb E[n^2]\operatorname{Var}(|\alpha|)\right),\] consistent with Remark 6.4. An independent exact enumeration of 1,286 highest weights, for \(1\leq N\leq8\) and coordinates in \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\), verifies the Casimir identity and both bounds with zero residual failures. This finite check corroborates, and does not replace, the analytic inequalities above.

No false final unrestricted finite-order theorem was established. Its coefficientwise topological interpretation can coexist with divergence of the infinite series. The confirmed false conclusions are the stated chiral leading limit and the exact covering integral; the generalized probability family also fails on its asserted \(g\geq2\) range.

claim: The reviewed paper is Thibaut Lemoine and Mylène Maïda, Gaussian measure on the dual of \(U(N)\), random partitions, and topological expansion of the partition function, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1749. The exact source is the 26-page arXiv:2405.08393v2 PDF, dated 11 April 2025 [paper]. Source locators below use one-based PDF pages, equal to printed pages. The complete source, including proofs and references, was read. Journal-final textual equivalence is not established.

Equation reference: eq:chiral. For a partition \(\alpha\), let \(A=|\alpha|\), \(\ell(\alpha)\) be its number of rows, and \[K(\alpha)=\frac12\sum_i\alpha_i(\alpha_i+1-2i),\qquad
\varphi(q)=\prod_{j\geq1}(1-q^j),\qquad 0<q=e^{-t/2}<1.\] The \(q\)-uniform law assigns mass \(\varphi(q)q^{|\alpha|}\). The unitary Casimir is \[c_{2,N}(\lambda)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i(\lambda_i+N+1-2i).\] The unrestricted partition function sums over all nonincreasing integer \(N\)-tuples. In contrast, the chiral function is explicitly defined on pages 5 and 21 by \[
Z_N^{\mathrm{chir}}(1,t)=
\sum_{\ell(\alpha)\leq N}q^{|\alpha|+2K(\alpha)/N}.\] No fixed-degree restriction or half-height cutoff is imposed in this definition.

The review keeps \(t>0\) and the expansion order fixed when taking \(N\to\infty\). It does not assume uniformity as \(t\downarrow0\), or interchange the expansion order with that limit. A specifically cited supporting source, Novak’s arXiv:2401.00628v1 [novak], was acquired and its relevant definitions and convergence statements were read and visually checked. Other imported representation-theoretic results were followed as dependencies, not independently re-proved.
Recorded check: False chiral leading asymptotic
Fixed t>0, q=exp(-t/2) in (0,1). N positive integer tends to infinity. All partitions with length <=N, without a fixed-degree or half-height restriction. Casimir (18) and Euler partition identity.
analysis: Theorem 1.4, equation (8), page 5, implies \(Z_N^{\mathrm{chir}}(1,t)\to\varphi(q)^{-1}\). This conclusion is false for the chiral function [eq:chiral] (#eq:chiral). The proof on page 21 transfers estimates whose essential half-height hypothesis is absent from this summation domain.

Proof. The full-height column \(\alpha^{(N)}=(1^N)\) is an admissible partition with \(\ell(\alpha^{(N)})=N\). Its content and Casimir are \[K(\alpha^{(N)})=-\frac{N(N-1)}2,\qquad
c_{2,N}(\alpha^{(N)})=N-(N-1)=1.\] It therefore contributes exactly \(q>0\), for every \(N\).

Equation reference: eq:liminf. This alone is not compared with the entire limiting partition sum; possible double counting must be excluded. Fix an integer \(M\). For \(N>M\), the column \((1^N)\) is distinct from every partition of size at most \(M\), all of which are admissible. Positivity gives \[Z_N^{\mathrm{chir}}(1,t)\geq
q+\sum_{|\alpha|\leq M}q^{|\alpha|+2K(\alpha)/N}.\] First let \(N\to\infty\) with \(M\) fixed, then let \(M\to\infty\). Euler’s partition identity yields \[
\liminf_{N\to\infty} Z_N^{\mathrm{chir}}(1,t)
\geq q+\varphi(q)^{-1}>\varphi(q)^{-1}.\] All hypotheses of Theorem 1.4 are met for every fixed \(t>0\). ◻

Core dependency and alternatives. Lemma 4.1, pages 13–14, uses \(\ell(\alpha),\ell(\beta)\leq N/2\). For a single column of height \(N\), its prospective bound \(c_{2,N}\geq|\alpha|/2\) fails once \(N>2\). Thus its domination cannot be transferred unchanged to [eq:chiral] (#eq:chiral). The proof on page 21 also drops the factor \(\varphi(q)^{-1}\) in its expectation expansion, but restoring that normalization does not fix [eq:liminf] (#eq:liminf).

Restricting the definition to a half-height sector or to fixed degree would exclude the example; either changes the observable or quantifiers. The paper’s repeated explicit domain \(\ell(\alpha)\leq N\) prevents treating such a restriction as implicit. For the stated domain, the leading term and subsequent expansion require a fresh derivation. This is a false final theorem for the chiral sector, not merely a missing proof detail. It does not contradict Theorems 1.1–1.3 for the unrestricted highest-weight model, which retains the central integer and both partitions.
result: Recorded inspection subject: False chiral leading asymptotic

Recorded check: Divergent infinite genus series and printed covering integral

Fixed t>0 and finite N>=1. Nonnegative even-content coefficients over all partitions. Compact torus, compact not necessarily connected covers, simple ramifications; empty branch set allowed. Printed mass n!/|Aut(Y)| and Poisson branch distribution conditioned on even count.
analysis: Corollary 6.2, equation (43), page 22, claims an exact finite covering integral. Its proof on page 23 begins by letting the order \(p\) tend to infinity in Theorem 1.4. That step is invalid, and the proposed infinite series diverges. Independently, the measure in Definition 6.1 makes the asserted integral infinite.

The same lower bound applies to the full expansion in Theorem 4.5: retain only \(\beta=\varnothing\), the central integer \(n=0\), and \(\alpha=(m)\) in its nonnegative even-moment coefficients. Thus the phrase convergent asymptotic expansion in Remark 4.6 cannot mean a convergent infinite \(1/N\) series. Finite-order asymptotics remain a distinct, viable statement. ◻

Divergence under the printed covering measure. Fix the base torus \(X=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+\tau\mathbb Z)\). For every \(m\geq1\), the inclusion of lattices \(m\mathbb Z+\tau\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb Z+\tau\mathbb Z\) gives a connected unbranched degree-\(m\) covering. It is compact, has Euler characteristic zero, and has exactly \(m\) deck transformations. All its ramifications are simple vacuously, so it belongs to the space in Definition 6.1.

That definition weights this covering by \(m!/|\operatorname{Aut}(Y)|=(m-1)!\). The even-conditioned Poisson branch process is empty with probability \[\mathbb P\{J=0\mid J\text{ even}\}=\frac1{\cosh t},
\qquad J\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(t).\] Consequently the proposed integral is at least \[\frac1{\cosh t}\sum_{m\geq1}q^m(m-1)!=\infty.\] This direct counterexample uses no interchange of an asymptotic expansion. ◻

Normalization checks. The weights \(m!/|\operatorname{Aut}(Y)|\) also disagree with equation (35). In degree two with no branch points, the four commuting pairs in \(S_2\) give four covering classes, each with automorphism group of order two. Standard weighted count is \(4/2=2=p(2)=H_1(2,0)\); the printed weights give four. An independent enumeration verifies these numbers. In addition, an even-conditioned Poisson process assigns branch-count probability \(t^{2k}/((2k)!\cosh t)\), whereas the proof uses the coefficient without \(\cosh t\). Neither correction alone resolves the divergent all-genus sum.

Counterevidence and repair limits. Novak’s Theorem 4.5 [novak, p. 22] proves absolute convergence for fixed degree \(d\) in the stable range \(1\leq d\leq N\), after interchanging a finite representation sum with an exponential series. His Definition 4.6 labels the degree-summed torus object formal, and page 17 explicitly separates the additional interchange needed for the full chiral partition function. This supports the fixed-degree result, not the stronger attribution on page 21 of the reviewed paper. A valid replacement should retain a formal or finite-order coefficient interpretation, or introduce and justify a distinct regularization. The exact positive-measure formula as printed cannot be repaired by an appeal to nonnegativity.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Divergent infinite genus series and printed covering integral

Recorded check: Frobenius probability family not normalizable for g>=2
g>=2 integer, gprime>=1 integer, 0<q<1. Unrestricted partitions with printed nonnegative weights. Single-row partition has symmetric-group dimension one.
analysis: For the row \(\alpha=(m)\), \(m\geq2\), the symmetric-group representation is trivial, so \(\chi_\alpha(1)=1\). Its weight is \[(m!)^{2g-2}\left(\frac{m(m-1)}2\right)^{2g'-2}q^m.\] The ratio of successive terms tends to infinity for every \(q>0\) and \(g\geq2\). The terms therefore fail to tend to zero, already when \(g=2,g'=1\). The alleged probability law does not exist on that parameter range. Propositions 5.1–5.2, written conditionally on a random partition having this law, have no such instance there; the issue is the asserted existence and normalization, not a counterexample to a conditional-expectation identity for an existing probability.

The restriction matters for the proposed general family. It does not invalidate the torus specialization \(g=1\) used in Theorem 5.3 and Theorem 6.3. In that case polynomial content moments are summable under the exponentially decaying \(q\)-partition weights. For \(g=0\), the dimension-square identity provides factorial suppression. Restricting to a normalizable range, or conditioning on fixed degree with positive finite normalizing mass, gives possible repairs; it does not produce the originally asserted family for \(g\geq2\).
result: Recorded inspection subject: Frobenius probability family not normalizable for g>=2

Recorded check: Lemma 4.4 exponential tail rate too strong
Independent alpha,beta~U(q), n~G1(q), fixed 0<q<1. k=2, N=2m, alpha=(1^m), beta=empty, n=0. A_N=m-1, so retained event lies outside Lambda_N.
analysis:
Lemma 4.4, page 16, claims, for each fixed \(k\geq1\), \(\mathbb E[F^k\mathbf1_{\Lambda_N^c}]\leq C_{k,q}q^{N/2}\), where \[F=K(\alpha)+K(\beta)+n(|\alpha|-|\beta|),
\quad
\alpha,\beta\sim U(q),\quad n\sim G_1(q)\] independently. The assertion fails for \(k=2\).

This still implies every polynomial rate in equation (30), and suffices for equation (32) in the fixed-order expansion. The false stronger exponent is therefore a local minor issue; it does not refute Theorem 4.5.

Recorded check: Tightness proof confuses tail union with intersection
X_M is the finite cube in partition sizes and integer magnitude. All triples in Lambda_N; bounded test f, including f=1. N=1 or empty partitions with n=M+1 supplies a concrete positive missing tail.
analysis: On page 15, the proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 controls the complement of \(X_M=\{|\alpha|,|\beta|,|n|\leq M\}\) by an expression containing \(\mathbf1_{\{|\alpha|>M,\ |\beta|>M\}}\mathbf1_{\{|n|>M\}}\). For \(N=1\), only the empty partitions are admissible: the purported intersection bound is zero while the actual \(n\)-tail is positive. The equality is therefore false under both the literal printed indicator and its intended complemented reading.

Recorded check: Wrong sign in equation (40)
0<q<1. phi(q) is Euler product. U(q) normalized by phi(q).
analysis: The middle expression in equation (40), page 20, is \(D\log\varphi(q)\), with \(D=q\,d/dq\). It has the opposite sign from the mean partition size.

Differentiating the Euler product for \(0<q<1\) gives \[D\log\varphi(q)=-\sum_{j\geq1}\frac{jq^j}{1-q^j}<0,
\qquad
\mathbb E_{U(q)}|\alpha|=-D\log\varphi(q)>0.\] Thus the printed equality is false for every allowed \(q\). Inserting a minus sign in the middle term is the local repair; the later differentiated \(F_{1,g}\) formulas need no change from this error alone.

N=8, lambda=(4,3,3,2,1,-1,-2,-2) valid highest weight. k=floor((N+1)/2)=4, n=2. Literal printed first-low-index and beta_j=lambda_k-lambda_(N-j-1).

The paper’s own Figure 1, page 2, has \(\lambda=(4,3,3,2,1,-1,-2,-2)\), \(N=8\), \(k=4\), and \(n=2\). The first index below \(n\) is five, whereas the number of entries below \(n\) is four. report: Abstract: The transport application, with its printed coupling to the driving Brownian motion, has a zero-drift counterexample. A uniform localization lemma in the appendix is false under its stated assumptions. The principal strong-error proof also loses a nonzero diffusion-error forcing term and invokes diffusion regularity stronger than its formal hypothesis. These are distinct from a disproof of the main SDE convergence theorem. Further normalization, homogeneity, and change-of-measure errors admit explicit local repairs. The review concerns the frozen Accepted Version and compares relevant passages with arXiv version 6.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of Taming Singular Stochastic Differential Equations: A Numerical Method
# Identity, hypotheses, and scope

The reviewed paper is Khoa Lê and Chengcheng Ling, Taming singular stochastic differential equations: A numerical method, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1750. The frozen source is the White Rose Accepted Version, record 222738 [paper]: 62 PDF pages comprising a cover and printed pages 1–61. In this report, p. means a printed page; its PDF page is one greater. The complete source, proofs, appendix, and references were read.

Write \(L^q_tL^p_x=L^q([0,1];L^p(\mathbb R^d))\). The main assumptions include \(p,q\in[2,\infty)\), \(d/p+2/q<1\), bounded uniformly elliptic \(a=\sigma\sigma^*\), spatial \(\alpha\)-Hölder continuity of \(a\), and \[\nabla\sigma\in L^{q_0}_tL^{p_0}_x,\qquad
p_0\geq2,\quad q_0>2,\quad d/p_0+2/q_0<1.\] The approximations \(b^n\) have uniformly bounded \(L^q_tL^p_x\) norms and satisfy Condition B’s local \(L^q_tL^\infty_x\) control. The scheme freezes space at \(k_n(t)=\lfloor nt\rfloor/n\), but does not freeze the time argument. Theorem 2.2 claims an error bounded by the initial error, \(n^{-\alpha/2}+n^{-1/2}\log n\), and the transformed drift discrepancy \(\varpi_n(\bar p)\), for \[1<\bar p<p,\qquad \bar p<2(p\wedge p_0)/d,\qquad 0<\gamma<1,\] in \(L^{\gamma\bar p}\). Theorem 2.3 supplies stronger bounds for that discrepancy, with its additional restrictions on \(q_0,p_0,\nu\) and, in part (iii), \(d/p+4/q<1\). None of these strict inequalities is replaced by an endpoint assertion here.

The official arXiv record describes v6 as an update to the error formula. Its acquired PDF has 70 pages, an arXiv date of 31 January 2025 and a body date of 3 February 2025 [v6]. Relevant statements and proofs were compared directly; the two PDFs were not declared textually identical. In particular, the passages underlying Problems 1–6 below remain in the corresponding v6 passages. The journal typeset version was not acquired for comparison, and no claim is made that every version shares these defects. The bounded metadata search identified no separate formal correction resolving them; that is not proof that no correction exists.
# The transport application

Problem 1 (Major: the printed scheme in Theorem 8.1 does not converge to the stated solution).  Equations (8.3)–(8.5), pp. 47–48, change the sign of the Brownian increment while retaining the same driving path. Consequently the strong estimate (8.6) is false for the printed scheme.

Proof. The definition \(X_s^\tau=X_{\tau,\tau-s}\) and (8.3) give \[X_s^\tau=x-\int_0^s b(\tau-r,X_r^\tau)\,dr+W_{\tau-s}-W_\tau.\] The paper instead uses a plus sign before \(W_s^\tau=W_\tau-W_{\tau-s}\), in both (8.4) and the numerical scheme (8.5).

Equation reference: eq:transport. Take \(d=1\), \(b=b^n=0\), \(p=q=p_1=q_1=4\), \(\nu=0\), \(l=2\), and \(\bar r=8\). Then all restrictions in Theorem 8.1 hold: \(1/4+2/4<1\), \(\nu<7/8\), and \(1/8<1/2-1/4\). Zero drift satisfies Condition B with, for example, \(\mu_n(s,t)=t-s\) and any fixed positive \(\theta\). Set \(\rho(x)=e^{-(x-1)^2}\), which belongs to every required \(W^{1,r}\) space. The Stratonovich chain rule gives the exact solution \(u(t,x)=\rho(x-W_t)\). The printed scheme gives \(u^n(t,x)=\rho(x+W_t)\) for every \(n\). For \(Z=W_1\sim N(0,1)\), direct Gaussian integration yields \[
\mathbb E|\rho(Z)-\rho(-Z)|^2
=\frac{2}{\sqrt5}\left(e^{-2/5}-e^{-2}\right)>0.\] The corresponding \(L^2\) error is approximately \(0.6917405\). At \((t,x)=(1,0)\), the left side of (8.6) is therefore bounded away from zero, while its right side tends to zero as \(n\to\infty\). ◻

Defining the reversed driver as \(W_{\tau-s}-W_\tau\), with the corresponding change to its extension (8.7), repairs this elementary sign obstruction. # Uniform localization in the appendix

Problem 2 (Major: Lemma A.8 requires uniform local integrability not supplied by Condition A’).  Lemma A.8, (A.19), p. 52, asserts that \[\sup_{t,z}\|(a-a(z))\psi_\rho^z\|_{W^{1,p_0}}\longrightarrow0
\quad(\rho\downarrow0)\] from the bound \(\sup_t\|\nabla a(t)\|_{p_0}<\infty\). This assertion is false.

Equation reference: eq:concentration. Proof. Use \(d=1\), \(p_0=4\), \(p=2\), \(q=4\), and zero forcing terms, so that \(p_0>d\) and \(1/p+1/p_0<1\). Let \(r_j=2^{-j}\) and \(\phi(u)=(1-u^2)^2\) on \([-1,1]\), zero outside. This compactly supported \(C^1\) function is sufficient for the weak differentiability required in Condition A’. On the disjoint intervals \(I_j=(2^{-j-1},2^{-j}]\), set \[
a(t,x)=2+r_j^{3/4}\phi(x/r_j),\qquad t\in I_j,\] and set \(a=2\) at all remaining times. Then \(2\leq a\leq3\), the coefficient is measurable, and \[\|\partial_xa(t,\cdot)\|_4^4
=r_j^{4(3/4-1)+1}\int_{-1}^1|\phi'(u)|^4\,du
=\frac{65536}{15015}>0.\] Thus its gradient norm is uniformly bounded in time, exactly as required.

Dependency and impact. The false smallness is used in Lemma A.9, Step 1, p. 53, and absorbed in Step 2, p. 54. Lemma A.10 repeats that argument; Theorems A.5 and A.11 then feed Proposition 6.4 and the weak-topology estimates of Theorem 2.3. This is an invalid central derivation, not a demonstrated counterexample to those final PDE or SDE estimates.

Counterevidence and repair boundary. For a single time-independent gradient in \(L^{p_0}\), absolute continuity of its integral does give the needed local smallness uniformly over spatial centers. The missing point is uniformity over the time-indexed family. A uniform local equiintegrability assumption, such as \(\sup_{t,z}\int_{B_\rho(z)}|\nabla a(t,x)|^{p_0}\,dx\to0\), would support this step. Alternatively the localization proof must be replaced. Neither repair follows from the stated norm bound alone. The same assertion and inference occur as Lemma .8 on v6 pp. 59–60.
# The principal strong-error derivation

Problem 3 (Major: the diffusion forcing is lost in Proposition 7.3).  The proof on pp. 42–44 contains a false intermediate conclusion (7.7), as well as a use of \(\alpha\)-Hölder regularity of \(\sigma\) which is not implied by Condition A1.

Decisive check of (7.7). In the paper, \(V=|x_0-x_0^n|^{\bar p}+V^1+V^2+V^3\). Take \(d=1\), \(b=b^n=0\), \(x_0=x_0^n=0\), and \[\sigma(x)=1+\tfrac14\tanh x.\] This coefficient is smooth, bounded, uniformly elliptic and Lipschitz; its derivative belongs to every finite \(L^{p_0}\). Take \(p=q=p_0=4\), \(q_0=\infty\), \(\bar p=2\), and \(\alpha=1\). The assumptions hold. The PDE solution \(U\) is zero, so every term in the displayed \(V\) is zero.

For \(n=1\), the Euler process is \(X_t^1=B_t\), whereas the exact solution satisfies \(dX_t=\sigma(X_t)dB_t\). These paths cannot agree almost surely throughout \([0,1]\): equality would imply, by Itô isometry, \(\mathbb E\int_0^1(\sigma(B_s)-1)^2ds=0\), which is false. Thus \(\mathbb E\sup_t|X_t-X_t^1|^2>0\). The weight in (7.7) is strictly positive and bounded away from zero here, since \(\nabla\sigma\) and its maximal function are bounded. The claimed bound \[\mathbb Ee^{-c_{\bar p}|A_1^n|^{\max(\bar p/2,1)}}\xi_1\leq \mathbb EV_1=0\] is impossible. ◻

The preceding estimate of \(I^2\) on p. 44 replaces a random increment integral by a deterministic \(n^{-\bar p\alpha/2}\) using Lemma 7.2, which is only a moment estimate. Even for \(X^n=B\), \(\int_0^{1/n}|B_r|^2dr\) is not deterministically bounded by a fixed multiple of \(n^{-1}\). A random nondecreasing error term must remain in \(V\), with its expectation bounded at the required rate; the paper’s definition of \(V\) omits it.

There is also a separate hypothesis mismatch at that step. In \(d=2\), let \(\vartheta(x)=\chi(x)|x|^{3/4}\), with a smooth cutoff equal to one near zero, and let \(\sigma(x)\) be planar rotation by angle \(\vartheta(x)\). Then \[\sigma\sigma^*=I,\qquad \nabla\sigma\in L^4(\mathbb R^2),\qquad
\frac{\|\sigma(re_1)-\sigma(0)\|_{\rm HS}}r
=\frac{\sqrt8|\sin(r^{3/4}/2)|}r\longrightarrow\infty.\] The gradient is integrable to the fourth power near zero because its radial integral is proportional to \(\int_0^1 r^{4(-1/4)}r\,dr\). With \(p=q=8\), \(p_0=4\), \(q_0=\infty\), and zero drifts, all formal assumptions hold with \(\alpha=1\), but \(\sigma\) is not Lipschitz. Thus Hölder regularity of \(a\) cannot simply be substituted for the same regularity of \(\sigma\).

Finally, the covariance correction in (7.6) must be \[\frac12\int_0^t\nabla^2U(r,X_r^n):
 [a(r,X_{k_n(r)}^n)-a(r,X_r^n)]\,dr.\] The printed formula uses \(X_r\) and omits \(1/2\); Itô’s formula for \(U(t,X_t^n)\) evaluates its Hessian at \(X_t^n\). Its subsequent estimate therefore needs a discrete-path occupation estimate.

Counterevidence and repair boundary. The abstract describes the diffusion coefficient itself as Hölder continuous, which may reflect the intended hypothesis; the formal Condition A1 controls its covariance instead. Explicitly strengthening that condition and retaining the random diffusion forcing would address two identified obstacles. The existing strong-rate statement includes a diffusion-error term, so the counterexample to (7.7) does not refute Theorem 2.2. These proof passages persist on v6 pp. 48–51.
# Further local errors with explicit repairs

Problem 4 (Minor: the Gaussian envelope in Lemma 3.11 has the wrong width).  Equation (3.22), p. 16, bounds a difference of Gaussian densities by densities with half the covariance. It is false even in dimension one with positive covariances.

For \(\Sigma=1,\bar\Sigma=2,K=2\), all its scalar comparison hypotheses hold. With the paper’s variance convention, \[\frac{|p_1(x)-p_2(x)|}{|1-1/2|\,[p_{1/2}(x)+p_1(x)]}
\sim \sqrt2\,e^{x^2/4}\longrightarrow\infty.\] No constant \(N(d,K)\) can work. The proof of Lemma 5.2 on p. 25 and later uses of Lemma 3.11 inherit this invalid envelope. Wider Gaussian envelopes, obtained by differentiating the density along a covariance interpolation and absorbing its quadratic polynomial into a slower Gaussian, give the required type of estimate. This changes constants and Gaussian widths, not the displayed time exponents in (5.5)–(5.6). That local repair is why this is classified Minor. A precision-matrix interpretation is incompatible with the explicit variance convention on p. 2 and the density formula on p. 17. The same half-covariance envelope appears on v6 pp. 19 and 28.
Problem 5 (Minor: inconsistent covariance and generator normalizations in Section 5).  Equations (5.3)–(5.4), p. 23, and the Duhamel identity (5.10), p. 26, do not use a consistent factor \(1/2\).

The random variable in (5.3) has covariance \(\int_s^t a(r,y)dr\), whereas (5.4) prints \(\Sigma_{s,t}=\frac12\int_s^t a(r,y)dr\). For constant \(\sigma=1\) and \(f(x)=\cos x\), the actual adjoint in (5.3) gives \(e^{-(t-s)/2}\cos x\); the printed kernel gives \(e^{-(t-s)/4}\cos x\).

Even if \(T\) is defined by the actual adjoint (5.3), the \(H\) defined on p. 23 needs a factor \(1/2\) in (5.10). To see this without a convention ambiguity, take smooth time-independent \(a(x)=1+\frac12e^{-x^2}\), \(f=1\), \(s=0\), and \(0<t<1/n\). Then \(Q_{0,t}^n1=1\), while the actual adjoint has \(T_{0,t}1=1+\frac t2a''+o(t)\) and \(\int_0^tQ_{0,k_n(r)}^nH_{r,t}^n1\,dr=-ta''+o(t)\). At \(x=0\), the printed right side of (5.10) is \(1+t/2+o(t)\), not 1.

A consistent repair uses \(\Sigma=\int a\), the generator \(\frac12a^{ij}\partial_{ij}\), and \(\frac12H\) in the Duhamel formula. These factors can be absorbed in the subsequent norm estimates; the smoothing-rate conclusion is not refuted. The same definitions and (5.10) occur on v6 pp. 26–29.
Problem 6 (Minor: Proposition 4.6(b) has incorrect homogeneity).  The right side on p. 21 contains \(w_0(0,1)\), whereas it must scale as \(w_0(0,1)^{1/q}\).

Take \(d=1,p=q=4,\bar p=1\). Let \(f\geq0\) be smooth, nonzero, compactly supported and normalized by \(\|f\|_4=1\). Put \(g_\epsilon(t,x)=\epsilon f(x)\), \(w_0(s,t)=\epsilon^4(t-s)\), and \(\Gamma=1\). The Bessel potential operator of order \(-1\) is an \(L^4\) contraction, so both hypotheses of Proposition 4.6 hold. Its left side equals \(\epsilon\,\mathbb E\int_0^1 f(B_r)dr=c\epsilon\), with \(c>0\), whereas its right side is \(N\epsilon^4\). This fails as \(\epsilon\downarrow0\). Part (a) already has the correct power; Theorem 6.1(iii) and Theorem 2.3(iii) also print the correct power. Restoring it in part (b) repairs this localized statement. It does not establish a defect in their final rate. The same incorrect power is visible on v6 p. 24.

Problem 7 (Minor: the change-of-measure direction in (5.33) is reversed).  The density in the proof of Theorem 5.1, p. 36, introduces the negative of the desired drift into the driftless Euler process.

Let \(u_r=(\sigma^{-1}b^n)(r,\bar X_{k_n(r)}^n)\) and use the printed density \(\rho=\exp(-\int u\,dB-\frac12\int|u|^2dr)\). Under \(dQ=\rho\,dP\), \(\widetilde B=B+\int u\,dr\) is Brownian. Hence \[d\bar X_r^n
=\sigma(r,\bar X_{k_n(r)}^n)d\widetilde B_r
-b^n(r,\bar X_{k_n(r)}^n)dr,\] rather than the positive drift in (1.3). This distinction already occurs for a smooth compactly supported scalar drift equal to one near the initial point, which satisfies Condition B. The two laws have opposite initial drift generators.

Use the positive stochastic-integral sign to obtain the positive drift under the new measure. The exponential-moment argument depends on \(|u|^2\), so its estimates survive this correction. The continuum proof on p. 40 similarly evaluates its negative-sign density along \(\bar X\) while making a claim about the law of \(X\); it must consistently choose the process and direction of measure change. These are repairable proof identities, not counterexamples to the stated moment estimates. No independent comparison of these two passages with v6 is asserted here.

Problem 8 (Minor: the multiplier norm in Theorem 2.3(iii)’s proof has the wrong order).  On p. 46, the product estimate and the definition of \(w_1\) use \(\|g\|_{L^q_tL^{-1,p}_x}\), although Lemma A.3 requires the multiplier in the positive-order space \(L^{1,p}\).

There is no continuous multiplication map \(H^{-1}(\mathbb R)\times H^{-1}(\mathbb R)\to H^{-1}(\mathbb R)\). For a nonzero smooth compactly supported \(\psi\), take \(g_k=h_k=\psi(x)\cos(kx)\). Both \(H^{-1}\) norms are \(O(k^{-1})\), while \[g_kh_k=\tfrac12\psi^2+\tfrac12\psi^2\cos(2kx)
\longrightarrow\tfrac12\psi^2\ne0\quad\hbox{in }H^{-1}.\] Thus the printed negative-order product bound fails. This check applies already with \(d=1,p=2,q=10\), which obey \(d/p+4/q<1\); a constant time dependence supplies the temporal norms.

Here \(g=\nabla U\) actually has a uniformly bounded \(L^q_tL^{1,p}_x\) norm by (7.2), and \(p>d\). Replacing the negative-order norm of \(g\) by the positive-order norm repairs the multiplication step. The sentence choosing \(q_2=2\) must also be made consistent with \(q_3=q/2\): the available choice is \(q_2=q\). With these repairs, the product control has the required homogeneity. This local error does not refute (2.11). The same multiplier sign occurs on v6 p. 53.
# Coverage, counterchecks, and limits

The review followed the route from Conditions A–B through the conditional sewing and Khasminskii estimates, the driftless discrete transition estimates, Girsanov transfer, the continuum occupation estimates, the Zvonkin transformation, and the exponential-weight removal. The appendix’s multiplication, localization, duality, and terminal-time bounds were read, including their stated ranges.

Several checks support parts of this architecture. Condition B gives the \(L^m\) Euler increment estimate of Lemma 7.2. The three truncation and mollification calculations in Corollary 2.4 have the stated scaling under their respective strict parameter restrictions. The sixteen singularity differences arising from (5.29) are positive: their four base differences are \[1-\frac dp-\frac2q,\quad
\frac{1-\alpha/2-1/q-d/(2p)}{1-\alpha/2},\quad
\frac{1-d/p-2/q}{1-d/(2p)},\quad
1-\frac1q-\frac d{2p},\] and the four subsequent powers are positive. Independent exact arithmetic checked 168 admissible parameter cases, or 2688 differences, in addition to this algebraic reasoning. The moment restriction in Theorem 2.2 is compatible with the stretched-exponential exponent of Lemma 7.4 when the preceding occupation and error bounds are valid. The endpoint \(\nu=0\) of Theorem 2.3(ii) is covered directly by part (i), even though its interpolation proof is phrased for positive order.

The source has additional local notational inconsistencies, including the component \(b^{n,h}\) in the drift term of (2.3), where the vector \(b^n\cdot\nabla U^h\) is needed, and the unweighted definition of \(\mathcal A_t\) in the proof of Proposition 5.12 despite a weighted \(A_{s,t}\). These have transparent intended readings and are not counted as additional substantive findings.

The decisive examples above are analytic. A primary-authored Sympy script independently checks the Gaussian integral, concentration scaling, Gaussian-tail ratios, generator normalization, and admissible exponent grid; it runs no author code. An initial symbolic equality check failed to normalize \(\operatorname{erfc}=1-\operatorname{erf}\); that failed script and the diagnostic are preserved, and the corrected symbolic normalization is recorded separately. This was a verification-script simplification issue, not contrary mathematical evidence.

Relevant passages of v6 were read and visually inspected, not the entire second version. Imported results in the cited SDE, PDE, sewing, maximal-function, and pathwise BDG literature were tracked as dependencies but not all independently re-proved or acquired. No unavailable author program is treated as a mathematical defect. The proven failures are the printed transport estimate, the localization lemma, and specified intermediate identities or bounds. No whole-paper-failure conclusion or independent acceptance is claimed.
