Weighted error is positive, contradicting (7.7). Moment bounds cannot replace a random increment integral by a deterministic value. In the second example covariance is constant but sigma is not Lipschitz, while its gradient is L4. Also Ito's formula requires 1/2 times Hessian U at Xn, not Hessian at X, in the covariance correction.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The final claimed rate contains a diffusion-error contribution; abstract language suggests sigma Holder regularity may have been intended. Neither observation validates the printed intermediate estimate.

problems.title: Gaussian difference bound uses an impossibly narrow envelope
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: Problem 4 (Minor: the Gaussian envelope in Lemma 3.11 has the wrong width).
claim: Recorded check: Gaussian difference bound uses an impossibly narrow envelope
d=1, positive scalar covariances Sigma=1 and barSigma=2, K=2, satisfying the lemma's comparability assumptions.
analysis: Equation (3.22), p. 16, bounds a difference of Gaussian densities by densities with half the covariance. It is false even in dimension one with positive covariances.

For \(\Sigma=1,\bar\Sigma=2,K=2\), all its scalar comparison hypotheses hold. With the paper’s variance convention, \[\frac{|p_1(x)-p_2(x)|}{|1-1/2|\,[p_{1/2}(x)+p_1(x)]}
\sim \sqrt2\,e^{x^2/4}\longrightarrow\infty.\] No constant \(N(d,K)\) can work. The proof of Lemma 5.2 on p. 25 and later uses of Lemma 3.11 inherit this invalid envelope. Wider Gaussian envelopes, obtained by differentiating the density along a covariance interpolation and absorbing its quadratic polynomial into a slower Gaussian, give the required type of estimate. This changes constants and Gaussian widths, not the displayed time exponents in (5.5)–(5.6). That local repair is why this is classified Minor. A precision-matrix interpretation is incompatible with the explicit variance convention on p. 2 and the density formula on p. 17. The same half-covariance envelope appears on v6 pp. 19 and 28.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: |p1-p2| / (0.5*(p_(1/2)+p1)) is asymptotic to sqrt(2)*exp(x^2/4), so no N(d,K) works. Analytic tail calculation and independent numerical evaluations retained.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Precision-matrix notation would change the direction, but the source explicitly uses variance/covariance notation.

problems.title: Covariance and Duhamel factors are inconsistent
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 5: Problem 5 (Minor: inconsistent covariance and generator normalizations in Section 5).
claim: Recorded check: Covariance and Duhamel factors are inconsistent
First test sigma=1, f=cos(x). Second test d=1, smooth a=1+exp(-x^2)/2, sigma=sqrt(a), f=1, s=0, 0<t<1/n. These are smooth bounded uniformly elliptic admissible coefficients.
analysis: Equations (5.3)–(5.4), p. 23, and the Duhamel identity (5.10), p. 26, do not use a consistent factor \(1/2\).

The random variable in (5.3) has covariance \(\int_s^t a(r,y)dr\), whereas (5.4) prints \(\Sigma_{s,t}=\frac12\int_s^t a(r,y)dr\). For constant \(\sigma=1\) and \(f(x)=\cos x\), the actual adjoint in (5.3) gives \(e^{-(t-s)/2}\cos x\); the printed kernel gives \(e^{-(t-s)/4}\cos x\).

Even if \(T\) is defined by the actual adjoint (5.3), the \(H\) defined on p. 23 needs a factor \(1/2\) in (5.10). To see this without a convention ambiguity, take smooth time-independent \(a(x)=1+\frac12e^{-x^2}\), \(f=1\), \(s=0\), and \(0<t<1/n\). Then \(Q_{0,t}^n1=1\), while the actual adjoint has \(T_{0,t}1=1+\frac t2a''+o(t)\) and \(\int_0^tQ_{0,k_n(r)}^nH_{r,t}^n1\,dr=-ta''+o(t)\). At \(x=0\), the printed right side of (5.10) is \(1+t/2+o(t)\), not 1.

A consistent repair uses \(\Sigma=\int a\), the generator \(\frac12a^{ij}\partial_{ij}\), and \(\frac12H\) in the Duhamel formula. These factors can be absorbed in the subsequent norm estimates; the smoothing-rate conclusion is not refuted. The same definitions and (5.10) occur on v6 pp. 26–29.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: Actual covariance is integral a, while printed Sigma is half that. Constant sigma gives exp(-t/2)cos(x) versus exp(-t/4)cos(x). For f=1, Q1=1, T1=1+(t/2)a''+o(t), integral QH1=-t a''+o(t); the printed RHS is 1+t/2+o(t) at x=0.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: A uniform covariance convention cannot reconcile both the actual random variable in (5.3) and the printed factors.

problems.title: Proposition 4.6(b) has the wrong control power
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: Problem 6 (Minor: Proposition 4.6(b) has incorrect homogeneity). The right side on p. 21 contains \(w_0(0,1)\), whereas it must scale as \(w_0(0,1)^{1/q}\).
claim: Recorded check: Proposition 4.6(b) has the wrong control power
d=1,p=q=4,pbar=1, g_epsilon=epsilon*f, f smooth compactly supported nonnegative nonzero with L4 norm one; w0(s,t)=epsilon^4(t-s), Gamma=1. Bessel potential order -1 is an L4 contraction.
analysis: The right side on p. 21 contains \(w_0(0,1)\), whereas it must scale as \(w_0(0,1)^{1/q}\).

Take \(d=1,p=q=4,\bar p=1\). Let \(f\geq0\) be smooth, nonzero, compactly supported and normalized by \(\|f\|_4=1\). Put \(g_\epsilon(t,x)=\epsilon f(x)\), \(w_0(s,t)=\epsilon^4(t-s)\), and \(\Gamma=1\). The Bessel potential operator of order \(-1\) is an \(L^4\) contraction, so both hypotheses of Proposition 4.6 hold. Its left side equals \(\epsilon\,\mathbb E\int_0^1 f(B_r)dr=c\epsilon\), with \(c>0\), whereas its right side is \(N\epsilon^4\). This fails as \(\epsilon\downarrow0\). Part (a) already has the correct power; Theorem 6.1(iii) and Theorem 2.3(iii) also print the correct power. Restoring it in part (b) repairs this localized statement. It does not establish a defect in their final rate. The same incorrect power is visible on v6 p. 24.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: The left side is c*epsilon with c>0, but printed right side N*w0(0,1) is N*epsilon^4. This fails as epsilon tends to zero.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: Part(a), Theorem6.1(iii), and Theorem2.3(iii) already print w0^(1/q).

problems.title: Girsanov density uses the wrong direction/process
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 7: Problem 7 (Minor: the change-of-measure direction in (5.33) is reversed).
claim: Recorded check: Girsanov density uses the wrong direction/process
Take sigma=1 and smooth compactly supported bn=b equal to one near the initial point; all drift integrability/local boundedness assumptions hold. Density is exp(-integral u dB -1/2 integral |u|2).
analysis: The density in the proof of Theorem 5.1, p. 36, introduces the negative of the desired drift into the driftless Euler process.

Let \(u_r=(\sigma^{-1}b^n)(r,\bar X_{k_n(r)}^n)\) and use the printed density \(\rho=\exp(-\int u\,dB-\frac12\int|u|^2dr)\). Under \(dQ=\rho\,dP\), \(\widetilde B=B+\int u\,dr\) is Brownian. Hence \[d\bar X_r^n
=\sigma(r,\bar X_{k_n(r)}^n)d\widetilde B_r
-b^n(r,\bar X_{k_n(r)}^n)dr,\] rather than the positive drift in (1.3). This distinction already occurs for a smooth compactly supported scalar drift equal to one near the initial point, which satisfies Condition B. The two laws have opposite initial drift generators.

Use the positive stochastic-integral sign to obtain the positive drift under the new measure. The exponential-moment argument depends on \(|u|^2\), so its estimates survive this correction. The continuum proof on p. 40 similarly evaluates its negative-sign density along \(\bar X\) while making a claim about the law of \(X\); it must consistently choose the process and direction of measure change. These are repairable proof identities, not counterexamples to the stated moment estimates. No independent comparison of these two passages with v6 is asserted here.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: Under Q=rho P, Btilde=B+integral u is Brownian. Hence the driftless Euler process has drift -bn under Q, not +bn as claimed. Their initial generators differ.

Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: One can consistently start from the drifted process with the negative density, or from the driftless process with the positive density. The printed process/direction choice does neither.

problems.title: Negative-order multiplier norm is used in place of positive order
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 8: Problem 8 (Minor: the multiplier norm in Theorem 2.3(iii)’s proof has the wrong order).
claim: Recorded check: Negative-order multiplier norm is used in place of positive order
d=1,p=2,q=10 satisfies d/p+4/q<1. For smooth compactly supported nonzero psi, gk=hk=psi cos(kx), constant in time.
analysis: On p. 46, the product estimate and the definition of \(w_1\) use \(\|g\|_{L^q_tL^{-1,p}_x}\), although Lemma A.3 requires the multiplier in the positive-order space \(L^{1,p}\).

There is no continuous multiplication map \(H^{-1}(\mathbb R)\times H^{-1}(\mathbb R)\to H^{-1}(\mathbb R)\). For a nonzero smooth compactly supported \(\psi\), take \(g_k=h_k=\psi(x)\cos(kx)\). Both \(H^{-1}\) norms are \(O(k^{-1})\), while \[g_kh_k=\tfrac12\psi^2+\tfrac12\psi^2\cos(2kx)
\longrightarrow\tfrac12\psi^2\ne0\quad\hbox{in }H^{-1}.\] Thus the printed negative-order product bound fails. This check applies already with \(d=1,p=2,q=10\), which obey \(d/p+4/q<1\); a constant time dependence supplies the temporal norms.

Here \(g=\nabla U\) actually has a uniformly bounded \(L^q_tL^{1,p}_x\) norm by (7.2), and \(p>d\). Replacing the negative-order norm of \(g\) by the positive-order norm repairs the multiplication step. The sentence choosing \(q_2=2\) must also be made consistent with \(q_3=q/2\): the available choice is \(q_2=q\). With these repairs, the product control has the required homogeneity. This local error does not refute (2.11). The same multiplier sign occurs on v6 p. 53.
result: Recorded evidence: Evidence: Both H^-1 norms are O(1/k), while product tends in H^-1 to psi^2/2. Thus two negative-order factors cannot obey the printed multiplier inequality.
Recorded evidence: Counterevidence: The actual g=grad U has the positive-order Lq_t L^(1,p)_x bound by (7.2), with p>d.

report: Abstract: The barrier argument and the mechanism preserving complementarity in the hydrodynamic limit were examined in the frozen journal version. Two core proof defects and five local corrections are identified, with explicit examples, dependency boundaries and repairs. They concern the time range of an auxiliary estimate, an overbroad density bound, boundary orientation, the initial-time density statement, the coupling construction, martingale formulas, and the hypotheses of an imported linear PDE result. No counterexample to the intended positive-time hydrodynamic limit or to weak-solution uniqueness is established.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of A Weak Formulation of Free Boundary Problems and Its Application to Hydrodynamic Limits of Particle Systems with Selection
# Identity, assumptions, and review scope

The reviewed paper is Rami Atar, A weak formulation of free boundary problems and its application to hydrodynamic limits of particle systems with selection, Annals of Probability 53(5) (2025), 1825–1856, DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1751 [atar]. The frozen author-hosted journal PDF has 32 pages. All its definitions, statements, proofs and references were read. Page numbers below are journal page numbers; PDF page \(k\) is page \(1824+k\).

The individual diffusion has bounded coefficients \(b,c\), with \(b\in C^1\), \(c\in C^2\), bounded \(c'\), and \(c\) bounded away from zero. Its branching rate is \(\kappa\geq0\), and its forward operator is \[L^*u=\partial_x^2(au)-\partial_x(bu)+\kappa u,\qquad a=c^2/2.\] The initial measure \(\xi_0\) is any probability measure, including an atomic one. The injection measure \(\alpha\) is nonnegative and locally finite in time. Its cumulative mass \(I\) satisfies either the spatial domination condition \(\alpha(dx,dt)\leq C\,dx\,dI_t\) with positive temporal Hölder regularity, or temporal Hölder regularity strictly greater than \(1/2\). The removal mass \(J\) is nondecreasing, absolutely continuous, Hölder continuous with a positive exponent and zero at zero. The mass equation \[m_t=1+\kappa\int_0^t m_s\,ds+I_t-J_t\] has a strictly positive global lower bound. The stochastic primitives satisfy the independence and adapted martingale requirements (S.6)–(S.7), and their normalized data converge in probability as in Assumption 2.3.

The weak formulation couples \(\partial_tu-L^*u=\alpha-\beta\) with \(\beta(\mathbb R\times[0,t])=J_t\), nonnegativity, and \[\beta\{(x,t):U(x,t)>0\}=0,\qquad
U(x,t)=\int_{-\infty}^x u(y,t)\,dy.\] This orientation describes removal on the left. Absolute continuity of \(J\) is operative: it makes this condition invariant under changing a density on a Lebesgue-null set of times.
# Two auxiliary estimates

Problem 1 (Minor: Lemma 3.8 needs a small-time restriction).  Lemma 3.8, pp. 1841–1842, is stated for every \(\delta>0\), but its proof uses (3.2), p. 1834, which is established only for times at most one. Its unrestricted statement is false.

Proof. Take \(b=1\), \(c=1\), \(\kappa>0\), no injection, and \(J_t=\kappa t\). Put \[\lambda=\sqrt{2\kappa},\qquad v=1+\lambda,\qquad
q(z)=2\kappa z e^{-\lambda z}\mathbf1_{\{z\geq0\}},\] and define \[u(x,t)=q(x-vt),\quad \xi_0(dx)=q(x)\,dx,\quad
\beta(dx,dt)=\kappa\delta_{vt}(dx)\,dt.\] These are admissible data with \(m_t=1\). In particular, \(J\) is Lipschitz and the first injection alternative holds trivially for \(\alpha=0\). Direct calculation gives \[\int q=1,\qquad
\tfrac12q''+(v-1)q'+\kappa q=0\quad(z>0),\qquad
\tfrac12q'(0)=\kappa.\] Since \(q(0)=0\), the distributional boundary term is precisely \(-\kappa\delta_{vt}\); thus this pair solves the weak equation and complementarity condition.

For the drift-one Brownian diffusion, \(\int_{-\infty}^x p_t(x,y)\,dy=\Phi(-\sqrt t)\). Hence \(c_*=\Phi(-1)\) is a valid constant in (3.2), and set \(C_*=2/c_*\), the constant denoted \(c^*\) in Lemma 3.8. For \(n=2\), \[j_2(\delta)=e^{\kappa\delta}-1,\qquad
\rho_{2,\delta}=2v\delta.\] Let \(F(z)=1-(1+z)e^{-z}\), the distribution function of a unit-rate Gamma distribution of shape two. When \(p=C_*(e^{\kappa\delta}-1)<1\), the lemma’s domain condition holds, but its proposed bound is \[\Lambda_p(u_\delta)=v\delta+\frac{F^{-1}(p)}{\sqrt{2\kappa}}.\] For \(\kappa=10^{-4}\), \(\delta=100\), independent high-precision evaluation gives \[p=0.1266918912,\qquad
\rho_{2,\delta}=202.8284271,\qquad
\Lambda_p(u_\delta)=144.8644698.\] The claimed inequality is reversed by about \(57.964\). This is not dependent on an optimized choice of \(c_*\): for any fixed valid \(c_*>0\), take \(\kappa\delta=h\) small enough that \(C_*(e^h-1)<1\), then let \(\kappa\downarrow0\). The boundary displacement grows like \(\kappa^{-1}\), whereas the quantile offset grows like \(\kappa^{-1/2}\). ◻

Counterevidence and impact. Proposition 3.7 uses Lemma 3.8 only for sufficiently small \(\delta\), and uniqueness takes \(\delta\downarrow0\). Restricting Lemma 3.8 to \(0<\delta\leq1\) repairs the displayed proof without changing that limit argument. Alternatively a constant depending on a specified time horizon can be used. The example disproves the unrestricted lemma, not Theorem 3.1.

Problem 2 (Minor: the \(v\)-bound in Lemma 3.3(iii) is too general).  On p. 1835, \(v\) is defined in part (i) using an arbitrary measure \(\gamma\) whose cumulative mass has some positive Hölder exponent. Part (iii)’s assertion \(v\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,\infty);L^\infty)\) does not follow for that \(v\).

Take standard Brownian motion, \(\kappa=0\), any probability initial measure, and \[\gamma(dx,ds)=\delta_0(dx)(1-s)^{-3/4}\mathbf1_{(0,1)}(s)\,ds.\] Its cumulative mass is \(K_t=4[1-(1-t)_+^{1/4}]\), a nondecreasing \(1/4\)-Hölder function starting at zero. For \(t=1-\varepsilon\), \(|x|\leq\sqrt\varepsilon\), and \(0<\varepsilon<1/3\), retaining only \(r=t-s\in[\varepsilon,2\varepsilon]\) gives \[(S*\gamma)(x,1-\varepsilon)
\geq
\frac{e^{-1/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sqrt2\,3^{3/4}}\,
\varepsilon^{-1/4}.\] Thus the essential supremum is unbounded near time one. This is a positive-measure phenomenon, not just an infinite value at a single point.

Counterevidence and repair. The proof on p. 1836 estimates \(S_t\xi_0+S*\alpha\), using the stronger admissibility alternatives for \(\alpha\). The \(v\) actually used in Lemmas 4.3–4.4 is explicitly this latter function. Setting \(v=S_t\xi_0+S*\alpha\) in part (iii), or adding the same admissibility conditions on \(\gamma\), removes the overstatement. The example does not refute the boundedness of that intended dominating density or part (i)’s \(L^1_tL^q_x\) assertion.
# Boundary orientation and initial time

Problem 3 (Minor: Remark 2.6(i) identifies the opposite selection boundary).  Remark 2.6(i), p. 1833, states that a classical solution of (1.2) produces a solution of (2.10) by taking \(\beta(dx,dt)=c_0\delta_{\ell_t}(dx)\,dt\). This is incompatible with the left-tail complementarity condition.

For a concrete classical solution of (1.2), p. 1826, set \(c_0=1\), \(\ell_t=1\) and \(u(x,t)=2(1-x)\) on \(0\leq x\leq1\), zero for \(x\geq1\), with this stationary initial density. It has mass one, zero second derivative in the interior and both specified flux values equal to one. If the density is extended by zero to \(x<0\), then \[U(1,t)=\int_{-\infty}^1u(x,t)\,dx=1,\qquad
\beta\{U>0\}\big|_{\mathbb R\times[0,T]}=T>0.\] Hence the proposed pair fails (2.10)(ii).

Counterevidence and repair. Equation (1.2) deliberately removes the rightmost particle and includes reflection at the origin; the main model removes the leftmost particle on the full line. A corresponding weak formulation must use the right tail and the appropriate half-line boundary flux, or explicitly transform the orientation and domain. Merely extending the half-line density by zero also introduces a distributional issue at the reflecting endpoint. The general idea of a complementary weak formulation remains useful; this direct identification with (1.2) is the incorrect statement.

Problem 4 (Minor: Theorem 2.5(ii)’s density formula must exclude time zero).  On p. 1833, the theorem sets \(\xi_t(dx)=u(x,t)\,dx\) and asserts continuity on \(\mathbb R_+=[0,\infty)\), although arbitrary probability initial measures are allowed.

Choose \(b=0,c=1,\kappa=0,\alpha=0,J=0,\xi_0=\delta_0\). These are admissible data, with mass identically one, and can be approximated by particles initially at zero and no injections or removals on each fixed finite horizon. At positive times the density is the heat kernel. At time zero there is no Lebesgue density of \(\delta_0\), whatever version of \(u\) is chosen. In particular, an absolutely continuous measure assigns zero to \(\{0\}\), whereas \(\delta_0\{0\}=1\).

Counterevidence and repair. The measure-valued path is nevertheless weakly continuous at zero. The proof of Lemma 4.3 on p. 1851 already makes the correct distinction: \(\xi_t=u(\cdot,t)\,dx\) for \(t>0\), and \(\xi_0\) is specified separately. Incorporating that convention in Theorem 2.5(ii) repairs the endpoint wording. This is not a counterexample to hydrodynamic convergence.
# The particle construction and martingale identities

Problem 5 (Major: the stated coupling does not establish the required pathwise domination).  The no-removal comparison on p. 1847 is said to use exactly the same stochastic primitives, changing only the removal times to infinity. With the chronological family labels prescribed on p. 1831, this does not imply \(\xi_t^N\leq\zeta_t^N\) as measures.

A finite genealogy showing the obstruction. Consider one root, with Brownian motion, positive branching rate and no injections before the comparison time. There is a positive-probability event on which the root first has child \(1\), that child is to its left at a deterministic removal time and is removed, and no other particle is removed before the comparison time. In the no-removal system, child \(1\) survives and has a child before the root’s next birth. That extra child receives chronological label \(2\).

At the root’s next birth, the original system gives the newborn label \(2\), whereas the no-removal system gives the corresponding newborn label \(3\). The first uses \(B^2\), while its genealogically corresponding counterpart uses \(B^3\). Moreover, the no-removal particle already labelled \(2\) started earlier at a different space-time location. At a later time before further events, with positive probability the original particle \(2\) occupies a point occupied by none of the finitely many no-removal particles. Atomic measure domination therefore fails. The required event is obtained by prescribing finitely many disjoint Poisson event windows and open Brownian path constraints. It can also be embedded in an \(N\)-particle configuration. ◻

Counterevidence and repair. A valid domination coupling does exist: construct a common unremoved genealogical forest, with drivers indexed by root, parent and child number, then prune the selected system without reassigning drivers on surviving vertices. Chronological numbers can subsequently be used as bookkeeping. Nonanticipation in (S.7) and independent fresh drivers preserve the required marginal law. This explicit coupling, rather than literal reuse of the chronological array, supports the domination used in Lemmas 4.2–4.3 and the many-to-one estimates. The finding concerns the stated construction, not a failure of stochastic domination under all couplings. The invalid comparison is used directly in the compact-containment estimate (4.8) and in the passage from (4.18) to absolute continuity of every limit of the selected system. Those are core steps of Lemmas 4.2–4.3 and Theorem 2.5. A replacement coupling with the correct marginal laws is therefore needed to complete that derivation. This core proof defect is Major even though the genealogical repair supports the intended result.

Problem 6 (Minor: three transcription errors in Lemma 4.1’s martingale derivation).  The formulas on pp. 1846–1847 require an indicator reversal, removal of an extra branching-rate factor, and retention of the terminal configuration term before setting \(t=T\).

The definition after (4.3) prints \(\mathbf1_{\{\sigma^i\geq t\}}\int_{\sigma^i}^{t\wedge\tau^i}c\,\partial_x\phi\,dB^i\). For an initial particle \(\sigma^i=0\), this is zero for every \(t>0\), whereas the preceding Itô integral is generally nonzero. For instance, take standard Brownian motion, no events on a short interval and a compactly supported test function with nonzero spatial derivative near the initial point. The correct indicator is \(\mathbf1_{\{t\geq\sigma^i\}}\).

Next, the printed definition \(M_t^{\#,N}=\sum_i\int_{\sigma^i}^{t\wedge\tau^i}d\widehat\pi_s^i\) gives \[Y_t^N=\kappa\int_0^t m_s^N\,ds+M_t^{\#,N},\] not (4.5)’s expression with \(\kappa M_t^{\#,N}\). With one initial particle, \(\kappa=2\), and no births or removals up to \(t\), the defined martingale equals \(-2t\). The printed right side is then \(2t-4t=-2t\), while \(Y_t^N=0\).

Finally, the finite-time sum at the bottom of p. 1846 requires \[\int_{\mathbb R\times[0,t]}\phi\,d\bar\beta^N
=\langle\phi_0,\bar\xi_0^N\rangle
+\int_{\mathbb R\times[0,t]}\phi\,d\bar\alpha^N
+\int_0^t\langle\partial_s\phi+L\phi,\bar\xi_s^N\rangle ds
+\bar M_t^N-\langle\phi_t,\bar\xi_t^N\rangle.\] The last term is omitted in the displayed expression.

Counterevidence and repair. The next page explicitly sets \(t=T\), where \(\phi_T=0\), and the quadratic-variation argument already uses the correct lifetime orientation. Correcting these three formulas restores the usual decomposition and its order \(N^{-1}\) quadratic variation. No failure of Lemma 4.1’s vanishing-noise conclusion is established.
# The cited linear PDE theory

Problem 7 (Major: the imported linear well-posedness argument lacks its required hypotheses).  The passage following (2.9), p. 1833, transforms the forward operator using \(\bar b=-b+a'\) and \(\bar\kappa=\kappa-b'\), then invokes Amann’s Theorems 1 and 13 and Remarks 1 and 2(b). The paper’s assumptions do not imply the explicit coefficient bounds in that reference.

The acquired original [amann], p. 105, assumes bounded uniformly smooth coefficients in its general elliptic operator; Remark 2(b), p. 116, explicitly permits a bounded measurable zeroth-order coefficient. But \(b(x)=\sin(x^2)\), \(c=1\) satisfy Assumption 2.1, while \[\bar\kappa(x)=\kappa-2x\cos(x^2)\] is unbounded. Thus the stated transformation does not by itself verify the cited sufficient conditions. The reference also mentions further relaxations; those should not be silently identified with the assumptions here.

A direct repair under the original assumptions. The underlying linear statement can instead be justified without a bound on \(b'\). Let \(h=|c|\), set \[y=F(x)=\int_0^x h(r)^{-1}\,dr,\qquad
w(y,t)=h(x)u(x,t),\quad x=F^{-1}(y).\] This is a global bi-Lipschitz change of variable, preserving the \(L^1_tL^q_x\) class for every finite \(q>1\). Applying the chain rule in the weak formulation, justified by local smooth approximation of tests, gives \[\partial_tw=\tfrac12\partial_y^2w-\partial_y(Bw)+\kappa w+\nu,
\quad
B(y)=\frac{b(x)}{h(x)}-\frac12h'(x),\] where \(B\) is bounded and \(\nu\) is the pushforward of the driving measure. Include the pushed initial measure at time zero in a measure \(\eta\). With \(G\) the standard heat kernel, the equation has the distributional Duhamel form \[w=G*\eta-(\partial_yG)*(Bw)+\kappa G*w.\] The measure term belongs to \(L^1([0,T];L^q)\), since \(\|G_t\|_q=C_qt^{-(q-1)/(2q)}\) and the exponent is less than one. The remaining linear operator is a contraction in the equivalent norm \(\int_0^T e^{-\lambda t}\|w_t\|_qdt\) for sufficiently large \(\lambda\), because \[\int_0^T e^{-\lambda t}\|\partial_yG_t\|_1dt
\leq C\lambda^{-1/2},\qquad
\int_0^T e^{-\lambda t}\|G_t\|_1dt\leq\lambda^{-1}.\] Heat-equation duality gives the same Duhamel identity for any distributional solution in this class. The contraction therefore supplies existence and uniqueness there; transforming back gives the needed linear result. Compatibility across \(q\) follows by performing the construction simultaneously in intersections of these spaces.

Dependency and severity. This repair addresses the imported linear uniqueness used to identify the mild version in Lemma 3.3 and the limit equation in Section 4. It explains why a citation-hypothesis mismatch should not be presented as a counterexample to the main theorem. A precise applicable reference or the direct argument should replace the unsupported application. The displayed invocation does not establish linear well-posedness for the stated coefficient class; Lemma 3.3 then uses this unsupported uniqueness to identify the mild representative, on which the barrier proof and limit identification depend. This is a Major gap in a core derivation. The direct argument above supplies a repair under the original assumptions; it does not turn the original invocation into a valid one or establish that the final theorem is false.
# Positive checks, coverage, and version limits

The six mass-transport inequalities of Lemma 3.5 were checked against their total-mass restrictions. For a density of mass \(m\) with tail \(H(r)\), the two cut operators have tails \[(C_d u)[r,\infty)=\min\{H(r),m-d\},\] \[(C_{D,d}u)[r,\infty)
=H(r)-\min\{d,\max\{0,H(r)-(m-D-d)\}\}.\] These identities give direct checks of the order and modulus calculations. An independent exact-rational program checked 149,529 admissible scalar cases of parts (ii), (iv) and (vi), with no failures; finite checks supplement the algebra and do not prove the general assertions.

In the convergence argument, the stopped population estimate, first and second moments of the dominating branching system, compact containment and the continuity modulus were traced. Density identification is a positive-time assertion. The complementarity step uses countably many rational space-time tests, absence of spatial atoms in the limit, and continuity of its measure-valued path. At the switch from \([r,\infty)\) to \((r,\infty)\) on p. 1854, retaining a strictly smaller rational threshold from the preceding approximation avoids any loss of a possible spatial atom of \(\beta\); this is an explicit intended reading, not an assumption that \(\beta\) has no spatial atoms.

The independent primary-authored calculations verify the traveling profile’s mass, interior PDE and boundary flux, the numerical quantile violation, and the cut-operator cases. No author code was run. The acquired Amann PDF was inspected at the relevant statements, coefficient assumptions and remarks; its complete abstract functional-analysis development was not independently re-proved.

The current official arXiv metadata identifies v4 of 15 November 2024 [arxiv], earlier than the reviewed 2025 journal PDF. No equivalence or later correction is inferred from it. The bounded official metadata check identified no formal correction resolving the reported items; the publisher page returned no usable correction content, and empty Crossref relation fields do not prove absence of corrections. These limits remain explicit. The coupling construction and imported linear well-posedness argument are classified Major because their invalid derivations are directly used in the core proof. The other five findings remain Minor: their demonstrated failures are outside the range actually needed, concern auxiliary wording, or have the correct identities already used at the decisive step. The existence of repairs is recorded separately from severity. No counterexample to the intended positive-time hydrodynamic limit or weak-solution uniqueness is established. Independent acceptance status is recorded in the accompanying provenance.

problems.title: Lemma3.8's unrestricted time range is false
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 1: Problem 1 (Minor: Lemma 3.8 needs a small-time restriction).
claim: Recorded check: Lemma3.8's unrestricted time range is false
analysis: Lemma 3.8, pp. 1841–1842, is stated for every \(\delta>0\), but its proof uses (3.2), p. 1834, which is established only for times at most one. Its unrestricted statement is false.

Proof. Take \(b=1\), \(c=1\), \(\kappa>0\), no injection, and \(J_t=\kappa t\). Put \[\lambda=\sqrt{2\kappa},\qquad v=1+\lambda,\qquad
q(z)=2\kappa z e^{-\lambda z}\mathbf1_{\{z\geq0\}},\] and define \[u(x,t)=q(x-vt),\quad \xi_0(dx)=q(x)\,dx,\quad
\beta(dx,dt)=\kappa\delta_{vt}(dx)\,dt.\] These are admissible data with \(m_t=1\). In particular, \(J\) is Lipschitz and the first injection alternative holds trivially for \(\alpha=0\). Direct calculation gives \[\int q=1,\qquad
\tfrac12q''+(v-1)q'+\kappa q=0\quad(z>0),\qquad
\tfrac12q'(0)=\kappa.\] Since \(q(0)=0\), the distributional boundary term is precisely \(-\kappa\delta_{vt}\); thus this pair solves the weak equation and complementarity condition.

For the drift-one Brownian diffusion, \(\int_{-\infty}^x p_t(x,y)\,dy=\Phi(-\sqrt t)\). Hence \(c_*=\Phi(-1)\) is a valid constant in (3.2), and set \(C_*=2/c_*\), the constant denoted \(c^*\) in Lemma 3.8. For \(n=2\), \[j_2(\delta)=e^{\kappa\delta}-1,\qquad
\rho_{2,\delta}=2v\delta.\] Let \(F(z)=1-(1+z)e^{-z}\), the distribution function of a unit-rate Gamma distribution of shape two. When \(p=C_*(e^{\kappa\delta}-1)<1\), the lemma’s domain condition holds, but its proposed bound is \[\Lambda_p(u_\delta)=v\delta+\frac{F^{-1}(p)}{\sqrt{2\kappa}}.\] For \(\kappa=10^{-4}\), \(\delta=100\), independent high-precision evaluation gives \[p=0.1266918912,\qquad
\rho_{2,\delta}=202.8284271,\qquad
\Lambda_p(u_\delta)=144.8644698.\] The claimed inequality is reversed by about \(57.964\). This is not dependent on an optimized choice of \(c_*\): for any fixed valid \(c_*>0\), take \(\kappa\delta=h\) small enough that \(C_*(e^h-1)<1\), then let \(\kappa\downarrow0\). The boundary displacement grows like \(\kappa^{-1}\), whereas the quantile offset grows like \(\kappa^{-1/2}\). ◻

Counterevidence and impact. Proposition 3.7 uses Lemma 3.8 only for sufficiently small \(\delta\), and uniqueness takes \(\delta\downarrow0\). Restricting Lemma 3.8 to \(0<\delta\leq1\) repairs the displayed proof without changing that limit argument. Alternatively a constant depending on a specified time horizon can be used. The example disproves the unrestricted lemma, not Theorem 3.1.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Lemma3.8's unrestricted time range is false

problems.title: Lemma3.3(iii) overstates boundedness for the general gamma from part(i)
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (Minor: the \(v\)-bound in Lemma 3.3(iii) is too general).
claim: Recorded check: Lemma3.3(iii) overstates boundedness for the general gamma from part(i)
analysis: On p. 1835, \(v\) is defined in part (i) using an arbitrary measure \(\gamma\) whose cumulative mass has some positive Hölder exponent. Part (iii)’s assertion \(v\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}((0,\infty);L^\infty)\) does not follow for that \(v\).

Take standard Brownian motion, \(\kappa=0\), any probability initial measure, and \[\gamma(dx,ds)=\delta_0(dx)(1-s)^{-3/4}\mathbf1_{(0,1)}(s)\,ds.\] Its cumulative mass is \(K_t=4[1-(1-t)_+^{1/4}]\), a nondecreasing \(1/4\)-Hölder function starting at zero. For \(t=1-\varepsilon\), \(|x|\leq\sqrt\varepsilon\), and \(0<\varepsilon<1/3\), retaining only \(r=t-s\in[\varepsilon,2\varepsilon]\) gives \[(S*\gamma)(x,1-\varepsilon)
\geq
\frac{e^{-1/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sqrt2\,3^{3/4}}\,
\varepsilon^{-1/4}.\] Thus the essential supremum is unbounded near time one. This is a positive-measure phenomenon, not just an infinite value at a single point.

Counterevidence and repair. The proof on p. 1836 estimates \(S_t\xi_0+S*\alpha\), using the stronger admissibility alternatives for \(\alpha\). The \(v\) actually used in Lemmas 4.3–4.4 is explicitly this latter function. Setting \(v=S_t\xi_0+S*\alpha\) in part (iii), or adding the same admissibility conditions on \(\gamma\), removes the overstatement. The example does not refute the boundedness of that intended dominating density or part (i)’s \(L^1_tL^q_x\) assertion.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Lemma3.3(iii) overstates boundedness for the general gamma from part(i)

problems.title: Remark2.6(i) applies left-tail complementarity to a right-boundary problem
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 3: Problem 3 (Minor: Remark 2.6(i) identifies the opposite selection boundary).
claim: Recorded check: Remark2.6(i) applies left-tail complementarity to a right-boundary problem
analysis: Remark 2.6(i), p. 1833, states that a classical solution of (1.2) produces a solution of (2.10) by taking \(\beta(dx,dt)=c_0\delta_{\ell_t}(dx)\,dt\). This is incompatible with the left-tail complementarity condition.

For a concrete classical solution of (1.2), p. 1826, set \(c_0=1\), \(\ell_t=1\) and \(u(x,t)=2(1-x)\) on \(0\leq x\leq1\), zero for \(x\geq1\), with this stationary initial density. It has mass one, zero second derivative in the interior and both specified flux values equal to one. If the density is extended by zero to \(x<0\), then \[U(1,t)=\int_{-\infty}^1u(x,t)\,dx=1,\qquad
\beta\{U>0\}\big|_{\mathbb R\times[0,T]}=T>0.\] Hence the proposed pair fails (2.10)(ii).

Counterevidence and repair. Equation (1.2) deliberately removes the rightmost particle and includes reflection at the origin; the main model removes the leftmost particle on the full line. A corresponding weak formulation must use the right tail and the appropriate half-line boundary flux, or explicitly transform the orientation and domain. Merely extending the half-line density by zero also introduces a distributional issue at the reflecting endpoint. The general idea of a complementary weak formulation remains useful; this direct identification with (1.2) is the incorrect statement.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Remark2.6(i) applies left-tail complementarity to a right-boundary problem

problems.title: Density representation at t=0 excludes allowed atomic initial measures
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 4: Problem 4 (Minor: Theorem 2.5(ii)’s density formula must exclude time zero).
claim: Recorded check: Density representation at t=0 excludes allowed atomic initial measures
analysis: On p. 1833, the theorem sets \(\xi_t(dx)=u(x,t)\,dx\) and asserts continuity on \(\mathbb R_+=[0,\infty)\), although arbitrary probability initial measures are allowed.

Choose \(b=0,c=1,\kappa=0,\alpha=0,J=0,\xi_0=\delta_0\). These are admissible data, with mass identically one, and can be approximated by particles initially at zero and no injections or removals on each fixed finite horizon. At positive times the density is the heat kernel. At time zero there is no Lebesgue density of \(\delta_0\), whatever version of \(u\) is chosen. In particular, an absolutely continuous measure assigns zero to \(\{0\}\), whereas \(\delta_0\{0\}=1\).

Counterevidence and repair. The measure-valued path is nevertheless weakly continuous at zero. The proof of Lemma 4.3 on p. 1851 already makes the correct distinction: \(\xi_t=u(\cdot,t)\,dx\) for \(t>0\), and \(\xi_0\) is specified separately. Incorporating that convention in Theorem 2.5(ii) repairs the endpoint wording. This is not a counterexample to hydrodynamic convergence.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Density representation at t=0 excludes allowed atomic initial measures

problems.title: Literal reuse of chronological label drivers fails pathwise domination
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 5: Problem 5 (Major: the stated coupling does not establish the required pathwise domination).
claim: Recorded check: Literal reuse of chronological label drivers fails pathwise domination
analysis: The no-removal comparison on p. 1847 is said to use exactly the same stochastic primitives, changing only the removal times to infinity. With the chronological family labels prescribed on p. 1831, this does not imply \(\xi_t^N\leq\zeta_t^N\) as measures.

A finite genealogy showing the obstruction. Consider one root, with Brownian motion, positive branching rate and no injections before the comparison time. There is a positive-probability event on which the root first has child \(1\), that child is to its left at a deterministic removal time and is removed, and no other particle is removed before the comparison time. In the no-removal system, child \(1\) survives and has a child before the root’s next birth. That extra child receives chronological label \(2\).

At the root’s next birth, the original system gives the newborn label \(2\), whereas the no-removal system gives the corresponding newborn label \(3\). The first uses \(B^2\), while its genealogically corresponding counterpart uses \(B^3\). Moreover, the no-removal particle already labelled \(2\) started earlier at a different space-time location. At a later time before further events, with positive probability the original particle \(2\) occupies a point occupied by none of the finitely many no-removal particles. Atomic measure domination therefore fails. The required event is obtained by prescribing finitely many disjoint Poisson event windows and open Brownian path constraints. It can also be embedded in an \(N\)-particle configuration. ◻

Counterevidence and repair. A valid domination coupling does exist: construct a common unremoved genealogical forest, with drivers indexed by root, parent and child number, then prune the selected system without reassigning drivers on surviving vertices. Chronological numbers can subsequently be used as bookkeeping. Nonanticipation in (S.7) and independent fresh drivers preserve the required marginal law. This explicit coupling, rather than literal reuse of the chronological array, supports the domination used in Lemmas 4.2–4.3 and the many-to-one estimates. The finding concerns the stated construction, not a failure of stochastic domination under all couplings. The invalid comparison is used directly in the compact-containment estimate (4.8) and in the passage from (4.18) to absolute continuity of every limit of the selected system. Those are core steps of Lemmas 4.2–4.3 and Theorem 2.5. A replacement coupling with the correct marginal laws is therefore needed to complete that derivation. This core proof defect is Major even though the genealogical repair supports the intended result.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Literal reuse of chronological label drivers fails pathwise domination

problems.title: Martingale derivation contains indicator, factor and terminal-term errors
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 6: Problem 6 (Minor: three transcription errors in Lemma 4.1’s martingale derivation).
claim: Recorded check: Martingale derivation contains indicator, factor and terminal-term errors
analysis: The formulas on pp. 1846–1847 require an indicator reversal, removal of an extra branching-rate factor, and retention of the terminal configuration term before setting \(t=T\).

The definition after (4.3) prints \(\mathbf1_{\{\sigma^i\geq t\}}\int_{\sigma^i}^{t\wedge\tau^i}c\,\partial_x\phi\,dB^i\). For an initial particle \(\sigma^i=0\), this is zero for every \(t>0\), whereas the preceding Itô integral is generally nonzero. For instance, take standard Brownian motion, no events on a short interval and a compactly supported test function with nonzero spatial derivative near the initial point. The correct indicator is \(\mathbf1_{\{t\geq\sigma^i\}}\).

Next, the printed definition \(M_t^{\#,N}=\sum_i\int_{\sigma^i}^{t\wedge\tau^i}d\widehat\pi_s^i\) gives \[Y_t^N=\kappa\int_0^t m_s^N\,ds+M_t^{\#,N},\] not (4.5)’s expression with \(\kappa M_t^{\#,N}\). With one initial particle, \(\kappa=2\), and no births or removals up to \(t\), the defined martingale equals \(-2t\). The printed right side is then \(2t-4t=-2t\), while \(Y_t^N=0\).

Finally, the finite-time sum at the bottom of p. 1846 requires \[\int_{\mathbb R\times[0,t]}\phi\,d\bar\beta^N
=\langle\phi_0,\bar\xi_0^N\rangle
+\int_{\mathbb R\times[0,t]}\phi\,d\bar\alpha^N
+\int_0^t\langle\partial_s\phi+L\phi,\bar\xi_s^N\rangle ds
+\bar M_t^N-\langle\phi_t,\bar\xi_t^N\rangle.\] The last term is omitted in the displayed expression.

Counterevidence and repair. The next page explicitly sets \(t=T\), where \(\phi_T=0\), and the quadratic-variation argument already uses the correct lifetime orientation. Correcting these three formulas restores the usual decomposition and its order \(N^{-1}\) quadratic variation. No failure of Lemma 4.1’s vanishing-noise conclusion is established.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Martingale derivation contains indicator, factor and terminal-term errors

problems.title: Imported linear PDE result's explicit coefficient hypotheses are not verified
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 7: Problem 7 (Major: the imported linear well-posedness argument lacks its required hypotheses).
claim: Recorded check: Imported linear PDE result's explicit coefficient hypotheses are not verified
analysis: The passage following (2.9), p. 1833, transforms the forward operator using \(\bar b=-b+a'\) and \(\bar\kappa=\kappa-b'\), then invokes Amann’s Theorems 1 and 13 and Remarks 1 and 2(b). The paper’s assumptions do not imply the explicit coefficient bounds in that reference.

The acquired original [amann], p. 105, assumes bounded uniformly smooth coefficients in its general elliptic operator; Remark 2(b), p. 116, explicitly permits a bounded measurable zeroth-order coefficient. But \(b(x)=\sin(x^2)\), \(c=1\) satisfy Assumption 2.1, while \[\bar\kappa(x)=\kappa-2x\cos(x^2)\] is unbounded. Thus the stated transformation does not by itself verify the cited sufficient conditions. The reference also mentions further relaxations; those should not be silently identified with the assumptions here.

A direct repair under the original assumptions. The underlying linear statement can instead be justified without a bound on \(b'\). Let \(h=|c|\), set \[y=F(x)=\int_0^x h(r)^{-1}\,dr,\qquad
w(y,t)=h(x)u(x,t),\quad x=F^{-1}(y).\] This is a global bi-Lipschitz change of variable, preserving the \(L^1_tL^q_x\) class for every finite \(q>1\). Applying the chain rule in the weak formulation, justified by local smooth approximation of tests, gives \[\partial_tw=\tfrac12\partial_y^2w-\partial_y(Bw)+\kappa w+\nu,
\quad
B(y)=\frac{b(x)}{h(x)}-\frac12h'(x),\] where \(B\) is bounded and \(\nu\) is the pushforward of the driving measure. Include the pushed initial measure at time zero in a measure \(\eta\). With \(G\) the standard heat kernel, the equation has the distributional Duhamel form \[w=G*\eta-(\partial_yG)*(Bw)+\kappa G*w.\] The measure term belongs to \(L^1([0,T];L^q)\), since \(\|G_t\|_q=C_qt^{-(q-1)/(2q)}\) and the exponent is less than one. The remaining linear operator is a contraction in the equivalent norm \(\int_0^T e^{-\lambda t}\|w_t\|_qdt\) for sufficiently large \(\lambda\), because \[\int_0^T e^{-\lambda t}\|\partial_yG_t\|_1dt
\leq C\lambda^{-1/2},\qquad
\int_0^T e^{-\lambda t}\|G_t\|_1dt\leq\lambda^{-1}.\] Heat-equation duality gives the same Duhamel identity for any distributional solution in this class. The contraction therefore supplies existence and uniqueness there; transforming back gives the needed linear result. Compatibility across \(q\) follows by performing the construction simultaneously in intersections of these spaces.

Dependency and severity. This repair addresses the imported linear uniqueness used to identify the mild version in Lemma 3.3 and the limit equation in Section 4. It explains why a citation-hypothesis mismatch should not be presented as a counterexample to the main theorem. A precise applicable reference or the direct argument should replace the unsupported application. The displayed invocation does not establish linear well-posedness for the stated coefficient class; Lemma 3.3 then uses this unsupported uniqueness to identify the mild representative, on which the barrier proof and limit identification depend. This is a Major gap in a core derivation. The direct argument above supplies a repair under the original assumptions; it does not turn the original invocation into a valid one or establish that the final theorem is false.
result: Recorded inspection subject: Imported linear PDE result's explicit coefficient hypotheses are not verified

report: Abstract: The frozen 2023 preprint was read in full. Three substantive proof defects concern the hydrodynamic profiles, the constrained variational argument, and the passage to the global upper bound. Explicit calculations distinguish these defects from the final large-deviation formula: corrected profiles have the stated entropy cost, and a direct convexity certificate supports the intended optimizer. Five further local issues are identified. This is a review of the acquired preprint, not a claim that every item persists in the later journal article.
Author: AI-assisted technical review
Title: Technical Review of Atypical Behaviors of a Tagged Particle in Asymmetric Simple Exclusion
# Identity, hypotheses, and scope

The reviewed source is Sunder Sethuraman and S.R.S. Varadhan, Atypical behaviors of a tagged particle in asymmetric simple exclusion, arXiv:2311.07800v1, submitted 13 November 2023, 39 PDF pages [sv]. The first page carries the internal date 15 November 2023. The assignment associates this work with DOI 10.1214/24-AOP1752; that bibliographic association is not a certificate of equality with the journal text. All page locators below refer to the frozen preprint, whose printed and PDF page numbers agree.

The process is nearest-neighbor exclusion on \(\mathbb Z\), with \(p\in(1/2,1]\), \(q=1-p\), \(\gamma=p-q>0\), density \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and a particle pinned at the origin. The observation time is \(N\), and the deviation threshold is \(A\). Results for negative \(A\) require \(q>0\); the nonentropic lower-tail construction is proved only for TASEP. The main explicit upper-tail rate is \[I_\gamma(A)=
 \begin{cases}
 A\log\!\dfrac{A}{\gamma(1-\rho)}-A+\gamma(1-\rho),
       &\gamma(1-\rho)<A<\gamma,\\[3pt]
 I^Z(A)-A\log(1-\rho)-\gamma\rho,&A\geq\gamma,
 \end{cases}
\quad
 I^Z(A)=A\log c-pc-q/c+1,\] where \(c=(A+\sqrt{A^2+4pq})/(2p)\). The boundary value at the typical speed is understood by continuity.

For profiles vanishing at the origin, conditioning on \(\eta(0)=1\) must mean the pinned product law \[\delta_1(d\eta(0))\bigotimes_{x\ne0}\operatorname{Bern}
       \bigl(\rho_0(x/N)\bigr).\] Literal conditioning on a null event does not define that law. Under this intended interpretation, the Radon–Nikodym product on p. 22 omits \(x=0\); its printed extra factor is an order-one normalization error and does not change an \(N\)-scale entropy. Compact truncations, integer threshold conventions, and the order \(N\to\infty\) before the truncation radius tends to infinity are also operative.
# The hydrodynamic lower-bound profiles

Equation reference: burgers. Problem 1 (Major: several printed rarefaction profiles do not solve the conservation law).  Equation (4.5), p. 18, and the displayed evolutions in Sections 4.4 and 4.5, p. 20, are asserted to be entropic solutions of \[
 \partial_t r+\gamma(1-2r)\partial_u r=0.\] Their rarefaction branches fail this equation even at smooth interior points. The first two profiles are used to identify the typical tagged position in the changed measure.

Proof. In (4.5), take \(\gamma=\rho=1/2\) and \(a=A_\epsilon=3/8\), for instance \(A=5/16\), \(\epsilon=1/16\). These satisfy Theorem 2.2’s strict parameter restrictions. The printed boundaries are \(m(t)=-t/4\), \(s(t)=3t/8\), and the intervening density is \[r(t,u)=\frac{2(t-u)}{5t}.\] Its residual in [burgers] (#burgers) is \[\partial_t r+\tfrac12(1-2r)\partial_u r
       =-\frac{t-6u}{25t^2}.\] At \((t,u)=(1/2,0)\), strictly inside the fan, this equals \(-2/25\). Thus the discrepancy is not a choice of shock convention or a value at a discontinuity.

For Section 4.4, choose \(\gamma=\rho=1/2\) and \(A_\epsilon=1/8\), realized by \(A=3/16\), \(\epsilon=1/3\). The printed fan is \[r(t,u)=\frac{3t-2u+1}{5t},\qquad
 \partial_t r+\tfrac12(1-2r)\partial_u r
       =\frac{t+6u-3}{25t^2}.\] At \((1/2,1/2)\) its residual is \(2/25\). For Section 4.5, take \(\gamma=\rho=1/2\), \(A=-1/4\), \(\epsilon=1/8\) and \(x_0=A-\gamma-\epsilon=-7/8\). The printed fan has residual \[-\frac{4t-8u-7}{36t^2},\] equal to \(-2/9\) at \((t,u)=(1/2,x_0)\). All three residuals were independently reproduced by symbolic differentiation. ◻

Repair and counterevidence. A rarefaction from left density \(L\) to right density \(R<L\), initially at \(x_0\), has boundaries \[x_0+\gamma(1-2L)t,\qquad x_0+\gamma(1-2R)t,
 \qquad
 r(t,u)=\frac12\left(1-\frac{u-x_0}{\gamma t}\right).\] Consequently, in (4.5) one should use \[m(t)=\gamma(1-2\rho)t,\qquad s(t)=(2a-\gamma)t,\] while retaining the printed compression boundaries \(\ell(t)=\gamma-a+(2a-\gamma)t\) and \(r_+(t)=a-\gamma+2\gamma\rho+\gamma(1-2\rho)t\). The trajectory \(u=at\) remains in the density \(1-a/\gamma\) plateau until its right endpoint at \(t=1\). The left fan edge is strictly behind it, and \(\ell(t)-at=(\gamma-a)(1-t)\geq0\).

In Section 4.4 the correct fan boundaries are \(\gamma+(2a-\gamma)t\) and \(\gamma+\gamma(1-2\rho)t\). The shock from the origin has speed \(a-\gamma\rho\). Before \(t=1\) it has not met the fan, and the path \(at\) is in the plateau. In Section 4.5 the left edge of the fan should be \(x_0+\gamma(1-2\rho)t\); the right edge \(x_0+\gamma t\) is already correct. The separate particle comparison on p. 21 uses this right edge.
# The variational proof

Problem 2 (Major: the Euler–Lagrange equation ignores active derivative constraints).  Section 6.2, pp. 26–29, imposes \(\epsilon\leq v'\leq1-\epsilon\), then derives an unconstrained Euler–Lagrange equality in Step 2 and (6.1) in Step 3. Under its stated assumptions that equality can be impossible for every admissible function.

Proof. Use the notation of Section 6.2 and take \[a=0,\quad b=1,\quad \delta=\epsilon=1/10,\quad \rho=1/2,\quad
 H(u)=u/10+u^2/1000,\quad \lambda=100.\] The function \(H\) is smooth, strictly increasing and strictly convex, with \(H(0)=0\) and \(H'(1)<\rho\). Also \(\epsilon\leq H'(\delta)=501/5000\), so this is within the third case of Proposition 6.1 and the specified regularization.

Every admissible \(v\) has \(v(\delta)\geq0\) and \(v(u)\geq(u-\delta)/10\). Hence \[H(u)-v(u)\leq 1/100+u^2/1000\leq11/1000.\] The asserted equality \((h_\rho'(v'))'=\lambda e^{-\lambda(H-v)}\) would imply \[h_\rho'(v'(1))-h_\rho'(v'(\delta))
 \geq 90e^{-1.1}>29.95.\] But \(v'\in[1/10,9/10]\) forces the left side to be at most \(h_\rho'(9/10)-h_\rho'(1/10)=2\log9<4.40\). The contradiction also applies to the claimed weak derivative, by integrating over interior subintervals and taking endpoints. The constrained minimizer exists by compactness and lower semicontinuity; it therefore cannot satisfy the printed equality. ◻

Dependency and repair. This is the foundation for the convexity and contact-set argument leading to Proposition 6.1, Proposition 2.9 and both upper bounds. A variational inequality or a proof that the constraints are inactive is required; the latter is false in the example. Thus the core derivation needs replacement.

Equation reference: certificate. There is direct counterevidence to a stronger allegation that the intended optimizer is wrong. For the corrected candidate \(v_*\), put \(\psi=h_\rho'(v_*')\). Its slope increases only while \(v_*=H\), and is constant on the initial tangent and final slope-\(\rho\) portions. For any admissible \(w\), convexity gives \[
 \int_a^b\!\bigl[h_\rho(w')-h_\rho(v_*')\bigr]\,du
 \geq [\psi(w-v_*)]_a^b-\int_{[a,b]}(w-v_*)\,d\psi\geq0.\] Here \(d\psi\geq0\) is supported on the contact set, where \(w-v_*\leq0\); the initial boundary difference is zero. At the right boundary either \(\psi=0\) or the candidate is still on \(H\) with \(\psi\leq0\), giving the same sign. For the quadratic obstacle used in Proposition 2.9, a zero initial slope is handled by truncation: the remaining boundary term is \(O(\delta|\log\delta|)\) and vanishes. Strict convexity gives uniqueness. This proves the required candidate optimality without the invalid regularization equation, after correcting the printed formulas below.
# The global upper-bound step

Problem 3 (Major: the displayed local bounds do not imply (5.7)).  Section 5.1, Step 2, p. 23, replaces a minimum containing an indicator by an infimum restricted to where that indicator is one. The preceding bound has already discarded the superexponential exclusion of the other cases. Its asserted compact cover is also not justified for the center-dependent neighborhoods used there.

Let \[F(\beta)=v_\beta(1,A)-v_\beta(0,0),\qquad
 J_i=\mathbf1_{\{F(\beta_i)<\epsilon+\delta\}}.\] The printed minimum is \(\min_i J_i(K(\beta_i)-2\delta)\). An inadmissible center contributes zero. Removing that center and taking a positive constrained infimum cannot follow from this expression: even the two values \(J_1=0\), \(J_2=1\), \(K(\beta_2)-2\delta=1\) give \(0\), not \(1\). The correct local conclusion for a strictly inadmissible center is a superexponential bound, or a logarithmic indicator equal to \(-\infty\), rather than the finite bound produced in (5.6).

The centers are continuous densities strictly between zero and one, while \(\mathcal M_R\) contains zero and saturated densities. Density of the centers does not make arbitrary center-dependent small balls a cover: choosing each radius less than half its distance from the zero measure excludes zero from every ball. Lemma 3.4 and (5.4) permit shrinking these radii, so the cover requires an additional construction. Further, the assertion on p. 22 that \(N\pi_t^N/(N+1)\in\mathcal M_R\) is false whenever the empirical measure has an atom: no positive atom satisfies \(\mu([a,b])\leq b-a\) on arbitrarily short intervals. A uniform neighborhood approximation by spreading each atom over its lattice cell would give the intended asymptotic compactness.

Repair route and impact. One can organize the argument around neighborhoods of every \(W\in\mathcal M_R\), using the Bernoulli entropy dual formula \[K(W)=\sup_{f\in C([-R,R])}
 \left\{\int f\,dW-\int_{-R}^R\log(1-\rho+\rho e^f)\,du\right\}.\] For each center choose a near-optimal bounded \(f\), then a neighborhood where its affine entropy lower bound persists. Keep the superexponential estimate for centers with \(F(W)>0\), with a separate tolerance near \(F=0\). The product Bernoulli moment generating function and the uniform quenched tagged-particle bound then yield the entropy cost on the remaining neighborhoods. A finite subcover of this actual cover, followed by the lower-semicontinuity argument in Step 3, is the appropriate route to (5.7). Extension of each local flux estimate to these neighborhoods must be stated.

This repairs the logic the proof needs; it is not a claim that the displayed chain already proves it. The defect is central to Theorems 2.7–2.8 and Corollary 2.10. No counterexample to those final conclusions is given. The step profile used in this repair is \(\mathbf1_{\{x\leq0\}}\), as in Proposition 3.3; the opposite inequality printed on p. 21 is a local orientation error. Also, the no-restriction assertion beyond \(A+\gamma\) follows directly by adding to \(\int_0^{A+\gamma}\rho_0\leq\gamma\), avoiding the unnecessary intermediate subtraction on p. 24.
# Local formula and hypothesis corrections

Problem 4 (Minor: the optimizer displays and the cost identity need normalization corrections).  Proposition 2.9, p. 12, has an incorrect translation in both terminal affine pieces. Theorem 2.7, p. 11, omits the initial empty-interval cost in its equality involving \(K_1\). The first case of Proposition 6.1, p. 26, omits the left-endpoint translation.

At \(z_\rho=A+\gamma(2\rho-1)\) the printed affine piece \(\rho(u-\gamma(2\rho-1)+A)+G(\gamma(2\rho-1))\) jumps upward by \(2\rho A\) from the obstacle branch. It is not even continuous and exceeds the obstacle near the join. The correct expression is \[\rho(u-z_\rho)+G(z_\rho-A).\] This expression already appears correctly in Section 6.1, p. 26, providing direct internal counterevidence to failure of the intended optimizer. The \(x\) in the initial branch of \(v_2\) should likewise be \(u\).

Even with the corrected optimizer, \[K_1(v_*)=-\gamma\log(1-\rho)-\gamma\rho,
\quad
 I_\gamma(A)=I^Z(A)+K_1(v_*)-(A-\gamma)\log(1-\rho)
 \quad(A\geq\gamma).\] For \(\gamma=\rho=1/2\), \(A=4/5\), the missing cost is \(0.20794415416798359\ldots>0\). Formula (5.11), p. 24, and Step 6, p. 25, already include it. Finally, the zero-cost candidate in Proposition 6.1 is \(\rho(u-a)\), with the corresponding obstacle condition. For example, \(a=1\), \(b=2\), \(\rho=1/2\), \(H(u)=1+u^2\) satisfies the printed assumptions but \(v(u)=\rho u\) violates \(v(a)=0\). These are false displayed assertions with local repairs, not a refutation of the rate after restoring the intended normalization.

Problem 5 (Minor: the preliminary exponential martingale has the wrong sign).  The last display of Section 3.3, p. 13, subtracts the left-jump contribution inside the compensator. For \(q>0\) this expression is not a martingale.

Writing \(a_\pm(s)=1-\eta_s(X_s\pm1)\), the correct compensator is \[p(e^\lambda-1)a_+(s)+q(e^{-\lambda}-1)a_-(s).\] For the printed expression, under the pinned equilibrium law its expectation has derivative at zero \(2q(e^{-\lambda}-1)(1-\rho)\). At \(p=3/4\), \(\rho=1/2\), \(\lambda=\log2\), this is \(-1/8\), whereas a martingale starting at one has constant expectation. Bounded jump rates justify the short-time generator calculation. Equation (4.3), p. 16, and the martingale actually used in Section 8, p. 33, have the correct sign. Thus the operative change-of-measure and step-profile upper bound survive this local correction.

Problem 6 (Minor: the stationary error in (1.3) is incompatible with the stated initialization).  Equation (1.3), p. 3, writes \(X_t=\operatorname{Poi}_t+\chi_t\), with \(\operatorname{Poi}\) a Poisson process and \(\chi\) stationary. Under the usual convention that the Poisson process starts at zero, and the paper’s \(X_0=0\), this cannot hold for genuine ASEP.

At zero the equality forces \(\chi_0=0\) almost surely; stationarity forces \(\chi_t=0\) almost surely at every fixed time. It would follow that \(X_t\) is nonnegative and Poisson. But for \(q>0\), the left neighbor is empty initially with probability \(1-\rho\), and \[\mathbb P_\rho(X_t=-1)=q(1-\rho)t+O(t^2)>0\] for sufficiently small \(t\). The claimed representation therefore needs the precise initialization/error formulation of its cited approximation result. A stationary coboundary or a separately specified random offset would avoid this elementary contradiction, but neither is printed or independently verified here. The authors explicitly develop the main upper-tail argument independently of this approximation; the present finding does not refute its LLN or CLT.

Problem 7 (Minor: the introductory path large-deviation formula has the wrong sign).  The display defining the path large-deviation cost on p. 5 has \(\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\lim_{N\to\infty}N^{-1}\log\mathbb P(B_\delta)=K(\rho_0)+I_{\rm JV}(\rho)\). Its right side must have a minus sign.

Both displayed costs are nonnegative, whereas the left side cannot exceed zero. Choose a nonconstant smooth compact perturbation of the background density, of sufficiently small amplitude and derivative that its entropic evolution is smooth up to time one. It is among the stated nice profiles, has strictly positive initial entropy and zero entropic dynamical cost. The printed equality would assign it a positive logarithmic probability. The negative-cost convention in the main theorem statements and the entropy argument on pp. 17–19 are consistent; this introductory sign error does not invalidate those calculations.

Problem 8 (Minor: the optional compactification proof uses an inadmissible generator test).  Section 7.3, p. 30, applies stationarity as \(0=\mathbb E_\mu L_{\rm ZR}\zeta(k)\) for every invariant measure on the compactified space allowing \(\zeta(k)=\infty\). This requires an additional domain and limiting argument.

The coordinate function \(\zeta(k)\) is neither bounded nor finite on that space. In particular, the point mass on the all-infinite configuration is invariant, but \(L_{\rm ZR}\zeta(k)\) is not defined there by differences of coordinate values. Thus stationarity alone cannot justify the printed equalities for every invariant measure. Bounded truncations give boundary terms at infinity which must be treated, rather than silently replaced by the finite-coordinate formula.

This is a gap in the optional self-contained LLN proof, not a demonstrated false invariant-measure classification or false speed \(\gamma\). The alternative cited by the paper was checked in the acquired Tracy–Widom preprint [tw], pp. 1–3. Its Theorem 2 assumes \(0<p_{\rm TW}<q_{\rm TW}\) and gives tight fluctuations of \(x_1(t/\gamma)+t\) on the square-root scale. Set \(p_{\rm TW}=q\), \(q_{\rm TW}=p\), and reflect by \(X_s=1-x_1(s)\). Its initial positive-integer step becomes the required step on \(x\leq0\), and \(X_s/s\to\gamma\) follows for \(0<q<p\). At \(q=0\) the leading TASEP particle has an unobstructed rate-one Poisson clock, so the same LLN follows directly. The bounded drift and vanishing scaled martingale in Lemma 7.1 upgrade fixed-time limits to the required uniform limit. This establishes the cited route’s applicability without re-proving its Fredholm asymptotics. A proof via compactification would still need bounded-test limits accounting for mass at infinity.
# Positive checks, boundaries, and review limits

The three lower-bound entropy mechanisms were traced separately. For \(A\geq\gamma\), the tilted birth–death rates \(pc,q/c\) have difference \(A\), and the empty interval contributes the cost isolated above. The signs of the blocking terms in (4.3)–(4.4) agree with the chosen direction of tilt. For the TASEP lower tail, the initial entropy in (4.7) plus the shock cost in (4.9) simplifies to \(A\log(A/(1-\rho))-A+1-\rho\); an independent numerical check agrees. The special \(A=0\) hole-clock construction yields \(1-\rho\) by cancellation of the two \(\rho\log\rho\) terms. The negative-\(A\) construction is restricted to \(q>0\).

The rate is continuous at \(A=\gamma\): both branches give \(-\gamma\log(1-\rho)-\gamma\rho\). Their first derivatives agree there, and the birth–death Legendre derivative is \(\log c\). At \(p=1\) the rate reduces to the Poisson formula throughout the nonnegative upper tail; the \(A<0\) construction is not extended to that endpoint.

The current/tagged-particle ordering, Hopf–Lax conjugate, and superexponential flux argument in Sections 3, 8, 9 and Appendix A were followed. Integer threshold discrepancies vanish after scaling. The LLN proof on p. 29 should compare levels strictly above and below the limiting quantile; convergence in probability does not determine a tail probability exactly at that quantile. In Section 9, the removable case \(b=L\) should be handled directly through the integral of \(F'\) rather than division by \(b-L\). In Section 8, attractiveness propagates monotonicity of the semigroup, which supplies the two-time correlation used in (8.1); equal-time association alone would not suffice. The exponential optimization is an infimum of \(-\lambda A+p(e^\lambda-1)+q(e^{-\lambda}-1)\), consistent with the final displayed rate despite the intervening typographical wording.

The one-block replacement, shock coupling, and construction of nonentropic process measures remain imported results; their complete proofs were not all independently reconstructed. The Tracy–Widom reference was examined at its definitions and Theorem 2, not read or re-proved in its entirety. No author code was executed, and lack of author code is not a mathematical finding. The independent symbolic calculations and high-precision integrations support the explicit certificates and do not replace the analytic proofs.

The official arXiv metadata inspected for this review still lists v1. The bounded correction search did not establish a formal resolving erratum; absence of a correction is not certified. The later journal version was not silently substituted for the acquired preprint. Three findings are Major because the printed derivations of central results fail; the other five are local corrections or a supplementary proof gap. No whole-paper failure, false final rate theorem or independent acceptance is asserted.

problems.title: Incorrect rarefaction fans
problems.source_location: Retained report inspection subject: Incorrect rarefaction fans
claim: Recorded check: Incorrect rarefaction fans
analysis:
Equation (4.5), p. 18, and the displayed evolutions in Sections 4.4 and 4.5, p. 20, are asserted to be entropic solutions of \[
 \partial_t r+\gamma(1-2r)\partial_u r=0.\] Their rarefaction branches fail this equation even at smooth interior points. The first two profiles are used to identify the typical tagged position in the changed measure.

Proof. In (4.5), take \(\gamma=\rho=1/2\) and \(a=A_\epsilon=3/8\), for instance \(A=5/16\), \(\epsilon=1/16\). These satisfy Theorem 2.2’s strict parameter restrictions. The printed boundaries are \(m(t)=-t/4\), \(s(t)=3t/8\), and the intervening density is \[r(t,u)=\frac{2(t-u)}{5t}.\] Its residual in [burgers] (#burgers) is \[\partial_t r+\tfrac12(1-2r)\partial_u r
       =-\frac{t-6u}{25t^2}.\] At \((t,u)=(1/2,0)\), strictly inside the fan, this equals \(-2/25\). Thus the discrepancy is not a choice of shock convention or a value at a discontinuity.

For Section 4.4, choose \(\gamma=\rho=1/2\) and \(A_\epsilon=1/8\), realized by \(A=3/16\), \(\epsilon=1/3\). The printed fan is \[r(t,u)=\frac{3t-2u+1}{5t},\qquad
 \partial_t r+\tfrac12(1-2r)\partial_u r
       =\frac{t+6u-3}{25t^2}.\] At \((1/2,1/2)\) its residual is \(2/25\). For Section 4.5, take \(\gamma=\rho=1/2\), \(A=-1/4\), \(\epsilon=1/8\) and \(x_0=A-\gamma-\epsilon=-7/8\). The printed fan has residual \[-\frac{4t-8u-7}{36t^2},\] equal to \(-2/9\) at \((t,u)=(1/2,x_0)\). All three residuals were independently reproduced by symbolic differentiation. ◻

Repair and counterevidence. A rarefaction from left density \(L\) to right density \(R<L\), initially at \(x_0\), has boundaries \[x_0+\gamma(1-2L)t,\qquad x_0+\gamma(1-2R)t,
 \qquad
 r(t,u)=\frac12\left(1-\frac{u-x_0}{\gamma t}\right).\] Consequently, in (4.5) one should use \[m(t)=\gamma(1-2\rho)t,\qquad s(t)=(2a-\gamma)t,\] while retaining the printed compression boundaries \(\ell(t)=\gamma-a+(2a-\gamma)t\) and \(r_+(t)=a-\gamma+2\gamma\rho+\gamma(1-2\rho)t\). The trajectory \(u=at\) remains in the density \(1-a/\gamma\) plateau until its right endpoint at \(t=1\). The left fan edge is strictly behind it, and \(\ell(t)-at=(\gamma-a)(1-t)\geq0\).

In Section 4.4 the correct fan boundaries are \(\gamma+(2a-\gamma)t\) and \(\gamma+\gamma(1-2\rho)t\). The shock from the origin has speed \(a-\gamma\rho\). Before \(t=1\) it has not met the fan, and the path \(at\) is in the plateau. In Section 4.5 the left edge of the fan should be \(x_0+\gamma(1-2\rho)t\); the right edge \(x_0+\gamma t\) is already correct. The separate particle comparison on p. 21 uses this right edge.

problems.title: Euler-Lagrange equality ignores active constraints
problems.source_location: Retained report, Problem 2: Problem 2 (Major: the Euler–Lagrange equation ignores active derivative constraints).
claim: Recorded check: Euler-Lagrange equality ignores active constraints
analysis: Section 6.2, pp. 26–29, imposes \(\epsilon\leq v'\leq1-\epsilon\), then derives an unconstrained Euler–Lagrange equality in Step 2 and (6.1) in Step 3. Under its stated assumptions that equality can be impossible for every admissible function.

Proof. Use the notation of Section 6.2 and take \[a=0,\quad b=1,\quad \delta=\epsilon=1/10,\quad \rho=1/2,\quad
 H(u)=u/10+u^2/1000,\quad \lambda=100.\] The function \(H\) is smooth, strictly increasing and strictly convex, with \(H(0)=0\) and \(H'(1)<\rho\). Also \(\epsilon\leq H'(\delta)=501/5000\), so this is within the third case of Proposition 6.1 and the specified regularization.

Every admissible \(v\) has \(v(\delta)\geq0\) and \(v(u)\geq(u-\delta)/10\). Hence \[H(u)-v(u)\leq 1/100+u^2/1000\leq11/1000.\] The asserted equality \((h_\rho'(v'))'=\lambda e^{-\lambda(H-v)}\) would imply \[h_\rho'(v'(1))-h_\rho'(v'(\delta))
 \geq 90e^{-1.1}>29.95.\] But \(v'\in[1/10,9/10]\) forces the left side to be at most \(h_\rho'(9/10)-h_\rho'(1/10)=2\log9<4.40\). The contradiction also applies to the claimed weak derivative, by integrating over interior subintervals and taking endpoints. The constrained minimizer exists by compactness and lower semicontinuity; it therefore cannot satisfy the printed equality. ◻

Dependency and repair. This is the foundation for the convexity and contact-set argument leading to Proposition 6.1, Proposition 2.9 and both upper bounds. A variational inequality or a proof that the constraints are inactive is required; the latter is false in the example. Thus the core derivation needs replacement.

Equation reference: certificate. There is direct counterevidence to a stronger allegation that the intended optimizer is wrong. For the corrected candidate \(v_*\), put \(\psi=h_\rho'(v_*')\). Its slope increases only while \(v_*=H\), and is constant on the initial tangent and final slope-\(\rho\) portions. For any admissible \(w\), convexity gives \[
 \int_a^b\!\bigl[h_\rho(w')-h_\rho(v_*')\bigr]\,du
 \geq [\psi(w-v_*)]_a^b-\int_{[a,b]}(w-v_*)\,d\psi\geq0.\] Here \(d\psi\geq0\) is supported on the contact set, where \(w-v_*\leq0\); the initial boundary difference is zero. At the right boundary either \(\psi=0\) or the candidate is still on \(H\) with \(\psi\leq0\), giving the same sign. For the quadratic obstacle used in Proposition 2.9, a zero initial slope is handled by truncation: the remaining boundary term is \(O(\delta|\log\delta|)\) and vanishes. Strict convexity gives uniqueness. This proves the required candidate optimality without the invalid regularization equation, after correcting the printed formulas below.

report: Abstract: This review concerns the 49-page arXiv version 2402.00767v2 of the paper by Pierre Perruchaud and Isao Sauzedde. A missing heat-kernel factor makes the displayed Symanzik identity in Theorem 6.8 false even for a trivial line bundle on a unit flat torus. An explicit spectral calculation establishes the discrepancy and verifies the natural correction. A separate step in the proof of Theorem 7.1 substitutes a squared scalar trace defect for a matrix-norm estimate. An admissible winding-bridge example disproves the corresponding displayed inequality. The correct matrix estimate repairs that part of the argument. Neither issue is a counterexample to the determinant representation in Theorem 2.1. The assessment is an initial review of the identified version, not an independent acceptance decision.
