# The missing transition density in Theorem 6.8

Problem 1 (Major: a false displayed Symanzik formula).  In Theorem 6.8, page 37, both the real and complex displayed identities omit \(p_t(x,y)\) from each integral representing a covariance. The required factor is present in Lemma 6.5, page 35, and in the Feynman–Kac representation of Theorem 3.3, page 13. The bridge notation in Section 2.2, page 10, does not absorb this factor.
## Hypotheses and the exact assertion under examination

Section 6 assumes a compact connected smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension \(d\in\{2,3\}\), without boundary, with smooth nonnegative mass \(m\) that is not identically zero. The real or complex metric vector bundle has finite rank, and the connections are smooth and compatible with the bundle metric. A connection has an arbitrary probability law \(P\). Definition 6.7 weights that law by the positive loop-soup expectation \[w(
abla)=\mathbb E^{\mathcal L}_{n/2}[Z_{
abla,\mathcal L}],
 \qquad
 Z_{
abla,\mathcal L}=\prod_{\ell\in\mathcal L}\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Hol}^
abla(\ell).\] Here the trace is normalized, as explicitly defined on page 7. Theorem 6.8 concerns moments of the resulting mixture of Gaussian free fields, smooth test sections, and a measurable functional \(f\) of the connection. The counterexample below uses \(f=1\), so no integrability ambiguity is involved.

Equation reference: eq:printed, eq:correct. For the real case with \(k=1\), the covariance integral printed in Theorem 6.8 is \[
 \widetilde C_\nabla(s_1,s_2)
 =\int_0^\infty\!\int_{M^2}
 \mathbb E^m_{t,x,y}\!
 \left[\left\langle s_1(x),\operatorname{Hol}^\nabla_{t,0}(W)s_2(y)\right\rangle\right]
 \,dx\,dy\,dt .\] By contrast, Lemma 6.5 identifies the actual covariance as \[
 C_\nabla(s_1,s_2)
 =\int_0^\infty\!\int_{M^2}p_t(x,y)
 \mathbb E^m_{t,x,y}\!
 \left[\left\langle s_1(x),\operatorname{Hol}^\nabla_{t,0}(W)s_2(y)\right\rangle\right]
 \,dx\,dy\,dt .\] The bridge expectation is the usual normalized bridge expectation, multiplied by the mass/killing weight. The density \(p_t\) is a separate factor. The original PDF images on pages 10, 35, and 37 were inspected to exclude a text-extraction omission.
## An admissible exact counterexample

Let \(M=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2\) with its standard flat metric and volume one. Let \(E=M\times\mathbb R\), let \(\nabla=d\), and set \(m\equiv1\). Take \(P=\delta_d\), \(f\equiv1\), \(k=1\), and \[s_1(x)=s_2(x)=s(x)=\cos(2\pi x_1).\] The manifold is smooth, compact, connected, closed, and two-dimensional; the bundle and connection are smooth and metric-compatible; the mass is strictly positive; and the sections are smooth and periodic. Thus all operative assumptions for this instance are satisfied.

Equation reference: eq:variance, eq:zero. Holonomy equals the identity for every path. Every loop-product cutoff equals one, so \(Z_{\nabla,\mathcal L}=w(\nabla)=1\), and the normalization in Definition 6.7 is also one. Equation (3), page 7, gives \[L=-\tfrac12(\partial_1^2+\partial_2^2)+1,\qquad
 Ls=(1+2\pi^2)s,\qquad
 \int_M s\,dx=0,\qquad \|s\|_{L^2(M)}^2=\tfrac12.\] Consequently the actual Gaussian variance is \[
 \mathbb E[\Phi(s)^2]=\langle s,L^{-1}s\rangle
 =\frac{1}{2(1+2\pi^2)}>0.\] For constant mass one, \(\mathbb E^m_{t,x,y}[1]=e^{-t}\). The right-hand side of the printed formula instead becomes \[
 \widetilde C_d(s,s)
 =\int_0^\infty e^{-t}\,dt
   \left(\int_M s(x)\,dx\right)^2=0.\] Equations [eq:variance] (#eq:variance) and [eq:zero] (#eq:zero) contradict the displayed assertion of Theorem 6.8.

This calculation is exact. An independently written SymPy check verified the eigenfunction equation, both integrals of \(s\), the zero printed answer, and the positive variance \(0.024108923574146834\ldots\). It also verified that inserting the missing heat kernel yields \[\int_0^\infty \tfrac12 e^{-(1+2\pi^2)t}\,dt
 =\frac{1}{2(1+2\pi^2)}.\] No author code was executed.
## Alternative readings, repair, and impact

An implicit unit-volume convention cannot explain the discrepancy: the counterexample already has volume one. A convention putting the transition density inside \(\mathbb E^m_{t,x,y}\) would conflict with the explicit definition on page 10 and with Lemma 6.5. A determinant weight or random connection effect cannot correct it: both are trivial in this example.

Equation reference: eq:wick. There is strong internal evidence for the intended repair. Theorem 3.3, Lemma 6.5, and the one-paragraph Wick argument following Theorem 6.8 all require [eq:correct] (#eq:correct). For bounded measurable \(f\), replace every occurrence of [eq:printed] (#eq:printed) by [eq:correct] (#eq:correct). The corrected real formula is \[
 \mathbb E^{\mathrm{GFF}}_P
 \!\left[f(\nabla)\prod_{i=1}^{2k}\Phi(s_i)\right]
 =
 \frac{\displaystyle
 \mathbb E_P\!\left[f(\nabla)w(\nabla)
   \sum_{\pi}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in\pi}C_\nabla(s_i,s_j)\right]}
 {\mathbb E_P[w(\nabla)]},\] where \(\pi\) ranges over pairings.

Verification of the repair. Condition on \(\nabla\) in Definition 6.7. The conditional field is centered Gaussian with covariance [eq:correct] (#eq:correct); Wick’s formula therefore gives the sum over pairings in [eq:wick] (#eq:wick). Integrating against \(w(\nabla)dP/\mathbb E_Pw\) gives the result. The scalar massive Green bound used in Lemma 6.5 bounds the covariance uniformly in the metric connection for fixed smooth sections. The loop products have absolute value at most one; their positive expectations give \(0<w\leq1\) and \(\mathbb E_Pw>0\). Thus bounded \(f\) makes these finite moments integrable. The complex pairing formula requires the same missing density in each covariance, with the conjugation convention of the paper. ◻

For an arbitrary unbounded measurable \(f\), suitable integrability is still needed to interpret signed expectations; the bounded-\(f\) repair does not certify an unrestricted formula. The demonstrated failure is of the displayed Symanzik identity in this version. It does not invalidate the construction of the conditional Gaussian field, the loop representation of determinants, or the corrected covariance formula.
# A matrix estimate replaced by a scalar trace square

Problem 2 (Major: a false cutoff inequality in a core proof).  In the proof of Theorem 7.1, page 40, the first estimate of \(-\log\mathbb EX_\delta\) cites equation (20), page 32, and replaces the trace defect by \(\tfrac12|1-\operatorname{tr}U|^2\), where \(U\) is holonomy. Equation (20) controls the matrix \(I-U\); it does not provide this scalar replacement for a normalized trace in rank greater than one.
## Assumptions and a decisive algebraic check

Theorem 7.1, page 38, works in dimension two with a smooth metric bundle of arbitrary finite rank and a compatible smooth connection. The Riemannian metric, conformal factor, and nonnegative mass are smooth, and either the boundary is nonempty or the mass is not identically zero. Its proof compares products with different duration cutoffs after a conformal time change. The relevant event in the first moment is invariant under time reversal.

Equation reference: eq:traceid. For a unitary or orthogonal \(U\), set \(z=\operatorname{tr}U\), with normalized trace. Then \(|z|\leq1\), and \[
 2\operatorname{Re}(1-z)
 =|1-z|^2+1-|z|^2.\] Hence the pointwise inequality \(\operatorname{Re}(1-\operatorname{tr}U)\leq\tfrac12|1-\operatorname{tr}U|^2\), which would justify the displayed substitution, has the wrong direction whenever \(|\operatorname{tr}U|<1\).

For example, take the real orthogonal matrix \[U=J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.\] Then \(\operatorname{tr}U=0\), so the two sides are \(1\) and \(1/2\). Moreover \((I-U)^*(I-U)=2I\), which confirms that the matrix estimate itself is consistent. This is not an inadmissible class of holonomies: on the trivial rank-two real bundle over the flat two-torus, the smooth metric connection \(d-(\pi/2)J\,dx_1\) has holonomy \(J\) along a winding-one loop. All matrix equalities were also checked independently in SymPy.

This finite-dimensional example disproves the proposed pointwise matrix-to-trace-square substitution. By itself it is not a counterexample to the averaged cutoff inequality for a specified Brownian event, and it is not a counterexample to the final conformal-invariance theorem. The cited estimate does not justify the displayed scalar bound. The following construction also disproves the averaged inequality itself.
## An admissible counterexample to the integral inequality

Retain the flat unit torus and rank-two connection just described, and set \(m=1\). Choose the smooth conformal factor \[f(x)=\tfrac12\log a(x),\qquad a(x)=2+\cos(2\pi x_1).\] Since \(1\leq a\leq3\), this is globally smooth and \(\|e^{-2f}\|_\infty=1\). Formula (22), page 39, gives \(\widehat T=\int_0^t a(W_s)\,ds\). Thus the event in the first moment on page 40 is \(A=\{\widehat T>\delta\}\). The manifold is closed and \(m=1\) is nonzero; all assumptions of Theorem 7.1 are satisfied.

Equation reference: eq:Ldelta, eq:Rdelta. Let \(L_\delta\) and \(R_\delta\) denote respectively the two sides of the first inequality following the exact Campbell integral on page 40: \[\begin{aligned}
 L_\delta&=\int_0^\delta\!\int_M\frac{p_t(x,x)}t
 \mathbb E^1_{t,x,x}\bigl[\mathbf1_A(1-\operatorname{tr}U)\bigr]\,dx\,dt,
 \\
 R_\delta&=\frac12\int_0^\delta\!\int_M\frac{p_t(x,x)}t
 \mathbb E^1_{t,x,x}\bigl[|1-\operatorname{tr}U|^2\bigr]\,dx\,dt.
 \end{aligned}\] The asserted inequality is \(L_\delta\leq R_\delta\).

The lifted torus bridge has winding \(k=(k_1,k_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\), with unnormalized density \[g_t(k)=(2\pi t)^{-1}e^{-|k|^2/(2t)}.\] Indeed, the torus transition density is the sum of the Euclidean Gaussian densities, and conditioning on a lift divides each by that sum. Multiplication by \(p_t(x,x)\) in [eq:Ldelta] (#eq:Ldelta)–[eq:Rdelta] (#eq:Rdelta) cancels this normalizer. The mass weight is \(e^{-t}\), and the normalized holonomy trace is \[z_k=\cos(\pi k_1/2).\] In particular, the two windings \(k=(1,0),(-1,0)\) both have \(1-z_k=1\).

Equation reference: eq:Llower. For either of these two windings, the first lifted coordinate at time \(tu\) has the form \(x_1\pm u+\sqrt t\,b(u)\), where \(b\) is a standard unit Brownian bridge. Since \(a\) is \(2\pi\)-Lipschitz and \(\int_0^1 a(x_1\pm u)\,du=2\), \[\left|\frac{\widehat T}{t}-2\right|
 \leq2\pi\sqrt t\int_0^1|b(u)|\,du.\] Writing \(b(u)=B(u)-uB(1)\) gives \(\mathbb Eb(u)^2=u(1-u)\) and hence \[\mathbb E\int_0^1|b(u)|\,du
 \leq\left(\int_0^1u(1-u)\,du\right)^{1/2}
 =\frac1{\sqrt6}.\] Set \(\delta=1/100\). Uniformly in \(x\) and \(3\delta/4\leq t\leq\delta\), Markov’s inequality gives \[\mathbb P(\widehat T\leq\delta\mid k)
 \leq\frac{3\pi\sqrt\delta}{\sqrt6}
 <\frac{11}{28},\] where \(\pi<22/7\) and \(\sqrt6>12/5\) suffice for the last bound. Thus the probability of \(A\) is at least \(17/28\). All terms of \(L_\delta\) are nonnegative, so retaining these two windings yields \[
 L_\delta\geq\frac{17}{28}\frac{99}{100}\frac1\pi
 \int_{3\delta/4}^{\delta}t^{-2}e^{-1/(2t)}\,dt.\]
## A valid local repair

Equation reference: eq:matrixrepair, eq:cutoffrepair. The valid identity and bound are \[
 \operatorname{Re}(1-\operatorname{tr}U)
 =\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}\bigl((I-U)^*(I-U)\bigr)
 \leq\tfrac12\|I-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2.\] For fixed rank, equivalent matrix norms only change a constant. Let \(A\) denote the cutoff event occurring in the first moment on page 40. Reversing the bridge sends \(U\) to \(U^*\) and preserves \(A\) and the mass weight. Its expectation is therefore real. Taking real parts before dropping the indicator gives \[\begin{aligned}
 0&\leq \mathbb E^m_{t,x,x}
       [\mathbf1_A(1-\operatorname{tr}U)]\notag\\
  &\leq\tfrac12\mathbb E^m_{t,x,x}\|I-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
   \leq Ct^2. \end{aligned}\] The last bound is Proposition 3.1, page 13, with exponent two. In dimension two, the diagonal heat kernel is \(O(t^{-1})\) at small time, so \[\int_0^\delta\!\int_M
       \frac{p_t(x,x)}{t}\,Ct^2\,dx\,dt=O(\delta).\] This proves the required first-moment convergence by the matrix estimate, without the false scalar substitution.

For the second moment the inequality printed on page 40, \(1-|z|^2\leq2\operatorname{Re}(1-z)\), is valid for \(|z|\leq1\). Using [eq:matrixrepair] (#eq:matrixrepair) gives the same \(O(\delta)\) control. Thus \(\mathbb EX_\delta\to1\) and \(\mathbb E|X_\delta|^2\to1\), whence \(\mathbb E|X_\delta-1|^2\to0\). The remaining comparison uses the already established bound \(|Q_\delta|\leq1\).
## Counterevidence and boundaries

For a rank-one unitary holonomy, \(|\operatorname{tr}U|=1\), and [eq:traceid] (#eq:traceid) is an equality without the additional term. That special case explains why a scalar formula can look plausible, but Theorem 7.1 allows arbitrary rank. Equation (20) and the matrix estimates elsewhere in the paper provide the needed repair. The original images on pages 13, 32, 38–40 were inspected; the issue is present in the PDF and is not a conversion artifact. The repair addresses this cutoff step under the theorem’s hypotheses, conditional on the preceding loop-measure and holonomy results. It does not independently reprove every external ingredient of the conformal-invariance theorem.
# Coverage, dependencies, and limits of this review

The complete extracted text of all 49 source pages was read in this scientific conversation, including both appendices and the reference list. The source identity and all four manifest-listed payload files were hash-checked. Text reading, file parsing, visual inspection, and independent calculation are recorded separately.

The principal dependency chain examined was the following. The covariant Feynman–Kac formula identifies the heat kernel. Proposition 3.1 provides an \(O(t)\) holonomy fluctuation and an \(O(t^2)\) mean defect, the latter using reversal and the isometry property. Together with \(p_t(x,x)=O(t^{-d/2})\), these give the integrable small-loop power \(t^{1-d/2}\) for \(d<4\). The normalized Poisson products are controlled in even moments, leading to the determinant representation. The normalized kernel-dimension equality in the first part of Theorem 2.1 must be retained; the stronger nonzero-mass or nonempty-boundary condition is used for the loop-product assertion and the large-time behavior. The Gaussian covariance and mixture then lead to the Symanzik identities. The conformal result requires an additional cutoff comparison because the products are not absolutely convergent.

The boundary cases checked include trivial holonomy, deterministic connection laws, a constant positive mass, nonconstant mean-zero test sections, normalized versus unnormalized traces, rank one versus rank two, and the distinction between zero-mode assumptions and the stronger mass/boundary condition. In particular, the counterexample in Problem 1 lies wholly inside the assumptions; it does not rely on a zero-mass limit, a boundary singularity, or an unbounded test functional.

No further substantive defect is asserted. Reading the full text does not amount to independent certification of every stochastic-analysis estimate or cited theorem. The small-time rough-path arguments and the external heat-kernel and loop-measure results were examined as dependencies, but their original external proofs were not all reconstructed. The report’s decisive evidence is the two explicit counterexamples and the local repair arguments above. The reviewed arXiv PDF has not been established to be identical to the final journal article.

 \mathbb E^1_{t,x,x}\bigl[|1-\operatorname{tr}U|^2\bigr]\,dx\,dt.
 \end{aligned}\] The asserted inequality is \(L_\delta\leq R_\delta\).

The lifted torus bridge has winding \(k=(k_1,k_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\), with unnormalized density \[g_t(k)=(2\pi t)^{-1}e^{-|k|^2/(2t)}.\] Indeed, the torus transition density is the sum of the Euclidean Gaussian densities, and conditioning on a lift divides each by that sum. Multiplication by \(p_t(x,x)\) in [eq:Ldelta] (#eq:Ldelta)–[eq:Rdelta] (#eq:Rdelta) cancels this normalizer. The mass weight is \(e^{-t}\), and the normalized holonomy trace is \[z_k=\cos(\pi k_1/2).\] In particular, the two windings \(k=(1,0),(-1,0)\) both have \(1-z_k=1\).

Equation reference: eq:Llower. For either of these two windings, the first lifted coordinate at time \(tu\) has the form \(x_1\pm u+\sqrt t\,b(u)\), where \(b\) is a standard unit Brownian bridge. Since \(a\) is \(2\pi\)-Lipschitz and \(\int_0^1 a(x_1\pm u)\,du=2\), \[\left|\frac{\widehat T}{t}-2\right|
 \leq2\pi\sqrt t\int_0^1|b(u)|\,du.\] Writing \(b(u)=B(u)-uB(1)\) gives \(\mathbb Eb(u)^2=u(1-u)\) and hence \[\mathbb E\int_0^1|b(u)|\,du
 \leq\left(\int_0^1u(1-u)\,du\right)^{1/2}
 =\frac1{\sqrt6}.\] Set \(\delta=1/100\). Uniformly in \(x\) and \(3\delta/4\leq t\leq\delta\), Markov’s inequality gives \[\mathbb P(\widehat T\leq\delta\mid k)
 \leq\frac{3\pi\sqrt\delta}{\sqrt6}
 <\frac{11}{28},\] where \(\pi<22/7\) and \(\sqrt6>12/5\) suffice for the last bound. Thus the probability of \(A\) is at least \(17/28\). All terms of \(L_\delta\) are nonnegative, so retaining these two windings yields \[
 L_\delta\geq\frac{17}{28}\frac{99}{100}\frac1\pi
 \int_{3\delta/4}^{\delta}t^{-2}e^{-1/(2t)}\,dt.\]

 \operatorname{Re}(1-\operatorname{tr}U)
 =\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}\bigl((I-U)^*(I-U)\bigr)
 \leq\tfrac12\|I-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2.\] For fixed rank, equivalent matrix norms only change a constant. Let \(A\) denote the cutoff event occurring in the first moment on page 40. Reversing the bridge sends \(U\) to \(U^*\) and preserves \(A\) and the mass weight. Its expectation is therefore real. Taking real parts before dropping the indicator gives \[\begin{aligned}

       [\mathbf1_A(1-\operatorname{tr}U)]\notag\\
  &\leq\tfrac12\mathbb E^m_{t,x,x}\|I-U\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
   \leq Ct^2. \end{aligned}\] The last bound is Proposition 3.1, page 13, with exponent two. In dimension two, the diagonal heat kernel is \(O(t^{-1})\) at small time, so \[\int_0^\delta\!\int_M

report: Abstract: Two substantive issues are established in the reviewed journal-formatted version. The stated white-noise variational constant is contradicted by an explicit normalized function; an elementary sharp inequality gives the correct constant and exposes a separate inconsistency in Corollary 1.4. An unequal-parameter maximization in the proof of Lemma 5.1 is false, with a strictly positive finite-dimensional counterexample. That step feeds the concentration argument used for the long-time moment lower bound. Equal-parameter estimates and the separate high-moment argument must be distinguished from this failure. These findings do not constitute a counterexample to the general long-time asymptotic formula.
Author: AI-assisted technical review

Title: Initial technical review of
Hyperbolic Anderson equations with general
time-independent Gaussian noise: Stratonovich regime
# Reviewed source and scope

The subject is Xia Chen and Yaozhong Hu, Hyperbolic Anderson equations with general time-independent Gaussian noise: Stratonovich regime, Annals of Probability 53(6) (2025), 2144–2195, DOI https://doi.org/10.1214/24-AOP1758 [CH]. The frozen author-hosted journal-formatted PDF has 52 pages. Its SHA256 is `58b152d78cd0d54d82b991933b3eaece86e1ed2b44fe09882c14eba921e97e22`. The review identifier is M25-0532. All 52 source pages were personally read, including the appendix and references. Printed page numbers below are accompanied by PDF page numbers where a finding is localized.

The equation is \[\partial_t^2u=\Delta u+\dot W(x)u,\qquad u(0,x)=1,\quad
 \partial_tu(0,x)=0,\] in dimensions \(d=1,2,3\), with stationary mean-zero Gaussian noise. The covariance \(\gamma\) is both nonnegative and positive definite, possibly distribution-valued, with convention \(\gamma(x)=\int e^{i\xi\cdot x}\mu(d\xi)\). Theorem 1.1 gives existence under \(\int(1+|\xi|^2)^{-1}\mu(d\xi)<\infty\) in the sense of Definition 2.1. Its necessity statement assumes a square-integrable solution admitting the stated Stratonovich expansion. It is not an unrestricted uniqueness assertion.
# Problem 1: inconsistent white-noise constants

Problem 1 (Major: false variational value and inconsistent specialization).  On printed p. 2147 (PDF p. 4), immediately after (1.11), the source states that for \(\gamma=\delta_0\), \[\mathcal M_{\mathrm{printed}}=\frac14\left(\frac32\right)^{1/3}.\] On the same page, Corollary 1.4 gives coefficient \(C_{\mathrm{cor}}=\frac12(3/4)^{1/4}\) in both asymptotic displays. The first value is false under [eq:variational] (#eq:variational); the second does not follow from [eq:calpha] (#eq:calpha) with either the printed or the correct variational value.
## Admissible counterexample and sharp evaluation

Equation reference: eq:sech. Take \(d=\alpha=1\), \(\gamma=\delta_0\) and \(\mu(d\xi)=d\xi/(2\pi)\). These are exactly the white-noise assumptions of Corollary 1.4 and satisfy Dalang’s condition. For every \(b>0\), let \[g_b(x)=\sqrt{b/2}\,\operatorname{sech}(bx).\] This is a real smooth member of \(W^{1,2}(\mathbb R)\), and substitution \(z=\tanh(bx)\) gives \[
 \int g_b^2=1,\qquad \int g_b^4=b/3,\qquad
 \int(g_b')^2=b^2/3.\] In particular, \(b=1/2\) yields \[\mathcal M\ge\frac1{\sqrt6}-\frac1{12}>\frac3{10}>
        \frac14(3/2)^{1/3}.\] The strict inequalities need no numerical approximation: \(1/6>(23/60)^2\) proves the first, and \(3/128<(3/10)^3\) proves the second. Thus the printed value is already refuted by one admissible function.
The exact value can also be obtained without the unavailable book page cited in the source.

Equation reference: eq:mcorrect. Claim 1.  With the normalization [eq:variational] (#eq:variational) and \(\gamma=\delta_0\), \[
 \mathcal M=\frac{3^{2/3}}{2^{8/3}},\qquad \mathcal M^3=\frac9{256}.\]

Equation reference: eq:sharpGN. Proof. For real \(g\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R)\) with \(\int g^2=1\), set \(F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xg^2(y)\,dy\) and \(B=\int(g')^2\). The one-dimensional Sobolev representative is continuous and tends to zero at infinity; integration by parts and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[\begin{aligned}
 \int g^4
 &=-\int(2F-1)gg'\nonumber\\
 &\le
   \left(\int(2F-1)^2g^2\right)^{1/2} B^{1/2}
   =\frac1{\sqrt3}B^{1/2}. \end{aligned}\] The last equality follows from \(\int_0^1(2v-1)^2\,dv=1/3\). The argument applies directly to \(H^1\) representatives, or by smooth approximation. It follows that \[\left(\int g^4\right)^{1/2}-B
 \le 3^{-1/4}B^{1/4}-B
 \le \frac{3^{2/3}}{2^{8/3}}.\] The family [eq:sech] (#eq:sech) attains equality when \(b=(3/16)^{1/3}\), since it saturates [eq:sharpGN] (#eq:sharpGN) and maximizes \(\sqrt{b/3}-b^2/3\). This proves [eq:mcorrect] (#eq:mcorrect). ◻
## Consequences and alternative normalizations

Equation reference: eq:coeff. At \(\alpha=1\), [eq:calpha] (#eq:calpha) becomes \(C_1=(2\sqrt{\mathcal M}/3)^{3/2}\). Consequently, \[\begin{aligned}
 C_1(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{correct}})&=\frac1{3\sqrt2},
 &C_1(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{correct}})^4&=\frac1{324},\\
 C_1(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{printed}})^4&=\frac1{486},
 &C_{\mathrm{cor}}^4&=\frac3{64}. \nonumber\end{aligned}\] All three fourth powers are distinct. The discrepancy cannot be resolved merely by inserting the printed \(\mathcal M\) into Theorem 1.2.

A plausible alternative is a factor of \(1/2\) in front of the Dirichlet energy. That is indeed the convention of Balan, Chen and Chen [Retained latex: \cite[p.~1592, (1.7)]{BCC}]; their displayed white-noise constant is \(\frac34(1/6)^{1/3}\). Spatial scaling changes this half-energy quantity by \(2^{-1/3}\) when passing to the energy in [eq:variational] (#eq:variational). The result is exactly [eq:mcorrect] (#eq:mcorrect), not the source’s printed value. Thus the common alternative convention does not rescue the statement.
## Severity, repair and limits

This is a substantive error in an explicitly evaluated special case, not a discrepancy due to floating-point rounding or an inadmissible test function. The proof above establishes the corrected variational constant. It also gives the coefficient [eq:coeff] (#eq:coeff) required for consistency with Theorem 1.2. It does not by itself prove either stochastic limit: the affected long-time proof must additionally be repaired as discussed in Problem 2.

The value of \(\mathcal M\) in its defining variational form need not be changed. The printed evaluation, the two displays of Corollary 1.4, and the cited normalization should be corrected together. The source’s general existence statement is not refuted by this calculation.
# Problem 2: a false maximization enters the long-time lower bound

Problem 2 (Major: invalid core derivation for unequal parameters).  Lemma 5.1(1), source (5.6), printed p. 2174 (PDF p. 31), is stated for every \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p>0\). The maximization at the bottom of p. 2177 and top of p. 2178 (PDF pp. 34–35) is false when these parameters are unequal. The asserted uniform bound feeds (5.11) and (5.6), then (5.23)–(5.26) and Lemma 5.3 on pp. 2183–2185 (PDF pp. 40–42). It therefore enters a core lower-bound argument.
## Exact counterexample within the stated domain

Equation reference: eq:objective. Let \[\beta=\frac{2-\alpha}{2}>0,\qquad
 \theta_j=\frac{\lambda_j^{-2}}{\sum_k\lambda_k^{-2}}.\] The objective in the source is \[
 H(x,y)=\prod_{j=1}^p
 \left(\frac{x_j+y_j}{x_j}\right)^{x_j}
 \left(\frac{x_j+y_j}{y_j}\right)^{y_j}
 \theta_j^{x_j+y_j},
 \qquad \sum_jx_j=n,\quad\sum_jy_j=\beta n,\] with every \(x_j,y_j\) strictly positive. The source asserts that the maximum occurs at \(x_j=\theta_jn\), \(y_j=\beta\theta_jn\).
## Correct maximization and an internal consistency test

Equation reference: eq:sup. The correct supremum of [eq:objective] (#eq:objective) is \[
 \sup H=
 \left(\frac{(1+\beta)^{1+\beta}}{\beta^\beta}\right)^n
 \theta_{\max}^{(1+\beta)n}.\] To see this, the log-sum inequality bounds the logarithm of the first two factors by \(n[(1+\beta)\log(1+\beta)-\beta\log\beta]\). The remaining logarithm is at most \((1+\beta)n\log\theta_{\max}\). Concentrating mass on an index with maximal \(\theta_j\) and imposing \(y_j=\beta x_j\) approaches equality. Under strict positivity the supremum need not be attained. If all \(\theta_j\) are equal, every positive allocation with this common ratio attains equality. In that special case the source’s selected allocation is valid, although not unique.
## Dependency, counterevidence and repair boundary

The source explicitly explains on p. 2183 that different \(\lambda_j\) are retained for the proof of Lemma 5.3. The bound (5.6) is used to control a tilted moment-generating function in (5.23). Its particular smooth expression is then used to isolate \(((4-\alpha)/p,\ldots,(4-\alpha)/p)\) as the sole zero-cost point, establish (5.26), and derive (5.22). That lower coefficient asymptotic is used in (5.3)–(5.4) to obtain the fixed-\(p\), long-time limit (1.9). The demonstrated failure occurs before the large-deviation argument; it is not repaired by changing the formulation of the Gärtner–Ellis theorem.

Using [eq:sup] (#eq:sup) in the same exponential estimate gives dependence on \(\max_j\lambda_j^{-2}\) in place of the displayed weighted logarithm. That bound does not supply the claimed differentiable concentration argument at equal parameters. A new lower-bound proof, or an explicitly restricted conclusion, is required.

There is substantial counterevidence to any claim of total failure. The equal-parameter specialization \(\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_p\) survives this particular maximization check. Hence this finding does not invalidate the equal-parameter steps (5.13)–(5.15), or the high-moment upper bound (5.7), on this ground. The high-moment lower bound (5.27) is developed separately through Gaussian exponential tilting in Section 5.3 and is not based on (5.23). Nor does the counterexample refute the final stochastic limit (1.9); it establishes an invalid core derivation of that limit in the reviewed version. The existence proof in Section 4 has a different dependency chain.
# Additional checks, coverage and unresolved limits

The reading covered the positivity and measure-valued interpretation of the wave kernel, the \(L^2\) mollification definition, Wick pairings, Laplace transforms, the continuity and stochastic Fubini arguments, existence and expansion-class necessity, both asymptotic regimes, and the Hu–Meyer appendix. In dimension three the kernel is a positive surface measure, not an ordinary density. The upper endpoint \(\alpha=2\) is excluded. No extension to that endpoint, to unrestricted initial data, or to all possible solution notions is inferred.

Several independent calculations were retained alongside the report. For constant Gaussian potential \(\dot W(x)=Z\) (a valid Dalang example, but outside the positive-homogeneity assumptions of Theorem 1.2), the \(n\)th term is \(Z^nt^{2n}/(2n)!\). Both sides of Theorem 3.3, source (3.10), give \(Z^n\lambda^{-2n-1}\) after Laplace transformation. The independent exact checks covered \(n=0,\ldots,6\), and the factorial identity proves the general expression. For the necessity argument on p. 2172, integrating its time kernel gives \[\frac{t^2}{2r^2}-\frac{1-\cos(rt)}{r^4},\qquad r=|\xi|.\] Its limit at \(r=0\) is \(t^4/24\); at large \(r\) it is comparable to \(t^2/(2r^2)\). This supports the claimed Dalang necessity within the stated expansion class.

The operative normalization in Chen’s Brownian self-intersection theorem [Retained latex: \cite[Theorem 1.1]{C23}] was checked against the use on source p. 2175: that reference has half the Dirichlet energy, and spatial scaling yields the factor \(2^{\alpha/(4-\alpha)}\) used in the source. The variational identity in source (5.20) was also checked directly with a unitary Fourier transform: the resolvent denominator imposes \(\|h\|_2^2+\|\nabla h\|_2^2=1\), and amplitude and spatial scaling give the exponent \((4-\alpha)/2\). Fourier factors must be retained when consulting the earlier Riesz-potential formulation [BCR]. The Mittag–Leffler statement used in (5.5) was checked in [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma A.3, p.~1617]{BCC}]; its parameter is positive here.

Reference checks were targeted, not complete rereviews of the cited literature. The acquired reference PDFs and the actual pages read and viewed are recorded separately. In particular, Theorem C.4 on p. 307 of the book cited for the white-noise value [Cbook] was not acquired through the available legitimate primary routes. The independent proof of Claim Claim 1 (#cl:sharp) does not rely on that unavailable page. The author-hosted 2023 reference contains 17 article pages plus a promotional eighteenth PDF page and retains a placeholder running header; it was not silently equated with a separately obtained publisher file.

Bounded searches of the title, DOI, author publication list, arXiv metadata and primary publisher records found no matching correction. That is a discovery result, not proof that no correction exists. The frozen reviewed PDF was not replaced by a different version. No author code was executed, and code availability was not treated as a mathematical defect. Exact symbolic checks were performed by reviewer-written code; the decisive arguments are given in full above.

The findings establish the errors stated in Problems 1 and 2. They do not certify every auxiliary statement or every cited theorem, and no additional error is inferred merely from these limits. This is an initial technical report. Scientific decision remains pending and no independent human acceptance is recorded.

The remaining logarithm is at most \((1+\beta)n\log\theta_{\max}\). Concentrating mass on an index with maximal \(\theta_j\) and imposing \(y_j=\beta x_j\) approaches equality. Under strict positivity the supremum need not be attained. If all \(\theta_j\) are equal, every positive allocation with this common ratio attains equality. In that special case the source’s selected allocation is valid, although not unique.

The source explicitly explains on p. 2183 that different \(\lambda_j\) are retained for the proof of Lemma 5.3. The bound (5.6) is used to control a tilted moment-generating function in (5.23). Its particular smooth expression is then used to isolate \(((4-\alpha)/p,\ldots,(4-\alpha)/p)\) as the sole zero-cost point, establish (5.26), and derive (5.22). That lower coefficient asymptotic is used in (5.3)–(5.4) to obtain the fixed-\(p\), long-time limit (1.9). The demonstrated failure occurs before the large-deviation argument; it is not repaired by changing the formulation of the Gärtner–Ellis theorem.

Using [eq:sup] (#eq:sup) in the same exponential estimate gives dependence on \(\max_j\lambda_j^{-2}\) in place of the displayed weighted logarithm. That bound does not supply the claimed differentiable concentration argument at equal parameters. A new lower-bound proof, or an explicitly restricted conclusion, is required.

There is substantial counterevidence to any claim of total failure. The equal-parameter specialization \(\lambda_1=\cdots=\lambda_p\) survives this particular maximization check. Hence this finding does not invalidate the equal-parameter steps (5.13)–(5.15), or the high-moment upper bound (5.7), on this ground. The high-moment lower bound (5.27) is developed separately through Gaussian exponential tilting in Section 5.3 and is not based on (5.23). Nor does the counterexample refute the final stochastic limit (1.9); it establishes an invalid core derivation of that limit in the reviewed version. The existence proof in Section 4 has a different dependency chain.

report: Abstract: This review identifies one false supporting estimate in the multiline classification proof and one peripheral overstatement of uniformity. The heavy-path envelope of Lemma 6.8 has an incorrect boundary-layer width; an admissible parameter family makes its asserted high-probability event have probability tending to zero. The all-positive-tilt version of (2.3) also fails under its own scaling relation. These conclusions concern the stated estimates and their uses. They do not disprove the final classification theorems. Possible repairs, counterevidence and the limits of this initial review are stated separately.
Author: Math2025 review record M25-0533
Date: 29 October 2026

Title: Initial scientific review of
Characterizing Gibbs states for area-tilted Brownian lines
# Reviewed source, framework and assessment

The reviewed paper is by Mriganka Basu Roy Chowdhury, Pietro Caputo and Shirshendu Ganguly, The Annals of Probability 53(6) (2025), 2196–2255, DOI 10.1214/25-AOP1760 (https://doi.org/10.1214/25-AOP1760) [BCG]. The frozen source is the 60-page institutional PDF designated as the version of record by the acquisition manifest. Its SHA256 begins `df44a62d47f5de6e`; the complete digest, exact bytes and acquisition origin are retained in the accompanying provenance. The institutional record labels the file an editorial version. A separate byte-equivalence claim about every publisher-hosted copy is not made. Physical PDF page numbers are used throughout for source locations.

The primary scientific executor read all 60 source pages, including the definitions, proof arguments and references. The source image checks include all pages supporting the findings below. Reference reading was targeted, with the exact acquired versions and page subsets recorded; it was not a complete review of the cited literature. The assessment retains the initial review scope, with the interval-maximum candidate finding withdrawn after independent verification of the source formula and its length factor. Scientific disposition remains pending and no independent acceptance or human review is represented by this report.
## Definitions and hypotheses retained

Equation reference: eq:pbr. The one-line measure \(\mathcal L^{a;x,y}_{\ell,r}\) is the Brownian bridge from \(x>0\) to \(y>0\) on \([\ell,r]\), weighted by \(\exp(-a\int_\ell^r X(s)\,ds)\) and conditioned to remain positive (Definition 1.1, PDF p. 4). Thus, for strength \(2a\), the parabolic barrier representation is \[
 X(t)=Y(t)+at^2,\qquad
 Y\ \text{a standard Brownian bridge above }-at^2.\] This normalization follows directly from Lemma 2.4, PDF p. 13; using strength \(a\) instead would give the parabola \(at^2/2\). The Brownian variance convention is the one in the paper.

In the infinite ensemble, \(\lambda>1\) is fixed, the area strengths are \(2\lambda^{i-1}\), the curves are strictly ordered and positive, and the Brownian–Gibbs property resamples only finitely many curves on a bounded interval. Definition 1.7 additionally requires asymptotic pinning to zero. This assumption cannot be dropped: an upward translation preserves the Gibbs specification but changes the floor selected at infinity (PDF p. 8).

Theorems 1.3 and 1.8 classify extremal states by \((L,R)\in[-\infty,\infty)^2\) with \(L+R<0\); finite slopes, one slope equal to \(-\infty\), and both slopes equal to \(-\infty\) are distinct cases. Positive infinity is excluded. The parabolic coefficient is fixed by the tilt normalization. Time translation changes the slopes by \((L,R)\mapsto(L+2h,R-2h)\) at strength 2. Theorem 1.9 concerns lower lines and includes the time-scale term \(\lambda^{2k/3}\) inside the interval-maximum expectation. None of the counterexamples below violates these distinctions.
## Proof dependencies

For the multiline argument, the decisive chain runs from the heavy and light path estimates (Lemmas 6.1–6.3) to Proposition 5.5, then to confinement in Lemma 5.6, top-line fluctuation control in Lemma 5.7 and the reverse coupling used for uniqueness. Lemma 6.8 is explicitly applied in the heavy-path induction (PDF pp. 56–58). Equation (5.9) is also invoked in Lemma 5.7 (PDF p. 40), but the source formula includes the factor \(S\). That factor is precisely the interval-length dependence expected from the union-bound step; the initial report omitted it when transcribing the claim. No defect is asserted for (5.9). The remaining false supporting estimate does not by itself establish a false final classification theorem.
# Problem 1: the heavy-path envelope starts too early
## Locator, assertion and hypotheses

Equation reference: eq:printedwidth. Lemma 6.8, PDF pp. 56–57, journal pp. 2251–2252, takes \[X\sim\mathcal L_T^{2a;H},\qquad a=\lambda^{k-1},\quad k>n_0(T),
 \quad H\leq 2T^2,\quad 0<\delta<1/20,\] where \(n_0(T)\) is the largest integer \(j\) such that \(T^{-15}\leq T\lambda^{-(j-1)/2}\) (PDF p. 47). The asserted envelope is \(H+\Delta_2\) in the two endpoint strips and \(\Delta_2\) in the central interval, with \[
 \Delta_1=T\lambda^{-k/2},\qquad
 \Delta_2=T^\delta\lambda^{-(k-n_0)/5}.\] Its probability is claimed to be at least \(1-\exp(-\Theta(\lambda^{k\delta/2}))\). The failure below occurs strictly inside the central interval, so the overlap of the piecewise definition at its endpoints is immaterial.
## An admissible family and an exact lower comparison

Equation reference: eq:parameters, eq:tangent. Fix \[
 \lambda=4,\quad \delta=\frac1{40},\quad T=2^m,\quad m\geq2,
 \quad n_0=16m+1,\quad k=16m+2,\quad H=T^2.\] The formula for \(n_0\) follows by comparing powers of 2 in its defining inequality. All the hypotheses above hold, with a positive boundary height. Put \[d=\Delta_1=T2^{-k}=\frac14T^{-15},
 \qquad a=4^{k-1}.\] Then \(ad^2=T^2/4\) and the true tangency point from \((T,H-aT^2)\) to the barrier \(-at^2\) is \[
 \xi=T-\sqrt{H/a}=T-2d.\] Consider \(t_0=T-5d/4\). It satisfies \(\xi<t_0<T-d\) and belongs to the central interval in the printed envelope.
Proposition 1.  For the family [eq:parameters] (#eq:parameters), the probability of the envelope event in Lemma 6.8 tends to zero as \(m\to\infty\).

Equation reference: eq:probupper, eq:chernoff. Proof. At \(t_0\) the envelope requires \(X(t_0)\leq
T^{1/40}4^{-1/5}\). Hence, with \(\Phi\) the standard Gaussian distribution function, \[
 \mathbb P(X\leq\mathrm{Envelope})
 \leq
 \Phi\!\left(
 \frac{T^{1/40}4^{-1/5}-9T^2/64}
      {\sqrt{15T^{-15}/128}}\right)\longrightarrow0.\] For \(T\geq4\), the threshold is at most \(\mu_m/2\). The elementary Gaussian Chernoff bound consequently gives the more explicit estimate \[
 \mathbb P(X\leq\mathrm{Envelope})
 \leq \exp\!\left(-\frac{27}{1280}T^{19}\right).\] In contrast, \(\lambda^{k\delta/2}=2^{1/20}T^{2/5}\to\infty\), so the claimed lower probability tends to one for every positive constant hidden in \(\Theta\). ◻

This is a probabilistic counterexample proved by exact Gaussian comparison, not a simulation. Independent symbolic checks verified the tangency identity, mean, variance, threshold index and Chernoff coefficient. For example, \(T=16\) gives \(n_0=65\), \(k=66\), \(d=2^{-62}\), \(\mu_m=36\), \(\sigma_m^2=15/2^{67}\), and a printed bulk ceiling approximately \(0.8122523964\).
## The actual induction also encounters the defect

Equation reference: eq:inductionmean. The application in the proof of Lemma 6.1, PDF p. 58, uses boundary height \(H=T^2-2KT\), not an arbitrary unused endpoint of the lemma’s range. The same test point works for every fixed \(K>0\) and all sufficiently large \(T\) in [eq:parameters] (#eq:parameters). Its tangency width is \[\sqrt{H/a}=2d\sqrt{1-2K/T}.\] The Gaussian comparison now has mean \[
 T^2\left(\sqrt{1-2K/T}-\frac58\right)^2
 \sim\frac9{64}T^2,\] and variance of order \(d\). Thus it again exceeds the claimed bulk ceiling with probability tending to one. This rules out the defense that only irrelevant values near \(2T^2\) caused the contradiction.
## Counterevidence, repair and impact

The proof itself locates tangency only up to \(\xi=T(1-O(\lambda^{-k/2}))\). That statement does not put tangency after the specific point \(T-\Delta_1\) with coefficient 1. For all \(H\leq2T^2\), the geometric boundary-layer width is bounded by \[\sqrt{H/a}\leq\sqrt{2\lambda}\,T\lambda^{-k/2}.\] A plausible repair is to replace \(\Delta_1\) by \(C_\lambda T\lambda^{-k/2}\) with \(C_\lambda>\sqrt{2\lambda}\) and then propagate that constant through the induction. This is consistent with the proof’s order-of-magnitude geometry. For fixed \(\lambda>1\), the cumulative heavy-layer widths remain \(O_\lambda(T^{-15})\), which is smaller than \(T^{-10}\) for large \(T\). Thus the downstream domain margin does not itself obstruct such a repair.

This observation is counterevidence against a claim that the final theorem is false. It is not a substitute proof of the repaired probability estimate: the excursion comparison, fluctuation allowance and substitution of shortened domains in the induction must still be checked with the corrected constant. The finding is Major: a false lemma is used explicitly to establish the heavy-path input to Proposition 5.5. No assertion of failure of Theorems 1.3, 1.8 or 1.9 follows.
# Problem 2: the Ferrari–Spohn maximum bound overstates small-tilt uniformity
## Locator and an admissible scaling limit

Equation reference: eq:badFS, eq:smalllower. Lemma 2.6(5), equation (2.3), PDF p. 15, journal p. 2210, claims constants \(C,c>0\) independent of all \(T\geq1\), \(t>0\), \(a>0\) such that, for \(X_a\sim\mu^{a,\mathrm{FS}}\), \[
 \mathbb P\!\left(\max_{s\in[-T,T]}X_a(s)>t\right)
 \leq CTa^{2/3}\exp(-c\sqrt a\,t^{3/2}).\] The same lemma’s item 3 gives the exact scaling, with \(X\sim\mu^\mathrm{FS}=\mu^{2,\mathrm{FS}}\), \[X_a(s)\ \stackrel{\rm law}{=}\
 (a/2)^{-1/3}X\big((a/2)^{2/3}s\big).\] Set \(a_n=2n^{-3}\) and \(T=t=1\). Since \(X(0)>0\) almost surely, \[
 \mathbb P\!\left(\max_{[-1,1]}X_{a_n}>1\right)
 \geq \mathbb P(X(0)>1/n)\longrightarrow1.\] For any fixed positive \(C,c\), the right-hand side of [eq:badFS] (#eq:badFS) equals \[C2^{2/3}n^{-2}\exp(-c\sqrt2\,n^{-3/2})\longrightarrow0.\] All tested parameters lie within the printed range. This is a contradiction to uniformity in \(a\), rather than a failure of the fixed-tilt Ferrari–Spohn tail estimate.
## A bounded repair and its limited impact

Equation reference: eq:repairedFS. The cited fixed-tilt result [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma~5.3, PDF pp.~22--23]{CG}] requires a time interval of length at least the fixed natural scale. Under scaling, the relevant half-length is \(T'=T(a/2)^{2/3}\), which can be smaller than 1. Apply the fixed-tilt bound on the larger interval of half-length \(\max(1,T')\) and use the scaled threshold \((a/2)^{1/3}t\). After changing absolute constants, this proves the corrected form \[
 \mathbb P\!\left(\max_{[-T,T]}X_a>t\right)
 \leq C(1+Ta^{2/3})\exp(-c\sqrt a\,t^{3/2}).\] Alternatively one can restrict the original form to the range \(T(a/2)^{2/3}\geq1\), or to a uniformly comparable range with constants adjusted.

The paper’s coming-down estimates in Corollary 2.8 and Lemma 2.9 impose \(a\geq1\) (PDF pp. 16–17). In the checked large-\(T\) applications, including the heavy-path argument, \(Ta^{2/3}\geq1\), so \(1+Ta^{2/3}\leq2Ta^{2/3}\) and the added constant is absorbed in the prefactor. The condition \(a\geq1\) alone would not justify this absorption for arbitrarily short time intervals; no such unrestricted claim is made here. The classification at arbitrary positive overall tilt also has the separate deterministic scaling reduction. Accordingly, this finding is Minor: the universally quantified auxiliary estimate is false, but no failure of a core conclusion from the small-\(a\) regime is demonstrated. Constants depending on \(a\) would be a different statement and cannot be read into the explicit independence claim.
# Coverage, counterevidence and remaining work

The initial review followed the one-line slope/existence/uniqueness argument in Sections 3–4 and the multiline approximation, confinement and reverse-coupling argument in Sections 5–6. It checked the distinction between a finite interval law and an infinite Gibbs state; endpoint positivity and zero-boundary limiting conventions; the role of asymptotic pinning; tail triviality for extremal states; admissible slope pairs and the two infinite-slope limits; the parabolic normalization; and the order in which \(n\), \(T\), fixed compact windows and small failure probabilities are used.

The initial independent algebra file contains 27 passing checks, including four admissible parameter instances, the exact Brownian bridge variance and the small-tilt spatial/time rescaling. These calculations support current Problems 1 and 2 (initial Problems 1 and 3). The withdrawn interval-maximum candidate was not among those checks; its withdrawal rests on direct verification of the source formula, including the factor \(S\).

Several apparent local defects were considered but are not additional substantive findings. In particular, the absent additive constant in (5.11) is inconsistent at a zero window, while the stated (5.8) and the relevant reference’s more precise estimate retain the appropriate constant. This is treated as a local transcription issue, not an independent theorem failure. The comparison of an unconditional coupling error with a stronger conditional formulation, and the uniform-in-\(T\) wording near a boundary in (5.5)–(5.6), were also examined. The current report does not establish an additional defect from them. It does not certify every possible reformulation of those steps.

For external dependencies, the acquired [CG] PDF has 48 physical pages including its cover; the DOI-bearing article begins on physical page 2. The relevant statements and selected proof passages on mixing, maximum tails, uniform confinement and growing boundary data were read and their evidence pages viewed. For [CIW], the attempted institutional postprint download timed out. A separately acquired 20-page arXiv v1 was used for targeted checks of the tightness, Gibbs-property and monotonicity statements on physical pages 6–8. It is not asserted to be byte-identical or theorem-by-theorem identical to the cited Springer chapter. In particular, its Theorem 1.4 is stated for free and zero boundary ensembles; extending that input to the growing top boundary in the reviewed paper requires the additional compact confinement argument the authors discuss, rather than a verbatim application.

Bounded searches of the exact title, correction/erratum terms, the institutional record, the author publication listing and the arXiv record found no applicable correction that resolves these findings. The arXiv record inspected exposes v1 from 10 October 2023; it does not substitute for the frozen institutional source. An author-page fetch timed out, while its indexed listing was available. These observations do not prove that no correction exists. No applicable separate computational supplement was found in the recorded search, and no author code was executed. Missing code is not treated as a mathematical defect.
Finding | Established judgment | Repair, adoption and remaining check

Problem 1: Major | The printed heavy-path envelope is false, including in its induction regime. | Enlarge the boundary-layer constant and recheck the probability bound and induction. The geometric repair is plausible but not adopted as a completed proof.

Problem 2: Minor | The stated all-positive-tilt uniform bound fails as \(a\downarrow0\). | Use [eq:repairedFS] (#eq:repairedFS) or restrict the scaled interval range. The displayed correction follows from scaling; core applications checked here avoid the failing regime.

The report requests correction and verification of the Lemma 6.8 heavy-path estimate. It also records the bounded correction to the small-tilt auxiliary Ferrari–Spohn estimate. The initial interval- maximum finding has been withdrawn: the source states the factor \(S\) in (5.9), and its union-bound derivation is consistent with that form. A false supporting assertion is distinguished from a false final theorem throughout.

Theorems 1.3 and 1.8 classify extremal states by \((L,R)\in[-\infty,\infty)^2\) with \(L+R<0\); finite slopes, one slope equal to \(-\infty\), and both slopes equal to \(-\infty\) are distinct cases. Positive infinity is excluded. The parabolic coefficient is fixed by the tilt normalization. Time translation changes the slopes by \((L,R)\mapsto(L+2h,R-2h)\) at strength 2. Theorem 1.9 concerns lower lines and includes the time-scale term \(\lambda^{2k/3}\) inside the interval-maximum expectation. None of the counterexamples below violates these distinctions.

Equation reference: eq:badFS, eq:smalllower. Lemma 2.6(5), equation (2.3), PDF p. 15, journal p. 2210, claims constants \(C,c>0\) independent of all \(T\geq1\), \(t>0\), \(a>0\) such that, for \(X_a\sim\mu^{a,\mathrm{FS}}\), \[
 \mathbb P\!\left(\max_{s\in[-T,T]}X_a(s)>t\right)
 \leq CTa^{2/3}\exp(-c\sqrt a\,t^{3/2}).\] The same lemma’s item 3 gives the exact scaling, with \(X\sim\mu^\mathrm{FS}=\mu^{2,\mathrm{FS}}\), \[X_a(s)\ \stackrel{\rm law}{=}\
 (a/2)^{-1/3}X\big((a/2)^{2/3}s\big).\] Set \(a_n=2n^{-3}\) and \(T=t=1\). Since \(X(0)>0\) almost surely, \[
 \mathbb P\!\left(\max_{[-1,1]}X_{a_n}>1\right)
 \geq \mathbb P(X(0)>1/n)\longrightarrow1.\] For any fixed positive \(C,c\), the right-hand side of [eq:badFS] (#eq:badFS) equals \[C2^{2/3}n^{-2}\exp(-c\sqrt2\,n^{-3/2})\longrightarrow0.\] All tested parameters lie within the printed range. This is a contradiction to uniformity in \(a\), rather than a failure of the fixed-tilt Ferrari–Spohn tail estimate.

Equation reference: eq:repairedFS. The cited fixed-tilt result [Retained latex: \cite[Lemma~5.3, PDF pp.~22--23]{CG}] requires a time interval of length at least the fixed natural scale. Under scaling, the relevant half-length is \(T'=T(a/2)^{2/3}\), which can be smaller than 1. Apply the fixed-tilt bound on the larger interval of half-length \(\max(1,T')\) and use the scaled threshold \((a/2)^{1/3}t\). After changing absolute constants, this proves the corrected form \[
 \mathbb P\!\left(\max_{[-T,T]}X_a>t\right)
 \leq C(1+Ta^{2/3})\exp(-c\sqrt a\,t^{3/2}).\] Alternatively one can restrict the original form to the range \(T(a/2)^{2/3}\geq1\), or to a uniformly comparable range with constants adjusted.

The paper’s coming-down estimates in Corollary 2.8 and Lemma 2.9 impose \(a\geq1\) (PDF pp. 16–17). In the checked large-\(T\) applications, including the heavy-path argument, \(Ta^{2/3}\geq1\), so \(1+Ta^{2/3}\leq2Ta^{2/3}\) and the added constant is absorbed in the prefactor. The condition \(a\geq1\) alone would not justify this absorption for arbitrarily short time intervals; no such unrestricted claim is made here. The classification at arbitrary positive overall tilt also has the separate deterministic scaling reduction. Accordingly, this finding is Minor: the universally quantified auxiliary estimate is false, but no failure of a core conclusion from the small-\(a\) regime is demonstrated. Constants depending on \(a\) would be a different statement and cannot be read into the explicit independence claim.
